Title: LLMday Montevideo bets that the harness matters more than the model
Description: LLMday Montevideo, December 5 at World Trade Center Montevideo - Zyte, IBM, Abstracta, Marvik and Blizzard on agents, RAG and AI security. CONF42 = 42% off.
Body:
LLMday Montevideo is on December 5, 2026, at the World Trade Center Montevideo, and a good part of the programme argues one thing: what makes an agent work in production is everything around the model. Speakers come from Zyte, IBM, Abstracta, Marvik, Nubiral, Loopstudio, TCS and Blizzard Entertainment, and the code **CONF42** takes **42% off** the ticket.

The day has two rooms: the Main Stage all day, and the Ephemeral Stage opening after lunch.

## Three talks with "harness" in the title

That is not a coincidence. **Joaquin Bonifacino (Zyte)** gives *Long Running Agents: The Harness Is the Product*, drawn from an agentic data-QA engine running at 20B+ tokens per week. His point: demos run for thirty seconds, production agents run for hours, and most of what breaks at that timescale has nothing to do with the model.

**Martin Brian (Marvik)** turns the same question into a game in *The Harness Auction: What Makes an AI Agent Actually Work?*. Every audience member gets a limited budget and bids on components: a better model, tools, skills, more context, subagents or a verification loop. Bring a strategy.

**Lucia Hernandez (Metodica Digital)** widens the definition in *The User Is Part of the Harness: A Year Running an Agent That Adapts to Cognitive Load*, built around her own inconsistent executive function after an autism diagnosis at 35.

## RAG, documents and the boring wins

**Josefina R. Casanova (IBM)** shares *From PDFs to Production RAG: Lessons from Building Document Pipelines with Docling*, and **Leon Achata (TCS)** argues *RAG Is Not a Search Problem*, since exact identifiers, jargon and paraphrases all need different retrieval. **Marcos Martinez (Loopstudio)** has the most concrete number on the bill: *From 1 Hour to 10 Minutes: Automating Purchase Orders with AI*, for a US food and beverage distributor that received about 100 purchase orders a day by email, each in its own layout.

**Roger Abelenda (Abstracta)** presents Tero, an open-source agent platform for quality intelligence, and **Gorka Ludlow (Karma Digital)** ships *Apps, not chats*: macOS products that run models on-device.

## Security and the bigger picture

**Martin Rojas** breaks the GenAI data pipeline with OWASP guidance, and **Federico Novelli (Protect Group)** asks how to turn prompt injection and excessive agent permissions into business risk a security team can act on. **Axel Labruna and Maika de Jesus Esteves (Nubiral)** cover AgentOps, **Fede Rodrigo** insists *AI Is Never the Starting Point*, and **Marcelo B San Martin (Blizzard Entertainment)** closes the Ephemeral Stage with *The Great AI Role Rewrite*.

For a change of pace, **Mark Pawlikowski and Marcos Novelli Harispe (Reliaburger)** run a workshop that is openly a non-LLM break: set up, test and break a production cluster in seconds.

## Why a Conf42 viewer should go

If you followed the agent and RAG talks at [Conf42 Large Language Models 2026](https://www.conf42.com/llms2026), Montevideo is where you can bid against the people who gave them. The local community shows up too, with OWU, AWS Girls User Group Uruguay and DOUG Brazil on the supporters list.

Registration opens at 08:00. Tickets are on [Luma](https://luma.com/event/evt-THcPEG50zx51MsC) with **CONF42** for 42% off, and the two-stage schedule is on the [LLMday Montevideo page](https://llmday.com/2026-montevideo-q4).

Title: Test your agents for permission leaks like any other regression
Description: Ajay Munjuluru of JPMorgan Chase at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on authorization evals that catch agents revealing data a user isn't entitled to see.
Body:
Your agent eval suite probably scores accuracy, helpfulness and task completion. It probably doesn't check whether the agent just told an analyst something only their manager may see. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Ajay Munjuluru, Sr. Lead Software Engineer at JPMorgan Chase, shows how to treat authorization as a testable property of an agent system and run it in the delivery pipeline like any other regression suite.

In a regulated environment, he argues, that missing test is the one that matters most.

## Why access control at the tool isn't enough

The obvious defense is to enforce permissions in each tool the agent calls. Necessary, and not sufficient. Agents summarize, combine and paraphrase. A fact can escape in a summary even when no single tool call returned it verbatim, and two individually permitted results can add up to something the user should never see.

Ajay's experience comes from building multi-agent systems over enterprise banking CRM data, which is about as unforgiving a test bed for this as exists.

## Personas, assertions and combinations

The blueprint in the talk has a few moving parts:

- **Persona-based test users.** Several test identities with different entitlements run the same tasks, so you can compare what each one gets back.
- **Leak assertions.** Checks that inspect responses, summaries and tool calls for restricted facts, not just the final answer.
- **Combination tests.** These catch disclosures created when individually permitted results are joined. This is the clever bit, because it targets the leak that no per-tool permission check can see.

Each of those is plain test engineering applied to a new kind of system. That's the appeal: no exotic tooling, just the discipline you already apply to code.

## Run it when anything changes

Authorization evals only help if they run at the right moments. Ajay covers regression triggers for model upgrades, prompt changes and new tools, the three changes most likely to shift what an agent will say. A model swap that improves helpfulness can just as easily improve its helpfulness to the wrong person.

The last piece is making failures debuggable by linking each leak to the tool call and context that caused it. A red test that just says "leak" is a ticket nobody can close.

## Who should watch

Engineers shipping agents over data with entitlements: finance, healthcare, HR, legal, any internal CRM. Teams that already have an eval pipeline and want to add a security axis to it. Platform teams defining release gates for agent changes. You'll come away with a blueprint for adding authorization evals to an agent release process.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Securing AI-Driven Financial Operations: RAG & Agentic Systems at Scale](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Swamy_Biru_finance_rag_ai) by Swamy Biru (JPMorganChase & Co).
- [A Policy-as-Code Approach to RBAC Authorization](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Graziano_Casto_policy_rbac_authorization) by Graziano Casto (Mia-Platform), for the authorization model underneath.

Title: Your ranking model is learning from items nobody saw
Description: Devavrat Khanolkar of Cisco at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on fixing exposure bias in recommenders by replacing server-side proxy signals with measured exposure.
Body:
If your logs say an item was shown, but it sat below the fold and nobody scrolled there, your ranking model just learned that users didn't want it. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Devavrat Khanolkar, Machine Learning Engineering Technical Leader at Cisco Systems, presents an MLOps case study on finding and fixing exactly that kind of exposure bias in large-scale ranking systems.

The bug lives in the training data pipeline, which is why it can go unnoticed for a long time while the model quietly gets worse at diversity.

## Server-side tracking lies politely

The root cause in the talk is traditional server-side tracking. The server knows what it sent, so it records everything it sent as an exposure. Some of that content was never actually seen. Those unseen items become negative training examples, telling the model that users rejected things they never had a chance to reject.

The effects compound. Misleading negatives distort what the model learns and push it toward historically popular content, which then gets shown more, which makes it look even more popular. A feedback loop with good intentions and bad data.

## Replace the proxy with a measurement

The engineering fix is to swap the inaccurate proxy signal for directly measured exposure data. Simple to state, fiddly to ship, and Devavrat covers the fiddly parts:

- validating the new data source before trusting it,
- running the legacy and corrected pipelines in parallel so you can compare them,
- removing invalid training labels,
- adjusting the model training strategy for the cleaner data.

Running both pipelines side by side is the step people are tempted to skip, and it's the one that lets you prove the new signal is better instead of just different.

## Precision and diversity pull in different directions

The evaluation half of the talk covers offline evaluation, controlled online experimentation, and the trade-off between recommendation precision and exposure diversity. Fixing the labels may change what "good" looks like on your existing metrics, so the talk pays attention to validating model behavior before production rollout rather than declaring victory on one offline number.

Devavrat also credits cross-team collaboration as part of the fix. Measuring true exposure usually means a client-side change owned by someone other than the ML team.

## Who should watch

Anyone training rankers or recommenders on implicit feedback: feeds, search, e-commerce, content platforms. Data and MLOps engineers who own logging pipelines and suspect their labels. If you've ever wondered why your recommendations keep converging on the same few items, this talk offers one very plausible culprit.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Real-Time Personalization at Scale: Neural Ranking Systems and Operational Breakthroughs](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vedant_Agarwal_personalization_ranking_systems) by Vedant Agarwal (Walmart Global Tech).
- [Making recommendations explainable](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Lev_Fedorov_optimization_performance_efficiency) by Lev Fedorov (Amazon).
- [ML-Powered Search & Recommendation 101: From Core Concepts to Scalable Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sergey_Polyashov_recommendation_search_scalable) by Sergey Polyashov (Microsoft), a good primer first.

Title: One threat and one fix per layer of the AI stack
Description: Kriti Faujdar of Yelp at Conf42 MLOps 2026 gives a four-layer defense-in-depth map for production AI, from prompt injection to model egress.
Body:
Teams stall on AI security less from a lack of tools than from a lack of a map. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Kriti Faujdar, Lead Product Manager at Yelp, gives a lightning talk that is exactly that: a four-layer defense-in-depth framework for production AI, with the single threat and the single fix that matter most at each layer.

It's short by design, and it ends with homework: a 16-question checklist, four per layer, to run against your own pipeline.

## Training is the easy part

Kriti opens where many production AI projects get stuck. Shipping a system you would trust with real data, real tools and real actions is the hard bit, and teams freeze because nobody can say where the risks actually live. A layered view turns one scary question into four answerable ones.

## The four layers

Here's the map as the talk lays it out.

**Model.** The threat is indirect prompt injection: instructions smuggled in through content the model reads, not through the user. The fix is to validate every output before it drives an action. The model can read whatever it likes; it just doesn't get to act on it unchecked.

**Agents.** The threat is the over-permissioned agent. The fix is tool allowlists plus approval gates for irreversible actions. Deleting a record and drafting a reply should not share a permission.

**Tools and MCP.** The threat is poisoned or unvetted tool servers. The fix will feel familiar to anyone who has been burned by a dependency: allowlist them, schema-validate them, and pin them like dependencies. An MCP server is code you run on someone else's behalf, so treat it with the same suspicion as a new package in your lockfile.

**Infrastructure.** The threats are poisoned weights and silent exfiltration. The fix is to scan models in CI/CD and restrict egress, so a compromised model has nowhere to send what it finds.

## Why stacking beats perfecting

The argument behind the framework is the classic Swiss-cheese one. Every layer has holes. Stacked together, they leave no straight path from attacker to impact. That's a healthier goal than chasing a perfect prompt-injection filter, which is a race nobody has won yet.

## Who should watch

Product and engineering leads who need to explain AI risk to their team in ten minutes. Engineers wiring agents to MCP tool servers for the first time. Security folks looking for a shared vocabulary with the ML team. If you want deep exploit walkthroughs, pair it with the related talks below; this one is the map, not the terrain.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [RAGged and Compromised: Hacking Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Blaize_Stewart_rag_security_injection) by Blaize Stewart (GBLI), the model layer from the attacker's side.
- [Cloud MCP Servers Under Fire: Security Risks, Vulnerability Patterns, and Practical Defenses](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Aleksandr_Pinaev_security_vulnerabilities_compliance) by Aleksandr Pinaev (Swordfish Security).
- [Gate the Action, Not the Alert: Checking an Agent Before It Runs](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Artemis_Leonardou_agents_guardrails_policy) by Artemis Leonardou (NOFire AI).

[Watch Kriti Faujdar's talk](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Kriti_Faujdar_securing_agents_infrastructure) at [Conf42 MLOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/mlops2026).

Title: Which workload called your model, for whom, and can you revoke it?
Description: Bhavik Thakkar of Okta at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on workload identity, delegated OAuth access and MCP authorization for AI agents and ML pipelines.
Body:
Three questions most ML platforms can't answer about a single API call: which workload made it, on whose behalf, and how do you revoke it? At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Bhavik Thakkar, Senior Product Manager at Okta, lays out a practical identity architecture for ML pipelines and AI agents, drawing on lessons from building identity products for AI agents.

The starting observation is uncomfortable and accurate. Your ML platform is full of non-human actors, and most of them log in with shared API keys or over-privileged service accounts.

## Count the robots on your platform

Bhavik's list of non-human actors is worth reading slowly: training jobs pulling data, inference services calling feature stores, CI pipelines pushing models, and now AI agents calling tools through the Model Context Protocol on behalf of real users. Each one is an identity whether you modelled it or not. The ones you didn't model are the ones holding a long-lived key in an environment variable.

## Workload identity instead of secrets

The first part of the architecture gives pipelines, model servers and agents verifiable identities, SPIFFE/SPIRE-style, and short-lived credentials in place of long-lived keys. The appeal is operational as much as security: nothing to rotate by hand, nothing to leak from a config file, and a clear answer to "who is this?" in every log line.

## Agents should borrow access, not own it

The agent section is where the talk gets most current. An agent acting for a user should get scoped, user-bound access to tools and APIs, not a master key. Bhavik covers the building blocks: OAuth token exchange, MCP authorization, and registering agent clients with Client ID Metadata Documents.

He then places the guardrails: where human approval, step-up authentication and revocation belong once agents take real actions. If the agent is about to do something irreversible, that's the moment to ask a human, not the post-incident review.

## The failure catalogue

The part to bookmark is "what goes wrong", with a fix for each:

- over-scoped tokens that let an agent do far more than its task needs,
- confused-deputy calls between services, where a trusted service is tricked into acting for an untrusted caller,
- invisible agent-to-agent hops that break the audit trail,
- the missing kill switch.

That last one is a good test of any agent platform. If you can't name the button that stops a misbehaving agent right now, you don't have one.

## Who should watch

Platform and MLOps engineers running shared ML infrastructure. Anyone exposing internal tools to agents over MCP. Security architects who need a reference architecture to argue from. You'll leave with that architecture plus a checklist for your own platform and agent deployments. Expect a product perspective from someone who builds identity tooling, so the concepts lead and the vendor stays in the background.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Secretless Multi-Cloud Authentication with Workload Identity for DevSecOps Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Venkata_Velavarthipati_workloadidentity_oidc_secretless) by Venkata Velavarthipati.
- [Don't Give the Agent a Shell: Tool and Identity Boundaries for AI Agents in Cloud Operations](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Ahmed_Tariq_identity_permissions_cloud) by Ahmed Tariq (Simplify9).
- [Your AI Has Too Much Access: Deterministic Authorization for Coding Agents](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Sohan_Maheshwar_deterministic_authorization_agents) by Sohan Maheshwar (AuthZed).

Title: SecMLOps, or how to stop treating the ML pipeline as a soft target
Description: Jose Manuel Ortega of Alicante University at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on data poisoning, registry tampering, Python supply chain risk and endpoint attacks.
Body:
Security reviews tend to stop at the API gateway, and the ML pipeline behind it gets waved through as "data science stuff". At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Jose Manuel Ortega, Security Researcher at Alicante University, walks the whole machine learning lifecycle stage by stage and shows where attackers get in: ingestion, the model registry, Python dependencies and the deployed endpoint.

His framing is SecMLOps, security in machine learning operations, and his argument is that standard DevOps security does not cover the parts of the lifecycle that are unique to ML.

## Why a model is a different kind of artifact

Once a model graduates from a notebook into a production system, it becomes something worth attacking. It's also an odd artifact: shaped by training data you may not fully control, stored as a binary blob most scanners don't understand, and served from an endpoint that leaks information with every answer.

A container scanner and a WAF don't see any of that. Hence the talk.

## Four places the pipeline breaks

Jose organizes the session around the stages of the pipeline, each with its own threat:

- **Data ingestion and data poisoning.** If an attacker can influence what you train on, they can influence what the model does, and nothing in your CI will flag a cleanly formatted malicious row.
- **Model registries and tampering.** The registry is where a model becomes "the one we ship". Unauthorized writes there are a direct path to production.
- **Python dependencies and the supply chain.** ML stacks pull in a long tail of packages, and each one is a trust decision someone made once and nobody revisited.
- **Deployed endpoints, adversarial inputs and extraction.** Inputs crafted to fool the model, and query patterns designed to copy it.

Covering the pipeline end to end is the useful part. Most teams have thought hard about one of these and not at all about the other three.

## Security that doesn't stall delivery

The talk is pitched as intermediate level, and it promises real-world architectural patterns and practical toolchains rather than threat taxonomy for its own sake. The stated goal is resilient, secure and compliant AI systems without slowing developers down. That constraint matters: a control that adds a week to every model release is one the data science team will route around by Friday.

## Who should watch

MLOps and platform engineers who own the path from training to serving. Security engineers who have been handed "the ML platform" and need a map of what is different about it. Data scientists curious why their registry suddenly needs signed artifacts. If you already run a mature model-security program, treat it as a checklist to compare against.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Zero Trust MLOps: Securing AI Pipelines from Development to Production](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Sudheer_Obbu_zero_trust_mlops) by Sudheer Obbu (JPMorgan Chase).
- [A Beginner's Guide to Adversarial Machine Learning](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Anmol_Agarwal_beginners_guide_adversarial) by Anmol Agarwal (Nokia), good background for the endpoint attacks section.
- [Supply Chain Defense by Default: SBOMs, SLSA, and Provenance in CI/CD](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Bhaskar_Bharat_Sawant_supply_chain_ci) by Bhaskar Bharat Sawant (Cornerstone Building Brands).

Title: SREday Campinas asks when AI should touch production
Description: SREday Campinas, December 2-3 at Kyndryl HQ - two days with Bradesco, IBM, 3M, QuintoAndar and Sicredi on SRE, Kubernetes and AI agents. CONF42 = 42% off.
Body:
SREday Campinas runs for two days, December 2-3, 2026, at Kyndryl HQ in Campinas / Hortolândia, and the question hanging over the programme is how much of an SRE's job an AI agent should be allowed to do. Speakers come from Banco Bradesco, IBM, 3M, QuintoAndar, Sicredi, Microsoft, Bosch Digital and Orca Security, and Conf42 readers get **42% off** with the code **CONF42**.

The lineup mixes English and Portuguese sessions on a single track, so every talk has the whole room.

## Copilot, autopilot, or neither

Several talks circle the same decision from different angles:

- **Rod Anami (3M)**, *Can I hire AI agents to do my SRE work?*, builds a Copilot CLI harness to analyse months of ITSM history, because preventing the next failure needs context that lives in tickets.
- **Leandro Fachinelli (IBM)**, *From Copilot to Autopilot: When Should an SRE Let AI Touch Production*.
- **Marcelo Capile (IBM)**, *Diagnose, Approve, Remediate, Verify: A Two-Agent AIOps Loop for Kubernetes*, with a human approval step between hypothesis and action.
- **Lara Xavier (JLCP)**, *Quem observa o observador?*, on SRE for the AI agents that now do the observing. Somebody has to page the pager.

**Gabriel Dantas Gomes (QuintoAndar)** shows how to turn a cluster into an agentic one with kagent, and **Fabricio Veronez** and **Felipe Pereira (Máquina de Dados)** both talk harness engineering: what the environment around an agent needs before its pull requests are worth reviewing.

## Bradesco brings the postmortems

Banco Bradesco has three sessions. **Leonardo Camara, Pedro Alex da Costa and Henrique Gense** present *Além do RCA*, on moving from root-cause hunts to a blameless postmortem culture. **Joao Gabriel Franchi Briotto and Leonardo Camara** describe the Resilience Sprint, where devs, SRE, observability, architecture, ITSM and infra sit in one room with one application per month and look for single points of failure. **Luiz Siqueira and Maria Luiza de Queiroz** cover SRE as a Service.

## Platforms, supply chain and the scheduler

**Igor Estevan Jasinski (Sicredi)** explains how Sicredi turned monitoring into a self-service platform. **Camilla Martins** translates PhD research on ML-driven Kubernetes scheduling into tests on GCP. **Flavio Meira (Orca Security)** signs everything with Sigstore and Cosign in GitOps pipelines, **Emerson Silva (4Linux)** introduces Talos Linux, the Kubernetes OS with no SSH, and **Derick Rodrigues (Ana Gaming)** goes from manual deploys to golden paths with Backstage. **Igor Muralhes (ZenerIM)** takes SRE out of the cloud entirely, into industrial critical systems.

On day two, Rod Anami also runs a hands-on workshop, *Kill It and Watch It Come Back: Hands-on with Reliaburger*.

## Why a Conf42 viewer should go

If [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026](https://www.conf42.com/sre2026) is your yearly habit, this is the same conversation with a banking-heavy accent and two days of hallway time. Kyndryl hosts, with DOUG Brazil and Harness among the supporters.

Title: Taking agentic AI from demo to 600+ stores at Walmart Global Tech
Description: Meher Bhaskar Madiraju of Walmart Global Tech at Conf42 MLOps 2026: the evals, data contracts and ownership that got an agent system into production.
Body:
Most agent demos die quietly a few weeks after the applause. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Meher Bhaskar Madiraju, Senior Data Scientist at Walmart Global Tech, presents a case study of one that didn't: a multi-agent system for assortment planning and optimization, taken from prototype to a production deployment serving merchants across more than 600 retail locations.

The useful twist is in the takeaways. Meher argues that the organizational changes (ownership, on-call, stakeholder trust) mattered as much as the technology. Anyone who has tried to hand an LLM project to a team that didn't build it will nod here.

## Why prototypes don't survive

The abstract lists the usual causes of death, and it reads like a post-mortem template: brittle prompts, no evaluation harness, no guardrails, no ownership model. Each one is survivable on demo day. Together they guarantee that the first unexpected input, model update or reorg ends the project.

The talk is framed around fixing each of those in turn, with a real system rather than a reference diagram.

## Evals and data contracts belong in CI

The architecture is multi-agent orchestration for assortment planning, which means several agents reading and writing business data that merchants act on. Meher covers how the team runs evaluation and data-contract testing in CI, so a change to a prompt, a model or an upstream table gets caught before it reaches a merchant.

The promise worth holding him to: which gates actually caught bugs. Plenty of talks list the checks you could run. Fewer tell you which ones paid for themselves, and that is the list you want before you build your own pipeline.

## Default-deny for data, budgets for cost and latency

Two more production concerns get their own section. First, a default-deny data governance layer, the sensible stance when agents can query data on behalf of people with very different access. Second, monitoring with explicit cost and latency trade-offs, because a planning agent that is right but takes too long, or costs too much per run, still fails the merchant.

He also covers the failure modes that only appear at scale. If your agent has only ever met your own test cases, that section is the preview of your next quarter.

## A checklist you can steal

Attendees are promised a concrete checklist for moving their own prototypes into production: what to instrument first, which gates matter, and the people side of running an agent system. That last part is the bit most engineering talks skip. An agent with no on-call owner is a demo that happens to have a production URL.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and ML engineers holding a promising agent prototype and a vague mandate to "productionize it". Engineering managers deciding who owns an AI system once it ships. If you want a framework comparison, look elsewhere; this is a case study about process, testing and ownership.

Title: When ground truth changes after your AI already decided
Description: Avneesh Sharma of Amazon at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on evidence versioning, temporal consistency and claim-level checks for AI that works on late, stale data.
Body:
Your AI system made a decision at 10:00 using the data it had. At 10:20 the data changed. Was the decision wrong? At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Avneesh Sharma, Machine Learning Engineer at Amazon, takes on that question: how to build AI systems that stay reliable when ground truth arrives late, evidence conflicts and information goes stale.

It's a problem that model accuracy metrics are structurally blind to, which is exactly why it deserves a talk.

## Accuracy assumes the answer key is fixed

Classic evaluation compares a prediction to a label. That works when the label exists at prediction time and never moves. Modern AI systems rarely live in that world. They make decisions from information scattered across databases, APIs and continuously changing pipelines, and some of those sources will disagree with each other, or catch up hours later.

Avneesh frames the engineering challenge around three situations: data that arrives late, evidence that conflicts, and information that is stale by the time anyone acts on it. Each one makes a correct system look wrong, or a wrong one look fine, if you only score against today's truth.

## Version the evidence, not just the model

The patterns the talk covers start with evidence versioning: keeping track of which version of which data a decision was based on. Without it, you can't tell a bad decision from a good decision overtaken by events. With it, an audit becomes a lookup instead of an archaeology project.

Next comes temporal consistency, making sure the pieces of evidence a system combines actually belong to the same point in time. A join across two sources that refresh at different cadences is a classic way to produce an answer that was never true at any moment.

## Validate claims, one at a time

The third idea is claim-level validation. Rather than grading an AI output as a whole, you break it into the individual claims it makes and check each against the evidence. That's more work, and it's also the only way to say which part of an answer went stale when the data underneath moved.

Avneesh pairs this with evaluation strategies that go beyond traditional model accuracy, drawn from his experience building large-scale ML and AI infrastructure. Expect architecture patterns over math.

## Who should watch

Engineers whose models or agents act on operational data that keeps changing: fraud, pricing, inventory, support, anything with a pipeline and an SLA. Teams adding LLMs on top of live data sources will get the most from the claim-level material. If your training labels arrive weeks after inference, you are the target audience; you just may not have called it a reliability problem yet.

Title: Building and grading DevMate, an agentic LLM platform for Android code
Description: Anay Paul describes DevMate's architecture and evaluation pipeline for agentic coding on AOSP codebases at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
A coding agent that cannot be measured cannot be improved, only argued about. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Anay Paul (listed in stealth, with an Arizona State University background) presents DevMate, a centralised agentic LLM platform built to support developer workflows across complex Android Open Source Project codebases at Meta, with a strong focus on how it is evaluated.

## Why AOSP is a hard test

Android Open Source Project code is large, old in places and full of cross-module dependencies. That makes it a demanding target for agents: the context they need is spread out, and a plausible-looking change can be wrong for reasons three directories away. DevMate's approach combines static code understanding with dynamic contextual signals to support agentic tasks including code transformation, debugging assistance and architectural reasoning.

The session looks at the architecture behind those workflows and the engineering involved in running them consistently across very different development scenarios.

## Evaluation is the product

The centre of the talk is DevMate's evaluation infrastructure. It uses graders, benchmarking pipelines and feedback loops to assess model outputs, compare performance across tasks and align model behaviour with what developers expect. Building evaluation and observability into the platform is what lets the team make improvements measurable and reproducible while keeping quality standards.

That matters more for agents than for chat. An agent's output is a sequence of actions and a code change, and the question is whether the change is correct, not whether the explanation sounds right. Graders that check task outcomes, and benchmarks that can be rerun when the model or prompt changes, are the only way to tell a real improvement from a lucky week.

## Autonomy versus trust

The final theme is balance: how much autonomy to give the agent, how reliable it has to be, and how to keep developer trust. Developers forgive a tool that is sometimes unhelpful. They stop using one that is confidently wrong. The session promises practical insights on designing agentic LLM platforms, building evaluation pipelines and monitoring model behaviour with that trade-off in mind.

## Centralised on purpose

DevMate is described as a centralised platform rather than a set of per-team bots. The benefit of that choice is shared evaluation: one set of graders and benchmarks means a change to the model or the orchestration is measured the same way for every workflow that depends on it.

## Who should watch

Teams building internal coding agents or developer assistants, MLOps engineers responsible for evaluation pipelines, and anyone who has been asked whether the new model is better and wanted a number rather than a vibe. If you only consume a commercial coding assistant, the evaluation ideas still apply to choosing between them.

Title: Taking an enterprise RAG assistant from pilot to regulated production
Description: Arzoo Mittal (TransUnion) covers permission-aware, auditable RAG for regulated enterprises at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
Connecting an LLM to a vector database takes an afternoon. Making the result trustworthy, permission-aware and auditable in a regulated company takes the rest of the year. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Arzoo Mittal, Product Advisor at TransUnion, walks through how to design and operate a retrieval-augmented generation knowledge assistant for exactly that setting.

## Knowledge lives everywhere

The starting point is familiar to anyone who has searched an intranet: enterprise knowledge is fragmented across documents, internal wikis, policies, technical documentation and legacy systems. An LLM makes it possible to put a conversational interface over all of it. Arzoo's point is that a reliable assistant requires far more than that connection.

## The full pipeline, end to end

The talk walks the architecture in order: document ingestion, chunking, embeddings, hybrid retrieval, reranking, grounded generation and source attribution. Each step is a place where answers go wrong. Bad chunking splits the clause that mattered, weak retrieval finds the old policy, and missing attribution leaves the user unable to check the answer.

Source attribution is the regulated-industry detail to watch. An answer that cites the paragraph it came from can be audited. An answer that just sounds confident cannot.

## Permissions are the hard part

Two problems get special attention: preserving document-level access controls, and handling permissions that change. A knowledge assistant that politely summarises a document the user was never allowed to open is a data incident with good grammar. The talk also covers reducing hallucinations, evaluating retrieval quality and building observability across the RAG pipeline.

## Hybrid retrieval and reranking earn their place

Pure vector search is good at meaning and bad at exact strings, and enterprise questions are full of exact strings: policy numbers, product codes, internal acronyms. That is why the architecture combines hybrid retrieval with a reranking step before generation. Arzoo also covers evaluating retrieval quality on its own, which is the habit that separates teams who can debug a wrong answer from teams who can only shrug at it.

## What breaks after the pilot

The operational section is about life after the prototype: keeping knowledge fresh, monitoring retrieval failures, managing latency and inference costs, and measuring whether the assistant actually improves employee productivity. That last question is the one sponsors ask and engineers dread, and it is good to see it treated as an engineering requirement.

Attendees leave with a practical framework for moving an assistant from pilot to production, plus an evaluation scorecard and architectural patterns to adapt.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people building internal assistants in finance, healthcare, insurance or any field with auditors; platform teams asked to make one RAG stack serve many departments with different access rights; and anyone whose pilot impressed leadership and now has to survive real users.

Title: A voice AI tutor in production, with LangGraph, RAG and real evals
Description: Arjun Thakur at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on taking a voice-first LangGraph and RAG tutor past the prototype, with evals, tracing and a latency budget.
Body:
A voice agent has a problem a chat agent can hide: silence. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Arjun Thakur, an independent Principal AI Engineer, shares what it took to run a voice-first AI tutoring system built on LangGraph, RAG and OpenAI Realtime as a real product, and why "the answer looks good" is not an evaluation strategy.

His opening premise is one most of us have learned the expensive way: building the agent is the easy part. Making it fast, reliable, observable and useful once real users start talking to it is where the work lives.

## The stack is boring on purpose

The system Arjun describes is assembled from parts many teams already run: LangGraph for the agent workflow, FastAPI in front, PostgreSQL with pgvector for retrieval, and OpenAI Realtime for the voice loop. That's a feature. When the components are familiar, the interesting questions move to how they're wired together and what happens when one of them is slow.

In the talk he walks through how retrieval, agent workflows, semantic caching, verification and conversational memory fit together in one pipeline. Each of those layers adds a useful property and a few milliseconds, and in a voice product the user hears every one of them.

## Latency is a product requirement, not a dashboard

In a text UI, a two-second pause reads as "thinking". On a call it reads as "did it hang up?". So the design choices Arjun covers are framed by one constraint: keep latency low enough for a real-time conversation while still retrieving the right material and checking the answer.

That's where semantic caching earns its keep, and where verification has to be cheap enough to sit in the hot path. Expect the talk to be specific about the trade-offs: what you check every turn, what you cache, and what you give up in exchange for responding before the student loses interest.

## Evaluate the retriever and the agent separately

The part MLOps folks will care about most is how evaluation and observability get built into the development lifecycle instead of bolted on after the first angry user. Arjun's approach uses three instruments:

- **Retrieval metrics**, so you know whether the right context arrived before you blame the model.
- **Agent traces**, so a bad answer can be followed back through the graph to the node that went wrong.
- **Systematic testing**, so a prompt tweak or model swap is a regression run, not a vibe check.

He also covers the operational problems that only show up once a prototype meets people: retrieval quality drifting, agent failures, tracing gaps, and cost. If you've ever watched a demo-quality RAG app fall over on its first week of real questions, this section is the reason to watch.

## Who should watch

Engineers shipping RAG or agent-based apps that need to answer in real time, voice or not. Platform and MLOps teams asked to "add observability" to an LLM product without a clear idea of what to measure. Skip it if you want a LangGraph tutorial from zero; this one assumes you have built a prototype and now have to keep it alive.

Title: Can agentic LLMs correlate microservice telemetry better than we do?
Description: Nishanth Vepachedu examines agentic LLMs for telemetry correlation, root cause analysis and remediation at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
Microservices give you more logs, metrics and traces than any human can read during an outage. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Nishanth Vepachedu (in stealth, NIT Warangal alumnus) looks at how agentic large language models can help: semantic analysis of telemetry, correlation across services, automated causal reasoning and closed-loop remediation.

## Correlation is the bottleneck

The problem statement will be familiar to anyone who has carried a pager for a service mesh. Massive volumes of telemetry make incident detection, root cause analysis and reliability work harder, and traditional observability tools often struggle to correlate signals across complex service dependencies. The result, in Nishanth's words, is delayed investigations and operational blind spots. The data was there; nobody joined it in time.

That is the gap the talk aims LLM agents at. Reading a stack trace, a latency spike and a deploy event as one story is a language task as much as a statistics task.

## Fit it into the workflow you have

The talk focuses on architecture and operational practice: how to integrate LLM-driven analysis into existing observability workflows instead of replacing them. That is the sensible stance. Your dashboards, alerts and runbooks are not going away, and an agent that cannot read from them is a demo.

Nishanth draws on published research and industry findings to discuss improvements in event correlation, service dependency mapping, alert accuracy and incident response, including reductions in mean time to detection and mean time to resolution. Expect a synthesis of the literature rather than results from one production system; the abstract frames it that way and so do we.

## The questions you should ask before turning it on

The second half covers the parts that decide whether this survives contact with a security review: scalability, performance optimisation, debugging, security, data privacy and governance. Telemetry is full of customer identifiers and internal hostnames, and shipping it to a model raises questions your data protection officer will ask even if you do not. Closed-loop remediation also needs a clear answer to who approved the change when the agent made it.

## Who should watch

SREs and observability engineers curious whether LLM-based correlation is worth piloting, and platform teams building an AIOps roadmap who want a structured overview of the benefits and the risks. Engineers who have already shipped an LLM triage assistant may find it more useful as a checklist than as new material.

Title: How OpenAI connects Codex to Flyte through MCP for ML workflows
Description: Phoebe Wang (OpenAI) shows Codex driving reproducible Flyte training and eval workflows over MCP at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
AI coding tools can write ML code; getting that code to run reliably still needs an orchestrator. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Phoebe Wang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, shows how to connect Codex to Flyte through the Model Context Protocol for a reproducible training or evaluation workflow, and how OpenAI hosts Flyte for internal training.

## Writing the code was never the hard part

Anyone who has asked a coding assistant for a training script knows the next problem. The script looks right, then it runs on someone's laptop, against some version of the data, with whatever GPU was free. Nothing about that run is reproducible. The talk's premise is that reliable execution needs orchestration, and that the coding tool should hand work to the orchestrator instead of trying to be one.

Flyte is the orchestrator here: workflows defined in code, versioned, run on managed infrastructure. Codex is the author. MCP is the contract between them.

## MCP as the bridge

Phoebe covers how OpenAI developed MCP integration so Codex can work with Flyte. The appeal of doing it through MCP rather than a pile of shell commands is that the agent gets a defined set of operations with defined inputs and outputs. That makes it much easier to see what the agent asked for, rerun it, and stop it from doing things it should not.

It is also a rare look at internal plumbing at a frontier lab: how OpenAI hosts Flyte for its own training work. Expect specifics on the integration pattern rather than on model training itself.

## Leave with a checklist

The promised takeaway is concrete: a practical workflow pattern and a checklist covering debugging, reproducibility and safe execution. Those three are exactly where agent-written ML code tends to fail. Debugging asks whether you can tell what happened. Reproducibility asks whether you can do it again. Safe execution asks whether the agent can launch a cluster-sized job by accident, and the answer should be a firm no.

## Who should watch

ML engineers already using coding agents and wondering how to make the results run somewhere sensible; platform teams running Flyte, Airflow or similar who are getting requests to expose them to agents; and anyone building MCP servers for internal tools. Since the talk shows OpenAI's own tools (Codex) together with open-source Flyte, note that the pattern is about the integration, and similar ideas should carry over to other agents.

Title: What cloud infrastructure needs before agents can heal it
Description: Amit Anand looks at Kubernetes, multi-cloud and self-healing operations for agentic AI workloads at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
Agentic AI workloads are bursty, latency-sensitive and hard to predict, which is a polite way of saying they stress-test whatever infrastructure you put under them. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Amit Anand (currently in stealth, with a National Institute of Technology Jamshedpur background) surveys how to build cloud infrastructure for agentic AI with MLOps principles, and how AI agents themselves can help that infrastructure heal.

This is an architecture overview. Go in expecting patterns and considerations across a broad area rather than a single system's war story.

## Agents make capacity planning harder

Systems that perceive, reason and act generate workloads that do not look like a web service's daily curve. Amit points to the specific pressure points: unpredictable workloads, low-latency requirements and dynamic resource demands. Traditional cloud architectures were tuned for steadier traffic, and an agent that decides to call five tools in parallel does not ask the autoscaler first.

The talk looks at how Kubernetes, multi-cloud environments and orchestration frameworks such as LangChain can carry agentic AI workloads, with attention to resource scaling, workload orchestration, infrastructure automation and operational efficiency.

## Agents on the ops side, too

The other half flips the direction. Here AI agents are part of the operations team: collaborative agents assisting with incident detection, automated remediation and system recovery. Self-healing systems have been discussed at Conf42 for years; the agentic version adds reasoning to the loop instead of fixed runbooks.

Amit pairs that with an honest look at the maturity gaps in observability and automation that hurt reliability, performance and service-level objectives. That is the right order. An agent cannot fix what the telemetry cannot see, and a remediation loop built on patchy signals is just a faster way to make the wrong change.

## Governance comes with the territory

Letting software act on production raises questions that infrastructure teams cannot skip. The session covers designing agentic AI infrastructure with security, governance, compliance and cost optimisation in mind, and practical considerations for adding autonomous operations to existing cloud environments rather than greenfield ones. That last part matters: few teams get to rebuild their cloud to suit their agents.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams early in the process of hosting agent workloads, engineers evaluating automated remediation, and anyone who wants a structured map of the topic before committing to a design. If you already run an agent-driven remediation system in production, this will read as a checklist to compare against.

Title: Shipping LLM features on a page rendered millions of times a day
Description: Artem Zamarajev (Amazon) covers latency budgets, fallbacks, quality gates and kill switches for LLM features at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
An LLM feature that works in a demo is a weekend. The same feature on a high-traffic e-commerce page, millions of times a day, without hurting latency or showing a customer a bad answer, is a job. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Artem Zamarajev, Senior Software Engineer at Amazon, covers the operational side of that job, drawing on AI shopping features he shipped that reached millions of daily page renders with zero faults.

## Real time or precomputed?

The first decision in the talk is the one that shapes everything after it: when content should be generated in real time and when it can be precomputed. Not every piece of generated text needs to know who is looking at it this second. Precomputing what you can moves the model off the critical path, which is the cheapest latency fix there is.

## The page never waits on a model

For what does run live, Artem covers latency budgets, timeouts and fallbacks designed so the page never waits on a model. That rule is easy to say and hard to keep once product managers fall in love with a slow but clever answer. A fallback that renders something sensible when the model is late is what lets a critical page carry a generative feature at all.

He also covers integrating with an existing AI assistant's orchestration without becoming its bottleneck. On a large platform your feature is a guest in someone else's request path, and a slow guest gets uninvited.

## Catch bad output before customers do

Speed is half of it. The other half is quality: gates and monitoring that catch bad output before customers see it. With generative features, "the service returned 200" tells you almost nothing about whether the answer was right, so monitoring has to look at the content as well as the transport.

## Launch like you might need to unlaunch

The last section is about launching safely: gradual dial-ups, kill switches, and the metrics that matter during rollout. A kill switch is the most honest feature in any LLM launch plan. It admits that you will meet an output you did not predict and promises you can turn it off in seconds rather than in a deploy cycle.

Attendees leave with a practical checklist for taking an LLM feature from prototype to production traffic.

## Who should watch

Backend and ML engineers putting generative features on customer-facing pages, product teams negotiating latency budgets with model owners, and release engineers who will own the dial-up. If your LLM work lives in internal tools with patient users, the checklist still helps; the tolerances are just looser.

Title: Your rollback is a feature, and nobody has tested it
Description: Artemis Leonardou (NOFire AI) explains how to bound changes and test revert paths before an incident at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
"Ship fast, we can always revert" is the sentence that makes a lot of risky deploys feel safe. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Artemis Leonardou, Software Engineer and DevRel at NOFire AI, explains why she stopped believing it: the night she tried to revert an automated deployment and found the revert did not work either.

## The change an agent wrote

The story at the centre of the talk is specific. The change had been written by an agent. It touched more than she expected, in ways that were each reasonable on their own, and undoing it turned out to be a careful manual unwind instead of one command. Learning that while a service is down is the worst possible time to learn it.

That night is why she no longer accepts "we can always revert" as a reason to let anything automated ship something unbounded. Agents make this sharper because they are productive: they will happily touch config, schema and code in one change, and each edit looks fine in review.

## Treat the revert path like any other dependency

Her answer is to test the rollback path on purpose, the same way you would test anything else you rely on in an emergency. The talk covers three practices:

- Bounding a change so that reverting it really is one step.
- Verifying the revert actually runs, instead of assuming it will.
- Deliberately breaking things to see whether recovery behaves as expected, and reporting what she found when she did.

The third one is where the good stories usually live. A rollback that has never been executed is a hypothesis, and production is an expensive lab.

## It costs you speed, so choose

Artemis is upfront that this slows you down. The useful question, she argues, is not whether to do it but which changes deserve it, and she explains where she draws that line and why. That is the part most reliability advice skips: a rule you cannot afford to apply everywhere needs a clear rule for where it does apply.

## Who should watch

The abstract names the audience well: anyone whose pipeline has a revert path nobody has ever exercised in anger. Add teams letting coding agents open deployable pull requests, and ML teams whose model rollouts come bundled with feature pipeline and config changes. If your rollbacks are drilled quarterly, you will still pick up her line-drawing heuristics.

Title: Edge MLOps from PyTorch training to on-device ExecuTorch inference
Description: RanjithKumar Ragavan (T-Mobile) walks through an edge MLOps pipeline built around Meta's ExecuTorch runtime at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
Most MLOps pipelines stop at a cloud endpoint. A phone has no autoscaler, a thermal budget and a user who notices the battery. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, RanjithKumar Ragavan, Member of Technical Staff at T-Mobile, walks through what a pipeline needs when the deployment target is a consumer mobile device, drawing on his contributions to Meta's open-source PyTorch ExecuTorch runtime.

## The constraints move into the pipeline

On a server, memory and heat are someone else's problem. On a phone they are release blockers. RanjithKumar lists the constraints the pipeline has to respect: memory limits, thermal budgets, battery drain, and a fleet of devices with very different hardware. You cannot test once and ship everywhere when "everywhere" includes several generations of chips.

The talk starts with export: getting a PyTorch model into a mobile runtime built from a model loader, an execution planner, a memory manager and an operator registry. Knowing those parts is the difference between a cryptic failure on device and a fixable one.

## Compression is a pipeline stage, not a cleanup job

The second idea is that compression belongs inside the pipeline. The talk covers quantization-aware training, structured pruning and knowledge distillation as steps you run every time, not tricks you apply once a model is too big.

There is a specific claim worth hearing argued: quantization-aware training preserves accuracy better than post-training quantization alone. Plenty of teams start with post-training quantization because it is one command. The talk explains why that first step may not be the last one if accuracy matters.

## Validate per device tier

The release gate on edge is a matrix. RanjithKumar covers validating models across device tiers, including NPU versus CPU execution paths, and fitting models inside binary-size and thermal limits before release. An NPU path that is fast on a flagship and falls back to CPU on a mid-range phone is a different product, and the pipeline should know that before your users do.

Attendees get a reference pipeline for taking models from training to production on consumer mobile devices.

## Who should watch

ML engineers asked to "just put it on the phone", mobile engineers who have inherited a model they did not train, and MLOps folks whose tooling assumes a GPU in a rack. If you only ever serve from the cloud, the compression section still pays for itself.

Title: One anomaly detection pipeline for any retail KPI, not one per metric
Description: Priyank Jain (Boost Mobile / EchoStar) builds a KPI-agnostic anomaly pipeline for ~3,000 stores at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
Most anomaly detectors are built for one metric and rebuilt every time the business asks a new question. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Priyank Jain, Data Scientist II at Boost Mobile / EchoStar Corporation, walks through a KPI-agnostic pipeline designed for a retail network of roughly 3,000 stores: it starts with foot traffic and is built to take any time-series KPI with minimal changes.

## The real cost is the rebuild

A single-metric detector is easy to ship and expensive to own. The second request, the same thing for a different metric, means a second pipeline, a second set of thresholds and a second on-call conversation. Priyank's design goal is to make that second request a configuration change. Foot traffic is the first tenant, not the only one.

That framing is what makes this an MLOps talk rather than a modelling talk. The question is how to build something the analytics team can reuse across metrics, not which model scores best on a single chart.

## Three models, because each one misses different things

The pipeline uses an ensemble of Prophet, Isolation Forest and an autoencoder, and the talk explains why that three-model combination outperformed any single approach. Each family looks at the data differently: Prophet models trend and seasonality, Isolation Forest isolates points that are easy to separate, and an autoencoder flags what it cannot reconstruct. A store with a holiday spike, a store with a broken counter and a store that quietly changed its opening hours are three different shapes of weird.

On top of the ensemble sit severity scoring and automated reason-labelling, so an alert says how bad something is and gives a first guess at why. That is the difference between a dashboard full of red dots and a list someone can act on.

## The data fights back

Priyank is upfront about the practical data quality problems that appeared along the way, from zero-traffic days to extreme outliers. A zero might be a closed store, a broken sensor or a real disaster, and the pipeline has to decide which before it pages anyone. Those cases tend to consume more engineering time than the models, and it is useful to hear them discussed openly.

## What comes next

The talk closes with the roadmap: adding LLM-based root cause reasoning to explain anomalies automatically. It is presented as a plan, so expect design thinking there rather than production results.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and ML engineers who own anomaly detection for operations teams, especially in retail or any business with many similar locations. Also useful for anyone whose alerting stack has quietly become one bespoke detector per metric.

Title: Why logistic regression beat a CNN and an LSTM on noisy product names
Description: Vladimir Beskorovainyi (Besk Tech) explains trie rules, n-gram models and weighted labels for price statistics at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
Vladimir Beskorovainyi ran a 1D-CNN, an LSTM and a character n-gram logistic regression against each other on the same noisy product-name task, under one matched training protocol, and the logistic regression won every category. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, the CTO and CPO of Besk Tech explains why, and what that means for anyone classifying short, messy text.

## Receipts are not sentences

The setting is consumer price statistics built from alternative data: scanner exports, scraped listings, transaction and receipt records. These sources promise broader coverage than a surveyor with a clipboard, but they arrive as short, abbreviated, inconsistently spelled product names with no standard product code. Before any price can be compared, every item has to be mapped to a consumption classification such as COICOP.

In an abbreviated receipt line, word order barely matters and character fragments carry most of the signal. That is a strong hint about which model will win before anyone trains anything.

## Rules first, then a model that checks the rules

The pipeline runs in steps. Domain-specific normalisation and tokenisation come first. Then a prefix-tree (trie) pre-classifier, driven by per-category key phrases and stop phrases, proposes a category. Then a per-category binary confirmation model decides whether the item really belongs where the rules put it. Vladimir explains why binary confirmation per category beats one multiclass model here, and what that choice costs.

The operational lesson he flags as worth the ticket on its own: rules look like they are solving the problem, and then they are not. They cover only 32 to 50 percent of items, and coverage erodes as new product names appear. The learned stage is permanent infrastructure, not a stopgap you delete once the rule set matures. Anyone who has maintained a regex classifier for more than a year will nod here.

## Labels that compound

The other half is annotation. Several annotators give a binary valid or reject judgement, and votes are aggregated by a reliability weight that updates as annotation goes on. The model sits inside the same loop, so fine-tuning is continual instead of a periodic project. Around 66 labelled examples per category turn out to be enough.

## The numbers, with honest caveats

The headline result is mean F1 of 0.997 for the character n-gram logistic regression, with word-order features adding nothing and the neural baselines behind. The benchmark is synthetic and public, and Vladimir says plainly what that does and does not establish. The method has separately run in production on data that cannot be released; everything measured in the talk comes from the public benchmark. The method, benchmark and reproducibility package are on arXiv (2606.02004).

## Who should watch

Anyone classifying short text such as product titles, transaction descriptions or log lines; teams about to reach for a transformer by reflex; and people designing annotation workflows that should get better over time instead of decaying.

Title: A six-stage MLOps loop for municipal bond research and trading
Description: Tenny Enoch Devadas (Fidelity) maps MLOps onto the municipal bond lifecycle, from document AI to trade execution, at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
Municipal bonds pay for roads, schools and water systems, and they generate a mountain of PDFs. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Tenny Enoch Devadas, Principal Engineer at Fidelity, presents an architecture that applies MLOps practice to the whole municipal bond lifecycle, chaining document AI, credit analysis, portfolio decisions and trading into one monitored feedback loop.

## The input is a document problem

The lifecycle produces official statements, financial reports, continuing disclosures, ratings and security information, spread across municipalities, advisors, underwriters, investors and trading desks. The talk starts with an AI Document Intelligence Assistant that reads those sources (EMMA/MSRB and Bloomberg are named) and extracts the attributes analysts care about: CUSIP, coupon, maturity, call provisions, revenues, outstanding debt, debt-service coverage, pension obligations and covenants.

Extraction is only half of it. The output is validated against prior filings and reference data, which supports credit and anomaly detection: spotting material changes, disclosure inconsistencies, financial deterioration or improving credit. In other words, the model's work is checked against what the issuer said last year before anyone builds on it.

## Three assistants, one human in charge

That intelligence feeds a Portfolio Manager AI Assistant, which weighs credit quality alongside yield curves, relative value, duration, liquidity, ratings, portfolio exposure, investment guidelines, and state and sector concentration. It proposes Buy, Hold, Sell or Review, and the portfolio manager stays the final decision-maker.

After approval, a Trader AI Assistant evaluates fair value and liquidity, supports dealer and RFQ strategy, analyses quotes and helps document explainable best-execution decisions. In a regulated market, "the model said so" is not a best-execution record, so the explainability part is load-bearing.

## The loop is the MLOps part

The architecture ends in a six-stage operational loop: Document AI, Credit Intelligence, Portfolio Manager AI, Trader AI, Post-Trade AI and Continuous Monitoring. Each stage feeds the next and the monitoring stage feeds back. The talk focuses on the operational concerns around that loop: automation, validation, monitoring, explainability and continuous feedback. Expect architecture and practice rather than return figures; the abstract makes no performance claims, and neither will we.

## Who should watch

Engineers building ML systems in capital markets or any domain where decisions must be explained afterwards, and MLOps teams who want an example of chaining several models into one governed workflow. If fixed income is new to you, the talk is a decent tour of what data a bond desk actually uses.

Title: Treat loan valuation models like production software you can replay
Description: Ankur Mehra lays out a reproducible, auditable MLOps architecture for valuing illiquid loan portfolios at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
If you cannot rerun last quarter's valuation and get last quarter's number, you have a spreadsheet with extra steps. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, independent researcher Ankur Mehra presents an MLOps architecture for valuing mortgages, commercial loans and other illiquid lending assets, where reproducibility, traceability and reliability are treated as core requirements instead of audit-season chores.

## Accurate is the easy part

Financial institutions already have models that value illiquid loans under changing market conditions. Ankur's point is that accuracy on a workstation does not make a production system. Moving the models into production takes scalable pipelines, reproducibility, observability and strong controls around data and model changes. Illiquid assets have no market price to check against, which makes the model's own trail of evidence the thing everyone relies on.

## The valuation as a pipeline

The talk breaks the work into repeatable stages: market data ingestion, configurable economic scenarios, prepayment assumptions, cash-flow models and discounting. Organised that way, each stage has inputs and outputs that can be tested and versioned on their own, and a change to a prepayment assumption does not have to mean rerunning everything by hand.

## Version the assumptions, not only the code

The section most teams will steal is about versioning. Ankur covers versioning data, model configurations and assumptions together, so a team can reproduce a historical valuation, investigate an unexpected result and introduce a model update safely. Code in Git is not enough when the answer depends on which rate curve and which scenario file were loaded that morning.

## Operations: tests, lineage, failure handling

The operational half covers automated testing, pipeline monitoring, data lineage, failure handling, model validation and auditability. Event-driven processing comes up as a way to react to changes in market data and portfolio positions efficiently instead of rerunning the world on a timer, while still scaling the computation.

This is an architecture talk. It offers principles and structure, not a vendor product or a benchmark, and that is the right shape for the topic.

## Why replay matters more here

In most ML systems a bad prediction shows up as a bad outcome soon enough: a click that did not happen, a fraud case that slipped through. A loan valuation can sit on a balance sheet for months before anyone questions it, and by then the market data, the scenario set and the model version have all moved on. The only defence is being able to put the world back the way it was on the day the number was produced. That is what the versioning and lineage sections are for, and why Ankur treats them as requirements rather than nice extras.

## Who should watch

Quant developers and engineers who maintain valuation or risk models, MLOps teams entering finance from other industries, and anyone who has had to explain a number to an auditor six months after it was produced.

Title: Extend your ML platform for GenAI instead of building a second one
Description: Naveen Kumar Vedurupaka shows a shared control plane for predictive ML and generative AI workloads at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
Plenty of companies answered generative AI by standing up a second platform next to the ML platform they already had. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, independent researcher Naveen Kumar Vedurupaka argues for the opposite: extend the existing ML platform with a shared control plane that serves both predictive and generative workloads, while each keeps its own runtime optimisations.

## Two platforms, twice the plumbing

The cost of the side-by-side approach is duplication. Naveen lists what gets built twice: governance, observability, lineage, model registries, deployment pipelines and operating processes. Two registries means two sources of truth, and two sets of promotion rules means someone eventually ships through the one with fewer checks.

## Share the boring parts

The proposal splits a platform into what is common and what is workload-specific. Common capabilities that can serve both sides: model registry, lineage, observability, identity, governance, rollout strategies and cost attribution. Those are the parts auditors and finance care about, and they do not care whether the model is a gradient-boosted tree or an LLM.

The runtime layer is where the workloads differ. Extensions there cover LLM serving, retrieval-augmented generation, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, token streaming, continuous batching, multi-node inference and unified evaluation workflows. Classical and generative workloads run across online, near-real-time and batch serving environments without a full platform redesign.

## Contracts and gates make it hold

A shared control plane only works if the rules are written down. The talk covers Kubernetes-based reference architecture patterns, deployment contracts, promotion gates, policy enforcement, security controls, operational governance and cost management. Deployment contracts are the quiet hero here: they let a platform team say what any workload must provide before it can go live, regardless of what is inside.

The goal, in Naveen's framing, is to absorb generative AI into existing ML ecosystems with less duplication, while balancing scalability, safety, observability, performance and efficiency.

## Where the line falls

The practical value of the talk is in the boundary. Put too much in the shared layer and LLM serving inherits constraints built for batch scoring; put too little and you are back to two platforms with a shared login page. Token streaming and continuous batching, for example, have no real equivalent in classical model serving, so they belong in the runtime extension. Cost attribution, on the other hand, matters just as much for a GPU-hungry LLM as for a fleet of small models, so it belongs in the shared plane. That is exactly how the session divides them.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers and ML platform owners who are being asked where LLMs should live, architects reviewing a proposal for a separate GenAI stack, and anyone paying for two model registries. If you are starting from nothing, the common-versus-specific split is still a useful way to design.

Title: Run Vision on the Store's CCTV and Send Only Metadata to the Cloud
Description: At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Aleem Khan shows a retail computer-vision system on NVIDIA edge devices that ships anonymised metadata instead of video.
Body:
Small and mid-sized retailers already own the cameras. What they can't afford is streaming all that video to the cloud, and in many markets the internet connection couldn't carry it anyway. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, independent builder and serial entrepreneur Aleem Khan shows how his team built a computer-vision analytics system for physical stores that runs on NVIDIA edge devices on site and sends only anonymised metadata to the cloud.

## What runs in the store

The system does people counting, age and gender estimation, queue monitoring and heatmaps, all on existing CCTV feeds. The inference happens on NVIDIA edge hardware inside the store. What leaves the building is a stream of numbers and events, not pixels.

The title says it best: send metadata, not video. Bandwidth drops from video-sized to telemetry-sized, which turns a poor connection from a blocker into a non-issue.

## The pipeline, edge versus cloud

Aleem walks through the pipeline architecture: DeepStream modules, ONNX conversion of the models, and the split between what runs at the edge and what runs in the cloud. That split is the main design decision in any system like this, and the talk offers a reference for multi-camera computer vision you can compare your own against.

## When public datasets don't look like your stores

One of the more practical sections covers training data. Public datasets didn't match the stores' environments, so the team built and annotated its own on a startup budget. Anyone who has watched a model trained on clean benchmark photos meet a low-ceiling shop with a fisheye camera and fluorescent lighting knows why this matters.

## Running a fleet of edge devices

Once models live in dozens of stores, updating them becomes an operations problem rather than a data science one. The talk covers how the team kept models updated across distributed devices, the MLOps part that rarely gets slides. There's an honest note too: Aleem includes the mistakes made along the way.

## Privacy as an architecture choice

The privacy benefit falls out of the design. Video never moves off site, so there's no central archive of shoppers' faces to secure, leak or explain to a regulator. That is a far easier conversation than promising your cloud storage is locked down well enough.

## Who should watch

Engineers building computer vision for physical spaces: retail, warehouses, venues. Anyone deploying models to fleets of edge devices on unreliable networks. Startups without a big data-labelling budget, for the dataset section alone. If your cameras already sit in a data centre next to your GPUs, the edge story matters less, but the dataset and fleet-update lessons still carry.

Title: Follow One Token from Agent to GPU and Back in a Self-Hosted Stack
Description: Alessandro Vozza of Volt Datacenters at Conf42 MLOps 2026 traces a token through a gateway, an inference-aware router and vLLM on bare-metal GPUs.
Body:
Every agent call ends up as tokens on a GPU somewhere, and most developers never see the trip. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Alessandro Vozza, AI Architect at Volt Datacenters, follows a single token from an agent running in Kubernetes down to vLLM on bare-metal GPUs and back, and explains along the way why LLM traffic breaks the load balancing you're used to.

## The route

The talk is structured as a journey, which makes it a good map of a self-hosted AI stack:

1. An agent running in Kubernetes makes a call.
2. An AI gateway enforces identity and policy.
3. An inference-aware router decides where the request should go.
4. vLLM serves the model on bare-metal GPUs.
5. The tokens come all the way back.

If you've only ever called a hosted API, every one of those hops is something somebody else runs for you. This talk is about what it takes to run all of it on infrastructure you control.

## Why round-robin doesn't cut it

The most transferable lesson is why LLM traffic breaks traditional load balancing. Classic balancers assume requests are roughly similar in cost. LLM requests are not: a short prompt with a short answer and a long prompt with a long generation can differ enormously in GPU time, and spreading them evenly by count does not spread the load evenly. That's the job of the inference-aware router in the middle of the path, and Alessandro explains what it has to know to do it.

Anyone who has watched one pod melt while its siblings idle will feel seen.

## Prefill and decode, the two halves of latency

The talk also covers what prefill and decode mean for latency and cost. Prefill processes the prompt; decode generates the output token by token. They stress the hardware differently, which is why a long context and a long answer hurt in different ways, and why the numbers you tune for one don't help the other. Understanding the split is the difference between guessing at your GPU bill and reasoning about it.

## Gateway first, GPU later

Putting identity and policy at the gateway, before anything reaches a GPU, is a design choice worth noting. It means agents get authenticated and governed in one place, and the expensive hardware only sees requests that should be there. For teams self-hosting partly for control and compliance reasons, this is where that control actually lives.

## Who should watch

Platform and infrastructure engineers considering self-hosted inference, or already running vLLM and wondering why the load balancer doesn't help. Agent developers who want a mental model of what their calls cost below the API. If your stack is entirely hosted model APIs and staying that way, this is still a good explanation of what you're paying for.
