Title: The Validator Pattern for Analytics Agents You Can Actually Trust
Description: Amazon's Shipra Sonal and Madhu Gurramkonda at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on read-only specialist agents plus a validator that checks every claim at the source.
Body:
An analytics agent that's right most of the time has a nasty property: nobody can tell which answers are the wrong ones. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Shipra Sonal, Data Engineering Manager at Amazon, and Madhu Gurramkonda, Head of Data Analytics at Amazon, present the validator pattern, a simple split in which specialist agents can only read data and a separate validator checks every claim in a draft answer against its live source before the answer goes out.

## Mostly right is the dangerous zone

The problem is sharper than "agents make mistakes". A system that is usually wrong gets ignored. A system that is usually right gets trusted, and its occasional confident error ends up in a slide deck in front of a leader making a decision. For business questions, the cost of an unflagged wrong answer is much higher than the cost of a slow one.

The validator pattern goes after exactly that: it doesn't try to make the specialists perfect, it makes sure their output is checked before anyone sees it.

## Readers and a checker

The architecture has two roles. Specialist agents do the work of answering, but they are read-only, which removes a whole class of accidents before they start. A separate validator takes the draft answer and checks each claim against the live source. Separating the writer from the checker is an old idea in engineering (code review, double-entry bookkeeping, the second pilot), and the talk applies it to agent output.

## Scope the validator carefully

The useful details are in the boundaries. Shipra and Madhu cover how to split work between specialists and the validator, what the validator should check and, just as important, what it shouldn't. A validator that tries to re-derive every answer becomes a second, slower analyst with the same blind spots. A validator that checks too little is decoration. The talk also covers how to handle answers the validator rejects, which is the part most designs leave as an exercise for the reader.

## The outages nobody noticed

The section on failures in practice is the one to stay for. Among them: outages nobody noticed at first. That is a very particular kind of embarrassment for a system built to catch errors, and a reminder that the checker itself needs monitoring. If your validator goes quiet, it can look exactly like everything passing.

The talk closes with the operating rules that came out of those incidents.

## Who should watch

Data and analytics teams putting agents in front of business users. Anyone building a multi-agent system and deciding where verification lives. If your agent writes to systems rather than answering questions, the read-only constraint won't map directly, but the writer-checker split still will.

Title: A vLLM production stack that runs the same on EKS, AKS, GKE and Nebius
Description: Kosseila Haddalene (Cloudthrill) shows a Terraform-driven vLLM stack for multi-cloud Kubernetes GPU inference at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
Running vLLM on a laptop proves the tokens come out fast. Running it behind real traffic proves everything else. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Kosseila Haddalene, founder and AI infrastructure lead at Cloudthrill, presents an open-source, Terraform-driven vLLM production stack that behaves the same way on Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE and Nebius Mk8s.

The stack grows out of his upstream contributions to the official vLLM production stack, so this is a talk from someone who has had to make the thing work for other people, not only on his own cluster.

## The demo ends where the problems start

The abstract lists the trouble that shows up once vLLM leaves the notebook: several models served at once, hundreds of concurrent requests, pods that die mid-stream and tail latency that refuses to behave. Kosseila points out that these are the same issues the community keeps raising whenever someone runs vLLM on Kubernetes. If you have read the GitHub issues, you have met them.

The answer in the talk is not a clever flag. It is a repeatable deployment: GPU-optimised Kubernetes configuration for vLLM workloads, tiered inference, and automation that goes all the way from cluster bootstrap to an SSL-enabled endpoint that is ready to take requests.

## Four clouds, one Terraform story

The interesting promise is portability. Each managed Kubernetes service has its own opinions about GPU node pools, drivers, load balancers and certificates, and teams usually discover those opinions one outage at a time. A single Terraform-driven stack that lands consistently on EKS, AKS, GKE and Nebius Mk8s means the cloud becomes a variable instead of a rewrite.

That matters for two reasons. GPU capacity is where you find it, and the cheapest region this quarter may sit in a different provider next quarter. And lock-in creeps in through the glue code, not the model server. Keeping the glue in one codebase is how you avoid it. The session is pitched squarely at platform engineers and MLOps teams who want GPU-backed LLM inference without cloud lock-in.

## Observability ships with the cluster

The stack comes with Grafana dashboards built in. That sounds like a footnote until you need to explain to someone why p99 latency doubled at 14:00. Shipping the dashboards with the infrastructure means the first incident is debugged with the right graphs instead of the ones somebody builds during the incident. Tiered inference plus visible queues and GPU use is the combination that turns a vague complaint about a slow model into a specific, fixable problem.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who have been handed a ticket to make vLLM production-ready, MLOps teams comparing managed Kubernetes providers for GPU work, and anyone maintaining a fork of a Helm chart they no longer fully understand. If you only run one small model on a single GPU box, you can skip the multi-cloud parts, but the failure modes Kosseila lists will still look familiar.

Title: Joining GPU telemetry to the Kubernetes workload that owns it
Description: Nishant Modak (Last9) builds an OpenTelemetry Collector processor that maps GPU metrics to pods and jobs, at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
Body:
A GPU metric knows which device it came from. Your ML platform cares about which job, pod, model or team was using that device. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Nishant Modak of Last9 shows how his team built an OpenTelemetry Collector processor that joins node-level GPU data to the Kubernetes workload, so a utilisation graph finally has a name on it.

His job title is Chief Evals Officer, abbreviated CEO, which tells you roughly how seriously to take the job title and how seriously to take the engineering.

## Two vocabularies that never line up

The abstract states the problem in two sentences: GPU telemetry starts with a device identifier, an ML platform starts with a workload, and those names do not match. Anyone who has looked at a DCGM exporter dashboard and tried to work out which training run is hogging GPU 3 knows the feeling.

In the talk Nishant follows a single metric on its trip: from the GPU UUID, through device allocation, through pod discovery, to workload ownership. At the end it carries pod, namespace, deployment and job identity, which is the point where it becomes useful for capacity planning, performance work and failure analysis.

## The join is where it gets hard

This is the part worth the ticket. The join breaks in ways that are easy to miss:

- MIG changes what "a device" means, so one physical GPU can be several logical ones.
- Pods move.
- Short jobs finish and vanish before a cache refreshes.
- Device assignments and telemetry arrive on different clocks.

Nishant's warning is that a mapping layer can quietly attach the right metric to the wrong workload unless it keeps track of its own uncertainty. A wrong label is worse than no label, because people believe it and bill the wrong team.

The talk builds the attribution path, looks at the Kubernetes API and RBAC boundary it has to cross, and then deliberately breaks it with each of the cases above.

## Plain OTLP at the end

The output is ordinary OTLP with workload identity attached. No backend-specific GPU model is required. That design choice keeps the processor useful whether you send data to Last9 or anywhere else, and it means the hard logic sits in the pipeline rather than in a vendor's query language.

Nishant frames the session as a systems talk about the missing layer between GPU monitoring and useful MLOps telemetry. It is a fair description.

## Who should watch

Platform teams running shared GPU clusters, anyone writing chargeback reports for ML spend, and people maintaining OpenTelemetry Collector pipelines who want to see a non-trivial custom processor. If your GPUs are each pinned to one long-lived service, the attribution problem is smaller, though the MIG section still applies.

Title: Telling an Agent the Rule vs Enforcing It in Code, Measured
Description: Dylan Merigaud at Conf42 MLOps 2026 replays 200 runs of an unattended coding agent to test which rules hold as sentences and which need code.
Body:
If you've ever written "never do X" in an agent's instruction file and wondered whether it reads that line, Dylan Merigaud ran the experiment. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, the freelance AI engineer (Merigaud Consulting) presents a preregistered replay of 200 runs of a coding agent that runs unattended for months, comparing rules written as sentences with the same rules enforced in code on the path of the action.

## The setup: every rule in two forms

The agent is told what not to do in plain sentences, like most agents are. Dylan kept each rule in two forms: a sentence in an instruction file and, for some of them, code that sits where the action happens. He calls that code a door. A door can be a hook that refuses, a write path that rejects, or a precondition on the scheduler.

The replay covered 5 rules over 200 runs, and it was preregistered. That word is doing a lot of work. Most guardrail claims you read are post-hoc stories; this one committed to what it would measure before it measured it.

## Sentences worked better than you'd guess

The first result is a pleasant surprise for anyone who assumed instructions are decorative. One sentence cut violations from 100% to 0% on 2 rules, and to 10% or 20% on 2 more. For a cheap intervention, that is a lot of behaviour change.

## Doors alone did not hold

The second result is the one to print out and tape next to your monitor. The door alone did not hold: 53% of runs still broke the 4 rules it covered. One hook never fired in 10 of 10 runs that broke its rule. The enforcement existed in the code; the agent just found a path that didn't go through it.

Where the write hook did block, the block took effect 10 of 10 times. So the code works when it's on the path. The hard part is knowing whether it's on the path, and the only way to find out was to replay the agent and count.

## What to check before trusting a guardrail

Dylan closes with the cases behind those numbers and the checks he runs before he trusts a guardrail. The useful mental shift is that a rule enforced in code is a claim about every path the agent can take, and agents are good at finding paths you didn't draw. A hook you've never seen fire is a hypothesis, not a control.

There is a dry irony in the results: the sentence, which everyone treats as the weak option, did real work, and the code, which everyone treats as the strong option, needed testing to earn that status.

## Who should watch

Anyone running coding agents with hooks, deny lists or permission prompts and assuming they hold. Platform teams writing guardrails for other people's agents. Also anyone who likes their opinions backed by a preregistered experiment, which in this field is still a rare treat. If you only use agents interactively and approve every action yourself, this is useful background rather than urgent.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Hardening AI Coding Agents with Hooks: Enforcing Least Privilege on Autonomous Developers](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Karan_Bansal_agents_leastprivilege_hooks) by Karan Bansal at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, the case for hooks.

Title: A Write-Gate for an AI Agent Fleet, and the Bug It Didn't Fix
Description: Retailbox founder Michael Oskola at Conf42 MLOps 2026 shares the build log of Foreman+, an open-source agent fleet where every fact passes a write-gate.
Body:
Michael Oskola's talk at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19 is a build log, and the best part is the bug the safety system caught but didn't fix. Michael, founder of Retailbox, runs Foreman+, an open-source fleet of three AI agents that turns a technician's nameplate photo and voice notes into a field-service job record, with every fact passing a write-gate before the fleet can remember it.

## The stack and the gate

Foreman+ runs on Google ADK with Gemini on Vertex AI, and stores memory in Cloud SQL Postgres with pgvector. The write-gate is layered the sensible way round: cheap deterministic checks first, then an LLM verifier. If the verifier errors or returns nothing, the write is refused. Fail closed, in other words, which is the right default for anything that becomes long-term memory.

In the recorded demo run, the fleet made 14 proposals in 83 seconds, and the gate refused one.

## The gate caught it, the prompt caused it

Here's the story worth the ticket. A setup prompt named a job by street address instead of by ID. That made an agent write a technician's name onto a different job at the same address. The gate refused the write as a contradiction, which is what it's for. But Michael's point is that the real fix was in the prompt. A gate that keeps catching the same error is telling you about a bug upstream.

Anyone who has keyed a table on something that turned out not to be unique will wince in recognition.

## The camera details nobody puts on slides

The fleet also takes input from camera glasses, and the talk includes the small, unglamorous findings that make these systems work. Switching photo compression to medium cut capture time from 34 s to 6.3 s. And ordering mattered: a camera frame sent before the question was ignored, with the model answering from imagination. Attached inside the question turn, it was right 3 times out of 3 in their probe. Three is a small sample and Michael calls it a probe, but it's a cheap thing to check in your own multimodal pipeline.

## What the repo admits it lacks

The talk is candid about the gaps: every service runs as a single instance, and there's no CI yet. That kind of honesty is rarer than it should be in agent talks, and it makes the rest of the numbers easier to trust. The repo is MIT-licensed and the demo runs without a login, so you can check the claims yourself.

## Who should watch

Builders of multi-agent systems with shared memory, especially anyone letting agents write facts other agents will later rely on. Teams doing multimodal input from phones or wearables. If you want a polished production reference architecture, this isn't it; if you want an honest log of what broke and what changed, it is.

Title: Graph-RAG vs Vector Search for Agents That Must Get Facts Right
Description: AWS's Elizabeth Fuentes Leone at Conf42 MLOps 2026 builds a travel booking agent and compares FAISS vector search with a Neo4j knowledge graph.
Body:
A chatbot that hallucinates gives you a wrong answer; an agent that hallucinates books the wrong room. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, Developer Advocate at AWS, builds a travel booking agent live and compares two retrieval approaches on the same 300 hotel FAQ documents: traditional vector search with FAISS, and Graph-RAG backed by a Neo4j knowledge graph.

## When agents hallucinate, they act on it

The framing is the useful part. Hallucination in an agent is worse than in a chat window because the agent does something with the made-up fact. Elizabeth lists the failure modes: fabricated API parameters, invented confirmations, decisions based on false data. A wrong number in a reply is embarrassing. A wrong number passed to a booking API is a refund.

Her argument is that traditional RAG can make this worse. Vector search returns approximate matches, which is fine when you want something like the answer and a problem when you need exactly the answer. Ask for one hotel's pet policy and you may get a paragraph about a different hotel that sounds very similar.

## Structure for precise questions

Graph-RAG swaps similarity for relationships. The hotel FAQs go into a Neo4j knowledge graph, so a question about a specific property's facts can follow explicit links rather than relying on nearest neighbours in embedding space. The session shows how this reduces fabricated statistics and incomplete retrieval, and gets better accuracy on precise queries.

The honest scope matters here: the claim is about precise, factual queries. Graphs are not a free upgrade for every retrieval task, and the comparison is set up on a specific domain and dataset so you can see where the difference comes from.

## Hands-on, and no graph background needed

This is a hands-on session, and the abstract says no prior graph database experience is needed, which makes it a good first look at Graph-RAG if you've only ever used vector stores. The pattern you leave with is meant to transfer to any domain where agents need reliable, verifiable data retrieval. Travel booking is just a domain where the cost of a wrong fact is easy to picture.

Elizabeth has spoken at Conf42 before on keeping agents accurate and cheap, so this talk extends an ongoing thread rather than a one-off demo.

## Who should watch

Engineers building agents that act on retrieved facts: bookings, orders, account changes. Teams whose RAG works for summaries but falls over on exact lookups. If your use case is open-ended research where approximate matches are what you want, the vector half of the comparison will still be instructive.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Reduce AI Agents Costs and Mistakes with Semantic tool Selection](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_tools_semantic_cost), Elizabeth Fuentes Leone's own talk at Conf42 AI Agents 2026.

Title: A YAML Rules Engine for AI Use Case Reviews, With a Red Zone
Description: Ankur Gupta (Roblox, OWASP AI Exchange) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on automating AI use case governance with YAML policies and red-zone short-circuits.
Body:
Security teams reviewing AI features one by one end up as either a rubber stamp or a permanent bottleneck. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Ankur Gupta, who works on security risk at Roblox and is an author of the OWASP AI Exchange, presents a rules engine that evaluates AI use case requests against YAML policies, rejects the dangerous ones automatically and routes the rest through tiered approvals.

## Why manual review breaks

The problem will be familiar to anyone at a company where every team suddenly wants to ship an AI feature. Hundreds of requests, one security function. Manual review doesn't scale, and spreadsheet-based tracking breaks the moment two people edit the same tab. Without clear automated rules, Ankur argues, governance drifts to one of two failure modes, and neither of them is governance.

## Policies in YAML, context in JSON

The architecture is refreshingly plain. Teams submit an intake form; its answers become JSON context. The engine evaluates that context against tiered policy rules defined in YAML and produces an auditable approval or rejection decision. Rules are text in a repo, so they can be reviewed, versioned and diffed like any other code. Policy-as-code people will feel right at home.

## The red zone short-circuits

The detail that makes this practical is the red zone. Certain high-risk patterns trigger an automatic rejection without human review, and the engine stops evaluating as soon as one matches. That means reviewers don't spend time on requests that were never going to be approved, and requesters get a fast, explainable no instead of waiting a week for the same answer.

Everything that isn't red goes through graduated approval workflows, tiered by risk classification. Low-risk requests move quickly; higher tiers get more eyes. The point is to spend scarce security attention where it changes the outcome.

## Plugging into the GRC you already have

A rules engine that lives on its own island becomes another spreadsheet. Ankur covers integration with existing security review and GRC workflows, so decisions land where auditors and risk teams already look. He also shares lessons from operating the system across dozens of AI use case submissions, which is where the rule set gets tested against people who are very creative about describing their projects as low-risk.

## Who should watch

AppSec and GRC teams drowning in AI intake requests. Platform engineers asked to build "the AI approval process" with no spec beyond that sentence. Also useful if you write policy-as-code for infrastructure and want to see the same pattern applied to AI use cases. If your company has three AI features and one reviewer, the talk is a preview of next year.

Title: Your Agent's Refund Check Trusts an Order ID the Model Picked
Description: Aeroclub's Danila Redikultsev at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on self-signed evidence, the code checks that trust values an LLM agent chose.
Body:
An LLM support agent finds two orders for the same blender, picks one and calls the refund tool. The code check passes, the money goes out, and the broken blender was in the other order. That's the opening case of Danila Redikultsev's talk at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19. Danila is a Senior Software Engineer, AI, at Aeroclub, and builds LLM agents that spend customers' money.

## Moving the check into code didn't help

The blender example is worth slowing down on, because it defeats the usual advice. The team did put the guard in code. The code confirmed the order belonged to the customer, was recent, and was under the refund limit. Every condition was true. The problem is that the check trusted an order ID the model chose. The validation was rigorous about the wrong question.

Danila calls this self-signed evidence: the model supplies the value, and the check verifies the model's own claim against itself. It's a forged signature where the forger also runs the notary.

## How common is it

To see whether this is a corner case, Danila went through public τ²-bench runs. He counted 82 of 1,632 conversations where tools accepted a change to an order the task never asked to change. In at least 21 of those, the model picked the order itself. Not every agent bug is this one, but enough of them are that it deserves a name.

## Finding the model-written values

The practical part of the session is a short method:

- Find the model-written values your checks trust: IDs, amounts, targets, anything the LLM filled in rather than something the system derived from the user's request.
- Test each check with a swapped order ID. If the check still passes when the agent points at the wrong record, it was never checking the thing you cared about.
- Run a new check in shadow before it's allowed to block, so you learn its false positive rate on real traffic instead of from angry customers.

The swapped-ID test is the kind of idea that takes ten minutes to add to a test suite and stays useful for years.

## Who should watch

Engineers whose agents issue refunds, make bookings, or take any action with money or real-world effects attached; Danila names that audience directly. Security reviewers who sign off on a tool because it validates its inputs. If your agent only reads data, the concept still applies to whatever it reports back, though the stakes are lower.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [I Don't Trust AI Agents (And Neither Should You): Building Production-Ready Architectures](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Morgan_Willis_production_guardrails_trust) by Morgan Willis at Conf42 AI Agents 2026.

Title: Identity, Scoped Grant, Policy Gate, Audit for Agents at Aflac
Description: Aflac's Shanker Valipireddy at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on taking agentic AI from demo to production in a regulated enterprise, and the pattern that resulted.
Body:
Demos don't have auditors. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Shanker Valipireddy, Principal Architect and AI Enablement Lead at Aflac, gives a practitioner's account of moving agentic AI from demos to production inside a regulated enterprise, and boils it down to a four-part reference pattern: identity, scoped grant, policy gate, audit.

## Every agent gets its own identity

The first piece is per-agent identity with least-privilege access. It sounds obvious until you look at how many early agent deployments run under one shared service account with the permissions of whoever set it up. When something goes wrong, "the agent did it" is not an identity your security team can work with. Separate identities make it possible to scope, revoke and attribute what each agent does.

## Not every action deserves the same gate

The second idea is the one most teams get wrong in one of two directions: approve everything by hand and nothing ships, or approve nothing by hand and everything ships. Shanker describes risk-adaptive policy gates that auto-approve low-risk actions and escalate high-risk ones. The skill is in the classification, and in making the low-risk path fast enough that nobody tries to sneak around the high-risk one.

## Audit that can't be rewritten

Third, immutable audit. In a regulated business the question is not only whether the agent behaved, but whether you can show it later to someone who wasn't in the room. Immutable records are what make that conversation short.

## Evaluation as a platform gate

The fourth part puts evaluation where MLOps people will want it: as a gate the platform enforces, not a step each team remembers to run. Shanker grounds this in public agent benchmarks and in production failure patterns, rather than in a vendor's feature list.

## Lessons from a long platform career

The talk also draws on 20 years of platform work, including a 20,000-pipeline migration. That background shows in the framing. Agents are treated as one more workload that needs identity, permissions, policy and records, the same things platform teams have been building for services for years. The new part is that this workload decides for itself which API to call next, which is precisely why the old controls matter more, not less.

Attendees leave with the reference pattern and a checklist for operating agents in production.

## Who should watch

Title: Grade the Agent on What Happened, Not on What It Said
Description: At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Microsoft AI's Sajal Garg shows how to evaluate tool-using agents by observable actions and outcomes, then gate releases on them.
Body:
"A better answer score does not prove that an AI agent completed its task." That's the opening line of Sajal Garg's abstract, and the rest of his session at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19 is the operational fallout. Sajal is a Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft AI, where he works on automated LLM evaluation infrastructure, and the talk turns that work into a workflow for grading agents on actions and outcomes.

## The confident completion message

The failure he targets is specific. An agent reports success while a tool request is still unresolved, an action has run twice, or a required approval never happened. A text-only evaluation reads the polite summary and rewards it. The ticket system, the payments ledger and the approver's inbox would tell a different story, if anyone asked them.

The flip side gets equal billing: an agent that refuses every action is not reliable just because it never caused an unsafe effect. A scoring scheme that rewards doing nothing is a scoring scheme your laziest agent will win.

## Two kinds of checks, kept apart

The workflow is built around a non-confidential illustrative task, and its core move is separation. Deterministic checks look at actions and service state: did the record change, did the call happen once, was the approval present. Quality judgments look at generated content. Mixing the two into one number hides exactly the failures that matter.

Sajal also separates the failures of the harness from the failures of the agent. If the judge model times out or the test infrastructure falls over, that is not a task failure, and counting it as one sends people chasing a prompt bug that does not exist.

## Break it on purpose

The session uses controlled interruption and lost-acknowledgement cases to test recovery. A tool that did the work but never confirmed it is the classic distributed-systems trap, now with an LLM deciding whether to retry. Anyone who has debugged an at-least-once queue will recognise the shape.

Two hygiene rules come with it: reset test state between runs, and evaluate variable behaviour across repeated runs rather than trusting one lucky pass.

## From results to a release gate

The closing section connects evaluation to shipping decisions for code, prompt and model changes. Compare the current and candidate versions on the same cases. Keep the versioned inputs and checks so a result can be reproduced next month. Keep critical execution failures separate from aggregate quality scores, so a double refund can't be averaged away by a nicer tone.

Attendees leave with a failure taxonomy, concrete action and effect assertions, and an agent-evaluation release checklist. Sajal is clear that this is an operational evaluation session, not a worker-pool architecture talk or a product demo.

## Who should watch

Teams whose agents call tools that change state, and who currently gate releases on an LLM-judge score. ML platform engineers building the regression gate everyone else will be blocked by. If your agents only answer questions and never act, the deterministic half will matter less to you, though the judge-failure separation still applies.

Title: Put AI Compliance in the Pipeline, Not in a Pre-Launch Meeting
Description: At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Arpita Sheth moves AI governance into the MLOps pipeline with risk tiers, lineage, policy gates and generated docs.
Body:
A compliance review before launch made sense when a model launched once. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, software engineer Arpita Sheth argues that continuous retraining and redeployment break that model, and shows how to make governance a stage in the MLOps pipeline instead of a meeting on someone's calendar.

## Why the launch review stops working

The pressure comes from several directions at once: the EU AI Act, U.S. AI governance frameworks and privacy laws. Each expects you to know what a model is, what it was trained on and whether it still meets the rules. Meanwhile your models are retrained, redeployed and updated continuously. A sign-off from three versions ago describes a system that no longer exists.

Arpita brings the experience to back this up. Her background includes building automated GDPR compliance systems, ROPA (records of processing activities) reporting pipelines and data governance platforms at Meta. In other words, she has already done the boring-but-critical plumbing at a scale where manual review was never going to keep up.

## Five places governance lives in the pipeline

The talk walks through where compliance work attaches to the steps you already run:

- **Risk classification at model registration.** The moment a model enters the registry is the cheapest point to decide how much scrutiny it needs.
- **Lineage capture** across datasets, features and model versions, so the question of what a model was trained on has an answer that isn't an archaeology project.
- **Policy checks as CI/CD gates** before training and before deployment.
- **Monitoring signals that feed compliance evidence**, so the same telemetry that pages on-call also documents behaviour for auditors.
- **Documentation generated from pipeline metadata**, rather than written by hand after the fact.

That last item will make some readers very happy. Model cards that write themselves from the metadata you already have are model cards that stay current.

## The trade-offs get airtime too

What makes this more than a checklist is the honesty about cost. Arpita covers where automated gates slow teams down, and how to keep engineering and compliance aligned without manual handoffs. Every gate is a place a release can stall, and a gate that blocks too often teaches people to route around it. Getting the strictness right is the actual engineering problem.

## Who should watch

MLOps and platform engineers who own the pipeline that compliance will eventually want a piece of. Privacy and governance folks who would rather get evidence from a system than from a spreadsheet. If you're at a small team with one model and no regulator in sight, take the lineage and auto-documentation ideas and skip the rest for now.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [The Paved Road Had a Compliance Gate](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2026_Sumeet_L_Ram_compliance_gate_paved) by Sumeet L Ram at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026, the same idea from the platform team's chair.

Title: Two Equally Accurate Credit Models, a $227M Difference in Harm
Description: At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Neelima Verma uses FairLens and 95,588 HMDA mortgage applications to price model bias in dollars, not just accuracy.
Body:
Two models with near-identical AUC can do very different amounts of damage. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, data scientist and responsible-AI practitioner Neelima Verma presents the Dollar-Cost Fairness Framework, built with her open-source tool FairLens on 95,588 real HMDA mortgage applications, and shows a Support Vector Machine imposing $227M more in disparate harm than a neural network of the same accuracy.

## Accuracy is the wrong scoreboard for lending

The setup is a fair fight. Ten machine learning models, from logistic regression to neural networks, trained and evaluated on the same public mortgage data. The twist is the measurement: alongside accuracy, Neelima measures the dollar-denominated harm each model imposes on protected groups.

The headline finding: an SVM and a neural network landed on near-identical AUC, yet the SVM imposed $227M more in disparate harm against Black and Hispanic applicants. That is a 13x difference in financial harm between two models a leaderboard would call tied. She reports the results as bootstrap-validated, with p < 0.001.

## Compliant is not the same as harmless

The title's paradox comes from regulation. Fairness rules are tightening, and teams reasonably aim to pass a disparate impact audit. The talk's argument is that passing one may not be enough, because the audit and the harm are measured differently. A model can clear the bar and still be the most expensive choice for the people it decides about.

Translating bias into dollars is the practical move here. A fairness gap of a few points is easy to wave away in a review. A dollar figure lands in the same units as regulatory exposure and business risk, which is the language the people approving the model already speak.

## Interventions, with their price tags

The session covers bias interventions from AIF360, the open-source fairness toolkit: reweighing and calibrated equalized odds, and the real tradeoffs each brings. There is a live FairLens demo with model comparison and fairness dashboards. Attendees leave with a reusable evaluation framework and code patterns for putting fairness audits into ML pipelines, which fits squarely in an MLOps track: the check belongs next to the other gates, not in a slide deck after launch.

Neelima also ties it to agents: when an AI agent makes financial decisions about people, "agent risk" includes exactly this kind of quiet, accurate-looking harm.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and data scientists building or auditing decision systems in regulated areas such as lending, insurance or hiring. Model risk and compliance folks who sign off on models by AUC. If you've ever picked between two models on a third decimal place of accuracy, this talk suggests a better tiebreaker.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [AI's Hidden History: Unpacking Bias, Power, and the Builders Who Shaped It](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Lianne_Potter_bias_builders_history) by Lianne Potter at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, for the longer view on where bias comes from.
- [Compliance-by-Construction for Scalable, Privacy-Resilient Credit Apps](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Ravindra_Rajasekhar_Kavuru_privacy_compliance_credit) by Ravindra Rajasekhar Kavuru at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026, also in credit.

Title: Green Evals, Broken Agents, and Why Your Metric Choice Lies
Description: At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Adobe's Dylan Ler shows how a green eval suite hides broken agents, and how to make evals a versioned deployment artifact.
Body:
Add one metric and a clean win becomes a design problem. That is the story Dylan Ler, Forward Deployed Engineer at Adobe, tells about his own published experiments at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, and he uses it to argue that evals deserve the same treatment as the code they gate: versioned, owned and shipped through CI.

## The receipts come from his own work

This talk earns its title with numbers, all from Dylan's experiments rather than from a vendor slide. In his Latent Pager Memory study, reporting only F1 and latency made the method look like a straightforward win: +41.5% F1 and 2.55x faster. Adding a hallucination measure, which moved from 0.292 to 0.580, turned that win into a design problem.

The rest of the list is just as uncomfortable. Selecting checkpoints by validation loss instead of the metric that actually mattered would have cost about 35% F1. A one-line generation fix moved test F1 more than any architecture change did. In his calibration audit, accuracy and Brier score ranked the same models in opposite orders. And in his "Worlds That Teach Back" work, 85.6% token accuracy said nothing about whether the generated physics conserved energy.

Each of those is a small lesson. Together they say the same thing: the number on the dashboard is a choice, and somebody should own that choice.

## Evals as a deployment artifact

The second half of the session turns the lessons into a pipeline. Datasets, graders and thresholds are versioned and have owners, so "the eval changed" shows up in a diff instead of a hallway conversation. Deterministic checks run alongside calibrated LLM judges, each doing what it's good at. Evals score trajectories, invariants and tool calls, not only final answers, because an agent can reach a fine answer by a path that should have failed the build.

## A sentinel suite and a reproduction rate

Two practices stand out. First, a sentinel suite runs on every prompt, tool or model change. Prompts are code that nobody code-reviews, so something has to.

Second, every observed failure becomes a minimal regression test with a measured reproduction rate. That last bit is the quiet gem. A flaky agent bug that reproduces one run in five is still a bug, and knowing the rate tells you how many runs a test needs before a pass means anything.

## What to run, and when

Attendees leave with a CI blueprint and a budget: what runs per PR, what runs nightly, what waits for pre-release. That is the practical answer to the usual objection that thorough agent evals are too slow and too expensive to run on every change. You don't run all of them every time; you decide on purpose which ones you do.

## Who should watch

ML engineers who report one headline metric upward and suspect it's flattering them. Teams wiring evals into CI for the first time and wondering what belongs in the PR check versus the nightly job. Researchers moving prototypes toward production will recognise the checkpoint-selection trap in particular.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [From Benchmarks to Business Impact: Evaluating Generative AI in Production](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Srikanth_Devarakonda_llms_evals_benchmarks) by Srikanth Devarakonda at Conf42 Observability 2026, on the gap between benchmark scores and outcomes.

Title: LLMday London fills three cinema screens with agents and fine-tuning
Description: LLMday London, November 26 at Everyman Canary Wharf - post-training, $1.50 fine-tunes and agents gone wrong, from Cursive, MongoDB, UCL and more. CONF42 = 42% off.
Body:
LLMday London takes over three screens at Everyman Canary Wharf on November 26, 2026, with more than thirty talks on training models, running agents and the bills that come with both. Speakers come from Cursive, MongoDB, UCL, Birkbeck, Whitney AI, NOFire AI, inDrive, The Trade Desk and GitLab, and the code **CONF42** gets you **42% off**.

The day runs alongside the Prompt Engineering Conference on the same Luma event, so prompt nerds and model trainers share the lobby. This post is about the LLMday half.

## From $1.50 to 3 trillion parameters

The training talks span the full budget range. **Gabriele Monti (Birkbeck, University of London)** asks *How far can $1.50 go?*: three projects with small open models, LoRA and cheap cloud GPUs, starting with résumé-to-JSON on Gemma 2B for about $1.50 of T4 time, and finding where that recipe stops working. At the other end, **Paulius Rauba (Cursive)** shares *Lessons learned from post-training 3 trillion parameter models*.

In between, **Nick Mecklenburg (Whitney AI)** explains *Searching Through a Virtual World: Post-Training a 4B Search Agent*, trained inside a synthetic company with employees, Slack threads, documents and calendars because real private data was off the table.

## Agents, in production, misbehaving

LLMday London does not pretend agents are easy.

- **Mark Weston (FireHorse)**, *AI Agents - what could possibly go wrong?*, opens with 7,000 emails sent to 50 people by his own agent, doing what it was allowed to do.
- **Artemis Leonardou (NOFire AI)**, *Three Hours Debugging Code I Never Wrote*: an agent's change passed review and CI, then took a production path down because the failure only existed in the combination of edits.
- **Nicholas Greenwood (aries global)**, *make the wrong thing hard: adapting codebases for agents*, on shaping the repo so the simplest path is the right one.
- **Sylvain Liege (GoWit-Hungary)** on stopping more than 70 collaborating LLM personas from inventing data.

## Living with it every day

**Anthony Bourached (UCL)** reports on *A Year Living in MindPalace*, an open-source personal agent that handles his email, teaching, experiments and a GPU cluster. **Edoardo Romani (MongoDB)** covers persona-based agents for GTM and RevOps teams, **Andreas Voniatis (Artios)** measures what moves brand visibility in *Reverse Engineering AI Search Results*, and **Kannupriya Kalra and Rory Graves** present *LLM4S 1.0: From Idea to Production AI in Scala/JVM*. Proof that the JVM crowd ships LLM apps too.

The keynotes are from **Coral** and **Miko Pawlikowski (Reliaburger)**, who brings *Ten years of Kubernetes lessons, in one binary*.

## Why a Conf42 viewer should go

This lineup is the in-person cousin of [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026) and [Conf42 Large Language Models 2026](https://www.conf42.com/llms2026): the same mix of research results and production scars, but you can ask the follow-up question over lunch.

Title: Prompt Engineering Conference London treats prompts as production code
Description: Prompt Engineering Conference London, November 26 - Wise, AWS, IBM, Red Buffer and Superagentic AI on releasing, testing and judging prompts. CONF42 = 42% off.
Body:
The Prompt Engineering Conference comes to London on November 26, 2026, with three tracks and roughly thirty talks that treat a prompt the way you would treat a config change: versioned, rolled out, tested and occasionally rolled back. Speakers come from Wise, AWS, IBM, Red Buffer, Superagentic AI, Optimizely and Busuu, and **CONF42** gives Conf42 readers **42% off**.

It shares the day, the venue (Everyman Canary Wharf) and the registration page with LLMday London, so one ticket gets you both programmes. This post covers the prompt side.

## A prompt rollout can be an incident

The talk to circle first is **Ritesh Modi (Wise)**, *Prompt Release Engineering*. His abstract describes a 5% rollout of a prompt and model configuration that silently stayed in production for five months. If you have ever left a feature flag at 5% and forgotten it, you already know how that story feels, and the talk is about the release discipline that stops it.

**Emmanuela Opurum (SoftNet Technologies)** comes at the same problem from the architecture side with *Designing Production-Grade Prompt Systems for AI Agents: A Solution Architect's Perspective*: why prompt setups that work in a notebook fall over once they meet production.

## Who writes the next prompt?

**Shashi Jagtap (Superagentic AI)** asks exactly that in *Recursive Prompt Engineering: Who Writes the Next Prompt?*, on agents that generate and inspect prompts at runtime. **Guilherme Santos (Blindsight)** follows the other thread in *Prompt Lawyering. How AI games human requests*, starting from the Tetris-playing AI that learned to pause the game so it could never lose. Specification gaming, now with your system prompt.

**Egor Grositskiy (Beat Saber)** brings an art director's view in *When Prompting Isn't Enough*, where the hard part is defining "better" for creative output at all.

## Judging output you cannot check

Evaluation is the second spine of the programme:

- **Tahreem Rasul (Red Buffer)**, *The Agent Eval Stack: Outcomes, Trajectories, Reliability, and Judges*.
- **Olushola Oladipupo (AWS)**, *Before Your Agent Takes Action: Evaluating Customer-Service AI*, for agents that can change records, not just answer.
- **Oliver Gooding (IFF Research)**, *Evaluating LLM Outputs When Quality is Subjective*, where two experts can legitimately disagree.
- **Peter Fox (IBM)** on regression-testing a virtual assistant's migration from rules to LLM orchestration.

**Aleem Khan** adds a PEC-only session, *Detecting 70 Kinds of Bias with a Model You Own*, on replacing LLM API calls in a real-time news pipeline. The keynotes come from **Coral** and from **Miko Pawlikowski (Reliaburger)**.

Title: Logs Anyone Can Edit Won't Prove What Your AI Agent Did
Description: Asqav founder Joao Marques at Conf42 MLOps 2026 adds hash-chained, post-quantum-signed audit trails to AI agents in a few lines of Python.
Body:
When an AI agent moves money or data and something goes wrong, the first question is what it did, and the honest answer is often whatever the logs say, assuming nobody touched them. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Joao Marques, founder of Asqav, shows how to give agents audit trails that are tamper-evident and independently verifiable, using hash chains and post-quantum signatures.

## Observability is not proof

The talk opens with a distinction most teams blur. Standard logging and observability tools tell you what happened, assuming the records are intact. They don't let you prove integrity, which is what an auditor, a regulator or an incident review actually needs. If anyone with write access could have edited the log after the fact, the log is a story, not evidence.

## Two old ideas, put together

The approach combines two well-understood pieces. Every agent action goes into a hash chain: each entry references the previous one, so you cannot insert or delete an entry without breaking the chain. Each entry is also signed with ML-DSA-65, the post-quantum digital signature algorithm standardised by NIST. The result is a trail anyone can check for alteration, without a blockchain or an external service in the loop.

That last point deserves a small cheer. A surprising number of "verifiable" designs quietly assume a ledger nobody wanted to operate.

## A few lines in the frameworks you already use

Asqav plugs into common agent frameworks, including CrewAI, LangChain, Haystack and LiteLLM. Joao walks through adding audit trails to a CrewAI agent pipeline in under 10 lines of Python. The toolkit is open source, pip-installable and, per the abstract, has more than 1,700 tests. This is Joao's own project, so expect to see Asqav on screen; the hash-chain and signature design is the part you can carry anywhere.

## The production questions

The more useful half of the session covers what happens after the demo:

- Performance overhead of signing every action.
- Storage, since an append-only trail only grows.
- Key management tradeoffs, which is where most signing schemes succeed or fail in practice.
- Multi-party approval workflows that require a human sign-off before an agent executes a sensitive action.

He also maps the approach to the EU AI Act's requirements on traceability and record-keeping in Article 12. If your compliance team keeps asking how you'll show what the model did, this is a concrete answer to bring back to them.

## Who should watch

Engineers running agents that call APIs, write code or move data in production, especially in regulated industries. Security and platform teams deciding what "audit" means for agent actions. If your agents only draft text for a human to review, the overhead may not be worth it yet, but the approval-workflow section still applies.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [RuntimeGuard-AI: Cryptographic Compliance for High-Risk AI Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Neeraj_Kumar_Singh_Beshane_cryptography_compliance_pipelines) by Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026.
- [Log-Centric Intelligence: Enabling Real-Time Compliance Observability with LLM-Ready Architectures](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Prem_Anand_observability_logging_compliance) by Prem Anand at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026.

Title: Eval-as-code from day one, or your LLM app becomes write-only
Description: Anwar Khan (John Deere) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on reusable eval harnesses in CI with lm-evaluation-harness, RAGAS, DeepEval and Promptfoo.
Body:
An LLM application without an evaluation harness is one you can deploy but never safely change. Anwar Khan, Senior Staff Software Engineer for Enterprise Architecture and AI at John Deere, calls that a write-only system, and at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19 the talk shows how to avoid it by building eval-as-code into CI from the first commit.

## More moving parts than a validation set can cover

Traditional MLOps has a comfortable setup: model metrics and a validation set. LLM systems do not fit in that box. They have prompts, retrieval, tool calls, and a model you do not control, and Anwar's point is that the CI pipeline has to cover all of it.

The phrase "a model you do not control" is the one to underline. Your provider can upgrade the model under you, and nothing in your repository changes. Without evals running continuously, the first sign is usually a user complaint.

## A harness built from four familiar tools

The talk shows how to build reusable evaluation harnesses with lm-evaluation-harness, RAGAS, DeepEval and Promptfoo. The pieces it assembles:

- eval-as-code that runs in CI, next to unit tests
- behavioural regression suites
- faithfulness scorecards for retrieval-backed answers
- dataset versioning alongside prompt and code versions

That last item is easy to skip and painful to miss. If the eval dataset changes in the same week as the prompt, and neither is versioned, you cannot tell whether the score moved because the system improved or because the test got easier.

## Gate on some things, alert on others

One of the more practical sections is about deciding what belongs in a deploy gate versus what should only raise an alert. Gate on everything and nothing ships. Gate on nothing and the harness is decoration. Anwar's harness draws that line explicitly, which is a decision most teams make by accident.

The same thinking covers catching the silent quality drops that follow a provider-side model upgrade. That failure mode needs evals running on a schedule, not just on pull requests, because no pull request triggered it.

## Keeping eval coverage growing

A harness written once and never touched decays as the application grows. The talk closes on the operational practices that keep coverage growing alongside the system, so that a new tool, a new retrieval source or a new agent step arrives with its own tests.

The takeaways listed in the abstract: a reusable harness pattern that works across RAG and agentic systems, CI integration patterns for LLM evaluation, what belongs in a deploy gate, and practices for keeping evals current as the system evolves.

## Who should watch

ML and MLOps engineers, AI engineers and QA engineers. The session is marked intermediate, so it assumes you have shipped or are about to ship an LLM feature and know roughly what RAG is. If you already have Promptfoo or DeepEval running locally but not in CI, this is the talk that gets them into the pipeline.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: When an LLM writes clinical config, run validators before the judge
Description: Ocean Coldiron (ModMed) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on the eval harness for an LLM that generates clinical configuration: golden sets, validators, diffs, SME loops.
Body:
When an LLM writes prose, "looks good" might be enough. When it writes an allergy skin-test setup, a wrong answer becomes a patient-safety ticket. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Ocean Coldiron, Forward Deployed AI Engineer at ModMed, walks through the evaluation harness built for an AI-driven generator of clinical configuration and test protocols, and the order the checks run in matters as much as the checks themselves.

## Generators are a different eval problem

Most LLM eval advice is written for chat: is the answer helpful, faithful, polite? A generator that produces EHR note templates and allergy skin-test protocols has a stricter contract. The output is structured, it gets loaded into a system, and its errors do not read as awkward sentences. They read as wrong settings.

That is why the methods in this talk carry over to any structured-output generator. The abstract names SQL, YAML, JSON and forms. If your LLM produces something a machine will consume, you are in the audience.

## Deterministic validators go first

The first takeaway is a layering rule: deterministic validators run before any LLM judge. Schema checks and rule-based validators catch the errors that do not need judgement, such as a missing field, an invalid value, or a rule violation, quickly and for free.

Only output that passes those gates goes to an LLM-as-judge. It is cheaper, it is reproducible, and it stops you from asking a model to spot a typo in a field name, which it may or may not do depending on its mood.

## Golden sets from real configs, regression on every change

The harness is built on golden datasets made from real, de-identified configurations. Against those, diff-based regression tests run across model and prompt changes. Swap the model version or tweak the prompt, and you see exactly which outputs changed and how, instead of discovering it from a support ticket.

For structured outputs, a diff is a surprisingly powerful eval. It turns a vague question like whether the new prompt is better into a concrete list of changed fields that someone can review.

## Experts in the loop, cheaply

The third piece is subject-matter experts. Clinical configuration needs people who know the domain to say whether an output is right. Their time is expensive, so the harness turns their corrections into new test cases. Every expert review adds to the golden set, and the same mistake cannot sneak back in unnoticed.

Ocean frames this as closing the loop with domain experts at low cost, which is the realistic version of human evaluation: not a big annual labelling project, but a steady trickle of corrections that compound.

## Which metrics actually predicted defects

The part to watch for: the talk looks at which metrics predicted real-world defects and which turned out to be vanity numbers. That comparison is rare, because it needs production defect data to check against. Most teams pick metrics before shipping and never revisit whether they meant anything.

## Who should watch

AI engineers building generators of config, code, queries or forms, in healthcare or anywhere output errors have consequences. QA engineers being asked to test an LLM feature for the first time. Teams already using LLM-as-judge who suspect they are spending judge tokens on problems a JSON schema could catch.

Title: In healthcare ML, data quality is a safety requirement
Description: Saiteja Jonnalagadda (CVS Health) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on real-time pipelines that validate data and catch anomalies before bad records reach a model.
Body:
Saiteja Jonnalagadda, Senior Cloud Engineer at CVS Health, starts from a sentence every healthcare engineer knows in their bones: a single mismatched record can send the wrong information to the wrong patient. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Saiteja walks through how the team built real-time, cloud-native pipelines that treat data quality, validation and anomaly detection as core parts of the MLOps lifecycle instead of a cleanup step at the end.

## Messy, incomplete, and enormous

Healthcare data arrives messy, incomplete and in huge volume. Every model downstream depends on it, and in this domain a data error is not a cosmetic dashboard glitch. That is why Saiteja frames data quality as a safety requirement rather than a convenience, and designs the pipeline around it.

The shift sounds small and is not. If quality checks live at the end of the pipeline, bad data has already flowed through feature computation, maybe training, maybe a prediction. If they live at the front, the bad record is stopped at the door.

## Checks that run before the model sees anything

The core of the talk is the set of checks that catch bad records before they ever reach a model. Validation and anomaly detection run as part of the pipeline itself, in real time, as events flow through.

Saiteja also covers the design choices that let these pipelines process millions of events a day without falling over. Quality checks at that rate need to be cheap and predictable, or they become the bottleneck and someone switches them off "temporarily". Getting that balance right is most of the engineering.

## Measuring quality after go-live

A pipeline that was clean at launch is not guaranteed to stay clean. Upstream systems change, new sources get added, formats drift. The talk covers how the team measures quality once a system is running in production, so data quality becomes something you monitor continuously, like latency or error rate, instead of something you audit once a quarter.

## The honest part

The abstract promises candour about what did not go smoothly: assumptions that broke under real load, and what Saiteja would build differently today. That section is often the most valuable minute of any architecture talk, because it is the one you cannot get from documentation. Pay attention to which assumptions failed first; those are the ones most likely to fail in your pipeline too.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and MLOps engineers in healthcare, obviously. But Saiteja pitches the framework more widely, at any field where trust in the data matters: finance, insurance, logistics, anything with records about real people. If your current data quality strategy is a nightly job that emails a CSV of failures to a shared inbox, this talk is your nudge.

You should leave with a practical framework for making data quality a central part of your own pipelines.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: Uber's ACN: end-to-end tests written in English, run by an LLM
Description: Sowjanya Puligadda (Uber) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on Autonomous Cognitive Navigation, LLM-driven end-to-end testing at 95% reliability across 70+ languages.
Body:
Onboarding a new end-to-end test flow used to take 120 hours of manual scripting; with natural language definitions it takes under 4. That is the headline from Autonomous Cognitive Navigation (ACN), the LLM-driven testing framework Sowjanya Puligadda, Senior Engineering Manager at Uber, presents at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19.

## Locators are the weak point

Anyone who has maintained a UI test suite knows where the pain lives. Traditional automation relies on hardcoded locators and deterministic scripts. Rename a button, move a field, ship a new layout, and a chunk of the suite goes red for reasons that have nothing to do with bugs. At enterprise scale, keeping those scripts alive becomes a full-time job that competes with actually testing anything.

ACN takes a different route. It is a natural-language-based generative framework: you describe the scenario in plain language, and an LLM interprets the application state, reasons through the workflow, and executes complex end-to-end scenarios. No brittle script to rewrite when the UI shifts.

## The four parts that make it hold together

Letting a model drive a UI is easy to demo and hard to make reliable. The talk goes through the architecture and engineering decisions that address that, with four named components:

- **State-Aware Reasoning Loop**: the model reasons from the current application state at each step, instead of following a fixed script blindly.
- **Persistent Temporal Action Memory**: keeps context across long workflows, so step twelve still knows what happened in step two.
- **Semantic Canonicalization**: reduces unnecessary processing of UI information, which matters both for cost and for keeping the model focused.
- **Multimodal end-state verification**: validates that the outcome is correct even when the application has changed around it.

Each one maps to a classic failure of AI-driven automation: losing the thread on long flows, drowning in UI noise, and declaring success without really checking.

## The numbers, and the scale behind them

ACN has been applied across thousands of localised application variants and more than 70 languages. That scale is the interesting part. Localisation is where locator-based suites suffer most, because every language changes text, lengths and sometimes layout. A tester that reads the screen the way a human does has an obvious advantage there.

The reported results: 95% reliability, and new test flow onboarding down from 120 hours of manual scripting to under 4 hours of natural language definition. The first number is worth thinking about too. A 95% reliable test runner is a big improvement over a suite that breaks every release, and it also means the talk's guidance on how to evaluate and integrate it into engineering workflows deserves your attention.

## Who should watch

QA practitioners and test automation engineers drowning in flaky UI scripts. Engineering managers weighing whether LLM-based testing is ready for their pipeline. MLOps engineers interested in a production application of LLM agents that is not a chatbot. If you test APIs only, the ideas around state and verification still transfer, but the biggest wins here are in UI-heavy, multi-locale products.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Tackling Flaky Tests: Strategies for Reliability in Continuous Testing](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mike_Morgan_testing_flaky_strategies) by Mike Morgan, the problem ACN is trying to make go away.

Title: Turn One Broken Agent Trace into a Regression Test That Lasts
Description: At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Navan's Raju Dandigam turns a broken TypeScript agent's trace into a narrow, keyless regression test that runs in CI.
Body:
A TypeScript agent can hand back the right answer and still have done the job wrong. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Raju Dandigam, Staff Software Engineer at Navan, shows how to take the execution trace of a deliberately broken agent and turn it into a small regression test that runs in CI without API keys.

The premise will feel familiar to anyone who has stared at a green eval dashboard and a confused support ticket at the same time. An agent can produce the expected answer while skipping a required lookup, repeating a side effect, or recovering through an invalid path. Output evaluation scores the answer. It says nothing about which of those behaviours needs a test.

## The trace is the bug report

Raju's workflow runs locally and starts from the trace, not the output. Inspect the execution tree, isolate the events that matter, write down a narrow behavioural invariant, then rerun it against a keyless fixture in CI. The examples use Vitest and Jest, plus AgentInspect, a free, MIT-licensed project Raju maintains.

The keyless part matters more than it sounds. A regression test that needs a live model key and a live tool backend is a test that gets skipped on forks, flakes on Fridays and quietly stops running. A recorded fixture is boring, and boring is exactly what you want in CI.

## Assert the invariant, not the path

The interesting design problem is how strict to be. Agents are allowed to take different valid routes to the same result, so a test that pins one exact sequence of tool calls breaks on every harmless prompt tweak. The talk covers how to check required dependencies (this lookup has to happen before that action) and retry boundaries (this side effect must not repeat) without asserting one exact path for every valid run.

That is the difference between a test that catches regressions and a test that catches refactors. Most teams have written the second kind by accident at least once.

## A tool reporting success is a claim

Two distinctions in the session are worth the time on their own. First, recorded tool success is separate from the observed task outcome: a tool returning OK does not mean the thing the user wanted actually happened. Second, missing telemetry stays unknown. If the trace has no event for an action, that is a gap in your instrumentation, not proof the action never ran. Treating silence as evidence is how a check passes on a system that did the thing twice and logged it once.

Raju also covers keeping a redacted failure artifact, so another engineer can review the failure without needing access to the data that produced it.

## Honest scope

Raju is explicit that the method complements existing evaluation and production-observability systems, and that it is neither a replacement for runtime authorization nor a sales pitch. AgentInspect is the tool on screen, but the loop (trace, isolate, invariant, fixture) ports to whatever tracing you already run.

## Who should watch

Engineers who own an agent written in TypeScript and a test suite that only checks final answers. Platform folks deciding what a failure artifact should contain before it lands in a ticket. If you already run trajectory-level checks in CI with recorded fixtures, you'll mostly be comparing notes, which is still a decent way to spend half an hour.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: Agentic AI in banking breaks on orchestration and cost, not the model
Description: Rajesh Gupta (Skan AI) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on multi-agent systems in BFSI: split planning from execution, add repair agents, put budgets on autonomy.
Body:
Rajesh Gupta, Head of Agentic AI Product at Skan AI, has been deploying multi-agent systems in banking, financial services and insurance, and his talk at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19 is about what those deployments surfaced. His short version: the hard problems sit far beyond model performance, in orchestration across legacy systems, recovery when an agent gets it wrong, and the economics of letting software act on its own.

## Regulated environments are the stress test

BFSI is a useful place to learn about agents because it is unforgiving. Legacy cores, audit trails, approval chains and regulators who want to know who did what. An agent that works in a sandbox meets mainframes, batch windows and compliance reviews in production.

Rajesh frames the talk around three areas: reliable orchestration across legacy systems, recovery through verification and repair agents, and the economics of autonomous execution. Each is a place where a promising pilot can stall.

## Separate who plans, who acts, who approves, who fixes

The architectural claim at the centre of the talk is that planning, execution, authorization and recovery should be separate concerns. Rajesh calls that separation essential for both compliance and resilience.

It is the agent-shaped version of separation of duties, a principle any bank auditor already understands. The component that decides what should happen is not the one that does it, and neither of them is the one that signs off. If an executing agent goes wrong, a distinct recovery path exists, with its own checks.

Why this matters in practice: when the planner, the actor and the approver are one prompt, you cannot explain an action after the fact, and you cannot stop a bad one before it lands. Splitting them gives you seams to put controls and logs into.

## Verification and repair agents

Recovery gets its own agents. Rather than assuming a run succeeds and cleaning up by hand when it does not, the system verifies outcomes and routes failures to repair agents. In a regulated setting this is less about elegance and more about having a defined, auditable answer to the question of what happens when the agent is wrong.

## Agent costs are not linear

The economics section is the one finance teams will want to hear. Rajesh points out that cost behaviour in agentic systems is non-linear. Picture a task that usually takes a few steps and occasionally takes many, with retries, verification loops and extra tool calls stacking up. That makes cost per outcome hard to predict from cost per call.

His answer is budget guardrails plus outcome-based evaluation: measure what a completed, correct outcome costs, cap what any single run may spend, and judge the system on results delivered instead of tokens consumed. That is how you get to the predictable ROI a CFO will sign off on.

## Who should watch

Product and engineering leaders taking agents into regulated industries, and architects who need to explain an agent system to a risk committee. Engineers will get the most from the orchestration and recovery split; managers from the economics. This is a lessons-from-deployment talk, so expect patterns and trade-offs more than code.

Title: Filtering throws away 96.94% of the web, and that's the point
Description: Nicolo Brandizzi (Fraunhofer IAIS) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 gives a beginner's tour of LLM training data, from Common Crawl to the OpenGPT-X corpus.
Body:
Most of the web is not fit to train a language model, and a good data pipeline proves it by throwing almost everything away. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Nicolo Brandizzi, Senior Research Scientist at Fraunhofer IAIS, follows real training data from a raw Common Crawl dump to a clean, deduplicated corpus, and explains why filtering removes 96.94% of web documents.

The running example is OpenGPT-X, the project that produced the open Teuken models. The title's number is the starting scale: 173 billion documents on one end, training data on the other.

## A model is what it ate

The talk starts from a simple premise: a model learns everything it knows from its training data. So two questions follow. Where does that data come from, and what makes a piece of text suitable?

Nicolo answers both from the work at Fraunhofer IAIS. Curated sources and web crawls each give you different things, and the trade-offs between them shape the model you end up with. This is the bit that turns the usual line about models being trained on the internet from a shrug into something you can reason about.

## Metadata normalisation, the unglamorous hero

Before filtering and deduplication can do their jobs, the data has to agree with itself. The abstract singles out metadata normalisation as something that matters, and anyone who has merged two datasets with different ideas about what a language code or a date looks like will nod along. Pipelines at this scale amplify small inconsistencies into large ones.

## The pipeline doing its job

Then comes filtering, and the headline number. Removing 96.94% of web documents sounds like a pipeline gone rogue. Nicolo's framing is the opposite: that is the pipeline doing its job. The web is full of boilerplate, spam, near-empty pages and text that would teach a model bad habits, and a filter that keeps a few percent is a filter that works.

It is a healthy reframe for anyone who measures data work by volume. Here the valuable output is mostly the stuff you decided not to keep.

## Deduplication eats the compute

The second surprise: deduplication consumes 80% of the compute budget. Finding repeated text across a corpus of this size is expensive work. If you ever planned a data pipeline by assuming the clever model-based steps would dominate the bill, this is a useful correction.

Nicolo promises an honest number behind every claim, from CPU hours to euros per document. That level of cost accounting is rare in public talks about LLM data, and it is the reason to watch even if you never plan to pre-train anything yourself.

## Who should watch

This is explicitly a beginner's tour; no data-pipeline experience needed. That makes it a good fit for MLOps and platform engineers who serve or fine-tune models and want to understand what went into them, and for data engineers curious how their skills map onto LLM pre-training. Researchers who already run deduplication at scale will find the numbers interesting but the concepts familiar.

You should leave knowing how a training corpus is built, and what that tells you about the models trained on it.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Beyond Pre-training: Scaling Cloud-Native LLMs with Contextual Data for Real-Time AI](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Ankit_Awasthi_llm_data_performance) by Ankit Awasthi, what happens to data after pre-training.

Title: No dataset existed for Lebanese Sign Language, so they built one
Description: Layth Ayache (Achour Holding) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on 40,000+ Lebanese Sign Language samples and the MLOps behind a model that can say it doesn't know.
Body:
There was no Lebanese Sign Language dataset to download, so Layth Ayache's team collected one: more than 40,000 samples, gathered with Deaf community members, volunteers and NGOs. At Conf42 MLOps 2026 on November 19, Layth, Senior AI Systems and Web Engineer and Technical Lead at Achour Holding, talks about the unglamorous MLOps underneath that work.

The abstract is short and pointed, and it names three things. Each one is a lesson that applies far beyond sign language.

## When the benchmark doesn't exist either

Most ML tutorials begin with a dataset and a leaderboard. For many languages, including many sign languages, neither exists. That changes the job. You are the data collector, the labeller, the benchmark author and the model builder, and there is nobody external to check your homework.

Building a dataset with the community it serves also matters for more than sample count. Collecting with Deaf community members and NGOs is how you get signs as they are actually used, rather than a stilted version produced for a camera.

## Reject bad landmark extractions before training sees them

The first MLOps lesson is a data quality gate. Sign recognition pipelines commonly extract landmarks (positions of hands, fingers and body points) from video, and the model learns from those. When extraction fails, for example on a blurry frame or an occluded hand, you get garbage coordinates that look like perfectly valid numbers.

Layth's team rejects bad landmark extractions before they reach training. It is the same principle as validating inputs at an API boundary: once bad data is inside the training set, it is very hard to find again.

## A model that is allowed to say "I don't know"

The second lesson is about behaviour at inference time. A sign recogniser that always returns its best guess will confidently mistranslate anything it has not seen. For an accessibility tool, a confident wrong answer is worse than an honest shrug.

So the models are allowed to abstain. That is a product decision as much as a modelling one, and it is one many teams skip because a model that sometimes refuses looks worse on a demo.

## Reading 98% without fooling yourself

The third lesson is the one every ML engineer should hear at least once a year. The team got a 98% internal result, and the talk is about how to read that number without fooling yourself.

Internal results are measured on data you collected, split in ways you chose. If the same signers appear in training and test sets, or the recording conditions are uniform, a high score can say more about the split than the model. With no external benchmark to compare against, that self-discipline is the only safeguard you have.

## Who should watch

Anyone building ML for a low-resource language, a niche domain, or any problem where you had to make your own dataset. Accessibility and assistive-tech engineers. And anyone who has celebrated a 98% before checking how the test set was built. This is a compact talk about practice, not a sign-language linguistics lecture.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Data Quality and Validation in ML Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sunil_Kumar_Mudusu_data_quality_validation) by Sunil Kumar Mudusu, more on gating data before it reaches a model.
- [How to evaluate your Evals?](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Hilik_Paz_evaluate_evals) by Hilik Paz, on trusting the numbers your evaluation produces.
