Title: AI pricing in SAP works when the model can recommend but never write
Description: At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Sirisha Ayyagari shows a zero-trust pattern for AI pricing in SAP: stateless AI, BAdI hooks, ABAP guardrails, full audit.
Body:
The safest AI integration in a financial system is one where the model never holds a pen. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, software developer Sirisha Ayyagari walked through an architecture for plugging an external AI pricing engine into SAP, built on one rule she repeats throughout: "AI recommends, SAP validates, and SAP decides."

## Why pricing is the dangerous place to start

Pricing sits inside order-to-cash. A price lands on a sales order, then an invoice, then revenue recognition and financial reporting. Ayyagari's opening point is that most AI conversations ask what the model can do, and in ERP you also have to ask what it must never be allowed to do. Her three concerns are system integrity, auditability and financial control, and she is blunt that security has to be in the design from day one rather than retrofitted after the first audit finding.

## Stateless AI, stateful SAP

The boundary is drawn before any model is picked. The AI engine receives pricing context and returns a recommendation. It does not own the transaction, does not update the sales order or the billing document, and has zero write access to core financial objects. SAP keeps sole authority over transactional consistency and validation.

Her threat model explains why. An AI service account with write access is an external system with too much authority. Model output that is not sanitised can fall outside the expected range or arrive in the wrong structure. Security deferred "until later" is how financial controls end up full of exceptions. And without a rollback path, a model that starts producing bad numbers keeps doing so across thousands of orders before anyone pulls the plug.

## Clean core: BAdIs and an HTTP boundary

Technically, SAP sends context over an authenticated HTTP API, and the recommendation comes back through a BAdI extension point. That matters for two reasons. BAdIs are SAP-sanctioned extensibility, so no standard object is modified and upgrades stay safe. And the extension has its own life cycle, so it can be audited or replaced independently of the AI vendor.

The API boundary itself carries the security: mutual authentication, least privilege so the AI service only sees the context it needs, strict request and response schemas, and rate limiting at the gateway. The design does not rely on the model to protect the enterprise system. Anyone who has been asked to trust an LLM's self-restraint will appreciate that.

## Four guardrails and an ABAP sequence

At runtime she layers four controls: authenticated, logged and rate-limited calls; output validation against price boundaries, business rules and the schema; least-privilege access that keeps the AI out of SD and FI write paths; and circuit breakers. If the service goes down, latency spikes or recommendations drift out of range, the breaker trips and pricing falls back to native rule-based SAP pricing, so order-to-cash keeps running.

On the ABAP side the sequence is short and worth copying. Call the API with a hard timeout. Validate the response: out-of-range values are rejected, not shown as a warning, and a malformed structure raises an exception before it reaches the pricing transaction. Apply or fall back. Log the outcome either way.

## The audit trail answers "why this price?"

Logging here means a business audit trail, not HTTP status codes. For each decision she records the input context sent to the model, the raw recommendation, the validation outcome (accepted, rejected or fallback), the price SAP actually applied, the SAP document where it was committed, plus timestamp and service identity. When an auditor asks why a transaction got a particular price, there is a chain from recommendation to commit.

Her closing blueprint: threat-model first and decide what AI can read and never write; use BAdI plus HTTP for a clean core pattern; build failure into the design; log and justify every decision.

## Who should watch

SAP architects and ABAP developers being asked to "add AI" to pricing, discounting or any other money-moving process, and security reviewers who need a reference pattern to hold vendors to. It is a design talk without a live demo; the value is the boundary and the order of checks.

Title: In agentic logistics, confidence is a routing signal, not a permission
Description: Walmart's Pavan Boppidi at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 on combining feature flags with confidence, stakes and novelty gates to grant AI agents authority.
Body:
A routing agent proposes a reroute at 99% confidence, built on a thin history, and with no gate in the way, 99% gets treated as permission. At Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, Pavan Boppidi, Staff Software Engineer at Walmart, walked through a control plane for agentic logistics where a feature flag decides whether an autonomous capability is exposed at all, and a separate per-decision gate decides whether the agent may act on this specific case right now. He notes the views are his own, not his employer's.

His framing: the goal isn't full automation, it's controlled autonomy.

## Two questions a Boolean can't answer

Pavan starts from the feature flag crowd's comfort zone: roll out to 1% of traffic, watch telemetry, roll back without redeploying. Now put something else behind the flag. It isn't a button colour anymore; it's an agent that chooses tools, spends money and reroutes a fleet. On or off says nothing about who may act on which decision, with what confidence, under what conditions.

So he splits the problem. Should this capability be exposed? That's a flag question. Given it is exposed, should the agent execute this decision now? That's governance. His airport analogy works: the flag decides whether the terminal is open; the gate checks every boarding pass.

Logistics makes it urgent because decisions chain. A carrier suspends a lane, which changes routing, which changes when inventory arrives, which changes replenishment and what you can promise a customer. One event, four decision loops.

## The autonomy flag is a versioned policy object

The useful flag, in his design, isn't true or false. It's a policy: enabled, a mode such as delegative, a rollout percentage, a confidence floor, an allow-list of tools, a cost ceiling, a kill-switch condition and an expiry date. He's careful to say the schema is a pattern proposed for the talk, not a standard; the standard part is OpenFeature underneath, so the application code stays portable across flag platforms. Once autonomy is a policy, you can review it, diff it, audit who changed it, canary it and roll it back, which looks a lot more like running production config than talking about model behaviour.

## Confidence, stakes and novelty decide together

A governance layer intercepts every agent-proposed action and routes it. Routine, non-safety-critical decisions that clear the threshold execute autonomously. Broader ones go to a person with a structured evidence package. Safety-critical, time-sensitive ones go to a pre-validated edge rule set rather than waiting on a human or a cloud round trip. If a human doesn't respond, the default is safe inaction: silence never turns into permission.

Confidence alone is not the policy. Stakes say how much error you can tolerate; novelty says how far the situation sits from anything the system has seen. A very confident score on an irreversible action should still escalate, and scores are only useful if calibrated and watched for drift. He also lays out four authority modes, from advisory (human decides) to supervised autonomy (people supervise the policy, not every event), instead of a single human-in-the-loop switch. Nobody wants a job clicking approve on whatever the AI says.

## The tool is the trust boundary

Two failure modes from the opening scenario get their own sections. Flipping the flag stops new runs but not the ones in flight, so a real kill switch drains active runs, revokes tool leases, invalidates cached authorisation and then verifies tool calls have actually dropped. And shadow AI: an agent nobody registered calling the same carrier API. His answer is identity at the tool boundary, with a security sidecar doing signed identity, policy checks and MCP schema validation, so the unregistered agent's call is blocked, logged and reported. The model can ask for an action; it can't grant itself the authority.

He closes with a staged rollout (shadow, advisory, guarded delegation to a 1-10% cohort, then scale), an authority trail in every event record (agent identity, flag version, confidence, decision, tool scope, outcome), a 90-day path that starts with the control surface rather than the model, and five SLOs of which only one, decision quality, is a classic model metric. Human review queues get treated as a finite resource too.

## Who should watch

Platform and operations engineers being asked to let agents act on real systems, in logistics or anywhere with expensive side effects. It's architecture-heavy and dense, with a useful six-question self-check near the end.

Title: Mobile analytics security: cache the permission, never the data
Description: At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Tesla's Ashwin Kumar treats identity, authorization and latency as one problem for analytics on personal phones.
Body:
When the plant manager checks shift numbers on a personal phone, your perimeter has already lost. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Ashwin Kumar, Senior Manager of Data Engineering and Analytics at Tesla, argued that identity, authorization and performance for mobile analytics are one design problem, and that splitting them across three teams is exactly where the gaps appear. He notes up front that the views are his own and were not reviewed by Tesla.

## Three teams, three seams

The usual org chart hands login to the identity team, data permissions to the data team and responsiveness to the app team. Each solves its slice. Kumar's point is that the seams between those slices are where attackers live, and that mobile makes the seams wider, because operational leaders now read dashboards on the floor, in meetings and at home, on devices nobody enrolled in management.

The talk is short and tightly structured: five areas, each with a concrete mechanism.

## Bind identity, not the device

He starts from a principle: a personal phone touching operational data must carry the same trust guarantee as a managed laptop. Asking everyone to enrol their own phone in MDM fails socially, and he thinks it should fail. So trust is layered instead. Device attestation checks the OS has not been tampered with and uses hardware-backed keys. Corporate identity federation adds SSO with certificate-backed tokens. Continuous session validation re-evaluates risk signals on every request rather than once at login.

His summary line is a good one: trust is an envelope that travels with every call, not a gate you pass once.

## Strict and fast means caching the decision

On desktop a half-second permission check goes unnoticed. On a phone it feels broken, and users either quit or invent workarounds, which is worse. Kumar's answer has three parts. Pre-compute role resolution and cache it at the edge, keyed to the identity token and the data scope. Give every entry a strict TTL and force revalidation when a role or policy changes. And fail closed: a cache miss or a degraded network means deny.

The trick in one phrase from the talk: cache the permission decision, not the data. That is how you get strictness the device context demands and speed the user expects.

## Enforce policy where data is joined

A mobile dashboard can pull manufacturing, sales, service and workforce data, each with its own owner and access rules. The common mistake is to join it all and hide what the user should not see in the UI. That means the sensitive data already sits in a payload on a personal device. His rule: enforce policy at integration, not presentation.

Drill-down sharpens it. Broad authorization is enough for the enterprise summary. Tapping into a facility revalidates regional or departmental scope. Tapping into individual performance data triggers a final check. A broad grant at the top must never quietly open restricted detail at the bottom.

Freshness gets the same treatment. Queries are scoped at read time in the distributed warehouse, so access changes show up on the next query. Payloads carry a permission fingerprint that is invalidated if policy changes mid-session. Push alerts are permission-checked on the server before they leave.

## Authorize the query, not just the user

The last section is about natural language querying and AI-generated alerts. An AI summary can aggregate across scope boundaries without anyone noticing, and a RAG pipeline that retrieves everything and filters afterwards has already touched data it should not have. His fix is query-scoped authorization: map the identity token to permitted data domains before retrieval, run retrieval only against those partitions, vector search included, and generate the answer from that scoped context alone. He calls it a first-class architectural concern, not a filter bolted onto the output.

## Who should watch

Anyone building internal analytics or RAG features that reach phones, and identity engineers who have been asked to make BYOD safe without MDM. It is an architecture talk at around twenty minutes, with patterns rather than code, so it suits a lunch break.

- [Graziano Casto on a policy-as-code approach to RBAC](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Graziano_Casto_policy_rbac_authorization).
- [Sheshananda Reddy Kandula on automating mobile app security assessments with MobSF and Jenkins](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Sheshananda_Reddy_Kandula_mobile_security_automation).

Title: Small tools, small credentials. Don't give the ops agent a shell
Description: Ahmed Tariq (Simplify9) at Conf42 AI Agents 2026: typed tools, split observer and executor identities, and approvals tied to credentials.
Body:
The first prototype of a cloud operations agent usually has one tool called something like RunShell and a credential strong enough to make the demo work. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Ahmed Tariq, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Simplify9, took that design apart and replaced it with patterns DevOps teams already use for CI/CD pipelines: typed tools, two identities, short-lived credentials, plan-first changes and policy outside the model.

## The model can't be its own guard

Once an agent can restart a service, trigger a pipeline or change infrastructure, it is operating production, so Tariq treats it like any other privileged production identity. His central point is that a safety rule living only in a prompt is guidance, not enforcement. The model picks its next action from whatever context it was given, and that context can push it off course. Real controls have to live outside it: IAM, tool validation, policy checks and approval gates. The model can request an action; the infrastructure decides whether it's allowed.

He frames the agent's blast radius as two things. Its tools define what it can ask for; its credentials define what the cloud will permit. Shrink either and you shrink the radius. Shrink both and you have a much safer architecture.

## Typed tools with contracts the model can't edit

Instead of a shell, expose narrow tools: get pod logs, describe alerts, get recent changes, and one carefully controlled mutation such as restart deployment. Now the capability list is inspectable, versioned and reviewed in pull requests, and you know which tools are read-only and which mutate state.

A typed tool is more than a wrapper around bash. The restart tool's contract says the namespace must match a valid pattern, the target must be on an allowlist, the effect is declared as a mutation, a plan approval is required, and it carries idempotency, a timeout and an audit record. The model supplies the arguments but can't change the contract. In front of every mutation sits a deny-by-default policy check (OPA, Cedar, a cloud-native policy service or your own small layer) asking whether this is an approved tool, an in-scope environment, a valid approval and the right execution window.

## Observer, executor, and an approval that changes permissions

The identity pattern splits the agent in two. The observer reads logs, metrics, traces, alerts and infrastructure state and can change nothing. The executor holds only the few actions needed and becomes available only after a human approves. Credentials come from workload identity federation (AWS STS, Azure federated credentials, GCP workload identity federation): no static key inside the agent, nothing long-lived waiting to leak. If your agent's role name contains "administrator", he notes, the boundary is probably too wide.

The distinction he draws on approvals is the sharpest idea in the talk. A weak design tells the model to ask a human before doing anything dangerous, which leaves the model deciding what counts as dangerous. A stronger design ties approval to the credential itself: approving one specific plan releases the executor identity or a role assumption, expires quickly and records who approved it. Like a Terraform plan, the agent's output should be a recommendation of changes, never a report that it already made them.

## What permissions can't see

Correct access control still allows wrong targets, duplicate runs, unsafe retries, timeouts after the cloud already accepted a request, and half-finished multi-step changes. His answer is ordinary distributed-systems engineering: validate inputs at the boundary, use idempotency, retry only tools designed to be repeated, set clear timeouts and checkpoint multi-step work. Every tool call, denials included, becomes an audit record with the agent identity, approver, run ID, policy decision and a link back to the plan.

Finally, prompt injection through operational data. Logs, tickets, alerts and commit messages can carry attacker-controlled text, like a log line telling the AI to delete old backups. Treat all of it as untrusted data, return structured values from tools where possible, and assume the model will eventually be fooled. Then the architecture does the work: a missing tool is denied, an out-of-scope target is denied, and a valid-looking plan still stops at a human.

The short demo shows the flow end to end: the observer investigates, the plan waits for approval, a "no" stops it cold, and a "yes" grants a temporary permission and writes the audit entry.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers wiring agents into AWS, Azure or GCP. His rollout order is practical: inventory every tool and credential, replace shell access with typed tools, split identities, move to federation, gate mutations on plans, audit everything. You don't have to do it all on day one.

Title: In agent systems, retries multiply. Give every request a budget
Description: Yamini Rathamsetty and Karthik Akula (AWS) at Conf42 AI Agents 2026: how nested retries and fan-out burn agent budgets, and the fixes.
Body:
At 2 a.m., with no customers online and every dashboard green, the bill was climbing by multiples. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Yamini Rathamsetty, Senior Delivery Tech Leader at AWS Professional Services, and Karthik Akula, Senior Technical Account Manager at AWS, traced that kind of overnight spend to three ordinary things combined: nested retries, agent fan-out and no per-request budget. Their fix list fits on one slide.

## Fan-out is cheap only while everything succeeds

The system in the story was a multi-agent design that worked beautifully on stage. An orchestrator split a goal into pieces for specialist agents, each called tools, and some spawned workers of their own. One request became three agents, three became nine. That parallelism is the point, but it rests on a hidden assumption: almost every call succeeds on the first try. A demo runs the happy path twice; production runs it millions of times and hits every slow, flaky dependency along the way.

Then add retries. There were three layers, each sensible on its own. The AWS SDK retries failed calls by default with backoff. The application wrapped calls in its own resilience logic. And the agent itself, when a call failed, re-reasoned with a fresh model turn and often spawned a helper. Stack those and you don't add, you multiply.

## A dependency that stayed up and still did the damage

The speakers stress that their figures are illustrative, but they are the shape of what they saw: a steady few hundred dollars a day jumping to roughly twenty times normal overnight, with a single traced request fanned out into thousands of downstream calls. The trigger was not an outage. An outage would have paged someone. It was a dependency that was slow and failing about one call in five, up enough that no alarm fired, broken enough that every agent independently decided to try harder at the same moment.

That's the part that makes this an agent problem rather than an old retry problem. In a classic system, a retry reruns a cheap code path. In an agentic system, it reruns the model's reasoning, which is the most expensive thing you do, and that reasoning can decide to create more work. Autonomy is the feature you wanted, and it is also the multiplier.

## Your error rate is hiding the failures

The storm was hard to find for two reasons. The cost was smeared across dozens of agents, each doing a small, reasonable amount of extra work, so no single one looked guilty. And retried calls eventually succeeded, so the failures sat inside the success numbers. The breakthrough was to stop counting errors and start counting volume: agent turns per request and tool calls per request. One request with thousands of calls was the fingerprint.

Akula's organisational lesson is the most quotable part: nobody did anything wrong. Three teams made three locally sensible decisions at different times, and no one owned retries end to end. The real fix is to create an owner, one budget and one witness for the whole request path.

## The playbook

- **Budget every request**: a ceiling on total agent turns, tool calls and spawns. Not a timeout, a limit on the things that cost money.
- **Cap fan-out depth centrally**: the orchestrator may spawn workers, but a worker three levels down doesn't get its own tree.
- **Fail loud**: when a request hits its budget, stop and surface it. A loud failure is a page; a silent overrun is a mystery.
- **One retry layer**: pick the SDK, the app or the agent, and turn the other two off.
- **Circuit breakers** on every external dependency, with a half-open probe before closing again.
- **Idempotency keys**, so repeated work returns the cached result instead of paying again.
- **Cost as a first-class signal**: tokens and tool calls per request emitted live next to latency and errors, one trace spanning the whole agent tree, and alerts on volume rather than failures alone.

Their summary is that agents don't fall over the way old systems do. They get quietly, enthusiastically busy all night and hand you the bill in the morning.

## Who should watch

Anyone running autonomous or multi-agent workloads in production, and anyone whose cloud bill is reviewed monthly while latency is reviewed every minute. It's a story-driven talk with no live demo, and the checklist is ready to apply.

Title: How to prove data masking worked when the table has no primary key
Description: At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, CSC's Siyuan Feng shows how to catch masking failures with row counts, element checks and SQL INTERSECT.
Body:
Copying production into dev is the fastest way to get realistic test data, and the fastest way to put real customer records behind weaker locks. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Siyuan Feng, Data Analyst at CSC working on test data management, showed how to verify that masking actually happened, including the nasty case where source and target share no key to join on.

## Why test environments are the soft spot

Feng's framing is practical. Developers, QA and demo teams want production volume and production shape, because code that handles a hundred rows in dev may fall over at ten thousand. So teams copy prod. But production has strict access control, audit trails, MFA and firewalls, while dev and UAT have broader access for developers, contractors and vendors, lighter logging and lower security by design. Same customer data, weaker protection.

Masking is the fix: replace real values with useful fakes that keep the format, so an email stays an email and the @ sign stays put. The harder question is how you know the masking ran on every row, not just most of them.

## Three questions before test data ships

Feng reduces delivery to three checks.

**Row counts match, per table.** If the source has 30,000 rows and the target 29,800, two hundred rows probably failed. He stresses comparing table by table: totals can agree while two individual tables are off.

**Database elements match.** Indexes, constraints, triggers and grants must survive the trip. A missing index makes the app slow. A missing foreign key breaks the link between orders and customers. A dropped trigger stops counters updating. A lost grant means a QA engineer who should only read can suddenly change things, which is how a basic test turns into somebody else's outage.

**Every sensitive value changed.** The interesting one. Masking tools fail quietly when a server runs out of memory or a transform chokes on special characters or non-Latin text. His own example is his Chinese name: the tool could not process it, skipped the row, and the original value sailed through to the target untouched.

## Validation depends on what keys you have

With a stable primary key, it is a join: match customer 101 in source and target and compare the email. If they are identical, masking failed.

Without one, build a composite key from stable unmasked columns, such as a batch ID plus a record reference. That works, but searching for a unique combination across a wide table gets expensive fast, and there is no guarantee one exists.

Then there is the case with no usable key at all: decade-old legacy tables, append-only logs that keep duplicates on purpose, small tables where every column is sensitive. Here Feng swaps JOIN for INTERSECT. If passwords were replaced with random strings, the source and target password columns should share nothing. Any overlapping value is a failed row, and a simple lookup on that value finds the rest of the record.

## Dictionary replacement makes overlap legitimate

Random replacement is the easy version. Dictionary replacement is trickier, because the dictionary may already contain real values. Apple can become Oracle, which is good, or Apple can become Apple, which looks exactly like a failure. Intersection alone cannot tell them apart.

His answer is to use intersection as step one, isolate the overlapping candidates, then compare the non-masked columns of those rows. If the same company name now sits next to a different customer name, the row was masked and the collision is legitimate. If everything around it is unchanged, it is a real miss. You only build identifiers for the narrowed subset, not for hundreds of millions of rows.

## The tool and the scope

Feng closes with DBmask, his open-source, MIT-licensed masking tool, at version 0.1.1 and described as an initial framework. It is configured in YAML, targets SQLAlchemy databases including PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server, and produces a validation report covering row counts, element checks and masking completeness.

This is a hands-on talk with SQL-level examples. Test data managers, QA leads and data engineers who sign off on masked copies will get the most from it. If your masking already runs inside a tool with built-in verification, it is still a useful audit of what that verification should be checking.

Title: An AI kill switch that only closes the front door is not one
Description: Capital One's Parthiban Rajasekaran at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 on why a disabled flag doesn't stop in-flight agent work, and how to prove containment.
Body:
The dashboard said Disabled, a new request was rejected one second later, and fifteen seconds after that the agent sent the customer email anyway. At Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, Parthiban Rajasekaran, Principal Dev Engineer at Capital One, staged that drill against a running agent loop to make one point: a feature flag is an admission control, and a real kill switch also needs cancellation.

The drill is simulated, with mock tools and a mocked SMTP server, but he is clear that the mechanisms are real. Execution 47 looked up a customer, filed a Jira ticket and queued a follow-up job before the kill. The worker that picked up the job never checked the flag again. In production, as he puts it, there is no unsend.

## A flag value is intent, not a stop

The flag answered whether new work may start. The operators heard an answer to whether existing work had stopped. Once work is past that decision, you're no longer selecting features, you're cancelling a running system. Parthiban reminds the audience the industry already paid for this lesson without any AI involved: Knight Capital in 2012, where a repurposed flag triggered obsolete trading code left on one server and engineers spent about 45 minutes trying to make it stop.

Agents add a twist. The thing doing the work picks its own next step.

## Five jobs a kill switch has to do

He lays out a contract for what stop has to mean: admission (no new autonomous work), propagation (tell running executions cancellation was requested), interruption (stop what can still safely be stopped), compensation (reconcile what already happened) and verification (prove activity ceased within what you can observe). None of the mechanisms are new, he notes: cancellation tokens, fencing tokens, the saga pattern. What's new is where they have to live.

The concrete design: every execution gets an identity and a generation number. When the flag flips, a listener marks active executions as cancel requested and bumps the generation from 18 to 19; a reconciler sweeps up whatever the listener missed. The generation travels as a fencing token, so the downstream resource can reject stale work itself.

The subtle bit is timing. Checking the flag before every tool call is better than nothing, but the same worker can produce two outcomes depending on whether cancellation lands before or after its check. In the drill the window wasn't milliseconds, it was fifteen seconds of a job sitting in a queue. Revalidate as close to the side effect as you can, and use idempotency keys where the downstream supports them.

## Classify every tool before you grant it

Work comes in three kinds. Reversible (a draft: delete it). Compensatable (the Jira ticket: close it through deterministic, pre-approved code, never back through the agent you just cancelled). Irreversible (the email). If you can't classify a tool your agent can call, Parthiban says that's your first finding.

There's an agent-specific trap here too. A tool call that returns a cancelled status can look like a transient error to the model, which may then try a different tool. So cancellation is never the model's call: enforce it in the harness before the model's next turn. Routing around your own off switch is a very agentic kind of creativity.

## Containment is a metric you can test

The rerun shows the difference. The worker sees generation 18 against 19 and refuses to cross the boundary, the reasoning loop exits at its next safe point, the ticket is closed through the compensation path, and after a five-second quiet window the run counts as contained at 24 seconds. An OpenTelemetry trace of the single execution backs up the console output.

He defines "time to containment" (explicitly his own metric, not an industry standard) as zero active executions, zero unresolved compensations and a quiet window with no unauthorised side effects. He is equally honest about the limits: the GenAI semantic conventions are still in development, and if trace context doesn't survive the SQS hop, the trace doesn't prove end-to-end containment. Turning the flag back on gets its own warning: resume, replay and flush each make different assumptions, and flush is often the safest.

## Who should watch

Anyone who has put an agent behind a flag and called it a kill switch. It's a tight lightning talk that ends on three questions worth taking into your next design review: what happens to in-flight work when the flag changes, which side effects are interruptible, and what evidence would convince you mid-incident that the agent has stopped.

Title: Text-to-SQL on open models: self-correct, don't vote, measure linking
Description: Vladimir Beskorovainyi (Besk Tech) at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 tests text-to-SQL tricks on open models: self-correction pays, voting and schema linking don't.
Body:
Everyone has a text-to-SQL demo; few people have to answer for the number it produces at 9 a.m. Vladimir Beskorovainyi, Enterprise AI architect and CTO at Besk Tech, runs one of those systems, with 500 data marts on-prem, open models, and 30 million users who can't read SQL to check it. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026 he tested the popular tricks on the public BIRD benchmark and came back with a short list: pick a recent model family, add a self-correction pass, and measure everything else before you trust it.

## Two kinds of numbers, never mixed

He is unusually careful about sources. Production numbers come from his own system, with closed data and his own definition of correct, so you can't check them. Benchmark numbers come from BIRD dev (all 1,534 questions, execution accuracy), with open code you can rerun. He labels every number with its kind and never compares the two.

The test covered three families on his own servers with identical prompts and settings: Qwen 2.5 Coder at 7B, 14B and 32B, CodeLlama at 7B, 13B and 34B, and Llama 3.1 8B and 3.3 70B. Because every model answers the same questions, he compares pairs with McNemar's test, and his warning is that at this sample size a gap of two and a half points can still be noise. That paragraph alone is worth sending to whoever wrote your last internal benchmark slide.

## The year beats the size

Qwen climbs from 39 to 47 to 50 percent as it grows, and gains flatten quickly after 14B. CodeLlama barely moves, from 21 to 24.5. At 7B the gap between the families is 18 points, larger than any size effect. To check that this wasn't just a 2023 versus 2024 artefact, he added Llama 3.3 70B, which also came out strong. The lesson he draws is not "Qwen wins" but that a recent model beats an old big one: choose the family first, the size second.

## One fix-up pass helps; five votes don't

The cheapest trick was the best: let the model look at its own query and fix it. It helped every family, by about three points on CodeLlama 7B, 3.7 on Llama 8B and 1.2 on Qwen 32B, and it never made results worse. The stronger the model, the smaller the gain, because there is less to fix. The typical repairs were a wrong join key and a dropped filter.

Self-consistency (generate five answers and vote) gained 0.13 points, not significant, for five times the tokens and slow queries stretching from ten seconds to fifty. He measures cost in GPU seconds rather than tokens, because the person paying the bill pays for time. By that measure self-correction on CodeLlama 34B went from 12 to 22 cents per thousand queries for a real gain, a trade he takes every time.

## Schema linking: measure it, don't copy it

The result he didn't believe at first: cutting the schema down to the relevant tables, a step in every tutorial, made things worse on BIRD, by as much as 3.7 points on Llama 70B. A better embedding-based linker with 96.5 percent recall didn't help either. BIRD schemas are small, so the prompt was never the problem, and linking only adds the risk of dropping a table you need.

This is not a contradiction of his own production system, where every query goes through retrieval across 500 marts. There the schema doesn't fit in the context window, so routing is the only way the query works at all. Same name, two different jobs. His complaint is about teams with small schemas copying a trick that only exists because someone else's schema didn't fit. He is also clear that wide-schema routing is his next study, not a claim he makes yet.

## The model may be wrong, just not silently

In production, guardrails are blunt and cheap: read-only access, a whitelist of objects and a row limit on every query. None of that catches a valid query that answers the wrong question, which he calls a meaning problem rather than a security one, so a person still sees the number before it becomes a decision. He is open about limits too: his clean baseline scores 50.4 percent, below strong cloud models and fine-tuned systems.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers moving text-to-SQL from demo to something people rely on, especially on-prem with open-weight models. It's a short, dense talk, and the code, settings and per-question answers are published.

Title: Sensitive data discovery has to run as often as your schema changes
Description: At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, T-Mobile's Mary Sirisha Duggimpudi layers metadata, ML and runtime telemetry into continuous PII discovery.
Body:
A compliance inventory is a photograph of a system that keeps moving. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Mary Sirisha Duggimpudi, Senior Software Engineer at T-Mobile USA, laid out a layered design for finding sensitive data continuously, and for turning each finding into a ticket, a policy check or a blocked promotion instead of a line in next year's audit.

## The audit snapshot is already stale

Her starting point is familiar to anyone who has owned a data platform. Regulated data does not sit in one control database. It leaks into object storage, analytics platforms, SaaS APIs, temporary tables created during a migration, and, most often forgotten, logs. One careless debug line and a customer identifier is now flowing into the observability stack.

She names two gaps. The visibility gap: an audit captures one moment, while containers, datasets and schemas change in hours. The ownership gap: the security team spots the risk, but only the application team knows what the field means for the business. Discovery that ignores either one produces findings nobody can act on.

## Read the metadata before you read the rows

The design stacks independent signals rather than trusting one scanner. Layer one is metadata intelligence, and her phrase for it is "signal before sampling". A column called customer SSN tells you plenty without reading a million rows. Schema fingerprints match structures that resemble previously classified ones. Lineage flags derived tables that probably inherited their parent's sensitivity. Access patterns reveal stores that suddenly receive sensitive traffic.

The point is cost. Metadata is cheap, so it decides where the expensive deep scans go first.

Layer two is classification, and she is firm that it is not a choice between AI and rules. Regex and validation algorithms catch Social Security numbers, card numbers and IBANs with high precision. ML classifiers add context when values are masked or encoded oddly. NLP entity detection covers the free text in support tickets, comments and JSON blobs. Confidence scores then route work: a 99% finding and a 65% finding should not land in the same queue.

Layer three is runtime telemetry: API traces showing sensitive fields crossing service boundaries, query logs exposing shadow access paths, and continuous checks on application logs. Her example is the classic regression: masking works today, a dependency bump disables it tomorrow, and only runtime validation notices.

## Explainability is an adoption requirement

The sharpest part of the talk is about trust. A platform that raises hundreds of alerts a day, half of them wrong, trains engineers to ignore it. So every finding should carry its evidence: which pattern matched, which metadata contributed, the model's confidence, what was sampled. High-confidence findings can be remediated automatically, medium ones go to a human, and the human's verdict feeds back into the classifier.

She also walks through schema drift as a four-step loop: detect the change from DDL logs or catalog events, classify the new columns, assign the finding to an owner from metadata, and govern it with policy as code. A developer adding a date-of-birth field ships working code and a changed privacy risk profile in the same commit. The architecture catches the second part near the moment it happens.

## Findings that do something

Discovery only matters when it drives action. Findings open Jira or GitHub issues with evidence and a remediation SLA. OPA or Sentinel enforce requirements before deployment, Vault or KMS integrations validate encryption, and the same pipeline assembles evidence packages for auditors. She maps four control points onto delivery: pre-commit hooks, pull request schema diffs, deployment gates that demand classification, encryption attestation and a retention label, and post-deployment drift detection.

Her trade-offs are honest. Full content scanning costs more than metadata triage. In regulated environments she would rather favour recall and spend human review on the ambiguous cases. And she is careful to say automation does not make an organisation compliant; it gives continuous visibility and evidence that support compliance.

## Who should watch

Platform and data engineers being asked for a PII inventory, and security teams whose discovery tool has become an alert firehose. It is an architecture talk with no product pitch, so expect patterns rather than a demo.

Title: Confidently wrong agents need inline sources and separate states
Description: Microsoft's Girish Konda at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 on a year of running AI agents on real engineering work, and the guardrails that held up.
Body:
The dangerous agent output doesn't look like an error. It looks like a confident, well-formatted answer with a number in it that nobody can trace. At Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, Girish Konda, Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft and tech lead and architect for capacity management in Microsoft Fabric, shared what a year of running AI agents against his real job taught him about trusting what they give back, and which guardrails survived.

The promise of the talk is refreshingly contrarian: most agentic AI talks show the demo that worked; this one is about the ones that didn't, and what he changed afterwards.

## Real work, live platform

The setting matters. These weren't toy tasks. According to the talk's abstract, Girish used agents for incident triage, digging through telemetry, code review and multi-step operational runbooks on a live multi-tenant platform. That's exactly the kind of work where a plausible wrong answer costs more than an obvious failure, because someone acts on it.

He's clear that the capability is real. So are the failure modes, and they aren't the ones demos prepare you for.

## Five ways an agent goes quietly wrong

The abstract lists the failure modes he ran into, and every engineer who has used an agent for more than an afternoon will recognise at least one:

- **Unsourced numbers.** The agent hands over a figure with no source, and it reads like arithmetic.
- **Phantom citations.** It cites documents that don't exist.
- **Error propagation.** One wrong fact spreads into every artifact it touches.
- **Arguing back.** When challenged, it defends the wrong fact.
- **Session drift.** Long sessions wander away from the facts.

The common thread is presentation. A tidy table with a wrong number in it is more expensive to catch than a stack trace, which is the agentic equivalent of a test suite that passes because it asserts nothing.

## The guardrails that held up

The discipline Girish describes is practical and mostly process, not tooling:

- **Force sources inline**, so a claim with no source can't survive the answer it appears in.
- **Verify before recommending, not after.** Checking happens before the agent's conclusion becomes advice, rather than as a cleanup step once someone has already acted.
- **Make corrections visible.** The agent writes its corrections down where you can see them, so a fixed mistake leaves a trace instead of silently reappearing.
- **Keep submitted and confirmed separate** in anything an agent tracks. In his experience, an agent will collapse the two, reporting work as done because it was requested.

That last one is the sharpest, and it echoes a theme that ran through Conf42 Feature Flags 2026: the gap between what a system intends and what it has actually done. A flag that says disabled isn't proof an agent stopped; a ticket marked submitted isn't proof the change landed.

In the talk he goes through what he ended up with, the guardrails that held, and the ones he dropped. The goal he sets is a test you can apply yourself: can you tell whether your agent is working, or whether it just sounds like it is?

## Who should watch

Engineers using coding or operations agents on real systems, especially for triage and runbooks, and leads deciding how much to trust agent output in reviews. It's experience-led rather than framework-led, which makes it a useful counterweight to vendor demos.

Title: In ML compliance monitoring, an anomaly score is not a verdict
Description: Vinay Puri of Amazon at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 builds a working-hours alert system where ML flags unusual patterns and human investigators decide.
Body:
The hard part of ML-based compliance monitoring isn't the model. It's building a system that spots unusual behaviour at enterprise scale, explains why it looks unusual, and still leaves the decision with a human. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Vinay Puri, Systems Development Manager at Amazon, used a Working Hours Alert System (WHAS) as the case study: rules for known policy violations, anomaly detection for patterns nobody wrote a rule for, and a firm line that a score measures unusualness, not guilt.

The domain is workforce time and attendance, but Vinay is clear the same architecture fits security events, access behaviour and transaction monitoring.

## Rules catch what you can describe

Traditional compliance monitoring asks deterministic questions: did someone exceed a set number of hours, did they miss a required break? Those rules stay. What they miss are patterns where every single event is technically valid, yet over several weeks you see odd start times, abnormal durations, repeated gaps or a sharp change from that person's own history. Anomaly detection asks a different question, whether this behaviour looks unusual compared with what we'd expect, and the design combines both.

## Four stages, separate jobs

WHAS is a four-stage pipeline: ingest operational data, validate and clean it, turn raw events into behavioural features, then score them. The separation is the point. Model code shouldn't compensate for bad timestamp parsing, and policy logic shouldn't hide inside feature engineering.

Data quality gets the most airtime, deservedly. Attendance, schedules, approved leave and HR records live in different systems with different time zones, duplicates, late updates and conflicting states. Feed that straight in and, in Vinay's words, "The model will happily detect your data pipeline problems as employee anomalies." Normalise and validate relationships between records before anything reaches features.

## Compare people with themselves

Features fall into four groups: duration and timing, recurrence (one odd day is noise, the same pattern for a week is interesting), a historical baseline per individual rather than one global definition of normal, and context such as leave, travel, shift changes or operational incidents. Normal looks different across job functions, shifts and geographies, so the per-person baseline does a lot of work.

On algorithms, Vinay steers away from treating this as classification. There's a mountain of ordinary behaviour and very few confirmed violations, often too few reliable labels to train on. Anomaly detection learns what expected looks like instead. The ladder runs from interpretable statistical baselines through clustering and tree-based methods to representation learning, with interpretability dropping as you climb. In compliance, the most accurate model isn't automatically the best one, because investigators stop trusting alerts they can't understand.

## An alert must say why

A high score can mean a legitimate schedule change, an emergency, missing data, an integration failure or something worth investigating. So an alert carries the observed pattern, the contributing signals, the comparison with history and the available context, not just "0.87". Prioritise by anomaly strength, recurrence, how many independent signals agree, and whether context already explains it. Ten thousand alerts every morning is technically anomaly detection and operationally useless.

Reviewer feedback improves thresholds and features, but through validation, versioning and controlled deployment, never by retraining production straight from investigator clicks.

## Degrade gracefully, monitor the monitor

Production reliability means watching data freshness, feature validity, source distributions and model behaviour, not just CPU. His graceful-degradation example is a good one: if the scheduling feed fails while attendance keeps flowing, the system must mark the analysis incomplete rather than read missing schedules as unusual employee behaviour. Every transformation, model version and threshold change goes in an audit trail so an alert can be reconstructed months later.

Because this is workforce data, privacy and governance cover the platform itself: data minimisation, and clear answers on who can change a threshold, deploy a model or read an alert. When drift appears, diagnose before retraining, since a source system changing its timestamp format looks a lot like behaviour change.

## Who should watch

Engineers building any detection system that points at people, whether insider risk, fraud or access anomalies, and teams arguing about how much to automate. The closing principle is the one to keep: appropriate automation, not maximum automation.

Title: Six readiness checklists don't add up to one go-live decision
Description: Shubham Sharma (Microsoft) at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 presents MCRF, one readiness framework with evidence gates for mission-critical AI agents.
Body:
When the security team, the platform team and the AI team each sign off on an agent separately, the go-live decision ends up reflecting a negotiation rather than evidence. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Shubham Sharma, Senior Technical Program Manager at Microsoft, presented the Mission-Critical Readiness Framework (MCRF): one governance model that scores an agent platform across six domains and blocks deployment until the evidence is in.

## The problem is the seams

An enterprise agent is not one system. Sharma walks the stack: foundation models as the reasoning core, retrieval systems (vector stores, knowledge bases, RAG pipelines) for grounding, orchestration frameworks that run agent loops and route tools, security and compliance services, human-in-the-loop checkpoints with escalation paths and approval gates, and the cloud infrastructure under all of it. Each layer usually has an owner and a checklist. His point is that when those checklists are evaluated independently, governance fragments, deployment decisions become inconsistent, and the risk compounds in exactly the settings where a failure carries real downstream consequences.

Anyone who has watched a launch stall because three teams each assumed another had tested the retry path will recognise the shape.

## Six domains, measured before production

MCRF groups readiness into six domains: technical, operational, infrastructure, security, organisational and AI-specific. Before any production deployment it sets measurable gates on:

- **Agent reliability**: task completion rates and failure recovery, including adversarial and edge-case conditions.
- **Model governance**: evaluation, alignment testing, drift detection and version control for foundation models.
- **Tool connectivity**: validated integration contracts, API stability and latency SLAs for external tools.
- **Workflow resilience**: graceful degradation, retry logic and failure isolation across orchestration layers.
- **Observability**: end-to-end tracing, structured logging, alerting coverage and explainability for decision traces.
- **Compliance and operational preparedness**: regulatory alignment, audit readiness and verified on-call staffing.

The last item deserves attention: whether anyone is actually on call for the agent is a readiness question that rarely appears on an AI checklist.

## A lifecycle, not a gate

Sharma is explicit that MCRF is not a single sign-off. It runs as a loop: scope and classify (what the agent is, its risk tier, its stakeholders), assess the six domains, collect evidence (tests, artefacts, audit trails), then decide, either governance sign-off or remediation. Every phase leaves a structured record: assessment reports, evidence packages and decision records that stay with the agent.

Three mechanisms keep it honest. Readiness scorecards score each domain against predefined thresholds instead of judgement calls. Mandatory evidence gates block deployment until test results, audit logs and runbooks are submitted and reviewed. Cross-functional sign-off requires acknowledgement from engineering and operations leads, so approval no longer rests on one team that becomes the bottleneck.

## Who should watch

This is a governance and program-management talk, not an engineering walkthrough: there's no demo, no code and no case-study numbers. It suits TPMs, platform leads and architects who need a shared vocabulary for go/no-go reviews of agent platforms, or who are building the readiness template their organisation doesn't have yet. Engineers looking for implementation detail on any single domain will get more from talks focused on evals, tracing or identity, and the related picks below cover some of those.

Title: Compile it, judge it, attack it, on every PR that touches the agent
Description: Liran Yushinsky (JFrog) at Conf42 AI Agents 2026: a three-layer CI gate of compile checks, LLM-as-judge and Garak red-teaming for code agents.
Body:
If you check AI-generated code with a regex and a couple of unit tests, Liran Yushinsky would say you aren't testing, you're hoping. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, the automation lead in JFrog's AppTrust group showed a three-layer gate that runs on every pull request touching an agent's system prompt or tools: a deterministic compile check, an LLM judge scoring meaning against a golden dataset, and a Garak red-team scan. Any layer can block the merge.

## Why your old assertions stop working

A deterministic API is a peaceful contract: send a payload, assert on the response. An agent that turns natural language into code through a chain of tool calls gives you a different valid answer each run, so "actual equals expected" has nothing to hold on to. He also dismisses BLEU and ROUGE for code. They count word overlap, so renaming a variable or swapping a while loop for a for loop fails a correct function, and he cites research by Dan Hendrycks and colleagues showing such scores can rise while the code gets more broken.

His framing of the bigger picture: the gap in enterprise AI is not generation but verification. An agent's output is shippable only if you can prove, automatically and on every change, that it is correct.

## Making the judge trustworthy

LLM-as-judge means a strong model grades another model's output against a rubric you write. He cites the MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena work by Lianmin Zheng and colleagues, where a GPT-4 judge agreed with human reviewers on clear-cut cases about as often as humans agreed with each other. That was the point he stopped being a skeptic.

His four rules for a reliable judge are concrete:

- Let it reason step by step, then turn that into a series of yes/no checks (he names G-Eval, DAG and QAG).
- Don't ask for a score from one to ten; ask for labels such as pass, partial, fail.
- Anchor it with a golden reference and a couple of examples. For code, one good example often beats ten.
- Never let a model grade its own homework: if GPT wrote it, a different model family judges it.

He is honest about the blind spots: verbosity bias, position bias, self-enhancement bias, run-to-run wobble and model drift over time. Swap the order in head-to-head comparisons, log every score and alert on slips. His favourite trick is treating the wobble as a map, since the judge disagrees with itself exactly where your instructions are unclear. The judge in turn gets checked by meta-evaluation: run it over a human-labelled golden set, measure agreement, read every miss, tighten the rubric, repeat.

## Each layer catches what the others miss

Layer one strips the nice markdown and tries to compile or parse the output, or validates it against the real API spec. Hallucinated endpoints and broken JSON fail instantly, no LLM involved. Layer two runs the agent over 30+ curated natural-language-to-code pairs, with Promptfoo running the evaluation and Helicone tracing the calls, and blocks when the meaning score falls below threshold. Layer three uses Garak, NVIDIA's open-source LLM vulnerability scanner, to fire known jailbreaks and injections; if the agent takes the bait even once, the merge is blocked.

His comparison table makes the case: a missing colon is caught only by layer one, valid code that ignores a business rule only by the judge, and a "print your system prompt" injection only by the red team. Every row has a different hero.

The live demo runs the same gate against the JFrog AI assistant on the docs site and against ChatGPT writing Python. The interesting run is valid Python that blocks on low severity instead of critical: it compiles, layer one is happy, and the judge blocks it. As JFrog's own talk, it also points to AppTrust and JFrog Xray along the way.

## Who should watch

Test automation engineers and anyone shipping an agent that writes code, queries or policy. Mind his cost caveat: judge calls burn tokens, so the deterministic layer runs on every commit and the expensive LLM checks can run on a schedule.

Title: Pipelines should prove who they are, not carry cloud keys
Description: Venkata Velavarthipati at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 replaces long-lived CI and MLOps cloud keys with OIDC workload identity, scoped claims and fail-closed design.
Body:
The usual question about pipeline credentials is where to store them safely. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Venkata Velavarthipati, a lead cloud solution architect with about twelve years in cloud architecture and security, asked the better one: does the workload need a permanent credential at all? His answer is OpenID Connect workload identity federation, where each CI/CD or MLOps job proves who it is at runtime and receives cloud access that expires in minutes.

It's an architecture and security-model talk rather than a code walkthrough, backed by an AWS proof built with Terraform and GitHub, with the same pattern sketched for GCP and Azure.

## Rotation debt is the real cost

The traditional approach stores an access key in a secrets manager or parameter store and hands it to the pipeline. That works for one environment. Multiply it by clouds, accounts, data engineering and ML pipelines and runners, and the key ends up referenced in places nobody can list. Venkata's example will be familiar to anyone who has owned an IAM user: you lose track of where the old key is used, so you mint a second one on the same user to keep things running, and the first one lives on. Add contractors and a leaked key that sits exposed for months, and you have credential sprawl.

## Identity over credentials

The flow is short. The workload starts and gets a short-lived OIDC token describing itself. The target cloud validates the issuer, audience and workload-specific claims against a trust policy. If everything matches, it issues temporary credentials scoped to what that job needs (create one S3 bucket, nothing more) and they expire when the session ends. On AWS that's IAM and STS; on GCP, Workload Identity Federation; on Azure, Microsoft Entra federation. One identity source, several clouds, no stored keys.

Authentication alone isn't the control, though. Just because GitHub can issue a token doesn't mean every GitHub workflow deserves the same AWS access. His trust policy pins the subject to a specific repository and GitHub environment, and you can go further: only `main` reaches production, lower branches reach lower accounts. Add a session duration of 900 seconds and you get claim-level trust combined with short-lived authorization.

## The 99.99 percent number, read carefully

Venkata puts one number on the model: compare a key valid for 365 days with a 15-minute session, and the credential validity window shrinks by around 99.99 percent. What makes this section good is the caveat that follows. He's explicit that this is an exposure-window metric, not a breach probability metric. A long-lived key isn't guaranteed to be stolen, and a short one isn't guaranteed safe; the shorter window just gives least privilege, claim validation and monitoring much more to work with.

## Same pattern for training jobs

The MLOps case is the one worth stealing. A training job that reads data from another cloud or an on-prem store usually gets a secrets manager ARN baked into its environment, which is one more place for a long-lived credential to live. With workload identity, access is decided by the job's identity and can be scoped to the job, the environment and even the dataset. He deliberately shows no latency numbers here, since they vary by cloud, and calls it a reference pattern rather than a benchmark.

## Fail closed, and make it visible

Secretless doesn't mean failure-free. The identity provider can be down, STS can be slow, a runner's clock can drift, or a trust policy can be wrong. His rule: fail closed. When federation breaks, don't quietly fall back to a static key to keep the deploy moving; stop, make the failure visible and fix the trust configuration. The temptation to paste a secret back in is exactly how the old model returns.

Observability completes it. Capture identity and claim context at the federation boundary, use CloudTrail for role and API activity, and correlate each temporary session with the pipeline run that created it, so an API call is never from an anonymous-looking credential. Then watch for unexpected claims and unusual token requests. Trust relationships themselves are managed as code.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps teams still rotating CI access keys by hand, and ML engineers whose training jobs reach across clouds for data. If you already run OIDC federation for deploys, the MLOps section and the fail-closed argument are the parts to take back to your team.

Title: Send your agent three tools, not twenty-nine
Description: Elizabeth Fuentes Leone (AWS) at Conf42 AI Agents 2026: semantic tool selection with a vector search cuts token spend and wrong tool picks.
Body:
Every call your agent makes to the model carries the description of every tool it owns, whether the question needs them or not. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, Developer Advocate at AWS, showed the fix in a single Jupyter notebook: put the tool descriptions in a vector store, retrieve the top three for each query, and give the model only those.

## Two bills from one design choice

Her framing is a dual problem. The first is cost. With 29 tools, all 29 descriptions are serialised into the context on every invocation, and if the agent has memory, that context keeps growing. A one-line question still pays for the whole toolbox. The second is accuracy: the more similar and generic the tool descriptions, the more often the model picks the wrong one, and a wrong tool means a wrong answer.

Semantic tool selection attacks both at once. The query goes to a FAISS index of tool names and descriptions first, the index returns three candidates, and only those reach the LLM. Her example is a travel assistant asked about a price, which gets back the pricing and comparison tools rather than the hotel search. Her slide put the token saving at almost 85 percent against the traditional approach.

## Two agents, same queries, measured against ground truth

The demo builds the same travel agent twice with the Strands Agents SDK, the open-source, model-agnostic framework that AWS maintains (she runs it against OpenAI to make the point that it works with other providers). The first agent receives all 29 dummy tools on every query. The second runs the semantic search first. Each test query carries the tools that should answer it, so the notebook scores tool choices against ground truth instead of eyeballing them, and Strands' built-in usage metrics report the tokens per call.

She is candid about the results. The token saving is large and obvious. Accuracy improved but is not perfect, because the 29 tools were deliberately simple, with vague descriptions. That turns into one of her takeaways: retrieval can only be as good as the descriptions you index, so write tool descriptions like they matter. They are now search documents.

## Keep the memory, swap the tools

The first version builds a new agent per query, which is fine for benchmarking and useless in production, because each fresh agent forgets the conversation. The second version keeps one agent and uses Strands' tool registry to clear and re-register only the three retrieved tools before each turn. The chat history survives, the context holds only the tools for the current question, and the token count grows only with the history itself. If you use LangChain or LangGraph, she notes, you will need to find the equivalent mechanism in that framework.

## From notebook to managed service

A local FAISS index is right for learning and prototyping, and wrong for running a fleet of agents. For production she points to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a managed service that does the semantic tool search behind an MCP-style interface. You register tools from Lambda functions, external code or MCP servers, and the gateway returns the best matches with no embedding model or index for you to maintain. Her repository includes the infrastructure as code for that setup, and the talk is part of a series on stopping agent hallucinations, so related techniques sit in the same code.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose agent has grown past a dozen tools, or whose token bill grows with every new integration. It is a practical, code-first talk, and the second half is an AWS product pointer, which she flags herself. The pattern itself works with any vector store and any framework that lets you swap tools per turn.

## Related talks

- [From 150K to 22K Tokens: Context Engineering for MCP Tool-Calling](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2026_Nishant_Kumar_Thakur_Sonam_Raj_mcp_tokens_context) by Nishant Kumar Thakur and Sonam Raj
- [Stop AI Agents from Making Up Facts: Graph-RAG for Reliable Data Retrieval](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_graph_rag_retrieval), another part of her series
- [Beyond the Context Window: Building a "Mental Model" for Your AI Agents](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Lior_Schejter_context_agents_reasoning) by Lior Schejter

[Watch Elizabeth Fuentes Leone's talk](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_tools_semantic_cost)

Title: Multi-cloud Terraform security is four stages, not one gate
Description: Perumalsamy Ravindran at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 splits Terraform security into author, plan, apply and operate, with federated identity and plan-time policy.
Body:
Terraform won't let you write one network block and deploy it to three clouds, and pretending otherwise is how platform teams end up with a lowest-common-denominator module nobody wants. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Perumalsamy Ravindran, a Staff Software Engineer who has run Terraform as the backbone of multi-cloud enterprise platforms, argued that Terraform's real multi-cloud value is one workflow, and that security belongs in four stages of it: author, plan, apply and operate.

It's a dense twenty minutes with a source behind every statistic, and the practical bits outnumber the slides.

## The breaches are boring

Perumalsamy's starting point is that cloud intrusions rarely need anything exotic: an exposed secret, a misconfiguration, an unpatched vulnerability. His examples are familiar. Capital One's over-permissive IAM role behind a misconfigured proxy. A Microsoft AI research storage token with an expiry date in 2051. Location data for 800,000 Volkswagen electric cars in misconfigured storage. Every one, he notes, was a setting that could have been declared, reviewed and enforced in code. Meanwhile, IaC adoption is high but coverage is thin, with Firefly reporting only six percent of organisations fully codified.

## Modules are the security control plane

The architecture has three layers: foundations (accounts, identity federation, network backbone, central logging), a private module registry, and per-application, per-environment workload stacks. The registry holds per-cloud modules that share a contract: the same input names, tag schema and security defaults. Product teams ship on that paved road, and security reviews the road rather than every car.

His six module rules: secure by default (encryption on, public access off, opting out needs an explicit variable that policy can see), small validated interfaces, semantic versioning pinned by consumers, unit tests with mocked providers on every pull request, publishing through the private registry, and flat composition with no provider blocks inside reusable modules.

## State is a secrets database

Because Terraform state is plaintext, Perumalsamy treats it as a secrets store: one state per environment per domain, its own backend and identity to bound blast radius, encryption with your own key, native locking, versioning so corruption is a rollback rather than an incident, and access limited to the pipeline's plan and apply roles plus a break-glass role that pages someone. Log every read, because a state download is a data exfiltration event. CLI workspaces share one backend and credentials, so they are not an isolation boundary.

For secrets themselves, ephemeral resources and write-only arguments keep values out of plan and state entirely. Before those existed, every database password sat in the state bucket in plain text.

## Plan with one identity, apply with another

The pipeline is the same shape on any CI: format, validate, lint and static scanning first; then a plan with a read-only identity, exported as JSON; then policy (OPA, Sentinel or native Terraform policy) evaluated against what will actually change; a cost delta; human approval for production; and finally apply with a separate write-capable identity on the exact saved plan, so what was reviewed is what shipped.

Identity is the first thing he fixes: OIDC federation from CI to cloud, with the trust policy bound to repository and branch so a fork can't assume the production role. Setting the session name to the pipeline run ID makes every cloud audit entry trace back to a commit and an approval.

On policy, his advice is to start with the ten rules you'd be embarrassed to violate (public storage, unencrypted data, wildcard IAM, open management ports, missing ownership tags) and run them in advisory mode for two sprints before making them mandatory.

## The pipeline is now the target

The section that dates fastest, and matters most: attackers now go after the delivery path itself. His examples include a compromised GitHub Action rewritten to dump CI secrets into build logs, malicious releases of a security scanner, and tampered modules and providers on public registries. A provider runs at `init` with your credentials before any plan. The defences are boring and effective: commit the lock file with hashes, pin providers and CI actions to commit hashes, serve from a private mirror with an allowlist, accept only signed providers, and use ephemeral runners.

## Drift needs an owner

The best story is about drift. An engineer opened a security group rule by hand on a Friday; the scheduled drift plan flagged it on Sunday into a shared channel nobody owned; two weeks later the next apply quietly reverted it and broke a vendor integration mid-release. The fix: every drift alert becomes a ticket with a named owner and a one-day SLA, every drift is either codified or reverted, and plan-time policy rejects manual exceptions not in code. Drift is a decision, not a notification.

## Who should watch

Platform and cloud security engineers running Terraform or OpenTofu across more than one provider, especially if your CI still holds static cloud keys. The closing 90-day plan (remote encrypted state and federation first, then modules and split roles, then drift and audit) is a ready-made roadmap.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [How to hack a cloud production environment with external Terraform manipulation](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Uri_Aronovici_cloud_terraform_hack) by Uri Aronovici of ZEST Security at Conf42 DevOps 2025.
- [Terraform and Ansible Are Not an Architecture](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2026_Jeleel_Muibi_terraform_ansible_architecture) by Jeleel Muibi of HybridOps at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026.
- [Your Agent Can Write Terraform. It Can't Feel What It Breaks.](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2026_Kevin_Brown_agent_terraform_break) by Kevin Brown of Cloud World Model at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026.
