Title: Conf42 Observability 2026 - when green stopped meaning healthy
Description: Conf42 Observability 2026 in review, 20 talks on tracing AI agents, dashboards that lie, eBPF, telemetry pipelines and using signals to test.
Body:
[Conf42 Observability 2026](https://www.conf42.com/obs2026) went out on September 10, 2026 with 20 talks, and a single complaint kept surfacing in different accents: the dashboard said everything was fine. Sometimes the culprit was an AI agent reporting 200 OK while answering wrong, sometimes a payment provider, sometimes a fallback path nobody had ever exercised. Speakers from PagerDuty, Adobe, Google, Snowflake, ServiceNow, General Motors, Harness and a crowd of observability vendors showed what to measure instead.

## Green is a claim, not a proof

Diamond sponsor Harness opened with [Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise), head of resilience testing and LitmusChaos co-founder, on why dashboards can only show paths that have already run. His case study is a third-party API failing over to a redundant path that never carried traffic, a retry storm turning a partial outage into a full one, and a team debugging an hour nobody instrumented. The cure is an inventory of untested paths and controlled experiments to fill it.

[Eleftheria Batsou](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Eleftheria_Batsou_healthchecks_outages_dependencies) (UptimeRobot) took the outside-in version: your app returns a healthy 200 while customers can't pay because Stripe is degraded. The thing that broke is the payment provider, the identity provider, the CDN or the LLM API you added last quarter. [Victoria Nduka](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Victoria_Nduka_accessibility_slos_goldensignals) (VictoriaMetrics) proposed accessibility as a fifth golden signal, so regressions show up in SLOs instead of in an audit weeks later. And [Sylvain Kalache](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Sylvain_Kalache_burnout_oncall_sre) (Rootly) pointed the same discipline at people: we have liveness probes for every service, but the engineer holding the pager gets "How are you doing?" and always answers "Fine."

## Agents need traces of their own

The busiest track was agent observability. [Sabith K Soopy](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Sabith_K_Soopy_agents_debugging_tracing) (Stackgen) put it best in one line of his abstract: traditional APM won't tell you an agent burned 40k tokens narrating a wrong answer. He showed the spans Stackgen uses to follow an agent through plan, gather and present, with per-tool cost and latency. [Emerson Braun](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Emerson_Braun_agents_llms_observability) (Plan A Technologies) followed one agent run from request to outcome and instrumented the context it received, the decisions it made and where it started to drift.

[Elliot Gardiner](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Elliot_Gardiner_agents_codegeneration_tracing) (Code Telemetry) treated coding agents as long-running processes that search, edit, test, retry and delegate to subagents, and argued that token counts and adoption are the wrong metrics for them. [Princewill Kalio](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Princewill_Kalio_llms_rag_distributedsystems) (Dockie) said the quiet part out loud in his title: AI systems are distributed systems now, with retrieval pipelines, vector stores and background workers, and they deserve distributed-systems tracing rather than print statements.

## The 3am page for code no human wrote

Two talks dealt with the operational aftermath. [Ralph Bird](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Ralph_Bird_sre_agents_incidentresponse) (PagerDuty) opens at 03:47 with a pager firing over code written by one agent, shipped by another, never seen by a human, after the SRE agent has already failed. [Artemis Leonardou](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Artemis_Leonardou_debugging_agents_codegeneration) (NOFire AI) lived it: an agent-written change passed review and CI, then took a production path down for about three hours. Nothing in the diff was wrong on its own; the failure lived in the combination, and the dashboards could say what and where but not why.

## Measuring whether the AI was right

[Srikanth Devarakonda](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Srikanth_Devarakonda_llms_evals_benchmarks) (Adobe) connected generative AI evaluation (factual accuracy, grounding, safety, task completion) to observable system performance and business outcomes instead of static benchmarks. [Arjun D Sureshbabu](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Arjun_D_Sureshbabu_llms_hallucinations_nlp) (Snowflake) shared lessons from a human-in-the-loop architecture for legal, compliance and privacy NLP, where a hallucination has a regulatory cost. [Ravi Chandra](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Ravi_Chandra_llms_analytics_semanticlayer) (Google) went after the semantic layer behind analytics agents, using feedback to keep a static, expert-curated ontology from missing the long tail of what users actually ask.

## Pipelines, kernels and the bill

On the plumbing side, [Anais Dotis](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Anais_Dotis_ebpf_linux_networking) (groundcover) gave a hype-free explanation of eBPF and how kernel programming escaped the kernel into monitoring and security. [Rita Lopes](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Rita_Lopes_metrics_logging_tracing) (Gigapipe) started from the familiar four-backend stack of Prometheus, Loki, Tempo and Pyroscope, and the trade-off between observing everything and paying for it. [Diana Todea](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Diana_Todea_opensource_observability_sustainability) (VictoriaMetrics) built a green observability pipeline entirely from open source and described how she got there by contributing upstream. [Emmanuela Opurum](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Emmanuela_Opurum_cloudnative_architecture_tracing) (SoftNet Technologies) argued for designing observability into cloud architectures rather than bolting it on, and [Joshua Fox](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Joshua_Fox_kubernetes_autoscaling_reliability) (DoiT International) went beyond HPA and VPA for Kubernetes autoscaling that cuts waste without hurting reliability.

## Telemetry as test input

Two talks turned signals into tests. [Vasuki Uday Kiran Vudathala](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Vasuki_Uday_Kiran_Vudathala_loadtesting_performance_capacityplanning) (ServiceNow) replaced interviews and spreadsheet guesses about peak traffic with workload models built from observability data. [Sumaiyya Fatima](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Sumaiyya_Fatima_automotive_embedded_simulation) (General Motors) applied observability-driven validation to hardware-in-the-loop testing for software-defined vehicles, where functionality emerges from many domains talking to each other.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), the Diamond sponsor, and [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) at Gold. Every talk is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/obs2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBA6AiE2f0hmsnFk5oGfFjb).

The series continues with [Conf42 Observability 2027](https://www.conf42.com/obs2027). Bring the dashboards you trust least.

Title: Stream security findings fast, then reconcile them with anti-entropy
Description: Rahul Kizhakkepachilamakol of AWS at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 pairs streaming with Merkle trees, read-repair and hinted handoff so findings don't vanish.
Body:
A vulnerability finding that silently disappears in transit can be as dangerous as an outage, and a streaming pipeline is very good at losing things quietly. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Rahul Kizhakkepachilamakol, Principal Software Engineer at Amazon Web Services working on the security data platform behind vulnerability management for AWS and Amazon, explained how his team gets speed and correctness at once: stream every finding, and run an anti-entropy layer beside the stream that compares, detects, repairs and verifies.

It's a compact architecture talk that borrows well-known tricks from distributed databases and points them at security data.

## Late findings are open windows

Rahul's case for latency is straightforward. A finding only has value once it reaches the team that can act on it. Every delay stretches exposure time and slows detection, triage, incident response and containment. It also creates compliance risk, which matters a lot when your customers build their own compliance on top of yours, and it piles up a remediation backlog for security engineers.

The platform has three requirements that pull against each other: fast delivery no matter how distributed the cloud is (AWS runs in 40-plus regions), high availability even when parts of that cloud fail, and strong correctness in the data it hands out.

## Streaming for speed, anti-entropy for truth

The fast path is streaming. Scanner results are emitted as events the moment they're produced, enriched with business logic (severity, asset context, ownership), run through further risk detection and delivered to the people who remediate. Streaming keeps the pipe fast, but unlike a synchronous call it gives you no built-in guarantee that what the producer sent is what the consumer got.

So a second path runs in parallel. Between each producer and consumer, which are often systems owned by different teams, a feed goes to a reconciliation system. It follows the classic anti-entropy loop: compare the data sets, detect what's missing or wrong, repair it, then verify that producer and consumer now agree.

## Hash attributes, not just IDs

Comparing everything at this volume would be ruinously expensive, so the reconciler partitions data into Merkle trees as it collects it. If the hashes match, there's nothing to inspect; only a mismatch sends it deeper.

The detail that makes this security-grade is where the hashing happens. An existence check isn't enough, because a record can be present in both systems and still be wrong. Rahul's example: system A says a vulnerability is critical, system B has the same record at medium. Matching IDs would call that consistent. Hashing at the attribute level catches missing or null fields and changed ownership or context, so the layer finds silent corruption as well as missing findings. If you've ever trusted a dashboard because the row counts matched, this is the paragraph to reread.

## Two repairs, and a receipt for each

Repairs borrow two database techniques. Read-repair re-drives the correct record from the producer to a consumer that holds a wrong version. Hinted handoff covers a consumer that is down: the reconciler waits for it to recover and then replays what it missed, so an infrastructure blip doesn't become a permanent hole in security data.

In a regulated environment the repair itself has to be auditable, because automated corrections without records are their own compliance risk. Every reconciliation action is captured: the restored finding identifier, the source of truth used, the action taken, when it happened and the verification result.

## Who should watch

Platform architects and security engineers who own a findings pipeline, and anyone running event-driven systems where "eventually" needs a bound. The talk stays at architecture level, so don't expect code or benchmark numbers; do expect a pattern you can lift into any producer-consumer pipeline where a lost or mangled record has consequences.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Modern Database Architectures: From SQL to NoSQL and Distributed SQL](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Andrei_Manakov_tradeoffs_distributed_nosql) by Andrei Manakov of ShareChat at Conf42 SRE 2025.
- [Platform Engineering for FinTech: Database Sharding, Replication & Scale](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Karthickram_Vailraj_sharding_replication_database) by Karthickram Vailraj of Charles Schwab at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025.
- [Keep Calm and Run on AWS: Engineering Compliance Without Abandoning Your Stack](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Dmytro_Hlotenko_distributed_systems_resilience) by Dmytro Hlotenko of Sage Austria at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026.

[Watch Rahul Kizhakkepachilamakol's talk](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Rahul_Kizhakkepachilamakol_distributedsystems_vulnerabilities_latency) from [Conf42 DevSecOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2026).

Title: Your agent did nothing wrong. Your master data lied to it
Description: Vishwak Thatikonda (Starbucks) at Conf42 AI Agents 2026: why MDM built for dashboards breaks under agents that act, and the action-grade design that fixes it.
Body:
A replenishment agent placed about 9,400 duplicate orders over two days, worth roughly $41,000, and not one line of agent code was at fault. That anonymised incident opens the Conf42 AI Agents 2026 talk by Vishwak Thatikonda, Lead Engineer at Starbucks, and his argument follows from it: master data management built for reporting can't safely feed agents that take actions, so it has to be rebuilt as an action-grade layer.

## Act three has no human in front of the data

He frames the history of enterprise data in three acts. First the data observed (dashboards), then it recommended (churn scores, reorder suggestions), and now it acts: agents place the reorder and issue the retention offer with nobody reviewing each decision. In the first two acts, bad data produced a bad chart that a person could catch. In the third, it produces an action that has already happened by the time anyone looks.

The duplicate-orders story shows how small the trigger can be. An improved address normalisation step, a good change on its own, made one store resolve to two golden records. To the agent, two golden records meant two stores, so it ordered opening inventory twice. Every order looked valid on its own, which is exactly why nothing alerted.

## Four failure modes, four principles

He names the ways the substrate breaks: staleness from batch refreshes, near-match identity errors, duplicate entities, and slow drift that never throws an error. Each maps to a principle:

- **Immutability**: append instead of overwrite, so you can reconstruct what the agent saw when it decided.
- **Versioned contracts**: schema, allowed values and freshness guarantees, explicit and versioned at every point an agent reads.
- **Real-time resolution**: identity resolved in milliseconds when the event arrives, not overnight.
- **Event-driven execution**: state changes flow the moment they happen.

The reference system is a master data platform for a global retailer with about 38,000 locations, with a target of resolving an entity end to end in under 200 milliseconds and executing every agent action exactly once.

## Blocking, confidence bands, and refusing to guess

Comparing every incoming record against every existing one is fine for a thousand records and impossible at that scale. The trick is blocking: cheap keys produce a tiny candidate set before any expensive comparison, which in his telling turns a billion comparisons into about five. Matching then combines weighted, explainable signals (name similarity, address geometry, distance, contact fields) and returns a confidence band instead of a yes or no. High confidence auto-merges, low stays separate, and the middle goes to a human. The agent is always told which band it is in.

The stack is deliberately boring: AWS Lambda for stateless resolution that reruns safely, DynamoDB as the golden record store with change streams for capture, and EventBridge as a schema-registered bus that fans changes out to the inventory agent, the orchestration layer and the rewards engine. Idempotency is enforced in three places: deterministic request IDs, conditional writes in DynamoDB, and deduplication windows on the bus. Failures land in a dead-letter queue you can replay, which is how you reconstruct an agent's view of the world when debugging it.

## The demo makes the case

The live demo runs one event stream into two lanes: a legacy last-write-wins setup and the action-grade design, with the same agent on top. A re-registered store ships opening inventory twice on the left and merges on the right. A retried loyalty event credits a member twice on the left and is rejected as already committed on the right. Late, stale snapshots, look-alike customers and a record missing a required field all go wrong on the left and get refused, routed or dead-lettered on the right. A burst of low-confidence merges trips a circuit breaker and pauses the agent.

He also lists three traps: a cache in front of a batch warehouse (fast access to stale truth, which the agent trusts completely), treating data quality as a one-off clean-up project, and over-merging. For an agent that acts, a false merge is worse than an honest duplicate. As a database person might put it, the duplicate is a bug; the false merge is someone else's loyalty points.

## Who should watch

Data architects, platform teams and anyone whose agents write to systems of record. The roadmap (assess, harden, stream, operate) starts with the entities your agents already touch, which makes it easy to begin without a rewrite.

## Related talks

- [Cloud-Native MDM: Kubernetes Orchestration for Enterprise Data Quality at Scale](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Rahul_Ameria_mdm_quality_orchestration) by Rahul Ameria
- [Data Quality and Validation in ML Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sunil_Kumar_Mudusu_data_quality_validation) by Sunil Kumar Mudusu
- [Building Resilient Data Platforms: Implementing Blockchain-Based Master Data Management](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Chandra_Adapa_data_master_management) by Chandra Adapa

Title: Green dashboards only show the paths you have already tested
Description: Uma Mukkara of Harness at Conf42 Observability 2026 on why green dashboards can't prove resilience, and a four-step loop to test the untested paths.
Body:
Your dashboards can only show the paths your system has actually walked. At Conf42 Observability 2026, [Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise), who leads resilience testing at Harness and co-founded LitmusChaos and OpenEBS, argued that the fallback route, the retry path and the DR plan are exactly the ones nobody instrumented, and that the only way to see them is to break things on purpose first.

The keynote is short and practical. It is also a Harness talk: the last section demos Harness Resilience Testing. The first two thirds stand on their own as an argument for any observability team.

## The gap is widening, and he names three accelerants

The premise: the observability system says green, and incidents keep happening anyway. Not one or two, but a steady stream in large organisations. Mukkara blames three accelerants. Systems keep getting more distributed and dynamic, with more dependencies. Releases happen all the time, and AI-assisted coding has pushed some teams to tens of releases a day. And agents are now in the loop, which brings a failure shape of its own.

Observability, in his framing, tells you what is happening. It does not tell you what would happen.

## Four things a dashboard never shows

He lists the blind spots plainly:

- **Single points of failure.** A dashboard shows what is instrumented and exercised. An untested dependency stays invisible until it goes.
- **Timeouts and retries that trigger new paths.** The code has been green for months because that branch never ran.
- **Degraded mode.** If the system has never been degraded, nobody knows what degraded looks like on screen.
- **Recovery.** If you never ran a DR test, you have no idea what your dashboards will say during one.

The uncomfortable part is timing. These are precisely the dashboards you need when a single point of failure trips, timeouts pile up and the system drops into degraded mode or DR.

## A retry storm in a path that never carried traffic

His case study is the pattern most on-call engineers will recognise. Everything is green. A third-party API stops responding, and the system fails over to a redundant path that has never carried traffic, so nobody instrumented it. Retries on the new path turn a partial outage into a full one within the next thirty minutes to an hour, and when the full outage lands, the team is debugging blind because nothing captured that hour.

The fix he prescribes is boring in the best way: find that failover path ahead of time, exercise it in a lower environment, and build the dashboards for it before production needs them.

## Agents can report healthy while doing the wrong thing

The new failure shape is the AI agent. A health check can return 200 OK while the model behind it is slow but not down, and Mukkara's point is that a slow model is as bad as a broken one. A tool call can time out silently while the agent keeps answering 200. His suggestion: inject latency between the model endpoint and the agent and check whether your observability reports the agent's real health, or just its HTTP status.

## The four-step loop

The method fits on an index card:

1. Inventory tested versus untested paths. For every "what happens if this network fails", ask whether you have seen it or assumed it.
2. Run controlled experiments with a small blast radius against the untested ones.
3. Add the missing dashboards and metrics the experiments reveal.
4. Repeat it, quarterly or more often.

For a next step he suggests starting with your most critical service, listing every assumption never observed in production, and putting your agentic systems into degraded mode to see if the dashboards tell the truth.

## What the demo shows

The closing demo covers Harness Resilience Testing, which runs chaos experiments, load tests and DR tests from one place. AI-assisted risk scanners read deployment metadata, logs, configuration and runtime events to flag likely risks before you run anything, and a resilience testing agent recommends and creates the experiments to confirm them.

SREs and observability owners who have ever had to explain a green dashboard in a postmortem. Platform teams adding AI agents to production will get the most from the agent section, which is short but specific.

Title: Multi-tenant Kubernetes needs a named boundary, not more rules
Description: Lahiru De Silva of WSO2 at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 shows how OpenChoreo turns tenants into cells with four directional gateways instead of hand-written network policies.
Body:
In year one, a tenant is one namespace, three services and one network policy. By year three it's four namespaces, cross-namespace calls, a shared platform service and an external SaaS API, multiplied by every tenant you host. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Lahiru De Silva, Associate Technical Lead at WSO2 and a maintainer of the CNCF Sandbox project OpenChoreo, argued that the problem isn't missing rules. The tenant was never modelled in the cluster in the first place, so the fix is to give the boundary a name, a shape and a default: a cell.

The second half uses OpenChoreo, WSO2's open source internal developer platform, as the reference implementation, so expect a product walkthrough.

## "Tenant" means three different things

Lahiru starts by pinning down the word. Internal teams as tenants is the soft form: implicit trust, boundaries by convention, and a conversation if someone crosses one. Business units or partners bring contracts, budgets and compliance, so boundaries start to carry weight. External SaaS customers are mutually untrusted, and one tenant reaching another's data can end the contract or start a lawsuit.

Kubernetes gives you building blocks rather than tenant isolation. On the control plane side that's namespaces, RBAC and resource quotas. On the data plane side it's storage and network isolation, gVisor or Kata Containers sandboxing, and node isolation with taints, tolerations or dedicated pools.

## Why network isolation is the hard one

Most of those knobs are set once by the platform team: a namespace per tenant, a node pool choice, a sandbox technology, a quota number. Network isolation is different, because who talks to whom is a property of the application, decided by the developers. A platform team can't template it in advance.

So teams reach for micro-segmentation with NetworkPolicies, which works fine while a tenant is one namespace. As applications spread out, Lahiru lists what's broken. There are no defaults: deny is something you must remember to write. There's no identity, because policies match labels and IPs, and reachability isn't authentication. Rules multiply with tenants instead of composing. And the result can't be reviewed: when an app times out, you can't point at the policy responsible without working through all of them. The tenant exists in the docs and the billing system, but not in the cluster.

## Cells: self-contained, with a gateway

Cell-based architecture comes from WSO2's reference architecture, co-authored in 2018 by Asanka Abeysinghe and Paul Fremantle. A cell is self-contained: components inside talk freely, and anything from outside comes through the cell gateway. It's one bounded context owned by one team, versioned and immutable, replaced as a unit rather than patched.

Traffic gets four named directions: northbound for public ingress, westbound for ingress from the tenant's other cells, southbound for egress to the outside world, and eastbound for egress to other cells in the organisation. Compared with a pile of rules, Lahiru's scorecard is clear. Scaling is additive (a new tenant is a new cell), the default comes built in, you can tell what a workload can reach by reading the cell config instead of running experiments, and the boundary is an object you can point at.

## Developers declare intent, the platform writes the policy

In OpenChoreo, creating a project creates a cell per environment, so two tenants with three projects across three environments get nine cells, and nobody hand-writes a network policy. The cell is rendered as a standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, or a Cilium policy when Cilium is installed. Developers declare endpoints at project, namespace, internal or external scope, and the platform translates that into gateways, listeners, hostnames and certificates.

Observability is scoped to the cell: logs, metrics and traces labelled with namespace, project, environment and component, plus Layer 7 visibility and TCP-level wire logs with Cilium, which the demo shows down to SYN and ACK. Tenancy itself is flexible, from a data plane (cluster) per tenant, through a namespace per tenant, to a project per sub-team.

The abstract also promises egress controls such as credential injection and quotas, the RBAC/ABAC handover and multi-cluster trade-offs; the recorded talk spends its time on the cell model and the walkthrough instead.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers running shared clusters for many teams or customers, especially if your tenant boundary today lives in a spreadsheet of NetworkPolicies. The first half, on why network policies don't compose, is useful whether or not you ever touch OpenChoreo.

Title: SAP alerts need agents that investigate before a human wakes up
Description: Pon Murugesh Devendren (Deloitte) at Conf42 AI Agents 2026: five event-driven agents on SAP BTP that turn a Cloud ALM alert into an approved fix.
Body:
SAP Cloud ALM is good at saying something broke and silent on what to do next. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Pon Murugesh Devendren, a Manager at Deloitte working as an AI architect on a large US utility engagement, showed a multi-agent design on SAP Business Technology Platform that does the investigation before the operator opens a single log, then stops and waits for a human to approve the fix.

## The alert is where the work starts

His framing of the problem is one every on-call engineer will recognise. When an alert fires, four things still have to happen by hand: figuring out which systems, interfaces, jobs or business processes are actually affected; searching logs, runbooks and old tickets across tools that each want their own login; working out who the right resolver group and approver are; and digging up the fix someone found at 2 a.m. six months ago, which now lives in a ticket comment nobody will read.

The goal, as he put it, is not to replace operators. It is to hand them an incident where the first round of investigation is already done.

## Five agents, one job each

Instead of one large assistant, the architecture splits the work into five specialised agents: triage and classification, context and correlation, knowledge and root cause, resolution and coordination, and remediation and validation. Each one gets a narrow set of permissions and a clean handoff to the next, so it can be tested on its own, and the line between recommending and executing sits exactly where the governance needs it.

The agents are not polling. A qualifying alert created or updated in Cloud ALM triggers the workflow on demand, and the workflow keeps a correlation ID and shared incident state that every agent reads and writes. Without that shared state, in his words, you would have five agents having five separate conversations. The same framework covers integration failures (IDocs, RFCs, proxies), ABAP dumps and failed jobs, and connectivity or authorisation problems. Between those categories only the runbook and the allowlisted actions change, never the architecture.

## Most of an incident is investigation

The worked example is a failed IDoc posting to SAP ERP after retries ran out. The agents pull the IDoc payload, the ERP posting logs, recent GL account changes, known errors and a similar incident from months earlier. They propose a hypothesis with evidence attached: the GL account was locked for month-end close, so release the lock and reprocess the IDoc. An operator checks that in Microsoft Teams, approves, the action runs, and the validation agent confirms the order is now posted with no downstream errors. His point: the fix took five minutes, while finding it used to take an hour.

Grounding is strict. Retrieval runs through SAP AI Core and the Generative AI Hub with a vector engine over a curated corpus of runbooks, known-error articles and incident history, and nothing is answered from the model's memory. The operator gets a decision-ready briefing in Teams (scope, evidence, recommended action, risk level, who must approve) and can ask follow-up questions in the same thread. Tickets and coordination go through ServiceNow.

## Approval is architecture, not a checkbox

The slide he asked the audience to remember is the governance one. Remediation is limited to allowlisted, parameterised workflows; the system never generates and runs arbitrary commands. Anything that could touch production needs an authorised human, and every alert, piece of evidence, approval and outcome lands in an audit trail.

The rollout plan is just as cautious: start with notification only for a few high-value alert categories, then add investigation and recommendations, then a small set of low-risk approved actions, and only then expand. For metrics he adds a third category teams usually forget, governance and adoption, and he treats a rising override rate as the earliest sign that the grounding is going stale.

## Who should watch

SAP Basis and integration teams, SREs running ServiceNow-heavy operations, and anyone designing agents for regulated enterprises will get a reusable pattern here. It is an architecture talk, not a code walkthrough, and it shows how SAP's own tooling fits together rather than introducing a new product.

Title: Hardware-in-the-loop for software-defined cars needs observability built in
Description: Sumaiyya Fatima of General Motors at Conf42 Observability 2026 on a five-layer HIL platform with embedded diagnostics and closed-loop validation.
Body:
A pass/fail result tells a vehicle validation engineer almost nothing when the failing feature spans a dozen controllers. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Sumaiyya Fatima, Senior Software Engineer at General Motors, proposed treating hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing as shared infrastructure with observability designed in, so every test run records the signals, timings and diagnostics needed to explain a failure, not just report it.

It's an architecture talk rather than a tooling demo, and an unusual one for an observability conference: the system under observation is the test rig and the car's software, not a web service.

## One kick, many systems

Her example is a hands-free power liftgate. The customer kicks under the bumper and expects the tailgate to open. Behind that, the vehicle detects the motion, validates sensors, confirms a key fob is present, checks operating state and security conditions, passes messages across modules, and finally commands an actuator. When it doesn't open, the question is which of those broke: sensor, network, software service, configuration, or a diagnostic state blocking the action.

Fatima names three pressures on validation teams in software-defined vehicles: cross-domain dependencies like the liftgate, runtime variability from CI/CD and over-the-air updates changing behaviour after release, and scale, where more scripts and benches stop keeping up. She was careful to credit traditional HIL as a big reason embedded quality improved; it was built for single-controller architectures.

## Intermittent bugs need context, not a red cross

The motivating failure is the classic intermittent one: a ten-millisecond delay between two services that's harmless most of the time but causes a timeout under one startup condition. A traditional test reports that an expected output didn't arrive. What engineers need is what messages were exchanged, which services were active, the timing relationships and the diagnostics present at the moment.

## Five layers, observability at the centre

Her framework replaces per-program test benches with a shared validation platform, closer to how companies run cloud infrastructure than how they build one-off rigs. The five layers:

1. **Hardware abstraction.** Tests say send the lock command; the framework works out how that reaches whichever controller this program uses.
2. **Real-time simulation.** Deterministic recreation of rare conditions, such as low battery plus heavy network load at startup.
3. **Signal governance.** One standard name, scaling, owner and version per signal, ending the vehicle-speed-versus-speed-value arguments.
4. **Embedded diagnostics.** Every run records signal transitions, diagnostic trouble codes, network and service-to-service traffic, so the context exists before anyone asks.
5. **Automation orchestration.** The framework controls timing and collection, removing operator variability. Three engineers waiting five versus six seconds between steps can disagree about whether a timing bug is real.

None of the layers is new on its own, she noted. The integration is the contribution.

## Closed-loop validation asks how it passed

The part most transferable to other domains: tests that watch behaviour while running and react. An overnight software drop triggers regression tests; a service responds slower than baseline but still passes; the framework flags it, stores the telemetry and can launch extra scenarios. Her question for it: "How did the system behave while it passed?"

She closed with where this heads: using months of run data to prioritise risky test areas and spot latency trends drifting towards a failure threshold, with machine learning helping engineers find patterns. Her point was that none of that works without observability collecting the right data first.

## Who should watch

Automotive and embedded validation engineers, obviously. Backend engineers who own flaky integration suites will recognise the closed-loop and signal-governance ideas too. Expect concepts and examples, not code or benchmarks.

Title: Enterprise RAG needs authorization inside retrieval, not at the UI
Description: Ananda Kumar Dey of Quadrant Technologies at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 treats enterprise RAG as a knowledge security problem, with access filters before ranking.
Body:
When production goes down, the answer is usually spread across Jira, ServiceNow, GitHub, Confluence and a security platform, plus whatever lives in one senior engineer's head. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Ananda Kumar Dey, who leads AI strategy and solution architecture at Quadrant Technologies, argued that pointing an LLM at all of that is a knowledge security and trust problem first, and that the single most important control is filtering what a user may see before retrieval ranks anything.

It's an architecture overview of a production RAG system, aimed at teams moving past the demo, and it's refreshingly firm about measuring before tuning.

## The LLM is the small box

Ananda's diagram is familiar: query processing, retrieval, prompt augmentation, generation. His point is where the effort goes. The model is one component; ingestion, retrieval, access control, observability and grounding are the enterprise work. A wrong, stale or unauthorized retrieval produces an answer that is convincing and still wrong.

Governance starts at ingestion, well before anyone types a question. Pull from GitHub, Jira, Confluence and ServiceNow through governed pipelines, attach metadata on owner, sensitivity and source while chunking, and detect PII and secrets before creating embeddings. Bad data in the knowledge layer doesn't stay put; retrieval amplifies it.

## Index hygiene and hybrid search

Retrieval quality comes down to three choices: the embedding model, a vector store that supports filtering and enterprise controls, and index hygiene. Documents change, permissions change, content goes stale, so you need versioning, deletion propagation and lifecycle management, the same discipline as any other data platform.

On the vector database question (Pinecone, pgvector, Weaviate, Azure AI Search and friends) he refuses to pick a benchmark winner. Choose on hybrid search, metadata filtering, security integration and what you already operate. It's an architectural decision, not a speed contest.

The technical-content point every DevSecOps team will recognise: semantic search is good at concepts and paraphrase, and weak on exact identifiers like a CVE number, incident ID or config key. Combine dense retrieval with sparse BM25 and merge the rankings. Then re-rank: retrieve broadly (say the top fifty), score with a cross-encoder, and send only the best few chunks to the model. Retrieve broadly, re-rank intelligently, generate narrowly.

## Don't retrieve it and then hide it

The core security principle is that authorization can't live in the UI. The user's identity and policies have to shape retrieval itself: a policy engine evaluates the request and chunk metadata, and filters drop unauthorized chunks before they enter ranking. The system never fetches sensitive content and then tries to hide it afterwards.

Around that sit corpus protection (encryption, secret scanning, classification, retention and deletion) and an audit trail of who asked what, what was retrieved, what was generated and which sources backed it. Trust needs evidence that the controls ran, not just the controls.

## Measure retrieval separately from generation

On hallucinations, Ananda reframes the goal: rather than eliminating them, design controls that make unsupported answers hard to produce and easy to detect. That means authoritative sources, answers tied to retrieved evidence, and human review when confidence is low or the stakes are high.

Then evaluate in two layers. First ask whether retrieval found the right evidence (precision, recall, MRR), then whether generation used it well (RAGAS faithfulness and answer relevance), against a baseline of representative questions. His line: don't tune RAG by intuition, measure it.

## Graphs and agents come later

Some questions aren't answered by the three most similar paragraphs: which apps depend on this service, who owns it, are there related incidents or vulnerabilities. That's where graph retrieval, agentic RAG that splits a question into retrieval steps, and tool-augmented RAG pulling live API data come in. His production lessons put them in order: fix the data before tuning the model, enforce authorization inside retrieval, measure before changing models, chunking or prompts, and operate RAG as versioned, monitored, tested software. Twice, for emphasis: "RAG is not a prompt engineering project, it's a production system."

## Who should watch

Architects and platform teams building an internal knowledge assistant for engineering or security, especially where documents carry different access levels. If you've already shipped hybrid search with permission-aware filtering and a golden dataset, this will confirm your choices rather than surprise you.

Title: A health agent that acts, built on Home Assistant and a skill file
Description: Nick Rezaee of Harvard at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 wires wearable, phone and smart home data through Home Assistant so an AI skill can send personal nudges.
Body:
Uploading your Fitbit export to a chatbot and asking for insights is old news; getting an agent to notice a pattern and nudge you at the right moment is the open problem. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Nick Rezaee, technical research staff at a Harvard lab and a computational biology master's student at Harvard, showed a home setup that does the second part, and the surprising answer to the hardest piece is not a swarm of agents but Home Assistant.

It is a short, introductory talk with a clear architecture you can rebuild on a spare Linux box.

## Most health tech stops at the dashboard

The abstract states the problem well: most personal health technology collects data, computes a few metrics and tells you what already happened. Nick's goal is the next step, an agent that reads your data and your goal (say, walking more) and sends an intervention personalised to your patterns, so your notification differs from someone else's.

That needs something always on. Your laptop sleeps, so he puts a Linux server at home that syncs data, runs the AI on a schedule, sends phone notifications and keeps the history of what it sent for later improvement.

## The hard part is plumbing, and Home Assistant already did it

Once you add more context than the wearable (phone data, then smart home data), you can look for associations: less activity when you're on the phone, a higher heart rate with music. But every device has its own API and data format. Nick tried the obvious move first, top models running as a swarm of agents to do the integration, and found it needed a lot of steering and context, still tripped over data formats, and kept warning him that personal data might not be safe to handle.

His fix is Home Assistant, the popular open source home automation project. It pulls all those sources into a unified SQL database, sends phone notifications, runs automations, installs on Linux or Windows and is configured in the browser, so you don't need to be technical to set it up. It's a nice reminder that the agent doesn't have to do the boring integration work if a mature project already does it.

## The skill file is the product

With data in one place, the agent is a daily loop driven by a skill file, and Nick stresses that the details in that file matter. It decides which data streams to read (reading everything costs time and tokens, so you can prioritise), how messages are designed, and how to judge whether past notifications worked so the next ones improve. The flow becomes: personal data, Home Assistant, the daily skill, an intervention decision, a phone notification.

He runs this at home himself and reports that it works relatively well. Because Home Assistant also reaches speakers and computers, interventions don't have to be phone pings, and changing the goal (sleep, meditation, diet, other habits) is a matter of editing text in the skill file rather than writing software.

## What the abstract adds

The abstract goes further than the talk has time for: memory of what the agent has seen and tried, keeping analysis separate from action, limiting what the agent is allowed to do, evaluating whether interventions help, and the real risk of an annoying notification generator that thinks every pattern means something. Its example question (does staying on the computer late lead to worse sleep, and does a wind-down reminder change that?) is the right shape for a first experiment. Nick is explicit that the goal is not an AI doctor.

## Who should watch

Builders interested in agents that act on real-world feedback, quantified-self tinkerers, and anyone who already runs Home Assistant and wants to add an AI layer. If you are looking for clinical validation or an evaluation framework, this is not that talk; it's a working pattern and a starting point.

Title: An HTTP 200 doesn't mean the AI-backed request was safe
Description: Jayakumar Ramalingam of SiriusXM at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 secures AI-backed APIs hop by hop with deterministic checks around a probabilistic model.
Body:
"Can you explain this charge on my bill?" looks like one API call. Behind it sit identity, private account data, a model inference, a policy decision and possibly a refund in the system of record. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Jayakumar Ramalingam, Staff Software Engineer at SiriusXM, used that billing assistant as a running example to show how to secure an API once AI joins the request path: keep the model in the middle, and make every check around it deterministic.

This is a checklist talk in the best sense. No new framework, just the boundaries you already have, drawn more carefully.

## Draw the path before you defend it

Jayakumar splits the request into six hops: client, gateway, context, model, tools, response. Each hop can add data, change authority, time out or return half an answer. A valid identity at the gateway doesn't prove every retrieved document belongs to that customer, and a model suggesting a tool doesn't mean it may run one.

His first exercise is cheap: pick one endpoint, draw the whole path, and mark where untrusted data enters, where private data is added, where credentials are used and where state changes elsewhere. That gives you a threat model and a shared picture for design reviews and incident reports, so people point at a hop instead of talking about "the AI" as one box.

The classic controls stay: authentication, object-level authorization, request size and rate limits, an endpoint inventory, the OWASP API Top 10. AI makes them matter more, because a weak authorization check now leaks into retrieval, logs and downstream actions.

## A valid request can still end badly

The new problem is ambiguity inside a perfectly valid request. The response can be well formed and still reveal too much. Retrieved text can carry instructions aimed at the model. A fallback can run with weaker controls than the main path. An HTTP 200 tells you the transport completed, not that the right documents arrived or the action was authorized.

His sharpest example: the model returns a valid tool name and a $900 refund amount. The JSON passes the schema. The application still has to check the customer's entitlement, the amount limit, the account state and whether confirmation is needed. The schema tells you the answer has the right shape, not whether the action is allowed. So validation happens before inference (limit what context can be retrieved, send only what's needed) and after it (structure, allowed fields, sensitive data, policy), with permission decisions in code and policy systems rather than prompts.

## Authorization is a chain, not a front door

The confused deputy shows up here: an agent with broad credentials acting for a user with narrow rights, while taking instructions from text it retrieved. The fix is a check at every hop: endpoint, object, context, tool and downstream service, with the downstream service enforcing its own rules even after the broker approved. A household member may see their own bill but not another account's, and may ask for an explanation without being allowed to change a payment.

Retrieved content is data, not instructions. Filter by tenant before retrieval, keep source and chunk IDs, and remember that citations are evidence, not permissions. He also flags the quieter risk: write access to the index deserves the same attention as read access, because whoever can publish material can steer later answers.

## Narrow tools, one budget, honest fallbacks

Tools go through a narrow broker that checks the tool, validates arguments, confirms the caller's permission, applies limits and picks a scoped credential. A tool that fetches one order's status is far safer than one that can call any URL. State-changing calls get an idempotency key so a retry doesn't refund twice.

Rate limits count requests, but one AI request can cost far more than another, so Jayakumar wants one budget per request covering tokens, retrieval fan-out, model latency and tool calls. When it runs out, fail usefully. Fallbacks should do less under the same authorization rules; never quietly switch to a less protected model or a more privileged credential to finish the job.

The rest is operational: log trace IDs, policy outcomes, prompt and model versions and source IDs without copying documents into logs; alert on shifts in policy denials or stale retrieval, not just latency; version prompts, policies and retrieval config together, because rolling back only the model won't restore old behaviour; and run a regression corpus with a pass-rate threshold, since a flaky security gate eventually gets switched off.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers adding an LLM call to an existing API, and AppSec folks reviewing one. You'll recognise most controls; the value is seeing where each one goes on a request that now has a probabilistic step in the middle.

Title: An 80% accurate agent pipeline, and the 20% that needs QA
Description: Suneet Malhotra of Motorola Solutions at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 on running Claude Code and MCP from requirements to tests, and governing the chain, not the file.
Body:
An agent that reports success on a checkout test has told you almost nothing about whether you can release. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Suneet Malhotra, Senior Manager of Test Engineering at Motorola Solutions with around 20 years in software quality, looked at an agent pipeline built on Claude Code and MCP from the QA leader's chair, and argued that the unit of governance is the whole chain from requirement to release, not the code artifact the agent hands back.

The talk is short and conceptual. Its abstract carries the hard numbers from the pipeline itself; the talk spends its time on the questions a release owner has to answer.

## What the pipeline does

Per the abstract, the system runs at a Fortune 500 telecom and earlier ran at a top-25 consumer mobile app. Three MCP servers (Confluence and Jira, a structured test-case repository, and the automation codebase) let the model turn product requirements into Jira stories, test cases and executable Appium and TypeScript code. In the talk Suneet lists the wider MCP layer around it: Confluence, Jira, TestRail, GitHub, Firebase, Slack and Salesforce, with MCP defining tool contracts and routing requests so the requirement document, tickets and test cases no longer have to be written by hand.

The headline is roughly 80% accuracy: about 80% of generated automation runs the intended scenario without edits after generation. Suneet is careful on stage that he isn't claiming every agent produces exactly 80% correct code. He uses the figure to describe a system that works often enough to look useful and fails often enough that the remaining work is where QA lives.

## Five questions before you trust the green tick

His recurring checklist: what did the agent see, what context did we give it, what tools did it call, what changed, and what evidence supports the result? If you can't answer them, you can't call the release good.

He frames the agentic lifecycle as five stages: specify (requirements, constraints, acceptance criteria), plan (tickets and task sequences), build (code and config changes), verify (do the tests actually run correctly) and operate (monitor, roll back). A file can look right while the chain is broken. A test can pass with a hallucinated locator. A ticket can be closed against acceptance criteria that were never precise enough to evaluate.

## Record enough for someone who wasn't in the room

Observability here means reconstructing a decision later: what the agent received, which model, which tool versions, which permissions, what evidence, and which human approved or rejected what in Jira. That evidence trail is what turns an agent into something an engineering team can inspect, instead of a box that announces its own final state.

## Put humans where the risk is

The last 20% is edge cases, context, test data quality and decisions that depend on consequences rather than syntax. Common failures are sparse specs, unclear acceptance criteria, hallucinated API or parameter names, schema drift and lost context. Suneet tiers the response by risk: production configuration, payments and authentication keep a human in the loop; medium-risk regression changes can be automated with reliable review; low-risk changes can lean on unit tests and documentation. The pipeline creates specifications and tests, but there is no autonomous path to release approval.

The abstract adds the scars from a year of running it: don't ask the model to do deterministic work such as flaky-test detection, constrain output to a JSON schema or review time blows up, keep the human PR gate after a silent regression caused a multi-week mess, measure quality before cutting cost (a 25% token cut came with more hotfixes), and layer agents on top of the existing automation runtime instead of replacing it. With guardrails, the ratio of cheap failures to expensive ones went to 4:1, from 1:1 without.

## Measure rework, not output

The metric advice is the part to take back to your team. Track rollback frequency, defect escape rate, unsafe tool call rate and audit trail completeness, not how much the agents generated. Agents earn more autonomy by showing reliable behaviour under clear controls.

## Who should watch

QA and test engineering leads being asked to sign off on agent-generated tests, and engineering managers deciding how much of the delivery pipeline to hand to agents. If you want implementation detail, read the abstract alongside the video; the talk is the governance layer on top.

Title: Model weights pass every pipeline gate without being read
Description: Emmy Eide of Realign Labs at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 walks a model-bearing image through six pipeline gates and shows where "no findings" is mistaken for clean.
Body:
A scanner that can't parse an artifact doesn't return an error. It returns zero findings, and zero findings looks exactly like clean. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Emmy Eide, engineering and cybersecurity lead at Realign Labs and formerly director of product security for SDLC and supply chain security at Red Hat, pushed a model-bearing image through a competent pipeline gate by gate and showed which controls go quiet, which answer the wrong question, and which keep working perfectly while meaning less than you think.

It's the clearest framing of the AI supply chain gap you're likely to find, and it's generous to the tooling we already have.

## A missing decision, not a skipped one

Emmy's core point is about what supply chain security is for: turning risk into a decision somebody makes, with a name and a date. When a CVE ships unnoticed, that's a process failure you can fix. Model risk is worse, because there was never a decision point at all. The tooling came back green, and green says no decision is needed. In her words, "Silence isn't the absence of risk in scanners. It's the absence of a decision."

## The assumption nobody wrote down

Everything in modern DevSecOps (scanning, SBOMs, licence checks, even signing) assumes the artifact is code you can read, enumerate and diff. For twenty years identity stood in for behaviour: name the package version and you knew what it would do. Weights break that three ways. Nothing reads a few billion floating point numbers in any CVE-shaped sense. Behaviour comes from training, not reviewable source. And a version no longer pins behaviour, because the output also depends on the prompt, the retrieved context, the tools and sampling.

The more common case is worse still: you don't ship the model, you call one over an API. Then there's no blob to hash and your SBOM can at best point at a URL whose behaviour can change without a rebuild. Emmy is firm that this doesn't move the obligation; under the EU AI Act and GDPR, the deployer or controller still answers for the output.

## Six gates, six different failures

The walk is the heart of the talk:

1. **Dependency scanning** sees an eight-gigabyte file with no package URL or CPE, files it next to fonts and fixtures, and reports nothing. Failure mode: silence.
2. **SBOM generation** produces a valid, beautiful document where the model is one line at best. Incompleteness presented as completeness.
3. **Licence compliance** finds Apache 2.0 and MIT and misses the bespoke community licence and the training-data provenance. True, but the wrong scope.
4. **Signing** keeps working, and you should keep doing it. It proves who built the bytes, and with non-deterministic behaviour you lose the testing that used to cover the rest.
5. **Provenance-based admission** correctly answers "did this come from us?", a question that used to be a usable proxy for behaviour.
6. **Runtime** becomes the only place behaviour can be observed, on a security budget sized for a backstop.

She's fair to the new model scanners too (Checkmarx, HiddenLayer's engine, ModelScan, Fickling): they catch weaponised packages and pickle gadget chains, which is a real attack class. By their own scope statements, they cover the file, not what the model does when it works as intended.

## The G7 SBOM for AI helps, then hands off

The G7's SBOM for AI defines solid minimum elements, but many are links to model cards and prose, and a pipeline gate checks that a link exists, not that it's true. The level of autonomy was considered and left out. More record without more verification renders as more green.

## What to do this quarter

Emmy's asks are concrete. Request an SBOM for AI against the G7 elements and ask which fields are attested versus declared. Read your model scanner's scope statement and find the sentence about what it doesn't cover. Keep signing, but stop letting a green tick read as a safety verdict, and invest in runtime evidence of what the model called, reached and emitted. The afternoon task: point your scanner at a model image and check whether it read the thing at all. The real task: get someone to answer the autonomy question in writing, with a name and a date.

## Who should watch

Supply chain and AppSec engineers who own the scanner dashboard, and anyone signing off releases of AI features. Platform folks running self-hosted open-weight models will get the most out of the gate walk.

Title: Build load-test models from APM data, not planning-meeting guesses
Description: Vasuki Uday Kiran Vudathala of ServiceNow at Conf42 Observability 2026 derives peak RPS, concurrency and scenario mix from production telemetry.
Body:
Load tests rarely fail because the tool is weak; they fail because the workload model was a guess. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Vasuki Uday Kiran Vudathala, Staff Performance Engineer at ServiceNow, showed a six-query method that derives every number in a peak-readiness test from APM telemetry you already collect. His one-line summary: "Peak readiness should be computed, not negotiated."

## A green test on the wrong workload is the dangerous outcome

The familiar ritual: a few weeks before Black Friday or a launch, people sit in a room and agree on round numbers for concurrent users because round numbers feel safe. The test passes. The real peak arrives in a different shape, say browse-heavy instead of checkout-heavy, or a one-minute spike hidden inside an hourly average, and the system falls over anyway.

Vudathala's framing is that a failing test is a gift: it tells you to fix something. A passing test on the wrong model hands you false confidence with a check mark on it. He estimated the manual process at thirteen to twenty-four hours across two to four people, versus under five minutes for one engineer with automation, and was quick to add that speed is the bonus. Traceability is the point.

## Six queries, from a year down to one minute

The method treats observability data as a workload specification. He demonstrated it in New Relic's NRQL and pointed out Dynatrace DQL or anything exposing transaction and session telemetry works the same way.

1. **Peak day.** Count transactions per day over the season, with sessions, response time and errors.
2. **Peak hour.** Bucket that day by hour with p95 latency. This tells you whether the peak is a plateau or a spike, which sets the test duration.
3. **Peak minute.** A one-minute time series to find the worst sixty seconds. In his example that came to about 82 requests per second.
4. **Scenario mix.** What users actually did in the peak hour, cross-checked by transaction volume, top routes and funnel. Homepage-to-browse was 28 percent; checkout-to-payment only 6.
5. **Concurrency.** Average sessions times average session duration in seconds, divided by 3,600.
6. **Session population.** Distinct sessions in the hour, kept separate from concurrency.

His sharpest technical point sits in step three: don't size from an average. Infrastructure fails on the worst minute, not the mean one. He also flagged the boring traps: filter bots and synthetic traffic, watch for sampling, lock the time zone across queries, and on single-page apps use browser interaction events rather than page views.

## Two numbers people mix up

Steps five and six are where teams get burned. In his example, 529 users were active at once, while 4,280 distinct sessions passed through the hour. The first drives how many virtual users hammer the system; the second sizes your test data pool. Configure 4,280 virtual users and you run a test about eight times heavier than reality and spend a week fixing a problem that only exists in the test.

Growth gets the same discipline. Observed peaks come from data; growth multipliers come from your own year-over-year trend (1.2 to 1.3 for 20 to 30 percent growth, more for a big campaign), with a separate safety buffer. Each multiplier stays visible, so anyone can see which part was observed and which was assumed.

## Test the unhappy paths, then check yourself

Session telemetry also shows where journeys drop off, at discovery, at the cart, at payment. Each drop-off is its own scenario, often hitting the weakest part of the stack. In his words: "If you only test the happy paths, we are testing the demos, not our users."

After the real peak, rerun the same queries and compare against the model. That closes the loop and hands you next year's real growth number. He wrapped the method in a Java and Spring Boot tool, the Peak Workload Analyzer, which outputs a dashboard and a JSON report for your load tool, with New Relic and Dynatrace examples.

## Who should watch

Performance engineers, SREs and anyone who has sat in a peak-planning meeting and wondered where the numbers came from. If you don't have session-level APM data yet, the talk doubles as an argument for collecting it.

Title: Four signals, one backend - why Gigapipe stores everything in ClickHouse
Description: Rita Lopes, founder of Gigapipe, at Conf42 Observability 2026 on unifying logs, metrics, traces and profiles in one open source backend.
Body:
Putting Prometheus, Loki, Tempo and Pyroscope behind one Grafana doesn't give you one system; it gives you four backends and one browser tab. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Rita Lopes, founder and CEO of Gigapipe, made that argument and presented her company's answer: an open source, AGPLv3 observability stack that ingests all four signals through their existing protocols and stores them together in ClickHouse.

This is a founder talking about her own product, and she says so from the first sentence. It's still worth the time for the architecture reasoning, which applies whichever tool you end up running.

## The 3 AM tab shuffle

The opening is an incident walk-through. Metrics show the spike but not the cause. Logs show a flood of errors but not which request. Traces need timestamps you line up by hand. Fifteen minutes in, you know what broke and haven't started fixing it.

Lopes's sharper point is aimed at teams who think Grafana solved this. Open the data source config and there's a separate backend per signal, so the log panel doesn't know about the metrics spike and nobody hands you the trace ID from the log line. One UI, same manual correlation.

## The trade-off triangle

She frames the market as a triangle: complete coverage, affordable, operationally simple, pick two. Coverage plus cheap means self-hosting four systems and a part-time job as an observability engineer. Coverage plus simple means a vendor bill. Cheap plus simple means cutting signals, longer scrape intervals and shorter retention, until the one incident that needed the data. She added that AI workloads generate far more telemetry, which makes per-event pricing hurt more.

## The architecture: polyglot in, columnar underneath

Gigapipe's claims, as presented:

- **Polyglot writes.** OTLP, Prometheus remote write, Loki push, Tempo, Pyroscope, plus InfluxDB, Datadog and Elastic agents, so you can point an existing proprietary agent at a staging install and compare.
- **Polyglot reads.** PromQL, LogQL, TraceQL and FlameQL, plus InfluxDB and SQL, so Grafana and Perses dashboards work unchanged.
- **Clean-room code.** In her words, "Not a fork, not a wrapper", with no translation layer on the hot path.
- **Single binary.** Runs on Kubernetes, VMs or bare metal; your data stays where you put it.

ClickHouse is the deliberate choice underneath. Observability data is write-heavy, read in time ranges and rarely updated, and a columnar engine reads only the columns a query needs. Labels become columns rather than in-memory series, which she argued sidesteps the high-cardinality limits Prometheus hits. Cold data tiers to any S3-compatible store by TTL or space rules, without downsampling. She also said the next version is moving to a self-contained, Parquet-based data-lake design with no external database.

## Migration as a config change

The adoption path is incremental: start with one signal, usually logs, check data lands within seconds, repoint the data source, confirm dashboards still work, then move the next signal. The layers are independently replaceable, so you can adopt only the storage or only the query layer. She said teams report doing the full move in a single sprint.

Her performance and savings figures (billions of points a day on a single standalone deployment, sub-second historical queries, a 50 to 90 percent cost reduction) are customer-reported claims from the talk; benchmark them on your own data before quoting them to finance.

## Who should watch

SREs running the full Grafana LGTM-plus-profiling stack who are tired of operating four storage systems, and anyone evaluating ClickHouse-backed observability. If you want a neutral comparison of options, this isn't it; it's one team's case for its design.

Title: Green CI, broken game: a harness that checks behaviour, not form
Description: Ruben Marcus Luz Paschoarelli of MultiVM Labs at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 breaks a small typed harness three times to show what stops agent fiction from shipping.
Body:
Type check green, build green, deploy gate green, and the play button dead for every player. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Ruben Marcus Luz Paschoarelli, Senior AI Fullstack Engineer at MultiVM Labs, opened with that incident from CS Brazil, the browser FPS he runs, and argued that the thing deciding whether AI-written code is real is the harness around the model, not the model.

His name for the failure mode is fiction: output that is plausible, well-formed, confident and wrong.

## Every check in your pipeline checks form

The CS Brazil bug was a temporal dead zone: a `const` read before initialisation after the bundle order changed. It only exists at runtime, on that path, in that order. The game painted a red banner and reported nothing, no error tracker, no log line. Players told them.

Ruben's diagnosis is the useful bit. Type checks, builds, diff review and even a tired human reviewer at 6 PM all check form. That worked when the author also understood the behaviour. When the author is a model, form is the one thing that is always perfect, so those checks stop discriminating. His list of fiction shapes will be familiar: the import that looks right and doesn't exist, the flaky-test fix that deletes the test, tests that assert the mock, a final number no tool ever computed. The model isn't lying; it's completing.

Better models move the error rate, not the shape of failure. Reliability comes from structure, the way cars got brakes and belts rather than better drivers. He does the arithmetic: two percent fiction at two hundred merges a week is four incidents a week.

## Break it three times

The demo is a small typed harness in TypeScript with a deterministic step provider: no API key, so what you see is the harness, not model luck. Each break is an npm script from his public repo.

- **The model ships fiction.** It requests a nonexistent deploy-to-prod tool and gets a typed invalid-output failure with zero tools run. It calls a calculator with garbage arguments, including a `DROP TABLE users`, and the Zod schema rejects them. It then claims the answer is 96 anyway. The scorer reads the trace, sees the calculator never returned, and fails the run. Steps and results are discriminated unions, so you can't read a value without proving it's OK. Make illegal states unrepresentable; never trust input.
- **Fail closed.** A tool that mutates state is refused under the default policy, and the model has to admit it couldn't save. Only when a human sets `allowsWrite` does the write run. The policy is data set per run or per eval case, with a loop cap and per-step timeouts. Default deny, like firewalls and IAM.
- **One word versus the gate.** A coding agent gets a blocked-write test to pass by flipping one flag with a perfectly reasonable comment. Type check passes and a reviewer would approve it. The eval gate goes from four of four to three of four, exits non-zero, CI goes red. The gate is a golden dataset, deterministic scorers and a process exit code.

## Rulers that can fail, and judges as canaries

Two traps he calls out. Tests that can't fail: every ruler should ship with a mutant, so you've watched it go red. And trusting the report over the record: a check passes only if the trace holds a successful result from that tool, whatever the prose says. LLM-as-judge scores but doesn't gate until you've measured its agreement with human labels. Deterministic checks are the gate; the judge is a canary.

For teams who write harnesses in prompts rather than TypeScript, the same five rules apply: type the output contract with evidence labelled confirmed, inferred or unknown; ban wrong answers with literal examples; give critics no write tools and permission to find nothing; grade against rubrics; and pin prompts like dependencies, with a hash.

## Two production systems, same rule

His PR reviewer bot, Estraga Código ("code wrecker" in Portuguese), reviews diffs and opens issues but never merges. Merging is decided by 61 deterministic invariants about the game. And a fleet of nine agent roles across seven providers in a collaborative algorithm challenge submits only when the trusted eval is clean, heartbeats are live and the worktree is clean. It topped the leaderboard many times and fed an arXiv paper he co-authored, which he credits to the closed gate rather than clever agents.

He also lists the costs: golden datasets rot, judges drift, model versions change under you, and every gate needs an owner with authority to keep it closed the day before a deadline.

## Who should watch

Anyone merging agent-written code at volume, and especially anyone whose quality gate amounts to a reviewer glancing at the diff. The demos are short, reproducible and keyless, which makes them good material for a team session.

Title: Uber's driver onboarding team let agents build test accounts
Description: Kemet Dugue of Uber at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 shows the skills and the test-account agent that took onboarding setup from minutes to under 30 seconds.
Body:
Testing a driver onboarding feature at Uber means getting an account into one exact state out of more than 50,000 possible ones. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Kemet Dugue, software engineer on Uber's Driver Onboarding team, walked through how the team swapped run books and manual API calls for an agent that does it from a sentence, plus four smaller agent skills that removed everyday friction first.

The useful part of the talk is the order of operations: fix your own developer pain points with small, deterministic skills, then build the bigger agent on a platform that already exists.

## Why onboarding is a hard testing problem

Kemet calls driver onboarding the regulatory gateway to Uber's marketplace. Before anyone earns, they pass compliance and screening (criminal and motor vehicle checks with outside vendors), lifecycle tracking before and after activation, multi-channel onboarding for rideshare, couriers, fleets and rentals across thousands of jurisdictions, and document verification for licences, registrations and inspections. Fifteen-plus background check error states and dozens of document rejection reasons multiply into that state space.

## Four small skills before the big agent

The team first pointed agents at their own workflow:

- **Worktree skill.** Coding agents bottlenecked on one branch in one directory. Stashing Agent A's work so Agent B can make an urgent metadata fix forces language servers to re-index and the agent to rebuild context. A skill built on Git worktrees gives each agent its own directory, so both run in parallel.
- **Branch-to-diff skill.** Uber's pull requests ("diffs") have rigid CI templates demanding test evidence, linked tickets and template-aligned summaries. Generic LLM drafts were verbose and failed formatting checks. The skill inspects the Git changes, pulls context from Jira, checks local unit test coverage and formats the summary so it passes CI the first time.
- **EngiWiki sync.** Agents are only as good as the context they retrieve, and the repo had testing docs from 2023 that no longer matched reality. A sync skill keeps the internal EngiWiki aligned with the code as it changes.
- **Jira lifecycle rule.** Ticket transitions through the Jira REST API, such as moving a ticket to In Review when a diff is generated, plus fetching related historical tickets for context.

None of these is glamorous. All of them are the sort of thing that quietly costs a team hours each week, which is the point.

## The platform underneath

Kemet gives a quick tour of Uber's internal AI stack. At the bottom, an AI platform on Michelangelo, Uber's ML platform, with a model gateway, runtime SDKs and an agent registry. Above it, context engineering: code context infrastructure, memory hierarchies and an MCP gateway. Then industry and custom agents, from Claude Code to internal SDLC agents for test generation and code review. At the top, engineering enablement for cost, token telemetry and adoption.

Two pieces matter for the case study. The Agent Builder is a no-code web workspace where engineers and domain specialists configure agents in plain text, with MCP tools built in and handoffs between sub-agents. The MCP gateway exposes internal RPCs as standard MCP tool schemas, so agents query schemas at runtime and API changes don't require prompt rewrites, with observability and audit trails included.

## The test account agent

Previously, one test account took a multi-page run book and manual calls across several tools: five to ten minutes at minimum. The agent splits the job into two phases. Phase one provisions a base test account. Phase two transitions it into the requested state (a specific document rejection, a background check status), calling the right services through the MCP gateway. The UI is built in Agent Builder.

Results Kemet reports: setup time under 30 seconds, a 95% end-to-end success rate on their evaluation suites, and self-serve use by engineers and product managers.

## The takeaways are the design

Kemet closes with four rules that are worth more than the numbers. Decouple reasoning from state mutation: the LLM maps intent to parameters and a deterministic workflow does the changes. Let agents work in parallel. Benchmark tool calls with deterministic metrics, not vibe checks. And keep safety in code and at the gateway, not in the system prompt.

## Who should watch

Platform and product engineers in large organisations deciding where agents should start, and anyone whose test setup lives in a wiki page nobody trusts. If you only have five minutes, watch the takeaways.
