Title: Geography is not jurisdiction: EU compliance on AWS without theatre
Description: Dmytro Hlotenko (Sage Austria) at Conf42 Remix 2026 on CLOUD Act, DORA, NIS2, the European Sovereign Cloud and what AWS Outposts fails to solve.
Body:
Putting a rack in a Munich bunker doesn't change who holds the admin keys. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Dmytro Hlotenko, Senior Cloud Operations Engineer at Sage in Austria and an AWS user group leader in Vienna, gave a practitioner's defence of running AWS in regulated European environments, built around one question: who operates the control plane?

He opens with a disclaimer worth repeating: he is an engineer, not a lawyer, and the talk is a map for conversations with your legal team, not a replacement for one. His abstract puts the thesis bluntly: "Sovereignty without operational maturity is just compliance theater."

## Jurisdiction attaches to whoever runs it

His central distinction is between data residency and sovereignty. Residency is about where the bytes sit, and it's the easy part. Sovereignty is about operational control: the management plane, admin credentials, telemetry access. His reading of the CLOUD Act is that it targets service providers and the entities that hold or control data, not the people who wrote the software. So self-hosted software on your own metal, run by your own staff, is in a different position from a "local" managed service whose operators sit under US jurisdiction. Hardware in the EU with a remote admin in Seattle is not the safe option it looks like.

He also asks teams to separate capability from probability: a risk being possible doesn't by itself justify a multi-year redesign.

## DORA and NIS2 don't ban hyperscalers

Every new EU regulation, he says, triggers a wave of panic and expensive migrations. His reading: DORA cares about concentration risk and exit strategies for financial institutions, NIS2 about supply chain security for critical entities, and neither forbids AWS, Azure or GCP. What they demand is that you stop using them blindly: documented risk assessments, an exit strategy, strong encryption, real governance. If your compliance officer says DORA means leaving AWS, his advice is a new compliance officer.

The spreadsheet case for swapping one well-governed account for seven EU vendors misses the human cost: seven SLAs, seven escalation paths, retraining, slower recovery, and senior engineers who don't want to join to run a stack nobody else knows.

## The European Sovereign Cloud moves the needle, partly

AWS European Sovereign Cloud, launched in January 2026, gets a fair hearing. It's a separate partition run by a new legal entity, with metadata, CloudTrail and IAM staying in the Brandenburg region rather than touching us-east-1. He walks through a table of which GDPR, DORA and NIS2 concerns a normal EU region already covers and where ESC adds to it. His verdict: a large improvement and probably enough for most companies, but the parent is still a US company, which is why some European authorities still treat it with caution.

## What Outposts quietly doesn't solve

This is the case study that prompted the talk. A regulated customer wanted data to stay in Austria, and Outposts looked like the answer: AWS APIs in your own data centre. Dmytro's team benchmarked it properly, replaying real user behaviour with Locust and Playwright from Azure in Vienna against identical stacks.

The findings stack up. Outposts' control plane metadata lives in the parent region, so its CLOUD Act exposure matches a normal region. Many services are missing or stripped down: no Lambda, no Glue, no SageMaker, limited S3 at extra cost. A vCPU is often an SMT thread, so four physical VMware cores can mean roughly eight vCPUs, with licensing knock-ons. Storage tops out around 16,000 IOPS against the hundreds of thousands a SAN gave them, and some internal database jobs took two to three times longer. Then there's the backup trap: EBS snapshots go to the parent region, so your "local" data has backups in Frankfurt. Add power, cooling and a second rack for high availability, and you're building a data centre to keep the AWS APIs.

## Who should watch

Platform and cloud ops engineers in Europe fielding sovereignty questions from sales, legal or customers, and anyone pricing Outposts for compliance reasons. It's long and dense, and the benchmarking section alone justifies the time. His closing decision tree, from "standard region" through ESC to ESC plus Outposts to bare metal, is a good template for your own.

Title: When agents code and ship it, on-call needs simulator time
Description: Ralph Bird of PagerDuty at Conf42 Observability 2026 on owning incidents in AI-written code, the automation paradox and practice for on-call.
Body:
PagerDuty's mantra is "code it, ship it, own it". At Conf42 Observability 2026, Ralph Bird, Principal Machine Learning Engineer at PagerDuty, argued that AI is taking over the first two, and that the third has not gone anywhere. His fix borrows from civil aviation: if agents handle the routine incidents, humans need deliberate simulator time so they are not cold when the big one lands.

## 03:47, and the agent has already failed

The talk opens on a night in the near future. The pager fires at 03:47, a SEV 1, revenue bleeding. The difference from today: an SRE agent has already tried. The easy fixes, a restart or a rollback of the last deploy, are gone. You open a code base you have not read in two years, because an agent wrote it, another agent shipped it, and the minor incidents that used to teach you the system were handled overnight without you. The agent cannot fix this. Can you?

Bird is not a doom merchant about it. He expects more code to mean more incidents, and AI-written code to fail in different ways even with guardrails. He also expects agents to handle minor incidents, and thinks that is good: nobody needs a human to restart something at night if the agent can do it and leave a note in the morning. He also rejects both loud predictions, that it will all be agent ops, or that agents write everything and humans absorb the incident wave. Teams will own more services than they wrote, and that changes what ownership means.

## The automation paradox

The core idea is the automation paradox: the more reliable the automation, the rustier and rarer the humans who can handle what it cannot. When agents take the routine work, engineers lose the cheap practice that routine incidents provided, and meet the gnarly ones with less context, less recent practice and higher stakes.

Bird, a former nuclear safety engineer, walks through industries that already faced this. Top Gun exists because naval aviators came to rely on missiles and lost dogfighting skills. Civil aviation responded to autopilot dependence with recurrent simulator time, manual segments and standardised scenarios based on real faults. NASA trains for everything imaginable. Security teams red team their own systems. The lesson he draws for SRE is simple: reactive incident response is not training, so practice has to be routine, scheduled, realistic and aimed at the faults that actually hurt. There is no point drilling Kubernetes failures if you do not run Kubernetes.

## Know how your tools fail

Practice does not remove black swans, and Bird is honest about that, citing the cascading power outage that took out Portugal, where he lives, and Fukushima. His sharpest example is Aeroflot Flight 593, as he tells it: a pilot let his teenage son take the controls, yanking them disengaged the autopilot, and the pilot did not know his tool worked that way. The parallel for SRE agents: learn how they fail, especially when they fail confidently, because following a confident wrong answer is how you walk down the wrong path at 3 a.m.

For tooling, he wants an SRE agent that is both autopilot (take the routine, well-understood work) and co-pilot (assist on complex incidents while the human stays in command), plus incident history used to guide training. Replacement is not the goal.

## What to do tomorrow morning

The advice is concrete. Use agents to read, not just write: pick an unfamiliar code base in your organisation and have the agent help you understand it. Rehearse in low-stakes settings, with game days, drills, failure Fridays and chaos experiments, and bring the SRE agent into those drills so you learn its failure modes. Prioritise scenarios that scare you: the EC2 instance that dies, the read replica that fails, the Kafka queue that stops. Learn from near misses, not only the bad incidents. And treat ownership of the services you inherited as a conscious choice, using the time agents save to learn them.

## Who should watch

On-call engineers and engineering managers whose teams are adopting coding or SRE agents, and anyone building incident tooling. There is no product demo; it is a culture and practice talk from someone who builds incident response tooling. If you already run game days, watch it for the argument you need to keep funding them.

Title: Analytics platforms need a seven-layer design system, not three
Description: Sonali Priya (Local Backhaul Networks) at Conf42 Remix 2026 extends tokens, components and patterns with data, viz, semantics, workflow and governance layers.
Body:
Three dashboards, one metric called revenue, three different calculations. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Sonali Priya, Creative Design Director at Local Backhaul Networks, argued that the classic three-layer design system (tokens, components, patterns) was built for consumer apps and quietly fails on enterprise analytics, and she proposed a seven-layer model to fix it.

She has spent over a decade on enterprise platforms in telecom, finance, healthcare and infrastructure, and the talk reads like a list of things she has watched break.

## Three layers stop where the data starts

Her diagnosis has three symptoms. Fragmentation: teams rebuild the same charts, so you end up with five slightly different line charts. Visual drift: with no shared rules for colours, scales, axis labels and thresholds, two dashboards in one product look like they came from two companies. Governance gaps: nobody owns a metric definition or a component version, and access control gets bolted on later.

Then the specific failures. A standard table component is designed for a few hundred rows; analytics platforms routinely have hundreds of thousands or millions, and virtualization, streaming and lazy loading aren't in the box. A chart that looks elegant with a hundred points becomes noise with a hundred thousand, and the three-layer model says nothing about aggregation or sampling. So teams build their own, and the shared system stops being shared.

## The four layers she adds

Layers one and two are familiar, with a twist. Tokens need data-viz palettes (sequential, diverging, categorical), density modes for packed dashboards, and semantic tokens that encode intent such as "threshold exceeded" or "anomaly detected" rather than just blue and red, compiled from one source to CSS, iOS, Android and Figma. UI components stay deliberately unaware of data.

Layer three is data components: the virtualized table, query builder, filter panel and metric picker, stateful by design, handling loading, empty, partial and error states. Layer four is visualization primitives, the scales, legends, grids and tooltips that charts are assembled from, with accessible palettes and rules for what to show when there's more data than pixels.

Layer five, semantics, is the one she calls most underappreciated: a single definition of each metric, its units, its thresholds and targets, so "churn rate" means the same thing to the designer, the data engineer and the PM. Layer six is workflow patterns such as drill-down, cross-filtering, explore-to-dashboard and period-over-period comparison, codified once instead of reinvented per team.

## Governance goes on top, on purpose

Layer seven has four parts: a named owner for every metric and component (a person, not a team or a Slack channel), semantic versioning for metric definitions because changing one rewrites history, access and sensitivity controls inside the system, and a contribution workflow with quality gates for proposing and retiring components. Her summary line: a design system without governance is just a component library with good intentions.

The adoption order is the practical bit. Start with tokens and governance, the cheapest layers with the most leverage. Then data components and viz primitives, where users feel the pain. Then semantics, which is as much organisational work as technical. Patterns come last: wait until you see the same flow in three teams before codifying it. Measure reuse rates, consistency scores and time to dashboard, or you won't know it's working.

## Who should watch

Design system leads and front-end engineers on internal analytics or observability products, and data platform people who keep getting asked why two dashboards disagree. It's a framework talk with no code or live demo, delivered in a brisk twenty-odd minutes. Note that the abstract describes five pillars while the talk itself presents the seven layers.

Title: AI writes more of the code, so SREs have to own the failure odds
Description: Sylvain Kalache, Head of AI Labs at Rootly, on how AI-assisted coding raises change volume and incident rates, and where AI helps SREs, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
Incidents scale with the number of changes times the chance each one breaks something, and AI-assisted coding is turning up the first number fast. That is the framing [Sylvain Kalache](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Sylvain_Kalache_vibes_outages_writes), Head of AI Labs at Rootly and a former SRE, builds his Conf42 Remix 2026 talk around: you can't control how much code the world ships, but the probability of failure per change is still the SRE's job.

Rootly is an on-call and incident management platform with its own AI SRE, and Sylvain says so early. Most of the talk, though, is about patterns rather than product.

## C goes up, and help goes down

His formula is a baseline failure rate plus C, the number of changes in a period, multiplied by P, the probability that a change introduces a failure. He cites a run of industry figures on AI-written code and a study of 5,000 engineers at Microsoft, Accenture and another large company in which GenAI users produced 15% more commits and completed 25% more tasks. More output means more C.

Rootly's own data points the same way: Sylvain saw a threefold increase in average incidents per customer between 2023 and the time of the talk. Meanwhile the help available in an incident is shrinking. The developer you page may say they didn't really write that code, their agent did. Specialists such as database or networking experts are harder to find as practitioners become generalists. More incidents, less help, and a manager asking why AI hasn't made you faster.

## A field guide to AI slop

The examples are the fun part. Unit tests that pass because they faithfully reproduce broken logic. A Terraform test that is technically correct but checks the wrong intent. A case reported to Vercel where an agent hallucinated a GitHub repository and deployed it into a customer environment. Slopsquatting: researchers published a package under a name LLMs tend to hallucinate and it was downloaded 30,000 times in three months, even showing up in big companies' READMEs. And the cat-facts experiment, where adding an irrelevant line about cats to a maths problem doubled LLM error rates.

A friend who is an SRE at Airbnb told him every AI screw-up has a human equivalent, and Sylvain agrees: curling a random script into bash, fat-fingering `rm`, being distracted by cats. The difference is pace. So he argues for applying blameless culture to LLMs: the question is which guardrail was missing, not whose fault it was.

## Keeping P low, with AI's help

His message to sceptical practitioners is to try the tools, because they are where software is going. The fundamentals (testing, progressive delivery and the rest) matter more than ever because C keeps climbing. On the AI side he highlights mutation testing, citing Meta's automated compliance hardening work, where engineers accepted over 70% of LLM-generated tests across Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. He suggests LLMs as code review helpers, the same way linters and static analysis already are, since review is becoming the bottleneck.

During incidents, MCP gives agents access to the same tools engineers use, and AI SRE agents pull from GitHub, telemetry and past postmortems to propose root causes. He says Rootly's handles some lower-severity incidents without anyone looking, and gives a head start on complex ones. Two easy wins: let agents draft postmortems, and let them make your ugly internal tools look decent.

## Who should watch

SREs and on-call leads seeing incident counts rise alongside AI adoption, and engineering leaders who want a simple model for explaining why. Expect a vendor's perspective on AI SRE tooling, balanced by a lot of practical, vendor-neutral advice.

Title: For AI agents, cost is the canary and evidence is the grade
Description: Sabith K Soopy of StackGen at Conf42 Observability 2026 on spend caps, plan-gather-present traces and grading agents on evidence.
Body:
Agents rarely crash. They loop, burn tokens and write a fluent root cause analysis about the wrong service. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Sabith K Soopy, Principal Software Engineer at StackGen, shared what his team instruments on its DevOps and SRE agents, and his headline lesson came from invoices rather than white papers: watch spend first, because cost is the earliest signal that an agent has gone sideways.

## Green APM, wrong answer

The scenario is familiar to anyone who has tried an SRE agent. A 3 a.m. page, the agent reads logs, metrics and traces, and produces a confident RCA with all the right service names. Then the human on-call looks and says it is the wrong service. Nothing crashed. CPU, memory and p99 were all fine. What changed was that yesterday's run cost a few thousand tokens and today's cost three times that, and five tool calls became fifteen.

Traditional APM answers whether the service is up. Soopy's point is that agents need extra primitives to answer why the agent did that: session traces across multi-step reasoning, per-tool attribution of cost and latency, token budgets as first-class signals, and evidence checks.

## Put a hard stop in the path before you scale

Soopy describes runaway retry loops as the failure that shows up on the bill. A few hundred near-identical calls in ten minutes add up, and normal rate limits do not fire because each call looks legitimate. StackGen's answer is a set of limits: max steps, max spend per tool, a page when one run looks odd next to last week's average for that agent, and an alert on tool call count as well as dollars. A healthy run makes a handful of calls; a sick one makes dozens, each fine on its own. Ship the spend cap and the loop cap before you scale the traffic.

## Plan, gather, present

StackGen models an agent run as three chapters: plan what problem to solve, gather by calling tools, and present an answer. Most of the work and most of the trouble live in the middle. The team stitches hops with OpenTelemetry and inspects the LLM trees in Langfuse. If you only instrument the final HTTP response, he warns, you will never find where the reasoning went wrong.

The correlation details are the kind you only learn by getting them wrong. The agents are written in Go and send data to three places on purpose: the LLM trace store gets the chat and tool tree, the normal metrics stack gets budget and health counters, and logs carry the same OpenTelemetry trace ID. Use the real OpenTelemetry hex ID in logs, not your web framework's request ID, because the two look alike and break the join. Tool and agent names are fine as metric labels; a session ID in Prometheus is not. And add business labels to child spans (session, workflow, stage, agent) when you start, because retrofitting them after an incident is painful.

## Missing data is not a passing grade

The best story in the talk is a failure. The team built an agent quality scorecard that looked professional and was wrong. The formulas were fine; the population was not. Most of the spans it scored were tiny helper calls with almost no session context, and the healthy score nearly became an argument that the fleet was ready. The rule they took from it: measure telemetry quality before agent quality, and when data is incomplete, report unknown instead of a high score.

The grading itself is about evidence, not prose. In the present step the question is whether the answer cites what the gather step actually returned. Soopy notes they had seen automated graders score polished answers highly when the trace showed the tool was never called. For support, StackGen bundles a whole conversation into one debug zip (manifest with agent version, the execution DAG, the event stream) so a bad session can be replayed offline and batch-graded.

## Who should watch

Teams running LLM agents in operations, or anyone who has opened an LLM bill and winced. The talk is grounded in StackGen's own setup, with Langfuse and Grafana as the examples, but nothing depends on those tools. The two things to do next week, per Soopy: alert on sessions that cost far more than the agent's average or make far more tool calls than normal, and do not mark a run good unless the answer cites what was gathered.

Title: GraphRAG answers the counting questions vector RAG fakes
Description: Elizabeth Fuentes Leone (AWS) at Conf42 Remix 2026 builds a vector RAG agent and a GraphRAG agent side by side to show where retrieval invents numbers.
Body:
Ask a RAG agent "how many hotels have swimming pools?" and it will read three chunks and give you a confident estimate. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, Developer Advocate at AWS, showed why that happens and fixed it by swapping similarity search for a knowledge graph: the database counts, the model only writes the query.

A note on scope before you press play. The talk page carries the title of her semantic tool selection session, but the recording is the first part of a five-technique series on stopping agent hallucinations, and it is about GraphRAG. Semantic tool selection appears as technique number two, with a short preview: put every tool description in a FAISS vector store so the agent only sees the tools that match the query. If that is what you came for, her [AI Agents 2026 talk on semantic tool selection](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_tools_semantic_cost) is the full version.

## Vector search answers from the top-k, not from the data

Her framing of the failure is precise. Vector search returns the most similar documents, not all of them, so an aggregation question gets answered from a sliver of the corpus. The agent then does arithmetic on whatever it retrieved and reports the result as fact. She called it "fabricate numbers delivered with full confidence", and listed the three shapes it takes: fabricated statistics, incomplete retrieval, and out-of-domain answers where the model fills the gap from its training data.

The part worth remembering is that nothing is broken. Retrieval did its job. The question just wasn't a similarity question.

## Let the database do the maths

The GraphRAG side uses the Neo4j simple knowledge graph pipeline. An LLM reads each hotel document, discovers the entity types itself (hotels, rooms, amenities, policies, services), extracts relationships, and runs entity resolution so that "outdoor pool" and "swimming pool" collapse into one node. That deduplication, she pointed out, is what makes a count query accurate at all.

At question time the agent reads the graph schema from the tool's docstring and writes a Cypher query. The database executes it across every node and hands back the result. The model never sees a pile of chunks to summarise, so it has nothing to invent from. When the data isn't there, the query returns empty.

There's a cost angle too. Normal RAG pushes every retrieved chunk into the context, and every chunk is tokens you pay for. A query result is small.

## Four questions, two agents

The demo builds both agents with Strands Agents, the open source AWS agent SDK, running against OpenAI models, a local Neo4j and a FAISS store with an open source sentence-transformer embedding model. The dataset is a set of hotel documents; she recommends the lighter build for testing over the full 300-hotel version.

Then the same prompts go to both agents: an average rating across Paris hotels, a count of hotels with pools, a multi-hop question about room types and prices, and the trap, "tell me about hotels in Antarctica". Vector RAG found two Paris hotels and did the averaging itself, then offered a friendly general overview of Antarctic hotels it had no data about. The graph agent answered from the query results and said plainly that there are no hotels in Antarctica in the database. Antarctica, for the record, remains under-served by the hospitality industry.

## When to keep plain RAG

She doesn't pitch GraphRAG as a replacement. Semantic search over unstructured text, fuzzy matching and simple lookups are still RAG's job. Counting, aggregation and multi-hop reasoning across entities are where the graph earns its setup cost, and her suggestion for production is both: graph for structured questions, vectors for open-ended search.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose RAG app gets asked "how many" or "which ones" and answers with suspicious confidence. It's a short, code-first session with a notebook you can rerun, aimed at people who build agents rather than evaluate vendors. The tooling shown is AWS's own (Strands, with AgentCore mentioned for deployment), but Neo4j and the pattern are portable.

Title: Your agent said "done". Make it prove it with an evidence chain
Description: Emerson Braun of Plan A Technologies at Conf42 Observability 2026 on tracing agent context, decisions, actions and verified outcomes.
Body:
An agent that replies "Done. The issue is resolved." has made a claim, not delivered a result. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Emerson Braun, Staff Engineer and Regional Director at Plan A Technologies and creator of the AgentsKit side project, laid out an observability model for agents built on one rule: record context, decision, action and verified outcome, or you are guessing.

## A confident answer is just a claim

Braun's opening example is a refund. A customer asks for money back on a purchase from 20 days ago. The agent loads a policy with a 30-day window, approves the refund, and everyone is happy. Except the current policy says something else, and the question that matters in production is whether you can prove which version of the policy the agent actually used. If you cannot, you do not have observability.

The same "done" can hide three different failures, he argued: the wrong context (an outdated policy), a failed action (the refund never went through), or an unverified outcome (the customer is still waiting). A trace of the final chat message tells you none of that.

## Technical success and task success are different metrics

Anyone who has consumed a flaky API knows the pattern: a 200 response with a body that is not valid JSON, or valid JSON missing the field you need. Braun applies the same layered check to agent tool calls. Did the call return? Can the response be parsed and used? Does it contain what the workflow expects? And finally, did the intended state actually change in the world? Only the last one counts as the task succeeding.

## Failure is a state, not a conclusion

The most practical part of the talk is the case for state machines. Model each agent step as an explicit state, and a failure stops being the end of the story. You preserve the error and the execution state, classify what failed (timeout or invalid result), check what actually happened, then choose a recovery: retry, reroute, compensate, or escalate to a human.

Two details make this work. Idempotency keys, so a retried refund does not hit the customer twice. And an append-only ledger of every agent action, because if you only update the current state you cannot reconstruct the steps later. His summary of the principle: automate the recovery decisions, not the retries.

The demo makes the point with a scripted adapter, no model calls. The same refund conversation runs twice. Without observability, the agent says the refund happened and you have to take its word for it. With the trace, you see the context version, the policy version, a tool timeout, the agent treating the state as uncertain, and a status check that confirms the refund. Same outcome, but only one of them is evidence.

## Autonomy needs a control boundary

Braun sorts proposed actions by risk. Low-risk reads, searches and classification run autonomously, otherwise why have agents at all. Reversible actions run within limits and budgets. High-impact actions, like a change that touches many users in a database, always go to a human, and the human gets enough context to decide. An agent saying it wants to drop a table is not enough; which table, in which environment, is.

He also warns against the opposite failure: logging everything. Raw executions carry payloads, credentials and PII. Put a privacy boundary in the middle (allowlists, redaction, masking) and keep versions, routes, statuses, validations and outcomes. Collect enough to explain the system, not enough to recreate the user.

The talk closes with a ten-point checklist, from versioning instructions and context, through tracing every external boundary and binding approvals to exact actions, to linking metrics back to traces. Cost gets its own warning: the model call is rarely the whole bill once retries, tool calls and waiting are counted.

## Who should watch

Engineers putting agents in front of customers or production systems, especially anyone whose agent can move money or change data. It is a framework talk with a small scripted demo, not a product pitch; AgentsKit appears as the speaker's own example code. If you already run state machines for workflows, the novelty is applying that discipline to the parts of the agent you cannot see.

Title: Spotify's abstraction paradox: abstractions should teach, not hide
Description: Stuart Clark of Spotify on how 2014 hyper-growth made clean abstractions opaque during incidents, and how Backstage was built to fix it, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
The abstraction that makes shipping easy is often the one that makes a 3am incident impossible. At Conf42 Remix 2026, [Stuart Clark](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Stuart_Clark_scale_fail_spotify), Senior Developer Advocate at Spotify, tells the story of how Spotify's 2014 hyper-growth turned clean APIs into opaque walls, and how the fix (eventually open-sourced as Backstage) rests on one rule: an abstraction should teach complexity rather than hide it.

This is a story-driven talk about operational knowledge, not code. It's also the origin story of a tool many platform teams now use, told from the inside.

## 60 days to a tenth pull request

In 2014 Spotify was moving from a music streaming app to a personalised audio platform and hiring fast under a ship-fast, ship-often mantra. The user numbers looked great. Internally, engineering productivity was falling: the time for a new engineer to reach their tenth pull request, a milestone Spotify tracked, had grown to almost 60 days. Stuart calls that archaeological excavation rather than onboarding.

The odd part is that the systems looked good. Senior engineers had built clean APIs, documented interfaces and tidy abstractions that made common tasks simple, exactly as asked. New engineers could ship on the happy path. The moment something failed, they hit what Stuart calls a cognitive brick wall.

## The abstraction trap

Picture the incident room: the service is down, the person who built the component is on holiday, and the abstraction tells you only that something failed in the data layer. What, where and why are all hidden. The abstractions were optimised for the 90% of normal operations, and incidents live in the 10% of edge conditions they were never designed to illuminate.

The hidden cost Stuart names is knowledge atrophy. Seniors were relieved that juniors could ship without interrupting them, and gradually the people who truly understood the system became knowledge silos disguised as good engineering practice. His distinction is the heart of the talk: abstraction reduces cognitive load while preserving the ability to dig deeper; oversimplification hides complexity until it blows up in your face.

## Three layers, like a good technical book

The answer was Backstage, a unified developer portal. Stuart compares it to a good technical book, where chapter one gives the basics and the appendix has depth when you need it. Layer one is the happy path, covering what users need most of the time. Layer two is context, showing what is happening under the hood. Layer three is full system access when things break. Each layer should lead naturally to the next.

Three components carry it. Golden Path software templates encode operational lessons, not just boilerplate. The service catalog shows the nature of dependencies, their reliability and metrics, and what happens downstream if one breaks. TechDocs keeps documentation next to the systems. A plugin architecture allows customisation, and if you deviate from the defaults, the system helps you understand the implications.

## Knowledge as infrastructure

The scaling lesson is to treat operational knowledge like infrastructure: you wouldn't build a system without thinking about how it scales, so don't build abstractions without thinking about how the knowledge behind them scales. The outcomes he lists are new engineers following expert debugging paths, every interaction becoming a learning opportunity, and knowledge kept fresh as systems change, which prevents documentation rot. Spotify open-sourced Backstage in 2020 and donated it to the CNCF.

He ends with three questions to ask before building your next abstraction: can I trace through this when something goes wrong, does it teach me something about the system, and is there a natural path from basic use to deep understanding?

## Who should watch

Platform engineers building golden paths or an internal developer portal, and SRE leads who have watched a newer engineer freeze in front of a well-designed but opaque tool. If you want Backstage configuration details, look elsewhere; this is about the why.

Title: Score the risk before it pages you
Description: Oreoluwa Omoike, SRE at JPMorgan Chase, on an observe-score-decide-act loop that cut detection time and false alerts, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
Most alerting tells you loudly that something broke and says nothing about what is about to. At Conf42 Remix 2026, [Oreoluwa Omoike](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Oreoluwa_Omoike_driven_risk_aware), Site Reliability Engineer at JPMorgan Chase, presents a risk-aware decision loop that scores failure probability against business impact and time, then lets a policy engine decide whether to log, autoscale or page.

It's a compact talk with a formula, three ML patterns, a production case study with numbers, and a refreshingly specific list of ways it goes wrong.

## Reactive SRE is the same incident in a new disguise

The opening story is familiar: a 2am page, 45 minutes to root cause, a hotfix, bed, and the same class of failure two weeks later. The numbers he puts on reactive SRE are 14 minutes on average just to detect an incident, 45 minutes to mitigate, and 70% of alerts being noise. That last one is the quiet killer, because it trains engineers to stop caring. The deeper problem, he argues, is the mental model: our systems scream after something breaks and are poor at saying it probably will.

## Observe, score, decide, act

The framework has four steps, and the first is deliberately boring. Observe is your existing stack of metrics, traces, logs and burn rates. Score is where AI enters: risk equals probability of failure, times business impact, divided by time to impact. The failure probability comes from your model; business impact might be a checkout outage costing $5,000 an hour; time to impact is urgency, so a risk ten minutes out scores far higher than one six hours away. Decide is a policy engine, effectively a tiered response playbook run in milliseconds instead of by a sleepy human. Act executes it consistently, including at 3am.

## Three ML patterns that sit on top of what you have

Anomaly detection uses isolation forests or LSTMs trained on baseline traffic, catching drift rather than threshold crossings. Oreoluwa likes isolation forests because they are light and engineers can usually tell why one fired; LSTMs are worth it for subtler temporal patterns. SLO burn-rate forecasting tells you the error budget will be gone in about 40 minutes, which is 40 minutes to scale or shift traffic. Change risk scoring gives every deploy, config change and feature flag a blast-radius score before it reaches production, with gradient boosting learning from incident history.

All three run as sidecars plugged into Prometheus, OpenTelemetry and Grafana. He is blunt that proposing to replace the observability stack would kill the project on arrival.

## The case study numbers

The system ran for six months on an e-commerce platform processing 50 million events a day, through Black Friday-style spikes and flash sales. Mean time to detect fell to 2.3 minutes, which he puts as an 84% improvement. False positives dropped from 70% to 18%. Mean time to resolve went from 45 to 11 minutes. SLO breaches per month fell from 22 to four. On-call satisfaction surveys improved too, and one engineer called the AI scorer the most trusted member of the on-call team.

## The pitfalls nobody mentions

This section is the reason to watch. Models drift after campaigns, launches and seasonal spikes, so retrain weekly on a rolling window and track drift with the population stability index. Don't wire it straight to paging or you have rebuilt the alert storm: run log-only for two weeks, then allow autoscaling, then paging, and always keep a human override. Keep scoring under five milliseconds with async batching and feature caching for high-cardinality labels. And if 30% of the metric data is missing, don't score at all; a bad score is worse than no score. Build data quality monitoring before the model.

## Who should watch

SREs drowning in noisy alerts who want a concrete path toward predictive operations, and engineering managers who need numbers to justify trying it. His starting advice is small: one isolation forest and one Prometheus metric.

Title: Beyond send-time optimization: should we send at all?
Description: Adobe's Murthy Chandrapaty and Chakravarthy Kalva reframe send-time optimization as an AI decision layer that can send, defer or skip, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
A model that predicts the perfect send time will still happily send the fourth email of the day to someone who has stopped reading. At Conf42 Remix 2026, [Murthy Chandrapaty](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Murthy_Chandrapaty_Chakravarthy_Kalva_decisioning_b2c_marketing), Principal Engineer and Architect at Adobe, and Chakravarthy Kalva, Senior Product Manager at Adobe, argue that send-time optimization should become a decision system whose most valuable output is sometimes "don't send."

The talk splits neatly in two. Chakravarthy makes the product case; Murthy shows a demo and the three-layer architecture behind it.

## Prediction was the right answer to an old question

Send-time optimization (STO) trains a model on past opens and clicks to predict, per person, the moment they are most likely to engage. Chakravarthy is fair to it: in the era of batch campaigns and weekly newsletters it gave marketers a real advantage, and plenty of marketing tech still works this way.

The world it was built for has changed. Inboxes and phones are a constant stream of notifications, brands compete with each other and with their own other campaigns, and engagement has flattened. His line for the gap: high probability does not equal high wisdom. If 10:30am is your best time, it is probably everyone's best time, and the model has no idea how many messages that person has already received or where they are in their journey.

## Best action, not best time

The reframing moves from when to send to what the best action is right now, where the options are send, postpone or cancel. The predicted time is still an input, "one voice at a very crowded table" in Chakravarthy's phrase, alongside journey stage, how many messages the customer has had that day or week, quiet hours, fatigue rules and business priorities. Marketers keep a choice in the loop.

The business argument is about the long game. Holding a message protects the audience from burnout, lowers churn from annoyed unsubscribes and builds trust by respecting people's time.

## The demo: five users, one agent

Murthy's half starts from the same gap in engineering terms: a model can output an engagement likelihood or a relevance score, and a perfect prediction can still lead to the wrong decision. His demo runs five email scenarios through the decision layer, which returns an action plus its reasoning. The framework is channel-agnostic; email just keeps the demo simple.

A fresh user with high engagement and low fatigue gets the flash sale. The same campaign to a user with high engagement but a fatigue score of 0.80 is deferred, the case a prediction-only system would have sent anyway. A low-urgency newsletter to a fresh user goes out, and a high-urgency product update is sent on the user's preferred channel. The last scenario returns to the fatigued user with a different campaign: the agent remembers the fatigue across campaigns and defers again. Across the run, 60% were sent and 40% deferred, which Murthy frames as optimising for relationships rather than volume.

## Three layers: predict, decide, protect

The architecture is an ML prediction layer of four models producing scores with confidence, an AI decisioning layer that reasons over those signals and constraints, and a state manager that tracks user history and enforces limits. Murthy's takeaways: ML outputs signals and AI makes the decision; the decisioning layer is a first-class system rather than a pile of business rules; and scale is a distributed systems problem, with state contention when several campaigns compete for the same user. He says it runs millions of decisions a day at under 100 milliseconds of latency.

## Who should watch

ML engineers working on engagement or notification systems, product managers for marketing platforms, and anyone who has watched an "optimised" campaign train its users to ignore it. The demo code is on GitHub, linked from the talk.

Title: Prompts are guidelines, not guardrails, so put the agent in a box
Description: Marat Kenzhebulatov of Booking.com on sandboxes, multi-model review councils and audit logs for AI agents in payment code, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
Marat Kenzhebulatov's AI agent was asked to update dependencies and run the tests. Thirty seconds later it had left the project folder and was rewriting his global Maven configuration. In this Conf42 Remix 2026 pick, [Marat](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Marat_Kenzhebulatov_vision_computer_imaging), a Software Engineer at Booking.com who builds and maintains payment systems, turns that near miss into a practical design: contain the agent, review its work with a council of models, and log everything.

In payments, he notes, breaking things means people don't get on flights and hotels don't get paid. So the talk is about building a system where an agent's mistakes don't matter much.

## Myth one: you can prompt an agent into being good

His first instinct was better rules, skills and prompts: follow SOLID, never hard-code secrets, respect PCI requirements. It doesn't hold. Prompt injection is always possible, models are non-deterministic, and they can hallucinate past every instruction. His summary is that prompts are guidelines, not guardrails. Relying on a prompt to stop a bad commit isn't a security strategy.

If you can't trust the brain, contain the body. His playground is a Docker container with a restricted file system, an allow-list of commands and websites, and a secrets manager the agent can use but whose credentials never land in its context. Treat the environment as hostile and the agent's intent stops mattering: malicious or merely over-eager, the action is denied. Where to draw the allow-list line is your call; too tight and the agent can't work, too loose and it can do damage.

## Myth two: AI will replace security review (or never could)

Some people think the agent can review its own code; others think only humans can. Marat thinks both are wrong and uses a council instead, an idea he credits to Andrej Karpathy. Several agents with different roles each run on a different model: a PCI expert working from PCI DSS, a code-quality reviewer explicitly prompted to be mean, and an arbiter that weighs their opinions. Using different models matters because a single model can reward-hack its way through a review without actually doing one. If they can't agree in time, each writes a report and a human decides.

The feature workflow wraps around that. A brainstorm phase where the agent asks questions until it understands the feature, a plan that splits the design into small tasks, sub-agents executing them one by one with a light single-agent review after each, then the full council at the end. Marat stays in the loop throughout; the agents amplify his input rather than replace it.

## Audit everything, because something will go wrong

Ten years in fintech taught him that something eventually breaks. You can't debug an agent like a normal program, so record the session and the chain of reasoning. If an agent tries to escape the playground, you want to know exactly what it tried.

## Myth three: this is too much to build

You don't start with councils. Start by having the agent describe your project in an `AGENTS.md` file, and review what it wrote. Then turn your team's routine tasks into skills for predictable results, and only then add councils and multi-agent setups. His checklist: no secrets in agent context, a physical playground rather than rules alone, a human approving critical actions (you can't blame the LLM for something you approved), and cross-validation across models.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers in regulated domains who want to use coding agents without explaining an incident to compliance, and security teams writing the first policy for agent use. It's concise and opinionated, with patterns you can adopt in a day.

Title: ISO 42001 for beginners: the 16 documents an auditor asks for
Description: Security engineer and ISO 42001 lead auditor Aleksandra Drobnjak lists the minimum docs for an audit-ready AI management system, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
Experimenting with LLMs is fun until someone asks who approved the change, what data was used and whether you can explain the result. At Conf42 Remix 2026, security engineer [Aleksandra Drobnjak](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Aleksandra_Drobnjak_documentation_artifacts_beginners), a trained ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 lead auditor, walks through her "Minimum Viable AIMS": the 16 documentation artifacts auditors expect before they will accept that an organisation manages its AI systems in a controlled, repeatable way.

The emphasis is on how the standard is implemented and audited in practice, not how it reads on paper. As she puts it, the goal is auditable clarity around risk, ownership, change and accountability, not perfect documentation.

## What ISO 42001 is, briefly

ISO/IEC 42001, published in 2023, is a voluntary, certifiable standard and the first aimed at managing AI at the organisational level. It doesn't prescribe models or tools. Clauses 4 to 10 hold the auditable requirements, and Annex A lists 38 controls across nine objectives, chosen according to your risk profile rather than all mandatory. It follows the plan-do-check-act cycle, so it fits next to ISO 27001.

Aleksandra also places it among neighbours: ISO 22989 for AI terminology and roles (relevant even if you only consume AI), ISO 42005 for impact assessments, the NIST AI RMF as non-certifiable guidance, and the EU AI Act as binding law. Certification runs as a stage one documentation audit, a stage two effectiveness audit and annual surveillance over a three-year cycle. She doesn't show the standard itself for copyright reasons, which tells you something about how carefully she works.

## Why engineers should care

Her motivation is shadow AI. Well-meaning people paste company data into personal AI accounts whose defaults may allow training on that content, and lab environments running Jupyter, Kubeflow or MLflow end up reachable from production. Most of those problems are ordinary infrastructure mistakes applied to powerful systems, not sophisticated attacks. The scope and policy documents give engineers something they often lack: the mandate to say these tools are approved, these defaults are forbidden, these models need extra sign-off.

There is a business angle too. She points to AWS services such as Amazon Bedrock, Textract, Transcribe and Q Business operating under ISO 42001 certified units, and invites viewers to verify a certificate themselves through AWS Artifact and the IAF search.

## Sixteen artifacts, clause by clause

The core of the talk walks the list using the acronym for clauses 4 to 10: context, leadership, planning, support, operations, performance evaluation, improvement. Some highlights:

- **AIMS scope (4.3):** which AI systems are governed, which aren't, who is responsible. A notebook that quietly becomes part of a production workflow is exactly the gap this closes.
- **AI policy:** approved by leadership; it stops every team inventing its own workflow.
- **Risk planning, assessment and treatment (6.1.x):** each risk gets an owner, a decision and a next step, assessed with a repeatable method before models are promoted. Model artifacts behave like executable components, not just data.
- **Statement of applicability:** her example control on societal impact covers environmental footprint, economic effects, recourse, wellbeing and fairness.
- **Objectives, competence and documented information:** measurable targets, role-appropriate training records, and permission to document what lives in Slack DMs and someone's head.
- **Operations, risk register, treatment plans and impact assessment (clause 8).**
- **Monitoring results, internal audit and management review (clause 9),** then **nonconformities and corrective actions (10.2),** where minor versus major findings can delay or suspend certification.

## Who should watch

MLOps and security engineers who have been told the company is going for ISO 42001 and want to know what will actually be asked of them, and anyone building an AI policy from scratch. It's long and dense; keep the slides open and treat it as a reference. Her closing point is that most AI failures are governance failures, and that certification costs time and budget, so prioritise by risk instead of boiling the ocean.

Title: Reliability starts at what changed, not at the alert
Description: Spiros Economakis, founder of NOFire AI, on why AI should give production a memory of change so SREs act before customers feel it, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
Every incident investigation starts from zero because context doesn't survive change. That is the problem [Spiros Economakis](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Spiros_Economakis_sre_experience_ai), Founder and CEO of NOFire AI, puts at the centre of his Conf42 Remix 2026 talk, and his answer is to stop asking "what broke?" and start asking what changed and what that change affected

Spiros has spent over a decade running production and being the person people DM at 3am. He is clear that this isn't a talk about replacing SREs, and also clear, with some self-awareness, that the slides will probably look different in a year.

## Systems now change faster than people can model them

His diagnosis is that reliability got harder because systems change faster than humans can build a stable mental model, and AI-generated code has sped that up. His map of production has services, infrastructure, telemetry and knowledge at the bottom, workflows like releases, incidents, security and cost on top, and teams each owning a slice. Nobody sees all of it. Every incident cuts across those boundaries and each handoff loses context.

The customer side follows directly. Incidents take hours, customers report problems before monitoring does, and a few engineers carry the full mental model until they burn out or leave. What customers feel, as he puts it, is the external result of internal confusion.

## Three traps teams fall into

Spiros names the fixes most teams have already tried. The visibility trap: more dashboards and alerts, which add mental load without structure. The correlation trap: smarter-looking pattern detection that helps you react but doesn't explain why this incident happened this time. The tooling trap: a new tool per problem, now including AI tools, each solving a slice while adding handoffs and ownership gaps. The result is a system that is operable but not understandable.

## Give production a memory

The shift he describes is from raw signals to meaning, and from reconstructing understanding after the fact to having it in the moment. If you continuously track what changed (code, config, dependencies, infrastructure, traffic), where it landed and how behaviour shifted, every incident adds knowledge instead of wiping the slate clean.

That moves reliability earlier. Analysis runs on every pull request, using how the service normally behaves, how often it changes and what tends to go wrong after similar changes. Engineers don't have to remember everything; the system brings the context to them, in the IDE as well as in the incident channel. Spiros calls the loop of change, incident and outcome feeding back into understanding a context graph.

What's new compared to past attempts, in his account, is that systems can now track change over time rather than snapshots, link changes to outcomes as cause and effect rather than co-movement, and keep learning across incidents, architecture docs and chat. No reset button after the postmortem.

## The customer is the point

The payoff he lists is fewer surprises because risky changes get caught earlier, faster recovery because engineers act with full context, and more predictable releases. Customer experience improves as a direct result. For engineers, the job shifts from whack-a-mole with alerts to deciding when to ship, when to wait and how to manage risk before users feel it. His closing line: reliability doesn't live in alerts, it lives in understanding how production changes over time.

## Who should watch

SRE leads and engineering managers who feel their team is always reconstructing context from scratch, and anyone evaluating AI SRE tools who wants a framework for what "context" should mean. NOFire AI is Spiros's company, but the talk stays at the level of ideas rather than a product demo.

Title: Your infrastructure is a graph, so give the LLM the graph
Description: Roxane Fischer, co-founder of Anyshift, on why LLMs fail at infrastructure work without live context and how a knowledge graph fixes it, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
Ask an LLM to write a Terraform VPC peering connection and it will produce tidy, plausible code that references a VPC that doesn't exist. At Conf42 Remix 2026, [Roxane Fischer](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Roxane_Fischer_context_reasoning_infrastructure), co-founder of Anyshift, explains why: the model lacks the live context of your infrastructure, and the most useful shape for that context is a knowledge graph.

Anyshift builds AI on-call engineers, and Roxane says up front that she is not pitching the product layer. The talk is about the graph underneath it, and it's useful whether you build your own or not.

## The VPC peering test

Her example is deliberately small. A junior developer copies IDs from the AWS console and hard-codes them into the peering resource, which works today and breaks dependencies as the estate grows. GitHub Copilot does better on style: it knows hard-coded values are bad practice and uses references. But it doesn't know where your VPC is defined, often in another repository, so it creates a brand-new one. Complete as code, she points out, and completely unrealistic.

An AI IDE that reads multiple repositories gets closer. It can reference the remote state of the repo that owns your VPC. But it still fails on the junior developer's hard-coded ID, because that string points at a cloud resource, not at any code. Reconciling cloud data with code is exactly the context the tool doesn't have.

## Infrastructure already is a graph

A graph database stores entities as nodes and relationships as edges, which maps directly onto infrastructure: an IAM role attached to an EC2 instance, the instance inside a VPC, pods, containers, accounts and providers linked by typed connections. Add metadata (where each resource is defined in code, who owns it, who last committed to it, the timeline of changes) and you can ask questions like which instances or pods have had high CPU over the last 24 hours and what depends on them.

Roxane notes that real graphs at Anyshift reach tens of millions of nodes once versioning is included, which is why this is harder than it looks on a slide.

## Building it: database, ontology, ingestion

The recipe has three steps. Pick a graph database (Anyshift uses Neo4j; Amazon Neptune is another option). Define an ontology, which is the hard intellectual part: a common model of nodes and edges that lets AWS, GCP and Azure resources be treated as equivalent even when their definitions differ. Then populate and update it per integration, for example scanning AWS APIs and using CloudTrail to keep the graph fresh. Clean, structured data is where most of the effort goes, and it is ongoing maintenance.

Her worked example maps AWS resources to Terraform state to Terraform code, matching IDs across all three. Once those links exist, drift and shadow IT fall out of the graph: anything in the cloud without a state entry or code definition is a finding.

## When MCP is enough, and when it isn't

The cheaper alternative is MCP servers: connect your LLM to cloud providers' MCP endpoints with your credentials and let it query live. Roxane thinks that is a good option for startups and smaller estates. The limit is that each call is an API request returning a bounded amount of data. If you need every dependency, relationship and bit of history in one question, you need the pre-built cache that the graph provides.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers trying AI on infrastructure code and getting confident nonsense back, and anyone deciding between "just add MCP" and building a resource graph. It's a 15-minute talk (the live demo was cut for time), so expect concepts and architecture rather than code.

Title: Put an AI gateway in front of your LLM bill
Description: Michael Levan of Solo.io routes agent and MCP traffic through Agent Gateway on Kubernetes and charts token costs per gateway in Grafana, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
If every agent in your cluster calls an LLM directly, the first time you learn what it costs is the invoice. In a demo chosen for Conf42 Remix 2026, [Michael Levan](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Michael_Levan_agents_telemetry_costs), AI Architect and Solutions Engineer at Solo.io, routes LLM traffic through Agent Gateway on Kubernetes and builds a Grafana dashboard that shows cost, token usage and model per gateway.

This is a terminal-first walkthrough, short and practical. There are no slides about the future of agents; there is `kubectl`, `curl` and a dashboard at the end.

## One choke point for agent, model and MCP traffic

Michael's framing covers three kinds of traffic: agent to LLM, agent to MCP server and agent to agent. Put a gateway in the path of all of it and you get one place to route, observe and eventually control spend. He uses Anthropic because that is where he has a subscription, and notes that any provider works.

The setup is plain Kubernetes Gateway API. A secret holds the Anthropic API key. A `Gateway` object uses the agent gateway class and, for the demo, accepts routes from all namespaces. A backend resource tells the gateway what to route to (a Claude model here, though it could be an MCP server). An `HTTPRoute` ties the gateway to the backend and rewrites the OpenAI-style `/v1/chat/completions` path to a shorter `/anthropic`, which works because Claude accepts the OpenAI API format.

He creates three identical gateways. The number doesn't matter; three just makes a per-gateway cost breakdown worth looking at.

## Generate traffic, then scrape it

With the load balancer IPs exported into environment variables, a `curl` to each gateway confirms it works and produces metrics. Then comes kube-prometheus, which Michael prefers over a bare Prometheus and Grafana install because it ships Kubernetes dashboards out of the box. Port-forward both, pull the Grafana admin secret, log in.

The glue is a `PodMonitor` per gateway, scraping `/metrics` every 30 seconds. There's a small, honest moment where he has to fix the namespace because the project moved from one system namespace to another, the kind of thing that only shows up in a live demo.

## The dashboard is the deliverable

After another round of traffic, he imports a custom dashboard from his GitHub and the costs appear, per gateway and in total. "Luckily I haven't spent too much money," he notes. The same data is in Prometheus directly: search for the gateway's metrics and you can break token usage down by gateway, model and origin of the request.

That last view is what makes the setup useful beyond the demo. Once requests carry that metadata, cost attribution stops being a monthly spreadsheet exercise and becomes a query. The abstract promises cost control as well as observability; the demo covers the observing half, leaving budgets and limits as the obvious next step.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who have been asked who is spending the LLM budget, and Kubernetes teams already using Gateway API who want to see how an AI gateway fits the same model. If you want a conceptual talk on agent architecture, this isn't it; it's a recipe you can follow along with.

Title: When the device pays: microservices for IoT payment systems
Description: Silpa Potluri of GoodLeap explains how payment platforms split into microservices to handle machine-initiated micro-transactions, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
Payment systems were built for a human tapping a card a few times a day, and IoT devices tap thousands of times without asking anyone. At Conf42 Remix 2026, [Silpa Potluri](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Silpa_Potluri_payments_microservices_architecture), Software Developer at GoodLeap with more than 20 years in software and over a decade in payments, explains why that breaks monolithic payment platforms and how a microservices design handles devices that pay on their own.

It is a short, structured architecture talk. No code, but a clean map of the services a machine-to-machine payment flow needs and the order they run in.

## The assumptions IoT breaks

Smart meters reporting usage, vehicles paying tolls, appliances reordering supplies: in each case the device decides and triggers the transaction. Traditional systems assumed human interaction, infrequent transactions and relatively large amounts. IoT reverses all three.

Silpa names three monolith problems. Vertical scaling doesn't cope when thousands of devices come online at once. Waiting weeks to deploy a security fix is unacceptable when hardware is already in the field. And older stacks struggle to adopt modern cryptography or machine learning. Add the operational risk of one failure cascading across the platform, and a single database trying to absorb telemetry, micro-transactions, fraud signals and settlement records at the same time.

## One capability per service

The fix follows four familiar principles: single responsibility, independent deployment, technology flexibility and fault isolation. Her example of the last is a good one to keep: a failure in analytics shouldn't stop payments from going through.

The flow then runs service by service. Device authentication relies on cryptographic credentials embedded at manufacturing, secure elements for tamper resistance and full lifecycle management, including ownership changes and decommissioning, so credentials can be rotated without touching the device. Authorization has to finish in milliseconds: checking balances, subscriptions and usage limits, scoring risk, validating location to catch impossible scenarios, and enforcing idempotency so a flaky connection doesn't charge twice.

## Aggregate the tiny payments

The detail that makes IoT payments their own problem is size. Many transactions are fractions of a cent, so processing each one individually doesn't make sense. A smart meter's thousands of daily usage records are accumulated and settled as one payment on a threshold or schedule, while the detailed records are kept for transparency.

Settlement is the most regulated piece, needing strong consistency, multi-stage flows, continuous reconciliation and banking network integration. Machine learning fraud detection runs alongside it, watching device behaviour for coordinated attacks without slowing normal traffic.

## Events in the middle, a gateway at the edge

Services talk through events rather than direct calls: a device authenticates, an event is published, and fraud detection, analytics and notifications each consume it. Kafka is the example platform. At the front, an API gateway translates the many protocols devices speak (MQTT, CoAP, HTTP and automotive protocols), enforces security, rate-limits and routes, shielding the backend from spikes and malformed requests.

Her smart city scenario ties it together: parking meters, vehicles and charging stations generating payments automatically, with revenue split across agencies that each have their own rules. Running it takes distributed tracing, metrics and intelligent alerting, plus layered security: secrets management, service authentication, tokenisation and network segmentation.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving a payment monolith toward services, and IoT teams about to add billing to a device fleet who haven't thought about micro-transaction aggregation or idempotency yet. If you already run event-driven payments, the value is the IoT-specific concerns: device identity lifecycle and sub-cent batching.

Title: IoT data platforms fail on cost, not collection
Description: Bhanudeepti Chinta of Dave on lakehouse table formats, medallion layers and feature stores that keep IoT telemetry costs in line, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
Collecting sensor data is the easy part; paying for it is where IoT platforms get into trouble. In a talk selected for Conf42 Remix 2026, [Bhanudeepti Chinta](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Bhanudeepti_Chinta_lakehouse_analytics_scalable), Engineering Manager for Data at Dave with 14 years of building large data platforms, argues that the cost and complexity of IoT data tend to grow faster than the value teams extract, and that lakehouse architecture is first a cost containment strategy.

The session is a compact architecture overview rather than a hands-on build. Its value is in the ordering of decisions: which choices quietly pile up storage and compute bills, and which ones keep them proportional to what the business actually uses.

## Why IoT data breaks traditional architectures

Bhanudeepti lists the traits that make telemetry different. Sensors stream continuously, often at millisecond intervals, so volumes reach petabyte scale within months. The schema never sits still: firmware updates add fields and different vendors send, in her words, "consistently inconsistent telemetry formats." And the same data has three very different audiences. Operations wants real-time dashboards, data scientists want history for modelling, and business users want aggregates.

Classic warehouses give performance and consistency but get expensive and rigid with semi-structured data. Plain data lakes are cheap but lack reliability, governance and transactions. The lakehouse sits between them: warehouse-grade guarantees on top of low-cost object storage.

## Separate storage, table format and compute

The core technologies are Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi, which add transactional semantics, schema evolution and efficient metadata to cloud storage. Without them, she says, IoT platforms accumulate hidden operational and storage costs over time.

The physical design splits three layers. Object storage holds the data with effectively unlimited capacity, the table format manages metadata and transactions, and engines like Spark or Trino scale independently. That separation lets you pay for compute only when you run it, instead of keeping fixed infrastructure warm for workloads that come in bursts.

## Most cost overruns are design decisions

Streaming sits at the centre, with Kafka, Kinesis or Event Hubs feeding Spark or Flink. The decisions that decide the bill are mundane: partition by time to match how telemetry is queried, manage hot, warm and cold tiers deliberately, and absorb schema changes without rewriting history. Bhanudeepti's view is that many IoT cost overruns trace back to getting these wrong.

The medallion pattern gives the structure. Bronze keeps raw readings exactly as received for audit and replay, silver validates and normalises, gold serves business-ready datasets for dashboards. Expensive compute only runs where there is business value. Rather than separate batch and streaming stacks, she points to a Kappa-style approach: one streaming pipeline, with incremental processing and materialised views covering both.

Machine learning is where costs creep in quietly, because feature engineering gets duplicated across teams. Snowflake feature stores are her answer: reusable, governed features that stay consistent between training and inference.

## Four places it pays off

The case studies are brief: predictive maintenance in manufacturing, route optimisation and vehicle health in connected fleets, traffic and environmental monitoring in smart cities, and smart meter analytics for utilities, including energy theft detection and peak demand forecasting. Looking ahead she expects lower-latency streaming, better time series performance, stronger governance and more edge analytics to cut bandwidth. Her closing line sums up the talk: success comes from systems that align cost with value.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects designing or inheriting an IoT pipeline, and engineering managers who need a vocabulary for why the telemetry bill keeps growing. If you already run Iceberg with a medallion layout in production, treat it as a checklist rather than new material.

Title: Teaching observability to an 8-year-old with a thirsty houseplant
Description: Marie Cruz of Grafana Labs wires a soil moisture sensor to an ESP32, Prometheus and Grafana Cloud alerts with her daughter, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
The best explanation of monitoring versus observability you will hear this year involves a houseplant and a curious eight-year-old. In this Conf42 Remix 2026 pick, [Marie Cruz](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Marie_Cruz_sensors_gardening_analytics), Senior Developer Advocate at Grafana Labs, walks through the weekend project she built with her daughter: a soil moisture sensor on an ESP32 board, readings shipped to Prometheus, a Grafana Cloud dashboard, and a Telegram alert when the plant gets thirsty.

Marie set herself a goal for the year of no plant casualties, and used it as an excuse to teach STEM at home. The result is a beginner-level IoT build and a lesson in explaining technical ideas without jargon.

## Monitoring answers yes or no, observability answers why

The conceptual half of the talk is the gardening analogy, and it works on adults too. Monitoring is checking whether the soil is dry and watering it if so: reactive, a yes-or-no check. If the plant still looks unwell after watering, monitoring has nothing more to say.

Observability is looking at all the signals over time to understand why the plant's health changes. Does moisture drop at a certain time of day? Should room temperature and humidity be part of the picture? Is one of the dogs doing something it shouldn't? Without signals you are guessing on hunches; with them, Marie says, the black box becomes a clear box and you act before the plant suffers. Swap "plant" for "checkout service" and you have the talk most SREs give their managers.

## The hardware is cheap and the wiring is three pins

The build list is short: a soil moisture sensor, an ESP32-S3 dev kit, a breadboard, jumper wires and a USB-C cable, plus the Arduino IDE and a Grafana Cloud account on the free plan. The sensor's two metal prongs conduct better when the soil is wet, so its analog output is a number that goes up as the soil dries.

Wiring is VCC to 3.3V, ground to ground and analog out to pin 11. Marie explains each one to her daughter as parts of a battery, and explains baud rate as friends agreeing to speak at the same speed. The first program just reads the pin every five seconds and prints "dry" above 500 and "wet" below it to the serial monitor.

## From serial logs to a dashboard with alerts

Nobody watches a serial monitor all day, so the next step sends readings to the managed Prometheus that comes with Grafana Cloud. Prometheus becomes the gardener who writes every reading into a time series toolbox, and PromQL is how you ask it questions. The Arduino side needs a few libraries (Protobuf, Snappy, Loki transport and the Prometheus Arduino client), a config file with the instance URL, username, API token and Wi-Fi details, and a certificates file. Marie copied the example from the Prometheus Arduino project and adapted it; when her daughter asked whether that was cheating, she got a lesson in how programming actually works.

The dashboard uses a text panel with a picture of the plant, a stat panel for health, a gauge with the 500 threshold, and a time series. Value mappings turn green to red when the soil dries out, which made the dashboard readable for an eight-year-old. A Grafana alert rule on the same query fires to a Telegram contact point. As a last flourish Marie asks Grafana Assistant, the AI agent built into Grafana Cloud, to polish the dashboard's look.

## Who should watch

Parents and mentors looking for a first IoT project with real tooling; anyone new to Prometheus and Grafana who wants the whole metrics-to-alert path in one sitting; and engineers who need better analogies for explaining observability to non-engineers. If you run Prometheus at scale, the technical parts will be familiar, but the explanations are worth borrowing.
