Title: Decision latency is the new bottleneck in LLM delivery
Description: Senior engineering manager Lakshmi Priya Gopalsamy at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on SLOs for human approvals, policy as code and golden paths for LLM teams.
Body:
LLMs made writing code, tests and docs take minutes, but the approvals around them still take days. Lakshmi Priya Gopalsamy, a senior engineering manager with over 20 years of building large distributed systems, argued at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026 that the bottleneck in enterprise AI has moved from the machine to the human, and that decision latency and cognitive load deserve the same treatment as throughput and error rate.

Her reframing of the classic SRE question: "What happens when system succeeds faster than human can govern it?"

## The checkpoints never got the memo

Every AI output that touches production still crosses human gates: model approvals, prompt reviews, data governance, security and safety checks, incident response. Gopalsamy's opening scenario will be familiar: the model is ready, testing looks great, and the launch stalls because nobody knows who signs off.

She defines two properties. Decision latency is the time between an AI output being ready and a human making a call on it. Cognitive load is the stack of choices engineers juggle at once: model and provider selection, evaluation frameworks, hallucination mitigation, prompt versioning, prompt injection, data leakage and audit trails. Each is manageable alone. All at once, at LLM speed, they lead to burnout, and burnt-out engineers build fragile systems.

## Put SLOs on human loops

The useful move is borrowing SRE vocabulary for people. Do you know the p95 for a model approval? Is there a runbook when a safety validation fails, or does it go to a Slack channel and hope? Manual AI governance is toil in the strict sense, because it grows linearly with every new model, prompt and use case. Your team's capacity for manual governance decisions per sprint works like an error budget.

## Three tiers instead of one queue

The first pattern replaces the default of sending everything to a human review queue with three tiers borrowed from access control:

- **Pre-authorized** for low-stakes, reversible changes such as well-tested prompt templates or internal tooling suggestions. No human gate.
- **Async review** for medium-stakes changes such as new prompt patterns within an approved model family, reviewed within a clear SLO (she suggests something like four hours).
- **Explicit approval** for high-risk, irreversible moves: new model families, data classification changes, public APIs with regulatory exposure.

She compares it to a circuit breaker: the response to overload is built in, not remembered from a meeting two years ago.

## Owners, not committees

AI initiatives often launch with a cross-functional committee and no team owning production reliability, so incidents go to everyone, meaning nobody. Her fix is plain engineering management: one team owns each production LLM, carries the pager and the SLO, and has the authority to decide. For every model in production you should be able to say who owns it, what the SLO is, who gets paged and how architecture decisions are made.

## Governance you can unit test

The pattern she knows best comes from building a generative AI support system for a data platform with thousands of internal users and over a hundred thousand Spark jobs a day. Any governance decision that could be a rule lived in the pipeline, not in Slack. Prompt boundary checks, data classification and output safety thresholds ran in milliseconds and wrote an audit log with model version, timestamp and policy version.

"You cannot unit test a Slack approval, but you can absolutely unit test a policy engine." When an auditor asks how a decision was made, you point at a versioned policy and a log.

## Golden paths, including model choice

The last pattern is the opinionated golden path: an approved model catalog with version pinning, a standard evaluation framework, prompt templates with safety checks and observability hooks built in. Adoption is maths, not culture, because the paved road is faster. She singles out model selection: pick by task profile, risk profile and operational constraints, not by public benchmark score, and treat every model version bump as a governance event rather than a routine dependency upgrade.

Her homework for next week: map and time your decision loops, name an owning team for every production LLM, automate one governance decision this sprint, and write a one-page golden path.

## Who should watch

Title: The Kubernetes platform decides how reliable your LLM service is
Description: Sergey Speranskiy at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on BGP anycast control planes, routable pod networks, GPU scheduling and canary rollouts for LLM workloads.
Body:
An LLM service is only as reliable as the cluster under it. Sergey Speranskiy, a senior infrastructure platform engineer, made that case at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026 in a compact talk on what breaks first when LLM workloads move from one experimental node to production Kubernetes, especially on-prem.

His closing line sums it up: "The model is important, but the platform decides how the model behaves under failure."

## LLM workloads expose weak platforms faster

A typical web service is CPU-bound, has short requests and scales by adding replicas. LLM services need scarce GPUs and lots of memory, run long requests, and have latency that depends on model size, prompt length, generated tokens, batching and queue time. So bad scheduling, flaky networking or an unexpected restart turns into a user-visible problem quickly.

The experiment phase hides all this. One node, manual deploys and SSH debugging are fine until production asks for redundancy across failure domains. Losing one node, switch or rack can take a big share of your GPU capacity with it.

## Anycast the API server, run BGP on the host

The control plane is not on the request path, but scheduling, rollouts and autoscaling all depend on it. Speranskiy's preferred design gives the Kubernetes API a virtual IP announced by BGP anycast from every healthy control plane node. Each node checks its local API server and withdraws the route if it is unhealthy, so failover happens at the network level. etcd members go in separate physical failure domains to keep quorum.

He runs BGP routing (BIRD) on the host rather than in a pod, for a reason that is obvious once said: Kubernetes needs networking to start pods, so basic networking must not depend on pods.

## Make the packet path boring

Default overlay and NAT designs work, but during an incident you end up staring at translated addresses instead of real pod-to-pod flows. In his routable design, each node peers with two top-of-rack switches over BGP and advertises its pod CIDR into the data center fabric. No overlay, no NAT, and iproute, traceroute and tcpdump show what actually happens.

ECMP uses both uplinks at once, so redundancy also means active-active capacity, and BFD pulls a failed path quickly instead of waiting on long BGP timers.

## Treat GPUs as explicit, scheduled capacity

GPU nodes need the right NVIDIA driver, container runtime integration, device plugin, labels, monitoring and a safe upgrade process; many teams use the NVIDIA GPU operator for this. Kubernetes never assigns a GPU on its own: the device plugin exposes it and the pod has to request it.

From there it is scheduling discipline. Requests declare CPU, memory and GPU. Node selectors or affinity target the GPU pool. Anti-affinity and topology spread keep replicas out of a single failure domain. Taints and tolerations stop ordinary workloads from squatting on expensive GPU servers. Deployments suit simple serving, while training, fine-tuning and batch work fit jobs or queues with controlled concurrency.

## Roll out by traffic weight

A new model version, prompt template, runtime image or config can change latency, cost and error rate. Gateway API HTTPRoutes let you split traffic, for example 90 percent stable and 10 percent new, then shift it forward if metrics hold or back if they do not.

Observability has to cover more than application errors: GPU utilization and memory, scheduling problems, network behaviour, API server latency and etcd health.

## Who should watch

Platform and infrastructure engineers running or about to run model serving on their own Kubernetes, particularly on-prem or in tightly controlled environments. It is short and dense; cloud-managed-cluster users can skip the BGP section but should keep the scheduling checklist.

Title: Azure API Management as a leash for your AI endpoints
Description: Leo Visser of OGD at Conf42 LLMs 2026 demos token limits, content safety blocklists and semantic caching in Azure API Management in front of Foundry.
Body:
The cheapest LLM call is the one that never reaches the model. Leo Visser, a consultant at OGD ICT-diensten in the Netherlands and an Azure and PowerShell MVP, showed at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026 how putting Azure API Management in front of Azure AI Foundry gives you three practical controls: token-aware rate limits, content safety blocklists and semantic caching. It is a Microsoft-stack demo from start to finish, and a very hands-on one.

## A nature reserve that wanted less AI

The case behind the talk is unusual. A client, lightly disguised as a nature reserve management group, wanted an AI chatbot for staff and systems but also wanted to use it sparingly. They depend on donations, and supporters ask awkward questions about the energy and water that AI uses. They also wanted certain politically sensitive topics kept out of the chatbot entirely.

So the brief was a sustainable, restricted AI: useful, but on a leash. Visser says it was the first time a client asked him to limit topics, and that it made sense once he thought about it.

## The gateway in the middle

API Management, now also marketed as the AI gateway, sits between the application and the Foundry deployments. Visser walks through importing a Foundry endpoint as an API (there are dedicated options for Foundry, language model APIs and the newer A2A API), wiring the backend, and testing a gpt-5-mini chat completion from the portal. A small Power App drives the demos.

One detail worth noting from the demo: with gpt-5-mini he had to remove the max tokens parameter from the test body because that model does not support it.

## Limit tokens per consumer

The first control is the LLM token limit policy. Policies are XML, and in the demo he sets 60 tokens per minute, with optional quotas per hour, day, week, month or year, scoped per subscription key or IP address. Subscription keys are the useful unit: give each app, process or monitored area its own key and its own budget.

The demo also shows a gotcha. Three parallel requests all went through before the first response came back, because the gateway only knows the token count after the model answers. The fourth call was the one that got the limit-exceeded response.

## Block topics before the model sees them

The second control is AI content safety. You create an Azure Content Safety resource, then build a blocklist through its API, since the portal offers little to configure. Visser loops over a CSV of terms (for the demo, Azure service names such as App Service and Azure Functions), creates the list and adds each item. In API Management the content safety policy references the list by name.

The payoff is where the block happens. Asking about a blocked topic fails in the gateway, so the request never reaches the model, never burns reasoning tokens and never spends the energy. A system prompt telling the model to avoid a topic still runs the whole LLM.

## Cache answers that do not change

The third control is semantic caching. Before a prompt goes to the completion model, API Management embeds it with a small embedding model (text-embedding-ada-002 in the demo) and looks for a close enough vector in a Redis cache. A hit returns the stored answer; a miss calls the model and stores the result.

The settings are a similarity threshold and a cache duration, both tuned by trial and error. Static archives tolerate long durations; agents with RAG, tools or MCP servers need shorter ones. In the demo, the uncached version produces three slightly different answers slowly, while the cached version produces one slow answer and two instant, identical ones.

The setup notes are the kind you only get from someone who hit them: Azure Managed Redis needs the enterprise tier with RediSearch enabled, the connection string sometimes shows up without a port, only access keys work for the connection, and the AI gateway features need the Basic v2 tier. A confusing "role assignment already exists" error usually means the wrong tier.

## Who should watch

Azure teams putting Foundry models into production who need cost and content controls without writing them into every app, and platform teams that want one central gateway for many teams' models and MCP servers. If you are on another cloud, the patterns travel even if the clicks do not.

Title: Performance signatures that gate every LLM and RAG commit
Description: Kandasamy Selvaraj of ADP at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on statistical CI/CD gates that catch LLM latency, token and tool-call regressions before production.
Body:
Most LLM teams write the prompt, commit, build and run inference, then find out about the latency regression from users. Kandasamy Selvaraj, Principal Architect who leads performance engineering at ADP, argued at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026 that the missing step is a gate: a statistical performance signature evaluated on every commit, with a verdict back to the developer in about 15 to 20 minutes.

## Why LLM performance bugs hide

Selvaraj lists what makes these defects different. Latency varies with every model update, so you cannot tell whether time to first token got worse because of your code or your provider. RAG pipeline failures show up first in production. Token throughput and time to first token need different instrumentation from ordinary API metrics. Agents are probabilistic, so failures cascade silently along a chain. And developers get no feedback when they commit.

He cites research suggesting that agent failures in complex workflows mostly come from orchestration and tool-call sequencing rather than the model itself, which is exactly where his framework looks.

## Normal beats acceptable

The core idea is a deviation score: the observed metric minus the learned baseline, divided by the baseline's standard deviation. A static threshold tells you whether a number is acceptable. The deviation score tells you whether it is normal for this system. A 50 ms jump in p90 with a 20 ms standard deviation gets flagged at the two-sigma gate because it is 2.5 deviations out, even though 50 ms sounds harmless.

The baseline is not fixed. It is recalibrated as models, prompts and data change across commits, so the gate keeps up with the system it guards.

## Five dimensions, all must pass

For agents, time to first token is not enough. The signature tracks five dimensions:

- total trace latency across every LLM call and tool invocation
- per-tool response time, each tool with its own baseline
- LLM calls per trace, which catches looping and context loss (with a baseline of two calls, three is flagged and four is blocked)
- tokens per trace, where small changes compound: 200 extra output tokens per call, three calls per trace and 60,000 requests an hour adds up to 36 million extra tokens an hour
- tool error and retry rate, because a silent retry still costs latency and tokens

In his worked trace, the LLM calls pass but a code-executor tool lands 4.3 sigma out and the whole build is blocked. "One slow tool blocks the entire build."

## Tag every request with its build

The integration trick that makes root cause automatic is simple: inject build ID, commit ID, model version and prompt hash into every LLM request. Tools such as Langfuse, LangSmith or Arize can then tie a slow trace to the exact prompt change that caused it. The reference stack in the talk uses JMeter-style load generation, Jenkins for orchestration, Prometheus and Grafana for visibility, LangChain behind an AI gateway, and PostgreSQL and Redis on Kubernetes.

The demo shows a `/perf gate` chatbot running the same checks: one commit passes at 218 tokens per request against a 500 limit, then with the limit dropped to 100 the same pipeline blocks the build and explains why.

## Results and the honest caveats

Over an eight-week rollout he reports 30 to 40 percent fewer production performance issues per month, around 200 percent more defects found in development, mean time to detect down from most of a day to under an hour, and automated root cause for 91 percent of failures. The lessons are useful too: LLM non-determinism needs a wider sigma band than deterministic services, the gate needs 10 to 20 runs of baseline before it is trustworthy, and every team still needed a two-to-three-hour onboarding session.

He is explicit that the commit gate is an add-on to full-scale load and soak testing, not a replacement. The pipeline catches the change; the big test validates the system.

## Who should watch

Performance engineers, platform teams owning CI/CD for AI services, and anyone whose token bill has surprised the finance team. If you already run load tests and want them to say something useful per commit, this is the playbook.

Title: LLM moderation works as a system, not as one big model
Description: Andrei Shcherbinin of Social Discovery Group at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on rules, small classifiers, LLM judges and human reviewers in dating-app moderation.
Body:
Once scammers can generate a hundred polite variations of the same pitch, keyword filters stop being enough. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2026, Andrei Shcherbinin, who leads machine learning work at Social Discovery Group, walked through the production auto-moderation system his team built for user-to-user messaging on dating platforms. His thesis: LLM-powered moderation works when it is designed as a system of rules, lightweight models, LLMs and humans, each handling the risk it is best at.

## Dating raises the stakes

In dating products, safety is the product. Users share private and emotionally vulnerable content, romance fraud and payment manipulation are constant, and the hardest violations (grooming-like behaviour, coded language, attempts to move the chat off-platform) look harmless in any single message. Ten messages in a row can show a pattern that one message never does.

He also notes how LLMs changed the abuse itself. Old spam repeated itself. LLM-assisted abuse is fluent, varied and paraphrased, and on agentic platforms the risk extends to actions, not just text.

## Accuracy is the wrong scoreboard

With violations around one percent of traffic, a model that labels everything normal scores 99 percent accuracy and catches nothing. Shcherbinin's goal is controlled risk instead: category-specific thresholds, severity-aware evaluation, precision at low recall, recall on high-severity classes and false positive rates per category. Missing mild toxicity and missing a scam are different failures with different costs.

Policy is part of the model specification. Severity maps to a risk score, confidence to a threshold, context to features or prompt information, and reviewer decisions become corrected labels. If a label like suspicious off-platform behaviour is vague in the policy, the model will be vague too.

## Deduplicate or you train a template detector

The data section is the most practical part. Without deduplication, thousands of near-identical "help me with my phone bill" messages teach the model the template instead of the intent. It looks brilliant offline and fails the moment wording changes. "You have built a very expensive template historian," as he puts it.

His pipeline uses exact, normalized and near-duplicate deduplication, and treats it as evaluation hygiene that also cuts train-test leakage. For rare classes, progress is measured in positives found, not rows processed: sample a batch, skip anything already scored via a hash journal, pull few-shot examples from a human golden set, and let an LLM label each message as clear normal, clear violation or borderline.

The LLM is a pre-annotator, never the authority. It suggests a label, a reason and the supporting fragment; a human accepts or rejects; only validated labels enter the golden set. He likens the LLM to a very confident intern: fast, often right, and not the one who writes company policy.

## Each layer gets the risk it is good at

The production stack has four layers. Rules and keywords handle links, obfuscation and deterministic checks. Lightweight BERT-style classifiers handle high-volume categories cheaply. LLM judges take the grey zones where context and reasoning matter. Humans stay the policy authority for edge cases, appeals and high-severity categories. He expects more work to move to specialised LLM layers as they get cheaper, so the hybrid stack doubles as a migration path.

A score is not a decision. The same 0.82 can mean low-priority review for spam and immediate escalation for grooming-like behaviour, depending on severity, user risk and how full the reviewer queue is. "Prediction is machine learning. Decisioning is product engineering." Thresholds get recalibrated whenever policy, abuse mix, model or reviewer capacity changes.

## Honest about the headline numbers

The system handles millions of messages a day, with reviewer load down 60 percent and over 90 percent of violations caught. Shcherbinin spends a slide warning that such numbers mean nothing without the methodology behind them: which policy classes, what time window, how borderline cases count and what counts as caught. Rollout follows the same caution: offline validation, shadow mode, then monitoring of category mix, queue backlog and drift, because users adapt against the system and "scam evolves faster than static benchmarks".

## Who should watch

Trust and safety engineers, ML engineers working on rare-class problems and anyone tempted to point a frontier model at a moderation queue and call it done. It is a production talk with real trade-offs, light on code.

Title: Agile as the safety net for AI in regulated healthcare IT
Description: Independent researcher ShubhaPriya Muthuramalingam at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on why short sprints, shadow mode and embedded compliance make clinical AI safer.
Body:
Shipping an AI clinical engine as one big release is the riskiest way to do it. That is the core argument ShubhaPriya Muthuramalingam, an independent researcher, made at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026: short sprints with clinicians in the room, compliance written into the backlog and AI rolled out through shadow mode first are what keep healthcare IT both fast and safe.

This is a strategy talk, not a code walkthrough. If you want a Helm chart, look elsewhere. If you need words to convince a hospital steering committee that sprints and HIPAA can coexist, it is a good half hour.

## The expensive failure is the right project shipped too late

Healthcare organizations are running electronic health record modernization, FHIR interoperability, prior authorization automation and AI-assisted clinical decision support all at once. Muthuramalingam points out that waterfall programs assume requirements hold still for years, while a single policy update or regulatory mandate can invalidate months of work.

Her framing of the cost is sharp: "The real risk is in delivering the wrong solution after spending years or months in building it." Schedule overruns hurt, but building something clinicians no longer need hurts more.

## Compliance belongs in the backlog, not the final gate

The biggest misconception she tackles is that agile means less governance. In her version, HIPAA controls, access management, audit logging, data lineage and security requirements become backlog items and acceptance criteria. Compliance officers take part in every cycle instead of reviewing a finished system and finding the gaps after the money is spent.

That matters more once AI arrives, because explainability, traceability and accountability are hard to bolt on. A sprint review where a compliance expert sees working software every few weeks catches problems while they are still cheap.

## Roll clinical AI out in stages

The slide she calls the most important one for an LLM audience is about validation. Picture an AI clinical engine that no clinician touches until launch day: the likely results are alert fatigue, workflow disruption and patient safety concerns. Her alternative is a ladder: shadow mode first, then limited pilots, then controlled expansion, with every sprint used to check model outputs and gather feedback.

"Agile effectively becomes the safety mechanism for responsible AI adoption," she says. Engineers who have shipped canary releases will recognize the shape: never send all the traffic to a version nobody has watched.

## Deliver the architecture in layers

The talk also sketches a layered delivery order: patient portals, then interoperability APIs, then analytics, then AI-powered decision support. Each layer delivers value on its own and becomes the foundation for the next, which beats trying to land everything in one go.

For programs with hundreds of stakeholders she points to SAFe, the Scaled Agile Framework, with agile release trains and program increments to keep multiple teams planning together.

## Measure outcomes, and watch for fake agile

Muthuramalingam lists the usual ways transformations fail: resistance to change, misaligned expectations, weak DevOps capability, compliance as an afterthought, and teams that hold stand-ups but still decide everything the waterfall way. Ceremonies without the mindset are just more meetings.

For measuring success she suggests time to value, sprint predictability, defect escape rate and compliance coverage, plus AI-specific signals for clinical systems: model accuracy, clinical adoption, alert acceptance, false positive rates and provider satisfaction.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, architects and delivery leads in healthcare, insurance or any regulated domain who are about to put an LLM in front of clinicians or auditors. Engineers looking for implementation detail on model serving or evaluation can skip it; this one is about the operating model around the code.

Title: Compliance risk lives between the documents, not inside them
Description: Varsha Shah at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on correlating payroll, tax and procurement records with graphs, risk scoring and LLMs to catch hidden compliance risk.
Body:
A payroll record can be correct, a tax filing can be correct, and the company can still be out of compliance. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2026, Varsha Shah, an enterprise technical architect, showed a framework that connects payroll, tax, procurement and transaction data so the risk that sits between systems becomes visible.

Her one-line diagnosis of most compliance failures: "The organization did not lack the data, the organization lacked correlation."

## The employee who moved

The example that makes the talk click is small and very familiar to anyone who has touched HR systems. An employee relocates. HR records the new work location. Payroll pays them correctly. The tax filing system submits the required filing on time. Every system, checked on its own, is green.

Connect the records and the problem appears: the new location puts the employee under a different tax jurisdiction with different reporting rules and deadlines, and the filing was based on the old one. No rule engine looking at one document at a time would flag it, because no single document is wrong.

## Three questions, three components

Shah structures the architecture around three questions: what is connected, what is risky, and what does the risk mean in this regulatory context.

- **A graph-based entity correlation engine** links employees to payroll records, payroll to tax filings, vendors to procurement, and transactions to the wider business process. LLMs help resolve ambiguous references, so the same entity spelled two ways in two systems ends up as one node.
- **An adaptive probabilistic risk model** combines signals such as unusual transaction patterns, jurisdictional inconsistencies, entity relationships, history and prior audits into a confidence-weighted risk score, so investigators work the highest-exposure cases first.
- **A jurisdictional normalization layer** aligns currencies, tax codes and reporting requirements across countries, which she describes as a translation layer for compliance intelligence.

The feedback loop ties them together: every audit outcome and investigation result goes back into the risk model, so the system learns which patterns were real.

## The LLM is the reasoning layer, not the chat window

The part most relevant to an LLM audience is where the model sits. In this design the LLM is not the user interface. It reads the unstructured material that rule engines ignore (contracts, policies, audit notes, regulatory guidance), connects it to the structured records, and writes the explanation an auditor will read.

Shah's point is that finding a risk is only half the job. Explaining why the risk exists is what lets a compliance team act on it, and that is where the language model earns its place.

## Evaluated on enterprise-shaped data

The framework was tested on about three million anonymized records spanning payroll, tax, procurement and transactions, across four jurisdictions and five years of history. She reports stronger detection of cross-system patterns, fewer false positives than rule-based systems and less auditor time spent gathering evidence. She does not put exact precision and recall figures on screen, so treat the results as directional.

She is also candid about the limits: LLM hallucination means every finding must be grounded in verified evidence, legacy data is messy and inconsistent, and regulations keep moving. Her conclusion is that AI is a force multiplier for compliance experts, not a replacement.

## Who should watch

Architects and data engineers building compliance, audit or fraud platforms in multi-country organizations, and anyone who has been asked to "add AI" to a rule engine and wants a sensible place to put it. If you are looking for model internals or code, this is an architecture talk rather than an implementation one.

Title: Structured logs with business correlation IDs as a compliance layer
Description: Prem Anand at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on stitching AML and screening workflows from structured logs, not cross-database joins, and making them LLM-ready.
Body:
When a regulator asks what happened to one customer's transaction, the answer usually sits in five systems that don't join cheaply. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Prem Anand, a software engineer lead who has spent over two decades on compliance systems, argues for not building another database or dashboard to fix that, and instead treating structured application logs as the primary intelligence layer for AML, sanctions screening and customer verification, and as the groundwork any LLM on top will need.

## Why the database-centric approach breaks

His picture of a typical financial stack: customer data in Oracle or SQL Server, transactions in MongoDB or Cassandra, identity checks in a third-party system you can't even query, message queues and microservices across several environments. An alert fires at 10 AM and the analyst needs to know whether it's a false positive, what preceded it and whether the response was on time.

The old fix is compliance queries with heavy cross-database joins. They are slow, they compete with production for connection pools, and dirty or phantom reads mean decisions get made on wrong state. Failures that span services never show up in any single query, so they surface when a customer calls about a stuck payment, or when a regulator finds them first.

## Four layers, no schema changes

The architecture he walks through:

1. **A wrapper library.** Developers import one JAR; it wraps methods and emits a structured log for requests, responses, errors and business events, with no logging code in the business logic.
2. **One log schema.** Predictable fields in the same places, so machines, search engines and eventually LLMs can read them.
3. **A business correlation ID.** Tag the customer account, screening case or transaction rather than an infrastructure trace ID, and one customer's journey can be rebuilt without a single join.
4. **A decoupled ingestion pipeline.** Logs flow to a central layer off the transaction path.

Each layer is independently deployable, so you instrument one service, see the benefit, then do the next. No big-bang migration.

## The transaction never waits for the logger

Compliance telemetry must never become an availability risk. The logger writes into a lock-free, pre-allocated ring buffer and the transaction carries on; background workers drain it to ingestion. If the buffer fills, old telemetry events are dropped, never transaction data. If ingestion is down, the application doesn't notice. He quotes ring-buffer insertion at two to five hundred nanoseconds and under a microsecond of overhead per application.

Once the ingestion layer groups events by correlation ID and sorts by timestamp, the analyst gets a chronological narrative: transaction in, potential hit, enrichment score, alert, case assigned, cleared as a false positive. That one feed drives a live dashboard and statistical alerting with escalation paths, so an on-call engineer starts with context rather than a grep across five services.

## Logs come before LLMs

His most transferable point: an LLM handed a pile of inconsistent text from several systems will produce a plausible, wrong root cause, while the same incident as structured, business-tagged, time-ordered events gives it something it can reason about. He sketches three uses: natural-language investigations for analysts who aren't SQL experts, automatic incident summaries, and root-cause analysis across latency and queue metrics.

The safeguards are part of the design. Fields are masked before logs reach the observability layer, access is role-based and audited, retrieval sends the model only the relevant slice of masked logs, and the most sensitive environments run private models on their own hardware.

The cost, savings and scale figures in the talk come from his experience rather than a published benchmark; the architecture is the part to take away.

## Who should watch

Engineers on AML, KYC or payments platforms, SREs fighting cross-system investigations, and anyone planning to point an LLM at operational data who hasn't fixed the data yet.

Title: For LLM products, trust is a functional requirement
Description: Vijayalakshmi Narasimhan at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on product management for production LLMs, from trust-aware requirements to monitoring trust signals.
Body:
For web products the thing to manage was scalability, for mobile it was user experience, and for AI products it is trust. That's how independent researcher Vijayalakshmi Narasimhan closes her talk at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, and the half hour before it argues that the product development lifecycle most teams use was built for deterministic software and needs rework once an LLM ships.

This is a product management talk, not an engineering one. It is aimed at the people who write requirements and own outcomes, which is exactly why engineers on LLM teams may want to see it.

## The demo-to-production cliff

Her description of the typical enterprise journey will sound familiar: build a chatbot proof of concept, impress stakeholders, then hit the wall of deploying it safely at scale. A hallucinated answer in a demo is a funny slide. In production it can be a compliance, financial or reputational problem.

Traditional software gives the same output for the same input, so "does the feature work?" was most of the question. With an LLM you also have to ask whether it is fair, safe, explainable and auditable, and whether you can still answer that after launch. Prompts, context, data sources and model settings all move the output.

## Write trust into the requirements

Vijayalakshmi's main move is reclassification. Trust, compliance and security are usually filed as non-functional requirements and deprioritized. For LLM products she argues they are functional, because what the user experiences is the model's behaviour. A strong requirement says the system must give explainable responses, cite sources where appropriate and protect sensitive data, and it says so in measurable terms.

Compliance by design follows: identify regulatory, privacy, security and ethical constraints early and turn them into acceptance criteria and evaluation gates. Her example is a financial advisory assistant that needs transaction context, domain context, audit logs and decision traceability from day one, because retrofitting end-to-end audit into a mixed human and AI workflow is hard.

Governance artifacts make it visible: model cards for intended use, limitations and known risks, and datasheets for datasets covering origin, purpose and what the AI may do with the data.

## Test how it fails, not whether it fails

Classic QA isn't enough. She pushes scenario-based and behaviour-based validation, bias testing, ambiguous prompts (different users describe the same problem very differently) and adversarial cases. The aim isn't identical wording on every run; it is the same outcome for the same scenario. The useful question, in her framing, is how the model will fail and why.

## Monitor trust, not just latency

Models get updated, prompts evolve, data and policy change, so a passing validation result says little about next month. Monitoring has to cover technical metrics (latency, cost, error rate, hallucination rate, retrieval quality) and product metrics (task completion, satisfaction, adoption, business impact). The ones teams skip are trust signals, which are hard to quantify and often come from feedback sessions and dogfooding: ask users whether they trust the answers and, if not, whether the cause is the data, the response or the experience.

For structure she points PMs to the OECD AI Principles for what trustworthy AI looks like and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (govern, map, measure, manage) to put it into practice. Human oversight should scale with the stakes: light for low-risk tasks, verification checkpoints and override paths for healthcare, finance or hiring decisions.

## Who should watch

Product managers taking an LLM feature from pilot to production, and engineering leads who need a shared vocabulary with them for requirements, evaluation gates and post-launch monitoring. Engineers looking for implementation detail should pair it with something more hands-on.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [GenOps: A Governance-Driven Model for Safe, High-Velocity AI in CI/CD Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Neeraj_Kumar_Singh_Beshane_governance_genai_velocity) by Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane (Meta), governance from the delivery pipeline side.
- [Responsible AI with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Mohamed_Najaaf_guardrails_responsible_bedrock) by Mohamed Najaaf (AWS), on enforcing some of these controls in code.
- [A Product Manager's Take on the "AI-fication" in the World of Fintech](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Adhikar_Babu_product_manager_aification) by Adhikar Babu (Worldpay), another PM's view from a regulated industry.

Title: Conf42 Database DevOps 2026: migrations, operators and AI on call
Description: Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 roundup - safe schema migrations, a 30-day Kubernetes operator test, serverless database lessons and AI-assisted tuning.
Body:
Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 ran online on June 4, 2026, with 25 talks about the part of the stack that does not roll back cleanly. The schedule was split into AI, automation, delivery, governance, and scale tracks, but one question ran through all of them: now that AI can write your migrations and tune your queries, which parts of database operations can you safely hand over, and which still need a human with a pager?

Every talk is on the [Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 event page](https://www.conf42.com/dbd2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCwmGmMnd2P7QS42DFYdMUU).

## The riskiest deploy you ship

Schema migrations got the most attention, and for good reason. [Ahmed Tariq](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Ahmed_Tariq_postgres_mysql_scaling), a Cloud DevOps Engineer, opened his abstract with the line every DBA nods at: application releases can be rolled forward and back, but a migration that locks a 2TB table for an hour, or quietly loses data on rollback, cannot. His field guide covers expand-and-contract, migration tests, approval gates, and post-deploy checks, then adds AI where it earns its keep (drafting forward and rollback DDL, flagging unsafe operations) and is honest about where it breaks, such as hallucinated Postgres flags that are really MySQL flags.

Diamond sponsor Harness showed the pattern end to end. [Stephen Atwell](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Stephen_Atwell_cd_stateful_applications), Director of Product at Harness, had AI write a trigger-based Postgres migration that splits a JSON blob column into real columns, then shipped it through blue-green in staging and canary in production with no downtime, with policy checks, production data cloned to staging, and an AI-written test confirming that both app versions saw the same orders.

[Niraj Katkamwar](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Niraj_Katkamwar_llm_agents_delivery) of Intuit presented independent research on a prompt-driven framework that turns natural-language requirements into microservice and schema changes.

## Can the operator replace the DBA?

[Amarachi Iheanacho](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Amarachi_Iheanacho_postgres_k8s_tuning) of SideroLabs ran the experiment many teams argue about but never run: hand day-to-day operations of a PostgreSQL cluster to the CloudNativePG operator for 30 days, then deliberately inject node failures, pod crashes, storage pressure, replication issues, upgrades, and restores. Some problems were fixed automatically within seconds; others needed a human. The week-by-week walkthrough is the most honest answer to the title you will find.

[Renato Losio](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Renato_Losio_mistakes_lessons_scaling) brought five lessons from five years of so-called serverless databases on AWS. He once drew the New York City skyline with Aurora Serverless v2 capacity at re:Invent, and says fifteen years with AWS does not make him an expert, it just makes him old. Among them: serverless is just an adjective, and storage usually matters more than CPU. His key message: serverless databases remove capacity management, but they don't remove database engineering.

## AI as the junior DBA

Several talks put AI into the tuning loop. [Naga Bellamkonda](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Naga_Bellamkonda_alerts_incident_platform) of Gartner and [Ellavarasan Asokan](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Ellavarasan_Asokan_monitoring_reliability_platform) of Capital One, both long-time Oracle and Postgres administrators, shared lessons from AI-driven optimisation in production, from predictive tuning towards more autonomous operations. [Sampath Rao Madarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Sampath_Rao_Madarapu_azure_cloud_monitoring) of Microsoft showed Copilot in Azure for diagnostics and resource control.

On the AI application side, [Alejandro Duarte](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Alejandro_Duarte_llm_vectors_semantic) of MariaDB covered RAG in production, starting from the infamous glue-on-pizza answers, and [Ankur Aggarwal](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Ankur_Aggarwal_llm_inference_models) of Meta tackled a hard gap: how an LLM running in a trusted execution environment can query databases through MCP without exposing sensitive data.

## Same SQL, different answers

The governance track had the talk most data engineers should watch. [Muthupalaniappan Ramanathan](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Muthupalaniappan_Ramanathan_queries_monitoring_sql) of DoorDash showed how identical queries can return different results on Spark, Trino, and Snowflake because of type handling, null semantics, and optimiser behaviour, and proposed a canonical semantic layer with CI-integrated validation to catch the drift.

[Sheena Yap Chan](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Sheena_Yap_Chan_incident_reliability_platform) argued that the real risk is often not missing data but database signals that never reach the right people in time. [Muthu Saravanan](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Muthu_Saravanan_alerts_telemetry_platform) of Mind-Pros and [Dharmendra Ahuja](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Dharmendra_Ahuja_monitoring_analytics_platform) of IBM looked at intentional delivery and ethical validation inside AI-driven data pipelines.

## Always on, at scale

The scale track was heavy on finance. [Priyatham Nagaiya Seenu Naidu](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Priyatham_Nagaiya_Seenu_Naidu_kafka_pipelines_clusters) of Mastercard covered real-time payment networks like FedNow, UPI, PIX, and SEPA Instant, where the database must be up around the clock with sub-second processing. [Ritvik Pandya](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Ritvik_Pandya_monitoring_telemetry_reliability) of JPMorgan Chase started from a sudden p99 spike at peak hours and traced it to the ingress layer, fixing it with deterministic routing for cache locality. [Srikanth Uddanti](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Srikanth_Uddanti_distributed_systems_delivery) of Charles Schwab walked through the trade-offs of distributed databases, and [Surya Lankalapalli](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Surya_Lankalapalli_telemetry_analytics_delivery) of Microsoft made the case for active-active, multi-provider DNS, the dependency that quietly delays database failover.

Elsewhere in the lineup: [Jason Lester](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Jason_Lester_productivity_teams_efficiency) of Capgemini on loading cloud API output into a database for analysis the console cannot do, [Sulabh Jain](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Sulabh_Jain_kafka_streams_k8s) on modernising insurance core systems, [Sirisha Ayyagari](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Sirisha_Ayyagari_telemetry_tracing_platform) of IBM on real-time SAP pricing, [Kamini Murugaboopathy](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Kamini_Murugaboopathy_agents_pipelines_o11y) on real-time marketing analytics, [Bharat Kumar Reddy Karumuri](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Bharat_Kumar_Reddy_Karumuri_models_training_telemetry) of General Motors on operationalising ML and GenAI, [Zeeshan Khan](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Zeeshan_Khan_vectors_recruiting_semantic) on hiring as a data infrastructure problem, and [Harsha Vardhani Talluri](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Harsha_Vardhani_Talluri_metrics_telemetry_unified) on multi-vendor DOCSIS deployments.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to diamond sponsor [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), gold sponsor [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

This was the first Conf42 Database DevOps. The second, [Conf42 Database DevOps 2027](https://www.conf42.com/dbd2027), is set for May 27, 2027. Bring your rollback scripts.

Title: Compliance by construction for co-branded credit card platforms
Description: Ravindra Rajasekhar Kavuru (Expedia Group) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on building PCI, privacy and audit controls into credit platforms by design.
Body:
Retrofitting compliance onto a production system costs far more than designing it in, so make non-compliance architecturally hard. That is the thesis Ravindra Rajasekhar Kavuru, a software engineering manager at Expedia Group, puts forward at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026 for co-branded credit card platforms, where regulated banking infrastructure meets high-volume consumer traffic.

He opens with a disclaimer that the views are his own and based on general industry knowledge, not his employer's systems. Read it as a reference architecture, not a case study.

## Two worlds, one transaction

A co-branded card sits between a consumer platform that cares about throughput and a bank that cares about regulation, and every transaction has to satisfy both. Ravindra's framing of compliance by construction has four phases: regulatory constraints become system invariants at design time, enforcement is woven into service contracts and data flows at build time, policy is evaluated continuously against live telemetry at runtime, and audit evidence falls out of normal operation instead of being assembled once a year.

## Spend where the expected loss is

Security budgets should follow math, not fear. The talk proposes estimating breach probability per component and integration point from incident history, threat intelligence and system topology, then funding controls where the reduction in expected breach cost exceeds what the control costs, and spotting diminishing returns before over-investing in low-risk areas.

Technical controls alone aren't enough either. Drawing on behavioral compliance research, he lists what makes people actually follow policy: believing violations will be detected, security as a shared norm, compliant paths that are the easiest ones, and fast feedback on near misses.

## The stack, bottom to top

The architecture is presented as a pyramid:

- **Networking** built for very low latency and high throughput, with active-active regional deployment.
- **Distributed transactions** via sagas with compensating steps and outbox-based publishing, since two-phase commit is too slow at scale. A payment that succeeds but fails to record its compliance event is a regulatory liability, so the compliance record captures both the attempt and any compensation.
- **Event-driven services** on a bus such as Kafka, with schema-enforced, tamper-evident audit logs written to append-only sinks and enriched in-stream with risk scores and regulatory tags.
- **Security controls**: PCI DSS-aligned microsegmentation into cardholder-data, connected and out-of-scope zones, mTLS on every service call, network policy as code checked in CI, and tokenization using format-preserving encryption so tokens look like card numbers and downstream schemas don't change. ML predicts which tokens will be hot and keeps them in fast memory.
- **Real-time intelligence**: underwriting on precomputed features with no synchronous bureau calls on the critical path, streaming fraud scoring, and partner data checked at the ingestion boundary so partners can't inject non-compliant state.
- **Observability and governance** at the top.

## Where the LLMs come in

The LLM layer sits at the peak. Models learn normal behaviour from streaming telemetry and flag deviations with a plain-language explanation for analysts, aimed at novel fraud and violations that signature rules miss. Policy engines check operational behaviour against declared policy, and LLM components parse regulatory updates into proposed policy diffs. Every one of those proposals goes to a human, and Ravindra's last takeaway is to design the human-in-the-loop explicitly rather than as an afterthought.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineers on payments, cards or lending platforms, especially anyone preparing for a PCI DSS scope review. It is a dense architecture overview; LLMs are one layer, not the subject.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [AI-Powered Fraud Detection in Cloud-Native Digital Payments](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Sandeep_Katuri_fraud_detection_digital_payments_security) by Sandeep Katuri, on the fraud-scoring layer.
- [IoT Payment Systems: Microservices Architecture for Connected Devices](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Silpa_Potluri_payments_microservices_architecture) by Silpa Potluri (GoodLeap), on payment gateways moving to microservices.
- [AI-Driven Sensitive Data Discovery for Secure DevSecOps and Privacy Compliance](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Mary_Sirisha_Duggimpudi_datadiscovery_privacy_compliance) by Mary Sirisha Duggimpudi (T-Mobile USA), on finding regulated data before you can protect it.

[Watch Ravindra Rajasekhar Kavuru's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Ravindra_Rajasekhar_Kavuru_privacy_compliance_credit)

[Watch the talk on YouTube](https://youtu.be/lccAwOE5HG4).

Title: Database DevOps: CD for Stateful Applications
Body:
## Database DevOps: Bringing Continuous Delivery to Stateful Applications

Modern software delivery pipelines are remarkably good at deploying stateless applications. Teams can push application updates multiple times a day, automate testing, validate rollouts, and quickly roll back when something goes wrong.

Databases are often a different story.

While application deployments have embraced continuous delivery, database changes frequently remain manual, infrequent, and high-risk. Many organizations that deploy application code daily still schedule database releases monthly or quarterly because schema changes introduce challenges that traditional CI/CD workflows struggle to address.

In his session *Database DevOps: CD for Stateful Applications*, Stephen Atwell explored how engineering teams can apply modern delivery practices to databases, making stateful systems just as testable, repeatable, and automatable as the applications that depend on them.

### Why Databases Remain a Deployment Bottleneck

The core challenge of database delivery is state.

Stateless applications can be replaced, scaled, or rolled back relatively easily because their state lives elsewhere. Databases contain the data that applications depend on, making every structural change potentially risky.

Simple schema updates can become surprisingly complex when applications remain online throughout the deployment process.

Consider a scenario where a single database column needs to be split into multiple fields. During deployment, both the old and new versions of the application may run simultaneously. If each version reads and writes data differently, inconsistencies can emerge immediately.

This challenge often forces teams into maintenance windows, deployment freezes, or highly manual release processes.

As a result, database changes frequently become the limiting factor in otherwise mature continuous delivery environments.

### Continuous Delivery Requires Backwards Compatibility

Modern deployment patterns such as blue-green and canary releases depend on running multiple versions of an application simultaneously.

This creates a requirement that many database migrations fail to consider: backwards compatibility.

If version A of an application and version B of an application are both serving traffic, the underlying database must support both versions throughout the transition.

Database changes therefore cannot simply focus on the final desired schema. They must also account for the intermediate states that exist while deployments are in progress.

Successful database delivery requires teams to think about migrations as a series of controlled steps rather than a single change.

### The Hidden Complexity of Zero-Downtime Database Migrations

Zero-downtime deployments are relatively common at the application layer. Achieving the same outcome at the database layer is significantly harder.

The challenge becomes particularly apparent when restructuring data.

During the session, Atwell demonstrated a migration that transformed a PostgreSQL table storing serialized JSON data into a properly structured relational schema.

The goal was straightforward: extract fields from a JSON document and store them in dedicated database columns.

The execution, however, required careful planning.

The migration needed to ensure:

- No downtime
- No data loss
- Full backwards compatibility
- Support for old and new application versions
- Safe rollback capabilities

Achieving all of these requirements simultaneously demands more than simply writing migration scripts.

### Using Database Triggers to Maintain Consistency

One of the key techniques demonstrated during the session involved database triggers.

When introducing new columns, the existing application still expects the original data structure. New application versions, meanwhile, expect the updated schema.

Rather than forcing an immediate switch, synchronization mechanisms can keep both representations aligned.

In the demonstrated migration, triggers ensured that updates to the original JSON field automatically updated the new relational columns.

Additional triggers performed the reverse operation, keeping the original structure synchronized whenever the new schema was modified.

This approach allowed both versions of the application to operate simultaneously while observing the same data.

By maintaining consistency in both directions, teams gain the flexibility needed to deploy, test, validate, and roll back safely.

### Large Data Migrations Require More Than Correct SQL

Database migrations often fail not because the migration logic is incorrect, but because operational realities are ignored.

A script that performs well on a development database may behave very differently against production datasets.

Tables may contain millions or billions of rows. Long-running transactions can create lock contention, impact performance, or introduce unexpected downtime.

For this reason, migration strategies must account for scale from the beginning.

Instead of processing entire datasets in a single transaction, modern migration workflows often break work into smaller batches that can execute incrementally and safely.

This reduces risk while allowing migrations to proceed without disrupting production workloads.

### AI-Assisted Database Development

One of the more interesting aspects of the demonstration was the use of generative AI to create migration logic.

Rather than manually writing complex PostgreSQL migration code, the schema transformation was generated through natural language prompts.

The generated migration created new columns, built synchronization triggers, and produced the necessary data migration logic.

While AI-generated code still requires validation, it introduces a new workflow for database teams.

Instead of spending hours building migration scripts manually, engineers can focus on reviewing, validating, and testing generated solutions.

The result is a faster iteration cycle while still maintaining governance and operational controls.

### Governance Matters as Much as Automation

Automation alone does not make database deployments safe.

Every automated process still requires guardrails.

Throughout the deployment workflow demonstrated during the session, database changes passed through governance checks before being applied.

These checks verified that deployments complied with predefined policies and prevented potentially destructive operations from reaching production environments.

Examples include:

- Preventing accidental data loss
- Blocking unsafe schema operations
- Enforcing deployment policies
- Creating rollback checkpoints
- Validating generated SQL before execution

As organizations increase deployment velocity, governance becomes increasingly important because manual review alone cannot scale indefinitely.

### Testing Database Changes Against Production Data

One of the biggest challenges in database testing is reproducing production behavior.

Many database issues only appear when migrations encounter real customer data, realistic workloads, or unusual edge cases.

Traditional testing environments often fail to capture these conditions.

To address this challenge, Atwell demonstrated a workflow that clones production data into staging environments before running migration tests.

This approach allows teams to validate schema changes against realistic datasets while still operating within controlled environments.

When combined with automated testing, production-like data significantly improves confidence in deployment outcomes.

Organizations implementing this strategy must ensure that security controls, access policies, and compliance requirements remain consistent between production and staging environments.

### Verifying Data Consistency During Deployment

Testing database migrations requires more than simply checking whether a deployment completed successfully.

Teams must verify that data remains consistent throughout the transition.

In the demonstrated workflow, automated tests interacted with both the old and new versions of the application.

Actions performed through one version were immediately validated through the other version.

This process confirmed that both applications continued to observe identical data despite significant schema changes occurring underneath them.

These consistency tests become especially valuable when supporting parallel deployments through blue-green or canary release strategies.

Without this validation, subtle synchronization issues can remain hidden until they affect production users.

### Combining Database Migrations with Progressive Delivery

Application delivery practices such as blue-green deployments and canary releases have become common across cloud-native environments.

Database changes can benefit from the same principles.

During the session, schema updates were deployed alongside controlled application rollouts.

In staging environments, blue-green deployments allowed old and new versions to operate simultaneously while automated tests verified compatibility.

In production environments, canary deployments gradually increased traffic to the new version while monitoring system health and behavior.

This progressive approach reduces risk by limiting exposure and creating multiple opportunities to detect issues before they impact all users.

### The Future of Database Delivery

For years, databases have been treated as a special case within software delivery pipelines.

Application teams embraced automation while database changes remained manual, infrequent, and operationally risky.

That distinction is beginning to disappear.

Advances in infrastructure automation, Kubernetes-native workflows, AI-assisted development, automated testing, and database-focused CI/CD tooling are making it possible to manage stateful systems using many of the same practices that transformed application delivery.

The goal is not simply faster deployments.

It is creating a delivery process that is more predictable, more repeatable, easier to test, and safer to operate.

### Bringing Stateful Applications into Modern CI/CD

Database delivery will always require additional care because data cannot simply be redeployed when something goes wrong.

However, that does not mean databases must remain outside modern delivery practices.

By combining backwards-compatible schema changes, automated testing, governance controls, production-like environments, and progressive deployment strategies, organizations can bring databases into the same continuous delivery workflows that already power their applications.

The result is a more unified software delivery process where both application code and data evolve together, safely and repeatedly, without sacrificing reliability or availability.

Title: Validating an LLM judge for summaries with deliberately broken ones
Description: Liliya Imasheva and Michael Banf (Perelyn) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on an LLM-as-judge pipeline for high-stakes summaries, checked against expert scores.
Body:
To trust an LLM judge, feed it summaries you broke on purpose and see if it notices. That's one of the three changes that did most of the work in the validation pipeline Liliya Imasheva, LLM Engineer at Perelyn, presents at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, from work she did with Michael Banf, Perelyn's Chief AI Architect. The task is summarization in high-stakes environments, where one flawed summary has real consequences.

It's a lightning talk, and a tidy one: a clear question, a measurement method, and the handful of things that moved the number.

## The question is drift, not a leaderboard

The goal isn't to crown a model. It is to detect whether summary quality stays stable or quietly degrades when something changes: a model upgrade, a new dataset, more scale. To answer that you need a measurement you can repeat, and one that agrees with the experts.

The starting point was a dataset of pipeline-generated summaries that experts had scored from one to five on five carefully defined dimensions: completeness, correctness, conciseness, harmlessness and readability.

## Why ROUGE and BLEU didn't make it

The team first tried reference-based metrics: ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore and cosine similarity. They performed poorly on the task, and there was a deeper mismatch. Those metrics produce one continuous number, while the experts gave categorical Likert scores per dimension, and any mapping from one to the other adds its own uncertainty. They also reward overlap with a reference, when what a high-stakes summary needs is to be correct and safe.

So the judge became an LLM scoring the same five dimensions on the same one-to-five scale, with a written reason for each score. Same criteria for humans and machine is what makes the comparison meaningful.

## Agreement on a binary verdict, not exact scores

Nobody expects the judge to give exactly the score an expert gave. What matters is separating good summaries from bad ones and tracking the share of good ones. So scores of one to three count as bad and four to five as good, and agreement is how often the pipeline's verdict matches the expert's. An expert five and a judge four is a match; an expert four and a judge two is not.

## What moved the number

The levers are the usual ones: the model, temperature and sampling parameters, the prompt (a fixed template with each dimension's definition dropped into a placeholder), few-shot examples and the reference dataset. Prompt engineering with expert help, hyperparameter tuning and model upgrades gave marginal gains. Three things made the real difference:

- **Few-shot with both a good and a bad example.** Two or three well-chosen examples helped a lot; more than four started to confuse the model.
- **Negative controls.** About a third of the expert-scored test set was deliberately broken in three ways: negated facts (the hardest to catch, since they read almost like the original, so most controls were these), numbers swapped for random ones, and scrambled text (the easiest).
- **Asking for reasoning.** Making the judge justify every score improved agreement. On correctness, which matters most here alongside harmlessness, agreement improved by more than ten percent; completeness dipped by about three percent but stayed above 90 percent.

## Experts shrink, but never to zero

The pipeline is trustworthy only because it was validated against human judgment, and that baseline is what lets you improve the summarizer itself in a repeatable, automated way. Expert involvement can go down over time; Liliya is clear it can't go to zero.

## Who should watch

Anyone running an LLM-as-judge in production for summaries, extraction or any task where the eval itself needs evaluating. The negative-control recipe transfers to almost any task.

Title: Nine ways SOX audit teams use AI, and the sign-offs each one needs
Description: Karishma Velisetty at Conf42 LLMs 2026 maps nine AI use cases in SOX and ICFR audit work to their risks and the human controls that make them reliable.
Body:
AI tools are good at producing text that sounds right, and in a SOX audit that is precisely the danger. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, independent researcher Karishma Velisetty walks through nine places internal audit teams now use AI, from reviewing analytics scripts to drafting control narratives, and for each one names the risk and the control that makes the output fit for reliance.

If you build tooling for finance or audit teams, this is a rare look at how auditors themselves think about your output.

## Three kinds of tools, three risk profiles

Karishma groups the tools in use: code and analytics assistants (Copilot, Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT) used by data-savvy auditors to write and review scripts; language and document AI for drafting, reviewing and summarizing; and specialist audit AI wired directly into SOX workflows. Each carries a different risk, and the governance has to match.

## The five that are already common

- **Reviewing audit analytics scripts.** The big risk is over-reliance. If an auditor accepts an AI's explanation of a script without understanding the logic, human review becomes a rubber stamp. Her controls: a formal human sign-off on AI findings, a log of each AI review session (tool, date, findings) for external auditors and PCAOB purposes, and a second-level reviewer.
- **Contract review.** Contracts are confidential and often hold material non-public information. Her rule is simple: consumer AI never touches them, and enterprise AI is used only in a private, controlled deployment. Then check for misread clauses and hallucinated lease or accounting terms.
- **Invoice matching and reconciliation.** One of the highest-return uses, with one condition external auditors test first: population completeness. Run the match on an incomplete population and the results aren't audit evidence.
- **Control narratives.** This is where she sees the most enthusiasm and the most quiet quality loss. The fix is mandatory process-owner validation that the described steps match what actually happens.
- **Test sheets and workpapers.** The concern is coverage of the relevant assertions, and numbers the AI makes up. A suggested sample size has to come from your sampling policy and materiality, not from the model.

## Four that are growing fast

Journal entry testing, user access review, flux analysis and walkthrough documentation are earlier in adoption. AI makes full-population journal entry analysis feasible, but again only if you can prove it ran on the full population. Segregation-of-duties analysis is only as good as the role matrix; a stale matrix gives confident nonsense, and certification decisions can't be delegated to AI. For flux analysis she warns about well-written AI drafts containing assertions management never reviewed. Walkthrough recordings bring a legal question before an audit one: recording consent.

## Validation is not the same as review

The closing message is one sentence long and worth pinning above the desk: review means reading the output, validation means an accountable person formally signs off that it is correct and complete. Technical controls matter most for code and analytics, people and process controls for contracts and narratives, and monitoring keeps the whole framework honest. Confidentiality is non-negotiable: one material non-public information leak into a consumer tool is a regulatory and legal problem.

Note on scope: the abstract also mentions security scanners such as Bandit, SonarQube and CodeQL. The recorded talk spends its time on the nine use cases and the governance controls.

## Who should watch

Internal audit and SOX teams adopting AI, engineers building analytics or AI tools for finance functions, and anyone writing a policy for AI use in a regulated workflow.

Title: Your database failover is only as fast as your DNS
Description: Surya Lankalapalli (Microsoft) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on active-active multi-provider DNS, deep health checks and records as code for database failover.
Body:
Replication is solid, failover is tested, and then the outage hits and clients keep resolving the dead primary. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Surya Lankalapalli, Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft, argues that DNS is the database dependency nobody talks about, and that a single DNS provider is a silent single point of failure that can outlast the database failure itself by minutes.

His fix is active-active DNS across multiple providers, driven by health checks that reflect what the database is actually doing. It's a short, pattern-level talk with no vendor names, and a useful list of pitfalls.

## Two providers, both serving

Traditional setups rely on one DNS provider. When it degrades (DDoS, outage), teams flip to a secondary by hand, and in the meantime clients see stale records for minutes or hours. Active-active means two or more providers serve authoritative answers simultaneously, not one waiting on standby. If one degrades, the other keeps answering without intervention, and each provider's anycast network cuts latency for clients spread around the world.

Surya recommends two providers as the standard. More than two isn't unusual, but operational cost and differences between providers' routing features make it hard to scale beyond that.

## Three endpoints, three routing rules

The integration with replication is a health-check-driven sequence: continuous checks, detect an unhealthy primary, promote a replica, update DNS, reroute clients. He splits DNS into three endpoint types:

- **Write endpoint:** a single CNAME or weighted record that always points at the current primary and must update immediately on promotion.
- **Read endpoint:** round-robin or latency-weighted records across healthy replicas, so reads scale without application changes.
- **Regional endpoint:** geo-routing to the nearest healthy replica to cut cross-region read latency.

His line is that DNS isn't just a naming layer; it's a traffic control plane.

## Health checks are the engine

Active-active DNS is only as fast and reliable as the checks driving it. A real check combines TCP and HTTP probes, replication lag monitoring and node drain detection. Replication lag thresholds stop you promoting a stale replica; role detection stops writes going to a read-only one. The check interval and failure threshold effectively set your RTO. And checks must go to the application level: a shallow probe will cheerfully report healthy while the database isn't.

## Records as code, and the TTL trap

Both providers must hold the same records, so Surya treats DNS records as code in version control, deployed through CI/CD, with a sync engine keeping providers aligned and drift detection alerting on divergence. Manual changes during incidents are too slow and invite fat-fingered mistakes.

His favourite pitfall: lower TTL does not automatically mean faster failover. Low TTLs multiply resolver traffic and can run into provider rate limits, which can cause the outage you were trying to avoid. Set a low SOA TTL so NXDOMAIN answers aren't cached for long, keep replica records pre-warmed and live before you need them, and remember that providers' API limits differ.

## Fencing and the manual fallback

For multi-region setups, write fencing ensures only one region accepts writes after a failover. DNS alone can't prevent split brain, so coordinate it with the database's own fencing. Geo-routed reads trade latency against replication lag, and the acceptable lag depends on your customers. Finally, active-active removes DNS as a single point of failure, but providers can still degrade together, so keep a documented manual runbook.

Observability ties it together: resolution success rates per provider, replication lag exposed as a metric both database monitoring and health checks consume, and a log of every DNS change with timestamp, trigger and database state.

## Who should watch

SREs and database engineers who have tested failover end to end except for the part where clients find the new primary. If you've never looked at the TTL on your write endpoint, start here.
