Title: Turning tax law into code with agents and a DSL in the middle
Description: Abdul Basit Iqbal (Amazon) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on a multi-agent pipeline that turns regulatory changes into validated, auditable tax logic.
Body:
A tax jurisdiction changes a rule, and the enterprise typically takes three to six months to get it into production. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Abdul Basit Iqbal, a Senior Software Development Engineer and lead architect of Amazon's global tax engine, lays out an agentic architecture meant to shrink that cycle to hours, and spends as much time on the governance around the models as on the models.

## Compliance drift lives in the handoffs

Abdul names the problem compliance drift. Between a law changing and the system applying it there are four human handoffs: legal interpretation, compliance translation, developer implementation, QA. Each is slow and lossy, and while they run you are over-collecting, under-collecting or applying the wrong rule. His examples are mundane on purpose: a Canadian First Nations exemption, a ZIP code boundary shift in Tennessee.

Classic rule engines never fixed this because tax law isn't written to be structured. Phrases like substance over form have been argued over in court for decades, one regulation can reference treaties and a guidance document from 1998, and the same transaction can be taxed differently depending on entity structure or where a billing address falls. That is the opening for LLMs: the first technology that can read legal prose and emit structured output.

## Four stages, each allowed to say "not sure"

The architecture, which he calls Autonomous Compliance Infrastructure, is a set of purpose-built agents rather than one model:

1. **Monitoring** watches gazettes, tax authority sites and treaty databases continuously and classifies each change by tax type, jurisdiction and effective date.
2. **Legal NLP** extracts the semantics and scores its own confidence. A clear rate change with a date proceeds; ambiguous language or a contested ruling goes to a human before any rule is extracted.
3. **A domain-specific language** captures conditions, thresholds, rates and exemptions in a human-readable, technology-independent form.
4. **A Tax-to-Code engine** uses fine-tuned coding models to generate implementations from the DSL.

Isolation is the point. A low-confidence interpretation escalates instead of flowing downstream, and a failed validation stops the pipeline, so failures stay contained.

## The DSL is the real product

Abdul calls the DSL the strategic centre. Natural language is ambiguous and code is tied to one system; the DSL sits between them. One DSL rule can generate compliant code for a Java billing system, a Python microservice and a TypeScript front end, and because it's version-controlled like source, you can always ask what a rule looked like on January 1st and why it changed. His second lesson is that DSL design is strategic intellectual property: get it wrong and everything downstream is wrong too.

## Nothing generated ships unvalidated

Generated code goes through static analysis, regression tests, differential tests that compare old and new rule outputs, and formal property checks on boundary conditions. Then the rollout is staged: shadow mode, canary, gradual activation, full deployment with rollback kept live. Humans keep three kinds of decision: novel or low-confidence interpretations, changes spanning many jurisdictions, and anything touching an active audit or disputed position. Every rule traces back to the statute that produced it, and every approval is tied to an authenticated identity.

His lessons are refreshingly unglamorous. Confidence estimation matters more than accuracy. Some governments publish machine-readable rules and others publish scanned PDFs. And governance maturity decides success more than model quality: if nobody has defined who approves a rule change, the system stalls at the first hard call. Start with simple single-rate VAT regimes before cross-border complexity.

## Who should watch

Engineers building LLM systems for any regulated domain (tax, finance, insurance, legal), and architects who want a concrete pattern for confidence-gated escalation. It is an architecture talk, with no live demo or code.

Title: vLLM-Omni serves diffusion models and LLMs from one engine
Description: Kosseila Haddalene (Cloudthrill) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 explains how vLLM-Omni puts diffusion transformers and autoregressive LLMs behind one serving stack.
Body:
Diffusion transformers don't generate token by token, they denoise, and they're compute-bound where LLM decoding is memory-bound. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Kosseila Haddalene, founder and AI infrastructure lead at Cloudthrill, takes on the question that follows: can you serve images and video from the same inference engine and pipelines as your LLMs? His answer is vLLM-Omni, and the talk walks through how it is put together.

## Why this is a real problem

Most teams that serve LLMs have built their mental model, and their infrastructure, around autoregressive decoding: batching, KV cache, tokens per second. A diffusion model breaks those assumptions. It runs a denoising loop over a fixed number of timesteps, every step is heavy on compute, and the output is pixels, not a token stream. Bolting a separate image or video service next to the LLM fleet works, but it doubles the operational surface. The pitch for vLLM-Omni is one engine for both.

## Just enough diffusion first

Kosseila's plan is to start with just enough diffusion fundamentals for an LLM engineer, from noise to pixel: the denoising loop, why timesteps matter, and how a diffusion transformer (DiT) differs at its core from an autoregressive (AR) model. That framing is the useful part if you've only ever served text models; it explains why the usual LLM serving tricks don't carry over unchanged.

## How vLLM-Omni joins the two worlds

The architecture section in the talk covers the pieces that let both kinds of model live together:

- **Disaggregated AR and DiT stages.** The autoregressive and diffusion parts run as separate stages, natively, rather than one forced through the other's execution model.
- **OmniRouter.** The dispatch logic that decides where each request goes.
- **Diffusion acceleration.** The speed-ups available for the diffusion side.
- **OpenAI-compatible endpoints.** Text, images, video and audio come out of one engine behind an API most clients already speak.

The stated goal is a clear mental model of where multimodal inference is heading and what it actually takes to serve it in production. Treat this post as the map; the talk has the details.

## Who should watch

Platform and ML infrastructure engineers already running vLLM who are being asked to add image or video generation, and LLM engineers who have never had to think about diffusion and want the short version. If you serve only text models and plan to keep it that way, the diffusion primer is still a good half hour on how the other half of generative AI runs.

Title: Distributed databases, from CAP trade-offs to GitOps rollouts
Description: Srikanth Uddanti (Charles Schwab) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on replication, sharding, Raft vs Paxos, automation and zero trust for database clusters.
Body:
Picking a distributed database starts with deciding what you're willing to lose when the network splits. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Srikanth Uddanti, Senior Manager of Software Development and Engineering at Charles Schwab, where he runs multi-terabyte database clusters, walks through the fundamentals behind modern distributed databases and the DevOps and security practices that keep them running.

This is a good first talk on the subject: a structured tour from the CAP theorem to mutual TLS, with MongoDB as the recurring example. Engineers who already operate Cassandra or CockroachDB in anger will know most of it.

## Why monoliths run out of road

Srikanth frames three limits of the monolithic database. It scales vertically but not horizontally, which makes it a single point of failure. Global distribution brings latency and consistency problems across regions. And applications handling millions of transactions a day hit a throughput ceiling on a vertically scaled box.

## CAP, as a design decision

He uses the CAP theorem as the base for everything else: consistency, availability and partition tolerance, pick two. Traditional relational databases sit on consistency and availability; the horizontally scaled NoSQL systems he names, MongoDB, DynamoDB and Cassandra, are built to tolerate partitions. His practical framing of consistency: with a replication factor of two, a write isn't acknowledged to the user until it has been written twice.

## Three replication models, three sharding schemes

The replication section compares single leader, multi-leader and leaderless designs. Single leader, which MongoDB uses, sends all writes to a primary. It's simple, but it's a bottleneck, and writes not yet replicated when the primary dies are lost; you have to handle that edge case. Multi-leader enables geo-distributed writes at the price of conflict resolution. Leaderless accepts reads and writes on any node with quorums, maximising availability but needing careful quorum tuning.

For sharding: range-based keeps contiguous keys together (his example is querying people aged one to twenty), hash-based spreads load evenly (Amazon order IDs looked up from anywhere), and directory-based uses a lookup table, which is flexible but turns the table into a critical dependency.

## Raft is the one you can explain to on-call

On consensus, he walks through Raft leader election using MongoDB, where operators can set election priority and geography, followed by oplog replication to secondaries in the same or different zones, then commit and apply. Paxos, used in multi-master designs, is mathematically proven and flexible but harder to implement, and needs Multi-Paxos for practical log replication.

## Automate the cluster like any other infrastructure

The DevOps section treats database infrastructure as versioned, declarative code: Terraform or Pulumi to provision, Ansible and Helm charts to configure and enforce tuning parameters, and GitOps pipelines for schema migrations, rolling upgrades and canary rollouts with automated rollback gates. His deployment pattern is zone isolation: do maintenance one zone per region at a time, prove it works, and touch the other zones on a different day. Automated runbooks, he argues, shorten MTTR compared to manual response and remove the toil.

## Zero trust inside the cluster

Security comes in three parts: mutual TLS between clients and the database and between nodes; identity-based, least-privilege access so an application can read or write only the tables it needs; and audit logging of every admin action and schema change for root cause analysis. Certificates need lifecycle management (he mentions Venafi), and keys belong in a key management system or secrets manager.

His closing advice is to start from the use case: work out whether you need strong consistency or high availability, align it with your business SLAs, then automate and secure everything around that choice.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to running distributed databases, or DBAs moving from a single relational primary to a sharded cluster, who want the vocabulary in one sitting.

- [Modern Database Architectures: From SQL to NoSQL and Distributed SQL](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Andrei_Manakov_tradeoffs_distributed_nosql) by Andrei Manakov, the same trade-offs with distributed SQL in the mix.
- [Building a K8s Operator for a Distributed Database](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Natalie_Pistunovich_k8s_operator_distributed_database) by Natalie Pistunovich, for automating cluster operations on Kubernetes.

Title: Modernizing a .NET 4.8 app by writing the specs first
Description: Marco Antonio Silva (Microsoft) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 takes a legacy .NET app to .NET 10 with the GHCP Modernization CLI, then reverse-engineers specs with Spec2Cloud.
Body:
Legacy modernization usually dies on the business case: three to five years of migration work with few new features to show for it. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Marco Antonio Silva, a Senior Global Black Belt in Microsoft's EMEA migrate and modernize team, argues that LLMs can do most of the heavy lifting if you stop prompting your way through the code and make the specification the centre of the work.

The talk is two live demos on the same sample app, Contoso University: an ASP.NET MVC application on .NET Framework 4.8 with an old Entity Framework, SQL Server, IIS and Microsoft Message Queuing for notifications. Both tools shown are Microsoft's (one open source), so expect product on screen; Marco frames it as approaches rather than a pitch.

## Specs become the oracle, code the byproduct

The core idea is spec-driven development. Instead of vibe coding, you build human-readable and machine-readable documents first: features, acceptance criteria, business rules, schemas, APIs, architecture, tech stack. The model works against those, retrying until the acceptance criteria pass. The prompt matters less, the spec matters more, and specs can be reverse-engineered from existing code. Nothing about this is new for human teams, he notes; good documentation always made the target easier to hit.

## Path one: a deterministic assessment, then agents

The GitHub Copilot (GHCP) Modernization CLI handles Java and .NET. Its first step isn't an LLM at all: it downloads deterministic assessment tools such as AppCat that understand the frameworks and their dependencies. On Contoso University the assessment flagged the local file system, MSMQ that should move to Service Bus, Windows AD that should move to Microsoft Entra, and the framework itself, grouped into three waves with T-shirt sizes.

Only then do agentic skills take over. The plan step produced five tasks (messaging, authentication, the database, local files to Azure Storage, connection strings to Key Vault), written to a plan file you can read and edit before anything runs. Execution follows the critical path first, builds after each task and feeds compiler errors back into the loop. By the end of the demo the same app runs on .NET 10 with modern app settings and packages.

## Path two: get the documentation you never had

Spec2Cloud is the open-source option for when there's no tooling for your stack, or you want a deeper refactor than a framework upgrade. Run it in a brownfield repo and it installs dozens of skills into GitHub Copilot. The approach is fully agentic and, as Marco says plainly, non-deterministic but grounded.

On the same app it found the main issues the deterministic tool had found, then wrote architecture decision records with options, pros and cons and a recommended choice for a human to approve. Next it reverse-engineered product and feature requirement documents: student, course, instructor and department management, each with user stories, acceptance criteria and a pointer to where the current code implements them, plus Mermaid diagrams of the workflows. A state file and audit log keep the context in the repo, so a new session can pick up where the last stopped.

His point about that step is the one worth stealing. Even if you never modernize, a legacy system whose builders have left now has specs, and a new feature becomes one more requirement document on top of the rest.

## Keep the boring checks

Not everything should be agentic. Compiling, linting and CI checks you already run for humans should keep running for agents. Spec validation stays human-readable, an LLM can judge output against the acceptance criteria, and a human still signs off the pull request.

## Who should watch

Teams sitting on .NET Framework or old Java estates, architects writing a modernization business case, and anyone curious how spec-driven development works on code that already exists. If you're on a stack neither tool covers, the Spec2Cloud half is the part for you.

Title: Adding nodes made p99 worse, so they routed to the data instead
Description: Ritvik Pandya (JP Morgan Chase) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on deterministic routing and thread affinity that cut p99 from 47 ms to 19 ms on the same hardware.
Body:
When p99 latency quadrupled at peak and the team added nodes, it got slightly worse. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Ritvik Pandya, Engineering Manager at JP Morgan Chase, explains why: the problem wasn't capacity but coordination. Routing each transaction to the node that already owns its data, plus a few unglamorous Kubernetes settings, took p99 from 47 ms to 19 ms on the same hardware and database.

This is one of the most concrete talks of the event: a production story with a latency breakdown, the fix, the numbers and the places it doesn't work.

## The cluster was busy coordinating, not working

The baseline p99 was about 12 ms; at peak it hit 47 ms. Around 3.2% of requests timed out, clients retried, and the retries piled into a retry storm. With transaction volume expected to roughly double and the infrastructure budget not doubling with it, more hardware wasn't the answer anyway.

Tracing showed where the 47 ms went: roughly 12 ms resolving metadata to find where the data lived, 18 ms on cross-node coordination and replication acknowledgements, about 8 ms on lock contention, and about 4 ms on connections and network. Ritvik is careful to call these representative attributions from span-level analysis rather than exact maths, but the proportions were reproducible. Very little of the request path was actual transaction work. His analogy is a hospital where each visit gets a random doctor who first has to fetch your file from another department.

## Hash the key, land on the owner

The fix is deterministic routing: hash the transaction's primary key with the same partition key the database uses, and send it to the node most likely to hold that range. He's clear the idea isn't new; Dynamo-style partition-aware routing and Calvin's deterministic scheduling came first. What's different is applying it early, at the application and routing layer. The database (CockroachDB in their case, but the principle carries to Spanner, YugabyteDB, TiDB and DynamoDB) still handles correctness, replication and consensus. Routing just makes expensive coordination rarer on the hot path.

Two details matter. Use consistent hashing with virtual nodes, not modulo, so adding a node doesn't remap most of the keyspace and churn every cache. And choose the key carefully: stable, high cardinality, aligned with access patterns.

## Shared connection pools ate the gains

Routing was half the story. Their first multithreaded version shared a connection pool across threads and performed worse than the single-threaded baseline, because threads spent their time fighting over pooled connections. The fix was thread-to-node affinity: each worker thread owns a dedicated pool for its node group, with round-robin scheduling, async I/O and persistent connections.

## Burstable QoS was the hidden 15 ms

The best debugging story: staging benchmarks looked excellent, but production ran about 15 ms slower at comparable traffic. After weeks chasing network paths, database tuning and garbage collection, the culprit was Linux CPU throttling of containers in burstable QoS. Setting CPU requests equal to limits (guaranteed QoS) for latency-sensitive pods stabilised the tail. They also used StatefulSets for the database layer, co-located application pods near database nodes (same zone, sometimes same rack) and scaled on latency-aware signals instead of CPU.

The results: p50 from 18 ms to 8 ms, p95 from 34 ms to 14 ms, p99 from 47 ms to 19 ms, with throughput improving even more.

## Where determinism hurts

Ritvik spends real time on limits. Routing without resilience is fragile: when a node failed, every request mapped to it failed within seconds, so they added replica-aware failover and small queues for in-flight requests. Hot partitions still hash to one place and need splitting or dedicated capacity. Leaseholders move during rebalancing, so routing works on probability and must tolerate misses. Multi-key transactions see smaller gains. His homework for viewers: check your partition strategy, set requests equal to limits on latency-critical pods, measure p95 and p99 before and after, and track the share of requests landing on the right node.

## Who should watch

Anyone running a distributed SQL database behind a random load balancer, and anyone whose staging and production latencies mysteriously disagree on Kubernetes.

Title: Real-time payments leave no 2 a.m. maintenance window
Description: Priyatham Nagaiya Seenu Naidu (Mastercard) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on Kafka, consistency choices and zero-downtime schemas for 24/7 payment rails.
Body:
Batch settlement had one quiet luxury: a maintenance window at 2 or 3 in the morning. Real-time payment rails took it away. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Priyatham Nagaiya Seenu Naidu, Lead Software Engineer at Mastercard, walks through what that means for databases and DevOps when RTP, FedNow, UPI, Pix and SEPA Instant all run 24/7/365 with sub-second expectations and no off-peak hours.

It's a broad survey of the architecture, from streaming to compliance, rather than a single war story. Useful as a map of the moving parts and the decisions each one forces.

## Every transaction is an event now

The shift is from processing data on a schedule to processing each transaction the moment it happens. Priyatham puts event streaming at the centre: Apache Kafka for durable, distributed event logs with exactly-once semantics, and NATS or RabbitMQ for lightweight low-latency messaging. Kafka's partition model matters most to him because it scales horizontally while preserving per-account ordering. You can't process a debit before the credit it depends on, and you can't reorder events. Ingestion, validation, fraud scoring, settlement and notification all hang off the stream.

## Pick your consistency model on purpose

The database section is the core of the talk, with three rules:

- **Consistency is a deliberate choice.** Ledger updates and transactional flows need strong consistency; downstream analytics and notifications can often live with eventual consistency. His line: don't let the database choose for you.
- **Schema evolution happens with traffic flowing.** You can't take the system offline for migrations, so you rely on backward compatibility, strict schema change rules, feature flags, schema registries and rolling deployments.
- **High write pressure needs idempotency.** Write-optimised storage and connection pooling help, but in a distributed system retries are inevitable, so idempotency keys and retry-safe operations make sure a transaction is processed once even if the request arrives several times.

He also covers ISO 20022, which he describes as more than a message format: a schema-driven data model for rich remittance data, straight-through processing and real-time validation, adopted by FedNow and RTP among others.

## Always-on infrastructure, in three patterns

Microservices isolate failure domains, so a fraud service outage doesn't take settlement down with it. Kubernetes supplies auto-recovery, rolling deployments and horizontal pod scaling. And multi-region active-active databases accept writes in more than one region with consensus-based conflict resolution, so a regional outage doesn't stop payments. He contrasts Raft, with its leader-follower model that is easier to reason about operationally, and Paxos, which underpins systems like Spanner.

## Observability, fraud and security

"You cannot secure what you cannot see" runs through the last third. OpenTelemetry tracing follows a payment across dozens of microservices; latency percentiles, throughput and error rates become the primary SLAs; every log line carries a correlation ID, and adding region, country and city to log records shortens diagnosis from hours to seconds. Fraud detection gets its own constraint: the model has to run inside the transaction's latency budget, which pushes you to streaming feature engineering and lightweight models. Security is zero trust (network location is not a trust boundary), PCI DSS encryption and tokenisation, and PSD2 strong customer authentication, all treated as architectural constraints from day one rather than later additions.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving a payments or ledger platform from batch to streaming, and database teams asked to support one. If you've already built real-time rails, it's a good checklist; if you're new to the domain, it shows where the hard decisions are.

Title: Continuous Agentic Deployment runs a Kanban board of AI agents
Description: Denis Ermakov at Conf42 LLMs 2026 shows CAD, an open-source GitHub-only pipeline where agents analyse, code and test, and a human kicks the deploy.
Body:
Getting a model to write code is the easy ten percent; the other ninety is retries, validation, cost control and a clear point where a human stays in charge. That is the claim Denis Ermakov, Lead Software Engineer at Tehpotok, makes at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, and he backs it with a live, open-source pipeline called Continuous Agentic Deployment (CAD) that keeps shipping features while he talks.

The talk opens on a project board where cards move with nobody touching a keyboard. The app those agents built, CAD Console, is the dashboard that visualises the pipeline itself, which is a pleasingly recursive demo.

## GitHub is the whole runtime

There's no orchestrator service: no Temporal, no Airflow, no database. A GitHub Project board is the state machine (columns are states, moving a card is a transition), GitHub Actions is the agent runtime (each agent is one workflow run, with the secrets and logs you already trust), and issue comments are the context bus. Every station writes its output as a comment the next one reads, so the comment thread doubles as the audit trail.

The board has eight columns: to do, ready, SABA (system and business analysis), dev, test, human review, deploy, done. A one-line request like "show a KPI card naming the quickest shipped feature" goes in; the analysis agent turns it into affected files, approach, acceptance criteria and edge cases for the agents downstream.

## Work in progress limits make it a pull system

A dispatcher ticks over the board, checks each station's WIP limit and spawns a workflow run for any free slot. In the demo dev has a limit of one and analysis two, so analysis stalls when dev is busy, exactly like a human Kanban team. Idle agents don't exist, so idle capacity costs nothing.

Models and WIP limits live in repository variables, not code. Denis shows Claude Sonnet 4.6 on analysis and test, with pricier models reserved for dev and for the fixer and merge-conflict agents. Changing the economics of the line is editing a variable.

Every station has the same five-part shape: workflow, prompt file, WIP limit, model, board column. Adding a security-review stage means a new prompt, a copied workflow, a column and one hop in the dispatcher, with no changes to existing stations. That inversion of control is why he calls it a framework rather than a clever repo.

## Reliable lines from unreliable parts

Agents get things wrong, so the conventions carry the reliability:

- The spec lives in the tests. Acceptance criteria from analysis become the test suite, and code moves only when it passes.
- Self-correction is bounded. A failing card gets up to three fix attempts; as Denis puts it, "Three, not infinite, because infinite is just a way to burn money and stack the problem." After that the line stops and hands it to him.
- Every card works on its own branch, so parallel agents never share a working copy. When two features edited the same stylesheet, a resolver agent rebased and fixed the conflict without him.
- The deploy has no model in it. It is a deterministic script that merges, builds, ships and then checks that the live URL reports the exact commit it just built. A human presses the button, by design.

He is candid about the limits too. Agents do well on small, well-scoped, test-backed changes and struggle with ambiguous specs and big cross-cutting refactors. The real bottleneck was good issues on a codebase where features are additive, not the model. And today the engine is still fused to the one app it builds; pulling them apart is next.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers wondering how to put coding agents into CI/CD without buying an orchestration product, and anyone who has run Kanban and wants to see WIP limits applied to agents. If you only want a prompt library, skip it; the prompts are the least interesting part.

Title: The more experience you gain, the less freedom you give the model
Description: Andrii Veremiienko (Revolut) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on AI-assisted Android work: rules files, a core UI module and no code you cannot explain.
Body:
"The more experience I gain, the less freedom I gave to the model." Andrii Veremiienko, an Android engineer at Revolut, calls that sentence the main lesson of his talk at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026. He reached it by using AI coding tools in two very different places: a large fintech Android codebase, and his own indie apps, Loggia and Padel Coach.

The comparison is the interesting part. The symptoms in each world were different, but the root cause was the same: a model that is allowed to make architectural decisions will make a lot of them.

Note on scope: the abstract frames the session around LLM features inside mobile apps. The talk itself is mostly about building apps with AI assistance, and how to stay in charge of the code while doing it.

## Fast code, slower understanding

The speed-up was real. Andrii estimates each indie app would have taken around six months the traditional way; with AI the first production version took roughly two, on weekends and evenings. Custom animations and canvas components that once took days got easy, and basic tests became cheap enough to write early.

But the bottleneck moved. He shipped more code than before, which meant more code to read, review and own. In his words, AI did not make engineering discipline less important; it made it more important.

## Freedom shows up as anarchy

His early prompts were "build a feature" plus a few screenshots. It worked, which was the trap. The happy path ran, and weeks later the bill arrived: the model had invented its own abstractions and managers, and solved local problems without the global picture. In the indie apps, where nobody else enforced an architecture, every task got its own little design. He calls the result solid suffering: single responsibilities split so finely that several pieces did the same job.

The UI suffered the same way. Treated as separate tasks, screens got different back buttons, different navigation animations, and errors shown as a toast on one screen, a snackbar on another and a dialog on a third.

At Revolut the failure looked different. The architecture already exists, and the model's code often made sense in isolation but wouldn't survive a serious review, because a big codebase has several ways to do the same thing and only some are current. He also saw over-testing: valid but fragile, implementation-specific tests that cost time to review and to run.

## The fixes are boring on purpose

- **Context before code.** Study how similar problems were solved, note what's legacy or deprecated, and store it in project notes or the model's memory. His workflow is notes, understanding, plan, then the smallest reasonable change.
- **Rules files early.** Pick the architecture, package structure, core libraries, error handling, navigation, offline behaviour and dark theme up front. Adding offline support later with AI, he warns, is close to impossible.
- **A strict testing prompt.** Ask for behaviour-focused tests, then turn the preferences into a reusable skill. A useless test generated quickly is still useless, so delete it.
- **A core UI module first.** Colours, typography, spacing, buttons, sheets, error pop-ups. A screenshot tells the model what to build; a design system tells it how the product behaves everywhere.

The rule underneath all of it: don't merge code you can't explain. If a library call or decision is unfamiliar, stop and ask the model to explain it, and write the lesson down.

## Who should watch

Mobile developers using Claude, Codex or similar tools day to day, especially anyone running a side project where they are the only architect. Engineering leads deciding how much autonomy to give coding agents will find a useful counterweight to the more-autonomy-is-better pitch.

Title: Database DevOps with Cortex Code starts with a role that can't drop
Description: Tim Spann (Snowflake) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 runs database operations from the Cortex Code CLI and starts by locking down what the agent may touch.
Body:
Before you type a single prompt into a database agent, decide what it is not allowed to do. That is the first piece of advice Tim Spann, Senior Solution Engineer at Snowflake, gives at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, in a demo-heavy tour of Cortex Code, Snowflake's coding agent, doing day-to-day database operations from natural language.

This is a vendor talk and says so: it shows Snowflake's own tool, on Tim's own demo account, with his cat making a cameo. What makes it useful beyond Snowflake shops is how he sets the agent up and what he trusts it with.

## Permissions first, prompts second

Tim's rule is blunt. If you don't want the agent dropping objects, give it a role that cannot drop objects. If it should only see one database or one schema, scope it to that. Read-only is an option. Don't hand it your own credentials and don't give it full access.

In the demo the agent runs under a dedicated key-pair user that can only reach demo data, on a warehouse assigned just to it, so its compute cost shows up on its own line. He also runs Cortex Code on a Raspberry Pi 500 on an isolated network with no root access, which is the hardware version of the same idea. Only inside that kind of fenced-off environment does he switch to the mode where it stops asking for confirmation on every step.

## Give the agent house rules, not just a chat box

Consistency matters more to data teams than cleverness, so Tim leans on the standard pieces: an agents markdown file that records his preferences (users, directories, what he likes), MCP connections to the other systems he uses, and skills. His install listed 102 skills, from data quality to Iceberg table management, and there's a skill for writing your own skills. The point of skills, as he puts it, is that they carry the best practices so each session doesn't reinvent them.

There are two versions of the tool. One lives inside Snowsight and pops up when a query fails or a typo breaks something; Tim compares it to Clippy, but one that actually works. The one he spends the talk in is the command line, which can also run one-off commands so you can wire it into other systems the way you would the Snow CLI.

## What the demos actually did

The live part is a run of small, real admin chores against his transit and traffic data:

- Find the five largest tables in a schema (the New York MTA bus tracking table came out on top at about 22 million rows), then pull the ten most recent rows, with the agent working out which column is the timestamp.
- Run a "know your data" skill that profiled tables for quality and freshness, with the agent planning six tasks and fixing its own failed queries along the way.
- List running queries, agents, services, dynamic tables, tasks and pipelines, which turned up objects that last ran a year ago and were worth dropping.
- Write those findings to a markdown report, because session memory is handy but a document survives.

He also shows SQL the agent wrote to send a video sitting in a Snowflake stage to a Gemini model and get structured JSON back; it counted 25 vehicles on a busy New York street.

The wider claim is about pace. Tim describes handing the agent a source and having it build tables, tests, a semantic view, Cortex Search, agents and a dashboard in about an hour, while he validates and says yes or no. Treat that as one practitioner's workflow, not a benchmark.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and part-time database admins on Snowflake who want to see what an agent can do with their schema, and anyone outside Snowflake who needs a concrete checklist for giving a database agent a safe sandbox. If you want a vendor-neutral architecture talk, this isn't it.

Title: Continuous reconciliation for insurance ledgers with Kafka and ML
Description: Rakesh Jha (DXC Technology) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on AI general ledgers for life and annuity insurers, from Kafka ingestion to ML anomaly detection.
Body:
How long does your month-end close take? At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Rakesh Jha of DXC Technology, who works on finance systems for life and annuity insurers, argues that a close measured in days is a system design problem, and walks through an AI-enabled general ledger that reconciles each transaction as it posts instead of saving them all for the weekend.

A note on scope: despite the event, this is mostly a talk about event streaming and classic machine learning (LSTMs, random forests, isolation forests) applied to accounting. Language models appear at the edges, chiefly natural language processing of contracts on his watch list. If you work anywhere near insurance finance, that's a feature.

## The numbers he anchors on

Rakesh opens with three figures he attributes to KPMG-published analysis of AI in insurance: around 30% less time on routine reconciliation, 40% less manual intervention in routine accounting, and a 35% faster month-end close. He is careful about the 40%: it means 40% of the work is automated, not 40% fewer people, and the best organisations he works with use the time to make teams smarter rather than smaller. The close gets faster because validation runs all month, so less is left to investigate at the end.

## Four layers of ingestion before any model

Traditional ledgers batch the day overnight, so morning decisions run on stale numbers. His design processes transactions as they happen: a lapse, a death claim or an annuity payment hits the ledger immediately. Apache Kafka carries every financial transaction as an event. A normalisation layer reconciles formats from policy admin, investment, claims and reinsurance systems. Buffer management absorbs the spike from a typical 200,000 transactions a day to two or three million at quarter end without losing any.

## An ensemble of specialists

The ML pipeline runs feature engineering, models, an inference engine that applies regulatory rules in the same step, and an analytics layer that feeds improvements back.

Feature engineering gets the most attention, with a good analogy: a 3 a.m. call from an unknown number means little until you know it's the third in ten minutes from a country you never deal with. Same with money. A premium on the 1st and the same amount on the 28th are different events.

Then the specialists. An LSTM remembers sequences: a policyholder who paid on the 5th for eight years, 96 payments, suddenly paying on the 28th is a pattern break worth flagging. A random forest classifies which account a transaction belongs to and copes with imperfect data. An isolation forest finds the odd one out, like one suspicious death claim among three million transactions.

## Reconcile continuously, not on Fridays

The reconciliation section will feel familiar to finance teams: thousands of items on a Friday spreadsheet, the oldest the hardest to trace, weekend work, then Monday starts again. His point is that the system was designed to accumulate differences, so fix the design. Check every transaction as it posts and flag mismatches immediately. He cites research suggesting roughly 80% less processing time when moving from manual batch to continuous reconciliation. A sliding window learns recurring patterns, like a reinsurance treaty that always produces a timing difference on the 15th, and stops flagging them.

Anomaly detection has two layers: statistical checks such as z-scores on every transaction, and semi-supervised learning from past fraud cases and reserve errors. Compliance validates each transaction against current rules (NAIC regulations, state requirements, Sarbanes-Oxley) before posting, with immutable logs and versioned rules so auditors can see exactly what applied when.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects in insurance and fintech, especially anyone who owns a batch ledger. LLM specialists looking for prompt patterns won't find them here. The closing watch list of blockchain for reinsurance, NLP over treaties and edge computing at agencies is speculative and labelled as such.

Title: Multi-vendor DOCSIS fleets need one behaviour contract
Description: Harsha Vardhani Talluri at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on standardising chipset behaviour and telemetry across DOCSIS vendors to speed validation and triage.
Body:
Two cable modems can both pass the DOCSIS spec and still behave completely differently under the same load. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Harsha Vardhani Talluri, a senior network engineer, makes the case for a unified chipset development approach: keep multiple vendors, but standardise how their hardware expresses itself to your systems.

Honest scope first: this is a broadband networking talk, not a database one. It earns its place at a DevOps event through its argument about telemetry schemas, validation pipelines and incident triage, which transfers to any heterogeneous fleet. It's also short, around fifteen minutes, and stays at strategy level.

## Spec compliance is not behaviour compliance

Large DOCSIS footprints use several chipset suppliers on purpose, to protect the supply chain. The cost, Harsha explains, is operational fragmentation. Industry standards verify compliance but don't mandate how code executes internally or how faults are handled. Small differences in traffic queuing or error recovery loops get amplified every time firmware changes.

The practical damage shows up in two places. During outages, triage slows down because engineers first have to work out whether they're looking at a network break or a vendor quirk. And operations teams carry a separate mental model and special-case logic for every hardware family.

## Coexistence, not elimination

The proposal isn't to cut vendors. It's bounded innovation: the operator defines strict guardrails for observable behaviour, and suppliers stay free to innovate beneath that abstraction boundary. The functions to unify:

- **PHY and MAC conventions** for channel bonding, symbol rates and burst timing.
- **Dynamic control:** how hardware reacts to automated load balancing, impairments and frequency assignment.
- **Observability:** every chipset maps telemetry, event logs and counters into a single vendor-agnostic namespace.

That last one is the idea most engineers outside broadband can use. If a counter means the same thing on every device, the NOC can pull metrics from one observability stack without custom parsers, alarms become definitive, and mean time to resolution comes down.

## Define, enforce, operate

Harsha frames unification as a continuous discipline across the chipset lifecycle, not a one-time spec: define cross-vendor behaviour rules, enforce them through automated gating, and operate with shared dashboards.

The pipeline effects follow. Test teams move from separate per-vendor validation plans to unified, repeatable suites and reusable artifacts. Certification gets faster because engineers only validate the small, well-understood firmware differences. Provisioning drops device-specific rule branches, and mass firmware pushes run with repeatable upgrade and fallback guardrails.

## Why it matters before the next upgrade

She ties it to network evolution. High-split upgrades extend the upstream spectrum and demand uniform handling of frequency band shifts; next-generation DOCSIS work depends on aligned echo cancellation and profile configuration. Her view is that unification has to come before those launches, because fixing behavioural differences after scale is the expensive way round. The takeaways: standardise early, force one telemetry schema across the fleet, and treat consistency as a design target.

## Who should watch

Network and platform engineers at broadband operators, and anyone running a mixed-vendor fleet (storage arrays, switches, edge devices) who is tired of vendor-specific dashboards. Database engineers looking for database content should look elsewhere on the event playlist.

Title: Four layers for turning LLM experiments into real-time decisions
Description: Mohanraj Varatharaj at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on streaming data, RAG, decision engines and observability for real-time LLM decision systems.
Body:
Most enterprises already run AI somewhere. The hard part is getting a model's output into a decision that happens in seconds instead of after a weekly report. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Mohanraj Varatharaj, a lead software engineer with more than fourteen years on Spring Boot, Kafka and Flink backends, lays out a reference architecture for real-time decision systems built on LLMs, and the places it tends to break.

It's a broad overview with no single case study, which makes it a useful checklist for teams moving from pilots to production.

## From dashboards to decisions

Mohanraj traces the familiar path: static reporting (dashboards a human reads), batch ML (scheduled predictions), streaming analytics (near-real-time alerts, still handed to a human), and finally LLMs in the loop, building context from live streams and recommending decisions directly. Each step removes a manual handoff that turned a minutes-long decision into a days-long one.

## Four layers

His architecture has four components:

1. **Data ingestion.** Streaming pipelines such as Kafka, Kinesis or Flink normalise events from fragmented enterprise sources in real time.
2. **LLM reasoning.** Models with retrieval-based context generate structured recommendations from live operational signals.
3. **Decision engine.** Orchestration logic checks LLM output against business rules, confidence thresholds and governance constraints before anything acts.
4. **Observability.** Every decision is logged and traced, with drift, latency and decision quality tracked over time.

The decision engine is the layer worth copying first: the model recommends, and something deterministic decides whether that recommendation is allowed to act.

## Bad data, bad outcome

The data problems he lists will be familiar to anyone in a large organisation. The same customer transaction or product SKU lives under different schemas in different systems, and an LLM fed both gets confused. Real-time events joined to batch reference data create temporary inconsistencies: yesterday's inventory against today's demand. And when data comes from many teams, nobody is clearly accountable for its freshness or quality.

Governance comes in three tiers. Assisted means the AI suggests and a human decides (slow but safe). Supervised means the AI acts and humans review exceptions. Autonomous means the AI acts alone, with an audit trail so you can find and fix what went wrong.

## Where it breaks at scale

Four bottlenecks get named: provider rate limits that collapse under enterprise volumes, context window management, cold-start latency from serverless deployments that rules out tight SLAs, and the scaling pain of keeping session state across distributed services.

His design principles are concrete. Decouple inference from orchestration. Cache deterministic LLM outputs aggressively. Use async patterns for non-critical decisions. Set hard latency budgets per decision type. Add circuit breakers so a model call can't run forever.

On retrieval, he warns against over-fetching (noise) and under-fetching (missing context), recommends hybrid retrieval with re-ranking, and ties index updates to data changes. Semantic caching and hybrid routing, with local models for common cases and large ones for edge cases, keep cost and latency in check.

For failure, he wants deterministic fallbacks and graceful degradation to simpler models, because silent failure is the bigger risk. Input guardrails block prompt injection and out-of-scope requests; output checks use schema or regex validation plus quality scoring.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers being asked to put an LLM on top of an existing event stream. The talk stays at architecture level, so pair it with something hands-on, but the closing advice holds: audit the data foundations first, define decision tiers before you build, and build observability from day one.

Title: Your hiring problem is a data infrastructure problem
Description: Zeeshan Khan (STV) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on five layers from a legacy ATS to predictive hiring, with skills graphs, vector search and governance.
Body:
Every resume, interview note and candidate email is data, and in most companies it sits in a system built for compliance paperwork. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Zeeshan Khan, HRIS Manager at STV, argues that organisations which think they have a hiring problem usually have an infrastructure problem, and lays out five layers that take recruiting from an applicant tracking system (ATS) to a predictive, self-improving pipeline.

It's an architecture-and-strategy talk from the HR technology side. Expect concepts and examples rather than schemas or code.

## The ATS was never meant to be smart

Zeeshan's starting point: traditional ATS platforms were built for compliance and administrative workflow, not intelligence. Sourcing, resume parsing, interviews and compliance training each store data in a different place, and those stores rarely talk to each other. There are dashboards and reports, but no real-time insight and no prediction. Buying a newer ATS doesn't fix it, he says, because the missing piece is the data foundation, not the product.

## Five layers, each built on the last

His maturity model runs from the basics to what he calls the north star:

1. **Administrative.** The core ATS: job posts, interviews, hires.
2. **Data enrichment.** HRIS, ATS and CRM connected so the process lives in one place. Still descriptive, not predictive.
3. **NLP and embeddings.** Systems that understand the intent of a job description or a resume instead of filtering on keywords.
4. **Skills graphs and vector search.** Skills attached to jobs, employees, tasks and learning, so search works on meaning.
5. **Predictive hiring,** ending in a self-optimising ecosystem where every decision feeds the next.

## Search by meaning, not by filter

The vector search examples are the most concrete part. A keyword filter for Python, New York and a product manager title returns exactly what you typed. A query describing someone with ownership of a product from design through implementation to output surfaces people whose experience matches, even if their titles don't. His other example: an electrician can be matched to a technician role on shared skills and certifications that a title search would never connect.

The catch is the one every data engineer expects. It only works with good data, proper indexing and properly categorised records. In his words, garbage in, garbage out is real.

## From a won contract to a requisition

The predictive layer is easiest to picture through his workforce planning scenario. A company wins a project starting in six months. An agent reads the project's tasks, checks which skills exist in the organisation and who is available, finds the gap, searches internal employees for mobility candidates, then the existing candidate pool, and only then opens a new requisition. Event-driven architecture keeps it current: instead of batch jobs, signals such as a high-priority candidate losing interest trigger a notification with the reason, so recruiters can act before the offer is lost.

Skills graphs also feed internal mobility and retention. Tailored learning paths for every employee in a company of a hundred thousand are impossible by hand, he notes, but realistic when the infrastructure holds the skills data.

## Governance is not optional here

Hiring is a high-stakes automated decision area, and the abstract notes that algorithmic screening tools face active regulatory scrutiny and litigation. Zeeshan's governance list: bias detection, explainability (the system must say why it recommended a candidate, with the evidence), model auditing for accuracy and compliance, and human oversight. He is emphatic that AI supports recruiters and does not replace them. His closing line: the future of hiring is infrastructure plus judgment.

## Who should watch

HRIS and people-analytics engineers planning what to build after the ATS, and data engineers asked to support a recruiting team's AI ambitions. If you want vector database internals, pick one of the talks below.

Title: Your LLM judge is failing silently, and it should be the strongest model
Description: Vsevolod Voropaev at Conf42 LLMs 2026 argues the verifier is an agent system's hardest part and routes cross-family judges with bandits.
Body:
When your agent is wrong, you lose a task. When your judge is wrong, you lose the ability to know anything is wrong at all. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Vsevolod Voropaev, a founding engineer at an early-stage multi-agent startup with two years of production LLM work across three companies behind him, argues that the verifier is the hardest component in an agentic system, not the easiest, and that most teams have their intuition about it exactly backwards.

## Silence is the failure mode we can't see

The story is familiar. The agent works in the demo, someone asks how you know the output is correct, and you bolt on a second model call that rates the answer. For a while the judge and your own eyes agree, so you stop reading outputs. That's when the rot starts: a broken judge and a working judge emit the same artifact, a number.

No exception fires when a judge approves a bad answer. Logs, alerts and dashboards surface events, and a silently wrong verdict is the absence of one. The verifier, in his phrase, is the one component whose failures are invisible by construction.

## The biases are measured, and they compound

Vsevolod walks through findings from the LLM-as-judge literature. Position bias and verbosity bias appear in the original LLM-as-judge paper from Zheng and colleagues in 2023 and have survived every model generation since. Self-preference is worse: work by Wataoka and colleagues found it tracks perplexity, meaning judges favour text that reads like their own. On Arena Hard, he cites a self-preference effect ranging from -38% to +90% across judges. If agent and judge share a model family, you're getting a model nodding at its reflection.

Putting a human on top doesn't close the gap. Dietz and colleagues documented a rubber-stamp effect: people asked to check an LLM's verdict tend to agree with it, even when it's demonstrably wrong. That stacks two correlated verifiers and calls it defence in depth. None of this shows in a ten-example demo; the biases are statistical and appear at scale, exactly where you stopped looking.

## The judge should usually be smarter than the agent

The common setup puts the big model on the agent and a cheap one on the judge, because checking feels easier than doing. Vsevolod takes the verification-asymmetry argument seriously, then shows where it breaks. Checking is cheap only when there is a certificate: multiply the factors, run the code, execute the query. Most agentic tasks have none. Was the summary faithful to the contract? Will this plan reach the goal? Verifying means redoing the reasoning, and a judge can't reliably catch a mistake on a problem it couldn't solve.

His conditional rule: with a cheap certificate, a cheaper judge plus the tool can verify a stronger generator, so lean on the tool. Without one, the judge must be at least as strong as the agent.

Self-verification doesn't rescue you. He cites research showing generation and self-verification don't improve together, and that much apparent self-checking is fake verification: the model writes the words of checking with almost no effect on the answer. Real verification needs independent purchase on the problem: a different model, a tool, a ground-truth outcome.

## Route judges, don't average them

Three judges from one family averaged together give you sharper confidence, not better accuracy. Judges from genuinely different families (Claude, GPT, Gemini) disagree in systematic, measurable ways, and the cases where they split are a live map of where your risk is. Never let a model be the only judge of itself.

Since running a full panel on every output is unaffordable, he frames judge selection as a multi-armed bandit. Each judge or combination is an arm; downstream signals (spot checks, tests, escalations) are rewards. Thompson sampling, dating to 1933, explores early and concentrates on judges that keep being right per task type, and keeps relearning as models and traffic drift. The economics follow: verification at full strength can be the largest line in your inference bill, so you pay for strong judges only on the fraction of tasks near a decision boundary.

## Who should watch

Anyone running LLM-as-judge in production, or about to. The talk is dense with citations and he shares a reading list at the end, so keep the slides handy.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Who Judges the AI Agent? LLM-as-Judge for Testing Non-Deterministic Code Generation](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Liran_Yushinsky_testing_judge_codegen) by Liran Yushinsky, for judges in a code generation setting, where certificates exist.
- [Self-Signed Evidence: Why Your LLM Agent's Green Checks Prove Nothing](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Danila_Redikultsev_evidence_agent_checks) by Danila Redikultsev, a close cousin of the fake-verification argument.

Title: The database risk someone saw but never said out loud
Description: Sheena Yap Chan at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on the VISIBLE framework for getting database risks to decision-makers before they get expensive.
Body:
Most postmortems ask what broke. Sheena Yap Chan wants them to ask what stayed hidden too long. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, the founder of The Tao of Self-Confidence argues that the most expensive database risks are often already known to someone on the team; they just never reach the people who can act in time.

This is the non-technical talk of the event, and it says so. There's no SQL in it. It's about the human path a signal takes from the DBA who spots it to the leader who signs off on the fix.

## The gap sits between seeing and deciding

Sheena defines the visibility gap as the distance between what the technical team sees and what decision-makers understood in time to act. Risks hide in incident response, migration planning, performance conversations, reliability reviews, postmortems and handoffs. She compares it to a child hiding a mistake from their parents: the longer it stays hidden, the bigger and more expensive it gets.

Her reframe is that visibility isn't about attention, it's about protection, for you, the organisation and the customer. And confidence isn't about being loud; it's about saying what needs to be said when it needs to be said.

## Three ways a signal dies

The most practical slide lists three failure modes:

1. **Seen but not shared.** Someone noticed, assumed someone else had it, or was afraid to speak.
2. **Shared but not understood.** The concern was raised in language the listener couldn't parse.
3. **Understood but not acted on.** No owner, no channel, no spotlight.

Anyone who has read an incident timeline with a message from three days earlier saying "this looks odd" will recognise all three.

## VISIBLE, letter by letter

Her framework spells out seven pillars. Voice: can people raise concerns early, and if speaking up is hard, are there other routes such as one-to-ones or anonymous channels? Identity: do people see themselves as part of reliability? Spotlight: what deserves attention right now? Inner work: what keeps people silent? She calls this 80% of the work and draws on her own upbringing, where she was taught to stay in the background. Belief: do people think raising a concern will change anything? If the first one went nowhere, there won't be a second. Leverage: teams working in silos, one person doing everything until burnout. Elevation: turning a technical concern into something a decision can be made from.

## Templates you can steal

The concrete takeaways are phrasing. For migrations, replace "we should be fine" with the risks, the impact and the decision needed. During incidents, people need clear updates, next steps and owners, not more noise. And a five-line visibility statement for any escalation: here is what we are seeing, why it matters, the possible impact, the options, and the decision we need.

For leaders she offers four questions: what are we not seeing yet, what are people afraid to say, where are signals getting stuck, and who needs this information sooner?

## Who should watch

Team leads, incident commanders and the engineer who always notices the slow query first but doesn't like to make a fuss. Engineers after technical depth should skip it; those whose last outage had a Slack message nobody read should not.

Title: Put LLM agents in decision systems as copilots, not deciders
Description: Mazdul Choudhury (Walmart) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 lays out a three-layer architecture for LLM copilots in forecasting and planning workflows.
Body:
The hard question about LLMs in the enterprise has moved on from whether a model can answer a question. It is whether it can support thousands of business decisions a day within cost, latency, governance and stability limits. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Mazdul Choudhury, Staff Product Manager at Walmart, answers with an architecture: LLM agents as copilots inside decision workflows, with humans keeping the judgment and the accountability.

This is a product manager's framework talk. There's no code and no Walmart-specific numbers; what you get is a clean structure for taking an agent from demo to something an operations team will actually use.

## Copilot is a job description

Mazdul's definition is precise. A copilot gathers information, evaluates options, highlights tasks and surfaces recommendations. It doesn't replace people and doesn't make autonomous decisions. Humans own the call; the agent helps them process complexity faster and more consistently.

He uses forecasting and operational planning as the running example, because it mixes structured data (demand signals, operational metrics) with unstructured inputs (external events, market conditions, human expertise). The same pattern, he says, carries over to supply chain, capacity planning and risk management.

## Three layers that can change independently

The architecture matters more than the model choice, in his view, and it has three layers:

1. **Signal aggregation.** Continuously collect structured data (transactions, forecasts, metrics) and unstructured data (documents, reports, logs, communications) into one queryable context layer. Without good context, model sophistication doesn't help.
2. **Agent reasoning.** The LLM evaluates the context, generates forecasts, detects anomalies and recommends actions, and every output carries its rationale. If users can't see why, they won't act on it.
3. **Human interaction.** Users query the system, explore scenarios, validate assumptions and give feedback. This is the layer that stops the system being a black box, and where trust gets built.

Keeping the layers separate makes the whole thing more resilient and easier to deploy.

## Four production problems that tests won't show

Hallucination, decision consistency, latency and cost show up in production however well the model did in testing. His answers:

- **Grounding** is the most important hallucination fix: RAG, structured queries and authoritative internal sources, treated as an ongoing discipline around freshness and monitoring.
- **Multi-step orchestration**: retrieve context, plan, call tools, synthesise. It mirrors how an analyst works, but runs continuously.
- **Additive integration**: wrap existing systems instead of replacing them, deploy in shadow mode, and keep deterministic fallbacks.
- **Progressive maturity**: focused prototype, shadow deployment, human-in-the-loop validation, then scale with monitoring and governance. Jumping straight from prototype to production is, in his telling, why most AI initiatives fail.

His four takeaways fit on a sticky note: architecture before models, ground everything in enterprise data, integrate additively, and measure accuracy, latency, cost and human trust continuously.

## Who should watch

Product managers and engineering leads scoping their first agent inside an existing planning or operations workflow, especially if stakeholders are nervous about autonomy. Engineers after implementation detail should treat this as the map and look elsewhere for the territory.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Human-in-the-Loop MLOps: Production Patterns](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Tejasvi_Nuthalapati_human_loop_mlops) by Tejasvi Nuthalapati, on the human layer in practice.
- [Transforming Inventory Forecasting with Production ML](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Pallab_Haldar_orchestration_workflows_ai) by Pallab Haldar, the forecasting use case with classic ML.
- [AgentCast: Autonomous AI-Driven Time Series Forecasting for DevOps at Scale](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Premanand_Tiwari_forecasting_time_autonomy) by Premanand Tiwari, a more autonomous take on agents that forecast.

Title: Same SQL, three engines, three answers
Description: Muthupalaniappan Ramanathan (DoorDash) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on catching semantic drift across Spark, Trino and Snowflake in CI.
Body:
A query that compiles and runs on every engine in your stack can still return a different number on each one. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Muthupalaniappan Ramanathan, Senior Software Developer at DoorDash, makes the case that "SQL compatibility does not equal semantic consistency", and shows a DevOps framework for catching the difference at commit time instead of on a dashboard.

It's a compact talk, under twenty minutes, and it stays at framework level: no code walkthrough, but a clear testing strategy you can copy.

## Why you have three engines in the first place

Muthupalaniappan starts from the multi-engine reality: teams run Spark, Trino and Snowflake side by side because ETL pipelines, ad hoc exploration and real-time dashboards each favour a different runtime. That flexibility is reasonable. The cost is that the same SQL string can produce three answers, and standard SQL linting and schema tests won't notice.

## Where the divergence hides

The engines aren't buggy; they made different, deliberate design choices. He groups the differences into four:

- **Type handling:** implicit casts, numeric precision and integer overflow.
- **Null semantics:** how nulls propagate through joins and aggregations.
- **Aggregation behaviour:** floating point summation order and distinct-count edge cases.
- **Optimizer decisions:** rewrites that can silently change which rows are included or how results are ordered.

Each is small. Compounded across a few hundred pipelines and an engine upgrade or two, they become analytical drift: two teams with two "correct" revenue numbers.

## Write the meaning once

The core idea is analytical intent as a first-class abstraction. Instead of writing engine-specific SQL, you declare what the query means in engine-agnostic terms. A canonical semantic layer translates that intent into each dialect using deterministic rules, and humans never write dialect-specific SQL by hand. That removes handcrafted drift between copies and keeps one source of logical truth.

## Then make CI prove it

A semantic layer alone isn't enough, he argues; it has to be enforced. Every commit or schema change triggers a semantic diff and a cross-engine dry run, and an equivalence assertion has to pass before merge. Drift becomes a PR blocker rather than a production data incident.

The four test types are the most reusable part of the talk:

1. **Equivalence tests** assert identical results across engine pairs on a reference dataset.
2. **Null boundary tests** exercise rare but critical null paths.
3. **Precision regression tests** keep floating point aggregations within a set tolerance across engine upgrades.
4. **Translation snapshot tests** pin the generated SQL so an unintended compiler change shows up as a diff.

Merge-time checks don't end the job. In production he runs queries across engine pairs, compares result fingerprints, alerts on metric divergence and uses lineage-aware attribution to find the source of a drift. Trust in the numbers, in his framing, is an operational property you enforce, not a feature you ship once.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers running more than one query engine, and anyone planning an engine migration who wants a test harness for "did the numbers change?". If you run a single warehouse, the null and precision tests still make a good checklist for your next upgrade.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Closing the Semantic Gap with Feedback-Driven Ontology Learning](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Ravi_Chandra_llms_analytics_semanticlayer) by Ravi Chandra, another approach to keeping analytical meaning consistent.
- [Data Quality and Validation in ML Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sunil_Kumar_Mudusu_data_quality_validation) by Sunil Kumar Mudusu, validation patterns for the data feeding those queries.
- [Effective Observability in PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Other SQL Databases](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Adam_Furmanek_observability_postgresql_mysql) by Adam Furmanek, for watching what the engines actually do.

Title: An AI-maintained architecture hub so agents can reason across services
Description: Lior Schejter at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on a Git repo of AI-written markdown facets that gives agents system-wide context across many microservices.
Body:
Drop a coding agent into one repository and it feels like magic. Ask it to fix a bug spanning six microservices and it's flying blind. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Lior Schejter, Lead R&D Architect, shows how he fixed that with an Application Architecture Hub: a plain Git repo of markdown files that AI agents write, keep current on every merge, and read when they need the system-level picture.

The best part is how little infrastructure it needs. No graph database, no wiki platform, no servers.

## The same AI that's hungry for context can write it

The underlying problem predates AI. In a large microservice system, tracing a flow across services, or finding where data is used and changed, is possible but slow and doesn't scale. Humans are notoriously bad at keeping documentation current. Agents raise the stakes because they need that documentation to work well, and they also happen to be good at producing it: reading code, matching semantics, doing it tirelessly.

## Flat files beat the graph database

Lior's team did prototype graph databases first, because modelling a system as a graph feels natural. Flat markdown won. Agents read it natively, Git provides versioning, diffs and pull requests for free, and there is nothing to operate. He calls the robust architecture a temptation the team decided was premature optimisation.

The unit of ingestion is one repo, but documentation is split into facets: domain models, exposed APIs, events, dependencies and more. Questions to the hub tend to cut across services along one facet. Tracing a bug wants events and APIs for a set of services; assessing blast radius wants dependencies. Facets also make ingestion parallel and retries cheap.

A strict naming convention maps a repo and a facet to exactly one file path. If you know what you're looking for, you know the file name, with no search or lookup in between.

## Agents write it, scripts check it, citations keep it honest

An orchestrator agent dispatches one sub-agent per facet. Each reads the same repo, extracts its slice, and writes its own file, so they run concurrently without polluting each other's context, and a failure retries only that facet.

Early on, the ingestion agent was asked to lint its own output. That was unreliable, and since every check was mechanical (file locations, broken links, front matter), it moved into a script. His summary is an old lesson: don't use AI where you don't need it.

A GitHub Actions workflow triggers updates on merges to main for relevant repos, and opens a pull request for human review. Those reviews caught real gaps, like a non-standard Kafka publishing pattern in some repos that left events undocumented; the skill was updated to recognise it. With confidence built up, updates can merge automatically.

The single most effective measure against hallucination and run-to-run drift: requiring every claim to cite a file name and line numbers. Structured templates helped too, and repos built on consistent frameworks such as NestJS produced noticeably better documentation than older, looser code. To control cost, an update skill diffs the code against the hub and rewrites only what changed.

## Querying is where the value is

Query skills, distributed as a plugin to the team's Cursor installations, tell agents how to navigate the hub and connect files. An incident troubleshooting agent uses the hub alongside its log, Jira and Slack tools. Ready-made reports turn common questions into one prompt: a dependency map for a repo (including implicit dependencies through a shared database), flow descriptions with a plain-English variant for product managers, and architecture overviews for onboarding.

The latest step maps business terms to the repos that own or consume them. Because those mappings can't be anchored in code, low-confidence ones go to a human audit, and confirmed mappings survive future updates.

He says the initial prototype took one or two weeks, built mostly by one person.

## Who should watch

Teams with dozens or hundreds of services who want agents to help beyond a single repo. It's also a good reference for anyone tempted to build a knowledge platform before trying a folder of markdown.

- [Context Engineering for DevOps: Turning Your Infrastructure into a Reasoning Graph](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Roxane_Fischer_context_reasoning_infrastructure) by Roxane Fischer, the graph approach Lior decided against, applied to infrastructure.
