Title: Your GPUs are mostly waiting, and a Go profiler can show why
Description: Amol Lele of Hewlett Packard Enterprise at Conf42 Golang 2026 on a low-overhead Go profiler that finds ML training bottlenecks while jobs still run.
Body:
The most expensive line on an ML training bill is often a GPU doing nothing while it waits for the next batch. [Amol Lele](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Amol_Lele_real_time_training), Sr. Principal Cloud Developer at Hewlett Packard Enterprise, used his Conf42 Golang 2026 talk to walk through a multi-layer profiling system written in Go that makes those bottlenecks visible while training jobs are still running, rather than after the budget is spent.

The talk's title promises cutting costs by 50%. The abstract frames the outcome as training costs reduced by 30-50%, with profiler overhead of 2-5%, so keep that range in mind rather than a single headline number.

## Why existing profilers don't help in production

Amol's diagnosis is that teams debug reactively: failures surface after an expensive run, budget is gone before the root cause is known, and each failed experiment gets pricier. The usual tools each miss something. Framework profilers carry heavy memory overhead and huge trace files, fine for short sessions but not for continuous production use. Infrastructure dashboards show cluster-wide utilisation but not causality; low GPU utilisation doesn't tell you why. Log-based analysis adds overhead and arrives after the run is over.

## Why Go

The design goals are low overhead, visibility across application, system and infrastructure layers at once, real-time anomaly detection, horizontal aggregation across clusters, and modular support for new hardware. Go fits the collector side neatly: each subsystem runs as its own goroutine feeding shared aggregation channels; channels provide structured telemetry transport with backpressure; gRPC streaming and connection pooling come without low-level tuning; and static, cross-compiled binaries deploy easily onto heterogeneous fleets. Edge collectors sit close to the training job, with local aggregation and a recommendation engine above.

## Three failure modes worth paying for

The talk organises its findings around the three most costly patterns:

- **Data pipeline bottlenecks.** GPUs idle while waiting for data, hidden under averages that look acceptable. Causes include storage latency spikes, CPU saturation during augmentation, garbage-collection pauses in Python workers and serialisation overhead. Fixes: asynchronous prefetching, adaptive worker scaling on queue pressure, locality-aware scheduling, and dashboards that show queue depth, preprocessing latency and GPU idle time together.
- **Communication overhead.** As clusters grow, synchronisation dominates, and minor network jitter cascades into cluster-wide stalls. Remedies: gradient compression, hierarchical synchronisation, topology-aware scheduling, overlapping communication with computation.
- **Stragglers.** A distributed job moves at the speed of its slowest worker. The hard part is why it's slow: thermal throttling, network instability, data imbalance or contention.

The abstract attributes 40-50% of GPU underutilisation cases to the data pipeline, which matches the talk's emphasis that it's the most common and expensive one.

## Answers, not dashboards

The recommendation engine combines deterministic rules, statistical thresholds, time-series analysis and historical comparison, and outputs actions such as increasing preprocessing workers, enabling gradient compression, checking thermal instability on specific nodes or rebalancing shards. The abstract reports 85% accuracy in root-cause identification and an average 32% throughput improvement.

A profiler must not become the bottleneck, so overhead is engineered down with object pooling and reusable buffers to ease GC pressure, adaptive sampling, non-blocking buffered channels so collectors never block training, and graceful degradation that drops low-priority telemetry under heavy load. Amol also notes the energy angle: idle accelerators still draw substantial power, so shorter, better-fed runs cut energy and cooling too.

## Who should watch

ML platform engineers, MLOps teams paying for GPU clusters, and Go developers building low-overhead telemetry agents. There is no code on screen, but the failure taxonomy and overhead techniques transfer directly.

Title: Breaking an insurance monolith into Go services without breaking compliance
Description: Sulabh Jain at Conf42 Golang 2026 lays out a roadmap from legacy insurance core to Go microservices, Kubernetes and event-driven claims.
Body:
A hurricane makes landfall, claims volume spikes, the claims intake service waits synchronously on fraud detection, fraud detection slows under load, and the mobile app times out for everyone. [Sulabh Jain](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sulabh_Jain_building_cloud_native), a business applications supervisor, used that scenario at Conf42 Golang 2026 to make the case for decomposing legacy insurance core systems into Go microservices that talk through events.

The talk is a practical roadmap for Go engineers handed an insurance modernisation, covering architecture, operations and the organisational part he calls the hardest.

## Why monoliths hurt insurers in particular

Carriers are squeezed three ways: customers who know what a good digital product feels like (and are handed a twelve-step portal with a PDF upload), rising regulatory demands on a platform that can take six months to ship a change, and insurtechs who, in Sulabh's words, aren't smarter than your engineers but don't carry the same architectural constraints. Monoliths add quarterly releases, all-or-nothing scaling and deployments that can take the whole system down.

## Why Go for the core

His three reasons are specific to the domain. Performance: single binaries with no JVM, low memory overhead and many concurrent requests at low latency. Simplicity: a deliberately constrained syntax that stays readable across years of staff turnover on a financial system. And explicit error handling, because in insurance an unhandled error can mean a wrong premium or a wrong claim decision. Add that Docker, Kubernetes and Prometheus are themselves written in Go, and the toolchain fits.

## Cut along the business, not the stack

Service decomposition is where he says modernisation succeeds or fails. Split along bounded contexts (policy, claims, billing, underwriting), not front end, back end and database, or you build a distributed monolith with all the complexity and none of the independence. Each service owns its data store, which he calls non-negotiable, and exposes a versioned API contract. To find the boundaries, put engineers, business stakeholders and subject-matter experts in a room and map domain events: policy bound, claim received, payment processed.

## Events break the cascade

Back to the hurricane. Instead of calling fraud detection and waiting, claims intake publishes a claim-received event to a durable stream (Kafka, EventBridge or Pub/Sub; the pattern matters more than the product). Fraud scoring, adjuster assignment and customer notification each consume at their own pace, and if fraud detection falls behind, intake doesn't care and nothing is lost.

Without shared databases, cross-service consistency needs patterns such as Sagas with compensating events or an outbox, rather than distributed locks and two-phase commits, which he says introduce worse failure modes than they solve.

## Operations, partners and the slow part

Kubernetes provides autoscaling for claim spikes, self-healing and canary or blue-green delivery; Terraform, Helm and Argo CD make environments reproducible; CI/CD runs functional tests, SAST, dependency audits and performance gates on every commit. Partners such as MGAs and aggregators get API-first contracts with version bumps for breaking changes and centralised OAuth 2.0 or mutual TLS at the gateway.

The hardest change is organisational: teams organised by technical function will reproduce that structure in their services, which is Conway's law collecting its fee. Sulabh's mitigations are domain-aligned teams with end-to-end ownership, a platform team that hides Kubernetes complexity, service meshes for mTLS and retries, and running the legacy system in parallel behind an API facade so there is never a non-compliant window mid-migration.

## Who should watch

Go engineers and architects in insurance or any regulated, monolith-heavy domain. Experienced microservice teams will know most patterns; the value is seeing them mapped onto policy, claims and billing.

- [An Introduction to Saga Pattern for Distributed Transactions](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Dmitry_Khorev_saga_pattern_distributed_transactions) by Dmitry Khorev, for the consistency pattern the roadmap relies on.

Title: AI test agents on top of go test, with confidence thresholds
Description: Rejenish Kiran of Citizens Property Insurance at Conf42 Golang 2026 on adding AI test agents to Go suites under escalation and audit rules.
Body:
A deterministic test either passes or fails. An AI test agent gives you an answer with a confidence level, and in an insurance company that difference has consequences. [Rejenish Kiran](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Rejenish_Kiran_assisted_test_execution), QA engineering manager at Citizens Property Insurance Corporation in Florida, used his Conf42 Golang 2026 talk to argue that AI belongs as an augmentation layer above existing Go test suites, and only with explicit thresholds, escalation paths and fallbacks.

It's a short talk, roughly ten minutes, and it's a governance framework more than a tooling demo. That brevity suits the message: the hard part isn't the agent, it's deciding what you let it decide.

## Augment, don't replace

The agents he describes interpret plain-language requirements, turn business intent into executable validation steps, and navigate interfaces adaptively, which makes them more resilient when DOM structures, identifiers or content change. Rejenish cites research showing context-aware locator techniques hold up better under that drift, moving maintenance away from fixing broken locators and towards checking genuine behaviour changes.

He is equally clear about the limits: large-scale enterprise validation of these approaches remains thin, especially in regulated industries like insurance and banking. So the Go side stays in charge. Table-driven tests, benchmark suites and integration harnesses remain the core execution layer, and go test remains the source of truth. AI adds orchestration, telemetry, confidence scoring and escalation, mostly in system and acceptance testing, integrated into GitHub Actions, GitLab or Jenkins.

## Confidence decides what happens next

The most reusable idea is confidence-based escalation. A mature setup shouldn't emit only pass or fail:

- high-confidence outcomes proceed automatically;
- medium-confidence results go to an engineer for review;
- low-confidence cases escalate to humans or block the release;
- if classification itself fails, deterministic execution is the fallback.

Thresholds and escalation policies have to be defined before anything probabilistic runs in a regulated pipeline. Think of it as a circuit breaker for judgement.

## Test artifacts are compliance evidence

In regulated environments, Rejenish notes, test execution records double as compliance evidence. So every AI action has to be explainable, attributable and reproducible: decision logs, traceability from requirement through execution, replayable sessions for audit. Failure has to be safe too. When confidence drops, the system moves along defined fallback paths (pause for human input, fall back to deterministic Go scripts, open an escalation ticket) instead of landing in an undefined state.

He also points to learning-based defect prediction: models trained on historical execution data to rank which tests are most likely to fail, so the riskiest run first and time to first failure shrinks.

## Adopt in phases

The rollout advice is incremental: start in observation mode, add augmentation where it pays, then scale across the portfolio, with governance and evidence collection maturing alongside.

## Who should watch

QA leads and Go teams in finance, insurance or healthcare evaluating AI test agents, and anyone who has to explain a probabilistic test result to an auditor. If you want a hands-on framework walkthrough, this isn't it; take the escalation model and build your own.

Title: Self-healing infrastructure starts with telemetry, not with AI
Description: Sudhakar Pallaprolu at Conf42 Golang 2026 on Go control planes that detect, diagnose and remediate failures, with observability built first.
Body:
Systems don't fail politely: they fail at 3am, in cascades, faster than whoever holds the pager can open the runbook. [Sudhakar Pallaprolu](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sudhakar_Pallaprolu_autonomous_cloud_infrastructure), speaking for the Indian Institute of Engineering Science and Technology at Conf42 Golang 2026, asked what it would take for infrastructure to detect, diagnose and repair itself without waiting for a human, and why Go is a good language for the control plane that does it.

It is a fifteen-minute overview of AIOps patterns rather than a build-along, but its ordering of priorities is the useful part, and it puts telemetry first.

## Humans are the slowest step in the loop

The argument opens on reaction time. With a person in the loop for every remediation step, recovery is capped by how fast someone reads an alert. A modern Go deployment is dozens of interdependent microservices, and a failure in one can spread across the dependency graph before detection even fires. The window between incident and resolution is what self-healing tries to shrink.

Sudhakar's model has three pillars: detect (real-time anomaly detection on logs, metrics and traces), diagnose (ML-driven root cause analysis across all those signals at once, rather than a human reading one service at a time), and remediate (automated but policy-gated responses), with a learning loop feeding past resolutions back in.

## Go fits the pipeline, garbage in still wins

The Go case is the concurrency model: goroutines fan out across thousands of concurrent signal streams, channels hand data cleanly between detection, analysis and remediation phases, and context propagation cancels work for an incident that is already handled.

But he is explicit that speed is useless without good input. The observability layer, built with OpenTelemetry in Go services, needs structured, machine-parsable logs, time-series metrics for latency, errors and saturation, and distributed traces that follow one user's transaction across the dependency graph. If the data is incomplete, no pipeline will find the root cause, however fast it runs.

## Predict on trends, not thresholds

The predictive section is the most practical. Rather than alerting when something is already broken, models watch leading indicators such as memory pressure, connection pool saturation and disk I/O trends. Sliding-window aggregations compare each window to the previous one to surface degradation, which is a trend, not an alert. That triggers pre-emptive actions: pod restarts, shifting traffic between nodes or sites, scaling capacity. And the models need continuous retraining, because services change and yesterday's normal drifts.

## From runbooks to closed loops

Orchestration, in his telling, has moved from static IaC templates with manual gates, to event-driven automation on thresholds, to closed-loop orchestration where policies are evaluated against runtime context and corrective actions are dispatched deterministically. Cloud tools such as Azure Automanage, AWS Fault Injection Simulator and GCP Active Assist are presented as building blocks you wire into your own Go control plane. Reconciliation loops written in Go enforce declared state and revert unauthorised drift; policy as code keeps non-compliant deployments out of production. Kubernetes operators have been doing a version of this for years, and the talk extends the same idea upward.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers sketching the case for automated remediation, and teams who want an ordered checklist: observability, then policy, then prediction. It stays at the pattern level, with no code or incident numbers, so experienced operator authors will find it familiar.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Self Healing Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Nick_Hodges_self_healing_systems) by Nick Hodges, the earlier, broader take on the same goal.
- [Securing the Future: How AIOps Drives Operational Resilience on AWS](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Indika_Wimalasuriya_aiops_resilience_aws) by Indika Wimalasuriya, AIOps applied on one cloud in detail.
- [Chaos Engineering + Generic Mitigations: The Path to Self-Healing Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Leonid_Belkind_generic_mitigations_self_healing_systems) by Leonid Belkind, on testing the remediations you automate.

Title: One Go codebase, many binaries, and a vulnerability scanner problem
Description: Akshaya Jayaram of Salesforce at Conf42 Golang 2026 presents AMMF, attention-based fusion for spotting the same vulnerability across architectures.
Body:
Go's party trick is that one codebase cross-compiles for every GOOS and GOARCH you care about. [Akshaya Jayaram](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Akshaya_Jayaram_ammf_attention_based), M&A Security Principal at Salesforce, pointed out at Conf42 Golang 2026 that the same trick is a blind spot for security: identical logic produces very different binaries, so signature-based vulnerability detection struggles, and false positives pile up for whoever does the triage.

Her talk presents AMMF, an attention-driven multi-feature fusion approach for finding vulnerable functions across architectures, compilers and optimisation levels. It is a research-method talk, closer to a paper walkthrough than a tooling demo.

## Why the binaries don't match

Compilers reorder instruction sequences and calling conventions. Optimisation flags reshape control flow. Architecture differences hide semantic equivalence. The result is that a signature written for one build often says nothing useful about another, and keeping signatures per OS and architecture doesn't scale. For a security team doing due diligence on acquired code, as Akshaya does, that translates into a lot of noise and very little trust in the alerts.

## Three streams, weighted by attention

AMMF builds a function embedding from three kinds of evidence:

- **Semantic stream:** instruction-level embeddings that surface any code resembling a given vulnerability class, tagged by architecture.
- **Flow stream:** a gated recurrent unit (GRU), a network suited to sequences, models how instructions and data move, with self-attention correlating those flows to how a vulnerability class typically behaves. The point is that the bug often isn't one instruction but the way a function is called or how values pass between functions.
- **Function-level features:** argument counts and positions, call frequency, return behaviour, fused with control-flow features through an attention-augmented convolutional network.

Attention decides how much each stream contributes to the final call. If only some of the expected behaviours appear, the finding is downgraded rather than raised at full severity.

## Cast wide, then verify with the graph

Detection runs in two stages. Stage one uses a neural similarity model and nearest-neighbour search to pull every candidate function that might be related, deliberately broad. Stage two runs control-flow graph matching on those candidates only, comparing branching and sequence structure to confirm the real vulnerabilities. The graph acts as the verifier, which is where false positives drop, and because the expensive matching only runs on stage-one candidates, it saves compute. Haystack first, needle second.

The claim is that this holds across ARM and MIPS, GCC and Clang, and optimisation levels from O0 to O3, because the method reasons about instruction sets and control flow rather than byte patterns. The abstract reports strong accuracy and recall in those scenarios; the session itself doesn't present a results table, so read the specifics in the underlying work.

## Who should watch

Security engineers who audit third-party or acquired Go binaries, researchers working on binary similarity, and anyone whose SCA tooling flags the same issue differently per platform. Go developers looking for a scanner to install today won't find one here; it is a method, not a product.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Bridging the Security Tool Gap for Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Munawar_Hafiz_bridging_security_tool) by Munawar Hafiz, on why Go has historically been underserved by security tools.
- [From Pain to Gain: Vulnerability Management that developers won't hate](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Anthony_Laiuppa_vulnerability_management_developers) by Anthony Laiuppa, for what happens after a finding lands.
- [Malware Hunting - Using python as attack weapon](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2022_Filipi_Pires_malware_hunting_attack_weapon) by Filipi Pires, a hands-on look at binaries from the attacker's side.

Title: Catching project cost overruns before they hit the ledger
Description: Venkat Kamma of StarGroup Innovations at Conf42 Golang 2026 on Go microservices that add ML-based governance to Oracle Cloud PPM with zero ERP changes.
Body:
In most Oracle Cloud PPM shops, a cost overrun is something you read about in a report after the money has gone. [Venkat Kamma](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Venkat_Kamma_from_reactive_predictive), Senior Oracle Cloud PPM Solution Architect at StarGroup Innovations LLC, used his Conf42 Golang 2026 talk to describe a framework that moves that check to before a transaction posts: concurrent Go microservices that embed ML inference into project financial workflows without modifying Oracle Cloud at all.

That last constraint is the most interesting design choice. Anyone who has tried to customise an ERP knows that the cheapest customisation is the one you never make.

## Reactive governance fails three ways

Venkat frames the problem around grants, capital projects and large portfolios. Cost overruns surface only after budget thresholds are breached, when recovery options are thin. Revenue leakage, missed billing opportunities, goes unnoticed until the financial cycle closes. And compliance violations against federal grant rules, ASC 606 and contract-specific terms get found in audits instead of being stopped at entry.

## Five layers around an untouched ERP

The architecture is event-driven. Oracle Cloud emits events; a Go API gateway handles intake, routing and orchestration; concurrent Go validation pipelines check transactions in real time; ML models score events and flag anomalies; and a governance layer turns that into decisions. Oracle keeps running on its standard APIs and event streams. All the intelligence lives in the Go service layer, which Venkat argues also makes the pattern portable to other ERPs.

On top of that sit the named engines:

- **Allowability Intelligence Engine:** intercepts transactions before posting and evaluates them against grant regulations, contract cost structures and internal policy, so non-compliant costs never reach the ledger.
- **Forecast Drift Learning Engine:** learns from historical spend, utilisation and forecast deviations and recalibrates projections before drift turns into a material variance.
- **Funding-to-Forecast Intelligence:** predicts burn-rate risk across overlapping awards and can recommend reallocating funding between them before an overrun escalates.
- **Revenue Leakage Sentinel:** streams transactions to spot unbilled milestones, missed cost transfers and revenue recognition timing issues instead of waiting for month-end reconciliation.

A decision-intelligence layer adds scenario modelling and what-if simulations for executives.

## Where Go fits

The Go argument is the throughput one: goroutine fan-out for parallel transaction evaluation at ingestion, stateless HTTP clients calling ML endpoints that scale horizontally, and clean API boundaries per engine. Nothing exotic, which is rather the point for financial systems that auditors will read about.

The talk reports outcomes in qualitative terms: faster invoice cycles, better revenue capture, progressively improving forecast accuracy and fewer compliance incidents. There are no published figures in the session, so read it as an architecture pattern rather than a benchmark.

## Who should watch

ERP and finance-systems architects, especially in grant-funded or project-based organisations, and Go engineers asked to bolt intelligence onto a system of record they are not allowed to touch. If you want model details or code, you'll need to follow up with the speaker.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Advancing Security and Compliance in Revenue Management Systems with AI and Cloud Solutions](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Vikas_Vallakonda__security_compliance_revenue) by Vikas Vallakonda, the revenue-compliance angle from the previous Golang edition.
- [Transforming Financial Workflows: Harnessing Automation in Multi-Cloud Ecosystems](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Naveen_Gowda_financial_automation_ecosystems) by Naveen Gowda, on automating finance workflows across clouds.
- [So You Want To Build An Event Driven System?](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_James_Eastham_event_driven_system) by James Eastham, for the event-driven groundwork this framework assumes.

Title: Go as the orchestration layer for LLM-driven grocery commerce
Description: Sanjay Basu of TCS at Conf42 Golang 2026 maps where Go services sit in LLM commerce, from search and catalog enrichment to substitution and agents.
Body:
When a shopper types something like "quick high protein for tonight", someone has to turn that into structured filters, a vector lookup, an inventory check and a ranked answer before the shopper gives up. [Sanjay Basu](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sanjay_Basu_building_cognitive_commerce), Global Head for AI and GenAI Products at TCS, argued at Conf42 Golang 2026 that this is an architecture problem first and a model problem second, and that Go is a natural fit for the layer that does the coordinating.

It's a compact architecture tour, short on code and long on patterns. Treat it as a map of where Go services sit in an LLM-backed grocery and e-commerce stack, not as a build guide.

## Three layers, and Go owns the outer one

Sanjay's stack has a data layer at the core (vector store, point-of-sale feeds, everything else the models need), an LLM inference layer for model calls and streaming responses, and an orchestration layer of Go services around both. That outer layer does intent routing at the gateway, assembles context from user history and inventory state, and streams tokens straight to the client with no intermediary.

His reasons for Go are the familiar three: goroutines and channels for fanning out many simultaneous LLM calls, predictable low latency, and the operational simplicity of a single static binary. A single commerce request, he notes, may fan out into several model calls (classification, personalisation scoring, inventory-aware checks), and bounded worker pools plus context propagation keep that tractable without an external orchestrator.

## Four places the models earn their keep

The use cases are where the talk is most concrete:

- **Search and personalisation.** Natural-language queries become structured filters; clickstream, basket history and loyalty data are assembled in Go and injected into the prompt to ground it. Embedding generation runs on backend worker pools, and popular query embeddings get cached with a short TTL.
- **Catalog work at scale.** LLMs classify new SKUs into category trees and extract attributes from messy descriptions, images and spec sheets; Go pipelines then validate those attributes against the catalog schema and backfill gaps such as nutrition data and allergen flags.
- **Substitution and demand sensing.** When an item is out of stock, an LLM-backed service ranks alternatives by semantic similarity, dietary compatibility and price or margin delta, with a target of under 200 milliseconds.
- **Fulfilment and agents.** Order, picking, dispatch and last-mile stages pass events over channels with queues and circuit breakers between them. LLM agents interpret pick exceptions and slot conflicts, while Go services execute the approved actions with full audit trails.

## Autonomy needs more guardrails, not fewer

The closing caveats are the part to remember. Design for streaming, fan-out and context assembly before choosing a model. Autonomous agents need stronger observability and stricter circuit breaking, and Go services are the enforcement layer. And govern cost from day one: trace every LLM call end to end with OpenTelemetry, tie token spend to business outcomes, and build token budgets, model tiering and per-intent routing into the gateway before the first production deployment. Every CIO complaining about token bills is the joke, and it isn't really one.

## Who should watch

Architects and Go engineers adding LLM features to retail or marketplace backends who want a vocabulary for the moving parts. If you need benchmarks, code or a case study with numbers, this isn't that talk.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Golang-Powered Retail Distribution: Transforming Supply Chains Through Cloud-Native Innovation](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Ankam_retail_distribution_supply) by Srinivas Ankam, the supply-chain end of the same retail stack.
- [The Retry Storm That Ate My Budget](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Yamini_Rathamsetty_Karthik_Akula_cost_loops_tokens) by Yamini Rathamsetty and Karthik Akula, on what ungoverned token spend looks like.
- [Cloud-Powered Retail: Serving Future Needs Today](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Rustam_Orudzhev_retail_services_optimization) by Rustam Orudzhev, for the cloud side of retail platforms.

Title: Conf42 Cloud Native 2026: agents become infrastructure
Description: Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 roundup: 29 talks on running AI agents like services, securing MCP and cloud automation, migrations and EU compliance on AWS.
Body:
Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 ran online on April 23, 2026, with 29 talks under the familiar promise of *everything Cloud Native and Cloud Security*. The thread running through the day: AI agents and MCP servers are turning into ordinary infrastructure, with all the lifecycle, security and cost problems that implies, while the older cloud questions of migration, compliance and observability haven't gone anywhere. The full lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2026) and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrAk91tnHP48BKjDFW9jzf1V).

## Agents need the tooling pods already have

[Andrew Espira](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Andrew_Espira_ai_agents_automation) of Kustode asked the question several other speakers circled: you have `kubectl` for pods, `docker` for containers and `helm` for charts, so what do you use for the agents and MCP servers piling up on your machine and in your cluster? His answer is `agentctl`, a zero-dependency Go CLI that registers, health-checks, starts, stops and discovers them like any other managed service, with a live TUI dashboard on top.

[Elizabeth Fuentes Leone](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_ai_llm_applications) of AWS tackled a cost problem that grows with every tool you add: agents serialise every tool description into the context on every call, then pick the wrong tool anyway. Her semantic tool selection uses vector search to filter tools before they reach the model. [Sandeep Mannapur](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Sandeep_Mannapur_ai_agents_workflows) of ServiceNow covered what changes when a single chat interface becomes a distributed system of collaborating agents running real workflows, and [Dhivya Dhayakar](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Dhivya_Dhayakar_ai_llm_prompts) of Zscaler proposed intent-based orchestration as the fix for enterprises with a dozen isolated copilots and no shared governance.

## The new plumbing is a new attack surface

If agents are infrastructure, so are their connectors. [Aleksandr Pinaev](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Aleksandr_Pinaev_security_vulnerabilities_compliance), founder of Swordfish Security, catalogued how cloud MCP servers fail: misplaced trust boundaries, excessive privileges, weak isolation and vulnerable connector logic, plus the defences that work.

Older automation got the same scrutiny. [Leo Visser](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Leo_Visser_cloudarchitecture_infra_design) of OGD ICT-diensten asked whether your PowerShell and other cloud automation is quietly creating attack surface of its own. Security engineer [Aleksandra Drobnjak](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Aleksandra_Drobnjak_security_zerotrust_encryption) walked through real Azure attack techniques from Microsoft's Digital Defense Report, from hybrid identity abuse to trusted relationships, with demos. And [Rajasingh Gandhi Ramdas](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Rajasingh_Gandhi_Ramdas_distributed_systems_architecture) of IBM looked further out, at moving multi-cloud APIs off RSA and elliptic curve cryptography before quantum computers make that urgent.

## Migrations without the big bang

Harness's keynote came from [Ryan Vila](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Ryan_Vila_feature_flags_migration), who argued that migrations fail because of how they're released, not how they're coded. Flags route traffic gradually from old service to new, and measuring from the point of change makes regressions visible that fleet-wide dashboards would hide. His case study from Split, the company Harness acquired, moved a batch pipeline to streaming behind a flag and cut processing time from 10 hours to 15 minutes.

[Ran Tao](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Ran_Tao_data_analytics_insights) of AWS explained why lift and shift doesn't work for messaging systems moving from on-premises to the cloud. [Devinder Tokas](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Devinder_Tokas_cloudarchitecture_backend_systems) of Microsoft made the case for interoperability by design to avoid lock-in across clusters and clouds, and [Purushotham Jinka](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Purushotham_Jinka_ai_llm_optimization) of Citi traced how partitioning and indexing strategies change when databases go cloud-native.

## Compliance as an engineering problem

The most opinionated talk of the day was [Dmytro Hlotenko's](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Dmytro_Hlotenko_distributed_systems_resilience) "Keep Calm and Run on AWS". Dmytro, a senior cloud operations engineer at Sage in Austria, offered a practitioner's defence of running AWS in regulated European environments: what actually needs solving, what is compliance theatre, where Outposts helps and where it quietly fails, and how to keep a stack your team can still operate at 3am. He opened with a disclaimer that he's an engineer, not a lawyer, which is more than most sovereignty debates manage.

[Manasa Uppula](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Manasa_Uppula_data_streaming_realtime) treated digital onboarding in financial services as an architecture problem, where consent boundaries and interaction integrity have to be audit-ready by design. [Karthik Ravva](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Karthik_Ravva_ai_agents_reasoning) of Austin Energy argued that data governance has to be embedded in the lifecycle once AI-powered BI depends on it.

## Operations and real systems in production

[Uudit Misra](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Uudit_Misra_distributed_systems_reliability) of Salesforce asked why dashboards show green while users see failures, and answered with eBPF-based network observability for Kubernetes, deployed as DaemonSets instead of relying on iptables and sidecars. [Sampath Rao Madarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Sampath_Rao_Madarapu_distributed_systems_scaling) of Microsoft showed Copilot in Azure as an assistant for diagnostics and resource management.

Two case studies stood out for being about systems that run today. [Anton Solomonov](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Anton_Solomonov_computer_vision_verification) of SIMPLE described a computer vision system that verifies spare parts at warehouse receiving for a manufacturer supplying the mining industry, with confidence thresholds, exception handling and human-in-the-loop checks for parts that look nearly identical. [Gautham Paspala](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Gautham_Paspala_data_warehousing_analytics) of ServiceNow tackled friendly fraud, where a legitimate purchase becomes a fraudulent dispute weeks later, using temporal graph attention and transformers.

## Sponsors

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), our diamond sponsor, to gold sponsors [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) and [Virtana](https://www.virtana.com/), and to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) for the podcast partnership.

## What's next

All 29 talks are linked from the [Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 page](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2026). The series returns with [Conf42 Cloud Native 2027](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2027) on April 8, 2027, by which point your MCP servers will presumably need their own on-call rotation.

Title: Beyond the Toggle: Feature Flags as Your Cloud-Native Migration Safety Net
Body:
## Beyond the Toggle: Using Feature Flags to De-Risk Cloud-Native Migrations

Cloud migrations, API rewrites, and large-scale architecture transformations rarely fail because engineers cannot build the new system. More often, they fail because organizations attempt to release too much change at once.

A cloud migration often combines infrastructure changes, application updates, data movement, routing changes, and new operational processes. When all of these elements are introduced simultaneously, teams create a single high-risk event where identifying and recovering from problems becomes significantly more difficult.

During his session, *Beyond the Toggle: Feature Flags as Your Cloud-Native Migration Safety Net*, Ryan Vila, Americas Advisory Director at Harness, explored how feature management enables organizations to replace risky cutovers with gradual, observable, and reversible migration strategies.

### Why Cloud Migrations Create So Much Risk

Many migration initiatives begin with good intentions but quickly become coupled to a traditional release mindset.

Teams often build a new service, deploy it, and then switch all traffic to the new system in a single event. This approach creates several common failure modes.

The first is the "big bang" release. Multiple changes are bundled together and activated simultaneously, making it difficult to isolate the source of problems when issues emerge.

The second challenge is the lack of a practical rollback path. Organizations frequently discover that moving forward is easy, but moving backward is complex, time-consuming, or impossible without disruption.

The third problem is uncontrolled blast radius. If every user is exposed to a migration immediately, even minor issues can quickly become major incidents.

Successful migrations require teams to treat releases differently. Instead of viewing migration as a single event, they need a framework for introducing change gradually while maintaining the ability to observe, pause, and reverse progress when necessary.

### The Strangler Fig Pattern in Modern Architectures

One of the most widely adopted migration approaches is the Strangler Fig Pattern, originally popularized by Martin Fowler.

Rather than replacing an existing application all at once, teams introduce new services alongside existing systems and progressively redirect traffic toward the new implementation.

This creates a period where both systems operate in parallel.

The value of this approach is not simply technical flexibility. It provides an opportunity to compare old and new behavior in real-world conditions. Teams can evaluate performance, reliability, cost, and user experience before fully committing to the new architecture.

Once confidence has been established, the legacy service can be retired and the technical debt associated with maintaining parallel systems can be eliminated.

Feature flags provide the control layer that makes this gradual transition practical.

### Decoupling Deployment from Release

A key principle of modern feature management is separating deployment from release.

Deployment simply places code into production. Release determines who can actually use it.

By introducing feature flags, engineering teams gain the ability to deploy new functionality without immediately exposing it to every customer.

This enables a progression such as:

- Internal users and engineering teams
- Test accounts and synthetic traffic
- Designated customer groups
- Small production cohorts
- Gradually increasing percentages of traffic
- General availability

Each stage creates an opportunity to validate assumptions before moving forward.

Instead of asking whether the migration succeeds or fails, teams can continuously evaluate whether the migration is producing the desired outcomes.

### Progressive Rollouts Reduce Migration Risk

Canary releases and percentage-based rollouts are often discussed in the context of application features, but they are equally valuable for infrastructure and platform transformations.

A small rollout may mean exposing 1% of traffic to a new service.

For another organization, it could mean routing a specific region, customer segment, or internal department through the new architecture.

The exact definition depends on business requirements and risk tolerance.

The important principle is that every increase in exposure should be accompanied by measurement.

A migration that performs well at 5% traffic may behave very differently at 50% or 100%.

Scaling is itself a test, and each expansion should be treated as a validation step rather than an automatic progression.

### Measuring More Than Deployment Success

Traditional migration programs often focus on a simple question:

**Did the deployment complete successfully?**

Modern engineering teams should evaluate migrations against business and operational outcomes.

#### Performance

Latency, throughput, and response times provide immediate feedback on whether the new implementation delivers improvements over the existing system.

#### Reliability

Error rates and service-level objectives help determine whether stability improves or deteriorates as traffic increases.

#### Cost

Cloud migrations are frequently justified by efficiency gains. Measuring infrastructure consumption and operational expenses throughout the rollout helps validate whether expected savings are actually being realized.

#### Customer Experience

Aggregate metrics can hide problems affecting specific user groups.

Engineering teams should analyze behavior across different cohorts, platforms, regions, and usage patterns to identify issues that may not appear in overall statistics.

A migration that looks healthy at a global level may still introduce significant friction for a specific segment of users.

### Monitoring Versus Measurement

One of the most important distinctions highlighted during the session is the difference between monitoring and measurement.

Most organizations already have dashboards, alerts, and observability platforms.

However, observability alone does not necessarily reveal the impact of a specific change.

In production environments, background noise is constant. Small increases in error rates or latency may be difficult to detect when viewed across the entire system.

Measuring from the point of change creates a different perspective.

Instead of asking how the application is behaving overall, teams can evaluate how the newly introduced migration path is performing relative to the baseline.

This approach makes it easier to identify signals that would otherwise be hidden inside broader operational metrics.

The result is faster detection, clearer attribution, and more informed release decisions.

### A Real-World Migration Example

Ryan Vila shared an example from Split, the feature management and experimentation platform later acquired by Harness.

The company operated a data processing pipeline responsible for handling massive volumes of customer telemetry.

As customer adoption increased, costs grew linearly with traffic volume. Processing times also became a concern, while customers demanded greater visibility into data quality and ingestion reliability.

The engineering team redesigned the pipeline architecture to support more scalable processing patterns.

Feature flags were used to route traffic between the legacy pipeline and the new implementation.

Rather than performing a risky cutover, traffic could be progressively redirected and evaluated throughout the migration.

The results were substantial:

- Approximately 80% reduction in operational costs
- Processing time reduced from roughly 10 hours to 15 minutes
- Migration completed within a single quarter
- No customer-facing disruption during rollout
- Improved visibility and quality controls for customers

The example demonstrates that feature flags are not limited to user-facing features. They can also become a critical mechanism for controlling infrastructure evolution behind the scenes.

### Avoiding Common Feature Flag Pitfalls

Feature flags introduce flexibility, but they also require governance.

#### Stale Flags

Flags created for temporary migrations should not remain indefinitely.

Unused flags increase complexity, create confusion, and may introduce future operational risk.

#### Untested States

Every flag includes multiple potential states, including fallback behaviors.

Teams should validate each possible outcome rather than testing only the primary path.

#### Configuration Drift

Flag definitions must remain consistent across staging, production, and disaster recovery environments.

Differences between environments can create unexpected behavior during critical incidents.

#### Ownership Ambiguity

Every flag should have a clearly defined owner.

When an incident occurs, teams must know who is responsible for evaluating, modifying, or disabling the flag.

Without ownership, response times increase and operational risk grows.

### Building a Safer Migration Strategy

Feature flags are often introduced as a way to control application functionality.

Their broader value lies in helping organizations transform how they manage change.

By decoupling deployment from release, engineering teams gain the ability to:

- Introduce change gradually
- Reduce blast radius
- Validate outcomes continuously
- Roll back safely when needed
- Measure business and technical impact
- Modernize systems without disrupting customers

Cloud migrations will always involve risk. The goal is not to eliminate that risk entirely, but to manage it through controlled experimentation and progressive delivery.

Organizations that treat migrations as a series of measurable steps rather than a single release event are better positioned to deliver successful transformations while maintaining reliability, performance, and customer trust.

Title: An MCP server in Go should be narrow, gated and boring
Description: Shadi Elyafi at Conf42 Golang 2026 on a Go MCP server over AppSync GraphQL for 1M+ company profiles, with default-deny mutations and TDD.
Body:
Most MCP demos end the moment a model successfully calls a tool. [Shadi Elyafi](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Shadi_Elyafi_mcp_b2b_workflow), Lead Golang Developer at METRO AG, starts his Conf42 Golang 2026 talk exactly there and asks what happens when the tool touches real business data: a company intelligence platform with more than one million company profiles, reached through GraphQL on AWS AppSync, with Claude as the client.

His answer is that the protocol is the easy part. The production question is how much power each tool gets and how precisely its behaviour is defined.

## The server is a contract-enforcing layer

The architecture is three boxes. Claude, or any MCP client, handles user intent and picks a tool. The Go MCP server sits in the middle, built on MCP Go, doing dispatch, schemas, validation, mutation gating and response shaping. AppSync stays the GraphQL boundary into the backend, and the platform stays the system of record. Claude never talks to GraphQL directly.

So a request like finding SaaS companies in Germany with 50 to 100 employees never travels as a sentence. The client selects a search tool, the server parses typed parameters, trims input, resolves "DE" to the backend's value for Germany, and caps limits: default 10 results, never more than 100, because a valid query over a million profiles can still be useless. On the way back, nested backend responses get flattened into one stable record shape (ID, name, country, employee range, domain, industry text) so the model isn't guessing which nested field matters.

Authentication stays inside that boundary too. With OIDC bearer tokens the client acts on behalf of a specific user, so backend authorisation, audit trails and data scoping behave as if that user called the API directly. The MCP layer inherits the access model rather than routing around it.

## Mutations are off until someone proves they're safe

Nine tools were implemented; eight ship. Six are read-only (search, lookups, AI-assisted search, collections), two can write (add to collection, request email discovery). Read-only tools are constructed without the mutation flag at all, so there is no write path to accidentally open. Write-capable tools receive an explicit allow-mutations flag and fail before any backend work without it.

Shadi is clear that this is not an authorisation model, which still belongs to the backend. It is an operational switch that flips the default question from why not let the client write to what evidence makes this write path safe.

## Test the request, not just the response

The mutation gate was built test-first. The test builds the tool with mutations disabled, calls it, and asserts an error, no result, and, most importantly, that the mock GraphQL client was never called. That last assertion fails the moment someone moves the backend call above the guard.

Mocks also capture the GraphQL variables each tool sends, so tests check limit capping and country resolution, not only whatever the mock returns. A Go interface with one small Execute method (context, query, variables, result pointer) makes that cheap.

Then the honest bit: the ninth tool, Create Collection, passed its mocked tests and then hit a Lambda null pointer failure in the backend when exercised against the real AppSync endpoint through MCP Inspector. The code stayed; the tool was simply not registered. Mocks and real-system validation answer different questions, and you need both.

Rate limits round it out, because conversational follow-ups turn into bursts: AI search at five requests per minute, email discovery at ten per hour.

## Who should watch

Anyone wiring an LLM client into a production API, especially Go teams. It is one of the more concrete MCP talks on the Conf42 shelf: real tool counts, real limits, a real failure. Teams already running per-tool telemetry and default-deny writes will find it confirms rather than surprises.

Title: Correct code can still fail the car, so validate behaviour early
Description: Sana Fatima of General Motors at Conf42 Golang 2026 on behaviour-driven validation that catches cross-module defects before vehicle-level testing.
Body:
A chassis control module can be correctly written, compile cleanly, pass every unit test and still misbehave once it shares a bus with the brakes and the steering. [Sana Fatima](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sana_Fatima_from_code_correctness), Software System Test Engineer at General Motors, spent her Conf42 Golang 2026 talk on that gap: the defects that matter in software-defined vehicles are increasingly behavioural mismatches between correct modules, and the fix is to make expected behaviour an executable artifact from the design phase on.

Despite the conference, this is not a Go talk. It is a validation-process talk from someone with more than ten years in automotive software and system validation, and it applies to any system built from modules that each "work".

## Unit tests stop at the boundary

Sana's framing is that validation falls short in three places. Unit testing ends at the module edge, so cross-module assumptions are never stated, let alone checked. Behavioural intent lives in documents and tribal knowledge instead of anything a pipeline can run. And integration gets tested late, at system or vehicle level, which is exactly where diagnosis and rework are most expensive.

The stakes she describes are structural: modern vehicles carry over a hundred ECUs and tens of millions of lines of code from multiple suppliers, sharing buses and dependencies. One violated assumption can cascade into something safety relevant. Defects found at vehicle validation can trigger regression cycles across supplier teams and even hardware re-spins.

## Coding errors are the easy class now

The sharpest point in the talk is the distinction between coding errors and behavioural mismatches. Modern toolchains, and increasingly AI tools, are good at catching the first. The second is individually correct modules producing an incorrect system outcome, and it needs a different kind of validation.

The classes she lists are worth stealing for any test strategy review: timing violations across module boundaries that isolated tests can't see, violated interface contracts (mismatched assumptions about signal ranges or error handling between producer and consumer), invalid state combinations that only appear under specific input sequences, and faults handled locally that propagate differently once integrated.

## Specs as the single source of truth

Behaviour-driven validation, as Sana lays it out, starts with explicit behavioural specifications treated as a first-class engineering artifact: expected responses, state transitions and timing constraints. They are written in structured natural language such as Gherkin-style given-when-then, or as state machines, and broken down to module level so that software and tests are built from the same source in parallel.

Those specs become executable tests that run on every build and integration event in CI, not once at vehicle level. When a test fails, you check the code and the requirement together, because traceability runs from requirement to test to implementation. That same trace gives you the auditable evidence that ISO safety work and ASPICE expect, which is the quiet business case: the test record doubles as compliance paperwork.

## Who should watch

Test and validation engineers in automotive, aerospace, medical or industrial control, and anyone whose integration phase keeps producing surprises that unit tests swore weren't there. It is conceptual rather than hands-on: no framework demo, no code. If you already run BDD-style specs in CI with requirement traceability, you can skim it.

Title: Design systems that keep up with a fast Go backend
Description: Sonali Priya of LB Networks at Conf42 Golang 2026 on five pillars (modular components, tokens, versioning, governance) that stop analytics UIs splintering.
Body:
Your Go service can slice through millions of rows in real time and the dashboard on top of it can still feel like five products glued together. That mismatch is the starting point for [Sonali Priya](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sonali_Priya_scalable_design_systems), Creative Design Director at LB Networks, at Conf42 Golang 2026: the backend scales, the front end drifts, and a design system is the fix only if it is built like infrastructure.

It is a short, structured talk, about fifteen minutes, and it is a design-architecture talk at a Go conference. There is no Go code in it. What it has is a clean model that backend engineers who own platforms will recognise immediately.

## Fragmentation compounds quietly

Sonali names three patterns she sees almost everywhere. Inconsistency: the button on one dashboard doesn't quite match the button on another, and charts behave differently page to page. Duplication: three teams build the same filter panel three ways, and now you maintain three slightly broken versions. Governance gaps: things get added, nothing gets retired, and accessibility depends on goodwill.

None of these is dramatic on day one. Her point is that they compound, and the bigger the platform, the more each one costs. Anyone who has watched a monolith grow will recognise the shape.

## Tokens are an API contract with three layers

The most transferable idea is the token architecture. Global tokens hold raw values: hex codes, pixel scales, font weights. Semantic tokens map intent onto them, so a component asks for "color primary" or a large spacing step instead of a literal value. Component tokens are scoped to one component and reference the semantic layer.

That layering is what lets you repaint the global palette without touching component code, override one semantic token for one team, or tune a single button in isolation. Platform adapters then compile the same tokens to CSS variables on the web, native values on iOS and Android, and variables in Figma. It is the same trick as keeping config out of your binaries, applied to colour and spacing.

## One system, three surfaces

Analytics products rarely live in one place. Sonali splits them into standalone dashboards (the full system), embedded analytics inside someone else's product (where style isolation matters, so Shadow DOM earns its keep), and density-optimised operational tools for internal teams. Her insistence is that these are not three design systems but one, expressed differently, held together by the shared token layer. Responsive behaviour moves into viewport-specific token values rather than breakpoint logic scattered across components.

## Versioning and governance are where systems live or die

Pillar four is plain semantic versioning plus stable and beta release channels and real deprecation workflows with migration guides. If consumers can't predict what an upgrade breaks, they stop upgrading, and the system is effectively dead.

Pillar five is governance, which she argues decides whether everything else holds. Mature governance means a contribution workflow, review standards covering API design, a11y, tests and docs, accessibility checks automated in CI, and written decision frameworks for disagreements. Her preferred shape is a federated model: a platform team owns primitives, tokens and release infrastructure, product teams own domain extensions built on top of that core, not next to it. Platform engineers will notice this is the paved-road argument wearing a different outfit.

## Who should watch

Engineers who own a shared UI library, platform teams who keep getting asked why two dashboards look different, and backend leads who want vocabulary for front-end drift. If you already run a token pipeline and a federated contribution model, this will mostly confirm your choices.

Title: Computer vision that cut warehouse receiving errors by 99%
Description: Anton Solomonov of SIMPLE at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on a production computer vision check for near-identical spare parts in a mining supplier's warehouse.
Body:
Two spare parts that differ by a millimetre or two in thread or geometry look identical to a warehouse operator on a deadline, and are entirely different SKUs to the mining customer waiting for them. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Anton Solomonov](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Anton_Solomonov_computer_vision_verification), Lead Data & AI Architect at SIMPLE, presented a case study of a computer vision verification step built into warehouse receiving that reduced spare-part mismatches by 99%.

His framing is refreshingly unflashy: the interesting AI cases aren't the impressive demos, they are the ones embedded in a real process that keep working.

## The problem was the process, not the people

The client manufactures equipment and spare parts for the mining industry and receives high volumes of shipments from overseas suppliers. The paperwork said which part numbers should arrive. Reality kept delivering a very similar, different part: supplier mistakes, mixed-up part numbers, one item shipped under another's description.

The usual reaction is to tell people to be more careful and add a manual check. Solomonov argues that couldn't work. Under volume, time pressure and a complex catalog, nobody can measure every part and dig through technical documentation and still hit receiving targets. The business wanted both speed and accuracy, and manual work couldn't deliver both. So the brief became: reduce the probability of error exactly where the error happens. Starting from the process, not the technology, is what kept the design practical.

## A verification service, not an image classifier

The system compares more than pixels. Its data layer combines part photos, catalog images, text descriptions, technical specifications, item master data, historical receiving and error records, and the expected part number for the shipment. Images alone weren't enough, because some differences are too subtle to see. Context like SKU, product family and catalog attributes is what stops the model making a confident wrong call.

The recognition engine compares the photo against reference patterns for the expected item and its closest alternatives. Crucially it doesn't answer only yes or no. It returns a confidence level, the most likely part number, a list of similar alternatives, and the distinguishing features the operator should check. In production, he says, the dangerous system isn't the one that hesitates; it's the one that is confidently wrong.

## Confidence thresholds route the work

The operator takes a photo, the service pulls the shipment context, and the answer comes back in a form that's easy to read. High confidence confirms the match. Medium confidence flags risk and asks for extra verification, like a measurement or a catalog check. Low confidence routes the item to an exception flow. That human-in-the-loop design improved reliability, built trust with warehouse staff faster, and turned every ambiguous case into a new training example.

## Four trade-offs he made on purpose

The engineering section is the best part of the talk:

- **Accuracy versus speed.** Deep validation on every part would wreck receiving throughput, so the system was tuned for usefulness inside the process: accurate enough to catch problem cases, fast enough not to break the rhythm.
- **Automatic decisions versus controlled escalation.** Forcing a final verdict would create dangerous false positives and negatives in edge cases. Thresholds and escalation paths were less magical and more correct.
- **Scalability versus maintainability.** The model, reference data, matching logic, workflow, exception handling and quality monitoring were kept separate so a growing catalog didn't turn the system into a monolith.
- **Trust versus black box.** A bare "not a match" kills adoption. Showing why an item was flagged made the tool an assistant rather than a barrier.

## Production means living by the warehouse's rules

His definition of working in production is operational: available during shifts, fast responses, integration errors that never block receiving, fallback scenarios, monitored quality, and catalog and master-data updates that the system absorbs. Beyond the 99% figure, he points to less dependence on specific experienced employees, more consistent receiving quality and fewer disputes.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and architects taking a vision model out of a notebook and into an operational workflow, especially where errors are expensive and users are busy. The talk has no code but plenty of decisions worth copying.

Title: Stablecoin payment rails need the same SRE discipline as your cloud
Description: Murtuza J Merchant of Yellow at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on stablecoins as payment infrastructure: Polygon's upgrades, Chivo's failures, and five patterns.
Body:
Sending money from London to a supplier in Jakarta through correspondent banks takes two to five business days and $20 to $40 in fees; a USDC transfer on Polygon takes seconds. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Murtuza J Merchant](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Murtuza_J_Merchant_stablecoins_payment), Senior Editor and blockchain analyst at Yellow, argued that stablecoins are cloud-native payment infrastructure, and that running them needs the reliability engineering cloud teams already practise.

Scope note: Merchant is an analyst, and the talk is a mix of market overview and architecture patterns. The market figures, volumes and regulatory timelines are his, quoted as presented; check them before putting them in a slide.

## What makes a payment rail cloud-native

His first-principles argument contrasts SWIFT, ACH and card networks, built in the 1970s and 80s for batch processing with business hours and cut-off times, with a stablecoin: a token pegged one-to-one to a fiat currency on a programmable chain. Four properties make it cloud-native in his view: settlement logic in smart contracts, 24/7 availability, any wallet address as a valid destination, and composability, building financial products on stablecoins the way you build services on APIs.

## Polygon as the scale-up case study

He uses Polygon to show a chain growing from a cheap Ethereum sidechain into payment rails, and maps its upgrades onto familiar infrastructure work. Heimdall v2 moved consensus from Tendermint to CometBFT, which he likens to a database engine swap, cutting finality from minutes to about five seconds. The Rio upgrade introduced stateless validation and removed reorgs; he describes a reorg as a distributed-system rollback you didn't ask for, which is the last thing a payment needs. Raising the gas limit pushed capacity further. The AggLayer, Polygon's cross-chain protocol, is his analogy for multi-cloud: users shouldn't care which chain they are on.

## Chivo is the post-mortem

The counter-example is El Salvador's Chivo Wallet, built for the 2021 Bitcoin rollout. He reads it as a list of missing engineering practices: no load testing for a national launch with a sign-up incentive, no graduated rollout, a single point of failure on the national ID integration that killed onboarding when it failed, no observability into Lightning channel liquidity or routing, volatility exposure from holding Bitcoin, and no offline fallback for a population with patchy connectivity. His conclusion: you cannot ship an MVP for a country's payment system.

## The stack, layer by layer

The production stack he sketches has four layers. On-chain observability: The Graph indexes contract events into subgraphs with a GraphQL API, and Chainlink Proof of Reserve reports verified off-chain collateral on-chain, a continuous check instead of monthly attestations. Compliance as code: KYC rules, jurisdiction restrictions and counterparty eligibility live in smart contracts, enforced across chains with Chainlink CCIP. Custody and settlement: multi-signature and MPC key management (he names Fireblocks and BitGo) or chartered custodians such as Anchorage Digital. API and event streaming: a payment hub routing each transaction to bank or stablecoin rails by cost, speed and destination.

## Five patterns to take home

This is the part for cloud architects:

1. **Multi-region validators** across providers, with health checks, failover and stateless validation so nodes can be replaced without disrupting consensus.
2. **Reserve monitoring as SRE.** Combine Proof of Reserve feeds with subgraph supply data and alert when verified reserves drop below 99.5% of circulating supply. That's a PagerDuty event.
3. **Compliance rules in version control**, run through CI/CD and tested on a Hardhat testnet before mainnet. Terraform for compliance, in his phrase.
4. **Subscribe, don't poll.** Listen to node WebSocket APIs for confirmation events and emit a settlement event to your order system, treasury ledger or ERP once finality is reached.
5. **Hybrid custody**: hot wallets with MPC for low-value, high-frequency payments, cold storage with multisig approvals for high-value transfers, which mirrors tiered storage.

## Who should watch

Cloud architects at banks, fintechs or treasury teams who are being asked about stablecoin rails, and SREs curious what observability means when the ledger is public. Skip it if you want a critique of crypto; this is an advocate's talk with practical patterns.

- [Securing Payment Gateway Evolution: DevSecOps in Microservices Migration](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Silpa_Potluri_payment_api_secure) by Silpa Potluri at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025.
- [Feature Flags as a Migration Engine: De-risking Domain-Driven Decomposition of Monolithic Payment Platforms](https://www.conf42.com/Feature_Flags_2026_Jaya_Chand_Bandi_migration_payment_platforms) by Jaya Chand Bandi at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026.

Title: Harvest now, decrypt later means your API traffic is already at risk
Description: Rajasingh Gandhi Ramdas of IBM at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on post-quantum migration for multi-cloud APIs: ML-KEM, hybrid TLS and crypto agility.
Body:
If your data has to stay secret for ten years, an attacker recording your TLS traffic today is already a problem. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Rajasingh Gandhi Ramdas](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Rajasingh_Gandhi_Ramdas_distributed_systems_architecture), Senior Technical Architect at IBM, laid out how to move multi-cloud API estates to post-quantum cryptography: what to prioritise, which NIST algorithms to use, and why the answer is hybrid TLS plus crypto agility rather than a big-bang swap.

It's a concise strategy talk, about 15 minutes, aimed at architects planning a multi-year programme.

## The threat is retroactive

The motivation is harvest now, decrypt later: adversaries capture encrypted traffic now and wait for cryptographically relevant quantum computers. RSA and elliptic curve cryptography fall to Shor's algorithm. AES-256 and hash functions hold up if you use larger key sizes. So the urgent work is public-key infrastructure: handshakes, signatures and certificates. Trade secrets, health records and strategic plans with a long confidentiality horizon are at risk today.

## The hallways matter as much as the front door

His best point is about where teams look. Everyone thinks of north-south traffic at the gateway, but east-west traffic inside the network is just as exposed to harvesting by an attacker already inside. Hybrid connectivity from cloud to on-prem often runs on legacy VPNs, among the most neglected parts of the estate. Internal CAs and mTLS have to migrate too, or the trust model collapses from the bottom up. In his words, "a quantum proof front door is useless" if the hallways are wide open.

He also stresses there is no single migration path: cloud platforms, mobile apps, third-party integrations and legacy systems all use different TLS stacks.

## Prioritise on three axes

The risk assessment starts with discovery (find the cryptography you actually use), then prioritisation and a migration backlog. Priority is three-dimensional: confidentiality lifetime of the data, with decades-long secrets first; API criticality, meaning revenue impact, regulatory scope and sensitivity; and migration feasibility, separating near-term items from ones needing vendor coordination or redesign.

## The algorithms are settled

NIST's post-quantum standards are published as FIPS 203, 204 and 205, which he sees as the end of the wait-and-see excuse. The portfolio he walks through: ML-KEM (Kyber) replaces RSA and ECDH for key exchange; ML-DSA (Dilithium) for digital signatures; SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) as a hash-based backup with different assumptions; and FN-DSA (Falcon) for compact lattice signatures.

His recommendation is hybrid: derive session keys from both ECDH and ML-KEM, so an attacker has to break both. Classical crypto covers you if the new algorithms have an undiscovered flaw, and post-quantum covers you once quantum attacks arrive.

## Crypto agility is the real deliverable

He frames agility as a five-level maturity model: hard-coded algorithms, a library abstraction layer, centralised certificate management, algorithm choice as configuration, and automated agility with full observability. The goal is to change algorithms through configuration, not code rewrites.

Performance isn't free. Bigger keys mean bigger handshakes, which hurt on high-latency links. His abstract cites public keys 3 to 10 times larger than ECC and 10 to 30% latency overhead. Session resumption, connection pooling and HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 multiplexing offset some of it, and he insists on benchmarking in real production conditions.

## A four-phase roadmap, measured in years

Phase one builds the foundation: inventory, frameworks, library choice. Phase two puts hybrid TLS on sensitive external gateways and critical east-west service mesh traffic. Phase three rolls out to lower-priority APIs and partners. Phase four handles legacy systems and long-tail clients. The abstract puts the timeline at 24 to 36 months, and he calls it a programme touching networking, security, platform engineering, development, partner management and procurement.

## Who should watch

Security architects and platform leads who own TLS termination, service meshes or internal PKI and need a defensible order of work.

Title: Four levels of Azure automation, and the secret each one leaks
Description: Leo Visser of OGD ICT-diensten at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 demos PowerShell automation on Azure, from VM scripts to Functions behind API Management.
Body:
Every step up the Azure automation ladder makes your script easier to run and gives you a new secret to lose. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Leo Visser](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Leo_Visser_cloudarchitecture_infra_design), a consultant at OGD ICT-diensten in the Netherlands and Azure MVP for PowerShell, demoed the same small automation four ways, a scheduled script, an Automation runbook, an Azure Function and a Function behind API Management, and showed how to lock down each one.

It's a hands-on demo talk in the Azure portal and VS Code. The examples are Azure and PowerShell, but he notes most of it has equivalents on AWS and GCP.

## Why automate in the cloud at all

Visser's case is practical. Automation lets you shift tasks left: something that needed a high-privilege sysadmin can be wrapped so a service desk colleague with fewer rights can run it. In the cloud you pay per run instead of keeping compute sized for peak load, and it is easy to connect ticketing, monitoring and security systems.

## Level one: a script on a VM, made stateless

The first demo is a PowerShell script that reads the last hour of entries from a Storage table. Two improvements before anything fancy. Give the VM a managed identity and the script authenticates as that identity with a one-word change, no stored credentials. And fix the silent failure mode: if the job fails once and succeeds an hour later, a query for the last hour has skipped a whole hour of data.

His fix is a watermark. The script reads the last successful check date from Azure Key Vault, queries everything since then, and only writes a new value after success. He takes the new timestamp right after the query, not at the end of a long script, so entries added mid-run aren't skipped. Telemetry goes to Application Insights through the PowerShell module Telemetry Helper, which gives traces, alerts and run durations almost for free. With state in Key Vault, the script no longer cares which machine runs it.

## Level two: Automation runbooks and the webhook token

An Azure Automation account runs PowerShell or Python runbooks on shared infrastructure with managed identities and built-in logs kept for 90 days. Runbooks can be started by a webhook, which is handy for ticketing systems like TopDesk that trigger automation on a button press. The catch is that the webhook URL contains a token, a secret in the URL. Move it into Key Vault so it's out of your code and source control, and remember that arguments travel over the internet unless you add network integration for sensitive data.

## Level three: Azure Functions and rotatable keys

Azure Functions on the consumption tier start almost instantly, have live log streaming and send logs to Application Insights. Authentication is by function key, which works like an API key. You can issue different keys to different callers and revoke or renew one if it leaks. Better than one shared token, but still not a user identity.

## Level four: API Management in front

For user-level authentication, he puts API Management in front of the Function. The function key is stored inside APIM, and a validate-jwt policy on all operations rejects calls without a valid JWT. The demo hit a fun snag: the first call without a token still succeeded because headers were cached in his PowerShell session. After clearing them, the call returned unauthorised as intended. Tokens can then come from a service principal or user sign-in.

## Not every script needs level four

His closing advice is proportionality. A script on a management VM can be fine for something you run rarely. What makes automation resilient is combining the building blocks (managed identity, Key Vault, Application Insights, API Management) where the risk justifies it. His long-term goal, he admits, is a holiday while his automation keeps working.

## Who should watch

Ops engineers and Azure admins who write PowerShell to manage their platform and suspect some of those scripts have tokens in them. If you've ever pasted a webhook URL into a ticketing system, start here.
