Title: Azure attackers don't break MFA, they borrow your legitimate flows
Description: Security engineer Aleksandra Drobnjak at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 walks through ten Azure and Entra ID attack techniques from Microsoft's MDDR 2025, with defenses.
Body:
In device code phishing, the login page is real, the certificate is valid and MFA works perfectly, and the attacker still gets your tokens. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, security engineer [Aleksandra Drobnjak](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Aleksandra_Drobnjak_security_zerotrust_encryption), who works across Entra ID, Defender XDR and Purview in Microsoft 365 environments, walked through ten attack techniques highlighted in the Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2025, each paired with concrete defenses.

It's a long, dense talk, built on the report but translated into settings you can check on Monday.

## Passwords still get sprayed

The report's baseline: modern MFA still cuts compromise risk by more than 99%, yet over 97% of identity attacks are still password spray or brute force. Drobnjak describes what that looks like in logs: waves of failed sign-ins from different IPs and countries, often with the BAV2ROPC user agent that signals legacy authentication, which bypasses modern MFA by design. Her first checklist covers spotting brute force in Defender for Cloud Apps, filtering Entra sign-in logs for legacy auth clients, checking basic auth protocols like SMTP, POP3 and IMAP, and conditional access policies that block legacy auth. Turning it off can break old scripts and integrations, which is exactly the window attackers wait for.

## Social engineering moved into Teams and the Run dialog

Two techniques target people. In the first, attackers flood an inbox with spam, then message on Teams or call, posing as IT support, and talk the user into a Quick Assist session. She names Storm-1811 as linked to such campaigns. Defenses: limit external Teams communication, tell users plainly that IT never asks for Quick Assist through Teams, let them report suspicious messages and calls, and approve only specific remote management tools.

The second is ClickFix: a fake error or "verify you are human" prompt tells the user to press Win+R and paste a command the page put on their clipboard. It runs PowerShell or mshta and pulls a payload into memory with no file on disk. She cites Storm-1865 and phishing that impersonated booking.com. Defenses include awareness training, PowerShell constrained language mode, and hardened enterprise browsers.

## Device codes, sessions and consent: no password needed

The identity section is the core. In device code phishing (Storm-2372), the attacker starts a sign-in, gets a device code, and persuades the victim to enter it on the genuine Microsoft page. The victim completes MFA for the attacker's session. Block the device code flow in conditional access if you don't need it, and watch sign-in logs for it.

Session hijacking skips authentication altogether by stealing tokens through adversary-in-the-middle phishing, infostealers, malicious extensions or tokens left in code. Her layers: conditional access requiring compliant devices, token protection that binds tokens to a device, Continuous Access Evaluation, Credential Guard and LSA protection, then revoke and force re-authentication when in doubt.

Consent phishing gets an attacker's app granted permissions like reading mail, and that access survives a password reset. Her takeaway: "Attackers don't always need credentials. Sometimes they just need your permission." Restrict user consent, require admin approval for sensitive scopes, review app permissions regularly, and report malicious apps to MSRC.

## Help desks, SMS codes and identities that can't do MFA

Temporary Access Passes count as strong authentication, so a convinced help desk can hand an attacker the whole chain. SMS one-time codes fall to callers asking victims to read them back, and to SIM swaps, including cases with insiders at carriers. Workload identities (service principals, managed identities) can't do MFA, often hold broad rights and rarely get reviewed; she cites Storm-0558 forging tokens. Then come proximity tricks and MFA fatigue, countered with number matching, risk-based conditional access and at least two break-glass accounts.

## After the break-in, it looks like admin work

Post-exploitation in Azure often means living off the tenant: Azure Run Command executes scripts on VMs through the agent with no open ports, which looks like an admin troubleshooting. Restrict who can run it, monitor activity logs for it and for role and service principal changes, keep logs tamper-proof and backups isolated and tested.

## Who should watch

Anyone who owns an Entra ID tenant or responds to Microsoft 365 incidents. Even if you know half the techniques, the defense checklists per technique make it a good audit companion.

Title: A cloud MCP server is privileged infrastructure, not a connector
Description: Aleksandr Pinaev of Swordfish Security at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on where MCP security risk comes from, a classification of MCP flaws, and defenses.
Body:
The moment an MCP server advertises tools to an AI client, it joins your trust boundary. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Aleksandr Pinaev](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Aleksandr_Pinaev_security_vulnerabilities_compliance), founder of Swordfish Security, argued that cloud-hosted MCP servers concentrate access, execution and privilege behind one interface, and that the worst MCP bugs are design choices, not coding mistakes.

It's a focused 15-minute threat-modeling talk: where the risk comes from, a classification you can use in reviews, and a list of defenses.

## A capability container is also a risk container

Pinaev's model of an MCP server is a capability container. It tells the client what it can do (scan code, validate policies, read resources, trigger actions) and offers one protocol to discover and invoke all of it. That is elegant for interoperability. It also means trust, permissions, execution logic and external reach now sit behind a single boundary, which centralises risk very efficiently if you draw that boundary badly.

So he treats MCP as a control layer between models, tools and cloud services. It doesn't just move data; it shapes what a simple request can eventually turn into.

## Intent has to be constrained across the whole chain

Classic cloud security reasons about one API calling another. MCP chains are more fluid: a user talks to a model, the model uses an agent, the agent uses an MCP client, the client calls an MCP server, and the server reaches a tool or API. At every hop parameters can change, scope can widen and privileges can quietly expand. The question is less whether one endpoint is secure and more whether intent stays constrained end to end.

That's why he says a system can be unsafe even when the code is fine, authentication exists and the connectors are tested. Too much power in the wrong place, or trust mixed between the wrong components, produces systemic risk anyway.

## Six classes of MCP weakness

His classification gives security teams something to assess and prioritise:

1. Identity and access: weak authentication, token misuse, confused identity, broad scopes.
2. Trust boundary failures and unsafe delegation: hidden privilege changes, implicit trust between model, client, server and tools.
3. Tool and connector exposure: too many callable actions, overly powerful connectors, weak control over what gets registered.
4. Isolation failures: cross-tenant leakage, drift between environments, shared context abuse.
5. Validation and execution flaws: prompt injection, context injection, unsafe parameter handling, dangerous writes.
6. Visibility and control gaps: weak auditability, weak approval logic, weak monitoring.

Real attacks chain these. Injected context steers the model, the model picks a tool, and the MCP server performs a risky read that leaks data. Each step looks small; together they are high impact. Cloud hosting makes it worse: public reachability, harder forensics on ephemeral infrastructure, tokens spread across agents and automation, and trust that drifts between dev and prod.

## Defenses: split reads from writes, gate the dangerous ones

On design, he recommends treating MCP as a privileged execution path, separating read paths from write paths with much stronger controls on writes, constraining tool choices, scopes and allowed parameters, validating execution intent and not only input shape, adding explicit confirmation gates for dangerous or irreversible operations, and isolating tenants, agents, services and environments by default.

Operationally: strong authentication with short-lived credentials, scoped authorisation per tool and connector, allowlists for actions and resource classes where realistic, audit trails covering both MCP calls and their downstream effects, and monitoring tuned to AI-enabled abuse rather than ordinary API errors. His parting advice: "Do not ask only can the model call the tool." Also ask what authority that connection creates and how tightly it is controlled.

## Who should watch

Security engineers, cloud architects and AI platform teams about to put MCP servers in front of production systems. The classification alone is worth stealing for your next design review.

Title: Small businesses run cloud-native stacks without a security team
Description: Vaishali Mahavratayajula of Wells Fargo at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on Security in Your Pocket, a six-layer AI risk framework for small online businesses.
Body:
A one-person online shop today runs a Shopify store, a payment processor, a few SaaS tools, an Instagram DM bot and probably an AI assistant or two. That's a distributed cloud-native estate, and its owner usually doesn't know it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Vaishali Mahavratayajula](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Vaishali_Mahavratayajula_distributed_systems_performance), AI Security Architect at Wells Fargo, presented Security in Your Pocket, a mobile-first, AI-driven risk assessment framework aimed at exactly those owners.

Honest scope: she introduces it as her product idea. The abstract says it is implemented through the securemystore.ai platform for SKRM Technologies and evaluated in simulated small-business cloud environments, so treat it as a framework with early results rather than a field report.

## Too small for enterprise tools, too big for consumer ones

Her framing is a gap. Enterprise security platforms assume dedicated security teams, DevSecOps pipelines and clear ownership models. Consumer tools protect a person, not a business. A small owner who is also the marketer, the accountant and the support desk fits neither, and often can't say what a vulnerability is, what it would cost the business, or how to fix it.

She names four systemic gaps the framework targets: no visibility into cloud assets (forgotten APIs, unmonitored buckets, shadow AI from tools like ChatGPT and Perplexity), no clear security ownership between owner, web developer and anyone else, uncontrolled third-party and AI tool exposure through plugins and integrations, and security tools that don't match how these businesses actually work.

## Six layers, from discovery to attestation

The architecture runs in six layers:

1. **Asset discovery.** You can't protect what you can't see. Continuously find websites, APIs, SaaS tools, store pages and small AI apps, and track how the footprint changes as integrations get added.
2. **Vulnerability detection.** Known vulnerability patterns, misconfigurations, weak authentication, exposed services and overly permissive IAM roles.
3. **Continuous monitoring.** A one-time scan is a snapshot. Plugins update, permissions drift and new endpoints appear, so the framework baselines, detects deviations and notifies the owner in plain language.
4. **AI correlation.** This is the most interesting layer. A publicly reachable API might be a moderate risk on its own, and so might an over-scoped token. If that token can reach that API, the combination is much more severe than either signal suggests.
5. **Business-aligned risk scoring.** Instead of CVSS numbers, scores reflect revenue exposure, customer trust, regulatory obligations and downtime. For an owner, the useful question is how long the shop would be offline.
6. **Continuous attestation.** Automated evidence that the posture holds, so auditing is built in rather than done on demand.

## Plain language is a security control

A theme across the talk is translation. She wants findings free of CVE and CVSS jargon, phrased around one question: why does this risk matter to me? She also argues it reduces friction between developers and security people, who otherwise argue about whether a finding applies at all. Humans stay in the loop for risk ownership; the AI does the noisy work of scanning, correlating and translating.

## Who should watch

Builders of security products for SMBs, and engineers who look after a friend's or family member's online business and suspect its attack surface is bigger than anyone thinks. If you want implementation detail or detection rates, the talk stays at framework level.

Title: How you type and click is a fraud signal, in real time
Description: Sharath Reddy Polu at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on behavioral analytics for fraud prevention: signatures, contextual signals and a real-time scoring pipeline.
Body:
A stolen password gets an attacker into an account, but it doesn't teach them how the real owner types. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Sharath Reddy Polu](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Sharath_Reddy_Polu_cloudarchitecture_backend_infra), a University of Southern California alumnus, presented his published research on behavioral analytics for real-time fraud prevention: building dynamic profiles from navigation, keystrokes, devices and spending, and scoring every transaction against them.

Honest scope: this is a research overview, not a walkthrough of a specific production system. It's useful as a map of the techniques and how they fit together.

## From static rules to behavioral profiles

The starting point is the classic rule: flag a transaction over a certain amount or from an unusual location. Polu puts those systems at about 45% detection, false alerts close to 37% of the time, and an average response of 95 seconds. Behavioral systems in his research reach 87% detection with around 7% false alerts and an eight-second average response, and he reports cost savings rising from 22% to 76%. Those figures come from the research he presented; the talk doesn't break down the underlying datasets.

## Four dimensions of a behavioral signature

The profile is built from four kinds of signal:

- **Navigation patterns**: click sequences, page-flow preferences and interaction timing, which form a distinctive footprint of how a person moves through an app.
- **Keystroke dynamics**: how long each key is held, the flight time between keys, and how someone corrects mistakes. Typing rhythm turns out to be a biometric.
- **Device fingerprints**: OS, browser configuration, screen resolution and installed plugins, checked against devices the user has transacted from before.
- **Transaction sequences**: merchant preferences, timing and amount distributions, so the system can spot activity that drifts from past behaviour.

## Three layers of models, plus explanations

The analytical stack is layered. Supervised models such as decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting learn from labelled legitimate and fraudulent examples. Unsupervised clustering watches for new patterns that don't match established ones, the kind designed to slip past rules. Deep learning models, LSTMs and CNNs, look for sequential deviations and relationships in multidimensional data.

On top sits SHAP for explainability, so an analyst can see why a transaction was scored the way it was. In fraud, where a false positive means a real customer stuck at checkout, that matters.

## Context turns a signal into a decision

Behaviour alone isn't enough, so the systems add context. Location consistency catches impossible travel, like a transaction in New York followed by one in London 30 minutes later, while allowing for real travel and VPN use. Environmental context looks at time zones, connection types, unfamiliar networks and IPs from high-risk regions. Device identifiers flag unknown hardware.

## The real-time pipeline

The architecture he describes has four stages. A collection layer captures behavioral signals at every touchpoint, which he estimates at over 50 signals per transaction. An analysis engine runs neural models, with edge computing pushing some analysis toward endpoints to cut latency. Risk scoring computes a fraud probability per transaction against dynamic thresholds tuned to the individual or their peer group. Then an automated response either blocks the transaction or challenges it with step-up authentication.

The models keep learning from feedback, which he says lets them adapt in days rather than the months-long manual update cycles of rule-based systems.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people in fintech who own fraud rules and are curious what a behavioral approach adds, and security teams thinking about step-up authentication as a risk-scored decision rather than a blanket rule. Expect concepts and reported results rather than code.

Title: Friendly fraud happens weeks after checkout, so model the graph and time
Description: Gautham Paspala of ServiceNow at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on catching friendly fraud with temporal graph attention, transformers and human review.
Body:
Friendly fraud is the one where nothing looks wrong at checkout: a real customer, a valid card, an authorised transaction, delivered goods, and then a dispute weeks later. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Gautham Paspala](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Gautham_Paspala_data_warehousing_analytics), Staff Software Engineer at ServiceNow working on dispute operations for banks, proposed catching it with two attention models working together: a temporal graph attention network over the payment ecosystem and a transformer over each cardholder's history.

It's a short talk, around 15 minutes, that moves from problem framing to architecture to deployment concerns.

## Point-of-sale controls look at the wrong moment

The difficulty is the time gap. Traditional fraud controls try to stop a bad transaction before it clears. With friendly fraud the bad act, filing the dispute, happens long after the sale, when the merchant has already shipped. His abstract puts friendly fraud at 60 to 75% of chargeback volume and more than $48B in annual global losses, as industry estimates.

The baselines he cites are rule-based systems catching 23 to 31% of confirmed friendly fraud, with rigid thresholds fraudsters learn to step around, and traditional machine learning reaching roughly 38 to 47%. The ML ceiling, in his framing, comes from hand-crafted features and a weak grip on relationships between cardholders, merchants and devices, and on how those relationships change over time.

## The payment ecosystem is a graph with timestamps

The first model treats payments as a heterogeneous graph: accounts, devices and merchants, then transactions and IP addresses, then physical and digital addresses. The scale in the talk is issuer-sized: 50 to 100 million cardholder accounts, 15 to 25 million merchants, 10 to 50 billion edges, and 100 to 500 million new edges a day.

Every edge carries a timestamp: when a purchase happened, when a device was used, when an address was linked to an account. That's what lets the model see patterns that develop over weeks. Graph attention then learns which relationships deserve weight. Several accounts sharing one device or IP points to a coordinated ring. One cardholder disputing across many unrelated merchants is a cross-merchant pattern. Nobody writes a rule for either; the attention scores surface them.

## A transformer reads the cardholder's history

The second model processes each cardholder's transactions as a sequence, using self-attention to find which earlier transactions matter most when predicting whether a new one will be disputed. Combined, he argues, the two catch patterns neither finds alone: the graph sees structure, the sequence sees behaviour over time.

## The numbers, and how they were measured

He evaluates with precision, recall, AUC, and cost-sensitive threshold tuning that weighs annoying a real customer against missing a real loss. Against traditional ML, he reports the combined approach reaching 67 to 78% detection, a 40 to 65% relative improvement, and 35 to 45% fewer false positives than rule-based systems. The talk presents these as benchmark results without detailing the dataset, so read them as the framework's claim rather than a production report.

## Deploying it is the hard part

Keeping a graph with tens of billions of edges fresh while hundreds of millions arrive daily, and running transformer inference in near real time, is where the cloud-native part comes in. Three principles: distributed graph databases with partitioned storage and compute; segment-level calibration, with separate thresholds per merchant category and transaction type instead of one global cut-off, which he says sharply reduces false positives; and Kubernetes autoscaling for traffic spikes.

The last piece is human review. Fraud teams decide whether flagged cases really were fraud, and that feedback goes back into training. It keeps false positives falling and helps the model follow fraudsters to new tactics.

## Who should watch

Engineers and data scientists in payments or dispute operations who are past rules and gradient-boosted features and wondering whether graph models are worth the infrastructure. It's a framework talk, not a code walkthrough.

Title: Retina or Cilium? eBPF network observability, benchmarked on EKS
Description: Uudit Misra of Salesforce at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on why dashboards stay green during network failures, and Retina vs Cilium on a real EKS cluster.
Body:
Your dashboards are green, error rate is near zero, and users are getting 500s, because a network policy is dropping packets between two services without telling anyone. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Uudit Misra](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Uudit_Misra_distributed_systems_reliability), who works on the Kubernetes platform team at Salesforce, explained why that happens at the network layer and compared two open-source eBPF tools, Retina and Cilium, on a real AWS EKS cluster.

## Three failures your monitoring can't see

Misra lists three failure modes he has seen in production. Silent drops, where a policy blocks traffic and leaves no log, trace or alert. DNS timeouts in the few seconds while a pod starts up and lookups fail. And wrong backends, where a label change somewhere routes traffic to the wrong place. They share a cause: monitoring only watches what you told it to watch in advance.

His analogy is the car. Monitoring is the check-engine light someone wired to a threshold. Observability is the mechanic who can look under the hood for things nobody predicted. At the network layer that means flow-level records: source pod, destination pod, verdict, and the exact drop reason.

## Why iptables can't get you there

Traditional Kubernetes networking relies on iptables, a long linear list every packet walks. Misra gives four problems. It slows down as rules grow. It is shallow: layer 3 and 4 only, with no HTTP paths, DNS queries or gRPC service names. It has no identity, just IPs instead of pod names. And its drops are silent. None of the questions you ask mid-incident (why did traffic between these pods stop? which DNS query is timing out?) can be answered from iptables alone.

eBPF agents fix that from the kernel. They run as a DaemonSet, one per node, attach small programs to kernel hook points, and export flows to Hubble Relay, metrics to Prometheus and dashboards to Grafana, without sidecars, code changes or restarts.

## Retina sees the packet, Cilium knows who sent it

Retina, open-sourced by Microsoft in 2024, is observability only. It doesn't replace your CNI or enforce policy. It hooks TC for ingress and egress packets, kprobes for TCP, a socket filter for DNS and XDP for drops, and emits data in Hubble format, so an existing Hubble CLI works with it straight away. The catch is that it maps IPs to pods in user space, after the fact. In his screenshots, Retina flows show the destination as `world` with a raw IP instead of a pod name.

Cilium gives each pod a cryptographic identity derived from its labels when the pod starts, and the eBPF programs in the kernel carry that identity, so both ends of every flow are resolved. It also parses layer 7, giving you HTTP method, path and status, plus gRPC service names.

## The benchmark: identity costs CPU

Both tools ran one after the other on the same EKS cluster with around 500 QPS of sustained pod-to-pod traffic. Retina used 47% less memory per node and its CPU stayed flat. Cilium showed a 31% CPU spike under the same load, because it does per-flow identity work on every packet. The numbers come from `kubectl top`, not a simulator.

## A three-step blueprint

His recommendation is incremental. Install Retina with two Helm commands and have Prometheus scrape it, which gives you TCP flows and DNS in about five minutes. During an incident, run `hubble observe` filtered to your pod, and with a dropped-verdict filter to catch silent blocks. When you need pod identity on both sides or L7 detail, add Cilium in chaining mode. On EKS he set `cni.chainingMode=aws-cni`, so the VPC CNI keeps doing IP address management and Cilium adds identity-aware visibility on top.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers and on-call SREs running Kubernetes who have lost an evening to a packet that vanished without a log line. It's also a clear, well-measured comparison if you are choosing between the two tools.

Title: Copilot in Azure is only useful because it's grounded in your telemetry
Description: Sampath Rao Madarapu of Microsoft at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on Copilot in Azure: grounding in live telemetry, read-first safeguards and a staged rollout.
Body:
The interesting part of an ops copilot isn't the chat box, it's what the answers are grounded in. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Sampath Rao Madarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Sampath_Rao_Madarapu_distributed_systems_scaling), Senior Technical Advisor at Microsoft working in Azure infrastructure support, walked through how Copilot in Azure combines an LLM with live resource data, and why he insists on "augmented", not automated or autonomous.

This is a Microsoft engineer talking about a Microsoft product, from the support side rather than the marketing side. There's no live demo; it's architecture, scenarios and adoption advice.

## You are the integration layer

He starts with the toil. Diagnosing one VM issue can mean ten or more portal blades: the VM config, attached disks, network security groups, Azure Monitor metrics, Log Analytics queries, then dependencies across resource groups, all before root-cause analysis begins. Metrics, logs and configuration live in different tools that don't talk to each other in context, so the engineer stitches them together by hand. At scale, he argues, operational toil costs more than the infrastructure.

## Three layers, and the outer one matters most

He describes Copilot as three concentric layers. The core is the LLM engine that interprets intent and reasons. Around it sits the natural-language interface that captures context, like which resource you are looking at. The outer layer is the Azure control plane itself: live telemetry, Resource Manager APIs and resource data.

That outer ring is the point of the talk. His line: "Grounding is what makes AI operationally useful." A generic model can list what might cause high CPU. A grounded one can tell you this VM is hitting its uncached throughput limit because these specific disks are at their IOPS ceiling. The sources he lists are Azure Resource Graph for inventory and relationships, Azure Monitor and Log Analytics for metrics and logs, Resource Manager APIs for configuration and policy state, and diagnostic telemetry for edge and cloud health.

## What it looks like on a normal day

The scenarios are concrete. Ask why an App Service shows elevated latency and get metrics, recent config changes and dependency health in one reply. List every storage account without private endpoints across subscriptions without writing KQL. Find dev VMs that have been underutilised for three days and get right-sizing suggestions. The same model extends to Arc-enabled infrastructure at the edge.

## The safeguards are the product

He is direct that engineers stay in the loop. Humans validate that the telemetry Copilot cites reflects real behaviour, judge whether a design suggestion fits the customer's SLAs, and write the runbooks that steer it. Three safeguards make it enterprise-ready in his view: explainable responses that show data sources, a read-first design where Copilot queries and explains but every change is started and confirmed by a human, and Azure RBAC, so it can't surface data you aren't allowed to see.

## Start where the risk is low

His rollout advice is four steps. First, fix your telemetry baseline (Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, Resource Graph), because Copilot is only as good as that data. Then use it for diagnostics, config queries and policy reviews. Then build internal prompt patterns and playbooks. Only then move to cost optimisation and capacity planning, with human review at each step.

## Who should watch

Azure operators and SRE teams weighing AI-assisted tooling, and anyone building an internal ops assistant on another cloud: the grounding and read-first lessons transfer directly.

Title: A consent checkbox stored as a boolean won't survive an audit
Description: Manasa Uppula at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on designing financial onboarding as evidence: append-only consent, propagated identity assurance, audited sagas.
Body:
Most onboarding flows store consent as a boolean and call it done. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Manasa Uppula](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Manasa_Uppula_data_streaming_realtime), an enterprise web architect with nearly 14 years on large financial platforms, argued that this is exactly where regulated systems fail: the record exists, but it can't prove what the customer saw, when, and in what system state.

It's a compact talk, about 15 minutes, built around one framework and a worked example.

## Storing data versus proving what happened

Onboarding is where the legal relationship starts. You set consent boundaries, grant access to regulated services, and create a record a regulator might read years later. Uppula's point is that regulators have moved on from whether you collected the data to how a disclosure was presented, which version the customer saw, and what the system state was at that exact moment. KYC, AML, GDPR, CCPA and E-SIGN each turn into a specific architectural obligation. Her line: "The system must be able to prove what happened, not just store data."

The common failure she describes is compliance as surface: checkboxes and form validation on top of mutable database state, with exception paths as an afterthought. Every service ends up with its own version of what happened, and audits turn into manual reconstruction under pressure.

## Interaction integrity in three pillars

Her approach, which she calls interaction integrity, makes every material interaction produce verifiable evidence as a first-class output:

- **Consent and disclosure as artifacts.** Each disclosure event carries the disclosure version, a timestamp, the user's explicit response and the system state. Events go into append-only logs (she names Apache Kafka) backed by immutable storage. Nothing is updated; everything is appended.
- **Progressive identity assurance.** Verification is gradual: email, then document upload, maybe biometrics. Low-risk access comes early and higher capabilities open as confidence grows. In microservices, the trap is stale identity state in some services. Her fix is to carry the assurance level as a JWT claim and emit an event when verification succeeds, so downstream services update their enforcement instead of guessing.
- **Exception handling as compliance.** Session timeouts and a third-party KYC provider going down are not edge cases; they happen every Tuesday. A half-finished flow leaves legal ambiguity about whether the customer is onboarded at all. So she uses saga patterns with compensating transactions, orchestrated by AWS Step Functions or Temporal, and logs every failure path with the same rigour as the happy path.

## The savings account walkthrough

The example ties it together. A customer reads the terms and GDPR disclosure, and each view is an immutable event. Email verification grants low-risk access. An ID upload raises the assurance level in the JWT claims, which enables funds transfer. Then the KYC provider times out: the saga fires a compensating transaction, partial state is preserved, the customer gets a clear notification, and both the cause and the resolution are logged. No gap for an auditor to fall into.

## Governance has to change with the system

Her last point is the one platform teams tend to skip. Cloud-native systems change constantly, and every service update or migration is a chance for compliance to erode quietly. Treat compliance as an explicit, versioned architectural input, not something each team is assumed to preserve.

## Who should watch

Architects and backend engineers building onboarding, KYC or any consent-heavy flow in a distributed system. If your consent table has an `UPDATE` statement anywhere near it, this is worth 15 minutes.

Title: Your AI outage model failed because of governance, not the model
Description: Karthik Ravva of Austin Energy at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on embedding data governance in every lifecycle stage, from ingestion to auditable deletion.
Body:
A utility rolls out an AI model to predict outages, it misses a big one, and the post-mortem finds nothing wrong with the algorithm. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Karthik Ravva](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Karthik_Ravva_ai_agents_reasoning), Senior Product Manager at Austin Energy, used that story to argue that most AI failures are data governance failures, and that governance has to be built into each stage of the data lifecycle rather than bolted on after deployment.

It's a short, framework-level talk from someone who runs emergency data platforms at a utility. Expect a blueprint and a phased plan, not code.

## Teams build first and ask how to govern it later

Ravva's diagnosis is about sequencing. Organisations deploy models across several cloud providers, ship them to production, and only then work backwards to the governance question. The result is fragmented ownership, compliance gaps under GDPR, CCPA, TCPA and HIPAA that need provable lineage, and AI and BI output nobody fully trusts. His summary line: "AI that everybody's talking about is only as good as the data behind it."

## Four layers, one chain of custody

The blueprint has four layers, and the point is that governance lives inside each of them:

1. **Ingestion.** The first and most important control point. Validate, encrypt and record provenance at the gate, enforce structure at the schema and transformation level, and catalog every attribute before bad data spreads. Skip this and you scale bad metadata faster.
2. **Classification and cataloging.** Use ML models to classify data as it lands, because humans can't keep up with the volume. Classification is continuous, not a one-off.
3. **Access control and ownership.** If asking who owns a dataset gets several answers, you don't have ownership. He names the usual roles (data steward, data owner, domain owner, platform team) and pairs them with role-based access control.
4. **Tiered storage.** Archive (long-term, immutable, cryptographic audit trails), cold (rare access with lifecycle policies), warm (operational data for scheduled BI loads) and hot (active AI pipelines, strict RBAC, real-time monitoring). His utility example for hot data is the ADMS platform that utilities lean on to predict the next outage.

## Deletion is where governance gets tested

The sharpest section is about the end of the lifecycle. Data lives in many places at once, so the real audit question is whether you can prove it's gone. Ravva's answer is retention policy by design: when AI classifies data into a tier, attach the compliance flags right there, and make every deletion or retention decision auditable. Automating that is what shortens regulatory response times and takes manual work off the compliance team.

He also wants observability at each of the four layers, so schema drift and behavioural changes in the data get caught by the pipeline instead of by the outage model.

## Stage it, don't boil the ocean

The implementation plan has four phases: foundation (ownership, metadata, classification taxonomy), ingestion and access, the AI intelligence layer, then lifecycle automation. The order matters. AI classification can't work without the rules you defined in the foundation phase, so doing everything at once mostly produces confident mislabels. For multi-cloud and hybrid estates, he wants policies defined as code, one audit platform and one catalog across clouds. As he put it: "Governance maturity is built, not acquired after deployment."

## Who should watch

Product managers and data platform leads who have to convince leadership that a governance programme is worth doing before the next model goes live. Engineers looking for implementation detail will want to pair it with something more hands-on.

Title: Sovereignty is about who runs the control plane, not where the rack is
Description: Dmytro Hlotenko of Sage Austria at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on EU compliance on AWS: Cloud Act, DORA, NIS2, the Sovereign Cloud and the Outposts trap.
Body:
Putting servers in a European bunker does not make your data European. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, [Dmytro Hlotenko](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Dmytro_Hlotenko_distributed_systems_resilience), Senior Cloud Operations Engineer at Sage in Austria, argued that jurisdiction follows operational control, and then took AWS Outposts apart with benchmark numbers to show what keeping it on-prem actually costs.

He opens with a disclaimer worth repeating: he is an engineer, not a lawyer, and the talk is a starting point for your own conversation with legal and compliance. That honesty runs through the whole session. His abstract sums up the stance: "Sovereignty without operational maturity is just compliance theater."

## Geography is not jurisdiction

The core argument is about the Cloud Act. It targets service providers and the entities that manage data, not the people who wrote the software. So if you run licensed software on your own metal with your own staff, there is little for a US warrant to grab. Hand the management plane, the admin credentials or the telemetry to a US-controlled managed service, and your hardware in Munich is exposed exactly like a public cloud region would be.

That leads to his one question for every vendor pitch: who operates the control plane? Bring-your-own-key and bring-your-own-hardware do not change the answer if someone outside your jurisdiction holds root.

## DORA and NIS2 don't ban hyperscalers

Hlotenko spends a good chunk of the talk de-escalating regulatory panic. DORA cares about concentration risk and exit strategies for financial services. NIS2 cares about supply-chain security. Neither says you cannot use AWS, Azure or GCP. They ask you to stop doing it blindly: impact assessment, documented exit strategy, strong encryption, governance. A three-year migration plan is not a requirement.

He also makes the case against swapping one well-run AWS estate for a patchwork of smaller providers. The spreadsheet counts compute and storage. It misses hiring for a stack nobody knows, lost velocity, and mean time to recovery when you have, in his abstract's words, "seven SLAs, seven blast radiuses, and seven on-call rotations."

## The European Sovereign Cloud moves the needle, partly

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud, launched in January 2026, is a separate partition with its own legal entity, run by EU-resident staff, with metadata, CloudTrail and IAM staying in the Brandenburg region. He calls partition-as-perimeter a fundamental change compared to the regular EU regions, where some data still travels to us-east-1. The gap he flags: the ultimate parent is still a US company, which is why German and French authorities read it differently.

## Outposts solve physics, not law

The case study is the reason the talk exists. A regulated Austrian workload, a team with years of AWS muscle memory, and a business asking: why not put an Outpost in our own data center? Because Outposts were built for low-latency edge compute, and compliance came later. The control-plane metadata lives in the parent region, so Cloud Act exposure is the same as Frankfurt.

Then the service list shrinks: no Lambda, no Glue, no SageMaker, no Redshift, no Transit Gateway, a stripped-down ALB and EKS, and S3 that is limited and costs extra. What's left is plain compute that looks like AWS.

The team benchmarked it properly. They replayed real user behaviour with Locust and Playwright, generating load from Azure in Vienna so they weren't benchmarking AWS from inside AWS. Two findings stand out. A vCPU is often an SMT thread, so four real VMware cores can mean roughly eight vCPUs on AWS, with knock-on effects for database and OS licensing. And storage hurt: no io1 or io2, a ceiling of 16,000 IOPS against the 200K to 300K a SAN gave them, and internal database jobs that took two to three times longer.

The last trap is backups. EBS snapshots go to the parent region by default, which quietly undoes the data-residency story. Fixing that means local S3 from another provider and a more complex restore path.

## Who should watch

Platform and cloud ops engineers in the EU who keep getting forwarded articles about sovereignty, and anyone pricing Outposts as a compliance fix. The talk closes with a decision tree rather than a verdict, which is the right answer for a question this dependent on your regulator.

Title: Validate on every event, not on a schedule, in healthcare cloud
Description: Mohiadeen Ameer of Dell Technologies at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on SupportPlus, an event-driven framework for continuous validation, remediation and audit on AKS.
Body:
Traditional validation asks whether something already broke; event-driven validation asks what changed, what is now at risk and what to verify right away. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Mohiadeen Ameer, Software Principal Engineer at Dell Technologies, presented SupportPlus, an event-driven automation framework that turns validation in healthcare cloud platforms from a manual, periodic check into a continuous capability that detects, remediates and records evidence for auditors.

It is a talk about one framework built by the speaker's team, running on microservices, serverless components and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). The design ideas carry over; the framework itself is internal.

## Too dynamic to check by hand

Mohiadeen's starting point is the environment. A healthcare enterprise links EHR systems, telemetry platforms, lab systems, pharmacy and multiple interface engines through protocols such as gRPC and HL7, across many microservices, APIs, containers and asynchronous pipelines that never stop changing. The problem is less raw scale than dynamic complexity: everything is always updating, always depending on something else, and failures spread along those chains. In healthcare, a failed interface or a missed upstream dependency disrupts clinical workflows and creates compliance exposure, exactly when people need the system most.

He names three limits of traditional validation. It is reactive, kicking in after an alert fires or a user is already affected. It cannot scale with Kubernetes deployment velocity, because the dependency graph grows faster than anyone can check it by hand. And it creates compliance risk: stale or incomplete validation means late detection and fragmented evidence when you need to prove a control was working.

## The trigger is the change

SupportPlus begins with ingesting high-volume event streams: deployment signals, telemetry changes, queue behaviour, workload drift, dependency status. Those feed metadata-driven validation rules, so a check is a policy that knows the protocol type, service criticality and expected interface behaviour, rather than something hard-coded per service. Distributed orchestration then runs validation workflows in parallel across services, APIs and data layers, with serverless components where elastic scale helps and AKS keeping the framework close to the workloads it validates.

The real shift is the trigger model. A workflow starts because the system saw an event that warrants it, such as a deployment, a patch cycle, a configuration change, a latency anomaly or a blocked queue, not because a human noticed a symptom or a cron job came around.

## Detect, remediate, document

The framework does three things with what it finds:

- **Detection** combines real-time monitoring with machine learning that learns baseline interface behaviour over time and flags deviations before they become hard outages.
- **Remediation** uses protocol-aware logic instead of one action for everything: one failure type gets retry logic with a circuit breaker, another a queue consumer restart, another a service recycle.
- **Compliance** treats validation evidence as a normal byproduct of operation, so audit readiness is continuous rather than reconstructed afterwards.

Mohiadeen reports a 30% improvement in system availability, and is careful to point at the cause rather than the number: automated, event-driven validation catches issues earlier and stops conditions from maturing into visible outages. Consolidating validation, monitoring and remediation into one platform also removes handoffs between disconnected tools.

## Roll it out in four phases

Adoption is incremental: a pilot that integrates event streams and sets the first control points; expansion across more service domains; then automated remediation and compliance measures; then continuous improvement as the environment changes. Looking ahead, he expects AI and ML to make validation more predictive, correlating signals across dependencies to act before performance or compliance suffers.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers in regulated industries, especially anyone running interface-heavy healthcare or finance estates on Kubernetes. Teams already doing chaos engineering or continuous verification will recognize the ideas and may want the remediation-by-protocol detail most.

Title: Robots, drones and driverless trucks need one modality-agnostic brain
Description: Cijin Lonappan Kappani of Walmart at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on autonomous last-mile and middle-mile delivery and the cloud-edge architecture that runs it.
Body:
Last-mile delivery accounts for 40 to 50 percent of total logistics cost, which makes it, in Cijin Lonappan Kappani's words, a structural tax on every e-commerce transaction. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Cijin, Principal Technical Program Manager at Walmart working on drone and autonomous vehicle delivery with partners including Wing, Zipline and DroneUp, explained how sidewalk robots, drones and driverless trucks fit together, and why the hard part is the cloud-native orchestration layer that coordinates them.

It is a practitioner's overview from inside a retailer running these systems, with real deployments named, rather than a code-level tour of one platform.

## Three machines, three sweet spots

- **Sidewalk robots** run on existing pedestrian infrastructure, typically one to five miles from a fulfilment node with payloads around 15 pounds: groceries, pharmacy items, convenience goods. They depend on low-latency 5G or LTE for obstacle detection, remote supervision and routing, so losing connectivity is a failure mode the platform must handle. Curbs, snow and construction make path planning hard, and GPS degrades in urban canyons, so they rely on sensor fusion of lidar, cameras and odometry.
- **Drones** skip ground congestion entirely, targeting delivery in under 30 minutes for light items, typically around five pounds. Weather and regulation are the constraints, and the cloud integration point is unmanned traffic management: real-time airspace conflict resolution, weather monitoring and rerouting.
- **Autonomous trucks** are the most mature, because highway driving on fixed warehouse-to-store routes has far fewer edge cases. Walmart and Gatik run fully driverless box trucks on middle-mile routes in Arkansas, with no safety drivers. Cijin is emphatic that this is production, not a pilot.

## Hand-offs are where it gets hard

The most interesting case is multimodal. In the Serve Robotics and Wing pilot in Dallas, a sidewalk robot picks up packages from a micro-fulfilment node and carries them to an autoloader station, where a drone takes them for the final aerial leg. Each machine does the segment it is good at. The cost is coordination: transfer hand-offs need sub-minute arrival precision, scheduling has to weigh order velocity, robot availability, weather and drone capacity at once, every agent needs a consistent view of state, and when one modality fails the system must reroute without dropping orders. If that sounds like event-driven architecture with shared state and fault tolerance, that is exactly his point.

## Cloud, edge, fleet

The reference architecture has three layers. The cloud orchestration layer is the brain: fleet management, order state, telemetry ingestion, route optimization and remote supervision, horizontally scalable and observable. The edge coordination layer makes the low-latency calls (a robot dodging a pedestrian cannot wait for a cloud round trip) and must keep working on partial connectivity. The fleet layer is the robots, drones and trucks with their own onboard compute, executing locally and reporting state continuously.

His four design principles are the takeaway engineers can use anywhere: abstract the modality so orchestration does not care which vehicle delivers, degrade gracefully so one modality's failure does not cascade, coordinate through events so subsystems scale independently, and keep unified observability so any order can be traced across any agent.

## Regulation is a software requirement

Unlike technical problems, regulation cannot be engineered away. Drones in the US need FAA Part 107 certification, beyond-visual-line-of-sight waivers granted inconsistently by corridor, and now Remote ID. Trucks need state-level permits, with Arkansas and Texas leading. Sidewalk robots face a city-by-city patchwork. The engineering consequence is geofencing that enforces regulatory boundaries in real time, with different rule sets applied per jurisdiction. Weather adds another dependency: when wind grounds drones, the platform must reroute to ground modes and adjust delivery promises dynamically, because static SLAs do not survive weather-dependent fleets.

Walmart evaluates deployments with a four-quadrant risk framework (operational, technical, strategic, market) and takes a portfolio approach across technologies and partners rather than betting on one.

## Who should watch

Engineers building fleet, IoT or logistics platforms, and anyone who likes seeing distributed systems patterns applied to physical machines. If you want the economics of retail automation, the closing section on cost curves and a phased outlook to 2035 covers it; if you want code, this talk does not show any.

Title: Three-layer design systems break on a million-row table
Description: Sonali Priya of LB Networks at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on a seven-layer design system for analytics, adding data components, semantics and governance.
Body:
Your design system's table component was built for a few hundred rows; your analytics platform hands it a million. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Sonali Priya, Creative Design Director at LB Networks (Local Backhaul Networks), argued that the standard three-layer design system model breaks under enterprise analytics, and proposed a seven-layer model that adds data-aware components, visualization primitives, metric semantics, workflow patterns and governance.

## Five line charts, all slightly different

Sonali opens with three patterns anyone who has worked on an analytics product will recognize. Fragmentation: teams rebuild the same charts and dashboards from scratch, so you end up with five versions of one line chart. Visual drift: with no shared rules for colours, scales, axis labels or thresholds, two dashboards in the same product look as if two companies built them. Governance gaps: nobody owns a metric's definition or a component's versioning, and access control is bolted on later.

## Why tokens, components and patterns are not enough

The classic model (primitives such as tokens, then components, then patterns) works very well for consumer apps. It falls apart on analytics because it ignores data volume. Tables need virtualization, streaming and lazy loading. A chart that is clean at a hundred points is an unreadable smear at a hundred thousand, and the model says nothing about aggregation, sampling or progressive disclosure. Nothing drops in and works with your data pipeline, metric layer and access controls, so teams stitch libraries together and the shared system loses its point.

## The seven layers

1. **Design tokens**, extended for analytics: dataviz palettes (sequential, diverging, categorical), density modes for packed dashboards, and semantic tokens such as threshold exceeded or anomaly detected that encode intent, not just appearance. One definition compiles to CSS, iOS, Android and Figma.
2. **UI components**: buttons, inputs, tabs and so on, built only from tokens and deliberately unaware of data.
3. **Data components**: the virtualized table, query builder, filter panel, metric picker. Stateful by design, with loading, empty, partial and error states, plus saved views and column choices that do not break the shared definition.
4. **Visualization primitives**: scales, legends, grids and tooltips that charts are assembled from, with accessibility built in (colour-blind-safe palettes, pattern fallbacks, screen reader support) and encoded rules for when there is more data than pixels.
5. **Semantics and interpretation**: one definition of each metric, its units, thresholds and targets.
6. **Workflow patterns**: drill-down and drill-across, cross-filtering, saving an exploration as a dashboard, period-over-period comparisons.
7. **Governance**: named owners, versioning, access and sensitivity controls, and a contribution workflow with quality gates.

## Three teams, three definitions of revenue

Layer five is the one Sonali calls the most underappreciated. Her scenario: three teams build three dashboards, each with a metric called revenue, and none calculate it the same way. One includes refunds, one uses net and another gross, one runs daily and another weekly. A semantic layer makes it one definition with one set of thresholds, so when a designer, a data engineer and a product manager say churn rate they mean the same thing.

On governance her line is equally firm: every metric and component gets a named owner, not a team and not a Slack channel, a person. Changing a metric definition is not a bug fix; it is a change to history and needs semantic versioning and a migration path.

## Adopt it from the edges inward

You do not build all seven at once. Start with tokens and governance, the cheapest layers with the highest leverage. Then data components and visualization primitives, where users feel the most pain. Then semantics, which is as much organizational work as technical. Patterns come last: codify a flow once you see three teams repeating it. Measure reuse rates, consistency and time to dashboard, or you cannot tell whether it is working.

## Who should watch

Front-end platform teams, design system maintainers and data product leads on dashboard-heavy products. Consumer-app design system teams can skip the middle layers but will still get value from the governance section.

Title: Static partitions and B-trees assume a workload the cloud won't give you
Description: Purushotham Jinka of Citi at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on adaptive partitioning, learned indexes and ML query engines, plus guardrails for self-tuning databases.
Body:
Classic database design assumes stable workloads, fixed hardware and a DBA who retunes things every quarter; a cloud-native system offers none of the three. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Purushotham Jinka, Vice President at Citi focused on large-scale data and cloud platforms, traced how partitioning and indexing are moving from one-time design decisions to adaptive, increasingly self-optimizing mechanisms, with machine learning moving into the query engine.

It is a survey of where database architecture is heading rather than a hands-on tuning session, and it ends with a sensible order of operations for adopting automation.

## The mismatch

Traditional databases were built for predictability. Cloud environments are the opposite: workloads shift constantly, infrastructure is elastic, and availability expectations are very high. Purushotham's list of symptoms is short and recognizable: latency spikes, operational overhead and manual tuning that never catches up.

## Partitioning that keeps moving

His first claim is that partitioning is no longer a one-time decision. Range, hash or list partitions chosen up front go stale as query patterns drift and traffic creates hotspots. Newer systems watch real-time query patterns and rebalance data placement without downtime.

The strategies themselves are not exotic: range partitioning for time-based queries, hash for even distribution, composite schemes for mixed workloads. The change is combining them deliberately rather than picking one. Add partition-level replication, dynamic shard splitting and geo-aware placement, and you get horizontal scaling where capacity is added without repartitioning the whole dataset or taking it offline.

## Indexes stop being a static guess

Static B-tree indexes force teams to predict query patterns in advance and then maintain the structures by hand as schemas evolve. He describes a progression from static indexes, to adaptive ones (partial indexing, automated suggestions, online rebuilds), to learned indexes, where a model replaces part of the tree. In between sit the tools many teams already have: partial, covering, multi-column, spatial and inverted indexes, chosen from observed query behaviour.

The reminder engineers need most: indexes are not free. Every index speeds up reads and costs storage and write overhead, so indexing is an ongoing optimization problem. Cloud-native engines increasingly run index advisors that suggest additions and removals and rebuild in the background without blocking live transactions.

## ML inside the engine

The third chapter covers machine learning in the database itself. Workload managers classify queries and allocate resources before contention builds, and spot anomalies early, which matters most in multi-tenant systems. Adaptive query processing learns from execution history instead of trusting static cost models whose statistics go stale. To measure any of this he points to OLTP-Bench for simulating realistic workloads and iTuned for ML-driven configuration tuning. The pieces reinforce each other: partitioning reduces skew, indexing speeds queries, and ML keeps tuning both.

## Let it observe before it acts

The section that keeps this grounded is on guardrails. Self-optimizing systems bring new failure modes along with their benefits, so production adoption needs governance over when the system may act on its own: rollback safety, a human-in-the-loop mode, threshold guardrails and an observation-first stance. His rollout path is three steps: observe, then enable advisory mode, then automate selectively. That is the right order for any team that has watched an automatic tuner make a confident, wrong decision at peak load.

The abstract lists a set of benchmark percentages for these techniques; the recording does not walk through them, so check the slides if you need the figures.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers and DBAs moving workloads to managed or distributed databases, and architects deciding how much autonomy to grant a self-tuning engine. If you want query plans and EXPLAIN output, this talk stays at the architecture level.

Title: Moving RabbitMQ to the cloud? Choose rehost, replatform or refactor
Description: Ran Tao of AWS at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on migrating on-prem message brokers to EC2, Amazon MQ or SQS/SNS, and what changes in client code.
Body:
Lift-and-shift your message broker to a VM and you have moved the hardware, not the work: patching, broker monitoring and capacity planning still land on your team. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Ran Tao, Cloud Support Engineer at AWS, gave an introductory walkthrough of the three paths for moving an on-prem messaging system to the cloud (rehost, replatform, refactor), with Python code comparing a RabbitMQ client to Amazon SQS.

Honest scope: Ran says up front it is an introductory session, and the cloud side is AWS throughout, covering EC2, Amazon MQ, SQS and SNS. The decision framework transfers to other clouds; the service names do not.

## Two kinds of messaging system

On one side sit traditional message brokers such as IBM MQ, ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ: dedicated infrastructure connecting upstream and downstream services. On the other sit serverless messaging services, in AWS terms SQS for queuing and SNS for broadcasting. Industries lean on them differently. Retail sees peaks on weekdays and quiet nights and weekends, so it cares about scaling. Financial and government customers care most about durability and recovery during incidents.

On-prem, you pay for both capacity and specialists: doubling throughput means buying hardware, and running the brokers needs engineers with specific skills.

## Three paths and who owns what

- **Rehost** onto EC2. Quickest, with full control over OS, broker engine and version, and application logic barely changes. But security, patching and broker monitoring stay with you, and metrics such as connected clients are not natively wired into CloudWatch or IAM.
- **Replatform** onto Amazon MQ. You choose single-node or cluster deployment and an instance size instead of tuning OS, memory and CPU. CloudWatch integration is on by default, TLS is enforced, KMS can encrypt data at rest, and patching runs in a weekly maintenance window you pick. Scaling up is an instance-size edit and a reboot, rather than reworking the RabbitMQ config file by hand.
- **Refactor** to SQS and SNS. Your team owns only the business logic; capacity and scaling belong to the provider, pricing follows API calls, and the retail-at-midnight problem disappears because nothing sits idle.

His single-node versus cluster advice is worth repeating: one instance in one availability zone is fine for proofs of concept and development, but for production, use the cluster deployment, which mirrors messages across three nodes in three availability zones so losing one zone loses no data.

## What the client code shows

The RabbitMQ side uses the Pika library: set connection parameters (TLS 1.2), open a connection and channel, declare a queue, publish, and close the connection when you are done or it keeps eating broker resources. Consumers must acknowledge each message with a basic ack, or the broker will eventually treat the consumer as inactive and close the connection.

The SQS side has no connection management at all. Create a queue with properties like retention period, get a handle by name, `send_message`, `receive_message`, and then delete the message using its receipt handle. Forget the delete and the message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout, which is SQS's version of the missing ack.

## The refactor checklist

When moving to serverless, Ran's list is practical:

- **Separate producers from consumers** so each scales on its own; a backlog means more consumers, not more producer connections.
- **Pick the delivery model.** One broker can do both point-to-point and publish-subscribe; in AWS those become two services, SQS for once-only processing and SNS for fan-out.
- **Protocols change** from connection-based AMQP, WebSockets or OpenWire to HTTPS API calls.
- **Ordering versus scale.** FIFO queues preserve order; standard queues give best-effort ordering and scale much further.
- **Payload size.** The default limit is 1 MB, but AWS's extended client libraries for Java and Python store the body in S3 and pass a pointer, allowing up to 2 GB.
- **Identity and audit.** IAM replaces the LDAP setup you might still need for RabbitMQ on Amazon MQ, and CloudTrail can log data requests per message.

## Who should watch

Teams sizing up a broker migration who want the trade-offs laid out plainly, and developers who know RabbitMQ and want to see how SQS semantics map onto it. Messaging veterans will find the first half familiar; the client-code comparison and the refactor checklist are the parts worth the time.

Title: Design workflow interoperability in five planes, not adapters
Description: Devinder Tokas of Microsoft at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on a five-plane framework built on CNCF standards to keep cloud-native workflows portable.
Body:
If your team spends more time maintaining glue code between workflow engines than shipping features, interoperability was treated as an integration task instead of an architecture decision. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Devinder Tokas, Software Engineer at Microsoft with more than 20 years on large-scale platform systems, presented a five-plane framework for designing portability into cloud-native workflows using open standards from the CNCF ecosystem.

It is a framework talk: a structured checklist with the standards that fit each layer, plus a migration roadmap. There is no live demo.

## Where the integration debt comes from

Devinder lists three patterns that fragment cloud-native estates. Vendor lock-in, where proprietary APIs or managed services make migration costly and constrain future choices. Incompatible tooling, where different platforms run different workflow engines and data formats, so teams write custom adapters to connect basic pieces. And siloed workflows, isolated per cluster, cloud or team, which blocks unified observability and consistent governance. The net effect is engineering time drifting from features toward integration upkeep.

Standardized contracts are one of the few strategies that systematically reduce that debt, and they buy portability: workflows can move between providers when cost, performance or compliance requirements change, without rewriting the platform.

## The five planes

The model splits a workflow system into five layers, each with a clear contract and deliberately chosen standards:

1. **Workflow definition.** Declare workflows in a portable, versioned format rather than a runtime-specific one: the CNCF Serverless Workflow specification, OpenAPI for service interfaces, JSON Schema for validation. Contract-first, kept in source control, with schema evolution managed on purpose.
2. **Execution and state.** Durable state, checkpointing and recovery, with exactly-once semantics where possible and well-defined idempotency where it is not. CloudEvents helps different engines read state transitions the same way.
3. **Integration.** CloudEvents as the event envelope, AsyncAPI for message-driven interfaces, OpenAPI for request-response, with a service mesh and API gateways for consistent connectivity, security and routing.
4. **Observability and lineage.** OpenTelemetry for traces, metrics and logs, W3C Trace Context to correlate across vendors and runtimes, and data lineage to show what produced, transformed and consumed each piece of data.
5. **Packaging and deployment.** OCI images, Helm charts, Kustomize overlays and GitOps for repeatable, declarative deployments with predictable rollbacks.

His point about the first plane applies to the rest: if the definition is not portable, you pay for it in every plane downstream.

## Outcomes, with an honest caveat

The abstract cites benchmark figures for event-driven throughput and OpenTelemetry Collector performance. In the talk itself Devinder is careful to present performance and reliability gains as representative outcomes that depend on architecture, workload and implementation. The mechanisms are plausible enough on their own: standard contracts cut translation overhead between components, consistent event formats help throughput, shared observability removes duplicate agents and pipelines, and durable state lets workflows resume from the last safe point after a failure. His summary is that ambiguity is often the enemy of reliability, and standard contracts reduce ambiguity.

## A blueprint and a migration path

The reference architecture is an API gateway as the entry point, a service mesh for service-to-service identity and traffic policy, a CloudEvents-compliant messaging backbone, an orchestrator connected through standard APIs, cloud-agnostic state storage, and OpenTelemetry instrumentation throughout. Because the contracts are fixed, implementations can be swapped.

For existing systems: audit definitions against standards, replace bespoke adapters at the integration points, migrate one plane at a time, and instrument observability early so you can measure progress and catch regressions. For greenfield systems: adopt all five planes from day one.

## Who should watch

Platform and architecture teams facing a multi-engine, multi-cloud workflow estate, or planning one. If you already standardize on CloudEvents and OpenTelemetry, the value is the plane-by-plane checklist for spotting the gap you have not covered.

Title: The intelligent farm is a data pipeline with tractors attached
Description: Mallikarjuna Muchu at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on cloud-native AI in agriculture, from IoT and drone data pipelines to yield models, robots and traceability.
Body:
Farms already produce plenty of data from soil sensors, drones and satellites; what they lack is a system that turns it into decisions. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Mallikarjuna Muchu, a DevOps architect speaking for Andhra University, gave a compact tour of how cloud-native data pipelines, machine learning, robotics and blockchain fit together into one architecture for precision agriculture.

Set expectations accordingly: this is a short, high-level overview of the domain, roughly ten minutes, with no code or deployment walkthrough. It is a good map of the territory for engineers who have never thought about agriculture as a distributed systems problem.

## The problem: swimming in data, starving for decisions

The pressure on agriculture is familiar from any industry under strain: a growing population to feed, labour shortages, climate change and thin margins. Mallikarjuna's diagnosis is that the data is already there; farmers generate large volumes of it but have no unified system to act on it. His phrase for this is that farmers are swimming in data while starving for intelligence.

## The pipeline comes first

Everything in the talk hangs off what he calls the nervous system of the farm: continuous streams from IoT sensors, drones and satellites, processed in near real time by cloud-native pipelines. Without that backbone, he argues, none of the AI on top would be possible. Engineers will recognize the shape: high-volume, bursty ingest from unreliable edge devices into a platform that has to stay up when the network does not.

On top of it sit the use cases:

- **Precision farming.** Real-time analysis of soil health and irrigation needs, so action is targeted per field rather than one size fits all, reducing waste.
- **Yield prediction.** Models trained on multi-season data (weather, soil, planting history) produce forecasts that feed logistics, stocking and pricing.
- **Smart irrigation.** Water is applied only when the crop needs it, systems respond to soil conditions, and cycles can be delayed when rain is forecast.
- **Quality control.** Imaging and AI catch defects and contamination on high-volume production lines faster than manual inspection.

## Robots, ledgers and deep learning

Labour shortages are where robotics comes in: autonomous machines take repetitive and precision tasks around the clock, and because they are cloud connected, a whole fleet can be managed remotely. Blockchain provides an immutable record from seed to shelf, covering planting, processing and logistics, which he presents as a way to build consumer trust and speed up food safety responses. Deep learning is the tool for agricultural data that is too high-dimensional for people to read directly.

The architectural point he wants you to keep is that these are not separate gadgets. They are layers of one design: data flows from sensors through the infrastructure into models and out to business systems.

## The safeguards, and the order of operations

Two cautions stand out. Recommendations must be explainable, because operators need to trust what the system tells them before they act on a field. And the system has to stay resilient even when the pumps go offline, which for anyone who has run edge workloads means designing for partial connectivity from day one, plus strong data governance.

His implementation path is phased: connect the sensors, then analyse with AI, then automate with robotics, then integrate across the supply chain, each phase laying groundwork for the next. The three takeaways are that data is the most strategic asset, that automation solves real operational pain, and that sustainability and productivity go together.

## Who should watch

Engineers curious about IoT and data platforms outside the usual web and fintech examples, and anyone scoping an agritech project who wants the component list in one place. If you need architecture diagrams with specific services or numbers from a deployment, this overview will not supply them.

Title: Stateless AI coding tools need a team memory you version
Description: Gaurav Kumar of Amazon at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on context loss in AI development: living context artifacts, shared prompt templates, session handoffs.
Body:
Every new session with an AI coding assistant starts with you explaining, again, the architecture, the conventions and why that weird retry exists. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Gaurav Kumar, Software Development Manager at Amazon with 15 years at the company, called context loss the critical bottleneck in AI-assisted development and proposed a three-pillar fix: living context artifacts, standardized prompt templates and structured session handoffs.

It is a practice-and-process talk from an engineering manager, not a tool demo, and it is aimed as much at team leads as at individual developers.

## The bottleneck is continuity, not capability

Gaurav's diagnosis is that most AI development happens in stateless environments. The tool has no memory of the project's architecture, trade-offs, standards or business use cases, so developers rebuild the same mental model before the tool is useful. The same thing happens without AI when a teammate picks up work after a few weeks: the decisions live in spreadsheets, documents or someone's head.

He names three costs. Repeated re-establishment of structure and conventions at the start of every interaction. Lost architectural memory, so earlier design decisions are invisible and suggestions drift. And shallow collaboration in larger teams, where the assistant cannot reason about how the project evolved or enforce team conventions. His summary: until AI can retain project context over time, it stays strong at isolated tasks and weak at sustained engineering work.

## Pillar one: living context artifacts

Keep continuously updated documents that act as the project's persistent memory for AI: architecture decision records kept current, a domain glossary, and a prompt catalogue, all reviewed and version-controlled alongside the code. The key move is treating them as first-class engineering assets rather than optional docs. Do that, he argues, and the AI can answer the way a senior teammate would, which cuts meetings with senior engineers and shortens onboarding.

## Pillar two: prompts as a team practice

Replace ad hoc prompting with structured templates that embed architecture and domain knowledge, shared and versioned across the team. His examples are the repetitive jobs: on-call tickets, digging through logs, working out why threads are eating a service's resources. A template also solves the blank-page problem; as he puts it, once you have a way to start, the work is rarely the hard part.

## Pillar three: deliberate session handoffs

At the end of a session, write a summary of the decisions made. At the start of the next, reload context in a standard sequence. Store the handoff artifacts in the team repository so anyone can pick up where someone else left off. This is the piece that makes progress carry across sessions and people.

## Compound interest, and what is coming

Gaurav's metaphor is simple versus compound interest: plain AI use gives linear gains, while context carried across coding, testing, documentation and review compounds. He points at emerging stateful AI environments, with agents that retain memory, tool-use state and decision history across sessions, and argues that teams with good context habits now will adopt those fastest.

His starter kit is pleasantly small: audit where people keep re-explaining project context, build templates for the three most common AI tasks on your team, create the living artifacts (ADRs and glossary, co-located with code, reviewed every sprint) and agree a lightweight end-of-session summary format.

## Who should watch

Team leads rolling out AI coding assistants across more than a handful of developers, and anyone whose CLAUDE.md or rules file has grown by accident rather than design. Engineers looking for tool-specific configuration will need to translate the patterns themselves.
