Title: AI's best job in enterprise teams is carrying the mental model
Description: Dreema Patel of Adobe at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on three ways AI eases invisible complexity: RAG over internal knowledge, assisted coding, and failure-led tests.
Body:
In a platform with hundreds of services, nobody holds the whole map, and the gaps only show up when a deployment fails at 2 a.m. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Dreema Patel, Software Engineer at Adobe, argued that the real bottleneck in cloud-native enterprises is human cognition rather than infrastructure, and laid out three places where AI helps carry that load: knowledge retrieval, assisted development and data-driven testing and onboarding.

It is an overview talk aimed at engineering teams rather than a product walkthrough, and it works best as a framing for where to point AI first.

## Invisible complexity

Dreema's term for the problem is invisible complexity. Microservices, micro-frontends and real-time distributed systems let teams scale and deploy continuously, but they replaced one system with hundreds of interconnected parts. Each engineer knows their own services and a few dependencies; past that it gets fuzzy. That complexity does not go away because nobody looks at it. It builds up, and it becomes visible exactly when something times out or a dependency breaks. When system complexity grows faster than team understanding, she says, you get slower cycles, longer debugging and more incidents.

## Pillar one: make institutional knowledge queryable

Every organization piles up API contracts, design docs, PRDs and tickets. The answers usually exist somewhere; finding them costs time and focus, because every hop between docs, code, old tickets and a colleague's calendar is a context switch. Teams end up re-solving problems that were already solved.

Her answer is retrieval-based systems over your actual internal sources. Generic answers are useless inside an enterprise; you need ones that know your architecture and dependencies. RAG bridges static documentation and live context, so engineers start from accumulated experience instead of a blank page.

## Pillar two: move engineers up a level

Much development time goes to boilerplate, test plans, small fixes and repeated validation. AI can generate service scaffolding, complete complex logic, write unit tests and validate patterns while you code, which keeps engineers in flow. Dreema is careful about the limit: AI can generate code, but it does not grasp long-term system behaviour, business context or architectural trade-offs. The shift she wants is from asking how to write this code to asking what the right design is, which trade-offs to make, and how it will scale.

## Pillar three: test what actually broke before

The testing argument is the most concrete. Traditional tests are predictive: we test what we imagine might fail, while production fails in ways we did not imagine. AI can turn that around by mining history. Which combinations of services have failed together? Which files change constantly and are therefore likely unstable? She breaks it into three steps: analyse historical defects, generate scenarios aimed at failure-prone logic and service interactions, and validate over time which tests earn their keep and which are redundant.

Onboarding gets the same treatment. Instead of a new engineer spending weeks working out which services exist and who owns what, they ask how authentication works and get a walkthrough of the services, dependencies and key pieces, without waiting for a senior engineer to free up.

## The summary in one line

Knowledge becomes queryable, development becomes higher-level, testing follows real failures, and onboarding speeds up because context is always available. AI here is an intelligent layer across the platform, with engineers as the decision makers.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and platform leads deciding where AI investment pays off first, and engineers new to applying RAG inside a company. If you are looking for benchmarks or a specific implementation, the talk stays conceptual.

Title: Multi-agent systems fail in the architecture, not the prompt
Description: Sandeep Mannapur of ServiceNow at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on taking a chatbot to orchestrated agents: circuit breakers, timeout budgets, decision-aware traces.
Body:
A four-agent system can turn a two-second request into a twenty-second one, and its dashboards can be all green while it confidently returns the wrong answer. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Sandeep Mannapur, AI and ML Engineer at ServiceNow, walked through how an order-support platform grew from a monolithic chatbot into a centrally orchestrated multi-agent system, and why the fix was architecture rather than a smarter model or a better prompt.

## What the demo hides

Sandeep lists the problems every team hits after the prototype: orchestration logic that spreads across services and becomes the most fragile part of the system, latency that compounds with every agent hop, and failures that propagate when one agent's half-wrong output is passed downstream as if it were valid input.

The monolith failed in a specific order. Conversations that worked at 10 turns broke at 40 because the model was reasoning over tens of thousands of tokens of history. One agent asked to do order lookup, escalation logic, resolution drafting and customer communication became mediocre at all of them. And with no isolation, a single failed tool call took down the whole interaction, with no way to scale escalation separately from status lookups.

## Pick the boring orchestrator

On centralized orchestration versus decentralized swarms, his verdict is clear for operational workflows: centralize. Swarms look good on paper, with more parallelism and no single point of failure, but emergent behaviour is hard to predict, conflicting outputs have no resolution path, and tracing a fault through peer-to-peer chatter is miserable. If agents update real records, you want deterministic control flow and someone clearly accountable.

The resulting design has five layers: an orchestrator that only decomposes, routes and assembles (it never runs domain logic itself); specialist agents that get only the context they need and never read a sibling's state; tools exposed through MCP; agent-to-agent calls over A2A so a LangGraph agent can call a CrewAI agent through the same interface; and a response aggregator that validates everything before it reaches production.

## Four ways to stop one bad agent sinking the rest

- **Circuit breakers** around every agent call, so the orchestrator stops hammering a degraded agent with retries and routes to a fallback.
- **Sandboxing**: no shared in-memory state; inter-agent traffic goes through a durable message bus.
- **Timeout budgets** propagated from the orchestrator, with a degraded mode when an agent overruns.
- **Fallback reasoning paths**: a simpler, lower-capability agent with minimal tooling that keeps critical flows answering when the primary fails.

None of this is new to anyone who has run microservices. That is rather the point: agents are distributed systems with an unusually creative failure mode.

## Trace the decision, not just the call

The sharpest section is on observability. CPU, memory, latency and error rates can all look healthy while outputs are wrong, because correctness depends on the reasoning path. Sandeep wants traces that record which agent was invoked and why, what context it received and what was left out, which tools it called with which parameters, and how the orchestrator resolved conflicting answers. A shared identifier propagates across hops so you can rebuild the full chain. Jaeger and Zipkin will tell you Agent B was called; they will not tell you what Agent B decided. You need both layers.

## Laptop to cloud is a different problem

Locally it is SQLite checkpoints, in-process tools and a local model. In production it becomes Postgres, containerized MCP microservices, A2A servers on cloud functions or Kubernetes pods, stateless orchestrator containers and managed inference behind a gateway such as LiteLLM. He flags three cloud-only traps: token cost compounding (four agents with five tool calls each is 20 or more LLM calls per request, so per-agent token budgets must be hard limits), checkpoint formats that break in-flight workflows during rolling deploys (version them like public APIs), and agent containers that can take 30 to 60 seconds to cold start.

His validated stack is LangGraph, MCP, A2A, LiteLLM, Langfuse and DeepEval, with the caveat that the patterns matter more than the logos. Governance closes it out: schema validation gates on every output, human approval thresholds for high-risk actions, and immutable audit logs.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose agent prototype is about to meet real traffic, and SREs asked to run one. If you have built resilient microservices, much of it will feel familiar, which makes it a fast and useful translation guide.

Title: Vector RAG can't count, so let the graph database do it
Description: Elizabeth Fuentes Leone of AWS at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 shows graph RAG with Neo4j and Strands Agents answering counts that vector RAG makes up.
Body:
Ask a vector-RAG agent how many hotels have swimming pools and it will read three chunks, count what it sees and tell you "approximately four or five" with a straight face. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, Developer Advocate at AWS, shows why that happens and how graph RAG fixes it: turn the documents into a knowledge graph, have the model write a Cypher query, and let the database do the counting.

The session is listed under the title "Reduce AI Agents Costs and Mistakes with Semantic tool Selection". The session as recorded is about graph RAG: she introduces a five-part series on stopping agent failures, mentions semantic tool selection as the second technique, and spends the talk on the first one.

## Similarity search answers from a sample

Her framing is blunt. Vector search returns the most similar documents, not all of them, so on an aggregate question "your agent answered from 1% of the data". The real answer to the pool question on her slide is 133. The model never had the data to get there, so it estimated, and an estimate delivered with full confidence is a fabricated number.

She groups the failure modes into three: fabricated statistics, incomplete retrieval, and out-of-domain fabrication, where the agent cheerfully answers about things the knowledge base has never heard of.

## Build the graph, then let the LLM write queries

The demo uses a hotel dataset of 300 documents (with a lighter 10% version she recommends for trying it yourself). Neo4j's knowledge-graph pipeline has an LLM read each document and discover the entity types on its own (hotels, rooms, amenities, policies, services) along with the relationships between them, so there is no hand-written schema. Entity resolution then merges near-duplicates such as outdoor pools and swimming pools into one node, which is exactly what makes a count query come out right.

At question time the agent doesn't search by similarity. The tool's docstring carries the graph schema, the model reads it and generates a Cypher query, and the database executes it across every node. The model only writes the query and phrases the result. A useful side effect: instead of paying tokens for a pile of retrieved chunks the model has to aggregate in its head, it receives just the rows it asked for. And, in her words, "when the data does not exist, graph RAG returns empty".

## Four questions, two agents

The agents are built with Strands Agents, the open-source SDK that AWS maintains, here running on OpenAI as the model provider to show the provider is swappable. The baseline agent gets a FAISS vector store with an open-source sentence-transformers embedding model; the second gets the Cypher tool. Same prompt, four tests:

- **Aggregation:** the average guest rating across hotels in Paris. Vector RAG found two hotels and did the arithmetic itself.
- **Counting:** hotels with swimming pools in Paris. One short, grounded answer from the graph.
- **Multi-hop:** room types and prices of the highest-rated hotel. The dataset has no prices; the graph agent traverses to room data and says price is not available.
- **Out of domain:** hotels in Antarctica. Vector RAG offers a general overview it invented; the graph agent says there are none in the database.

She is fair to plain RAG at the end. Keep it for semantic search over unstructured text and fuzzy matching; reach for graph RAG for counts, aggregations and multi-hop reasoning; in production you probably want both.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose RAG agent gets asked "how many" or "which is the highest" questions by real users. It's a short, demo-led session with a notebook rather than a production case study, and the repository she shares covers the rest of the series, including deployment to production on AgentCore. If you wanted the semantic tool selection material, it gets a brief mention here and its own session elsewhere.

Title: One intent layer instead of a dozen disconnected copilots
Description: Dhivya Dhayakar of Zscaler at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on intent-based orchestration, smart model routing and trajectory evals for enterprise agents.
Body:
Every business unit built its own bot, none of them talk to each other, and the human manager has become the integration layer. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Dhivya Dhayakar, Senior AI Product Manager at Zscaler, presented intent-based orchestration as the architectural answer: a single layer that interprets what the user wants, plans the steps and routes them to specialist agents, with a human gate in front of anything high-stakes.

It is an architecture talk from a product manager's seat, so expect patterns and a phased roadmap rather than code.

## The tangled cables and the intelligence tax

Dhivya names two failure modes of today's copilot sprawl. The first is brittleness: point solutions that break when a process changes slightly or a query gets complicated. The second she calls the intelligence tax, the cost and latency of sending simple, repetitive tasks to a large model when a small one would do. Users, meanwhile, give up on remembering which of many agents does what.

Her running example is employee onboarding. Today the manager stitches together IT, HR and finance automations, some integrated and some not, and any step off the predetermined path breaks the flow. In the orchestrated version, the agent understands the goal (onboard this person) and adapts when individual steps change, while the manager moves from coordinator to overseer.

## Six parts of the middle layer

The architecture is a layer cake: enterprise tools and data at the bottom, channels and UX on top, and a unified orchestration layer in the middle that she calls the brain. Inside it she lists six components:

- intent intelligence that decomposes a complex request and plans steps;
- a multi-agent orchestrator acting as the harness for task-specific agents;
- a specialized agent pool;
- a tools and skills registry, one catalogue for the enterprise;
- adaptive memory so context survives handoffs and pauses;
- a human-in-the-loop policy gate for high-stakes actions.

The orchestrator plans through prompt chaining, then runs a self-reflection loop where the reasoning engine critiques its own plan before any tool is called. Memory has three tiers: session context, an experience store that remembers reasoning paths that worked before, and retrieval for live facts.

## Route by reasoning depth, not by habit

The fix for the intelligence tax is a smart router with a cost logic fork: simple, low-reasoning work goes to cheaper small language models, while ambiguous tasks on critical workflows go to large models with deeper reasoning. Her point is predictability as much as savings: no surprise bills once the system is in production.

## The onboarding flow, with a pause in the middle

The demo scenario is the best part. A supervisor agent issues formal contracts to task-specific agents, and those contracts bound resource use so agents do not fall into expensive infinite loops. At each handoff the harness checks for gaps. If the IT agent requests confidential system access without justification, the harness asks for clarification of intent; because the access is high-stakes, it then triggers a cascading human-in-the-loop pause, persists the distributed state of the whole agent hierarchy, and shows the reviewer an immutable audit trail of what has happened so far. After approval, the supervisor finishes provisioning and payroll on its own.

She also argues for generative UI, treating front-end components as skills in the registry, so a finance risk question renders as a dashboard and an HR checklist renders as a document view.

## Evals that score the path, not just the answer

Accountability rests on trajectory evals: score the route an agent actually took against a predetermined policy graph, so an agent that reached the right answer by an unapproved path still fails. Combined with immutable audit trails, that gives regulators and internal reviewers something to inspect. Her roadmap runs in four phases: intent and retrieval, then orchestration with registries, then high-stakes actions with human accountability, then scale and governance.

## Who should watch

Architects and platform teams inheriting a zoo of departmental bots, and anyone designing human approval into agent workflows. If you already run multi-agent systems with trajectory evaluation, the talk is a tidy reference model rather than new ground.

Title: Telecom AI will copy old investment bias unless you code against it
Description: Researcher Bhavika Reddy Jalli at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on algorithmic redlining in 5G/6G automation and putting fairness and carbon checks into pipelines.
Body:
Train a capacity-planning agent on ten years of telecom investment data and it will learn, very efficiently, that rural regions do not matter. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, independent researcher Bhavika Reddy Jalli argued that as 5G gives way to 6G and algorithms take over spectrum allocation, fault detection and power management, fairness and carbon accounting have to be engineered into cloud-native network pipelines rather than written into a policy PDF.

This is a research talk, not a tooling demo. It draws on her work on the societal effects of deep learning and agentic AI in telecommunications, and it is upfront that its central example is hypothetical, though grounded in documented patterns.

## Low usage is not the same as low demand

The starting point is the connectivity divide. Bhavika cites figures of 4.5 billion people with high-speed access, 1.5 billion with limited connectivity and 1.1 billion with none, much of the last group in Sub-Saharan Africa. (The talk abstract gives 4.0 billion for the first figure; the recording says 4.5.) Operators have historically invested in high-revenue urban areas. An allocation model trained on that history reads thin usage in an underserved region as weak demand, when the real cause is that nobody built the infrastructure.

The paper behind the talk calls this algorithmic redlining. The cloud-native twist is speed: skewed training data produces skewed allocation policies, those policies get deployed automatically across edge nodes, and the resulting coverage gaps feed back into the next round of training data. Each layer amplifies the one upstream, and it happens before a human gets a chance to notice.

## The worked example: 500 edge nodes and one reward function

The hypothetical is concrete enough to reason about. A national operator trains a reinforcement learning agent on a decade of investment data to automate base station capacity planning across 500 edge nodes. Rural regions with historically low usage get deprioritized, because a skewed reward signal tells the agent that is the efficient choice.

The fixes she proposes are equally concrete: coverage equity thresholds as hard constraints inside the RL reward function, geographic fairness audits at each deployment stage, and demographic parity checks before and after rollout. She reports that such interventions have shown rural coverage improving by 23% while urban efficiency gains were preserved. Her blunt summary of the alternative is that without these guardrails, optimization defaults to the high-revenue areas.

## Net carbon, not gross savings

The second thread is what she calls the sustainability paradox. Reinforcement learning can cut idle base station energy by replacing static, peak-power capacity planning with dynamic optimization, and digital twins let operators test strategies before touching real hardware. But training and continuous inference across edge and cloud cost real compute. Whether the network ends up greener depends on whether the efficiency gains outweigh the AI footprint, and that varies by deployment.

Hence her takeaway that sustainability requires net accounting. Measure the energy cost of training, inference and continuous relearning across the whole lifecycle, not only the watts saved at the base station.

## Governance as four things in the pipeline

The framework has four parts: transparency for regulators and operators, fairness evaluation that tests models against geographic and demographic equity metrics, accountability mapping so every automated decision traces to a responsible owner across microservices, and carbon reporting wired into CI/CD so each model update and inference workload carries a measured cost. The engineering message is that this runs continuously from training data curation through post-deployment observability, not as a gate at the end.

She also pushes back on the idea that governance slows teams down. Building auditability in from day one makes new regulation cheaper to absorb than retrofitting, and transparency becomes a trust asset with regulators, communities and enterprise customers.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects working on network automation, RL-driven resource allocation, or any system where historical data encodes past underinvestment. Platform teams thinking about carbon metrics in CI will find the net-accounting framing useful. If you want code or a reference implementation, this talk stays at the framework level.

Title: agentctl treats AI agents and MCP servers like pods
Description: Andrew Espira of Kustode at Conf42 Cloud Native 2026 on agentctl, a Go CLI that registers, health-checks and discovers AI agents and MCP servers.
Body:
You have `kubectl` for pods and `docker` for containers, but the Ollama instance, the three MCP servers wired into your editor and the agent somebody left running in a terminal tab have no common control plane at all. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2026, Andrew Espira, Founding Engineer at Kustode, showed agentctl, a zero-dependency Go CLI his team built to register, start, stop, health-check and discover AI agents and MCP servers as if they were ordinary infrastructure.

It is a short, demo-led talk about a tool the speaker's own team wrote, so treat it as a working pattern rather than a survey of the field.

## The agent layer is load-bearing and nobody is paging on it

The abstract paints a familiar mess: Ollama locally, MCP servers spread across Cursor and Claude Desktop, a LiteLLM proxy, a couple of custom agents. Some run in Docker, some as Node processes, some only exist because a terminal tab is still open. There is no unified view, health checks are manual, and when one dies overnight you find out the hard way.

In the talk Andrew frames the operational question more broadly. Once agents fan out across environments and make parallel tool calls, the people running them need to see which tools each agent calls, which data it touches, which services it hits, and why it chose operation X over operation Y. That last part, auditing the reasoning, is what separates this from a process manager.

## Registration, lifecycle and a state file you can read

agentctl keeps everything in a single JSON state file: no database, no daemon. You register agents and MCP servers with typed metadata (transport such as stdio, SSE or HTTP, endpoints, commands, tags), and `agentctl agent start` launches the process, records the PID and streams logs to `~/.agentctl/logs/`. `agentctl mcp health` probes HTTP endpoints, or checks PIDs for stdio servers that have no endpoint to probe.

The demo walks through `agentctl agent list`, a health check across everything registered locally, and pulling logs for a single agent with a line limit. Nothing exotic, which is the point: the verbs are the ones you already type for every other service you run.

## Discovery beats remembering what you installed

The part worth stealing is `agentctl discover`. Per the abstract, it scans three sources in parallel: running processes against roughly 30 known signatures (Ollama, LM Studio, CrewAI, LangServe, and any `node` process with "mcp" in its name), well-known ports such as 11434 and 1234, and the MCP config files of Claude Desktop, Cursor and VS Code. New services get registered automatically and re-runs are idempotent. If you have ever grepped three different JSON configs to remember which MCP servers your laptop is running, you can see why.

`agentctl dashboard` then renders a live terminal UI refreshing every few seconds: agents, MCP servers, recent calls, health and confidence scores. Andrew compares it to running `htop` on a Linux box, only pointed at the agent layer instead of RAM and disk.

## Confidence scores as a gate, SRE practice as the frame

Each agent carries a confidence score from 0 to 1, mapped to tiers in the abstract: green at 0.85 and above proceeds automatically, yellow between 0.60 and 0.85 notifies and proceeds, red below 0.60 escalates to a human. In the talk Andrew ties this to guardrails: validating that the data an agent used and the decision it made fit the context, and alerting on hallucinations at the stage where they appear in the reasoning chain.

The wider argument is that agent workflows deserve the same SRE treatment as any service. Kustode pushes the telemetry into its monitoring tools and Slack, and Andrew points at Grafana dashboards, SLOs and SLIs, token usage and hallucination rates as the things to track.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE engineers whose developers are quietly accumulating local models, MCP servers and agents, and anyone who wants a concrete shape for "agent observability" before buying a product for it. If you want deep internals of the reasoning-trace pipeline, the talk only sketches it; the abstract and the repo carry more detail than the recording.

Title: Conf42 SRE 2026 roundup: quiet failures, agentic ops, resilience
Description: Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026 in review, from HTTP/2 load balancing traps and in-place pod resize to MCP incident agents and resilience testing.
Body:
The best incident stories at [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026](https://www.conf42.com/sre2026) were the ones where nothing was technically down. One pod melting while its siblings idled, a security team slowed down by missing signals, a pricing cache that drifted. The event streamed online on March 19, 2026, with 35 talks from Harness, Virtana, Spotify, Rootly, Bloomberg, gridX, Walmart, Oracle, Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo and others, and it balanced those field stories against a strong thread on letting AI agents into operations.

## Failures that don't show up on the dashboard

[Mariem Sboui](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Mariem_Sboui_kubernetes_default_load) (gridX) told the kind of story that saves other teams a week. After HTTP/2 traffic arrived in their Kubernetes cluster, one backend pod ran hot on CPU and latency while the others sat nearly idle, and node metrics said there was plenty of capacity. The cause: Kubernetes Services and kube-proxy balance at Layer 4, per connection, and HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one long-lived connection. If you've ever wondered why your gRPC service has a favourite pod, watch this one.

[Abhimanyu Narwal](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Abhimanyu_Narwal_failures_dashboards_reliability) (Bloomberg) presented a case study from security operations where systems stayed up, yet missing signals and reduced clarity slowed people's diagnosis and response without triggering a single alarm. [Stuart Clark](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Stuart_Clark_scale_fail_spotify) (Spotify) went back to Spotify's 2014 hyper-growth, when abstractions oversimplified the system and hurt incident response; the lesson was that a good abstraction teaches complexity instead of hiding it. [Khushboo Nigam](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Khushboo_Nigam_correlation_over_collection) (Oracle) made the same argument for telemetry: SREs have a clarity problem, not a data problem, so organise signals by decision value and make "what changed?" the easy question.

## Agents in the incident channel, with guardrails

Several speakers put LLMs to work on diagnosis. [Makarand Gujarathi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Makarand_Gujarathi_assisted_incident_response) (Walmart) started from a familiar cost: engineers spending two to four hours and writing 15 to 30 SQL queries to correlate logs, metrics and traces across 5 to 10 backend components with skewed timestamps. His approach uses LLMs and MCP to do the correlation. [David McNerney and Daniel Raskin](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_David_McNerney_Daniel_Raskin_root_cause_distributed_systems) (Virtana) argued that outages are system problems, not application problems, and demoed agents investigating incidents over an automatically discovered dependency graph spanning services, Kubernetes, network and storage. [Savi Grover](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Savi_Grover_alerts_answers_modern) (Tekskills) and [Rohit Wadhwa](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Rohit_Wadhwa_predictive_workflow_integrity) (Walmart) covered agentic ops and autonomous triage across regions.

The counterweight came from talks about limits. [Ajay Athitya Ramanathan](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Ajay_Athitya_Ramanathan_autonomy_guardrails_operating) (FourthSquare) noted that agentic failures in finance and operations rarely look like model errors; they show up as exception backlogs, repeated overrides and escalations. [Suganya Nagarajan](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Suganya_Nagarajan_human_governed_automation) (Amazon) described human-governed automation loops for systems where autonomy makes failures spread faster, and [Vishal Shah](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Vishal_Shah_reliable_support_human) (Visa) kept a human in the loop of an agentic RAG system for API support.

[Sylvain Kalache](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Sylvain_Kalache_vibes_outages_writes) (Rootly) took the other side of AI in production: code written by assistants, tests that mirror the same flawed logic, hallucinated dependencies, more churn and bigger batches, landing on leaner SRE teams whose developers know their own code less well.

## Resilience you test, not resilience you hope for

[Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise), who leads resilience testing at Harness and co-created LitmusChaos, gave the keynote: outages are inevitable, untested resilience accumulates like technical debt, and chaos, load and disaster recovery testing work better as one practice run with every delivery than as three teams' separate projects.

[Bhargavaram Potharaju](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Bhargavaram_Potharaju_national_scale_regulatory) (Wells Fargo) covered HA, DR and audit-ready design for national-scale regulatory reporting, [Rajesh Kumar Balusu](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Rajesh_Kumar_Balusu_building_highly_available) (AGAP Technologies) highly available databases, and [Shruthi Sepuri](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Shruthi_Sepuri_testing_reliability_strengthening) (TCS) the gap between functional testing and reliability in regulated systems.

## Platform mechanics: CPU, VMs, caches and queues

[Raman Tehlan](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Raman_Tehlan_Shubham_Rai_unlocking_just_time) (Zurich Lab) and Shubham Rai (Truefoundry) combined Kubernetes in-place pod resize with PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics to adjust CPU requests without restarts, aimed at clusters that are over-provisioned and throttled at the same time. [Shruthi Rajashekar](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Shruthi_Rajashekar_reducing_call_pain) (Broadcom) made VMs first-class Kubernetes resources to cut on-call pain on hybrid platforms. [Mukul Kumar Gaur](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Mukul_Kumar_Gaur_ready_shopping_caching) (Accelya) explained how airline NDC shopping platforms cache offers for metasearch traffic without letting prices drift. Title: Resilience Testing Is Non-Negotiable in the Enterprise SDLC
Description: Outages in distributed systems are inevitable, making resilience testing essential in the SDLC. It must be continuous, covering failures, load, and disasters. Delayed validation creates “resilience debt,” increasing risk. A holistic approach—combining chaos, load, and DR testing—plus cross-team collaboration and AI-driven insights improves reliability and reduces impact.
Body:
### Resilience Testing Is Non-Negotiable in the Enterprise SDLC

Outages in distributed systems are inevitable, making resilience testing essential in the SDLC. It must be continuous, covering failures, load, and disasters. Delayed validation creates “resilience debt,” increasing risk. A holistic approach combining chaos, load, and disaster recovery testing, along with cross-team collaboration and AI-driven insights, improves reliability and reduces impact.

Modern software delivery has dramatically accelerated. AI-assisted development, automated CI/CD pipelines, and cloud-native architectures now enable teams to deploy software dozens of times per day.

But speed alone does not guarantee reliability.

At [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026](https://www.conf42.com), Uma Mukkara, Head of Resilience Testing at Harness and co-creator of LitmusChaos, delivered a clear message: outages are inevitable. In modern distributed systems, assuming your design will always work is not just optimistic, it is risky.

Failure in distributed systems is a mathematical certainty.

That is why resilience testing must become a core, continuous practice in the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).

---

### The Reality of Inevitable Outages

Even the most reliable cloud providers experience outages.

Examples of unpredictable failures include:

- Physical disruptions such as drone strikes impacting AWS Middle East data centers  
- Policy or configuration errors triggering cascading outages in platforms like Azure  
- Retry storms and load spikes overwhelming services under unexpected demand  

These incidents highlight a critical reality: failure patterns constantly evolve.

A system validated during design may not be resilient against tomorrow’s failure scenarios. Architecture may remain stable, but surrounding failure conditions change continuously.

Resilience cannot rely on assumptions.

**Hope is not a strategy. Verification is.**

For a broader perspective, explore how [chaos engineering, load testing, and disaster recovery testing](https://developer.harness.io/docs/chaos-engineering/) work together.

---

### What Resilience Really Means

Resilience is often misunderstood as simply keeping systems online.

But uptime alone is not enough.

**Resilience is the grace with which systems handle failure and return to an active state.**

A resilient system must handle three categories of disruption:

#### System Failures
Pod crashes, node failures, infrastructure disruptions, and network faults.

#### Load Conditions
Traffic spikes or sudden demand pushing systems to their limits.

#### Disasters
Regional outages, multi-AZ failures, and infrastructure loss requiring recovery mechanisms.

Testing only one dimension leaves critical risks undiscovered.

True resilience requires validation across all three.

---

### Continuous Verification in the SDLC

Many organizations still treat resilience as a “day-two problem” handled after deployment.

Others assume that once validated during design, resilience is solved.

Both assumptions are flawed.

Resilience must be continuously verified.

As systems evolve with each release, so do their failure modes. Effective teams:

- Test resilience continuously  
- Verify resilience with every delivery  
- Document results across releases  

This shifts resilience testing into the outer loop of the SDLC, alongside functional and performance testing.

Instead of reacting to production incidents, teams proactively identify weaknesses before customers experience them.

---

### Understanding Resilience Debt

Resilience debt is similar to technical debt.

When teams delay resilience validation, they accumulate hidden risks.

Over time, this debt compounds.

When failure inevitably occurs, business impact scales with the amount of unresolved resilience debt.

The solution is consistent expansion of resilience testing coverage.

As testing matures over time, teams gain:

- Better system feedback  
- Earlier risk detection  
- Reduced likelihood of severe outages  

---

### A Holistic Approach to Resilience Testing

Resilience testing should not exist in silos.

Many organizations separate:

- Chaos testing  
- Load testing  
- Disaster recovery validation  

But real-world failures often occur at their intersection.

Examples:

- Resource bottlenecks emerging only under combined load and failure conditions  
- Chaos experiments reused for disaster recovery validation  
- Combined chaos and load testing revealing system limits  

A holistic approach integrates:

- **Chaos Engineering**  
- **Load Testing**  
- **Disaster Recovery (DR) Validation**

Learn more in the [Harness Resilience Testing documentation](https://developer.harness.io/docs/chaos-engineering/).

---

### Collaboration Across Teams

Resilience testing requires cross-functional collaboration.

Key contributors include:

- Developers  
- QA engineers  
- SREs  
- Platform teams  

Many organizations already share infrastructure but run isolated experiments.

By coordinating efforts, teams can:

- Reuse testing environments  
- Share chaos experiments  
- Validate DR workflows more frequently  
- Improve overall efficiency  

Resilience improves significantly when teams share assets instead of operating in silos.

---

### The Role of AI in Resilience Testing

As systems grow more complex, determining what to test and when becomes challenging.

Large organizations may have hundreds of possible experiments.

Agentic AI systems can help prioritize testing by analyzing:

- Incident data  
- CI/CD pipeline history  
- Infrastructure configuration  
- Operational documentation  

AI can recommend:

- Relevant chaos experiments  
- Appropriate load scenarios  
- Timely disaster recovery tests  

This ensures teams run the right tests at the right time without overwhelming engineering capacity.

---

### A Unified Platform for Resilience Testing

Harness has expanded its chaos engineering capabilities into a unified platform: **Harness Resilience Testing**.

This platform enables teams to:

- Design chaos experiments  
- Run load tests  
- Validate disaster recovery workflows  
- Observe system risk patterns  

All within a single environment.

This unified approach provides a **single pane of glass** for identifying and tracking resilience risks across the SDLC.

---

### Resilience Is a Core Practice for Modern SRE Teams

Resilience testing is not optional.

Outages will happen. Infrastructure will fail. Dependencies will break.

What matters is whether systems have been continuously validated against those failures.

As resilience testing coverage increases:

- Feedback improves  
- Risk visibility grows  
- Business impact decreases  

In modern software delivery, resilience is no longer just a reliability practice.

It is a **core discipline of the enterprise SDLC**.

---

### Get Started

Ready to validate your system’s resilience?

Title: When every dashboard blames someone else, map the dependencies
Description: David McNerney and Daniel Raskin of Virtana at Conf42 SRE 2026 on finding root cause with a live system dependency graph and investigating agents.
Body:
Modern outages are system problems, not application problems. That is the thesis David McNerney, Director of Product Management at Virtana, and Daniel Raskin, Virtana's Chief Marketing Officer, brought to Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026. Their answer to the familiar incident where every tool points at a different culprit is a system dependency graph, discovered automatically and kept current, which both humans and AI agents can use as context while they hunt for root cause.

## The incident where every tool is right and nobody is

Every SRE has been on this call. A service slows down, the dashboards light up, application metrics say one thing and infrastructure metrics say another. Each team's view is accurate for its own layer, and none of them explains the outage, because the cause lives in the interaction between layers.

The examples in the talk are the kind that cost hours. A spike in a storage queue throttles Kubernetes pods, and the pods look like the problem. Network contention shows up as application latency, so the application team starts profiling code. A GPU pipeline stalls, but the real bottleneck is the upstream data feeding it. In each case the symptom appears in one place and the cause in another, and traditional APM, built around services, plus telemetry split across tools, makes the jump between them hard.

## A graph of how the system actually behaves

The approach Virtana presents in the talk is a System Dependency Graph: a continuously updated map of the relationships between services, Kubernetes objects, infrastructure, networks and storage, discovered from production rather than drawn from an architecture diagram. The difference matters. The diagram in your wiki shows how the system was meant to work. A discovered graph shows how it is wired today, including the dependency someone added during last quarter's migration and never documented.

Once you have that map, the question during an incident stops being which dashboard is right. It becomes what this slow service depends on, and which of those dependencies changed. Following edges from symptom to cause is what an experienced SRE does in their head. The graph makes that path explicit and gives everyone on the call the same picture.

## Agents that use the graph as context

The second half of the talk, per the abstract, is a demo of autonomous agents using the dependency graph as operational context: investigating incidents, tracing cascading failures across layers and surfacing root cause faster. This is the same pattern several Conf42 speakers arrived at in 2026. An LLM agent with access to metrics alone tends to produce plausible stories. An agent that can walk a relationship graph has a structure to reason over, so its conclusions can be checked against real dependencies instead of taken on trust.

If you are evaluating any tool in this space, the talk suggests some good questions to ask: how the graph is discovered and how fresh it stays, whether it reaches below Kubernetes into network and storage, and whether the agent's investigation can be traced edge by edge so an engineer can verify it.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who run Kubernetes on shared infrastructure and keep losing the first hour of incidents to blame between layers. It is a vendor talk: the graph and the agents shown are Virtana's. The framing of outages as system behaviour, and the habit of following dependencies rather than dashboards, are useful whatever you run.

[Watch David McNerney and Daniel Raskin's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_David_McNerney_Daniel_Raskin_root_cause_distributed_systems) ([YouTube](https://youtu.be/z9mjbWbV8eo)).

Title: AI-written code raises the change rate, so SREs must cut the odds
Description: Sylvain Kalache of Rootly at Conf42 SRE 2026 on how AI coding multiplies changes and incidents, slopsquatting, and using AI back against the failure rate.
Body:
If incidents scale with the number of changes times the chance each change breaks something, AI coding tools just turned up the first number. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Sylvain Kalache, Head of AI Labs at Rootly and a former SRE, built his talk around that simple model: developers now ship far more change, SREs cannot control that, but they can and must drive down the probability of failure per change.

Disclosure he makes himself: Rootly sells on-call and incident management, including an AI SRE, so part of the remedies section is his own product category. The diagnosis stands without it.

## C is going up whether you like it or not

He anchors the talk in a rough formula: a constant baseline failure rate plus C, the number of changes in a time window, times P, the probability that a change causes a failure. Then he stacks the evidence on C: survey data that most engineers already use AI tools, vendors reporting large shares of their code written by AI, Cursor's founder citing a billion accepted lines a day in mid 2025, and research across 5,000 engineers at Microsoft, Accenture and another large company showing more commits and more completed tasks.

His own data point is from Rootly customers: from 2023 to the time of the talk, a three times increase in the average number of incidents per customer. And the help is thinning. Ask the author about a broken service and the honest answer may be that their agent wrote it. Specialists are getting rarer as practitioners become generalists. More incidents, less help, and a manager asking why the AI has not made you faster.

## AI fails like humans do, only faster

The catalogue of failure modes is fun and slightly alarming. Unit tests generated to match broken logic, so they pass. A test for Terraform that technically tests something but not the intent. An agent that hallucinated a GitHub repo and deployed it into a customer environment, a case he attributes to Vercel. Slopsquatting: researchers published a package under a name LLMs tend to hallucinate, a huggingface-cli package, and saw about 30,000 downloads in three months with no promotion at all. And a study where an irrelevant line about cats sleeping most of their lives doubled an LLM's error rate on a maths problem.

A friend at Airbnb gave him the counterpoint: for every AI screw-up there is a human equivalent. Slopsquatting is curl-to-bash; deleted files are a fat-fingered rm. We have also been distracted by cats for a long time. His conclusion is to extend blameless culture to LLMs: the question is still which guardrail was missing, not whose prompt it was.

## P is the SRE's job, and the fundamentals matter more

He does not list new magic. The usual tools for keeping P low (testing, review, progressive delivery, rollback and the rest) matter more than ever, because if they were weak before, more change makes it worse. Then he points AI back at the problem:

- **Mutation testing**, long a nice theory, becomes practical. He cites Meta's automated compliance hardening experiment across Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp: 9,000 mutants, 500 privacy test cases, and engineers accepting more than 70% of the generated tests.
- **LLMs as code review helpers**, the next step after linters and static analysis, since review is becoming the bottleneck.
- **MCP** to give agents the same data sources you use in an incident, and AI SRE agents that pull from GitHub, telemetry and past postmortems to propose root causes. At Rootly, he says, some lower-severity incidents are now handled fully automatically.
- **Toil**: let the agent write postmortem timelines and give the ugly internal tools some CSS.

## Who should watch

SREs and engineering leads watching change volume climb since the team adopted coding agents, and sceptics of AI in production. His advice to the latter is blunt: try it. The C times P framing alone is worth a slide in your next reliability review.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Verification Timing: Why Checking AI-Written Code at the Gate Is Already Too Late](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Yunhao_Jiao_aicoding_verification_gates) by Yunhao Jiao.
- [Not Just Syntax: How AI is Changing Code Review](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Shubham_Singh_ai_code_review) by Shubham Singh.
- [LLM Copilots for SRE: Transforming Incident Response and Auto-Remediation](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Susanta_Kumar_Sahoo_copilots_sre_remediation) by Susanta Kumar Sahoo.

Title: Spotify learned that good abstractions teach complexity
Description: Stuart Clark of Spotify at Conf42 SRE 2026 on the abstraction paradox from 2014 hyper-growth, and how Backstage turned operational knowledge into infrastructure.
Body:
The abstraction that makes shipping easy is often the one that makes a 3am incident impossible. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Stuart Clark, Senior Developer Advocate at Spotify, told the story of how Spotify's 2014 hyper-growth exposed that paradox, and how the fix grew into Backstage, the developer portal Spotify later open sourced and donated to the CNCF.

The story is Spotify's own and so is the tool, but the talk is mostly about a design principle you can apply to any internal platform, dashboard or runbook.

## Ten pull requests in sixty days

Around 2014 Spotify was moving from a music streaming app to a personalised audio platform and hiring at breakneck speed, with a ship fast, ship often mantra. User numbers looked great. Internally, engineering productivity was sliding: the time for a new engineer to reach their tenth pull request, a milestone Spotify tracked, had ballooned to almost 60 days. Onboarding had turned into what he calls archaeological excavation.

The odd part was that the systems looked excellent. Clean APIs, documented interfaces, elegant abstractions hiding the mess underneath. Senior engineers had done exactly what was asked.

## Abstractions optimised for the 90% fail you in the 10%

Then came the incidents. A new engineer could follow the happy path, but the moment something broke, the abstraction became an opaque wall: it said something failed in the data layer, and nothing about what, where or why. The person who built it was on holiday. The tool that made development fast made recovery nearly impossible. He calls it the abstraction trap.

The diagnosis is crisp: abstractions were optimised for the 90% of normal operations, while incidents live in the 10% of edge conditions they were never designed to illuminate. The hidden cost was knowledge atrophy. Seniors were relieved juniors no longer needed them, and the understanding of how things actually worked quietly concentrated in fewer heads. Knowledge silos, disguised as good engineering.

## Abstraction is not oversimplification

The distinction he draws is the takeaway. Abstraction should reduce cognitive load while keeping the ability to dig deeper when needed. Oversimplification hides complexity until it explodes. His analogy is a good technical book: chapter one gives you the basics, the appendix is there when you need it.

So Spotify's abstractions got three layers: a happy path covering 80% of what users need 80% of the time, a context layer showing what is happening under the hood, and full system access for when things break. Each level leads naturally to the next instead of being hidden behind it.

## Treat knowledge as infrastructure

Backstage carries that idea through three components. Golden Path software templates encode operational lessons, not just boilerplate. The service catalog shows not only that service A depends on B, but the nature of the dependency, its reliability metrics and what fails downstream when it breaks. TechDocs keeps documentation next to the code. A plugin architecture lets teams customise while sensible defaults carry the collective wisdom; you can deviate, but the system shows you the implications.

The outcomes he describes are qualitative: onboarding metrics improved dramatically, seniors spent less time interrupted, juniors built understanding instead of waiting on help, and knowledge freshness kept documentation from rotting. As he puts it, "Abstractions should be bridges to understanding not solid walls around it."

## Three questions before your next abstraction

He closes with a framework for any deployment tool, dashboard or incident process: can I trace through this when something goes wrong; does it teach me something about the system, or just a rote procedure; and can I graduate from basic usage to deep understanding along a natural path?

## Who should watch

Platform teams building internal developer portals, SRE leads who keep discovering that only one person can debug a critical service, and anyone writing a wrapper that will someday be paged at 3am. It is a story-driven talk rather than a Backstage tutorial.

Title: Crisis-ready platforms should be edge-first and equity-aware
Description: Rakesh Kumar Kavsari Gopal at Conf42 SRE 2026 on AI platforms that keep health and financial services running in disasters - predictive scaling, edge, fallbacks.
Body:
Systems built for average load fail on exactly the day everyone needs them. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, technical architect Rakesh Kumar Kavsari Gopal, who brings 17 years across healthcare, banking and e-commerce, presented a reference architecture for health and financial platforms that must stay up through hurricanes, pandemics and economic shocks, and argued that keeping them up is an ethical obligation as much as a technical one.

It is a broad architecture talk covering software, hardware, SRE practice and migration, aimed at the people who would have to build such a platform rather than a single product.

## Legacy platforms are tuned for an ordinary day

He groups crisis failures into three recurring patterns: demand spikes, loss of capacity and connectivity, and compliance gaps. Hospitals in a regional disaster face surges well above baseline; payment networks and aid distribution platforms buckle precisely when vulnerable communities rely on them. The common thread is architecture designed for average load, with no ability to anticipate surges, no offline-first mode when networks degrade, no routing that prioritises the most vulnerable, and no way to reconfigure without a human in the loop.

## Predict, then reconfigure by crisis type

The intelligence layer has four parts. Predictive load balancing uses historical crisis data plus real-time signals to pre-scale capacity before demand peaks, not after things start failing. Context-aware reconfiguration reprioritises workloads by crisis type, so a hurricane, a pandemic and an economic shock each trigger a different response profile. Edge intelligence runs local inference so essential services continue when central cloud connectivity degrades or disappears. A fallback protocol engine, backed by SLAs, defines graceful degradation: critical functions stay alive while non-essential services are shed.

The design rule that holds it together is layer independence. A failure in one layer should not cascade into another, which any SRE who has watched a shared dependency take down five teams will appreciate.

## The hardware is part of the reliability story

Unusually for an SRE talk, he goes down to the metal: resilient edge clusters near hospitals, relief centres and bank branches; ruggedised servers rated for heat, humidity and intermittent power; mesh networking that picks the best path across satellite, LTE and fibre; and an offline-first sync protocol that reconciles edge state with the cloud once connectivity returns. Data is encrypted end to end and distributed across cloud and edge so a regional outage is not a single point of data loss, with HIPAA, GDPR and local data rules enforced at the infrastructure layer rather than bolted on after deployment.

## Equity as a routing rule

The most distinctive idea is the disaster equity protocol: prioritisation for elderly, disabled and low-income users encoded directly into service logic, with bandwidth and compute allocated accordingly, aid apps optimised for low-end devices and weak networks, and offline-first design so access survives infrastructure failure. Putting that into code rather than leaving it to manual decisions during a crisis is, in his framing, the right thing to do.

## Migrate in stages, let the AI earn trust

Replacing critical systems overnight is neither feasible nor safe. His three stages: offline-first modules run alongside existing platforms with no disruption; AI-driven modules take over non-critical, then mission-critical workloads with continuous validation; finally legacy systems retire and the SLA-backed fallbacks and equity protocols run fully. The talk cites outcomes from adopting organisations, including up to 60% faster service delivery during crises and 20 to 30% financial improvement, alongside a 99.9% availability target and three times provisioned headroom for surges; treat these as the speaker's reported figures rather than a benchmark you can reproduce from the talk.

## Who should watch

Architects and SREs working on public-sector, humanitarian, healthcare or payments infrastructure in disaster-prone regions. It is wide rather than deep, with no code or detailed case study, so its value is the checklist: predict rather than react, treat edge as required, model vulnerable populations explicitly, and migrate in stages.

Title: Tesla vs GM margins as a lesson in reliability trade-offs
Description: Sonali Galhotra of Sony Pictures at Conf42 SRE 2026 reads Tesla and General Motors profit ratios as telemetry for innovation speed versus stability.
Body:
Profit margins are a lagging indicator, and so is your error budget burn. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Sonali Galhotra, Senior Engineering Program Manager at Sony Pictures, compared Tesla and General Motors through their gross, operating and net profit ratios, and used the contrast to argue that organisational signals say as much about a platform's reliability as its dashboards do.

She flags it herself as slightly different from a typical SRE talk. It is a socio-technical analogy, not a finance lecture and not a tooling talk, and it is short.

## Reliability is an organisational property

Her starting point is one program leaders know well. Systems do not run in isolation; they run inside organisations that must sustain themselves. How resources get allocated, how hard the company pushes innovation, how much goes into infrastructure and how leadership balances speed against stability all shape what reliability is achievable. Program managers sit right in the middle of those tensions, which is why she wants them reading organisational signals the way an SRE reads CPU, memory pressure and queue depth.

The hypothesis is simple: financial and operational patterns can act as very high-level telemetry. She picks three ratios. Gross margin as a hint of production efficiency and architectural integration, operating margin as operational discipline and cost control, and net margin as long-term sustainability.

## Two architectures, two telemetry shapes

Tesla, in her reading, runs a tightly integrated stack: hardware, software, manufacturing and distribution closely connected. In platform terms, a vertically integrated system optimised for innovation velocity, where decisions propagate quickly. General Motors is the mature, diversified system: a large portfolio, geographically distributed operations, highly standardised processes. Closer to a stable modular ecosystem optimised for predictability over decades.

The numbers behave accordingly. According to the analysis summarised in the abstract, the gross profitability gap between the two is statistically significant, with Tesla stronger, consistent with tighter control of the value chain and fewer external dependencies. Operating and net margins show more volatility at Tesla, tied to aggressive investment and rapid scaling, and more stability at GM. Those operating and net differences were not statistically distinct, which is a nice reminder that variance and average are different questions.

## Neither shape is the right answer

The SRE translation is the payoff. Innovation-heavy architectures deliver strong top-line efficiency but introduce variability; continuous iteration creates operational fluctuation. She draws the parallel to AI platforms, where training cycles, infrastructure scaling and experimentation pipelines inject variance into production. Mature systems trade peak performance for resilience under pressure, and large enterprise platforms tend to drift toward that model as they start carrying mission-critical load.

So reliability goals have to match the organisation's risk tolerance. An AI platform in experimentation mode can accept more volatility; a customer-facing platform serving millions of users cannot experiment as freely. Setting the same SLO philosophy for both is how you end up either slow or on fire.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, program leads and senior SREs who negotiate reliability targets with the business, and anyone trying to explain to leadership why the experimental platform and the billing system should not share an error budget. If you want tooling or incident tactics, skip it; if you want vocabulary for the speed-versus-stability conversation, it is a quick, unusual angle.

Title: Regulated systems can be up and still make the wrong decisions
Description: Shruthi Sepuri of TCS at Conf42 SRE 2026 on workflow-level reliability for insurance and finance - decision accuracy SLIs and testing that continues in production.
Body:
A rule configuration change can quietly move an approval threshold and leave every dashboard green. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Shruthi Sepuri, Software Developer Engineer at TATA Consultancy Services, showed how that kind of silent workflow failure slips past infrastructure monitoring in regulated systems, and how to extend testing into production so you catch wrong decisions, not just slow ones.

Her one-line summary is the talk in miniature: "A system can be up and still be wrong."

## The factory machine that hums while making bad parts

She opens with an analogy: a factory machine that runs perfectly, nothing overheating, panel all normal, while the parts coming out are wrong. Her first slide puts that into software. On the left, the view on-call engineers are used to: four nines of uptime, tiny error rate, low latency, CPU and memory comfortable. On the right, the business workflow: ingestion passes, the rule engine errors, the decision output is wrong, compliance validation is skipped and the audit log has a gap. The footnote says it all: a rule misconfiguration, and no infrastructure alert triggered.

Uptime, error rates and latency measure technical health. None of them measure decision correctness, and in insurance or financial services, a wrong approval at scale is a compliance event, not a minor defect.

## There is a missing layer in most monitoring stacks

She breaks systems into layers. Infrastructure and application services (servers, databases, APIs, queues, caches) are usually monitored well. The business workflow layer (claims processing, underwriting, policy adjustments, compliance validation, audit logging) is under-monitored. The compliance outcomes layer (correct decisions, audit trails, risk controls) is often not measured at all.

Her worked example is a claims system where a config change silently alters approval thresholds. Infrastructure stays green throughout, decisions drift, incorrect approvals or rejections go through at scale, and the audit trail may be incomplete. The listed causes are all mundane: rule misconfigurations, data mapping issues, threshold drift, missing compliance attributes. None of them crash anything.

## Four indicators for decision correctness

Reliability has to be defined at the workflow level, with a check at each step: is the input validated, are the right rules in use, is the outcome in the expected range, are required fields complete, is the audit record immutable and complete. From those come four indicators:

- **Decision accuracy rate**: share of automated decisions within the expected outcome range.
- **Approval and rejection deviation**: statistical drift from the historical baseline, so a sudden spike or drop becomes a signal.
- **Compliance field completion**: required audit attributes populated per transaction.
- **Rule execution correctness**: rules behaving as configured, checked against known test cases.

## Testing does not stop at the release

The bridge to QA is the part testers will appreciate. Testing feeds deployment, deployment feeds monitoring, incidents feed learning, and learning feeds better tests. Her four methods: synthetic business transactions replayed continuously against live rule engines, real-time monitoring of decision outcomes and rule execution, comparing rule engine output against expected baselines after every deployment, and alerting on statistical anomalies in outcomes rather than only on technical errors. Production decision distributions then flow back to update test cases and thresholds before the next rule change ships.

Her formula for it is testing plus observability equals workflow reliability. Neither half is enough alone.

## Who should watch

QA engineers moving toward reliability work, and SREs on rule-heavy platforms in insurance, banking or anywhere a config file can change an outcome. It is an accessible, framework-level talk with illustrative dashboards; bring your own rule engine and you will leave with a short list of SLIs to add.

Title: AI for clinical handoffs has to fail safely before it helps
Description: Abhiram Potharaju of Wells Fargo at Conf42 SRE 2026 on SBAR-aligned AI handoff summaries built with SRE habits - safe degradation, explainability, governance.
Body:
A shift change in a hospital is an on-call handover where the system being handed over is a person. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Abhiram Potharaju, Senior Software Engineer at Wells Fargo, looked at AI-augmented clinical handoffs through an SRE lens: how to build an assistant that summarises patient data reliably, stays honest about uncertainty, and leaves every clinical decision with the clinician.

It is a design and governance talk rather than a system demo, and it is careful not to oversell: the goal is fewer missed details, not automated medicine.

## Handoffs fail for three boring reasons

Communication breakdowns during handoffs are a known contributor to adverse events, and he narrows the causes to three. Cognitive overload: clinicians juggle many patients under time pressure. Fragmented EHR data: the facts exist but are scattered across notes, labs, vitals and medication lists. Variable quality: even with SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) in place, execution differs between clinicians and shifts.

Any SRE who has received a one-line handover note that says all good, watch the queue, will recognise the pattern. His point is that this is a patient safety and reliability problem, not a documentation one.

## Use the format clinicians already trust

The proposed system ingests structured data (vitals, medications, orders, labs) and unstructured notes, and produces a concise summary aligned to SBAR. That alignment is the clever, unglamorous choice: it fits a framework clinicians already use instead of inventing a new one. Situation carries current status and the immediate concern, Background the relevant history, Assessment the meaningful trends, and Recommendation the next steps that need attention.

The abstract adds the monitoring side: continuously watching vital sign trends, medication changes and lab deviations to highlight early signs of deterioration. The aim is to reduce variability and speed up situational awareness, so less time is spent searching records.

## Reliability here means degrading safely

This is where the SRE framing earns its place. In healthcare, being useful is not enough; the assistant has to stay dependable when data is incomplete, inconsistent or late. He lists the familiar toolkit (observability, fault tolerance, incident awareness, proactive maintenance) and adds the healthcare-specific requirements: safe behaviour under uncertainty and safe degradation, so that a gap in the input shows up as a gap in the summary rather than a confident fabrication.

Explainability is treated as a reliability property too. If the system flags a risk, the clinician should be able to see what drove it. That builds appropriate trust and guards against over-reliance, which in this domain is its own failure mode.

## Governance is part of the system, not paperwork around it

The deployment section reads like a production readiness review. Validate carefully before broad rollout, keep monitoring accuracy, reliability and workflow impact afterwards, train staff on how and when to use it, and set clear escalation paths and oversight for when outputs look wrong. He recommends starting with pilot programs on clearly defined use cases, involving clinicians early in workflow design, and measuring outcomes from real workflow behaviour. Adoption, in his framing, is not a one-time event.

## Who should watch

Engineers building AI features for clinical, legal or other high-stakes workflows, and SREs asked to put an LLM summary in front of people who will act on it. It stays at the level of principles, with no metrics or architecture diagrams to copy, so treat it as a framework for your design review rather than a blueprint.

Title: Green dashboards, slow humans - measure workflow latency instead
Description: Abhimanyu Narwal of Bloomberg at Conf42 SRE 2026 on silent telemetry gaps, workflow SLIs, count invariants and canaries that prove a pipeline is working.
Body:
The edge gateway said 100,000 events arrived; the analysis engine showed 90,000; every service was green. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Abhimanyu Narwal, Engineering Team Lead for security services at Bloomberg, used that gap to argue that the expensive reliability failures are often not outages but the quiet ones that slow humans down, and he left a short checklist for catching them.

He is clear about scope up front: an anonymised case study and a reusable SRE pattern, not a breach story and not a description of Bloomberg's proprietary architecture.

## The fog of war is ambiguity, not panic

The pipeline is a familiar shape: events enter, get processed, results surface in a UI, a human analyst validates them and acts. For a long time it looked perfect. Then an analyst raised a low-severity alert because counts diverged between stages.

Nothing had crashed. The question was whether the gap was expected transformation lag or a visibility hole, and in a security workflow that uncertainty is costly. Management kept asking whether threats were being missed. After a lot of digging the answer was reassuring and annoying in equal measure: processing and safety checks had worked fine, but a telemetry agent had silently failed and dropped logs before they reached the UI. Compute health was 100%. The team's confidence was not.

## The four golden signals answered the wrong question

Latency, traffic, errors and saturation were all fine. They answer whether the system is alive, and miss whether the workflow is explainable. His key distinction: service latency is milliseconds between request and response; workflow latency is the time for a human to go from seeing a signal to confidently acting on it. When telemetry drops, the second one explodes while the first stays flat.

So the team stopped treating this as a logging bug and started treating the whole human workflow like a distributed trace, human validation step included.

## Three SLIs worth stealing

- **End-to-end duration**: p50 and p95 from ingestion to visible in the UI, alerting when it is consistently worse than the workflow needs. That catches slow degradation behind healthy services.
- **Count integrity**: compare counts between stages against an explicit model of expected deltas and lag. His example: 2% divergence for five minutes is normal; 10% for an hour means the invariant is broken.
- **Liveness via canary**: a known-good synthetic event injected continuously and verified at every stage. If you take one thing from the talk, he says, take this.

## Systems should confess their own blind spots

On the design side he proposes what he calls a fifth golden signal for the system to reveal its own coverage gaps. When telemetry is missing, the UI should say so. Treat partial degradation as a first-class state instead of a binary up or down, so reduced coverage shows as reduced coverage rather than a reassuringly normal screen. And make invariants (everything received is eventually surfaced within a known window) observable contracts.

His last tactic is the most human one: if people are a reliability endpoint, measure their friction. Repeated queries, pivots, escalations and reopen rates are proxies. Before the fix, tier-one analysts did not trust the UI and escalated to engineering for manual database queries; that escalation loop was, in his words, the true error rate.

## Who should watch

SREs and observability folks supporting any human-in-the-loop pipeline: security operations, fraud review, moderation, support tooling. The checklist is deliberately small: pick one key workflow, define its invariants, add one synthetic canary, write one workflow SLO. A cheap Monday morning, and you get to stop guessing.

Title: Airline shopping traffic is mostly repeats, so cache it carefully
Description: Mukul Kumar Gaur of Accelya Group at Conf42 SRE 2026 on caching NDC airline offers at scale with freshness rules that stop pricing drift.
Body:
Many of the searches hitting an airline's offer engine are the same question asked by different robots a few seconds apart. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Mukul Kumar Gaur, Senior Principal in Product Management and Product Engineering at Accelya Group, explained how NDC shopping platforms can serve that repeat demand from cache without quoting a price the airline no longer offers.

If NDC is new to you: it is the airline industry's move to offer- and order-based retailing, where offers are built dynamically per request instead of being pulled from static fare filings. That flexibility is exactly what makes every request expensive.

## You are scaling to process repetition

The problem, in his framing, is redundancy. Requests arrive from airline websites, online travel agencies, metasearch sites and automated repricing systems, and a large share are repetitive or near-duplicate searches for the same origin and destination. Meanwhile each one now triggers real-time offer generation: fares, taxes, inventory availability and merchandising rules.

Without caching, the platform recomputes the full offer every time. His phrase for it is that platforms end up scaling infrastructure to process repetition rather than incremental revenue. The bill shows up as latency and cloud cost, and the risk shows up during traffic spikes. The fix is not a bigger engine but recognising repeat demand and reusing work already done.

## Pick the cache by how fast the price moves

The talk lays out three strategies, with the trade-off stated plainly: performance versus flexibility versus pricing freshness.

- **Full offer caching** stores the complete offer as generated and returns it instantly on a matching request. Fastest option, best for markets where prices are fairly stable or the cache window is tightly controlled.
- **Hybrid anchored caching** keeps stable parts (say, the fare structure) and recalculates the volatile parts, such as availability and dynamic price adjustments, per request.
- **Partial component caching** caches individual pipeline pieces independently, such as tax calculations, fare rules or schedule data. Less speed-up, less stale-data risk.

His recommendation is to layer them rather than choose one. Most real platforms have markets in all three categories.

## Governance is what keeps a cache honest

The obvious worry is pricing drift: a cached offer that outlives the inventory or price it was built on. The abstract also names the downstream pain, settlement discrepancies, which is the kind of bug finance finds weeks after engineering shipped it.

The controls he lists are freshness thresholds that cap how long an offer stays valid, real-time invalidation triggers that evict cached data when pricing or availability changes, special handling for high-elasticity markets, and elastic controls that hold consistency under spikes. The abstract adds request quality scoring and partner-level cache controls, so a noisy aggregator does not get the same treatment as a channel that converts.

Monitoring closes the loop: BI dashboards on cache hit rates, system performance and pricing alignment, plus automated alerts when discrepancies appear. Cache invalidation is famously one of the two hard problems; this talk is mostly about making its failures visible fast.

## Peak sales are the real test

His worked scenario is a high-demand promotion, when shopping traffic can jump within minutes. Without caching, every request hits the offer engine and performance degrades exactly when the airline most wants to sell. With layered caching, most of those requests are served from offers already computed, and the engine keeps capacity for the ones that need fresh pricing.

## Who should watch

Engineers on travel, e-commerce or any dynamic pricing system where reads vastly outnumber purchases. It is a conceptual talk with no code or benchmark numbers, so expect a clear mental model and a checklist (layered caching, explicit invalidation policy, observability on pricing accuracy) rather than an implementation.
