Title: In regulatory reporting, a missed deadline is a compliance failure
Description: Bhargavaram Potharaju of Wells Fargo at Conf42 SRE 2026 on high availability, deadline-aware disaster recovery and audit replay for regulatory reporting.
Body:
When a regulatory report is late, nobody files it under operations. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Bhargavaram Potharaju, Senior Infrastructure Engineer at Wells Fargo, argued that on national-scale reporting platforms SRE directly decides compliance outcomes, and that high availability, disaster recovery and audit readiness have to be designed in from day one rather than added after the first audit finding.

It is a short, architecture-level talk with no vendor in it: a reference model, the principles behind it, and a path to adopt it one layer at a time.

## Your SLOs should be written in filing deadlines

The pressure he describes comes from two directions: data volumes grow each reporting cycle while submission windows shrink. In that world a delay is not a service issue and a wrong output is not a data issue; both can turn into penalties. So service level objectives, incident response and error budgets all need to line up with regulatory deadlines, not generic IT targets.

He names five places legacy platforms struggle: high availability, peak-load performance, data accuracy, auditable outcomes and disaster resilience. Most enterprise systems are tuned for an average Tuesday. Reporting platforms live and die in the crunch right before cutoff.

## Recovery time is measured backwards from the cutoff

The most useful idea is deadline-aware disaster recovery. Recovery objectives cannot be picked in isolation; they depend on how much time is left before submission. If an outage hits close to a deadline, the platform still needs time to recover, reprocess, validate and submit, and ideally time to validate the results before sending them. An RTO that looks fine on paper can be useless an hour before the filing window closes.

That is also why he insists failover be tested under realistic load. Availability tested only under daily traffic tells you nothing about burst traffic and peak concurrency, and a DR plan that has never run at peak is, in his framing, a theoretical design exercise.

## Prove how the number was made, not just the number

Audit readiness gets its own section. The platform has to show exactly how a submission was created: immutable logs, full data lineage and deterministic replay, so you can rerun the process and reproduce the same result when asked. The pipeline he sketches runs ingestion, validation, transformation, submission, monitoring and audit replay, with fault isolation between stages so that a problem in one stage cannot silently corrupt the next.

## Business telemetry catches what server metrics miss

Server metrics will tell you a machine is stressed. They will not tell you the deadline is at risk. He wants observability at the business-process level: record counts, validation pass and fail rates, queue depth, per-stage latency, submission timing and acknowledgement status.

The failure mode he flags as most dangerous is the silent one: records dropped, validations skipped, acknowledgements never confirmed, all while the platform looks healthy, and nobody finds out until the audit. His answer is end-to-end validation gates and explicit confirmation that each record reached a correct outcome. He also accepts that many of these platforms cannot go fully cloud native because of security, data residency or legacy integrations, so the controls have to work in hybrid setups too.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects on finance, insurance or government reporting systems, and anyone whose batch pipeline has a hard external deadline. It is high level and light on tooling; the value is the framing and the checklist: identify current failure modes, define compliance-aligned SLOs, improve telemetry, test DR in realistic scenarios, then harden submission gates step by step.

Title: CruiseKube right-sizes Kubernetes pods in place, minute by minute
Description: Shubham Rai (Truefoundry) and Raman Tehlan (Zurich Lab) at Conf42 SRE 2026 show CruiseKube, open source CPU right-sizing with in-place pod resize and PSI.
Body:
Everyone knows lower CPU requests mean a cheaper cluster, and almost nobody lowers them. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Shubham Rai of Truefoundry and Raman Tehlan, Cloud Native Consultant at Zurich Lab, presented CruiseKube, an open source controller that keeps correcting pod requests in place, using two features that only recently became usable in Kubernetes.

It is a builders' talk: the problem, the design choices, the components and a dashboard demo, closing with an honest list of where not to turn it on.

## Over-provisioning is a fear problem, not a knowledge problem

Shubham opens with why clusters stay expensive. Teams fear CPU throttling and OOM kills, because an under-provisioned pod that gets killed is a business outage. So they pad requests. Then nobody wants to keep re-analysing workloads and editing YAML. The padding compounds: inflated requests force the cluster autoscaler to add nodes that sit half empty.

His point about where to fix it is worth hearing. You cannot solve this at the node level, because node over-provisioning is downstream of request over-provisioning. Fix requests first, or the node autoscaler is just efficiently buying the wrong amount of hardware.

## Predict a little, correct often

The contrast with the Vertical Pod Autoscaler is the core idea. VPA does periodic analysis and produces a recommendation that has to hold for a long time, per workload, across whatever nodes its pods landed on. CruiseKube runs a continuous feedback loop that only needs to be right for a short window ahead, and it decides per pod, in the context of the node that pod is on.

Two things make that viable. In-place pod resource updates went GA in Kubernetes 1.35, so a request can change without a restart. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) metrics, beta in 1.34, give per-container contention data on each node, even when you set no CPU limits. CruiseKube combines CPU usage with CPU PSI to pick the request.

The node view matters because of headroom, the gap between a pod's base need and its bursts. Bursts are big and rare, so the gap between the 75th percentile and the maximum is large. Instead of every pod reserving its own worst case, CruiseKube reserves the largest headroom among the pods on a node and lets them share it. It is the same bet as a shared on-call rota: not everyone has a bad night at once.

## Two entry points and a lot of guardrails

Raman walks through the loop: observe the cluster from Prometheus, store stats, learn patterns (a peak at the same time over the last seven days), then apply. Changes land in two places. A mutating admission webhook sets requests when a pod is created, informed by history, so a pod that was OOM-killed comes back with more memory. A continuous optimizer applies recommendations to running pods in place, evicting only when a pod needs more than its node can give.

The guardrails are the part SREs will check first. Everything starts in recommend-only mode; nothing changes until you enable cruise mode per workload. Eviction respects criticality (a single-replica workload ranks higher than one with fifty pods) and you can edit priorities. OOM kills feed back into memory sizing. There is also a disruption window for Karpenter users whose do-not-disrupt annotations block node consolidation.

The demo dashboard shows monthly cost, current and untapped savings, allocatable versus requested versus recommended resources, per-workload recommendations and an event log of every change. On the demo cluster, enabling it for all workloads showed savings of about 60%.

## Where they say not to use it (yet)

Their recommendation is stateless services, dev and staging, and short-lived jobs. Latency-sensitive services, stateful apps like databases and queues, and workloads under HPA should stay in recommend mode for now; HPA support was still in progress at the time of the talk.

## Who should watch

Platform and FinOps engineers who have tried VPA, found it too slow or too disruptive, and still pay for idle cores. It is a short, practical tour with a demo; you will come away knowing whether to install it in recommend mode and look.

Title: AI personalisation fails silently, so give it circuit breakers
Description: Yury Lysak of Lionsoul Global at Conf42 SRE 2026 on proactive SRE for AI personalisation: drift signals, small-data methods and black swan circuit breakers.
Body:
A recommendation engine can be 100% available, return zero errors and still lose you a client. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Yury Lysak, Head of Strategic Projects at Lionsoul Global, a digital asset wealth manager, made the case that AI personalisation needs its own SRE playbook, because its failures never page anyone.

He brings a useful career arc to it: personalisation and commercial analytics for telcos at VEON and for retailers via McKinsey, now applied to wealth tech, where the client list is short and every client matters.

## Loud failures get fixed, quiet ones get quarterly reviews

His framing is the sharpest part of the talk. Traditional failures are loud: a 500, a timeout, a crash, and everyone mobilises. Personalisation failures are gradual. Features decay, embeddings go stale, recommendations get a little worse each week, and the dashboard stays green. He describes client lifetime value slipping a percent or two per month, unnoticed until a complaint or a quarterly review shows months of lost revenue.

Then there are the events no model was trained for. He cites the October 2025 crypto liquidation cascade and the February 2026 Bitcoin crash as moments when the engineering was fine and the models' assumptions about liquidity and correlation were catastrophically wrong. No latency alert catches a model that is confidently describing a market that no longer exists.

## When you have 50 clients, A/B testing is a fantasy

What transfers from telco and retail is a lot: next best action becomes fund allocation, churn prediction becomes attrition scoring, basket analysis becomes spotting which clients might fit a new strategy. What does not transfer is the sample size. With a few dozen clients you cannot A/B test or train a standard model.

His substitutes are concrete: Bayesian methods that start from priors learned elsewhere and update per client, Thompson sampling for exploration on tiny samples, transfer learning where similar data exists, and the relationship manager as a human sensor whose qualitative notes feed the loop. The architecture he shows layers this: data sources (including RM notes), an ML pipeline producing ranked recommendations with confidence intervals, an LLM layer that writes the client-facing narrative, and a guardrail layer with a rules engine and an RM review gate. The LLM drafts; it never has the last word.

## Three levels of admitting the model does not know

The circuit breaker design is the part to copy. Level one is an always-on market regime detector: volatility above twice the 90-day average, or correlations moving sharply, widens uncertainty bounds and escalates to humans. Level two watches confidence per recommendation and suppresses automation when inputs drift too far from training data. Level three, when both trip, switches off ML recommendations and falls back to conservative, pre-approved defaults. His guiding principle: silence beats a confident wrong answer.

Monitoring is tiered too: daily data quality and confidence, weekly PSI drift per feature plus the RM override rate (above 30% means the model is misaligned), monthly business metrics against a non-personalised baseline. And every alert should speak business, naming revenue at risk rather than just a threshold crossed.

## Compliance as a pipeline step

In regulated finance each recommendation is a potential regulatory event, so his pipeline logs inputs, model version and confidence at generation time, validates against concentration limits and client restrictions, has an LLM write a feature-referencing explanation, routes it through an RM, then archives it. Answering a regulator, he says, went from weeks of digging to a download.

## Who should watch

Anyone running ML in production where the feedback loop is slow and the dataset small: wealth, B2B, healthcare, anything with dozens of customers instead of millions. The business impact figures in the talk are his own, so treat them as one firm's experience; the circuit breaker and alert-design patterns stand on their own.

Title: From alerts to answers with context-driven observability and agents
Description: Savi Grover (Tekskills) at Conf42 SRE 2026 gives a quick tour of turning alert noise into context, with an agent loop that rolls back a bad canary.
Body:
SRE teams don't need more alerts, they need answers, and the gap between the two is context. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Savi Grover, Site Reliability Engineer at Tekskills, gave a brisk tour of context-driven observability and ended with an agent that notices a spike in 500s, traces it to a bad canary and rolls it back before reporting to a human.

It's one of the shortest talks of the event, closer to a lightning talk than a workshop. Watch it as a checklist, not a tutorial.

## Data rich, information poor

Savi's starting point is the paradox most on-call engineers recognize. The move from monoliths to microservices multiplied telemetry volume (she puts it at a hundred times), and SREs are now drowning in high-cardinality noise. Traditional monitoring identifies the symptom and leaves the engineer to hunt for the cause by hand.

She names four reasons the old way fails:

- **Siloed data.** Metrics, logs and traces live in separate tools with no correlation.
- **The dashboard mirage.** Flipping through dozens of dashboards during an outage adds cognitive load instead of removing it.
- **Static thresholds.** She says they lead to 80% flapping, non-actionable alerts.
- **Knowledge leakage.** Resolution depends on tribal knowledge rather than encoded patterns.

## Signal to context

Her framework shifts attention from raw data to meaningful, contextual events. Golden signals (latency, errors, traffic, saturation) are still the base, but read through SLOs rather than as raw thresholds. Distributed tracing is the backbone, with trace IDs stitching the user journey together across the mesh. And AI does dimensionality reduction: a thousand connection-refused log lines become one "database connectivity" cluster event.

The supporting practices are the ones that make all of that possible:

- consistent tags and metadata on all telemetry (application, environment, service tier, owner),
- end-to-end lineage, so you can see which downstream assets an upstream issue affects,
- anomaly detection that learns normal behaviour instead of relying only on static thresholds,
- correlation that links logs, metrics and traces to code changes, infrastructure and business impact,
- automated root cause analysis that goes past detection to triage and suggested fixes.

## The agent loop

The agentic ops part is a four-step loop. **Observe:** watch golden signals through tools like Prometheus and Grafana and notice an anomaly, say a spike in 500 errors. **Analyze:** query traces and find that a downstream API is timing out or down. **Act:** check recent CI/CD logs, identify a bad canary deployment and trigger a rollback. **Report:** tell the team in Slack or email what caused it, what was done and the details of the anomaly.

It's a clean picture of where agents fit in incident response. What the talk doesn't cover is the hard part: guardrails, how much autonomy the agent gets before a human approves, and what happens when it rolls back the wrong thing. Pair it with a longer talk if you're about to build one.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to observability who want the vocabulary in one sitting, or a team lead looking for a short talk to kick off an alert-fatigue discussion. Experienced SREs will know most of it already.

Title: Three telemetry layers that answer "what changed?" in an incident
Description: Khushboo Nigam (Oracle) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on organizing traces, Kubernetes signals and CI/CD telemetry so incident triage follows evidence.
Body:
The alert already tells you something is wrong; the question you actually ask next is "what changed?" At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Khushboo Nigam, Principal Cloud Architect at Oracle, presented a layered observability framework that sorts telemetry by the investigation question it answers, so an engineer can move from user impact to platform health to the deployment that caused it without becoming the manual integration layer.

Her one-line thesis is the talk's title: correlation over collection.

## A clarity problem, not a data problem

Khushboo's diagnosis is that most teams already collect plenty: infrastructure metrics, logs, traces, deployment events, a pile of alerts. Each signal has value, but on its own it doesn't tell a story. During an incident they all compete for attention at once, and the on-call engineer ends up stitching them together by hand under pressure.

She draws the usual line between monitoring and observability, and it's a useful refresher. Monitoring catches known failure conditions: CPU above 90%, latency above 500 milliseconds, the known knowns. Observability is for the unknown unknowns, the failures nobody wrote an alert for. Neither helps if the telemetry has no shared context linking a latency spike, a timeout in the logs, a slow span and last night's release.

## Organize signals by the question they answer

The framework has three layers, each tied to one question:

1. **Application traces: where is it failing?** Follow the request across services and find the slow or failing span.
2. **Kubernetes metrics and events: is the platform healthy?** Node resource pressure, pod restarts, crash loops, scheduling problems.
3. **CI/CD telemetry: what changed?** Deployments, version bumps, configuration changes, pipeline results.

The order matters. You narrow from the whole system to one component, then decide whether the platform or the application is at fault, then look for the change.

## Enrich spans so you can pivot

The demo uses a retail microservices app on managed Kubernetes: a load balancer, a web frontend, an API backend with a payment operation, and an external database. Telemetry flows through the OpenTelemetry Collector plus cloud-native services into separate backends for application monitoring, logs and metrics.

The key move is in the collector: it enriches application spans with Kubernetes metadata, so the payment span that shows the error and high latency also carries the node name, pod name and pod IP. That's the pivot from layer one to layer two; you jump straight to that node's resource usage and that pod's events. Further down the same span sits the service version and the error message from the application's instrumentation. If the platform looks healthy and errors began right after a deploy, the version in the span tells you which release to look at.

Put together, telemetry becomes what she calls a structured hierarchy of evidence, with each layer narrowing the search rather than adding more noise.

## Know what your provider owns

One aside is easy to skip and shouldn't be. On managed Kubernetes, the control plane (API server, etcd) is usually the cloud provider's responsibility, while nodes and workloads are yours. Khushboo's advice: read your provider's policy, find out which metrics and logs they expose for the parts they manage, and know in advance when to escalate rather than debug.

## Who should watch

SREs whose incident response still starts with opening five dashboards, and platform teams setting up OpenTelemetry who want a reason to enrich spans with Kubernetes and deployment metadata. The framework is platform-agnostic and clearly explained; it's not a vendor pitch.

Title: Watch the business workflow, not the service, to detect faster
Description: Rohit Wadhwa (Walmart) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on Predictive Workflow Integrity, which models workflows as state machines and cut detection time below a minute.
Body:
A burnt pizza alarm fires after the damage is done; a better system checks the oven temperature and the dough on the way. That analogy opens the talk by Rohit Wadhwa, Senior Software Engineer at Walmart, at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026. His model, Predictive Workflow Integrity (PWI), moves observability from individual services to end-to-end business workflows, and he reports mean time to detection dropping from about 12 minutes to 58 seconds.

It's a short talk, more of a model and results summary than an implementation guide, but the reframing is worth the time.

## Service signals miss workflow failures

Event-driven microservices across regions bring three problems Rohit sees in practice. State divergence, where services stop agreeing about what's going on. Latency variability, where one slow service compounds across the whole call path. And cascading failures, where one failing component ripples into a wide outage. Service-level dashboards can look fine while a business workflow is stuck halfway, and with a 12-minute detection time you're only starting to fix things after customers have noticed.

## Workflows as state machines

PWI models each workflow as a distributed state machine and keeps evaluating its transitions. It looks for three red flags:

- **Delayed convergence.** The workflow doesn't reach its expected state within the expected time, a sign some service didn't follow its instructions.
- **Conflicting ownership.** Several teams acting on the same workflow or platform, which slows down resolution.
- **Abnormal execution paths.** A service routes the workflow down an unexpected path, which leads to degraded performance and then failure.

None of these are visible from a single service's latency graph, which is the point.

## Autonomous triage on a causal graph

To act on those signals, PWI correlates logs, metrics and traces into one map of the system (the abstract calls it an event-driven causal graph) and applies machine learning on top to prioritize incidents by severity. From there it moves to automated remediation. Rohit claims it predicts likely issues and fixes some before they surface, which reduced incident creation and level-two escalations. He doesn't walk through the models themselves, so treat this part as the outline of an approach rather than a recipe.

The numbers, from the talk and its abstract: MTTD went from roughly 12 minutes to under one minute (58 seconds in his example), mean time to mitigation from about 45 to 50 minutes down to 10 to 12, and false-positive alerts from around 18% to about 4%. That last one matters most for on-call morale.

## Rings by geography

The second idea is Ring-Based Geolocation Routing. If users are on the East Coast and servers on the West Coast, you pay latency on every call, and a regional failure can take down the whole application. Rohit's team localized event processing and decisions into rings per region. He reports edge-to-cloud latency falling from about five seconds to under one, roughly an 80% improvement, and says PWI runs across thousands of nodes at edge and cloud.

## Who should watch

SREs whose dashboards are green while customers report stuck orders, and teams thinking about workflow-level SLIs. If you want implementation detail (which models, how the state machines are defined), you will need to follow up with the speaker; the value here is the reframing and the before/after numbers.

Title: Moving a message broker to AWS: rehost, replatform or refactor
Description: Ran Tao (AWS) at Conf42 SRE 2026 compares lifting RabbitMQ to EC2, Amazon MQ, and refactoring clients for SQS and SNS, with Python code.
Body:
Lift-and-shift is the fastest way to move a message broker to the cloud and the one that keeps the most work on your team. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Ran Tao, Cloud Support Engineer at Amazon Web Services, compared three migration paths for on-prem messaging (rehost on EC2, replatform onto Amazon MQ, refactor for SQS and SNS) and showed Python client code for RabbitMQ and SQS side by side.

He calls it an introductory session, and it is: a structured map of the options on AWS, from an AWS engineer, useful if you're about to make this decision.

## Two kinds of messaging

On one side sit traditional message brokers such as IBM MQ or RabbitMQ, dedicated infrastructure connecting producers and consumers. On the other sit cloud-native serverless services: on AWS, SQS for queueing and SNS for broadcasting. Ran notes how requirements differ by industry: retail needs elasticity for peaks and quiet nights, while financial and government customers care most about durability and recovery during incidents.

Running brokers on-prem means paying for capacity up front, provisioning more to scale, and keeping engineers with specialist skills to run and monitor them.

## Three paths and who owns what

**Rehost.** Mirror the OS, broker engine and configs on EC2. Few application changes and full control, but you still own patching, broker monitoring and security configuration, and native integration with IAM or CloudWatch is limited.

**Replatform.** Move to Amazon MQ, a managed broker. Configuration shrinks to deployment mode and instance size; CloudWatch metrics (connections, channels, memory, per-queue message counts) and broker logs come enabled. Scaling up is a bigger instance size and a reboot instead of editing RabbitMQ config files. TLS is enforced, data at rest can be encrypted with a KMS key, and patching happens in a weekly maintenance window you pick, for example midnight for a retailer. Single-node brokers live in one Availability Zone and suit proofs of concept; for production Ran recommends cluster mode, which mirrors messages across three nodes in three AZs so losing one doesn't lose data.

**Refactor.** Rewrite clients for SQS and SNS. Scaling and capacity become the provider's problem and pricing is per API call, so a retailer isn't paying for an idle broker fleet at night. Your team's responsibility shrinks to business logic.

## What the code actually changes

The RabbitMQ example uses Pika: set TLS 1.2 connection parameters, open a connection and channel, declare a queue, publish, then close the connection. Ran stresses closing connections, because leaked ones show up as broker memory and CPU creeping up over time. Consumers must call `basic_ack`, or the broker eventually treats them as inactive.

The SQS version has no connection management at all. Create the queue, get its URL, send and receive messages through API calls, and delete each message after processing using its receipt handle; skip that and the message reappears after the visibility timeout.

## The refactor checklist

- **Separate producers from consumers** so they scale independently; draining a backlog shouldn't require more producers.
- **Know your delivery model.** A broker does point-to-point and publish-subscribe in one place. On AWS they split: SQS is point-to-point, SNS is publish-subscribe.
- **Protocols change.** AMQP and other persistent-connection protocols become HTTPS API calls.
- **Ordering versus scale.** SQS FIFO queues keep strict order; standard queues give best-effort ordering and scale much further.
- **Payload limits.** Messages are capped at one megabyte by default; AWS extended client libraries for Java and Python store the body in S3 and send a pointer, up to two gigabytes.
- **Auth and audit.** SQS and SNS use IAM and can log requests in CloudTrail, whereas RabbitMQ, even on Amazon MQ, may need something like an LDAP server.
- **Lost knobs.** Managed services remove some settings; you can't turn TLS off on an Amazon MQ RabbitMQ broker.

## Who should watch

Teams running RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ on-prem with a cloud migration on the roadmap, and SREs who want to know what they will still own after each option. If you already run SQS in production, you can skip it.

Title: Why HTTP/2 sent all our Kubernetes traffic to one pod
Description: Mariem Sboui (gridX) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on an incident where kube-proxy's connection-level balancing pinned HTTP/2 traffic to a single pod.
Body:
One pod at full CPU, its siblings idle, plenty of cluster capacity, and the autoscaler perfectly happy: that was the picture after Mariem Sboui's team switched some critical services to HTTP/2. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Mariem, Senior Site Reliability Engineer at gridX, walked through the incident and its cause: Kubernetes Services balance TCP connections, not requests, and HTTP/2 puts many requests on one long-lived connection.

It is a short, focused incident review, and the kind of talk that saves someone a very confusing afternoon.

## The symptoms didn't add up

External users saw extra latency, which Mariem put at more than 300 milliseconds. Not catastrophic, but real. Looking at the backends, one pod was serving essentially all incoming traffic while the others sat idle.

What made it confusing was everything that looked fine. Nodes and pods had idle capacity. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler was working normally. And killing the hot pod didn't help: the traffic simply landed on another single pod, with no redistribution. Mariem is candid about the team's mistake. They assumed HTTP/2 would behave like HTTP/1.1 inside Kubernetes, without knowing what happens one layer down.

## Layer 4 balancing meets multiplexing

By default a Kubernetes Service does Layer 4 load balancing. When a new TCP connection arrives, kube-proxy picks a backend pod and every request on that connection goes to that pod. Nothing looks at individual requests.

That works for HTTP/1.x because clients typically open many short-lived connections, and each new connection can land on a different pod. HTTP/2 changes the deal: a client multiplexes many requests over a single connection, and those connections tend to stay open for a long time. So kube-proxy makes one choice and the whole stream follows it. One pod gets everything, its CPU spikes and throttles, and latency climbs for users.

## A quick patch, then a six-month fix

The short-term changes were all at the application level: tuning keep-alive settings, reducing connection reuse in the HTTP/2 clients, and increasing the number of active connections. That spread traffic out enough to stop the bleeding, and Mariem is clear that it was only a stopgap.

The permanent fix is Layer 7 routing: a service mesh, an HTTP-aware proxy, or an API gateway or ingress that routes per request. Her team chose a service mesh, specifically Istio, and the rollout took about six months. The proxy inspects each HTTP request and decides per request, taking into account paths, headers, routing rules, backend latency and health. Distribution afterwards isn't perfectly equal, but it is far better than the default.

That six-month number is worth remembering. The incident fix took days; the architectural fix took two quarters.

## The takeaways

- Don't rely on default kube-proxy load balancing for HTTP/2-based traffic. That includes gRPC and anything else that keeps connections open.
- Put Layer 7 load balancing in front of those services.
- Run enough backend pods that capacity can actually absorb the distribution.

## Who should watch

Anyone about to enable HTTP/2 or gRPC inside a Kubernetes cluster, and anyone staring at one hot pod with an autoscaler that sees no problem. Platform teams debating whether a mesh is worth the cost will find a concrete reason here. It's short, practical, and has a real incident at its centre.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Developing custom Load Balancer using Envoy](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Sandeep_Bhat_custom_load_balancer_envoy) by Sandeep Bhat (Harness), for the proxy-level view.

Title: Run VMs as Kubernetes resources to cut hybrid on-call pain
Description: Shruthi Rajashekar (Broadcom) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on VM Service in VCF, which manages virtual machines and containers through one Kubernetes control plane.
Body:
If your on-call rotation covers containers in Kubernetes and VMs in a separate virtualization stack, you are on call for two platforms with two sets of alerts, dashboards and runbooks. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Shruthi Rajashekar, Engineering Manager at Broadcom who leads VM Service in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), argued for managing both through one Kubernetes control plane, with VMs declared and reconciled like any other resource.

To be clear about scope: this is a talk about a Broadcom product, VM Service in VCF, from the team that builds it. Shruthi has spent a decade at VMware and Broadcom and worked on vMotion, so the hybrid problem is home turf.

## Two worlds, one pager

The pain she describes is operational fragmentation. Containers live in Kubernetes-native tooling; VMs live in another stack with different APIs and consoles. During an incident, SREs correlate alerts from different systems and switch context to troubleshoot, and automation is hard to standardize when every workload type has its own lifecycle model. Most enterprises still run critical workloads on VMs while newer services run in containers, so this split isn't going away on its own.

## A VM as a first-class Kubernetes resource

VM Service makes a virtual machine something you declare, deploy, scale and manage with the same Kubernetes primitives as a pod or a deployment. You write the desired state in a manifest; the platform provisions it and keeps reconciling. That brings the usual Kubernetes benefits to VMs:

- VM specs can live in Git next to application code, so GitOps workflows apply to them too.
- Provisioning becomes repeatable and auditable instead of a console click or a one-off script.
- Engineers stop asking which system owns a workload during an incident; they interact with Kubernetes either way.

The same automation, policies and playbooks then apply across both workload types.

## Where reliability actually improves

Shruthi's list of reliability gains is concrete enough to test against your own setup:

- **Consistent alerts and metrics.** When VMs and containers sit under the same orchestration layer, alerts are generated the same way and metrics follow the same patterns, so incident response becomes predictable.
- **Capacity planning as one pool.** Instead of reasoning about separate resource pools for VMs and containers, teams can plan holistically.
- **Policy-driven rollouts and isolation.** Rollout safety, resource isolation and security policies can be enforced programmatically for VMs, and Kubernetes scheduling and policy help limit blast radius.
- **Unified telemetry.** Correlating CPU pressure, network anomalies or latency spikes across VMs and containers in one view, rather than across two monitoring pipelines.

## Modernize without rewriting

Her closing point is the most persuasive for teams with real legacy estates: you don't have to containerize everything to adopt cloud-native operations. Bring existing VM workloads under Kubernetes governance, keep newer services in containers, and modernize incrementally. The legacy application that nobody wants to rewrite gets declarative management and safer rollouts without a migration project.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams on VMware or VCF who run mixed VM and container estates and are tired of two operational models. If you're not in the VMware world, the talk still frames the case for unifying control planes, but the mechanics are specific to VM Service. It is an overview talk; expect architecture and benefits rather than a demo or incident numbers.

Title: AI answers for API support should pass an expert before developers
Description: Vishal Shah (Visa) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on agentic RAG for API support where owners approve every answer and each correction trains the system.
Body:
A developer hits a 401 on an OAuth 2 call, searches, and finds a Stack Overflow answer from 2021 describing an auth flow that has since been deprecated. By the time a human expert sees the ticket, the misconfiguration is already in production. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Vishal Shah, a staff software engineer at Visa who works on LLMs and agent systems, presented Reliable API Support: an agentic RAG framework where the API owners approve every AI answer before a developer sees it, and every correction feeds back into the system.

## Too slow or too fast and wrong

Vishal calls the status quo a structural failure, not a documentation one. Support either waits on human bandwidth, which is slow, or runs a chatbot that produces confident, fluent answers with no grounding in current API behaviour. Docs go stale after a fast release; a model trained before the change will happily describe behaviour that no longer exists. For SREs, both paths end in incidents caused by your own support channel.

## Three components

**Multi-source retrieval.** The knowledge base is federated: API docs, versioned changelogs, internal incident reports, curated FAQs and verified community examples, each indexed with version, confidence tier and last-verified date. Retrieval is hybrid, dense embeddings plus sparse keyword search, because exact error codes need exact matching. With one such collection per product API, the corpus gets large fast.

**Provisional answers with a confidence score.** The agent runs a ReAct-style reason-act-observe loop until it has enough context, reconciles conflicting sources, and produces a proposed solution, the evidence behind it and a calibrated low, medium or high confidence. High confidence can be fast-tracked; low confidence is escalated as a priority.

**The expert gate.** Senior engineers on the owning team review the draft against the live API spec and approve, edit or reject. Vishal's preference is to push these reviews into Microsoft Teams, Slack or Discord so owners can approve from a phone. The corrected answer goes to the developer and is stored as a labelled example for the next retrieval re-ranking or fine-tuning cycle.

## The feedback loop is the product

The part Vishal is most excited about: every expert edit is a labelled signal (the agent proposed A, the expert changed it to B). Developer thumbs up or down adds another layer. More queries produce more corrections, which improve retrieval, which raises confidence, which lowers review load. The system earns autonomy through demonstrated accuracy rather than being granted it on day one.

He adds a realistic caveat: a product in early development with lots of new API features will produce low confidence for a while, while stable APIs get high scores quickly.

## A roadmap in three phases

He deliberately frames this as a slow build. Phase one is plumbing: the retrieval pipeline, initial indexing, a review interface, and baseline retrieval metrics (precision at K, mean reciprocal rank) measured before touching the LLM layer. Phase two puts real queries through, tunes confidence thresholds and wires corrections back in; that's where they first saw repeat ticket volume drop. Phase three is scale and dashboards for accuracy, satisfaction and expert review time.

His four principles are worth pinning up: ground every response, calibrate confidence explicitly, make human review a first-class component, and close the loop. The warning attached to the third is the most practical line in the talk: if reviewing a draft takes more effort than writing the answer, experts will route around your system.

To start, he suggests pulling the last three months of support tickets, finding the top 10 recurring error types, and building the retrieval layer for those first.

## Who should watch

Platform and developer-experience teams running internal API support, and anyone shipping RAG where a wrong answer causes an outage rather than an awkward reply. It is an architecture talk; there are no published results beyond the qualitative drop in repeat tickets.

Title: ETL or a unified data platform? Pick by scale and reliability target
Description: Venkata Kundavaram (Goodwill Easter Seals Minnesota) at Conf42 SRE 2026 compares batch ETL with unified data platforms through an SRE lens.
Body:
For an SRE, "is the service up" is only half the question; the other half is whether the data it serves is correct and fresh enough to act on. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Venkata Kundavaram, IT Development Manager at Goodwill Easter Seals Minnesota, compared traditional ETL tools with unified data platforms and offered a short decision framework: choose by scale, reliability targets and integration needs, not by what is fashionable.

This is a compact, introductory talk built on a review of published research and industry reports. Treat it as a framework for a whiteboard conversation, not a benchmark.

## Data reliability is service reliability

Venkata's framing is practical. Enterprise data is no longer only structured transactions; SRE teams also handle logs, traces and customer behaviour signals, in different formats arriving at different speeds. The more types you ingest, the harder reliability guarantees get. A pipeline fails, a schema changes upstream, and suddenly incident response depends on data nobody fully trusts.

His example is an e-commerce slowdown. If your pipeline can't correlate application latency with checkout and inventory updates quickly, you lose time during the incident. When the data platform can't keep up with a spike, you get blind spots: delayed dashboards and missing metrics, exactly when you need them.

## What ETL is good at

Traditional extract-transform-load is predictable. You know what runs, when it runs and what it outputs. That makes it a good fit for stable reporting: end-of-day finance summaries, compliance reporting, weekly business dashboards. Upfront cost is usually lower.

The catch is the assumption baked into it: schemas rarely change, workloads are predictable and latency doesn't matter much. ETL tends to scale vertically (a bigger machine until you hit the ceiling), and batch processing adds latency that can collide with real-time reliability objectives. Maintenance costs also grow as volumes and complexity grow.

## What unified platforms buy you

Unified data platforms put ingestion, processing and governance on distributed, horizontally scalable architecture. You add nodes instead of upgrading a server, which handles spikes more gracefully and supports near real-time processing. They handle structured and unstructured data, fit event-driven systems better, and often build in monitoring and governance, which can shorten detection and recovery.

The price is a higher upfront investment and more operational complexity. Venkata's warning here is the most useful line of the talk in substance: a powerful platform nobody on the team can operate will fail operationally.

## Count people in the cost

His cost lens is total cost of ownership: tooling, compute, people, incident time, training and vendor support. Two platforms can look similar on licensing while one demands constant manual fixes that cost far more over a year in engineering time.

The decision framework then comes down to three lenses:

- **Scale and performance.** Predictable workloads that tolerate some latency suit batch ETL. Real elasticity and high-volume ingestion point to a unified platform.
- **Reliability.** How much fault tolerance and observability do you need from the data layer itself?
- **Integration.** If you plan anomaly detection, forecasting or recommendations on top, pick a platform that supports those integrations.

His closing scenario is a mid-sized e-commerce company whose transaction volume is surging: promotions spike, support tickets spike, and leaders can't tell in real time whether checkout is failing or whether inventory is right. That's the tipping point where the unified approach usually wins.

## Who should watch

SRE leads and engineering managers about to argue for (or against) a data platform migration, who want a neutral structure for the decision. If you already run streaming platforms at scale, you'll know most of this; the TCO framing is still worth stealing for the budget meeting.

Title: Healthcare denial letters are a reliability problem, then an AI one
Description: Prakash Easwaran (ZeOmega) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on automating utilization management letters, then using AI with human review to make denials readable.
Body:
"How hard can it be?" is what Prakash Easwaran, Implementation Manager at ZeOmega, says engineers think when they first hear about generating a letter, and his talk at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026 is the answer. In healthcare utilization management, every approval or denial must reach the member as a legally binding letter within tight deadlines, and his team first made that pipeline reliable with automation inside ZeOmega's Jiva platform, then added generative AI to make denials understandable, with a human reviewing every one.

## A letter is a regulatory artifact

Utilization management is how health insurers review and authorize care. Each decision (approved, denied, extended, more information needed) produces a letter governed by CMS, state insurance departments and NCQA standards. Prakash says turnaround windows can be as tight as 24 to 72 hours, and a member may be waiting on that letter to schedule surgery.

The complexity is a matrix: decision types crossed with state rules crossed with plans. The same denial needs different appeal language in New York than in Texas. Before automation, staff picked templates by hand from a library, pasted clinical rationale from other systems, saved PDFs to shared drives and emailed them to print vendors. Nobody could say in real time whether a letter had been generated, sent to fulfillment or mailed. Problems surfaced as complaints or audit flags. Every manual hop was also a place where protected health information could leak.

He cites the regulatory reality that even a small slip, one missing required statement or a one-day delay, can push compliance violations up by 75%. Small process gaps, not outages, were the risk.

## Automate the easy letters first

The rollout was phased over years rather than a big bang: letter configuration in 2023, the denial matrix in 2024, approval letter automation in 2025, and denial, extension and additional-information letters plus the start of AI in 2026.

Approval letters went first because they are structurally simpler. Now a decision in the clinical system triggers generation automatically, the template is chosen by rules, fields are populated programmatically, and the letter goes straight to the printing and fulfillment system. Work that sat in a queue for hours or days happens in seconds or minutes. Every step logs a timestamp (decision, generation, transmission), so when a regulator asks for the audit trail it exists already.

Denials are harder: they must carry the clinical rationale, regulatory citations, appeal rights and state language. The denial matrix is the rules engine that maps decision type, state and plan to the right template and language blocks. Unlike approvals, denials keep a human review step before print dispatch, but the reviewer now checks a correctly assembled letter instead of building one from scratch.

## Then make it readable

A letter can be correct, compliant and on time and still be useless to the person reading it. Members who can't understand a denial don't file the appeals they are entitled to. The AI layer works on top of the compliant letter:

- rewrites dense clinical and legal language into plain English without dropping required content,
- adjusts tone so the letter is respectful rather than bureaucratic,
- explains this member's specific decision instead of a generic statement,
- flags missing or unclear appeal language for the reviewer.

The guardrails are the part SREs should copy. The AI can suggest, enhance and flag, but it cannot publish a letter on its own. Everything it changed is logged with when and why. Templates and rules are versioned as regulations change, and dashboards track turnaround, error rates and review queues. Next on the roadmap: compliance scoring at generation time, predictive risk flags before dispatch, and confirmation of actual delivery.

## Who should watch

Anyone automating documents or workflows in a regulated industry, and teams trying to add an LLM to a process where a wrong answer is a legal problem. The order of work (deterministic automation first, AI on top, human review where impact is highest) is the reusable lesson. It is a domain-heavy talk with no code.

Title: Semantic contracts catch the data bugs schema registries miss
Description: Jyothish Sreedharan at Conf42 SRE 2026 on AI-governed lakehouse ingestion with Apache Flink on Kubernetes that adapts to schema drift without breaking.
Body:
A column that switches from dollars to cents passes every schema check and quietly corrupts every dashboard downstream. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, independent researcher Jyothish Sreedharan, who works on distributed data engineering, presented an ingestion architecture for lakehouses that validates what data means, not just its shape, and runs on Apache Flink and Kubernetes so the pipeline keeps going while it adapts.

## Two ways an upstream team breaks you

Jyothish starts with the failures every data platform team knows. Schema drift: someone upstream renames `customer_id` to `user_id` during a deploy, a small change for them, an immediate failure for the pipeline that expected the old name. Then the nastier one, the semantic gap, where structure stays valid but the meaning moves. The dollars-to-cents switch is his example.

Both end the same way: SREs and data engineers diagnosing by hand, patching transformations and redeploying. A schema registry helps with the first kind only, and only by saying yes or no. It has no idea that a renamed field is the same concept, so the pipeline stays broken until a person reconciles it.

## Contracts that learn what normal looks like

The core idea is a semantic contract, learned from history, with three parts:

- **Value distributions.** Each attribute gets a statistical baseline; a sudden jump outside the expected range is flagged.
- **Attribute relationships.** Tax should track the purchase total. If it stops tracking, something is wrong even though both columns are valid numbers.
- **Temporal patterns.** Hourly traffic, daily volumes and seasonality, so spikes, drops and late events stand out.

On top sits a schema intelligence layer that works in three steps. Detect an evolution event (a field appears, disappears or changes structure). Infer whether the new element means the same as an old one using embedding similarity. Then have an LLM generate the transformation that maps the new shape into the existing lakehouse model. Structured CDC streams from MySQL or Postgres, semi-structured JSON and Parquet, and unstructured text (logs, emails, documents parsed by LLMs) are all aligned on event time with the Dataflow model.

## The boring parts are what make it safe

This is where the talk earns its slot at an SRE conference. Flink provides exactly-once delivery to the lakehouse through checkpointing and two-phase commit. Operator state, including the contract baselines and temporal models, lives in RocksDB. Asynchronous snapshots based on the Chandy-Lamport algorithm capture consistent state without pausing processing, and Flink jobs upgrade from savepoints without losing that state.

On Kubernetes, KEDA scales the pipeline on Kafka consumer lag instead of CPU, so capacity follows the actual backlog.

And because adding AI adds new ways to fail, there are three resilience patterns. A circuit breaker falls back to the last known good contracts if the inference service goes away. A dead letter queue takes records that fail semantic validation, with lineage metadata, instead of stopping the pipeline. Flink's credit-based backpressure slows producers when AI scoring adds latency, so memory doesn't overflow.

## The tradeoffs he admits

Jyothish is upfront about the costs. Deeper semantic analysis is more accurate and slower, so scoring often runs asynchronously. Every LLM-generated mapping has to be logged, versioned and reviewable, because an autonomous pipeline nobody can audit is a liability. Contract models are versioned separately from the Flink job so a bad model can be rolled back without touching the running pipeline.

Production surprises: a brand-new source has no history, so it needs a short supervised warm-up before autonomous governance means anything. Baselines for thousands of attributes can inflate RocksDB state, which calls for TTL eviction and tiered storage. And bursts of schema changes can exhaust LLM API quotas; local embedding models and caching reduce that dependency.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers and SREs who run streaming ingestion and are tired of being the schema reconciliation service. The Flink and Kubernetes reliability details stand on their own even if you never let an LLM write a transformation. It is an architecture talk; there is no live demo.

Title: Every AI feature in a pharmacy app needs a tested fallback
Description: Dipta Rakshit (Walmart Global Tech) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on running AI-driven healthcare and retail in one mobile platform without missed doses.
Body:
When the refill prediction model in a pharmacy app fails and the app sends nothing, a patient misses a dose. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Dipta Rakshit, Staff Software Engineer at Walmart Global Tech, explained how one mobile platform serves prescriptions and retail (eyewear try-on, pet care, promotions) at once, and why every AI feature on it ships with a degraded mode that has already been tested.

## One app, two very different blast radii

The setup is unusual. On one side sit HIPAA-governed prescription lifecycles, insurance integrations and pharmacy partners, each with its own API quirks. On the other sit commerce features where the failure mode is a lost sale, not a health event. Dipta's answer is domain-scoped microservices: pharmacy, retail and user management deploy independently, with circuit breakers and bulkheads so a retail traffic surge can't starve pharmacy services of compute.

He gave a production example. When a pharmacy integration partner's API went down, the system saw the error rate climb within 30 seconds, tripped the circuit breakers and switched to a backup partner. On-call got a notification and had nothing to do. That is the goal state he describes: detection and isolation happen before a human reads the page.

The same split goes all the way down to data. Health and commerce data travel through separate encrypted pipelines with separate audit controls, even on shared cloud infrastructure. When a data access issue came up, the team could show quickly that it was confined to the commerce plane, which turned a compliance investigation of days into hours.

## Failing closed is the worst default

The sharpest lesson came from early in their ML rollout. When the refill prediction model failed, the system returned nothing, so no reminders went out at all. A dumb rule based on fill dates would have been better. Now every AI feature has a defined fallback chain before launch: ML prediction, then rule-based reminders from prescription history, then fixed-interval reminders. The AR eyewear try-on drops from full AR rendering to a 2D overlay to a plain product image.

They don't trust those fallbacks on paper. They break the AR service on purpose with chaos experiments and check that customers can still finish a purchase. With the ML models running, Dipta reported a 40% reduction in missed doses compared with fixed-interval reminders, which is exactly why falling back silently to nothing would hurt.

## Measure the outcome, not just the API

Observability for AI here covers inference latency per request path, feature drift, prediction confidence (low confidence triggers the fallback) and fallback activation rates by service. Tracking those found a surprise: refill predictions slowed down at peak hours because of feature computation, not inference. Fixing the feature pipeline cut that latency by 60%.

The bigger shift is the SLIs. Refill completion rate is a primary SLI; if it drops below 95%, the team investigates even when CPU and latency look fine. Dipta said these outcome SLIs catch problems 30 to 60 minutes earlier than operational metrics alone.

## Accessibility and localization are reliability work

Two examples make the point better than any slogan. A date-format mismatch sent prescription reminders on the wrong day for some users; the fix was ISO 8601 everywhere. A Spanish translation error in prescription instructions could have led to wrong medication timing, so translated content now goes through code review, automated tests and staging like any other change, plus a native speaker review. Screen reader failures are treated as SLO breaches with the same incident response as an API outage. If a user can't complete the task, the service failed, whatever the status page says.

## Who should watch

Engineers running mobile platforms in regulated domains, and anyone shipping ML features to production who hasn't yet decided what happens when the model is down. The patterns (separate data planes, tested fallbacks, outcome SLIs) carry over well beyond pharmacy. It is a broad architecture talk rather than a code walkthrough.

Title: A risk score that pages you before the SLO breaks, not after
Description: Oreoluwa Omoike of JPMorgan Chase at Conf42 SRE 2026 on risk-aware SRE scoring failure x impact / time to impact, with real before-and-after numbers.
Body:
Most alerting is very good at screaming after something breaks and bad at noticing that something is about to. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Oreoluwa Omoike, Site Reliability Engineer at JPMorgan Chase, presented a risk-aware decision framework that scores each risk as probability of failure times business impact, divided by time to impact, and lets a policy engine decide whether to log, scale or page.

In the case study he shares, mean time to detect fell from 14 minutes to 2.3, and false positives dropped from 70% of alerts to 18%.

## The 2am loop you have already lived

Omoike opens with the story every on-call engineer knows: the 2am page, 45 minutes to find the root cause, a hotfix, back to bed, and two weeks later the same class of failure in a slightly different disguise. His three baseline numbers frame the problem: 14 minutes on average just to detect an incident, 70% of alerts that turn out to be noise, and 45 minutes to mitigate once you know. The 70% is what slowly trains engineers to stop caring, which is how the real alerts get buried.

His argument is that the deeper issue is the mental model, not the tooling.

## Observe, score, decide, act

The framework has four steps, and the first is deliberately boring: observe with the stack you already run (metrics, traces, logs, burn rate). Scoring is where AI comes in. Instead of watching for threshold breaches, the system computes a live risk score: failure probability from an ML model, multiplied by business impact (his example is a checkout outage costing a set amount per hour), divided by time to impact. A risk six hours out scores very differently from one ten minutes away.

A policy engine then decides, like a tiered response playbook that runs in milliseconds rather than a human flipping through a runbook at 2am. Then the system acts, consistently, including when nobody is watching.

## Three AI patterns, bolted on the side

The scoring rests on three patterns. Anomaly detection with isolation forests or LSTMs trained on baseline traffic catches behaviour that drifts rather than crossing a line. He likes isolation forests because they are lightweight and engineers can usually tell why one fired; LSTMs earn their keep with richer sequential signals. SLO burn rate prediction forecasts when the error budget runs out, which turns "we're burning" into a deadline you can act on. Change risk scoring gives every deploy, config change and feature flag a blast-radius score before it reaches production, using gradient-boosted models trained on historical incidents.

All three run as sidecars that plug into Prometheus, OpenTelemetry and Grafana. He is emphatic on this: pitch a replacement of the whole observability stack and the project is dead on arrival.

## The numbers, and the pitfalls

The case study is an e-commerce platform handling 50 million events a day, run for six months through the kind of peaks that include Black Friday and flash sales. Mean time to detect went from 14 minutes to 2.3 (84%), false positives from 70% to 18%, mean time to resolve from 45 minutes to 11 (76%), and SLO breaches from 22 a month to four (82%). On-call satisfaction surveys improved too.

The pitfalls section is the part worth taking notes on. Models drift with campaigns, launches and seasons, so retrain weekly on a rolling window and track the population stability index. Don't wire it straight to paging, or you rebuild the alert storm you set out to kill: run log-only for two weeks, then auto-scaling, then paging, with a human override always available. Keep scoring under about five milliseconds with batching, asynchronous evaluation and feature caching for high-cardinality labels. And mind data quality: if 30% of a metric's data is missing, don't score it, because "a bad score is worse than no score." Build data quality monitoring before the scoring model.

## Who should watch

Teams drowning in noisy alerts, and anyone trying to get from SLO dashboards to action, will find a concrete, incremental recipe. His advice for starting is pleasingly small: one isolation forest model and one Prometheus metric. "Perfection is the enemy of shipping."

Title: Give the on-call LLM read-only MCP access and a very good schema doc
Description: Makarand Gujarathi of Walmart at Conf42 SRE 2026 on AI-assisted incident response, where LLMs query telemetry over MCP, grounded by context engineering.
Body:
The slow part of most incidents is not the fix, it's the two to four hours of finding where the problem actually is. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Makarand Gujarathi, Senior Software Engineer at Walmart, presented an incident response pattern where an LLM, connected to telemetry through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), turns a plain-language description of the incident into investigative SQL, refines it in a loop and proposes a hypothesis while the on-call engineer steers.

His claim about what makes it work is the useful part: AI assistance is only as good as the context you provide.

## The human is the only integration layer

Gujarathi's diagnosis will be familiar to anyone who has been on call for microservices. A single request can touch five to 10 services, each with its own database, cache, queue and pipeline. During an incident the engineer jumps between a data warehouse, Kibana or Splunk, Grafana or Datadog dashboards, a tracing UI, deploy logs and feature flag dashboards. None of these share a mental model; the person on the bridge is the only thing joining them.

Expertise is the other bottleneck. Senior engineers know which dashboards to trust and which service really sits behind an API. Juniors wait for them to join the call. And the problem is never a lack of telemetry, it's making sense of too much of it under time pressure. The abstract puts numbers on the manual version: 15 to 30 SQL queries for a moderate incident, with timestamp skew from hundreds of milliseconds to several seconds.

## MCP is what makes the chatbot safe to point at production

The LLM brings natural language and structured-data skills. MCP gives it a standard, controlled way to reach telemetry, which Gujarathi breaks into three jobs. Schema introspection lets the agent ask which tables, columns and metrics exist, so it works from the real schema, not a guessed one. Controlled execution exposes only safe, read-only operations, enforces query patterns and filters or masks personal data, which gives you guardrails and an audit log. And a standard protocol means the same agent can query BigQuery, Snowflake, a lakehouse, Prometheus or a log store without a custom integration per system.

His walkthrough uses a checkout service throwing HTTP 500s in one region shortly after a deployment. The agent extracts the service, region, time window and the deploy, then queries error rates by endpoint, latency before and after, and traffic by version. It narrows the spike to one region, one version and the payment endpoint, notices payment provider timeouts rising after the rollout, and suggests the payment integration change as the cause. The engineer can interrupt or redirect at any point; the AI does the query-writing grunt work.

## Context engineering is the actual project

Connect an LLM to a production database with no documentation and, he warns, expect poor results and possibly unsafe behaviour. Three ingredients fix that:

- **Schema documentation** that explains meaning, not just names: what a column represents, whether timestamps are seconds or milliseconds, how logs and metrics join for one request.
- **Curated query libraries** of pre-tested investigations (error rate by endpoint, P95 latency before and after a deploy, top services by error volume) that the agent adapts instead of reinventing.
- **Architecture diagrams** in machine-readable form, so knowing that checkout depends on payments, inventory and user profile becomes a suggested next query.

Telemetry quality still sets the ceiling: inconsistent metric names, mixed tracing libraries, one-minute versus five-minute buckets and sampled traces all hurt the AI as much as the human.

## What changes, and what stays human

He is careful about results. The exact percentage gains depend on telemetry maturity, context work and how comfortable engineers are with the assistant, so he describes the qualitative pattern instead: plausible root causes sooner, far more queries run in the first 10 to 15 minutes, and junior engineers driving investigations without waiting for an expert. Critical actions such as rollbacks, traffic shifts, declaring a major incident and external comms stay under human control. The rule of thumb is to have AI recommend and explain, not silently act, starting with read-only automations like pre-running standard diagnostics when an alert fires.

His adoption path is refreshingly unglamorous: assess telemetry maturity first (if it's poor, fix that before any AI), then build the context materials, then pilot read-only on one or two services during real incidents and iterate.

## Who should watch

SRE and observability teams thinking about an LLM in their incident tooling will get a sober, buildable pattern here, along with the reasons a weekend demo tends to disappoint. It's an architecture talk with a worked scenario, not a product pitch.

Title: SRE habits in a biologics lab cut manual work 40% per AMBR run
Description: Amogha Tenneti of Eurofins PSS at Conf42 SRE 2026 on automating AMBR250 lab analytics with FLEX2 via phase gates, equivalency tests and super users.
Body:
Toil, single points of failure and controlled migrations are not only software problems. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Amogha Tenneti, Senior Associate Scientist at Eurofins PSS supporting Janssen, a Johnson & Johnson company, showed how SRE-style thinking guided the move of a regulated upstream biologics lab from manual analytics to an automated analyzer, cutting manual labour per AMBR250 run by about 40%.

This is one of the more unusual talks at the event: no Kubernetes, no pager, and a very familiar shape anyway.

## High toil and a big error surface

The setting is upstream biologics process development at Janssen's Malvern, Pennsylvania site. The Sartorius AMBR250 runs many parallel 250 ml microbioreactors for rapid process screening, which means lots of small samples and dense data. The analytics behind it were still manual: each sample went through several instruments by hand.

Tenneti lists three resulting problems: reliability risk from operator-dependent sampling variability, operational overhead that capped throughput, and a compliance burden that widened audit and data integrity exposure. In her words, from an SRE perspective the system had high toil and a large error surface area.

The fix was the BioProfile FLEX2 analyzer, which measures metabolites, blood gases, electrolytes, osmolality and cell health metrics from a single small sample in one automated run, with structured, audit-ready output suited to GxP requirements. One instrument replacing several also removed the throughput mismatch between the bioreactor and its analytics.

## A phase-gated rollout that looks like a production migration

What makes it an SRE talk is how the change was made. From December 2022 to August 2024 the integration followed a phase-gated model: independent analytical evaluation, instrument qualification through IQ, OQ and PQ (installation, operational and performance qualification), equivalency studies, validation, super user deployment, and full operational implementation in August 2024. Tenneti draws the parallel herself: it mirrors a controlled production migration in software.

The equivalency studies are the lab's version of running old and new systems side by side before cutting over. Four structured comparability experiments tested each AMBR-derived sample on both the FLEX2 and the existing standard analyzers, across pH, pCO2, glucose, lactate, glutamine, glutamate, ammonium, osmolality, viable cell density and viability. Acceptance criteria were set in advance from internal validation and regulatory standards. All four studies met them, and only then were the old analyzers decommissioned. Picture a canary release where the canary has to pass a regulatory review.

## Removing the human single point of failure

Automation also changed the day. Instead of someone coming into the lab to sample and walk each sample across several instruments, sampling could be scheduled sensibly, with a full analytical panel from one run per sampling event. Fewer touch points meant fewer handling errors and data that could be reviewed and trended.

The scale-out plan is the part most engineering orgs could copy. Twelve super users were trained: eight at Malvern and four at Spring House, Pennsylvania, so both sites could troubleshoot independently without relying on one subject-matter expert. That is distributed ownership aimed squarely at knowledge silos.

## Who should watch

Engineers working in regulated industries (pharma, medical devices, anything with GxP or audit trails) will find a rare worked example of SRE principles outside software. SREs who want a fresh way to explain toil, change management and bus factor to non-software colleagues will also get something from it. It is a short case study from a lab scientist, so expect process and validation detail rather than code. Her summary: eliminate toil, protect reliability through controlled change, improve observability with structured data, and distribute ownership.

Title: Set RTO, RPO and SLOs before you migrate a single database
Description: Rajesh Kumar Balusu of AGAP Technologies at Conf42 SRE 2026 on database high availability via SLO-first planning, Kubernetes self-healing and the 6 Rs of migration.
Body:
Databases are often the last mile of availability: the application tier can be redundant three times over and a single standalone database node still decides your uptime. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Rajesh Kumar Balusu, Database Architect at AGAP Technologies, laid out a three-phase approach to highly available databases, and his first rule is simple: define the reliability targets before touching the architecture.

Balusu brings 20 years of database engineering and cloud architecture across Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, AWS and Google Cloud, much of it spent on migrations from on-premises data centres for public sector, university, retail and pharmaceutical customers. The talk is a structured checklist built from that experience.

## Targets come from the business, not from hope

Phase one is assessment and planning. Before any change, an SRE team should pin down four numbers: an uptime SLO (five nines leaves roughly five minutes of downtime a year), a recovery time objective for how long a restore may take, a recovery point objective for how much data you can afford to lose, and P99 query latency targets for reads and writes. His point is that every later decision, from replication mode to backup frequency, should trace back to these.

Then comes the infrastructure review, which is where the hidden single points of failure live: standalone database nodes, single-region deployments, storage nobody meters. He adds aging components (end-of-support software and hardware), workload saturation (CPU spikes, memory pressure, IOPS ceilings) and security gaps such as unencrypted connections, overprivileged service accounts and missing audit logs. Most of these surface only during an incident, which is an expensive way to do an audit.

Capacity planning should be driven by metrics rather than instinct: utilisation trends, peak transaction rates and concurrency, storage growth and IOPS headroom, connection pool saturation. The goal is reliability headroom without paying for idle capacity. Traffic control uses battle-tested tools: NGINX for layer 7 load balancing, health checks and read-replica routing, HAProxy for TCP-level proxying and active-passive failover.

## Kubernetes as an SRE tool, not a developer convenience

Phase two maps cloud native practices onto reliability outcomes. Immutable container images remove environment drift between development, QA and production. Kubernetes liveness probes detect pod failures and restart automatically, cutting MTTR. HPA and KEDA scale replicas on CPU, memory or custom signals such as queue depth. CI/CD pipelines carry quality gates and rollback triggers tied to error-rate breaches. He measures it all against the DORA metrics: deployment frequency, mean time to recovery and change failure rate.

## The 6 Rs stop you refactoring everything

Phase three is migration, using the 6 Rs: rehost (lift and shift), replatform (for example moving to managed RDS or Aurora), repurchase (move to a SaaS database), refactor (microservices, event sourcing, CQRS), retain (stay on-premises where latency, compliance or cost justify it) and retire (decommission databases nobody uses, which also shrinks the attack surface). His takeaway: not every database needs refactoring, and picking the right path protects stability.

Execution means mapping every upstream and downstream consumer before touching a schema or a connection string, costing compute, storage, egress, licensing and operations rather than just instance prices, and tuning and right-sizing after the move.

## HA you haven't tested is a rumour

The high availability principles are the classics, stated plainly: multi-zone or multi-region replicas, health-check-driven automatic failover, synchronous replication where you need zero RPO and asynchronous for distribution and scale, and regular chaos experiments and failover drills. His final takeaway is the one to tape to the runbook: HA must be tested, not assumed.

## Who should watch

This is a broad, methodical overview rather than a close look at one engine. It suits teams planning a database migration to the cloud, SREs inheriting database ownership, and anyone who needs a checklist to run an infrastructure review. Experienced DBAs will recognise most of it, and may still find the 6 Rs framing handy for the next "should we rewrite it?" meeting.
