Title: Frontend latency is a reliability problem; Galileo moved work server-side
Description: Murali Varma of Galileo Financial Technologies at Conf42 SRE 2026 on server components, streaming SSR and Turbopack as reliability tools for B2B web apps.
Body:
Most SRE teams stop caring at the load balancer. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Murali Varma, Senior Staff Software Engineer at Galileo Financial Technologies (part of SoFi), made the case that the browser belongs in scope too, and showed what happened when Galileo treated frontend latency as an operational reliability problem: a 60% smaller JavaScript bundle, 45% faster initial page loads and server response times cut from 300 ms to 150 ms.

## Users who can't leave still pay for slow pages

The industry statistic he opens with is well known: 53% of users abandon an app that takes more than three seconds to load, rising to 71% beyond four. Galileo's twist is that its users can't abandon anything. Galileo builds B2B operational platforms for more than 200 enterprise clients, used all day by customer service agents and relationship managers.

That makes slowness worse, not better, because the damage is silent and cumulative. Every extra second multiplies across hundreds of agents and thousands of interactions a day: longer handle times, more errors under time pressure, fatigue over eight-hour sessions, and extra API pressure and compute spend across a multi-tenant environment. It just doesn't show up on the dashboard anyone is watching.

## Variance was the real killer

The legacy stack was a classic single-page application: download the full bundle, render everything client-side, call the APIs after hydration, and only then show something meaningful. Bundles ran two to three megabytes, first contentful paint hit three to four seconds on constrained networks, and the cache hit rate sat around 65%.

Varma's sharpest point is about the spread, not the average. On degraded networks, client-heavy rendering collapsed unpredictably, and you cannot set a reliable SLO against that kind of variance. His principle for fixing it is very SRE: move computation off infrastructure you don't control, the user's browser, and onto infrastructure you do.

## Three ways to move the work

**Server components.** Business logic that used to run in the browser now runs on the server, and only minimal serialized UI payloads reach the client. Hydration becomes surgical instead of wholesale, which cuts client CPU and memory and makes behaviour more stable across the mixed corporate hardware agents actually use.

**Streaming SSR.** Instead of waiting for the whole page to be computed, the server sends HTML progressively, decoupling time to first byte from time to interactive. For SREs, he stresses, the win is predictability: lower variance is what makes a meaningful SLO possible. Galileo measured a 42% improvement in time to first meaningful paint and 45% faster initial loads across production routes.

**Hybrid rendering.** Different content gets different modes: static generation where data is stable (cache-friendly and close to failure-proof), server components for dynamic, personalized data, and client JavaScript only for genuinely interactive elements.

## The build system is part of the blast radius

The section people usually skip is build tooling. Legacy tooling was a hidden constraint on evolving the architecture, so Galileo introduced Rust-based Turbopack, with a 10x improvement in cold-start build speed. The SRE link is direct: faster builds mean shorter feedback loops and faster rollbacks, and better tree shaking means smaller payloads, so a bad deploy ships less code.

Across production, cache hit rate went from 65% to 89%. The organisational effects in the abstract are a 35% reduction in time to market and a 47% increase in developer productivity, plus fewer rollbacks. The talk notes that the production metrics came from Galileo's own monitoring and observability systems.

## Who should watch

SREs whose SLOs end at the API gateway, and frontend leads trying to get infrastructure budget for a rendering rewrite, both get ammunition here. It's framework-level rather than a code walkthrough, and the stack is the React Server Components and Next.js ecosystem, so teams on other frameworks will need to translate. His three closing principles: frontend reliability belongs in SRE, server-centric architecture scales, and performance engineering starts at the architecture layer, not with band-aids on top.

Title: Your recommendation model should never be able to slow checkout
Description: Ajay Srinivas Kiran Gemidi of Valuguard Solutions at Conf42 SRE 2026 on isolation, execution limits and lineage for AI analytics in critical platforms.
Body:
In one production environment, a recommendation service took 40% of the shared compute during peak traffic and checkout got slower. The model was accurate; the architecture had no resource limits. That story sits at the centre of Ajay Srinivas Kiran Gemidi's talk at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, where the Sr Systems Engineer at Valuguard Solutions argues that AI analytics inside production platforms is a reliability problem first and a modelling problem second.

Gemidi brings 20 years across systems engineering, DevOps and enterprise data platforms, and the talk reads like it: four architectural guardrails, each with the mechanisms that enforce it.

## Why AI workloads show up in postmortems

Analytics used to run overnight, safely away from the transactional path. Now models power fraud detection, recommendations and real-time analytics inside the platform. Three things make that awkward. Inference compute demand is bursty, with feature extraction, pre-processing and model execution all competing for the same resources. Execution is opaque, so you cannot simply read the code path when the output looks wrong. And data dependencies sprawl across feature pipelines and upstream services.

In incident reviews this surfaces as three recurring patterns: latency amplification when inference competes for compute, cascading failures when a slow inference service pushes delay and load upstream, and observability gaps because CPU, memory and request latency say nothing about prediction confidence or feature drift.

## Guardrail one: isolation

Analytical workloads should not compete with transactional ones for compute. The fixes are familiar container-platform tools used on purpose: dedicated compute pools for inference, namespace resource quotas, separate execution queues, network segmentation to shrink the blast radius, and priority-aware scheduling so mission-critical services win during contention. In the checkout story, the remedy was dedicated pools, CPU limits and circuit breakers. Nothing exotic, which is rather the point.

## Guardrail two: deterministic execution

Inference pipelines get treated as system components with hard edges: validate inputs and reject malformed ones early, put execution timeouts on long-running requests, validate output schemas, and define performance budgets at design time. Those budgets include maximum inference latency, capacity headroom and rate limits on inference APIs.

## Guardrail three: lineage you can replay

When an automated decision triggers an incident, the investigator needs to know what input data the model saw, which model version answered and which feature values drove the result. Gemidi's operational lineage is input snapshots, version-pinned model artifacts and distributed trace IDs, which together allow replaying a prediction during the investigation. Replay is where he puts the gain in time to resolution. He also folds security into reliability: access controls limit blast radius, so they belong in the same design conversation.

## Guardrail four: operating it for years

Models drift because users and data change. His toolkit is continuous monitoring on AI-specific signals such as confidence distributions, feature distributions and inference latency percentiles, plus shadow deployments, canary releases and champion-challenger testing before full rollout, with automated rollback triggers. Human oversight stays in: confidence thresholds route uncertain predictions to human review, and feature flags let engineers switch a model off quickly during an incident.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who have just been told a model is moving into the request path will get a clear checklist. Data scientists will find it a useful preview of the questions operations will ask. It is a principles talk with one worked example, delivered clearly but without code. His four takeaways fit on a sticky note: isolate AI workloads early, enforce execution constraints, build lineage from day one, and engineer for drift.

Title: Conf42 Machine Learning 2026: shipping models is the hard part
Description: Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 roundup - why models fail after deployment, switchback tests, explainable recommenders, ML security and agents, in 35 talks.
Body:
Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 ran online on February 19, 2026, with 35 talks, and very few of them were about training a better model. The lineup was about everything that happens after the notebook: drift, data skew, failing pipelines, experiments that lie, recommendations nobody can explain, and the identities and compliance rules wrapped around the whole thing. The abstract of a talk by Ancilia Dmello of Ford summed up the mood in six words: shipping ML is harder than training it.

All sessions are on the [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 event page](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrAxRHbUdOPlp1-OnsVso-nC).

## Good models, bad production

[Oleksandr Pyvovar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Oleksandr_Pyvovar_robustness_reliability_models), a machine learning engineer at Meta, opened with the scenario every ML team knows: a model hits 95% accuracy in the lab and six months later barely beats random guessing. His explanation is that good models rarely fail because they were wrong; the world changes after deployment. The talk walks through data drift (train a self-driving car only on sunny days, then send it to a foggy city), concept drift, label drift, feature pipeline degradation, training-serving skew, and feedback loops that amplify bias, followed by a monitoring framework and a remediation playbook.

[Ancilia Dmello](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Ancilia_Dmello_forecasting_inventory_retail) of Ford Motor Company laid out an observable MLOps framework on Google Cloud covering real-time, batch, and streaming inference, drift detection, CI/CD, and retraining. [Srihari Godleti](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Srihari_Godleti_fairness_bias_mitigation) of Roku made the case that slow training is often data skew rather than bad code, with three Apache Spark techniques to fix it. [Kiran Ramanna](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Kiran_Ramanna_retraining_lifecycle_models) of ServiceNow and [Srinivas Talasila](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Srinivas_Talasila_compliance_governance_ai) of SAP covered the organisational and infrastructure halves of the same problem: readiness to stop pilot sprawl, and HA, DR, and zero trust for the platforms models run on.

## Predict the failure before it burns compute

[Pavel Solikov](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Pavel_Solikov_security_adversarial_attacks) of J.P. Morgan had one of the most practical talks of the day. His team's Prefect flows can run for 30 minutes or two hours and fail at the end. Since Prefect already knows the parameters, environment, and metadata at the start, and the first tasks can cheaply fingerprint data quality, a gradient boosting model can score the risk of failure in the first minute or two and abort, reroute, or warn the developer with a reason.

[Tim Markin](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Tim_Markin_feature_stores_management) of GiftHorse turned the same idea on software delivery: a production ML system that scores pull requests for risk and estimates delivery time before coding starts, using repo metadata, AST features, and CI signals.

## Experiments and recommendations you can trust

[Sergei Nasibian](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sergei_Nasibian_knowledge_graphs_reasoning), a Quantitative Strategist at Rothesay, explained why classic A/B tests break for delivery pricing in food tech: when you change prices, you change courier supply and other users' experience too. Switchback testing, which alternates treatments over time rather than splitting users, is the alternative.

[Lev Fedorov](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Lev_Fedorov_optimization_performance_efficiency) of Amazon showed how his team turned a black-box recommender into a traceable ranking system, with per-user recommendation traces and user-facing reasons, such as a productivity video shown because you once liked one about effective planning. The trigger was users reporting irrelevant content and developers unable to say why it appeared. [Rohan Mitra](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Rohan_Mitra_experimentation_reproducibility_science) of PhonePe gave a hands-on tutorial on writing the spec for a recommendation system, and [Murthy Chandrapaty and Chakravarthy Kalva](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Murthy_Chandrapaty_Chakravarthy_Kalva_decisioning_b2c_marketing) of Adobe argued that send-time optimisation should grow from a prediction problem into decisioning.

## ML in money and markets

Finance and marketing filled two tracks. [Avaneendra Kanaparti](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Avaneendra_Kanaparti_experimentation_abtesting_optimization) of American Express covered customer lifetime value models for approvals and credit lines, [Balakumaran Sugumar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Balakumaran_Sugumar_anomaly_detection_signals) of Synchrony mapped where ML sits in payment platforms, and [Vivek Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Vivek_Kumar_responsible_ethics_ai) of Majesco used telemetry to predict performance problems in high-volume transaction systems. [Abhinay Kumar Reddy Seella](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Abhinay_Kumar_Reddy_Seella_satisfaction_prediction_telemetry) of Roku predicted user satisfaction in real time from LLMs and behavioural telemetry instead of waiting for surveys, and [Ashutosh Verma](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Ashutosh_Verma_scalability_architecture_distributed) of Meta connected online and offline journeys for attribution.

## Securing the pipeline, and the people with access to it

The security track treated ML platforms like any other production system. [Reshma Vemula](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Reshma_Vemula_pipelines_orchestration_mlops) of Loma Linda University Health showed how PHI leaks into development environments, and [Neha Asthana](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Neha_Asthana_simulation_synthetic_data) of Abbott argued that ML platforms are only as secure as the identities behind them. [Aleksandra Drobnjak](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Aleksandra_Drobnjak_documentation_artifacts_beginners) gave a beginner-friendly guide to the minimum ISO 42001 documentation for an AI management system, for the moment someone asks who approved this model and what data it used. [Sagar Sudhir Behere](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sagar_Sudhir_Behere_streaming_realtime_analytics) of Circle and [Sudheer Kumar Aluvala](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sudheer_Kumar_Aluvala_optimization_hyperparameters_tuning) of HCL America applied ML to third-party risk and zero trust compliance.

## Agents arrive, carefully

Agents had their own track, with an emphasis on guardrails. [Sumit Kaul](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sumit_Kaul_architecture_design_patterns) of PayJoy designed incident response agents that propose root causes and mitigations while humans keep decision authority. [Marat Kenzhebulatov](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Marat_Kenzhebulatov_vision_computer_imaging) of Booking.com covered AI agents in security-critical backend work, [Rajeshwari Sah](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Rajeshwari_Sah_labeling_annotation_quality) of Apple built a clinical documentation scribe as a LangGraph state machine, and [Sujith Vadakkepati](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sujith_Vadakkepati_deployment_containers_kubernetes) of Oracle combined RAG with ERP data for explainable supplier risk.

Further afield, [Sowmiya Narayanan Govindaraj](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sowmiya_Narayanan_Govindaraj_risk_modeling_assessment) of Motional covered unified perception models for autonomous driving, and [Mohamed Najaaf](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Mohamed_Najaaf_recommendation_ranking_systems) of AWS showed how to cut the carbon footprint of generative AI workloads. Operations talks from [Anu Arora](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Anu_Arora_personalization_recommendation_platforms) of ServiceNow, [Dinesh Garg](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Dinesh_Garg_evaluation_benchmarks_metrics) of Honeywell, and [Pallab Haldar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Pallab_Haldar_orchestration_workflows_ai) of Cognizant covered autonomous IT support, IoT warehouse data, and inventory forecasting.

Title: Let agents think freely, but make every action pass a gate
Description: Ajay Athitya Ramanathan of FourthSquare at Conf42 SRE 2026 maps the guardrail stack for AI agents in high-risk production, from Pydantic to OPA and Temporal.
Body:
A model that suggests something wrong is usually harmless; a model that executes something wrong touches real systems, data and users. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Ajay Athitya Ramanathan, Data & AI Engineer at FourthSquare, turned that gap into a design rule for agentic automation: "maximum reasoning freedom, but with strict execution boundaries." Then he spent most of the talk naming the actual tools that enforce it.

## Old automation assumes you know every step

Ramanathan's diagnosis is that existing automation was built for deterministic software. ETL pipelines, batch jobs and rule-based workflow engines follow predefined decision trees, static scripts and fixed actions. Agents do the opposite: they plan dynamically, reason probabilistically and discover which tools to call. Plug an agent into infrastructure built for predictable workflows and you inherit the risks without the controls: hallucinated actions, prompt injection, unauthorized data access, cascading automation failures and, in regulated industries, compliance violations.

His answer is not to remove the autonomy, since reasoning is what makes agents useful. It is to make sure an agent never talks to production directly. Requests flow from a user or workflow into the agent framework, then through guardrails and policy engines, and only then into enterprise systems via secure tool APIs, with monitoring across the whole path.

## Five pillars, each with tools you can install

The second half is a practical catalogue, organised in five groups.

**Programmable safety.** Prompt injection defence (think SQL injection, but for prompts) with tools such as Guardrails Hub and NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails. Structured output so the agent always returns typed, machine-readable data, with Pydantic validating on the receiving end. Business-rule validations, with an example anyone in finance will recognise: check that the invoice line items plus tax and charges add up to the grand total. And LLM-as-a-judge, using a second model to evaluate the first, made measurable with tools like LangSmith.

**Identity and access.** Agents need identities like employees do, starting from least privilege. Open Policy Agent for fine-grained access control, cloud managed identities such as Azure managed identity, session-bound JWT or OAuth 2.0 tokens, and time-bound credentials that expire with the session. If the agent only needs to read, it should not hold write access to the database.

**Privacy.** Microsoft Presidio for detecting and redacting PII, AWS Comprehend as a managed alternative, Faker for masking with realistic values, Ollama for running models entirely on-prem, and synthetic data tools such as Mostly AI.

**Human in the loop**, which he calls the most underrated pillar. LangGraph supports interrupt-and-resume so execution pauses until a human approves, Temporal handles longer, durable approval flows, OPA allow lists define which actions are permitted at all, and irreversible actions get explicit checkpoints that require confirmation.

**Observability and evals.** Per-step traces with LangSmith or Weights & Biases, logging of prompts, responses, latency and token counts with Azure Monitor or Datadog, OpenTelemetry for vendor-neutral instrumentation, LLM Guard for real-time input and output checks, DeepEval and RAGAS for offline evals that catch drift, and Grafana or Elastic to pull it all into one audit timeline. If you can't observe it, you can't trust it.

## Who should watch

This is a survey talk, wide rather than deep: no single tool gets a long demo, but you leave with a shopping list sorted by the risk it addresses. It suits platform and SRE teams about to give an agent write access to anything that matters, and anyone who needs to explain to a compliance team what stands between the model and the database. His closing claim is the one to test against your own stack: safety and autonomy are not opposites if the guardrails are real.

Title: Batch SIEM gives attackers a head start; shard the compute instead
Description: Abhishek Suman of Microsoft at Conf42 SRE 2026 on compute-sharded stream processing with consistent hashing for petabyte-scale security detection.
Body:
"A bad actor does not wait for your batch job." That is the premise of Abhishek Suman's talk at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026. Suman, a Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft who works on real-time data pipelines and security analytics infrastructure, argues that detection latency in a batch-based SIEM is architectural, and the fix is a compute-sharded stream processing design where every event is evaluated as it arrives.

## The latency is baked in, not tunable

Lateral movement, credential harvesting and persistence can be done in minutes, often inside a single batch window. By the time a scheduled cycle runs and an alert fires, the attacker may already be settled in. Suman's point is that you cannot tune this away. Scheduled batch cycles put structural latency into every layer, and at petabyte volume the problems compound: ingestion queues back up, correlation windows grow, and alert fidelity drops under load. These pipelines were designed for gigabyte-scale data, and it shows.

## Shard the compute, not only the data

The core design distributes both data and computation across independent processing nodes using consistent hashing. Streams and compute workloads get mapped onto nodes in a virtual ring, which buys a few properties SREs care about:

- Deterministic shard assignment, so you can predict where a key lives.
- Elasticity: adding or removing a node remaps only a small subset of keys, so scaling out does not mean a full reshuffle.
- Fault isolation: a failed node affects only its own key range.
- Stateful correlation per shard, without a global correlation step that becomes the next bottleneck.

Each shard runs on its own, which is how the design avoids a central choke point and scales horizontally as volume grows. If you have ever watched one overloaded correlator hold a whole SOC hostage, this is the part to rewind.

## Schema-agnostic ingestion keeps coverage moving

Security telemetry is a zoo: firewall logs, EDR events, cloud audit trails, network flows, identity signals. Requiring predefined schemas for each one turns every new source into a project. Suman's design infers structure at runtime and applies only lightweight normalization at the ingestion boundary, so new sources can be onboarded without pipeline halts or schema migration cycles. Faster onboarding is a reliability concern here, because a source you cannot ingest is a blind spot.

## Rules for the known, ML for the novel

Detection is hybrid. Rule-based detection covers known signatures, compliance checks and thresholds, with low latency and high precision. An ML anomaly layer adds behavioural baselines, statistical deviation and unsupervised clustering to catch novel behaviour and zero-day techniques that have no signature yet.

Multi-region deployment is treated as both a resilience and a compliance requirement: region failure isolation so one outage does not blind global detection, localized processing for data residency, distributed consensus to keep detection rules and state consistent across regions, and automatic shard reassignment and failover for node or zone failures.

## What it delivered, and the SRE checklist

The results are reported qualitatively: detection latency down by an order of magnitude against scheduled batch cycles, stable throughput as workload grew, better compute utilization per unit of telemetry than centralized designs, and measurably faster time to respond across the case-study deployments. The talk does not share exact figures.

His four lessons are the reusable part. Design for horizontal scale from day one, because sharding is hard to retrofit. Decouple ingestion from processing. Alert on SLO metrics such as processing lag, shard rebalance duration and pipeline depth, and define those SLOs before rollout. Test failure modes, not just the happy path: node loss, region partitions and back-pressure cascades. Or, as he put it, "resilience is not emergent, it is engineered."

## Who should watch

Engineers building or operating security analytics pipelines, and anyone running stream processing at serious volume, will get a compact architecture overview. It is a design talk with no code or product demo, so treat it as a blueprint to compare against your own pipeline.

Title: An LLM that estimates delivery time from your Git history
Description: Tim Markin (GiftHorse) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 demos a pipeline that estimates feature delivery time from past work and scores every commit for risk.
Body:
Every product manager has asked "how long will this take?" and every engineer has guessed. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Tim Markin, Technical Product Manager at GiftHorse, showed a pipeline that answers with an estimate built from the team's own Git history, then reviews each commit and pull request for risk before a human reviewer has to.

It is a demo-driven talk from a former game developer turned PM. The demo is a from-scratch rebuild, not the internal tool, and Markin says plainly that it is not production ready, so treat it as a blueprint.

## Estimates come from what the team actually shipped

The problem he has fought his whole career is wrong delivery estimates. Before, his team relied on engineers' judgement corrected by past Jira sprints. Now, when the discovery team brings a feature to the delivery team, the tool produces an estimate first.

The pipeline has three steps. Feature extraction reads the Git history. Retrieval-augmented generation looks up similar past work, which is what makes the estimate better than a cold guess. An LLM analysis step then reasons about complexity and risk and returns a time estimate with a confidence level, risk scores and recommendations.

To show it, he points the tool at a three-repository Web3 hackathon project: a NestJS and Postgres backend, a frontend in the Cocos game engine, and a smart contract. Static analysis reports files, lines of code, complexity and a risk score per repository. The well-structured backend scores low risk; the Cocos frontend scores higher because so much of it is wiring UI to scripts in the editor, which the model struggles to read. Markin's aside that a React frontend would likely have scored lower is a quiet reminder that these tools reward code they have seen a lot of.

## A risk score on every commit

The second half is review. Each commit and PR gets an AI review, and if the feedback is useful the engineer can act on it immediately instead of waiting for a colleague. In his team's production setup, a risk score above 50% or quality below 50% notifies team leads and stakeholders, who will ask about it at the feature demo. If an engineer shows the AI got it wrong, they carry on and the model gets tuned.

The demo makes the point with a deliberately bad commit: a hardcoded secret key, no input validation, command injection. The tool rates it maximum risk and unsafe for production, which is the right call and also the easy one. The more interesting case is the AI-written NFT service commit that also comes back high risk and low quality.

## Closing the loop on estimates

The tool also compares estimates with what actually happened. In the demo it filters out overnight gaps of eight hours, counts the rest as working time, and uses commit timing to see when work stopped. The estimates line up except for backend setup, which went faster because it was done with AI help.

Markin reports that after adoption his team's delivery estimate accuracy rose from 60% to up to 80%, security issues were caught before merge, PMs could prioritise without long meetings, and PRs arriving for human review were noticeably better. The demo stack is Python with FastAPI, ChromaDB and the Claude API, which he says matches production apart from hardening. The repository is linked at the end of the talk; you will need a Claude or OpenRouter API key to run it.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and PMs tired of estimates that drift, and platform teams thinking about AI review as a CI gate. Watch it for the RAG-over-past-work idea and the feedback loop on estimates; bring your own skepticism about any model's confidence on unfamiliar codebases.

Title: Put a rule engine on both sides of the LLM in grocery retail
Description: Sanjay Basu of TCS at Conf42 SRE 2026 on running LLMs in grocery retail with new SLOs, hybrid rule-plus-LLM decisions and a five-stage AI incident playbook.
Body:
When an LLM recommends a substitute for an out-of-stock item, a wrong answer costs a sale and maybe a customer. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Sanjay Basu, Global Head for AI / GenAI Products at TCS, laid out a framework for running LLMs in grocery retail: redefine the SLOs for probabilistic systems, wrap the model in deterministic rules, and give AI failures their own incident playbook.

## Why LLMs break the usual SRE assumptions

He starts with the three properties that make LLM services awkward to run. Outputs are non-deterministic, so the same prompt can give different results across calls, which undermines traditional notions of correctness. Latency varies at the token level and grows with output length. And the dependencies keep moving: prompts, embeddings and context windows change continuously.

Retail raises the stakes. Traffic spikes around flash sales such as Cyber Monday, substitutions have to be the right substitution, personalization runs at an audience of one, and inventory accuracy has to be predicted rather than assumed.

## SLOs for a system that is allowed to be a little wrong

His answer is to extend the SLO set rather than abandon it. Alongside the usual availability, he proposes semantic accuracy (the share of responses that pass automated semantic evaluation against ground truth or intent), time to first token, a hallucination rate budget treated like an error budget, and cost per inference as a first-class reliability signal. The last one is the quiet troublemaker: tokens behave like infrastructure spend, so scaling decisions have a bill attached.

## The rule engine goes before and after the model

The architectural centrepiece is a hybrid decision layer. A rule engine enforces the hard business constraints, which are deterministic. The LLM works as a reasoning layer inside that decision space. Then a post-inference validation step checks the output against the rule engine again before it reaches a customer or a downstream system. The point is to keep hallucinations from surfacing, and to make sure every call has a deterministic fallback so the customer experience does not degrade when the model does. Resilience, he insists, is designed in, not bolted on after the first production incident.

## AI incidents get their own five stages

For AI-induced failures he outlines a five-stage response:

1. Detection, via the semantic evaluation pipeline alerting on hallucinations and quality drops.
2. Containment, by shifting traffic automatically to the rule-based fallback layer and throttling model traffic.
3. Diagnosis, by replaying prompt telemetry to isolate the offending template version or embedding refresh.
4. Remediation, by rolling back the prompt version or restoring traffic through a shadow model.
5. Post-incident hardening, by reviewing the SLO breach and the evaluation pipeline itself.

That only works if you log every prompt and template version, which is why observability features so heavily: prompt telemetry, embedding-based similarity checks between output and retrieval context, and drift monitoring on semantic distributions.

Guardrails round it out: pattern classifiers for prompt injection before the model is invoked, named entity recognition to strip personal data from the context window, toxicity and bias screening, and regulatory filters that hard-block things like alcohol, pharmacy and age-restricted products in recommendations.

## Agents get budgets, not blank cheques

The last section covers agentic LLMs in logistics, fulfilment and last-mile delivery, where models plan, call tools and act. His constraint is that this autonomy is bounded at the orchestration layer: action budgets, rollback triggers and human evaluation ratios for every agent workflow.

## Who should watch

This is a short, dense framework talk rather than a war story, so expect a checklist more than a postmortem. It suits SREs and platform leads who have been handed an LLM feature in a high-traffic commerce system and need a vocabulary for SLOs, fallbacks and incidents. If you already run semantic evals in production, the hybrid rule-engine pattern and the incident stages are the parts to compare against your own setup.

Title: One shared perception model beats a stack of single-task models
Description: Sowmiya Narayanan Govindaraj (Motional) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on unified, transformer-based perception that fuses camera and lidar for self-driving.
Body:
A self-driving stack that runs one model for detection, another for segmentation and a third for depth is reading the same scene three times and never agreeing on what it saw. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Sowmiya Narayanan Govindaraj, Senior Machine Learning Engineer at Motional, explained why the autonomous vehicle industry is moving to unified end-to-end perception models, and what changes once those models leave the lab.

It is a compact, conceptual talk from someone who takes perception models from research into safety-critical deployment. No code, but a clear architecture and a useful list of production lessons.

## Fragmented stacks duplicate work and cascade errors

The classic perception pipeline trains separate models per task, and sometimes per sensor. Each processes the same inputs independently, which means duplicated computation, higher latency and errors that cascade from one stage to the next. The deeper problem, as Govindaraj frames it, is that the modules are optimised locally rather than globally, so the system never forms a cohesive understanding of the scene and becomes brittle and hard to maintain over time.

## Shared encoders, light task heads

The unified alternative trains one system that jointly learns spatial, semantic and temporal representations. All sensors feed shared encoders, and lightweight heads branch off for each output. Because features are shared, improving one task helps the others: segmentation informs depth, detection benefits from both. Fewer models, better accuracy.

Transformers make this practical. Self-attention captures long-range context across the scene, cross-modal attention aligns camera appearance with lidar geometry without hand-written fusion rules, and token representations cope with different sensor resolutions. The architecture has three parts: a shared backbone, cross-modal alignment into a common latent space, and temporal fusion over multiple frames, since one frame can be ambiguous but motion reveals intent. Images bring texture and semantics, point clouds bring precise geometry, and training 2D and 3D together gives steadier boxes and depth for tracking and planning downstream.

## Sensors fail unevenly, so fusion has to adapt

The most practical lesson: rain and darkness hurt cameras, while fog and sparse returns hurt lidar. Static fusion weights cannot handle that, so the model uses adaptive attention that weights each sensor by its current reliability and leans on the others when one degrades. The goal is graceful degradation rather than sudden failure.

Outside controlled settings come weather, geography, domain shift and the long tail: construction zones, emergency vehicles, unusual pedestrian behaviour. These matter most for safety and appear least in training data, so the team relies on targeted collection, balanced sampling and continual learning. For new cities, domain adaptation techniques such as adversarial feature alignment, test-time adaptation and rapid fine-tuning keep the model adjusting. Perception, Govindaraj says, is not something you train once and freeze.

## Labels are the bottleneck, so learn without them

Labelling driving data at scale is very expensive, so self-supervised methods (contrastive alignment, temporal consistency, cross-sensor reconstruction) let training scale on unlabelled data. That leads into foundation models pre-trained on large driving datasets, with lightweight heads for detection, tracking or prediction, and zero-shot generalisation to scenarios nobody labelled.

The engineering payoff is a single forward pass: lower latency, simpler deployment and easier debugging. It is rare for an architecture change to cut complexity and improve accuracy at once, and the talk ties both back to safety through fewer disengagements and more consistent behaviour.

## Who should watch

ML engineers in robotics, autonomy or any multi-sensor system who are weighing a multi-task model against a zoo of specialists. Newcomers get a clear map of the modern perception stack; specialists get a short list of what tends to break in deployment.

Title: A 96% accurate forecast is worth nothing if it arrives late
Description: Prajakta Talathi of College Ave at Conf42 SRE 2026 on running predictive analytics in education finance as a production service with SLOs and fallbacks.
Body:
A model can score 96% offline and still deliver zero decision value if its forecast is stale when the cash planning meeting starts. That is the opening argument of Prajakta Talathi, Marketing Analytics Manager at College Ave, at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026: treat predictive analytics in education finance as a production service, with SLIs, SLOs and a plan for when things degrade.

Her one-line version: "the model might be right, but it's right in the wrong universe."

## The disbursement-week story

The talk runs on a hypothetical that will feel uncomfortably familiar. It is peak disbursement season for student loans. Teams have to plan cash availability against fixed enrollment timelines and payment commitments. Inputs shift under them: school calendars, certification timing, enrollment changes. Everything has to be explainable to auditors.

Then a feed arrives with a slightly drifted format. Nobody catches the early warning. The models run, the scores come back, the dashboards look alive. Anomalies surface later, and the team spends the week diagnosing instead of deciding. Do that twice and the business stops trusting the prediction service, which is harder to fix than any schema.

She calls this failure mode silent wrongness, and she is blunt about its cost: "silent wrongness is the most expensive failure mode."

## Accuracy is one SLO among several

The shift she argues for is from optimising offline accuracy and hoping production behaves, to defining targets, observing behaviour and planning fallbacks. The forecast needs three properties: availability when planning decisions are made, observability of drift, latency and data quality, and trustworthiness, meaning outputs stay correct and explainable under stress or degrade safely.

She makes those concrete with example targets, framed as starting points you tune to your business: P99 forecast latency at or under 120 seconds at peak, data age at or under 24 hours, and drift kept within bounds using the population stability index, around 0.2 over a rolling window. High availability matters most during the disbursement window. None of these measure accuracy. All of them measure whether the forecast is usable right now.

## A degradation ladder beats going dark

The operating model is a pipeline (ingestion, transformation, model, serving, decision) with an independent control at every stage: schema and null checks, drift and health checks, access governance, fallbacks with confidence levels. The rule she sets is that a degraded upstream step must never turn into a silent downstream prediction error.

When live inference fails, the system walks down a ladder instead of switching off: short-lived snapshots as fallback, confidence flags that annotate freshness and uncertainty, and rule-based fallback once model health drops below its SLO. Recovery comes from runbooks, rollback, retraining triggers and audit logs.

On alerting she has the line every on-call engineer has learned the hard way: if every alert is urgent, eventually none of them are, including the ones that matter. So alerts go on SLO burn rate, data quality gates block bad batches, and anomaly detection watches output distributions to catch the wrongness nobody would otherwise see.

## Who should watch

Data and analytics teams who ship models and then hand them over to "production" will get the most from this, especially in regulated finance. SREs who have been asked to own an ML service will find it a clear map of which SRE habits transfer directly. It is a framework talk built around a hypothetical, not a case study with internal metrics, and it says so.

Title: Let the AI propose, let governance decide what actually runs
Description: Suganya Nagarajan of Amazon at Conf42 SRE 2026 on Human-Governed Automation Loops, which split decision generation from authorization to cap blast radius.
Body:
Automation that can act on millions of requests can also break millions of requests, and it does it at network speed. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Suganya Nagarajan, Software Development Manager at Amazon, presented Human-Governed Automation Loops (HGAL): an architecture where AI components propose actions and a separate, human-defined governance layer decides which of them may execute.

Her framing of the problem is one every SRE will recognise: as systems scale, "manual interventions become a bottleneck, but blind automation is a liability." HGAL is her attempt to keep the speed of the first option without inheriting the second.

## Postmortems are governance that arrives a week late

The reliability gap she describes is about timing. Most governance today is offline or asynchronous: reviews, approvals, the postmortem that explains last week's outage. Useful for next time, useless for the retry storm happening now. Her example is a plain one: an automated service retries failed requests and accidentally DDoSes its own backend, burning the error budget in seconds while the safety net is still reading the ticket.

What she wants instead is governance that watches the service level indicators live, notices that failures jumped after a bad deployment, and reverts the change before the outage lands.

## Proposing and authorizing are two different jobs

The core move in HGAL is separating decision generation from decision authorization. The AI engines keep generating actions continuously, so the system never blocks waiting for a human. A control plane sits between those proposals and production and acts as a gatekeeper for every automated action, which she likens to policy as code.

Her running example is dynamic pricing or traffic shaping: the model proposes shifts every minute to match demand, and the governance layer refuses the ones that would breach the SLOs. The humans never review each decision. They write, observe and evolve the rules that do.

## Delegation boundaries decide who gets paged

Since nobody can approve every action, the interesting design work is in what she calls decision delegation boundaries: the line between acting alone and escalating. The dimensions are confidence, impact, historical reliability and context. A disk cleanup at 80% usage is an independent task. A database failover hits an escalation boundary.

Context is the part people tend to skip. If the system is already fragile, for example running with high latency, HGAL tightens the boundaries and asks for more human authorization. Her policy example is the kind you could paste into a config file: no automated restarts if the error budget is below 10%. In her words, designing these boundaries well "is the difference between building a self-healing system and a runaway failure."

A side benefit she points out: blameless postmortems get better evidence. Instead of asking why the automation failed, you can audit exactly why a decision was authorized or denied, given the SLIs at that moment.

## The honest part: it costs something

The talk does not pretend this is free. She lists latency trade-offs, governance models that have to keep evolving, and the work of training staff to run automation rather than fight fires by hand. Her takeaways boil down to three: monitor continuously, design boundaries around the thresholds that keep you accountable, and embed governance in the control plane rather than bolting it on at the edge.

## Who should watch

This is an architecture talk, not a product demo or a code walkthrough. Watch it if you run auto-remediation, experimentation platforms, recommendations or notification systems and are trying to decide how much autonomy to hand over. If you already have policy-as-code gates in front of your automation, the delegation-boundary vocabulary is still worth stealing for your next design review. It closes on a line worth pinning above the deploy button: "Let's build systems that are safe as they are fast."

Title: The greenest GenAI request is the one served by a smaller model
Description: Mohamed Najaaf (AWS) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on cutting GenAI's energy use with right-sized models, cheap customisation, efficient silicon and monitoring.
Body:
You probably do not need the biggest model on the leaderboard, and your electricity bill and carbon footprint both know it. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Mohamed Najaaf, Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, walked through the design choices that shrink the energy cost of generative AI applications, from model selection and customisation to silicon and observability.

To be clear about scope: this is an AWS talk, and the tools and figures are AWS's. The decision order it teaches transfers to any cloud.

## The demand curve is the motivation

Najaaf opens with published research from firms including Deloitte, Gartner and Goldman Sachs: model training size has grown enormously over the last decade, data centre electricity demand climbs steeply from 2022 on, and he cites a Goldman Sachs forecast that about 60% of that new demand would be met by burning fossil fuels, plus a World Economic Forum estimate that the compute needed for AI doubles roughly every hundred days. Whatever your view of the exact numbers, the direction is not in dispute.

## Start with managed services and the right-sized model

The first two levers are architectural. He recommends managed or serverless services (Amazon Bedrock for foundation models behind one API, SageMaker, EKS) so the provider carries the hardware, networking and patching, and AWS's position is that moving workloads off premises into its data centres can cut their carbon footprint by up to 99%.

The more portable lever is model selection. Evaluate against your real criteria (language support, open or proprietary, size, generalist or domain-specific) and pick the lightest model that passes. His example: a use case might not need Claude Opus 4.6 when Claude Haiku 4.5 does the job, and the smaller model is both cheaper and needs fewer resources per inference. Bedrock Evaluations can score candidates on helpfulness, faithfulness, correctness, harmfulness and refusal, plus your own metrics, and you redo it as new model versions ship.

## Customise from the cheap end of the ladder

Najaaf orders customisation by energy cost. Prompt engineering is the cheapest and should come first. Retrieval-augmented generation adds your own data through a vector store. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning touches a subset of weights, full fine-tuning touches all of them, and training from scratch is the most expensive and carbon-heavy option, which few organisations need.

That ladder is a good default for any team: climb only as far as the evaluation results force you.

## Silicon, compression and watching the meters

For training, he points to AWS Trainium, which he says is up to 25% more energy efficient than comparable EC2 instances, with Trainium2 about three times more efficient than the first generation and Trainium3 (announced too late for the slides) about four times better again. For inference that does not need a GPU, Graviton is quoted at up to 60% less energy.

Deployment optimisations do the rest: model compilation for the target hardware, compression and pruning, and distillation, where a large teacher model trains a small student to handle most queries with close to the same quality.

Finally, observability. CloudWatch for Bedrock metrics and guardrails, SageMaker Profiler and the AWS Neuron monitor for training, and NVIDIA's System Management Interface on GPU hosts. Sustainability, in his framing, is a loop: monitor, re-evaluate models as they change, and adjust.

## Who should watch

Teams building on Bedrock or SageMaker who want a checklist that lowers cost and energy at the same time, and architects who need a structured argument for "use the smaller model" in the next design review. If you are not on AWS, the model selection and customisation sections still apply as is.

Title: Zero Trust compliance can't run on rules refreshed once a quarter
Description: Sudheer Kumar Aluvala (HCL America) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on a closed-loop ML compliance engine that scores risk in real time inside ZTNA.
Body:
Plenty of companies have bought Zero Trust network access and then fed it hand-written policies updated on a fixed schedule. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Sudheer Kumar Aluvala, Client Delivery Director for Engineering at HCL America, argued that this pairing leaves gaps between refresh cycles and proposed a machine-learning compliance engine that adjusts access decisions as risk changes.

It is a short, architecture-level talk drawn from his team's ZTNA and AI compliance work for enterprise and SMB customers. Expect a design and reported outcomes, not code.

## Three ways static policy fails

Aluvala groups the problems he keeps meeting into three. Periodic policy refreshes leave windows where threats have moved and the rules have not. Manually defined rules invite misconfigurations and inconsistencies, each a potential hole. And as the footprint spreads across hybrid and multi-cloud environments, maintaining thousands of individual and group rules stops being operationally sustainable.

None of that is surprising, which is the point: the architecture is Zero Trust, but the policy process is still on a calendar.

## A closed loop in four stages

His alternative is a loop with four repeating stages. Data ingestion gathers telemetry across the enterprise. Model training turns that into usable risk signals. Predictive enforcement makes access decisions from projected risk instead of a static rule. Automated feedback feeds every outcome back in, so the system learns from both successful interventions and false positives.

The inputs come from three places: endpoint telemetry (device health, configuration state, patch level), user behaviour analytics (access patterns and authentication history that produce a contextual risk score per person), and threat intelligence feeds with industry-specific vulnerability data. Combined, they replace point-in-time snapshots with a risk assessment that tracks current conditions, and he describes predictive analytics flagging likely compliance violations before they happen.

## What his team reports from production

From their deployments, Aluvala reports around 40% faster incident response through automated enforcement, a 98% reduction in critical policy errors with ML-generated controls, and a 60% decrease in manual effort that freed the team for other work. These are his figures from customer projects; the talk does not break down the baselines, so read them as directional.

## Automation still needs a human with a veto

The enterprise section is where the talk is most grounded. Adoption depends on explainability: clear decision rationale and complete audit trails so automated decisions still satisfy regulators. He lists bias detection to keep access decisions non-discriminatory, human oversight with the ability to review and override, and privacy-preserving analytics through anonymisation and purpose limits.

Deployment is split by size. SMEs get a lightweight setup on managed ML services for quick time to value. Large enterprises get hybrid deployments integrated with existing SIEM and SOAR platforms, which is where most of them will already have their alerts.

## Who should watch

Security architects running ZTNA who suspect their policy refresh cadence is the weak link, and ML engineers asked to build risk scoring for access decisions. If you want implementation details, use this as the map and look elsewhere for the territory.

Title: Third-party risk was built for annual reviews; ML makes it continuous
Description: Sagar Sudhir Behere (Circle) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on rebuilding vendor risk management with NLP, semantic dedup, model ensembles and event-driven monitoring.
Body:
Risk does not wait for your annual vendor review. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Sagar Sudhir Behere, Head of Third Party Risk Management at stablecoin issuer Circle, described how his team re-architected third-party risk management (TPRM) as a machine-learning system, replacing calendar reviews and static questionnaires with document extraction, adaptive questions and event-driven monitoring.

He pitches it as a playbook rather than a theory or a vendor pitch, and it is refreshingly specific about where humans stay in the loop.

## The process was designed for a slower world

Behere names three structural problems. Calendar-based reviews assume risk politely waits its turn, so a change in month two surfaces in month twelve, if you are lucky. Static questionnaires ask every vendor the same questions in the same order, burying low-risk vendors and under-examining high-risk ones. Manual evidence review has analysts reading stacks of policies and SOC reports, and two analysts can read the same PDF and reach different conclusions without either being wrong.

Meanwhile a modern enterprise depends on hundreds or thousands of third parties (cloud providers, SaaS, payment processors, data vendors, open-source dependencies) and regulators want more transparency and continuous oversight, not less. His summary: risk now moves at the speed of software, not audit cycles.

## Read the documents with NLP, keep the receipts

The architecture has four parts: continuous data ingestion, intelligent processing, dynamic risk evaluation and continuous monitoring. The first bottleneck they attacked was evidence review. NLP models extract and normalise control evidence from unstructured vendor artefacts, asking whether a document demonstrates the specific control rather than whether it looks fine.

The detail that matters for auditors is traceability: every extracted data point links back to the sentence in the source document, so you can click from a risk conclusion to the evidence. Humans moved from reading documents to validating judgements.

## Ask each question once

Next came questionnaire redundancy. Different frameworks (SOC, ISO, internal policy, regulatory requirements) ask for the same control in different words, so semantic similarity models cluster questions by meaning. Instead of five near-identical questions, the vendor sees one. Follow-ups adapt to the answers, digging deeper only where a control looks weak or ambiguous, and context-aware routing sends security questions to security people and finance questions to finance. Behere describes this as the point where vendors stopped calling the process painful.

## Never trust a single model

For the obvious "what if the model is wrong" question, the answer is ensembles. Multiple independent models evaluate the same risk signal; agreement raises confidence, disagreement flags the case. Every output carries a confidence score: high confidence moves the workflow forward, low confidence sends it to a person. That also answers the governance worries about single-model bias and black boxes, because you can explain both the conclusion and how sure the system is.

## From periodic reviews to listening for events

The bigger shift was to stop reassessing on a schedule and react to material events instead: threat intelligence, security advisories and CVEs, financial indicators such as credit ratings and market stress, public disclosures like breach notices and enforcement actions, and behavioural anomalies. Reassessing everything continuously would just create noise faster, so the system listens for meaningful changes and triggers action only then.

Models trained on historical cyber, operational and financial incidents look for the weak signals that tend to precede trouble (missed patches, delayed disclosures, financial stress) so the team can ask targeted questions or escalate controls early. Every score comes with its contributing factors and a full audit trail, built with regulatory expectations in mind from the start.

## Who should watch

Risk, compliance and security engineers in regulated companies, and ML engineers asked to build tooling for them. His closing advice is a sensible starting order: automate evidence extraction, cut redundant questions, then add signal-driven monitoring. No perfect model required.

Title: An ML platform is only as secure as the identities that can touch it
Description: Neha Asthana (Abbott) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on identity lifecycle, access reviews, RBAC and privileged access management for enterprise ML platforms.
Body:
The quickest way to steal a model is often to borrow the service account that trains it. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Neha Asthana, Identity Solutions Architect at Abbott, walked through the identity and access management foundations an enterprise ML platform needs: lifecycle automation, access certification, role-based access and privileged access management, tied together under one governance view.

This is an IAM fundamentals talk applied to ML, from someone who works in a regulated industry. If identity has always been somebody else's job on your platform, it is a compact correction.

## ML platforms multiply identities

Asthana's framing is growth. As organisations scale ML and data-heavy workloads, the population of users and service accounts expands faster than traditional controls can keep up with. Data access patterns span pipelines and analytical tools, automation needs elevated privileges, and regulated industries keep raising the bar. The result is three familiar failures: access sprawl across platforms, compliance gaps at audit time, and privileged accounts used without proper controls.

## Let HR be the source of truth

The first fix is identity lifecycle management connected to an authoritative source, usually the HR system. Four events drive everything: onboarding creates accounts and roles from job title and department, role changes adjust access on transfer or promotion, offboarding revokes access immediately, and rehires reactivate an identity instead of minting a duplicate. Automating these removes manual steps and, with them, the orphan accounts that linger after someone leaves.

## Review access, then model it as roles

Access certification campaigns ask managers and data owners to periodically confirm that each person still needs what they hold. That is how privilege creep and dormant accounts get found and removed, and it is the evidence auditors ask for.

RBAC then ties permissions to roles rather than people. Her examples map neatly onto an ML team: a data scientist needs the ML platform, training environments and approved datasets; a business analyst running dashboards can usually make do with read-only access; the infrastructure team needs admin rights for logging and monitoring. Get the roles right and most access requests answer themselves.

## Privileged accounts are where ML is most exposed

The section that makes this an ML talk is privileged access management. Service accounts run training jobs, CI/CD pipelines deploy models to production, and data engineers administer infrastructure holding huge volumes of data. Every one of those needs elevated permissions, which makes each an attack path to models, training data and pipelines.

The PAM capabilities she lists are concrete: credential vaulting to get secrets out of code, automated password rotation, session brokering so humans use privileged sessions without ever seeing the credential, session recording for anomaly detection and forensics, and just-in-time access with time-bound elevation and automatic revocation. Applied to ML, that means protecting proprietary models and training data, securing automated workflows, and controlling who can modify or export sensitive datasets.

## One governance view for humans and machines

The finish is integration: IAM governance (she mentions SailPoint IdentityIQ) combined with a PAM execution layer, so human and non-human identities sit in one inventory, privileged and service accounts get certified alongside people, and the same policy applies everywhere. For healthcare and other regulated sectors, that produces the audit logs, attestations, separation of duties and documentation that HIPAA, SOX and GDPR reviews look for.

## Who should watch

ML platform owners who have never been through an access review, security engineers newly assigned to an ML team, and anyone counting the long-lived tokens in their training pipelines. Identity specialists will find the fundamentals familiar; the value is in mapping them onto ML roles and service accounts.

Title: In healthcare ML, PHI leaks from dev environments, not production
Description: Reshma Vemula (Loma Linda University Health) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on why ML dev copies leak PHI and a five-step plan built on synthetic data.
Body:
Every healthcare ML project starts the same way: someone copies production data into a dev environment so the model has something to learn from. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Reshma Vemula, a Visualization Developer at Loma Linda University Health who specialises in EHR data security and compliance, argued that those copies are where protected health information actually escapes.

It is a short, focused talk: the risk, the numbers she presents, and a roadmap. Good for a lunch break.

## Your production data has several unmonitored twins

The core observation is multiplication. Production data gets copied into development, testing, training, validation and UAT, and Vemula says most healthcare organisations keep at least three to five copies of production data in non-production workflows, each carrying dozens of PHI elements per patient record. Every copy is another place to secure, and the non-production ones rarely get production-grade monitoring.

Her slides put the share of breaches occurring in development environments at 51.3%, and she reports that organisations relying on real PHI in dev and test face remediation costs roughly three times higher than those using synthetic data, once regulatory penalties, legal costs, disruption and reputational damage are counted.

## Mask it, or better, never copy it

The controls come in layers. Advanced data masking and encryption reduce unauthorised access while keeping data useful for testing, and deterministic masking matters for ML specifically: the same input always maps to the same masked value, so validation and model performance tests stay consistent across runs.

The stronger move is synthetic data generation. It preserves the statistical properties a model needs, keeps patients out of the training set entirely, and in her framing is the foundation of the whole roadmap. You cannot leak a record that was never real.

## Shift the security work left

The second half covers process. DevSecOps puts scanning into code writing, testing and deployment rather than after release, and she cites teams on this approach fixing over 95% of vulnerabilities during development. AI-driven monitoring watches activity across ML pipelines for anomalies to shorten response time. Across the pipeline she wants automated PHI detection at ingestion, isolated and encrypted training environments, secure validation, controlled deployment, and logging at every phase.

## The five-step roadmap

Her plan is incremental by design: start with synthetic data generation, then encryption and access controls, then secure training pipelines, then DevSecOps integration, and finally automated compliance. Each step can land without stopping the data science team, which is usually the objection that keeps real PHI in dev in the first place.

## Who should watch

Healthcare data engineers, ML platform owners and security or compliance leads in organisations bound by HIPAA. It is an overview rather than a tooling walkthrough, so pair it with something hands-on if you need to pick a masking or synthesis tool next week.

Title: Production ML needs HA, DR and Zero Trust designed in from day one
Description: Srinivas Talasila (SAP) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on the infrastructure pillars that keep ML training and serving available, secure and auditable.
Body:
A model that works in the lab still has to survive a zone outage, a traffic spike and an auditor. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Srinivas Talasila, Director of Cloud Operations at SAP, argued that availability, recovery and security for ML platforms have to be settled in the planning phase, because bolting them on after launch is how you get both downtime and audit findings.

It is a high-level architecture talk from someone with nearly two decades in IT operations (AT&T, Adobe, HP, now SAP), aimed at the people who sign off on production readiness rather than the people tuning learning rates.

## The lab hides the hard parts

Talasila's starting contrast: in the lab the data is clean and the focus is benchmark metrics. In production you meet drift, use cases that keep changing, scalability and latency requirements, and availability targets. Each of those is an infrastructure decision, and each is harder to change once the architecture is locked.

He uses IBM Cloud SoftLayer as a worked example of what to look for in a provider (bare metal and virtual compute, global availability zones, a network backbone tuned for moving large datasets) while keeping the advice provider-neutral: benchmark throughput, IOPS and latency for your own use case before you commit.

## Resilience pillars, in plain terms

**High availability** means multi-zone deployments, load balancing across zones, stateless model servers so a failed instance takes no state with it, fault detection with automated failover, and a defined path back once the zone recovers. **Disaster recovery** means an off-site strategy with air-gapped or immutable backups and a recovery time you have actually checked against what the provider offers. **Rate limits** keep one tenant's unpredictable spike (or a DDoS) from taking down everyone else's real-time serving.

**Zero Trust segmentation** gets the most airtime. Training, QA and production environments are isolated, changes only flow upward after testing and security clearance, serving endpoints sit behind API authentication and rate limiting, and network rules or ACLs are defined up front. Drift management applies to infrastructure too: rate limits, allowed ports and software versions should not change quietly.

## Controls an auditor will ask about

The operational-controls section reads like a checklist for regulated ML: asset management for versions and releases, identity and privileged access management for model registries and pipelines (integrated with your existing directory where you have one), audit logging across training and serving so you can tell what ran where and why it failed, compliance validation for regulated workloads, and automated scanning of container images before they enter a repository.

## Ownership is the missing pillar

The closing argument is about people. Resilience stops being the infrastructure team's job alone and becomes shared across data scientists, ML engineers, MLOps practitioners and platform engineers, with a clear RACI, vendor and change management in the loop, and SLOs for availability, performance and security that you measure and iterate on. The point is that a vendor's maintenance window should never be the first time anyone checks whether a model endpoint is actually highly available.

## Who should watch

Platform and cloud operations leads planning where ML workloads will run, and anyone writing the production-readiness checklist for an ML platform. If you want benchmarks or reference configurations, this is a framework overview rather than a build log.

Title: Your ML pipeline is slow because of data skew, not bad code
Description: Srihari Godleti (Roku) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 shows how repartitioning, key salting and broadcast joins tame Spark data skew in ML pipelines.
Body:
A Spark stage finishes when its slowest task finishes, and in a streaming company one power user can be that task. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Srihari Godleti, a data and ML engineering leader at Roku, explained how data skew turned retraining jobs that ran in about 40 minutes into nearly three-hour runs with no code or infrastructure change, and the three techniques his team uses to fix it.

This is a practical, code-snippet talk about Apache Spark in ML feature pipelines. Bring your Spark UI.

## The symptom is one executor doing all the work

Roku processes billions of watch events and ad impressions a day, and every play, pause and ad click feeds Spark pipelines for personalisation, embedding generation and ad ranking. When the jobs slowed down, the Spark UI told the story: around 95% of tasks finished quickly while one executor ran far longer, processing more than ten times the shuffle data of its peers. Shuffle spills went up, garbage collection paused, that one CPU sat at 100% and everyone else idled.

The cause is the mismatch between Spark's hash partitioning and real behaviour, which follows a power law. One viewer has two interactions, another has 150. Group by user and the heavy one owns a partition. Godleti adds that in ad ranking his team has seen skew cost around 20% efficiency, which at that scale becomes a real line on the cloud bill, plus stale recommendations because retraining finishes late.

## Skew comes from three places

He sorts root causes into natural imbalance, join and aggregation keys, and computational skew. Natural imbalance is the world being lumpy: the Super Bowl, a Formula One race, a viral show, regional and seasonal patterns. Join-key skew appears when user features meet behavioural data and a few very active IDs dominate, and groupBy or reduceByKey aggregations (especially daily and weekly rollups) concentrate it further. Computational skew is the sneaky one: even with evenly sized partitions, variable-length documents, embedding generation or high-cardinality transformations make some rows far more expensive than others.

His point is that skew is a property of the data, not a bug in the system, so it belongs in the pipeline design from the start.

## Three fixes, in order of escalation

**Repartition** for moderate skew: explicitly redistribute on a column with a chosen partition count before expensive joins and aggregations. His rules of thumb are a partition count of two to three times the total cores and partitions of roughly 100 to 200 MB. It adds a shuffle and does nothing about key frequency, but his team saw about a 30% improvement in preprocessing stages.

**Salt the hot keys** when one value dominates: append a small random suffix to heavy user IDs so a single key becomes several, aggregate, then aggregate again. That second stage is the price. In Roku's case a large partition dropped from about 8 GB to around 600 MB and some training runtimes fell by nearly half.

**Broadcast the small side** of a join so the large behavioural table never shuffles. Keep the broadcast table small (he cites 10 MB as the typical limit) and below roughly a fifth to a quarter of executor memory to avoid GC pressure. One enrichment stage went from about 90 minutes to close to 10.

The abstract's headline is pipeline times cut by about 40%. The talk's own advice is to apply these selectively to the stages that are actually skewed instead of over-engineering the whole pipeline.

## Where it goes next

Godleti closes with work in progress: models trained on historical Spark metrics to predict skew risk before a stage runs and recommend partition counts, salting factors and broadcast strategies. It is framed as an experiment, so treat it as a direction rather than a result.

## Who should watch

Data and ML engineers who own Spark feature pipelines and keep seeing one task bar stretch across the timeline. If you already salt keys in your sleep, the numbers are still a nice sanity check. If you have never opened the Spark UI's stage view, watch this and then open it.

Title: Good models fail after deployment because the world keeps moving
Description: Oleksandr Pyvovar (Meta) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 maps five production failure modes, from data drift to feedback loops, with a fix for each.
Body:
A model that scores well in the lab can be close to a coin flip six months later, and nothing in the code changed. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Oleksandr Pyvovar, a machine learning engineer at Meta, catalogued why that happens, how to detect each cause and what to do about it, all in one tidy taxonomy.

The abstract puts the thesis well: great models "don't usually fail because they're wrong" but because the world changes after they ship. The talk then earns that line with detection methods you can actually implement.

## Five ways production quietly breaks a model

Pyvovar walks through data drift, concept drift, label drift, feature pipeline degradation with training-serving skew, and feedback loops with bias amplification. Each gets an analogy, a real incident and a detect-then-resolve pair.

Data drift is the self-driving car trained on sunny days and deployed in fog; his real-world example is Zillow Offers and its pricing model failing to adapt to post-pandemic market volatility. Concept drift keeps the inputs but changes their meaning, which is the daily life of fraud models whose adversaries simply move to a VPN or shift their attack hours. Label drift is the add-to-cart model calibrated on a normal week meeting Black Friday, or a loan-default model trained in a calm economy meeting a recession.

## Every failure mode gets its own detector

What makes the talk useful is that the detectors differ per failure mode. For input drift he covers Population Stability Index for tracking key features over time, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for numerical features and Jensen-Shannon for categorical ones. Concept drift needs performance monitoring against labels, adaptive sliding windows that grow or shrink as the data shifts, or error-rate thresholds. Label drift is caught by watching the class distribution, a chi-square test, or simply the share of positive predictions.

The fixes are equally specific: Platt scaling or isotonic regression to recalibrate after label drift, class weighting and cost-sensitive learning, online learning or windowed ensembles for concept drift, and domain adaptation when relabelling is not an option.

## Your pipeline is part of the model

The feature pipeline section is the one platform teams should bookmark. His example is Google's diabetic retinopathy model, which matched specialists on clean lab images and then struggled in clinics in Thailand where photos were taken in poor light. Same model, worse ingredients.

The prescriptions are the ones you know you should already have: Great Expectations or Deequ for data validation, schema monitoring, logging inputs and outputs in both training and serving to catch skew, data contracts between teams, containers for environment parity, and a feature store as the industry standard that removes a whole class of skew bugs.

Feedback loops get the heaviest example, the COMPAS recidivism tool, and three countermeasures: deliberate exploration (a random slot or two in a recommendation batch), positional debiasing, and fairness constraints at training time.

## Retrain on signals, not on the calendar

On retraining, he compares time-based schedules (simple but wasteful), performance triggers (precise but reactive, since the losses already happened), drift triggers (proactive but noisy) and a hybrid policy, which he recommends while admitting it needs a lot of threshold tuning. Monitoring is split into model performance, data health and system health, with open-source options like Evidently AI, NannyML and Alibi Detect alongside commercial platforms.

The closing practices are the kind you tape to a monitor: design for drift from day one, keep training-serving parity, roll out gradually starting with a small slice of traffic, instrument for ground truth, document everything, and treat ML as a product rather than a project.

## Who should watch

ML engineers shipping their first or fifth model, and SREs who inherited a model and want a mental checklist for the week a model got worse while nobody deployed anything. Seasoned MLOps folks will know most of the tools, but the per-failure-mode mapping of detector to fix is a handy reference.

- [AI Model Monitoring: Building Reliable Alert Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muddassar_Sharif_ai_model_systems) by Muddassar Sharif (Virtuans.ai) turns detection into alerting.
