Title: Conf42 DevOps 2026 - agents joined the pipeline, failover got boring
Description: Conf42 DevOps 2026 in review, 47 talks on agents in CI/CD and on-call, infrastructure as a graph, boring failover, CI-gated SLOs and what green CI misses.
Body:
[Conf42 DevOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/devops2026) opened the Conf42 year on January 22, 2026 with 47 talks. The loudest question was what happens when AI agents get commit rights, pipeline access and a seat on the on-call rota. The quieter, equally useful one was how to make the old hard things (region failover, migrations, compliance) dull enough that nobody needs a hero. Speakers came from Intuit, Google, Disney, Meta, Microsoft, Cisco, Splunk, Twilio, Workday, Oracle, ASML, Harness and more.

## Agents in CI/CD and on call, with the brakes attached

Diamond sponsor Harness set the frame. [Chinmay Gaikwad](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Chinmay_Gaikwad_cicd_agentic_ai) argued that AI made writing code cheap and moved the bottleneck after the commit, then laid out an enterprise-ready pipeline built by agents: a knowledge graph for context, policies enforced outside the prompt, and RBAC that treats the AI as an extension of the user, so if you can't deploy to production, neither can your agent.

[Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Neeraj_Kumar_Singh_Beshane_governance_genai_velocity) (Meta) proposed GenOps, a governance-first model for letting generative agents act inside CI/CD. [Vladyslav Budichenko](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Vladyslav_Budichenko_incidents_agents_security) (Vocaly AI) gave agents in incident response the good, the bad and the ugly treatment, including how to use them safely with MCP. [Neal Iyer](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Neal_Iyer_guardrails_ai_accountability) (Splunk) brought the same "guardrails first" stance to agents in the security operations centre, keeping human control in the loop. On the infrastructure side, [Praneeth Patil](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Praneeth_Patil_autonomous_infrastructure_cloud) (Equinix) described LLM-driven multi-cloud infrastructure that catches misconfigurations, and [Premanand Tiwari](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Premanand_Tiwari_forecasting_time_autonomy) (Amazon) demoed autonomous time-series forecasting for capacity planning.

## Infrastructure is a graph, so give the model the graph

Context engineering got its own cluster. [Roxane Fischer](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Roxane_Fischer_context_reasoning_infrastructure) (Anyshift) explained why LLMs fail at infrastructure: they can't see live dependencies or multi-hop relationships. Her answer is to model infrastructure as a graph, query it with Graph RAG and natural-language-to-Cypher, and measure context quality. [Pronnoy Goswami](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Pronnoy_Goswami_observability_queries_context) (Workday) used the Model Context Protocol to make telemetry queryable, and [Michael Levan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Michael_Levan_agents_telemetry_costs) (Solo.io) asked the two questions every platform team now hears about agentic and MCP traffic: how do we observe it, and how do we keep the bill sane. [Tina Kanth](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Tina_Kanth_finops_streaming_prompts) (Microsoft) showed prompt templates that turn streaming financial events into structured, auditable triage decisions.

## Make failover boring

The most satisfying talks were about removing drama. [Akshay Pratinav](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Akshay_Pratinav_failover_resilience_workloads) (Intuit) described a Kubernetes-native platform where services onboard declaratively to region failover: pre-scale from live traffic, promote standby databases, shift routes through Route53 and Istio. The goal, in his words, is to make failover boring, which is the highest compliment in operations.

[Harris Baskaran](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Harris_Baskaran_kubernetes_modernization_containers) (Google) walked a high-volume ticketing monolith from VMware and Oracle to GCE, then rebuilt it cloud-native on GKE and PostgreSQL, with dependency mapping, replication and multi-region DR lessons along the way. [Kalyan Inturi](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Kalyan_Inturi_availability_migration_gateways) (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure) used shadow traffic and phased rollouts for a zero-downtime gateway migration. [Nikhil Kokal](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Nikhil_Kokal_apis_scalability_reliability) (The Walt Disney Company) covered architectures for APIs at billions of requests, and [Srinivas Pagadala Sekar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Srinivas_Pagadala_Sekar_gitops_resilience_automation) (Karsun Solutions) built self-healing pipelines with Tekton and Argo CD.

## Observability as a contract, not a nice-to-have

[Sumit Kaul](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Sumit_Kaul_slos_instrumentation_observability) (Payjoy) made observability a platform contract: zero-code instrumentation and SLOs gated in CI/CD, so a service cannot ship without traces and metrics. [Mohit Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Mohit_Gupta_gpu_ci_validation) (Intel) applied the same idea to GPU performance, catching compute and memory bottlenecks in the pipeline instead of in production. [Aravind Sekar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Aravind_Sekar_reliability_prevention_ai) (Twilio) and [Raghu Bhupatiraju](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Raghu_Bhupatiraju_predictive_analytics_outages) (Expeditors) both pushed from firefighting towards prediction, the latter for supply chain systems.

## Green checkmarks are not the whole story

[Tilda Udufo](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Tilda_Udufo_cicd_quality_testing) (Outreachy) gave one of the event's sharpest reminders: passing tests don't guarantee quality, as the XZ Utils incident showed, and review practice and culture have to cover what automation misses. [Bhaskar Sawant](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Bhaskar_Sawant_security_automation_pipelines) mapped how AI-driven development changes the pipeline attack surface. [Gian Wild](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gian_Wild_accessibility_security_inclusion) (AccessibilityOz) took apart the idea that security and accessibility must trade off against each other. Hands-on security tooling came from [Nikolay Milyaev](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Nikolay_Milyaev_xdr_security_analytics) (Microsoft) on Defender XDR alert fatigue, [Gareth Emslie](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gareth_Emslie_sentinel_security_automation) (Dynatrace) on extending Microsoft Sentinel, and [Gurdeep Gill](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gurdeep_Gill_firewalls_ai_protection) (Cisco) on NGFWs for AI workloads. [Imran Abdul](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Imran_Abdul_sdwan_networking_automation) (Pace University) brought GitOps to the enterprise network, SD-WAN and zero trust included.

## Regulated and physical systems

Compliance and industry talks rounded out the programme: [Pooja Ranjan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Pooja_Ranjan_compliance_saas_governance) (Oracle) on continuous compliance for SaaS, [Vivek Chittireddy](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Vivek_Chittireddy_privacy_regulation_security) (Meta) on privacy by design with differential privacy and anonymisation in the pipeline, [Swapna Chimanchodkar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Swapna_Chimanchodkar_clinical_healthcare_ai) (Cognizant) on deploying real-time sepsis detection, and [Rasmi Ranjan Nayak](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Rasmi_Ranjan_Nayak_embedded_robotics_ai) (ASML) on deterministic embedded AI for robotics.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), the Diamond sponsor, and [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) at Gold. All 47 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/devops2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrB6SG3pv3bmTo7NWFlCGiNx).

The series returns with [Conf42 DevOps 2027](https://www.conf42.com/devops2027).

Title: Active inference as a first-principles path to next-generation agents
Description: QF Network CEO Alex Vyatkin at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on active inference and the free energy principle as a basis for adaptive AI agents.
Body:
Today's agents are LLMs in a loop, and they still struggle the moment a scenario is genuinely new. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Alex Vyatkin, co-founder and CEO of deep tech startup QF Network, pointed past the hype to a different foundation: active inference, a framework from neuroscience built on Karl Friston's free energy principle, in which agents act to reduce surprise about their world.

He calls it "quite a deep rabbit hole" and means it as an invitation. This is a research-frontier talk: no benchmarks, no product demo, but a clear explanation of the ideas and a reading list to get started.

## The reality check behind the agent boom

Vyatkin opens by taking stock of the year of the agent: lots of new projects, some of them wild, and even talk of Mac Mini shortages from people running agents at home. The market is growing fast. But in his assessment, current agents still fail in novel scenarios, remain hungry for data and compute, and get harder to run as tasks grow more complex, with many projects at risk from unexpected costs. The gap between promised autonomy and delivered autonomy is where he wants engineers to look.

## Agents that minimise surprise

The core idea: an adaptive system survives by minimising variational free energy, a bound on surprise, meaning the mismatch between its internal model of the world and what it senses. It can close that gap two ways. Perception updates the internal model. Action changes the world so it matches the model. In active inference, perception and action are two sides of one loop.

Agents choose policies by minimising expected free energy, which bundles two values. Epistemic value rewards exploring to reduce uncertainty. Pragmatic value rewards reaching preferred states. That gives a principled answer to the exploration-exploitation dilemma, instead of a reward function bolted on afterwards, and Vyatkin argues it produces goal-seeking and curious behaviour from first principles.

## What that buys you, on paper

The claimed advantages are the ones current agents lack. Adaptation to novel scenarios without massive retraining. Much lower data and compute for learning. And explainability: you can inspect an agent's beliefs and the policies it is weighing, which makes governance easier than with a black-box model. He also flags robotics, where controlling a body in a changing environment remains a hard problem.

## Many agents, no central controller

Active inference is multi-scale. Agents keep their own boundaries (Markov blankets in the jargon), share world models, and coordinate through belief propagation and message passing, minimising expected free energy as a team. Orchestration can emerge from collective behaviour with no central controller. Vyatkin stretches this toward enterprise systems with traceable, adaptive workflows and, more speculatively, toward agents that act like researchers testing hypotheses.

## Where to start digging

His resource list is the practical takeaway: the textbook by Parr, Pezzulo and Friston, available free from MIT Press; a forthcoming fundamentals book aimed at engineers; libraries in Julia and Python with example agents; and the Active Inference Institute for courses and community.

## Who should watch

Engineers who suspect LLM-in-a-loop agents are not the end state and want a serious alternative to read about, and anyone in robotics or control looking for a principled take on exploration. If you need something to ship next sprint, this is background reading, not a recipe.

Title: Shipping faster without losing sleep
Description: This is the practice
Body:
# DevOps, but now it thinks for itself

DevOps has always been about automation.

In 2026, the automation talks back.

Conf42 DevOps 2026 is a very clear signal that agentic AI has moved from experiments to infrastructure. CI/CD pipelines are making decisions. Compliance is running in real time. Incident response is increasingly autonomous. And somehow, it all still needs to be observable, secure, and affordable.

This conference is packed. The agenda spans agents, AI, architecture, compliance, data, FinOps, MLOps, observability, security, SRE, and sustainability. If DevOps touches it, it’s probably here. Often with an AI-powered opinion.

AI agents are everywhere. From enterprise-ready CI/CD pipelines and autonomous cloud engineering to self-healing operations and AI-driven incident response, many talks focus on what happens when systems stop waiting for humans to intervene. There’s excitement, but also a lot of healthy caution.

Compliance and governance get serious attention. Compliance-as-code, continuous regulatory validation, privacy-by-design pipelines, and real-time compliance copilots show how DevOps is adapting to regulated environments like finance, healthcare, and critical infrastructure. This is DevOps where audits are not theoretical.

Data and FinOps show up in force. Medallion data lakes, blockchain-driven BI, read-intensive architectures, streaming financial events, and cost-aware observability all point to a world where DevOps teams are responsible not just for uptime, but for economics and trust.

Observability and SRE round things out. AI-powered observability, predictive reliability, agent traffic monitoring, and multi-workload failover reflect how complex systems have become. The focus shifts from reacting faster to preventing problems before users notice.

If DevOps is your job, your craft, or the thing that quietly connects everything else you do, this one’s for you. In 2026, DevOps isn’t just shipping software anymore. It’s running intelligent systems at scale.

Title: Machine learning as the layer that lets automation adapt
Description: Amazon BI engineer Aditi Namdeo at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on ML as the intelligence layer for self-optimising factories, fleets and grids.
Body:
Rule-based automation works until the world changes, and then it is the thing causing the downtime. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Aditi Namdeo, a business intelligence engineer at Amazon, made the case for machine learning as the intelligence layer that sits on top of industrial automation and lets it adapt: learning from new data, catching faults early and tuning itself against the KPIs that matter.

This is an introductory, framework-level talk. It doesn't walk through code or a single system in depth. What it gives you is a clean mental model of where ML fits in automation, and a checklist for making it trustworthy.

## From static rules to systems that learn

Namdeo frames the shift as moving from static, rule-based automation to dynamic systems that keep improving. She cites the figure that 70% of unplanned downtime is linked to inflexible automation, which is the problem statement in one number.

Three techniques do most of the work in her model. Reinforcement learning lets a system learn from interaction and trial and error in changing environments. Predictive modelling uses history to forecast what comes next so processes can be tuned ahead of time. Anomaly detection spots irregular patterns in real-time data so the system can respond before a small fault becomes an outage.

## Three places it pays off

She walks through manufacturing, logistics and energy:

- **Manufacturing:** data-driven workflow optimisation, higher throughput and less downtime through predictive maintenance.
- **Logistics:** route planning on real-time data to cut fuel and delivery time, and smarter load balancing to use vehicle capacity better.
- **Energy:** predictive load management to forecast demand, distribution tuned to predicted usage, and real-time anomaly detection across the grid.

The common thread is self-healing automation. Manual anomaly detection means delays and extended downtime; ML-driven detection allows immediate identification and, in her framing, autonomous corrective action.

## Keep the AI and the OT apart

The architectural advice is the part engineers will recognise. Separate the AI layer from the operational technology layer so either can change without destabilising the other. Manage the data flow between them for real-time responsiveness. Build modular so the system grows incrementally instead of being redesigned.

Explainability gets equal billing. In critical industries, people need to understand why a model made a call before they let it act. She argues for explainable pipelines, standardised model validation against benchmarks, cross-functional teams that pair data scientists with operations experts, and continuous feedback so human reviews and corrections flow back into the model. The balance she describes is honest: overly complex models hurt interpretability, overly simple ones miss the patterns that matter.

## Measure the right things

Her closing advice is to pick KPIs tied to operational goals, not model metrics in isolation. Throughput, downtime reduction and energy efficiency are the three she highlights, because they map straight to revenue, cost and sustainability targets.

## Who should watch

Engineers and analysts new to industrial or operations ML who want the big picture before picking tools, and managers who need vocabulary for a predictive-maintenance proposal. If you already run anomaly detection on plant telemetry, the related talks below go deeper on implementation.

Title: Multi-cloud ML meets data sovereignty law, and governance has to adapt
Description: EY's Sapna Pillai at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on keeping multi-cloud ML compliant with GDPR, the CLOUD Act and data localisation rules.
Body:
Running machine learning across several clouds is the easy part now. Doing it while every jurisdiction tightens the rules on where data lives and who can reach it is harder. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Sapna Pillai of EY's Technology Consulting practice gave a compact tour of where governance breaks down in distributed, multi-cloud ML systems, and the four tools she reaches for to fix it: sovereign cloud zones, zero trust, compliance automation and unified cross-region governance.

It's a short talk and an overview, not a build-along. Its value is the map: which laws pull in which direction, which standards give you a shared vocabulary, and where in the ML lifecycle the gaps open up.

## Why multi-cloud makes compliance harder

Pillai starts with the case for multi-cloud ML: best-of-breed services, less vendor lock-in, better disaster recovery and the ability to shift resources with demand. The cost of that flexibility is governance complexity. Governments increasingly assert control over where data is stored, processed and accessed, especially when it crosses borders, and that collides with workloads designed to move freely.

She names three recurring problems. Keeping data residency lawful across several providers. Keeping full auditability of data movement when lineage spans clouds. And staying consistent when the laws themselves disagree.

## Three laws that pull in different directions

The examples are the ones that keep architects awake. GDPR sets strict data protection standards in the EU and has shaped governance practice well beyond it. The US CLOUD Act lets law enforcement reach data held by US-based companies even when that data is stored overseas. China's Cybersecurity Law imposes strong localisation and cross-border transfer requirements. Put a training pipeline, a feature store and an inference endpoint in three regions and you can trip over all three.

For a common language across platforms she points to ISO 27018 for personal data in public clouds, the Cloud Security Alliance STAR programme for evaluating and certifying cloud controls, and NIST 800-53 for security and privacy controls in regulated and government-aligned systems.

## Visibility first, then controls

The gap she keeps returning to is visibility. Many organisations can't say how data moves between providers, and without that, unauthorised access, accidental cross-border transfers and failed audits become likely. Her toolkit, in order:

- **Sovereign cloud zones** keep storage and processing inside a jurisdiction while still giving you cloud scale, and they help with trust from local customers and partners.
- **Zero trust** assumes no implicit trust and verifies every access request, so data stays protected as it moves across clouds and regions, with least-privilege access throughout.
- **Compliance automation** covers real-time monitoring of regulatory requirements, consistent policy enforcement across providers and automatically generated audit trails, because manual compliance doesn't scale across clouds.
- **Cross-region ML governance** means one framework for residency, access and security from training to inference to retraining, not a separate patchwork per region.

Her balancing rule is worth pinning above the architecture board: "Compliance should enable the business not slow it down." Governance has to bend with new regulations instead of freezing the platform.

## Who should watch

Platform and ML engineers who have just been told the next model must serve EU and US customers from shared infrastructure, and architects who need a quick refresher on which regulations and standards matter before a design review. If you already run sovereign regions in production, this one will mostly confirm your checklist.

Title: Treat climate risk models for food systems like software
Description: Poshan Kumar of Kyndryl at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on generative AI climate scenarios, adaptation advice and stakeholder briefs run as GitOps pipelines.
Body:
A climate model that informs a planting decision should be versioned, tested and rolled back like any other production service. That's the thesis [Poshan Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Poshan_Kumar_climate_modeling_food), Senior Lead and Managing Consultant at Kyndryl, brought to the sustainability track at Conf42 DevOps 2026: generative AI can simulate climate risk, propose local adaptations and write briefs for decision-makers, and DevOps practice is what makes those outputs reliable enough to act on.

The talk is short and dense, a reference architecture packed with dataset and model names rather than a demo. Kumar describes himself as an analytics architect working where enterprise platforms meet climate resilience, and the talk sits at that crossing.

## The operational backdrop changed

He opens with 2024, likely the first calendar year above 1.5 degrees over the pre-industrial baseline, with compounding floods and heat stress hitting production, storage and transport. Food insecurity stays high, with around 2.3 billion people facing moderate or severe food insecurity in the figures he cites. The engineering takeaway he draws is that data and ML systems for food have to anticipate extremes, quantify uncertainty and keep adapting.

## The inputs are better than most teams realise

The convergence he describes has three parts. First, data: ERA5 reanalysis gives hourly global data back to 1940 at roughly 31 km with uncertainty estimates; Sentinel-2 provides multispectral surface imagery at 10 to 20 m, useful for vegetation stress; CMIP6 scenarios define possible futures for stress testing. Second, ML weather and climate models: GraphCast for 10-day global forecasts, NeuralGCM as a hybrid physics-ML model that runs stably over decades, and generative downscaling to kilometre scale for precipitation and near-surface fields, which is what a farm-level decision needs. Third, DevOps maturity: containers, GitOps and policy as code.

## Three capabilities, one pipeline

The core of the talk is three generative capabilities. Climate scenario generation builds synthetic extreme-event ensembles conditioned on emissions pathways, downscales them, and validates them against historical analogues from ERA5. Adaptation strategy generation uses LLM agent workflows to suggest local interventions, such as crop rotation, irrigation timing tied to soil moisture and seed selection for drought, conditioned on hydrology, soils and economics. Automated brief generation writes stakeholder-specific briefs for farmers, buyers and NGOs, including uncertainty bands, scenario IDs and data provenance so the output can be audited.

Between them sit the unglamorous steps: ingest from the Copernicus data APIs and soil databases, link weather stress indices such as heat degree days to yield models, and render farmer-friendly maps.

## The DevOps stack is the familiar one

The architecture uses Argo Workflows for the container DAG (ingest, generate, downscale, evaluate, brief), Kubeflow Pipelines v2 for reusable ML components and experiment tracking, KServe for autoscaled inference with canary rollouts for both predictive models and LLM endpoints, Argo CD for cluster state and drift detection, and a model registry (Azure ML or SageMaker) for promotion, lineage and approval gates. Pipelines fail on significant data or prediction drift, and dataset and model version IDs travel in metadata. Nothing in that list will surprise an MLOps engineer, which is the point: the climate part is new, the plumbing is not.

## Governance built in

For trust, Kumar maps the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (govern, map, measure, manage) and its 2024 generative AI profile onto pipeline stages, and wants a model card for each climate and LLM component. His closing advice: integrate AI into pipelines, treat climate LLM artifacts like versioned, tested software, promote them through GitOps, and keep outputs practical.

## Who should watch

MLOps and platform engineers working with geospatial or agricultural data, and climate-tech teams that need a production architecture rather than a notebook. The auto-generated captions struggle with the dataset names, so keep the slides at hand.

Title: ISO 42001 for beginners: the 16 documents an AI audit asks for
Description: Security engineer Aleksandra Drobnjak at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 maps the minimum ISO 42001 paperwork that makes an AI management system auditable.
Body:
Sooner or later someone asks who approved a model change, what data went into it, and whether anyone can explain it. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), security engineer Aleksandra Drobnjak answered that question with a short list: the 16 documentation artifacts an ISO 42001 auditor expects to see before concluding that an organisation manages its AI systems in a controlled, repeatable way. She calls it "Minimum Viable AIMS", and the point is clarity about risk, ownership and change, not perfect paperwork.

Drobnjak comes at this from both sides of the table. She has spent more than ten years in engineering roles across multi-cloud and container security, supported ISO and SOC 2 audits, and trained as an ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 lead auditor. So the talk reads less like a summary of the standard and more like a walk through what an auditor actually opens first.

## The standard in one paragraph

ISO 42001 was published in 2023 and is the first certifiable standard for managing AI at the organisational level. It doesn't tell you which models or tools to use. It has ten clauses, with clauses 4 to 10 holding the auditable requirements, plus Annex A with 38 controls across nine control objectives. Not every control is mandatory: you pick them by risk, scope and context. It follows the plan-do-check-act cycle, so it sits comfortably next to ISO 27001. Certification runs as a stage one documentation audit, a stage two effectiveness audit, then annual surveillance audits inside a three-year cycle.

A nice practical aside: you can pull the ISO 42001 certificates behind AWS services such as Amazon Bedrock, Transcribe and Textract from AWS Artifact, then check the certificate number yourself on IAF CertSearch. Drobnjak says it takes a couple of minutes.

## Scope is where shadow AI gets caught

The first artifact, the AIMS scope (clause 4.3), sounds dull and does the most work. Her MLOps example is familiar: a model starts in a notebook, someone wires it into a pipeline, and it is influencing real workflows before anyone decided whether it belongs inside governance. The same gap covers engineers pasting company material into personal AI accounts whose default settings may let the vendor train on it.

She also points at ordinary infrastructure mistakes: Jupyter, Kubeflow or MLflow instances left reachable from outside or from production networks. A written scope forces the question of which ML tools may run in production and which environments need authentication, logging and approvals.

## Risks that never become tickets don't count

The planning artifacts (clause 6) exist because risks get discussed, even documented, and then nothing changes. Each risk or opportunity needs an owner, a decision and a concrete next step that lands on someone's board. A repeatable risk assessment method stops one team calling a model change low risk while another blocks the same change outright. She treats model artifacts as executable components, not just data, which is why promotion shouldn't be "just another commit".

The statement of applicability example she shows is control A.5.5 on societal impact, and she makes it concrete: energy use and carbon footprint, who gains or loses access to tools, whether a decision can be understood and challenged, and effects on health and wellbeing.

## Operations, audits and the closing loop

The rest of the list follows the lifecycle: competence records (7.2), the documentation your teams actually rely on (7.5, the place for release notes and prompt changes that otherwise live in Slack DMs), operational controls (8.1), the risk register, treatment plans (8.3), AI system impact assessments (8.4), monitoring results (9.1), internal audit (9.2), management review (9.3), and nonconformities with corrective actions (10.2). She explains the difference between a minor nonconformity, such as a missing approval record, and a major one that signals a systemic breakdown and can delay or suspend certification.

Her strongest takeaway is the one engineers tend to nod at: "advanced models rarely cause problems by themselves." Missing ownership, missing traceability and missing feedback loops do. She is also frank that certification costs time, attention and budget, so a risk-based approach beats trying to do everything at once.

## Who should watch

Watch it if you run ML platforms or security and someone has just said the word "audit" in a meeting, or if you need a checklist to start an AIMS without boiling the ocean. It is a beginner-friendly talk by design; if you have already been through an ISO 42001 stage two audit, you'll mostly be checking your own list against hers.

Title: A medical scribe as a LangGraph state machine, not one big prompt
Description: Apple ML engineer Rajeshwari Sah at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 builds a four-agent LangGraph scribe that turns doctor-patient talk into checked SOAP notes.
Body:
One huge prompt that turns a doctor-patient conversation into a clinical note will produce something that looks right. When it isn't, you can't tell which part failed. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Rajeshwari Sah, a machine learning engineer at Apple, rebuilt the task as a LangGraph state machine with four narrow agents, a typed shared state and a consistency checker, and ran it live on a 7B model on her laptop.

Her definition of "agentic" is pleasantly unromantic: break a complex task into specialised, testable steps, make each step a node that transforms a shared state, and let the graph decide what happens next. The agency lives in workflow design, routing, retries and quality checks.

## Why clinical notes punish shortcuts

The output format is SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan). The input is a messy human conversation where patients jump topics and a critical fact may appear once. Clinical language adds traps: negation ("denies chest pain"), temporality ("started last week"), uncertainty ("possible viral URI") and context ("family history of diabetes"). Ask one prompt to transcribe, extract, prioritise, format and validate at once and it fails quietly. Her line for the whole design: "plausible but wrong is worse than no output."

She is clear that this is an educational prototype. Real clinical use needs validation, privacy controls and clinician oversight.

## Four agents, one typed state

The pipeline is transcription (Whisper for audio, or text input), information extraction, summarisation into SOAP, and a consistency check. Every node reads and writes a single state object holding the transcript, the extracted encounter, the SOAP note, the consistency report, logs and errors. Nodes behave like pure functions: state in, state out. That makes them unit-testable, replayable and diffable across versions.

Extraction is treated as an API contract. Pydantic models describe symptoms, vitals, diagnoses, medications, tests and follow-ups, combined into a `ClinicalEncounter`. The schema guides the model and validates its output. If validation fails, the node retries once with a stricter prompt; if it fails again, it sets an error and stops cleanly. Nodes never crash the workflow, they record the failure and let the router decide.

## Summarise from facts, then check the facts

Summarisation reads the structured encounter, not the raw transcript, with temperature zero and a no-new-facts rule. The consistency agent then compares the note against the encounter, combining cheap deterministic checks (does the blood pressure in Objective match the extracted value?), semantic checks with an LLM as judge, and safety checks for invented medications or labs. The report flags issues for a clinician or triggers a revision; it never replaces human review.

## The demo, on a laptop

The recorded demo runs the whole graph in Streamlit against Qwen 2.5 7B served locally through Ollama. From a respiratory-infection conversation it extracted six symptoms, three vital signs, one diagnosis and two prescriptions, wrote the SOAP note, and the consistency agent caught that difficulty breathing was missing from the Subjective section. The code is on her GitHub, linked from the slides.

## Measure each agent, not just the note

Evaluation is per node: entity-level precision, recall and F1 by category for extraction; ROUGE-L plus omissions, contradictions and readability for summaries; consistency issues per note over time. She suggests starting with 20 to 50 annotated conversations, simulated if needed. Extensions include a grounding node for ICD-10 and SNOMED codes, and a redaction node before logs are persisted.

## Who should watch

Anyone building multi-step LLM workflows in a regulated domain, healthcare or not. The state-plus-router pattern transfers directly to claims, contracts or support tickets. If you already run LangGraph in production, the evaluation and failure-handling sections are the useful bits.

Title: Extending Microsoft Sentinel with your own codeless connector
Description: Gareth Emslie of Dynatrace at Conf42 DevOps 2026 builds a Microsoft Sentinel solution with a codeless connector, KQL analytics rules and packaging.
Body:
If the SIEM your security team lives in doesn't know about your tool, you can teach it. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, [Gareth Emslie](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gareth_Emslie_sentinel_security_automation), Senior Product Manager and Tech Evangelist at Dynatrace, showed how to extend Microsoft Sentinel end to end: a Codeless Connector Framework data connector that polls a REST API, data collection rules that shape the data on ingest, KQL analytics rules that raise incidents, and the packaging that turns it all into a Content Hub solution.

The worked example is Dynatrace's own Sentinel solution, which pulls attacks detected by Dynatrace Runtime Application Protection, so this is a vendor's integration used as a tutorial. The steps apply to any product with a REST API, and the demo is detailed enough to follow along.

## Why a DevOps engineer should care about the SOC's tools

Emslie opens with the pressure on security operations: data breaches at a record high in the Identity Theft Resource Center's 2023 report, human error behind most of them, and SOC teams buried in alerts from fragmented tools. He also cites a Threat Stack report in which 52% of companies admitted cutting security corners to hit deadlines. His argument is that speed and security aren't mutually exclusive, and that DevOps people are well placed to build the automation that connects the two.

Sentinel is the stage for that: analytics rules for detection, SOAR-style playbooks and automation rules for response, hunting queries grouped by MITRE ATT&CK tactics, and a Content Hub where partners publish connectors and solutions.

## Pick the connector type that doesn't bill your customer

There are three ways to build a connector that calls a REST API. Logic Apps give you a what-you-see-is-what-you-get interface, and Azure Functions give you full code, but both deploy extra Azure resources into the customer's environment. The Codeless Connector Framework (CCF) has more limited REST support, but Microsoft hosts and runs it, so the customer deploys nothing. That's why he recommends CCF.

Data then goes through data collection rules at ingest: a KQL transformation filters, enriches and restructures the raw JSON into a defined table schema (the custom table keeps its `_CL` suffix, and `TimeGenerated` is required). At query time, ASIM parsers normalise data from different sources into one schema. He reminds viewers that billing follows the volume of data analysed and stored, which is a good reason to filter at ingest.

## The demo, file by file

The live part works in Microsoft's public Azure-Sentinel GitHub repository, where every solution lives under `Solutions/<Vendor>`. Emslie walks through the files a CCF connector needs:

- the data collection rule, with table schema, destinations and the transformation query;
- the polling configuration: endpoint URL built from the customer's environment URL, HTTP method, retries, time format for the start and end query window, headers, where the data sits in the JSON response (an attacks array here), and `nextPageKey` token paging;
- the table definition with typed fields and no type suffixes;
- the connector definition that drives the portal UI, with publisher, sample queries, permissions, prerequisites such as an access token, and a connect toggle.

He adds an analytics rule template in YAML: query frequency and period, MITRE tactics and techniques, a KQL query for attacks that aren't allow-listed, a custom alert name built from Dynatrace fields, incident creation, and grouping of alerts over seven days when entities match. In the portal, he creates a rule from that template, tweaking severity, entity mapping for IPs and hostnames, schedule and threshold.

## Package it, or side-load it to test

Packaging uses a PowerShell script from the repo's tools folder, `createSolutionV3`, which produces a versioned zip for Microsoft Partner Center plus an ARM template and UI definition. That ARM template is the handy bit: deploy it as a custom template in your own subscription to test the solution without publishing, which is how he ran the demo.

## Who should watch

DevOps and platform engineers who own an internal tool or product that the security team wants inside Sentinel, and anyone writing their first CCF connector. It's long and detailed, so keep the Azure-Sentinel repo open alongside it.

Title: Scoring every 5G session for risk before it reaches the UPF
Description: Binu Govindan of Microsoft at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on multi-factor AI risk scoring and a tiered mitigation pipeline for the 5G user plane function.
Body:
Signature-based detection catches the attacks you have already seen. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, [Binu Govindan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Binu_Govindan_network_screening_mitigation), Principal SDET at Microsoft working on 5G and Azure, described a different approach for the 5G user plane function: give every session a risk score from several behavioural factors, then let a tiered pipeline shape, isolate or terminate it, with an analyst in the loop.

Govindan was clear that the talk reflects his own views, not his employer's. It's an architecture overview of about 15 minutes, aimed at people who run telecom or cloud-native network infrastructure and wonder how to secure UPF at scale.

## Why the user plane is the target

The UPF is the heart of the network, he explains: it carries the bulk of user traffic from devices out to external networks. And 5G gives attackers more to work with than earlier generations. The protocols are complex, with loopholes in signalling and the data plane. The core is virtualised and service-based, running on cloud and Kubernetes, which adds the usual cloud-native attack surfaces. And slice misconfigurations have historically opened doors to exploitation.

## Five signals instead of one signature

His risk scoring framework weighs five kinds of evidence for each session:

- **Behavioural analysis**: how the session behaves over time, including duration and packet sizes.
- **Geographic context**: sessions from areas where threats have been seen before score higher.
- **Temporal indicators**: time-based patterns of activity.
- **Volumetric metrics**: how much data and usage, which is where DDoS and resource congestion show up.
- **Historical intelligence**: a database of past attacks and their nature.

The model combines them into a high, medium or low score per session. The real-time loop collects traffic and telemetry, including CDR-style records from calls, scores sessions, classifies threats and triggers responses, and keeps learning as attack patterns evolve.

## Mitigation is a pipeline with escalating steps

The part DevOps teams will recognise is the response, written as an automated, tiered pipeline. Level one is enhanced monitoring, pulling data from Prometheus and call records. When a session looks risky, the pipeline applies traffic shaping and QoS adjustments. A high-risk session gets isolated, and the last step terminates it. The policies live as rules in the pipeline, and the AI can propose new rules too.

Humans stay involved: a trained analyst executes response actions for sessions classified as threats. The operational benefits he lists are the ones you'd expect: less alert fatigue, because some automated action has already happened before an alert reaches an analyst, faster incident response and more consistent operations. Think of it as a circuit breaker for subscribers rather than services.

## Fitting into a DevOps workflow

For integration, Govindan describes a GitOps-compatible, containerised deployment with Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry, an API-first design that plugs into CI/CD, and Kubernetes-friendly packaging. His rollout advice is the right kind of cautious: establish a baseline first, letting the system observe the network for one to several weeks to learn what good and bad sessions look like; then define policies on top of the telemetry pipeline and train analysts; and only then scale gradually towards full automation. He calls the end state 5G SecOps.

## Who should watch

Telecom engineers, network security teams and SREs running a 5G core on Kubernetes. The talk stays at the architecture level, with no model details or evaluation results, so treat it as a blueprint to compare against your own design.

Title: Outages start quietly, so build systems that fail fast
Description: Justice Eziefule of Metastable Labs at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on retry storms, pool exhaustion, timeouts that cancel work and failing fast under load.
Body:
Most outages don't announce themselves with a wall of 500s. They start with a dependency that gets a little slower while every dashboard still looks fine. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, [Justice Eziefule](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Justice_Eziefule_availability_resilience_operations), co-founder and CTO of Metastable Labs and formerly a senior software engineer at Paystack, walked through how that quiet start turns into a full outage, and the habits that keep a system standing while it is failing.

Eziefule spent years at Paystack, the African payments company later acquired by Stripe, running systems that processed hundreds of millions of dollars a month. He promised not to make the talk a shopping list, and kept the promise: it's about failure mechanisms that behave the same on any cloud.

## The incident that looks like a normal Tuesday

His example starts with a traffic bump from a launch or a campaign. Twenty minutes in, one dependency slows down: Postgres under heavier reads, a hot Redis, a third-party provider rate-limiting you. Average query time climbs from about 15 ms to about 150 ms. Nothing is down yet.

Then the maths arrives. One dashboard load fans out to six internal services, each hitting the database, so 100 ms per call becomes 600 ms per request. And averages lie at scale: if p50 is 100 ms but p99 is five seconds, someone is always living in that p99.

## Retries multiply load at the worst moment

Things slow down, so everyone adds retries: the client, the service, the SDK. One request becomes two or three. His point is blunt: retries don't reduce load, they multiply it, at exactly the wrong time. That's the retry storm, and it turns a slow dependency into a death spiral.

Next comes connection pool exhaustion. Slower queries hold connections longer, the pool of 50 fills, and new requests queue for a connection that never frees up. CPU and memory look fine. The service is up but frozen, which he calls a zombie. Then timeouts fire, and many are badly designed: no timeout at all, a 30-second timeout that blocks everything, or a timeout that doesn't cancel the work underneath. That last one means the database keeps grinding on queries for requests the client has already given up on. Systems, as he puts it, die politely.

## Stabilise first, investigate later

During an incident, his first goal is not root cause. It's to stabilise the system and protect users, and the toolkit is ordered:

- **Limit concurrency.** Cap concurrent requests per endpoint and concurrent DB queries. Returning a 429 beats accepting everything and collapsing.
- **Layered timeouts that cancel.** Short and consistent: two to three seconds for a user request, roughly 500 ms to 1.5 s between services, and when a request times out, cancel its pending queries and downstream calls.
- **Circuit breakers.** Stop calling a sick dependency for a while, giving it room to recover and keeping your service from being dragged down.
- **Graceful degradation.** In payments, auth and placing an order are critical; a recommendations widget is not. Serve cached data, return partial results, and never block a payment because analytics is slow.
- **Load shedding.** Reject early, drop non-critical background tasks, sample logs. Fail fast, because slow failure is what kills you.

## Alert on burn rates, not CPU

For detection he uses the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation), with latency as percentiles. Quiet incidents show up as a stable p50, a creeping p95 and a spiking p99, with queue depth and pool usage rising before any errors. So alert on p99 burn rate, queue growth, error budget burn and pool exhaustion, not on whether CPU is high. Add correlation IDs and structured logs even without full tracing, so you can follow one request through the stack.

His controversial claim is that many outages are prolonged by a messy response rather than bad code: five engineers deploying fixes with nobody in charge. His playbook names an incident lead, freezes non-essential changes, stabilises, restores via rollback, and only then investigates. Before the next outage, design for idempotency so retries can't double-charge, move heavy work to queues, add bulkheads and rate limits.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers and SREs running anything with fan-out and a shared database. If you have ever watched a healthy-looking service stop answering, this half hour explains why, in plain language.

Title: Your system recovers only as fast as its slowest workload
Description: Akshay Pratinav of Intuit at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on a Kubernetes-native DR platform built on declarative intent, pre-scaling and staged failover.
Body:
At Conf42 DevOps 2026, [Akshay Pratinav](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Akshay_Pratinav_failover_resilience_workloads), Staff Software Engineer at Intuit, described how his team set out to make regional failover boring. The lesson that shaped the design: your system only recovers as fast as the slowest workload in the stack, so APIs, async workers, databases and routing have to fail over together, as one declared, staged workflow.

He says up front that this isn't a product pitch but patterns learned on the way. Then, helpfully, he shows the system anyway: the YAML teams write, the architecture behind it and the guardrails that keep it safe.

## Recovery is the outage customers remember

Pratinav starts from the premise that outages are normal: regions fail and managed services have bad days. What erodes customer trust is slow, manual, chaotic recovery. In a microservice estate, recovery is lopsided. APIs come back quickly, background workers lag, databases need promotion and async pipelines replay or stall.

Two organisational problems make it worse. Failover evolves team by team, so you end up with dozens or hundreds of DR strategies that are each fine and don't compose. And runbooks get followed by stressed, tired engineers with incomplete information, which is the worst time to work through a multi-page checklist. Nobody, he says, should be manually scaling clusters at 3 AM.

## Declare intent, let the platform own the mechanics

The biggest shift was from imperative procedures to declarative intent. Teams declare capacity, dependencies, data requirements and criticality; the platform executes. A customer-facing API and a nightly batch job can declare very different needs inside the same framework.

Two other principles carry a lot of weight. Fail over the whole stack, because a partial failover can be worse than none: move the API without its async workers and you corrupt state or build huge backlogs. And pre-scale the standby region from live primary traffic, so failover becomes a traffic move rather than a wait for cold capacity.

## A DR plan is a workflow with four stages

The concrete example is a DR procedure in YAML for an active-passive service with a database. Stage one pre-scales Kubernetes pods in the failover region by updating HPA and replica values to match the primary. Stage two promotes the standby database. Stage three dials traffic over. Stage four resets HPA and replicas to their original values, so nobody pays for idle compute afterwards. Each stage starts only when the previous one completes.

Under the hood, a UI calls a backend API that starts a state machine. The state machine publishes each stage to a Kafka topic, where agents pick it up: a database agent for promotion, a capacity agent for scaling, and an in-cluster add-on on every Kubernetes cluster that does the pre-scaling. Each agent takes a lock in a semaphore service and releases it only after an external monitoring tool confirms the action, and the state machine polls that lock before sending the next stage. The frontend is React; the backend is Go and Python. Routing shifts through Route53 or Istio, based on health signals rather than someone's judgement call.

His line on the design deserves a sticky note: toggles don't recover systems, workflows do.

## Safety rails, then practise until it's dull

Speed without safety can be worse than staying down, so moves are gated on health checks, dependency validation and drift detection, and every step is reversible. He wants no DR-only configuration and no special flag flipped once a year: production should always be ready to fail over. Regular game days, low-stress because the process is automated, mean the first failover never happens during a real outage.

The payoff he describes is partly cultural. Once engineers trust the system, they practise more, and failover becomes something they understand rather than fear.

## Who should watch

Platform teams running many microservices across regions, and SREs tired of DR plans that live in a wiki. If you are designing a DR orchestrator, the Kafka-plus-semaphore stage gating is the part to study.

Title: Reliability lives in what changed, not in what broke
Description: Spiros Economakis, founder of NOFire AI, at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on using AI to give production a memory and move SRE from firefighting to foresight.
Body:
Every incident investigation starts from zero because context doesn't survive change. That is the problem [Spiros Economakis](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Spiros_Economakis_sre_experience_ai), Founder and CEO of NOFire AI, put at the centre of his Conf42 DevOps 2026 talk. His answer is to stop asking "what broke?" and start asking what changed, where it landed and what it affected, with AI keeping a persistent memory of production so the question can be answered before customers notice.

Economakis spent over a decade on call for production systems, and the talk is a conceptual one: diagrams and arguments, no product demo. It's worth knowing that he builds a company in this space, so the vision lines up with what NOFire AI works on, though the talk never turns into a pitch.

## Systems now change faster than anyone can model them

The opening is a recognition, not a critique. Most engineering work happens in exceptions, edge cases and half-known systems. AI-generated code and vibe coding mean teams ship faster than ever, so production changes faster than humans can build a stable mental model. AI didn't create the problem, he says; it accelerated it.

His picture of production is three layers: services and infrastructure at the bottom, workflows such as releases, incidents, security and cost in the middle, and teams on top, each owning a slice and nobody seeing the whole. Every incident cuts across those boundaries, every handoff loses context, and the pain lives in the gaps. Customers feel the result: they report problems before monitoring does, and a few engineers who carry the full model of production become single points of failure until they burn out or leave.

## Three traps we already fell into

He names the fixes we've all tried. The visibility trap: more dashboards, metrics and alerts, which add mental load without structure. The correlation trap: smarter-looking pattern matching that helps you react but doesn't tell you why it happened this time. The tooling trap: a new tool or process for every new problem, each solving a slice while adding handoffs and ownership gaps. His summary is that the system became operable but not understandable. If your incident channel has more bots than humans, you know the feeling.

## From raw signals to a memory of change

What's different now, he argues, is that systems can hold meaning rather than emit fragments. Instead of reconstructing understanding after the fact from logs, traces, commits and deploys, AI can keep it close to production: a continuous view of what changed (code, config, dependencies, infrastructure, traffic), where it landed and how behaviour shifted. Every incident adds to that understanding instead of wiping the slate.

That moves reliability earlier. A deployment analysis can run on every PR, using the service's own history: how often it changes, what tends to go wrong after those changes, what is already unstable. Spotting risky changes in the IDE, finding the real cause during an incident, and feeding every outcome back becomes one loop rather than a deploy, an incident, a postmortem and some forgotten tickets.

## Customer experience is the downstream metric

The customer case follows: fewer surprises because risky changes are caught early, faster recovery because engineers act with full context, and more predictable releases. The engineer's job shifts too, from whack-a-mole with alerts to deciding when to ship, when to wait and how to manage risk before users feel it.

He closes on a strong claim. SRE has been optimised for speed (faster detection, faster response, faster RCA), but speed alone doesn't reduce risk; understanding does. He also predicts the talk itself will look different in a year, which is refreshingly honest for a talk about AI.

## Who should watch

SRE leads and engineering managers thinking about where AI belongs in reliability work beyond chatbot-assisted RCA. If you want implementation detail, this is the wrong talk. If you want a clear argument for change-centric reliability, it's a good one.

Title: A warehouse is a production system, so give it SLOs
Description: Vishnu Prasad of ERP Initiatives Group at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on applying SLIs, error budgets, IoT observability and digital twins to warehouses.
Body:
An empty bin that the system swears is full is a data consistency bug, and a forklift picker finds it the way an on-call engineer finds a stale cache. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, [Vishnu Prasad](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Vishnu_Prasad_supplychain_reliability_warehouses) of ERP Initiatives Group, a supply chain solution architect focused on warehouse management, made the case that warehouses deserve the same reliability discipline as cloud systems: service level indicators, error budgets, observability pipelines and automated remediation with a human in the loop.

This is a talk for people on either side of that wall. Platform engineers get a tour of how a modern warehouse actually runs; supply chain teams get SRE vocabulary applied to their world. There's no code, and the framework stays at the level of principles.

## The stack nobody puts on the reliability roadmap

Prasad describes the modern warehouse as layers of integrated systems: inventory management, transportation management, third-party logistics, procurement, sales, maintenance and production, all wired into the warehouse and the wider supply chain. Add robotic picking, automated storage and retrieval systems climbing high racks, AI route planning and demand forecasting, and you have a distributed system with physical consequences.

His complaint is that organisations give this far less attention than their cloud systems, and try to optimise it later. Traditional monitoring relies on someone walking the floor and judging how a machine, a component or a stock level is doing. At high volume there is too much data for that, and the subtle drifts that matter later get missed.

## Start with an SLI, then decide what you can tolerate

The SRE mapping is the most useful part. Pick the indicator first: picking accuracy, inventory accuracy, or how often a picker reaches a bin that is empty even though the system says otherwise. Then set an error budget, a tolerated variance the system knows about.

Then build automated remediation for the failure you just defined. In his empty-bin example, the bin gets blocked, an exception is raised, and an investigation workflow runs. Swap "bin" for "shard" and it's a runbook any SRE would recognise.

## Sensors, KPIs and the case for fixing it before it breaks

On observability, Prasad leans on IoT sensors for temperature, motion, weight and similar signals, monitoring equipment around the clock. The argument for predictive maintenance is logistics, not theory: when a machine breaks you need parts, the parts may not be in stock, and a site that runs 24/7 sits idle until they arrive. Train models on the sensor data and you fix things before they fail.

Alongside the machines, he tracks the flow: time from customer order to pick to the goods leaving the site, so bottlenecks show up as a measurable KPI.

## Rehearse demand spikes on a digital twin

For change, he recommends a digital twin of the warehouse: a copy where you simulate a demand surge, or a sudden drop caused by anything from a natural disaster to geopolitics, and watch how your processes and systems cope before the real thing arrives. Change itself follows familiar rules: version control so you can revert, unit, integration, acceptance, load and performance testing, and incremental rollouts with observation between phases, because downtime in a high-volume warehouse is expensive.

## Self-healing still needs a supervisor

His remediation loop runs detection, diagnosis, remediation and verification. The system can take some actions itself, but Prasad builds human judgement into the verification step, since throwing resources at a problem is not the same as solving it. When an automated suggestion fails, he wants a manual fail-safe workflow, root cause analysis that asks whether the model, the integration or training was at fault, validation after restoration, a gradual return to automated mode, and a post-incident review.

## Who should watch

Platform teams who support ERP and warehouse systems, and supply chain engineers who want a reliability vocabulary to argue for budget. If you want deep technical detail on any single piece, pair it with a more specialised talk.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: Your SOC will ask for AI agents. Ship the guardrails first
Description: Neal Iyer of Splunk at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on a guardrails-first framework for SOC AI agents, from org context and policy gates to shadow mode.
Body:
Neal Iyer, Director of Product Management at Splunk (a Cisco company), opened his Conf42 DevOps 2026 talk with a bet: your security operations colleagues will come to you, the DevOps person, asking for help building and deploying AI agents. His [Guardrails First framework](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Neal_Iyer_guardrails_ai_accountability) is what he wants you to have in your pocket when they do: four pillars and a six-phase rollout that keep a non-deterministic model away from your domain controllers.

Iyer is a product manager who says he talks to over 150 SOC teams a year, and the talk reads like it. It's a framework talk, not a product demo, and it applies whether you buy an AI SOC platform or build one in-house.

## Security pays you to be right every time

The tension is stated plainly. SOC teams already had alert fatigue, tool sprawl and a skills shortage; generative AI then made attacks faster, cheaper and easier to launch. Agents look like the only way to keep up. But security is a job where you are paid to be right every single time, and LLMs are variable and sometimes wrong.

His observation about the market is the useful part: the startups and the in-house prototypes all demo very similarly and very well. The hard part is earning enough trust to put one in production. Buy versus build, he argues, is not the fundamental decision.

## Context first: your SOPs are training data

The first pillar is organisational context. The same alert gets triaged differently in two companies, depending on their tools, how their data is laid out and their standard operating procedures. So the agent's curriculum should be your own case notes and the SOPs your lead analysts write.

Two practical warnings come with it. Writing for an agent exposes gaps in existing SOPs, including steps buried in corporate jargon an agent has no way to decode. And every increment needs a back-testing pipeline that runs the agent against alerts your team has already labelled by hand. If you have shipped ML before, that's just an eval set with a security badge.

## Scope the tools, gate the actions

The second pillar is policy constraints. Decide whether an agent enriches, updates tickets or takes response actions, and give it only the tools for that job. An enrichment agent that can't lock accounts can't lock out a domain controller and send the company dark when it reaches the wrong conclusion.

On top of scoping, Iyer wants policy-driven gating: the agent proposes, the proposal is evaluated against policy, and the gate decides whether it executes automatically, escalates to a human, or gets checked after the fact. DevOps engineers will recognise the shape. It's an admission controller for decisions.

## Audit everything, then earn autonomy

Trust comes from a full audit trail: the data the agent used, how it reasoned over it, every action and the final recommendation. He treats complete traceability as a must-have for anything you build or buy.

Autonomy then arrives in stages. Start in shadow mode, visible only to a few SOC leads who judge whether the reasoning holds up. Move to suggestions in the analysts' UI that nobody is obliged to accept. Then grant bounded autonomy for low-risk actions, and keep widening it with feedback. He doesn't see fully autonomous, high-impact actions as sensible with today's technology.

The six-phase blueprint follows the same logic: assess your documentation, pick a narrow low-risk scope (employee-reported phishing emails come up as a common first candidate), design guardrails, build, run in shadow mode, then expose suggestions and grow autonomy. Measure false positives removed, time to analyse, analyst productivity and the accuracy of both recommendations and reasoning.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers who will host, wire up or gate a SOC team's agents, and security leads deciding how much autonomy to grant. There's no code here, so if you want implementation detail, pair it with a hands-on agent security talk.

Title: When AI writes the code, provenance is the review you can trust
Description: Bhaskar Sawant at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on securing AI-era CI/CD with SBOMs, SLSA provenance, policy as code, hardened builds and pipeline monitoring.
Body:
Our pipelines now ship code that no single human fully wrote or reviewed end to end. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, [Bhaskar Sawant](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Bhaskar_Sawant_security_automation_pipelines), Lead Engineer at Cornerstone Building Brands and IEEE Senior Member, laid out a DevSecOps playbook built on that fact: shift security left into the developer workflow, shield production on the right with verifiable trust, and use SBOMs and provenance to prove that what you deploy is what you meant to build.

Sawant brings 15 years of CI/CD and enterprise delivery experience, and the talk is a structured blueprint rather than a demo. If you saw his supply chain talk at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, this one extends the same ideas to AI-assisted development.

## The old assumption was that humans wrote the code

For decades, he points out, software security assumed people wrote the code: you hired developers, trained them, reviewed their work and held them accountable. GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT broke that assumption. Generated snippets, automated dependency updates and machine-suggested configuration now flow through pipelines, often with less scrutiny than a junior engineer's first PR.

He names four AI-specific threats: prompt injection through crafted comments and docs, training data that teaches insecure patterns or leaked credentials, dependency confusion when an assistant suggests a package name an attacker has typosquatted, and obfuscated malicious code that slips past reviewers who trust the generator. He also quotes industry estimates (78% of organisations hit by a supply chain incident, around 40% of new enterprise code generated by AI) to size the blast radius. Treat those as context, not benchmarks.

## SBOMs say what's inside, provenance says where it came from

The foundation is two artefacts. A software bill of materials lists every dependency and build-time tool, generated automatically and checked against vulnerability databases, so policies can decide what is allowed in. Build provenance, using the SLSA framework, records who built an artifact, when and under what conditions, as signed attestations. His one-line summary is the most quotable part of the talk: SBOMs tell us what is inside; provenance tells us where it came from.

## Policy as code, builds as cattle

Once you can see, you enforce. Security requirements become versioned, testable code, tested in CI and enforced at commit, build, deploy and runtime. "Security becomes engineering, not the paperwork," as he puts it.

Then he turns to the build system itself, which he calls a high-value target: compromise it and you can inject code into every artifact you ship. The defences are layered. Each job gets a clean, ephemeral container with minimal privileges, destroyed and recreated per run. Credentials are scoped and time-limited. Build networks are segmented from production and limited to approved sources. Artifacts are signed with Cosign or Sigstore, and only verified artifacts move forward. Isolation limits the blast radius; signing gives you provenance you can verify.

## Watch the pipeline like production

The shield-right half is detection. Sawant maps checks to each stage: signature validation at commit, checksum and typosquat checks at dependency resolution, anomaly monitoring during the build, SBOM and provenance validation at publishing, and signature and policy enforcement at deploy. The indicators he lists are worth turning into alerts: unusual build durations, unexpected network traffic from runners, changes to build scripts, unsigned commits, mismatched checksums, missing SBOM data, artifacts without valid provenance.

He keeps developer speed in the frame throughout: scans in the IDE, security checks parallelised with functional tests, and feedback that tells a developer how to fix the problem. His targets include detecting issues in under two minutes and close to full artifact signature coverage.

## Who should watch

Platform and CI/CD owners whose repositories now take a steady stream of AI-generated code and bot-authored dependency bumps. If you already run SLSA level attestations and ephemeral runners, the threat list for AI assistants is the new part.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Your SBOM Stops at the model](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Emmy_Eide_sbom_models_supplychain) by Emmy Eide at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026.

Title: Zero trust in a 5G pipeline means every stage proves itself
Description: Vijayakumar Venganti of Cisco at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on embedding zero-trust checks into every CI/CD stage of 5G and cloud-native delivery.
Body:
If your pipeline deploys several times a day, a security review at the end is a speed bump nobody slows down for. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, [Vijayakumar Venganti](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Vijayakumar_Venganti_zerotrust_security_networks), Software Engineer at Cisco Systems, argued that the only check that keeps up with machine-speed delivery is one that runs at machine speed: zero-trust verification wired into every stage, from the commit to the network slice.

This is a compact framework talk, about a quarter of an hour, with no live demo. Its value is the map: what to verify at each layer, and why 5G makes the old perimeter model collapse faster than it does elsewhere.

## The perimeter dissolved before anyone noticed

Venganti's starting point is that perimeter security assumes threats stay outside, and cloud-native architecture removed the outside. 5G adds edge computing, network slicing and swarms of IoT devices on top, so the attack surface grows with each push. He cites survey figures for the shift (over 60% of organisations adopting zero trust, with plans pointing to 81%) and a private 5G penetration test in which industrial networks without zero trust were exposed to insider threats in under 30 minutes.

The failure modes he lists will be familiar to anyone who has audited an old CI setup: static rule-based access control that can't follow changing infrastructure, one-time authentication that leaves unverified windows, and lateral movement that nobody sees once an attacker is in.

## Verify at four levels, automatically

The core of the talk is a checklist for CI/CD, split by level:

- **Code**: sign every commit, run static analysis, scan dependencies.
- **Container**: scan images, verify provenance, apply runtime policy.
- **Infrastructure**: validate infrastructure as code, detect configuration drift, enforce immutability.
- **Network**: a service mesh with mutual TLS and microsegmentation.

None of that is exotic. The point he presses is that manual review won't work at this scale, so each check has to execute automatically and consistently. Remove static credentials, and have every step produce a cryptographic attestation, so the chain runs unbroken from developer to production. He calls it an immutable chain of custody, which is also a good test for your own pipeline: could you prove, for the artifact running right now, who built it and what checked it?

## A four-layer architecture for 5G

For the 5G side, Venganti proposes four layers. The access layer does continuous identity verification with MFA, mutual TLS, container attestation and behavioural monitoring. The transport and segmentation layer uses 5G slicing policies and zero-trust gateways to stop lateral movement. A policy intelligence layer learns baselines for users, services and infrastructure and adapts policy in real time when behaviour deviates. On top sits a control and orchestration layer: a central zero-trust controller with policy as code, immutable audit records for every run, and a feedback loop so risk insights update the security posture.

He also suggests using 5G slicing itself for pipeline isolation, and edge intelligence for low-latency detection. That is the most telecom-specific idea in the talk, and the one platform teams outside 5G can skip.

## The hard part is people

The talk is honest about cost: operational complexity, new attack surfaces from the AI components themselves, performance overhead, a skills gap and a cultural shift. His answer is training and phased adoption, and a closing line that zero trust is a continuous process rather than a destination. Anyone who has rolled out mTLS across a few hundred services will nod at "phased".

## Who should watch

Engineers building delivery pipelines for telecom or edge workloads, and anyone who needs a one-page mental model of where zero-trust controls belong in CI/CD. If you already run signed commits, SLSA provenance and a mesh with mTLS, treat it as a sanity check rather than new material.
