Title: Adaptive learning for students with disabilities needs DevSecOps first
Description: Raghav Sai Cheedalla of Meta at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on building AI learning pathways for special-needs students that stay private, fair and accessible.
Body:
More than 7.5 million US students receive services under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, and traditional instruction was never built to adapt to each of them. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Raghav Sai Cheedalla, Senior Software Engineer at Meta, showed how adaptive AI can personalise their learning, and argued that in education the pipeline around the model (security, privacy, accessibility and bias checks) matters as much as the model itself.

His core belief, stated at the start: AI in education has to be secure, transparent and equitable if it is going to change lives.

## Three ways a system adapts

Raghav describes three mechanisms for personalised learning. **Modality adaptation** works out whether a student learns best visually, by ear or another way. **Difficulty calibration** keeps tasks in the student's optimal zone so skills come faster. **Scaffolding intelligence** gives hints, examples and explanations at the right moment and fades them out as mastery grows, which he says reduces learned helplessness and builds confidence.

The outcomes he cites are large: skill acquisition up 41%, engagement up 35%, and reading challenges detected as early as seven months. With accessible design such as screen readers and speech-to-text, he reports close to a 50% increase in independent task completion.

## The threat model is a child's file

The security section is what earns this talk its slot at a DevSecOps event. AI in education carries particular risks: exposure of sensitive student data, model inversion attacks, biased outcomes, spoofing of assistive technology interfaces and insider threats. Those risks, he says, define the guardrails you have to build from day one.

His design rules: meet FERPA and GDPR, encrypt the data, use zero-trust security, and continuously monitor both access and model behaviour, so students never have to trade privacy for personalisation. For the data lifecycle: collect minimally, encrypt thoroughly, get consent, keep logs only for a set period, and let families revoke consent.

## Explainable, audited, and still the teacher's call

Trust, in his framing, needs interpretable models, audits, dashboards for teachers and clear explanations for families, so no decision feels like a black box. Bias in educational AI has real consequences, so he wants diverse training data, fairness metrics, routine audits and inclusive design, all built into the development lifecycle as a continuous responsibility rather than a checkbox.

He is clear that AI should not replace educators. Automating grading and content adaptation frees teachers for the emotional connection, context and individual support that only humans give.

## The pipeline that makes it real

The DevSecOps blueprint is concrete: infrastructure as code, automated security and accessibility testing, model signing and tamper detection, continuous monitoring and feedback-driven iteration. In the ML pipeline he adds secrets scanning, FERPA and GDPR checks, fairness tests for bias and drift, and model behaviour monitoring. Compliance checks for FERPA, GDPR, the ADA and WCAG run directly in CI/CD, so compliance becomes proactive instead of reactive.

One lesson stands out for anyone in a regulated sector: treat accessibility issues as severity one. For this audience, an inaccessible feature is a broken feature.

## Who should watch

Engineers building edtech, health or any product where users are vulnerable and regulated, plus accessibility advocates looking for language that lands with platform teams. The numbers come from the speaker's slides rather than a study he walks through, so treat them as his summary of the field.

Title: Banking AI ships at the speed of its data lineage
Description: Vinaya Nadig of Amazon at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on a unified data governance framework that makes AI in banking traceable from source data to decision.
Body:
Banks already run fleets of automated decision-makers, and the thing slowing new ones down is rarely the model; it's proving where the data came from. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Vinaya Nadig, Principal Engineer in Amazon's Last Mile Transportation organization, made the case for a unified AI data governance framework that bakes lineage, quality and access control into the model lifecycle.

Vinaya calls governance the least exciting word in AI, then spends the talk showing why it decides what reaches production.

## Machines decide in milliseconds, reviews take months

The setup starts with 2008: opaque algorithms on incomplete data, long before generative AI. Today AI approves loans, flags fraud and suggests investments in real time. Vinaya cites survey figures that most financial institutions call governance their main barrier to scaling AI, and puts the typical deployment delay from compliance review at six to nine months. The talk's best line sums up the gap: "AI moves at milliseconds, but our controls move at human speed."

The war stories carry it. When GDPR arrived, banks paused projects to trace how customer data flowed into ML pipelines; one European bank found 30 versions of the same data set across models, with no consistent consent tracking. After the LIBOR scandal, regulators asked for lineage in risk models and most banks couldn't produce it.

## Four pillars, one catalogue

Legacy governance tools came from the 1990s warehouse era: batch, monthly reports, Excel exports, blind to model lineage. The proposed framework embeds governance from feature engineering through deployment and monitoring, on four pillars:

- **Metadata management**, a central catalogue for every data asset and model.
- **Lineage tracking**, every transformation and dependency visible end to end.
- **Quality monitoring**, automated checks for drift, anomalies and bias.
- **Cloud-native oversight**, with targets of sub-200 ms query response while tracking thousands of model updates a day.

Security is the other half: role-based access for tens of thousands of users, a full audit trail for every access, integration with enterprise identity. Vinaya flags data-lineage hijacking, tampered upstream data silently corrupting models, as the AI version of the SolarWinds supply-chain lesson. The frameworks on the checklist are GDPR, CCPA, Basel III and BCBS 239, whose demand for accurate, complete and timely risk data is close to impossible without automated lineage.

Vinaya's analogy for the framework: less a gatekeeper, more an air traffic controller for thousands of models.

## A weeks-long trace became one query

The case study is a tier-one global bank, unnamed, that adopted the framework in 2025. Vinaya reported 30% faster AI deployment, 40% stronger audit readiness and full compliance across GDPR, Basel III and BCBS standards. The anecdote that sticks: a regulator asked to trace a fraud model back to its 2019 training data, a job that used to take weeks, and the answer came from one governance query in 0.3 seconds. We only have the speaker's account of the bank, but the shape of the win, lineage as a query instead of an investigation, is the point.

## Governance first, not governance later

The rollout is foundation (cloud-native with governance built in), integration (wire ML lifecycle tools into governance pipelines), automation (continuous bias, drift and compliance monitoring), then scale. Vinaya's comparison is Netflix building observability into its cloud migration from day one.

## Who should watch

Data platform and ML engineers in financial services, risk and compliance technologists, and anyone who has watched a finished model sit in review for a quarter. Engineers outside banking will still recognise the lineage problem; regulated industries just make it louder.

Title: Self-service BI works when security is neither too tight nor too loose
Description: Mallikarjun Bussa of Dropbox at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on letting everyone query data with AI-powered BI while least privilege, masking and lineage keep it safe.
Body:
Everyone wants answers from the data, and nobody wants to wait a week for a report. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Mallikarjun Bussa, Lead Business Intelligence Engineer at Dropbox, made the case that self-service BI and DevSecOps belong together: give people direct, AI-assisted access to data, and build the security in from the start so that access does not turn into a leak.

It is a short, plain-spoken talk from someone with 18 years in BI and data, aimed at the balance point rather than at any one tool.

## Too much data, too few answers

Mallikarjun's diagnosis is familiar to anyone who has owned a reporting backlog. Companies have more data than ever and still struggle to answer simple questions, because the data sits in too many systems and silos and every report takes too long. Self-service BI is his answer: marketing, HR, finance and operations open a dashboard and get the insight in minutes instead of filing a ticket and waiting.

The catch is obvious. Hand more people access and you widen the blast radius. That is where he brings in DevSecOps: build security into development, deployment and daily operations instead of patching it on at the end. His analogy: you put the seatbelt on before driving, not after.

## Why most BI projects fail

He cites studies saying 70% of BI projects fail, and the reasons he lists are about people and governance rather than technology: no governance, untrained users, access that is either too open or too restricted, and systems too complicated to use. The 30% that succeed balance security with easy access. Too tight and people route around it; too loose and you end up in an incident review.

## AI makes it easier, which raises the stakes

Natural language querying changes who can ask questions. Instead of SQL, users ask for this month's revenue or for the top reasons for churn, and the system finds patterns, predicts outcomes and guides them. He likens it to a small data analyst sitting on your shoulder. The more powerful the tool, he warns, the more the security matters.

His two examples keep it grounded. A marketing team using AI-powered BI saw campaign reporting drop from hours to minutes, cut costs and improved ROI while staying compliant with privacy law. An HR team used predictive analytics to spot employees likely to leave so it could offer help early, which only worked because the sensitive details were visible to HR alone and every access was audited.

## The controls are simple on purpose

The security baseline he recommends is deliberately unexciting: least-privilege access, masking sensitive data for people who should not see it, multi-factor authentication, and sessions that time out automatically. On top of that sits lineage, the story of where a number came from, what transformed it and who touched it, so that when a leader asks about a figure on a dashboard, you have an answer, and the auditors stay happy.

He closes on culture: leadership support, trained users, clear policies, continuous improvement. His roadmap is four steps (assess the current state, design the architecture with security and automation in mind, enable and train users, monitor and optimise), and he says it works for small teams and large enterprises alike.

## Who should watch

Data platform and analytics engineers rolling out self-service tooling or natural-language querying, and security teams asked to approve it. It is an overview, so treat it as a checklist for the conversation rather than an implementation guide.

Title: AI promises to end the speed-versus-security standoff in DevSecOps
Description: Venkatesh Kata of CGI at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on moving cloud security from manual gates to predictive, AI-driven and eventually autonomous protection.
Body:
Developers want to ship today; security wants to read the diff first. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Venkatesh Kata, Senior Middleware/DevOps Engineer at CGI, argued that AI resolves that old standoff by turning security from a final checkpoint into something predictive and continuous, built into every stage from design to operations.

It is a vision talk from someone with more than twelve years in DevOps and middleware automation: short on demos, long on where the field is going and what teams need to get there.

## The security velocity paradox

Venkatesh calls the core tension the security velocity paradox. Teams want fast releases; security teams want precision and deep analysis. The result is manual gates, slow scanners and security teams buried in thousands of alerts, while compliance delays stall whole releases. With threats evolving faster than ever, he says, you cannot give up either side.

His answer is to change the nature of the work. Instead of reacting to vulnerabilities, AI predicts them. Instead of waiting for reports, it analyses continuously. Instead of humans sifting false positives, it triages, prioritises and fixes common issues automatically. The abstract claims 40% fewer production vulnerabilities and 25% faster deployment cycles for this shift-left approach.

## From procedural automation to adaptive intelligence

He traces the history in four steps: security bolted on at the end, early shift-left that improved timing but stayed manual, tool sprawl that multiplied alerts without context, and now AI that adds prediction and reduces noise.

The technical core is a short tour of the models. Machine learning trained on large code corpora spots vulnerability patterns. Neural networks look at cloud configurations as a whole instead of resource by resource. Reinforcement learning improves decisions with each iteration. Graph neural networks get special attention: attackers do not compromise one resource, they chain misconfigurations to move laterally, and GNNs can find those multi-step attack paths at a scale humans cannot.

That leads to his most practical point: settings that each look fine on their own can be dangerous together, and AI analysis of those interactions is how many organisations find issues they had missed for years.

## Remediation in minutes, explained decisions

Traditional remediation runs scan, ticket, developer rework, review and retest, a loop that can take weeks. AI shortens it by fixing common vulnerabilities automatically while keeping controls in place. Predictive security reads behaviour patterns, commit histories, deployment trends and infrastructure changes to guess where the next vulnerability will appear, which he frames as moving from firefighting to foresight.

He insists AI decisions be explainable, naming adversarial training, differential privacy, federated learning and explainability frameworks such as LIME and SHAP.

## People and the road there

Two closing sections matter for anyone planning adoption. Security engineers need ML basics, ML engineers need security, and cross-functional teams become the default; AI is framed as augmentation, not a threat to jobs. The roadmap: assess maturity, start with high-value pilots, decide build versus buy, measure outcomes, scale what works. The endpoint he sketches is autonomous security operations, with AI agents investigating threats and generating policies while humans own strategy, ethics and the hard calls.

## Who should watch

Engineering leaders building a case for AI in their security programme and engineers curious where graph-based cloud analysis is heading. If you want code, a reference architecture or vendor comparisons, this one stays at strategy level.

Title: Blue/green on AWS with Lambda@Edge, cookies and a cache that cooperates
Description: Rayenn Hamrouni of Lenstra at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on cookie-based blue/green routing with Lambda@Edge, SSM and CloudFront caching.
Body:
Rollbacks that take ages are the tax you pay for release days you dread. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Rayenn Hamrouni, DevOps Engineer at the Paris cloud consultancy Lenstra, showed how his team built cookie-based blue/green deployments at the edge with Lambda@Edge, and then made it survive CloudFront caching. Since adopting it, he reports zero production incidents during releases and promotions or rollbacks in under a minute.

This is a field report from a client project, which makes it one of the more hands-on talks of the event.

## The starting point was ordinary

The architecture is textbook AWS: CloudFront serving a static front end from S3 and forwarding API calls to an Application Load Balancer in front of ECS on Fargate. It looked fine on a diagram, but production releases kept causing incidents, rollbacks were slow and painful, and deployments sometimes meant downtime.

Blue/green fixes that in principle: two identical environments, test the new release on green, switch traffic, flip back if it breaks. Rayenn is upfront about the costs too: you run two environments for a while, state and database schema changes need careful thought (his project had no database to manage, which helped), and routing gets more complex.

## Five ways to switch, one that fit

He walks through the AWS options before revealing the one they picked:

- **Route 53**, including weighted routing. Simple and works with any architecture, but DNS caching means the switch is never instant and you cannot route per request.
- **API Gateway**, flexible per header or cookie, but no help for a static S3 front end.
- **ALB weighted target groups**, fast to switch and roll back, again no S3 and less routing logic.
- **CodeDeploy**, a full blue/green workflow with health checks and automatic rollback, at a real setup cost.
- **Lambda@Edge**, functions that run in CloudFront edge locations and can rewrite the origin or S3 prefix before a request hits your backend.

They chose Lambda@Edge for per-user control and low latency.

## Cookies decide who sees which colour

Each colour gets its own ALB and ECS cluster, and the front ends live under different prefixes in the same bucket. A cookie, holding something hard to guess like the release commit hash, pins a user to a version so they do not bounce between releases mid-session. No cookie, or a full reload of the app, assigns the currently active release. A developer override cookie always wins, so QA can force a version in their browser.

The catch: changing the active version in the function code meant redeploying Lambda@Edge to every edge location, which is slow and unpredictable. Iteration two moved the active version to SSM Parameter Store and cached it in memory for a short time, so a switch is a parameter change, not a deploy.

## Make the cache work for you

The best part of the talk is the caching explanation. CloudFront has four hook points (viewer request, origin request, origin response, viewer response) and the cache sits between viewer and origin. If an object is cached, the origin hooks never run, so where you put your logic decides whether blue/green works at all.

Their final flow: at viewer request, a developer cookie injects a unique identifier to bypass the cache. On a miss, origin request routes to the right prefix using the cookie or the active release from SSM. Origin response sets the release cookie when the app loads. Every switch triggers a cache invalidation, so the next load reaches the origin hooks and gets assigned correctly. Getting caching right is half the design here.

He flags what the talk leaves out: coordinating colours across multiple backends and databases, progressive rollout to a subset of users, and CI/CD automation of promotion and rollback.

## Who should watch

Anyone running a CloudFront-fronted app on AWS who wants safer releases without adopting a full deployment platform. If your stack is all API Gateway or ALB, the comparison of options is still useful.

Title: Surgical robots need a data pipeline before they need a smarter arm
Description: Srinivasa SKN Ambati of Anthem at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on a five-layer analytics architecture that feeds clinical robots real-time patient data.
Body:
A surgical robot is only as good as the data reaching it, and hospital data lives in systems that rarely talk to each other. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Srinivasa SKN Ambati, Engineer Lead at Anthem, laid out an architecture that connects EHRs, IoT devices and robotic telemetry into one pipeline, so clinical robots and the clinicians beside them act on the same near-real-time picture.

The talk is a wide overview, from history to ethics, with a clear technical spine in the middle.

## From reactive care to closed loops

Srinivasa frames the shift as moving from treating illness to predicting and preventing it, powered by a mix of imaging, genomics, wearables, IoT and electronic health records. He sketches the robotics timeline too: PUMA 560 and later the da Vinci surgical system for minimally invasive surgery, robotic rehabilitation in the 2010s, AI-assisted robotics across surgery, pharmacy and hospital logistics by 2020. What comes next, he argues, is an integration era where robotic data feeds patient analytics and the loop closes.

Analytics follows the same arc: descriptive (what happened), predictive (what will happen), and now prescriptive (what to do next).

## Five layers between a sensor and a surgeon

The core of the talk is a five-layer framework:

1. **Acquisition** from robots, EHRs, IoT sensors and medical devices.
2. **Processing** that turns raw feeds into structured, usable records.
3. **AI and analytics**, where statistical and ML models produce insight.
4. **Integration** through APIs and middleware, so the pieces combine.
5. **Presentation**: dashboards, alerts and decision support at the point of care.

In motion, that is Apache Kafka streaming robotic telemetry and patient vitals, Apache Spark processing across a cluster, Hadoop HDFS storing structured and unstructured data, SAS Viya for modelling and forecasting, and HL7 and FHIR for talking to hospital EHR systems. Srinivasa calls the result the digital nervous system of modern healthcare, which is a fair description of a Kafka cluster nobody is allowed to restart.

## The model zoo has a job for everyone

The ML infrastructure runs on an automated lifecycle, a hybrid cloud that keeps sensitive PHI under tighter on-prem control while bursting to the cloud for scale, GPU clusters for imaging and containerized deployment. Models are monitored for drift, fairness and performance, with retraining triggered on drift. The algorithm map is tidy: CNNs for images, RNNs for patient time series, transformers for clinical text and reinforcement learning for robotic control.

Governance is non-negotiable here: HIPAA controls with role-based access, AES-256 encryption and audit logging, GDPR-style consent tracking, MFA, network segmentation and lineage. His one-liner: "trust is the ultimate currency".

## Before, during and after the incision

The clinical walkthrough covers preoperative 3D maps for planning, intraoperative tissue classification and postoperative models that flag complications early. The talk cites a 23% cut in operating times, roughly a third fewer complications, and predictive maintenance on robotic components at over 90% accuracy with downtime down nearly 40%; it doesn't name the studies behind them, so treat them as the speaker's figures.

Srinivasa is candid about the limits: inconsistent data quality, interoperability gaps, compute cost, clinician resistance, algorithmic bias and the need for real-world validation. His advice is to pilot small, adopt HL7 and FHIR, monitor for bias, set up ethics committees, and keep clinicians, engineers and patients in the same conversation.

## Who should watch

Data engineers moving into healthcare, architects designing PHI-heavy pipelines, and robotics teams who need to know what clinical data integration really involves. Expect breadth over depth; it's a map rather than a build guide.

Title: Stop running migrations as projects and build a migration platform
Description: Meenu Venkataarangam of Recode Solutions at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on automating discovery, transformation, orchestration and compliance in migrations.
Body:
The dependency nobody mapped is what usually sinks a migration. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Meenu Venkataarangam, Program Manager at Recode Solutions, showed how an automation framework built on DevSecOps principles turns enterprise migrations from risky one-off projects into a repeatable, compliant capability.

Meenu leads enterprise-scale migration programmes covering data platform modernisation and transformation pipelines, and the talk is a compact, structured overview: why manual migrations fail, the four automation components every framework needs, where security fits, and what comes next.

## Lift and shift was the easy era

Migrations used to be physical-to-virtual moves with minimal transformation. Today they span mainframes still carrying mission-critical workloads, AWS migrations with multi-account governance and containerisation, Hadoop estates being replatformed to cloud-native systems, and consolidation into Snowflake. Hybrid ecosystems, compliance constraints and cross-team alignment all come along. Her verdict on the manual approach: long timelines, coordination failures, security gaps and compliance trouble. It simply cannot keep up.

## Four components, one backbone

Meenu's framework has four building blocks:

- **Discovery tools** that automatically map applications, data flows, security policies and performance baselines. She calls unknown dependencies the biggest cause of migration setbacks, which is why discovery is where automation pays off first.
- **A data transformation engine** in four stages: parallel extraction with minimal load on the source, automated schema conversion and cleansing, real-time reconciliation to stop data drift, and optimised loading with rollback.
- **Workflow orchestration** that sequences dependencies, runs tasks in parallel, handles exceptions and shows progress live, removing the manual hand-offs that cause most delays.
- **Automated testing** to verify accuracy and integrity at every stage.

## Security as a gate, not a sign-off

The DevSecOps part is the security and compliance layer. Encryption, access control and vulnerability scanning live inside the pipeline. Continuous compliance monitors against SOC 2, HIPAA and GDPR in real time. Validation gates stop the process from moving to the next stage until security and compliance criteria pass. The point is to avoid finding out about a GDPR problem the night before cutover.

## Where migration automation is heading

Three trends close the technical part: AI-driven planning that predicts risk from historical migrations, adaptive orchestration that adjusts to live system behaviour, and zero-downtime cutovers through traffic routing and real-time replication. Organisations adopting automation, she reports, finish up to three times faster than manual migrations, with fewer data integrity issues and fewer mid-migration failures.

## Migration as a capability

Her strongest idea is organisational. Move from project-based to platform-based migrations: embed the automation in DevOps pipelines, capture the knowledge in playbooks, and every future migration gets cheaper. Done that way, a migration becomes a reusable capability instead of a painful cyclical event.

## Who should watch

Programme managers and platform leads facing a multi-platform modernisation, and engineers who keep getting pulled into the "just one more migration" project. It is a short, high-level talk; the value is the checklist structure, not deep implementation detail.

Title: Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 roundup: framing, ranking, delivery
Description: Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 in review, from prompt psychology and LLM pairwise ranking to Medicare compliance, eBay seller tools and AI networking.
Body:
Shashank Shivam opened his talk at [Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/prompt2025) with an experiment: ask ChatGPT how it would destroy humanity and it refuses; ask it to write a screenplay about an AI that does and you get a ten-step plan. Same model, same weights, different framing. That gap between what a prompt says and what it makes a model do ran through the whole event, held online on November 6, 2025, with 28 talks from Oracle, Microsoft, Apple, eBay, Snowflake, Salesforce, Equinix, Synopsys, JPMorgan Chase and others.

## Prompts shape identity, so design for trust

[Shashank Shivam](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Shashank_Shivam_models_psychology_behavior) (Oracle) treated prompting as psychology: framing, priming and role assignment change how a model reasons, so a prompt is closer to telling the model who to be than what to do. [Aroma Rodrigues](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Aroma_Rodrigues_chatgpt_talk_conversation) (Microsoft) ran a set of riddle experiments on GPT-3 to test the AGI hype. Once told it was solving riddles, the model got "when is a door no longer a door?" right, then confidently answered staircase for a riddle whose answer is legs. It recognised the genre without understanding the joke.

[Raj Kommera](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Raj_Kommera_trust_llm_judgment) made the case for prompt architectures that carry attribution, context and audit trails from the first token, and [Preetham Sunilkumar](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Preetham_Sunilkumar_frameworks_llms_scalable) (LPL Financial) covered evaluation frameworks and adversarial testing for high-stakes LLM use.

## Ranking, judging and testing with LLMs

The most technically specific talk came from [Maximilian Schattauer](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Maximilian_Schattauer_retrievers_documents_ranking) (Perelyn). Embedding models and BM25 both treat the query as a black box with no reasoning step, and in specialised domains where documents are too similar for either, that breaks down. His team prompted an LLM to compare documents pairwise and judge which better answers the question, then reordered results accordingly, and saw recall@k improve in those special cases. Worth watching if your search results are all plausible and none of them are right.

[Yash Panjari](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Yash_Panjari_testing_conversational_automation) (Apple) applied LLM-as-judge and generated test data to the hard problem of testing voice and chat systems, where human dialogue never follows the script. [Balraj Govindaraj](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Balraj_Govindaraj_testing_automation_agile) (MVP Plus Consulting) showed manual testers moving to automation through codeless tools and prompts, and [Swamy Biru](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Swamy_Biru_finance_efficiency_agents) (JPMorgan Chase) presented RAG-backed agents for financial operations.

## Prompts in the delivery and data pipeline

[Bandanawaz Mulla](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Bandanawaz_Mulla_healthcare_cloud_solutions) (Health Care Service Corporation) had a deadline-shaped story: a 2024 CMS mandate for Medicare Advantage supplemental benefit reporting meant consolidating 102 benefit types from more than ten systems for two million members. LLMs were used across the development lifecycle, including rapid prototyping of the ETL logic. [Janak Bhalla](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Janak_Bhalla_code_developers_scale) (Microsoft) covered LLM tooling for code migrations and fixing compile errors at scale.

On the data side, [Jimish Kadakia](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Jimish_Kadakia_data_cloud_access) (Snowflake) showed natural-language interfaces for querying data and triggering pipelines, [Siva Kumar Raju Bhupathiraju](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Siva_Kumar_Raju_Bhupathiraju_sql_infrastructure_hybrid) (Paycor) prepared SQL backends with Azure SQL Managed Instance for LLM workloads, [Annapurneswar Putrevu](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Annapurneswar_Putrevu_pipelines_learning_systems) (Bloom Energy) combined prompts with reinforcement learning for self-healing pipelines, and [Richa Solanki](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Richa_Solanki_data_lakehouse_enterprise) (Ally Bank) covered lakehouse architecture. [Bhavana Reddy Chadagonda](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Bhavana_Reddy_Chadagonda_science_testing_experimentation) argued that experimentation skills remain a data scientist's edge in AI-heavy roles.

## The infrastructure under the prompt

A cluster of talks went below the API. [Praneeth Patil](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Praneeth_Patil_agents_infrastructure_multicloud) (Equinix) looked at LLMs moving from writing infrastructure snippets to acting as multi-cloud agents, with hallucinations, misconfigurations and cost as the risks to design around. [Rahul Thakur](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Rahul_Thakur_infrastructure_resilience_scale) (Salesforce) sharded AI services across zones for resilience. [Rajesh Arsid](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Rajesh_Arsid_ethernet_performance_scaling) (Synopsys) explained how Ultra Ethernet and UALink affect inference throughput and latency across distributed systems, a reminder that prompt engineering at scale is also a networking problem. [Vamsi Gadireddy](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Vamsi_Gadireddy_network_protocols_reliability) (Microsoft Azure) covered AI in network engineering itself.

## Industry case studies

The remaining talks applied prompt engineering domain by domain: seller tools at eBay ([Sureshkumar Karuppuchamy](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Sureshkumar_Karuppuchamy_ecommerce_tools_ai)), insurance claims triage and underwriting ([Chetan Prakash Ratnawat](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Chetan_Prakash_Ratnawat_insurance_transformation_workflows), Capgemini), Power BI supply chain analytics at Kellogg's ([Victor Gabriel](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Victor_Gabriel_supplychain_savings_bi), GEP Worldwide), multi-agent ERP design ([Kasee Palaniappan](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Kasee_Palaniappan_enterprise_erp_intelligence), SAP Ariba), fleet telematics ([Preeti Sali](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Preeti_Sali_fleet_management_telematics), Ford), supply chain automation ([Kunal Dixit](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Kunal_Dixit_supplychain_automation_resilience), Zensar), Security Copilot for Conditional Access and Zero Trust ([Cynthia Akiotu](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Cynthia_Akiotu_security_defense_cyber)), agile delivery ([Hema Yalamancheli](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Hema_Yalamancheli_agile_delivery_prompt), Tyler Technologies) and enterprise migrations ([Meenu Venkataarangam](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Meenu_Venkataarangam_migrations_automation_innovation), Recode Solutions).

Thanks to [LLMday](https://llmday.com/) and the [Prompt Engineering Conference](https://promptengineering.rocks/), the gold sponsors, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) as newsletter partner, [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and the media partners. Every talk is on the [Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrC9ZgozU8V1FhRF147_HDjp) and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/prompt2025).

Title: Let the pipeline learn which tests matter
Description: Baradwaj Bandi Sudakara of Ascension Health at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on generative AI test creation, ML risk-based testing and anomaly alerts.
Body:
Deployments went continuous years ago; most QA and security reviews did not. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Baradwaj Bandi Sudakara, Senior Software Engineer at Ascension Health, argued that the gap closes when generative AI writes the tests and machine learning decides which ones to run, without replacing the CI/CD pipeline or security policies you already have.

## Static checks against a moving system

His framing: teams ship daily into distributed microservices with shifting attack surfaces, while test suites, security reviews and scripted automation stay static. Rigid tests and predefined rules cannot keep pace with systems that behave in fluid, unpredictable ways, so the distance between deployment speed and assurance keeps growing. The move he proposes is from reactive to predictive, manual to automated, gatekeeping to acceleration.

## Generative AI as the test author

The first lever is test and security script generation. Baradwaj describes what he sees GitHub Copilot doing day to day: reading user stories, understanding code context, generating complete test suites and security validation scripts, and even adding stories to Jira through plugins. The value he stresses is coverage of scenarios humans tend to skip, rather than raw speed.

The test data case study is the more interesting one. Realistic, interconnected test data for microservices is notoriously painful to build. AI reads the schemas, studies production data patterns, synthesises realistic datasets and generates boundary and edge-case values. Data preparation time drops sharply while coverage across service boundaries goes up.

## Machine learning as the test scheduler

The second lever is predictive quality engineering. Models trained on production logs, historical defects, code changes and system behaviour predict which modules are risky and which areas are likely to break. That feeds a risk-based testing pyramid: critical paths and high-risk modules first, then recently changed code and integration boundaries, with stable low-risk areas last. You run less and catch more, and the pipeline gets smarter with each release.

The same idea powers his anomaly detection example. ML learns what normal looks like across services and flags performance drift, suspicious access patterns, latency spikes and unusual memory use. In his setup an anomaly fires a Slack alert, and if it is bad enough, a phone call. If your on-call rotation already ignores half its alerts, this is the part to watch carefully.

He also covers AI-assisted static analysis, runtime behaviour monitoring and dependency intelligence that ranks patches by exploitability and impact.

## Adopt it in phases, not in one weekend

Baradwaj is emphatic that this is no overhaul. His four phases: assess and pilot (start with AI test generation and vulnerability scanning), integrate and train (connect tools to CI/CD, train models on historical logs and incidents), scale and optimise (more services, feedback loops), and finally autonomous operation where AI makes real-time calls like test prioritisation. Security policies and the CI/CD pipeline stay as they are; AI goes where manual effort and risk are highest.

His takeaways: start with one pilot, fix data quality, build cross-functional teams, feed production incidents back into the models, and position AI as an enabler rather than a replacement.

## Who should watch

QA leads and SDETs drowning in flaky suites, and DevSecOps engineers looking for a phased argument to take to their managers. It is a strategy talk with a few concrete cases rather than a tooling walkthrough, so bring your own stack.

## Related talks

- [Machine Learning in the DevSecOps Pipeline](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Srikanth_Potla_pipeline_security_devsecops) by Srikanth Potla, on predictive security for cloud-native apps.

Title: Small changes in phrasing, massive shifts in results
Description: Design the prompt
Body:
# So yes, prompts are infrastructure now

There was a brief moment when prompt engineering felt like a party trick.

You typed a clever sentence, the model did something impressive, everyone nodded, and we moved on. That moment is very much over.

Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 is about what happens when prompts stop being experiments and start running real systems.

This conference brings together twenty four talks across seven tracks, covering prompting, data, infrastructure, testing, finance, culture, and commerce. The focus is not on clever phrasing, but on building prompt-driven systems that are secure, scalable, and actually useful.

Security shows up early and often. From prompt injection and zero trust enforcement to using prompts as part of cyber defense workflows, several sessions explore what it means to protect systems where words can trigger actions. When prompts touch infrastructure, governance stops being optional.

Enterprise use cases take center stage. Insurance workflows, healthcare compliance, supply chain automation, ERP systems, finance platforms, and e-commerce tooling all appear, powered by prompt-driven AI. These talks are about scale, regulation, and measurable impact, not demos that only work once.

Agents are everywhere. Multi-agent systems, autonomous workflows, RAG pipelines, and prompt-driven orchestration show how LLMs are moving beyond responses and into coordinated action. Alongside that comes a lot of discussion about trust, transparency, and keeping humans in the loop when systems start making decisions.

Testing and evaluation round things out. LLM-as-judge, automated QA, prompt psychology, and performance optimization all show up, because once prompts become part of production systems, “it feels right” is no longer a valid test strategy.

If prompt engineering is part of your job now, whether you planned it or not, this one’s for you. Prompts aren’t just instructions anymore. They’re becoming the interface between humans, machines, and the systems we rely on.

Title: The wall itself can be part of the IoT network
Description: Rahul Pingale of Wallquest at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on PVC-free non-woven wall surfaces that carry RFID, sensors and robot navigation markers.
Body:
Here's a talk you won't find at many software conferences: wallcoverings as infrastructure. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Rahul Pingale, Technical Director at Wallquest, showed how a PVC-free non-woven surface can carry RFID antennas, sensors and machine-readable markers, so the wall stops being decoration and starts being part of a building's IoT and robotics stack.

It's a materials engineering talk, and a vendor one: the platform is Wallquest's. The reasoning is still worth an engineer's time, because it starts from a problem software people rarely think about.

## Vinyl walls get in the way of the network

Rahul's opening complaint is about traditional vinyl wallcoverings in smart buildings. They emit VOCs, they can block wireless signals, and they're hard to remove when sensors or automation hardware need upgrading. The physical layer, quite literally, holds back the digital one.

## Three material tricks make the surface useful

The platform rests on three pieces of engineering:

- **Water-based nano-barrier coatings** that replace solvent-based vinyl coatings for moisture protection. Rahul says the barrier is validated to ASTM E96 for moisture vapour transmission, with zero solvent and so no VOC emissions from it.
- **Microsphere pressure-sensitive adhesive.** Instead of a solid glue layer, tiny contact points give strong hold but allow clean removal. Sensors, panels or displays can be repositioned without repairing the wall. Anyone who has peeled a cable clip off fresh paint will appreciate the idea.
- **Multi-method printability.** The substrate works with gravure, flexo and UV digital printing, so RFID antennas, QR codes and conductive inks can be printed straight onto the surface.

## A navigation map printed on the corridor

The robotics angle is the most interesting part. Rahul lists three things such walls give connected spaces: wireless transparency, so signal strength holds for robots and sensors; embedded sensors such as temperature or occupancy detectors; and machine-readable markers, QR codes and NFC chips, that help autonomous systems navigate. In his framing the surface becomes a navigation map, a data network and compliant infrastructure at once, with asset tracking and damage-free updates as a bonus.

His summary line: "material engineering is infrastructure engineering" for connected spaces.

## Standards do the persuading

Because these walls go into hospitals and schools, compliance carries much of the talk. Rahul cites CDPH emissions testing for low VOC, ASTM E84 Class A fire safety, REACH and WELL building alignment, freedom from heavy metals, and simulated five-year durability across climates. He reports adoption in more than 15 facilities across North America and Europe, spanning hospitals, schools and smart offices.

The rollout advice will sound familiar to anyone who has shipped software: align material capability with the automation needs, bring facilities, IT and sustainability teams in early, pilot small, then scale on the data.

## Who should watch

Facilities and smart-building engineers, robotics teams working on indoor navigation and fiducial markers, and anyone who designs IoT deployments and has never asked what the wall is made of. If you only want code, skip it; if you like learning how the physical layer gets built, it is a refreshing watch.

- [Youhana Hana: Build your Smart Robot with AWS IoT](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Youhana_Hana_build_smart_robot_aws) is the software half of a connected robot.

Title: Your ML pipeline needs a security gate before the model exists
Description: Rajkumar Sukumar of AT&T at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on an AI-native DevSecOps framework, from trusted data ingestion to bias tests and audit trails.
Body:
A handful of manipulated images slipped into a training set can sink a multimillion-dollar model, and a standard CI/CD pipeline will wave it straight through. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Rajkumar Sukumar, Lead Data/AI Engineering at AT&T Services, laid out a layered DevSecOps framework for machine learning that starts checking at data ingestion, long before anyone trains anything.

## Fast AI deployments ship their own failure modes

Rajkumar opens with a retail story: a visual quality inspection model works fine at launch, then product defects climb for weeks. The cause turns out to be a small amount of deliberately poisoned training data, and nobody noticed because the pipeline had no controls aimed at the model itself.

His second example is a 2023 loan approval system pulled within weeks because it kept rejecting applicants from one group. Nothing was broken in the code. The model had simply been trained on too narrow a set of people. Data poisoning, adversarial attacks, prompt injection, privacy leaks and ethical risk all arrive bundled with the speed of modern AI rollout, he argues, and classic DevOps has no gate for any of them.

## Six layers, starting with the data

The framework has six parts: secure data ingestion, privacy-preserving training, automated security testing, protected inference endpoints, ethical governance gates and continuous monitoring.

Ingestion is where trust starts. That means cryptographic verification of data sources, real-time anomaly detection, automatic PII detection and redaction, audit logs and data lineage. His lineage anecdote is the most relatable moment in the talk: an enterprise traced a model failure back to a single corrupted CSV file whose origin nobody could name.

For training on sensitive data he walks through three techniques: differential privacy (add noise so the model cannot memorise individuals), federated learning (the data stays at the source and only model updates travel, like learning from ten hospitals without moving patient records) and homomorphic encryption (banks collaborating on fraud detection without sharing raw customer data).

## Test the model like you test the code

The ML-specific CI stage adds adversarial testing that generates hostile inputs, static analysis, model hardening, input validation and dependency scanning of the ML frameworks. At inference time, he puts a web application firewall in front of the endpoint to filter bots, injection attempts and malformed requests, and to defend against model extraction.

## Ethics as a pipeline gate

The part that separates this from a generic security talk is governance by design. Rajkumar adds a pre-training ethical review, bias testing across demographic groups rather than in one isolated slice, and human-in-the-loop approval until the model is stable. One recent deployment he cites performed about 20% worse for a minority group; neither the data scientists nor the business knew why until they checked how little training data that group had.

To make governance scale he suggests policy as code with version-controlled rules and automated compliance checks on every ML pipeline, plus immutable audit trails (he mentions blockchain) so lineage is tamper-proof and regulator-ready evidence exists before anyone asks for it. A healthcare company that adopted the approach, he reports, saw zero security incidents, faster deployments and clean HIPAA and SOC audits.

His one-line takeaway: security and ethics cannot be bolted on to AI systems, they have to be built in.

## Who should watch

Platform and MLOps engineers who own the path from data lake to endpoint, security teams asked to sign off on a model they cannot read, and anyone who still treats the training set as somebody else's problem. It is a framework talk, so expect checklists rather than code.

## Related talks

- [DevSecOps for AI: Introducing MLSecOps for Software 2.0](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Eugene_Neelou_ai_introducing_mlsecops_for_software_20) by Eugene Neelou, an earlier take on the same problem.
- [A Beginner's Guide to Adversarial Machine Learning](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Anmol_Agarwal_beginners_guide_adversarial) by Anmol Agarwal, for the attacks the testing stage should simulate.

Title: Snowflake turned weeks of CSAT triage into an overnight job
Description: Rajanikant Vellaturi of Snowflake at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on starting AI customer experience small: classify survey feedback inside the workflow you have.
Body:
Thousands of free-text survey answers a week, three people reading them by hand, and the insight arriving after it stopped mattering. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Rajanikant Vellaturi, Senior Support Communications Manager at Snowflake, showed how his team plugged an AI classifier into its existing feedback pipeline and turned weeks of manual tagging into a job that finishes overnight.

The talk is broad, covering personalisation, AI agents and predictive support across retail, finance, healthcare, telecom, SaaS and manufacturing, but the Snowflake case study is the part with real engineering in it.

## The CSAT problem, in the speaker's words

When a support ticket closes, Snowflake sends a survey with an open text box. Customers use it for anything: feature complaints, service quality, a thank-you to the engineer who fixed their issue. That is thousands of responses every week, and a team of three was reading each one, tagging sentiment as positive, negative or neutral, and mapping it to an issue type such as product feature, service quality or technical issue.

It did not scale. Rajanikant describes the work as repetitive data entry that burned the team out, and by the time a bucket of feedback reached the team that owned the problem, it was stale.

## Plug the model in, don't rebuild the house

The fix is deliberately boring. Survey responses already landed in a Snowflake table. The team added an AI classification step that reads that table, assigns sentiment and issue type at scale, and writes the results to another table. The job is scheduled for Sunday night, so on Monday morning the teams find last week's feedback sorted and ready to act on.

Results, as he reports them: processing time dropped from weeks to hours, CSAT and response times improved, and the people who used to tag rows now spend that time on cross-functional fixes and closing the loop with customers. The lesson he keeps repeating is that nothing was built from scratch. The workflow stayed; one manual step became a model call.

## Agents, prediction and the creepy line

Beyond the case study, Rajanikant contrasts script-based chatbots that answer "what are your store hours" with agents that keep context, notice frustration and hand off to a human with the full history, so the customer never starts over. His airline example: miss a flight, and the app's agent rebooks you and you just click accept.

On prediction, he lists telecom companies spotting signal drops before customers notice, SaaS products spotting unused features and sending tailored tutorials, IoT sensors scheduling maintenance before machines fail, and payment systems issuing refunds before anyone complains.

He is candid about the challenges: data scattered across CRM, transaction systems and warehouses, bias from narrow training data, and over-personalisation that unsettles customers. His answers are data integration and governance first, fairness testing across segments, telling customers you use AI with an opt-out, and a human in the loop for critical decisions.

## Five practices worth copying

His closing list: data first; integrate AI into existing workflows; keep a human in the loop; measure continuously (before and after CSAT, resolution times, retention); be transparent with customers. Start small, he says, find where people do the most manual work, and put the model there.

## Who should watch

Support and CX leads who are being asked for an AI strategy and want a first project that will actually ship, and data engineers who own the tables those projects will read. If you want architecture diagrams or model choices, this is not that talk; it is a practitioner's playbook.

## Related talks

- Dmitry Kindrya asks whether LLMs [rescue customer support or ring its death knell](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Dmitry_Kindrya_customer_support_revolutionizing), the sceptic's take on the same question.
- [Reliable API Support: Human-in-the-Loop Agentic RAG for SRE](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Vishal_Shah_reliable_support_human) by Vishal Shah, for the human handoff done in an engineering context.

Title: AI can clear the forensic backlog, but it can't testify for you
Description: Cybersecurity analyst Victor Agboola at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on where AI speeds up digital forensics and why investigators stay in charge.
Body:
Digital evidence now arrives faster than humans can read it. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, cybersecurity analyst Victor Agboola walked through how machine learning, deep learning and NLP shrink forensic backlogs from weeks to days, and why the human investigator still has to sign off on every conclusion that ends up in front of a court.

It is a survey talk rather than a tool demo: a map of where AI fits in the forensic workflow, a handful of real-world use cases, and a frank list of the ways it can go wrong.

## The problem is volume, not cleverness

Evidence used to mean a laptop. Victor's list now includes phones, cloud accounts, vehicles and IoT devices, and he describes investigators facing three to four week backlogs because every seized gadget has to be examined. The job AI does first is unglamorous: automate the repetitive work, surface the patterns humans miss and push the high-value items to the top of the pile.

He splits the techniques by data type. Machine learning spots anomalies in system behaviour and network traffic, clusters artefacts into campaigns and classifies malware families. Deep learning handles images and video. NLP pulls names, places and transaction details out of emails and chats, and summarises long message threads.

## Triage is where the days come back

The most concrete example is device triage. Agencies routinely receive piles of phones, laptops, tablets and USB drives at once. An AI triage system scans each device as it is ingested, flags deleted messages, suspicious media, unusual communication patterns and encrypted containers, and produces a structured preview so investigators can decide which devices need a full examination. In some agencies, Victor says, that shift cut turnaround from three to four weeks to a few days.

Two other cases stand out. For child sexual abuse material, deep learning classifiers do the first screening pass, which he puts at accuracy rates as high as 95%, so humans only see content already triaged as relevant and carry less of the trauma. For fraud cases spread across SMS, WhatsApp, email and social media, NLP maps who talks to whom and flags sudden shifts in sentiment or the repeated phrasing scammers tend to use.

He also mentions deep-learning file carving that rebuilds fragmented files where pattern matching fails, and tools such as Cellebrite Pathfinder and Magnet's copilot.

## A black box is a gift to the defence

The second half is the part worth the watch. Victor lists six risks: biased training data that over-prioritises one population, privacy and warrant constraints on massive personal datasets, explainability in court, hallucination, governance, and the irreplaceable human expert.

The courtroom point is the sharp one. Courts want workflows that are transparent, reproducible and auditable, and if an investigator cannot explain how a model reached an output, the defence will challenge it. His fix is procedural: validate every AI finding against the raw data, re-test models when they are retrained, alert on low confidence scores, and write down who may run which AI process and how its output is read. A hallucinated lead in a forensic report has a name and an address attached to it.

## Where it is heading

The closing section covers LLM copilots that summarise artefacts and draft preliminary reports, automated evidence capture across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, IoT and vehicle forensics, models that detect anti-forensic tricks like wiping and timestamp tampering, and AI-generated training for a workforce that cannot hire fast enough. His summary is that the best results come from machine efficiency combined with human expertise.

## Who should watch

Security engineers who end up handing evidence to legal or law enforcement, DFIR newcomers who want a map of the field, and anyone building AI features whose output may one day be cross-examined. If you already run AI triage in a forensics lab, the use cases will be familiar, but the governance checklist is still worth stealing.

Title: Testing conversational AI with LLM judges and generated utterances
Description: Yash Panjari of Apple at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on QA for voice and chat assistants with LLM-as-judge, generated test data and CI/CD gating.
Body:
Users will ask an assistant to set an alarm in more ways than any test plan lists. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Yash Panjari, Senior Software Development Engineer at Apple, who has spent a decade on voice assistants such as Alexa and Siri, presented an end-to-end QA framework for conversational AI: LLMs that judge responses, LLMs that generate test data, and both wired into CI/CD.

## Why enumerated test cases fail here

Traditional QA assumes you can list the inputs. Conversational AI breaks that: set an alarm for seven, wake me up at seven sharp and get me up before sunrise are the same intent. Manual review is expensive, inconsistent and slower than the pace of model updates, so the gap between how smart the bots are and how they are tested keeps growing.

## The judge, calibrated

Yash describes LLM-as-judge as an automated senior QA engineer that scores semantic accuracy, contextual relevance, safety and compliance, and user experience (tone, helpfulness, naturalness). His example: a bot replies that a package arrives next week, and the judge checks that against context showing it was due tomorrow.

The four components are what make it trustworthy rather than a vibe check:

- **Standardised prompts:** structured rubrics, for example rating a response on accuracy, tone and user satisfaction.
- **Calibration datasets:** aligning judge scores with human expert ratings.
- **Statistical validation:** checking correlation with human reviewers.
- **Multi-judge consensus:** several models (he names GPT-4, Claude and Gemini) score the same dialogue independently, and only agreement counts.

He adds bias-aware validation across demographics and scenarios, transparent rubrics for audit, and periodic human calibration. His phrase for it is reliability insurance.

## Generated test data, with a schema

The other half is generative QA. Instead of authoring cases by hand, models produce paraphrases, multilingual variants, adversarial inputs and noisy utterances. His examples are good fun: asking whether you need a jacket or an umbrella in Paris as paraphrases of a weather query; booking the cheapest non-cheap flight; sarcasm about airlines never being delayed; real-world typos and speech errors.

To keep that from becoming chaos, generation is schema-driven: each schema defines intents, entities, languages, tone and difficulty, so you can regenerate consistent sets for regression across releases. The same models produce expected intents and entities as labels, with multi-model consensus, and low-confidence cases go to a human. That closes the loop from generation to evaluation.

## Gates in the pipeline

In CI/CD, a commit triggers fresh test generation, the judge scores responses, regression detection flags quality drops, and deployment gating lets only validated builds reach production. The benefits he lists are less manual effort, faster releases, wider long-tail coverage and continuous monitoring.

His practical advice is the part to keep: start with high-impact user journeys, define quantitative KPIs such as accuracy and safety scores, keep humans in the loop for emerging topics, version-control prompts and schemas like production code, and update judge models as LLMs improve.

## Who should watch

Teams shipping chat or voice assistants who still rely on hand-written test cases, and anyone setting up LLM-as-judge who wants a checklist for calibrating it. The talk describes the framework rather than Apple internals or specific numbers, so expect a design, not a case study.

Title: Rerank documents by asking an LLM which of two is better
Description: Maximilian Schattauer of Perelyn at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on pairwise LLM document ranking for specialised corpora where embeddings fall short.
Body:
When every document in your corpus looks alike to an embedding model, cosine similarity stops being an answer. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Maximilian Schattauer, Technical Consultant for Data and AI at Perelyn in Munich, showed how his team improved retrieval for a client by using an LLM as a pairwise judge: show it two documents and a query, ask which answers better, and build the ranking from the votes.

It is a short, focused talk based on one client project, and Maximilian is upfront that the evidence is anecdotal. The method is simple enough to try on your own data.

## Where conventional retrievers break

A classic retriever takes a query and returns documents ranked by semantic relatedness (embeddings) or keyword overlap (BM25). The results might feed an LLM, but Maximilian's case is the one where they do not: they go straight to a user or a downstream data application, so ranking quality is the product.

His list of limits: the retriever always considers the whole query, so you cannot tell it to focus on one aspect; it is a black box you cannot steer; and there is no reasoning in the ordering. In specialised domains where documents are too similar for embeddings or keywords to tell apart, you need something that can reason about small differences. The client project hit exactly that, and the retrieval metrics showed it.

## Retrieve first, then let the LLM reorder

The pipeline keeps a classic retriever for a preliminary candidate set, then uses an LLM to refine the set and its order. The second stage adds a text input you can control: focus on certain aspects of the query, inject metadata, or add rules that a non-LLM retriever cannot capture. You can use a regular model or a reasoning model at this step.

## The LLM as a binary operator

The core idea is how the LLM is used. Rather than pasting all candidates into one prompt and asking for a ranking, Maximilian's team put two documents and the query into each prompt, described the domain, and asked for a single verdict: A or B. Running that over every pair yields a comparison matrix, and counting wins gives an order.

Two refinements matter. Running each comparison several times at non-zero temperature gives statistics to ground the ordering instead of a single coin flip. And pairwise comparison avoids the needle-in-a-haystack problem of one big prompt, where documents get lost when the candidate list is long. In their project, the pairwise setup was quantitatively better than one-shot LLM ranking, and the abstract reports gains in recall@k over traditional retrievers in these specialised scenarios.

## The bill

He does not hide the cost. The number of LLM calls grows with the square of the number of candidates, so this is far slower and more expensive than an embedding lookup, a keyword search or even a single LLM reranking call. Keep the preliminary set small, and save the method for domains where ranking errors are costly. Quadratic is fine for twenty documents and a budget meeting for two thousand.

## Who should watch

Engineers building search or RAG over narrow, look-alike corpora (legal, technical standards, internal policy) who have hit the ceiling of embedding similarity. If your retriever already does well on general web-like text, a cross-encoder reranker is probably the cheaper next step; this talk is for when that is not enough.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Zain Hasan on chatbots with advanced retrieval-augmented generation techniques](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Zain_Hasan_chatbots_retrievalaugmented_building) at Conf42 LLMs 2024.

Title: Multicore avionics fail certification on timing, not features
Description: Charles Antony Raj of Collins Aerospace at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on certifying multicore flight software under DO-178C and CAST-32A for electric aircraft.
Body:
Two cores sharing an L2 cache can make a flight control task late in ways no single-core analysis predicts, and that is what slows multicore avionics programs down. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Charles Antony Raj, Senior Manager for Systems and Software Engineering at Collins Aerospace, explained how electric aircraft teams get multicore processors through DO-178C certification without losing determinism.

Charles brings about two decades in aerospace, and the talk reads like a certification plan you could hand to a new program lead.

## Why electric aircraft want more cores

The case for multicore is threefold: computing power for sensor fusion, flight management and onboard AI in real time; integration of several avionics functions onto fewer boxes, which cuts weight and wiring; and power efficiency, leaving more energy for propulsion. On an electric aircraft every kilogram and watt has a job.

## Shared hardware is the real adversary

The catch is that cores share caches, memory buses and IO. Charles lists the interference channels: shared L2 or L3 cache evictions, simultaneous memory access creating wait states, contention on IO controllers and DMA, and latency across the interconnect fabric. Each one makes worst-case execution time, WCET, much harder to bound. His first pitfall follows directly: never assume single-core WCET numbers carry over.

## DO-178C says what, CAST-32A says how

DO-178C remains the foundation: design assurance levels A to E, verification, configuration management, traceability. CAST-32A adds the multicore-specific objectives around interference mitigation, timing analysis and resource usage. Charles also notes that EASA's AMC 20-193 supersedes CAST-32A for applicants in its jurisdiction, and the FAA's AC 20-193 from 2024 aligns with it.

The objectives boil down to: plan and characterize the hardware early, budget and partition resources, demonstrate WCET bounds under interference, handle multicore-specific faults, and deliver a multicore accomplishment summary to the authority.

## Partition in space and in time

The engineering answer is partitioning. Spatial partitioning gives each function its own memory region. Temporal partitioning time-slices execution so every critical task gets guaranteed CPU access. Careful core and cache allocation cuts interference between partitions, and stress testing proves the boundaries hold.

For robotic control the rules get specific: put sensor fusion from IMUs, cameras and lidar on dedicated cores, keep path planning and other heavy autonomy away from low-level control loops, and run safety monitors and watchdogs on separate cores or partitions. As Charles puts it, "Even microsecond delays can affect stability."

The tooling list is concrete too: a partitioning RTOS such as Green Hills INTEGRITY-178 tuMP, timing tools from vendors like Rapita and LDRA, structured test harnesses, and ETM or PTM hardware tracing.

## Somebody already got to DAL A

The case study is CMC Electronics' PU-3000, which Charles describes as one of the first platforms to reach civil multicore certification to DO-178C DAL A, running INTEGRITY-178 tuMP and producing evidence against CAST-32A objectives. The lesson he draws: it's achievable, provided you pick the platform early, start interference characterization in parallel with development, bring in hardware-in-the-loop testing early and talk to the certification authority from the start.

## Who should watch

Avionics and safety-critical embedded engineers, anyone building drones or autonomous vehicles on multicore SoCs, and managers who need to explain to their own management why the timing analysis takes so long. If you have never met a DAL, it's a dense but readable first tour.

Title: Manual testers already write prompts; codeless tools make them run
Description: Balraj Govindaraj of MVP Plus Consulting at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on a four-phase plan to move manual testers to codeless, prompt-driven automation.
Body:
A good bug report is already a prompt. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Balraj Govindaraj, QA architect and IT Specialist Expert at MVP Plus Consulting, argued that manual testers can become automation contributors through codeless platforms and natural-language prompts, and laid out a four-phase framework for getting a QA team there without throwing away its domain knowledge.

## The widening gap

Balraj starts with the job market. Postings ask for automation skills, and script-based tools such as Selenium and Cypress remain out of reach for many testers who do not code. The people with the deepest product knowledge get sidelined just as AI-driven development and fast CI/CD raise the bar for feedback speed and coverage.

He names three traditional barriers: coding prerequisites (Java, Python, JavaScript), complex frameworks that shift focus from what to test to how to code the test, and the maintenance tax of scripts that break with every UI change.

## Plain language as the test spec

The bridge, in his telling, is prompt engineering. Testers have spent years writing test cases and bug reports in precise natural language, and codeless platforms with AI features can now execute that kind of text. His examples are close to what a tester would write anyway: navigate to checkout and confirm the total matches the cart; find the submit button in the login form even if its ID or class changes between releases; confirm an error message appears when the email format is invalid and that it includes helpful guidance.

The locator example is the quiet win. Self-healing locators described in words cut the maintenance burden that sinks so many Selenium suites, because the test describes intent instead of a CSS path.

## Four phases

Balraj's framework:

1. **Platform evaluation.** Choose tools with native prompt-driven test generation, visual workflow builders that mirror how testers think, integrations with Jira, CI/CD and test management, self-healing, and team features such as version control and shared libraries. Avoid tools that merely hide code or need heavy scripting for advanced cases.
2. **Knowledge transfer.** Present visual workflows as an extension of manual test cases, teach prompt basics with simple examples first, give testers a sandbox environment, and celebrate early wins publicly.
3. **Standardisation.** Build prompt libraries for common flows (login, form validation, data checks), test templates for regression, smoke and integration suites, and quality guidelines for naming and review.
4. **Scaling.** Run the tests in CI/CD on commits and pull requests, expand from critical journeys to edge cases, and track execution time, pass rates, maintenance effort and time to feedback.

## The examples

He illustrates each phase with team stories. A financial services QA team generated 120 login and dashboard tests from plain English prompts in a week. A government QA team converted 50 manual UI flows into visual workflows. One team kept a central prompt library in Confluence covering 12 microservices, so one improved prompt updated every linked test. On an insurance modernisation project, suites ran from GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps pipelines on every commit, and within three sprints 80% of regression checks ran automatically. Another team started with a handful of critical flows (registration, payments, reports) and used prompt-based generation to reach more than 45 edge scenarios.

## The objections, answered

Will AI replace testers? Balraj says no: it supports judgment but cannot replicate the critical thinking and context experienced testers bring. Are codeless tools strong enough? He points to API testing, database validation and conditional logic. Vendor lock-in? Pick platforms with export and open integrations. His summary is that encoding tester knowledge into reusable prompts turns tribal wisdom into documentation that survives turnover.

## Who should watch

QA leads with strong manual testers and a mandate to automate, and engineering managers deciding whether to retrain or replace. Test automation engineers who live in code will find the tooling advice generic, but the change-management plan is worth borrowing.

Title: LLM-assisted ETL for a Medicare benefits mandate, 102 benefit types
Description: Bandanawaz Mulla of Health Care Service Corporation at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on using prompts to build CMS supplemental benefit reporting on AWS.
Body:
Regulators set deadlines, not data models. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Bandanawaz Mulla, Senior Manager of Platform Strategy at Health Care Service Corporation, described how his team used LLMs across the development lifecycle to meet a CMS mandate on Medicare Advantage supplemental benefits: 102 benefit types, more than ten source systems and over two million members.

The interesting part is where prompts were used. This is AI-assisted engineering of a compliance pipeline, not an AI product facing members.

## The mandate and the mess

The CMS requirement, due in December 2024, asked Medicare organisations to reach members who are entitled to supplemental benefits but have not used them, and tell them what is available and for how long. Doing that means knowing, per member, which of the benefits apply and what has been used.

The data problem Bandanawaz lays out: 102 supplemental benefits, each with its own structure; more than ten vendor source systems, some overlapping in what they cover; and two million plus members across medical and pharmacy (PDP) plans. Before anyone writes outreach, someone has to integrate and standardise all of it.

## Where the prompts went

The abstract lists the uses most clearly, and the talk follows it:

- Prototyping ETL logic for complex healthcare data transformations.
- Generating SQL for the dimensional model of a health event data mart.
- Creating test scenarios for edge cases in benefit utilisation patterns.
- Translating HIPAA and federal regulatory language into technical specifications, and generating audit logging frameworks.

The stack underneath is plain AWS: EC2 and Lambda for processing, S3 as the data lake for raw and processed data, and RDS for structured benefit and member data.

## Results, as reported

Bandanawaz reports 100% on-time federal reporting and a 40% reduction in development time from the prompt engineering approach. The longer-term payoff he describes is a single source of truth for benefits data, which removed redundant processing and now feeds member communication triggers for unused benefits and reusable components for future mandates.

## Lessons for regulated shops

His takeaways are the reason to watch if you work under HIPAA or similar rules:

- Prompts that combine domain knowledge with precise technical specifications produced more usable code than generic requests.
- AI-generated code needed repeated refinement to meet security and HIPAA standards; the first output was a draft, never the deliverable.
- LLMs helped bridge clinical, technical and business stakeholders by translating between their vocabularies.
- Put regulation and precise legal and clinical terminology into the prompt, demand audit trails, validate output against frameworks such as NIST and ISO, and refine prompts with clinical and legal experts.

He also maps AI help onto phases: discovery (analysing existing systems for integration points and hidden dependencies), design (generating architecture options), implementation (prototyping ETL pipelines), testing (edge-case scenarios) and documentation (technical and compliance reports).

Fair warning: the delivery leans on superlatives, and the talk stays at the strategy level, without showing a prompt or a schema. Read the abstract alongside it for the concrete list.

## Who should watch

Data engineering leads and architects in healthcare payers, or any regulated organisation facing a reporting mandate on a tight deadline, who want to know where LLM assistance helped and where humans still had to check every line.
