Title: Conf42 JavaScript 2025 - give the main thread a break, give the AI the docs
Description: Conf42 JavaScript 2025 in review, 25 talks on scheduler.yield(), testing pain, accessible JS, web games, docs-as-context for AI and privacy in the browser.
Body:
[Conf42 JavaScript 2025](https://www.conf42.com/js2025) streamed on October 30, 2025 with 25 talks, and the programme split neatly in two. Half was about the browser itself: a main thread that needs to breathe, tests that still hurt, forms that still lock people out. The other half was about JavaScript as the glue around AI, from docs wired into the IDE to NLP running client-side. Speakers came from PagerDuty, Cloudinary, Playtech, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, Nike, ADP, UBS and the game studio Hology.

## The main thread is a shared resource

[Aleksandr Tkachenko](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Aleksandr_Tkachenko_let_browser_take) (Playtech) gave the most immediately useful talk of the day on `scheduler.yield()`, part of the new Prioritized Task Scheduling API. You call it inside a long task and the browser gets to handle the clicks and keystrokes that piled up, then resumes your code where it left off, which helps Interaction to Next Paint. He is upfront that the API is experimental and not in every browser yet, and spends time on the imperfect alternatives you can use in the meantime. Think of it as a polite `await` for the main thread.

[Deepika Annam](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Deepika_Annam_revolutionizing_performance_intelligent) (Nike) covered optimisation techniques across Node.js backends and React frontends, and [Lakshmi Bhargavi Mullapudi](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Lakshmi_Bhargavi_Mullapudi_real_time_engineering) (Techstar Group) looked at the architectures behind real-time systems for fraud detection and personalisation.

## Testing still hurts, and the survey says where

[Daniel Afonso](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Daniel_Afonso_state_testing_tech) (PagerDuty) built his state of JavaScript testing around the State of JS survey. Mocking came out as the number one pain point, ahead of configuration, performance, the ESM versus CommonJS mess, excessive complexity and flakiness, and satisfaction with testing sat at 2.5 out of 4. From there he traced a decade of change in test runners, testing libraries, mocking and production practices, and where AI-based tools fit. Come for the history, stay for the honest scorecard.

## Accessibility is a JavaScript problem with JavaScript fixes

Two talks argued that accessible front ends are mostly a matter of knowing the rules. [Gian Wild](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Gian_Wild_accessible_easier_than) (AccessibilityOz) gave concrete code examples, the three types of JavaScript functionality, and ten principles for accessible JavaScript and forms, starting from the fact that around twenty percent of people have a disability. [Anisat Ahmed](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Anisat_Ahmed_introduction_aria_guide) delivered a good first talk on ARIA, cutting a confusing set of attributes down to how to use them well.

## Docs are the context your AI is missing

[Sharon Yelenik](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Sharon_Yelenik_ai_docs_accuracy) (Cloudinary) worked on turning Cloudinary's APIs into MCP servers and came away convinced that the thing holding AI back in the IDE is the context it gets as much as its accuracy. Her talk shows what happens when documentation is connected directly to the LLM client in the editor, with examples across Cloudinary, Auth0 and Firebase. It is one of the more grounded takes on agentic coding from the docs side of the house.

Agents showed up elsewhere too. [Jyoti Kunal Shah](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Jyoti_Kunal_Shah_agentic_autonomous_micro) (ADP) proposed an agentic framework that co-evolves React micro-frontends with the microservices behind them, [Ajitha Buvanachandran](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Ajitha_Buvanachandran_agentic_search_multi) built multi-agent search that decomposes queries, and [Linga Annela](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Linga_Annela_micro_frontends_fast) used Module Federation micro frontends to ship AI features without touching the monolith. [Ujjwala Modepalli](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Ujjwala_Modepalli_client_side_nlp) (Wells Fargo) kept the text analytics in the browser with Natural.js and TensorFlow.js, no backend required.

## Securing the stack from npm to the VM

[Srinivasa Rao Gunda](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Srinivasa_Rao_Gunda_securing_framework_frontend) (UBS) laid out a vulnerability management framework for full-stack JavaScript, from npm dependencies to DOM-based attacks. [Vivekananda Chittireddy](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Vivekananda_Chittireddy_privacy_design_building) (Meta) brought privacy by design to JavaScript data systems with differential privacy, anonymisation and encryption. [Annie Tsai and Adam Ringhede](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Annie_Tsai_Adam_Ringhede_level_why_typescript) (Hology) made the case for TypeScript and JavaScript as game development languages. Title: Tuning Oracle and SQL Server on AWS and Azure, layer by layer
Description: Adithya Sirimalla of Enliven Technologies at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on a practical framework for Oracle and SQL Server performance and cost in the cloud.
Body:
Moving Oracle or SQL Server to the cloud doesn't retire the DBA playbook; it adds a second set of tools on top. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Adithya Sirimalla, Software Developer and DBA at Enliven Technologies, walked through a framework that pairs classic database tuning with what AWS and Azure provide, framed for automation workloads where every millisecond of latency feeds a real-time decision.

Fair warning on scope: this is a brisk survey, more checklist than demo. As a checklist it's a good one.

## The fundamentals still come first

Before any cloud console, Adithya starts with the tools DBAs already trust: SQL Plan Management and AWR analysis on Oracle, Query Store on SQL Server. They keep plans stable, show where the bottlenecks are and track performance over time. The cloud tools sit on top of that history, they don't replace it.

## Pin the plan before it regresses

Plan stability gets its own slide, and rightly so. Capturing and enforcing known-good plans with SQL Plan Management in Oracle and Query Store plan forcing in SQL Server prevents the classic regression where a statistics refresh picks a worse plan on a busy Tuesday. Pinning the plan is the database equivalent of a lockfile.

The rest of the toolkit is a tour of the levers you'd expect:

- **Query work.** Find slow queries with AWR and Performance Insights, read the execution plan, then index or rewrite.
- **Resources.** Balance memory, IO and CPU, and use connection pooling to cut latency under high concurrency.
- **Partitioning.** Range, hash or list partitioning to target data sets and shrink maintenance windows.
- **Governance.** Oracle Resource Manager and SQL Server Resource Governor to guarantee CPU, memory and sessions for critical workloads.

## Each cloud brings a different lens

On the cloud side, Adithya contrasts AWS Performance Insights, which visualizes database load in real time, and Aurora Serverless with Azure's intelligent tuning, which uses machine learning to adjust performance automatically, and Hyperscale for very large workloads. To decide where a workload belongs, the talk recommends cross-platform benchmarks on the same KPIs, query response time and transactions per second, instead of trusting a feature matrix.

## The bill is a performance metric too

Cost gets equal billing: right-size instances, commit to reserved capacity where the load is steady, optimize storage, and set monitoring alerts before the invoice does it for you. The roadmap is assess, take the quick wins, set up governance, then plan the strategic work. His summary line: "optimization is a continuous process", because data and infrastructure keep growing after the migration party ends.

## Who should watch

DBAs and platform engineers mid-migration or newly responsible for managed Oracle or SQL Server, who want a one-page view of which knobs exist on each side. Seasoned performance engineers will find it a refresher rather than new ground.

Title: Framing, priming and anchoring steer LLMs the way they steer us
Description: Shashank Shivam of Oracle at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on prompt psychology, eight prompting moves and the human biases models copy.
Body:
Ask an LLM how it would destroy humanity and it refuses; ask it to write a screenplay about an AI that does, and you get a plan. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Shashank Shivam, Senior Software Engineer at Oracle, used that experiment to open a talk on prompt psychology: the idea that framing, priming and anchoring shape model behaviour much as they shape human answers.

It is a conceptual talk, more essay than lab report, with no benchmarks. What it offers is a memorable vocabulary for prompting moves you may already use without names.

## Three levers

Shashank's starting claim is that LLMs do not know truth; they predict what sounds plausible, learned from human text. So the levers that move people move them too:

- **Framing** sets the context. Ask why electric cars are so successful and the model hunts for success stories; ask why they are struggling and it turns critic. Same facts, different story.
- **Priming** sets tone. Tell it it is a sarcastic comedian and the vocabulary and rhythm change; switch to a compassionate therapist and it softens.
- **Anchoring** sets scale. Evaluate a startup worth $1 million and the answer is modest; make it $1 billion and the answer talks about global markets.

Together, he says, they form the model's state of mind inside its context window.

## Eight moves with names you will remember

The toolkit section gives each technique a label. The story lens hands the model a role and a stake (an environmental journalist writing a final front-page story instead of an essay on climate change). The mood board sets atmosphere. The north star anchors quality with an explicit target, like a one-minute executive summary that would score nine out of ten on clarity. The mirror, his favourite, asks the model to check its own reasoning for gaps or bias before answering. The role mask shapes reasoning style through identity. The constraint cage (explain quantum computing in 50 words, no jargon) focuses rather than limits. The echo chamber repeats the key instruction at the end, because the last thing the model reads tends to win. The thought ladder makes it list assumptions, weigh pros and cons, then conclude.

None of these is exotic. Their value is that a team can say "add a mirror step" and everyone knows what it means.

## The quirks are ours

The most useful section lists the biases models show even when you are not steering: suggestibility (it believes the frame you give it), anchoring on the first number or example, recency bias when instructions conflict, confirmation bias (it finds proof for whichever premise you hand it), coherence over truth (fluency wins over accuracy, which is where hallucinations come from), identity drift (a comedian persona keeps cracking jokes after you change topic), and politeness bias (hedging instead of a clear no).

His explanation is that none of this comes from code; it comes from the human text the models learned from. That is also a practical warning. If you test a prompt only with friendly phrasings, you are testing your own framing as much as the model.

## Who should watch

Prompt writers who want a shared language for techniques, and anyone designing evals who needs a reminder of how question wording biases results. If you want measured effects or ablations, this talk will not give them; its closing on cognitive design and thinking with models is closer to philosophy than engineering.

- [Sachin Gupta on prompt drift and keeping prompts stable](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2026_Sachin_Gupta_drift_prompts_stable), for what happens when small wording changes bite in production.

Title: Written in moments of optimism and caffeine
Description: Still shipping the modern web
Body:
# JavaScript is still running the internet

JavaScript has been “overused” for at least a decade now.

And yet, here it is. Powering browsers, servers, APIs, data pipelines, AI workflows, accessibility tooling, and entire businesses that would quietly fall apart without it. Funny how that works.

Conf42 JavaScript 2025 is a snapshot of what JavaScript looks like today. Big. Mature. Everywhere.

This conference brings together twenty talks across five tracks, covering foundations, integrations, intelligence, security, and systems. From core browser APIs and performance tuning to JavaScript running serious workloads in healthcare, finance, and enterprise platforms, the focus is firmly on real-world use.

AI is woven throughout the program. Generative AI for claims and fraud, agentic search, client-side NLP, AI-assisted documentation, and micro frontends designed to integrate intelligence directly into web apps all make an appearance. These sessions focus less on demos and more on how JavaScript fits into AI systems that actually ship.

Accessibility and performance get proper attention too. Talks cover ARIA, inclusive JavaScript patterns, testing practices, browser scheduling, and keeping applications responsive as they grow more complex. Because fast and accessible still matters, even when everything else is getting smarter.

Security is not an afterthought. Rate limiting, API security, vulnerability management, privacy by design, zero trust architectures, and protecting both frontend and Node.js systems show up across the schedule. JavaScript may be flexible, but production systems still need guardrails.

If JavaScript is part of your stack, your job, or your long-running love-hate relationship, this one’s for you. The language keeps evolving, and somehow, it keeps ending up right in the middle of everything.

Title: UALink scales GPUs up, Ultra Ethernet scales them out
Description: Rajesh Arsid of Synopsys at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 with a short primer on UALink and Ultra Ethernet, the interconnects behind fast token exchange.
Body:
Every clever prompt ends up as tokens moving between GPUs, and the wires decide how fast. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Rajesh Arsid, ASIC Physical Design Principal Engineer at Synopsys, gave a compact primer on the two open interconnect standards aimed at AI clusters: UALink for scaling accelerators up inside a pod, and Ultra Ethernet for scaling clusters out.

Set expectations before you click: this is a brief talk, a few slides long, and it is about hardware. Prompt engineering appears in the title and the framing, not in the content. As a two-term vocabulary lesson for software people who keep hearing these names, it does the job quickly.

## Compute grew faster than the plumbing

Rajesh opens with the bottleneck. Compute demand is growing exponentially, and despite parallelisation, training times have stretched from weeks to months. His slide shows model parameter counts doubling every three to four months. The strain lands on every dimension at once: network bandwidth and latency, memory bandwidth and capacity, and compute. He points to the memory and interconnect standards (DDR, HBM, PCIe and others) racing to keep up.

He ties this back to the ML lifecycle: prepare data, build, train, test, fine-tune, repeat. Through that loop, data is split and fed to many GPUs, often across many machines, so GPU-to-GPU performance shapes the whole timeline.

## Scale up: make many GPUs look like one

UALink is an open interconnect for scaling up accelerators. Picture a pod of racks, each with GPUs, wired together so they behave like one giant GPU. The goal is memory sharing and synchronisation between accelerators, with direct load, store and atomic operations across them. Rajesh says UALink can connect from hundreds up to thousands of GPUs.

For inference, this is the layer that matters when one model is split across several accelerators: the faster they share memory, the faster tokens pass between them.

## Scale out: connect the pods

Ultra Ethernet, developed by the Ultra Ethernet Consortium, is the open, high-performance networking answer for AI and HPC at the next level up: linking clusters to each other. Rajesh describes it as high bandwidth, multipath, open and highly configurable, with a new transport layer that brings better congestion control and stronger RDMA. The scale he cites is millions of GPUs.

The split is the takeaway. UALink is the inside-the-pod fabric, Ultra Ethernet is the between-pods network, and both are open standards rather than a single vendor's fabric.

## Why a prompt engineer might care

Rajesh's conclusion links both to token-to-token performance. UALink's memory synchronisation suits the rapid token passing inside a sharded model; Ultra Ethernet's low latency and high throughput handle token exchange at cluster scale. If you own inference latency budgets, the interconnect is one more term in the equation, and it helps to know which layer a vendor is talking about.

## Who should watch

Software and platform engineers who want a quick orientation on AI cluster networking before a capacity planning meeting or a hardware vendor pitch. If you design interconnects for a living, it is too short to teach you anything new; if you came for prompt techniques, look elsewhere in the event.

Title: Users act on AI answers they can check, so prompt for that
Description: Raj Kommera at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on trust-building prompts with confidence tags, source attribution, clarifying questions and audit trails.
Body:
An accurate model that nobody acts on is a very expensive autocomplete. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Raj Kommera, a Salesforce engineer and platform architect, argued that the enterprise AI adoption gap is about trust, and that trust is designed at the prompt layer: confidence tags, source attribution, clarifying questions and audit metadata built into every response.

## The trust gap

Raj's framing: LLMs already sit inside chatbots, copilots and decision tools, but if users cannot see how or why a model reached its answer, they will not act on it. You end up with systems that are technically capable and quietly unused. The challenge is human confidence, not model capability.

## Five principles for trustworthy prompts

The core of the talk is a short list:

1. **Confidence tagging:** have the model label outputs, for example as ready to act on, needs review, or needs an expert.
2. **Source attribution:** make the model cite the documents or reasoning behind each claim.
3. **Adaptive clarification:** let the model ask for more information when the request is ambiguous.
4. **Progressive disclosure:** high-level insight first, details on request.
5. **Audit trail integration:** embed metadata so every decision can be traced later.

His example of confidence tagging: rather than a raw number, the model reports a defect rate as moderate in confidence and recommends inspecting part of the batch. The user knows both how sure the system is and what to do next.

He adds context scaffolding: inject domain vocabulary (what counts as a qualified lead or a material risk), regulatory rules such as GDPR or SOC requirements, and thresholds for when to escalate or send to a human. Generic models do not know your organisation's words, and that mismatch is a common reason trust breaks.

## Same model, different prompts, different adoption

Raj walks through three cases. In a lead qualification assistant, sales reps ignored AI lead scores. The scores were fine; the explanation was missing. After redesigning prompts to include confidence tags, citations and visible reasoning, he reports 71% more follow-up actions and a 34% improvement in conversions, with no change to the model.

In a legal summarisation pipeline, teams refused summaries they could not trace to a clause. Section-level attribution and flags for clauses that deviate from standard templates cut review time sharply, and he reports user confidence rising to near 90%.

The third is a decision-support bot asked whether to approve a vendor contract. The old version answered at once. The new one first asked whether the vendor was new or a renewal and what the contract value was, then checked spend thresholds and compliance before recommending. Asking first turned out to be the trustworthy move, which anyone who has worked with a good senior colleague already knew.

## Making it scale

The techniques underneath are schema-driven outputs (JSON the system can validate automatically), chain-of-thought prompting so reasoning is visible, and conditional instructions for edge cases such as missing data. Feedback loops capture user corrections in the chat or orchestration layer, so prompts can be refined and failure modes found. His roadmap: audit current prompts for ambiguity, redesign for transparency, test with real users, and keep iterating.

## Who should watch

Product engineers and architects shipping LLM features to business users who are polite about the AI and then ignore it. If your team argues about model choice while adoption stalls, this talk points at the cheaper lever.

Title: One JavaScript feature pipeline from Kafka to in-browser inference
Description: Apple data engineer Venkata Chandra Sekhar Sastry Chilkuri showed at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 how Node.js, Redis and TensorFlow.js serve fresh ML features.
Body:
Personalisation that updates overnight feels broken to users who expect the page to react to what they just did. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Venkata Chandra Sekhar Sastry Chilkuri, Senior Data Engineer at Apple, showed how to build the whole feature pipeline in JavaScript: Node.js consumers on Kafka compute features, Redis serves them, WebSockets push them, and TensorFlow.js runs the model in the browser.

## Three hard problems

He frames real-time feature pipelines around three problems: computing features fast at scale, caching them so they stay fresh without hurting performance, and keeping the logic identical across Node.js servers, edge workers and browsers. Miss one and you get stale experiences, jittery latency, or training-serving skew, where the model in production sees features computed differently from the ones it trained on.

His argument for JavaScript is that one language runs in all three places. Async/await and non-blocking I/O suit event-driven workloads, and the ecosystem covers every stage, from Kafka clients to TensorFlow.js.

## The four building blocks

1. **Feature computation in Node.js**: microservices consume user events from Kafka, compute rolling counts and session stats, and publish features downstream. Transforms are kept idempotent and windowed so retries and back pressure don't corrupt results.
2. **Redis as the feature store**: computed features are cached with configurable TTLs for sub-millisecond reads during online inference.
3. **WebSockets**: push updates instead of polling.
4. **Edge or browser inference**: the app uses cached features with TensorFlow.js or ONNX.js to run models locally, skipping the server round trip.

Caching is layered by access pattern: browser memory for hot features on the current page, Redis for shared online reads, and an edge cache for global reach. TTLs plus pub/sub or WebSocket refreshes keep features fresh just in time. He also mentioned OpenAI's Atlas browser as a sign of how far local AI in the browser has come.

## Isomorphic feature code kills training-serving skew

The most useful section is about consistency. Ship isomorphic modules for feature logic so the same code computes a feature in Node.js and in the browser. Test both with the same fixtures. Lock schemas with TypeScript types or JSON Schema. Monitor feature distributions so drift shows up before model quality drops. It's the JavaScript version of the feature-store promise, without needing a separate platform team.

## Measure before you scale

Metrics he tracks: p50, p95 and p99 latency for computation, retrieval and inference; features per second; cache hit ratio; WebSocket delivery success; and skew between training and serving. Those numbers drive window sizes, TTLs, model size and fan-out strategy, and tell you whether to scale up for peak hours or down to save money.

Use cases: recommendations that update with every interaction, personalised UI with predictive prefetching and adaptive notification timing, and live analytics aggregated client-side and streamed over WebSockets.

His rollout order is sensible: ship offline features with a cache first, add real-time computation with Kafka, then client-side inference with small models, and scale based on observed metrics, not assumptions. Decouple compute from serving, design fallbacks and graceful TTLs for failures, and version features like APIs so you can roll back.

## Who should watch

Full-stack JavaScript developers working with data teams on personalisation, and ML engineers whose features keep drifting between offline training and online serving. It's an architecture walk-through with small code examples, not a production case study.

Title: A prompt constitution: decompose, guard early, version everything
Description: Preetham Sunilkumar of LPL Financial at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on a prompt constitution framework with modular chains, guardrails and red teaming.
Body:
Change one word in a prompt and an LLM can hand you a different answer, or a dangerous one. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Preetham Sunilkumar, Vice President and Software Development Manager at LPL Financial, presented what he calls a prompt constitution: a framework that treats prompts as modular, versioned software with safety built in from the first step.

## Three walls you hit in production

Preetham calls the starting problem the prompting paradox: the same model that looks like a magician pulling a rabbit from a hat can turn chaotic with a small change in wording. Traditional systems are deterministic business logic; LLMs are not. He groups the failures into three walls:

- **Safety:** prompt injection, jailbreaking and biased outputs.
- **Consistency:** two phrasings of the same question (his example: the best way to learn Python versus how a beginner should start with Python) get different, even contradictory answers.
- **Complexity:** prompts stacked on prompts, nested conditions and role play in one block, impossible to reuse or debug. His image is building a skyscraper with sticky notes.

## Pillar one: split the monolithic prompt

The structural integrity pillar breaks one do-everything prompt into a chain of specialists. His example is a customer review. The monolithic version asks the model to read the review, give the sentiment and topics, and write a reply, all at once. It works for a handful of reviews, then accuracy and bias drift as volume grows.

The fix is a router plus three specialists: one for sentiment, one for key topics and concerns, one that drafts the reply from the other two outputs, with evaluation at each stage. The bonus is reuse. Next project needs sentiment analysis? Specialist A is already built.

## Pillar two: guard the input, not just the output

The safety net pillar moves from filtering outputs to guarding before the core model ever sees the request. His banking bot example takes a message that combines a valid billing complaint with a request to hack someone else's account. A pre-processing guardian (another LLM or agent) splits it, passes the billing issue through and declines the rest with a safe response. The harmful part is neutralised before the response generator runs.

## Pillar three: prompts are code

The scalable assembly pillar is the one most teams skip. Keep a catalogue of prompts separate from the engine that runs them, version every change, test at unit and integration level, A/B test versions, and make rollback a one-line change. If a new model version behaves worse than the old one, swap back the same way you would roll back a build.

## Constitution, critique, revision, reinforcement

The framework runs in four steps: define the constitution from organisational values, regulation (FINRA in finance, health rules in healthcare), ethical principles and behaviour guidelines; self-critique each stage's output against it; revise; and feed results back as reinforcement.

The evaluation section is practical. Define the objective first (factual accuracy, reasoning, bias, robustness to adversarial input, multi-turn behaviour, refusals), then generate and label synthetic data for that objective rather than reusing 10 or 15 favourite questions. Red teaming covers threat modelling, adversarial generation, stress testing, vulnerability analysis and hardening. He also points to the EU AI Act's requirements on risk management, data governance, documentation, transparency, human oversight and accuracy, and closes on human in the loop as the feedback mechanism that holds it together.

## Who should watch

Teams moving LLM features from prototype to a regulated production system, especially in finance or healthcare. Platform engineers building prompt registries will find a useful checklist. If you already run versioned prompts with eval suites and input guards, this confirms your design more than it extends it.

- [Josh Armitage on red teaming AWS](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Josh_Armitage_red_teaming_aws_practice_preach), the security tradition Preetham borrows from.

Title: Microservices, edge and serverless from a JavaScript architect's view
Description: Ford Credit tech lead Surya Prabha Busi surveyed microservices, edge, multi-cloud, serverless and zero trust for JS teams at Conf42 JavaScript 2025.
Body:
JavaScript started as the language of the browser and now runs a good share of the cloud. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Surya Prabha Busi, Technical Lead at Ford Credit with more than 18 years of building cloud-native applications, gave a tour of the architecture choices JavaScript teams now face: microservices, edge computing, multi-cloud, serverless, a look at quantum computing, and the zero trust security that has to wrap all of it.

This is a survey talk. It covers a lot of ground quickly, with industry figures on each slide, and works best as a briefing for someone stepping into architecture decisions.

## From monolith to services, and the hard part in between

She starts with the familiar story. A monolith ships frontend, backend and business logic as one unit, which is simple until the app grows and every update becomes risky. Microservices split that into independent services with their own logic, easier to deploy, update and scale where traffic actually is.

She cited adoption rising from 45% in 2019 to 91% in 2024, a 76% reduction in deployment time and around 50% operational cost savings from smaller, containerised services. The challenge she highlighted is the one every team hits: drawing the service boundaries. Decomposing business logic into services takes real domain knowledge, and she put the share of teams struggling with it at 67%.

## Edge computing belongs in the first design

Edge computing moves computation closer to where data is produced, which matters most where data is time-sensitive, such as healthcare and manufacturing. Her figures: 45% faster processing, 42% better real-time data handling, a 33% efficiency boost in healthcare and 56% faster emergency response in manufacturing. Her practical point is that edge has to be planned from the start of an application's design, not retrofitted.

## Multi-cloud: flexibility you pay for in governance

On multi-cloud she was candid about the trade-off. Early adopters ran into integration problems, and choosing between public, private and hybrid cloud is a real decision: public is cheaper because you share it, private costs more but is yours alone, hybrid mixes both. With structured governance she cited up to 41% reduction in governance overhead and 32% cost optimisation. Success, in her framing, depends on orchestrating public, private and edge resources based on how critical the data is.

## Serverless, quantum, and zero trust

Serverless cuts development cycles (she cited 33%) by removing infrastructure work, with automatic scaling and pay-per-execution pricing. Quantum computing got an honest label: still research, with quantum-inspired algorithms starting to show up in JavaScript libraries, worth knowing about rather than planning around.

Security closes the talk. More services and more clouds mean more surface, so she recommends zero trust: least privilege, access granted on need, and continuous authentication and authorisation for every service integration.

## Who should watch

Developers moving into a lead or architect role who want one session that names the main architectural options and their trade-offs. Experienced platform engineers will know the material; the figures are useful conversation starters, but the talk doesn't break down where each one comes from, so check sources before putting them in a business case.

Title: Build compliance into the data model, not the audit week
Description: Sneha Nallapu of J.B. Hunt at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on compliance-by-design with event sourcing, bitemporal data, graph lineage, CQRS and ABAC.
Body:
Most compliance work arrives after the system is built, as a late patch with a deadline attached. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Sneha Nallapu, Senior Software Engineer at J.B. Hunt Transport Services, argued for the opposite: pick architecture patterns that make a system auditable by construction, so regulation becomes a design input like security or scalability.

It's a compact pattern catalogue aimed at automated financial systems, and every pattern on it is something you can put on a whiteboard on Monday.

## Event sourcing is a diary you never edit

The first of three foundational patterns is event sourcing: every change captured as an event, never overwritten. Sneha's analogy lands: "It's like keeping a diary instead of editing yesterday's entry." Technically that means an append-only log with replayable history and cryptographic integrity. For a regulator it means full traceability and non-repudiation, because nothing gets quietly deleted.

## Two clocks beat one

The second pattern, bitemporal modelling, keeps two timelines for every fact: when something happened in the real world and when the system recorded it. With both, you can reconstruct what was true at any moment and what you believed at that moment, even after corrections. Anyone who has had to explain what a report showed before last month's backfill knows why this matters.

## Lineage as a graph, not a spreadsheet

The third is graph-based lineage. Nodes and edges map how data moves across microservices, so an auditor can trace a reported number back to its source and an engineer can see what a schema change will break before shipping it.

## Separate the writes, label the readers

On top of the foundation, Sneha adds three more patterns:

- **CQRS.** The command side validates transactions and enforces rules; the query side is tuned for audits, monitoring and reporting. Accuracy and read speed stop fighting over the same tables.
- **ABAC.** Attribute-based access control decides on user attributes, data sensitivity and context in real time. Her example: an analyst in Europe can see European data under GDPR while a contractor gets a narrower view. Policies are declarative, which also makes them auditable.
- **Adaptive exception handling.** Reinforcement learning watches compliance exceptions, picks responses and improves over time, so recurring issues shrink as rules change.

## Don't adopt all six at once

The most useful slide may be the effort map. Event sourcing and CQRS are heavy lifts; ABAC and bitemporal models are lighter. So the roadmap is phased: assess gaps and map current obligations, design around the core patterns, pilot one domain, then scale. Starting with the cheap patterns gets you evidence that the expensive ones are worth it.

## Who should watch

Engineers building ledgers, payment flows, trading or logistics systems under regulation, and architects who get asked to prove what happened more often than they'd like. It's an overview, so expect breadth across six patterns rather than code for any one of them.

Title: AI can run the network, but you still need to know BGP
Description: Vamsi Gadireddy of Microsoft Azure at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on AI-driven network engineering, self-healing networks and the skills that still matter.
Body:
The 2 AM router failure used to mean a phone call. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Vamsi Gadireddy, Senior Network Engineer on Microsoft Azure, described how AI is moving network operations from monitor-and-react to anticipate-and-adapt, and argued that this makes protocol fundamentals more important, not less.

It is a career-and-strategy talk for network engineers rather than a prompt engineering deep cut. Expect a roadmap and a skills list, with real examples sprinkled in.

## Three kinds of network, one engineer

Vamsi says the modern network engineer has to be fluent in three worlds. Enterprises care about compliance, uptime and security (think a bank keeping trading live around the clock, or a healthcare company keeping HIPAA intact across clouds without slowing doctors down). Cloud providers care about automation and elasticity at continental scale. Telecom operators carry enormous traffic and billions of IoT connections. His image for enterprise work is renovating an old house while keeping the lights on, because the legacy systems never expected to talk to cloud services.

## The fundamentals are your compass

The part worth underlining: AI can optimise configurations, but it cannot replace understanding of BGP, OSPF and MPLS. When a model recommends a route change, someone has to tell whether it really improves latency or hides a topology problem. IPv6, security and observability join that core list as IoT pushes past what IPv4 can address.

On top of that, he wants programming fluency, AI literacy and data interpretation. If a model suggests reallocating bandwidth based on telemetry, you should know what it learned from and what biases it may carry. The new command line, in his telling, is Python, YAML, JSON and Git, driving Ansible, Terraform, Netmiko-style libraries, NAPALM and SDN controllers. You push a commit, and validated changes roll across hundreds of devices.

## Where AI already pays

Vamsi lists anomaly detection (traffic spikes that might be an attack), predictive maintenance (ports and links likely to fail) and root cause analysis that correlates thousands of logs in seconds. His example is a global telco that used AI to detect Wi-Fi degradation across regions before customers noticed.

Self-optimising networks are the next step: systems that diagnose themselves and reroute around failures, such as shifting traffic from a failed Singapore link through Tokyo without anyone touching a console. He is clear that autonomy needs guardrails, with engineers defining what the AI is allowed to change.

## Humans keep the context

His best example of why: an AI might flag a huge data transfer as a security threat, while a human knows it is the sanctioned quarterly backup. AI speeds up analysis; people supply business context, regulation and judgment.

He closes with design principles (API-first, microservices, declarative configuration, observability by default, horizontal scaling, stateless design, graceful degradation, chaos engineering in the spirit of Netflix's Chaos Monkey) and a five-step roadmap: assess, automate and collect telemetry, pilot AI in low-risk areas such as anomaly detection, scale what works, and keep learning.

## Who should watch

Network engineers wondering which skills to invest in next, and engineering managers planning a NetDevOps or AIOps programme. If you already run intent-based networking in production, the material will be review; the framing is still handy for explaining it to leadership.

Title: Real-time data systems that decide on fraud in milliseconds
Description: Lakshmi Bhargavi Mullapudi of Techstar Group mapped the Kafka, Flink and ClickHouse stack behind real-time apps at Conf42 JavaScript 2025.
Body:
A card transaction can be ingested, enriched, scored by a model and blocked in 80 to 120 milliseconds, if every stage of the pipeline is built for it. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Lakshmi Bhargavi Mullapudi, a software engineer at Techstar Group, walked through the architecture that makes that possible, from event ingestion to the WebSocket that updates the dashboard.

It's a short, dense reference talk: one slide per layer, with the trade-offs named.

## Five layers, one latency budget

Her pipeline is ingest, process, store, deliver. For ingestion she compares Apache Kafka (a distributed log with strong ordering per partition and a big connector ecosystem) with AWS Kinesis (managed, auto-scaling, less to operate, built-in retention and replay). Both handle millions of events per second when configured well; the choice comes down to throughput needs, operational appetite and what you already run.

For stream processing: Apache Flink as a true streaming engine with exactly-once semantics, stateful operators and event-time processing, against Spark Structured Streaming's micro-batches with good SQL support for teams already on Spark.

For serving queries, Apache Druid for time-series aggregations across billions of events behind live dashboards, and ClickHouse for analytical SQL at scale with strong compression and vectorised execution.

## The fraud case study

The worked example shows where the milliseconds go. Transactions land in Kafka topics with about 10 ms latency. They're joined in flight with user profiles, historical patterns and risk codes. A lightweight model scores the feature vector within 50 ms. High-risk transactions are blocked and the security team is alerted. End to end: 80 to 120 ms from transaction to decision.

## Where latency actually hides

Her low-latency rules are the part to keep:

- **Minimise network hops.** Each round trip adds roughly 1 to 5 ms, so co-locate processing and storage and avoid cross-datacentre calls.
- **Pick a better serialisation format.** Avro or Protocol Buffers instead of JSON; she noted serialisation can eat 20 to 30% of processing time in high-throughput systems. JavaScript developers, that one is aimed at you.
- **Batch small.** Micro-batches with 10 to 50 ms windows usually balance throughput and latency.
- **Cache strategically.** In-memory caches for hot data and lookup tables serve reads in microseconds.

For scale: partition with consistent hashing or range partitioning, keep services stateless and push state to Redis or a distributed store, and autoscale on consumer lag rather than CPU.

## Pick consistency per data type

She treats consistency as a business decision. Strong consistency for financial transactions, eventual consistency for analytics and recommendations, and tunable quorum reads and writes where the importance of a request varies. Many systems mix all three. Fault tolerance comes from checkpointing, replication, retries and circuit breakers that fail fast when downstream services degrade.

On the frontend, WebSockets or server-sent events push updates to the browser, GraphQL subscriptions fit teams already on GraphQL, and Redux, NgRx or Zustand handle streaming state in React, with normalised data to avoid unnecessary re-renders.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers who are about to own a real-time feature and need a map of the backend it depends on, and anyone choosing between Kafka and Kinesis or Flink and Spark. Her closing advice works for everyone: define latency targets before picking tools, because not everything needs sub-second processing, and measure every stage, since latency in one component is latency for the whole system.

## Related talks

- [Demystifying Event-Driven Architectures with Apache Kafka](https://www.conf42.com/Enterprise_Software_2021_Bogdan_Sucaciu_event_driven_architectures_apache_kafka) explains the ingestion layer properly.
- [Cloud-Native Analytics: Transforming Big Data into Real-Time Product Insights](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Nimit_Bhardwaj_big_data_analytics_realtime_insights) covers the analytics end of the pipeline.

Title: Shard your AI service, but keep the conversation state central
Description: Rahul Thakur of Salesforce at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on sharding AI services across zones, with routing, session affinity and migration.
Body:
A single deployment serving all your LLM traffic is one bad node away from an outage. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Rahul Thakur, Lead Member of Technical Staff at Salesforce, made the case for running AI services as many independent shards behind a metadata-aware router, with compute sharded and conversation state kept in a central store.

It is a short, design-level talk: no benchmarks or code, but a clear component list you can hold your own architecture against.

## Why AI traffic is awkward

Rahul starts with what makes AI services different from a typical stateless API. Traffic is extremely variable. Conversations are stateful, so you carry context and customer settings between requests. Some requests need far more resources than others. And failures arrive unannounced. Put all of that on one deployment and you get bottlenecks, resource contention and a single point of failure.

## The pieces of a sharded AI service

His proposal splits traffic across shards that each serve a share of requests, with smart routing and failover on top. The components:

- **AI service shards**, each working independently.
- **A metadata service** that knows every shard and its dependencies. This is the brain of the setup.
- **A routing layer** that sends each request to the right shard.
- **Multi-zone placement**, so losing one availability zone does not take the service down.
- **State management**, because conversations carry context.
- **Observability**, which matters more once you are debugging across many shards instead of one.

## Affinity, then load, then priority

Routing gets the most detail. The first rule is session affinity: the same user should land on the same shard every time, and the metadata service tracks which shard already serves them. Next, if some shards are overloaded, the router steers new traffic to quieter ones. Priority routing can sit on top, keyed on subscription tier or workload type, and geographic routing sends users to nearby shards.

## Shard the compute, not the context

The design choice to remember is about state. Rahul keeps conversation context in a centralised database while the compute is sharded. When a shard misbehaves and a conversation has to move, the migration is a short sequence: retrieve the state, pick a new shard, update the routing, and optionally pre-warm. Because the context never lived on the failed shard, there is nothing to rescue from it.

That is the part of the talk most likely to save you a postmortem. Sticky sessions without a plan for moving them are a pager waiting to go off.

## Scaling signals

For scaling he lists horizontal (more shards), vertical (bigger shards where one shard naturally carries more load), capacity reservation, and cost optimisation through reserved capacity. Autoscaling triggers include request queue depth, latency thresholds, predictive models trained on past usage, and cost-aware triggers that retire underused shards. Health checks per shard, disaster recovery and automatic failover round it out.

The abstract sets the goal at 99.99% uptime; in the talk Rahul describes the payoff as getting close to full availability, independent scaling and lower cost from right-sizing each shard. His rollout advice is to build a few shards first, confirm that scale-up, scale-down and the metadata service all work, and only then expand.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers who own an LLM-backed service that has outgrown one deployment, or who are designing one and want the failure modes on the table early. If you already run cell-based architecture, this will feel familiar, applied to stateful AI chat.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Andrew Robinson on fault isolation with shuffle sharding](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Andrew_Robinson_fault_isolation_shuffle_sharding) at Conf42 SRE 2021, the classic way to limit blast radius.
- [Trista Pan on sharding and scaling out traditional databases on Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Trista_Pan_automatically_shard_scaleout_databases_kubernetes), for the state side of the story.

Title: Adaptive optimisation for Node.js backends and React frontends
Description: Nike's Deepika Annam argued at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 for runtime-adaptive tuning across Node.js and React, citing up to 2.29x throughput gains.
Body:
Static performance tuning is driving a car stuck in one gear: fine on the flat, painful on hills. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Deepika Annam, Senior Data Engineer at Nike, made the case for "intelligent optimisation", where Node.js backends and React, Vue and Angular frontends adjust their own resources at runtime, and cited results of up to 2.29x throughput.

It's a high-level talk: lots of analogies, a checklist of techniques, and headline numbers. Good for framing a performance programme, less so for copying code.

## Why static configs lose under real traffic

Her scenario is a retailer during a big sale: thousands of users hit the site in different ways, the backend strains and the frontend falls behind. Fixed configurations and manual tweaks don't keep up when load changes minute to minute. The alternative she describes is a system that watches memory pressure and request spikes and adapts while running, like streaming players that switch video quality to match bandwidth.

## Node.js: pools that resize themselves

On the backend, the levers are adaptive worker pools, connection pools and event loop monitoring, so the server can shift resources when traffic jumps and keep latency down. She compares it to a head chef watching orders and moving staff around the kitchen. These patterns matter most where API throughput is the business, such as finance, retail and logistics.

## React: only the actors who are needed on stage

On the frontend, the problem is unnecessary re-renders. The fixes are familiar ones applied deliberately: watch render cycles, memoise components, lazy-load, and give critical UI updates priority while deferring the rest. She also covers framework-specific angles: rendering and state management in React, the reactivity system and templates in Vue, change detection and ahead-of-time compilation in Angular.

## The numbers, and how to read them

The headline results she presented: 2.29x throughput, 40% smaller bundles, 60% faster load times, and 3x better API response. She also mentioned retailers reporting checkout times dropping from several seconds to under two during peak sales. The talk doesn't attach these to a named application or a published benchmark, so treat them as the scale of improvement to aim for, not a guarantee.

Her point about architecture is that none of this needs heavy infrastructure: a light runtime layer with low CPU and memory overhead can deliver most of the gain.

## The usual suspects, with fixes

The challenges section works as a checklist:

- **Bundle size**: code splitting, tree shaking, dynamic imports with loading priorities.
- **Runtime efficiency under peak load**: adaptive resource allocation and caching.
- **DOM update overhead**: batch operations, an efficient virtual DOM, render what's visible first.
- **API bottlenecks**: request prioritisation, caching, and predictive prefetching (her example: travel sites loading flight data before the user searches).

She also recommends TypeScript for optimisation code that has to scale, with generics, type guards, decorators and union types, and decorators for performance monitoring.

Her closing advice is the right order of operations: measure a baseline first, then move from static config to runtime adaptation, keep the optimisation layer light, and test in production because that's the performance users actually get.

## Who should watch

Engineering leads planning a performance push across a full JavaScript stack, and developers who want a structured list of techniques to check their app against. If you already profile your event loop and React renders, you'll know most of the tools; the value is in seeing them as one system.

## Related talks

- [React is Killing your Performance and it's Your Fault](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Assaf_Krintza_React_Performance) goes much deeper on re-renders.
- [Mission: Performance Impossible – Real time chat webapp's performance with 100k active users](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Mohammed_Zubair_Ahmed_41_realtimechat_performance_100kusers) is a concrete case study under real load.
- [Intelligent Kubernetes Workload Optimization: Applying Deep Reinforcement Learning for Cloud-Native Performance](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Deepika_Annam_optimization_reinforcement_performance) is the same speaker on adaptive tuning at the infrastructure layer.

Title: An LLM agent for multi-cloud should act like a guarded junior SRE
Description: Praneeth Patil of Equinix at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on moving LLMs from one-off Terraform snippets to RAG-grounded agents that fix multi-cloud drift.
Body:
Asking a chatbot for a Terraform module is fast, and sometimes fast in the wrong direction. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Praneeth Patil, Senior Staff Engineer at Equinix, sketched how LLMs can move from reactive snippet generators to agents that watch multi-cloud state, detect drift and propose fixes, and what verification has to surround them before anyone lets them touch production.

## The VPC module that opened everything

Praneeth's cautionary tale is worth the price of admission. A chat assistant wrote a clean VPC module in minutes. It also opened up all traffic, because nobody had mentioned the bastion host restriction. Nice code, wrong outcome. His lesson: without context and checks, you speed up right and wrong changes equally.

The wider problem is familiar to anyone running AWS, Azure, GCP and colocation side by side. Each has its own IAM, network model, APIs and billing knobs. The result is config sprawl, policy divergence and drift, and the glue (Terraform, Crossplane, scripts) becomes a second platform to maintain, or worse, tribal knowledge.

## RAG is the difference between fiction and grounded action

The agent he describes behaves like a junior SRE with excellent recall of the docs, wrapped in strict guardrails. It keeps continuous awareness (snapshots of state, drift and quotas across clouds), detects misconfigurations, vulnerabilities and cost anomalies, and proposes or executes fixes with approvals and rollbacks.

Retrieval is the core. Before changing a security group, the agent pulls the desired state from infrastructure as code, the actual rules from the cloud API, the change history from logs and PRs, your own security and FinOps policies, and provider best practices such as the AWS Well-Architected material. The output is a proposed diff plus the reasoning behind it.

## Four checks before anything applies

The verification pipeline is the part to steal:

1. Syntax validation, linting and formatting for YAML, JSON and Terraform.
2. Semantic analysis: does this change do what was intended? Reasoning models help here.
3. Policy guardrails: compliance, budgets, tagging, encryption, data residency.
4. Dry runs: `terraform plan`, `kubectl diff`, smoke tests in staging.

He also recommends dual-model verification, where a second model or a rules engine critiques the plan and asks why it is needed and what could go wrong. Red teaming, built into the pipeline.

## The real value is between deployments

Praneeth argues that the agent earns its keep after the deploy, watching for IAM changes, route table edits, load balancer health, quotas and pricing. His anecdote: a teammate with account access modified a security group, and the whole team went looking for what broke. An agent holding the desired state could have spotted the change, explained it and proposed the rollback.

He is candid about risks: hallucinated configurations, over-privileged agents and runaway cost, including the cost of the agent's own inference. The mitigations are least privilege granted on demand, tests that confirm the agent behaves as expected, logging every decision and its reasoning, tiered human approvals with time-boxed change windows (not at 2 AM), and a versioned artifact behind every action so rollback is instant.

## Start small

His adoption path has four steps: keep your current flow and add retrieval and validation around LLM-generated artifacts; add RAG over your docs, IaC and runbooks; let agents detect and report drift; only then allow autonomous actions, with humans in the loop.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams who already use Terraform or Crossplane across more than one provider and are being asked what agentic AI means for them. It is architecture and practice, not a product demo.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Stephane Jourdan on why infrastructure drift deserves attention](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Stephane_Jourdan_infrastructure_drift) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021, the problem before agents.
- [Peter O'Neill on securing terraform apply with Open Policy Agent](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2022_Peter_ONeill_terraform_apply_secured_open_policy_agent), one way to build the guardrail stage.

Title: Robots shipped today will still be running when quantum breaks RSA
Description: Nehal Singh of California State University, Long Beach at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on moving robot fleets to post-quantum crypto with hybrid TLS and Dilithium.
Body:
A warehouse robot bought this year may still be on the floor in fifteen years, which is long enough for a quantum computer to read everything it ever sent. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Nehal Singh, Senior Manager for IT Infrastructure and Productivity Apps at California State University, Long Beach, laid out how to move robot networks to post-quantum cryptography without breaking real-time behaviour.

The talk is short and practical: threat model, the NIST algorithms, a reference architecture, and a migration checklist.

## Harvest now, decrypt later already applies to robots

Shor's algorithm is expected to break RSA and ECC, the schemes that protect robot command channels and firmware today. Nehal's sharper point is timing. Attackers can collect encrypted telemetry, maps, sensor logs and firmware blobs now and decrypt them once the hardware exists. Robots produce exactly that kind of long-lived data, and they receive updates and commands that must stay trustworthy for years.

Robots also widen the blast radius. A breach isn't only a data leak; spoofed control channels or manipulated lidar and camera input can make a machine do something physical. Add OTA updates, cloud APIs, message brokers and containerized services, and every layer is its own door.

## Kyber for keys, Dilithium for trust

The NIST post-quantum standards give two lattice-based workhorses. Kyber is a key encapsulation mechanism that replaces RSA and ECC key exchange. Dilithium is a signature scheme, and Nehal maps it to the jobs robots care about most: command authentication and firmware signing, so a robot trusts an update fifteen years from now just as it does today. Open-source libraries exist and hardware support is starting to land.

## Run both until one breaks

Nobody swaps a fleet's crypto overnight. The recommended bridge is hybrid cryptography: classical and post-quantum algorithms side by side, so if either one falls the other still holds. Hybrid TLS or SSH lets you upgrade links without stranding legacy components. It's belt and braces, and in this case wearing both is the design.

The architecture spreads the load sensibly. Robots, with tight compute and power budgets, do lightweight local verification. Edge gateways take on the heavier PQC operations. Cloud APIs, remote debugging and management channels run PQC-enabled TLS or SSH. Zero trust sits across all of it: every device, action and packet verified continuously, with quantum-safe signatures making identities hard to forge later.

## Start with an inventory, not an algorithm

The plan Nehal proposes is refreshingly unglamorous:

1. Build a cryptographic inventory across devices, gateways and cloud pipelines.
2. Prioritize firmware, command channels and OTA.
3. Pilot hybrid TLS on one gateway-to-cloud link and watch handshake latency and compatibility.
4. Check that HSMs, TPMs and secure enclaves can support PQC.
5. Write down governance and incident response.

The pitfalls are just as practical: silent fallback to a weaker algorithm unless policy forbids it, legacy boxes that need wrapping in a secure gateway, vendors without a PQC roadmap, and crypto code that needs independent testing. The closing line is worth stealing for your next budget slide: the "best time to secure these systems was yesterday."

## Who should watch

Title: Power BI plus Copilot found $30M hiding in food scrap rates
Description: Victor Gabriel of GEP Worldwide at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on pairing Power BI dashboards with Copilot prompts to cut a food maker's supply chain costs.
Body:
Sometimes the most valuable prompt is a plain question about scrap. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Victor Gabriel, a supply chain consultant at GEP Worldwide, told how his team gave a large food manufacturer a Power BI foundation with a Microsoft Copilot prompt layer on top, and how the questions analysts could suddenly ask led to about $30 million in savings on scrap and conversion costs.

The talk title names Kellogg's; in the recording Victor describes the client as a $15 billion food manufacturer with many contract manufacturers across North America. It is a consulting case study, short and practical, with the lessons stated plainly at the end.

## Excel dashboards were not enough

The starting point will sound familiar: data scattered across systems, little real-time visibility into cost, slow detection of margin leakage, and a hard time turning numbers into decisions. The client had dashboards. What it lacked was a fast way to ask why.

## Three pillars, one source of truth

Victor's framework has three parts:

- **Power BI foundation:** real-time dashboards that present the facts.
- **Prompt engineering layer:** Microsoft Copilot for scenario modelling and questions in plain language.
- **Integration engine:** connections to manufacturing systems, supplier portals and finance data, merged into a single source of truth.

The prompt layer is the point of the talk. Instead of filing a request with the data team, an analyst can ask which factors contributed most to scrap variance in Q3 and get visuals and a summary back. Victor's line is that this made advanced analytics usable by people who are not data scientists.

## The answer was in the recipes

The focus stayed on two levers: margin performance (conversion cost, yield, profitability per product) and cost optimisation (supplier cost benchmarking, packaging efficiency, process improvements). Timing helped too: the platform went live during a corporate restructuring, so its numbers fed directly into decisions about which suppliers to consolidate, grow or move production to.

The headline finding was that scrap rates were 15% above industry benchmarks. The prompt-driven analysis traced part of it to product recipes that were not consistent across suppliers. The fixes were unglamorous: standardise the formulas, renegotiate supplier contracts and add live supplier performance alerts. Within 18 months, raw material and packaging scrap reached industry-best levels, and that is where the $30 million comes from.

It is a good reminder that the LLM did not save the money. It shortened the path from a hunch to the spreadsheet row that proved it.

## Lessons that travel

Victor's takeaways apply well beyond food manufacturing:

- Start with business questions, not tools.
- Fix data quality early, because poor data kills good analytics.
- Work cross-functionally; the integration engine only works if finance, operations and procurement share data.
- Use AI to support human judgment, not to replace it.

His getting-started blueprint is incremental: pick three to five high-impact areas, build a simple Power BI dashboard, add Copilot (or another LLM) gradually, track which insights lead to actions, then scale and standardise once value is proven.

## Who should watch

Analytics leads and data engineers in manufacturing, retail or procurement who already have a BI stack and wonder what an LLM layer adds. It is light on implementation detail (no prompt templates, no data model), so treat it as a business case, not a how-to.

Title: Privacy by design for JavaScript data pipelines, layer by layer
Description: Meta data engineer Vivekananda Chittireddy showed at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 how k-anonymity, differential privacy and tokenisation fit JS stacks.
Body:
Three attributes, zip code, date of birth and gender, are enough to identify most people in the US, which is why "we removed the names" isn't anonymisation. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Vivekananda Chittireddy, a data engineer at Meta, showed how to build privacy into JavaScript data systems from the browser to the analytics layer, with the techniques that actually hold up: k-anonymity, differential privacy, tokenisation and a five-layer architecture.

He's clear that this is his own experience building privacy-aware systems, not a description of how Meta does it.

## The four principles, applied to code

He frames privacy by design with four principles: be proactive, not reactive; make maximum privacy the default without waiting for users to opt in; build privacy into the design from day one instead of bolting it on; and keep full functionality, because a private product nobody can use helps no one. For JavaScript developers that means controls at every stage, from client-side collection through Node.js backends to processing and analytics.

## Techniques that survive contact with an attacker

- **K-anonymity**: every record looks identical to at least k-1 others on identifying fields. With k of 5, any individual blends in with four others.
- **L-diversity**: each of those groups also needs varied sensitive values. If every patient in a group has the same diagnosis, being hidden in the group protects nothing.
- **Differential privacy**: add calibrated noise to query results so that any one person's presence barely changes the output. He suggested epsilon values between 0.1 and 1.0 as the practical range, and pointed to Node.js libraries that can apply local differential privacy in the browser.
- **Pseudonymisation and tokenisation**: replace identifiers like social security numbers with internal IDs that keep joins working, or with random tokens mapped in a separate vault, so the analytics pipeline never touches real PII.

For the ambitious, he covered homomorphic encryption (computing on data without decrypting it) and secure multi-party computation, where several organisations compute over combined data without seeing each other's records.

## Two case studies

In healthcare, a consortium wanted medical research across institutions without exposing patient data. Using JavaScript-based federated learning with differential privacy, records stayed on hospital servers, models trained locally, and only differentially private updates were shared, keeping the setup within HIPAA and GDPR.

In financial services, card details were tokenised at the point of collection, so real-time fraud detection ran on streaming pipelines without seeing card numbers, while behaviour analytics used k-anonymous cohorts of 25 to 50 people.

## A five-layer blueprint

1. **Collection**: consent management, minimal scope, pseudonymise immediately using browser APIs.
2. **Storage**: encrypt at rest, keep identifying data in separate databases from transactional data, strict access controls between them.
3. **Processing**: differential privacy on queries, secure enclaves for sensitive operations, aggregate instead of working per user.
4. **Analytics**: insights only from de-identified data, with full audit trails for breach investigations and certifications.
5. **Access**: role-based access, purpose limitation and least privilege.

Tools: Node.js's built-in `crypto` module, JSON Web Tokens for token handling, and the browser's SubtleCrypto API for client-side encryption.

## The pitfalls list is the part to print

PII in plain-text logs (one stack trace with user data undoes the rest). Treating MD5 hashes or sequential IDs as anonymisation, when they're trivially reversible. Collecting everything just in case. Privacy controls only on the client, where any developer with devtools can bypass them. And keeping data forever, which conflicts with GDPR and California privacy law and makes any breach more expensive.

## Who should watch

Node.js and data engineers handling user data in regulated sectors, and anyone who has to argue for privacy work in a design review. It's a broad overview with real techniques; you'll still need the library docs to implement them.

## Related talks

- [Privacy by Design for DevOps: Building Scalable, Secure, Regulation-Ready Data Systems](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Vivek_Chittireddy_privacy_regulation_security) brings the same principles to DevOps pipelines.
- [Building Privacy Aware Infrastructure](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Natalia_Grybovska_privacy_aware_infrastructure) looks at the platform layer.
- [Advanced Security Strategies for Protecting PII in Cloud Environments](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Sharath_Chandra_Adupa_security_pii_cloud) covers PII protection from a Go backend's view.

Title: RAG agents for investment banking reconciliation, trade by trade
Description: Swamy Biru of JPMorgan Chase at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on RAG-backed multi-agent systems for trade processing, reconciliation and compliance.
Body:
Reconciliation is the job nobody in a bank brags about and everybody depends on. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Swamy Biru, a Vice President of Software Engineering at JPMorgan Chase, laid out how retrieval-augmented generation plus a set of specialised agents can move trade validation, reconciliation and compliance checks from overnight batches to something close to real time.

This is an architecture talk, not a demo. It is a map of where LLMs fit in front, middle and back office systems, and which guardrails a regulated shop needs around them.

## The problem: the same trade, ten slightly different records

Swamy frames the pain in three parts: data inconsistency, manual processes and real-time risk. A single trade generates data points that must agree across front-office trading systems, middle-office risk platforms and back-office settlement. The inputs come from internal systems, market data vendors, regulatory platforms and counterparty messages, each with its own format and update rhythm.

Batch processing leaves windows where systems disagree. Highly paid people then spend their days hunting discrepancies that add little strategic value but cannot be skipped. And regulators want audit trails and data lineage on top of all of it.

## Retrieval first, then specialised agents

The architecture he shows routes a query (a trade, in whatever format it arrives) to an LLM that first pulls context from a vector database, then hands work to specialised agents: trade processing, risk assessment, compliance monitoring and settlement reconciliation. Each agent owns one domain and they coordinate through defined interfaces, which keeps the system modular.

Why retrieval matters here: the model answers from transaction databases, settlement platforms and counterparty communications rather than from what it absorbed in training. That gives you current information and an audit trail. Semantic search over embeddings handles the fact that financial terminology varies across desks, counterparties and time periods, so the system can find the relevant rule or record even when the query is phrased differently.

Prompt engineering sits in the middle of the data flow: templates, intent classification and prompt optimisation turn market data, internal reports and regulatory documents into compliance alerts, recommendations and client reports. Swamy's claim is that engineered prompts reduce hallucination and keep answers within the domain.

## Reconciliation that knows what equivalent means

The sharpest section compares traditional and AI-assisted reconciliation. Traditional: overnight batches, discrepancies found late, and lots of false positives from format differences, each one investigated by hand. The AI version runs continuously and, crucially, understands context: different spellings of a counterparty name, a settlement date shifted for a holiday, a price difference within tolerance. Those are not real breaks, and treating them as such is what buries reconciliation teams.

He extends the same idea to risk (spotting correlations across positions that standard models miss) and compliance (flagging patterns before they become violations, and tracking regulatory changes across jurisdictions).

## The guardrails a bank will ask about

Swamy lists six security and compliance pieces: encryption at rest, in transit and in use; role- and attribute-based access control; tamper-proof audit logging; an explanation for every AI decision that a human reviewer can check; ongoing model validation as markets shift; and automated incident response. The microservice layout lets services scale independently during volatile market periods and keeps a failure in one component from taking down the rest.

The abstract puts the results at 40% efficiency gains and 95% accuracy at major investment banks; the talk itself focuses on the architecture rather than walking through those measurements.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects in financial services sketching where LLMs go in a trade lifecycle, and anyone who needs a vocabulary for talking to compliance about RAG. If you want code, benchmarks or a live system, this is a whiteboard session.

Title: A vulnerability management framework for full-stack JavaScript
Description: UBS's Srinivasa Rao Gunda walked Conf42 JavaScript 2025 through XSS, dependency confusion, Node.js hardening and risk-based patch deadlines.
Body:
A JavaScript app gets attacked from both ends: the browser that renders whatever you put in `innerHTML`, and the Node.js server that trusts whatever arrives in a query string. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Srinivasa Rao Gunda, a technical architect at UBS with a background in wealth management systems, presented a framework for handling both: assess, prevent, detect, respond, and patch by risk instead of by mood.

It's a broad survey aimed at teams that want a checklist for the whole stack, from React components to container images.

## Where the attacks come in

He opens with four attack types that keep showing up in JavaScript codebases:

- **DOM-based XSS**: reading a value from the URL and dropping it into `innerHTML` is an invitation.
- **Prototype pollution**: tampering with shared object prototypes so the whole app inherits the attacker's properties.
- **Dependency confusion**: attackers publish packages with names close to your internal ones to public registries and wait for a build to pull the wrong one.
- **Server-side injection**: unvalidated input that changes SQL or NoSQL queries to read, change or delete data.

His point is that traditional perimeter security doesn't cover all of these, so you need a systematic approach.

## Score your dependencies before they score against you

The framework has four parts: assessment (find and quantify risk across the stack), prevention (security patterns and controls), detection (continuous monitoring and automated scanning with alerts), and response (incident workflow and patching).

The assessment criteria for third-party packages are a useful list: vulnerability history and how fast past issues were fixed, maintenance activity (commit frequency, response to issues), the security posture of the transitive dependency chain, and download metrics as a proxy for community adoption. Automated auditing tools make those decisions consistent across projects instead of depending on whoever reviews the PR.

## Frontend and Node.js patterns

On the client: HTTPS everywhere, proper CORS policies, validate and sanitise every input from outside, and use tokens or certificates for authentication. In React, avoid `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`; when you really need raw HTML, sanitise it with DOMPurify or similar first. TypeScript and prop types help enforce type safety and control data flowing between components.

On the server, the examples are the ones that hurt in finance: a query parameter that flips `isAdmin` to true, or a changed account number on a withdrawal. Validate every parameter, handle exceptions without leaking internals in error messages, add rate limiting and throttling, keep environment variables and secrets out of code, apply least privilege, and run `npm audit` regularly.

For containers: minimal base images such as Alpine to cut the attack surface, run Node.js as a non-root user, scan images in CI/CD before deployment, and never bake secrets into images; use the orchestrator's secret management.

## Patch by severity, on a clock

The response part is the most reusable slide. His risk-based deadlines:

- Critical or zero-day, actively exploited: patch within 24 hours.
- High severity affecting production, not yet exploited: within seven days.
- Medium risk: within 30 days.
- Low priority, such as issues needing local access: fold into regular maintenance.

Automation runs through the whole pipeline: secret scanning before commit, automated dependency audits and security tests on every pull request, gates in CI/CD (he mentions failing the build when SonarQube finds vulnerabilities), and runtime monitoring in production. He adds that TypeScript is not a silver bullet; it doesn't replace runtime validation or secure coding, it's one layer of defence in depth.

## Who should watch

Full-stack JavaScript teams that need a shared baseline for security work, and tech leads writing their first patching policy. Security specialists won't find new attack research; the value is in the structure and the patch-deadline table.

## Related talks

- [Supply Chain Attacks: Focused on NPM attacks](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Danish_Tariq_Hassan_Khan_Yusufzai_supply_chain_npm_attacks) goes deeper on the dependency side.
