Title: A good prompt has four parts, and most people skip three
Description: Chetan Prakash Ratnawat of Capgemini at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 with a beginner's tour of prompt structure, core techniques and AI ethics.
Body:
Most bad AI output starts with a prompt that only states the task. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Chetan Prakash Ratnawat, Senior Manager at Capgemini, gave a ground-floor tour of prompt engineering built around one formula: give the model context, a task, constraints and any extra information, and the quality of the answer follows.

A note on scope before you press play. The talk's title points to insurance workflows, but the recording is a general introduction to prompting; claims triage and underwriting do not come up. Treat it as a first talk on the subject, delivered by someone who has rolled AI tools out to enterprise clients, and you will get what it offers.

## Prompting went from keywords to roles in four years

Chetan opens with a short history. Around 2020, prompts were bags of keywords and you hoped for the best. Then came few-shot prompting, where you hand the model a template or examples to imitate. Role prompts (*act as an analyst*) and chain of thought followed, and now multimodal prompts mix text, images and audio. It is a tidy way to see that each technique was a fix for the previous one being too vague.

He also reminds the audience that the model behind the prompt matters as much as the prompt. His version of garbage in, garbage out runs both ways: a poor model or a poor prompt will waste your time and can hand you biased answers.

## The four-part prompt, with a washing liquid

The most reusable slide is the structure. Chetan's worked example is a marketing brief:

- **Context:** you are the marketing manager for a new product launch in the FMCG sector.
- **Task:** write a short paragraph describing the target audience and the key marketing messages.
- **Constraints:** keep it short and focused on the most important messages.
- **Additional information:** the product is a liquid for washing machines, aimed at urban and semi-urban households.

Compare that with *write an email for me*, which he uses as the bad example alongside *tell me about cybersecurity*. The weak versions are not wrong, just unbounded, so the model fills the gaps with generic filler. His fix for the cybersecurity one is to ask for three common threats and how Microsoft Defender mitigates them. Same topic, a fraction of the guesswork.

He adds a list of "power words" that steer output: act as, summarize, generate, predict, elaborate, simplify. Then the core techniques: role prompting, chain of thought, few-shot and zero-shot. None of this is new to a daily LLM user, but it is laid out in an order that a team new to the tools can follow.

## The failure stories are the better half

Chetan balances the success stories with incidents worth remembering: an airline chatbot that gave a customer misleading information and ended in a legal case, staff pasting confidential code into a public chatbot until the employer blocked it, and a hiring tool that showed bias. He also mentions a financial reporting chatbot from his own client work, where he reports productivity and reporting-accuracy gains and points to his article for the details.

The lesson he draws is procedural. Validate every AI-generated output, label AI-assisted work as such with clients, write retention and data-handling rules down, and train colleagues on them. Governance is the boring part of the talk and probably the part your security team will thank you for.

## Who should watch

Managers, analysts and engineers who are about to roll an AI assistant out to a team and need a shared vocabulary for what a good prompt looks like. If you already write structured system prompts and run evals, you can skip to the failure cases and the governance section. If you came for insurance-specific workflows, they are not in this recording.

Title: Rate limiting that reads behaviour instead of counting requests
Description: Rehana Sultana Khan of Versa Networks showed at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 how 27 behavioural features and tree ensembles replace static API limits.
Body:
A product launch that goes viral on Hacker News and a DDoS look exactly the same to a static rate limiter: lots of requests, fast. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Rehana Sultana Khan, Technical Program Manager and Engineering Manager at Versa Networks, showed how to swap that request counter for a model that reads 27 behavioural features per client, scores the threat, and slows bots down without slamming the door on real users.

## The fixed threshold is wrong both ways

Set the limit low and you block your best customers mid-flash-sale with HTTP 429s; she cited a figure of 41% of legitimate traffic blocked by overly aggressive static rules. Set it high and abuse walks in, while you over-provision infrastructure for the worst case and pay for servers that sit idle most of the time.

She named three flaws: rigid thresholds that can't tell a good spike from an attack, no context (a user who has logged in from the same office for two years looks like a script from a foreign data centre), and the operational cost of not trusting your limiter.

The threat that exploits all three is the low-and-slow application-layer DDoS. A botnet of thousands of devices sends a few requests per minute each, staying just under your limit, aimed at the expensive endpoints: login, search, checkout. Each IP looks like a quiet user. Together they drain database connections and CPU while the rate limiter waves them through.

## Collect, engineer, train, deploy

Her pipeline has four steps. First, instrument API gateways and load balancers to capture what she calls the digital DNA of each interaction: request frequency and burst patterns, the milliseconds between calls (humans are irregular, scripts keep metronome time), the sequence of endpoints, what happened after each request, login success and failure rates, session token behaviour, response times and 5xx rates, geolocation, IP reputation, and device fingerprints.

The outcome signals are the clever part. A run of 404s suggests a scanner. A run of 401s followed by a single 200 could be credential stuffing in progress.

Second, turn those facts into 27 features in four groups:

- **Temporal**: request-rate volatility, a burst score, time-of-day anomalies.
- **Access behaviour**: endpoint entropy (a shopper goes home, search, product, cart; a scanner jumps between login, admin and export) and a flag for known malicious sequences.
- **Network**: a "geographically impossible" score for New York to London between two requests, IP reputation, a source anomaly index.
- **User context**: a session confidence score, and failed-login velocity normalised against the user's own 90-day baseline. A forgetful typist failing three times means less than a user who never fails suddenly failing twenty.

## A committee and an investigator

Third, training. She uses a decision tree ensemble: a random forest as a committee of specialists, each looking at a different slice of features and voting, plus gradient boosting as the investigator for subtle edge cases. She reported 97.5% model accuracy, inference in microseconds, and interpretability good enough to see which features drive a decision. Retraining runs continuously on new labelled production traffic.

Fourth, deployment: the model runs as a serverless function (AWS Lambda or Azure Functions) behind the API gateway, which computes features, asks for a score and enforces the answer. Scale-to-zero billing, automatic fan-out during spikes, multi-zone availability by default, and blue-green deployments for model updates.

## Slow them down instead of blocking

Her strongest idea is progressive throttling. The model assigns a threat score from 0 to 100. Scores from 0 to 30 get full speed. From 31 to 70, small added delays: a 500 millisecond pause cripples a script and a human barely notices. From 71 to 99, much stricter limits. Confirmed threats are blocked. Graceful slowdown is what keeps false positives from turning into angry customers.

Across production deployments on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud she reported 96% detection accuracy, a 68% drop in false positives and over 27% infrastructure cost savings.

## Who should watch

API platform and security teams tired of tuning one number per endpoint, and anyone who has had a marketing launch blocked by their own WAF. You'll want an ML-literate colleague to build the training pipeline, but the feature list alone is worth stealing for rule-based systems.

Title: Recommendation engines quietly decide what a business builds next
Description: Ankita Saxena of Amazon at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on how recommendation systems grew from a carousel into infrastructure that steers inventory and investment.
Body:
The "you may also like" row is the visible tip of a system that now tells retailers what to stock, streamers what to commission and marketplaces who to match. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Ankita Saxena, Senior Product Manager at Amazon and a Carnegie Mellon alum, walked through four industries where recommendation engines have turned from a feature into the layer business decisions sit on.

It's a strategy talk with architecture diagrams, not a code walkthrough. If you build or run recommenders, it's a useful map of where your model's output ends up after the click.

## The click stream is a supply chain signal

Ankita starts with e-commerce. The pipeline is familiar: real-time capture of behaviour and transactions, item-to-item collaborative filtering to find purchase affinities, a personalization engine, and then a step many teams forget to own, aggregation into business intelligence for inventory planning, supplier management and product development.

Her examples are small and concrete. If shoppers keep buying a reusable water bottle with fitness gear, the pattern can push a retailer to bundle them, order more, or launch a private-label version. If people view a jacket and don't buy it, the system flags friction, and the team tries a new price, better images or different messaging. The recommender becomes a product manager that never sleeps and never asks for headcount.

## Streaming recommends by mood, not just by genre

Streaming gets the most technical section. On top of collaborative filtering, she describes micro-genre tagging (her example: not just "romantic", but romance with multiple couples and a Christmas theme), computer vision and audio analysis for cinematographic style, pacing and mood, and NLP over plot and character arcs.

The payoff she points to: a viewer who prefers warm colour balance and slower pacing gets visually similar shows even when the stories differ. And when millions binge one style of light comedy-drama, that demand signal feeds commissioning and licensing decisions. The model's taste becomes the studio's budget.

## Virtual try-on attacks the return label

Digital retail is Ankita's favourite case, and the one with numbers. Fit uncertainty drives returns, so visual-similarity models and AR try-on narrow the choices a shopper has to make. She cited return rates down by roughly 5 to 8% where those features are used, conversion up 15 to 25% on average across retailers, session duration up 20 to 30%, and order value up 8 to 12%. Treat them as the ranges she reported rather than a controlled study, but they show which metrics the business watches.

## Marketplaces need four agents at the table

The hardest case is the two-sided enterprise marketplace. Ankita frames it as multi-agent reinforcement learning with four roles: a seller agent chasing visibility and inventory turnover, a buyer agent hunting relevant suppliers and value, a platform agent guarding marketplace health and liquidity, and a regulatory agent keeping matches inside regional law, logistics and payment rules.

Her example: a buyer wants cheap shipping, a seller wants to clear excess stock, and the system learns to pair the buyer with a nearby supplier so both win. Her closing line on the whole topic: "It becomes a foundation and not a feature."

## Who should watch

Product managers and ML engineers who own a recommender and want to argue for it in a planning meeting, and anyone curious how the same collaborative-filtering core stretches across retail, media and B2B. If you want loss functions and feature stores, pair it with something more hands-on.

Title: Give your LLM a read replica, not your production SQL Server
Description: Siva Kumar Raju Bhupathiraju (Paycor) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on Azure SQL Managed Instance and MI Link as a low-latency, governed data source for LLMs.
Body:
Point a chatbot at the on-prem SQL Server that runs payroll and you've built a load test nobody scheduled. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Siva Kumar Raju Bhupathiraju, a principal database administrator at Paycor (now a Paychex company), showed how Azure SQL Managed Instance with Managed Instance Link gives LLM workloads a near-real-time, governed copy of on-prem data without a full migration, and how to tune it for prompt traffic.

It's a focused DBA talk on the Microsoft stack: specific features, a reference architecture, and a tuning checklist, rather than LLM theory.

## Legacy SQL wasn't built for prompt traffic

Siva lists what goes wrong when traditional SQL Server meets LLM applications: high-latency data access, limited scalability under many concurrent AI requests, complex replication across environments, and bottlenecks in real-time scenarios. LLM apps, meanwhile, want sub-second responses per prompt, continuous data sync, elastic scale and enterprise security. The gap between how fast the AI app moves and how fast the database answers is where the user experience dies.

## MI Link: replicate, don't migrate

The core of the talk is Managed Instance Link. It connects an on-prem SQL Server to an Azure SQL Managed Instance using log-based synchronisation, which Siva compares to an Always On availability group configuration, with near-zero latency. The managed instance then holds current, consistent data that LLM workloads can read, while production keeps doing its day job.

The same link doubles as disaster recovery. The managed instance serves AI reads and acts as a DR target, so in a disaster you can fail workloads over from on-prem to Azure. One setup, two jobs.

For global organisations, he shows multiple MI Links from one source database feeding regional managed instances, so LLMs serve users from the nearest copy and cross-region latency drops. His worked example is a global bank building a customer chatbot over mostly on-prem data: regional instances answer the bot, and the on-prem source isn't hammered by every conversation.

## Tune for prompt queries

Siva's tuning list is the most directly useful section for DBAs:

- Enable Query Store to capture query history, spot slow queries and fix plans before they hit LLM response times.
- Configure Resource Governor to classify workloads, so prompt-serving queries get dedicated memory and compute separate from everything else.
- Follow connection pooling best practices and tune parallelism and isolation levels for hundreds of simultaneous requests.
- Size the buffer pool to the workload, and index for read-heavy patterns.
- Monitor MI Link health so replication stays in sync.

For analytical prompt context, he points to Azure Synapse Link: pre-aggregate and index frequently used context in Synapse, keeping analytical preparation separate from transactional workloads and avoiding traditional ETL.

## Governance follows the data

Security travels with replication: automated discovery and labelling of sensitive data used in prompts, row-level and column-level security enforced on each target, comprehensive audit logging of AI-driven data access, and Always Encrypted columns plus TDE for data at rest and in transit.

His phased plan: assess current SQL workloads and AI integration points, optimise with MI replication tuned for low latency, scale to multi-region with integrated analytics, then build new AI applications on the hybrid base.

## Who should watch

SQL Server DBAs and data platform engineers being asked to feed an LLM app from on-prem data, and architects weighing hybrid replication against a full cloud migration. If you're not on Microsoft's stack, the separation-of-workloads idea still applies; the feature names won't.

Title: Protect data in use with confidential VMs, trusted launch and zero trust
Description: Microsoft's Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu showed at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 how TEEs, TPM-backed boot and zero trust stack up to secure cloud VMs.
Body:
Encryption at rest and in transit stop helping the moment your data is loaded into memory on someone else's hardware. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Priyadarshni Shanmugavadivelu, Principal Product Manager at Microsoft, laid out three layers that close that gap for cloud VMs: confidential computing for data in use, trusted launch for boot integrity, and zero trust for everything that talks to the VM afterwards.

It's a security architecture talk drawing on her work on Azure's VM platform, not a JavaScript one, and it works as a clear overview of how the pieces fit.

## Data in use was the missing third

Her framing: cross-tenant attacks, memory scraping and hypervisor breaches all target data while it is being processed, and perimeter-based VM security wasn't built for that. Confidential computing uses hardware trusted execution environments (TEEs) that keep data encrypted while the CPU works on it, invisible even to the cloud provider and system administrators.

The two main technologies she covered:

- **AMD SEV-SNP** (Secure Encrypted Virtualization with Secure Nested Paging): per-VM memory encryption with integrity checks, protection against hypervisor-level attacks, and attestation of boot integrity.
- **Intel TDX** (Trust Domain Extensions): workload isolation at the CPU level, "trust domains" enforced by hardware boundaries, with remote attestation.

Use cases: analytics across organisations that can't share raw data, training models on medical or financial data, and key management where keys never appear in plain text.

## Trusted launch: a chain of trust before the first process runs

TEEs protect a running VM, while trusted launch protects the boot. It builds on four steps: a TPM 2.0 chip as hardware root of trust, measured boot that records every boot component in platform configuration registers, remote attestation that compares those measurements to known-good baselines, and orchestrator policies that only let trusted VMs run. If a component was tampered with, attestation fails and the VM doesn't start. That's how you catch rootkits before the workload is even up.

The DevOps part is the most practical. Put attestation into CI/CD: write policy as code saying which images must be verified, attest each VM automatically before containers are deployed, and monitor continuously so integrity drift raises an alert. Trust becomes something checked on every deployment instead of once at setup.

## Zero trust between VMs

Then the network. "Never trust, always verify" applied to VMs means none is trusted for being on the same network. She gave three mechanisms: microsegmentation tied to workload identities instead of IP addresses, continuous re-authentication of every request with cryptographic identity, and behavioural monitoring that triggers an automated response to unusual connections or privilege escalations. The payoff is limiting lateral movement: an attacker with stolen credentials still can't hop across VMs, and an admin pulling unusual data volumes at odd hours gets noticed.

## What it costs

She tied the layers to compliance: network segmentation and cardholder data protection for PCI DSS 4.0, protected health information under HIPAA, and data minimisation and encryption for GDPR. On performance, she put TEE overhead at roughly 2 to 10 percent depending on workload, with remote attestation adding hundreds of milliseconds that caching and using TEEs only where needed can reduce. Looking ahead: post-quantum cryptography in TEEs, homomorphic encryption for computing on encrypted data, and ML-based anomaly detection for zero-day attacks.

## Who should watch

Cloud and platform engineers handling regulated workloads, security architects comparing SEV-SNP and TDX, and anyone who has to explain to compliance why "encrypted at rest" isn't the whole answer. If you build Node.js services, it's useful context on what your VM is doing underneath, but you won't see code.

## Related talks

- [Scaling Secure Enclaves: Confidential Computing in Go-Powered Distributed Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Vallabhaneni_enclaves_security_confidential) takes TEEs into application code.
- [Cloud Network Segmentation in pursuit of Zero Trust](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Atif_Siddiqui_cloud_network_segmentation_in_pursuit_of_zero_trust) goes further into the segmentation layer.
- [Real Zero Trust Security for Containerized Environments](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Ammar_Khan_zero_trust_security) applies the same principle to containers.

Title: RLHF at scale is a data problem and a network problem
Description: Votal AI CTO Jyotirmoy Sundi explained at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 how RLHF training runs on Kubernetes GPU clusters and where it gets stuck.
Body:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback is why chat models follow instructions, and running it across a GPU cluster is mostly a fight with networking, checkpoints and the slow supply of good human labels. That was the argument Jyotirmoy Sundi, co-founder and CTO of Votal AI, made at Conf42 JavaScript 2025, in a talk that maps the distributed RL stack from policy algorithms down to NVLink.

Fair warning: despite the venue, there is no JavaScript here. This is an ML infrastructure talk, and a useful one if you're the person asked to keep the training cluster alive.

## From MDPs to transformers, and why the reward function bites

He starts with the shift from classic reinforcement learning, built on Markov decision processes that maximise reward step by step, to transformer-based networks that can learn far richer functions across text, images, video and audio.

The training loop he describes for language models: pre-train on a large cluster, then supervised fine-tuning on instruction data (question and answer pairs written by domain experts such as doctors or maths olympiad winners), then optimise against a reward model using policy algorithms like PPO or GRPO, or actor-critic setups. The warning he repeats is about reward hacking. If the reward function is defined loosely, the model will find a way to score well without doing what you meant, and the consequences can be unpleasant. Every engineer who has written a metric and then watched a team optimise it will recognise the pattern.

## Data parallel, model parallel, and checkpoint everything

On the infrastructure side, most of these runs live on large Kubernetes clusters. With data parallelism, every pod holds the same model and gets a slice of the data; workers send updated weights back to a main server after each batch, which combines them and sends them out again. When the model is too big for one GPU, model parallelism splits the network itself across pods.

Runs can take weeks, so checkpointing is not optional: losing a run halfway and restarting from zero burns compute you won't get back. Replay buffers, actor-critic state and terabytes of data all need state management that survives pod restarts.

## The cluster plumbing

The concrete bits are worth having in one place:

- Kubernetes doesn't schedule GPUs natively; you install NVIDIA's device plugin and request GPUs per pod (four is typical, up to eight).
- Fast GPU-to-GPU communication needs NVLink and the NCCL library, because moving weights and state between pods quickly becomes the bottleneck.
- Frameworks he mentioned include IMPALA, Ray (with Ray Train from Anyscale), Microsoft's DeepSpeed for models too big for one GPU, PyTorch DDP for data parallelism, and Kubeflow's PyTorchJob and TFJob operators.

In production he stresses GPU monitoring (he mentions tools like Datadog), because a bad data split leaves some GPUs underused while others work hard. Add circuit breakers for unstable policies and failover that resumes from the last checkpoint instead of killing the whole run.

## Human feedback is the bottleneck

His main point is that the hardest part isn't the frameworks; it's getting enough high-quality human feedback. Feedback loops can take months, and companies such as Scale AI exist to produce labelled examples at volume. That's why he sees reinforcement fine-tuning as promising: start from a seed dataset, define a solid reward function, and let the model generate new training examples itself instead of waiting on experts.

Other open problems he lists: communication overhead between nodes, preferences that change over time, and consistency, since retraining should give results close to the last run even if they're not identical. Emerging directions include federated RLHF, where learning happens on edge devices and only weights sync to a central server, multimodal training, and feedback collected inside the product and used either for fine-tuning or as context in RAG prompts.

## Who should watch

Platform and MLOps engineers who run or are about to run GPU training on Kubernetes, and ML engineers who want a single overview of the RLHF pipeline and its failure points. Frontend developers looking for JavaScript can skip this one.

- [Scaling Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback in Distributed Cloud Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Jyotirmoy_Sundi_reinforcement_learning_distributed) is the same speaker on the same subject at Conf42 Kube Native 2025.

Title: Self-healing data pipelines swap static rules for an RL agent
Description: Annapurneswar Putrevu at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on RL agents and prompts that detect, explain and fix data pipeline failures on AWS.
Body:
Every data team has a runbook rule along the lines of add a node when CPU runs hot, and every data team has been paged for the failure the runbook didn't list. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Annapurneswar Putrevu, a software engineer with 22 years in the industry spanning Java, middleware and cloud, laid out a design for self-healing data pipelines: telemetry feeds anomaly detection, a reinforcement learning agent picks the recovery action, and natural-language prompts let engineers ask what broke and tell the system what to do.

It's an architecture walkthrough on an AWS reference stack, with a gentle introduction to reinforcement learning for people who know classic ML but not RL.

## Why rules run out

Annapurneswar's starting point is that demand for data has exploded. Stakeholders want dashboards, analytics and training data, so data engineers build pipelines constantly, and when one breaks, decisions stall. The traditional fix is rule-based: if CPU crosses a threshold, scale; if a system hangs, restart; if the network fails, alert.

He names three recurring pain points. Schema drift: the source schema changes and the ETL transformations break until someone rewrites them. Resource contention: a sudden influx overwhelms Airflow, Glue jobs, VMs or the warehouse. System anomalies: unseen errors and network failures. Static rules are rigid, can't adapt to new failure patterns, need manual updates and downtime, and struggle with complex scenarios.

## The reference pipeline

His example flow starts with an Oracle database as the external source. AWS DMS pulls changes using CDC; an Airflow DAG handles pre- and post-processing ETL, with Glue jobs alongside; the data lands in Redshift or another warehouse such as Snowflake. A monitoring layer, CloudWatch metrics in the AWS case, watches every node.

On top he stacks five layers. Monitoring tracks health, resource use and data quality. Analysis runs anomaly detection; he suggests isolation forest. The RL agent layer evaluates pipeline state and picks a recovery action such as rescheduling jobs, scaling Glue resources, remapping schemas or retrying DMS loads. Execution applies those actions across AWS services. Feedback checks whether the fix worked and feeds the result back so the agent improves.

## RL in one table

The teaching section is the talk's best part. In supervised ML you predict a target from features. In RL, think of the feature row as a state (error type, pipeline stage, latency), then add an action (retry, restart), a reward, and the next state. That state-action-reward-next-state tuple is the core data structure. If the next state is healthy, reward plus one; a retry that times out again earns zero or a penalty. The agent keeps a Q-table of these values and learns, by trial and error, which action maximises long-term reward. He likens the reward to a professor handing out extra marks and penalties.

The actions he describes include dynamic resource reallocation, ETL workflow adjustments, schema remapping (crawl the new source schema, regenerate the mapping with an LLM, deploy through CI/CD), exponential backoff instead of hammering a dead target every 30 seconds, and adaptive back pressure that throttles ingestion before failures cascade.

## Prompts as the operator console

Prompt engineering is the human interface. Ask in plain language for the last 24 hours of CPU use or how many errors an Airflow DAG has thrown, then ask for a root cause and let an agent read logs, traces and metrics to explain it. Then instruct it: spin up another worker node. No dashboard clicking required.

## Build it slowly

His adoption advice is grounded. Deploy full observability (metrics, logs, traces) first, since that's what the agent learns from. Build a simulation environment that mirrors production and generate failure scenarios there before trusting the agent live. Define the recovery actions and rewards explicitly. Then tackle one problem at a time, say schema drift, then resource contention, then network latency, rather than a big-bang rollout.

## Who should watch

Data engineers on AWS tired of brittle runbooks, and ML-curious platform engineers who want a clear mental model of RL applied to operations. It's a design proposal rather than a production post-mortem, so treat the architecture as a starting point.

Title: A lakehouse ends the choice between governed and cheap data
Description: Richa Solanki (Ally Bank) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on lakehouse zones, Data Vault, ELT, open table formats and automated governance at scale.
Body:
For years the data team's choice was a governed, expensive warehouse or a cheap lake that slowly turned into a swamp. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Richa Solanki, Manager of Data Management at Ally Bank, explained how lakehouse architecture removes that trade-off, and walked through the patterns that make it work at enterprise scale: raw, refined and curated zones, Data Vault modelling, ELT in place, and governance that runs itself.

It's a compact architecture primer from someone running enterprise data management in banking, with a sensible implementation checklist at the end.

## Two flawed options

Richa frames the problem first. Data now arrives structured, semi-structured and unstructured from many systems, and fragmented environments make governance, security and efficiency harder. Warehouses give reliability, consistency and strong governance, but they're expensive and rigid. Lakes are cheap and scalable, but drift into swamps with unclear ownership and no transactional consistency. Enterprises have been forced to pick structure or flexibility.

The lakehouse, in her telling, combines warehouse governance with lake economics, and runs batch analytics, streaming and machine learning on one platform: build once, govern centrally, serve many use cases.

## Four capabilities that make it a lakehouse

She lists four pillars. ACID transactions keep integrity as you scale to billions of records. Schema enforcement supports both schema-on-read and schema-on-write as business data evolves. Real-time analytics query batch and streaming data together without complex ETL. Unified governance gives one place for metadata, lineage and compliance, which is what enterprise adoption hinges on.

## Zones and vaults

The structural pattern is three zones. Raw stores data exactly as it arrives, for auditability. Refined is where cleansing, validation, standardisation and business rules happen. Curated holds analytics-ready datasets for reporting and machine learning. The layering is what lets people trust a number: you can always trace it back to what arrived.

Inside, she recommends Data Vault modelling for flexibility and history. Hubs hold core business entities and their identifiers, links capture relationships between them, and satellites store descriptive attributes with full history. Schemas can evolve without breaking downstream systems, and you can see how data changed over time, which auditors in a bank tend to ask about.

## Performance and ELT

Scale is pointless if queries crawl, so she covers the performance trio: columnar formats like Parquet and ORC that compress well and read only needed columns; intelligent caching for frequently accessed data; and dynamic partitioning by time, geography or other dimensions for pruning and parallelism.

The pipeline shift is from ETL to ELT. Instead of extracting, transforming and loading across several systems, with latency and failure points at each hop, you extract and load first, then transform in place. Fewer copies, less maintenance, and more time analysing data instead of fixing pipelines.

## Governance can't be manual

At scale, governance has to be automated: data quality checks that flag anomalies before they reach analytics, complete lineage and audit trails, role-based access control and encryption. Richa cited results from lakehouse implementations of around 60% less maintenance effort, ETL workflows about 45% faster and total cost of ownership down roughly 40%, and says the bigger gain is agility.

Her implementation advice: choose platforms that support open table formats such as Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg or Apache Hudi to avoid lock-in; migrate in phases, starting with non-critical workloads; and train engineers and analysts in both warehouse and lake thinking, because it's as much about people and process as technology.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects planning a move off a separate lake and warehouse, and data managers in regulated industries who need the governance story to hold up. If you already run Iceberg with Data Vault, it's a refresher; the related talks go into DataOps and ingestion.

Title: Sentiment analysis that never leaves the browser
Description: Ujjwala Modepalli of Wells Fargo showed at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 how TensorFlow.js, Web Workers and IndexedDB run text analytics client-side.
Body:
Your analytics know a user clicked "Contact support". The message they typed afterwards knows they were furious. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Ujjwala Modepalli, Senior Credit Risk Specialist at Wells Fargo, showed how to read that text with NLP that runs entirely in the browser, so the raw words never reach your servers.

## Clicks tell you what, text tells you why

Her starting point: traditional analytics track clicks, scrolls and time on page, but every form, chat message, search query and feedback comment carries signals about emotion, intent, confusion and satisfaction. Those signals have mostly been ignored because processing language meant expensive server-side pipelines.

Moving the work to the client gives three wins in her framing: privacy (the text stays on the device, which simplifies compliance), real-time feedback (sentiment can update as the user types, so the interface can offer help), and efficiency (users "bring their own compute", with GPU acceleration in the browser, so server costs and latency drop).

## The toolkit and the architecture

The libraries are small and familiar:

- **Natural** and **Compromise** for tokenisation, part-of-speech tagging and entity recognition, with no external dependencies.
- **TensorFlow.js**, using WebGL for GPU acceleration, for sentiment scoring and text classification with pre-trained models.
- **Web Workers** to keep NLP off the main thread so the UI never freezes, and **IndexedDB** to store results locally across sessions.

Service workers cache models for offline use, and results flow into a state layer (Redux or Context API) that updates React components. She described it as distributed computing at the browser level.

## Real-time sentiment without analysing every keystroke

The pipeline loads a lightweight pre-trained model (a small transformer or LSTM variant) at startup. Input events are debounced so analysis runs after the user pauses, not on every key. Text is normalised, tokenised (stop words removed, stemming applied) and vectorised with TF-IDF or embeddings, then scored. The score shows up in the UI as a colour, an emoji or a gauge.

On top of that she showed topic modelling with k-means or hierarchical clustering on vectorised snippets, so clusters like billing issues or feature requests form and update as new messages arrive. Custom React hooks talk to the workers, context providers share results across the app, and D3.js draws timelines, word clouds and cluster graphs.

## Four kinds of users hiding in your text boxes

The segmentation section is the most product-friendly part. Language separates hesitant users ("maybe", "I think", lots of questions), competitive switchers who name other products or pricing, high-intent prospects with decisive phrasing, and at-risk users whose negative sentiment and cancellation words signal churn early. She layers that into features (polarity, readability, emotional intensity), behavioural metrics (how often and how fast people write, whether their tone shifts) and finally scores such as a satisfaction index or churn probability.

## Performance and consent are part of the design

Client-side models are heavy, so she lazy-loads TensorFlow models only when needed, batches inference to use the GPU better, debounces input and caches results in IndexedDB under hashed keys so repeated text isn't re-analysed. On privacy: explicit opt-in that explains what's analysed, users can view, export or delete their data, stored text is encrypted, and analytics switch off in private browsing.

Use cases she listed: routing frustrated or urgent support chats to live agents, finding content gaps from search intent, and auto-tagging feedback as bugs, feature requests or praise.

## Who should watch

Frontend and product engineers who want sentiment or intent signals without building a data pipeline, and anyone whose privacy review blocks sending free text to a server. It's an architecture and pattern talk rather than a live coding session.

Title: Conf42 Kube Native 2025: GPUs, fewer clusters and regulated AI
Description: Conf42 Kube Native 2025 roundup - GPU sharing with vCluster, fewer environments, Dapr and eBPF, defence in depth, and AI in regulated industries on Kubernetes.
Body:
Conf42 Kube Native 2025 ran online on October 16, 2025, with 53 talks, which makes it one of the larger events in the series. Two conversations ran side by side. One was about Kubernetes itself: sharing GPUs, cutting environment sprawl, observing clusters with eBPF, and securing them in depth. The other was about what enterprises now run on it, above all AI workloads in banks, insurers, and hospitals, where compliance is part of the architecture.

Every session is on the [Conf42 Kube Native 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/kubenative2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBfaAPyif8OXN3e1XcXeO2A).

## GPUs are the new scarce resource

[Piotr Zaniewski](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Piotr_Zaniewski_sandboxes_gpu_multitenant), Head of Engineering Enablement at vCluster, had the most hands-on pitch of the day: in 30 minutes, spin up vCluster sandboxes, drop NVIDIA's open-source KAI Scheduler inside, and use fractional GPUs to share expensive hardware across tenants without deadlocks or a cluster per team. Multi-tenant, multi-scheduler, with the YAML to copy.

[Deepika Annam](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Deepika_Annam_optimization_reinforcement_performance) of Nike went further up the stack, applying deep reinforcement learning to pod scheduling, autoscaling, and resource management. [Jyotirmoy Sundi](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Jyotirmoy_Sundi_reinforcement_learning_distributed), co-founder and CTO of Votal.ai, covered scaling reinforcement learning with human feedback across distributed cloud systems.

## How many clusters do you really need?

[Arsh Sharma](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Arsh_Sharma_kubernetes_environments_scalability), Senior DevRel Engineer at MetalBear, asked the question in the title that every platform team should ask: one environment for production, one for staging, one for CI, one per developer so nobody blocks staging. Do you need them all? The talk shows how to reuse existing environments for development and CI, lowering cloud costs and cluster sprawl.

Platform developers also got two takes on simplifying the code itself. [Christophe Gigax](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Christophe_Gigax_dapr_architectures_cloudnative), Cloud Solution Architect at Hager Group, showed how Dapr exposes state management, pub/sub, and other building blocks as standard APIs, so microservices stop reimplementing them. [Anupama Pathirage](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Anupama_Pathirage_ballerina_integration_opensource), Head of Engineering for integration at WSO2, presented Ballerina, an open-source language with cloud deployment constructs built into the code.

## Resilience patterns that hold up

The architecture track was strong on concrete patterns. [Rahul Singh Thakur](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Rahul_Singh_Thakur_sharding_uptime_architecture) of Salesforce gave a practical guide to multi-zone sharded microservices with intelligent request routing. [Karthik Reddy Beereddy](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Karthik_Reddy_Beereddy_streaming_redis_selfhealing) of LexisNexis Risk Solutions covered self-healing streaming with Redis Streams and Azure Event Hubs, and [Shalini Katyayani Koney](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Shalini_Katyayani_Koney_kafka_streaming_scalable) of Walmart scaled Kafka on Kubernetes with StatefulSet tuning, autoscaling, and GitOps. [Ashif Anwar](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Ashif_Anwar_azure_eventdriven_patterns) of Wolters Kluwer and [Dhruvesh Talati](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Dhruvesh_Talati_resilience_design_recovery) of Ally added event-driven patterns on AKS and architectures for crisis response.

On the observability side, [Alejandro Mercado](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Alejandro_Mercado_observability_kubernetes_ebpf), DevOps Lead at Michael Page, made the case for eBPF-powered observability for incident detection and root cause analysis, and [Srinivas Pagadala Sekar](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Srinivas_Pagadala_Sekar_observability_llms_paas) of Karsun Solutions looked at LLM-assisted diagnostics to cut MTTR and alert noise.

## Defence in depth, and the post-quantum clock

[Karthikeyan Thirumalaisamy](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Karthikeyan_Thirumalaisamy_security_missioncritical_kubernetes), a Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft, laid out a defence-in-depth blueprint for mission-critical services on AKS, EKS, and GKE, covering insider threats, supply chain attacks, and runtime exploits. [Derek Asir Muthurajan Caleb](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Derek_Asir_Muthurajan_Caleb_quantum_security_infrastructure) of Broadcom looked further ahead, at moving Kubernetes clusters and service-to-service traffic to quantum-resistant cryptography. [Vivek Koodakkara Shanmughan](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Vivek_Koodakkara_Shanmughan_identity_keycloak_deployment) of Aryaka Networks described a regional hub model for running Keycloak identity across a global SASE deployment, and [Satya Purella](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Satya_Purella_integration_fintech_platforms) of Fifth Third Bank covered secure integration platforms for fintech.

## AI in regulated industries

The biggest cluster of talks was about running AI on Kubernetes where regulators are watching. In finance, [Ashish Dibouliya](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Ashish_Dibouliya_banking_compliance_governance) of Webster Bank presented a Kubernetes-ready AI data governance framework with drift detection, [Jaydeep Taralkar](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Jaydeep_Taralkar_finance_ml_orchestration) of UBS focused on responsible ML at scale, [Kiran Purushotham](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Kiran_Purushotham_trading_llm_insight) of JPMorgan Chase showed swarms of LLM agents for market insight, and [Manoj Kalakoti](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Manoj_Kalakoti_finops_costgovernance_autonomous) of Apple embedded FinOps cost governance into the delivery pipeline. [Manisha Sengupta](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Manisha_Sengupta_finance_risks_modernization) of Brown Brothers Harriman covered the attack vectors that come with AI in finance.

In healthcare, [Tharun Nallamothu](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Tharun_Nallamothu_copilot_clinical_workflows) of Microsoft presented Dragon Copilot, an AI clinical assistant built around ambient recording for documentation. [Manikesh Iruku](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Manikesh_Iruku_ehr_pipelines_accuracy) of Amazon built LLM auditing for EHR pipelines, [Amala Umakanth](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Amala_Umakanth_genai_healthcare_fraud) of McKinsey applied GenAI to claims processing and fraud, and [Venus Garg](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Venus_Garg_ethical_ai_trust) of Boston University asked whether Kube-native stacks are ready for the bias, privacy, and trust questions healthcare AI raises.

## The rest of the lineup

Data engineering got its own track, including [Sruthi Erra Hareram](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Sruthi_Erra_Hareram_etl_airflow_optimization) of TELUS Digital on tuning PySpark and Airflow on Kubernetes and [Vamsi Pulusu](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Vamsi_Pulusu_datapipeline_streaming_modern) of Ford on moving from legacy ETL to streaming and lakehouses. [Bhavana Reddy Chadagonda](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Bhavana_Reddy_Chadagonda_abtesting_experimentation_careers) of Intuit offered career advice through A/B testing techniques like CUPED. And for something different, [Chandan Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Chandan_Kumar_lighting_immersion_responsive) of Google explained pre-computed surround lighting that reacts in under 100ms, while [Preeti Sali](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Preeti_Sali_ev_charging_infrastructure) of Ford covered cloud-native EV charging infrastructure.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to gold sponsor [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

For earlier editions, start with [Conf42 Kube Native 2024](https://www.conf42.com/kubenative2024). Then go and count your clusters.

Title: Experiment design, not dashboards, is the data science career moat
Description: Bhavana Reddy Chadagonda at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on picking experiment designs, CUPED variance reduction, A/B testing LLM prompts and career growth.
Body:
To find out whether weights slow runners down, don't compare raw mile times; compare each runner to their own baseline. That small example carries much of Bhavana Reddy Chadagonda's talk at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025. Bhavana, an independent researcher with over a decade designing and scaling experimentation, argued that experiment design (picking the right method, cutting variance, avoiding the classic traps) is one of the most valuable skills in data science, and now essential for evaluating prompts and LLMs.

She pitches it as a field guide: part methods, part platform, part career advice. The statistics stay practical and the career section is unusually specific.

## Let constraints pick the design

Bhavana's rule is that business constraints choose the experiment design, not the other way round. Her menu: classic A/B tests for features and UI changes; multivariate and factorial designs to learn interaction effects; holdout studies for long-term and network effects that build over weeks or months. When traffic patterns complicate things, switchback experiments rotate the same unit through both variants over time, which suits marketplaces and two-sided platforms. Geo experiments randomise by region when user-level randomisation would spill over.

When randomisation isn't possible at all, she walks through the credible alternatives: difference-in-differences, interrupted time series (look for a level or slope break exactly at the intervention), and synthetic control (build a weighted virtual twin of the treated city or state from untreated ones).

## Statistics as business skills

Rather than re-teach p-values, she ties each concept to why a business should care. Hypothesis testing forces clear success criteria before launch. Communicating uncertainty honestly builds trust, because leaders expect ranges and risk, not perfection. Effect size and power keep you on changes that matter. Multiple-testing discipline protects against false wins when a company runs many experiments a month. Sequential methods support faster, adaptive learning.

## Cut variance, ship faster

The most practical section is variance reduction. Sample size scales with variance, so halving variance roughly halves the sample you need and the time you wait. Her toolkit: regression adjustment with pre-period covariates (the umbrella for CUPED); blocking or stratification at assignment; metric engineering such as winsorising outliers and log-transforming skewed metrics; cluster-aware analysis for geo and switchback tests; and exposure hygiene, counting only eligible, actually exposed users and freezing event definitions before launch.

CUPED gets the runner example. Experiment mile time is driven largely by how fast each runner already was, so using baseline mile time from before the experiment strips out that explainable variance and isolates the effect of the weights. Her best practices: pick covariates highly correlated with the metric, use more than one if they help, make sure they come strictly from before the experiment, and impute missing values. She also points to CUPAC, which swaps the regression for a machine learning model that predicts the baseline.

## Experiments for prompts and models

The section that earns the event slot applies all of this to LLMs: comparing prompt templates, few-shot examples and system instructions; benchmarking models or fine-tuned versions; testing RAG retrieval strategies, chunking and ranking; measuring personalisation; and systematically probing for harmful outputs, bias and hallucination. Online, that means A/B, multivariate or contextual bandits; offline, automated frameworks, synthetic data and LLM-as-judge for faster iteration.

Her warning list is worth pinning up: sample ratio mismatch, logging gaps, a unit of randomisation that differs from the unit of analysis, interference between groups, peeking, metric drift and seasonality. If it seems too good to be true, it probably is.

## The career map

She closes with a portfolio plan (document realistic experiments end to end, contribute to libraries such as statsmodels or PyMC, show business impact) and an IC ladder from solid A/B fundamentals at entry level to shaping the experimentation platform and roadmap at staff level.

## Who should watch

Analysts and data scientists who want to specialise, engineers building experiment-ready systems, and anyone A/B testing prompts with more enthusiasm than statistics. Seasoned experimentation leads will find the methods familiar but the career framing useful for mentoring.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [A/B testing platform at scale](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2023_Riteek_Srivastava_ab_testing_platform_at_scale) by Riteek Srivastava at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023, for the platform side.
- [AI-Driven Testing for Conversational AI: LLM-as-Judge, Generative QA, and Scalable Automation](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Yash_Panjari_testing_conversational_automation) by Yash Panjari at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025.
- [Fast Confidence Estimation for Classification and Regression models](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Andrei_Stroganov_Andrei_Visochan_estimation_regression_confidence) by Andrei Stroganov and Andrei Visochan at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.

Title: From single pods to planetary scale
Description: This is how modern infrastructure lives
Body:
# Kubernetes is no longer just infrastructure

Kubernetes used to be the thing you learned so you could deploy containers “properly”.

Now it’s where streaming platforms live. Where AI runs. Where healthcare systems process claims. Where finance does fraud detection. Where compliance, security, data, and automation all collide. No pressure.

Conf42 Kube Native 2025 is a snapshot of that reality.

This conference brings together forty seven talks across ten tracks, covering Kubernetes, AI, LLMs, data, security, compliance, healthcare, IoT, and cloud-native architecture at scale. It’s not about getting started. It’s about what happens after Kubernetes becomes the backbone of everything.

AI is deeply embedded throughout the program. Container-native ML, GenAI pipelines, ethical AI in healthcare, predictive maintenance, churn detection, and AI-driven finance all show up, running directly on Kubernetes. These sessions focus on production systems, not experiments.

Architecture and scalability are front and center. From scaling Kafka to hundreds of thousands of messages per second, to event-driven patterns, multi-zone sharding, API gateways, and self-healing streaming platforms, this is Kubernetes pushed hard in real environments.

Security, governance, and compliance get serious attention too. Zero trust, AI data governance, regulated workloads, quantum-resistant infrastructure, and cloud-native risk management appear across industries like finance, healthcare, and public services.

If Kubernetes is the foundation your systems are built on, this one’s for you. Cloud native keeps expanding, and Kubernetes is right in the middle of it. Still.

Title: An agentic control plane that keeps micro-frontends in sync
Description: Jyoti Kunal Shah of ADP showed at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 how AI agents detect API drift and patch micro-frontends behind canary releases.
Body:
Microservices let teams ship independently, until one of them renames a field and three React micro-frontends start rendering blanks. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Jyoti Kunal Shah, Director of Application Development at ADP, proposed an "agentic control plane": AI agents that spot that kind of API drift, write the adapter, and ship it behind a canary with automatic rollback.

## The moving target problem

Her starting point will be familiar to anyone in a large frontend org. Micro-frontends bring the microservice idea to the UI: teams build modules in React or Angular and plug them into a shared container. Every team has its own framework, release cycle and dependencies.

So when a backend adds an endpoint, changes a payload or gets slower, the frontends that depend on it have to adapt right away. If they don't, users hit runtime mismatches and broken screens. She calls it the moving target problem: the architecture is decentralised on paper, but the dependencies stay tightly coupled in practice. With 25 or more services and 10 or more micro-frontends, the number of version combinations explodes, and coordinating through email, tickets and manual QA stops scaling.

## Four planes: see, think, act, stay inside the lines

The control plane she described has four layers:

- **Observation**: telemetry from OpenTelemetry, API gateway logs and real user monitoring. This is how the system sees itself.
- **Cognition**: reinforcement learning agents tune scaling and configuration, LLM agents generate code or config patches, and contract agents watch schema compatibility.
- **Execution**: GitOps pipelines and service mesh controllers apply changes through canary and blue-green releases, with automatic rollback.
- **Policy and governance**: safety envelopes, approval thresholds and audit logs.

The loop runs from perception through reasoning to action. A renamed field is detected by the observation plane, the cognition plane finds which UI components read it, an LLM agent proposes a minimal diff or adapter, and the execution plane deploys it to a canary. If service level objectives hold, the change is promoted; if not, it rolls back. Nobody files a ticket.

## The case study numbers

She described a global e-commerce company with 25 microservices and 10 micro-frontends that adopted the approach. Before, API changes regularly broke frontends and delayed deployments. Afterwards she reported adaptation latency improved by 35% and frontend errors dropped by 40%, with less manual coordination and an audit trail for every automated change. The talk doesn't go into how those numbers were measured, so treat them as one organisation's results.

## Trust is the hard part

The challenges section is the most honest part of the talk. Reinforcement learning needs good telemetry to train on. LLM-generated code needs sandbox validation before anyone trusts it. Governance is complicated, because someone has to write policies that balance agent freedom against safety. Her conclusion is that AI should augment engineering teams rather than replace them, which is also the reason the policy plane exists.

Looking ahead, she pointed to explainable reinforcement learning, knowledge graphs that map dependencies between services and UIs so drift can be predicted before it happens, and federated learning so teams can share adaptation strategies without sharing sensitive data.

## Who should watch

Platform and frontend architects running micro-frontends at scale, especially if contract breakage between backend and UI teams is a recurring incident theme. It's a framework talk without code, so bring your own implementation ideas. The governance section is worth showing to whoever has to sign off on agents that write code.

## Related talks

- [Destructuring frontend monoliths with Microfrontends](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Trishul_Goel_monolith_Microfrontends) covers how teams get into micro-frontends in the first place.
- [Harnessing Microfrontends: Building Scalable, Reliable, and Secure Platforms for Complex Web Applications](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Venkata_Sai_Manoj_Pasupuleti_microfrontends_platforms_applications) looks at the platform side of the same architecture.
- [Engineering Cloud Infrastructure for Agentic AI: MLOps and Self-Healing Systems](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Amit_Anand_agentic_cloud_healing) takes the self-healing idea down to the infrastructure layer.

[Watch Jyoti Kunal Shah's talk](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Jyoti_Kunal_Shah_agentic_autonomous_micro)

Title: Multi-agent AI fits ERP when autonomy is bounded and logged
Description: Kasee Palaniappan (Ariba, SAP America) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on multi-agent AI for ERP and hybrid IT, from frameworks to bounded autonomy.
Body:
A marketing chatbot here, a finance tool there, an onboarding bot somewhere else, and a human copying data between them: that's how Kasee Palaniappan describes most enterprise AI so far. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Kasee, from Ariba Inc (SAP America), made the case for coordinated multi-agent systems across ERP and hybrid IT, plugged into existing systems through APIs, with bounded autonomy, audit logs and a human on every critical decision.

It's a concise strategy talk for people who own enterprise systems. It names real frameworks and use cases, and spends as much time on the brakes as on the engine.

## Think team, not chatbot

Kasee's definition of a multi-agent system is helpfully plain. Stop picturing one AI and picture a team of specialists: a data analyst agent, a compliance agent, an inventory agent, each with a role, sometimes subdivided further. They communicate, collaborate and delegate, and they work towards a high-level business objective. His example goal: reduce procurement cost by 10%, with agents splitting the work and minimal human intervention.

## Four pillars of orchestration

He organises the architecture into four pillars. Goal-directed planning breaks a big objective into executable tasks per agent, and he calls it the most important. Dynamic reflection lets the system review its own successes and failures and improve. Tool orchestration gives agents access to real APIs, databases and ERPs; without it they're just chatting. Collaborative problem solving lets agents share insights across departmental silos.

For building it today he points to three frameworks: LangGraph for graph-based, cyclical workflows where agents may need to rethink a step; AutoGen from Microsoft for conversational agents that solve tasks together; and CrewAI for role-based crews defined like a team with a hierarchy.

## Where it lands in the business

The use cases are the back-office ones where ERP lives. Procurement: supplier evaluation and contract compliance monitoring around the clock across global supply chains. Finance: invoice processing, real-time expense reconciliation, and anomaly detection that also generates the audit trail. HR: onboarding workflows and conversational answers to employee questions. Document management: classify, extract, structure and route documents to the right person. He cited figures from multi-agent deployments of a 68% reduction in processing time, 92% better accuracy on tasks like data extraction and 45% better cost efficiency.

## Don't rip and replace

The question every ERP owner asks is how this works with a massive SAP or Oracle estate. Kasee's answer is modularity: agents connect to existing cloud and on-prem systems through standard APIs and middleware, so you can automate one small piece of a process first. That lowers risk and gets value earlier without betting the ERP on it.

## Bounded autonomy is the safety model

He's direct about the three hard problems: security and data privacy when agents touch sensitive data; scalability in compute and cost as you go from ten agents to a thousand; and governance, because when an agent decides on someone's behalf, regulators will want to know what it considered and why. His three safeguards: comprehensive audit logging of every decision, action and piece of data an agent touches; bounded autonomy, with clear operational limits and programmed escalation paths to humans; and incremental deployment, starting with a low-risk, high-value use case. His recurring line: don't try to boil the ocean.

The roadmap follows: foundation, pilot, scale, optimise, ending in what he calls a self-optimising digital ecosystem.

## Who should watch

Enterprise architects and ERP owners being asked about agents, and IT leaders who need a shared vocabulary for agent roles, frameworks and governance before a vendor supplies one. If you've already shipped LangGraph or CrewAI in production, the related talks get into implementation patterns.

- [AI Orchestration: Getting Super Agents to Complete a Mission](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Batandwa_Mgutsi_ai_orchestration_superagents) by Batandwa Mgutsi at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024.

Title: Agentic search splits one question across four kinds of agents
Description: At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Ajitha Buvanachandran showed how research, analysis, domain and QA agents in Node.js turn search into answers.
Body:
Search engines hand you a pile of documents and wish you luck. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Ajitha Buvanachandran, a principal machine learning and generative AI engineer at an investment firm (listed on the talk page with Anna University), argued that the fix is to stop retrieving and start investigating: split the question across specialised agents, and let Node.js do the coordinating.

The talk is an architecture overview with one worked example, which makes it a good map before you start wiring agents together yourself.

## The question nobody's keyword index can answer

Her running example is a financial company whose leadership asks why mobile banking satisfaction went down and what to do about it. A keyword search matches every document that contains "mobile", "banking", "satisfaction" and "decline", including hardware specs for mobile phones. Someone then spends days reading.

Semantic search does better: it understands that the question is about customer experience and returns survey results, NPS scores and feedback analysis. But a human still has to put the story together.

The third generation, agentic search, aims to hand back the story itself. In her example the agents pull metrics from CRM data, app store reviews, support tickets and social media monitoring, notice that the satisfaction drop lines up with a mobile app release, tie user complaints to navigation complexity from a UI redesign, and check the finding against seasonal effects and sampling bias before anyone sees a report.

## Four roles, four phases

The architecture has four agent types:

- **Research agents** break the query into parts and fetch data from databases, documents and external sources.
- **Analysis agents** look for patterns and correlations using statistics and ML.
- **Domain expert agents** add industry context, such as how similar dips played out at other banks.
- **Quality checking agents** look for bias, accuracy problems and gaps.

They work in four phases: query interpretation, distributed execution (research and early analysis run in parallel), collaborative synthesis, and quality validation before delivery. The validation step is the part most hand-rolled agent demos skip, and here it has its own agent.

## Why JavaScript gets the coordinator job

Her case for JavaScript is about the event loop, not about raw model performance. Coordinating agents mostly means waiting: on LLM calls, vector lookups and other services. Node.js's non-blocking I/O handles many concurrent agent requests without stalling, and Express or NestJS give you the microservice scaffolding. The building blocks she lists are LangChain.js for chains, agents and streaming; a vector database for retrieval-augmented generation over private data; message queues and event buses for passing messages between agents; and a validation pipeline at the end.

The rollout path is practical: define agent personas and protocols, build an event-driven orchestration layer, connect vector stores, semantic search and LLM APIs, then add quality pipelines before production.

## The bill comes in latency and tokens

She doesn't pretend multi-agent setups are free. Coordination adds overhead, which she suggests fighting with caching, parallel execution and streaming partial results. LLM costs pile up fast, so batch calls, cache results and pick the model per task. Debugging a distributed agent pipeline needs logging and tracing across the whole orchestration path, and the QA agents have to catch bias in the data as well as in the model output. Her framing is that these are engineering problems with known fixes, not reasons to stay away.

## Who should watch

JavaScript and Node.js developers asked to "add AI search" to an internal data platform, and architects deciding whether agent orchestration belongs in their existing Node services. If you want code walkthroughs, this one stays at diagram level; pair it with something hands-on.

## Related talks

- [Implementing Agentic AI Solutions in Python from scratch](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Craig_West_agentic_ai_django) builds the agent loop by hand, the hands-on follow-up to this architecture.
- [Beyond Text Generation: The Rise of Agentic AI and Its Transformative Potential](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Naman_Goyal_generation_text_agentic) steps back to what makes a system agentic at all.
- [Langchain with Golang](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Alexandre_Evangelista_de_Souza_langchain) shows the same chain-and-agent ideas outside JavaScript.

[Watch Ajitha Buvanachandran's talk](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Ajitha_Buvanachandran_agentic_search_multi)

Title: Four layers of defense for mission-critical managed Kubernetes
Description: Karthikeyan Thirumalaisamy of Microsoft lays out at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 a cloud, cluster, container and code defense-in-depth model for AKS, EKS and GKE.
Body:
Managed Kubernetes takes the control plane off your hands; it doesn't take the cluster admin with stolen credentials off your threat model. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Karthikeyan Thirumalaisamy, Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft, presented a defense-in-depth model for mission-critical services on AKS, EKS and GKE, built on the four Cs of cloud-native security: cloud, cluster, container and code.

The structure is the selling point. After each layer he asks the same question, what gap is still open, and the next layer answers it.

## What counts as mission-critical

He defines mission-critical services as systems whose failure has serious financial, safety or reputational consequences: payment processing and fraud detection in finance, EHR platforms and medical monitoring in healthcare, secure communications in defence, and code signing, security scanning and package verification in the software supply chain. All handle sensitive or regulated data.

The threats in managed Kubernetes are a familiar list taken seriously: insider risk at cloud, cluster and tenant admin level; misconfigurations such as permissive rules, public control-plane endpoints or missing encryption; malware injected through base images, registries or CI/CD; runtime exploits and container escapes; and supply-chain attacks on build systems and dependencies. His point is that the default protections from your cloud provider cover only part of that list.

## Cloud and cluster: shrink the surface

At the cloud layer the tools are network design: a hub-and-spoke topology with the hub handling routing, inspection and policy while spokes isolate workloads; strict firewall rules on both inbound and outbound traffic; and private clusters and endpoints so the control plane and container registry talk only over internal IPs.

That only protects the perimeter, so the cluster layer goes inside. A private API server with RBAC and least privilege. etcd encrypted at rest with a key management service, so a stolen disk doesn't hand over your secrets. Kubelet anonymous access disabled and ports restricted. Network policies to limit pod-to-pod and namespace traffic, cutting lateral movement. And OPA Gatekeeper as an admission controller to block privileged pods, require signed images and enforce configuration standards before anything runs.

## Container: trust the hardware, not the host

Even a well-secured cluster can lose a container to a kernel exploit or a breakout. Thirumalaisamy's answer is confidential computing. Confidential VMs use hardware-backed trusted execution environments to encrypt memory and isolate the VM from the hypervisor and host. Confidential containers extend that to individual workloads, running them in secure enclaves so code and data in use stay protected even if the kernel, container runtime or host is compromised. This is also the layer that answers the insider question: a privileged cloud operator can't read what the hardware won't decrypt for them.

## Code: lock down what actually runs

The last gap is the application itself: code that downloads packages, spawns processes or runs unverified scripts at runtime. The controls here are signed images from trusted registries, distroless images with no shell or package manager for attackers to use, immutable containers that are rebuilt rather than patched in place, seccomp profiles restricting system calls, and Falco for real-time detection of privilege escalation, unexpected file access and unknown processes.

He presents the four layers together as closing the known gaps, so that a breach of one layer still leaves three standing. That is the model's promise rather than a guarantee, but the layered argument holds up.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers running regulated workloads on managed Kubernetes, and anyone who needs a clear structure to audit a cluster against. If you already run confidential containers in production, the earlier sections will be review.

Title: Natural-language data access only works on top of a semantic layer
Description: Jimish Kadakia (Snowflake) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on LLMs for SQL generation, conversational pipelines and the governance that keeps them honest.
Body:
Asking for customer retention rates by region for quarter four is a lovely prompt, right up until the model guesses what your company means by retention. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Jimish Kadakia, a solutions architect at Snowflake with around 12 years in data and analytics, argued that LLMs can open cloud data to business users, but only when context, validation, governance and feedback loops are built in first.

It's a practitioner's overview rather than a product demo. He mentions Snowflake's Cortex Analyst and Snowflake Intelligence, and dbt's use of LLMs, as examples, but the advice applies to any warehouse.

## From SQL tickets to plain questions

Jimish starts with the traditional setup: data engineers write complex SQL views and stored procedures, script and babysit pipelines, and handle monitoring, security and governance. Business users file a ticket and wait. LLMs, he argues, go well beyond chatbots and content generation here; they can bridge the gap between business users and technical data infrastructure.

His three applications: query generation (natural language to optimised SQL), pipeline orchestration through conversation (rerun last night's job after a source fix), and real-time analytics (where are sales high, which region is hurting).

## Four components, and context comes first

The core of the talk is four components that make this work.

**Context optimisation.** Give the model business information and data relationships. His concrete recommendation is a semantic layer: semantic views or models that capture business terms, calculation logic and how entities relate. The more useful context the model has, the more accurate the query.

**Prompt design patterns.** The way a question is written shapes the answer, so build reusable templates that guide business users to consistent results.

**Validation.** Safeguards that check data integrity and output quality, with rigorous testing before anything reaches business users in production.

**Feedback loops.** Humans refine prompts based on real usage and model performance, so accuracy improves over time.

## Three things you can actually build

His examples make it concrete. Ad hoc querying: a user asks for retention by region; the system generates SQL that a technical user can review before it runs, or, for non-technical users, returns a table or chart directly. Pipeline management for developers and admins: run the nightly customer aggregation pipeline by asking for it, instead of hunting through a scheduler. Data exploration embedded in BI tools, with a natural-language search bar that reshapes existing views.

The review-before-run option is the quiet good idea here. You get the speed without letting an LLM fire unchecked SQL at production.

## The hard parts

He doesn't skip them. Accuracy and hallucination need validation frameworks and guardrails, because a model that starts down a wrong path can keep confidently producing wrong answers. Governance and security are independent of LLMs but more urgent with them: privacy regulations, reviewed permissions, and keeping PII and policy-restricted company data out of what the model sees. Fine-tuning on domain schemas and business terminology helps. Performance at scale needs enough compute without wasting it. His governance checklist: access control, automatic column masking, role-based access, complete audit trails of LLM-generated queries, and human approval before execution where required.

His rollout mantra: start small with one domain or process, collaborate across business, engineering, security and compliance, test rigorously, scale incrementally.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and analytics leads being asked to put a chat box on the warehouse, and platform owners who need a checklist for doing it without leaking data or trust. If you've already shipped text-to-SQL in production, the related talks go deeper into orchestration and semantic consistency.
