Title: Riddles show where ChatGPT predicts instead of understanding
Description: Aroma Rodrigues (Microsoft) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 probes GPT-3-era ChatGPT with riddles, translated Hindi puzzles and word problems to test AGI claims.
Body:
Ask ChatGPT "when is a door no longer a door?" and it gives you a dictionary answer. Tell it the question is a riddle and it says: when it's ajar. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Aroma Rodrigues of Microsoft used dozens of riddles like that one to probe what a pure language model actually does, and her conclusion is blunt: ChatGPT is not AGI, and the places it fails tell you why.

The experiments were run on the GPT-3 version of ChatGPT on a free personal account, which she flags up front. That's the point rather than a weakness: before retrieval and tool layers were bolted on, you could watch the language model think without it looking things up.

## Riddle mode is a context, and it sticks

Once ChatGPT decides it's in a riddle conversation, it stays there. It answers classic riddles well (all twelve months have at least 28 days; a hole makes a bucket lighter; today comes before yesterday in a dictionary) and Aroma suspects most of those were simply in the training data. The interesting part is what happens off the beaten path. Asked what has a bottom at the top, it said a staircase. The answer is legs. Prompted for another answer, it invented a second, equally confident story. She describes the model spinning an imaginative narrative and then bending the answer to fit it.

The same sticky context breaks maths. Asked how many apples ten rabbits eat in ten minutes if five eat five in five, it stayed in riddle mode and produced reasoning she calls incredibly weird. A bus-passenger word problem fell apart as the model lost track of its own running total, which she compares to young children losing count across multiple steps.

## Translated riddles strip away the memory

Her best methodological move: to get riddles the model probably hadn't seen, she took riddles from Hindi and regional sources with no common English translation. The results got much stranger. One crude translation produced the claim that ducks give both milk and eggs. A riddle about ants (two ants ahead, two behind) got the wrong answer, and she bets the classic version with ducks would have got the right one. A question about ten birds on a wall, one shot with an arrow, got the arithmetic answer of nine, as if birds were inanimate objects that don't fly away.

The pattern she draws out: the model handles a familiar surface form, and stumbles when the same logic arrives in unfamiliar words. Your parents have six sons and each has a sister; it added six and six, twice.

## What would count as AGI, anyway

The second half takes the historical definitions one by one: the Turing test, the coffee test, the robot college student test, the employment test. Her view is that several of them are either already passed or not very meaningful, which says more about the tests than about the models. Her own definition leans on observation. Humans learn by perceiving the physical world, not only by reading about it; the model relies on available knowledge, from training or from search.

She closes with her own heavy ChatGPT use: good at context-linked creative writing in theory, but in practice it loses the thread, and a travel itinerary it wrote assumed she could cover a half-hour cab ride in about ten minutes. Retrieval helps today's versions answer her riddles correctly, but she calls that cheating in the riddle-game sense: looking up the answer isn't solving it.

## Who should watch

Anyone building on LLMs who wants an intuitive feel for failure modes before reading the papers: context lock-in, multi-step arithmetic drift, surface-form matching. It's a long, conversational talk built on examples rather than benchmarks, so treat it as a field notebook, not a study. People who want rigorous evaluation methods should pair it with the related talks.

Title: Ship AI features as micro frontends, not monolith releases
Description: Linga Annela at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on Module Federation, edge-side composition and WebAssembly for adding AI features to large web apps.
Body:
Adding a chatbot to a big monolithic front end usually means touching shared code, rerunning the whole regression suite and waiting for the next release train. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Linga Annela argued that micro frontends let teams ship AI features (a chatbot, a recommendation widget, a predictive dashboard) as independent units with their own stack and schedule, and walked through the techniques that make that practical.

It is an architecture overview rather than a hands-on demo: one pattern per slide, explained at the level you would use to brief a team before a migration.

## Micro frontends are microservices for the browser

Linga's definition is the familiar one: split one big JavaScript app into smaller, independently deployable pieces, each owned by a team or domain, each free to pick React, Vue, Angular or plain JavaScript. The AI angle is that a feature team can put a conversational assistant or a personalisation engine live without touching the core application, and run experiments in isolation. The talk also cites industry figures for faster delivery and A/B testing; it doesn't name the studies, so treat them as directional.

## The toolkit, one technique at a time

- **Module Federation in Webpack 5.** Applications, even ones built with different frameworks, share code at runtime. You expose a component, say the recommendation widget, from one project and consume it in another without rebuilding or redeploying, and share common dependencies like React to keep bundles down.
- **Edge-side composition.** Instead of assembling micro frontends in the browser, the CDN stitches together only the pieces each route needs, which helps time to interactive and lets each piece cache independently.
- **WebAssembly for inference.** Compile models from TensorFlow or PyTorch to WebAssembly and run predictions, image classification or sentiment analysis on the client, with no server round trip and sensitive data staying on the device.
- **API patterns.** Plain REST endpoints owned by each micro frontend, so teams can update models independently, or GraphQL Federation, where each micro frontend contributes a subgraph to one typed schema.

## State is the hard part

Linga flags state management as the most important piece of distributed front ends. The layered approach in the talk: keep state local to each micro frontend where possible, use custom events or a lightweight shared store for what must be shared, and use optimistic rendering so the UI stays consistent when AI features are loaded or swapped at runtime. Anyone who has watched two micro frontends disagree about who the logged-in user is will appreciate the emphasis.

Performance comes next: lazy-load components on demand, share common dependencies instead of duplicating them, cache API responses and predictions in service workers, and deploy to edge runtimes.

## Start with one widget

The roadmap is sensible and modest. Find where the monolith blocks AI work, draw boundaries around business domains, set up Module Federation with shared dependencies and pipelines, then ship one small AI feature, like a chatbot or analytics widget, as a proof of concept before scaling. Linga mentions applying the approach to an e-commerce project with customer, admin and driver apps, still in progress at the time of the talk.

## Who should watch

Front-end leads with a large single-page app and a queue of AI feature requests, and architects weighing micro frontends for team autonomy. If your app is small and one team owns it, the coordination problem this solves may not exist for you yet.

Title: Treat migration as a standing capability, not a one-off project
Description: Meenu Venkataarangam (Recode Solutions) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on four automation pillars and AI that make enterprise migrations repeatable.
Body:
Most enterprises run a big migration, swear never again, and then start the next one with the same spreadsheets. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Meenu Venkataarangam, a program manager at Recode Solutions, argued for the opposite: make migration a continuous, automated capability, built on four pillars (discovery, transformation, orchestration and testing) with AI on top for prediction.

It's a short, framework-level talk aimed at people who plan and run migrations rather than at engineers looking for tool configs. Think of it as a checklist with a spine.

## From lift-and-shift to a permanent muscle

Meenu traces migration's history in three steps. It used to be lift and shift: move the workload, done. Today it involves many teams, tools and compliance frameworks. The future she describes treats migration as a strategic capacity, where systems keep evolving without disrupting the business.

Manual migrations, in her framing, fail in predictable ways: long timelines, unpredictable results, high error risk. Automation's job is to shorten delivery, raise predictability, improve data quality and free specialists from repetitive migration work. Her line is that this is about reliability, consistency and governance as much as speed.

## The four pillars

**Discovery automation.** Automatically map dependencies, data lineage and system interconnections. What used to take weeks or months of documentation becomes a visual map of how every data source and service affects the others, so the plan starts from reality.

**Transformation engine.** Schema conversion, code refactoring and bulk data movement at scale. Her examples: converting an Oracle schema to PostgreSQL, rewriting stored procedures, and moving terabytes with validation built in. She names three common patterns: cloud migration to AWS, Azure or GCP; Hadoop to modern cloud platforms; and data warehouse modernisation onto platforms like Snowflake with automated schema and query translation.

**Intelligent orchestration.** Even fully automated steps need sequencing and monitoring. Her metaphor is an air traffic controller: define the workflows, execute them, adapt to conditions in real time, validate each stage.

**Automated testing.** Differential testing compares source and target systems to catch hidden logic or data issues early, and real-time monitoring plus automated rollback lets teams recover quickly when something slips. This is the pillar that turns a migration from a leap of faith into something you can measure.

## Where the AI comes in

The AI layer is modest and sensible. Machine learning looks at previous migrations to predict effort, cost and risk. AI-driven automation adjusts workflows when issues appear. Predictive analytics forecasts bottlenecks before they arrive. If your organisation has done five migrations and kept the data, the sixth one should be easier to estimate, and that's the whole idea.

She also covers zero-downtime strategies: continuous replication, intelligent routing and instant rollback, so the migration happens while the business keeps running. No weekend cutover, which anyone who has spent a Saturday night watching a progress bar will appreciate.

## Start small, then compound

Her roadmap is four steps: assess your current migration process, define a target automation vision, implement gradually starting with high-impact use cases, and measure and optimise continuously. The enterprises that get this right, she argues, adapt to new technology faster because moving is no longer an event.

## Who should watch

Programme and delivery managers planning a portfolio of migrations, and architects who need a vocabulary for pitching migration tooling as an investment rather than a project cost. Engineers after deep detail on, say, stored procedure translation will want to pair it with something more hands-on, like the talks below.

Title: Reinforcement learning agents can tune Kubernetes better than thresholds
Description: Deepika Annam (Nike) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on DQN, PPO and SAC agents for Kubernetes scheduling and autoscaling, with safe rollout guardrails.
Body:
A flash sale hits, the static HPA thresholds react too late, some services fall over while others sit on idle capacity, and someone edits configs at midnight. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Deepika Annam, Senior Data Engineer at Nike, used that retail story to make the case for deep reinforcement learning in Kubernetes: agents that learn workload patterns and adjust scheduling and resources ahead of the spike instead of after it. In her experiments, RL-optimised clusters cut application response time by 30% compared with static autoscaling.

The talk covers the algorithms, how they plug into Kubernetes, and, most usefully, how to stop a learning agent from breaking production.

## Thresholds react; agents anticipate

Deepika's critique of standard autoscaling is that it is reactive: a metric crosses a line, the system responds, and it never learns from last week. An RL agent observes the cluster, learns cyclical spikes, seasonal trends and correlations between microservices, and adjusts proactively. One result she called surprising was agents anticipating traffic surges before they happened, from patterns in historical data. She also saw fewer scaling events overall, which makes resource management calmer and cheaper.

She targets four areas: pod scheduling, resource allocation, traffic routing in the service mesh, and multi-cluster orchestration.

## Pick the algorithm by the shape of the decision

The algorithm section is a good primer on matching method to problem:

- **Deep Q-Networks** for discrete choices: which node gets this pod, which resource tier. Experience replay keeps training stable by sampling past experiences at random.
- **PPO** for continuous allocation such as CPU and memory, because its clipped objective keeps policy updates gradual, so resources don't lurch.
- **Soft Actor-Critic** for multi-objective work. Entropy regularisation keeps the agent exploring, and the reward can weigh cost, performance and reliability together. In her experiments SAC did best on highly variable, multi-service workloads, with lower response times and better cost efficiency than DQN and PPO.

The hard part in every case was the reward function. Reward only CPU utilisation and the agent will happily ignore latency. Weighting several metrics correctly was the key to getting the behaviour they wanted.

## Custom controllers do the translating

Integration runs through custom controllers that collect cluster metrics, feed them to the agent, and turn its recommended actions into Kubernetes API calls, with error handling and rollback so every action is reversible. The pain points she lists are honest: metric latency, Kubernetes API changes, and RBAC so the agent can only take safe, authorised actions. Debugging an agent whose decisions look counter-intuitive needs detailed logs of state and reward calculations.

Multi-cluster adds state synchronisation and network latency to the mix. Her suggestion there is federated learning: each cluster trains locally and shares only model updates, so raw data never leaves the cluster.

## Guardrails before glory

The production section is the one to bookmark. Circuit breakers halt the agent if it starts behaving unexpectedly. New policies roll out as canaries on a small subset of workloads, with automated rollback if performance drops. Models are versioned and A/B tested against each other. And everything is visible in Prometheus and Grafana, so humans can audit what the agent did. Her adoption advice is to start with non-critical workloads and capture baseline metrics first, so the improvement is provable.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who have tuned HPA thresholds one too many times, and ML engineers looking for a well-scoped infrastructure problem. The talk is conceptual on the algorithms and practical on the safety rails; you won't get code, but you will get the architecture and the questions to answer before trying it.

Title: One staging cluster can replace your dev and CI clusters
Description: Arsh Sharma (MetalBear) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 shows mirrord running local code in a shared staging cluster to stop Kubernetes cluster sprawl.
Body:
Kubernetes adoption starts with one production cluster and somehow ends with a cluster per developer. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Arsh Sharma, Senior DevRel Engineer at MetalBear, traced how that sprawl happens and showed MetalBear's open source tool mirrord letting developers and CI share a single staging cluster safely, by running local code as if it were inside the cluster.

Honest scope: this is a vendor talk showing MetalBear's own project, with a live demo. The problem framing is useful even if you never install it.

## How one cluster becomes forty

Arsh's story will be familiar. Production gets a cluster. Shipping straight to production is scary, so staging gets one or two. Staging deploys are slow and one team's deploy blocks the others, so CI starts spinning up clusters. CI gets slow too, so developers get personal environments mirroring production. Then they want ephemeral on-demand environments, so you either provision many clusters or carve one huge cluster into namespaces. Either way, the outcome is the same: more environments than the DevOps team can manage and a cloud bill nobody can defend.

The costs he lists go beyond money: DevOps time spent maintaining environments instead of improving things, sometimes extra hires just to run them, and developers waiting 15 to 20 minutes for an ephemeral environment every time they want feedback.

## Run locally, behave as if remote

mirrord's idea is to keep the process on your laptop while mirroring its context from the cluster: incoming and outgoing traffic, the file system and environment variables. Your local process thinks it is running in the cluster. Outgoing requests go out via the cluster, so other services see them as coming from the target pod. All the dependencies, the databases and queues, are already in staging, so nothing needs to be set up locally.

## The demo: mirror, then steal

The demo uses an IP visit counter service backed by Redis, an IP info service and Kafka, all deployed in a staging cluster with nothing running locally. Arsh uses the mirrord extension in Cursor (there are extensions for VS Code, Windsurf and JetBrains IDEs, plus a CLI), picks the target deployment, and sets a breakpoint. A request to the cluster endpoint hits the breakpoint on his laptop. The config loads environment variables from the cluster, and the code reads a response file that exists only in the cluster.

Then he switches from mirror mode to steal mode in the mirrord JSON config, adding an HTTP header filter so only requests carrying his header come to his machine. He edits the response string, sends a request with the header, and gets his local change back from the shared cluster. Everyone else's requests still reach the deployed version.

That filter is the point. It is what lets many developers, CI jobs or, as he notes, AI agents share one staging cluster without stepping on each other.

## What keeps sharing safe

The obvious objection is safety, and Arsh addresses it after the demo:

- HTTP filters route each request to the right developer, once
- queue splitting lets several developers consume from the same Kafka or SQS queue without disrupting each other
- mirrord policies block forbidden actions, such as writing to a sensitive database
- any dependency can run locally instead, for example a database when you're testing a migration

The CLI also runs in CI, so CI jobs can use the staging cluster too. The end state he proposes: one production cluster and one production-like staging cluster that the platform team actually maintains.

## Who should watch

Platform teams staring at a growing pile of dev and preview environments, and developers tired of waiting on deploys to test a one-line change. If your org already runs ephemeral environments happily, the queue-splitting and policy features are still worth seeing.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Designing Staging Environments: A Blueprint for Pre-production](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Lucas_da_Costa_staging_environments_blueprint_preproduction) helps you build the one staging cluster worth sharing.

Title: A five-layer blueprint for generative AI in healthcare claims
Description: Amala Arul Malar Umakanth of McKinsey & Company at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on layered GenAI for claims processing and multimodal fraud detection.
Body:
Static fraud rules, such as flagging any claim above a dollar threshold or any duplicate within 30 days, are easy to write and just as easy to dodge. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Amala Arul Malar Umakanth, a principal data engineer at McKinsey & Company, laid out how generative AI can sit inside healthcare insurance workflows, from reading clinical notes to spotting fraud rings, and what has to be true about the data first.

Fair warning for the JavaScript crowd: this is an architecture and strategy talk about healthcare data, not a code walkthrough. Its value is the structure it puts around a messy domain.

## The problem is volume and fragmentation

Amala frames the starting point plainly. Tens of millions of claims move through payers and providers every day, and much of the review is still manual: people reading notes and checking codes line by line. The data lives in PDFs, portals, EHR systems, HL7 messages and DICOM images that don't talk to each other, and fraud detection relies on rigid rules that evolve slower than the fraudsters.

## Five layers, bottom up

Her blueprint stacks five layers:

- **Ingestion and pre-processing.** Pull every format in, then clean, deduplicate and enrich it into structured data. No model rescues dirty inputs.
- **Clinical language understanding.** NLP extracts diagnoses, procedures and medications from physician notes and discharge summaries, and builds context. Her example: telling a follow-up visit for diabetes from a new diabetes diagnosis, a distinction that changes billing.
- **Validation.** Check correctness against medical standards, with the goal of improving claim quality before submission rather than rejecting bad claims after.
- **Risk detection**, where the fraud models live.
- **Orchestration.** High-confidence claims auto-approve; questionable ones escalate to people, so human judgement goes where it is needed.

## Fraud detection gets several lenses at once

The fraud section is the most concrete. Instead of single rules, she describes multimodal analysis that combines structured claim data, narratives and behaviour:

- Graph neural networks map relationships between claims, patients, providers and transactions, so a provider unusually connected to clusters of questionable claims stands out. Her description: a social network for claims data.
- Temporal pattern analysis watches for odd timing, such as charges at strange hours or bursts of identical procedures.
- Document authenticity checks look for tampering or forgery in invoices and paperwork.
- Anomaly scoring combines the signals and ranks claims, so investigators start with the truly suspicious ones instead of drowning in false alarms.

Her favourite idea is synthetic fraud scenario generation: use generative models to invent fraud patterns that haven't happened yet and stress-test the detection pipeline before a new tactic reaches production.

## Responsible AI and a phased rollout

She treats trust as a prerequisite: keep PHI private, explain decisions about denials and fraud alerts, monitor for bias, and meet HIPAA and audit requirements. The adoption hurdles she lists are data silos, model drift (models need retraining as diseases, regulations and populations change, which means a real MLOps practice) and workforce resistance.

The roadmap has four phases: foundation (secure pipelines, NLP models, validation rules), development (fraud models run in shadow mode alongside existing systems, with explainability tools for adjusters and A/B testing), integration (connect to core platforms, automate routing, add dashboards) and optimisation (continuous learning, more claim types, synthetic fraud generation, federated learning). Start small, show value, then grow.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects at payers or health-tech vendors, and anyone asked to put AI into claims without a clear picture of the pipeline it needs. Engineers looking for JavaScript, model code or measured results from a specific deployment will not find them here.

Title: Pre-computed surround lighting beats the camera pointed at your TV
Description: Chandan Kumar (Google) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on pre-computing ambient light signals from the video stream to sync smart lights in ~60 ms.
Body:
Anyone who has set up sync lighting knows the scene: the police chase ends, and only then does the room start flashing red and blue. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Chandan Kumar, a software engineer at Google, presented a fix: stop watching the screen with a camera, and pre-compute the light signals from the video signal itself, ahead of time. His benchmark put the result at about 60.7 ms end to end, against the 200 to 300 ms he measured for conventional systems.

This is a design talk based on a defensive publication he wrote under the same name. It sits a long way from Kubernetes, and it is one of the more fun talks on the event's IoT track.

## Why today's sync lights lag

Chandan's critique of the conventional setup is precise. A camera points at the screen, a small box processes what it sees, decides on colours and brightness, then sends commands to bulbs, usually over Zigbee. Every step happens live, so every step adds latency. Worse, because heavier computation would add even more delay, those boxes play it safe: a limited palette of mostly primary colours and conservative brightness. The system is boxed in by physics and its own processing budget.

The result, in his experience and the internal test users he surveyed, is lighting that feels disconnected from what's on screen, the opposite of immersion.

## Read the signal, look ahead

The core idea is to process the content from the signal pass-through instead of from a camera, and to use a predictive buffer that looks a few seconds ahead. If the system knows the next scene is a police chase, it can prepare the red-and-blue sequence and send it so it lands as the scene starts. He describes buffering the light state about two seconds before the scene appears, which also smooths transitions when a stream rebuffers.

Because the work is decoupled from the display, frame rate stops being the limit. A 120 Hz or 240 Hz monitor that outruns a camera-based system is fine when the lights are computed from the content in advance. Game engines could even pre-encode lighting for parts of a map: head towards snow and the room goes white, towards the sea and it goes blue.

## Smarter than the dominant colour

Two refinements make the output better, not just faster. Scene classification picks the subject instead of the dominant colour: a character looking at a rainbow in a blue sky should get rainbow light in the room, not sky blue. And because the system checks its own predictions, it can use the full RGB gamut and the full zero-to-100% brightness range: properly dark for a horror game, fully bright for a colourful blockbuster.

Distance calibration is another neat trick. If a bulb at the back of a large room takes a second to receive its signal, the system just sends that bulb's command a second earlier. A camera-based system can't do that, because it only knows what's on screen now.

## The architecture and where it goes

The pipeline has four parts: content input, a frame analysis engine that decodes content into light states, the predictive buffer, and a node controller that sends commands to strips, bulbs or virtual devices for testing. Better GPUs deepen the look-ahead.

Chandan's bigger vision is an ecosystem like surround sound mixing, where content producers pre-compute a lighting track once and every viewer's device simply plays it, the same way subtitles ship with a film. He sketches uses from home theatres and consoles to commercial cinemas converted cheaply with smart lights, plus calmer focus modes and accessibility for viewers with impaired vision.

## Who should watch

Smart-home and IoT engineers, game and media developers, and anyone who likes a clean latency argument: move the work out of the critical path and into a buffer. Kubernetes operators won't find their cluster in it, but they will recognise the pattern.

Title: Security Copilot finds the users your Conditional Access forgot
Description: Cynthia Akiotu at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 demos Microsoft Security Copilot fixing Conditional Access drift and summarising DLP alerts with prompts.
Body:
The most dangerous gap in a Microsoft tenant is often a policy nobody remembers writing, or a user nobody added to it. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Cynthia Akiotu, a cybersecurity architect who works on identity and access management and data security, showed how Microsoft Security Copilot turns plain-language prompts into fixes for exactly that kind of quiet drift, with two live demos in Entra and Purview.

It's a Microsoft-stack talk, and an honest one: the product on screen is Security Copilot, and the case is that defenders should use AI at least as fluently as attackers already do.

## The pressure cooker

Cynthia opens with the defender's problem as she sees it. Attackers use AI to write better phishing emails and probe faster; analysts drown in alerts, false positives and real ones alike; and employees paste sensitive data into AI tools, which keeps executives up at night. Her framing is that defenders don't lose for lack of skill so much as lack of context and speed. Nobody reads every alert, and nobody eyeballs every policy.

Her answer is what she calls augmentation rather than automation: the analyst stays in charge, but asks questions in natural language (who are the riskiest users in this tenant?) instead of hunting through consoles.

## Drift is the silent hole

The sharpest part of the talk is about Conditional Access drift. In a large organisation, people join, change roles and leave, picking up admin rights on the way. New applications get deployed without Conditional Access coverage. Policies pile up: duplicates, obsolete ones, conflicting ones. Each of these is a door an attacker can walk through, and she points out they're hard for the human eye to spot.

The demo shows the Conditional Access Optimization agent in a Microsoft Entra tenant. It scans for users not covered by policies such as MFA, applications outside policy coverage, and policies that could be merged. The concrete moment: a suggestion that two users were missing from an existing policy requiring MFA for a financial application. One click applies it, with an explanation of what the policy does. That's the whole pitch in miniature: the agent spots the gap, the analyst approves the fix.

## DLP alerts you can actually read

The second demo moves to Microsoft Purview and data loss prevention. Cynthia asks Copilot for insight into existing DLP policies by location (endpoint devices in her example), then opens an alert about a sensitive document being downloaded to a device and asks for a summary of the user's activity.

What comes back reads like an insider-risk timeline: the same user emailed attachments outside the organisation, uploaded sensitive files to cloud storage, collected an unusual volume of sensitive files, then deleted files. She reads it, plausibly, as a disgruntled employee on the way out. The point is the turnaround: a sequence that would take an analyst a while to reconstruct arrives as a paragraph.

## The prompt is now a perimeter

She closes with a warning that keeps the talk from being a pure product tour. If prompts can change policies, prompts are an attack surface. Her rules: audit every prompt and action analysts run, treat Security Copilot as a privileged access surface, and cover it with the same policies as any other admin tool. Speed without visibility just moves the risk.

## Who should watch

Security analysts and identity admins in Microsoft 365 shops who want to see what Security Copilot looks like on real tenant screens, and security leads weighing whether an AI assistant earns its privileged access. If you're on another stack, the drift checklist (users, apps, redundant policies) still travels well; the clicks won't.

Title: Knowledge bases fail when nobody measures how people search them
Description: Harshita Dubey of Apex Fintech Solutions at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on rebuilding a SharePoint knowledge system with embedded analytics and JS microservices.
Body:
If finding an answer in the company wiki is harder than asking on Slack, people will ask on Slack. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Harshita Dubey of Apex Fintech Solutions told the story of a 24-month effort to turn a static enterprise knowledge system into one that watches how it is used and adapts, built on SharePoint Online with custom JavaScript microservices on top.

It is a short talk, roughly a lightning-length case study, and it is mostly about approach and results rather than code. Think of it as the slide deck you would want before pitching the same project internally.

## Why knowledge systems die quietly

Harshita opens with the claim that more than half of enterprise knowledge systems fail to deliver real value, even at organisations with over 100,000 employees spread across many countries. She names three causes: static architectures that can't keep up with how teams work, content scattered across silos, and a user experience so poor that self-service loses to asking a colleague.

Her team's fix was to treat it as a data-driven product, not an IT project. Embed analytics to see behaviour, mine search patterns for intent, build real-time feedback loops, and stop guessing.

## JavaScript as the adaptive layer

The architecture is deliberately unglamorous. SharePoint Online is the secure base. On top sit JavaScript microservices for analytics, search and personalisation, plus dynamic UI components that respond to user behaviour, context-aware filtering so people see what is relevant to their role, and natural-language search so users can ask questions the way humans do. Three engines carry it: NLP-backed search, a personalisation engine tuned to behaviour and role, and live dashboards that make the whole thing visible.

The governance angle is the part many teams skip. Dashboards tracked engagement, showed where users abandoned searches (a polite way of saying where the content failed them), and surfaced emerging needs before anyone filed a request.

## The numbers she reports

Harshita reports that information retrieval time fell by 33%, self-service resolution rose 22 points from 62% to 84%, onboarding time dropped 21%, support tickets fell 35%, and efficiency gains saved $3.7M a year. The talk does not break down how each figure was measured, so read them as the outcome of this one programme rather than a benchmark.

## Four principles and a roadmap

She distils it into modularity (independent services that grow without breaking each other), analytics first (measure from day one), scalability (assume success and design for it) and user-centric development (tools fail when users aren't part of the build). The roadmap is assess, lay the analytics foundation, add JavaScript-powered intelligence, optimise from feedback, then scale. The lesson she says travels to any stack: invest in microservices and you get flexibility without replatforming.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product owners stuck with an intranet or SharePoint estate that nobody loves, and anyone who needs a short, metrics-led argument for instrumenting internal tools. If you want implementation detail, such as which search stack or how the microservices talk to SharePoint, this talk stays at the architecture level.

Title: ARIA is translation notes for screen readers, so use it sparingly
Description: Anisat Ahmed at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 introduces ARIA roles, properties and states, when native HTML is enough, and the mistakes to avoid.
Body:
A `div` styled to look like a button is, to a screen reader, just something clickable called "Click me". At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Anisat Ahmed gave a beginner-friendly introduction to ARIA built around that gap, and her most useful advice was about when not to reach for it at all.

This is an intro talk and says so: half an hour, three core concepts, a handful of code examples, then best practices, common mistakes and testing tools. If you have shipped accessible custom widgets before, it is a refresher. If ARIA attributes feel like magic incantations copied from Stack Overflow, it is a good place to start.

## HTML speaks two languages

Anisat's framing is that every page speaks a visual language (colours, layout, hover effects) for sighted users and a semantic language (this is a button, a level-one heading, a navigation region) for assistive technology. Accessibility bugs happen when the two disagree: something looks like a button but doesn't say it is one. ARIA, Accessible Rich Internet Applications, exists to make them agree when plain HTML can't. Her analogy is translation notes for screen readers: they don't change how the code looks, they add meaning.

She is also clear on motivation. Building accessibly is not a compliance checkbox or lawsuit avoidance; a product people can't navigate is simply unfinished.

## Roles, properties, states

The three concepts in her own short definitions:

- **Role** says what an element is, such as `role='button'` or `role='dialog'`.
- **Properties** describe it, such as `aria-label='Close dialog'`, `aria-labelledby` and `aria-describedby`.
- **States** say what is happening now, such as `aria-pressed='true'`, `aria-expanded` or `aria-selected`.

## Native HTML first, always

Her golden rule is the one the W3C repeats too: no ARIA is better than bad ARIA. Use `button` for buttons, `nav` for navigation, `input` for inputs, and only add ARIA when no semantic element exists, such as for tabs, carousels, modals and notifications. Rebuilding built-in behaviour on a `div` and then patching it with ARIA usually creates more problems than it fixes.

## Two examples worth copying

The first is a toast. A `div` that says "Message sent successfully" is visible to sighted users and silent to screen reader users. Add `role='status'` and `aria-live='polite'` and the message is announced when it appears, without interrupting the user.

The second is a confirm-delete modal. Visually it is obvious; to a screen reader it may not exist. Give the container `role='dialog'`, point `aria-labelledby` at its heading and `aria-describedby` at the paragraph asking whether you are sure, and the user hears what the dialog is for before they reach the Cancel and Delete buttons.

## The mistakes she keeps seeing

- ARIA on every element, just in case.
- `aria-hidden='true'` on interactive elements, which tells the screen reader to ignore something the user needs.
- Assuming ARIA adds keyboard support. It doesn't: you still write the key handlers.
- Conflicting roles, such as a button given a dialog role.

For testing, she recommends unplugging the mouse and tabbing through the page, listening with NVDA on Windows or VoiceOver on a Mac, and running automated checkers like axe DevTools, WAVE and Lighthouse, then retesting by hand. Her workflow advice is to bake accessibility checks into pull requests and the design system so it stops feeling like extra work.

## Who should watch

Junior and mid-level front-end developers, designers who hand off component specs, and reviewers who want a shared vocabulary for why a modal is not being announced. Senior accessibility folks can skip it, or send it to the colleague who keeps writing `div onclick`.

Title: Dragon Copilot hands the clinical note-taking to ambient AI
Description: Tharun Nallamothu (Microsoft) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on how Dragon Copilot turns doctor-patient conversations into clinical notes with ambient AI.
Body:
Doctors finish a visit, then spend the evening on the paperwork, and the next patient gets a tired physician. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Tharun Nallamothu, Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft, presented Dragon Copilot, the AI clinical assistant he works on: it records the doctor-patient conversation ambiently, turns it into a structured note, and lets the doctor fix it by voice, so the hours go back to patients.

Honest scope: this is a product talk from an engineer on the team, covering Microsoft's own product, its architecture at a high level and his part in building it. Tharun has spent five to six years in healthcare software across Nuance Communications and Microsoft.

## The problem started before COVID and got worse during it

Tharun tells the origin story plainly. Every visit ends with documentation and prescriptions, which eats time, produces imperfect notes that bring patients back, and burns physicians out. The pandemic made it acute. The goal was to automate the documentation so the doctor's attention stays in the room.

## How it works

The pipeline he describes has four stages:

1. Ambient recording captures the conversation between physician and patient in real time.
2. Natural language understanding extracts the medically relevant information from the spoken conversation.
3. Generative models turn that unstructured input into structured clinical documentation: the note and the transcript, delivered back to the doctor.
4. Voice dictation lets the doctor review and edit the note hands-free when something is wrong or missing.

It also integrates with electronic health record systems, Epic in particular, which is where the note has to end up for the workflow to change at all. Multilingual transcription covers cases where doctor and patient speak different languages.

The figure he quotes on patient experience: 93% of patients said their physician seemed more attentive and personable with Dragon Copilot in the room.

## Healthcare means the security slide is the main slide

The implementation section is where the healthcare constraints show. Voice dictation and ambient recordings are encrypted and stored securely. The platform follows HIPAA, with strict separation so one doctor's patient information never reaches another doctor. Accessibility matters too: Tharun points out the app supports visually impaired users.

The challenges he lists are the ones anyone in clinical AI will recognise: robust multilingual transcription accuracy, secure data migration without loss or breaches, and fitting the whole thing into healthcare compliance and accessibility frameworks.

## What he built

Tharun's own contributions were on the client side and the architecture around it: leading end-to-end features on mobile and web, native mobile work on Apple's Cocoa frameworks, web work in React, Redux and TypeScript, RESTful APIs, and testing against Epic's environment. His point about scale is fair: anything designed at Microsoft has to work for millions of users.

## Who should watch

Engineers building AI features into regulated workflows, and anyone curious how an ambient-AI product is put together end to end. If you want model internals, evaluation methodology or the Kubernetes deployment, the talk doesn't go there; it stays at product and architecture level.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: EV charging networks need cloud-native design to keep up
Description: Preeti Sali (Ford Motor Company) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on microservices, predictive maintenance, smart routing and V2G for EV charging.
Body:
Range anxiety is mostly a data problem: drivers don't know whether the charger ahead works or is free. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Preeti Sali, Senior Technical Program Manager at Ford Motor Company, laid out how cloud-native design (microservices, Kubernetes and open APIs) turns EV charging from a patchy network of boxes into a system that predicts failures, routes drivers and talks to the grid.

It is a vision-and-architecture talk from a program manager with an electrical engineering background, aimed at the why and the what more than the YAML.

## Adoption is outrunning infrastructure

Preeti's starting point is the gap. She cites 14 million EVs sold globally last year, nearly one in five cars sold worldwide, and drivers who expect chargers to be as reliable as gas stations always were. The goal, in her framing, is smarter chargers, not merely more of them.

She names three hurdles in today's networks:

- scalability: traditional networks weren't designed for exponential growth or global coverage
- grid integration: legacy systems handle dynamic load management and renewables poorly
- user experience: patchy availability, poor visibility and too much downtime

## The cloud-native answer is the usual one, applied somewhere new

The architecture will look familiar to anyone at a Kubernetes conference. Microservices split the system into payments, routing, user interfaces and the rest. Kubernetes orchestrates and scales them as demand spikes. Open APIs connect vehicles, utilities and third-party apps. What makes it interesting is the domain: the services sit between cars, drivers and a power grid.

## Predict failures, route drivers, spread the load

Reliability gets the first application. With predictive maintenance, IoT sensors monitor charger health, machine learning predicts failures, and cloud systems schedule repairs, which she says can cut downtime by as much as 40%. Fewer surprises for drivers, better use of technicians.

Convenience comes next. Real-time charger status and queue lengths feed routing that sends drivers to the best station by traffic, charging speed and availability. Distributed load balancing uses chargers evenly while easing grid strain. The pay-off is the one in the title of most EV marketing decks: drivers know before they arrive.

Energy management is the third. Cloud-native scheduling shifts sessions to off-peak times using pricing, grid conditions and user preferences, cheaper for consumers and gentler on the grid.

## Cars as batteries

The most ambitious part is vehicle-to-grid (V2G). Treat millions of parked EVs as distributed storage: absorb excess solar or wind when supply is high, feed power back when demand spikes. Preeti's argument is that only a cloud-native platform can orchestrate that at scale, and it is where mobility and energy systems converge.

## Roll it out in waves

Scaling, she says, needs phases: core charging platform first, Kubernetes for horizontal scaling across sites, then advanced features like V2G and AI-driven optimisation once the network is stable. She points to the International Energy Agency projection of roughly four times as many public chargers needed by 2030 as the reason the approach has to be operationally simple. Analytics, edge computing for local low-latency decisions, and machine learning that keeps improving routing and maintenance predictions sit underneath it all.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people working on EV, energy or IoT platforms who want a structured map of where cloud-native patterns apply, and Kubernetes engineers curious about a domain where a failed pod might strand a driver. Expect a framework, not an implementation.

Title: FHIR and Kubernetes microservices are closing healthcare access gaps
Description: Geetha Sharanya Bolla (Apexon) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on data integration, FHIR and cloud-native microservices for rural and underserved care.
Body:
A diabetic patient visits a rural clinic, then a city hospital, then a specialist, and if those systems can't share data the tests get repeated and the history goes missing. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Geetha Sharanya Bolla, Lead Engineer at Apexon, made the case that fixing this is an integration problem, and that FHIR plus Kubernetes-based microservices is the combination that finally makes healthcare systems speak the same language.

The talk is an overview with a mission: the technology matters because of who it reaches, especially rural and underserved patients.

## Fragmented data means fragmented care

Geetha's opening statistic is that nearly 80% of critical patient data sits siloed across disconnected systems: records, lab results and prescriptions in separate databases that don't talk. Her framing is that this is a human problem as much as a technical one. When data is fragmented, care becomes fragmented, and every repeated test and delayed treatment follows from it.

The modernisation imperative she describes has three parts: infrastructure that handles large data volumes and many simultaneous users, interoperability so data moves securely between providers, payers and patients, and access for places where geography means weeks of waiting for a specialist.

## Lego bricks and a conductor

Her architecture metaphor is a friendly one. A monolithic hospital system is a giant rigid block; microservices turn it into Lego pieces for patient management, billing and scheduling that can be rearranged, reused and scaled independently. Kubernetes is the conductor that keeps them healthy and available. Standardised APIs, FHIR in particular, are how the pieces talk.

She tracks FHIR's rise as the quiet revolution behind it: adoption growing from 14.8% in 2017 to 58.3% by 2022, by the figures she cites. FHIR gives healthcare data a common grammar, so information flows between electronic health records, telehealth systems and mobile apps instead of staying locked in silos.

## What integration bought, in numbers she reports

The impact section collects figures from health information exchanges and implementations she reports on. Integrated HIEs, she says, cut preventable readmissions by 30% and duplicate lab tests by 52%. Moving to containerised, Kubernetes-native microservices brought, in her numbers, 62% higher transaction throughput, 47% faster responses at peak load, infrastructure costs down by up to 57% and deployment times improved by 74%.

COVID-19 was the stress test. Telehealth went from about 1% of visits before 2020 to 35.3%, and her argument is that systems already on cloud-native, API-based architectures were the ones that could absorb that overnight. The rural story is the one she clearly cares most about: a Kubernetes-based telehealth platform in rural India that, she reports, improved specialist access by 58% and cut urgent care delays by 43%.

## Four design principles

Her closing checklist is short enough to pin above a desk:

1. Cloud-native architecture: containerised microservices orchestrated by Kubernetes.
2. Standards compliance: FHIR and other interoperability standards from the start, not retrofitted.
3. Scalability: systems that expand elastically with demand.
4. Security and compliance across the whole development lifecycle.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects new to healthcare who want the shape of the domain in one sitting, and healthcare IT teams making the case for interoperability work. Engineers already deep in FHIR will know the material; the value is the equity framing and the collected numbers.

Title: Kubernetes automation as a public good for government services
Description: Mahesh Jalukuri (Envoy Global) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on Kubernetes-native automation for equitable, resilient healthcare, legal and utility services.
Body:
Tax deadlines, vaccine registrations and benefit applications at midnight are load tests that governments don't get to schedule. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Mahesh Jalukuri, Senior DevOps Engineer at Envoy Global, argued that Kubernetes-native automation is how public services survive those spikes, and that the payoff is measured in fairness as much as uptime: the same quality of service for someone in a capital city and someone in a remote village.

It is a short policy-meets-platform talk. The technology is familiar; the lens is the citizen.

## Four pillars, one of them unusual

Mahesh frames the case on four pillars. Scalability for surges like filing deadlines. Reliability so services stay up at the moment citizens need them. Efficiency because public budgets are always tight. And equity, the one you rarely see on a Kubernetes slide: everyone should get the same quality of service regardless of where they live or which language they speak.

That fourth pillar changes what you measure. A portal with great p99 latency in English and a broken translated flow is not a reliable service for a large part of the population.

## Results across three sectors

The talk reports findings across healthcare, legal services and public utilities. The figures, all from the research he presents:

- system availability up 37% for public sector organisations using Kubernetes automation
- telemedicine consultations up 430%, with feature rollout times cut from 45 days to seven
- court backlogs down 23%, and access for non-English speakers up 52% thanks to multilingual automation
- 99.999% uptime for emergency services on self-healing infrastructure, and 76% fewer outages in rural deployments
- costs down by up to 34% within two years and 42% by year three

The one he dwells on most is about people. Before automation, only 23% of staff time was available for innovation; afterwards it was 58%. The rest had been firefighting and manual processes. That shift, from troubleshooting servers to designing better services, is the real return.

## The obstacles are human too

Mahesh doesn't pretend it's easy. The challenges he names are a Kubernetes skills gap in many public sector teams, legacy systems that won't disappear overnight and need careful migration, and the risk of a digital divide where automation leaves vulnerable groups behind instead of serving them.

His policy recommendations map onto those: cross-agency standards for security and operations, structured workforce training, inclusive and accessible design in every project, and private partnerships that bring in expertise while keeping essential services under public control.

## A phased plan

The implementation framework is a four-phase timeline. Months one to three: assess infrastructure and set baseline metrics. Months four to eight: pilot Kubernetes on low-risk services. Months nine to 18: scale critical services with citizen feedback loops. Then continuous optimisation. His closing advice is the classic platform-team mantra applied to government: start small, scale smart, and let small wins build into systemic change.

He ties it back to trust. Transparent service status, consistent quality, proactive communication and accessible design make citizens more willing to engage with digital government, which is a reliability outcome worth having on the dashboard.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers in the public sector or at govtech vendors, and anyone who needs to explain to non-technical stakeholders why self-healing infrastructure and automated rollouts matter for citizens. Engineers looking for implementation detail will find the talk light on it.

Title: Datacenter buildouts get faster when nothing waits in line
Description: Vamsi Gadireddy (Microsoft Azure) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on parallel workflows, early power and fiber planning, and pre-staged racks.
Body:
A late fiber trench permit delays network installation, which delays testing, which delays production. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Vamsi Gadireddy, Senior Network Engineer on Microsoft's Azure cloud infrastructure team, explained how hyperscale datacenter buildouts get faster by breaking that chain: run land, power, network, compute and compliance as parallel streams, and never let one workflow block another.

It is the most physical talk you will find at a Kubernetes conference. No YAML, lots of transformers. If your clusters run in someone else's building, this is a rare look at what has to happen before the first node boots.

## Linear thinking is the bottleneck

Vamsi's core claim is simple: a modern datacenter is not a single-threaded project. Land, power, cooling, networking, compute and compliance move together, and a delay in one domain cascades into the rest. Acceleration means breaking sequential dependencies, not working faster on each step in turn.

That starts early. Site selection, land acquisition and permitting, in his experience, need to begin 18 to 24 months before the target operational date. Waiting for design approval before starting zoning or utility negotiations already costs months.

## Power and fiber are the pacing items

Two lead times dominate his talk. Utility coordination alone can take more than 18 months, from negotiating connections to securing substation permits, and AI racks keep pushing power density up. His lever is pre-ordering long-lead components such as generators, transformers and UPS systems before the final electrical design is locked. Yes, that's a risk; his argument is that slight over-provisioning costs far less than a six-month delay.

Network is the second bottleneck. Fiber installation can take six to 12 months, longer when right-of-way permits drag. So carrier engagement starts alongside land and power planning, existing fiber gets assessed before final site selection, and options like dark fiber are on the table. He calls connectivity delays preventable if addressed early, which is the kind of sentence you only get from someone who has been burned.

## The dependency matrix is the single source of truth

To keep parallel teams from colliding, Vamsi uses a dependency matrix that maps every component and milestone and how they connect: power readiness affects rack delivery, which affects network turn-up and validation. It is revisited continuously, not filed. In his words it separates reactive teams from proactive ones, and it is how project managers see a bottleneck before it lands.

## Pre-stage everything you can

The compute section is where the timeline really compresses. Traditionally, servers went in after the building was complete. Instead, racks are pre-staged and validated off-site, shipped ready to deploy, and configured by automation, which moves deployment from months to weeks.

The software layer follows the same idea: infrastructure as code for network, storage and compute, versioned and tested through CI/CD; containerisation to decouple services from hardware; thousands of automated checks across clusters; and progressive rollouts so the site becomes productive in stages while construction finishes. Commissioning gets the same treatment, with component-level testing during installation and availability zones commissioned in parallel.

Compliance, often treated as the last gate, moves to day one: security and compliance experts embedded from the start, preliminary audits during construction, automated policy validation.

## Measure it

His closing metrics are worth copying: overall project duration, time to production, how quickly the site starts generating value, and the percentage of work executed in parallel. That last one is the honest measure of whether the strategy is working.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure and network engineers, capacity planners and anyone running large physical rollouts, including edge sites and on-prem clusters at smaller scale. Kubernetes engineers will recognise the progressive-rollout and IaC ideas, applied to concrete and copper.

- [Pitfalls of Infrastructure as Code](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Tim_Davis_pitfalls_Infrastructure_as_Code) covers what goes wrong in the IaC layer Vamsi relies on.
- [Simplifying Cluster Provisioning at Scale](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Bharath_Nallapeta_cluster_provisioning_scale) shows k0rdent provisioning the clusters that land on the racks.

Title: Healthcare fraud detection fails on data before it fails on models
Description: Triveni Kolla (Cotiviti) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 makes the case for data-centric AI in healthcare fraud detection: clean, governed data first.
Body:
A provider bills two insurers for the same service under slightly different patient details, and the duplicate slips through because the identifiers don't match. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Triveni Kolla, Senior Business Intelligence Developer at Cotiviti, used scenarios like that to argue that healthcare fraud detection is a data quality problem first. Bigger models on messy claims data hit diminishing returns; governed, clean data is what lets AI deliver.

The talk is a strategy overview from someone with a decade in healthcare data warehousing and BI. It is not a code walkthrough.

## The scale of the problem

Triveni opens with the size of it. She cites estimates of around $300 billion a year lost to healthcare fraud in the US, up to 10% of total healthcare spending, with roughly three quarters of healthcare data unstructured and, in the figure she quotes, four out of five medical bills containing errors. Those errors are not all fraud, but they are all places fraud can hide.

## Model-centric versus data-centric

The central slide contrasts two approaches. The traditional, model-centric one treats data as a fixed input and keeps refining algorithms and adding complexity. The data-centric one treats data quality as the main lever: systematic governance, continuous quality monitoring and proactive enrichment.

Her three failure scenarios make it concrete:

- a duplicate bill missed because patient identifiers are inconsistent across systems
- a model trained on incomplete records that produces skewed risk scores
- a telehealth session billed while the patient record is incomplete, so the fraud goes unnoticed

The line most engineers will nod at: a well-labelled, high-quality dataset can let a simple logistic regression beat a deep neural network trained on messy or biased data. The abstract puts numbers on the payoff, crediting clean, governed datasets with detection accuracy up to 95%, 85% fewer false positives and 70% shorter investigations.

## Data as a living asset

Her continuous quality framework has four steps that loop: profile and assess every source, define quantifiable standards for completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness, monitor in real time so deviations are caught before they reach a model, and feed model outcomes back into the quality process.

On the modelling side she favours random forests for this domain, for pattern recognition across many decision trees and, importantly in healthcare, interpretability that survives regulatory review and audit. Other ideas in the toolkit: blockchain-style immutable audit trails for data integrity, and AutoML pipelines that automate preprocessing and model selection for teams without deep in-house ML expertise.

## Where cloud-native fits

The Kubernetes Native angle is the platform under all of this. Elastic scaling lets fraud workloads grow from routine monitoring to an investigation surge. Integration happens through standard healthcare interoperability, FHIR and HL7 messaging, with electronic health records, claims and health information systems. Security and compliance (HIPAA, GDPR) are built into the platform instead of patched on.

Her roadmap is staged: assessment and data audit in the first months, then data quality improvement and governance, then a pilot across key fraud scenarios, then full deployment with continuous monitoring. The KPIs pair financial measures (fraud losses, recoveries, investigation cost) with operational ones (accuracy, false positive rate, investigation cycle time).

## Who should watch

Data engineers and BI teams in healthcare payers and claims processing, and ML engineers who keep getting asked for a better model when the data is the problem. If you need the argument for funding data governance before the next model, Triveni has made it for you.

Title: One await scheduler.yield() can unfreeze a page stuck on long tasks
Description: Aleksandr Tkachenko of Playtech at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on scheduler.yield(), why setTimeout yielding loses its place, and a frozen banking demo.
Body:
A loop that spends 10 ms on each of 200 items sounds harmless, right up to the moment the page freezes for two full seconds. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Aleksandr Tkachenko, a front-end engineer at Playtech, showed how the experimental `scheduler.yield()` API lets a long task pause, hand the browser its turn, and resume ahead of the queue, often with a one-line change.

He is upfront about scope: the API is still early, not every browser supports it, and a polyfill exists. The talk is a careful explanation of why it behaves differently from the tricks we already use, plus a demo you will recognise from your own app.

## The event loop, briefly and correctly

Aleksandr starts with a refresher worth the time. Synchronous code runs on the call stack; async callbacks wait in the microtask queue (promises) or the task queue (timers); when the stack empties, the loop drains all microtasks, then picks one runnable task, and repeats. Task queues are not strict FIFO, and the event loop is defined in the HTML standard, not in ECMAScript. Anything holding the main thread past 50 ms is a long task, and while it runs the browser cannot repaint or respond.

## The two-second freeze you can feel

His toy demo makes it visceral. A `blockingTask(ms)` burns CPU on purpose, and a `heavyWork()` loop calls it for 10 ms on each of 200 items. Click OK and the button stays visually pressed; click Log four times and nothing happens until the work ends, then all four timestamps print at once; click the close icon three times and the window vanishes only afterwards. Events are queued, not lost, which is somehow worse for the user who keeps clicking.

## Why setTimeout(0) is a polite but unreliable pause

The classic fix is to chunk the loop and `await` a promise resolved by `setTimeout(fn, 0)` every so often, here about every 25% of the work. It helps, but your continuation goes to the back of the task queue. If something else on the page has a `setInterval` firing, those callbacks can run first, so you never know when you get control back. `requestAnimationFrame` has similar drawbacks, and `requestIdleCallback` suits background work, not resuming a user-triggered job.

`scheduler.yield()` changes the ordering. After the pending user input is handled, your continuation is prioritised and runs before already queued timer tasks. His diagram contrasts the three cases: no yielding (the click waits for the whole task), setTimeout (the click runs, then a queued timer, then your work), and `scheduler.yield()` (the click runs, then your work continues).

## Priorities made explicit

The Prioritized Task Scheduling API names three levels: `user-blocking` for input and critical UI, `user-visible` for things the user sees but that are not urgent, and `background` for work nobody is waiting on. `scheduler.yield()` defaults to user-visible, and when called inside a `scheduler.postTask()` callback it inherits that task's priority. Aleksandr deliberately stops short of a full postTask tour.

## The banking demo

The finale is a fictional banking app: hidden balance, a card that flips to show details, and a Generate report button that runs the heavy loop over 1,000 items. Without yielding, the button sticks and the card and balance controls ignore every click. With `scheduler.yield()` every 5% of the work, the button renders, a loading animation appears and the user can flip the card and reveal the balance while the report builds. Animations are a little less smooth, and he says so.

## Who should watch

Front-end engineers chasing Interaction to Next Paint (INP), anyone maintaining legacy code with heavy synchronous loops they can't rewrite this sprint, and people who have sprinkled `setTimeout(0)` around and wondered why it sometimes doesn't help. If you already use `postTask` in production, the event loop section will be review.

Title: Conf42 Incident Management 2025: work the incident, not the tools
Description: Conf42 Incident Management 2025 roundup: Twilio on incident comms, AI for detection and RCA, incidents under HIPAA and GDPR, and the platforms underneath.
Body:
Conf42 Incident Management 2025 took place on October 2, 2025, with 22 talks about the moment something breaks and everything that decides how badly it goes. AI showed up in most of them, as a summariser, a detector, a root cause assistant and a tester, but the talk that stuck was about something older: telling people what is going on. The lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/im2025) and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBU25vUS7hZWANfG6r4D4oK).

## Communication is the incident customers see

[Gandhi Mathi Nathan Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Gandhi_Mathi_Nathan_Kumar_ai_automation_resilience), Principal Incident Commander at Twilio, chose incident communications because, as he put it, there is plenty of content on detection and resiliency and very little on how responders keep everyone informed. He walked through the tool stack a single Twilio incident touches: FireHydrant to declare and run it, PagerDuty to page, Zoom for the bridge, Slack for the asynchronous work where most incidents actually happen, Datadog, Atlassian Statuspage, Google Docs for retrospectives, Confluence and Slack canvases for action items.

His warning applies to any shop with that many tabs open: the trouble starts when "You end up working the tools instead of working the incident". From the customer's side, the status page is still green, nobody has told them anything, and support tickets start to flood in. He then demoed how AI can take on the updates and bring late joiners up to speed so the incident commander can keep the room focused on mitigation.

Two more talks looked at the screens responders stare at. [Priyanshi Deshwal](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Priyanshi_Deshwal_visual_interfaces_intelligence) of Mode argued for AI-powered visual interfaces that replace static dashboards with real-time insight, and [Sujit Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Sujit_Kumar_contactcenters_automation_scale), VP of Technology at Copart, covered contact centres built to stay calm and coordinated when incidents push call volume up.

## AI for detection and root cause, with receipts

[Mallikarjun Ramasani](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Mallikarjun_Ramasani_intelligence_cloud_future) of Barclays surveyed ML-driven detection, root cause analysis and auto-remediation in cloud operations. [Vasanth Mudavatu](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Vasanth_Mudavatu_transparency_algorithms_ai) of Dell Technologies asked the question every on-call engineer should ask of these tools: can you trust your AI during a breach? His answer was algorithmic transparency, so responders can see why the model flagged something before they act on it.

[Pushap Goyal](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Pushap_Goyal_graph_spanner_security) of Google showed Spanner Graph tracing security incidents across distributed systems, turning scattered events into a connected attack story. [Mahmood Nawaz](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Mahmood_Nawaz_knowledge_cloud_resilience) of LTIMindtree focused on knowledge systems that turn each incident into something the next responder can find, which is the part of the postmortem that usually goes missing.

## When the regulator is on the other line

[Nisheedh Raveendran](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Nisheedh_Raveendran_compliance_hipaa_gdpr), Senior Staff Engineer at LinkedIn, opened with three short sentences every compliance-adjacent engineer will recognise: system down, regulators calling, patients waiting. His talk covered why normal incident response fails when HIPAA, GDPR or the EU's Digital Markets Act are in play, and the playbooks that work instead.

[Nirup Baer](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Nirup_Baer_finance_modernization_resilience) of Wells Fargo looked at how financial firms embed compliance into cloud architecture so resilience and speed don't trade off against each other. In healthcare, [Sreenivasul Reddy Meegada](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Sreenivasul_Reddy_Meegada_healthcare_biometrics_security) drew on deployments of NICE and Omilia voice biometrics to tighten security without slowing patient workflows.

## The platforms underneath the incident

A good chunk of the day was about systems that shouldn't need an incident commander in the first place. [Sruthi Erra Hareram](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Sruthi_Erra_Hareram_databricks_analytics_reliability) presented a cross-cloud analytics pipeline on Azure Databricks and AWS built with incident-aware orchestration. [Adithya Sirimalla](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Adithya_Sirimalla_multicloud_databases_resilience) of Enliven Technologies covered running Oracle and SQL Server across AWS, Azure and OCI with automation, monitoring and disaster recovery. [Vijaykumar Pasunoori](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Vijaykumar_Pasunoori_apigateways_microservices_serverless) of Valet Living made API gateways part of detection and recovery, and [Rehana Sultana Khan](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Rehana_Sultana_Khan_ratelimiting_api_protection) of Versa Networks showed AI-driven rate limiting that adapts to malicious traffic instead of relying on fixed thresholds.

## Preventing the next one

Prevention got its own track of sorts. [Vijay Kumar Kola](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Vijay_Kumar_Kola_sap_salesforce_testing) of Intuitive used AI-powered testing to catch SAP and Salesforce failures before production, [Gobinath Kasimayan](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Gobinath_Kasimayan_sap_governance_agility) of Deloitte Consulting treated SAP master data governance as an incident prevention tool, and [Krishna Chaitanya Yarlagadda](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Krishna_Chaitanya_Yarlagadda_supplychain_automation_prevention) of Mercury Financial applied anomaly detection to supply chain disruptions that cascade into incidents within hours.

## Sponsors

Thanks to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), our gold sponsor, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) for the newsletter and to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) for the podcast partnership.

## What's next

All 22 talks are linked from the [Conf42 Incident Management 2025 page](https://www.conf42.com/im2025). Next in the series is [Conf42 Kube Native 2025](https://www.conf42.com/kubenative2025) on October 16, and the reliability conversation picks up again at [Conf42 SRE 2026](https://www.conf42.com/sre2026) on March 19, 2026. Meanwhile, check whether your status page knows about your last incident.

Title: JavaScript testing is heading back to the real browser
Description: Daniel Afonso of PagerDuty at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on the state of JS testing, from Vitest browser mode and MSW to Playwright and AI.
Body:
Ten years ago we ran component tests in a real browser with Karma and Jasmine, hated how flaky they were, and fled to jsdom. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Daniel Afonso, developer advocate at PagerDuty, argued that the industry is now walking back into the browser, this time with tools that make it bearable, and laid out the rest of the 2025 JavaScript testing picture on the way.

Daniel is on the SolidJS DX team and wrote a book on React Query, so he speaks as someone who writes and migrates a lot of tests. He grounds the talk in two sources: the State of JS survey (mocking is the top pain point; overall testing happiness sits at 2.5 out of 4) and an informal poll of eight friends about how their companies actually test.

## Eight companies, eight definitions of "unit"

The friend poll is the most relatable section. Jest plus React Testing Library dominates unit and integration work; Cypress or Playwright handle end-to-end; Storybook shows up as a component catalogue; one team still runs Karma and Jasmine; one writes BDD tests in Gherkin. Only one person counted static analysis (TypeScript and ESLint) as part of testing, and one team has a tidy migration rule: new tests in Testing Library, old Enzyme tests get migrated whenever someone touches them.

Daniel's diagnosis is what he calls the backend fallacy. Testing Library's user-centric philosophy removed implementation details from front-end tests, so the backend definitions of unit and integration stopped fitting, and every organisation he has met now draws the lines differently.

## jsdom pretends to be a browser and ends up neither

The core of the talk is the test-runner story. Jest's TypeScript and ESM support are still experimental, and wiring it to Webpack is configuration pain. Vitest fixed that by sharing the bundler with your app. Then Artem Zakharchenko, creator of Mock Service Worker, wrote a post arguing that jsdom runs in Node and fakes browser APIs, and that the closer the test environment is to production, the more the test is worth. His recommendation: Vitest browser mode.

Daniel migrated and lists what changed: `queryBy` and `findBy` became `getBy`, the `waitFor` wrappers went away because browser mode retries assertions automatically, MSW switched to its service worker mode, tests went async, and mocks for things like localStorage were deleted because the real API is there. The cost was two to three seconds of extra runtime, which he happily pays. Testing Library's own author later wrote that he was glad to see people uninstalling it, because Playwright and Vitest had absorbed its ideas natively.

## End-to-end tools want to be the whole suite

Playwright is winning adoption with cross-browser support, codegen, tracing and free parallelism. Daniel's sharper observation is that end-to-end tools, and Storybook, now all offer visual, component, API and accessibility testing, so his updated testing trophy has static analysis at the base, then unit, then component and end-to-end, with visual and accessibility testing across the top. MSW, meanwhile, has become the default for network mocking across REST, GraphQL and WebSocket, in the browser, Node and React Native.

## AI speeds you up but won't close your knowledge gap

On AI, he is pragmatic. Copilots speed you up, but check their output, especially on newer patterns like browser mode. Playwright's MCP server can explore a site and generate a test. Natural-language test tools such as Midscene get close to self-healing tests (a moved logout button no longer fails the run), at the cost of speed, and vision models like UI-TARS take terser prompts than text-only models working from the DOM.

## Who should watch

Front-end teams still on Jest with jsdom, anyone deciding between Cypress and Playwright, and leads who need a map of 2025 testing tools to justify a migration. It is a survey talk, so depth varies, but the browser-mode migration checklist alone saves an afternoon.
