Title: Master data management is a stateful Kubernetes workload
Description: Rahul Ameria (Meta Platforms) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on rebuilding MDM as Kubernetes microservices with StatefulSets, Helm, GitOps and Kafka.
Body:
The fastest way to lose master data on Kubernetes is to treat it like a stateless web app. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Rahul Ameria, Data Analyst at Meta Platforms, walked through what cloud-native master data management (MDM) looks like when matching, merging, validation and governance each become their own containerised service, and which Kubernetes primitives keep the single source of truth from quietly forking.

It is an architecture overview, broad rather than deep, and useful as a map of the moving parts.

## Why MDM had to change

Traditional MDM systems, in Rahul's description, are heavyweight, stateful and slow to scale. That was tolerable when everything lived in one data centre. With hybrid and multi-cloud deployments and microservices that need customer, product, supplier and account data in real time, the old shape doesn't fit.

His key distinction: cloud-native MDM is a redesign of how data mastering works in distributed, elastic infrastructure, and containerising the legacy MDM product isn't the same thing. Each capability becomes a service with clear boundaries, declared in Kubernetes manifests, deployed through Helm and GitOps, and scaled by the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler when ingestion spikes.

## State is the whole game

The section on stateful workloads is the core of the talk. StatefulSets give the core MDM stores stable network identities and ordered deployment. Persistent volumes on cloud block storage (AWS EBS, Azure Disk, GCP persistent disk) mean data survives pod restarts. Consensus stores such as etcd or CockroachDB keep state consistent across nodes.

His pitfalls list makes the same point from the other direction. Stateless assumptions lead to data loss on restarts. Ignoring storage latency slows matching and merging under load. Underestimating service mesh overhead turns into a configuration nightmare later. Skipping observability makes debugging impossible while data quality degrades unnoticed. His advice on databases and consensus strategy: choose them up front, because changing them later is expensive refactoring.

## Governance rules belong in Git

The governance argument is the one regulated industries will like most. Match rules, survivorship rules and validation policies all go into version control, so every change has a history. CI/CD applies the manifests, cutting human error. If a governance update causes trouble, you roll back to a known good configuration.

Observability gets a specific treatment too. Prometheus exporters publish data-quality metrics such as validation throughput, matching latency and merge accuracy; Grafana dashboards show MDM health at a glance; Jaeger or OpenTelemetry trace a record across microservices. That turns MDM from a black box into something an on-call engineer can reason about.

## Integration and a retailer story

Rahul positions MDM as a hub: API gateways such as Kong or NGINX expose master data with rate limits and auth, Kafka or Pulsar stream raw data in and master updates out, adapters bridge mainframe and ERP systems, and dbt and Airflow feed warehouses. Security is zero trust with mutual TLS through the mesh, HashiCorp Vault for secrets, encryption in transit and at rest, and RBAC with audit logs for GDPR and CCPA.

He illustrates it with a global retailer whose legacy MDM downtime during seasonal peaks hurt order fulfilment. After moving to microservices on StatefulSets backed by block storage, with Kafka for ingestion, the talk reports 99.9% uptime through Black Friday, a 30% cost reduction from elastic scaling off-peak, and governance rule changes deployed via GitOps in minutes.

## Who should watch

Data platform and data governance teams weighing a move of MDM onto Kubernetes, and platform engineers who are about to be asked to host it. His first best practice is the right one: start with one domain, such as customer data, before expanding.

Title: Tuning PySpark and Airflow on Kubernetes, one variable at a time
Description: Sruthi Erra Hareram (TELUS Digital) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on executor sizing, joins, skew and Airflow patterns for Kubernetes-native ETL.
Body:
A 60 MB dimension table, switched to a broadcast join, took one Spark stage from 19 minutes to three. That story sits in the middle of Sruthi Erra Hareram's talk at Conf42 Kube Native 2025, and it sums up her approach: most ETL speed comes from a few boring, measurable changes. Sruthi, a Data Engineer at TELUS Digital, covers the architecture, the Spark tuning, the Airflow patterns and a four-week rollout plan for running PySpark and Airflow on Kubernetes.

She promised zero fluff and mostly delivered. This is a practitioner's checklist, not a product pitch.

## Why ETL breaks at scale

Sruthi names four recurring failures. Clusters sized by guesswork, either over-provisioned and expensive or under-provisioned and flaky. Poor visibility, so a job failing at 2 AM means manual recovery because nobody can see lineage or timing. Brittle monolithic scripts where a new column ripples through everything. And growing data volume that inflates shuffle cost, storage cost and the blast radius of bad input.

Her foundation has three pillars: containers so each pipeline declares its own dependencies, CPU, memory and JVM; Kubernetes as the compute fabric, with namespaces isolating teams and quotas keeping noisy neighbours in check; and infrastructure as code, with Terraform and Helm reviewed through pull requests and promoted via GitOps.

## Spark tuning lives in memory, joins and skew

The tuning section is the densest and most reusable. Her starting points:

- executors of roughly 4 to 8 GB as a pragmatic range
- persist only where reuse pays off
- memory fractions around 0.6 for execution and 0.2 for storage as a baseline, adjusted with real metrics
- broadcast hash joins for small dimensions, sort-merge for large fact-to-fact joins
- salting or pre-aggregation for hot keys

The skew story is the other memorable one: a single customer accounted for 40% of the rows in one pipeline, and salting into 16 buckets levelled the partitions and removed the straggler.

Her diagnostic trick is worth stealing. If median task time is low but p95 is awful, suspect skew. If both are high, you are under-resourced or over-shuffling. And the discipline around it: take a baseline, change one variable at a time, and when a change wins, bake it into project templates so the next pipeline inherits it.

## Airflow on Kubernetes needs a few patterns, not more people

Running Airflow on Kubernetes aligns the control plane with the data plane: pod-level isolation per task, workload identity and managed secrets. Her practical tip is to define a small set of pod templates (small, heavy joins, machine learning) and let tasks pick by convention.

The four patterns she recommends:

1. Dynamic DAG generation from configs kept in S3 or GCS, so hundreds of similar pipelines don't mean hundreds of copy-pasted files.
2. Branching with BranchPythonOperator to route around known bad data or choose a light or heavy path by input size.
3. Backfills driven by logical run dates, with every step idempotent.
4. SLA monitoring through custom callbacks into Datadog or Prometheus, alerting on leading indicators like rising retries instead of only failures.

Her micro-example ties it together: if today's volume is more than 1.5 times the seven-day median, the DAG branches to a wider executor profile and adds a checkpoint.

## Observability and the rollout

Prometheus for executor and shuffle metrics, structured JSON logs with correlation IDs, OpenTelemetry tracing across Airflow tasks and Spark jobs, Great Expectations for data quality, and per-app cost tracking. Then a migration that keeps risk low: one medium-impact pipeline per sprint, compare against the baseline, publish the result, repeat. Her pitfalls list includes the cheap win most teams still miss: move large datasets from CSV or JSON to Parquet or ORC.

## Who should watch

Data engineers running Spark and Airflow who are moving onto Kubernetes, or who already have and are paying for it. Platform engineers supporting data teams will get a clear picture of what those teams need from the cluster.

Title: A/B testing is the data science skill that compounds a career
Description: Bhavana Reddy Chadagonda (Intuit) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on experiment designs, CUPED variance reduction and the platform behind trustworthy A/B tests.
Body:
The fastest way to make a data scientist indispensable is to make them the person who can say whether a launch actually worked. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Bhavana Reddy Chadagonda, Staff Data Scientist at Intuit, laid out a field guide to experimentation: which design to pick, how CUPED cuts the sample size you need, the pitfalls that fake a win, and how all of it turns into career progression.

It is part statistics primer, part career talk, with a short section on the cloud-native platform that makes experiments cheap to run. The statistics stay at the level of intuition and business framing; she points to existing resources for the maths.

## Business constraints pick the design, not the other way round

Bhavana walks through the menu. Classic between-subjects A/B tests for feature releases and UI changes. Multivariate and factorial tests when you want interaction effects. Holdouts for effects that take weeks to show up. Switchback experiments that rotate treatment over time, the approach marketplaces like DoorDash, Uber and Lyft use because users on both sides of the market contaminate each other. Geo experiments when user-level randomisation would spill over.

When true randomisation isn't possible, she names the credible fallbacks: difference-in-differences, interrupted time series and synthetic control. The point running through this section is judgement. Knowing when to deviate from pure randomisation is the skill, and it is exactly what interviewers probe.

## Halve the variance, halve the sample

The most practical part of the talk is variance reduction. Required sample size is proportional to variance, so if you cut variance in half you need roughly half the users, which means faster decisions and more experiments per quarter.

She groups the techniques into five buckets: regression adjustment with pre-period covariates (the umbrella CUPED sits under), balanced assignment through blocking or stratification, metric engineering such as per-user aggregation, capping outliers and log transforms, cluster-aware estimation for geo and switchback tests, and the operational hygiene of counting only truly exposed users with event definitions frozen before launch.

CUPED gets a worked example: a test of whether runners are slower with weights attached. Each runner's mile time is already explained largely by how fast they were before the experiment, so adjusting by their baseline strips out the noise and leaves the effect of the weights. Her best practices are the ones people skip: pick covariates highly correlated with the outcome, use only data from before the experiment, and feel free to use more than one.

## If it looks too good, check the plumbing

The pitfalls section is a good pre-launch checklist. Sample ratio mismatch and logging gaps. Randomising on one unit and analysing on another, which inflates variance. Interference between treatment and control. Peeking without adjusting the false positive rate. Metric drift and seasonality. Her rule: if something seems too good to be true, it probably is, so check these before you celebrate.

## The career ladder, spelled out

Bhavana closes with a concrete IC ladder for experimentation specialists. Entry level means solid fundamentals, clean hypotheses, reproducible analysis and clear writing. Mid level means leading multiple tests, mentoring, sequential and Bayesian methods, and standard guardrails. Senior means setting experimentation strategy and partnering with engineering on the platform. Staff and principal shape the system: platform roadmaps, open source contributions and teaching the organisation to learn faster.

The portfolio advice is practical: document real scenarios end to end from hypothesis to recommendation, contribute to statistical libraries, and show iteration instead of one-and-done tests.

## Who should watch

Analysts and early-career data scientists planning their next step, engineers building feature-flag or experimentation platforms who want to know what the statisticians need, and product managers tired of arguing from opinion. Experienced experimenters will know most of it, though the variance-reduction taxonomy is a handy reference.

Title: Accessible JavaScript comes down to three types and ten principles
Description: Gian Wild of AccessibilityOz at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on making forms and scripted widgets accessible, from keyboard traps to error messages.
Body:
If you only remember one thing from Gian Wild's talk, she would like it to be this: don't use CAPTCHA. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, the AccessibilityOz founder walked through a compact framework for accessible JavaScript, three types of functionality and ten principles, illustrated with real sites that get it right and very real sites that get it wrong.

The talk is dense on purpose. Gian says so up front and points to the AccessibilityOz JavaScript fact sheet, which carries the same principles, a testing checklist, developer examples and a live demo appendix with copy-paste code. Think of the video as the guided tour of that fact sheet.

## Three kinds of JavaScript, three obligations

Her taxonomy is the useful frame. Type one binds behaviour to elements that are already interactive (links, buttons, text fields), so assistive technology can read their attributes and text. Type two presents information without interaction, such as a progress meter, and must have a text equivalent like a percentage. Type three builds custom widgets that are both, and those must be made from elements assistive tech already understands: a calendar widget with a label, a trigger button and table markup underneath.

## The keyboard is the test that catches most things

Principle two (everything works with every input device) gets a lot of airtime, because assistive technologies such as joysticks, head wands and switches usually mimic a mouse or keyboard. Her rules are concrete: tab moves between actionable items, escape closes, arrow keys move within menus, focus is always visible, and there are no keyboard traps. Except inside a modal, where focus must be trapped until the user closes it.

Her horror story is the late-2000s Firefox video player, which swallowed the tab key. Users who tabbed into it had to close the browser, reopen the page and try to steer around the video.

## Order, time and surprise

Several principles are about predictability:

- **Source order, focus order and visual order should agree.** Insert dynamic content in the DOM right after the element that triggered it. Never put information after a submit button: her examples include a ticket site that hides the accessible-tickets option below it, and a bookshop page that only mentions a title is unavailable in a corner nobody reads.
- **Timed activity can be controlled.** Warn before a session expires and let people extend it. A donation form with a 20-minute timeout gets the eye-roll it deserves.
- **Movement can be paused.** Carousels need pause controls, animated GIFs should stop within five seconds, and the blink and marquee elements stay buried. For flashing content she recommends the free PEAT analysis tool, with the 1997 Pokemon episode as the cautionary tale.
- **No unexpected changes.** No navigation on a select's change event, no timed client-side redirects, no popups that vanish after a few seconds.

## Forms are where JavaScript most often breaks things

Labels must be programmatically tied to fields (she inspects Amazon's sign-in field to show the `for`/`id` pairing). Fieldsets group fields that only make sense together, like an area code plus a phone number. Errors must be in text, not just red, because screen readers don't announce colour and red-blind users can't see it.

Validation gets specific rules: validate on submission, not per field; bind to the form's submit event, not the button's click; move focus to the first invalid field; insert the error message right after the field and in its label; and never force focus to stay in an invalid field.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers who build forms, menus, modals or carousels, which is most of them. Some parts are an intro (there is a pointer to her Accessibility Basics material if terms like "assistive technology" are new), but the form-validation and focus-order rules are the sort of checklist senior engineers get wrong too. Have the fact sheet open in another tab.

Title: Solution architects are what make a Kubernetes CRM resilient
Description: Chakra Gadige (Splunk) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on how Technical Solution Architects steer CRM platforms onto Kubernetes without new bottlenecks.
Body:
Moving a CRM onto Kubernetes is mostly an organisational problem with a YAML-shaped tail. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Chakra Gadige, Technical Lead for Salesforce at Splunk, argued that the role holding that move together is the Technical Solution Architect (TSA): the person who translates business goals into a cluster design and keeps today's shortcut from becoming next year's outage.

This is a short, high-level talk. There is no demo and no code; it is a framework for how to think about CRM modernisation and who should own it. If you lead a platform or CRM team and need a checklist to argue with, it is worth the time.

## The CRM stopped being a monolith, so the architect stopped being a diagrammer

Chakra's starting point is the shift he sees in CRM platforms: away from monolithic suites and towards containerised services, with Kubernetes as the default orchestration layer. That shift changes the job. In his framing, the TSA is a "business translator" who makes sure technical design lines up with what the organisation wants, and a manager of technical debt who designs systems that scale before they have to.

His most useful line is that TSAs are simplifiers. They reduce complexity by finding where technical debt comes from, designing a streamlined architecture, using a modular approach to scaling, and putting observability in early so problems surface before customers notice them. Anyone who has inherited a CRM integration layer with eleven point-to-point connectors knows exactly why that matters.

## Resilience comes from a short list of principles

The architecture section is a compact list of principles for a Kubernetes-native CRM:

- microservices for flexibility, so one team's change doesn't redeploy the world
- declarative configuration for consistency across environments
- deliberate stateful service management, because CRM data has to persist
- API-first design and integration
- a zero trust security model, end to end

None of these is new on its own. The value is in seeing them applied to CRM, where stateful data, multi-tenancy and integrations with every other system make shortcuts expensive.

## Before and after is the honest way to sell it

Chakra frames the change as a before-and-after. Before the TSA gets involved: monolithic CRMs, manual deployments, inconsistent environments and security gaps. After: a microservice-based CRM on Kubernetes, automated CI/CD pipelines, security built in by design, and full observability.

He also says how to know whether it worked. The metrics he lists are the DORA family: change failure rate, mean time to recovery, deployment frequency and lead time for changes. That's the right answer, because calling an architecture resilient is a claim and those four numbers are the evidence.

## The hard parts get named, briefly

The challenges slide covers the problems that bite in practice: stateful workload management, integration latency, database performance and multi-tenant complexity. The mitigations he pairs with them are the standard Kubernetes toolkit: StatefulSets, caching, service mesh adoption and namespace isolation. Security gets its own list: identity and access management, secret management, network policies between microservices, and continuous container scanning.

The roadmap is five stages: assessment, design of a Kubernetes-native blueprint, a pilot that proves core functionality, progressive migration, and continuous optimisation. A pilot before migration sounds obvious. Plenty of CRM programmes skip it anyway.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering managers planning a CRM or Salesforce-adjacent modernisation, and anyone who has to explain to leadership why a Kubernetes migration needs an owner and not just a ticket. Engineers looking for StatefulSet tuning or mesh configuration should look elsewhere; this talk stays at the level of principles and roles.

Title: Hallucinations are a symptom; missing context in the IDE is the bug
Description: Sharon Yelenik of Cloudinary at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on MCP servers, indexed docs, Context7 and rules files that make AI coding in the IDE accurate.
Body:
Your AI assistant does not hallucinate because it is dim. It guesses because nobody told it your project's rules. That is the core claim Sharon Yelenik, senior developer experience and API content writer at Cloudinary, made at Conf42 JavaScript 2025, and she backed it with a step-by-step setup that feeds documentation straight into the LLM client inside the IDE.

Sharon spent the previous year on a large Cloudinary team turning the company's APIs into Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. The talk is what that work taught her about documentation accuracy, with Cloudinary as the worked example and Cursor as the IDE. The same recipe applies to Auth0, Firebase, Supabase, Slack, Shopify and other APIs she lists at the end.

## Two jobs for the AI in your editor

She splits IDE AI into two use cases. The familiar one is code generation and refactoring. The second is agentic work: uploading assets, configuring environments, the backend chores you normally leave the editor to do. MCP servers handle the authentication, validation and execution so the agent can act on your behalf without you switching to a web console.

The motivation is trust. Sharon cites survey data that only 3.8% of developers report both low hallucination and high confidence, and that agent adoption is still a minority. Her reading: hallucinations are not the root problem, they are a symptom. The model does not know your architecture, your naming conventions or the documented rules of the product you are calling, so it guesses, and every bad guess erodes the team's willingness to use it.

## Four layers of context

The practical core is four habits, each demoed in Cursor:

- **Add the vendor's MCP servers.** She pastes Cloudinary's remote MCP server config into Cursor's tools settings, authenticates once per server, and the tools light up.
- **Index the docs site.** Cursor's docs indexing takes the documentation URL; then you attach those docs as context on each request.
- **Use Context7.** Its MCP server indexes the code snippets and examples from API docs, so generated code comes from documented examples, not guesses. Not every product is indexed yet, and she suggests asking vendors for it.
- **Write rules files.** MDC files in Cursor, with equivalents in JetBrains and VS Code. Some APIs ship them already; Cloudinary has one explaining transformation parameter order and invalid combinations.

## Rules files: compatibility, conventions, constraints, canon

Her mnemonic for writing your own rules is four Cs: compatibility notes (what plays well together), conventions (naming, folders, architecture), constraints (what the AI must never do, such as exposing secrets or calling admin APIs from the browser) and canon (short correct snippets to copy). Keep them one to three pages, review them often, link the official docs.

Her Cloudinary examples are refreshingly specific: always apply automatic format and quality, use named transformations for hero images and thumbnails instead of ad hoc ones, and only pair face gravity with automatic cropping because other combinations misbehave. These are exactly the bugs that are tedious to find later.

## The demo closes the loop

The finale runs the whole stack. From inside the IDE she uploads a portrait image to Cloudinary via MCP, asks for a wide hero version (the agent checks for an existing named transformation, finds one that does not match, creates a new one and wires the URL into the page), adds a text overlay that follows her rules file's font and placement standard, and crops a face-centred thumbnail that comes back with the right parameters. The thumbnail is a bit big, which she notes honestly: no rule said otherwise.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers and team leads trying to get colleagues to trust AI coding, and anyone writing docs for an API that agents will consume. It shows Cloudinary's own MCP servers, so it is partly a vendor walkthrough, but the habits transfer to any well-documented API. If you already run curated rules and MCP tools daily, the four Cs checklist is the part worth stealing.

Title: Predictive manufacturing service needs a CRM that scales like Kubernetes
Description: Jasmeer Singh (IBM) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on moving aftermarket service from reactive repairs to predictive analytics on Kubernetes-native CRM.
Body:
Manufacturers leave money on the table every time a machine breaks before anyone calls the customer. Jasmeer Singh, Senior Architect for Salesforce at IBM, used his Conf42 Kube Native 2025 talk to argue that aftermarket service (maintenance, spare parts) becomes a profit driver once it turns predictive, and that the CRM behind it has to be rebuilt on Kubernetes to handle the sensor data that makes prediction possible.

It is a short, focused architecture talk: the pipeline, the Kubernetes primitives and the mistakes to avoid.

## CRMs were built for contacts, not telemetry

The business problem is reactive service: equipment breaks, then the company responds. Many manufacturers have digital initiatives and still cannot scale predictive service models. Jasmeer's diagnosis is the system of record. Traditional CRMs were designed to track customer interactions, not billions of IoT signals. They are monolithic, struggle with real-time velocity, and buckle as customer data volume grows.

Breaking the analytics into containerised microservices lets each piece scale on its own, up when demand spikes and back down when it falls.

## Sensor noise in, service calls out

His real-time pipeline has four stages. IoT ingestion through containerised collectors capturing sensor streams nonstop. Service history (maintenance logs and repair records) analysed in a distributed way to surface patterns. Machine learning models in Kubernetes pods modelling customer behaviour and usage. Predictive insights served in real time through autoscaling services, pushed through APIs into the CRM and dashboards.

Underneath: containerised pipelines, Helm-managed ML deployments, event-driven triggers so predictions happen as data arrives, Jobs for batch analytics, CronJobs for recurring work, custom operators for ML workflows, and StatefulSets for persistence. The outcome he claims is longer customer retention, sharply lower downtime through predictive maintenance, and service revenue growth from putting resources in the right place at the right time. The talk does not break down the three-times figure in its title, so treat that as the headline rather than a measured result.

## Resource limits are where it lives or dies

The most practical section is about resources. CPU allocation should be dynamic. Memory needs limits and affinity rules so no single pod hogs the cluster. Persistent volumes hold model artifacts you must keep; ephemeral storage handles temporary work. Model training should be distributed across pods.

Monitoring covers two layers: model accuracy, drift, latency and data quality on the application side; pod resource use, scaling events and storage performance on the infrastructure side.

## Three pitfalls to plan for

Jasmeer names three failure modes. Without proper resource requests and limits, workloads compete and slow each other down. Without deliberate data access design, IO bottlenecks creep in fast. Without careful state management, models and intermediate data can vanish during scaling. Each is avoidable, but only if planned upfront, which is a polite way of saying the default settings will bite.

Resilience rounds it out: multi-zone deployments, circuit breakers, horizontal scaling policies, and backups of persistent volumes.

## Who should watch

Architects connecting IoT data to CRM and field-service systems, especially in manufacturing, and platform teams asked to host ML workloads for a business unit for the first time. If you already run stateful ML on Kubernetes, the pitfalls list is a quick sanity check.

Title: TypeScript is a serious language for building games on the web
Description: Annie Tsai and Adam Ringhede of Hology at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on why TypeScript, WebGPU and WebAssembly make browser games a real platform.
Body:
If your mental picture of a browser game is a Flash puzzle you hid from your parents in 2008, Annie Tsai and Adam Ringhede of Hology Interactive would like a word. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025 the two co-founders, who have spent around two years building a game engine on web technologies, made the case that TypeScript and JavaScript are now a sensible default for web and mobile games, not a compromise.

It is a short talk, closer to a well-argued pitch than a tutorial. Annie covers the market side, Adam the engineering side, and the whole thing fits in a coffee break.

## The audience already lives in the browser

Annie's opening argument is distribution. Traditional studios think in PC and console terms, while a huge number of players sit on phones, social platforms and web portals. She points to platforms like Poki, with players from over 100 countries, and CrazyGames, which recently published an FPS. Discord activities are another door: you ship the game to people who are already hanging out there.

The pitch is about friction. A web game needs no install, no 100 GB download and no new graphics card. The same stack also stretches beyond games into education, marketing, rapid prototypes and interactive overlays for live streams, where the chat can play along.

## The GPU is no longer locked behind a native app

Adam takes over with the platform. WebGL 2 has been in the big browsers for years, and WebGPU is now supported in all major ones too. His take is that WebGL already gets you surprisingly close to native graphics and that its capabilities have not been used to the full. WebGPU narrows the gap further and adds parallel compute on the GPU, which games can use for more than drawing triangles.

## Types are the bridge from C++ habits

The language argument is where the talk earns its title. JavaScript gives you fast iteration: no long compile step, easy sharing as a website or an itch.io upload, a good fit for prototypes. TypeScript adds what bigger game codebases need: static types that make a large codebase readable, behave a bit like self-documentation, and catch type errors before runtime. For developers coming from C# or C++, Adam frames TypeScript as a bridge between JavaScript's dynamic nature and the compile-time safety they are used to, with strictness you can dial up or down.

The detail engine builders will enjoy is hot reloading. Because it is a scripting language, Hology's editor watches your code, transpiles it on change and runs it inside the already-running application in a couple of hundred milliseconds. Anyone who has waited for a C++ engine to rebuild knows exactly what that is worth.

## Open source beats proprietary toolchains

Adam contrasts the npm world with traditional game development, where engines often ship their own languages, version control and file formats that resist diffing or integration with other tools. With TypeScript you get millions of packages, tools that transfer to non-game work, and an open source culture that makes collaboration easier.

On performance, he pushes back on the usual doubt. Written carefully, with typed array buffers and C-like patterns, JavaScript optimises very well under the JIT. When you need more, WebAssembly lets you compile C, C++ or AssemblyScript (a TypeScript-like language) and bring in pathfinding or physics libraries of the kind AAA engines use. Most game code never has to touch it, but the escape hatch exists.

## Who should watch

Web developers curious about games, game developers wondering whether the browser is worth a look, and anyone choosing a language for a small team's first 3D project. It is an overview with a clear point of view, and it is upfront that Hology builds an engine on this stack. If you want code-level detail on rendering or physics, treat it as the starting map, not the territory.

Title: Shift FinOps left so the cloud bill is a pipeline check, not a surprise
Description: Manoj Kalakoti (Apple) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on autonomous FinOps for financial services - pre-deploy cost estimates, budget gates and self-healing spend.
Body:
By the time a cost spike shows up on the monthly cloud bill, the money is already gone, and in a regulated bank that is a governance failure as much as a budget one. Manoj Kalakoti, Senior Site Reliability Engineer at Apple, argued at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 that FinOps for cloud-native financial services has to move into the engineering lifecycle: cost estimated before deploy, budgets enforced as policy, anomalies caught and fixed by automation.

It is a blueprint talk. No vendor pitch, no tool demo, but a clear sequence of controls you could build one at a time.

## Retrospective FinOps is always late

Manoj's critique of traditional FinOps is that it reviews bills after the fact. Finance and engineering systems are disconnected, feedback loops take weeks, and multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters running thousands of workloads with market-driven scaling make attribution hard. Add legacy systems, regulators demanding cost transparency, and a skills gap between finance and cloud-native operations, and spend goes unchecked until it is a problem for the audit committee.

His fix is platform engineering: put financial intelligence where developers already work, through infrastructure-as-code templates, CI/CD gates, Kubernetes admission controls and real-time telemetry.

## Price it before you ship it

The first control is pre-deployment cost estimation. Static analysis of infrastructure-as-code templates computes the resource cost of a change, calibrated with historical usage and live cloud-provider pricing APIs, and factoring in reserved instances and savings plans. The output is a forecast with confidence intervals, plus an audit trail of who approved which cost.

The second is policy-based budget gating. Budgets are defined in YAML at project, team or application level and enforced at commit, build, deploy and scaling events. Exceptions go through an approval workflow with audit logging, and dashboards show budget consumption as it happens.

## Untagged resources get fixed by a bot

Cost attribution depends on tags, so the third control is automated tagging: enforced tag schemas at creation, tag inheritance, tags set from deployment context, validation gates in CI/CD that stop non-compliant deploys, and remediation bots that fix anything untagged or mistagged. Anyone who has tried to allocate a shared cluster's bill by hand will recognise the problem this solves.

## Detect anomalies, then remediate them

Real-time anomaly detection replaces static thresholds with ML: time-series analysis against historical and seasonal patterns, resource fingerprinting to baseline each workload's behaviour, correlation of cost spikes with deployments and application events, and forecasting with confidence intervals.

Self-healing remediation closes the loop. Once an anomaly is flagged, automated root-cause analysis finds the workload or change behind it, and a playbook runs in one of three modes: self-service, developer-approved, or fully automated with approvals and audit trails. Typical actions are rightsizing over-provisioned resources, applying reservation discounts, moving storage to cheaper tiers and recommending architecture changes.

## Built to survive the audit

For regulated environments, Manoj insists on immutable cost logs, standardised metadata schemas and tamper-proof records of approvals and attributions, with reporting aligned to frameworks such as SOX and PCI DSS. Success is measured on cost reduction, cost predictability against forecast ranges, policy compliance (every resource tagged and allocated) and anomaly response time.

His takeaways fit in a line each: shift FinOps left, give engineers self-service cost insight, replace manual reviews with automated policy, and design for compliance from the start.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams who get pulled into cost reviews, and FinOps practitioners in financial services trying to get engineering to care before the invoice arrives. The talk is long on structure and short on specifics, so treat it as a target architecture to compare against your own.

Title: How Informatica CLAIRE automates data integration in hybrid clouds
Description: Sathish Kuppan Pandurangan (Zurich North America) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on CLAIRE in Informatica IDMC for metadata discovery, anomaly detection and compliance.
Body:
Most data integration time goes into mappings, classification and chasing quality issues that a machine could have spotted. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Sathish Kuppan Pandurangan, an Informatica platform administrator at Zurich North America with 15 years in data platform engineering, walked through how CLAIRE, the AI engine inside Informatica's Intelligent Data Management Cloud (IDMC), automates that work across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and on-premises systems.

To be clear about scope: this is a product-focused talk about one vendor's platform, given by someone who runs it rather than someone who sells it. The abstract claims CLAIRE automates 80% of integration tasks; the talk itself is about how, not about benchmarks.

## Legacy integration hits three walls

Sathish's problem statement is short. Legacy integration platforms struggle with real-time operations, manual steps create bottlenecks, and compliance requirements pile more complexity onto every workflow. As organisations move to containerised, Kubernetes-based environments, the integration layer needs a different approach to orchestration, governance and scale.

## One engine across clouds and the data centre

CLAIRE sits on top of native connectors. On AWS that means S3, relational databases, Redshift and Lambda, inside AWS security and compliance frameworks. On Azure, Data Factory, Data Lake Storage, Synapse and Azure SQL. On-premises, it bridges legacy systems to the cloud with real-time synchronisation.

The automation story starts with pattern recognition over existing integrations: CLAIRE suggests transformation logic and generates mapping and workflow recommendations, so developers know where to look. It extends to predictive maintenance, anomaly detection and self-healing pipelines.

## Metadata discovery finds the sensitive columns

The section most relevant to regulated companies is metadata discovery. CLAIRE scans data across the estate and classifies it using pattern recognition and semantic analysis, identifying personal information and regulated content. It learns from user feedback over time, so classification improves as new sources and data types arrive.

Data quality gets the same treatment. The engine builds baselines of normal data behaviour, flags deviations before downstream processes are hit, and suggests corrective actions based on how similar issues were resolved before.

## Kubernetes does the scaling, CLAIRE predicts it

On the infrastructure side, Kubernetes integration provides pod-level scaling with data volume, load balancing, failure recovery, microservices behind an API gateway with circuit breakers, and native network policies, secret management and role-based access control. CLAIRE adds predictive resource allocation from historical usage, seasonal trends and business cycles, scaling up ahead of peaks and deprovisioning when demand drops.

For compliance, it maintains lineage, generates compliance reports, watches access patterns, flags potential violations in real time and applies remediation.

## Where it gets used

Sathish describes three industry patterns. In banking, risk data aggregation across trading systems and real-time fraud flagging that can trigger holds on accounts. In healthcare, unified electronic health records while keeping to HIPAA. In insurance, which is closest to his own employer's world, automated claims intake: classifying and routing claims by complexity, urgency and risk, cross-referencing documents against policies and claim history, and flagging fraud patterns for deeper review.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and administrators already on Informatica, or evaluating IDMC, who want a tour of what CLAIRE covers. If you are not in that ecosystem, the classification and anomaly-detection ideas still transfer, but expect product names throughout.

Title: Read the SAP transport and the pull request before you pick your tests
Description: Vijay Kumar Kola (Intuitive) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on AI-driven, risk-based testing that keeps SAP S/4HANA and Salesforce changes safe.
Body:
Most enterprise incidents in SAP and Salesforce estates start as a change somebody tested too little, or tested the wrong things very thoroughly. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Vijay Kumar Kola, Senior Analyst in IT at Intuitive who has worked as a senior QA lead on SAP S/4HANA and Salesforce programmes, showed how AI-assisted testing reads what actually changed and points the regression effort at the risky parts, so failures get caught before go-live rather than after.

## Static test suites cannot keep up with quarterly releases

Vijay's problem statement will be familiar to anyone on an ERP programme. S/4HANA modules (sales and distribution, materials management, finance, transport management) depend on each other, so a change in SD can break MM or finance. Salesforce adds layers of customisation, CPQ pricing rules and multi-cloud setups, plus integrations with legacy systems and external APIs. SAP ships quarterly and service-pack updates; Salesforce ships seasonal releases; the testing window keeps shrinking.

Meanwhile regulated processes under SOX and GxP demand near-total accuracy, and resource limits leave large parts of the suite untested. He describes one recent project where a model adjustment in Salesforce meant retesting 70% of the suite. Static scripts age badly: an assessment he led on S/4 found 60% of test cases redundant because the scripts were outdated.

## Let the change tell you what to test

The idea at the centre of the talk is change-driven test selection. His team built agents that read the SAP side (transports and LiveCompare reports) and the Salesforce side (GitHub pull requests and change summaries), work out which objects and business processes are affected, and determine the regression impact. On one project that cut manual testing by 40 to 50%. Doing the impact analysis up front on another saved the regression team 35% of testing time.

Around that sit three techniques. Predictive analytics trained on historical defects and production issues forecasts where defects are likely, so compliance-critical workflows get priority. Machine learning on execution results removes redundant tests and highlights the impactful ones. NLP turns requirements in specs, user stories and emails into test cases; he describes using it on a long Salesforce CPQ specification and on a 20-page change log during an S/4HANA implementation.

The tooling named is Tricentis Tosca for model-based regression across SAP modules and RPA bots for repetitive financial checks such as journal postings and reconciliations, which, he said, caught SOX discrepancies that manual review would have missed.

## Salesforce gets its own three checks

For Salesforce, Vijay describes three tailored approaches. Declarative configuration validation tests flows and validation rules, including a CPQ pricing flow where discounts changed by country and customer; the AI tests caught a logic error during the pilot. Third-party integration testing simulates traffic across the boundaries with SAP or payment gateways; an agent predicted a sync delay under peak load, and the team adjusted API call frequency before go-live. User experience impact prediction flagged lag for mobile users after a CPQ update, prompting a redesign.

## Quality gates that can say no

The framework is pragmatic: assess current testing and pain points, build a data strategy from test results, defect logs and user behaviour, pick tools that fit your ecosystem, and integrate with CI/CD pipelines, test management tools and automation frameworks such as Selenium. In the pipeline, real-time quality gates make deployment decisions from test results and risk scores, and automated rollback watches post-deployment metrics. He also mentions self-healing tests that propose fixes to broken automation and wait for a human to confirm before updating the library.

His advice for starting is small: pilot predictive analytics on one module, such as SD, MM or finance, in your next SAP update.

## Who should watch

QA leads, release managers and SAP or Salesforce platform owners who own the regression suite and the go-live call. The abstract headlines a 68% reduction in incidents; the talk itself is a practitioner's tour of how his teams got their gains, so expect project anecdotes rather than a controlled study.

Title: Bias scales with your cluster, so put ethics in the deploy pipeline
Description: Jaydeep Taralkar (UBS) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on scaling financial ML on Kubernetes with fairness gates, data residency and continuous bias monitoring.
Body:
A model that quietly penalises one demographic in one city becomes a model that penalises it across a continent the moment you scale it. Jaydeep Taralkar, Executive Director at UBS, made that the core warning of his Conf42 Kube Native 2025 talk on scaling AI-driven financial services with Kubernetes, and his answer is to make fairness a gate in the deployment pipeline rather than a slide in the ethics review.

The talk pairs the familiar scaling story with a less familiar goal: using cheap, elastic infrastructure to serve people the financial system has historically left out.

## Markets spike, monoliths don't stretch

Financial workloads are bursty. Jaydeep's examples are a market open, when a sudden spike needs massive resources that then fall away, and Black Friday traffic hitting a single application that also runs credit scoring for millions of users. A monolith becomes the bottleneck.

The Kubernetes answer has three parts: break the monolith into independently scalable microservices (his image is untangling a giant ball of yarn), scale horizontally in real time, and deploy across regions for performance, resilience and regional compliance.

## Elastic infrastructure reaches the unbanked

The part that sets this talk apart is financial inclusion. Jaydeep points to India's 2014 push to open bank accounts at scale as the kind of moment this architecture has to handle. Scalable cloud-native systems make it practical to run mobile-first credit scoring for emerging markets, use alternative data such as mobile phone usage and utility payments for people with no credit history, and serve dozens of languages through containerised NLP models.

That reach is also where the risk lives. Any underlying bias gets amplified across millions of users, so governance stops being a design consideration and becomes a requirement.

## Fairness as a failing test

His three governance mechanisms are all cloud-native habits pointed at ethics:

- **Policy as code**: fairness criteria encoded in the deployment pipeline, so a model that fails them is blocked before production.
- **Automated monitoring**: continuous bias detection and fairness checks, which he likens to a smoke detector that is always on.
- **Audit trails**: immutable logs of every model decision and governance action.

In practice that means CI/CD for models with clear versioning and automatic fairness tests in staging, canary deployments to a small user subset to watch for bias before full rollout, and custom metrics for model fairness next to CPU and memory, with alerts when bias crosses a threshold. Distributed tracing then shows the full path of a decision.

## Data residency without rebuilding

For multi-jurisdiction compliance, Kubernetes scheduling rules keep a country's data on servers inside that country, region-specific configurations adapt to local law without a rebuild, and a service mesh secures cross-border coordination.

The case study puts it together: a global fraud detection system handling a hundred million transactions a day across more than 30 countries, with response times under 100 milliseconds. Regional clusters, a service mesh between them, Prometheus, Grafana or AppDynamics tracking fairness alongside system metrics, and GitOps or Jenkins pipelines with ethical validation gates before any model goes live.

## Three things to remember

His closing list is short: start with governance before you scale, monitor fairness as continuously as latency, and automate everything, because without automation none of this holds up across regions.

## Who should watch

ML platform engineers and architects in financial services, and anyone building credit or fraud models that will run in more than one country. If fairness in your org lives in a policy PDF, this talk shows where it should live instead.

Title: Banks should run AI governance as microservices next to the models
Description: Ashish Dibouliya (Webster Bank) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on a Kubernetes-native framework for AI metadata, lineage, drift and regulatory compliance.
Body:
Governance built for a static data warehouse cannot keep up with fraud models that retrain continuously and run on containers that come and go by the minute. Ashish Dibouliya, Managing Director of Data Architecture at Webster Bank, used his Conf42 Kube Native 2025 talk to propose the fix: deploy governance itself as cloud-native microservices on Kubernetes, so it scales and moves at the same speed as the AI it watches.

It is an architecture talk with a case study at the end, pitched at the people who have to satisfy both the innovation team and the regulator.

## Containers made AI fast and governance blind

Ashish describes the dual pressure every bank feels: compliance failures cost money and reputation, while the business wants AI shipped quickly. Kubernetes gave AI workloads hybrid-cloud deployment, dynamic scaling and blue-green or canary updates. It also brought dynamic service meshes, distributed clusters and short-lived workloads that traditional monitoring and governance tools struggle to follow.

He lists four places the old model breaks: metadata (AI produces huge volumes of it, constantly changing), lineage (tracing where each model feature came from is nearly impossible at scale), real-time compliance (regulators expect continuous monitoring of bias, drift and quality), and regulatory complexity (explainable, fair AI as a standing obligation rather than a one-time box to tick).

## Three services do the governing

His unified AI data governance framework runs as microservices integrated with Kubernetes orchestration, built from three components:

- A **metadata orchestration engine**, the central nervous system, managing thousands of metadata events per second.
- An **intelligent lineage tracker**, using graph algorithms and instrumentation to trace dependencies across distributed AI systems.
- A **real-time compliance monitor**, checking AI decisions against internal policy and regulation as they happen.

The metadata layer has to be fast to be useful: relational and graph stores for different query types, hot data in memory, indexes for time-based, graph and full-text queries, and federation so you can query across sources without centralising everything.

## Drift and bias checks run all the time

The automation layer watches for data, concept and performance drift, checks fairness across demographic groups for protected attributes, and uses unsupervised ML for anomaly detection in models and data. Security is defence in depth: integration with enterprise IAM, attribute-based access control for fine-grained permissions, every governance operation logged with full context, and encryption including field-level encryption and tokenisation.

## Mapped to the rules banks actually face

The regulatory mapping is concrete. For GDPR, consent tracking and the right to be forgotten, which means finding every model trained on a given person's data. For CCPA, automated consumer-rights requests and data-sharing tracking. For Basel III, risk model validation tracking and stress testing. And it anticipates the EU AI Act by classifying AI systems by risk level and applying matching controls.

## The case study numbers

A global tier-one bank rolled the framework out in phases, starting with fraud detection, credit risk and regulatory reporting. Ashish reported 68% faster time to market for new AI models, roughly 75% less audit preparation time through automated reporting, and 42% fewer risk events thanks to earlier detection. His reading: good governance speeds innovation up rather than slowing it down.

The roadmap adds serverless compliance functions triggered by events, policies deployed alongside workloads, human-readable explanations of AI decisions, and federated governance across clouds and organisations.

## Who should watch

Data architects, AI platform owners and risk or compliance leads in banking, plus anyone who has been asked to list every model trained on one customer's data and could not.

- [Designing a Scalable Data Governance Framework for Multi-Tenant Cloud Contract Management](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Kushal_Shah_governance_framework_cloud) by Kushal Shah, another framework built for scale.

Title: Bad master data is an SAP incident waiting for a trigger
Description: Gobinath Kasimayan (Deloitte Consulting) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on AI master data governance in SAP that flags data incidents before they cascade.
Body:
A duplicate vendor record looks harmless until the payment run fails, and by then the incident is already in finance. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Gobinath Kasimayan, Specialist Master at Deloitte Consulting and a data architect focused on energy and oil and gas, walked through how AI-driven master data governance in SAP can catch that class of problem early, raising incidents from data patterns instead of waiting for a downstream process to break.

## Master data is the DNA, and it replicates

Gobinath's starting point is that customer, supplier, material, asset and employee master data is the bloodline of an SAP estate. When it is inaccurate or stale, it hits operational processes like supply chain, order to cash and finance, and it does not stop there: it replicates into every downstream system that consumes it. Fixing it today usually means someone files an incident, a data steward corrects the record, and the correction is replicated out again.

His asset management example makes the cascade concrete. Enterprise asset management data feeds a performance management system; if the source data is wrong, the performance rules calculate the wrong results, and preventive maintenance in an oil and gas operation goes off course. Globally managed objects such as customer master make it worse, because one bad record spreads to every location at once.

## Why rule-based MDM falls behind

Traditional master data management relies on static validation rules, central manual governance and batch processing. That copes when volume is low. With globalisation and multi-system estates, the rules do not adapt to consolidation or new product lines, and batch jobs find problems after they have landed. He cites research putting the cost of poor data at around $13 million a year for an average enterprise, with 41% of data professionals' time lost to it.

Today's workaround, as he describes it, is a data steward exporting a report to Power BI or Excel and scanning it for anomalies by eye. It is about as fun as it sounds.

## Three pillars: ML, NLP, prediction

The cognitive MDM he proposes rests on three capabilities. Machine learning for anomaly detection and automated classification. Natural language processing to read unstructured data, such as documents and user feedback, and let stewards ask why an error occurred in plain language. Predictive analytics on time-series and historical data to raise incidents before the issue materialises.

He connects this to SAP's own direction: SAP Master Data Governance gaining AI and ML capabilities, HANA's in-memory ML libraries and real-time replication, and Datasphere for semantic models across systems. One practical step he built himself is a small LLM-based tool that reads live or legacy data and generates profiling dashboards, so stewards can see where cleansing is needed during a transformation project.

## Real-time monitoring, faster root cause

On the incident side, two ideas stand out. Real-time monitoring with adaptive thresholds and pattern correlation: a sudden spike in rejected purchase orders can be traced to a faulty vendor master record before it reaches finance. And faster root cause analysis through automated lineage tracing that shows where an error started and how it spread, with multidimensional correlation to prioritise the investigation. Some fixes can be automatic, such as correcting a misclassified material code, with approvers notified and compliance logs updated.

His rollout advice is to avoid boiling the ocean: start with an assessment and data profiling, deploy domain-specific modules for the highest-severity use cases first, keep humans in the loop to train the models, and treat change management as seriously as the tooling.

## The numbers he reports

From his implementations, Gobinath reports cleansing effort down 75% with 95% clean data, around 90% classification accuracy as models mature, 60% less time spent, and 80% of incidents prevented through predictive analysis. His examples include a global retailer with 60% less manual effort and a 15% supply chain efficiency gain, and a bank where faster customer onboarding was worth about $5 million in revenue. These are his project results rather than a published study, so treat them as an experienced practitioner's benchmarks.

## Who should watch

Title: Regulated ML on Kubernetes works when compliance is in the pipeline
Description: Manisha Ponugoti at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on admission controllers, GitOps audit trails and GPU scheduling for AI in healthcare, banking and insurance.
Body:
"Who approved this change?" is a question an auditor will ask, and the right answer takes seconds, not a week of archaeology. Manisha Ponugoti, who designs cloud systems that combine AI with strict regulatory needs in healthcare, banking and insurance, built her Conf42 Kube Native 2025 talk around that idea: let Kubernetes and GitOps enforce the rules, and compliance stops slowing ML down.

She frames the tension simply: AI wants speed, regulators want control. A clinical prediction has to explain itself, a fraud flag has to be explainable to regulators, and every automated insurance claim decision needs a trail of who changed what, when and why.

## Every model is a container, every change is a commit

The architecture is deliberately plain. Each model ships as a container. Kubernetes handles deployment and version upgrades, StatefulSets let models with state roll back safely, and every configuration and model change goes through Git. Manisha's example: a regulator asked for the exact deployment history of a patient-data matching model, and because of GitOps the team could show it in seconds instead of days.

The self-healing basics also count as compliance in this world. One healthcare matching service used to need engineers for hours to redeploy after a failure; on Kubernetes it recovered by itself within minutes.

## Let the cluster say no

The strongest section is about enforcement before anything runs:

- Security rules forcing containers into a safe, read-only mode.
- Network policies blocking any traffic not explicitly allowed.
- Admission controllers rejecting workloads that violate policy.
- Persistent, uneditable audit logs.

Her anecdote: a developer tried to deploy a model that had not been code-reviewed, and the admission controller blocked it automatically. Nobody had to catch it in a meeting.

The GitOps flow wraps around that: every change starts as a pull request, automated checks validate security, fairness and data rules, Kubernetes applies the approved change, and rollback is instant. In one bank, updates that used to take five hours dropped to 12 minutes with no manual steps.

## Watch, explain, and turn GPUs off

Visibility comes from a service mesh for gradual rollouts and instant rollback, model explanation tools so a doctor asking why a patient was flagged high-risk sees the reasons, and Grafana dashboards for performance and cost. On cost, Kubernetes scales GPU nodes on demand, gives critical jobs GPUs first and puts background work on cheaper preemptible servers. In one insurance project that cut compute costs by 40%.

## Three case studies, one set of patterns

The case studies carry the numbers. A global patient-record matching system handled 10 million requests a day after migration, with inference 73% faster and healthcare privacy policies enforced at deploy time. A multinational bank moved from manual, error-prone deployments to pipelines measured in minutes, with fraud detection four times faster. A large insurer used namespaces to isolate clients, autoscaling for claim traffic and built-in explanations for each AI decision.

The repeating patterns: compliance as code, immutable audit trails, safe rollouts starting new models at 5% of traffic, and full separation of training and serving. Next on her list are policy-driven runtime compliance, serverless GPUs priced per prediction, and federated learning so private data stays where it is.

## Who should watch

MLOps and platform engineers in any regulated industry, and the compliance people who keep asking them for evidence. If your audit prep currently involves screenshots, this is the talk.

Title: Hyperautomation puts KYC, fraud and compliance on Kubernetes
Description: Mamatha Swamy (Microsoft) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on containerised ML, GitOps compliance rules and bias checks for financial services workloads.
Body:
Compliance rules kept in spreadsheets and Word documents cannot be versioned, diffed or rolled back, and that is how a regulatory change ends up taking months to implement. Mamatha Swamy, an architect at Microsoft who has worked with financial services for years, used her Conf42 Kube Native 2025 talk to show how hyperautomation (ML, NLP, RPA and computer vision orchestrated on Kubernetes) turns compliance and risk work into versioned, auditable pipelines.

The talk is organised around use cases, with Azure services as the examples, which makes it easier to follow than most "AI for finance" overviews.

## Kubernetes is the orchestration layer for everything

Mamatha defines hyperautomation as the convergence of machine learning, natural language processing, robotic process automation and cloud-native technology. ML models handle pattern recognition, anomaly detection and credit risk. NLP and LLMs read regulatory text and draft reports. RPA bots do routine validation and submissions. Computer vision handles document checks and biometrics.

Kubernetes ties them together: horizontal pod autoscaling for reporting peaks, a service mesh for zero-trust traffic between microservices, and GitOps workflows to push policy changes across global infrastructure in minutes instead of weeks.

## KYC as parallel containers

The first use case is know-your-customer verification. A user uploads an identity document and a selfie; Kubernetes runs document validation (computer vision with OpenCV and TensorFlow), facial matching (biometric APIs such as the Azure Face API) and behavioural analysis as independent microservices at the same time. The combined confidence score comes back in seconds rather than hours, which cuts onboarding friction.

Streaming fraud detection follows the same model: event-driven ingestion, containerised models detecting patterns, alerts at the end, with the aim of blocking a fraudulent transaction before it completes while keeping false positives low. A third case is AI customer service agents built on Azure OpenAI and deployed on Azure Kubernetes Service, keeping conversation context while staying inside privacy rules.

## Put the compliance rules in Git

The most transferable idea is GitOps for compliance itself. Extend infrastructure as code to regulatory logic: rules live in version control, LLM-based compliance pipelines run through GitOps workflows, every change is traceable, and environments cannot drift apart. Mamatha contrasts this with the fragmented manual process she sees today, where teams apply updates by hand, interpretations differ, and compliance teams cannot easily verify that production matches the latest standard.

## Credit models need bias checks built in

Credit risk modelling gets the most careful treatment. Containerised model serving makes A/B testing of risk models in production practical, and techniques like gradient boosting and ensembles can beat traditional score-based models. But Mamatha spends real time on bias: training data that reflects historical lending discrimination can make a model penalise people for factors correlated with gender, race, geography or socioeconomic status. Her remedy is bias detection, explainable AI, deliberate model selection and continuous monitoring of outcomes, because regulators will ask how a decision was made.

## Start with one high-impact use case

Her rollout advice: pick a high-impact case like KYC to prove return on investment, build the Kubernetes foundation with security and monitoring first, roll out gradually with canary deployments and A/B tests, and design audit trails and explainability in from day one. Multi-region deployment, model retraining pipelines and circuit breakers for ML service failures round out the risk list.

## Who should watch

Architects and platform teams in banks, insurers and fintechs scoping which compliance and risk workloads to containerise first. Anyone building credit models should watch the bias section even if they skip the rest.

Title: Financial risk governance starts with one shared view of the data
Description: Sreenivasulu Gajula at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on three pillars for bank risk governance - integrated data, automated compliance and AI fraud defence.
Body:
Most banks do not lack risk data; they have three copies of it in three departments that do not talk. Sreenivasulu Gajula, a Principal Full Stack Engineer, built his Conf42 Kube Native 2025 talk on that fragmentation problem and on an enterprise-architecture answer resting on three pillars: an integrated data ecosystem, adaptive compliance and AI-driven fraud defence.

It is a short, high-level talk aimed at people deciding how a financial organisation should be wired, more blueprint than code. He describes the goal as a kind of immune system for banks and financial companies.

## Three pressures, one fragmented estate

Sreenivasulu names three forces: regulation that changes often enough to be hard to keep up with, technology change that demands architectural agility, and fraudsters who are smart and go looking for vulnerabilities. Against that, the typical organisation has customer, trading and compliance departments each maintaining its own dataset. Nobody sees the full picture of how data flows, risks surface late, and important rules get missed.

His analogy for the traditional approach is three people in separate rooms trying to talk through slow, noisy lines. The target is everyone in one room on a live group chat: faster, more accurate, same page.

## Pillar one: connect trading, customer and compliance data

The first pillar breaks the department walls. Trading systems, customer data and compliance platforms feed a unified risk view, one real-time dashboard that shows all the risks. Underneath that sits a unified data fabric with real-time synchronisation and standardised governance, replacing isolated databases and manual reconciliation.

## Pillar two: rules in the system, not on a checklist

Adaptive compliance means embedded controls, continuous monitoring, automated reporting and the ability to adapt as regulation changes. Instead of people manually checking thousands of transactions for rule breaks, the rules live in the system, which checks around the clock, generates reports and raises alerts immediately.

## Pillar three: AI for fraud, humans for the hard calls

The fraud pillar combines machine-learning pattern recognition for abnormal behaviour, real-time analysis that flags anything strange, integration with legacy systems, and human oversight for the tricky cases. That last element is the one worth underlining: he keeps a person making the final call.

## Adoption is the real project

The implementation section is pragmatic about people. Organisational resistance is met with training and a slow rollout rather than everything at once; legacy integration with modern connectors, step by step; and the cost case made by showing savings from fewer frauds and cheaper compliance. The phases run foundation (agree on data governance), integration (connect the critical systems), intelligence (switch on the AI models) and optimisation.

For success measures he lists outcomes such as 60% faster compliance reports, 40% cost savings and 99% availability. He presents these as targets for measuring success; the talk does not tie them to a named deployment, so read them as goals rather than benchmarks.

## Who should watch

Enterprise architects and engineering leads in banks or fintechs who need to explain to non-engineers why the data silos are a risk problem and not just an IT annoyance. Engineers after implementation detail should pair it with the more hands-on talks below.

Title: In a subscription business, every outage is also a churn event
Description: Venkata Majeti at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on AI-driven incident resilience for subscription platforms, from anomaly detection to retention.
Body:
A subscription customer who hits an outage does not file a ticket; they quietly decide not to renew. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Venkata Majeti, a senior Salesforce consultant at HashiCorp, argued that subscription platforms should treat incidents as revenue events, and use AI both to catch them early and to hold on to the customers they touch.

## Downtime costs more than the downtime

Venkata sets the scene with the subscription economy at around $400 billion, growing at 18.2% a year since 2018 and driven mostly by digital services. In that model, reliability is tied directly to revenue retention. The figures he cites for the cost of downtime go beyond lost transactions: about $300K per hour for an average enterprise-size company, 15 to 35% higher churn after significant disruptions, wasted acquisition spend when new users hit errors, and brand damage that takes six to twelve months to recover from.

Then the reliability paradox every product org knows. Growth needs new features; each deployment and integration adds failure points; stability traditionally meant slowing releases. His pitch is that AI-driven resilience lets you keep shipping without paying for it in uptime.

## From thresholds to learned normal

The detection section contrasts static thresholds, which only fire after users are hurt, with models that learn normal behaviour across millions of transactions, catch subtle anomalies humans miss, predict failures before they cascade and improve through feedback loops.

The architecture he pairs with it is familiar but well assembled: horizontally scalable microservices with intelligent load balancing; event streaming with buffering and replay so no data is lost during an outage; active-active multi-region deployment with automatic traffic shifting; and stateful recovery of transactions and sessions after partial failures. On storage he lists predictive caching, data tiering that balances performance against cost, horizontally scaling read replicas, and graceful degradation that keeps core functions alive under resource pressure. He cites 99.99% availability for read operations at leading platforms even during significant backend incidents.

## Retention is part of incident response

The section that makes this talk different from a generic AIOps overview is what happens to the customer during and after the incident. Venkata describes churn models aimed specifically at incident windows: score in real time how an incident affects each user segment, reach out proactively with personalised messages and compensation, and watch post-incident usage for signs of disengagement.

He maps a user journey across the incident: before (normal personalised journeys), during (reroute users to features that still work, communicate transparently), initial recovery (restore with priority access for high-value customers), stabilisation (targeted re-engagement and satisfaction monitoring) and post-recovery (feature adoption with an emphasis on rebuilding trust). Dynamic pricing appears too, with targeted incentives for users who actually experienced the disruption rather than blanket discounts.

Treating a status page and a retention campaign as parts of the same runbook is the idea most worth taking away.

## A staged roadmap

His implementation plan is concrete about sequencing. Foundational data collection with unified logging and standard event formats, around one to two months. Baseline modelling of normal operation and the KPIs that correlate with user satisfaction, two to three months. First-generation anomaly detection with human verification feedback to cut false positives, three to four months. Then gradual response automation for well-understood incidents with clear remediation paths. The longer horizon covers user-impact correlation, predictive incident management and, eventually, self-healing systems. He recommends hybrid squads of SREs, data scientists and product engineers, five to seven people with executive sponsorship.

## Who should watch

SREs and product engineers at SaaS and media subscription companies, especially anyone who has had to explain an outage to the growth team. The numbers are industry-level figures rather than one company's results, so use them for the business case and measure your own.

Title: Shard customers across availability zones, and pay for it
Description: Rahul Singh Thakur (Salesforce) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on zone-sharded services, a metadata router, consistent hashing and the cost of 99.99% uptime.
Body:
Losing a whole availability zone should be a bad afternoon, not an outage. Rahul Singh Thakur, Lead Member of Technical Staff at Salesforce, walked through how to get there at Conf42 Kube Native 2025: shard customers across zones, route every request through a metadata service that knows who lives where, and accept the extra cost and debugging pain that buys.

Rahul came to this from infrastructure services his team needed to keep up even through a complete zone failure. The talk is a design guide rather than a war story, and it is refreshingly clear about trade-offs.

## A zone is a blast radius

Cloud availability zones are self-contained sets of infrastructure: something going wrong in one should not take down another. Spread a service across several and a single-zone outage leaves the service up. Rahul's principles follow from that: treat each zone independently, keep data from wandering between zones, design for partial failure, and monitor each zone on its own because "the service" is now several services.

Stateful services are where it gets hard. When they scale up or down, the state has to stay with the right customer.

## Something has to know which zone owns which customer

The central component is a metadata service. It assigns each new customer to a shard, remembers the mapping, tracks the health of each zone, and applies routing policy, so it acts as both intelligent router and load balancer. Sharding by customer also shrinks the blast radius: a bad zone affects its customers, not everyone.

Because the number of zones is not fixed, Rahul uses consistent hashing so adding or removing a zone moves only the data that has to move.

On Kubernetes, the supporting pieces are pod distribution across topology with affinity rules, persistent volume management for stateful pods, service registration that carries zone and capacity information, and zone-aware scaling so the survivors can absorb a failed zone's traffic.

## Pick availability, then live with eventual consistency

Rahul is direct about CAP. If every write must replicate to all zones before it succeeds, one unavailable zone blocks writes, and you have traded away the availability you came for. Since the goal is uptime, his recommendation is eventual consistency: let other zones catch up. Keep a customer's data partition inside its zone, and resolve conflicts with last-write-wins or something smarter if the domain needs it.

## High availability means paying for everything twice

The cost section is the most useful part. Going multi-zone duplicates infrastructure, so Rahul suggests rightsizing from load tests, reserved instances, choosing cross-zone communication options with cost in mind, and zone-aware autoscaling that grows only the zone that needs it. Debugging also gets harder, which is why distributed tracing and good logs are on the must-have list.

Operationally: canary deploys to one zone first, and changes that never assume a particular zone.

## Is it worth it?

His conclusion is measured: sharding across zones adds a metadata service to run, extra cost and harder debugging. It pays off for mission-critical and data services, such as a database where a down zone must not mean unreadable data. For a lot of other services, plain replication may be enough.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers designing tenant placement or planning for zone failure, and anyone about to promise four nines without having priced them.

- [Optimize end user connectivity for multi-region architectures](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2022_Christian_Elsen_Lerna_Ekmekcioglu_reliable_multiregion_arch) by Christian Elsen (AWS), the routing problem one level up.
