Title: No single data pipeline architecture wins, so migrate in pieces
Description: Vamsi Pulusu (Ford Motor Company) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 compares medallion, Lambda, Kappa, lakehouse and data mesh, then lays out how to leave legacy ETL.
Body:
Remember waiting overnight for the batch job so the morning report would exist? Vamsi Pulusu, Technical Architect and lead data engineer at Ford Motor Company with 16 years in the field, used that memory to open his Conf42 Kube Native 2025 talk, then compared the five architecture patterns that replaced it and argued that the right answer is a combination chosen per business context, reached incrementally.

The abstract is blunter: "Legacy ETL is dead." The talk itself is more nuanced, and better for it.

## Why the nightly batch had to go

Vamsi lists the constraints of traditional ETL: overnight batch windows that kept data stale when the business wanted real-time monitoring; single points of failure where recovery often meant reprocessing everything; scaling by buying bigger hardware; tools built for structured data facing logs, device streams and web events; and lock-in through proprietary query extensions.

The turning point, in his telling, was cloud object storage decoupling storage from compute. Before, more processing meant buying more storage, and vice versa. After, cheap and practically unlimited storage scales on its own, costs move from capital spend to pay-as-you-go, and schema-on-read lets you land raw data first and transform it later.

## Five patterns, five philosophies

The core of the talk is a side-by-side:

- **Medallion**: bronze for raw data as landed, silver for standardised and quality-checked data, gold for business-ready structures like star schemas and pre-aggregated metrics. Clear quality boundaries; a good fit where governance is strict.
- **Lambda**: a batch path for complete historical accuracy plus a speed path for fast preliminary answers. The cost is two code bases for the same transformation logic.
- **Kappa**: stream first, one processing engine, an append-only event log as the system of record. Batch is just streaming over a longer window. Simpler to maintain.
- **Lakehouse**: warehouse features such as ACID transactions and schema enforcement on top of cheap lake storage, so BI, ML and streaming share one copy of the data.
- **Data mesh**: less an architecture than an org chart. Domain teams own data as products on a self-serve platform under federated governance. Vamsi is clear that it is a socio-technical change, and that is the hard part.

The Lambda-versus-Kappa comparison alone is worth the time if your team keeps maintaining the same logic twice.

## Governance becomes a runtime job

Distributed pipelines make old periodic checks inadequate. Vamsi wants automated lineage at dataset, column and even record level, continuous quality validation at every transformation boundary, and data contracts between producers and consumers, implemented with versioned schema registries that check proposed changes against historical usage before they break someone downstream.

He also covers the tools timeline, from DataStage and Informatica through Hadoop to Airflow, Prefect, Kafka, Spark streaming and Flink, and argues that tool choice should weigh team skills, operational needs, cost model and integration, not just feature lists. Feature stores get a mention as the bridge between pipelines and ML, with point-in-time correctness as the requirement that matters.

## Migrate domain by domain

Big-bang replacement is rarely feasible, so his migration strategies are all incremental: modernise by recurring pattern, run hybrid behind gateway components that keep interfaces stable, bridge to existing sources with adapters, and go domain by domain starting with non-critical ones. Inventory your current state, pick a target pattern such as medallion or lakehouse, invest in lineage and quality early, and build streaming skills in the team.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects planning a move off batch ETL, and platform engineers who host those pipelines on Kubernetes and want to know why the data team keeps saying "medallion". It is a survey talk; you will leave with a map, not a migration runbook.

- [What is a Data mesh for god's sake !?](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Ismael_Hommani_CharlesAlban_Benezech_data_mesh) by Ismael Hommani (Wescale), more on the organisational pattern.
- [Build cloud native open format data lakehouse](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Satish_Mane_Rajeev_Jaiiswal_build_open_format_data_lakehouse) by Satish Mane (AWS), the lakehouse built out.

Title: An incident-ready contact centre keeps humans in reserve for the outage
Description: Sujit Kumar (Copart) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on designing AI-assisted contact centres that stay calm when the CRM is down and call volume spikes.
Body:
When the CRM goes down, your agents cannot see order history, customers repeat themselves, hold times grow and somebody posts about it. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Sujit Kumar, Vice President of Technology at Copart, described how to design customer support so it absorbs exactly that kind of incident, and the core idea is capacity: let automation handle the routine so humans are free when things get emotional.

Sujit's position is that incidents are inevitable, but how the support operation responds decides whether customers stay. The talk is an architecture and strategy overview, not a product demo.

## Resilience by design, not by chance

The foundation is cloud-native support architecture. Microservices isolate faults so one failing component does not take the whole platform down. Event-driven processing reacts to sudden change in real time. Auto-scaling adjusts resources when traffic spikes. Underneath sit the usual guards: circuit breakers to stop degraded components cascading, intelligent load distribution across available resources, and redundant systems so there is always an alternative path.

None of that is unique to contact centres, which is the point. A support platform is a production system with an unusually loud failure mode.

## Route by intent, and by mood

On top of the foundation, AI does triage. Intent detection with natural language processing and historical data works out what the caller wants from the first interaction; during an incident, misrouted calls only add friction. Sujit adds two refinements: detecting multiple intents in one conversation, and reading emotional state. His example: a customer who says they cannot log in and are really frustrated has both a login issue and an urgency signal, and the system should treat it accordingly.

Risk-based escalation scores cases using patterns, account history and behaviour to flag potential fraud or security concerns, so high-risk cases jump the queue and routine ones follow the standard path. AI-driven decision trees, unlike static flowcharts, adjust in real time; if one system is degraded, they reroute customers to an alternative resolution.

## Never make the customer start over

The handoff section is the one most support teams will recognise as their weak spot. Conversational AI handles routine requests (account updates, password resets, basic troubleshooting), which creates reserve capacity for agents. When a case does need a human, the context travels with it: interaction history, intent and emotional state, delivered as a briefing so the agent can pick up without asking the customer to repeat everything. During an outage, when patience is already thin, that continuity matters most.

Agents also get real-time assistance: suggested responses, compliance guidance and knowledge articles, with speech analytics flagging potential compliance violations before they become costly.

## The ticket queue is a monitoring signal

The idea SREs may steal: support data as early warning. Predictive models look at historical patterns, system metrics and external factors, and an unusual rise in password-reset tickets can be the first sign of a broader outage. Spot it early and you can communicate proactively, sometimes before the incident is formally an incident. Multimodal support helps resolution speed too, with customers sharing a photo of an error or a video of a malfunction.

Sujit ties it together as a four-phase roadmap: a cloud-native foundation, AI for intent and routing, predictive analytics and multimodal processing, then resilience optimisation with tuned load balancing, failover and incident procedures. He presents it as a roadmap, not a one-off project.

## Who should watch

Engineering leaders who own customer support platforms, and SREs who have never looked at their company's ticket volume as telemetry. If you want hard numbers from Copart's own rollout, the talk stays at the level of patterns.

Title: AI clusters now live or die by their SerDes links
Description: Phani Paladugu (Synopsys) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on why AI workloads push SerDes to 224G and beyond, and the power and signal-integrity bill that follows.
Body:
Your GPU cluster's bottleneck may be a few millimetres of copper. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Phani Paladugu, Executive Director of Product Management at Synopsys, explained why serializer/deserializer (SerDes) links, the high-speed interfaces behind Ethernet and PCIe, have become a design constraint for AI systems, and what chip designers are doing about it.

Fair warning for a Kubernetes crowd: this talk lives below the operating system, at the silicon and package level. That is exactly why it is interesting. Every pod you schedule on an AI node depends on these links.

## Compute grew faster than the wires

Phani's starting point: generative AI model sizes have been doubling every three to four months, training runs stretch into weeks and months despite parallelism, and memory and interconnect bandwidth have not kept pace with compute. So the links have to get faster. Ethernet SerDes are moving from 112G to 224G per lane, and PCIe from 64G to 128G with Gen 7.

Faster alone is not enough. Power efficiency has to stay around four to five picojoules per bit while driving long-reach channels with 45 to 50 dB of loss at 224G, or 35 to 40 dB for PCIe Gen 7. At those rates reflections, crosstalk, jitter and inter-symbol interference all get worse. He calls the combination a design paradox, and it is hard to disagree.

## Training and inference want different links

A point software people rarely hear: workload shape should drive SerDes design. Inference traffic is bursty, often asymmetric, more memory-bound than compute-bound, and latency-sensitive. Training is compute-bound and needs sustained high bandwidth, with latency still mattering. Phani's advice is to understand the exact use case before optimising for performance, power, area and latency, because no single design wins all four.

## PAM4, DSPs and machine-learned tuning

The signal chain has changed. Older NRZ SerDes used analogue equalisers: a feed-forward equaliser on transmit, and a continuous-time linear equaliser plus decision-feedback equaliser on receive. At today's rates the signalling moved to PAM4, and receivers became DSP-based, with multi-tap equalisers and high-performance data converters. That shift toward digital architectures also lets designers ride process scaling and voltage scaling for power.

Real-time adaptation tunes parameters to each channel, and machine learning algorithms now handle calibration and adaptation. Clock and data recovery uses digital bang-bang phase detectors and multi-phase sampling, and forward error correction (Reed-Solomon or LDPC) is chosen against the channel's loss, power and latency budget.

Configurability matters too: lanes configurable from one to sixteen, and multi-protocol SerDes that can serve Ethernet or PCIe on the same silicon.

## Hundreds of lanes, one power budget

AI chips use hundreds of SerDes lanes, so power is attacked at every level: supply scaling, adaptive biasing and clock gating in circuits; power islands and workload-aware power states in the architecture; dynamic voltage and frequency scaling and thermal-aware floorplanning at the system level. Placement on all four edges of the die and the package escape routing become part of the design.

Phani also maps links to topologies: Ultra Accelerator Link for scale-up inside a system, Ultra Ethernet for scale-out across the data centre.

## What comes after 224G

Ethernet is heading to 448G per lane within two to three years, with PCIe and UALink following. Co-packaged optics moves the optics next to switches and accelerators, cutting channel loss and the need for long-reach SerDes, and Phani cited five to eight times more bandwidth with two to three times less power from these technologies. Chiplets and 3D packaging bring their own SerDes requirements.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure and platform engineers who buy, rack or schedule AI hardware and want to understand why network and node specs look the way they do. Hardware engineers will find it a compact overview; Kubernetes operators will find it a useful look under the floor.

Title: Self-healing streaming on Kubernetes with Redis Streams and KEDA
Description: Karthik Reddy Beereddy (LexisNexis Risk Solutions) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on replayable logs, circuit breakers and lag-driven autoscaling for streams.
Body:
CPU is the wrong signal for scaling a stream consumer: the number that matters is how far behind it is. Karthik Reddy Beereddy, Senior Site Reliability Engineer at LexisNexis Risk Solutions, made that case at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 as part of a catalogue of self-healing patterns for streaming systems built on Azure Kubernetes Service, Redis Streams and Azure Event Hub.

The talk is a pattern catalogue drawn from his platform modernisation work, moving nightly batch jobs to event-driven services. It is broad rather than deep, but the pieces fit together into one coherent design.

## Start with a log you can replay

Every streaming system juggles throughput, consistency and availability, and Karthik is upfront that you trade them off rather than max all three. His foundation is Redis Streams as a replayable, append-only event log. Messages carry unique IDs and timestamps, so after a failure the sequence can be rebuilt deterministically.

Two properties make that log a resilience tool rather than just a queue. It buffers temporary downstream failures without losing data, with back-pressure so a long outage does not exhaust memory. And consumer groups distribute load and fail over: a crashed consumer's replacement resumes from the last acknowledged position.

## Replay only works if handlers are idempotent

Replaying events is how the system recovers state, which means handlers will see duplicates. Karthik's rules: use partition keys and sequence numbers to keep ordering deterministic, combine event sourcing with snapshots and incremental replay to shorten recovery, and make every handler idempotent so duplicates have no side effects. That last one is the difference between a clean recovery and a replay that bills every customer twice.

Circuit breakers sit around the downstream calls with the usual three states: closed while things are healthy, open to fail fast once error thresholds trip, half-open to probe recovery and restore traffic gradually.

## Partition for isolation, scale on lag

On Event Hub, partitions are both a performance lever and a failure boundary: each acts as an independent commit log, so a stuck partition or consumer group does not stall the others. In one implementation his team adjusted partition counts based on throughput trends, such as billing events peaking in business hours, to stay clear of throttling without over-provisioning.

Scaling is where KEDA comes in. Instead of the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler watching CPU, KEDA scales consumers on Event Hub consumer lag: backlog grows, pods appear; backlog drains, they go away. He likes that it builds on the HPA, reads Prometheus metrics, and leaves scaling events visible next to the system metrics they reacted to.

## The boring Kubernetes parts do the healing

The self-healing loop is mostly stock Kubernetes, configured with care: liveness probes that restart unresponsive containers, readiness probes that pull unhealthy pods out of service discovery, restart policies with exponential backoff, and HPA policies on custom metrics. A service mesh such as Linkerd adds mTLS, retries and canary routing without application changes.

Observability closes the loop. Baseline message throughput, consumer lag, error rates and resource usage in Prometheus, alert on deviation, and use Grafana heat maps to spot hot partitions and uneven load. Delivery uses blue-green and canary rollouts with Argo Rollouts.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers running consumers on Kubernetes, especially anyone whose stream autoscaling still keys off CPU. It is a good map of the patterns; for implementation detail on any one of them, follow the related talks.

Title: In banking, make the compliant path the fastest path to production
Description: Nirup Baer (Wells Fargo) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on building compliance into cloud platforms so incidents are rarer and leave their own audit trail.
Body:
Think of compliance as seat belts in a performance car: designed in from the start, not strapped on before the inspection. That is the image Nirup Baer, Program Manager at Wells Fargo, built his talk around at Conf42 Incident Management 2025, and the practical claim behind it is that when the safe path is also the fast path, teams stop negotiating with controls and incidents leave their own evidence behind.

## An incident in a bank is three incidents

Nirup starts with the stakes. Financial services move enormous sums every day, customers touch real balances, and when a system pauses the cost shows up in money and reputation at once. So an incident is technical, business and regulatory simultaneously, and the response has to respect all three. That is why, in his framing, incident management sits where reliability, regulation and brand meet.

His answer is modernisation as a way to set better defaults: repeatable patterns for network, identity, storage and compute; rules in the build and release steps so risky changes never reach customers; and unchangeable logs so the system can tell its own story afterwards.

He gives a quick field example. A fragile service was moved into a landing zone with strong guardrails, with the same team and the same code. The next incident felt like a drill they had already practised: they knew what changed, when, and the safe way back.

## Blast radius is an architecture decision

The architecture section stays at the level of principles, which suits a mixed audience. Manage policy and visibility centrally while keeping sensitive customer data in the region where it belongs. Design for small blast radius: clear service boundaries, sensible timeouts and retries, and fast ways to switch off risky features. Practise failovers until they are boring. Run the most critical systems in more than one place and keep a warm backup for the rest.

His highway analogy works: each service has its own lane with dividers and a shoulder, so a blown tyre in one lane does not close the road.

## Three stories where the audit trail came for free

The case studies are where the idea earns its keep. In regulatory reporting, overnight batches became real-time streams, so delays showed up in minutes instead of the next day, and every step wrote an unchangeable record. Reports that took days ran in minutes, and audit prep that took weeks took days.

In fraud detection, the turning point was managing the whole model lifecycle rather than just the score. Changes needed approval, a misbehaving version could be rolled back with one decision, and the team could explain what changed and why. False alarms and losses both dropped.

In trading, surveillance moved from after the fact to real time, with limits enforced as orders flowed and check records travelling alongside the trades. When the market surged, the system followed a safe playbook rather than calling a meeting.

## Policy in the pipeline, not in the quarterly review

The repeatable part is infrastructure as code plus rules in the delivery pipeline. If a setting would expose data or open a risky path, it does not pass, and the system says which rule failed and shows the approved pattern. Long review meetings become fast feedback while the work is still in progress, and the platform keeps a timestamped record of what fired, who changed what and how it was fixed.

His incident routine follows from that: confirm the signal, start a clean log immediately, pause risky change paths, use pre-approved moves (switch off a feature, limit traffic, fail over), communicate in plain language, let the system collect the facts, and do not call it fixed until the service holds steady for a meaningful window. Then promote the fix into the shared template so the next team never meets the same problem.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE leads in banks, insurers and trading firms, and anyone whose change process is a quarterly checklist. The closing advice is small enough to start on next sprint: pick one painful control, automate it end to end inside a golden path, and measure recovery time and audit hours saved.

Title: Design for the crisis before it arrives, not during the outage
Description: Dhruvesh Talati (Ally) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on cloud-native patterns that keep crisis-response systems up, scaled and talking to each other.
Body:
When a flood, a cyberattack or a pandemic hits, the systems people need most get their worst traffic day at the same moment the infrastructure underneath is least reliable. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Dhruvesh Talati, Senior Software Engineer at Ally with a background in cloud infrastructure and DevSecOps, argued that resilience for those systems has to be designed in from the first commit rather than bolted on after the first outage.

This is a strategy talk more than a hands-on one. Think of it as a checklist for an architecture review of anything that has to stay up when everything else is falling over.

## Three demands that legacy stacks fail at once

Dhruvesh frames crisis resilience as three pillars. Availability: emergency calls and medical services need near-perfect uptime, and he puts the target at 99.99%. Scalability: surges are unplanned, so the platform has to absorb something like ten times normal capacity within minutes. Interoperability: crisis response means public agencies, private companies and aid groups sharing data in real time, which only works if their systems can actually talk.

His point is that on-premise estates built for steady load struggle on all three together, and a weakness in one organisation spreads to everyone depending on it.

## The patterns are familiar; the stakes aren't

The building blocks will be known to any SRE: microservices so one failure stays local, Kubernetes for scheduling, scaling and self-healing, and infrastructure as code so a region can be rebuilt the same way twice. Then the four classic fault-tolerance patterns:

- Circuit breakers that isolate a failing dependency before it cascades.
- Timeouts that kill hung requests before they eat every thread.
- Retries with exponential backoff, so a flaky network does not become a self-inflicted load test.
- Bulkheads that partition resources so a noisy service cannot starve the critical one.

What the talk adds is the framing. In a normal product these are reliability hygiene. When the product is an emergency dispatch system, they decide whether the service survives the day it matters.

## Multi-region, edge and zero trust as one design

Beyond elastic scaling with real-time monitoring and smart traffic routing between zones, Dhruvesh pushes for active multi-region deployments with automated failover and strongly consistent replication, so disaster recovery stops being a scramble and becomes a property of the system.

Two less common points stood out. First, edge sites that keep working when the link to the central cloud drops, with local processing under 100 milliseconds for life-critical uses such as patient monitoring. Second, zero trust, because perimeter security tends to dissolve in exactly the chaos a crisis creates: continuous verification, strict least privilege and encryption in transit, at rest and in processing.

He also covers AI for predicting escalation and recommending resource allocation, though at a high level.

## Migrate in phases, start with what can break

The migration advice is pragmatic: assess and define resilience requirements, prove the architecture on non-critical systems, move core services using known patterns, then integrate and optimise with the legacy estate still in the picture. And treat resilience as an ongoing capability rather than a project with an end date.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leads in public-sector, healthcare, finance or utility platforms who need the vocabulary to argue for multi-region and failover budgets. If you want YAML and failure-injection demos, pair it with one of the talks below.

Title: Dapr moves the plumbing out of your microservices and into a sidecar
Description: Christophe Gigax (Hager Group) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 shows how Dapr's sidecar and building blocks keep state stores and brokers out of app code.
Body:
Your service should not know whether its orders land in Redis or Cosmos DB. That is the pitch Christophe Gigax, Cloud Solution Architect at Hager Group and a Microsoft MVP, made at Conf42 Kube Native 2025: put Dapr, the Distributed Application Runtime, next to every service as a sidecar, talk to it over plain HTTP or gRPC, and let YAML decide what sits behind it.

It is an introduction, and an honest one. If you have heard "Dapr" in a CNCF slide and never run it, this is a good first half hour.

## The pain is the glue code, not the services

Christophe starts where most microservice migrations hurt. Small, focused services buy team autonomy and independent deploys, but debugging a bug that spans five of them means running all five locally, and the interdependencies pile up until nobody can follow the flows. On top of that, most languages and frameworks were never designed with distributed systems in mind, and apps end up tied to one hosting platform.

Dapr's answer is to standardise the outside world. Service-to-service invocation, state management, pub/sub, resource bindings and triggers, actors, distributed tracing and secrets all become building blocks behind the same API, from any language. He counted more than a hundred pluggable components available off the shelf, and you can write your own.

## Your code only ever talks to localhost

The core idea is the sidecar pattern. Launch a service and a Dapr sidecar starts next to it; every external interaction goes through that sidecar. Saving state is a call to the state API with a store name. Calling another service is a call that names the target app ID and method, and Dapr does the service discovery.

The demo uses the official Dapr quickstarts repository. A Node.js app exposes endpoints to create and fetch orders, but its code never mentions a database: it posts to the Dapr port, 3500, with the name of a configured state store. `dapr init` had already pulled a Redis container locally, so `dapr run` with an app ID wires everything up and the logs show the Redis state store and pub/sub components loading. A small Python client then loops forever creating orders, calling the Node app through its own sidecar rather than directly. Neither app knows the other's address, and neither knows Redis exists.

That is the part worth watching: two short programs with zero infrastructure imports, still talking to each other and to a database.

## Swapping the broker is a YAML change

Every component (state store, pub/sub broker, binding, secret store) gets its own YAML file holding the connection details. Want Cosmos DB instead of Redis, or Azure Service Bus instead of RabbitMQ? Change the component file; the service code stays put. Pub/sub works the same way: a service publishes to Dapr, Dapr forwards to whichever broker is configured, and subscribers expose an endpoint Dapr calls with each new message.

Telemetry follows the same logic. Dapr speaks OpenTelemetry, so the backend you send traces to can change without touching the app.

## On Kubernetes, the injector does the work

For production Christophe recommends Kubernetes. Installing Dapr there adds four system pods, including the sidecar injector, the actor placement service and Sentry for security, plus the operator. The injector adds a sidecar to every pod you annotate, and from then on the app code is identical to what ran on your laptop. He also noted that Dapr became a graduated CNCF project in November 2024, which matters if your architecture review board asks about maturity before anything else.

## Who should watch

Developers and architects weighing how much distributed-systems plumbing to write themselves, and teams that keep rewriting the same Redis or Kafka client wrapper in three languages. If you already run Dapr in production, you will know most of this; the value here is a clear mental model you can hand to a new team.

Title: Event Grid, Service Bus and AKS for sub-two-second fraud checks
Description: Ashif Anwar (Wolters Kluwer) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on event-driven patterns on Azure and a fraud pipeline on Event Grid, Service Bus, Functions and AKS.
Body:
Kubernetes gives you the stage, but events are what make anything happen on it. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Ashif Anwar, Principal Engineer at Wolters Kluwer, explained how to combine Azure Kubernetes Service with Azure's event services, and walked through a fraud detection system that cut response time from minutes to under two seconds.

His argument for event-driven design is the letter-versus-phone-call analogy: you post the letter and get on with your day instead of waiting on the line. Services that communicate asynchronously through events are loosely coupled, scale with the flow of traffic, contain failures instead of cascading them, and react the moment something happens, with no polling.

## Each Azure service has one job

Anwar mapped the Azure toolkit onto distinct roles. Event Grid is the nervous system: a hyperscale pub/sub router with massive fan-out, attribute-based filtering, built-in retries and dead-lettering, suited to IoT telemetry or microservices that react to the same event. Service Bus is the circulatory system: durable queues and topics, sessions for first-in-first-out ordering, and dead-letter queues for messages that cannot be delivered. That matters wherever a lost or reordered message means money, such as high-value financial transactions.

Azure Functions are the reactive glue: serverless handlers triggered by Event Grid, Service Bus, HTTP or Blob Storage, scaling from zero to thousands of concurrent executions for enrichment, filtering and routing. AKS runs the heavy, long-lived workloads and integrates natively with the messaging services.

## Patterns matter more than products

The patterns section is a clear refresher. CQRS separates read and write models so each can be optimised. Event sourcing stores the sequence of events instead of only the latest state, which gives you a full audit trail and the ability to rebuild any past state. Sagas coordinate multi-service transactions with compensation, his example being a trip where a cancelled flight must undo the hotel and car booking. And he advised finding a balance between choreography, where services react independently, and orchestration, where a controller directs them.

## The fraud pipeline, step by step

The case study starts with legacy fraud detection that took minutes or hours, and a goal of under two seconds with 95% accuracy. Every transaction from payment services on AKS becomes an event. Event Grid routes it to Service Bus for reliable ordering. An Azure Function enriches it with customer history and context. A machine learning model on GPU-backed AKS pods scores it within milliseconds. A final function approves, rejects or flags the transaction for review.

For Black Friday-style peaks, Event Grid absorbs millions of events per second, Service Bus retries and dead-letters so no message is lost, Functions scale out instantly and the model pods scale horizontally. The results he reported: sub-two-second response, 15% fewer false positives, 100% uptime during peak periods, and correlation IDs that trace every event end to end.

## The lessons are the reusable part

Four lessons apply well beyond finance. Make handlers idempotent so a redelivered event does not charge someone twice. Version event schemas semantically so consumers can handle old and new. Always carry correlation IDs. And use managed identities and RBAC instead of hard-coded credentials. He closed with healthcare telemetry, retail inventory sync and insurance claims as other places the same patterns apply.

## Who should watch

Engineers building on Azure who are choosing between Event Grid, Service Bus and Functions, and architects moving a synchronous monolith towards events. Azure-specific, but the patterns and lessons travel to any cloud.

- [So You Want To Build An Event Driven System?](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_James_Eastham_event_driven_system) by James Eastham (AWS) covers the fundamentals from the AWS side.
- [An Introduction to Saga Pattern for Distributed Transactions](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Dmitry_Khorev_saga_pattern_distributed_transactions) by Dmitry Khorev (Mero) goes deeper on sagas and compensation.

Title: Supply chain incidents are cheaper predicted than fought
Description: Krishna Chaitanya Yarlagadda (Mercury Financial) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on ML, IoT and predictive escalation to stop supply chain disruptions.
Body:
One regional fulfilment centre goes sideways and a few hours later you have stockouts and broken delivery promises across the network. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Krishna Chaitanya Yarlagadda, Senior Manager for Data Science and Analytics at Mercury Financial, walked through how AI moves supply chain incident management from firefighting to prevention, drawing heavily on what he saw during his time at Amazon.

It is a broad tour rather than a single deep technique: about a dozen building blocks, each grounded in an example from large-scale operations.

## The incident starts upstream of the alert

Krishna's framing is that supply chains are fragile ecosystems. A delayed shipment or a warehouse breakdown ripples outward, and traditional approaches fix the problem after it lands, by which point customer trust and revenue are already at risk. At Amazon, he said, predictive analytics was used to forecast product-level problems before they disrupted sales, intervening before customers felt the pain.

The prerequisite is data breadth. Supplier metrics, transport timelines, inventory flows, weather, even geopolitical risk all need to land in one place. No analyst can join those fast enough by hand; a model can. He describes layering clickstream, supply chain and vendor data at Amazon to get a full view of operations.

## Baselines first, then everything weird stands out

The machine learning section is classic anomaly detection done for operations. Build a baseline of normal, then flag deviations: a spike in transit delays, supplier lead times drifting. His example is models spotting when a product class deviated from its usual demand and supply pattern so the team could adjust before it escalated.

IoT turns warehouses into what he calls a digital nervous system: sensors on temperature, humidity, vibration and equipment health. Amazon tracked conveyor performance and environmental conditions to catch bottlenecks before they hit order flow. Computer vision adds eyes, spotting wear on equipment, misaligned packages and early failure signs, and predictive maintenance on sortation equipment saved, in his words, countless hours of downtime. Anyone who has been paged for a jammed sorter at peak knows what that is worth.

## Predict the escalation, not just the incident

Two ideas will feel familiar to SREs. Reinforcement learning tunes the response: learning from historical incidents which actions worked, and routing alerts to the right team. At Amazon the alert-routing logic was refined to cut noise and avoid alert fatigue while critical incidents still got immediate attention.

Predictive escalation goes a step further. Models estimate when an incident is about to breach its SLA and trigger mitigation protocols faster than a human would. In a high-velocity fulfilment business, a few minutes of delay can turn into thousands of missed deliveries.

## Sharing without oversharing

The partner-network ideas are the less common part. Federated learning lets supply chain partners share disruption intelligence without exposing their raw data; he compares it to consortium data in finance. Blockchain-style immutable audit trails support compliance reporting. Krishna is candid that Amazon did not use blockchain directly for incident management, but invested heavily in immutable logging, which is the same principle.

His rollout advice is incremental: assess, pilot to validate, scale gradually, keep optimising as new risks and data patterns appear. Start small, prove the impact, expand.

## Who should watch

Engineers and data scientists supporting logistics, retail or manufacturing operations, and SREs curious how their alerting and escalation patterns translate to physical systems. If you want model architectures or metrics from a single deployment, this is a map of the territory instead.

Title: A knowledge base that measures its own failed searches gets better
Description: Harshita Dubey (Apex Fintech Solutions) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on turning a SharePoint knowledge base into a Kubernetes-backed system with embedded analytics.
Body:
Every company has a knowledge base, and most employees have learned to ask a colleague instead. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Harshita Dubey, Senior Technical Program Manager at Apex Fintech Solutions, described how an enterprise kept SharePoint as its content store but wrapped it in Kubernetes-hosted analytics, search and automation services, so the system could see where people got stuck and fix itself.

The case is a large one: a knowledge management system serving 15,000+ employees across global offices. Dubey opened with the claim that over half of enterprise knowledge systems miss their performance goals, and the root causes she listed will sound familiar.

## Why knowledge systems fail

Three causes. Siloed design, where each department builds its own fragmented repository. Outdated, monolithic architecture that cannot adapt to new business or user demands. And poor adoption, because people abandon tools that return irrelevant results or are painful to use. Her conclusion is that this needs an architectural rethink, not a new search box.

## Keep the content, replace everything around it

The contrast she drew is static repository versus containerised ecosystem. SharePoint Online stays as the content source. Around it, containerised services handle analytics, search and automation, and Kubernetes provides scaling, resilience and continuous deployment. Because services are decoupled from the content layer, each can scale or be modernised without disturbing the documents underneath.

The analytics layer has three parts: user behaviour analytics (engagement, click-throughs, navigation paths), search pattern mining (how people query, and where searches fail), and real-time feedback loops that adjust results and recommendations based on what users actually do. Failed searches are the gold here: they tell you exactly which content is missing.

## Smart features and a governance loop

On top of that, Kubernetes-hosted services add natural language search that tries to understand intent beyond keywords, context-aware filtering by role or project, and predictive analytics that anticipates what someone needs before they search. Automation extends to governance: tracking engagement and abandonment to find friction points, surfacing popular and missing topics, and promoting high-value content automatically, without someone curating by hand.

The roadmap runs in four phases: foundation (clusters, microservices, SharePoint API integration), analytics (tracking and early AI recommendations), intelligence (NLP and predictive analytics), and optimisation (automated governance, enterprise-wide scale).

## The results she reported

After full implementation: 33% faster information retrieval, 35% fewer support tickets and a 22% boost in self-service resolution. User satisfaction rose 37.5%, onboarding time fell from 14 weeks to 11, and the transformation delivered $3.7M in tangible gains from efficiency improvements.

Her starter advice is short: instrument everything for observability, modularise analytics as separate services, collect real-time user feedback, let data drive content lifecycles, and define success metrics up front.

## Who should watch

Internal tools teams, IT leaders and program managers who own a sprawling intranet or wiki and want an incremental path that does not start with a content migration. It is a brief case-study talk at the architecture level; it does not go into which NLP or search stack was used.

Title: AI data checks on Kubernetes cut SAP merger integrations to months
Description: Neelima Aderu (PwC) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on containerised AI for SAP M&A integrations, from automated mapping to preload data quality sign-off.
Body:
When two companies merge, their SAP systems do not, at least not without a year of consultants mapping fields by hand. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Neelima Aderu, Senior SAP Integration Architect Manager at PwC with more than 14 years in integration middleware, presented a case study where Kubernetes-orchestrated AI modules handled mapping, code analysis and data validation, and integration timelines shrank from 12 to 18 months to four to six.

The setting is the hardest kind of integration project. Two large SAP estates spanning regions, heavy customisation and terabytes of data, with GDPR and HIPAA requirements and a business that expects zero downtime. Traditional approaches mean long timelines, large consulting bills and risk to the customer experience.

## Integration as a cloud-native workload

Aderu's reframe is to treat integration as a parallel workload instead of a sequential manual process. AI models run as containerised microservices, each specialising in a task. Transformer networks identify complex master data patterns, CNNs analyse ABAP code for business logic, and graph neural networks optimise SAP dependencies. Kubernetes provides fault tolerance and autoscaling, and the system processed around half a million records per second across 10 TB datasets.

## The preload sign-off is the clever bit

The most practical part of the talk is about data quality, which she argued is where migrations really go wrong. Business teams supply the data, and it is easy for consultants to load whatever they were handed. Instead, her team collected validation prerequisites from each functional consultant (mandatory columns for vendor master, delivery dates within valid ranges, and so on) and built them into an AI-driven workflow that checks data before load. Nothing was loaded without a preload sign-off from those checks.

They applied it across master data (materials, vendors, customers, vendor banks, profit and cost centres, batch traceability, bills of material, routings, employee IDs), critical open transactional data such as open sales and purchase orders, and financial loads (AP, AR, fixed assets, GL balances) that must reconcile to the trial balance. Errors show up on the spot instead of after go-live, when they hurt operations.

## The numbers she reported

Timelines dropped 50 to 70%. Integration costs fell 78%, manual effort 85% and rework cycles 92%, which she attributed to the AI-driven quality validation. The AI suggested mappings and generated transformation logic, validated continuously, and caught 93% of potential issues before they affected operations. The abstract also cites 99.8% uptime.

## Integration as a long-term capability

The closing advice is about people as much as tools. Invest in data quality and governance, build internal AI and cloud-native expertise because the technology keeps moving, and keep business and IT working together, because the AI needs business context to know which of four issues is the real P1. And design every mapping as if the next customer is already coming, so it is reusable rather than one-off. Every SAP consultant who has rewritten the same EDI purchase order mapping will nod at that one.

## Who should watch

SAP integration architects, functional consultants and IT leads facing a merger, divestiture or large S/4HANA migration. The Kubernetes content is architectural; the real value is the preload validation workflow and the list of data objects that need it.

Title: Multi-cloud databases work when you pick per workload, not per vendor
Description: Adithya Sirimalla (Enliven Technologies) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 compares Oracle Autonomous Database, Azure SQL and RDS for SQL Server resilience.
Body:
Running Oracle and SQL Server across AWS, Azure and Oracle Cloud is not a strategy anyone chose on purpose, but plenty of DBAs live there anyway. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Adithya Sirimalla, software developer and DBA at Enliven Technologies, gave a practical overview of how to keep that estate resilient, and his headline advice is refreshingly blunt: choose the database platform per workload, not out of vendor loyalty or habit.

This is an overview talk for DBAs and platform engineers rather than a deep technical session. It covers four things in order: the three managed platforms, resilience strategy, automation and observability.

## Three managed platforms, three personalities

Adithya's comparison is the most useful part for anyone mid-decision.

Oracle Autonomous Database is the self-managing one: automated patching, upgrades and tuning, machine learning for performance optimisation, and automatic scaling. It can run serverless for variable workloads, or on dedicated infrastructure for steady, predictable ones.

Azure SQL Database leans on intelligent performance: AI-based recommendations and automatic tuning, with a Hyperscale tier that lets a database grow to 100 TB. Transparent data encryption and Azure identity integration cover security, and pricing comes as DTU-based, vCore-based or serverless.

Amazon RDS for SQL Server is the enterprise-reliability option: automated backups, point-in-time recovery, Multi-AZ deployments for high availability, read replicas, and support for SQL Server features such as Always On availability groups, SSIS and SSRS, with reserved or on-demand pricing.

His summary: Oracle for self-management, Azure for intelligent performance, RDS for dependable enterprise service. Each has a lane.

## A backup you have not restored is a rumour

The resilience section covers what goes wrong in practice. Multi-cloud backup with cross-cloud replication, scheduled to avoid performance impact, and validated regularly by actually restoring. Failover through active-passive setups with automated health checks and DNS-based routing, or active-active architectures if you need zero downtime.

Compliance gets equal billing with uptime. Data residency rules, encryption standards, centralised audit logging and consistent controls across clouds keep the auditors happy and stop the second cloud from becoming the compliance gap.

## Automate the toil, then watch everything

On automation, Adithya focuses on Terraform for infrastructure as code, keeping database infrastructure version-controlled and reproducible, combined with the AWS CLI, Azure CLI and OCI CLI to script snapshots, scaling, patching and performance checks. His framing is that automation is about cutting human error and making operations repeatable, not only about speed.

For monitoring, the question he poses is the right one: will you know something broke before your customers do? Track CPU, memory, I/O, availability and response times, plus threat detection, and build a unified view from tools like CloudWatch, Azure Monitor, Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog or Splunk. The more ambitious step is automated performance tuning: establish baselines, add ML-based anomaly detection, and wire predefined responses for common issues, with the goal of pushing MTTR down until incidents are barely noticeable.

## Who should watch

DBAs and platform engineers who inherited databases on more than one cloud, and architects deciding where the next Oracle or SQL Server workload should land. If you already run cross-cloud DR drills, the comparison section is the part to take away.

Title: An AI governance framework that speeds launches instead of blocking them
Description: Maurya Priyadarshi (Meta) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on a four-pillar framework for enterprise AI security, from governance boards to automated compliance.
Body:
Security reviews for AI projects often feel like a toll booth on the road to production. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Maurya Priyadarshi, Manager of Salesforce Applications at Meta, presented a framework for enterprise AI security and governance designed to flip that, so that a governed pipeline becomes the fast lane rather than the queue. He was clear that it comes from his own research, not a description of Meta's internal tooling.

The premise is that traditional security frameworks were built for static applications and do not fit how AI systems change, learn and pull from many data sources. That gap is where the risks live.

## Four risks every AI system brings along

Priyadarshi grouped the critical AI risks into four buckets. Data leakage, meaning unauthorised exposure of PII and trade secrets. Model manipulation, the malicious alteration of model behaviour, which depends on who builds the model, how and with access to what. Compliance failures, because building a model does not mean anyone checked it against regulation. And bias and fairness problems, which follow AI wherever it goes.

## The four pillars

The framework rests on governance structures, technical safeguards, compliance alignment and continuous monitoring.

Governance means named bodies with clear jobs. An AI governance board of senior executives and cross-functional leaders sets direction, ratifies policy and allocates resources. An AI ethics committee brings in legal counsel and cross-functional teams. A technical review panel of engineers, security specialists and compliance officers evaluates systems, because, as he noted, engineers alone are not equipped to judge all of it.

Technical safeguards start with identity and access management: multi-factor authentication for AI systems and granular role-based access fitted to AI development and deployment roles. His observation is that teams focus on building the model and nobody thinks about IAM, and that traditional IAM struggles with dynamic access patterns.

## Detect in real time, comply on autopilot

The monitoring loop has four steps: ingest data continuously from AI systems, analyse patterns with ML to spot deviations from operational baselines, generate high-priority alerts for security incidents, performance issues and potential compliance violations, and coordinate incident response and remediation.

Compliance is automated as a workflow. Map applicable regulations (GDPR, CCPA and industry-specific rules) to AI operations, deploy automated controls for data handling, consent management and audit trails, run continuous checks with remediation tracking, and generate compliance reports and regulatory submissions automatically. Model monitoring covers accuracy, drift, degradation alerts and output quality, with explainability features such as decision pathways and feature importance.

## Why this is supposed to be faster

The payoff he argued for is speed. Once controls and approval pathways are in place, a new AI initiative does not have to rebuild the security case from scratch each time. Add fewer incidents, less manual compliance work and more confidence from executives, regulators and employees, and governance turns into a competitive advantage rather than a cost.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, security leads and compliance teams setting up AI governance for the first time, especially in organisations where AI is spreading faster than policy. It is a high-level framework talk with no Kubernetes or tooling specifics, so engineers will want to pair it with something more hands-on.

- [DevSecOps for AI: Embedding Security and Ethics into the Machine Learning Pipeline](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Rajkumar_Sukumar_ai_ml_ethics) by Rajkumar Sukumar (AT&T) moves the controls into the ML pipeline.

Title: Catch churn while it happens with Kafka, Kubeflow and Knative
Description: Gaurav Sunkar (Google) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on real-time churn detection using LSTMs and ensembles served via Kafka, Kubeflow and Knative on Kubernetes.
Body:
By the time a monthly churn report flags a customer, that customer has usually already left. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Gaurav Sunkar of Google Cloud, who previously worked on digital marketplaces including eBay, Walmart and StockX, proposed a real-time retention engine on Kubernetes: Kafka to stream every interaction, Kubeflow to train and retrain the models, and Knative to score customers the moment behaviour changes.

Why bother? His four reasons are revenue tied to customer lifetime value, acquisition costing more than retention, targeted campaigns instead of broad ones, and freeing teams from manually spotting at-risk customers.

## Traditional churn models are late by design

Sunkar listed why the classic approach falls short. It is reactive: by the time patterns are processed, the customer is gone. It segments customers into homogeneous cohorts and misses individual trajectories. It mostly uses transactional data and ignores support tickets, communications, payment issues and product usage. And it runs on fixed rules and static thresholds that cannot follow seasonality or shifting expectations.

What AI adds, in his framing, is response time (act when the behaviour happens), continuous learning from new data streams, and multi-source inputs for a fuller risk picture.

## Pick the model by the memory you need

The model section is a useful quick comparison. Recurrent neural networks handle sequences of customer behaviour, like a drop in login frequency, but lean on recent history. LSTMs keep both immediate and distant signals, so they can catch gradual disengagement over weeks or months. Ensembles such as random forests and gradient boosting combine with deep learning for a fuller assessment. On features, he stressed micro-interactions like click-through rates and navigation patterns, which can precede visible churn by weeks and give you the intervention window.

## An orchestra with a stage manager

Sunkar explained the stack with an orchestra analogy that actually holds up. Kubernetes is the conductor. Kafka collects every event from mobile apps, web apps and backend services into a unified log, and Kafka Streams handles real-time feature extraction and aggregation. Kubeflow is the brain: training pipelines that retrain as data arrives, experiment tracking, hyperparameter tuning and model versioning, so data scientists iterate while DevOps manages deploys. Knative is the stage manager, scaling inference functions up for Black Friday and down on quiet days, triggered directly by Kafka events.

Production needs a unified data platform for batch and streaming, REST and GraphQL APIs for CRM integration so interventions carry full customer context, and autoscaling compute. Prometheus and Grafana watch accuracy, latency and drift, and new model versions are validated against production traffic before they take over.

## Retention means keeping trust too

The ethics section is more than a box tick. Audit predictions across segments so infrequent users are not systematically written off, use SHAP and LIME so customer success teams know why someone is flagged, and log model decisions and intervention triggers. Privacy by design under GDPR and CCPA means feature selection must adapt to each customer's consent, with consent checks and retention policies automated in the Kubeflow pipeline.

His roadmap has four steps: foundation (Kubernetes, Kubeflow, Kafka), model development on historical data, production on Knative with CRM integration, then A/B testing and scaling.

## Who should watch

ML and data platform engineers at marketplaces, subscription businesses or anyone with a churn dashboard that only explains the past. It is a blueprint talk without code, and a good overview of how the three CNCF-adjacent tools fit together.

Title: Voice biometrics can retire the date-of-birth check in healthcare
Description: Sreenivasul Reddy Meegada at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on replacing knowledge-based checks in healthcare with voice biometrics, and its limits.
Body:
If your security question is a date of birth and a zip code, an attacker with a search engine already knows the answer. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Sreenivasul Reddy Meegada, a technical lead and solutions architect, made the case for voice biometrics as the replacement for knowledge-based authentication in healthcare, with a frank list of where it breaks.

## Why attackers love healthcare records

He opens with the economics. On the black market, he said, a credit card record goes for around $5 while a healthcare record goes for around $250. That gap explains why healthcare is a favourite target, and why weak, password-based and knowledge-based authentication is a liability rather than a nuisance.

Healthcare also adds its own twist. Clinicians work under pressure with access to life-and-death information, and in an emergency a slow login is a clinical problem, not a UX complaint. Get authentication wrong in the other direction and you get medical identity theft, which can lead to incorrect treatment, insurance fraud and altered records.

## What a voiceprint actually measures

The useful explainer in the middle covers what a voiceprint is. Part of it is physiological: everyone's vocal tract produces a distinctive signature. Part of it is behavioural: pronunciation, rhythm and intonation patterns built up over years of speaking. Systems combine features such as fundamental frequency and spectral distribution with machine learning to build the print, which is why, in his telling, false accepts stay low and simple impersonation does not get far. He also notes systems can distinguish a live human from an automated playback.

The applications he lists are concrete: staff access control, fraud prevention on insurance claims, and authentication in the contact centre, where callers no longer need to recite member numbers and birthdays. The abstract points to real deployments built on NICE and Omilia.

## The results, and the honest caveats

Citing a recent survey of clinical deployments, he reports an 83% reduction in authentication time and a 67% reduction in support requests, most of which were authentication problems in the first place. Fewer "I can't log in" calls is an incident-reduction story in its own right.

Then the part many vendor decks skip. Background noise causes mismatches. People sound different when they are ill or emotional. Licensing, training and workflow disruption cost real money. Privacy rules (HIPAA, GDPR and others) apply to biometric data, so privacy and security teams belong in the strategy discussion from day one. And you have to pick a match threshold: accept only high-confidence matches, or allow medium ones, depending on the business requirement.

## How to roll it out without a new incident class

His deployment advice is conservative in a good way. Do a pre-rollout assessment with site surveys, infrastructure audits and user interviews. Keep multimodal fallback: when voice fails, drop back to knowledge-based authentication without blocking the clinician or the member. Pilot with one department, tune, then expand in phases. Check whether the vendor supports enrolment from historical recordings, so returning callers do not have to enrol again, and how well it integrates with your IVR and CRM.

On compliance he highlights a quieter benefit: voice authentication creates non-repudiable records of who accessed what, which supports HIPAA audit logging and fine-grained, least-privilege access.

## Who should watch

Security architects and contact-centre platform owners in healthcare and insurance weighing biometrics, and anyone running an identity verification flow that still asks for a birthday. It is a strategy and rollout talk, not a demo of a specific product.

Title: Users ignore AI they cannot inspect, so build trust into the stack
Description: Raj Kommera (ON24) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on five design pillars for trustworthy AI, from contextual confidence scores to OpenTelemetry audit trails.
Body:
An accurate model that nobody trusts has the same business value as no model at all. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Raj Kommera, Senior Engineer at ON24, presented what he calls Kube-Native Trust: five architectural pillars that make AI recommendations inspectable, and a mapping of each pillar onto tools Kubernetes teams already run.

The pattern he keeps seeing in enterprises is that users quietly ignore AI recommendations because they cannot scrutinise the logic, trace the data or judge how certain the model is. Millions get invested, and the tool ends up sidelined. His diagnosis: the real problem is transparency, not prediction.

## Why enterprise AI gets sidelined

Kommera named four causes. Models act like black boxes. They ignore business context like regulatory limits, budget thresholds and workflow quirks. Observability is too thin to trace an input to a prediction, so nobody can audit or debug it. And there is a trust gap between the engineers who build the model, the data scientists who tune it and the business users who are supposed to act on it. His fix is to treat trust as a first-class architectural concern.

## Five pillars, each one buildable

**Contextualised confidence scoring.** Instead of one flat percentage, tell users how confident the model is for this specific context, how this prediction compares with similar past cases, and how to read the score.

**Source traceability.** For any recommendation, answer which data was used, how it was processed, which features mattered and which business rules were applied. He likened it to turning on version history for every decision.

**Adaptive thresholds.** A static "act above 70%" rule is naive. Thresholds should move with use-case criticality, operational constraints and risk tolerance; a 60% confident prediction may be fine for marketing and unacceptable in healthcare.

**Progressive disclosure in the UI.** Level one is a summary and a confidence score, level two adds key drivers and alternatives, level three shows full lineage, parameters and feature importance. Users pick their depth.

**End-to-end audit trails.** Immutable logs of what was predicted, why and when, with OpenTelemetry integration, captured human feedback, outcome validation and compliance-ready reports.

## Mapping it to Kubernetes tools

The implementation blueprint reuses the platform you probably already have. A service mesh such as Istio or Linkerd captures model traffic, latency and request traces. GitOps with Argo CD or Flux version-controls models, so you can answer which version made which call. OpenTelemetry gives unified tracing from infrastructure up to business outcome. A policy layer enforces governance and adaptive thresholds and secures the pipeline. In his reference architecture, confidence scoring runs as its own microservice, thresholds are policy-driven, the UI exposes layered explanations and everything from prediction to outcome is logged.

His examples cover customer segmentation (why a user falls into a segment), lead routing (why a lead was prioritised), clinical patient risk scoring and infrastructure scaling decisions that show cost context.

## Who should watch

Engineers building AI features into enterprise products who keep hearing that users do not adopt them, and platform teams asked to make models auditable. It is a short framework talk; the starter checklist at the end (audit transparency gaps, add confidence scoring to one model, start tracing with OpenTelemetry, add feedback loops to the UI) is the part to steal.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: Conf42 MLOps 2025 roundup: where the lab meets production
Description: Conf42 MLOps 2025 in review, from warehouse robots and vendor lockouts to trillion-parameter training, AgentCore, zero trust pipelines and fintech ML.
Body:
Two days before Elementor launched its AI Site Planner, OpenAI locked the company's account. Dennis Nerush told that story at [Conf42 MLOps 2025](https://www.conf42.com/mlops2025), and the punchline was that it barely mattered, because the team had built for exactly that failure. The 37 talks at the event, streamed online on September 18, 2025, kept coming back to the same gap: models that work in the lab, in the notebook or in the demo, and what it takes to keep them working once real traffic, real dust and real vendors get involved. Speakers came from Meta, Amazon, AWS, Mastercard, Oracle, Intuit, JPMorgan Chase, Barclays, SiriusXM and many more.

## The real world is messier than the lab

[Shubham Beldar](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Shubham_Beldar_when_ai_automation) (Symbotic) brought the most physical failures of the event. Picking robots that look flawless in the lab meet transparent shrink wrap, irregular products and dust on their vision sensors, and accuracy drops from the mid-nineties to the low sixties. His diagnosis is an MLOps one: training data missing the messy cases, and validation done in the lab instead of on the warehouse floor.

[Dennis Nerush](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Dennis_Nerush_scaling_ai_fault) (Elementor) covered the vendor version of the same lesson. His team's infrastructure integrates several AI vendors and can switch between them, which is why an account lockout two days before launch turned into a manageable incident instead of a war room. [Madhavi Bhairavabhatla](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Madhavi_Bhairavabhatla_fail_fast_recover) (Mastercard) went one level down to timeouts: set too generously, they hold resources, delay failure detection and let one slow service drag down the rest, so the talk lays out cascading timeouts across system layers.

Several talks addressed the lab-to-production pipeline directly, including [Jimmy Katiyar](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Jimmy_Katiyar_model_production_building) (SiriusXM), [Srikanth Vissarapu](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Srikanth_Vissarapu_lab_production_building) (Meta), [Bharath Reddy Baddam](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Bharath_Reddy_Baddam_bridging_mlops_gap) (New York Life) and [Naveen Edapurath Vijayan](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Naveen_Edapurath_Vijayan_mlops_scale) (AWS), who covered CI/CD for ML, monitoring and governance.

## Scale at the largest platforms

[Anjan Dash](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Anjan_Dash_mlops_trillion_parameter) (Meta) talked about operating training pipelines for trillion-parameter LLMs, where failure recovery and cost are daily concerns. [Prabhakar Singh](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Prabhakar_Singh_production_mlops_spam) (Meta) covered real-time, multimodal spam detection at billion-user scale, including sampling strategies that cut labelling cost and privacy-preserving ML. [Mohan Singh](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Mohan_Singh_building_autonomous_mlops) (Amazon) presented self-healing ML infrastructure that predicts failures and scales itself.

On agents, [Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Samuel_Baruffi_poc_bedrock_agentcore) (AWS) addressed why so many agent projects stall at proof of concept: production needs identity, governed tool access and a runtime, which is what Amazon Bedrock AgentCore packages as managed services. [Nishanth Joseph Paulraj](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Nishanth_Joseph_Paulraj_deploying_ai_literature) (Thermo Fisher Scientific) deployed literature agents for biomedical research, and [Brian Irish](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Brian_Irish_embracing_sky_computing) (Ditto) made the case for sky computing across clouds.

## Humans, governance and security in the loop

[Tejasvi Nuthalapati](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Tejasvi_Nuthalapati_human_loop_mlops) (Amazon) argued for production patterns that keep humans in the loop to improve models rather than replace people. [Bhanu Maryala](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Bhanu_Maryala_automating_ai_ethics) (Informatica) automated data governance inside generative AI pipelines so compliance doesn't slow deployments. [Sudheer Obbu](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Sudheer_Obbu_zero_trust_mlops) (JPMorgan Chase) applied Zero Trust to ML pipelines from development to production, and [Arfi Siddik Mollashaik](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Arfi_Siddik_Mollashaik_ai_driven_cybersecurity) (Securiti) looked at threat detection and privacy with post-quantum defences in mind. Healthcare got its own governance angle from [Nikitha Edulakanti](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Nikitha_Edulakanti_mlops_scale_designing) (Fresenius Medical Care) and [Aishwarya Pai](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Aishwarya_Pai_mlops_healthcare_scaling) (Deloitte).

## Finance was the busiest track

No other domain came close. [Naresh Karri](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Naresh_Karri_production_mlops_finance) (Intuit) covered keeping fraud models alive under extreme load and drift, [Mallikarjun Ramasani](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Mallikarjun_Ramasani_operationalizing_ai_finance) (Barclays) ML-powered BI and real-time analytics, [Narasimha Rao Vanaparthi](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Narasimha_Rao_Vanaparthi_mlops_fintech_architecting) (State Street) responsible AI in regulated environments, and [Dileep Kumar Kanimetta](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Dileep_Kumar_Kanimetta_mlops_scale_operationalizing) (Microsoft) drift detection and automated governance for risk models. [Parul Purwar](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Parul_Purwar_scaling_ai_finance) (IMC Trading), [Pushpalika Chatterjee](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Pushpalika_Chatterjee_generative_ai_fintech) (Huntington National Bank) and [Naganarendar Chitturi](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Naganarendar_Chitturi_paperwork_pipeline_building) (Newrez), who built MLOps for autonomous mortgage processing, rounded it out. Insurance came via [Sameer Joshi](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Sameer_Joshi_ai_driven_insurance) (Cognizant) and [Sreelatha Pasuparthi](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Sreelatha_Pasuparthi_intelligent_error_response) (Liberty Mutual), whose ML-driven Slack integration predicts which errors matter across 17 enterprise systems.

## MLOps at the edges

Some of the most interesting constraints came from outside big tech. [Lalitha Potharalanka](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Lalitha_Potharalanka_scaling_educational_ai) (FDA) took educational AI to rural schools with poor connectivity through low-code platforms and edge inference, and [Anoosha Cherukuri](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Anoosha_Cherukuri_low_code_meets) (State of Tennessee) brought low-code automation to public sector systems. [Krishna Munnaluru](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Krishna_Munnaluru_production_ready_mlops) (Oracle) built a VoIP monitoring pipeline on Kafka, Kubeflow and MLflow, [Manoj Kumar Vunnava](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Manoj_Kumar_Vunnava_scaling_conversational_ai) (GoDaddy) scaled conversational AI in contact centres, [Muruga Angamuthu](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Muruga_Angamuthu_transforming_manufacturing_ai) (Techtronic Industries) covered predictive maintenance in manufacturing, and [Rajeev Chevuri](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Rajeev_Chevuri_scaling_mlops_self) (Freddie Mac) built self-service ML platforms.

## Partners and where to watch

Thanks to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) as newsletter partner, [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and the media partners who supported the event. Every talk is on the [Conf42 MLOps 2025 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCyZXSIA8uy6Fq0cdcNfl4f) and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/mlops2025).

The series continues with [Conf42 MLOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/mlops2026).

Title: Run a GPU scheduler per team by putting it in a virtual cluster
Description: Piotr Zaniewski (vCluster) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 demos NVIDIA's KAI Scheduler inside vCluster for fractional GPUs and per-team scheduler versions.
Body:
Upgrading the one scheduler every GPU team depends on is the kind of change that gets scheduled for a Friday and regretted by Saturday. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Piotr Zaniewski, Head of Engineering Enablement at vCluster, showed a way out: run NVIDIA's open-source KAI Scheduler inside a virtual cluster, so each team gets its own scheduler version and an upgrade's blast radius shrinks to one disposable pod.

This is a vendor talk in the honest sense. vCluster Labs makes vCluster, and the session is a live demo of it, run on a local kind cluster with an older NVIDIA consumer card passed through to Docker. The setup is published with the video so you can reproduce it on your own GPU.

## Kubernetes inside a pod, with a syncer in the middle

vCluster runs a full, certified Kubernetes control plane inside a pod on a host cluster: an API server, a controller manager, a data store (SQLite in the demo, with etcd or an external backend for high availability) and optionally its own scheduler. The key component is the syncer, which runs a reconciliation loop that copies resources between the virtual cluster and the host, handling name collisions along the way and configurable down to which resource types cross over.

The result is cheap. Zaniewski pointed out the virtual cluster pod in the demo using roughly 370 MB of memory, which is why spinning one up per team, per test or per CI run is realistic where a new EKS cluster is not.

## KAI Scheduler slices the GPU

NVIDIA open sourced the Kubernetes AI scheduler in 2025. It adds fractional GPU allocation, queue-based scheduling and topology awareness. In the demo, two pods asked for 20% and 10% of the same GPU through annotations, with the KAI scheduler name and the NVIDIA runtime class set, and both landed on the one card exactly as configured. The abstract cites utilisation going from 40% to 90% with fractional GPUs. There was also a small GPU-backed web app that wrote SRE horror-story haiku on request, which is the most on-brand demo app a Kubernetes conference has seen.

## Upgrades without a shared blast radius

The real argument is about risk. With one scheduler on a big shared cluster, a buggy release leaves every dependent pod pending, a bad CRD upgrade can corrupt namespaces, and teams wait on each other for features. He cited a New Relic 2024 figure of enterprise downtime costing up to a million dollars per hour.

Inside a virtual cluster, the scheduler is one more workload. The vCluster config enables a virtual scheduler, syncs nodes, node labels and runtime classes from the host so pods can target GPU nodes, and uses a setting that stops vCluster from taking ownership of pods when you want the host scheduler instead. He then created two virtual clusters, team stable and team beta, installed different KAI Scheduler versions in each, and ran the same fractional GPU pods in both, while a third team kept using the host cluster's default scheduler.

## Rollback is a delete

Testing a scheduler upgrade without a new host cluster takes minutes instead of hours. Rolling back took about 39 seconds in the demo: delete the virtual cluster, and nothing else on the host notices. That turns A/B testing of scheduler versions into something you can do in production, team by team.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers and SREs running shared GPU clusters for ML, research and inference teams with different version needs. You will get the most out of it if you already know Kubernetes scheduling basics; it moves quickly through vCluster internals into the demo.

- [Running vLLM Inference on Kubernetes Across Clouds](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Kosseila_Haddalene_vllm_kubernetes_gpu) by Kosseila Haddalene (Cloudthrill) covers what runs on those GPUs.
