Title: Let sensor data, not the calendar, write the maintenance work order
Description: Abhijit Joshi (Deloitte Consulting) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on using GenAI on IoT sensor data to drive ERP maintenance work orders in automotive plants.
Body:
Most factory maintenance still runs on the calendar: every three months, whether the robot worked hard or sat idle. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Abhijit Joshi of Deloitte Consulting, a supply chain transformation specialist with 20 years in automotive manufacturing who started his career in plant maintenance, made the case for letting generative AI read sensor data and decide when the ERP system should raise a work order.

The stakes he quoted are blunt: unplanned equipment downtime costing automotive manufacturers up to 22,000 per minute, and traditional strategies that cannot keep up. His claim is that putting GenAI between IoT data and ERP maintenance planning can cut unplanned downtime by around 40%.

## Calendar, usage and condition all miss something

Joshi walked through the three classic approaches, using the analogy of servicing your own car. Calendar-based maintenance services equipment at fixed intervals, regardless of how much it ran, so it is either too early or too late. Usage-based maintenance waits for a run count or cycle threshold. Condition-based maintenance acts when a monitored parameter crosses a limit. All three are reactive in practice, waste resources, and ignore most of the historical data the plant already has.

## Three drivers, one loop

His framework stacks three components. IoT sensors on the line capture vibration, temperature and pressure continuously, something no human inspector can do. The ERP system already knows inventory, work orders, parts, instructions and technician capacity. Generative AI sits on top: it models equipment behaviour, generates synthetic data to simulate operating conditions the plant has not seen yet, learns failure patterns from history plus live data, and tells the ERP when a work order is due based on actual deterioration.

The output is three actions: an automated maintenance work order to a technician, a plan that schedules work around expected downtime, and KPIs from the same data. ERP feedback then refines the model.

## Start with the robots and the paint shop

He named two target applications where failures hurt most in car plants: automated assembly and welding robots, where continuous monitoring of operating patterns catches early failure, and paint application lines, where predictive maintenance on booths and spray systems prevents both downtime and quality defects.

Implementation advice is deliberately low-drama. Use existing sensors and infrastructure rather than building new ones, feed the data through a warehouse into a readable format, plug predictions into the existing work order flow, and roll out one plant or even one line at a time.

## The numbers come with a caveat

Joshi presented ballpark results from studied deployments: downtime down 40%, forecasting accuracy improved by around 85%, false alarms cut by 50%, maintenance costs down 30%, and first-time fix rates reaching 90%. He was clear these vary by company and are expected outcomes rather than one client's figures. His end state is the zero-downtime factory, with systems that eventually self-diagnose.

## Who should watch

Manufacturing IT and ERP teams, maintenance planners and anyone scoping an industrial IoT project who needs to explain the business flow to plant leadership. Despite the conference name, the talk is about the maintenance and ERP workflow, not Kubernetes, so platform engineers looking for cluster patterns should pick one of the related talks below.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [AI Driven Vectorized Motor Health Monitoring for Reliable Industrial Operations](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Avinash_Sista_maintenance_industrial_ai) by Avinash Sista (MongoDB) zooms in on turning motor signals into predictions.

Title: Regulated incidents run on two clocks, and only one is technical
Description: Nisheedh Raveendran (LinkedIn) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on incident response under HIPAA, GDPR and DMA without sacrificing recovery or compliance.
Body:
Your incident commander wants the system back; your compliance officer wants evidence, timelines and a notification draft; and both are right. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Nisheedh Raveendran, Senior Staff Engineer at LinkedIn, laid out a compliance-aware incident framework for teams working under HIPAA, GDPR and the EU's Digital Markets Act, built on one idea: run the regulatory track in parallel from minute zero instead of bolting it on after the fix.

## The regulatory incident paradox

Nisheedh frames every regulated incident as a dual mandate. Technical recovery is about speed: restore functionality, stop data loss, prevent cascading failures. Regulatory obligations are about accuracy: reporting deadlines, documentation, evidence preservation, legal and forensic requirements. The same small responder team gets pulled both ways, and communication has to be transparent and timely while staying inside what legal will let you say.

Classic incident management optimises only the first clock. That is where it fails: deadlines that do not line up with recovery, documentation that slows the fix, legal, compliance and PR all joining the call, and data-access rules that stop responders from looking at the very production data they need.

## Three regimes, three different stopwatches

The regulatory section is a compact reference worth bookmarking. HIPAA covers protected health information: notify HHS (and potentially media, depending on scale) typically within 60 days, notify affected individuals without undue delay, and back the classification with a documented risk assessment.

GDPR is the tight one, with a 72-hour window to the supervisory authority. Nisheedh breaks it into phases. The first 24 hours are preliminary assessment: was personal data affected, and start collecting evidence now. Hours 24 to 48 are risk assessment for the data subjects and drafting the notifications. Hours 48 to 72 are the notification itself. Seeing it as a runbook rather than a deadline is the useful shift.

The DMA, aimed at gatekeeper platforms, adds obligations that bite during the incident: transparency about algorithmic failures, continued service and interoperability, fairness in which services get restored first, and strict rules on sensitive data access during recovery.

## Build the compliance track before you need it

The framework has three phases. Preparation means pre-approved notification templates, a map of which regulations apply to which systems, and privacy-preserving investigation tools. Response means parallel tracks for mitigation and compliance with synchronisation checkpoints, a regulatory triage step, and continuous documentation. Recovery adds compliance verification checkpoints and progressive service restoration.

Two ideas stand out. Documentation by design: evidence collection is automated inside the technical workflow, so logs and audit trails exist without anyone writing them up at 3 a.m., with a single source feeding multiple regulators. And decision frameworks: predefined criteria for classifying the incident, with notification triggers tied to impact thresholds, so nobody debates whether this counts as a breach while the clock runs.

## Responders who never touch production data

The privacy-preserving analysis section is the most concrete. Investigators need data to assess impact; regulators restrict access; collecting evidence can itself break data minimisation. Nisheedh's example is AWS Systems Manager: operators run mitigations through an automated, logged tool without direct production access, which preserves the audit trail and keeps sensitive data masked from on-call engineers. The regulator gets a log; the engineer never gets the patient record.

He closes with a playbook recipe: map the regulations that apply to you into a reference matrix of deadlines, embed a compliance liaison in incident teams, write the templates, define classification decision trees, and run game days on scenarios involving regulated data that test the notification timeline as well as the fix.

## Who should watch

Incident commanders and SRE leads in healthcare, fintech or any EU-facing platform, and the compliance people who keep getting paged into calls they were not briefed for. It is a framework talk, not a tooling demo, and that is its strength.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [GDPR and Beyond: Demystifying Data Governance Challenges](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Antonio_Murgia_Francesco_Valentini_gdpr_beyond_data) by Antonio Murgia and Francesco Valentini, for the data-governance groundwork.
- [SRE for National-Scale Regulatory Reporting: HA, DR, and Audit-Ready Design](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Bhargavaram_Potharaju_national_scale_regulatory) by Bhargavaram Potharaju, on audit-ready design from the SRE side.
- [Privacy by Design for DevOps](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Vivek_Chittireddy_privacy_regulation_security) by Vivek Chittireddy, on building the data systems so the incident is easier to begin with.

Title: Turning fragile models into dependable systems
Description: Machine learning, sustained
Body:
# MLOps: where models meet reality

Training a model is the easy part.

Getting it into production, keeping it running, making sure it behaves, scales, stays secure, and doesn’t quietly ruin someone’s day at 3 AM? That’s the real job.

Conf42 MLOps 2025 is all about that gap between “it works on my notebook” and “this powers a real system”.

This conference digs into MLOps at scale. Trillion-parameter models, governed pipelines, self-healing infrastructure, automated deployments, and AI systems that need to run reliably across cloud, enterprise, and regulated environments. From healthcare and finance to telecom, manufacturing, and public sector platforms, these talks focus on production, not demos.

There’s a strong emphasis on automation and resilience. Cascading timeouts, failure recovery, self-service MLOps platforms, AI-driven code evolution, and pipelines that can survive real traffic and real users. Several sessions look at what happens when automation goes wrong, and what teams learned the hard way.

LLMs and generative AI are everywhere, of course. Training pipelines, inference platforms, agent-based systems, RAG architectures, and scaling conversational AI all make an appearance. Alongside that comes governance, ethics, security, and making sure models don’t leak data, drift silently, or surprise regulators.

Finance and healthcare get plenty of attention, with talks on fraud detection, risk modeling, clinical workflows, and responsible AI in highly regulated environments. These sessions show what MLOps looks like when the cost of failure is measured in more than just uptime.

If you’re responsible for turning machine learning into something stable, repeatable, and trustworthy, this one’s for you. MLOps is no longer optional. It’s the difference between promising models and systems people can actually rely on.

Title: Why Kubernetes API gateways need a service mesh behind them
Description: Niharika Jha (Microsoft) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on pairing Kubernetes-native API gateways with Istio or Linkerd for traffic control, mTLS and observability.
Body:
A traditional API gateway in front of a few hundred microservices tends to become the one box everybody is afraid to restart. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Niharika Jha, Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft, gave a compact tour of the alternative: Kubernetes-native API gateways layered with a service mesh, so north-south and east-west traffic share policies, security and telemetry.

The talk runs about 15 minutes and works as a structured overview rather than a deep implementation session. It is a good map of the moving parts for teams that are hitting service sprawl and have not yet picked a mesh.

## The gateway was never built for this many services

Jha's problem statement is service sprawl: the number of services outpaces what a traditional gateway can manage. The symptoms are slow releases blocked on integration, gateways that become single points of failure, manual service discovery and static config that does not survive multi-cloud, and configuration drift between dev, staging and production. All of it adds operational load and slows teams down.

Her answer is a layered architecture. A Kubernetes-native gateway handles the edge, a service mesh handles service-to-service traffic, and together they give end-to-end traffic control, one place to enforce policy and a single view of what is happening, across Azure, AWS or Google Cloud.

## Istio if you need everything, Linkerd if you need less

On the mesh itself she covered Istio's split between a control plane that manages policy and discovery centrally and Envoy sidecars that do routing and load balancing per pod, with mutual TLS for zero-trust traffic between services. For teams that want a lighter footprint, Linkerd offers mTLS, routing and observability with less resource overhead.

The traffic patterns that make a mesh worth its sidecars are the ones she highlighted: automated canary deployments that shift traffic gradually and roll back when health checks fail, circuit breakers that stop one failing service from cascading, and load balancing driven by real-time metrics.

## Security and observability as defaults

Security gets two layers. Kubernetes RBAC with automated service accounts and least privilege controls who can do what in the cluster, while OAuth 2.0 and JWTs handle stateless authentication at the API level, wired to external identity providers. Observability is the standard trio of Prometheus for metrics, Grafana for dashboards and Jaeger or Zipkin for traces.

Helm charts standardise deployments as configuration-as-code across environments. Adaptive rate limiting throttles traffic based on downstream health, and it works together with HPA and VPA for scaling. Operators and custom resource definitions give developers self-service with GitOps principles.

## APIs as products

The less common angle is monetisation. Jha treated APIs as business products: usage-based pricing, analytics on consumption, namespace isolation for multi-tenant customers, and self-service developer portals for discovery. If your platform team is asked to justify its budget, that section gives you the vocabulary.

Her rollout framework has four steps: assess the current architecture, deploy Istio or Linkerd with the right security settings, integrate the gateway so traffic management and observability line up, then tune for production performance and scale.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects who own an ingress or gateway layer and are weighing whether to add a mesh, plus platform leads who need a one-slide-per-concept overview to share with their team. If you already run Istio in production, it will be familiar ground.

Title: The quiet attacks on AI in finance hide in cloud-native gaps
Description: Manisha Sengupta (Brown Brothers Harriman) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on adversarial attacks, data poisoning and Kubernetes misconfigurations in AI-driven finance.
Body:
The most dangerous attack on a financial AI system may be the one that looks like normal traffic. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Manisha Sengupta, Assistant Vice President for systems in Investor Services Technology at Brown Brothers Harriman, mapped how AI models for fraud, credit scoring and trading pick up new attack surfaces when they move to containers, microservices and public APIs, and what a layered defence looks like.

She opened with a story about a smart home app whose cloud-hosted AI detected unusual activity in the house. One leaked API key later, an attacker was querying the model to learn when the home was empty. Her takeaway: the real threat is often the quiet pattern nobody watches, not the big obvious hack.

## Four ways to break a model without breaking in

Sengupta grouped the AI-specific threats into four. Adversarial attacks craft inputs that look legitimate to humans but fool the model, for example transactions a fraud detector scores as safe, and black-box versions now work with very little insider knowledge. Data poisoning slips malicious records into training data, so a credit model can quietly discriminate against a group while still looking accurate. Model extraction and inversion reverse engineer a model from its outputs, leaking things like customer spending habits or proprietary trading logic, and offering models through APIs widens that surface.

The fourth is the platform itself. Misconfigured RBAC hands out privileges, public container images ship with vulnerabilities, weak network policies allow lateral movement, and short-lived containers are hard to monitor and audit.

## How a fraud system gets walked around

Her attack scenario chains those together: compromise a developer account, use weak network policies to reach the transaction data pipeline, corrupt it, and push real fraudulent transactions past detection without an alarm. For trading systems, adversaries study algorithm outputs to reverse engineer the logic and front-run the institution's own trades. In a distributed system, each step looks like ordinary activity.

## People are part of the attack surface

She gave the human factor equal weight. Data scientists optimise for accuracy and may use unvalidated public datasets or skip sanitisation. Developers grant broad permissions in shared environments and pull vulnerable open source libraries. DevOps teams under deadline pressure cut corners. And there is a global shortage of people who know both AI and security.

## Defence in depth, with explanations

Her resilience model has four pillars: zero trust across the AI pipeline, model governance with versioning and security checks, data security with integrity and lineage tracking, and infrastructure security with defence in depth tailored to AI. Explainable AI helps analysts understand why something was flagged, speeds up investigations and cuts false positives, though she warned it must be balanced against what explanations reveal.

The most practical idea is cross-layer anomaly correlation. A network spike alone is a glitch; a network spike plus model drift plus a data shift is probably an attack. Governance closes the loop with clear ownership across the model lifecycle, continuous audit, incident playbooks that cover AI events, and bias and fairness testing.

## Who should watch

Security engineers and platform teams at banks, asset managers and fintechs who run models in Kubernetes, and ML engineers who have never threat-modelled their own training pipeline. It is a risk-mapping talk without tooling demos, best paired with something hands-on.

Title: Your API gateway is the first responder in a microservices incident
Description: Vijaykumar Pasunoori at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on API gateways as incident control planes: service mesh, serverless, edge failover, zero trust.
Body:
When a request path crosses dozens of services, the one component that sees all of it is the gateway in front. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Vijaykumar Pasunoori, a technical lead with about two decades in cloud and microservices architecture, made the case that modern API gateways are the natural place to detect, isolate and recover from incidents, because they let you apply resilience patterns once instead of in every service.

The event lists him with Valet Living; in the talk he mentions his current role as a tech lead at Freddie Mac. Either way, the talk is a survey across six areas, packed with figures from the deployments he describes.

## Four generations, from proxy to reliability engine

Vijaykumar traces the gateway's career path. Generation one was the basic proxy: simple routing, basic auth, little visibility. Generation two added API management, with rate limiting, analytics and developer portals, which is where governance started. Generation three went cloud native, Kubernetes-native and integrated with the service mesh. Generation four is what he calls the reliability engine: AI-driven resilience, predictive scaling and autonomous recovery.

The financial-services example he returns to coordinates more than 850 microservices through a single gateway cluster, handling 180 million calls a day at around 47 ms latency. The number incident people will care about: MTTR dropped from 23 minutes to 4.3 minutes.

## The mesh multiplies what the gateway can see

Pairing the gateway with a service mesh gives you one control plane for traffic shaping, circuit breaking and observability. The figures he cites for the combination include 62% faster incident detection and 78% more accurate fault isolation. The practical point underneath the percentages is architectural: north-south traffic at the gateway and east-west traffic in the mesh, governed together, means an incident has fewer places to hide.

## Serverless and edge: different failure, same lever

For serverless workloads the gateway's job shifts to cold starts, scaling precision and request batching. He reports a 76% reduction in cold starts via pre-warming, and 43% fewer function invocations during spikes through intelligent batching.

At the edge, the pattern is regional gateway nodes, a central control plane for config and routing policy, health-aware traffic steering and automated fallback paths. His best story here is an e-commerce customer that rode out a major AWS us-east-1 outage by rerouting automatically to healthy regions, keeping 99.98% availability. Failures stay regional; customers stay online. That is the kind of incident review you want to write.

## Security cannot be the thing you drop under load

The zero trust section is a useful corrective. Under peak load, identity providers struggle too, and the temptation is to relax checks. Vijaykumar describes distributed token validation, local policy enforcement and graceful degradation so authentication keeps working even when the identity provider is restricted. Availability and compliance both hold, rather than one being traded for the other mid-incident.

## Tech is half of it

His implementation checklist is the bit to screenshot: clear ownership of what the gateway does versus the services, multi-layer observability with tracing, metrics and probes, failure isolation through circuit breakers, bulkheads and rate limits, automated remediation with fallback behaviour, and runbooks for gateway-specific failures. As he puts it, this is about operational discipline as much as technology.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams who own the edge of a microservices estate and want a compact tour of what a gateway can take off individual services. The numbers come from the deployments he describes rather than a controlled benchmark, so read them as direction, not a target. If you already run Envoy-based gateways with a mesh, the edge and zero trust sections still earn their minutes.

Title: Treat fairness, explainability and privacy as cluster infrastructure
Description: Venus Garg (Boston University) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on building fairness audits, explanation sidecars and federated learning into Kubernetes for healthcare AI.
Body:
Kubernetes already gives you admission controllers, canaries and automatic rollbacks, so why not point them at bias as well as bugs? At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Venus Garg of Boston University argued exactly that: in healthcare AI, fairness, explainability and privacy should be enforced by the deployment pipeline itself, using the same hooks platform teams already rely on.

Her starting point is that the properties which make Kubernetes good for ML (distributed pipelines, dynamic scaling, many small services) also make auditing harder. Training, ingestion, model updates and inference are spread across pods, and that is where documented failures such as dermatology models misclassifying darker skin tones can hide.

## A fairness audit is just another pipeline job

The first pillar is fairness. After every training job, an audit task runs using tools like Fairlearn or IBM AIF360, computing metrics per subgroup: are false negative rates higher for one group, does error vary across populations? If a metric crosses a threshold, the pipeline halts and the model is flagged for review or rolled back. On Kubernetes that is a Job or a step in an Argo workflow, versioned and repeatable.

Garg shared a story from one deployment where the continuous audit caught a subgroup's error rate drifting upward over time, and the system rolled back to the last known good model, buying time to retrain. Without automation, she noted, that drift might have gone unnoticed until harm was done.

## Put the explanation in a sidecar

The second pillar is explainability, both local (why this patient was scored high risk, via LIME or SHAP) and global (what the model relies on overall). Her pattern is an explainability sidecar or microservice next to the model server: the main service returns the prediction, the sidecar returns the explanation, and each scales independently.

She was candid about cost. Explanations add latency and compute, so compute them only for flagged or uncertain requests, cache them for repeated inputs, or return them asynchronously. And treat explanation output with the same access controls as predictions, because explanations can leak sensitive inputs.

## Keep patient data where it lives

The third pillar is privacy through federated learning: local training pods per hospital cluster, only model updates leave the premises, and a central aggregator pod combines them. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise before aggregation so individual contributions cannot be reverse engineered. Every step is versioned and logged.

## Make the cluster say no

Scaling this means not building one monolithic ethics module. Run the fairness auditor, explanation service and privacy aggregator as separate services, cache what you can, monitor fairness drift alongside performance, and fail safe when a check itself breaks. For regulation (HIPAA, GDPR, FDA rules, the EU AI Act), admission controllers such as OPA Gatekeeper can refuse a deployment whose fairness audit did not pass or whose explanation mechanism is not active.

Her rollout advice is incremental: assess current models for bias with baseline metrics, integrate checks into CI/CD and dashboards, then scale with reusable Helm charts or operators. Start with one fairness check, then add an explanation sidecar, then pilot federated training.

## Who should watch

ML platform engineers in healthcare or any regulated field who need a concrete place to put fairness and explainability checks. It is a patterns talk rather than a demo, and the hospital examples are illustrative, but the mapping of each ethical control to a Kubernetes primitive is useful on its own.

Title: A five-layer GenAI pipeline for healthcare claims and fraud
Description: Amala Umakanth (McKinsey & Company) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on GenAI claims processing, from ingestion and NLP to adjudication, explainability and fraud detection.
Body:
Healthcare claims fail in boring ways long before they fail in fraudulent ones: a missing document, an inconsistent code, a follow-up visit billed like a new diagnosis. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Amala Umakanth, a data engineer at McKinsey & Company, walked through a five-layer generative AI architecture for claims processing that targets both problems, faster and more accurate claims on one side and proactive fraud detection on the other.

She framed the scale first. Tens of millions of claims move daily through eligibility, coding, validation, adjudication and audit, and each layer adds room for error. She cited studies putting around 15% of claims as denied or delayed, and fraud such as upcoding, phantom billing and collusive provider networks costing the industry over a hundred billion dollars a year. Rule engines with fixed thresholds cannot keep up with patterns that keep changing.

## Clean data first, then understand it

Layer one is ingestion and preprocessing. Claims arrive as PDFs, HL7 messages and DICOM images, and the pipeline converts them into structured data with cleaning, deduplication and enrichment. Without that foundation, as she put it, no model delivers reliable outcomes.

Layer two is semantic understanding. NLP reads physician notes, discharge summaries and claim narratives, extracts diagnosis codes, procedures and medications, and builds context. Her example: telling a follow-up visit for diabetes apart from a new diabetes diagnosis, a subtle difference that changes billing accuracy.

## Validate, decide, and know when to ask a human

Layer three validates claims against ICD-10 and CPT coding standards, cross-checks medical necessity and provider credentials, and enriches each claim with labs and prior encounters. The aim is to fix bad claims before submission, not just reject them.

Layer four is AI-driven adjudication: approve, deny or flag, with reinforcement learning from expert feedback. Edge cases the system cannot decide confidently go to human reviewers. Layer five is orchestration, the control plane that ties models, external data and business rules together, compares AI summaries against source documents and keeps the audit trail regulators expect.

## Fraud moves, so the detector has to

The fraud section is the most interesting part. Static rules (flag claims over a dollar amount, duplicates within 30 days) are easy for fraudsters to step around. Umakanth described three evolving scheme types: pattern evolution, including GenAI-forged MRI scans and clinical notes; collusive networks, caught by mapping relationships between providers, patients and clinics, such as shared addresses or circular referrals; and behavioural anomalies, caught by baselining each provider and flagging sudden spikes in high-cost procedures.

She also proposed using generative models to simulate synthetic fraud scenarios, such as claims from fabricated identities, to stress-test the detection pipeline before attackers try them for real.

## The enterprise part is the hard part

Prototypes are quick; production is not. Her list of hurdles is honest: data silos across legacy systems, the need to explain why a claim was denied, and teams that need data and AI literacy to work with the pipeline. Compliance has to be built in: explainable decisions, federated learning across institutions, bias monitoring and alignment with HIPAA and GDPR.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects at payers, providers or insurance tech firms scoping where GenAI fits in a claims workflow. Despite the conference, the talk is light on Kubernetes specifics and heavy on the claims domain and the fraud taxonomy, which is where its value is.

Title: Spanner Graph turns scattered security alerts into one attack story
Description: Pushap Goyal (Google) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on modelling security incidents as a graph in Spanner Graph, with TrueTime keeping the timeline honest.
Body:
A security incident is a graph whether your tooling admits it or not: a user touched a machine, the machine talked to an IP, a process spawned another process. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Pushap Goyal, a software engineer at Google, argued that investigators should store it that way, in Spanner Graph, so the questions responders ask first (how far did this spread, and in what order) become queries rather than an afternoon of dashboard archaeology.

It is a short, architecture-level talk, and Pushap opens with a disclaimer that it reflects his own experience and public information rather than an official Google position. Treat it as a well-organised map of the idea, not a product walkthrough.

## Four ways traditional incident tooling lets you down

Pushap sorts the pain into four buckets. Data is fragmented across systems that were never meant to be joined. Every system stamps events with its own clock, so reconstructing the forensic timeline is guesswork. Relational and log-centric models miss the relationships between entities. And the gap gets filled by people: he describes SRE engineers correlating dashboards by hand, which is slow and leaks detail.

The outcome is the familiar one. Detection takes longer, investigations end incomplete, and the operational bill grows.

## Nodes, edges, properties: the incident as a data model

The graph model is simple to state. Nodes are users, machines, IP addresses and processes. Edges are the relationships between them: accessed, created, communicated with. Properties carry the context, such as timestamps, severity and classification. Put network, application, endpoint, cloud and identity data into one model and you get a single semantic layer you can query across, instead of five consoles you alt-tab between.

From there the investigation patterns fall out naturally. Traverse outward from the breach point and you have the blast radius. Follow edges through systems and you have the lateral movement path. Look for links between events that looked unrelated and you find the connections traditional tools miss.

## Why Spanner specifically: the clock

The interesting part of the pitch is time. Spanner's TrueTime gives globally consistent timestamps with bounded uncertainty, so there is a known maximum skew between events in different regions and their order can be trusted. For incident forensics that is the whole game: an attack timeline where step three appears before step two is worse than no timeline at all.

Pushap also points out that Spanner Graph sits on the same database you might already use for transactional workloads, with Spanner's horizontal scaling and automatic sharding and replication, so the security graph does not have to be a separate island.

The query side covers what responders reach for: path analysis between compromised assets, pattern matching, centrality measures to find critical assets and choke points, and community detection to group related events into one campaign.

## The boring parts that decide whether it works

The implementation slide is the most practical one: collect from every source, normalise, fit the data into the graph model, store it, then investigate. He flags three design challenges up front. Schema design is a trade-off between how many entity and relationship types you model and how fast queries run. Ingestion means choosing real-time or batch and handling out-of-order events. And query performance needs tuning, planning or caching to keep responses inside your threshold. Anyone who has watched a graph query fan out across a supernode will nod at that last one.

## Who should watch

Security engineers and incident responders who spend investigations stitching logs together, and platform teams deciding where security telemetry should live. If you want benchmarks or a live demo, this is not that talk; it is the case for the model and the checklist for building it.

Title: Zero trust for ML pipelines, stage by stage
Description: Sudheer Obbu of JPMorgan Chase at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on applying never-trust-always-verify to data, training, serving and monitoring in MLOps.
Body:
An ML pipeline has more ways in than a web app: the training data, the model artifact, the training infrastructure and the live inference endpoint are all targets. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Sudheer Obbu, Senior Lead Software Engineer at JPMorgan Chase and a DevSecOps and multi-cloud architect with 19 years in the field, argued that traditional DevSecOps misses those threats and showed how to apply zero trust at each of four stages of the ML lifecycle.

The talk is a framework with a practical tool list at the end. The 73% reduction in security incidents he cites is his headline result for organisations adopting the approach; the reusable part is the stage-by-stage control set.

## The threats that DevSecOps doesn't cover

Sudheer singled out three ML-specific threats and ranked them by risk. Data poisoning sits highest: feed a fraud model bad data and it becomes a fraud enabler. Inference attacks come next, manipulating a live model for desired outputs or extracting confidential training data. Model theft goes straight at the proprietary asset. None of these is fixed by scanning your code, which is why the attack surface needs its own strategy.

## Data and training: lineage, sandboxes, signatures

Zero trust here means never trusting by default, even inside your network, and verifying every request to read data or deploy a model. For data ingestion he described a security pyramid: strict identity and access management for data sources at the base, encryption in transit and at rest in the middle, and data lineage with checksums at the top so you can prove nothing was tampered with on the way in. Garbage in, garbage out turns into something nastier when the garbage was planted.

Training jobs run in isolated sandbox containers with locked-down network access and scanned dependencies. Training scripts get least privilege: read access to the data they need, write access to one artifact location. Every trained model is digitally signed, versioned and stored in an audited registry with its own access controls.

## Serving and monitoring: hardened endpoints, assumed breach

At serving time, models run on hardened minimal container images behind network policies, every inference request is authenticated and authorised, and rate limiting and input validation are standard. Secrets go into a dedicated manager such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager, never into code. Monitoring then assumes breach: log every request, response and access event, watch for anomalies such as performance drift and data skew that may signal a subtle attack, and trigger automated responses like revoking access and alerting the security team.

His two case studies make it concrete. A fintech that enforced strict IAM and signed all model artifacts cleared its major audit findings on data access and spent 40% less time on manual compliance reporting. A healthcare platform used isolated model environments with token-based API authentication to reach HIPAA compliance on diagnostic models.

## The pitfalls are mostly human

The closing advice is sharp. Too much friction and data scientists will build insecure shadow IT, so automate security into CI/CD and ship secure-by-default project templates. Zero trust is continuous: review logs, rotate credentials, run security drills. And treat models differently from code: a signed container doesn't stop a model being stolen or poisoned, so sign the artifact itself and monitor for drift.

The toolbox he listed: Okta, Azure Active Directory and cloud secret managers for identity; Snyk, Trivy and Dependabot for code and containers; Istio or Linkerd for service-mesh encryption and policy, with Falco for runtime threats; and DVC, MLflow or ClearML for data lineage and model registries. The four-step start: map your pipeline and its access controls, give every user and service a unique identity with MFA, enforce least privilege with just-in-time access, and monitor continuously.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers responsible for ML infrastructure in regulated industries, and MLOps teams whose security review consists of a container scan. If you already run a service mesh and signed artifacts, the threat model section is the new part.

Title: Splitting a monolithic segmentation pipeline into Kubernetes services
Description: Ujjwala Modepalli (Wells Fargo) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on rebuilding segmentation ML as microservices with Helm, drift-triggered retraining and a feature store.
Body:
A monolithic analytics pipeline scales the way a single-lane bridge does: everything waits for the slowest truck. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Ujjwala Modepalli, Senior Credit Risk Specialist at Wells Fargo with around 14 years in analytics and predictive modelling, described how her team re-engineered a predictive customer segmentation system into a set of Kubernetes services, and why the biggest win was being able to scale each stage on its own.

The problem she started from is familiar to anyone who has run batch scoring in a bank. As data volumes grew, processing times stretched, insights arrived late, and adding servers did not help because the pipeline was one rigid unit. Data scientists, ML engineers and DevOps worked in separate silos on top of it.

## Four layers, each with its own scaling knob

The architecture splits into data ingestion, feature engineering, model training and inference. Ingestion services pull from CRM, digital interactions and transactions using event-driven ingestion. Feature engineering services clean and validate raw data into standard features. Training runs distributed across the cluster for gradient boosting, neural networks and clustering. Inference serves real-time segment predictions with Redis caching in front.

Her point is that the split matters more than any individual component. If training spikes, you scale training. If inference needs compute, you add inference pods. Different teams can ship changes to their stage without breaking the whole pipeline, which is the real productivity gain.

## Helm for consistency, CRDs for the ML-shaped parts

With dozens of services, every deploy needs to look the same. The team versions deployments as Helm charts with environment-specific overrides, so one chart goes to dev, staging and production and rolls back cleanly. For needs that plain Kubernetes does not model well, such as scheduling training jobs, managing GPU resources and automating retraining lifecycles, they extended the cluster with custom resource definitions.

## Let drift trigger the retrain

Customer behaviour shifts with promotions, seasons and product launches. Instead of retraining on a calendar, monitoring watches for data drift, and when behaviour no longer matches the model, Kubernetes kicks off a retraining pipeline. The new model is validated and deployed without manual steps or downtime.

A container-based feature store backs this up. Training and inference read the same versioned features, with Redis for fast retrieval, so A/B tests on new features and rollbacks to old ones stay traceable. Anyone who has debugged a training-serving skew will appreciate that line item.

## Sidecars, init containers and the GPU budget

She also walked through the Kubernetes patterns they leaned on: init containers that check data integrity and dependencies before the main container starts, sidecars that collect latency and drift metrics for Prometheus and Grafana, and multi-container pods for tightly coupled steps like preprocessing plus serving. GPU scheduling policies give deep learning jobs priority access, and tuned memory allocation stops large clustering jobs from crashing out of memory.

The reported outcomes: 85% GPU utilisation, roughly three times better memory efficiency, a 60% cost reduction, 99.9% uptime and 40% faster processing. The rollout ran in four phases (containerise, orchestrate, optimise, production), each iterated before going enterprise-wide.

## Who should watch

Data science and ML platform teams at enterprises still running segmentation or scoring as one large batch job. It is a case-study talk at the architecture level, with no code on screen, so it works best as a map of which pieces to break out first.

- [AI-Powered Customer Insights for Financial Services](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Neha_Thakur_insights_financial_customer) by Neha Thakur (AWS) focuses on what the segments are used for.

Title: Kafka on Kubernetes lives or dies on storage and consumer lag
Description: Shalini Katyayani Koney (Walmart) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on Kafka on Kubernetes at 100,000+ msg/s with StatefulSets, fast disks and lag-based scaling.
Body:
Running Kafka on Kubernetes is easy to start and easy to get wrong, and the place it usually goes wrong is the disk. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Shalini Katyayani Koney, Senior Engineering Manager at Walmart, laid out the patterns behind a Kafka platform that sustains over a hundred thousand messages per second in production, and argued that storage, resource sizing and lag-aware scaling matter more than any single clever trick.

The framing is practical. Kubernetes gives you self-healing, scheduling and autoscaling for free, but Kafka brokers are stateful, and every one of those conveniences has to be bent around that fact.

## Brokers are pets, so give them StatefulSets

The foundation is three pieces. Brokers run as StatefulSets, which gives ordered rollout, stable network identities and a persistent volume that follows each broker. Volumes come from SSD-backed storage classes with high IOPS, because Kafka's log segments want fast sequential writes. And a service mesh handles encrypted pod-to-pod traffic and metrics without touching application code.

On sizing she gave concrete starting points: two to four CPU cores per broker, and 8 to 16 GB of heap, tuned to partition count and retention. Critical Kafka pods run in the Guaranteed QoS class so the scheduler does not evict them when the cluster gets crowded. In a shared cluster, a noisy neighbour is a polite name for an outage.

## Storage is where most deployments fail

This was the most opinionated part of the talk. Size persistent volume claims from your retention policy and replication factor, not from a guess, because undersized volumes lead to disk pressure and unstable brokers. Then tune the file system: Koney reported that XFS with the right mount options can improve write performance by 30 to 40% over default configurations.

Networking gets the same treatment. Isolated network policies for the Kafka namespace, load balancing with session affinity (clients like sticky connections to the brokers that lead their partitions), and TCP buffer tuning or even dedicated interfaces when throughput demands it.

## Scale on lag, and respect partition leadership

CPU and memory do not tell you when Kafka needs help. Her horizontal pod autoscaling keys off Kafka-specific signals such as consumer lag and partition throughput. The catch is that you cannot just kill a broker on scale-down: leadership has to move and replicas have to be reassigned first, and partitions must stay balanced or hotspots eat the capacity you just added.

For multiple clusters she uses Helm charts for consistent installs across regions, MirrorMaker for cross-region replication, and a GitOps workflow where every cluster config lives in Git with automated rollbacks when a change destabilises a cluster.

## Measure lag before your users notice it

The monitoring stack is Prometheus scraping JMX metrics, Grafana dashboards for throughput and latency, and alerts on consumer lag spikes, under-replicated partitions and disk thresholds. Disaster recovery uses Kubernetes operators for backup and failover, cross-region copies of topic configs, consumer offsets and ACLs, and chaos experiments that break components on purpose to prove recovery works.

The headline production numbers she shared: a sustained hundred thousand messages per second, 99.9% availability with zero-downtime rolling upgrades, and P99 latency under five milliseconds even under heavy load. Note that the abstract talks about million+ msg/sec, while the talk itself sticks to the hundred-thousand figure.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who have been asked to move Kafka off VMs and onto a shared cluster, and SREs who inherited a Strimzi or Helm-based setup that pages on disk pressure. It is an architecture talk with no live demo, so treat it as a checklist to compare against your own cluster rather than a tutorial.

Title: ML threat detection and crypto agility for the post-quantum era
Description: Arfi Siddik Mollashaik of Securiti at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on multimodal ML threat detection, privacy-preserving training and post-quantum readiness.
Body:
Signature-based security tools struggle against zero-days, polymorphic and fileless malware and supply chain attacks, because there is no signature yet. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Arfi Siddik Mollashaik, a solution architect in professional services at Securiti (securiti.ai) with 18-plus years in data security and privacy, made the case for layered ML threat detection, privacy-preserving training, and building crypto agility into ML pipelines before quantum computers force the issue.

It is a broad survey that covers a lot of ground quickly: detection architecture, feature engineering, privacy techniques, a rollout plan and a post-quantum outlook. Good as a map of the problem space; thin on implementation detail.

## No single model catches everything

Arfi's detection architecture combines three families. Supervised learning (random forests, gradient boosting, support vector machines) classifies known threats from labelled data. Unsupervised learning (isolation forests, one-class SVMs, DBSCAN clustering) flags deviations from normal behaviour, the route to catching what nobody has labelled yet. Deep learning (LSTMs, transformers, convolutional networks) handles complex patterns. Combining them, he argued, gives higher accuracy and fewer false positives than any one alone, and he cited a 93% detection rate for the combined approach.

The ML layer does four jobs: behavioural detection of anomalous users and systems, prediction of emerging threats from threat intelligence, adaptive response as the models learn from new data, and resource optimisation by prioritising alerts on risk and context.

## Features come from three places

Network traffic features cover protocol anomalies, flow metadata and volumes, temporal bursts and new destinations. User behaviour features look at authentication patterns, when people access what, data movement and command frequency. Host features watch process execution chains, system call sequences, resource usage, and registry and file system changes. Good feature selection, by his figure, raises model performance by 40% while cutting compute overhead. The real-time pipeline then runs ingestion from sensors, logs and network taps, streaming feature extraction, ensemble scoring into risk scores, and automated responses.

## Train on sensitive data without moving it

Security telemetry is full of sensitive data under GDPR, HIPAA, PCI and CCPA, so Arfi covered three privacy-preserving techniques. Federated learning trains on local data and exchanges no raw records. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise so outputs carry mathematical privacy guarantees while remaining useful. Homomorphic encryption allows computation on encrypted data without decrypting it.

## Shadow mode first, then post-quantum planning

His rollout is three phases: build data collection, labelling and feature engineering and integrate with existing SOC tools; deploy models in shadow mode next to current systems, tune thresholds against baselines and train the security team; then retire legacy detection gradually with CI/CD-driven model updates and automated retraining. The KPIs he tracks: classification latency, false positive rate, coverage of known attack vectors and zero-day detection success.

The post-quantum section looks further ahead. Shor's algorithm threatens RSA, ECC and Diffie-Hellman, NIST has standardised post-quantum algorithms (he named the CRYSTALS key encapsulation and Dilithium signature schemes), and he expects the transition over the next five to six years. His advice is crypto agility and hybrid classical plus post-quantum approaches, wired into ML pipelines now.

## Who should watch

Security engineers evaluating ML-based detection, and ML teams asked to work with security telemetry under privacy rules. If you need a deep treatment of any one area, use this as the index and follow up elsewhere.

Title: The LLM era needs more MLOps, not less
Description: Naveen Edapurath Vijayan of AWS at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on automation, CI/CD, governance and monitoring for classic models and LLMs alike.
Body:
A model in a Jupyter notebook is an experiment; a model in production, monitored and governed at scale, is a business solution. That was the starting line for Naveen Edapurath Vijayan, Head of Engineering for AWS Central Economics, at Conf42 MLOps 2025, and his answer to whether large language models make MLOps obsolete was an emphatic no: they make it more necessary.

Naveen has 15-plus years in data analytics and ML, building petabyte-scale warehouses and models for finance and HR, and more recently agentic AI. He opened with a disclaimer that the views were his own, not Amazon's or AWS's. The talk is a crisp conceptual overview that maps each MLOps pillar onto its LLM equivalent, which is its most useful feature.

## Models fail silently when nobody watches

His cautionary tale was a credit risk model trained on pre-2020 data. When COVID changed consumer behaviour overnight (job losses, defaults, relief cheques), the model kept running unmonitored and misclassified risk for months, with heavy financial losses. Add the other usual suspects: brittle pipelines where a renamed column breaks the feature store, manual deployments where someone copies a model file and hopes, and models in production that haven't been retrained in months or years. LLMs then add cost explosions, hallucinations and compliance gaps on top.

## MLOps is DevOps plus data and models

Naveen's definition is tidy: MLOps applies continuous integration, delivery and infrastructure automation to machine learning, but where DevOps deals with code, MLOps deals with code, data and models. The lifecycle is a loop: ingest and validate data, train and fine-tune (tracked in MLflow or SageMaker), validate for accuracy, fairness, robustness and interpretability, deploy, then monitor and retrain automatically when metrics drift out of bounds. His retail example retrains recommendation models daily, validates them on test sets and rolls them out through shadow deployments.

## Every pillar has an LLM twin

This is the part worth bookmarking. Feature pipelines become prompt pipelines, with prompts and prompt chains version-controlled and tested. Automation that reruns preprocessing with Airflow or Kubeflow also refreshes a retrieval index when new documents are published and triggers evaluations, with nobody intervening by hand. CI/CD tools like DVC and MLflow run regression, bias and feature unit tests; for LLMs, each new prompt template is tested against historical customer interactions and shadow-deployed beside the old one. Fine-tuning is expensive, so automated evaluation pipelines keep you from retraining when you don't need to.

Monitoring widens from accuracy, latency, drift and infrastructure cost to hallucination rate, toxicity, bias and grounding, meaning whether answers tie back to real sources. He described enterprises running red teaming in production and flagging unsafe outputs for human review, and gave the example of a healthcare chatbot drifting into advice not grounded in medical sources, which guardrails need to catch instantly.

## Governance is the price of doing business

Enterprises need to answer which model made a decision, what data trained it and whether it was biased; a financial regulator may ask why a loan was denied. MLOps governance lets you produce the data set, the model version and the code. For LLMs, add provenance for fine-tuning data, red-teaming results, and the transparency obligations of GDPR and the EU AI Act. His best practices: infrastructure as code, feature stores and the emerging prompt stores, bias and safety evaluation inside CI/CD, and cross-functional teams that include compliance and business owners.

## Who should watch

Teams adding LLM features on top of an existing ML platform, and leaders deciding whether "LLMOps" needs a separate org chart. Practitioners after tooling depth will find a framework here, not a tutorial.

Title: When a hurricane hits, the claims portal is the incident
Description: Chandra Prakash Kathroju (Citizens Property Insurance) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on AI, edge computing and serverless for insurance incident response.
Body:
For an insurer, the worst day for the systems is the worst day for the customers: a hurricane makes landfall, thousands of policyholders file claims at once, and the portal falls over. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Chandra Prakash Kathroju, Software Engineer at Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, gave a short overview of how AI, edge computing and serverless architecture change incident response in insurance, where the incident is often a physical event and the system's job is to keep up with it.

It is a compact, high-level talk that maps technologies onto insurance problems rather than walking through one implementation.

## Four ways insurers fall behind

Kathroju starts with the pain points. Incidents can go unnoticed for hours or days, delaying recovery and adding cost. Claims processing is manual, so adjusters are overloaded and policyholders wait in backlogs. Without real-time data, insurers react to losses instead of preventing them. And during disasters, systems built for normal demand collapse under the surge. All four hit customer trust and operating cost directly.

## Process at the source, scale in the cloud

The three technologies each cover a different gap.

**AI** is already in underwriting (IoT sensor data, driving behaviour and property data for risk assessment), claims (chatbots gather information, models triage severity, human adjusters handle exceptions) and fraud detection, catching patterns before payout. For incidents it adds real-time monitoring of underwriting and claims data, early detection of unusual patterns and alerts routed to the right team with a severity level and suggested action. It also supports root cause analysis, pulling data from several systems to tell weather damage from equipment failure from human error.

**Edge computing** processes data where it is created. A flood sensor in a home can raise an alert immediately even if the connection to the cloud is slow; accident data from a car's telematics can be analysed locally so the insurer can act right away. Less latency, less bandwidth, faster response.

**Serverless** he compares to electricity: you use what you need and don't worry about the power plant. For insurers that means claim portals that scale with a disaster surge instead of crashing, and new tools like claim apps shipped in days.

The layered model joins them: sensors capture data, edge processing gives instant local insight, cloud analytics finds patterns across sources, and the result feeds decisions from claim approvals to fraud prevention.

## Disaster mode and the compliance line

For large disruptions he lists the standard toolkit: autoscaling, dynamic allocation that moves workloads across regions, failover with backups, and load balancing to smooth spikes. Two insurance-specific points follow. Blockchain fits reinsurance, where smart contracts can automate settlements and an immutable trail builds trust between insurers and reinsurers. And hybrid cloud is how insurers square scale with regulation: sensitive regulated data stays in private or on-premises systems, while analytics and other elastic workloads run in public cloud, with logging, monitoring and automated governance keeping GDPR and HIPAA obligations covered.

The roadmap is assess, design, pilot in a small controlled environment, then scale and optimise.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects at insurers, or anyone building systems whose load follows the weather. It is an overview, not a deep technical session, so treat it as a map of where each technology fits in an insurance incident.

Title: How Elementor's GenAI stack shrugged off an OpenAI account lockout
Description: Dennis Nerush of Elementor at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on multi-org rate limits, circuit breakers, a one-switch Claude fallback and the insert-rate metric.
Body:
Two days before Elementor launched its AI Site Planner, OpenAI locked the company's account and every call stopped. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Dennis Nerush, Director of AI Engineering at Elementor, explained why that turned out to be a minor event instead of a war room: a GenAI infrastructure built for rate limits, sick vendors and switching providers with a single key.

Elementor powers more than 19 million websites, and Dennis put its AI footprint at over 2 million users, more than 40 AI features, around 10 billion tokens a month and about a million AI requests a day. This is one of the most practical talks of the event: real incidents, real design decisions, and an honest list of what still hurts.

## Rate limits shape the architecture first

Elementor shipped its first AI features roughly four months after ChatGPT launched, when GPT-3.5 Turbo allowed 60 requests per minute. That pushed them to Microsoft Azure for higher limits and better support, which worked for about a year until the Elementor Copilot arrived. Like GitHub Copilot for layouts, it predicts the next section of a page and fires events on almost every user interaction.

Azure's limits weren't enough, and its developer experience got heavy: models available only in some regions, a dedicated resource and deployment per region, quotas shared across deployments, and a portal form to request more. So they moved back to OpenAI, where switching models is a line of code. To go beyond one organisation's limits without committing to an enterprise tier, they created several OpenAI organisations and extended the SDK so a call first fetches the next organisation from a round-robin pool. Developers don't know or care which org serves them.

## Sick organisations get benched automatically

Identical organisations do not behave identically. Dennis showed that latency and error rates mostly track each other and then diverge, with one org slowing or failing while others are fine, and provider status pages are rarely as green as you'd hope. Users don't care; they expect the product to work.

The fix is a circuit breaker on top of the pool. If an organisation crosses a threshold, such as hitting its rate limit or returning errors three times within a window, it is marked unhealthy and removed; after a while the system tries it again and restores it if it behaves. State lives in Redis so every Kubernetes pod sees the same pool rather than each pod rediscovering the failure, and every open and close posts to Slack. Nobody deploys a hotfix to remove a resource and sets a reminder to add it back the next morning.

## The fallback vendor needs its own prompts, and drills

The lockout is where the second vendor paid off. From day one Elementor also built on Anthropic's Claude, and Dennis was frank that migrating is harder than it sounds: structured output and validation features differ, and the same system prompt gives different results on different models. They keep provider-specific prompts and instructions so a single configuration key moves the whole system to Claude and back. It is deliberately manual, since the scenario is rare. His extra tip: practise the switch regularly, because fallbacks quietly rot while the main path keeps improving. He also mentioned the team was working on open-sourcing the framework.

## Insert rate beats vibes for evaluating images and layouts

Text evals are fairly direct; Dennis's example was the AI writing a whole paragraph for a button, fixed by evals on length per widget type. Images and full page structures need taste, so Elementor defined a success metric it calls insert rate: did the user actually insert the result, or regenerate or close the page? Every interaction is stored with the raw input, the enhanced prompt, the full prompt, the output and the inserted flag.

They started by reading failures manually, then built AI-powered offline clustering jobs that post weekly findings to Slack. One cluster found that requests mentioning transparent backgrounds were almost always rejected because the image model couldn't produce them; the fix was a hint telling users so. Others surfaced the long button text and weaker Japanese understanding than they had assumed.

## Who should watch

Anyone shipping LLM features to real users at volume, especially if your whole product sits on a single provider key. Platform engineers will want the circuit-breaker section; product teams, the insert-rate one. Smaller products can skip the multi-org gymnastics, and Dennis said as much: size the resilience to the need.

Title: An immutable ledger for payment incidents, from Visa's SRE side
Description: Sai Krishna Gurram (Visa) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on recording incident events to a blockchain ledger and encoding playbooks as smart contracts.
Body:
Payment networks get audited, and the incident timeline is usually the weakest piece of evidence in the room: a ticket, a spreadsheet and a Slack thread somebody edited later. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Sai Krishna Gurram, a senior Site Reliability Engineer consultant at Visa, proposed pairing a blockchain ledger with cloud-native infrastructure and AI so that every detection, escalation and recovery step lands in a tamper-evident record, and the common responses run as smart contracts.

It is a concept-and-rollout talk. Gurram describes the architecture, the automation patterns and a phased plan; he doesn't walk through a production system or its internals.

## The pain is blind spots, slow hand-offs and audits

He groups the problems of high-volume payment operations into three. Manual ticketing and spreadsheet tracking leave gaps where emerging failures hide until late. Reactive response adds delay at every hand-off, and missed alerts turn into customer impact. Manual, fragmented reporting makes audits slower and the evidence weaker, which raises regulatory exposure. With outages costing serious money per hour through lost interchange, chargebacks and reputation, preventing incidents and recovering faster is a business requirement.

## Ledger for the record, cloud for the muscle

The thesis has three parts:

- **Immutable audit trails.** Every notable event in an incident is timestamped and written to the ledger with cryptographic verification, giving a tamper-proof history for postmortems and regulators that survives tool changes and later edits.
- **Elastic response.** Cloud resources expand and contract with incident severity, keeping performance stable under load without paying for peak all year.
- **Smart contracts as playbooks.** Predefined rules that page the right people, flip flags, shift traffic or roll back, reducing human error and time to restore.

On top sits AI anomaly detection across traffic, latency, error rates, dependencies and security events. One detail stands out as useful whether or not you ever touch a blockchain: watch for drift in p50 latency, which can precede p99 spikes, and correlate it with deploys, feature flags and infrastructure changes.

## Zero-touch, with guardrails

The automation he describes is severity-aware routing to on-call, leadership and partner teams with deduplication to avoid alert floods; scaling replicas, warming caches or moving workloads to healthier zones when degradation appears; and restoring the last known good state when rollback or failover criteria are met, including config versions, traffic shifting and dependency gating. Predictive work rounds it out: forecasting saturation during weekend peaks and scheduling preventive maintenance like node replacement or canary restarts before a minor issue becomes an incident.

## Pilot it on something boring first

The rollout plan is the part to keep. Map your services and integration points, then pick a non-critical but representative service and start by recording detection and response events to the ledger. Measure the latency and storage overhead before going further. Next, encode common playbooks (degraded latency rollback, circuit breaking on dependency saturation, surge scaling) as contracts with clear guardrails and approvals. Only then expand to mission-critical services and cross-team dashboards.

That order matters because the hard question with this design is cost: what writing every incident event to a ledger adds in latency and complexity compared with an append-only log you already trust. The pilot is where you find out.

Further out he mentions quantum-resistant encryption and decentralised validation of threat indicators, which shift the talk toward security operations.

## Who should watch

SREs and compliance-minded engineers in payments and other regulated industries, especially if audit evidence is a recurring pain. Go in expecting an architectural proposal rather than a case study with numbers; the pilot plan and the p50-before-p99 heuristic are the practical takeaways.

Title: An MLOps maturity model from ad hoc notebooks to full automation
Description: Srikanth Vissarapu of Meta at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on maturity levels, validation layers, canary and A/B rollouts, and cost levers for ML pipelines.
Body:
Most ML projects never reach production, and many that do fail to deliver. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Srikanth Vissarapu, a software engineer at Meta, laid out a maturity model for ML pipelines and the architecture patterns that move a team from ad hoc experiments to end-to-end automation. His argument: data quality and collaboration sink more ML initiatives than models do.

The talk is a broad blueprint rather than a Meta case study. Srikanth described several of his failure statistics as ballpark figures, which is a fair way to read them: directional evidence that most production ML trouble starts upstream of the model.

## Four levels of maturity

Level zero is ad hoc experimentation: manual work, no standard workflow, fragmented collaboration, no success metrics. Level one adds basic pipeline automation, maybe a few scheduled jobs, but governance is thin, teams are siloed and monitoring can't spot drift. Level two brings continuous integration with repeatable pipelines, version control for every model, automated testing and proactive monitoring. Level three is end-to-end automation with centralised pipelines, governance and compliance baked in, and metrics captured at every stage.

His reading of the obstacles puts data quality on top, which he linked to more than half of production ML failures, followed by lack of standardisation, insufficient monitoring and governance gaps. Garbage in, garbage out never retires.

## Four validation layers before a model ships

The validation framework is the most practical section. Data validation comes first: schema enforcement, distribution checks and drift detection on the data set. Then model accuracy measured against real production data and business KPIs, not just the training split. Then operational checks: a model that is accurate but slow still disappoints users, so latency, throughput and resource use get validated too. Last, ethical validation for bias and consistency.

His best practices: write clear pass/fail thresholds for each step, enforce them inside the CI/CD pipeline rather than by hand, and keep a history of validation results as a measure of how your MLOps practice is maturing.

## Canary, blue-green and A/B are different questions

On delivery, Srikanth separated the strategies cleanly. A canary exposes a small slice of traffic to the new model and promotes it as metrics hold up. Blue-green runs a parallel environment and switches over when it looks good. A/B testing exposes users to two versions and lets business and technical metrics decide. Around them sit model artifact versioning, dependency management, containerised model serving in Docker, and infrastructure as code.

## Cost is part of the architecture

The cost section is a welcome inclusion. Compute (GPUs above all), data storage and processing for pipelines and feature stores, tooling, and operational overhead are the main drivers. The levers he listed: autoscaling to match workload, model pruning, quantisation and distillation to shrink models with similar performance, end-to-end automation, and visibility into where the money goes. He finished with organisational advice: cross-functional MLOps teams, joint ownership of model performance and business outcomes, and a centre of excellence that offers self-service tooling.

## Who should watch

Teams trying to place themselves on a maturity curve, and leads writing an MLOps strategy document. The talk is long and general; engineers after a specific stack should treat it as a checklist to compare against.

Title: SiriusXM cut model deployments from 45 days to four hours
Description: Jimmy Katiyar of SiriusXM at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on validation gates, CI/CD, monitoring and Kubernetes behind a jump from MLOps level one to three.
Body:
Machine learning projects rarely fail because the model is bad; they fail when someone tries to run it in production at scale. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Jimmy Katiyar, Senior Product Manager at SiriusXM, showed how his organisation went from MLOps maturity level one to level three in 18 months, bringing model deployments down from 45 days to four hours while serving millions of daily transactions.

It is a product manager's view of an ML platform, which is a feature: the talk spends as much time on shared KPIs and team habits as on pipelines, and the numbers come with the organisational changes that produced them.

## Months to production is a business problem

Jimmy started with the familiar enterprise picture: deployments done by hand, environments that don't match between development and production, teams in silos, frequent incidents and painful compliance. When a model takes 60 to 90 days to reach production, competitors who iterate faster win. He framed maturity in four levels, from fully manual and ad hoc (level zero) through partial automation and continuous delivery to level three, where everything is automated and systems heal themselves.

## Four pillars, and the gate that mattered most

SiriusXM's architecture rests on four pillars: automated model validation, CI/CD pipelines, monitoring, and scalable infrastructure. The validation framework is the part worth copying. Every model passes three gates before going live: statistical performance (accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and business KPIs), operational readiness (latency, scalability, throughput) and compliance (explainability, bias detection, regulatory alignment). Jimmy credited those gates with a 94% reduction in production issues.

The CI/CD pipeline versions data sets, configurations and artifacts alongside code. Build and test covers containerisation, performance benchmarks and security scanning. Staging runs shadow deployments and A/B tests under load, and production relies on canary releases, automated rollbacks and audit logs. That pipeline is where 45 days became four hours.

## Monitoring that pays for itself early

Monitoring spans four dimensions: model performance, data quality, system operations and business impact, the last measured in revenue or conversion. In its first year the system caught 28 critical drift incidents before customers felt them. On the infrastructure side, Kubernetes handles orchestration and autoscaling, Apache Spark does distributed data processing, and load-balanced inference services sit behind strict access controls, encryption and audit logging. He reported 3.5 million inference requests a day at 99.99% uptime and under 50 ms latency.

## The hardest pillar is the one without a diagram

Jimmy was candid that technology doesn't solve mismatched skills, fragmented tools and inconsistent success metrics. Data scientists and engineers often don't speak the same language. SiriusXM unified development environments, standardised workflows and created shared KPIs, and he relayed that their VP of AI engineering considered getting both sides speaking one language the biggest win.

His roadmap has four phases: foundation (standard environments, version control, basic pipelines), automation (CI/CD, validation dashboards, model registry, metadata tracking), scale (Kubernetes orchestration, drift detection, automated rollback), and optimisation (feature stores, self-healing infrastructure, governance). The pitfalls are the ones every platform team has hit at least once: tool obsession, underestimating culture change, and over-complicating the first step. Start with one high-value use case.

## Who should watch

Product and engineering managers building an internal ML platform, and teams stuck at level one wondering what level three looks like in practice. Engineers wanting pipeline code will find the outline here and the details elsewhere.
