Title: When developer experience becomes an engineering problem
Description: Platforms evolve
Body:
# Platforms: because glue code became a career

Platform engineering usually starts with good intentions.

“We’ll make this easier for teams.”  
“We’ll standardize things.”  
“We’ll reduce cognitive load.”

Next thing you know, you’re running dozens of services, managing policies across clouds, supporting AI workloads, and explaining to developers why the platform exists in the first place.

Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 is all about that reality.

This is a big conference. Seventy plus talks across architecture, APIs, automation, developer experience, security, reliability, AI, compliance, and transformation. If your job involves building internal platforms that other teams depend on, this one speaks directly to you.

AI is deeply woven into the program. Agentic platforms, self-healing infrastructure, anomaly detection, AI-driven CI/CD, and ML platforms at scale all show up. There are sessions on building AI platforms that actually deliver value, and others on keeping them reliable, observable, and secure once they hit production.

The use cases are very real. Financial systems processing massive volumes with low latency. Healthcare platforms operating under strict regulation. Smart cities, subscription payments, fraud detection, industrial IoT, and enterprise data platforms that move hundreds of terabytes a month. These are not toy examples.

Developer experience gets serious attention too. Talks cover internal developer platforms, cloud IDEs, unified Git policies, design systems as platform infrastructure, and using automation to reduce friction instead of adding more dashboards.

Security, compliance, and resilience are baked throughout. Zero trust, identity governance, multi-tenant platforms, regulated environments, and building systems that stay upright even as usage and complexity grow. Because platforms are only useful if people trust them.

If you’re building the foundations that everyone else stands on, this one’s for you. Platform engineering is hard, invisible work. At least here, you’ll be among people who get it.

Title: Generative AI turns bank transactions into stories customers read
Description: Pushpalika Chatterjee (Huntington National Bank) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on generative AI for financial narratives, personalisation and synthetic fraud data.
Body:
Nobody reads their bank statement, but plenty of people would read one sentence telling them their coffee habit just ate into this month's savings. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Pushpalika Chatterjee, Senior Software Engineering Manager for Enterprise Payments at The Huntington National Bank, argued that generative AI moves banking from recording transactions to telling customers what they mean, and she showed where that helps personalisation, fraud defence and stress testing.

## From ledger rows to narratives

For decades, banks treated each transaction as an isolated event in a structured ledger. Pushpalika's point is that generative AI can combine structured data (spending history) with unstructured data (even voice) into contextual insight. Her running example: instead of just recording a $50 spend at Starbucks, the system can explain how that spend raised this month's expenditure and dented savings. She calls the shift financial storytelling.

She is candid about the audience for this: younger customers who never open a statement, and people outside finance for whom 30 days of transactions are "just random numbers." A plain-language explanation reaches them where a dashboard does not.

## A short history of AI in banking

The talk traces the arc quickly. Rule-based fraud alerts and credit scoring in the 1990s and 2000s, rigid and full of false positives. Machine learning for personalisation and risk scoring in the 2010s. Deep learning for real-time fraud detection and NLP chatbots later that decade. Then generative AI, which does not only predict a problem but proposes what to do next: what-if simulations, tailored loan and investment offers, personalised reports.

The mortgage example lands well. If you pay a thousand dollars more each month, or a hundred thousand up front, how much shorter is the loan and what happens to the payment? That kind of tailored answer is what she means by personalisation, as opposed to picking from five predefined products.

## Synthetic fraud as a vaccine

The most engineering-relevant idea is defensive. Attackers already use AI, so Pushpalika proposes using generative models to create synthetic fraud patterns and adversarial transactions to train more robust detectors, and to stress-test liquidity and credit crises before they happen. Her metaphor is a digital vaccine: expose the system to the one-in-a-million edge cases deliberately, rather than learning about them in production.

## The bill comes due: bias, privacy, explainability, security

She does not skip the hard part. Bias, so that better protection does not flow only to the financially privileged. Privacy under laws like GDPR and CCPA, where banking data is among the most sensitive there is. Explainability, because regulators will not accept black-box answers. Security, where prompt injection is the new SQL injection.

Her mitigations: federated learning so banks can collaborate without sharing raw data, differential privacy so outputs cannot expose individuals, and explainable AI so regulators and customers can see why a decision was made.

## A pilot and a look ahead

The case study is a personalised wealth management assistant her team piloted. It ingested spending, saving and investment data, generated what-if projections and tax-optimisation suggestions in plain language. She reports customer engagement up 40% and noticeably better financial literacy scores.

Looking forward, she sketches multi-agent systems (separate agents for risk, liquidity and compliance that negotiate trade-offs), a personal finance copilot that schedules payments and moves funds the way GPS handles navigation, and large-scale simulations that let regulators stress-test something like a digital currency before launch.

## Who should watch

Product engineers and ML teams in banking thinking about customer-facing generative AI, and anyone building fraud models who wants an argument for synthetic adversarial data. It is a broad, strategy-level talk with one pilot, not an implementation walkthrough.

Title: Running a 10TB-a-day Databricks pipeline like an SRE service
Description: Sruthi Erra Hareram at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on freshness SLIs, circuit breakers and Z-ordering for a cross-cloud Azure Databricks pipeline.
Body:
Data pipelines rarely get the SRE treatment that APIs do, which is odd, because a stale dashboard is an outage to the people staring at it. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, data engineer Sruthi Erra Hareram walked through a case study of an analytics pipeline on Azure Databricks and Amazon S3 handling more than 10 TB a day, and the single idea that held it together: treat freshness as an SLI with an error budget, and let that budget decide what gets paused.

The workload was ad campaign telemetry, billions of events a day across regions, feeding user-facing dashboards that had to stay fresh within minutes. With many interdependent ETL jobs, one upstream blip could cascade through the lot.

## Freshness is the SLI that matters

The team's working targets were p95 freshness under 15 minutes and p99 under 30, with back-pressure rules when those drift. They tracked three SLIs: freshness from ingest to the gold layer, p95 query latency on key workloads, and end-to-end success rate. Error budgets triggered graceful degradation. If seven-day rolling freshness blew its budget, non-critical enrichments were paused so the core tables kept up.

Toil came first in the backlog. They automated the most common failure classes, aiming to keep auto-resolution above 70%, on the reasoning that humans should not be babysitting pipelines.

## Retries only work when writes are idempotent

The stack is Azure Databricks with Delta Lake for ACID semantics, schema evolution and time travel, Azure Data Factory for orchestration, and S3 for durable versioned storage where it was needed. On top of that she describes four standard patterns:

- **Checkpointing.** Every stage can resume from known offsets, and offsets are committed only after idempotent writes succeed.
- **Circuit breakers at integration points.** One example threshold: trip if the error rate stays above 10% for five minutes, or freshness breaches for three consecutive checks.
- **Exponential backoff with jitter.** Random jitter of up to three seconds, so retries don't stampede.
- **Idempotent writes.** All merges are keyed and retries have no side effects.

Her one-line summary of the section is the bit to pin above your desk: retries only work when your operations are idempotent.

## Z-order from query logs, not intuition

Before tuning, the pipeline did full scans, big shuffles and spiky latencies. The fix was aligning storage to real access patterns: partitioning that prunes (by event date, for instance), Z-ordering on high-selectivity keys queried together (campaign ID, region, device), and regular OPTIMIZE plus small-file compaction so Spark isn't drowning in tiny files.

How they chose Z-order keys is the most transferable detail. They mined query logs for the most frequent multi-column filters with high cardinality, validated with A/B runs on representative workloads, and revisited the keys quarterly because dashboards change what people query. Z-ordering itself ran weekly on hot tables and monthly on warm ones, and compaction kicked in when average file size dropped below 128 MB. Fixed clusters gave way to workload-aware autoscaling with hard cost guards per priority tier.

## An incident, step by step

The playbook runs detection (SLI-driven, freshness and success rate, not just CPU), classification, containment, remediation and recovery. Her example is S3 cross-region replication lag. Freshness monitors flagged the drift, downstream joins paused, users were served the last consistent slice with a clear stale-data banner, and non-critical work was diverted. Once replication recovered, the team validated consistency on boundary tables, burst-scaled to clear the backlog and returned to steady state. On-call only approved predefined steps; everything else was automated.

She also shows how to read metrics together: a rising data-quality error rate with flat compute points at schema drift, not capacity, while a widening p95 at flat volume points at partition skew or small-file bloat.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers who get paged for late tables, and SREs who inherit a lakehouse and want a vocabulary for it. It is a compact case study, dense with thresholds you can argue about, and light on slides of architecture boxes. The closing blueprint (SLIs and budgets, breakers at every seam, checkpoints at every hand-off, two failure-mode drills per quarter) is a solid starting checklist.

Title: Make identity the control plane of your cloud platform
Description: Sony Interactive Entertainment's Anjan Kaleru at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on zero trust IAM, continuous compliance and self-service access for developers.
Body:
Developers want access quickly, security wants tight control, and auditors want evidence. Anjan Kaleru, Staff IAM Engineer at Sony Interactive Entertainment with more than ten years in identity and access management, opened his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 talk with that three-way tug of war, and his answer is to put identity at the centre of the platform so all three get what they need from the same automation.

His framing is borrowed from Gartner and repeated for good reason: identity is the new security boundary. Every login, every API call, every device check is an access decision.

## Why the old tools stopped fitting

VPNs and firewalls assumed a network you could draw a line around. Cloud platforms broke that, and the usual response, a patchwork of tools bolted on one at a time, adds confusion instead of fixing anything. Anjan traces identity through three phases: the centralised Active Directory and VPN era, the cloud disruption where hundreds of microservices brought their own rules, and the infrastructure-as-code era where access rules change as fast as the code. Most breaches, he notes, come down to weak or unmanaged identities, which is why the last phase needs zero trust and API-first identity platforms.

## What zero trust IAM looks like day to day

Zero trust here means every request is checked, every time. His examples are concrete. Contractors get temporary access with MFA and just-in-time provisioning through an access request system. If an application is connected to the identity platform, access is granted right away; if not, a service request is created automatically so it is still tracked. In multi-cloud setups, identity governance (IGA), privileged access management (PAM) and single sign-on work together as one control plane.

The patterns that produce results are automated access reviews, PAM vaulting for admin accounts, and SSO integrations. In Kubernetes environments, teams add namespace isolation and automated policy validation. The principle underneath is the same everywhere: enforce least privilege and validate access before it is granted, not after.

## Compliance that is always on

The section with the most practical value is about turning compliance from an annual event into a continuous property. Instead of big review cycles and spreadsheets, checklists live in workflows, reminders are automated and reports are audit-ready at any moment. Anjan reports zero audit flags thanks to automated reviews, and hundreds of hours saved per business cycle on reporting. Identity intelligence adds access recommendations so reviewers can make a sensible keep-or-revoke decision instead of rubber-stamping a long list of entitlements.

Self-service is the developer half of the deal. Service catalogues, automated key management and simple web-based account creation mean developers do not wait weeks for access, and security keeps control because the paths are pre-approved.

## A healthcare example and the next three trends

His case study is a healthcare organisation managing access to patient data under compliance rules. With zero trust, automated provisioning and self-service, provisioning time dropped from days to under 12 hours, incidents went down and audit preparation got much faster. (The abstract's headline is 48-hour requests becoming 12-minute flows; the talk itself reports the under-12-hours figure.)

Looking ahead, Anjan sees three trends: converged IAM where IGA and PAM merge into one platform covering human and machine identities; automation-first governance where reviews, evidence collection and policy checks run continuously; and identity for AI, where non-human identities and intelligent agents need governing just like people. As agents get spun up daily, that last one is coming for every platform team soon.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers who own access requests and audits, and anyone about to give AI agents credentials. It is a strategy-level talk with concrete patterns rather than a product demo, though Anjan's background is in Saviynt and SailPoint.

Title: Platform engineering when a dropped frame can hide a lesion
Description: Johnson & Johnson's Santosh Suresh at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on endoscopy imaging platforms with sub-200 ms video, tiered storage and 99.99% uptime.
Body:
In most systems a moment of lag is an annoyance. In bronchoscopy, Santosh Suresh pointed out, it could mean missing a critical airway lesion. Santosh, a Principal Engineer at Johnson & Johnson, used his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 talk to walk through the infrastructure behind advanced flexible endoscopy: real-time video with end-to-end latency under 200 milliseconds, 99.99% uptime, and storage that never loses an image it cannot recreate.

At about eight minutes it moves fast, close to a narrated reference architecture. That makes it dense, and useful as a checklist.

## The requirements are unusually unforgiving

A single procedure produces massive uncompressed data. The target is end-to-end photon latency below 200 ms, and Santosh says their best systems sit at 90 to 120 ms. Uptime has to be 99.99%. Multiple imaging modalities (RGB, near-infrared, fluorescence) each produce their own data stream with their own processing needs, and modern endoscopes are at least HD. A storage failure is not a retry: the diagnostic imagery is gone.

## Compute, network and a video pipeline

The core infrastructure is clusters with hundreds of CPU cores and multiple high-end GPUs for real-time processing, with dedicated resources for encoding and transcoding, and separate compute pools so batch jobs never steal from live procedures. The network has a 10 Gbps backbone, quality-of-service rules that prioritise endoscopic traffic, multiple edge ingestion points with automatic failover, and low-latency paths for clinical workflows.

The video pipeline runs ingestion, then image enhancement (noise reduction, enhancement, colour correction), then H.265 encoding to save bandwidth while keeping quality, then multi-protocol streaming with adaptive bitrate to viewing stations.

## Three storage tiers, by age

Storage is tiered by how recently a procedure happened:

- **Hot:** NVMe for active and recent examinations, sub-millisecond access.
- **Warm:** SSD for procedures up to 30 days old.
- **Cold:** historical procedures with intelligent compression for cheap long-term retention.

Scaling relies on stateless microservices on Kubernetes with automatic pod scaling, load balancing that considers data locality and network topology, and session affinity so a procedure's stream stays on consistent processing. Performance tricks include GPU acceleration, zero-copy buffer management to minimise memory transfers, caching for hot content, and time-series databases for procedure metrics.

## Designing for failure during a procedure

High availability means no single points of failure (redundant power and network), continuous health monitoring with very fast failure detection, automated failover and geographic resilience. Santosh calls chaos engineering and regular failover testing essential, including partial failures, network partitions and cascading failures under controlled conditions.

Data flows through Kafka buffering for the high-bandwidth feeds, stream processing for validation and enrichment, and a lambda architecture combining stream and batch. Security covers HIPAA with AES-256 at rest, hardware security modules, tamper-proof audit logs with cryptographic signatures, end-to-end encryption from capture to archive, and context-aware authorisation with MFA and SSO. Hospital integration uses DICOM interfaces that turn video into multi-frame objects, PACS connectivity, DICOMweb for REST access, and cross-enterprise sharing.

## The case study

At a 1,200-bed academic medical center running 50,000 endoscopic procedures, the platform brought latency under 200 ms, handled 200-plus concurrent procedures at peak, integrated with the EMR through a federated architecture that preserved video quality, and cut operational cost by about 40% through performance optimisation. Next on his list: deeper AI and ML integration, edge computing, ultra-high-definition and 8K imaging, and 3D reconstruction from endoscopic video for navigation assistance.

## Who should watch

Engineers on real-time video, medical devices or any platform where latency is a safety property. Pause often; the slides carry more than the narration.

Title: Rate limits that watch behaviour instead of counting requests
Description: Rehana Sultana Khan (Versa Networks) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on ML rate limiting that lets real traffic spikes in and slows the bots down.
Body:
A fixed rate limit fails twice: it slams the door on the crowd your marketing team worked hard to attract, and it waves through the patient bot that spreads its requests across a hundred IP addresses. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Rehana Sultana Khan, Software Engineer at Versa Networks, made the case for rate limiting that classifies behaviour rather than counting requests, and walked through how to build it on the big three clouds.

She tells it as a story, which is unusual for a talk this close to security engineering, and it works. A shop door with a "five people per hour" rule, and a friend called Sarah who runs a travel app with the same kind of static threshold.

## The static threshold is wrong in both directions

Sarah's first bad day: an influencer writes about her app, real users flood in, the limit kicks in and blocks them for an hour. No revenue, lots of angry people. Her second bad day: a scraper comes in from many IP addresses, each one politely staying under the limit, and walks off with all the flight and hotel data. The threshold saw nothing wrong.

Khan names the two failure modes plainly. False positives turn into abandoned transactions and damaged customer relationships. Sophisticated attackers who distribute traffic across IPs and time never trip the rule in the first place, so there is nothing to respond to.

## Hire a committee, not a bouncer

The fix is to replace the counter with something closer to a security guard who watches how people behave. Instead of a single number, the model looks at request timing patterns, payload characteristics, geographic distribution, user agent diversity and response code sequences, plus the temporal dimension: what a session does over time. A real shopper logs in, browses and adds to a cart. A scraper hits the same endpoints with perfect spacing and never buys anything.

Her "committee of experts" is a friendly description of decision tree ensembles such as random forests and gradient boosting: one tree is good at geography, another at timing, another at browsers, and the majority vote wins. She picks them because they handle mixed data types, capture non-linear relationships and stay relatively interpretable. Class imbalance (legitimate traffic vastly outnumbers attacks) is handled with sampling techniques and cost-sensitive learning, and the models keep learning through online updates and periodic retraining.

## Slow them down before you block them

The most practical idea is progressive throttling. Rather than a binary allow or deny, the system applies subtle delays, then rate reductions, and only blocks outright when confidence is high. Users are grouped into behavioural cohorts that they can move between, earning more headroom with legitimate use or losing it with suspicious activity.

She maps three attack types onto this: credential stuffing (rapid failures from many IPs, followed by forced password resets for affected accounts), API scraping (robotic browse patterns with no purchases) and low-and-slow account takeover (a valid account that only ever views personal and payment details).

For the build, she lists the cloud pieces: API Gateway, Lambda and SageMaker on AWS; API Management with Azure Machine Learning; API Gateway with Vertex AI on Google Cloud. Multi-cloud setups get one central policy source pushed to every region, with Kubernetes helping keep deployments consistent.

## The numbers, with a caveat

Khan cites figures for organisations that adopt this approach, including 30% lower infrastructure costs from not serving junk traffic, and an e-commerce case study with a 92% drop in false positives while handling 300% traffic spikes during flash sales. The case study is not named, so read these as the shape of the payoff rather than a benchmark. Her measurement advice holds regardless: track detection accuracy and adaptation rates next to business metrics like blocked legitimate users and support tickets, because security metrics alone tell half the story.

## Who should watch

Platform and API teams who own gateway configuration, and anyone who has had to explain why the launch-day spike got a wall of 429s. It is an accessible, analogy-heavy introduction, so security specialists will want to pair it with something more hands-on.

Title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: the primitives between PoC and production
Description: Samuel Baruffi (AWS) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on AgentCore runtime, identity, gateway, memory and observability for shipping enterprise AI agents.
Body:
Most agent projects work fine on one developer's laptop. The trouble starts when they need auth, scale, memory and an audit trail. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Samuel Baruffi, Principal Global Solutions Architect at AWS, toured Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a set of pick-and-choose primitives for running agents in production, from serverless runtime and identity to an MCP gateway with semantic tool search.

This is an AWS product talk, and Samuel is upfront about it. It was recorded on September 5, 2025, while AgentCore was still in preview, so check current docs for what has changed since.

## Why PoCs stall

The pattern Samuel kept hearing from customers: an agent PoC runs locally, then hits four walls on the way to production. Performance, scalability, security and governance. AgentCore is AWS's answer, and the key design choice is that each piece can be used on its own. You do not have to buy the whole ecosystem; you can bring your own framework (Strands, LangGraph, LangChain, CrewAI or your own) and your own model, including non-Bedrock ones.

He also clarifies a common confusion: Bedrock Agents, which has existed for about two years, is the more opinionated option. AgentCore is the lower-level, more flexible set of building blocks.

## Runtime and identity

**AgentCore Runtime** is serverless compute for agents. You add a decorator, package a Docker image to ECR, and invoke the agent through an API. Sessions get true isolation, scale from zero, and can run for up to eight hours. Runtime can also host a remote MCP server, for example one built with FastMCP.

**AgentCore Identity** handles both directions of auth. Inbound: who may invoke this agent, using existing providers like Okta, Azure AD or Amazon Cognito over OAuth 2.0, without migrating users. Outbound: how the agent gets IAM permissions for AWS resources, or API keys and OAuth flows for third parties like Salesforce or Google Drive.

## The gateway and its tool search

**AgentCore Gateway** is a managed MCP server. Point it at an OpenAPI schema or a Lambda function, and those endpoints become MCP tools behind authenticated access. One gateway can have many targets, and each target many tools.

The feature Samuel clearly enjoys is semantic search over tools. If your gateway exposes 360 tools, a plain list-tools call returns all of them, which bloats context. Instead the agent can ask the gateway for tools relevant to a task (his example: creating a social media post) and get back four. His reasoning is the right one: "the more tools you provide, the less accuracy you have", plus more latency and more tokens billed. It is essentially a small RAG system over your tool catalogue.

## Memory, browser, code and traces

**AgentCore Memory** splits short-term memory (raw conversation turns, stored for a configurable period) from long-term memory, which is extracted asynchronously as semantic facts, user preferences or summaries. Storage is per-customer with namespaces and bring-your-own encryption.

**Browser** gives agents isolated, serverless headless browsers with live-view streaming and session replay. **Code Interpreter** runs model-generated code in isolated sandboxes with no root access. **Observability** ships prebuilt CloudWatch dashboards and traces of every model and tool call, and exports OpenTelemetry if you use another backend.

Samuel closes by pointing to the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub, the docs and the blog.

## Who should watch

Teams on AWS with an agent stuck at PoC, and anyone designing agent infrastructure who wants a checklist of the primitives production needs, whatever cloud you use. If you are not on AWS, the identity and tool-search sections still transfer.

Title: Getting patients to appointments by wiring Epic to Uber and Lyft
Description: Sai Sharan Reddy Mittapelly at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on a HIPAA-compliant link from Epic EHR to rideshare APIs, with provider failover.
Body:
One in five patients in the United States misses or delays care because they have no reliable way to get there, and for a dialysis or chemotherapy patient a missed appointment is not a scheduling nuisance. Sai Sharan Reddy Mittapelly, a healthcare integration engineer with ten-plus years in the field (he mentioned Henry Ford Health as his current employer), spent his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 talk on the platform that connects Epic EHR scheduling to Uber and Lyft so the ride is booked with the appointment.

It is a nice change from yet another generic microservices talk: the domain constraints are unusual, the failure mode is a patient not getting treatment, and the architecture decisions follow directly from that.

## Two APIs that were never meant to meet

On one side sits Epic, speaking SMART on FHIR: REST APIs carrying patient data as JSON or XML resources, replacing the older HL7 v2 and v3 messages. On the other side, rideshare APIs designed for consumers: quick pickups, arrival estimates, and no built-in compliance for medical data. The integration layer between them is, in Sai's description, a translator and a security guard combined.

## The three hard problems

**Bidirectional flow.** Epic shares appointment details; the rideshare side sends back driver location, ETA and drop-off confirmation. Both systems, and the patient's app, need to stay in sync throughout.

**Provider failover.** If Lyft goes down, the system switches to Uber without the patient noticing, the way a GPS reroutes you around a closed road. Care does not wait for a vendor's status page to turn green.

**HIPAA in every request.** Each ride request carries more than 47 sensitive fields: patient name, appointment type, pickup address, notes and mobility needs. Every one must be encrypted, logged and auditable.

## The architecture that follows

The platform splits into microservices (Epic integration, transport orchestration, a provider gateway, patient profiles and compliance) around a Kafka event bus. Kafka carries transport requests and their state changes, appointment updates from Epic, driver location and ETA updates, and compliance audit events. PostgreSQL handles the transactional side: the ride registry, billing reconciliation, compliance documentation and configuration. A cache holds patient transport profiles, so details like wheelchair access are on hand instantly.

Sai's hospital analogy works: separate wings for emergency, lab and radiology, each with its own team, connected by secure hallways. During flu season the ride-matching service scales up without dragging the rest of the system along.

It runs on Kubernetes across multiple AWS regions with predictive autoscaling driven by historical clinic load, active-active clusters, and canary deployments. Security is zero trust: rotating tokens, AES-256 encryption, OAuth 2 with PKCE, TLS and a web application firewall.

## Monitor the clinic, not just the cluster

The most transferable idea is the split in observability. If an API slows down, that is an IT problem. If a dialysis ride is late, that is a clinical problem that could harm a patient, and it should page a different team. So they define custom SLOs tied to medical schedules, not just latency percentiles.

There is an ML layer too: a pipeline from data collection through feature engineering to monitored deployment, with the healthcare caveats of incomplete data and the need for clinicians to understand recommendations. His example is a model that learns a patient often cancels Monday-morning rides and schedules a backup plus a reminder. He credits AI with cutting no-shows by 42%, and describes a Chicago hospital where dialysis patients had been missing appointments because of transport: after the integration, no-shows fell, patients were happier, and clinicians got back about 20 hours a month of manual transport coordination. The transcript is a bit tangled on the exact percentages for that case, so watch the slides for the figures.

## Who should watch

Engineers working on healthcare integrations, and anyone building a platform where an outage has a human cost and SLOs need a domain meaning. His closing line sums up the stance: in healthcare, uptime is a lifeline.

Title: ML that ranks errors by business impact cut MTTR at Liberty Mutual
Description: Sreelatha Pasuparthi (Liberty Mutual) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on ML-driven alert triage and Slack routing across 17 enterprise systems.
Body:
When customers find two thirds of your critical issues before you do, the alerting is not working. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Sreelatha Pasuparthi, Principal Software Engineer at Liberty Mutual Insurance, described how her team built an ML system that classifies errors by business impact and routes them to the right person over Slack, Teams or email, and she reports mean time to resolution falling from 162 to 18.6 minutes across 17 enterprise systems.

## The cost of noise at scale

The starting numbers are the kind that make an on-call engineer wince. Seventeen production systems supporting about 230,000 daily active users and 3.7 million daily transactions produced over 12,000 error events a day. Average detection took 162 minutes, 68.2% of critical issues were first discovered by customers, and SLA compliance sat at 62.3%. Engineers spent 23% of their time triaging alerts instead of building.

Alert fatigue is usually described as a morale problem. Here it is a measurable tax on delivery.

## Capture everything, cheaply

The first layer is middleware that captures exceptions across all systems. Sreelatha cites a 99.7% capture rate with only 3.2 milliseconds of overhead per transaction, distributed tracing to preserve context, an event-driven architecture on a Kafka backbone, and containerised ML inference endpoints. If the capture layer is expensive, someone turns it off; keeping it cheap is what makes everything after it possible.

## An ensemble that asks "does this matter?"

The classifier is an ensemble: random forest for categorical features, LSTM for stack-trace analysis and gradient boosting for time-series patterns, with continuous retraining fed by human feedback. She reports 93.8% accuracy at prioritising errors by business impact.

The features are the interesting part, grouped into four families:

- **Exception characteristics**: stack-trace patterns, exception type, message semantics, code-path frequency.
- **Business context**: estimated affected users, transaction financial value, process criticality, data integrity impact.
- **Temporal patterns**: time-of-day correlation, error frequency trends, business-hour weighting, seasonality.
- **Historical response**: prior resolution times, SLA breach prediction, escalation rates, developer response patterns.

The models were trained on 18 months of history covering 12,387 resolved incidents with full resolution workflows.

## Right alert, right channel, fewer storms

Routing evaluates each alert across 14 parameters, including severity, system impact, time of day and team workload, then picks the channel and urgency: a Slack DM, Microsoft Teams or email. Intelligent rate limiting clusters related errors and suppresses predicted cascades, which she says cut alert volume during major incidents by 68.2% while still catching 99.8% of unique issues.

Reported outcomes: an 88.5% reduction in MTTR, $2.3 million in annual savings from reduced downtime, a 23.5% gain in developer productivity and a 73.4% drop in overall alert volume.

## The MLOps lessons

Sreelatha's practices are refreshingly unglamorous. Start with one high-volume system and expand as models mature. Build explicit human feedback loops. Measure business outcomes like MTTR and cost, not just model accuracy. And build for transparency, so engineers understand why an alert fired and how it was routed. A classifier nobody trusts is just a new source of noise.

## Who should watch

SRE and platform teams drowning in alerts, and ML engineers looking for an applied problem with a clear success metric. It is a results-focused talk; the slides describe the architecture rather than show code.

Title: Incident dashboards should interpret the data, not just show it
Description: Priyanshi Deshwal (Mode) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on AI incident views that rank alerts, pick visuals and write plain-language summaries.
Body:
Five people on a bridge call, five different dashboards, everyone squinting at time ranges that don't line up. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Priyanshi Deshwal, Senior Software Engineer at Mode (she introduced herself as a frontend engineer at ThoughtSpot, working on data visualisation and analytics products), argued that the classic dashboard is a monitoring tool we keep misusing as a crisis tool, and laid out what an AI-assisted incident view should do instead.

Her framing is a visualisation engineer's, which makes it a useful counterweight to the usual AIOps talk about models and pipelines. The question she keeps returning to is simple: during your last big incident, how much time went into finding the right data rather than acting on it?

## Dashboards were built to watch, not to fight fires

Deshwal's critique of dashboards has three parts. They are reactive by design, showing history and forcing you to reconstruct the present. They overload you: twenty charts refreshing every few seconds while you try to work out which change came first and whether you're looking at a symptom or a cause. And they demand manual work, with someone clicking filters and widening time windows at exactly the moment human error is most expensive.

Underneath that sits the data problem. Logs live in one tool, metrics in another, deployment history somewhere else, and responders swivel between them correlating by hand. Traditional tools sample, add latency and leave blind spots, which is the last thing you want during a high-severity incident.

## From a map to a GPS

The analogy she uses is a good one. A map tells you where the roads are; a GPS reroutes you when traffic builds. AI-powered visual intelligence should do the second job: interpret the data, group related anomalies, and suggest probable root causes with confidence scores, while the layout reconfigures itself so the most relevant metrics bubble up.

She breaks this into three capabilities:

- **Alert prioritisation.** Learn from historical incidents so that instead of triaging 500 alerts by hand, you get a ranked list of the few that matter.
- **Automated visual recommendations.** Pick the right chart for the problem. During a network outage, generate a topology map with affected nodes in red so the blast radius is visible at a glance.
- **Contextual summaries.** Turn technical data into a plain-language summary for stakeholders, so a responder isn't spending a chunk of every hour writing status updates.

Further out she sketches natural-language queries ("show me all error spikes for the checkout service in the last 30 minutes"), voice control and shared interfaces where several teams explore the same data live. The split of work stays clear: the machine crunches data at scale, humans keep judgment and communication.

## Shadow mode before trust

The implementation section is the part to steal. Measure first: time to detection, time to resolution and the number of hand-offs per incident. Unify logs, metrics and alerts into one pipeline, because a model with half the picture gives half an answer. Train on historical incidents, design role-based views (deep detail for SREs, business impact for executives), and treat the AI like a team member who should get smarter after every retrospective.

Her advice on adoption is pragmatic. Fix data quality and naming conventions before blaming the model. Run the AI in shadow mode, making recommendations alongside human decisions, so responders can compare and build confidence. Roll out gradually and bring incident commanders in early. And keep the visualisation layer fast under load, because a dashboard that freezes while everything is on fire is its own incident.

## Who should watch

Engineers building internal incident tooling, observability product teams, and anyone who owns the dashboards their on-call rotation actually opens at 3am. It is a vision-and-roadmap talk rather than a product demo or a code walkthrough, so come for the design principles and the rollout checklist. The closing question is worth taking back to your team: if your next P1 happened tomorrow, what should the screen show you first?

Title: Scaling a biopharma data platform from 15 TB to 140 TB a month
Description: Ritesh Kumar Sinha at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on a platform-as-a-product rebuild of biopharma analytics on AWS, with compliance written as code.
Body:
A Fortune 500 biopharma company could reach only 15% of its available healthcare data sources, and its researchers were waiting hours for queries. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Ritesh Kumar Sinha, Associate Vice President at Kotak Mahindra Bank with two decades in technology and engineering, showed how a platform-as-a-product rebuild took that analytics stack from 15 TB to 140 TB of monthly processing on AWS, with HIPAA and GDPR controls built into the infrastructure code.

It is a compact talk (under eight minutes) and mostly a case study with the numbers up front, so it suits a quick watch between meetings.

## Why healthcare data platforms are their own kind of hard

Ritesh lists the constraints: hundreds of terabytes of sensitive data a month, HIPAA and GDPR on top, legacy systems that will not scale, researchers who want self-service analytics, and very different data domains to join. The legacy setup was a monolith that could not grow with demand, which in this industry means slower research, not just slower reports.

## Researchers are the customers

The shift he puts at the centre is treating infrastructure as a product, with research and clinical teams as its customers. In practice that meant self-service capabilities and automation so teams could get resources without waiting for an engineer, and compliance requirements written directly into infrastructure code instead of checked afterwards.

The platform runs on AWS, with automated ETL pipelines, a multi-zone data architecture and dynamic scaling. A metadata-driven framework keeps data quality consistent. Data lands in Amazon S3 and loads into Amazon Redshift with the COPY command, which is about as plain as a data platform gets and is probably why it scaled.

## The numbers he reports

Ritesh puts the outcomes in a list, and they are worth quoting as reported:

- monthly processing capacity from 15 TB to 140 TB;
- an 80% reduction in processing time;
- 67% faster developer velocity through self-service;
- $2.3 million in annual cost savings;
- drug discovery timelines shortened by 4.2 months per compound;
- a 23% higher clinical trial success rate through better data access.

The abstract frames the query change as 12 hours to 2.4 hours. Since the talk does not show the measurement method behind the research outcomes, read those as the team's own assessment.

## How the migration was run

The legacy-to-cloud-native move came in five phases: assessment of current capabilities and target architecture; a foundation of cloud environment plus compliance frameworks; migration using blue-green deployments; optimisation of the architecture and self-service; and then innovation with advanced analytics and ML.

The challenges were mostly human: organisational resistance, skill gaps, legacy integration, compliance worries, and the tension between standardisation and flexibility. The fixes Ritesh lists are the ones that tend to work: executive champions, platform engineers embedded with the teams, phased migration with clear metrics, compliance as code, and golden paths with escape hatches for edge cases. That last pairing is the detail to take home; a golden path with no escape hatch is just a wall.

His four strategies for anyone repeating this: start small with a high-value use case and scale fast, put compliance into automation and CI/CD, measure platform value with KPIs such as developer velocity and resource utilisation, and build an internal community through feedback forums and training.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers in regulated industries, and platform teams whose customers are scientists or analysts rather than application developers. It is a results-first case study with an AWS reference shape, not a deep architecture walkthrough.

Title: Dashboards don't act, so eBay built systems that do
Description: eBay's Sureshkumar Karuppuchamy at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on SLO-driven alerts, adaptive rate limiting and auto-rollbacks that earn trust.
Body:
Adaptive rate limiting alone prevented nearly 30% of major incidents on the platform Sureshkumar Karuppuchamy works on. Sureshkumar, an Engineering Lead at eBay, told that story at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 as part of a bigger argument: dashboards show you problems but never fix them, so at billions of requests the reliability has to live in the system, with humans paged only for what truly needs them.

The talk opens with the scene everyone knows: 2 AM, phone buzzing, squinting at graphs while trying to contain something. Then it spends half an hour explaining how to stop being the control loop.

## Observability built for machines to act on

The old way was to collect everything, build endless dashboards and hope someone noticed the right spike. The new way is SLO-driven signals tied to user experience: p95 latency, availability, checkout success rate. Error budgets decide when to ship fast and when to slow down.

The supporting patterns are concrete. One golden dashboard per service, not ten. OpenTelemetry first, so metrics, traces and logs share a pipeline, with trace IDs on metrics so an engineer can jump from a latency spike straight to the trace behind it. W3C trace context propagated everywhere, with tail-based sampling that keeps the errors and outliers. Structured JSON logs, with sensitive data redacted at the collector and routing by severity. Deployments and feature flag toggles appear as annotations on dashboards. Real user monitoring and CDN metrics extend the view past the backend, and capacity and cost are tracked per owning team.

## Alerts are control signals

Static thresholds fail because normal keeps moving, so the team built anomaly detectors that learn usage patterns and warn before capacity limits, plus models that forecast latency spikes and correlate logs, metrics and traces. The nicest trick is using browser JavaScript errors as a release signal: if a rollout pushes JS errors up, it rolls back before users notice.

From there, alerts trigger actions. A slow dependency trips a circuit breaker. An error budget burning too fast rolls back the deployment. Multi-burn-rate alerts catch both fast spikes and slow leaks, and only real user impact pages a human; the rest goes to chat or tickets.

Automation comes in tiers. Tier one, safe and reversible actions like throttling and circuit breakers, always runs automatically. Tier two, progressive changes like shifting regional traffic, can start on its own but leaves room for human oversight. Tier three, complex or novel incidents, notifies a person and hands them runbooks and context. In his words, automation handles the easy 80% while humans take the hard 20%.

## Every scar becomes a safeguard

Many of their incidents were not infrastructure failures but workload anomalies: a buggy client spamming requests, an internal batch flooding an API. Static limits could not adapt, so they built throttling that learns normal traffic per client and per endpoint and contains runaway workloads automatically. That is the 30% figure above.

The cultural rule behind it is the line worth stealing. Every postmortem asks two questions: could this have been auto-detected, and could it have been auto-mitigated? If yes, they build it. A cascading outage gave them circuit breakers; a bad config rollout gave them progressive deployment. Deployment approval moved from pre-release sign-off to post-deployment analysis, with canaries, progressive rollouts and automatic rollback on SLO breaches doing the gating.

## Trust gets earned, not declared

Engineers worry automation will make things worse, so it ships in stages: first a mode where it only logs what it has done, a suggest mode where it recommends and waits for approval, then autonomous mode within guardrails, with every action transparent, reversible and explainable. Over time the team saw it was more reliable than a tired human at 2 AM. Business KPIs close the loop too: if a release looks fine technically but cart abandonment spikes, it rolls back.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who own an on-call rotation and want a concrete ladder from dashboards to closed-loop remediation. The tiered automation model and the log, suggest, then act rollout are directly reusable.

Title: Teaching Oracle Cloud databases to see outages coming
Description: Sunil Yadav at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 makes a three-minute case for ML anomaly detection, RL tuning and predictive scaling for 99.98% Oracle uptime.
Body:
Database downtime is expensive enough that waiting for the pager is the costly option. Sunil Yadav, a database administrator who has worked across multinationals in several countries, used his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 slot to argue that machine learning can spot the trouble early enough on Oracle Cloud to hold availability at 99.98%.

Set expectations first: this is a lightning talk. The recording runs about three minutes, so think of it as an elevator pitch for ML-driven database resilience, with the slides doing much of the talking. It is a good way to see the shape of the idea before you go looking for the details.

## The money argument

Sunil opens on the cost of downtime: by his figure, more than $9,000 for every minute a database is down (the abstract puts it at $9,375). Over a year the financial impact is large, which is why he frames prevention, not faster recovery, as the goal. If a model can flag an anomaly before it turns into an outage, you get to fix it during working hours instead of at three in the morning.

## The loop: monitor, learn, optimise, validate

The technical idea comes in a few steps:

- **Anomaly detection on performance metrics.** A deep learning model first learns the normal patterns in the database's performance metrics, then keeps judging new samples at five-second intervals to catch drift early.
- **Reinforcement learning for the Oracle cluster.** Tuning runs as a cycle: monitor, learn, optimise, validate, and repeat.
- **Data Guard tuning.** Neural networks help tune Oracle Data Guard for high availability and scalability, using synchronised replication with minimal performance impact and failover within seconds.
- **Predictive auto-scaling.** Since the model already knows the load patterns, it can scale ahead of demand. The aim is lower cost without giving up availability or performance.

He also notes that the framework scales horizontally and vertically, works across architectures, and leaves engineers more productive because the anomaly detection is automated.

## The numbers, with a caveat

Sunil quotes a 287% return on investment with an eight-month payback alongside 99.98% availability, and mentions case studies in financial services, healthcare and retail. The abstract adds sub-3-second failovers, predictive monitoring that prevents 83% of outages, 60% cost cuts and a footprint across 750-plus enterprises. A three-minute talk has no time to show the methodology behind any of these, so treat them as the speaker's claims. He is candid that some unforeseen issues will always remain: close to a hundred percent, not quite there.

## Who should watch

DBAs and SREs responsible for Oracle estates who are wondering whether ML-based anomaly detection is worth a pilot, and anyone who needs a short framing to share with a manager. If you want implementation detail (features, model types, how the RL agent is constrained in production), use this as a starting point and pair it with a longer talk.

Title: Swap the AI monolith for a team of specialised agents
Description: Okta's Sidhanta Panigrahy at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 lays out a four-layer multi-agent architecture for AI platforms that fail in pieces, not all at once.
Body:
Monolithic AI platforms fail the way monolithic apps always have: one bad change, one exhausted resource, and everything goes down together. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Sidhanta Panigrahy, Director of Business Technology at Okta, argued for breaking the "one big AI system" into many small, specialised agents he calls microminds, coordinated by a dedicated layer so that a failure stays local.

It is an architecture talk at the level of patterns, not a framework demo. If you lived through the microservices migration, a lot of it will rhyme, and that is rather the point.

## Why the monolith stops scaling

Sidhanta's description of the bottleneck will be painfully familiar. As the codebase grows, an update that took a week stretches into a month because everyone competes for the same architecture and resources. A minor feature triggers regression testing across unrelated parts of the system. Tightly coupled systems fail completely. And there is an organisational cost: different business units have different AI needs, and one centralised system turns into a queue they all wait in.

## Four layers of agents

The core idea is that complex intelligence does not require one complex system. Instead you build many focused agents, each tuned for a specific problem, and connect them with a standard communication protocol (he points at MCP for agent communication), an intelligent coordination layer, and natural fault tolerance. He structures it as four layers:

- **Perception:** data ingestion, processing and first interpretation.
- **Cognition:** analysis, reasoning, decision making and domain-specific insight.
- **Action:** turning those decisions into concrete operations on external systems and business processes.
- **Coordination:** orchestrating the agents across all layers and adapting collaboration patterns to current conditions.

That split is the useful takeaway even if you never adopt the vocabulary. It gives you a place to put each responsibility and a boundary to fail at.

## Fail in pieces, recover in pieces

On performance, agents run in parallel on different resources, scale with actual demand, and idle when not needed, connected through message queues with compression so communication does not eat the gains. On reliability, the familiar patterns come back: graceful degradation, circuit breakers, continuous health monitoring and self-healing. The difference from a monolith is granular recovery. You restart one agent rather than the whole platform, and restore functionality incrementally while keeping downtime small.

Operating it is harder, and he says so. You need distributed tracing to follow one request across many agents, and correlation-based alerting that can tell a problem the system can absorb from one that needs a human. Security moves to zero trust between agents: each one has its own identity and dynamic permissions, there are distributed audit trails, and behavioural baselines flag anomalies.

## Getting there from here

Nobody rewrites a production AI platform over a weekend, so the legacy integration section matters. Sidhanta lists four strategies: adapter layers so agents and legacy systems can talk, data synchronisation between old and new components, an API gateway to centralise security and protocol translation, and event-driven messaging so the two worlds coordinate asynchronously. He is just as firm that the change is about people: skills programmes for running distributed systems, development processes adapted for interdependence, and pilots that prove value while keeping risk small.

## Who should watch

Architects and platform leads sketching how an AI platform should be decomposed, especially those already fighting a shared model service that every team depends on. The abstract promises live demos and Fortune 500 data; the recording is mostly the architecture and the patterns, which is where its value is.

Title: Warehouse AI that aces the lab can still fail on the floor
Description: Shubham Beldar (Symbotic) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on four warehouse automation failure patterns and the MLOps habits that prevent them.
Body:
A picking robot that scores above 90% in the lab can drop to the low 60s the first time it meets shrink wrap. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Shubham Beldar, Solutions Engineer at Symbotic, walked through four ways AI fails in real warehouses and the MLOps practices that stop it: validate on the live floor, monitor across systems, deploy in phases, and never underestimate the people who have to use it.

Shubham has spent over six years designing automated distribution centres for large retailers across grocery, healthcare, apparel and food, and the talk is grounded in that floor-level experience.

## Failure one: the physical reality gap

The lab never had transparent shrink wrap on a robot-built pallet, irregularly shaped products, or dust on the vision sensors. Real warehouses have all three. Shubham describes accuracy falling from around 95% to the low 60s when systems hit those conditions.

His diagnosis is pure MLOps: training data lacked messy real-world cases, validation happened only in the lab, and no feedback loop pushed floor errors back into retraining. Teams optimised for benchmarks instead of reality.

## Failure two: forecasts that never noticed the market moved

Demand forecasting models worked until market volatility hit. Then came overstock of the wrong SKUs, empty shelves at peak demand and errors compounding unchecked. The root causes he lists are no drift detection, stale ground truth, no human verification points, and no fallback plan. His image: the model keeps steering even as it heads off the cliff.

## Failure three: seven middlewares and a schema mismatch

Many warehouses run seven or eight middleware systems. Each looks fine in isolation, but when traffic spikes, latency cascades across them, and a single schema mismatch becomes the single point of failure that brings the deployment down. The fixes: shared monitoring across teams, testing the full integrated system instead of components, and graceful degradation plans. Anyone who has debugged a distributed system will nod along; the warehouse just adds forklifts.

## Failure four: the people said no

The most striking story is about trust. One parts distributor invested about $7 million in an automated system, the workforce rejected it after early failures, and the whole thing was abandoned. Operators with 20 years of experience often believe they are more productive doing it their way, and some fear for their jobs. If they do not trust the system, they route around it.

## What actually works

Shubham's strategies map one-to-one onto the failures:

- **Phased deployment.** Start with controlled pilots in shadow mode next to existing operations, and scale when metrics hold. He cites a large US retailer rolling out one phase at a time, which he says reduced integration risk by nearly 40% compared with big-bang launches.
- **Comprehensive testing.** Adversarial tests, worst-case scenarios, chaos engineering, synthetic edge cases, and load tests timed for peaks like Christmas and Black Friday.
- **Hybrid human-AI operation.** Clear human-in-the-loop protocols, human corrections fed back into training, and AI designed to augment workers rather than replace them. The best results he has seen paired high inventory accuracy with better workforce morale.

His closing point is worth taping to a monitor: the most successful warehouse projects do not always have the most advanced algorithms. They follow ML operations practices.

## Who should watch

Robotics and supply chain engineers, and any MLOps team deploying models into the physical world where sensors get dirty and people have opinions. It is a lessons-learned talk, not an architecture deep-dive.

Title: Zero trust for AI platforms, one layer at a time
Description: JPMorgan Chase's Sudheer Obbu at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on zero trust for ML pipelines, from service identity and mTLS to lineage and runtime monitoring.
Body:
A training job that scales from one node to hundreds of workers in a few minutes is a nightmare for an identity system built around people logging in. Sudheer Obbu, Senior Lead Software Engineer at JPMorgan Chase, built his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 talk on that mismatch: AI platforms need zero trust, and they need it applied to services, models and data, not just users.

Sudheer has spent 19 years on DevSecOps and multi-cloud architecture, and the talk reads like a layered reference architecture. The abstract's headline figure of 73% fewer incidents is not broken down in the talk itself; what you get instead is the framework and the order to build it in.

## The perimeter assumed your models lived in one building

The old model trusted anything inside the network. AI platforms span clouds, edge locations and hybrid environments, so there is no inside. They also bring their own attacks: model poisoning and data poisoning during training, adversarial inputs designed to force a misclassification, and model extraction, where an attacker rebuilds a proprietary model by watching its outputs. The cost of getting it wrong is a compromised model, stolen IP or a regulatory problem.

The zero trust principles are the standard three: verify explicitly, use least privilege, assume breach. What makes AI different is the shape of the system. One ML pipeline can involve dozens of services, from ingestion and feature stores to training orchestrators and model registries, and every hop needs the principles applied.

## Five layers, in build order

**Identity and access.** Every service gets a cryptographically verifiable identity. Mutual TLS between microservices means only authorised services can talk to each other, and certificate issuance, rotation and revocation have to be automated because the workloads appear and vanish at training-job speed.

**Network segmentation.** Microsegmentation isolates workloads, tenants and processing stages. The catch is that GPU-to-GPU traffic needs high throughput, and traditional network controls can add latency the training job will not tolerate. Sudheer's answer is software-defined networking that opens authorised channels on demand.

**Data and model protection.** This is the layer he calls the most critical, because a model is only as trustworthy as its training data. Lineage tracking with cryptographic integrity checks back to the source is the main defence against poisoning. Feature stores need permissions at the feature level. For the most sensitive computations he points at homomorphic encryption and secure multi-party computation, with the honest caveat that they are complex.

**Runtime security and observability.** AI jobs run long, burn resources and need privileged GPU access, so monitoring has to tell a legitimate burst from a breach. Signals worth watching include model accuracy degradation and unusual query patterns, alongside log aggregation that can cope with the volume from training jobs and model serving.

**Incident response.** Runbooks specific to AI: model rollback, handling a breach that touched training data, and automated quarantine of compromised workloads.

## Start with mTLS, and bring the data scientists

The rollout advice is incremental. Begin with service identity and mutual TLS, which pays off immediately. Move to broad network policies, then tighten into microsegmentation as you learn the traffic. Do data classification and lineage before anything exotic. And remember the cultural half: data scientists may see security controls as obstacles, so the controls have to help their productivity rather than hinder it.

On tooling he names Istio or AWS App Mesh for service-to-service auth, Kubernetes with specialised GPU node pools, and observability that tracks GPU utilisation, training loss and serving latency. Performance gets its own section: hardware-accelerated encryption, cached auth tokens, a trusted proxy for high-frequency calls, and sampling plus asynchronous logging so monitoring does not become the bottleneck. He ends on what is coming: confidential computing, federated learning, AI-assisted policy enforcement, and post-quantum cryptography.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who just inherited a GPU cluster and a security review, and security engineers who need a map of where ML systems differ from web services. It is a framework talk, so pair it with your own threat model.

Title: Put AI data governance inside the CI/CD pipeline
Description: Bhanu Maryala (Informatica) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on Training Data Declarations, a framework that runs compliance checks inside MLOps pipelines.
Body:
Governance that lives in a review meeting will always lose to a deadline. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Bhanu Maryala, Senior Solution Architect at Informatica, presented Training Data Declarations (TDD), a framework that embeds data governance for generative AI directly into CI/CD so compliance checks run automatically instead of queuing for a human.

The talk is about twenty minutes and aimed at teams shipping generative AI under real regulatory pressure.

## Speed or compliance is a false choice

Bhanu opens with three tensions every enterprise AI team knows: speed versus compliance, provenance tracking that gets harder as datasets grow, and the regulatory burden of operating in several jurisdictions at once. The usual framing is "move fast or stay compliant." His answer is both, and the way to get both is to stop treating governance as a gate outside the pipeline.

(Yes, the acronym collides with test-driven development. Same instinct, though: write the rules down first and let the machine enforce them.)

## What the framework actually contains

TDD has four core pieces:

- A **four-tier classification system** that sorts datasets by risk and provenance, from highly trusted to restricted sources.
- A **standard metadata schema**, so every dataset carries the same governance information, including licensing and transformation history.
- **Real-time risk assessment** that runs continuously from ingestion through training and into runtime.
- **Comprehensive audit trails** that leave regulators a complete record.

The design principle that ties them together: governance travels with the model wherever it is deployed. Bhanu shows it running across AWS (S3, Lambda, SageMaker), Azure (Blob Storage, Functions, Azure Machine Learning), GCP (Cloud Storage, Functions, Vertex AI) and Snowflake through native procedures. Container-native governance tools and Kubernetes-based policy enforcement handle checks before, during and after deployment, with dashboards giving near-instant feedback.

## Licensing is the gap nobody budgets for

The most concrete section is about licensing. Many training datasets include copyrighted or ambiguously licensed material, and in generative AI that turns into legal exposure the moment the model ships. TDD adds automated license detection, risk evaluation and remediation, all before deployment. Bhanu shows a short Python snippet that scans directories, validates policies and flags risky files before they reach training.

There is also jurisdiction-specific automation: different regions have different rules, and the framework adapts checks to regional requirements and cross-border data flows rather than forcing one global policy.

## A case study in review time

The financial services example is a large institution that wanted generative AI in customer service under strict regulation. With TDD and industry-specific rules, Bhanu says the team cut compliance review time by 87% while keeping full regulatory adherence. That is the claim of the talk in one number: governance automation should make releases faster, not slower.

He maps the framework onto the pipeline stage by stage. Metadata collection starts at ingestion, governance checks run during pre-processing, lineage is tracked through training, compliance is verified before validation and deployment, and monitoring continues in production.

## Who should watch

Title: How a CNN-LSTM pipeline cut VoIP fault detection to minutes
Description: Krishna Munnaluru (Oracle) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on a Kafka, Kubeflow and MLflow pipeline that monitors carrier-grade VoIP with neural networks.
Body:
In telecom, a 15-to-30-minute delay in spotting a problem means thousands of dropped calls. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Krishna Munnaluru, Senior Principal Architect at Oracle, walked through a production MLOps pipeline for voice-over-IP monitoring: Kafka for streaming, Kubeflow for training, MLflow for the registry, and a CNN-LSTM model that he says reached 88% prediction accuracy and brought fault detection down to two to five minutes.

This is one of the more concrete talks of the event: real components, real numbers, and a clear view of where each piece sits.

## Traditional monitoring sees less than half the network

Krishna's starting point is the state of conventional VoIP monitoring. By his figures, traditional tools give about 40% visibility into the network, react in 15 to 30 minutes, and statistical models for call-quality prediction reach around 65% accuracy. Blind spots plus slow reaction plus mediocre prediction is a bad combination when every minute is customer-visible.

## The model reads packets like a sequence

The neural network combines CNN layers that extract features from packet sequences with LSTM layers that pick up temporal patterns across sessions. On top of that sit a custom embedding layer for protocol-specific features, an attention mechanism that focuses on anomalies, and a hierarchical feature extractor that works across timescales. Krishna reports a 23-point improvement over the traditional statistical approach.

Features come from edge collectors capturing SIP, RTP and QoS metrics. Apache Beam processes more than 10,000 events per second and extracts 45-plus features, recursive feature elimination handles selection, and Feast serves as the feature store so training and inference see the same values. That last detail is the one that saves you from the classic training-serving skew bug.

## Every piece is wired to the next

The architecture point Krishna keeps returning to is that the components are tied together, so models are not just trained but continuously deployed, observed and improved. Kafka ingests events at sub-100-millisecond latency. Kubeflow pipelines run TensorFlow Data Validation for schema checks and drift detection, then distributed GPU training with hyperparameter tuning. MLflow tracks every experiment's parameters, metrics and artifacts, and versioned models go through approval workflows so teams can roll forward or back.

Serving uses TensorFlow Serving in containers on Kubernetes with horizontal autoscaling, blue-green deployments for zero downtime and instant rollback, and edge inference nodes across regions answering in under 50 milliseconds. In production he cites 96% anomaly detection accuracy and 99.99% availability.

## Monitoring that retrains itself

Monitoring covers model metrics (precision, recall), data quality (feature drift, missing values) and system health (latency, throughput). When drift is detected, retraining triggers automatically. The team also runs A/B tests in production and self-healing mechanisms for infrastructure faults.

Because operators have to trust the output, explainability is built in: SHAP values for feature importance, counterfactual explanations, dashboards tracking feature attribution over time, and automated model cards and audit logs, so an engineer can trace a prediction back to its cause.

The rollout went in four phases: foundation (data collection, features, first model), automation (CI/CD, testing, registry, dashboards), scale (distributed training, geographic deployment), then ongoing optimisation with ensembles and tuning. He also notes reduced licensing costs from using open-source tooling.

## Who should watch

Telecom and network engineers thinking about ML for service assurance, and any MLOps engineer who wants a reference architecture with named tools at each stage. The talk stays at architecture level, so do not expect code.

Title: Untangling SAP integration with OData services
Description: Volkswagen's Venkateswaran Petchiappan at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on swapping SAP middleware tangles for tuned RESTful OData APIs.
Body:
Every new system you bolt onto SAP makes integration worse at more than a linear rate. Venkateswaran Petchiappan, Senior Solution Architect Lead at Volkswagen, made that the starting point of his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 talk, and his way out is to expose SAP data through OData services: standard REST over HTTP, with the platform handling security, monitoring and errors centrally instead of in every point-to-point connector.

If your mental model of SAP integration is a batch job written in a hurry in 2009 and a middleware licence nobody dares to cancel, this talk is a tidy tour of the alternative.

## How SAP integration got here

Venkateswaran walks through the stages. Early SAP integration meant custom programs and batch jobs: fine for basic needs, useless for anything real time. Then came middleware layers and connectors, which needed specialised skills and tended to create silos. OData services shifted things to RESTful, standardised APIs. The last step is a platform-first model where the cross-cutting concerns live at the platform level rather than at each integration point.

The problems he lists will be familiar to anyone who has stared at an SAP interface diagram. Large organisations run five to 15 distinct systems. Middleware dependencies drive up cost. Huge data volumes bottleneck at interface boundaries. Exposing confidential data to cloud apps opens security gaps. And different systems model the same business concept in entirely different ways, so every connection carries its own translation logic. Pile enough of that up and you get the fragile web he calls integration debt.

## Why OData fits SAP

OData extends REST principles to SAP's shape of data. Entity models line up with the SAP application layer, metadata descriptions make services self-documenting, and the usual HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) work as expected. Third-party applications can consume the definitions while keeping the business semantics intact. The principle he repeats is connect once, reuse often: one well-defined service instead of a new bespoke interface per consumer. He adds flexible querying and a simpler entity relationship model that can make full use of SAP HANA's in-memory processing.

## Ask for less data

The performance section is the practical core. The techniques are simple and the gains come from using all of them:

- Server-side filtering with `$filter`, so only the rows you need leave SAP.
- Pagination with `$skip` and `$top`, so large result sets arrive in manageable chunks.
- Response compression to cut bandwidth.
- Batch requests that fold multiple operations into one call.
- Field projection with `$select`, returning only the columns you asked for.
- Delta queries that fetch only what changed since the last sync.

With those in place, he says response times can drop to around 700 milliseconds even for complex data scenarios. None of it is exotic; the point is that most slow SAP integrations skip half of these because the connector made it easy to pull everything.

## Results by industry, and the mobile angle

He closes with sector numbers from case studies: 32% fewer parts shortages in manufacturing through real-time supply chain sync, retail inventory accuracy up from 82% to 98.5%, and an 80% drop in integration-related data errors for healthcare providers. He also shows a layered mobile architecture where apps consume SAP data over JSON and HTTP through a security layer, without legacy RFC-based plumbing in the middle.

## Who should watch

Integration architects and platform engineers who own the boundary between SAP and everything else, and developers whose backlog is full of requests for one more field out of SAP. It is an overview of the approach and its tuning knobs rather than a live build, so bring your own OData endpoint to try the query options on.
