Title: Build your developer platform around one pain point first
Description: Anil Kumar Veldurthi (US Bank) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 says treat infrastructure as a product, start with one pain point, measure from week one.
Body:
How much of last week did your developers spend fighting infrastructure instead of shipping features? Anil Kumar Veldurthi, a cloud architect whose two decades include Wells Fargo, First Republic Bank and US Bank, opened his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 talk with that question, and his answer for the 40%-or-more crowd is an internal developer platform built like a product, one painful problem at a time.

This is a strategy talk with a roadmap attached. If you already run Backstage and Argo CD in anger, you will recognise most of it. If you are the person who has to convince a VP to fund a platform team, it is close to a ready-made pitch.

## DevOps hit a scaling wall, and developers are paying for it

Anil's diagnosis: practices that work for a team of ten become miserable at a hundred-plus microservices across several clouds. He has seen organisations where a test environment needs sign-off from six teams and takes about three weeks. Meanwhile the competition deploys several times a day.

Platform engineering, in his telling, does not replace DevOps. It stops asking every developer to be an infrastructure expert. Infrastructure becomes a product and developers become its customers, so you measure their satisfaction and iterate on their feedback. The example he uses lands well: instead of two days of learning Terraform, security groups and networking to get a database, a developer answers a few questions and has one in minutes.

## Hide Kubernetes, compose the rest

The technology section is refreshingly opinionated. Kubernetes is the default substrate, but his golden rule is not to expose it to developers. They should be able to ask for a scalable web service, not learn storage classes. GitOps is the operational backbone, so every change to infrastructure and config is auditable and reversible. A service mesh takes service-to-service auth, circuit breaking and observability off each team's plate.

His summary is "composition over creation": Backstage for the portal, Argo CD for GitOps, Istio for the mesh, and custom code only where the business is genuinely different. On build versus buy, he warns that a custom platform needs at least 10 to 15 full-time engineers, and that organisations routinely underestimate that by half. The hybrid route (off-the-shelf portal and GitOps, custom glue) is where most successful teams end up.

## The roadmap, and the traps

Phase one is a quick win on the worst pain, usually CI/CD or environment provisioning, owned by an actual product owner rather than a committee of engineers. Phase two adds self-service observability, automated security and templates. Phase three brings the advanced deployment strategies. Skipping the first two to build "the ultimate platform" is the failure he has watched most often: one organisation spent 18 months on it, launched, and watched developers go back to their old tools because it was too complex.

The other traps are familiar and still worth hearing: building for theoretical problems instead of real ones, not-invented-here syndrome (do not write your own service mesh), and governance that is either too rigid or too loose. He also hands out homework: send a developer survey this week with one question, what is the most frustrating part of getting code from laptop to production, and start tracking environment creation time, deployment frequency and satisfaction even if the numbers are embarrassing.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and staff engineers making the case for a platform team, and new platform teams deciding what to build first. The back half includes an ROI framework and a pre-flight checklist (executive sponsor, product owner, pilot application), which is the part to send to your manager.

Title: Real-time translation is a systems problem, not a model problem
Description: At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Amit Arora showed that sub-200 ms speech translation rests on modular pipelines, edge nodes and GPU scheduling.
Body:
A translation model that scores well on a benchmark is the easy part. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Amit Arora, a software engineering manager with more than 20 years in the trade, argued that the hard part is the platform around the model: hitting a response time under 200 milliseconds for millions of daily conversations in 40-plus languages, without the meaning falling out somewhere between Mumbai and a data centre in Virginia.

His framing is useful for anyone running AI in production, not just translation teams. Four requirements pull against each other: latency, scale, reliability and accuracy. Optimise one in isolation and you break another. The talk is about getting all four to hold at once.

## Five services, each doing one job

The pipeline Amit describes is a chain of separate microservices: automatic speech recognition turns audio into text, a pre-processing step normalises it, neural machine translation converts it, post-processing cleans it up, and text-to-speech produces the audio on the other side. Keeping these apart is the whole point. Each stage can be scaled, upgraded and monitored on its own, so a better speech recogniser does not require redeploying the translator.

The models ship as containers on Kubernetes, which gives version control and lets domain-specific models (medical vocabulary, say) run next to general-purpose ones. New models go out with blue-green and canary releases: a small slice of users first, a check on how it performs, then everyone. For a system where a mistranslation can land in a hospital, an instant rollback is a feature, not an afterthought.

## The speed of light is a product requirement

The section worth the price of admission is on edge computing. If a user in India or Africa needs a sub-200 ms round trip and every request travels to a US region, the budget is gone before the model even runs. Amit's answer is to push the ASR, MT and TTS components out to edge nodes close to users. In his numbers that cut latency by 40% and upstream bandwidth by almost 60%, and it keeps sensitive audio inside the local jurisdiction, which makes the compliance team happier than any slide deck could.

Under that sits the plumbing: Kafka and Flink for low-latency streaming ingestion, batch pipelines for retraining and analytics, careful GPU scheduling so models do not collide at peak load, and aggressive caching of common phrases, domain terms and user dictionaries. GPUs are the bottleneck, so when they run short the platform degrades gracefully to simpler models instead of falling over.

## Telemetry as the nervous system

Amit treats observability as the core of the platform: latency, throughput, accuracy and error rates per stage, distributed tracing to find which microservice is slow, and user corrections fed back into the models. Fault tolerance is designed in from day one, with redundancy across regions, self-healing restarts and load balancing. His point is that resilience is never an accident; it has to be engineered in at the start.

## Where it matters

The case studies are the reason the talk sticks. A hospital system put domain-specific medical translation models on edge nodes inside its hospitals and saw a 35% reduction in critical medical communication errors. Online classrooms added live captioning and translation to video calls. Enterprises embedded translation into Teams and Slack for international meetings. He closes on what comes next: personalised and context-aware translation models, federated learning at the edge, multimodal input, and lower energy use for GPU-heavy workloads.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE engineers who have been handed an "AI feature" with a hard latency budget, and ML engineers who want a checklist of everything their model will depend on in production. It is an architecture overview rather than a code walkthrough, so expect diagrams and principles, not Helm charts.

Title: Healthcare AI fails at deployment, so build the deployment first
Description: Aishwarya Pai (Deloitte) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on a four-phase MLOps framework for getting clinical models into hospitals safely.
Body:
Most healthcare AI projects do not die in the notebook. They die on the way to the ward. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Aishwarya Pai, Senior Consultant at Deloitte, opened with that gap and a blunt figure from her abstract: 68% of healthcare ML projects fail in production. Her answer is a four-phase framework that treats model assessment, infrastructure, pipelines and monitoring as one programme.

It is a short, structured talk, closer to a consultant's playbook than a code walkthrough, and it is honest about that.

## The hard part is not the model

Aishwarya asks the audience a question that frames the rest: which is harder, building the AI model or getting it safely into production? Her view, and probably yours, is deployment. Healthcare adds four hurdles most industries do not stack together:

- **Regulation**, meaning FDA and HIPAA requirements.
- **Sensitive data**, where patient privacy is non-negotiable.
- **Workflow fit**, because doctors cannot be slowed down by clunky systems.
- **Monitoring at scale** across many hospitals, not one tidy environment.

## Four phases, explained as building a hospital

The framework is model assessment, infrastructure readiness, pipeline automation and monitoring. Her analogy is a construction project: check the materials, make sure the building is safe and compliant, automate the elevators and security, then keep the whole thing under round-the-clock surveillance.

**Model assessment** goes past accuracy. Does the model work across different patient groups? Is it fair? Can clinicians understand its decisions, and can you prove all of that to regulators?

**Infrastructure readiness** is about compute, security and HIPAA-compliant data flows, plus integration with EHR systems so the model shows up inside the clinician's existing workflow. Her line here is memorable: trying to run MRI scans on a laptop just won't work.

**Pipeline automation** handles pre-processing and de-identification, training with version control, safe deployments with canary tests and rollbacks, and automatic generation of documentation for regulators. That last item is the one teams forget until an audit arrives.

**Monitoring** tracks accuracy in real time, watches for data drift as patient populations change, and alerts clinicians when something looks wrong. Aishwarya calls this the most critical phase, because it is the one that keeps patients safe after launch.

## A plain stack and a year-long rollout

For the engineers in the room she names the tooling: Git for version control, CI/CD pipelines with approvals, Docker and Kubernetes for deployment, Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring. Nothing exotic, which is rather the point. The difficulty is in the process around the tools, not the tools themselves.

The rollout plan takes about a year. Months one and two assess and plan, three and four build the foundation, five and six pilot a single model, and seven to twelve scale to more hospitals. She leaves the audience with a real trade-off to argue about: a faster pilot, or a more cautious system-wide rollout?

The abstract and slides cite improvements from structured MLOps (higher success rates, faster deployment, annual savings). Treat those as the research figures she presents rather than a single case study you can reproduce; the framework itself is the useful takeaway.

## Who should watch

Engineering leads and consultants starting MLOps work in a hospital system, and anyone who has to explain to a clinical stakeholder why "the model works" is not the same as "the model is ready". If you want deep implementation detail on drift detection or de-identification, pair it with something more hands-on.

Title: A Data Platform Is Abstraction, Automation and a Chargeback Model
Description: Meta engineer Rahul Joshi at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on multi-tenant, self-service data platforms from Hadoop to the lakehouse.
Body:
Rahul Joshi, a software engineer at Meta, used his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 talk to make the case that a shared enterprise data platform lives or dies on four things: abstraction, automation, observability and user experience. Underneath sits a less glamorous requirement that most self-service platforms discover the hard way: a chargeback model, because self-service on a cloud bill with no ceiling is a budget incident waiting to happen.

The talk is a general framework drawn from industry patterns, not a tour of Meta's internal systems, and it's pitched at architects designing or reshaping a multi-tenant data platform.

## Three eras, three lessons

Rahul opens with history. The big data era, from around 2006, built data lakes on Hadoop clusters of commodity hardware, and platform engineers spent their days keeping them running. The cloud era moved that work to managed services such as Redshift, BigQuery and Snowflake, removing operational toil but adding cost optimisation and vendor management. The lakehouse era, with Delta Lake, Iceberg and Hudi, lets one platform serve analytical and operational workloads with strong consistency and governance. Each phase left a lesson that modern designs carry.

## Self-service needs standard patterns and a catalog

The principles section starts with personas: business users, analysts, data scientists and engineers all need interfaces that hide the implementation without hiding the capability. From there:

- **Platform APIs** with clear documentation and versioning, so contracts between producers, consumers and the platform survive schema changes.
- **Standardised processing patterns**, so a thousand use cases don't each re-implement the same reads, joins and flattening.
- **A shared data catalog**, because with hundreds of producing systems, finding data is the first problem.
- **Infrastructure and pipeline automation** for provisioning, promotion from dev through QA and UAT to production, and consistent configuration across environments.

## Tenants, isolation and who pays

Multi-tenancy is the core of the enterprise case: one platform serving many lines of business instead of one platform each. Every tenant gets its own workspace, access controls, compute allocation and data-sharing rules, including geographic restrictions, with both logical and physical isolation of storage and compute where needed.

The cost section names the drivers plainly: compute when data is queried, storage for raw, refined and use-case layers (he references the medallion pattern), and network for transfers. The answer is tracking that attributes cost to teams through chargeback, so each line of business sees what it spends and what it could trim. The levers are scheduling, autoscaling when demand is predictable, and tiered storage such as S3 Intelligent-Tiering or explicit lifecycle and retention rules.

## Observability means data quality, too

Infrastructure monitoring covers health, throughput and utilisation. Data observability adds freshness, schema evolution, missing and duplicate records, schema violations and statistical anomalies, with quality rules run inside the pipelines and tiered alerting by issue type. Security covers encryption at rest, in transit and in memory, masking and tokenisation, and access control from role- and attribute-based down to row and column level. One practical point: SQL access on table formats like Delta Lake or Snowflake gives you usage audit for free, while raw file consumption needs extra tracking.

## Avoid the lock-in you can see coming

For future-proofing, Rahul advises open formats and an abstraction layer so consumers don't notice when storage or compute underneath changes. Plan for terabytes turning into petabytes, as AI workloads keep the data growing, and for governance needs that will change with the business.

## Who should watch

Architects and leads running a central data platform for several teams, especially if the cloud bill and the catalog are both getting out of hand. It's a framework talk; there's no code, but the checklists are solid.

Title: Fraud Hides in the Sequence of Events, So Build a Platform
Description: Rahul Ganti at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on a real-time fraud platform with Kafka, Flink, a feature store and graph features.
Body:
The fraud in Rahul Ganti's case study wasn't in any single transaction. It was in six days of behaviour: small test payments, new payees with names close to existing ones, then a new device and an odd login location. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Rahul, who builds fraud detection at a financial institution he doesn't name, walked through the end-to-end platform that caught it, and argued that beating modern fraud is about engineering platforms, not writing better rules.

## Why rule engines lose

Rules were the long game of cat and mouse played in slow motion: a pattern emerges, analysts write a rule, criminals move on. Rigid thresholds generate false positives that block legitimate customers, a cost his team put at nearly $5 million a year. Rules see one transaction at a time, not the pattern around it, and they didn't scale with digital payments. Rahul also cites FTC data showing that while fraud report counts held steady, the share of people who actually lost money rose from 27% to 38% in a year: attackers are getting better per attempt.

## Five layers that decide in milliseconds

- **Ingestion** of transactions, customer profiles, device data and external threat feeds.
- **Stream processing** with Apache Kafka as the durable log and Apache Flink computing on the streams, so analysis happens in flight.
- **A feature store** with offline and online sides, so training and serving use the same feature logic. This is the guard against training-serving skew, the bug that quietly degrades models without throwing an error.
- **A model registry** as the control plane: multiple live models, A/B tests, gradual rollouts and instant rollbacks.
- **A decision engine** that combines model scores with configurable business rules, so analysts can trigger step-up authentication or flag an account without writing code.

Kafka between all of them keeps the components decoupled.

## Graphs find the network behind the account

The feature engineering is where the case study gets interesting. Streaming aggregations capture behaviour over windows (transaction count in five minutes, average amount over 24 hours). Graph features model customers, accounts and devices as nodes and transactions as edges. In the case study, the payees led to a network of 47 accounts across 12 institutions created in the same two-week window, with circular money flows and shared device fingerprints. Meanwhile login velocity was up 400% against the six-month baseline and behavioural biometrics showed an 85% deviation in mouse patterns. Rahul estimates the response prevented $2.3 million in losses across the affected institutions.

## The rest of the platform

Multi-cloud is deliberate: portability through containers and Kubernetes, failover between providers for a 99.99% availability target, and data residency per jurisdiction. The ML side has a sandbox, distributed GPU training, automated retraining pipelines and serving replicas across zones. Security is defence in depth: zero trust and microsegmentation, encryption, least privilege and full audit logs. Event sourcing gives regulators an append-only history, and sagas keep cross-service transactions consistent without two-phase commits. Federated learning lets institutions train a shared model without exchanging raw customer data, and Rahul is clear it's a big undertaking.

He reports p50 latency of 47 ms and p99 of 89 ms against a 100 ms SLA, and, for a mid-sized bank processing close to $50 billion a year, $27.2 million in prevented annual losses and 52,000 fewer legitimate transactions blocked each day.

## Who should watch

ML and platform engineers in payments or banking, and anyone building real-time decisioning where latency budgets and audit both bite. The feature store and decision engine sections apply well beyond fraud.

Title: ML Network Routing Should Start in Shadow Mode
Description: Rahul Tavva of Kairos Technologies at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on a phased rollout of ML-based routing with BGP and OSPF as the fallback.
Body:
Nobody sane hands their network to a model overnight. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Rahul Tavva, a senior network delivery lead at Kairos Technologies in Dallas, laid out how to bring ML-based routing into production the careful way: telemetry first, then shadow mode, then advisory mode, then automation for low-risk traffic, with classic protocols kept as the safety net throughout.

The talk is short and high level. Its value is the rollout plan and the operational questions, which apply to putting any model in a control loop.

## Why BGP and OSPF aren't enough on their own

Rahul's framing: BGP and OSPF have been reliable for decades, but they run on fixed rules, react only after something breaks, take a while to converge and lean on manual tuning. Cloud, microservices and real-time apps want routing that adapts. ML systems learn from network data, spot patterns, predict trouble and reroute before it happens, balancing speed, cost and reliability, and they can flag unusual patterns that hint at a failure or a security problem.

## The pipeline

The architecture has four parts: telemetry collection (latency, packet loss, throughput, link usage, application patterns, even time of day and scheduled maintenance), a data pipeline that cleans it, a training system that builds, tests and stores models, and an inference system that makes routing decisions in real time. Fallbacks and safety switches sit around all of it.

Training options include supervised learning on past good decisions, reinforcement learning from feedback, and a hybrid that mixes ML with traditional routing, which he recommends as the best fit today.

## Four phases, and the first one changes nothing

1. **Shadow mode**: the model makes decisions on paper only.
2. **Advisory mode**: the model suggests routes and engineers approve them.
3. **Selective automation**: the model takes over certain traffic classes or low-criticality regions.
4. **Full automation**: the model runs routing, with the classic protocols as backup.

If you've done progressive delivery for application code, this is the same idea pointed at the control plane. The difference is that the blast radius is the network.

## The operational questions are the real content

Monitoring an ML router means watching the model, not just the links: accuracy, drift, confidence per decision. Dashboards should show ML and traditional routes side by side and explain why a path was chosen, which is how operators come to trust it.

Security gets its own section: poisoned telemetry can steer routes, and a reverse-engineered model can be exploited, so encrypt telemetry, validate inputs, run anomaly detection and always keep a human override. Runbooks need new entries for what to do when the model makes strange choices, when confidence drops or when telemetry breaks: how to roll back, shift traffic gradually and retrain after an incident.

He cites examples from financial services (latency spikes cut by almost 70%) and e-commerce (page load times down 30% at peak, far fewer manual interventions), alongside the challenges they hit: compliance concerns, false alarms and models degrading during unusual events.

## Who should watch

Network engineers being asked about AIOps, and platform teams that will end up hosting the models. It needs network engineers, data scientists, platform and ops people working together, with cross-training, which is perhaps the most realistic slide in the deck.

Title: Mobile Test Infrastructure Should Be a Product, Not a Service
Description: Cognizant's Charanpreet Singh Hora at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on device clouds, GitOps, feature flags and AI test selection for mobile.
Body:
Every month brings new iOS and Android releases and new devices, and no QA team can buy all of them. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Charanpreet Singh Hora, a Senior Manager at Cognizant with over ten years in mobile automation on device clouds such as Perfecto and BrowserStack, argued that mobile testing should be run as an internal platform product: self-service, API-driven, multi-tenant and governed.

It's an overview talk that maps platform engineering practice onto mobile QA. The abstract promises live demos and data from hundreds of enterprises; the recording is a slide walkthrough, so come for the structure rather than a demo.

## Why siloed QA can't keep up

The problem is combinatorial. Diverse OS versions, native and web apps, a wide spread of screen sizes, varying network conditions, and continuous delivery on top. Siloed QA teams with manually managed devices can't keep pace. The platform answer is devices on demand and testing as a capability teams consume through an API.

## The foundations look like any other platform

Charanpreet's architecture will be familiar to cloud teams:

- **Infrastructure as code** with Terraform across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, with Kubernetes running isolated test containers, so test environments stop drifting.
- **GitOps** for test configuration, automation scripts and infrastructure definitions, with peer review, staging first and progressive rollout of new testing capabilities.
- **Multi-tenancy** with a namespace, resource quota and access controls per team, network segmentation for sensitive test data, and role-based access tied to the enterprise directory, denied by default.

## Run fewer tests, smarter

The AI section focuses on two practical ideas. Predictive models use historical test patterns, release schedules and seasonal traffic to provision device capacity before a crunch and release it in quiet periods. Intelligent test selection picks the minimum suite needed to validate a specific change, so critical flows get tested without running everything on every device.

Compatibility testing goes past functional checks into performance, accessibility and visual regression across device sizes. Device clouds let you pick real devices by region: if your customers are in Australia, test from Australian devices and see their latency.

## Testing doesn't stop at release

The progressive delivery section ties testing to production. Feature flags roll a change to a small percentage of Android or iOS users and widen over weeks. Canary analysis compares control and experiment groups for performance regressions, crash rates and UX degradation. Automated rollback triggers revert a bad change when metrics slip. In other words, the release is the last test stage, and it should have a kill switch.

Industry examples cover financial services (PCI DSS and SOX checks automated as policy as code, generating audit evidence) and e-commerce (traffic simulation of browse, search, cart and checkout journeys, performance budgets that block regressions, and test environments scaled to production load ahead of peaks like Thanksgiving).

## Observability and governance for the test platform itself

The platform needs its own SLOs and error budgets, distributed tracing through test workflows to find bottlenecks, and governance that balances developer autonomy with control: admission policies, resource quotas, budget alerts and regular policy reviews. Developer experience gets REST and GraphQL APIs, SDKs and interactive docs. Future directions include 5G and edge testing and carbon-aware scheduling of heavy test runs.

## Who should watch

QA leads and mobile platform teams planning a move from a device drawer and a shared spreadsheet to a self-service test platform. Experienced platform engineers will know the patterns; the value is seeing them applied to mobile.

Title: Wiring HR Events to Financial Wellness Without Leaking Pay Data
Description: Intuit's Hitesh Pahuja at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on event-driven, privacy-first HCM and FinTech integration for employee financial wellness.
Body:
A raise, a new benefits window or a family change is a moment when an employee's money decisions matter, and the HR system knows about it first. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Hitesh Pahuja, Senior Software Engineering Manager at Intuit working on HCM and FinTech products for small and medium businesses, showed how to connect human capital management (HCM) systems to financial wellness tools with an event-driven, privacy-first architecture, so help arrives at that moment instead of months later.

## Two systems that should talk and usually don't

Hitesh's starting point: financial stress reduces focus, raises healthcare use and drives turnover, yet most enterprise architectures treat workforce management and financial wellness as separate domains. The result is missed chances to intervene when it counts. Any fix has to respect strict privacy rules and still feel smooth across many cross-functional use cases.

## The architecture in four moves

**An orchestration layer that goes beyond ETL**, with privacy by design from day one, because employee pay data is about as sensitive as data gets.

**Event-driven communication.** Salary changes, benefit enrolments, moves (with their effective dates) and performance reviews are events that can trigger a wellness nudge. Kafka is the backbone for a hybrid of synchronous and asynchronous calls. Event sourcing keeps the full history of an employee's journey, stream processing analyses workforce events as they happen, and event schemas are designed to evolve.

**Well-worn integration patterns.** A hexagonal-style core that keeps business logic independent of the many provider integrations, an API gateway for authentication, throttling and monitoring, and circuit breakers so one flaky provider degrades gracefully instead of cascading. Data mesh comes up for organisations with complex data needs.

**Microservices cut by business capability** rather than technical layer, with eventual consistency where the data type allows it and service discovery for scaling.

## Privacy is a design input

The security section is strict, and rightly so. Zero trust: authenticate and authorise every request whatever its source. Encrypt at rest, in transit and, where possible, in use. Use token-based auth with scopes tied to specific data types. And practise data minimisation, exchanging only what a given business function needs. Consent management, retention policies and immutable audit trails are treated as architecture, not paperwork bolted on later.

## AI that nudges instead of nags

The AI section aims at turning reactive programmes into proactive ones: models that spot employees at risk of financial stress from workforce and financial patterns, federated learning so sensitive data doesn't have to be centralised, real-time scoring and a feedback loop that keeps refining accuracy. Personalised nudges then use context (a promotion might mean revisiting retirement contributions; a deadline means a reminder) and reach people through SMS, mobile apps or notifications.

It's the part of the talk where a reader might want more on the guardrails: using sick leave or communication patterns as stress signals is powerful and sensitive, which is exactly why the consent and minimisation sections matter.

## Legacy and load

Most HCM cores are legacy and expensive to upgrade, with old data formats and little real-time integration. The approach is change data capture, a transformation layer between legacy formats and modern APIs, adapters that isolate legacy logic, caching for batch windows, and solid retry and error handling. Performance planning targets payroll runs, quarter end and year end, with multi-tier caching, sharding and CDNs for education content.

Examples are anonymised: a healthcare organisation that started by linking emergency savings to payroll, a tech company with event-driven responses to promotions and equity events, a manufacturer that used adapters to avoid disrupting HR processes, and a financial services firm that leaned on consent management.

## Who should watch

Engineers building integrations between HR, payroll and financial products, and anyone designing event-driven systems over sensitive personal data. The closing principles are a good checklist: start with a core use case and success metrics, design for privacy from the start, use events for responsiveness, keep it modular.

Title: Real-time enterprise intelligence is an MLOps problem, not a BI one
Description: Terance Joseph Paulraj (SQA Concepts) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on moving from backward-looking reports to streaming, governed AI decisions.
Body:
Traditional business intelligence answers "what happened?" and leaves you to work out what to do about it, usually after the moment has passed. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Terance Joseph Paulraj, Senior Data and BI Architect at SQA Concepts, argued that real-time enterprise intelligence only works when models, MLOps practice, streaming and governance are built as one system, and he laid out a staged roadmap for getting there.

Terance brings close to 25 years of building data systems for large organisations, and the talk reads like it: less about any single model, more about the plumbing and the order you build it in.

## The weekly report is already out of date

The framing is simple. A daily, weekly or monthly report describes a world that has already changed by the time a leader reads it. Real-time intelligence processes continuous data streams as they arrive, layers predictive analytics (what is likely to happen) and prescriptive analytics (what to do next) on top, and automates some of the resulting actions. His example is the obvious one: a fraud system that blocks suspicious activity without waiting for a human to open a dashboard.

The building blocks he names are familiar to anyone who has run a streaming stack: distributed processing with tools like Kafka and Spark Streaming, models ranging from plain statistics to deep learning, and automated decision workflows driven by rule engines and reinforcement learning.

## Four parts, and missing one breaks the lot

The sharpest slide in the talk is a four-way intersection: AI models, MLOps practices, real-time processing and governance. Models without MLOps stay in research. Real-time processing without governance gives you fast decisions nobody can explain. Terance's point is that all four have to meet, and that "missing even one piece weakens the system."

He pairs this with a maturity path most enterprises will recognise. First come scattered pilots owned by different teams, duplicating effort. Then integrated platforms with shared infrastructure and connected pipelines. Only at the last stage do insights from one domain, say supply chain, feed directly into another, like finance.

## Match the automation to the risk

The most practical part is a three-tier model for how much a machine should decide on its own:

- **Full automation** for high-volume, low-risk calls such as spam filtering or flagging duplicate records.
- **Human in the loop** for medium-risk decisions like loan approvals, where the model recommends and a person approves.
- **AI-augmented** decisions for high stakes, where the model highlights areas on a scan and the doctor still makes the call.

It is a useful antidote to the "automate everything" pitch, and it maps cleanly onto how you would design approval gates in a pipeline.

On the delivery side he walks through CI for models and data pipelines, CD with validation gates, feature flags and canary deployments for new models, and monitoring that tracks business outcomes and data drift, not just uptime. The architecture slide stacks containers, Kubernetes, serverless and infrastructure as code under an event-streaming backbone, feature stores, lakehouse patterns and data contracts.

## A roadmap in months, not slogans

Terance closes with a phased plan: foundation in three to six months (MLOps infrastructure, governance, streaming, a first model catalogue), integration in six to twelve (connect models to real systems, automate low-risk decisions, add monitoring and retraining), then expansion in twelve to twenty-four months with reinforcement learning and natural language interfaces. The advice underneath is to start small, prove value on early use cases and expand step by step, which is boring and correct.

He also covers natural language interfaces as the bridge for people who would rather ask "what were our sales last week?" than write SQL, and a section on responsible AI: governance, bias testing, explainability and compliance with rules like GDPR, plus the honest admission that the most accurate model is not always the fairest.

## Who should watch

Data and BI architects trying to turn a dashboard estate into something that acts, and platform leads who need a vocabulary for selling a phased MLOps programme upward. If you already run streaming feature pipelines in production, this is a high-level overview rather than an implementation guide.

Title: Self-service ML platforms work when governance is built in first
Description: Rajeev Chevuri (Freddie Mac) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on self-service ML platforms for financial services, with governance designed into every layer.
Body:
Data scientists want to ship models without filing tickets, and regulators want to know who approved every model and which data trained it. Rajeev Chevuri, a senior cloud DevOps engineer on Freddie Mac's enterprise data science platform, argues at Conf42 MLOps 2025 that a self-service ML platform can satisfy both, as long as governance is designed in from the start rather than bolted on later.

It is an architecture talk aimed at banks and other regulated institutions, with a build-versus-buy section and a 90-day roadmap at the end.

## From laptop experiments to platforms

Rajeev describes the usual maturity path in financial services. Teams start with siloed experiments: models built in isolation with no path to production, manual and error-prone deployments, and results nobody can reproduce, because what worked on one laptop fails in production. Governance is ad hoc. Integrated platforms that cover the whole ML lifecycle bring consistency, automation and auditability, and he credits them with big reductions in data preparation time and training cost and better deployment success rates.

## Three layers and four pillars

His reference architecture has three layers. The foundation is infrastructure: scalable CPUs and GPUs, resilient storage and secure networking, with Kubernetes doing the standardising whether you run in the cloud, on-premises or hybrid. Above it sits data and feature management: ingestion, validation, versioning and a feature store for consistency and reuse, all auditable. On top is ML lifecycle management: experimentation, training, versioning, deployment and monitoring.

Four components carry the weight. Container orchestration schedules ML workloads as custom resources so they run the same everywhere, with isolation between tenants. Distributed compute with Spark and Dask handles large data with lineage tracking, so every transformation can be traced. A model registry stores models with compliance metadata (who trained them, on what data, when) and cryptographic checks so nothing tampered goes live. CI/CD gates deployments behind tests, security scans and approvals.

## Governance is a layer, not a review meeting

The governance layer has three parts. Automated policy enforcement applies access controls and security at runtime, so a misconfiguration by a data scientist does not become a compliance incident. Compliance documentation, including model cards, lineage diagrams and validation reports, is generated automatically as evidence instead of written by hand. Audit observability captures logs, monitoring data and explainability outputs, so when a regulator asks why a model made a decision, the answer is already there.

For developers, the experience is curated environments with pre-approved packages, templates for consistency, and one-click deployment to staging with compliance checks and monitoring wired in.

## Build, buy or both

Rajeev's build-versus-buy comparison is useful for planning. Building in-house gives full customisation and legacy integration but typically takes 12 to 18 months and a specialised team. Commercial platforms deliver in three to six months with compliance features built in, at the price of vendor lock-in. A hybrid (vendor core plus your own governance and integrations) lands in six to nine months, and he sees it as the best balance for most financial organisations.

He closes with what is next, including edge inference, enterprise AutoML with explainability built in, serverless training and privacy-preserving ML with federated learning. His 90-day roadmap is practical: audit current ML workflows and compliance gaps, design requirements with both technical and regulatory teams, prototype with a small team, and deliver a minimum viable platform focused on the highest-friction areas, measured by deployment time and user satisfaction.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers and ML infrastructure leads in banking, insurance or any audited industry, and anyone writing the business case for an internal ML platform. If you already run one, the governance layer and build-buy numbers make a good checklist.

Title: Regulatory Submissions Speed Up When Documents Become Components
Description: Satish Babu Golla at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on structured content, reusable blocks and workflow automation for life sciences submissions.
Body:
In drug development, the bottleneck often isn't the science but the paperwork. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Satish Babu Golla, who has spent nine-plus of his 17 years in IT implementing Veeva Vault for pharma clients including BMS and Pfizer, argued that treating regulatory documents as structured, reusable components (and running them on a shared platform) is what shortens the road from trial to patient.

It's a short talk and an unusual one for a platform engineering conference: the platform here is a content platform, and the users are regulatory and clinical teams rather than developers.

## Documents are the slow path

Satish starts with the cost of the status quo. In his telling, about 40% of a therapy's long road to market goes to managing documentation, a single clinical document can go through six to eight review cycles, and every day of delay costs money and keeps patients waiting. Clinical, regulatory and commercial teams work in isolation, so a small content change triggers a full re-approval, and each country needs its own localised version.

Anyone who has watched a monolithic config file get re-reviewed from top to bottom for a one-line change will recognise the pattern.

## Content as components

The fix borrows directly from software. Break documents into reusable building blocks that adapt to each market without starting from scratch. Automate workflows so reviews run in parallel instead of in sequence. Add an integration layer that connects clinical, regulatory, safety and commercial functions. On top, AI-powered quality checks catch errors before they block a submission, cloud collaboration lets global teams edit the same content in real time, and real-world data lets documents update as safety data changes.

## Two case studies

The first is a submission during a global health emergency that would normally take six months and was completed in eight days, using pre-approved templates, parallel workflows across 22 agencies, real-time collaboration and automated localisation. The second is a mid-sized biopharma launching in 18 markets with a small regulatory team, cutting localisation timelines by 40% through platform authoring, reusable submission components and automated translation. The talk doesn't name the companies.

He also lists headline impact figures (faster document lifecycles, fewer findings, savings per therapy) and a forecast that AI-drafted structured content will save a large share of authoring time. Treat those as his estimates rather than measured results from a specific rollout.

## Rare diseases and the roadmap

For rare diseases, where speed matters most, he describes adaptive trial documents that update as patient data changes, patient-reported outcomes integrated directly, and real-time reviews with agencies.

The roadmap is sensibly incremental: assess pain points, build the platform foundation and governance, integrate clinical, safety and regulatory systems, then scale and bring in AI. He's candid that the hard part is cultural. Authors become content engineers and have to learn structured authoring and new workflows, which needs executive backing.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects working in or selling into pharma, and platform teams curious how "golden paths" and reuse look outside software delivery. If you want Kubernetes manifests, this isn't that talk. His practical homework: benchmark your document cycle times, find reuse opportunities, map your stack, start with high-value areas and roll out in phases.

Title: LabCorp Put Master Data Management on a Permissioned Blockchain
Description: LabCorp's Chandra Adapa at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on Hyperledger Fabric, IPFS and attribute-based encryption for enterprise MDM.
Body:
Master data (patient identities, customer and product records) is the layer every other system trusts, which makes a centralised MDM database both a bottleneck and a single, very attractive target. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Chandra Adapa, Principal Enterprise Architect at LabCorp, described how his team rebuilt MDM on a permissioned blockchain, and reported production figures of over 3,000 transactions per second at 99.9% uptime.

Blockchain talks often stay theoretical. This one is a production architecture with a phased rollout, deployment strategy and incident process, which is why it's worth the time even if you're a sceptic.

## Four problems with centralised MDM

Chandra lists the pain points of traditional MDM once an enterprise spans geographies, clouds and dozens of applications. Consistency: two systems update the same customer at once and you get conflicts and drift. Security: one breach of the central store hands an attacker all master data. Performance: the system slows as data grows. Compliance: regulated industries need audit trails and lineage that legacy platforms bolt on afterwards.

His argument is that a ledger's core properties map onto those one by one: immutability for audit, consensus so no single system (or administrator) decides alone, cryptography for authenticity, and shared visibility so parties stop arguing over whose copy is right.

## The stack

- **Hyperledger Fabric** as the permissioned ledger, with business logic in chaincode smart contracts.
- **PBFT consensus**, which he notes tolerates up to a third of nodes being compromised.
- **Attribute-based encryption** so policy decides access at the data level. His example: only doctors with an oncology specialisation and an active licence can read oncology data, and access changes the moment someone's status does.
- **IPFS** for large objects, with only their cryptographic fingerprints on-chain to keep the ledger lean.
- **OAuth 2.0, JWT and TLS 1.3** for authentication, sessions and transport; AES-256 at rest.
- REST and GraphQL APIs on top, Redis caches in the data layer, and Kubernetes across availability zones underneath.

Zero-knowledge proofs cover the most sensitive operations, letting someone prove authorisation without revealing the data.

## Rolled out like any risky platform change

The team didn't jump straight to production. A proof of concept tested CRUD operations, consensus and performance; a pilot ran real workloads, tuned throughput and introduced attribute-based encryption; production added infrastructure as code, monitoring and disaster recovery.

Deployments use blue-green environments, canary releases for new smart contracts with automatic rollback, and feature flags. Monitoring covers infrastructure, application metrics and blockchain-specific signals such as consensus participation, block propagation times and chain growth. Incidents get ML-based anomaly detection, clear escalation paths and post-mortems that feed the runbooks.

On compliance, smart contracts enforce retention rules automatically, every access is logged immutably, and lineage traces each record from creation to use. He mentions right-to-be-forgotten support through cryptographic deletion, which answers the obvious question about immutable ledgers and GDPR. Results he quotes, beyond throughput and uptime, include a 60% improvement in data access.

## Who should watch

Data platform architects in healthcare, finance or supply chains who need tamper-evident audit and multi-party trust, and anyone who wants to see what a production Hyperledger Fabric deployment looks like end to end. If your MDM lives inside one organisation with one trusted admin team, you may decide the consensus overhead isn't worth it; the talk gives you enough detail to make that call.

Title: Treat the Cache as Self-Healing Infrastructure, Not a Tweak
Description: Roku's Shailin Saraiya at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on layered, ML-tuned caching that heals itself and stays simple for developers.
Body:
Caching usually gets filed under small optimisations to tune later. Shailin Saraiya, Senior Software Engineering Manager at Roku, spent his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 talk arguing the opposite: treated as a platform, caching becomes a self-healing infrastructure component that cuts latency, protects databases and lets traffic grow without the on-call rota growing with it.

His opening lesson sets the tone: anyone can provision more servers, but real scale comes from systems that are resilient, adaptive and simple for developers to use.

## Static TTLs are where the pain starts

The problem list will be familiar to anyone who has run a busy service. Databases hit connection limits at peak. APIs that were fast at low load start timing out. Teams lose days firefighting instead of shipping. Traditional caching helps a bit, but static TTLs either expire data too soon (wasted recomputation) or keep it too long (stale answers). Scaling is manual and reactive, and observability is poor enough that users notice before engineers do.

## Five principles for a cache that runs itself

Shailin's target state rests on five ideas:

1. **Self-service**: adding caching to an API should be a config change or an annotation, not weeks of distributed-systems work.
2. **Intelligence**: when a launch in Europe sends traffic surging at 3 AM local time, the system rebalances on its own.
3. **Self-healing**: when a node dies or a replica lags, the platform promotes replicas, reroutes and rebuilds state from logs instead of paging someone at 2 AM.
4. **Observability**: automation with dashboards, metrics and recommendations, never blind.
5. **Effortless scaling**: double the traffic should not mean double the operational work.

## Layers, events and a mesh

The architecture stacks four caching tiers: database caches, a distributed key-value tier (Redis is his example), in-memory application caches, and edge caches near users. Four principles hold it together: service-mesh integration for discovery, retries and circuit breaking; event-driven updates from streams rather than polling, which enables async warming and state reconstruction from event logs; directory-based coherency for invalidation across thousands of nodes; and the layering itself, so no single tier becomes the bottleneck.

Implementation follows the same theme. Cache infrastructure is declared and rolled out through GitOps with zero downtime. Developers get annotation-style APIs. Failures are detected in milliseconds and handled by replica promotion and rerouting.

## Let models set the TTL

The ML section is the distinctive part. Predictive warming loads data before the request arrives, based on history, popularity and time of day. Adaptive TTLs adjust expiry to how volatile the data is. Anomaly detection catches odd traffic, potential cache-poisoning attempts and degradations early. He mentions neural networks for access prediction, reinforcement learning to tune eviction for hit ratio, and clustering to group workloads for targeted warming.

At the edge, the hard parts are coherency (eventual consistency, vector clocks, read repair), small nodes (dynamic sizing, smarter eviction, compression) and partitions, where edge caches keep serving and reconcile later.

Observability goes past p50/p95/p99 and hit ratios into insight: flagging that hit rates fell after a deploy, or suggesting an endpoint worth caching. The abstract quotes an 83% latency drop, 6.5x user growth and 97% hit rates; the talk itself stays at the level of patterns, so watch it for the design rather than a benchmark breakdown.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers whose databases sweat at peak, and anyone building caching as a shared service. The culture section (shared ownership, data-driven decisions, incremental migration with legacy support) is short but on point: hot keys are solvable, organisational resistance takes longer.

Title: Mortgage MLOps can't move fast and break things
Description: Naganarendar Chitturi (Newrez) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on MLOps for autonomous mortgage AI, where explainability is legally required and models shadow whole loans.
Body:
In mortgage lending, breaking things means someone does not get their home or your company faces fair-lending fines. Naganarendar Chitturi, Senior Automation Architect at Newrez, uses that to explain at Conf42 MLOps 2025 why standard MLOps had to be reworked for autonomous mortgage AI, and how it can still shrink a 30-to-60-day loan process to three to five days.

This is one of the more grounded talks of the event: a regulated domain, legacy systems, and concrete patterns for each.

## 47 steps and a weekend in a queue

Naganarendar starts with the process. A straightforward purchase loan has 47 distinct steps. An application submitted on Friday evening waits in a queue until Monday, employment verification means calling an HR department that may reply on Tuesday, the appraisal is booked for the following week, and bank statements are reviewed line by line. Every step touches different people and systems that do not talk to each other.

The data is just as messy: structured credit bureau feeds, unstructured tax returns and bank statements, real-time property valuations, and loan data in mainframe systems from the 1980s with batch files and formats older than the web. Much of the AI, he says, exists purely to translate between modern pipelines and those systems.

## Explainability is the law here

The regulatory point is what makes mortgage ML different. If you deny a loan, you must give specific, understandable reasons that regulators can audit, so every decision must trace back through the pipeline with full lineage. He recalls an examiner asking about one loan decision from 18 months earlier. With the right architecture he could pull up, in seconds, which models were involved, what data they used, which business rules fired, and the exact versions that were live.

His team's answer is compliance-first feature engineering: every feature pipeline automatically includes bias detection, PII anonymisation and audit trail generation, and the feature code produces documentation compliance officers can use in regulatory submissions.

## Validate across groups, shadow across loan lifecycles

Training is optimised for fairness, explainability and compliance alongside accuracy. He describes regulatory-aware cross-validation, where validation sets are built to test performance across demographic groups, geographic regions and market conditions.

The deployment pattern is the one to remember. Because a loan takes weeks to close, a bad model may not show its damage for weeks. So new models run in extended shadow mode next to production for complete loan lifecycles before any traffic moves. That is a much longer canary than most teams would tolerate, and in this domain it is the right one.

## Documents are the hard part

Document processing is, in his words, one of the most complex parts of the system. PDFs arrive scanned at odd angles, bank statements come in hundreds of formats, pay stubs vary by employer and by year. They use an ensemble of OCR models because no single one handles every document type, plus named entity recognition trained for financial documents that knows gross from net income. Separate model versions handle older and newer document layouts, since applicants submit historical paperwork.

Privacy-by-design pipelines identify and mask PII automatically and log every access. The credit scoring model never sees raw bank statements, only engineered financial-behaviour features from the feature store. Storage is tiered into hot (under 50 ms retrieval for live decisions), warm for training, and cold for long-term regulatory retention. During peaks they make tens of thousands of external API calls an hour to bureaus and verification services, each with its own quirks and outages.

He also mentions results from his work: savings he puts at $8 million, and a generative AI chatbot that handles about 60% of customer service inquiries.

## Who should watch

ML engineers in lending, insurance, banking or any field where a model decision can be challenged in front of a regulator. The shadow-for-a-full-lifecycle pattern and compliance-first features are useful well beyond mortgages.

Title: Architect for Provability, Not Just Compliance
Description: UBS's Satish Manchana at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025: policy engines, golden images and CI gates that make compliance provable in hybrid cloud.
Body:
Satish Manchana, a product owner at UBS with more than two decades in financial organisations, put the core idea of his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 talk in one sentence: we architect for high availability and performance, so we should also architect for provability. Applying a control is half the job; the platform has to show how and when it was applied, to a regulator, on demand.

Most platform engineers already know how to automate infrastructure. His point is that the hard part is doing it under SOX, GDPR, MiFID II and DORA at the same time, across continents.

## Regulations turn into engineering requirements

The talk gets specific fast. MiFID II wants trade events timestamped with millisecond accuracy, which means "NTP is running" is not an answer. You need timestamp logging, regular validation of NTP drift and retained logs for audit. Nobody verifies that by hand across hundreds of thousands of servers, so Satish's framing is that compliance is a data problem: the right telemetry, stored the right way, at the right time.

He's also honest about how they got here. Silos first, then shadow PowerShell scripts and Ansible roles to dodge the bottlenecks, then DevOps pipelines that were fast but each one bespoke (Jenkins here, GitLab there, AWS and VMware in between). At audit time there was no single baseline to point at. Platform engineering was the step that made the baseline a product.

## Four building blocks

**Provisioning frameworks.** Nothing gets deployed outside a policy-enforced path. Requests are declared as code (Terraform, plus Bicep and ARM templates on Azure) and pass through a policy engine: encryption at rest disabled means rejected; a public IP on a regulated subnet means rejected. Predefined landing zones ship with network topology, IAM, monitoring and logging already wired in. The lesson he stresses most: keep the policy engine independent of the IaC code, in its own repository, so when a regulator changes an encryption rule you update one place instead of rewriting Terraform modules everywhere.

**Golden images.** The pipeline starts from a vendor ISO, applies CIS Level 1 hardening and logging configuration, embeds agents for malware, file integrity, time sync, backup and endpoint protection, then runs vulnerability scans. Only passing images get versioned, signed, timestamped and published. Images rebuild on a fixed cadence (every two weeks in his example) with emergency rebuilds for events like WannaCry, so live servers get replaced rather than patched in place. Drift control uses PowerShell DSC, Azure DSC and Ansible.

**CI/CD gates.** Policy tests run like unit tests on every IaC change and fail with a precise reason, which also teaches engineers the regulatory intent. The same policies run periodically against deployed workloads to catch drift.

**Policy as code.** Rules live in Git with pull requests, reviews and tests, using tools such as HashiCorp Sentinel, OPA, AWS Config and Azure Policy. When a regulator asks when a rule changed and why, the answer is the commit history. A nice side effect: risk teams and engineers finally share one artifact, so neither has to read the other's native format.

## Self-service is the enforcement mechanism

The catalog offers pre-approved environment types, each a wrapper around the compliant provisioning path, golden image and policy runtime. Every resource carries metadata: who requested it, which policy version applied, which controls ran. His sharpest observation is that the faster self-service gets, the less incentive anyone has to bypass it.

In the case study, one type of server had been built at least six different ways depending on the region. Consolidating into one image pipeline and one policy engine cut provisioning from days to under an hour and reduced audit findings, and the risk function grew comfortable delegating control to engineering.

## Who should watch

Platform teams in banking, insurance, healthcare or anywhere with external auditors. If you're designing a policy-as-code rollout, the "separate policy from IaC" advice alone justifies the time.

Title: Before you repatriate, consider sky computing
Description: Brian Irish (Ditto) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on sky computing and SkyPilot, an intercloud broker approach to vendor lock-in, egress fees and GPU scarcity.
Body:
Plenty of companies hit by a shocking cloud bill are moving workloads back on-prem. Brian Irish, an engineering lead at Ditto with years as an SRE behind him, argues at Conf42 MLOps 2025 that many of them never set up basic cost controls in the first place, and that the better answer is sky computing: treat all clouds as one pool and let a broker place each workload where it runs best.

The talk introduces the idea from Ion Stoica's paper at UC Berkeley, frames it in three pillars of Brian's own, and then shows what it looks like in practice with SkyPilot, the open-source intercloud broker from Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab.

## Repatriation is often a missed cost review

Brian credits the cloud with keeping its promises of on-demand scale, pay-as-you-go pricing and global reach, then lists the drawbacks: vendor lock-in, data gravity and egress charges that surprise everyone. He cites a survey finding that 42% of US organisations are considering or have already moved at least half their cloud workloads back on-premises.

His question is whether those companies planned their cloud usage with cost in mind or just reacted to the invoice. He suspects the latter: no automatic shutdown of dev environments after hours, no spot instances for batch work, no resource quotas. Stepping back to on-prem, he suggests, might not be a step forward.

## Three pillars of sky computing

These are Brian's framing, and he is clear they are his, not the paper's. Abstraction is the glue: Kubernetes, Ray and S3-compatible APIs hide which cloud your data and compute live on, across AWS, GCP and Azure and neoclouds like Lambda Labs and CoreWeave. Automation is the intercloud broker deciding workload placement on price, availability and regulatory needs. He calls it the largest pillar and the hardest to get right. Agility depends on reciprocal peering agreements between providers that make data transfer free or cheap, which would break down egress fees and data gravity.

## SkyPilot is the broker you can use today

SkyPilot is where the talk becomes practical. Brian walks through its claims, which come from the project and its case studies rather than his own benchmarks: a unified interface to many clouds plus Kubernetes and on-prem, big savings from spot orchestration, fast GPU provisioning, faster checkpointing with cached mounts, and no code changes for existing ML workloads. You write one YAML file and run one launch command.

He quotes the Abridge case study, where a team moving off a Slurm cluster got interactive GPU shells with a single launch command, Jupyter notebooks on GPU clusters, managed jobs that restart automatically on failure, and models exposed as FastAPI services for quick evaluation, which Slurm does not offer natively. The distributed training YAML he shows is short: plain PyTorch and Hugging Face, with SkyPilot filling in node counts, GPUs and IP addresses.

## Split the pipeline across clouds

The payoff for ML is placing each stage where it fits best. His example: training on Google Cloud TPUs, inference on AWS Inferentia for lower latency, and preprocessing on Azure because it is often cheaper, with data residency rules respected along the way. That is hard to do by hand and routine with a broker.

He ends with honest obstacles. Universal standards across clouds are unlikely given competitive interests, though Kubernetes, Ray and S3 APIs get you a long way. Hyperscalers have every reason to resist peering agreements that cut egress revenue. Sky computing works with that friction rather than waiting for it to vanish.

## Who should watch

ML platform teams fighting GPU scarcity or single-cloud bills, and SREs asked to evaluate repatriation. It is part concept talk, part SkyPilot introduction, and Brian is upfront that it was his first time recording with OBS, so forgive a glitch or two.

Title: An Internal Developer Platform Playbook That Starts Narrow
Description: Micron's Kommireddy Veera Venkata Subrahmanyam at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025: IDP components, tooling, metrics and why to start small.
Body:
Kommireddy Veera Venkata Subrahmanyam, a senior manager at Micron Technologies, opened his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 talk with a claim most platform teams will recognise: engineering teams spend around 40% of their time on infrastructure work, and an internal developer platform (IDP) can claw a large part of that back. The rest of the talk is a compact playbook for building one, ending on the advice that matters most: start with a narrow scope and grow.

His day job gives the talk a practical slant. His team supports enterprise applications such as Teamcenter and Rapid Response, builds RPA bots with UiPath and ships Power BI and Tableau dashboards, which is a lot of different toolchains for one group to keep consistent.

## The tax developers pay before writing code

The problem section lists the familiar costs: disconnected tools, repetitive manual tasks, no standardisation (so quality varies and knowledge stays in heads), resistance to new workflows, and the extra complexity of microservices and multi-cloud deployments across AWS, Azure and the rest. All of it lands as cognitive overhead, which slows delivery and stretches time to market.

The IDP answer is to put developers "in the driver's seat": automate the manual work, offer clear APIs and interfaces, ship prebuilt services and workflows, and instrument everything so the platform team can see what helps.

## Three components, then a shopping list

Kommireddy breaks an IDP into three core pieces:

1. **Self-service infrastructure**, to cut wait times and remove ticket-shaped bottlenecks.
2. **An integrated toolkit**: version control, security scanning, performance testing, compliance checks and deployment automation in one path.
3. **Observability**: logs, metrics and traces, plus anomaly detection and proactive alerting.

He then maps tools to each layer. Kubernetes, Terraform and Crossplane for infrastructure; Argo CD, Tekton, GitHub Actions and Jenkins X for CI/CD; Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry and Datadog for observability; Backstage for the service catalog; Vault, OPA and Snyk for security. It's a sensible default stack if you need a starting list to argue about.

## Measure the platform like a product

The strategy section is where the talk earns its keep. Track active users, deployment time and platform usage, but also productivity and satisfaction. Run a feedback loop: collect usage data, errors and performance metrics, gather developer feedback, analyse the patterns, communicate the plan, deliver, repeat. Platform teams that skip the "communicate the plan" step tend to discover their roadmap was a secret.

He also draws a clean line between disciplines. Platform engineering measures productivity and adoption, SRE measures uptime and latency, DevOps measures MTTR and deploy frequency. They overlap, but each has its own scoreboard.

## Three stories, light on detail

The success stories are anonymised: an e-commerce chain that standardised environments, CI/CD and observability and reported tripled feature velocity and 75% fewer production bugs; a financial services firm that embedded compliance as policy as code and halved its regulatory overhead; and a startup that invested early in golden paths and automated onboarding while growing from 10 to a hundred users. Treat these as illustrations of the pattern rather than case studies you can audit.

## Who should watch

Managers and leads making the case for a platform team, or teams in their first year of one. It's an overview, not a build log, so experienced Backstage operators can skip it. The closing advice is the part to keep: clear vision, narrow scope, measure, iterate.

Title: Forecasting Models Fail in Deployment, Not in the Notebook
Description: Amazon's Shivendra Kumar at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on platform-first forecasting: microservices, APIs and asymmetric error costs.
Body:
Shivendra Kumar, who leads a team of demand planners and forecasters at Amazon, made one argument at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 that is worth the whole talk: a moderately accurate forecast that ships reliably every week beats a brilliant model that never leaves a research notebook. Everything else in "Platform-First Forecasting" is about building the platform that gets models out of the notebook and into decisions.

He comes at it with about 13 years in planning, supply chain and S&OP across Caterpillar, Dell and Amazon, so the framing is practitioner first.

## Accuracy is one metric among five

Most forecasting teams report MAPE or RMSE and call it a day. Shivendra lists what the business actually judges a forecast on:

- **Business alignment**: does the number come with context? Is it high against last week, low against the same week last year, growing at the rate the business expects?
- **Operational efficiency**: good science with a bad deployment gets perceived as a bad model.
- **Reliability and consistency**: output every week, through peak and off-peak, with a plan for the periods where it degrades.
- **User satisfaction**: are planners using it to make decisions?

The line about bad deployments is the one that will sting anyone who has watched a strong model lose trust because the Monday run failed twice.

## Put the business's risk appetite in the loss function

The most useful section is on asymmetric error handling. A single-number forecast hides the fact that over-forecasting and under-forecasting cost different amounts. For some products stockouts are expensive and spare inventory is cheap; for others excess stock is the disaster. Capacity planning has the same shape: overbuild and you carry depreciation, underbuild and service degrades. Financial forecasting trades compliance effort against speed.

His conclusion is that loss functions should reflect real business consequences, not mathematical convenience, and that the platform has to take that feedback in. If your model treats a missed sale and an overstocked pallet as the same error, it is optimising something nobody asked for.

## Decompose the monolith into four services

The architecture section splits a forecasting system into microservices: data ingestion (sources with daily or hourly cadence, quality checks), feature engineering, model training, and prediction serving with low-latency interfaces. Supporting pieces include Kafka-style stream processing, security controls and feature stores. Containerisation follows the workload: horizontal pod autoscaling, persistent storage planned for a dataset that will keep growing for years, and batch jobs where consumers only need yesterday's published version rather than a fresh query over billions of rows.

APIs get the same discipline: versioned, RESTful, with flexible request schemas, per-profile authorisation and progressive disclosure of complexity, so a new user isn't handed every knob on day one.

## Lego blocks for very different SKUs

In the e-commerce example, forecasting pens and forecasting couches need different methods, data and users. Building the system as reusable blocks lets each use case assemble only what it needs. Logistics works the same way: first, middle and last mile each have their own customers, on shared foundations. The abstract's revenue figure isn't something the talk walks through, so take the architecture as the takeaway.

## Who should watch

Data scientists who wonder why their models aren't adopted, and platform engineers asked to host ML workloads. It moves fast (he admits the time was short for the topic), so expect principles over code.

Title: Self-healing data pipelines detect, diagnose and fix with AI
Description: Lakshmi Srinivasarao Kothamasu (Fidelity Investments) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on AI anomaly detection, LLM root cause and automated pipeline repair.
Body:
With enough interconnected jobs, at least one pipeline failure a day is close to guaranteed. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Lakshmi Srinivasarao Kothamasu, Principal Data Engineer at Fidelity Investments, made the case for pipelines that detect their own anomalies, diagnose the root cause with language models and apply the fix, turning data engineers from firefighters into supervisors of an autonomous system.

## Firefighting is the default, and it's expensive

Lakshmi draws on more than 20 years of building enterprise data lakes and analytics platforms, on-premises and in the cloud. His starting point: even with modern orchestrators and cloud-native platforms, pipeline failures remain a constant production pain. A small schema mismatch, a network blip or a configuration change breaks downstream workflows, and the cost lands as lost revenue, compliance violations and decisions made on stale data. He says around 60% of platform engineers' operational bandwidth goes on troubleshooting and recovery. Traditional monitoring tells you something failed; the remediation is still manual, and the logs you need are scattered across systems for an engineer to stitch together.

## Four capabilities, one loop

The self-healing pipeline he describes runs a detect, analyse, fix, learn loop:

- **Anomaly detection.** Transformer-based models watch metrics, logs and data quality checks for abnormal behaviour.
- **Root cause analysis.** Language models such as GPT-4 read logs, trace dependency graphs and propose the most probable cause.
- **Autonomous remediation.** Reinforcement learning agents or rule-based automation take the corrective action.
- **Continuous learning** from past failures, successful repairs and human feedback.

Architecturally, he offers three ways to deploy it: a centralised AI layer, decentralised agents embedded in pipelines, or a hybrid.

## Three domains, three flavours of failure

The case studies show how the same loop adapts. A global retailer ingesting around two terabytes of data kept hitting failures from schema changes and traffic spikes, delaying product availability online. With AI detection identifying schema mismatches and automated workflow recovery, Lakshmi reports recovery dropping from about two hours to five minutes.

In healthcare, an LLM parses logs to find authentication failures and misconfigured policies, the system isolates failing nodes and reroutes data, and higher-risk actions go to engineers for review. Recovery time fell by 70%, and because every AI-driven action was logged, compliance audits held up.

In a fintech running real-time fraud detection, where even short outages are dangerous, reinforcement learning agents shift compute to fraud models when volume spikes and fail over to backup pipelines without human intervention.

## Guardrails are part of the design

Lakshmi is clear that autonomy needs supervision. Every remediation is logged with an explanation, industry regulations shape what the system may do on its own, and engineers keep a supervisory role over high-impact fixes. Building trust takes transparency, continuous monitoring and cultural change, not just a better model.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers who own on-call for pipelines and want a structure for automating the routine fixes without losing auditability. It's a short talk that stays at the architecture and case-study level; the domain comparisons are the most useful part.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [AI-Driven Self-Healing Infrastructure: The Next Evolution of SRE](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Vijaybhasker_Pagidoju_selfhealing_infrastructure) by Vijaybhasker Pagidoju, the same idea one layer down.
