Title: Healthcare Interoperability Is a Platform Problem, Built in Layers
Description: Gunjan Desai Rajendrakumar (UT Austin) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on a layered, FHIR-first platform for healthcare data exchange.
Body:
A patient arrives in the emergency room and nobody can see their allergies. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Gunjan Desai Rajendrakumar of The University of Texas at Austin argued that this is a platform engineering problem: point-to-point integrations between hospital systems don't scale, and the fix is a layered exchange platform that speaks FHIR at the edge and keeps every concern in its own lane.

It's a short, architecture-level talk, closer to a reference design than a war story, and that's what makes it useful as a map.

## Point-to-point integration is the thing that breaks

The opening framing is blunt. Healthcare data lives in legacy EHRs, lab systems, imaging systems and personal apps, in formats ranging from HL7 FHIR to custom schemas. Wiring each system to every other one works for a clinic and collapses for a regional network. The cost of that collapse shows up as duplicate tests and doctors deciding without the history in front of them.

So the talk treats interoperability the way a platform team treats any shared capability: build it once, expose it through a contract, and let applications rely on the contract instead of the plumbing.

## Four layers, four jobs

The architecture splits into layers that each own one problem:

- **Ingestion** connects to the diverse source systems through standardized connectors.
- **Transformation** normalizes formats, and this is where AI earns its place: machine learning and NLP speed up schema mapping, which is traditionally slow manual work, and turn free-text clinical notes into something searchable.
- **Orchestration** validates business rules, checks consent and resolves conflicts.
- **Application interface** exposes FHIR-compliant APIs that apps can build on, including SMART-on-FHIR patient apps.

The point of the separation is that a specialist, a family doctor and an ER physician end up reading the same record instead of three partial copies. Underneath sit the usual cloud-native tools: microservices on Kubernetes, serverless for spiky workloads, and infrastructure as code for consistency and compliance.

## Security is role-shaped, because care is role-shaped

The security section is the most healthcare-specific part. Access is fine-grained and role-based because an emergency physician may need broad access while a specialist needs only the relevant slice. Data is encrypted end to end with automated key rotation, and audit logging records every read and write so compliance reports don't require a human to assemble them. Gunjan frames the whole thing as trust between providers and with patients, which is a nicer way of saying the auditors will ask.

## Run it like any other production platform

The back half applies familiar operations practice to a domain that often lags on it. Monitoring tracks API response times and transformation throughput; data-flow monitoring follows messages through the pipeline with processing and success rates; anomaly detection flags bad data. Automated deployment pipelines with rollback replace manual releases, which the talk calls error prone for integration systems this tangled. Performance work covers parallel processing, caching repeated lookups, database partitioning and auto-scaling.

The case studies are described in outline rather than numbers: a regional health information exchange giving ER doctors patient histories in minutes, hospital consolidations migrating gradually without disrupting care, and patient-facing apps built on FHIR APIs. Looking ahead, Gunjan points to blockchain for tamper-proof audit trails and patient-controlled sharing, and to LLMs for clinical documentation, while noting that performance and compliance questions remain open.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to healthcare who need the vocabulary and the shape of an exchange platform in one sitting: the layers, where FHIR sits, and why consent and audit are first-class. If you already run an HIE, this will be familiar ground. If you build integration platforms in any regulated domain, the layering transfers well beyond hospitals.

Title: Contact center AI fails on day one without the backstage crew
Description: Manoj Kumar Vunnava (GoDaddy) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on the MLOps that keeps contact center conversational AI reliable, from feature stores to drift.
Body:
A telecom chatbot that answers a network outage by telling customers to restart their router is a demo that met production. Manoj Kumar Vunnava, a senior telecom engineer at GoDaddy, opens his Conf42 MLOps 2025 talk with exactly that story and spends the rest explaining the MLOps that would have prevented it: consistent features, repeatable training, careful rollouts, monitoring at four levels and automated retraining when the world shifts.

It is an accessible talk, full of analogies, aimed at people building or running AI in customer support.

## Why contact centers are harder than they look

Manoj lists what makes this domain unusual. Volume runs to millions of conversations a day. The AI works next to human agents as a co-pilot, so it has to fit into their workflow. Errors are expensive in public: one bad answer can turn into a social media pile-on within hours. And every industry has its own vocabulary, so one generic model will not cover healthcare, insurance, retail and banking.

His metaphor for MLOps is a theatre's backstage crew. The actors get the applause, but someone has to make sure the lights work and the show starts on time.

## Features are context, not just text

For conversational AI, features include what was said earlier in the conversation, timing signals such as how quickly a customer replies and how often they contact support, and language signals like sentiment, intent and domain keywords. He manages these through a feature store, which he compares to a well-organised pantry: you do not want to discover halfway through cooking that the salt is gone. Teams that skip it, he says, end up with models that work in the lab and fall apart in production.

Training has to be robust and automated: data quality checks, synthetic data for rare but important cases like fraud, bias detection across languages and industries, experiment tracking, and validation against business KPIs like customer satisfaction and resolution time rather than accuracy alone.

## Shadow first, then canary, then everyone

Rollout follows a familiar ladder: shadow testing where the model predicts silently, canary releases on a sliver of traffic, staged rollouts as confidence builds, and a rollback switch always ready. His analogy is teaching someone to drive, from the passenger seat to the parking lot to the freeway.

CI/CD treats models like software. Code, configuration and features live in Git, tests run on every change, models are registered with metadata, and deployments are containerised and rolled out gradually. In his experience this cut deployment time from weeks to hours.

## Drift arrives on schedule and by surprise

Monitoring runs at four levels: technical metrics (latency, error rates), data quality, model performance (accuracy, agent overrides) and business outcomes. Drift gets special attention. Holiday seasons flood support with package questions, outages bring a sudden wave of identical calls, and language itself changes. A year earlier nobody asked support about ChatGPT; now it is a routine question. When drift shows up, retraining should be automatic: collect new interactions, verify them with agents, retrain, validate against old and new scenarios, and roll out carefully.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product owners building support bots, agent-assist tools or voice AI, and MLOps teams new to conversational systems. It is not a deep technical dive, but the four-level monitoring model and drift examples are practical. His golden rule: AI should free agents for empathy and complex cases, not replace them.

Title: Schools need MLOps that works offline and needs no ML engineer
Description: Lalitha Potharalanka (FDA) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on low-code, privacy-first, offline-ready MLOps for schools with tight budgets and patchy internet.
Body:
Most MLOps advice assumes a cloud account, a platform team and a fast network. A rural school district has none of those. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Lalitha Potharalanka, a senior Appian developer at the US Food and Drug Administration, makes the case that bringing AI to classrooms takes a different stack: low-code platforms teachers can configure themselves, privacy designed in from the start, and architectures that keep working when the internet does not.

It is a long, example-heavy talk organised around challenges, low-code enablers, privacy techniques and implementation strategies.

## Schools are not small enterprises

Lalitha's list of constraints is specific to education. Infrastructure varies wildly between well-connected urban schools and rural ones with weak connectivity and old hardware. Most educators are not trained in DevOps or ML engineering, so a tool that needs retraining or troubleshooting becomes shelfware. Student data falls under FERPA in the US, GDPR in Europe and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act. And budgets rarely stretch to dedicated infrastructure or specialist staff, given that hiring a full-time ML engineer in the US costs more than many schools can justify.

## Low-code moves the controls to the teacher

The low-code section is the heart of the talk. Prebuilt AI components let educators deploy things like student risk scoring or adaptive learning recommendations without writing code. Visual dashboards in tools like Azure ML Studio let staff set thresholds and watch data drift. Platforms like Google Vertex AI automate retraining and redeployment when new data arrives.

She backs each point with a deployment she cites: a district where most teachers could configure models on their own after two weeks of training, a school system that cut false-positive alerts by adjusting monitoring thresholds visually so counselors could focus on genuine cases, a Midwestern district that took retraining from two weeks to one day, and a rural district that ran predictive analytics for student retention on a low-code platform for a fraction of the cost of a custom build. The pattern across them is that the people closest to the classroom can tune the model without filing a ticket.

## Privacy is a pipeline property

Lalitha treats privacy as architecture. Data minimisation comes first: a dropout-risk model may not need names, addresses or years-old attendance logs. Differential privacy adds statistical noise so individuals cannot be re-identified, which matters most in small classroom datasets. Federated learning trains models on school servers or even teacher laptops and sends back only learned weights, and she cites a Canadian province where 42 schools used a federated model to identify post-COVID learning delays. On-device inference goes further, so student data never leaves the tablet at runtime.

## Offline is a feature, not a fallback

The implementation strategies tie it together: containerisation so the same model runs on whatever hardware a school has, edge inference for places with poor connectivity, automated bias detection, and governance with role-based access and audit trails built into the workflow rather than added for the auditor. Picture an AI tool that has to hold up through a week of flaky Wi-Fi during exam season.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects in edtech, public sector or nonprofit settings, and anyone designing ML for users who will never hire an ML engineer. The privacy section is a good primer even if your users are not students. If you already run federated learning in production, the value here is the education-specific context and examples.

Title: Fraud detection as a platform problem with a sub-second deadline
Description: Shivam Tiwari (The University of Texas at Dallas) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on platform patterns for real-time financial crime analytics.
Body:
Catching a fraudulent transaction after it settles is bookkeeping; catching it before it completes is engineering. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Shivam Tiwari of The University of Texas at Dallas presented platform engineering patterns for real-time analytics systems built to detect financial crime, aimed at processing millions of transactions with sub-second detection.

We don't have a transcript of this session yet, so this post sticks to what the talk set out to cover and why the problem is worth your time. Watch the recording for Shivam's specific architecture and choices.

## Why this is a platform problem, not just a model problem

Fraud detection is often discussed as a modelling challenge: which features, which algorithm, which threshold. Shivam's framing puts the weight on the infrastructure underneath. A model that scores well offline is useless if the platform can't feed it fresh data and return a verdict before the transaction completes. The abstract's promise is about exactly that layer: the analytics platform that has to ingest a constant stream of transactions, enrich them, score them and act on the result, all at high volume and inside a latency budget measured in fractions of a second.

That combination is what makes it high-stakes engineering. Throughput and latency pull against each other, false positives block legitimate customers, false negatives cost money, and the whole thing has to stay up because a detection outage is a gap criminals can drive through.

## The questions a talk like this answers

The session sits in the high-scale track of the event, and the abstract positions it as practical patterns rather than theory. If you're building or evaluating such a system, these are the questions to watch it with:

- How transactions flow from ingestion to a decision, and where state lives along the way.
- How the platform keeps detection under a second as volume grows to millions of transactions.
- How analytics and detection logic can change without slowing the pipeline down.
- How the system behaves when a component fails, given that fraud doesn't pause for incidents.

## Who should watch

Platform and data engineers in payments, banking or e-commerce who own the infrastructure behind risk and fraud teams, and engineers from other domains curious how hard real-time gets when money is on the line. Expect an architecture-pattern talk from an academic speaker rather than a production war story from a specific bank.

Several Conf42 speakers have tackled the same problem from different angles, and they pair well with this session:

Title: Aircraft digital twins are a platform, not a 3D model
Description: Divakar Duraiyan (Tata Consultancy Services) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on the edge, data and compliance layers behind predictive aviation maintenance.
Body:
A modern airliner is a flying data centre, and its digital twin is only as good as the platform that turns that telemetry into a maintenance decision. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Divakar Duraiyan, Technical Architect at Tata Consultancy Services, walked through what that platform needs: tiered edge computing from the aircraft to the ground, hybrid stream and batch processing, legacy integration through APIs, and audit trails strict enough for aviation regulators.

## A twin is a living replica, not a dashboard

Divakar starts by clearing up the term. A digital twin isn't a 3D model or a pretty dashboard; it's a virtual replica of an aircraft's physical systems that keeps updating from real-world data. Three capabilities make it useful: data collection from thousands of onboard sensors, dynamic simulation so engineers can test scenarios without touching the aircraft, and predictive maintenance that flags failures weeks ahead.

## The architecture underneath

Data quality comes first, because the accuracy of every prediction depends on it. The platform validates incoming telemetry, runs anomaly detection on it and scores its quality before it feeds the twin. On the compute side Divakar describes container-based analytical workloads orchestrated by Kubernetes, scaling with demand. Processing is hybrid: streaming for real-time monitoring, batch for deeper analysis of time-series data and large binary flight recordings. Storage is tiered, with hot storage for recent data and warm and cold tiers for the history that trend analysis and model training need. Zero trust networking, encrypted transmission and strong authentication run through every layer.

## Edge computing in three layers

The real-time requirement drives a three-layer edge design. Onboard computing does initial analysis in flight and can flag anomalies before the aircraft lands. Ground-based edge systems take over at the gate for heavier analysis and detailed maintenance recommendations. Centralised processing correlates insights across the whole fleet and runs deep historical analysis off-peak. Event-driven architecture and message queues keep those layers consistent, which is harder than it sounds when one of your nodes is at 35,000 feet.

## Legacy systems and regulators set the constraints

Airlines run maintenance management, inventory, scheduling and compliance systems that have been in place for decades. Divakar's answer is a carefully designed API layer that abstracts those systems, exposing maintenance history, parts inventory and maintenance windows to the twin without disturbing existing workflows.

Regulation shapes everything else. Bodies such as the FAA and EASA impose requirements on maintenance practice and documentation, so the platform must keep records for decades and keep an audit trail linking every predictive recommendation to the maintenance action actually taken. Predictive models move through four stages: historical data collection across failure modes, model development, validation against real maintenance outcomes, and actionable recommendations.

His reference case is Lufthansa's AVIATAR platform, which he describes as combining a large fleet data foundation, API-layer legacy integration and predictive algorithms validated to spot component issues weeks before traditional inspection would.

## What else rides on the twin

Augmented reality puts twin data in the technician's view: step-by-step instructions, component identification and live sensor health overlaid on the actual part. Running globally adds fleet-level analytics, time-zone coordination, local caching for low-bandwidth airports and localised interfaces. The business case rests on fewer unscheduled events and aircraft-on-ground situations, better parts forecasting and components replaced neither too early nor too late.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers working on IoT, industrial or other safety-critical telemetry, where edge layers, long retention and auditability matter as much as the model. It's an architecture survey without code, and it pairs well with Divakar's own observability-focused talk on the same subject.

Title: Self-service ETL platforms generate the DAGs so developers don't
Description: Batchu Krishna (Fidelity Investments) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on metadata-driven ETL, generated Airflow DAGs and GitOps for data platforms.
Body:
Most developers who need a data pipeline don't want to write an Airflow DAG by hand, and a good platform shouldn't make them. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Batchu Krishna, a Software Engineer at Fidelity Investments with around two decades of data migration and ETL work behind him (banking projects included), described how to turn traditional ETL operations into a self-service data platform: metadata-driven pipelines, generated DAGs, infrastructure as code and the guardrails enterprises need.

## ETL as a product, not a ticket queue

Batchu frames platform engineering as a shift from managing infrastructure to building internal products. A data platform should feel natural to application developers: it plugs into the CI/CD they already use and follows patterns they already know. It also has to handle enterprise-scale processing, large legacy migrations and live transaction volumes while staying simple enough for general-purpose developers. Done well, that removes the handoffs where one team waits for the next to finish its stage.

## Declare the pipeline, let the platform write it

The central idea is metadata-driven ETL. Instead of imperative code per pipeline, pipelines are defined as structured metadata describing the transformations, the data quality requirements and operational parameters such as how to handle bulk loads or real-time feeds. At runtime the platform interprets that metadata and generates the workflows.

He grounds it in a familiar Azure layout from earlier projects: data moves from sources into a landing zone, then integration, then curated, with a pipeline and transformation step at each hop. In a metadata-driven platform those hops are described rather than hand-built, and Airflow DAGs are generated from the definitions so users never write Python DAG code directly. The payoff is maintainability: the definitions focus on business requirements, not implementation details, which removes a whole class of implementation errors.

The architecture underneath is microservices on Kubernetes with Apache Airflow as the orchestration backbone. The hard part, in his words, is hiding Kubernetes complexity from users while still giving them access to its scheduling and resource management, without handing permissions to people who shouldn't have them.

## The rest of the stack is software engineering applied to data

The supporting practices will look familiar:

- **CI/CD for pipelines:** version control, automated tests on pre-loaded test data, staged deployments with approvals, and rollback to the previous version when a release misbehaves.
- **Cloud integration:** templates over Azure Data Factory, careful cluster, notebook and job management for Databricks, and REST or GraphQL APIs with consistent error handling.
- **Infrastructure as code:** Terraform modules and Helm charts, with GitOps through Argo CD or Flux giving an audit trail and approval workflow.
- **Data testing at four levels:** generated test data, integration tests in containers, schema compatibility checks and performance regression against a baseline.
- **Observability:** distributed tracing with Jaeger or Zipkin, metrics in InfluxDB, logs in Elasticsearch or Splunk, and ML-based anomaly alerting.

Governance closes the list: automatic lineage capture, RBAC tied to enterprise identity, audit logs of every action, and privacy controls for GDPR and CCPA such as classification and deletion.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving an ETL team from hand-built jobs to a platform model, especially on Azure and Airflow. The delivery is conversational and wide-ranging rather than tightly scripted; the metadata-to-DAG section is the part to watch closely.

Title: A fixed-income index system goes from 30-minute runs to under 5
Description: Tarun Chataraju (JPMorganChase) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on moving a monolithic index system to Kubernetes, Airflow and Kafka.
Body:
Monthly index rebalancing used to mean a maintenance window during which clients couldn't see their data. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Tarun Chataraju, Senior Lead Software Engineer at JPMorganChase, described how his team moved a legacy fixed-income index system to Kubernetes, Apache Airflow and Kafka, cutting calculation time by 88% (from 30 minutes or more to under five) and removing scheduled downtime altogether.

## The monolith was failing on three fronts

The legacy system was one code base, deployed by hand, scaled by buying bigger boxes and run as nightly batches. Rebalancing needed ever longer windows, which hurt SLAs. Data volumes grew five times in three years. Index calculations took 30 minutes or more at peak, when clients wanted near real-time numbers, and quarter-end reporting or a volatile market day could swamp it. Tarun's point is that this was a business problem, touching client satisfaction and revenue, not just an IT one.

## Kubernetes is the engine, Airflow the conductor

The new architecture splits responsibilities cleanly. "Think of Kubernetes as the engine and airflow as the conductor, making sure the orchestra plays in the right order."

Airflow runs the index workflow as a DAG: pull issuer and bond metadata from providers such as Bloomberg through stateless, containerised adapters; collect real-time and end-of-day prices with data quality checks before anything proceeds; trigger calculation pods; generate reports and validations; publish to APIs and downstream consumers. Every step is visible, retriable and auditable, and if pricing data fails, calculations pause until it's corrected. At month-end the calculation engine scales out to around 30 pods, then back down overnight.

Around that sit domain-driven services (pricing logic decoupled from reporting), time-series databases tuned for financial tick data, REST and GraphQL APIs with compliance masking of restricted securities at the API layer, and a service mesh for traffic control, encryption and tracing.

## Kafka and Redis absorb the spikes

Kafka decouples processing so spikes queue gracefully and state survives a node failure; in one stress test it handled three times the expected peak without dropping a message. Redis cut database reads by 90%, with cross-region replication. StatefulSets, network policies for regulatory boundaries and horizontal pod autoscaling let the system handle 20 times more concurrent calculations on volatile days.

## The migration was strangled, not switched

The part worth stealing is the migration plan. Phase one built cloud infrastructure with compliance, IaC, CI/CD and monitoring baked in. Phase two moved historical data with dual writes and a validation framework that checked every bond reference record and price across old and new systems. Phase three peeled services off the monolith with the strangler pattern, with Airflow orchestrating across both worlds while reference data still lived in the legacy database and calculations had moved to Kubernetes. Phase four cut over with blue-green deployments and ran both systems in parallel until the team trusted the new one. Clients never saw a disruption; the system just got faster.

Tarun also credits the organisational side: a platform team acting as an internal service provider, a self-service portal for databases and dev environments, internal tech talks and runbooks. Custom product time to market dropped by 70%.

## Who should watch

Anyone modernising a batch-heavy system in a regulated industry, especially if Airflow is already on your shortlist. The next steps he lists (ML anomaly detection on market data, streaming DAGs for intraday triggers) show where the design goes next.

Title: Spam detection at billion-user scale is an ensemble and a graph
Description: Prabhakar Singh (Meta) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on production MLOps for multi-modal spam detection, from smart sampling to graph-based campaign detection.
Body:
At billion-user scale, a 0.1% false positive rate sounds tiny until you realise it means millions of legitimate people waking up to find their posts blocked. Prabhakar Singh, a software engineer at Meta, uses that arithmetic to open his Conf42 MLOps 2025 talk on production spam detection, and then lays out the blueprint: a hierarchical ensemble across text, images, video and behaviour, smart sampling to keep labelling affordable, and graph analysis to catch coordinated campaigns.

He describes the patterns of large-scale systems in general rather than disclosing internal Meta specifics, which keeps it portable to smaller platforms.

## The constraints are brutal

Billions of pieces of content, millions of evaluations per second at peak, and user-facing decisions that must return in under 100 ms. Spam here means fraud, phishing, scams and harmful content, across hundreds of languages, under GDPR and CCPA, against attackers who change tactics daily. His line for it is playing chess with millions of opponents who all change strategy overnight.

## Cheap filters first, specialists second

The model architecture is a hierarchical ensemble. Fast, lightweight pre-filters process the bulk of the volume and are tuned for high recall. Suspicious items go to specialist models for text, images, video and behaviour. A multimodal fusion stage combines signals with cross-attention, catching cases where the text looks fine but the image makes it obviously spam. A meta-learner weighs everything by historical reliability. His analogy is airport security: a quick scan for every bag, a closer look for the suspicious ones.

The features are where the signal lives: transformer embeddings and entity recognition for text, CNNs and OCR for images and memes, and behavioural and contextual signals like posting frequency, device fingerprints and account age. A post at 2 a.m. from a new device linked to a trending spam topic reads very differently from the same post on an old account.

## Label the samples that teach the model something

Labelling billions of samples is impossible, so the question is which ones matter. Prabhakar lists uncertainty sampling (send low-confidence cases to humans), diversity sampling (do not miss underrepresented languages and formats), adversarial sampling (seek out where the model fails), and time-sensitive sampling for new attack vectors. When attackers started hiding spam in memes, adversarial sampling surfaced it early enough to retrain.

## A campaign only shows up as a graph

Coordinated attacks are the interesting part. A single post looks normal; thousands of accounts acting together do not. Real-time streaming analysis spots activity anomalies, and graph neural networks model user-content interactions as dynamic graphs to expose suspicious clusters. His example is 10,000 accounts piling onto one post in under a minute: invisible individually, obvious as a graph. Countermeasures include throttling, CAPTCHAs and flagging clusters for review.

## Privacy and shipping discipline

Privacy is built in through federated learning, differential privacy, and cryptographic techniques such as homomorphic encryption, multi-party computation and zero-knowledge proofs. Models retrain daily, are validated against golden datasets, fairness slices and adversarial examples, run in shadow mode before progressive rollout, and can roll back instantly. Monitoring covers model performance, system performance, data drift and business impact, including false-positive appeals, with structured incident playbooks and post-mortems.

## Who should watch

Trust and safety engineers, anyone running abuse detection on a marketplace or social product, and ML engineers interested in cascaded inference under tight latency budgets. It is a dense overview; take notes on the sampling section.

Title: Your supply chain AI is only as good as the ERP beneath it
Description: Vinod Nagarahalli (Illumina) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on rebuilding ERP as a composable, API-first platform for AI-driven supply chains.
Body:
Most supply chain AI projects fail before the model is trained, because the data lives in an ERP built for transactions, not intelligence. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Vinod Nagarahalli, Director of IT at Illumina, made the case for treating ERP as a platform: modular services, API-first interfaces and event-driven flows, so forecasting, predictive maintenance and contract intelligence have a clean, connected foundation to run on.

## Legacy ERP: highways built for cars, asked to carry high-speed trains

Vinod's diagnosis has three parts. Years of customisation and bolt-ons leave planning, logistics, asset management, HR, finance and sourcing fragmented, so data is siloed and decisions lag. The data that does exist is often incomplete and inconsistent, which starves AI of exactly the clean, integrated input it needs. And the architecture is rigid, so every integration with a cloud service, ML framework or digital twin turns into its own expensive project. His image: roads built for cars, now expected to carry high-speed trains.

## Platform engineering applied to the back office

The fix is to apply platform engineering principles to ERP itself. Break functionality into microservices (finance, procurement, planning, logistics) that can scale and change independently. Make it API-first, with versioned, documented interfaces that partners, internal systems and AI services can call. Move from batch to event-driven processing, so inventory updates, demand signals and disruptions are handled as they happen.

On top of that he argues for a unified architecture with a common data model and shared governance. His example of why it matters: maintenance scheduling that automatically accounts for production plans, inventory and transport constraints, because those systems finally share data.

Integration is the other half. Vinod sketches a real-world shape: SAP S/4HANA as the core, with Ariba, extended warehouse management, transportation management, integrated business planning and financial supply chain modules around it, plus Teamcenter for product lifecycle, Camstar for manufacturing execution and LabVantage for lab data. The goal is to turn the ERP from a system of record into what he calls a system of intelligence.

## Three use cases on the same foundation

- **Predictive maintenance.** IoT sensors stream temperature, vibration and pressure; the ERP adds context; ML spots early signs of wear so repairs happen in planned downtime with parts ordered ahead.
- **Demand forecasting.** Models combine sales history, market trends, sentiment, weather and IoT data, keep learning as data arrives, and run what-if scenarios for demand surges or supply disruption.
- **Contract intelligence.** NLP extracts payment terms, delivery obligations and compliance clauses; ML flags risky terms. Wired into the ERP, a supplier missing a critical delivery can trigger a production-plan change or alternative sourcing automatically.

## Governance and people

He closes with the less glamorous parts: data lineage and quality, model lifecycle management with versioning and retraining, privacy techniques such as differential privacy and federated learning, and defences against data poisoning and model extraction. Then people: redesigned processes, upskilling and leaders who can run hybrid human and automated teams. His implementation advice is to start with clean governed data and a few high-impact domains rather than boiling the ocean.

## Who should watch

Engineers and IT leaders in manufacturing or life sciences who are being asked for AI on top of an ERP that barely talks to itself. It's a strategy-level talk with a vendor-heavy reference architecture; there's no code, but the integration map is useful.

Title: Make metadata the nervous system of your data platform
Description: Terance Joseph Paulraj (Western Governors University) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on metadata-driven, self-healing data pipelines.
Body:
One new field in an upstream table, a dozen broken pipelines, and an empty dashboard waiting for the morning meeting. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Terance Joseph Paulraj of Western Governors University argued that this isn't bad luck or sloppy code but an architecture problem, and that the fix is to make metadata (schemas, rules, lineage, configuration) the foundation the platform reacts to, rather than documentation scattered across wikis and people's heads.

## The hidden tax of classic ETL

Terance itemises what traditional extract-transform-load really costs. Velocity drops because a small change, like adding a customer field, needs coordination across several teams. Operational complexity grows faster than the pipeline count. Quality problems surface late, after the data has fed a business decision, and fixing them feels like detective work. Then the costs people forget: a steep learning curve for new engineers, senior engineers turned into bottlenecks because only they know the fragile parts, and scaling that makes the system heavier rather than smoother. He calls it a tax on every new feature.

## Reflexes instead of runbooks

His metaphor is the nervous system. Your hand pulls back from a hot stove before your brain writes a memo; a metadata-driven platform should react to change the same way. Once metadata is first-class, a schema change is something the system understands and propagates downstream instead of a breakage. Lineage lets you trace any value back to its source and see what an incident touched. Quality rules travel with the data and fire before bad data reaches a report. Documentation regenerates itself.

## Four patterns that make it real

He names four building blocks:

- **A metadata repository** as the central brain: schemas, lineage, quality rules and operational details in one connected place.
- **Event-driven architecture**, so a schema change, a finished job or a failed quality check triggers events the system adapts to.
- **A service mesh for data**: many small services with clear interfaces instead of large, fragile ETL jobs.
- **Policy as code** for governance, privacy and retention rules, tested and deployed like any other software.

For developers that turns into declarative data contracts (say what data you need, let the platform work out how), single-command test environments and intelligent discovery of relevant datasets. For operations it means checks on business logic rather than only CPU and job status (revenue numbers that should match across sources, say), predictive alerts on unusual drops in volume, and automated root cause analysis that points to where an issue started and what sits downstream.

The same metadata layer also keeps processing logic separate from the cloud it runs on, so workloads can be placed by cost, performance or compliance across AWS, Azure or Google Cloud.

## Migrate without a big bang

Terance recommends the strangler fig pattern, or a metadata bootstrap that first harvests metadata from existing systems without changing them, which gives you lineage and documentation early. A small centre of excellence builds reference implementations, and rollout starts with high-value areas such as schema management. From his enterprise implementations he reports an 85% drop in manual fixes, 99.9% reliability for mission-critical BI and 40% lower cost, with figures stated in the talk rather than broken down.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers who are tired of being the human schema-change handler. The talk is conceptual and pattern-level rather than a code walkthrough, so pair it with a tool-specific session if you want implementation detail.

Title: Autonomous MLOps is a four-phase climb, not a switch
Description: Mohan Singh (Amazon) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on self-healing infrastructure, predictive scaling and AI-driven code modernization as the path to autonomous ops.
Body:
The 2 a.m. pipeline page is the thing every ML platform team wants to retire, and Mohan Singh, a software development manager at Amazon Web Services, spends his Conf42 MLOps 2025 talk on how you get there. His model is three pillars (self-healing infrastructure, intelligent scaling and AI-driven code evolution) climbed in four phases over 18 to 36 months, with each phase paying for itself before full autonomy arrives.

It is a short, high-level talk with a clear structure, more strategy map than implementation guide.

## From firefighting to systems that fix themselves

Mohan's history of MLOps has three stages. First it was manual: engineers on call in the middle of the night patching broken pipelines. Then automation made workflows faster and cut errors, but still needed constant supervision. The next stage is systems that learn, adapt and repair themselves. His analogy is the human immune system: detect, respond, adapt to new threats.

## Self-healing is a loop with four parts

A self-healing system, in his breakdown, has monitoring that uses ML to spot anomalies, diagnosis that pinpoints root causes across logs and signals, resolution through automated playbooks, and a feedback loop that makes the system smarter after every incident. He compares it to an aircraft autopilot that stabilises the plane rather than just alerting the pilot.

The implementation pieces are observability-driven AI that catches small deviations before they become incidents, cross-service intelligence that understands dependencies so failures are diagnosed in context, and automated patching that finds and fixes vulnerabilities without waiting for a human.

## Scale before the spike, not after

Traditional autoscaling reacts once demand has already arrived, which Mohan likens to braking after you have run the red light. Predictive resource management flips that: forecast demand hours or days out and provision ahead, then scale back down when the load passes.

His five-step loop is worth noting: collect telemetry beyond CPU and memory (request patterns and business metrics), analyse it with time-series models to find cycles and seasonality, forecast demand from minutes to days ahead, turn forecasts into allocation plans, then automate execution through infrastructure as code with feedback to correct in real time.

## Code that maintains itself

The third pillar treats the codebase as a living system. Mohan describes three approaches powered by LLMs, code analysis and reinforcement learning: performance optimisation that detects bottlenecks and validates fixes with A/B tests, dependency management that assesses library risk and performs safe upgrades, and architecture evolution where ML tools recommend structural changes. He says his own team at AWS used to spend around 30% of its time on cleanup and migration work of this kind.

He quotes large improvements in recovery time, operational overhead and infrastructure cost for organisations adopting these systems. The talk does not show the methodology behind those figures, so read them as the speaker's reported results rather than benchmarks.

## The roadmap is the takeaway

The four phases are the most reusable part. Foundation: observability and standardised infrastructure as code, because nothing autonomous works without good telemetry. Augmentation: AI-assisted monitoring, anomaly detection and early predictive scaling with humans in the loop. Autonomy: remediation and predictive scaling with minimal intervention, plus early code optimisation. Evolution: self-improving systems that adapt architecture through reinforcement learning.

He closes on what comes next: multi-agent systems sharing infrastructure decisions, explainable AI operations for accountability, cross-platform optimisation over hybrid and multi-cloud, and infrastructure that learns from patterns across industries.

## Who should watch

Platform leads and engineering managers building a case for investing in AIOps, and SREs who want a staged plan to point at. If you want config files and code, pair it with one of the talks below.

- [Vijaybhasker Pagidoju on AI-driven self-healing infrastructure as the next step for SRE](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Vijaybhasker_Pagidoju_selfhealing_infrastructure) at Conf42 SRE 2025.

Title: Treat an AI fairness failure like a failing unit test
Description: Dharmendra Ahuja (IBM) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on putting bias checks, model cards and fairness monitoring into the platform's CI/CD.
Body:
If a model fails a bias check, the pipeline should go red exactly as it would for a broken unit test. That's the core of Dharmendra Ahuja's talk at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025. Dharmendra, a DevOps Lead at IBM, argues that ethical AI is a platform engineering problem: the safeguards belong in the shared pipeline and tooling, not in a checklist each product team reinvents.

## Velocity versus responsibility is a false trade

He frames the dilemma most platform teams feel. On one side, pressure to ship faster and support more models. On the other, a non-negotiable mandate for fairness, privacy and compliance, with reputational damage and regulatory fines waiting if you get it wrong. The old mantra of going fast and breaking things ages badly when, as he puts it, breaking things means breaking people.

His claim is that automation dissolves the trade. Catching issues early avoids the late, expensive rework that slows releases down. The talk's headline figures (a 286% gain in deployment efficiency and 89% of bias issues detected before production) are presented as results for organisations taking this approach; the talk doesn't break down how they were measured, so treat them as directional.

## Shift fairness left, then make it mandatory

The mechanics are familiar to anyone who has added a quality gate. As soon as a model is committed, the pipeline runs a battery of fairness tests, such as statistical parity difference and equal opportunity, using toolkits like IBM's AI Fairness 360. If the model fails, the build fails. Ethics becomes part of the definition of done rather than a review meeting.

The platform piece is what makes it scale. Instead of every team picking its own libraries, the platform offers curated ethical tooling as a service: standard model cards that auto-populate fairness metrics, pre-built compliance data pipelines with anonymisation built in, and approved bias-mitigation libraries. The right way becomes the easy way, which is the oldest trick in platform engineering applied to a newer problem.

## Fair yesterday is not fair today

Deployment isn't the finish line. Models drift and data drifts, so a model that passed its fairness gate can stop being fair in production. Dharmendra describes real-time ethical monitoring that checks live traffic for drift and violations against baselines, with automated alerting and remediation workflows routing issues to the right team. He mentions Fiddler as one option for the monitoring stack.

## Someone has to decide what "fair" means

The most useful slide is about people. Fairness thresholds and the definition of bias can't be invented by engineers alone, so he recommends a lightweight council with legal, compliance, ethics and business representatives. The platform team's job is to encode their decisions as policy as code, turning human judgement into automated pipeline gates.

His rollout plan is refreshingly incremental. Pick one high-visibility model and audit a single metric, such as gender bias. Try one open-source framework by hand. Add one non-blocking check to the pipeline so developers see the report. Only then make it blocking for critical applications, add more tests, and formalise monitoring and governance.

## Who should watch

Platform and MLOps engineers who've been asked to make the AI responsible and want a concrete pipeline shape for it. It's a short, high-level talk; the four-step rollout is the part to take back to your team.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [The Fairness Paradox: Why Your Compliant ML Model May Be Causing the Most Harm](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Neelima_Verma_fairness_compliant_harm) by Neelima Verma (FairLens), a useful counterweight on what passing a check actually proves.
- [Ethical Data Engineering: Addressing Privacy, Bias, and Fairness in AI Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Arun_Vivek_Supramanian_privacy_engineering_ethical) by Arun Vivek Supramanian (Amazon), the data pipeline view.

Title: AI in the platform should earn autonomy like a new hire
Description: Manoj Kumar Vunnava (GoDaddy) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on smarter pipelines, predictive ops and ML-driven scaling, rolled out gradually.
Body:
You wouldn't give a new team member production admin on day one, so don't give it to your AI either. That's the most practical idea in Manoj Kumar Vunnava's talk at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025. Manoj, a Senior Telecom Engineer at GoDaddy, walks through where AI and machine learning fit into an internal platform, and argues for introducing them in stages: recommendations first, semi-automation next, full automation last.

## Why the old platform model stopped scaling

Manoj starts with a short history. Platform engineering began as a standard kit of pipelines, deployment scripts and dashboards, and it worked until the estate grew from a few servers to thousands of containers across regions. He names four resulting problems: mental overload from dozens of dashboards and alerts, maintenance overhead that eats the platform team's time, scaling bottlenecks (ten times the traffic can't mean ten times the engineers), and cloud bills growing faster than the business. His analogy is a manual gearbox in rush hour versus a car with adaptive cruise control: you still choose the destination, the system does the tedious work.

## Five places AI earns its keep

He breaks the AI-driven platform into building blocks:

- **Smarter CI/CD.** Pipelines that pick the tests a change actually needs, predict deployment risk, and roll back automatically before customers notice. His kitchen analogy: a chef who knows which steps matter for this dish, instead of running the same ten-step recipe every time.
- **Predictive analysis and incident resolution.** Spotting unusual patterns, doing root cause analysis across logs and metrics faster than a human, filtering alert noise, and applying safe routine fixes such as adding CPU or memory to a struggling process.
- **Automated remediation**, for the fixes that are routine enough to trust.
- **Dynamic resource optimisation.** ML that forecasts demand from past usage and right-sizes capacity instead of overprovisioning "just to be safe". He cites 15 to 30% cloud cost savings reported by companies doing this.
- **Intelligent observability** that feeds all of the above.

## Two case studies, told as scenarios

Manoj illustrates the ideas with two unnamed organisations, presented as illustrative scenarios rather than named customers. A global financial services firm with slow deployments and frequent incidents adds predictive scaling, ML anomaly detection and staged rollouts, and reports 65% faster deployments, 42% fewer production incidents and 22% lower infrastructure cost. A fast-growing e-commerce platform uses AI-assisted self-service configuration and auto-troubleshooting observability so its platform team supports three times the developers without new headcount.

## The rollout is the real content

The implementation advice is where the talk is strongest. Start small with something high-value and low-risk, like test optimisation or autoscaling. Get the data foundation right first, because AI only sees what your logs and metrics show it. Keep humans in the loop at the start: if the system recommends scaling down, an engineer approves it. Architect for modularity (AI as plug-in components, not a rip-and-replace), explainability, manual fallbacks and continuous learning.

He's also candid about the obstacles: data quality, legacy integration, keeping models current, skill gaps and teams worried about losing control. His remedy is upskilling, small pilots and clear communication about what the AI will and won't do.

## Who should watch

Platform leads deciding where to start with AI and wanting a sensible order of operations. If you already run ML-driven autoscaling and AIOps, this is an overview you can skip; if you're pitching it internally, the staged-autonomy argument is worth borrowing.

Title: What a card swipe asks of a payment platform in 200 milliseconds
Description: Tapan Vijay (Meta) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on the latency, fraud, settlement and key-management design behind planet-scale card processing.
Body:
Buying a coffee with a card gives a dozen systems roughly 100 to 200 milliseconds to agree with each other. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Tapan Vijay, Head of Payment Engine and Gateway at Meta, took that single swipe apart and showed what a payment platform has to get right inside that window: routing across gateways, a chain of fraud checks, issuer approval and a consistent answer for every party involved.

## A web of parties, each with its own fraud check

The complexity starts with the cast. Cardholder, merchant, acquirer, network, gateway and issuer all sit in the path of one authorisation, across multiple data centres, geographies and dozens of regulatory frameworks. Each party wants to reduce its own liability, so each runs its own fraud checks. Tapan puts numbers on the stakes: in the region he describes, around 150 billion card transactions a year, holiday peaks around 65,000 transactions per second, and roughly $31,000 lost per second of downtime.

## Eventual consistency is not an option at checkout

Most of the architecture advice is classic distributed systems, sharpened by money. Scale horizontally rather than buying bigger machines. Isolate critical components in a service-oriented design so a failure stays local and upgrades don't take the whole system down. Distribute geographically for disasters, but keep transactions from bouncing between continents and blowing the latency budget.

The point he stresses most is consistency. Plenty of systems tolerate eventual consistency; a payment has to complete or not happen at all, within a time bound, with no ambiguity. The nightmare is the bank saying approved while the gateway says failed.

To hit the latency target, authorisation systems use connection pooling and persistent connections to skip TCP handshakes, compact protocols instead of XML, adaptive load balancing that watches server health and queue depth, and circuit breakers. Static reference data is cached, and distributed caches need careful invalidation, because overly aggressive invalidation causes a thundering herd.

## Fraud detection gets 10 to 20 milliseconds

Within the end-to-end budget, fraud scoring gets roughly 10 to 20 milliseconds to analyse hundreds of parameters: device fingerprints, behavioural patterns, velocity checks, geographic anomalies. Models have to be deployed in every region rather than called centrally, which drags in versioning, A/B testing and monitoring problems, plus hot-swapping models without disrupting traffic. New fraud patterns should be expressible as rules in a domain-specific language, so detection can change without a code deploy.

## Settlement, keys and reconciliation run on a different clock

Authorisation is milliseconds; settlement usually runs daily, although real-time payment rails are pushing it toward immediate transfer. That calls for careful state management (authorised, captured, batched, submitted, settled) consistent across every partner. Cross-border payments add FX risk, rate locking and liquidity relationships. Reconciliation at this volume moves from batch to continuous.

On security Tapan covers defence in depth, hardware security modules, zero trust and tokenisation, plus hierarchical key management: a master key in the HSM encrypts data keys stored with the data, so rotation touches only key-encryption keys instead of re-encrypting everything. He also calls out insider controls, because the platform must stop its own staff from pushing through an unauthorised transaction.

## Who should watch

Engineers building anything where correctness and latency both matter, payments or not. It's a dense survey rather than a case study of Meta's own systems, and the closing look at real-time rails, open banking APIs and stablecoins is a good map of what's coming.

Title: Running AI literature agents over 30 million biomedical citations
Description: Nishanth Joseph Paulraj (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on the MLOps behind RAG literature agents for biomedical researchers.
Body:
Biomedical research publishes more than a million papers a year, and every new project still starts with a literature review. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Nishanth Joseph Paulraj, a senior data engineer at Thermo Fisher Scientific, shows the MLOps architecture behind AI literature agents that search a corpus of more than 30 million citations, and argues that domain experts have to be part of the pipeline, not just its customers.

The talk is a tour of the full stack, from microservices and model registry to vector database scaling and A/B testing.

## The problem is a tsunami of citations

Nishanth frames it from the researcher's chair. Relevant work can be hidden from search, reading everything is impossible, and by his account researchers spend a large share of their time on the review alone. His solution combines four parts: domain-adapted LLMs, an advanced retrieval-augmented generation system, a precision named entity recognition system for genes, proteins and drug interactions, and robust MLOps to keep it all running.

## General NLP breaks on biomedical language

The domain adaptation section explains why off-the-shelf pipelines struggle. Biomedical text has highly specialised vocabulary that differs across sub-disciplines, entity relationships like gene-protein interactions that need expert understanding, meanings that shift between research areas, and a constant stream of new discoveries. Evaluation therefore needs biomedical accuracy metrics plus domain expert review, not only standard test sets.

## The architecture separates embedding from retrieval

His blueprint for an effective setup is concrete: containerised microservices for modular scaling and versioning, a model registry because the models keep changing, asynchronous processing pipelines for batch citation updates (citation counts change daily), a clean separation of embedding generation from retrieval services, a real-time inference API layer built for sub-second responses, and a dedicated evaluation environment for scientific validation.

Scaling the vector database is its own chapter. The challenges are generating embeddings efficiently for a huge corpus, balancing recall against compute cost, and updating indexes without downtime. His answers are asynchronous batch embedding pipelines, hierarchical indexing, read replicas with staged updates, and query caching. On the RAG side he lists domain-specific embedding models, multi-stage retrieval, citation network enrichment and context window optimisation.

## Speed alone is not a success metric

The KPIs he reports are sub-second query latency, 90% accuracy in entity recognition and citation relevance scores above 85%, with an A/B testing framework reporting an 80% reduction in literature search time. The point he keeps returning to is that faster search is not proof the system is better. Scientific validation pipelines must measure the research outcome too.

Monitoring covers model drift, citation accuracy, system health, query patterns and resource use, on dashboards built for both ML engineers and scientists. Infrastructure has a baseline sized to average load with redundancy, autoscaling inference endpoints, scheduled scaling for predictable peaks like the academic calendar, and dedicated GPU allocation for embedding and inference.

## Who should watch

Engineers building RAG over specialised corpora (legal, patents, clinical, biomedical) where generic embeddings miss the point, and data teams scaling a vector store from a demo to tens of millions of documents. His closing lessons apply well outside biology: bring in domain experts, validate scientifically, keep the corpus updating, and prioritise explainability, because researchers will not trust a citation they cannot trace.

Title: Conf42 Rustlang 2025: Rust leaves the systems niche
Description: Conf42 Rustlang 2025 roundup - Rust in data lakes, AWS Lambda, networks, 5G, factory vision, security pipelines and carbon-aware Kubernetes, in 27 talks.
Body:
Conf42 Rustlang 2025 ran online on August 21, 2025, with 27 talks, and the striking thing was who gave them. Very few speakers were compiler hackers or crate maintainers; most were data engineers, network engineers, security engineers, and architects at banks, carmakers, telcos, and retailers, explaining why Rust ended up in their production stack. The borrow checker has clearly left the systems programming niche and found a job in the enterprise.

All sessions are on the [Conf42 Rustlang 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/rustlang2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBMebMWQQ03iUNjed9luMsp).

## Rust under the data stack

Data infrastructure was the most convincing track. [Rahul Joshi](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Rahul_Joshi_memory_rust_tech), a Distinguished Data Engineer at Capital One, walked through three eras of enterprise data: on-prem Hadoop with its JVM garbage collection and memory overheads, cloud warehouses like Snowflake and Redshift, and today's lakehouses built on open formats with storage separated from compute. His argument is that Rust, through projects like Apache Arrow and DataFusion, has become a critical piece of that third era because it offers memory safety without a garbage collector.

[Venkata Appalapuram](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Venkata_Appalapuram_systems_architecture_ai) of Ritepros gave the most transferable talk for library authors. Starting from a Spark JMS connector built at Capital One to read from ActiveMQ, IBM MQ, and Amazon SQS, he mapped JVM library patterns to Rust crate design: provider interfaces become traits, exception handling becomes `Result`, plus testing and documentation strategies that work across both ecosystems.

[Narendra Reddy Mudiyala](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Narendra_Reddy_Mudiyala_memory_safety_systems) of Accenture applied Rust to data mesh, and [Ritesh Kumar Sinha](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Ritesh_Kumar_Sinha_memory_safety_zero) of Kotak Mahindra Bank to large-scale pipelines for climate data.

## Rust in the cloud

[Vamsi Praveen Karanam](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Vamsi_Praveen_Karanam_aws_cloud_scale), a Software Development Engineer at Amazon, gave a practical tour of the AWS SDK for Rust. His comparison is a fair one: Go is strong on Lambda but carries a bigger runtime, Java has the ecosystem but pays for cold starts and memory, Python wins at prototyping but slows at scale. Rust's small binaries mean faster Lambda cold starts, and with Tokio you can run thousands of async calls to AWS services.

[Bandhavi Sakhamuri](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Bandhavi_Sakhamuri_cloud_ai_rust), a Senior SRE at SolarWinds, built a carbon-aware Kubernetes scheduler in Rust. Default schedulers weigh performance and availability but not where the electricity comes from; the framework adds that signal, whether you run on EKS, AKS, or GKE. [Uday Kiran Yedluri](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Uday_Kiran_Yedluri_cloud_security_rust) covered Rust across multi-cloud enterprise environments, and [Karthik Mohan Muralidharan](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Karthik_Mohan_Muralidharan_edge_cloud_divide) of Walmart Global Tech looked at orchestration patterns between the edge and the cloud.

## Packets, radios and robots

Rust's home turf, low-latency systems, still had a strong showing. [Rahul Tavva](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Rahul_Tavva_memory_code_zero) of Kairos Technologies covered zero-copy packet processing and async routing, [Prasanth Kosaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Prasanth_Kosaraju_memory_safety_systems) of Dataquest applied Rust to network infrastructure in educational and industrial settings, and [Riddhi Patel](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Riddhi_Patel_memory_safety_zero) of DRC System explored how the ownership model fits ultra-low-latency 5G systems. [Venu Madhav Nadella](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Venu_Madhav_Nadella_memory_safety_zero) of Spectrum moved telecom operations from reactive to predictive.

On the factory floor, [Sankar Subramanian](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Sankar_Subramanian_memory_safety_zero), a Staff Engineer at Lucid Motors with over 20 years in control and automation, showed zero-copy machine vision pipelines for spotting battery defects in EV manufacturing. [Anushree Nagvekar](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Anushree_Nagvekar_edge_memory_safety) of AEye looked at edge AI for autonomous vehicles, where zero-cost abstractions and memory safety both matter.

## When a crash is not an option

Several talks made the safety argument where it hits hardest. [Lakshmi Vara Prasad Adusumilli](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Lakshmi_Vara_Prasad_Adusumilli_memory_safety_systems) of Conduent started from a blunt premise, that when 911 systems crash, people die, and showed compile-time guarantees in emergency response systems. [Raphael Shobi Thomas](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Raphael_Shobi_Thomas_memory_safety_code) covered a healthcare and travel safety platform for seniors, and [Prabhakar Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Prabhakar_Singh_memory_safety_systems) of Meta built real-time fraud prevention for gig platforms.

Security engineers had their say too. [Naresh Yelkoti](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Naresh_Yelkoti_memory_security_cloud) of U.S. Bank built security scanning pipelines in Rust, [Sachin Kapoor](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Sachin_Kapoor_memory_security_safety) walked through zero trust fundamentals implemented in Rust, and [Ketankumar Patel](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Ketankumar_Patel_memory_safety_zero) of Wind River proposed a framework for ethical AI in Rust.

## Agents, dashboards and business systems

Rust for AI agents appeared too. [Sidhanta Panigrahy](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Sidhanta_Panigrahy_memory_safety_zero) of Okta built a Tokio-based multi-agent system, and [Sarat Piridi](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Sarat_Piridi_agents_zero_systems) of Hanwha Qcells covered Rust-powered process automation across industries. Dashboards got two takes: [Tashi Garg](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Tashi_Garg_cloud_ai_rust) of Juniper Networks on dynamic UIs for cloud infrastructure, and [Shahzeb Akhtar](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Shahzeb_Akhtar_memory_security_rust) of UnitedLex on business intelligence.

The business-systems corner rounded it out: [Swetha Priya Sathiyam](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Swetha_Priya_Sathiyam_systems_memory_code) of ADP on HR tech, [Nageswara Rao Nelloru](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Nageswara_Rao_Nelloru_memory_ai_zero) on claims management APIs, and [Shikha Duttyal](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Shikha_Duttyal_ml_ai_rust) of Meta on digital twins for supply chains.

## Partners and what's next

Conf42 Rustlang 2025 was supported by the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners listed on the event page.

For more, the earlier editions are still online, starting with [Conf42 Rustlang 2024](https://www.conf42.com/rustlang2024). Fair warning: you may come out wanting to rewrite something.

Title: Emergency response platforms where a new service ships in 3 minutes
Description: Lakshmi Vara Prasad Adusumilli (Conduent) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on golden paths, GitOps and multi-region failover for 911-grade systems.
Body:
Most platform teams measure success in developer hours saved. Lakshmi Vara Prasad Adusumilli, Senior DevOps Lead and Cloud Lead at Conduent, measures it against a hurricane making landfall while 911 call volume surges. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 he showed how a 12-person platform team supporting more than 80 developers took emergency-service deployments from two weeks to three minutes, using the same building blocks most internal developer platforms use, held to a much stricter bar.

## Downtime during the disaster is the one outage that matters

The setup is simple and grim. Emergency systems have to scale instantly in a crisis, talk to legacy and government systems, stay compliant, and never go down in the exact moment demand peaks. Before the platform work, Lakshmi describes the usual pain: two-week deployments, frequent configuration errors, limited redundancy, isolated ops teams and geographic failover that needed specialist knowledge. Long release cycles and manual steps cannot keep up when a call spike arrives with no warning.

## Golden paths do the thinking nobody has time for

The developer portal is the centre of his platform, and golden paths are its main feature. During a disaster nobody should be working out TLS, network policy or logging by hand, so the pre-approved templates ship with all of it. A new emergency microservice built from a golden path comes pre-wired with centralised logging, TLS and dashboards. He names Backstage as the kind of portal that hosts this, with Helm charts, Terraform modules and Kubernetes YAML blueprints underneath.

Two more portal pieces round it out. A service catalogue lets teams pick databases, queues, caches and object storage without opening tickets; his example is an engineer provisioning a pre-configured Kafka cluster from the catalogue during an incident instead of waiting days. Service scorecards give every microservice a report card for uptime, error rates, recovery time, security posture and latency, fed by Prometheus, Grafana and OpenTelemetry.

## GitOps as the drift alarm

Everything is code and everything goes through Git. Terraform provisions clusters across regions with identical settings; Argo CD or Flux reconciles live state against what is committed, and reverts anything changed directly in the cluster. Lakshmi reports full drift-detection coverage with 73% of deviations auto-remediated. For a regulated emergency system the audit trail is a feature in its own right: every change has a commit, a history and an approval.

## Failover at every layer

The resilience design is layered all the way up. Multiple Kubernetes clusters per region run active-active, regional load balancers are themselves redundant, and individual services such as dispatch or geolocation fail over from cluster A to cluster B without manual intervention. Global traffic management routes users to the nearest healthy region and fails over a whole region if a flood takes a data centre offline. A service mesh adds circuit breaking and mutual TLS so partial failures stay partial. He cites an 800% spike in emergency calls as the kind of load this design spreads across clusters.

Policy as code closes the loop: a deployment that violates a security rule is blocked automatically, without a human gate slowing the team down.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who already run a portal and want a reference for what "production-grade" means when the users are first responders. It's a broad architecture walkthrough rather than a deep implementation session, and its best advice is the closing one: start with one golden path, measure rigorously, then expand.

- [Enhancing Business Resilience with Azure Site Recovery](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Somaning_Turwale_resilience_disaster_mitigation) by Somaning Turwale (Microsoft), on cloud disaster recovery tooling.
- [Predicting and Mitigating Emergency Situations on the Roads: A Data-Driven Approach](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Maksim_Kariagin_data_road_emergency) by Maksim Kariagin (Metyis), the data side of emergencies.

Title: At trillion-parameter scale, cost is a training metric
Description: Anjan Dash (Meta) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on operating trillion-parameter LLM training runs, from parallelism and checkpoints to early warnings and cost.
Body:
When a training run lasts weeks on thousands of synchronised GPUs, every idle hour is money you will not get back, and you only learn whether the model is any good at the end. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Anjan Dash, a technical leader at Meta who works on ads ranking systems, walks through what it takes to operate trillion-parameter LLM training, and his conclusion is that MLOps here is the foundation that makes training possible at all.

It is an overview talk that covers the whole stack: infrastructure, orchestration, failure recovery, monitoring and cost. Good if you need the map before you go deep on any one piece.

## The scale problem in five lines

Anjan lists the challenges plainly. Training cycles are so long that feedback arrives weeks late. Thousands of GPUs must stay in sync or nothing trains. Hardware, power and specialist people all cost a lot. The models are data hungry, so the data pipeline has to keep up. And checkpoints of a trillion-parameter model are huge, so even saving a snapshot is an engineering problem.

The financial framing matters: weekly training cost, the cost of every failed hour while GPUs sit idle, waste when data or power is not arriving, and the total duration of the run. Each one is a lever MLOps can pull.

## Parallelism is a stack, not a choice

His infrastructure section covers distributed training clusters, high-bandwidth interconnects between GPUs and clusters, custom kernels that exploit hardware-specific acceleration, a data pipeline system to feed the cluster, GPU-aware orchestration, and monitoring.

He compares two frameworks. NVIDIA's Megatron brings tensor parallelism to split layers efficiently and sequence parallelism to chunk long input sequences across GPUs to manage memory footprint. Microsoft's DeepSpeed brings the ZeRO optimizer for memory, pipeline parallelism, and offloading to CPU and NVMe. Real trillion-parameter training, he notes, combines tensor, pipeline, data and sequence parallelism at once.

## Recovery has to be automatic

The failure-recovery section is the most operationally useful. Detection watches for hardware failures, gradient explosions and data corruption. Checkpoint management decides how often to save and how far back you can fall. Resource reallocation reconfigures the cluster around failed hardware. Training should resume on its own; a human fixing things by hand during a multi-week run is not a plan.

Monitoring runs at two levels. System metrics cover GPU utilisation, network bandwidth, disk IO and power. Training metrics cover loss, gradients, learning rate and parameter norms. Alerting needs anomaly detection, multiple channels (phone, Slack, email) and automated escalation if nobody answers.

## Watch the gradients before they bite

Anjan's early-warning list is the part to copy into a runbook: gradient spikes, shifts in activation distributions across layers, a widening gap between training and validation, and unexpected loss behaviour when the learning rate changes. Each is a signal that lets you intervene before a catastrophic failure wastes days of compute.

His takeaways close the loop: invest in distributed systems and the people who understand them, automate everything, monitor at multiple levels, and treat cost as a first-class metric tracked as seriously as model quality. The GPU bill, after all, does not care how elegant the loss curve looks.

## Who should watch

ML platform and infrastructure engineers moving from single-node or modest multi-node training toward large distributed runs, and engineering managers who need to explain where the money goes. Researchers already living inside Megatron or DeepSpeed configs will find it a summary rather than new detail.
