Title: Rust from wearable to hospital, a health platform for older travellers
Description: Raphael Shobi Thomas at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on a Rust healthcare AI stack for senior travellers, from no_std biosensors to WebAssembly translation.
Body:
By 2030, about 703 million travellers worldwide will be 60 or older, and many carry chronic conditions into places where they do not speak the language. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Raphael Shobi Thomas](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Raphael_Shobi_Thomas_memory_safety_code), a senior software engineer and independent researcher, presented a health and safety platform for those travellers with Rust at every layer: biosensor firmware, data pipelines, risk models, in-browser translation and medical records.

## One language from the sensor to the cloud

The pitch for Rust is the usual trio (memory safety, native performance, compile-time thread safety) plus one that matters a lot here: cross-compilation to Windows, Linux, embedded targets, iOS and Android. A single language across devices is a real simplification when the same health record moves from a wrist to a hospital.

He described the platform handling 2,847 concurrent users, each with more than 47 health variables, at sub-millisecond latency, operating under GDPR across 34 countries.

## Firmware that survives bad connectivity

The embedded layer runs `no_std` Rust with embedded-hal on biosensors, which means no standard library, no OS services and tight memory. On top sits a custom protocol built for poor or intermittent connectivity: data is buffered locally and forwarded when the link returns, end-to-end cryptographic checks guard against tampering, and medical data gets priority. That is the right design for a traveller who walks out of mobile coverage mid-arrhythmia.

## The data and ML pipeline

On the server side, Tokio handles continuous health streams, zero-copy parsing reads biosensor data straight from byte buffers, and a custom Serde serialization pipeline processes medical records about 340% faster than a comparable Python implementation, by his measurement. Schema evolution relies on Rust's type system to keep old and new data formats compatible.

Risk assessment uses Candle and the tch-rs bindings, plus ONNX Runtime for pre-trained models on CPU or GPU. The predictor shares the model across threads behind `Arc` and `Mutex`, a deliberately simple pattern for safe concurrent access, and evaluates around 150 risk factors per assessment.

## Translation that never leaves the device

The WebAssembly piece is the most interesting design choice. Medical terminology translation runs as Rust compiled to WebAssembly in the browser or on the device, covering 23 languages at a reported 94% accuracy, with about 60% lower latency than server-side translation. Sensitive health data never goes to a server just to be translated.

Records use the Substrate framework to log every access on a blockchain, with patients managing permissions on chain and smart contracts enforcing consent.

## The Portugal scenario

His case study ties it together: a 72-year-old traveller in rural Portugal, a sensor detecting an irregular heart rhythm and elevated blood pressure, the model flagging a potential cardiac event with 92% confidence, the system finding the nearest medical facility, translating the medical history into Portuguese and sharing verified records with the receiving hospital.

## The honest part

He is upfront about the costs: few medical-domain crates compared with Python or Java, FFI work to reach existing healthcare systems, slow certification under GDPR, HIPAA and MDR for new tech, long early build times, and the ownership learning curve. His answers were custom domain crates, type-safe bindings, compliance checks in CI/CD, build tuning and team training.

## Who should watch

Engineers building health, wearable or edge-AI systems who want to see one Rust stack stretched from firmware to the browser. Compliance-minded teams will appreciate the challenges section.

Title: Fraud checks in milliseconds, a five-layer Rust pipeline for gig apps
Description: Prabhakar Singh of Meta at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on real-time fraud prevention for gig platforms in Rust, with Tokio, Candle and petgraph.
Body:
On a food delivery or ride-sharing app, the money leaves the moment the job is done, so a fraud check that is late is a fraud check that did not happen. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Prabhakar Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Prabhakar_Singh_memory_safety_systems), a software engineer at Meta, walked through a five-layer fraud prevention architecture for gig platforms, written end to end in Rust, including the ML inference.

## Why gig fraud is harder than bank fraud

"Fraud prevention in gig platforms is a game of millisecond." Singh's point is that every constraint is tighter than in banking. Approve a transaction slowly and the customer abandons the order or the driver assignment times out. Workers and customers are scattered across cities and countries, so fraud patterns vary by geography and change weekly. Payouts are instant, with no hold period to investigate. And the models have to analyse thousands of transactions a minute without choking.

The attacks he lists will look familiar: account takeover with leaked credentials, synthetic identities stitched from real and fake details, driver-customer collusion to fake trips, GPS spoofing, and stolen cards used for instant payouts.

## Five layers, each a safety net

The architecture stacks five detectors, each catching what the others miss:

1. **Stream processing** with Tokio, ingesting transactions asynchronously.
2. **Rules** using Rust pattern matching for known signals, such as the same card used in three countries within an hour.
3. **Statistical anomaly detection** with time-series models for unusual spikes or dips in behaviour.
4. **ML classification** with Candle, Hugging Face's pure-Rust ML framework, which imports models from PyTorch or TensorFlow via ONNX and runs on CUDA or Metal.
5. **Graph analysis** with petgraph, looking for connected components, centrality and structural similarity.

Two implementation details made the biggest difference, he said: Tokio's async streams, and zero-copy deserialization with Serde so JSON or protobuf is parsed straight from bytes. Those are what keep the pipeline inside its latency budget.

## No Python in production

Running inference in Candle means the whole pipeline stays in one memory-safe language: no language boundary, no GIL and no extra process hop. It is the most opinionated part of the talk and the most interesting, because most fraud stacks still keep Python for the model.

## The graph catches the ring

The graph layer has the best story. A group of 32 drivers and 18 customers ran a fake-order scam for weeks without tripping the standard ML models; graph analysis in petgraph surfaced them as a cluster. Fraud rings are relationships, and per-transaction features cannot see them.

## The numbers he reported

From a major food delivery company's production benchmarks, he reported Rust at 93% of C++ performance, 6.2x faster than Java and 2.4x faster than Python with TensorFlow, with tail latency consistently under 35 ms and much lower CPU use than Python. In a ride-sharing case, a platform losing about $3.2 million a month to GPS spoofing and fake identities replaced its Python fraud stack with Rust microservices, WebAssembly rule modules and Candle, and saw 87% less fraud loss, 65% fewer false positives and 99.98% uptime over 12 months. The companies are not named.

He also covers privacy-preserving techniques (homomorphic encryption, federated learning, differential privacy, secure enclaves) and a roadmap toward behavioural biometrics and SHAP or LIME-style explanations in Rust.

## Who should watch

Fraud, risk and payments engineers on marketplace platforms, and ML engineers curious whether Rust-native inference is ready for production. The petgraph section is worth it on its own.

Title: A RAG platform for keeping up with research literature
Description: Nishanth Joseph Paulraj (Western Governors University) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on RAG for research literature, from vector shards to knowledge graphs.
Body:
More than 10,000 biomedical papers are published every day, which means the discovery your experiment needs may already exist, buried under yesterday's output. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Nishanth Joseph Paulraj (Western Governors University) laid out the architecture patterns for an AI literature processing platform built on retrieval-augmented generation, with the engineering around the LLM doing most of the work.

## Accuracy first, then speed, then freshness

Paulraj's requirements come in three layers. Researchers need correct answers, so RAG grounds the model's reasoning in authoritative references instead of letting it improvise. They need them fast, so retrieval has to be sub-second at scale. And they need them current, because research moves and yesterday's conclusion may be outdated.

## Embeddings over keywords, shards over one big index

The retrieval tier is a distributed vector database. Embeddings capture context that keyword search misses; sharding the index across nodes gives parallel processing and fault tolerance; optimised nearest-neighbour search keeps latency flat as the corpus grows.

Around it sits an event-driven microservice architecture, with Kafka as one option, stateless services and independent scaling, so a surge of new documents does not slow down queries. He is explicitly tool-agnostic here: the architecture matters more than the brand names.

## Spend GPUs like they cost money

Inference cost gets its own section, with three techniques:

- **Batching** several requests together to keep GPUs busy.
- **Response caching** so common queries skip the pipeline entirely.
- **Model quantisation** to shrink models without losing too much quality.

Caching appears again at the platform level: embedding, retrieval and response caches mean a popular query does not need fresh computation every time. Some answers can wait for the next incremental update. Horizontal scaling across GPU pools, rather than ever-bigger machines, lets the platform shrink when demand drops.

## Freshness and knowledge graphs

The research-specific part is real-time knowledge synchronisation: continuous ingestion, incremental updates, conflict resolution when new findings disagree with old ones. On top, domain-specific models extract entities such as genes, proteins and diseases, and their relationships (what causes what), and merge them into knowledge graphs. That turns a pile of PDFs into something you can traverse by relationship, not just search by similarity.

## Production hygiene

The rest is the checklist you would want for any production AI system: end-to-end monitoring of throughput, latency, error rates and inference quality with distributed tracing; circuit breakers, retries with backoff and graceful degradation (a simpler fallback model, cached responses, partial results) instead of hard failure; Terraform, CloudFormation and Kubernetes manifests deployed through CI/CD with canary and blue-green rollouts; and explicit benchmarks for latency, throughput, accuracy and uptime to validate the design and plan capacity.

He closes on reuse: the same blueprint works for case law, financial filings, technical manuals and historical archives. His summary is the right one for the whole topic: it is not about deploying an LLM, it is about engineering an ecosystem around it.

## Honest scope

The abstract promises demos and code; the recording is a slide-led architecture overview without either, and it does not walk through measured results. Watch it for the shape of the system and the checklist, not for benchmarks.

## Who should watch

Engineers building search or question answering over large, fast-moving document collections, in research, legal, finance or internal knowledge bases. If you are new to the retrieval side, pair it with an embeddings primer first.

Title: What platform teams can borrow from a century of car platforms
Description: Nikunj Karoliya of Pebble Mobility at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 maps VW's MQB, Ford's shared platforms and Tesla OTA onto internal developer platforms.
Body:
Car makers solved the problem of many products built from shared parts decades before anyone wrote an internal developer platform. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Nikunj Karoliya, Lead Engineer at Pebble Mobility, walked through how automotive manufacturing handles modularity, standardisation, versioning and technical debt, and what each lesson means for software platform teams.

This is an analogy talk, and a well-chosen one. There is no code; the value is in the mental models and the concrete automotive examples behind them.

## Shared chassis, different cars

Early car makers built every model as a one-off with its own components and assembly lines: duplication, siloed expertise, slow and expensive scaling. The shift to shared platforms (common chassis, interchangeable parts, unified processes across vehicle lines) is the same shift software made towards shared services and internal platforms. His motto for it: build once, reuse often.

Karoliya grounds the parallel in three architecture principles:

- **Separation of concerns.** Chassis, powertrain and user-facing features are designed by independent teams who meet at well-defined interfaces, just as infrastructure, backend and frontend teams meet at API contracts.
- **A flexible foundation.** Volkswagen's MQB platform supports both combustion and electric powertrains through standardised mounting points. The software equivalent is one API layer over both containers and serverless functions.
- **Standard interfaces.** Hundreds of electronic control units talk over protocols such as CAN and FlexRay so a brake system from one supplier works with traction control from another. In software that is gRPC, REST and event buses.

## Standardise the suspension bolts, not the interior

The sharpest section is on what to standardise. Car makers standardise chassis frames, suspension mounting points and crash structures: heavy engineering, strict regulation, and nobody buys a car for its rear suspension bolts. They keep freedom for the interior, the driving feel and infotainment.

Translated: authentication, logging, monitoring and deployment pipelines are your chassis. Rebuilding them per team adds cost and no value. Recommendation engines and UI personalisation are your interior. His example is a company with both a food delivery and a ride-hailing app: share payment processing, let each product own its matching algorithm and tracking UI.

## Versioning for things that live 20 years

Cars stay on the road for 10 to 20 years, so replacement parts must stay compatible across generations. Karoliya uses that to argue for architecture review boards that keep a platform coherent, explicit backward-compatibility and long-term support policies, and stability guarantees for components like identity and billing that other teams depend on. Moving fast is fine for features; your logging library should be boring for years.

Across product lines, that means dependency tracking to see the ripple effect of a change, coordinated phased releases, and extensive compatibility testing. Ford introducing a new part to the F-150 line through testing, pilot runs and phased rollout is, in his telling, a canary release with a supply chain attached.

## Technical debt measured by impact, not age

Automakers cannot wipe the slate clean with each model; tooling, training and supply chains represent decades of investment. They modernise behind abstraction layers so new components fit old platforms. Karoliya recommends the same for software (APIs, adapters and bridges instead of a big-bang rewrite) and a definition of debt that counts code that slows you down or blocks integration, not merely old code.

## Platform teams and product teams, Ford edition

The organisational example is Ford moving from vehicle-line teams (one for the F-150, another for the Mustang) to cross-functional platform teams owning shared architecture, with the F-150 and Ranger sharing much of their platform while product teams focus on model-specific features. Add centres of excellence, training and internal conferences to spread the knowledge, and you have the platform-team operating model in sheet metal. Tesla's over-the-air updates and Volkswagen's MEB electric platform close the talk as the point where cars became software platforms in their own right.

## Who should watch

Platform leads who need to explain to leadership why shared components, governance and versioning policies matter; the automotive vocabulary lands well with non-engineers. If you already run a mature platform org, the standardisation and versioning sections are still a good sanity check.

Title: How Slack built its own cloud dev environments, and when you should
Description: Jayant Tyagi of Salesforce (Slack) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on remote dev VMs, 90-second warm pools, SSH agent forwarding and frontend grafting.
Body:
"Works on my machine" stops being a joke when your product spans two code bases in two GitHub Enterprise accounts and no laptop can build both. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Jayant Tyagi, Software Engineer at Salesforce on the Slack engineering team, described the remote development platform he led at Slack: one CLI command, a provisioned VM in about 90 seconds, and features no off-the-shelf cloud IDE offered.

This is a build-it-yourself story. If you use Gitpod or Codespaces you will recognise the shape; the interesting parts are the choices Slack made because it controlled the whole stack.

## Two code bases, one product

The trigger was integration after acquisitions. One product had features living in multiple repositories, some in different GitHub Enterprise accounts. Changing one side, waiting for a sync, then changing the other, glued together with feature flags, was slow. Slack's dev environment runs both code bases side by side in two Docker containers that talk to each other port to port, so the product can be tested end to end on one machine with both tool chains installed.

The broader case for cloud development environments is familiar but well put: large code bases make laptop builds take minutes or hours, iOS, Android, web and ML tool chains break with every OS patch, confidential code ends up on laptops, and new hires spend their first days installing things.

## Ninety seconds, because the VM already exists

Each developer gets an isolated workspace VM reached over an encrypted SSH tunnel, built from hardened base images that bake in whatever all flavours share. SSO, the corporate firewall and role-based access come along by default.

Speed comes from not starting cold. Slack runs on AWS Auto Scaling Groups with a warm pool of pre-provisioned VMs, prebuilt images and cached dependencies and builds, giving roughly 90-second startup. The developer runs a command with a branch name and a configuration (frontend, backend, ML), and Chef recipes and shell scripts mount volumes, fetch secrets from the secret store and install linters, hooks and utilities. Then you connect from VS Code or Cursor and the branch is already checked out. The configuration also picks the instance size, so ML work gets more cores and RAM than someone editing HTML.

## SSH agent forwarding beat OAuth tokens

A small decision worth copying: how the VM talks to GitHub. Slack evaluated a GitHub OAuth app (managed and easy, but you own token scopes, expiry, rotation and the blast radius of a leaked token) against SSH agent forwarding, where the VM uses the developer's laptop credentials over the encrypted connection. They chose agent forwarding: nothing to rotate, and git behaves exactly as it does locally.

## Frontend grafting is the custom feature

The feature Tyagi is proudest of is frontend grafting. With special query parameters, a staging or production page loads its frontend bundles (HTML, JavaScript, React) from a developer's remote VM instead of its own. You get to test your unshipped frontend against production-shaped data and configuration, which dev environments rarely have. It only works inside the company firewall, and it only exists because the platform was built in-house.

## Treat it like a product and watch the bill

The rollout advice: pilot team first, take their feedback, onboard teams in phases, and write runbooks, since some developers have never lived in a Linux terminal. On cost: environments are ephemeral with a lifetime of a week or two, they suspend after idle periods, instance sizes map to the use case, and billing dashboards with budget alerts catch growth. Environment flavours help here; he notes Uber runs six, and Slack has at least four.

The results he reported: about 75% shorter build times thanks to bigger machines and remote caching, and developers productive from day one. For this product, almost nobody develops locally any more.

His honest caveat is the best line of advice in the talk. This is a non-trivial investment; if your laptops still cope, it may not pay off yet.

## Who should watch

Platform and developer-experience teams deciding between buying a cloud IDE and building one, and anyone stuck with a multi-repo product that is painful to run locally. Small teams with one tidy repo can skip it for now.

Title: Rust AI copilots for loans, shelves and SCADA, from reusable parts
Description: Sarat Piridi of Hanwha Qcells at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on Rust AI copilots for finance, retail, manufacturing and utilities, and the patterns behind them.
Body:
Enterprise automation usually dies in the integration layer, somewhere between a modern API and a point-of-sale terminal that has never heard of one. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Sarat Piridi](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Sarat_Piridi_agents_zero_systems), a senior engineer at Hanwha Qcells, showed how he would build AI copilots in Rust for loan processing, retail inventory, procurement and utilities, and which design patterns keep them maintainable.

It is a long, wide-ranging talk. The industry examples are described in general terms rather than as named deployments; the architecture and the patterns are the parts worth your time.

## Three building blocks

Piridi's copilot has three parts:

- **A data extraction engine** that pulls from spreadsheets, documents, databases and older file formats, processing many streams at once without wasting memory.
- **An agent system**, the brain, which uses AI models to understand data, make decisions, coordinate tasks and roll back actions when something goes wrong.
- **An integration layer** that connects to modern systems through APIs and to legacy systems that have none.

His reuse argument is that Rust's type system and modules make these parts behave like building blocks: a parser or decision model built for a finance project can be configured for healthcare or retail later, much like a modular ERP where each customer enables a different subset of features.

## Four industries, one shape

- **Finance:** loan processing that checks documents, verifies information and applies regulatory rules, with the core analysis in Rust and approvals left in tools like Power Platform.
- **Retail:** real-time inventory across hundreds of stores without two systems overwriting each other, predictive reordering, and an integration layer that pulls transaction data out of legacy POS systems.
- **Manufacturing:** procurement agents that check supplier availability, compare prices and place orders in parallel.
- **Utilities:** extending SCADA systems without replacing them, with fault-tolerant monitoring and automated regulatory reporting for audits.

## Patterns that make the compiler do the review

The design-pattern section is the best part. The actor model lets components run independently without stepping on each other's data. The command pattern packages each task so it can be undone, which is exactly what a copilot that takes actions needs. The repository pattern hides storage so you can switch databases without rewriting logic. Feature flags control rollouts.

The standout is the typestate pattern, which encodes the steps of a workflow in types so that, in his words, "we can't accidentally run the process in the wrong sequence". For loan approvals and audits, a compile error beats a post-incident review. His crate list: Tokio for concurrency, Serde for data formats, rust-bert for NLP, Rayon for parallel processing and Tonic for gRPC.

## The claimed payoff

Piridi cites 60 to 75% less development time for new workflows once the core components exist, 89% fewer production incidents and 83% faster overall process times, along with about 30% lower memory use. These are presented as typical results, not tied to a named system. His advice for starting is sensible: pick one process where reliability really matters, pilot a Rust copilot there, and reuse what you built in the next project.

## Who should watch

Engineers building AI-assisted business automation that must talk to legacy systems, and anyone who wants a quick tour of typestate and command patterns applied to agents.

Title: Zero trust at enterprise scale is a staged journey, not a product
Description: Naveen Kumar Birru of Palo Alto Networks at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on identity, microsegmentation, service mesh mTLS and API gateways for zero trust.
Body:
The castle-and-moat model assumes the attacker is outside the wall. Most traffic now never crosses the wall at all. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Naveen Kumar Birru, Senior Principal Software Engineer at Palo Alto Networks, walked through what zero trust means once you strip the marketing off: verify every request, base trust on identity instead of network location, and enforce policy at every layer of the stack.

## Why the perimeter stopped working

Birru opens with the numbers he uses to make the case: most enterprises run several cloud providers, the large majority of breaches still come from human error such as phishing and misconfiguration, and average breach costs keep rising. He adds that around 70% of traffic now flows east-west, inside the perimeter, where the moat does nothing. The model he argues for assumes breaches will happen and focuses on limiting the damage.

The three principles are short: continuous verification, identity-based trust and no default trust. His summary of the shift is the most quotable line in the talk: trust becomes something you earn, not something you inherit.

## Identity is the new perimeter

Identity, whether a person, a device or a workload, carries most of the weight. Following the NIST zero trust guidance, authentication and authorisation are dynamic and enforced before every access. The difficulty is that most enterprises run several identity systems, and machine identities now outnumber human ones in a majority of organisations. His recommendations are federated identity across environments, privileged identity management, and continuous authentication that rechecks identity during a session rather than only at login.

Access decisions then become contextual: identity and behaviour patterns, device health, location, time and data sensitivity combined into an adaptive risk decision rather than a static role check.

## Contain the blast radius

Microsegmentation applies controls at the workload level instead of network zones, so only explicitly allowed services can talk. Birru cites a large reduction in breach scope for segmented environments; the mechanism is the useful part: a compromised service cannot wander sideways, so a potential company-wide breach becomes a contained incident.

Encryption follows the same logic. Data in transit, at rest, in API calls and in east-west microservice traffic is encrypted with proper key management, so an intercepted packet is still useless.

## Enforce at three layers

The platform-engineering section maps zero trust onto the stack:

- **Network:** secure gateways, next-generation firewalls and SASE.
- **Service mesh:** Istio, Linkerd or AWS App Mesh providing mTLS on every service-to-service call, explicit policies on which services may talk, telemetry on communication patterns, and cryptographic workload identities that are hard to spoof.
- **Application:** API gateways that authenticate every consumer regardless of network origin, rate-limit, detect anomalies and validate schemas to block malformed payloads.

His warning on APIs is blunt: a zero trust architecture is only as strong as its weakest API. And he stresses that inconsistent enforcement across distributed environments is where attackers look first.

## You cannot secure what you cannot see

Observability gets a full section: security events collected across cloud and on-prem, behavioural baselines to spot deviations, automated responses that contain threats when detected, and feedback loops that tune policies over time. Built in from the start, not bolted on.

## Start with high-value targets

The closing advice is the honest bit. Only a small minority of organisations have fully implemented zero trust; most are partway or still planning. Legacy systems that were never designed for continuous verification are the top obstacle, followed by tool sprawl, skills gaps and culture. Successful programmes start with high-value targets, prove impact, then expand, with leadership, operations and business units aligned. Zero trust is a strategic commitment, not something you buy and tick off.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers who need a structured overview to plan a programme or brief leadership. It is a broad survey backed by industry statistics rather than a Kubernetes walkthrough, so do not expect YAML.

Title: VoIP monitoring that predicts call problems and fixes them itself
Description: Krishna Munnaluru of Oracle at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on a Kafka and ML monitoring platform for VoIP with lambda processing and guarded auto-remediation.
Body:
Voice is the least forgiving workload on the network: a web page can load half a second late, a sentence cannot arrive half a second late. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Krishna Munnaluru, Senior Principal Architect at Oracle, presented a monitoring platform for VoIP systems that learns what normal call quality looks like, predicts degradation before callers notice, and runs validated fixes automatically.

It is a short, architecture-level talk. Think of it as a blueprint with the reasoning attached, not a code walkthrough.

## Monitoring is a product, not a dashboard

Munnaluru starts with the familiar mess of distributed telephony: disconnected tools, alarms that are mostly false positives, and manual remediation that stretches recovery. His framing is platform engineering's: monitoring infrastructure is a product with users, and like good infrastructure it should be invisible, reliable and low maintenance. In real-time communications there is no tolerance for delay, so reliability has to be close to absolute.

## Kafka in the middle, plugins at the edge

The architecture is deliberately built from proven open-source parts:

- **A plugin-based ingestion layer** collecting call-quality metrics, network indicators and system performance from varied VoIP environments.
- **Apache Kafka** as the backbone for high-throughput, fault-tolerant telemetry streaming.
- **Microservices** for modularity and independent scaling.
- **Prometheus and the Elastic Stack** for metrics, logging and visualisation.

Data flows from raw VoIP telemetry through Kafka into ML models, and comes out as dashboards, alerts or automatic fixes, surfaced to developers through APIs and IDE plugins where they already work.

## Baselines beat thresholds

The machine-learning layer establishes baseline performance patterns and flags subtle degradation early. Its main job is separating normal variation from real problems, which is how you cut false positives: if call quality dips, the system decides whether it is a blip or an incident before it pages anyone. Quality prediction models forecast trends so teams can act before users are affected.

Processing uses a lambda architecture: millisecond-level streaming for urgent alerts alongside batch analytics for deeper trends. Built-in back-pressure prevents overload during traffic spikes, circuit breakers keep components steady, and event correlation finds the root cause so one failure does not produce a hundred alerts.

## Auto-remediation with guardrails

Detection triggers action. Remediation steps are chosen by severity and by how well they worked historically, checked for safety, then executed through canary deployments with rollback. Every outcome feeds back into future choices, so the system's playbook improves with use. A self-healing system that cannot undo its own fix would just be a faster way to make things worse; the canary-and-rollback guardrail is what makes the automation trustworthy.

## Cheap enough to keep

Munnaluru is direct that intelligent monitoring has to pay for itself. He reported intelligent data lifecycle management cutting storage costs by 65%, stream-processing optimisation giving 40% higher efficiency and right-sizing saving 30% on resources. The platform's own reliability is checked with load testing, chaos engineering and meta-monitoring: the monitor gets monitored too.

Rollout advice is the standard good list: infrastructure as code for repeatable deployments, realistic integration testing, training so teams can operate it themselves, and incremental adoption for early wins. Next on his roadmap: smarter models to push false positives down further, service mesh, serverless and eBPF observability, and edge support for constrained environments.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform teams running telephony, contact-centre or other real-time media systems, and anyone designing an alerting pipeline that pages too often. It is a high-level overview, so pair it with a hands-on talk if you want implementation detail.

Title: Why the big public clouds left multicast behind, and what to use
Description: Srinivas Shamkura of SADA explains at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 why clouds skip native multicast and how overlays, pub/sub and CDNs fill the gap.
Body:
Multicast is one of those protocols that works beautifully in your data centre and then quietly fails to exist in the cloud you are migrating to. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Srinivas Shamkura, Senior Cloud Infrastructure Engineer at SADA, explained why most major cloud providers don't support it natively, what that does to infrastructure automation, and which workarounds are worth their cost.

## One sender, many listeners, no sessions

Shamkura starts with the case for multicast. With unicast, one sender serving a thousand receivers holds a thousand TCP sessions, which burns CPU on the sender for nothing but bookkeeping. With multicast the sender pushes packets to a group, receivers join and leave, and there are no per-receiver sessions at all. His analogy is a radio station: tune to the frequency and you hear what everyone else hears. Financial market data, telecom and media streaming are built on it for exactly that reason.

## Five reasons the cloud said no

The heart of the talk is a list of five barriers:

1. **State explosion in software-defined networks.** Every join and leave means recalculating forwarding tables consistently across a huge virtual network, which loads the control plane.
2. **Multi-tenancy.** Multicast assumes one administrative domain; a shared physical fabric serving many customers cannot risk group traffic leaking between tenants.
3. **Operational complexity.** Unicast can be routed statically and predicted. Multicast membership changes constantly and is hard to automate.
4. **Performance in virtualised networks.** The cost of processing multicast through virtual switches can eat the bandwidth savings it was supposed to bring.
5. **Architecture mismatch.** Microservices prize loose coupling and explicit service boundaries; multicast couples publishers and subscribers implicitly.

## The automation bill arrives later

For platform engineers the pain is downstream. A legacy app that relied on multicast cannot be lifted and shifted. Terraform and CloudFormation have no native multicast resource, so teams end up with custom scripts beside their declarative code, which breaks the consistent, state-file-driven workflow they rely on.

Kubernetes adds its own wrinkles. Service discovery is DNS and point to point, so apps that discovered peers via multicast must be rewritten for the Service abstraction. Network policies govern pod-to-pod traffic but not multicast, leaving a security gap. And pods may be created and destroyed faster than multicast trees can be recalculated. A protocol designed for long-lived routers meets workloads that live for minutes.

## Three ways out, each with a cost

Shamkura is candid that every option has trade-offs:

- **Application-level replication.** The app manages group membership, delivery and error handling itself. It lets you migrate, but now the network is the developers' problem, and performance can suffer.
- **Overlay networks.** Deploy a marketplace router, build GRE tunnels from senders and receivers to it, run BGP between the hosts and that router, and let PIM handle the multicast. It moves the work back into the network layer, at the price of more moving parts to run.
- **Cloud-native rewrites.** Use managed messaging such as Amazon SQS or Google Cloud Pub/Sub, or a CDN when the workload is content distribution rather than real-time data.

His own lean is clear: the workarounds bring monitoring complexity, harder capacity planning, longer incidents and inconsistent environments between on-prem and cloud. Redesigning toward cloud-native and serverless event architectures is usually where the total cost of ownership comes out ahead.

## What might change

Looking ahead he points at SDN-native multicast scoped to specific use cases, SmartNICs and DPUs taking the per-packet burden off virtualised hosts, and service meshes such as Istio and Consul possibly growing multicast-like features. None of those exist as a drop-in answer today, which is why the talk's practical advice is about design choices you can make now.

## Who should watch

Anyone planning a migration of trading, telecom or media systems to AWS, Azure or Google Cloud should watch before the design review, not after. Platform teams already fully on Kubernetes with no legacy multicast can treat it as a well-explained piece of networking history.

Title: Four layers of agents, building multi-agent AI systems on Tokio
Description: Sidhanta Panigrahy of Okta at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on a four-layer multi-agent AI architecture in Rust, with Tokio coordination and a manufacturing case study.
Body:
A single monolithic AI service is a single point of failure with a very expensive GPU bill attached. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Sidhanta Panigrahy](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Sidhanta_Panigrahy_memory_safety_zero), Director of Business Technology at Okta, presented a four-layer multi-agent architecture written in Rust and argued that memory safety and Tokio's async runtime are what keep a system of many cooperating agents stable under load.

## The monolith problem

Panigrahy opens with the bottleneck he sees in enterprise AI programmes: most organisations build one centralized AI system, the design itself creates a single point of failure, and garbage-collected runtimes add unpredictable latency spikes and memory overhead on top. Splitting the work across specialised agents fixes the first issue. Rust, he argues, fixes the second.

## Perception, cognition, action, coordination

The architecture has four layers, each made of specialised agents:

- **Perception** agents ingest data, filter it and normalise it.
- **Cognitive** agents run model inference and decision logic.
- **Action** agents execute business logic inside transactional flows.
- **Coordination** agents orchestrate workflows across the distributed system.

The split is a useful template even outside Rust: it separates the noisy input side from the decision side, and makes coordination a first-class job rather than something every agent improvises.

## Why Tokio, and why traits

Agent coordination runs on Tokio, with non-blocking I/O across agent boundaries and priority-based scheduling of agent tasks. He reported handling about 250% more concurrent agents than an equivalent Python or Go system. For the agents themselves he uses custom traits with static dispatch where agent types are known at compile time, so polymorphism costs nothing at runtime, and efficient serialization for messages between agents. He also names actor, embedded-database and ML crates as options beyond Tokio.

The safety argument is about the bugs that plague distributed agents: race conditions, parallel state updates, inconsistent error handling and protocol violations. His claim is that the Rust compiler catches the bulk of them before deployment, and that his systems showed zero memory leaks across more than 50 million agent interactions.

## The manufacturing case

The case study is a global manufacturer whose AI quality-control system had unpredictable latency, causing about 12% production delays. The Rust rebuild used 22 specialised agents across the four layers, integrated with legacy systems through PyO3 and WebAssembly bindings. Panigrahy reported a 43% reduction in quality inspection time with no increase in defects, and latency under 50 ms at three times normal load. The company is not named. His implementation roadmap runs for about 20 weeks, from architecture assessment through core infrastructure and integration to production rollout.

## Who should watch

Architects designing agent systems who worry about what happens at scale, and teams with Python agent prototypes that are starting to fall over. Expect architecture and results rather than code. For a different angle on the same architecture, Panigrahy also gave a platform-focused talk at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025.

Title: AI workloads break networks that were built for web apps
Description: Bhaskararao Vakamullu of Hewlett Packard Enterprise at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on spine-leaf, ECMP, RDMA and network observability for AI scale.
Body:
A web app talks to a handful of backends and shrugs at a few hundred milliseconds of latency. A distributed training job talks to hundreds of nodes at once and stalls if the fabric hiccups. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Bhaskararao Vakamullu, Senior Network Software Engineer at Hewlett Packard Enterprise, argued that this gap makes the network a core platform capability, and walked through the design principles that keep it from becoming the weakest link.

It is a compact talk, close to a lecture in data-centre networking for platform people, and it moves fast.

## East-west traffic changed the shape of the network

Vakamullu traces the evolution from the classic three-tier core, distribution and access design to spine-leaf, which is optimised for east-west traffic between servers. AI made that traffic dominant: before a response ever goes back to the user, a lot of computation happens inside the data centre.

He contrasts the two worlds. Web applications typically need two to four backend connections and predictable traffic. AI workloads span 128 to 256 or more nodes, need terabit-scale bandwidth, want latency under 10 milliseconds, and are bursty and unpredictable. Software-defined networking and purpose-built ASICs with low-latency fabrics are the response.

## Incast is the failure you should know by name

His cascading-failure example is a financial AI platform hitting timeouts under peak load. The culprit is TCP incast: many servers answer one aggregator node at the same moment, buffers overflow, packets drop, retransmissions pile up and the service degrades. The fix he describes is RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) with flow control, so the fabric prevents the collapse instead of reacting to it.

The other bottlenecks on his list are worth checking against your own network: bufferbloat adding latency, switches that cannot process enough packets per second, oversubscription ratios that break AI workloads, and ML training saturating links within seconds.

## Design for the link that will fail

The fault-tolerance principles are classic, and stated crisply:

- **Path diversity** with ECMP (equal-cost multipath), so traffic spreads across several routes.
- **Fast failure detection** with BFD (bidirectional forwarding detection), so a dead link is noticed in under a second and traffic moves.
- **Segment routing** for traffic engineering.
- **Isolated failure domains** and graceful degradation, so a fault hits a slice of traffic rather than all of it.

For spine-leaf specifically: keep oversubscription below 3:1, size buffers for microbursts, and consider RDMA where latency really matters.

## Find problems before users do

On observability he recommends regular-interval telemetry, watching latency distributions, utilisation and retransmissions, ML-based anomaly detection, and digital twins for what-if analysis before you change production.

His case for caring is cost. He cited figures on how small amounts of latency add minutes to training runs, waste GPU cycles and multiply infrastructure cost, and an e-commerce platform that moved to a spine-leaf design with a 400 Gbps backbone and cut incidents by 98.5%. The talk gives the numbers without the methodology, so take them as illustrations of the direction. The underlying point holds regardless: idle GPUs waiting on a congested network are the most expensive way to do nothing.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who own Kubernetes or ML infrastructure but treat the network as somebody else's box will get a fast vocabulary for that conversation: incast, oversubscription, ECMP, BFD, RoCE. Network engineers will know all of it already.

Title: Treat subscription payments as a platform and failed charges come back
Description: George Thomas of Chegg at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on payment gateways, smart retries, tokenisation and usage-based billing as self-service.
Body:
Every subscription business has a quiet revenue leak: the card that expired, the charge that bounced, the retry that went out at the wrong time. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, George Thomas, Engineering Manager and Enterprise Integration Architect at Chegg, showed how treating payments as an internal platform (unified gateway, event-driven services, smart retries) turns that leak into recovered revenue and lets product teams ship pricing changes without an engineering ticket.

Thomas has worked across Zuora, Recurly, Stripe, Oracle and Salesforce, and it shows: this is a talk about the plumbing between those systems.

## From one processor to an event-driven platform

He sketches the evolution most companies lived through. A monolithic integration with one processor. Then several providers such as Braintree, Stripe and Adyen, each with its own custom integration code. Then API-first providers with abstraction layers, though teams still handled every failure themselves. And finally event-driven payment platforms where recovery and self-service are designed in from the start.

## Four building blocks

The architecture he describes has four parts:

- **A payment gateway** that hides the differences between providers behind one interface, so product code never cares whether a charge goes to Stripe or Braintree.
- **A subscription engine** owning the lifecycle: monthly, annual, bundles, price points, discounts and taxes, billing the right customer for the right period.
- **Event processing.** A renewal is an event; notifications, payment collection, general-ledger posting and revenue allocation react to it asynchronously instead of sitting in one synchronous transaction.
- **Revenue recovery** with automatic retries, because cards expire and balances run low.

The principles around them are the platform-engineering staples: abstract the card-network details away from product teams, make launches and pricing changes configuration-driven, build compliance into the APIs with audit logging, and offer a paved road for common payment scenarios while allowing deviations.

## Retries are a model, not a loop

The best section is the case study on failed payments. Before the platform, about 15% of subscription payments failed on the first attempt, retries were manual best guesses, error codes were not handled properly and only about 40% of failed payments were recovered.

You cannot just retry forever: Thomas points out that card networks such as Visa and Mastercard can fine merchants who keep retrying when they should not, so you get a handful of attempts over a few weeks. The platform version learns from the error codes and historical patterns which failures are retryable and when a retry is likely to succeed, A/B tests retry strategies against each other, and monitors the model in real time in case success rates start sliding. He reported recovery rising to 78%, which translated to millions in recovered revenue.

## Compliance and usage billing as self-service

On compliance, the trick is to never touch card numbers. Hosted payment fields from Stripe, Zuora or Recurly collect and tokenise the card, your systems keep only the token, and PCI scope shrinks accordingly. Infrastructure as code with Terraform keeps humans out of production consoles and gives auditors a change history.

Usage-based billing gets extra time because, as he notes, token-priced AI products made it mainstream. The hard parts are high-volume event ingestion, aggregation across systems and metering abstractions. His platform answer: predefined dimensions and metrics, self-service registration of new ones, and a usage-estimation API so customers can see what the next bill will be.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects running subscription billing, especially anyone stitching several payment providers together or about to launch usage-based pricing. If you have never had to reconcile a renewal event with the general ledger, some of it will feel like inside baseball, in the best sense.

Title: Production RAG at enterprise scale is a platform engineering job
Description: Srinivas Chennupati of Fannie Mae at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on scaling enterprise RAG: vector stores, caching, model routing, cost per query.
Body:
Getting a retrieval-augmented generation demo to answer one question is an afternoon. Getting it to answer ten thousand people in under two seconds without leaking a document is a platform. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Srinivas Chennupati, a platform architect at Fannie Mae with over 14 years in the industry, laid out the infrastructure strategies that take RAG from notebook to enterprise knowledge service.

## Why RAG, and why it is hard at scale

Chennupati starts with a short primer: retrieve relevant snippets from internal documents, PDFs and emails, pass them to the LLM as context, and the answer is grounded in your facts instead of stale training data. He cites hallucination rates as high as 27% as the reason enterprises reach for it.

Then the hard part. A production system has to cover terabytes of repositories, keep queries under a second or two, stay up, and serve 10,000-plus concurrent users. None of that is solved by a better prompt.

## Four pillars under the vector store

The infrastructure section builds on four ideas:

1. **Distributed vector databases.** Shard embeddings across nodes for horizontal scale; Weaviate, Pinecone and similar systems trade off scalability, latency and cost differently.
2. **Load balancing** that routes queries across database clusters, pipelines and LLM instances so no single tier becomes the bottleneck.
3. **Hybrid storage.** Hot embeddings on SSD, the rest on cheaper cold storage.
4. **Elastic scaling.** On Kubernetes, the vector store, retrievers, rerankers and LLMs scale independently, because they never get busy at the same time.

## From 12 seconds to under two

The performance section is the one to steal from. Chennupati describes cutting query times from eight to twelve seconds down to under two with layered tricks:

- **Caching at two levels:** query-level caching (hashed) for repeated questions, embedding-level caching for frequently retrieved documents.
- **Hierarchical retrieval:** a cheap coarse filter first, fine-grained ranking second, so you compare far fewer vectors.
- **Dynamic model routing:** small LLMs for lightweight queries, large ones only for the complex ones.
- **Placement:** retrieval and inference closer to the data, via edge or regional clusters.

Model routing doubles as the main cost lever. Together with autoscaled inference endpoints, open-source models for routine queries, volume discounts from vector database and cloud vendors, and careful placement across on-prem GPUs and cloud, he puts the achievable saving at up to 60%.

## Treat it like any other tier-one service

The reliability advice will sound familiar to SREs, which is the point. Metrics on embedding throughput, vector search latency and inference time in Prometheus and Grafana. Replicated clusters with automatic failover. Checkpointing embeddings so an outage does not mean re-indexing everything. Chaos testing of the retrieval pipeline with simulated node failures and network partitions. Version-controlled pipelines deployed through CI/CD and Terraform.

Security gets the same treatment: zero trust between RAG components, encryption of embeddings at rest and in transit, role-based access that respects existing enterprise data governance, audit logs for SOC 2 and ISO 27001, and masking sensitive data in logs. An embedding of a confidential memo is still a confidential memo.

## Benchmark five things before you ship

His closing framework is a short list worth pinning to a wall. Measure end-to-end query latency under different loads, retrieval accuracy against ground truth, throughput at peak concurrency, resource utilisation across compute, memory and storage, and cost per query at different scales. Then set SLAs before launch.

From more than 50 enterprise implementations he reported adoption around 85% when RAG lives inside existing tools (Slack bots, CRM plugins, knowledge portals) and ROI of 200 to 400% within 18 months. Those are aggregate claims rather than a single walked-through case, so treat them as direction, not a benchmark.

## Who should watch

Platform and infrastructure engineers who just inherited "the AI knowledge base" from a data science team will get a sane checklist. If you want code, retrieval evaluation methods or a specific vendor comparison, this is the wrong talk: it is an architecture overview, delivered quickly.

Title: An AI-powered CPQ platform, layer by layer
Description: Kishore Epuri at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 lays out a microservices blueprint for AI quoting and pricing, from Kafka events to GitOps and SLOs.
Body:
Configure, price, quote sounds like a form with a total at the bottom, until you have thousands of product options, discount approvals and a sales team waiting on a number. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Kishore Epuri, a CPQ solution architect with more than 15 years in the field, walked through a microservices platform that puts machine learning behind every quote and still answers in about 200 milliseconds.

## Three kinds of model, three kinds of service

The core of the design is not one big model. Epuri splits the AI work into three integration patterns, each behind its own service:

- **Gradient boosting** for pricing optimisation, exposed through standard APIs.
- **Neural networks** for configuration recommendations: guided selling and bundles, the backend telling the user what most customers buy with this configuration and what a bundle would save.
- **Real-time adjustment** that nudges prices based on current market conditions.

Data scientists pick the serving framework per model type (he names TensorFlow Serving and MLflow), while the platform gives one monitoring and management layer across all of them. That separation is the platform-engineering point of the talk: the model team chooses its tools, ops still gets one dashboard.

## Every price is an event

Between services sits Kafka, carrying what he describes as millions of pricing events a day, with standardised schemas so the platform can evolve without breaking consumers. Topics are organised by business domain and carry timestamps and correlation IDs.

The useful twist is event sourcing. Because every pricing decision and configuration change is kept as an event, you get a full history for free: what price was offered last week, which configurations users built over time, and an audit trail for compliance and debugging. When finance asks why a customer got that discount, the answer is a replay, not an archaeology project.

## GPUs only when the neural nets need them

The infrastructure section covers Terraform modules across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud to avoid vendor lock-in, a service mesh for encrypted service-to-service traffic and canary releases, and GitOps with Argo CD doing blue-green deploys of new model versions.

Two cost ideas stand out. The autoscaling feeds on model-serving metrics as well as CPU, so scaling reflects actual model performance. And node selection weighs cost against performance, provisioning GPU nodes only when neural-network workloads ask for them. Batch work runs on spot instances with fallback to on-demand, and training jobs run off-peak.

## SLOs that include the model

Epuri's SLO framework starts with the usual 99.9% availability and adds latency targets: 95% of pricing calculations within 200 ms, and an average ML inference latency of 50 ms. On top he puts AI-specific indicators: inference accuracy, prediction consistency across replicas and feature freshness for real-time predictions. That last trio is the bit most platforms still lack.

The rest of the stack is what you would hope for in enterprise software: mutual TLS with certificates rotated by cert-manager, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, secrets in Vault, a feature store shared by training and serving, Docker Compose environments with mock models for local development, and automated runbooks for incident response.

## The results he reported

For the case study, Epuri said the platform scaled from 10,000 to over 100,000 monthly requests through horizontal scaling, response times fell from around 800 ms to under 200 ms, and time to market for new features dropped by 65%. The talk presents these as headline outcomes rather than walking through the measurement, so read them as one team's report.

## Who should watch

Architects building ML into transactional enterprise systems (CPQ, ERP, order management) will get a complete checklist in one place. It is a slide walkthrough of the architecture rather than a demo or code, and it moves quickly across many layers; if you only care about one, jump to the event-driven or SLO sections.

Title: Rust for multi-cloud tooling, small binaries and explicit errors
Description: Uday Kiran Yedluri at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on why Rust suits multi-cloud tooling across AWS, Azure and GCP, and how to start with low-hanging services.
Body:
One cloud is easy, two are manageable, and somewhere after that the tooling starts to fray. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Uday Kiran Yedluri](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Uday_Kiran_Yedluri_cloud_security_rust), a cloud architect with 20 years in IT across AWS, Azure and GCP, argued that Rust is a strong fit for the tools that have to behave the same way in every one of those environments.

This is a strategy-level talk aimed at architects and engineering leads, not a code session. Its value is in the framing and the adoption plan.

## The fourth house problem

Yedluri's analogy lands well. "Also, think of it like managing multiple houses." The first house is fine, a vacation house is okay, and by the third or fourth the maintenance never stops. Multi-cloud is the same: companies adopt it to avoid lock-in, cut costs, meet compliance and improve resilience, and then pay in performance bottlenecks, a larger attack surface and operational load, plus how much each person has to know about each provider.

## Where Rust pays off across clouds

He groups the benefits into four areas:

- **Containers.** Rust services start faster, use less memory and avoid garbage-collector delays, and smaller binaries mean quicker deployments and cheaper storage.
- **Infrastructure as code.** Strict compile-time checks catch mistakes before provisioning, and he cited Rust-based tooling provisioning three to four times faster than older approaches.
- **Resilience.** The `Result` type forces explicit error handling, pattern matching covers every case, and the `?` operator keeps propagation readable. Ownership guarantees resource cleanup even during failures, which matters when a service spans providers.
- **Security.** He repeated the commonly cited figure that around 70% of high-severity CVEs in infrastructure components come from memory safety issues, and added stronger dependency verification, reproducible builds and compile-time help against leaking secrets between environments.

## The case studies

His main example is a global financial institution that replaced Java services with Rust and, he said, saw roughly 30 to 40% lower latency on the critical components, higher uptime, smaller deployments and no serious security issues for months after launch. He also mentions healthcare (faster data processing and HIPAA compliance) and manufacturing (better quality control and smaller device updates). None of these are named, and the talk gives few details on how the numbers were measured, so read them as direction rather than proof.

## Start where it hurts, then make it reusable

The roadmap is the part to keep:

1. Start small with non-critical services, picking the one with the highest pain and the lowest risk.
2. Build reusable libraries that work across all your clouds, so the second service is cheaper than the first.
3. Measure from day one and keep measuring.
4. Scale the patterns that work, with internal advocates who can show the results.

He also lists the trends he expects to grow: Rust as a default for secure cloud services, WebAssembly apps that run the same on any provider, and edge computing.

## Who should watch

Cloud architects and engineering managers building the case for Rust in a multi-cloud estate. Developers looking for crates and code samples should pair it with something more hands-on.

Title: Healthcare AI only pays off once the FHIR plumbing is in place
Description: Srimurali Krishna Chillara of Boston Children's Hospital shows at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 how FHIR, NLP and BI turn clinical data into outcomes.
Body:
The flashy part of healthcare AI is a model beating a dermatologist. The part that decides whether it ever helps a patient is an integration layer nobody puts on a slide. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Srimurali Krishna Chillara, Senior MicroStrategy Architect at Boston Children's Hospital, made that case: BI and AI only deliver outcomes in hospitals once platform engineers have unified the data underneath them.

## Sixteen platforms and no common language

Chillara opens with the mess. By his figures the average health system runs more than 16 platforms, most with incompatible data models; over 80% of healthcare data is unstructured (physician notes, imaging, scanned PDFs); and only about 30% of hospitals have achieved meaningful integration despite regulatory mandates. Add HIPAA, GDPR and newer AI rules on top, and "let's add some AI" becomes a multi-year project before the first prediction.

His proposed shape is a three-layer platform:

1. **Data integration:** FHIR-based APIs, real-time streaming and ETL/ELT pipelines pulling structured and unstructured data together.
2. **Analytics processing:** NLP over clinical text, dashboards for operations, machine learning for patient risk and resource needs.
3. **Delivery:** role-based access, integration into clinical workflows, and explainable AI so clinicians actually trust what they see.

## FHIR is the boring hero

The most engineering-heavy section is about FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources). Its pitch to developers is that it is plain RESTful APIs instead of the rigid message formats of older standards. Chillara cited integration projects finishing 63% faster on FHIR than on HL7 v2, and roughly three times the return on investment because data moves between systems instead of being re-keyed. If you have ever parsed a pipe-delimited HL7 message by hand, that speedup will not surprise you.

## Models matter less than where they land

He walks through the clinical numbers that usually headline these talks, from AI diagnostic accuracy in dermatology to fewer missed lung nodules in radiology and faster pathology. The point he draws from them is a platform one: none of it helps unless the model is embedded in the clinician's workflow, showing decision support inside the systems they already use rather than in a separate research tool.

Two case studies make it concrete. An emergency department fighting overcrowding combined real-time capacity management, predictive analytics and ML triage on one platform; he reported boarding times for admitted patients down 32%, triage 41% faster and about $4.2 million a year saved. On the money side, NLP pulling billing-critical details out of clinical notes, plus models that flag claims likely to be denied before submission, cut denied claims by 67% and lifted revenue by 12% in his example.

## NLP turns notes into FHIR resources

The unstructured-data section is the bridge between the two worlds. Named entity recognition and medical concept detection turn discharge summaries and referral letters into structured, FHIR-compliant resources, which can then feed population health analytics, quality reporting or decision support. In other words, the notes stop being a write-only database.

## Match ambition to readiness

The adoption advice is refreshingly modest. Low-readiness organisations should start with small pilots and simpler tools while fixing data quality and culture; high-readiness ones can go for enterprise-wide ML. The pitfalls he names are the classic ones: leading with technology instead of the problem, underestimating data quality, and building tools that sit outside clinical workflows. He closes on what comes next: federated learning across institutions without sharing raw data, ambient documentation, multimodal models, and AI regulation that demands every system be explainable and auditable.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers moving into healthcare, or BI teams being asked to "add AI", will get a sensible architecture and a vocabulary for the conversation with clinicians. It is an overview talk: expect the reasoning and the reported results, not code or FHIR resource walkthroughs.

Title: Healthcare apps need native code, on-device AI and HIPAA by design
Description: Srikanth Puram of General Motors at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on native mobile platforms with embedded AI for HIPAA-compliant, offline-ready healthcare.
Body:
When a patient's heart rate drops, a loading spinner is not an acceptable state. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Srikanth Puram, a senior software engineer at General Motors, made the case that healthcare apps should be built as platforms on native mobile code with embedded AI, so they stay fast, private and useful even when the network isn't there.

The talk is a broad tour rather than a code walkthrough, and each section is anchored by a real-world example from a different country.

## Platforms, not one-off apps

Srikanth's starting point is pressure on health systems: ageing populations, more chronic illness and stretched capacity. Building isolated apps doesn't scale, so he argues for platforms of reusable components, standardised interfaces for hospitals, devices and insurers, and architectures that handle millions of patients. Reliability, observability and maintainability matter even more in a domain that needs safe, auditable systems.

His example is a UK hospital network that built one shared platform for appointments, telemedicine and vaccination tracking and reused components across apps, cutting development time.

## Why native

Native development, in his framing, is about performance and reliability: real-time responsiveness for alerts, deeper OS-level security with encryption and secure storage, direct integration with glucose monitors, ECGs and blood pressure cuffs, and offline capability for rural areas with poor connectivity.

The example is an Android diabetes app connected directly to Bluetooth glucose monitors. Patients get instant alerts on abnormal readings and doctors get accurate, secure data streams. He argues that immediacy would have been hard with a hybrid app.

## AI on the device

Embedded AI shifts care from reactive to predictive. With frameworks like TensorFlow Lite, models run on the phone, so sensitive data stays local and analysis is faster. Uses include early warning of deterioration, personalised care recommendations and clinical decision support.

His examples range widely: a mobile eye-care app in India detecting diabetic retinopathy from smartphone images in clinics without eye specialists, connected ECG patches in Japan flagging abnormal rhythms, and an oncology decision-support system suggesting chemotherapy options while doctors keep the final call.

## Compliance is architecture

On HIPAA his line is that compliance is foundational, not optional: encryption at rest and in transit, role-based access with biometrics and multi-factor authentication, and audit trails for every data interaction. The best platforms bake these in so every app built on them gets them automatically. He cites a US telemedicine provider that restricted test results to physicians only, which helped with HIPAA and with patient trust.

## Rolling it out safely

The implementation section is the most grounded. Agile adapted for regulatory cycles, clinical validation with diverse patient groups, pilots in controlled settings, and real change management with staff training. His favourite example is a US children's hospital that piloted an asthma app with 50 families, refined it, then expanded to 10,000 patients.

Accessibility gets attention too: large fonts, voice input, high-contrast modes, translation and content tuned to literacy levels. Looking ahead he points to federated learning, AR in surgery and voice-first interfaces.

## Who should watch

Mobile engineers moving into health tech, and platform teams who need a checklist of what regulated, device-connected mobile apps require. Expect breadth over depth.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Nisheedh Raveendran on managing regulatory incidents in HIPAA, GDPR and DMA environments](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Nisheedh_Raveendran_compliance_hipaa_gdpr) covers what happens when compliance meets an incident.
- [Meghana Rao and Ananya M Gowda on attacking Bluetooth LE in mobile and wearables](https://www.conf42.com/Web_30_2022_Meghana_Rao_Ananya_M_Gowda_bluetooth_mobile_wearables_ecosystems) is the security flip side of device integration.
- [Ramakrishna Ambati on secure IoT edge architecture for medical diagnostic systems](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Ramakrishna_Ambati_maintenance_predictive_medical) applies edge AI to medical hardware.

Title: Platform-first cloud starts with pilot teams, not a big bang
Description: Srikanth Vissarapu (Crusoe) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on self-service infra, golden paths, hub-and-spoke multi-cloud and phased rollout.
Body:
A cloud migration that hands developers a console login and a wiki page is just a ticket queue with extra steps. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Srikanth Vissarapu, Staff Software Engineer at Crusoe, argued for a platform-first approach: self-service infrastructure, golden paths, policy as code, and a rollout that starts with a few pilot teams before the whole company is asked to move in.

The talk is a broad tour rather than a single case study. Think of it as a checklist of what an internal platform has to cover before it earns the name, delivered by someone who has clearly sat on both sides of the provision-me-a-VM ticket.

## The gap is between what developers build and what they must know

Vissarapu frames the problem as a mismatch. Developers want to ship features; classic DevOps models also make them carry infrastructure, networking and compliance in their heads. That cognitive load slows everything down.

His answer has three parts. Self-service, so engineers provision VMs, run workloads and manage configuration without going through a ticketing system. Golden paths, the predefined and optimised routes through common scenarios like building, testing and deploying a service. And central governance, because more freedom needs more guardrails: least-privilege access, security and privacy checks baked in, not bolted on.

## Multi-cloud needs a hub, a mesh and codified rules

Most companies he sees have drifted into more than one cloud, each picked for its own strengths. The pattern he recommends is hub and spoke: a central hub owns the shared foundations (authorisation, monitoring, governance) and teams build services on top.

Between those services sits a service mesh such as Istio on Kubernetes, so developers stop hand-rolling inter-service communication. Over everything sits policy as code: governance rules written down, versioned and enforced automatically, so compliance doesn't depend on someone remembering a spreadsheet.

## Self-healing deploys are part of developer experience

The developer experience section covers the expected ground (AI coding assistants like GitHub Copilot for boilerplate and tests, CI/CD with automated unit and integration tests) and then lands on a point worth stealing: a canary deployment that rolls itself back to the last healthy build is a developer-experience feature, not only an ops feature. Nobody codes confidently when a bad release means a weekend.

On the infrastructure side he lists reusable infrastructure-as-code modules and template libraries, autoscaling templates that kick in when workloads outgrow what you bought, GitOps workflows for an audit trail of what changed and what rolled back, and container scanning so known-vulnerable libraries never reach production.

## Measure the platform three ways

How do you know it worked? Vissarapu splits the scorecard into three:

- **Technical:** lead time for changes, mean time to recovery, change failure rate.
- **Business:** cloud spend, cost per deployment, time to market. His example: launching in a new country no longer means buying hardware there.
- **Developer:** surveys and feedback, because a platform people hate is a platform people route around.

## Roll it out in phases

The most practical slide is the adoption plan. Start with pilot teams and build the base layer with them: a consistent way to package and deploy, canary and blue-green as built-in options. Once the pilots are confident, widen to cross-functional teams and turn the platform into shared ownership, where other teams contribute and extend it. Then keep iterating on feedback. A platform is a product with users, and this plan treats it like one.

The abstract quotes headline gains for faster deployments and lower overhead; the talk itself spends its time on the patterns rather than on a measured case, so treat those figures as the goal, not a benchmark.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and architects starting an internal platform, or explaining one to leadership, will get a clean map of the territory in one sitting. If you already run Backstage, Crossplane and a mature GitOps setup, you will recognise most of it; skip to the rollout and metrics sections.
