Title: How Rust took over the lakehouse, from Arrow to DataFusion
Description: Rahul Joshi of Capital One at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 traces data platforms from Hadoop to lakehouses and shows where Rust components now sit in the stack.
Body:
The JVM carried big data for fifteen years; the newest layer of the lakehouse stack is increasingly written in Rust. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, Rahul Joshi, Distinguished Data Engineer and Director at Capital One, walked through three eras of enterprise data architecture and showed exactly which pieces of a modern lakehouse Rust now powers.

Rahul brings about 20 years of building data platforms in financial services, and it shows: the talk is a clear history lesson that ends in a practical adoption plan.

## Phase one: Hadoop and the JVM tax

The story starts in the on-premise Hadoop era: HDFS and MapReduce, everything on the JVM. It worked at scale, but Rahul listed the costs plainly. Each task needed its own heap, object headers added bytes to every record, data exchanged between map and reduce tasks had to be serialized and deserialized at every hop, and garbage collection pauses of seconds made run times inconsistent.

His benchmark slide compared word count, the hello world of big data, across Hadoop, Spark and DataFusion, with the Rust engine finishing far ahead. The point is not the toy workload; it is that removing GC and serialization overhead changes the resource profile of the whole job.

## Phase two: warehouses fixed usability and added lock-in

Cloud warehouses such as Snowflake and Redshift solved much of Hadoop's usability problem with SQL-friendly analytics. The catch, as Rahul framed it, was proprietary storage formats: you pay compute to load data, compute to query it, and egress to take it out again. Storage and compute were coupled, and ML workloads usually meant copying data somewhere else, creating silos.

## Phase three: the lakehouse, with Rust in the engine room

The lakehouse merges the two with open table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi) on object storage, ACID transactions, schema evolution, time travel, and separate scaling of storage and compute.

This is where the Rust inventory comes in, and it is the slide worth screenshotting:

- **Table formats**: Rust libraries for Delta and Iceberg that let you read and write tables without spinning up Spark.
- **Columnar storage**: Apache Arrow's Rust implementation for zero-copy columnar memory, plus parquet-rs and Lance for storage.
- **Query processing**: Apache DataFusion for SQL and DataFrame APIs with parallel execution and a small footprint.
- **DataFrames**: Polars on top of Arrow.

Rahul quoted recent benchmarks for these: big query-speed gains for DataFusion over Spark on the same hardware, large memory savings for Polars over pandas on a 100 GB dataset, and much faster Parquet loading with arrow-rs than with PyArrow. These come from published and internal tests rather than a live demo, and as always your workload will have opinions.

## Start with the bottleneck, not the rewrite

The practical section is the strongest. Rahul described three integration styles: Rust microservices for the critical processing components, native extensions for Python or JVM code that keep the existing interface, and full replacement of a pipeline for maximum benefit.

His recommendation is the boring correct one. Most organizations start by replacing components already identified as bottlenecks, such as high-throughput ingestion, heavy feature engineering for ML, or interactive SQL that needs sub-second response, and only then consider rewriting more. Measure first, swap the hot path, repeat.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers and architects deciding where Rust belongs in their stack, and anyone who wants a crisp narrative of how we got from MapReduce to the lakehouse. It is light on code and heavy on architecture.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [LanceDB: an OSS serverless vector database in Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Lei_Xu_lancedb_oss_serverless_vector_db) by Lei Xu: the Lance format Rahul mentions, from the people who build it.
- [Bring your DataOps to the Data Lakehouse](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Jorge_LoaicigaRodriguez_dataops_lakehouse_challenges) by Jorge Loaiciga Rodriguez: running a lakehouse once it exists.
- [Enterprise Data with Lakehouse Architecture at Scale](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Richa_Solanki_data_lakehouse_enterprise) by Richa Solanki: another enterprise migration story.

Title: Porting JVM library design to Rust crates, pattern by pattern
Description: Venkata Appalapuram of Ritepros at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on mapping a Spark JMS connector's provider interfaces and exceptions to Rust traits and Results.
Body:
Good library design survives a change of language; only the syntax moves. That is the thesis of Venkata Appalapuram's talk at Conf42 Rustlang 2025. Venkata, of Ritepros Inc, used the Spark JMS connector built for Capital One as a case study and walked through how each of its JVM design decisions translates into Rust crate design.

If you write libraries in Java or Scala and are starting on Rust, this is a practical side-by-side: provider interfaces next to traits, exception hierarchies next to `Result`, Mockito next to trait mocks.

## The connector that set the requirements

The project background gives the patterns their weight. The Spark JMS connector reads financial transactions from several message queue providers (ActiveMQ, IBM MQ and others), feeds real-time pipelines including fraud detection, and is reused across departments. It has to be fast and it cannot lose messages, because a customer whose transaction vanished does not care which broker was at fault.

The other hard requirement was normalizing many different message patterns into one schema before handing them on. From that, Venkata drew five universal design challenges: abstraction boundaries, configuration, error propagation, extensibility without breaking compatibility, and performance overhead.

## Provider interfaces become traits

On the JVM side, the connector used provider interfaces with dependency injection, so the implementation for a given broker can be swapped based on the user's configuration. Venkata's point is that this pattern has a natural counterpart in Rust's trait system, with the bonus of compile-time polymorphism and zero-cost dispatch, and trait objects available when you genuinely need runtime choice.

Separation of concerns carries over the same way. In the JVM connector, message consumers do not know which queue a message came from, acknowledgement is handled by the connection layer rather than the processing code, and error handlers plug in and out. In Rust, the module system enforces those boundaries, ownership makes it explicit who is responsible for a connection, and the borrow checker discourages leaky abstractions.

## Exceptions become Results, and the compiler checks your homework

The error-handling section is the most useful comparison. The JVM version uses checked and unchecked exceptions with detailed messages and stack traces, with some care about the cost of throwing. The Rust version encodes success or failure in `Result`, uses custom error enums for composable error types, adds context with the `anyhow` and `thiserror` crates, and relies on exhaustive `match` so no error case is silently ignored.

Configuration follows a similar arc. Both sides use a builder pattern with sensible defaults and validation at construction time. Rust can push more of that validation into the type system, including const generics for static configuration.

## Testing and docs travel well too

Testing strategies map almost one to one: Mockito against trait mock implementations, Testcontainers for real broker instances in integration tests, and property-based testing with JUnit theories or jqwik on the JVM against proptest and quickcheck in Rust. Documentation goes from Javadoc and example classes to rustdoc with doc tests that are compiled and run, so examples cannot rot.

Venkata reported a 10x performance improvement and a 99.9% reliability target met for the work. The closing lessons are the parts to keep: abstraction principles are language-neutral, use each language's strengths, testing strategy is portable even when test code is not, and document intent, not just implementation.

## Who should watch

JVM engineers building their first serious Rust crate, and anyone maintaining a library across two ecosystems. Seasoned Rust library authors will find the patterns familiar but may enjoy the JVM mirror.

- [Rust for Java Programmers: a Personal Perspective](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Ovidiu_Ionescu_java_programmers_personal_perspective) by Ovidiu Ionescu: the same migration, from the individual developer's side.

Title: Why Rust fits HR tech, from payroll runs to open enrollment
Description: Swetha Priya Sathiyam of ADP at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on how Rust's safety and concurrency map onto HRIS systems that touch every employee.
Body:
HR systems are one of the few enterprise platforms that touch every person in a company, from the day they are recruited to their last paycheck. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, Swetha Priya Sathiyam, Director of Solution Design for ADP Lyric HCM at ADP, made the case that Rust's safety and concurrency guarantees line up unusually well with what an HRIS has to get right.

Be clear on the scope: this is an architect's argument for where Rust could fit in HR technology, built on domain experience and published case studies, not a tour of a Rust codebase at ADP. Taken that way, it is a useful map of a domain most Rust talks never visit.

## Open enrollment is a load test with a deadline

Swetha traced HR tech through three eras: paper files and timecards, mainframe and on-premise HRIS (with core payroll still in COBOL at many large companies, reliable but expensive to change), and today's cloud suites like Workday, SAP SuccessFactors and Oracle Cloud HCM.

Her point is that even the modern platforms hit scaling walls. She described open-enrollment windows where a benefits page took minutes to load because everyone logged in at once. Every HR engineer knows the calendar: the traffic spike is scheduled, and so is the outage if you are unlucky.

## The domain maps neatly onto Rust's features

The most interesting part of the talk is how specific the mapping gets.

Memory safety matters more than usual because the data is Social Security numbers, bank details and medical information. Fearless concurrency matters because payroll, benefits processing and a performance cycle can all be running at once for tens of thousands of employees. Explicit error handling forces you to decide what happens when a tax rate file is missing or a benefits vendor API is down, instead of finding out on payday.

Her best example is the type system. A job grade, she noted, is not a number: it is tied to bands, locations and rules. Rust lets you model that in types so invalid combinations do not compile. The same goes for workflows: a state machine can make it impossible to mark a candidate as hired before the background check completes.

## A reference architecture in layers

Swetha sketched a modular Rust HRIS: a data layer with compile-time checked queries, an API layer on Actix Web for employee self-service portals that must absorb spikes, authentication with strong cryptography and role-based access control modelled in code rather than config, and async background jobs for payroll batches and compliance reports. Her payroll example runs tax calculations per jurisdiction concurrently and merges the results.

Security got its own section: RBAC in the code, tamper-evident audit logging of every access to sensitive data, and the ownership model as a natural fit for data lifecycle rules like deletion after a retention period, which matters for GDPR and HIPAA.

## The case studies, and the practices

She cited case studies she researched, including a financial services firm moving payroll from COBOL to Rust with a large cut in processing time, a tech company replacing a Java onboarding app that crashed during graduate hiring, and a healthcare platform meeting HIPAA requirements. The companies are not named, so treat these as illustrations.

The best-practice list is solid and transferable: domain-driven design to model HR processes, consistent error handling so payroll failures surface early, end-to-end tests for compliance and data integrity, minimal `unsafe`, audited third-party crates, and documented HR logic so the next team can onboard.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects in HR, payroll or other regulated enterprise systems who are weighing Rust for a new service. Rust specialists will not learn new language tricks here, but they will get a sharp picture of a domain where correctness has a payday.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [SBB: Secure Building Blocks in Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Yashwanth_Singh_M_sbb_secure_building_blocks) by Yashwanth Singh M: security primitives for the PII-heavy parts.
- [Employee Self-Service in SAP HR with SAPUI5 and JavaScript](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Lakshmi_Gogula_ess_sap_hr_sapui5) by Lakshmi Gogula: the self-service portal side from the SAP world.
- [Fall in LOVE with Unit Testing!](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Joe_Skeen_love_unit_testing) by Joe Skeen: for the "comprehensive tests" part of the checklist.

Title: A Rust 5G traffic manager built on zero-copy and safe DMA
Description: Riddhi Patel of DRC System LLC at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on a Rust 5G traffic manager that targets sub-5 ms latency without C++ memory risks.
Body:
5G systems want end-to-end latency under five milliseconds, and the two classic ways to get there both hurt: C and C++ are fast but leak and overflow, while Java and Go are safe but pause for garbage collection at the worst moment. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, Riddhi Patel of DRC System LLC made the case that Rust is the exit from that trade-off, using the architecture of a Rust 5G traffic manager as the example.

It is one of the shortest talks of the event, closer to a well-organized briefing than a tutorial. If you want the shape of a Rust packet-processing system on one page, it delivers.

## The trade-off Rust is meant to break

Riddhi laid out the problem plainly. Network functions for 5G need massive concurrency and near-perfect reliability at very low latency. Manual memory management in C and C++ brings buffer overflows and slows development; garbage-collected languages bring unpredictable pauses that real-time workloads cannot absorb.

Rust's answer, in her framing, is the usual four pillars applied to packets: ownership gives memory safety with no collector, zero-cost abstractions give high-level code with C-like performance, the compiler rejects data races, and when you do need low-level control, `unsafe` is scoped to small, auditable blocks.

## Four layers of a smart network manager

The architecture slide is the core of the talk. A radio interface layer processes packets asynchronously using zero-copy buffers. A traffic classification engine leans on Rust's type system for compile-time optimized matching. A routing core handles lock-free concurrency. Underneath sits memory-safe DMA for moving data quickly.

The zero-copy point is explained well. In C or C++ you hand out pointers and hope everyone frees memory correctly. In Rust you hand out slices, views into the same buffer that the borrow checker tracks, and memory is released when it goes out of scope. Less copying means less memory bandwidth used, which Riddhi tied to running on resource-constrained hardware at the edge.

## Types as a performance tool

Two patterns stand out. Compile-time polymorphism through generics lets one piece of code compile into specialized, optimized routines with no runtime dispatch cost. The type-state pattern encodes the state of a connection or buffer in its type, so whole classes of wrong-state bugs become compile errors.

The DMA example is the most interesting for systems people. DMA access is traditionally the scary part of the codebase. Riddhi showed wrapping DMA buffers in a struct with safe cleanup behind a Rust abstraction, so direct hardware access comes with the same guarantees as the rest of the program. On the async side, futures and stream combinators replace callback chains, avoiding the spaghetti that callback-heavy network code tends to grow.

## The numbers she reported

For her system, Riddhi reported around 4.2 ms end-to-end latency under heavy load, a 300% throughput gain over a comparable C++ implementation, lower CPU usage, and no memory-safety incidents across 18 months of deployment. The talk does not walk through the benchmark setup, so read these as the speaker's results rather than a reproducible comparison.

Her adoption advice is the sensible kind: replace critical components of an existing C or C++ system incrementally rather than attempting a full rewrite.

## Who should watch

Network and telecom engineers curious about Rust, and systems programmers who want a compact picture of zero-copy, type-state and safe hardware access in one design. Experienced Rust networking folks will find it an overview rather than new technique.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Software-Defined Networking for IoT and 5G](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Sai_Charan_Madugula_networking_iot_5g) by Sai Charan Madugula: the network side of the same 5G story.
- [Get maximum benefit from zero-cost abstractions](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2022_Tim_McNamara_maximum_benefit_zerocost_abstractions) by Tim McNamara: what "zero-cost" actually buys you.
- [Empowering Fearless Programming and Data Engineering](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Vishnu_Chilukoori_Srikanth_Gangarapu_empowering_fearless_programming) by Vishnu Chilukoori and Srikanth Gangarapu: Rust's concurrency model in practice.

Title: Supply chain digital twins in Rust, and why predictable beats fast
Description: Shikha Duttyal of Meta at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on digital twins, variance-based route optimization and a Rust infrastructure built for always-on monitoring.
Body:
The fastest shipping route is not always the best one; the most predictable one often is. That is the idea at the centre of Shikha Duttyal's talk at Conf42 Rustlang 2025. Shikha, a Supply Chain Solutions Program Manager at Meta, walked through digital twins for supply chains, variance-based route optimization, and why the engine underneath was built in Rust.

This is a talk from the operations side of the house. It speaks the language of inventory, safety stock and payback periods, with Rust appearing as the infrastructure choice that makes the twin trustworthy enough to run for months.

## A digital twin is a control tower that can simulate

Shikha drew a line between the traditional supply chain control tower, which mostly shows historical data on a dashboard, and a digital twin: a live virtual replica of the physical network that you can run scenarios against. Test a new product launch or a supplier change in the twin, find the bottleneck there, and only then commit trucks and contracts.

She listed the gains organizations report from this: faster launches, constraints found before they cost money, and better resource utilization from continuous automated scenario planning. The figures she quoted are industry results and case-study numbers rather than a benchmark she ran live, so treat them as direction, not a promise.

## Optimise for variance, not just the average

The sharpest section is the maritime routing case study. Traditional route optimization asks for the fastest or the cheapest path. Shikha's argument is that what planners actually need is the route that arrives in the most predictable time, every time.

The logic is tidy. A route with low transit variance makes arrival estimates accurate, accurate estimates make inventory planning precise, and precise planning lets you carry less expensive safety stock. In her example, the algorithms found lanes with much lower variance than others with similar average transit times, and a Fortune 500 manufacturer turned that into savings by cutting safety stock. Anyone who has padded an SLA to cover a flaky dependency will recognize the pattern: the p99 drives the buffer, not the mean.

## Where Rust earns its place

Supply chain monitoring applications run for months or years without a restart, so Shikha led with memory safety: the ownership model rules out the slow leaks that make long-running services degrade. Her code examples were small and illustrative. A function that takes ownership of a container record frees it when done, with no use-after-free possible. A `RouteOptimizer` trait lets you swap a variance-based optimizer for another implementation with static dispatch and no runtime cost.

She also pointed at fearless concurrency for high-velocity IoT streams and at WebAssembly as a way to run the same Rust code from low-power shipping sensors up to cloud servers. Her description of the organizational pattern is one many teams will recognize: Python for exploration and data science, Rust for the production services where failure is not acceptable.

## The second case study, and the roadmap

A global shipping company with a fleet of container vessels ran a twin on Rust-based edge computing, monitoring more than 1,200 parameters per vessel. Shikha highlighted a small memory footprint and efficient compression that cut satellite transmission costs, which matters when your bandwidth bill is priced per byte from mid-ocean.

The talk closes with an 18-month, four-phase roadmap: foundation and pilot choice, a first limited twin on ERP and WMS data, expansion with IoT sensors and a control tower, then optimization with ML and partner integration. She stressed change management as one of the three pillars, next to data integration and algorithms.

## Who should watch

Engineers building logistics or operations platforms, and technical leads who need to explain a Rust investment in business terms. If you want deep Rust internals, this is not that talk; it is about why the language choice matters to the outcome.

Title: Rust event-driven dashboards that stop polling for incidents
Description: Tashi Garg of Juniper Networks at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on replacing polling dashboards with a Rust telemetry pipeline that pushes events to the UI.
Body:
A dashboard that polls every 30 seconds is a dashboard that is, by design, up to 30 seconds wrong. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, Tashi Garg, Senior Staff Software Engineer at Juniper Networks, argued that this staleness is where incidents hide, and that a Rust-built, event-driven telemetry pipeline is how you get the delay out of the loop.

It is a short, focused talk: the problem, why Rust fits, one case study, and a phased rollout plan. Good value for anyone who has watched a graph turn red a few minutes after the customer tickets arrived.

## Polling dashboards are blind by construction

Tashi's framing starts with mechanics. Most static dashboards collect data at a fixed interval, often 30 seconds or a minute depending on the widget, so an event can happen well before it shows up on screen. Add binary or threshold-based health checks on top, and the slow, intermittent failures (packet loss that comes and goes, latency that degrades without crossing a line) never get flagged at all.

Tashi presented figures for both effects: detection delays averaging around 8.5 minutes from onset to first visibility, and a large share of anomalies that threshold checks simply missed. Combine staleness with missed anomalies and you get what the talk calls the reactive monitoring trap: teams only respond once the issue is already hurting customers.

## Why the backend has to be Rust-shaped

The fix is a push model: process telemetry as it arrives and stream updates to the UI instead of waiting for the next poll. That only works if the pipeline keeps latency flat under load, and that is the case Tashi makes for Rust.

The list is the familiar one, but it is pointed at a specific failure mode. No garbage collector means no GC pause at the exact moment a telemetry spike hits. The borrow checker rules out data races in concurrent ingestion code. Zero-cost abstractions let you write readable stream processing without paying for it at runtime.

The ecosystem named in the talk is concrete: Tokio for async ingestion across many concurrent IO-bound tasks, zero-copy serialization for big JSON, protobuf or Avro payloads, a low-latency web framework to push live updates, and crossbeam for multi-core concurrency primitives.

## The reference stack is small and boring, in a good way

The suggested architecture has four layers. Lightweight Rust agents on hosts (the talk cites a target of under 15 MB and under 2% CPU) ship telemetry over gRPC or WebSockets. An async streaming pipeline processes it across cores. A real-time API layer pushes updates to the dashboard within tens of milliseconds. The UI subscribes over WebSockets or server-sent events instead of polling.

In the case study, a global financial services provider running more than 12,000 instances across several clouds, Tashi reported the Rust backend handling 3.2 million telemetry data points per second, with incident detection dropping from about 11 minutes to 47 seconds. Those are the speaker's numbers from that deployment; the talk does not show the code or the methodology in depth.

## Roll it out in phases, not in one heroic rewrite

The most practical slide is the adoption plan. Spend the first month auditing blind spots and recording baseline MTTR and downtime. Run agents in staging for a couple of months and validate latency, throughput and detection accuracy. Roll to production over a quarter, wired into the incident tooling, and only then layer on ML anomaly detection or natural-language query interfaces.

Tashi also named the three predictable obstacles: legacy systems (bridge with FFI or gRPC rather than replacing everything), the Rust skill gap (start with one self-contained component), and data volume (filter and aggregate at the agent before sending upstream).

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who own monitoring and suspect their dashboards are lagging reality. It is more architecture pitch than code walkthrough, so Rust experts looking for implementation detail will want to pair it with something hands-on.

- [Perses, the GitOps native dashboard visualization tool](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Erwin_de_Keijzer_gitops_perses_dashboard_visualization) by Erwin de Keijzer: dashboards as code, the other half of the dashboard problem.
- [The Failures You Don't See on Dashboards](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Abhimanyu_Narwal_failures_dashboards_reliability) by Abhimanyu Narwal: a reliability case study about what graphs hide.
- [Business Insights with OpenTelemetry](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Brian_Loomis_observability_insights_telemetry) by Brian Loomis: what to put into the telemetry stream in the first place.

Title: Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025: hybrid sidecars, cloud QPUs and PQC
Description: Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 roundup: 19 talks on preparing architecture and cryptography, cloud quantum services, hybrid sidecars and finance use cases.
Body:
Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 ran on June 19, 2025, with 19 talks and a useful tension between them. Some speakers treated quantum advantage as a business plan for this year; the most practical ones treated it as an engineering problem: wrap a small, noisy quantum core in classical systems you already run, and get your architecture and cryptography ready before the hardware forces the issue. The full lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/quantum2025) and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDLJsZ2QLy2_0A5YjP6CaRq).

## Get ready before the hardware is

[Laxmikanth Mukund Sethu Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Laxmikanth_Mukund_Sethu_Kumar_classical_quantum_enterprise), Executive Director at JPMorgan Chase, gave the most grounded framing of the day. Quantum isn't production-ready for every enterprise use case, he said, but architects can lay groundwork now with patterns they already know: event-driven design, hybrid orchestration and API-driven interfaces that a quantum service could slot into later. He drew on platforms he has designed for banks, airlines and government systems, and kept the quantum mechanics to a minimum.

The cryptography side got its own warning. [Pavan Nutalapati](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Pavan_Nutalapati_quantum_cloud_security) laid out how quantum computing threatens today's encryption in the cloud, the emerging standards, and how to build a quantum-safe strategy. [Sarah Choudhary](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Sarah_Choudhary_quantum_algorithms_problem) covered the algorithms behind the cryptography and optimisation headlines for anyone who wants to know what the machines would actually run.

## Quantum arrives as a cloud service

Most engineers will meet quantum hardware through an API. [Naga Murali Krishna Koneru](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Naga_Murali_Krishna_Koneru_cloud_aws) of Hexaware Technologies walked through Amazon Braket and hybrid quantum-classical workflows on AWS. [Srinivas Sriram Mantrala](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Srinivas_Sriram_Mantrala_quantum_cloudops_devops) explored what quantum-enhanced DevOps and hybrid cloud integration could look like, and [Srikar Kompella](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Srikar_Kompella_quantum_saas_architecture) of Twilio looked at multi-tenant SaaS architecture where quantum and edge processing meet.

Then [Denish Tomar](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Denish_Tomar_quantum_cloud_qum) of Qumulus asked the question nobody else did: who is going to understand the bill? He opened with a founder whose usual monthly cloud spend jumped several times over because an autoscaling setting sent a cluster to 50 servers instead of five, for three days instead of two hours. If we can't predict classical cloud costs, he argued, usage-based pricing for quantum will be worse, and bundled, predictable resource models are the way out. The only quantum talk of the year where the scariest number was on an invoice.

## Hybrid sidecars and research tooling

Two talks showed what a sensible first step looks like. [Pradeep Karanam](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Pradeep_Karanam_plm_teamcenter) of Facebook described a small sidecar for Siemens Teamcenter, the product lifecycle management system, that sends only the hardest part of a "what if" question about product options or purchase plans to a cloud quantum computer. Everyone's daily workflow stays the same, and the classical system does everything else. He also explained why today's noisy machines are always wrapped in classical code.

[Vamsi Praveen Karanam](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Vamsi_Praveen_Karanam_low_code_experimentation) of Amazon tackled the research side with a schema-driven approach: one JSON schema, stored versioned and immutable, generates a React control panel, a serverless Step Functions workflow that runs and post-processes circuits, and a lineage tracker that tags every run. Researchers edit a manifest instead of copying notebooks, and the audit trail comes for free.

## Finance wants to go first

Financial services supplied the most use cases, and the most optimism. [Nikhil Kassetty](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Nikhil_Kassetty_quantum_payments_latency) of Intuit looked at how quantum could affect real-time payments, fraud detection and settlement, based on emerging pilots and experiments. [Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Venkateswarlu_Boggavarapu_finance_optimization) of JPMorganChase covered data engineering for quantum-enhanced personalisation, and [Siva Prakash](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Siva_Prakash_quantum_data_streaming) and [Ganesh Marimuthu](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Ganesh_Marimuthu_quantum_trading_systems) took on streaming feature stores and trading systems. [Sai Kaushik Ponnekanti](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Sai_Kaushik_Ponnekanti_quantum_business_value) of Meta argued that business value is available in the NISQ era already, with today's noisy machines.

## Edge and IoT

Two speakers pushed quantum toward the edge. [Anushree Nagvekar](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Anushree_Nagvekar_quantum_edge_ai) of AEye presented a hybrid quantum-classical architecture for embedded edge AI, and [Gayathri Jeganmohan](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Gayathri_Jeganmohan_quantum_iot_security) of Microsoft looked at what quantum means for IoT security and optimisation as device counts keep climbing.

## Sponsors

Thanks to [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), our gold sponsor, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) for the newsletter and to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) for the podcast partnership.

## What's next

All 19 talks are linked from the [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 page](https://www.conf42.com/quantum2025). Next on the Conf42 calendar is [Conf42 Rustlang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/rustlang2025) on August 21, a good place to rewrite your classical half in something memory-safe while the qubits settle down.

Title: Where bits become possibilities
Description: And math bends reality
Body:
# Quantum computing, but make it real

Quantum computing has a reputation.

It’s mysterious. It’s powerful. It’s either “the future of everything” or “not ready yet”, depending on who you ask and how much coffee they’ve had.

Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 lives right in that tension.

This conference brings quantum out of the abstract and into real systems. There are talks on quantum algorithms, hybrid quantum classical architectures, and what it actually means to run quantum workloads alongside the cloud platforms we already depend on.

AI and data play a big role. You’ll hear about quantum-enhanced edge AI, personalization in finance, real-time data engineering, and how quantum techniques could reshape optimization, machine learning, and decision-making at scale. Not someday. Actively being explored now.

Security and infrastructure show up early and often. Quantum-safe cryptography, cloud security, DevOps for quantum systems, and preparing enterprise architectures for a post-quantum world are all on the agenda. Because when encryption changes, everything else has to change with it.

The use cases are surprisingly practical. Finance, supply chains, IoT, SaaS platforms, storage systems, and enterprise data architectures all make appearances. From shaving microseconds off payments to rethinking how data moves and is protected, these sessions focus on where quantum could deliver real advantage first.

If quantum computing has ever felt too distant, too theoretical, or too confusing to engage with, this one’s for you. No hype. No hand-waving. Just a clear look at how quantum is starting to plug into the systems we already build and run.

Title: Quantum-accelerated trading should start with one Treasury book
Description: Ganesh Marimuthu at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on hybrid quantum-classical trading systems, what firms measured, and why to start with a narrow use case.
Body:
The best place to try quantum in a trading stack is not the whole stack. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, Ganesh Marimuthu, a trading technologist with a background in fixed income, argued for hybrid quantum-classical trading systems and closed on the advice that makes the rest credible: start with one bottleneck, such as portfolio optimisation for a slice of US Treasuries, and grow from there.

Marimuthu has worked on fixed income and commodity trading platforms, market-making and risk-adjusted strategies, and products such as ION and Bloomberg, across US Treasuries, swaps, credit and equities. That desk-side view shapes the talk more than the physics does.

## The data has outgrown the latency budget

He opens with the scale: leading exchanges generate around 342 billion market data messages a day, and classical architectures have fundamental limits in processing that within trading-grade latency. In high-frequency trading, nanoseconds decide profit or loss, so every model you add has to fit inside the same response time.

His argument for quantum techniques is parameter capacity. More parameters inside the same latency window means trading models that can weigh a wider range of market factors and signals at once, instead of trading on a simplified picture.

## What the firms measured

The talk presents a set of headline figures: a 78% reduction in complex calculation time, 67% lower computational resource requirements with quantum-inspired algorithms, a 41% reduction in forecasting error rates, and 99.9% execution reliability for the hybrid framework. It also follows three trading firms through a four-step process: find computational bottlenecks in the existing infrastructure, develop quantum-inspired optimisation algorithms for portfolio management, deploy a hybrid architecture, and evaluate.

By asset class, he reports the largest gains in derivatives, where complex mathematical models benefit most from optimisation, with equities, FX and commodities also improving. Note the wording: much of this is quantum-inspired algorithms on classical and accelerated hardware, and the talk doesn't detail the baselines or the hardware, so read the numbers as the speaker's results rather than reproducible benchmarks.

## Each layer does what it's good at

The architecture is a clean division of labour. Classical systems ingest high-throughput market data. Quantum processors take the complex optimisation problems. Hardware acceleration provides deterministic, minimal-latency execution for the algorithms that have to run on every tick. Anyone who has worked with FPGA-accelerated order paths will recognise the shape; the new tenant is the optimiser.

He also makes a time-to-market argument: firms using these frameworks can develop and deploy advanced strategies faster, which matters most during periods of high volatility.

## Four obstacles, honestly named

The challenges section is practical:

- **Talent.** People who understand both quantum computing and financial markets are rare; firms are building training programmes and academic partnerships.
- **Reliability.** Early quantum processors have higher error rates, so hybrid designs add error correction and verification.
- **Integration.** Connecting quantum processing to existing trading systems through APIs without losing performance.
- **Regulation.** Frameworks for quantum-enhanced trading are still being developed, and trade surveillance and spoofing analysis are part of that conversation.

## Start narrow, then scale

His closing recommendations are the useful part. Apply quantum-enhanced algorithms to one specific computational bottleneck rather than across rates, commodities and credit at once; build internal capability in hybrid design; and prepare systems so that, as hardware matures over the next three to five years, the firm can scale quickly.

## Who should watch

Trading technologists and quants who want a business-side map of where quantum and quantum-inspired methods fit in a trading stack. It's strategy and results, not circuits.

Title: In streaming finance, the QPU is a co-processor for the hardest 1%
Description: Siva Prakash of Bharathidasan University sketches a hybrid Kafka, Flink and feature store stack with a QPU on top at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025.
Body:
Nobody is going to push every card swipe through a dilution refrigerator. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, Siva Prakash of Bharathidasan University, who has spent over two decades in IT, sketched what a sensible hybrid looks like for ultra-low-latency finance: Kafka and Flink streams and a feature store doing the everyday work, with a quantum processor acting as a co-processor for the few problems that would choke a classical system.

It's an architecture-and-vision talk. There's no demo; the value is a clear layering you can reason about, and an unusually direct list of what makes it hard.

## Complexity, not volume, is the wall

Prakash's problem statement is that finance now demands microsecond-level decisions in high-frequency trading, fraud prevention and dynamic risk, while data keeps flowing in from market feeds, news and alternative sources. Volume is one challenge; he argues the bigger one is complexity. Correlating hundreds of risk factors or finding patterns across millions of transactions grows far faster than linearly, and at some point real-time processing becomes impractical no matter how big the data centre gets.

## A four-layer hybrid stack

The architecture slide is the part to keep:

- **Classical infrastructure** at the bottom: compute, network fabric, databases. In his telling it handles 99% of tasks.
- **Stream processing** with Apache Kafka and Apache Flink, extended with quantum-aware connectors that decide when to route a computationally intensive task away from the classical path.
- **A feature store** on platforms like Feast or AWS SageMaker, built to store and serve features produced by, or meant for, quantum processes.
- **The QPU** at the top, receiving only the hardest problems: complex optimisation, simulation and pattern recognition, with answers fed back into the stream.

That last point is the whole design philosophy. The classical system runs the workflow; the quantum part is a specialised accelerator.

## Three use cases on top

He applies the stack to algorithmic trading (quantum signal processing to separate signal from noise, faster pattern recognition, many trading scenarios evaluated at once), fraud detection (spotting subtle deviations spread across accounts and scoring risk before a transaction completes), and personalised advice (quantum clustering for customer segments, and portfolio optimisation recalculated continuously instead of overnight). The speedups he quotes are forward-looking claims about where the technology is headed, not measurements from a production system.

## The engineering bill is steep

The section most talks skip is the strongest here. Qubits have to be kept colder than deep space, below 20 millikelvin, to maintain coherence. Moving data between classical and quantum worlds adds latency that has to be optimised carefully. Error correction is, in his words, arguably the biggest hurdle. And integration between quantum processors and classical systems is a serious project in itself.

He adds a data-quality angle: garbage in, garbage out applies even more to quantum systems, so you need noise mitigation, continuous calibration to keep the two worlds in sync, and fault-tolerant designs for anything mission critical.

## Feature stores you can build today

The practical takeaway is that the feature store can be re-architected now: compute the heaviest features (derivatives pricing, complex risk metrics) with specialised algorithms, optimise how features are routed and cached based on real usage, and generate rarely used but expensive features on demand. Do that, and plugging in a QPU later is a connector change rather than a rewrite.

His roadmap runs from early, narrow quantum advantage now, to mature hybrid systems in two to three years, quantum financial networks in five or more, and quantum-native finance beyond ten. "The journey of quantum advantage is a marathon, not a sprint."

## Who should watch

Data and ML platform engineers in finance who own streaming pipelines or feature stores and want a mental model for where quantum might plug in. If you need benchmarks, this is the wrong talk; if you need a diagram for an architecture review, it's a good one.

- Sridhar Muthineni on [AI-Driven Fraud Detection and Personalization in Go Fintech Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sridhar_Muthineni_driven_fraud_detection).

Title: One JSON schema can generate the UI and pipeline for quantum runs
Description: Amazon's Vamsi Praveen Karanam at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 turns a JSON schema into a React form, a Step Functions pipeline and lineage for Braket jobs.
Body:
Quantum research has a notebook problem: every new experiment starts as a copy of the last one, with a parameter changed and a dependency nobody wrote down. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, Vamsi Praveen Karanam, Software Development Engineer at Amazon, showed a fix borrowed from platform engineering: describe the experiment in one JSON schema and generate the UI, the pipeline and the lineage tracking from it.

It's the most software-engineering-shaped talk of the event, and a compact one: one architecture, real numbers.

## The manifest replaces the monolith

Karanam's diagnosis is that research tooling lags the science. Hardware and error mitigation techniques change constantly, so notebooks get cloned, logic hides in scripts, documentation drifts and auditing becomes nearly impossible, which hurts most in regulated industries.

The framework puts a single JSON schema at the centre, "a machine readable contract that defines what an experiment can and cannot accept". From it, the system generates three things: a React form so scientists never touch HTML or JavaScript, an AWS Step Functions workflow that runs circuits and post-processes results serverlessly, and a lineage tracker that tags and versions every run. In his comparison, about 30 lines of schema replace a hand-coded notebook.

## A small, serverless architecture

The plumbing is pure AWS. The schema lives in S3 with Object Lock, so it is versioned and immutable. A CI/CD pipeline triggers two generators: one builds the React portal, the other compiles the Step Functions state machine. The state machine calls Amazon Braket to run quantum jobs, invokes Fargate containers for post-processing and stores results in S3. OpenTelemetry feeds Grafana dashboards.

The engineering numbers are pleasingly tiny. Three CDK stacks (portal, pipeline, observability). A schema file of about 375 bytes. A React bundle of 1.2 KB gzipped. A state machine of 23 states with no Lambda functions at all. Local testing runs on LocalStack, deploys go through GitHub Actions, and most dev and test work fits within the AWS free tier.

## Validation up front is the real win

Karanam lists four benefits, and the third is the one any SRE will recognise: configuration errors drop to zero because schema validation runs before anything is submitted. Researchers fill a form that is guaranteed to be valid instead of discovering a typo after a queue wait. Schemas also live in git with pull requests and diffs, and new team members can run experiments without learning internal SDKs.

## The VQE sweep numbers

To test it, his team ran a one-million-shot VQE sweep and compared the schema portal with the notebook baseline across five metrics:

- Setup time per parameter variant: 18 minutes down to 3.
- Wall-clock time for the suite: from 13.4 to 11.8 hours, thanks to better concurrency and simulator fallback when QPU queues back up.
- Configuration errors: 7 down to 0.
- Cost: about 200 USD saved, mostly from fewer retries.
- Learnability: researchers rated the portal 4.8 out of 5, against 3.1 for notebooks.

He stresses these came from real jobs on Braket with simulator fallback and Fargate post-processing, not synthetic benchmarks.

## What comes next

The roadmap has three items: chaining multiple experiments so one stage's output feeds the next, encrypting results with post-quantum algorithms aligned with NIST standards, and portable backends for Azure Quantum and Google Cirq using the same schema and UI.

## Who should watch

Anyone building internal tooling for researchers or data scientists, quantum or not. The pattern (schema as contract, generated UI, generated workflow) works for ML experiments and load tests too. Quantum specialists will get the most from the VQE sweep comparison.

- Karthikeyan Rajamani on [Site Reliability at the Quantum Frontier](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Karthikeyan_Rajamani_site_reliability_quantum), keeping hybrid quantum-classical systems robust.

Title: NISQ-era quantum value comes from small, well-scoped pilots
Description: Meta's Sai Kaushik Ponnekanti at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on getting real value from noisy quantum hardware with hybrid workflows and tight scope.
Body:
Today's quantum computers are noisy, small and expensive per shot, and they can still earn their keep if you ask them a small enough question. That was the argument Sai Kaushik Ponnekanti, Software Engineer at Meta, made at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025: in the NISQ era, value comes from slicing a business problem down to tens of qubits, wrapping it in classical pre- and post-processing, and celebrating modest wins.

The abstract promises big gains; the talk itself is refreshingly restrained. Ponnekanti repeatedly stops to say a result was a pilot, a proof of concept, or "small wins", which makes his examples easier to trust.

## Scope the problem until it fits the machine

The core idea is that NISQ hardware (tens to low hundreds of qubits, noisy gates, short coherence times) only helps on scoped problems. A logistics network becomes a regional slice with a dozen stops. A portfolio becomes 30 to 40 assets. A molecule becomes a small one. If a problem needs 60 qubits and the device offers 30 with good fidelity, you find a reduced instance or partition it.

He compares it to learning to sail in calm water before tackling the ocean, and the analogy holds: the point of today's pilots is mostly the skill you build.

## Hybrid is the default, not a compromise

Every example in the talk is a hybrid loop. Classical pre-processing narrows a candidate set, a quantum circuit refines or evaluates the short list, and classical post-processing interprets the output. In the pharma example, classical docking produced 50 candidate ligands, quantum-enhanced evaluation trimmed them to 15, and the top five went to lab assays. In logistics, classical solvers handle the broad layout while quantum routines refine specific legs.

Algorithms like QAOA encode an optimisation objective into a shallow circuit and sample candidate solutions; the classical side keeps the best ones.

## Noise is something you engineer around

The most practical section is on error mitigation. Ponnekanti describes zero-noise extrapolation: run the same circuit with gate durations stretched to amplify noise, then extrapolate back toward a zero-noise estimate. He also mentions randomised compiling. Both cost extra circuit runs and classical compute, which is the price of usable output.

The engineering hygiene list is one any team can adopt today: prototype on simulators with noise models, run only final circuits on hardware, keep circuits in version control, and log run metadata (date, device, calibration metrics, circuit version) so you can compare results as hardware changes. He has juggled SDKs across Qiskit, Cirq and an ion-trap system via AWS, and the quirks are real.

## Pilots need a business metric

The organisational advice is blunt. Pick use cases with clear metrics, build a small team, define success criteria up front. One organisation he describes treated matching classical results within 5% as a worthwhile stepping stone. The anti-pattern is months of random circuits with no business problem attached, ending in reports "full of technical jargon, but little business insight."

## Who should watch

Engineers and tech leads who have been told to "look into quantum" and want a sane way to start: what to pick, how to run it, what to expect. Physicists will find the theory light, by design.

Title: The business case for quantum data management, and what to ask of it
Description: Sampath Kumar Varanasi at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 pitches quantum-enhanced data quality, reconciliation and governance with a 198% ROI headline.
Body:
Every data team knows the feeling of spending the week on ETL and the Friday afternoon on analysis. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, Sampath Kumar Varanasi argued that quantum-enhanced data management can flip that ratio, and put a number on it in the title: 198% return on investment for enterprises that adopt it early.

This is an executive-level pitch, not an engineering walkthrough. It is useful as a picture of how quantum is being sold to data leaders, and as a checklist of questions to bring when someone sells it to you.

## Data volume is outgrowing the legacy stack

Varanasi's starting point is growth. With the AI wave and the GPUs behind it, enterprise data has moved from terabytes to petabytes spread across many interconnected systems, and he expects it to keep doubling. His claim is that traditional computing methods struggle to extract value from that much data efficiently, and that legacy systems can't keep up with validation and reconciliation at this scale.

The competitive framing follows: organisations without a quantum data strategy, in his view, risk falling behind those that start now.

## Where he puts quantum to work

The talk organises the use cases around the daily chores of data management:

- **Validation.** Quantum algorithms that check several data-quality dimensions in a single computation instead of one pass per rule, which he credits with cutting validation time sharply.
- **Pattern and anomaly detection.** Spotting inconsistencies that conventional frameworks miss.
- **Master data and reconciliation.** Breaking down departmental silos into a central repository, with faster resolution of synchronisation issues across distributed systems.
- **Security and compliance.** Quantum-grade encryption, random number generation, and detecting likely policy violations before they happen. "Prevention is better than cure" is his summary.
- **Continuous monitoring.** Tracking many quality parameters at once instead of in nightly batches.

## An implementation plan with four pillars

The roadmap section is the most transferable part. Varanasi breaks adoption into quantum infrastructure (hardware and software requirements), classical integration, quantum-safe security, and change management, and wraps it in an ROI framework: enhanced operations, improved processing and a future-proof architecture. His action plan is short: start a quantum data assessment now, then implement with integration, security and change management planned from the start. He says early implementers see the return within 24 months.

## Read the numbers like an engineer

The talk is dense with percentages for error reduction, processing time, detection rates and savings. It doesn't name the hardware, the algorithms or the data sets behind them, and much of what it describes (deduplication, reconciliation, rule checks) runs on classical systems today. That doesn't make the ambition wrong, but it does mean the right follow-up is a pilot with your own baseline, not a budget line based on a slide. Ask which steps run on a QPU, which are quantum-inspired code on CPUs, and what the classical comparison was.

## Who should watch

Data leaders being pitched quantum for the first time, and architects who want to understand the vocabulary their executives are hearing. Engineers looking for circuits or benchmarks should start with the related talks below instead.

Title: Storage tiering is a QUBO problem, and annealers can take a swing
Description: Gopinath Govindarajan of Deloitte Consulting maps quantum annealing, QML and post-quantum crypto onto enterprise storage at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025.
Body:
Deciding which data block lives on NVMe and which goes to tape is an optimisation problem, and optimisation is the thing quantum annealers are built for. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, Gopinath Govindarajan, Senior Solutions Specialist for Cloud Managed Services at Deloitte Consulting, laid out how quantum techniques could slot into enterprise storage: annealing for tiering, quantum machine learning for retrieval, and post-quantum cryptography for the data at rest.

Govindarajan brings 17 years of data engineering across healthcare, insurance and financial services, and the talk reads like an architect's reference deck: broad, layered, and with a phased roadmap at the end.

## The crisis is scale, retrieval and energy

He starts with why classical storage is straining. Architectures designed for sequential, predictable workloads now face petabytes a day from big data, IoT and real-time analytics. He names three limits: scaling bottlenecks where more storage brings more latency and management overhead, inefficient retrieval over high-dimensional or fragmented data, and the energy and infrastructure cost of keeping it all spinning.

## Tiering as a cost function

The most concrete idea is storage tiering. Tier 0 is NVMe for caching and real-time streams, tier 1 is SSD for frequently accessed files, tier 2 is HDD for archives and backups, and the last stop is tape or cold storage. The hard part is assigning each data object to the right tier dynamically.

Govindarajan frames that assignment as a QUBO (quadratic unconstrained binary optimisation) problem: minimise total storage cost and access latency by mapping data blocks to tiers, subject to performance requirements and capacity limits. Quantum annealing, which finds low-energy states through tunnelling and superposition, is the solver he points to, with D-Wave-style systems as the example. Anyone who has hand-tuned a lifecycle policy in S3 will see why a solver is attractive.

## QML for retrieval, PQC for the archive

Two more pieces round out the architecture. On the machine learning side he covers quantum k-nearest neighbours for similarity-based retrieval and quantum support vector machines for classifying data for compression, deduplication or hot-versus-cold tiering.

On security, the argument is about long-lived data. Stored data might be decrypted later by a quantum computer, so storage systems should adopt post-quantum cryptography (lattice-based schemes such as CRYSTALS, plus code-based, multivariate and hash-based families), quantum random number generation for better keys, and quantum watermarking for tamper detection and provenance.

He is careful that hybrid systems "do not store quantum data directly", since quantum memory doesn't scale yet. The quantum part optimises and secures classical storage; it doesn't replace it.

## Results and a roadmap

The talk reports implementation results by industry, including, for financial services, a 41% reduction in operational storage spending while handling four times the transaction volume at sub-5 ms retrieval latency. Treat those as the speaker's figures: the talk doesn't walk through the benchmark setup, and the case studies elsewhere describe quantum-inspired algorithms running on classical hardware.

The roadmap is the most reusable part. Phase one is awareness: assess risks, find sensitive workloads, train teams, set goals. Phase two is a proof of concept, such as lattice-based encryption for backups, watermarks on sensitive files, or annealing for tiering. Phase three is testing for latency, throughput, compatibility and security under simulated threats. Phase four is enterprise rollout, starting from low-risk targets like archival storage and backups.

## Who should watch

Storage and data platform architects who want a map of where quantum ideas touch their systems, and anyone writing a quantum-readiness plan for a data estate. It's a survey, not a demo; you won't see a QUBO formulated line by line.

- Nehal Singh on [Securing Robot Networks for the Quantum Era](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Nehal_Singh_robotics_quantum_security).

Title: Quantum payments need post-quantum security before they need speed
Description: Intuit's Nikhil Kassetty at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on quantum routing, fraud detection and settlement for real-time payments, and the security catch.
Body:
The same machine that could route a payment in microseconds could also read the payment's encryption. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, Nikhil Kassetty, Software Engineer at Intuit, made the case that quantum computing will reshape real-time payments, routing, fraud detection and risk, and that the industry has to build quantum-safe infrastructure in parallel or the upside turns into exposure.

It's a forward-looking talk rather than a build log. Kassetty is clear that the field is in what he calls the experimentation era: pilots, not production.

## From batch windows to path search

The problem he starts from is familiar to anyone who has waited three days for a bank transfer. Payments still move in batch cycles, held up by processing windows, settlement queues and routing inefficiencies. His thesis is that quantum-enhanced routing could evaluate a huge number of possible paths at once, weighing currency conversion, regulatory constraints and network conditions, and pick the most efficient one.

Settlement is where he sees the biggest change: work that takes hours or days today shrinking towards milliseconds, which improves liquidity and cuts risk along the way. He grounds the claim in a real initiative, the Bank for International Settlements working with the central banks of France and Germany on a project around cross-border settlement and monetary infrastructure.

## Fraud detection before the transaction completes

The second use case is fraud. Kassetty describes quantum sorting and analytics over massive financial data sets to spot anomalies and patterns in real time, flagging suspicious activity before a transaction finishes rather than after. He extends the same idea to anti-money laundering, where tracing behaviour across complex transaction chains and hidden networks is a graph problem that grows ugly fast on classical hardware.

Risk management gets its own pass: portfolio optimisation across many assets and constraints, asset pricing models that keep more variables instead of simplifying them away, market and credit risk simulated at scale, and consumer analytics for more personalised services.

## The quantum security paradox

The section that makes this talk more than a hype reel is the one Kassetty names the Quantum Security Paradox. Payment systems rely on RSA and ECC, both of which a capable quantum computer can break. Worse, harvest attacks are already possible: collect encrypted transactions, personal data and interbank traffic now, decrypt them once the hardware catches up.

His conclusion is that post-quantum cryptography has to arrive before quantum computers reach maturity, and that security "must evolve parallel with innovation". If you work on payments, that is the slide to take back to your team.

## A phased path, not a switch

The preparation advice is practical. Build a strategic roadmap that assesses talent and where quantum creates the most value. Expect regulators, central banks and industry bodies to shape the standards. And plan the transition in phases, starting with hybrid models and gradually introducing post-quantum cryptography, because nobody flips a global payment network from old to new overnight.

He is also honest about the limits: qubits remain fragile, the hardware is still evolving and timelines are uncertain.

## Who should watch

Payment and fintech engineers who want a structured map of where quantum might matter in their domain, and security folks who need the harvest-now argument framed for a payments audience. If you want algorithms and benchmarks, this isn't that talk; it's the strategy layer.

Title: Conf42 Observability 2025 roundup: instrument, tame OTel, cut costs
Description: Conf42 Observability 2025 in review, from config-driven instrumentation and eBPF to honest OpenTelemetry lessons, smaller bills, Kafka signals and identity.
Body:
Auto-instrumentation gets you about 80% of the way; the last 20% is manual work, and at Wave, Jean-Mark Wright estimated it at roughly ten years of it. That is where his talk title, "Instrumenting at 10 years per second", comes from, and it set up the main tension of [Conf42 Observability 2025](https://www.conf42.com/obs2025): teams want deeper telemetry, and they want to spend less effort and less money getting it. With 61 talks streamed online on June 5, 2025, it was one of the largest Conf42 events of the year, with speakers from Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Meta, Salesforce, Confluent, Adobe, WSO2, Palo Alto Networks, AT&T and Telstra.

## Better instrumentation for less effort

[Jean-Mark Wright](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_JeanMark_Wright_instrumenting_second_months) (Wave) opened with an on-call story: the system was quietly giving a premium feature, bank transaction import, to customers who hadn't paid for it, and only detailed manual instrumentation made the cause findable. His team's answer is Config-Accelerated Custom Instrumentation, which captures telemetry from function inputs through configuration instead of hand-written spans.

[Isala Piyarisi and Nilushan Costa](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Isala_Piyarisi_Nilushan_Costa_fluent_opensearch_zero) (WSO2) went further and rebuilt their platform's observability on Fluent Bit, OpenSearch and Prometheus with zero-instrumentation telemetry via eBPF, reporting log latency under five seconds and large cost savings. If you want to write the eBPF yourself, [Sooter Saalu](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Sooter_Saalu_writing_programs_ebpf) (Draft.dev) covered custom programs for tracing syscalls and profiling latency. [Divya Darshana](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Divya_Darshana_clarity_gofr_grpc) showed how the open source Go framework GoFr builds tracing, logging and metrics into gRPC services, and [Dharmendra Ahuja](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Dharmendra_Ahuja_fluent_eks_aws) walked through Fluent Bit on EKS.

## OpenTelemetry, with the caveats left in

Two talks gave OpenTelemetry an honest review. [Narendra Reddy Sanikommu](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Narendra_Reddy_Sanikommu_opentelemetry_messy_problems) (NVIDIA) credited it with removing vendor lock-in and unifying OpenTracing and OpenCensus into one standard across languages, then spent the rest of the talk on the new problems it creates and how to tame them. [Meletius Mgbeodichimma Igbokwe](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Meletius_Mgbeodichimma_Igbokwe_lessons_field_bullet) collected field lessons from teams that tried to make it work in production. Between them you get a realistic adoption plan, not a brochure. [Vignesh Iyer](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Vignesh_Iyer_lightweight_teams_system) (NVIDIA) added an open source pipeline for lean teams, and [Neel Shah](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Neel_Shah_logs_metrics_traces) (Middleware) looked at what comes after the three pillars.

## The bill is an observability signal too

Cost had its own track in all but name. [Aritra Ghosh](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Aritra_Ghosh_shrinking_kubernetes_cost) (Microsoft) shared techniques to cut Kubernetes monitoring spend without losing visibility, and [Venkata Madhu Prateek Reddy Kambala](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Venkata_Madhu_Prateek_Reddy_Kambala_logging_cost_cutting) (Synapsis) traced rising logging bills to their root causes. [Yury Nino](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Yury_Nino_series_cost_anomalies) (Google) turned the problem around, running time series analysis on logs to catch billing anomalies before the invoice does. [Denish Tomar](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Denish_Tomar_dashboards_clouds_fun) (Qumulus) argued for fixed-cost infrastructure so dashboards stop being a monthly surprise, and [Ganeshkumar Palanisamy](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Ganeshkumar_Palanisamy_platforms_scale_finops) (Reltio) combined AIOps with FinOps on multi-cloud data platforms.

## Find the signals that matter in your system

The most reusable talks picked one kind of system and asked which signals actually matter. [Abhishek Walia](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Abhishek_Walia_kafka_visibility_scale) (Confluent) pointed out that Kafka doesn't fail cleanly; it stalls and lags, so you need the few signals that catch that early. [Vamsi Praveen Karanam](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Vamsi_Praveen_Karanam_aws_serverless_workflows) (Amazon) tackled Step Functions fan-outs that launch thousands of Lambdas, streaming telemetry into a graph neural network to spot hot branches. [Sudeep Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Sudeep_Kumar_traces_user_synthetic) (Salesforce) aggregated synthetic traces into critical user journeys, and [Palak Bhawsar](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Palak_Bhawsar_synthetic_monitoring_outage) (Telstra) made the case for synthetic monitoring that catches the outage while you sleep.

Data and frontend teams got their turn. [Chaitanya Reddy Krishnama](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Chaitanya_Reddy_Krishnama_dashboards_qa_nightmares) (MoneyGram) described dashboards that looked great until they started lying because of silent pipeline failures and schema drift. [Vadim Tsaregorodtsev](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Vadim_Tsaregorodtsev_passport_frontend_navigating) (ETG) gave every frontend project an Observability Passport linking its logs, Sentry and security tools. [Alexandru Hang](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Alexandru_Hang_logs_behaviour_experience) (ING Tech Romania) used activity logs to predict what users will do next and prefetch assets. [Ashwin Das Gururaja and Devang Gaur](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Ashwin_Das_Gururaja_Devang_Gaur_dashboard_payment_commerce) (Adobe) covered end-to-end observability for checkout and payments.

## Identity and security belong in the telemetry

[Cynthia Akiotu](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Cynthia_Akiotu_identity_access_breach) (Tesco Bank) argued that most observability ignores who is doing what, and that privilege misuse and insider threats only show up when identity is part of the picture. [Srikanth Potla](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Srikanth_Potla_modeling_insight_spots) (SoFi) threat-modelled the observability stack itself, since logs, metrics and traces leak too. [Krishna Ganeriwal](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Krishna_Ganeriwal_privacy_infrastructure) (Meta) looked at observability for privacy infrastructure, [Chintan Udeshi](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Chintan_Udeshi_edge_realtime_security) (Palo Alto Networks) at edge security monitoring, and [Onyebuchi Mark Irozuru](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Onyebuchi_Mark_Irozuru_signatures_observability_federated) (Botanixlabs) at monitoring federated multisig node operators with Grafana Alloy.

## Further afield

Observability ideas also travelled: AI-assisted pipelines to reduce noise and MTTR at Informatica ([Kirti Ranjan Parida and Sarav Jagadeesan](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Kirti_Ranjan_Parida_Sarav_Jagadeesan_mttr_pipelines_reduce)), generative models on Amazon Bedrock ([Hazel Andrea Saenz Giron](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Hazel_Andrea_Saenz_Giron_serverless_bedrock_generative), Caylent), aircraft digital twins ([Divakar Duraiyan](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Divakar_Duraiyan_aircraft_digital_twins), TCS), and event-driven collaboration between electronic and mechanical hardware design teams ([Pradeep Karanam](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Pradeep_Karanam_ecad_mcad)). For something different, [Anastasiia Zvenigorodskaia](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Anastasiia_Zvenigorodskaia_opensource_profitable_making) (Epicmax) talked about making open source profitable.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/) and [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), the gold sponsors, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) as newsletter partner, [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and the media partners. Every talk is on the [Conf42 Observability 2025 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDEJMKwPJN2wRgGdf8sIpnn) and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/obs2025).

The series continued with [Conf42 Observability 2026](https://www.conf42.com/obs2026).

Title: A quantum-safe cloud starts with knowing where your crypto lives
Description: Pavan Nutalapati at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on how Shor's algorithm threatens cloud encryption and the five moves to make before it lands.
Body:
The data an attacker steals from your cloud today doesn't have to be readable today. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, Pavan Nutalapati, a senior technical lead, argued that cloud teams should start their post-quantum migration now, and that the first step is an unglamorous one: a cryptographic inventory of where RSA and ECC actually sit in your stack.

It's a short, structured talk, close to a briefing you could hand a security lead. The value is in the ordering: the threat, five strategies, three obstacles, and a to-do list.

## Shor breaks the keys, Grover dents the rest

Nutalapati starts from the mechanics. Qubits in superposition and entanglement let quantum machines run algorithms that are fundamentally different from classical ones, and two of them matter for security. Shor's algorithm factors large numbers exponentially faster than classical methods, which is a direct hit on RSA and ECC, the public-key cryptography behind identity, key exchange and TLS in nearly every cloud system. Grover's algorithm weakens symmetric encryption too, though less dramatically.

His point is that the cloud is built on exactly these primitives. Once a sufficiently powerful machine exists, the protections around RSA-2048 stop meaning much.

## Harvest now, decrypt later is the urgent part

Of the three risks he lists, Nutalapati calls the third the scariest. Attackers are already collecting encrypted traffic and archives, betting that a future quantum computer will open them. That makes the deadline for long-lived data (healthcare records, financial data, government secrets) much earlier than the arrival of the hardware. If your data needs to stay secret for ten years, your migration timeline is set by the attacker's storage budget, not by IBM's roadmap.

## Five strategies, from standards to inventory

The core of the talk is a five-part playbook:

- **Post-quantum cryptography.** NIST selected four algorithms in 2022: CRYSTALS-Kyber for key exchange, and CRYSTALS-Dilithium, Falcon and SPHINCS+ for digital signatures.
- **Quantum key distribution.** Secure by physics, since eavesdropping disturbs the quantum state, but expensive and range-limited. He sees it mostly in defence, finance and government.
- **Hybrid cryptography.** Pair a classical algorithm with a quantum-safe one for backward compatibility. He points to Google and Microsoft testing Kyber alongside traditional TLS in Chrome and Azure environments.
- **Cloud vendor initiatives.** Azure's quantum-safe VPN options, IBM Cloud's post-quantum testing, AWS's inventory tools and migration guidance.
- **Cryptographic inventory and risk assessment.** Find where encryption is used, which keys and algorithms are in place, and where sensitive data resides, then prioritise long-lived data. He adds zero trust as the safety net for weak spots you haven't fixed yet.

## The hard part is legacy, not math

Nutalapati is candid about why this is slow. Many quantum-safe algorithms don't play well with legacy systems and devices, and migration is a significant investment. His counter is the cost of doing nothing: he cites an average cloud breach at around $4.4 million before quantum attacks are even practical. "So doing nothing is the riskiest choice."

The path forward is four concrete steps: implement hybrid encryption, track the NIST standards as they mature, work with your cloud vendors, and run crypto audits.

## Who should watch

Security architects and platform leads who need a vocabulary and a plan to bring to a steering meeting. It's an overview, not an implementation guide; you won't see code or a migration of a real service. If you want the engineering detail, pair it with the talks below.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Mathilde Raynal on [Quantum-Resistant Native Go Programs](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Mathilde_Raynal_quantumresistant_native_go_programs), post-quantum crypto at the code level.
- Derek Asir Muthurajan Caleb on [Quantum-Resistant Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Derek_Asir_Muthurajan_Caleb_quantum_security_infrastructure), the same migration inside a cluster.
- Robert Slade on [Quantum Computing: Implications for Security](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2022_Robert_Slade_implications_for_security).
