Title: When metrics, logs, and traces tell a story
Description: Insight follows
Body:
# You can’t fix what you can’t see (and sometimes you still can’t)

Observability always sounds straightforward.

Collect some logs. Add a few metrics. Throw in traces. Build a dashboard. Feel accomplished.

And then production happens.

Conf42 Observability 2025 is for everyone who has stared at a perfectly green dashboard while users were very clearly not having a good time.

This conference goes deep into what observability actually looks like in modern systems. Distributed architectures, serverless workflows, event-driven platforms, cloud-native everything, and systems that span multiple clouds, regions, and teams. There are talks on logs, metrics, traces, telemetry, and what to do when all of them still leave blind spots.

AI shows up everywhere. AI-powered anomaly detection, cost analysis, AIOps, predictive monitoring, and observability for ML systems themselves. Some sessions focus on catching issues earlier. Others focus on reducing noise, cutting observability bills, and figuring out which signals actually matter at 3 AM.

Identity, security, and trust are big themes too. From observable identity systems and threat modeling to monitoring access patterns and preventing breaches before they happen, observability is treated as a security concern, not just an ops one.

The use cases go wide. Finance, healthcare, telecom, retail, public sector, e-commerce, and high-frequency systems all make an appearance. You’ll hear about Kafka at scale, OpenTelemetry in the real world, synthetic monitoring, edge observability, and what happens when your monitoring strategy grows faster than your infrastructure.

If you’ve ever asked “why didn’t we see this sooner” or “why is this alert firing again”, this one’s for you. Observability isn’t about having more data. It’s about finally understanding what your systems are trying to tell you.

Title: Amazon Braket makes quantum hardware a pay-as-you-go AWS service
Description: Naga Murali Krishna Koneru of Hexaware Technologies tours Amazon Braket at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, from hybrid jobs to shots and hardware.
Body:
You don't need a dilution refrigerator in the server room to run a quantum circuit; you need an AWS account. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, Naga Murali Krishna Koneru, Technical Architect at Hexaware Technologies, gave a cloud engineer's introduction to quantum computing through Amazon Braket, AWS's managed service for running quantum algorithms on real hardware and simulators. It's an intro talk and says so: the value is in how cleanly it maps quantum vocabulary onto things an AWS person already knows.

Koneru comes at the subject with 11 years of AWS, DevOps and automation behind him, and it shows. Superposition and qubits get a slide each; the architecture diagram gets the attention.

## The classical computer stays in charge

The most useful framing in the talk is the hybrid model. A classical machine does the setup, the pre-processing and the final analysis, and drives the quantum device like a co-processor. The quantum side only gets the routines where superposition and entanglement help, then hands results back for interpretation. If you have ever offloaded a hot loop to a GPU, the shape is familiar.

Koneru also gives the scaling argument in one line: doubling a classical computer's power means doubling its bits, while a quantum computer gains that with one more qubit. That's the pitch for why anyone bothers with hardware this fragile.

## One SDK, several kinds of qubits

The talk lists the four SDKs most people will meet: Qiskit from IBM (which he calls the most used), Q# from Microsoft, Cirq from Google, and the Amazon Braket SDK. Then it walks the hardware Braket fronts:

- **Superconducting qubits**, among the most mature technologies, from IQM and Rigetti.
- **Ion traps** from IonQ.
- **Neutral-atom processors**, arrays of atoms manipulated by lasers, from QuEra.
- **Managed simulators** from AWS itself, for checking an algorithm before paying for real hardware time.

The practical point: Braket is a single front door to several qubit technologies, so you can switch hardware with minor code changes and compare results. Koneru also mentions AWS's February 2025 chip announcement (Ocelot), built on cat qubits that resist errors better than regular ones, which the talk credits with cutting error correction by 90%.

## Shots, tasks and hybrid jobs

The section worth bookmarking explains Braket's units of work. A shot is a single execution of a circuit on a device. A task bundles a series of shots and submits them together. A hybrid job is the classical-plus-quantum loop from earlier, run as one managed unit. You reach all of it through managed notebooks, the SDK or the Braket console, and it plugs into the usual AWS services: CloudWatch for notifications, S3 for results, IAM for permissions, KMS for encryption.

The billing model is pay as you go, which is the real democratisation argument here. No upfront hardware, no lab, just a bill that grows with the number of shots. Plan your experiments the way you plan your Lambda invocations.

## Who should watch

Cloud and platform engineers who have been asked whether the company should look at quantum and want a mental model in under half an hour. It's light on algorithms and heavy on service anatomy, which is exactly right for that audience. If you already write Qiskit for fun, skip to the Braket console walkthrough near the end, then go back to work.

The closing section looks ahead: fault-tolerant systems with fewer errors, cryptography use cases, quantum education and workforce development, and one day a quantum computer that fits on a desk.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Vincent van Wingerden on [High level programming for quantum circuits](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Vincent_van_Wingerden_programming_quantum_circuits), the step after "hello, qubit".
- Daniel Goldsmith and Pippa Spencer-Williams on [Journey into Quantum](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Daniel_Goldsmith_Pippa_Spencer_Williams_business_benefits), the business side of getting started.

Title: Generate, predict, self-heal - AI's three jobs in testing
Description: Jyotheeswara Reddy Gottam of Walmart Global Tech at Conf42 Observability 2025 on generative tests, predictive risk analytics and self-healing automation.
Body:
Jyotheeswara Reddy Gottam of Walmart Global Tech, who has worked in development and quality engineering for more than 13 years, used his Conf42 Observability 2025 talk to make a case for combining three AI techniques in QA: generative test creation, predictive analytics that point testing at risky code, and self-healing automation that repairs tests when the UI changes. His claim is that the three together do more than any one of them alone.

It is a compact, strategy-level talk. If you want to see a specific tool in action, this is not that; if you need a structure for pitching AI-assisted testing to your organisation, it is.

## The three costs of traditional testing

Jyotheeswara starts with what goes wrong today. Manual test scripting eats engineering time and leaves coverage gaps. Defect detection is reactive, so critical issues reach production, where a P1 damages customer trust and revenue. And automation suites carry a maintenance tax: scripts break with UI changes, and false positives drain both time and confidence in the suite. Everyone who has babysat a flaky end-to-end test knows the third one personally.

## One technique per problem

His "AI testing triangle" pairs each problem with a technique:

- **Generative AI** writes test scripts and finds edge cases human testers often miss, turning days of script writing into minutes and keeping quality consistent across suites rather than only where the experts sit.
- **Predictive analytics** uses historical data, such as where P1 bugs clustered, to flag high-risk modules before deployment and send testing effort there.
- **Self-healing frameworks** detect UI changes that break tests, update the scripts and verify the fix without manual work.

He also shared improvement figures across healthcare, fintech and e-commerce, including test creation time down by about 70% and maintenance hours down sharply. Treat them as the speaker's reported results rather than a benchmark; the talk does not break down the underlying projects.

## Integrate in stages

The implementation advice is the part most teams can use directly. Start with standalone tools and test each AI component on its own. Move to partial integration with limited scope to build confidence. Only then connect everything into one feedback loop where components share data. On the tooling side, he suggests REST APIs between tools, embedding them in CI/CD pipelines, a central metrics store such as Elasticsearch, and unified dashboards in Grafana, Splunk or similar.

His roadmap follows the same shape: pick tools and set baseline metrics, pilot individual components against control groups, connect the feedback loops, then scale across teams and document what worked.

## Keep a human with the veto

The governance section keeps the talk grounded. Jyotheeswara asks for transparency (documented, explainable test generation and auditable predictions), regular validation against human experts, continuous retraining with confidence scores, and QA leads keeping final authority with override capability on every automated action. His closing point: AI should enhance human testers, not replace them.

## Who should watch

QA leads, test automation engineers and engineering managers weighing where AI fits in their testing budget. The connection to observability is the metrics loop: predictive testing runs on the same historical defect and quality data observability teams already collect.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Mike Morgan's [Tackling Flaky Tests](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mike_Morgan_testing_flaky_strategies), the problem self-healing frameworks aim at.
- Liran Yushinsky's [Who Judges the AI Agent?](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Liran_Yushinsky_testing_judge_codegen) on testing non-deterministic, AI-generated code.
- Vitali Shchur's [The QA Ownership Mindset](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vitali_Shchur_qa_mindset_startup) for the human side of quality.

Title: Commerce observability starts where green dashboards stop
Description: Adobe's Ashwin Das Gururaja and Devang Gaur at Conf42 Observability 2025 on tracking checkout, payments and renewals as business signals.
Body:
Revenue drops, every dashboard is green, and the APIs keep returning 200. That is the failure mode Ashwin Das Gururaja, senior engineering manager at Adobe, and Devang Gaur, a payments product manager at Adobe, built their Conf42 Observability 2025 talk around. Their argument: in commerce and subscription businesses, the question is whether customers can buy, pay and renew, and service health only answers part of it.

The talk comes in two halves, engineering first and product second, which is a nice structure. Most observability talks never hear from the person who owns the renewal rate.

## Ask whether customers can buy

Ashwin contrasts traditional monitoring (is the service up, CPU, memory, response times, 4xx and 5xx rates) with commerce observability, which asks questions that map to money. Can customers complete a purchase, even when the checkout API returns 200 but the payment flow has a bug? Is fraud detection blocking good customers? Are payment forms actually loading in the browser? Are failed payments causing involuntary churn? Can customers update their wallets?

He then walks the full funnel (product discovery, add to cart, checkout, authorisation and fraud, fulfilment and confirmation) and the subscription lifecycle (trial signup, free-to-paid conversion, billing cycle, payment processing, renewal, usage and expansion), naming what to watch at each step. One detail worth keeping: a missed billing event can lead an entitlement system to remove access after a grace period from a customer who did nothing wrong.

## The three pillars, with a revenue column

The pillars stay the same, but each gets a business twist. Metrics include payment success rate per processor, conversion and churn alongside system health, because two processors can perform very differently on the same traffic. Logs capture why things happened: the processor's decline reason, the customer's journey breadcrumbs, why the fraud engine blocked a transaction, and error classification weighted by revenue. Traces follow a transaction from the click to settlement, including third-party gateways like Adyen or PayPal.

## Hunt for the failure you did not think to monitor

The section on unknown unknowns has the best example. 3-D Secure might start failing in France for certain card types. The dip is small for the whole system, so health checks stay calm, but it is still lost revenue. Ashwin's prescription is anomaly detection on business metrics, cross-system correlation and automated root cause analysis, so the system can ask why conversion dropped instead of whether services are healthy.

His practical do and don't lists are short and worth screenshotting: start from the subscriber journey, not the architecture; build runbooks with churn impact; test observability during billing cycles; don't alert on everything; don't ignore processor dependencies, in-app mobile metrics or the customer success team, who often hear first.

## The product manager's half

Devang's part is the reason to watch. He describes A/B tests that looked like failures until observability showed a silent JavaScript error on mobile, and a US churn creep with no alerts at all, traced to a config change that broke wallet updates with one payment processor. Customers could not update cards, so renewals failed. The team fixed it in under 48 hours.

His proposal: write observability into acceptance criteria like a product spec. For a new billing flow, can you see payment success by method, wallet errors by region, retry success by card type? Start with the golden flows (free-to-paid conversion, wallet updates, recurring billing and renewal). Adobe began by instrumenting retry success rate. You do not need hundreds of metrics, just the few that matter.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product managers in commerce, payments or subscription businesses, and anyone whose incident reviews keep concluding that the dashboards looked fine. The talk opens with industry-wide statistics; the stronger material is the Adobe examples in the second half.

## Related Conf42 talks

- George Thomas on [Platform Engineering for Subscription Payment Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_George_Thomas_subscription_payment_service).
- Venkata Majeti's [AI-Driven Incident Resilience](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Venkata_Majeti_subscriptions_scale_uptime) on subscription systems without losing uptime.
- Sandeep Katuri on [fraud detection for digital payments](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Sandeep_Katuri_fraud_detection_digital_payments_security), the other side of the approval-rate balance.

Title: Quantum jobs will make cloud bills even harder to predict
Description: Qumulus developer relations engineer Denish Tomar argues at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 that metered pricing breaks down for quantum workloads.
Body:
Nobody can say exactly what their cloud bill will be next month, and quantum workloads will make that worse. That is the argument Denish Tomar, Developer Relations Engineer at Qumulus, made at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025: usage-based pricing already confuses teams running well-understood CPUs and memory, and a quantum job whose runtime, retries and error correction are unknowable in advance turns metering into a guessing game.

This is a vendor talk and it says whose product it shows: the second half presents Qumulus's fixed-resource model as the alternative.

## The $10,000 autoscaling surprise

Tomar opens with a story worth the price of admission. A startup founder's AWS bill came in around $10,000 against a usual $2,000. The cause was one autoscaling mistake: instead of scaling up to five servers it scaled to 50, and instead of running for two hours it ran for three days before anyone noticed. Then came the line items nobody could explain: NAT gateway processing charges, CloudWatch logs, load balancer capacity units, cross-availability-zone transfer, API gateway requests and Lambda cold starts.

His challenge to the audience: open your cloud dashboard and state exactly what you will spend next month. Not approximately. You can't, and that's with technology we have optimised for decades.

## Why quantum makes metering worse

The quantum section explains superposition and entanglement for a general audience (spinning coins, mazes explored in parallel), then gets to the billing point. A quantum algorithm might finish in 30 seconds or 30 hours. It might need one run or 500, because results are probabilistic. It might use cheap basic operations or need error correction that costs a hundred times more. Tomar's example: the same quantum job could cost anywhere from $500 to $5,000, and you wouldn't know which until the bill arrives.

His view is that the big providers are struggling with this too: classical bills meter known quantities, while quantum bills meter unknown time, unknown errors and unknown retries.

## The Qumulus pitch

The alternative he presents is predefined, fixed resources at a fixed price instead of metering each operation, compared to a subscription you use without watching the meter. Qumulus is built on OpenStack, which he argues means no vendor lock-in to anyone's quantum ecosystem. He shares a before-and-after from a startup that moved from AWS: before, a bill that swung widely month to month and a fifth of engineering time spent on cost optimisation; after, a predictable bill and no time spent chasing it. The founder's line, as he tells it, was that the best part was building things instead of optimising for AWS pricing.

His closing line sums it up: "your cloud bill doesn't have to be quantum chaotic".

## How to take it

The diagnosis is the strongest part: unpredictable cost is already an engineering tax, and probabilistic workloads with variable retries make it heavier. Whether fixed-resource pricing is the answer for your team depends on how bursty your workloads are, which the talk doesn't model. The quantum billing figures are projections, not quotes from a provider's price list, so read them as the shape of the problem.

## Who should watch

FinOps practitioners, startup CTOs and platform teams who own the cloud bill, plus anyone planning to experiment with quantum services and wondering how to budget for them. If you already run strict cost controls on AWS, the first half will feel familiar; the quantum billing argument is the new part.

- [Real-time FinOps intelligence for streaming financial events](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Tina_Kanth_finops_streaming_prompts) by Tina Kanth, for watching spend as it happens.
- [Your cloud emits CO2](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Olivier_Bierlaire_your_cloud_emits_co2) by Olivier Bierlaire, another bill your cloud runs up quietly.

Title: An observability passport for every frontend project
Description: Vadim Tsaregorodtsev of ETG at Conf42 Observability 2025 on one page of links per app covering Sentry, SLOs, error budgets, logs and traces.
Body:
Vadim Tsaregorodtsev's team once restarted a broken service, found nothing in Sentry, and only later learned the cause was another team's release: their CPU usage jumped and dragged his product down through a shared integration layer. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Vadim, who leads a frontend team at ETG, presented his answer to the question of how you know a product works, and works properly: an observability passport, a single page per project that links every signal you need.

It is a refreshingly practical talk from the frontend side of the house, where observability content is thinner than it should be.

## Works, and works properly, are two questions

The talk splits the question in two. Knowing that the app works is monitoring: requests go through, no errors, an alert fires if load climbs. Knowing that it works properly is observability: being able to explain why the system behaves as it does, such as knowing that load rises after launch time and that is a bad window to release. Monitoring tells you something broke; observability helps you figure out why.

When his team launched a new car rental product for B2B partners and corporate clients, Vadim used it as the chance to build this properly rather than waiting for support to say everything is broken.

## Metrics, sorted by who cares about them

Vadim sorts metrics into technical (CPU, RAM, response time), business (conversion, retention, revenue per user) and hybrid metrics that matter to both, with Google's Web Vitals as the prime example: page load speed is technical, but it shapes user experience and search ranking, which hits the business.

He then gives one of the clearer explanations of SLA, SLO and SLI you will hear in a frontend talk. The SLA formalises business expectations; the SLO is the internal target, such as API response time under 200 ms for 95% of requests; the SLI is the measured share of requests that actually met it. The error budget sits on top: at a 99.9% target, the budget is 0.1%, and when it is nearly gone, feature work freezes and the team fixes reliability. He pitches it as a sprint planning tool and a way to tell the business, in its own language, why a risky feature can wait.

## What goes in the passport

The passport began as a Confluence page of links. Over the talk it fills up:

- **Error tracking** with Sentry (or anything that tells you what went wrong and how to fix it).
- **Vulnerability analysis** with DefectDojo, where the team set an SLO of zero critical vulnerabilities in production and seven days to fix found ones, which he notes is the tool's default.
- **Basic metrics** such as memory and CPU, exported via a Prometheus client package.
- **Logs**, plus **traces** for the cases where one component's logs cannot explain a failure; request IDs tie events together, and OpenTelemetry with Jaeger draws the graph.
- **Profiling** in Sentry to find the slowest endpoints and pages.
- **Product analytics**, which caught real bugs: a currency switcher firing an extra event, and an event meant for the listing page firing on the booking page because of a cache issue.
- **The availability SLA, test coverage and the Swagger docs** for other services.

## A repeatable recipe

Whatever the tool, Vadim reduces each passport entry to the same steps: pick the area to watch, define what counts as deviation, set an error budget, collect the data, visualise it, add alerts where needed, and assign owners with a response protocol. That recipe travels well beyond frontends.

## Who should watch

Frontend leads who own production apps and want a cheap, concrete way to make their reliability visible to the team and the business. Backend SREs will find the SLO material familiar, but the passport idea and the product-analytics examples are worth stealing.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Joe Blubaugh's [Don't get out of bed for anything less than an SLO](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Joe_Blubaugh_bed_less_slo) takes the SLO argument into on-call.
- Sumit Kaul's [Observability as a Platform Contract](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Sumit_Kaul_slos_instrumentation_observability) enforces SLOs in CI/CD.
- Michael Haberman's [Distributed tracing for Node.js using OpenTelemetry](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Michael_Haberman_distributed_tracing_OpenTelemetry) for the tracing entry in the passport.

Title: How WSO2 rebuilt Choreo observability on open source for 70% less
Description: Isala Piyarisi and Nilushan Costa of WSO2 at Conf42 Observability 2025 on Fluent Bit, OpenSearch, Prometheus and eBPF zero-instrumentation metrics.
Body:
WSO2 moved the observability behind its Choreo internal developer platform off Azure-native services and onto Fluent Bit, OpenSearch and Prometheus, and the abstract claims log latency under five seconds with roughly 70% lower cost. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Nilushan Costa, associate technical lead, and Isala Piyarisi, senior software engineer, both on the Choreo observability team, explained the migration, the eBPF-based zero-instrumentation metrics, and the lessons they paid for along the way.

This is one of the more detailed architecture talks of the event, with real component names, failure stories and a cost breakdown.

## Why they left an Azure-only setup

Choreo started on Azure, with logs going through Azure agents into Log Analytics, and traces and metrics through an OpenTelemetry Collector into Azure Data Explorer. Three things pushed them off it. Cost: publishing and querying telemetry in a cloud platform is expensive. Portability: customers wanted Choreo data planes on AWS, on Vultr and on-premises, and each cloud has its own query language and APIs. Control: owning the stack meant they could build features on top of it.

## Logs: Fluent Bit, OpenSearch, and an operator

Fluent Bit runs as a DaemonSet collecting container logs into OpenSearch, which they had already used as a short-lived cache alongside Log Analytics and liked. The new setup runs OpenSearch as a distributed deployment with separate master and data nodes, managed by the OpenSearch operator, because Choreo also runs private data planes per customer and manual upgrades across many clusters would be slow and error-prone. Primary and replica shards are spread across availability zones, so a lost pod or deleted volume recovers from its peers.

## Metrics without asking anyone to instrument

The zero-instrumentation side is the part many teams will want to copy. Prometheus, managed by the Prometheus operator and backed by Thanos for retention and high availability, scrapes three sources: kube-state-metrics for Kubernetes context like labels and resource requests, cAdvisor in the kubelet for per-container CPU and memory, and Hubble from Cilium for HTTP-level and layer 3/4 metrics such as status codes and latencies, with no code changes from users. They described routing traffic through an Envoy proxy on the node with eBPF to extract RED metrics without the overhead of a full service mesh. All of it feeds a dynamically generated service diagram showing error rates and latency between components, and clicking a spike pulls the related logs.

## The lessons they learned the hard way

The war stories are the best part:

- **Prometheus counts are estimates.** Send 15 requests and the diagram might show 13.8. Their older event-based system showed exact counts; Prometheus gives aggregated data, so use something else if you need exact numbers, for billing for example.
- **Order of operations matters.** Taking a rate over a recording rule that had already summed data produced wrong results.
- **Storage is part of observability.** An AWS deployment on EFS underperformed; switching to EBS fixed it, and Fluent Bit's metrics alone would not have told you why.
- **Config details bite.** The inotify watcher in Fluent Bit's tail plugin stopped collecting logs after a while; switching to the stat-based watcher fixed it. They also wrote a Lua script for log throttling so Fluent Bit cannot overwhelm OpenSearch.

## The cost numbers

Per data plane, the old setup cost around $1,200 a month for Azure Data Explorer and about $1,000 for Log Analytics. The open-source stack costs roughly $250 for compute and $100 for storage, which they put at about 70% overall savings, plus more control and better performance.

## Who should watch

Platform teams running Kubernetes across several clouds or on-premises, and anyone with an expensive managed observability bill wondering what self-hosting really involves. You will leave with a component list and a short catalogue of traps.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Nikolay Sivko's [Zero-instrumentation observability based on eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2024_Nikolay_Sivko_zeroinstrumentation_observability_ebpf) on the same idea from another angle.
- Pranshu Srivastava's [The Power of Cilium For eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Pranshu_Srivastava_cilium_ebpf_networking) for the Cilium side that Hubble comes from.
- Alejandro Mercado's [Observability in Kubernetes with eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Alejandro_Mercado_observability_kubernetes_ebpf).

Title: Observability 2.0 trades firefighting for forecasting
Description: Neel Shah of Middleware at Conf42 Observability 2025 on OpenTelemetry collectors, ML anomaly detection, smarter ingestion and AI-assisted root cause.
Body:
The 2 a.m. outage with terabytes of telemetry and no idea where to look is the scenario Neel Shah built his talk around. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Neel, a DevRel at Middleware and a DevOps community organiser, argued that observability is shifting from reactive troubleshooting to predictive operations, with OpenTelemetry as the foundation, ML and LLMs on top, and smarter ingestion to keep the bill sane.

It is a broad overview rather than a single technique, and it is a vendor-adjacent talk: Neel shows where Middleware's own features fit, which he flags openly.

## A short history of too much data

Neel sketches three eras. Around 2015, monoliths and classic tools like Grafana. Then the telemetry explosion, where microservices produced so much data from apps and infrastructure that teams had plenty of signals and little understanding. Then, from about 2023, AI arriving to make sense of it. The shift he wants: from manual troubleshooting to incidents that explain themselves, and from finding risk during the outage to having it flagged before.

## OpenTelemetry is the floor, the collector is the engine

The middle of the talk explains why OpenTelemetry matters. Before it, everyone collected data in different formats, so sharing between teams or tools was painful. OTel created a vendor-neutral, standard way to instrument, easier correlation between signals, and freedom to route data to multiple backends. Neel notes it is one of the largest CNCF projects after Kubernetes.

He walks through the collector's three parts: receivers that take data in, processors that transform it, and exporters that send it to a backend. If you have never looked inside a collector pipeline, this is a clean explanation.

## ML for patterns, LLMs for summaries

On the AI side, Neel separates two jobs. ML models detect anomalies and incident patterns that were previously invisible, and help prioritise incidents by severity and impact. LLMs summarise incidents in plain language and can predict likely issues from historical patterns. He also lists the data types he considers part of the 2.0 picture beyond the classic three: events, profiles, dependencies and eBPF, which reads from the kernel which ports are open and how packets move.

His example of where this goes is a little cheeky: an alert says CPU is above 80%, and the alert itself offers a button to double the capacity. Whether you want that button in production is a separate conversation with your change board.

## The cost problem has a pipeline answer

The section on cost is the most practical. Neel names the drivers: massive telemetry growth from microservices, storing every log, metric and trace even when much of it is irrelevant, high-cardinality metrics and oversampled traces. The results are higher infrastructure spend, slower queries and noise.

The answer is to filter before you store. He lists dynamic sampling, filtering, deduplication, aggregation and edge processing, and shows Middleware's ingestion control pipeline as one implementation that keeps unnecessary logs out of storage.

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads who want a quick map of where observability tooling is heading, and anyone new to the OpenTelemetry collector. If you already run sampling and ML-based alerting in production, the talk is mostly confirmation; the value is in the framing and the cost checklist.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Shahar Azulay's [True Kubernetes Observability with eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Shahar_Azulay_kubernetes_observability_ebpf) expands on the eBPF data type Neel lists.
- Michael Levan's [Observing Agentic/MCP Traffic & Keeping Costs Low](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Michael_Levan_agents_telemetry_costs) applies the cost discipline to AI agent traffic.

Title: A four-tool observability stack for small teams on Kubernetes
Description: Vignesh Iyer of NVIDIA at Conf42 Observability 2025 builds a low-cost stack from Fluentd, Prometheus, Jaeger and Grafana, plus three pitfalls to avoid.
Body:
You do not need an enterprise contract to see inside a distributed system. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Vignesh Iyer of NVIDIA showed small teams how to stand up a working observability stack on Kubernetes from four open-source tools (Fluentd, Prometheus, Jaeger and Grafana) with a handful of commands each, and then spent the most valuable minutes on how teams drown in their own signals.

It is pitched squarely at teams with little budget and a cluster to look after, and it says so in its first sentence. Think of it as a good first talk on assembling the pieces, with opinions attached.

## Four pillars, one tool each

Vignesh frames the stack around four pillars, each answering one question:

- **Logging** tells you what is happening in the system right now. His pick is Fluentd as the log aggregator.
- **Metrics** show how the system behaves over time. Prometheus, which he calls one of the most used components in Kubernetes clusters.
- **Tracing** finds the bottleneck in a request's path. He chose Jaeger over OpenTelemetry here because it is easier for a small team to set up.
- **Dashboards** decide how quickly you can act on all of it. Grafana, pulling data from the other three.

The Jaeger-over-OTel choice is worth noticing. It is a deliberate trade of future flexibility for setup speed, and for a three-person team that can be the right call.

## Install paths you can copy

For each tool he shows both the `kubectl apply` route, using the manifests the project maintains so you stay on the latest version, and the Helm route. Then the small details that trip people up: point applications at Fluentd's forward port and emit JSON logs so parsing stays easy; override the Prometheus Helm values to declare scrape targets for your services; send spans from the client libraries to the Jaeger agent by its in-cluster service name (his Python example used port 6831); and register Prometheus, Jaeger and your logs as Grafana data sources in the Helm config.

None of this is novel, but having it in one place in the right order saves an afternoon of tab-hopping.

## Alert on everything and you will hear nothing

The pitfalls section is where the talk earns its slot. First, alert fatigue. Vignesh described a previous company where alerts were set up for every issue; the team mailbox filled so fast that people stopped receiving alerts altogether and missed the ones that mattered. His rule: alert only on the specific issues you need to act on, and leave the rest to logging.

## Sample less, show less

Second, do not oversample metrics. Sending data every second turns signal into noise and grows your storage for no insight; he suggests something like once a minute as a reasonable balance, depending on the system.

Third, dashboard hygiene. The instinct that more panels mean more insight is, in his words, far from the truth. Build each dashboard for its audience: a high-level view of system health for a manager, deeper application detail and log access for a developer. A dashboard that tries to serve everyone serves the screenshot in the incident review.

## Who should watch

Small teams, side projects, startups and anyone who has been told there is no budget for observability and needs a credible starting point. Teams already running a mature OpenTelemetry pipeline will know the material, though the alerting and dashboard advice is a useful reminder for anyone.

Title: Quantum CloudOps means deciding which parts of an app go quantum
Description: Srinivas Sriram Mantrala at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on what DevOps and CloudOps teams must change when quantum joins the cloud.
Body:
The most expensive mistake in a hybrid quantum system will be putting the wrong part of the application on the quantum side. Srinivas Sriram Mantrala made that his closing point at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, in a talk on "Quantum CloudOps": what DevOps and CloudOps teams need to change as quantum processing arrives through cloud providers, which he expects within about five years.

It's a conceptual talk, delivered conversationally, with no demo. Think of it as an operations team's checklist for a technology that isn't on their pager yet.

## Thinking ten moves ahead

Mantrala explains superposition with chess. A strong player can hold maybe ten candidate moves in their head; then for each one, ten replies, and the tree explodes. His pitch for quantum is the ability to process that whole tree of combinations at once and surface the risky branch early. He applies the idea to security, where you want to anticipate the next attack and the one after it, and to operations, finance and medicine, anywhere a wider search beats a sequential one.

## The hybrid infrastructure has three parts

His architecture keeps today's cloud in charge:

- **Quantum processing units**, built on qubits, superposition and entanglement, for the complex algorithms.
- **Classical infrastructure**, the existing cloud that already handles conventional tasks and orchestration.
- **An integration layer** with translators, workload schedulers and real-time processing that distributes work between the two for the best performance.

The integration layer is where operations teams will spend their time, because load balancing now has two very different kinds of backend.

## What DevOps has to learn

The most useful section lists what changes for the people running the platform:

- **CI/CD** pipelines need quantum deployment and testing stages.
- **Observability** (logs, metrics and the analytics on top) has to cover quantum workloads too.
- **Operating models** need updating, and people need training to run quantum-backed applications.
- **Automation** has to extend to quantum resource allocation.
- **APIs** for quantum processing won't look like today's request-response endpoints, and programming models for concurrency may shift with them.

None of this is exotic; it's the same muscle teams built moving from on-prem to cloud. That is the reassuring subtext.

## Where it pays and how to start

Mantrala's list of beneficiaries: security (quantum-resistant encryption to protect sensitive data against future attacks), AI algorithms redesigned for quantum parallelism, pharmaceuticals (running clinical study computations concurrently instead of step by step) and finance (market prediction, portfolio and risk assessment).

Adoption follows the usual path: partner with a cloud provider that offers quantum infrastructure, build proofs of concept, then build the hybrid integration with APIs between quantum and classical services, find the limits, automate workload distribution, measure and improve.

## The design decision that decides the bill

The closing point is the reason to watch. Not everything should run on quantum. Put too much there and you pay for complexity you don't need; put too little and you miss the speed-up where it matters. The new design skill is drawing that line inside each application, per requirement. Every cloud migration has a team that lifted and shifted everything; this is the warning not to do it again.

## Who should watch

DevOps, SRE and platform engineers who want to know what quantum would mean for their pipelines and runbooks, explained without maths. If you want circuit-level detail or architecture diagrams, pair it with a more technical talk.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Principium: the quantum hardware ecosystem](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Archit_Srivastava_principium_hardware_ecosystem) by Archit Srivastava, for what sits behind the cloud API.

Title: When OpenTelemetry is worth the mess it brings
Description: NVIDIA's Narendra Reddy Sanikommu at Conf42 Observability 2025 on what OpenTelemetry fixes, the new problems it creates, and when it pays off.
Body:
OpenTelemetry fixes vendor lock-in and fragmented instrumentation, and in exchange hands you a stack of SDKs, exporters and YAML. Narendra Reddy Sanikommu, a senior software engineer at NVIDIA, made that trade explicit at Conf42 Observability 2025 in a short, balanced talk: what OTel solves, which problems it creates, and how to decide whether your organisation is on the right side of the ledger.

The title asks "OpenTelemetry or OpenTeleMessy?" and the answer is honest: both, depending on what you run.

## What it genuinely fixed

Narendra starts with the wins, and they are real. Before OpenTelemetry, every vendor shipped its own agent and SDK; now you instrument once and send the data to whichever backend you like. OTel merged OpenTracing and OpenCensus into one standard across languages, covers metrics, traces and logs, and lets you correlate them. The collector decouples collection from analysis, and auto-instrumentation removes a lot of boilerplate. He also pointed to its community: one of the most active CNCF projects, with a busy roadmap.

## And what it broke

Then the bill. The documentation throws a newcomer straight into APIs, SDKs and layers of abstraction. Each component has its own configuration. Language implementations are inconsistent, which undercuts the polyglot promise: the standard is shared, the quirks are not. Signals sit at different maturity levels, with tracing the most mature, metrics next, and logging the recent arrival. Debugging is hard when a problem could live in instrumentation, collection or export. And collector configurations grow into large YAML files with mismatched component names, authentication you wire up yourself, and connectivity issues. Filing an issue can mean bouncing between repositories.

Anyone who has chased a missing span through three config files will recognise every slide.

## The test for whether it pays off

The most useful section is his decision rule. OpenTelemetry makes sense when:

- your organisation has a large, diverse technology stack you want to standardise;
- the value exceeds the implementation complexity, which you have to judge honestly;
- you want vendor-neutral collection and export as a long-term investment;
- you run cloud-native, distributed, containerised workloads such as Kubernetes;
- you need control over data routing and filtering to cut noise and cost.

If none of those apply, the mess may outweigh the benefits.

## How to tame it

His strategies are incremental. Begin with language-specific auto-instrumentation, and use what your platform already ships (he mentioned Amazon EKS offering OpenTelemetry collectors). Start with tracing, the most mature signal, and add metrics and logs later. Follow semantic conventions and keep attributes and labels tidy. Use local exporters to speed up troubleshooting. Roll out to critical user flows first instead of a big-bang migration, lean on community blogs and talks beyond the official docs, and consider vendor distributions such as Grafana Alloy that smooth adoption.

The outlook section notes semantic conventions reaching stability, the collector approaching version 1, profiling arriving as a signal, and generative AI observability joining the ecosystem. His conclusion: still the first choice if you want a vendor-neutral, comprehensive solution.

## Who should watch

Architects deciding whether to adopt OpenTelemetry, and teams halfway through an adoption who want a sanity check. It is a compact overview rather than a hands-on lab, so it suits a lunch break.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Prathamesh Sonpatki's [The Complete Handbook to OpenTelemetry Metrics](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Prathamesh_Sonpatki_handbook_opentelemetry_metrics) for the signal this talk calls less mature than tracing.
- Nicolas Fränkel's [Practical introduction to OpenTelemetry tracing](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Nicolas_Frankel_opentelemetry_tracing), a good first step for the "start with tracing" advice.
- Pranay Prateek's [Scaling Opentelemetry Collectors using Kafka](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2024_Pranay_Prateek_scaling_opentelemetry_kafka) for when collectors become the bottleneck.

Title: OpenTelemetry is a toolkit, so budget for the rest of the build
Description: Meletius Mgbeodichimma Igbokwe at Conf42 Observability 2025 on field lessons from OpenTelemetry: collector sizing, version drift, docs and training.
Body:
OpenTelemetry gives you the plumbing for traces, metrics and logs; it does not give you a finished observability system. That is the thread through Meletius Mgbeodichimma Igbokwe's talk at Conf42 Observability 2025, a practitioner's list of what goes wrong once a team moves from the OpenTelemetry pitch to running collectors in production, and what he would do differently.

The talk starts with the promise: a single standard across clouds and on-premises, freedom from vendor-specific agents, and broad adoption across the big cloud providers and established tools like Datadog and LogicMonitor. Then it spends most of its time on the gap between that promise and a Tuesday afternoon with a full disk.

## The pain starts before the first span

Meletius groups the early problems into three. Documentation that drifts out of date, so teams follow instructions for a version they are not running. SDK and library burden across languages, where outdated libraries quietly break instrumentation. And version conflicts between components, which he described as a constant source of friction when teams try to ingest or trace anything. None of these is exotic. All of them eat weeks.

His fix for the documentation problem is cultural rather than technical: treat internal docs as a regular activity owned by everyone, not something one person updates once in a while.

## Collectors need real hardware and someone watching them

The most memorable part is a story from his own environment. A cluster used for support servers and data warehousing filled its storage, nobody had a collector watching it, the server disks filled too, and the environment crashed, at real cost to the business. The lesson is the obvious one that teams still skip: monitor the thing that stores your telemetry.

He also warned against putting collectors on undersized, burstable servers meant for dev and test. Processing pipelines that cannot keep up with data volume, and single points of failure in the telemetry path, turn into dropped or delayed data exactly when the environment is busiest. Observability that goes dark under load is a smoke alarm that only works when nothing is burning.

## Set it up, then test that it works

A recurring complaint in the talk is the "configure and walk away" pattern: monitoring gets installed, the ticket closes, and nobody checks the dashboards, the schemas or whether the alerts fire. Meletius calls these monitoring blind spots and pairs them with collector crashes under peak load and version drift, where weeks go into triaging library updates that did not match the codebase.

His advice: verify monitoring end to end before handing it off, and schedule regular reviews of schemas, resources and integration points rather than waiting for an incident to do the review for you.

## What he says actually works

The closing recommendations are pragmatic:

- Start small, on critical systems, and limit the initial scope.
- Write documentation and training tailored to your own stack.
- Expand gradually as the team gets comfortable.
- Treat OpenTelemetry as a foundation and build alerting and visualisation layers on top of it.
- Accept that observability needs ongoing investment in people and infrastructure, not a one-time setup.

## Who should watch

Teams early in an OpenTelemetry rollout, and managers who need a plain-language case for why "we adopted OTel" is the start of the budget conversation, not the end. Engineers looking for collector configuration snippets or benchmark numbers will not find them here; this is an experience talk about process and ownership.

- Bruno Ferreira's [Optimizing Observability with OpenTelemetry Collector for Budget-Friendly Insights](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Bruno_Ferreira_observability_opentelemetry_collector) gets into the collector configuration this talk leaves out.

Title: Quantum-ready architecture is mostly event queues and job routers
Description: JPMorgan Chase's Laxmikanth Mukund Sethu Kumar at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on hybrid patterns that prepare enterprise systems for quantum.
Body:
If your platform already runs on event queues, APIs and Kubernetes jobs, you are closer to quantum-ready than you think. Laxmikanth Mukund Sethu Kumar, Executive Director at JPMorgan Chase, argued exactly that at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025: quantum will coexist with classical computing, not compete with it, and the work enterprise architects can do today is integration, not physics.

The abstract promises a systems view drawn from platforms built for banks, airlines and government, and the talk sticks to it. Quantum mechanics gets one slide; architecture gets the rest.

## What today's DevOps stack is missing

The useful starting point is the gap list. Quantum workloads don't fit existing DevOps stacks yet, and Sethu Kumar names three missing pieces: job orchestration, state isolation for quantum workloads, and latency tolerance. He also asks architects to stop thinking in either/or terms: a qubit's state is probabilistic, and so are its results, so the systems around it should expect distributions, not single answers.

The supply side is already there. AWS Braket, IBM Quantum and Azure Quantum all expose quantum hardware through cloud-native APIs.

## Three tiers and a clean seam

His hybrid architecture is three layers:

- **Application tier**: microservices and APIs, unchanged.
- **Orchestration tier**: quantum job routers and queues.
- **Backend tier**: classical compute, quantum compute, or both.

The rule for the middle layer is the line to remember: decouple the quantum logic from the orchestration logic. Middleware owns session management, job queuing, error retries and result normalisation, so a flaky quantum backend never leaks into your business code.

## Patterns you already know

The design patterns are deliberately familiar:

- **Quantum as a service**, alongside IaaS and SaaS.
- **Quantum triggers from classical event queues** such as Kafka: a classical service publishes, a quantum consumer reacts.
- **Serverless quantum microservices**, for example an AWS Lambda function that kicks off a Braket job.
- **Cloud-native abstractions**: containers for local quantum simulation, Kubernetes job runners for orchestrating quantum flows, and CI/CD pipelines for quantum kernels.

Tools named include the Braket SDK and gRPC bridges. Security is zero trust across both worlds; interoperability depends on vendor-neutral interfaces and standards such as QIR; and observability means quantum job telemetry flowing into Prometheus and OpenTelemetry like everything else. If your quantum job can't be seen on the same dashboard as the rest of the system, it isn't production-ready, whatever the qubit count.

## A five-step roadmap with a safe middle

The roadmap is the most reusable slide: identify quantum-able problems (scheduling, ML model tuning), build a dev sandbox on emulators, integrate with job orchestration and message buses, pilot a hybrid service on a non-critical path, then promote gradually to production workflows. The goal, in his framing, is to experiment without rewriting the stack, using modular adapter layers, simulators and mature hybrid CI/CD.

## Who should watch

Enterprise and platform architects, engineering leads and anyone who has been asked for a quantum strategy and wants one that fits on an architecture diagram. It's short, clear and free of hype. Physicists will find nothing new; integrators will find a checklist.

Title: Your recommender did not crash. It quietly served default content
Description: Sai Kumar Bitra of AT&T at Conf42 Observability 2025 on observing real-time personalization engines, with model metrics, traces and a silent drift story.
Body:
The worst personalization incident is the one where nothing crashes. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Sai Kumar Bitra, a principal software engineer at AT&T, walked through how to observe a real-time personalization engine, and illustrated it with a scenario where engagement slid for a week while every service stayed green.

The answer to that scenario turned out to be a missing profile attribute upstream, and finding it took metrics, traces and logs together.

## Why personalization is hard to observe

Sai lists the challenges. Personalization runs on distributed pipelines of services, data pipelines and ML models, so end-to-end tracking is a must. Event volume is high, and telemetry must be captured without adding latency to responses that users expect in milliseconds. Model decisions are a black box: when recommendations get worse, is it the model, the rules or the source data? And users hop between web, mobile and store, so their journey has to be stitched across channels.

## The architecture and the metrics that matter

His reference architecture is a request entering through APIs, a decision engine calling a model service that executes models and rules, a data layer holding profiles and content, and event ingestion (for example through Kafka) feeding the model. Everything ships telemetry to one centralised observability pipeline, instrumented once with the OpenTelemetry SDK.

The metrics he cares about go beyond latency:

- **Latency and throughput** per API, model call and data call.
- **Error rates and timeouts**, including how often the system falls back to default recommendations.
- **Engagement metrics** such as click-through, conversion and dwell time, tied to observability so a drop shows up as a signal.
- **Model indicators**: confidence score distribution, frequency of each model variant, and drift between live inputs and training data.
- **Resources**, including Kafka topic throughput and consumer lag.

## Traces and logs for the black box

Tracing follows each personalization request through API, decision engine, model and database, with a span per segment, so you can see which layer is eating the milliseconds. Tracing every request is not feasible, so sample normal traffic and keep a representative slice. Logs should be structured and rich: user segment, relevant features, perhaps a reason or explanation score, plus trace IDs for correlation. And anonymise: GDPR concerns mean engineers get enough to troubleshoot without logging sensitive customer data.

On scale, he warns against metric overload from per-user labels (aggregate by category or percentile instead), recommends batching and buffering telemetry exports so applications are not blocked, tiered storage, and monitoring the observability pipeline itself, because a lagging log forwarder during an incident is its own outage.

## The silent drift incident

The case study is the memorable part. Engagement on a personalized component dropped gradually over a week. Nothing crashed. An alert on click-through rate falling below baseline fired, and the model drift metric showed live inputs had shifted from the training data. Traces showed normal latency, but many sessions were getting default content: the model was unsure and falling back. Logs, which recorded whether each response was personalized or default, showed users not landing in any segment. The cause was upstream: the ETL had stopped collecting an age attribute that segment rules depended on. Fix the ETL, and the recommendations come back.

The lesson: monitoring isn't just an ops concern when the product is the model's output.

## Who should watch

Engineers running recommendation or ranking systems in production, and ML teams whose models are monitored only for uptime. It is a broad overview with one strong story; the tool stack at the end (OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger, the ELK stack, plus commercial APM) is standard.

Title: Watching a treasury trading floor that moves in microseconds
Description: Ganesh Marimuthu at Conf42 Observability 2025 on tracing, ML anomaly detection and telemetry pipelines for high-frequency treasury trading.
Body:
In a treasury trading platform, the monitoring itself can be the incident. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Ganesh Marimuthu, who has spent more than two decades in investment banking technology, walked through how distributed tracing, machine-learning anomaly detection and cloud-native telemetry pipelines change operations for systems that execute trades in microseconds, and why every one of them has to justify its own overhead.

The talk is a tour of a domain most observability content never visits: US Treasuries, dealer-to-dealer markets, smart order routers, KDB databases and settlement reconciliation. If your usual pager problem is a slow checkout page, this is a useful look at a world where a few microseconds of tracing overhead is a line item.

## The scale is the problem statement

Ganesh opened with the numbers his platforms deal with: around 8.4 TB of market data a day, algorithms executing a large share of the treasury flow, and market data peaking in the tens of thousands of messages per second. His point is that traditional monitoring was built for a slower world. When a minor performance degradation can turn into a financial loss before a human finishes reading the alert, the observability system has to work at the same tempo as the trading engine.

## Tracing earns its keep, if it stays out of the way

The section on distributed tracing is the most concretely useful. Ganesh described tracing across trading microservices cutting mean time to resolution by 78%, and latency analytics finding bottlenecks in the pipeline that led to a 23% improvement in average execution times. The part that matters for anyone in a latency-sensitive shop: the tracing added less than 2.5 microseconds of overhead. That is the bar. A tracer that costs more than the trade it observes gets switched off by the desk, and nobody files a ticket about it.

He also covered smart order router monitoring: round-trip times to each venue, venue responsiveness, and real-time comparison of expected against actual execution prices. That last one is observability in its business-outcome form. The router can return success and still have filled the order at the wrong price.

## Anomaly detection with a feedback loop

The ML part of the talk describes anomaly detection that spots deviations in trading patterns (market dislocations, execution anomalies, compliance issues) and keeps learning from both normal operations and the anomalies it has already flagged. Ganesh quoted 85% accuracy for that system and tied it to trade surveillance and spoofing detection, where regulators care as much about the audit trail as engineers care about the latency graph.

## Pipelines that survive the market open

The cloud-native pipeline he described separates collection, enrichment, storage and alerting, so a volatile market open, when telemetry matters most, does not knock over the system that is supposed to explain it. He showed latency swinging by up to 20% around market openings, economic announcements and auctions, and argued the observability stack has to absorb those swings without adding its own. Tiered storage (hot data in memory, cold data archived) and KDB for time series came up as the practical answers to data volume.

The closing third goes further out: quantum-resistant cryptography for monitoring data, homomorphic encryption for alerting on encrypted metrics, and blockchain-based audit trails that he credited with an 82% cut in reconciliation cost. Treat this part as a look at where the field is heading rather than a how-to.

## Who should watch

Engineers and SREs in trading, payments or any system where the observability budget is measured in microseconds. If you have never had to argue about the latency cost of a span, the talk is a good calibration of how differently finance thinks about telemetry. If you want step-by-step configuration, look elsewhere: this is an architecture and outcomes talk.

- Janardhan Chejarla's [Securing High-Frequency Trading at Scale](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Janardhan_Chejarla_trading_cloud_scale) covers event-driven order management from the security side.
- Srinivas Reddy Mosali's [Zero Downtime, Zero Excuses](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Reddy_Mosali_fintech_infrastructure_scaling) on fintech infrastructure that cannot blink.

Title: Sample synthetic tests at 100% and aggregate the traces
Description: Sudeep Kumar of Salesforce at Conf42 Observability 2025 on turning fully sampled synthetic traces into aggregated views of critical user journeys.
Body:
Synthetic tests tell you a user journey failed; traces tell you which of the many services in that journey did it. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Sudeep Kumar, a principal engineer in Salesforce's Monitoring Cloud organisation, showed how his team traces every synthetic test run at full sampling and then aggregates those traces into views that point straight at the slow or failing service.

The scale is the first thing he puts on the table: observability for over a million hosts and containers, more than 2,000 teams and 13,000 developers, and more than 300 billion spans a day.

## Critical user journeys are hero flows

Sudeep defines critical user journeys (CUJs) as "hero flows": high-value, customer-facing, business-critical request paths, often revenue-impacting. In a microservices estate those paths cross many services, so when an incident hits, finding the guilty hop is the slow part. Distributed tracing answers the key questions: which services sit on the critical path, how healthy those transactions are, and where the bottleneck is. Because journeys change as features ship, tracing also exposes new and unwanted access patterns.

His advice on instrumentation is unglamorous and correct: on CUJ paths, add spans manually, one at a time, where they add value. Those spans become your best signals.

## A refresher that sets up the trick

He walks through the semantics: each service emits spans with a start time, duration and operation, all tied to one trace ID and assembled into a waterfall. Context propagates through transport headers (Salesforce uses B3 headers for legacy reasons; OpenTelemetry headers work too). The detail that matters later is the sampling flag: if it is zero, downstream services propagate context but do not emit spans, which is how most platforms keep trace volume affordable.

## Synthetic tests get 100% sampling

That is the core idea. Ordinary traffic is sampled; synthetic tests that emulate a CUJ are always sampled at 100%, so every run is captured end to end. Each test is a set of templated steps, each step emitting its own trace tied to the test ID, and variables let the same definition run from Europe, Japan or the US. The result is an outside-in view of performance and availability: browser, APM and DNS monitoring included.

Drilling into one failed run, linking to its trace IDs and opening the waterfall works. But looking at runs one by one does not scale.

## Aggregation is where the gold is

The payoff is aggregation across similar traces:

- **Latency contributors:** a "create account" transaction takes around 85 milliseconds, and the metric alone does not say where. Aggregating similar traces into a time series shows which operation (here, authentication) dominates.
- **Slice and compare:** the same view for errors, per step, per region variable, against a baseline for week-over-week trends.
- **Directed graphs:** an aggregated graph of the request flow with per-edge health, such as 72 runs of a test with 12 failing on the call to one app. Since synthetic traces are fully sampled, nothing is missing from that picture.

He finishes with three on-demand options for when synthetic coverage is not enough: tracing for one specific user, long-running tracing to catch sporadic issues, and per-instance tracing for a single tenant's instance.

## Who should watch

SREs and observability platform engineers who run synthetic checks and tracing as separate tools and suspect they should talk to each other. You need a tracing back end you control to build the aggregation views; the design ideas transfer anyway.

Title: Kafka stalls quietly. Metrics, events, logs and traces catch it
Description: Abhishek Walia of Confluent at Conf42 Observability 2025 on the MELT stack for Kafka, with the broker metrics that matter, JMX, KIP-714, JSON logs and traces.
Body:
"Kafka doesn’t fail cleanly: it stalls, lags, and misfires beneath the surface." That is how Abhishek Walia, a staff customer success technical architect at Confluent, framed his talk at Conf42 Observability 2025. His answer is the MELT stack (metrics, events, logs, traces) applied to Kafka: which signals actually matter, how to collect them, and which ones you can postpone.

His opinionated short version: start with metrics and logs, then graduate to events and traces.

## The MELT pyramid, applied to Kafka

Abhishek stacks the signals as a pyramid:

- **Metrics** are the base: numerical measurements exposed by brokers, such as request counts, disk back pressure, network thread usage, replication lag and consumer lag.
- **Events** are discrete state changes: a broker crash, a rolling restart, a disk hitting 70%, a pod moving on Kubernetes. Kafka does not expose events directly, so you derive them from logs and metrics.
- **Logs** are not optional. Errors, stack traces, controller elections, client disconnections: root cause analysis cannot finish without them.
- **Traces** live at the client and business layer: a watermark in the Kafka message header that follows the message through every producer, broker and consumer.

His example of why events matter is a good one: during a rolling restart, producer latency spikes for no apparent reason in the metrics. Overlay the rollout event and the spike explains itself.

## Pick metrics carefully, because Kafka has thousands

He recalls counting about 3,500 MBeans on a small home-server cluster a few years ago. Most are noise. The ones he starts with are replication health, partition and leader distribution (no hot broker while others idle), error rates for fetch, produce and replication requests, and network utilisation, which he calls the most precious resource in a Kafka cluster. His sizing aside makes the point: produce at around 125 megabytes per second and a one-gigabit port is already close to full.

Collection is JMX on brokers and clients, a Prometheus JMX exporter to turn MBeans into a scrapable HTTP endpoint, Prometheus to store, and Grafana to graph. The newer piece is KIP-714 in Kafka 3.7 and later, which lets clients push their key metrics to the brokers, so you can collect client metrics centrally without instrumenting every producer and consumer with JMX.

## Logs: JSON, central, and kept longer than you think

The logging advice is concrete. Configure Log4j to emit structured JSON so machines can parse it without hand-built parsers; yes, the volume grows. Ship logs with Filebeat or an OpenTelemetry Collector to one central store, filterable by broker and cluster; he likes Grafana Loki. And do not set retention to seven days. He did, years ago, and regretted it. Size retention to how long application teams can come back with questions: if that is 30 days, keep around 45, tiering to warm and cold storage instead of deleting.

## Traces through message headers

For tracing, propagate context in Kafka headers so consumers continue the same trace, use OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation, and store spans in Jaeger, Zipkin or similar. His example trace breaks a message's life into producer time, time waiting in the broker, consumer fetch and processing, which shows where the hot spot is when processing slows down.

He also points viewers at a JMX monitoring stack with tuned Kafka dashboards that he and friends maintain.

## Who should watch

Anyone running Kafka in production who has a Grafana dashboard full of panels and no idea which three to look at during an incident. The tool choices are his preferences and he says so; swap them for what your organisation already runs.

Title: Four patterns for putting quantum inside a multi-tenant SaaS
Description: Srikar Kompella of Twilio sketches quantum, edge and multi-tenancy patterns for SaaS at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, from federated learning onward.
Body:
Multi-tenancy started as a way to save money on shared servers; Srikar Kompella thinks its next stage is quantum-aware resource allocation across tenants. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, the Twilio Senior Software Engineer laid out an architecture vision for SaaS built on three pillars (quantum compute, edge processing and advanced multi-tenancy) and four integration patterns that combine them.

It's a forward-looking architecture talk rather than a build log. The value is in the patterns, which are concrete enough to reason about now.

## Three pillars, one platform

Kompella's pillars split the work by what each is good at. Quantum computing, reached on demand through the cloud, takes the optimisation, simulation and pattern-finding problems. Edge processing brings those results close to users so decisions happen in real time and less raw data travels. Multi-tenancy is the delivery framework: fair, cost-effective sharing of scarce quantum processors with strict isolation of each tenant's data in a mixed classical, quantum and edge environment.

The edge piece has one idea worth stealing: train a complex model on the quantum side, then deploy it to local edge runtimes. A factory robot then adjusts on the spot instead of waiting on a central server, and a traffic grid tunes signal timing at each intersection.

## Multi-tenancy grows up in three steps

The talk frames multi-tenancy as an evolution: basic resource sharing with minimal isolation and a focus on cost, then advanced segmentation where tenants share services but keep data and workflows separate, then quantum-aware architectures that allocate resources dynamically across tenant boundaries while still isolating them.

## The four integration patterns

This is the section to watch closely:

1. **Quantum federated learning.** Each tenant (his example: a hospital and a research institute) trains a quantum ML model on its own data inside its own perimeter. Only model updates leave, protected by quantum-resistant cryptography. The platform aggregates them into a better global model and sends it back. Raw data never moves.
2. **Customised quantum edge deployments.** Tenant-specific quantum algorithms go to edge locations based on each tenant's needs, with workloads routed between edge nodes and central quantum machines as demand shifts.
3. **QML-driven resource orchestration.** A quantum ML model forecasts each tenant's resource demand from live metrics, and the platform allocates capacity before the tenant needs it. Think autoscaling that reads ahead.
4. **Secure tenant collaboration.** Quantum-resistant data exchange plus privacy-preserving joint processing, so competitors can pool insights without sharing raw data. His example is rival retailers finding supply-chain inefficiencies that hurt them all, leading to industry consortiums hosted on the platform.

Pattern one is the most grounded: federated learning already exists classically, and the quantum part slots into the model and the crypto rather than the workflow.

## From selling software to selling answers

Kompella's business point is that quantum lets a SaaS company sell results such as optimisation or materials discovery as a service, not just tools. His roadmap is sober: assess the current architecture and find computationally heavy workloads, pick one pattern for a single pilot and measure it, then scale and invest in in-house expertise. He calls it an evolution, not an overnight revolution, which is the right tone.

## Who should watch

SaaS architects and platform engineers who own tenancy, isolation and capacity planning, and who want a vocabulary for where quantum might enter their stack. Skip it if you want benchmarks or code; it's patterns and diagrams.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Optimizing multi-tenant SaaS: scalable architectures for performance, security and cost](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Shinu_Pushpan_saas_multitenancy_security) by Shinu Pushpan, the classical baseline these patterns extend.
- [Quantum-resistant Kubernetes for the post-quantum era](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Derek_Asir_Muthurajan_Caleb_quantum_security_infrastructure) by Derek Asir Muthurajan Caleb, on the crypto the patterns assume.
- [Product management with multi-tenancy architecture](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Waqas_Khan_multitenancy_optimization_strategy) by Waqas Khan, for the product side of tenancy decisions.

Title: Monitoring says it broke; OpenTelemetry helps you find out why
Description: Naga Murali Krishna Koneru of Hexaware at Conf42 Observability 2025 explains observability basics and the OpenTelemetry Collector with Loki, Mimir and Grafana.
Body:
"Monitoring shows you're broken - observability tells you why." That line from the abstract is the thesis of Naga Murali Krishna Koneru's talk at Conf42 Observability 2025. Naga, a technical architect at Hexaware Technologies working on AWS, DevOps and DevSecOps, walked from the vocabulary of observability to a working OpenTelemetry Collector setup that hides Loki, Mimir and Grafana behind a single endpoint.

It is a primer, and a well-organised one: if you are the person on your team who has to explain OpenTelemetry to everyone else, this is a good script.

## The methods you measure with

Naga grounds everything in two outcomes: mean time to detection and mean time to resolution. Then he lines up the standard measurement methods side by side:

- **RED:** rate, errors and duration, for request-driven services.
- **USE:** utilisation, saturation and errors, for resources such as CPU, disk and network queues.
- **Google's four golden signals:** latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
- **Core Web Vitals:** LCP, FID and CLS, for what the user's browser experiences.

His distinction between monitoring and observability is practical: monitoring tracks known issues and suits small or monolithic systems; observability uncovers unknown unknowns in complex systems and tells you where, when and why.

## Four signal types, two ways to collect

He covers the signal types with a one-line job for each: metrics say what is happening, logs say what happened and when, traces show where in the request path the bottleneck is, and profiles explain why at the resource level (CPU, garbage collection).

Push versus scrape gets a decision rule. Scrape, as Prometheus does, when running on Kubernetes or other dynamic environments and apps can expose an HTTP endpoint. Push, as with StatsD to Graphite, when apps are short-lived, need real-time metrics, or sit in restricted networks where nothing can scrape them.

## The Collector is the part to understand

The OpenTelemetry section explains the project (a CNCF project, vendor-neutral, multi-language) and then focuses on the Collector: receivers as entry points, processors that filter, enrich or sample, exporters that ship to back ends, plus connectors that link pipelines and extensions that add capabilities. A pipeline can have several of each.

He lists where telemetry comes from in a typical Kubernetes setup: SDK-instrumented apps, service meshes such as Istio, node and pod metrics, cluster events, Fluentd and Fluent Bit for container logs, cloud provider metrics, liveness and readiness probes, and container runtime data. On instrumentation, auto-instrumentation gets you visibility quickly with little effort, while manual instrumentation gives precise control over business-specific signals.

## One endpoint, many back ends

The closing architecture is the takeaway. Two VMs run Fluent Bit for logs and node exporter for metrics. Both talk only to the OpenTelemetry Collector, which routes logs to Loki and metrics to Mimir, with Grafana on top (Tempo is the tracing piece of the same stack). The applications never need to know which back ends exist, so swapping one later does not touch application code. The full stack, from bottom to top, is instrumentation, collection, storage and visualisation.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to OpenTelemetry, and leads who need a structured overview to onboard a team. Experienced Collector operators will find it introductory.
