Title: Fluent Bit on EKS, from empty cluster to CloudWatch logs
Description: Dharmendra Ahuja at Conf42 Observability 2025 demos Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet on AWS EKS, shipping enriched container logs to CloudWatch, plus five use cases.
Body:
Fluent Bit is the small log processor that ends up on most Kubernetes nodes, and the setup is easier to learn by watching than by reading the Helm chart. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Dharmendra Ahuja, a DevOps architect and data engineer, built the whole pipeline live on AWS EKS: cluster, IAM, Fluent Bit and a sample app, ending with container logs in CloudWatch.

It is a practical, step-by-step demo, followed by five real-world patterns that reuse the same building blocks.

## What Fluent Bit does in the pipeline

Before the demo, Dharmendra lays out Fluent Bit's four jobs: **collect** logs from containers and endpoints, **enrich** them with Kubernetes metadata and custom tags, **transform** them by structuring, filtering and masking sensitive fields, and **route** them to destinations based on content, namespace or other attributes.

The internals map to a plain pipeline: input plugins read from containers, files or systemd; parsers turn lines into structured JSON; filters enrich or drop data; buffers hold logs in memory or on disk during spikes or network delays; output plugins push to CloudWatch, S3, Kinesis Data Firehose, OpenSearch, Elasticsearch or Kafka.

## The demo, step by step

The demo is the reason to watch, because it shows the parts people get wrong. In order:

1. Create the EKS cluster from an `eksctl` config file and watch the CloudFormation stacks build the VPC pieces, control plane and add-ons.
2. Update the kubeconfig and create a `fluent-bit` namespace.
3. Associate an IAM OIDC provider with the cluster, then create an IAM service account bound to a pre-made policy that grants CloudWatch Logs access. This is how the pods get permissions without node-wide credentials.
4. Add the Fluent Bit Helm repo and install the chart with the existing service account, CloudWatch output, region, log group and a log stream prefix.
5. Edit the Fluent Bit ConfigMap to swap the default Elasticsearch output for CloudWatch, then restart the DaemonSet so it picks up the change. The restart is the step people forget.
6. Deploy an NGINX "log server" in a demo namespace, port-forward it, and hit it with `curl` while tailing logs locally in a second terminal.

The payoff is a new log group in CloudWatch with the expected streams, and a CloudWatch dashboard showing the requests as they arrive. The demo is honest about waiting for CloudFormation, which anyone who has run `eksctl create cluster` will recognise.

## Five patterns from the field

The closing section takes the same DaemonSet and points it at different problems:

- **FinTech audit trail:** tail container logs, enrich with Kubernetes metadata, ship to CloudWatch for centralised logging that satisfies financial audits.
- **SaaS search:** stream to Amazon OpenSearch with Kibana dashboards for near-real-time log queries.
- **Gaming platform to Datadog:** use the HTTP output plugin with filters that trim log volume and ingestion cost without hurting cluster performance.
- **Healthcare compliance:** add Linux audit logs via the systemd input, archive to a dedicated S3 bucket for long retention under HIPAA, and let the security team pull into Splunk for forensics.
- **Multi-tenant isolation:** add tenant labels by namespace and route each tenant to its own Grafana Loki tenant, so one cluster serves several customers without mixing logs.

## Who should watch

Engineers about to put logging on their first EKS cluster, or anyone who has copied a Fluent Bit Helm values file without knowing what the IRSA steps were for. If you already run Fluent Bit in production, skip to the use cases.

- [Alok Ranjan on going from fragmented logs to unified insights](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Alok_Ranjan_fragmented_logs_unified) (SRE 2025).
- [Leonid Yankulin on anonymizing application logs the DevOps way](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Leonid_Yankulin_structured_logging_google_cloud) (DevSecOps 2022), for the masking step in practice.

Title: Cut the Kubernetes observability bill by collecting better signals
Description: Aritra Ghosh of Microsoft at Conf42 Observability 2025 on trimming Kubernetes monitoring costs layer by layer, from control plane to network, with budgets.
Body:
Observability can eat up to 40% of a cloud bill, and in Kubernetes a lot of that data shows up whether you asked for it or not. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Aritra Ghosh, a senior product manager at Microsoft working on cloud-native monitoring, walked through where that money goes and how to cut it layer by layer without going blind.

His closing mantra sums up the talk: better signals mean lower cost and happier engineers.

## Where the money actually goes

Aritra names four spending sinks he sees in enterprises:

- **High-cardinality custom metrics**, priced separately by most tools and inflated by labels like user ID.
- **Long log retention and verbose logging**, with debug logs left on and kept for 30 or 90 days.
- **The same data shipped to several destinations**, paying storage more than once.
- **Cross-region and cross-network traffic**, which adds egress on top of storage.

Cloud-native makes this worse because pods spin up and down constantly and some telemetry is generated outside your direct control.

## Start from SLOs, then rank the signals

The framework is: collect what matters, choose the right signal, tune retention and aggregation, and consolidate or offload the rest. Start with service level objectives, because that is what users feel. Then rank by value: metrics first (they drive alerting), traces second (they show the path between services), logs last (they explain what went wrong inside one service). That ranking is a useful corrective for teams whose bill is 80% logs.

## Four layers, four diets

The Kubernetes-specific part splits monitoring into four components:

- **Control plane:** ingest managed-service metrics such as API server latency and health checks instead of full logs, and alert on deviation from expected behaviour rather than static thresholds.
- **Nodes:** track CPU, memory and disk IO, watch heartbeats and node-ready transitions, and skip per-process metrics unless you are actively debugging.
- **Pods:** filter health checks and static endpoints at the source, and use labels and OpenTelemetry auto-tagging to tie telemetry to services.
- **Network:** focus on connection failures and DNS resolution problems, sample flow records such as NetFlow or IPFIX, and prefer eBPF-based tooling.

On OpenTelemetry he recommends explicit aggregation temporality, dropping labels to cut cardinality, and limiting custom metrics to business-critical paths.

## A budget, not just a dashboard

The organisational advice is the part many cost talks skip. Build a cost-aware dashboard showing spend per telemetry type, then attribute it to teams with tags so chargebacks are at least visible. Then set an observability budget: a monthly cap per cluster, with quotas on log volume and custom metrics enforced through tools like Fluent Bit and Loki.

His checklist runs drop, shorten retention, filter at source, consolidate tools, tune alerts. On cardinality: keep user IDs and UUIDs out of metric labels and use tier, region or status code. On alerts: funnel raw data to filtered to routed to actionable, and page only on SLO violations or customer impact.

He illustrates the result with an explicitly fictional customer that reached a 40% saving by dropping health check logs, lowering verbosity, replacing raw latency logs with Prometheus histograms and moving cold data to object storage. It is labelled as an illustration, not a benchmark, and the trade-off curve that follows makes the real point: past a certain volume, more telemetry adds cost but not insight.

## Who should watch

Kubernetes platform teams and engineering managers who own the monitoring line item. The tool list at the end (Prometheus with Thanos or Cortex, Fluent Bit, the OpenTelemetry Collector, Grafana, Cilium) is a sensible open-source baseline.

- [Roman Khavronenko on measuring PromQL and MetricsQL expression complexity](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2024_Roman_Khavronenko_measure_promql_metricsql) (Observability 2024), for what cardinality does to your queries.

Title: Edge devices sit outside your monitoring, and attackers know it
Description: Chintan Udeshi of Palo Alto Networks at Conf42 Observability 2025 on real-time observability for edge devices as the first step in edge security.
Body:
Edge devices live outside the network boundary your monitoring tools were built for, which makes them an attractive way in. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Chintan Udeshi, a principal product manager at Palo Alto Networks, made the case that real-time observability of edge devices is where edge security starts, and laid out a roadmap from one device to a global fleet.

He is clear that monitoring is only the first step, and the talk spends real time on what has to come after it.

## Why the edge keeps growing

Chintan opens with the three reasons workloads move to the edge: latency drops to milliseconds for near-real-time applications; operations keep working when the internet does not (his example is a self-driving car in a remote area that still has to make critical decisions); and local processing saves bandwidth. He cites market projections showing steep growth through the next decade, which is why the security problem is getting bigger.

## Three ways in

The threat section explains why edge is different. Devices operate outside traditional network boundaries, so the cloud and on-prem monitoring stack does not see them. Legacy tools lack edge-specific threat detection. And edge hardware has limited CPU and memory, so teams often trade security capability for speed. He cites a study finding that 45% of organisations had at least one significant edge security incident in the past year.

The attack patterns follow from that:

- **Entry point and lateral movement:** compromise an edge device, then move into cloud and on-prem systems.
- **Data breaches:** poorly secured devices often hold unencrypted data.
- **DDoS:** limited devices cannot fend off sophisticated botnet traffic.

## What edge observability needs to do

His spec has three parts. Equip devices with small micro-agents that watch behaviour alongside CPU and memory use, so subtle deviations from known-normal stand out. Correlate those signals across all edge devices, not one at a time, so an attack shows up as a pattern. And automate the response, isolating a compromised device within milliseconds instead of waiting for a human, so threats do not move laterally.

The case study is a large automotive manufacturing plant that ran edge security monitoring for three months. Chintan reports fewer incident escalations, most unauthorised access attempts between edge and core infrastructure identified, and mean time to detection falling from 197 hours to about four.

## Monitoring is the start, not the finish

The section worth pausing on is his list of controls that must sit on top of visibility: continuous authentication in line with zero trust, least-privilege access, micro-segmentation so one infected device cannot reach everything, and runtime protection against unknown vulnerabilities. His reminder for that last one is Log4j, disclosed in December 2021 after sitting in software for years.

## The rollout roadmap

The implementation advice is incremental: inventory edge devices and their weak points, pick the most critical device, instrument it, and measure mean time to detection and lateral movement. Then integrate edge telemetry with the rest of the platform (public cloud, private cloud, on-prem, network fabric and IoT) for a single view, and finally expand to the whole worldwide fleet.

## Who should watch

Security and platform engineers responsible for factories, retail sites, vehicles or any fleet of devices that never touches the data centre. It is a product manager's strategic overview, vendor-neutral in content, without product demos or config.

- [Venukumar Chirlawar on Rust in edge computing for performance and security](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Venukumar_Chirlawar_edge_computing_security) (Rustlang 2024).

Title: A quantum sidecar for Teamcenter, not a PLM rewrite
Description: Pradeep Karanam at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on sending only the hardest PLM questions from Siemens Teamcenter to cloud quantum hardware.
Body:
Your PLM system already knows every part and option in the product; it just takes forever to answer a big "what if". Pradeep Karanam, Solutions Architect, used his talk at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 to show a small sidecar that sends only the hardest parts of those questions from Siemens Teamcenter (or any PLM tool) to a cloud quantum computer and writes the answer back. Nothing rewrites Teamcenter's core.

The abstract states the goal plainly: option lists that appear 8x faster and purchase plans that cut shortage risk by one third, without changing anyone's daily workflow.

## The pain is measured in dollars per day

Karanam opens with the business case. He cites a study putting the average cost of a major supply-chain disruption around $22 million, and a stopped production line burning roughly $1.5 million a day. Then the complexity problem: a car like the BMW Mini has trillions of valid option combinations, and the rule engines inside PLM check options close to one by one. His goal is to turn overnight batch jobs into answers you get over a coffee break.

## Four steps over REST

The architecture is the reason to watch. Teamcenter already sends heavy jobs to HPC clusters, so quantum is just another remote backend:

1. Pull the bill of materials or supply data through the Active Workspace REST API.
2. Convert it into the maths a quantum machine understands: a QUBO matrix for optimisation, or a probability model for simulation.
3. Send it to the cloud and wait a few seconds for the best answer.
4. Write the new configuration or risk score back into Teamcenter, where everyone already works.

He calls it a bolt-on microservice, not a rip and replace. For configuration, every rule becomes an energy penalty, and the annealer settles into a valid, low-energy build.

## The hardware list is refreshingly specific

Instead of a generic qubit diagram, the talk names what was reachable through cloud APIs at the time: D-Wave's Advantage2 annealer, Pasqal's neutral-atom machine on Google Cloud, IBM's 127-qubit Eagle, and Fujitsu's Digital Annealer, which he says is already in daily use at a Toyota plant. Gate-model chips, annealers and neutral-atom arrays get one line each on what they are good for. Because today's machines are noisy, the quantum core is always wrapped in classical code.

## Fewer Monte Carlo runs, more design iterations

For supply risk, planners run Monte Carlo simulations when a port closes. Karanam's point is that quantum amplitude estimation reaches the same confidence with about 10,000 scenarios instead of a million, and he cites D-Wave tests where scenario throughput rose sharply. The same pattern applies to engineering: the talk cites faster battery-cooling CFD, fewer crash FEA runs and overnight polymer simulations, all feeding the Teamcenter digital twin.

## Protect while you innovate

Two pieces of advice stand out because they apply even if you never buy quantum time. First, quantum computers threaten today's encryption, and NIST published its first post-quantum standards in 2024, so audit the Teamcenter supplier portal for RSA-2048 and plan the cutover. Second, his risk table: hybrid error-aware code for decoherence, open standards like QIR against vendor lock-in, a "quantum translator" role that speaks both PLM and quantum, and phase-gated ROI checkpoints so projects live or die on real numbers.

The roadmap is staged: a cloud proof of concept on one high-value use case in the first three months, a production microservice benchmarked against CPUs by month twelve, then more sites and post-quantum TLS on the supplier portal by month 24.

## Who should watch

PLM architects, manufacturing IT leads and supply-chain planners who want a quantum pilot small enough to get approved. The talk is short and dense; the four-step REST flow and the risk table are the parts to screenshot.

Title: Seven signatures needed, three signers showed up. Now what?
Description: Onyebuchi Mark Irozuru of Botanix Labs at Conf42 Observability 2025 on monitoring a federated Bitcoin multisig with Grafana Alloy, Loki, Prometheus and Tempo.
Body:
A multisig is secure because its signers are spread across operators, hardware vendors and continents, and that is exactly what makes it hard to debug. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Onyebuchi Mark Irozuru, DevOps lead at Botanix Labs, a Bitcoin layer-2 startup, showed how his team built shared observability for a federated multisig without taking control away from the independent operators who run the nodes.

The setup is Grafana Alloy on each operator's side, shipping to central Loki, Prometheus and Tempo endpoints.

## The invisible complexity of distributed signing

Mark opens with the Bitcoin motto about keys and coins, then gets to the operational problem. A multisig spreads the attack surface by requiring signatures from multiple locations, states, hardware vendors and validator sets. Now picture seven signatures needed from 12 validators on four continents, and only three show up. Is a validator offline? Did it receive the transaction? Is the mempool full? Is it a network problem, a protocol problem, or an attack?

Without good telemetry, he says, you have no answers to any of those questions.

## What usually gets monitored, and what does not

Teams already watch the easy things: transactions, signature counts, hot and cold wallet balances. What stays hidden is the interesting part: the signature collection pattern (who signed what, and when), which nodes have been active and pushing the most transactions, network topology health, cryptographic performance and bottlenecks in proof generation. He walks through the flow of a 3-of-3 signing (initialisation, hash, signature collection, aggregation and verification) to show how many steps users never see.

In a federation, operational silence means slow recovery. Timeouts and slow signers translate directly into slow block production.

## Federated observability keeps the federation federated

The design principle is the part worth stealing for any multi-party system: each operator stays independent, with their own configuration on Kubernetes, Docker, bare metal or cloud, while contributing to a shared visibility layer. Nobody hands over the keys to their infrastructure to get a shared dashboard.

Grafana Alloy is the collector of choice because it combines logs, metrics, traces and profiling in one open-source agent and can run as a sidecar. Each operator tunes Alloy locally; all data flows to shared endpoints: Loki for logs, Prometheus for metrics, Tempo for traces. Access to those endpoints is secured with tokens, so the shared layer does not become the weak point.

## Before and after

The before picture is grim and familiar: blind spots in signature collection, hours of debugging a failed transaction by asking operators to send logs over various channels, unstructured logs, network issues found too late, and malicious nodes participating unchecked.

After, the team can see who the slow signer is, trace how requests propagate across signers, catch failures in real time and set alerts on service level indicators before users notice.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure engineers in Web3, and anyone running a system where several independent organisations each own a piece, such as consortiums, partner networks or federated platforms. It is short and architectural; bring your own Alloy config. Mark closes with open questions for the audience, including how to find the monitoring gaps specific to your own network.

Title: Why enterprise data integration moved to serverless cloud platforms
Description: Sudhakar Guduri at Conf42 Observability 2025 surveys the move from on-prem ETL to serverless cloud data integration, with industry examples.
Body:
On-premises ETL tools once owned enterprise data integration; cloud platforms now do much of that work. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Sudhakar Guduri, a senior ETL data quality engineer with a background in SSIS, Informatica and reporting tools, gave an overview of that shift: why serverless, event-driven integration displaced the traditional stack, and what made migrations succeed in finance, healthcare and manufacturing.

Set expectations up front: this is a market and architecture survey, not a hands-on build. It is useful as orientation for someone who grew up on classic ETL and wants the big picture before picking a platform.

## From the ETL era to cloud-native integration

Sudhakar frames the history in four stages: the traditional ETL era with manual, developer-heavy pipelines on-premises; a transition period; cloud-native integration; and a future where most organisations treat a cloud-based platform as their primary integration strategy. The on-premises systems, he says, hit scalability limits and integration failures at peak periods, while cloud platforms absorb large swings in workload.

His cost comparison breaks the case into infrastructure, maintenance, development and total cost of ownership, with the cloud side lower in each category. The argument is the familiar one, made with a table: you stop paying for idle capacity and for the people who babysit it.

## The platforms in the frame

He names the three that come up in most enterprise shortlists: AWS Glue, Microsoft Azure Data Factory and Google Cloud Dataflow, and compares customer satisfaction across them. He notes all three keep adding features such as machine-learning-based data quality monitoring and automated lineage tracking, the parts that matter to a data quality engineer.

## Serverless and event-driven are the actual change

The architectural core of the talk is two ideas. Serverless integration scales automatically with data volume and lets teams focus on development rather than infrastructure management. Event-driven integration triggers pipelines from data changes or scheduled events, runs workflows without manual intervention, and feeds real-time analytics within minutes instead of overnight batches.

That second point is where this talk touches its host conference: once pipelines fire on events instead of a nightly schedule, knowing when one silently stopped firing becomes the operational problem.

## Industry examples and success factors

Sudhakar walks through implementations in three sectors. Financial services shows the approach working in a heavily regulated environment, with faster time to insight than the previous on-premises systems. Healthcare organisations adopt cloud services for applications and infrastructure to improve operational efficiency and quality of care. A multinational manufacturer uses cloud integration for IoT data collection and predictive analytics.

The success factors he draws out are sensible and transferable:

- **Phased migration** rather than a big-bang cutover.
- **Hybrid architecture during the transition**, so old and new run side by side.
- **Data governance designed in**, not retrofitted.
- **Executive sponsorship**, because integration projects cross every department.

## Where it goes next

The closing section points at AI-assisted data mapping and quality management to reduce manual effort, integration strategies that span multiple clouds, and a shift from batch to streaming architectures for decisions on current data.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and ETL developers planning or justifying a move off on-premises integration tools, and managers who need the vocabulary. Engineers looking for pipeline code or failure stories will want something more hands-on.

Title: What SAP AI on BTP actually does, industry by industry
Description: Levi Strauss & Co. SAP project manager Venkata Kalyan Chakravarthy Mandavilli tours SAP AI use cases at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025.
Body:
Most ERP users meet SAP's AI as a recommendation in a screen they already use, not as a model they deploy. Venkata Kalyan Chakravarthy Mandavilli, SAP Project Manager at Levi Strauss & Co., spent his session at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 mapping which techniques sit behind those features on SAP's Business Technology Platform (BTP), across retail, healthcare, manufacturing, finance, supply chain, energy and agriculture.

Fair warning on scope: this is an SAP AI talk that happened to land at a quantum conference. There are no qubits in it. What it offers instead is a catalogue of classical ML patterns mapped onto the ERP processes they serve, from someone who has spent years leading SAP implementations across manufacturing, pharma, food and beverage and more.

## The stack: BTP underneath, AI core on top

Mandavilli starts with the architecture. BTP provides the integration layer, API management and data orchestration. On top, SAP's AI core offers machine learning services (classification, regression, clustering, anomaly detection), natural language processing (entity extraction, sentiment, document understanding) and computer vision (object detection, defect identification, visual inspection). The pitch is that these plug into existing SAP systems rather than living in a separate data science silo.

## Retail and healthcare: familiar models, specific inputs

For retail, recommendations come from hybrid models that combine collaborative filtering with content-based filtering, using purchase history and browsing patterns. Demand forecasting ensembles LSTM networks with classical ARIMA models and adds external signals like seasonality, market trends and social media sentiment.

Healthcare is the more interesting example. Admission prediction uses regression and classification over historical admissions, seasonal illness patterns, population demographics, facility utilisation and the local event calendar, which is a neat reminder that a marathon in town is a capacity-planning input. NLP mines unstructured clinical notes alongside structured data, with HIPAA compliance kept in the loop.

## Manufacturing gets the numbers

The manufacturing section has the talk's firmest figures, presented as industry results for predictive maintenance: unplanned downtime reduced by up to 50% and maintenance costs down 10 to 40% compared with scheduled maintenance. The loop is IoT sensor data collection, pattern analysis to predict failures, maintenance scheduling before they happen, then continuous learning. For quality, CNN-based visual inspection is cited as catching up to 99% of surface defects against 80 to 90% for traditional machine vision and human inspectors.

## Finance, supply chain, energy, fields

The rest of the tour moves quickly:

- **Finance**: graph neural networks that model relationships between entities to flag fraud, with SHAP and LIME for explainable decisions, and reinforcement learning for forecasting.
- **Supply chain**: multi-objective evolutionary algorithms balancing cost, time and environmental impact, early-warning ensembles, digital twins and automatic rerouting.
- **Energy and utilities**: reinforcement learning for consumption optimisation, hybrid physics-plus-ML renewable forecasting, storage charge cycles and microgrid balancing.
- **Agriculture**: multispectral satellite imagery for moisture stress and pest detection, field sensors, and gradient-boosted trees for yield prediction.

## Who should watch

SAP functional leads, solution architects and project managers who need a vocabulary for which model fits which SAP process, and data scientists joining an SAP shop. If you were hoping for quantum, pick another talk from the same event; if you have an SAP roadmap on your desk, this one is a useful checklist.

Title: In healthcare IT, a slow service is a patient waiting
Description: Brahmanand Reddy Bhavanam of Info Way Solutions at Conf42 Observability 2025 on tying distributed tracing and telemetry to clinical workflows and compliance.
Body:
When a hospital system slows down, the incident ticket is the least of it: somewhere a clinician is waiting on a screen. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Brahmanand Reddy Bhavanam, a developer at Info Way Solutions, argued that healthcare observability has to measure system health in terms of patient care, and that it has to be designed in from the start rather than bolted on.

It is a short, framework-level talk of about 15 minutes, built around one case study and a three-layer model you can borrow.

## CPU graphs do not know about patients

Brahmanand's starting point is the gap between traditional monitoring and what healthcare actually needs. Basic system metrics like CPU usage, without context, give fragmented visibility and reactive troubleshooting, with no link to clinical workflows. A crash might only be noticed once it has already delayed care.

The alternative he describes is end-to-end visibility across care pathways: unified tracing of a patient's journey through the systems, so an engineer can see which clinical step a slow service is holding up. He cites a figure that 73% of healthcare organisations lack comprehensive visibility into their distributed systems, which is the blind spot the rest of the talk addresses.

## Compliance is part of the observability spec

In this domain the telemetry itself is sensitive. Brahmanand lists the non-negotiables: HIPAA- and GDPR-compliant monitoring, encryption, audit trails and role-based access to the data the observability stack collects. The pipeline that watches the system also has to survive the system's bad days, so he asks for fault-tolerant monitoring with automated failover, so visibility stays up during outages.

## The case study: tracing across clinical service boundaries

The concrete example is a critical care scenario where unpredictable latency across interconnected services was slowing responses. The fix was end-to-end distributed tracing with custom instrumentation across all clinical service boundaries. The talk reports a 67% reduction in troubleshooting time afterwards, so issues were resolved before they turned into clinical disruptions.

He also looks at peak load, when patient volume spikes and reliability drops, and describes advanced telemetry collection and real-time adjustments keeping services from degrading.

## AIOps and the edge, briefly

Two forward-looking sections cover predictive analytics that anticipate failures hours ahead, filtering to cut false alarms so teams focus on clinically significant alerts, and automated remediation. Edge observability brings monitoring closer to the point of care, keeps watching through network disruptions, and processes sensitive data locally, which helps with privacy.

## A three-layer framework

The most reusable part is the model:

- **Technical metrics layer:** infrastructure, applications and network, with healthcare-specific thresholds for critical care.
- **Business impact layer:** correlates system performance with patient outcomes.
- **Compliance layer:** continuous HIPAA and GDPR compliance with automated reporting.

Implementation follows a plain sequence: assess existing systems and clinical workflow gaps, deploy tracing and unify metrics, logs and traces with compliance in place, then train clinical and IT staff together.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects new to healthcare who need a vocabulary for talking to clinical stakeholders, or teams writing the case for budget. It stays at the strategy level, so expect a framework and headline results rather than tool configs.

Title: QA for health insurance should watch the claim, not just test it
Description: Subash Lekshmi Velayudhan at Conf42 Observability 2025 on moving health insurance QA from testing to observing claims, portals and compliance.
Body:
A parent logs into a member portal to check coverage for their child's surgery, and the portal crashes. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Subash Lekshmi Velayudhan, a quality engineer with 22 years in health plan systems, used that scene to argue that QA in health insurance has to move from testing before release to observing what members and claims go through in production.

His phrase for the goal is a shift "from defect detection to experience protection", and the talk is a roadmap for getting there.

## Why testing alone falls short

Subash's view is that traditional QA does not keep up with fast-moving, heavily regulated healthcare platforms. Test suites catch defects before release; they do not tell you that open enrolment just made the portal crawl or that one microservice in the claims path is failing. He compares mean time to resolve with and without observability tooling, and frames observability as a survival tool rather than a luxury.

## Metrics, logs and traces, in claims language

The best part is how he maps the three signals onto the domain:

- **Metrics:** claims processing by complexity, prior authorisation approval rates, member portal latency during open enrolment.
- **Logs:** the story behind events, including which protected health data was accessed and why a provider lookup failed. They are the audit trail too.
- **Traces:** a claim's journey through 20 or more microservices, checking eligibility, provider validity, pricing, applied benefits, authorisation and status.

That last one is the case for tracing in insurance in one sentence: claims hop across APIs, third-party systems and legacy bridges, and without traces nobody can say which hop stalled.

## Observability as legal armour

Subash pushes the compliance angle further than most talks do. Observability lets you show who accessed protected health information and when, trace every step of a claim, and preserve evidence automatically during a regulatory investigation. It proves you are doing the right things, not only fixing them fast. He points out that QA teams often miss this part.

He also lists domain KPIs worth wiring into dashboards: auto-adjudication rate, first-pass resolution, average processing time and error rate by claim type for claims; portal availability, authentication success and provider search accuracy for members; and query and API response times, resource use and batch completion for the platform.

## A case study and the hard parts

He walks through a case study at a large US health insurer, where portal outages and claim delays were addressed with distributed tracing across more than 200 services and real-time dashboards on the claims pipelines, cutting time to resolution and processing time.

The challenges section is candid: protected health data must stay protected inside the telemetry, storing logs and traces costs money and needs retention policies, legacy systems were not built to be observed, and teams need training. His advice is to pace yourself: pilot one critical service such as claims, eligibility or the member portal, prove value, then scale. QA, operations, security and product all have to own it together.

## Who should watch

QA leads and test architects in healthcare or any regulated domain who want to make the case for observability inside the QA function. It is a strategy talk, light on tooling, heavy on the domain.

Title: Teach the browser to guess your next click, then prefetch it
Description: Alexandru Hang of ING Tech Romania at Conf42 Observability 2025 on training a TensorFlow.js model on activity logs to predict and prefetch the next page.
Body:
Your activity logs already know where most users go after the home page. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Alexandru Hang, a software engineer at ING Tech Romania, showed how to turn that history into a small neural network that predicts a user's next page and lets the app fetch its data before the click lands.

It is an observability talk with an unusual angle: the logs are not there to explain an outage after the fact, they are training data for making the app feel faster in the moment.

## The problem: pages that load a lot of stuff

Web apps keep getting heavier, and each page pulls in more assets and API calls. Alexandru's goal is twofold: give the user an instant page, and give the server a heads-up about the load that is coming. If you know the user is about to open messages, you can request that data while the app is idle, and the click finds everything already in memory.

He considers the boring option first, and it is a fair one. A statistical approach would tell you that a large share of users go from home to the newsfeed and then to messages. That works, but it is the same guess for everyone. He wants a per-user prediction, which is where the neural network comes in.

## A machine learning primer for software engineers

The first half is a gentle tour aimed at people who are "not AI engineers", in his words. He walks through linear regression (good for extrapolating a trend, wrong for picking a next action), decision trees and random forests (classification), and then neural networks, which he picks because they adapt to patterns and can even mimic the simpler models. He demonstrates that last point by having a small network approximate a linear function from a handful of points.

The cats-versus-dogs example carries the explanation of training and testing: feed labelled data, hold some back, and measure accuracy. If 80 of 100 test images come back right, the accuracy is 80%, and you either ship or go back to training. Senior ML folks can skip ahead; everyone else gets a clear mental model in a few minutes.

## TensorFlow.js moves the guessing to the client

The tool choice is the interesting design call. Alexandru uses TensorFlow, and specifically TensorFlow.js, so the model can run in the browser. Since the prediction is per user anyway, running it on the user's own device keeps that work off the server. He also notes you can start from a pre-trained model (for example from Hugging Face), retrain one for a more specific case, or build your own when neither fits.

## The model is small and readable

The code walkthrough is short:

- **Encode the pages.** Neural networks do not take strings, so each page (home, newsfeed, messages, shop) gets a number and becomes a one-hot vector, the shape TensorFlow expects.
- **Define a sequential model.** Two dense layers: a ReLU hidden layer and a softmax output layer that turns the result into a choice of next page.
- **Train with `model.fit`.** The activity log is the input, the following page is the label, with 100 epochs and a chosen batch size.
- **Predict with `model.predict`.** Pass the current history, get the likely next page, and prefetch its assets.

For the demo the activity log is an in-memory array, which keeps the network out of the picture. He points to the full source on GitHub for the whole loop. The same predictions, he adds, can feed anomaly detection on user flows or forecasts of server workload.

## Who should watch

Frontend and full-stack engineers who have never trained a model and want a first, concrete use for one in their own app. It is an intro, and it says so. If you already run recommendation models in production, the primer will feel slow, but the prefetch framing might still give you an idea for your access logs.

- [Anton Kalik on AI meeting Node.js](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Anton_Kalik_ai_nodejs_custom_sports_activity) (JavaScript 2023), another JavaScript-first take on putting a model in your app.

Title: Most of your logs are never read, and you pay for them twice
Description: Venkata Madhu Prateek Reddy Kambala of Synapsis at Conf42 Observability 2025 on cutting logging bills with sampling, filtering, tiered storage and compression.
Body:
Cloud vendors charge you once to ingest a log line and again to keep it, and most of those lines are never queried. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Venkata Madhu Prateek Reddy Kambala, a senior DevOps engineer at Synapsis, laid out four ways to shrink a logging bill without losing the logs you need at 3am: sampling, filtering, tiered storage and cheaper tooling.

The talk leans on public engineering write-ups from Uber, Slack, Shopify and Razorpay, so it reads as a field guide to what other teams already tried.

## Why the bill keeps growing

Venkata names the usual suspects. Microservices multiplied the number of log streams. Pricing hits both ingestion and storage, so every line is charged twice. Debug logging gets left on in production, where it generates huge volume that almost nobody reads. And without governance, nobody decides what should be collected in the first place. He cites research that only about 30% of generated logs are ever used for queries or monitoring; the rest just sits in storage.

## Sample debug, never sample errors

The first strategy is sampling. He describes Uber keeping only 5% of its debug logs, and walks through three approaches: head-based (decide at the source), tail-based (decide after the trace completes) and level-based (different rates per log level). The rule he repeats is the one worth remembering: never sample error or fatal logs. Start debug and info sampling around 10% and tune from there, and keep the sampling consistent across service boundaries.

To avoid sampling bias hiding a rare event, he suggests trace-aware sampling and a safety switch: when an alert fires, stop sampling so the incident gets full fidelity.

## Drop the noise at ingestion

Filtering removes logs that carry no value at all. His example is Slack dropping health check logs with Fluent Bit. The common noise list is familiar: health and ping endpoints, repeated non-critical connection timeouts, every successful authentication, chatty service-to-service calls. Filtering at the ingestion layer saves twice, because the line is never ingested and never stored.

## Hot, warm, cold

Storage tiering matches retention to how often data is read: roughly the last seven days in Elasticsearch for fast queries, seven to 30 days in standard S3, and anything older in Glacier for compliance. He flags the catch honestly: querying cold storage is slow and painful, so design queries to stay on hot and warm data, and build rehydration workflows for the rare deep look back.

## Tooling and compression

The fourth lever is moving to open-source stacks such as Grafana Loki, with the trade-off spelled out: you swap a vendor bill for the cost of people who can run the system. The case study that gets the most airtime is Uber's CLP (Compressed Log Processor), which compressed huge volumes of Spark job logs while still allowing queries without decompressing them.

Structured JSON logging runs through all of it. It makes filtering precise, compresses better and makes queries faster, so it is the cheapest change on the list.

## A roadmap, with baselines first

Venkata closes with a plan: audit volumes, find the five to ten streams that generate most of the data, put cost dashboards in place, then roll out filtering and sampling, then tiering, then longer-term moves like compression and log-based metrics. Track financial, operational and volume metrics, and set the baseline before you change anything, or you will never know what worked.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams who just got the observability invoice and need a structured list of options to bring to a FinOps review. If you already sample and tier, the case studies are still useful ammunition.

Title: Quantum personalisation in banking starts with a customer data platform
Description: JPMorganChase's Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on the data engineering under quantum-enhanced, real-time financial personalisation.
Body:
Before any qubit touches a bank's recommendation engine, someone has to resolve which of five customer records is the same person. Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu, Vice President and Senior Lead Data Engineer at JPMorganChase, made that the spine of his talk at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on quantum AI-driven personalisation in financial services. The quantum layer sits on top; the customer data platform underneath does most of the work.

## Personalisation as a requirement, not a feature

Boggavarapu's opening argument is commercial: customers expect a bank to anticipate their goals, not just answer their questions. He cites machine learning approaches such as XGBoost and neural networks beating traditional segmentation, and a reference architecture with API-driven microservices serving 15-plus touchpoints in under 200 milliseconds, event processing at more than 50,000 transactions per second and a data lake of five petabytes or more. Those are the targets the rest of the talk designs for.

## The CDP is the central nervous system

The most practical section is the customer data platform. In his telling, a CDP does four jobs:

- **Aggregation**: structured and unstructured data from digital and physical touchpoints, through APIs and ETL.
- **A unified view**: a 360-degree profile built with entity resolution, persistent identifiers and cross-channel attribution.
- **Actionable insight**: recommendations and predictive scoring on top of that profile.
- **Compliance by design**: granular consent management, automated governance workflows and encryption, so GDPR and CCPA are built in, not bolted on.

He calls the CDP the central nervous system for customer data, and every later slide depends on it.

## Where the quantum part comes in

The quantum layer is pitched as pattern recognition across many variables at once. The talk describes a tensor-network architecture analysing hundreds of financial variables simultaneously, quantum annealing for portfolio optimisation and quantum-accelerated gradient descent for faster training. These are presented as capabilities rather than shown in a demo, so this is the part to watch critically.

Generative AI gets equal billing: tailored financial education content, chatbots built on retrieval-augmented generation over a financial knowledge base, and synthetic data generated with differential privacy so models can train without exposing personal data.

## The data engineering problems are the real ones

The section engineers will get the most from is the list of hard problems, all classical:

- **Latency**: memory-mapped databases with non-blocking IO, edge computing and predictive caching.
- **Volume**: auto-scaling microservices on Kubernetes, polyglot storage, stream processing.
- **Security**: post-quantum cryptographic algorithms, zero-knowledge proofs for identity checks and homomorphic encryption.
- **Governance**: graph-based metadata for automated lineage, attribute-based access control and immutable audit trails.

His roadmap is equally grounded: assess the existing data architecture, deploy the CDP and secure API connections, pilot with selected customer segments, then scale across products and channels. If your bank does only the first three steps, you still end up with a better platform, quantum or not.

The talk closes with outcome figures (engagement, conversion and satisfaction gains) presented as results of effective implementations; it doesn't detail the deployments behind them.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects at financial institutions planning real-time personalisation, and anyone who wants to see where quantum might plug into an existing data stack. If you came for quantum circuits, this isn't that talk; if you came for how a bank structures customer data, it is.

Title: AI clusters need networks that observe and heal themselves
Description: Bhaskararao Vakamullu at Conf42 Observability 2025 traces network observability from ARPANET to streaming telemetry and self-healing AI networks.
Body:
When a single switch moves 51.2 Tbps and ports run at 800G, polling SNMP every few minutes is like checking a Formula 1 car with a sundial. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Bhaskararao Vakamullu, an Anna University graduate who has worked at networking and observability companies, made the case that AI workloads have turned the network into the critical path, and that the network now has to observe and repair itself in real time.

## Sixty years of watching packets

The first section is a history lesson, and a good one for anyone who started with Datadog. In the 1960s ARPANET, the packet-switching research network that became the internet, had rudimentary tools: interface message processor consoles, a network control centre, ping-like utilities. From the 1980s to 2000, SNMP became the standard for performance and health metrics. Then came agent-based monitoring on VMs and containers, SaaS dashboards from New Relic, Datadog and Stackdriver, threshold and anomaly alerts in CloudWatch, and integrations with PagerDuty, Slack and CI/CD. Today's stack adds Grafana, Prometheus and Loki, OpenTelemetry as the open standard, Dynatrace, ML monitoring tools for drift and explainability, and native tooling from AWS, GCP and Azure.

## Why AI raises the stakes

Bhaskararao lists four reasons network observability matters more for AI: performance guarantees that hold under real workloads, failure domain isolation so a fault in ingestion, training or inference does not cascade, resource optimisation across expensive compute, and security, since AI systems are attractive targets for data breaches and model theft.

The hardware numbers explain the urgency. Ports that were a revolution at 100G are now built at 800G; a single networking box processes 51.2 Tbps. Training and inference need ultra-low latency to stay synchronised and near-perfect availability, because an interrupted training run is expensive.

## Streaming telemetry replaces polling

The shift he calls the programmable telemetry revolution is the practical core. Traditional monitoring collects predefined metrics such as CPU, memory, disk and traffic, mostly through periodic checks and thresholds. That works for basic health but lacks the context distributed AI systems need. Modern telemetry, with gRPC streaming as his example, continuously pushes high-resolution metrics, logs, events and traces from every layer, and feeds analytics and ML that can predict problems before users see them.

## Detect, analyse, decide, execute

The self-healing architecture is a closed loop. Real-time telemetry detects faults, degradations and threats. Analysis correlates metrics, logs and traces across components with ML to find the root cause. The decide phase weighs policy rules and historical incidents to pick a remediation: isolate a component, fail over, change a configuration. Execution then runs it automatically through playbooks and orchestration tools: reroute traffic, restart services, scale resources. The goal is a network that does not wait for a human at 3 AM.

## Still hard: opaque hardware and sheer scale

He is honest that visibility gaps remain. GPUs, TPUs and accelerators from different vendors follow different protocols, so hardware is often a black box. Correlating user behaviour, system logs and network metrics across domains is difficult. And AI systems generate so much telemetry that collecting and processing it without adding latency requires sampling and aggregation.

The future section points at chip-level telemetry (power, temperature, clock speed, cache misses), AI-powered analysis, digital twin networks for testing changes safely, and intent-based observability. His example of intent is the best line in the talk: instead of asking how the CPU is doing, ask whether important users in the EU region are getting 4K quality, and act on that.

## Who should watch

Network and infrastructure engineers moving into AI clusters, and SREs who want the history of their tools in one place. This is a broad survey, heavy on definitions and history, with no demos; watch it for the big picture and the intent-based framing.

Title: Stop passing CAD files around and start streaming design events
Description: Pradeep Karanam at Conf42 Observability 2025 on replacing ECAD and MCAD file snapshots with Kafka events so design conflicts surface in minutes.
Body:
Hardware teams still collaborate the way software teams did before CI: electrical and mechanical engineers exchange files at gated milestones and find conflicts weeks later. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Pradeep Karanam, a solutions architect at Facebook, showed how an event-driven observability layer between ECAD and MCAD tools makes cross-domain changes visible in real time. In his pilots, revision lead time dropped from seven days to three.

## Three millimetres, six weeks

The story that frames the talk: mid-program, the mechanical team moves a chassis rib by three millimetres. The ECAD side keeps routing the board, unaware. A week later the conflict surfaces, and the team is staring at a costly respin and a six-week slip. The root cause is not bad tools, Pradeep argues; the information arrived too late to matter.

He backs this with the wider pattern: a study across eight boards found more than ten file snapshots per spin, each one a possible reroute, and industry data puts late rework at an 8 to 10% cost increase and four to six weeks of schedule. Engineers end up doing forensics on which file version changed which part, instead of design.

## Why events instead of files

Events are push-based: a tool emits a lightweight message the moment something meaningful happens. They are context-rich, carrying geometry hashes, user IDs and variant tags. They allow automatic downstream checks. And they flow through a broker that tolerates outages: if the MCAD side is down, ECAD keeps publishing and the broker replays when it returns. Decisions that waited for the next milestone now happen in minutes.

## Three building blocks

- **A shared schema**: every ECAD change and MCAD update follows one contract with item ID, revision ID, geometry hash, user and timestamp, plus optional blocks for BOM variants. Tools validate events locally, so malformed ones never leave the workstation.
- **Audit logging**: every event also lands in an immutable store recording who changed what and when, exportable to CSV for compliance reviews in regulated domains like medical and automotive hardware.
- **Library sync**: exports and multi-revision check-ins keep symbols and footprints aligned across tools such as OrCAD, Allegro and NX, and the sync status becomes another event so stale footprints get caught before they reach a schematic.

Two cross-cutting enablers sit on top. A taxonomy separates geometry events (board outline, keep-outs, mounting holes), component events (placement moves, part swaps) and analysis events (DFM or thermal results); simple heuristics there cut irrelevant chatter by 54%. And resilience: back pressure and replay, compensating transactions for partial writes, a checksum verifier for corrupt payloads, and a circuit breaker around flaky PLM APIs.

## The pipeline end to end

ECAD and MCAD publish to a Kafka broker. A stream processor compares geometry deltas and BOM differences, and violations go to dashboards and chat channels, while the audit store keeps everything. Pradeep stresses that every component is off the shelf. The keep-out example shows the loop: MCAD publishes an update adding a rib, the processor compares geometry hashes, the rule engine flags a keep-out breach, and both teams get an alert with a 3D overlay within a minute.

Pilot results: revision lead time from seven days to three, part number approvals from four days to a day and a half, and board spins from three to two. The pipeline watches itself too, with Grafana tracking event volume and broker lag and Kibana for inspecting payloads.

## Start small

The rollout runs in four phases, starting with low-noise BOM and outline events and ending with suppliers and manufacturing on the same streams. The advice is hard-won: too many events too soon erodes trust, version the schema because silent field changes break integrations fastest, align ECAD and MCAD naming on day one, and watch broker lag early.

## Who should watch

Hardware and PLM engineers, and software engineers who like seeing event-driven patterns applied outside their usual habitat. It is a fast, dense talk; the architecture is generic enough to reuse anywhere two teams share an artefact through file drops.

Title: Hybrid quantum-classical edge AI, with the numbers on the slides
Description: Anushree Nagvekar of AEye shows a hybrid quantum-classical split for edge AI at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, with latency, power and capacity figures.
Body:
Give the quantum side the optimisation and leave the IO and control loops to classical hardware. That is the split Anushree Nagvekar, Manager Software Engineering at AEye, argued for at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, in a short, number-dense talk on hybrid quantum-classical processing for edge AI. Her headline claim: neural networks with 3.2x more parameters while staying under 15 milliseconds of latency, against a classical-only ceiling of 1.4x.

## The edge is running out of headroom

The setup is familiar to anyone shipping embedded ML. Nagvekar cites a projection of 75 billion IoT devices by 2027, and data at the edge getting heavier: high-resolution video, medical scans, autonomous vehicle telemetry. Classical edge systems have to trade model complexity against real-time performance, and past a point latency becomes unmanageable. Her framing is that you shouldn't pick a side. The architecture is "not purely classical and not purely quantum", and the division of labour is the interesting part.

## Who does what in the hybrid

The split in the talk is clean enough to sketch on a whiteboard:

- **Quantum**: optimisation-heavy, high-dimensional work such as routing, scheduling and training complex networks.
- **Classical**: deterministic, routine tasks such as IO operations and simple control loops.

The same idea extends to resource allocation. Quantum units optimise across compute, memory, bandwidth and storage, and the talk says they react to changes in under 30 milliseconds, 4.2x faster than classical methods. The pipeline has four steps: detect complex dependencies, explore many configurations in parallel, execute, then predict and adjust as conditions change.

## The numbers, and how to read them

Nagvekar presents a lot of figures: 78% faster optimisation, 67% lower power consumption, latency down to 30 ms from a 120 ms baseline, 41% lower operational cost, and case studies with 82% anomaly detection and 43% fewer false alarms in manufacturing, 91% accuracy in real-time medical imaging with HIPAA compliance maintained, and 37% power savings in smart-infrastructure energy distribution. She says these come from real-world case studies rather than the lab.

The talk doesn't walk through the benchmark setups behind them (hardware, baselines, workloads), so treat them as the claims to go verify, not as a spec sheet. The architecture holds up without them.

On security, the hybrid stack uses lattice-based key exchange, tamper-evident signatures and multivariate polynomial encryption, the post-quantum families that run on ordinary chips, which is the right choice for a device with a battery.

## The roadmap starts on classical hardware

The most useful slide for a team that wants to try this is the rollout plan. Review the current infrastructure and find tasks worth optimising. Then test quantum-inspired algorithms on classical hardware and validate the boost before any real quantum integration. Only then move to hybrid workflows, tune task delegation and data flows, and scale with monitoring feedback loops. It is a gradual, low-risk path, and the classical-first step means you learn something even if the quantum part never pays off.

Future directions in the talk: domain-specific quantum hardware for edge devices, a quantum cloud at the edge, and quantum neural networks.

## Who should watch

Embedded and edge ML engineers who keep bumping into the latency-versus-model-size wall, and architects building industrial, automotive or smart-city systems. It is a quick talk, so it suits a lunch break; budget extra time for checking the numbers.

Title: Privacy observability means answering who touched this data, and why
Description: Krishna Ganeriwal of Meta at Conf42 Observability 2025 on lineage, consent propagation and audit trails for privacy infrastructure at hyperscale.
Body:
In most systems observability answers "is it up and is it fast?". In privacy infrastructure it has to answer something harder: who touched this user's data, why, and were they allowed to? At Conf42 Observability 2025, Krishna Ganeriwal, an engineer on Meta's ads privacy infrastructure team, explained why that question makes observability foundational to privacy-aware systems at hyperscale, and which architectural patterns make it answerable.

## A black box recorder for every interaction

Krishna defines privacy observability as the ability to reconstruct a privacy black box recording for every interaction with user data. The stakes are regulatory, with GDPR, CCPA and India's DPDP in play and fines that can reach 4% of global revenue, but he argues trust matters more than fines. Users stop using services that cannot tell them what happened to their data.

## Five questions you need to answer daily

The use cases he walks through are the heart of the talk:

- **Data lineage**: where user data was generated, who processed it, whether it was shared externally.
- **Consent propagation**: when a user revokes consent in one UI, every system must respond, in real time. His example: a user who allowed location for personalised ads and later turns it off. Wherever that location data fed models or training, it has to be wiped. One lagging cache is enough for a compliance failure.
- **Purpose limitation**: data collected for personalisation must not quietly feed targeting or model training without explicit consent.
- **Anomaly detection**: a login from a new location or a sudden access to full history; is that expected, or a policy mismatch?
- **Policy drift**: over time, does enforcement silently bypass updated constraints?

None of these can be answered from uptime dashboards.

## Speed, scale and secrecy at once

The design challenges stack up. Volume means billions of log events a day and petabytes of data. Speed means sub-second processing, because the services behind it are real-time. Granularity means tracking per user, sometimes per impression, since every user's privacy settings differ. And security: the observability data itself describes how users interacted with the system, so it must never leak personally identifiable information. Krishna's summary is that you have to design for speed, scale and security simultaneously.

## Four patterns from production

The architecture section names patterns he says privacy teams across big tech run in production:

1. **Event-driven lineage**: Kafka or another pub-sub system tracks data flows as they happen.
2. **Consent-aware tagging**: each payload is tagged with the purposes and scopes allowed to consume it, so location data can be marked as off limits to ads systems but usable elsewhere.
3. **Embedded policy engines**: runtime guards check that every access matches consent.
4. **Cryptographic audit trails**: Merkle trees or blockchain-style structures for immutable, verifiable logs.

At Meta, lineage systems track data across thousands of internal sources, consent status travels with the data, and policy engines enforce compliance along the way. Auditors, legal and engineering use the same real-time views of how data moves. Krishna reports a 40 to 50% reduction in audit prep time across several internal teams where this was applied well.

## What it buys and what is still open

Beyond faster audits and lower fine risk, he lists two benefits engineers will appreciate: developers can finally see how their own systems handle data, and only compliant data reaches downstream ML models. The open problems are just as interesting. Can ML detect privacy anomalies in real time? Can a system be observed and enforce policy at once? And should policy observability get a standard, the way OpenTelemetry standardised traces? Right now there is none. His closing line works as a slogan: "If you can't see it, you can't enforce it."

## Who should watch

Engineers building data platforms that touch personal data, and anyone who has had to answer a data subject access request by hand. It is an architecture talk without code, but the use-case list makes a good checklist for your own system.

Title: RAG support bots should know when they do not know
Description: Vaibhav Fanindra Mahajan at Conf42 Observability 2025 on RAG for customer support, with confidence thresholds, fresh indexes and clean human handoffs.
Body:
A support bot that guesses is worse than no bot at all. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Vaibhav Fanindra Mahajan walked through how retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves on classic support chatbots, and the feature that matters most for trust: a RAG system can score its own confidence from retrieval results and escalate or ask a clarifying question instead of making something up.

## Why the old bots break

Vaibhav starts with the problems of traditional chatbots, including the ones with intent classification and basic NLP. They rely on rule-based flows that break on edge cases, they are trained on a snapshot of data that goes stale quickly, and their session state is brittle, so multi-turn context is weak. Every policy change means a manual knowledge update, unusual questions fall through the dialogue tree, and when the model does not know, it tends to guess.

## Retrieval first, generation second

RAG puts retrieval before the answer. The query is embedded with BERT or sentence transformers, matched against a vector store such as FAISS, Pinecone or Weaviate to fetch the top-k passages, and those passages go into the prompt, so the output is grounded in current enterprise knowledge instead of the model's memory.

For multi-part questions, which linear dialogue flows handle badly, the input is split into smaller sub-questions, each is retrieved separately, possibly from different knowledge clusters, and the snippets are fused through concatenation or a fusion-in-decoder layer before one combined answer is generated.

## Confidence is the observable part

The section that fits the conference theme is about knowing when to stop. RAG systems can estimate confidence from retrieval scores and response entropy. Set a threshold, and below it the bot asks a clarifying question or escalates. If no relevant documents come back for, say, an outage question, it returns a fallback or an explicit uncertainty signal rather than a confident invention. Those scores are also exactly what you want on a dashboard.

Session-level memory, using embeddings or key-value stores, tracks intent and previous turns. When a human does take over, the bot hands over a package: conversation history, retrieved documents and generated responses, with the intent chain. The agent does not have to ask the customer to repeat everything, which Vaibhav ties to lower handling time and better first-contact resolution.

## Keep the index fresh, and clean

A RAG bot is only as current as its index, so he describes a continuous update pipeline. When a policy document or support article changes in Confluence or a CMS, it is queued, re-embedded by a background job with a model such as BGE or MiniLM, and the vector index is updated. The next query sees the new content the same day, with no fine-tuning.

He is blunt that this is garbage in, garbage out. Remove duplicates and near-duplicates, reconcile conflicting entries that confuse retrieval, organise the knowledge base with a clear taxonomy and tag everything with metadata for filtering. And keep an access-control and query-filtering layer after retrieval so unauthorised data never reaches a customer.

## Where it goes next

The future section includes per-customer index segments for personalised support, multilingual answers drawn from the same knowledge base, and multimodal RAG with vision encoders such as CLIP and BLIP-2, so a photo of a damaged product or an error screenshot can be matched against visual knowledge. His team is also working on feeding usage logs to the bot to spot anomalies and surface help before an outage hits. He closes with a comparison of first-contact resolution, around 75 to 85% with RAG against 45 to 55% for traditional bots.

## Who should watch

Teams building or buying an AI support assistant who want a clear architecture walkthrough. The observability angle is lighter than the title suggests, centred on confidence scores and knowledge freshness rather than tracing, and the talk is conceptual rather than a demo.

Title: Wave turned ten years of manual instrumentation into a config file
Description: Jean-Mark Wright of Wave at Conf42 Observability 2025 on CACI, Python metaclasses that capture span attributes from config instead of hand-written code.
Body:
Auto-instrumentation gets you the databases, caches and HTTP calls. The attributes that actually explain your business logic, which plan, which feature group, which customer, have to be added by hand, and at Wave that hand-work added up to about ten years. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Jean-Mark Wright, staff engineer leading observability at Wave, showed how his team replaced most of it with configuration and Python metaclasses. They call it Config-Accelerated Custom Instrumentation, or CACI.

## The 15-minute fix that started it

The talk opens with an incident. An on-call engineer noticed that Wave was giving away Transaction Import, a premium feature that lets small businesses pull bank transactions into the accounting product, to users on the free starter plan.

The service involved had excellent manual instrumentation in Datadog, so the team could interrogate traces directly. Were users being put on the right plan? Graphing traces by plan said yes, the starter plan. Opening a single trace showed a span attribute nobody had thought about: the feature group was the legacy one. Plans point to feature groups, and the starter plan was pointing to the legacy group, which includes Transaction Import. Graphing feature group over time showed exactly when it started. It was data corruption in the database. Jean-Mark says they found it within 12 minutes and had the leak fixed in 15.

## The bad news: one service like that, 40 without

That service had taken roughly three months of engineering effort to instrument this well over its year and a half of development. Wave has about 40 other microservices. Three months times 40 is 120 months, hence the title. Parallelising helps, but it would still take years.

## Instrument the data, not the call sites

CACI starts from two observations. First, requests flow through a predictable stack of components: API, then service with business logic, then repositories for persistence. Second, data passes between them as arguments: business ID, user ID, country, business name. If engineers can say which data they care about, a framework can wrap every component and capture it wherever it appears.

So engineers write a telemetry capture configuration with allowed and disallowed field names and field types, with support for data classes and dictionaries. They do not have to know which component handles which field.

## Metaclasses do the wrapping

The implementation uses a Python metaclass, a class that creates classes. When a component declares the service metaclass, the metaclass loops over its methods, replaces each with a wrapper that inspects the inputs, captures any that match the configuration as span attributes, and then calls the original function. Application code stays untouched. Because the result is a little magical, they also generate a coverage report listing every component, method and input with a tick for whether it is captured.

## What the pilot showed

On a new microservice, CACI took instrumentation coverage from 1% to about 60%, and getting the configuration in place took less than a week instead of months. The captured fields show up in traces, logs and errors alike, so the team can break errors down by event type or latency by Kafka topic, the same kind of slicing that solved the premium leak.

Next on the list: a component-agnostic metaclass beyond services, capturing outputs as well as inputs, using LLMs to speed up rollout across the fleet, and Datadog's dd-trace support for propagating attributes between spans.

## Who should watch

Python teams with good auto-instrumentation and poor answers to the question of which customers are affected. This is one of the most concrete talks of the event: a real incident, a clear design and code you can picture writing. If your stack is not Python, the idea of declaring data of interest once and capturing it at component boundaries still transfers.

Title: A first eBPF program for observability, in C and in Python
Description: Sooter Saalu of Draft.dev at Conf42 Observability 2025 introduces custom eBPF programs with two demos, packet counting in C and file tracing with BCC.
Body:
eBPF lets you run your own sandboxed code inside the Linux kernel without patching the kernel or loading a risky module, which is exactly why every observability vendor now ships something built on it. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Sooter Saalu, technical writer at Draft.dev, gave a compact introduction to writing custom eBPF programs, with two demos that show the round trip from kernel hook to a number you can graph.

## How a program gets into the kernel

Sooter starts with the pipeline every eBPF program goes through. You write the program, usually in C, compile it to bytecode, and hand it to the loader. Before it runs, the verifier checks it: no unbounded loops, no out-of-bounds memory access, nothing that could crash or compromise the kernel. Once accepted, it is compiled to machine code and attached to a hook, an event or a system call.

That path explains the three benefits he lists for observability: kernel-level visibility, often before any user-space application sees the event; no code changes to the applications you are watching; and low overhead, because what runs is native machine code next to the operations it observes.

## Demo one: counting packets in C

The first demo runs on a small AWS instance. A C program parses packet information from incoming traffic and writes it into BPF maps, one for packet counters and one for packet events, recording things like packet size. After compiling and loading it onto a network interface, Sooter sends traffic and shows the maps filling up.

The key concept is the map itself. It lives in kernel space but is readable from user space, so a user-space process can export its contents to Prometheus and Grafana. Kernel collects, user space ships.

## Demo two: tracing file access with BCC

The second demo trades C for Python using BCC. The Python script embeds the eBPF logic, and BCC compiles, loads and attaches it at runtime, with no manual load step. The target is an Nginx web server with a few HTML files; a load test sends a hundred requests across the pages and the program reports each file access as it happens.

What you do with those events is up to you: custom metrics, logs, or a direct feed into your analysis tools. Sooter's point is that eBPF gives you the access, and the logic is yours.

He is honest about the trade-off. Higher-level options, such as the Python, Go and Rust libraries, BCC and the Cilium libraries, make programs much easier to write but cost something in performance: slower execution and a larger footprint than native C.

## You probably do not have to write it all yourself

The last section maps the ecosystem built on eBPF: Pixie for Kubernetes observability without manual instrumentation, Parca and Pyroscope for continuous profiling, DeepFlow for automated tracing, Cilium for Kubernetes networking, plus eBPF-based tooling from OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Grafana. There are also tools for managing and loading programs. Sooter points to write-ups of how companies such as Netflix and Apple use eBPF, and the demo code is on GitHub.

## Who should watch

This is an intro, and a good first talk on eBPF if you know what a syscall is but have never written a kernel program. It is short and demo-driven. If you already run Cilium or Pixie in production, skip to the related talks below for more depth.
