Title: IoT devices outlive RSA, so quantum-safe security starts now
Description: Gayathri Jeganmohan of Microsoft maps quantum computing onto IoT intelligence and security at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, from QKD to quantum signatures.
Body:
A satellite or a medical implant shipped today may still be talking to the network when a quantum computer can read its traffic. That is the sharpest thread in Gayathri Jeganmohan's talk at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, where the Microsoft software engineer split the quantum-meets-IoT story into two halves: what quantum computing can do for IoT intelligence, and what it does to (and for) IoT security.

It's a survey talk, broad rather than deep, and a good map for anyone who owns a fleet of connected devices and keeps hearing the word "quantum" in vendor decks.

## IoT has a data problem before it has a quantum problem

Jeganmohan's starting point is that IoT data is huge, unstructured and noisy: temperature, pressure and a dozen other sensor streams per factory, every second. Her claim is that quantum algorithms can find patterns in that kind of high-dimensional data more efficiently than classical ones, and she walks through where that is being tried:

- **Traffic analytics**: Volkswagen using a quantum algorithm to spot dense traffic areas and optimise urban flow.
- **Anomaly detection**: Cambridge Quantum's tooling for spotting unusual patterns in network traffic.
- **Recommendations**: research at Netflix and Amazon into quantum-inspired collaborative filtering.
- **Fraud**: quantum Monte Carlo methods, with Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan investing.
- **Genomics**: D-Wave working with healthcare startups on DNA analysis workflows.

## Keep the edge small, put the heavy model somewhere else

The machine learning section has the most architectural meat. Edge devices have limited power and energy, so today they lean on the cloud for inference and post-processing. Jeganmohan's picture is a backend where quantum resources handle training (quantum support vector machines and quantum kernel estimation get named) and fast inference, with results offloaded back to the device for real-time decisions. Her target use case is predictive maintenance in factories, plus quantum sensors fusing multiple signals for smart cities, agriculture and autonomous vehicles.

## Four security techniques, one deadline

Security is where the talk gets concrete. RSA and ECC, which today's classical machines can't break, become vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a large enough quantum computer, and IoT was never designed with security in mind to begin with. Jeganmohan lists four responses:

1. **Defence against quantum attacks**: quantum-safe protocols, most urgent for long-lifecycle devices such as vehicles, medical implants and satellites.
2. **Quantum key distribution**: key exchange built on quantum mechanics that detects eavesdropping, with secure links between autonomous vehicles and roadside units as the example.
3. **Quantum random number generation**: truly random keys for secure session start-up on industrial sensors, instead of the pseudo-random output of a `rand` call.
4. **Tamper-proof identity**: quantum signatures, so only authenticated, quantum-signed devices can send actuation signals to critical infrastructure.

One thing worth keeping straight while you watch: post-quantum cryptography runs on ordinary classical chips, while QKD and QRNG need quantum hardware in the loop. For a constrained sensor, that difference decides what you can ship this decade. The talk's first point, protecting long-lived devices against future attacks, is the one you can act on with today's hardware.

## Who should watch

IoT architects, embedded security people and product owners with devices in the field for ten years or more. It is an overview, so expect breadth: if you want protocol detail on QKD, use this as the map and find the specialist talk next.

Title: Measure multi-cloud data integration by risk avoided, not only cost
Description: Ravi Kumar Amaresam of Minisoft Technologies at Conf42 Observability 2025 on unifying multi-cloud data and measuring the ROI in five categories.
Body:
Ask a finance team to justify a cross-cloud data project and they will look at the cost line first. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Ravi Kumar Amaresam, senior lead software engineer at Minisoft Technologies (previously IBM and TCS), argued that cost is usually not where the biggest return sits. In his ROI framework, the largest payoff from unifying data across clouds tends to come from risk mitigation, through better security and compliance, with customer experience close behind.

## The problem: data spread over AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and the basement

Ravi starts where most enterprises are: several cloud providers, plus some on-premises systems, with data scattered across all of them. Multi-cloud brings real benefits, such as avoiding lock-in, choosing the best cloud per workload and resilience, but he cites a figure that 42% of organisations face significant cross-cloud data barriers. The result is duplicated data, slow pipelines and no single view of anything.

## A three-layer integration framework

The core of the talk is the framework his team uses:

- **Standardised connectors**: pre-built and custom API integrations that act, in his words, as universal translators between platforms.
- **Adaptive security**: automated compliance checks and threat detection that keep up as requirements change.
- **Intelligent orchestration**: workflows tuned automatically from real-time performance metrics and business needs.

Security runs through it. Data is classified by sensitivity automatically and encrypted at rest and in transit across every cloud boundary, zero trust secures the touch points, and AI-based anomaly detection monitors continuously with real-time alerts. Compliance is centralised as policy definitions that get translated into cloud-specific controls, enforced continuously, and reported with evidence ready for auditors.

For speed, Ravi describes event-driven workflows that automate routine responses, and an 81% decrease in data transfer time through optimised traffic routing and smart caching.

## The case study

The anchor example is a global financial institution operating in 43 countries, with data across six clouds and therefore no unified customer view. The fix was a cross-cloud data fabric with AI-driven integration, producing a unified customer data platform with real-time analytics. Ravi reports a 421% ROI in the first year, mainly from fraud prevention, operational efficiency and customer retention, and fraud detection 92% faster.

He also gives sector results: in healthcare, faster patient data retrieval and unified records for care coordination; in financial services, faster fraud detection; in government, better data sharing between agencies. The figures come from his firm's deployments and are not broken down further in the talk.

## ROI in five columns

The measurement framework is the part to take away. Instead of a single savings number, track five categories: cost reduction, operational efficiency, decision velocity, risk mitigation and customer experience. A project that barely moves the cloud bill but halves the time to spot fraud is a good project, and this framing lets you show it. Happy customers who stay longer count too.

## Phase it

The roadmap has three phases: assessment and strategy (cloud inventory, data flow analysis, ROI targets), foundation building (data fabric, security controls, governance), then gradual expansion to more workloads and clouds. He calls it a journey, not a destination, which is the honest description of any integration project.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leads building the business case for a data integration or data fabric project. It is a strategy-level talk presenting Ravi's own framework, light on implementation detail, so watch it for the ROI model and the case study rather than for how to wire the connectors.

Title: Your dashboards are lying, and your pipeline tests are why
Description: Chaitanya Reddy Krishnama of MoneyGram at Conf42 Observability 2025 on fixing silent pipeline failures and schema drift with data observability.
Body:
The worst dashboard is not the broken one; it is the one that looks polished and is quietly wrong. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Chaitanya Reddy Krishnama of MoneyGram told the story of how silent pipeline failures and schema drift corrupted his team's analytics, and how they fixed it by treating data pipelines like production software: instrumented, tested continuously and on call.

## How a dashboard learns to lie

The failure modes will be familiar to anyone who has owned a warehouse:

- **Silent pipeline failures**: jobs that failed or only partly succeeded without loud errors, so some records simply never loaded.
- **Schema drift**: an upstream column renamed or a format changed, pipelines kept running, and key fields misaligned without a single alert.
- **Brittle validations**: the few quality rules that existed broke whenever volume spiked or new fields appeared.
- **Thin coverage**: a couple of critical tables tested, hundreds not.

Detection came from stakeholders, typically the Monday 8 AM Slack message about broken data. Chaitanya sums up the cost in one line: "Once a dashboard tells a lie, every report becomes a suspect." Team morale went with it, as more time went into firefighting than delivering.

## Why the old QA could not keep up

Traditionally, data QA was a checkbox at development time: if the pipeline ran without errors, the data was assumed fine. Tests were static while the data changed every month, and writing even five checks for each of a thousand tables by hand meant thousands of tests to maintain. QA lived before deployment with no feedback loop from production, and the rest was people eyeballing reports.

## The pivot: telemetry on every stage

The turning point was asking why they ran data systems in the dark when nobody would deploy an app without monitoring. The team added logging at each ETL stage, measured row counts and processing times, and traced data flows from source to dashboard. A few principles came with it:

- **Fail fast**: some tests are marked critical, and when they fail the pipeline stops and alerts instead of pushing bad data downstream.
- **Lineage**: a map from source to target, so a bad data set points to its likely upstream cause and to the reports it will affect.
- **Checks as code**: expectations such as no nulls in critical columns or transaction amounts within a sane range, run on every update.
- **Data health monitoring**: freshness, volume, distribution and schema changes, watched around the clock.

The alert example is the kind you can copy straight away: a daily sales table that normally has around 100K rows and today has zero should page someone, and so should an ETL job that has not run by its scheduled time.

## The toolchain

The stack is open source and ordinary in the best sense. Great Expectations runs checkpoints after loads to verify row counts, ranges and null percentages. dbt handles transformations and SQL tests, with tests code-reviewed and versioned like the models. OpenTelemetry instruments custom pipeline code, propagating a trace ID so every event in a pipeline run is linked. Prometheus stores pipeline metrics and Grafana became their pipeline control centre. In BigQuery, the information schema tables help detect schema changes and track bytes processed.

At the end of the chain, dashboards carry an implicit trust score: if it is live, every upstream check passed. If upstream data is stale or under investigation, the report gets an annotation saying so.

## The cultural half

The lessons are as much about people as tools. Trust but verify, at every step. Make observability a team sport across data engineers, QA and analysts. Start with your worst pain point, such as the dashboard that breaks every quarter, and win there first. Treat data incidents like software incidents, with on-call rotations, root cause analysis and a new test after every miss. And celebrate catches, because a prevented bad dashboard is invisible unless someone points at it.

## Who should watch

Analytics engineers, data platform teams and anyone whose stakeholders have stopped trusting the numbers. The talk is practical and tool-specific enough to act on; you could set up a freshness alert and a first Great Expectations suite the same afternoon.

Title: A plain-language tour of Shor, Grover, QAOA and VQE
Description: Sarah Choudhary walks through the four quantum algorithms worth knowing at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, plus where pilots run and where the hype is.
Body:
Four algorithms carry most of the weight in quantum computing today, and you can understand all four without a physics degree. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, Sarah Choudhary, a Principal SME architect and data scientist with two decades in data and AI systems, gave a 30-minute tour of Shor, Grover, QAOA and VQE, then spent just as long on what the hardware still can't do. It is an introduction and it says so up front: the promise is clarity for researchers, cloud architects and the merely curious.

## Classical computers aren't wrong, they're the wrong tool sometimes

Choudhary starts with the von Neumann architecture, the 1940s design that took us from floppies to the cloud, and its limit: nature doesn't compute in ones and zeros. Simulating a molecule with classical logic is, in her words, "trying to paint the ocean with a pencil". Later she offers an even better one: modelling quantum systems on a classical machine is like translating poetry with a calculator.

The argument isn't that quantum replaces anything. She is explicit that a quantum computer will not run your spreadsheet faster or replace your phone's processor. It complements classical machines on a specific class of problems that lean on superposition, entanglement and interference. The talk also tells the 2019 Google Sycamore random circuit sampling story honestly, including IBM's rebuttal that a classical supercomputer could have done it in days rather than millennia.

## The four algorithms, one sentence each

The core of the talk is a compact field guide:

- **Shor (1994)** factors large integers exponentially faster than classical methods, which is why RSA has an expiry date and why post-quantum cryptography is now a national security topic.
- **Grover (1996)** searches unsorted data in square-root time. Her haystack example: a million possibilities in about a thousand steps.
- **QAOA** is a hybrid classical-quantum optimiser aimed at routing, load balancing and portfolio problems, where classical solvers settle into a local minimum.
- **VQE** estimates the ground-state energy of molecules, the route to faster drug and materials design.

She ties each to who is testing it: Roche and AstraZeneca on molecular simulation, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase on portfolio optimisation and Monte Carlo, Volkswagen and DHL on traffic and route planning, ExxonMobil and BASF on catalysts.

## Light might beat the fridge

The section most intros skip is photonic quantum computing. Instead of superconducting circuits cooled near absolute zero, photonic machines encode qubits in particles of light, run at room temperature and reuse fibre-optic components that are already mass-produced. Xanadu's Borealis and PsiQuantum get named, along with the honest catch: generating single photons reliably and building logic gates from light is still less mature than superconducting tech.

She then lines up the four hardware families (superconducting at IBM and Google, trapped ions at IonQ and Honeywell, photonics, and the earlier-stage neutral-atom and topological approaches, Microsoft among them) and admits nobody knows which one wins.

## The hype section is the best part

Choudhary is blunt about the NISQ era. Qubits decohere in microseconds, one reliable logical qubit may need hundreds or thousands of physical ones, and for many real-world problems nobody has yet proven a quantum solution beats classical. She also warns that some companies sell quantum solutions that are not quantum at all. Her timeline: hybrid models common in R&D by about 2028, error-corrected systems after that, and quantum as an API call in the cloud after 2032. Treat the dates as a forecast, not a promise.

The closing advice is practical: you can start now with Qiskit, Cirq, Azure Quantum's Q#, Amazon Braket and PennyLane, most of them free to try in the cloud.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects who need one talk that maps the vocabulary (qubits, interference, NISQ, QAOA) to real problems and real companies. If you already write Qiskit circuits, the history section will be familiar; jump to the hardware comparison and the hype warning.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Quantum inspired algorithms as a means of getting quantum benefit in the NISQ era](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Abhigyan_Mishra_algorithms_quantum_benefit_nisq_era) by Abhigyan Mishra, for what you can run before the hardware matures.
- [High level programming for quantum circuits](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Vincent_van_Wingerden_programming_quantum_circuits) by Vincent van Wingerden, the next step once the algorithms make sense.
- [Quantum computing: is it real or just hype?](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Michal_Jankowski_real_or_hype) by Michal Jankowski, a second opinion on the hype question.

Title: Put cost signals in the same engine as your alerts
Description: Ganeshkumar Palanisamy of Reltio at Conf42 Observability 2025 on merging AIOps and FinOps into one observability platform for multi-cloud data systems.
Body:
Most teams keep the cloud bill in one tool and the pager in another, then wonder why nobody can say which feature made last month expensive. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Ganeshkumar Palanisamy, principal software architect at Reltio, argued for one correlation engine that sees tenant, platform, subsystem, cloud and cost signals together, so AIOps and FinOps stop being separate projects.

## No, you cannot just buy it

Ganeshkumar opens with the multi-cloud bargain: cherry-pick the best of AWS, GCP and Azure, avoid lock-in, and in exchange get fragmented tools, inconsistent metrics and siloed teams. He asks the question every budget holder asks, whether there is a single tool that fixes this, and answers it straight away: no. Observability at this scale is an engine you build, starting with a unified platform that collects metrics, logs and traces consistently across providers and a documented inventory of every cloud resource it covers.

## Smart alerts carry context

The most practical section is on alerting. His example: a latency alert that fires when latency rises 20%. On its own it produces a stream of false positives, because latency also rises while the system is autoscaling, during unusual but legitimate customer load, or while a subsystem hiccups and recovers on its own. Add that context to the rule and the alert fires only when something is going on beyond auto-recovery. Fewer pages, and the ones that remain mean something.

From there the talk stacks three more capabilities:

- **Anomaly detection** that keeps up as new customers bring new usage patterns.
- **Predictive analytics**: at Reltio, data is aggregated every five minutes, and with enough history a model predicts the next five minutes, so you can scale ahead of demand or warn a human when automation cannot fix it.
- **A correlation engine** across multi-tenant signals: per tenant, per platform, per subsystem, per cloud, and then cost.

## FinOps as another signal type

The FinOps half is about joining cost to usage. Once cost data sits next to the operational data, you can see which kind of usage drives which cost, budget from usage and cost trends together, right-size intelligently and attribute spend to the business that caused it. Ganeshkumar reports a 28 to 37% reduction in cloud spend through resource placement and right-sizing, and a 43% drop in underutilised instances. On the operations side he cites incidents detected 67% faster, resolution 51% faster, and teams managing 3.4 times more infrastructure without extra staff.

## Tags are a design decision

The best practices include one worth underlining: standardised tagging across all clouds. His point is that the number of tags matters less than the value each one carries and how consistently it is managed, so everyone can tell what an application is and what it is for. He also wants observability as code, deployed alongside the infrastructure, and part of the design from the first day rather than added after launch.

## Start with the current state, not the ideal one

The action plan is refreshingly unglamorous. Assess what you already have, because most systems already have some observability. Document the tools in use and the baseline you need. Define a target architecture for your own workloads; he explicitly declines to hand out a blueprint because every system differs. Then pick the highest-impact workload first, prove the savings and the scaling gains there, and use that win to fund the next step.

## Who should watch

Platform and data-platform engineers in multi-cloud, multi-tenant setups, and anyone trying to get engineering and finance to read the same dashboard. The talk is strategy with a few concrete examples rather than a tool demo; the alerting and five-minute prediction sections are the parts you can apply next week.

Title: Aircraft digital twins spot failures weeks before they ground a plane
Description: Divakar Duraiyan of Tata Consultancy Services at Conf42 Observability 2025 on digital twins that turn flight telemetry into predictive maintenance.
Body:
A modern aircraft produces more than 200,000 data points and up to 1.2 TB of operational data a day, and most of it used to be read only after something broke. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Divakar Duraiyan, a technical architect at Tata Consultancy Services who has spent the last ten years on aviation technology, showed how digital twins turn that firehose into maintenance warnings that arrive weeks early. His headline: twins can identify failure patterns 28 days in advance.

## A twin is observability for a physical system

A digital twin is a virtual replica of aircraft systems, mechanical, electrical and environmental, fed by live telemetry. Divakar's four properties will sound familiar to anyone who runs software observability: complete visibility across components, predictive analysis, integration of thousands of sensors into one operational picture, and continuous monitoring across the whole flight rather than only at inspection time.

He reports the impact in the same vocabulary SREs use: mean time to detect down by nearly 90%, mean time to resolve down by more than 76%, 61.8% less emergency maintenance and an 84.6% drop in aircraft-on-ground (AOG) events, the costly disruptions that strand a plane.

## Three senses, fused

The detail that makes the talk interesting is the multimodal telemetry:

- **Vibration**: high-frequency sensors sampling at 20 kHz pick up deviations down to 0.05 mm, often an early sign of bearing wear.
- **Thermal imaging**: 0.1 °C resolution to find electrical faults or fluid leaks.
- **Acoustic monitoring**: algorithms listen beyond human hearing for ultrasonic anomalies.

The fusion layer is the real trick. Algorithms combine vibration, heat and sound into one signal and can flag a pattern that predicts failure even when each individual sensor looks normal. That is correlation across signal types, the same argument the observability world makes for joining metrics, logs and traces.

## Edge first, cloud second

An aircraft is the ultimate flaky network, so the architecture pushes computation onto the plane. Onboard nodes process raw data mid-flight and detect anomalies immediately. Filtering algorithms cut transmission by 87%, sending only what matters. Multi-channel secure transmission adds resilience, and cloud integration handles fleet-wide aggregation on the ground. Observability keeps working through connectivity gaps.

The output reaches technicians through augmented reality: risk maps per component, analytics turned into overlays, and repair procedures in the technician's field of view. Divakar says AR guidance reduced error rates by 76.2%.

## Three airlines, three results

The case studies give the claims some texture. A European carrier ran twins across 137 aircraft for a year, saw a 93% drop in unexpected component failures and prevented 18 cancellations by catching early signs of fuel pump problems, saving roughly 4.3 million euros in AOG costs. A North American cargo operator, despite legacy integration pain, cut maintenance costs by 23% and extended component life by 14%. An Asian regional airline caught an APU failure pattern 21 days earlier than its traditional systems and cut maintenance turnaround by 42%.

## The hard parts

Divakar is clear that this is not an overnight project. Data accuracy has to exceed 98.7%, so sensors need constant calibration; a small drift means a false alert or a missed fault. Most airlines run 14 or more legacy systems, some decades old, so APIs and middleware are essential. In-flight telemetry faces extreme temperatures and vibration. A full rollout takes 18 to 24 months, though he says many airlines see a return within seven to nine months.

## Who should watch

Anyone building monitoring for physical systems: IoT, manufacturing, energy. The closing section shows the same techniques moving into power generation turbines, medical scanners and production lines. Software-only SREs will also enjoy seeing their own MTTD and MTTR vocabulary applied to jet engines.

Title: In cloud banking, the trace is the security control
Description: Subrahmanyam Mamidi at Conf42 Observability 2025 on using metrics, logs and traces to catch breaches early and keep cloud banking audit-ready.
Body:
A payment breach that sits undetected for 72 hours is the scenario Subrahmanyam Mamidi builds his Conf42 Observability 2025 talk around. His argument: once a bank runs on microservices across several clouds, observability stops being an operations nicety and becomes a security and compliance control. The same traces that explain a slow payment also show where an attacker went.

## Why banks lose sight of their own systems

Subrahmanyam starts with the migration path most banks are somewhere along: fully on-premises data centres with total control, then hybrid setups where selected workloads move to cloud providers, then cloud-native banking built on distributed microservices and serverless. Each step buys agility and gives up a bit of visibility.

He lists the pressures that make that trade painful in finance:

- Regulation that does not care about your architecture: Basel III, GDPR and regional banking authorities.
- Distributed dependencies that traditional monitoring was never built to follow.
- An attack surface that grows with every new provider and region.
- Data sovereignty: a bank must know exactly where customer financial data flows.

## Three signals, two jobs

The framework is the classic trio. Metrics track system performance, resource use and transaction volumes. Logs give a chronological record of events, incidents and financial transactions, which doubles as the audit trail. Traces follow a transaction end to end across microservices, capturing the dependencies and latencies in payment processing.

What makes the talk worth a listen is how he maps those signals onto security work. Suspicious patterns surface before they become a breach. Traces let you find the source and scope of an incident across distributed systems quickly. A live dependency map doubles as an attack surface map. And after the incident, a complete audit trail makes forensics a query instead of a scavenger hunt.

On the compliance side the same data supports continuous, automated validation against Basel III and GDPR, plus immutable audit artefacts that examiners can actually use.

## Four steps to build it

His implementation recipe is short:

1. **Instrumentation**: put telemetry into the critical banking services so the code reports on itself.
2. **Collection**: a fault-tolerant pipeline that gathers and normalises metrics, logs and traces from very different systems.
3. **Storage**: regulatory-compliant, secure repositories with granular retention policies that satisfy both operations and compliance.
4. **Analysis**: machine learning to correlate the streams and flag security anomalies.

Storage is the step people underestimate. In a bank, telemetry is itself sensitive data with its own retention rules.

## The case study and the numbers

The anchor example is a retail bank whose payment processing breach went undetected for 72 hours under traditional monitoring. After adding distributed tracing across its cloud microservices with anomaly detection, Subrahmanyam says the bank detected incidents in under five minutes and prevented about $4.2 million in fraud losses while staying compliant. He also cites a 62% reduction in incidents, 78% faster response and a 41% cut in compliance documentation effort after observability programmes like this one. No bank or data source is named for those figures, so read them as illustrations of the shape of the payoff.

## Practical advice that survives the slides

The best practices are sensible and specific to the domain: design observability into the architecture from the start, map technical metrics to banking outcomes and customer experience, use ML for anomaly detection in complex transaction flows, and control cost with sampling, because full-fidelity telemetry on every transaction gets expensive fast. The rollout he suggests starts with an assessment focused on high-risk transaction paths, then a pilot in one critical service, then enterprise scale, then continuous tuning as threats change.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects in financial services who need to explain to a security or compliance team why tracing deserves budget. It is an overview rather than a hands-on session, so you get a framework and a vocabulary, not a reference implementation.

Title: Four building blocks for wiring multiple clouds together safely
Description: Naga Swetha Kattula (IEEE) at Conf42 Observability 2025 on AI-driven API management, confidential computing, zero trust and event-driven integration.
Body:
Running on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud at once avoids vendor lock-in and buys you three security models, three API styles and three ideas of what a data format is. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Naga Swetha Kattula, a Senior Member of IEEE, walked through four building blocks for integrating those platforms without leaving gaps: AI-driven API management, confidential computing, zero trust and event-driven architecture.

## The integration tax grows with every cloud

Naga frames the problem with the trade-off everyone in a multi-cloud shop knows. You pick each provider for what it does best, then pay for it in integration work: data synchronisation hurdles that cause delays and budget overruns, inconsistent API structures and auth mechanisms, different storage formats, and a separate security policy per provider. Her claim is that each added cloud raises integration complexity by at least 70%, and that the fix is a unified security and integration strategy instead of per-cloud glue.

## AI in the API gateway

The first block is API management that uses machine learning for design, documentation, traffic optimisation and attack detection. The talk compares traditional and AI-enhanced approaches on false-positive rate, attack detection and successful exploitation. Naga reports that ML models can detect up to 93% of API-based attacks while keeping false positives below 4%. It is the part of the talk closest to observability: the detector is only as good as the telemetry it watches.

## Protecting data in use, not just at rest

Confidential computing gets the most detail. Data at rest is covered by encryption, data in transit by TLS. Data in use, while it is being computed on, is the gap. Hardware-based trusted execution environments create enclaves that keep data encrypted during computation, so even system administrators and the cloud provider cannot read it. Naga notes that Intel SGX implementations have grown secure memory from 128 MB to 512 GB, which widens the set of workloads that fit inside an enclave.

The use cases are concrete: healthcare teams processing PHI in the cloud under HIPAA, financial institutions running analytics on sensitive data, and federated learning where several organisations train a model on combined data without seeing each other's raw records.

## Zero trust as the default posture

Zero trust appears in its standard form: never trust, always verify. Every entity is authenticated and authorised continuously regardless of network location, access follows least privilege, workloads sit in isolated zones, and real-time behaviour analytics watch for anything odd. The model assumes breach and treats each request as if it came from an untrusted network. Naga cites a 43% reduction in successful network intrusions and a 37% reduction in incident response costs for organisations that adopted such frameworks, and says real-time behaviour analytics spotted suspicious activity 73% faster than periodic scanning.

## Events instead of batch jobs

The last block is event-driven architecture: sources emit events, a bus routes them, subscribers react, and state is kept consistent across services. Loose coupling makes it a good fit for keeping data in sync across clouds in real time. Naga reports a 58% reduction in integration latency compared with scheduled batch processing, and gives an industrial IoT example of processing data from over 25,000 sensors with sub-second response.

## Who should watch

Architects drawing the first diagram of a multi-cloud integration strategy and wanting a checklist of the security pieces. This is a broad survey: each of the four topics gets a few slides, the figures are cited without naming the deployments behind them, and there is no code. Treat it as a map and go to the related talks below for the territory.

Title: Trace the risk score, not just the request
Description: Diliprao Boinapally of G2 Risk Solutions at Conf42 Observability 2025 on rebuilding bankruptcy monitoring as a traced, serverless pipeline.
Body:
A bankruptcy filing that reaches the analyst two days late is a loss nobody pages for. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Diliprao Boinapally of G2 Risk Solutions showed how his team rebuilt bankruptcy monitoring from a slow, reactive black box into a serverless pipeline where every risk score can be traced back to the documents that produced it. The idea worth stealing: instrument the business signal (case type, risk level, client) with the same care as latency and errors.

## The before picture was a visibility crisis

Diliprao is candid about where they started. Legacy systems were siloed and manual. When something broke, nobody could trace the root cause. Risk signals took hours or days to surface, and compliance teams spent weeks stitching together audit trails after the fact. Every blind spot, in his framing, was a chance to lose money.

That crisis forced the mindset shift that runs through the whole talk: observability could not be bolted on later. It had to be part of the architecture from the first commit.

## The pipeline, layer by layer

The architecture is a familiar data-engineering stack, which is part of why the talk is useful:

- **Ingestion**: serverless, event-driven functions pull legal filings, credit scores, transactional databases and third-party feeds, normalising data as it arrives. Each document gets quality metrics: format issues, missing fields, delays.
- **Entity resolution**: Apache Spark matches names, identifiers and patterns across data sets to produce risk scores. Every transformation is traced, so the team can watch matching precision and spot bottlenecks.
- **Orchestration**: Apache Airflow runs the dependencies and schedules, and each step logs its validation status, error category, retry rate and regulatory checkpoints.

Across all three, OpenTelemetry carries a trace from the entry point to the final risk score. That is the detail that turns "the score looks wrong" from a week of archaeology into a query.

## Logs that speak compliance

The second move is enriching logs with business context instead of leaving them as purely technical records. A log line that says which client, which case type and which risk level it belongs to is one a compliance officer can read. Diliprao ties system KPIs such as latency and throughput to business outcomes such as detection accuracy and compliance completeness, so engineering and compliance end up looking at the same dashboards and arguing about the same numbers.

Dashboards are split by audience: executives get KPIs and financial impact, engineers get task failures and latency, compliance gets traceability and alert logs. One pane of glass, three different windows.

## The numbers he reports

The talk is generous with results from the rollout. Average processing time fell from two hours 40 minutes to 31 minutes. Risk alerts reach decision makers in under 45 seconds. False positives dropped by 87% and false negatives, which he rightly calls the dangerous ones, by 94%. On the compliance side, he reports documentation completeness at 97% and audit preparation time down by 71%. These are his team's figures for their system; treat them as a direction of travel rather than a benchmark for yours.

## Roll it out in four steps

The implementation roadmap is the most reusable part: a telemetry gap assessment across technical and business layers, then instrumentation (logging, tracing, metrics across the serverless, Spark and Airflow pieces), then role-specific dashboards built with stakeholder feedback, then enablement through training and playbooks. Each step is meant to pay for itself before the next starts.

## Who should watch

Data engineers running Spark or Airflow pipelines in regulated industries, and anyone who has had to rebuild an audit trail from Slack history. It is a short, architecture-level talk rather than a code walkthrough, so come for the design and the framing, not the config files.

Title: Enterprise interfaces that notice cognitive overload, ethically
Description: Karthik Mohan Muralidharan at Conf42 Observability 2025 on inferring user stress from typing, mouse and workflow signals and adapting enterprise UIs, with consent.
Body:
Your typing slows down, you start correcting more mistakes and you wander off the usual path through a form. To an emotionally aware interface, that pattern says overload, and it can respond by simplifying the screen or offering help. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Karthik Mohan Muralidharan, a software engineer with about eight years in full-stack Salesforce development, presented research on adaptive enterprise interfaces that infer cognitive and emotional state without cameras or biometrics, and the ethical guardrails they need.

This is a research survey rather than a product demo. It turns observability inward: instead of watching the system, the system watches how people are coping with it.

## Enterprise software is behind consumer apps

The opening gap is striking. Citing research, Muralidharan says only around 18% of enterprise systems use any affective computing principles, against nearly 69% of consumer applications with adaptive elements, and adoption is lowest where stakes are highest: financial platforms, healthcare management and critical infrastructure. His view is that the hurdles are now more organisational than technical.

The cited benefits are what make the case: studies he references report fewer diagnostic errors and higher decision confidence for clinicians using emotionally responsive interfaces, lower cognitive load and better task accuracy across sectors.

## Reading state from ordinary interaction

The detection methods are all non-invasive. Typing rhythm correlates with cognitive load; a drop in keyboard speed is a consistent signal of increased mental demand. Error patterns are telling: clustered errors predict fatigue, a jump in corrections often signals frustration, and navigation errors versus data entry errors carry different signatures. Workflow sequencing shows hesitation when users drift from optimal task paths. Mouse movement and dwell time add more: longer dwell on a complex element correlates with confusion, and more frequent attention switching indicates information overload. Ensemble models then classify five emotional states, with accuracy he puts in the high 70s.

He also notes that cloud processing has cut inference latency sharply since 2020, and that federated learning keeps most of a centralised model's accuracy without pooling sensitive data.

## How the interface adapts

Once a state is inferred, the interface responds in five ways. Information density modulation reduces complexity during overload. Contextual assistance offers help when confusion is detected, which he links to fewer support tickets and less task abandonment. Workflow simplification restructures complex tasks during stressful periods. Contrast enhancement directs attention to critical elements. And intelligent timing of notifications cuts interruptions. The architecture is four layers: data collection, inference engine, adaptation rules and the interface itself, fast enough to adapt in real time.

## Support, not surveillance

The ethics section is the reason to watch. Transparent consent and granular opt-in permissions raise acceptance far above blanket consent. Low-confidence inferences should fall back to a static interface rather than guess. Unmitigated models show accuracy gaps across cultural backgrounds and age groups, which balanced training data and cultural calibration reduce. Most enterprise users worry this data will be used for performance reviews, so technical safeguards that prevent extracting individual performance metrics are essential, along with easy user overrides. His summary is that ethics by design is also the path to adoption.

## Who should watch

Product designers and front-end engineers building internal tools for high-stakes work, and anyone curious about affective computing beyond webcams and wearables. The talk leans heavily on cited study figures, so follow up on the sources before quoting them in a design review.

Title: Graph topology plus learned baselines for financial anomaly detection
Description: Siva Prakash at Conf42 Observability 2025 on dependency graphs and behavioural baselines replacing static thresholds in financial system monitoring.
Body:
Static thresholds do not know that a Monday morning looks different from a Friday afternoon during options expiry. Siva Prakash, who has spent two decades in IT and the last four years in financial and insurance systems, made that the starting point of his Conf42 Observability 2025 talk: combine a live dependency graph of your services with machine-learned behavioural baselines, and you catch anomalies thresholds miss while sending fewer false alerts.

The talk's headline claims are big: 99.4% anomaly detection accuracy and 87% fewer false alerts. They come from the speaker's own solution and unnamed case studies, so read the method as the takeaway and the figures as claims.

## Why thresholds fail in finance

Prakash's diagnosis has four parts. Low detection rates for critical anomalies, so issues surface after customers or financial processes are hit. Alert fatigue, with operators he describes as drowning in false positives and missing the real alert. System complexity, with thousands of interdependencies across microservices, APIs and distributed databases. And the financial impact: downtime, reputational damage and regulatory penalties. Static limits on CPU or response time ignore context and relationships, which is exactly what a distributed system is made of.

## Step one: a living graph of the system

The first technique is graph-based topology analysis. Collect logs, metrics and traces from every application, microservice, database and infrastructure component. Build a graph of service dependencies from that telemetry; he compares it to a social network for your services, showing who talks to whom and how often. Then analyse interaction patterns to spot deviations, such as a service suddenly calling another it has never talked to, or a critical path with unusual latency. Because the graph knows the relationships, alerts carry blast radius and upstream and downstream impact, which helps with prioritisation and root cause.

## Step two: baselines instead of thresholds

The second technique is behavioural analytics as a continuous loop. Collect hundreds of system metrics in real time. Use machine learning to learn what normal looks like for your environment, with dynamic baselines that adapt to seasonality. Evaluate deviations in context: is this an isolated blip or part of a pattern? Then flag subtle anomalies early, often before anything would breach a static limit. The graph says how components connect; the baselines say how they should behave within that structure.

## Data volume is its own engineering problem

Financial systems are data factories, as he puts it, so the platform needs intelligent filtering to prioritise relevant telemetry, adaptive compression to keep storage costs down while preserving history, and real-time analysis on top. Integration covers AWS, Azure, GCP and on-prem, language-agnostic instrumentation with OpenTelemetry support to avoid lock-in, SQL and NoSQL connectors, and security requirements that are non-negotiable in the sector: SOC 2, PCI and GDPR alignment, end-to-end encryption and role-based access.

## A phased rollout

His implementation plan is concrete in its timing: an assessment phase of two to three weeks for topology mapping and a monitoring gap analysis, a pilot of three to four weeks on the most critical services to set baselines, an expanded rollout of four to six weeks with alert tuning, and ongoing optimisation. The case studies he cites, a global investment bank, a regional credit union and an insurer, are presented as anonymised examples of reduced MTTR and fewer false alerts.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform teams in banking, payments or insurance who are still alerting on fixed thresholds, and anyone wondering how topology and ML baselines fit together. Expect a solution pitch in the second half rather than code.

Title: Cloud-native observability, from API gateway to capacity planning
Description: Vamsi Krishna Munnangi of Walmart at Conf42 Observability 2025 on pillars, stateless vs stateful signals, API gateway telemetry and HA pipelines for peak traffic.
Body:
Monitoring tells you something is wrong; observability tells you why and how to fix it. That is the line Vamsi Krishna Munnangi, a senior software engineer in infrastructure engineering at Walmart, builds his Conf42 Observability 2025 talk on, using lessons from systems that have to survive Thanksgiving, Black Friday and holiday peaks.

It is a structured survey that covers a lot of ground in 30 minutes. The best sections are the practical ones on API gateways and on keeping the observability pipeline itself highly available.

## Stateless and stateful services need different signals

Munnangi makes a distinction many overviews skip. For stateless services such as load-balanced APIs, watch throughput, latency and resource use with horizontal scaling in mind, and lean on tracing individual requests and analysing errors. For stateful services such as databases, track persistence signals: replication health, consistency and storage performance. His example is Google Cloud Spanner and keeping data durable across regions. Health probes and anomaly detection are the shared patterns across both.

## Tracing done with intent

His tracing recipe has four steps. Instrument code and propagate trace context with OpenTelemetry. Configure intelligent sampling: keep 100% of critical paths, sample the rest (he suggests something like one in a thousand) and make sure both normal and exceptional patterns are represented. Centralise the pipeline on scalable transport such as Kafka or GCP Pub/Sub. Then visualise traces in Jaeger to find bottlenecks. For the three pillars he names Prometheus for metrics, the ELK stack for logs and Jaeger for traces.

## The API gateway is an observability hub

The gateway section is the one to watch. As the point where external traffic enters the internal world, the gateway sees request volumes, service dependencies, rate-limiting effectiveness, authentication events and attack patterns worth handing to the security team. He mentions traffic ranging from a few hundred to tens of thousands of requests per second at peak, and tooling combinations such as Azure API Management with Application Insights, Apigee with Stackdriver, and Kong or NGINX with Prometheus and Grafana.

The best practices are a usable checklist: structured access logs with correlation IDs, rate limiting and circuit breakers that expose metrics, tracing headers instrumented at the gateway, and latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) for SLO enforcement.

## Keep the observability pipeline highly available

A pipeline that goes down with the system it watches is not much use. Munnangi's four-stage pipeline (collection, processing and filtering, tiered hot and cold storage, visualisation) is backed by HA practices: collectors and storage across multiple availability zones, monitoring at node, zone and region level, tracking failover events and MTTR, correlating signals across clouds and auditing cross-cloud failover and data sync. Local buffering keeps metrics when a connection drops, and multi-channel alerting through Slack, email and PagerDuty means one dead channel does not silence a page.

## Capacity planning from the same data

Finally, the telemetry feeds capacity planning: aggregate months of utilisation data, forecast seasonal spikes with machine learning, autoscale to balance cost and performance, and compare forecasts with actual consumption to refine the models. His roadmap ends where most good ones do: Prometheus and centralised logging first, SLIs and SLOs for core services, then tracing and team dashboards, then automated detection and remediation. Start with one service and scale.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE engineers designing observability for high-traffic microservices, especially anyone who owns an API gateway. Parts of the talk cite percentage improvements from studies and production systems without much detail, so value it for the patterns more than the numbers.

Title: Salesforce Nonprofit Cloud as a fix for nonprofit data silos
Description: Sekhar Midathana of Northern Trust at Conf42 Observability 2025 on how Salesforce Nonprofit Cloud centralises donor, program and volunteer data.
Body:
Nonprofits often run on a patchwork of spreadsheets and single-purpose tools, which means nobody can see the whole organisation at once. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Sekhar Midathana, Salesforce Consultant at Northern Trust Corporation, presented Salesforce Nonprofit Cloud as the way out: one cloud-based platform for donors, programs, volunteers and reporting, with the manual admin automated away.

Honest scope first. This is a product overview of a CRM, and it sits a long way from tracing and metrics. The observability angle is organisational visibility: getting leadership and program staff to look at the same data in real time.

## Three problems the talk starts from

Midathana names time constraints, data silos and communication gaps. Small teams with tight budgets lose hours to manual data entry and admin, leaving less time for the mission. Donor management, program tracking and outreach live in different tools, so there is no comprehensive view. And program staff lack real-time visibility into outcomes while leadership struggles to coordinate and track progress across the organisation, which also makes it harder to show impact to funders.

## What the platform does

The talk describes Nonprofit Cloud as a purpose-built layer on top of Salesforce rather than a generic CRM. Being hosted by Salesforce gives remote access from any device, scaling without hardware, automatic updates and the vendor's availability and disaster recovery. It is also highly configurable, so organisations can fit it to their own workflows, reporting needs and existing systems.

The operational features he walks through are the practical part. Automated donation receipts, scheduled recurring payments and personalised acknowledgements. Real-time dashboards for program progress, from program managers up to executives. A single searchable home for donor contacts, program outcomes and volunteer history. And prebuilt plus custom reports for donors and grant makers.

## Donors and teams

On donor relations, he covers centralised donor profiles with giving history, communication preferences and interests; online, mobile and recurring giving with gift matching tracked automatically; segmentation for targeted campaigns; and donor analytics such as lifetime value and acquisition cost. On collaboration, task assignments, activity feeds and real-time updates sit on the same shared data, so teams stop asking each other which spreadsheet is current.

## Implementation, the unglamorous part

The implementation section is the most transferable to any platform rollout. Discovery sessions with stakeholders and an honest audit of current tools. Configuration to the organisation's workflows, then data migration from legacy systems with accuracy checks, integrations with donation and volunteer platforms, and access controls and data governance for sensitive records. Training with super users who act as champions, and ongoing support with regular check-ins as goals change.

He illustrates the approach with two unnamed success stories, an environmental nonprofit with multiple chapters and a youth education fund, and before-and-after percentages for donor retention, program efficiency, reporting speed and staff satisfaction. The talk does not say where those figures come from, so read them as illustrations rather than benchmarks.

## Who should watch

Nonprofit operations leads evaluating a CRM, and Salesforce practitioners who want a feature tour of Nonprofit Cloud. Engineers looking for observability tooling will not find it here; the takeaway for them is the reminder that visibility problems are often data-silo problems first.

Title: Pick AWS observability tools by function, not by familiarity
Description: Prudhvi Raj Atluri of Quantiphi at Conf42 Observability 2025 maps CloudWatch, X-Ray, Managed Grafana, QuickSight and OpenTelemetry to the jobs they fit.
Body:
Using QuickSight as a real-time monitoring tool is a good way to learn what "periodic refresh" means during an outage. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Prudhvi Raj Atluri, Associate Architect for Data at Quantiphi with more than ten years building analytics platforms on AWS, built his talk around that kind of mismatch: managed services picked for the wrong job create blind spots, alert fatigue and ballooning costs.

His lens is simple and reusable. A tool adds function when it speeds up insight and integrates at scale. It adds friction when it brings noise, lag and complexity.

## The AWS toolbox, sorted by job

Atluri walks through the core services and what each is for. CloudWatch is the general-purpose foundation: log collection, metric aggregation, dashboards, alarms and automated actions. X-Ray traces requests end to end through distributed applications, the tool for finding which microservice is slow. Amazon Managed Grafana is for rich, real-time visualisation across AWS services and open source data sources. QuickSight is BI: interactive dashboards and natural language queries, with periodic data refresh, explicitly not real time. And AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry gives vendor-neutral, standardised instrumentation across stacks.

He then widens the list to the governance and optimisation side: CloudTrail for auditing every API action, AWS Config for continuous resource configuration checks, DevOps Guru for ML-based anomaly detection with suggested root causes, Trusted Advisor for best-practice checks, Compute Optimizer for right-sizing, and Inspector for automated security scans on EC2, Lambda and containers.

## Function, by example

The function examples are the recommended defaults. CloudWatch alarms for real-time alerts on EC2, Lambda metrics and Container Insights. X-Ray to pinpoint bottlenecks across API Gateway and Lambda flows using service maps. Grafana, his favourite, for live dashboards over CloudWatch, Prometheus and other sources, including SLO tracking. And OpenTelemetry for unified instrumentation across ECS, EKS or hybrid environments, sending data to CloudWatch or third-party tools.

## Friction, by example

The friction examples are the ones worth remembering. QuickSight for real-time monitoring, where batch refresh guarantees lag. CloudWatch Logs at scale without structured queries, which turns unstructured log data into reduced visibility. And overlapping tools without integration, which fragments data and slows collaboration. Tool sprawl rarely looks like a decision; it looks like five teams each making a reasonable one.

## Architecture patterns and where AI fits

For architecture he describes four patterns: a centralised telemetry pipeline using S3 and OpenSearch; real-time monitoring with Grafana and CloudWatch plus SNS or SES notifications; AI/ML integration through SageMaker and Bedrock for predictive analysis and anomaly detection; and automated response with Lambda and EventBridge for remediation and scaling. His view of GenAI in observability is measured: predictive analytics, automated root cause suggestions, natural language questions about system behaviour, and smarter alert filtering to cut noise.

## Best practices

The closing advice is short. Build observability in at design time rather than bolting it on. Align SLOs and SLIs with business KPIs. Automate alert generation and root cause analysis where you can. And keep reviewing the pipeline and tool choices so they stay relevant as the system changes.

## Who should watch

Teams designing or cleaning up an AWS observability stack, and architects who need a quick map of which native service does what. It stays high level by design, so experienced CloudWatch and X-Ray users will mostly get the framework, not new tricks.

Title: DataOps treats data pipelines with the rigour of code deploys
Description: Lakshmi Narayana Gupta Koralla of Starbucks at Conf42 Observability 2025 on DataOps principles, governance as code, data CI/CD and observability for pipelines.
Body:
DataOps takes the habits that made DevOps work, automation, CI/CD, version control and monitoring, and applies them to data pipelines. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Lakshmi Narayana Gupta Koralla, Senior Data Engineer at Starbucks with 14 years in IT, gave a broad survey of the methodology: where it came from, its core principles, the architecture components and how to measure whether it is working.

It is a wide-angle overview rather than a walkthrough of one Starbucks pipeline. Treat it as a syllabus: each section names the tools and patterns to go and read about.

## Where DataOps came from

Koralla traces the line from centralised data warehouses with rigid ETL, through the big data era that added volume and complexity, to DataOps emerging around 2015 as practitioners borrowed from software engineering. The old model had siloed teams, manual handoffs and data projects that ran for months or years. The new one asks why a schema change should be harder to ship than an API change.

## Four principles

The conceptual core is four principles. Automation and orchestration across the data lifecycle, with dependencies and sequencing managed explicitly. CI/CD for data, so changes are integrated, tested for validity and impact, and deployed through standard processes. Version control and reproducibility for transformation logic and models, so any previous state can be recreated. And quality by design, with validation built into pipelines so anomalies are caught before downstream consumers see them.

## The architecture, component by component

This is the most useful part for practitioners. Monitoring and observability for data covers quality, lineage, performance and business alignment, often with statistical baselines to detect anomalies, and in mature teams as observability as code so monitoring evolves with the pipelines. Governance as code means policies are codified, versioned and enforced inside pipelines, with a federated model where a central team sets frameworks and domain teams own their rules.

For data CI/CD he points to blue-green and canary releases for pipelines and the expand-contract pattern for non-breaking schema changes. The automation layer is the familiar stack: Docker for consistent environments, Apache Airflow, Prefect and Dagster for workflows as code, dbt for transformations, Kafka and Flink for streaming. On organisation, he mentions data mesh, DataOps centres of excellence, data product teams and guilds, all relying on clear ownership and SLAs between producers and consumers.

## Measuring it, and rolling it out

Koralla proposes four measurement areas: pipeline performance, data quality, time to insight and resource utilisation, and a maturity model running from ad hoc at level one to optimised at level five. The rollout runs through assessment, pilot, expansion and maturity phases, starting with a high-value use case that produces proof points for stakeholders. He is clear that executive sponsorship matters because DataOps is a business initiative, not just a technical project, and that legacy integration, skills gaps and cultural resistance are the usual blockers.

## Beyond the basics

The later sections cover the frontier: the overlap with MLOps (feature stores, drift detection, explainability that traces predictions back to data transformations), store-and-forward patterns for edge data, Lambda and Kappa architectures for streaming, and privacy by design with data minimisation, dynamic masking and jurisdiction-aware routing. He also lists emerging trends such as declarative pipelines, data contracts between producers and consumers, and self-healing pipelines.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and platform teams building a DataOps practice from scratch, and engineering managers who need a structured overview to plan against. If you already run dbt with CI and data contracts, you will mostly be nodding along, though the governance-as-code section is a good checklist.

Title: The monitoring fear cycle, and how fixed-cost clouds break it
Description: Denish Tomar of Qumulus at Conf42 Observability 2025 on why metered observability makes teams self-censor dashboards, and a fixed-cost alternative.
Body:
You are halfway through debugging a production incident when finance pings you: the cloud bill just went up by $5,000, what happened? Denish Tomar, Developer Relations Engineer at Qumulus, opens his Conf42 Observability 2025 talk with that moment and argues that per-unit observability pricing quietly makes systems less observable, because engineers start rationing the very data they need.

This is a short talk from a vendor. The diagnosis applies to any metered stack; the proposed fix is the fixed-cost platform Tomar works with.

## The monitoring fear cycle

Tomar's central diagram is a loop most teams have lived through. Deploy a service with basic monitoring. An incident shows visibility is not enough, so add metrics, logs and traces. The bill spikes, finance asks for cuts, monitoring gets scaled back. Another incident. Repeat.

He gives an example from a team he worked with: great dashboards covering response times, error rates and database behaviour, until the service grew from 10 to 50 and monitoring costs climbed so much that they deleted dashboards and sampled metrics at 10%.

## What rationing costs you

The list of side effects is the strongest part of the talk. Self-censoring, where engineers do not build the dashboards they need. Delayed detection, because the right data is not collected. Blind debugging when an incident hits. Crisis monitoring, where full telemetry only gets switched on during an emergency. And a knowledge gap, because new team members never learn tools that are treated as scarce.

His incident timeline makes it concrete: users report slowness at 10:00, the team checks basic metrics at 10:15, asks permission to enable detailed monitoring, waits for data, and pinpoints a database bottleneck at 11:15. Nearly two hours of impact, most of it spent waiting for visibility. The next day, detailed monitoring is scaled back again. He also recalls a senior engineer spending three hours optimising monitoring to save $200 a month, which is a strange use of a senior engineer.

## Four meters on every byte

Tomar breaks the cost down to the architecture: agents collect data, ship it to a central service, which stores and indexes it and runs queries for dashboards and alerts. That creates four separate cost drivers. Data transfer, especially across regions or to third-party tools. Ingest processing for parsing and indexing. Storage, particularly at high resolution. And query costs, where you can end up paying to read your own data. Add unpredictability from traffic spikes or a chatty bug, and teams build deliberately compromised monitoring.

## Observability as a platform feature

His alternative is to make observability part of the infrastructure rather than a metered add-on. In a fixed-cost model, metrics and logs are collected automatically, with no transfer fees, predictable included retention and no charge for querying. He demos the platform he works with: a new server comes with dashboards for CPU, memory, disk I/O and network, 30 days of high-resolution history, and logs, with no setup step. Replaying the same incident, the alert fires within minutes, the database connection issue is found quickly and the fix lands in about 25 minutes, after which the team adds a dashboard for that scenario without asking anyone's permission.

## Who should watch

Engineers and engineering managers who have ever dropped a log level, shortened retention or killed a dashboard to save money. Even if you stay on a metered platform, the fear-cycle diagram is a useful thing to show the person who signs off the bill.

Title: An observability maturity roadmap written for analytics leaders
Description: Raghavender Puchhakayala of JPMorgan Chase at Conf42 Observability 2025 on four pillars, four pitfalls and a reactive-to-predictive maturity path for distributed systems.
Body:
Most observability talks are pitched at the engineer holding the pager. Raghavender Puchhakayala's talk at Conf42 Observability 2025 is pitched at the person who has to justify the budget. Puchhakayala, of JPMorgan Chase and a Senior Member of the IEEE, treats observability as a strategic data product and offers analytics leaders a four-stage maturity roadmap, from reactive to predictive, for distributed systems.

Honest scope: this is a short overview, not a hands-on session. It is useful as a shared vocabulary for a planning meeting, less so as a how-to.

## Monitoring knows what to look for; observability doesn't need to

The framing is the standard distinction, stated cleanly. Traditional monitoring watches known issues with predefined metrics and threshold alerts. Observability aims at the unknown unknowns, through high-cardinality telemetry and context-rich data. He also puts a number on why the distinction matters: a 99.99% availability target leaves roughly 22 minutes of downtime a month, which is not much time to discover you were watching the wrong graph.

He splits the value three ways: business insight into user journeys, operational intelligence for spotting anomalies, and the telemetry foundation that feeds both.

## Four pillars, with events added

Puchhakayala uses four pillars rather than three. Metrics for quantities over time like CPU, memory, latency and throughput. Logs for timestamped, structured event records. Traces for request flows across services. And events for state changes such as deployments and configuration changes, the pillar that most often explains why the other three suddenly look different.

On top of the pillars he places analytics: interactive exploration across all telemetry, ML-driven pattern recognition for anomalies, correlation of business and technical data for impact, and predictive analytics.

## A reference architecture in four layers

The architecture slide is a tidy checklist. An instrumentation layer with OpenTelemetry agents and SDKs. A collection and transport layer using streaming tools such as Kafka and Flink. A storage and processing layer of time-series databases and tracing backends. And an analysis layer of dashboards, notebooks and alerting. He then surveys the usual tools (Prometheus, Grafana, Elasticsearch, OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace) and suggests choosing by ease of use, scalability, integrations and overall cost and complexity.

## The four pitfalls

This is the slide to bring to your next retro. Data deluge: collecting everything without a purpose, so signal drowns in noise. Tool sprawl: fragmented visibility across platforms that do not correlate. Siloed ownership: platform teams working in isolation from the people who need the insight. And alert fatigue: too many low-value notifications, so the important one gets ignored.

## The maturity path and the leader's job

The roadmap has four stages: reactive (respond after impact), proactive (catch issues as they emerge), analytical (understand patterns and dependencies) and predictive (forecast before they occur). The leader's role, as he describes it, is translating telemetry into business impact, building feedback loops from insight to action, and driving data literacy across teams. His closing advice is to define business outcomes first, start with high-impact services, build teams that mix analytics and operations, and climb the maturity ladder one step at a time.

## Who should watch

Analytics and engineering leaders who need a framework to explain observability to the business, and teams writing their first observability strategy document. Practitioners who already run OpenTelemetry in production can skip to the pitfalls slide.

Title: Public sector observability through BI dashboards and AI alerts
Description: Power BI analyst Indraneel Madabhushini at Conf42 Observability 2025 on merging legacy and cloud telemetry into role-based dashboards for agencies.
Body:
A slow backend tax-processing system often goes unnoticed until citizens start waiting. Indraneel Madabhushini's talk at Conf42 Observability 2025 starts from that kind of visibility gap and argues for treating public sector observability as a business intelligence problem as much as a monitoring one. Madabhushini, a Power BI data analyst with more than 12 years in SAP BusinessObjects, SAP BW and the Microsoft Power BI stack, lays out a four-pillar framework and a phased roadmap for agencies.

This is the view from the BI side of the house. If you want collector configs, look elsewhere; if you need executives to actually look at your telemetry, this is the right angle.

## Three problems agencies share

He names them plainly. Complexity overload: data spread across mainframes, cloud platforms and customer databases with no full picture. Visibility gaps: insight buried inside individual systems, so nobody sees the end-to-end flow of a service. And reactive operations: problems discovered after the disruption, which costs service quality and public trust.

## Four pillars, BI first

The framework stacks business intelligence (Power BI turning raw data into dashboards and scorecards), AI for predicting behaviour and flagging anomalies, data integration that merges every system into one view regardless of vendor or format, and core monitoring of metrics, logs, traces and events. Without that last telemetry foundation, he says, real visibility is impossible.

The technical layout is a modern data stack: connectors and agents pulling telemetry from on-prem, cloud, third-party APIs and IoT devices; an analytics engine on Spark or Databricks correlating logs with performance metrics; secure storage in Azure Data Lake or Snowflake with encryption and role-based access; and visualisation in Power BI, Tableau or SAP BusinessObjects with separate executive, operational and technical dashboards.

## Results he cites from enterprise work

Madabhushini illustrates the framework with three projects from his private sector career. At a food manufacturer, replacing an ageing monitoring system that could not scale, he reports 40% faster incident response. At an industrial technology company, merging more than 12 data streams into one view, a 35% cut in downtime. At a medical device maker, an AI anomaly detection system that he says prevented 28 major incidents in a year and around $1.5 million in potential downtime costs. These are his reported outcomes, not independent benchmarks, but they show the kind of win that gets a BI-led approach funded.

## A roadmap that avoids analysis paralysis

The phases are assessment (inventory tools, data sources and workflows, involve cross-functional teams), architecture (decide which signals to collect, ETL, models, schemas and interfaces, modular by design), implementation (a proof of concept on one high-priority service, then agile sprints) and adoption (training, documentation, executive champions, feedback loops). His practical next step is a two-to-four-week internal review and a pilot on a high-visibility service such as a customer portal, with results inside 30 to 60 days.

## Compliance and culture are the hard parts

The challenges slide is honest. Agencies need FedRAMP and FISMA-compliant tools and strict access control. Legacy systems often lack APIs, so integration means custom ETL, middleware and sometimes reverse-engineering logs; he calls it the hardest and most rewarding part. Some teams resist the transparency observability brings, which is why executive sponsorship matters. And tight budgets favour a high-ROI pilot that funds the next phase.

## Who should watch

Data and BI teams in government or regulated organisations who are being asked to "do observability", and platform teams who need their telemetry to reach decision makers. Engineers looking for tracing internals can skip it.

Title: Observability costs money, so map it to business KPIs first
Description: Srinivas Sriram Mantrala at Conf42 Observability 2025 traces observability from threshold alerts to AI and GenAI, and why SLOs tied to KPIs fund it.
Body:
Srinivas Sriram Mantrala's talk at Conf42 Observability 2025 is a tour of how microservices monitoring grew up, from "the database is down" emails to AI-assisted, self-healing operations. Mantrala, a senior manager, keeps returning to one practical point along the way: observability comes with a cost, and nobody approves that cost unless you can show what it buys in business terms.

It is a conversational, experience-driven talk rather than a technical deep cut, and it works best as a map of where AI fits into an observability practice.

## Four stages, from alerts to self-healing

Mantrala lays the history out as a sequence. Traditional monitoring was threshold alerts for monoliths: something is up or down, an administrator reacts. Basic observability split the data into the familiar three pillars, with metrics for the high-level view, logs for granular events and traces for how a request moves through services. Still reactive, but much richer.

The next step, which he calls AI-enhanced observability, came with cloud platforms: pattern analysis on that data to learn peak hours, quiet hours and sensible maintenance windows, and to plan resources ahead. The last step is self-healing, where the same analysis drives horizontal or vertical autoscaling for events like Thanksgiving traffic without anyone touching a console.

## No KPI mapping, no budget

The section that earns the talk its place is about SLOs. Mantrala argues that unless you correlate technical metrics with business KPIs, there is no buy-in to invest in observability at all. His examples are plain: customer satisfaction depends on latency, so you need latency data to say anything about satisfaction; revenue per transaction depends on knowing how long orders take and whether the system scaled in time. Business approves the spend when it can see that link, and only then can the practice survive past the first budget review. Every SRE who has had a tracing project cut will nod along.

## Make observability part of the build

He describes a layered implementation framework: collect the data, then add validation checks so new microservices cannot reach production without the required logging, metrics and tracing, enforced in CI/CD alongside the usual quality gates. Intelligent analysis with ML models sits on top, and AIOps remediation on top of that. The point is that observability is a discipline applied to every new service, not a one-off project.

For tooling he names Grafana as his personal favourite, mainly for dashboards each role can build for itself and for its query language over historical data.

## Contextual alerts and a chatbot for the on-call

The forward-looking part is about incident response. Contextual alerting, as he describes it, means the alert arrives on your phone with the history of similar incidents, the actions taken last time and the person who fixed it, so the on-call engineer can delegate to someone who has seen it before. Intelligent routing sends specific alerts to the people with the right experience.

Then GenAI: a chatbot over historical incident data that suggests steps, summarises similar incidents and points to the most common fix, so a new team member can get going without weeks of knowledge-transfer sessions.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers building the case for observability investment, and teams early in their AIOps thinking who want a framework for where each capability fits. If you already run SLO-based alerting and incident similarity search, much of this will be familiar.
