Title: In async commerce, failures whisper, so design for tracing first
Description: Anup Raja Sarabu of T-Mobile at Conf42 Observability 2025 on async payments, BOPIS events, eventual consistency and the observability that keeps it honest.
Body:
On a new iPhone launch day, T-Mobile's payment system went down in the first 15 minutes and customers sat on "oops, something went wrong" with orders they could not submit. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Anup Raja Sarabu, Senior Technical Product Manager at T-Mobile, used that incident to explain why the team is decoupling payments from order submission, and why observability has to be designed in before the first event is published.

His one-line summary of the trade-off: synchronous systems fail loudly, while in async flows failures don't scream, they whisper. Miss the whisper and you find out from a customer.

## The launch-day incident that started it

New product introductions, especially September Apple launches, are T-Mobile's busiest days, with Sarabu citing around 100,000 orders. Checkout was synchronous: build the cart, pay, and only then submit the order. Circuit breakers kept the rest of the system up, but with payments broken nobody could finish. That raised the question of whether payment really needs to block the order at all.

The redesign he describes puts payment on a queue. The customer gets an order number and confirmation immediately; card validity, fraud and funds checks happen behind the scenes; the order is only submitted once payment clears. If payment fails, the customer gets a text or email asking them to re-enter card details. T-Mobile already ran buy online, pick up in store (BOPIS) this way, with inventory validation, store notification and pickup scheduling as independent events working in parallel.

## Four things to observe in async systems

Sarabu's pillars for async observability are specific. Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry context injected into requests and events, so spans correlate even across Kafka hops. Event audit and replay: structured events with user ID, order ID, timestamp and type, so you can reconstruct what happened and retry failed processing. Consistency monitoring that checks whole business transactions complete (inventory reserved, payment confirmed, shipment initiated) even when events arrive out of order. And domain dashboards in business language, so product managers and support see orders and payment states instead of raw traces.

On tooling he names OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Grafana and AWS X-Ray for traces, Burrow for Kafka consumer lag, and Kibana, Metabase and Power BI for the order dashboards. The Kafka metrics that matter are queue depth, consumer lag, throughput and handler error rates.

## Eventual consistency, engineered on purpose

The CAP section is the most useful part for architects. In high-scale commerce, partition tolerance is non-negotiable, so T-Mobile chose availability and accepted eventual consistency. That only works with three techniques: idempotent handlers so a duplicated payment confirmation never charges twice, version numbers on orders and payments to resolve concurrent updates, and compensating transactions instead of rollbacks, such as a cancellation event that restores inventory when payment fails after confirmation. His warning about dashboards is worth framing: in async systems, every service can be green while the flow is broken.

## Lessons he closes on

Design for traceability from day one, because tracing cannot be bolted on later. Plan for eventual consistency rather than chasing real-time consistency. Align metrics to business events so observability becomes an organisational asset, not just a dev tool. He also reported BOPIS carts converting to orders at a markedly higher rate than standard online carts, and close to full availability during launch and promotional peaks.

## Who should watch

Anyone moving checkout, payments or fulfilment from synchronous calls to events, and product managers who want to understand what their engineers mean by eventual consistency. It is long and conversational, but the incident is real and the patterns are concrete.

Title: Telecom reliability needs better signals, not more alerts
Description: Ajay Averineni of IBM at Conf42 Observability 2025 on moving telecom monitoring from reactive alerts to AI anomaly detection with LSTMs, NLP and closed loops.
Body:
The outage that starts Ajay Averineni's talk is a familiar one: dozens of alerts from different systems, none of them clear, hours spent finding the root cause, and the signals sitting in the data days earlier. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Averineni, Lead Application Developer at IBM, walked through how a telecom operations team moved from reactive monitoring to AI-assisted anomaly detection, and why the hardest part was getting the operators to trust it.

His takeaway from that outage fits in one line: "We don't need more alerts." What the team needed was better intelligence on top of the alerts they already had.

## Telecom data is big, siloed and short on context

Averineni frames the problem with scale. He cited telecom networks generating up to 25 terabytes of operational data a day, a number growing with 5G and IoT, and the claim that most outages are preventable if the early signals get caught. Traditional monitoring fails in three ways in his telling: it is reactive (users notice first), siloed (network, infrastructure and applications watched separately) and short on context (alerts fire on narrow metrics with no bigger picture). He compares troubleshooting under those conditions to solving a puzzle with half the pieces missing.

The fix he describes is the observability one: collect metrics, logs and traces across domains, replace fixed thresholds with dynamic baselines so normal fluctuations stop triggering alert storms, and let self-learning models keep adjusting those baselines.

## Two models for two kinds of data

The technical core is short and concrete. For metrics, the team used LSTM-based models to catch temporal anomalies in high-dimensional time series. For logs, they applied natural language processing to pull patterns out of unstructured text. Correlating the two, structured time series plus unstructured logs, is what he says traditional tools could not match.

The build order matters too. They started by aggregating 18 months of telemetry, trained deep learning models on telecom-specific patterns (which he stresses look very different from standard enterprise data), and then added tracing through every layer from hardware to virtual network functions.

## Trust was the real bottleneck

The section worth the watch is the one on culture. Operations engineers were sceptical, so the team brought them in from day one: operators tested the models, flagged false positives and suggested new inputs. Averineni says that buy-in changed everything, and it is the bit most AIOps rollouts skip.

Two engineering choices supported that trust. A unified entity model tied infrastructure, virtual functions and services together so an anomaly could be placed in context. And an explainable AI layer with visual tools showed operators why an alert fired, which he credits with cutting false positives by 27%. Edge filtering and intelligent sampling kept the terabytes-a-day problem manageable.

## The architecture closes the loop

The final design has three layers: distributed agents collecting telemetry, a stream processing layer running ML pipelines in real time, and a knowledge and automation layer driving auto-remediation and model refinement. Each incident feeds back into the models, so detection, root cause analysis and remediation become a loop instead of a ticket queue. His closing roadmap is sensible: assess the current stack, pilot one domain, scale gradually while unifying data, and only then automate remediation.

## Who should watch

Operations and SRE teams in telecom or any network-heavy business drowning in alerts, and anyone planning an AIOps pilot who wants a realistic order of operations. It is a short, high-level talk; you will not get model hyperparameters, but you will get a sensible sequence and an honest note on adoption.

Title: A graph neural network that tunes Step Functions fan-outs live
Description: Vamsi Praveen Karanam of Amazon at Conf42 Observability 2025 on OpenTelemetry plus a small GNN that resizes Step Functions map chunks mid-run, with guardrails.
Body:
When an AWS Step Functions map state fans out into thousands of Lambda invocations, one slow branch can hold up the whole workflow. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Vamsi Praveen Karanam, Software Development Engineer at Amazon, presented Adaptive Parallelism Insights (APIX): OpenTelemetry spans on every branch, a compact graph neural network that reads them, and a controller that changes chunk sizes on a running workflow without touching business code.

It is one of the more concrete AI-for-observability talks of the event: a named architecture, a model size, explicit guardrails and a results table.

## Three pains of big fan-outs

Karanam lists the failure modes anyone who has run large map states will recognise. Latency cliffs, where a few slow branches delay the entire execution. Tracing gaps, because high-level dashboards average away branch-specific anomalies and the native execution history only shows coarse events. And cost spikes from hidden retries and cold starts. Those turn into three questions: how to capture per-branch telemetry cheaply, whether a small model can digest it fast enough, and how to act on its advice mid-run without blowing through limits.

## The pipeline, top to bottom

Every task gets an OpenTelemetry span; map and parallel branch spans carry a chunk ID. The same wrapper writes counters such as payload size, retry count and cold start time through CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format, so no agent is needed inside Lambda. Spans travel over OTLP to a collector on AWS Fargate, then into Kinesis Data Firehose, which feeds live heat maps in Amazon Managed Grafana and lands raw records as Parquet in S3.

SageMaker Serverless hosts a two-layer GNN of about 1.2 million parameters. Every 60 seconds it reads the latest window of branch metrics and predicts an ideal chunk size, with a confidence score and projected cost and latency impact. EventBridge passes the inference to a Lambda callback that checks guardrails and patches the running map state. Each decision is hashed, stored in Systems Manager Parameter Store and written into later spans, so auditors can follow a change from inference to outcome.

Span emission adds about two milliseconds per invocation, which he calls negligible for tasks that run for seconds.

## Guardrails make the automation shippable

The part to steal even if you never train a GNN is the controller's three boundaries. Chunk size can change by at most 25% within five minutes, which prevents oscillation. A concurrency cap keeps total Lambda concurrency below the account quota minus a safety buffer. And a rollback trigger reverts to the previous chunk size if p95 latency and errors both rise for two consecutive windows.

## The numbers he showed

The evaluation compared static batching at 1,000 items and dynamic S3 partitioning against adaptive chunking on three workloads: a uniform 10 TB synthetic set, a skewed 10 TB set with larger records mixed in, and 3 TB of anonymised production data. Adaptive chunking had the lowest latency and cost on every workload. On the skewed set, throttle errors fell from 47 under static batching to five; on the live data, from 24 to three.

He is upfront about the limits: cold start jitter can exaggerate latency gains, synthetic workloads may miss extreme patterns, and model drift means weekly retraining plus drift alerts.

## Who should watch

Teams running data enrichment, ETL or compliance jobs on Step Functions distributed maps, and anyone who wants a worked example of putting a model in a control loop safely. The five lessons at the end (sample generously during peaks, keep guardrails, publish dollar deltas next to trace IDs, watch retry patterns, retrain weekly) apply well beyond AWS.

Title: Chip design gets the observability treatment, in seven layers
Description: Naveen Desai of Marvell Technology sketches at Conf42 Observability 2025 how AI-driven monitoring could shorten semiconductor design cycles.
Body:
Observability usually means pods, queries and p99s. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Naveen Desai, Principal Engineer at Marvell Technology, pointed the same idea at chip development: instrument the design flow, the simulations, the fab and even the chips in the field, then let AI find the patterns. His headline claim is that AI-driven observability can cut semiconductor design cycles by up to 40%. Fair warning: this is a lightning-length overview of a few minutes, a map of the territory rather than a walkthrough of any one technique.

## The problem is schedule, not curiosity

Desai opens with the pain: in his figures, 87% of semiconductor projects run late and over budget, often by several million dollars. In an industry where a slipped tape-out pushes back a product launch, that hits time to market, profitability and how fast the next generation arrives. The pitch for observability here is business-first: faster launches, lower operating cost, and chips that perform better once deployed.

The abstract adds a 22% yield improvement to the 40% cycle-time figure. The talk presents both as the potential of the approach rather than results from a single named project.

## Seven places to put the sensors

The core of the talk is a list of seven areas where monitoring plus AI applies:

1. **Design automation monitoring**: real-time feedback during design so issues surface early, with workloads optimised dynamically for compute efficiency.
2. **Predictive telemetry**: pattern recognition over multidimensional sensor data to detect critical design anomalies and reduce physical testing.
3. **Automated design rule verification**: tools that keep learning from complex design patterns, flagging errors and suggesting context-aware fixes.
4. **Performance and power optimisation**: adaptive frequency scaling and proactive thermal management, which low-power designs live or die by.
5. **Simulation with digital twins**: near-complete test coverage across electrical, thermal and mechanical domains.
6. **Yield optimisation**: manufacturing telemetry across more than a hundred process parameters, with ML spotting defect patterns.
7. **Edge device performance**: telemetry from deployed chips under real-world conditions, used to tune ML performance and battery life.

For software observability people, the shape is familiar. Items 1 to 3 are shift-left testing, item 5 is staging, item 6 is production metrics, and item 7 is real user monitoring for silicon.

## Roll it out like any other platform

The implementation roadmap is three phases: an assessment with gap analysis and measurable KPIs, an integration phase that brings in observability tools with minimal workflow disruption and team training, and an optimisation phase where AI insights refine processes, feed predictive models and spread knowledge across product lines. Desai closes by calling AI-powered observability practical today, not a future concept.

## Who should watch

Engineers in or near hardware (EDA, verification, test, product engineering) who want a compact framing for where AI monitoring fits in their flow, and software observability folks curious how their ideas travel to silicon. If you want implementation detail, pair it with one of the deeper hardware talks below; this one is the table of contents.

Title: Your observability stack is an attack surface, so threat model it
Description: SoFi security engineer Srikanth Potla applies STRIDE to logs, metrics and traces at Conf42 Observability 2025 and sets hard baselines for monitoring pipelines.
Body:
The tool that can scrape every environment in your company is also the best lateral movement path an attacker could ask for. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Srikanth Potla, Senior Product Security Engineer at SoFi, turned the threat-modelling lens on observability itself: agents, transport, storage, dashboards and alerting. His argument is that monitoring infrastructure usually sits in a security blind spot, and that a few non-negotiable baselines close most of it.

## Telemetry is reconnaissance for the other side

Potla starts from the attacker's view. Adversaries look for the dark corners where their activity won't be logged. Worse, your observability data is intelligence for them: metrics, logs and traces reveal architecture, service dependencies and entry points. His image: a blueprint of your house left on the front porch. And because systems change, a dashboard deployed six months ago may be exposing data nobody anticipated.

Each of the three pillars leaks differently. Metrics expose architecture, logs may contain sensitive data, and traces reveal business logic and data flows.

## Three layers of risk, four motives

He describes observability pipelines as a three-layer cake. At collection, outdated agents run with excessive privileges and send data unencrypted. In transport, missing TLS, poor certificate management and weak cipher suites invite interception. In storage, the central system becomes a high-value target, with weak access controls and unpatched time series databases.

Attackers come for four reasons: reconnaissance through exposed dashboards; exfiltration of PII and secrets that ended up in logs (he's seen API keys and database credentials in plain text); alert flooding, triggering false positives so the real incident drowns; and living off the land, using your monitoring tools' privileges for lateral movement.

## STRIDE, mapped to monitoring

The centrepiece applies STRIDE to observability:

- **Spoofing**: fake metrics injected to skew data or hide activity. Authenticate every agent.
- **Tampering**: telemetry altered in transit or at rest. Use cryptographic integrity checks.
- **Repudiation**: audit logs deleted or modified. Build immutable logging pipelines.
- **Information disclosure**: sensitive metrics visible to the wrong people. Lock down dashboards and APIs.
- **Denial of service**: overloaded collectors blind you during an attack. Rate limit and add redundancy.
- **Elevation of privilege**: over-permissioned agents. Apply least privilege.

Before STRIDE, he recommends mapping the attack surface: list every observability component and data flow, mark trust boundaries (a Prometheus server reaching into several environments is one), catalogue entry points such as APIs, dashboards, agent channels and webhook receivers, and prioritise by impact, since a compromised central logging system is not the same as a compromised edge agent.

## One plausible breach, four steps

His scenario is uncomfortably believable. An outdated Grafana instance with public dashboards gives initial access and a map of the network. API keys logged in plain text, plus broadly permissioned monitoring service accounts, provide credentials. Prometheus, which already has network access everywhere for scraping, becomes the pivot into production. Then data leaves through custom metric queries, which look exactly like normal monitoring traffic.

## Baselines with numbers on them

Potla's minimums are concrete: 100% of telemetry encrypted in transit, multi-factor authentication on every monitoring dashboard, a 30-day maximum rotation for monitoring credentials, and zero secrets in logs, enforced with scrubbing and secret detection. For alerting, he treats the notification path as critical infrastructure: correlation rules to cut false positives, severity tiers where security alerts bypass throttling, and the same rigour for Slack webhooks, email servers and pagers as for public apps. The action plan: run an observability threat assessment, secure collection, transport and storage by risk, feed observability into the SOC, and track metrics like failed dashboard logins and credential rotation compliance.

## Who should watch

Anyone who runs Grafana, Prometheus or an OpenTelemetry collector fleet, and security engineers who've never been invited into the observability design review. It's a framework talk, but the baselines and the attack chain are easy to turn into tickets this week.

Title: Informatica filters telemetry at the source and lets AI run the pipes
Description: Kirti Ranjan Parida and Sarav Jagadeesan show at Conf42 Observability 2025 how Informatica cut telemetry noise with OpenTelemetry filters and AI agents.
Body:
Sixty terabytes of logs a day is the point where every unnecessary log line has a network bill attached. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Sarav Jagadeesan, Director of Platform Engineering and Infrastructure, and Kirti Ranjan Parida, DevOps Architect, both at Informatica, described how they rebuilt the company's telemetry pipeline: filter at the agent, shape data centrally, and use AI agents (with a human approving) to build and maintain the pipelines themselves. The payoff they describe is lower cost, faster dashboards and lower MTTR.

## The scale that forced the rethink

Jagadeesan opens with Informatica's footprint: four hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle), around 20 regions, more than 600 Kubernetes clusters and thousands of nodes and VMs. That produces about 60 TB of logs every day and 3.8 trillion documents ingested a month, with roughly 15 PB stored on S3.

The old design shipped logs from every region and availability zone into a central Kafka queue, then into the data store, visualised in Kibana, Grafana and a homegrown analytics tool. At that volume it meant rising cost, operational overhead and slow dashboards.

## The expensive part is the collector, not the backend

Parida's key finding: after adding a central telemetry pipeline, they realised most of the cost came from the agents collecting logs and shipping them across the network, where NAT gateway and transfer fees pile up. So the fix moved left. They standardised on an OpenTelemetry-based agent with filters (and ML models) at the source to drop noise before it ever crosses the network; the talk credits that step with about a 20% reduction.

The central pipeline then reshapes what's left:

- **Logs that are really metrics** get converted and stored in the metrics system, which is far cheaper than storing them as logs.
- **High-volume, low-value data** such as health checks gets downsampled to a summary.
- **PII** gets masked in one central place before long-term storage.

Less data means lower cardinality, faster search and dashboards, and lower storage and backup costs. A single agent covers all telemetry signals and is managed by fleet management, so config changes don't mean touching every host.

## AI agents build the pipelines, humans approve them

The catch with all this control was the human effort to create pipelines, maintain them and keep up with new data patterns. Informatica's answer is an AI agent that takes a natural language request, knows the pipeline transforms and query languages, and can create or modify pipelines and recommend optimisations based on the shape of the data. It doesn't deploy on its own: a human reviews and approves, then the agent rolls it out. That human-in-the-loop design is the detail worth stealing.

A second AI assistant faces the people investigating incidents. Ask in plain language, and it translates to the observability system's query language, correlates traces, metrics and logs, draws a basic visualisation, and can run routine runbooks. Combined with APM context propagation, service maps and ML anomaly detection on response times and error rates, it means you don't need the one expert who knows which dashboard to open on every incident call. That's where the MTTR improvement comes from.

## Who should watch

Platform and observability teams paying for telemetry at multi-cloud scale, especially anyone who has only optimised the backend. The talk is architectural rather than a code walkthrough, but the sequence (filter at source, convert logs to metrics, downsample, mask, then automate with a human gate) is directly reusable.

Title: GoFr wires tracing, metrics and health checks into gRPC for you
Description: GoFr contributor Divya Darshana demos at Conf42 Observability 2025 how the Go framework makes gRPC servers, clients and streams observable with zero instrumentation.
Body:
gRPC is fast, strongly typed and great at streaming, and out of the box it tells you almost nothing about what's happening inside those binary pipes. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Divya Darshana, an open source contributor to GoFr, the opinionated Go framework from GoFr.dev, demoed how GoFr closes that gap: every gRPC call, unary or streaming, gets logged, traced and measured, and health checks are registered, without writing a line of instrumentation code. It's a framework talk by a contributor, so expect GoFr front and centre.

## Why gRPC needs help

Darshana starts with the reasons teams pick gRPC: HTTP/2 multiplexing, protobuf binary serialisation, language-agnostic contracts that make schema mismatches rare, and bidirectional, client and server streaming. Then the catch: by default there's no request visibility and no health checks. Her analogy is driving blindfolded at night, fast and with no idea what's ahead.

The blind spots she lists are familiar to anyone who has run gRPC in production. No distributed tracing, so a request that touches 5, 10 or 20 services leaves a fragmented picture. Unstructured, context-free logs that turn a simple bug into a day of grepping. No latency, error rate or volume metrics, so a latency spike on a payment service or a silently failing streaming pipeline goes unnoticed until something downstream complains. Teams then spend weeks hand-instrumenting services to stitch the story together.

## The demo: proto in, observable server out

The live part is short and concrete. Start with a `greet.proto` service definition and run the protobuf compiler, which produces the usual `greet.pb.go` and `greet_grpc.pb.go`. Those files work, but they carry no observability and no health checks.

Then install the GoFr CLI and run its `wrap grpc server` command against the proto file. It generates several files next to the proto; the only one you edit is the server template, already wired with GoFr's context, observability hooks and health checks. Implement the handler (here, take a user's info and reply with a greeting), register the service with the GoFr app in `main.go`, and run it.

Call it from Postman and the request shows up in the logs. Metrics are exposed on a `/metrics` endpoint on port 2121, and traces, both built-in and custom, appear in the configured trace exporter. The GoFr context inside each handler also gives access to connected databases, metrics, logs and traces, so custom spans and DB calls don't need extra plumbing.

## Health checks that Kubernetes can use

GoFr adds a health service to every gRPC server, registered for the server as a whole and for each individual service. A health request against the server returns overall status; one against a named service returns just that service. You can also set a service's serving status at runtime, temporarily marking it unfit to serve and bringing it back, which maps neatly onto Kubernetes readiness checks.

## Streams get spans per message

The section that will interest gRPC veterans is streaming, where observability is usually weakest. GoFr instruments server, client and bidirectional streams the same way. In a chat service example, each message sent or received becomes its own span, and stream duration, message counts and in-stream errors are captured automatically. Clients built with GoFr's client wrapper get auto-instrumented upstream calls too, so the call graph is traceable across services.

## Who should watch

Go developers building gRPC microservices who are tired of copy-pasting interceptors, and teams evaluating Go frameworks. If you already have a mature OpenTelemetry interceptor setup, the streaming and health check parts are still worth a look. The docs and examples live at gofr.dev, and the project invites contributors.

Title: Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 - when "don't" means nothing to your embeddings
Description: Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 in review, 136 talks on embedding blind spots, LLM evaluation, tiny models, agents, guardrails and ML in finance and health.
Body:
[Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) went out on May 8, 2025 with 136 talks, enough to fill a long weekend of viewing. Under the volume sat a sensible mood: less awe at what models can do, more scrutiny of where they quietly fail and what it takes to run them somewhere real. Speakers came from Google DeepMind, Microsoft, Meta, AWS, NVIDIA, Dropbox, Samsung Research, Expedia Group, Palo Alto Networks, Walmart, JPMorgan Chase and many more.

## Your model is more confident than it should be

The talk most likely to change how you build RAG came from [Ritesh Modi](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Ritesh_Modi_embedding_models_language) (Microsoft). In *Hallucination by Design* he shows test results where embedding models treat "take medication" and "don't take medication" as the same thing, then walks through the patterns that cause it and how to make GenAI systems more reliable anyway. Negation, it turns out, is a rounding error in vector space.

[Alok Ranjan and Saurabh Suman](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Alok_Ranjan_Saurabh_Suman_modern_approaches_bleu) (Dropbox, San José State University) argued that BLEU and ROUGE can't measure what modern LLMs do, and moved through benchmarks like MMLU and TruthfulQA to real-world and human-in-the-loop evaluation. [Andrei Stroganov and Andrei Visochan](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Andrei_Stroganov_Andrei_Visochan_estimation_regression_confidence) (Samsung Research) took the mathematical route: fast, real-time confidence estimation for classification and regression models using C++ compile-time numerical integration. [Gaurav Bansal](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Gaurav_Bansal_evaluation_enterprise_language) covered scalable evaluation and QA for enterprise LLMs.

## Small models, tight budgets

Not every model gets an H100. [Max Navrotsky and Oleksandr Gordieiev](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Max_Navrotsky_Oleksandr_Gordieiev_llms_optimization_devices) (VGS, Lutsk National Technical University) shrank GPT-2 for very weak hardware with pruning, quantisation and fine-tuning. [Hitesh Saai Mananchery](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Hitesh_Saai_Mananchery_compression_pixel_video) (Expedia Group) presented R2S, an ML approach to video compression that removes frame redundancy by tracking pixel shifts. At the other end of the scale, [Praneel Madabushini](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Praneel_Madabushini_tesla_openai) (NVIDIA) looked at how Kubernetes handles resource-hungry AI and ML workloads, with lessons drawn from Tesla and OpenAI, and [Bhaskar Goyal](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Bhaskar_Goyal_enterprise_cloud_patterns) (Google) covered architectural patterns for cloud-native AI at scale.

## Agents, with and without guardrails

[Naman Goyal](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Naman_Goyal_generation_text_agentic) (Google DeepMind) traced the move from passive text generators to agents that make decisions and act on their environment. [Alex Shershebnev](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Alex_Shershebnev_code_agents_coding) (Zencoder) got practical about AI coding agents and how to build them, and [Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Samuel_Baruffi_chatbots_bedrock_enterprise) (AWS) showed Amazon Bedrock Agents orchestrating enterprise workflows with access to business data and APIs. [Mohamed Najaaf](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Mohamed_Najaaf_guardrails_responsible_bedrock) (AWS) followed with the brakes: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for responsible AI. [Laly Bar-Ilan](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Laly_BarIlan_language_components_understand) (Bit) proposed composable components as the shared language between developers, non-technical teams and AI, so an agent can build features from product intent while humans stay in the loop.

For anyone still fuzzy on the basics, [Veliswa Boya](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Veliswa_Boya_rag_embeddings_vector) (AWS) gave a good first talk on vector embeddings and RAG, and [Sergey Polyashov](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sergey_Polyashov_recommendation_search_scalable) (Microsoft) did the same for search and recommendation systems, trade-offs and pitfalls included.

## ML where mistakes have consequences

Trust and safety got serious treatment. [Georgina Tryfou](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Georgina_Tryfou_moderation_scalable_safety) (Gcore) described an AI system for detecting and moderating harmful content such as CSAM in near real time, with privacy built into the design. [Lianne Potter](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Lianne_Potter_bias_builders_history) (Compromising Positions) went back to the early builders of AI to show how their choices about bias and power still shape what we build. [Arun Vivek Supramanian](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Arun_Vivek_Supramanian_privacy_engineering_ethical) (Amazon) covered privacy, bias and fairness from the data engineering side.

Finance and healthcare filled whole tracks. Highlights include [Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Venkateswarlu_Boggavarapu_fraud_detection_db_graph) (JPMorganChase) on graph databases for fraud detection, [Surendra Lakkaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Surendra_Lakkaraju_ecommerce_fraud) (Amazon) on real-time e-commerce fraud detection, [Sandeep Gourneni](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sandeep_Gourneni_banking_optimization) (Hitachi Digital Services) on LLM-assisted legacy banking code transformation, and [Sachin Telalwar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sachin_Telalwar_compliance_healthcare) (Zocdoc) on secure distributed healthcare systems.

## ML out in the world

Some of the most memorable talks left the data centre. [Aroma Rodrigues](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Aroma_Rodrigues_imagination_source_journey) (Microsoft) told the story of an open source journey that began in 2016 with a shoe for visually impaired people, built from an Arduino, an Android phone and an unreasonable amount of optimism. [Dmytro Hlotenko](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Dmytro_Hlotenko_photography_community_serverless) (APA-IT) processed 8,000 event photos in real time on AWS AI and serverless at Community Day DACH 2024, sorting them and delivering them back to the community. [Avraam Tolmidis](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Avraam_Tolmidis_traffic_smart_systems) (Meta) applied multi-agent systems and predictive optimisation to urban traffic, and [Karthikeyan Rajamani](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Karthikeyan_Rajamani_iot_accoustic_analysis) (Thomson Reuters) listened to machines, literally, with IoT acoustic analysis for predictive maintenance.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/) at Gold and [APA Tech](https://apa.at/about/apa-tech/) at Silver. All 136 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDbH1VBaoA60lLAAVqmiLPe). Start with Modi's embedding tests; you will look at your retrieval results differently afterwards.

Title: Let a robot customer find the outage before a real one does
Description: Telstra DevOps engineer Palak Bhawsar explains synthetic monitoring at Conf42 Observability 2025, from monitor types to thresholds that won't bury you in alerts.
Body:
Palak Bhawsar's team once had a payment gateway API crash at 2 AM and only found out when 50 customers complained. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Bhawsar, a DevOps Engineer at Telstra and technical blogger, used that night as the case for synthetic monitoring: scripted robots that click, submit and call your APIs around the clock from around the world, so the first person to notice a failure is on your team. It's a clear introduction, aimed at people setting up their first synthetic checks.

## Traditional monitoring waits for something to break

The contrast she draws is simple. Classic monitoring is reactive: it tells you once the thing is broken, often once a user has already hit it. Synthetic monitoring simulates the user's interaction every minute, every five minutes, or whatever interval you pick, from multiple regions. Think of it as a robot customer that never sleeps and never files angry support tickets.

Why now? Bhawsar gives three reasons: systems made of microservices, serverless functions and APIs have more ways to fail; users expect instant responses (she cites a 2024 study claiming a two-second delay makes 20% of customers leave); and your users are spread across countries, so a check from one region proves very little. She also cites market forecasts for synthetic monitoring growing from $1.42 billion in 2024 to about $3.78 billion by 2033, driven by cloud adoption, AI in monitoring tools and the shift from reactive to proactive.

## Five monitors, five questions

The talk's taxonomy is a handy checklist:

- **API monitors**: is the endpoint up and returning a 200?
- **Browser monitors**: can a simulated user add to cart and pay?
- **Scripted monitors**: does a fixed multi-step journey (log in, add to cart, place the order) work end to end?
- **Ping monitors**: is the server reachable at all?
- **SSL/TLS certificate monitors**: is the certificate still valid, or did it quietly expire on a Sunday?

## Start from the journey you can't afford to lose

Her implementation steps start with the business, not the tool. Identify the critical user journeys: for a healthcare app that's booking an appointment or reaching a prescription, for a bank it's moving money between accounts. Script those flows end to end, pick a tool that fits (she names New Relic, Dynatrace and Datadog), schedule runs around the clock from the locations your users are in, and review the results regularly so last night's failure becomes next sprint's fix.

What to look for in a tool: multi-region testing, integration with the rest of your observability stack (logs, traces, metrics), custom scripting in the languages your team uses, and AI-driven insights. Bhawsar gives a personal example of the last one: a null pointer exception buried in a large Java codebase that an AI feature pinned to the exact method.

## Thresholds decide whether anyone reads the alerts

The best-practice section is where the experience shows. Set realistic thresholds: a non-critical app can fail once or twice a day, a payment or banking flow can't fail even once. Alert only on critical issues, because alerting on everything is how the one that matters gets missed. And validate full flows, not single features: add-to-cart working doesn't mean a customer can complete a payment.

## Who should watch

Developers and junior SREs who own uptime but don't yet have synthetic checks, and teams who have them but only ping the homepage. Experienced observability engineers will find it introductory. Either way, it's a good prompt to write down your top three critical journeys and check whether anything tests them at 2 AM.

- Natalie Lunbeck on [E2E Test Before Merge](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Natalie_Lunbeck_e2e_test_merge), the same journeys tested earlier in the pipeline.
- Gil Zilberfeld on [Playwright In An Hour](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Gil_Zilberfeld_26_playwright_automation_testing), a common engine for scripted browser checks.
- Amith Reddy Ravuru on [Platform SLOs Beyond Uptime: Measuring the Journey from Request to Value](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2026_Amith_Reddy_Ravuru_slos_uptime_journey).

Title: Serverless ML inference pays off until the cold start bites
Description: Shreya Gupta of the University of Southern California weighs serverless AI deployment at Conf42 Observability 2025, from platform benchmarks to cold starts.
Body:
Thirty-eight dedicated servers running at about a third of their capacity is the kind of number that makes a finance team ask questions. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Shreya Gupta of the University of Southern California made the case for serverless AI, where ML models run as stateless functions that scale with demand and bill only for execution time. She backs it with benchmark figures, two industry case studies and, to her credit, a full section on where serverless falls over.

The numbers in the talk come from the studies and case reports she presents; treat them as the speaker's sources rather than your next SLA.

## Event in, prediction out

Gupta's architecture is the standard serverless loop applied to ML. Event sources (an API request, a data change, a scheduled job) trigger function containers that hold the model code. Because each invocation is stateless, the platform can run them in parallel and scale automatically, while managed services handle authentication, storage and monitoring. Her analogy: power is only on while you hold the light switch.

The implementation cycle is model encapsulation (package the model in a function, usually behind an HTTP inference endpoint), deployment with its trigger configuration, execution, and automatic scaling up and down. She notes that models from 75 MB up to 1.8 GB are being served this way.

## The platform choice is mostly a cold start choice

The most practical slide compares the big clouds using benchmark studies with identical models (ResNet-50, BERT base, YOLOv4). In those numbers, Google Cloud Functions had the lowest average inference latency for image classification at 112 ms and the fastest cold start, AWS Lambda followed at 136 ms with SnapStart helping Java cold starts and GPU support limited to T4, Azure Functions had the most consistent cold starts plus container-based GPU support, and IBM Cloud Functions trailed on both counts without direct GPU support.

The lesson she draws is about cold starts: the delay when a function wakes after idling matters most for GPU-accelerated functions, so your latency sensitivity should drive the platform pick.

## Two migrations, told with numbers

The case studies are where the cost story lives. A global investment bank moved risk analysis off those 38 underused servers over about four and a half months; the talk reports 68.2% lower infrastructure cost and average risk-analysis latency falling from 8.2 to 3.1 seconds, plus better audit trails for regulators. A healthcare diagnostics provider, previously waiting an average of 86 days to expand capacity, moved containerised imaging models to serverless over seven months; model update cycles reportedly dropped from 36 days to 4.8, with autoscaling handling swings from 50 to 5,000 images an hour without manual intervention.

## Where serverless still hurts

Gupta lists the limits plainly. Cold starts for complex deep learning models can reach 6.2 seconds. Memory caps constrain model size. Execution time limits cut off long-running jobs. Vendor lock-in makes moving from one cloud to another expensive. And CPU and memory options per function are narrower than a dedicated VM, which matters for large or specialised models. On security, she points to function isolation, fine-grained IAM at the function level and short-lived credentials as the defences that carry most of the weight.

Her future section sketches "nano functions" that execute parts of a computational graph instead of a whole model, standardised function interfaces to ease lock-in, and lighter container formats for AI.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and platform teams deciding where to host inference for spiky, request-driven workloads. If your models are huge, long-running or latency-critical on first request, the limitations section is the part to take to your design review. If they're small and bursty, the case studies are your business case.

- Gangadharan Venkataraman on [developer-centric ML inference platforms on Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Gangadharan_Venkataraman_inference_orchestration_kubernetes), the non-serverless alternative.
- Murali Krishna Reddy Mandalapu on [optimizing real-time AI inference at the edge](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Murali_Krishna_Reddy_Mandalapu_ai_inference_edge).

Title: Teaching machines to recognize the unseen
Description: Prediction in motion
Body:
# Machine learning is doing… a lot

Machine learning used to be a niche.

Now it’s everywhere. Finance, healthcare, retail, cloud, security, HR, supply chains, marketing, manufacturing, smart cities, and probably something involving your fridge. Subtle.

Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 leans fully into that scale.

This is a big conference. One hundred plus talks across twenty tracks, covering everything from core ML concepts to full-blown AI systems running in production. You’ll find sessions on agents, generative AI, analytics, architecture, cloud, data engineering, security, testing, and the slightly terrifying joy of putting models where real decisions are made.

There’s a strong focus on real-world ML. Fraud detection at scale, healthcare platforms, financial risk modeling, recommendation systems, supply chain forecasting, and enterprise data pipelines all show up. Less “look what the model can do” and more “here’s how we made this work without breaking everything”.

Generative AI and LLMs are everywhere, of course. Evaluation, hallucinations, embeddings, RAG, agents, optimization, and running models on everything from massive clusters to very small devices. Several talks focus on keeping things safe, explainable, and compliant once the hype wears off.

The program also makes room for the human side of ML. Ethics, bias, accessibility, trust, governance, and what happens when AI systems start influencing people, products, and policies at scale. There are talks that zoom out, and others that go deep into very specific problems.

If machine learning is part of your job, your roadmap, or your long-term existential questions, this one’s for you. It’s broad, practical, and very honest about the fact that ML is no longer optional or simple.

Welcome to the mess.

Title: Trace every step of identity verification, not just the login
Description: Shikha Gurjar of Guidewire Software shows at Conf42 Observability 2025 how tracing, correlation and behavioural baselines make identity checks observable.
Body:
A document scan that passes, a selfie match that's slightly off and a database check that's a little inconsistent each look fine on their own. Together they can be a spoofing attempt. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Shikha Gurjar, Technical Project Manager for Essential Services at Guidewire Software and ten years into the property and casualty insurance industry, explained how instrumenting identity verification end to end turns that black box into something teams can see, correlate and act on in real time.

## Identity verification is a distributed system

Gurjar's framing is that a modern identity check is a pipeline of services: biometrics (fingerprint, face or voice), AI analysis of the process, sometimes blockchain for an audit trail, and a lot of third-party calls. Observable identity systems instrument each step, capturing biometric results, response times and error patterns, and feed them into monitoring and alerting so a failed verification or a suspicious login shows up in minutes rather than days.

The talk puts a number on the payoff: an 87% cut in the time it takes to identify a problem. It also credits modern observable systems with catching sophisticated spoofing, fake IDs and deepfakes, at 99.99% accuracy. Those are the speaker's figures for the industry; the talk doesn't break down where they were measured.

## Five spans that tell the whole story

The clearest section is a worked distributed tracing example for an online verification:

1. **Document upload**: how long it took, whether the file arrived, logs on errors.
2. **Document validation**: authenticity, expiry and tamper checks, pass or fail, processing time.
3. **Biometric matching**: the selfie comparison time and the match confidence score.
4. **Data verification**: each external call to government databases or credit bureaus, timed, so third-party delays stand out.
5. **Risk assessment**: how the inputs flowed into the trust score and which rule raised a flag.

With that trace you can tell that biometric matching is consistently the slow step, or that document validation crashes intermittently, before customers notice. It's the same playbook as tracing a checkout flow, applied to a domain where a slow step is also a fraud signal.

## Baselines catch the attacker with the right password

Two techniques sit on top of the traces. Correlation engines link events across steps and learn normal patterns (time taken, device type, match scores), so small deviations get flagged together instead of being dismissed one by one. Behavioural anomaly detection goes further: learn what normal looks like per user or group (login times, devices, locations, upload habits), score each action by how far it strays, and trigger adaptive authentication when the score crosses a threshold. That can mean an OTP, a manual review or blocking the action outright. The point is catching attacks where the credentials are correct.

## Privacy is a design constraint, not a footnote

All this telemetry is sensitive by definition, and Gurjar spends real time on it: collect only what's needed, anonymise or encrypt personal data, be transparent about what's collected, and design for privacy by default. Her roadmap is phased: assess current telemetry and blind spots, instrument the identity workflow, integrate alerts and adaptive responses, then refine the models and baselines. A full rollout takes six to twelve months in her estimate, with benefits visible after two to three if you go incrementally.

## Who should watch

Engineers building onboarding or KYC flows in insurance, banking or anywhere fraud is a cost line, and SREs who already trace payments and want to extend the habit to identity. It's a strategy talk without code. If you only take one thing, take the five-span trace and draw it for your own verification flow.

Title: From MELT data to AIOps, one AWS service at a time
Description: Manik Kashikar of Thoughtworks maps full-stack observability and AIOps onto CloudWatch, X-Ray and DevOps Guru at Conf42 Observability 2025.
Body:
A checkout spike is rarely a frontend problem; it's often a database lock timeout or a flaky third-party payment API that nobody connected to the user's spinning button. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Manik Kashikar of Thoughtworks walked through how to get from siloed monitoring to full-stack observability and then to AIOps, with the AWS services that cover each step. It's a strategy-level talk with an AWS reference stack, not a hands-on demo.

## Visibility is the thing most teams don't have

Kashikar opens with a figure from a state of observability report: 89% of organisations say they still lack complete visibility into their systems, despite running several tools. Tool sprawl, long MTTR and exploding telemetry volume all push costs up. His ask is to treat observability as a first-class citizen, which means understanding why the system behaves as it does in real time, and ideally what it will do next.

The foundation is the MELT stack (metrics, events, logs, traces), but the value appears when you correlate those across application, infrastructure, business and user experience domains.

## The maturity curve ends at business context

His maturity model goes from siloed monitoring (logs and metrics without context) to telemetry tied to business KPIs like uptime, revenue impact and churn, and finally to full-stack observability, where infrastructure, applications, digital experience and business context are stitched together. The illustrative example: a 40 millisecond rise in response time that costs 2% in conversions is a business problem, not a graph.

To get there, he argues for two lenses at once. Outside-in captures what users experience: slow pages, failed transactions, latency. Inside-out surfaces backend response times, slow database queries, memory spikes and API gateway bottlenecks. Real observability joins the two, so the checkout spike points straight at the lock timeout.

## The AWS kit, layer by layer

For the observability layer, the talk maps the pieces: CloudWatch for native metrics and logs, X-Ray for distributed tracing across microservices, CloudWatch Synthetics to mimic user journeys and catch issues before customers do, and CloudWatch RUM for frontend latency and Core Web Vitals. The value, he says, is in composite dashboards that correlate them, for instance CloudWatch alarms with X-Ray traces to isolate bottlenecks.

## AIOps is observe, learn, act

Once telemetry is flowing in volume, AIOps is the natural next step. Kashikar breaks it into three pillars: observe (ingest clean, structured MELT data), learn (ML models for outliers, seasonality and failure prediction) and act (alert suppression, ticketing, dynamic scaling, even rollbacks). The example: if CPU spikes are always followed by database timeouts, the system learns the relationship, suppresses the noise and highlights the root cause.

On AWS, that means DevOps Guru for ML-powered operational insights, CloudWatch anomaly detection on time series metrics, and X-Ray Insights to tie traces to error rates. Chained together, DevOps Guru can spot a performance anomaly, link it to the failing X-Ray segment and fire an SNS alert into your incident management system.

He's candid about what slows teams down (data quality, integration complexity, resistance to change) and frames the outcome as fewer tickets and faster root cause, with every incident becoming training data.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and architects on AWS who need a maturity model and a service map to justify the next observability investment. If you already run DevOps Guru in anger, you'll know most of this; if you're still on per-team dashboards, it's a solid roadmap. Other clouds have equivalents, and he says so.

- Mandi Walls on [Tackling Alert Fatigue with SLOs](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Mandi_Walls_tackling_alert_fatigue), the non-ML way to cut noise.

Title: Modular architecture is a boundary problem before a tooling one
Description: Wayfair engineer Anusha Reddy Guntakandla lays out modular architecture at Conf42 Observability 2025, from encapsulation to modular monoliths and incremental migration.
Body:
If your order module also sends customer notifications, you don't have modules, you have folders. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Anusha Reddy Guntakandla, Software Engineer at Wayfair, gave a compact tour of modular architecture for enterprise platforms: how to draw module boundaries, which implementation path fits which team, and why the migration should happen one module at a time. It's a short, survey-style talk, best treated as a checklist rather than a war story.

## A module owns a business capability

Guntakandla's definition is the useful starting point: a large application broken into discrete, self-contained modules, each covering one business capability and talking to others through stable interfaces, APIs or message brokers. Think of each module as a bounded context in domain-driven design terms. It owns its own logic and can evolve, build, deploy and scale independently, which also shrinks the blast radius of any one change in CI/CD.

The four traits she lists are textbook but well illustrated:

- **Encapsulation**: a customer module exposes a profile API and hides how it aggregates loyalty points.
- **High cohesion**: everything in a module serves one purpose (hence the order module that shouldn't send notifications).
- **Loose coupling**: asynchronous messages or stable contracts, which nudges you towards event-driven designs.
- **Interface stability**: REST, GraphQL or gRPC contracts kept backward compatible with OpenAPI or protobuf schemas.

## Fault isolation is the design goal you'll feel

Of the design principles, two stand out. Scalability by design: a payments module can scale three times as far as a mostly static help centre module, so you pay for capacity where the load is. And fault isolation: if the inventory service fails, checkout should still proceed on estimated quantities or cached data. That one sentence is a better argument for modularity than most architecture diagrams.

Maintainability gets a concrete example too: refactoring one module from PHP to Node.js without touching the rest.

## Three ways to get there

The talk compares three implementation paths. Microservices give each service its own codebase, database and pipeline, and suit domains with strong service boundaries. A modular monolith is a single deployable unit organised internally as modules, which she recommends for early-stage teams or when deployment overhead needs to stay low, with the option to split later. Plugin architectures, common in CMS and e-commerce engines, load features at runtime. Her advice is to choose with a decision matrix based on deployment frequency, team size and service criticality.

The illustrative e-commerce case reports a product catalogue moved to a standalone Elasticsearch-backed service with 47% faster queries, a CQRS-based order module with retries and circuit breakers, and a plug-in recommendation engine credited with a 15% lift in product discovery.

## The costs are real, so migrate incrementally

Guntakandla doesn't oversell it. Defining boundaries, contracts and pipelines takes effort up front; too many chatty services add latency (bulkheads, caching, batching and connection pooling help); and without clear ownership, teams re-couple modules by accident, which is where tools like Backstage or Compass come in. Her adoption rules: start with domain modelling (event storming, context maps), govern interfaces with registries and contract testing, and never big-bang. Extract one module, define KPIs, validate, then move on.

## Who should watch

Engineers about to propose breaking up a monolith who want a tidy vocabulary and a list of trade-offs to put in the design doc. It's a 101-to-201 overview without code, so senior architects will recognise most of it. The modular-monolith-first advice is the bit worth repeating in meetings.

- Swetha Lakkaraju on [Decoupling Legacy Banking: Modular Core Strategies for Speed, Scale, and Innovation](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Swetha_Lakkaraju_banking_modular_modernization).

Title: Treating a city's 5G network as code, not as ladder work
Description: Anil Thimmapuram at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on applying DevOps and infrastructure as code to 5G small cells, edge nodes and IoT for smart cities.
Body:
In one city, Anil Thimmapuram recalls, updating a traffic light meant sending a person out with a USB stick. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Thimmapuram, a DevOps engineer, made the case that 5G is less about faster video and more about giving cities a network that can be deployed, tested and rolled back like software.

It is a short, upbeat talk built around one deployment story. The numbers he shares he calls approximate, and he does not name the city, so read it as a practitioner's account rather than a case study with an appendix.

## The problem is cities running on timers

The opening picture is easy to recognize: traffic lights on fixed timers from another decade, power grids that are always on whether anyone needs them or not, and emergency vehicles following a GPS route with no live data about the jam ahead. Inefficient, he says, but also dangerous and expensive, since every change needs someone on site.

His fix combines three things: 5G small cells and edge computing for low latency, a dense IoT layer for sensing, and DevOps practice for running all of it.

## DevOps for routers, not just microservices

This is the sharpest idea in the talk. Usually DevOps means CI/CD for application code. Thimmapuram's team pointed it at the network itself. Every router, switch and edge node was defined as code. Terraform plans spun up 5G clusters on AWS, Helm charts configured edge services, and pipelines automatically tested latency, bandwidth and even failure cases before anything went live.

The cultural change fits in one line: instead of sending someone up a ladder, push to prod. He credits the automation with cutting deployment time by 85% and, just as important, giving the network rollback options that traditional networking did not have. Anyone who has ever reverted a bad router config by driving to the data center will appreciate that last part.

## Sub-10 ms needs the compute on the light pole

For a city to react in real time, he targets latency under 10 milliseconds. That meant small cells on light poles, buildings and buses (anywhere with power and fiber backhaul) and edge nodes doing local processing instead of a round trip to a distant cloud region. That is what enables live video analytics and instant alerts: a camera spots a fire, traffic is rerouted and ambulances get a clear path.

On top sits the IoT layer, up to 10,000 connected endpoints per square mile: smart meters, pollution sensors, cameras, emergency buttons, EV chargers. His favourite example: sensors picked up an air-quality spike and school buses were rerouted away from it with no human in the loop.

## Traffic, power and the rollout

With AI-driven video analysis, traffic lights adapted to conditions instead of timers, green waves reduced stop-and-go, and emergency corridors opened dynamically. On the power side, IoT meters balanced the grid: charging EV stations when solar output was high, running street lights from stored batteries at night, and shifting load when a neighbourhood surged.

The rollout was deliberately phased: an assessment that mapped every duct, pole and antenna; an automation framework with CI/CD pipelines for infrastructure; a pilot in dense downtown zones; then a parallel citywide rollout using infrastructure as code, with each deployment validating itself.

The approximate results he reports: commute times down about a quarter, emergency response 42% faster, 35% energy savings, a 28% drop in carbon output and a 64% rise in resident satisfaction. The team then open-sourced the blueprint as modular, vendor-neutral playbooks with a training program, and he says they are working with more than 15 cities, adding privacy-focused designs.

## Who should watch

Platform and network engineers curious about infrastructure as code beyond the usual cloud estate, and anyone working on smart-city or telecom programs who needs a short, motivating story. If you want architecture diagrams, Terraform modules or a methodology for those percentages, the talk stays high level.

Title: Sorting 8,000 conference photos with Rekognition, Lambda and $50
Description: Dmytro Hlotenko at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on the serverless AWS pipeline that culled and edited 8,000 AWS Community Day DACH photos for about $50.
Body:
Every event photographer knows the real work starts after the event: thousands of frames, most of them blinks and blur. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Dmytro Hlotenko, cloud architect at APA-IT, AWS Community Builder and AWS user group leader in Vienna, showed the serverless pipeline he built to cull and edit more than 8,000 photos from AWS Community Day DACH 2024. It cost about $50 to run and turned roughly 4,200 usable candidates over to the marketing team.

It is a personal project told by someone who is both a serious photographer and an AWS engineer, which is exactly why the details are good.

## Getting the files off the camera is half the architecture

Hlotenko shot the day on two Sony bodies at once, an Alpha 9 III and an Alpha 7 IV, in RAW. The first trick is the upload path. Sony cameras can push files over FTPS, a feature built for press photographers at sports events, so he pointed them at an AWS Transfer Family endpoint that writes straight into S3. From there it is standard event-driven plumbing: S3 events, EventBridge, SQS with a dead-letter queue, and two Step Functions workflows (one for processing, one for metadata).

One warning he gives with feeling: Transfer Family is not priced like a serverless service. Leaving the endpoint up cost him over $220 before he noticed. Turn it off when the shoot ends.

## Claude could not tell if eyes were open; Rekognition could

The selection logic copies his own cognitive process: is the main face sharp, are the eyes open, is the pose something anyone would post on LinkedIn. His first attempt handed that judgment to Claude 3.5 through Amazon Bedrock with a picture-editor prompt. It failed on the most basic check. People wearing glasses confused it, and it could not reliably tell open eyes from closed.

So he went back to Amazon Rekognition, which returns the boring numbers he actually needed: sharpness, exposure, face confidence, eyes-open scores. He ran his archive of past community-day and meetup photos through it, compared the scores of shots he had kept against shots he had rejected, and stored the resulting thresholds in DynamoDB for the processing Lambda to read. Speakers needed a higher sharpness bar than general crowd shots. No custom training was needed.

He also kept the Rekognition bill small: DetectFaces and DetectLabels for scoring, DetectModerationLabels as a secondary filter, no IndexFaces, jittered calls to stay under API limits, and burst sequences sent as a batch so four near-identical frames did not cost four full analyses.

## RAW editing in a Lambda beats Fargate here

Culling is only half the job; editing takes longer. Hlotenko wanted the highlight and shadow recovery that only 14-bit RAW files allow, since he shot speakers against bright slides without flash. No commercial editor he uses offered an API, so he wrote a Lambda around the open-source LibRaw library, through a Python wrapper, that reads Sony ARW files directly.

Two details stand out. The Lambda first pulls the small JPEG preview embedded in every RAW file, roughly 1,200 pixels wide, and sends that to Rekognition, which is enough to judge a face and much cheaper than the full frame. And at 1.5 GB of memory the Lambda outperformed a comparable container on Fargate, with the first processed image landing in about ten seconds. Claude Haiku on Bedrock does get a job after all: given the metadata and calibration weights, it suggests the editing strategy, and he was happy with its white balance and highlight decisions.

## The numbers

About 15 to 20 relaxed hours to build, against what he estimates as more than 60 hours of manual sorting and editing saved. Roughly $20 on Rekognition and $30 on Lambda, Step Functions, DynamoDB and Transfer Family for the day, which works out to under a cent per picture. Accepted and rejected shots land in separate buckets, because the machine can still be wrong and a human gets the last look.

## Who should watch

Anyone building event-driven pipelines on AWS who wants a real, small, end-to-end example with costs attached. Photographers who code will enjoy the RAW details. If you need a reason to keep a cheap, specialized vision API around instead of throwing a general LLM at every image task, this talk is a good one.

Title: Letting cars bid for road segments to beat congestion
Description: Avraam Tolmidis of Meta at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on multi-agent traffic routing where vehicles take bids from intersections and re-plan as conditions change.
Body:
What if every car and every intersection negotiated? At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Avraam Tolmidis, Software Engineering Manager at Meta with a PhD focused on multi-objective optimization and four years in automated driving, presented a decentralized traffic system in which vehicle agents ask nearby intersections for bids on the next road segment and keep re-planning as the city changes around them.

It is a research-flavoured talk with a clear algorithm and simulation results, not a product pitch, and Tolmidis (a former teacher) explains it step by step.

## Central traffic control reacts too late

The problem is the one you sat in this morning. Congestion grows with urban population and vehicle counts, infrastructure is outdated or was never built for today's load, and when something happens on the road the response is slow because a human has to detect it and a human has to intervene. The cost is time, fuel and, in the worst cases, lives.

His proposal flips the model. Instead of one system timing lights for everyone, each vehicle is a mobile agent and each intersection a stationary agent. Decisions are mostly local, with optional centralized policies when you want to optimize for a wider area.

## Routing as an auction with weighted objectives

He calls the approach AMOR: adaptive multi-objective optimized routing agents. A vehicle approaching a decision point sends its route request to nearby stationary agents, along with weights for the objectives it cares about: travel time, distance, monetary cost (tolls), emissions, or anything else that makes sense.

Each stationary agent pulls segment data, refreshes estimates when the data is stale, normalizes the values and scores each segment with the weighted objective function. For time, distance and cost, that is simply each weight times its normalized value, summed. A route's cost is the sum of its segments, found with Dijkstra or something fancier, and the agent's bid is its cheapest route. No route, and it returns a negative value. The vehicle picks the lowest positive bid and drives the first segments of that route.

The key word is adaptive. Every few nodes, or whenever congestion or an emergency appears ahead, the vehicle starts a new auction. Stationary agents can also exchange data to sharpen their estimates. Routes evolve with the traffic instead of being fixed at departure, which is roughly what a good taxi driver does with a radio, minus the opinions.

## Re-planning is where the gains show up

Tolmidis ran a few hundred simulations in NetLogo with congestion, emergencies and mixed vehicle types over a fixed distance, comparing three strategies: plain distance-based routing, multi-objective routing planned once at the start, and AMOR with dynamic re-planning.

Both multi-objective approaches came out cheaper than distance-only routing, and both were faster. AMOR was faster still. The biggest difference showed up when congestion hit mid-trip: the other two strategies saw trip duration climb sharply, while AMOR kept the increase under 20%. Planning well at the start helps; being able to change your mind helps more.

## What a city would need

The infrastructure list is concrete. V2X (vehicle-to-everything) communication so vehicles can talk to each other, to smart traffic lights, to adaptive road signs, and even to a pedestrian's phone around the corner. Roadside units acting as the stationary agents. V2X-capable vehicles running the agent software. Local edge terminals for fast computation and a city traffic management center if you want a central view.

He is explicit about the assumptions: the map is known (no live mapping), road segments can carry tolls, historical traffic data exists and keeps being collected, and vehicles know their global position.

The benefits he lists follow from the design: smoother flow and fewer bottlenecks, shorter trips, priority lanes on demand for buses and emergency vehicles (an ambulance negotiating its own green wave), faster rerouting around closures, and lower emissions because there is less stop-and-go.

## Who should watch

Engineers interested in multi-agent systems, optimization or mobility will like the clean auction design and the honest simulation framing. If you want field deployment data, this talk does not claim any; it is a well-explained model with simulated results.

Title: Open source without a strategy is an expensive hobby
Description: Epicmax COO Anastasiia Zvenigorodskaia prices her team's Vue.js open source work at Conf42 Observability 2025 and maps seven ways to make it pay.
Body:
Ten thousand GitHub stars feel like success until you multiply the hours by a developer's rate. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Anastasiia Zvenigorodskaia, co-founder and Chief Operating Officer at Epicmax, did that sum in public for her company's Vue.js projects and arrived at a blunt verdict: without a strategy, any open source project is an expensive hobby. The rest of the talk is the strategy she wishes they had started with, from seven monetisation models to which one fits which stage.

It's an odd one out at an observability conference, and a refreshingly honest one.

## The bill for eight years of stars

Epicmax started open source for a very practical reason: its client work was under NDA, so there was no portfolio. Vuestic Admin, a set of ready-to-use dashboard pages, took off fast, brought in the first commercial clients, and today sits at around 2,000 forks and more than 10,000 stars. Epic Spinners, CSS-only loading animations built because the team wanted to play with CSS, has nearly 4,000 stars. Vuestic UI, the component library extracted from the admin panel, has about 3,600.

Then she prices it, using an average mid-level developer rate for Spain. Vuestic Admin took more than 4,000 hours, roughly 90,000 euros, because "one project" really meant three versions, redesigns as trends changed, bug fixing, Discord support and docs. Epic Spinners, the side project, still cost around 470 hours. Her estimate for Vuestic UI runs to almost half a million euros. Her conclusion after all that: more visibility and a better-looking agency, but they could have achieved much more.

## Seven models, explained with shoes

The monetisation section uses one analogy throughout, which makes it easy to remember:

- **Open core**: free shoes, paid comfort (GitLab, Grafana, Elastic). Attracts users, but drawing the free/paid line is hard and you maintain two versions.
- **SaaS**: free shoes, paid cleaning and delivery (Docker Hub and similar). Recurring revenue, heavy infrastructure and support costs.
- **Dual licensing**: free for a walk in the park, paid if you're a waiter on your feet for 12 hours (MySQL). Protects you from cloud resellers, needs lawyers.
- **Support and consulting**: the shoes are free, the fitting is paid (Red Hat). High-value clients, but you're still selling hours.
- **Plugins and marketplace**: basic black shoes free, red laces extra (WordPress, Grafana).
- **Sponsorship**: people donate because they love your shoes (Blender). Fully open, unstable income.
- **Courses and education**: teach others to make shoes (Linux Foundation, Vue School).

Her observation is that successful projects combine two or three of these.

## Match the model to the stage

Early stage is about users and trust: sponsorship, education and consulting with clear boundaries, and sharing the story long before you hit 1,000 stars. The growing stage needs a clear reason to pay, simple pricing and recurring income, so open core, SaaS or a marketplace. The business stage means licensing, security, compliance, contracts and, yes, sales people doing calls, demos and onboarding, because now you compete with commercial products.

## The mistakes are the useful part

Epicmax's self-diagnosis is specific: no goals before investing, one strategy for three different projects, developers picking tasks by interest because nobody had defined business impact, too little real use of their own products, and a belief that users would simply come. What went right: the projects became an onboarding sandbox for new hires, the team stayed focused on Vue.js, and partnerships with other Vue ecosystem players followed.

## Who should watch

Maintainers wondering whether their side project could pay for itself, and engineering leaders deciding whether to fund one. No code here; the value is the numbers and the frameworks. If you have ever postponed monetisation until later, this is the talk telling you when later is.
