Title: Edge AI for IoT comes down to deploying, updating and shrinking models
Description: Gayathri Jegan Mohan of Microsoft at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on running ML at the IoT edge with portable runtimes, OTA updates, quantization and cloud pipelines.
Body:
Running inference next to the sensor sounds simple until you have ten thousand sensors from six vendors and a new model to ship. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Gayathri Jegan Mohan, Software Engineer at Microsoft, gave a structured introduction to edge AI for IoT: why inference is moving off the cloud, what breaks when it does, and four practices that keep a fleet of constrained devices manageable.

It is a good first talk on the subject. Engineers already shipping TFLite models to Jetsons will recognize most of it; everyone else gets a clean map.

## Why push inference to the edge at all

In the usual IoT setup, devices send data to the cloud, the cloud runs the model, and the result comes back. Edge AI removes those hops by running a pre-trained model on the device. Jegan Mohan lists the payoffs: lower latency for things like traffic-light control or spotting a failing appliance, less bandwidth, better privacy because raw data does not travel (or cross borders), operation with weak or no connectivity, and lower energy use. Her examples are everyday ones: a surveillance camera flagging anomalies locally, a factory robot inspecting parts without uploading images, a smart speaker recognizing your voice on the device.

Her framing number, from the abstract: by 2025, 75% of enterprise data will be processed at the edge.

## What makes the edge hard

The challenge list is honest. Devices have little compute, memory and storage, and many run on batteries, so a full-size ResNet is out. Pushing updates to a large fleet is hard, and version drift is a real risk. Devices on public networks need secure boot and lightweight secure protocols. Connectivity is intermittent, which complicates syncing results back. Compressed models trade away some accuracy. Observability shrinks to simple logs, because a heavy telemetry stack does not fit. And hardware diversity means every vendor brings its own OS and protocols.

## Four practices for running a fleet

**Deploy for portability.** Use portable model formats such as ONNX or TensorFlow Lite so the same model runs across hardware. Target accelerators with unified runtimes (NVIDIA Jetson, Intel, Arm NPUs) and package model plus dependencies in containers so every device behaves the same way. Walmart is her example here: thousands of store cameras running edge-optimized vision models on compact servers such as NVIDIA Jetson to track inventory and restocking.

**Update like a release, not a hotfix.** Over-the-air updates with version control, A/B rollouts to a slice of devices before the rest, and digital twins to test a new model against a virtual copy of the device first. Tesla's OTA pipeline for Autopilot models, with rollback, is her example.

**Shrink the model on purpose.** Quantization from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers for smaller, faster inference on something like a Raspberry Pi; pruning insignificant weights and neurons; and knowledge distillation, where a small student model learns from a larger teacher. Google's MobileNet family, built with quantization and pruning for on-phone image classification that works in airplane mode, illustrates the payoff.

**Keep the cloud for the lifecycle.** The cloud does not leave the picture; it moves behind it. Cloud MLOps pipelines (she names Azure ML and AWS SageMaker) retrain on telemetry collected from the edge, CI/CD automates testing and rollout, and the improved model goes back out. Siemens' predictive maintenance on Azure IoT is the example, with a reported cut in machine downtime.

Each practice gets one real-world example, which makes the talk easy to follow.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects starting an IoT or edge ML project who want the whole problem in one sitting. Teams already running a fleet may find the update and observability sections the most useful checklists. If you came for benchmarks or code, this is not that talk.

Title: How a solo startup designer used Midjourney, Sora and Figma
Description: Nikita Poloznikov, Head of Design at Jazari, at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on the AI image tools that let one designer cover a whole startup.
Body:
Being the only designer at a startup means owning pitch decks, ad creatives, user flows and the app UI at the same time, plus the occasional backend logic discussion. Nikita Poloznikov, Head of Design at Jazari, a remit-now-pay-later financial service, told the story at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) of how he stopped trying to work harder and built an AI image toolkit instead: Stable Diffusion first, then Midjourney 6.1, then OpenAI's image generation in ChatGPT, with Figma for the cleanup.

This is a practitioner's experience report, not an ML talk. There are no benchmarks; there are honest notes on what each tool was good and bad at, from someone who shipped the results in real campaigns.

## Stable Diffusion: good enough for the first pitch deck

In early 2024, Midjourney's web interface was still in closed beta and the main way in was a Discord chat, which Poloznikov found stiff for creative work. He settled on DreamStudio, running Stable Diffusion XL 1.0, for its clean interface and easy prompt experiments. It produced the first assets for early pitch decks and a mock-up of the company's first limited-edition payment card, a prototyping step he calls pivotal for the brand.

The limits were real. Even with negative prompts, getting realistic, non-stereotyped images of people was hard, and outputs came with broken hand anatomy and awkward details that needed heavy retouching. A start, but not something that scaled with a growing company.

## Midjourney 6.1: taste becomes a setting

Version 6.1 and the move to a full web app changed the experience. Two features stand out in his account. Personalisation: rating images during onboarding teaches the model your taste. Aesthetic tuning: stylisation, weirdness and variety controls set how unusual results get. Style references, each with a code, work like a Pinterest board the model can read, so a whole folder of visual DNA can steer new images.

One of his early Midjourney images went into a performance ad on Meta and, by his account, clearly beat the team's standard creatives on click-through. That result pushed the team toward a broader generative content strategy.

The frustration is just as candid. Midjourney often misreads specific instructions about objects, their relationships and textures. At one point he wondered whether hiring a photographer and buying cricket balls would be faster than persuading the model, and the usable image arrived after around 120 variants. Anyone who has argued with a prompt for an afternoon will feel seen.

## Retouch in Figma, because speed matters

Whatever the generator, Poloznikov says the output always needs fixing: weird hands, awkward shadows, inconsistent textures. His advice is to skip heavyweight tools and do quick fixes directly in Figma, which is lightweight and collaborative, since the value comes from iterating quickly rather than perfecting one image. Figma's built-in background remover helps too.

## ChatGPT images: the tool that finally got the brief

OpenAI's image generation, built into ChatGPT, was the breakthrough in his story. With a minimal interface (dimensions, number of outputs, references) and Midjourney-style prompts adapted for it, he found it captured natural skin tones, intentional camera angles, believable expressions and coherent backgrounds without endless re-prompting. That mattered because the brand had shifted toward representing people from many backgrounds. It still struggled with complex scenes of several people interacting in motion, but once controlled it produced polished marketing assets with little editing, plus upscaling and transparent PNG output.

## Lessons that outlast the tool versions

His closing lessons are the reason to watch. Models change fast, so your mindset has to change faster. AI tools empower designers rather than replace them; what separates experts from dabblers is how well they use them. Do not get attached to one tool. And creative intuition, not the gadget, is where a designer's value lies.

## Who should watch

Designers and founders at early-stage companies who need marketing and product visuals without a team, and engineers curious how generative image tools hold up in daily production work. Tool versions will date; the workflow advice will not.

Title: A microphone on the machine can hear the failure coming
Description: Karthikeyan Rajamani, Lead SRE at Thomson Reuters, at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on IoT, acoustic sensing and ML for predictive maintenance.
Body:
Scheduled maintenance assumes machines fail on a calendar. Karthikeyan Rajamani, Lead SRE at Thomson Reuters, opened his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk with a study he attributes to PTC finding that more than 80% of equipment failures are random, which is why preventive schedules alone cannot catch them. His answer is predictive maintenance: cheap IoT sensors, including plain microphones, feeding signal processing and ML models that flag a failure before it becomes downtime.

The talk is an accessible introduction that covers the whole pipeline from sensor to dashboard. If you run services rather than turbines, the structure will still feel familiar: it is observability for things with bearings.

## Three kinds of maintenance

Rajamani lays out the options. Breakdown maintenance reacts after the failure. Preventive maintenance runs on a schedule, like an oil change, quarterly or yearly. Predictive maintenance watches the equipment continuously and acts when the data says something is wrong. The benefits he lists are practical: downtime can be scheduled outside business hours, the technician arrives with the right spare part instead of diagnosing on site, maintenance costs fall, equipment lasts longer, and the failure data goes back to the design team for the next product.

## Why sound is a good signal

Sensors have become cheaper, lower power and more accurate, and can measure vibration, temperature, pressure, humidity and sound in real time. The acoustic angle is the most interesting part. He describes PTC's microphone-based monitoring as non-invasive: you place a microphone on a benign spot on existing machinery, without modifying it, and build an acoustic footprint of normal operation. Combined with vibration and temperature profiles, that multimodal picture is far more specific than any single sensor, and comparing it against previous failures reduces false positives.

## From waveform to prediction

The pipeline has five parts: data acquisition, signal processing, an ML model, edge computing, and feedback for model refinement. Signal processing converts the raw signal into the frequency domain so the model can look at where the peaks are, not just how loud the machine is. Models such as random forests and CNNs are trained to predict anomalies and maintenance needs.

Edge computing earns its place because sensors can sample every second or every few milliseconds. Processing locally and sending only what matters keeps the network from drowning and cuts latency. A supervised feedback loop improves accuracy over time, and the output lands on dashboards and as mobile alerts for service engineers. Any SRE who has tuned an alert to stop paging on noise will recognise the job.

## Where it applies and what gets in the way

Applications span manufacturing lines, energy (turbines and transformers), logistics fleets, automotive, oil and gas, railways and utilities. He cites market growth and studies reporting large reductions in downtime and maintenance costs.

The challenges section is honest. Factories with a "my system is working fine" mindset resist acting before failure. Skills in IoT, data analytics and acoustics are scarce. IoT devices are often fit-and-forget, with no regular updates and expiring certificates, which makes them a security liability. The data volume needs object storage such as Amazon S3. And retrofitting old equipment with no baseline profile takes real homework.

## What comes next

He closes on AR-guided repairs with remote experts, digital twins, models that learn with less supervision, and third-party cloud platforms offering predictive maintenance as a service.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to industrial IoT who want the end-to-end shape of a predictive maintenance system, and SREs curious how their alerting instincts translate to physical equipment. Specialists in vibration analysis will want more depth than an overview gives.

Title: Your dashboards show what broke, not who broke it
Description: Cynthia Akiotu of Tesco Bank argues at Conf42 Observability 2025 that identity belongs inside observability, from privilege misuse to ghost access.
Body:
Most observability stacks can tell you the API spiked at 14:02. Very few can tell you which identity was holding elevated permissions at 14:01. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Cynthia Akiotu, Cyber Risk Analyst at Tesco Bank, made the case that this gap is where modern breaches live, and that identity has to be a first-class signal next to logs, metrics and traces. Her opening line sets the tone: observability without identity is like a map without landmarks.

It's a security talk aimed at observability people, which is exactly the audience that needs it.

## Attackers log in, they don't break in

Akiotu's core claim is that identity is now the perimeter. The firewall-and-perimeter era assumed attackers had to force their way through; today they sign in with valid credentials and move laterally without tripping anything. And "identity" no longer means a person: managed identities, service principals, bots acting on behalf of users and, increasingly, AI agents all hold credentials.

She lists the usual identity-shaped incidents: insider threats (employees, vendors, third parties, malicious or careless), unauthorised access, audit violations and privilege misuse, the last one being an admin quietly raising their own rights. The Tesla insider leak of 2023, where former employees handed staff data to the media, is her example of people with legitimate access doing illegitimate things.

## Four quadrants of not knowing

The most memorable part of the talk is a quadrant that crosses identity visibility with risk awareness. The interesting cells are the uncomfortable ones:

- **Unsanctioned SaaS**: an employee finds a free tool online and signs in with office credentials, unseen.
- **Ghost access** (the unknown known): unused roles, misconfigurations and policy gaps. Akiotu describes it as a dashboard on fire without knowing who lit the match, and points to the third-party route into Marks & Spencer's ransomware incident.
- **Invisible identities** (the unknown unknown): the CISO's worst case, like the abandoned legacy system behind the Legal Aid Agency breach, or the NHS trusts exposed through a third-party mobile device management tool.

She also names the reasons teams don't fix this: hybrid estates where on-prem Active Directory isn't synced with Entra ID, tools that don't talk to each other, and licensing costs that keep growing until a breach makes the budget appear.

## Correlate first, buy tools second

The practical section is a short checklist. Correlate identity with system events, so your SIEM (she mentions Microsoft Sentinel) and identity platform (Entra ID) actually share data. Audit permissions in real time using signals like location and device compliance, instead of static role-based rules checked once a quarter. Detect insider threats and shadow AI, add data loss prevention, align with Zero Trust (assume breach, verify every identity), and enforce least privilege under whatever regime applies to you: GDPR, HIPAA, NIST and friends.

Her sharpest point is that the tooling list matters less than whether the tools are wired together. Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, Sentinel and Purview get a mention, but the warning is about silos, not products. And because some breaches are unavoidable, she closes on incident response: mature security is also measured by how fast you contain and recover.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who own the logging pipeline but have never been asked to join identity data to it, and security analysts who want vocabulary to pitch that work to them. It's conceptual rather than hands-on, so don't expect queries or a demo. Start with her opening question, which is when your organisation last ran an access review, and whether anyone would admit the answer.

Title: Catch the log bill spike with ARIMA in BigQuery ML
Description: Yury Nino of Google shows at Conf42 Observability 2025 how time series anomaly detection on Cloud Logging data flags cost spikes before the invoice.
Body:
Turning on every log you can find during an incident feels responsible right up until the bill arrives. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Yury Nino, Cloud Applications Modernization Engineer at Google, told exactly that story: an incident with too little logging, a decision to enable all the available audit logs, and a 700% jump in billing from one month to the next. Her fix is to point time series analysis at the logs themselves, so the next spike shows up as an anomaly before it shows up as an invoice.

The premise is neat and a little ironic. If logs are part of the cost problem, they also carry the signal you need to see it coming.

## The reactive tax is bigger than the bill

Nino frames the cost of doing nothing in four buckets: downtime (lost revenue, churn, reputation), inefficient resource use, security breaches, and wasted engineering time spent firefighting. The billing spike is just the most visible symptom. Proactive cost management, in her definition, means continuous monitoring and optimisation, predictive analytics for right-sizing, elasticity, picking the right pricing models, and above all visibility. The talk focuses on that last one.

Cloud logs are harder to reason about than on-prem logs because the infrastructure is distributed, dynamic and often ephemeral. That makes simple thresholds brittle. You need something that knows what normal looks like for your workload.

## A fast tour of the anomaly detection toolbox

Before the demo, Nino gives a compact map of the machine learning options SRE teams use for anomaly detection:

- **Unsupervised** methods such as clustering and autoencoders, which fit cloud data well because nobody has labelled your logs.
- **Supervised** classifiers such as support vector machines and random forests, which need historical labelled anomalies.
- **Semi-supervised** approaches trained on normal data only, plus isolation forest.
- **Time series** techniques like seasonal decomposition into trend, season and residual.

Because most cost and log signals have a time component and are rarely stationary, she lands on ARIMA (autoregressive, integrated, moving average). It's an introduction to the ideas, and she says as much, but it's enough to understand why the model choice isn't arbitrary.

## The pipeline is three clicks and two queries

The architecture is pleasingly boring. A Cloud Logging log router sink sends logs to a BigQuery dataset (the sink can also target a Cloud Logging bucket, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub or another project). In BigQuery ML, a SQL query builds the training set from a subset of fields: timestamps truncated to the minute, grouped so each time unit has a count. A second query runs the ARIMA-based anomaly detection over that series.

For charts, Nino exports the results to CSV and opens them in Google Sheets, which is a refreshingly honest choice for a demo. The flagged days line up with the extra logs being generated, and those match the behaviour in Cloud Billing. Once the pattern is known, you can forecast the next jump in log volume, and with it the next jump in cost.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE folks on Google Cloud who own the logging budget, or who have been asked why it doubled. The demo is short enough to reproduce in an afternoon, and the SQL-only approach means nobody has to stand up a separate ML stack. If you already run anomaly detection on billing exports, the interesting part is applying it one step earlier, to log volume. Your finance team will not thank you, because they will never find out there was a problem. That's the point.

Title: Probabilistic apps need observability you switch on yourself
Description: AWS Serverless Hero Hazel Saenz of Caylent shows at Conf42 Observability 2025 how to measure Bedrock-backed serverless apps with CloudWatch and X-Ray.
Body:
Send the same prompt to a model a hundred times and you may get a hundred different answers. At Conf42 Observability 2025, Hazel Andrea Saenz Giron, Cloud Software Architect at Caylent and an AWS Serverless Hero from Guatemala, built her talk on that fact: generative AI apps are probabilistic, so the only way to keep quality, speed and cost in balance is to measure every interaction. Her demo shows how to do that on AWS with Amazon Bedrock, Lambda, CloudWatch and X-Ray, including the bit nobody tells you: Bedrock's model invocation logging is off until you turn it on.

## Deterministic habits break on probabilistic systems

Saenz starts with a story every GenAI tinkerer knows: the ad shows a perfect image, your attempt has a character with three mouths. The reason is architectural. Banking and e-commerce systems she built before were deterministic, a pile of ifs where the same input gives the same output. A model returns the most probable answer, which may not be the one this user wanted, and each model behaves differently because it was trained on different data. So model choice becomes a business variable, not a detail.

From there she defines three objectives that pull against each other: quality (no three-mouthed characters), performance (users leave slow apps) and cost (models are expensive, and not every task needs the smartest one).

## The building blocks of a GenAI app

The talk maps a GenAI application into layers: a foundation model hub (your own models or ones reached through the Bedrock API), a data foundation (RAG, fed from ETL jobs, Confluence, Jira, GitHub, PDFs, CSVs, APIs and databases, landing in a Bedrock knowledge base), model adaptation and prompting, GenAI ops for deployment and versioning, integration with existing apps, and governance with a control plan. Bedrock Guardrails sits in the data path to keep sensitive customer data out of answers.

Observability is the thread through all of it. Her argument is that decisions like switching models, rewriting prompts or fixing the data have to be made on numbers, and observability is where the numbers come from.

## Four layers, in this order

Saenz proposes an incremental path:

1. **Component metrics**: invocation errors, latency and utilisation for the infrastructure.
2. **Model metrics and traces**: what happened between the user's request and the answer, step by step.
3. **Guardrail metrics**: how many users tried to pull sensitive data or probe for information they shouldn't get.
4. **User feedback**: the thumbs up, thumbs down signal that tells you whether a different answer each time is a good answer.

## The demo: tokens are your cost meter

The demo uses a small music-expert API from her GitHub repo that you can deploy into your own account. After enabling Bedrock invocation logging to CloudWatch (or an S3 bucket), each request shows which model ran, the question, the answer and the tokens used. Tokens are the useful part: send the same request to two models and you can compare cost and latency directly. X-Ray traces on the Lambda then split total duration from the time spent waiting on the model, so you know whether to tune your code or your model choice.

## Who should watch

Developers on AWS moving a GenAI prototype towards production, and SREs who've inherited one. It's an approachable talk, more about building the right habits than about advanced tracing. If you already instrument LLM calls with OpenTelemetry, the four-layer ordering is still a handy checklist for what you're missing.

Title: Legacy modernization works in phases, and people decide if it sticks
Description: Sasidhar Reddy Somula of Accenture at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on modernizing legacy systems in phases, with change management as the real budget line.
Body:
Most legacy systems are not broken. They are expensive, slow to change and impossible to retire, which is worse. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Sasidhar Reddy Somula, Technology Architect and Application Development Manager at Accenture, argued that modernization succeeds when it is phased, measured and planned around the people who have to use the result, and that the technology choice is the easier half.

This is a strategy talk, not a code walkthrough. If you want Terraform, look elsewhere. If you are the person who has to explain to a steering committee why the mainframe migration needs a training budget, keep reading.

## The maintenance bill eats the innovation budget

Somula opens with the number every architect in a large enterprise has heard in some form: his slides put legacy upkeep at 60 to 80% of IT budgets. Whatever the exact figure in your shop, the shape is familiar. The money goes to keeping the old thing alive, and the new thing waits.

He frames three challenges that keep teams stuck. First, the financial one: transformation costs money before it returns any. Second, organizational culture, which resists change at least as hard as the code does. Third, the balancing act between stability and new capability. His analogy is fixing an airplane while it is still flying, which anyone who has done a zero-downtime cutover will recognize as optimistic about how much room there is in the cabin.

## Pick a migration pattern per application, not per company

The architecture section is the most practical part. Somula walks through the "six R" approach to cloud migration (rehost, replatform, refactor and friends) and makes the point that it is a per-application decision. Each system gets weighed on business criticality, technical debt and the performance it has to keep.

He singles out the strangler fig pattern as the safer route for systems that cannot go dark: replace functionality piece by piece behind a stable interface instead of a big-bang rewrite. His slides cite studies showing a meaningful risk reduction compared with big-bang approaches. The underlying logic needs no citation: a cutover you can roll back one slice at a time is a cutover you can survive.

Lift and shift gets a fair hearing too, with a caveat. Moving a problem to the cloud does not solve it. You just pay for it by the hour now.

## The failure mode is change management, not technology

The part worth the watch is the turn from architecture to people. Somula cites the oft-repeated figure that most digital transformations fail on change management rather than technology, then gets specific about what helps:

- incremental interface changes instead of an all-at-once UI swap
- change champions embedded in departments, who his slides credit with far higher adoption than rollouts without them
- digital adoption platforms and modern documentation (videos, interactive guides) instead of a PDF nobody opens
- real-time feedback channels so users can say what broke before they quietly route around it

His recommendation is concrete: set aside 15 to 20% of the modernization budget for training, support and adoption. That line item is the first thing cut in most project plans, which may explain a lot.

## Measure the outcome, not the migration

Somula closes with how to keep stakeholders on board: track business outcomes (cost, response time, adaptability, user satisfaction) alongside technical metrics, and show progress visually so the business side sees value before the final cutover. He also mentions using large language models for code analysis and dependency mapping during migration planning, which is the one place the talk touches the conference's machine learning theme directly.

His closing takeaways are short: balance stability with innovation, prioritize people, measure holistically, go phased. Transformation is a marathon, he says, not a sprint.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering managers about to pitch, scope or rescue a modernization program will get a tidy framework and a vocabulary for the meeting. Engineers hoping for implementation detail on the strangler pattern or a migration war story can skip it; the talk stays at the strategy level, and many of its numbers come from industry studies on slides rather than one project.

Title: SAP plus machine learning in insurance starts with the data migration
Description: Satish Puram of Deloitte at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on pairing SAP S/4HANA with ML for insurance claims and underwriting, and why migration decides it.
Body:
Insurance runs on claims, policies and very old systems. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Satish Puram, a Specialist Leader at Deloitte Consulting with 22 years of SAP implementations behind him, laid out how insurers combine SAP S/4HANA with machine learning for claims, underwriting and customer service, and why the unglamorous parts (data migration, integration, leadership) decide whether any of it works.

It is a leadership-perspective talk from a consultant who has done this many times. Expect frameworks and SAP module names, not model architectures.

## Why insurers are under pressure

Puram names four forces. Digital-first insurtech competitors move faster with lighter operations. Legacy infrastructure creates data silos and drives up operating cost. Cyberattacks against policyholder data keep getting more sophisticated. And customers now expect the same frictionless, personalized service they get everywhere else, which is a high bar for a claims process designed around paper.

His answer is the SAP stack, and he is upfront about it: S/4HANA as the real-time data and analytics foundation, SAP Insurance Analyzer for risk analysis and insurance-specific regulatory needs, a data management suite for integration and governance, and SAP CRM for the policyholder side. The headline numbers on his slides (processing-time cuts, efficiency gains, a return on investment within two years) are framed as industry results for SAP deployments, so treat them as the vendor-ecosystem view rather than one audited project.

## Where the machine learning goes

The ML part is three applications, each familiar to anyone who has worked near an insurer:

- **Claims automation.** Models review claim documents, flag fraud indicators and auto-approve the straightforward cases, which Puram says takes processing from days to minutes for those claims.
- **Dynamic underwriting.** Predictive models build personalized risk profiles and premiums, which also opens coverage to segments that were previously underserved.
- **AI-driven service.** Virtual assistants and sentiment analysis for round-the-clock support and proactive issue spotting.

None of this is exotic. The interesting part is what has to be true underneath for it to run.

## The pyramid, and the migration nobody budgets for

Puram's integration model is a pyramid: business value alignment at the base, then API-first architecture, then a data governance framework, then security by design. Start from the business case and build upward, so integration effort goes where it pays.

Then he says the quiet part: across his whole career, in insurance and every other industry, the biggest challenge has been data migration. His recipe has four steps. Discovery and assessment (audit every source and map it to the target SAP structures). Cleansing and enrichment (kill duplicates, fix quality, add attributes). Testing and validation over multiple cycles with representative samples. And post-migration monitoring, because the job does not end at cutover. If your ML model is trained on the claims history, this is the step that decides whether it learns from signal or from twenty years of duplicate customer records.

## Automation is a loop, and leadership is the hard part

His process automation framework runs from discovery (find candidates, compute ROI per process, align stakeholders) through design (RPA bots, ML models at decision points, SAP integration), phased testing and deployment, into continuous improvement with regular retraining on new data.

The leadership section covers three challenges he deals with daily: managing cross-functional teams of IT, business units and outside consultants; keeping claims and policy operations running during the transition; and building problem-solving frameworks for the technical surprises that always arrive. He closes with a case study of a midsize regional insurer that moved to S/4HANA with ML in phases, starting with claims and policy administration, and reports shorter processing times, lower costs and improved customer satisfaction.

## Who should watch

IT leaders and architects at insurers, and consultants scoping SAP programs, will find a clear map of where ML fits and what to sequence first. ML engineers looking for model detail will not find it here; the talk is about the program around the models.

Title: Your parked car is still burning power, and software can fix it
Description: Ravinder Katla, infotainment integration engineer at General Motors, at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on power moding across a vehicle's ECUs.
Body:
Charge an electric car to 280 miles of range, leave it in the garage overnight, and it can show 270 in the morning. Ravinder Katla, an advanced infotainment systems integration engineer at General Motors with 12 years across embedded, firmware and integration roles, explained at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) where that missing range goes: dozens of electronic control units that keep drawing power when nobody is driving. His case is that power moding, the software that decides which ECUs are awake and when, is one of the cheapest sustainability levers a carmaker has.

It is an engineer's walkthrough from inside the industry rather than an ML talk. AI shows up mainly as the next step for power management, and the talk does not describe GM's internal implementation.

## A car is 16 to 32 computers with opinions

Katla starts with the architecture. A modern vehicle has roughly 16 to 32 ECUs depending on the manufacturer, each owning a function: the body control module handles lighting, brakes and other body functions, others handle infotainment, telematics and so on. Each draws power differently, and some need power constantly. The power states that matter are propulsion (driving), run, and sleep, and the problem lives in sleep: a parked car whose modules keep running background work drains the battery and shortens its life.

## Sense, analyse, adjust, repeat

His model for power moding has four steps. Environmental sensing: monitor usage patterns, driver behaviour and conditions. Real-time analysis: measure how much each component draws in each power state. Dynamic adjustment: rebalance power between ECUs, especially in sleep. Continuous optimisation: keep cutting consumption as data accumulates.

For EVs, the benefits are efficiency, range (he notes that HVAC alone noticeably affects range) and battery lifespan, which is also why manufacturers recommend charging to 80%. For combustion vehicles, less electrical load means less fuel burned to generate it; he cites fuel consumption reductions of a few percent and CO2 savings per vehicle per year. Multiply small per-car gains by millions of cars a year and the numbers stop being small.

## Updates while you sleep

The implementation section is the most concrete. Over-the-air updates and ECU firmware upgrades often have to run while the vehicle sleeps, so power moding has to allow critical updates without leaving the car awake all night. His rollout model goes from software updates on a test fleet, through power management protocol integration, to algorithm tuning from fleet data, driving patterns and environment, then a monitoring period (he gives 12 months as an example) to find which ECUs consume the most and verify improvements.

## Some modules must never nap

The challenges are what make this harder than "turn things off". ECUs come from different suppliers with different mechanisms, and they talk to each other and to the outside world, such as the telematics module reaching carrier networks, so a unified power model is genuinely hard. Safety-critical functions, such as theft detection, crash response or an alarm when a door opens, have to stay awake, and ISO 26262 functional safety requirements must be respected across every power transition. Cybersecurity functions that prevent unauthorised control also stay on. Older platforms may lack the hardware for advanced power states, so retrofits raise costs.

He calls for standardised ECU power management architectures across manufacturers and suppliers, and cross-industry working groups with semiconductor and software companies.

## Where AI comes in

The future section is where the ML angle appears. Today's power modes are discrete states triggered by predefined conditions. Next comes AI-driven optimisation that asks, per ECU, whether the power it is drawing is necessary right now and shuts it down if not; vehicle-to-everything integration for coordinated power with infrastructure and other vehicles; and distributed intelligence where each component decides for itself whether to wake. His key takeaway: unlike hardware improvements, this ships through software updates to cars already on the road.

## Who should watch

Embedded and automotive software engineers, and anyone in IoT who has to keep a battery-powered device both responsive and asleep. ML practitioners looking for models will find the AI part brief; the systems problem is the reason to watch.

Title: In AI messaging, the assistant drafts and the human decides
Description: Gagan Shah, Head of Product at Intuit and former lead of LinkedIn's messaging revamp, at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on AI-assisted professional messaging.
Body:
Migrating 17 years of messages with zero downtime is the kind of sentence that makes a platform engineer sit up. Gagan Shah, Head of Product at Intuit, opened his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk with the LinkedIn messaging revamp he led, then made a product argument for where AI belongs in professional messaging: the best experiences are AI-assisted, not AI-authored, and the human stays in charge of what gets sent.

It is a short, opinionated product talk rather than an ML engineering session. There are no model architectures here; there is a clear point of view from someone who has shipped messaging at scale, and plenty of Douglas Adams.

## A UI change that was really a backend rebuild

Shah describes LinkedIn moving from a rigid InMail inbox to a dynamic chat interface. The visible change was the UI. The real work was rebuilding the backend for speed and scale, migrating 17 years of message history without downtime, and adjusting to new norms around tone and responsiveness. The result, in his telling, was more conversations and more frequent reconnection: messaging became a live network instead of a slow email proxy.

## Messaging is where work happens now

His case for why this matters: messaging is the backbone of modern work across Slack, Teams, LinkedIn and Facebook Messenger, it compresses decisions from hours of email to minutes of chat, and it is where mentorship, networking and deals usually start. Professional messaging has also become less formal, with a quick "got five minutes?" replacing long outreach. That cultural shift is part of the product, not a side effect.

## Scaling trust is harder than scaling servers

The section engineers will nod along to is on growth. As a platform grows, the problems become social: noise, spam and drifting etiquette. LinkedIn's answers were features that scale trust: spam filters, rate limits, message invitations, read receipts and do-not-disturb statuses. Shah's point is that scaling communication means shaping the invisible rules of interaction and responding as those norms change, which is a product job as much as an infrastructure one.

## AI assists, the human decides

The core of the talk is the loop. Smart replies, tone checks, live translation and summaries are already in the tools we use. AI brings scale and speed, humans bring nuance and meaning. Looking five years out, he expects AI assistants that triage, draft and schedule; real-time multilingual conversation with tone-aware translation; context-aware chat that pulls up relevant documents and flags risks; new media such as voice, gestures and even AR; and, most importantly, systems that verify authenticity. He pushes back on the idea that messaging ends up as AI talking to AI. His bet is that the tools amplify human connection and strip out formality.

## The product rules have not changed

His advice to product leaders is refreshingly plain. Keep it simple: if it takes four clicks, it is too much. Build for trust and let users control their data and inbox. Use AI to enhance the human voice, not replace it. Plan for billions of messages without degrading the experience. Optimise for message quality and human connection rather than raw volume. And make the product feel like a superpower, not one more inbox to clear.

The closer: AI is the Babel fish, translating and suggesting, but people still set the destination. Bring a towel.

## Who should watch

Product managers and designers adding AI features to any communication product, and engineers who want the product reasoning behind human-in-the-loop design. If you need the infrastructure story of a messaging migration in detail, pair it with the related talks.

Title: Self-healing tests aim at integration testing's maintenance tax
Description: Siva Yachamaneni, Quality Engineering Manager at Infosys, at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on AI test generation, self-healing suites and smarter runs.
Body:
The expensive part of test automation is rarely writing the tests. It is keeping them alive while the application changes underneath. Siva Yachamaneni, Quality Engineering Manager at Infosys with close to 18 years in software development and quality engineering, used his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk to show where AI can cut that maintenance tax in enterprise integration testing: generated test cases, self-healing frameworks, autonomous execution, anomaly detection and coverage gap analysis.

It is a survey of techniques and industry research rather than a walkthrough of one framework, and the figures come from market and research reports he cites. The structure is clear, though, and each technique comes with its key capabilities spelled out.

## Static scripts versus a moving target

Yachamaneni names three problems with traditional integration testing. Growing complexity: enterprise systems form a web of connections that static scripts and predefined scenarios cannot keep up with. Maintenance burden: by his figures, maintenance takes around 30% of total testing effort. Limited coverage: traditional approaches typically reach 40-60%, missing integration scenarios that multiply as systems interact. Anyone who has watched a suite go red because a button moved three pixels knows the third problem is really the second one in disguise.

## Five places AI helps

**Test case generation.** Models analyse code, requirements and user stories to propose scenarios, including edge cases manual design misses. NLP lets non-technical stakeholders describe tests in plain language.

**Self-healing frameworks.** The framework detects changes in the UI, data structures or business logic, works out which scripts and execution paths are affected, and updates them automatically. He cites research suggesting this can cut maintenance requirements substantially, with visual AI particularly useful for UI tests.

**Autonomous execution and monitoring.** Smart scheduling orders runs by dependency and risk, intelligent parallelisation spreads them across infrastructure, and predictive monitoring looks for subtle patterns that precede failures.

**Anomaly detection and root cause analysis.** ML correlates data across systems to spot unexpected behaviour, diagnose root causes that span services, and suggest fixes based on history.

**Coverage optimisation.** Risk-based prioritisation, discovery of untested paths from code structure and runtime behaviour, and smaller suites that cover more.

## Adoption follows regulation

The industry slide is a useful reality check. Banking and finance lead adoption, which he ties to regulation and the cost of a broken integration in a payments system. Healthcare, manufacturing and retail follow with their own drivers.

## Where it goes next

The future section names four trends: digital twins for testing integrated systems in production-like environments without production risk, explainable AI so test tooling can say why it picked a test or predicted a defect, natural-language interfaces for test definition, and federated learning so organisations can share testing insights across supply chains without exposing sensitive data. Explainability is the one to watch: a self-healing test that silently rewrites itself is only useful if you can see what it changed.

## Who should watch

QA managers and test architects building a case for AI tooling, and engineering leaders who want a vocabulary for evaluating vendors. Practitioners who already run self-healing suites will want more depth than a survey offers, so pick from the related talks.

Title: Putting a different ML model at every DevSecOps pipeline stage
Description: Srikanth Potla, Senior Product Security Engineer at SoFi, at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 maps supervised, unsupervised and NLP models onto CI/CD.
Body:
Security reviews that take a month are a release blocker with a badge. Srikanth Potla, Senior Product Security Engineer at SoFi, argued at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) that machine learning can close the gap between development speed and security review, as long as you match the model type to the pipeline stage: supervised models for known vulnerabilities, unsupervised models for runtime anomalies, and NLP for infrastructure-as-code.

The talk is a framework plus figures from industry data and a case study. It names Snyk as one example tool, but it is not a product pitch, and it does not show Potla's own pipeline at SoFi.

## The security development gap

Potla's opening is that conventional security cannot keep up with modern delivery cycles. He cites 94% of enterprises using cloud services and a sharp rise in AI-powered attacks since 2022, and calls the result a "security development gap": every week between writing code and reviewing it is a window for an attacker. The figures he leads with, from what he describes as data across more than 500 enterprise implementations, are fewer security incidents, faster secure deployments, and mean time to remediate dropping from 38 days to just over four.

## Pick the model for the threat you know (and the one you don't)

**Supervised learning for known vulnerabilities.** Models trained on large datasets of known vulnerable code patterns flag similar issues in new code before deployment, and get better as new vulnerability data arrives. His example is Snyk's ML-enhanced scanning in 2024, which he says caught far more vulnerabilities before production than traditional static analysis.

**Unsupervised learning for the unknown.** Baselines of normal behaviour per environment, continuous monitoring, and self-learning models that flag deviations. This is where novel attacks and zero-days show up, and he says it has been especially effective for runtime detection in containers.

**Container security across the lifecycle.** Image scanning, behavioural runtime protection, network monitoring for unexpected connections, and configuration checks against best practice.

**NLP for infrastructure-as-code.** The most interesting idea in the talk. Regex-based IaC scanners match patterns; NLP-based analysis tries to understand what a Terraform or CloudFormation file intends, so it can catch overly permissive policies or insecure defaults that a pattern match would miss, and suggest code-level fixes.

## Wire it into every stage

Put together, the pipeline looks like this: ML-powered pre-commit analysis at commit, supervised scanning of container images and dependencies at build, ML-generated security tests aimed at likely weak points in test, NLP infrastructure scanning before provisioning, and unsupervised runtime monitoring in production.

The case study is a financial services company whose mobile banking releases waited around 27 days for security review. After adding an ML pipeline that prioritised vulnerabilities and opened pull requests for common issues automatically, reviews dropped to two days, and the automated remediation now handles most common issues without a human. That frees the security team for the problems that need judgment.

## Start small

The implementation advice is modest: document existing controls and gaps, define success metrics, build a cross-functional team, start with code scanning in CI and container monitoring, set up feedback loops, then add unsupervised runtime models and automated remediation. Pick one tool, measure it, then expand.

## Who should watch

AppSec and platform engineers building a case for ML-assisted scanning, and security leaders who want a stage-by-stage map. Teams already running mature DevSecOps tooling will find the framework familiar; the IaC section is the part most likely to give them a new idea.

Title: Hyper-personalization is a latency problem and a privacy problem
Description: Lakshmi Narayana Gupta Koralla, Senior Data Engineer at Starbucks, at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on the data and ML stack behind hyper-personalization.
Body:
An offer that arrives ten seconds after the customer stopped caring is just noise with your logo on it. Lakshmi Narayana Gupta Koralla, Senior Data Engineer at Starbucks, used his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk to break hyper-personalization into the layers that make it work: multi-source data, real-time triggers, ML models, cross-channel identity, and the privacy architecture that decides whether customers put up with any of it.

Fair warning on format: this is a dense, research-heavy survey. Most of the figures come from published industry studies and anonymised company examples (a streaming service, an airline, a department store, a coffeehouse chain), not from Starbucks internals. Watch it for the structure and the vocabulary, and treat the numbers as citations you can chase.

## Preferences move, so the model has to

The core premise is what Koralla calls dynamic identity recognition: a customer's preferences are contextual and shift with time, place and situation, so personalization built on fixed segments misses the moment. Hyper-personalization replaces segments with real-time analytics and ML that recalibrate on micro feedback loops. His opening example from the abstract is Salesforce's platform, which he says processes more than 80 billion AI predictions a day.

## The plumbing comes first

The technical infrastructure section is the most useful part for engineers. It starts with multi-source data orchestration, a "signal fusion" layer that joins heterogeneous sources into one customer view. He notes that most organisations name data integration as their primary obstacle, and gives a healthcare example where unifying more than 70 data sources cut preparation time from weeks to hours.

On top of that sits real-time processing: contextual triggers that react to the customer's current situation, such as a financial services app using location and transaction history to time advice. Then the ML layer, where one media company runs 16 separate models coordinated as one experience.

## Seconds matter more than features

The delivery section introduces the idea Koralla calls attention decay: personalization effectiveness falls off quickly with delay. He cites leading companies delivering a personalised experience within 1.8 seconds of a trigger, against industry averages above 10 seconds. That turns personalization into a latency engineering problem, which is a much more tractable conversation for a data team than "be more relevant".

He also covers modular content assembly (experiences broken into separately personalised components), dynamic pricing based on individual price sensitivity, and cross-channel identity resolution, with a department store example reconciling 43 million customer profiles across eight or more channels.

## The personalization paradox

The privacy section names the tension directly: consumers want tailored experiences and are anxious about the data collection that makes them possible. With multinational enterprises juggling many separate privacy frameworks, Koralla argues for privacy by design, built into the architecture instead of added after a regulator asks. He points to Apple's App Tracking Transparency, with only 18% of users opting in, as the event that forced consumer brands toward first-party, consent-based data. The privacy-preserving techniques he lists include data minimisation, differential privacy and federated learning, plus explainable recommendations so customers can see why they got an offer.

## Measure the relationship, not the click

The closing sections are on attribution and lifetime value: multi-touch attribution that sees how touchpoints amplify each other, journey analytics, and lifetime value models that measure whether personalization strengthens the relationship over time. His coffeehouse example uses consumption pattern modelling to spot early signals in spending behaviour and protect high-value customers before they drift.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and ML engineers asked to "do personalization" who want a layer-by-layer map of the stack, and product leads who need the privacy argument in their pocket. If you want implementation detail on ranking models, pair it with the related talks.

Title: AI identity verification has to work for everyone, not just the average face
Description: Venkata Krishna Ramesh Kumar Koppireddy of UV Cyber at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 surveys AI-driven identity checks, from biometrics to consent and inclusion.
Body:
Opening a bank account in two minutes with a face scan and a fingerprint sounds like pure convenience until you ask who it fails. Venkata Krishna Ramesh Kumar Koppireddy, Principal Architect at UV Cyber, gave a primer at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) on how AI is reshaping digital identity: the core biometric techniques, the fraud systems around them, and the privacy and inclusivity work that decides whether any of it is acceptable.

It is a short, survey-style talk. Expect a structured tour of the field with one example per slide, not a reference architecture or a deployment story.

## Four ways a machine decides it is you

The core technologies get one slide each. Facial recognition maps facial features into mathematical representations and needs anti-spoofing so a photo of your face does not count as your face (airport e-gates are the example). Fingerprint analysis uses deep learning on ridge patterns and minutiae (the way your phone opens). Voice identification builds a signature from pitch, tone and other vocal characteristics (phone banking). Behavioural analytics watches typing rhythm, navigation habits and device handling to keep verifying you in the background while you use an app.

That last one is the interesting shift. Identity stops being a single gate at login and becomes a continuous signal, which is also why the privacy section later in the talk matters so much.

## Fraud prevention is the other half of identity

Koppireddy pairs verification with fraud prevention: real-time transaction monitoring, pattern recognition over historical data, multi-factor authentication that mixes biometric, behavioural and knowledge-based checks, and adaptive models that keep learning from new attacks. His example is a card fraud attempt flagged because the geolocation and behaviour did not match the customer. He then walks through applications in financial services, healthcare (correct patient identification to prevent treatment errors) and border control, where touchless face scans shorten customs queues.

## Collect less, ask first, offer another way in

The section that lifts the talk above a vendor pitch is privacy and inclusion. Data minimisation: collect only what verification needs, because every extra field is extra breach surface and extra regulatory risk. Consent management: give users granular, understandable control over how identity data is shared and stored. Surveillance: biometric systems can drift into mass surveillance, so ethical frameworks and technical safeguards have to be designed in, not bolted on.

On inclusion he argues for equitable verification across age, income and technical skill, cultural sensitivity around biometrics, and alternative paths for people with visual, auditory or motor impairments, or with old devices and poor connectivity. The concrete example: offer voice verification to a visually impaired user instead of forcing a face or fingerprint flow. A system that only works on a new phone in good lighting is an availability bug with a compliance problem attached.

## Regulation and rollout

He maps the regulatory side (GDPR, CCPA, the EU's eIDAS and Canada's digital identity frameworks, emerging rules on algorithmic bias) and gives a four-step rollout: audit existing identity systems, build an encrypted and API-friendly foundation, pilot with a small user group, then scale with monitoring. The talk ends on self-sovereign, decentralised identity with user-controlled wallets, and a short coda on using AI for network security, secure coding and log review.

## Who should watch

Product managers and engineers scoping a first AI-based verification flow who want the vocabulary and the risks on one page. Security architects already running biometrics in production will know most of it, but the inclusion checklist is a useful thing to hold your current flow up against.

Title: Shift-left and shift-right testing work better as one loop
Description: Jyotheeswara Reddy Gottam of Walmart Global Tech at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 joins pre-release testing and production signals into one quality loop.
Body:
Your unit tests and your Grafana dashboards are probably owned by different people who rarely compare notes. Jyotheeswara Reddy Gottam, Senior Software Engineer at Walmart Global Tech with 13 years in development and quality engineering, argued at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) that this split is the real quality problem: shift-left testing and shift-right validation should feed each other as one continuous loop, so production signals shape what gets tested and test results shape what gets watched.

This is a framework talk with a case study and published figures, not a tool demo. It is practical in places, though, and names plenty of real tools.

## The bug you find in UAT costs more than the one you find in a PR

Gottam opens with four symptoms. Development and functional testing happen in one silo, operations in another, so production feedback rarely reaches the developer. Bugs that slip past early testing surface in UAT or production, where they are far more expensive to fix. And the fragmented process slows releases. None of this is new, which is the point: most teams know it and still run four disconnected quality activities.

His continuous quality loop has four stations: preventive shift-left testing during development, continuous monitoring through deployment, reactive shift-right validation in production, and feedback that turns production insight into development priorities. The goal is to shorten the time it takes to go round.

## What each side brings

On the left he lays out a testing pyramid with numbers attached: roughly half the effort in developer-written unit tests, around 30% in automated CI integration checks, 15% functional tests (Cucumber, WebDriver, Playwright), and 5% end-to-end. Pre-commit hooks and CI validation on merge do the gatekeeping.

On the right he lists observability tools (Dynatrace, Splunk, Grafana), chaos engineering (AWS Fault Injection Simulator, Azure Chaos Studio, Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos), canary deployments that start with 1-2% of users or A/B switches before widening the rollout, and performance monitoring with Prometheus, InfluxDB, CloudWatch or Azure Monitor. A canary that only ever hits 2% of users is also the cheapest apology you will ever issue.

## Treat each tool as an agent, then make them talk

The idea that gives the talk its edge is orchestration. Gottam suggests thinking of each quality activity (unit testing, integration testing, functional testing, Git checks, observability, chaos experiments) as an agent with one targeted job, then wiring them together with agent-to-agent communication. When a fault shows up anywhere in the chain, the signal reaches the developer faster and the fix ships sooner. It is an architecture for feedback, not a single product.

## People are the hard part

He is candid that tooling is the easy bit. Quality has to become everyone's job, from product to SRE. He argues for T-shaped quality professionals: deep in one area such as test automation or CI/CD, and broad enough to understand observability, performance analysis and chaos engineering. Adoption should be phased: baseline current metrics, connect development and production tooling with proofs of concept, add AI-augmented testing, then aim for a self-improving system.

The case study is a financial services team that moved from 12-week release cycles, mostly manual testing and separate QA and SRE groups to two-week releases, a majority of automated coverage and fewer incidents. He also mentions AI-assisted tools such as self-healing tests and test selection from design or requirement documents.

## Who should watch

QA leads and engineering managers trying to justify merging test and operations feedback, and SREs who want developers to care about what production is telling them. Experienced chaos practitioners will find the right-hand side familiar; the value is in the loop.

Title: Fraud, collections and payments through one AI risk lens
Description: Deepu Komati, Lead Engineer at PenFed Credit Union, at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on AI for fraud detection, loan collections, payments and compliance.
Body:
Ten small transfers across different accounts look boring one at a time. Together they can look like a fraud ring. Deepu Komati, Lead Engineer at PenFed Credit Union, built his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk around that idea: AI earns its place in financial risk management by seeing patterns across transactions that rules and humans miss, and the same lens applies to fraud, loan collections, payment routing and regulatory work.

It is an overview of where AI fits in a financial institution's risk stack, with figures drawn from industry results. There is no code and no single system under the microscope, so treat it as a map with Komati's priorities marked on it.

## Rules catch yesterday's fraud

The problem framing is familiar but well put. Traditional risk management combed through records and reacted after an incident. Static rules and models trained once on history fall behind fraudsters who change tactics. Komati's alternative is a system that compares every transaction against the customer's own baseline (amount, time, location, device) and against wider historical patterns, then acts in the moment: hold the payment or route it for extra verification before it completes.

He cites three gains for that approach: better detection accuracy, fewer false positives, and much faster responses than traditional systems. The false-positive point deserves the emphasis he gives it. Every legitimate card declined is a customer annoyed and a support call queued, so a model that only gets more paranoid is not an improvement.

## Collections that call at the right moment

The most distinctive section is loan collections, an area most ML talks skip. Instead of one-size-fits-all reminders, models use borrowing history, payment behaviour, seasonal spending and wider economic factors to estimate each borrower's likelihood of repayment, then personalise the timing and content of outreach, for example a reminder shortly after a borrower's usual pay cycle, or an alternative payment plan when their situation changes. Komati reports recovery improvements for personal loans and a large jump for business loans, which are usually the hardest to recover. His framing is that collections become less of a confrontation and more of a conversation, which is good for recovery and for the relationship.

## Payments that route themselves

On payment processing, he contrasts batch systems with manual exception handling against AI-assisted processing that runs adaptive authentication checks, routes each transaction along the path that best balances speed and security, and resolves many exceptions automatically. The payoff is lower processing time and operating cost, plus fewer stalled payments.

## Explain every flag

The ethics and regulation half of the talk is where engineers should pay attention. Fairness means auditing decisions across demographics so models do not reinforce historical bias. Transparency means every flagged transaction or declined loan comes with a documented reason. Privacy means encryption and anonymisation. Accountability means governance, review committees and audit trails. Komati also describes AI that scans regulatory changes and flags compliance gaps, and decision logs that give regulators a readable path through each automated call. The rollout he recommends is the sensible one: assess, pilot with real feedback, develop skills, and keep retraining as threats evolve.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people new to financial ML who want a tour of use cases beyond fraud, and anyone who has to explain to a compliance team why a model said no. Practitioners after architecture diagrams or model details will want to pair it with the talks below.

Title: AI in police CRM systems needs public dashboards and audits
Description: Chiranjeevi Dubaguntla of PruTech Solutions at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 weighs AI CRM in policing and proposes a community transparency framework.
Body:
A model that learns from historical policing data will learn historical policing habits, including the bad ones. Chiranjeevi Dubaguntla, a Salesforce developer at PruTech Solutions with more than 14 years in CRM systems, used his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk to look at both sides of AI-driven CRM in community policing: real gains in response and engagement, and real risks of bias and surveillance. His proposed fix is a Community Algorithmic Transparency Framework built on public dashboards, citizen-readable logs and quarterly third-party audits.

It is a short talk, closer to a policy brief than an engineering session, and it does not walk through a specific product. That is fine: the questions it raises apply to any team building decision support for the public sector.

## What the systems actually do

Dubaguntla describes CRM platforms that ingest 911 calls, case management records and citizen complaints, then run sentiment analysis to flag rising community tensions, predictive alerts to direct resources to high-risk areas, and officer engagement scorecards. He reports departments seeing shorter emergency response times, more positive citizen interactions, and higher community satisfaction where the systems are transparent. That last qualifier carries much of the talk.

## The feedback loop nobody asked for

The "shadow side" section is the part to watch. Documented cases show minority communities flagged more often by algorithms despite similar incident rates. Systems trained on historical data tend to perpetuate the patterns in that data, so more flags lead to more enforcement, which leads to more data that justifies more flags. Most predictive tools offer little auditability, and citizens rarely know what data is collected about them or how it shapes decisions. In communities with a history of over-policing, he points out, that opacity makes trust almost impossible to build.

Anyone who has watched a recommender system amplify its own early guesses will recognise the shape of the problem. The difference is that here the output is a patrol car, not a playlist.

## Four principles: visibility, documentation, participation, review

The framework has four parts. Visibility: public-facing dashboards that show how algorithms make recommendations. Documentation: engagement logs that citizens can access, so they can see how their case was routed, who resolved it and on what basis. Participation: community involvement in system design, through public workshops and town halls. Review: mandatory quarterly third-party algorithm audits, which he compares to the independent financial audits companies already accept.

He reports pilot results from Boston, Oakland and Denver, including higher trust in police technology after dashboards launched, a community oversight committee that reviews algorithm changes, and more engagement with a police portal after transparency measures. The implementation path runs from auditing existing AI systems, to technical changes that make algorithms explainable, to formal channels for citizen feedback, to independent audits that repeat.

## Engineering recommendations

The technical asks are specific enough to act on: open-source the critical algorithms for public review while protecting security-sensitive parts, collect only necessary data with clear retention rules, test regularly against diverse datasets to find and correct bias, and let individuals view and manage their data within reasonable limits.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product managers building analytics or CRM tools for government, and anyone designing a model whose decisions land on people who never opted in. If you want technical depth on bias testing methods, pair it with the talks below.

Title: Keeping Oracle SOA Suite while moving to Spring Boot microservices
Description: Vasipally Nagireddy of Creoal + SMX at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 maps integration patterns for running Oracle SOA Suite alongside cloud-native Spring Boot.
Body:
Most enterprises do not get to rip out their service bus on a Tuesday. Vasipally Nagireddy, a Principal Consultant at Creoal + SMX with 17 years in enterprise integration, used his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk to map how Oracle SOA Suite and cloud-native Spring Boot microservices can live together: who routes what, how data stays consistent, and how identity travels across the boundary.

Despite the event's name, there is no machine learning here. This is an enterprise integration architecture talk, framed as research, and it moves quickly through a lot of components. Watch it with the slides in mind as a checklist rather than expecting a demo.

## The hybrid is the destination for a long time

Nagireddy's starting point is realistic: cloud adoption pushes teams from monoliths to distributed services, but the systems that run the business still sit behind Oracle SOA Suite, with its enterprise service bus, business process management and business activity monitoring. Spring Boot gives you service discovery, circuit breaking and distributed configuration for the new services. The question is how to make the two talk without the bus becoming either a bottleneck or an orphan.

His answer is to keep Oracle Service Bus as the integration backbone for orchestration and transformation, and to put a deliberate mediation layer around it. That layer does content-based routing with protocol transformation, load balancing across backends, and error handling built from configurable retry policies, adaptive circuit breakers and persistent dead-letter queues. If you have ever debugged a failed SOAP call that silently vanished, the dead-letter queue is the line item to underline.

## Govern the API edge and the data between systems

The API management section centres on an API gateway that handles versioning so old consumers keep working while new ones move on, rate limiting and throttling so a spike from one consumer does not flatten a backend, and dashboards over consumption, latency and security anomalies. For data synchronisation he points to cache topologies, optimistic locking and configurable consistency models, trading performance against integrity per use case rather than picking one rule for the whole estate.

## Identity has to survive the trip

Security is where hybrids usually leak, and the talk is specific about the layers. WS-Security with SAML token profiles and X.509 certificate validation on the SOA side, OAuth 2.0 for federated identity on the microservice side, role- and attribute-based access control with central policy administration, AES-256 at rest and TLS 1.3 in transit with HSM-backed key management. The piece that ties it together is identity propagation through Oracle's security token service, plus correlation IDs and audit logging so a single request can be traced end to end across both worlds.

## Results and what is next

He closes with CI pipelines that build SOA artefacts and Spring Boot services together, multi-level caching, horizontal and vertical scaling, and container resource quotas with predictive autoscaling. His comparison of patterns finds event-driven integration gave the lowest response times and highest throughput, while service-bus integration offered the richest feature set at slightly higher latency. Future work points at service mesh and hybrid-cloud management.

## Who should watch

Integration architects and platform teams who own an Oracle middleware estate and are being asked to "go cloud-native" without breaking the order flow. If you have never touched SOA Suite, the vocabulary density will be high; if you have, it is a compact list of the decisions you will need to make.

Title: Healthcare security that treats HIPAA as the floor, not the goal
Description: Sachin Telalwar of Zocdoc at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 sketches a blueprint for healthcare systems that are secure, available and fast under stress.
Body:
Passing a HIPAA audit tells you the paperwork is in order. It says little about whether a clinician gets a patient record in under two seconds during an emergency, or whether an intruder is spotted in minutes instead of hours. Sachin Telalwar, Senior Software Engineer at Zocdoc, used his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk to lay out a blueprint for healthcare systems that go past the compliance checklist: layered security, near five-nines availability, tamper-evident audit trails and ML-driven threat detection.

This is an architecture overview built from published research and existing implementations, not a tour of Zocdoc's own stack. Telalwar says so up front: the numbers on his slides come from papers and studies, and he presents them as targets rather than as results from one system.

## Speed is a security requirement in a hospital

The framing that makes the talk worth watching is that availability and access speed belong in the same conversation as security. In most industries a slow lookup is a UX bug. In emergency care, Telalwar argues, sub-two-second access to critical patient data can be lifesaving, so the architecture has to protect data integrity without putting a slow gate in front of it.

He breaks the target system into four layers. A distributed data layer that orchestrates encrypted patient data at very large volumes with strict validation. A microservice core designed to absorb huge numbers of concurrent API requests with failover so a node going down does not take the service with it. Security middleware that runs real-time behavioural analysis to stop threats before they get deeper in. And a user interface layer that has to stay compliant while still answering fast enough for clinical work.

## Make the audit trail hard to lie to

The audit section borrows from blockchain without insisting you run one. Every interaction is recorded into cryptographically sealed blocks, a distributed consensus step validates those records, anomaly detection flags unauthorised modifications quickly, and the result is a chronological trail that is tamper-evident. For regulated teams the appeal is obvious: an audit log that an attacker (or a nervous insider) cannot quietly rewrite is worth more than a bigger log.

## Detection belongs at the edge

On threat detection, Telalwar pushes ML-based models close to where the data is generated, with edge nodes distributed across healthcare facilities so analysis happens near the source and detection times shrink. He cites research that puts traditional breach detection and response at around 167 minutes and argues a well-built system should bring that down to roughly 12 minutes. The other metric he keeps returning to is false positives: a security model that floods the operations team with noise is a model nobody trusts by the second week.

## Count the money and the trust

Two slides deal with outcomes that rarely show up in architecture talks. One covers patient trust and privacy satisfaction before and after a security programme. The other covers the business case: avoided breach costs and penalties, automated compliance reporting that cuts audit preparation work, and security operations that spend less time on manual triage. The rollout advice is pragmatic: assess the existing infrastructure and seasonal load patterns first, write a facility-specific plan, deploy in phases so patient care is never disrupted, and keep tuning with live threat intelligence. He closes with forward-looking items such as quantum-resistant encryption and planning for petabyte-scale data.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects building or inheriting healthcare platforms who need a checklist of what "secure enough" should mean beyond the regulation, and security leads who have to argue for budget with something other than fear. If you want implementation detail, benchmarks or code, treat this as the map and look elsewhere for the terrain.
