Title: Low-code ships apps faster, then needs a governance plan
Description: T-Mobile Salesforce architect Balaji Bodicherla covered low-code and no-code at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, from citizen developers to centres of excellence.
Body:
The pitch for low-code is that a business analyst can change a workflow without filing a ticket. The catch is that a hundred analysts changing a hundred workflows is its own kind of incident. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Balaji Bodicherla, a Salesforce Solution Architect at T-Mobile with 17 years in IT, covered both halves: why Salesforce and other platforms are moving towards low-code and no-code, and the governance you need before citizen developers multiply.

It's a short, slide-led overview, about 13 minutes, aimed at teams deciding whether to open the platform up to business users.

## Drag and drop replaces Apex for the small stuff

Bodicherla grounds the talk in his own platform. Complex Salesforce logic is written in Apex code today, which keeps even small changes in the developers' queue. Salesforce is taking steps towards low-code now, and perhaps no-code later, with drag-and-drop configuration and visual workflows that let business teams make minimal changes themselves. The figures on his slides are ambitious: applications built up to 10 times faster than with traditional methods, and development timelines cut by about 70%. Treat those as industry headline numbers rather than T-Mobile measurements.

His demographics slide is the interesting one: business professionals make up 42% of platform users and IT developers 38%, with analysts at 12% and other roles at 8%. In other words, the users are already mostly not engineers, which is exactly why the second half of the talk matters.

## The four ways it goes wrong

The challenges section names the failure modes plainly:

- **Governance**: per his figures, 67% of enterprises struggle to oversee and control the spread of citizen-built apps across departments.
- **Security**: 64% struggle to keep consistent security standards and compliance across their low-code estate.
- **Scalability**: complex business logic and high-volume data processing can outgrow what some platforms handle.
- **Integration**: connecting to legacy enterprise systems usually needs specialist skills that aren't in a typical low-code toolkit, so it becomes the bottleneck.

## A centre of excellence before a thousand apps

His governance framework has three pillars. Centralised oversight means a dedicated centre of excellence, an inventory of every application, real-time usage analytics and enforceable quality standards. Security protocols mean role-based access control, end-to-end encryption and automated compliance checks. Development guidelines give citizen developers room while requiring standard design patterns, structured testing and validation, and mandatory documentation and change management.

The rollout path is the familiar, sensible one: assess your needs, choose a platform that balances capability, security and usability, run a targeted pilot with clear success metrics, then expand across departments with governance in place. Build a training programme for citizen developers alongside it.

## Who should watch

Salesforce admins and architects, and IT leads whose business teams are asking for more self-service. It's light on technical depth and heavy on slides and survey numbers, so engineers looking for platform internals or code will want the related talks. It sat in the security track, and the governance section is where that fits best.

- [Low-Code Meets Public Code: Automating with Minimal Engineering](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Anoosha_Cherukuri_low_code_meets) by Anoosha Cherukuri shows low-code automation in practice.

Title: GPU edge AI answers in milliseconds and keeps data where it lives
Description: Info Keys architect Sai Prasad Mukala made the case for GPU-accelerated AI at the edge at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025: latency, sovereignty, self-healing.
Body:
Picture a wind turbine in a remote field that reads its own vibration, temperature and blade speed, predicts a failure, and never sends a byte to the cloud. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Sai Prasad Mukala, Enterprise Architect at Info Keys, used that image to argue that GPU-accelerated AI at the edge solves two problems at once: latency, and keeping data inside the jurisdiction it came from.

## Flip the factory: process on site, ship only the summary

The core architecture shift is easy to picture. In the traditional model, every machine in a smart factory streams raw sensor data to the cloud, which loads the network, adds latency and can create compliance trouble for regulated data. In the model Mukala describes, each machine has a GPU-enabled industrial computer that detects anomalies and adjusts parameters on site within milliseconds, and only high-value insights or summaries go to the cloud. Long-range work like trend forecasting can stay central; the time-critical loop moves to the edge.

The performance claims are the talk's headline: up to 15x over CPU-only setups, inference below 10 milliseconds for production deep learning models, and up to 60% lower power by pairing GPUs with energy-efficient ARM architectures. As with any benchmark slide, read them as the upper end of what the talk reports, not a promise for your workload.

## Retail, factories and 5G all want the same thing

Three industries carry the examples. In retail, edge processing of in-store sensor and camera data drives inventory replenishment, faster personalised recommendations and dynamic pricing, plus video analytics that flag possible theft in under a second; the talk cites a 28% cut in operating costs and a 65% drop in latency. In manufacturing, predictive maintenance on machine health data reduces unplanned downtime by 43%, and computer vision catches defects before a part moves further down the line. In telecom, cloud-dependent architectures with response times in the tens to a hundred milliseconds can't serve autonomous vehicle coordination, factory robots or AR, so providers put GPU compute at cell sites and aggregation points to get single-digit millisecond responses.

## Sovereignty is the non-technical blocker

Mukala calls data sovereignty one of the biggest non-technical challenges for global AI. Cross-border transfer rules like the GDPR's make it hard to build one central model on data from everywhere, and non-compliance is expensive. Edge processing helps by keeping data in its jurisdiction of origin, but it trades one problem for another: consistent governance across many nodes in many countries. You need a framework that enforces the same policy everywhere.

Security gets the same treatment. A distributed fleet is a bigger attack surface, so he lists zero trust for every interaction, quantum-resistant encryption ahead of future threats, continuous vulnerability scanning across nodes, and secure hardware enclaves for sensitive workloads.

## Remote nodes have to fix themselves

Since nobody drives out to a remote node to reboot it, Mukala describes autonomous edge infrastructure with three properties: self-optimising (rebalancing workloads and resources on demand), self-healing (detecting failures and rerouting or reconfiguring), and self-defending (isolating a compromised node or blocking malicious traffic without a human). His rollout framework is four steps: assess which workloads genuinely need the edge (latency, data volume, processing needs), deploy standardised GPU-equipped nodes, migrate applications with containers and orchestration, then optimise continuously on latency, throughput and utilisation.

## Who should watch

Architects weighing edge versus cloud for an industrial, retail or telecom use case, and anyone whose AI plans keep running into data residency rules. It's a strategy talk with industry figures, not a hardware or code walkthrough.

Title: Signature-based security can't see a zero-day; baselines can
Description: Amazon's Dinesh Rajasekharan explained at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 how anomaly detection, pattern mining and threat intel make security predictive.
Body:
If your defence works by matching known attack signatures, a brand-new tactic sails straight through it. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Dinesh Rajasekharan, a product management leader for security and developer experience at Amazon, made the case for moving security from reactive to predictive with machine learning, and was candid about the parts that still don't work well.

It's a brisk talk, around ten minutes, that works as an executive-level map of AI in security operations.

## Three reasons the old model runs out of road

Rajasekharan frames the problem with the projected global cost of cybercrime, $10.5 trillion a year by 2025, then lists why traditional security can't keep up. It's reactive and only kicks in after damage is done. The volume of data in modern networks overwhelms static rules. And signature-based detection depends on known attack vectors, so a zero-day leaves you blind. His image for it is using a map of the past to navigate terrain that keeps moving.

As examples of what ML can do, he cites MIT's AI2 platform detecting 85% of attacks, and a financial firm seeing a 60% drop in false positives after adopting AI.

## Learn normal, then flag the 3 AM database dump

The pipeline he describes is collect, pre-process, model, act: gather everything from firewall logs to user behaviour, clean and structure it, let models find patterns and anomalies, then hand security teams actionable insights or trigger automated containment.

Three techniques carry it. Anomaly detection builds a baseline of who logs in when and what they do, then flags deviations: an employee suddenly reading an entire database at 3 AM gets noticed. Crucially, the baseline keeps adapting as normal behaviour changes, which is how false positives come down over time. Pattern recognition mines historical logs for attack fingerprints, such as login anomalies followed by privilege escalation, and graph-based analysis can link coordinated campaigns across distributed systems. Real-time threat intelligence correlates activity across endpoints, servers and cloud apps with global feeds, and some systems isolate infected machines automatically.

He also maps model types to jobs: supervised learning on labelled past attacks (say, phishing) to catch similar ones, unsupervised clustering to spot new kinds of threat, and deep learning for high-volume, high-complexity environments like cloud infrastructure. His case studies include a bank detecting more new fraud types, an e-commerce company using AI against DDoS, and a healthcare provider catching insider threats through unusual patient-record access.

## Garbage labels make garbage detectors

The honest section is the one to remember. ML needs clean, labelled data, and getting it is often the bottleneck. Black-box models create a trust and compliance gap when nobody can explain why something was flagged. False positives still happen, and frequent ones desensitise analysts into alert fatigue. Surveillance and data-use ethics need deliberate handling. His outlook covers explainable AI, adversarial ML to defend against AI-powered attacks, federated learning for privacy-preserving analytics, and more autonomous security systems, which he notes are already in research labs and startups rather than a decade away.

## Who should watch

Security leads and product managers who need a quick, balanced framing of where ML helps a SOC and where it bites. There's no tooling demo, so engineers wanting detection-engineering detail should go straight to the related talks.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Synergizing Threat-Informed Defense: When Cloud Attack Emulation Meets Detection Engineering](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Kennedy_Torkura_threat_informed_defense) by Kennedy Torkura is the hands-on detection side.
- [Atomic Red Team - Closing the Gap with Threat Actors](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Christopher_Haller_atomic_red_team_threat_actors) by Christopher Haller tests whether your detections fire at all.

Title: Shor's algorithm is coming for RSA, and the migration starts now
Description: Cloud advisor Vishnuvardhana Reddy Veeraballi gave a primer on post-quantum cryptography, QKD and the NIST picks at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.
Body:
RSA rests on how hard it is to factor large numbers, and ECC on discrete logarithms over elliptic curves; Shor's algorithm solves both efficiently on a big enough quantum computer. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Vishnuvardhana Reddy Veeraballi, a cloud advisor, gave a compact primer on what replaces them: post-quantum cryptography you can run today, quantum key distribution that needs new hardware, and the NIST standards that tie it together.

It's a short overview talk, around 12 minutes, so treat it as an orientation map rather than an implementation guide.

## Three families of math that quantum computers don't break

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) means algorithms that resist both classical and quantum attacks and still run on ordinary hardware. Veeraballi walks through three families:

- **Code-based cryptography** builds on the difficulty of decoding messages deliberately corrupted with errors, with security resting on problems like syndrome decoding and learning parity with noise.
- **Hash-based signatures** rely only on the strength of cryptographic hash functions, not on factoring, which makes them a conservative choice.
- **Lattice-based cryptography** uses hard problems over lattices, the grids you get by combining vectors. The textbook pictures are in 2D or 3D; real schemes use far more dimensions than anyone can draw.

The catch is cost. PQC typically needs more processing power and memory, and keys and signatures are larger, which hits bandwidth and storage. His comparison table puts it plainly: traditional crypto is efficient and well studied but quantum-vulnerable; PQC resists quantum attacks but is younger and heavier.

## QKD detects eavesdroppers, but only within range

Quantum key distribution takes the physics route. In his walkthrough, Alice encodes random bits into photon states and sends them to Bob, who measures with randomly chosen bases. They compare basis choices over a classical channel, keep the matching results, and check error rates. Any interception disturbs the quantum states, so an eavesdropper shows up as a raised error rate before the key is finalised with error correction and privacy amplification.

The flagship deployment is China's 2,000 km Beijing-Shanghai quantum link, alongside satellite-based QKD. The limits are real: distance constrained by quantum state degradation, slower key generation, specialised and expensive hardware, side-channel risk in the classical components, and awkward integration with existing networks.

## NIST has picked, so the excuses are shrinking

The standardisation timeline is the most actionable slide. NIST launched its post-quantum process in 2016, collected and evaluated candidates from 2017 to 2022, and in July 2022 announced its first selections: CRYSTALS-Kyber for encryption, and CRYSTALS-Dilithium, Falcon and SPHINCS+ for digital signatures. Kyber and Dilithium are lattice-based with good performance and reasonable key sizes, Falcon gives compact lattice signatures, and SPHINCS+ is the conservative hash-based option.

## Hybrid first, and test before you trust

For organisations, the hurdles are legacy compatibility, the performance hit of bigger keys, the risk of the transition period itself, and a shortage of people who can implement this correctly. His recommended path is hybrid encryption that combines a classical and a post-quantum algorithm, so you're protected against both today's and tomorrow's attackers, and still covered if a newer algorithm turns out to have a flaw. Adopt a forward-looking plan for data that could be harvested now and decrypted later, but test PQC carefully before full rollout so you don't swap one weakness for another.

## Who should watch

Security engineers and architects who need a fast refresher before a crypto-agility discussion, and anyone who has heard Kyber mentioned and wants the context. Skip it if you've already started a PQC migration; the related talks go further.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Quantum Cybersecurity: Securing the Future in the Age of Quantum Computing](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Husayn_Gokal_securing_future) by Husayn Gokal covers the same threat from a strategy angle.
- [Preparing for the Impact of Quantum Computing on Cloud Security](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Pavan_Nutalapati_quantum_cloud_security) by Pavan Nutalapati maps it onto cloud estates.
- [AI-Driven Cybersecurity: Intelligent Threat Detection and Privacy in the Post-Quantum Era](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Arfi_Siddik_Mollashaik_ai_driven_cybersecurity) by Arfi Siddik Mollashaik joins post-quantum privacy with ML defence.

Title: Only 8% have finished zero trust; here's what the rest are stuck on
Description: Palo Alto Networks' Naveen Kumar Birru covered zero trust at enterprise scale at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, from identity sprawl to service meshes and APIs.
Body:
By the figures Naveen Kumar Birru cited, only 8% of organisations have fully implemented zero trust across the enterprise, while 49% are applying it in key areas and 34% are still planning. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Birru, Senior Principal Software Engineer at Palo Alto Networks, spent his talk on the gap between the pilot and the whole estate, and on the layers where it usually opens.

If you've already heard the never-trust-always-verify pitch, this is the follow-up about doing it across many clouds, many identity systems and a lot of legacy.

## Identity sprawl is the real perimeter problem

Birru's numbers set the scene: multi-cloud estates averaging 3.7 providers, most breaches traced to human error such as phishing and misconfiguration, and 70% of traffic moving east-west inside the network where the old perimeter never looked. His answer is that identity becomes the perimeter, for people, devices and workloads alike, checked continuously during a session rather than once at login.

The hard part is that most enterprises run several identity systems at once, and, per the figures he quoted, machine identities now outnumber human ones in most organisations. Federated identity and privileged identity management stop being nice-to-haves. His summary of the cultural shift: trust becomes something you earn, not something you inherit.

## Enforce at every layer, or attackers find the one you skipped

The architecture section is where the talk earns its title. Policy enforcement has to happen at three layers at once:

- **Network**: secure gateways, next-generation firewalls and SASE.
- **Service mesh**: mTLS between services and fine-grained policies in containerised environments.
- **Application**: API gateways that authenticate and authorise every request.

Any layer without consistent enforcement is where attackers look. Encryption runs through all of it: data in transit and at rest, east-west microservice traffic, API calls, and proper key management, so intercepted data stays useless.

## Service meshes are the connective tissue

Birru gives service meshes such as Istio, Linkerd and AWS App Mesh a central role in cloud-native zero trust. They provide mTLS so every service-to-service call is authenticated and encrypted, explicit policies on which services may talk, cryptographic workload identities that are hard to spoof, and telemetry on communication patterns that exposes anomalies. Without one, he argues, zero trust in microservice environments tends to fall short.

APIs get the same first-class treatment: gateways as central enforcement points, authentication for every consumer regardless of network origin, rate limiting and anomaly detection against abuse, and schema validation to reject malformed or malicious payloads before they reach the backend. Your zero trust strategy is only as strong as your weakest API.

## Legacy is the blocker everyone names

Around 60% of security leaders, he said, cite legacy compatibility as their biggest obstacle: older systems were never built for continuous verification. Add tool sprawl, skills gaps and cultural resistance. The organisations that get further treat it as a staged programme, starting with high-value targets and expanding, with leadership buy-in rather than as a security team side project. Observability ties it together, because you cannot secure what you cannot see.

## Who should watch

Security architects and platform engineers past the zero trust 101 stage who are now facing identity federation, mesh rollout or API gateways. It's a framework talk heavy on survey figures rather than a demo. Birru gave the same talk title at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, so pick whichever recording suits you.

Title: Fraud detection's other job is not declining good customers
Description: Amazon engineer Surendra Lakkaraju laid out ML fraud detection at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025: supervised and unsupervised models, features, scale.
Body:
A falsely declined card doesn't just lose one sale; that customer may never come back. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Surendra Lakkaraju, Senior Software Development Engineer at Amazon, explained why rule-based fraud systems now hurt both sides of the ledger, and how machine learning systems catch more fraud while turning away fewer real shoppers.

It's a short, dense overview of a modern fraud stack, with industry figures rather than Amazon internals.

## The rule that blocks a thousand dollars from a new device

Lakkaraju opens with the classic rule: block every transaction over a thousand dollars from a new device. It worked when fraud was simple. Today's fraud is faster and more coordinated, rules can't adapt, and the false-positive rate he cites for rule-based systems is above 28%. His figure for the cost of false declines is over $3.6 billion a year in lost transactions. Meanwhile fraud keeps growing by more than 20% a year.

ML systems, by the abstract's numbers, process hundreds of thousands of transactions per second against thousands of features each, with detection accuracy above 96% and false positives down by 81%.

## Pick the model by what you need to explain

The supervised section is a practical guide to choosing:

- **Random forests** are interpretable, which matters when you have to explain a decision to a regulator.
- **Gradient boosting** handles imbalanced data well, and fraud is the textbook imbalanced problem.
- **Neural networks** find complex patterns humans can't articulate.

All of them need to answer in real time; the abstract cites sub-70 millisecond inference across more than 100,000 concurrent sessions. In practice you pick by fraud pattern, data volume and explainability requirements, or combine them.

For fraud you've never seen, there are no labels, so unsupervised methods take over: isolation forests separate odd behaviour, autoencoders flag anything they can't reconstruct as normal, and clustering finds groups such as fraud rings. He credits these with catching over 26% of novel fraud patterns that traditional filters would have missed.

## Features are where fraudsters get caught

The feature engineering section is the most transferable part. Temporal features catch timing anomalies, like 500 gift cards bought in five seconds. Network features link users, devices and IPs. Behavioural features such as cursor movement and typing speed separate bots from humans. The best signals combine domains, so a fraudster can't fake all of them at once, and they have to keep evolving because static feature sets become targets.

Scale is its own problem. Black Friday means millions of transactions in minutes, decisions in under 150 milliseconds, and a system that can't go down: distributed, fault-tolerant microservices with failover infrastructure.

## Rules and humans stay in the loop

Lakkaraju doesn't argue for ripping out rules. Hybrid systems use rules as guardrails that encode business expertise, with ML finding the subtle patterns, like a pilot on autopilot who can still take the controls. He puts hybrid detection accuracy above 97%, with the bonus of explainability for regulators. For the cases automation can't settle, ML prioritises and routes them to the right analyst, highlights the suspicious signals, and learns from the analyst's decision.

Looking ahead, he points to explainable AI for auditable decisions, federated learning so companies can fight fraud together without sharing sensitive data, and models that update within seconds of a new attack pattern.

## Who should watch

Engineers building or inheriting a payments risk system, and product people who need to argue that false declines are a revenue problem. It's an architecture-and-concepts talk without code.

Title: Network and security teams belong on the same stack
Description: Cisco product manager Sharanya Prasad argued at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 for converging networking and security with SDN, SASE and zero trust.
Body:
When the network team and the security team run separate tools, separate policies and separate on-call rotations, the attacker gets to work in the gap between them. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Sharanya Prasad, Senior Product Manager at Cisco, argued that the two functions should converge into one framework, so visibility, detection and response all come from the same place.

It's a strategy talk from a product manager, about 15 minutes long, and best read as a briefing for the people who set the roadmap rather than the people who write the firewall rules.

## Silos are a security vulnerability

Prasad's starting point is organisational. Isolated networking and security teams produce fragmented systems, inconsistent policies and slow incident detection, which adds up to business risk. Building security into the network infrastructure itself gives unified visibility, faster detection and automated response. Her examples of what that buys are drawn from organisations that did it: a Fortune 500 bank cutting security incidents by 35% with integrated software-defined networking, a hospital taking breach containment from over 48 hours to under 60 minutes after rolling out SASE, and a manufacturer reaching 99.8% uptime on its OT systems with zero trust principles.

## Four technologies carry the convergence

She names four pillars:

- **Software-defined networking**, which routes traffic dynamically based on real-time security needs.
- **Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)**, her favourite topic, which unifies networking and security at the edge so the same policy follows the user wherever they connect.
- **Zero trust architecture**, verifying every user and device to cut lateral movement.
- **AI-powered security**, using machine learning to spot anomalies and automate responses, which is how this talk earns its slot at an ML conference.

## The pyramid is about people, not boxes

The most useful slide is an organisational pyramid. Consolidated infrastructure sits at the base, integrated toolsets that bridge networking and security workflows come next, then cross-functional teams with shared accountability and success metrics, and strategic alignment between business and security goals at the top. The point is that buying a converged product does nothing if the two teams still don't talk.

Prasad is straightforward about why this is hard. The biggest gap is skills: few people understand both domains deeply. Then come teams clinging to old roles, legacy infrastructure that was never designed for converged architectures, and budgets that lose to other priorities even when the ROI looks good on paper.

## Assess, pilot, then expand

Her roadmap is phased: assess the current infrastructure and vulnerabilities, align goals with business outcomes, break down silos with unified platforms and cross-training, then deploy in phases with analytics and feedback loops. For cloud, it starts with visibility into the full footprint, then multi-layer access policies across hybrid and multi-cloud, converged control systems, and continuous monitoring. Start small, think big, review regularly.

## Who should watch

Security and network leads making the case for SASE or a platform consolidation, and engineers who want to understand the vocabulary their leadership is using. It's high-level and vendor-neutral in tone, with no product demo. If you need configuration detail, the related talks below go lower down the stack.

Title: Zero trust starts where the castle and moat stop working
Description: AWS's Vaibhav Anil Vora walked through zero trust at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, from least privilege and microsegmentation to adaptive authentication.
Body:
For decades the security model was a castle with a moat: strong walls, and once you were inside, everyone trusted you. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Vaibhav Anil Vora, Senior Cloud Technical Account Manager at AWS, explained what replaces it when cloud, remote work and supply chains drain the moat: continuous verification of every request, from every user and device, every time.

It's a thorough, well-structured overview of the zero trust model, and a good choice if you need the whole picture in one sitting.

## Verified a minute ago means nothing now

Vora's core point is that zero trust treats each access request as potentially hostile, even if the same user was verified a minute earlier. Identity becomes the main control point. He rests it on three foundations: continuous verification, least privilege, and comprehensive monitoring, because you can't verify what you can't see.

The history section explains why the old model failed in practice. Attackers who got past the perimeter could move laterally with little resistance and then linger undetected for long periods. The response was a conceptual shift from asking where a request came from to asking who or what is making it and what it wants to reach. The working assumption becomes: assume breach.

## Least privilege has a clock on it

The least-privilege section is more detailed than most. Just-in-time access grants elevated rights only for a specific task and only for its duration, shrinking the window an attacker can use. Attribute-based controls decide access on device health, location, time of day and data sensitivity, not just role. Identity governance keeps checking whether permissions are still needed after people change teams.

Microsegmentation gets similar care. Software-defined networking sets policy centrally, independent of the physical network. Application-layer segmentation restricts traffic by the identity of the software rather than IPs and ports, which holds up when the network changes underneath. Workload isolation goes down to individual containers or processes. None of it works without dependency mapping: you need to know which services legitimately talk to which before you write the rules.

## Risk scores decide how hard to ask

The adaptive authentication walkthrough is the most practical part. Establish a baseline of normal behaviour, monitor telemetry from endpoints, networks, apps and identity systems in real time, score each access attempt on behaviour, device, location, time and resource sensitivity, then respond. Low risk means standard MFA. High risk, such as sensitive data from a new location at an odd hour, means extra steps, a block, or an alert. Data gets its own track: discover sensitive data, classify it against rules like GDPR and HIPAA, protect it with encryption and DLP, then govern its use.

For rollout, he recommends assess, plan, phase and integrate: start with high-value or high-risk environments, and adapt the security gateways and proxies you already own rather than ripping everything out. Zero trust, in his words, is a journey rather than a destination.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects who keep hearing zero trust in planning meetings and want a structured, vendor-light explanation. There's no product demo despite the AWS badge. If you already run JIT access and service identity everywhere, the future-trends section on ML behavioural analytics and DevSecOps is the part to skip to.

Title: Batch, micro-batch or stream? Let the latency budget decide
Description: Meta engineer Sai Kaushik Ponnekanti walked through real-time ML pipelines at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025: Kafka, Flink, event time and drift.
Body:
A fraud alert for a card swipe that happened two hours ago is a history lesson, not a defence. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Sai Kaushik Ponnekanti, a senior software engineer at Meta with earlier stints at Google and Walmart Labs, explained how to build sub-second analytics pipelines for machine learning, and, just as usefully, when you shouldn't bother.

## Not every business needs a stream

The talk's best section is the honest one. Ponnekanti lines up three options. Batch runs hourly or daily and is perfectly fine for the ad-tech team that wants last week's campaign performance; building a heavy streaming pipeline for that is engineering for its own sake. Micro-batching sits in the middle. Real-time streaming pushes latency under 10 milliseconds for things like live stock trading, real-time gaming and dynamic content.

His micro-batching example is pleasingly specific. When an Amazon purchase event for diapers arrives, you want the user's path that led there: homepage, product page, add to cart. So you look back a few windows to reconstruct the session. That is a micro-batch problem, not a sub-10ms one.

## Fraud, carts and factory floors

The use cases span three industries. In banking, he describes his own card being used in Tennessee an hour after a transaction in California, which an hourly batch would spot only after the thief had finished shopping. In e-commerce, real-time pipelines update recommendations within a session and warn shoppers before a Black Friday iPad deal sells out under them, a scenario he knows from Walmart's Thanksgiving traffic. In manufacturing, machines stream temperature, vibration and speed so models can flag a failing line before your kid's birthday toy ships five weeks late.

The abstract carries headline figures, such as fraud losses cut by $15M and conversions up 18%; treat those as the talk's cited industry numbers rather than Meta production data.

## Event time is where streaming gets hard

The technical core is the gap between when an event happens and when it is recorded. Click add-to-cart, the backend gets it minutes later, and the event still happened when you clicked. Ponnekanti puts out-of-order arrival at around 15% of streaming data and walks through the standard defences: sliding windows that wait a minute or two for the homepage and product-page events, and watermarking. If an add-to-cart shows up before the homepage visit, your pipeline needs to wait, not panic.

Model drift gets the same treatment. Summer clothes sell in summer, winter clothes in winter, and a model trained on one season quietly degrades in the next. Real-time systems should detect distribution shifts and retrain automatically.

## Kafka in, Flink through, and pick hybrid on purpose

On frameworks he compares Apache Kafka, Apache Flink, AWS Kinesis and Azure Event Hubs, noting that the managed cloud services integrate more easily but add latency. His own career has mostly meant hybrids: Kafka for ingestion, Flink for processing, then a real-time feature store feeding an optimised model-serving layer that retrains when accuracy drops. The fastest framework is not automatically the right one; team count, tolerated latency, integration effort and learning curve all count.

## Who should watch

Data and ML engineers deciding whether a use case needs streaming at all will get the most from it. It's an architecture overview with personal examples rather than a code walkthrough. Start, as he suggests, with your most latency-sensitive application and grow from there.

Title: Your logs already know what broke; ML helps you hear it
Description: SRE architect Vijaybhasker Pagidoju showed at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 how clustering, embeddings and LSTMs turn noisy logs into faster debugging.
Body:
Most log lines are noise, and the one line that matters tends to show up once, quietly, at the worst possible time. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Vijaybhasker Pagidoju, a Lead Site Reliability Engineer and SRE architect, made the case for machine learning as the thing that reads logs at a scale humans can't, then spent equal time on what it can't do without an engineer next to it.

It's a compact talk, roughly 15 minutes, and a good primer for an SRE team weighing ML-assisted log analysis.

## Logs are the most honest telemetry you have

Pagidoju's framing flips logs from chore to asset. They are raw, authentic records of user activity, system behaviour and failure traces, with no modelling guesswork in between. The problem is volume and mess: a brutal signal-to-noise ratio, JSON next to plain text next to semi-structured lines, timestamps that don't line up so cause and effect drift apart, and rare events that never cluster into a convenient spike. Meanwhile MTTR keeps climbing, and with it pager fatigue. His line for it: finding the right entry is like trying to find a single sentence in a dictionary the size of Australia.

## Four techniques do most of the work

The toolkit is classic and well chosen:

- **Clustering** groups similar log entries so the algorithm can say these events look related.
- **Embeddings** turn unstructured text into numbers that carry meaning.
- **Dimensionality reduction** such as PCA strips noise and keeps the features that matter.
- **Sequence models** such as LSTMs catch patterns across time, which is how you see the slow-building failure.

For anomaly detection he separates statistical baselines (z-scores, moving averages) for known patterns from ML models like isolation forests, autoencoders and one-class SVMs for the hidden ones. In production, his recommendation is a hybrid: rule-based filters first, ML verification on top, and feedback loops so the system improves.

The reference pipeline is four boxes: collect from every service and infrastructure layer, pre-process into a machine-readable shape, run the ML stage, then an insight engine that produces alerts and dashboards people actually act on. He cites Estonia's Health and Welfare Information System Centre reporting a 40% MTTR reduction after adopting Elastic's observability platform.

## The model doesn't know it's Black Friday

The section worth the watch is the one about limits. ML surfaces patterns but lacks context: it can't tell whether a traffic spike is Black Friday or an incident. Engineers validate findings, tune alerts and correct the system, and that loop is what makes it trustworthy. He lists three risks: black-box models nobody can explain (and an alert you can't explain is an alert you won't trust), drift as system behaviour changes, and bias, for example alerting that only cares about revenue-critical services while the rest go dark.

## Who should watch

On-call engineers drowning in alerts, and SRE leads who've been sold an AIOps product and want the vocabulary to question it. It's conceptual rather than a demo. His closing advice is the right one: adopt incrementally, prove value on a small slice, then expand.

Title: From coffee and tea vectors to RAG on Amazon Bedrock
Description: Veliswa Boya of AWS gave a beginner-friendly tour of vector embeddings and RAG at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, ending in Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
Body:
Models only understand numbers, so before an LLM can finish *the capital of France is*, your text has to become vectors. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Veliswa Boya, Senior Developer Advocate at AWS, used under 30 minutes to explain vector embeddings, retrieval augmented generation, and how the two fit together, with a short Boto3 demo on Amazon Bedrock.

She says up front it's a high-level introduction, and that's exactly what it is: a clean first talk on the topic, not a tuning session.

## Coffee sits near tea, cappuccino sits nearer coffee

The embedding explanation is built from a café menu. Put *coffee* and *tea* into a toy vector space and they land close together because both are hot drinks. Add *cappuccino* and it lands closer to coffee, since there's coffee in it. Where words end up comes from training and from how the words are used in the training text.

Boya then shrinks the idea to a sheet of paper: words as arrows from one corner, their direction carrying meaning, their coordinates turning words into numbers. Two dimensions are nowhere near enough for a real vocabulary, so real embeddings use hundreds or thousands of them. It's the clearest mental model you'll find for why *similar* becomes *close* in a vector database, and why music and shopping apps can recommend things that match your taste.

## RAG answers the questions your model was never trained on

Her RAG example is a PDF of internal staff training courses. A foundation model knows nothing about it, so it can't tell you which course is most popular or how long people take to finish one. RAG fixes that by pulling from an authoritative knowledge base outside the training data before generating the answer, and it does so without retraining the model. She frames it as a cost-effective way to keep output relevant and accurate for a specific organisation.

She's also honest about the plumbing that makes people hesitate: multiple data sources, embedding large volumes of data, incremental updates to the vector store, scaling retrieval, and orchestrating it all.

## The AWS part, clearly labelled

This is an AWS talk and it says so. The demo initialises a Boto3 session, creates a Bedrock Runtime client and defines a `get_embedding` function that calls the Amazon Titan Embeddings model and returns the vector. The managed answer to the plumbing problem is Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which connects foundation models and agents to private data sources, augments prompts via the Retrieve API, and offers RetrieveAndGenerate for the full loop with source attribution.

## Who should watch

Watch it if RAG is on your roadmap and you want the concepts straight before you pick a vector store, or if you need a short explainer to share with a team that's new to it. If you already run hybrid search with rerankers in production, this one will feel like a refresher; skip to the related talks.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: NLP from bag-of-words to GPT, told through the benchmark numbers
Description: UnitedLex director Shahzeb Akhtar traced NLP from n-grams to multimodal models at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, one perplexity and BLEU score at a time.
Body:
GPT-1 was trained on about 5 GB of unpublished books; GPT-4's training set has been reported at around 13 trillion tokens. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Shahzeb Akhtar, Director of IP Strategy and Technology at UnitedLex, retold the history of natural language processing using the metrics each era was judged by, which turns a familiar story into a useful one.

Akhtar leads an IP data science team whose platform, Vantage for IP, processes hundreds of thousands of patents with NLP, so he has a practitioner's reason to care what each generation of models could actually do.

## Counting words had a ceiling, and perplexity showed it

The early part covers bag-of-words and TF-IDF: text as an unordered pile of words, good enough for classification and retrieval, blind to grammar. N-gram models added a little context, but perplexity, the measure of how surprised a model is by the next word, stayed above 120. Then the curse of dimensionality: with a 10,000-word vocabulary each document becomes a 10,000-dimensional vector that is mostly zeros, distances stop meaning much, and memory runs out. It's a tidy explanation of why the field had to move on.

## Each architecture fixed the last one's bug

Word2vec and GloVe gave dense embeddings where king sits near queen. RNNs added memory but lost it over long sequences thanks to vanishing gradients; LSTMs fixed that with gated memory cells and pushed Penn Treebank perplexity into the forties, at the cost of slow, sequential training. The 2017 transformer paper replaced recurrence with attention, enabling parallel training and a BLEU score of 41.8 on English-to-French translation. Akhtar shows the paper's attention-head visualisations, including heads resolving which noun a pronoun refers to, which is a nice touch for anyone who has only seen the architecture diagram.

BERT gets its own section: bidirectional context (so *bank* means different things by a river and in a city), masked language modelling with about 15% of tokens hidden, and the pre-train then fine-tune pattern that cut the need for big labelled datasets. Then the GPT line: 125 million parameters, then 1.5 billion, then 175 billion, with SuperGLUE moving from 45.2 to 71.8.

## Smaller, cheaper and greener is the next scoreboard

The last third looks forward. Multimodal models in medical imaging, visual question answering and video reasoning; then the efficiency toolkit: pruning, knowledge distillation into student models, quantisation down to 8 or 4 bits for edge devices, and sparse attention to tame the quadratic cost of long contexts. His prediction for future benchmarks is that energy use, causal reasoning and ethical alignment will matter alongside accuracy, citing a University of Massachusetts Amherst estimate of around 300 tons of CO2 to train a single large model.

## Who should watch

Engineers who arrived in NLP via ChatGPT and want the backstory in one sitting, and anyone who has to explain to a manager why perplexity and BLEU aren't the whole story. It's a history-and-concepts talk; there's no code. If you lived through the LSTM years, the transformer and efficiency sections are the part to keep.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Superposition in LLM Feature Representations](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Boluwatife_BenAdeola_superposition_feature_representations) by Boluwatife Ben-Adeola looks inside the models this talk ends with.

Title: You can't assertEqual an LLM, so evaluate it instead
Description: At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Gaurav Bansal explained why LLM apps need scored evaluation, golden datasets and humans in the loop, not plain asserts.
Body:
Ask a model about the weather twice and you get 62 degrees the first time and 74 the second, both phrased differently. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Gaurav Bansal, a test infrastructure engineer who said in the talk he has spent about a decade at Amazon, used that tiny example to make one point: with LLM applications, "we don't test it. We evaluate it."

It's a short, practical talk aimed at people who own quality for services that now have a model somewhere in the request path.

## The unit test you grew up with stops working

Bansal starts from the most boring test in the world: a `sum` method, two and two in, four out, `assertEqual`, done. Then he swaps the method for an LLM. Same input, different output, and both answers might be fine. The assert fails while the product works, which is the worst kind of red build.

His fix is a doctor's-office analogy. A doctor asks how you feel on a scale from one to ten; nobody expects an exact string back. Evaluation works the same way: you score responses for accuracy, semantic similarity to an expected answer, context relevance, safety, logical coherence and instruction-following, then decide what score is good enough.

## Golden datasets go stale, so keep a human near them

The implementation roadmap he lays out is refreshingly unglamorous:

- Define the evaluation criteria first: which metrics, which thresholds.
- Build the infrastructure: a service with access to the model and your knowledge bases, plus a UI that shows how the golden dataset ran and whether it met the criteria.
- Keep humans in the loop, because the golden dataset itself can go stale and somebody has to notice.
- Automate the whole thing and put it in the CI/CD pipeline, because evaluation you run by hand is evaluation you stop running.

The before-and-after comparison is the bit that matters when you swap models. Run the evaluation on the current model, run it on the new one, compare, and alert if quality drops. Model upgrades become a diff you can read instead of a vibe.

## Break it on purpose before someone else does

Bansal spends a good chunk of time on adversarial work. Edge-case generation should throw strange and hostile inputs at the system so the guardrails get exercised. Red-team exercises try to mislead or break the model and check that confidential project data doesn't leak out of it. Stress testing checks that the service survives a high volume of complex queries, not just the happy path.

He also folds compliance into the testing job: document the evaluation methodology and its limitations, keep old and new evaluation results side by side, audit the data regularly, and follow the regulations of each country you operate in. Not thrilling, but it's the part auditors will ask about.

## Who should watch

Watch it if you're a QA or platform engineer who just inherited an LLM feature and your test suite is flaky in new and exciting ways. It's a framework talk rather than a tooling demo: no specific evaluation library is shown, so pair it with something hands-on. If you already run evals in CI with a curated golden set, you'll mostly be nodding along.

One honest note on the data: the event listing shows Uttar Pradesh Technical University as his affiliation, while in the talk he describes his roughly ten years at Amazon.

Title: Your embedding model thinks "effective" and "ineffective" match
Description: Ritesh Modi (Microsoft) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on the 38 ways off-the-shelf embedding models misread language, and how fine-tuning fixes most of them.
Body:
"The treatment was completely ineffective" and "the treatment was absolutely effective" scored 96% cosine similarity with an off-the-shelf embedding model. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Ritesh Modi, Principal AI Engineer at Microsoft, used that result to open a systematic look at how embedding models misunderstand language, tested across 38 failure scenarios, and showed how domain models, preprocessing and fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers bring the scores back in line with meaning.

If your RAG system retrieves by embeddings, and most do, this is the talk that will make you go and test yours.

## A quick, practical primer

Ritesh starts with the basics, done well. Embeddings turn text into vectors that carry meaning, so dog sits near puppy. He covers dimensionality (from 32 to 4,096; more captures nuance, fewer is faster and cheaper to store), max sequence length (tokens past the limit are silently dropped, so know your model's), vocabulary size (out-of-vocabulary words have no meaning to preserve), and the comparison metrics, with cosine similarity as the default. A live demo with an MPNet model scores "What's the weather like in New York today?" against "Can you tell me the current weather in New York?" at 88%: different words, same intent, which is the whole point of embeddings.

## The quiz that breaks your trust

Then the quiz. Effective versus ineffective treatment: 96% similar. Hypertension versus hypotension, two opposite conditions, are next to each other too. His wider test set covers 38 scenarios, including capitalisation, whitespace, negation, word order, temporal order (finishing a degree before starting a job, or the other way round), hypotheticals versus facts, units (a procedure taking five minutes versus five hours), numeric ranges, and dates written 10/12 versus 12/10, which came out 99% similar despite two months between them. The lowest similarity across the whole set was around 80%, for spelling and typos. Every pair should have scored much lower.

He explains the causes plainly. Models weight words they consider important, reward word overlap regardless of order, and lean on sentiment words, so a sentence saying something was not enjoyed still looks like one saying it was. Picture that in a retrieval system serving medical guidance, where the opposite instruction comes back as the best match.

## Three fixes, in the right order

His remedies, to combine as needed:

- **Choose a domain model.** A medical or legal embedding model trained on that vocabulary, many of which are on Hugging Face.
- **Preprocess on ingestion.** Expand numbers and dates into words, spell out abbreviations, add metadata to disambiguate entities like Apple the fruit and Apple the brand.
- **Fine-tune.** Build sentence pairs labelled with target similarity (generated with an LLM and curated, or your own data), split into train, validation and test, then fit with Sentence Transformers using a loss function and an embedding similarity evaluator.

After fine-tuning, the same 38 scenarios drop sharply, some into negative cosine scores; the negation case falls to 46%. A few stay high, which he treats honestly: more data, different epochs, or maybe it doesn't matter for your use case (capitalisation might not).

## Fine-tuning is the last step, not the first

His closing advice is the senior-engineer part. Know your data, evaluate the base model on your own examples before trusting it, prefer a model someone has already tuned, and fine-tune only if needed. Keep a baseline, evaluate systematically and keep iterating. The demo code is on GitHub.

## Who should watch

Anyone building RAG, semantic search or recommendations, especially in medical, legal or financial domains where a negation is the whole meaning.

Title: Shrinking GPT-2 for tiny devices works only if you fine-tune first
Description: Max Navrotsky (VGS) and Oleksandr Gordieiev at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on trimming, pruning and quantising GPT-2, and why distillation broke.
Body:
The compression trick that made GPT-2 fit on weak hardware was not a compression trick at all. It was fine-tuning. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Max Navrotsky, Senior Software Engineer at VGS, presented joint research with Oleksandr Gordieiev, Professor at the Software Engineering Department of Lutsk National Technical University, on aggressively optimising GPT-2 for low-end, CPU-only devices, and found that a model focused on one task survives compression that wrecks a general one.

It is a clear, experiment-driven talk with a refreshingly honest failure in the middle.

## Why GPT-2, and what "tiny" means

The target is field operations, offline systems and embedded devices: hardware where a modern LLM is out of the question. They picked GPT-2 because it is open source (no licence or API limits), small at 117 million parameters and around 500 MB, not already compressed, well documented, and still good at coherent generation for its age. The test task is concrete: fine-tune it to generate ISO-compliant software requirements, then measure perplexity, CPU usage, memory, inference speed and model size. In Max's words, if they could carry one model into a forest on an old laptop, it would be GPT-2.

## Three aggressive cuts, one gentle one

The talk sorts techniques into aggressive ones, which change the model's structure or weights, and a non-aggressive one:

- **Architecture trimming.** Half the layers removed (12 to 6) and hidden size halved (768 to 384). Layers were removed symmetrically from the centre, keeping the bottom layers for syntax and token-level understanding and the top layers for higher-level structure.
- **Pruning.** Rank weights by absolute value and drop the smallest, 40% in the final setup. Max's analogy: muting the quietest voices in a noisy room.
- **Quantisation.** Weights from float32 to int8. Nothing deleted, just less precision, and a big drop in CPU load.
- **Knowledge distillation.** The student mimics the teacher without architecture changes.

## Distillation failed, and that is the interesting result

After trimming, the student was too small to understand the teacher's outputs. It compensated the only way it could, with hallucinations and repetition, and the output was unusable. The conclusion: non-aggressive methods don't stack on top of aggressive ones, so distillation was dropped from the final pipeline. Reporting the thing that didn't work is worth the price of admission on its own.

## The combined result, and the memory trade-off

The final model is fine-tuned GPT-2 trimmed to six layers, 40% pruned and int8-quantised. Compared with raw GPT-2, CPU load roughly halves, the model is about five times smaller, inference is faster and perplexity barely moves. The catch is RAM, which went up by about 200 MB, as the optimisations trade CPU time for larger tensors, caching and parallel processing. Max argues that is the right trade for battery-powered devices, where CPU is the biggest power draw, though it matters on microcontrollers with very little memory.

## Fine-tuning creates "resistance"

The key idea is what the authors call model resistance: how well a model keeps output quality under compression. A model fine-tuned for one clear task has strong internal signal and degrades slowly even under heavy pruning and quantisation. A general model has many overlapping skills and breaks fast; when they applied the same cuts to raw GPT-2, results were unusable and perplexity shot up. Fine-tuning, in their framing, is what makes optimisation possible at all.

## Who should watch

Engineers deploying language models on edge, offline or embedded hardware, and anyone choosing between a big general model and a small specialised one. The results are on GPT-2 and one task, so test before generalising to newer models.

Title: Confidence without ground truth, via p-values and compile-time C++
Description: Andrei Stroganov (Samsung Research) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on a p-value confidence metric for predictions with a constant-time, compile-time C++ lookup.
Body:
Your model predicts that 8,000 of an app's 300,000 methods are hot. With no labels to check against, is that believable? At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Andrei Stroganov, Expert Software Engineer at Samsung Research, presented joint work with Andrei Visochan on a confidence metric for exactly this case: a p-value score that says how plausible a prediction looks against the known distribution, computed in constant time from a lookup table that C++ builds at compile time.

It is a compact, math-forward talk, and the most hands-on numerical code of the event.

## The problem: no test set in production

During tuning you have labels, so F1 and AUC work. In production you often don't. Andrei's motivating case is the team's ML method for profile-guided optimisation on Android. Apps ship Java bytecode, and only frequently used ("hot") classes and methods are compiled ahead of time, listed in a profile. A model predicts which ones are hot and builds that profile. When no reference profile exists, you can't validate the prediction directly.

What you can do is ask whether the result is statistically reasonable. Their examples: does almost 8,000 hot methods look right for a Solitaire app, or almost 10% hot methods for SofaScore? They set three goals for the metric: easy to interpret (near one means probable, near zero improbable), fast to evaluate, and easy to verify without a mountain of unit tests.

## The metric is a doubled tail probability

From training data they plot the ratio of hot methods to total methods per app. It roughly follows a normal distribution, with a cubic spline interpolation as a more precise alternative. Given a cumulative distribution function F and a measured value t, the confidence is twice the smaller of F(t) and 1 minus F(t). If t sits in the middle of the distribution, the two tails are equal and confidence is one; if it's far out in either tail, confidence heads to zero. Applied to their examples, one app's hot-method count looks about right, another's looks very suspicious, and Solitaire lands somewhere in between, depending on your threshold.

The talk is honest that this definition is arguable for some distributions, which is the kind of caveat more ML talks should include.

## Make the compiler do the integration

The engineering half is where it gets fun. To evaluate the CDF quickly, they integrate the PDF numerically on an even grid with the trapezoid rule and store the cumulative values in a lookup table, so a query is just an index computation: constant time.

Where to build the table? At startup costs launch time and needs tests. Pasting values from Python is simple but painful every time the distribution changes. Their choice is C++ generic programming: generate the table during compilation, with compile-time error checks, and plug in any distribution, whether a formula or a piecewise approximation.

There is one snag. In C++17 the standard exponential isn't a constant expression, so they write their own: a Taylor series for arguments below one, and for larger values a split into integer and fractional parts, with fast binary exponentiation for the integer power to avoid overflow. The full source is on GitHub.

## Who should watch

ML engineers who ship models where labels arrive late or never, and C++ developers who enjoy constexpr tricks. One note: the abstract frames this around LLM predictions, while the talk itself works through classification and regression on the Android profiling case.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Salman Saeed Khan on probabilistic programming in Python](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2024_Salman_Saeed_Khan_probabilistic_programming), for more on reasoning with distributions instead of point estimates.
- [Hariharan Ragothaman on offloading compute-heavy workloads from Python to C++](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Hariharan_Ragothaman_cpp_python_workloads), the other side of the C++ performance story.

Title: Why BLEU gives a perfect answer 0.016, and what to measure instead
Description: Alok Ranjan (Dropbox) and Saurabh Suman at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on replacing n-gram metrics with FactScore, LLM-as-judge, G-Eval and RAG evaluation.
Body:
A shopper asks a support bot what size a jacket is, the bot answers "34", and BLEU scores that correct reply at 0.016. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Alok Ranjan, Engineering Manager at Dropbox, and Saurabh Suman of San José State University used examples like that to argue that n-gram metrics measure the wrong thing for LLMs, and walked through the evaluation toolkit that should replace them: atomic fact checking, human preference rankings, LLM judges, G-Eval and separate retriever and generator metrics for RAG.

It is a long, thorough talk, and one of the best overviews of LLM evaluation from the event.

## What BLEU and ROUGE actually measure

The first section is a fair-minded refresher. BLEU is precision-oriented n-gram overlap, a staple of machine translation; ROUGE is recall-oriented, built for summarisation. Both are fast, language-agnostic and need no human labels, which is why they spread.

Then the failure cases. Besides the jacket, their HR policy example pairs a reference ("employees are permitted to work remotely up to three days per week") with a paraphrase about staff telecommuting with supervisor approval. Same meaning, BLEU score of zero. The list of sins: surface-level, easy to game by repeating reference phrases, blind to factuality and coherence, and prone to penalising longer, more fluent answers. A metric that prefers the wrong answer with the right words is a regression test for vocabulary, not quality.

## What to measure instead

They define the dimensions a modern evaluation should cover: factual accuracy, semantic coherence, answer relevance, context precision and context recall, plus bias mitigation and reliability across prompts and personas.

For factuality, the method is FactScore: break a response into atomic facts (the Eiffel Tower is in Paris; it was built in 1889), check each against a trusted source, and score the supported fraction. The model-based version layers sentence-embedding alignment, natural language inference to label each fact as entailed or contradicted, and weighted aggregation.

Human evaluation stays in the loop, but structured: rubric-based scoring plus pairwise A-versus-B comparisons aggregated with a Bradley-Terry model into a global ranking, then compared against automated metrics to see where they disagree.

## Letting an LLM grade the LLM

Saurabh's half is about automation. An LLM judge brings context awareness, scale and consistency; humans audit the judge and feed corrections back. He demos the OpenAI Evals framework running GPT-3.5 Turbo on 25 Spider SQL samples from a single CLI command: 20 correct, 80% accuracy. One "failure" is instructive: the model used a LIKE pattern where the reference used exact equality, which is often right but not what was asked.

G-Eval gets the most attention. Define criteria, let the model write its own evaluation steps with chain of thought, then score. Assertions work like unit tests for LLMs, such as a rubric that fails any reply mentioning it is an AI assistant, which changes from fail to pass with a different persona prompt. On correlation with human judgment across coherence, consistency, fluency and relevance, the ROUGE variants trail, embedding metrics like BERTScore and MoverScore do better, and LLM-based evaluators such as G-Eval correlate best.

## RAG needs two report cards

For retrieval-augmented generation, evaluate the retriever and the generator separately: contextual precision, recall and relevancy for retrieval, and answer relevance and faithfulness for generation. A great generator still hallucinates when retrieval fails. They compare basic RAG, multi-query and RAG fusion across models and conclude no single metric is enough. The talk closes with a synthetic dataset pipeline (chunk documents, generate contexts and "goldens", evolve harder queries) and a practical checklist: clear objectives, mixed methods, representative datasets, continuous evaluation, strong baselines.

## Who should watch

Anyone shipping an LLM feature who still reports BLEU to their manager, and teams building their first eval harness. It is long, but it is the whole map in one sitting.

- [Liran Yushinsky (JFrog) on LLM-as-judge for non-deterministic code generation](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Liran_Yushinsky_testing_judge_codegen), the judge pattern applied to agents.

Title: Azure ML for document management, from extraction to compliance
Description: Harsha Vardhan Reddy Yeddula at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on Azure AI Document Intelligence, semantic search, Logic Apps workflows and PII redaction.
Body:
Every regulated company runs on documents nobody wants to read twice: invoices, contracts, claims, SOPs, audit reports. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Harsha Vardhan Reddy Yeddula, a Microsoft certified professional and Microsoft 365 cloud architect with 17 years in IT, showed how Azure Machine Learning and the surrounding Azure services automate that pile end to end, from pulling fields out of a scanned form to redacting PII before a file leaves the building.

This is an Azure-stack talk through and through, with SharePoint as the repository in most examples, so it is most useful if that is your world.

## Extraction and classification come first

Harsha starts where the manual work is heaviest. Azure AI Document Intelligence (formerly Form Recognizer) extracts structured data such as dates, amounts, names, product details and ID card fields from invoices, contracts and regulatory forms. Classification models then tag documents by content into groups like financial, legal or medical so they can be found later. He cites a 30 to 50% reduction in operational costs on data entry tasks for companies using AI document processing.

## Search should understand the question

Keyword search fails the moment a user doesn't know the exact phrasing in the document. Harsha's answer is semantic search through Azure AI Search, which works from the context and intent of the query and returns relevant documents even for incomplete search terms. He ties search to access control too: HR documents should not appear for regular employees, and internal business documents should not appear for customers. A search box that leaks the salary spreadsheet is worse than no search box.

## Upload triggers the workflow

The automation section is the most practical. When a document lands in SharePoint or Azure Blob Storage, the ML model analyses, classifies and extracts key data, and that becomes a workflow trigger. Power Automate, Azure Logic Apps and Azure Functions then send notifications, update records, start approvals or call external B2B connectors, with minimal human intervention. He cites up to 40% operational efficiency gains from automating workflows, and stresses that metadata, sensitivity classification and record retention are what make the hand-offs between departments work.

## Compliance as a model output

For regulated industries, ML models scan documents against rules like HIPAA and FDA requirements, flag sensitive or non-compliant content, and use NLP to identify and redact PII such as social security numbers, addresses and phone numbers. He quotes research that automated compliance monitoring can cut the likelihood of regulatory violations by up to 70%.

The industry examples make it concrete. In insurance, models speed claims processing and flag likely fraud from historical patterns. In life sciences, they help run quality management systems: tracking SOP revisions, audit reports and CAPA (corrective and preventive actions) against regulatory standards. Power BI dashboards then show audit findings, risk assessments and document status, from draft to approved.

## Security and the rollout plan

Underneath sit role-based access control, encryption and secure storage, with Azure Kubernetes Service hosting models for real-time inference at scale. His roadmap has four stages: assess current document processes and pick the workflows that benefit most, develop and train models for those document types, integrate and deploy with monitoring and security controls, then optimise accuracy and expand to more document types based on measured results.

## Who should watch

Architects and developers running document-heavy processes on Microsoft 365 and Azure, particularly in insurance, healthcare and life sciences. If you are on another cloud the patterns still apply, but the product names won't.

- [Vladimir Pesterev on extracting structured data from images with OCR and an LLM](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Vladimir_Pesterev_ocr_llm_data), the LLM-era take on extraction.
- [Mohit Sachdeva on AI-driven OCR for efficiency, accuracy and compliance](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Mohit_Sachdeva_ocr_ai_automation), the same goals built in Go.
- [Siddharth Pratap Singh on vector-based semantic search for information retrieval](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Siddharth_Pratap_Singh_search_vector_semantic), how the search half works under the hood.

Title: Cloud-native AI patterns, from containers to drift detection
Description: Bhaskar Goyal (Google) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on the cloud-native patterns behind enterprise AI, from IaC and layered stacks to split training and inference.
Body:
Getting a model to work in a notebook is a weekend. Getting it to production reliably, many times a week, is an architecture. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Bhaskar Goyal, Software Engineer at Google, walked through the cloud-native patterns that make that second part repeatable: containers, infrastructure as code, a layered stack, separate training and inference environments, feature stores, ML-aware Kubernetes, accelerator scheduling, CI/CD for models and automated monitoring.

It is a well-organised tour of the whole stack in about twenty minutes, so think of it as a checklist you can hold your own platform against.

## Containers and IaC kill "works on my machine"

Bhaskar starts with the contrast everyone in ML has lived: manual steps, handoffs between data science and ops, and deployment cycles measured in weeks. The first two fixes are old DevOps ideas applied to ML. Containers bundle code, libraries and dependencies so the environment is identical from development to production, and minimal inference images cut both latency and attack surface. Infrastructure as code, with Terraform or Pulumi, makes clusters and networks declarative, version-controlled and easy to roll back. He cites industry and project figures like a 90% reduction in configuration drift and 65% faster disaster recovery, presented as typical outcomes rather than a single case study.

## Training and inference want opposite things

The idea most worth stealing is the split. Training wants massive GPU clusters, batch optimisation and cheap interruptible spot instances, and can be ephemeral: spin up, train, tear down. Inference wants low latency, autoscaling, right-sized compute and high availability. Running both on one environment means one of them is always configured wrong. Bhaskar connects the split to 99.9% or higher inference uptime as a common SLA target, and to lower cloud costs from using spot capacity only where restarts are acceptable.

## Feature stores fix training-serving skew

His feature store section is a clean explanation of why the component exists: standard feature definitions, versioned storage with metadata, point-in-time correct retrieval for reproducible training, and low-latency serving for real-time predictions. The headline benefit is the notorious training-serving skew, when the feature computed in training differs from the one computed in production. Anyone who has chased a model that was great offline and mediocre online will nod here.

## Kubernetes needs ML-shaped extensions

On orchestration he lists the patterns that make Kubernetes ML-aware: custom resources like TFJob and PyTorchJob for distributed training, operators that encode the ML lifecycle, horizontal pod autoscaling on request volume or GPU utilisation, and a service mesh such as Istio for canary releases, A/B testing models and mutual TLS. For accelerators: device plugins, multi-tenant GPU sharing, NUMA-aware scheduling, mixed-precision inference, and hibernating idle GPUs and TPUs, which matters given what they cost per hour.

## Deployment is not the end

The last stretch covers MLOps pipelines (continuous integration with data and model validation gates, continuous delivery that packages models with Helm charts, continuous deployment with blue-green or canary rollouts and automated rollback) and monitoring. Models degrade as data drifts, so monitoring has to watch inputs and predictions, trigger retraining, and tie ML metrics to business KPIs so the value of the model stays visible.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers inheriting an ML workload and ML engineers who want the ops vocabulary. It is a broad, vendor-neutral overview, not a Google product talk and not a hands-on demo; the numbers are industry-reported ranges, so benchmark your own.
