Title: What Tesla and OpenAI show about Kubernetes for AI workloads
Description: Praneel Madabushini (NVIDIA) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on GPU scheduling, self-healing and distributed training on Kubernetes, via Tesla and OpenAI.
Body:
A cluster sized for last year's models is underprovisioned today. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Praneel Madabushini, Senior DevOps Engineer at NVIDIA with around ten years in DevOps, explained why Kubernetes became the default home for AI and ML workloads, then used Tesla and OpenAI as case studies of what the pattern looks like at extreme scale.

The case studies are drawn from public material about both companies, not inside knowledge, and the talk is upfront that it is about patterns you can copy.

## AI workloads break static clusters

Praneel's opening is a list of ways AI differs from a web service. Training is resource-hungry enough to eat a large share of a data centre's power budget. Data volumes and parameter counts keep compounding, so static infrastructure is always behind. Distributed pipelines spanning object stores, message queues and GPU nodes multiply failure modes, and without automated recovery the mean time to repair stretches into hours or days. Thousands of GPUs and no self-healing is how you lose a weekend of training.

## What Kubernetes brings to the table

The middle section maps each problem to a Kubernetes feature:

- **Declarative GPU provisioning.** Describe GPU type, driver and CUDA base image in YAML; the NVIDIA device plugin handles the rest.
- **Scaling.** The horizontal pod autoscaler fed by NVIDIA metrics, the vertical pod autoscaler for right-sizing, and KEDA for event-driven bursts.
- **Self-healing.** If a GPU node panics, the scheduler restarts the pod on healthy hardware and pod disruption budgets keep training jobs at quorum. Liveness and readiness probes catch hung processes.
- **Multi-tenancy.** Namespaces, quotas, taints and node selectors let you reserve one pool of A100s for a research team and a pool of H100s for production inference.
- **Monitoring.** Prometheus and Grafana dashboards for GPU temperature, power draw, PCIe throughput and network I/O.

He backs these with CNCF survey numbers and aggregated adoption statistics; the point is less any single figure than how normal running AI on Kubernetes has become.

## Tesla: hybrid cloud and over-the-air models

In Praneel's account, Tesla's autonomous driving pipeline processes video from eight cameras per car, roughly 1.5 TB of data per vehicle a year, with Kubernetes orchestrating thousands of containers for training. The stack he describes is PyTorch and TensorFlow for training, Triton Inference Server for inference, NVIDIA GPUs plus custom chips, data parallelism across GPUs, and a hybrid of on-prem and cloud capacity to balance cost and performance. The detail that stands out is deployment: model improvements ship over the air as new container images, so the fleet runs current weights.

## OpenAI: scheduling as the competitive edge

For OpenAI, the case is about scheduling at scale. Praneel describes Horovod on Kubeflow for distributed training, Spark on Kubernetes for petabyte-scale ETL, Triton plus custom operators for serving at sub-50 ms latency, priority-based preemption so critical research runs keep their SLAs, and pods moving between CPU-only preprocessing and GPU training stages as the pipeline progresses. Distributed tracing and GPU telemetry raise alerts in under a second.

## The ecosystem around it

He closes with the tooling: Kubeflow for pipelines, Katib for hyperparameter tuning, TensorFlow operators, KServe, Seldon Core and Triton for serving, and security from SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identity, mutual TLS and Kata Containers for hardware-virtualised isolation of high-value models.

## Who should watch

DevOps and platform engineers about to put GPUs into a cluster for the first time, or anyone who has to justify Kubernetes for ML to leadership. If you already run Kubeflow in production, the case studies are the main new material.

Title: Fleet logistics on Kafka, Kubernetes and edge computing
Description: Venkata Anil Kumar Nilisetty (Cognizant) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on event-driven microservices for GPS tracking, route optimisation and fleet management.
Body:
A delivery truck does not wait for your monolith's four-hour deploy window. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Venkata Anil Kumar Nilisetty, a manager at Cognizant Technology Solutions with more than 15 years building enterprise applications, showed how an event-driven microservices architecture on Spring Boot, Kafka and Kubernetes changed fleet management and logistics, with results across tracking, maintenance, warehouses and last-mile delivery.

It is a short talk, and almost every slide carries a number.

## Why the monolith had to go

Venkata starts with the state of logistics IT. He says 60 to 80% of IT budgets in the sector go into maintaining legacy systems that take four to six hours for minor changes, go down for two to three hours per update cycle, and degrade sharply beyond about a thousand users. Add rising fuel costs, tight delivery windows and complex urban routing, and the case for a rewrite makes itself.

The replacement is textbook: Spring Boot for modular services, Kafka for event streaming, Kubernetes for autoscaling and resilience. Services deploy independently, scale on demand and keep failures local.

## Tracking and edge: put the compute near the truck

Three use cases carry the talk. The first is GPS tracking with a hybrid active-passive model, reaching five to ten metres accuracy in cities and 15 to 20 metres in rural areas. Kafka handles up to 25,000 updates per vehicle per hour with 95% transmission success even in poor signal areas.

The second is edge computing for traffic management. Speed and behaviour checks run on the vehicle side rather than in the cloud, responding to speed violations in 85 milliseconds and to complex behaviour in 120. That cuts false alarms and bandwidth use by up to 78%. It is the right call: a speeding alert that arrives after the driver has slowed down is just a log line.

The third is AI route optimisation using historical data, live traffic and customer delivery windows, which he reports gives 40% faster route planning, 25% more deliveries per vehicle and up to 20% lower delivery costs.

## The business results

The numbers Venkata reports are broad: 45% fewer vehicle breakdowns, 25% lower maintenance costs, 98.5% fleet tracking accuracy, 35% better driving behaviour, 30% fewer accidents and 20% lower insurance premiums. For a 100-vehicle fleet he puts savings at over $350,000 a year from fuel and maintenance alone.

Warehouses get the same treatment: intelligent order batching cut picking times by 38%, real-time inventory improved space use by 42%, and better route planning and load consolidation reduced last-mile costs by 30% and carbon emissions by 28%.

## Resilience by design

The infrastructure slide is the one platform engineers will want to pause on. Pods autoscale between three and ten instances around 70% CPU, uptime holds at 99.95% even during updates, load shedding prevents cascading failures, and active replication recovers from outages in under 30 seconds.

## Who should watch

Engineers modernising a logistics or fleet platform, and anyone pitching Kafka-plus-Kubernetes to a business that still deploys on Sundays. The talk shows results rather than code, so expect architecture and outcomes, not configs.

Title: Healthcare enterprise architecture, built in four phases
Description: Suresh Kumar Gundala at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on FHIR, blockchain, cloud and compliance as code as the layers of a connected healthcare stack.
Body:
Hospitals rarely suffer from a lack of systems. They suffer from too many that don't talk to each other. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Suresh Kumar Gundala, an enterprise architect with more than 17 years in distributed systems, APIs and micro-frontend applications, laid out how enterprise architecture turns that pile of systems into one connected healthcare platform, and why it has to be done in phases rather than as a single big migration.

It is an architecture survey with case studies, aimed at people who build the plumbing that clinical software sits on.

## Three components hold the stack up

Suresh starts with the three components he sees in every modern healthcare infrastructure. Distributed systems link hospitals, clinics, labs and specialist centres so data moves between them in real time. Standardised APIs act as the common language between EHRs, lab systems and pharmacy systems. And security, meaning encryption, access controls and continuous monitoring, is what keeps all of that compliant with HIPAA.

On top of those he places three technologies, each with a clear job:

- **FHIR** for interoperability. Its RESTful design is what makes it practical for developers, and it lets legacy systems join newer applications without a rewrite.
- **Blockchain** for integrity. Records that can't be altered without detection, no single point of failure for attackers to aim at, and smart contracts to automate rules such as insurance claim steps.
- **Cloud** for elasticity and recovery: scaling with patient volumes, paying for what you use, and geographically distributed backups for when a region goes dark.

## The numbers he attaches to it

Suresh reports measurable gains from EA implementations: a 37% workflow improvement, 54% better system reliability, 89% better data consistency and a 42% overall cost reduction. His success stories are more concrete. A metro health system cut data retrieval time by 68% and saw patient satisfaction rise about 29%. A rural care network connected 24 previously isolated clinics and cut patient transfer coordination time by about 41%. A research hospital group used secure data sharing with partners to grow clinical trial enrolment by 35%. The talk names these as examples, not as peer-reviewed studies.

## Compliance belongs in the architecture

The most useful idea for engineers is how he handles regulation. HIPAA, GDPR and the 21st Century Cures Act keep changing, and checking them by hand doesn't scale. His answer is compliance as code: frameworks that automate monitoring, documentation and enforcement of policy, so audit trails stay current without a quarterly scramble. If you have ever reconstructed an audit trail from Slack messages, you know why this matters.

The other two challenges get equally practical answers. Legacy systems get middleware adapters and standard APIs instead of disruptive replacements. Staff adoption gets role-specific, incremental training built into daily workflows.

## Foundation, integration, optimisation, innovation

The phased model is the spine of the talk. First comes a secure foundation, then integration of isolated systems through standard interfaces, then optimisation driven by real usage data, and only then innovation with AI, IoT, predictive analytics and LLMs. Looking ahead, Suresh expects predictive analytics to flag patient deterioration up to 72 hours earlier, edge computing to remove latency from telemedicine and emergency care, and zero trust to replace perimeter security.

## Who should watch

Architects and platform engineers in healthcare IT who need a vocabulary for the whole stack, or a sequence to argue for with leadership. If you want implementation detail on FHIR servers or a specific ledger, look elsewhere; this is the map.

Title: Value-based care is a data integration problem first
Description: Bandanawaz Mulla (Health Care Service Corporation) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on how cloud platforms tackle the data and reporting work behind value-based care.
Body:
If you get paid for patient outcomes instead of procedures, you have to be able to measure outcomes, and most healthcare data is not ready for that. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Bandanawaz Mulla, Senior Manager Platform Strategy at Health Care Service Corporation with more than 19 years in IT, walked through the challenges of value-based care (VBC) and the cloud patterns that address each one, ending with a system his team built on AWS.

It is a payer-side view of the problem, which makes it a useful counterweight to the many provider-side healthcare AI talks.

## From fee-for-service to quality metrics

Bandanawaz frames VBC as the move from fee-for-service, where more services equal more revenue, to reimbursement tied to benchmarks, cost and patient satisfaction. That means preventive care, chronic disease management and coordinated care across providers. It also means tracking a lot of quality metrics: HEDIS measures, STAR ratings, ACO performance. The model promises better care at lower cost, but it demands changes in workflows, infrastructure and culture.

## Fragmentation is the root problem

Patient data lives in separate EHRs, lab systems, pharmacy databases, billing platforms and specialty records. Each silo creates a blind spot for clinical decisions and makes quality reporting close to impossible. His fix is the familiar but correct one: a cloud data lake that pulls disparate sources into one repository, FHIR APIs and HL7 integration engines for two-way data sharing, and normalisation services so the data is usable for analytics.

Reporting follows from there. He names AWS HealthLake, Microsoft Azure for Health and the Google Cloud Healthcare API as platforms that automate extraction, normalisation and metric calculation, with dashboards that find care gaps while there is still time to act, rather than in a retrospective review months later.

## Coordination, engagement and risk

The middle of the talk maps the remaining challenges to cloud capabilities:

- **Care coordination**: role-based shared care plans that specialists, primary care, nurses and social workers update at the same time, plus alerts for missed appointments or care plan deviations.
- **Patient engagement**: automated SMS, email and app reminders, secure messaging, wearables for remote monitoring, and patient portals tailored to language and literacy.
- **Risk stratification**: machine learning on clinical data, claims history and social determinants of health, using cloud compute to find high-risk patients early.
- **Compliance**: HIPAA, HITRUST and SOC 2 frameworks available from the cloud provider, with automated audit logging.

## The engine his team built

The most concrete part is a value-based care data enablement engine Bandanawaz's team implemented on AWS. It aggregates data into a unified view of contract performance against key metrics. He reports that it cut provider onboarding and implementation costs by 25% or more, reduced reporting time by 75% and improved accuracy by 30%. That is the bit of the talk you can take to a planning meeting.

His best-practice advice is incremental: assess current systems, define specific VBC goals, start with the highest-impact use case, involve stakeholders early, and use FHIR APIs to standardise exchange. Nobody migrates a payer's data estate in one quarter.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers at payers, ACOs or health systems moving into value-based contracts, and anyone who needs to explain to a non-technical sponsor why the data lake comes before the AI. It is a strategy talk with one real system in it, not a hands-on tutorial.

Title: Multimodal AI in patient care means four data streams, not one
Description: Hari Suresh Babu Gummadi (Frontier Internet) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on fusing EHRs, patient-reported outcomes, genomics and wearables for care.
Body:
A clinical model that only reads the EHR sees the patient on the days they visit the clinic. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Hari Suresh Babu Gummadi, an IT solutions architect at Frontier Internet with a background in enterprise workflow automation across telecom, finance and insurance, argued that patient-centred AI needs four streams at once: electronic health records, patient-reported outcomes, genomic profiles and wearable sensor data.

The talk is a framework overview, not a code walkthrough. Its value is in how it puts the pieces together and which clinical problems each stream is supposed to solve.

## Each stream covers a different blind spot

Hari's framing is that every data source fills a gap the others leave open. The EHR is the backbone: medical history, clinical notes, diagnostics. Patient-reported outcomes capture what the chart misses, such as pain levels and emotional wellbeing, the things a lab panel never shows. Genomic profiles bring in individual variants and biomarkers, so therapy choice can be targeted rather than averaged. Wearables fill the time between visits with heart rate, sleep and activity.

Put together, the model gets a continuous picture instead of a series of snapshots. Anyone who has debugged a system from hourly metrics alone, and then got per-second data and saw what was actually happening, will recognise the argument.

## The first payoff is clinician time

Before outcomes, Hari puts the clinician's workload. Automating routine analysis and surfacing the most relevant clinical information is pitched as reducing documentation time by 42%, giving clinicians about 3.5 extra hours a week with patients, and he reports 89% provider satisfaction with clinicians citing better work-life balance. On the patient side, he describes higher engagement, with patients more involved in treatment planning and more willing to trust their providers when AI-driven insights are shared and explained openly.

The point worth keeping: a model that adds clicks to a clinician's day will be ignored, however accurate it is. Workload comes first.

## Prediction is where multimodal earns its keep

The sharpest section is on early deterioration. Hari describes a prediction system that looks for subtle physiological changes across several parameters at once and flags critical deterioration up to 48 hours before conventional monitoring would. His examples are the kind of slow drift a single threshold alarm misses, like small but consistent changes in respiration or sleep quality preceding something like sepsis.

The same data feeds the shift from reactive to proactive care: personalised risk profiles built from genetics, lifestyle and environment; alerts when the expected pattern breaks, for example when refill activity drops; and treatment pathways tailored in oncology to reduce adverse effects. He closes with results from a five-year study across 27 healthcare systems, reporting a 34% increase in clinical efficiency and a 41% reduction in adverse events. The talk gives the headline figures rather than the study design, so treat them as the speaker's summary.

## The communication layer is underrated

One part that often gets skipped in AI healthcare talks is communication. Hari spends time on how the framework gives specialists and primary care the same consistent data, and turns complex results into clear recommendations a patient can follow. Prediction is useless if the referring GP never sees it.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects starting on healthcare data platforms who want a map of which data sources matter and why. If you need model architectures, fusion techniques or validation methods, this talk stays at the framework level. One data note: the abstract on the talk page describes a different session on population health BI, so go by the video.

Title: Population health with risk tiers, gradient boosting and maps
Description: Satya Manesh Veerapaneni (Dazzlon) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on predictive BI, four-tier risk stratification and geospatial analytics for population health.
Body:
Most population health programmes fail at the first step: knowing which patients to call. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Satya Manesh Veerapaneni, Senior Business Intelligence Consultant at Dazzlon, showed how predictive BI turns EHR, claims and social determinants data into four risk tiers, and how a map can be as useful as a model when deciding where care should go.

It is a short, dense talk and one of the more concrete healthcare sessions of the event.

## The problem is targeting, not effort

Satya opens with a statistic from the abstract: over 60% of healthcare organisations struggle to identify high-risk populations, predict chronic disease trends and allocate resources efficiently. In the talk he is clear that this is not a lack of will. It is data silos, outdated infrastructure and limited access to integrated tools.

## Build the 360-degree view first

Before any model, he combines three data types: clinical records from EHRs, utilisation and cost data from claims, and social determinants of health such as income, education and housing stability. ETL pipelines, secure API gateways and HL7 FHIR compliance keep it clean, and he reports the integrated data validated at over 99.7% accuracy. Garbage in, garbage risk score out, so this ordering is right.

## Four tiers from supervised models

The risk stratification models are supervised, trained on over 8.5 million patient records with more than 3,000 variables: labs, medication adherence, utilisation patterns and socioeconomic inputs. Random forest and gradient boosting beat traditional logistic regression, reaching 87 to 92% accuracy at predicting hospitalisation within six months. Patients land in one of four buckets (high risk, rising risk, low risk, healthy), each with its own intervention plan, from intensive care management down to wellness education.

He backs it with evaluation that goes beyond a holdout set. In studies covering over 30,000 patients, compared with traditional care, he reports readmissions down 20%, ER visits down 30%, costs down 20% and engagement up 40%, measured with A/B testing and propensity score matching. Seeing a healthcare BI talk mention propensity matching is a small joy.

He also stresses interpretability: clinicians need to see why a model flagged someone. One example model flags readmission risk from subtle combinations of refill patterns and prior claims.

## Geography is a feature too

The most distinctive section is geospatial analytics. Using GIS, the team maps disease prevalence, resource use and care access across regions to find healthcare deserts, plan mobile outreach and choose sites for new clinics. With catchment area modelling and isochrone maps, he reports facility placement efficiency improving by over 40%.

## A diabetes case study and the equity angle

His case study is a regional health system serving 150,000 people, mostly aged 45 to 75, with a high diabetes burden. Using HbA1c trends, adherence and social data over 18 months, diabetic admissions dropped 42%, saving $3.2 million a year. Outcomes fed back into the system to adjust care plans, which is what separates a learning system from a dashboard.

Equity runs through all of it: zip code, ethnicity, income and access data to find underserved groups, culturally sensitive outreach with local partners, and equity KPIs tracked over time. The roadmap ends with Plan-Do-Study-Act loops to recalibrate the models.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and BI engineers in healthcare analytics, especially anyone building risk scores who has not yet thought about geography or equity metrics. It moves fast, so keep the pause button handy.

- [Satya Manesh Veerapaneni on AI-powered healthcare BI with Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Satya_Manesh_Veerapaneni_healthcare_bi_analytics), the same speaker on the real-time analytics engineering side.

Title: Where AI pays off in healthcare, from paperwork to precision medicine
Description: Peeyush Khandelwal at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on AI in documentation, claims, pharmacy, imaging and precision medicine, plus ethics and a rollout roadmap.
Body:
The least glamorous AI in a hospital is often the one that pays for the rest. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Peeyush Khandelwal toured the places AI is already changing healthcare: clinical documentation, claims processing, pharmacy, diagnostic imaging and precision medicine, and then closed with the parts most tours skip, workforce training, ethics and a phased rollout plan.

Treat it as a broad briefing for engineers and leaders deciding where to start, rather than a technical deep look at one model.

## Start with the paperwork

Peeyush opens on documentation and admin, because that is where clinicians lose their week. In his figures, AI-assisted documentation reduces medication errors by about 30% and saves providers around six hours a week. Documentation systems reach 93% accuracy at organising clinical notes, cross-check medications and suggest corrections against clinical guidelines.

Claims get the same treatment. AI pre-scans claims for coding errors, missing documentation and compliance issues before submission, handles routine claims without human touch, and flags the ones likely to be denied. He cites 42% faster processing and 28% fewer denials, with claims turnaround dropping from weeks to days. For anyone who has worked on a billing pipeline, the shift-left idea is familiar: validate before the expensive round trip, not after.

## Pharmacy and imaging: AI as a second check

The pharmacy section is about safety. AI performs first-pass prescription verification, scans the full record (prescriptions, labs, allergies) for harmful interactions, suggests dosing from age, weight, renal function and genetic markers, and keeps watching for adverse events after the prescription is filled.

Imaging is where Peeyush is careful with his framing. Models trained on CT, MRI and X-ray datasets detect abnormalities with high sensitivity and specificity and never get tired at the end of a shift. He reports a 28% reduction in radiologist workload, but not because radiologists are replaced: the model sorts normal scans from urgent ones so humans spend their attention where it matters. His phrase for it is a second set of eyes.

## Precision medicine is the long game

In precision medicine, deep learning finds biomarkers that reveal disease pathways and new therapeutic targets. Decision support shortens time to the right treatment, which Peeyush puts at 35%, and outcome prediction uses labs, imaging history and wearable data to adjust a care plan early. Earlier in the talk he credits ML with speeding the discovery of treatment options up to 200 times compared with conventional research methods.

## People, ethics and the roadmap

The second half is what makes the talk more than a list of wins. Adoption needs AI literacy across the organisation, role-specific training (clinicians, administrators and technical staff need different things), hands-on practice in simulated environments, and continuous learning. The ethics section covers four non-negotiables: fairness tested across diverse populations, privacy, transparency so a clinician can see why a model flagged a risk, and human oversight. In his words, AI is "a tool, not a replacement of clinical judgment".

On money, he reports positive ROI typically within nine to 14 months for institutions (with claims automation alone paying back in four to six), about $1.2 million a year saved on documentation for a mid-size hospital, and a 9.3% increase in patient throughput. The roadmap is sensible and boring in the best way: find the biggest pain point, build champions, pilot in one department, measure error rates and time saved, then expand.

## Who should watch

Healthcare IT leads and ML engineers picking a first AI project, and anyone who needs to make the case to finance. Engineers wanting architecture details should pair it with a more hands-on talk.

Title: Bolting generative AI onto cloud ERP without breaking it
Description: Pavan Kumar Bollineni (Deloitte) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on a layered architecture, data prep and model governance for AI forecasting in ERP.
Body:
ERP systems hold the most valuable data in a company and are the last place anyone wants to experiment. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Pavan Kumar Bollineni](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Pavan_Kumar_Bollineni_cloud_erp), a Manager at Deloitte with 12 years in SAP ERP solutions, lays out how to add generative and predictive AI to cloud ERP: a layered architecture, a loosely coupled integration, disciplined data preparation and a model lifecycle with a retirement plan.

The talk is broad and example-heavy, mixing an implementation framework with a long list of industry use cases. The framework is the part to keep.

## Why ERP is where forecasting lives

Pavan's starting point is that forecasting, inventory, production scheduling and financial planning all already run through the ERP, so that's where AI pays off. His focus is generative adversarial networks alongside more familiar machine learning, used to improve forecasting accuracy across business functions.

He cites market figures for AI-in-ERP growth and adoption, plus a stream of company examples, from Walmart's inventory management to Toyota using reinforcement learning to cut production lead times by 18%. Treat these as illustrations of where the pattern shows up; the talk doesn't go deep on any single deployment except one.

## Five layers, clear boundaries

The architecture is a five-layer stack:

1. **Security**: data protection and compliance at the integration boundary.
2. **Technology**: the compute infrastructure that makes AI workloads possible.
3. **Data**: information flow and storage.
4. **Application**: business logic and processing.
5. **Presentation**: the user interface.

The point of the layering, he says, is clarity about system boundaries, integration points and information flows. Cloud deployment, infrastructure as code for repeatability, and canonical data models that normalize terminology across business units sit underneath.

## Keep AI loosely coupled to the ERP

The integration advice is the most useful engineering takeaway. Successful projects isolate AI components from the underlying ERP through middleware that abstracts the ERP's complexity and exposes standardized interfaces, with event-driven patterns and explicit error handling. That way the model can evolve on its own schedule and the core system keeps its functional integrity. Anyone who has tried to upgrade an ERP with custom code welded into it will appreciate the instinct.

## Data prep and model lifecycle are the real work

Pavan's data preparation pipeline has four steps: validate against quality thresholds, standardize formats across sources, enrich with derived features and context, and verify readiness before model ingestion. The challenges he names are inconsistency across sources, incomplete historical records and semantic ambiguity, and he notes that systematic preparation beats ad hoc approaches.

Model governance runs develop, validate against business requirements, deploy with monitoring, monitor with alerts on degradation thresholds, and retire outdated models in favour of better ones. That last step gets skipped surprisingly often.

## One worked case

The deepest example is an automotive parts manufacturer on SAP S/4HANA using GAN-based forecasting, which he reports delivered a 37.88% improvement in forecast accuracy and 4.7 million in annual inventory savings. He also cites an average 23% forecasting improvement over traditional time-series approaches when ERP data is combined with external factors.

## What comes next

His future directions: multimodal AI that combines structured ERP data with text, images, audio and video; edge computing at factories, stores and logistics centers; and model optimization through quantization, pruning and distillation. The roadmap: assess readiness, pick high-value use cases with success metrics, go proof of concept to scale, and set up a center of excellence that mixes technical, domain and change management people.

## Who should watch

SAP and Oracle ERP architects being asked to "add AI", and data engineers who will own the integration. If you want GAN internals or code, look elsewhere; this is an enterprise architecture talk.

Title: Vibe marketing is vibe coding for campaigns, data leaks included
Description: Udipta Basumatari (Thravos.io) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 demos vibe marketing with LLMs, and the data safety framework it still needs.
Body:
If vibe coding is prompting your way to a working app, vibe marketing is prompting your way to a working campaign. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Udipta Basumatari](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Udipta_Basumatari_vibe_marketing_genai), Chief Marketing Officer at Thravos.io, explains what the term actually means, demos it with ChatGPT and Canva, and then spends a welcome chunk of the talk on where it goes wrong.

Udipta has 16 years in marketing, MarTech and go-to-market, including running Adobe Media Optimizer from 2014 to 2019, so he has watched marketing move from predictive machine learning to generative models first-hand.

## The vibe is the smallest part

He opens by admitting he doesn't love the name, because it suggests the job is matching your audience's mood. That's maybe 20% of it, he says. The term borrows from Andrej Karpathy's "vibe coding", and Udipta proves the point with a travel-map website he vibe coded in about eight hours after 15 years away from programming.

Applied to marketing, the idea is that anyone, not only marketers, can work with LLMs to shrink the loop from campaign planning to execution, iteration, reporting and re-optimization. That means personalization down to the individual, rapid content creation and testing, and feeding customer reviews and comments straight into a model to decide the next move.

## Real campaigns, real numbers

The examples are the fun part. Coca-Cola let fans generate art with DALL-E inspired by its branding and got over 120,000 submissions and over 7 million social impressions. Heinz used image generation for ketchup bottle visuals and saw a 40% higher ROI on AI-generated video ads. Mango used virtual models for a summer collection. Virgin Voyages sent personalized video invitations from a deepfake Jennifer Lopez, which is either delightful or unsettling depending on your relationship with your inbox.

## The demo: fast, then human

The live demo pretends Udipta runs a campaign for Hoka. His best practice: open a separate ChatGPT thread per channel (X, in this case), seed it with instructions, then paste a refined brief with audience, brand guidelines, key phrases and colour palette. He asks for three ad copy variations and three images, and gets copy he'd happily ship.

Then the honesty. One generated image has text that doesn't contrast with the background, so a human has to catch it. The work is maybe five or six times faster, not hands-off. He also runs out of image credits mid-demo, which is the most relatable moment of the conference. Canva covers the manual fallback with AI background removal and templates.

Two smaller demos land harder. A sentiment analysis of customer reviews, built with free Python libraries and ChatGPT-written code, took about 20 minutes and revealed that login issues were the top complaint. A segmentation for a gaming company suggested nudging players towards "whale" spending levels.

## The ecosystem is fragmented

The first problem: tools that push ads to Facebook and Google over APIs don't generate the copy, and tools that generate copy don't push. You can't automate end to end yet, so someone experienced still glues it together.

## Data safety is the serious one

The second problem is bigger. Udipta recalls the Samsung developer who pasted product source code into ChatGPT. His answer is a data security framework from his time at Salesforce:

- **Secure data retrieval**, so only sanctioned data reaches the model.
- **Grounding**, where personalization happens, with masking and encryption. His example: Ticketmaster should send pop concert offers to him and jazz offers to his wife, without leaking either profile.
- **A gateway** with contractual or technical zero retention at the LLM provider, or locally hosted models if you can afford them.
- **Generation guardrails** against hallucination and toxicity.
- **An audit trail** to know what happened, when, and who was at the wheel.

His warning to smaller companies is that skipping this now will haunt them later.

## Who should watch

Marketers and growth engineers experimenting with LLMs, and the platform or security engineers who will be asked to make it safe. It's a broad, practical tour rather than a deep technical build.

Title: An HD camera and LED on a 5 mm tip change flexible endoscopy
Description: Santosh Suresh (Johnson & Johnson) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on CMOS sensors, LED-on-tip lighting and imaging modes in modern flexible endoscopes.
Body:
Any computer vision model is only as good as the camera feeding it, and inside a human lung that camera has to fit on the tip of a tube. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Santosh Suresh](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Santosh_Suresh_flexible_endoscopy), Principal Engineer at Johnson & Johnson, explains how flexible endoscopes went from fiber-optic light and small CCD sensors to HD CMOS cameras with LEDs on the tip, and what that changes for diagnosis and treatment.

Honest scope: this is a medical hardware and imaging talk at an ML conference. Machine learning appears in the future directions, as the thing all this better imaging makes possible. For ML engineers who might one day train on endoscopy video, that makes it useful background.

## From fiber bundles to an HD revolution

About ten years ago, Santosh says, the state of the art was a small CCD sensor at the tip of the scope, with light shone onto tissue through a fiber-optic bundle from an external light engine. Surgeons and pulmonologists could finally see hard-to-reach anatomy such as the lungs, but the picture had limits.

What changed is the sensor. CMOS technology brought higher resolution and better light sensitivity, so clinicians can identify and evaluate lesions with more confidence. Today's scopes deliver 1080p HD imaging with a 170-degree field of view, very low latency, and 60 frames per second, smooth enough to follow a beating pulse or trace vasculature in detail.

## Shrinking everything at once

The engineering story is miniaturisation. The endoscope tip has shrunk from 10 to 15 outer diameter to about 5, which matters a great deal for patient comfort. Small LEDs now put out on the order of five to 10 lumens across a wide cone. And the LED on the tip went from two to three millimetres to about 0.57, with the same light output.

Moving the light source into the body creates a new problem: heat next to living tissue. So the designs include heat dissipation and temperature regulation to protect the surrounding tissue from thermal exposure. Anyone who has managed thermals on a tiny board will sympathise; here the enclosure is a patient.

## Four ways to see

Santosh walks through the imaging modalities:

- **RGB**, the standard full-colour view and by far the most common, for natural colour reproduction during routine exams.
- **Near-infrared**, which reveals subsurface vascular networks and structural abnormalities.
- **Clear Pixel**, for challenging light-starved environments, keeping images usable even with bodily fluids or other obstructions in view.
- **Narrow band imaging**, an optical filter that isolates specific blue and green wavelengths to bring out mucosal surface patterns and microvascular structure for early detection of disease.

Beside the camera and LED, the tip leaves room for working tools: biopsy tools to extract a lesion, injection devices for therapeutic agents, irrigation to clear fluids, and energy delivery, such as a laser to ablate a kidney stone.

## What it does for patients and hospitals

Across gastroenterology, pulmonology, urology and ENT, he cites a 15 to 20% rise in sensitivity and specificity moving from standard to enhanced HD endoscopy. For patients, a lung biopsy can mean hours in hospital instead of days, with less pain medication and faster recovery. For institutions, he reports a 30% decrease in average procedure time, a 25% increase in daily procedures per endoscopy suite, 92% positive patient feedback, and equipment costs recovered within 16 months.

The implementation section is refreshingly practical: capital costs from tens of thousands to half a million depending on configuration, staff training, service intervals and sterilization protocols, and EMR integration for archiving images and findings.

## Where ML comes in

The future directions are where this audience perks up: machine learning for lesion detection and classification, automated analysis that flags abnormalities during procedures, robotic manipulation and autonomous navigation, single-use scopes to remove cross-contamination risk, and AR and VR for 3D mapping.

## Who should watch

ML engineers working on medical imaging who want to understand the hardware behind their data, and anyone curious how a modern endoscope works. If you want model architectures, this isn't the talk.

Title: Five pillars for securing enterprise generative AI workloads
Description: Kalyan Madicharla (AWS) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on a five-pillar security framework for GenAI, from IAM and prompt injection to the EU AI Act.
Body:
Your existing cloud security framework was written before anyone could talk your application into leaking its system prompt. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Kalyan Madicharla](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Kalyan_Madicharla_securing_genai), Senior Technical Account Manager at AWS, presents a five-pillar framework for generative AI workloads: infrastructure security, data protection, application security, responsible AI and regulatory compliance.

It's a short, dense talk that works as a checklist you can hold your own GenAI rollout against. Kalyan frames the pillars as interdependent layers, not separate boxes to tick.

## Why the old framework isn't enough

The opening is the market argument: generative AI growing from 13.8 billion in 2023 to a projected 118 billion by 2032, with new security, privacy and ethical risks that existing cloud frameworks don't fully cover. Each pillar, he says, maps to problems seen in real field deployments, from access control breaches to AI outputs nobody was watching.

## Pillar 1: infrastructure, starting with identity

Identity and access management is the number one attack vector, and he cites 67% of organizations reporting unauthorized AI access attempts. So: least privilege and multi-factor authentication first. Encrypt every model endpoint and internal API end to end with TLS 1.3 or higher, consider HSM-backed key storage, and use infrastructure as code with embedded guardrails to prevent drift. Run automated security posture assessments quarterly. Defense in depth, not a perimeter.

## Pillar 2: data is both fuel and liability

Classify training and inference data by sensitivity, and minimize what the model can reach. Protect intellectual property with watermarking, provenance tracking and legal frameworks for AI-generated output. For personal data, lean on synthetic data, federated learning and differential privacy.

## Pillar 3: inputs and outputs are a new attack surface

This is the section most teams underinvest in. GenAI apps aren't traditional apps, and prompt injection lets users steer model behaviour with crafted input. Kalyan's answer is input sanitization and contextual validation on the way in, and output scanning on the way out: real-time toxicity detection, context filtering and safety classifiers. He cites an MIT Technology Review study finding 72% of GenAI adopters have already had at least one unsafe output incident.

## Pillars 4 and 5: ethics and regulators

Responsible AI means clear usage policies with risk categories per use case, routine red teaming, and automated bias detection paired with human review. Prompt security gets its own threat modeling: instruction leakage, boundary enforcement, controlled prompt chaining and context filtering.

On regulation, the EU AI Act treats GenAI in critical sectors as high risk, demanding explainability, risk controls and human oversight, while in the US the FDA, FTC and NIST each offer sector-specific guidance. The practical ask is an audit trail for every GenAI interaction (input, output, user identity and system response) in tamper-evident storage.

## Making it real

The implementation steps are concrete. Run a GenAI-specific security assessment that maps your models, APIs, data sets and endpoints. Write policies with business, legal and technical owners together. Secure APIs with OAuth 2.0 plus PKCE, which protects against token interception in client-side and mobile scenarios. Add rate limiting and usage monitoring to catch abuse.

Looking ahead, he expects adversarial prompts, data poisoning, prompt injection chaining, model inversion and evasion attacks, which push security from static controls towards real-time prompt inspection and output monitoring.

## Who should watch

Security architects, platform engineers and cloud teams who have just been told the company is "doing GenAI" and need a structure for the conversation. It's a framework talk without a demo, so pair it with something hands-on.

- [Manvitha Potluri on why single-layer LLM guardrails fail](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2026_Manvitha_Potluri_injection_guardrails_bedrock) tests hundreds of prompt injection attacks against the input and output pillar.
- [Blaize Stewart on hacking RAG systems](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Blaize_Stewart_rag_security_injection) shows what the attacker side looks like.

Title: Where AI's return actually shows up in financial services
Description: Sampath Varanasi (Microsoft) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 tours AI's measurable impact in finance, from loan approvals and AML to financial inclusion.
Body:
"Show me the ROI" is the sentence that ends most AI pilots. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Sampath Varanasi](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sampath_Varanasi_services_financial_roi), Technical Program Manager at Microsoft, tries to answer it for financial services, walking domain by domain through where AI has produced numbers a CFO would recognise: efficiency, forecasting, anti-money laundering, lending and inclusion.

This is a big-picture survey rather than a single case study. The figures come from the industry and from named institutions' public efforts, and Sampath narrates them conversationally, with plenty of personal asides.

## Efficiency first, because it's easiest to count

The opening slide puts AI-driven automation at a 35% operational efficiency gain across routine work: account creation, consolidation, transaction processing, data entry. His example is JPMorganChase automating loan approvals and account verification. In his telling, the initial loan process that used to take two to five weeks now takes under one, which saves time for the bank and the borrower alike.

Forecasting is next, with Goldman Sachs as the example of AI applied to market prediction and budgeting, and a cited reduction in data processing errors of about 20%.

## Three technical pillars

Sampath frames the architecture behind these results around three ideas:

- **Generative AI** for customer interaction. He quotes systems handling 1.2 million tokens per second and points to HSBC's customer service chatbots giving immediate answers grounded in a customer's profile and history, where a request used to take 24 to 48 hours.
- **Predictive analytics** over the roughly 2.5 petabytes of financial data generated daily, with BlackRock spotting trends and managing portfolio risk.
- **Security**, which he insists is not optional: multi-layered encryption, AI-driven cybersecurity of the kind Visa uses, and strict compliance whenever personal data passes through a chatbot or agent.

## AML is where the numbers get loud

The anti-money laundering section carries the headline figure from the abstract: 83.5% accuracy in threat detection, catching sophisticated financial crimes that previously went unnoticed. He adds a 65% reduction in false positives at one bank, which matters as much as the detection rate. Every false positive is an analyst's afternoon spent on an innocent customer.

Looking further out, he expects AI to handle a large share of routine banking transactions by 2027, with Wells Fargo cited as moving that way so human advisors can spend their time on complex financial planning instead of paperwork.

## The social return

The most interesting turn in the talk is the argument that ROI isn't only financial. Sampath cites AI-driven banking access reaching 1.7 billion previously unbanked people, mobile payment platforms in Kenya, fraud detection preventing consumer losses, and lenders such as Kabbage and Fundbox using AI to assess small business credit and approve more loans to underserved communities. Fintechs like Affirm and Square appear as examples of risk models built for fairer lending.

## How to get your own numbers

The closing advice is the part you can apply on Monday: define clear objectives and measurable outcomes before deploying, invest in talent and skills, set up governance and ethical guidelines, monitor continuously like any other production service, and measure ROI on an ongoing basis rather than once at launch. His own example is documentation: work that used to take him two to three hours a day now takes under an hour.

## Who should watch

Program and product leaders in financial services building the business case for AI, or anyone who wants a quick catalogue of public examples to cite. Engineers after architecture details or a single deployment measured end to end will want something more hands-on.

Title: A financial data pipeline built for the day the market panics
Description: Anandan Dhanaraj (BNY) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on a normalize, enrich, store pipeline that keeps latency flat during market bursts.
Body:
Financial data pipelines are judged on their worst day, not their average one. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Anandan Dhanaraj](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Anandan_Dhanaraj_financial_architecture_market), Vice President and Back-End Engineer at BNY, walks through a pipeline designed around market volatility: normalize everything into one schema, enrich it once, store it flat, and scale before the spike arrives.

It's a compact architecture talk from someone who has spent years building high-performance microservices. No ML models on stage; the machine learning shows up as the next step for scaling and anomaly detection.

## Three ways legacy pipelines fail

Anandan names three constraints. **Volume:** legacy systems that cope with thousands of transactions a second on a normal day fall over when market volatility multiplies traffic by an order of magnitude. **Latency:** trading platforms work in microseconds, so millisecond delays cost real money. **Heterogeneity:** data arrives as SWIFT messages, JSON and files, over FTP, MQ channels and Kafka topics, each with its own field structure, time zones and date formats.

The last one is the sneaky one. Every format quirk you handle downstream is a performance tax you pay on every message.

## Normalize first, enrich once

The pipeline has five layers:

1. **Canonical schema normalization.** A transformation engine maps incoming fields to a predefined schema, a validation layer enforces types, and configurable exception handling protects data integrity. Everything downstream sees one shape.
2. **Ingestion** that reads fast, with automatic failover to a backup when the primary fails, and retries.
3. **Enrichment**, which joins in reference data such as security details, account details and FX conversion, so analysts don't have to query multiple platforms to assemble one record.
4. **Storage**, where enriched data is flattened into Oracle with partitioning and custom indexes chosen by analysing each data set's query patterns and volumes at onboarding.
5. **Analytical consumption**, with real-time dashboards backed by query patterns tuned for speed.

Each data set gets its own MQ channel, which keeps a noisy feed from starving a quiet one.

## Scale before the spike

The detail worth stealing is predictive autoscaling. Instead of reacting when queues back up, the scaling logic looks at historical patterns and current market conditions and provisions resources before demand materializes, so latency targets hold even during extreme volume. Benchmarks were run under simulated conditions matching historical flash crash scenarios, which is a much better test than a synthetic steady load.

## Results, as reported

Anandan cites a 78% reduction in average query latency for mission-critical operations. In the benchmark section he describes processing 300K transactions per minute normally and bursts of 450K messages with 8 to 10 millisecond response times, at 99.99% availability. The abstract quotes 100K+ transactions per second, so check the talk itself for which unit applies where.

Elsewhere he reports a 450% increase in processing capacity, unplanned downtime cut from a few hours to under three minutes, and per-transaction infrastructure costs down 68%.

## The trade-offs he admits to

The takeaways are sensible rather than flashy. Start with an audit of current data flows, find the worst bottleneck, and modernize incrementally with measurable gains at each step. Expect to balance latency against throughput, complexity against maintainability, and specialised optimization against flexibility. Next on his list: machine learning for predictive scaling and anomaly detection, graph databases for relationship modeling, and zero-downtime upgrade paths.

## Who should watch

Data and back-end engineers in trading, custody or payments who own a pipeline with too many input formats, and anyone who wants a clear example of canonical-schema-first design. If your stack is streaming-native, the layering still applies even though the storage choice here is Oracle.

Title: Change metadata, not code: modernizing enterprise finance systems
Description: Srinivasa Rao Akyana at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on consolidating enterprise finance systems on Azure, adding AI, and making metadata the design principle.
Body:
Quarter close is when you find out how many spreadsheets your finance stack really runs on. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Srinivasa Rao Akyana](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Srinivasa_Rao_Akyana_metadata_financial_reduction), who leads engineering efforts in a large enterprise finance organization, tells how his team consolidated a patchwork of legacy financial systems, moved them to Azure, layered AI on top, and made metadata the thing you change instead of code.

It's a transformation story with clear steps and specific before-and-after figures, told by someone who clearly sat through the painful closes.

## Patches, silos and quarter-close anxiety

The starting point: decades-old reporting tools on ageing servers, hard-coded logic that couldn't take new use cases, data warehouses that didn't talk to each other, and finance teams spending hours reconciling numbers between them. The cost wasn't only technical. It showed up as missed deadlines, poor insights and anxiety during quarter close.

## Clean the attic before you move house

The first move was consolidation, which Srinivasa compares to clearing out a cluttered attic: five tools doing similar things, spreadsheets with conflicting formulas, pipelines running on legacy jobs. The four steps:

- **Audit** every financial application, report and integration, mapped to business value, with telemetry to find underused tools.
- **Map** a unified architecture with clear integration points.
- **Consolidate** redundant tools and standardize pipelines on reusable components.
- **Validate** every rebuilt feature for performance, security and compliance.

His example: three separate systems all producing headcount reports, merged into one, cutting the effort by 60% and ending the argument about whose number is right.

## Then the cloud, then the models

Only after consolidation did the platform move to Azure. Reported results: 50% faster time to market, with forecasting models that took months to deploy now going live in weeks, 35% cost optimization from retiring redundant storage and legacy VMs, and 99.9% availability. The anecdote that sticks: a year-end close reporting environment that took nearly 12 hours to prepare became ready in under 20 minutes.

AI came third, aimed at real pain points rather than demos. Forecasting models built on time series and historical signals reached 85% accuracy for predicting operating expense trends, hiring spikes and vendor spend. Automating invoice matching, report scheduling and cost reconciliation cut manual effort by 75%. Real-time anomaly detection flags duplicate payments, cost spikes and misclassified expenses with 30% better precision than the old rule-based checks.

## Metadata as the hidden superpower

The idea that gives the talk its title is that the platform is metadata-driven. Every data set, transformation and business rule is described and governed by metadata. That buys three things: systems that document themselves so new engineers ramp up faster, dynamic data models where a regulatory change means editing metadata rather than shipping code, and full lineage so a change to report logic can be traced everywhere it propagates. Compliance audits get easier as a side effect.

The end-to-end figures he shares: report generation from 24 hours to three, data errors from 12% to 3%, operational costs down 25%, and time to insight from 48 hours to 12. The CFO's office now treats the platform as the source of truth for executive dashboards, which in finance engineering is about as high as praise goes.

## Lessons, including the boring ones

Start small and scale fast. Put finance experts inside the development process, because engineers alone can't solve financial systems. Prioritize data quality, since the best model in the world still obeys garbage in, garbage out. Don't skip governance.

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads in finance IT, FP&A platforms or any internal data platform where reconciliation eats the calendar. It's especially useful if you are trying to sequence consolidation, cloud and AI and keep getting asked to do all three at once.

Title: Digital twins leave the factory floor for financial risk
Description: Nikhil Kassetty (Intuit) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 builds AI digital twins of financial systems with random forests, LSTMs and reinforcement learning.
Body:
Digital twins grew up modelling jet engines and production lines. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Nikhil Kassetty](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Nikhil_Kassetty_optimization_twins_decisions), Software Engineer at Intuit working across AI, cloud and fintech, points the idea at money instead: a live, continuously updated replica of a portfolio, a payment network or a credit pipeline, with machine learning models predicting where it will break.

It's a framework talk with a model comparison, pitched at people who build risk and monitoring systems in finance.

## Static reports see yesterday

Nikhil's problem statement is one most finance engineers will nod along to. Risk scoring, asset tracking and operational reporting usually happen after the fact, in silos, on periodic snapshots. Even where digital twins exist in finance, he says, they tend to be static, fragmented and domain-specific, with no live data feed and no way to learn.

A twin in his sense is the opposite: it can represent a portfolio, a payment network, a risk model or an entire business process, it updates from live data streams, and it can simulate both the current state and possible futures. Think of it as a staging environment for your balance sheet.

## The pipeline: from feeds to features

The framework starts with real-time data: payments, loans and trades; portfolio metrics like exposure and risk scores; liquidity indicators, both internal reserve ratios and external funding availability; and market data such as volatility, interest rates and sentiment indexes pulled from APIs.

Then the unglamorous work: cleaning missing records, catching anomalies like a transaction spike that is really a system error, fixing format mismatches, and normalizing and scaling inputs so the models train properly. Feature engineering adds rolling averages, transaction patterns, liquidity shifts over time, portfolio drift and synthetic risk flags.

## Four models, two winners

Nikhil compares four models on financial data, predicting risk signals such as anomalies in transaction flow, portfolio stress and credit utilization drift:

- **Random forest classifier** for risk classification. It leads on accuracy at 95.5%, plus precision, recall and F1.
- **LSTM** for time-series patterns. Close behind, and especially strong on recall, which suits slow-building risks like liquidity dips and credit defaults.
- **Support vector machine** for separating risk tiers. Moderate, with lower recall, though still useful for binary problems with clear patterns.
- **Autoencoder** for anomaly detection without labels. Reasonable, considering it is unsupervised.

His emphasis on precision and recall is the right one for finance. A false positive blocks a good customer; a false negative lets a real risk through. You want a model that respects both.

## A twin that tunes itself

The step that makes this more than a dashboard is reinforcement learning on top. The system learns from outcomes to adjust thresholds, reallocate capital and change strategy, using feedback such as cost savings or successful risk mitigation as the reward.

Nikhil reports a 25% reduction in unplanned operational downtime, an 18% decrease in maintenance and overhead costs, a 20% improvement in asset utilization, and a 145% return on investment. He is upfront that twins need serious investment at the start and pay back over time.

## What's still hard

He lists the open problems honestly: scaling across large, multi-layered financial systems; real-time synchronization when data sources are diverse; and compatibility with legacy infrastructure. Solvable, he says, but they need continued cross-functional work.

## Who should watch

Engineers and data scientists building risk monitoring, treasury or fraud systems who want a structured way to think about simulation plus prediction. It's a framework overview, so expect architecture diagrams and model comparisons rather than code.

- [Divakar Duraiyan on aircraft digital twins](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Divakar_Duraiyan_aircraft_digital_twins) turns flight data into predictive maintenance.

Title: How one legacy bank platform was rebuilt in 18 months
Description: Srinivas Allam (Core ITS) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on moving an iSeries-era banking platform to microservices, APIs and cloud without downtime.
Body:
Migrating a bank is like changing the engine on a plane that has passengers' savings in the hold. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Srinivas Allam](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Srinivas_Allam_transforming_banking), IBM iSeries Senior Program Analyst at Core ITS, tells the story of an 18-month modernization of a legacy banking platform: microservices, cloud infrastructure, API-first design, and a migration he describes as running without data loss.

Despite the machine learning in the title, the transcript is mostly a platform modernization story. AI-driven personalization is where the team heads next. The value is in the sequencing and the risk controls, which apply to any big migration.

## Four phases, one question

The journey ran in four phases: planning (assess the legacy systems, pick priorities), migration (move customer accounts with minimal disruption), implementation (cloud-native architecture and API-first principles) and optimization (keep measuring and iterating after go-live). Every change, Srinivas says, was judged by one question: does this make the experience better for customers and easier for the teams?

## What was wrong with the old platform

The starting point will sound familiar to anyone near an iSeries estate. Transactions took 3.2 seconds, which sounds fine until you compare it with every other app on a customer's phone. Systems couldn't talk to each other, so there was no unified view of a customer. Security protocols were outdated enough to be a compliance risk. And maintenance needed specialised support just to keep the lights on.

## Rebuild, don't patch

The new architecture combined microservices that deploy independently, cloud infrastructure that scales with load, API-first interfaces reusable inside and outside the bank, and a zero-trust model where nothing is trusted until proven otherwise. An API gateway unified access to old and new services, a service mesh handled service-to-service traffic, and a data integration layer kept legacy and modern systems consistent. That layering is what let them modernize gradually instead of forcing a weekend cutover.

## The numbers, as reported

Srinivas puts a figure on almost everything:

- Transaction time fell from 3.2 seconds to 0.8 seconds.
- Account opening went from 48 hours with branch visits to four hours with partial automation, then to 15 minutes, fully digital with biometric verification.
- Audit preparation shrank from two weeks to three days, with continuous compliance monitoring.
- 1.2 million automated test cases covered 98.7% of the platform, and deployments went from a 72-hour weekend outage to 25 minutes with CI/CD.
- Infrastructure costs fell 42% and support tickets fell 72%.

He also reports net promoter score rising from 28 to 52 and customer retention from 76% to 92%. Banking customers rarely switch, so a retention jump is the number that will interest the business side.

## The risk controls are the reusable part

The section to bookmark is risk mitigation. Old and new systems ran in parallel with synchronized data. Canary deployments sent new features to a small slice of traffic first. Every change could be rolled back instantly. Real-time monitoring covered performance, security and health. And cross-functional teams brought technical, business and compliance people into the same room.

People got the same attention: communication campaigns explaining why, hands-on training, dedicated support during the transition, and a platform tuned on employee feedback. He reports 89% staff adoption within three months.

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads facing a legacy core banking migration, especially on IBM i, who want a realistic phase plan and a checklist of safety nets. If you came for neural networks on iSeries, that's mostly the next chapter, not this one.

Title: AI takes first pass on financial marketing review, humans finish
Description: Vijayakumar Jayaseelan (Cognizant) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on a dual-persona AI and human workflow for financial marketing compliance.
Body:
In a bank, a marketing email can spend longer with compliance than it took to write. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Vijayakumar Jayaseelan](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Vijayakumar_Jayaseelan_marketing_compliance_financial), Senior Manager and Principal Architect at Cognizant, argues for a split workflow where AI does the first compliance pass on marketing content and human reviewers make the final call.

Be warned: this is a numbers talk. Almost every slide is a statistic drawn from industry analyses and annual reports, and the delivery moves fast. The architecture is light; the argument is the business case.

## The bottleneck is the review queue

Financial marketing is regulated content. Every brochure, landing page and campaign email has to pass a review that checks claims, disclosures and wording against the rules. That review is slow, manual and expensive, and it scales with headcount.

The abstract frames the payoff in three numbers: review times cut by 73%, regulatory violations down 67%, and content production up 42%. In the talk, the most concrete version of the first one is the time to review a complex marketing piece, dropping from 32 hours to 8.5 hours.

## Two personas: an approver and a refiner

The idea worth taking away is what Vijayakumar calls the dual-persona approach. Instead of one AI system that either approves or rejects, the workflow has two roles:

- An **approver** agent assesses the initial content and flags compliance issues.
- A **refiner** stage, with human oversight, reworks the content and takes the final decision.

The machine handles volume and the routine checks. People focus on the complex scenarios where judgement and context matter. In his figures, AI handles roughly 73% of initial processing while human reviewers, doing final verification, keep accuracy high.

It's the same pattern that shows up in code review bots and fraud triage: let the model clear the obvious cases so humans spend their attention where it's actually needed.

## What the AI layer does

Three capabilities carry the system in the talk:

- **Natural language processing** that reads content and identifies likely violations. He cites 93% accuracy in identifying compliance issues against 76% for traditional manual review, with a lower false positive rate.
- **Intelligent version control** for every draft of every piece, with an audit trail regulators can follow.
- **Throughput** to run many compliance checks concurrently, with fast responses for standard checks.

The audit trail point is easy to skip and shouldn't be. In a regulated industry, being right is not enough; you have to show how you were right, for every version.

## The business case, as presented

The back half of the talk stacks up cost and ROI figures attributed to industry research: reductions in compliance operating costs, regulatory penalties, revision cycles and time to market, implementation costs recovered within months, and RegTech market growth forecasts. Treat these as the industry's own scorecard rather than results from a single deployment; the talk doesn't walk through one system end to end.

## Who should watch

Architects and product owners in financial services who are pitching AI-assisted compliance internally and want a vocabulary for the human-in-the-loop design, plus the stats their stakeholders will ask about. Engineers looking for model choices, prompts or a reference stack should pair it with something more hands-on.

Title: Every bank call analysed, not sampled, on serverless AWS
Description: Neha Thakur (AWS) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 builds a serverless pipeline that turns bank calls and chats into sentiment and topic dashboards.
Body:
Most contact centers learn what went wrong on Monday sometime around Tuesday night. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Neha Thakur](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Neha_Thakur_insights_financial_customer), Associate Solutions Architect at AWS in London, shows a serverless pipeline that transcribes every call, reads every chat, and puts sentiment and topics on a dashboard within minutes. No sampling, no manual QA queue.

It's a reference architecture with a live console demo, aimed at banks and fintechs. If you have ever wired S3 events to Lambda, you already know half of it. The interesting half is what she bolts on top.

## The bank call center, hour by hour

Neha opens with a day in a bank's contact center. At 9:00 a surge of calls arrives and nobody knows why. By 11:00 agents sense a pattern but can't prove it. At 2:00 the quality team is still reviewing yesterday's calls. At 4:00 management sees the metrics sliding with no root cause in sight.

Her point is that the data was there the whole time, sitting in recordings and chat logs nobody had time to read. Repeat calls about the same issue are the cost of that blindness: each one is a problem that could have been fixed earlier.

## S3 events all the way down

The architecture is a chain of event triggers, and that is its charm:

- Audio files and their metadata JSON land in an S3 bucket.
- The upload triggers a Lambda that calls Amazon Transcribe.
- The transcript lands in another S3 folder, which triggers a second Lambda.
- That Lambda sends transcripts and chat logs to Amazon Comprehend for sentiment and topic modeling.
- The combined output goes to Amazon QuickSight for dashboards, with Athena available for SQL straight on the bucket.

In the demo, Comprehend tags one conversation as negative with a 99.5% confidence score, and a topic modeling job pulls out ten topics with their related terms. The QuickSight board covers 61 sample conversations: sentiment distribution, sentiment by account type, dominant topics, and per-agent performance.

Nothing waits on a schedule. A call recording arrives, analysis starts. Neha's pitch for serverless is the familiar one, put plainly: no capacity planning, scale with volume, pay for processing time and nothing else.

## Dashboards that change behaviour

The part worth stealing is what the dashboards are for. If one topic, say opening or closing an account, dominates the calls, write an FAQ so customers can serve themselves and the phone stops ringing. If one agent's conversations trend negative, that's a training conversation, not a mystery.

She also shows QuickSight generating an executive summary and a "data story" from selected visuals, which she pitches at whoever reports to leadership at the end of the month or quarter. Whether your CFO wants a machine-written narrative is between you and your CFO.

## Security is in the diagram, not the appendix

For a bank, the pipeline is only as good as its controls. Neha walks through them: S3 encryption at rest, encryption in transit, AWS KMS for key management, tightly scoped IAM roles per Lambda, Transcribe's ability to identify and redact sensitive information, CloudTrail for audit logs, and services running inside your VPC. None of it is exotic. All of it is the reason the compliance team will sign off.

## Who should watch

Engineers at banks, insurers or any regulated business with a contact center, especially if your current "analytics" is a supervisor listening to five random calls a week. It's also a tidy example of composing managed AI services without training a single model. If you want custom models or on-prem speech recognition, this isn't that talk.

- [Vishal Khadake on NLP for incident management](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Vishal_Khadake_49_nlp_sentiment_language) applies sentiment analysis to a very different kind of complaint.

Title: LLMs translate the COBOL, humans sign off on every rule
Description: Sandeep Gourneni (Hitachi Digital Services) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on modernizing COBOL banking code with LLMs and role-based human review.
Body:
Banks don't keep COBOL because they love it. They keep it because every previous attempt to replace it went badly. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Sandeep Gourneni](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sandeep_Gourneni_banking_optimization), Technical Program Manager at Hitachi Digital Services in Dallas, lays out a framework where LLMs do the bulk translation of legacy code and engineers, compliance officers and domain experts review what comes out.

It's a short, slide-driven talk: a framework overview with a case study, not a code walkthrough. Sandeep brings 17 years of banking transformation projects across several geographies, and the war stories are the best part.

## The legacy burden, in his numbers

Sandeep's opening slide claims legacy maintenance eats up to 65% of IT budgets at most financial institutions. Two thirds of the spend, just keeping the lights on. Meanwhile the pool of COBOL developers keeps shrinking and the demand for new digital services keeps growing.

He quotes a CIO who told him the bank spent so much maintaining legacy systems that it couldn't invest in what customers were asking for. Anyone who has sat in a budget meeting next to a mainframe line item will recognise the mood.

## Why rip-and-replace keeps failing

The "modernization paradox" slide is the heart of the problem. Traditional transformation projects, in Sandeep's figures, fail 85% of the time, run past 24 months on average, and he has personally seen budgets overrun by three to five times. One project he consulted on was planned for 18 months and took over four years.

Manual code conversion doesn't scale, and big-bang replacement is a non-starter when the system moves money and the tolerance for errors is zero. So the question becomes how to go faster without betting the bank. Literally.

## A four-stage pipeline with people at the end

The architecture has four stages:

1. Legacy code ingestion: COBOL parsing and mapping the code to banking domain concepts.
2. LLM translation with models specialised for banking.
3. Verification of behavioural equivalence through testing.
4. Human review for expert validation and refinement.

Three model choices carry the translation step. Extended context windows let the model see an entire banking module at once, so relationships between functions survive. Fine-tuning on the financial domain teaches it accounting principles, transaction processing and regulatory requirements. Multi-language output targets Java, Python and other modern languages.

## The review is role-based, and it feeds back

The human oversight system is what makes this palatable for a regulated shop. Engineers, compliance officers and domain experts each validate a different aspect of the translated code. Automated compliance flagging pushes potential regulatory issues to a human. Side-by-side runtime comparison checks that the new code behaves like the old. And human corrections flow back into the model, so the same mistake should get rarer over time.

That last loop is the detail worth copying even if you never touch COBOL: review effort that trains the tool instead of evaporating.

## Results, as reported

Sandeep presents figures from early implementations: an 80% reduction in human effort for code translation, 60% faster testing and verification cycles, 75% fewer regression defects after go-live, and a 35% lower total cost of ownership. One regional bank projected over $12 million in savings across five years.

The case study is a major bank's transaction system: 10 million lines of 30-year-old COBOL processing 3 million transactions a day, migrated to containerized microservices. The roadmap he recommends is incremental: assess, pilot on non-critical modules, scale, then keep refining.

## Who should watch

Tech leaders at banks staring down a COBOL estate, and anyone selling or evaluating LLM code migration who wants a sensible shape for human review. If you want benchmarks, prompts or a look at the generated Java, the talk stays at the slide level.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Swetha Lakkaraju on decoupling legacy banking](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Swetha_Lakkaraju_banking_modular_modernization) argues for modular cores instead of one big migration.
