Title: Fraud rings hide in joins; graph databases follow the money
Description: Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu (JPMorganChase) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on graph algorithms, GNNs and embeddings for financial fraud detection.
Body:
A money laundering ring is a graph problem pretending to be a table. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, [Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Venkateswarlu_Boggavarapu_fraud_detection_db_graph), Vice President and Senior Lead Data Engineer at JPMorganChase, explains why fraud detection gets easier once accounts, customers, devices and transactions are nodes and edges, and walks from classic graph algorithms to graph neural networks.

It's a broad, well-structured survey with 16 years of database and cloud experience behind it. If you have never run PageRank on anything but a homework assignment, this is a good map of the territory.

## Relational databases make you pay per hop

The core argument: fraudsters exploit relationships. Shell companies, fake identities, mule accounts. Tracing those through a relational schema means join after join, and deep connections get slow and expensive on large data sets. A graph database stores the relationships directly, so following a money trail five hops out is the normal case instead of the query that times out.

In his model, nodes are checking and savings accounts, customers, transactions, merchants, devices and IP addresses. A device used to access several unrelated accounts is suddenly visible as a single node with too many edges.

## Three algorithm families do the heavy lifting

Venkateswarlu groups the useful algorithms into three families:

- **Community detection** finds clusters that trade heavily among themselves and barely touch anyone else. Several accounts moving funds rapidly in a closed loop is the textbook pattern for collusion.
- **Centrality** ranks nodes by importance. Betweenness centrality flags nodes that sit on many shortest paths, which is exactly where a money mule lives. Degree centrality flags hubs, which could be a busy legitimate business or a fraud hub, so context matters.
- **Pathfinding** traces how funds move between two accounts. Short paths suggest direct transfers; long, convoluted ones suggest layering.

## Graph features make ordinary models smarter

You don't have to throw away your existing fraud models. Network metrics such as degree and PageRank, path lengths, repeated path patterns, timing of fund flows, and community size and density all become features for conventional classifiers. He cites improvements of up to 35% in detection accuracy in some cases when graph-based features are added.

Then come graph neural networks, which skip the hand-crafted features entirely. The intuition he gives for message passing is that each node is a little messenger, combining what its neighbours tell it with what it knows and passing it on. GNNs handle node classification (is this account fraudulent?) and graph classification (is this whole network?). For teams that still want familiar tools, graph embeddings such as Node2Vec, graph autoencoders, TransE and GraphSAGE turn nodes into vectors for clustering and classification. GraphSAGE gets a special mention because it can embed nodes it hasn't seen yet, which matters when new accounts appear every second.

## A case study and the unglamorous parts

The case study is a laundering operation hidden across seemingly unrelated accounts linked by over 200 structured transactions. Temporal analysis exposed the layering, and the investigation led to the recovery of $4.7 million and the identification of a previously unknown criminal network.

The implementation advice is refreshingly practical. Data integration needs ETL pipelines and entity resolution, so that "John Smith" and "J Smith" become one node. Scale needs indexing, caching, sharding and distributed processing, with streaming for real-time detection and batch for deeper analysis. Privacy rules such as GDPR and CCPA call for granular access controls and anonymization. Start with a pilot on one use case, train your analysts, and integrate with the fraud tools you already run rather than replacing them.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and fraud analysts at financial institutions who are weighing a graph database, and ML engineers curious where GNNs actually earn their keep. It's conceptual rather than hands-on: no query language or vendor demo.

- [Vinod Upputuri on AI-powered fraud detection](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Vinod_Upputuri_ai_fraud_machine) covers the machine learning side of the same fight.
- [Vijaya Kumar Guntumadugu on cloud-based anti-money laundering](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Vijaya_Kumar_Guntumadugu_banking_compliance_money) shows where AML compliance meets AI.

Title: An AI tutor that refuses to write the essay for you
Description: Universitio founder Vahid Mohammadi at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on students, AI detectors and humanizers, and AI that teaches instead.
Body:
86% of students already use AI in their studies, according to a Digital Education Council survey of more than 3,800 students in 16 countries. Vahid Mohammadi, founder of Universitio, a UK-based international student recruitment company, opened his Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 talk with that figure and a sharper question: are students using AI to learn, or to replace learning? His answer is a design brief for an AI that guides a student through the work and refuses to do it for them.

## Detectors, humanizers, and an arms race nobody wins

Mohammadi walks through the cycle every university now lives with. Schools deploy AI detectors such as GPTZero and Grammarly's checks; the detectors misfire, sometimes flagging human writing. Professors compensate by comparing new work against a student's earlier writing, checking references (he cites a study where only 7% of ChatGPT-generated references were accurate and verifiable), and listening for a voice that doesn't sound like the student. Students respond with AI humanizers that rewrite text to slip past detectors, often successfully.

His point is that winning that round changes nothing. The professor still notices the disconnect, and the student still knows they didn't do the work. University policies vary widely, from outright bans to allowed-with-disclosure, and he sides with educators who redesign assignments to be personal, reflective or tied to events, so the thinking is harder to outsource.

## The mentor, not the ghostwriter

The core of the talk is a thought experiment. A student says they don't know how to start, and instead of producing an essay the AI breaks the problem down, explains what makes an introduction work, points out weaknesses and guides the next draft. Mohammadi contrasts two assistants: one that does whatever it is asked, and one that declines to write the assignment but teaches the student to write it. Only the second, in his view, belongs in education.

## Humans in the training loop

He then describes the platform his team is building along those lines. Each student gets a personal AI companion focused first on academic writing: it reads drafts, gives feedback and explains what went wrong, without doing the work. The interesting design choice is what happens at the edges. When the assistant isn't confident, it doesn't guess; it flags the question to a human academic, who answers and teaches the system how to respond next time. Over time he wants it to learn institution-specific expectations, and eventually help international students with life abroad, from housing to paperwork.

This is a founder describing a product in progress, so treat it as a vision and a design philosophy rather than a set of results. The detector-and-humanizer section is the most broadly useful part.

## Who should watch

Engineers building LLM features for education or training, product teams thinking about refusal as a feature, and anyone in a university wrestling with AI policy. ML practitioners looking for model internals won't find them here.

Title: Block storage that predicts its own capacity and moves its own data
Description: Venkatachala Nivas Chainuru at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on ML for block storage, from predictive capacity and intelligent tiering to phased rollout.
Body:
Most block storage arrays are configured once and then left alone until someone files a ticket. Venkatachala Nivas Chainuru, of California State University Northridge, argued at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 that static configuration and manual management can't keep up with enterprise data growth, and that ML-driven storage, which forecasts capacity, places data by access pattern and tunes itself, is the way out.

## Why static stops working

He points at the sectors under the most pressure: healthcare, manufacturing with IoT telemetry, and financial institutions with transaction records and compliance archives. They combine fast growth with mission-critical workloads and regulation, which is the worst mix for a storage team adjusting LUNs by hand.

## Forecast before you buy

The first pillar is predictive analytics over historical usage, workload characteristics and infrastructure telemetry. Chainuru cites storage utilisation rising from an industry average of 48% to 72%, with procurement costs reduced by up to 35% through more precise capacity planning. That is the most persuasive figure for anyone who has bought a shelf of disks "just in case".

## Let the system shuffle the tiers

The second pillar is intelligent tiering. His model is a hybrid pool: 5 to 15% high-performance drives, a mix of standard SSDs and high-capacity drives, and cheap archival storage, presented as one system. Models move data between tiers based on access patterns and performance needs. He cites storage cost reductions of 19 to 37% for organisations that adopt it. A performance optimisation engine then adjusts configuration parameters in real time as workloads shift.

## Three kinds of learning, three jobs

The talk's clearest section maps ML families to storage problems:

- **Supervised learning** for predictive failure analysis, reading device health metrics to spot failing hardware before it hurts, with accuracy improving as failure history accumulates.
- **Unsupervised learning** for workload characterisation, clustering I/O by request size, read/write ratio and timing, which matters when new applications appear often.
- **Reinforcement learning** for tuning, treating storage management as a sequence of decisions scored by their effect on performance.

The data to feed this comes from multi-layered monitoring that combines infrastructure and application metrics, block-level metadata (timestamps, operation types, latencies), and local aggregation with adaptive sampling so telemetry doesn't eat the bandwidth it is meant to save.

## Roll it out in phases

Integration advice is pragmatic. Add a storage virtualisation layer so optimisation can target specific workloads while the rest runs as before; integrate through APIs with existing IT automation; and start with monitoring and analytics before letting the system take automated actions, keeping clear fallback procedures while you build confidence in the models. That last step is the one most worth copying: let it recommend for a while before you let it act.

## Who should watch

Storage and infrastructure engineers, and SREs who own capacity planning, who want a structured view of where ML fits into block storage. It is a conceptual overview without a product demo, so pair it with your vendor's documentation.

Title: How the Salesforce ecosystem runs on partners and Trailhead
Description: Northern Trust's Sekhar Midathana at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on AppExchange, Trailhead, the Trailblazer Community and Salesforce partner types.
Body:
Salesforce is as much a marketplace and a training academy as a CRM. Sekhar Midathana, a Salesforce consultant at Northern Trust Corporation with seven years on the platform, spent his Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 talk explaining how those pieces fit: AppExchange for distribution, Trailhead for skills, the Trailblazer Community for support, and a set of partner types that build, integrate and run it all.

Fair warning on scope: this is a business-ecosystem talk, not a machine learning one. AI shows up near the end as Einstein and a direction of travel. If you work in or around Salesforce, it is a clear orientation.

## AppExchange as the distribution layer

Midathana's argument is that the ecosystem is a multi-party win: partners get access to a large customer base and a trusted brand, customers get prebuilt, integrated solutions instead of custom builds. The figures he gives for AppExchange: more than 8,000 apps and solutions, over 90 million installs, used by 80% of the Fortune 500 and available in more than 150 countries. He also cites partner revenue generated through it, though the abstract and the talk use different totals ($3B+ versus 6.2 billion), so treat the exact figure with care.

For customers, the case is time to value, lower cost of ownership versus custom development, industry-specific apps, and a steady stream of new ones.

## Trailhead as the talent pipeline

The most interesting point for engineering leaders is Trailhead's role as a hiring funnel. Learning paths with hands-on challenges in sandbox orgs, badges and leaderboards, and recommendations based on role and progress. His numbers: around 15 million learners, about 1,200 hours of content, 35 million badges earned, and 73% of learners reporting career growth. Partners and customers use it to upskill staff, which in turn widens the pool of people who can build on the platform. It is a model other platform companies have copied, with mixed success.

## Who does what in the ecosystem

He lays out the partner types: consulting partners like Accenture and Deloitte that implement; independent software vendors such as Slack, Tableau, DocuSign and Conga that extend the platform; technology partners like AWS, Google and Microsoft; system integrators; managed service providers that run orgs day to day; AppExchange publishers; and Trailhead partners that create learning content. The Trailblazer Community, with user groups in more than 90 countries plus online forums and recognition programmes, connects them.

## Collaboration stories, and what's next

His success stories follow a three-step pattern of identifying a market need, co-developing a solution and delivering it integrated. Industry clouds such as Financial Services Cloud and Health Cloud came from that collaboration. Vlocity's insurance work, he says, cut a client's policy processing time by 50% and raised satisfaction by 20%; a Deloitte retail project lifted sales by 25%. He looks ahead to deeper Einstein AI integration, more industry clouds such as manufacturing, and cross-cloud integration across Sales, Service and Marketing Cloud.

## Who should watch

Developers and architects new to Salesforce who need the map before the code, and consultancies weighing which partner path to pursue. Engineers looking for ML depth should pick another session.

Title: Compressing video by tracking where the pixels went
Description: Expedia's Hitesh Saai Mananchery at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on R2S, an ML compression method that drops pixels a point tracker says are redundant.
Body:
If the camera pans four pixels to the right, the next frame only contains a four-pixel-wide strip of anything new. Hitesh Saai Mananchery, Senior Machine Learning Engineer at Expedia Group, built a compression method on that observation and presented it at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025. R2S, Redundancy Removal using Shift, uses a learned point tracker to work out how far each frame moved, stores only the new pixels and rebuilds the rest from the previous frame on decode.

This is a research talk about a proof of concept, backed by a paper on arXiv (2406.19630), and Mananchery is clear about what works today and what is still future work.

## Why bother when H.265 exists

He frames it with scale: video is around 85% of internet traffic, and social media alone pushes petabytes into cloud storage every day. Established codecs (H.264, H.265, AV1, VP8) are rule-based and lossy. The ML research thread (autoencoders, VAEs, deep contextual networks) is attractive because a learned approach can work across video formats and isn't tied to one framework. R2S is also lossy; the question is whether the loss is visible.

## Track a pixel, not an object

The mechanism uses Persistent Independent Particles, PIPs, an existing point-tracking model, and its successor PIPs++. Pick an arbitrary point in the first frame and track it frame by frame. The displacement tells you which region of the next frame is new and which is a shifted copy of what you already stored. The redundant region is zeroed out, and its coordinates go into a side array. Decoding reverses it: the first frame is always stored intact, and each subsequent frame is rebuilt by pulling the redundant region from the previous reconstructed frame using those coordinates.

His demo tracks the nose of a running dog, which is a good reminder that the method follows pixels rather than recognising objects.

## Single point now, grids later

The proof of concept uses single-point trajectories, which work when the scene is static and the camera moves. Moving objects with a moving camera need multi-point trajectories: an 8x8 grid of tracked points that separates camera motion from object motion. That is the next paper, alongside object masking and similarity-search approaches for reusing pixels.

## The numbers, and the trade-off

Results from the single-point version: about 15 ms per frame to compress, frames shrinking from around 238 KB to 36 KB, and roughly 84% size reduction at about 4% loss. The interesting trade-off is in the prediction window. Predicting across eight frames at once is faster and compresses harder, but tracking accuracy falls and loss climbs steeply; one frame at a time keeps loss near 4%. It is also slow for now: a two-minute video takes around a minute to compress, so this is a storage-side idea, not a live-streaming one.

Mananchery's closing point is a neat inversion: ML consumes enormous amounts of stored data, so it may as well help store that data more cheaply.

## Who should watch

Computer vision and ML engineers curious about learned compression, and media or storage teams wondering what the research looks like below the codec layer. Expect diagrams and results, not production code.

Title: Great Expectations, Deequ or TFDV, picking a data validator for ML
Description: Sunil Kumar Mudusu of Church Mutual at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 compares three open-source data validation tools for ML pipelines.
Body:
Bad data doesn't crash your model; it quietly makes it worse, and you find out from a business user. Sunil Kumar Mudusu, Lead AI Engineer and Data Engineer at Church Mutual Insurance Company, gave a short, practical talk at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 comparing three open-source tools that catch those problems before training: Great Expectations, Amazon's Deequ and TensorFlow Data Validation.

It is a brisk introduction rather than a hands-on workshop, and that is its strength: in a few minutes you get a decision rule for which validator fits your stack.

## The problems you are guarding against

Mudusu lists the usual suspects: missing values, numbers stored as text, formats that change over time, extreme or strange values, and duplicate rows. The abstract adds the two that hurt ML the most: schema drift and unexpected distributions. Any of them can survive a pipeline run without an error and still degrade predictions. His point is simple: don't spend all your effort on the model and none on what feeds it, and make the checks automatic.

## Three tools, three sweet spots

**Great Expectations** is the Python-first option. You declare rules about what your data should look like, it runs against pandas, SQL and Spark, and it produces readable reports. Mudusu recommends it for Python teams and small to medium datasets, and warns that it is not ideal for very large or real-time data.

**Deequ** comes from Amazon and runs on Apache Spark. It is built for big, frequently changing datasets and can track data quality metrics over time. It suits AWS users and Spark teams, and is overkill for small projects or beginners.

**TensorFlow Data Validation** is his favourite. It is part of the TensorFlow ecosystem, profiles datasets before training and detects anomalies automatically. It fits TensorFlow and production ML pipelines well, and is less useful if you train with something else.

## The decision rule

His summary is easy to remember: Great Expectations for flexible rules and clear reports, Deequ when data is big or always changing, TFDV when you are on TensorFlow. The abstract frames the same choice by workload: batch pipelines, streaming systems or end-to-end ML platforms. Check early, check often, and pick the tool that matches the team rather than the one with the most stars.

What the talk doesn't cover is equally worth knowing: there's no live demo and no configuration walkthrough, so plan to read each tool's docs after watching. Think of it as the five-minute briefing before you open three browser tabs.

## Who should watch

Data and ML engineers adding validation to a pipeline for the first time, and leads who need to justify one tool over another. Teams already running one of these in production will find little new.

Title: Notifications that know when, where and whether to arrive
Description: Microsoft's Ankita Kamat at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on ML filtering, send-time prediction and adaptive throttling for notifications at scale.
Body:
The cheapest notification is the one you decide not to send. Ankita Kamat, Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft, built her Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 talk around that idea: a high-throughput notification platform where ML decides whether a message is worth sending, which channel it goes to, and what hour it lands, so that pings become engagement instead of uninstalls.

## The plumbing comes first

Kamat starts with the infrastructure, because no model saves a system that drops messages on Black Friday. Her architecture is microservices on Kubernetes (event receivers such as a Kafka consumer, a router, channel adapters for push, email and SMS, and analytics pipelines), autoscaled on queue length, talking gRPC and Protobuf internally, built around CQRS and event sourcing. An enrichment layer pulls user preferences, location and history from Redis.

Her broker comparison is practical: Kafka for durable high-volume ingestion, RabbitMQ for complex routing and dead-letter queues, Redis Streams for low-latency fire-and-forget pushes, Pulsar for geo-replication and backlogs, and often Kafka plus Redis Streams together. Resilience comes from readiness and liveness probes, circuit breakers, active-active geo-distributed clusters and periodic chaos tests with Gremlin.

## Should this message exist at all?

The ML layer starts with smart filtering: a binary classifier (XGBoost or LightGBM) trained on opened, clicked, dismissed and ignored outcomes, with features like message type, device, region, historical responsiveness and time of day. Only messages scoring above a threshold for that user get delivered. Then comes personalised content with template-based or fine-tuned language models, and a closed feedback loop where every click, mute and dismissal becomes a label for daily retraining, with new models shadowed against production first.

## Timing is the multiplier

The section on predictive delivery timing is the best part. Engagement logs are clustered with K-means plus dynamic time warping, or DBSCAN, revealing cohorts such as office workers who open at lunch, students in the evening and parents late at night. A gradient-boosting or LSTM model then produces an hourly heat map of open likelihood for the next 24 to 48 hours, and a lightweight scheduler enqueues each message at its best predicted slot, with a fallback to the second-best slot if it goes unread.

Kamat reports open rates up by as much as 35%, engagement up 45% and mute and uninstall rates down 18% compared with random delivery windows. She adds the operational caveats that matter: make scheduled messages idempotent with TTLs, add jitter to avoid notification storms, and combine timing with adaptive rate limiting so a user who keeps dismissing a category hears from it less often.

## The cart-abandonment case

Her e-commerce case study replaced a nightly batch email (around 4% open rate) with real-time events, a model predicting purchase intent within one to three hours, and personalised subject lines. The result she reports: 42% more recovered carts, 28% fewer messages sent and 37% higher click-through. Fewer messages and more revenue is the whole argument in one line.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers who own a notification or messaging service, and ML engineers asked to "improve engagement" without drowning users. It covers both the systems and the models, which is rarer than it should be.

Title: AI in DevOps, from Copilot in the IDE to automatic rollbacks
Description: Kowshik Sakinala at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 surveys AI across DevOps, from coding assistants and predictive CI/CD to security and DORA metrics.
Body:
Kowshik Sakinala, a senior DevOps engineer, used his Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 talk to follow AI through the whole delivery lifecycle: the IDE, the CI/CD pipeline, the security scanners, the incident channel. His thesis is that DevOps plus AI moves teams from reacting to predicting, and that the engineer's job changes shape rather than disappearing.

## The assistant in the editor

He starts where most engineers first met AI at work: coding assistants. GitHub Copilot, Amazon CodeWhisperer and Tabnine complete whole functions, suggest names and fixes, write unit tests and docstrings, and adapt to a codebase's style over time. His Copilot example is small and relatable: start writing a CSV-processing function and it proposes error handling for malformed fields, along with the header parsing. He cites 30 to 50% faster development, smoother onboarding and less technical debt as the claimed upside, and pitches Copilot as a pair programmer and living documentation.

## Pipelines that see failure coming

The more interesting section is predictive pipeline management. By mining build histories, commit metadata and job patterns, models flag flaky tests and unstable branches, reorder jobs for speed, catch regressions before a merge to main and size resources to cut waste. Sakinala cites up to 40% faster pipelines and 20% fewer failed builds, plus a confidence score attached to every commit.

His worked example is Sigma Solve, an AI layer on top of CI/CD that analyses commits, test coverage and file volatility, scores each build from 0 to 100 for deployment readiness and routes high-risk builds to staging or QA. A build that resembles past bad builds gets a second look, which is what a good release manager already does by instinct.

## Security and the metrics that move

On security, the threats he lists are specific: secrets hard-coded in pull requests, overly permissive IAM policies, drift between Terraform and what is running in AWS, and anomalous service-to-service calls. AI's contribution is scanning patterns across large log volumes, clustering alerts to cut false positives, and suggesting remediations, with NLP summaries of incident reports and git hooks that enforce posture early.

He then ties it to DORA-style numbers reported by teams using AI in the pipeline: deployment frequency doubled, lead time for changes cut by 50%, change failure rate down 30%. Observability becomes action when the system links a latency spike to the commit that caused it and suggests rolling back or scaling up.

## Two industries, one theme

The finance examples focus on predicting overnight batch delays, flagging unusual API usage and unauthorised config changes, and generating audit trails from CI/CD metadata. The e-commerce ones are about milliseconds: forecasting traffic for cache preloading, catching slow queries, and automatically aborting a rollout of a new cart service if conversions drop just before a flash sale.

## Humans still own the trade-offs

His closing is sensible: AI takes test generation, alert prioritisation and summaries; people keep architecture, trade-offs, business logic and crisis communication. He sketches conversational DevOps, generated runbooks and self-tuning pipelines as the next step.

## Who should watch

Team leads and platform engineers who want a broad map of where AI already shows up in delivery, with figures to bring to a planning meeting. It is an overview, not a build guide, and the numbers are cited rather than measured on stage.

Title: One DITA source, many partner brands, no copy-paste docs
Description: RingCentral's Rakesh Konda at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on co-branded documentation with DITA, AEM Guides, key maps and DITAVAL filters.
Body:
When AT&T and Vodafone both resell your product under different names, with different feature sets, your documentation team either copies everything or gets clever. Rakesh Konda, Engineering Team Lead at RingCentral, showed the clever route at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025: a single-source DITA content system on Adobe Experience Manager Guides that rebrands and filters itself per partner and publishes to web, PDF and JSON without duplicating source.

This is a documentation-architecture talk rather than an ML one, and it is upfront about that. If you have ever maintained a fork of the user guide for one customer, keep reading.

## How docs sprawl happens

Konda describes the usual mess: organisations acquire products, each arrives with its own content system and publishing process, tribal knowledge fills the gaps, and every partner wants their own name, logo, screenshots, support contacts and feature subset. Each new partner multiplies the work. Channels add more: website, chatbot, mobile app, PDF, each with its own format.

His prescription is a single source of truth with modular, reusable content blocks, automated brand controls and multi-channel publishing. When picking a platform, he looks for structure, scalability, omnichannel output and a short learning curve for new authors, and AEM Guides with native DITA support is his choice.

## Three mechanisms do the work

The middle of the talk is the useful part, because it names the moving pieces:

- **Key maps** swap product names and assets per partner. His example: partner A calls the product Smart Meet, partner B calls it Global Connect, and each has its own key map defining the product name, logo, UI screenshots and support contact. The topics reference the key; publishing resolves it.
- **Conditional attributes and DITAVAL files** control which content appears for which audience. Tag a section with a feature or audience attribute, then include or exclude it per brand in a DITAVAL file. Features one partner lacks simply vanish from their output.
- **Output presets** tie it together: one preset per partner and channel, each linking the right DITAVAL and key map, so producing a partner's PDF or HTML is one click.

Content then assembles like Lego: modular topics combine into maps that become user guides or troubleshooting docs, with AEM providing version control underneath. Platform differences (Android versus iOS) fit the same filtering model as partner differences.

## The payoff

Konda reports faster time to market, lower error rates and easier partner onboarding from teams that adopt this model, with branding consistent and updates reflected everywhere at once. He doesn't give hard numbers, so judge it on the mechanism, which is sound and widely used in technical publishing.

## Who should watch

Technical writers, docs engineers and anyone building documentation pipelines for white-label or partner products. Engineers who have only seen Markdown docs-as-code will find the DITA vocabulary (key maps, DITAVAL, presets) a useful addition to their toolkit.

Title: AI is moving upstream, from data consumer into the ETL itself
Description: Janardhan Reddy Kasireddy (Reveal Global Consulting) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on schema mapping, self-healing pipelines and starting small.
Body:
For most of its life, ML has been a downstream customer of the data warehouse. Janardhan Reddy Kasireddy of Reveal Global Consulting used his Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 talk to describe the reverse: AI embedded inside the pipelines, mapping schemas, catching anomalies before they land and tuning jobs while they run. His evidence comes from a decade of building data platforms at Capital One, FINRA and the US Department of Transportation's FMCSA.

## Where the time actually goes

Kasireddy opens with the numbers that made it click for him: 68% of engineering time on maintenance rather than new work, four and a half hours a day on debugging and fixing pipelines, and data quality problems discovered only once they hit production. His version of the 3am question is familiar: was that failure a schema change, a quality issue, or something upstream that nobody announced?

The scale of his background makes the argument concrete. At FINRA he worked on a pipeline ingesting over 250 billion daily trade events with zero tolerance for data loss. At FMCSA, inspection and violation reporting for all 50 states had to be right because public safety decisions depend on it.

## Rigid rules versus learned mappings

The core comparison is traditional ETL against an AI-assisted version, four rows deep:

- Manual mapping between schemas becomes automatic schema discovery that infers types and proposes mappings, even for nested JSON.
- Hard-coded if-then transformations become patterns learned from the data.
- Reactive error handling, where you find out after downstream data is corrupted, becomes prediction of errors before execution.
- Static Spark tuning, set once and forgotten, becomes real-time adjustment of partitioning, parallelism and memory.

The tools he names are concrete: AWS Glue for ML-assisted schema detection and mapping, Databricks Auto Loader for schema evolution on ingestion, and ML-based anomaly detection on data flows. At FMCSA his team used PyDeequ for automated data quality checks and explored models to flag suspicious inspection records.

## Self-healing is a loop, not a feature

His self-healing pipeline is a four-stage cycle: detect anomalies, diagnose root cause, apply a fix from a library of known corrections, then record the outcome so the next similar failure resolves faster. The quality framework around it follows the same shape: define expectations (hand-written or discovered), validate at every stage rather than only at the end, auto-remediate common issues, and track quality scores over time.

The headline figures from his slides: 85% less manual schema mapping, 92% of anomalies intercepted before production reports, and a 43% cut in pipeline maintenance cost.

## Start small, measure, then scale

His adoption framework is refreshingly modest. Find the most repetitive work (schema mapping, validation, debugging), automate one critical pipeline, measure time saved and quality gained, and only then expand. He also lays out an adoption timeline running toward fully autonomous data platforms; that last stage is a forecast, and he presents it as one.

## Who should watch

Data engineers running Spark, Glue or Databricks pipelines who spend more time on break-fix than building. The regulated-industry examples make it especially relevant for finance and government teams.

Title: Security as code in Jenkins, and why the design phase is cheapest
Description: CGI's Sarathe Krisshnan Jutoo Vijayaraghavan at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on security as code in Jenkins pipelines and the adoption curve.
Body:
A vulnerability caught at design costs about $25 to fix; the same bug found in production costs about $75,000. Sarathe Krisshnan Jutoo Vijayaraghavan, Senior Consultant at CGI Technologies, put that 3,000-fold gap at the centre of his Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 talk on security as code in Jenkins. The argument: write security controls as versioned, reviewed, tested code inside the pipeline, and speed and safety stop being opposites.

## Controls are artifacts too

With 15 years in CI/CD automation and infrastructure as code, Vijayaraghavan treats security exactly like infrastructure. Controls are codified, version-controlled and peer reviewed. They follow shift-left, moving checks to the start of the lifecycle. And they are immutable: defined once and deployed identically to every environment. He cites research that immutable security controls bring 94% fewer misconfigurations across environments and 78% less compliance verification effort.

## What goes in the Jenkinsfile

The implementation section maps four integrations onto a declarative Jenkins pipeline:

- **Security scanning stages**: SAST, software composition analysis, DAST and container scanning, triggered on every build.
- **Policy as code**: security requirements expressed declaratively and enforced automatically across environments.
- **Secret management**: secure credential storage and retrieval so nothing sensitive leaks through the pipeline.
- **Compliance verification**: compliance rules as code, validated during execution, with feedback to developers.

The figures he gives for why each matters: automated scanning finds vulnerabilities 17 times faster than periodic manual reviews, SAST surfaces an average of 26 potential issues per thousand lines, third-party dependencies make up around 80% of modern application code, and container scanning prevents 60% of incidents that stem from unscanned images.

## People change more than tools

The organisational section is where the talk earns its time. Security teams move from gatekeepers to enablers, spending far less time on manual checks; developers resolve most security issues themselves with the right tooling. He is candid about the obstacles too: tool integration is the top technical hurdle, with only 36% of security tools offering APIs good enough for CI/CD; 82% of organisations report a skills gap; auditors in regulated industries are often unfamiliar with automated controls; and both security staff and developers resist, for opposite reasons.

His adoption journey is a useful planning aid: a resistance phase in the first 90 days, targeted pilots with two or three baseline tools up to day 180, broad rollout of SAST, DAST and SCA by the end of year one, and optimisation after that, where false positives drop sharply. High performers set up a centre of excellence, invest about 32 hours of security training per developer per year and reward secure coding.

## Where AI comes in

Despite the title, AI is the closing chapter rather than the core. He sketches the next stage as security chaos engineering and continuous verification inside the pipeline, followed by AI-driven predictive vulnerability detection, automated remediation suggestions and context-aware policies. Watch it for the Jenkins security-as-code playbook; the ML part is a forward look.

## Who should watch

DevOps and platform engineers running Jenkins who need to add security without adding a week to every release, and security leads building the business case. The cost-of-delay numbers will work well in a slide deck.

Title: Split the ML monolith, but stop at four or five services
Description: Abhishek Walia of Confluent at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on microservices for ML systems, with communication patterns, deployment options and observability.
Body:
If your data processing, training, serving and inference all ship as one executable, a segfault anywhere takes down everything. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Abhishek Walia of Confluent explains how to break ML systems into microservices for independent scaling and fault isolation, which communication and deployment patterns to use, and why you shouldn't decompose too far.

It's an engineer's talk, opinionated and practical, with the occasional aside from his home lab.

## What the monolith costs an ML team

Walia starts with the monolith. Everything goes into one deployable unit, so when one layer becomes a hotspot you scale the whole thing, and RAM and CPU are sized for the hungriest component. Fault isolation is close to zero. Microservices fix both: if inference needs more CPU and RAM, scale only inference.

He adds two less obvious benefits. Technology flexibility: rewrite only the API layer in Go, because Go is faster and easier to parallelise, without touching the Python training code. And deployment independence: each service gets its own CI/CD schedule, so refreshing the API doesn't redeploy training modules.

The costs are real too. Data consistency across service boundaries becomes your problem. In-process calls become TCP or gRPC calls with network overhead. Debugging means following one failure across six services in time order. It's not a free buffet, as he puts it.

## Pick the communication pattern for the data

Walia walks through four options. Direct REST or gRPC calls are simple with strong consistency; with gRPC over HTTP/2 you open a connection once and reuse it instead of building one per request. Event streaming suits the continuous, never-ending data many ML systems consume as model input. A shared data store with stateless instances works but leans hard on one service, so be careful. Message queues decouple services for asynchronous processing with independent scaling. His own preference is event streaming (this happened, here is the current state, update everywhere), while he stresses that the use case decides.

## Containers, serverless or a serving platform

For deployment, containers and Kubernetes handle networking, load balancing, ingress, scheduling, blue-green deployments and A/B tests in codified YAML, but Kubernetes is operationally demanding, so have someone who can debug DNS. (It's always DNS.) Serverless functions such as AWS Lambda and Google Cloud Functions remove infrastructure management entirely. Specialised serving platforms like KServe, formerly KFServing, and SageMaker are optimised for model serving. His advice: start with serverless, then consider specialised platforms, then container orchestration if you have to.

## Observability first, and don't over-decompose

Monitoring one monolithic process was easy; microservice sprawl isn't. Walia wants model performance metrics in Prometheus with Grafana on top, distributed tracing with Jaeger or Zipkin so a single trace ID follows an event through the services, plus centralised, time-ordered logging and resource tracking to find hotspots. On trends, he points to service meshes like Istio, deployed as sidecars, for zero-trust security and fault tolerance with little code, and to AI-driven orchestration as agent frameworks mature.

The takeaways are the bit to pin on the wall. Start with the service that gives the most gain for the least decomposition effort, roughly 80% of the benefit for 20% of the work, not the most painful one. Don't split one process into 15 services; start with four or five and add more only if needed. Measure after decomposing to see whether you've gone too far. His top three: identifying the right service, sound decomposition boundaries, and observability. Infrastructure modernisation and CI/CD-driven continuous evolution can come after.

## Who should watch

ML platform engineers and backend teams moving model serving out of a monolith. If you've already run microservices at scale, the ML-specific framing and decomposition advice are still worth the time.

Title: Fairness belongs in the data pipeline, not the model review
Description: Amazon's Arun Vivek Supramanian at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on privacy, bias and four ethics gates built into data pipelines.
Body:
"I just build the pipeline" stops being a defence once the pipeline feeds a model that decides who gets a loan. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Arun Vivek Supramanian, Senior Data Engineer at Amazon, argued that privacy and fairness are data engineering problems first, and that the place to enforce them is a set of gates inside the pipeline rather than a one-off audit at the end.

## Bias is in the data before it is in the model

Supramanian's examples are the familiar ones, told from the plumbing side. Cambridge Analytica, in his framing, was a breakdown of governance and consent before it was a model failure. The resume-screening model that penalised applications mentioning "women's" learned it from historical hiring data. A chatbot trained on internal company data leaked social security numbers when prompted cleverly. The common thread: nobody upstream asked what the data carried.

His point is that bias can enter at collection, preprocessing and labelling, so treating fairness as a property of the trained model is checking the wrong layer.

## Noise with a budget

On privacy, the talk sticks to two techniques with real deployments behind them. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise so aggregates survive while individuals don't: Supramanian cites Apple collecting phone usage statistics with epsilon values between two and four, and Google using values as low as 0.3. K-anonymity makes each record indistinguishable from at least k-1 others. His recommendation is to combine them, since anonymisation alone has a long history of being undone by a clever join.

## Two case studies with before and after

The e-commerce case: a recommendation engine served women suggestions 18% less aligned with their preferences, because training data skewed toward male purchase behaviour. Stratified sampling, fairness-aware feature engineering and retraining narrowed the gap and lifted satisfaction scores overall.

The healthcare case is the stronger one. A readmission model underperformed for non-white patients because they were underrepresented. The team redesigned collection with targeted outreach, raising non-white representation from 24.7% to 49%, used federated learning across five institutions, and generated synthetic records with GANs for rare subgroups. Performance disparity dropped by 68%. Supramanian's line is that this is fairer and clinically better at the same time.

He also flags intersectional testing: a credit model can look fair by gender and by race separately and still disadvantage Black women. He cites that only 29% of organisations test for this.

## Four gates and a paper trail

The practical core is an ethics-by-design model with four checkpoints: a collection gate (consent, representation), a processing gate (does a transformation introduce bias), an output gate (are results privacy-safe and fair) and a monitoring gate (new risks after deployment). Around that sits documentation that goes past lineage to record trade-offs, discovered biases and known limitations, such as a dataset that excludes under-18s. Toolkits like IBM's AI Fairness 360 help, but he is clear they are not silver bullets and need validating in production, not only in test suites.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who own pipelines feeding ML, and anyone facing GDPR, HIPAA or the EU AI Act questions about where fairness checks live. It is a concise overview rather than a code walkthrough, so bring your own implementation details.

Title: A tour of where AI fits in an enterprise data pipeline
Description: Deloitte's Gopinath Govindarajan at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 maps AI onto feature engineering, data cleansing, MLOps, enrichment and versioning.
Body:
Gopinath Govindarajan, Senior Solutions Specialist for cloud managed services at Deloitte Consulting, spent his Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 slot walking an enterprise data pipeline stage by stage and asking, at each one, what a model can take off an engineer's plate. With 15 years in data engineering behind him, his answer covers feature engineering, cleansing, MLOps, quality monitoring, enrichment and version control, and ends with a roadmap for teams starting out.

## Five ways pipelines hurt

He frames the problem with five pain points most data teams will recognise: data silos that make engineers spend their days locating and normalising data; poor quality (duplicates, gaps, inconsistent formats, schema changes); orchestration across ETL and ELT jobs where one failure cascades; legacy pipelines that can't scale horizontally; and governance under GDPR, HIPAA and CCPA, where lineage, role-based access and sensitivity classification all need tracking.

## Let the machine propose features

Automated feature engineering gets the most detail. Instead of hand-building inputs, tools analyse data types and relationships, generate candidates such as ratios, time aggregates and encodings, then rank and prune them. Govindarajan names Featuretools, SageMaker Autopilot and DataRobot, and the techniques underneath: deep feature synthesis over relational data, recursive transformations for layered features, embeddings for categorical and text fields, and selection by correlation or mutual information.

## Cleansing that learns

His contrast between traditional and intelligent cleansing is concrete. Instead of static scripts that drop duplicates and fill nulls, models impute missing values with KNN or regression, flag outliers statistically rather than by fixed threshold, learn normalisation patterns for dates and addresses, and resolve entities with fuzzy matching, his example being "IBM Corp" versus International Business Machines. Anyone who has written that regex knows why a learned approach appeals.

## MLOps as the glue

The middle of the talk describes the MLOps layer: CI/CD for models, a model registry for versions and lineage, a feature store so training and inference use the same features, and retraining triggered by drift or decay. Predictive quality monitoring and data enrichment (NLP on text, computer vision tagging for product images, geospatial attributes) follow, along with intelligent version control using tools like DVC and MLflow.

## The numbers

The abstract headlines 85% efficiency gains, 62% less development time, 95% of anomalies detected automatically and 3.5x more deployments. The case studies in the talk add a financial services firm that lifted analyst productivity by 37%, a healthcare provider that automated 73% of critical classifications while staying compliant, and a firm that delivered market data 2.8 times faster. These are reported results without named clients, so treat them as direction rather than benchmarks.

## Start with observability

The closing roadmap is the most actionable part: adopt a modern data stack, add data observability that tracks freshness, accuracy, volume and lineage, version data and models as well as code, automate ingestion and quality checks where you can, and treat data as a product rather than a byproduct.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and architects who want a map of where AI applies across a data platform before choosing tools. It is a broad survey, so engineers looking for one technique in depth will want a narrower talk.

Title: ML expense forecasting starts with your cost-centre hierarchy
Description: Mizuho's Vishal Gangarapu at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on structuring expense data so ML can classify, flag anomalies and forecast costs.
Body:
Before any model touches your expense data, someone has to decide which cost centre owns the data subscription fee. That is the unglamorous starting point of Vishal Gangarapu's talk at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025. Gangarapu, Executive Director for Finance Data Analytics and Transformation at Mizuho, makes the case that ML expense management lives or dies on taxonomy, and only then on algorithms.

## Why the old way misses

He opens with the baseline: forecasts built without historical patterns drift far from actuals, expenses land in the wrong categories, and budgets swing between the start of the cycle and the end. Finance teams lose their time to reconciliations instead of decisions. His examples come from financial services, but he says the ideas apply to any industry with a budget.

## Get the hierarchy right first

The most useful section for engineers is a short lesson in how finance actually models money. Cost centres are where expenses are booked; profit centres generate revenue. Every profit centre needs a matching cost centre, but pure cost centres like HR, IT and facilities have no profit centre at all. Expenses then fall into three buckets in his framework: direct (tied to revenue activity, about 38% of the total), allocated overhead that waterfalls one way from shared functions to front-office units (about 45%), and variable costs that scale with revenue and book straight to profit centres.

If you have ever been handed a "just predict the costs" ticket, this ten-minute primer is worth the watch on its own. Your features are only as clean as the chart of accounts behind them.

## Three models, in order of ambition

The data foundation comes next: transaction metadata, historical categorisation, normalised vendor information, primary and foreign keys, and 12 to 18 months of history before you trust a forecast.

Then the use cases, starting small:

- **Automated classification** of transactions into categories using amounts, vendor timing patterns and payment methods as features.
- **Anomaly detection** for spikes and misallocations, with dynamic thresholds that respect seasonality and a human review loop that feeds back to cut false positives.
- **Time-series forecasting**, matched to horizon: ARIMA for stable short-term costs like IT, other approaches for volatile ones like compliance, and ensembles beyond a year, measured with MAPE.

The abstract promises 91% accurate cost allocation, 87% anomaly precision and hidden savings of 12-18%. In the closing case study, a financial firm cut its misclassification rate from 30% to 6% and processing time by 76%, over an 18-month programme.

## The team is the hard part

Gangarapu's implementation roadmap puts the cross-functional team (engineers, data specialists, financial analysts) ahead of deployment, and says that is where many organisations fumble: buying a model is quick, getting value from it is not. Start with classification and anomaly detection, give time-series forecasting a couple of months, and budget for continuous recalibration as the organisation changes.

## Who should watch

Data and ML engineers who support FP&A or controllership teams, and finance leads wondering what "add ML" actually requires. It is a practitioner overview, light on code and heavy on domain structure, which is the part engineers usually lack.

Title: Users don't report bugs, they leave, and analytics shows where
Description: Raju Dandigam of Navan at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on front-end analytics with Amplitude, from event planning to funnels, A/B tests and debugging.
Body:
Most users never report a bug or a confusing form. They just leave. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Raju Dandigam, a staff engineer at Navan, explains how front-end analytics catches those silent failures, using Amplitude as the worked example: plan your events, build funnels, run A/B tests and debug a conversion drop from real user behaviour.

It's a practical introduction aimed at the whole product team, not just data folks, and it's refreshingly honest that tracking everything is a mistake.

## Seeing the app through the user's eyes

Dandigam's definition is a good one: front-end analytics is like putting on glasses that show the app through the user's eyes. Where they click, how far they scroll, how long they stay, and where they rage-click out of frustration. The value is fast, reliable feedback; launch a new pricing page and you can see whether it helps or hurts signups without waiting for a gut feeling or a complaint.

Everyone benefits differently. Product teams prioritise features that matter. Engineers debug based on real usage instead of guessing. Growth teams run experiments and optimise flows. Designers validate layouts against behaviour. The shared data gives all of them the same picture.

## Four kinds of analytics

He sorts the field into four types. Behavioural: what users did, clicked, dropped or stayed. Technical: load time, JavaScript errors and anything that stops a user proceeding. Experimental: A/B testing which variant performs better. Session replay: watching what the user saw, which is great for debugging and UX reviews. The aim is to capture intent (searching for a product, starting a signup, hovering on a help icon), not just clicks.

He names Amplitude, Mixpanel, PostHog and Sentry among the popular tools, and picks Amplitude for the talk because it is easy to set up and self-serve: a product manager can build a funnel or cohort and share a dashboard without writing SQL.

## Plan the events before you log them

The integration itself is short. Import the library for your framework, initialise it with the API key, and call a log function with an event name and properties when the user acts; his example is React. The more important advice is about what to log. Don't track everything: it bloats the data, and most tools charge by volume. Start with a clean event list and the properties you think you'll need, use consistent names, and group related actions. Pass the user ID at login so a person's actions connect across sessions, letting you see anonymous and logged-in behaviour together.

## Funnels, experiments and time-travel debugging

The signup funnel is the central example: signup start, email entered, signup success. If 70% start and only 20% finish, there's friction. Test a shorter form, an accordion or a single page, roll variants to segments, and compare. Amplitude Experiment splits users into A (old design) and B (new call to action) and reports conversion per cohort, so you can say which version wins with numbers instead of opinions.

For engineers, the debugging use case is the hook. A feature ships and conversion drops. Filter by browser or version, correlate with the deployment, then use session replay to watch where users got stuck. Dandigam calls it time travel for debugging, which is about right. His conclusion: analytics isn't about dashboards, it's about closing the feedback loop between what you build and what users experience.

## Who should watch

Front-end engineers, PMs and tech leads setting up product analytics for the first time, or cleaning up a tracking plan that grew without one. Experienced experimentation teams will know the material.

Title: Public sector AI earns trust through audits, appeals and plain English
Description: Sanjiv Kumar Bhagat at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on privacy, fairness and interpretability frameworks for AI-enhanced public sector ERP systems.
Body:
When a government system makes an automated decision about you, you need to know why and you need a way to appeal. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Sanjiv Kumar Bhagat, who has 21 years in IT, more than 12 full-lifecycle ERP implementations and a long stretch in higher education systems, presents a framework for building trust into AI-enhanced public sector systems: privacy, algorithmic fairness and interpretability, backed by audits and human oversight.

It's a framework talk aimed at people planning public sector AI programmes, not a technical deep look at any one model.

## Three pillars

Bhagat sets up three pillars. Comprehensive data privacy, with protection that evolves as threats do. Ethical algorithmic fairness, with bias detection and mitigation across demographics. And interpretability: decision processes that are transparent and come with explanations people can actually follow. He opens with the improvements he associates with AI in the public sector: a 60% reduction in privacy incidents, 75% less administrative overhead and 82% better service accuracy.

## Privacy and fairness as processes

The privacy framework has three components. A comprehensive data audit that inventories and classifies every sensitive source and repository. Granular access control with multifactor authentication, role-based permissions and transaction logging. And automated de-identification that removes personally identifiable information with cryptographic safeguards.

Fairness is a loop, not a checkbox. Define fairness metrics with quantifiable equity measures for each demographic group. Measure outcomes across population segments to find disparate impact. Bring in stakeholder feedback from diverse communities to check real-world equity. Then adjust the model and go around again. The abstract cites a 40% bias reduction for the practical frameworks he describes.

## Explain it to a citizen, then let a human overrule it

Interpretability has the most practical guidance. Technical transparency means documented architecture, accessible code repositories and detailed process workflows. Decision explanation means translating algorithmic decisions into rationales citizens can understand, with examples. And human oversight means review channels with guaranteed human intervention and a clear appeal process for every automated decision.

That last requirement is what separates government systems from most commercial ones. A recommendation engine that gets it wrong costs a click. A benefits system that gets it wrong costs someone their rent, so the appeal path is part of the design, not an afterthought.

## What government adds on top

Bhagat lists public-sector-specific requirements: enhanced security with more resources for critical protection, hardened infrastructure and data sovereignty across jurisdictions; mandatory quarterly bias audits with documented remediation, review panels that include citizens, and public reporting of findings; and regulatory compliance aligned across federal, state and local rules, with audit trails for automated decisions and structured reporting to oversight committees and legislators.

The implementation roadmap moves from assessment (an ethics audit of current systems, stakeholder needs, technical readiness) to framework design (customised ethical principles, governance structure, success metrics) to iterative rollout with phased technology integration, staff training and public communication. His four success factors: inclusive development from day one, continuous ethics training, transparent communication about how AI is used, and adaptive governance with regular reviews. His closing claim is that trust is measurable, because public confidence tracks transparency.

## Who should watch

Programme leads, architects and policy teams scoping AI in government or higher education ERP. Engineers looking for bias-detection code won't find it here; they will find the requirements their system will be judged against.

Title: One ETL tool got you hired; the second one gets you promoted
Description: Sudhakar Guduri at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on why data engineers should master several integration platforms, from Informatica to NiFi and Talend.
Body:
Plenty of data engineers built a career on one integration tool and then found every job ad listing three. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Sudhakar Guduri, who has 14 years with tools such as Informatica, DataStage and Matillion, reporting tools like SSRS and Cognos, and databases from SQL Server to Snowflake, argues that proficiency across several integration platforms is what moves a data engineering career forward, and lays out a plan for getting there.

This is a career talk, not a technical one. It's short, personal in places, and ends with a concrete learning schedule.

## From specialist to integrator

Guduri starts with his own experience: he began focused on Informatica, which served him well, until he noticed roles demanding breadth across platforms, especially in hybrid and cloud environments. The reason is the shape of modern data work. Sources multiply (APIs, streaming, IoT, on-prem and cloud) and so do consumers (BI tools, ML pipelines, business apps). One tool rarely fits every job, so employers move to multi-tool strategies.

His example of that in practice: a retailer using Informatica for bulk data warehousing, Apache NiFi for streaming and Talend for cleansing and governance. Each tool doing the part it's good at.

## The platforms on the shortlist

He highlights three platforms and two cloud services. Informatica, strong in healthcare, with AI-powered features, deep health integrations and enterprise scale. Talend, enterprise-grade with broad connectivity, a unified platform, robust governance and cloud-native options. Apache NiFi, with a drag-and-drop visual interface, real-time processing and provenance tracking. Plus AWS Glue (serverless, Spark-based transformation, a metadata catalogue and schema discovery) and Azure Data Factory.

## What the case studies claim

Guduri presents two case studies. A fintech with a complex legacy setup of 200 data sources adopted a multi-tool integration approach orchestrated with Talend, which he credits with 2.8 million dollars in savings. A healthcare example moved from Informatica batch processing that took around 48 hours, with frequent errors, to real-time integration, reducing errors by 75% at 98.8% accuracy. On the career side, he cites figures of up to 42% higher salaries for multi-tool professionals and faster career growth. The talk doesn't detail the methodology behind those numbers, so treat them as the speaker's benchmarks rather than a published study.

## A learning plan you can put in a calendar

The most usable part is the framework. Foundation: get one platform to a complete level, with certification and practice projects. Expansion: add a second platform, look for the same patterns, and solve familiar problems a different way. Integration mastery: build projects that combine tools. Around that runs a loop of learning (structured courses and documentation), practice (hands-on projects), applying it at work, and sharing it back through community and mentoring.

The action plan is equally plain. Assess where you are with your current tools. Pick complementary platforms based on market demand. Set aside five to ten hours a week for the new platform. And build a cross-platform project that demonstrates integrated solutions, because a working pipeline that spans two tools is a better interview answer than a list of logos on a CV.

## Who should watch

Early and mid-career data engineers deciding what to learn next, and managers designing a skills plan for an integration team. Senior engineers already fluent in several platforms won't learn much new.

Title: Your support chatbot shouldn't know why the sky is blue
Description: Mohamed Najaaf of AWS at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on responsible AI and how Amazon Bedrock Guardrails filter prompts, PII and off-topic questions.
Body:
A customer-service chatbot that happily explains why the sky is blue is burning your tokens on someone else's homework. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Mohamed Najaaf, a solutions architect at Amazon Web Services, walks through the dimensions of responsible AI and then shows how Amazon Bedrock Guardrails blocks the queries a business chatbot should never answer.

It's an AWS talk about an AWS feature, and it says so. The useful part is how concrete the failure cases are, and the reminder that guardrails are the second line of defence, not the first.

## Eight dimensions, one lifecycle

Najaaf starts with how AWS defines responsible AI: fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, veracity and robustness, governance, and transparency. Controllability means you can monitor and steer the system's behaviour. Veracity and robustness means correct outputs even with adversarial or unexpected inputs. Transparency means you can tell stakeholders how the system reached an answer.

He maps these across the ML lifecycle, from problem formulation (is an algorithm even the ethical solution here?) through training data (is it representative or skewed toward one group?) to deployment and monitoring. The point he keeps returning to: this is not a one-time check. You keep watching for unfair, harmful or inappropriate responses after launch.

## Meet Sarah and her viral clothing brand

The demo scenario is a small business owner, Sarah, whose clothing brand went viral and who adds a chatbot to her website to keep up with customer questions. Without guardrails, the obvious attacks (how to build a weapon, run my malicious script) are mostly refused by the model providers' built-in safety. The subtle ones are not. An impersonator says they're Sarah and asks for the company ID. Someone asks for Q3 profits. If the model is connected to a data source holding that information, it answers. And generic questions about the sky or the US president get answered too, turning your support bot into a free general-purpose assistant on your bill.

The consequences he lists are the ones that end up in the news: leaked proprietary data, inconsistent brand voice, regulatory non-compliance and hallucinations, such as inventing a refund policy that doesn't exist.

## The guardrail controls

Bedrock Guardrails is a feature of Amazon Bedrock for application-specific safeguards, and Najaaf runs through its filters. Prompt attack detection, with a strength slider from none to high, blocks inputs trying to override system instructions. A profanity filter covers both inputs and outputs. Harmful-category filters for hate, insults, sexual content, violence and misconduct can each be tuned. Sensitive information filters mask or block PII such as card numbers, addresses, emails, ages and IP addresses. And denied topics are defined in natural language: for Sarah, anything not related to buying her products, with sample phrases like why the sky is blue.

With the guardrail applied, the impersonation request, the profit question and the off-topic queries all get a polite refusal.

## Don't feed the model what it shouldn't say

The best advice in the talk isn't about the product. If a data source holds confidential information, don't connect it to a public-facing chatbot at all; even a tiny leak probability is too much. Mask or redact sensitive data at the storage level, in the S3 bucket, before it ever reaches a knowledge base. Guardrails then sit on top as an extra layer. And test thoroughly, because overly strict settings create false positives that refuse genuine product questions, which hurts the brand just as much.

## Who should watch

Teams building customer-facing assistants on Bedrock, or anyone who wants a clear catalogue of guardrail categories to compare against their own stack. If you need a vendor-neutral treatment of LLM safety, pair it with something broader.

Title: You may not need a separate vector database for product search
Description: Sowjanya Pandruju of AWS at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on product similarity search with Bedrock embeddings and PostgreSQL pgvector on RDS or Aurora.
Body:
If your product catalogue already lives in PostgreSQL, the vectors can live there too. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Sowjanya Pandruju, a cloud application architect at Amazon Web Services, builds up from generative AI basics to a product similarity search that stores embeddings next to product metadata with the pgvector extension on Amazon RDS or Aurora PostgreSQL.

The first half is a gentle primer on foundation models, vectors and embeddings; the second half compares AWS vector stores and ends with working SQL. It's an AWS talk using AWS services, and it says so up front.

## From foundation models to vectors

Pandruju starts with the vocabulary. Foundation models are pre-trained on large amounts of unstructured data and can be customised three ways: instruction-based fine-tuning on example prompts and desired outputs, domain adaptation on specialised data like medical, legal or financial text, and information retrieval that connects the model to external data so answers stay current without retraining. She notes that the retrieval route is popular precisely because most organisations can't afford to keep retraining.

Then vectors: an ordered list of numbers that turns real-world data into something a model can compare. An embedding is a vector that captures meaning, so similar items land close together, like two similar movies in a recommendation system. Her pipeline sketch: raw documents, images and audio go through Amazon Bedrock to produce embeddings, which are stored in a vector database for similarity search.

## Picking a vector store on AWS

The comparison is the most useful slide for anyone choosing. Amazon Kendra suits low-code teams who want rapid deployment: semantic search with 40-plus connectors, and it handles chunking, embeddings and algorithm choice for you. Amazon OpenSearch Service supports dense vector fields and k-nearest-neighbour search, a good fit if you already run OpenSearch, prefer NoSQL and want low latency. And Amazon RDS or Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector suits teams that prefer SQL and want application data and AI vectors in the same database for governance and speed.

## Why Postgres

Her case for PostgreSQL is practical. pgvector adds a native vector type and similarity search. You can store structured data like product metadata alongside vectors and run hybrid queries that combine filters with similarity. Postgres is mature and trusted for critical workloads. And it can be cost-effective because you skip running a separate specialised vector database for many use cases.

pgvector supports three similarity metrics, each with its own operator: Euclidean distance for straight-line closeness, cosine similarity for direction rather than magnitude (the usual choice for text embeddings), and inner product for normalised embeddings, where a higher dot product means more similar.

## The SQL is the demo

The example is deliberately small. Create a table with a product ID and an embedding column of type vector. Insert a few rows with toy embeddings (in production these come from your model). Then select products ordered by Euclidean distance to a query vector, limited to two results. That's a nearest-neighbour search written as an ORDER BY, which is the whole pitch: if your team already knows SQL, the learning curve is short.

Her summary of the benefits: unified storage of metadata and embeddings, flexible similarity metrics, hybrid queries that mix SQL filters with semantic matching, and no extra database to operate.

## Who should watch

Developers and architects on AWS who are adding semantic or similarity search to an existing Postgres-backed product. If you already know embeddings well, skip ahead to the vector store comparison and the pgvector section.

Title: From scripts to self-managing clouds, and the data that has to be right
Description: Rahul Amte of Nivid Technologies at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on AI-powered cloud automation, from predictive scaling to automated remediation.
Body:
Rule-based automation does exactly what you told it, which is the problem once your cloud outgrows your rules. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Rahul Amte, a cloud architect at Nivid Technologies working across AI infrastructure, DevOps and security, gives an introduction to AI-powered cloud automation: systems that learn from historical and real-time data to scale, optimise cost and fix incidents before a human gets paged.

It's a short overview talk, a good first stop for someone mapping where ML fits in cloud operations, rather than an implementation guide.

## Why rules run out

Amte's starting point is scale. Provisioning, scaling and monitoring are repetitive, and multi-cloud and hybrid strategies multiply the operational burden. Traditional automation follows fixed rules; AI-driven automation learns from data and adapts. In his list of core capabilities, AI detects anomalies such as traffic surges or failures, predicts future resource needs, optimises resource placement and triggers automated responses. Put together, that's his picture of a self-managing, self-healing environment.

## Three use cases worth stealing

Predictive scaling comes first. AI looks at historical usage to forecast demand and scales ahead of time; his example is an e-commerce flash sale over Thanksgiving or Christmas, where resources go up before the traffic arrives, keeping customers happy without paying for idle capacity the rest of the year.

Cost optimisation is second, and Amte makes a sharp point about it: most cost work today is reactive. Someone notices the bill, decides, then acts. AI can make it proactive by suggesting rightsizing, shutting down idle resources or moving to reserved instances, which matters after a decade of teams spinning up infrastructure left and right.

The third is incident management. AI can cut mean time to repair by detecting failures, correlating logs and metrics, and applying fixes or rerouting traffic, such as restarting a service or provisioning a new instance when a node fails. His framing is memorable: we already have monitoring as a service and alerting as a service, so why not remediation as a service?

## The tools already exist

Amte maps the providers' offerings: AWS DevOps Guru and CloudWatch anomaly detection, Azure Monitor and Advisor with AI built in, GCP AutoML and cloud operations tooling, plus third-party AIOps platforms such as Dynatrace and Splunk. None of this requires inventing a new platform; much of it is a matter of switching on and tuning what your provider ships.

## The catch is the data

The benefits he lists are the expected ones: higher uptime through proactive management, savings through smarter allocation, better security through anomaly detection, and DevOps teams spending time on improvements instead of firefighting. The challenges are more interesting. AI is only as good as its training data, and poor data quality leads to wrong decisions. Integration with legacy systems is hard. And blindly trusting automated decisions is risky, especially in regulated industries. That's the right caveat to end on: the automation that restarts your service at 3am needs to have learned from the right history.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers new to AIOps who want a quick map of use cases and tools. If you already run predictive autoscaling and automated remediation, you can skip it.
