Title: Catching the data that turns a weird shade of green
Description: Santosh Kumar Sana at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on an ensemble of statistics, VAEs and LSTMs that flags subtle anomalies in cloud data pipelines.
Body:
Threshold alerts catch the pipe that bursts. They miss the slow leak. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Santosh Kumar Sana, a senior database administrator at Insight Global, presents an AI-driven anomaly detection system for cloud data pipelines that combines classic statistics with deep learning so it can flag drift that never crosses a fixed line.

His running metaphor is a river: data flowing in from everywhere, and a monitoring system that knows what clean water looks like, so it notices when the water slowly changes colour instead of waiting for obvious rubbish to float past.

## Why fixed alarms aren't enough

Modern pipelines, in Sana's framing, are sprawling networks of sources, transformations and stores spread across cloud services. Every hop is a chance for data to be transferred incorrectly, lost in transit, or interpreted differently (what one system thinks a date is, another disagrees with). Traditional monitoring is a handful of thresholds. A gradual decline or a subtle shift in distribution trips none of them, and at today's volumes nobody can spot those by eye. He cites studies putting the cost of poor data quality at around 20% of company revenue, which is why he treats this as a business problem.

## No single magic algorithm

The detection layer is an ensemble, and that's the core idea. On the statistical side: control charts with upper and lower limits, time-series forecasting that flags deviations from expected values, distribution-based methods such as Gaussian mixture models, and proximity-based methods that flag points far from their neighbours. On the deep-learning side: variational autoencoders that learn the structure of normal data and flag records they struggle to reconstruct, and LSTM networks that catch odd sequences and trend shifts over time.

The ensemble combines them with weighted averaging (weights based on each model's track record for a given anomaly type), majority voting and stacking with a meta-learner. Sana's example of why: a statistical model quickly flags a large outlier, while a deep model picks up a persistent drift in a complex relationship. Each covers the other's blind spot.

## Collect the data about the data

Monitoring coverage goes beyond the records themselves. The system collects metadata (schemas, types, timestamps, lineage), operational metrics from pipeline components (processing time, CPU, memory, network latency, error rates) and samples of the actual data at points along the pipeline. Metadata changes, he notes, are often the earliest sign something is wrong. Then comes the unglamorous part: feature engineering with cleaning, scaling, encoding, derived features like rates of change, PCA for dimensionality reduction, and per-model formatting such as sequences for the LSTMs and input vectors for the VAEs. Garbage in, garbage out still applies to the thing that detects garbage.

Architecturally it's containerised microservices (ingestion, feature engineering, statistical analysis, deep-learning inference, alerting, feedback) designed to run on AWS, Azure, GCP or hybrid setups and to scale horizontally.

## Thresholds that move with the data

Two details make the system livable. Users label flagged anomalies as right or wrong, and that feedback adjusts the models. And detection thresholds adjust dynamically as data characteristics change, which keeps false alarms down. Rollout was gradual: less critical pipelines first, using those tests to find edge cases like sudden schema changes or brand-new pipelines, then wider.

Sana reports a 40% reduction in data quality issues, 84% fewer false positives and incident detection that went from hours or days of log digging to near-instant. For a financial institution's trading data pipelines he cites a 43.7% reduction in data issues and 3.27 million dollars in annual savings. Next on his list: concept drift handling, so a new normal isn't flagged forever, better compute efficiency, and automated remediation.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and platform teams who own pipelines and are tired of learning about bad data from a dashboard consumer. ML practitioners will recognise the models; the value is in how they're combined and fed.

Title: Making generative AI fit on the edge, one bit at a time
Description: Sai KR Pentaparthi of ST Engineering iDirect at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on quantization, pruning and distillation for low-latency edge GenAI.
Body:
Going from FP32 to INT8 can make a model about four times smaller and three to four times faster, and that's before you prune anything. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Sai KR Pentaparthi, principal software engineer at ST Engineering iDirect, where he works on IP satellite network infrastructure, lays out a systematic approach to running generative AI on resource-constrained edge devices: pick the right hardware and runtime, then stack quantization, pruning and knowledge distillation.

This is one of the more technical talks of the event and a solid survey for anyone who has to ship a model to a box with a power budget.

## The edge says no four ways

Pentaparthi starts with the constraints. Edge devices have far less compute, memory and storage than cloud servers. Connectivity is spotty or absent. Many run on batteries or tight power budgets. And the applications (autonomous vehicles, industrial monitoring) want answers now. Demand is growing anyway; he cites an edge AI accelerator market growing at around 39% a year, low latency as the top adoption driver for over 78% of organisations, data privacy for almost 65%, and model optimisation already used in 82% of deployments.

## Hardware and runtime are half the answer

Before any compression, he surveys the hardware: NPUs with 10 to 15 times the energy efficiency of a CPU for typical neural network work, Google's Edge TPUs at up to four TOPS in roughly two watts, mobile GPUs and FPGAs, plus the Jetson, Ryzen AI, Core Ultra and Snapdragon families. The NVIDIA A10 spec sheet makes the INT8 case vividly: 31.2 teraflops at FP32 against 250 TOPS for INT8 on its tensor cores, up to 500 with sparsity.

Runtimes matter as much. In his comparison, TensorFlow Lite wins on hardware support through delegates, ONNX Runtime on raw speed and portability, PyTorch Mobile on developer experience, and Apache TVM on peak performance at the cost of much harder deployment. For LLMs specifically, optimised stacks such as TensorRT-LLM clearly outperform less optimised ones like llama.cpp on the same hardware, and 7B models at INT4 are becoming feasible on edge platforms, though standard benchmarks there are still thin.

## Quantize smart, not uniformly

Quantization gets the most time. Post-training quantization is simple and needs no retraining, just a calibration dataset, and for many models INT8 PTQ costs less than 2% accuracy. Quantization-aware training simulates low precision during training, typically holding degradation under 1.5% at INT8, but needs the training pipeline and data. Dynamic-range quantization picks scaling at runtime. And mixed precision keeps sensitive layers at FP16 or FP32 while pushing robust ones to INT8 or INT4, which he says can reach large compression with under 1% accuracy loss. The practical trick is the sensitivity analysis: find which layers hurt when squeezed and leave those alone.

## Prune, fine-tune, repeat; then teach a student

Pruning removes redundant weights or whole structures. Unstructured pruning gives high compression but sparse matrices that need special support to run faster; structured pruning removes filters or neurons and speeds up ordinary hardware. Iterative magnitude pruning, with fine-tuning between rounds, preserves accuracy best, and the lottery ticket hypothesis offers the theory for why so much of a network can go. Knowledge distillation trains a small student on a big teacher's soft targets, in response-based, feature-based, offline, online and self-distillation flavours. He also points to architectures built for efficiency from the start: MobileNet, ShuffleNet, SqueezeNet and EfficientNet.

The case study ties it together: an edge voice assistant with 98.2% wake-word accuracy, under 0.5% false activations, 87.3% command recognition in noisy environments, a 76 MB footprint (73% smaller than baseline) and 85 ms end-to-end latency.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and embedded developers moving models onto devices. His closing checklist is worth copying: set latency, accuracy, power and size targets first, combine techniques, benchmark on the actual target hardware, and keep collecting real-world data after deployment.

Title: Multi-tenant governance that runs all year, not just at audit time
Description: Kushal Shah at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on a data governance framework for multi-tenant cloud contract management with tenant keys and automated compliance.
Body:
In a multi-tenant system, every tenant's data sits next to someone else's, and every regulator expects you to prove it never leaks. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Kushal Shah, a data management professional with more than 15 years in data governance, architecture and business intelligence, explains how his team built a governance framework for multi-tenant cloud contract management that isolates tenants, automates compliance and keeps performance intact.

It's a short, tight talk, a case study more than a tutorial, and it covers the whole stack from row-level security to audit trails.

## Three problems, three continents

Shah names three core challenges. Data isolation: keep each tenant's data separate while still allowing shared analytics. Regulatory complexity: GDPR, HIPAA and CCPA, varying by region. Operational efficiency: strong controls that don't slow down authorised access. The detail that makes it real is where the problems came from. The cloud infrastructure team in North America flagged data boundary issues, the legal team in Europe found compliance gaps, and DevOps in Asia-Pacific worried security would slow deployments. One framework had to answer all three.

The framework sits on three pillars: tenant-specific controls so each organisation sets its own security posture, a secure data architecture, and resilient infrastructure built for redundancy and scale. The point, he stresses, was to design governance into the system, not bolt it on later.

## Isolation by default

The isolation strategy has three parts. Row-level security in the shared environment so access is restricted unless granted. Tenant-specific encryption with dedicated keys, so data stays unreadable even to privileged users. And ownership metadata embedded in every data element, which drives dynamic access policies across the system. That last one is the clever bit: once every record knows whose it is, policy becomes a lookup rather than a guess.

## A compliance engine that fixes things

The compliance engine runs continuously. It watches for discrepancies in real time, validates against regulations, alerts teams to likely violations and, importantly, remediates automatically by triggering corrective workflows and documenting each action. Security is layered: identity and access management with MFA and defined roles, masking and tokenisation for sensitive fields, encryption in transit, and encryption at rest with distributed key management. If one barrier fails, the next one holds.

For global operations, data is routed by jurisdiction, with region-specific retention and deletion policies, and the documentation system generates audit-ready reports aligned to several standards at once. Every access is logged with who, what, when and why, contracts and data changes are version-controlled, and exports are tracked with anomalies raising alerts.

## What changed

Shah reports a 40% drop in compliance violations across regions, a 30% improvement in operational efficiency through automation, a 65% reduction in audit cycle time and 99.9% system uptime. The platform scaled from thousands to tens of thousands of users without degradation. The rollout followed a phased path: assess gaps and risks, design the architecture for the business and regulatory profile, build the access, encryption and compliance layers, then deploy gradually across functions and regions while measuring.

## Who should watch

Architects and data leads running SaaS or shared platforms with regulated customers, especially anyone facing multiple jurisdictions. It's high level on implementation detail, so treat it as a checklist to compare against your own design.

Title: APIs that see the incident coming, and the rollout plan to get there
Description: Vamsi Krishna Munnangi of Walmart at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on AI-driven API resilience, from intelligent optimization to self-healing.
Body:
An API that only reacts to failure has already failed somebody. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Vamsi Krishna Munnangi, a senior software engineer in infrastructure engineering at Walmart, makes the case for moving API operations from reactive to predictive, with AI handling optimisation, threat detection and a growing share of incident resolution.

The talk is part vision, part playbook. The vision is a stack of impressive percentages; the playbook at the end is the part you can take to a planning meeting.

## Three pillars of a predictive API

Munnangi organises the idea into three pillars. Intelligent optimisation: algorithms that tune performance, balance traffic and allocate resources against real-time demand. Preemptive security: detecting threats before they escalate, using threat intelligence, behavioural analysis and context-aware authentication. And autonomous healing: systems that monitor continuously, predict failure points and apply corrective measures before users notice.

For the optimisation pillar he describes an API gateway scaling dynamically to 3,500 requests per second with a 67% throughput increase, deep-learning load balancing with 25% lower latency under heavy traffic, and reinforcement-learning-based caching that predicts frequently accessed content and cuts database load by 35%. The caching idea is the most transferable: if a model can guess what will be read next, your database doesn't have to answer the same question twice.

## Security at a million events a second

On the security side, Munnangi describes real-time analysis of a million security events per second, AI-powered contextual authentication that cuts unauthorised access attempts by up to 73%, and predictive threat detection that improves recognition speed by 58%. The framing is that traditional security waits for an attack to happen, while the predictive version looks for the early signal.

## Learn what normal looks like, then act early

The self-healing architecture starts with baseline models that analyse 50,000 events per second to learn normal system behaviour. From there, the early-warning layer flags problems 30 minutes before conventional tools, and recovery actions deploy in milliseconds. In his figures, automated resolution handles 70% of critical incidents and cuts mean time to resolution by 85%, with predictive models improving incident response by 12 to 15% a quarter as they learn from historical incidents.

Munnangi presents these as the gains from AI-driven API management in general rather than a single Walmart case study, so read them as targets, not a benchmark you'll hit on day one.

## Canary first, then everything

The roadmap is the strongest section, and it's pure SRE common sense applied to ML. Start with assessment: analyse your API infrastructure, find the resilience gaps and agree measurable objectives with stakeholders. Then a pilot on non-critical APIs only, deployed with canary techniques, to establish baselines and detection thresholds and check prediction accuracy against real incidents. Then gradual expansion across production, integrated with existing monitoring, with team training and a rollback plan ready. Finally, continuous optimisation with real operational data and measured ROI in downtime reduction.

His practical advice for getting started: assess your resilience maturity, identify the APIs that need the highest availability, begin with monitoring and analytics before adding prediction, and build a cross-functional team of API developers, ML specialists and site reliability engineers. Start small, scale fast.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams responsible for API gateways who are being asked what AI can do for availability. The phased rollout is useful on its own; the numbers are best treated as motivation.

Title: Predicting Oracle outages before the archive logs fill up
Description: Sunil Yadav at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on using pattern recognition, Data Guard tuning and predictive autoscaling to keep Oracle Cloud databases up.
Body:
Most database outages announce themselves: a tablespace filling, archive logs piling up at month end, CPU pinned near 100%. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Sunil Yadav, a database administrator with years of Oracle E-Business Suite and core database work across telecom, banking and retail, argues that machine learning should spot those patterns early enough to act, and walks through how that applies to Oracle Cloud availability.

It's a DBA's talk about ML, not an ML researcher's talk about databases, which is the right way round for this topic.

## The bill for a bad hour

Yadav opens with the money. He puts the cost of database downtime for a large enterprise at more than 9,000 US dollars a minute, and notes that even a modest production problem tends to take around an hour from detection to fix. Multiply those and you get his per-incident figure of roughly 700,000 dollars, which is the argument for spending on prevention instead of faster firefighting.

The ML part rests on three pillars: early detection, preventive action and, as the outcome of the first two, better uptime. His claim is that most problems can be seen coming, often 30 minutes or more in advance, and that the patterns are not mysterious. Month-end and quarter-end loads, archive and transaction logs that grow on predictable days, CPU climbing toward saturation.

## Recognise the pattern in seconds, not in the post-mortem

The practical detail worth keeping: pattern recognition is only useful if it runs on a short interval. Yadav suggests checking every five to ten seconds, not every 30 minutes or hour, so action can follow immediately. Beyond the obvious signals, he describes using neural networks to find correlated patterns in monitoring logs that a person scanning dashboards would miss.

He frames the loop in four steps: monitor every log continuously, learn the patterns and anomalies from what the logs contain, optimise by choosing the remediation, then validate whether the fix actually solved the problem. The validation feeds back into the model. On top of that sits Oracle RAC (Real Application Clusters) for availability and scalability, so a failed node or network problem is absorbed by the rest of the cluster.

## Data Guard: no lag, no hit on the primary

The section on Oracle Data Guard is where the DBA experience shows. Yadav sets two requirements for ML-assisted tuning of standby replication. The lag between primary and standby has to stay in the sub-millisecond range so a failover loses no committed transactions, because a standby that drops transactions is not much of a standby. And the replication must not slow down the primary to get there. Add fast-start failover so the standby comes up within minutes, ideally under one, and you have the three goals he works toward: no data loss, minimal impact, fast recovery.

He's refreshingly realistic about the target. Very few enterprise applications truly need 100% uptime; a few minutes of downtime a year is what 99.98% availability allows, and that is what the title promises.

## Scale for month end, not for every day

Predictive autoscaling gets a concrete example. As month end approaches and CPU starts climbing, add CPUs as demand grows, and do the same for memory and storage growth, or at least alert an engineer to provision space before it runs out. Then scale back down. Yadav cites a 47% reduction in over-provisioning from ML models and up to 60% lower cost from storage tiering based on access patterns, plus an ROI of more than 280% over three years and an 8.4-month payback. Those are the figures he presents for ML-based resilience in Oracle Cloud; the talk doesn't break down where they were measured.

## Who should watch

Oracle DBAs and platform teams running Oracle Cloud who want to move from alerts to prediction. ML engineers will find the modelling side light; the value is in which database signals are worth predicting.

Title: Let AI map customer_id to customer_number across your clouds
Description: Prakash Vanga of Sriven Technologies at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on AI-driven data integration across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.
Body:
Your customer records live in Amazon S3, your application logs in Azure Monitor and your analytics in Google BigQuery, and none of them speak to each other natively. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Prakash Vanga of Sriven Technologies, an AWS data engineer with 13 years of experience in cloud engineering and identity and access management, argued that AI can absorb much of the integration grind: mapping fields, routing data, enforcing policy and finding the broken pipe before users do.

The talk covers both the problem and a phased roadmap, with the numbers framed as results his slides attribute to AI-driven integration programmes.

## Four ways multi-cloud hurts

Vanga's opening diagnosis is specific. **Fragmented data**: different formats and APIs per cloud. **Inconsistent security**: AWS IAM roles and policies, Azure role-based access control and GCP IAM bindings tied to resource hierarchies aren't interoperable, so one over-permissive role or inconsistent MFA policy becomes the way in. **Manual integration**: human-driven connections between services that are slow and error-prone. **Compliance complexity**: data landing in the wrong region by default, and audit trails split across CloudTrail, Azure Monitor and Cloud Audit Logs, which makes HIPAA or SOX evidence painful to assemble.

## Where AI does the work

The core of the talk is four capabilities:

- **Automated data mapping.** Models scan datasets from different systems, detect that `customer_id` in AWS is `customer_number` in Azure, and generate the mapping logic. He reports an 85% reduction in manual mapping effort.
- **Intelligent data routing.** Instead of fixed routes, the system watches bandwidth, latency and server load and picks the fastest path for each transfer.
- **Governance enforcement.** Self-learning policy engines apply rules consistently across clouds; he cites up to 70% less compliance monitoring workload.
- **Issue detection and troubleshooting.** Continuous scanning of logs and data flows, pattern recognition and correlated root-cause analysis across clouds, with a reported 94% improvement in early detection and much shorter troubleshooting.

The operational payoff he describes is a single pane of glass across AWS, Azure and GCP with alerts that say what broke and how to fix it, rather than a tour of three consoles.

## Choosing a platform that won't trap you

Platform selection rests on four criteria: interoperability with every cloud API, data format and protocol (including on-prem); built-in ML for prediction and pattern recognition; scalability with growing data and users; and vendor independence so you can move later. Performance optimisation then adds predictive resource allocation, AI-based data filtering so less moves between systems, edge processing near the data source, and adaptive compression tuned to content and network conditions.

He includes a financial-services case study in which integration time and data errors fell sharply and uptime improved; the transcript is clear on direction, less so on the methodology.

## A phased roadmap

The plan is unusually concrete about duration: discovery for four to six weeks, foundation (core integration platform, primary systems connected, basic flows and monitoring) for eight to ten weeks, AI enhancement (automated mapping, routing, self-learning policies, predictive monitoring) for six to eight weeks, then ongoing optimisation. Looking ahead, he points to self-healing operations, blockchain-backed audit trails across providers and natural-language control of cloud operations.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects stitching together AWS, Azure and GCP, especially in regulated industries where audit trails span providers. It's a strategy talk with no live demo; take the roadmap durations as a starting point for your own estimates.

Title: Shard the service, not just the database
Description: Salesforce engineer Rahul Singh Thakur at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on sharding service instances for high availability and fault isolation.
Body:
Replicas protect you from a dead pod, not from a bad deploy or a broken availability zone that takes every replica with it. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Rahul Singh Thakur, Lead Member of Technical Staff at Salesforce, proposed taking sharding up a level: run several independent instances of the whole service, give each a slice of customers, and route every request consistently to its shard.

It's a short architecture talk without slides full of numbers, and it's more practical than most because he spends half of it on what gets harder.

## One instance is one blast radius

His starting point: without sharding, everything flows to one place. That's a single point of failure, there's no room for intelligent load distribution, and any problem hits all incoming traffic at once. With, say, five shards each serving 20% of customers, losing one instance costs 20% of capacity rather than all of it.

## The metadata service does the routing

The key new component is a metadata service. Its job is consistent routing: identify a request (by IP address or customer credentials) and always send it to the same shard. It also knows which shards exist and holds metadata about the services taking part. Around it sit two more pieces: a provisioning service that spins shard instances up or down as the product grows or shrinks, and a configuration service, because shards of the same service may need different runtime properties.

## What you get for the trouble

Thakur's benefit list goes beyond availability:

- **Better caching**: each shard sees the same customers repeatedly, so a local cache is far more effective.
- **Safer deployments**: release to one shard first, validate, then roll on, so a regression hits a fraction of customers.
- **Targeted scaling**: if one shard serves current-day data and others serve historical data, scale the hot one independently.
- **Fault isolation**: put shards in different availability zones and an AZ outage takes out one shard, not the service.
- **Cost flexibility**: scale shards up and down at different times instead of keeping one giant instance at peak size.

## What gets harder

This is the part worth the watch. Debugging gets more complex because you first have to know which shard a customer lives on and what configuration it runs. Infrastructure complexity grows with the provisioning layer. Moving customers between shards is the biggest challenge, especially for stateful services, and live data migration brings consistency and latency risk.

His mitigations are concrete. For moves, use dual ingestion: keep writing to the old shard, start writing to the new one, switch reads once they're in sync, then clean up, ideally with retention-based cleanup so old data ages out on its own. Customers shouldn't notice the switch. For routing latency, cache the shard map in the metadata service, since adding or removing shards is rare, and invalidate on change. For debugging, give every shard proper dashboards and alarms and make the customer-to-shard mapping visible.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers whose replicated service still fails as one unit, and SREs looking for a cell-style architecture explained without a vendor attached. Note that despite the conference track there's no machine learning in it; it's a distributed-systems talk.

Title: Zero-touch migration starts with the system nobody documented
Description: Narendra Chennupati at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on an AI middleware framework that discovers, maps and migrates legacy workflows to the cloud.
Body:
The hardest part of a legacy migration is usually the knowledge that walked out the door with the people who built the system. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Narendra Chennupati, a senior software engineer with more than ten years in enterprise architecture across healthcare, banking, finance and insurance, proposes a zero-touch, AI-driven middleware that discovers, maps and migrates legacy workflows with as little manual work as possible.

It's a framework talk: layers, stages and industry patterns rather than a live demo. If you're scoping a mainframe exit, it gives you a decent vocabulary for the parts a migration needs to automate.

## Why lift-and-shift keeps hurting

Chennupati starts with the three classic routes: lift and shift, re-platforming and refactoring. All three, he argues, still lean on manual integration work, and that brings the same failure modes every time. Specialists who understand both the old and the new stack are rare. Documentation is outdated or missing. Migration happens step by step, which limits parallel work. And human error creeps in during the transition.

His list of pain points will look familiar to anyone who has run one of these projects. The original architects have retired or moved on. Dependencies surface only mid-migration, so the scope grows while the timeline slips. Data quality problems show up late and need cleaning nobody planned for. And testing grows with system size until doing it by hand stops being realistic.

## Six layers between the old system and the new one

The core of the talk is a layered architecture borrowed in spirit from zero-touch network orchestration. A perception layer watches the legacy system through non-invasive methods. An intelligence layer builds a model of what the system actually does. An orchestration layer coordinates the transformation, an execution layer carries out migration tasks through APIs, a governance layer enforces organisational policy, and an optimization layer keeps tuning performance and resource allocation.

Feeding those layers are the technologies he names: NLP to pull domain knowledge out of unstructured docs, code comments and user manuals; machine learning to find patterns in system behaviour; knowledge graphs to represent components and their relationships; computer vision to map user interactions in systems that have no API at all; and ensemble methods to make the whole thing more robust.

## Mine the logs, find the shadow workflows

The four-stage methodology is the most practical part. First, system analysis: monitor without disruption and build an inventory of components, interactions and dependencies. Second, workflow discovery: process-mining algorithms read event logs to reconstruct the business processes people actually run, including the shadow workflows and exception paths nobody wrote down. Third, code transformation into modern languages while preserving behaviour and generating equivalent APIs. Fourth, continuous validation, with a digital simulation to test migration plans and automated comparison of responses between legacy and migrated components.

That second stage is the one to steal even if you never automate the rest. The process the business thinks it has and the one in the event logs are rarely the same process.

## Same idea, four industries

Chennupati walks through sector patterns: mainframe COBOL to microservices in finance (transaction integrity and regulatory compliance), customised on-prem ERP to cloud-native ERP with IoT in manufacturing, departmental patient systems to a unified platform in healthcare (privacy and fragmentation), and network management systems to cloud-native orchestration in telecom (hardware dependencies and old protocols). He closes with headline figures of 70% cost reduction, 60% time savings and 90% lower risk compared with traditional approaches; the talk presents them as the framework's results rather than walking through a specific measured project.

He is also candid about the limits. Heavily customised proprietary systems resist standard analysis, hardware dependencies and non-deterministic behaviour remain hard, security-through-obscurity in old systems clashes with modern requirements, and complex scenarios still need a human-AI collaboration model.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering managers planning a large modernisation who want a structured way to think about discovery and validation. Engineers looking for tooling recommendations or code will find it high level.

Title: Conf42 SRE 2025: postmortems, pit stops and SLOs over alerts
Description: Conf42 SRE 2025 roundup - postmortem lessons from reality TV and Formula 1, SLOs against alert fatigue, databases without DBAs, and AI in incident response.
Body:
Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025 ran online on April 17, 2025, with 107 talks, one of the largest lineups Conf42 has run. With that many sessions, the tracks covered almost everything that can page you: observability, SLOs, resilience, databases, cloud, fintech, healthcare, and a growing pile of AI. The talks worth starting with, though, were the ones about people: how teams review incidents, decide what deserves an alert, and stay curious about their systems.

Every session is on the [Conf42 SRE 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCu4WV3_Ve7-ChGVhr_-DbU). Below is a guided path through it.

## Incident reviews, from unexpected teachers

[Paige Cruz](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Paige_Cruz_what_real_housewives), Principal Developer Advocate at Chronosphere, gave the most quotable title of the event: what The Real Housewives taught her about postmortem meetings. Bringing "receipts" and holding "the meeting before the meeting" turn out to be useful habits for structured, blame-aware incident reviews. It is funnier than most postmortems and more useful than most postmortem templates.

[Ricardo Castro](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Ricardo_Castro_what_can_we), Principal Engineer and SRE at FanDuel, found his teacher in Formula 1: the race where Red Bull Racing repaired Max Verstappen's car in Hungary and turned a potential disaster into a podium finish. The talk pulls out the incident management lessons that apply when your outage has no pit wall.

[Saurabh Phaltane](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Saurabh_Phaltane_curious_sre_cultivating), a Senior SRE at Google, argued for curiosity as the core SRE skill, balancing breadth and depth and thinking about the system as a whole. [Shaalmali Raychaudhury](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Shaalmali_Raychaudhury_navigating_sre_incident) of PayPal and [Pradeep Gaddamidi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Pradeep_Gaddamidi_deployments_downtime_unexpected) added practitioner stories about incident management and deploy-day fires.

## Alert on what users feel

[Mandi Walls](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Mandi_Walls_tackling_alert_fatigue), DevOps Advocate at PagerDuty, took on alert fatigue with SLOs: metrics centred on the user experience give teams a focus, and give them permission to disable alerts that contribute nothing to customer happiness. [Siddharth Joshi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Siddharth_Joshi_reliability_excellence_slo) of Nagarro covered the tooling side of SLO management, and [Gaurav Mittal](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Gaurav_Mittal_slos_failute_prediction) of Nordstrom went beyond SLOs to anomaly detection, finding the signals hidden in your data before they become outages.

[Veliswa Boya](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Veliswa_Boya_application_resilience_whose), Senior Developer Advocate at AWS, asked whose job application resilience is anyway, and how resilience and innovation can coexist through both culture and technical choices. [Sai Sahiti Nemalikanti](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Sai_Sahiti_Nemalikanti_designing_failure_using) of AWS followed with patterns for designing for failure.

## Observability you can actually use

[Alok Ranjan](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Alok_Ranjan_fragmented_logs_unified), an Engineering Manager at Dropbox, told the story of unifying fragmented container logs with open-source tools, along with what it taught him about DevOps culture. [Swapnil Kulkarni](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Swapnil_Kulkarni_observe_or_not) of Kloudfuse reframed the debate: whether to observe is not the question; whether observability solves the right use cases is. [Sai KR Pentaparthi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Sai_KR_Pentaparthi_xray_ebpf_o11y) showed eBPF for network-level visibility in cloud-native systems, and [Mohit Menghnani](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Mohit_Menghnani_unlocking_observability_react) of Twilio brought observability to React and Node.js applications.

## Databases without a DBA

[Renato Losio](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Renato_Losio_things_fall_apart), Principal Cloud Architect at Funambol, shared a decade of running managed production databases without DBA expertise, from crashing managed instances to storage costs that grew far faster than planned, plus a warning about trusting benchmarks. [Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Samuel_Baruffi_amazon_aurora_dsql), Principal Global Solutions Architect at AWS, introduced Amazon Aurora DSQL, a serverless distributed SQL database with active-active availability. [Andrei Manakov](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Andrei_Manakov_tradeoffs_distributed_nosql) of ShareChat walked through the real-world CAP trade-offs in distributed NoSQL design.

## Real-time systems with no second chances

Some talks dealt with systems where reliability is not abstract. [Vlad Onetiu](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Vlad_Onetiu_serverless_confluent_kafka) of DataIceberg built a real-time earthquake alert system with Lambda functions and Confluent Kafka that checks for event changes every second and sends SMS and email notifications. [Bhushan Gopala Reddy](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Bhushan_Gopala_Reddy_resilient_health_monitoring) of Aruba Networks engineered Bluetooth Low Energy health monitoring for disaster zones. [Srihari Pakalapati](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Srihari_Pakalapati_ransomware_readiness_backup) of Trader Interactive covered ransomware readiness with immutable backups and automated recovery, and [Payal Godhani](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Payal_Godhani_zero_downtime_ml) of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure applied SRE techniques to zero-downtime ML deployments.

## AI on call

AI was everywhere, and the most practical uses were small. [David Asamu](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_David_Asamu_ai_sre_prometheus_nl), who leads the SRE team at Nomba, started from a wish every on-call engineer has had: "What if you could chat with your monitoring metrics?" The talk shows asking Prometheus questions in natural language instead of writing queries mid-incident. [Smita Verma](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Smita_Verma_alerts_action_building) of Adobe built AI-powered autonomous incident response at scale, and [Rahul Amte](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Rahul_Amte_smarter_failure_testing) of Nivid Technologies combined AI with chaos engineering for smarter failure testing. Title: Multi-cloud ERP needs a canonical model for shared data
Description: SPL Consulting's Srinivasan Pakkirisamy at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on syncing data across Oracle Cloud ERP, Workday, Salesforce and Blue Yonder.
Body:
The same company you buy from is a supplier in Oracle Cloud ERP, an account in Salesforce and a vendor in Blue Yonder, and each system cares about different attributes. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Srinivasan Pakkirisamy, Director of Technology Portfolio at SPL Consulting, laid out a framework for integrating best-of-breed cloud ERP stacks, and his answer to that naming mess is a canonical data model agreed up front.

He opens with the cost of getting it wrong: his slides claim that over 67% of multi-cloud integration projects overrun because of data and integration complexity.

## Best-of-breed means many schemas

Enterprises increasingly pick a specialist per domain: Oracle Cloud ERP for finance, Workday for human capital management, Salesforce for CRM and Blue Yonder for supply chain. Each is strong in its lane, and each was designed with its own data philosophy. Oracle brings complex chart-of-account segments and business rules, Workday employee records span 23 related objects with 200-plus attributes and SOAP-based services, and Salesforce runs an event-driven architecture that emits millions of event notifications a day in large deployments.

Pakkirisamy separates two problems. **Schema heterogeneity** is structural: different shapes for overlapping data. **Semantic mapping** is subtler: the supplier/account/vendor example, where the entity is the same but the meaning, hierarchy and rules differ. He says semantic reconciliation can consume around 43% of development effort.

## Three ways to normalise

The options he compares:

- **ETL**: extract, transform, load. Simple and widely used, but the mapping logic piles up in the transform layer.
- **Schema mapping engines**: tools that hold mappings for many ERPs so integrations reuse them.
- **Canonical data models**: each system of record agrees a standard format and publishes it, pub/sub style, so consumers get one shape. Expensive to design, cheaper to live with.

He clearly favours the third, and he's honest about the bill: expect a 25 to 30% increase in initial effort, offset later by lower maintenance costs.

## Timing and conflicts are the real bugs

Synchronisation brings its own failure modes. He cites eight to 15 seconds of propagation delay for standard transactions and up to minutes for complex ones, and many data elements operate under eventual consistency. In bidirectional sync, he reports that 6 to 8% of records hit update conflicts, rising to 12 to 15% with frequent modifications.

His conflict-resolution menu: timestamp-based (last write wins), domain-specific rules (the system of record wins, so Oracle owns the supplier, Salesforce the customer), manual reconciliation where neither works, and conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) as the direction the industry is heading. Building blocks he names include Salesforce change data capture, which slashes data volume compared to full synchronisation, and Kafka as an event-streaming backbone.

## Security and drift

Data in flight between clouds widens the attack surface. He covers cross-platform authentication with OAuth 2.0, automated compliance monitoring, layered encryption in transit (outdated cipher suites and TLS misconfigurations show up in the incident stats), and automated detection of schema drift, since undetected schema changes cause a good share of integration failures.

## Phase it

The implementation path is sequential on purpose: data profiling and mapping (tools plus domain experts in the room), canonical model design, integration pattern selection per data element (timing, volume, transformation complexity, recovery), synchronisation, then monitoring and governance. A typical large implementation, he says, ends up with five to eight distinct integration patterns. Looking ahead, he expects ML-assisted mapping tools and smarter, context-aware conflict resolution.

## Who should watch

Enterprise architects and integration engineers living between Oracle, Workday and Salesforce, and anyone about to propose point-to-point integrations as a temporary fix. Despite the conference, there's little machine learning here; it's a solid data-integration talk.

Title: Edge ML pays off when you place each workload deliberately
Description: Minisoft Technologies' Ravi Kumar Amaresam at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on where ML belongs between edge devices and multiple clouds.
Body:
Sending every sensor reading to a cloud region and waiting for the model to answer is fine until the network blinks or the answer arrives too late. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Ravi Kumar Amaresam, Senior Lead Software Engineer at Minisoft Technologies (after 15 years at IBM), argued that the return on ML investment depends on placement: inference at the edge where latency or connectivity demands it, training in the cloud, and a multi-cloud layer that keeps the two connected.

The talk is short and structured as a playbook, with two case studies and a placement framework you can borrow.

## Why the edge, in numbers

Amaresam contrasts centralised cloud ML, which brings latency and bandwidth costs, with edge ML running inference on or near the device. The benefits he cites are concrete: up to 60% lower maintenance costs and latency cut from over 300 milliseconds to 14. The point he calls most important is quieter: edge systems keep working when the cloud link drops. A factory line doesn't stop because a WAN circuit did.

## Two case studies

**Healthcare point-of-care analytics.** A provider's patient data was overwhelming its network. Moving lightweight models on site allowed real-time processing of vital signs, and federated learning let the models improve without centralising sensitive data, so critical events were detected sooner.

**Manufacturing predictive maintenance.** Unplanned downtime is expensive. Anomaly detection models running on local factory sensors spotted issues days before failure, and the manufacturer cut maintenance costs by 60%. Data from the edge flowed back to the cloud to refine models over time, which is the loop that keeps the edge models from going stale.

## A placement framework

The most reusable slide is the workload placement framework. Not everything belongs on the edge. His questions:

- **Latency**: if the system needs sub-100 ms responses, the edge is the answer.
- **Data gravity**: process data where it's generated.
- **Privacy and compliance**: keep regulated data local when you can.
- **Compute needs**: heavy training stays in the cloud.

The usual result is a hybrid: lightweight models at the edge, heavy training centrally.

## Making models small and keeping them current

Edge devices need compact models, so he lists quantisation, pruning and neural architecture search to cut size without losing too much accuracy, plus federated learning for training across devices without moving raw data. The operational challenges are model update logistics and security; his answers are containerised deployment, differential (delta) updates and proper version control for model artifacts.

On the cloud side he wants an abstraction layer with unified APIs to avoid vendor lock-in, workloads orchestrated dynamically on real-time performance and cost, and governance plus DevOps pipelines covering deployment from edge to cloud. The roadmap is the familiar one: assess goals and metrics, build foundations and governance, then automate optimisation as you scale, starting with one high-impact use case.

## Who should watch

Architects deciding which models leave the data centre, IoT teams in manufacturing or healthcare, and anyone asked to justify an edge ML budget. It's a compact overview; for the toolchain itself, pair it with one of the hands-on talks below.

Title: Make the platform cloud-native before you add the ML
Description: Tejaswi Katta of Logicgate Technologies at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on embedding ML into microservices, containers and serverless architectures.
Body:
Bolting a model onto a monolith gets you a demo; embedding it in a cloud-native platform gets you a system that learns. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Tejaswi Katta of Logicgate Technologies, who has spent about 15 years in enterprise integration and AI, made the case for ML as the catalyst of cloud-native transformation, and one of his four closing priorities is the one most teams skip: get the platform genuinely cloud-native before layering ML on top.

It's a brisk, high-level talk that works as a map of the territory more than a build guide.

## Four steps of cloud architecture

Katta's evolution story has four stages. Monolithic applications were static, tightly coupled and hard to scale. Lift-and-shift migration improved resource utilisation but changed little architecturally. Cloud-native design broke systems into microservices and containers under orchestration, adding resilience and flexibility. The fourth stage embeds ML into that architecture, so the system predicts and automates decisions instead of just running them.

## What distributed computing buys ML

Running ML in a cloud-native environment lets you lean on distributed computing. He cites 10 to 20 times faster training through parallelised pipelines, elastic scaling that matches resources to demand, routine petabyte-scale processing and pay-for-what-you-use economics. On the operations side, ML-driven automation adds predictive scaling ahead of spikes, continuous self-optimisation of parameters and automated threat detection; he reports organisations seeing 45 to 60% less downtime and 30 to 40% better resource efficiency.

For hybrid and multi-cloud estates his checklist is short and sensible: centralised governance for model management and security policies, edge deployment for latency-sensitive inference, provider choice based on accelerators or pricing, and failover so predictions keep flowing when a region goes down.

## The hard parts, named plainly

The challenges slide is the most useful one for practitioners:

- **Model drift** as real-world data changes, which means continuous monitoring and retraining.
- **Black-box models** that make interpretability and audit difficult.
- **Data quality** across distributed services, a perennial struggle.
- **New attack surfaces**: adversarial attacks, model poisoning and privacy leaks.

His emerging answers map one to one: MLOps platforms that automate the lifecycle from data prep to deployment (he cites deployment times cut by almost 80%), explainability frameworks such as SHAP and LIME for trust and compliance, and federated learning to train on decentralised data without moving it.

## A four-step plan

The implementation framework is assessment (align ML initiatives with business priorities), architecture design (microservices, data pipelines, governance), a focused proof of concept that demonstrates return on investment, then scaling the successful patterns enterprise-wide. On impact he reports features reaching market 65% faster and leaders growing 20 to 30% faster than peers on conventional architectures, while noting the revenue percentages look modest and the absolute gains don't.

His closing priorities: tie every ML initiative to clear business metrics, make sure the platform really is cloud-native (containers, microservices, infrastructure as code), invest in DataOps and MLOps, and build cross-functional squads that combine data science, cloud engineering and domain knowledge.

## Who should watch

Engineering leaders sequencing a modernisation programme, and architects who need a crisp slide on why ML on a shaky platform is a bad idea. Practitioners already running MLOps pipelines will recognise most of it; the drift and security list is still a good review.

Title: Write the data strategy before you migrate a single table
Description: UK Research and Innovation's Raman Kapoor at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on the data strategy that makes cloud migration safe and AI-ready.
Body:
Lift and shift without a data strategy moves your duplicates, silos and mystery spreadsheets to someone else's data centre, at a monthly rate. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Raman Kapoor, Head of Data, MI and Analytics at UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), set out the blueprint he uses to make cloud migrations secure, scalable and ready for AI, and it starts with an inventory of everything you're about to move.

Kapoor has 20 years in the field, including IBM, Experian and the Scottish Government, and the talk reads like it: little hype, lots of governance.

## What goes wrong without one

His list of migration risks without a clear data strategy is worth printing: data silos and inconsistencies, security vulnerabilities, compliance failures against GDPR and sector rules, multi-vendor performance problems, slower time to value, cost overruns from unknowns, and duplicate systems carrying duplicate data in different formats through your new pipelines. Without that foundation, he says, getting value from AI is close to impossible.

## Inventory the legacy before it ambushes you

The practical heart of the talk is the legacy inventory. Record every process that needs to change and has an impact on the migration: old ETLs, integrations with no monitoring, logging or resilience, manual data processes waiting to be automated, inconsistent file formats, access dependencies held by different data owners, front-end journeys built on Power Apps. Map each to lineage and to the critical systems, then act on them in the order your roadmap needs, not when they break.

## The pillars

The strategy itself rests on a familiar set of pillars, with Kapoor's emphasis on trust:

- **Governance and ownership** from day one: data stewards and owners, usage policies, data-sharing agreements for internal and third-party flows, regulatory alignment.
- **Metadata management**, with a centralised catalogue that he likens to a Google search for your data.
- **Quality and lineage**, down to column-level lineage and impact analysis so you see the ripple effect of a change.
- **Data quality checks built into pipelines** from the start, instead of fixing data after the fact.
- **Security by design**: zero trust, encryption at rest and in transit, fine-grained access, and automated compliance audits that run all the time rather than once a year.
- **Integration frameworks** and **AI and analytics enablement** planned from the beginning.

## The cloud building blocks

For the platform he points to serverless pipelines with AWS Lambda and Athena, a data lake for raw data without predefined structures, event-driven ingestion, and containerised workloads. His migration path: discovery and assessment, governance and security models, modernised ETLs and APIs with deployment pipelines, phased migration starting with critical processes, and data quality frameworks in the pipelines so AI is possible from the first day.

## A migration that landed on time

He closes with a recent project that followed this path. Legacy APIs moved to AWS API Gateway, ETLs were rebuilt as Lambda functions that kept feeding business reporting, and legacy reports were replicated in Power BI and rolled out to users, without slippage. His summary is to spend more time at discovery, which makes the rest of the journey faster.

## Who should watch

Data leaders and architects in the public sector or any regulated organisation about to start (or restart) a migration. Engineers looking for implementation detail will find the platform section brief; the value is the checklist and the order of operations.

Title: When availability becomes a feature
Description: SRE makes it measurable
Body:
# Reliability is everyone’s job (but somehow also yours)

Site Reliability Engineering sounds calm and responsible.

In practice, it’s alerts at odd hours, dashboards you don’t fully trust, postmortems that could have been emails, and a deep, personal relationship with latency. Still, someone has to keep the lights on.

Conf42 SRE 2025 is for the people doing exactly that.

This is a big one. One hundred talks across reliability, observability, incidents, automation, architecture, security, cloud, data, AI, healthcare, fintech, hardware, and just about every place where failure is not an option. If a system needs to stay up, it probably shows up here.

AI plays a starring role. From self-healing infrastructure and anomaly detection to AI-assisted monitoring, chaos engineering, and SRE practices for ML systems, the program digs into how automation is changing reliability work. Sometimes for the better. Sometimes with new things to worry about.

But SRE isn’t just about tools. There are talks on culture, postmortems, ownership, accessibility, inclusion, and the very human side of running complex systems. You’ll hear about quiet engineers, impostor syndrome, and what reliability looks like across different organizations and industries.

The real-world use cases go deep. Healthcare platforms, financial systems, gaming infrastructure, supply chains, cloud migrations, legacy modernization, and systems operating at global scale all make an appearance. From sub-50ms architectures to multi-cloud resilience, this is SRE in production, not theory.

If your job involves preventing outages, responding to incidents, or explaining why five nines is harder than it sounds, this one’s for you. Reliability is a moving target. At least here, you don’t have to chase it alone.

Title: A checklist for ML systems that span several clouds
Description: Naga Swetha Kattula at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on secure, scalable and recoverable ML integrations across multiple cloud providers.
Body:
Most ML teams don't choose multi-cloud; they wake up in it. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Naga Swetha Kattula, a Senior Member of IEEE, laid out a practical checklist for ML systems that span providers: which deployment model to pick, which API style fits which prediction pattern, how to lock down identity and training data, and what to do when a region disappears.

She opens with the trade. Multiple clouds get you out of vendor lock-in, and in return you pay with operational overhead, compliance work and a bigger attack surface. Her slides cite that 78% of ML deployments already span more than one cloud.

## Pick the layer you want to own

The first decision is how much of the stack you run. IaaS (EC2-style VMs and networks) gives full control for custom frameworks and specialised workloads. PaaS (SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML, IBM Watson Studio) manages the frameworks and scaling so teams can focus on models. SaaS (Rekognition, Azure Cognitive Services, Google Vision AI) is close to drag-and-drop for well-defined use cases. Each step up trades flexibility for less undifferentiated plumbing.

## Match the API to the prediction

Kattula maps four integration styles to their jobs. REST is stateless, lightweight and works with almost anything. GraphQL reduces over-fetching with precise queries behind a single endpoint. gRPC brings binary, low-latency streaming for large volumes. Event-driven integration (pub/sub, queues, serverless triggers) handles asynchronous ML at scale. Later she turns that into three runtime patterns: synchronous request/response for immediate predictions under 100 ms, queue-based asynchronous inference for batch and background work, and stream processing for continuous inference.

## Identity and training data are the crown jewels

The security section is the densest. Least privilege sits at the top of her IAM pyramid, with MFA, role-based access and centralised identity underneath. Zero trust means verifying every identity and device, granting just-in-time and just-enough permissions, and monitoring behaviour continuously.

For training data she lists end-to-end encryption with key rotation, data sovereignty controls that respect regional rules, monitoring of who touches which dataset, and differential privacy to protect individual records at some cost to accuracy. Then comes the compliance alphabet: GDPR, HIPAA, the EU AI Act's risk-based approach, PCI for payment data in fraud models, and CCPA's rights to access and deletion, which reach into how you retrain.

## Spend less, recover faster

Cost advice is practical: run non-critical training on spot instances, move cold training data to cheaper storage tiers, autoscale on predicted demand and right-size instances to the workload. She cites 30 to 40% savings for properly configured ML environments. For portability she recommends containers on Docker and Kubernetes, serverless inference where you pay per prediction, and consistent versioning and monitoring across providers.

Disaster recovery closes the talk: replicate the model registry across regions with version-controlled artifacts, run multi-region deployments behind global load balancers with regular health checks and isolation tests, and design degraded modes (simplified fallback models, cached recent predictions, rules-based alternatives, retries and dead-letter queues) so a failing region means worse predictions, not none.

## Who should watch

ML platform engineers and architects formalising a multi-cloud setup, or anyone writing the non-functional requirements page of an ML design doc. Experienced cloud security folks will find the IAM material familiar, but the degraded-mode section is a useful prompt.

Title: What Starbucks, Mayo Clinic and Capital One teach about ML security
Description: Okta's Nagasruthi Kattula at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on ML-driven security in cloud CRM systems, from Starbucks to the Capital One breach.
Body:
The 2019 Capital One breach started with a misconfigured web application firewall and a server-side request forgery against the AWS metadata service. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Nagasruthi Kattula, Manager of Software Engineering at Okta, used it as the cautionary middle of a talk about ML-driven security in cloud CRM systems, with Starbucks, Mayo Clinic and JPMorgan Chase as the case studies on the other side of the ledger.

The thesis is the shift from reactive to proactive: rules that wait for a human to update them versus models that learn behaviour, predict threats and adjust access on the fly.

## Four building blocks

Kattula's architecture has four components that recur in every case study: **threat detection** (models flagging anomalous behaviour), **access intelligence** (adaptive authentication that tightens requirements as risk rises), **data protection** (automatic classification of sensitive data plus encryption) and **security orchestration** (coordinated response across systems). She contrasts them with the status quo of manual threat detection, static access controls and security tools that work in silos per platform.

## Starbucks: classify at ingestion

The Starbucks example runs on Salesforce. Data is classified as it's ingested, field-level encryption follows the classification, and Einstein Analytics models correlate security events with customer behaviour. The talk cites more than 30,000 locations, over 87 million customer records and anomaly detection across more than 250,000 user accounts, built on Salesforce Shield with custom extensions. The design idea worth stealing: protection scales with customer interactions because it's attached to the data, not bolted onto the app.

## Capital One: what a model might have caught

Kattula's reading of the breach is specific. The attacker used SSRF to reach the metadata service, obtained temporary IAM credentials and exfiltrated over 100 million customer records without being detected. Her argument is that three ML-backed controls could have broken that chain: behavioural analysis of unusual IAM credential use, continuous scanning for misconfiguration and drift (the firewall), and context-aware access decisions that demand extra verification when a request pattern looks wrong. That's a hypothesis rather than a post-mortem finding, and she presents it as such: analysis suggests ML could have prevented it.

## Mayo Clinic and JPMorgan Chase: scale and plumbing

The healthcare case, on Microsoft Cloud for Healthcare, reports automatic classification of protected health information at 99.3% accuracy across 23 million patient records, continuous HIPAA compliance scanning over 8.4 TB of daily data, and models that improved from 76% to over 98% accuracy through operational feedback. The JPMorgan Chase case is a multi-cloud split: AWS for transaction anomaly detection, Google Cloud for model training with federated learning, Azure for customer-facing adaptive authentication, all tied together by a central orchestration layer that normalises telemetry from each provider. Kattula cites more than 5,000 security models and an average of three minutes to act on an identified threat. These are reported figures from the talk; there's no source slide to check them against.

## Start with one well-defined problem

Her implementation framework is four steps: assess current controls and data flows, develop and baseline the models, design the integration architecture, and stand up governance with guardrails, performance monitoring and bias detection. Her advice is to pick a well-defined problem, set success metrics, and grow from there.

## Who should watch

Security and CRM platform teams, especially anyone running Salesforce or a multi-cloud estate, who want named examples to bring into an architecture review. It's a case-study tour, not a hands-on build; you'll leave with patterns, not configs.

Title: Detect, then respond is too slow for multi-cloud attacks
Description: Trace3 Principal Architect Pradeep Kurra at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on AI-driven, autonomous threat defense across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.
Body:
Polymorphic malware rewrites itself each time it runs, and the gap between an exploit being written and being used keeps shrinking. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Pradeep Kurra, Principal Architect at Trace3, argued that the classic detect-then-respond loop can't keep up across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, and that AI has to take over the first moves: correlating signals, isolating machines and locking accounts before a human opens the ticket.

He's careful about the human part, though. His closing point is that AI is a force multiplier for skilled security teams, not a magic box.

## Three capabilities, not one

Kurra splits the "AI security advantage" into three distinct things. **Real-time analysis** chews through logs, network traffic and user behaviour at a scale no analyst can. **Autonomous response** acts on detection directly, isolating infected machines or killing processes, often without waiting for approval. **Adaptive defence** learns from every attack and anomaly, where signature-based tools stay frozen until the next update.

The numbers he cites are operational ones: alert queues where most alerts are noise, a 30% cut in false positives, response times halved and incident resolution 40% faster. He presents them as typical outcomes rather than a single study, and the argument doesn't depend on the exact percentages. Fewer junk alerts means less burnout and faster attention on the real ones.

## Normal is learned, not written down

The behavioural analytics section is the clearest. Static rules ("if X, block") are known to attackers, who route around them. A model learns what normal looks like by observation instead. His examples are the ones you'd want in a runbook: a user who always logs in from Austin during working hours suddenly signs in from Singapore at midnight, or a database starts sending unusually large volumes of data outside business hours. The system flags it and acts, locking the account or isolating the device.

Zero trust is the policy frame around it: verify every user, device and request, apply least privilege, assume breach and microsegment the network to limit blast radius. AI's contribution is continuous trust evaluation through the whole session, not just at login.

## Correlation is the killer feature

Where AI earns its keep is across platforms. Kurra's example: a strange authentication attempt in Azure Active Directory, abnormal API calls in AWS and a suspicious download from a GitHub repository look like three unrelated events in three consoles. A SIEM with AI correlation tells them as one coordinated attack. SOAR then automates the response; for a phishing email that means quarantine, account lock, flagging similar messages and notifying an analyst within seconds. Alerts also arrive enriched, for example matched to the known tactics of a group like APT29, so the analyst starts with context.

He also names the native tooling: Amazon GuardDuty scanning CloudTrail for odd API activity (an admin call at 2 a.m. from a country where you have no staff), Microsoft's security center assessing vulnerabilities across compute, storage and identity, and Google Cloud Security Command Center watching containerised workloads.

## Where it's going

The industry examples cover finance (authentication anomaly detection that stopped fraudulent logins before they succeeded), healthcare (ransomware behaviour caught and endpoints isolated mid-execution) and e-commerce (separating bot traffic from shoppers during holiday DDoS). The future section points to predictive defence that closes likely attack paths early, self-healing infrastructure that rolls back to a known-good snapshot, and AI-managed quantum-resistant encryption.

His advice on getting there is incremental: start with AI-enhanced monitoring and detection, build confidence, and move towards autonomous response, while investing in the people who oversee it.

## Who should watch

Security architects and SOC leads making the case for automated response across several clouds, and platform engineers who want to know what the security team's tools are doing with their logs. It's a strategic overview rather than a detection-engineering lab.

Title: Environmental regulators need platforms, not paperwork
Description: Sneha Deepika Kalagarla of Cleveland State University at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on digital platforms for environmental compliance and monitoring.
Body:
Environmental protection still runs on a surprising amount of paper: permit applications, inspection reports and compliance filings that sit in different agencies' drawers. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Sneha Deepika Kalagarla of Cleveland State University made the case for replacing that with integrated digital platforms (cloud-native systems fed by IoT sensors, with AI on top) and showed the outcomes reported by projects that already made the switch.

It's a short, high-level talk, and an unusual one for a machine learning conference: the users are regulators, field teams and citizen scientists, not data scientists.

## From drawers to dashboards

Kalagarla's starting picture is the contrast between paper-based, fragmented systems and platforms where regulators, businesses and communities see the same environmental data in real time. The benefit she keeps returning to is shared visibility: when everyone works from the same live data, decisions get made on evidence instead of last quarter's PDF.

The headline improvements she reports include 67% faster permit review and approval, 42% faster emergency response, and gains in data accuracy and compliance reporting quality. She mentions projects such as Terra Watch as examples. The talk doesn't break down the underlying studies, so these are best read as the range digital programmes report, not a guarantee.

## The stack is boring, which is good

The technology she describes is familiar to anyone who has built a telemetry pipeline:

- **Cloud-native infrastructure** that scales as monitoring demands grow.
- **IoT environmental sensors** streaming continuous data from the field.
- **Integrated data management**, centralised and secure, with cross-agency access.

The interesting part is who consumes it. A regulator's dashboard has to work for people across all levels of technical skill, so she spends real time on accessibility, intuitive navigation and clear visualisation. Mobile access gives field teams live data on site, and citizen-science programmes let the public contribute measurements. She reports higher stakeholder participation and better data quality where those programmes are sustained with ongoing education.

## AI, blockchain and digital twins, each with a job

Three technologies get a specific role rather than a buzzword slot. Machine learning spots patterns that anticipate compliance violations, with a reported 31% gain in violation detection accuracy. Blockchain provides tamper-proof ledgers for compliance records, which she ties to stakeholder confidence. Digital twins create virtual replicas of ecosystems so agencies can test interventions without risking the real river.

## Three case studies

The close is a trio of examples: a river basin restoration where an integrated platform coordinated several agencies and cut restoration timelines by 40%; a coastal monitoring network whose early warning system mobilised a response three hours faster than conventional methods and prevented a contamination event; and a community-driven urban air quality initiative that found pollution hotspots and reduced harmful particulate matter by 27%.

Her implementation advice is a three-step loop: assess the environment and set measurable objectives tied to the agency's mission, build in agile iterations with input from regulators, field staff and communities, then deploy with training and careful integration with legacy databases.

## Who should watch

Engineers working in govtech, utilities or ESG reporting who need an overview of what environmental agencies want from a platform. If you're after sensor-network architecture or model details, this stays at the overview level; it's a good brief before a stakeholder meeting rather than a design doc.

Title: Oracle-to-AWS migrations fail on dependencies you didn't map
Description: LTIMindtree's Krishna Anumula at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on a phased framework for migrating Oracle databases to AWS, from assessment to cost tuning.
Body:
Most database migrations don't fail on the copy; they fail on the system nobody knew was reading that table. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Krishna Anumula, Specialist in System Management at LTIMindtree, walked through the framework behind an Oracle-to-AWS migration he recently delivered, and the stage he spends the most time on is the one before any data moves.

His framing is that a migration is a business change as much as a technical one: you're trading capital-heavy hardware cycles for consumption-based pricing, and that only pays off if the move is planned around how the business works.

## Assess first, and more than once

The pre-migration assessment has three parts. Workload performance analysis looks at compute requirements, data integration and system capabilities; his abstract cites that 62% of enterprises struggle with data complexity during migration. Dependency mapping is the big one: he puts 47% of migration failures down to gaps in understanding how systems interact. Readiness evaluation closes it out, and his practical advice is to plan on three to five assessment iterations before the real cutover. The more thorough the preparation, the quieter the weekend.

## RDS or EC2 is a licensing question as much as a technical one

AWS gives Oracle shops two main paths. Amazon RDS is the managed option: backups, patching and scaling are automated, and Anumula cites up to 45% less database management overhead. Self-managed Oracle on EC2 suits complex requirements that need fine-grained configuration, and it supports Bring Your Own License, which matters if you already own Oracle licences.

## Pick the migration type deliberately

He distinguishes three techniques:

- **Homogeneous** (Oracle to Oracle): the least complex, with minimal compatibility risk.
- **Heterogeneous** (Oracle to MySQL, or even MongoDB): needs schema conversion and data transformation up front, but is also a chance to modernise.
- **Hybrid**: a phased mix of the two, migrated incrementally to reduce risk. This is the one his team defaults to.

The overall flow is assessment, preparation (aligning the plan with business objectives), migration with AWS Database Migration Service to keep downtime minimal, and validation of data integrity, performance and functionality afterwards. He's emphatic about testing through every environment (dev, UAT, pre-prod) before production.

## Network and security come before the first byte

The security model is layered: encryption at rest and in transit, access policies and continuous monitoring; AWS Direct Connect for dedicated private links, with VPN tunnels on top; and VPCs with subnets and security groups to control which resources can reach the database. AWS's native controls cover Oracle-specific needs such as database-level encryption and access control.

## Cost tuning never ends

Post-migration, the work turns into a loop: analyse resources for under-use, scale dynamically with real demand, monitor with Amazon CloudWatch to catch bottlenecks early, and keep refining because the cloud bill moves with the workload. He closes on organisational readiness (training teams on AWS, change management) and treating the migration as an ongoing programme rather than a one-off project.

## Who should watch

DBAs and infrastructure leads planning an Oracle exit or a lift to RDS, and project managers who need a phase plan to put in front of stakeholders. It's a methodology talk; there's no DMS configuration walkthrough, so bring your own runbook.
