Title: AI workloads break the resource management you already have
Description: Shreya Gupta of the University of Southern California at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on profiling, scheduling and autoscaling AI workloads in the cloud.
Body:
A training job and an inference endpoint built on the same model can want completely different hardware an hour apart, and most cloud schedulers were never designed for that. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Shreya Gupta of the University of Southern California surveyed how resource allocation for AI workloads works today: profiling, scheduling, autoscaling, virtualisation, cost and security, plus the honest bit about where prediction accuracy falls apart.

It's a survey talk, closer to a well-organised literature review than a war story, and it's useful precisely because it puts every layer of the stack on one page.

## Know the workload before you place it

Gupta starts with why AI is different: big swings in resource needs, dependence on GPUs or TPUs, sensitivity to latency and throughput, and behaviour that changes by phase (training versus inference). Allocation therefore starts with profiling, and she walks through four approaches:

- **Static analysis** of the model architecture and hyperparameters before execution, which she puts at roughly 80 to 85% precision for established workloads.
- **Historical pattern analysis** on past telemetry, using time-series methods to forecast demand.
- **Online monitoring** of compute saturation, memory bandwidth and I/O at runtime.
- **Hybrid approaches** combining the three.

The caveat she flags is the interesting one: for genuinely new workload patterns, accuracy can slide to the 60 to 65% range. Your profiler is only as good as its memory of jobs like this one.

## Scheduling is NP-hard, so everyone cheats politely

The scheduler section covers priority-based preemption, fair-share allocation for multi-tenant clusters, deadline-aware scheduling for production pipelines and approximation algorithms for the multi-dimensional packing problem. Optimal allocation across CPU, GPU, memory and network is NP-hard, so real systems run heuristics that trade theoretical guarantees for decisions made in time. That's a candid framing for a field that tends to oversell "intelligent" schedulers.

## Autoscalers that ace the lab and stumble in prod

Her autoscaling architecture has three layers: monitoring that collects multi-dimensional telemetry, an analysis engine (often reinforcement learning) that decides when to scale, and an execution layer that adds VMs, changes replica counts or edits limits. She notes these systems can reach around 95% prediction accuracy in controlled tests and drop as low as 72% when real traffic does something unexpected.

She also separates vertical scaling (bigger instances, GPU partitioning, memory ballooning, limited by hardware and by applications that dislike resources shifting under them) from horizontal scaling (more instances, limited by coordination overhead and diminishing throughput gains).

## Kubernetes wins, and you pay for it

Kubernetes is her default orchestrator for AI, outperforming alternatives such as Docker Swarm at large scale, but with real operational complexity and a training burden. The virtualisation section covers hardware-assisted CPU virtualisation, second-level address translation and NUMA awareness, SR-IOV for I/O, and GPU sharing via partitioning and time-slicing, with the warning that I/O-heavy jobs still feel the overhead.

## Cost and security close the loop

On cost she lists VM allocation policies, workload placement across zones and regions, right-sizing and commitment discounts, and notes that typical cloud utilisation of 30 to 45% can rise to 65 to 75% with better policies, while admitting those figures assume idealised flexibility. On security: isolation, least-privilege authorisation for whatever makes allocation decisions, continuous validation, and side-channel protection when tenants share GPUs.

The closing look ahead is worth the wait: automated workload fingerprinting, energy-aware scheduling, and carbon-aware computing that runs jobs when the grid is greenest.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers starting to host GPU workloads, and anyone who needs a vocabulary map before reading the scheduling papers. If you already run Kueue or Volcano in anger, you'll know most of it, but the accuracy caveats are a good sanity check against vendor slides.

Title: AI for customer experience starts with one view of the customer
Description: Upwork's Mohan Krishna Mannava lays out a data-driven CX framework at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, from integrated data to AI and measured outcomes.
Body:
Most companies already have the data to personalise customer experience; it just lives in six systems that have never met. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Mohan Krishna Mannava, Customer Analytics and Insights Leader at Upwork with over 12 years in data and AI, presented a framework for turning that scattered data into better customer experience (CX): integrate first, extract insights, add AI, then measure and repeat.

It is a strategy talk aimed at analytics leaders and the people who fund them. There is no code and no single company case study, but the framework is clear and the order of operations is the point.

## The bottleneck is silos, not models

Mannava's diagnosis is that the last decade's data explosion did not translate into better experiences. The data is fragmented across siloed systems, so no one has a single view of a customer. Strategies stay reactive instead of anticipating needs. Personalisation suffers, and so does satisfaction. Some companies also hesitate to adopt new technology at all, which he warns costs them later.

The root issue, in his framing, is the silos. Poor personalisation is the symptom.

## Integrate at the customer grain

The first step is data integration, and he is specific about what goes in: behavioural data from tools like Adobe Analytics or Google Analytics (which features and buttons customers use), feedback and sentiment from reviews, support interactions and social mentions, profile data such as demographics, preferences and segment, contextual data like location and device, and above all transaction data.

The key detail is that everything gets joined at the customer level. For any customer you should be able to answer how many transactions they made in the last 30 or 60 days, what they buy most often and what they do in the app. That 360-degree view is the foundation every later step stands on.

## Insights only count once someone acts on them

Step two is a four-stage path from raw data to action: refine the data (clean and structure it), analyse it for patterns, turn patterns into business-relevant insights, then act on them. Mannava stresses the last stage. Generating insights is the easy part; acting on them is where CSAT and NPS actually move.

## Where AI fits in the loop

Only then does AI come in. His examples are familiar but well placed: chatbots and virtual assistants that resolve issues before they reach a contact centre, personalised recommendations built on past behaviour and transactions, proactive service alerts that predict problems before customers hit them, and NLP sentiment analysis that routes unhappy customers to the right team early.

He also describes three broader patterns: predictive experiences that anticipate needs, omnichannel journey orchestration that keeps personalisation consistent across every touchpoint, and augmented human service, where support agents get customer context in front of them during the conversation. Automation of repetitive service tasks frees agents for complex problems and more empathetic support.

The whole thing is a loop. Measure outcomes, find where you still miss customer expectations, and refine.

## The organisational part is half the work

The closing section is about readiness. Mannava lists a cultural shift towards a customer-centric, data-driven mindset, training employees on the new AI tools, strong data governance covering quality and privacy, and KPIs that prove the transformation worked: CSAT, NPS and effort score, alongside revenue metrics before and after. It needs executive sponsorship, cross-functional teams from IT, marketing, support and product, and frontline staff who can see the insights, since they are the ones talking to customers.

## Who should watch

Analytics and CX leaders planning an AI programme, and data engineers who need to explain to stakeholders why integration comes before the chatbot. Practitioners looking for model architectures will find this too high-level.

Title: High availability is not disaster recovery for cloud SAP systems
Description: Naveen Karuturi of Pacific Gas and Electric explains at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 how to layer HA and DR for cloud SAP, with HANA, Oracle and SQL Server options.
Body:
Many SAP teams have high availability and assume they are covered; Naveen Karuturi's point is that a regional outage does not care. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Karuturi, Senior SAP Basis Administrator at Pacific Gas and Electric Company, explained why high availability (HA) and disaster recovery (DR) solve different problems, and walked layer by layer through building both for SAP in the cloud.

## Downtime is a supply chain problem within hours

Karuturi sets the stakes with cited figures. SAP underpins ERP at about 84% of Fortune 500 companies. A minute of core SAP downtime costs an average of $8,750, and incidents without proper HA can stretch past four hours and $2.2 million. The operational impact arrives fast: 87% of organisations see significant supply chain disruption within eight hours of SAP downtime, and 64% see customer-facing impact within the first two.

## Same region versus another region

The distinction is the core of the talk:

- **High availability** keeps the system running through component failures inside the primary environment, using redundancy and automated failover across availability zones in one region. He puts it at 15 to 22% on top of base infrastructure cost. A failed server or storage device should go unnoticed by users.
- **Disaster recovery** covers events that take out a whole environment, like a data-centre outage or a hurricane, by recovering in a geographically separate region. Depending on recovery objectives, it adds 28 to 47% to total cost.

Then the uncomfortable statistic: 87% of production SAP environments have some basic HA, but only 53% have fully documented and tested DR plans, even though 76% call SAP business critical. Organisations running both report 35% fewer operational disruptions than those with partial setups.

## HA is built in three layers

**Infrastructure**: compute spread across availability zones, redundant network paths and load balancers, and replicated cloud storage.

**Database**: the replication option depends on your platform. SAP HANA System Replication keeps a real-time standby and recovers in two to five minutes; Karuturi says about 84% of HANA deployments use it. Oracle Data Guard gives synchronous or near-synchronous replication with three-to-seven-minute recovery. SQL Server Always On availability groups average around four minutes.

**Application**: load-balanced SAP application servers that keep about 95% of normal throughput when one fails, clustering for the ABAP and Java central services (ASCS and SCS) with recovery around 2.5 minutes, enqueue replication so in-flight locks survive an enqueue server failure, and automated failure detection that starts recovery within 12 to 30 seconds.

## DR is backups, replication and orchestration

DR stacks three more pieces: regular backups, cross-region replication and automated recovery orchestration that removes manual steps under pressure. Done properly, he says mature DR cuts recovery time by 72%, from an average of 18.7 hours to 5.2.

On providers, he compares AWS (multi-AZ deployments, EBS snapshots and Elastic Disaster Recovery, with RPOs of one to five minutes), Azure (availability zones, Site Recovery and Azure Backup, with RPOs of five to fifteen minutes) and GCP (regional persistent disks and cross-region backup copies). Every cloud has the building blocks; the job is picking the right ones for your SAP estate.

## Practise until it is boring

His implementation advice: start from a business impact analysis (organisations typically spend 8 to 15% of SAP infrastructure budget on resilience), protect every layer, automate wherever possible, and test regularly. Organisations running quarterly recovery drills nearly double their success rate in real events compared with annual testers. Define RTO and RPO explicitly; he cites teams that do recovering 2.6 times faster, from 12.3 hours to 4.7.

The best line is about muscle memory: when a real crisis hits, practice is what makes the system resilient.

## Who should watch

SAP Basis administrators, infrastructure architects moving SAP to the cloud, and anyone whose DR plan has not been tested since it was written. It is a structured overview rather than a hands-on runbook.

Title: Intelligent platforms start with governance, not models
Description: Walmart's Baba Prasad Pendyala at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on turning cloud infrastructure into ML-driven platforms that predict and self-heal.
Body:
Cloud gave us elastic infrastructure; machine learning is supposed to make it think. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Baba Prasad Pendyala, Staff Technical Program Manager for infrastructure engineering and CI/CD at Walmart, argued that the next step after migration is a platform that predicts, optimises and heals itself, and that the work that makes or breaks it is governance and organisational readiness rather than the model.

This is a strategy talk aimed at the people who fund and run platform teams. There's no code on screen. What you get is a map of the journey and a checklist of where these programmes tend to stall.

## Three eras of infrastructure

Pendyala frames the story in three steps. Traditional infrastructure meant manual provisioning, fixed capacity and reactive management. Cloud migration brought elasticity and automation. The third step is ML integration: systems that forecast load, tune themselves and recover without a human in the loop. He lingers on self-healing because, in his view, it's what enterprise buyers ask for now.

That shift, he says, needs a different kind of architect, one who can align ML with business goals, build models that suit cloud environments and still knows the infrastructure underneath. Infrastructure mastery is the foundation in his list, not an afterthought.

## The toolbox is ordinary on purpose

The frameworks he names are the familiar ones: TensorFlow scaling training across distributed infrastructure, Kubeflow orchestrating ML workflows on Kubernetes, MLOps platforms covering the lifecycle from development to monitoring, and managed cloud ML APIs for vision, language and prediction. The point isn't novelty. It's that these pieces already exist, so the hard part has moved elsewhere.

## Governance comes before scale

"Innovation without governance invites chaos" is the line that carries the middle of the talk. His governance loop has four parts: define architectural standards for ML across the enterprise, enforce compliance with security, regulatory and ethical-AI requirements, measure outcomes against business objectives, and feed those outcomes back into the standards.

He then maps learning styles to infrastructure jobs. Supervised learning handles anomaly detection and capacity forecasting from labelled history. Unsupervised learning finds clusters and correlations in telemetry nobody thought to label. Reinforcement learning drives auto-scaling, network tuning and adaptive security response, the self-healing part. His summary: humans guide machines, machines learn from operations.

## A healthcare case and the numbers behind it

The concrete example is a healthcare provider with a 30% readmission rate and 65% diagnostic accuracy. Cloud ML models wired into the existing EHR systems analysed vitals, labs, medication data and social determinants of health to flag deterioration risk early. Pendyala reports readmissions down 47%, accuracy up to 92% and savings above $3 million a year. He also cites cross-enterprise figures such as 31% lower cloud costs and 67% faster issue resolution. The talk doesn't detail the methodology behind them, so treat them as the speaker's benchmarks rather than a study.

## Where it breaks

The most useful slide for practitioners is the list of failure modes: data quality (garbage in, garbage out), legacy integration friction, scarce ML talent and cultural inertia. His remedies are unglamorous: data governance and preprocessing, APIs and microservices in front of legacy systems, upskilling plus targeted hiring, and executive champions. The roadmap that follows is equally plain: assess readiness, pick high-value use cases, start with small pilots, document what worked, then scale the patterns.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and platform leads building the business case for ML in operations, especially in regulated industries. If you want Kubeflow manifests or a self-healing controller design, this one stays at the whiteboard level; pair it with something hands-on.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Indika Wimalasuriya on [how AIOps drives operational resilience on AWS](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Indika_Wimalasuriya_aiops_resilience_aws), a more operational take on the same promise.
- Yogesh Pugazhendhi and Duraisamy Rajamani on [self-healing real-time streaming pipelines with Go and AI](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Yogesh_Pugazhendhi_Duraisamy_Rajamani_building_self_healing).
- Aishwarya Pai on [MLOps in healthcare](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Aishwarya_Pai_mlops_healthcare_scaling), for the deployment side of clinical models.

Title: Specialist AI agents for B2B integration, with an orchestrator on top
Description: Balaprabunath Coimbatore Ramalingam of Pfizer at Conf42 SRE 2025 proposes agentic AI for EAI and EDI integration, with specialist agents and self-healing.
Body:
Every enterprise has an integration team that finds out about a broken partner feed when finance calls. Balaprabunath Coimbatore Ramalingam, Lead Analyst at Pfizer, used his Conf42 SRE 2025 talk to propose an agentic AI framework for enterprise application integration (EAI) and EDI: a set of narrowly scoped AI agents, coordinated by an orchestrator, that validate, translate, monitor and repair the flows between trading partners and internal systems such as ERP and CRM.

It is an architecture proposal mapped onto SRE principles, not a walkthrough of a specific product.

## Three pressures on integration teams

He frames the problem with three challenges. Scale: new applications and models arrive constantly, and each one is a new integration point. Complexity: large enterprises run hundreds or thousands of interconnected, heterogeneous applications. Time sensitivity: when a business-critical interface fails, the cost is immediate, so integration fixes are always urgent.

## One agent, one job

The framework has four parts: specialist agents, collaborative intelligence, self-healing and continuous optimisation. The specialists are deliberately narrow so their responsibilities do not overlap:

- **Validation agent**: data integrity and schema compliance for formats such as IDoc, EDIFACT or HIPAA transactions.
- **Translation agent**: converts between formats.
- **Monitoring and detection agent**: spots anomalies and failures, including an agent hallucinating.
- **Orchestration agent**: builds the workflow in which agents collaborate.
- **Connector agent**: sets up connections to a new system, including generating firewall change requests.
- **Security agent**: data encryption and user security, in the role IAM plays in the cloud.

## Agents ride on top of the business flow

The architecture diagram is the clearest part. The existing business flow stays: external partners (customers, suppliers, banks, government agencies) send data through B2B software, which transforms it into what ERP and CRM systems expect, and acknowledgements, invoices and payments flow back. On top sits the agent flow: a customer service agent takes requests in natural language, splits them into tasks and hands them to an AI orchestrator, which refines them and dispatches specialist agents. A governance layer covers security, data and AI policy, and transaction data lands in a data lake that feeds training for the agents.

## Self-healing, then write it down

The self-healing loop is detect, find the root cause, generate a remediation checklist, run it automatically, and log the whole episode in a knowledge base so the next agent does not repeat the failure. He ties this to SRE pillars: automation, SLOs, incident management, observability, capacity planning and shared responsibility, with a push for business-aligned SLOs that reflect business impact rather than purely technical metrics.

On adoption barriers he is realistic. Data privacy is the first worry, which he addresses with federated learning and encryption. Many legacy systems have no API at all. His answer to both is to avoid a big-bang rollout: start with one agent, expose only non-sensitive data, prove value, then expand. He closes with evaluation figures, including a 92% reduction in MTTR, presented without methodology.

## Who should watch

Integration and EDI engineers wondering where agents could fit in their stack, and SREs supporting B2B platforms. Expect diagrams and a proposed design, not code or a live system.

Title: The SRE job in hybrid quantum-classical neural networks is the handoff
Description: Karthikeyan Rajamani, Lead SRE at Thomson Reuters, explains hybrid quantum-classical neural networks at Conf42 SRE 2025 and what SREs would need to run them.
Body:
How do you put a dashboard on a qubit? Karthikeyan Rajamani, Lead SRE at Thomson Reuters, ends his Conf42 SRE 2025 talk on that kind of question. The talk explains hybrid quantum-classical neural networks (HQCNNs), models that hand part of the work to quantum circuits and the rest to classical hardware, and then asks what reliability engineering looks like when half your system obeys quantum mechanics.

Set expectations: about two thirds of the talk is a quantum and HQCNN primer, and the SRE section comes at the end. It is a forward-looking talk about systems that today run mostly in labs, which Rajamani says plainly.

## Why mix quantum and classical at all

Quantum computing brings superposition (a qubit can be zero, one or both until observed), entanglement (one qubit's state tied to another's at any distance) and the ability to model states in Hilbert spaces. Classical computing brings the mature GPU stack behind today's neural networks. The hybrid pattern: pose the problem classically, encode it into quantum states, compute, then return and validate the result classically. Rajamani opens by pointing to recent quantum chips from Google (Willow) and Amazon as the reason this is getting practical attention.

## Parameterised circuits are the trainable part

The building block is the parameterised quantum circuit: quantum gates with tunable parameters. A feature map encodes classical features into quantum states, for example as amplitude or phase. The circuit runs a forward pass, results go back to the classical side for backpropagation, and gradient descent adjusts the circuit parameters in a quantum-classical feedback loop. Training steps he lists are circuit initialisation, parameter optimisation, error mitigation, and evaluation against a known classical benchmark.

Applications he highlights include medical imaging diagnostics, drug discovery, personalised medicine combining clinical, environmental and genomic data, financial modelling, and supply chain optimisation.

## The problems are physical, not just software

The challenges section is candid. Qubits suffer decoherence and stay unstable; error mitigation is still work in progress; scaling is hard. Barren plateaus, where gradients vanish as circuits get deeper, are a known training problem for parameterised circuits. And the classical-quantum interface creates data transfer bottlenecks that hybrid algorithms must keep to a minimum.

## What an SRE would own

The last section is the reason it was at an SRE conference. Rajamani's list of reliability concerns:

- **Handoffs** between classical and quantum are a point of failure, so interfaces must not lose or distort data.
- **Observability** of quantum state, quantum noise, decoherence and latency, plus model drift, has no ready-made tooling.
- **Error mitigation** when encoding or handoff goes wrong.
- **Deployment and orchestration** of new models into quantum environments, which may need techniques nobody has written yet.
- **Repeatability under load**: consistent results even when heavily loaded, and scaling quickly on demand.

He closes with references from IBM on parameterised circuits and reliability, and a University of Texas at Austin result on using classical computers to test whether quantum-generated numbers are truly random.

## Who should watch

SREs and ML engineers who want a readable introduction to HQCNNs and a first list of operational questions. If you want production war stories, there are none yet; this is a map of the territory ahead.

Title: Adding AI to SRE practice is an evolution, so start small and scale
Description: Umamaheswarareddy Chintam of Calance at Conf42 SRE 2025 on AI for observability, anomaly detection, chaos testing and postmortems in cloud-native platforms.
Body:
Static thresholds tell you a disk is 90% full; they do not tell you it will be full on Thursday. Umamaheswarareddy Chintam, a solutions architect at Calance, built his Conf42 SRE 2025 talk around that gap: how AI moves SRE practice from reactive, rule-based alerting towards predictive and automated operations on cloud-native platforms, and why the rollout should be "evolution, not a revolution."

## From static rules to learned baselines

He contrasts the two worlds. Traditional SRE means manual incident workflows, monitoring that only reflects current status, static rule-based alerts and after-the-fact historical analysis. The AI-assisted version adds automation and self-healing, forecasting of likely issues, intelligent alerting with dynamic priorities, and pattern recognition. He quotes improvements of 25% in MTTR and around 30% in service availability, figures from the talk's abstract and slides rather than a measured case of his own.

## A pyramid for observability

His model for AI-driven observability is a pyramid, built bottom up: comprehensive telemetry that keeps the signal-to-noise ratio high, machine learning that sets automated baselines with dynamic thresholds that adapt to seasonality and growth, pattern recognition that finds non-obvious links between seemingly unrelated services, and at the top context-aware dashboards that highlight the metrics that matter. Anomaly detection follows the same loop: learn normal operation, monitor continuously, detect deviations, refine the model from feedback to cut false positives.

## Let AI pick the chaos experiments

The section that stands out applies AI to chaos engineering. Algorithms analyse service dependencies to find critical failure points and design experiments with the most learning value. Experiments run in low-traffic windows with safety mechanisms against cascading impact. Real-time analysis compares actual resilience against what the models predicted, and discovered weaknesses trigger remediation workflows.

He pairs it with NLP for postmortems: transcribing and organising incident communication, matching incidents to earlier ones, extracting causal relationships from technical discussion for root cause analysis, and updating runbooks and documentation automatically.

## A payments case and a rollout plan

The case study is a financial services payment platform where, in his figures, downtime cost around $150K per hour, MTTR dropped from 45 to 12 minutes after predictive models were added, and savings came to $3.2 million. He then covers capacity planning as a loop: historical analysis, demand prediction, scenario modelling, automated provisioning.

The adoption plan is the part to keep: assess current SRE maturity and find gaps, start with small experiments, build cross-functional skills, then scale across the organisation. Measure the impact as you go.

## Integration is part of reliability

The final section draws on his integration background: APIs between front ends and back ends, iPaaS options such as MuleSoft and Azure Logic Apps, SAP Integration Suite, and API management as an SRE concern for uptime and scale. AI helps here too, for example by correlating latency across microservices to find the slow one.

## Who should watch

SRE leads drafting an AI roadmap who want a broad catalogue of use cases and a staged adoption plan. It is a survey across many topics rather than a deep build on one, with no demos.

Title: Augment the legacy retail system instead of ripping it out
Description: Rajkumar Chindanuru of Tailored Brands presents at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 a framework for layering AI onto legacy retail systems instead of replacing them.
Body:
The 15-year-old merchandising system that everyone wants to replace is also the only place that knows how the business actually works. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Rajkumar Chindanuru, Senior Software Engineer at Tailored Brands with around 20 years of legacy modernisation work behind him, argued for keeping that system and wrapping AI capabilities around it, and showed a grocery chain case study where that beat the rip-and-replace estimate by a wide margin.

## Why the usual playbooks disappoint

Chindanuru starts with the numbers that make retail CIOs wince. Citing research and his own survey, he says around 70% of major retailers still run on systems more than 20 years old, 70 to 80% of IT budgets go to maintaining them, and only 20 to 25% of the data they hold feeds decisions.

He then names three failure modes of conventional modernisation. Rip-and-replace carries high risk because mission-critical business logic can get lost in translation. Lift-and-shift produces migration without transformation, a legacy system on newer hardware. And phased rewrites without a clear vision drift into incremental improvements that never add up to an integrated picture.

## Four layers on top of the old core

His Cognitive Retail Transformation framework adds four layers to the existing system rather than rebuilding it:

1. **Cognitive layer integration**: pull data out of the legacy system through APIs and streams so it can be processed at all.
2. **Predictive analytics**: run machine learning on that data for forecasting and decision support.
3. **Hyper-personalisation**: use the results to tailor how the business reaches and converts customers.
4. **Intelligent process automation**: automate the processes the new insights show can be refined, without re-engineering the core.

The rollout runs in phases: a cognitive foundation (data pipelines and core infrastructure), intelligent augmentation (wiring predictions into operational systems), and autonomous optimisation (closed-loop systems that tune themselves). The abstract adds a fourth phase, continuous learning, and the talk returns to that idea when describing how predictive accuracy improves over time.

## The grocery chain numbers

The case study is a regional grocery chain with a 15-year-old merchandising management system and the usual problems: out-of-stocks, overstock and promotions of uncertain value. Chindanuru reports an implementation cost of about $3.2 million, roughly 0.4% of the retailer's annual revenue, against an estimated $12 to 15 million for a conventional replacement. First-year benefits came to about $5.8 million, a 181% return on investment, with positive ROI inside eight months. He breaks that down into about $3.5 million from inventory (lower carrying costs, less shrinkage, better availability), $1.2 million from marketing and promotion efficiency, and $1.1 million from operational efficiency.

Whatever you think of the exact figures, the comparison is the argument: same business outcome, a fraction of the risk, and the institutional knowledge in the old system survives.

## The risks he does not skip

Chindanuru is clear that augmentation brings its own problems. Poor data quality produces poor predictions. Integrating AI platforms with legacy systems adds complexity. Skills are scarce in a fast-moving field. Change management is needed because people's workflows change. And technical debt accumulates when the AI layer is added without architectural discipline. His mitigations follow directly: clear architecture standards, data governance with master data management, a talent strategy (build or hire), and change management as a first-class workstream.

## Who should watch

Enterprise architects and engineering managers in retail or any industry sitting on a decades-old system of record. It is a strategy talk with a case study, not a code walkthrough, and it pairs well with Chindanuru's own talk on legacy modernisation strategies at Conf42 Golang 2025.

Title: Where AI earns its keep inside SAP and ERP systems
Description: SAP project manager Venkata Kalyan Chakravarthy Mandavilli of ITEK Software tours AI use in SAP and ERP at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, from invoices to Joule.
Body:
ERP systems run the invoices, orders and compliance checks that everything else depends on, which makes them the place where small automation wins add up fastest. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Venkata Kalyan Chakravarthy Mandavilli, SAP Project Manager at ITEK Software with 21 years of SAP work going back to R/3, gave a business-level tour of where AI is changing SAP and ERP: repetitive task automation, forecasting, decision support, natural language interfaces and generative AI for reports and code.

Honest scope first: this is an overview for people deciding where to invest, not an implementation guide. Most figures are cited from industry research, and there are no demos.

## Start with the boring, repetitive work

The first and most convincing section is automation of repetitive tasks:

- **Invoice processing**: AI matching instead of manual keying, with fewer errors and shorter cycle times, and systems that learn from corrections.
- **Order management**: faster order processing and better accuracy, which saves money on returns, corrections and customer service follow-ups.
- **Compliance monitoring**: AI-based monitoring catches more reportable incidents than rule-based systems and cuts audit preparation time.

The abstract adds the SAP-specific example: SAP Intelligent Robotic Process Automation (iRPA) reducing manual processing times by up to 30% in multinational enterprises. Mandavilli also cites research that companies implementing AI-enhanced SAP solutions saw an average 32% reduction in operational cost in the first year, with up to 40% of manual workload automated.

## Forecasting is where the money hides

The predictive analytics section covers demand forecasting that beats traditional time-series methods, transaction monitoring that catches fraudulent activity before payment execution, and supply chain models that spot bottlenecks and supplier risks before they hit operations. The abstract credits AI models with up to 40% better demand forecasting accuracy, which flows straight into lower excess stock.

From his current project, Mandavilli mentions working with Levi's distribution centres, where order volumes are large enough that better accuracy across the network matters.

## Natural language lowers the bar to use ERP

The user experience section is where the change is easiest to see. Conversational interfaces such as SAP Joule and Copilot let users get through complex workflows without memorising menu paths. Mandavilli's point from implementation projects: many client users have no SAP background, and natural language reduces the knowledge barrier that has historically limited ERP adoption. Context-aware assistants add proactive suggestions in complex areas like financial consolidation.

## Generative AI writes the reports and some of the code

Generative AI shows up in three ways: automated creation of business reports with consistent formatting, code generation for SAP development that follows standard architectural patterns, and chatbots that resolve most user inquiries without a human and keep context across a conversation. He adds AI-assisted analytics such as summarisation and natural-language filtering, and claims AI-enhanced analytics let organisations respond about 40% faster to changing business conditions than traditional BI reports.

## A timeline for what comes next

He closes with expected horizons: predictive maintenance (2025 to 2027), self-optimising supply chains (2025 to 2027), autonomous operations (2026 to 2028) and cross-system intelligence (2026 to 2029). Treat those as one practitioner's forecast rather than a roadmap.

## Who should watch

SAP project managers, ERP owners and business stakeholders who need a map of where AI fits before talking to vendors. Developers wanting technical depth should look elsewhere, starting with Mandavilli's more technical SAP AI talk at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025.

Title: Start with a modular monolith, extract microservices on purpose
Description: Freeport's Asif Mehboob weighs monoliths against microservices on latency, failure modes, cost and team size at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.
Body:
The architecture you pick on day one is the one you will still be explaining in year five, because switching later usually means a rebuild. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Asif Mehboob, Senior Manager of Software and Business Intelligence Engineering at Freeport, laid out the trade-offs between monoliths and microservices and landed on a pragmatic default: a modular monolith first, with services extracted where the business actually needs them.

Mehboob opens by admitting this decision has kept him up at night more than once, which is the most relatable sentence in any architecture talk.

## Two shapes, plainly defined

A monolith is one codebase, deployed as one unit, with tightly coupled components sharing memory and a database, calling each other through direct function calls on a single technology stack. Microservices split the application into small independent services, each owning one business capability and its own database, talking through well-defined APIs, deployable and scalable on their own, and free to use different languages. He sums microservices up as service-oriented architecture done right.

## Network calls are the bill you pay for independence

The performance section puts numbers on what everyone hand-waves. An internal function call in a monolith takes around a millisecond. An API call between microservices takes 50 to 100 milliseconds, and service-to-service communication adds five to ten times the processing overhead because of serialisation and network cost. If a user request fans out across several services, those numbers stack. Designing microservices without budgeting for that latency is how teams end up with a slower system that is also harder to debug.

## Failures stay local, if you design for it

The other side of the ledger is resilience. In a monolith, one critical bug can take the whole application down, because it is one unit. In a microservices system, failures can stay isolated and the system can degrade gracefully, using patterns such as circuit breakers and fallbacks. The same logic applies to scaling: a monolith scales as a single heavy block even when one component is the bottleneck, while microservices scale the hot path only.

## Cost depends on which year you are looking at

Mehboob compares relative costs category by category. Microservices cost more for initial development, infrastructure and team onboarding. They cost less for maintenance and much less for scaling. Updates follow the same pattern: changing a monolith means modifying the shared codebase, retesting the whole application and redeploying everything, while a microservice can be tested against its own integration points and shipped alone. Monoliths are faster to deliver at the start; microservices sustain feature delivery later, at the price of more coordination and distributed systems knowledge.

## Four questions decide it

His decision framework is short enough to put on a whiteboard:

1. **Complexity**: simple applications suit a monolith; complex domains with distinct bounded contexts suit microservices.
2. **Scale**: high-volume or variable workloads benefit from targeted scaling.
3. **Team structure**: large, distributed teams work better with service ownership boundaries.
4. **Growth trajectory**: map the next three to five years, not the next sprint.

Monoliths fit small applications, early-stage startups that need to validate the idea before perfecting the infrastructure, and teams with tight budgets. Microservices fit large enterprises with many teams, high-traffic apps and organisations that need independent releases. The Netflix example illustrates the path: a monolithic Java application, a database corruption that caused a multi-day outage, and a gradual decomposition into more than 700 microservices.

His conclusion is the useful one. Be pragmatic rather than dogmatic, start with a modular monolith, and extract services strategically instead of following the fashion of the day.

## Who should watch

Tech leads and architects about to start a new system, and teams arguing about whether to split an existing one. It is an overview without code, and a good shared reference before an architecture review.

Title: An eight-hour ETL job cut to 45 minutes with Azure Data Factory
Description: Lokeshkumar Madabathula of Webilent Technology explains Azure Data Factory components, reusable pipelines, triggers and retries at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.
Body:
An ETL job that runs for eight hours is a job that fails at hour seven. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Lokeshkumar Madabathula, Lead Data Scientist and Data Engineer at Webilent Technology, gave a short introduction to Azure Data Factory (ADF) and how its reusable pipelines, event triggers and retry handling cut processing time and maintenance work, including a financial services case where a legacy pipeline dropped from eight hours to 45 minutes.

This is a brief talk, about seven minutes, and an introduction rather than an advanced tuning session. If you have never opened ADF, it is a quick way to learn its vocabulary.

## The problem is many sources that do not talk to each other

Madabathula's starting point is familiar to anyone who runs data pipelines: data arrives from streaming systems, files, relational and NoSQL databases and APIs, and none of those systems know about each other. Stitching them together by hand delays processing, slows decisions and drives up maintenance cost. ADF is Azure's cloud data integration service for connecting those sources and loading them into the destination you choose.

## Four building blocks

The talk explains ADF's core components clearly:

- **Linked services**: the connections, for example from ADF to Salesforce on one side and your data lake on the other.
- **Datasets**: the data structures you read and write, the tables, files and columns the target needs.
- **Activities**: the configurable steps where transformations and business rules live.
- **Pipelines**: the end-to-end orchestration that sequences linked services, datasets and activities into one solution.

If you know Airflow, the mental mapping is roughly connections, assets, tasks and DAGs.

## Where the maintenance savings come from

Madabathula highlights three features that reduce hand work:

1. **Reusable pipeline templates**: build a pipeline once for sales data and reuse it, with small tweaks, for HR or CRM data.
2. **Event-triggered execution**: when source data is added or updated, the pipeline runs on its own, so nobody logs in to rerun it.
3. **Error handling**: retries that resume from a checkpoint instead of starting over, with alerts through email, messages or Teams channels.

He quotes improvements of 78% faster processing, 63% cost reduction, 42% better resource efficiency and up to 90% automation. The case study is the concrete one: the financial services ETL pipeline that took eight hours on legacy tools ran in 45 minutes on ADF with the same transformations and business logic, a 91% improvement, and maintenance cost fell by 70%.

## Best practices, briefly

His checklist is short: organise pipelines by domain (sales, HR, CRM), commit code to Git regularly, use integration runtimes appropriately, and turn on Azure Monitor so failures get a prompt response. His advice to teams is to look at existing pipelines first, find out what makes them slow and expensive, and migrate those.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and analysts evaluating ADF or inheriting an estate of hand-built ETL scripts on Azure. Experienced ADF users will not find new techniques here, and the talk does not cover machine learning workloads, but it is a fast orientation for newcomers.

Title: Automate the tester's hardest jobs, not every test case
Description: Capgemini test architect Sujeeth Manchikanti argues at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 for small, reusable test utilities over chasing full automation coverage.
Body:
Test automation suites have a habit of becoming white elephants: expensive to build, expensive to feed, and not much use day to day. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Sujeeth Manchikanti, Test Architect at Capgemini, proposed a different scope: stop trying to automate the whole test catalogue and build small, independent utilities that take the heaviest manual work off testers.

## Why automation keeps disappointing

Manchikanti traces automation from the simple record-and-replay tools of the early 2000s, through the Page Object Model and open-source frameworks of the 2010s, to today's self-healing scripts and visual recognition. The tools improved; the success rates, he argues, did not move much.

His figures on the common pitfalls are blunt. Teams attempting to automate more than 60% of test cases in the first year see a 78% failure rate. Teams managing over a thousand test cases spend four to five hours a week on maintenance. And 67% of automation projects fail because of poor test case selection. On the ground, he says, organisations expecting a full first-run pass rate see 62%, coverage targets of 80% land at 54%, and suites that are not maintained decay quickly.

## Counting the cost of the elephant

The white elephant metaphor carries the cost section. A suite is not done when it is built; it has to be fed every day. Manchikanti points to around 2.5 full-time engineers spent on maintenance in a typical project, plus tool licences, infrastructure, failed-run triage and migrations every time the technology shifts. The abstract puts annual automation infrastructure spend at $100,000 to $300,000 for many enterprises. His sharpest number: the cost per test case execution rising from $2 to $3 at the start to $8 to $10 within two years.

## Utilities with one entry and one exit

The proposal is what he calls the utility model. Each utility solves one painful testing job and has a clear entry and exit point. His example: validating a dataset of a million records might take a manual tester five or six days with sampling. A utility written in whatever technology suits the job, Python for instance, validates the whole set and returns the result in a standard format.

Utilities then plug into a keyword-driven enterprise framework with shared logging, so one utility's output can be the next one's input. That is the trick that keeps them small without making them isolated scripts nobody can chain.

Two strategic choices come with it. He focuses on API-level testing, since that is where most integration failures occur, and keeps separate tools for UI testing. And he deliberately reduces scope: instead of planning 100% automation and achieving a quarter of it, he defines a narrower target and automates all of that.

## What the narrower scope bought

Manchikanti reports an 85% reduction in maintenance cost, faster execution because database, API and UI layers are tested separately, sanity checks of an application in minutes, and utilities reused across teams. Independent utilities in his projects returned around 300% ROI within the first few months. Because the strategy is independent of the tool, migrating between tools later is less painful; he notes that assistants like GitHub Copilot make porting a utility to a new stack easier.

His implementation steps are simple: set clear objectives on what to automate, get stakeholder buy-in, implement gradually, define KPIs and track ROI, and keep watching execution results.

## Who should watch

QA leads and test architects whose automation suite is growing faster than its value, and engineering managers being asked to fund another framework rewrite. There is little machine learning in it despite the conference; it is a strategy talk about where automation effort pays.

Title: Block misconfigured cloud resources at the provider with native policy
Description: Santosh Bompally of Humana demos Azure Policy and GCP org policies blocking bad deployments at Conf42 SRE 2025, as one pillar of cloud security posture.
Body:
Scanning Terraform in CI catches the misconfigurations that go through CI. Santosh Bompally's talk at Conf42 SRE 2025 is about the rest: the storage account someone clicks together in the portal at 5pm on a Friday. Bompally, Cloud Security Engineering Team Lead at Humana, shows how cloud-native policy engines (Azure Policy, GCP organization policies, AWS service control policies) deny bad resources at the provider, whatever path they arrived by, and where that fits in a full cloud security posture management setup.

## Four pillars, one gap

He structures CSPM as four layers:

1. **Infrastructure as code scanning**: policies in the pipeline and on pull requests, so misconfigurations are caught before merge. He covered this in an earlier session using an OPA agent to author IaC policies.
2. **Cloud-native validation**: provider-level policies that check every deployment, from IaC or the console. This is the focus of the talk.
3. **Runtime remediation**: event-driven functions that fix what slipped past the first two.
4. **Compliance reporting**: tying it all together so you can see the attack surface and prove compliance.

The argument for layer 2 is simple: shifting left is cheaper, but it only covers changes that go through your pipeline.

## The demo: TLS 1.0 gets through, then it does not

The Azure demo is worth watching because it shows the friction honestly. Bompally creates a storage account with minimum TLS 1.0 and networking open to all networks. Azure accepts it and only recommends TLS 1.2. He then assigns the built-in minimum TLS policy, first finds it is still in audit mode (it records one non-compliant resource but blocks nothing), switches the effect to deny, adds a custom message for developers, and tries again. This time validation fails until he picks TLS 1.2. Audit versus deny is the difference between a dashboard and a guardrail, and the demo makes that concrete.

He also shows compliance packs in Azure Policy: assign an initiative for a standard such as FedRAMP, ISO or NIST and every mapped policy applies at that scope.

On GCP, he opens organization policies under IAM, shows constraints such as public access prevention for storage, and demonstrates a custom machine type constraint: an oversized VM is rejected with a compliance violation, a default-sized one deploys. AWS gets a mention via service control policies.

## Remediation has a price tag

For runtime remediation, he asks a question teams often skip: what MTTR do you actually need for a misconfiguration, a day or ten minutes? Real-time event processing and auto-fix functions cost money, and the bill grows with event volume, so the target should be a deliberate trade between cost and risk. He adds anomaly detection and AI-driven insights for spotting permission creep in machine identities and for prioritising vulnerabilities by exposure.

## Exceptions need scopes and paperwork

The closing section is on exception management: when the business accepts a risk, make the exception temporary, risk-assessed, documented and approved, and watch for scope creep from one resource to several.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers running Azure or GCP who rely on pipeline scanning alone. The live demos make this more useful than a slide talk; you will see exact menus and the audit-versus-deny trap.

Title: Clean up your alerts first, then let SLOs decide what wakes you
Description: Mandi Walls of PagerDuty at Conf42 SRE 2025 on cutting alert fatigue. Delete junk alerts, route the rest, and page on error budget, not every 500.
Body:
One 500 error out of 10,000 requests should not wake anyone at 3am. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Mandi Walls, DevOps advocate at PagerDuty, makes the case that alert fatigue is solved in two passes: first a ruthless cleanup of alerts that were never worth a page, then SLOs and error budgets to decide when the remaining signals become urgent. Apart from a pointer to PagerDuty's community forum and one product setting, the talk is vendor-neutral.

## What fatigue costs

Walls defines alerts narrowly: real-time notifications that reach a human and should need action now. Too many of them and you get the familiar list: slower response, missed alerts (the ninth one that looked like the other eight but was not), ignored false positives, stress and burnout, lower productivity, and incident reviews that never get written because nobody has time. She notes that people about to join on-call worry most about exactly this: how often they will be pulled away from work, and from sleep.

## Six kinds of alert to delete or demote

Before any SLO work, the baseline cleanup:

- **Success notifications**: unless you truly need to know in real time, send them to chat, not the pager. As she puts it, "get your dopamine hit on Instagram" or somewhere else, not from your monitoring.
- **Non-actionable alerts**: chronic issues the responder cannot fix. Track them as a metric and use the trend to win engineering time from product managers.
- **Misrouted alerts**: if your team has no access to fix it, have the conversation with the team that does.
- **Low urgency**: route to a channel, a ticket, or a low-urgency queue that a "goalie" triages each morning. In PagerDuty you can make low-urgency alerts skip SMS and push.
- **Features nobody uses**: lower the urgency and revisit it.
- **Broken alerts**: if the code changed and the monitor no longer reflects it, disable it.

Her suggested mechanism is an alert cleanup sprint: sort by frequency, start with the ten noisiest, and for each one ask whether it is actionable, urgent and telling you something about service performance. Then check that what remains is readable from its first line, because a list of incidents with identical opening lines hides the one that matters. She also explains why SMS will not carry more detail: country-by-country rules push global senders to the lowest common denominator.

## Error budgets are permission to wait

With the junk gone, SLOs handle what is left. SLOs are the team's goals for production metrics, set inside whatever SLA the lawyers signed, and based on what users actually care about. The magic, in her framing, is that they let you absorb some failures before anyone's phone lights up. A single isolated error on a busy service can be recorded as low urgency, and escalate to high urgency only when a cluster of them starts eating the budget. If your SLO is 95% success, you might start paging at 97% rather than at the first failure. That cuts volume and sets urgency in one move.

## Who should watch

Team leads with a noisy rotation, new on-call engineers, and anyone who needs arguments for a cleanup sprint. Her line for managers: more than a handful of major alerts in a week-long shift means you are drowning people. Resources she points to include the SLO chapter of the Google SRE workbook and Nobl9's material, which PagerDuty uses for its own SLOs.

Title: Anomaly detection starts with knowing what normal looks like
Description: Gaurav Mittal of Nordstrom at Conf42 SRE 2025 maps point, contextual and collective anomalies, the methods that find them and the tools to start with.
Body:
A CPU spike at 2pm is Tuesday; the same spike at 3am is a question. That contrast sits at the centre of Gaurav Mittal's talk at Conf42 SRE 2025. Mittal, a software development engineer at Nordstrom, argues that SLO-based monitoring tells you when things have already gone wrong, and that anomaly detection, done carefully, moves some of that discovery earlier. His talk is a structured primer on what anomalies are, how to find them, and how to adopt AI in SRE without trying to boil the ocean.

## Too many signals is its own outage

The starting problem is the monitoring explosion: teams collect so many metrics that the noise hides the signal, alert fatigue sets in, and response slows. Mittal lists what AI can help with here: filtering alerts, predicting failures from historical patterns, automated remediation, capacity planning, faster root cause analysis, incident triage, and ChatOps that runs diagnostics from chat.

## Three shapes of weird

The core of the talk is a taxonomy worth keeping:

- **Point anomalies**: a single data point far from the rest, like one server's sudden CPU spike.
- **Contextual anomalies**: normal in one context, abnormal in another. Busy CPU on a workday is fine; the same at 3am is not.
- **Collective anomalies**: no single point is odd, but together they are, like latency creeping up across several services over time.

The third is the one static thresholds never catch, and the reason to bother with any of this.

## Statistics before deep learning

For detection, Mittal starts with plain statistics: z-scores against the mean, median absolute deviation against the median, moving averages and exponential smoothing. If average response time is 100 ms, a 500 ms reading stands out without any neural network. Then come machine learning methods: clustering, where a point outside the usual cluster is the outlier, and time series forecasting. He covers supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, and notes unsupervised learning is the natural fit for anomaly detection because you rarely have labelled incidents.

The hard parts are honest ones: seasonality changes what normal means by hour and month, noisy data needs preprocessing, normal drifts as systems grow, so models need ongoing retraining, and AI is only as good as the data it sees.

## Overlay first, replace later

On adoption, he describes three models: an overlay that runs AI alongside existing monitoring, embedded AI features inside the platforms you already use, and automated remediation that acts on what it detects. The overlay is his recommended on-ramp, because nothing existing has to be ripped out.

For tooling he lists Prometheus, Grafana, the ELK stack, Facebook's Prophet for forecasting, and scikit-learn or TensorFlow if you build your own, alongside commercial options such as Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace and Splunk, plus the cloud providers' built-in tools. Case studies are public ones from Netflix, LinkedIn and Uber.

## Who should watch

SREs who keep hearing "AIOps" and want a clear map of the terms before talking to vendors, and teams with a specific noise problem. It is a primer, not a build log: there is no Nordstrom system shown. The advice to pick one high-value use case, such as alert fatigue, get the data foundation right first, and iterate is the part to take away.

Title: AutoML for SRE teams that do not have a data scientist on call
Description: Swapna Anugu at Conf42 SRE 2025 on using AutoML for incident prediction, alert tuning and capacity planning, with a pilot-first rollout plan.
Body:
Most SRE teams have years of metrics and logs and nobody with time to train a model on them. Swapna Anugu's pitch at Conf42 SRE 2025 is that AutoML closes that gap. Anugu, a cloud architect, lead data engineer and data scientist at Manasi Information Technologies, explains how automated machine learning turns operational data into predictions about failures, noisy alerts and capacity, and lays out a pilot-first path for adopting it.

## The pipeline you no longer hand-build

The core contrast is with traditional ML. There, someone works through data exploration, preparation, feature engineering, model selection, training, hyperparameter tuning and evaluation by hand. With AutoML, you supply the data and the target metric, optionally a time or cost budget, and the platform tries algorithms and parameters, evaluates them on train and test splits, and returns a ranked list with accuracy scores. You pick the winner. If you know which features or algorithms you want, you can pin them; if not, the platform proposes them.

Anugu names Azure AutoML plus the Google Cloud and AWS equivalents as the main platforms, and says they work in broadly similar ways, so the choice usually follows your existing cloud.

## Five places it earns its keep

The SRE use cases she lists:

- **Incident prediction**: spot server failures or traffic and error spikes in advance.
- **Root cause analysis**: correlate metrics, log patterns and recurring events so the fix is found faster.
- **Capacity planning**: forecast surges and overloads, scale ahead of them and scale down when demand drops, which is where cloud money is saved.
- **Automated alert tuning**: learn which alerts are real and which are noise, so engineers only see the meaningful ones.
- **Self-healing**: rules that, for example, restart a service once a threshold is reached, without a human.

She also walks through domain examples: market-hours load in financial services, Black Friday spikes and failed payments in e-commerce, IoT device and patient record systems in healthcare, and outage detection and bandwidth forecasting in telecom.

## Pilot it next to the humans

The rollout plan is sensible and conservative. Assess your SRE maturity and document current processes, prepare monitoring data with quality baselines and labels for supervised learning, choose a platform, then run a modest pilot and compare automated results with manual ones before scaling. She quotes outcome figures for organisations that have done this, including a 91% alert accuracy rate and detection time down 68%, without detail on where they come from.

The challenges section is the most practical part. Inconsistent monitoring data needs validation pipelines before it reaches a model. SRE teams are reluctant to trust automated decisions, so start with non-critical systems and run side-by-side comparisons. Integration with existing monitoring tools is messy, so use standard APIs and loosely coupled integration points.

## Who should watch

SRE leads curious whether AutoML could take some prediction work off their plate, and teams that already store good telemetry but have no ML engineers. It is a conceptual walkthrough with no live demo or platform screens. Her conclusion is the right frame: AutoML does not replace SRE, it takes over routine analysis so engineers can focus on the strategic work.

Title: How 300+ APIs connected Moderna's vaccine pipeline end to end
Description: Rishi Nareshbhai Lad of ModernaTx shows at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 how API-led integration across 110+ systems sped up pharma operations.
Body:
No single piece of software runs a pharmaceutical company, so the integration layer ends up being the company's nervous system. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Rishi Nareshbhai Lad, Principal Integration Engineer at ModernaTx, described how his team built more than 300 integrations connecting 110-plus internal and external systems, and what that did for mRNA vaccine development, manufacturing and clinical trials.

## Start with how a vaccine gets made

Lad opens with a short primer that makes the rest of the talk land: identify the virus and decode its RNA, design the mRNA instructions, run clinical trials across diverse populations, scale up manufacturing under FDA scrutiny, then ship through a cold-chain supply network. Each of those stages lives in different departments using different tools. Before the integration work, that meant legacy systems, manual processes and data that did not move between them.

## Four patterns, chosen per partner

There is no single integration style in the talk, and that is the useful part. Lad uses:

- **REST APIs** for secure, real-time system-to-system calls.
- **Pub/sub** for event-driven updates, especially in manufacturing where something happening on the line should reach other systems immediately.
- **ETL** for heavy batch syncs such as financial and clinical data.
- **Hybrid API plus file transfer** for partners who cannot integrate through APIs at all.

That last one is the honest bit. Every enterprise architecture diagram has a partner who still sends files, and Lad designs for them instead of pretending they do not exist.

## Clinical trials move at the speed of the CRO feed

The example that shows the business value best is clinical trials. Trials run worldwide through contract research organisations, and if their data reaches the sponsor late, scientists decide late. Integrating directly with CRO systems in real time cut delays by 30 to 40% in his account, and helped scientists judge sooner whether a candidate was working, which doses to test and which populations to enrol, while staying GxP compliant.

On the manufacturing side, the move from manual data entry to integrated, event-driven systems removed paper workflows and built audit tracking and validation into the system rather than bolting it on later.

## Where the hours went

Lad's figures on automation are concrete: eliminating manual data entry saved about 90,000 hours a year and reduced errors by 78%, and automated workflows saved roughly 35 minutes per executed protocol. He says researchers now spend 40% more time on scientific work. The abstract adds the headline outcomes for the programme: 60% faster time-to-market for an mRNA cancer vaccine, 99.1% data validation accuracy and a 38% shorter trial duration.

## Compliance shapes the platform

The platform runs on AWS, with Molecule clusters on EC2 instances sized for GxP and enterprise workloads. A modular architecture with reusable components and API templates made deployments five times faster. Security is split by regime: GxP, non-GxP and SOX workflows are kept separate, compliance is validated against 21 CFR Part 11, and access goes through OAuth 2.0, Okta and a web application firewall. In a regulated industry, those separation lines are what lets you move quickly without an auditor stopping you.

## Who should watch

Integration engineers and enterprise architects in regulated industries, particularly life sciences. There is no deep machine learning content despite the conference, so come for the integration patterns and the compliance boundaries. A short talk, and a good one to send to anyone who thinks integration is plumbing nobody needs to plan.

Title: Recommenders are a funnel: millions of items in, about 50 out
Description: Microsoft's Sergey Polyashov explains at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 how search and recommendation systems retrieve, rank and scale, and why they scale unlike LLMs.
Body:
A recommender system is a funnel that starts with millions or billions of items and ends with roughly 50 on your screen. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Sergey Polyashov, Principal Software Engineering Manager at Microsoft, who has led video search, personalised video recommendations and product search at Yandex and Microsoft, walked through each stage of that funnel and explained why the tricks that scale LLMs do not simply carry over to recommendations.

It is billed as a 101, and it is one: compact, well organised, and dense enough that experienced engineers will still pick up a few names to look up.

## Short-term clicks are easy to measure and easy to overfit

Polyashov starts with why the systems matter (he cites recommendations driving about 30% of YouTube views, 35% of Amazon purchases and 80% of what people watch on Netflix) and then with what to optimise. Short-term targets such as clicks, watch time and purchases give fast feedback but tempt you into chasing immediate interest. Long-term targets such as retention, subscription renewal and content diversity are harder to measure and closer to real user value. A system that only optimises clicks eventually learns to serve the same five things forever.

He also makes a point many intro talks skip: logging is part of the model. Every click, scroll and dwell feeds offline training and evaluation, and if you log incorrectly you train on biased, broken labels.

## The funnel, stage by stage

The multi-stage pipeline he describes:

1. **Query and user understanding**: what this user has done, and what they want right now.
2. **Candidate generation**: high recall, around 10,000 items, with diversity, freshness and popularity in the mix.
3. **Pre-ranking**: lightweight models, often gradient boosted trees or small neural networks, cut that to about 1,000.
4. **Heavy ranking (L2/L3)**: deep networks or transformers score each remaining candidate to pick the top 50 or so, judged by NDCG.
5. **Final re-ranking**: business rules for category diversity, boosting new items, sponsored content and policy compliance.

Cheap models early for speed, expensive models late for accuracy. That ordering is the whole performance budget.

## Candidate generation is a mix, not a choice

For retrieval, Polyashov lists approximate nearest neighbour search with libraries such as FAISS from Meta and ScaNN from Google and algorithms like HNSW, fed by embeddings from collaborative filtering (ALS is fast but weak on cold start) or content-based two-tower models. Random walks over item graphs help diversity and cold start. Search systems lean on inverted indexes with BM25, which scale to trillions of documents through sharding. And simple heuristics like popularity, recency and subscriptions still earn their place when latency matters. Production systems combine several.

## Gradient boosting still owns the last mile

On ranking, his summary is pragmatic. Gradient boosted trees such as XGBoost and LightGBM remain the common final ranker: fast, debuggable, good on structured features. Deep networks capture richer interactions, handle sequences and high-cardinality features, and scale better with data, but cost more and are harder to explain. A typical hybrid uses neural networks upstream for embeddings and features, then separate boosted models predicting relevance, click probability and conversion, combined by business goal.

For scaling neural recommenders he covers two-tower late fusion (item embeddings computed offline), contrastive learning with hard negative mining, embedding compression through hashing, quantisation and distillation, bias correction with a context-aware tower used in training and dropped at inference, and transformer encoders for user behaviour sequences.

## Why recommenders do not scale like LLMs

The most thought-provoking slide contrasts the two worlds. LLMs and vision models get long dense inputs, strong supervision, a universal pretraining task and tolerance for seconds of latency. Recommenders deal with huge embedding tables, millisecond budgets, short sparse behaviour sequences and implicit feedback, with no clean scaling law. Making the model bigger runs into bias, noise and diminishing returns. He closes with the trends pushing on that limit: Meta's 2024 research on trillion-parameter sequential transducers, graph neural networks for the long tail, and reinforcement learning for long-term goals and exploration.

## Who should watch

Engineers joining a search or recommendations team, or backend developers who want the vocabulary before their first design review with one. Specialists will know the material but may enjoy the scaling comparison.

Title: Predicting cardiac events early starts with boring data quality
Description: Darshan Patel explains at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 the data pipeline and explainability work behind predictive healthcare AI.
Body:
What if a model could flag a heart attack days before it happens? That question opens Darshan Patel's talk at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025. Patel, a data engineer specialising in healthcare data compliance and analytics, spends most of it on the unglamorous answer: predictive healthcare works only when the data pipeline underneath it is clean, harmonised and fast, and when clinicians can see why the model raised an alert.

## Healthcare collected the data, then mostly ignored it

Patel frames the field in three phases. Traditional care was reactive and largely on paper. The digital phase, driven by electronic health records from the 2000s, captured vitals, labs, medications and notes, but most of that data went no further than billing and record keeping. The current phase uses machine learning on the same data to predict risk, sometimes days or weeks ahead, increasingly with signals from consumer devices like the Apple Watch.

He cites research showing a 70% improvement in early cardiovascular risk detection, roughly a week or more of advance warning, and about a one-third reduction in emergency room visits from interventions based on those alerts.

## The pipeline has four stages and the model is the third

His integration architecture runs:

1. **Source integration**: EHRs, wearables, genetic testing, lab information systems and image archives.
2. **Harmonisation**: aligning units, terminologies and formats. One hospital reports glucose in one unit, another in a different one; diagnosis codes vary between ICD and SNOMED.
3. **AI processing**: models trained on the unified data.
4. **Clinical insight delivery**: alerts inside the EHR, dashboards or mobile apps, so the prediction reaches someone who can act on it.

The fourth stage is the one projects forget. A correct prediction that lands in a dashboard nobody opens is the same as no prediction.

## A missing decimal point is a clinical risk

The data quality section is the strongest part of the talk. Patel's framework has four steps: cleansing (typos, unit errors, duplicate records), normalisation (unit conversion, terminology mapping, consistent timestamps), integration (linking a patient's lab results, medications and wearable data into one profile) and validation (statistical checks, logic rules and clinical review). His examples are memorable: a temperature of 103.0 Fahrenheit losing its decimal point, or a male patient listed as pregnant. In most domains, bad data gives you a bad dashboard. In healthcare it can give you an unsafe recommendation.

He lists four technical challenges up front as well: privacy and HIPAA compliance (with de-identification, masking and federated learning as tools), interoperability across Epic, Cerner and proprietary device formats, latency (a sepsis alert that arrives 20 minutes late may be useless), and data quality.

## Explainability is what gets the model used

On modelling, Patel recommends ensembles for structured EHR data, deep learning for imaging, and probabilistic models where uncertainty has to be expressed, with version control so clinical audits can trace which model made which call. Then comes the adoption problem: if a clinician does not trust an output, it will not be used. His four techniques are feature attribution (show that rising white blood cell count drove the sepsis flag), visual dashboards with trend lines and confidence bars, contextual explanations tied to medical knowledge, and confidence metrics so a 95% prediction is treated differently from a 60% one.

He closes with a regional hospital case where cardiac readmissions fell by about a third after the model was embedded in the EHR and staff were trained on reading its alerts.

## Who should watch

Data engineers moving into healthcare, and ML teams whose models work in notebooks but stall at clinical adoption. It is a broad overview rather than a technical walkthrough of one model, and the explainability section is the part worth stealing for any regulated domain.
