Title: Catching fake-review rings in real time with Kafka, Flink and GNNs
Description: Satyanandam Kotha explains at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 a hybrid streaming and graph architecture that flags coordinated fake reviews in milliseconds.
Body:
A five-star toaster review claiming the appliance changed someone's life is either a very good toaster or a fraud ring at work. Satyanandam Kotha opened his Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 talk with that joke, then showed the system behind it: a real-time fraud detection pipeline on Apache Kafka and Apache Flink that combines four detection methods, including graph neural networks, to catch coordinated fake reviews as they are posted.

Kotha presents it as a system running in production across 12 e-commerce platforms, and the talk is a tour of how it is built.

## Speed matters because fraud is coordinated

The threat model is the useful starting point. Fake reviews are rarely random; they come from campaigns run through many well-prepared fake accounts that post in a way designed to look natural. Every hour a fake review stays up, it shifts buying decisions, buries honest sellers and costs the platform credibility. So detection has to happen while the review is arriving, not in a weekly batch job.

## Kafka in, Flink through, graphs on the side

The architecture has four parts. Kafka carries the stream of reviews with fault tolerance. Flink processes it with very low latency and, importantly, keeps state: with RocksDB as the state backend, the system remembers user behaviour over long periods, which is how it catches an account that behaves for months and then turns. Detection models are deployed horizontally so throughput grows by adding servers. And a custom graph database maps relationships between accounts, reviews and products to expose clusters.

Kotha also describes custom sparse graph representations that skip unnecessary edges, which he says cut memory by 40% and made graph queries three times faster.

## Four detectors that cover each other's blind spots

The detection layer is hybrid on purpose, because fraud does not look the same twice:

- **Ensemble models** where each member watches a different signal, such as posting time, review content or account history.
- **Graph neural networks** that look at who is connected to whom, so ten accounts reviewing the same products at the same times with similar ratings stand out as a group.
- **Behavioural analytics** for odd posting rates, unusual hours or an account that only ever reviews one seller's products.
- **NLP** for templated phrasing, overly positive language and machine-generated text, which matters more now that fraudsters use AI tools too.

He is candid about why one method is not enough: NLP alone misses natural-sounding fakes, behavioural models miss quiet accounts, and graph models need data before they kick in. Combined, they lift precision and recall together, which is the hard part. A strict system flags real reviews and annoys users; a loose one lets fraud through.

## Eight accounts are enough to spot a campaign

The coordinated-campaign section is the sharpest idea. Rather than waiting until hundreds of accounts are obviously involved, the system uses thresholds and temporal pattern analysis to flag groups as small as eight accounts, for instance eight accounts reviewing the same product in a short window with no prior interaction with it.

## Privacy is designed in, not added

Kotha covers three privacy techniques: federated learning so raw data stays where it was collected, differential privacy noise on aggregated results, and homomorphic encryption so inference can run on encrypted data. On operations, he reports around 10 ms detection latency, handling five times normal traffic at peaks like Black Friday, near-linear scaling with about 5% overhead, daily retraining that adapts to new patterns within 24 hours, and microservices with CI/CD, A/B tests and canary rollouts so a new detector ships without touching the rest. The production results he cites are a 78% drop in fake reviews and uptime above 99%.

## Who should watch

Trust and safety engineers, anyone building streaming ML with Flink, and teams who need fraud signals that survive adversaries adapting. The talk is architecture-level; you will not see model code, but you will get a clear map of which component does which job.

Title: MFA and zero trust, rolled out in phases starting with critical assets
Description: Sandeep Jarugula of U.S. Bank at Conf42 SRE 2025 on why identity is the weak point and how to phase in MFA and zero-trust controls.
Body:
Most breaches start with someone logging in who should not. That is the premise of Sandeep Jarugula's talk at Conf42 SRE 2025: Jarugula, a Senior Lead Java Full Stack Developer at U.S. Bank, makes the data-driven case for multi-factor authentication plus a zero-trust architecture, and sketches a phased rollout that protects the most valuable systems first.

It is a compact overview, around ten minutes, aimed at teams building the business case rather than configuring an identity provider.

## Identity is the attack surface

Jarugula frames the problem with cost. He cites an average breach cost of $4.45 million globally for 2023, with 83% of breaches tied to compromised identity, and $3.92 million in annual savings for organisations that combine MFA with zero trust. The point for engineers is less the exact figures than the target: if most attacks walk in with stolen credentials, the login flow is your perimeter.

## Three kinds of proof

MFA layers different kinds of evidence: something you know (passwords, PINs), something you have (tokens, cards) and something you are (biometrics). Each factor is another barrier, and he quotes a 99.9% reduction in account compromise when MFA is properly implemented. The operative word is "properly": a second factor that can be skipped or phished back is mostly decoration.

## Verify every request, wherever it comes from

Zero trust drops the idea of a trusted inside. Every access request is verified and authenticated continuously, whether it comes from inside or outside the network. The payoffs he lists are a smaller attack surface, blocked lateral movement and better containment when something does get in. He then walks through sector results he has collected for finance, healthcare and government, including fewer account takeovers in financial services and faster HIPAA compliance in healthcare.

## Roll it out like any risky change

The most transferable part is the integration plan, which reads like a change-management playbook an SRE would recognise:

1. **Assessment**: a full security audit to find vulnerabilities and access risks.
2. **Strategy**: a tailored plan with goals, milestones, resources and stakeholder buy-in.
3. **Pilot**: a controlled trial in selected departments and critical systems.
4. **Phased implementation**: expand gradually, critical assets first, adjusting from feedback.
5. **Continuous optimisation**: keep monitoring and refining as threats change.

## Less friction, not more

The closing section looks at where authentication is heading: passwordless login with biometrics or trusted devices, stronger biometrics with anti-spoofing, behavioural authentication that uses machine learning on user patterns for continuous checks, and adaptive risk assessment that raises or lowers requirements by location, device and activity. His takeaway is that security and user experience have to be designed together, or users will route around the controls.

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads who need to explain MFA and zero trust to stakeholders, or who are planning the order of a rollout. If you already run a zero-trust program, the talk will be familiar ground; for implementation detail, pair it with one of the talks below.

Title: Keeping Hyperledger Fabric up when orderers, peers and certs fail
Description: Umegbewe Nwebedu of Botanix Labs at Conf42 SRE 2025 on Raft vs BFT ordering, partitions, endorsement policies and cert expiry in Hyperledger Fabric.
Body:
A permissioned blockchain is a distributed system with extra paperwork, and it fails in the same boring ways: a node dies, the network splits, a certificate expires. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Umegbewe Nwebedu, an SRE at Botanix Labs who has spent three years running Hyperledger Fabric networks, walked through the patterns that keep a Fabric network available, from Raft clusters to endorsement policies that do not freeze the chain when one organization goes dark.

## Know the moving parts first

Fabric is a modular, permissioned framework for settings where participants are known: government, finance, supply chain. Peers host the ledger and the chaincode (smart contracts) that endorse transactions. The ordering service batches transactions into blocks. Certificate authorities issue identities. Peers keep each other in sync over a gossip protocol, and consensus is configurable: Raft, BFT or solo, with Kafka deprecated.

Nwebedu's baseline topology is two to three peers per organization for redundancy and three to five orderers in a Raft cluster. On Kubernetes, use anti-affinity so the pods do not all land on the same node, and spread nodes across failure domains: region, data center, rack.

## Raft forgives crashes, not liars

With Raft, one orderer leads and proposes batches; a block commits when a majority of followers acknowledge it. Lose the leader and a follower steps up. Three orderers survive one crash, five survive two. He warns against adding nodes without reason, since each one adds coordination overhead.

Raft only handles crash faults. If a node actively misbehaves, say by reordering transactions, you need Byzantine fault tolerance, which Fabric now offers as a BFT ordering service. The arithmetic is 3f + 1: tolerating one malicious node needs four orderers, two needs seven. It costs more resources and messages, and he notes it is still new in Fabric, so most deployments should only reach for it when participants genuinely do not trust each other.

## Partitions and the minority that waits

When orderers split, only the side with a Raft majority keeps producing blocks. The minority stops rather than forking, then catches up when the partition heals. Isolated peers stop receiving blocks and pull what they missed from healthy peers over gossip once connectivity returns. The design lesson is placement: distribute orderers so a majority survives losing any one region.

## Your endorsement policy can be the outage

This is the most useful section for anyone running Fabric. A policy that requires all three organizations to endorse means one org going offline stops transactions for everyone. A policy like "any two of three" keeps the network running. Other tuning tips: size blocks for your workload while watching latency, choose LevelDB for speed or CouchDB when you need rich queries, use channels to isolate workloads, tune Raft's tick interval, election tick and heartbeat for high-latency global deployments, and upgrade one node at a time.

His incident list is refreshingly unglamorous: orderer crashes Raft handles on its own, peers out of sync, strict endorsement policies freezing the network, chaincode containers panicking, proposal floods that need rate limits, and certificate expiry, which he says caused real trouble on a Fabric-based chain he worked on at Gala.

## Who should watch

Anyone operating Fabric or evaluating it, and SREs curious how classic consensus trade-offs show up in a ledger. It is practical and config-aware, with sample Raft and endorsement policy snippets. Monitoring advice is standard Prometheus plus Grafana, alerting on block production stalls, ledger height lag, Raft leader changes and certificate expiry.

Title: Where AI touches enterprise revenue systems, from forecasts to pricing
Description: Vikas Vallakonda, an SAP BRIM program manager, surveys AI for forecasting, dynamic pricing, lead scoring and retention at Conf42 SRE 2025.
Body:
Revenue systems are where enterprise architecture meets the CFO, and Vikas Vallakonda's talk at Conf42 SRE 2025 is a short tour of where AI plugs into them. Vallakonda, a technical program manager at Discovery Analytics with 14 years as an SAP consultant across S/4HANA, BRIM, CRM and SD, maps AI onto five revenue functions: demand forecasting, pricing, lead conversion, personalisation and retention, then closes with the data infrastructure and ethics questions that come with them.

Be clear on scope: this is a business-side overview, about ten minutes long, delivered from the perspective of someone who implements subscription management, convergent charging and billing on SAP. It is not an SRE deep technical session, and there are no architectures or code on screen.

## Forecasts and prices that move with the market

The first two areas carry the most numbers. On forecasting, Vallakonda cites a 45% reduction in forecasting error from AI-powered tools and a 30% increase in inventory turnover, which he ties directly to cash flow and lower carrying costs. On pricing, he describes systems that adjust to market conditions, inventory levels and customer behaviour, with retailers reporting 8 to 12% improvements on average and up to 16% in peak seasons. Treat these as figures he quotes, not results from his own projects; the talk does not show where they come from.

## Spend sales effort on the leads that convert

Lead scoring is the third area: models that learn from past successful conversions rank incoming leads so teams focus on high-potential ones, and keep getting more accurate as the conversion history grows. He reports around 30% higher conversion rates for organisations that do this.

## Next best action and churn

The retention section covers churn-risk detection from customer behaviour and "next best action" engines that weigh many possible steps for each customer and pick one that balances short-term revenue against the long-term relationship. He pairs that with personalised recommendations and interfaces that match each customer's interests.

## The plumbing has to be real time

The part an SRE audience will care about most is the infrastructure requirement. Dynamic pricing and personalisation only work if the data platform answers fast, and he describes enterprise-grade implementations processing on the order of nine to ten million records per hour. Underneath that sits a unified data architecture, plus compliance and governance so the systems stay fair, transparent and privacy-respecting as they make decisions that affect what customers pay.

## Who should watch

Engineers who support billing, CRM or SAP revenue stacks and want the business vocabulary for why the AI projects landing on their platform matter. If you want reliability patterns for running those systems, look elsewhere; this talk covers the reasons and the use cases, not the implementation.

Title: In finance, privacy-aware AI sends the model to the data
Description: Raghavender Puchhakayala of JPMorgan Chase explains federated learning and differential privacy for banking, wealth and insurance at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.
Body:
Two banks want a better fraud model, and neither is allowed to show the other a single customer transaction. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Raghavender Puchhakayala of JPMorgan Chase, a senior IEEE member who leads AI-driven analytics with more than a decade in banking data warehousing and BI, explains the toolkit that makes that possible: federated learning, differential privacy and secure multi-party computation. His thesis is that privacy and model performance don't have to be a trade-off in regulated finance.

It's a strategy-level talk aimed at people who build and approve analytics in banks, wealth managers and insurers. It explains the techniques clearly without getting into the maths.

## Why the old pipeline stops working

Puchhakayala traces analytics in finance from basic reporting to predictive and prescriptive models, and now to what he calls responsible AI. Regulations like GDPR and India's DPDP Act force institutions to be intentional about how data is used, customers want personalisation without giving up privacy, and models can no longer be black boxes. Copying every dataset into one lake is getting harder to defend.

## Three techniques, one toolkit

The core of the talk is a clean explanation of three methods.

**Federated learning** trains a model across many data sources without moving the data. In his words, "The model travels to the data, not vice versa." Sensitive records stay where they live.

**Differential privacy** adds mathematical guarantees that individuals can't be identified even in aggregate results, which is stronger than a procedural promise.

**Secure multi-party computation** lets departments or institutions compute together without revealing their inputs. That's the two-banks fraud model from the opening.

Together they cover both the technical and the compliance requirements, which is the combination regulated teams need.

## Where it lands in finance

In banking, he points to credit risk models trained across global branches, fraud detection that learns patterns across payment channels while staying within compliance boundaries, and anti-money-laundering monitoring with fewer false positives, so fewer legitimate transactions get flagged for review. In wealth management, federated training across client segments supports personalised portfolio advice without centralising anyone's life goals or risk tolerance. In insurance, which mixes health, property and behavioural data under rules like Solvency II, privacy-preserving models help with pricing and with catching false claims.

## The research behind it

He also references a paper he co-authored, accepted for publication by IEEE: an AI-driven scheduling framework for cloud ETL that uses LSTM networks to predict workloads and isolation forests to detect anomalies. Tested on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud with real workload traces, it cut cloud infrastructure cost by up to 40% with better autoscaling. The next phase of that research extends it with federated learning for compliance-heavy financial workloads.

## How to start

The obstacles are organisational as much as technical: inconsistent data quality, silos, legacy systems and strict compliance. His advice is to set up governance before writing any code, defining roles and escalation paths. The tooling has matured: major clouds support federated learning alongside confidential computing, and open-source differential privacy libraries come from Google, IBM and OpenMined.

The starting plan is concrete. Pilot one federated use case where privacy matters (fraud detection is his pick), staff it with analytics, legal and IT together, define success as regulatory alignment and risk reduction as well as accuracy, and build a centre of excellence to capture what you learn.

## Who should watch

Data and ML leads in banks and insurers, compliance-minded architects, and anyone who has had a promising model blocked by a data-sharing rule. Practitioners who've already shipped federated training won't find implementation detail here.

Title: Summarising a four-person email thread is an architecture problem
Description: eBay engineer Swapnil Hemant Thorat breaks down AI message summarisation at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, from text pipelines to hallucination checks and context.
Body:
You email support about a refund, get passed to a supervisor, then to another department, and end up explaining everything again. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Swapnil Hemant Thorat, Member of Technical Staff 2 at eBay, uses that familiar mess to show why AI summarisation of business conversations gets harder with every person who joins a thread, and how to design a system that keeps the context intact.

It's an architecture talk aimed at engineers building summarisation for customer service and internal communication, rather than a model benchmark.

## Why summarisation matters to the business

Thorat splits business communication into external conversations (customers with sales, marketing and support over chat, email or a shopping assistant) and internal ones between colleagues. A customer service agent, he says, spends about five and a half hours of an eight-hour day on active communication. Instant messaging through Messenger, WhatsApp and iMessage only adds more text. A good summary saves agent time, and it saves the customer from repeating themselves at every handoff. His abstract cites a 23.7% reduction in time spent on routine communication for businesses using AI summarisation.

## Three layers, bottom up

His architecture is a stack, and the top depends on the bottom.

**Text processing.** Normalisation lowercases, strips punctuation, expands abbreviations and turns numbers, currencies and dates into words, all to reduce ambiguity. Tokenisation splits text into characters, words or sentences depending on the use case.

**Semantic analysis.** Works out the grammatical structure and the relationships between terms: who the actors in a conversation are and how they relate.

**Summary generation.** Only as good as the two layers beneath it.

For scale he adds message queues and a divide-and-conquer approach: break a large job into threads that run in parallel, with a governing thread that stitches the results together.

## Hallucinations, metrics and bias

The second half covers what breaks. Hallucination is fine when you ask a model for a poem, and costly when it invents a fact in a customer's refund history, so detection belongs in the architecture. Quality needs structured evaluation of both accuracy and usability, automated regression tests so a prompt tweak doesn't break existing behaviour, and humans reviewing outputs. He also notes that research shows the link between compute spent and summary quality isn't linear: horizontal scaling won't fix a quality problem.

On bias he argues for neutral training data, thorough cleaning and preprocessing to neutralise skew.

## Context needs checkpoints

The sharpest idea is logical checkpoints: metadata added during processing, based on timestamps and actors, that tells the summariser what situation it is in. His example is a flight booking. An email before departure is about an upcoming trip. A follow-up the day after is probably about a missed flight, a cancellation or lost baggage. Same thread, different context, and the timestamp is what tells them apart.

He shows accuracy dipping as complexity grows: single-topic threads summarise well, multi-actor threads less so, cross-department threads less again, while short time-critical messages come out well because there's less text and tighter context.

## Shipping it

The operational checklist: CI/CD, checkpointing, automated regressions, bias and hallucination detection built into the data pipeline, a hybrid of caching and long-term storage tuned per use case, and AI governance for security as use cases multiply.

## Who should watch

Engineers building summarisation or agent-assist features for support teams, and anyone who needs to explain to a product manager why the multi-threaded case is the hard one.

Title: Serverless ML pays off first on spiky inference workloads
Description: Presidio's Tarun Kumar Chatterjee shows at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 where serverless ML cuts cost and deploy time, and how to migrate in three phases.
Body:
Most ML models spend their lives idle, then get hammered. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Tarun Kumar Chatterjee, .NET Senior Lead Developer at Presidio, argued that this traffic shape is exactly why serverless fits model serving, and gave a three-phase plan for moving inference workloads over without betting the business on it.

The talk leans on industry research figures rather than a single case study. The headline numbers he cites: around 40% lower cost than traditional ML deployments, a 65% reduction in infrastructure management overhead, and organisations shipping 3.4 times more models a year once deployment stops being a ticket queue.

## Weeks to hours is the real story

The slide that sticks is deployment time. Chatterjee describes three stages. Traditional deployment takes two to three weeks of provisioning, environment setup and manual scaling. A transitional setup, where teams configure an API gateway and containerise functions, gets that to three to five days. Fully serverless, with everything automated, he puts at two to four hours.

That is the argument for platform work in general: the savings on the bill are nice, but the bigger change is that a data scientist can try an idea on Tuesday and see it in production on Tuesday.

## Pay-per-use matches how ML actually behaves

On cost, the case is the pay-per-use model. Training and inference spike, then sit quiet, and a provisioned cluster bills you for the quiet part too. Serverless bills for the spikes. Chatterjee breaks the savings into infrastructure, maintenance, scaling and DevOps effort, and he describes elastic scaling holding stable, low-latency responses through a tenfold traffic surge.

## A four-layer reference architecture

He sketches a layered pattern for serverless ML:

1. **Data ingestion**: event-driven, with streaming input, automatic feature extraction and optimised storage.
2. **Training**: ephemeral compute that spins up on demand, including GPU access, hyperparameter tuning and distributed training jobs.
3. **Inference**: containerised models behind an API gateway, with auto-scaling endpoints, model versioning and A/B testing, and caching for hot queries.
4. **Monitoring**: performance metrics, drift detection and automated retraining triggers.

The benefit of the split is that each layer scales and gets optimised on its own schedule.

## Cold starts and package size are the tax

Serverless has known costs, and the optimisation section addresses them directly. Model compression through quantisation, pruning and knowledge distillation can shrink models by 60 to 80%, which matters when your function has a size limit. Cold starts get handled with warm pools, preloaded models and managed concurrency. Memory gets right-sized per model and combined with adaptive batching. Caching at the gateway, function and database layers removes repeated work. Chatterjee reports that teams combining these saw a further 25% cost reduction on top of the initial serverless savings.

## Migrate the boring models first

The roadmap is sensible and low-drama. Start with an assessment: find inference workloads with variable traffic or frequent updates, and do a cost-benefit pass. Then pilot with non-critical models, refactor them for serverless, set a performance baseline and wire up CI/CD. Only then scale out to higher-value models and write down what you learned. He cites research that 87% of pilots following this phased approach reached full production within three months.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and platform teams who run inference on always-on clusters and suspect they are paying for idle GPUs. It is an overview with research-backed figures rather than a provider-specific demo, so bring your own AWS, Azure or GCP details. Teams with steady, high-volume inference traffic may find the cost argument weaker for them, and the talk is honest that the first candidates are variable-traffic workloads.

Title: A tiny slice of queries caused most of the database load
Description: DBA Solomon Chigurupati shows at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 how reinforcement learning and historical analysis can tune enterprise databases with DBAs in the loop.
Body:
On one e-commerce platform, just 0.03% of distinct queries generated over 70% of the database load at peak. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Solomon Chigurupati, a senior Oracle database administrator who has spent years tuning databases for financial clients, uses that finding to sell a simple idea: let an AI framework find those queries and propose fixes before peak traffic does, and keep the DBA in charge of approving them.

The talk presents a framework and a case study, combining historical pattern analysis with reinforcement learning, rather than a specific product.

## Why reactive tuning keeps losing

Chigurupati starts with the mess every DBA knows: relational databases like Oracle and MySQL next to NoSQL stores like MongoDB and Cassandra, spread across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, each with its own optimiser, indexing and storage. Traditional tuning is reactive. Someone notices slow queries, walks through execution plans, runs tests and tweaks settings after users have felt it.

His numbers on the cost: misconfigurations behind a large share of service disruptions, about a quarter of DBA time spent on tuning and most of that on trial and error, and 87% of configuration parameters never changed even though workloads swing with business cycles. Static configuration means you're either over-provisioned and paying for it, or under-provisioned and paging for it.

## A four-layer framework

The architecture has four layers. A data collection layer gathers telemetry: query execution statistics, resource usage and system logs. An analysis engine builds a historical knowledge base and spots recurring patterns. An optimisation engine generates recommendations such as index tuning, memory distribution and resource allocation. An implementation layer applies low-risk changes automatically and routes complex ones through human review. Abstraction layers keep it working across relational, NoSQL and cloud systems.

At the centre is a reinforcement learning model that keeps learning from outcomes, so recommendations improve as workloads shift. He cites research showing RL approaches cutting query latency sharply against traditional optimisers and handling join ordering for far more tables than classic optimisers manage.

## Humans keep the veto

The part that should reassure DBAs is the collaboration model. The AI processes huge volumes of metrics, automates index management and spots anomalies well before traditional alerts. Humans bring business context, risk assessment and long-term capacity planning. The loop runs: AI proposes, the DBA evaluates against business context, impact is measured against the prediction, approved changes ship with safeguards. He reports teams using this approach completing more strategic projects and spending far less time on routine maintenance.

## The e-commerce case

The case study is a platform whose query latency rose three to five times during peak shopping, with checkout responses over ten seconds. The framework ran alongside existing systems and analysed three months of history to find baselines and recurring bottlenecks, which is where the 0.03% finding came from. After six months, his abstract and talk report a 40% reduction in over-provisioning, a 28% drop in average query latency at peak and 17 potential bottlenecks headed off before customers noticed.

Next on his roadmap: cross-platform optimisation across heterogeneous databases, explainable recommendations so DBAs see why and not just what, a natural-language interface, and models specialised for OLTP, analytics and IoT workloads.

## Who should watch

DBAs who wonder whether AI tuning is a threat or a tool (it's pitched as a tool), and platform teams running mixed database estates. The case study is the most concrete part; the framework is a blueprint rather than open-source code.

Title: A layer-by-layer blueprint for a central patient data repository
Description: Optum's Vishal Kumar Jaiswal maps the storage, FHIR integration, matching and security layers of a central patient record at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.
Body:
A patient's story usually lives in four places at once: the EHR, the lab system, the pharmacy and the insurer's claims database. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Vishal Kumar Jaiswal, Senior Manager of Software Engineering at Optum and a database architect with around two decades in the field, laid out how to pull those fragments into one secure, queryable repository, layer by layer, from the storage engines up to the audit trail.

The talk works like an architecture review checklist. Each layer comes with the components Jaiswal would pick and the figures he cites from published studies of public hospital deployments, so treat it as a survey of what the research reports rather than a single production war story.

## Pick the store per data shape, then put FHIR in front

The storage layer splits by data type. PostgreSQL holds structured clinical data, MongoDB takes the unstructured material, and a cloud archive tier keeps rarely touched records cheap while still answering quickly. Above that sits the integration layer: a FHIR API gateway, an HL7 message processor for the older feeds, ETL pipelines for bulk loads and a real-time event bus for clinical workflows that cannot wait for a nightly batch.

The point Jaiswal keeps returning to is that FHIR is the contract. Once every source speaks it, the rest of the system stops caring whether a record started life as an HL7 v2 message or a CSV export from a claims vendor. He also covers SMART on FHIR for authorisation, which is what lets third-party apps read the repository without each one inventing its own login.

## Patient matching is a machine learning problem in disguise

The most ML-shaped part of the talk is deduplication. The same person shows up with a typo in one system and a maiden name in another, and a central repository is only as good as its ability to decide that two rows are one human. Jaiswal walks through both families of approach:

- **Deterministic matching**: combine identifiers with rules, and improve it by looking at temporal patterns (how a record changed over time). He cites a 15-institution study where multifactor deterministic matching pushed false positives down to 0.03%.
- **Probabilistic matching**: machine learning models that score how likely two records are the same patient. The cited research reports a 92.4% match rate even when demographic data is incomplete.

In practice you run both: rules for the obvious matches, a model for the messy middle.

## Keep copies in sync with CDC, not cron jobs

For real-time synchronisation he recommends change data capture feeding an event publication layer through message queues, plus explicit conflict resolution when two systems update the same record. His suggestion is a version-vector style mechanism, which is the distributed systems answer to the question of who wins when the lab and the clinic both edit the allergy list.

## Security is four separate jobs

The security section is the most practical part of the talk. Jaiswal separates it into:

1. **Encryption**: AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.3 in transit, and field-level encryption for the most sensitive elements.
2. **Access control**: role-based access control combined with attribute-based rules, because a role alone cannot express this nurse, this ward, this shift.
3. **Break-glass access**: an emergency path to critical patient data, which the cited research says can work within 30 seconds while staying audited.
4. **Audit trails**: tamper-evident logging, including blockchain-based trails some organisations use to prove nothing was rewritten.

The break-glass point deserves more attention than it usually gets. A system that is perfectly locked down and blocks a doctor in an emergency has failed at its actual job.

## Performance comes from boring, well-placed indexes

The closing sections cover composite and partial indexes for frequent clinical query paths, full-text search for clinical notes, write-through caching to keep cached data consistent, horizontal sharding by patient ID, and monitoring and alerting tuned to catch problems before users do. None of this is exotic; the value is in seeing it applied to clinical data volumes in one place.

## Who should watch

Data architects and platform engineers in healthcare who are scoping a central repository or a FHIR integration layer will get a solid checklist. If you work outside healthcare, the patient-matching and break-glass sections are the parts that transfer best. Engineers looking for a code-level FHIR walkthrough should pair it with something more hands-on.

Title: Migrate a monolith one bounded context at a time, not in a big bang
Description: Amlan Ghosh at Conf42 SRE 2025 lays out a four-phase, event-sourced path from monolith to event-driven microservices with zero-downtime traffic shifting.
Body:
The riskiest moment in a monolith migration is the cutover weekend, so Amlan Ghosh's answer is to never have one. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Ghosh, an architect with over two decades of modernization work, walked through a framework for moving from a monolith to event-driven microservices in small, reversible steps, with event sourcing as the safety net.

He opens with the reasons migrations hurt. In his figures, 68% of enterprises name stability as their main migration worry, 43% of migrations fail on the first attempt because of thin architecture planning, and 37% run over budget. The fix he proposes is less about new technology and more about order of operations.

## Draw the boundaries before you cut

The framework starts with domain-driven design. Bounded contexts give each future service a clear edge around one piece of business logic, and a ubiquitous language keeps developers and domain experts talking about the same thing. Ghosh recommends context mapping and event storming sessions with the domain experts to find the subdomains and the events that flow between them. If you skip this, you tend to rebuild the monolith as a set of services that all call each other, which is the same ball of mud with more network hops.

## The event log is your undo button

Event sourcing carries most of the reliability argument. Every state change is captured as an immutable, timestamped event in an append-only log, and that log becomes the system's source of truth. Current state is rebuilt by replaying the stream, and projections build read models from the same events. For an SRE that means debugging by replay, audit trails for compliance, and a way to recover from a bad deploy by reconstructing state at a known point. Ghosh names Apache Kafka, EventStore and the Axon Framework as the usual tools.

His schema rules are practical: put an explicit version in the event metadata, name events in the domain's language, carry creation timestamps and causal metadata, and make each event self-contained so consumers do not need to call back for context.

## Run old and new side by side

The case study is a Fortune 500 retailer, migrated in four phases:

1. **Assessment**: model the domains and identify service boundaries.
2. **Event schema design**: the team defined 47 distinct event types plus a versioning strategy.
3. **Parallel run**: build the microservices alongside the legacy monolith, which stays in service.
4. **Progressive migration**: shift traffic incrementally, which he reports was done with zero downtime.

He contrasts this with the traditional approach: a big-bang cutover, an extended downtime window, a migrated monolithic database, manual verification and limited rollback. The event-driven route instead uses event-based data synchronisation, automated canary analysis and instant rollback.

## Patterns that keep the new system standing

Once services exist, the usual resilience kit applies: circuit breakers that fail fast when a dependency is unhealthy, bulkheads with separate resource and thread pools, and retries with exponential backoff, jitter and dead letter queues. Monitoring ties it together with correlation IDs across services, alerts on SLO violations, distributed tracing and telemetry in every event flow.

## Who should watch

Architects and SREs staring at a monolith migration plan who want a checklist for sequencing it. This is a framework talk at the slide level: you get the phases, patterns and a case study summary, not code or Kafka configuration. If you already run event sourcing in production, the roadmap at the end (domain analysis, event storming, schema design, infrastructure, then one bounded context at a time) is a good sanity check for your own plan.

Title: Factories can run SRE too, with SLOs on the assembly line
Description: Kumar Nayan at Conf42 SRE 2025 on bringing SLOs, observability and a four-phase rollout to manufacturing, from PLCs on the shop floor to the cloud.
Body:
A robotic welding station can have an SLO. That's the premise of Kumar Nayan's talk at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025: the practices Google built for web services (service level objectives, observability, blameless incident culture) transfer to manufacturing, provided you treat the factory as one stack running from PLCs on the shop floor to analytics in the cloud. He pairs the argument with an automotive case study and a four-phase rollout plan.

It's a structured half-hour talk aimed at people who'll have to sell SRE to plant managers as much as engineers.

## The reliability crisis is a firefighting habit

Nayan starts with the cost of the status quo, citing research that an hour of unplanned downtime can cost upward of $260,000 across industries, before counting backlogs, late deliveries and lost trust. He blames three habits: break-fix maintenance that waits for failure, operational data scattered across legacy and modern systems with no unified view, and uptime metrics that look fine on paper while hiding constant small disruptions. His line for it is building a resilient vessel instead of patching leaks in a sinking ship.

## One stack from PLC to cloud

The holistic model is the key idea. Manufacturing reliability spans four layers: shop floor systems (PLCs, HMIs, robotics and machine controllers, each with its own protocols and timing), edge computing such as manufacturing execution systems running near the line, core infrastructure (on-prem servers, databases and networks handling everything from batch scheduling to MRP), and cloud services hosting analytics, digital twins and multi-plant enterprise apps.

Each layer needs aligned, measured reliability goals. His example: if a cloud digital twin predicts machine failures from real-time feeds, those feeds need their own uptime SLO, because when the feed fails, predictive maintenance silently stops working. Reliability stops being an engineering problem or an IT problem and becomes a shared objective.

## Observability as a pyramid

He presents monitoring as four layers: comprehensive data collection from PLCs, edge devices, server logs and cloud apps at the base; real-time dashboards showing overall equipment effectiveness, machine states and SLO compliance; contextual correlation, such as tying a slowing robotic arm to an upstream jam sensor or an out-of-spec batch of raw material; and predictive analytics on vibration, temperature, throughput and cycle times at the top. The practical payoff is scheduling a maintenance window when a machine trends out of tolerance instead of waiting for it to break.

Three manufacturing-specific patterns come out of this: reliability for industrial control systems that can't simply be patched or rebooted, so they get redundancy and protocol-aware monitoring instead; a framework that unifies OT and IT observability and accountability; and digital twins as a safe place to simulate failures and train incident response.

## An automaker's numbers

The case study is an unnamed automotive manufacturer that defined SLOs for robotic welding, paint shops and final assembly, its three repeat trouble spots, and consolidated sensor, controller and enterprise data into one dashboard. He reports mean time to recovery down 62%, unplanned downtime down by around 45 to 47%, and an estimated $3.2 million a year saved. He calls the cultural shift the biggest outcome: management began tracking how reliably output was achieved, not just how much was produced.

## Four phases, and the obstacles

The rollout runs assess (inventory, pain points, baselines), pilot (one or two critical systems, an SLO such as 99% or 99.9% uptime, monitoring and incident response), scale (more lines, automation, cross-functional OT/IT teams), then optimise (machine learning and digital twins for prediction). The challenges are honest ones: machines 20 to 50 years old with no telemetry, which need industrial gateways, protocol converters and retrofitted sensors; picking metrics that reflect real production goals, which needs operations, maintenance and quality in the room; and long-tenured staff sceptical of a new methodology. He frames it as a marathon, not a sprint.

## Who should watch

SREs moving into industrial or IoT companies, OT engineers who keep hearing the word SLO, and anyone building the business case for observability on a factory floor.

Title: Integration platforms need SLOs for messages, not just endpoints
Description: Logicgate's Tejaswi Katta at Conf42 SRE 2025 on applying SRE to cloud-native integration with SLOs, tracing, chaos tests and SLO-gated rollbacks.
Body:
The integration layer is where every other team's outage becomes your incident. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Tejaswi Katta, Lead Software Engineer at Logicgate Technologies, laid out how SRE principles apply to cloud-native integration platforms: SLOs that cover asynchronous message delivery as well as synchronous calls, tracing at every integration boundary, chaos experiments against brokers and gateways, and deployments that roll themselves back when SLOs slip.

It's a short framework talk with one financial services case study.

## From ESB to SRE-driven integration

Katta traces the evolution: monolithic point-to-point connections, then service-oriented architecture with enterprise service buses and better reuse, then cloud-native integration with distributed microservices and containers. Each step multiplied the number of services and data sources, and complexity grew with them. The next step, in his framing, is an SRE-driven approach built on observability and automated operations, because traditional monitoring struggles with dynamic scaling and cross-cloud dependencies.

## SLOs that understand asynchronous work

The most useful section is on defining service level objectives for integration. He splits them three ways:

- **Availability** for integration endpoints, message brokers and API gateways, measured both as synchronous request success rates and as asynchronous message delivery guarantees.
- **Latency** for data processing pipelines, with averages and percentiles, plus context-aware thresholds that account for payload size and complexity. A large batch file and a tiny event shouldn't share a latency target.
- **Throughput** for message rates, concurrent connections and transaction volume, including elasticity: how quickly the system scales to meet a spike.

That second point is the one most integration teams miss. A single latency SLO across wildly different payloads either alerts constantly or never.

## Trace every boundary, then break things on purpose

On observability, Katta wants instrumentation at every integration boundary, with tracing, metrics and logs aggregated centrally, dashboards for end-to-end flow health, and alerting tied to SLOs to cut mean time to diagnose. Chaos engineering follows the scientific method: form a hypothesis, inject a controlled failure such as API rate limiting or a message broker outage, measure the response against your SLOs, refine the design. The output is integration flows that heal themselves and keep running under pressure.

## A case study with big numbers

His example is a global financial services firm that moved a legacy integration architecture to a cloud-native platform supporting over 3,000 APIs and more than 500 million daily transactions. The reported results: 99.99% availability, incident response times down 70%, five times the throughput, and 85% of incident remediation automated. He credits comprehensive observability and automated canary analysis. The firm isn't named, so take the figures as a description of the target state rather than a benchmark.

## Security and automation in the same breath

Security gets a zero-trust treatment: service-to-service authentication regardless of network location, centralised secrets with automated credential rotation, data lineage for sensitive fields flowing through pipelines, and API gateways with threat detection for unusual traffic. Automation covers configuration as code managed through GitOps, blue-green and canary deployments that roll back automatically when SLOs are breached, predefined runbooks, and predictive capacity scaling from historical patterns. The culture piece is shared accountability between development, operations and business teams, with blameless postmortems.

His roadmap is four steps: assess current flows and reliability metrics, define business-aligned SLOs, instrument everything with consistent telemetry, then automate operations with reliability gates in CI/CD.

## Who should watch

Teams that own an ESB, an iPaaS or a homegrown integration hub and have never been sure what their SLO should be. It's an outline rather than a build-along, but the SLO breakdown is worth stealing.

Title: Enterprise blockchain buys tamper evidence and pays in throughput
Description: Sharath Chandra Adupa at Conf42 SRE 2025 on blockchain for data integrity in finance, supply chain, healthcare and IoT, and the costs that slow adoption.
Body:
A ledger that every node keeps a copy of is hard to quietly edit, and that is the entire security pitch. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Sharath Chandra Adupa, who has more than 20 years in IT across the financial and health sectors, gave an overview of blockchain as an enterprise data integrity tool: what the architecture guarantees, where finance, supply chain, healthcare and IoT use it, and the governance, interoperability and throughput problems that keep projects late and over budget.

It's a short introductory talk, and its most useful part is the second half, where the costs get as much airtime as the benefits.

## What the architecture actually guarantees

Adupa grounds blockchain in distributed ledger technology: synchronised, cryptographically secured copies of the entire transaction history held by many independent participants, so no single entity controls the data and there's no single point of failure to attack. The four properties he lists are cryptographic security, immutability, transparency and smart contracts.

On immutability he's specific: a transaction only becomes effectively permanent after consensus validation, and he cites Bitcoin's convention of six confirmations. On privacy, he describes the balance public chains strike: every transaction is visible, but participants appear as addresses rather than real identities. The two cryptographic workhorses are hashing and digital signatures.

For an SRE audience, the useful translation is that blockchain gives you tamper evidence and decentralised trust. It doesn't make your data correct; it makes changes to it detectable.

## Where it's used, by industry

The talk tours four sectors with reported figures:

- **Financial services:** settlement moving from T+3 toward near real time, cross-border payments in minutes instead of three to five days, and KYC/AML checks automated through smart contracts.
- **Supply chain:** product tracking in seconds, fewer documentation errors, provenance to fight counterfeit pharmaceuticals and food, and recalls handled in hours rather than weeks.
- **Healthcare:** HIPAA-compliant sharing of electronic health records between providers, with less reconciliation work.
- **IoT:** fewer vulnerabilities than centralised designs, supply chain traceability and less unplanned downtime in smart factories.

The percentages come thick and fast and aren't tied to named deployments, so treat them as illustrations of the claimed upside.

## The bill arrives in the second half

This is where the talk earns its slot. Adupa lists what he presents as the real constraints:

- **Integration:** 30 to 40% of project timelines spent on legacy compatibility, and timelines running 50 to 60% beyond projections.
- **Regulation:** 40 to 50% of implementation budgets going to compliance.
- **Throughput:** enterprise architectures limited to around 100 to 300 transactions per second, with final settlement averaging three to five minutes.
- **People and money:** most enterprises struggling to hire blockchain expertise, and comprehensive deployments costing from around $500,000 up to $1 million.
- **Governance and interoperability:** 40% of projects delayed by governance decisions, and only 15% achieving cross-chain functionality.

If you've been asked whether blockchain should back your audit log, that list is your first conversation. A throughput ceiling in the hundreds of transactions per second and minutes to finality are reliability properties, and they rule out a lot of workloads before the security argument starts.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leads asked to evaluate blockchain for integrity or audit use cases, especially in finance and healthcare. Engineers looking for implementation detail, consensus internals or code will want a hands-on talk instead.

Title: Healthcare payers can price provider contracts with data, not paper
Description: Uday Bag of Cognizant shows at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 how predictive models can set provider contract rates and cut payment discrepancies.
Body:
In US healthcare, the rate an insurer pays for an office visit is often settled through paper contracts, back-and-forth emails and manual data entry, and every manual step is a chance for a payment error. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Uday Bag, Lead Product Consultant at Cognizant, makes the case for replacing that process with predictive models that propose fair rates from historical data and feed them straight into claims workflows.

It's a domain talk rather than an ML one. You won't see model architectures, but you will get a clear picture of a corner of health insurance most engineers never see, and why it's ripe for automation.

## The problem: contracts by hand

Bag explains the setup for outsiders. Healthcare payers (insurers) negotiate rates with providers: individual practitioners, provider groups and hospitals. Hospital contracts are especially complex, and a payer may need to contract with many hospitals in a single county. The process is largely manual. Contracts are reviewed, rates go back and forth, and agreed numbers are keyed into systems by hand.

The knock-on effects stack up: human errors become payment discrepancies, providers get paid late or wrong, a whole department carries the administrative load, and the payer-provider relationship sours.

## What AI changes

His proposal has three parts. Predictive analysis forecasts an optimal rate for a service, such as an office visit or a specialist visit in a given specialty, from historical data, market trends and patterns, so negotiations start from a defensible number. Real-time adjustment lets contracts update dynamically instead of waiting for someone to correct a rate that claims processing picks up later. And error prevention follows from the first two: fewer hand-keyed numbers, fewer discrepancies.

The integration point matters. Payer systems are often silos: capitation, claims adjudication, validation and clinical edits each run their own engine. Bag argues that data-driven rates built into the workflow let those engines talk to each other during adjudication.

## Who's already doing it

His industry examples include his own employer's tooling: Cognizant's NetworX Modeler models future price changes so both sides can see what a rate will look like next year. He also points to Medicaid payers using AI-driven approaches to shorten negotiations, and to UnitedHealthcare as an example of the scale involved, with 110 billion dollars in Q1 2025 revenue. He mentions case studies reporting contracts locked in roughly 42% faster, though from smaller pilots rather than full-scale rollouts. Bring your own scepticism to vendor examples.

## Rolling it out

The implementation plan is pragmatic. Assess the current state (legacy systems, data quality, whether data can move between systems), define the strategy and pick the tool, set up governance because healthcare data is heavily regulated, pilot on a small set of contracts and measure, then scale. Train the staff who'll run it. Measure the outcome in KPIs and ROI.

## What's next

Bag's future list: NLP to read contract language and remove manual review, closed in-house blockchain systems with smart contracts for payments, contracts that adapt as CMS and state regulations change, and value-based payment tied to outcomes rather than volume.

## Who should watch

Engineers who've joined a health insurer or a healthtech vendor and need the domain primer, and product people scoping automation in payer operations. If you came for model details, this isn't that talk.

Title: Auto-WEKA, IBM AutoAI or Microsoft NNI? Picking an AutoML tool
Description: Senior data scientist Suresh Kumar Maddala compares AutoML frameworks at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 and shows where automation needs governance.
Body:
Every data scientist has lost a week to a grid search. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, senior data scientist Suresh Kumar Maddala explains how AutoML takes that week back, compares three frameworks (Auto-WEKA, IBM's AutoAI and Microsoft's Neural Network Intelligence) by what each is good and bad at, and argues that the real work moves from tuning models to governing them. His abstract puts the payoff at 60 to 80% less model development time.

Maddala brings 11 years across retail, healthcare, manufacturing and finance.

## The problem AutoML solves

Building a predictive model the old way means trying several algorithms, each with many hyperparameters, each taking many values, then comparing everything by hand. AutoML automates the pipeline from preprocessing and feature engineering through algorithm selection and hyperparameter optimisation. Maddala grounds it in three ideas: optimisation theory (search the configuration space efficiently, with Bayesian optimisation, genetic algorithms or gradient-based methods), meta-learning (carry knowledge across datasets and tasks), and computational efficiency (balance exploration against exploitation).

The second benefit is organisational. AutoML lets business analysts and domain experts build models without deep ML expertise, which is how many companies run citizen data scientist programmes.

## Three frameworks, three personalities

The comparison is the most useful part of the talk.

**Auto-WEKA** pioneered combined algorithm selection and hyperparameter optimisation, using sequential model-based configuration with Bayesian optimisation. Strong academic foundation; weak end-to-end automation, deep learning support and enterprise integration. Best for research, proofs of concept and teams already invested in WEKA.

**IBM AutoAI** covers the whole lifecycle with data preparation, feature engineering, built-in fairness checks and explainability, integrated with the Watson ecosystem. The trade-offs are vendor lock-in, cost and implementation complexity. Best for regulated industries and shops already running IBM.

**Microsoft NNI** focuses on neural networks: architecture search, hyperparameter tuning and model compression in a modular framework that supports TensorFlow and PyTorch. Steep learning curve, less help with classical ML. Best for deep learning teams with strong engineers.

He also points to end-to-end platforms such as Google Cloud AutoML and H2O Driverless AI.

## Automation creates new debts

The challenges section is honest. Automated searches produce complex models that resist explanation. They amplify bad data instead of fixing it. Generic searches struggle with specialised domains. And unmanaged adoption breeds model sprawl and technical debt. His fixes: pair AutoML with explainable AI and set interpretability thresholds per application, gate automated modelling behind data quality checks, and customise pipelines and objectives with domain knowledge. Many organisations, he notes, use tiers: AutoML for straightforward predictions, more human oversight for mission-critical ones.

His abstract adds a case of a global automotive supplier using AutoML for predictive maintenance and cutting unplanned downtime by 35%, with most enterprises seeing positive ROI within 12 to 18 months.

## Who should watch

Data science leads evaluating AutoML platforms and managers planning a citizen data science programme. The phased roadmap at the end (assess, pilot, scale, integrate) is a reasonable project plan. Practitioners who already run Optuna or Ray Tune daily will find the theory section familiar.

Title: Generative AI in factories should start on the packaging line
Description: Kumar Nayan of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign argues at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 that generative AI moves manufacturing beyond prediction.
Body:
A predictive model tells you a press brake will probably fail in the next 24 hours. A generative model asks what press-brake configuration would raise throughput and avoid the failure altogether, then hands you a toolpath for your CAM system. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Kumar Nayan of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign uses that contrast to explain why generative AI is a different kind of tool on the factory floor, and why the first project should be a packaging line rather than the flagship process.

Nayan says up front that this isn't a technical talk. It's a business picture: results, challenges and a four-phase playbook, aimed at people who have to justify the investment.

## The numbers he leads with

His case examples come with big figures. An aerospace supplier cut a part's concept-to-certification cycle from about 18 months to around 11 using generative design, while still meeting FAA standards. A consumer packaged goods plant used a generative scheduling agent and saw unplanned downtime drop by roughly a third. A tier-one auto supplier commercialised more of its concepts because generative simulation flagged manufacturability problems before the first prototype. He says a meta-analysis across more than 60 plants on three continents shows gains of similar magnitude. The cases are anonymised, so take them as illustrations rather than benchmarks.

## Three floor-level wins

On the shop floor he picks three things plant managers care about. Bottlenecks: real-time layout engines that use sensor feeds to rebalance material flow and autonomous mobile robot routes, with plants reporting fewer micro-stops. Energy: a European glass manufacturer used a generative optimiser that predicted furnace thermal inertia hours in advance, so power draw follows demand, saving around 2 million euros a year. Changeovers: during Covid, an electronics line switching from automotive sensors to ventilator boards got new SMT recipes overnight from a generative process planner instead of a two-week revalidation.

Supply chains get the same treatment: models that blend weather, traffic and supplier-health signals to flag shortages weeks ahead, AI-compiled and risk-scored alternative suppliers, and automatic logistics rerouting.

## The hurdles are about data and secrets

Nayan doesn't sugarcoat the problems. Data quality comes first: legacy machines without sensors, PLC timestamps out of sync, and ten different spellings of the same part ID. His fix is a modern data fabric with a single data owner. Second is IP: generative models ingest process know-how, so without strict access controls and federated options you risk leaking trade secrets, which makes zero trust a requirement. Third is bias and drift: a model trained on history may favour old plastics over new recyclable designs and quietly undermine sustainability targets.

## The playbook

His rollout has four phases: assessment (two to six weeks), data preparation (six to eight), a pilot on one contained use case (eight to twelve), then ongoing scaling with AIOps monitoring, change-management training, regular stakeholder demos and a rollback plan you hope to never use.

The three actions to take home: run a readiness assessment covering data, talent and culture; choose a lighthouse pilot with high value and low political resistance (the packaging line, not the flagship); and publish a 12-month roadmap tied to financial and ESG KPIs.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and plant or operations leaders building a business case for generative AI, and data teams who need to speak the language of OEE and changeovers. Engineers looking for model internals should know it's a strategy talk.

Title: Six models, one Walmart dataset, and why XGBoost won the forecast
Description: Jubin Thomas of Signet Jewelers compares six regressors on Walmart weekly sales at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025; XGBoost tops the test set.
Body:
K-nearest neighbours scored a perfect 100% on the training data and then lost to XGBoost on the data it hadn't seen. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Jubin Thomas, Technical Architect at Signet Jewelers with 15 years in supply chain and retail and a senior IEEE member, runs six regression models against public Walmart sales data and shows why gradient boosting came out on top for demand forecasting.

It's a short, focused talk: one dataset, one comparison, one recommendation. That makes it a clean worked example for anyone learning to evaluate forecasting models.

## Demand forecasting versus sales forecasting

Thomas separates the two. Demand forecasting estimates customer demand per store-and-item combination from history, and drives inventory planning and fewer stockouts. Sales forecasting estimates future sales from history, market trends, seasonality and external factors, and drives staffing, budgets and marketing. Both are the same maths with different consumers.

## The dataset

The Walmart dataset is publicly available and covers 45 US stores. Each row has the store, the week, weekly sales (the target), a holiday flag, temperature, fuel price, the consumer price index and unemployment. The economic indicators are what make it more interesting than a plain time series: you can test whether CPI or fuel prices carry signal beyond the calendar. The abstract notes the usual preparation, handling missing values and encoding categorical features, before a train and test split.

## The bake-off

Six models, all available off the shelf in Python. The scores are as the slides present them, training first, then test:

- **Linear regression** with degree-3 polynomial features: 97.7 and 95.8.
- **Ridge regression**, also degree 3: the same 97.7 and 95.8.
- **KNN** with three neighbours: 100 and 91.9, the classic overfitting picture.
- **Decision tree**: 97.3 and 93.3.
- **Random forest** with 75 trees: 99.1 and 95.6.
- **XGBoost regressor**: 99.9 and 97.2, the best test score in the experiment.

The abstract adds that XGBoost also beat decision tree and linear regression across MAE, MSE and RMSE. The gap between the train and test columns is the lesson as much as the winner: the model that memorises best isn't the one that forecasts best.

## What the data says

The correlation matrix shows weekly sales moving with the holiday flag, and temperature moving with fuel price. XGBoost's feature importance ranks the store and CPI as the strongest predictors, ahead of temperature and holidays. So where you sell and how prices are moving matter more than whether it was hot that week.

## Why gradient boosting won

Thomas gives three reasons: gradient boosting with regularisation that limits overfitting, effective handling of missing values and skewed distributions, and a highly tunable model with strong cross-validation support. His recommendations follow from that. Simple models are faster but less accurate. XGBoost is the pick for accurate, scalable forecasting. And since this run used basic parameters, ensembling and hyperparameter tuning should squeeze out more on harder data.

## Who should watch

Analysts and engineers starting out in retail forecasting who want a concrete model-comparison template, and students who need a reminder that a perfect training score is a warning sign. If you already tune LightGBM against Prophet for a living, this is a refresher, not a revelation.

Title: Microservices resilience comes from patterns, tests and a slow migration
Description: Suresh Kumar Gundala at Conf42 SRE 2025 on circuit breakers, sagas, contract tests and strangling a monolith one service at a time.
Body:
In a monolith, one bad component takes the whole shop down. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Suresh Kumar Gundala, an enterprise architect with more than 17 years designing distributed systems, APIs and micro-UI applications, made the case that microservices buy resilience through fault isolation, and laid out the patterns, testing layers and migration steps that make the isolation real.

It's a broad survey aimed at teams considering or early in a migration. If you've run microservices in production for years, much of it will be familiar; the testing and migration sections are the most useful parts.

## Fault isolation is the resilience argument

Gundala's opening contrast: when a monolith fails, customers lose the entire application; when one microservice fails, only its feature degrades and users keep working with the rest. The core principles follow from that: service independence, modularity around business capabilities (user management, payments, inventory), fault isolation and loose coupling through well-defined APIs. Add decentralised data ownership, independent scaling, a CI/CD pipeline per service and observability per team.

## Four patterns doing the heavy lifting

- **Circuit breaker.** Like its electrical namesake, it stops calls to a failing service and routes them to fallback logic, so one failure doesn't cascade.
- **Saga.** Distributed transactions become a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions if a step fails, which keeps data consistent under high concurrency such as e-commerce peaks.
- **API gateway.** One entry point that handles routing, authentication, rate limiting and protocol translation.
- **Containerisation.** Docker and Kubernetes for consistency across environments and dynamic orchestration.

Each comes with an improvement percentage in the talk. They're presented as industry figures without sources, so the patterns are the takeaway, not the numbers.

## A luxury retailer's monolith

The case study is an anonymised luxury e-commerce retailer whose monolith needed up to six weeks to roll out a feature and had to be duplicated wholesale to scale, running infrastructure utilisation at 87%. After breaking it into services, utilisation dropped to 42% and operational costs fell by 35%, while the site handled peak shopping traffic. The lesson that transfers: scaling a monolith means paying for copies of everything, including the parts that aren't busy.

## Testing is where distributed systems bite

Gundala is candid that testing gets harder: in a monolith you test one thing, in microservices you test many things talking to each other in dynamic ways. His layers:

- **Unit tests** per service, without external dependencies.
- **Integration tests** for protocols, data flows and shared APIs between deployed services.
- **Contract tests** so providers and consumers agree on API behaviour before a deploy breaks someone.
- **Chaos tests** that inject failures to prove the resilience you designed for.

Observability gets the same treatment: metrics per service, distributed tracing to pinpoint the failing hop, centralised logging and proactive alerting.

## Migrate like a strangler fig

The migration advice is the part to keep. Start with decomposition analysis to find bounded contexts inside the monolith. Use the strangler pattern to replace functionality incrementally rather than attempting a big-bang rewrite. Pick a non-critical pilot service so the team learns deployment, management and monitoring on something that can fail safely. Build the supporting ecosystem (infrastructure, tooling, processes) before you need it. He's also direct about the human cost: team restructuring, coordination between services and a real learning curve for engineers used to monoliths.

## Who should watch

Architects and tech leads planning a monolith breakup, and developers who've been told they're "moving to microservices" and want the vocabulary. Teams already deep into service meshes can skip to the testing and migration sections.

Title: Cloud-native uptime in one checklist, from failover to SLOs
Description: Adobe's Viralkumar Ahire at Conf42 SRE 2025 gives a lightning tour of multi-region failover, self-healing automation and AI-assisted reliability.
Body:
Redundancy you haven't tested is a rumour. That's the sharpest line of thinking in Viralkumar Ahire's talk at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, where the Senior Cloud Platform Developer at Adobe, with over 20 years in the industry, compressed cloud-native reliability into a few minutes: multi-region failover you actually drill, self-healing automation so a human isn't paged for the routine, AI to cut alert noise, and SLOs to keep everyone honest.

This is a lightning talk, a handful of minutes long. Think of it as a checklist you can hand to a team starting out, not a case study.

## Reliability is an architecture goal

Ahire's starting point is that downtime is a business risk before it's a technical one: revenue, customer satisfaction and brand trust all take the hit. In always-on systems, reliability has to be intentional. Reacting to incidents isn't enough; you need to prevent them, detect them early and recover fast, which starts with treating reliability as a core architectural goal rather than an operations afterthought.

He names the familiar cloud-native pains: latency spikes from autoscaling, cascading failures between services, and fatigue from noisy alerts, all amplified by ephemeral infrastructure. The fix he points to is visibility: knowing what is happening, when and why.

## Multi-region only counts if you drill it

Geographic redundancy protects against zone outages, network disruption and provider failures. Ahire's caveat is the useful part: redundancy isn't enough, you have to test it, with regular failover drills, chaos engineering and synthetic traffic before a real incident does the testing for you. Active-active gives the best availability but costs more engineering effort, a trade-off worth making explicit.

## Humans don't scale, runbooks can

On self-healing he lists the toolbox: Kubernetes restarting containers, Terraform rebuilding infrastructure declaratively, Ansible automating incident responses. The goal is detect, react and recover, ideally without paging anyone at 3am.

He's measured about AI. Models can forecast anomalies, filter alerts to reduce fatigue and speed up root cause analysis, and he names New Relic AI, Dynatrace and Azure Monitor as platforms already embedding it. His framing is that this is about giving engineers superpowers, not replacing them.

## The checklist

His closing list is worth pinning:

- Design for failure and simulate it with chaos tools.
- Automate deployments.
- Observe everything: logs, metrics, traces and real user data.
- Make reliability a shared responsibility, not just the SRE team's job.
- Define SLIs, SLOs and error budgets.
- Adopt infrastructure as code and GitOps workflows.

The takeaway he leaves with is that resilience is ultimately about earning users' trust, and that cloud-native reliability is a continuous journey of better design, smarter automation and a collaborative culture.

## Who should watch

Teams early in their cloud-native reliability journey and managers who need a five-minute primer before a planning session. Experienced SREs won't find new material here, but it's a tidy summary to share.
