Title: An LLM can write your PromQL if your metrics are documented
Description: Nomba's David Asamu at Conf42 SRE 2025 on PromChat, an open-source tool that turns plain questions into PromQL and answers back in natural language.
Body:
Mid-incident, nobody wants to remember whether that metric is a counter or a histogram. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, David Asamu, Tech Lead Manager of the SRE team at Nomba, showed an open-source project that lets you ask Prometheus questions in plain English: an LLM agent reads the metric metadata, writes the PromQL, runs it, and explains the result. His headline finding is that off-the-shelf models can already write PromQL with no fine-tuning, and that the real bottleneck is how well your metrics are documented.

This is a builder's talk, with architecture, real queries from the backend logs, and a candid look at where it failed.

## The loop, end to end

The flow starts and ends in natural language. A question arrives from a web app or a Slack app, hits a REST backend, and goes to an AI agent. The agent sends the question to the LLM along with metadata from the Prometheus metadata API, which lists every metric, its type and its help text, effectively the schema of your monitoring data. Via function calling, the LLM uses two tools: one to fetch metadata and one to run a query. The result goes back through the LLM to be phrased as an answer.

Asamu's motivation came from the chat-with-your-database projects in the data world. Why not metrics? The payoffs he lists: lower cognitive load during incidents, fewer bespoke Grafana dashboards for every new question, and a gentler PromQL learning curve.

## Two data sources, one surprise

He demoed against two Prometheus instances. The first scraped node exporter on his own Mac, answering questions about CPU, disk, memory and, yes, battery percentage. The second was the public demo Prometheus from PromLabs, whose demo service exposes custom metrics including one that reports whether today is a holiday.

Asking whether today is a holiday produced a query on the holiday gauge, got back 1, and the model used the help text to know that 1 means yes. Asking how many items had shipped today was the better trick: the model wrote an increase over one day on the shipped-items counter, got three series back (one per demo service instance), and correctly summed them into one total.

## When the cheap model got it wrong

The third question, whether the demo API was slower than usual, came back empty. The query was valid PromQL; it just didn't answer the question. On Gemini 1.5 Flash, the model misread intent. Switching to the Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking model produced a rate-based query over the histogram, and the answer identified one API path with far more 500s and much higher latency than the rest. That's an incident lead you'd want in seconds.

## What he learned

- **No fine-tuning needed.** The only prompt change was one-shot prompting with an example, so the model returned bare PromQL instead of wrapping it in extra characters that Prometheus rejected.
- **Bigger thinking models write better complex queries;** lighter ones handle the simple cases.
- **Documentation is the ceiling.** Without help text saying what 1 and 0 mean for the holiday metric, the model couldn't interpret the answer. Labels are the bigger gap, because the metadata API rarely describes them, which is exactly what you need for filtering.
- **Phrasing changes results.** Leave out the time window and the model picks one; ask with an explicit window and the answers become consistent.

Next on his list: visualisations alongside text answers, sources beyond Prometheus, and memory so the system learns from user corrections. The code is open source on GitHub and there is a hosted web version running on his personal API key, so expect rate limits.

## Who should watch

SREs curious about LLM copilots for observability, and anyone who maintains Prometheus exporters, because this talk is the best argument yet for writing proper HELP strings.

Title: Securing enterprise AI is mostly zero trust you should already have
Description: Chintan Udeshi of Palo Alto Networks lays out AI threats and controls at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, from model poisoning to runtime protection.
Body:
Log4j sat in production software for more than seven years before anyone noticed it, and Chintan Udeshi uses that fact to explain why AI security can't stop at patching. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Udeshi, Principal Product Manager at Palo Alto Networks working on AI, container and runtime security, walks through the new threats AI brings and argues that most of the defence is the zero trust discipline enterprises should already practise, applied to models and their data.

It's a vendor-neutral talk: he works at a security company but doesn't pitch a product. It reads as a structured checklist for teams about to put AI into critical systems.

## Why the stakes went up

Udeshi cites a PwC report in which around 86% of executives expected AI to become mainstream technology in 2025, with 60% of organisations planning to put it into mission-critical infrastructure. Put a model into the core and its exposure grows with it. He also brings field notes from the RSA Conference in San Francisco, where many companies he spoke to had already shipped customer-facing chatbots and virtual assistants.

## The new attack surface

He sorts AI threats into two tiers. The first tier is the obvious one: poisoned training data that corrupts the system's integrity, privacy failures (picture a chatbot handing out a customer's Social Security number), AI-generated misinformation and deepfakes at scale, and regulatory exposure that varies by industry and region.

The second tier is where it gets uncomfortable. Realistic impersonations aimed at executives. Phishing personalised for every recipient, then lateral movement once inside. Model poisoning, which bends outputs rather than data. And adversarial probing, where attackers feed varied inputs to map what a model reveals and then reverse-engineer its weaknesses. Your model's error messages are now part of your attack surface.

## The controls, layer by layer

The defensive half is methodical. Protect the model itself against DDoS, prompt injection and data leakage, and secure traffic between application and model. Encrypt data at rest so a stolen database is useless. Use role-based access control to shrink who can touch what.

Then zero trust. Udeshi contrasts it with the old perimeter model, where anything from inside the network was trusted: with data spread across data centres and public clouds, every request gets authenticated, MFA is the default, and every user and service gets least privilege. Micro-segmentation stops malware from spreading laterally when one part is compromised. Runtime protection watches live traffic for anomalies, because some vulnerabilities, Log4j-style, are unknown until they aren't. His concrete monitoring example: if all your offices are in the US, an access attempt from another continent should be flagged.

## Security from day one, regulation all the way through

On the lifecycle he is blunt: security is usually an afterthought in architecture, and it shouldn't be. Write security requirements up front, enforce secure coding standards and strict access control, run penetration and stress tests, schedule vulnerability assessments and attack simulations, and keep tested backups and a recovery plan.

The compliance tour covers HIPAA for healthcare, FIPS for finance, FedRAMP, GDPR's consent, data minimisation and explanations for automated decisions, and the EU AI Act's risk categories and prohibited practices. He ends on ethics: balanced training data, documented controls, data minimisation and humans who can override the model.

## Who should watch

Engineering leads and architects about to put AI into a regulated or mission-critical path, and security people who need a shared vocabulary with ML teams. Seasoned AppSec engineers will know the controls; the threat taxonomy is the part to borrow.

Title: Retail AI is a data problem wearing a chatbot costume
Description: Hari Prasad Bomma of Risamsoft maps retail AI at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, from inventory forecasting to the six kinds of data that feed it.
Body:
A chatbot answering a question about stock is also recording a demand signal. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Hari Prasad Bomma, Senior Data Engineer at Risamsoft with 18 years in the field, presents AI in retail as one connected system: the assistant collects intent, intent feeds forecasting, forecasting drives restocking. His point is that the value comes from wiring the pieces together, and that the wiring is made of data.

It's an overview talk based on his published article of the same name, and it covers a lot of ground: trends, applications, technologies, frameworks, data types and a case study.

## Three trends, one expectation

Bomma frames the market with a projection of AI in retail growing from 26.9 billion dollars in 2023 to over 60 billion by 2030, then names three trends. Hyper-personalisation uses purchase history, location and other touchpoints to tailor the experience. Real-time dynamic pricing, long used by airlines and hotels, arrives in stores; a grocery shop can move prices with expiry dates or foot traffic. And physical stores catch up with e-commerce through footfall analytics, automated checkout and computer vision that tracks shelf interactions.

The applications are the familiar list done in order: inventory management that predicts buying trends weeks ahead, time-series demand forecasting (stock raincoats before the wet season), recommendations, NLP assistants that handle FAQs and returns around the clock, fraud detection and sentiment analysis of reviews.

## Pick the framework by the problem

The technology section pairs core capabilities with the data they need: NLP with text and speech, computer vision with images and video, predictive analytics with structured sales and transactions, recommendation engines with behaviour. Then the frameworks. TensorFlow for forecasting and shelf-image stock detection. PyTorch for chatbots, dynamic pricing and sentiment. Azure AI for managed deployment with anomaly detection and product tagging. Amazon SageMaker for personalisation, supply chain and search ranking.

His rule of thumb: optimising logistics points at TensorFlow or SageMaker, building a conversational assistant points at PyTorch. You don't need to reinvent the wheel.

## Six kinds of data, one quality bar

The most useful slide breaks retail data into six types: time series (sales, foot traffic, seasonality, for LSTM or ARIMA forecasting), transactions (SKUs, payments, discounts, store and customer IDs), text (reviews and social posts), visual (camera feeds for theft detection and product categorisation), audio (voice commerce), and clickstream (every click, scroll and exit). Without clean, well-labelled and regularly refreshed data, he says, even the strongest tools aren't much use.

## The case study

Bomma's own analysis used an open retail dataset with sales history, customer demographics and transactions. He segmented customers for targeted campaigns, used regression to find seasonal and regional patterns that informed product placement and ad timing, applied predictive models to stores that kept overstocking low-demand items, ran sentiment analysis on reviews to prioritise quality control, and evaluated promotions with uplift modelling. It's a sensible template for a first retail ML project with open tools and Python.

## Who should watch

Data engineers moving into retail and retail teams scoping their first ML projects. It's a survey: experienced retail data scientists will recognise every slide, but the data-type breakdown is a good checklist to hand to a new hire.

Title: A local LLM dev stack, from Ollama to Continue in VS Code
Description: Hashnode engineer Ayodele Samuel Adebayo shows at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 how open-source LLMs run locally to take boilerplate off your plate.
Body:
Your slowest hour of the week is probably not the hard algorithm. It's wiring up state management for the fifth time. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Ayodele Samuel Adebayo, software engineer at Hashnode and technical educator (Uncle Big Bay online), makes the case that open-source LLMs running on your own machine are the cheapest way to delete that boilerplate, and he names the exact tools to do it.

The talk is practical and aimed at working developers, not ML specialists. It moves from why productivity matters, through the adoption numbers, to a concrete local setup and the rules for not getting burned.

## The adoption curve is already behind you

Adebayo leans on the 2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey: 76% of developers were using or planning to use AI tools, actual use rose to 62% from 44% a year earlier, and 81% named higher productivity as the top benefit. His read is that AI has moved into the same slot Git and Stack Overflow once took in the daily workflow. The useful question is no longer whether to use it but where.

## Why run the model yourself

The case for open-source models is control. No API quotas or rate limits, no vendor deciding your roadmap, data that stays on your hardware, and models you can tune for your own codebase. For a solo developer or a small team, that also means no surprise cloud bill and no outage on someone else's status page.

What you do with it is ordinary engineering work: generating repetitive endpoints and UI components, refactoring, writing unit tests, drafting commit messages, documenting code, producing architecture diagrams for a README, and onboarding onto an unfamiliar repository by asking it questions. He also points at AI in the Chrome console for debugging network errors, and at MCP integrations (Supabase is his example) for letting models talk to your database.

## The stack, piece by piece

His architecture is simple. A local runner serves the model: Ollama, LM Studio, or vLLM when you need optimised serving. An editor extension connects it to your IDE: Continue.dev gives Copilot-style suggestions in VS Code powered by your local model, and Tabby ML is a lightweight open-source autocomplete. For bigger ambitions, LangChain builds apps on top and OpenDevin builds autonomous dev agents with your own prompts, rules and data.

Setup follows the same order: pick a runner, plug it into the editor, point the config at your local endpoint, then write prompt templates for your stack, whether that's Next.js or plain HTML and CSS.

## Treat it like a fast, confident junior

The cautions section is the part to keep. Models hallucinate and are blind to their own mistakes, so every suggestion gets reviewed, especially around sensitive logic. Local or not, don't paste production API keys or internal code into tools you don't understand; read how the tool works and what its community says first.

His best practices: start from the real bottleneck instead of using AI because it's cool, prompt with clear context, validate everything, pick tools that fit your stack for the long term. His closing line puts it neatly: "AI is your turbo charger and not your brain."

## Who should watch

Developers who've only used hosted assistants and want to try a self-hosted setup, and team leads weighing privacy against convenience. It's an introduction, so ML engineers who already serve models with vLLM won't learn much new. Adebayo's own challenge is the right takeaway: try one open-source LLM tool for a week and see what it changes.

Title: Moving fraud detection from rules to a real-time ML pipeline
Description: Sudhakar Kandhikonda of Lord Abbett walks through an AI fraud detection build at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, from Kafka ingestion to graph analysis of fraud rings.
Body:
Fraud that takes 27 hours to spot has usually left the building. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Sudhakar Kandhikonda, Senior Software Engineer at Lord Abbett with 18 years in data engineering, presents a case study of a financial institution replacing rule-based fraud detection with a real-time, multi-layered ML system, and the headline is detection time falling from hours to seconds, early enough to stop most fraudulent funds before they move.

He presents it as an implementation at a leading financial institution, without naming it. The talk is dense with metrics; the architecture is the part that transfers.

## What was broken

The legacy setup had four problems: high false positive rates, data siloed across systems, long detection delays, and customers paying for all of it in friction. Annual fraud losses ran above 25 million dollars and satisfaction was sliding. He cites research that siloed data misses the connection patterns behind a large share of complex fraud, and the ACFE estimate that organisations lose about 5% of revenue to fraud each year, with financial services the most targeted sector.

## Three layers of plumbing

The data integration framework unified 17 disparate systems, including core banking, card processing, digital channels and CRM. It has three layers: a standardisation layer whose ETL pipelines normalise 14 different data formats, Apache Kafka streaming across a cluster of brokers, and a data lake holding 37 months of history for analytics. The legacy mess explains the effort: 23 timestamp conventions and nine incompatible transaction classification schemes. Anyone who has joined two banking systems on a date field will wince in sympathy.

## The ML pipeline and decision engine

The ML core has four parts. Feature engineering tracks 237 behavioural indicators across transactions, user behaviour, devices and network patterns. Continuous retraining feeds confirmed fraud cases back in with updates every eight hours. Ensemble modelling combines supervised algorithms (a gradient-boosting model performed best) with unsupervised anomaly detection that looks for statistical outliers across many dimensions at once.

A real-time decision engine turns scores into millisecond-level actions. The point is timing: intervention before funds leave the institution, in the large majority of fraudulent attempts, against a tiny fraction with the old system.

## The hard parts

Three challenges get their own slide. Data quality, which needed hundreds of normalisation rules and quality checks. Latency, solved by profiling bottlenecks and parallel processing until evaluation fit the real-time budget. And explainability: regulators across 17 jurisdictions wanted clear reasons for declined transactions, so the team built a custom framework that produces human-readable explanations of model decisions.

## Graphs, federation and what comes next

The innovations section is the most interesting technically. Adaptive feature engineering proposes and tests new indicators every month. Federated learning lets seven participating institutions train together on a much larger pool of fraud examples without sharing raw data, using secure multi-party computation. Graph-based network analysis maps relationships between accounts and found 34 previously undetected fraud rings.

Next on his list: behavioural biometrics such as typing patterns and device handling, voice analysis to catch social engineering in call centres, cross-channel correlation, and post-quantum cryptography with the NIST-standardised CRYSTALS-Kyber and Dilithium algorithms.

## Who should watch

Data engineers building streaming fraud or risk platforms, and fintech architects who need a reference design for ingestion through decisioning. The auto-transcript garbles some of the figures, so check the slides if you plan to cite a number.

Title: Cognitive accessibility is the gap screen readers left open
Description: Vignesh Kuppa Amarnath of MSRcosmos shows at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 how adaptive voice, colour and layout AI can support users with cognitive disabilities.
Body:
Screen readers and keyboard navigation have had decades to mature. Tools for people with cognitive disabilities have not. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Vignesh Kuppa Amarnath, software engineer at MSRcosmos, argues that this is where AI earns its keep in accessibility: interfaces that learn how a person thinks and reshape voice, colour and layout around them.

It's a short, slide-driven talk, closer to a briefing than a tutorial. It's worth watching for the framing and the roadmap rather than for implementation detail.

## Accessibility as a translation problem

Amarnath opens with a data-mapping analogy from his day job. Two servers that speak different languages need a translator in between; now imagine that translator understood context and intent instead of swapping words. Point the same idea at people and you get speech turned into live text for users with hearing impairments, visuals described as audio for blind users, and colours mapped to patterns or labels for people with colour blindness. A cognitive system goes one step further and learns each user's preferences.

He works across tax, health insurance and payroll clients in the US, and the talk carries that enterprise lens: accessibility is moving into the development lifecycle as a requirement, and accessible design makes clearer interfaces for everyone.

## Three adaptive levers

The talk groups the technology into three modalities.

**Voice interaction.** Natural language processing lets users with cognitive disabilities navigate by spoken command, with recognition tuned for speech variation and alternative communication patterns, and models that keep refining from real usage.

**Colour optimisation.** Convolutional neural networks analyse an individual's colour perception and remap the palette, building a profile within two to three sessions. He cites clinical studies showing a 47% drop in eye strain during long screen use.

**Adaptive layout.** Interfaces that restructure themselves around a user's cognitive patterns and interaction history. His figures include navigation time cut by up to 47% for users with cognitive differences and interface-related support tickets down 73%.

The deck reports several overlapping metrics for task completion and support reduction, so treat the individual percentages as directional and watch for the pattern: fewer tickets, more independent users.

## The healthcare portal case

The most concrete section is a case study of a regional healthcare system whose patient portal had low adoption among users with cognitive disabilities, blocked by dense information and confusing navigation. The fix combined voice interaction, adaptive layout and personalised colour, with the AI learning from each user to simplify screens and surface what mattered. He reports support requests falling by 64% and medication adherence improving by 27%. That second number is the reminder that accessibility failures in healthcare aren't cosmetic.

## A roadmap that keeps users in the loop

His implementation plan has four steps: assess existing barriers and user needs, choose technology aimed specifically at cognitive accessibility, integrate and test with users of varying cognitive abilities throughout, then deploy with monitoring so the system keeps adapting. The second step matters most: involve the people you're designing for while you build, not after.

## Who should watch

Product and frontend teams who already meet WCAG basics and want to think about the next layer, and healthcare or public-sector teams with low portal adoption. Engineers looking for code, model architectures or evaluation methods won't find them here.

Title: Healthcare claims are a rules engine waiting for RPA, ML and NLP
Description: Cognizant's Uday Bag at Conf42 SRE 2025 on applying RPA, machine learning and NLP to US healthcare claims adjudication and early fraud detection.
Body:
Roughly every third US healthcare claim still gets touched by a human, according to the figures Uday Bag opened with. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, the Lead Product Consultant (Technical) at Cognizant made the case for layering robotic process automation, machine learning and NLP onto claims adjudication, and for catching suspicious claims at the EDI gateway before they ever reach full adjudication.

This is a domain overview for payers rather than an implementation guide: a stack of four techniques, three anonymised case studies, a rollout plan and an honest list of what makes healthcare hard.

## Why claims are worth automating

Bag sets the scale with the numbers he presented: US healthcare spending of roughly $4.9 trillion in 2024, about 17.6% of GDP; around 30% of claims processed manually; about $350 billion a year in administrative cost; an average 45-day cycle from submission to payment; and an error rate near 7.5% that feeds denials and resubmissions. When the base is that large, he argues, even a small percentage of waste is a lot of money.

## Four layers, each doing a different job

His stack:

- **RPA** for routine, rule-based, repetitive claims with predictable logic.
- **Machine learning** to find patterns and anomalies and to learn from past adjudication outcomes.
- **NLP** to pull structured data out of unstructured clinical notes, which matters in an industry where every entity keeps its own systems and formats.
- **An AI-based rules engine** that applies payer policies dynamically, so whatever the models decide still gets validated against policy.

The fourth layer is the one engineers should notice. The models propose; policy still disposes.

## What the case studies claim

He describes three payer examples without naming them: machine learning on specialty pharmacy claims (high-dollar, authorisation-heavy) pushing auto-adjudication up by almost 80%; NLP on clinical documentation cutting processing time by 65% and improving fraud detection; and RPA adding capacity for 1.5 million more claims a month. Across adopters he cites adjudication time down by up to 75% and error rates down by up to 80%. These are reported results, not his own measurements, so read them as the upper end of what's possible.

## Fraud is cheaper to catch at the gate

The fraud section is the most practically useful. Unusual billing behaviour can be flagged as claim files (UB-04, CMS-1500) come through the EDI gateway, compared against the same provider's history and against peers. Flagging suspicious claims early in the cycle, before full adjudication, both catches more and reduces load on the adjudication system. He cites up to 60% better fraud detection accuracy than rule-based systems.

## The hard parts

Bag doesn't pretend it's easy. Data quality comes first, because AI needs clean, consistent, standardised input and healthcare data is anything but. Then regulatory compliance and privacy, staff training as job roles change, and ethics: algorithms that touch healthcare decisions must be transparent, explainable and free of bias. His outlook is a hybrid model where AI handles the bulk of rule-based decisions and human experts take the complex ones, with self-learning models and blockchain-based validation as longer-term bets. He puts typical ROI at 12 to 18 months after full implementation.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people at payers, TPAs and health-tech vendors who need the shape of the problem before choosing tools. If you already run an ML adjudication pipeline, the challenges section is the part worth your time.

Title: Generative AI as an operator for hybrid cloud, from scaling to fixes
Description: Cognizant's Vijayakumar Jayaseelan at Conf42 SRE 2025 on using generative AI for predictive scaling, security and self-healing across on-prem and cloud.
Body:
Black Friday is the oldest capacity planning problem in the book, and Vijayakumar Jayaseelan used it to frame a newer answer. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, the Senior Manager and Principal Architect at Cognizant argued that generative AI can move hybrid cloud operations from reactive to proactive: forecasting demand from historical metrics and logs, scaling resources across on-prem and public cloud before the spike, and remediating issues it finds in the logs.

It's a short, high-level talk, closer to an architecture briefing than a demo. No specific product is shown.

## Why the old way falls short in hybrid

Jayaseelan describes the hybrid setup most enterprises have: on-prem data centres with high control and limited scalability, public cloud (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) with consumption pricing, and a network topology between them that needs careful tuning and consistent security policy. Traditional management fails it in three ways: manual provisioning that can't keep pace with demand, static allocation that leaves either idle capacity or bottlenecks, and reactive troubleshooting that only starts after users notice.

## Four jobs for the model

The talk splits AI's role into four areas:

- **Predictive workload management.** Models read historical metrics and logs, forecast demand before it spikes, and scale resources up and down across the hybrid estate.
- **Security.** Behavioural anomaly detection, continuous verification in a zero-trust model, automated containment, and generative AI producing synthetic attack scenarios to test defences.
- **Network optimisation.** Real-time analysis of traffic between on-prem and cloud, with dynamic path selection and distribution across regions or zones.
- **Automated decisions.** Generating and tuning infrastructure-as-code templates (Terraform, Ansible, Kubernetes), detecting errors in logs and remediating them, and spotting resource-hungry long-running queries for tuning.

The synthetic attack idea is the most interesting of the four: using the model's generative side to rehearse attacks rather than only to classify logs.

## The figures to check against your own estate

The talk cites up to 35% lower infrastructure cost from predictive scaling, up to 40% lower latency from network optimisation and up to 80% less manual intervention, plus three anonymised examples: a bank cutting infrastructure cost by 30%, a hospital network speeding patient data access by 45%, and an auto parts maker reaching 99.99% production uptime. None of the setups are described in detail, so treat the numbers as motivation for a pilot rather than a benchmark.

## Start small and keep a human in the loop

The challenges section is the part worth copying into a design doc. Integration complexity: adopt incrementally, starting with one well-defined workload that has measurable optimisation potential. Skill gaps: train internally, use managed services for the specialised AI parts, and build cross-functional teams. Trust: make AI decisions transparent with human oversight during the initial phase. Data quality: governance, cleansing and continuous validation, because the model is only as good as the telemetry it reads. He ends with edge computing converging with AI-optimised hybrid cloud as the next step.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure leads in enterprises running both data centres and public cloud who want a map of where AI could plug into operations. Hands-on SREs will want to pair it with something more concrete.

Title: Observability pays off when app metrics line up with business ones
Description: Kloudfuse's Swapnil Kulkarni at Conf42 SRE 2025 on the six contexts of observability and why correlating app and business metrics matters most.
Body:
Nobody is debating whether to have observability anymore. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Swapnil Kulkarni, founding member and customer success and solutions architect at Kloudfuse, argued that the real question is whether your telemetry answers the questions each team in the company is actually asking, and that the answer depends on correlating application metrics with business ones.

It's a compact, vendor-neutral talk. Kloudfuse is an observability company, but no product appears on screen; the content is a framework for thinking about who uses the data.

## Six audiences for the same telemetry

Kulkarni walks through the contexts one by one:

- **Technical:** metrics, logs and traces, the raw material. After a deploy, you look at request duration, logs and the processes that are failing.
- **Operational:** SLOs, SLIs, error budgets and incident response, where the question is how errors translate into degradation.
- **Development:** the feedback loop from production to developers: how CI behaves, how a feature flag performs at each stage.
- **User experience:** real user monitoring and synthetic checks. Are customers abandoning carts because of frontend timeouts? Does the site load in five seconds instead of two?
- **Business:** linking a 5xx spike in the checkout service to lost revenue.
- **Security and compliance:** spotting a burst of login attempts from one IP, plus audit trails, access logs and retention rules for GDPR, HIPAA and SOC 2.

The point isn't that every company needs all six. It's that each group consumes the same signals differently, and a dashboard built for one is noise to the others.

## Correlation is the whole game

The core of the talk is the gap between application metrics (latency, error rate, CPU, query time) and business metrics (daily active users, feature adoption, revenue per transaction, conversion, churn). On their own, the first set tells engineers the system is unwell; the second tells leadership that something is costing money. Joined up, they tell you which error is losing which revenue.

His worked example is a payment service across regions throwing 5xx errors that hurt the overall SLO. If the success metrics for purchases and signups carry labels such as user type, region, plan and feature flag, you can slice by those and see that one region on one device type is the problem, then act on it.

## Alert on what the business would page you for

That correlation changes alerting. Instead of a bare alert that the error rate hit 50% over the last five minutes, Kulkarni argues for composite alerts that combine an error spike with a drop in conversions, checkouts or signups. The SLO, in his framing, should mix system health and user experience. The prerequisite is a unified view: when you look at a burst of 500s, you want the time series, the logs and the triggering events side by side rather than in three tools.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform teams trying to get business stakeholders to care about telemetry, and anyone writing SLOs who suspects theirs measure the servers instead of the customers. It's an overview, so it pairs well with a hands-on talk on implementing business metrics.

Title: An AI hiring pipeline built on the Microsoft stack, step by step
Description: Tential Solutions' Sudeep Shanubhog at Conf42 SRE 2025 walks through an AI recruitment flow, from resume parsing and voice screening to Azure AI and Dynamics 365.
Body:
Hiring a senior full-stack .NET developer by scrolling job portals is slow, and Sudeep Shanubhog thinks most of it can be automated. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, the Technical Lead and Senior Full Stack Developer at Tential Solutions sketched an AI-driven recruitment pipeline on the Microsoft ecosystem: NLP resume screening, an AI voice call to qualify candidates, automated assessments and scheduling, all the way to the offer email.

Fair warning on scope: this is an overview talk about recruitment technology, not site reliability. It's short, and it's built around a worked example plus a set of headline metrics.

## Six steps from resume to offer

The example is a role needing ten-plus years in Microsoft technologies: .NET Core, Angular or React, SQL Server or MongoDB. The pipeline he describes:

1. **Profile filtering.** The model reads thousands of resumes for context, not just keywords, looking at project history and growth to separate people who used a technology from people who merely listed it.
2. **AI voice engagement.** For a match, an AI voice call verifies background, recent projects and salary expectations.
3. **Automated skill assessment,** emailed and tailored to the role and the candidate's experience.
4. **Real-time scoring,** followed by another AI voice interaction to book interviews.
5. **Multi-round coordination,** with the system handling scheduling against hiring managers' availability.
6. **Outcome and offer,** sent automatically with terms and conditions.

## Semantics over keyword matching

The most transferable idea is in the resume screening section. Keyword search is rigid; NLP can recognise that a DevOps engineer and a cloud automation specialist might mean the same thing in context, pick out certifications and career progression, and parse PDFs, documents or scanned files alike. He cites a 43% improvement in resume matching accuracy from that approach.

Beyond screening he covers adaptive cognitive tests, technical simulations for coding and design, predictive models trained on past hiring outcomes, and chatbots plus automated status updates so candidates aren't left in the application black hole.

## The numbers, and how to read them

The talk leans on headline figures: 45% less time to hire, 37% better quality of hire, 32% lower hiring cost, 58% less unconscious bias, 41% higher candidate satisfaction and up to 25 hours a week saved per recruiter. They're presented as industry results rather than measurements from a named deployment, so treat them as the case for a pilot, not a forecast. The bias figure in particular deserves your own audit, because a model trained on past hiring outcomes learns whatever those outcomes encoded.

## Where Microsoft fits

The ecosystem slide connects three pieces: LinkedIn Talent Solutions for passive candidates, Dynamics 365 HR for applicant tracking, onboarding and performance, and Azure AI services for custom skills-matching models, resume parsing and chatbots. The rollout advice is sensible: assess the current process, pick one use case such as screening, pilot it on one role or department, then scale and keep tracking KPIs.

## Who should watch

HR tech teams and engineers building internal tooling on Microsoft 365 and Azure who want a reference flow to argue about. SREs looking for reliability content can skip this one; it's a recruitment talk that happened to land in an SRE conference.

Title: Agentic AI in layers, and why autonomy should be a dial
Description: Google DeepMind ML engineer Naman Goyal at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 maps agentic AI: planning, memory, tools, ReAct vs plan-and-execute, graduated autonomy.
Body:
An agent that asks permission for every step is safe and useless; one that never asks is useful until it isn't. Naman Goyal, a machine learning engineer at Google DeepMind, gave a research-level map of agentic AI at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), and the idea most worth taking home is that autonomy should be a context-sensitive dial, set by risk and reversibility, rather than a single switch.

This is a survey talk. No code, no demo; instead a structured tour of the technical foundations, the two dominant operating frameworks, the research frontiers and the ethics, with figures drawn from published studies.

## From text generators to goal-driven systems

Goyal traces the arc in three steps. Early LLMs like the first GPT-3 were powerful but reactive: prompt in, text out. Then came deeper contextual understanding, still inside the input-output paradigm. Now there are systems you give an objective and they work out the steps, coordinating across tools, platforms and APIs with minimal human guidance.

## Four layers that make agency possible

He stacks the foundations bottom up:

- **Hierarchical planning:** break goals into sub-goals, tasks and operational steps, sometimes with recursive refinement. He cites studies where this beats flat planning on complex tasks, with success rates around 45% higher.
- **Long-term memory:** episodic memory for events, semantic knowledge bases for concepts and working memory for the current context, to get past the context window. Explicit semantic knowledge has shown accuracy gains of up to 37% on some domain tasks.
- **Tool integration:** web search, code execution, document analysis and other software. Tool-using implementations reached nearly three times the success rate on complex information-gathering tasks.
- **Decision autonomy:** on top, the agent decides when and how to use the layers below.

## ReAct or plan-and-execute: it depends on the weather

ReAct, formalised around late 2022, runs tight loops of observe, reason, act and observe again. It shines in dynamic environments and on multi-hop information gathering; Goyal cites 31% higher completion rates on benchmarks such as HotpotQA and WebShop, and better error recovery because feedback arrives immediately.

Plan-and-execute writes a detailed plan first and executes it methodically, replanning only when something big goes wrong. It suits stable, structured environments and avoids the overhead of constant reasoning; he cites stakeholder ratings about 24% higher on consistency in domains like urban planning. His conclusion: neither wins everywhere, hybrids are emerging, and choosing the framework for the context matters.

## Autonomy as a graduated framework

The levels run from suggest-only, where a human approves every step, through supervised operation with verification at key points, to bounded independence inside predefined safety parameters, and finally near-full autonomy where humans set goals and handle major exceptions. The right level depends on task risk, reversibility of actions, the agent's confidence and domain sensitivity. He reports studies where such context-sensitive boundaries cut unnecessary human interventions by as much as 64% while maintaining safety. For anyone shipping agents, that is the slide to screenshot.

## The frontiers

Multi-agent systems assign roles, as MetaGPT does with product manager, architect and programmer; experiments with AutoGen found structured agent-to-agent communication improved completion by about 37% over centralised approaches. Embodied agents connect LLM reasoning to robots through vision-language-action models, with systems like RT-1 and RT-2 following natural-language instructions. Continual learning needs to avoid catastrophic forgetting, and he cites 24 to 38% higher success after repeated interaction cycles. Meta-learning aims at agents that pick their own learning strategies and might need 40 to 65% fewer examples for new tasks.

## Ethics is a design input

The last section groups risks into alignment (value drift, purpose validation), control (kill switches, behaviour boundaries, human-AI protocols), societal impact (displacement, equitable access) and accountability (decision audit trails, recourse). He argues for value-sensitive design throughout the lifecycle, and notes that ethics and governance research still trails capability work.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product leads who want a structured mental model of agent architectures before choosing a framework, and researchers looking for an overview with pointers. Treat the percentages as figures from the studies he cites, each in its own setting, not as general guarantees.

Title: An enterprise AI tour, and why the loan model ran in shadow mode
Description: Balakrishna Sudabathula of Delta Dental Ins. maps enterprise AI at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, from pipelines and decision support to chatbots and risks.
Body:
The most useful story in this talk is about a model that never went live on schedule. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, Balakrishna Sudabathula, Expert Software Engineer at Delta Dental Ins., walks through how enterprises wire AI into daily operations, and his best example is a lender that tested a loan-approval model in shadow mode, found it scoring recent immigrants lower, paused it and fixed it before launch. That is the whole argument for decision support with a human in the loop, told in one anecdote.

This is a broad, beginner-friendly tour rather than a build log. If you want one map of where AI shows up in a company (HR, finance, operations, support) and the plumbing it needs, it does that job in about half an hour.

## AI needs a body, not just a brain

Sudabathula compares an AI system to a car: the model is not much use without an engine, fuel and a driver. His reference architecture has five parts. Data ingestion pulls from websites, sensors and forms. Processing modules find patterns and make predictions. An analytics layer turns results into scores and charts. Integration pushes those results into apps and dashboards. Presentation is where a person sees the warning, recommendation or report.

His bank example runs every transaction through that chain: the fraud model flags something odd and an analyst gets the alert straight away. Nothing exotic, which is the point. Most enterprise AI value sits in the boring connective tissue.

## From helper to decision partner

The middle of the talk covers what he calls decision intelligence. In a hospital, a system reads symptoms, test results and history and suggests diagnoses, while doctors still make the call. In retail, it tells managers what is running low and when to restock. A good decision system, in his framing, combines four inputs: rules you must follow, historical and live data, the models, and feedback from humans.

The HR and finance examples are where the time savings show up. He describes one company cutting its hiring cycle from 30 days to eight with AI resume screening that also checks for bias, and a bank whose compliance-document review went from three weeks for a team to two days.

## Real time is an integration problem

Sudabathula lists four integration patterns: real-time streaming with tools like Kafka, event-driven systems that react when a user logs in, streaming analytics that work on data as it arrives, and hybrid setups where some models score live while others retrain overnight. The aviation example sticks: engine data checked mid-flight so the ground team hears about an anomaly before the plane lands.

He also breaks a support chatbot into its layers (interface, natural language understanding, a dialogue manager that remembers context, backend connections to real systems, and logging and security), with a telecom bot in four languages handling 68% of customer requests without a human.

## The risks are the usual suspects, done properly

The challenges list is familiar but honest: personal data under GDPR and HIPAA, model drift as the world changes, scaling from 10 users to 10,000, biased training data, and knowing when a human must make the final call. The infrastructure answer is equally standard: Airflow and Kubeflow pipelines, CI/CD for models, edge models (a drone that spots pipeline cracks on the device itself), feature stores and human review.

He closes on AutoML and explainable AI, with a bank using SHAP to show customers why a credit application was approved or denied. Explaining the "no" is cheaper than handling the complaint.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers new to enterprise AI who want the whole picture on one page, and anyone writing an internal pitch who needs a clean architecture diagram plus examples. If you already run feature stores and shadow deployments in production, you'll know most of this; skip to the risks section for a tidy checklist.

Title: Build a coding agent in four steps, from ReAct loop to agent team
Description: Zencoder's Alex Shershebnev at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 live-codes coding agents, from a ReAct prompt to MCP tools and a LangGraph agent team.
Body:
The quickest way to stop being mystified by AI coding agents is to build a bad one, then a less bad one. Alex Shershebnev, ML and DevOps lead at Zencoder, did exactly that live at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025): a plain LLM call, then a ReAct loop with three hand-written tools, then MCP servers, then a four-agent LangGraph team, before showing Zencoder's own agent solving a Jira ticket.

The first three quarters are vendor-neutral and come with a public notebook repository. The last part is a demo of Zencoder's IDE plugin, and he says so.

## Benchmarks are single files; work is not

Shershebnev starts with the headlines that AI will replace mid-level engineers, and with new models beating each other on coding benchmarks. His caution: many benchmarks ask a model to write a function or class for a task, a single-file change. Real work spans many files and sometimes several repositories, so benchmark gains don't transfer one to one.

He also cites a study from about ten years ago finding developers spend around 70% of their time understanding code, requirements and tasks rather than writing code. Agent design patterns line up with that: tool use, planning, reflection and multi-agent collaboration. His analogy is a Roomba, which needs brushes and wheels as well as software to clean a room.

## Step one and two: an LLM, then a loop

The baseline is GPT-4.1 with no tools. Asked for Google's response time, the packages installed locally, or what's new in Python 3.14, it offers commands to run and stale knowledge, because it lives in the cloud with a training cut-off.

Then comes ReAct (reason and act) in a single system prompt: thought, action, pause, observation, answer, with three actions available, ping, bash and a basic web search, plus an example session (how many islands make up Madeira). A short loop parses actions from the model output, runs them and feeds results back. Now it pings google.com, runs pip list and summarises the Python 3.14 release notes. One prompt turned a knowledge base into something that acts.

## Step three: let MCP describe the tools

Hand-defining every action does not scale; imagine one per git subcommand. So he switches to the Model Context Protocol, introduced by Anthropic at the end of November 2024: a JSON-RPC protocol where MCP servers wrap tools and clients like an LLM app or IDE discover their names, descriptions and input schemas. A bash server in Python takes about three lines with the FastMCP class and a decorator.

With Claude 3.7 Sonnet as the model and a JSON config listing four servers, a filesystem server from npm, Brave web search in Docker, a fetch server as a Python package and his bash server, the agent searches the web for release notes and writes a hello-world file to disk. MCP registries already list servers for tools like Grafana and Jira.

## Step four: a supervisor and three virtual engineers

The final notebook uses LangChain and LangGraph to build a hierarchy: a supervisor (think product manager) that routes work to front-end, back-end and DevOps agents, each a ReAct agent with shell, Brave search, filesystem and a human tool for asking the client questions. Subordinates only talk through the supervisor. He notes that in real life you would give each agent different tools, Prometheus or Datadog for the DevOps agent, Figma for the front-end one.

The task: a conference website with an intro page, a talk submission page and a page listing submissions, a React front end, a back-end API, Postgres storage, and Docker Compose. On camera, the agents check installed tools, scaffold directories, run npm installs and start writing code.

## The vendor part

Zencoder ships as a plugin for VS Code and JetBrains IDEs. In the demo it pulls a Jira ticket that needs changes across Python, Go and TypeScript, analyses the repository, creates a branch, commits through a Git MCP server and posts to Slack when finished.

His view of the future is developers as reviewers and managers of virtual junior developers, offloading documentation and tests while keeping enough understanding to debug mission-critical code. Or, as he jokes, finally becoming the goose farmer you always wanted to be.

## Who should watch

Developers who use coding assistants but have never looked under the hood, and anyone who wants a gentle, code-first explanation of ReAct, MCP and multi-agent graphs. If you already run LangGraph in production, the early stages will feel familiar.

Title: Amazon Bedrock Agents in practice, a 43-step multi-agent research run
Description: AWS principal architect Samuel Baruffi at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 shows Amazon Bedrock Agents and a supervisor-led multi-agent investment research demo.
Body:
One API call, three minutes, 43 traced steps across four agents: that's what a single investment research question cost in Samuel Baruffi's demo. Baruffi, a principal global solutions architect at AWS, used his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk to explain what Amazon Bedrock Agents manages for you and to walk through a supervisor agent orchestrating specialists over a 10-K, web news and live stock data.

This is a product talk about AWS services, presented by AWS. The architecture patterns transfer to any stack, and the trace walkthrough is the most useful part even if you never touch Bedrock.

## What he means by agent

Baruffi pins the term down: autonomous systems that reason, plan and complete multi-step tasks on behalf of humans. They break an objective into tasks (planning), use tools and knowledge to do them (actions), and watch the results to update the plan until the goal is met (reasoning). His example: instead of checking whether a meeting room is free, an agent checks everyone's calendar, sends invites, monitors replies and follows up with key people who decline.

He quotes Gartner predictions that 33% of enterprise software applications will include agentic AI by 2028, up from under 1% in 2024, and that 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously by then. The evolution he sketches goes from simple assistants, to deterministic flows with a router, to single autonomous agents with several tools, to teams of expert agents acting as virtual workers.

## Where Bedrock Agents sits in the AWS stack

The AWS generative AI stack has three layers: infrastructure (SageMaker AI, NVIDIA GPUs, AWS Trainium and Inferentia), Amazon Bedrock as the building blocks, and Amazon Q as the application layer for business users and developers. Bedrock offers serverless access to Amazon and third-party models priced on input and output tokens, plus knowledge bases for managed RAG, data automation for PDFs, guardrails, evaluations including LLM-as-a-judge, prompt caching, intelligent prompt routing and cross-region inference.

Bedrock Agents is the fully managed option for building and deploying agents. Alongside it AWS offers Q agents for productivity and the do-it-yourself route with open source frameworks on Lambda and Step Functions.

## The production problems a managed service targets

Baruffi lists what customers struggle with when moving from proof of concept to production: a fast-changing framework ecosystem, the operational complexity of orchestrating and scaling multiple agents, entitlements so data isn't shared too widely, governance and compliance, and above all observability, meaning tracing every step and running evaluations. His pitch is that the managed service takes on the heavy lifting, while being honest that "You still need to put a lot of work".

Agents get action groups to call your APIs, knowledge base access, a sandboxed code interpreter, managed memory and sessions, guardrails and step-level traces. Multi-agent collaboration, released late in 2024, lets a supervisor delegate to collaborator agents with built-in intent classification for handoffs. Inline agents can also act as MCP clients, treating MCP servers as action groups.

## The demo: a supervisor and three specialists

The Investment Research Assistant supervises three agents. A financial news agent has a web search API and a knowledge base of Amazon's 10-K and 10-Q filings, prepared with Bedrock Data Automation and embedded into an OpenSearch Serverless index. A quantitative analysis agent calls a Yahoo Finance API for prices and ranges. A summariser condenses findings for the supervisor.

The prompt asks for growth opportunities from the latest 10-K, related news, competitors in each area, analyst price ranges for the next 12 months and the past 30 days of price movement. The trace shows the supervisor writing its plan, handing off to the news agent, which searches the knowledge base, then the web for growth initiatives and analyst targets, before reporting back; then the quant agent pulls stock data and recent volatility; then the supervisor synthesises. Step 43 is the final answer, covering AI, AWS, healthcare and Project Kuiper with competitors and analyst ranges.

## Who should watch

Teams on AWS evaluating managed agents versus rolling their own, and anyone who wants to see what a real multi-agent trace looks like step by step. If you are cloud-agnostic, watch for the trace and the production checklist and skip the service tour.

Title: Ransomware goes after your backups first, so lock and test them
Description: Trader Interactive's Srihari Pakalapati at Conf42 SRE 2025 on the 3-2-1-1-0 rule, logically air-gapped vaults and restoring into a clean room account.
Body:
If your recovery plan assumes the backups are fine, the attacker has already read it. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Srihari Pakalapati, Principal Cloud and Security Architect at Trader Interactive, laid out a cloud backup architecture built for ransomware: immutable copies in a logically air-gapped vault in a separate account, keys the attacker can't touch, and restores into a fresh "clean room" account instead of the production account that just got owned.

It's a long, practical talk, and the reference architecture alone is worth the time.

## The attacker reads your backup plan too

Pakalapati opens with figures from the Sophos 2024 ransomware report: 59% of organisations surveyed were hit in the past year, and 94% of victims said the attackers targeted their backups. Encryption is the visible part; exfiltration usually comes first, so the attacker can threaten a leak as well as a lockout. He also notes that attackers can sit quietly in a network for two to three months before they start encrypting.

His list of response pitfalls is a good tabletop agenda on its own: no practised crisis communication plan, logging too thin to build a timeline, nobody knowing who can authorise a ransom payment (or whether paying a sanctioned group is even legal), wildly optimistic recovery estimates, and the worst one, discovering mid-incident that the backups are encrypted, incomplete or too old.

## Classify the data, then pick the RPO and RTO

Recovery planning starts with four questions: scope (how much data), RPO (how much you can afford to lose), RTO (how fast you must be back) and copies (how many you keep). You only answer them well after data classification, and he walks through a simple flow chart: if the business can't move forward without the data and it can't be recreated, it's truly critical.

He then maps tiers to targets: mission-critical systems such as payment processing under 10 minutes, business-critical ERP and customer-facing apps under an hour, operational tools under eight hours, administrative systems 24 to 48 hours. Each tier lands on a different point of the cost curve, from plain backup and restore through pilot light and warm standby up to active-active, where you pay for production twice.

## 3-2-1 grows two more digits

The traditional 3-2-1 rule becomes 3-2-1-1-0: three copies including production, two storage types, one copy offsite, one copy offline or immutable, and zero errors on restore verification. The fourth digit is the ransomware answer; the fifth is the one teams skip. He cites a Veeam survey finding that 40% of recovery attempts fail.

## The architecture: a bunker and a clean room

The reference design has three parts:

- **A local backup vault** in the production account for everyday operational restores, like rolling back a bad deployment.
- **A logically air-gapped vault** in a dedicated "data bunker" account, possibly in another region, with no network path from production. Backups are immutable and encrypted with service-provider-owned keys, so stealing customer key material doesn't help. In compliance mode the vault lock can't be lifted by anyone, root user included, once the cooling-off period ends.
- **A clean room account** for restores. Sharing works through AWS Resource Access Manager, so backups restore directly into another account without copying first.

He names AWS Backup and Google Cloud as offering logically air-gapped vaults, with Veeam among the third-party options. On top come MFA, least-privilege RBAC, geofencing on backup access, audit logs and anomaly detection on backup behaviour.

## A backup isn't a backup until you've restored it

The part most teams skip is automated restore testing: restore into a forensic account on a schedule, validate integrity and recovery metrics, scan the restored data for malware, alert on the result, then tear the resources down so the test doesn't quietly become a second bill. The talk ends on the human side: a cross-functional incident team, out-of-band communication channels in case your chat tool is the thing that got encrypted, step-by-step recovery playbooks, quarterly tabletops and at least an annual full recovery simulation.

## Who should watch

Cloud and platform engineers who own backups, security architects designing account structure, and SREs whose DR plan was written before ransomware gangs learned to delete snapshots. The examples are AWS-flavoured, but the account isolation pattern travels.

Title: The SRE mindset starts with the customer and assumes failure
Description: Google's Saurabh Phaltane at Conf42 SRE 2025 on the habits behind reliable systems: customer-first metrics, designing for failure, T-shaped learning.
Body:
Before you pick a tool, pick a mindset. That was the pitch from Saurabh Phaltane, Senior Site Reliability Engineer on Google Search infrastructure, at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025. His argument: reliability work starts with what the customer actually expects, assumes that everything will break, and gets better through small, continuous steps rather than one heroic project.

This is a talk about thinking, not tooling. There are no dashboards or YAML on screen. What you get is a senior SRE's checklist for how to frame a reliability problem, drawn from a career that runs from small startups to Google.

## Reliability is defined by the person on the other end

Phaltane's first principle is to ask what the end user is expecting and build the reliability story around that. He contrasts two jobs. At Google Search, the critical promise is delivering a page of results accurately and fast, so most of the optimisation energy goes into latency. At a previous company, latency mattered much less; the promise there was uptime, published on a status page as 99.99% over the last 30 days.

Same discipline, different target. Once you know which one your customer cares about, the tools, the metrics and the SLOs follow. Pick them first and you end up measuring whatever your monitoring vendor made easy.

## Define before you dive

The second habit is planning: write down the metrics of success, the end goals and the SLO definitions before taking on a project. Phaltane is honest that this doesn't solve the problem by itself. What it does is keep you from getting distracted by work you shouldn't be doing, and it gives other people something to review.

He pairs this with balancing velocity against reliability. As an organisation grows, its reliability bar should rise with it, but there is always a trade-off with shipping speed, and real people depend on the result.

## You can't build for success, only design for failure

The core of the talk is failure-first design. Things will fail, and some failure modes will be ones nobody considered. At Google, he describes running through failure scenarios before a feature reaches production, with three questions: does the failure degrade the customer experience, do we have alerting that fires before the customer notices, and do we have a mitigation ready before customers "feel the heat"?

His earlier company ran multi-availability-zone, multi-data-center infrastructure with replication, standby backups and a third backup on top, all coming from the same instinct.

## Hacky scripts count as progress

Phaltane frames reliability as a curve that never reaches the goal: every improvement takes you closer, none finishes the job. His advice for getting started is refreshingly unglamorous. Every great piece of automation began as a hacky script someone wrote the third time they did something by hand, and that's fine. Start at 99%, then push to 99.9% next year; he notes that each extra nine is a much bigger investment than the last.

## Learn T-shaped, write things down, go blameless

The last section covers how an SRE grows. With a field that spans kernel interrupts, TCP/IP and now agentic AI applications, he recommends a T model: breadth through talks, conferences and reading, and one domain where you go deep. Admitting you can't know everything beats pretending you can fix everything.

On incidents, he pushes blameless postmortems, a shift from firefighting to fire prevention (the second time a fire happens, invest in the long-term fix rather than another short-term mitigation), principles over tools, and writing your standards down so the next SRE inherits them. He closes on community: share what you learn, because everyone is building on layers other people made.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into SRE, and team leads who want a vocabulary for why their team should define SLOs before buying an observability platform. Veterans will recognise most of the principles; the value is in hearing how a Google SRE prioritises them.

Title: Read the replication SLA before the data centre catches fire
Description: RADAR DevOps engineer Pradeep Gaddamidi at Conf42 SRE 2025 on real SRE incidents with GCS replication, certificate chains, missing logs and Terraform habits.
Body:
A dual-region bucket sounds like your data is in two places. Pradeep Gaddamidi, DevOps engineer at RADAR with a background in banking and financial services, learned at the worst possible moment that it isn't always, yet. At [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) he shared a set of real incidents and near misses, from a data centre fire to a missing intermediate certificate, each with the concrete fix he'd apply next time.

This is the good kind of war-story talk: specific, a little self-deprecating, and full of checklist items you can steal. His own summary of the job: "Deploying infrastructure is always a mix of planning and firefighting."

## The bucket that was dual-region, eventually

His team used Google Cloud Storage dual-region buckets and assumed replication between regions was instant. Then a data centre fire made objects in their bucket unavailable for up to two hours. Only afterwards did they find that default replication, as he describes it, guarantees 99.9% of newly written objects within one hour and 100% within 12 hours. Google's recommendation was turbo replication, which targets 100% replication to both regions within 15 minutes regardless of object size.

The lesson is boring and essential: before production, check that the product's terms actually meet your RPO and SLA needs, and read the conditions seriously. The feature they needed existed; nobody had turned it on.

## Certificates: the outage you can calendar

Public certificate validity dropped to one year, which means more renewals, and wildcard certificates reused across many places are hard to track. Gaddamidi's suggestions: Datadog synthetic monitoring to watch endpoints and expiry dates, or the Infinity plugin in Grafana to query endpoints for certificate information, plus documentation of where each certificate is installed.

His sharper story is a financial client's outage caused by a missing intermediate certificate. The server certificate is signed by an intermediate, which is signed by a trusted root, and if the chain is incomplete visitors get an error. The fix is a post-renewal habit: check the chain with SSL Labs, or run openssl against the endpoint with the showcerts option and confirm the verify return code is zero.

## Logs you can't reach are logs you don't have

An investigation into records missing from a database stalled because the database wasn't configured to emit useful logs, and the VMs that connected to it kept logs locally instead of forwarding them. The team had to hunt across machines. His rule: logging enabled and shipped to a central platform such as Datadog or Elasticsearch belongs on the pre-deployment checklist.

He's honest about his own miss. He set up an Elasticsearch logging system but, under time pressure, skipped the disk alert, and Elasticsearch stops ingesting when disk usage hits its watermark at 80%. The fix is to install monitoring and logging agents through configuration management like Ansible or Puppet as part of provisioning, so nobody has to remember.

## Terraform, and the free tier surprise

No Terraform incident here, but two habits. Prefer well-maintained public modules from the Terraform Registry over hand-written ones unless the use case is truly unique; he replaced many custom modules he'd written. And run plan and apply through CI/CD rather than from laptops, so teammates review changes before infrastructure appears, with a scanner checking the code for misconfigurations and exposed secrets.

The last stories are about scope creep in the SRE role: writing a Python cloud function to convert protobuf-formatted data into something Prometheus could ingest, and discovering that Slack alerting in their Elastic setup sat behind a paid tier, so they scripted their own. Hence his final rule: pilot tools in dev before production, so you learn the requirements before they become incidents.

## Who should watch

Early and mid-career SREs and DevOps engineers, and anyone writing a production-readiness checklist. Seasoned operators will recognise every story, which is exactly why the checklist items are worth copying.

Title: 1980s AI labs built shelfware by deleting the social
Description: Lianne Potter at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 revisits anthropologist Diana Forsythe's fieldwork in AI labs, and why its lessons on bias and power still apply.
Body:
Ask why a lab's carefully built medical AI never got used, and in the 1980s the answer was "it's all on the shelf". Lianne Potter, digital anthropologist, cybersecurity practitioner and co-founder of Compromising Positions, used her [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk to bring back the fieldwork of anthropologist Diana E. Forsythe, who spent about eight years observing four US medical AI labs, and to argue that the same habits that produced that shelfware are still with us.

It is a history talk with a sharp edge and a good sense of humour (there is a Lady Terminator detour and an Indiana Jones jab). No code, but plenty that should change how you run your next requirements session.

## What counts as real work

Forsythe asked the researchers what doing AI meant. Their answer: writing code, solving problems, building systems. Then she logged what they actually did all day: lab meetings, seminars, more meetings, conferences, teaching, papers, admin. Coding came last. Potter's point lands immediately for anyone who has looked at their own calendar.

Because the social parts of their own work didn't count, the researchers didn't value them, and they weren't good at them. Disciplines like anthropology, psychology and philosophy were dismissed as soft or unscientific. One lab member called Forsythe, a highly educated researcher herself, a "Dictaphone with legs". Potter's phrase for the result is deleting the social.

## One expert, one textbook, invisible power

The knowledge engineers of the era saw expertise as something to extract and make machine readable. In practice that meant one- or two-hour interviews, once or twice a fortnight, with a single expert, often a senior white man such as a heart surgeon, whose view stood in for a whole field. They wanted surgery by the book, not surgery as it happens. Warm people switched to a cold, transactional style in interviews because it felt like a technical task; one expert said they felt treated like a dog.

The end users, like the doctor down the line, never knew the system rested on a handful of sources. Nurses weren't considered valid experts at all. Potter connects this directly to black-box models today, to thumbs-up feedback deciding whose answers count, and to scandals like the Amazon recruiting tool.

## Blame the user, ship to the shelf

Flush with funding after the AI winter, the labs built with few constraints and little interest in whether anyone liked the results. When systems went unused, researchers blamed naive or computer-phobic users. One said usefulness wasn't quantifiable. They rarely observed clinicians at work; one designer, asked whether they had visited a hospital site, said they couldn't stand the sight of blood.

The systems encoded the ideal path, so knowledge fell off a cliff, the researchers' own term, the moment reality deviated. Potter's favourite example: a system suggesting a male patient had an infection that only occurs in pregnant women. Nobody had coded that men don't get pregnant.

## The pipeline problem is a culture problem

Women made up about 8% of academic computer science in the US in that period; Potter puts it at about 15% now. Forsythe documented teasing and harassment, and colleagues who insisted science was gender neutral and so they couldn't be sexist. Her observation that diversity efforts treat this as a pipeline issue, while ignoring how women already in the field are treated, could have been written last week.

Potter's call to action: bring anthropologists and other outsiders into AI development, observe real users in real settings, and design for deviation from the happy path. Forsythe died in 1997; her book is Studying Those Who Study Us, and Potter's project has the blessing of Forsythe's widower.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and product people building tools for domain experts, anyone running user research for AI products, and leaders thinking about who sits in the room when requirements are written. It is equally good for people who think they've heard every AI ethics talk.

Title: Formal proofs, simulation and ML together for PCIe and USB4 verification
Description: Intel's Jena Abraham at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on hybrid hardware verification: formal methods, FPGA-accelerated simulation and ML test targeting.
Body:
Every new generation of PCIe or USB multiplies the states a verification team has to cover, and the tape-out date does not move to compensate. Jena Abraham, senior design verification engineer and technical program manager at Intel, showed at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) how her team layers formal methods, FPGA-accelerated simulation and machine learning so the expensive testing goes where bugs actually live.

For software engineers this is a peek into a world where a missed edge case costs a re-spin of silicon. For hardware folks, it's a compact tour of where ML has earned a seat in the verification flow.

## Three walls: time, coverage, scale

Abraham names the constraints up front. Timelines shrink while protocol complexity grows, and manual test creation can't keep up. Large test suites still miss rare edge cases at protocol boundaries and during state transitions, which is exactly where field failures come from. And standards like PCIe Gen 5 and Gen 6 and USB4 bring far more states, configurations and timing requirements than their predecessors, so the number of test vectors needed grows by orders of magnitude.

## Each layer covers the others' blind spots

The approach is hybrid. Formal verification, using symbolic execution and theorem proving, explores the full state space and gives no false negatives for the bug classes it covers, which matters for spec compliance at the architecture level. But formal models abstract away electrical noise, race conditions and timing violations, so dynamic simulation runs the implementation under real traffic and varied configurations. ML sits between the two, reading verification results and coverage data and reprioritising tests, with insights flowing in both directions.

## FPGAs for raw speed

Offloading packet parsing, protocol state monitoring and real-time error detection onto FPGAs is where the headline numbers sit: Abraham reports an 85% reduction in overall verification time compared with CPU-based methods and a 12x increase in transaction throughput, thanks to the parallelism of FPGA fabric. Lower latency also means the system can react to protocol events as they happen, which helps when chasing transient faults.

## Models trained on old bugs find new ones

The ML core is supervised learning on historical verification outcomes, passing and failing, with past defects classified by experts so the labels mean something. Each protocol gets its own neural network tuned to its timing, sequencing and encoding behaviour, with hyperparameter tuning aimed at generalisation rather than memorising old failures.

The architecture she shows is specific. Inputs combine protocol parameters (encoding schemes, error-checking rules, flow control), timing and synchronisation data, state-transition vectors and historical defect patterns. Hidden layers mix temporal convolutional networks for waveform and transaction streams, bidirectional LSTMs for handshakes and error recovery that make sense read both ways, and multi-head attention to focus on state transitions. Outputs rank test vectors by confidence, map which parts of the spec are under-tested, flag violations in real time and give a probability distribution over likely defect types.

She cites 94% accuracy in predicting high-risk edge cases and 97% precision in picking high-yield test vectors, with the models retrained on every new round of verification data.

## Generated tests and smarter features

ML-driven test generation replaces some expert-written and constrained-random scenarios, aiming for more vectors with less redundancy and adjusting output as coverage gaps appear. Feature selection extracts the parameters that matter from the spec, detects correlations (a violation that only shows up under a specific timing condition), ranks parameters by their bug-finding potential and keeps refining.

## Where it goes next

Her outlook: reinforcement learning so verification strategies optimise themselves, predictive models that flag design flaws before implementation, knowledge transfer across Ethernet, PCIe and USB, and verification that shifts left to guide design from the start.

## Who should watch

Design verification engineers and EDA tool builders, plus ML engineers looking for a domain where labelled failure data is rich and precision is everything. The talk shows architectures and results, not code or tooling names, so treat the numbers as the team's reported figures.
