Title: Four pillars of a self-driving data platform
Description: Microsoft engineer Madhuri Koripalli at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on metadata intelligence, self-healing pipelines, predictive scaling and embedded governance.
Body:
The 2am page for a pipeline that broke because someone upstream added a column is the job most data engineers would happily hand to a machine. Madhuri Koripalli, a software engineer at Microsoft, made the case at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) for a self-driving data platform built on four pillars: metadata intelligence, self-healing pipelines, predictive resource optimisation and embedded governance.

It is a conceptual, framework-level talk with plenty of reported metrics and friendly analogies (a librarian, an immune system, an autopilot, a guardian). There is no reference implementation, so take it as a design vocabulary and a set of targets.

## Why manual data management loses

The argument starts with growth. Global data volumes are heading for zettabytes, a large share of new data needs real-time processing, and IoT streams don't wait for a nightly batch. You can't hire enough people or write enough static scripts to keep up, so the platform itself has to take on the routine work.

## Metadata stops being documentation

The first pillar turns metadata from a passive catalog into an active layer that tags, classifies and connects data sets automatically. Koripalli reports outcomes organisations have seen: 62% faster data discovery, 72% fewer data quality issues, 43% more stakeholder trust in data and project delivery 2.7 times faster.

Her case study is an e-commerce retailer that used AI-generated product metadata. Search for "waterproof jacket" and the engine understands synonyms and related features. Reported results: 37% better search relevance, a 24% higher conversion rate, 19% fewer returns and 29% larger orders. It's a nice reminder that metadata work shows up on the revenue line, not only in the data team's backlog.

## Pipelines that fix the boring failures themselves

The self-healing pillar has four steps. Detect anomalies against a learned normal, such as a batch half its usual size or a file that never arrived. Adapt to changes like a new upstream column by mapping schemas from metadata or ignoring extra fields until it learns how to handle them. Remediate known failure patterns automatically, for example retrying a timed-out job on a backup server or switching to a secondary source when data arrives corrupted. Then learn from each incident.

The pay-off she describes is fewer overnight alerts, dashboards that are still fresh at 6am, faster recovery because the system has already isolated the problem, and ops teams that don't grow linearly with data volume. She cites a McKinsey finding that advanced self-healing systems can cut operational costs by up to 30%.

## Scale before the spike, not after

Predictive optimisation learns usage cycles (the 9am dashboard rush, month-end batch jobs), forecasts demand, provisions ahead of time and scales down on quiet weekends, then compares prediction to reality and retrains. Her umbrella analogy fits: you pack it because the forecast said rain.

The reported numbers are bold: 43.8% better resource utilisation than threshold-based autoscaling, over-provisioning down from about 61% to 12.3%, about $476K a year saved for mid-sized deployments, 380% first-year ROI, 76.2% fewer SLA violations and 3.2 times more workload variability absorbed without degradation.

## Governance as a glass box

The fourth pillar automates detection and classification of sensitive data (columns that look like social security numbers, data sets with health information), enforces masking, encryption and role-based access at runtime, monitors for odd access like heavy sensitive queries at 2am, and explains every automated action. Her phrase for the goal is a glass box rather than a black box.

Reported metrics include 67% less audit preparation time, 94.8% accuracy in classifying sensitive data, data access requests dropping from about nine and a half days to about 12 minutes, and new regulations implemented in 26 days instead of 97.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers and architects building the case for automation, and managers who need numbers to frame it. Treat the metrics as figures gathered from various reports and studies rather than from one system you can inspect; the talk doesn't break down where each comes from.

Title: Global HR system rollouts need a global core and local slack
Description: ADP implementation leader Swetha Priya Sathiyam at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on deploying global HCM systems, with AI for risk and data quality.
Body:
Replacing the HR system of a company that operates in dozens of countries is less a software project than a negotiation between headquarters and every local payroll rule. Swetha Priya Sathiyam, senior manager for implementation and solution design on ADP's Lyric HCM with close to 15 years in HR transformation, laid out at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) a why-what-how framework for deploying global human capital management systems, with AI and ML used mainly to spot risk early and keep migrated data clean.

Scope note for engineers: this is a programme-delivery talk. There is no model architecture here; the ML appears as a capability of the platforms and a tool for implementation risk. If you've been pulled into an HCM migration, that's exactly the angle you need.

## Why companies rip out their HR stack

Sathiyam opens with figures she cites from industry research: 93% of companies planning to overhaul HR systems within three years, 42% of them chasing operational efficiency, and 82% moving to cloud-based solutions. Fragmented, outdated HR tech across countries makes it harder to attract, develop and keep people.

Her advice on the business case is pragmatic: don't sell it to executives as cost cutting alone. Frame it as a pyramid with strategic value at the top, operational efficiency in the middle and data-driven talent insights at the base, then recruit allies in finance, IT and regional HR who can argue the cross-functional benefits and absorb resistance.

## Governance before configuration

The collaboration section reads like a checklist you'd want pinned to the project wiki: identify and mobilise stakeholders, define who holds decision power and who holds operational power, build a responsibility matrix for who acts, who is consulted and who is informed, and revisit it regularly. She recommends dedicated collaboration platforms for real-time documentation, issue resolution and decision records, so accountability doesn't stop at the headquarters time zone.

## Where AI actually helps the rollout

Three uses stand out. Predictive risk identification learns from implementation patterns at similar organisations to forecast trouble before it shows up. Real-time monitoring watches system interactions for anomalies. Automated data validation checks integrity during migration, which anyone who has moved employee records between systems will recognise as the part that quietly eats months.

On the platform side, ML-driven predictive and talent analytics turn the HCM from a data repository into something that advises HR on retention and engagement.

## Cloud, with sovereignty

Her case for SaaS HCM is the familiar one: no on-premise servers or in-house infrastructure team, scaling that flexes as companies grow and shrink, vendor-managed updates, and strong security with encryption and granular access controls. She names Workday, SAP and Oracle Cloud Fusion as examples. Larger organisations increasingly go hybrid, keeping the most sensitive personal data in private clouds while using public cloud for processing.

Data governance is the non-negotiable. Data residency features keep records inside the borders the law requires while still feeding consolidated global analytics.

## The equilibrium is the job

The heart of the talk is balancing global standards with local flexibility. Design fundamental global processes, then tailored regional adaptations for local compliance. Govern on outcomes rather than rigid process, giving regional teams controlled autonomy within agreed parameters. Change management runs in three layers: awareness of why, capability building for the people who'll use it, and adoption support through SOPs and job aids, tuned with persona-based journeys from the C-suite down to individual contributors.

Her roadmap: assessment and strategy with ROI metrics, design and configuration with integration and migration plans, deployment in big-bang, regional waves or targeted journeys depending on the client, and then a centre of excellence that keeps improving the system after go-live.

## Who should watch

Engineers, architects and programme managers about to work on an HCM or ERP migration, and HR technology leads who need a structure to present to executives. Skip it if you want ML internals.

Title: What a decade of scrappy NLP side projects teaches about AI
Description: Microsoft engineer Aroma Rodrigues at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 replays her open source NLP projects, from blame parsers to SNLI bullshit detectors.
Body:
If you want to see how fast NLP moved, look at what one curious engineer had to hand-build in 2018 versus what an LLM does for free now. Aroma Rodrigues, a software engineer at Microsoft and a regular on the PyCon circuit, used her [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk to replay about ten of her open source projects, from shoes for the visually impaired to a contradiction detector for friends who are "15 minutes away".

It is a story talk, not a tutorial. Each project gets the goal, the method of its day, what went wrong, and what she would do with today's tools. That last part is what makes it useful.

## No dataset? Make one, then let an LLM make more

Her 2018 project at PyCon India tried to read terms and conditions for you: extract obligations, permissions and risks, and highlight the risky lines in red. The idea came from work on retirement accounts at Fidelity Investments, where legal rules and machine-readable rules lived side by side with no mapping between them. The problem was the usual one: no labelled data. She hand-annotated sentences into an SNLI-style dataset from first principles, which was far too small to train a strong classifier. Her modern fix: use those sentences to prompt an LLM, or have an LLM generate thousands of synthetic examples to train a better one.

## Parsing blame before transformers

The 2019 PyCon South Africa project went after misinformation in noisy, multilingual WhatsApp forwards, aiming to trace who was being blamed rather than only flag what was fake. With little training data, she leaned on spaCy and NLTK: part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, active versus passive voice, entity and emotion tracking, and a linguistic path model of blame. Verification used keyword extraction, a news API to cross-check coverage, reverse image search and fact-checking sites. Hand-written parse patterns are tedious, and she says plainly that LLMs now offer much richer context for this.

A related 2020 project measured gender bias in children's educational materials using little more than pronoun counts, entity-to-gender mapping and adjective associations, a reminder that dictionary-and-score methods still find real patterns.

## A bullshit detector built on SNLI

The crowd-pleaser is her PyCon Estonia 2023 talk: spotting when friends contradict themselves. She used SNLI, the dataset of 570,000 human-written sentence pairs labelled entailment, contradiction or neutral, with BERT and GPT-2 embeddings feeding a new classifier. A pair of headlines about Bernie Sanders, one calling his victories grand and one modest, scored as a light contradiction. Her argument for why this still matters: checking whether a new instruction contradicts an earlier one is exactly what you want from an LLM, and it helps with hallucinations and contradictory news.

## Poking at generative models with honest test cases

The 2024 PyCon US project, written during a week waiting at home for a visa, asked which jobs AI would take. She tested image generation on descriptions of character actors from a Kaggle dataset, a forensic sketch artist's job in miniature. Vague descriptions produced wrong faces; very descriptive ones came close. Captions for her travel photos from China were factual and flat, focusing on a passing car instead of the colourful street. A virtual try-on experiment after watching Clueless produced mostly odd results. Her 2023 tests of ChatGPT with riddles found it improved a lot once told it was in riddle mode, but struggled then with word problems, Venn diagrams and sensory experiences like hearing an egg crack.

## Where it started: ultrasound shoes

The oldest project, from 2016, was a pair of shoes with ultrasonic sensors that detected obstructions in front, behind and to the sides, sending data over Bluetooth to an Android app built with MIT App Inventor and PhoneGap. Feedback came as voice through a headset; she would now want haptics. Her closing point fits the whole talk: synthetic data from LLMs is great for creative tasks where factual accuracy isn't the goal, like tautologies, metaphors or photo captions.

## Who should watch

Python developers who want project ideas, early-career engineers wondering whether side projects are worth it, and anyone teaching NLP who needs a before-and-after of classic parsing versus LLMs. If you want one technique explained thoroughly, this deliberately skims.

Title: Environmental regulators are moving from paper files to live platforms
Description: Sneha Kalagarla of Cleveland State University at Conf42 SRE 2025 on cloud platforms, sensors and community data for environmental compliance.
Body:
Environmental enforcement used to run on clipboards and filing cabinets, which is a poor interface for an air-quality spike. Sneha Kalagarla of Cleveland State University made the case at [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) that cloud-based platforms with real-time monitoring, automated reporting and analytics are changing how regulators, industry and citizens protect the environment, and that the gains show up in faster incident response and lower operating costs.

Scope note: this is a domain and strategy talk about public-sector platforms, not an SRE deep technical session. Its reliability content is the requirements such a platform must meet; the rest is about why the shift matters and how agencies roll it out.

## From paper delay to real-time data

Kalagarla describes the old model: paper records, manual collection and fragmented data management, leading to inconsistent collection, analysis errors and slow responses. The new model replaces static records with systems that capture, store and process large volumes of data in real time, and the next step is AI that predicts environmental incidents before they happen.

She cites studies showing improvements in compliance monitoring, a 42% reduction in time to respond to critical environmental events, and much faster permit processing through digital workflows. On cost, the talk attributes savings to sensors and automated collection, cloud storage replacing on-premises servers, mobile tools for field visits, and automated workflows replacing paper processing.

## The architecture regulators need

The technology stack is the part SREs will recognise. Cloud hosting with 99.9% uptime and automatic disaster recovery. Responsive web and native mobile apps that support field work in remote places with limited connectivity, which is a sync problem as much as a UI one. Integrated databases that give agencies a single environmental data repository for cross-agency sharing and historical trends. An analytics engine with dashboards and automated compliance alerts on top.

The monitoring section lists the inputs: air-quality sensors with parts-per-billion detection and threshold-triggered notifications, continuous multi-parameter water monitoring tied to watershed management and flood prediction, satellite and drone imagery analysed for ecosystem shifts, soil composition tracking, radiation sensor networks with instant alerts, and compliance checks against emission standards with tamper-proof digital audit trails. Anyone who has run IoT ingestion will spot the hard problems hiding in that list: calibration, gaps and data you can defend in court.

## Citizens as a data source

One of the more interesting threads is community science. Mobile apps let residents contribute environmental observations, and Kalagarla reports a 57% rise in participation across pilot locations. The obvious worry is data quality, and her answer is AI validation and smart verification protocols to turn crowdsourced input into research-grade datasets, plus neighbourhood dashboards that show residents their local conditions.

The stakeholder map is broad: agencies get faster decisions, regulated industries get clearer guidance and proactive notifications, the public gets data portals, and researchers get standardised datasets and APIs.

## Roll it out like any platform

The implementation path is a sensible four-phase plan: assess current systems and set baseline metrics, pilot core functions with selected user groups and refine, integrate enterprise-wide with training and governance, then optimise continuously. Looking further out, she points to better ML for violation detection with fewer false positives, environmental DNA monitoring for biodiversity, AR and VR visualisation, and distributed ledgers for verifiable compliance records.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people building public-sector or compliance platforms, and anyone curious how civic monitoring systems are designed. If you came to Conf42 SRE for incident tooling or Kubernetes, this is a change of scenery rather than a technique to copy.

Title: Battery chips need power estimates that update as the design does
Description: Block's Puneet Gupta at Conf42 SRE 2025 on adaptive power calculation in battery-operated chip design, from architecture to sign-off.
Body:
A power budget fixed at the architecture stage is a forecast, and chip designs never stop changing after the forecast is made. Puneet Gupta, principal ASIC physical design engineer at Block, argued at [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) that power calculation for battery-operated chips should be adaptive: re-estimated at every design milestone from the best data available, with automation flagging gaps and feeding mismatches back to the teams that can fix them.

Fair warning for the SRE crowd: this is a hardware talk about ASIC flows, toggle files and power grids. The reliability lesson is general, though. It is the hardware cousin of a capacity plan that goes stale the moment it is written.

## Why static power numbers drift

Gupta walks through the stages of a chip project (architecture, RTL, physical design, sign-off) and the parameters that move between them: switching activity files, load capacitance, frequency and voltage. Features added late, especially high-frequency switching ones, change the power picture and cascade. A design that grows in area needs more current, which means a more robust power network, which adds load capacitance and power again.

The current practice he describes is a fixed calculation from the architecture spec plus static assumptions about area growth. His example of how that goes wrong: during area recovery a designer swaps in leakier low-threshold cells that shrink area but raise power. Mix enough of those decisions together and you get a suboptimal design with higher consumption, lower performance and a battery that drains fast.

## Recalculate at every milestone

The adaptive method starts with a comprehensive estimate from the preliminary spec, padded with statistical models built from prior designs and technology experience. Then it refines as real data arrives: workload analysis and simulation once RTL exists, more realistic load capacitance and toggle rates after placement, clock tree synthesis and routing, and rigorous checks at sign-off across functional and DFT activity files and every operating mode.

He gives input-quality thresholds for each phase. Early on, at least 45% of sequential elements and I/Os should have annotated activity, with parasitic data assumed to be mostly modelled. By the end of place and route he expects toggle-rate coverage in the 95 to 100% range and parasitic completeness of 85 to 100%. Tracking those numbers tells you how much to trust the estimate in front of you.

## Automate the nagging

The automation layer is the part that will look familiar to anyone who has built CI. The flow uses an activity file if it exists and falls back to a pessimistic toggle rate if not. It flags missing activity files, missing libraries or suspiciously low toggle rates and routes the report to the right owner, whether that's architecture, RTL or physical design. Predictive models fill gaps, for example estimating activity when the DFT file is missing, and a shared dashboard keeps all teams looking at the same numbers. Checkpoints in synthesis and place and route write power reports automatically, so a jump between phases is easy to trace to its cause.

## The results, and a nice feedback story

Power distribution network work rides on the better estimates: size the grid to the real current demand, avoid IR drop and electromigration, leave routing room for clocks and signals, and use power gating and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling where logic can idle.

Gupta reports savings in the 30 to 40% range from these techniques, 37% in his own case, along with a 42% performance-efficiency improvement with no area penalty and 2.8 times better battery longevity on a high-frequency battery-operated device. His favourite example of feedback in action: four cores switching simultaneously drew too much power, so the architecture team staggered turning them on by load, and spread the switching when all four were needed. He also notes the honest cost: ML-assisted calculation needs compute and runtime.

## Who should watch

Physical design and power engineers working on battery-operated silicon, and platform or EDA tooling engineers who build flows for them. Software SREs can watch it as a well-argued case for treating estimates as living data, but there is no cloud content here.

Title: Famous outages make a good syllabus for failure-resilient systems
Description: Botanixlabs DevOps lead Onyebuchi Mark Irozuru at Conf42 SRE 2025 on antifragility, chaos engineering and the failure patterns behind public outages.
Body:
Onyebuchi Mark Irozuru, DevOps lead at Botanixlabs, opened his talk at [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) with a confession: he loves failures, because "each failure teaches us something profound about our system that success could never teach us." What follows is a tour of resilience engineering built on that idea: five pillars for designing systems that expect to break, and a catalogue of well-known public outages grouped by the failure pattern behind them.

He says up front that he kept it high-level. This is an overview and a reading list, not a hands-on session, and it works best as the latter.

## Uptime is a lagging indicator

The talk starts at 3am with red dashboards, a disconnected microservice and a boss on the line, then zooms out. In a system with thousands of components something is always failing, so the useful questions are when, how, and at what cost. Irozuru's example of cost is the 2017 Amazon S3 outage, which he says cost companies more than $150 million and rippled through every industry that leaned on it.

His argument is that classic reliability engineering, maximum uptime through redundancy and fault tolerance, is necessary but no longer sufficient. Uptime and availability metrics tell you how you did; they don't tell you how the system will behave under a failure you haven't seen.

## Five pillars, one of them borrowed from Taleb

The pillars he proposes are antifragile architecture, chaos engineering, circuit breaker design, dynamic resource allocation, and monitoring and observability.

Antifragility is the most interesting framing: resilient systems resist disruption, while antifragile ones get stronger from it, using chaos input, real-time feedback and diversification. Chaos engineering is the practical route there, and he points to Netflix's Chaos Monkey terminating production instances as the origin story. The reasoning is simple: traffic spikes and failures will happen anyway, so better to cause them yourself while you are watching.

Circuit breakers isolate unhealthy nodes so traffic goes only to healthy ones and failures don't cascade. Dynamic resource allocation covers Kubernetes pod autoscaling, predictive scaling from historical patterns, resource pools that redistribute capacity during degradation, and load management that prioritises traffic by business impact. Monitoring needs baselines, automatic anomaly detection and a hard line between noise and actionable signals, because waking engineers for unactionable alerts is its own reliability problem.

## Outages, sorted by cause

The middle of the talk is the part to bookmark. Irozuru sorts public incidents into three families and names examples for each:

- **Cascading failures and retry storms:** Slack's 2021 global outage, the Netflix Christmas Eve outage in 2012, and the 2020 Robinhood trading outage as resource contention.
- **Operational failures:** configuration drift (a Salesforce database outage in 2019), deployment and migration problems (the TSB Bank migration in 2018, the Knight Capital trading loss in 2012, the 2017 S3 outage), and human error, with the 2017 GitLab incident in which an engineer deleted a production database.
- **Software failures:** resource exhaustion (a GitHub incident in 2018, a Reddit outage in 2016) and dependency failures (a Stripe API outage in 2019, the Fastly CDN outage in 2021).

Reading the public postmortems for that list is a solid weekend of resilience education.

## What five nines actually asks for

He closes on 99.999% availability, which is about five minutes of downtime a year, and what it demands: no single points of failure, zero-downtime deployments with rollback, partial availability during degradation, redundant infrastructure and network paths, comprehensive monitoring, and resilience patterns in the code. The toolkit to get there: architecture reviews and failure modelling to find fragile dependencies, sound foundational code patterns, and SLIs, SLOs and error budgets with real-time dashboards.

## Who should watch

Engineers building their first resilience programme who want a structured vocabulary and a list of famous incidents to study, and team leads who need material for a lunch-and-learn. If you've already read most of those postmortems, skip to the failure-pattern section.

Title: Stop chasing zero failures and design systems that absorb them
Description: AWS senior engineer Sai Sahiti Nemalikanti at Conf42 SRE 2025 on designing for failure with redundancy, bulkheads, circuit breakers and graceful degradation.
Body:
Picture tax day, the last hour before the deadline, and the service that files returns drops off the map. Sai Sahiti Nemalikanti, senior software engineer at AWS, used that scenario at [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) to argue that preventing every failure is a losing battle, and that the reliable move is to assume parts will break and design so the blast radius stays small: redundancy, isolation, circuit breakers, careful timeouts and retries, and graceful degradation, all watched by real monitoring.

It is a short, focused primer, around ten minutes of content by the speaker's own estimate. If you're new to resilience patterns, it's a clean first pass; if you've read the classics, it's a crisp refresher you can hand to a junior engineer.

## The last nine costs the most

Nemalikanti's first argument is economic. Chasing 100% uptime by prevention alone gives diminishing returns, with each step becoming exponentially harder, more complex and more expensive. Her second is about consequences: in an unprepared system a small glitch cascades, domino-style, into a full outage with a long tail of customer impact.

Designing for failure flips the goal. Systems should withstand turbulence without collapsing, degrade functionality rather than stop, and recover quickly. She is careful to say this doesn't mean giving up on stability; it means getting real reliability by planning for imperfection.

## Five patterns that do most of the work

**Redundancy.** No single point of failure for critical components. Run multiple instances of services, databases and load balancers, ideally across availability zones, so traffic can move when one instance dies.

**Isolation.** The bulkhead analogy: a flooded compartment shouldn't sink the ship. A failing user profile service should not take down payment processing. Separate resource pools, microservice boundaries and queue-based communication are the tools she names.

**Circuit breakers.** Hammering a service that is already struggling makes it worse for everyone and can make it unrecoverable. Once failures pass a threshold the breaker trips, callers get an immediate error or fallback, the struggling service gets room to recover, and a few trial requests later decide whether to close the circuit again.

**Timeouts and retries.** Never wait indefinitely. Use aggressive timeouts, and retry only with exponential backoff and a limited count, or you build your own retry storm and turn one problem into two.

**Graceful degradation.** Partial service beats none. Her example is a news site where the related-articles widget can fail without stopping anyone from reading the main story, which works only if core and non-core features were separated at design time.

## You still have to see it

Monitoring and observability sit underneath all five. Logs, metrics and failure detection tell you the impact, help you find the root cause, and, the part teams forget, verify that the resilience mechanisms behave as intended. A circuit breaker you can't observe is a guess with a config file.

## A habit, not a library

The closing section is about culture. Developers, testers, operations and SREs should keep asking the same question: "what happens if this part that I'm working on fails?" Chaos engineering is how you check the answer, by injecting controlled failures to find weaknesses before real outages do.

Her suggested starting point is pleasantly small: pick one critical component, analyse its failure modes, add one resilience pattern, then test it by injecting failure. Repeat until the muscle is built.

## Who should watch

Engineers early in their distributed systems career, teams writing their first resilience guidelines, and anyone who needs a short, well-ordered explainer to share in a design review. Experienced SREs will find no surprises, though the ordering makes a good checklist.

Title: A first map of GenAI apps, from unstructured data to a RAG chatbot
Description: Snowflake solutions consultant Shivali Naik at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 gives an intro to RAG chatbots and a crawl-walk-deploy path to adoption.
Body:
Most of the data a company owns has no schema, and that is the whole reason generative AI got interesting for enterprises. Shivali Naik, a solutions consultant at Snowflake, used her [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) session to lay out the basic shape of a retrieval-augmented chatbot, show one she built over her own PDFs, and suggest a staged way to adopt it without trying to do everything in week one.

Set expectations correctly: this is an introductory talk. If you've already shipped a RAG system, you'll recognise every box on the diagram. If you're the person who has to explain those boxes to a team or a manager, it's a tidy twenty minutes.

## AI was already here; ChatGPT changed the adoption curve

Naik opens with a short history: IBM's machine beating Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, games that tuned themselves to win, Netflix and social feeds recommending what to watch next. Then the chart everyone has seen: ChatGPT reaching a million users in five days, against roughly two and a half months for Instagram. Threads got there faster still, but her point is that ChatGPT is used for work by researchers and office workers alike, which is a different kind of adoption than a social feed.

## The problem is the 90% with no schema

Her framing of why this matters: most enterprise data is unstructured. Emails, chat logs, clinical notes, pathology reports, images, audio, video. Without a predefined schema you can't write a simple SELECT and start your analysis, so traditional databases struggle. Generative models fill the gap with text understanding, summarisation, document classification and conversation that keeps context across follow-up questions.

She contrasts old-style bots, predefined and unable to learn, with LLM-backed ones that are context aware and improve with data and feedback.

## The stack fits on one slide

The architecture is the classic one. A question gets embedded, the embedding is matched against a vector store of chunked documents, the relevant chunks come back, and the LLM turns them into an answer. Her shopping list: a large language model, an embedding store, vector search functions, and a framework for the UI on top.

Her own demo was a chatbot over a stage of PDFs, one of them her resume. She chunked the files into a vector store, wrote a function to fetch relevant chunks, kept chat history so follow-up questions could be summarised with context, and wrapped prompt and completion functions around it. Anyone who has asked a model about their own CV will appreciate the choice of test document.

## Clean the input, then expect a training period

The practical warnings are worth hearing. Ingest from every source into one staging location and transform it first, because stray special characters will break your Python scripts. After deployment, plan for a three-to-six-month period where real user questions teach you what the bot gets wrong. Add thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback so bad answers become signal.

Her adoption path is crawl, walk, deploy. Crawl: get the data in, clean it, chunk and vectorise. Walk: build the decision engine that defines which parameters matter and what a good versus a bad answer looks like. Then put it in front of users and watch.

## Where she sees it going

Multimodal bots that mix voice and text, agents that act (her example: GPT-4 finding a highly rated hotel deal for her dates and offering to book it), AI-built data engineering workflows, and more governance and safety tooling so cautious companies can adopt it inside a framework. She closes with WALL-E's idle humans versus a new era of discovery, and leaves the choice to the audience.

## Who should watch

Analysts, data engineers and managers getting their first bearings on GenAI applications, and anyone planning a pilot chatbot over internal documents. Experienced RAG builders can skip to the related talks.

Title: Plain SMS as the workhorse of population health outreach
Description: ZeOmega's Roja Perumandla at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on a HIPAA-compliant, event-driven SMS framework for closing care gaps between visits.
Body:
The cheapest channel in healthcare IT might also be the one that reaches the most patients between appointments. Roja Perumandla, director of professional services and client success at ZeOmega, a population health management company, argued at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) that an SMS framework with intelligent message routing and an event-driven back end can close care gaps that portals and phone calls leave open.

It is a short, domain-first talk. The value is in the map of where care breaks down and which message fixes which break, more than in any model or code.

## The gaps are timing problems

Perumandla lists the usual suspects in population health: patients not sticking to treatment plans, missed appointments that break continuity of care, medication non-adherence, and social factors like food, transport and housing that never show up in the chart. Her sharpest number is about speed: traditional outreach, she says, reaches only 38% of patients within 24 hours, which is a long time when the intervention is time-sensitive. Another: traditional one-way channels reach only up to 62% of high-risk patients, and tell care teams little about what happens between visits.

The common thread is that care happens in clinic, and the problems happen at home.

## The architecture, layer by layer

The system she describes sits on four layers. A healthcare integration layer talks to EHRs over HL7 and FHIR interfaces and feeds quality reporting. A clinical message processing engine decides what goes to whom and when. A protected health information database holds the sensitive data. A compliance layer wraps it all for HIPAA. The talk abstract adds AES-256 encryption and multi-factor authentication, and claims 99.99% uptime, up to 50,000 clinical alerts per hour and delivery latency under 200 milliseconds.

The FHIR link is what makes it more than a reminder service: care gaps can be identified automatically from clinical data and turned into outreach.

## One channel, many care pathways

Most of the talk walks through use cases, each a structured message sequence rather than a single text:

- **Chronic disease:** for diabetes, pathways aligned with American Diabetes Association guidelines, with blood glucose monitoring prompts and adherence support.
- **Care transitions:** discharge instructions reinforced over several messages, follow-up appointment reminders with preparation steps, medication reconciliation check-ins, and post-discharge symptom assessments with alert thresholds that escalate to the care team.
- **Prevention:** risk-stratified cancer screening reminders, structured immunisation outreach and pre-visit guidance so wellness visits cover more ground.
- **Social determinants:** structured assessments that connect vulnerable patients with community resources; she cites up to 35% more patients connected.

There is a sensible equity argument underneath. Rural and low-income patients, with transport limits and inflexible appointment systems, are exactly the ones a text message can still reach, and tailored messaging can work around literacy and language barriers.

## About the numbers

The abstract lists a long set of outcome figures, including a 42% improvement in treatment-plan adherence, a 37% reduction in missed appointments and a 51% increase in medication adherence. The talk itself does not walk through how they were measured or over which populations, so read them as the speaker's reported results rather than a study you can reproduce.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people building patient engagement, care management or health messaging, especially anyone integrating with EHRs over FHIR. If you came for machine learning internals, there aren't any: the intelligence here is in routing and clinical pathways.

Title: A tour of neural networks in banking risk, fraud and investing
Description: Data scientist Swapna Anugu at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 surveys where AI and ML meet financial decisions, from dynamic risk scores to fraud rings.
Body:
A customer who suddenly spends far more than usual, logs in from two states at once and types unusually slowly is three weak signals that add up to one strong one. Swapna Anugu, an AI-driven cloud data lead and data scientist at Manasi Information Technologies, used her [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk to survey how neural networks and classic ML combine in banking: risk assessment, anomaly detection, investment strategy and executive decision support.

This is a broad overview from someone who has worked on banking and finance use cases, not a walkthrough of one production system. Treat it as a map of where the models sit and what each is for.

## Pick the network for the data shape

Anugu starts with the toolbox. Recurrent networks for time-series prediction, CNNs for recognising chart patterns, transformers for sequential data with complex relationships. The reasons to bother with neural networks in finance are the usual ones, stated plainly: large data sets, non-linear relationships, noisy or incomplete inputs, and decisions needed in real time, from credit scoring to loan approvals.

She points out that structured transaction data is the easy part. Semi-structured and unstructured inputs are where standalone systems struggle and cloud-hosted ML earns its keep. Transfer learning gets a mention too: a pattern that preceded defaults in one product or region can warn about the same pattern elsewhere.

## Risk scores that move with the customer

The risk section has three parts. Dynamic risk scoring updates a person's or company's risk level as new data arrives, instead of leaning only on a static credit report. Scenario simulation runs what-ifs, such as a market crash, rising interest rates or a major slowdown, against the bank's portfolio to plan safety measures ahead of time. And explainable outputs: if a loan is denied, the system should say why, for example income too low, too many recent credit inquiries, or late payments in the past six months. That last one is less about elegance and more about not getting a regulator's letter.

## Fraud lives in the patterns between signals

The anomaly-detection framework is the most concrete part of the talk. Behavioural biometrics watch how someone interacts with their device: typing speed, hesitation, urgency. Transaction stress analysis compares spending to the usual pattern, like the regular local shopper who suddenly spends big at odd hours. Cross-channel tracking spots the same account active on several devices in different states at once. Network analysis looks for fraud rings, such as many accounts making similar purchases or two unrelated customers bouncing money back and forth. The stated goals are catching fraud early, cutting false alerts and not slowing down legitimate transactions.

## Investment and executive intelligence

On the investing side she covers reinforcement learning strategies that keep learning from market conditions and outcomes, NLP sentiment analysis over text, and personalised portfolios aligned to risk tolerance and objectives. For leadership, predictive analytics, scenario planning and decision support let executives act on current data instead of waiting weeks for an analysis.

## The rollout advice is the useful bit

Her implementation path is sober. First check whether the problem belongs in ML at all, because not every problem statement fits. Then prepare infrastructure on a cloud platform, run a pilot on sample data, monitor it for a while to see whether patterns hold, and only then scale with governance in place. Mask sensitive fields such as social security numbers before they reach a model. Keep humans in the loop for judgment calls, and keep measuring after launch, since a model is never done. Her headline takeaways: hybrid approaches beat a single model, good data comes first, and people and process matter as much as technology.

## Who should watch

Analysts and engineers new to financial ML who want the vocabulary and the main use cases in one place, and managers scoping a first fraud or risk pilot. Practitioners looking for architectures, benchmarks or code will want the related talks.

Title: Harmful-content moderation at scale lives or dies on the pipeline
Description: Gcore ML engineer Georgina Tryfou at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on a modular, privacy-first AI pipeline that catches CSAM and abuse in video.
Body:
A moderation model that is 99.999% accurate can also be completely useless, because harmful content is so rare that "everything is fine" scores that well. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025), Georgina Tryfou, a machine learning engineer at Gcore who builds real-time AI systems for video and speech, walked through how her team detects child sexual abuse material and other high-risk content, and why most of the hard work sits around the models.

It is a systems talk with an ethics spine. No code, but a full pipeline diagram, the failure modes that shaped it, and the privacy rules baked in from the start.

## Four problems before you write a line of model code

Tryfou lists them plainly. Class imbalance: the positives are vanishingly rare, so it has to be handled in system design, training and monitoring, not patched at the end. Volume: a ten-minute HD video can be 500 MB or more, and YouTube alone takes in over 500 hours of video a minute. Privacy: GDPR and plain ethics mean you can't hoover every upload into a central server. And adversaries: abusive content hidden behind innocent-looking cat memes, translucent overlays, TikTok-style filters, even tucked into the audio track with steganography. Static, surface-level features don't survive that.

## Decide what to scan before you scan it

The pipeline starts with a trigger, and this is the part worth stealing. Random sampling covers stored libraries. Metadata triggers fire on things like a sudden spike of uploads from one account or a filename resembling known hashes. Customer signals feed in post-publish moderation requests. Scanning less, but smarter, cuts cost and preserves privacy at the same time, which is a rare two-for-one.

Behind it sits a task engine on Celery (a distributed task queue), which prioritises by urgency, retries failed steps and balances across workers. A live-stream segment that needs a verdict within five seconds jumps ahead of a batch job. Jobs are sharded by modality, so vision, audio and sequence models scale independently. A preprocessing layer then splits video into short segments, normalises audio, re-encodes odd codecs and deduplicates content already scanned.

## An ensemble, then a decision you can explain

Inference runs several models in parallel: CNN frame classifiers fine-tuned on stricter data than typical NSFW filters, a Whisper-style transcription pipeline with keyword spotting, and lightweight temporal models (GRU or 3D CNN) for actions that unfold over five or ten seconds. Each returns its own score and tag. A post-processing layer fuses them, either with score aggregation or a meta-classifier, and enriches with metadata like title and spoken language. One rule she mentions: down-weight NSFW scores when a video is clearly educational, such as an anatomy lecture.

The decision layer then flags for human review, auto-blocks, alerts the customer or logs silently for borderline cases, and it stores a decision trace: which model outputs contributed, when and why. Everything is loosely coupled, so a single component can be swapped without breaking the rest.

## Privacy is a design input

Original media is discarded after scanning; only tags, scores and timestamps are kept, and only when a flag is raised. Scanning is consent-based, retention follows regional law, and deployments differ by jurisdiction. Tryfou also admits an early model disproportionately flagged videos with darker lighting or skin tones; the team retrained on more balanced data and added bias-detection hooks to validation.

What's next, per the talk: running detection on CDN edge nodes, region-aware thresholds and model variants, models trimmed under 200 MB for edge servers, and customer dashboards for reviewing events and tuning thresholds. She is clear these are in active development and early rollout.

## The lessons are the best five minutes

Orchestration is key, because without queues, retries and monitoring the models fall over under load. False positives erode customer trust, so threshold tuning is product work. A queue once failed silently and nothing ran for hours, hence the emphasis on logging and fallbacks. And trust comes from transparency, not perfection.

## Who should watch

Anyone building trust-and-safety tooling, video or audio ML pipelines, or any classifier where the positive class is tiny and the cost of a miss is huge. If you want model architecture details, this stays at the block-diagram level.

Title: AI coding should compose components, not spit out snippets
Description: Bit chief scientist Laly Bar-Ilan at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 on components and the dependency graph as a shared language for devs, PMs and AI.
Body:
Ask your code assistant for a button twice and it will happily write you two buttons. Laly Bar-Ilan, chief scientist at Bit, used her [Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) talk to argue that the fix is architectural: teach AI to think in reusable components and their dependency graph, so it composes features from what already exists instead of generating fresh, isolated code every time.

It is a vendor talk in the honest sense. The ideas stand on their own, and the demo shows Bit's own platform and its model, Hope AI.

## Programming history is a story of bigger building blocks

Bar-Ilan opens with a quick tour: punch cards in the 1940s, assembly, Fortran and COBOL, C, then C++ and Java organising code around real-world objects, then JavaScript, Python and PHP hiding memory allocation and compilation. Each step moved further from the hardware and toward human intent, and each step made the unit of communication bigger. Her term for prompt-driven coding is a "semi-natural language": a dialect of English with domain jargon.

The punchline of the history lesson is that the next unit is the component. Not a register move, not a function, but a header, a shopping cart, a payment flow.

## Components are words; the dependency graph is the grammar

At Bit, components model the whole code base, front end and back end: every entity, database handler, algorithm and microservice. Each one hides its implementation, tests, configuration and versioning behind an API and docs. Her image is an iceberg: you see the tip, and the tip is all you or the model need.

The dependency graph is the syntax. A header depends on a logo, an avatar and a navigation menu; the menu uses a search box, which uses a button and a search service. Read that way, the graph is a live map of the organisation's product functionality, visible to non-engineers, and the first place to look before building anything new.

## Tokens versus a political map

The sharpest analogy in the talk: when a model reads code it sees tokens, like a topographical map with exact terrain and no borders. Humans see a political map, with features, boundaries and connections. Handing the model components and the graph gives it the political map directly, instead of making it infer meaning from import statements scattered across repositories.

That changes the task from generation to composition, which is easier. It also protects IP, since the model sees interfaces rather than implementations, and keeps context lean.

## Top down, then bottom up

The workflow she shows is hybrid. A prompt like "build a news platform" makes the model propose an architecture of components first. It searches the graph for ones to reuse, then goes bottom up: modify existing components where needed, generate the glue code, and generate new components only for what's missing. After human review, the new components join the graph and are reusable by everyone.

Because components are runnable and testable, you can check a change and its impact on the rest of the graph before it ships.

## Keeping humans in the loop

The closing section is about control, and it's the part worth arguing about. Reading a component's docs and tests is easier than reviewing a wall of generated lines. Isolated components give you granular permissions, so a misbehaving piece can be reviewed or replaced without risking the whole system. Product managers and designers can open and review pull requests on components, which pulls them into the development loop. Her closing line, roughly: git blame only tells half the story now.

## Who should watch

Tech leads worried about AI-generated duplication rotting a large code base, platform teams thinking about internal reuse, and anyone curious how architecture-first prompting differs from autocomplete. If you need evaluation numbers on code quality, the talk doesn't offer any.

Title: Using Splunk ML to turn alert floods into automated remediation
Description: Prabhu Govindasamy Varadaraj at Conf42 SRE 2025 on AI-powered observability with Splunk, cross-layer anomaly correlation and remediation loops.
Body:
Three dashboards shouting about the same outage make a choir, not an observability strategy. At [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), Prabhu Govindasamy Varadaraj laid out how machine learning in Splunk can correlate anomalies across metrics, logs and traces, find the likely root cause, and trigger remediation automatically, moving an operations team from reacting to thresholds toward predicting failures.

Honest scope: this is a Splunk-centred architecture talk. The ideas transfer to other platforms, but the pipeline, the agents and the ML features shown are Splunk's.

## The problem is uncorrelated noise

The talk opens with what Varadaraj calls an observability crisis in distributed architectures: siloed tools producing floods of uncorrelated alerts. Systems generate huge volumes of metrics, logs and traces, but capturing the right data in context, then detecting meaningful patterns across those signals, is where most teams stall.

He traces the history quickly. Early monitoring meant CPU, memory and disk thresholds. Then log aggregation with ELK and Splunk made logs the centre of debugging, though still siloed. Then full observability joined metrics, logs and traces to explain why, and now AI-assisted observability analyses trends and predicts failures. He cites industry figures that 94% of enterprises consider digital services critical to their core business while many still lack full-stack observability.

## One anomaly per layer, one story across them

The sharpest part of the talk is the layered detection model. In the metrics layer, Splunk learns normal behaviour, such as memory use or request rates, and adjusts thresholds automatically. In the log layer it uses NLP-style pattern analysis to surface rare entries like authentication failures. In the traces layer it flags abnormal latencies in microservices.

The value comes from correlating them. Varadaraj's example: a spike in response time, tied to a burst of error logs, traced back to one slow backend microservice. That is one incident with a suspect, instead of three alerts and a war room.

## The pipeline behind it

The architecture section is concrete. Collection uses Splunk universal forwarders and lightweight agents for on-prem logs, OpenTelemetry for metrics and traces, and native integrations for AWS, Azure and GCP. The processing pipeline does field extraction and enrichment (geolocation, device info), normalises data from every source, and injects correlation IDs so logs, metrics and traces can be joined across services. The ML layer then extracts features, baselines behaviour and runs anomaly detection, and results land in dashboards and alerts routed through Slack, PagerDuty or email.

On model design he makes a point worth stealing: feed the model more than CPU and memory. Combine infrastructure, application behaviour, user interactions and business performance, then tune against real past failures. Too sensitive and you get noise, too specific and you miss real problems.

## Remediation as a learning loop

Automated remediation follows a five-step loop: detect the anomaly, run root cause analysis with correlation engines, pick a response based on what worked historically (scaling, restarting a service), execute it, then verify the result and feed it back. The case study is an e-commerce company during an annual sale with traffic at ten times normal volume. Per the talk, the models spotted a payment-processing bottleneck 15 minutes before traditional alerting would have, triggered autoscaling, and prevented a slow checkout that could have cost $2.3 million in lost sales.

Varadaraj is upfront about the costs: you need a solid data strategy, integration with existing systems, continuous tuning, and patience while teams learn to trust predictive tooling. His rollout framework starts with critical services and instrumentation standards, adds retention policies, correlation agents, pipelines and a service map, and reaches maturity in roughly four to six months.

## Who should watch

Teams already on Splunk who want to go past saved searches and static alerts, and SRE leads making the case for AIOps with a concrete reference architecture. If you're on a different stack, the layered-correlation model and the remediation loop are still the parts to take away.

Title: An async success response is a promise your queue has to keep
Description: Vignesh Kuppa Amarnath of MSRCOSMOS at Conf42 SRE 2025 on zero data loss in async messaging via replication, acknowledgement protocols and recovery.
Body:
The user saw "success". The broker then fell over, and the event never got processed. Vignesh Kuppa Amarnath, a software engineer at MSRCOSMOS who works with clients in tax, health insurance and payroll, opened his talk at [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) with exactly that failure, and spent the rest of it on the patterns that close the gap: message replication with acknowledgements from every destination, durable persistence, structured recovery, and consistency levels chosen per business need.

It is a compact, conceptual talk. Expect definitions and design steps rather than broker configuration, which makes it a good primer before you go read your Kafka or RabbitMQ durability settings with fresh suspicion.

## Asynchronous means you answered before you knew

The opening example is the whole thesis. A web service accepts an event, drops it on a queue and returns success. In a synchronous system the user would learn about a failure in real time; in the async design the response goes out without any guarantee that the event was fully processed. If the messaging system goes down at the wrong moment, you have told someone something that is no longer true.

Kuppa Amarnath lists the distributed-system problems that make this worse: message tracking blind spots where the flow of messages becomes hard or impossible to follow, inadequate recovery mechanisms, and inconsistent state across nodes that should agree. For SREs the consequences are unpredictable recovery times, data integrity issues, and the dreaded post-failure reconciliation.

## Replicate, acknowledge, persist, verify

The prevention side is a four-step replication architecture: distribute the message across multiple nodes, get acknowledgements from all destinations, keep the replicas synchronised, and ensure durability during failures. The distributed acknowledgement protocol repeats the shape in more detail: send to every node involved, require a confirmation receipt from each, persist on multiple nodes for a durable period, and verify that distribution actually completed.

None of this is exotic. The value of the talk is in stating it as a checklist that you can hold a system against, especially one where an acknowledgement quietly means the message reached one broker's memory and nothing more.

## Three ways back after the crash

For recovery he describes three techniques. Snapshot-based recovery restores from consistent point-in-time backups, avoiding complex message reconstruction. Replay-based recovery rebuilds state systematically from transaction logs so nothing is lost during recovery. Peer-assisted recovery lets healthy nodes collaboratively rebuild a failed peer, spreading the recovery workload and cutting downtime.

He adds standardised message formats such as JSON or XML with schema enforcement, so that validation and transformation stay simple when messages cross team boundaries.

## Pick consistency like you pick a budget

The performance section is where the trade-offs live. Eventual consistency buys throughput and less synchronisation overhead at the cost of temporary staleness. Strategic caching lowers response times and backend load if invalidation is done carefully. Partitioning balances load, isolates failure domains and scales horizontally.

A chart walks the spectrum from strong consistency through quorum and read-your-writes to eventual consistency, with latency and throughput moving in opposite directions as you relax guarantees. The case study, described in outline, follows a team that lost data during a regional outage, redesigned around multi-region replication with quorum writes, and added end-to-end message tracking.

His closing advice fits on a sticky note: put data integrity ahead of raw performance, match the consistency level to the business need, start with the critical data path, and monitor everything. Without that last one, zero data loss is just a claim nobody can check.

## Who should watch

Engineers designing event-driven systems in domains where a lost message is a lost payment or a lost claim, and SREs who want a vocabulary for interrogating a messaging design. If you already run quorum writes with end-to-end message tracing, this is a review rather than new material.

Title: SRE for one-hour retail delivery starts with three layers of SLOs
Description: Srinivas Ankam of Cloud5 Solutions at Conf42 SRE 2025 on applying SLOs, observability, chaos engineering and incident practice to AI retail logistics.
Body:
When the promise to the customer is a one-hour delivery window, a slow API is a late van. Srinivas Ankam, a retail architect with two decades in the industry at Cloud5 Solutions, showed at [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) how classic SRE practice maps onto AI-driven retail logistics: SLOs written at the technical, customer and business level, observability that tracks fulfilment velocity per region, and chaos experiments that measure customer impact rather than just error counts.

It is a framework talk, broad rather than deep, and its strength is showing how one set of SRE tools fits a domain where software, warehouses and delivery fleets fail together.

## Retail logistics got fast, so reliability got physical

Ankam frames the evolution in four steps: traditional orders taking days through central warehouses, then omnichannel cutting fulfilment to about 24 hours, then AI-powered micro-fulfilment centres (MFCs) filling orders within hours, and next, predictive systems that start processing before the customer finishes ordering.

The MFC architecture he describes stacks an AI layer for predictive inventory placement and demand forecasting on top of fault-tolerant microservices with regional failover, all on Kubernetes. The business target he gives is 98.7% order accuracy within one-hour delivery windows.

## SLOs in three layers

The most reusable slide is the SLO framework, because it refuses to stop at the infrastructure. Technical SLOs target 99.99% availability, API responses under 100 milliseconds and order processing latency under 50 seconds. Customer-experience SLOs cover delivery-time accuracy within plus or minus five minutes, order accuracy above 99.5% and app transaction completion above 98%. Business SLOs track cart abandonment under 15%, repeat purchase above 65% and more than 12 orders per hour in delivery efficiency.

Whether you like each number is less important than the structure: an engineer can see which business outcome their latency budget protects, and an executive can see why an infrastructure incident shows up in the cart. Error budgets, SLOs, automation through CI/CD and observability are the four principles Ankam puts underneath it.

## Observability that speaks in orders per region

The observability section ties technical signals to fulfilment. Distributed tracing is meant to hold up through 10x traffic spikes at peak shopping times, anomaly detection alerts engineers before customers notice, and custom metrics track fulfilment velocity across regional MFC networks, with dashboards comparing actual and expected performance per geographic zone. SLO tracking feeds executive dashboards so infrastructure health is visible next to customer satisfaction.

Route optimisation for last-mile delivery gets its own slide: real-time GPS positions from the fleet, ML models forecasting congestion, and dynamic route computation through dense urban areas.

## Break it on purpose, then measure the customer

The incident framework is the familiar arc done properly: detection through PagerDuty alerts, customer feedback monitoring and synthetic transaction canaries; structured incident command with cross-functional teams and pre-defined channels; playbook-driven remediation including automated rollbacks; and blameless postmortems feeding a knowledge base.

Chaos engineering follows the same discipline. Form a precise hypothesis about steady state, run calibrated failures in production to test boundaries and recovery, and correlate technical metrics with customer-experience indicators to quantify what a degradation actually costs. The abstract promises strategies for when delivery robots go rogue; the talk's answer is that you find out how your system behaves before the robot does. Shift-left security rounds it out with IDE linting, SAST and dependency checks in CI, container image scanning at deploy and threat monitoring in production.

## Who should watch

SREs and architects in retail, e-commerce or logistics who need a template for SLOs that executives will read, and anyone building reliability programmes for systems where software failures turn into physical delays. Skip it if you want implementation detail for a specific tool.

Title: A guided tour of the Spring Boot toolbox, from Initializr to circuit breakers
Description: Krishna Rao Vemula of Ikon Tech Services at Conf42 SRE 2025 tours Spring Boot tooling, from start.spring.io and DevTools to Eureka and circuit breakers.
Body:
Spring Boot's real selling point is how much of a service you never have to write. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Krishna Rao Vemula of Ikon Tech Services walks through the tools that make that true, in the order you meet them on a project: generating it, running it locally, packaging it in Docker, splitting it into microservices, migrating its database and keeping it standing when a dependency falls over.

The talk is listed as "Spring Boot Observability: Building Self-Healing Microservices for Modern SRE Practices". The session as recorded is a broader tour of Spring Boot developer tooling; the resilience material that SREs will care about most arrives at the end, with circuit breakers and rate limiting.

## Start and iterate without ceremony

The tour begins at start.spring.io, the Spring Initializr, where you pick the starters you need (an embedded Tomcat web starter, Spring Data JPA and so on), choose jar packaging, download the project and open it in any IDE.

Then DevTools, which watches the classpath and restarts the app when classes change, with live reload so the browser picks up the latest changes. Krishna pairs that with per-environment property files and profiles: separate settings for dev, SIT and production, selected by profile name, so the same build reads the right configuration wherever it runs. He also spends a moment on IntelliJ IDEA's Spring support for code suggestions, navigation and running tests at method or class level.

## The fat jar makes Docker boring, in a good way

Because a Spring Boot application is self-contained, with the embedded server inside the jar, the Dockerfile shrinks to an OpenJDK base image, a copy of the jar and a start command. The same image then runs on a laptop, in the CI/CD pipeline, in test and in production, and profiles decide which properties each environment loads. Nothing exotic, which is exactly the point.

## Microservices, the Spring way

The middle of the talk covers the moving parts of a Spring microservice estate:

- **Bootstrapping.** The main class with `@SpringBootApplication` loads every component in its package at startup, and `@RestController` turns a class into a REST service.
- **Less boilerplate.** Annotations such as `@Data` generate the getters, setters, `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` that plain Java classes otherwise drown in.
- **Service independence.** His example is an employee service and a department service on separate servers and databases: when the department service is down, the employee service still answers.
- **Calling each other.** `RestTemplate` for inter-service HTTP calls, a Eureka registry for service discovery once you have more than a handful of services, and an API gateway as the single entry point for routing, load balancing and security.

## Schemas, tests and failing gracefully

The last stretch is where the SRE angle shows. Database changes are tracked as versioned migrations kept with the application code, including repeatable migrations, and applied automatically when the service starts, which closes the usual gap between a code deploy and a schema change. For testing, Spring Boot Test runs against real services instead of hand-built mocks, including database repositories.

Then circuit breakers: when calls to a dependency keep failing past a threshold, the circuit opens and stops sending it requests, so one sick service doesn't drag its callers down. Rate limiting protects services from traffic spikes by capping the request rate. That pair is the closest the recording gets to the self-healing story in the title.

## Who should watch

Java developers new to Spring Boot, or engineers moving from a monolith to their first Spring microservices, who want a map of the ecosystem in one sitting. It's an orientation rather than a close look at Actuator metrics or tracing, so SREs looking for observability internals should pair it with the talks below.

Title: Follow one trace from the React click to the Node.js backend
Description: Twilio staff engineer Mohit Menghnani at Conf42 SRE 2025 on unified full-stack observability for React and Node.js with trace propagation.
Body:
A slow page is a whodunit with four suspects: the React render, the network, the Node.js handler and the database. Mohit Menghnani, staff software engineer at Twilio working on the phone numbers product, made the case at [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) that you only solve it quickly when the frontend and backend share one trace, so a user's click can be followed through every hop instead of reconciled across two teams' dashboards.

This is an approachable, practical talk aimed at full-stack teams. It covers concepts, standards, KPIs and tooling choices rather than a deep code demo.

## Two dashboards, zero answers

Menghnani's analogy is a play: you can't follow it by watching only the actors or only reading the script. Treat a React frontend and a Node.js backend as isolated systems, each with its own dashboard, and the interaction between them is exactly what nobody sees. Unified full-stack observability is his name for a single view from the user's interaction in the UI through server logic down to the data layer, with the linking done by tooling rather than by an engineer squinting at timestamps.

The payoffs he lists are the ones that matter on call: lower MTTD and MTTR, shared context between frontend and backend teams, bottlenecks that span the boundary, and anomaly detection across the whole stack.

## Correlation is a header, not a meeting

The core technique is trace propagation. A user action gets a unique ID, and that ID rides along on every backend request it causes. Menghnani points to the W3C Trace Context headers, traceparent and tracestate, as the standard way to carry it, with correlation or session IDs embedded in logs as a complementary approach. Many platforms pair real user monitoring on the frontend with APM on the backend to automate that link, and OpenTelemetry gives you a vendor-neutral way to implement the propagation.

From there it is standard distributed tracing: each operation is a span, spans form a trace, and tools like Jaeger and Zipkin draw the waterfall. His examples are the useful kind. A payment failure that turns out to be the backend timing out on a third-party gateway. Product images loading slowly because the Node.js API that fetches their data is slow. A particular user path in the UI that drives CPU on one backend route.

## Pick KPIs both teams will argue about

The talk proposes a joint KPI set: user-perceived latency, error rates on both sides, end-to-end request latency, throughput, resource utilisation, user engagement metrics and Core Web Vitals. Menghnani's framing is that these numbers are conversation starters for frontend and backend teams, and that a shared dashboard makes it obvious when a change on one side hurt the other.

The best-practice list follows the same logic. Put frontend and backend metrics and traces in one dashboard. Alert on correlated signals, for example only when a spike in frontend errors coincides with rising backend latency, which is a good way to stop paging people for noise. Tag telemetry consistently, define SLOs so everyone knows what good looks like, and review dashboards and alerts regularly. His one-line summary: "we are not just collecting data, but we need to collect the right data."

## The tooling shelf is crowded

Menghnani runs through the field without picking a winner: Datadog and New Relic for full coverage of React and Node.js, Honeycomb, Dynatrace, Elastic Observability, Grafana Cloud, Observe, and OpenObserve as an open-source option, with OpenTelemetry underneath most of them. He mentions that his team at Twilio was evaluating OpenTelemetry, and recommends running a few proofs of concept with free trials and team feedback before committing.

## Who should watch

Full-stack teams running React and Node.js who still debug incidents by comparing two sets of graphs, and frontend engineers who want a gentle introduction to tracing vocabulary. If you already propagate traceparent from the browser and alert on joint signals, this will mostly confirm your setup.

Title: Middleware is the layer that lets legacy and cloud-native coexist
Description: Suman Neela of AppsTek at Conf42 SRE 2025 on middleware-driven hybrid integration, with ESBs, SOA, data consistency and security across old and new.
Body:
Nobody gets to rewrite the mainframe on a Tuesday, so the real question is what sits between it and the Kubernetes cluster. Suman Neela, integration developer at AppsTek, argued at [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) that the answer is a deliberate middleware layer: an orchestration tier that handles transformation, routing, consistency and security so that on-premises systems and cloud-native services can keep working as one business.

Scope note up front: this is an architecture overview, not a code walkthrough. It is built around industry figures and patterns rather than a single production system, and it works best as a map for someone about to own an integration programme.

## Four eras, one estate

Neela frames enterprise architecture as a sequence that most companies never fully finish: monolithic systems with tightly coupled functions and painful scaling, then service-oriented architecture with business-aligned services behind standard interfaces, then hybrid integration that synchronises data between on-premises and cloud platforms, and finally distributed microservices with autonomous deployment and dynamic scaling.

The useful point is that a real estate contains all four at once. The legacy database is still the source of truth, the SOA services still carry the business rules, and the new services want events. Middleware is how those layers talk without each one learning everyone else's protocol.

## The hard parts are timing and truth

The integration challenges the talk lists are the ones on-call engineers know by heart: growing complexity, real-time processing demands, and keeping data consistent from legacy databases all the way to cloud services. Neela cites survey figures that 72% of technology leaders rank system integration as a critical priority for digital transformation and that 65% of organisations are modernising integration infrastructure for real-time processing.

The argument is that point-to-point connections stop scaling long before the business stops adding systems. A middleware layer acting as an orchestration mechanism takes on the transformations, enforces security and compliance in one place, and gives you a single spot to look when two systems disagree about what a customer record says. Anyone who has debugged a nightly batch that silently dropped a field will appreciate having one suspect instead of twelve.

## ESBs grew up

The talk walks through the role of specialised middleware: hybrid solutions, cloud services, the enterprise service bus and legacy adapters, each scored by Neela on efficiency, communication reliability and message routing. The broader claim is that middleware has moved from a simple network communication layer into an integration platform that has to bridge old and new patterns while keeping performance and reliability up.

Looking ahead, Neela expects middleware to become more self-optimising: AI-driven automation and self-healing for routine integration work, edge computing integration to cut latency for time-critical applications, and IoT support for high-volume device data.

## Results depend on the domain

One of the more practical slides compares business intelligence integration across industries, with healthcare and finance reported as more effective than education and manufacturing. Neela reads the gap as a sign that integration requirements differ sharply by domain, so the middleware strategy should be domain-specific rather than copied from a vendor reference architecture.

On security, the talk cites 84% of surveyed organisations naming security as their primary integration concern, and treats compliance monitoring and data governance as core middleware responsibilities, especially in regulated industries.

## The checklist before you buy anything

The closing best practices are sensible and unglamorous: analyse existing systems and future scalability needs before implementation, pick tools that fit your technical requirements for scalability, security and monitoring, build comprehensive logging and monitoring from day one, and train the teams who will run the thing. The SRE translation: if the integration layer has no telemetry, it becomes the place incidents go to hide.

## Who should watch

Architects and integration engineers inheriting a hybrid estate, and SREs who keep getting paged for problems that turn out to live between systems. Skip it if you want implementation detail for a specific ESB or message broker.
