Title: eBPF turns the Kubernetes network from blind spot to live map
Description: Sai KR Pentaparthi at Conf42 SRE 2025 on eBPF network observability for Kubernetes, from dependency maps and anomaly detection to egress savings.
Body:
The service map in your wiki describes the cluster you meant to build; the kernel sees the one you actually run. At [Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), Sai KR Pentaparthi showed how eBPF gives SREs that kernel-level view of Kubernetes networking: continuous, event-driven capture of service-to-service traffic, with dependency maps, anomaly detection and cost insights built on top, and without the overhead of packet capture or chatty sidecars.

It is a strategy talk with a practical adoption path at the end, pitched so that you don't need to have written a kernel module to follow it.

## Sampling loses the interesting part

Pentaparthi starts with the blind spot. With hundreds of microservices, and often a service mesh, the communication paths are dynamic and rarely match static configuration or infrastructure-as-code definitions. Traditional monitoring samples or aggregates, which is fine for trends but throws away the fine-grained sequence of events you need for transient network problems. His image for it: debugging a tangled mess of wire with the lights partially off.

eBPF flips the model. Small programs run in a sandboxed virtual machine inside the Linux kernel and fire on events such as packets being processed, system calls or kernel function entry and exit. That gives microsecond-resolution data at the source. The safety story matters for production: every program passes the kernel verifier, which checks for problems like unbounded loops and out-of-bounds memory access before it is allowed to load.

## What the kernel's view buys you

The talk contrasts eBPF with agent-based monitoring on collection model, overhead, depth, implementation and real-time analysis, then lists what teams do with the data.

Dependency discovery is the headline. Because eBPF sees all traffic, it can build a live topology of which services talk, how often and with what latency, including the undocumented and legacy relationships nobody wrote into a manifest. Watch that map over time and you see how behaviour changes under load or during deployments, and you can spot chatty services or caching opportunities.

Anomaly detection comes next: learn a baseline for latency, error rates, protocols and connection frequency per path, flag statistically significant deviations instead of maintaining brittle static thresholds, and send alerts with real context, such as which two services and which path, rather than a bare "high latency". Those detections can trigger automated responses like restarting a pod, rerouting traffic or collecting extra diagnostics.

## The case study, and the money

Pentaparthi describes a global payment processor running more than 200 interdependent microservices on Kubernetes. Per the talk, eBPF-based observability brought 70% faster troubleshooting of critical payment issues, a complete map of the service dependencies including previously unknown interactions, and automated self-healing for roughly 85% of common network issues.

The cost section is where finance starts paying attention. Precise visibility into cross-availability-zone and internet egress lets teams reroute expensive traffic, and the talk cites egress reductions of up to 43%, resource savings from trimming chatty communication, and faster scaling decisions based on observed demand rather than coarse metrics.

## Start with one cluster

The adoption advice is refreshingly modest: start small with a single cluster or even one namespace and one pain point. Pick tools from the open-source ecosystem, naming Cilium, Hubble and Pixie, or commercial platforms built on them. Check kernel support; Pentaparthi gives 4.18 or later as the general baseline, with newer kernels better for broad features. Then feed the data into what you already run, such as Grafana or Datadog for dashboards and PagerDuty or Opsgenie for alerts. His sequence is learn (ebpf.io and project docs), experiment on a kind cluster, measure against a known issue, then scale.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who own Kubernetes networking and are tired of reconstructing incidents from aggregated metrics. If you already run Cilium with Hubble in production, the first half will be familiar, but the cost and anomaly sections are a good checklist.

Title: Generate test automation from the manual test case itself
Description: Sujeeth Manchikanti of Capgemini at Conf42 SRE 2025 presents a tool-agnostic framework that turns manual test cases into keyword-driven automation.
Body:
Most test automation dies of maintenance, not of bad ideas. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Sujeeth Manchikanti, Test Architect at Capgemini with about 15 years across manufacturing, banking, retail, telecom and CRM projects, presented his Universal Automation Framework (UAF), a tool-agnostic design that generates keyword-driven automation straight from manual test cases, so there is far less script code to rot.

This is a talk about the speaker's own framework, and he says so. Watch it for the architecture idea, which is portable whether or not you adopt UAF.

## The problem: code that tests code

Manchikanti's diagnosis is blunt. Testing takes a large share of project cost, and test automation is writing one piece of code to test another. As the application grows, so does the test code, until it becomes unmanageable. Testers are not professional developers, and developers rarely bring a tester's creativity. Add tool fragmentation across the stack, scripts constantly under maintenance and the skills needed to hold it together, and he calls test automation, as practised today, a loss-making business.

He is also explicit that he does not think AI is close to replacing software testing, because testing is creative work.

## Virtual application modelling

The core idea is a virtual application. The pipeline goes:

1. **A tool-agnostic object repository** describes the application's UI elements, built with existing open source tools.
2. **The framework generates a virtual application** from that repository. Manual testers write test cases by entering data, validation points and sequences into this model instead of free text.
3. **Routines** capture repeated steps, so common flows are picked rather than retyped.
4. **A keyword-driven data sheet** is generated from what the tester entered.
5. **A generic framework**, small and common to most automation stacks, executes that sheet through whichever automation tool you already use.

The pay-off is what he calls instant automation: update the manual test case and the automation is ready, with no script edits. Because nearly every automation tool can run a keyword-driven framework, the tool becomes a plug-in rather than the centre of the design. Reporting is generic too, saving results down to leaf level for any third-party reporting tool.

## What it changes for teams

The organisational argument is as strong as the technical one. With one standard core framework, people can move between projects knowing only the functional side plus basic troubleshooting. One central architect maintains the framework instead of a lead per team. Licences drop because tools are used for less of the development time.

He shares figures for maintenance reduction, development speed, coverage and cost from his implementations, plus three short case summaries from financial services, healthcare and retail clients. They come from the speaker's own projects, without client names, so read them as practitioner reports rather than independent benchmarks.

## Where AI fits, in his view

Manchikanti's future section puts AI around testing rather than in place of it: generating tests from usage patterns, migrating scripts between tool versions or technology stacks, predicting failure points from reports, and using the saved time for harder work such as IoT device testing across many devices.

## Who should watch

QA leads drowning in brittle UI scripts, and SRE or platform teams who own the release pipeline and want test coverage that does not collapse every sprint. If you already run a mature keyword-driven framework, the virtual application layer is the part that is new.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Tackling Flaky Tests: Strategies for Reliability in Continuous Testing](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mike_Morgan_testing_flaky_strategies) by Mike Morgan deals with the other half of automation pain.
- [API Testing Made Easy](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Barkatul_Mujauddin_api_testing) by Barkatul Mujauddin covers a layer UAF also targets.

Title: Observability in distributed systems, and the four traps to skip
Description: Hardik Patel of PayPal at Conf42 SRE 2025 on metrics, logs and traces, the signals that matter, and pitfalls from alert fatigue to vanity metrics.
Body:
Distributed systems hide their bugs at production scale, which is exactly where your test environment isn't. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Hardik Patel, Manager of Software Development at PayPal, gave a compact introduction to observability for large distributed systems: the three pillars, the metrics worth tracking, a roadmap for rolling it out, and the pitfalls that turn observability into noise and cost.

It is a concise, well-organised overview from someone with roughly 20 years across Yahoo, Symantec, Groupon and PayPal. Good for setting shared vocabulary on a team; light on implementation detail.

## Why monitoring alone runs out

Patel lists three reasons traditional monitoring falls short. Distributed systems present one system view over tens or hundreds of interconnected services. They change constantly with continuous deployment, so yesterday's baseline is stale. And some issues only surface at scale, which test systems usually cannot mimic. If you cannot reproduce the bug, you have to be able to see it where it happens.

## Three pillars, four signals

The pillars are standard and explained crisply. Metrics are numeric data points at regular intervals, good for trends and catching bottlenecks early. Logs are timestamped records of discrete events, good for context and forensics. Traces follow one request end to end across services, good for latency and dependency problems.

The four metrics he says matter most:

- **Latency** across service boundaries, tracked at P95 and P99.
- **Error rates,** with thresholds that depend on business impact: tighter for mission-critical services, looser elsewhere.
- **Resource utilisation** (compute, memory, network IO, storage), watched to prevent exhaustion before it happens.
- **User experience** metrics, to connect backend performance to what users actually feel.

His tracing example walks a request from a frontend interaction with a correlation ID, through context propagation into downstream microservices, to a database span that flags a 200 ms query exceeding its threshold. Simple, but a good picture to show anyone who has never opened a trace view.

## A roadmap in four steps

The implementation path is short: define key metrics tied to business outcomes, instrument code with standard conventions, centralise collection so signals from different services can be correlated, then build dashboards and alert rules and keep pruning noise and false positives. Above it sits an alerting pyramid that starts from capacity trends at the bottom, moves through early-warning thresholds and critical infrastructure health, and ends with alerts on business metrics that affect customers.

## The four pitfalls

This is the slide to screenshot:

1. **Alert fatigue.** Too many alerts, and the critical ones get ignored. Keep alerts actionable, with a clear corrective action.
2. **Cost overruns.** Collecting and storing everything is expensive, in storage and in code that computes metrics next to business logic. Sample high-volume telemetry.
3. **Tool overload.** Too many disparate tools are hard to adopt; consolidate where possible.
4. **Vanity metrics.** Tracking everything because everything feels important. Track what ties to business outcomes.

The business-impact numbers on root-cause time, MTTR and uptime are given as general expectations rather than PayPal measurements, so read them as the case for investing, not as a benchmark. His closing point is cultural and right: train teams to actually use the signals, or the dashboards just decorate the wall.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers starting an observability programme, or teams that have metrics and logs but no tracing yet. Experienced observability folks will find it familiar; the pitfalls list still makes a tidy review checklist.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Observability 2.0: much more than just logs, metrics and traces](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Neel_Shah_logs_metrics_traces) by Neel Shah argues for moving past the three-pillar model.
- [Practical introduction to OpenTelemetry tracing](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Nicolas_Frankel_opentelemetry_tracing) by Nicolas Frankel turns the tracing slide into running code.
- [Observability Maturity Model for AWS](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Indika_Wimalasuriya_observability_maturity_model) by Indika Wimalasuriya gives a way to measure where you are on Patel's roadmap.

Title: Blockchain as a tamper-proof audit trail for regulated test data
Description: Sridhar Dachepelly of Dell Technologies at Conf42 SRE 2025 on using blockchain audit trails and smart contracts for test data compliance under HIPAA, SOX and FDA rules.
Body:
A database audit log has an awkward weakness: whoever can write to the database can usually rewrite the log too. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Sridhar Dachepelly, Senior Principal Software Engineer at Dell Technologies, argued that blockchain fixes exactly that for test data in regulated industries, and walked through how it applies in healthcare, finance and pharmaceuticals.

It is a short, high-level talk. The useful part is the audit trail design and the phased adoption advice; the industry statistics are best read as context.

## The compliance problem, framed by regulation

Dachepelly opens with the cost of getting compliance wrong: rising regulatory spending, the cost of data breaches, and tightening data integrity requirements. The frameworks he names are the ones engineers in those sectors already live with: HIPAA in healthcare, Sarbanes-Oxley in finance, and FDA 21 CFR Part 11 for electronic records in pharma. Part 11 in particular demands authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation, which is close to a description of what a ledger does.

## Three properties doing the work

He leans on three core features:

- **Immutability.** Once recorded, data cannot be altered or deleted, so the audit trail is reliable.
- **Decentralisation.** Distributing data across nodes removes the single point of failure.
- **Smart contracts.** Compliance rules encoded so that checks run automatically instead of by manual audit.

For test data this matters more than it first seems. In pharma and healthcare, test results feed regulatory submissions and approvals, so proving that nobody touched them after the fact is a real requirement, not a nice-to-have.

## What an audit trail on a ledger looks like

The most concrete slide is the audit trail flow:

1. **Data creation.** Test data is generated with a cryptographic signature and timestamp.
2. **Consensus.** The network verifies data integrity.
3. **Secure storage.** Data sits in tamper-proof blocks, cryptographically linked.
4. **Permissioned access** controlled through smart contracts.
5. **Audit verification,** with the complete history available to authorised auditors.

Every transaction records what changed, who changed it and when. His key contrast: traditional database logs can be altered, while a distributed consensus mechanism makes the audit trail itself tamper-resistant.

## Adopt it in slices

Dachepelly does not pretend this is easy. Integration with legacy systems, scalability in high-transaction environments, organisational readiness and regulatory uncertainty are all on his challenges slide. His mitigations are pragmatic: hybrid solutions with APIs bridging blockchain and existing systems, newer consensus mechanisms and sidechains for throughput, training and change management, and early engagement with regulators.

The adoption path is the same advice you would give for any risky platform change: assess your compliance pain points, run a controlled proof of concept in one regulatory area with clear success metrics, then scale based on measured results. Looking ahead, he points to AI for predictive compliance and zero-knowledge proofs for verifying compliance without exposing sensitive data.

## A note on the figures

The talk cites large percentage improvements in compliance cost, audit preparation time and data integrity errors. They are not tied to named deployments in the talk, so treat them as the case for a pilot, not as expected results.

## Who should watch

Test and QA leads in pharma, healthcare or financial services who own audit evidence, and architects asked whether blockchain belongs in their compliance stack. It will not teach you to build a ledger; it will help you decide whether a pilot is worth scoping.

- [Compliance As Code with Cloud Custodian](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2021_Ismael_Hommani_Tanguy_Combe_compliance_as_code_cloud_custodian) by Ismael Hommani and Tanguy Combe shows a non-ledger route to automated compliance.

Title: Fintech ML on Kubernetes is a GPU utilisation problem first
Description: Srinivas Reddy Mosali of Visa at Conf42 SRE 2025 on SRE strategies for ML workloads on Kubernetes, from MIG partitioning and custom autoscaling to spot instances.
Body:
The most expensive thing in your ML cluster is often a GPU doing nothing. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Srinivas Reddy Mosali, Senior Consultant and Systems Engineer at Visa, framed fintech reliability as an infrastructure efficiency problem: AI and ML workloads on Kubernetes are resource-hungry and unpredictable, and running the containers is easy while running them well is not.

Despite the title, this is not a startup war story. It is a dense catalogue of techniques for GPU-backed ML platforms, with a financial-services lens on availability and cost.

## Squeeze the GPU before buying another one

Mosali starts at the hardware. Three levers:

- **Multi-instance GPU (MIG)** on NVIDIA A100 and H100 cards, carving one GPU into isolated instances so several inference workloads can share it.
- **CUDA-level memory management** to cut fragmentation and use tensor cores better, which he says matters most for vision-heavy models such as ID verification and biometric fraud detection.
- **Lower precision for inference.** FP32 is often unnecessary; FP16 or INT8 shrinks the memory footprint substantially.

## The HPA doesn't know what a model is

The autoscaling section is the most practical. The out-of-the-box Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler knows CPU and pod counts, not machine learning. His fix is a custom metrics pipeline through Prometheus adapters, exposing ML signals such as queue depth, batch processing duration and GPU memory pressure to the autoscaler.

Around that he layers workload profiling from historical telemetry, predictive scaling with warm pools for recurring jobs like end-of-day retraining and batch scoring, and buffer management: deliberately keeping some GPU headroom during critical windows such as trading sessions or holiday peaks, then scaling down harder afterwards. That last one is an SRE trade-off stated plainly; a little waste is the price of availability in finance.

## Schedule like the network is the bottleneck

For distributed training, Mosali focuses on orchestration. Topology-aware scheduling uses node affinity to keep jobs on nodes linked by NVLink or fast PCIe. Distributed frameworks such as TensorFlow multi-worker get tuned to the actual infrastructure. Priority-based preemption keeps high-priority jobs from queuing behind low-priority ones on shared clusters; he calls it air traffic control for GPUs.

Node pools follow the same logic: separate pools per GPU type (A100s in one, V100s in another) enforced with taints and tolerations, CPU-to-GPU-to-memory ratios matched to inference versus training, and nodes with InfiniBand or NVLink grouped together. Multi-team fairness comes from namespaces, resource quotas and guaranteed minimums for every team.

## Storage, spot and observability

Two more sections round it out. Storage: distributed file systems like GPFS for small, fragmented ML files, in-memory caching between persistent storage and compute, and automated hot/cold tiering behind a unified namespace. Cost: classify jobs by fault tolerance, checkpoint so reclaimed spot instances resume cleanly, and mix spot and on-demand dynamically.

The observability model is a four-layer pyramid: historical data for capacity planning, resource utilisation, ML-specific performance insights such as throughput and training loss, and root cause analysis that correlates GPU spikes with specific training phases.

The talk's improvement figures (cost, training speed, GPU usage, SLA attainment) are credited to a case study and real-world tests that are not detailed further, so take them as motivation.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE engineers running GPU workloads on Kubernetes, especially in shared, multi-team clusters. The four-step roadmap at the end (baseline metrics, quick wins like right-sized limits, then advanced tactics, then continuous refinement) is a sensible order of work.

Title: Monitoring has its own overhead, so budget for it
Description: Sanjeev Kumar of Delta Dental at Conf42 SRE 2025 compares Prometheus, Datadog and New Relic, and measures what monitoring itself costs in CPU and cloud spend.
Body:
Your monitoring stack is also a workload, and it has a bill. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Sanjeev Kumar, a DevOps Specialist at Delta Dental Insurance, compared Prometheus, Datadog and New Relic across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, and stood out from the usual monitoring talk by putting numbers on the other side of the ledger: how much CPU and money the monitoring itself consumed.

That trade-off slide is the reason to watch. The rest is a solid, compact guide to actionable alerting.

## Three tools, three clouds, one real workload

Kumar evaluated three tools with distinct roles. Prometheus as the open source, metrics-based option that fits containerised environments like Kubernetes. Datadog as the SaaS platform with broad cloud integrations and strong dashboards. New Relic for application performance monitoring and user experience tracking.

Beyond simulated environments, the tools were also deployed at a health insurance company running on Microsoft Azure, under real load such as traffic spikes during claims processing and compliance-driven applications. He tracked four factors: latency, throughput, CPU and memory use, and operational cost. Putting cost on the same list as latency is the quiet insight here.

## The gains, and the tax

On the gains side, the talk reports AWS latency dropping from 100 ms to 80 ms and Azure throughput rising from 1,900 to 2,400 requests per second after integrating Datadog and New Relic, with downtime down by around 15% across platforms. Kumar's comment is fair: these look modest, but on high-traffic, regulated systems a few milliseconds and a few points of uptime are what users and auditors notice.

Then the tax. CPU usage went up by 5 to 8% across platforms once monitoring was integrated, because the agents collect and process a lot of data in real time. Operational cost rose by about 12% on average, counting both tool fees and the extra cloud resources to run them.

His conclusion is not to monitor less but to monitor deliberately:

- Skip full-stack monitoring where application-level insight is enough.
- Tune collection intervals. Ask whether you need a metric every second or whether five minutes will do.
- Track the critical KPIs instead of everything.

Blindly switching on every feature, he warns, leads to wasted resources and unexpected bills. Anyone who has opened a surprise observability invoice will nod here.

## Alerts should guide, not overwhelm

The alerting section is short and practical. Do not page when CPU crosses 50%; page when it stays above 90% for a sustained period. Use dynamic baselines (Datadog and New Relic can learn what normal looks like) and alert on significant deviation. Group related alerts so responders see the incident, not a pile of symptoms. Route alerts to the right team with context, and plug them into incident workflows through PagerDuty, Slack or ServiceNow.

His last best practice is the one most teams skip: review alerts regularly, because what was critical six months ago might not be today.

## Who should watch

Teams choosing between Prometheus, Datadog and New Relic, and anyone who has to justify an observability budget to finance. It is a short talk, and the evaluation is summarised rather than shown in detail, but the overhead numbers are a useful counterweight to vendor slides that only show the upside.

- [How to set up reliable monitoring and alerts for cloud applications](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Israel_Heringer_reliable_monitoring_alerts) by Israel Heringer covers the setup side step by step.

Title: Healthcare data warehouses run on layers, partitions and tiers
Description: Vishal Jaiswal of Optum at Conf42 SRE 2025 on the layered architecture, partitioning and hot/warm/cold storage behind predictive analytics in hospitals.
Body:
A hospital produces two kinds of data: rows that fit a star schema and everything else, and the everything else is winning. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Vishal Jaiswal, Senior Manager Technology at Optum with around two decades in IT, walked through how to build a predictive analytics data warehouse for hospitals that stays fast and available while that unstructured share keeps growing.

This is an architecture talk with a healthcare accent, aimed at people who own ETL, data models and query performance rather than pagers. The SRE angle is availability and performance at scale for data that clinicians depend on.

## Three layers, each with a job

Jaiswal frames the warehouse as a multi-layer architecture:

- **Ingestion,** which has to take both real-time streams from patient monitoring systems and batch loads of administrative records.
- **Storage,** split between structured and unstructured data.
- **Analytics,** where stream processing, batch ETL and machine learning pipelines run.

The structured side leans on dimensional modelling, with star schemas for the transactional data and the goal of sub-second responses for most queries. The unstructured side, clinical narratives and documents, goes into document stores with flexible JSON schemas. The design detail that ties them together is reference pointers between structured and unstructured records, so a query can join a patient encounter to its clinical notes without forcing both into one shape.

## Partition by time, because most questions are about time

The performance section is the most transferable. Jaiswal notes that time-series analysis queries make up a large share of healthcare analytical workloads, so partitioning strategy matters more than almost anything else. He describes machine-learning-driven partition scheme selection, custom healthcare-specific indexing patterns based on how data is actually searched, column storage optimisation, compression, and intelligent query routing and caching in front of BI tools.

None of that is unique to healthcare. What makes it pressing there is the mix: thousands of concurrent query sessions from clinical and administrative departments, years of history kept for trend analysis, and peak loads that follow admission and discharge cycles.

## Hot, warm, cold, by clinical urgency

The storage tiering slide is the clearest. Hot data lives in memory for mission-critical patient information: real-time monitoring, active treatment protocols, emergency clinical decisions. Warm data sits on SSD and covers roughly the last 30 to 90 days of clinical history and upcoming appointments. Cold data goes to secure cloud archives with compliance-certified encryption and tamper-proof audit trails for regulatory records.

Tiering by clinical urgency rather than just access frequency is a nice touch. The cost of a slow query on an ICU dashboard is not the same as on last year's billing report.

## Challenges and the roadmap

He closes with the hard parts: EHR and legacy system integration, security and compliance, and unstructured data volume. The roadmap is assessment and planning, architecture design, pilot implementation, then full deployment and training, with stakeholder involvement throughout and security built into the foundation rather than added later.

The talk is heavy with percentage improvements credited to recent studies and healthcare organisations, without naming them. Use them as a sense of direction rather than as Optum's own metrics.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects building analytics platforms in healthcare or another regulated, document-heavy domain. SREs supporting a warehouse team will get useful vocabulary for the tiering and partitioning conversations. If you want code or a specific vendor stack, the talk stays at the architecture level.

- [Cloud-Native Data Engineering in Healthcare: Powering Precision Medicine](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Santhosh_Kumar_Rai_data_engineering_healthcare_precision) by Santhosh Kumar Rai covers the pipeline side for clinical data.
- [LLM-Audited EHR Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Manikesh_Iruku_ehr_pipelines_accuracy) by Manikesh Iruku looks at keeping EHR data accurate as it flows in.

Title: How Dropbox replaced SSH-and-grep with Grafana Loki
Description: Alok Ranjan of Dropbox at Conf42 SRE 2025 on moving unstructured logs to Grafana Loki, with per-service tenants, break-glass access and memberlist.
Body:
Before Loki, debugging at Dropbox meant SSHing into a host and hoping the logs were still there. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Alok Ranjan, Engineering Manager for the storage platform at Dropbox, told the story of how his team replaced that habit with Grafana Loki, and what it took to run it at Dropbox scale.

This is the best kind of conference talk: real requirements, real alternatives rejected for real reasons, and the operational scars from running the thing afterwards.

## The problem was a seven-day clock

Dropbox had no central solution for unstructured logs, the raw output from first-party code and third-party debug files sitting in local log directories on each host. Developers SSHed into boxes. Hosts were rotated out after seven days, taking their logs with them. Then came the move from standalone hosts to containers, which are even more ephemeral and more awkward to shell into.

So the requirements write themselves: at least a week of retention (the host rotation policy), ingest the entire production stream without changing application code, P99 ingestion under 30 seconds and queries under 10, 99% availability, mTLS from day one, access control by service ownership, encryption at rest, and a way to detect and redact PII if it ever leaks. The starting ingest was about 150 TB a day.

The non-goals are just as sharp. No mandated log format changes, no replacing structured logging, tracing or metrics, no new logging practices imposed on teams. Loki was to be a troubleshooting tool, not a new religion.

## Why not SaaS, cloud, enterprise or build

Ranjan walks through the options. External SaaS was out on cost and on the risk of shipping PII to a third party. Managed cloud logging was too expensive at their scale and the UX fell short. Self-hosted enterprise meant licensing costs plus running it on their own hardware anyway. Building in-house was tempting but not their core competency.

Loki won on low total cost of ownership, Grafana integration (engineers already lived there), a scale-out architecture and native multi-tenancy. The key design choice he explains well: Loki indexes only labels, not full text, so the index stays small. That is also why label cardinality is the thing to police; a trace ID or user ID as a label explodes your stream count.

## Running it: tenants, break glass and a write-heavy cluster

The deployment numbers are striking. Around 10 GB of logs per second, 30 days of retention taking about 10 PB of object storage, around 1,000 tenants, and fewer than one query per second. It is overwhelmingly a write system.

Some choices worth stealing:

- **Their own object store instead of S3** for chunks, cutting data transfer costs enough to raise retention from one week to four. Index files still go to S3.
- **Tenant equals service**, mirroring the existing permission model, with a custom query auth proxy instead of Grafana Enterprise RBAC.
- **Break glass access**: during an incident any user with a justified reason can temporarily read any service's logs, with an audit trail and limits on volume.
- **Write-ahead log disabled** on ingesters, trading durability for availability, plus conservative per-tenant rate limits with alerts and hot-reloaded overrides.

## etcd lost to memberlist

The best war story is the hash ring. Loki stored it in etcd as a single binary blob, and every ingester heartbeat rewrote the whole thing with a compare-and-swap. With a replication factor of three and 201 ingesters, write contention made deploys take hours, pushes failed on availability alerts, and etcd going down caused outages. Switching to memberlist, a gossip protocol that propagates deltas, removed the contention and the single point of failure, at the cost of eventual consistency. Ranjan reports no memberlist issues in the past year and double the ingesters afterwards.

## Who should watch

Anyone running or evaluating Loki at scale, and platform teams who need to replace SSH-based debugging without forcing every team onto a new log format. The talk assumes you know what an ingester is by the second half.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Logging in the Age of Cost-Cutting: Smart Strategies to Reduce Bills](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Venkata_Madhu_Prateek_Reddy_Kambala_logging_cost_cutting) by Venkata Madhu Prateek Reddy Kambala is all about the cost side that drove Dropbox's choice.
- [Anonymize application logs in DevOps way](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Leonid_Yankulin_structured_logging_google_cloud) by Leonid Yankulin covers the PII redaction requirement in depth.
- [Making Logs Work for you with Fluentd](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Phil_Wilkins_logs_fluentd) by Phil Wilkins looks at the shipping side of the pipeline.

Title: Conf42 Golang 2025: real dependencies in tests, hidden ones in go.mod
Description: Conf42 Golang 2025 roundup: 64 talks on testing Go services, dependency hygiene, Wasm and eBPF, confidential computing and Go in banking and fintech.
Body:
Conf42 Golang 2025 ran on April 3, 2025, with 64 talks, the biggest lineup of any Conf42 Golang so far, under the usual greeting to the gophers from outer space. Two ideas kept coming back: test against real dependencies instead of mocks, and know exactly which dependencies you're carrying. Around them, Go showed up at the edge, in the kernel, inside secure enclaves and in a lot of banks. The full lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025) and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDbxTLhVidTfS-6lJeAH6m-).

## Test against the real thing

Two talks made the same argument from different directions. [Manuel de la Pena](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Manuel_de_la_Pena_testing_go_integration), Staff Software Engineer at Docker and maintainer of Testcontainers for Go, showed a talk-rating service tested against real Postgres, Redis and Redpanda containers, plus an AWS Lambda running inside LocalStack. He then broke the average calculation on purpose and watched the test catch it in seconds. His tour of wait strategies is a good reason never to write `time.Sleep` in a test again.

[Nikolay Kuznetsov](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Nikolay_Kuznetsov_testing_go_services) of Zalando gave the companion piece: a practical guide to testing a Go service layer by layer. He leans on the testing trophy over the classic pyramid, since integration tests are now cheap enough to run more of them, and tests the repository layer against a real database rather than a mock. His toolkit covers Testcontainers, mocks generated with mockery, `httptest` for handlers, testify and go-cmp for comparing whole structs, and randomised test data. [Sridhar Dachepelly](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Sridhar_Dachepelly_testing_erp_orchestration) of Dell Technologies applied Go to test orchestration in large ERP systems.

## Know what's in your binary

[Andrii Raikov](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Andrii_Raikov_dependencies_code_management), Principal Software Engineer at Delivery Hero, asked the audience to name the indirect dependencies of their current project, then showed why most can't. Importing `fmt` silently pulls in `io`, `os`, `reflect` and more, and a few lines using the AWS SDK make a binary several times bigger. The second half covered patterns he has seen at Delivery Hero: a v2 client library that broke its v1 interfaces and stranded teams on the old version, and a `helpers` package that drifts into circular dependencies. His most practical advice: don't skip the import block in code review.

On the framework side, [Divya Darshana](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Divya_Darshana_http_communication_apis), an open source contributor to GoFr, showed circuit breakers, authentication and health monitoring for inter-service HTTP calls using the GoFr framework. And [Namkat Cedrick](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Namkat_Cedrick_career_experience_journey) of Iknite Studio gave the most personal talk of the day, "How Golang Changed My Life", revisiting old programming fears with a new mindset.

## Go beyond the server

[Alex Casalboni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Alex_Casalboni_cloud_edge_webassembly), Developer Advocate at Edgee, explained why WebAssembly suits edge computing, where logic in the request path has a budget of a few milliseconds. He traced Go's Wasm support from the `wasm` target in Go 1.11 to WASI preview 1 in Go 1.21, pointed to TinyGo for the component model, and showed how Edgee runs analytics SDKs as Wasm components at the edge.

[Pranshu Srivastava](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Pranshu_Srivastava_cilium_ebpf_networking) of Cloudera spoke to people starting with eBPF who don't want to write their user space code in Rust, sharing his experience with Cilium, why he chose it and which mistakes to avoid. [Brian Loomis](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Brian_Loomis_cloud_platforms_resilience), Director of Architecture at Progress, covered a distributed job runner designed to survive an unreliable network. [Utham Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Utham_Kumar_v2x_communication_vehicles) of Nanyang Technological University took Go into vehicle-to-everything networks for connected cars.

## Security in Go services

[Srinivas Vallabhaneni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Vallabhaneni_enclaves_security_confidential) of Walmart showed how Go fits confidential computing, keeping sensitive data inside secure enclaves in distributed systems without giving up performance. [Aditi Mallesh](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Aditi_Mallesh_identity_security_microservices) of Microsoft built identity orchestration as high-performance Go microservices across clouds, and [Santosh Bompally](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Santosh_Bompally_security_iac_threat) of Humana combined infrastructure as code with AI-driven threat detection. [Sudeep Shanubhog](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Sudeep_Shanubhog_security_cloud_adaptive) of Tential Solutions covered adaptive, real-time security for Microsoft cloud services written in Go.

## Go where the money moves

Finance had a strong showing. [Srinivas Allam](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Allam_banking_modernization_fintech) of Core ITS described Go modernising a tier-1 bank's legacy IBM iSeries infrastructure with zero-downtime migrations. [Deepu Komati](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Deepu_Komati_fintech_cloud_infrastructure) of PenFed Credit Union built financial decision systems in Go, and [Srinivas Reddy Mosali](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Reddy_Mosali_fintech_infrastructure_scaling) of Visa made the case for fintech infrastructure that never blinks. Beyond banking, [Ankita Kamat](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Ankita_Kamat_notification_latency_scaling) of Microsoft used Go's concurrency model for notification systems that handle millions of messages while keeping millisecond latency, [Hardik R Patel](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Hardik_R_Patel_data_pipelines_analytics) of PayPal designed multi-hop data pipelines for real-time analytics, and [Srikar Kompella](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srikar_Kompella_serverless_migration_aws) of Prime Video used Go for a serverless SaaS migration on AWS.

## Sponsors

Thanks to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), our diamond sponsor, and [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), our gold sponsor. Silver sponsors [Edgee](https://www.edgee.cloud/), [Tential](http://www.tential.com/), [Delivery Hero](https://careers.deliveryhero.com/deliveryhero-jobs) and [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) all joined in, each with a speaker on the lineup. Thanks also to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) for the newsletter.

## What's next

All 64 talks are linked from the [Conf42 Golang 2025 page](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025). The gophers return for [Conf42 Golang 2026](https://www.conf42.com/golang2026) on May 21, 2026. Until then, go read your `go.sum`.

Title: Put the database in the test, not in the CI config
Description: Manuel de la Pena of Docker, maintainer of Testcontainers for Go, at Conf42 Golang 2025 on integration tests against Postgres, Redis, Redpanda and LocalStack.
Body:
If reproducing one failing integration test means starting the whole application, the test setup is in the wrong place. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Manuel de la Pena](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Manuel_de_la_Pena_testing_go_integration), Staff Software Engineer at Docker and maintainer of Testcontainers for Go, showed how to move databases, brokers and even AWS Lambda out of the CI configuration and into the Go test that needs them.

The talk is mostly live code: one small service, four real dependencies, four test files, and timings on screen. It shows Docker's open source library, and it is about as practical as Go testing talks get.

## The CI server is a bad place for dependencies

Manuel starts with the setup many teams still run. A CI server, Jenkins or GitLab runners or GitHub Actions, is configured by you or a platform team to start every database, queue and cloud emulator your tests need. Those dependencies must match production versions and configuration, and the workers must be big enough to run all of them next to the tests.

Every dependency upgrade becomes a CI change, often in a system developers don't own. Each new service adds load to shared runners. And when a test fails, there's no easy way to run just that test on your laptop.

## Containers as test fixtures

Testcontainers for Go gives your test code programmatic access to the Docker engine: create, start, stop and terminate containers right where they're used. Testing the persistence layer means starting one Postgres container in that test, not the whole stack.

Each container's well-known port (5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL) is mapped to a random host port, so many containers can run in parallel. Manuel lists three benefits: consistency, because dependencies run in containers instead of on your host; test data isolation, because each container has its own data; and build speed. Onboarding shrinks to installing Docker and running the tests, which the project calls the clone and run experience.

## One service, four dependencies

The demo app rates conference talks in real time. It stores ratings in PostgreSQL through `pgx`, caches in Redis, streams events through Redpanda with the `franz-go` Kafka client, and calls an AWS Lambda to compute statistics.

Each repository takes a connection string, which is what makes it testable. The Postgres test uses the Postgres module with an init SQL script, database name and credentials, waits until a log line appears twice, and hands the connection string to the repository. On the Postgres 15 Alpine image it passes in about 10 seconds. Redis needs no customisation and passes in about seven. Redpanda, with topic auto-creation on, takes 14 seconds on the first run because it pulls the image, and five on the next.

The Lambda test is the clever one. A Makefile builds and zips the function. The test starts LocalStack, copies the zip into the container, and runs the create-function command inside it once the container is up. It then reads the function URL and swaps in the randomly mapped port. Then Manuel breaks the average calculation on purpose, reruns, and the test catches it in seconds: total count correct, average wrong. A Lambda tested end to end on a laptop, with no AWS account involved.

## The parts of the API worth knowing

The second half tours the building blocks behind the modules:

- **ContainerRequest** defines image, exposed ports, network and readiness conditions.
- **Lifecycle hooks** run your code before and after create, start, readiness, stop and terminate.
- **Files** are copied in after the container is created but before it starts, so a database can boot with a known state.
- **Ryuk**, the extra container you may have spotted in `docker ps`, cleans up containers, networks, volumes and images when tests finish.
- **Wait strategies** replace `time.Sleep`: wait for an exec result, an exit, a file, a health check, a listening port, an HTTP response with a given status or header, a log line or regex, a SQL query, or all of them together.

Testcontainers can also build an image from a Dockerfile and run it, which is handy when the dependency is your own service.

## Who should watch

Go developers whose integration tests either live only in CI or don't exist, and platform teams tired of maintaining test databases on shared runners. If you already use Testcontainers, the LocalStack Lambda pattern and the wait strategies list are the parts to steal.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [How to test your code with Testcontainers in Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Julien_Breux_test_testcontainers_container) by Julien Breux (Google Cloud), a gentler first container test.
- [Tackling Flaky Tests: Strategies for Reliability in Continuous Testing](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mike_Morgan_testing_flaky_strategies) by Mike Morgan (Buildkite).
- [Cloud Testing Without the Wait](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Anita_Ihuman_kubernetes_development_testing) by Anita Ihuman (MetalBear), on testing against real Kubernetes from your machine.

Title: A tour of the AI underwriting stack, from random forests to SharePoint
Description: Harsha Vardhan Reddy Yeddula at Conf42 SRE 2025 maps the ML, NLP and computer vision models behind AI insurance underwriting and where each one fits.
Body:
Underwriting is a document problem wearing a risk-model costume. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Harsha Vardhan Reddy Yeddula, who lists Osmania University Hyderabad and says he has more than ten years in insurance IT, gave a model-by-model tour of how AI is being wired into insurance underwriting, from classic classifiers to NLP on policy documents, computer vision on property photos, and Copilot inside SharePoint.

If you want a single map of which technique sits where in an underwriting pipeline, this is it. It is a survey, dense with figures, and it moves fast.

## Pick the model by what the regulator will ask

The first section compares three classic machine learning models for risk classification: random forests, logistic regression and gradient boosting. The comparison that matters is not raw accuracy. Yeddula singles out logistic regression for its complete algorithm transparency for regulatory compliance, even though the boosted models score higher in his figures.

That is the right framing for anyone building in a regulated domain. The model you can explain to an auditor often beats the one that wins the leaderboard, and a pipeline can use both: the transparent model for decisions that need justifying, the stronger one for triage.

## Most of the work is reading

The NLP section is where underwriting actually lives. Policies, riders and endorsements are long documents, and the talk describes BERT-based models, named entity recognition and coverage-gap detection pulling key facts out of them. The headline contrast is a standard policy analysed in seconds versus close to an hour by hand.

He also covers predictive models for fraud: time series for predicting claims, graph neural networks for fraud rings, and autoencoders for spotting claim patterns that no rule describes. The graph and autoencoder pieces are the ones worth noting if you build anomaly detection elsewhere; the techniques transfer directly to ops data.

## Computer vision for property, and the renewal nobody thinks about

Property assessment gets its own section. Image capture feeds detectors (he names YOLO and Faster R-CNN variants) that identify property features and structural damage, cutting inspection time from close to an hour per property to a few minutes in his numbers.

The underrated bit is policy renewal. Every policy comes up for renewal on a cycle, and robotic process automation plus models turn a manual, hours-long renewal review into minutes per policy. Renewals are boring, high volume and rule-heavy, which is exactly why they are a good first target.

## The SharePoint ending

The talk closes somewhere unexpected: Microsoft SharePoint and Copilot. Yeddula's argument is that insurance is all about content, metadata and file repositories, so the collaboration layer is where AI shows up for underwriters day to day, through summarisation, AI-assisted authoring, automatic content classification and SharePoint agents. It is clearly where his own consulting experience sits, and he offers help with moving content to the cloud.

## A note on the numbers

Almost every slide carries percentages for accuracy, speed and cost. They are not tied to a named carrier or study in the talk, so use them as rough orders of magnitude, not as targets for your own project.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects new to insurance who want the vocabulary: which model for risk scoring, which for documents, which for images. Teams on Microsoft 365 wondering where Copilot fits in an underwriting workflow. If you want implementation detail or failure stories, this survey will leave you wanting more.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [AI-Driven Insurance Operations: MLOps Strategies](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Sameer_Joshi_ai_driven_insurance) by Sameer Joshi covers running these models in production.
- [From Manual to Magical: How Rule-Based AI is Transforming Dental Insurance Claims](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Pravesh_Nikhare_insurance_rules_processing) by Pravesh Nikhare makes the case for rules next to models.
- [AI-Powered Fraud Detection in Cloud-Native Financial Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Sandeep_Jarugula_fraud_detection_analytics_security) by Sandeep Jarugula goes deeper on behavioural fraud analytics.

Title: Autonomous incident response has to earn its autonomy
Description: Smita Verma of Adobe at Conf42 SRE 2025 on rolling out AI incident response in phases, from observe-only to supervised actions to autonomy.
Body:
An AI that can roll back your production deploy at 3am had better be able to explain why. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Smita Verma of Adobe made the case for AI-powered autonomous incident response, and spent most of her time on the part vendors skip: how to roll it out so SREs actually trust it.

Her short version is in the closing line: "start small, start safely, but start now." The roadmap she gives for doing that is the reason to watch.

## Thousands of alerts a minute is a human-speed problem

The setup will be familiar. Microservices, containers and hybrid cloud add interdependencies, and alert volume can reach thousands per minute. One slow microservice ripples through its dependants, and finding the original fault by hand is, in her words, a needle in a haystack.

Autonomous systems answer that with pattern recognition across disparate data, contextual classification of what an anomaly means, and predefined playbooks executed at machine speed. The response actions she lists are concrete: isolate a compromised network segment, quarantine a suspicious container while redundant instances keep serving, redistribute compute during an incident, and roll back automatically when a deployment degrades performance.

## The 30-second timeline

The best slide is a timeline from a database case study. At T+0 an anomalous query pattern appears on the primary cluster. At T+1.5 seconds it is classified as likely resource exhaustion. At T+3 query throttling kicks in for non-critical services. At T+6 traffic moves to secondary replicas. At T+30 the SRE team gets an alert with the diagnostic data already attached.

Note the order. The humans are paged last, after the system has bought them time, and they arrive to a summary instead of a blank dashboard. That is the ergonomic win, regardless of what you think of the headline MTTR numbers.

A second case study covers a zero-day in a web framework, caught by behaviour anomalies rather than signatures, then contained and packaged into forensic data for the security team.

## Trust is a rollout plan

The section worth copying is the implementation path. Verma lays it out in five phases:

1. **Assessment.** Catalogue incident types and find high-volume, low-risk ones.
2. **Monitoring enhancement.** Improve telemetry, cut noise and tag data before automating anything.
3. **Passive learning.** Run the AI in observation-only mode. It predicts and recommends; humans compare its suggestions with what actually happened.
4. **Supervised automation.** The system acts, but only with human approval. Her analogy: supervised driving, with the SRE's hand still on the wheel.
5. **Full autonomy,** for well-understood incident types only, expanding as the system earns it.

Around that she adds guardrails: confidence scoring so an uncertain model escalates instead of guessing, read-only integrations at first, a tiered autonomy framework, full decision tracing (inputs, confidence, model used) and one-click override from the dashboard. Her first suggested use case is wonderfully unglamorous: automate the response to disk space alerts.

## Who should watch

SRE leads being pitched an AIOps product and wanting a sane adoption plan, and platform teams designing their own auto-remediation. The abstract's MTTR and false-positive figures come from enterprise deployments she does not name in detail, so the phased rollout is the takeaway, not the numbers.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [AI-Assisted Incident Response Using LLMs and MCP in Distributed Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Makarand_Gujarathi_assisted_incident_response) by Makarand Gujarathi shows the LLM-era version of the same idea.
- [AIOps: New Approaches to Reduce Alert Noise](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Birol_Yildiz_aiops_alert_noise) by Birol Yildiz tackles the alert flood that comes first.
- [Pragmatic Incident Response: 5 lessons learned from failures](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Robert_Ross_pragmatic_incident_response) by Robert Ross is the human-process baseline any automation should respect.

Title: Insurance AI takes the broken window, humans take the pile-up
Description: Balakrishna Sudabathula of Delta Dental at Conf42 SRE 2025 on splitting insurance work between AI automation and human adjusters, case by case.
Body:
The useful question about AI in insurance is not whether it works but which claims it should be allowed to decide. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Balakrishna Sudabathula, Expert Software Engineer at Delta Dental Insurance, laid out a working split: let the models clear the routine, high-volume cases in minutes, and route anything messy, contested or emotional to a person.

It is a business-facing overview rather than an engineering deep cut, and it is honest about that. Sudabathula opens by saying insurance is something everyone experiences, and that his goal is to show how much technology runs behind the scenes.

## A triage rule, not a replacement plan

The clearest idea in the talk is a triage boundary. A customer files a claim for a broken window: the system verifies the details and approves it within minutes. A multi-vehicle accident with a liability dispute: the system flags it for human review, and an adjuster makes the call.

That is the same shape SREs use for automated remediation. Automate the well-understood, low-blast-radius cases. Escalate the rest with context attached. The difference is that the "incident" here is someone's car, house or health, so the escalation path is also where empathy lives.

Sudabathula is explicit that the human side is not a temporary gap. Complex negotiations, legal disputes and situations where a customer has just had a major accident need a person, and he expects that to stay true.

## Where the models earn their keep

He walks through four areas where AI does the heavy lifting:

- **Underwriting and quotes.** Reading medical reports and risk factors to produce a premium quote in minutes instead of days.
- **Usage-based pricing.** Telematics in cars and fitness trackers feeding behaviour into pricing, so safe drivers and active customers can be priced differently.
- **Real-time risk alerts.** Weather data driving proactive warnings to customers ahead of floods or storms, and smart home security devices lowering theft risk.
- **Claims and fraud.** OCR on uploaded documents to extract data, network analysis to map relationships between claimants and providers and spot fraud rings, and language analysis to catch a story that changes between forms.

The fraud section is the most technical. Mapping claimant-provider graphs is a good reminder that many AI wins in insurance are really graph and pattern problems with a model on top.

## Read the numbers as directional

The talk quotes several improvement figures for claims speed, fraud detection, efficiency and market growth, attributed to "many companies" or to market reports. No single deployment is named, so treat them as the industry's pitch rather than Delta Dental's results. The structure of the argument holds up without them.

## Who should watch

Engineers joining an insurance or healthcare-payer team who want the business map before they touch the claims pipeline. Product people deciding where to put the human-review threshold. If you were hoping for model architectures or an SRE incident story, this one stays at the strategy level; pair it with something more hands-on below.

Title: A monitoring and alerting primer, from triggers to escalation
Description: Rishabh Srivastava of MRI Software at Conf42 SRE 2025 gives a first-principles tour of monitoring, alerting, escalation policies and the tools behind them.
Body:
If someone on your team keeps asking what the difference is between monitoring and alerting, send them this one. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Rishabh Srivastava, Manager of Technical Delivery and Integrations at MRI Software, gave a structured primer on both: what to watch, how alerts should be built, and why a badly tuned alert system can be worse than none.

It is a 101 talk and it behaves like one: definitions first, then components, then tools, then a worked scenario. That is a feature if you are onboarding people.

## Failures have real-world blast radius

Srivastava opens with a gallery of famous failures to establish stakes: the Knight Capital trading algorithm failure in 2012, the 2021 AWS outage, the 2003 North American blackout, the Colonial Pipeline attack and the 2017 Equifax breach. The list spans finance, infrastructure and security on purpose. The point is that "system reliability" is not a cloud-team concern; it shows up in fuel supply and bank balances.

## Monitoring watches, alerting interrupts

The core of the talk is a clean decomposition.

Monitoring has three components: data collection (logs, metrics and events), analysis (finding patterns and anomalies) and visualisation (dashboards and reports). He splits it into four areas: infrastructure (CPU, disk), application performance (response times, database queries), network (latency, packet loss) and security (anomaly and intrusion detection).

Alerting also has three: triggers (the conditions), notification channels (email, SMS, Slack, PagerDuty) and escalation policies (what happens when nobody acknowledges). That last one is the piece junior teams most often forget. An alert that nobody acknowledges and that never escalates is a log line with ambitions.

## The four ways alerting goes wrong

The most useful slide lists the failure modes of a poor alerting system:

- **Too many alerts,** leading to alert fatigue and ignored critical pages.
- **False positives and false negatives,** one wasting responders' time, the other hiding real issues.
- **Alerts without context,** forcing extra investigation before anyone can act.
- **Delayed responses,** turning minor issues into outages.

His fixes are the standard, correct ones: tune thresholds carefully, run structured on-call rotations to prevent burnout, use ML-based anomaly detection to cut false positives, and make sure logs and metrics give enough context to diagnose quickly. He also frames it as a five-step loop that ends with continuously refining alert rules, which is the step most teams skip after the initial setup.

## Tools and a dashboard walk-through

There is a quick survey of the usual suspects: Prometheus and Grafana on the open source side, Datadog and New Relic as commercial platforms, AWS CloudWatch, Azure Monitor and Google Cloud's operations suite from the providers, and PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Slack, VictorOps and Microsoft Teams for incident routing. The selection advice is sensible: match team expertise, budget and integration needs.

He finishes with an illustrative e-commerce holiday-sale scenario (no monitoring, slow pages, abandoned carts; then real-time tracking and anomaly detection) and a tour of an Azure Monitor dashboard for a retail app, reading out usage, failed requests, server response time and browser page load. The closing advice is worth keeping: when you move from a monolith to microservices, your monitoring has to start tracking inter-service communication too.

## Who should watch

New SREs, developers joining an on-call rotation for the first time, and managers who need shared vocabulary with their ops team. Experienced practitioners will recognise every slide; the failure-mode list is still a good checklist for your next alert review.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Praemonitus praemunitus: use actionable alerts to fix problems quickly](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2024_Leonid_Yankulin_actionable_alerts_fix) by Leonid Yankulin goes deeper on what makes an alert actionable.
- [Alerting on SLOs and Error Budget Policies](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2022_Ricardo_Castro_alerting_slos_error_budget_policies) by Ricardo Castro is the natural next step beyond threshold alerts.
- [Incident Response, Incident Management, and Alerts: where they fit in CloudOps](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Chris_Riley_incident_response_incident_management_alerts_CloudOps) by Chris Riley connects alerting to what happens after the page.

Title: Designed for servers, services, and scale
Description: Go runs quietly
Body:
# Go is calm. The systems are not.

Go has a reputation.

Simple. Clean. Predictable. The language you pick when you want fewer surprises and fewer late-night debugging sessions. Naturally, it ends up powering some of the most intense systems out there.

Conf42 Golang 2025 is all about that contrast.

This conference goes deep into building fast, reliable, very serious systems with Go. High-performance microservices, identity orchestration, notification systems handling millions of messages, and cloud-native platforms that really care about latency. If it needs to be fast and not fall over, Go is probably involved.

Security and resilience show up everywhere. From telemedicine platforms with military-grade protection to secure multi-cloud microservices and confidential computing, there’s a strong focus on building systems that can be trusted at scale. Not just in theory. In production.

AI is very much in the picture too. Go powering AI-driven ETL pipelines, edge computing, TinyML, OCR, and intelligent automation across finance, healthcare, IoT, and public sector platforms. It’s less “AI magic” and more “how do we ship this safely and make it fast”.

You’ll also find plenty of practical Go topics. Concurrency patterns, inter-service communication, dependency management, testing strategies, API design, and the occasional reminder that simplicity is a feature, not a limitation.

If Go is your language of choice, or you’re curious why so many critical systems quietly rely on it, this one’s for you. Solid engineering, real-world problems, and just enough chaos to keep things interesting.

Title: Why WebAssembly fits the edge, and where Go stands with it
Description: Alex Casalboni of Edgee at Conf42 Golang 2025 on how CDNs became compute platforms, why Wasm suits the edge, and Go's WASI support.
Body:
Code that runs before and after every HTTP request gets a budget of a few milliseconds, and that rules out most of the compute models we're used to. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Alex Casalboni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Alex_Casalboni_cloud_edge_webassembly), Developer Advocate at Edgee and previously six years at AWS, explained why WebAssembly is the runtime that fits that budget, how far Go's support has come, and how Edgee builds its edge platform on it.

It's a sponsor talk with a clear structure: history and fundamentals first, then Edgee's own architecture. The first part works as a solid primer on server-side Wasm even if you never touch Edgee.

## CDNs quietly became clouds

Alex's history lesson runs in two parallel tracks. On the cloud side: AWS from 2006, then virtual machines, then containers and Kubernetes, then serverless functions around 2014 and 2015. On the CDN side: companies as old as Akamai built for caching and DDoS protection, with limited custom logic through things like the Varnish Configuration Language.

Then, roughly between 2016 and 2019, the tracks crossed. Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge, CloudFront Functions and Fastly Compute put code on hundreds of points of presence. Key-value stores, databases, queues and object storage followed. His conclusion is that many CDN providers have become cloud providers, and the line between edge and cloud keeps blurring.

## Why Wasm and the edge match

WebAssembly was announced in 2015, shipped in 2017 and became a W3C recommendation in 2019. Alex focuses on the server side, where WASI, the WebAssembly System Interface, gives modules controlled access to files, sockets, clocks and HTTP. He also mentions the well-known remark from Docker's founder that Wasm plus WASI would have made Docker unnecessary.

The edge brings hard constraints. You get less memory and CPU than a VM or container, and because the logic sits in the path of every request, it needs to finish in single-digit milliseconds. Alex puts the target at five to ten. Containers that take seconds to start and serverless functions with hundreds of milliseconds of cold start don't fit.

Wasm's properties line up with that: near-native performance, small binaries with fast initialisation, and sandboxing by default. A module can't make an HTTP call or touch the filesystem unless the host grants it. That last one matters most if you're a platform running other people's untrusted code.

## Go and WebAssembly, version by version

For Gophers, this is the most useful section. Go has had a `wasm` target since Go 1.11 in 2018, with JavaScript glue for browser use. WASI preview 1 support arrived as experimental in Go 1.21 in 2023. For WASI preview 2 and the component model, Alex points to TinyGo plus `wit-bindgen-go`, which generates Go bindings from WIT, the interface definition language for components. Edgee defines its own WIT interfaces so developers can write components against them.

He also flags Go 1.24's expanded support for exporting Go functions to a Wasm host, and Google Cloud's announcement in the same post that its Application Load Balancer accepts service extensions written in Wasm, custom logic right in the request path. For runtimes, he recommends Wasmtime from the Bytecode Alliance rather than reinventing the host.

## What Edgee built

Edgee's first product is data collection and web analytics. The idea is to take heavy client-side SDKs, he names Google Analytics, Segment and Amplitude, and run them as Wasm components at the edge before the page reaches the browser. The proxy runs on Fastly today, with other CDNs such as Cloudflare planned, and talks to backend services, currently on AWS Lambda, for work that can't happen at the edge yet.

Around that sits a component registry for publishing and sharing public or private Wasm components, and an Edgee CLI that scaffolds, builds, tests and pushes components in Go, Rust, Python, C# and TypeScript. The proxy, the CLI and the components are open source. A/B testing, feature flags and AI inference were on the roadmap he described.

## Who should watch

Go developers curious about WebAssembly outside the browser, and platform engineers deciding what belongs at the edge versus in a region. If you already ship Wasm in production, skip to the Go version notes and the Edgee architecture. If you don't, the first half explains the "why" better than most docs.

- [Go Containerless on Kubernetes with WebAssembly and Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Deepu_K_Sasidharan_kubernetes_containerless_webassembly) by Deepu K Sasidharan (Auth0).

Title: How a serverless migration cut costs and failures together
Description: Tarun Kumar Chatterjee of Presidio at Conf42 SRE 2025 on moving to AWS Lambda, DynamoDB and API Gateway, from proof of concept to cold-start tuning.
Body:
Paying for servers that sit idle while also falling over on traffic spikes is the worst of both worlds, and it is where Tarun Kumar Chatterjee's team started. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Tarun, .NET Senior Lead Developer at Presidio, told the story of their move from traditional cloud services to a serverless architecture on AWS, and reported infrastructure costs down 62%, operational failures down 78% and deployment frequency up 3.5 times.

It is a practitioner's migration story, light on code and heavy on sequencing: what they used, how they won over sceptics, and what broke in observability and cost along the way.

## Why they moved

The problems were the familiar trio. Costs grew faster than business needs, with underutilised servers draining money. Engineers spent too much time managing servers instead of shipping features. And the architecture could not absorb sudden traffic spikes, which caused customer-facing failures.

Tarun is careful to say serverless was not picked as a one-size-fits-all answer. It was chosen for automatic scaling, pay-per-use pricing that removes over-provisioning, and time handed back to engineers.

## The AWS kit

The stack is standard AWS serverless: Lambda for business logic, DynamoDB as the managed NoSQL store, API Gateway for endpoints, S3 for static assets and data, CloudWatch Logs for monitoring, and Secrets Manager for credentials. Docker and Amazon EKS stayed in the picture for workloads that suited containers, which is a healthy sign; a migration that pretends everything fits in a function usually ends with a 15-minute timeout.

## Proofs of concept beat slide decks

Engineers doubted serverless on performance, scalability and risk. The team answered with proof-of-concept projects, early adopters inside the teams who became advocates, and metrics on cost, incidents and deployment frequency. The rollout followed the same caution: break the monolith into function-sized pieces, start with a pilot on non-critical workloads, refactor services to be stateless, and build serverless-specific CI/CD pipelines.

## Observability gets harder before it gets better

The most useful section covers what got worse. Distributed tracing across many functions is harder, each function's execution context is limited, cold starts add unpredictable latency, and resource use varies a lot. Their fixes: end-to-end correlation IDs on every request, centralised structured logging, per-function dashboards, and dynamic alerting based on statistical baselines rather than fixed thresholds.

## Cost tuning is a continuous job

On cost, Tarun lists four practices. Right-size memory per function with automated tests, because memory drives both speed and price. Reduce deployment package size and use provisioned concurrency on critical paths to tame cold starts. Watch execution durations so functions creeping toward their timeout get fixed before they cause costly timeout loops. And enforce tagging standards and deployment policies so the estate stays manageable.

Developer satisfaction, he reports, reached 94% as people spent their time on product work instead of infrastructure.

## Who should watch

Teams planning a move from VMs or containers to AWS serverless who want the order of operations and the observability and cost traps, not a Lambda tutorial. If you are already deep in serverless, the correlation-ID and memory-tuning sections are a useful checklist.

Title: SRE at the edge needs local SLOs, not a global average
Description: Srinivas Vallabhaneni at Conf42 SRE 2025 on adapting error budgets, CI/CD, observability and GitOps to edge devices with patchy networks.
Body:
Five nines is a cloud habit, and the edge does not care about your habits. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Srinivas Vallabhaneni, a senior software engineer, walked through what happens to SRE practice when the workload lives on a factory floor, in a vehicle or on a shipping container instead of in a region with three availability zones.

His answer is that the toolkit survives, but every tool has to be resized. Error budgets, SLOs, automation and observability all still apply. They just have to assume low power, flaky links and hardware you cannot walk up to.

## The edge is messy, so the SLO should be local

The shift he describes is simple to state. For years the default was to ship everything upstream, process it centrally and respond. That breaks down once you have millions of sensors, real-time feedback loops and limited bandwidth. So processing moves to where the data is born.

The reliability consequence is the interesting part. Vallabhaneni argues that SLOs should reflect what is realistic for each location or device type rather than one global average, and that error budgets may need to account for connectivity gaps and power limits. A device in a basement with one bar of signal is not failing its SLO; the SLO was written for the wrong device.

## Ship less, ship smarter

Most of the talk is about adapting the delivery and telemetry pipeline:

- **Containers on a diet.** Lightweight images, Alpine-based builds or distroless containers that strip out everything you don't need, to save memory and startup time on small hardware.
- **Rollouts that tolerate dropped connections.** Progressive rollouts, automated canaries, rollback mechanisms and sync pipelines that resume where they left off when the link drops.
- **Configs as versioned code.** GitOps-style workflows that sync and enforce config state across hundreds or thousands of devices.
- **Observability that summarises at the source.** Instead of forwarding every log line, detect anomalies locally and send only summarised or critical data, while keeping distributed tracing across the edge-to-cloud hop.

None of this is exotic on its own. The value is seeing it lined up as one design, where each choice assumes the network might vanish for a while.

## Policy as code is your rollback insurance

One point deserves more attention than it usually gets. On edge fleets, rollback might be slow or impossible, so Vallabhaneni puts policy as code in front of every deployment: validate against security, performance and reliability rules before anything leaves the building. Pair that with infrastructure as code and GitOps reconciliation, and drift on a device in the field gets corrected automatically. The bad config you never ship is the cheapest incident you will ever handle.

He also covers the resilience patterns you would expect, with an edge accent: circuit breaking to isolate unstable components, failover to backup nodes, smart data replication, and mesh networking so devices can route around failed links.

## Decide what runs where

The closing architecture question is the one teams actually argue about: what belongs on the device and what stays in the cloud. His split is practical. Real-time control, anomaly detection and basic analytics go local. Historical analysis and model training stay central. The winning design is a hybrid, local autonomy for fast reactions plus central coordination for learning and visibility.

The talk includes several industry examples with large percentages (defect rates, data transfer savings, latency cuts). They are presented as illustrations rather than as his own team's measurements, so treat them as motivation, not benchmarks.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE engineers who have just been handed an IoT or industrial fleet and want a checklist of what changes. It is an overview talk with no code or tool demos. If you already run GitOps at the edge, you will mostly be nodding along; if you don't, the "what runs where" framing and per-device SLOs are worth stealing.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Edge Intelligence Revolution: GPU-Accelerated AI at the Edge](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sai_Prasad_Mukala_intelligence_edge_gpu) by Sai Prasad Mukala looks at the hardware side of running models on the device.

- [Self Healing Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Nick_Hodges_self_healing_systems) by Nick Hodges goes deeper on the autonomous-recovery idea Vallabhaneni sketches.
