Title: A layered framework for putting AI into security operations
Description: Venkata Krishna Ramesh Kumar Koppireddy at Conf42 SRE 2025 on AI for anomaly detection, incident response, risk-based patching and compliance.
Body:
Security teams drown in alerts long before they run out of attackers, which makes triage the first job worth handing to AI. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Venkata Krishna Ramesh Kumar Koppireddy presented a strategic framework for AI in enterprise security, layered from data collection through anomaly detection and automated response up to predictive defence.

This is an introductory, framework-level talk. Each capability comes with a plain-language example, which makes it a good one to share with stakeholders outside the security team, and less of a fit for practitioners looking for model internals.

## Baselines, not signatures

The detection layer rests on behavioural baselines. Machine learning learns what normal looks like and flags deviations that signature-based tools miss. His examples are deliberately ordinary: an employee who always logs in from one location suddenly appearing in another country, or someone who works eight to five logging in at 3am. Neither is an attack yet; both deserve a look, and the system can block the account or weigh the application's criticality before deciding.

Adaptive learning keeps the baseline current as the threats change, which is the part rule sets struggle with.

## Automate the opening moves of an incident

The response layer follows a four-step loop: evaluate the alert by severity, context and potential impact; enrich it with threat intelligence and environment details; run predefined playbooks through orchestration; and verify the fix while generating documentation for compliance. The phishing example is the template: when someone clicks a suspicious link, the system assesses the risk and either warns the user or isolates the machine, without an analyst starting from scratch.

## Patch what attackers can actually reach

Vulnerability management is where the framework is most practical. Instead of ranking by CVSS score alone, AI weighs exploitability, attacker behaviour and asset criticality. His example: a flaw that is only exploitable from inside the network can wait behind one reachable from outside. Anyone who has stared at a scanner report full of critical findings will appreciate the idea.

Compliance gets the same treatment. Continuous checks of configurations against NIST, PCI DSS, HIPAA and ISO 27001, generated reports and audit trails, and drift detection when a configuration change breaks compliance.

## Threat intel and just-in-time controls

Threat intelligence is aggregated from commercial feeds, open-source intelligence, dark web monitoring and industry ISACs, with NLP reading unstructured sources like forums and blogs. Just-in-time remediation applies temporary access controls, adaptive boundaries and on-demand isolation only when risk rises, shrinking the always-on attack surface, which he argues suits cloud environments where perimeters are blurry.

He cites an 85% reduction in false positives, 67% faster incident response and 73% better resource utilisation from AI integration. His roadmap advice is measured: assess first, pilot in high-value areas such as phishing and endpoint protection, integrate with existing tools rather than replacing them, and keep re-evaluating.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, SREs and security leads building the case for AI in their security operations, or explaining it to non-specialists. Experienced detection engineers will find the concepts familiar; the risk-based patching and just-in-time sections are the most actionable.

Title: Read the import block, because that's where Go tech debt starts
Description: Andrii Raikov of Delivery Hero at Conf42 Golang 2025 on hidden Go dependencies, breaking v2 libraries and the helpers package that ate a codebase.
Body:
Can you name the indirect dependencies of the Go service you work on, and say why each one is there? At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Andrii Raikov](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Andrii_Raikov_dependencies_code_management), Principal Software Engineer at Delivery Hero, opened with that question and spent the rest of the talk showing why most of us can't, and how small package decisions turn into years of tech debt.

Delivery Hero runs a lot of Go, and Andrii's examples come from its own code base, good and bad. The talk has two halves: a set of binary-size experiments that make hidden dependencies visible, and three patterns from production that he has watched go wrong more than once.

## Your binary knows what you imported

Andrii starts with a hello world that prints with the built-in print function, then swaps in `fmt` and recompiles. The binary grows noticeably. Then he adds `os` to read a name from the arguments, and the size barely moves. The reason is in `fmt` itself: it already pulls in `io`, `os`, `reflect`, `strconv`, `sync` and `unicode`, so by the time you ask for `os` you already have it. Moving the code into an external module on GitHub changes almost nothing either.

The bigger experiment uses the AWS SDK to list S3 buckets in a few lines of code, and the binary jumps several times over. Andrii then had ChatGPT write the same call by hand, signing the request against the S3 API using only the standard library. That version is about six megabytes smaller, but still around eight. Commenting out imports one by one, he finds `crypto` and `encoding` barely matter on their own. A tiny program that only calls a URL with `net/http` already lands at about five megabytes.

He is explicit that the lesson isn't "rewrite net/http". The lesson is that nobody looks. You add one small library and have no idea what it drags in, or what its dependencies drag in.

## A v2 that breaks v1 can trap a team for years

The second half is about culture, and the first story will be familiar to anyone in a large company. A platform team owns a global service-to-service token service and ships client libraries in several languages, Go included. Version one works. Then version two changes the interfaces without a new module path.

Service teams look at the migration cost, decide "if it works, don't touch it", and stay on v1. The platform team has no capacity to support both and deprecates v1, so no more fixes or security updates. Then a different team builds a new shared library on top of v2. Any service still on v1 that tries to use it gets a conflict: two implementations under the same name. Andrii says he has seen this happen several times, and it takes a year or two to build up, by which point untangling it can cost more than a greenfield rewrite.

The fix he points to is the one the Go ecosystem already expects: a breaking change gets a separate major-version path with its own `go.mod`, so v1 and v2 can live side by side.

## The helpers package is a dependency magnet

The other two patterns are about DRY applied without thought. A `helpers` package grows a function that prints details of a `Gopher` type, so helpers now depends on the gopher package. The day the gopher package needs a helper, you have a cycle, and the usual workaround is a second helpers package, which brings back the duplication you were trying to remove. His fix is plain: that function should be a method on the type, with private fields if you like.

Scale the same habit across services and you get his worst case: the same helper code living in a service's own package, in a newly extracted shared library and again in a third dependency, with three slowly diverging implementations and three sets of vulnerabilities.

## What to do on Monday

Andrii's closing list is short: write a dependency policy and actually follow it, audit dependencies and update versions regularly, scan for vulnerabilities in transitive packages too, and work with product to prioritise the debt. His most practical tip: don't skip the import block during PR review. Several of his horror stories would have been caught there.

## Who should watch

Go developers in teams with more than a handful of services, and anyone maintaining a shared internal library. It's a good talk for mid-level engineers who haven't yet been burned by a breaking minor version. Seniors may know the theory, but the binary-size experiments are worth a look before your next `go get`.

Title: Error budgets and safe chaos for healthcare AI systems
Description: Peeyush Khandelwal at Conf42 SRE 2025 on SLOs, sandboxed chaos experiments, tiered error budgets and GitOps for AI systems in clinical settings.
Body:
A diagnostic model that drifts quietly is worse than one that crashes loudly, because nobody pages for it. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Peeyush Khandelwal, who has more than 20 years of IT experience in US healthcare, presented a playbook for running AI in clinical systems with SRE practice: SLIs that include clinical signals, chaos engineering in sandboxes, error budgets tiered by clinical risk, and GitOps for compliance.

The framing is that healthcare AI sits between two forces: AI evolves fast, and healthcare infrastructure is built on safety and stability. Regulators treat many of these systems as medical devices, which constrains how you update, monitor and test them.

## Measure clinician overrides, not just accuracy

The SLI section is the most original part. Peeyush groups indicators into three buckets:

- **Technical**: inference latency under 200 ms, model drift kept below 0.5%, batch completion at 99.9%, and supporting API availability at 99.95%.
- **Clinical**: diagnostic suggestion accuracy, documentation completeness, and clinician override frequency.
- **Operational**: time to detect variance, recovery time objectives, incident response time, change failure rate.

He reports that in one project, tracking how often clinicians overrode the model was more informative than raw model accuracy, because it directly measured trust and eventual adoption. That is a metric any team shipping AI to experts could steal.

## Chaos engineering, but in a sandbox first

He acknowledges that chaos engineering in a hospital sounds alarming. The approach is graduated: fault injection starts in isolated sandboxes with synthetic patient data, every step is reviewed by clinical experts before anything nears pre-production, and more aggressive failure modes are tried only as confidence grows. The payoff example is a cascading-failure risk in a sepsis decision model that would have gone unnoticed without simulated faults.

## Spend error budget where the risk is low

Error budgets are allocated by the clinical impact of each component. A model writing post-visit summaries gets a looser budget than one recommending oncology treatment. Alerting is tiered by burn rate, and deployment pace follows the remaining budget. One hospital saw a 64% reduction in non-actionable alerts after adopting it, and the tiering let teams move faster in low-risk areas while locking down components that influence clinical decisions.

## Models degrade, so verification never stops

Because real-world data keeps changing, Peeyush treats verification as a pipeline: validation against benchmark datasets before deployment, shadow deployments running new models alongside live ones, canary rollouts with rollback triggers, and live drift monitoring with edge-case flagging. Clinician panels review edge cases before full rollout. He cites a 72% drop in model-related incidents at one organisation using this multi-stage approach.

GitOps ties it together for auditors: versioned infrastructure as code, declarative configuration, automated compliance checks, clinical sign-off in the pipeline and automatic rollback on SLO violations, with Argo CD and Flux named as the tooling some hospital networks use.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform teams moving into regulated domains, and ML engineers whose models are about to meet clinicians. The case-study figures are aggregated across institutions, so take them as direction; the SLI taxonomy and the risk-tiered error budgets are the parts to copy.

Title: Reconciling supply chain orders on Hyperledger Fabric with Go chaincode
Description: Venkata Anil Kumar Nilisetty of Cognizant at Conf42 Golang 2025 on Hyperledger Fabric, Go smart contracts and Kafka for multi-company order reconciliation.
Body:
When a buyer, a supplier and a logistics firm each keep their own copy of an order, someone ends up reconciling three spreadsheets by email. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Venkata Anil Kumar Nilisetty](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Venkata_Anil_Kumar_Nilisetty_blockchain_supply_order), Java Full Stack Lead Developer at Cognizant, presented a design that replaces that loop with a shared Hyperledger Fabric ledger, smart contracts written in Go, and a cloud-native microservice stack around it.

This is one of the few blockchain talks where the chain is the boring, permissioned kind, which is exactly what multi-company back-office work needs.

## The cost of disagreeing about an order

Venkata frames the problem with figures from industry studies: large multinationals process millions of order transactions a year, discrepancies take two to three days to resolve on average, a meaningful share need heavy manual work, and companies spend hundreds of thousands of dollars a year on reconciliation. Supply chain complexity also raises coordination costs. None of that is surprising if you have ever chased a purchase order number through three ERPs.

## A ledger at the bottom, ordinary services on top

The architecture is layered. The base is a Hyperledger Fabric network in which each key supply chain participant runs as an organisation, using Fabric's channels to keep data private between participants. Smart contracts, written as chaincode in Go, hold the core business logic and automate order validation and reconciliation. That is the Go part of the story.

Above the ledger sits a fairly conventional enterprise stack: Spring Boot microservices for business logic and API exposure, Apache Kafka carrying events between modules, and a GraphQL API for flexible queries. Deployment is on AWS, with EKS for container orchestration, multi-AZ RDS for persistence with automated failover, and ElastiCache to take read load off the database.

He gives per-component performance figures, headlined by throughput of up to 2,800 transactions per second at around half a second of latency across organisations, plus numbers for chaincode execution, Kafka event latency and GraphQL query times.

## Security comes from the ledger as much as the network

The security section stacks several layers. TLS 1.3 with perfect forward secrecy on the network. Authentication that combines Fabric's blockchain-native identity with a traditional PKI, with access requests validated by consensus and fully auditable. Multi-signature protocols for critical operations, requiring sign-off from designated validator nodes. And tamper-proof audit logs, which come naturally when the log is a ledger.

## What changes for the business

The results Venkata presents are the reason anyone would take on a blockchain project. By his account, automated smart contracts eliminated most manual documentation work, dispute resolution dropped from an average of 45 days to five, and order processing error rates fell from 5% to 0.1%. He also covers lower transaction costs, reduced working capital needs and less compliance verification effort, though some of those figures read as drawn from published studies rather than this single system, so check the slides for which is which.

He closes with next steps: AI and ML integration, IoT feeds, cross-chain interoperability and mobile apps.

## Who should watch

Architects in supply chain, logistics or procurement weighing a permissioned ledger against yet another integration hub, and Go developers curious what chaincode is used for in real enterprise designs. If you want to write Fabric chaincode, this is the why, not the how.

Title: Precision medicine is a data engineering problem first
Description: Santhosh Kumar Rai at Conf42 SRE 2025 on the pipelines behind precision medicine, joining EHRs, genomics and wearables with governance and early warning.
Body:
Personalised treatment depends on one patient record that pulls together genomics, clinical history and wearable data, and building that record is mostly plumbing. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Santhosh Kumar Rai, SAP Lead Consultant at Xpress Global IT Solutions, gave an overview of how data engineering underpins precision medicine and diagnostics, and why reliability matters when the data drives clinical decisions.

This is a broad survey talk rather than an architecture deep-read. Its value is in mapping the problem: which data sources exist, why they resist integration, and what the infrastructure has to do before any model is trained.

## Four streams into one patient

Santhosh describes the foundation as four layers. Genomic information, with sequencing costs having fallen from around a hundred million dollars in 2001 to about a thousand in 2023. Clinical history pulled from records, treatments and diagnostics that used to live in separate systems. Lifestyle and environmental data from wearables and sensors, a big contributor to healthcare data volume growth. And the data engineering infrastructure that processes all of it.

## Fifty systems, fifty data models

The integration section explains why this is hard. Data arrives as EHR records, images, wearable streams, genomic sequences and patient-reported outcomes, each with its own formats and standards. Much of the clinically relevant information is unstructured text that needs natural language processing to become usable. And he notes that a single hospital typically manages over 50 distinct clinical information systems, each with its own data model and exchange protocols that must be reconciled into one patient view.

Anyone who has merged two customer databases can multiply that pain by 25 and add HIPAA.

## Quality and lineage before analytics

His governance process has four steps: lineage tracking, master data management, standardisation and validation. The analytics infrastructure on top combines high-performance computing, stream processing, MLOps pipelines and interactive visualisation, with genomic analysis for a single patient needing a large amount of CPU time.

He cites impact figures from the field: NLP systems extracting clinical concepts from narrative text at over 90% accuracy, data provenance frameworks reducing errors by 35%, FHIR-based data models improving query performance by about 50% over traditional relational models, and well-designed clinical visualisation reducing decision time by 25%.

## Early warning and faster genomics

Two applications carry the second half. Genomic pipelines that complete sequencing analysis in hours rather than weeks, filtering millions of variants down to a short list of clinically significant ones, which matters for critically ill newborns. And early warning systems that integrate hundreds of variables per patient, including continuous waveform data, apply time-series analytics, and keep retraining on new data to stay accurate.

His comparison table claims large gains over traditional approaches, including whole-genome analysis dropping from two or three days to around eight hours and a 23% reduction in in-hospital mortality.

## Who should watch

Data engineers moving into healthcare who want a map of the sources and constraints, and SREs supporting clinical data platforms who need to understand why their pipelines are on the critical path. Engineers looking for concrete pipeline designs should pair it with a more implementation-focused talk.

Title: Moving the power grid to the back of the chip frees the front for signals
Description: Intel physical design lead Ramalinga Reddy Kotapati at Conf42 Golang 2025 on backside power delivery, nano-TSVs and why sub-2nm chips need them.
Body:
For decades, chips have carried power and signals on the same side of the wafer, fighting over the same metal layers. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Ramalinga Reddy Kotapati](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Ramalinga_Reddy_Kotapati_semiconductor_power_efficiency), Technical Lead Physical Design Engineer at Intel, explained backside power delivery networks (BSPDN): move the power to the back of a thinned wafer, feed it through nano through-silicon vias, and give the front side back to signals.

Fair warning on scope: this is a semiconductor physical design talk, with no Go in it. It earns a place on a software engineer's watch list because it explains a change in the hardware your services will run on, and it is one of the more unusual sessions in the Conf42 Golang archive.

## The front side has run out of room

Ramalinga starts with how a conventional chip is wired. With, say, 15 metal layers, the top ones carry power, the next ones the clock, and only what is left is available for signal routing. At five nanometres and below, he says, power delivery can take around 40% of routing resources. As wires shrink, IR drop (the voltage lost along the power network) gets worse, supply voltages approach 0.7 volts so every millivolt of droop matters, and switching activity adds power supply noise that hurts timing predictability.

In short, the power grid has become the noisy neighbour that takes the best parking spots.

## Flip the wafer, drill tiny vias

Backside power delivery moves most of the power routing to the back of the chip. To make that possible, the silicon substrate is thinned dramatically, and power reaches the transistors through nano-TSVs: vias he describes as under 200 nanometres in diameter, with very high aspect ratios. A dedicated backside metal stack, built with advanced copper metallisation, carries the power network.

The payoff he walks through comes in three parts. Lower IR drop and a more stable supply, because the power network is short and wide. More routing resources for signals on the front, so interconnects get shorter and crosstalk drops. And fewer front-side metal layers for the same design, which he puts at roughly seven or eight instead of ten to fifteen.

## Manufacturing is the hard part

A good portion of the talk covers what has to go right in the fab: thinning wafers with tight thickness control across a 300-millimetre wafer, etching near-vertical TSV sidewalls, and placing TSVs to manage thermal gradients, since heat now has a different path out of the chip. On the design side, he describes machine learning used to optimise the power network and TSV placement, and 3D electromagnetic simulation that he says correlates closely with measurements on real silicon.

## Who is shipping it

Ramalinga surveys the big three. Intel's implementation is PowerVia, which he ties to its 18A generation. TSMC is investing in backside power for its two-nanometre-class process, and Samsung is working on vertical power delivery with its own TSV designs. He compares the three on power efficiency, TSV yield and current density, with Intel ahead in his figures, and closes on costs: higher manufacturing cost per wafer, balanced by efficiency gains that he expects to pay back for data-centre parts.

The audio is hard going in places and some of the figures are best read off the slides, so watch with them open.

## Who should watch

Hardware-curious software engineers who want to know why the next generation of server CPUs will look different, and anyone in performance or capacity planning who likes to know where efficiency gains come from. Chip designers will find it a compact survey.

Title: Clinical ML lives or dies on messy, unstructured data
Description: Arun Vivek Supramanian of Amazon at Conf42 SRE 2025 on the data lakes, ETL and ML models behind diagnostics, imaging and clinical NLP in healthcare.
Body:
Most healthcare data is images, notes and sensor streams, and the hard part of clinical machine learning is getting that into a shape a model can use. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Arun Vivek Supramanian, Senior Data Engineer at Amazon, walked through the data sources, processing frameworks and model families behind ML in healthcare, and the security and workflow problems that decide whether any of it reaches a clinician.

It is a compact survey aimed at engineers who know data platforms and want to see where healthcare differs.

## The data is big, varied and dirty

Arun's starting point: around 80% of healthcare data is unstructured, from imaging to clinical notes to wearable streams. He breaks down the sources. EHRs hold history, medications, labs and physician notes. Imaging makes up most of the volume, with a single radiology department generating up to a hundred thousand images a day. Each sequenced genome adds 200-plus GB. Wearables collect 10 to 20 biometric points per second.

Then the three problems. Heterogeneity: structured tables, free text, time series and images in the same patient record, so SQL alone will not cut it. Volume and velocity: he puts a 300-bed hospital at 50 TB a year from EHRs and an ICU monitor at 2,000-plus readings per second. Quality: smoking status missing in 60% of records, diagnosis codes varying between hospitals.

## Schema on read, because the schema keeps changing

The infrastructure section makes the case for frameworks that tolerate this mess. Apache Spark for in-memory batch and stream processing, with one provider cutting clinical model training time by 88% after moving off disk-based processing. Hadoop for semi-structured and unstructured data, used by a public health network to integrate radiology scans and clinical notes from more than ten hospitals.

Cloud data lakes are the main recommendation, because traditional warehouses force early schema decisions while healthcare data types keep shifting. One US network combined imaging, EHR and telemetry in a lake and got pipelines that took days down to around an hour.

## ETL that preserves clinical meaning

His best line of thought is that healthcare ETL is about meaning, not just movement. Extraction is followed by normalisation to clinical vocabularies such as SNOMED CT, LOINC and RxNorm, validation to catch missing and inconsistent entries, transformation for model readiness, and incremental loading for streaming data. One hospital cut pipeline latency from 2.5 days to 11 hours, enough for near real-time use in critical care.

## The models on top

With the data in place, the model examples cover familiar ground. A deep learning model for 30-day readmission reached an AUC of 0.87. LSTM networks on ICU time series flagged deterioration six to ten hours earlier than manual methods. CNNs for lung nodule detection performed comparably to expert radiologists, and segmentation architectures cut manual processing time by 60%. NLP extracts structure from discharge summaries and pathology reports and automates clinical trial matching.

## Trust is a deployment requirement

The closing section is the reality check. Security failures often come from access control misconfiguration, so HIPAA-grade protection means encryption, role-based access and audit logs. Clinicians already spend hours in EHRs, so any tool must live inside existing workflows. And if a model influences care, you must be able to explain why, which means explainable AI and clear accountability.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and SREs starting on healthcare platforms who want the map before the details. Experienced healthcare ML practitioners will know most of the examples; the ETL-for-meaning section is the part worth passing to a new team member.

Title: Health monitoring that keeps working when the grid is gone
Description: Bhushan Gopala Reddy of Aruba Networks at Conf42 SRE 2025 on BLE health monitors for disaster zones, with mesh links, power budgets and error budgets.
Body:
Hospital monitoring equipment assumes stable power and a network, which are the first two things an earthquake takes away. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Bhushan Gopala Reddy, an Embedded Software Engineer at Aruba Networks, presented research on Bluetooth Low Energy health monitors built for disaster zones, and on applying SRE ideas such as error budgets and graceful degradation to devices strapped to patients.

The target in the abstract is 99.99% uptime, in conditions with no grid, no internet, dust, debris and temperature extremes. Consumer fitness trackers can be wrong now and then. A device tracking heart rate, SpO2, temperature and respiration in a field hospital cannot.

## Make the radio link heal itself

The first set of techniques is about BLE connection resilience. Dynamic device discovery rebuilds connections automatically as patients are moved. Multi-path communication keeps a signal alive when the primary route fails, which Bhushan reports raised connection reliability from 92.4% to 99.7% in field testing. Devices keep transmitting core vitals at signal levels as low as -95 dBm.

The key design choice is that devices form a mesh and relay each other's data. A self-healing network routes around damaged or disconnected nodes, so one dead device does not create a monitoring blind spot.

## Power is the real SLO

Batteries decide how long the system lasts, so a lot of the talk is a power budget:

- **Adaptive sampling** by patient criticality and remaining charge; stable patients are sampled less often, cutting their power draw by 62.4%.
- **Edge processing** to analyse locally instead of transmitting raw data, taking idle current from 4.2 mA to 0.8 mA.
- **Coordinated transmission windows** across devices, a 28.3% overall power reduction against a standard BLE implementation.
- **Energy harvesting** from kinetic, thermal and ambient RF sources, extending operation by 18 to 26% in favourable conditions.

Sampling a stable patient less often to save battery for an unstable one is triage, applied to firmware.

## Firmware updates over a straw

Over-the-air updates in a disaster zone have to survive tiny bandwidth and dropped links. The team ships delta updates instead of full images, shrinking typical payloads from tens of kilobytes to around 8 to 12 KB, plus aggressive compression. Checkpointing lets an interrupted update resume where it stopped, and an automatic rollback reverts to the last stable version when an integrity check fails. Field testing showed a 92.2% first-attempt success rate.

## Error budgets per function

The SRE section is the most transferable. Instead of one reliability number, the system sets different targets per function: the strictest for critical alert delivery, a high one for the overall system, and a looser 98.5% for non-critical features so the team can still iterate on them. Healthcare-specific SLIs follow: vitals latency under one second, alert delivery under 200 ms, data accuracy at 99.5%, and battery-life prediction within plus or minus 5%.

When resources run short, graceful degradation sheds non-essential features first, scales data resolution with patient status, keeps local alerting running with no central system, and lets nearby devices take over monitoring for a failing unit.

Bhushan reports deployments after the Nepal earthquake and Hurricane Maria, including monitoring over 5,000 patients across 15 field hospitals at 99.3% uptime.

## Who should watch

Embedded and IoT engineers working on devices that must work offline, and SREs curious how error budgets and SLIs translate to hardware in hostile places. Some figures in the talk move quickly, so treat it as a tour of techniques, each worth looking up on its own.

Title: Your GPU cluster is waiting on the network, not the GPUs
Description: Murali Krishna Reddy Mandalapu of Renesas at Conf42 SRE 2025 on interconnect bottlenecks in GPU HPC clusters, RDMA, topologies and adaptive routing.
Body:
GPU compute has been growing much faster than the links between GPUs, and at scale the network becomes the computer's bottleneck. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Murali Krishna Reddy Mandalapu, Senior Director of Hardware Engineering at Renesas Electronics, laid out why interconnects throttle GPU-accelerated HPC clusters and which topologies, protocols and software tricks claw the performance back.

His headline framing: compute capacity outpaces interconnect bandwidth improvements by three to four times per hardware generation, and in modern HPC applications interconnect latency and congestion can eat 30 to 50% of total execution time, even in well-optimised workloads. You bought thousands of GPUs; a third of the time, some of them are waiting for a packet.

## Three ways the fabric fails you

Murali names three limits of traditional interconnects:

- **Bandwidth saturation.** GPUs produce data faster than the network drains it, buffers congest and compute pipelines stall.
- **Routing inefficiency.** Static routing cannot react to congestion, so traffic keeps taking the bad path during heavy workloads.
- **Synchronisation overhead.** Collective operations need barriers, and tiny latency variations compound as node counts reach the thousands.

The last one is the one that surprises people coming from web systems. In a collective, the slowest participant sets the pace for everyone.

## Pick the topology for your traffic pattern

The topology tour is a good refresher. Fat-tree gives non-blocking communication with full bisection bandwidth and predictable latency, at the cost of switch counts that grow steeply. A 3D torus wraps a mesh around itself for low hop counts and simpler wiring, well suited to nearest-neighbour patterns common in physics simulations. Dragonfly uses hierarchical groups of high-radix routers to shrink network diameter and cable length, trading local and global bandwidth more cheaply.

There is no winner, and that is the point: the right topology depends on what your application actually sends.

## Take the CPU out of the path

RDMA moves data memory to memory across the fabric without the CPU in the middle. Murali cites up to 55% lower end-to-end latency and 97% protocol efficiency for medium-sized messages.

Two case studies make it concrete. Frontier gained 24.8% from dynamic adaptive routing over static routing, using the Slingshot interconnect's congestion control on a dragonfly topology. NVIDIA's Selene pairs 200 Gb/s InfiniBand HDR with full bisection bandwidth, RDMA, and NCCL collectives tuned to the topology.

## Software still matters

On the software side he lists adaptive routing that reconfigures paths from live traffic, topology-aware algorithms that map communication onto physical layout to cut cross-switch traffic, NCCL tuning to eliminate redundant transfers, and load balancing across multiple paths.

The benchmark table is a handy mental model: traditional Ethernet at 12.5 GB/s and 10 microseconds, InfiniBand HDR at 25 GB/s and 3.5 microseconds, NVLink at 50 GB/s and 1.8 microseconds, with photonic interconnects projected at 100 GB/s and 0.5 microseconds. He closes on what is coming next: dedicated network processing units, silicon photonics and network interfaces co-packaged with the GPU.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure engineers and SREs who now run GPU clusters for training or simulation and have mostly worked with request-response systems. It is a hardware-leaning survey, not a tuning guide, but it gives you the vocabulary to ask why your scaling curve flattened at 64 nodes. His practical advice: profile your communication patterns before buying anything.

Title: Test Go services layer by layer, against a real Postgres
Description: Nikolay Kuznetsov of Zalando at Conf42 Golang 2025 on testing each layer of a Go service with Testcontainers, mockery, httptest, go-cmp and gofakeit.
Body:
A mocked database will happily accept SQL your real one rejects. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Nikolay Kuznetsov](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Nikolay_Kuznetsov_testing_go_services), Senior Golang Software Engineer at Zalando in Helsinki, showed how he tests a Go service one layer at a time: repositories against a real Postgres in a container, business logic against generated mocks, and HTTP handlers and routers with `httptest`, each with the library that makes it pleasant.

His running example is a shopping cart for Zalando's pre-owned business, where every item is unique, built with Postgres, the pgx driver and the Gin framework in a hexagonal layout: domain in the middle, ports as interfaces, adapters for the database and HTTP. Nikolay also maintains pgx-outbox, a transactional outbox library for pgx, so the Postgres focus is not an accident.

## Trophy, not pyramid

He starts with the testing trophy, which argues for more integration tests than the classic pyramid allows, because running real dependencies in containers is now cheap and unit tests tend to couple tightly to code. The trophy also adds a static layer at the bottom: linters catching what tests never should have to.

Then four principles for the rest of the talk: test layer by layer, use table tests everywhere, compare every field of the result rather than one or two, and feed tests randomised data instead of the same hardcoded values.

## Repositories get a real database

For the repository layer, the rule is to test against the same Postgres version you run in production, started from Go code so its lifecycle is tied to the tests. Nikolay uses testcontainers-go, which ships modules (he counts more than 30) including Postgres and LocalStack for AWS services like SNS, SQS and S3. A few lines start the container with the right wait strategy and init scripts, and the module hands back a connection string on a random local port, so suites can run in parallel without colliding.

Where to start the container? He recommends testify's `suite` package: `SetupSuite` starts Postgres and builds the pgx pool and repository once, `TearDownSuite` terminates it. He finds that cleaner than `TestMain` or `sync.Once`, and cheaper than a container per test. Even if you forget the teardown, Testcontainers' Ryuk sidecar cleans up stray containers after the run.

For assertions he reaches for go-cmp, which he describes as semantic equality and more powerful than `reflect.DeepEqual`. Its options do the fiddly parts: ignore a `CreatedAt` field, treat nil and empty slices as equal, handle unexported fields, or supply a custom comparer for currency values.

## Services get mocks, handlers and routers get different tests

At the service layer, depend on interfaces and generate mocks. Nikolay notes that golang/mock is deprecated, Uber's fork is incompatible with it, and mockery is now the popular choice: it generates testify-style mocks from interfaces via `go:generate`, with a simpler API. Each table-test case gets its own mock setup function, and `AssertExpectations` at the end confirms the calls happened.

For test data he likes gofakeit, which generates UUIDs, prices, currencies and much more. Because the values change on every run, it occasionally finds a bug a fixed fixture would have hidden.

At the HTTP layer he separates two kinds of test on purpose. Handler tests go deep: build a Gin context from an `httptest` recorder, inject the mocked service, and check status codes, error handling and the decoded body with go-cmp. Router tests stay on the happy path and check the wiring: the route path, parameter extraction and middleware.

He closes with coverage reports (local HTML, or Coveralls for open source), Pact Go for contract tests across services, and testifylint, a linter that flags misuse of testify's `assert` and `require`.

## Who should watch

Any Go developer whose test suite is either all mocks or all end-to-end. It is one of the most code-heavy talks of Conf42 Golang 2025, and you can lift the patterns straight into a service.

Title: Virtualised GPUs get close to bare metal for enterprise AI
Description: Venkatachala Nivas Chainuru at Conf42 SRE 2025 on the Dell, VMware and NVIDIA virtual GPU stack and how close it gets to bare-metal AI performance.
Body:
The usual objection to virtualising GPUs is the performance tax. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Venkatachala Nivas Chainuru argued that for most enterprise AI workloads the tax is small enough to be outweighed by better utilisation, faster provisioning and lower operating cost, using the joint Dell Technologies, VMware and NVIDIA virtual GPU stack as the example.

Be clear on scope: this is a talk about one vendor alliance's validated architecture, presented largely through performance and adoption figures, rather than a hands-on build. If you are deciding whether vGPU is worth piloting, that is exactly the kind of evidence you will want to look at.

## The overhead question

The talk takes on the objection directly. Venkatachala cites studies putting the average virtualisation overhead at about 18% across mixed workloads, then shows how much better the specific validated stack does. The headline numbers, as he presents them:

- Deep learning training at up to 96% of bare-metal performance.
- Inference at up to 98%.
- TensorFlow image classification at 95%, processing up to 4,500 images per second.
- Memory-intensive workloads at around 92%.

He also notes near-linear scaling from one to eight GPUs within a single server for training. Inference faring best is intuitive: shorter, more independent jobs suffer less from sharing.

## What the stack is

The architecture combines NVIDIA AI Enterprise software with VMware vSphere for virtualising and containerising AI workloads on Dell infrastructure. A virtualised deployment layer runs on premises or at a cloud provider, and workloads can be containerised on top. The pitch for platform teams is that GPUs become a pooled, schedulable resource instead of servers dedicated to one team.

## The operational case beats the benchmark case

The more persuasive part of the talk is operational. Provisioning that used to take weeks drops to days or hours, which he puts at up to 60% faster deployment. Organisations that already have VMware expertise reuse it, which he links to 83% greater operational efficiency and 30% less specialised training. Utilisation is around three times better than dedicated AI infrastructure, maintenance overhead falls by about 54%, and total cost of ownership drops by roughly 40% over five years.

The utilisation number is the one to take back to your capacity planning meeting. An idle dedicated GPU is the most expensive kind of idle there is.

## Departments, not silos

The second half looks at AI applications running on shared vGPU infrastructure across HR, IT security and customer service, with figures for faster hiring, fewer security incidents and higher customer-interaction capacity. The argument underneath is about platforms: one shared GPU pool serving many departments avoids each one building its own island of hardware, and he cites lower training costs and faster implementation from that shared approach.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure and platform engineers in VMware-heavy enterprises weighing vGPU against dedicated GPU servers, and anyone who needs the business-case numbers for that decision. Engineers already running Kubernetes-native GPU sharing will find it a useful comparison point rather than new technique.

Title: Risk analytics starts with metadata-driven Azure pipelines
Description: Lokeshkumar Madabathula at Conf42 SRE 2025 on Azure Data Factory pipelines, governance and real-time Power BI dashboards as the base for financial risk analytics.
Body:
Predictive risk models are only as current as the data feeding them, and in most enterprises that data is late. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Lokeshkumar Madabathula, a senior Azure data engineer with over 15 years in enterprise data, presented the architecture he built underneath AI-driven risk management: metadata-driven Azure Data Factory pipelines, strict governance and real-time dashboards.

A note on scope: the title promises predictive models for financial stability, but most of the talk is about the data platform those models depend on. That is arguably the more useful half. A model scoring yesterday's exposure is a history lesson.

## Code-heavy ETL cannot keep up with risk

The problem statement is about change. Data arrives from web, IoT, transactional systems and third-party APIs, in many formats, at different speeds, with varying schemas and business rules. Traditional ETL frameworks are code-heavy, error-prone and slow to maintain, so when the risk picture moves, the pipelines lag behind it.

Lokeshkumar's answer was Azure Data Factory, chosen for its visual pipeline design, prebuilt connectors to a hundred-plus sources, and reusable components. The more important decision was architectural: a metadata-driven design where business logic can change without changing code.

## Put the logic in metadata, not in pipelines

The best-practice section is the core of the talk and transfers well beyond Azure:

- **Modular design.** Pipelines split into functional units for ingestion, cleansing, transformation and loading.
- **Parameterised templates** so a new use case is a configuration, not a new pipeline.
- **Metadata-driven execution** controlling source file types, schema mappings and target tables from configuration.
- **Incremental loading** of only the delta, which cuts both runtime and compute.

He reports operational costs dropping 40% through dynamic scaling and scheduling, and pipeline success rates improving to 99.9%, virtually eliminating manual restarts. For anyone who has been paged for a broken chain of dependent jobs at 2am, the last number is the one that matters.

## Governance you can audit

Financial data brings auditors, and the talk takes that seriously. Every transformation is tracked with timestamped lineage. Every activity is logged, searchable and tied to user credentials. Operational dashboards built on Power BI and Log Analytics show pipeline health, with alerts on performance thresholds.

On the security side: encryption in transit, keys held in Azure Key Vault, least-privilege role-based access, version-controlled configuration for every change, plus data masking, right-to-be-forgotten handling and consent tracking for GDPR. He credits these controls with passing multiple compliance audits.

## From pipelines to dashboards

Once the platform was stable, the team built self-service analytics on Power BI and Azure Analysis Services connected directly to streaming sources, giving finance teams real-time views of exposure, risk, operational losses and market trends. Report generation time dropped by up to 70%.

His forward look is where the predictive part comes back: auto-tuned pipelines, failure alerts and embedded models forecasting financial risk from live data. It is presented as a direction rather than a delivered system, which is honest.

## Who should watch

Data engineers building on Azure for regulated industries, and SREs who own data platforms and want to argue for metadata-driven design over hand-coded jobs. If you came for model architectures for market risk, this is the plumbing talk, not the modelling one.

Title: Fraud models need circuit breakers and a rule-based fallback
Description: Prakash Vanga of Sriven Technologies at Conf42 SRE 2025 on SRE patterns for real-time AI fraud detection, from circuit breakers to multi-dimensional SLOs.
Body:
When the fraud model is slow, the customer's card payment is slow, so an ML model on the payment path has to be engineered like any other critical dependency. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Prakash Vanga of Sriven Technologies, an AWS data engineer with 13 years in cloud and identity, walked through the SRE patterns his team used for cloud-native AI fraud detection: streaming, circuit breakers, ML-aware observability and SLOs that measure more than uptime.

Where [Sasidhar Reddy Somula](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Sasidhar_Reddy_Somula_real_time_fraud) at the same event focused on which models catch what, this talk is about keeping those models running at payment speed.

## From batch to stream

The starting point was batch analysis that ran hours after transactions happened, producing late detection and frustrated customers caught by false positives. The team moved to a streaming architecture on Kafka, added a feature store for low-latency access to historical context, and served models as auto-scaling microservices for real-time inference.

None of that is exotic. The interesting part is what they had to add once models were in the hot path.

## AI systems fail in new ways

Prakash's resilience patterns are the heart of the talk:

- **Circuit breakers** that detect an overwhelmed model and fall back to a simpler rule-based system, so transactions keep flowing instead of cascading into timeouts.
- **Graceful degradation**: critical fraud checks always run, while deeper analysis can be paused under peak load.
- **Automated canary analysis**: new models get a small slice of traffic first, with latency and false-positive rates watched before full rollout.

The rule-based fallback is the quietly important idea. Teams spend years replacing rules with models, then discover the rules are still the best safety net when the model misbehaves.

## Observability for models, not just hosts

Standard monitoring could not explain model behaviour or tie it to business impact, so the team built a specialised stack. It tracks inference latency, prediction confidence and compute usage per model version; watches for data drift in input features; uses explainability tooling to show why a transaction was flagged; and correlates technical metrics with fraud losses and customer friction.

## SLOs with more than one axis

Uptime alone does not describe a fraud system, so their SLO framework combines availability at 99.9%, detection latency under 200 milliseconds, a false-positive rate below 0.5%, a detection rate above 98%, and explainability with reason codes for every decision. The value of writing all five down is that trade-offs between depth of analysis and real-time speed become explicit decisions instead of arguments.

## Chaos testing without losing real money

Breaking production is not an option when failures cost money immediately. The team runs hypothesis-driven chaos experiments in replica environments with synthetic transactions mimicking normal and fraudulent behaviour, checking that degradation paths, fallbacks and recovery actually work.

Reported results: a 78% reduction in detection time, false positives down 63%, 99.99% availability and a 42% cost reduction. The talk closes with compliance as code (infrastructure as code, model governance, automated audit trails) and a three-step plan: assess gaps, build foundational patterns, measure business impact.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who are about to put an ML model on a latency-critical path, in payments or anywhere else. The patterns are general; fraud just makes the stakes obvious.

Title: Read TLS traffic before it's encrypted, with eBPF uprobes and Go
Description: Pranshu Srivastava of Cloudera at Conf42 Golang 2025 on writing eBPF user space code in Go with cilium/ebpf, and probing OpenSSL to see plaintext.
Body:
If you probe the `send` system call to watch an app's HTTPS traffic, all you get is ciphertext. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Pranshu Srivastava](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Pranshu_Srivastava_cilium_ebpf_networking), Software Engineer at Cloudera, showed the fix: attach uprobes to OpenSSL's read and write functions instead, and write the user space side in Go with Cilium's eBPF library. It is a first-steps talk aimed at people who want eBPF without writing their user space code in Rust.

## eBPF in one paragraph

Pranshu's working definition: eBPF lets you attach your own functions to system calls and other hooks, so when an application calls them, your code runs too, with access to the arguments and data structures. It grew out of classic BPF, which could only filter packets. The selling point is overhead: probes are small and attach efficiently, so you can observe a busy application without slowing it down.

The kernel-side program collects the data; something in user space has to load it, attach it and read the results. That is where the choice of library comes in.

## Why Go and Cilium, not Rust or Python

His team picked the cilium/ebpf library for three reasons: the rest of their application was already Go, Go is a good language for observability tooling, and the Cilium project has active maintainers and a helpful community, which he says sped up their development noticeably.

He is fair to the alternatives. Aya in Rust gives you stronger memory safety, but with a steeper learning curve and less support, and eBPF itself is young enough that documentation is thin everywhere. BCC gives Python the libraries it needs. For the kernel side he compares BCC with libbpf: BCC compiles the eBPF program each time it runs, so the source has to ship with your project, while libbpf follows compile once, run everywhere, so you build once and carry only the object files. That was a deciding factor for them.

## Probe the library, not the syscall

The heart of the talk is a diagram borrowed from Pixie. An application making an HTTPS call hands its data to OpenSSL, which encrypts it inside `SSL_write` and decrypts inside `SSL_read`, and only then do the bytes reach `send` and `recv`. Probe the syscalls and you see gibberish. Probe the library functions and you see the plaintext.

Because OpenSSL lives in user space, these are uprobes, not kprobes. Pranshu attaches one probe at the entry and one at the exit of both `SSL_write` and `SSL_read` in the system's libssl, stores data in a hash map keyed by thread group ID, and submits events for the Go tracer to poll in a loop.

## The demo

He then runs Pixie's demo: a client and server exchange secrets over a TLS connection. He starts both, notes the PID, points the tracer at it, and the probes attach. The client's and the server's secrets appear in the tracer output in clear text, matching what the apps logged.

It is a tidy illustration of why eBPF-based observability tools can see inside encrypted traffic without touching application code, and also a reminder that root on a host means seeing everything on it.

## Who should watch

Go developers curious about eBPF who want a concrete first project, and SREs wondering how tools like Pixie see HTTPS payloads. Experienced eBPF authors will know the uprobe trick, though the library comparison is a handy summary.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Writing Custom eBPF Programs for Observability: What You Need to Know](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Sooter_Saalu_writing_programs_ebpf) by Sooter Saalu, the next step after your first probe.
- [How Kernel Programming Escaped the Kernel](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Anais_Dotis_ebpf_linux_networking) by Anais Dotis, on how eBPF reached networking and beyond.
- [Zero-instrumentation observability based on eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2024_Nikolay_Sivko_zeroinstrumentation_observability_ebpf) by Nikolay Sivko, the production version of the idea.

Title: Go as the glue for enterprise data pipelines, from ingest to governance
Description: Sanath Chilakala of NTT DATA at Conf42 Golang 2025 on Go-based ingestion, ETL and governance, with healthcare and finance case studies.
Body:
Enterprises are not short of data; they are short of data anyone can find. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Sanath Chilakala](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Sanath_Chilakala_data_architecture_scaling), Director of AI and Digital Solution Architecture at NTT DATA, opened with the figure that enterprise data grows 42.2% a year while 68% of it goes unused, and argued that Go is a strong backbone for the architecture that fixes the second number.

## Most companies are stuck at "collect" and "structure"

Sanath frames data maturity as four rungs. At the bottom is basic collection: many systems, fragmented and reactive. Next is structure: data in a database with some integrity, even without a formal model. Then advanced analytics on a purpose-built data model for your industry. At the top is AI readiness, where systems start to optimise themselves.

His claim is that most organisations are trapped on the first two rungs, and that a large share of a data professional's working day goes on finding and validating data instead of using it. If you have ever spent a sprint reconciling three definitions of "active customer", you have met this problem.

## Four pipeline stages, one language

The core of the talk walks a pipeline through ingestion, transformation, analysis and distribution, and says where Go earns its place in each:

- **Ingestion**: goroutines make it cheap to connect to many sources at once and handle high event rates with little CPU overhead.
- **Transformation**: lightweight concurrent ETL that scales across CPU cores, so complex transformations run in parallel on modest compute.
- **Analysis**: Go services interfacing with TensorFlow, Apache Spark or custom engines, so decisions can be made on streaming data close to when it arrives.
- **Distribution**: delivery to data lakes, warehouses and applications, with data verified cryptographically along the way.

The language case is the familiar one, made well: compiled performance close to C, faster than interpreted Python or JavaScript for this work, and native fit with Kubernetes, Docker and Prometheus plus first-party SDKs for AWS, GCP and Azure.

## Governance is a service, not a spreadsheet

Sanath spends real time on governance, which many data-platform talks skip. His framework has four parts: metadata management with a catalogue and lineage showing how an attribute moves and changes between systems; security and compliance that flags PHI and PII fields and keeps auditable definitions; quality controls that fail data which does not meet its definition; and role-based access control. His point is that a Go microservice architecture lets these governance services scale out and adapt as regulations change, instead of living in a central tool nobody can update.

## Two case studies

The healthcare example: an organisation with patient records scattered across departments, where a doctor's request for a patient history could take hours. The Go solution connected 17 disparate systems through microservices with a real-time HL7 FHIR translation engine and HIPAA-compliant verification, and Sanath reports an 83% cut in clinical data retrieval time, with histories available in seconds.

The finance example: compliance reporting spread across 28 systems, with each monthly report taking about 160 staff hours. A data fabric with cryptographically secured audit trails and automated anomaly detection cut reporting time by 94%, by his account.

He finishes with a library shortlist worth bookmarking, including Gonum, NATS, SPIFFE and SPIRE, Ory Hydra, Jaeger, BadgerDB and Terraform, and a rollout plan that starts with an audit and a tightly scoped pilot with clear KPIs before expanding.

## Who should watch

Data architects and platform leads making the case for Go in a data stack that is mostly Python and Java today. It is a strategy talk with numbers and case studies rather than code.

Title: How Cummins rebuilt a PLM data platform around Go concurrency
Description: Krishna Baride of Cummins at Conf42 Golang 2025 on goroutines, channels, zero-allocation parsing and gRPC behind a faster product lifecycle platform.
Body:
Product lifecycle management systems are where CAD files, specs, test results and regulatory paperwork go to wait in line. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Krishna Baride](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Krishna_Baride_plm_ai_scaling), Senior IT Leader for PLM and product owner at Cummins, described how his team replaced that queue with Go microservices built on goroutines, channels and some carefully avoided allocations, and fed the result into AI pipelines.

## The problem is a monolith with a sequential pipeline

Krishna names three pain points. Product data volume keeps growing with product complexity. Legacy PLM architectures sit on monolithic databases and process data sequentially, so they cannot scale. And engineering, manufacturing and quality each keep data in their own systems and formats, so cross-team handoffs stall.

The talk is the story of attacking all three with Go. It is a tour of the architecture rather than a code walkthrough, so expect boxes and patterns, not listings.

## Parse once, in parallel, without feeding the GC

The foundation is an ingestion and transformation engine. Specialised parsers convert proprietary CAD formats into standardised data for analysis and visualisation tools. Goroutines then process different sections of complex product hierarchies at the same time, with synchronisation primitives keeping the result consistent.

The detail Go engineers will appreciate is the zero-allocation strategy: custom memory management so transformations do not allocate new objects each time. Krishna credits it with cutting garbage collection pressure and improving throughput by 85%. Anyone who has watched pprof turn into a flame graph of `runtime.mallocgc` knows why that matters.

## Channels as the company notice board

To fix the cross-team silos, the team built an event-driven notification system on Go channels. Significant data changes publish events into a non-blocking, channel-based system, so producers never wait on consumers. A central dispatcher routes events by payload with acknowledgements, and aggregated streams feed real-time dashboards that show process status to every team at once.

Around that sit the usual scale-out companions: a multi-tier cache with local caches backed by Redis clusters, a machine learning model that predicts likely access patterns and prefetches data before the request arrives, and publish-subscribe invalidation to keep caches coherent across nodes.

## The concurrency kit for AI pipelines

Plugging AI into PLM pushed the team further into Go's lower levels. Krishna describes custom synchronisation primitives coordinating AI pipeline execution across services, memory pools of pre-allocated buffers for large batches, and lock-free data structures built on atomic operations for concurrent access that scales with cores.

Services talk over gRPC, with strongly typed protocol definitions, code generated from interfaces, bidirectional streaming over multiplexed connections and client-side load balancing. On the operations side he lists GC tuning, back-pressure to stop overload, continuous profiling with Go's built-in tools to steer resource allocation, mutual TLS between services, and rate limiting.

The headline outcome, per the talk title, is product launches about 40% faster, which Krishna ties to the combination of Go microservices, AI integration and the event-driven design rather than to any single trick.

## Who should watch

Engineers modernising heavy enterprise systems, especially in manufacturing, and Go developers looking for a real-world catalogue of which concurrency patterns earn their complexity. The recording's audio is rough in places, so keep the slides open.

Title: A tap-to-pay purchase is a distributed system that must never charge twice
Description: Likhit Mada of Intuit at Conf42 SRE 2025 traces a mobile wallet payment end to end, then covers idempotency keys, queues, webhooks and the SRE work behind them.
Body:
Tapping your phone at a till kicks off a chain involving at least six parties, and the whole thing has to behave as if it ran exactly once. At [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), Likhit Mada, a software engineer at Intuit, walks through how mobile payments actually flow, then spends the best part of the talk on the engineering that keeps them correct: idempotency, asynchronous processing with queues and webhooks, and the SRE practices around security, compliance and scale.

If you have never had to explain the difference between an acquirer and an issuer, this is a clear primer. If you have, skip to the idempotency section; it is a good checklist.

## Who is in the room when you tap

Mada introduces the cast. The customer pays with a phone. The merchant accepts payment through a point-of-sale terminal or online checkout. The acquirer processes payments for the merchant and eventually deposits funds. The issuer is the bank behind the customer's card, which checks balances and authorises. Payment networks such as Visa and Mastercard route between acquirer and issuer. A payment gateway connects the merchant to the processor and networks and runs fraud checks. A token service provider swaps the real card number for a token. And the wallet provider (Apple Pay, Google Pay, Samsung Pay and others) holds it all on the phone.

The core of a digital wallet is tokenization: the token service provider maps a random token to your real card in a token vault, and the token is tied to your device and stored at hardware level, so it is useless elsewhere. The end-to-end flow then runs from a biometric check, through NFC to the terminal (or a token to the website), the gateway, the network and the issuer, and back, with settlement and merchant deposits happening later in batches. QR-code payments (Alipay, WeChat Pay) and bank-transfer apps over rails like ACH or Faster Payments take shortcuts around parts of the card network.

## Idempotency is the whole game

Mobile networks drop, users double-tap, and clients retry. Each of those can turn one purchase into two. Mada lists the defences. The main one is an idempotency key: a unique identifier generated by the client (or sometimes the server) and carried through the request. If the key is new, process it; if it exists, return the stored result, whether in progress or complete, without reprocessing. That needs database constraints and persistent transaction state.

Around that sit a deduplication window that checks for identical requests by customer, merchant and amount within a time range; transaction state kept in persistent storage that survives crashes, with distributed caches for fast duplicate checks; retries with exponential backoff (one, two, four, eight seconds) to avoid hammering a struggling server; and client-side care like disabling the pay button after the first tap, with a safe retry path. Any engineer who has been paged about a customer charged twice will nod along.

## Queues for spikes, webhooks for truth

For scale, synchronous payment processing becomes the bottleneck, so Mada pushes work asynchronous. Message queues absorb traffic spikes, with dead letter queues catching failures. Status flows back two ways: callbacks, defined per request and typically used for immediate handling such as sending the user to a success page; and webhooks, registered once at account level, which push events like success or failure to the merchant's endpoint and retry when that endpoint is down. His summary: webhooks are the sturdier choice for anything beyond the immediate response.

He also covers tap to pay on iPhone and the Stripe Terminal Android SDK, which turn a merchant's phone into the terminal with no extra hardware.

## Where SRE earns its keep

The last third maps SRE practices onto payments: canary deployments for biometric verification services, automated secret rotation and certificate monitoring, chaos tests that check security holds up during infrastructure failures, automated rollbacks when a fraud model's false-positive rate crosses a threshold, and distributed rate limiting and circuit breakers protecting authentication during spikes. SLOs and SLIs should be payment-specific: transaction success rate, processing latency, uptime. Capacity planning has to anticipate Black Friday. For regions with patchy connectivity he suggests edge caching and offline transaction queuing; for legacy cores built on COBOL and batch jobs, resilient integration layers with circuit breakers and retries.

## Who should watch

Engineers joining a payments team, SREs supporting checkout or wallet services, and anyone designing an API that must never do the same thing twice. Payments veterans will know the flow but may enjoy the idempotency checklist.

Title: Treat the month-end close like a production service
Description: Pavan Kumar Bollineni of Deloitte at Conf42 SRE 2025 on applying SLOs, playbooks and blameless postmortems to SAP S/4HANA finance systems.
Body:
Finance systems get the strictest deadlines in the company and, often, the least reliability engineering. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Pavan Kumar Bollineni, a Manager at Deloitte, showed how SRE practice applies to an SAP S/4HANA finance implementation: define the close as a service, give it SLOs, and staff incidents with both IT and finance people.

The problems he starts from will sound familiar to anyone who has supported an ERP. During financial close, transaction response times climbed from about two seconds to 30 seconds. Users in Asia hit timeouts at peak while Europe was fine. Outages landed during month-end, leaving incomplete entries that took days of manual reconciliation to fix.

## Financial transactions are services too

The first move is a reframe. Treat financial transactions and reporting as services with reliability and performance targets, the way a customer-facing API would be treated. That sounds obvious, but it changes who gets attention and budget: the close process stops being something only finance worries about and becomes something with an owner, a dashboard and an error budget.

From there Pavan lays out finance-flavoured SLOs:

- **Availability** for critical functions such as ledger updates and reporting at 99.99%, roughly four minutes a month.
- **Latency**, with 95% of financial transactions completing within two seconds.
- **Business-aligned targets** that tighten during month-end close, when the tolerance for downtime drops further.
- **Quarterly review** of the SLOs against observed trends and business needs.

The month-end tightening is the clever bit. A finance system does not have uniform importance across the month, so its reliability target should not be uniform either.

## Alert on what blocks the close

Monitoring follows the same logic. Alerts that affect the close are prioritised over less critical functions. Latency increases trigger alerts before users notice. And coverage goes beyond uptime to business completion metrics: did reconciliations finish, did reports generate. A system can be up and still fail the close, and only the second kind of metric catches that.

## Incidents need an accountant in the room

The incident-response section has the most portable advice. Write finance-specific playbooks for common failures such as transaction failures and data inconsistencies, with step-by-step resolution and escalation paths. Form cross-functional response teams where a finance expert can say what an error means for the financial statements while engineers fix the cause. Run blameless postmortems focused on process and systems.

Pavan reports average incident resolution dropping from four hours to one, and most recovery procedures being automated. He also describes the cultural side: IT and finance attending joint reliability reviews, sharing the prioritisation of fixes, and finance engineers and SREs cross-training on each other's domains.

## Error budgets for ERP

His implementation lessons are a compact SRE primer translated for business systems: start with business metrics like close duration, use error budgets to balance feature velocity against stability, cross-train both teams, and measure business outcomes rather than just uptime. He ends by pointing the same approach at procurement, manufacturing, HR and customer service platforms.

## Who should watch

SREs who have inherited an SAP estate, and ERP or finance-systems leads who want vocabulary for asking for reliability investment. It is a framework talk with examples rather than a deep technical one; if you already run SLOs, the value is in the finance-specific SLIs and the cross-functional incident model.

Title: Catch insurance fraud before the payout, not after
Description: Sasidhar Reddy Somula at Conf42 SRE 2025 on streaming ML fraud screening for Michigan MCCA reimbursement claims, with privacy-preserving federated learning.
Body:
Most insurance fraud is found after the money has left the building, and recovering it is slow, expensive and often impossible. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2025, Sasidhar Reddy Somula made the case for moving the check upstream: score every claim in real time with machine learning, before payment, and treat the scoring pipeline as a production system with SRE discipline around it.

His example is a specific and unusual one: reimbursement claims to the Michigan Catastrophic Claims Association (MCCA), which covers auto insurance claims above standard coverage thresholds. High value per claim makes it a magnet for organised schemes involving providers, attorneys and claimants working together.

## Rules age faster than fraudsters

The talk opens with the familiar failure of legacy detection. Manual review does not scale to thousands of claims per week. Rule-based systems are outdated quickly and are easy to route around once someone learns the thresholds. Data sits in silos, so no single reviewer sees the pattern across claims. The result, as Sasidhar puts it, is that most fraud is detected post-payment and some is never caught.

Machine learning helps because it learns patterns rather than encoding yesterday's ones, and because it can link claims that look unrelated in isolation. That second point matters most for organised fraud, where each individual claim may look fine.

## Three model families, one claim

Sasidhar walks through the model types he sees in this kind of system:

- **Computer vision** over medical images, photos and scanned documents, to spot tampering and duplicates.
- **Sequence and pattern models** over claim histories, treatment sequences and billing, the patterns a human reviewer misses.
- **Transformer models** reading the narrative descriptions in claims for inconsistencies and suspicious language.

He cites a 23% improvement in detection accuracy for this combination compared with earlier methods. The point is less any single model than combining evidence from documents, histories and text on the same claim.

## Streaming is what makes it prevention

The architectural shift is the SRE-relevant part. With stream processing on Kafka and Flink, claims are screened as they arrive instead of in a nightly batch, and alerts fire before the payment is released. That turns fraud work from recovery into intervention, and it lets investigators spend their time on the high-risk queue rather than on every claim.

It also means the scoring path is now on the critical path for payments. A slow or broken model stalls legitimate claims, which is exactly the kind of dependency that needs SLOs, monitoring and a fallback.

## Federated learning for data you cannot share

The most interesting idea is cross-jurisdiction collaboration. Insurers, agencies and regulators each hold part of the picture but cannot pool raw claims data. Federated learning lets each party train locally and share only model updates. Sasidhar reports this reaching 85 to 90% of centralised detection accuracy while keeping sensitive data where it lives. Fraud rings that span regions show up without anyone violating privacy law.

He reports pilot results of a 50% drop in fraudulent payouts and a 70% reduction in manual review, plus fewer false positives, which means fewer delays for honest claimants.

## Explainability is a regulatory requirement

The closing section is a reminder that a fraud model has an audience beyond engineers. Decisions must be justifiable to regulators and policyholders, which means documented training data and decision factors, privacy compliance, regular bias audits, and human review of algorithmic decisions. His rollout advice is incremental: assess current vulnerabilities and data readiness, pilot on high-risk claim categories, then scale claim type by claim type.

## Who should watch

Engineers and data teams in insurance or payments who are moving from batch rules to real-time scoring, and anyone who needs a short tour of federated learning in a regulated setting. It is an overview rather than an implementation walkthrough, so do not expect Flink job configs.
