Title: Put only the sensitive services in the enclave, and write them in Go
Description: Srinivas Vallabhaneni of Walmart at Conf42 Golang 2025 on confidential computing with Go, covering TEEs, attestation, sealing and enclaves in microservices.
Body:
Firewalls protect you from people outside. Confidential computing is for the day the threat is the infrastructure itself. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Srinivas Vallabhaneni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Vallabhaneni_enclaves_security_confidential), a senior software engineer at Walmart Global Tech, made the case that trusted execution environments are now practical for production, and that Go is a better fit for them than its reputation in systems programming suggests.

## Why the perimeter is not enough

Srinivas opens with the attack surface: microservices, APIs, cloud and edge have multiplied the entry points, and he cites the figure that nearly 80% of data breaches involve misuse of privileged access. If attackers are mostly misusing what is already trusted, VPNs and IAM do not save you. You need data to stay protected even when the host is compromised.

That is the job of a trusted execution environment (TEE), which he describes as a lockbox inside the CPU. Three properties make it work: isolation (even someone with root cannot read the enclave's memory), attestation (you can prove only verified code is running inside) and encryption across the data's whole life, including during execution. His summary is that this is zero trust implemented in hardware.

## The overhead argument has mostly gone away

The usual objection to enclaves was speed. Srinivas puts numbers on the change: in 2018, running code inside an enclave could cost up to 35% in performance; on modern hardware five years later he puts it at around 4%. That moves TEEs from research prototypes into the set of things you can reasonably put on a production path.

Why Go, when TEEs are usually associated with C or Rust? His reasons: a small runtime footprint suits resource-constrained enclaves, type safety and simple syntax cut down on memory corruption bugs in code that must be trustworthy, and goroutines keep parallel work lightweight. Go's structure also makes it easy to write the enclave lifecycle as a clean state machine: initialise the enclave and its keys, attest, run the sensitive logic, then seal the results so they are encrypted before they leave.

## Not everything belongs in the lockbox

The most practical idea in the talk is selective placement. In a microservice architecture, Srinivas encrypts data at ingestion, runs only the services that touch PII or other sensitive logic inside an enclave, lets supporting services do blind processing on encrypted payloads, and decrypts results only for consumers that pass attestation. You pay the enclave cost only where a breach would actually hurt.

His worked scenario is analytics on encrypted data: encrypted input from users or edge devices flows into a TEE-based analytics engine, gets decrypted and analysed inside, and leaves sealed. He pitches that zero-trust pipeline at healthcare, finance and multi-tenant SaaS.

## It fits the DevOps toolchain now

He also answers the question he says comes up most: can this go into a normal delivery pipeline? His answer is yes. Attestation checks can gate deployments, Kubernetes operators can schedule enclave workloads through extended CRDs, and HashiCorp Vault can distribute secrets to enclaves.

He is honest about what remains hard: side-channel attacks, remote attestation across large or hybrid clusters, key distribution to isolated nodes, and keeping the API between enclave and non-enclave code small enough not to leak. He closes on multi-party computation, confidential containers and zero-knowledge proofs as where the field is going.

## Who should watch

Go engineers building services that handle regulated data, and security architects weighing whether confidential computing is worth piloting. It is an overview with an architecture sketch rather than a code walkthrough, so pair it with something hands-on if you want to write your first enclave.

Title: Investment-bank reconciliation belongs in a cloud pipeline, not spreadsheets
Description: Jaya Krishna Vemuri of State Street at Conf42 SRE 2025 on cloud reconciliation for investment banking - ingestion, matching rules, exceptions and audit trails.
Body:
Reconciliation is where investment banks find out whether their books agree with everyone else's, and too often it still runs on manual sheets and overnight batches. At [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), Jaya Krishna Vemuri, a vice president at State Street Bank and Trust Company with more than 14 years building high-volume investment products on Oracle, Sybase, Snowflake, Azure and AWS, lays out what a cloud-based reconciliation platform looks like and why it beats the legacy approach.

It is a domain talk for people who build or run financial back-office systems. The architecture section is the practical core; the stats-heavy middle is best read as the speaker's industry roundup.

## Five ways legacy reconciliation hurts

Vemuri's list of problems will look painfully familiar to anyone near a finance operations team. It is time-consuming: data analysis, preparing sheets, matching transactions, investigating breaks and building reports are mostly manual, which drags out period close. Every manual step invites human error: data-entry mistakes, missed transactions, wrong matches, and from there inaccurate financial statements. Systems are disjointed, with departments and outside partners on separate software and no unified view. Data is delayed because legacy processes run on batches, so decisions get made on stale information. And all of that makes audits harder; a failed audit means redoing the work.

## Four layers, one pipeline

The proposed architecture is a clean four-stage pipeline. A data ingestion layer uses APIs and connectors to pull trade confirmations, settlements, transactions and market data from banks, counterparties, custodians and trading platforms. A transformation engine runs ETL workflows to standardise and enrich the ingested data for the business's needs. A reconciliation engine applies configurable matching rules and algorithms across sources, flagging discrepancies for review. A reporting and analytics layer produces real-time dashboards, regulatory reports and predictive analytics.

Around that sit the features that make it worth migrating: automated matching of internal records against external statements and ledgers, real-time synchronisation so transactions reconcile as they happen instead of the next morning, integration with accounting software and custodian systems, and reporting that surfaces issues early. He describes the platform as microservices, each scaling independently.

## The number that tells the story

Vemuri compares metrics from before and after a cloud implementation. The one that sticks: exception-handling time dropping from around 360 minutes (six hours) to 18 minutes. That is the difference between an operations team that spends the day chasing breaks and one that reviews a short queue.

The rest of the talk layers on a long run of figures for data quality, compliance reporting, throughput and availability, plus forward-looking items such as blockchain-based audit trails and quantum-inspired algorithms. Some of these are from his own work and some, by his account, come from multiple outside sources. If you plan to cite any of them in a business case, ask where each came from first. Reconciliation people, of all people, will appreciate checking the numbers against a second source.

## Getting it into production

The implementation notes are where the SRE angle shows: hybrid and multi-cloud strategies, active configurations across geographic regions for disaster recovery, user training with certification during the first quarter, and AI-assisted support for routine incidents. He also points at how large the integration surface gets, with reconciliation platforms touching many internal systems and external services.

Looking ahead, he expects AI-driven pattern recognition for complex matching and real-time anomaly detection before errors reach operations, blockchain ledgers for transparency and fraud prevention, and richer interactive dashboards for spotting bottlenecks.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects in banking, custody or fund administration who own reconciliation, and SREs supporting those platforms who want the business context behind the pages. If you want implementation code or vendor comparisons, this stays at the architecture and outcomes level.

Title: Mask, tokenize or anonymize? Picking the right tool for PII in cloud
Description: Sharath Chandra Adupa of Fidelity Investments at Conf42 Golang 2025 maps encryption, masking, tokenization and differential privacy to the data you hold.
Body:
Encrypting everything is the easy part of protecting personal data. Deciding which records stay reversible, who holds the keys and how much analytical value you can afford to destroy is the hard part. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Sharath Chandra Adupa](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Sharath_Chandra_Adupa_security_pii_cloud), Principal Architect at Fidelity Investments, laid out a toolkit for PII in cloud environments and, more usefully, which tool fits which kind of data.

Scope note: this is an architecture and policy talk drawing on his 20 years across finance and healthcare. It is language-agnostic, with no Go code, so treat it as a reference for the design review rather than the pull request.

## PII is wider than the SSN column

Sharath starts with the basics: personally identifiable information is anything that uniquely identifies a person. Social Security numbers and credit card numbers are the obvious ones. The less obvious ones are combinations, such as name plus date of birth plus address, which identify someone even though no single field does. That is the trap for anyone who classifies columns one at a time.

Regulations like GDPR, CCPA and HIPAA set the floor, and he notes that most organisations go beyond them. Moving to the cloud adds multi-tenant infrastructure to the threat model, which is why he argues for an architecture designed around privacy rather than bolted on.

## Own the keys, and keep them in the right country

The encryption section covers the three layers you would expect: application-level, volume and file-level, and database encryption. The part worth noting is key ownership. Customer-managed keys and bring-your-own-key setups let an organisation generate and store keys in its own vaults, which keeps control of the encryption material and helps meet data residency rules. He adds geographic boundary controls: region-specific key storage and operations, so the keys live where the data is required to live.

## Reversible or not is the real question

The obfuscation section is the most practical part of the talk, because it sorts techniques by whether you can get the original data back:

- **Policy-driven obfuscation** applies predefined rules to mask or transform sensitive fields automatically, so the data stays usable for things like testing and development.
- **Data masking** is irreversible: the value becomes meaningless text.
- **Tokenization** is reversible under strict control. Tokenize at rest, detokenize on retrieval for callers who are allowed to see the real value.

He cites figures for the payoff: policy-driven masking cutting compliance violations by around 85% while keeping referential integrity, and tokenization shrinking the scope of compliance audits by up to 70%. The audit-scope point is the one to take to your compliance team, since every system that only ever sees tokens is a system the auditors care less about.

Beyond that come anonymization (irreversible, including handling quasi-identifiers that could lead to re-identification), pseudonymization (artificial identifiers that can be re-linked with extra information) and differential privacy, which offers mathematical guarantees while keeping data useful for analysis.

## Match the technique to the sector

A neat slide pairs sectors with approaches. Healthcare research wants anonymization plus differential privacy and HIPAA compliance. Academic research leans on differential privacy. Market analysis can live with pseudonymization. Financial services, Sharath's home turf, combines pseudonymization with encryption because regulators and the business both need the data.

He closes on governance: mature governance and change management, in the figures he presents, reduce security incidents and disruptions, and policy-driven controls keep protection consistent across a sprawling estate. In other words, the technology works only if somebody owns the policy.

## Who should watch

Architects and data engineers designing storage for regulated data, and anyone who has to explain to an auditor why the analytics warehouse holds tokens instead of card numbers. If you already run a tokenization vault, the sector mapping is the slide to screenshot.

Title: Most microservice slowness starts in the database layer
Description: Sudhakar Reddy Narra of ServiceNow at Conf42 SRE 2025 on query tuning, concurrency, layered caching, smart load balancing and chaos tests for fast, resilient services.
Body:
One composite index took a query from around two seconds to under 50 milliseconds. That is the kind of detail Sudhakar Reddy Narra, a senior staff performance engineer at ServiceNow with 17 years in the field, brings to [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025). His talk lays out a layered framework for fast, resilient cloud microservices, and most of it is built from fixes he shipped in production: query rewrites, connection pools, caches, routing and chaos experiments.

It is a long, dense talk, and one of the more concrete performance sessions you'll find. Each section ends with a number and a reason.

## A pyramid, with the database at the bottom

Narra frames the work as a pyramid. The foundation is architecture, code and infrastructure: clear service boundaries (an order service talking to billing through events instead of direct API calls), no N+1 queries, idempotent APIs that survive retries, Kubernetes autoscaling, Terraform and read replicas. On top of that sit engineering practices: performance tests in CI/CD, automated observability, SLOs enforced through the lifecycle. Then measurable results, and finally business value.

The results he reports: average response times cut from over 400 ms to under 100 ms through query tuning and caching, roughly three times the throughput at peak, a 75 percent cut in storage for a key table, and concurrent users scaled from about 1,000 to 5,000 on the same infrastructure. On one project, he says, cloud cost fell by about 40 percent while handling five times more users.

## Fix the queries before buying hardware

In his experience, 60 to 70 percent of performance bottlenecks live in the database layer, so he starts there. The classic N+1 pattern (one API call fanning out into N+1 queries) got collapsed into a single query. Slow and frequent queries were found with database logs, New Relic and Oracle AWR reports, then fixed with missing indexes, fewer joins and query hints. APIs were tuned to fetch what the UI shows: if a page lists ten records, don't fetch a hundred. Selective denormalisation of a reporting table removed three joins and made dashboard queries much faster. Oracle got optimizer hints and SQL plan baselines; MySQL got EXPLAIN-driven tuning. Query optimisation, he notes, isn't glamorous, but it is one of the highest-ROI efforts in performance engineering.

## Concurrency is a resilience feature

The concurrency section treats throughput and stability as the same problem. Default connection pool settings were replaced with dynamic pools, split for read-heavy and write-heavy services, which he says cut connection overhead by about 40 percent in the busiest services. An order service that blocked on inventory calls was rewritten as event-driven, using RxJava or Spring WebFlux. Custom thread pools and backpressure let the system shed load gracefully instead of failing in cascade. Cascading timeouts from the database up to HTTP clients, plus circuit breakers, kept a dead dependency from exhausting thread pools. Timeouts, in his words, are brakes.

## Cache every layer, invalidate carefully

Caching runs from client to database: cache-control headers, ETags and versioned static assets on the client; edge caching at the API gateway for slow-changing endpoints like product listings, with targeted invalidation; cache-aside with in-memory and Redis caches in the app, with TTLs set by how volatile each dataset is; and cached results for expensive reports, kept consistent with write-through. Load balancing got smarter too: requests classified by priority (a profile lookup outranks a monthly report), routing driven by health and capacity, weighted and geo-aware distribution, and graceful degradation with cached fallbacks.

## Test performance and failure on purpose

Observability ties it together: RED metrics for services, USE for infrastructure, structured logs with correlation IDs, OpenTelemetry or Jaeger tracing (which showed most checkout latency came from a downstream payment system), and SLO-driven alerting. Performance testing runs at four levels, from unit benchmarks in pull requests to production-like JMeter and Gatling runs that pause deployment when an SLO is missed. One end-to-end test found a two-second checkout delay caused by a synchronous email call.

Chaos engineering closes the loop: testable hypotheses about critical flows, a scoped blast radius, progressive rollout from dev to canary in production, auto-termination thresholds, and every finding turned into a fix. One experiment exposed a slow downstream API stalling the homepage; a timeout plus cached fallback cut failover from minutes to seconds.

## Who should watch

Backend and performance engineers, SREs who own latency SLOs, and anyone about to throw more pods at a problem that might be one missing index. Expect breadth over depth on any single technique, and no code on screen.

Title: A self-healing supply chain needs detection, action and a human
Description: Venkata Anil Kumar Nilisetty of Cognizant at Conf42 SRE 2025 on GNNs, transformers, Flink and Airflow for supply-chain anomaly detection and automated remediation.
Body:
Supply chains are graphs, so it makes sense to look for trouble with graph models. At [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), Venkata Anil Kumar Nilisetty, a Java full stack lead developer at Cognizant, presents an AI framework that detects supply-chain anomalies with graph neural networks and transformers, explains them, and then fixes what it can automatically through orchestrated workflows, with humans kept in the loop over chat.

It is a compact, architecture-level talk, packed with results figures. Think of it as a reference design for an SRE-style detect, analyse, remediate, learn loop applied to logistics.

## Disruption cascades

The problem statement is about interconnection. Large companies work with thousands of suppliers across many countries, so a failing node rarely stays local: Nilisetty cites research that a single disruption can cascade into nearly half of downstream operations. Reactive approaches, where someone notices a shortage after it happens, no longer keep up.

## Streams first, models second

The foundation is a real-time event processing layer: Apache Flink and Kafka Streams handling large event volumes at millisecond latencies, orchestrated on Kubernetes with Knative for event-driven scaling. Without fresh events, the cleverest model in the world is just writing history.

On top sit two model families. Graph neural networks fit the shape of the data, since suppliers, shipments and transactions form a network, and he reports high accuracy with far fewer false positives than traditional methods. Transformer models handle the time-series side, flagging many anomalies well ahead of conventional methods, and fine-tuning reportedly works with only a couple of hundred labelled anomalies, which matters in a domain where labelled incidents are scarce.

## Explain it, or nobody acts on it

The section on explainability is the one SREs should steal. Powerful models need to justify themselves to the operators who will act on their alerts. The framework uses SHAP values to show which features drove a prediction (a few top features usually dominate, which cuts investigation time), counterfactual explanations so operators can run what-if scenarios before intervening, and attention visualisations that highlight suspicious nodes in the transaction graph. An alert that says why is an alert that gets acted on.

## From alert to fix

Detection is only half the job. Apache Airflow orchestrates remediation workflows that adapt to the disruption scenario, and Nilisetty reports mean time to resolution falling from about 27 hours to under five. The same loop drives automated inventory rebalancing (fewer stockouts, less excess stock) and Hyperledger Fabric smart contracts that validate transactions between parties, enforce compliance checks automatically and shrink dispute counts and settlement times.

Humans stay in the picture through ChatOps bots in Slack and Microsoft Teams that cut the time to make people aware of an issue, a knowledge base that helps operators resolve recurring issues faster, and continuous learning loops that reduce false positives quarter over quarter.

## Read the numbers as the speaker's

The talk closes with headline results across fraud, disruption duration, inventory metrics and detection speed. They are presented as outcomes of the framework, without a detailed account of the datasets or deployments behind them. Useful as targets and talking points; verify against your own pilot before quoting them upward. His conclusion is the part that holds regardless of the figures: supply-chain resilience has to be automated, but also explainable, secure and human-centred.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers in logistics, retail or manufacturing, and SREs curious how the incident loop they know translates to physical operations. If you want implementation detail on the GNN or transformer models, this stays at the block-diagram level.

Title: Build composite SLOs from user journeys, then pick the tool
Description: Siddharth Joshi of Nagarro at Conf42 SRE 2025 on SLO management - critical user journeys, composite SLOs and how Harness and Nobl9 compare.
Body:
A checkout page and an order-confirmation email don't deserve the same SLO. At [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), Siddharth Joshi, a senior staff engineer and DevOps tech lead at Nagarro with 12 years in IT, argues that SLOs for complex systems should be designed from critical user journeys, combined into composite SLOs, and managed as a lifecycle, with dedicated SLO management products doing the heavy lifting.

The first third is a solid SRE refresher. The value is in the e-commerce worked example and the closing product comparison.

## The 100 percent myth, again

Joshi starts where SRE always starts: developers want to ship fast, operations want stability, and SRE (introduced at Google in the early 2000s) gives both a shared set of numbers. SLIs measure service quality (availability, throughput, latency), SLOs set internal targets, SLAs are the contract with consequences. Then the misconception he wants to kill: aiming for 100 percent reliability. Systems go down in practice, and chasing perfection means developers can't work on features or innovation. The error budget is the agreed amount of unavailability the team can tolerate: budget left means ship features, budget threatened means work on reliability.

The practices that make it real are monitoring with the right metrics and alerts on the error budget, demand forecasting and capacity planning, change management and emergency response, and managing operational toil.

## Why SLOs go wrong in microservices

The challenges list is the honest part. SLOs often don't line up with business goals, because teams measure what is easy instead of what the business cares about. Targets get set without historical data, so they end up unrealistic. In distributed systems with interdependent microservices and APIs, it is hard to pinpoint which service broke the SLO. Teams forget to prioritise components by what users actually do. Tooling has limits. And systems change constantly with continuous deployment, so SLOs must be revisited as features land.

His approach: understand the system, map critical user journeys, design SLOs for the critical services, set metrics, and use them effectively.

## Pre-purchase matters more than the email

The worked example is an online shop. Joshi splits the journey into pre-purchase (browse the store, add to cart, pay) and post-purchase (warehouse receives and dispatches, invoicing, email confirmation). In pre-purchase, availability matters more than latency, and website availability ranks slightly above payment availability, because if the site is down nobody gets as far as paying. In post-purchase, warehouse and invoicing outrank email: a confirmation that arrives late is fine, an order that never dispatches is not.

From there the method is mechanical in a good way. Identify the services (store website, payment, invoicing, emailing, warehousing), set individual SLOs per service for availability and latency, combine them into composite SLOs for the pre- and post-purchase experiences, and aggregate those into an overall picture of system reliability. A composite SLO answers the question your VP actually asks: is the shop working?

## Where the products fit

Joshi then surveys the market. He puts Harness and Nobl9 out front for SLO management specifically: both support composite SLOs and user journeys, Harness offers service reliability management and governance via Open Policy Agent, and Nobl9 keeps several years of historical data to inform decisions. He groups FireHydrant, Squadcast, ServiceNow and New Relic under monitoring and incident management rather than dedicated SLO tooling. His comparison grid covers real-time error budget tracking, mapping SLOs to business capabilities, RCA, custom dashboards and reports, automation and auditing. As with any vendor grid in a talk, it is one practitioner's view; run your own trial against your own journeys.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform leads whose SLOs exist on paper but don't drive decisions, and anyone evaluating SLO platforms. If you already run composite SLOs in Nobl9 or similar, the refresher will be familiar; the journey breakdown might still be worth stealing for your next workshop.

Title: AI threat detection in Go for Azure, from logs to containment
Description: Sudeep Shanubhog of Tential Solutions at Conf42 Golang 2025 on a Go-based, ML-driven security pipeline for Azure and preparing for quantum threats.
Body:
Signature-based detection is good at the attacks you already know and bad at the patient ones you don't. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Sudeep Shanubhog, Technical Lead and Senior Full-stack Developer at Tential Solutions, described a Go-based security framework for Microsoft Azure that uses machine learning to spot advanced persistent threats and automates containment, and looked ahead to quantum-resistant cryptography.

It is a short, high-level talk, under seven minutes, that sketches the system and its reported results rather than showing code.

## Why Go for the security pipeline

Sudeep starts with a quick Go primer for the audience: an open source language from Google, compiled to machine code, so faster than interpreted languages such as Python, with goroutines for running many tasks at once and garbage collection that handles large security data volumes without slowing down. For a system that must analyse events as they arrive, those properties are the requirement list.

## Static rules miss the patient attacker

The problem framing is the expanding attack surface of cloud adoption. Advanced persistent threats evolve beyond known patterns, so rule-based tools struggle. His framework uses machine learning and behavioural analysis to find suspicious activity, with continuous monitoring across Azure resources, anomaly detection, automated countermeasures and models that learn from every security event.

## Four stages from log to response

The architecture is the most reusable slide:

1. **Collect** Azure logs, telemetry and user activity.
2. **Pre-process** and enrich the data with threat intelligence, in parallel using Go's concurrency.
3. **Analyse** with machine learning models to detect and classify threats.
4. **Orchestrate the response**, automating containment within milliseconds to limit disruption.

It runs as a distributed system across multiple Azure regions for zero-downtime production. Sudeep reports a throughput of 12,000 security requests per second and 18.5 million security actions per day.

## The numbers, as reported

The results he cites: a 64% increase in threat detection accuracy, a 57% reduction in response time, 43% lower operational cost, 96.42% detection accuracy for advanced persistent threats and a 63% improvement in detecting novel threats. The talk does not show the evaluation behind them, so read them as the project's own figures.

## Getting ready for quantum

The forward-looking part covers three ideas: quantum-enhanced pattern recognition, predictive threat analytics, and quantum-resistant cryptography so encrypted data stays safe once quantum attacks are practical. The last is the one teams can act on today, by tracking post-quantum algorithms and planning a migration path.

## Roll it out in four steps

The adoption roadmap is short: assess to find security gaps, pilot on critical workloads, integrate across all Azure resources, then keep tuning the models with live threat intelligence.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects on Azure who are weighing ML-based detection and want a reference pipeline shape, and Go developers curious about security workloads. If you need model details or code, this talk stays at the overview level.

Title: CSPM starts with an inventory and a baseline, not a dashboard
Description: Cloud Advisor Vishnuvardhana Reddy Veeraballi at Conf42 Golang 2025 on rolling out Cloud Security Posture Management via inventory, baselines, alerts and auto-fix.
Body:
Most cloud breaches that make the news start with a setting somebody forgot, not a zero-day. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Cloud Advisor [Vishnuvardhana Reddy Veeraballi](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Vishnuvardhana_Reddy_Veeraballi_cloud_security_cspm) walked through Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) as a rollout plan: know what you run, write down what "secure" means for it, then let machines watch for drift and fix it.

Honest scope first: this is a vendor-neutral introduction to CSPM, and despite the Golang track there is no Go code in it. It is a short, structured talk, useful if your team is about to buy or build posture monitoring across AWS, Azure and GCP and you want the order of operations.

## The three moving parts

Vishnuvardhana splits CSPM into three components. Continuous monitoring pulls configuration metadata from the cloud providers' APIs, either from a SaaS vendor or a system you build yourself. A risk assessment layer scans that metadata against frameworks such as the CIS benchmarks, NIST and FedRAMP. Compliance monitoring then works with policy engines to enforce the organisation's own standards and report on them.

None of that is exotic. The value of the talk is in how he sequences it.

## Scope comes before rules

Step one is an inventory of every cloud asset, with two kinds of prioritisation. Qualitative: a service that backs a public-facing application gets attention first. Quantitative: a service you run hundreds of resources on matters more than one you touched once. That inventory also defines what is in and out of scope, and if you are using a third-party CSPM tool, it tells you which of the services you actually use the vendor does not cover at all. That gap is easy to miss when the sales demo looks complete.

Step two is the security baseline. He is clear that vendor rule packs and industry frameworks are templates, not gospel. Some default rules will not apply to your organisation, and severities need adjusting to your own risk tolerance. Treat the default rule pack the way you treat a default linter config: a starting point you are expected to argue with.

## Wire it into the tools people already watch

Only after the baseline does integration come in: SIEM, IAM tooling, and alert routing into something like Jira tickets, with severities you have customised. He describes two ways to connect to the cloud providers. Scheduled scans every 12 or 24 hours are simple. Event-driven integration reacts when a resource changes, updates the inventory and re-evaluates the rules straight away, which is what you want when someone opens a storage bucket at 4pm on a Friday.

The best-practice list that follows is familiar but worth having in one place: least-privilege IAM with MFA, regular vulnerability scans and pen tests, monitoring for unauthorised changes to the baseline itself, tested incident response playbooks with clear escalation paths, and role-based training with simulated phishing.

## Auto-remediation is the end state

The forward-looking part of the talk points at automated remediation playbooks that put a misconfigured resource back to the baseline without a human, plus AI-assisted threat detection, predictive analytics, and posture checks moved into DevOps pipelines so bad configuration is caught before it ships. He also flags zero trust, edge security and preparing cryptography for quantum threats as directions the field is heading. These are signposts rather than worked examples, so expect a map, not a tutorial.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers scoping a CSPM programme, and engineering managers who need a shared vocabulary before a vendor evaluation. If you already run Prowler, Security Hub or a commercial CSPM tool in anger, you will know most of this; the inventory-first and baseline-tuning advice is still a good checklist to compare against.

- [Compliance As Code with Cloud Custodian](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2021_Ismael_Hommani_Tanguy_Combe_compliance_as_code_cloud_custodian) by Ismael Hommani and Tanguy Combe, for turning baseline rules into code that can also fix things.

Title: GitOps: roll back the commit, not the server
Description: Kowshik Sakinala at Conf42 SRE 2025 on GitOps with Argo CD, Flux and Jenkins X - the four pillars, the pull-request workflow and a pilot-first roadmap.
Body:
When a GitOps deployment goes wrong, you don't SSH into the server; you revert the commit. At [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), Kowshik Sakinala, a senior DevOps engineer who has modernised deployments with Kubernetes, Helm and GitLab CI, makes the case for GitOps as the default way to run infrastructure: Git as the single source of truth, changes through pull requests, and a controller that keeps the cluster matching what is merged.

It is an introductory-to-intermediate talk. If you already run Argo CD across many clusters, the roadmap and challenges sections are the parts to watch. If you are still triggering Terraform by hand, the whole thing is for you.

## Why traditional infra management drifts

Sakinala starts with the familiar failure mode. Even with Terraform or Ansible, infrastructure changes often involve manual triggers, environments that slowly diverge, and poor visibility into what is actually running. The classic symptom: it worked in dev but not in prod. GitOps flips the model by routing infrastructure through the same review, approval and CI/CD flow as application code. He cites the 2023 State of Continuous Delivery report for the claim that around half of organisations had already started using GitOps.

## Four pillars, one loop

His definition is compact. Version control: Git tracks every infrastructure change. Declarative config: you describe the desired state in YAML or HCL. Continuous reconciliation: an agent like Argo CD checks whether the cluster matches Git and fixes drift. Collaboration: infra changes go through pull requests and approvals, bringing dev and ops into one workflow. He calls it infrastructure meeting software engineering principles, which is about right.

The workflow example is concrete. A developer changes a Kubernetes manifest (a memory limit, a new app version), opens a PR, it is reviewed and merged, the GitOps controller picks it up and updates the cluster. Rollback is a Git revert. Everything is versioned and auditable. He used this model on a multi-cluster retail system where every environment stayed in sync with Git, and even hotfixes went through the same path.

## Pick a tool, the idea stays the same

The tooling overview is short and fair. Argo CD has a strong UI showing what is deployed against what is in Git, good for teams starting out. Flux is lighter, integrates well with Kustomize and Helm, and suits GitOps at scale. Jenkins X combines GitOps with CI pipelines. Secrets go through a manager such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager. Because Kubernetes is already declarative, he describes Kubernetes and GitOps as peanut butter and jelly: you are layering a Git workflow on top of something that already wants desired state, and that covers namespaces, CRDs and more, not just apps.

## Numbers, and where they come from

Sakinala reports that on one of his own projects, post-deployment incidents fell by 40 percent in the first quarter after adopting GitOps, which he puts down to the end of guesswork: everyone knew exactly what was running and when. He also summarises public stories from Spotify (Flux CD plus Backstage for self-service deployments) and Capital One (Argo across thousands of apps). Treat those as his retelling and go to the original sources if you want to quote them.

## Start with one app

The challenges are the honest part: secrets and least-privilege access, multi-repo structure with templating via Helm or Kustomize, and organisational adoption, which needs training, integration with existing CI and some internal marketing. His team started with a small app, got quick wins and spread the results internally.

The roadmap follows from that: assess your current process, pick a pilot app and a GitOps tool, document the wins, scale gradually, and measure deployment frequency, MTTR and incident count. His summary: GitOps is a mindset shift, not just a tool adoption. Looking ahead, he expects AI to predict failing deployments, multi-cloud GitOps across AWS, GCP and on-prem, and GitOps extending to databases and APIs.

## Who should watch

Teams on Kubernetes who still deploy with pipelines that push to clusters, and leads who need a short, structured pitch for GitOps adoption. Seasoned Flux or Argo CD operators can skip to the challenges and roadmap.

Title: In-car AI assistants have to earn their place behind safety
Description: Ravinder Katla of General Motors at Conf42 SRE 2025 on AI in infotainment, from voice and driver monitoring to on-device privacy and a four-phase test regime.
Body:
Every feature in a car's infotainment system answers to the same boss: safety. At [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), Ravinder Katla, an advanced infotainment systems integration engineer at General Motors, walks through how AI is reshaping the screen and voice assistant in your dashboard, and why each capability has to fit inside hard limits on compute, power, privacy and driver attention.

It is an overview from someone who integrates these systems, not a model-architecture talk. The value is in seeing the constraints an automotive engineer works under, which look very different from a cloud team's.

## Voice is the interface that matters most

Katla starts with the basics: infotainment is information plus entertainment, the display in front of the driver or in the centre console where you play media, change vehicle settings and, when parked, even play games. Talking to it is the fastest and least distracting way to use it, so voice recognition gets top billing. He describes accuracy on voice commands climbing from the low 80s percent in 2020 to the mid 90s by 2023, so a failed command went from routine to rare.

## More silicon, same safety budget

The computing story is about consolidation and growth. A car is a network of electronic control units, each owning a slice of functionality: body control, lighting, vehicle control, audio amplification. Katla traces how the number of processing units dedicated to infotainment-class work grew over a few model years, with throughput rising into trillions of operations per second, and the cost of core hardware rising with it. All of it sits under tight constraints: space in the dash, power draw that eats into EV range, memory to manage, and safety-critical operations that need performance guarantees.

## A co-pilot that watches the driver

Beyond voice, AI uses the cabin camera. Katla describes driver monitoring that reads eye movement and facial expression to spot distraction, illness or distress, and, after a crash or sudden event, connects to back-office systems and emergency services. Neural networks learn routines from repeated routes to warn about traffic or road closures ahead.

He breaks context-awareness into four parts: temporal analysis (day-of-week patterns), geo-pattern intelligence (for example recommending charging stations to EV drivers), behavioural patterns (media suggestions based on mood and preference), and a feedback loop: when you reject a suggestion, the system learns not to repeat it. That last one is the difference between a helpful assistant and one you mute forever.

## Privacy by keeping data in the car

The privacy section is the most transferable part for engineers outside automotive. Katla lists four techniques: on-device processing so sensitive data stays in the vehicle and less goes to vendors; differential privacy, adding noise so aggregates stay useful while individuals stay protected; federated learning, training across the fleet while raw data stays local; and time-limited storage, with personal data deleted automatically (for example when the car changes owner).

## Test it like a car, not like an app

Distraction mitigation drives the interface design: workload-adaptive UIs that simplify during demanding driving, multimodal input (voice, touch) that doesn't pull eyes off the road, and interruption management that tells a distracted driver to look back at the road. Validation runs in four phases: NHTSA guidelines and brand interaction standards, controlled-environment behavioural testing, driving-simulator validation, and real-world testing with test-fleet drivers whose feedback feeds the next iteration.

His future list: multimodal deep learning combining vision, audio and sensors; AI that interacts sensibly with semi-autonomous driving; augmented-reality information on the windshield; emotion-aware responses; and V2X communication between vehicles, networks and charging infrastructure.

## Who should watch

Engineers curious about edge AI under real-world constraints, anyone working on in-vehicle software, and privacy engineers looking for a tidy set of patterns. Not much here for SREs looking for cloud reliability practices, and the numbers on the slides are best treated as the speaker's industry summary.

Title: AI-driven SRE, briefly: predict the outage, skip the page
Description: Sidhartha Velishala of Humana at Conf42 SRE 2025 gives a short intro to AI-driven SRE via anomaly detection, predictive maintenance and forecasting.
Body:
Most on-call pain comes from finding out about a problem at the same moment as your users. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Sidhartha Velishala, Technical SME at Humana, gives a compact introduction to AI-driven SRE: machine learning that watches metrics and logs, spots the pattern before the outage, and turns firefighting into scheduled work. His one-line version: "It's going from putting fires out to building systems that do not catch fire in the first place."

The talk is listed as "SRE and Healthcare Data Compliance: Balancing Security and Reliability". The session as recorded is a short, general overview of AI in SRE practice, without a healthcare or compliance angle, so treat it as a primer.

## Reactive ops doesn't scale

Sidhartha starts with the situation every SRE knows: things break out of nowhere, alerts don't make sense, root cause analysis takes forever, and the team is always playing catch-up. His point is less about tooling than about fatigue. Working that way is stressful, tiring and, as he puts it, it doesn't scale.

AI-driven SRE in his definition is the usual SRE toolkit (monitoring, alerting, reliability work) combined with machine learning for anomaly detection and forecasting. The system learns what normal looks like and gives you a heads-up when a familiar bad pattern starts to form, before users notice.

## Three techniques carry most of the value

The middle of the talk names the three building blocks:

- **Anomaly detection.** Watching thousands of metrics and logs at once and collapsing them into one clear signal, instead of a hundred alerts that all describe the same symptom. This is the part that attacks alert noise directly.
- **Predictive maintenance.** Using history and behaviour to estimate when a component is about to fail, with remaining useful life estimation and condition-based monitoring, so a disk or a misbehaving server gets replaced in a maintenance window you chose rather than one the outage chose.
- **Demand forecasting.** Reading past usage, traffic patterns and seasonality such as holiday spikes, so capacity is planned ahead and you neither under-provision and fall over nor over-provision and pay for idle machines.

Put together, he argues, you get more uptime, fewer outages and a calmer rota. The best outcome is the one customers never see: they don't know there was almost a problem.

## One case study, one number

He backs the pitch with a single story from a tech company he worked with. The team trained models to spot problems early, built dashboards and gave engineers more visibility. He reports that downtime dropped by over 60% in eight months, with fewer late-night incidents. The talk doesn't go into which models, which signals or how false positives were handled, so take it as a direction rather than a recipe.

He closes with where the field is heading: faster anomaly detection, better predictions, self-healing infrastructure, and systems that help keep SLOs on track automatically.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers new to the idea of applying ML to operations who want the vocabulary in under ten minutes: anomaly detection, remaining useful life, condition-based monitoring, forecasting. Experienced SREs already running AIOps tooling won't find new techniques here, and anyone who came for healthcare data compliance should look elsewhere; the related talks below go deeper on prediction in production.

Title: Salesforce integration works best with middleware in the middle
Description: Balaji Bodicherla of T-Mobile at Conf42 SRE 2025 on Salesforce APIs, MuleSoft, platform events and when batch beats real-time.
Body:
If Salesforce talks to another system directly and that system goes away, you rewrite the integration. That is the argument Balaji Bodicherla, a Salesforce solution architect at T-Mobile, opens with at [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025): put middleware between Salesforce and everything else, then choose between Bulk API, REST/SOAP and event-driven integration based on volume and latency, not habit.

It is a practitioner's tour of the Salesforce integration toolbox, aimed at people who build and run those integrations. It is also, by design, a Salesforce-and-MuleSoft talk: the tools are the ones that ship with the platform.

## Middleware is your insurance policy

Bodicherla's recommended default is to always have a middleware layer in place. His reasoning is practical rather than architectural purity: if an external system is replaced, the middleware absorbs the change and Salesforce doesn't need rework.

MuleSoft is the obvious candidate, and he walks through the Anypoint Platform pieces: Design Center for API-led connectivity, Exchange for reusable assets and templates, and Runtime Manager for deployment, with CloudHub, Runtime Fabric on Kubernetes, or on-premises when data has to stay put. The API-led approach organises APIs into three layers (system, process and experience) so new capabilities get composed from existing APIs instead of yet another point-to-point link.

Below that sit the prebuilt connectors: AppExchange apps certified by Salesforce (often paid), MuleSoft's catalogue of over 300 connectors, and External Services, which lets analysts call REST APIs from Flow Builder without custom code.

## Pick the API by the shape of the data

The API section is the part worth bookmarking. Bulk API is for large volumes and usually runs as a scheduled night job so it doesn't disrupt business hours; records go in batches, and batches are processed in parallel. REST and SOAP APIs handle records as they are created and need syncing. For real time there are four options: platform events (custom-schema business events over publish-subscribe), Apex triggers on data changes, Change Data Capture (record-level create, update and delete changes, broadcast only to subscribed systems) and the Streaming API with long polling.

His rule of thumb from the best-practices slide is blunt: if a huge amount of data has to move, don't go real-time. Check with the business whether a batch is good enough, and avoid paying for latency nobody needs.

## Measure page time, not just API time

Bodicherla spends a slide on performance measurement, because slow integrations show up as slow pages. Salesforce's Experienced Page Time (EPT) covers the full journey from request through server processing and DOM work to a fully interactive page, and the Lightning component framework tracks rendering times, server round trips and JavaScript execution. The workflow he describes is measure, change the code, then re-measure with the same framework.

## Resilience is boring on purpose

Security gets the expected but necessary list: OAuth 2.0 flows including JWT bearer and SAML assertion, a connected app per external system with granular API access, IP restrictions and session policies, TLS everywhere, Event Monitoring logs, and Shield Platform Encryption as a paid add-on. Governor limits keep tenants honest on the multi-tenant platform.

For reliability, his checklist is what an SRE would write: load test under varied conditions to find bottlenecks, establish throughput baselines for capacity planning, and handle errors with retries with exponential backoff, dead letter queues for manual intervention and detailed logging. Start with a small, well-defined integration, set standards for error handling and monitoring, then scale.

## Who should watch

Salesforce developers and architects, and the SREs and platform engineers who get paged when a nightly sync falls over. If you don't run Salesforce, the integration patterns transfer, but the product specifics won't. There is no live demo; it is slides and experience.

Title: REST is one option among six, and the best designs blend them
Description: Gokul Babu Kuttuva Ganesan of ComTec at Conf42 SRE 2025 compares GraphQL, events, API mesh, serverless, AI-assisted and hypermedia APIs.
Body:
REST served enterprise integration well, but it is no longer the automatic answer. That is the opening claim from Gokul Babu Kuttuva Ganesan of ComTec Information Systems at [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), who lines up six alternatives (GraphQL, event-driven architecture, API mesh, serverless APIs, AI-enhanced APIs and hypermedia APIs) and ends with a simple rule: no single paradigm fits everything, so blend them to match the use case.

It is a short talk, closer to a lightning overview than a workshop. That makes it a quick way to calibrate your own API strategy; just don't expect code.

## What hurts about REST at scale

Kuttuva Ganesan names four pain points that will be familiar to anyone who has maintained a large REST estate. Complex data means multiple endpoints and multiple calls, which slows development and frustrates developers. Responses tend to over-deliver data, which is wasteful for mobile and bandwidth-sensitive clients. Versioning becomes a nightmare as systems scale, with breaking changes rippling out to consumers. And REST wasn't designed for high-throughput, event-heavy environments, which shows under peak load.

## The client asks, the server answers exactly that

GraphQL gets the most attention, and for good reason: the client controls the shape of the response, so a single query returns what is needed and nothing more. Kuttuva Ganesan says some companies have seen 60 to 70 percent less data transferred and faster development cycles, and stresses that the bigger payoff is developer experience and maintainability rather than raw speed.

Event-driven architecture tackles the real-time side. Instead of polling or chaining synchronous calls, services publish events when state changes and consumers process them asynchronously. Loose coupling makes systems more scalable and resilient, especially in microservice estates.

## Tame the point-to-point sprawl

API mesh targets a problem every enterprise architect has drawn on a whiteboard at least once: dozens of teams building their own ad hoc integrations until the diagram looks like spaghetti. A mesh offers a unified gateway that routes, composes, secures and caches across microservices, acting as the orchestrator in the middle.

Serverless APIs scale to demand and disappear when idle, the pay-as-you-go model for compute. The talk quotes significant cost reductions alongside cold-start and warm-response figures; as always with serverless, measure cold starts on your own workload before promising latency to anyone.

## Smarter and self-describing APIs

Two less obvious entries round out the list. AI-enhanced APIs use intent recognition, anomaly detection and predictive caching, so a system starts anticipating what a user will need, not only answering what was asked. And hypermedia APIs, which he admits might seem old school, are self-documenting: they guide clients through resource discovery, which he says reduces breaking changes and makes client-side development more intuitive. It is a nice reminder that HATEOAS was never really dead, just under-marketed.

## Choosing is a strategy decision

The closing framing is the most useful part. Picking an API paradigm is a strategic decision as much as a technical one: look at business goals, data patterns, consumer expectations and scalability needs. His takeaways fit on a sticky note: no single solution fits all, so blend strategies as needed; every model has trade-offs, so evaluate them; start small by finding one pain point, implementing and learning; and tie your architecture to outcomes.

## Who should watch

Integration architects and tech leads deciding whether their next service should be REST, GraphQL or event-first, and anyone who needs a fast primer on the options before a design review. Engineers looking for implementation detail on any single paradigm will want one of the deeper talks below.

Title: Put policy as code into every Jenkins stage, starting in warn mode
Description: Sarathe Krisshnan Jutoo Vijayaraghavan of CGI at Conf42 SRE 2025 on wiring OPA, Conftest and Sentinel checks into Jenkins pipelines from IDE to runtime.
Body:
Most breaches in a DevOps shop don't need a zero-day; they need someone to forget to close a port. At [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), Sarathe Krisshnan Jutoo Vijayaraghavan, a senior consultant at CGI Technologies with 15 years in IT, makes the case for policy as code (PaC) inside Jenkins: write security and compliance rules as versioned code, run them at every pipeline stage, and let the build fail before a misconfiguration ships.

It is a structured, tool-level talk. You get the where (each stage of the lifecycle), the what (Open Policy Agent, Conftest, HashiCorp Sentinel) and a sample Jenkins pipeline, plus the decisions that make PaC livable rather than a wall of red builds.

## Misconfiguration is the threat model

He frames the problem around human error and speed. In infrastructure as code, a small mistake (a public S3 bucket, a forgotten environment variable, a bad firewall rule) replicates across dozens of environments instantly. Manual review can't keep up with modern delivery. The fix is to express the rules in machine-readable form (JSON, YAML, or Rego for OPA), keep them in Git like application code, and run them automatically.

Storing policies in version control is more than hygiene here. It gives auditors who changed what and when, lets you roll a bad policy back, and lets teams propose and review policy changes through pull requests.

## A gate at every stage, not one at the end

The core of the talk walks the lifecycle. At development time, commits are checked for open ports, unencrypted data and non-compliant configs, ideally inside the IDE (VS Code, IntelliJ) so developers see violations before the pipeline does. At build, software composition analysis flags vulnerable libraries, image scans catch containers running as root or with needless open ports, and PaC breaks the build if standards aren't met. At test, SAST, DAST and IAST run, and PaC enforces thresholds such as no critical vulnerabilities. At deploy, Terraform or CloudFormation plans are validated before provisioning. In production, runtime checks and SIEM alerting catch drift such as weak encryption or unauthorized access.

He also puts checks in pull requests, so only compliant code and configs reach the main branch and human reviewers can focus on logic and design.

## Jenkins, because it is already there

Why Jenkins? Mostly because many organisations already run it: plugins for nearly everything, policy checks insertable at any stage, a big community, and no new infrastructure to justify. The sample pipeline is a good template: check out code, run Conftest against the Terraform files, generate a Terraform plan, test the plan against policies again, and only then apply.

The tool roles are clear. OPA is the general-purpose engine with Rego. Conftest specialises in YAML and JSON configs for Kubernetes, Terraform and Helm. Sentinel is built into Terraform, Vault and Consul, so it suits teams already on the HashiCorp stack. Example policies include blocking public S3 buckets, requiring cost-tracking tags on cloud resources, refusing containers that run as root or carry known vulnerabilities, and least-privilege IAM.

## Not every violation should stop the line

The most practical section is on failure handling. Critical issues (a security vulnerability, a compliance breach) stop the pipeline by default. Non-critical ones like code style or minor configuration nits get reported while the pipeline carries on. Failure actions are customisable per policy, which is how you keep security and developer speed on speaking terms.

Compliance reporting closes the loop: automated records of each violation with timestamp, author and the specific policy, which is what GDPR or HIPAA audits ask for. His getting-started advice is the right kind of modest: pick the policies that cover your most common or critical risks, choose tools that fit your stack (OPA for most cases), start in non-production or in warn-only mode before enforcing hard failures, and add policies gradually.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevSecOps engineers running Jenkins who want a concrete map of where policy checks belong. If you are on GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, the stage-by-stage model transfers directly; only the plumbing differs.

Title: Rolling out HSM-backed encryption across 50 Oracle databases
Description: Krishna Anumula of LTIMindtree at Conf42 Golang 2025 on HSM-backed Oracle TDE across 50 databases, with automated key rotation and minimal downtime.
Body:
Encrypting one Oracle database is a change ticket. Encrypting 50 of them, across versions from 11g to 19c, with four teams who each hold part of the keys, is a project. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Krishna Anumula, an Oracle database engineer at LTIMindtree with about 13 years in the field, walked through how his team put hardware security module (HSM) backed Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) on 50-plus databases for a client and automated the rollout down to near-zero downtime.

It is a practitioner's case study from the database side. There is no Go in it, and the value is in the sequence and the cross-team mechanics.

## Why the HSM, not just a wallet file

The databases held customer and personal data, including social security numbers, health insurance details and home addresses. The solution combined an HSM with AES-256 encryption and a key management infrastructure in which the master keys live in tamper-resistant hardware rather than on the database host. Krishna maps it to the regulations the client had to meet: GDPR, PCI DSS for cardholder data, HIPAA for health information and SOX for financial reporting controls.

Alongside encryption, the team masked credit card and personal data when cloning production into non-production, so developers testing on copies never see the real values.

## Patch first, then encrypt

The rollout ran in phases: preparation, configuration, encryption, validation and maintenance. Preparation meant patching every database and upgrading the older ones to 19c before HSM integration was possible. Configuration meant integrating the HSM with Oracle TDE through authenticated channels. Encryption covered tablespaces and sensitive columns. Third-party security experts then tested whether the data could be reached. Maintenance put key rotation on an automated schedule.

The first one or two databases were done by hand; everything after was scripted.

## The hard parts were not the crypto

Krishna's list of challenges is the most useful slide. Legacy versions needed upgrades and patches. Network setup between databases and the HSM required careful routing and certificate-based authentication. Encryption added I/O latency on busy transactional systems, which took buffer and tablespace tuning to fix. Master key backup, restore and disaster recovery needed meticulous planning, because a lost key means lost data.

## One script instead of four people on a call

The manual process needed the database engineer, the HSM team, the CyberArk team, the network team and security all present for hours. The team wrote Python and Bash automation that runs the steps and prompts each team only at its moment, for example to approve a password from their own machine. That turned a three-to-four-hour, all-hands session into one monitored execution.

Key management follows a clear lifecycle: generation in the HSM, distribution to Oracle wallets through automated channels, use by TDE, automated rotation and offline backups, with key copies kept physically in a vault room and refreshed every quarter.

## Results, as reported

Krishna reports that about 150 to 200 terabytes of data are now encrypted, audit time dropped by 30% thanks to centralised key management and cleaner audit trails, and the automation framework cut implementation time by 60%. He also reports query performance improving after the project, which he attributes largely to removing unused and unwanted connections during the work rather than to encryption itself.

## Who should watch

DBAs and security engineers facing a TDE or HSM rollout across a fleet of databases, and anyone coordinating several teams that each hold part of a secret. Next on his list is the newer Oracle release and quarterly rotation with zero downtime.

Title: Catch cloud misconfigurations in the pipeline with IaC scans and OPA
Description: Santosh Bompally of Humana at Conf42 Golang 2025 on shift-left cloud security with IaC scanning in OPA and KICS, native policies and auto-remediation.
Body:
A storage account with public network access and HTTPS-only turned off should never reach the cloud, and with a policy check in CI it doesn't. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Santosh Bompally, Cloud Security Engineering Team Lead at Humana, laid out a layered approach to cloud security posture management (CSPM) and demoed the first layer live: Terraform and Bicep templates with deliberate misconfigurations failing a pipeline scan built on Open Policy Agent rules.

He opens with a disclaimer worth repeating: the material is his own research, not his employer's. The talk is about cloud security practice; Go is the community it was presented to, not the subject.

## Misconfiguration is the customer's side of the bargain

Santosh grounds the talk in the shared responsibility model. Providers secure their part; customers own IAM, encryption and service configuration. He cites the Cloud Security Alliance and Gartner on misconfiguration being the main cause of cloud incidents and largely the customer's fault, and points at the growing size of compliance fines, such as GDPR rules about where certain data may live. With tens or hundreds of services each having settings that change with every release, configuration complexity is the attack surface.

## Four pillars, each catching what the last missed

His model has four layers:

- **IaC scanning** before deployment, with policies wired into the version control system so every merge request is checked.
- **Cloud-native policies** (Azure Policy, GCP organisation policies, AWS organisation policies) for deployments that skip IaC, such as console clicks or a vendor provisioning into your tenant.
- **Runtime remediation** driven by events: a resource change triggers an Azure Function, Lambda or Cloud Function that fixes the drift, followed by a verification step.
- **Compliance monitoring and reporting** that maps posture to standards, prioritises risk and increasingly uses AI for anomaly detection and behavioural analysis.

## The demo: a pipeline that refuses bad templates

The demo app, Insights AI, has Terraform modules and an equivalent Bicep version. The storage module allows public network access, disables HTTPS-only traffic and opens blob access to the world, the kind of settings behind real breaches where exposed keys met open endpoints. The CI stage pulls the Checkmarx KICS image, runs a scan with both built-in and custom policies, prints the results and fails the build.

The custom policies are the interesting bit. For each rule there are positive and negative sample templates showing the misconfigured and expected shape, and the query itself is written in Rego. It checks the storage account attributes and reports which specific resource fails, which matters when a module deploys dozens of them. Developers see exactly what to fix before anything reaches the cloud.

## Why shift left pays for both sides

His argument for doing this in CI is about people as much as risk. Developers get feedback while they can still fix the code themselves, and security teams learn about problems before runtime. The alternative, security forcefully changing resources at runtime, causes drift and sometimes breaks applications.

## Exceptions need a process too

The closing section is mature advice. Pick tools that cover every cloud you actually run, not just the big three. Define which benchmarks are non-negotiable and which can take exceptions. Every exception, whether a missing capability or an accepted risk, needs documented approval from the business, the application owner and security, and must be applied consistently across IaC, proactive, reactive and monitoring layers. He promised a part two on cloud-native controls.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers setting up policy-as-code for Terraform or Bicep, and teams whose cloud findings keep getting fixed by hand after deploy. The demo is short but complete enough to copy the pattern.

Title: Pick distributed architecture patterns for fit, then plan to change them
Description: Ashis Chowdhury of Mastercard at Conf42 SRE 2025 tours microservices, event-driven design, CQRS and service mesh, and the trade-offs each one brings.
Body:
Every distributed architecture pattern buys you something and sends you an invoice. At [Conf42 SRE 2025](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025), Ashis Chowdhury, a Mastercard engineer who introduces himself as a data architect with 23 years in data engineering, walks through the patterns most teams reach for (microservices, event-driven architecture, CQRS and service mesh) and keeps returning to one point: choose by fit for the use case, and expect to revisit the choice as the system matures.

This is a survey talk, and a well-organised one. If you have run a few of these patterns in production, treat it as a checklist. If you are newer to distributed design, it is a tidy map of the territory with the downsides printed next to the upsides.

## Centralised is easy until it is the bottleneck

Chowdhury starts with the contrast that motivates everything else. A centralised system keeps data and compute in one place: simple to maintain and secure, but a single server that can choke when too many users arrive, or take everyone down when it fails. A distributed system spreads data and resources across servers, often across physical sites, so it keeps working when a component dies. The price is more points of interaction, which makes it harder to secure and to administer.

He grounds this in familiar names (Netflix, Amazon, Spotify) and in the terminology most of us already use loosely: client-server, three-tier, service-oriented, microservices.

## Every pattern comes with its own bill

The middle of the talk takes the patterns one by one, and the useful part is that each gets its drawbacks named out loud.

Microservices give independent deployment and scaling, but they need careful orchestration and monitoring, testing the whole as a coherent system is hard, data consistency across independent services is a real problem, and all that chatter between services adds latency.

Event-driven architecture decouples producers from consumers through a broker or event bus, using publish-subscribe. Producers don't need to know who listens; consumers don't need to ask. That buys parallel processing and real-time responsiveness, which is why Chowdhury points to financial transactions, fraud detection, IoT, telecoms and patient monitoring as natural fits. The bill: keeping events in order and the system consistent is complex, and debugging and tracing are harder than in other styles.

CQRS (command and query responsibility segregation) splits writes from reads so each side gets its own optimised model. Chowdhury lists independent scaling, read- or write-optimised schemas, tighter security on who can write, and much simpler read queries. Anyone who has stared at a twelve-way join on a shared model will feel that last one. He is careful to say it doesn't fit every scenario; use it where the design allows.

Service mesh moves service-to-service communication into a dedicated layer: sidecar proxies in the data plane, a control plane for routing rules, load-balancing policy and security settings. You get discovery, traffic management, security and observability. You also get performance overhead, operational effort and a steep learning curve.

## Design for failure, and invest in seeing it

The best-practice list will be familiar to SREs: design for failure from the start, prefer stateless components, CI/CD, fault tolerance, load balancing, domain events and chaos engineering. Scaling gets the usual horizontal versus vertical framing, with a push towards stateless designs.

Two points in the closing takeaways stand out. First, continuous refinement: an architecture chosen today will meet better options as the application grows, and the architect should be anticipating challenges three to four years out. Second, the thing he says comes through most strongly across microservices, event-driven systems and cloud deployment is the need to invest in strong monitoring and observability tooling. Patterns you can't observe are patterns you can't operate.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving from a monolith or a central data platform towards services, and anyone who needs a structured refresher before an architecture review. The talk stays at the concept level, with no code or benchmarks, so senior distributed-systems folks may prefer to skim the drawbacks sections and the takeaways.

Title: Observability 2.0 means one telemetry lake, not five tools
Description: Sivasubramanian Bagavathiappan of GuhaTek at Conf42 SRE 2025 on unified observability with OpenTelemetry, a telemetry data lake and the Grafana LGTM stack.
Body:
If finding the cause of an incident means opening a metrics tool, a tracing tool and a log search side by side and lining up timestamps by eye, you're doing the correlation that your platform should do. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Sivasubramanian Bagavathiappan, SRE leader and co-founder of GuhaTek, which offers SRE as a service, laid out a path from siloed monitoring to a single source of truth built on OpenTelemetry and the Grafana stack.

It's an architecture talk with a clear reference design. Good for teams planning a consolidation, less so for those who want a live demo.

## Observability 1.0 had the signals, not the connections

Siva first lists what the classic era already collected: metrics as time series, traces for call-tree views of latency and errors, logs, profiling (now viable in production with continuous profiling via eBPF), real user monitoring and APM runtime views such as JVM heap or goroutine counts.

The problem is the shape. Each signal came from its own tool and agent, analysis was reactive and after the fact, and correlation was manual. Miss instrumenting one layer and that component becomes a black box during the next incident.

## What 2.0 adds

The upgrade is context and structure:

- **Traces with context**: parent-child relationships and business attributes, so you can pull the trace for one user's order.
- **Events**: structured key-value records of critical changes, replacing unstructured logs for correlation.
- **User experience monitoring**: frame render times, app start time, crashes.
- **Data stream visibility** for Kafka-heavy and IoT systems.
- **Business metrics** such as conversion rates and checkout drop-offs.
- **Composite alarms** that combine failing layers into one alert and cut alert noise.

His observability funnel ties these together. Infrastructure at the bottom, then data stores, middleware and connectors (circuit breakers, retries), APIs with golden signals, customer journeys, and business outcomes at the top. When the business number drops, you trace it down to a technical layer.

## The reference architecture

Instrumented systems send signals to a collector, which feeds a data pipeline that adds context such as cluster name, masks PII and converts formats. Everything lands in an enterprise telemetry data lake, the single source of truth for metrics, traces, logs, events, profiles and front-end data. From there you get one view, composite alerts, synthetics, SLO tracking, and a clean dataset for ML models.

## OpenTelemetry in, Grafana out

OpenTelemetry provides the vendor-neutral standard, with auto-instrumentation for common languages such as Go, Java and Python that captures HTTP and gRPC calls with a few lines of configuration. Business metrics and custom spans still need SDK code. Collectors process and forward the data, and custom attributes like an order ID let you filter traces down to one customer.

Grafana handles visualisation, with prebuilt JSON dashboards for Kafka, Kubernetes and Linux. The full stack he describes is the LGTM set: Loki for logs, Grafana, Tempo for traces and Mimir for metrics, with Pyroscope for continuous profiling and collection via Prometheus exporters, OpenTelemetry and Fluent Bit. On top: service maps from traces, alerting, on-call, incident tracking, SLOs, and load and browser testing. If you'd rather not run the storage yourself, the collection layer can ship to commercial backends.

Alerting closes the loop. Composite, rule-based alerts across data sources trigger webhooks into workflows that walk service maps and knowledge graphs for automated root cause analysis.

## Who should watch

Teams paying for several monitoring tools that don't talk to each other, and anyone designing a telemetry pipeline on open standards. Experienced Grafana operators will know the stack; the funnel idea is the part to borrow.
