Title: Cloud data engineering, from four-week servers to autoscaling pipelines
Description: Sai Sravan Gudipati at Conf42 Golang 2025 on what cloud data engineering changes, from IaC and autoscaling pipelines to storage tiering and edge.
Body:
Procuring a Linux server used to take four to eight weeks of tickets and humans; now a reviewed config file builds it. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Sai Sravan Gudipati used that contrast as the opening move in a broad tour of cloud data engineering: infrastructure as code, modern data pipelines, elastic scaling, MLOps, cloud security, storage tiering and edge computing, ending with a migration roadmap.

It is a wide survey rather than a narrow technical talk, and despite the title, Go does not come up in the recording. Treat it as a primer on how the cloud reshapes data platforms.

## Data volume is the forcing function

Sai starts with scale: he cites roughly 463 million terabytes of data generated globally and a cloud computing market projected to reach about 2.84 trillion dollars by 2030. The examples are familiar: Netflix personalising content for millions of users on cloud infrastructure, healthcare organisations running analytics on patient records, and banks such as Capital One using cloud services for real-time fraud detection and transaction processing.

## Infrastructure as code turned weeks into a pull request

The IaC section is the most grounded part. Terraform and AWS CloudFormation replace manual provisioning, cut configuration errors and make disaster recovery repeatable. Mistakes in code still happen, so peer review and automated checks catch them before deploy. Sai describes his own organisation's version: the infrastructure code already exists, an engineer submits a small definition file, and a server appears. A ticket queue has never been so quiet.

## A pipeline that scales to the spike

His worked pipeline uses Snowflake on AWS. Several applications drop files in different formats (CSV, XML, JSON) into an S3 bucket; ingestion picks them up in near real time; transformations apply the business logic; data moves to cheaper storage tiers when it goes stale; and dashboards in tools such as Power BI consume the result. The point he keeps returning to is elasticity: warehouses and instances scale up from extra small to extra large for a sudden surge of users and scale back down, so nobody buys idle servers for a peak that happens twice a year.

## Storage needs retention rules, not just disks

On-prem storage tends to keep stale data forever because no one owns the clean-up. In the cloud, auto-tiering and retention policies move rarely used data to archive classes such as Glacier, with the trade-off of slower access. Sai shows that combining tiering, compression and smart placement cuts cost by about 30% compared with traditional storage.

## Security, MLOps and the edge

Three shorter sections round it out. MLOps on cloud platforms covers model development, CI with automated testing, deployment through test and production environments, and monitoring for drift. Security combines AI-driven threat detection, zero trust with continuous multi-factor verification, and compliance automation, which matters for firms that report to regulators. Edge computing keeps processing near the user for latency around 15 milliseconds, which is what time-critical work such as card transactions needs.

## A four-step migration roadmap

He closes with a path for legacy applications: assess the current data architecture through stakeholder interviews and system audits; develop a strategy and cost estimate; implement with cross-functional teams and DevOps practices; and track value realisation against what the old setup cost.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers new to cloud data platforms who want the whole map in one sitting. Experienced data engineers will know the pieces; the talk is a good one to send a stakeholder before a migration kick-off.

Title: A decade on Amazon RDS as a non-DBA, and what broke
Description: Renato Losio of Funambol at Conf42 SRE 2025 on storage autoscaling traps, backup costs, Graviton crashes, blue-green surprises and cold replicas on RDS.
Body:
Managed databases are managed right up until the moment an ALTER TABLE triggers storage autoscaling and eats the IOPS you needed to finish it. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Renato Losio, Principal Cloud Architect at Funambol, shared lessons from running production databases on Amazon RDS since 2011 without being a DBA, most of them learned through AWS support tickets.

This is the best kind of experience talk: specific failures, the reason behind each, and what he does differently now. If you run MySQL on RDS or Aurora, budget the full half hour.

## Why a Java developer picked RDS

Renato started as a Java developer who could install MySQL but had no idea how to run failover or replicas. Multi-AZ was the hook: one endpoint, and AWS handles replication, failover and backups. Back then RDS offered MySQL 5.1, magnetic storage and little else. Today's choice of engines, storage classes and instance families is better and cheaper, which leads to his first lesson: keep iterating. If your database deployment hasn't changed in two or three years, you're probably missing savings.

His second lesson is to use AWS support as a design review. Before a storage change that is slow or hard to revert, write the plan down and ask support what could go wrong.

## Storage autoscaling during an optimize is a trap

His most painful example: running OPTIMIZE or a copying ALTER TABLE on a large table pushed free storage below the threshold, autoscaling kicked in and added terabytes he didn't need, and the storage operation competed for IOPS with the very job that triggered it. Shrinking storage back is hard. Lesson: disable autoscaling before heavy schema work, and remember the table copy needs free space roughly the size of the table, plus binary logs if a replica is paused.

He covers three ways to make the change: directly on the primary, on a replica with replication paused and then swapped, or with RDS Blue/Green deployments. Tools like Percona's pt-online-schema-change help control the load.

## CPU is overrated, backups are not

A cost chart from one of his production databases shows backup costs almost matching CPU. RDS backups are incremental, but if writes are scattered across a fragmented table, each increment is large. Optimising tables cut the backup bill noticeably, in his example on the order of a couple of thousand euros a month.

## Graviton is transparent until your parameter group isn't

Moving from Intel to Graviton on RDS is a console switch, and he adopted early. Then an instance crashed. Beyond a bug, the real cause was memory: tuning such as an aggressive InnoDB buffer pool had been set for Intel instance memory ratios, and his own CloudWatch-driven autoscaling logic ran out of memory before it could scale. Lesson: don't over-tune the parameter group for short-term gain, and keep memory settings relative to the instance class.

## Smaller traps worth knowing

- **Aurora migration via replica** requires Aurora to support your MySQL minor version, which lags community releases. Stay on a minor Aurora supports if you want that escape hatch.
- **gp3 vs gp2**: same price; gp3 gives 12,000 IOPS above 400 GB and lets you tune throughput separately. Prefer io2 over io1 at the same price, and watch out for staging copies inheriting provisioned IOPS.
- **Blue/Green** loses Performance Insights history from the old instance, and backups of the retired instance follow their own retention clock.
- **New replicas start cold.** Data loads lazily from S3, lag can take hours or days to reach zero, and switching to a cold instance gave him hours of degraded performance.

## Benchmarks lie

His closing experiment inserts rows one at a time from a stored function. RDS MySQL took 5 minutes 49 seconds; Aurora took 2.7 seconds, purely from the storage layer. MariaDB matched MySQL, and io2 Block Express more than halved the io1 time. His point is that you can get wild results from simple benchmarks, so ask who ran one and what they want to sell you.

## Who should watch

Anyone running RDS or Aurora in production, especially without a dedicated DBA. Expect to leave with a checklist.

Title: Hybrid object storage works when tiering is automatic
Description: Venkatachala Nivas Chainuru at Conf42 Golang 2025 on hybrid object storage across on-prem and cloud, with policy-driven tiering and a finance case study.
Body:
The cheapest byte is the one sitting on the right tier, and nobody should have to move it there by hand. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Venkatachala Nivas Chainuru, a senior infrastructure engineer, explained how hybrid object storage spans on-premises hardware and multiple clouds behind one API, and why an orchestration layer that tiers data automatically is what makes the economics work.

This is an infrastructure strategy talk aimed at storage and platform teams, with no Go code in it.

## Unstructured data broke the old storage model

The starting point is the growth of unstructured data: video, images and IoT sensor readings from social media, healthcare and finance. Object storage handles large volumes of it more efficiently than file or block storage, and a hybrid design lets data live on-prem or in several clouds while applications see a single repository through industry-standard APIs.

## Four layers, one brain

His architecture has four layers. The management layer is the front end for the whole estate. The application layer is the user-facing services and APIs. The storage layer is the physical back end, local and cloud. The orchestration layer is the core: it reads metadata, access patterns, performance needs and cost parameters, then moves data between tiers on its own.

The tiers are hot (mission-critical, on-prem flash or fast SSD), warm (less frequent but still needed), cold (historical and reporting data in the cloud) and archive (long retention for regulators, typical in healthcare and finance).

## Cost optimisation is a loop, not a project

The cost advice is concrete: analyse the data lifecycle and access patterns, put hot data on fast storage and cold data on cheap storage, automate the moves with tiering policies, keep monitoring and adjust placement, and choose cloud tiers and regions with cost in mind. He reports that organisations using these strategies see 30% or greater reductions in cloud storage spend. On-prem hardware then only has to serve latency-sensitive work, which stretches the investment.

## Compliance is the reason hybrid exists

Regulation is why many teams cannot go all-cloud. A unified API layer lets sensitive workloads stay on-prem while less regulated data takes advantage of cloud pricing, with consistent data sovereignty, retention, encryption and audit trails across both.

## Start small, test the failover

The implementation path is a sensible checklist: assess the environment and compliance needs, design a blueprint with tiers and integration points, write automated tiering and governance policies, then deploy and test, including failover, data recovery and your RPO and RTO targets. Start with non-critical workloads and move sensitive ones later.

## A financial services case study

The worked example is a financial firm with five petabytes of growing data, an infrastructure it could not afford to scale, and regulations that pinned some data on-prem. It put active trading data and customer records on on-prem flash, sent historical and long-retention data to the cloud, and added intelligent tiering with consistent policy enforcement. Reported results: about 30% lower storage cost in the first year, around 35% better analytics performance, 40% less storage management overhead and 60% faster new application deployments.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure and storage engineers planning a hybrid estate, and anyone who has to justify a storage budget to finance and compliance at the same time. Cloud-only teams will find the tiering section useful on its own.

Title: Inside Aurora DSQL, where latency is paid only at commit
Description: Samuel Baruffi of AWS at Conf42 SRE 2025 explains Aurora DSQL internals, from Firecracker query processors to adjudicators, journals and witness regions.
Body:
A multi-region, active-active relational database usually means paying cross-region latency on every statement. Amazon Aurora DSQL pays it once, at commit. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Samuel Baruffi, Principal Global Solutions Architect at AWS, took the service apart component by component to show how optimistic concurrency, synchronised clocks and a replicated journal make that possible.

This is an AWS architect explaining an AWS product, announced at re:Invent in December 2024 and in public preview when he recorded. It's also a genuinely good distributed-systems lesson, because he spends most of the time on how it works rather than why to buy it.

## What problem it's aimed at

Samuel starts with the limits of a traditional Postgres box: one server caps capacity, a single instance hurts availability, read replicas help but are fiddly, and patching and tuning cost engineering time. DSQL is serverless and Postgres-compatible, scales reads, writes, compute and storage independently, and has no servers to patch.

## Single region or linked regions

A single-region cluster runs active across three availability zones, with compute, transaction logs and storage replicated independently, for 99.99% availability. A multi-region cluster offers 99.999%: two linked regions, each with its own endpoint, as equal peers with no leader. Reads stay local; writes replicate synchronously at commit, so RPO is zero. A third witness region holds only a copy of the journal so there is always a quorum, and has no endpoint.

## Follow a pizza order through the system

The components are a front end, query processors, adjudicators, a journal, a crossbar and storage. Samuel's example is a user ordering pizza in Virginia.

A read (select restaurants with rating 4) goes from the front end to a query processor, which takes a start time from the Amazon Time Sync Service, using GPS and atomic clock references so regions agree on time. It looks up the shard map and reads straight from storage. No adjudicator, no journal.

A read-write transaction (pick a restaurant, pick an item, insert the order) takes a snapshot at its start time. Every read and write then happens inside the query processor, which buffers writes in a private workspace and lets you read your own writes. Nothing touches storage, and nothing crosses regions, until commit. Then cross-region latency applies once: tens of milliseconds for nearby regions, a hundred or more for distant ones.

## Query processors are Firecracker microVMs

The query processor runs Postgres inside a Firecracker microVM, the same open-source technology built for Lambda in 2018, on bare metal hosts. Each transaction gets its own, so the fleet scales from zero to very large numbers as load demands. Isolation is snapshot isolation.

## The adjudicator decides who wins

At commit, the query processor sends the adjudicator its write set and start time, essentially asking it to pick a commit time if nobody else has written those keys since. If two transactions modified the same row, the first to commit wins and the second is aborted, and the application must retry. Transactions touching different rows, say item 93 and item 97, both commit. The result is no deadlocks, but your code needs retry logic, which is the practical takeaway for anyone building on it.

Durability lives in the journal, not storage. A transaction counts as committed once the journal acknowledges it; the crossbar uses the journal's ordering to apply updates to storage in sequence, even across several journals.

## When a region goes down

If one linked region fails, adjudicator leadership for its keys moves to the healthy region, the journal remains durable across the surviving region and the witness, and the healthy endpoint keeps serving reads and writes. You move traffic yourself, by switching endpoints or with Route 53 health-checked routing. You can place the witness between distant regions to optimise latency.

## Who should watch

Anyone evaluating distributed SQL, and engineers who like to know what happens between BEGIN and COMMIT. The adjudicator section alone is worth it.

Title: Timing ECOs that stop creating new violations
Description: Puneet Gupta of Block at Conf42 Golang 2025 on slack-aware post-routing cell legalisation, so chip timing fixes stop spawning fresh violations.
Body:
Every chip designer knows the loop: apply a timing fix, the tool legalises the new cell somewhere far away, the new wire creates a fresh violation, repeat. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Puneet Gupta, Principal ASIC Physical Design Engineer at Block, presented a slack-aware approach to post-routing cell legalisation that orders which cells may move by how critical their timing is, so an engineering change order (ECO) fixes what it was meant to fix and nothing else breaks.

To be clear about scope: this is a physical design talk about place and route, not about the Go language. If you write Go for a living, it is an unusually clear look at a very different kind of optimisation problem.

## Why the default legaliser hurts

ECOs arrive from many places: timing closure in scenarios the place-and-route run did not cover, logic fixes from design verification, and DRC or LVS clean-up. To insert a buffer or upsize a cell in a dense area, neighbouring cells must move. Puneet's point is that conventional legalisation works on net length and free space, not slack. It shoves cells wherever there is room, and in congested regions that can be far from the driver, so the new route causes setup or hold violations, sometimes through crosstalk.

## Sort cells by slack, then move the safe ones first

The method has a clear sequence:

1. Run full timing analysis around the ECO area.
2. Tag every nearby cell with its slack and filter.
3. Fix the critical cells in place.
4. Legalise the unfixed cells with relative placement: shift the neighbour by a track first, then the cell, so everything moves together.
5. Refine iteratively, updating timing only for the affected cells, until timing is clean.

He groups cells into four tiers. Most critical (flops, typically) are hard-fixed and only nudged for DRC. Moderately critical cells, like a three-input AND driving several critical loads, are also hard-fixed at first. Minor negative-slack cells are soft-fixed, and non-critical cells move freely. Legalisation then works from the least critical tier upwards. Because the most critical paths are never disturbed first, the process does not generate new violations.

## The results he reports

On a 7-nanometre mobile SoC and on dense CPU, GPU and neural network accelerator designs, Puneet reports worst negative slack improving by 15%, ECO cycle time down by 40 to 50% because fixes stop spawning new ones, fewer ECOs overall (about half), and less congestion in the ECO regions. The runtime cost stays low because only selected cells are legalised and timing updates are incremental.

## It slots into existing flows

The implementation is practical: Tcl scripts that report slack per cell, write the list to CSV, sort it, and feed it back into the tool, which already has the needed commands. That means no new EDA product, just a smarter order of operations. He also sees room to extend the same idea to power and area targets.

## Who should watch

Physical design and timing closure engineers on advanced nodes, especially anyone fighting high-utilisation blocks. Software engineers curious about how much of chip design is really a scheduling problem will enjoy it too. People expecting Go content should pick another session.

Title: University ERPs need error budgets that follow the semester
Description: Sanjiv Bhagat at Conf42 SRE 2025 on semester-aware SLOs, chaos game days and immutable infrastructure for cloud ERP systems in higher education.
Body:
Most systems have a peak season. University ERPs have one with a calendar printed on it: registration week, financial aid disbursement, grade submission. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Sanjiv Bhagat, a program manager with 21 years of project experience including higher-education work, showed how SRE practices turned fragmented campus ERPs into cloud systems that hold up through those peaks, with SLOs and error budgets that change across the semester.

The talk is a reference architecture from real implementations. Lots of named tools, few code samples.

## The headline numbers

Sanjiv puts two results up front: 99.99% uptime during peak registration periods and 78% fewer security incidents. The starting point was the usual campus mess of siloed departmental systems, legacy databases that don't share data across campuses, and plenty of sensitive student and staff data to protect.

## SLOs written for the academic year

This is the idea worth stealing. Instead of one SLO for all seasons, the targets track the calendar:

- **Student portal**: 99.99% uptime during registration with a 500 ms response time objective, and looser thresholds off-peak to save cost.
- **Financial systems**: 99.999% transaction consistency using two-phase commit, prioritised during disbursement cycles with dedicated resources.
- **Faculty services**: grade submission and course management at 1.5 seconds maximum response time and 99.9% availability, extended during non-teaching periods.

Error budgets vary through the semester as well. Quiet weeks allow more experimental deployments; critical academic events get strict change freezes. Dashboards show the remaining budget in real time and drive deployment and maintenance decisions. Anyone who has watched a Friday deploy meet Monday traffic will see the appeal of a calendar that says no for you.

## Architecture built for spikes

The platform is containerised microservices on Kubernetes with automated scaling policies, Istio for traffic management with encrypted east-west traffic, and zero-trust network policies with identity verification. Splitting the monolith let registration and financial aid scale independently when their season arrives, with automatic failover keeping services up when a primary has trouble.

An API gateway does a lot of work. It translates protocols for legacy systems, uses circuit breakers so a failing legacy component degrades gracefully instead of taking everything down, handles SAML federation with research institutions alongside OAuth, and applies rate limiting with fair scheduling so course registration gets priority. Canary deployments and A/B routing let modernisation happen incrementally while the old and new systems coexist.

## Observability that measures students, not just servers

The observability stack is Prometheus with education-specific gauges, a centralised ELK stack with PII-aware filtering, PagerDuty with role-based escalation, and Jaeger for distributed tracing. The detail that matters is the custom instrumentation: registration completion rates and form submission success alongside the technical metrics, plus monitoring of federated identity providers with alerts when single sign-on latency crosses a threshold.

## Break it on purpose, in the quiet weeks

Chaos engineering runs as game days with cross-functional teams during maintenance windows, automated fault injection during non-critical periods, and quarterly resilience tests that grow in complexity. Experiments simulate database loss during registration, identity provider outages and network partitions between services, and every experiment ends with updated runbooks.

Remediation is tiered. Level one fixes run automatically; levels two and three need progressively more approval. ML-based anomaly detection triggers playbooks from pod restarts to database failovers, which he credits with a 65% drop in MTTR.

Infrastructure is immutable: Terraform modules, Packer pipelines building hardened images with monitoring baked in, compliance and vulnerability scans in CI/CD, and blue-green deployments with automated rollback. Security as code uses OPA guardrails, Vault for dynamic credentials, and automated evidence collection for FERPA, GLBA and NIST 800-171.

## Who should watch

Anyone running systems with predictable, brutal peaks, which covers far more than universities. If you only take one thing, take the calendar-aware error budget.

Title: From Codd to ScyllaDB, every database step is a trade-off
Description: Andrei Manakov of ShareChat at Conf42 SRE 2025 on CAP, PACELC, replication, sharding, tunable consistency and when relational is still the right call.
Body:
If you serve a thousand requests a second, Andrei Manakov's advice is to use a relational database and stop reading about CAP. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Andrei, Senior Staff Software Engineer at ShareChat working on ML infrastructure, walked through the history of databases from hierarchical stores to NoSQL and distributed SQL, and showed that every step up the scaling ladder buys capacity by giving up something specific.

It's a clear, well-ordered tour that works as a refresher for experienced engineers and a map for anyone choosing a datastore for the first time.

## The ladder before you distribute

Andrei starts with the hierarchical databases that preceded Codd's relational model, where apps were coupled to physical storage and renaming a field could break everything. Codd's model gave a formal foundation in set theory and logic, then SQL, ACID transactions and normalisation followed.

When internet-scale load arrived, teams climbed a ladder of cheaper fixes first:

- **Vertical scaling**: bigger box, same architecture, a hard ceiling.
- **Split by domain**: separate databases for loosely coupled areas, no distributed transactions needed.
- **Denormalise**: accept copies of data and skip transactions where losing a like on a post in a failure is fine.
- **Local caching**: fast reads in app memory, at the cost of stale data.

None of those get you past one server's limit of cores and memory. Distribution does, and that's where the theory bites.

## CAP is for bad days, PACELC is for every day

He explains CAP plainly: during a network partition, you choose between consistency and availability. Single-instance Postgres or MySQL is the classic case that simply assumes no partitions. The more useful model is PACELC, which adds that even with a healthy network you trade latency against consistency, because strong consistency means waiting for replicas to acknowledge.

Asked when to use a relational database, he answers almost always, unless the load is extreme. Add mirroring or replicas so it isn't a single point of failure, and you keep transactions, consistency and normalisation without thinking about CAP at all.

## Replication, sharding and the price of each

Read replicas give near-unlimited read scaling but introduce replication lag, so a user can write to the primary and read stale data from a replica, and writes still bottleneck on one primary. Sharding scales writes too, using hash-based, lookup-table, geographic or domain keys, but a failed shard makes part of the data unavailable, cross-shard transactions disappear, and a simple count becomes hard.

NoSQL flips the design process: start from the queries the app will run and model data to serve them. Distributed transactions with two-phase commit or Paxos and Raft are possible but slow, block on the slowest participant, and get stuck when the coordinator fails at the wrong moment. Distributed SQL tries to keep the familiar interface and transactions while sharding automatically, but schema design matters as much as ever, because joins across shards are slow.

## Tunable consistency, shown on ScyllaDB

The practical section uses Redis and ScyllaDB. Redis Cluster with sharding but no replicas favours consistency; add replicas and reads may be stale but availability improves. ScyllaDB, inspired by Cassandra, lets you set consistency per query: ALL waits for every replica (strong, slow, fails on any partition), ONE returns after a single ack (fast, possibly stale), and QUORUM waits for a majority as the middle ground. ALL is for payments and bank transfers; ONE suits feeds, ads and analytics.

He finishes with storage engines (B-trees for read-heavy work, LSM trees with bloom filters for write-heavy) and the trend of rewriting proven databases in C++ with a thread-per-core, shared-nothing design that removes lock contention.

## Who should watch

Engineers picking a database for a new service, and SREs who want a shared vocabulary with their data teams. The core message: there's no perfect database, only one that fits your trade-offs.

Title: Merge the network and security teams before the tools
Description: Senior product manager Sharanya Prasad at Conf42 SRE 2025 on converging networking and security with SDN, SASE and zero trust, and why people and process come first.
Body:
When ransomware starts moving sideways through a network, the time lost between the network team noticing and the security team acting is time the attacker keeps. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Sharanya Prasad, a Senior Product Manager, argued for converging networking and security into one practice, built on software-defined networking, SASE and zero trust, and made the case that the convergence is mostly about people and process.

It's a strategy talk from a product manager's seat: frameworks, a case study and a roadmap rather than configs.

## Why bother converging

Sharanya's numbers frame the payoff: organisations with unified networking and security see a 15% reduction in breach costs, per the research she cites, along with faster containment and better incident management. Her ransomware example shows the mechanism. An integrated setup can segment the threat automatically, alert the right teams and block lateral movement, where siloed tools would need a human handoff at each step.

## Three technologies doing the heavy lifting

- **Software-defined networking** makes the network programmable, so it scales and adapts like the rest of your infrastructure. Her image: moving from a static road map to real-time traffic control.
- **SASE** (secure access service edge) puts networking and security together in the cloud, protecting users and apps at the edge without backhauling traffic to a data centre for inspection.
- **Zero trust** trusts nobody by default. Every user, device and request is verified each time, posture is tracked continuously, and policies are reapplied when posture changes.

She also points to strong market growth for security service edge, driven by hybrid work and cloud adoption.

## The pyramid: tools are only the second step

The most useful slide is a maturity pyramid. At the base, siloed operations: separate teams, separate tools, separate goals, and the blind spots and delays that come with them. Next, common tools, so both teams work from the same data. Then aligned processes, harmonised workflows, handoffs and incident response, which removes the finger-pointing. At the top, integrated teams that operate as one.

Her conclusion is that true convergence is about people and processes more than any product, which is a refreshing thing to hear from a vendor's product manager.

## AI as the fast path from alert to action

AI shows up as a four-stage loop. Detection scans traffic and behaviour for anomalies, analysis with machine learning filters noise and cuts false positives, response isolates devices or blocks traffic within seconds or escalates to a human, and adaptation retrains models and playbooks after each incident.

## What gets in the way

Sharanya is direct about the obstacles:

- **Skills.** Only 24% of IT professionals are proficient in both networking and security, by her figures.
- **Legacy systems.** Old infrastructure wasn't built to integrate with modern security frameworks. Her line about retrofitting a jet engine onto a propeller plane lands.
- **Organisational resistance.** Teams with their own priorities and tools need change management and executive sponsorship, not just a migration plan.

For cloud-native environments, identity becomes the control plane, security is distributed to every access point including east-west traffic, and protection is designed into the network architecture with microsegmentation, service meshes and cloud-native firewalls.

## A bank and a roadmap

The case study is a global bank whose real bottleneck was response, not threats. It rolled out a SASE framework with integrated SD-WAN and stood up a joint network operations center for both teams. Detection time dropped from hours to minutes, and redundant tools were retired.

Her roadmap: assess the current state and overlaps, define a unified framework with governance and roles, pilot in a controlled environment, then roll out fully with a continuous improvement loop. Start small, measure, expand.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform leads whose incident timelines include a handoff to a separate security team, and managers planning a SASE or zero-trust programme. Hands-on network engineers will want a deeper technical follow-up.

Title: Go for real-time NLP pipelines, and where Python still wins
Description: Sunil Kumar Mudusu of Church Mutual Insurance Company at Conf42 Golang 2025 on Go for real-time NLP with goroutines, Kafka and TensorFlow's Go API.
Body:
Python owns NLP research, but a chatbot or spam filter in production lives or dies on latency and throughput. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Sunil Kumar Mudusu, Lead AI Engineer and Data Engineer at Church Mutual Insurance Company, argued that Go is a strong choice for the real-time part of the text pipeline: goroutines for parallel processing, Kafka for streaming input, and the TensorFlow Go API to serve pre-trained models.

The session is listed as a talk about data transformation in AI workflows; the recording itself focuses on real-time NLP. It is short, about six minutes, and works as a survey.

## Why real-time NLP is a systems problem

Sunil opens with the three pressures on real-time NLP: latency, scalability and efficiency. Go's answers are its compiled speed, built-in concurrency, ability to scale and small memory footprint. None of these make a model smarter; they make the plumbing around the model cheaper and faster.

## The Go NLP toolbox is small but real

He names the libraries to know: spaGO, prose for classic NLP tasks, the TensorFlow Go API for running trained models, and Kafka clients for streaming. The use cases he lists are the familiar ones: chatbots and assistants, sentiment analysis, real-time stream processing with Kafka, spam filtering and content moderation, and speech-to-text pipelines.

## Goroutines plus Kafka is the pattern

The architecture idea is simple. Kafka delivers text messages as a stream; Go consumers fan them out to goroutines connected by channels so many documents get tokenised, classified or scored in parallel; the low memory use lets the service keep up with high throughput without falling over. Pre-trained models are loaded through the TensorFlow Go API and run inside that same pipeline, so the Go service does not need to call out to a separate Python server for every message.

## An honest comparison with Python

The comparison slide is the best part because it does not oversell. Go is faster, handles concurrency better, uses less memory and scales more easily. Python has many more NLP libraries, and Go has fewer options. Sunil's conclusion is that Go's ecosystem for NLP is still maturing, and the limitation will only go away with more library development and community growth.

In practice that suggests a split many teams already use: research and training in Python, high-volume inference and preprocessing in Go.

## Who should watch

Go developers who have been asked to put text classification or sentiment analysis behind a streaming system, and data engineers weighing Go for preprocessing. It is a quick overview with a code slide on goroutines for parallel NLP rather than a full tutorial, so plan to read the library docs afterwards.

Title: What Red Bull's 20-minute car rebuild teaches incident response
Description: Ricardo Castro (FanDuel / Blip.pt) at Conf42 SRE 2025 uses Red Bull's repair of Max Verstappen's crashed car in Hungary to teach incident management.
Body:
Max Verstappen crashed his Red Bull into the barrier on the way to the grid, and the team had about 20 minutes to make it raceable. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Ricardo Castro, Principal Engineer for SRE at FanDuel / Blip.pt, replayed that 2020 Hungarian Grand Prix incident clip by clip and pulled out the incident-management lessons software teams can copy.

It's a short, story-driven talk, and the most watchable entry in the SRE 2025 lineup if you want to explain incident response to someone who has never held a pager.

## Decide fast with a broken picture

The setup: wet track, formation lap, Max locks up while warming his tyres and hits the wall. A timer on the broadcast shows under 23 minutes left. Red Bull must choose between the pit lane, where every tool and part lives but Max starts last, and fixing the car on the grid, which means carrying the garage out there. No mechanic has seen the damage yet; they have telemetry and Max's description of a likely broken suspension.

They pick the grid. Ricardo's lesson is to act decisively without the full picture, to stop a small problem from becoming a big outage, and to accept that some of those calls will be suboptimal or plain wrong. Protect customers, revenue and trust first, and get comfortable with the discomfort.

## Calm voices, clear process

The next clips are mechanics asking for tools and parts. Nobody shouts. Who is doing what is spoken out loud. When an engineer asks for a front wing, the person coordinating points them back to the process.

Ricardo turns this into three practices:

- **Clear communication**: the right information to the right people at the right time, which prevents confusion and keeps stakeholders in the loop.
- **Clear processes**: predefined steps, planned and rehearsed before the incident, so response is fast and consistent.
- **Teamwork**: different skills on one problem, shared responsibility, no single hero.

The calmness clip is the best one. With under seven minutes left, Red Bull's Jonathan Wheatley asks for updates without raising his voice, knowing the car will be driven at over 300 km/h under heavy g-forces. Ricardo's takeaway is that calm teams make better decisions, and that toughness is trained through game days and chaos engineering, not discovered on the day.

## Skills you sharpen before you need them

Early in the incident, Red Bull concludes it has to do the repair faster than it ever has. That only works with deep technical proficiency, so the talk argues for teams that know their systems well and have the tools to act. Knowledge is the difference between a guess and a fix.

## Start with postmortems

The final lesson is the one Ricardo would begin with. F1 teams are known for brutal postmortems, run after good races as well as bad ones, and Mercedes-AMG publishes some of its own. He argues for blameless postmortems that dig for why, not just what, and use each incident to change process. Postmortems, he says, build the other capabilities over time, because every one is a lesson the team keeps.

The ending writes itself: the car was fixed in time and Max went from seventh on the grid to second at the finish.

## Who should watch

Incident commanders, new on-call engineers, and managers who need a ten-minute story to explain why process and calm matter. F1 fans get a bonus; non-fans won't be lost.

Title: Kubernetes plus ML models that scale before the spike lands
Description: Nikhil Kassetty of Intuit at Conf42 SRE 2025 on pairing Kubernetes with LSTM forecasting, isolation forests and RL placement for availability and low latency.
Body:
Reactive autoscaling has a built-in delay: by the time CPU spikes and the scaler reacts, users already feel the lag. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Nikhil Kassetty, a software engineer at Intuit working across cloud, AI and fintech, made the case for layering machine learning models on top of Kubernetes so the cluster scales, places workloads and fails over on predictions instead of alarms.

It's a short architecture talk with a clear structure. Expect a model zoo and a set of results, not a code walkthrough.

## Kubernetes is the muscle

Nikhil starts with what Kubernetes already gives you: autoscaling, self-healing when a container crashes, rolling updates without downtime, service discovery and load balancing, affinity rules to place pods on the right nodes, and security policies with resource limits as guardrails. His complaint is that all of it is reactive. Alerts fire, logs get read, users complain, then things get fixed.

## The brain: four models, four jobs

The architecture adds three layers. Live metrics and logs from the cluster (CPU, memory, pod status, traffic) feed an ML layer, which feeds a decision engine that triggers scaling, moves workloads or raises alerts, and learns from each decision. The models are specific:

- **LSTM** for forecasting resource spikes, so scale-up happens before load arrives.
- **Isolation forest** for anomaly detection, aimed at things like cryptojacking and container escapes.
- **PPO reinforcement learning** for workload placement, which he says improved resource usage by 18%, a number he defends as big at cluster scale.
- **Random forest** for predicting which components are likely to fail.

The pitch for forecasting is simple: scale up or down proactively, respond in sub-second time, and avoid over-provisioning at the same time.

## Security is an availability feature

Nikhil argues that security threats are what bring systems down fastest, so detection belongs in the reliability stack. Behavioural detection watches containers and pods for crypto mining, privilege escalation and odd file access. API monitoring flags deviations in how internal and external APIs are called. Network anomaly detection looks for exfiltration and DDoS patterns with a low false-positive rate. In his setup, threats are mitigated in under three seconds.

## Recovery plans written on the spot

The disaster recovery section replaces static playbooks with generated ones. The system scans for early warnings such as disk issues, memory leaks and degraded node health, a risk engine scores them, and a recovery plan is produced for the live cluster state. Failover runs on demand or automatically, with an RTO under 15 minutes and, thanks to real-time replication, an RPO under five minutes.

The results slide spans industries: an e-commerce platform cutting infrastructure costs by 31% at 99.99% uptime, a financial services deployment reducing incidents by 45%, IoT edge workloads cutting data transfer costs by 40%, and pharma supply chains kept stable during disruption.

He ends on autonomy: AI agents making live infrastructure decisions, explainable AI so every scaling or blocking action is traceable, and federated learning across clusters. Engineers move from operators to strategists, writing training data instead of rules.

## Who should watch

Platform teams curious about predictive autoscaling and ML-driven anomaly detection on Kubernetes. It is light on implementation detail, so treat it as a map of which model fits which job and go deeper from there.

Title: Migrating a monolithic SaaS to Go on AWS Lambda, one slice at a time
Description: Srikar Kompella of Prime Video & Amazon Studios at Conf42 Golang 2025 on moving a monolith to serverless Go on AWS with the strangler pattern.
Body:
On AWS Lambda you pay for every millisecond your function runs, so a language that starts fast and runs lean shows up straight on the bill. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Srikar Kompella, a senior software engineer at Prime Video & Amazon Studios, combined that argument for Go with a full playbook for breaking a monolithic SaaS into serverless pieces, finishing with an e-commerce migration that went from monthly releases to several deployments a day.

It is a long, methodical talk. The Go part is the why; the bulk is the how of the migration.

## Go and Lambda are a good match on cold starts

Srikar's Go case is about the economics of serverless. A compiled binary means fast execution and a small package. In the test he describes, Go cold starts measured 10 to 20 milliseconds against 100 to 200 for Python doing the same task. Goroutines let one function handle many concurrent events without threading headaches, and the garbage collector keeps memory, which Lambda also bills, under control.

He compares Go with the usual alternatives fairly: Java has a rich ecosystem but JVM start-up hurts rarely called functions; Node.js is popular but its single thread becomes a bottleneck on CPU-heavy work; Python is great for development speed but uses more memory and runs slower in production.

## Carve along domain boundaries first

The migration method starts with domain-driven design: find the logical boundaries, begin with the components that have the fewest dependencies, and prioritise by complexity and impact. Then extract microservices, each with its own data store, talking through versioned APIs on API Gateway. Then turn them into single-responsibility Lambda functions triggered by API Gateway, S3, DynamoDB or EventBridge events.

## Move traffic with the strangler pattern

Traffic moves gradually. The strangler pattern replaces monolith features one at a time, feature flags switch new paths on and off without a deploy, and canary releases send a small share of traffic to the new components first. Close monitoring and quick rollbacks make the whole thing reversible, which is the property that lets you sleep during a migration.

## The database is the hard part

Srikar is candid that the database is the biggest challenge. His mapping: MySQL or PostgreSQL to Aurora Serverless; heavier relational systems split between DynamoDB for high-throughput access and Aurora for complex queries; MongoDB to DocumentDB or DynamoDB; Redis or Memcached to ElastiCache or DAX. Going to DynamoDB means designing for access patterns instead of a relational schema, a rewrite of how you think, not just where data lives.

Not everything has to go serverless either. His hybrid model keeps stateful services on ECS or EKS, uses managed services like RDS and OpenSearch, and leaves long-running, GPU or legacy jobs on EC2.

## The e-commerce case study

The worked example is a platform whose transactions slowed by 400% at peak. The team prioritised inventory and payments, moved the product catalogue from MySQL to DynamoDB with a dual-write approach for zero downtime, then rebuilt payment processing as Lambda functions behind API Gateway with an event-driven design. That step alone gave a 30% infrastructure cost cut and 50% better peak response times. The completed serverless platform reached an 80% cost reduction in normal operation and handled 10x traffic surges.

## Who should watch

Teams planning to move a monolith to AWS serverless, especially if Go is on the table. The list of challenges, from cold starts and provisioned concurrency to eventual consistency, circuit breakers and least-privilege IAM per function, is a good pre-flight checklist.

Title: Breaking a .NET monolith into services without a rewrite
Description: Asif Mehboob of Freeport LNG at Conf42 SRE 2025 on moving legacy systems to .NET microservices via bounded contexts, CI/CD and four migration paths.
Body:
A monolith is a single long video recording: change one slide and you re-shoot or re-time everything after it. That's the analogy Asif Mehboob, Senior Manager of Software and Business Intelligence Engineering at Freeport LNG, used at Conf42 SRE 2025 to explain why his team moved legacy systems onto modern .NET and microservices, and how to do it without starting from scratch.

It's a structured modernisation talk aimed at teams with an aging .NET estate. Light on code, heavy on sequencing.

## Why the legacy system has to move

Asif's list of legacy pain is the familiar one, delivered from experience: systems that block new features, maintenance costs that keep rising, specialists who get harder and pricier to hire, and missing modern security protections that create compliance and cyber risk. His position is that modernisation is a business necessity, not an IT project.

The video analogy is worth the watch. Record one slide per clip, and fixing slide X means re-recording one clip and re-merging, with no script timings to rewrite. That's fault isolation and independent deployment explained to anyone in the room.

## One platform now

A quick history keeps the .NET part grounded: the Windows-only .NET Framework, then the open-source, cross-platform .NET Core, then the unified platform from .NET 5 onwards, which he puts at .NET 9 at the time of the talk. The upshot is that you can redesign on a modern runtime without abandoning the ecosystem.

At his organisation, the move delivered a development cycle that runs across three shifts, development speed up 67%, and compute efficiency up 40%, by his account.

## Pick the right path per component

Asif lays out four modernisation approaches, in rising order of effort:

- **Rehost** (lift and shift): new infrastructure, same code.
- **Refactor**: better internal structure, same external behaviour.
- **Re-architect**: real structural change that enables new capabilities.
- **Rebuild**: recreate the application with modern technology.

Before choosing, analyse the current system: identify stakeholders, draw architecture and dependency diagrams, and assess technical debt and bottlenecks. Then set business objectives and success metrics, choose a strategy per component, and write a roadmap with stakeholder buy-in.

## Bounded contexts first, then templates

The decomposition steps are practical. Map business domains to bounded contexts with clear edges. Design each service around one business capability. Define integration through APIs and messaging. Then create service templates so every team builds services the same way.

The data layer moves to scalable managed cloud databases, with repositories, ORMs and abstraction layers, eventual consistency where services share data, and encryption plus strict access control. Delivery runs through a CI/CD pipeline with automated builds and unit tests, containers, Kubernetes for orchestration, and release gates with monitoring. On the code side he points to SOLID, the repository and unit-of-work patterns, factory methods and dependency injection.

He's honest about the costs: skill gaps and a learning curve, resource balancing during the transition, and the difficulty of troubleshooting across distributed services. His advice from doing it recently: start with small pilots, train the team, embed security at every stage, and invest in observability early.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and architects planning a .NET modernisation, especially if they need the vocabulary to pitch it upward. Engineers already deep into microservices will find the patterns familiar.

Title: Multi-cloud needs one SRE playbook, not one per cloud
Description: Arun Pandiyan Perumal of Adobe at Conf42 SRE 2025 on SLOs, unified observability, IaC and shared IAM to tame multi-cloud operational overhead.
Body:
Every extra cloud provider brings its own APIs, its own monitoring console and its own IAM model, and the operational cost compounds. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Arun Pandiyan Perumal, Site Reliability Engineer at Adobe, argued that the fix is standardisation: one set of SLOs, one observability pipeline and one automation approach that spans every cloud you run.

It is a broad, survey-style talk that covers a lot of ground quickly. Treat it as a checklist for a multi-cloud reliability programme rather than a war story.

## Four ways multi-cloud hurts

Arun starts by naming the complexity precisely, which is more useful than it sounds:

- **Architectural complexity.** Different architectures, APIs and service offerings per provider.
- **Visibility gaps.** Each cloud ships different monitoring tools and standards.
- **Data silos.** Separate logging and monitoring per cloud fragments the data, so nobody gets a whole-system view.
- **Scalability and cost.** Data ingestion and retention across clouds grow faster than budgets.

If you have ever correlated an incident across two vendor consoles in two browser tabs with two clocks, you know which one stings most.

## SRE as the common language

The core argument is that SLIs, SLOs and error budgets give you a provider-neutral way to talk about reliability. SRE brings consistent processes, tools and practices across clouds, and cross-functional collaboration between ops, development, security and the providers themselves. Tie those objectives to business priorities, he says, and reliability work stops being a side quest.

On architecture he recommends microservices or modular designs that scale and update independently, active-active or active-passive strategies across clouds for failover, and regular tests of the fallback paths. Data consistency and replication across clouds get specific attention, with a warning about excessive replication overhead.

## Automate it once, run it everywhere

The overhead reduction comes from a few habits:

- **Infrastructure as code** to cut manual changes and configuration drift.
- **Standardised CI/CD pipelines** across providers, so a deploy looks the same wherever it lands.
- **Configuration management and policy enforcement** with Ansible, Chef, Puppet and Open Policy Agent.
- **Self-healing mechanisms** that detect and recover from failures without a human.
- **Platform engineering** with self-service portals, so developers can ship without infrastructure expertise.

For observability, he points to OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Grafana to aggregate metrics, logs and traces from every vendor into a single view, plus distributed tracing across services and unified incident workflows to keep alert noise down. Chaos-style fault injection across clouds is how you prove the failover strategy works before an outage proves it doesn't.

## Security that doesn't fork per provider

The security section mirrors the rest: unified scanning and continuous posture management for a consistent baseline, a centralised IAM with least-privilege access across clouds, encryption at rest and in transit with key management that works across providers, and zero trust for every communication between services and users.

He closes with trends: more serverless and function-as-a-service, AIOps for managing scale, continuous resilience testing, and stricter data governance regulation.

## Who should watch

Teams that have just gone from one cloud to two, and leads writing the case for a platform team. Seasoned multi-cloud operators will recognise most of the list; the value is in seeing it laid out as one connected programme rather than a pile of tools.

Title: IT operations moving from reactive to predictive, tool by tool
Description: Incident management engineer Jugnu Misal at Conf42 Golang 2025 on Prometheus, Nagios, Datadog and AIOps, and how to roll out automation in stages.
Body:
Most incident timelines start with a customer noticing first. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Jugnu Misal, an incident management engineer, gave a compact tour of how operations teams move from reacting after failure, to catching problems early, to predicting them, and which tools carry each step: Prometheus, Nagios, Datadog and AIOps platforms.

It is a short introductory talk, good for someone new to operations or for a manager who needs the vocabulary. It does not touch Go itself.

## Three eras of ops

The framing is a ladder. Reactive teams fix things after they break, with long downtime. Proactive teams use monitoring to spot failures early. Predictive teams use AI-driven analytics to forecast failures before users feel them. Jugnu's argument is that each rung depends on the one below: you cannot predict what you do not measure.

## Pick monitoring tools for the environment you have

He pairs the two classic monitors with the environments they suit. Prometheus does precise metric collection and alerting and fits dynamic cloud environments. Nagios, with its long-lived plugin ecosystem, is strong for broad infrastructure oversight. Datadog is the observability layer for multi-cloud and hybrid estates, with one view across infrastructure, applications and logs, from code-level tracing to AI-assisted log analysis.

The figures in the talk, such as cutting manual interventions by 78% and reaching five-nines availability, come from the studies and deployments he cites rather than from a measured case shown on screen.

## AIOps learns from the incidents you already had

The AIOps section is the most interesting. Instead of waiting for an alert, tools continuously analyse patterns, detect anomalies and trigger automated remediation, so routine failures heal themselves and fewer things get escalated to a human. The machine learning part matters because the models adapt with each incident and get more accurate over time. Anyone who has been woken up by the same flapping alert three nights in a row will see the appeal.

## Build a home lab before you automate production

A nice, practical aside: Jugnu recommends home labs as a risk-free place to learn these tools, try configurations and simulate real incidents. If you want to understand alert fatigue, break your own Raspberry Pi cluster first.

## Roll it out in five steps

The closing method is sensible and reusable:

1. Audit current monitoring to find the gaps.
2. Select tools that match the business needs.
3. Pilot before a full rollout.
4. Integrate so data flows across platforms.
5. Keep optimising based on what the metrics tell you.

## Who should watch

People early in an SRE, ops or incident management career, or anyone choosing between these tools for the first time. Seasoned SREs will know the material; it is a crisp primer, not an implementation guide.

Title: Azure Load Testing, from portal click to CI/CD gate
Description: Peter De Tender of Microsoft at Conf42 SRE 2025 demos Azure Load Testing with URL tests, JMeter and Locust scripts, and runs from CI/CD pipelines or REST.
Body:
Load testing is the part of SRE where you get to break things on purpose and call it diligence. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Peter De Tender, an Azure technical trainer at Microsoft, gave a demo-heavy tour of Azure Load Testing: build a test in the portal, see the JMeter script it generates, swap in Locust, then trigger the whole thing from a pipeline.

This is a vendor talk about a Microsoft managed service, and Peter says so cheerfully. It's also one of the more practical half hours on the topic, because most of it is a live portal session with real knobs.

## Hammer the staging environment, not production

Peter's framing of SRE is blunt: a large chunk of the job is stress testing, because making a workload highly available means knowing how it behaves under real load. Load, in his definition, can be users, sessions or raw traffic, as with a streaming service where bandwidth matters more than headcount.

Azure Load Testing is a managed service, so nothing to install. It can target anything reachable over HTTP or HTTPS: an App Service, a VM, an API endpoint, and not only workloads hosted in Azure. His advice is to aim it at test, acceptance or staging, since you don't want your experiment to become the incident.

## The portal writes your JMeter file for you

The first demo is the URL-based test. Peter adds a GET request against his own blog's homepage, shows how to add sub-paths and other HTTP methods, query parameters and headers, and chains a second request to another endpoint to simulate a flow.

A few details worth knowing:

- **Secrets and certificates** come from Key Vault, and the test needs a managed identity with role-based access to read them.
- **Each engine instance handles up to 250 users**, so simulating 1,000 users means four instances. The portal's display of this confused even Peter for a moment.
- **Load patterns** can be linear, step or spike. His example of a spike: a food-ordering platform at breakfast and lunch.
- **Test criteria** let you fail a run on a metric such as response time, and Application Insights adds server-side metrics.

The neat reveal: even though he started from the URL form, the service converted everything into a JMeter test plan behind the scenes. Download it, and you have the config, the JSON and the JMX XML ready to version and upload as a script-based test.

## JMeter or Locust, same dashboard

Azure Load Testing began on Apache JMeter and later added Locust. The difference, per Peter, is mostly how you write the test: JMeter uses JMX files, Locust uses Python. His Locust script pulls a to-do item and checks for a 200 response. Running it and reading the results look identical in the portal, so you can standardise on whichever framework your team already uses elsewhere.

## Then take the human out of it

The SRE point is automation. In Azure DevOps you install the Azure Load Testing extension from the Visual Studio Marketplace and add a stage that points at the load test resource, resource group and YAML config. In GitHub Actions, the equivalent is the azure/load-testing action. Neither is required: since it's just another Azure service, you can authenticate, get a token and trigger runs with plain REST calls and curl.

His live Azure DevOps run failed on permissions, which is the most realistic pipeline demo you'll see this year.

He closes by pointing to Azure Chaos Studio as the companion service for chaos experiments on Azure workloads.

## Who should watch

Teams on Azure that run load tests by hand today, and anyone who wants to see how a managed load-testing service maps onto JMeter and Locust. If you're on another cloud, the pipeline ideas transfer; the clicks don't.

Title: Automate the processes worth automating, not the easy ones
Description: Mohit Sachdeva at Conf42 SRE 2025 on pairing intelligent automation with BPM, picking processes by business value, and why governance decides scale.
Body:
The automation programmes that pay back are the ones that choose processes by business value, not by how easy they are to script. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Mohit Sachdeva of Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University, New Delhi, gave an overview of intelligent automation (IA) combined with business process management (BPM): why the pairing works, which tools lead, and the governance and change management that separate a scaled programme from a pile of pilots.

This is a business-level talk. It sits closer to the operations and enterprise architecture end of the conference than to SLOs and pagers, which is useful context if you are the engineer being asked to support the automation platform.

## The numbers behind the hype

Mohit opens with Deloitte research: 73% of organisations are already on an intelligent automation journey, 58% are using AI to scale automation platforms, average return on investment arrives in about 11 months, and 93% report outcomes that meet or exceed expectations. Whatever your view of survey data, that is a lot of companies already running bots against their business processes.

The benefits he attributes to combining IA with BPM fall into three areas. Process efficiency: cycle times cut by up to 90% and roughly 30% of employee time freed from repetitive tasks. Data utilisation: real-time analytics and faster retrieval, with business process integration keeping data consistent across previously siloed applications. Customer experience: satisfaction up 20 to 30% and service 40 to 60% faster.

## Machines take the grunt work, humans keep the steering wheel

The core argument is that IA is not about replacing people. Machine learning lets a BPM system monitor, analyse and adjust processes on the fly without manual intervention, while humans stay in the loop for strategic oversight. Natural language processing and conversational AI handle more of the customer journey, reading context and emotional signals to personalise support. Mohit's phrase for the combination of adaptive automation and human judgment is that it makes the pairing "very deadly", which is the most enthusiastic thing anyone has said about BPM in a while.

## Pick the tool for the process

He surveys the main platforms: UiPath for end-to-end automation with process mining, Automation Anywhere as a cloud-native platform built to scale, Pega Systems for orchestration and case management, and Kofax for document-heavy processes with RPA and advanced OCR. His advice is the right one: tool choice depends on your business needs and strategy, not on the vendor slide.

Process selection follows the same logic. His pyramid puts business value at the top, with finance, HR and tax departments as typical starting points, and recommends a formal selection framework so automation stays aligned with strategic goals.

## Governance and change management decide whether it scales

The section most engineers will nod along to is governance. Mohit says 69% of high-performing organisations run an automation centre of excellence, and success comes from balancing central standards with local execution and clear roles across business and technical teams. That is how a programme gets past its first pilots.

Change management is called foundational: involve teams early, be transparent about how roles will change, and invest in reskilling. He notes that leading companies redesign workflows so people and machines work together rather than in isolation. On architecture, he wants a modular stack with enterprise-wide standards and continuous refinement, citing 47% of successful organisations using process mining for continuous improvement.

The future he sketches is hyperautomation: AI, RPA, BPM and analytics integrated, process intelligence to find high-value targets, and self-healing, adaptive workflows. For an SRE audience, self-healing workflows are the familiar idea wearing a business suit.

## Who should watch

Engineering and operations leaders evaluating an automation programme, platform teams asked to support RPA and BPM tooling, and anyone who needs a vocabulary for talking to the business side. If you want implementation detail or SRE practice, this talk stays at the strategy level.

Title: Space missions run on data pipelines as much as on rockets
Description: Siddhartha Parimi of Dell Technologies at Conf42 SRE 2025 on the data engineering behind space missions, from onboard filtering to James Webb pipelines.
Body:
If rocket science is the body of a space mission, data engineering is the brain and nervous system. That is the framing Siddhartha Parimi, a product manager at Dell Technologies, used at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025 to walk through how missions collect, compress, filter and process the data they send home, and why so much of that work now happens on the spacecraft itself.

It is a light, accessible talk with plenty of analogies, closer to an engaging introduction than an engineering deep end. That makes it a good one to share with people outside the data team.

## The volumes are real

Siddhartha opens with scale. A single mission can send back hundreds of gigabytes a day, and he says the International Space Station alone generates nearly a terabyte daily. Storing that is the easy part. The hard part is collecting it efficiently over thin, distant links, processing it in near real time, and making it usable for scientists around the world.

His comparison for life without modern techniques: streaming Netflix over a dial-up connection. Anyone who has tried to pull logs from a remote site over a bad VPN will feel that one.

## Distributed systems and smart compression

The ground side runs on distributed architectures: instead of one big computer, many smaller nodes process in parallel, which lets agencies scale on demand and serve many simultaneous data requests from several missions. He likens it to a kitchen of chefs each preparing part of the meal.

Compression is treated as triage, not just shrinking. Data goes through initial cleanup, priority tagging, analysis and long-term storage, optimised for both speed and scientific value. He cites compression ratios as high as ten to one, which on a deep-space link is the difference between getting the picture today or next week.

## Decide on board, send only what matters

The most transferable section is edge processing. Spacecraft now filter and compress data on board, prioritise what matters most, make some mission adjustments autonomously, and transmit only the important parts. Siddhartha compares it to phone face recognition working without internet, and says this runs at under five watts per node.

The reason is latency. With round trips to Mars measured in many minutes, a spacecraft cannot wait for Earth to tell it how to respond to a solar flare or a fault. He describes onboard real-time processing with latency under 10 milliseconds: sensors capture, processing evaluates, the spacecraft acts, and only critical events are relayed home.

The compute picture has three tiers: small radiation-hardened processors in orbit, big supercomputers on the ground for heavy analysis, and cloud platforms in between coordinating the two.

## James Webb as the case study

The James Webb Space Telescope is the worked example. Siddhartha says it sends back around 40 GB of data a day, which goes through onboard filtering and then layered processing pipelines on Earth that turn raw light signals into images and discoveries. He ties the topic back to the economy too, citing satellite communications as the largest slice of a $423.8 billion space economy, from GPS and weather to agriculture and finance.

The look ahead includes AI-driven autonomous spacecraft, a delay-tolerant interplanetary internet, quantum computing for mission planning and encryption (which he labels early days), and orbital cloud computing where spacecraft share compute and storage. Literally a cloud in space.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers who enjoy a good analogy, anyone working on edge or bandwidth-constrained systems, and people curious about how space missions handle data. If you want detailed pipeline code or specific mission software, this overview stays above that level.

Title: Offline-first Oracle stacks for rural e-governance
Description: Vasipally Nagireddy (Creoal + SMX) at Conf42 SRE 2025 on using Oracle Cloud, APEX and SOA Suite to bring health, farming and land services to rural areas.
Body:
Reliability looks different when the user is a farmer three hours from the nearest clinic and the network drops twice a day. At Conf42 SRE 2025, Vasipally Nagireddy, Principal Consultant at Creoal + SMX with 17 years in enterprise integration architecture, walked through how Oracle technology is used for e-governance in rural areas, and why offline capability matters more than raw connection speed.

This is a short, research-framed talk rather than a hands-on build. It is useful if you work on public-sector systems or anything that has to keep working where the infrastructure doesn't.

## The digital divide is an availability problem

Vasipally opens with the scale of the gap: by his figures, 3.7 billion people without internet access, most of them in rural areas. Low population density makes connectivity expensive to deploy, and the people left offline lose access to education, healthcare, financial services and government resources.

Read that with an SRE hat on and it is a familiar shape. The service exists, but a large share of users can't reach it reliably. His answer is architecture, not just more towers.

## The stack: OCI at the bottom, APEX at the counter

The talk lays out the Oracle stack layer by layer:

- **Oracle Cloud Infrastructure** as the scalable foundation.
- **Oracle Database and analytics** for secure data management.
- **Oracle SOA Suite** as the integration framework that connects services.
- **Oracle APEX and E-Business Suite** for application development and business processes.

The point of an integrated stack, he argues, is that governments can roll out standard services quickly and still customise them for each community, and that the whole thing has to function with limited connectivity.

## Offline mode is the feature that carries the rest

The healthcare section is where the design idea is clearest. APEX applications provide patient record management that works offline, with telemedicine links connecting remote clinics to urban medical centres for consultations and referrals. He credits the offline mode as especially valuable where connectivity is intermittent, because it keeps the service available instead of failing whenever the link does.

Agriculture gets similar treatment: crop planning, input tracking, yield monitoring and market price access. He notes that adoption was strongest when the platforms arrived with hands-on training for farmers.

Administrative services round it out. Document digitisation, process automation through Oracle Business Process Management, and access across web, mobile and kiosk interfaces. The case study is land registration, where Oracle Blockchain holds land records and APEX powers the citizen-facing side; he reports the system handling over 50,000 transactions a month and fewer corruption complaints about land deals.

## People beat technology-only rollouts

The most transferable lesson is about humans. Vasipally names four barriers: connectivity, digital literacy, energy constraints and cultural adaptation. The mitigations are offline-capable applications and mesh networks, community training with simplified interfaces, low-power devices and alternative energy, and localised content.

Communities that ran digital literacy programmes alongside the new systems saw adoption 25% higher than technology-only approaches, in his study. The research behind the talk mixed stakeholder interviews with performance metrics from the Oracle systems, tracked over 24 months, so the claims come with a methodology rather than a single anecdote.

His closing policy points follow from that: invest in rural connectivity through public-private partnerships, prefer integrated platforms over siloed apps, build digital skills into education, and keep measuring long-term impact. Technology alone, he concludes, cannot close the divide.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects building government or NGO services, and anyone designing for intermittent networks. If you want Kubernetes manifests or failover drills, this isn't that talk; it's a high-level map of a stack and the human factors around it. If you care about why "works offline" belongs in your requirements, it's a solid 20 minutes.

Title: Why Go fits V2X networks for connected vehicles
Description: Utham Kumar at Conf42 Golang 2025 on building vehicle-to-everything systems in Go, from goroutines and channels to Kubernetes and pprof.
Body:
A connected intersection is a concurrency problem with brakes attached: thousands of vehicles, roadside units and pedestrians' phones all sending small, time-sensitive messages at once. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Utham Kumar, a program and product leader whose career runs through Visa, T-Mobile, Verizon, Lenovo and IBM, made the case that Go's goroutines, channels and standard library are a natural fit for vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication.

This is an overview of why Go suits the domain, pitched at architects and product people, rather than a walkthrough of a specific codebase.

## V2X is a message bus with lives on it

Utham starts with the definition: V2X covers vehicle-to-vehicle, vehicle-to-infrastructure and vehicle-to-pedestrian, one network where cars, traffic signals and people can talk. The industry figures he quotes are big: up to 40% fewer collisions, around 30% better traffic flow and faster emergency response. He also expects over half of new vehicles to ship with V2X capability by 2030.

## Goroutines and channels match the shape of the traffic

The Go argument is straightforward and well made. Goroutines are lightweight enough to hold thousands or even millions of simultaneous connections. Channels pass data between them safely, which prevents race conditions when several vehicles share time-sensitive state. The result is highly parallel event processing, which is what reading sensor data from many vehicles at once requires.

He adds the operational side: fast start-up, small memory per goroutine for edge devices, and pprof and tracing to find bottlenecks. His benchmark targets are concrete: under 100 milliseconds end to end for collision avoidance, 500,000-plus messages per second sustained, 99.99% uptime via circuit breakers, and a 25% performance gain from iterative profiling.

## The standard library is half the stack

A good chunk of the talk is a reminder of what Go gives you for free: networking and cryptography packages for authenticated, encrypted traffic between vehicles, and HTTP and JSON support for over-the-air updates, telemetry APIs and cloud calls. In safety work, fewer third-party dependencies is a feature, not a limitation.

## The reference architecture

The architecture slide is the most reusable part: API gateways for secure telemetry ingestion, real-time messaging over NATS, Kafka or MQTT, and specialised services for collision detection and route optimisation. The Go microservices run on Kubernetes, roll out through CI/CD with canary releases, and process data first on edge nodes before the cloud aggregates and sends instructions back. He cites horizontal scaling to around 600,000 messages per second.

## Security and the community

On security he lists TLS for transport, ephemeral key rotation against replay attacks, elliptic-curve cryptography and post-quantum work in the Go community. He also points out that built-in concurrency primitives make it less likely you introduce threading bugs that turn into security holes.

## Who should watch

Architects and technical product managers evaluating a language for connected-vehicle or IoT messaging. Experienced Go developers already know the concurrency pitch; the value for them is the domain framing and the reference architecture. There is no live code, and the crash-reduction figures come from pilot deployments the talk does not detail.
