Title: Self-driving cars need inference in the car, not the cloud
Description: Murali Krishna Reddy Mandalapu of Renesas Electronics at Conf42 Golang 2025 on edge AI inference for autonomous vehicles, from latency budgets to quantisation.
Body:
Every 10 milliseconds of processing delay adds roughly 0.3 to 0.5 metres to a car's stopping distance. That one number from Murali Krishna Reddy Mandalapu, Senior Director of Hardware Engineering at Renesas Electronics, explains why his Conf42 Golang 2025 talk argues that autonomous vehicles must run their safety-critical AI inference on board, with the cloud kept for jobs that can wait.

It is a hardware and ML systems talk rather than a Go talk, and it is a dense tour of where the compute budget in a self-driving car goes.

## The data firehose and the deadline

Murali frames the problem with three pressures. Volume: cameras at 30 to 60 frames per second, lidar producing hundreds of thousands to millions of points per frame and radar together generate terabytes of raw data per hour. Latency: the full perception, decision and action pipeline has to complete within 100 to 300 milliseconds to avoid a collision at speed. Variability: computational load can swing by up to 480% between an empty highway and a dense urban intersection, so the architecture has to adapt.

## Consumer GPUs were the wrong tool

The history slide is worth a look. First-generation prototypes used repurposed consumer GPUs that drew up to 300 watts, needed liquid cooling and lost up to 67% of processing time to data transfer. Second-generation automotive-grade accelerators were built for the job, with better performance per watt, less memory traffic through pruning and compression, and reduced-precision compute.

## Hybrid, with the edge owning safety

His comparison of edge and cloud is clear-eyed. The edge answers in 5 to 15 milliseconds against up to 500 for the cloud, keeps working when connectivity drops and keeps sensitive data inside the vehicle. The cloud has orders of magnitude more compute and no power limit, which suits HD map generation and fleet learning. The industry has converged on a hybrid in which mission-critical perception and control stay on the vehicle.

## Make the model smaller before you make the chip bigger

The practical core is model optimisation:

- **Quantisation** from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers: four times smaller weights, with an accuracy loss he puts at about 1.2%, and 8-bit operations using far less energy than floating point.
- **Pruning** of parameters that contribute little, with structured pruning giving large efficiency gains and around 2% accuracy loss after fine-tuning.
- **Knowledge distillation**, where a large teacher model trains a compact student with many fewer parameters.
- **Hardware-aware neural architecture search**, which models memory access and operator timing for the target chip.

He also describes multi-stage perception, where cheap region-proposal networks run first and the expensive classifier only looks at regions of interest.

## Neuromorphic and event-driven sensing is next

The forward-looking section covers event-driven processing, which handles changes instead of full frames and cuts power sharply, and neuromorphic processors that combine memory and compute in neuron-like structures at a few hundred milliwatts. He ends on distributed AI, continuous learning with small, safety-aware updates, and federated learning across fleets.

## Who should watch

Engineers working on embedded ML, robotics or automotive software who want a map of the latency budget and the optimisation toolbox. If you came for Go code, there is none; if you came for why the deadline shapes everything, it delivers.

Title: Go microservices around TensorFlow for clinical ML
Description: Kamal Gupta of Amazon at Conf42 Golang 2025 on using Go services to ingest medical data, wrap TensorFlow models and push predictions to clinicians.
Body:
Python trains the model; something still has to feed it 30-plus medical data formats and get the answer to a clinician before it stops mattering. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Kamal Gupta, Software Development Engineer at Amazon, walked through a healthcare ML system where that something is Go: microservices that ingest patient data, custom wrappers that orchestrate TensorFlow models, and WebSocket delivery of predictions to clinical workstations and mobile devices.

It is a short, results-heavy talk. Treat it as an architecture sketch with a scoreboard attached, not a code walkthrough.

## Go sits on the boring, critical path

Kamal's case for Go rests on three properties that matter in a hospital more than in most places. Goroutines let the system run thousands of concurrent analyses on patient data streams without much overhead. Go's security libraries and memory-safe design help keep data handling inside HIPAA rules. And the compiled binary with a predictable garbage collector gives the millisecond-level responsiveness that a critical decision needs.

The architecture has three stages. Ingestion: Go services that capture and normalise data from clinical devices, EHRs and wearables. ML orchestration: Go wrappers around TensorFlow that coordinate distributed model execution and parallel feature extraction. Delivery: real-time results pushed over WebSockets with Go's encryption libraries end to end.

## Wrapping TensorFlow from Go is the real engineering

The most honest slide is the one on implementation challenges. Integrating TensorFlow models with Go services needed custom bindings, so the team built framework-specific wrappers with careful memory management. Clinical data arrived from disparate systems in inconsistent formats, and Go's parsing was used to build adaptive normalisation that keeps the diagnostic meaning intact. Regulators want audit trails, so every system decision goes into immutable logs.

There is also a workflow point that engineers tend to forget: the interfaces were designed to map onto how clinicians already work, because a prediction nobody looks at is a very expensive log line.

## The numbers, as reported

The talk is generous with figures, all from the speaker's own deployment: 94% accuracy on cardiovascular disease markers, a roughly 68% cut in pneumonia diagnosis time, Go services processing 10,000-plus vital-sign data points per second, and edge code on IoT devices that reduced network bandwidth by 78%. The validation framework runs four stages (performance testing, accuracy validation against gold-standard clinical data, clinical integration studies and long-term monitoring of 27 metrics in production).

The talk does not show how those figures were measured, so read them as the team's results rather than benchmarks you can reproduce.

## Privacy is designed in, not bolted on

Kamal lists the privacy toolkit: differential privacy to protect individual records while keeping population-level signal, federated learning so training happens on-device without shipping raw patient data, and computation on encrypted data. It is a good checklist for anyone building ML near regulated data, whatever language they use.

## Who should watch

Go engineers who are asked to put ML into a regulated product and want to see where Go fits around the model rather than inside it. Health-tech architects will find the pipeline shape familiar. If you want code, profiling or the details of the TensorFlow bindings, this talk stays at the slide level.

Title: From software engineer to principal cloud architect, with AI in the mix
Description: Amlan Ghosh at Conf42 Golang 2025 on the skills ladder behind a principal cloud architect role, plus healthcare and retail migrations with AI.
Body:
Amlan Ghosh has spent over two decades in software engineering, and at Conf42 Golang 2025 he laid out the route he took from writing enterprise applications to working as a principal cloud architect. The talk mixes a career map with two case studies, a regional healthcare system and a retail omnichannel platform, where cloud migration and machine learning arrived together.

Fair warning for the Go crowd: there is no Go in it. This is a cloud architecture and career talk that happened to land on the Golang track.

## The skills stack is built like a skyscraper

Amlan's central image is a building that needs a deep foundation before it can go up. His layers, from the base:

- **Hands-on coding.** He started by building real applications on AWS: EC2, S3, Lambda, Step Functions, RDS.
- **Infrastructure as code.** CloudFormation and Terraform to stand infrastructure up from code instead of consoles.
- **Performance and cost.** Designing solutions that scale and stay cheap enough to keep running.
- **Security and compliance.** Zero trust architecture and governance.
- **AI integration.** Deploying ML services and custom models on top of everything else.

The order matters. His point is that architects who skip the hands-on floor end up drawing diagrams nobody can build, and the AI layer sits on top of all the boring ones.

## Healthcare: growth that the old EHR could not take

The first case study is a regional healthcare organisation whose patient numbers grew by 200% while its legacy electronic health record system choked. Any move had to satisfy HIPAA and GDPR, including data crossing borders. The answer was a secured hybrid cloud with end-to-end encryption and granular access control, plus machine learning modules for clinical decision support and predictive analytics for resource planning.

## Retail: one inventory instead of two

The retail case had siloed inventory, so online and in-store channels disagreed on prices and stock. The fix was a unified AWS data platform on microservices with event-driven synchronisation of inventory, ML forecasting for replenishment and behavioural personalisation. The reported results: 28% higher conversion, 45% fewer stock-outs and a 3x return on investment within 18 months.

Across his engagements Amlan also cites a 42% reduction in infrastructure cost and 68% faster time to market, which he attributes mostly to not waiting for hardware procurement.

## A four-phase migration you can actually reuse

The most practical slide is the migration method: assess (catalogue workloads, find what is broken, prioritise), plan (timeline, tools, compliance strategy), migrate (start with a pilot workload, then data, applications and security settings, then validate), and optimise (performance tuning, cost management, automation). Nothing exotic, which is the point: most failed migrations skipped the first box.

## Career advice, minus the fluff

He closes with what worked for him: specialise in areas in demand (serverless, Kubernetes, ML on cloud), keep a portfolio of real projects, contribute to open source, get the professional-level cloud certifications, and speak and write in public. Plus one habit worth stealing: explain your architecture in terms of return on investment, because that is the language the budget speaks.

## Who should watch

Engineers a few years in who are wondering what the architect track actually requires. Senior architects will recognise most of it; the two case studies are a handy template for selling a migration internally.

Title: Earthquake alerts in the minutes before the shaking arrives
Description: Vlad Onetiu of DataIceberg at Conf42 SRE 2025 on a serverless earthquake alert system built on AWS Lambda, Confluent Kafka and DynamoDB locks.
Body:
An earthquake alert that arrives after the earthquake is a history lesson. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Vlad Onetiu, Software Automation Engineer and DevSecOps at DataIceberg, showed the serverless system he built to turn seismic sensor data into SMS, email and Telegram notifications fast enough to use the minutes between a quake starting and its full waves reaching cities far from the epicentre.

It is a research project with a real architecture behind it: AWS Lambda producers and consumers, Confluent Kafka for parallel fan-out, DynamoDB for subscribers, and three iterations of a locking scheme that make the talk worth watching for anyone who has fought duplicate deliveries.

## The problem: a good alert system that is often late

Vlad's motivation is the Romanian government's alert application, which pushes warnings about weather, accidents and infrastructure failures to phones. His complaint is about timing: in many cases the alert lands after the event has unfolded. His example: if you are already looking at the rainbow, the storm warning is not much use.

Earthquakes cannot be predicted reliably, so he does not try. Instead he uses distance as the advantage. A government-linked seismic research institute runs a rapid alerting project with physical sensors in Romania's most active seismic area, emitting data on even very small movements. Because major cities sit hundreds of kilometres away, there are a couple of minutes between detection and the strongest shaking arriving. The system listens to that feed and fans the alert out to subscribers, whether people or critical infrastructure operators.

## Why serverless fits a system that is idle almost always

The serverless choice is practical. Nothing needs to run 24/7 between earthquakes; what matters is spinning up enough capacity in milliseconds when one hits, and not paying for idle servers the rest of the year.

The backbone is Lambda producers listening to the sensor data and writing to Kafka, with multithreading to use each instance's full CPU and a "topic roulette" so separate threads do not write into the same partitions. Each partition triggers Lambda consumers, which iterate the subscriber table in DynamoDB and send through Twilio for SMS, Amazon SES for email, and Telegram as a backup channel. Minor failures (network blips, latency) are retried; major failures land in an SQS dead-letter queue for manual investigation. Consumers are kept warm because cold starts in the final hop are exactly where you cannot afford them.

## Three versions of not notifying the same person twice

The best part is the concurrency story. Early on, parallel consumers raced: one subscriber could get several notifications while another got none.

Version one adds a custom timestamp lock per subscriber item in DynamoDB, plus optimistic locking with a version field, so an item that is being notified or was just notified is skipped. It works, but triggers waste time colliding on the same items. Vlad describes it as watching a row of dominoes from the front.

Version two segments the subscriber list, for example IDs 1 to 400, and locks per segment, so each Kafka-triggered worker owns its slice and race conditions disappear. The new problem: one worker per big segment is slow.

Version three allows a configurable maximum number of workers per segment, splitting the work inside it without conflicts. The dominoes are now viewed from the side, with several soldiers per row.

## Scaling by subscriber count, not by guessing

Since predicting the next quake is off the table, autoscaling keys on the number of subscribers: threads, Kafka topics and partitions, consumer triggers and warm instances all step up as the list grows. The first version used Python and AWS CLI scripts inside an orchestrating Lambda; the team is moving it to Terraform driven by GitHub Actions, which also gives them versioned snapshots of the infrastructure to roll back to. Vlad also mentions Amazon Kinesis as a possible Kafka replacement, to keep traffic inside AWS and cut latency.

## Who should watch

Anyone building fan-out notification systems, Lambda-plus-Kafka pipelines, or DynamoDB workloads with contention. The locking iterations are the transferable lesson. Note that the project is protected under licence; Vlad asks anyone wanting to build on it to contact him first.

Title: A five-step plan for reliability across more than one cloud
Description: Sai Prasad Mukala of Info Keys at Conf42 SRE 2025 on multi-cloud SRE, from removing single points of failure to SLO gates and chaos engineering.
Body:
Running on two clouds does not make you twice as reliable; it makes you reliable only if your observability, security and rollout practices span both. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Sai Prasad Mukala, Enterprise Architect at Info Keys Inc, laid out what site reliability looks like across a multi-cloud estate and finished with a five-step implementation framework that works as a project plan.

It is an architect's overview, broad rather than deep, that touches edge computing, AI-driven incident response and DevSecOps on the way. The framework at the end is the part to keep.

## Why go multi-cloud in the first place

Sai frames the reasons in three buckets. Strategic: eliminating single points of failure through diversified cloud partnerships and vendor-agnostic architecture, so one provider's outage does not stop the business. Technical: distributing workloads so the system keeps high availability and recovers quickly when something breaks. Cost: each provider prices differently, so one may be cheaper for storage while another suits compute-heavy work, and placement can follow the bill.

He walks through the familiar architecture arc from monoliths to microservices, containers and Kubernetes orchestration, with Kubernetes doing the heavy lifting on declarative configuration and built-in fault tolerance.

## Let models do the triage

On incident management, Sai cites a 68% reduction in MTTR, 47% lower operational costs and incident response 3.2 times faster with AI-powered tooling. The mechanisms are diagnostic engines that analyse telemetry in real time to find root causes, predictive models that spot anomalies before they become outages and trigger scaling or alerts, and neural-network-based triage that scores severity and routes incidents to the right team instead of someone sorting the queue by hand at 3am.

## Observability has to cross the cloud boundary

The distributed observability section names the four things that get hard at scale: uniform telemetry protocols across heterogeneous components, log aggregation from thousands of distributed edge points, request context propagation through multi-cloud service meshes, and machine-learning anomaly detection that catches subtle deviations before they cascade. Edge computing and 5G raise the stakes, because more processing moves to the network edge where failures are local and harder to see.

## Security belongs in the same pipeline

Sai contrasts the traditional model, where security teams sit in silos with fragmented monitoring and slow approval loops, with integrated DevSecOps: security controls embedded in infrastructure as code, unified toolchains, automated compliance checks in CI/CD, and shared metrics so incident response is collaborative. He backs it with a breach cost breakdown in which brand damage is the largest share, ahead of legal penalties, customer compensation and recovery.

For change management he recommends gradual feature rollouts with automated rollback, controlled A/B experiments, SLOs used as quality gates for deployment, and fully versioned infrastructure as code.

## The five steps

The framework that closes the talk:

1. **Assess current state**: audit the infrastructure and find critical reliability gaps across clouds.
2. **Define SLOs**: quantifiable reliability targets tied to business outcomes.
3. **Build an observability platform**: unified monitoring with cross-cloud visibility and contextual alerting.
4. **Automate remediation**: self-healing infrastructure with ML-driven prediction and recovery workflows.
5. **Practise chaos engineering**: controlled failures to validate resilience and expose hidden dependencies.

## Who should watch

Architects and SRE leads planning or inheriting a multi-cloud setup who want a checklist they can hand to a team. If you need provider-specific failover recipes, look elsewhere; this talk is about the shape of the programme.

Title: Micro-frontends let enterprise teams ship without waiting in line
Description: Nasir Sayed of FINRA at Conf42 SRE 2025 on micro-frontend architecture for enterprise apps, integration patterns, pitfalls, and where WebAssembly fits.
Body:
A monolithic frontend turns every release into a group project: one team's change waits on everyone else's tests. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Nasir Sayed, Senior Software Engineer at FINRA, explained how micro-frontends split an enterprise UI into independently owned and deployed pieces, which integration pattern to pick, what goes wrong, and why WebAssembly is a natural partner.

The talk's title points at ADP's Client Engagement Hub; the recording itself is a general walkthrough of the architecture with several industry examples rather than a detailed account of that one project.

## Why frontend monoliths hurt

Nasir's list is short and accurate. Tight coupling means changing one part can break another, so updates feel risky. Many teams on one codebase get in each other's way. Deployments need lots of testing and careful timing. Over time the technical debt piles up and everything slows down.

Micro-frontends break the UI into smaller parts with clear jobs. Each team can choose its own framework and libraries, own its slice of the product from build to launch, and ship it on its own schedule.

## Four principles before any code

He sets four ground rules. Domain-driven design: split the app along real business areas, not technical layers. Loose coupling: parts should not lean on each other so hard that one change breaks the rest. Resilient integration: if one piece goes down, the page keeps working. Team ownership: one team in charge of each piece end to end. That third rule is the one SREs will care about, since a dead widget should degrade a page, not page someone.

## Three ways to stitch the pieces together

Nasir compares the main integration options:

- **Web Components**: browser-native custom elements, isolated with Shadow DOM, framework-agnostic.
- **Module Federation**: the webpack feature that lets separate apps share JavaScript at runtime and load only what is needed.
- **Server-side composition**: the backend assembles the parts into one page, good for SEO and fast first loads on public sites.

For performance he recommends progressive lazy loading of what matters first, sharing common dependencies rather than bundling them repeatedly, shared component libraries, and real-time performance monitoring per micro-frontend, so you know which piece is slow rather than just that the page is.

## Results, examples and the catch

He cites teams cutting deployment time by around 60%, bugs dropping by about 40% because changes are smaller, and release speed roughly tripling. Industry examples include HSBC rebuilding online banking on micro-frontends, IKEA organising product pages by category with each team owning a section, and Providence splitting parts of a patient system to handle privacy rules.

Nasir is candid about the costs. User experience can feel inconsistent when teams design differently, so you need a shared design system, common components and a UX team keeping things aligned. Combining products at runtime can hurt performance, which is where load optimisation and caching shared modules come in. And independent teams still need clear APIs, good documentation and regular check-ins.

Migration is incremental: find the natural boundaries in the current app, pilot on a simple low-risk area, set up pipelines and tooling, then peel pieces off according to business features while watching performance.

## WebAssembly as the fast lane

The closing section pairs micro-frontends with WebAssembly. Wasm runs near-native code in the browser from languages like C, C++ and Rust, inside its own sandbox, which matches the isolation micro-frontends want. His suggestion is pragmatic: find the slowest part of your app and try moving that piece to WebAssembly first. Throughout, he sprinkles predictions about AI tooling helping teams choose boundaries and integration strategies; treat those as forecasts.

## Who should watch

Frontend leads and architects with a large shared UI and several teams fighting over the release train. Teams with one product and one squad can probably skip it; Nasir's own argument is that the benefits come from independent ownership.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [JavaScript Micro Frontends: Fast-Track AI Integration for Modern Web Apps](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Linga_Annela_micro_frontends_fast) by Linga Annela continues the AI angle.
- [Glorious Monolith: Scaling an application without microfrontends](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Maksim_Zemskov_glorious_monolith_scaling_application_microfrontends) by Maksim Zemskov makes the counter-argument, worth hearing before you split.

Title: A field guide to moving a monolithic SaaS app onto AWS Lambda
Description: Srikar Kompella of Prime Video & Amazon Studio at Conf42 SRE 2025 on migrating SaaS monoliths to serverless microservices on AWS, step by step.
Body:
Serverless migrations fail less often when you start with the right candidates: stateless services with spiky traffic, not the core of the monolith. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Srikar Kompella, Software Engineer at Prime Video & Amazon Studio, gave a long, structured tour of moving SaaS applications from monoliths to serverless microservices on AWS, covering decomposition, the service catalogue, CI/CD, security and analytics, and closing with a migration roadmap.

Set expectations correctly: this is a reference-style talk built on industry studies and anonymised case studies, not a war story from Prime Video's own systems. Its value is breadth, and the roadmap at the end.

## The monolith tax

Srikar's diagnosis of the monolith is one most SaaS teams will recognise. Tightly coupled components mean small changes trigger testing across the whole application, and release cycles stretch from days to weeks. He cites a study putting monolith feature releases at about 12 weeks versus three weeks with microservices.

Scaling is the other tax. Because you cannot scale components independently, you provision for the peak all year: his example is an e-commerce platform sized for Black Friday traffic in every month that is not November. Add technology lock-in, one shared database becoming a contention point, slower onboarding of new developers, and a single failure that can take everything down.

## Cut along business lines, then strangle

The decomposition advice is solid and familiar. Split by business domain rather than technical layer, using domain-driven design, event storming and context mapping to find natural service boundaries. Define versioned, well-documented API contracts (OpenAPI helps) so services evolve independently. Extract incrementally with the strangler pattern, high-value and low-risk pieces first. Add a service mesh for discovery, circuit breaking, retries and observability. And align the architecture with how the organisation is actually structured, because Conway's law does not care about your diagram.

## The AWS kit, piece by piece

The middle of the talk is a guided catalogue. AWS Lambda is the compute foundation, with event-driven execution, automatic scaling and per-millisecond billing. Around it: Aurora Serverless for databases with variable load, API Gateway for secure APIs with request validation and caching, EventBridge as the event bus between decoupled services and SaaS providers, S3 for storage and event triggers, and CloudWatch for logs, alarms and dashboards that can kick off automated remediation.

The anonymised case studies make the pitch concrete: a fintech that moved transaction processing to Lambda and DynamoDB and reports a 45% infrastructure cost cut, a healthcare analytics platform reporting 52% lower operating expenditure, and a retail recommendation engine brought down to 200 millisecond responses.

## Pipelines and least privilege are not optional

Srikar is firm that serverless needs mature DevOps. Infrastructure as code with CloudFormation or the Serverless Framework, builds with CodeBuild, CodePipeline deploying functions, API configuration and database changes together, ephemeral test environments, contract tests for APIs, and canary deployments combined with feature flags.

Security shifts to the function level: one tightly scoped IAM role per Lambda, secrets in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation, strict schema validation at the API Gateway boundary, dependency scanning in CI/CD, and KMS for encryption at rest and in transit. He also sketches a serverless analytics pipeline (EventBridge, Kinesis, Lambda, S3 and Redshift, QuickSight) for real-time business intelligence.

## Where to start

The roadmap is the part to take home. Assess the current architecture first. Pick stateless services such as API endpoints and data transformation tasks. Look for variable or unpredictable workloads; services with a peak-to-trough traffic ratio of five to one or higher benefit most from Lambda's scaling and pay-per-use model.

## Who should watch

Teams scoping a serverless migration for a SaaS product on AWS, and engineers who want one session that names every moving part. The statistics are numerous and come from cited studies rather than measurements shown in the talk, so use them as prompts for your own benchmarks.

Title: Event-driven middleware for healthcare claims and eligibility
Description: Suman Neela of AppsTek at Conf42 Golang 2025 on real-time integration for payors, with event-driven claim status, message brokers and edge processing.
Body:
Manual claims processing can take up to 30 days, and eligibility checks have been known to take hours. At [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Suman Neela](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Suman_Neela_payor_claims_integration) of AppsTek described how healthcare payors replace those waits with real-time data integration: middleware between legacy and modern systems, event-driven claim status updates, cloud message brokers and, eventually, processing at the point of care.

This is an integration architecture talk for the US healthcare payor world, with no Go content. It's most useful if you build claims, eligibility or provider-facing systems and want the target architecture in one place.

## Three problems in payor operations

Neela starts with manual processing bottlenecks, data scattered across systems (which causes eligibility errors and slow claims resolution), and the compliance burden of HIPAA and interoperability mandates on fragmented systems. The organisations that have adopted real-time integration, he said, report faster claims processing, fewer denials, shorter integration development with middleware such as Dell Boomi, and very high data accuracy.

## The layered architecture

His backbone for a modern payor system stacks business applications (claims engines, eligibility verification, member portals) on a secure REST API management layer, over a middleware layer for real-time transformation, intelligent message routing and workflow orchestration, on top of distributed databases and cloud warehouses, all running on a hybrid of elastic cloud and legacy on-prem infrastructure. Middleware is the piece that keeps legacy and new systems talking in both directions while enforcing security and compliance.

## Claims as a stream of events

The claim lifecycle he walks through is submission (electronic claims validated immediately against member data and provider contracts, including format checks), adjudication (business rules, benefit calculations and contract terms applied in real time), payment determination and status communication. The event-driven part is the status: when a claim changes state, the system publishes an event and every connected system and stakeholder gets the update.

The numbers he gave are the before-and-after targets of this approach: eligibility checks from about 1.5 hours to 0.3 seconds, claim status updates from three to four hours to half a second, prior authorisation from 48 hours to five seconds, and full adjudication from 72 hours to 30 seconds, with message brokers handling over 10,000 messages per second at peak. These are presented as achievable results, not measured on a named deployment. Open enrollment is the load test this design has to survive.

## AI and edge processing come next

Beyond the core, Neela sees ML predicting claim outcomes and routing, real-time fraud detection on claim patterns, NLP pulling clinical context from unstructured notes, and autonomous resolution of routine issues. Edge computing moves simple eligibility and claim checks into hospitals and clinics, cutting latency and bandwidth (useful in rural areas) and letting facilities keep working during network outages.

His roadmap: assess the integration architecture and add middleware connectors and brokers in the first six months, move claims to a fully event-driven design with AI-assisted adjudication and provider APIs by month 18, then aim for near-instant standard claims and predictive intervention.

## Who should watch

Integration engineers and architects at payors, TPAs or health tech vendors, and anyone who has to explain to leadership why the claims backlog is an architecture problem. Go developers can skip this one.

Title: Privacy-preserving search works, but it isn't free
Description: Siddharth Pratap Singh of Dell Technologies at Conf42 Golang 2025 on PIR, homomorphic encryption, federated learning and the latency they cost search.
Body:
Imagine checking a book out of a library without the library learning which book you took. That's private information retrieval, and at [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Siddharth Pratap Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Siddharth_Pratap_Singh_search_privacy_performance) of Dell Technologies used it to open a tour of privacy-preserving search: the cryptography that makes it possible, the machine learning techniques that keep training data private, and an honest look at what it does to relevance and latency.

It's a conceptual overview rather than a Go or code session, and a well-paced one. Its best quality is that it doesn't pretend privacy comes at no cost.

## Privacy by design, not by patch

Singh traces search from simple keyword matching to today's systems that analyse behaviour and predict intent. More personalisation means more data collected, and GDPR and CCPA pushed engineers to rethink the design. His three principles: privacy by design (built into every layer up front, no bandaid fixes), data minimisation (collect only what the function needs) and encryption at rest, in transit and during processing.

## The cryptographic toolkit

The technical core is a short catalogue:

- **Private information retrieval (PIR)**: fetch data from a server without revealing the query, built on lattice-based cryptography and homomorphic encryption.
- **Secure multi-party computation**: several parties compute a result together without sharing raw inputs. His image is solving a puzzle while keeping your pieces hidden.
- **Query obfuscation**: randomising searches so the pattern reveals less.
- **Distributed trust**: no single party or node holds the keys to everything.

## Keeping the ML pipeline private

For machine learning he covers federated learning (hospitals can train a diagnostic model together without sharing patient records), differential privacy (calibrated noise so no individual stands out), homomorphic encryption (math on a locked safe without opening it) and secure enclaves (hardware-isolated environments for sensitive operations). Together they cover training through deployment.

## The trade-offs

This is the section to watch. Singh was frank that stronger protections cost performance. Search relevance drops as privacy measures tighten; his metaphor is a librarian who whispers answers and sometimes gets them wrong. Query latency rises because every request passes through more systems, and computational costs climb. The mitigations he described are real-time accuracy monitoring, automated resource allocation and adaptive tuning: maximise privacy without turning search into a snail.

## Healthcare, law and finance

His use cases are the high-stakes ones. In healthcare, granular permissions let authorised clinicians retrieve the records they need in an emergency, with audit trails logging every access under HIPAA and GDPR. Legal discovery platforms search mountains of confidential documents during investigations. Financial systems let customers query portfolios and tax history over encrypted data. He reported high success rates across these sectors and suggested a rollout path: modular architecture, incremental upgrades around legacy systems, monitoring and incident response drills, and performance tuning.

## Who should watch

Engineers building search or retrieval over sensitive data (health records, legal documents, financial history) who need a vocabulary for the options and an honest sense of their cost. Cryptographers will find it introductory; that's the point.

- [Confidential computing with Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Moritz_Eckert_confidential_computing_Intel_SGX_security_cloud_native) by Moritz Eckert at Conf42 Golang 2021, the secure enclave idea in practice.
- [The Privacy Predicament: Averting the Perils of Data-Hungry Language Models](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Pratik_Thantharate_privacy_predicament_datahungry) by Pratik Thantharate at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

Title: Synthetic data works best mixed with real data, not instead of it
Description: Pradeep Kumar Vattumilli at Conf42 SRE 2025 on synthetic data for AI training in healthcare and autonomous vehicles, and why hybrid sets win.
Body:
Synthetic data solves the privacy and scarcity problems of AI training, but it does not escape the need for real data: the generators still have to learn from something. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Pradeep Kumar Vattumilli of JNTU Kakinada gave an overview of synthetic data in AI, with healthcare and autonomous vehicles as the main examples, and the most useful slide in the deck is the one where real and synthetic data are combined.

This is an introductory survey rather than a hands-on build. If you need a map of where synthetic data helps and where it bites, it covers the ground in a short watch.

## What synthetic data is for

Pradeep frames synthetic data as artificially generated records that mirror real-world scenarios, produced with techniques such as GANs, variational autoencoders and transformer-based models. The pitch has three parts: privacy, because there are no real personal identifiers in the output; scarcity, because you can generate volume on demand; and coverage, because you can create the rare and dangerous edge cases real collection rarely captures.

He cites a projection that 60% of AI training data would be synthetic by 2025, and reports that organisations see around 40% shorter development cycles. In healthcare, he says, synthetic data can keep up to 90% of the original patient data's statistical significance while removing re-identification risk.

## The use cases: hospitals and highways

Healthcare gets the most time: drug discovery, diagnostics and clinical trial simulations that need fewer participants while keeping statistical power. Autonomous vehicles are the second showcase. Synthetic pipelines generate more than 50,000 unique traffic scenarios, including rare events and adverse weather, which is the kind of test set nobody wants to collect by actually driving into a hailstorm.

## The catch: generators need good real data

The section on data quality and validation is the honest middle of the talk. In medical imaging, Pradeep says current generative models need a minimum of roughly one thousand diverse real patient cases before synthetic production scales well, and quality metrics drop significantly with smaller datasets. Garbage in, plausible-looking garbage out.

That leads to his strongest argument: hybrid approaches. Combining real and synthetic data, he reports CT accuracy rising from 82% to 94%, MRI fidelity from 78% to 96%, rare disease representation from 61% to 88%, and model generalisation from 70% to 93%. Whatever your domain, the shape of the lesson travels: use synthetic data to fill the gaps in a real dataset, not to replace it.

## Validation and standards close the loop

Pradeep ends with technology and process. On the technology side, neural-network-based validation frameworks continuously check the quality of generated data. On the process side, standardised approaches and quality frameworks are what let organisations scale synthetic data while staying compliant. For anyone in reliability, the parallel is obvious: a data generator is a production dependency and deserves the same monitoring as any other.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and data teams weighing synthetic data for regulated domains, and SREs who support ML pipelines and want the vocabulary. The figures in the talk are reported results without much detail on how they were measured, so treat them as direction rather than benchmarks.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [The Privacy Predicament: Averting the Perils of Data-Hungry Language Models](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Pratik_Thantharate_privacy_predicament_datahungry) by Pratik Thantharate covers the privacy pressure that makes synthetic data attractive.
- [Data Quality and Validation in ML Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sunil_Kumar_Mudusu_data_quality_validation) by Sunil Kumar Mudusu goes deeper on the validation step.
- [AI for Chaos-Resilient Data Quality](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Shashank_Reddy_Beeravelly_ai_data_quality) by Shashank Reddy Beeravelly treats data quality as a reliability problem.

Title: Surgical robots work best as partners that learn from surgeons
Description: Rajarshi Tarafdar of JP Morgan Chase at Conf42 SRE 2025 on human-AI symbiotic robotics, from tremor filtering to bidirectional learning in surgery.
Body:
The goal of an AI-assisted surgical robot is not to replace the surgeon; it is to steady the hand, sharpen the view and take on the mechanical work so the human can focus on judgment. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Rajarshi Tarafdar of JP Morgan Chase presented human-AI symbiotic robotics: systems built on a continuous feedback loop where both the person and the machine get better over time.

It is an unusual talk for an SRE conference, and that is part of its appeal. Swap "surgery" for "production" and many of the design questions (latency budgets, intent prediction, human override, accountability) are ones reliability engineers argue about every week.

## Four subsystems, one loop

Rajarshi describes the architecture as four integrated subsystems: multimodal perception through sensor fusion, an AI prediction engine built on machine learning, physical actuators for precise mechanical response, and bidirectional interfaces that carry communication both ways between human and AI. Sensors collect the environment, the models learn from real-time feedback, and the actuators turn computed decisions into physical movement.

The surgical use case is where the numbers live. He cites improvements in decision latency, tissue manipulation accuracy, minor complication rates and patient stay, plus about a 25% reduction in unnecessary instrument movements and a cognitive load reduction of around 28%. The point he draws is that the surgeon's attention moves from routine mechanics to critical decisions.

## Superhuman precision, human limits

The case for robotics in microsurgery starts from human limits: natural hand tremor, precision that degrades with fatigue, and limited visual perception at small scales. AI-assisted systems answer with tremor filtering, motion scaling and magnified visual feedback, holding sub-millimetre precision in the most demanding procedures. Rajarshi argues this makes some procedures possible that were previously too risky for patients.

## The hard parts are latency, intent and proof

He does not oversell. The technical challenges he lists are latency management for critical applications, which needs new communication protocols and computational architectures; intent prediction, where current algorithms reach about 94.2% accuracy in predictable scenarios but struggle with novel situations and expert techniques that deviate from training patterns; and safety verification, since formally verifying these systems remains hard.

That middle one should sound familiar. A model that is right 94% of the time on the happy path and unsure on the long tail is exactly the shape of every on-call problem with ML in it.

## Learning goes both ways

The most interesting idea is bidirectional learning. Surgeons teach the system their techniques, which get captured and encoded into the models, while the AI feeds back insights that improve human decision-making. Communication runs over several channels at once: voice commands and confirmations, gaze tracking for attention-based control, gesture recognition, and haptic feedback for force and touch.

Ethics gets its own section: clear boundaries on the AI's decision authority with meaningful human oversight, protocols for collecting surgical data with patient consent, frameworks for attributing responsibility when outcomes come from joint decisions, and equitable access across health systems and regions. Rajarshi closes by pointing the same principles at manufacturing, space exploration, disaster response and micro-scale scientific work.

## Who should watch

Engineers curious about human-in-the-loop AI beyond chat interfaces, anyone working on robotics or medical devices, and SREs who want a fresh angle on latency and override design. This is a high-level overview of the field rather than an implementation walkthrough, and it is not about running production systems.

Title: AI in the cloud lands on the SRE's desk, ethics included
Description: Sanjeev Pellikoduku of SLB at Conf42 SRE 2025 on the security, operations and ethics work SREs inherit when AI moves into cloud systems.
Body:
When a company bolts AI onto its cloud platform, the reliability team inherits three new problems at once: protecting training data and models, operating a stack that behaves less predictably, and answering for whether the system is fair. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Sanjeev Pellikoduku, Senior Cloud Software Engineer at SLB, mapped all three and argued that the fix is the same every time: get SRE involved at design time, not after launch.

This is a survey talk. It moves quickly across security, operations and governance rather than drilling into one implementation, so treat it as a checklist for an AI readiness review.

## Security means protecting the model, not just the box

Sanjeev puts data privacy at the top of the list. Teams struggle to protect sensitive training data while keeping models accurate, and the models themselves need defending against adversarial attacks that try to manipulate outputs or extract confidential information.

The countermeasures he walks through are the privacy-preserving toolkit: homomorphic encryption, which allows computation on encrypted data without decrypting it; secure enclaves that give hardware-level isolation for model inference; and differential privacy, a mathematical framework that limits how much any individual record leaks while keeping the data useful. None of these is free in performance terms, and part of the SRE job is keeping the system fast while they are switched on.

## Operating AI needs more AI

On the operations side, the challenges are familiar but sharper: integration debt, deployment difficulty, monitoring gaps and cost that is hard to predict. His operational answers are AI-powered monitoring with predictive anomaly detection and automated remediation, a service mesh for visibility and control across microservices, MLOps frameworks to streamline model deployment and versioning, and dynamic resource allocation to keep GPU and compute spend in check.

The slogan he uses for the AIOps piece is simple: use AI to manage AI. It is also the most quietly recursive idea of the conference, and it works only if someone still watches the watcher.

## Ethics is an operational concern

The section that sets this talk apart is ethics, framed as four pillars: fairness and bias mitigation, explainability and transparency, regulatory compliance, and human oversight. Sanjeev's point is that SREs cannot hand this off entirely. They need to work alongside ethics specialists and data scientists, because the controls (model documentation, bias detection, explainability tooling) live in the same pipelines SREs already run.

## What early involvement buys

The case study is a financial services AI transformation. The lesson Sanjeev draws is that the key to its success was involving SRE early in the AI system design, so reliability and security requirements were addressed from the start rather than retrofitted. He reports operational costs dropping by 31% alongside the improvements.

His best-practice list closes the loop: shift security left with automated scanning of AI components, define cloud resources and model deployments as infrastructure as code for versioning and fast recovery, integrate AIOps for intelligent monitoring and remediation, and set up regular knowledge sharing between data science and SRE teams.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform leads about to take on an AI workload, and engineering managers who need a structured list of what "AI-ready" should mean for security, operations and governance. Specialists in any one of these areas will want a deeper talk on their slice; the value here is seeing all three side by side.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Ethical Data Engineering: Privacy, Bias, and Fairness in AI Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Arun_Vivek_Supramanian_privacy_engineering_ethical) by Arun Vivek Supramanian goes deeper on the data side of the ethics pillars.
- [How AIOps Drives Operational Resilience on AWS](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Indika_Wimalasuriya_aiops_resilience_aws) by Indika Wimalasuriya shows the "AI managing AI" idea on a concrete cloud.
- [Ethical AI in Healthcare: Bias, Privacy, and Trust in Kube-Native Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Venus_Garg_ethical_ai_trust) by Venus Garg applies similar principles in a regulated domain.

Title: Conf42 LLMs 2025 roundup: evals, attacks and agents in production
Description: Conf42 Large Language Models 2025 in review, from evals and AI testing AI to BadGPT and prompt injection, hierarchical agents and fine-tuning economics.
Body:
In March 2025 the question at [Conf42 Large Language Models 2025](https://www.conf42.com/llms2025) was no longer whether to build on LLMs but how to know the thing you built works, and how someone might break it. The 39 talks, streamed online on March 20, 2025, split roughly into three camps: people measuring model behaviour, people attacking it, and people wiring models into agents and products. Speakers came from Arato.ai, Kusho, Palisade, Microsoft, AWS, PayPal, IBM, Lime, Warner Bros. Discovery and others.

## You can't ship what you can't measure

[Hilik Paz](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Hilik_Paz_evaluate_evals) (Arato.ai) laid out why testing changes with LLMs: well-defined outputs and errors give way to unpredictable ones, identical inputs can produce different answers, and pass or fail turns into scoring across several dimensions. Good evals, in his framing, are measurable, repeatable and actionable, and the talk covers building the test dataset that gets a prompt all the way to production.

[Sourabh Gawande](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Sourabh_Gawande_applications_practices_tradeoffs) (Kusho) brought the engineering view from 18 months of building Kusho's API-testing agent: retries and timeouts from day one, schema validation with Pydantic, Server-Sent Events for streaming, Redis-backed task queues for long jobs, and promptfoo evals in CI, which he called unit testing for prompts. [Robin Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Robin_Gupta_test_systems_process) (Testzeus) used AI to test AI, combining rule-based and model-based checks for bias, hallucinations and inconsistencies with open source tools, and [Ankush Sharma](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Ankush_Sharma_observability_models_predictions) applied SRE practices to observability for LLM systems.

## Attacks are cheaper than you think

The security track was the event's most sobering. [Dmitriy Volkov](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Dmitriy_Volkov_hacking_underrated_security) (Palisade) presented BadGPT, a fine-tuning poisoning attack that strips safety measures from a model without hurting its performance or adding token overhead. His title, "LLM hacking is underrated", was the thesis. [Jorrik Kiijnsma](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Jorrik_Kiijnsma_attacks_risks_security) (Sopra Steria) live-coded prompt injection attacks against LLM-powered web apps and the defences against them, the best kind of talk to send a frontend team.

[Kartheek Medhavi Penagamuri Shriram](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Kartheek_Medhavi_Penagamuri_Shriram_threats_risks_defenses) (Microsoft) walked through the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications, [Jose Manuel Ortega](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Jose_Manuel_Ortega_security_auditing_tools) surveyed security and auditing tools, and [Balaji Thadagam Kandavel](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Balaji_Thadagam_Kandavel_code_data_security) (Cox Automotive) made the case for deploying and fine-tuning in-house so your code and IP don't feed someone else's next model.

## Agents, RAG and the build-or-tune question

[Aleksandr Khramogin](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Aleksandr_Khramogin_sequential_agents_hierarchical) (LogicBoost) moved past sequential agent chains to hierarchical planning, with specialised agents that decompose complex tasks, built in Python with LangChain, CrewAI and OpenAI's API. [Sandeep Kumar P](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Sandeep_Kumar_P_data_insights_amazon) (AntStack) set out to show that RAG, vector databases and multi-stage flows only seem complex because they're explained badly, using Amazon Bedrock. [Manish Ballal](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Manish_Ballal_automation_process_operations) (AWS) looked at agentic automation in business process operations.

[Muddassar Sharif](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Muddassar_Sharif_fine_tuning_business) (Virtuans.ai) asked the question every team eventually faces: is fine-tuning worth the data, compute and people it needs, or is RAG the better fit? [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Peter_De_Tender_azure_models_management) (Microsoft) showed Azure AI Foundry hosting models from several vendors, [Graziano Casto](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Graziano_Casto_workloads_cloud_environments) (Mia-Platform) the gaps in running AI workloads on Kubernetes, and [Shoeb Bustani](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Shoeb_Bustani_aws_reviews_architecture) (AWS) generative AI speeding up Well-Architected reviews.

## LLMs inside real products

Some of the most concrete talks were product case studies. [Rustam Musin](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Rustam_Musin_automated_content_localization) built automated podcast localisation in Kotlin, chaining Whisper for transcription, GPT-4 for refinement and translation, and LLM-powered speech synthesis. [Kaan Tas](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Kaan_Tas_task_pricing_costs) (Lime) applied AI to pricing warehouse tasks dynamically by task density and demand. Title: Grounding a chat model in your documents with embeddings
Description: Pushpalatha KR of HP at Conf42 SRE 2025 on a retrieval approach that embeds uploaded documents, searches them semantically and feeds context to a chat model.
Body:
A general-purpose chat model knows a lot about the world and nothing about your documents. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Pushpalatha KR, Senior Software Engineer at HP, showed a retrieval approach that closes that gap: encode the user's documents and questions as high-dimensional embeddings, use semantic search to find the relevant passages, and put them in the prompt for a chat completion model.

This is a short talk, a few minutes long, and an introduction to the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pattern with a small demo. If you already run a RAG pipeline in production, you know this ground; if you are explaining the idea to a colleague, it is a compact walkthrough.

## The problem: lots of documents, no context

Her starting point is information overload. Reviewing and analysing large volumes of unstructured documents is slow, and generic models answer without the domain knowledge or context the business needs. She also argues that classic NLP models, such as sentiment analysis, are less accurate when the task depends on understanding context.

## The pipeline

The solution architecture is the standard RAG flow, described step by step:

1. A user uploads a document, which is converted to text.
2. A text embedding model turns that text into vectors, stored in a vector database.
3. When a new prompt arrives, it is embedded the same way and a similarity search pulls the closest passages.
4. A similarity threshold filters what counts as relevant context.
5. The chosen passages go into the prompt, and the chat completion model returns a domain-grounded answer.

She adds that fine-tuning can improve results further when large amounts of domain material are available up front, and that analysing sentiment and context in the uploaded content helps the responses fit the circumstances, not just the facts.

## The demo

The demo is a simple web app: upload a document (she uses a school English or science textbook), see its contents, then ask questions about it in a chat panel. Answers come back grounded in the uploaded material rather than the model's general knowledge. It is a modest demo, but it makes the moving parts concrete, which is what a first look at RAG needs.

## What the talk leaves for later

Since it is brief, several production questions are out of scope: chunking strategy, how the threshold is tuned, which embedding model and vector store were used, and how answer quality is evaluated. Those are the next things to look up before building your own.

## Who should watch

Developers and SREs who keep hearing about embeddings and vector search and want the shortest possible explanation of how the pieces connect. Anyone already debugging retrieval quality should go straight to the related talks below.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Veliswa Boya on vector embeddings and RAG, demystified](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Veliswa_Boya_rag_embeddings_vector), a fuller beginner-friendly explanation.
- [Zain Hasan on building chatbots with advanced RAG techniques](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Zain_Hasan_chatbots_retrievalaugmented_building).
- [Ofer Mendelevitch on measuring hallucinations in RAG](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Ofer_Mendelevitch_rag_measuring_hallucinations), for when the demo works and you need to know how well.

Title: SRE and DevOps share goals but solve different problems
Description: Tajudeen Oyindamola Tajudeen of JP Morgan Chase at Conf42 SRE 2025 on where SRE and DevOps differ, where they overlap, and how to stop them fighting.
Body:
SRE and DevOps are not two labels for the same job, and they are not rivals either. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Tajudeen Oyindamola Tajudeen, a software engineer at JP Morgan Chase & Co., argued that the two share the same goals but solve different problems, and that teams get the best results when they stop picking a side.

This is a short, beginner-friendly talk, and it says so by its pace: a crisp map of the two disciplines rather than a war story. If you have ever been in a meeting where someone asked what the difference really is, this is the answer you wish you had ready.

## Cousins with different personalities

Tajudeen's framing is that SRE and DevOps are cousins. DevOps grew out of the need to break down the silos between development and operations: move fast, automate everything, you build it, you run it. SRE was born at Google and asks a different question: how do we engineer reliability into the system, so that software does not just work but keeps working?

Both love automation. Both lean on the same tools, from Kubernetes to Terraform, and both depend on a blameless culture. The difference is the scoreboard. DevOps success is typically measured by deployment frequency; SRE cares about uptime and adds the metrics to prove it, starting with SLIs. DevOps lives in CI/CD tooling; SRE lives in monitoring dashboards. Put simply, DevOps tears down the walls while SRE builds the guardrails.

## Error budgets are where the friction starts

The part he calls the "secret weapon" is the error budget. It turns risk into a number. If a service burns through its allowed downtime for the month, SRE may hold feature releases until reliability recovers. From the DevOps side of the room that looks like a speed bump, and that is exactly where the arguments begin: one team says ship, the other says it is not reliable enough yet.

His fix is boring in the best way. Align the two perspectives early. Bring SREs into sprint planning, define SLOs together, and share both the blame and the credit. A release freeze that everyone agreed to in advance is a policy; one that arrives as a surprise is a turf war.

## Pick by stage, borrow from both

Tajudeen does not pretend there is one right answer. Startups often lean DevOps because getting the product to market comes first. Enterprises with complex systems tend to care more about reliability, and SRE practices pay off there. The best teams, he says, borrow from both, and he points to Netflix running SRE for streaming while using DevOps for its internal tools.

A short illustrative case study makes the point concrete: a SaaS company whose DevOps team is burning out on nightly outages brings in SRE to set SLOs and track error budgets in the CI/CD pipeline. The outcome he describes is fewer midnight outages, which is the only KPI on-call engineers truly care about. His rule of thumb follows naturally: if reliability issues keep piling up, that is a signal to add SRE thinking.

## Small first steps

The closing advice is practical. Add SLOs to your next sprint. Invite an SRE to a DevOps retro. Start measuring SLIs for critical services. Read the Google SRE books alongside the DevOps ones. Tiny steps, as he puts it, lead to big wins.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to reliability work, managers trying to decide whether they need an SRE team, and anyone who has to explain the difference to a hiring committee. Seasoned SREs will not find new techniques here, but they may find a cleaner way to explain error budgets to the people who resent them.

- [CICD: The SRE-DevOps Overlay](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Safeer_CM_Garima_Bajpai_cicd_sre_devops_overlay) by Safeer CM and Garima Bajpai looks at the same overlap through the delivery pipeline.

Title: Go in healthcare, education and sustainability projects
Description: Satish Puram of Deloitte at Conf42 Golang 2025 on Go-based systems for telemedicine, learning platforms and energy monitoring, and what made them land.
Body:
Most Go talks are about latency and throughput. At [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Satish Puram](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Satish_Puram_healthcare_sustainability_impact) of Deloitte, a specialist leader with 22 years of consulting experience in digital and financial transformation, pointed the same qualities at a different target: telemedicine platforms, learning management systems and energy monitoring, where uptime and concurrency translate into patients seen and classrooms that keep working.

It's a consultant's-eye view built on outcome metrics, with no code. Its real value is the second half, on why these projects succeed or stall.

## Telemedicine under a pandemic load

Puram's healthcare story is about scale arriving overnight. Before the pandemic, he said, telemedicine adoption sat around 8%, with large urban and rural gaps. When COVID-19 hit, platforms had to grow capacity within weeks. In his account, Go-based telemedicine infrastructure now reaches most previously underserved communities, kept 99.8% uptime while handling three times pre-pandemic patient volumes, and rural adoption has caught up with urban rates. He also credited Go-powered EHR implementations with reducing clinician burnout through better care coordination and real-time clinical data exchange.

## Learning platforms that stay up during exams

For education he described learning management systems with 99.7% uptime even at peak usage, more efficient teacher workflows, automated grading that shortens feedback cycles, and accessibility features: real-time translation across 47 languages and screen reader integration that increased participation among students with disabilities. The shared thread with healthcare is that the users most likely to give up on a slow or flaky system are the ones the project exists to reach.

## Concurrency for energy and supply chain monitoring

The sustainability section uses Go's concurrency model for energy management: track consumption with millisecond precision, let ML spot inefficiency patterns, and allocate resources automatically. Puram reported these systems finding 15-20% of previously undetected energy waste. He also described Go-based supply chain platforms with blockchain-backed records that improved end-to-end visibility and sped up supplier onboarding.

All the figures in the talk come from consulting engagements and are presented without methodology, so read them as case-study claims.

## What made the projects work

This part generalises beyond Go:

- **Agile delivery**: fast prototyping and short feedback loops to validate assumptions early.
- **User-centred design**: field testing with the actual beneficiaries, not proxies.
- **Cross-functional teams**: developers working directly with clinicians, educators and sustainability specialists.
- **Data governance**: privacy frameworks and data quality controls from the start.

On challenges, he named legacy integration (API-first design and phased migration), organisational change (training and transparent communication) and technical complexity (breaking problems into manageable services with good documentation).

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads working on public-interest, health or education projects who want examples of where Go shows up outside infrastructure tooling, and anyone making the case for a cross-functional team. If you want implementation detail, this is a talk about outcomes, not code.

Title: Using AI to read 5.2 million lines of COBOL before you migrate them
Description: Sanath Chilakala of NTT DATA at Conf42 SRE 2025 on AI-assisted mainframe modernization, from dependency mapping to generated tests.
Body:
The hardest part of a mainframe migration is not writing the new system; it is understanding the old one. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Sanath Chilakala, Director of Digital Solution Architecture at NTT DATA, made the case for using AI first as a reader: mapping dependencies, mining old documentation and generating tests, so that a legacy core can move without the downtime nobody is allowed to have.

The talk centres on a financial services case study: a 30-year-old core banking system, about 5.2 million lines of COBOL, roughly 400 mission-critical dependent applications, and a strict zero-downtime requirement.

## Four reasons these projects go sideways

Sanath opens with the usual suspects, and they are usual for good reason. Legacy dependencies: decades of logic with limited documentation and tangled interdependencies. The knowledge gap: COBOL skills are scarce, so few people can even explain what the current code does. Operational risk: these systems run transaction-heavy workloads where downtime is expensive. And performance expectations: the new platform is expected to beat the old one, at scale, from day one.

None of that is news to anyone who has stood near a mainframe. What the talk adds is where AI fits against each item.

## Let the model read the manuals

The most practical idea is applying NLP to the existing documentation. Manuals and design docs get ingested, the system builds semantic mappings between components, and a knowledge graph ties the sources together. In the case study, that drove automated dependency mapping across the estate, the part of the job that usually eats months of interviews with the last people who remember why a batch job runs at 2am.

Sanath also shows AI-driven capacity prediction for the target platform, comparing traditional estimates and AI estimates against actual usage. He puts AI-driven prediction accuracy at around 95%, against 60 to 70% for even mature traditional approaches.

## Testing is the real bottleneck

He is blunt that manual testing has always been the weak spot in migration planning. His AI testing framework has four parts: generating test scenarios from documentation, user stories and product docs; executing them automatically and pointing at the failing code; recognising patterns across test runs to inform later migrations; and refining the test set as the model learns, for better coverage over time.

For the banking case study, the outcomes he reports are a 72% reduction in critical production incidents, a migration timeline cut by 14 months, $4.3 million in cost savings, and 99.998% uptime maintained throughout.

## A phased rollout, and honest mitigations

The implementation framework is sensible and unglamorous: assess and catalogue systems with automated discovery, pilot on a small MVP, integrate AI tooling into existing SRE practice (code analysis, predictive monitoring, automated testing), then scale across the enterprise. The mitigations section is worth a listen too: data cleansing pipelines and quality scoring with human review for edge cases, using AI to quantify and prioritise technical debt, and pairing scarce mainframe veterans with AI specialists so knowledge actually transfers.

The closing segment turns to quantum computing as a future direction for optimisation, security and capacity planning. Sanath is clear that this is not here today, so treat it as a look ahead rather than a plan.

## Who should watch

Architects and SREs facing a mainframe or other legacy-core migration, especially in banking or insurance, and anyone who needs to argue for AI-assisted discovery and testing budget. If you want code-level COBOL refactoring techniques, this talk stays at the architecture and programme level.

Title: Keeping conversational AI under 300 ms when the model is a black box
Description: Raghu Chukkala of Verizon at Conf42 SRE 2025 on SRE for contact center AI with four-layer observability, automated remediation and AI-aware chaos tests.
Body:
A chatbot that fails is not a 500 page somebody retries later: it is an annoyed customer, live, on the phone or in the chat window. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Raghu Chukkala, Lead AI Chatbot Engineer and Architect at Verizon, walked through how his team runs Contact Center AI (CCAI) at a 99.99% uptime target and a 300 millisecond response ceiling, and why classic monitoring was not enough to get there.

The headline number in the talk is a 73% cut in mean time to recovery through automation. The more useful part is how they got it.

## Your dashboards do not understand your model

Raghu's starting point is that traditional monitoring was never built for AI systems. The transformer-based NLP models behind intent recognition and response generation are black boxes: you cannot inspect their internal state the way you inspect a microservice. Traffic is irregular, with spikes from product launches, seasonal sales or a random social media moment, so threshold-based alerting misfires. And a single conversation can touch CRMs, speech engines, databases and third-party APIs, so a small backend failure ripples through the whole AI stack.

His answer is a four-layer observability model:

- **Business impact**: conversation completion rate and customer satisfaction.
- **Model performance**: intent accuracy, fallback rate, entity extraction quality.
- **System performance**: latency, error rate, throughput.
- **Infrastructure**: CPU, memory, disk, saturation.

The point of stacking them is correlation. A rise in fallback responses can then be traced to its cause, whether that is model drift, a slow backend or a starved node.

## Failure modes that only AI systems have

The section on recurring failure patterns is the one to bookmark. Intent classification degrades gradually, for example when a new product name or new slang appears and accuracy slides over time. Small backend delays compound through the AI pipeline into latency cascades. A single edge-case query can eat enough memory or CPU to hurt every other session. And one external API going down can take out the entire conversational flow.

Naming these patterns matters because each one becomes something to detect, alert on and test for.

## Chaos engineering, aimed at the AI layer

Raghu's chaos experiments target the model, not just the infrastructure: corrupted conversation memory, misclassified intents in sequence, model components failing from memory overflow. The loop is the familiar one (hypothesis, targeted experiment with safety controls, analysis, hardening), pointed at the failure modes above.

Remediation is automated the same way: ML-based anomaly detection, automatic triage into known classes like intent degradation or resource starvation, then actions such as scaling, rerouting, throttling or restarting a service, with each incident feeding back into future detection. Under extreme load the team trades model weight for speed, switching to lighter models or temporarily reducing precision, alongside predictive autoscaling, token-based routing and conversation sharding across clusters.

## Ship models like you ship risky code

New models go through shadow testing (running beside production without serving users), then a canary slice of traffic, then a gradual ramp with automated rollback, then full rollout. Raghu also ties SLOs to cost: tracking latency, throughput, utilisation and intent accuracy lets the team right-size GPU capacity off-peak, and he reports 30 to 40% cost savings from aligning SLOs with real user needs.

## Who should watch

SREs inheriting an AI-powered product, especially chat or voice, and ML engineers who have never had to think about MTTR. If you already run LLM features in production, the failure-pattern list and the layered metrics are the takeaways.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Scaling Conversational AI in Production](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Manoj_Kumar_Vunnava_scaling_conversational_ai) by Manoj Kumar Vunnava covers the contact center problem from the MLOps side.

Title: Static BI dashboards can't keep up with healthcare data
Description: Satya Manesh Veerapaneni of Dazzlon at Conf42 Golang 2025 on AI-augmented BI in healthcare, from claims fraud to readmission prediction and KPI alerts.
Body:
Traditional business intelligence was built for data that doubles once a year. At [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Satya Manesh Veerapaneni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Satya_Manesh_Veerapaneni_healthcare_bi_analytics) of Dazzlon argued that healthcare data, by the estimate he cited, doubles every 73 days and is about 80% unstructured, so template-driven reports miss the patterns that matter. His answer is BI augmented with machine learning, NLP and computer vision, applied to claims fraud, chronic disease prediction and KPI monitoring.

One expectation to reset: although the event is Conf42 Golang and the abstract mentions Go, the talk itself is about healthcare analytics and doesn't discuss Go. It's an overview with ranges drawn from industry research, not a single system's results.

## From descriptive reports to predictive ones

Classic BI relies on predefined templates and queries. That's fine for monthly reporting and blind to anything you didn't think to ask. Veerapaneni's shift is to machine learning for pattern detection, NLP to read clinical documents and computer vision for images. As an example of the gap, he cited diabetic retinopathy detection with AI reaching over 90% sensitivity and specificity, against around 70% for traditional methods.

## Fraud detection that adapts

Healthcare fraud costs an estimated 3-10% of total spending, and rule-based systems get outsmarted by new schemes while generating plenty of false positives. AI-augmented BI analyses billing patterns for statistical anomalies. He cited 70-90% detection accuracy and 30-50% fewer false positives for such systems, with the key benefit that new fraud patterns can be caught without constant rule rewrites.

## Chronic disease and readmissions

For chronic disease management, deep learning models stratify patient risk, forecast treatment outcomes and predict readmissions. Veerapaneni cited 75-85% accuracy for readmission prediction, improved by 10-20% when social determinants of health data are included. The practical win is earlier intervention for the patients most likely to come back.

## KPI alerts that don't cry wolf

Manual tracking of dozens of KPIs leads to alert fatigue. AI-augmented monitoring adjusts thresholds based on historical and contextual factors and prioritises notifications; he cited 40-60% fewer low-value alerts. Natural language generation then turns numbers into short narrative explanations. Any on-call engineer will recognise the problem; this is the same fight, with hospital metrics instead of p99s.

## Data quality is the hard part

The most grounded section covers implementation. He noted that even established EHR systems can have critical fields missing in a large share of records, that organisations run many clinical and administrative systems that don't talk to each other, and that coding for the same clinical concept varies widely. Trust is the other barrier: clinicians want to know how a model reached its conclusion, so explainable AI, rigorous validation and continuous clinical input drive adoption. Looking ahead, he pointed to ambient intelligence, multimodal models and federated learning for privacy-preserving analytics.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and analysts in healthcare or insurance planning an AI layer over existing BI, and anyone who needs a quick map of where ML helps in hospital analytics. Go developers looking for code should skip it.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Transforming Population Health with Predictive BI, Risk Stratification & Geospatial Insights](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Satya_Manesh_Veerapaneni_predictive_bi_health), Veerapaneni's follow-up at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.
