Title: Teaching machines to work with meaning
Description: The next platform layer
Body:
# LLMs are no longer a side quest

There was a time when large language models felt like a fun experiment.

You tried a prompt, laughed at the output, maybe used it to rewrite an email, and moved on. That time is very much over.

Conf42 Large Language Models 2025 is all about what happens when LLMs move into production, decision-making, business workflows, and places where “oops” is not an acceptable outcome.

This conference covers the full LLM lifecycle. From how models are trained and evaluated, to fine-tuning, retrieval, agents, orchestration, and getting things safely into production. There are talks on evals, testing AI with AI, prompt injection, observability for LLMs, and what it actually takes to trust model output beyond demos.

Agents are a big theme. Hierarchical agents, agentic automation, task decomposition, and systems where models don’t just respond, but act. Some sessions focus on building these systems. Others focus on keeping them from doing something creative in all the wrong ways.

LLMs show up across real industries too. Finance, healthcare, payments, insurance, retail, media, and enterprise platforms all make an appearance. You’ll hear about fraud detection, compliance, customer experience, product management, and how businesses are trying to extract value without accidentally leaking data, IP, or sanity.

Security gets plenty of attention. LLM hacking, data leaks, auditing, threat models, and defending against prompt injection are all on the agenda. Because once LLMs touch real systems, they inherit all the same risks, plus a few new ones we’re still naming.

If LLMs are part of your stack, your roadmap, or your long-term anxiety, this one’s worth your time. The hype phase is fading. The real work has already started.

Title: Building LLM apps means retries, streaming, queues and evals
Description: Sourabh Gawande of Kusho AI at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on the plumbing every LLM app needs, from retries and schema checks to background jobs and evals.
Body:
Treat an LLM API like any other API and your app will break in production. That is the opening claim from Sourabh Gawande, co-founder and CTO of Kusho AI, at Conf42 Large Language Models 2025. Drawing on 18 months of building Kusho's AI agent for API testing, he walked through the unglamorous engineering that sits between a working prompt and a working product: retries, schema validation, streaming, background jobs and evals, with the specific libraries his team runs in production.

## Plan for the model to be wrong a few percent of the time

The root cause is simple: "LLMs are inherently non-deterministic." A stable REST API might fail around 0.1% of the time in his experience; even the most mature LLMs come in at roughly one to five percent depending on the task. Chain calls, feeding one response into the next prompt, and the error rate compounds. Sourabh's point is that this won't be fixed by waiting for better models. It's the application's job.

So retries and timeouts go in on day one, not after the first incident. In Python his team uses tenacity: a decorator on the function, with stop conditions (three attempts, ten seconds), fixed or random waits, and timeout decorators in the same package. LangChain users get a retry output parser that resends the prompt along with the failed output so the model knows what went wrong.

## Validate structure, then fix the prompt

Structured output is where most failures show up: extra fields, missing fields, a lost bracket. The fix is a schema library rather than hand-rolled checks. Pydantic on Python, Yup on JavaScript, with failed validation triggering a retry. Usually one or two retries clear it.

The useful nuance is cost in time. A call that should take five seconds can take 15 to 20 after retries, and users notice. If the same mistake keeps coming back (single quotes in JSON, say), put that rule in the prompt so the first answer is right. He also mentioned OpenAI's structured output mode, but prefers validation in the app: rely on one vendor's feature and switching to Claude or another provider gets harder.

## Stream short tasks, queue long ones

Users drop off well before ten seconds, and many LLM calls take five to ten. Streaming tokens as they arrive hides most of that. WebSockets work but mean a rewrite and possibly a different language; Server-Sent Events reuse your existing HTTP stack, and in Flask or FastAPI amount to a generator and a couple of headers. His recommendation: SSE, unless you truly need two-way traffic.

Streaming stops making sense when a task takes minutes. His example is an essay generator fed a hundred topics: do it in the request path and you tie up the backend for everyone else. Store the task, process it in the background, and notify the user by email or Slack, because they've left the tab. Start with a cron job polling the database. When you need more workers, move to a task queue. Kusho uses RQ (Redis Queue), which he says takes about 15 minutes to set up; they found Celery more than they needed.

## Evals are unit tests for prompts

The evals section is short and practical. Think of it, in his words, as "unit testing for your prompts": take a prompt template, run it against many inputs and several models, assert on the outputs, and compare cost. Hook it into CI so every build checks the prompts still behave. His team's pick is promptfoo, configured in YAML and available as open source or hosted.

## A provider tour with a timestamp on it

The talk closes with a quick tour of model APIs as they stood in early 2025: OpenAI as the versatile, reliable default; Anthropic's Claude for coding; Groq's custom chips for low latency; AWS Bedrock for keeping sensitive data inside AWS; Azure OpenAI, which was slightly faster in their tests but gated behind forms; and DeepSeek's open weights. The specific models have moved on since. The way of choosing (task fit, latency, data residency, reliability) still applies.

## Who should watch

Developers shipping their first LLM feature into an existing product, especially in Python. Experienced backend engineers will recognise every pattern; the value is in seeing which ones matter more with LLMs, and which libraries a small team found good enough. It is a talk by a vendor's CTO, but it's about engineering practice, not Kusho's product.

Title: Letting AI pick your chaos experiments
Description: Rahul Amte of Nivid Technologies at Conf42 SRE 2025 on adding ML to chaos engineering, from hypothesis generation to the tools that already support it.
Body:
Classic chaos engineering has a scaling problem: a human still has to decide what to break and then read the results. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Rahul Amte, Senior Cloud Engineer at Nivid Technologies, walked through how machine learning can take on both jobs, choosing experiments from observability data and analysing system behaviour as the experiment runs.

It's an introductory survey that starts from the basics, so it works well as a first talk on the topic for teams already doing some chaos work.

## The basics, briefly

Rahul recaps chaos engineering as controlled experiments that test whether a system holds up under turbulent conditions, a practice Netflix popularised with Chaos Monkey. The principles are the familiar list: define a steady-state hypothesis, introduce real-world disruptions, run in production, automate, and keep the blast radius small. The field has since grown from a single tool into an ecosystem including Gremlin, LitmusChaos and Chaos Toolkit, and it now plugs into CI/CD pipelines.

## Where the manual approach runs out

The limitation he names is human effort. Scenario selection is manual, analysis of results is barely automated, and that slows learning as systems grow. AI fits in at three points: generating dynamic test scenarios instead of a fixed library, predicting which components are likely to fail, and analysing behaviour in real time. The capabilities he lists are ML anomaly detection, failure forecasting, reinforcement learning for scenario planning, and NLP over past incident reports, which is a nicely underused data source.

## The workflow is a loop over your telemetry

His AI-assisted workflow runs from collecting observability data, to generating hypotheses, to designing experiments, injecting faults, and using real-time analytics for insight and remediation. The point he stresses is that the whole thing depends on the quality of your logging and monitoring data. He sketches a sample architecture on AWS that injects Chaos Monkey-style failures into EC2, with variants that take OpenTelemetry signals as input to anomaly detection models.

On tooling, his advice is to enhance rather than replace: Chaos Toolkit can use AI-based probes for validation, Gremlin can use ML insights to target attacks, and LitmusChaos supports AI-driven workflows.

## Keep a human in the loop

The challenges section is honest. AI adds complexity, models need tuning, data quality and governance become chaos engineering problems, and you have to decide how far to trust the model's choices. His best practices follow from that: start small in dev and sandbox environments, make the AI's decisions explainable, involve SRE, ML and DevOps teams together, and measure real impact with indicators such as availability and latency. He points to the awesome-chaos-engineering list on GitHub for tools, papers and community projects.

## Who should watch

Teams that run some chaos experiments and wonder what ML could add, and anyone who needs a broad map of the tools. Practitioners who want a detailed reinforcement learning setup or measured results won't find them here; the case studies are brief.

Title: Who gets left offline? Digital exclusion among older adults
Description: Rinku Mohan of Bettercoach at Conf42 SRE 2025 on research comparing digital exclusion of older adults across ten countries, and what drives it.
Body:
Every system we keep reliable assumes someone can actually use it. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Rinku Mohan, Senior Software Engineer at Bettercoach, presented research on how many older adults are digitally excluded, why, and how that changes between richer and poorer countries. The gap she found is wide: in her data, 11% of older adults in the United Kingdom were digitally excluded, against 91% in India.

This sat in the event's accessibility track, and it is a research talk rather than an engineering one. The abstract mentions tools like SSO; the talk itself spends its time on the study and its policy recommendations, so come for the evidence, not for an implementation.

## The study

Rinku compared five high-income countries (the United Kingdom, Germany, Austria, France and Estonia) with five lower and middle-income ones (India, Mexico, Brazil, Bulgaria and Romania), using ageing survey data from 2019 to 2023. The analysis combined principal component analysis to find the main drivers, chi-square tests to see whether exclusion tracks country type and age group, and ANOVA to compare life satisfaction and self-rated health between included and excluded people.

The context slide is sobering on its own. Internet use drops sharply in the older age bands, and old-age dependency ratios in most of the countries studied sit above 50 older people per 100 working-age adults (India is lower, at 37).

## Three drivers, not one

The factor analysis points to three groups of causes:

- **Socioeconomic**: country type, education and marital status. People without a partner (single, divorced or widowed) were more likely to be excluded everywhere, and the gap was wider in middle-income countries.
- **Health**: physical and health conditions are real barriers, which argues for folding digital literacy into healthcare support.
- **Age-related limitations**: the case for age-friendly design and accessibility improvements.

Among the high-income group, Estonia and France had the highest exclusion rates at around 30%. Among middle-income countries, Mexico had the lowest at 33%. The chi-square results confirm a strong association between country type and exclusion, with older groups in middle-income countries hit hardest.

## Why engineers should care

The consequences she lists are the ones product teams create without noticing: reduced access to essential services, social connection and banking. When a bank, a clinic or a government service goes digital-only, the excluded users are no longer counted in your error rate. They just stop showing up. Rinku also found that digitally included people reported better health ratings than excluded people in every country except Mexico.

Her recommendations are aimed at policymakers and organisations: expand digital literacy programs (she points to Austria's Digital Seniors among the promising ones) into remote areas, make devices and internet access affordable, focus on the most excluded groups, and back community-based and public-private efforts. She also calls for longitudinal studies to measure whether interventions work.

## Who should watch

Product engineers, designers and accessibility advocates who need data to argue for inclusive design, and anyone building services that are quietly becoming digital-only. Infrastructure-focused SREs looking for operational detail can skip this one.

Title: SRE for payment systems that must work on 2G and through blackouts
Description: Utham Kumar at Conf42 SRE 2025 on offline-first design, region-specific SLOs and phased SRE adoption for payment systems in emerging markets.
Body:
A 99.95% target means something different when the cell tower is on 2G and the power has been out since lunch. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Utham Kumar argued that SRE practices can carry payment systems in emerging markets, as long as you adapt them to local conditions instead of copying a datacentre playbook.

His setting is regions with thin banking infrastructure but wide mobile adoption, where digital payments are how underserved communities get financial services at all. The constraints are physical: power outages, slow and intermittent networks, and regulatory complexity that varies by country.

## Offline first, sync later

The architectural answer is a hybrid of cloud and edge. Process transactions locally, then synchronise once connectivity comes back. Utham presents this as what keeps transaction success rates at 97% or higher in difficult areas, and he links that number directly to trust: if a payment fails twice, the user goes back to cash. Edge computing, caching and robust synchronisation make up his second takeaway for tech leaders.

## Make SLOs fair to the conditions

The most transferable idea is context-adjusted SLIs and SLOs. A 99.95% success target might become 97% in rural zones where connectivity is outside the team's control. His reasoning is about people as much as numbers: targets that ignore reality demoralise teams, while regional targets keep them accountable for what they can influence. It's the error budget idea applied honestly to geography.

## The practices that moved the needle

He credits a set of standard SRE practices with cutting payment failures by more than 60%: distributed tracing across heterogeneous services, automated remediation so systems recover from regional failures without waiting for a human, and precise SLOs. Service mesh gets a mention for taking networking, security and observability out of application code, even alongside legacy systems; he reports faster incident resolution and fewer security incidents once policies were enforced uniformly.

His example is a rural healthcare payments platform on 2G with frequent power cuts, where an offline-first architecture and regional SLOs took transaction reliability from 78% to above 99%. The talk doesn't name the platform or the operator, so treat it as an illustration of the pattern.

## Roll it out in phases

The roadmap is deliberately incremental: start with baseline metrics and simple monitoring, then add distributed tracing and testing, and only then move to AI-driven predictive analytics. Machine learning shows up at that last stage, flagging unusual transaction patterns, routing data around poor networks and blocking suspicious activity in real time. Culture runs alongside: embed reliability champions in the development teams.

## Who should watch

Engineers building payments, mobile money or any transactional system for users with unreliable connectivity, and SRE leads wondering how to set SLOs for regions with very different realities. It's a short, high-level talk; the regional SLO argument is the part to take back to your team.

Title: Why Go fits the plumbing of enterprise AI platforms
Description: Baba Prasad Pendyala of Walmart Global Tech at Conf42 Golang 2025 on Go for AI cloud platforms, a healthcare case study and human-plus-AI decisions.
Body:
Models get the headlines, but someone has to write the services that feed them data and serve their answers. At [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Baba Prasad Pendyala](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Baba_Prasad_Pendyala_cloud_ai_platforms), a staff technical program manager at Walmart Global Tech, made the case that Go is a natural fit for that layer: compiled speed, goroutines for parallel work and small microservices that are easy to scale.

This is a strategy-level talk aimed at people deciding how to build AI platforms, not a coding session. It mixes the technical argument for Go with governance, team skills and a healthcare case study.

## What AI platforms need, and what Go brings

Pendyala lines up AI platform requirements against Go's strengths. AI platforms need high-throughput data pipelines for streaming data, microservices that spread work across clusters, and fault tolerance so the system recovers gracefully. Go brings near-C speed thanks to compilation, an optimised garbage collector, goroutines and channels for lightweight parallelism, and minimal per-service overhead.

He's clear about where Go sits: it's the core platform, ETL and API layer, with models executed through Go bindings for TensorFlow and ONNX, plus lightweight Go-native inference for edge and small services. That's a realistic division of labour; nobody is retraining a large model in Go this week.

## The stack in four layers

His integration model has four parts:

- **Core platform**: containerised Go microservices and low-latency APIs for inference.
- **AI libraries**: TensorFlow and ONNX bindings, and memory-efficient ingestion pipelines built with native Go libraries.
- **Operational tools**: real-time observability for both data pipelines and models, plus governance features that record how models behave and decide.
- **Business value**: faster insights, lower compute bills, better decisions.

He also mentioned Go connectors for AWS, Azure and GCP, and patterns like fallbacks, throttling and abstraction layers for multi-cloud portability.

## A healthcare case study

The example is clinical: IoT devices capture patient vitals, AI models on a Go backend analyse them continuously, and clinicians receive recommendations with probability scores. The platform learns from outcomes over time. Pendyala reported a 42% reduction in readmission rates and a 21% improvement in diagnostic accuracy from that implementation, along with fewer adverse events and faster decisions. The talk doesn't go into how those were measured, so take them as reported results.

## Humans stay in the loop

The section worth underlining is about people. Pendyala argued for human and AI together: clinicians bring intuition, ethics and context, models bring pattern recognition and scale, and human feedback refines the models. He paired it with a readiness checklist: assess infrastructure and skills, set governance rules, run small pilots to prove value, then roll out in phases. On skills, his point was that engineers need to understand goroutines, concurrency and memory profiling to get Go's benefits.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and architects choosing a language for AI platform services, and Go teams asked to justify Go next to a Python-first ML group. Hands-on developers will want to pair it with something that shows code.

Title: Multi-hop data pipelines and the three ways they break at scale
Description: Hardik R Patel of PayPal at Conf42 Golang 2025 on multi-hop pipelines, from Kafka and Flink to fixing data skew, state and back pressure.
Body:
Every big data pipeline hits the same three walls eventually: one partition gets all the data, state stops you scaling out, and a fast producer drowns a slow consumer. At [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Hardik R Patel](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Hardik_R_Patel_data_pipelines_analytics) of PayPal, with around 20 years in tech across Yahoo, Symantec, Groupon and PayPal, laid out how multi-hop pipelines are structured and how to get past each of those walls.

It's a compact, well-organised overview of real-time pipeline design. Despite the title, the talk itself stays language-agnostic; it's about architecture and tools, not Go code.

## Four hops, each with one job

Patel breaks a typical pipeline into stages:

1. **Extraction**: pull structured, semi-structured and unstructured data from many sources. The priorities are resilient connectors and data quality checks, so bad data never enters the pipeline.
2. **Transformation**: cleanse, normalise and enrich so later stages process faster and the overall data lag stays low.
3. **Analysis**: complex event processing and ML to extract insights in near real time.
4. **Action and storage**: trigger automated responses to key events and persist results with an efficient storage footprint.

Putting the quality gate at the first hop is the decision that saves the most pain. Garbage that gets past extraction gets enriched, analysed and stored, which is to say, it gets expensive.

## Design principles and the usual tools

The principles are parallelism through partitioned workloads, elastic horizontal and vertical scaling, fault tolerance with automated recovery, and throughput optimisation through less serialisation overhead and smarter partitioning. The tool tour names Apache Kafka for messaging with partitioning and replication, Spark for distributed processing with SQL and ML support, AWS Lambda for elastic pay-per-use compute, and Apache Flink for exactly-once semantics, event-time processing and windowing.

On performance he lists caching hot data, partitioning for parallelism, load balancing, right-sizing CPU, memory and network per workload, and columnar or binary formats to cut I/O.

## The three scaling walls and how to climb them

This is the most useful part:

- **Data skew**: uneven distribution creates hot nodes and idle ones. The fix is adaptive partitioning with real-time workload monitoring and dynamic rebalancing.
- **State management**: stateful operations limit horizontal scaling. Use fault-tolerant distributed state stores with tiered caching and configurable eviction.
- **Back pressure**: a fast producer overwhelms a slow consumer, causing instability or data loss. Add intelligent rate limiting, priority-based buffer queues and adaptive throttling.

## Watch every hop

He closes on observability: metrics for end-to-end latency and per-stage throughput, logs for error trends and faster root cause analysis, and distributed tracing to correlate behaviour across nodes. His final takeaway is to tie every pipeline to a business outcome, since a pipeline nobody needs is the cheapest one to optimise.

## Who should watch

Engineers designing or inheriting a streaming pipeline who want a clear vocabulary for its stages and failure modes. If you want Go-specific implementation, pair it with one of the Go talks below.

Title: Building social determinants of health into clinical workflows
Description: Roja Perumandla of ZeOmega at Conf42 SRE 2025 on screening, data standards and partnerships that bring social determinants of health into care systems.
Body:
A patient who misses three appointments may not have a compliance problem; they may not have a car. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Roja Perumandla, Director of Professional Services and Client Success at ZeOmega, made the case for treating social determinants of health (SDOH) as a systems problem: screen for them in a standard way, wire the results into clinical workflows and data platforms, and measure the outcomes.

Be clear on scope before you press play: this is a healthcare operations talk, not an SRE talk in the infrastructure sense. The engineering content is about data standards, integration and rollout, and the reliability framing is mostly in the abstract. For engineers building health platforms, that is exactly the useful part.

## Five factors, one standard screen

Roja focuses on five determinants: housing, food security, interpersonal safety, transportation and utilities. She ties each to care. Unstable housing links to more emergency visits and delayed care; food insecurity, which she puts at 10.2% of US households, makes chronic disease harder to manage; she cites 3.6 million Americans missing medical appointments because of transport; and without power, water or connectivity, medication storage and telehealth fall apart.

The fix starts with a standard questionnaire covering those five areas, a defined screening frequency (high-risk patients screened quarterly), screening embedded in EHR touch points such as annual wellness visits, transitions of care and chronic disease follow-ups, and proper training for staff on what to do with a positive screen.

## Change the team, not just the form

Her comparison of care teams is the organisational core. The traditional team of physicians, nurses and medical assistants focuses on diagnosis and treatment and has little capacity for social needs. The enhanced team adds social workers and community health workers, with clear protocols for screening, referral and follow-up, and ongoing measurement of completion rates and outcomes. She reports results from organisations that made the change, including an 86% screening completion rate and 28% fewer emergency visits in rural settings.

## The data plumbing matters most

For engineers, the standards section is the meat. Structured capture with coded terminologies such as SNOMED and ICD-10 keeps documentation consistent; FHIR-based APIs carry the data securely between health systems, community organisations and public health bodies; dashboards track referral completion and population trends; and automated alerts kick off an intervention pathway when a screen comes back positive. Analytics combine clinical, claims and community-level data, including geospatial risk mapping at neighbourhood level.

Her infrastructure checklist reads like any regulated platform: HIPAA-compliant cloud hosting with role-based access and end-to-end encryption, API management for exchanges between EHRs and referral tools, mobile and web access with offline capability for rural areas, and granular consent management so patients control what gets shared.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people working on EHR integrations, care management platforms or public health data, and anyone curious how reliability thinking transfers outside infrastructure. If you want SLOs and incident response, pick another talk from the event. Her rollout is phased: design in months one to three, infrastructure in four to six, a pilot in seven to nine, then expansion.

Title: Incident, problem and change management, and surviving the bridge
Description: Shaalmali Raychaudhury of PayPal at Conf42 SRE 2025 on how incident, problem and change management fit together, plus tips for tough bridges and interviews.
Body:
A user who has lost access to a tool will often file it as a priority-one incident. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Shaalmali Raychaudhury, an SRE at PayPal, used that everyday mix-up to open a clear tour of how incident, problem and change management connect, then added the practical bits nobody teaches graduates: how to handle a difficult incident bridge, and how to interview for SRE roles.

This is a foundations talk, and it says so. If you have run an incident program for years, you will know the model. If you are new to SRE or incident management, or you are the person explaining it to new hires, it is a tidy reference.

## Three processes, one loop

Shaalmali's model is a loop. **Incident management** restores service fast and within agreed SLAs; think of it as the emergency response team. Access requests are request tickets, not incidents, and keeping the two apart protects the queue. **Problem management** steps back to find root causes through RCA and to ship permanent fixes or workarounds; her example is repeated server outages that incident response patches each time until problem management traces them to a misconfigured application. **Change management** then gets that fix into production safely, with risk assessment and phased, tested rollouts (a database upgrade staged across environments, in her example), so the cure doesn't cause the next incident.

## Make priority mean the same thing to everyone

Her incident tips are short and correct. Standardise logging, categorisation and priority so a P1 for one engineer is never a P3 for another. Automate communications and escalation, because writing manual updates mid-bridge eats the time you need to hit SLAs. Review SLAs and priority matrices as the business changes, and chase the RCA actions assigned to other teams so their deadlines don't quietly slip.

## The bridge is a people problem

The section on difficult bridges is where her own experience shows. Understand the actual impact first: requesters often push for P1, and if the impact doesn't match the priority matrix, explain why rather than just flipping the label. Keep empathy even when the issue isn't yours or isn't urgent, and point people to next steps instead of leaving them stranded. And hold boundaries: when someone pushes back on priority rules and escalation procedures, be assertive so time goes where the impact is.

## Interview advice for new SREs

She closes with tips for fresh graduates: ask the recruiter as many questions as you need to understand the role (SRE means different things at different companies), research your interviewers where you can, prefer short focused courses on the job's required skills over week-long tutorials, and be honest about what you don't know.

## Who should watch

Graduates and career changers heading into SRE or incident management, new incident commanders, and team leads who want a crisp explainer of how the three processes hand off to each other. Seasoned responders can skip to the bridge section.

Title: A framework for moving infrastructure monitoring from reactive to predictive
Description: Jena Abraham of Intel at Conf42 SRE 2025 on a reliability framework of dynamic thresholds, alert consolidation and ML anomaly detection for fast-growing systems.
Body:
Most outages that drag on are outages nobody could see properly. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Jena Abraham, Senior Design Verification Engineer and Technical Program Manager at Intel Corporation, laid out a modern reliability framework for high-speed infrastructure whose goal is to catch degradation before it becomes an incident, and to stop drowning on-call engineers in duplicate alerts while doing it.

She opens with three problems. Monitoring gaps, which in her figures are behind 68% of extended service outages. Slow service degradation that stays invisible until it crosses a critical line. And detection delay: on average, she says, 42 minutes pass between an incident starting and an alert firing. That is a long time for a small fire to find the curtains.

## Static thresholds are the first thing to go

The framework's anomaly detection rests on dynamic thresholds that follow traffic patterns and system behaviour, so expected load swings stop paging people. On top of that sit ML-based analysis for subtle deviations and predictive alerts that warn on emerging patterns before a hard threshold is hit. SLOs are the backbone: she cites 93% of system components covered by SLOs, tracking of CPU, memory and IO, pre-production bottleneck detection and capacity forecasts 30 days ahead.

## One incident should produce one page

The section most teams can act on tomorrow is about multi-service noise. When one fault ripples through several services, alert consolidation folds the duplicates together (she reports a 75% reduction in duplicate notifications). Intelligent filtering ranks alerts by context. Automatic dependency mapping draws the service graph for you, and a correlation engine ties incidents across services into a single view of health, which is what you need to find the actual root cause instead of the loudest symptom.

## Stopping the cascade

Cascading failures get their own toolbox, and it is a solid list of classics: real-time anomaly detection to catch the first deviation, circuit breakers to isolate failing components, load shedding to protect mission-critical paths when capacity is short, and graceful recovery that brings services back in dependency order instead of all at once.

## Where AI fits, and how to roll it out

The AI-for-observability slide makes ambitious claims: anomaly classification at 90% accuracy, failure forecasts 24 to 48 hours ahead, 70% less root-cause investigation time and 60% fewer unnecessary escalations. The talk presents these as framework results without naming the systems or the measurement method, so read them as targets rather than benchmarks you can compare against.

The rollout plan is more grounded: an assessment phase (gap analysis of current monitoring, SLO workshops, forming the team), a deployment phase (core observability platform, service instrumentation, training the models), and an optimisation phase (tuning alerts until they are precise and actionable, and automating runbooks).

## Who should watch

Teams whose infrastructure has grown faster than their monitoring, and anyone building the business case for SLOs plus alert correlation. It's a concise, slide-driven overview at framework level, without tool names or configs, so treat it as a checklist to compare against your own stack.

Title: AI self-healing infrastructure and the SRE 3.0 job description
Description: Vijaybhasker Pagidoju at Conf42 SRE 2025 on AI that detects, predicts and remediates failures, the risks it brings, and how the SRE role shifts as a result.
Body:
If your infrastructure can restart, drain and scale itself, what is left for the person holding the pager? In his keynote at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Vijaybhasker Pagidoju, a Lead Site Reliability Engineer, argued that AI-driven self-healing is the next stage of SRE, and that it turns engineers from firefighters into the people who design, train and govern the systems that respond on their own.

He frames the history in three versions. SRE 1.0 was mostly manual: on-call, basic monitoring, reactive response, and the arrival of error budgets. SRE 2.0 brought infrastructure as code, scripted remediation, chaos engineering and the move from monitoring to observability. SRE 3.0, in his telling, is autonomous: predictive healing, with engineers architecting systems that respond themselves.

## Detect, predict, remediate, learn

The core of the talk is a four-stage loop. **Detection** watches logs, metrics and signals for anomalies a human would miss, like slowly building patterns that never quite break. **Prediction** trains models on historical data and live telemetry to forecast failures, sometimes days ahead. **Remediation** triggers corrective workflows without a human: restart a service, drain traffic from a failing node, scale a region. **Optimisation** feeds postmortem data back in to sharpen predictions and cut noise. Each stage builds on the one before, which is also a hint about rollout order: there is no point automating remediation for anomalies you can't yet detect reliably.

## The case studies, and how to read them

He walks through three examples. Netflix's ChAP (Chaos Automation Platform) uses risk models to choose where to inject faults instead of breaking things at random, which he summarises nicely as chaos with intent. Meta is described as migrating workloads off servers once a model is confident a failure is coming. Microsoft Azure is presented with big gains in noise reduction and auto-resolution. The talk quotes sizeable percentages and savings for each without citing sources on screen, so check the companies' own engineering write-ups before putting those numbers in a slide deck of your own.

## The risks get equal billing

The section on what can go wrong is the most useful part for practitioners. Explainability: AI remediation that acts like a black box creates accountability gaps exactly when an incident needs clarity. Human oversight: too little automation wastes the opportunity, too much creates over-reliance that fails at the edge cases. Security: an agent with infrastructure-level access is a new attack surface, and model poisoning is a real threat. Bias: a model trained on skewed history will give some systems worse reliability than others.

## Start small, keep humans in the loop

His timeline runs from today's assistive phase (anomaly detection and noise reduction) through auto-healing of known failure patterns in the next two to three years, towards AI-native platforms where SREs train models, review critical decisions and set governance. His bottom line: "AI doesn't replace us. It needs us." And his practical advice is the right one: pick your biggest pain point (observability, remediation or capacity) and start there, because "It's a force multiplier, not a substitute."

## Who should watch

SRE leads drafting an AIOps roadmap, and engineers who want a vocabulary for what self-healing actually involves. It is a vision keynote, not an implementation guide, so pair it with something hands-on.

Title: Putting a Go API layer in front of an iSeries core bank
Description: Srinivas Allam of Core ITS at Conf42 Golang 2025 on modernising IBM iSeries banking systems with Go microservices, EBCDIC conversion and zero-downtime rollout.
Body:
The fastest way to modernise a core bank is to leave the core alone. At [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Srinivas Allam](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Allam_banking_modernization_fintech) of Core ITS, who brings over 21 years of iSeries development and banking work, described how a tier-1 bank kept its IBM iSeries (AS/400) systems running COBOL and RPG while a layer of Go microservices took over the job of talking to web, mobile and partner APIs.

It's an architecture and results talk rather than a code walkthrough, but the shape of the solution is one many banks will recognise, and Go is central to it.

## Downtime is not an option, so don't migrate in one jump

Allam's framing of the problem is blunt. Legacy platforms process millions of transactions a day and have run for decades, but customers now expect real-time processing, open APIs and omnichannel apps. The modernisation has to happen around 24/7 operations, with security and regulatory compliance intact the whole time.

His answer is a four-part architecture: the iSeries keeps running mission-critical operations; a Go API layer transforms legacy data models and routes transactions; an integration hub on enterprise message brokers carries traffic between old and new; and APIs expose banking functions to web and mobile.

## Why Go for this job

Allam's case for Go is practical:

- **Goroutines** handle thousands of concurrent transactions with little memory, compared with traditional thread models.
- **Compile-time type checking** protects transaction integrity before anything ships.
- **Memory safety** removes the buffer overflow class of bugs from code that touches financial data.
- **A single static binary** with no external dependencies simplifies deployment and compliance reviews.

The last point is underrated. When an auditor asks what's running in production, "this one file" is a nice answer.

## The unglamorous technical work

The key implementation pieces were optimised Go drivers for iSeries DB2 with ACID-compliant transactions; binary converters from legacy EBCDIC records to JSON and XML without data loss; bridging the legacy access controls to OIDC authentication; and unified telemetry across old and new components. Anyone who has debugged a character encoding problem in a payment file will appreciate that EBCDIC got its own slide.

## How they shipped it without a maintenance window

The deployment pattern combines blue-green environments for instant failover, canary releases for progressive traffic migration, continuous validation that the legacy and modern systems agree, and automated rollback with circuit breakers that trip on failure.

The case study, as Allam described it: an audit of 15+ years of customisations, a Go processing framework handling 3,000+ transactions per second, secure pipelines migrating millions of records with a full audit trail, and 50+ Go microservices. He reported transaction processing time down 78% in the implementation, response times 96% lower than the legacy path, and lower CPU and memory usage. These are the project's own figures.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects at banks, insurers or retailers sitting on an iSeries, mainframe or AS/400 estate and looking for a strangler-pattern approach with Go. If you have never seen EBCDIC, count yourself lucky and maybe watch anyway.

Title: A zero-downtime checklist for FinTech infrastructure
Description: Srinivas Reddy Mosali of Visa at Conf42 Golang 2025 on high availability, scaling, disaster recovery, observability and Kubernetes for payment systems.
Body:
In payments, a few seconds of unavailability can mean lost money, a regulator's attention and customers who stop trusting you. At [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Srinivas Reddy Mosali](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Reddy_Mosali_fintech_infrastructure_scaling), a senior consultant systems engineer at Visa, walked through the practices that add up to zero downtime: active-active architecture, predictive scaling, cross-region recovery, chaos engineering, observability and careful maintenance.

It's an SRE fundamentals talk applied to FinTech, with no Go-specific content. Its strength is coverage: if you're auditing a payments platform, it's close to a checklist.

## Choose your availability model on purpose

Mosali starts with the trade-off most teams make implicitly. Active-active setups have several systems serving requests at once, so failover is instant. Active-passive keeps a standby, which costs less but adds a short delay on failover. Around that sit multi-region deployment, load balancing at several layers, and replicated object storage so customers can always reach their financial data.

## Scale before the spike, not during it

Payment traffic is spiky and predictable: market opens, holiday shopping. He recommends AI-driven predictive scaling that reads usage patterns and adds capacity ahead of the peak, combined with horizontal scaling for more servers and vertical scaling for bigger ones. Serverless computing and caching with Redis or a CDN take load off the backend. The idea is simple: your autoscaler shouldn't find out about Black Friday from the error rate.

## Assume failure, then rehearse it

The disaster recovery section covers cross-region backup replication against regional outages, multi-master databases so another node takes over when one fails, and automated rollback pipelines. Mosali also recommends chaos engineering: simulate failures in a controlled environment to find weak spots before a real incident does.

## Security can't cost you latency

He argues a breach can be worse than downtime, so zero trust, encryption at rest and in transit, and compliance with GDPR, PCI DSS and SOC 2 are mandatory. The twist he emphasises is that none of it should slow transactions down. AI-driven fraud detection on live transaction patterns is his example of security that runs inline without hurting speed.

## Observability, Kubernetes and maintenance windows that don't hurt

The rest of the talk covers:

- **Observability**: logs, metrics and traces as the three pillars, with AI anomaly detection, predictive analytics and self-healing for minor failures.
- **Kubernetes**: horizontal pod autoscaling for transaction surges, rescheduling pods off failed nodes, RBAC and network policies, and StatefulSets with persistent storage for databases.
- **Maintenance**: blue-green deployments, canary releases and feature flags; database schema versioning for backward compatibility; maintenance notices to customers; SRE playbooks and postmortems after every incident.

His closing point is that reliability is a core part of FinTech success, not a side goal for the infrastructure team.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into payments or banking infrastructure, and teams preparing for a reliability review who want a structured list of what to check. Seasoned SREs will recognise most of it; the value is in seeing it assembled for a regulated, always-on domain.

Title: AI in Hollywood and the Metaverse Is an Assistant, Not the Auteur
Description: Rahul Basu of Warner Bros. Discovery at Conf42 LLMs 2025 maps where AI fits in filmmaking, casting, distribution and metaverse storytelling.
Body:
Do not expect a fully AI-generated blockbuster, or a daydream piped straight from your brain into a TV series. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Rahul Basu, a Software Engineer at Warner Bros. Discovery, mapped where AI is already changing filmmaking and the metaverse, and drew a firm line: AI assists human creators, it does not replace them.

This is a vision and survey-of-tools talk rather than an engineering deep end, and it presents Rahul's own research and opinions, not a Warner Bros. Discovery product roadmap. Watch it for the system map and the predictions.

## Hollywood has always been an early adopter

Rahul's opening argument is historical. Studios pushed CGI, VFX and virtual reality before most industries touched them, so it is no surprise they are early on AI. He lists where it already shows up: script analysis and brainstorming, pre-visualisation, post-production tasks like colour grading, VFX and sound editing, removing unwanted objects from shots, music composition and adaptive scoring. On the metaverse side: AI-generated non-player characters, world-building tools, gesture recognition and eye tracking.

## A three-layer architecture for AI entertainment

The most structured part of the talk is a system design. Rahul proposes three layers:

1. **Content creation and production**, with AI tools for writing, storyboarding and post-production.
2. **Metaverse experience**, covering AI-driven storytelling, NPCs and immersive environments.
3. **Distribution and personalisation**, with recommendation engines and adaptive storytelling.

Key components include an AI script-writing engine, pre-visualisation and storyboarding, an interactive storytelling engine and AI-generated environments for VFX, plus real-time dubbing, digital humans and predictive analytics. He also shows a tech-stack slide of current tools per layer, with the honest caveat that many of these products will do something different, or better, in a year.

## Casting, dubbing and the trailer you see

The audience-facing predictions are the most concrete. AI casting tools analyse past performances and audience preferences to help directors shortlist actors. Facial recreation can bring an actor back for a flashback scene, which Rahul flags as raising ethical concerns. Real-time subtitles and dubbing make a film shot in English ready for audiences in China, Japan or Europe on day one. In marketing, predictive analytics forecasts box office and target demographics, and studios can cut multiple trailer versions for different audience segments. That last one means the trailer you saw and the one your neighbour saw may not be the same film, at least not in two and a half minutes.

## Where the line is

Interactive storytelling, where viewers make choices that shape the plot, gets a cautious yes. Brain-computer interfaces that turn imagination directly into film get a no for now. And the fully autonomous AI movie is the prediction Rahul is most confident about rejecting: AI will cut costs and speed up workflows, but the creative call stays human. Eye tracking for VR rendering, which focuses resolution where users look, is his example of AI making immersion cheaper rather than replacing artists.

## Who should watch

Engineers in media and streaming who want a structured overview of where AI fits in the production pipeline, and anyone building recommendation, dubbing or immersive features. If you want code, look elsewhere; this one is the map.

Title: Sub-50ms authentication with edge proxies and stateless JWTs
Description: Aditi Mallesh at Conf42 SRE 2025 on an IAM design for gaming and betting platforms that keeps login under 50ms with edge proxies and short-lived JWTs.
Body:
When a bet window closes in seconds, a slow login is lost revenue. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Aditi Mallesh presented an identity and access management architecture for online gaming and betting that keeps authentication under 50 milliseconds globally, built from edge-deployed identity proxies and stateless, short-lived JWTs that need no database lookup.

The premise is blunt: past roughly 100 ms of authentication time, she says, transaction completion drops sharply, and players in time-sensitive games notice every pause. So the design treats auth latency as a product metric, not a security tax.

## Move identity to the edge, take the database out

Two decisions do most of the work. First, identity proxies sit close to players, which in her numbers cut network transmission time by an average of 65 ms across markets. Second, tokens are short-lived JWTs signed with ES256, validated statelessly at the edge, so thousands of transactions per second need zero database lookups. The headline benchmark: 32 ms average response time globally for the edge JWT path, which she reports as three to seven times faster than the traditional approaches they compared against.

## The hard part is revocation

Anyone who has shipped JWTs knows the catch: you can't take a signed token back. Her answer is the standard one done properly. Tokens live five minutes, refresh silently in the background, and a distributed block list handles the compromised ones. The other two challenges she names are just as familiar to anyone running multi-region auth: keeping policy consistent across regions (centralised policy management with atomic, versioned updates pushed to edge nodes over a resilient messaging layer) and varying KYC rules per jurisdiction (region-specific compliance modules with local data residency, kept out of the core login flow).

## Keep the slow stuff off the critical path

The pattern repeats through the talk. Fraud detection runs on streaming behavioural data (interaction patterns, device fingerprints, transaction velocity) so legitimate users don't wait for it. KYC and trust scoring are offloaded rather than blocking login. WebAuthn and FIDO2 replace passwords with device biometrics and security keys, which removes friction and, she argues, closes the door on credential stuffing.

She shares outcome figures from the rollout, including a 92% drop in authentication-related support tickets, 43% lower infrastructure cost and a 67% reduction in account takeover attempts. These are the speaker's reported results; the talk doesn't name the platform or show the measurement setup, so treat them as directional.

## Who should watch

Engineers who own login for latency-sensitive products (gaming, betting, trading, checkout) and want a compact checklist of trade-offs. It's a short architecture overview rather than a code walkthrough. Her advice on rollout is sensible: pilot in your highest-value region, nail core auth speed first, and add biometrics and behavioural analysis later.

Title: What Real Housewives reunions teach about running postmortems
Description: Paige Cruz of Chronosphere at Conf42 SRE 2025 on seven Real Housewives lessons for postmortems: receipts, feelings, facilitation, and no blame games.
Body:
A good postmortem works like a good Real Housewives reunion: nobody gets crowned the owner of the truth, and the interesting part is why everyone remembers it differently. That is the argument Paige Cruz, Principal Developer Advocate at Chronosphere and self-declared Bravoholic, made at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, in one of the most fun talks of the event.

The trick is that the metaphor carries real weight. Paige starts from an off-camera argument between two cast members in the first Beverly Hills season, where each woman was sure of her own version and no tape existed. Incidents have the same shape. The on-call engineer, the manager, the bystander who only reads the report and the executive who wants a promise that it never happens again all hold partial, valid views. Even the telemetry is filtered, because someone decided earlier what was worth instrumenting.

## Receipts should be a portal, not a gotcha

Lesson one is *bring receipts*, but with a twist. On the show, receipts are saved for a dramatic reveal. In an incident write-up, Paige wants them to be a way in: instead of a dashboard screenshot, link the dashboard pinned to the incident's time range so a curious engineer two years later can rerun the query, change the window and follow the breadcrumbs. Add enough context that someone outside your team can follow along.

## Feelings are data too

Reports tend to dwell on stress and fear, which Paige frames as plain negativity bias. Her counterweights are three questions worth stealing for your template: what stopped this from getting worse, which part of the response are you proudest of, and where did we get lucky?

## The facilitator is the producer

Andy Cohen asking a cast member to finish her insult on camera is the anti-lesson: provocation for ratings, the opposite of psychological safety. Paige uses screen-time data from a fan account to show how an edit decides whose story gets told, and points out that a postmortem facilitator holds the same power. Balance airtime so seniority doesn't drown out the quiet responder, and ask *how* questions instead of *why* ones. "Why didn't you check the logs?" puts people on the defence; "how did you approach troubleshooting at that point?" gets you their context. She recommends Etsy's 2016 debriefing facilitation guide, and passes on a lovely idea from a SREcon speaker who opens every incident review with a song picked for the outage.

## The meeting before the meeting, and letting the mouse go

Where cast members self-produce through backroom texts, Paige recommends one-on-one debriefs (credited to Amy Tobey's SREcon talk) to hear from people who wouldn't speak up in a group. She ran them after a multi-hour data-loss incident her team gave an apocalyptic nickname and found layers the single group meeting would have missed. One question she highlights rarely appears in templates: did you practise self-care before and during the incident?

*Let the mouse go* is the warning against using an incident as proof that your pet reliability crusade was right all along. As she puts it, if you could predict incidents, "you would be called AIOps and at least triple your current take home pay."

The remaining lessons are time-boxing (no three-part reunion specials) and avoiding blame. Paige walks the arc from blame to blamelessness to blame-aware, and quotes Sidney Dekker's *Stop Blaming*: "People didn't make bad choices. They probably had bad choices".

## Who should watch

Anyone who runs incident reviews, writes the template, or has sat through a postmortem that felt like a trial. No Bravo knowledge needed; the clips explain themselves. If your org already does structured learning reviews, the facilitation and one-on-one sections are still worth the time.

Title: ML services fail silently, so SREs need drift metrics
Description: Payal Godhani of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure at Conf42 SRE 2025 on why green dashboards hide decaying ML models, and the four drifts SREs should track.
Body:
A model can be up, fast and inside its SLOs while it quietly recommends the wrong thing to every customer. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, Payal Godhani, Principal Engineer at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, argued that this is the core gap between ML and SRE: our standard signals say the service is healthy, and say nothing about whether the predictions are any good.

Her framing is two tribes. ML engineers live offline, iterate on experiments and care about accuracy. SREs live in production metrics and care about uptime and latency. When SREs inherit a model they didn't design, logs, metrics and traces tell them the pod is fine. They don't tell them the output has become biased, that the input data has shifted, or that the model has gone stale since its last retrain. As she put it, ML systems "don't always crash, but they decay".

## Put the monitor next to the model

The architecture she sketches is simple and worth copying. A model monitoring service sits beside the prediction service and ingests both the inputs and the predictions. It feeds the usual dashboards and alarms, and where ground truth eventually arrives, compares predictions against it on historical data. To an SRE it looks like any other service; the difference is that its correctness depends on live external data and its own history, not just the binary.

Her shopping-cart example mixes the two worlds on one screen: per-region latency, RMSE for how far predictions land from the truth, and real-user signals such as page views, add-to-cart and checkout conversion. That last chain is the one product people will ask about anyway.

## Four drifts, from obvious to sneaky

The most useful part of the talk is a clear taxonomy:

- **Prediction drift**: the shape of the output changes. A recommender that used to mix budget and premium items starts skewing premium, maybe because of a seasonal shopping event or an upstream change. You don't need ground truth to spot it, which makes it the first alarm bell.
- **Data drift**: live traffic no longer looks like training data, for example after the business expands into a new geography the model never saw.
- **Feature drift**: one feature's distribution moves. Her example is a location feature that flips from mostly urban to mostly rural after a regional ad campaign. Watch the features your model weighs most.
- **Feature attribution drift**: after retraining, the model starts leaning on a different feature (brand over price, in her example). Inputs can look stable while behaviour changes, so this one is the hardest to catch.

## Zero downtime means observability stays off the hot path

On deployment she keeps it practical: send live traffic to a shadow model and compare its decisions with production before flipping; run all monitoring asynchronously so it never adds inference latency; plan graceful degradation for when the model misbehaves; and make observability part of every CI/CD pipeline. For tooling she names Evidently on the open source side, and Vertex AI and Amazon SageMaker from the cloud providers.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who have been handed an inference service and a pager, and ML engineers who want to know what their on-call colleagues can and can't see. It is a conceptual talk with no live demo, so if you already run drift detection in production, you'll recognise most of it; the four-drift breakdown is still a good one to share with the team.

Title: Application resilience is everyone's job, not one team's
Description: Veliswa Boya of AWS at Conf42 SRE 2025 on breaking silos so resilience and innovation coexist, plus the CI/CD, IaC and telemetry practices behind it.
Body:
The question Veliswa Boya keeps getting after her continuous resilience talks is whether resilience slows down innovation. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025, the AWS Senior Developer Advocate answered it with an organisational claim: resilience and innovation coexist when resilience stops being one person's or one team's job and becomes a shared responsibility.

This is a culture-first talk, and a good primer. If you came for chaos experiments or failover diagrams, this isn't that talk; if you are the person trying to convince a siloed org to change, it gives you a clear structure and a reading list.

## Start from failure, not robustness

Veliswa recaps continuous resilience as a move away from robustness-centric thinking: accept that applications will fail at some point and build the capabilities to cope when they do. That acceptance is what makes the rest of the talk necessary, because coping with failure needs people who talk to each other.

## Silos are where not-my-job comes from

Her diagnosis of siloed development is familiar: roles that rarely interact, slower delivery, and conflicts that surface as *that is not my job*. Code quality alone doesn't make an application resilient; performance efficiency, security and functional suitability matter just as much, and splitting them across separate roles pulls teams straight back into silos. She paraphrases Eric Madar writing for DevOps.com: team members are equally responsible for resilience, and outdated structures put it on a single person, team or role. Organising around products rather than projects is her lever for fixing that.

She leans on Emily Freeman's *DevOps for Dummies* for the culture side (trust, collaboration, continuous improvement) and asks two pointed questions: is diversity of thought encouraged, and can team members make decisions without asking management every time?

## The technical scaffolding for shared ownership

Culture needs tooling to stick, and the second half maps it out:

- **Distributed architectures**: drawing on *Fundamentals of Software Architecture*, she contrasts a monolith's single deployment unit with microservices, so teams can own components independently.
- **Continuous integration and delivery**: GitHub Actions to build and test every pull request, framed by AWS's introductory DevOps white paper.
- **Infrastructure as code**: Terraform for provisioning across clouds.
- **Monitoring and logging**: OpenTelemetry to collect and export metrics, logs and traces.
- **Security as a cross-cutting concern**: protected pipelines, proper access controls, and the OWASP Top 10 as a cultural baseline.

Collaboration tools get a mention too: GitHub for reviews and pull request notifications, Trello boards so nobody has to ask what's in progress.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, team leads and developers early in a DevOps or SRE transition. Experienced SREs will know the practices; the value is in the framing, which works well as something to send to the people who still think resilience belongs to ops. She closes with three questions worth asking your own org: do you still have siloed functions, are you moving away from them, and have you finished?

- [Cristina Buenahora Bustamante on building a culture of reliability and ownership](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Cristina_Buenahora_Bustamante_evangelizing_culture_ownership).

Title: Building financial decision systems on Go microservices
Description: Deepu Komati of PenFed Credit Union at Conf42 Golang 2025 on Go microservices, ML fraud detection, APIs and DevOps for FinTech platforms.
Body:
Everyone has had a legitimate card payment declined by an overcautious fraud model. At [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Deepu Komati](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Deepu_Komati_fintech_cloud_infrastructure) of PenFed Credit Union used that moment to frame a whirlwind tour of a FinTech stack built on Go microservices: machine learning for risk and fraud, an API layer for partners, cloud migration, blue-green deploys and automated compliance checks.

It's a broad architecture overview rather than a walk through code. Think of it as a map of the pieces a modern financial platform needs, with Go as the service layer that ties them together.

## Go as the transaction highway

Komati's metaphor for the microservice layer is a highway where cars don't jam. Transaction processing is spread across Go services, and he credits Go's concurrency for handling thousands of requests per second at low latency where, in his framing, Java or Python services struggle under the same load. Resilience comes from routing traffic to backup nodes when a service fails, which he tied to a 99.99% uptime target, and from scaling for Black Friday or heavy trading days.

## The fraud model's real job is to stay out of the way

The machine learning section pulls in transaction histories, market feeds and spending patterns to predict loan defaults and flag fraud. The number he chose to highlight is about false positives: he reported a 78% reduction, so legitimate transactions go through without needless blocks. That's the right metric to care about. A fraud model that catches everything by blocking everyone is just an outage with extra steps.

Later he described real-time fraud detection that learns from past fraud cases and cited banks cutting fraud losses by nearly two thirds.

## APIs, cloud and the boring parts that make it work

The rest of the talk covers the platform around the models:

- **APIs**: REST and GraphQL endpoints so banks and FinTech partners can integrate in weeks, with a startup offering instant credit scoring as the example.
- **Cloud migration**: moving transactions off on-prem bank systems with zero downtime, using serverless to pay only for what runs, and multi-cloud for redundancy and regional data rules. He cited a 40% cost reduction.
- **DevOps**: 95% test coverage before deploys, blue-green releases and real-time monitoring.
- **Compliance**: automated AML screening and KYC onboarding in under a minute.

He also included a blockchain section on smart contracts and immutable transaction records. As with most of the numbers here, these are the speaker's reported outcomes, presented without the setup behind them.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to FinTech who want a checklist of what a financial platform has to cover, and architects pitching Go for the service layer in a bank. If you want benchmarks, code or the trade-offs behind the 99.99% figure, you'll want to pair this with something more hands-on.

Title: Bringing Go models to AWS SageMaker with your own container
Description: Likhit Mada of Intuit at Conf42 Golang 2025 on SageMaker for FinTech ML, its deployment options, and training Go models via custom Docker images.
Body:
SageMaker doesn't ship a Go kernel, but it doesn't need to. At [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Likhit Mada](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Likhit_Mada_fintech_aws_sagemaker) of Intuit, a senior software engineer in FinTech, walked through the whole AWS SageMaker lifecycle for financial ML and then showed the escape hatch: write your model in Go, put it in a Docker image, push it to ECR and let SageMaker train and serve it like anything else.

It's a long, thorough product tour of SageMaker, with the Go material concentrated in two places: the bring-your-own-container path and Go as the high-throughput glue around the models.

## Why FinTech teams reach for a managed ML platform

Mada lists the bottlenecks as talent (too few people who know both models and infrastructure), infrastructure complexity (GPUs and distributed compute), compliance and data security, and the gap between a trained model and production inference. SageMaker's answer is to manage the infrastructure so engineers spend their time on models. He said SageMaker gave his model development a roughly 40% boost.

The security pieces he highlighted are the ones a regulator will ask about: IAM for fine-grained access to data and models, a VPC so sensitive financial data never crosses the public internet, and encryption at rest and in transit.

## Three ways to build, from no-code to Go

The tour runs through data prep (JupyterLab, the visual Data Wrangler, EMR for terabyte-scale data, Glue interactive sessions) and then three development modes:

- **Built-in algorithms and JumpStart**: supply data, hyperparameters and compute; pick foundation models with a click.
- **Script mode**: your own Python or R script on supported frameworks like TensorFlow or scikit-learn, with SageMaker handling the rest.
- **Bring your own container**: for algorithms or languages SageMaker doesn't support. This is where Go comes in. You write the model in Go, add a Dockerfile with its dependencies, push to Elastic Container Registry, and create a training job that points at your image, your data and an S3 output path.

Since SageMaker is built on containers anyway, the Go model is a first-class citizen once it's packaged.

## Pick the inference mode by traffic shape

The deployment section is a handy decision table. Real-time endpoints suit continuous traffic and small payloads, like immediate fraud detection. Serverless inference fits bursty traffic that tolerates cold starts. Asynchronous inference handles payloads up to about 1 GB with longer processing. Batch transform covers large offline jobs such as churn prediction. Model Monitor and CloudWatch then watch for drift.

## Go around the model, not only inside it

Mada was candid that Go isn't the first language people think of for ML. He pointed to a growing set of Go ML libraries, Gonum for numerical computing, GoLearn and GoCV among them, and suggested Go for pre- and post-processing of large or streaming data, for calling SageMaker through the AWS SDK for Go, and for Go Lambda functions that trigger retraining when new data or a new image lands. His closing advice is honest: new to ML, start with Python and SageMaker; comfortable in Go and chasing efficiency, bring your own container.

## Who should watch

Engineers evaluating SageMaker for regulated workloads, and Go developers who've been told ML means Python. Skip it if you already run SageMaker in production; most of the tour will be familiar.

Title: Make Podcasts Searchable With LLM Diarization and Topic Segments
Description: Waseem Syed at Conf42 LLMs 2025 designs a four-layer system that makes long audio searchable by speaker and topic using Whisper, TF-IDF and LLMs.
Body:
You can Ctrl+F a document, but not a two-hour podcast. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Waseem Syed, a Senior Staff Software Engineer who leads generative AI mobile development, designed a system that turns long audio into something you can search by who spoke, what they talked about and when.

It is an architecture talk with pseudo-code: four layers, each with a clear input and output, that you could sketch on a whiteboard and start building. If you have a pile of meeting recordings, lectures or webinars, this is the blueprint.

## Audio is linear, and that is the problem

Waseem's framing is content overload. Podcasts, audiobooks and online courses have exploded, and listeners cannot skim them. Text lets you jump to the paragraph you need; audio makes you scrub. His goal is to close that gap with three capabilities: speaker diarization (who spoke when), topic segmentation (what each part is about) and a search interface that accepts text or voice questions.

## Layer one: transcripts with timestamps on every word

Everything starts with transcription, using OpenAI Whisper or Google Gemini. The detail that matters is word-level timestamps. Without them you can find a phrase in the transcript but not jump to the moment it was spoken. In Waseem's experience Whisper's timing tracked playback accurately, which is what makes "take me to that sentence" possible.

## Layer two: let the LLM decide who is speaking

The most interesting design choice is diarization. Classic diarization relies on acoustic features, and it struggles when voices sound alike or audio is poor. Waseem's approach starts from the transcript instead: chunk it on pauses, then send the chunks to an LLM with a structured prompt that uses context and conversation history to assign speakers, returning JSON. It trades a pure signal-processing problem for a language problem, which is exactly what LLMs are good at.

Topic segmentation uses older tools well. Chunks are converted to TF-IDF vectors, cosine similarity between adjacent chunks detects where the topic shifts, and an LLM such as GPT-4 writes a descriptive label for each segment. Cheap maths finds the boundaries; the expensive model only names them.

## Layers three and four: index once, query forever

The indexing layer stores each segment with its speaker, topic, start and end times, adds full-text search and caching, and optionally a vector database for retrieval-augmented queries. Waseem's point is that after this step queries hit metadata, not media, so they are fast. The interaction layer exposes it through questions like asking what John said about AI ethics, or jumping to every segment where Jill spoke, plus timestamped notes, follow-up links and per-segment ratings, so creators learn which parts of an episode landed rather than relying on one score for the whole thing.

He also flags accessibility: voice queries and structured navigation help listeners who cannot easily scrub through audio.

## Who should watch

Engineers building on meeting recordings, podcasts, lecture capture or call-centre audio. The diarization-by-LLM idea alone is worth the time. It is a design proposal rather than a production post-mortem, so bring your own evaluation plan.

Title: Resilient supply chains start with everyone reading the same forecast
Description: Madhusudan S Vadigicherla of Integra Lifesciences at Conf42 Golang 2025 on shared production forecasts, standard calendars and SKU segmentation.
Body:
A container can sit full of stock outside a warehouse door while customer service tells a buyer the item is out. At [Conf42 Golang 2025](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025), [Madhusudan S Vadigicherla](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Madhusudan_S_Vadigicherla_supply_chain_forecasting) of Integra Lifesciences argued that most supply chain fragility looks like that: the data exists, but the people who need it can't see it. His fix is shared production forecasts, one planning calendar and one set of metrics across distribution centres, plants and suppliers.

Fair warning for Gophers: this is a supply chain management talk with no Go in it. It's built around a case study from a consumer goods client, and it's most useful to engineers who build the planning and integration systems that sit under those processes.

## The forecast has to travel the whole chain

His model case is an intercompany network. A distribution centre in one country generates the forecast and sends it to a manufacturing plant in another. The plant then has to buy raw materials from its suppliers, build the product and ship it back. If any hop works from a different number, someone either overproduces or misses orders.

Shared visibility, in his definition, means the distribution centre, the plant and the suppliers all talk about the same SKU-level numbers: what you want to sell, what you want to produce and what you need to buy. Whether partners see it in your system or theirs matters less than that they see it at all. Industries call this synchronised or integrated business planning; the talk is a field report on making it actually happen.

## Standardise the calendar before you standardise the model

The less glamorous point is the important one. A thermometer and a hair dryer don't forecast the same way, so business units invent their own terms, calendars and KPIs. Vadigicherla's project spent much of its effort on a unified terminology, a common calendar for forecast generation timing, and shared performance indicators, so data from different units could be combined at all.

He was careful to say this isn't a one-size-fits-all model. You keep local calibration for each product portfolio, but the plumbing and vocabulary are common. Anyone who has tried to join two datasets with different fiscal weeks will feel this one.

## Segment, then spend your effort on the A items

The project used Pareto-style segmentation: classify SKUs as A, B or C by revenue contribution, then look at volatility and coefficient of variation. The high-value, critical components got the focus, with advance notifications to suppliers. That's where most of the lead-time gains came from.

## What the case study reported

In the talk, Vadigicherla reported these results once the implementation was done:

- Overall equipment effectiveness across manufacturing up 15%.
- Lead time for the A items cut by 25%.
- A 30% improvement in stockout reduction for mission-critical components.
- Communication across functions improved by 40%.

The abstract quotes slightly different figures (30% lead-time reduction), so treat the numbers as one project's self-reported outcome, not a benchmark. He also stressed that measurement and reinforcement keep it working: a KPI that's defined but never measured won't drive adoption, and segmentation done today will be stale in a few months.

## Who should watch

Engineers and analysts building ERP integrations, demand planning or S&OP tooling who want the business view of why the data contracts matter. If you came for goroutines, skip this one and come back when your planning team asks why their forecasts don't match the plant's.
