Title: Running LLMs in Production Needs the Same SRE Playbook, Plus Traces
Description: Ankush Sharma at Conf42 LLMs 2025 maps SLOs, metrics, logs, traces and runbooks onto large language models in production.
Body:
A language model in production is still a service: it has latency, an error rate, a capacity limit and somebody who gets paged. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, engineering leader Ankush Sharma, whose career runs from big tech to startups, gave a compact introduction to applying SRE practice and observability to LLM systems.

Set expectations correctly: this is a short primer, not a deep tooling session. It is useful precisely because it is short, and because it argues that you do not need a brand-new discipline to run models, just the existing one applied with care.

## What makes LLMs awkward to observe

Ankush named four problems. LLMs run on enormous data sets, which makes performance monitoring heavy. Their behaviour is dynamic and non-deterministic: the same input can produce different outputs. They are black boxes, so you cannot easily see why a response came out the way it did. And monitoring them needs infrastructure that scales with them. None of that makes the old pillars obsolete, but it changes what you log and what you alert on.

## A four-step implementation

The practical core of the talk is a step-by-step sequence:

1. **Define key metrics**: prediction latency, throughput and error rates.
2. **Add richer logging**: capture inputs, outputs and model behaviour, not just HTTP status codes.
3. **Use distributed tracing** to map end-to-end interactions and pinpoint where a request failed.
4. **Deploy real-time dashboards**, with Grafana as the example.

Step two is the one teams skip, and the one they regret skipping. When a user reports a bad answer, a 200 OK in the access log tells you precisely nothing.

## SRE responsibilities, translated

On the SRE side, Ankush mapped the familiar duties onto models: 24/7 availability through automated failover, runbooks for common incident scenarios, automatic scaling during high-demand periods, and toil reduction. He added one that matters more for ML systems than for most services: a feedback loop with the AI team, so model performance data from production flows back into iteration. SLIs, SLOs and error budgets frame all of it, with the usual goal of balancing reliability against speed.

## Case studies in brief

The case studies are sketches rather than war stories: monitoring response latency for an AI chatbot, keeping a healthcare AI within medical guidelines, and continuously tracking prediction accuracy for fraud detection in banking, where false positives cost real customers. Each one picks a different primary signal, which is a quiet lesson in itself: the right SLI depends on what failure means for that product.

He closed with reading recommendations, starting with Google's SRE book, free to read online.

## Who should watch

SREs who have just been handed an LLM-backed service, and ML engineers who have never written a runbook. If you already run OpenTelemetry traces through your model gateway, you can skip to the related talks for more depth.

Title: A data warehouse scales compute; a data mesh scales ownership
Description: Arun Vivek Supramanian of Amazon at Conf42 Golang 2025 on data mesh principles, the tooling behind them and why the hard part is cultural.
Body:
The central data team with a backlog of 150 feature requests is not short of engineers; it is short of owners. That is the thread running through Arun Vivek Supramanian's talk at Conf42 Golang 2025, where the Senior Data Engineer at Amazon walked through data mesh as an organizational change first and an architecture second.

Honest scope up front: despite the event, this is not a Go talk. It is a well-organized introduction to data mesh, with concrete examples for each principle, aimed at engineers and leads deciding whether the model fits their company.

## Four principles, each with an example you can picture

Arun goes through the four standard principles and attaches a scenario to each, which is what makes the talk easier to follow than most data mesh explainers:

- **Domain-oriented ownership.** The payments team at a fintech owns transaction data, because it understands settlement delays, reversals and fraud patterns better than a central team ever will.
- **Self-serve data infrastructure.** A marketing team publishes campaign performance as a data product through declarative config or a pipeline UI, instead of filing a ticket with data engineering.
- **Federated governance.** Every domain follows a common metadata model, lineage tracking and access control, but enforcement is automated. He describes it as GitOps for data: policies live in code, and deviations raise alerts or block a deployment.
- **Data as a product.** A monthly sales dataset ships with metadata, freshness indicators, a named data steward and alerting, and a failing pipeline gets treated like a broken production API.

## Warehouses, lakes and the five datasets called "customer reviews"

The comparison section is the best part. In a warehouse model, a healthcare company adding real-time lab results to dashboards needs coordination across data engineers, analysts and business teams, and a schema change can ripple through dozens of downstream jobs. In a mesh, the clinical lab domain publishes a versioned data product that patient care or billing can consume directly.

Lakes get a sharper critique. They made storage cheap and flexible, but ownership and documentation went missing. His example is a data scientist looking for customer feedback and finding five similarly named datasets, none documented, none guaranteed. The mesh answer is not a better lake; it is a named owner, a catalog entry, visible lineage and someone to raise an issue with.

## The stack underneath

For the platform layer, Arun names the usual building blocks and what each contributes: Apache Iceberg for schema evolution and time travel, Delta Lake for transactional integrity over a lake, Snowflake for sharing data products across regions without copying them, Amazon S3 as the storage foundation with versioning and IAM-based access, Airflow, Dagster and Prefect for orchestration, and DataHub and OpenMetadata for lineage and discovery. He also points to Zalando, JPMorgan Chase and Netflix as public examples of mesh-style organization, noting that Netflix follows the principles without using the label.

## The hard part is people

The challenges section is refreshingly blunt. Not every team wants to own data. A mesh launched before the platform is mature pushes toil onto domains and produces schema drift and broken pipelines. Distributed ownership widens the attack surface, so role-based access, audit logging and PII tagging have to be automated rather than requested.

His adoption advice follows from that: assess whether your teams already align by domain, pick one pilot domain with a clear business case and a motivated team, build the platform as a product with golden paths for ingestion, validation and publishing, and start governance with minimal policies that grow from feedback.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and platform leads at companies where the central data team is the bottleneck, and anyone who has to explain data mesh to leadership without hand-waving. If your data fits in one well-run warehouse with a happy team behind it, this is a talk about a problem you may not have yet.

Title: ERP testing breaks at the seams between modules, so orchestrate those
Description: Sridhar Dachepelly of Dell Technologies at Conf42 Golang 2025 on orchestrating per-module ERP test suites through one engine and a shared results database.
Body:
An ERP system is finance, HR, inventory, supply chain and a pile of in-house apps pretending to be one product, and most of its bugs live where those modules hand data to each other. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Sridhar Dachepelly, Senior Principal Software Engineer at Dell Technologies, argued that the fix is not one more test framework but an orchestration layer that runs every team's existing suites in business order and records the results in one place.

This is an architecture and process talk rather than a Go code walkthrough. It is most useful to anyone who has tried to run an end-to-end ERP regression across teams that each picked their own tools.

## The problem: every module tests itself, nobody tests the flow

Sridhar sets the scene with his own environment: an ERP made of dozens of modules, each with several test teams, each team with its own automation style, its own framework and its own Docker setup or grid to run scripts on. Each of those suites can be perfectly green while the end-to-end business process is broken.

He also cites industry figures to frame the stakes: most ERP projects run late, and a large share of those delays come from testing bottlenecks. Traditional, module-by-module testing, he says, simply has not kept up with how tightly the modules are now integrated.

## Orchestration is a contract, not a framework

The core idea is to leave each team's framework alone. The orchestration team works with the module owners and the business transformation team to collect the end-to-end scenarios, then chains the existing automation scripts to match them.

The glue is a centralized test database. Every module connects to it, and every run writes its results there automatically. When module one finishes, module two starts from module one's results rather than from hand-copied test data, so a scenario flows across modules the way a real transaction would.

His architecture has a few named parts:

- **An orchestration engine** acting as command central, triggering the GitLab pipelines for each module and recording each workflow's status.
- **An integration layer** holding pipeline information and test data.
- **Per-module execution frameworks**, deliberately left as each team built them.
- **Environment management** inside the orchestration layer, because copying production data down to SIT and dev environments is where validation rules and data quietly go missing when a separate team owns it.
- **Reporting and analytics** on top of the shared database.

That last point about environments is the most practical one in the talk. If the people orchestrating tests also own environment setup, the class of surprises where a test passes in one environment and fails in the next has one owner instead of three.

## Where AI fits, and where it is still a forecast

Sridhar lists four places to apply AI: test planning that ranks critical paths from user stories and past regression defects, test generation from your existing code repository and requirements, predictive analysis that flags likely failures when new code lands in GitLab, and self-healing scripts. He is upfront that the later stages are a roadmap: predictive quality first, then fully autonomous, self-configuring test systems toward the end of the decade, with QA engineers moving toward business-value work.

The talk quotes large percentage gains for environment setup time, execution time and delivery speed. Treat those as the targets the approach is aiming for in his context, and measure your own baseline before promising anyone the same numbers.

## Start with one module

His rollout advice is the least glamorous and most reusable part: start with a pilot on one critical ERP module, standardize naming and documentation so test assets can be reused, put API-first interfaces on the orchestration layer, build security checks into it, and invest in test data provisioning that can simulate real transactional flows. Then scale out over months, not weeks.

## Who should watch

QA leads and platform engineers on large ERP programmes, especially where several vendors or teams own different modules. If you test a single service with a single framework, the orchestration problem will feel abstract; if you have ever coordinated a cross-module regression by spreadsheet, it will feel very familiar.

Title: Dental Claims Run on Rule Engines First, Machine Learning Second
Description: Pravesh Nikhare of Delta Dental of California at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on rule-based AI for dental claims, from policy engines and validators to audit trails and costs.
Body:
Before any model gets to be clever about a dental claim, somebody has to turn a benefits policy into rules a machine can execute. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Pravesh Nikhare of Delta Dental of California walked through how rule-based AI processes dental insurance claims, which parts stay deterministic, and where machine learning and NLP get added on top.

It is an architecture overview, not a code walkthrough. If you build claims, billing or eligibility systems in any regulated industry, the shape will look familiar, and that is the point.

## The problem is paperwork with legal consequences

Traditional claims processing, as Pravesh framed it, is manual data entry plus human judgement applied unevenly. Two assessors read the same policy and reach different answers; patients and dentists wait; insurers pay for the rework. The fix he described starts with encoding: converting policy language (eligibility, limitations, reimbursement rules) into structured rules, so the same claim gets the same decision every time.

## Three components, four stages

The system he outlined has three parts:

- a **policy-driven rule engine** that codifies eligibility criteria, limitations and reimbursement policy;
- a **multi-stage claims validator** that checks each claim against patient eligibility, treatment history and policy terms;
- an **analytics engine** that uses machine learning to flag likely fraud and anomalies.

Claims then move through four stages: submission and initial checks on patient and provider details, rule application (treatment codes, benefit calculations, clinical necessity), cross-checking against the patient's previous treatments, and finally frequency limitations such as annual visit caps and lifetime maximums. Anyone who has debugged a billing system knows that last stage is where the edge cases live. "Two cleanings a year" sounds simple until someone asks which year.

## Compliance is a feature, and so is the audit trail

The section worth the most attention for engineers is compliance. Pravesh named the rulebooks the engine has to respect: American Dental Association guidelines, HIPAA and state-specific insurance policy. Because those change, the rule sets need to be updated dynamically rather than through a long manual release, and every automated decision should leave an audit trail that explains why it was made. That traceability is what lets an insurer defend a denial, and what makes the system trustworthy to the people on the receiving end.

## The honest part: cost, integration and the claims that don't fit

He did not pretend this is free. The talk put initial setup at 200,000 to 500,000 and integration with legacy systems at six to twelve months. Unusual or incomplete claims still need a human, and he stressed balancing automation with oversight to avoid wrongful denials. Bias and transparency get their own slide too: a rule engine that denies consistently is only fair if the rules are.

On benefits, the talk cites studies putting administrative cost savings around 50% and points to round-the-clock processing and faster reimbursement for dentists. Treat those as industry figures quoted in the talk rather than Delta Dental production numbers; the session does not break down its own results.

## Where it goes next

The forward-looking part covers NLP to read clinical notes, deep learning on dental x-rays to assess treatment necessity, blockchain for claims documentation, and extending the same framework to medical, pharmacy and behavioral health claims. This is where the LLM angle of the event comes in: language models are a natural fit for the unstructured parts (notes, attachments) that rule engines cannot read.

## Who should watch

Engineers and analysts working on claims, payments or any policy-heavy workflow, especially if you are being asked to "add AI" to a system whose real job is deterministic. It is a short, clear overview. If you want implementation detail, pair it with the related talks below.

Title: Running AI in the cloud needs security, ops and ethics together
Description: Sanjeev Pellikoduku of SLB at Conf42 Golang 2025 on AI in the cloud as three problems, from homomorphic encryption and enclaves to bias tests and ethics boards.
Body:
Putting a model in the cloud means trusting someone else's hardware with both your data and your model weights. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Sanjeev Pellikoduku of SLB argued that integrating AI with cloud computing is really three problems at once (security, operations and ethics) and that solving one while ignoring the other two is how projects stall.

It's a strategy-level talk, about twenty minutes, and despite the title and the event, the recording stays at the architecture level; Go itself doesn't feature. Think of it as a checklist for the design review.

## Problem one: your data and your model are both targets

Sanjeev leads with security as the main brake on AI adoption in the cloud: data privacy exposure when sensitive information is processed by AI systems, too few automated security tools, and models themselves becoming assets that can be stolen, reverse-engineered or attacked with adversarial inputs. Compliance violations complete the list.

His three countermeasures are the interesting part:

- **Homomorphic encryption**, so models compute on encrypted data without ever decrypting it.
- **Secure enclaves**, hardware-isolated execution environments that protect both the model and the data it processes.
- **Federated learning**, training across decentralised devices so sensitive data never pools in one cloud repository, with model quality close to centralised training.

None of these is free (homomorphic encryption in particular costs a lot of compute), but they're the right shortlist when the threat model includes the infrastructure provider.

## Problem two: operations at multi-cloud scale

The operational section covers technical debt from bolting AI onto legacy systems, monitoring model performance and drift across distributed environments, and keeping deployment pipelines consistent across clouds. The fixes are standard platform engineering applied to AI workloads: a service mesh to secure and observe service-to-service traffic, AI systems monitoring other AI deployments to catch degradation and drift earlier, and infrastructure as code for reproducible, version-controlled environments.

The meta-monitoring idea is worth a pause. Using a model to watch models is reasonable, as long as somebody is still watching the watcher.

## Problem three: ethics as an engineering requirement

Sanjeev treats ethics as operational, not decorative. The risks are discrimination against vulnerable groups, privacy violations, black-box decisions nobody can scrutinise, and environmental cost. His framework: systematic bias testing across demographic groups, explainable-AI techniques to make decisions inspectable, and cross-functional ethics review boards. He frames this as both a moral obligation and a business one, as regulation tightens and stakeholders ask harder questions.

## A bank that did all three

The case study is a global bank facing a rise in sophisticated fraud with fragmented legacy systems. It built a zero-trust AI cloud platform with homomorphic encryption for real-time analysis, secure microservices orchestration and an ethical governance framework with automated bias checks across dozens of demographic variables. He reports better fraud-detection accuracy, fewer false positives and much faster customer responses. Parts of the recording are hard to make out here and the bank isn't named, so take the specific figures as the speaker's report.

He closes with trends: quantum-enhanced machine learning, edge-cloud hybrids and self-optimising AI systems, plus the reminder that each brings new governance questions.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leads planning AI workloads in regulated industries who need one page that covers security, operations and governance. Practitioners looking for implementation detail on any single technique will want a deeper talk afterwards.

- [Moritz Eckert on confidential computing with Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Moritz_Eckert_confidential_computing_Intel_SGX_security_cloud_native), the enclave idea with actual Go in it.

Title: Moving telecom billing and support systems to Go microservices
Description: Bhaskara Beeraka of American Family Insurance at Conf42 Golang 2025 on rebuilding telecom BSS in Go with microservices, Kafka, gRPC and cloud-native deployment.
Body:
Telecom business support systems (BSS) are the unglamorous layer that bills you, manages your account and decides whether your top-up went through. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Bhaskara Beeraka of American Family Insurance walked through migrating legacy telecom BSS to Go microservices: why Go fits always-on, high-volume transaction systems, and the stack he'd use from Kafka to Grafana.

It's a migration playbook more than a code talk, and the delivery is conversational. The useful part is the concrete tool list and the order of operations.

## Why BSS is a Go-shaped problem

Bhaskara describes BSS as one layer in a stack: network at the bottom, operations support above it, BSS, then customer experience on top. The pressure on it comes from customers expecting real-time services and from digital-native competitors. His case for Go has four parts: compiled performance for high-volume transactions, goroutines and channels for millions of simultaneous connections, a garbage collector that keeps resource use low for always-on services, and cross-platform builds.

## Split by business function, scale by demand

The microservices section is about independence. Each business function (billing, customer management and so on) runs as its own service with its own data store and API. A failing service stays contained, with circuit breakers and timeouts keeping the rest operational. And scaling becomes targeted: billing can grow during a peak without scaling the whole estate. Go's small memory footprint and fast start-up make that rapid scaling practical. He reports the Go implementation handling around 2.5 million transactions an hour with very high uptime, against much lower throughput from the legacy system.

## Security for APIs that talk to everything

Every service exposes APIs to internal callers, external ones and third parties, so security is per call: authentication and authorisation, JWTs built with Go's crypto packages, identity management across services, and AES-256 for customer and financial data at rest and in transit. He also mentions real-time security event processing in Go and alignment with the ITU-T X.805 security architecture for telecom.

## The stack, named

The open-source tool list is the most bookmarkable slide:

- **Data:** CockroachDB for distributed storage, Redis via the go-redis client for caching.
- **APIs:** the Echo framework for high-performance REST, gRPC between internal services, OpenAPI for documentation.
- **Observability:** Prometheus for metrics, distributed tracing, Grafana for dashboards; he credits full observability with cutting time to resolve production issues from hours to minutes.
- **Structure:** Go modules for dependencies, domain-driven design for project layout.
- **Streaming:** Kafka with Go consumers for event-driven, real-time processing.

Containerised with Docker, he notes the Go services occupy roughly 15 to 20 MB each, which makes elastic scaling across clouds cheap. CI/CD with automated tests, cross-compilation, static analysis, security scanning and blue-green or canary deploys lets the team ship to production multiple times a day.

## How to start

His advice for a BSS migration is sensibly incremental: set clear business objectives, define services and their APIs carefully, start with a bounded context that has high business value and moderate risk, grow the Go footprint gradually, invest in training and pair programming, and set performance baselines so you can prove the gains with real telemetry.

## Who should watch

Engineers at telecoms or any transaction-heavy business planning a strangler-style migration off a monolith, and Go teams who want a reference stack for a large back office. If you already run Go microservices in production, the tool list will mostly confirm your choices.

Title: Moving anti-money laundering to the cloud with NICE Actimize
Description: Vijaya Kumar Guntumadugu of CitiusTech at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on a cloud AML rollout with NICE Actimize, from data model to fewer false positives.
Body:
Legacy anti-money laundering systems have a signature failure: they flood compliance teams with alerts on transactions that turn out to be perfectly legitimate. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Vijaya Kumar Guntumadugu, Technical Specialist at CitiusTech, presented a case study of a major financial institution moving its AML operations to the cloud on NICE Actimize, covering the data integration work, the detection scenarios and the results reported after go-live.

Be clear on scope: this is a case study of one vendor platform, NICE Actimize, and ends with a recommendation to consult NICE experts. The data integration section is the part that carries over to any AML stack.

## Why the legacy system had to go

Regulators keep adding requirements: KYC protocols, due diligence checks, expanded reporting, all varying by jurisdiction. Guntumadugu describes the traditional AML systems as built on outdated technology with fragmented data silos and manual processes. They generate a high volume of false positives and struggle to keep up with both new financial crime tactics and the pace of regulatory change.

## The modules

The platform pieces he covers are the standard AML trio. Suspicious activity monitoring analyses transactions continuously to detect laundering or fraud patterns. Watch list filtering screens transactions against global sanctions and regulatory lists for known individuals, companies or countries. Customer due diligence gathers and assesses client information to rate risk.

## The real work: one data model for everything

Detection is only as good as its inputs, so the project started with data. Sources included core banking systems, high-frequency trading platforms and global payment networks, merged into a single consolidated view of customers and transactions. A unified schema was designed to handle more than a million transactions a day from those sources, and more than 200 critical data points were mapped, including customer profiles, transaction patterns and risk indicators. Consistent formats reduce latency and make analytics more accurate; a well-designed model also makes it easier to absorb the next regulatory change.

Anyone who has tried to join payment-network data with core banking records will know this is the part of the project that eats the calendar.

## Scenarios, tuning and the feedback loop

On detection, the system integrated with global regulatory watch lists for instant screening and used ML to surface complex laundering patterns among millions of daily transactions. The institution built custom detection scenarios for its own business model and regulatory environment, each tested to confirm it caught suspicious behaviour without adding false positives. Scenarios are updated as tactics and rules change, with analyst feedback collected systematically to refine them.

## The reported results

The figures come from the case study as presented and match the abstract: false positives down 40% and detection improved by 60%. Guntumadugu also cites high system availability, most regulatory reports automated, a redesigned analyst interface with one-click access to key data, lower infrastructure costs from moving off on-prem hardware, and a full implementation finished ahead of the typical industry timeline. The success factors he names are partnership between business, compliance and IT; strong data governance; and continuous improvement.

## Who should watch

Engineers and compliance technologists at banks planning an AML modernisation, especially if NICE Actimize is on the shortlist. If it isn't, the data standardisation and scenario-testing sections are still a useful checklist.

Title: OCR accuracy is won in preprocessing and post-processing
Description: Mohit Sachdeva at Conf42 Golang 2025 walks through the OCR pipeline, from binarisation and deskewing to contextual correction, and its use in four industries.
Body:
The model that recognises characters gets the credit, but the cleanup before and after it decides whether an OCR system is usable. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Mohit Sachdeva, who has 17 years in IT, walked through how optical character recognition works stage by stage and where it pays off in healthcare, finance, legal and education.

It's an explainer, and a friendly one: Mohit stops to define the jargon on his own slides. Go doesn't come up, so this is for people who want to understand OCR rather than implement it in a particular language.

## Stage one: make the image worth reading

Preprocessing gets the most detail, and rightly. Mohit breaks it into four steps:

- **Binarisation:** greyscale to black and white with adaptive thresholding, so uneven lighting doesn't wipe out half a page.
- **Orientation correction:** detecting and fixing skew with the Hough transform and projection-profile analysis.
- **Noise reduction:** median filtering, Gaussian smoothing and morphological operations (erosion, dilation, opening, closing) to remove specks and artefacts.
- **Resolution enhancement:** super-resolution and interpolation for low-resolution scans.

He reports that preprocessing alone lifts accuracy substantially and cuts error rates sharply on degraded documents. Anyone who has fed a phone photo of a crumpled receipt into an OCR engine will believe him without the percentages.

## Stage two: features, segments, patterns

Feature extraction turns pixels into recognisable traits: geometric features such as strokes, angles and shapes, and topological ones such as holes, endpoints and junctions. Character segmentation isolates characters with connected-component analysis and clustering, which also helps with vertical and horizontal text. Recognition then uses template matching, adaptive algorithms, neural networks and multiple classifiers voting on the answer.

## Stage three: context fixes what pixels can't

Post-processing is the stage Mohit calls the one that takes OCR from functional to exceptional. Contextual understanding and probabilistic analysis correct the raw output, so a smudged character inside a known word or field format gets resolved. He credits this stage with the largest error reduction of the pipeline.

That matches practice: the cheapest accuracy gain is often a dictionary, a field schema or a checksum rather than a bigger model.

## Four industries, one comparison table

The application half covers:

- **Healthcare:** digitising patient records, prescriptions and insurance forms; giving clinicians fast access to history in emergencies; lab results handled with HIPAA compliance in mind.
- **Finance:** faster audit preparation, real-time flagging of regulatory issues, quicker customer identification and onboarding.
- **Legal:** digitising contracts and case files, faster discovery for litigation, easier legal research across historical documents.
- **Education:** text-to-speech for visually impaired readers, searchable archives, and help grading handwritten assignments.

He compares the sectors on efficiency, accuracy, time saved and satisfaction, with finance leading most columns and education scoring high on satisfaction despite lower efficiency. The figures aren't attributed to specific studies, so read the table as a relative picture.

## Where it goes next

The outlook is deeper integration with deep learning for feature extraction, multilingual recognition across scripts, edge deployment on constrained devices, better handling of document variation, and stronger security for sensitive content. His closing point is that OCR is heading beyond character recognition toward contextual understanding and analytics.

## Who should watch

Developers and analysts about to build or buy document processing who want the pipeline vocabulary, and product people who need to know why a vendor's demo document looks cleaner than theirs. Computer-vision engineers can skip it.

Title: TinyML and edge computing: models in kilobytes, not gigabytes
Description: Pradeep Kumar Vattumilli at Conf42 Golang 2025 gives a primer on edge computing and TinyML, from quantisation and pruning to microcontroller deployment.
Body:
A neural network that fits in a few kilobytes and runs for months on a coin cell sounds like a trick, but it's an engineering discipline with its own toolchain. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Pradeep Kumar Vattumilli gave a primer on edge computing and TinyML: why you'd move inference onto the device, how models get squeezed that small, and what you give up to do it.

This is an introductory talk, about twenty minutes, and Go doesn't come up. Think of it as a first lecture on the topic, useful if you're new to on-device machine learning.

## Compute where the data is

Pradeep defines edge computing as processing at or near where data is generated instead of shipping it to distant servers and back. The gains are latency in milliseconds, continued operation when connectivity drops, and privacy because sensitive data stays local. His examples are the classic ones: self-driving cars that can't wait for a round trip, factory equipment flagging anomalies on the spot, and wearables that analyse vital signs on the device and only transmit critical alerts.

## Three tiers, three budgets

The clearest slide is his comparison of cloud (remote data centres), edge (local gateways or servers) and TinyML (the end device itself):

| Tier | Latency | Power | Memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cloud | 100 ms to seconds | Kilowatts | Gigabytes+ |
| Edge | 10 to 100 ms | Watts | Megabytes |
| TinyML | 1 to 10 ms | Milliwatts | Kilobytes |

Each step down trades model size and flexibility for speed, power and independence from the network. Choosing the tier is most of the design decision.

## How a model shrinks to fit

TinyML relies on three compression techniques: quantisation (from 32-bit numbers down to 8-bit or lower while staying above the accuracy you need), pruning, and knowledge distillation. On the software side he names TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers, which targets boards with as little as 256 KB of flash. On the hardware side, newer microcontrollers include dedicated machine-learning accelerators.

The development workflow has four steps:

1. Collect representative sensor data that captures the edge cases, and label it carefully.
2. Train at full precision on proper infrastructure.
3. Optimise with quantisation, pruning and distillation until the model fits.
4. Deploy to the target microcontroller and verify speed, power and accuracy in the real world.

Step one is the one teams skimp on, and the one that decides whether step four works.

## What it's good for, and what bites

Applications span healthcare monitoring (fall detection without the cloud), agriculture (soil sensors driving irrigation), manufacturing (vibration and acoustic signatures for predictive maintenance) and consumer wearables with local voice commands. The challenges are equally concrete: very tight memory, compute and energy budgets; accuracy loss under aggressive optimisation; the need for embedded-systems expertise; and exposed devices that invite tampering and model theft.

He closes with trends to watch: federated learning, neuromorphic hardware, energy harvesting for battery-free inference, and compressed transformers small enough for microcontrollers.

## Who should watch

Developers and architects meeting edge AI for the first time, or IoT teams deciding whether a model belongs in the cloud, a gateway or the sensor itself. Embedded ML practitioners will know all of this; the comparison table is still a handy slide for explaining the trade-offs to a product manager.

- [Sai Prasad Mukala on GPU-accelerated AI at the edge](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sai_Prasad_Mukala_intelligence_edge_gpu), the heavier end of the edge tier.

Title: Why most AI models never reach production in finance
Description: Jitender Jain, ex-Capital One, at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on AI in financial services and a six-step document pipeline for loan income verification.
Body:
Jitender Jain, a former Principal Software Engineer at Capital One with 17 years in financial technology, opened with a striking statistic in his Conf42 Large Language Models 2025 talk: by the industry figures he cites, only about one in five AI models actually gets deployed to production. His reading is that the blockers are mostly not about model quality. Resistance from decision makers and integration with existing systems account for more of the failures than weak performance does.

From there the talk covers where AI pays off in financial services, a case study on automating income verification for loans, and the practices that get projects past the pilot stage. Jain notes the opinions are his own, not his employer's.

## Leadership buy-in beats model accuracy

The breakdown he shows splits the reasons models stall into three groups: decision makers resisting changes to existing operations, technical integration problems, and model performance that isn't strong enough. The lesson he draws is that polished demos don't survive contact with an organisation unless leadership is on board and the integration work is planned.

## Where AI earns its place in banking

Jain walks through a set of use cases. Object detection, with YOLO models for autonomous vehicles and shelf monitoring in retail, serves as the cross-industry example. In financial services, document processing is the big one: loan applications with complex forms and supporting materials, invoices and receipts, and KYC document verification across formats and legal frameworks. Then fraud detection through anomaly detection and real-time transaction monitoring, which should improve security while cutting false positives. Customer service bots and automated fraud alerts, personalisation from dynamic pricing to loan terms tailored to individual risk profiles, and investment management round out the list.

## The case study: income verification

Income verification is the foundation of responsible lending: for the lender it is risk management and compliance, for the customer it determines what they can borrow and on what terms. The manual process causes three problems Jain keeps returning to: errors when humans misread documents, delays that frustrate customers and push up abandonment, and inefficiency that costs institutions heavily.

The objective is to automate verification with AI-augmented document processing without removing humans entirely. The pipeline has six stages: capture the documents, classify the document type, extract the information, enrich the extracted data, review and validate with a human where needed, and pass verified data to downstream consumers. Humans handle exceptions and complex cases; the machine handles the repetitive reading.

It's the kind of pipeline that sounds obvious once drawn, which is usually a sign someone has built it more than once.

## Four practices for getting past the pilot

His best practices are pragmatic. Identify problems where AI clearly adds value: repetitive tasks, decision support, large data volumes. Plan and budget for data, infrastructure, talent and ongoing model maintenance, with security, compliance and ethics included from the start. Choose the model to fit the job; some problems need a decision tree, not deep learning. And use the ML SDKs and APIs from AWS, Google and Microsoft instead of building everything in-house.

He ends on the considerations that never go away in finance: data privacy, ethics, regulation, and organisational change, which he calls often harder than the technology.

## Who should watch

Engineers and technical leads in banks and fintechs planning an AI document-processing project, and anyone who needs to explain to leadership why a good model isn't enough. It is an overview with one worked example, not a code walkthrough.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: In AI reconciliation, the machine matches and humans judge
Description: Naveen Gowda of Couchbase at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on AI and RPA for financial reconciliation across ERPs, with people kept on exceptions and compliance.
Body:
Month-end close is where finance teams find out how badly their systems talk to each other. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Naveen Gowda, Director of Data Engineering at Couchbase, gave a compact talk on applying AI to financial reconciliation in large enterprises: pattern recognition for errors like duplicate invoices, RPA for the routine matching, predictive analytics for exceptions, and people kept firmly in charge of what the outputs mean.

At around ten minutes, this is a short overview rather than an implementation walkthrough. It is most useful as a map of where automation fits in a reconciliation process.

## The starting point: ERPs that don't integrate

Gowda opens with the problem most large finance organisations recognise. They run several complex ERP systems that don't integrate cleanly, teams reconcile between them by hand, and the manual handoffs become bottlenecks that delay the month-end close. As digital transaction volumes grow, he argues, a manual process simply can't keep up.

## Three jobs for AI

He splits the AI contribution into three parts. First, pattern recognition: machine learning and natural language processing to spot issues such as duplicate invoices in seconds, where a human search might take days. Second, robotic process automation paired with AI to remove manual touchpoints, so routine reconciliations run in the background without constant oversight. Third, exception handling: predictive analytics to forecast anomalies and shorten the time to resolve them, freeing the team for complex, higher-value work.

The point of the split is that each part is a different kind of tool. Matching is deterministic plumbing, anomaly prediction is statistics, and the remaining judgement calls stay with people.

## Integration first, then training, then iteration

The implementation section is the most practical. Gowda recommends an iPaaS layer such as MuleSoft with an API-led architecture and queuing to connect the ERPs for faster, closer to real-time reconciliation, which is a sensible reminder that most reconciliation pain is an integration problem before it's an AI problem. He then stresses training programmes for the finance team, phased rollout starting from a proof of concept, and short feedback loops; his team used biweekly sprint reviews to keep improving the system.

Throughout, he quotes percentage improvements for accuracy, close-cycle time, cost and compliance risk. The talk doesn't say which organisations or studies they come from, so treat them as the speaker's figures rather than benchmarks.

## Humans stay in the loop on purpose

The closing message is about balance. AI handles the data volume, but human insight is what checks that outputs match business needs and regulatory requirements. As regulations change, the AI systems have to change with them, and people are the ones who notice. Gowda frames it as empowering finance staff to do more meaningful work, not replacing them.

## Who should watch

Finance operations leads and data engineers scoping automation for reconciliation or close processes. If you already run RPA in finance, the integration-first advice and the split between matching and exception handling are the parts to take away.

Title: Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 - follow the packet, rotate the secret, read the bill
Description: Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 in review, 81 talks on EKS networking, dynamic secrets, edge APIs, Wasm on Kubernetes, microservices, cloud costs and databases.
Body:
[Conf42 Cloud Native 2025](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2025) ran on March 6, 2025 with 81 talks, and the best of them were refreshingly unglamorous. How does a packet actually reach a pod in EKS? How do you rotate a secret every two weeks without restarting the app? Why is the database still the one tier that doesn't scale? Speakers from AWS, HashiCorp, Microsoft, Meta, Mirantis, Fermyon, Comcast, Expedia Group, Booking.com, Salesforce and a strong group of sponsors answered with demos rather than diagrams.

## Know your plumbing

[Dumlu Timuralp](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Dumlu_Timuralp_networking_performance_optimization) (AWS) took the packet's-eye view of Amazon EKS, from the internet through Route53, the ALB and the VPC to the pod, pitched as the Magic School Bus for cloud networking. The point is practical: stop being stuck between teams during an outage because nobody can trace the path. [Roman Rastiehaiev](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Roman_Rastiehaiev_api_gateways_comparison) (HiBob) compared open source API gateways such as Kong, Traefik and Envoy, and [Akim Mamedov](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Akim_Mamedov_p2p_networks_decentralization) explained the principles behind P2P networks like BitTorrent and IPFS.

Sponsor Zuplo added the global angle. [Adrian Machado](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Adrian_Machado_api_network_distribution) argued for running auth, validation, rate limiting and caching at the edge while keeping data-bound services near the database, then debugged his own 1.3-second demo live. Sponsor Dimensigon's [Daniel Moya](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Daniel_Moya_automation_decentralization_orchestration) showed open source, decentralised automation that moves commands and files between networks that can't see each other, through a bridge node.

## Secrets, segments and the supply of trust

[Rosemary Wang](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Rosemary_Wang_secrets_handling_security) (HashiCorp) started from a requirement every security team writes and every app team dreads: rotate the secrets applications use every two weeks without manual restarts. Her answer is automation, comparing application-agnostic and application-aware ways to inject secrets. [Venkata Nedunoori](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Venkata_Nedunoori_security_segmentation_optimization) (dentsu international) covered micro-segmentation in cloud environments, and [FNU Parshant](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_FNU_Parshant_securing_hardware) (Arm) went down to the silicon with dual-state models for hardware security.

## The developer loop and the runtime

[Anita Ihuman](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Anita_Ihuman_kubernetes_development_testing) (MetalBear) made the case for "remocal" development: test against a realistic cloud environment from your laptop and cut the inner loop from hours to seconds. [Eti Ijeoma](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Eti_Ijeoma_docker_cache_efficiency) (Manufactured) gave a tidy talk on Docker build caching with layer ordering, bind mounts and cache mounts. [Mikkel Mork Hegnhoj](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Mikkel_Mork_Hegnhoj_kubernetes_architecture_extensions) (Fermyon) introduced Spin and SpinKube for running WebAssembly apps on Kubernetes, with an honest comparison against containers. [Bharath Nallapeta](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Bharath_Nallapeta_cluster_provisioning_scale) (Mirantis) presented k0rdent, which hides the hundreds of lines of YAML Cluster API normally demands, and [Siri Varma Vegiraju](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Siri_Varma_Vegiraju_workflow_dapr_failure) (Microsoft) used Dapr workflows so one failed step doesn't force a restart of a long-running process.

## Microservices, defended and questioned

[Chad Green](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Chad_Green_microservices_architecture_defense) (Jasper Engines & Transmissions) delivered "In Defense of Microservices", taking the complexity critiques head on with real implementations. [Asher Sterkin](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Asher_Sterkin_cloud_flexibility_ports__adapters) argued for applying Ports and Adapters systematically so today's cloud choices don't lock out tomorrow's. [Praful Konduru](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Praful_Konduru_resilience_scalability_faulttolerance) (Meta) covered fault-tolerant cloud-native design, and [Prithvi Raj](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Prithvi_Raj_community_tales_future) (Mirantis), former community manager of LitmusChaos, told the story of growing the chaos engineering community as the project became CNCF incubating.

## Every cloud has a bill

Cost came up from every direction. [Maksymilian Kalek](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Maksymilian_Kalek_aws_cost_efficiency) (Perelyn) built an ultra-budget AWS backend with Lambda and Powertools, self-hosted PostgreSQL on a cheap EC2 instance, and React on S3 and CloudFront. [Seshendranath Balla Venkata](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Seshendranath_Balla_Venkata_cost_cloud_efficiency) (Comcast) shared how his team optimised AWS EMR and Databricks workloads, and [Shinu Pushpan](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Shinu_Pushpan_saas_multitenancy_security) (Expedia Group) balanced performance, security and cost in multi-tenant SaaS. [Brian Loomis](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Brian_Loomis_observability_insights_telemetry) (Progress) used OpenTelemetry for something other than debugging: consumption-based pricing and showing customers what they use.

Gold sponsor Rapydo took on the most expensive tier. [Matan Nataf](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Matan_Nataf_rapydo_databases_broken) argued that developers own the queries while CloudOps owns the consequences, then demoed blocking, throttling and caching runaway queries across a fleet of MySQL and PostgreSQL instances.

## People and AI

Not everything was infrastructure. Sponsor Buildly's [Gregory Lind](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Gregory_Lind_teams_collaboration_efficiency) made the case for radical transparency in software teams, from one shared backlog to committing code on day one. On the AI side, [Shivay Lamba](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Shivay_Lamba_container_ecosystem_automation) (Couchbase) tackled AI projects whose datasets, models and weights live in separate places, using ModelKits to package them, and [Anant Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Anant_Kumar_apache_spark_clusters) (Salesforce) built resilient Apache Spark clusters on Kubernetes for AI workloads.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) at Platinum, [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/) at Gold, and [APA Tech](https://apa.at/about/apa-tech/), [Buildly](https://www.buildly.io/), [Dimensigon](https://www.dimensigon.com/), [Jozu](https://jozu.com/) and [Zuplo](https://zuplo.com/) at Silver. All 81 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDi1jv-thhvcy4pJ3sBeUJr).

The series returns with [Conf42 Cloud Native 2026](https://www.conf42.com/cloud2026).

Title: Commit on day one - radical transparency for software teams
Description: Gregory Lind of Buildly at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on radical transparency, one shared backlog, open decisions, admitted mistakes and fewer silos.
Body:
New developers at Buildly are expected to commit code on their first day, into their own branch, and get feedback on it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Gregory Lind](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Gregory_Lind_teams_collaboration_efficiency), CEO and founder of Buildly, used that ritual as the entry point to "radical therapy for software teams": a set of practices built on radical transparency, drawn from a book of the same name he co-wrote.

This is a culture talk, not a technical one, and it comes from a founder whose product (Buildly's AI-assisted product management, with humans in the loop) is built around the same ideas. No code on screen, a lot of hard-won management advice.

## Radical as in fundamental, therapy as in what managers end up doing

Lind defines his terms up front. Radical means a fundamental, far-reaching change, not the surfing kind. Therapy is a nod to what anyone who has managed a team already knows: a lot of the job is helping people through struggles and rebuilding trust and accountability. He is clear he is not a licensed therapist, he just plays one in product management.

## Four principles of transparency

The framework rests on open communication inside the team and with the wider organisation, data-driven decision making, continuous feedback from the team and later from customers, and inclusivity and diversity of perspectives. The practical move that ties them together is merging the product backlog with the developer backlog, so there is one process everyone can see. The payoff he claims: fewer silos, faster decisions, shorter conflicts (data settles arguments faster than seniority), and people who stay because they feel heard.

He points to Atlassian and to Google's habit of sharing engineers across cross-functional teams as examples, and to IBM's AI Fairness 360 and Netflix's responsible AI work as models for ethics tooling.

## Show your reasoning, not just your result

Transparency, in Lind's version, goes further than most teams are comfortable with:

- Share how a decision was made, not only what was decided, by opening the backlog to the team and even to customers.
- Ask for criticism, and keep it constructive inside the team.
- Make performance and compensation policies transparent, since that is where a lot of unhappiness actually comes from, along with reporting lines.
- Test AI features in production, not just the model that built them, and embed ethical checks in the process so nothing quietly skews what customers are shown.

## Run your product like a startup, and your startup like an open source project

The most memorable line in the talk is his summary of the method: run a product like a lean startup, and run a startup like an open source project. Share work openly, ask for feedback early, and build communities that contribute. He also defends building the better mousetrap: an existing tool that doesn't fit your needs is a reason to build in the open, not a reason to stop.

His counter-example is Theranos, built behind closed doors with fake-it-till-you-make-it secrecy and too much control in one person's hands. Transparency from the start, he argues, would have changed the story.

## Where Agile and Scrum fall short

Lind's critique of Scrum is that it separates roles (the pigs and chickens) when a cloud-native, multi-repo product needs everyone pulling together. His radical process brings development, product, marketing and design cycles into one, treats developers as stakeholders alongside management and marketing, and favours demo days and surveys over documentation for its own sake.

Two rules stand out. When you ship a bug that breaks part of the application, say so before users find it. And keep the CEO from going straight to individual developers; route questions through shared, consistently updated channels so nobody gets yanked out of focus.

He is also realistic about morale. The goal is not to be a cheerleader, but to build trust and safety, run daily check-ins people actually read, celebrate the occasional win, and notice who is struggling, including whether they are buried in too many tools.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, product managers and founders of small teams who suspect their process has more walls than it needs. Engineers looking for technical content can skip it.

- [The Future of Work: Engaged Leaders and Empowered Teams](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Leslie_Martinich_future_work_teams) by Leslie Martinich (Competitive Focus) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

Buildly was a Silver sponsor of Conf42 Cloud Native 2025. Lind describes it as a software architecture as a service company with open source products and Buildly Labs, AI-assisted product management with human oversight that now carries insights from the Radical Therapy book. He also runs OpenBuild, a mentorship programme for developers moving from junior to senior and from senior to CTO.

Title: Self-healing ETL pipelines and the metadata they need
Description: Sudhakar Kandhikonda of Lord Abbett at Conf42 Golang 2025 on AI across extract, transform and load, from source detection to self-healing pipelines.
Body:
Ask a data engineer where their week went and the honest answer is often a pipeline that broke because a column changed type. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Sudhakar Kandhikonda of Lord Abbett, who has 18 years in data warehousing and data engineering, walked through how machine learning is being applied to every phase of ETL, and why the most interesting piece is the pipeline that diagnoses and fixes its own failures.

It's a short, numbers-heavy survey talk. Go doesn't feature; the subject is data integration architecture, with a particular eye on Indian enterprises.

## The problem is preparation, not analysis

Sudhakar opens with the data explosion, framed around India: high AI adoption among Indian enterprises and fast-growing data volumes. The operational complaint is familiar anywhere. Engineers spend a large share of their time preparing data and troubleshooting ETL jobs designed when a gigabyte-scale warehouse counted as big. His argument is that those systems won't stretch to current volumes without rethinking.

He anchors the benefits in a 2024 study in the journal Decision Support Systems that analysed 287 enterprise data integration implementations, and reports processing-efficiency, error-reduction and cost figures from it.

## Four parts of an AI-enhanced pipeline

The architecture has four components:

- **Ingestion** that handles many formats at once, including nested JSON and industry-specific EDI variants.
- **A machine-learning subsystem** where transformer models predict the right transformation path for data structures they haven't seen before.
- **A metadata repository**, which he ties to much higher pipeline reliability.
- **Self-healing mechanisms**, which he credits with cutting average downtime per incident from 6.4 hours to 23.7 minutes.

## Extract, transform, load, each with a model

On extraction he covers machine-learning source discovery for onboarding new data sources faster, adaptive scheduling that balances load on source systems, and format recognition for unfamiliar formats after training on a modest set of examples. Transformation brings pattern recognition to automate recurring transformations, anomaly detection for data quality, and predictive cleansing that resolves issues which used to need a human. Loading becomes a decision engine: choosing the target, partitioning dynamically and optimising in real time, which he links to better query performance and lower storage cost.

## The pipeline that pages itself, then fixes it

The section worth watching is self-healing. Neural networks trained on pipeline telemetry predict integration failures before they hit downstream systems. Because most failures follow recognisable patterns, many can be fixed with predefined remediations. And reinforcement learning, in his telling, resolves more incidents autonomously than simpler machine-learning approaches. The upshot is fewer tickets that need a human at all.

The quiet dependency running through all of it is metadata. A self-healing pipeline is only as clever as what it knows about its sources, so his advice to build a solid metadata foundation first is the most practical line in the talk.

## Mind the technical debt and the skills gap

Sudhakar is candid about the obstacles. Large organisations carry thousands of transformation scripts, many with hardcoded business logic nobody has reviewed in a long time; skills in AI and machine learning are scarce, even in a talent hub; and automated processing invites more regulatory scrutiny. His recommended path: start with high-value use cases, enrich metadata, add feedback loops, keep humans over critical steps, and invest in skills. He closes with forecasts for reinforcement learning, natural-language integration interfaces and more autonomous data ecosystems by 2030.

The figures come thick and fast and aren't individually sourced beyond the study he names, so treat them as directional.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects planning a modernisation of legacy ETL, and managers who need a vocabulary for AI-assisted pipelines. If you want code or tool names, this isn't the talk; pair it with something hands-on.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Sruthi Erra Hareram on Kube-native ETL at scale with PySpark and Airflow](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Sruthi_Erra_Hareram_etl_airflow_optimization), the hands-on companion.
- [Gaurav Mittal on using AI to optimise ETL pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Gaurav_Mittal_etl_pieplines).
- [Srinivas Murri on smart data pipelines and AI automation in data engineering](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Srinivas_Murri_smart_data_pipelines).

Title: A Go framework for deciding what AI decides and humans keep
Description: Rajarshi Tarafdar of JP Morgan Chase at Conf42 Golang 2025 on CWIF, a Go-based framework that splits decisions between AI and humans in automation-heavy industries.
Body:
Most automation projects argue about which model to use. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Rajarshi Tarafdar of JP Morgan Chase argued about something more useful: where the line between machine and human decisions sits. He presented the Collaborative Workflow Intelligence Framework (CWIF), which uses Go for the high-throughput data paths and draws explicit boundaries for what AI may decide alone and what a person must sign off.

It's a framework overview with case studies, not a code walkthrough, and the audio is rough in places. The structure is what's worth taking away.

## Four problems with modern automation

Rajarshi starts with the tensions any automation-heavy business knows: keeping human oversight where safety and standards require it, processing large data volumes in real time, integrating complex existing systems, and helping the workforce collaborate with AI rather than compete with it. CWIF is pitched as the bridge: a bidirectional flow where AI recommends, humans make the ethically sensitive or context-dependent calls, and feedback on outcomes keeps improving the models.

## Why Go carries the hot path

The Go case is familiar but well placed. Goroutines handle many concurrent data streams; static typing catches the class of runtime errors that, in a factory or a bank, cost revenue; and Go's readability helps engineers and data scientists work in the same codebase. In the architecture (data-collection microservices, an AI processing core, human interface components), Go powers the collection and transformation layers where concurrency demand is highest. He shows benchmarks comparing Go with the previous systems and with Python and Java implementations, reporting large speed-ups and lower memory use, without detailing the test setup.

## Three industries, one pattern

The case studies all follow the same shape, which is the point:

- **Manufacturing:** Go microservices collect and normalise data from mixed sensor networks; models predict maintenance needs; alerts go out; humans make the final call on complex maintenance and quality issues. He reports fewer production delays and less unplanned downtime.
- **Logistics:** AI plans routes and balances loads; human dispatchers review recommendations in unusual or critical situations. A regional logistics provider saw lower costs and better on-time delivery.
- **Financial services:** AI extracts data from loan applications, Go services run risk calculations with very low latency, and underwriters focus on the complex cases the system flags. A mid-size regional bank improved loan approval efficiency while keeping its risk profile.

He also reports higher worker engagement, which matches the framework's premise: people keep the judgement work.

## Roll it out in recommendation-only mode first

The implementation path is the most transferable part:

1. Map current processes and decision boundaries.
2. Run an advisory pilot where AI only recommends.
3. Move to supervised automation, increasing autonomy under oversight.
4. Keep optimising from performance data and feedback.

Go's modularity helps here, he notes, because clear service boundaries let you promote one decision type at a time. Change management and education run alongside, so workers understand how the system complements their role.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leads designing human-in-the-loop systems in manufacturing, logistics or finance, and anyone who needs a staged plan to take AI from advisory to autonomous. If you want Go internals, there's little here; if you need the decision-boundary vocabulary, it's a solid starting point.

Title: Moving a scooter two blocks shouldn't pay like a rush-hour rescue
Description: Kaan Tas, General Manager at Lime, at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on replacing flat task prices with AI-driven dynamic pricing for micromobility operations.
Body:
Moving an e-scooter two blocks in a quiet area and retrieving a broken one from a congested city centre at rush hour are not the same job, yet flat pricing pays them the same. That example anchors Kaan Tas's Conf42 Large Language Models 2025 talk. Tas, General Manager at Lime, explained why fixed prices for street-based tasks like rebalancing bikes and scooters inflate costs and leave urgent work undone, and how AI-driven dynamic pricing addresses it.

The talk is short, about ten minutes by Tas's own estimate, and stays at the level of the pricing model's inputs and logic rather than the code behind it.

## A fast-growing industry that still has to make money

Tas came to micromobility via construction, hospitality startups and AI-driven property investment, which may explain why he frames everything in operational terms. Cities are adding bike lanes and backing shared mobility, and he cites a market projection of roughly fourfold growth by 2033. Growth doesn't mean profit, though. He lists four industry problems: limited parking infrastructure, vehicles piling up in low-demand areas, high operational costs from manual logistics decisions, and static pricing that ignores real conditions. Pricing, he argues, is the easiest lever to pull.

## Why flat prices fail

Set the price too high and costs inflate; too low and tasks go unfulfilled because workers won't take them. His four specific failures of fixed pricing: it ignores real-time labour availability, so you overpay when workers are plentiful and get delays when they're scarce; it doesn't vary by location, so some workers reject low-paid tasks while others are overpaid for easy ones; it ignores task density, so areas that urgently need redistribution get no extra attention; and it doesn't react to weather, traffic or events.

## The inputs: density, workers, urgency, conditions

The AI model he describes prices each task from four signals. Task density: a backlog in an area raises payouts to attract workers there. Worker availability: few workers means higher prices to balance supply. Time sensitivity: urgent jobs, such as pulling a scooter out of a no-parking zone, pay more so they get done fast. Environmental conditions: weather, traffic and city events that change the real cost of the work.

The process runs in four steps: collect real-time task, worker and citywide data; forecast demand with machine learning; adjust prices automatically; and learn from outcomes to refine the strategy.

## Borrowing from Uber and Amazon

Tas explicitly compares the approach to Uber's surge pricing, which raises fares when rider demand outpaces available drivers and adjusts for hotspots like airports and stadiums and for bad weather. He also points to Amazon's dynamic pricing on demand, competitor prices and inventory. The difference here is that the price is paid to a workforce, not charged to a customer, which turns surge logic into a tool for getting operational work done at the lowest cost that still gets it picked up.

The abstract mentions a Lime example where AI cut warehouse task costs by more than 20%; the recorded talk keeps to the model's logic and doesn't walk through that result in detail.

## Who should watch

Operations and product people running gig-style task marketplaces, whether that's fleet rebalancing, deliveries or field service. It's a short primer on the inputs to dynamic task pricing; engineers looking for modelling details won't find them here.

Title: Where software expects failure and keeps running
Description: Cloud native thinking
Body:
# Cloud native, but make it… manageable

Cloud native started as a promise.

You know the one. Faster deployments. Infinite scale. Fewer problems. More sleep.

Somewhere along the way, it turned into Kubernetes YAML, surprise cloud bills, fifteen dashboards, and a deep emotional relationship with latency. Growth.

Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 is here for everyone living that reality.

This is a big one. Seventy plus talks across Kubernetes, microservices, APIs, data, observability, security, AI, scaling, and all the tools that somehow became “essential”. From cloud testing without the wait to running ultra budget workloads for pennies, this conference covers the whole spectrum from scrappy to enterprise-grade.

AI is everywhere, naturally. Cloud-native LLMs, predictive analytics, AI-powered fraud detection, recommendation systems, digital twins, and AI-driven operations show up across industries like healthcare, finance, insurance, retail, manufacturing, and entertainment. There’s plenty of “this is cool”, and also a healthy dose of “here’s how this breaks in production”.

Kubernetes gets a lot of love. Real-world stories about running clusters at scale, improving uptime, reducing costs, simplifying connectivity, and making microservices behave. There are also talks questioning assumptions, defending simpler architectures, and reminding us that not every problem needs twelve services and a service mesh.

Security, resilience, and observability are baked throughout the program. Secrets management, zero trust, multi-cloud monitoring, chaos engineering, disaster recovery, and cost optimization all make an appearance. Because cloud native is not just about shipping faster, it’s about surviving success.

If your job involves containers, clouds, APIs, data pipelines, or explaining to someone why the architecture diagram looks like that, this one’s for you. Cloud native is powerful, messy, and still very much evolving.

Bring curiosity. And maybe your favorite kubectl alias.

Title: Put the API gateway at the edge and keep the data near the database
Description: Adrian Machado of Zuplo at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on which parts of an API belong at the edge, the data trade-offs, and a slow D1 demo debugged live.
Body:
Rejecting a missing API key should not require a round trip from Japan to Texas. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Adrian Machado](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Adrian_Machado_api_network_distribution), staff engineer at Zuplo, made the case for running the compute-heavy, data-light parts of an API (auth, validation, rate limiting, caching) on the worldwide edge, while the services that touch your database stay close to it.

It is an honest talk. Machado spends as much time on why the edge is not a silver bullet as on why APIs suit it, and his own demo comes out slower than the API it was copying, which he then debugs on stage.

## What "the edge" buys you, and what it costs

A typical API lives in one region, so a user far away pays for every undersea hop, sometimes adding up to seconds. CDNs fixed this for static files. Edge functions, pushed by Cloudflare, Vercel and others through the WinterCG working group, do the same for code: lightweight function-as-a-service runtimes deployed at the CDN's points of presence, typically with a zero millisecond cold start.

The trade-offs are real. Cloudflare's runtime is JavaScript plus some WebAssembly, so Python or Rust services need a Wasm build. Node.js compatibility is partial, and anything that needs raw TCP probably won't work. Bundle sizes are capped. Libraries built for the browser usually run, because the edge is essentially V8.

## Your data is the catch

The bigger problem is that compute is global and data usually isn't. A CRUD call from an edge function pays the edge-to-database round trip, which can be slower than co-locating function and database in one region. Thousands of edge invocations can also exhaust your database connections.

Machado lays out three answers in order of effort:

- **A database proxy** such as Prisma Accelerate or RDS Proxy, which pools connections and can cache, without changing the database.
- **A globally distributed data store** like Cassandra or CockroachDB, or read replicas near the edge, at the price of consistency: async writes give stale reads, sync writes give slow ones.
- **Data that lives at the edge**, such as Cloudflare R2 for blobs, D1 or Upstash for per-region SQLite (handy for GDPR locality), or edge key-value stores for configuration that rarely changes.

## Why APIs are a good fit

Public API users can be anywhere, because you have no control over where your customers deploy. And a lot of API work is compute, not data: authentication and authorisation (especially API keys you validate yourself), logging, request validation with libraries like Ajv or Zod, bot and bad-actor filtering, rate limiting and caching.

Rate limiting at the edge has a bonus effect he points out: rejected requests never reach your central services, which frees them up for legitimate traffic and soaks up some DDoS along the way. His recommended architecture follows from that. Run an edge API gateway for those concerns, and host the actual microservices near the data, ideally replicated across a few regions. The gateway layer is JavaScript or Wasm; your services can be Django or anything else.

## The demo that came out slow

The demo is an ATM locator, a good edge use case because ATM locations are regional, rarely written, and very cacheable. As a baseline he calls Capital One's Nessie hackathon API, which answers in roughly 100 milliseconds. His version uses a Next.js site on Vercel, a Zuplo edge function and route, an edge cache, and Cloudflare D1 holding ATM data he gathered from Capital One's dataset.

The first call took about 1.3 seconds. Rather than hide it, he walks the debugging checklist: is the D1 query itself slow (a latitude/longitude index would help), is the database placed too far away, or is gateway latency to blame. His most likely suspect is placement, since D1 won't necessarily put a low-traffic hobby database close to you, and the practical fix is to cache at the edge so the round trip happens as rarely as possible. It is a better lesson than a perfect demo would have been.

## Who should watch

API engineers modernising a public API, CTOs thinking about API developer experience, and anyone whose global users are paying latency for work that never needed the database. It is a high-level talk, not an introduction to serverless and not a deep tuning session.

Title: Where Salesforce AI fits in clinical trial management
Description: Harsha Vardhan Reddy Yeddula at Conf42 Golang 2025 on generative AI and Salesforce in clinical trial management: patient matching, documents, supply chains.
Body:
Clinical trials fail quietly long before the science does: not enough eligible patients, protocol amendments, sites running out of the drug. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Harsha Vardhan Reddy Yeddula, a software professional with 17 years in IT, surveyed how generative AI and Salesforce's AI capabilities apply to clinical trial management systems (CTMS), from patient recruitment and regulatory documents to supply chains and site resourcing.

Set expectations: this is a domain survey for life-sciences IT, and Go isn't part of it. There's no code or architecture diagram to copy; the value is a map of where AI touches a trial's lifecycle.

## Recruitment is the bottleneck worth automating

Harsha spends the most time on finding the right patients. Matching algorithms read electronic health records to identify eligible candidates, and natural language processing pulls clinical details out of unstructured medical notes, the part of a record that usually defeats keyword search. He argues AI-driven recruitment enrols several times more of the eligible pool than manual methods, and that predicting enrolment patterns shortens site selection.

He also covers EHR integration as a data-silo problem: AI helps move information between different EHR systems so trial teams see a fuller picture of each patient.

## Documents, compliance and the paperwork tax

The generative AI piece is mostly about documents. Connecting Salesforce data to large language models produces customised reports, and natural language generation drafts standard trial reports and regulatory submissions, with humans reviewing the output. Alongside that sit automated HIPAA compliance monitoring and real-time threat detection on trial data. In a regulated industry, cutting documentation time is the kind of win that pays for the project.

## Trials have a supply chain too

A less obvious section covers logistics. Machine-learning models forecast site-specific supply needs to cut stockouts and hold less inventory; reinforcement learning optimises delivery routes across international sites; and predictive maintenance keeps cold-chain products within temperature limits. Anyone who has watched a trial stall because a site ran out of investigational product will appreciate that this gets its own slide.

## Simulation before the first patient

Harsha also covers AI-powered trial simulations and protocol optimisation: predicting outcomes and patient responses to reduce early-phase enrolment needs, and assessing patient burden across a few hundred protocol factors to predict dropout risk. Resource forecasting per site rounds it out.

## Read the numbers as estimates

The talk is full of percentages for accuracy, error reduction, satisfaction and timelines. To his credit, Harsha says partway through that these figures come from research and proofs of concept and may vary in real deployments. Take him at his word and treat them as hypotheses to test in your own pilot.

## Who should watch

Developers and architects working on CTMS, CRM or data platforms in pharma and life sciences who want a quick inventory of AI use cases across a trial. If you're after implementation detail on Salesforce objects or model choices, you'll need to go further than this talk.
