Title: How Go cured one engineer's fear of C and pointers
Description: Namkat Cedrick of Iknite Studio at Conf42 Golang 2025 on writing C on paper, finally getting pointers in Go, and building a Go community in Central Africa.
Body:
Namkat Cedrick learned C by writing it on paper, closing his eyes and hoping it would compile. At Conf42 Golang 2025, the tech lead at Iknite Studio, who also runs the Central African Go community, told the story of how Go, a language that looks a lot like the C he had come to dislike, changed how he saw programming and opened up his career.

This is a personal talk, not a technical one. There are no benchmarks and no code on screen; it's about perspective, and it's warmer for it.

## The volatile memory incident

The story starts in a high school computer lab, with blinking lights that felt like Star Wars and a mouse he didn't yet know was called a mouse. He was one of three arts students in a class of science majors learning HTML and Pascal. Asked the difference between volatile and non-volatile memory, he gave a perfect definition of each, attached to the wrong one. The class laughed, and he seriously considered quitting.

Access was the other barrier. Students couldn't use the lab without a supervisor, and he had no computer at home, so practice time was scarce. In college the language became C, still without a laptop, and the class consensus was that C was hard, low-level, for embedded engineers only, and no way to start a career. Pointers in particular felt like black magic.

## Pointers, finally, without the dread

Then a first job asked him to write Go. What surprised him was that pointers suddenly made sense: a variable has an address, the address points to the value, and that's it. The concept hadn't changed; the surrounding language had stopped fighting him. If you've ever explained pointers to a junior, this part of the talk is worth hearing for how it lands from the learner's side.

## Why Go stuck

Namkat gives three reasons. First, simplicity as a design goal, which made the language approachable even though its way of doing things can look odd to people coming from object-oriented languages. Second, the origin story: Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson at Google, tired of long C++ build times, setting out to make something simple, readable and fast. He points to Rob Pike's 2015 talk on what the Go team did right and wrong as part of what drew him in. Third, batteries included: formatting, testing and an HTTP package in the standard toolchain, so you install Go and can start a local server without configuring anything.

His first Go project as a junior was an online ticketing system, with one week to learn the language before work started. Approaching it as which problem a language solves, rather than how scary its syntax looks, made the steep curve manageable. He later became a tech lead working in Go.

## Paying it forward

The future he describes is community work. Few developers in his area know Go, so he runs talks, workshops and meetups through the Central African Go community. He credits the Gophers he met online for answering questions on their own time, and recommends the Go community on X and the official Go Slack.

His takeaways are deliberately plain: perseverance, resourcefulness, consistency, lots of small projects, and people around you who pull you up.

## Who should watch

Early-career developers stuck between languages, mentors who want a reminder of what learning feels like without a laptop, and anyone organising a local Go group. Experienced Gophers won't learn new syntax here, but they might remember why they started.

Title: A CFO's case for LLMs, from fraud to cash flow to compliance
Description: CFO and CLO Andriy Bagryantsev at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on LLMs reading the unstructured text finance ignored, for fraud, cash flow and compliance.
Body:
Finance has always run on numbers in columns, while a lot of what actually moves the numbers sits in text: contracts, emails about late shipments, regulatory bulletins. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Andriy Bagryantsev, who serves as both CFO and CLO and has a background in engineering and web development, argued that LLMs matter to finance because they can finally read that text, and walked through three places it changed how his companies operate: fraud detection, cash flow and compliance.

It is a perspective talk from the business side, without architecture diagrams, and its value is in hearing what a finance leader actually wants from the technology.

## Before: spreadsheets, silos and month-end surprises

Bagryantsev paints the old world plainly. Data sat in silos and outdated databases that didn't talk to each other, so a real-time view of financial health was close to impossible. You waited for month-end or quarter-end close, saw what had happened, and only then decided how to respond. Unstructured information (regulatory documents, contracts, emails, invoices, even social media comments about the company) stayed out of reach because finance tools weren't built for natural language.

## Fraud: rules are a list fraudsters can read

Running online platforms that process large transaction volumes, he saw everything from stolen cards to elaborate identity theft. The old defence was rule-based: if-then conditions for unusual amounts, foreign IP addresses, location mismatches. Fraudsters adapt and the rules had to be updated by hand.

An LLM-based system can take in both structured transactions and unstructured signals, including the text users write, and pick up subtler warning signs like shifts in writing style or inconsistencies with a user's history. He reports a significant drop in fraudulent transactions after adopting one, together with fewer false alarms for legitimate customers, though he gives no figures.

## Cash flow as a continuous conversation

The second use case is forecasting. Monthly or quarterly forecasts can't react when a key supplier starts shipping late or sales spike. An LLM can parse emails about delays and contract changes alongside data from the resource planning system, supplier sites, markets and news, and feed that into the financial picture as it happens. His phrase for it is a continuous conversation with your cash flow. The practical payoff: keep just enough cash on hand and put the rest to work.

## Compliance: the LLM reads the bulletins first

As the person also responsible for legal, this is the use case he is most enthusiastic about. Companies operating across jurisdictions keep teams just to read regulatory updates and work out whether they apply. An LLM that monitors official sites and bulletins can match a change, say in data privacy or payment rules, against existing policies, flag what needs updating and draft a first version. Humans still confirm the final decision and stay accountable.

## The hurdles he didn't skip

He is careful not to oversell. Data preparation takes longer than you'd expect when financial information is scattered and poorly documented, and it can't be skipped. Stakeholders want to know why the system recommends something, so his team added explainability tools that show which data points drove an output. And staff need training on how to ask the system questions; adoption came once people saw the benefits.

Looking ahead, he sees multimodal inputs, agents working across departments, and autonomous handling of simple tasks like routine invoice approval under well-defined rules, with the CFO's role shifting towards designing financial intelligence systems and owning their governance.

## Who should watch

Finance leaders and the engineers who build tools for them. If you are pitching an LLM project to a CFO, this is a good preview of the questions you'll get.

Title: Everything in your stack autoscales except the database
Description: Matan Nataf of Rapydo at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on why managing database fleets is broken, and a demo of throttling, blocking and caching queries.
Body:
In a cloud-native stack, the database is usually the one tier that doesn't scale out when a noisy neighbour shows up. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Matan Nataf](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Matan_Nataf_rapydo_databases_broken), co-founder of Rapydo, called databases "the stepson of every CloudOps organization" and argued that the way teams run fleets of RDS instances is broken: the people who write the queries aren't the people who get paged for them.

This is a vendor talk with a long live demo of the Rapydo console. The diagnosis in the first half is worth hearing even if you never install anything.

## Developers own the queries, CloudOps owns the consequences

Nataf's framing is organisational before it is technical. Managed services like RDS pushed database responsibility towards developers: they write the queries, pick the ORM, and often a single dev team owns a given database. Developers live in days and sprints, and their code has close to 100% of the impact on the database.

CloudOps and SRE teams live in minutes. They own the infrastructure bill, the database SLA, uptime and performance, and when queries run slow, the customer-facing team calls them. So one group causes the load and another absorbs it, usually without a DBA on the team. He calls that situation not healthy, which is a polite way to describe most on-call rotations that include a database.

## Observability alone leaves you reactive

The first problem with a fleet is visibility. Which instance has the slowest query? Where was the last CPU spike? Which databases are creeping towards the edge of their SLA? He acknowledges the existing observability tools for this, naming Datadog DBM, SolarWinds and New Relic, and argues that seeing the problem is only half the job. The other half is automation: caching queries, shielding the database from CPU spikes, accelerating slow queries and right-sizing the underlying instances.

His case for why it matters is the RDS scaling ladder. Hit a CPU spike, double the instance size, hit the ceiling again, double again. Scaling up is always a 100% step.

## The customer story: from emergency to shrinking instances

Nataf showed a CPU graph from a customer running a couple of hundred RDS instances that had climbed to 8xlarge one emergency at a time. After inserting Rapydo with a few rules, he said, the CPU baseline dropped from 60-100% to 20-30%, and the team then shrank instances step by step until they were 75% smaller than on day one, still below 50% CPU. He put the customer's compute savings at more than half a million dollars a month. Those are the vendor's numbers from a single customer, so treat them as a story, not a benchmark.

## The demo: from bird's-eye view to the offending query

The live part follows one workflow. A master dashboard ranks average query time across the fleet, MySQL and PostgreSQL side by side. Drill into the slowest instance and you find a `SELECT SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS` running for 333 seconds. A locks view groups by locking thread and points to a single `UPDATE` causing most of the locks across the fleet.

Then he switches to real time on a database pinned at 100% CPU, with a view that refreshes every three seconds and can scroll back to watch the problem compound, from a handful of concurrent executions to around fifty. Killing the query helps for a minute, then the application sends it again. That is the moment for rules.

## Rules: block, throttle, or cache

Rapydo's rule engine matches query patterns with wildcards and applies an action. You can block a pattern outright, restrict it to certain hours or weekdays so an analytics query only runs at night, or throttle it so only a couple of executions run in parallel. In the demo, the throttle brings the database back from the edge. A second rule caches a query with table-based invalidation: when someone writes to the underlying table, the cache entry is dropped so results stay coherent. Other rules cover database connections and limiting specific users or tenants, which is where the noisy-neighbour problem from the opening gets its answer.

## Who should watch

CloudOps and SRE teams responsible for many MySQL or PostgreSQL instances without a dedicated DBA, especially in multi-tenant SaaS. If your scaling strategy for RDS is "next instance size up", the rule-based throttling and caching ideas are worth knowing whatever tool you use.

Title: Automating across networks that can't see each other, with Dimensigon
Description: Daniel Moya of Dimensigon at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 demos open source, decentralised automation with a REST API on every server and proxied transfers.
Body:
Most automation tools assume one control node that can reach every server. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Daniel Moya](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Daniel_Moya_automation_decentralization_orchestration) of Dimensigon demoed the opposite: an open source Python platform that puts a RESTful API on every server, lets any node manage the others, and routes commands and software through bridge nodes when two networks can't talk directly.

The talk is essentially a long hands-on tutorial in Docker, built and narrated live. If you want slides and theory, look elsewhere. If you want to see what using the tool feels like, keystroke by keystroke, this is it.

## A "dimension" is a cluster of servers across subnets

Dimensigon (DM for short) is both the company name and the tool's. It targets a specific, common headache: two or more subnets or data centres connected only through a few specific points, which you still want to manage as one group. That group is called a dimension, and Moya recommends one per lifecycle stage, so production, pre-production and development each get their own, for organisation and security.

The architecture lives in one GitHub repository with three components:

- **dmcore**, a Python Flask service that exposes the RESTful API on each server
- **the elevator**, which detects a new version anywhere in the network and spreads the upgrade
- **dshell**, a command-line client built on prompt_toolkit that turns commands into REST calls, with tab completion everywhere

A web UI is planned. Metadata lives in a distributed database built on SQLAlchemy, with logic to handle split brain during network instability and keep the surviving group consistent.

## The demo network: two subnets and a bridge

The setup is easy to reproduce. Two Docker networks stand in for two data centres, one container is attached to both as a bridge, and the rest live on one side or the other. A new dimension starts with one node, which issues single-use join tokens; every other server joins with its own token, generated from any node that is already a member. From then on, any node can administer the others.

A catalog of actions, orchestrations and software replicates across the dimension with a version watermark. When a node falls behind, `manager catalog refresh` pulls the newest one, and nodes also update automatically in the background.

## Actions, steps and orchestrations

The automation model is layered for reuse. An action is a reusable unit: a shell command, Python, an Ansible playbook, an HTTP request, or one of the built-in internal actions. Steps reference actions, orchestrations are made of steps, and orchestrations can themselves be steps in larger ones. Every step can have an undo, with conditions for when the orchestration counts as failed.

Changing an orchestration creates a new version rather than overwriting the old one, which keeps runs reproducible. Orchestrations export to and import from JSON, and Moya hopes to grow a shared orchestration library. Secrets go in a vault, scoped per environment, and are referenced with double curly braces in the code. The hello-world orchestration runs on three nodes at once and reports success, return code, parameters and elapsed time per server.

## Distributed commands and proxied software transfers

Two features stand out for day-to-day operations. Distributed commands open a shell against a set of target servers so every command you type runs on all of them, handy for pre-flight checks or troubleshooting many hosts. Moya says the idea came from a distributed shell he had used on Oracle Exadata.

The software library is the other. You register a file on any node, and it can be sent to any other node, either one-off or as a step in an orchestration. In the demo, a 200 MB file moves from a server on one network to a server on the other through the bridge, split into chunks and reassembled at the destination. His pitch for it is concrete: no NFS mounts between parts of the company, just a transfer that routes around the network gaps.

Other commands cover log federation (subscribing to a log or directory and replicating it elsewhere), locks for critical orchestrations, server routes and hop costs, and pings that check whether Dimensigon is alive on a node.

## Who should watch

Ops engineers and DBAs managing servers spread across segmented networks, on-prem and cloud, who find SSH jump hosts and a single Ansible control node limiting. It is a tool walkthrough, so watch it with a terminal open.

Title: AI that helps licensing staff instead of replacing them
Description: Sneha Kalagarla of Cleveland State University at Conf42 Golang 2025 on an AI framework for e-licensing and e-permitting that augments human case workers.
Body:
Moving a professional licence from one US state to another can add weeks of paperwork that nobody enjoys, least of all the staff checking it. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Sneha Kalagarla of Cleveland State University presented a framework for putting AI into e-licensing and e-permitting systems so it does the information gathering, document checks and case routing, while human officers keep the judgement calls.

A note on scope before you press play: despite the event, Go doesn't come up. This is an architecture-and-outcomes talk about public-sector case management, and it's most useful if that is your world.

## Where licensing work actually goes

Sneha starts with the state of digital government. Citing OECD data, she notes that many countries now have digital transformation offices and digital-first strategies for licensing, but maturity varies, and hybrid paper-and-digital systems are still common. The operational pain is concrete: staff spending most of their time on document verification and compliance checks, international applications taking weeks longer than domestic ones, state-to-state transfers (her example is a CPA licence) adding more, and backlogs at peak periods. When a regulation changes, updating the system can take months.

That last point is the one any engineer will recognise. The rules change faster than the software that enforces them.

## Augment, don't replace

The framing is the talk's best idea. AI handles the routine work and surfaces insights; officers review exceptions and make the calls. Everything else in the design follows from that boundary, including how much autonomy the system gets.

## Three layers and a three-pass pipeline

The architecture is microservices with AI components in three layers:

- **Intelligent data acquisition:** gathering and validating application data automatically.
- **Cognitive processing middleware:** real-time decision support and workflow routing.
- **Adaptive service delivery:** allocating resources as volumes shift, with predictive scaling for peaks.

Applications pass through a three-stage pipeline: an initial AI screening that classifies the submission and extracts key fields, a deeper machine-learning validation, and a contextual check where transformer models compare the application against the relevant regulations. All three run in seconds, so valid applications move on and problems get flagged early. The pipeline is meant to learn from each case and adapt to different document formats and jurisdiction rules.

## Security that adapts to context

Security gets its own layer: behavioural biometrics for continuous authentication, AI-driven authorisation that adjusts permissions by context and risk, and anomaly detection on data access. For a system holding personal records of every licensed professional in a state, that layer matters as much as the speed-ups.

## The numbers, with a caveat

The talk is dense with percentages: shorter processing times, higher accuracy, fewer compliance errors, more self-service, lower operating cost, and payback within roughly 14 to 15 months. They're presented as results from studies and early implementations, but the talk doesn't name the agencies or studies behind each figure, so treat them as directional rather than as benchmarks to quote in a budget request.

The implementation advice is more portable: set up governance and infrastructure first, integrate with legacy systems rather than replacing them, spend real budget on training and change management (she suggests a quarter of the project), and keep monitoring and iterating after launch.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people working on government or regulated case-management systems, and anyone scoping where AI fits in a document-heavy approval workflow. If you came to Conf42 Golang for Go code, skip this one; if you are about to automate a permit queue, it gives you a sensible shape.

Title: GoFr makes inter-service HTTP calls fail politely
Description: Divya Darshana of GoFr at Conf42 Golang 2025 demos registered HTTP services with auth, retries, health checks and a circuit breaker in the open-source GoFr framework.
Body:
Your order service calls the payment service, and the payment service doesn't answer. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Divya Darshana, an open-source contributor to GoFr, showed how the GoFr framework handles that moment and the boilerplate around it: register a downstream HTTP service once, then get authentication, default headers, health checks, retries and a circuit breaker by configuration rather than by hand-rolled middleware.

Honest scope: this is a framework talk from someone who works on it, with a live demo. If you already have your own HTTP client stack, it's still a tidy checklist of what that stack should do.

## Four ways an HTTP call goes wrong

Divya frames inter-service HTTP around four problems. Latency compounds, so one slow service drags every caller. Failures cascade, whether from hardware, traffic spikes or a misconfiguration. Each call is a security surface on a network you may not fully trust. And without observability, debugging turns into guessing. Her point is that these are business problems as much as technical ones; one outage or breach costs more than the plumbing to prevent it.

## Register once, call from anywhere

The demo is pleasantly small. In `main`, `app.AddHTTPService` registers a downstream service by name and address, and GoFr's container manages it. Inside any handler, the service comes back from the context with `GetHTTPService`, and you call `Get` on an endpoint.

She runs two projects locally on ports 8080 and 8081: a hello handler in one calls a name handler in the other and returns the combined greeting. The payoff is in the logs: GoFr logs the outbound call with the same correlation ID as the parent request, and the traces show the downstream call nested under the handler that made it. Logs, traces and metrics come by default, which she calls one of the framework's distinguishing points.

## Options for the failure you'll eventually have

Configuration is where GoFr does the work:

- **Authentication:** basic auth, API keys or OAuth with client ID, secret and token URL, set globally or per service.
- **Default headers:** declare `Content-Type: application/json` and friends once instead of on every request.
- **Health checks:** ping a service's health endpoint on an interval with a timeout; if it fails, GoFr marks the service unavailable and stops sending to it.
- **Retries:** for example up to five attempts before returning the error, for blips like timeouts.

## Retries alone are a self-inflicted DDoS

The sharpest part of the talk is the warning about retrying blindly. If a service is properly down, every client retrying in a loop wastes resources and piles load onto the thing that's already struggling; enough clients and you have an accidental denial-of-service attack on your own system. GoFr's answer is a circuit breaker: after failures cross a threshold the circuit opens, GoFr polls the health endpoint (by default `/.well-known/alive`) at the configured interval, and closes the circuit when the service recovers.

It's the electrical metaphor taken literally, and it's the right default: retries for transient faults, a breaker for real outages.

## Who should watch

Go developers building their first set of microservices who would rather not reinvent HTTP client resilience, and teams evaluating GoFr specifically. Seasoned distributed-systems folk can skip to the circuit-breaker section; the rest is a clear demo. The GoFr docs and Discord are where she points people for more.

Title: AI's first job in PLM is recovering tribal knowledge
Description: Krishna Baride of Cummins at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on legacy PLM, untraceable change orders, tribal knowledge and where AI fits in product development.
Body:
Every engineering org has one person who knows why a part was changed ten years ago, and that person is always on holiday when it matters. Krishna Baride, Senior IT Leader for PLM and Product Owner at Cummins, used that scenario to frame his Conf42 Large Language Models 2025 talk on how AI fits into product lifecycle management: less about futuristic design tools, more about making a decade of scattered engineering history searchable.

It is a short, high-level talk aimed at people who own PLM systems or the business processes around them. Expect analogies and strategy, not code.

## PLM is the life story of a product

Baride defines product lifecycle management as the story of a product from its first idea to retirement, including how it is serviced in the aftermarket. It ties together people, data, processes and business systems, the blueprint behind every step from first sketch to final assembly. When it works, nobody notices. When it doesn't, you get the problems the talk is really about.

## Legacy PLM is a house with no plumbing map

His central analogy: inheriting a legacy PLM system is like inheriting a house with complex plumbing and no map. Pipes go in all directions, some disconnected, some leaking. The concrete symptom is tracing an engineering change order: try to reconstruct a change made to a complex machine a decade ago when the records are split across departments, some in software and some on paper. The result is errors, delays, and a dependency on undocumented tribal knowledge.

That last one is the risk he stresses most. If the only person who can fix a critical issue is away, the organisation doesn't have a process; it has a person.

## What AI brings: the digital map

Here AI plays the expert plumber with a map. Baride describes AI analysing the change history to make traceable what changed, why, when it was approved, and what differed from one revision of a change order to the next. Captured tribal knowledge becomes searchable data rather than something that leaves with a retirement party. He adds familiar examples beyond the core PLM record: a centralised system that spots design flaws before they reach manufacturing, predictive maintenance from sensor data, and AI-powered digital twins for simulating product behaviour before building physical prototypes.

He also mentions industry case studies from aerospace and automotive manufacturers. The talk gives headline percentages for these without sources on screen, so they are better treated as illustrations than evidence.

## The hard parts are people and data models

The implementation advice is grounded. Start with small, focused projects where AI has the biggest impact. Invest in training and change management, because adoption is about people more than technology. Treat data security and ethics as non-negotiable, with regular audits.

The challenges he lists will sound familiar to anyone who has integrated enterprise systems. Data models in legacy PLM rarely match modern ones; a bill-of-materials format mismatch between PLM and an ERP like SAP can quietly wreck accuracy and the collaboration between engineering and procurement. People who understand both PLM and AI are hard to find. Implementation is expensive and the upfront investment is hard to justify. And users may not trust AI recommendations when a critical decision is on the line.

## Who should watch

PLM owners, engineering IT leaders and product owners in manufacturing who need a vocabulary for pitching AI internally. Engineers wanting architecture details should pair it with Baride's more technical Go talk below.

Title: In retail, you are either in the cloud or out of business
Description: Rustam Orudzhev at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 tours how Walmart, Nike, Netflix, Macy's, Alibaba and others use cloud for personalisation and omnichannel retail.
Body:
Rustam Orudzhev, a digital ecosystem products expert with a career in telecom and big tech, made a blunt claim at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025: "Retailer is either in the cloud or out of business." His talk backs it up with a fast tour of how a dozen big names, from Walmart and Nike to Macy's and Alibaba, use the cloud for personalisation, omnichannel shopping and real-time inventory.

This is a business and product talk, not an engineering one. You will not see architectures or code; you will see what the cloud is for, from the point of view of the people who sell to shoppers.

## Stores are now a choice

The storyline starts with a picture of a London market in the early 20th century and lands in the pandemic, which in Rustam's account sped up the shift online. Before COVID, physical stores dominated and online supported them; after, online is essential and the physical store becomes an experience hub. His first takeaway: we only go to a physical store if we want to.

Nike's live stores are the example. Staff carry cloud-connected devices and know from the customer's profile what to offer, members get tailored perks through the app, and a journey can start online and finish in the shop without a gap.

## Personalisation is the product

Much of the tour is about knowing the customer. Netflix tunes recommendations in near real time from what you watched and browsed, and even personalises artwork and layout. Target uses cloud analytics for targeted promotions, recommendations and dynamic pricing. Starbucks Rewards keeps offers in sync across app, web and store and scales through peak hours. Stitch Fix mixes machine learning with human stylists, which Rustam presents as a hybrid model for something as personal as fashion. H&M's virtual assistant uses natural language processing, the rare chatbot he does not mind.

## Omnichannel needs one copy of the truth

The operational examples are the ones engineers will appreciate most. Nordstrom unifies customer profiles and inventory across channels so buy-online-pick-up-in-store works and stores double as fulfilment centres that pick the best location to ship from. Macy's puts RFID on shelves for real-time inventory, gets automatic restock alerts when stock runs low, and uses Bluetooth beacons, with consent, for in-store offers. Alibaba's new retail initiative ties e-commerce, Hema Fresh stores, IoT inventory and apps like Taobao and Alipay into one ecosystem.

Every one of these is a data synchronisation problem wearing a shopping bag.

## The platform layer

At the bottom of the stack, Rustam points to Walmart's cloud migration, which he says began around 2010, is still ongoing, and includes a partnership with Microsoft Azure; to Shopify as the way small merchants get global infrastructure, payments and shipping without building it; and to Azure's retail offering for scaling compute and analytics without a data centre of your own. Amazon gets a nod as the benchmark for online retail.

His five takeaways: physical stores are optional, a retailer is only as good as its online and mobile experience, omnichannel integration defines the customer experience, predictive personalisation is imperative, and AI now runs from recommendation to support.

## Who should watch

Engineers building for retail who want the business context behind the tickets they get, and product managers who need case studies for a cloud business case. If you are after technical depth on how any of these systems are built, look elsewhere.

Title: Test your LLM app with rules first, then with a second LLM
Description: Robin Gupta of TestZeus at Conf42 LLMs 2025 builds a RAG quiz app and tests it with keyword checks, a format judge and a context-adherence evaluator.
Body:
Robin Gupta, co-founder and CEO of TestZeus, built a small RAG app live at Conf42 Large Language Models 2025 and then broke it the easy way: he asked his quiz generator to write a poem about conferences, and it cheerfully did. The rest of the talk is about catching that kind of failure automatically, first with plain Python rules and then with a second LLM whose only job is to judge the first one.

It is a hands-on notebook session using LangChain and GPT-4o at temperature zero, so you can follow along line by line.

## Why traditional assertions run out

Gupta starts with a comparison table. Traditional software follows predefined rules and gives one output for one input; tests are right or wrong. LLM-based apps behave probabilistically and can give different outputs for the same question, so they need evaluating on accuracy, quality, bias, consistency and toxicity. He lists what to check (context adherence, context relevance, correctness, bias, toxicity) and borrows when from regular CI: after every change or data update, before deployment in SIT or UAT, and as smoke tests after release.

## Ring one: dumb rules catch a lot

The app under test generates quizzes from a small quiz bank covering topics such as Leonardo da Vinci, Paris, telescopes, The Starry Night and physics. The first evals are deliberately boring. Does a science quiz contain the expected words? Does a request for an off-topic quiz (bread making, in the demo) produce the refusal the system prompt asks for? No AI involved, as Gupta stresses, just string checks wrapped in functions.

Those checks pass for the happy path and catch a missing refusal. They don't catch the poem, because nothing in a keyword list says "this isn't a quiz".

## Ring two: an LLM checks the format

So he adds an evaluator chain with its own system prompt: read the response and output Y if it looks like a quiz, N if it doesn't. He hardens the app's prompt too (only use facts from the quiz bank, match categories explicitly, say you don't know otherwise) and feeds the evaluator a known bad response to make sure it fails. The pieces end up as pytest-style tests, which is the moment this stops being a demo and starts looking like something you could put in a pipeline.

## Ring three: the judge has to explain itself

The last evaluator checks context adherence. It receives the same quiz bank as the app and must flag any quiz that contains facts not in the bank. Gupta then extends the prompt so the evaluator returns a decision plus a brief explanation referencing the facts it used, and runs it over a small dataset with Pandas to display the results. Science and geography pass with reasons; bread making fails with an explanation that the bank covers none of it.

One practical observation from his experiments: instructions written in bold in the system prompt were followed more strictly by the model.

## Who tests the testers

He closes with a CI/CT pipeline: per-commit evals on feature branches, pre-release format checks, post-release smoke runs with the evaluator, reading the explanations and not just pass/fail. When an audience member once asked who checks both AI systems, his answer was humans, today and forever. He also points to Infosys's responsible AI toolkit for red teaming and to TestZeus's open source testing agent on GitHub.

## Who should watch

QA engineers and developers shipping their first RAG or chatbot feature who need a starting test strategy. The layered approach (cheap rules, then an LLM judge with explanations) scales up to customer support bots, which Gupta mentions as the obvious next use.

Title: IoT and 5G need networks you program, not networks you rewire
Description: Sai Charan Madugula at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on software-defined networking for IoT and 5G, from network slicing and OpenFlow to edge computing.
Body:
Hardware-centric networks were designed for a world where you could schedule a change window. Sai Charan Madugula argued at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 that IoT and 5G have ended that world, and that software-defined networking, which separates the control plane from the data plane, is what lets networks keep up with billions of devices and sub-millisecond latency targets.

It is a short conceptual overview, around 15 minutes, built on use cases and industry figures rather than a lab demo. Good as a refresher on why SDN matters for cloud-native systems at the edge.

## The rigid network problem

Sai Charan's opening statistic is that over 127 new devices connect to the internet every second, and he cites a forecast of more than 75 billion connected devices by 2025. 5G raises the bar further with latency under one millisecond, which is what autonomous driving and remote surgery need, and speeds above 20 Gbps for streaming and AR/VR.

Traditional networks, configured box by box in hardware, cannot reallocate themselves fast enough for that. SDN's move is to pull the decisions out of the switches into a centralised, programmable control plane. That gives three things he keeps returning to: centralised control with real-time programmability, dynamic allocation of bandwidth and compute where demand is, and flexibility because configuration is software rather than hardware.

## Slicing one network into many

The most useful section for cloud engineers is 5G network slicing, which SDN makes possible: several virtual networks on the same physical infrastructure, each tuned for its traffic. Sai Charan describes two slices:

- **Enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB)**: high throughput for HD streaming, VR and gaming.
- **Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC)**: for autonomous vehicles, remote surgery and industrial automation.

His metaphor is virtual lanes, each with its own quality of service. If you have ever argued for separate node pools in Kubernetes, the idea will feel familiar.

He walks through smart cities (smart grids, faster fault detection, adaptive traffic management) and industrial IoT (fine-grained monitoring, predictive maintenance, automated control across thousands of sensors and actuators) as the places SDN pays off. The percentages he quotes for those are industry claims, not results from a named deployment.

## Centralised control has a latency cost

The talk is candid about SDN's weak spots: integrating with legacy systems and mixed protocols, latency from a centralised controller in time-sensitive applications, and keeping performance as distributed networks grow.

His fix for latency is edge computing. Processing data close to where it is generated cuts round trips and supports real-time decisions for IoT and 5G workloads. OpenFlow appears as the standard that makes this workable across vendors: one protocol between controller and switches, so you can mix equipment and push policy changes centrally. Dynamic spectrum allocation rounds it out, squeezing more devices onto the same airwaves.

## Who should watch

Cloud and platform engineers whose workloads are moving to the edge or onto telco infrastructure and who want the networking vocabulary: control plane, slicing, OpenFlow. Network engineers who already run SDN will find it introductory.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Andrey Slastenov on the role of IoT and 5G devices in DDoS attacks](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Andrey_Slastenov_iot_5g_devices_ddos_threat_landscape) is the security flip side of all those devices.
- [Ravi Theja Kambhampati on routing and switching foundations for network resilience](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Ravi_Theja_Kambhampati_38_network_resilience_scalability) covers what sits underneath SDN.

Title: Notification systems that survive a flash sale
Description: Ankita Kamat of Microsoft at Conf42 Golang 2025 on scaling notifications with events, Kafka and RabbitMQ, sharding, adaptive rate limits and three cache tiers.
Body:
Nobody praises a push notification that arrives on time, but everyone notices the bank alert that shows up an hour late. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Ankita Kamat of Microsoft walked through the architecture of real-time notification systems at very large scale, from event-driven microservices and message brokers to sharding, adaptive rate limiting and a three-tier cache, with the goal of keeping delivery in the low milliseconds when traffic spikes.

It's a broad systems-design tour rather than a Go-specific talk: Go appears as the language for the performance-critical pieces, next to Node.js for delivery and Python for analytics.

## Before you optimise, survive

Ankita opens with the scale challenge. She cites Facebook at around 8 billion notifications a day, close to a hundred thousand a second, with latency targets under 75 milliseconds. Then come the spikes: breaking news, a celebrity livestream, a flash sale, traffic several times above baseline. Her design rule is to build for five to ten times the expected peak, because the peak you planned for is never the one you get.

## Events in, brokers in the middle

The architecture splits notifications into small services: user preferences, device tokens, queueing, sending. Each deploys and scales on its own, so the delivery service can grow during a campaign without dragging the rest along. Services emit events instead of calling each other; when someone likes a photo, the app fires an event and the notification system picks it up in the background.

For the broker she draws a clear line. Kafka for high-throughput ingestion, RabbitMQ for rich routing with topic routing, conditional delivery and priority queues. Many systems run both, Kafka taking events in and RabbitMQ deciding where they go.

## Failure is a certainty, so contain it

The resiliency section covers circuit breakers and retries with exponential backoff plus jitter, so a recovering service isn't flattened by every client retrying at once (the thundering herd). The point isn't to avoid failure but to shrink its blast radius and degrade gracefully.

## Shard by more than one key

The sharding section is the most practical part. Ankita layers four strategies:

- **By user**, so one user's notifications stay ordered, which matters for security alerts and messaging.
- **By geography**, routing European users to an EU cluster and US users to a US one to cut round trips.
- **By time**, keeping today's messages hot and archives on cheaper storage.
- **By function**, so a suspicious-login alert never queues behind a promotional banner.

## Rate limits that read the room

Static rate limits don't fit spiky systems, so she describes adaptive ones: watch CPU, memory, request latency, queue depth and downstream success rates; derive a soft ceiling from history (for instance where a service has degraded before); anticipate recurring bursts like a weekly Friday-evening spike. Under pressure, throttle ingress, put 2FA codes and alerts first, and drop newsletters if you must. A closed feedback loop on retries, latency and drop counts tunes the limits over time.

## Three caches, one source of truth

The caching hierarchy is L1 in-process memory for hot data like templates and flags, L2 a distributed cache such as Redis or Memcached for device tokens and rate-limit metadata with per-key TTLs, and L3 the database (PostgreSQL, Cosmos DB, Cassandra) as fallback. She reports offloading 95% of reads from the database this way. The talk ends on engagement: timing, personalisation, frequency caps and cross-channel fallback, such as following an unseen push with an email.

## Who should watch

Engineers designing anything fan-out shaped: notifications, alerts, webhooks, activity feeds. It's a solid checklist talk; seniors will know the individual patterns, but the way the four sharding strategies and adaptive rate limiting fit together is worth the time.

Title: Five security layers for a Go telemedicine platform
Description: Smita Verma of Adobe at Conf42 Golang 2025 on a defence-in-depth model for telemedicine apps in Go: TLS 1.3, AES-256, MFA, JWT, zero trust.
Body:
A video consultation is a stream of the most private data a person has, travelling over networks nobody in the call controls. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Smita Verma, a senior product manager for security and compliance at Adobe, laid out how she would build a telemedicine platform in Go: five stacked security layers, Go's standard library doing the cryptography, and microservices to keep a breach in one corner from becoming a breach everywhere.

She comes at it from both sides of the table. Before product management she spent six years as a developer in security, legal and banking software, and the talk reads like someone who has had to explain HIPAA to engineers and goroutines to compliance officers.

## The threat model is the network you don't own

Smita frames the problem around telemedicine's growth after COVID-19: patient data now crosses many networks, some of them hostile, and attackers have noticed. Her list of hard problems is practical. Data in transit. Authentication that's strong without making a doctor fight a login screen between patients. HIPAA and GDPR. And the third-party integrations (cloud services, payment gateways, electronic health records) that each add an attack vector you didn't write.

## Why she reaches for Go

Her case for Go is about removing whole categories of risk. Memory safety closes off the buffer-overflow class of exploits. Goroutines let one service hold thousands of concurrent patient sessions without a thread-per-connection bill. And the standard library ships the crypto, so you can do strong encryption without pulling in third-party packages, each of which is one more thing to audit.

That last point is the underrated one. In a regulated system, every dependency is a supply-chain question somebody has to answer in writing.

## Defence in depth, layer by layer

The core of the talk is a five-layer model:

- **Application:** input validation, context-aware output encoding, OWASP guidance against SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
- **Data:** AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.3 in transit.
- **Access:** granular role-based permissions plus multi-factor authentication.
- **Network:** mutual TLS, zero-trust segmentation, next-generation firewalls.
- **Infrastructure:** hardened cloud configuration, immutable infrastructure, continuous monitoring.

On authentication she maps four mechanisms onto Go: MFA wired through the `context` package, JWTs signed with the native crypto libraries, lightweight session tracking with strict expiry, and SSO federation over OAuth, OpenID and SAML. Key management goes to hardware security modules, so keys can be rotated and recovered without a migration project.

## Microservices as blast-radius control

Smita's argument for microservices is security-first rather than velocity-first. Isolated services mean a compromised one doesn't hand over the rest. Security-critical components scale on their own. Patches ship to one service without downtime, which matters when the alternative is postponing a fix until nobody is mid-consultation. And telemetry collected per service makes detection sharper.

She backs this with figures for incident reductions, compliance timelines and three anonymised case studies (a hospital network, a virtual-care startup, a health insurer). The talk doesn't name its sources or the organisations, so treat the numbers as the speaker's framing and the architecture as the takeaway.

## A roadmap you could put in a ticket

The closing section is the most reusable: assess, design, prototype a proof-of-concept microservice, pen-test and harden, then roll out progressively with automated scanning and live threat detection. Nothing exotic, which is the point; regulated systems reward boring sequences.

## Who should watch

Go developers who have just joined a healthcare or other regulated team and need the security vocabulary fast, and architects writing the security section of a design doc. It's an overview rather than a code walkthrough, so if you want `crypto/tls` config snippets you'll be writing them yourself afterwards.

Title: Identity orchestration in Go across 30-plus clouds
Description: Aditi Mallesh of Microsoft at Conf42 Golang 2025 on a four-stage Go identity service with zero trust, goroutine-heavy policy checks and an identity query DSL.
Body:
When an enterprise runs workloads on several clouds plus its own data centres, every environment ships its own idea of who a user is. At Conf42 Golang 2025, Aditi Mallesh of Microsoft showed how her team rebuilt identity orchestration as a set of Go microservices: one pipeline that authenticates and authorises every request, fast enough that security stops being the excuse for a slow page.

It's a short talk (around fifteen minutes) and an architecture overview rather than a code session, so it works best as a map you can check your own design against.

## The problem is inconsistency, not missing features

Aditi's starting point is that multi-cloud organisations rarely lack security controls. They have too many, each with a different authentication mechanism and a different policy language. The result is gaps between environments, performance bottlenecks where the systems meet, and resource overhead from running all of it. Traditional fixes, in her framing, make you trade security against speed against operating cost.

## Four stages, every request, zero trust

The system splits identity into four components: request ingestion, policy resolution, token management and access enforcement. Every request goes through the full chain, so there's no trusted inside network. Separating the stages means each can scale and change on its own; her best-practice list adds that keeping policy rules apart from enforcement lets you change rules without redeploying the enforcement points.

That last design choice is the one worth stealing. If a policy tweak needs a redeploy of every gateway, people stop tweaking policy.

## Goroutines do the heavy lifting

Go earns its place through concurrency. The authorisation service evaluates thousands of policy decisions in parallel on goroutines and channels instead of OS threads. The team added a custom scheduler to manage goroutine lifecycles and avoid leaks, plus purpose-built synchronisation primitives to cut lock contention on the hot path.

Policies are written in an identity query language, a domain-specific language whose parser and matcher are tuned for fast, parallel access decisions. It plugs into the usual cloud-native kit: Open Policy Agent, Kubernetes operators and a service mesh. Each service exposes Prometheus metrics and shuts down gracefully so rolling updates don't drop requests mid-decision.

## The numbers she reports

Aditi claims 300% faster policy resolution than the previous approach, sub-millisecond responses under peak load, and lower resource use, validated in production on millions of authentication requests a day. The case study is a global financial institution with more than 30 separate cloud environments: after a 12-week rollout, she reports 99.9997% availability, 72% fewer security incidents and 65% lower identity infrastructure cost. The talk doesn't show the benchmark setup, so read these as the team's results rather than something you can reproduce from the slides.

## Practices that travel

The closing advice is good Go hygiene in any domain:

- Profile before you optimise.
- Design for distributed workloads from day one.
- Prefer channels to locks for coordinating goroutines.
- Thread `context` through everything, so cancellation propagates and shutdowns don't leak goroutines.
- Test security as rigorously as features.

She mentions an open-source implementation and documentation, though the talk itself doesn't name the repository.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers consolidating authentication across clouds, and Go developers who want to see concurrency patterns applied to policy evaluation. If you want line-by-line code, this isn't that talk; if you are drawing the boxes for an identity layer, it's a useful fifteen minutes.

Title: An Azure landing zone is the foundation you pour before workloads
Description: Srinivasarao Thumala of Microsoft at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 explains Azure landing zones, management groups and the accelerator for greenfield and brownfield.
Body:
Nobody builds a stadium and then wonders about the foundations, yet plenty of cloud estates start with one subscription and a credit card. Srinivasarao Thumala, Senior Customer Engineer at Microsoft, gave a clear introduction to Azure landing zones at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025: the reference structure of management groups, subscriptions and policies that makes an Azure estate governable before the first big migration lands.

This is a Microsoft engineer explaining Microsoft's own guidance, and it is an intro. If you have never drawn a management group hierarchy, it is a good 20 minutes.

## Where the landing zone sits in the journey

Srinivasarao places it in the Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework, which runs through define strategy, plan, ready, adopt, govern, manage and secure. The landing zone belongs to the ready phase: after you know why you are moving and what depends on what, and before tools such as Azure Migrate, Azure Site Recovery and Database Migration Service start moving workloads.

He is frank about why customers struggle. Teams used to traditional IT lose concepts in translation to the cloud model, their operating models do not fit cloud delivery, and they want control and a compliant platform they can trust.

## One subscription is a trap

A recurring customer conversation, he says, is single versus multiple subscriptions. Subscriptions have limits for some resource types (virtual networks are his example), so a growing estate eventually needs more of them. Management groups sit above subscriptions and let you apply access, policy and compliance to many at once, segmented by environment (prod, pre-prod, dev, QA) instead of subscription by subscription. RBAC gets easier for the same reason.

## The reference shape

The conceptual architecture starts at the tenant and identity, then a root management group with platform, landing zone and sandbox groups beneath it. Platform splits into three subscriptions:

- **Identity**: for example Active Directory servers.
- **Management**: Log Analytics, Azure Policy and related tooling.
- **Connectivity**: VPN, ExpressRoute and the hub of the network.

Application teams then deploy into their own landing zones under the landing zone group. Srinivasarao stresses that not everyone needs the full design. A small organisation might keep identity, management and networking in one platform subscription with a couple of landing zones; a large one might have hundreds of subscriptions.

## Start, align or enhance

Organisations arrive at different stages. Greenfield ones, with nothing in production on Azure yet, can use the Azure landing zone accelerator: a portal-based deployment of the full conceptual architecture, or the same thing via ARM templates, Bicep or Terraform, optionally with a partner's automation. Brownfield ones, for instance an estate designed for ten applications that now needs to host a hundred, align with the reference by adding policies, building the management group hierarchy, tightening RBAC, improving the network and centralising security, which can mean moving resources between subscriptions. Mature estates enhance: turn business risks into policies, monitor violations, remediate.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects starting an Azure estate or inheriting a messy one, and platform teams who need a shared vocabulary with their Microsoft account team. Seasoned Azure platform engineers will know it already.

- [Carlos Solis Salazar on management and security with Azure Arc](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Carlos_Solis_Salazar_azure_management_security) extends governance to servers outside Azure.

Title: Dapr workflows let a crashed job resume instead of restarting
Description: Siri Varma Vegiraju of Microsoft at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on Dapr workflows, activities and replay for long-running jobs that survive pod failures.
Body:
Your ETL job has processed one and a half files out of ten when the pod dies. Does it start again from row zero? At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Siri Varma Vegiraju, a software engineer at Microsoft, showed how his team uses Dapr workflows so long-running jobs resume from the last completed step, without the team having to build and run a checkpointing engine of its own.

It is a focused talk with a working .NET demo and a look at the production setup on Kubernetes.

## The scenario everyone has lived through

Siri's example is concrete. A storage account holds ten files of 100,000 rows each, every row a VM ID that needs to be looked up to find which service it belongs to. The job finishes the first file, gets 50,000 rows into the second, and the pod dies. Restart from the start of the second file and you redo 50,000 rows. At 20 or 30 files a day, fine. At hundreds or thousands, failures are an inherent part of cloud workloads and that strategy does not scale.

The obvious fix is checkpointing every offset. The less obvious cost is everything behind it: schema, transactions, the database, schema versioning, observability, and what happens when the checkpoint store fails. Building that generically, Siri says, is a multi-month effort, and checkpointing is hardly a new problem. Hence looking for something off the shelf.

## Sidecar plus state store

Dapr, the Distributed Application Runtime, runs as a sidecar next to your service, one per pod. Your service talks to it over HTTP or gRPC, so the app can be in Go, Node, Python, .NET or Java. Besides workflows, Siri points out the service-to-service invocation building block (retries and permissions handled by the sidecar) and publish/subscribe to the broker of your choice.

The workflow building block has three parts: an SDK that enforces the contracts the engine needs, the workflow engine itself, and a state store. The store can be Cosmos DB, Redis, Cassandra and others, and swapping it is a change to a YAML component file, because the SDK never sees the store's internals.

## Activities are the unit of replay

In a Dapr workflow, an activity does the actual work (call an API, run business logic) and the workflow orchestrates activities. Each has an input and an output. In Siri's scenario, one activity reads a file and returns its rows; then one activity per row takes a VM ID and returns a service name, so 100,000 rows mean 100,000 activities.

For each input and activity combination, the engine stores the output. When the workflow restarts after a crash, Dapr sees that a combination already has an output and returns it instead of running the activity again. That is the checkpoint, for free.

The demo proves it with console logging: run the sidecar (HTTP port 3500, gRPC 4001), start the workflow, watch both activities log, kill the app, restart without rescheduling, and the file-reading activity no longer logs. Only the VM metadata step runs.

## What production looks like

The Kubernetes setup Siri's team runs includes the Dapr Sentry service for certificates, the Placement service to distribute workflows and activities across Dapr hosts, Azure Cosmos DB as the state store reached via managed identity, Prometheus for metrics and Application Insights for logs. One gotcha worth the price of admission: authenticating with managed identity makes the Dapr container slower to start, so the default timeout is not enough and needs raising.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers writing batch or ETL jobs that take hours, and anyone about to hand-roll a checkpoint table. If you already use Temporal or Durable Functions, this shows how Dapr's model compares.

Title: kconnect turns kubeconfig juggling into one login command
Description: Sai Sandeep Ogety of PeopleCert at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 demos kconnect, an open-source CLI for discovering and logging into EKS, AKS and Rancher clusters.
Body:
Somewhere, an SRE is pasting a kubeconfig into the wrong file during an incident. Sai Sandeep Ogety, DevOps Institute Ambassador with PeopleCert, presented kconnect at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025: an open-source CLI that discovers Kubernetes clusters across EKS, AKS and Rancher, authenticates you with your existing identity provider, and writes the kubeconfig for you.

It is a tool walkthrough with a live demo, short and practical. Sai is a user and advocate of the project, which he says is owned by Fidelity, with docs at fidelity.github.io/kconnect.

## A thousand clusters, one CLI

The motivation is scale. Sai describes an environment of roughly a thousand clusters, across on-prem and cloud. For every SRE, platform and DevOps engineer, reaching a cluster meant finding the right config, switching context, and dealing with each provider's own authentication. Multiply by a thousand and it eats real time.

kconnect replaces that with one flow: authenticate, discover the clusters your credentials can see, pick one, and get a generated kubeconfig. The supported platforms are AWS EKS, Azure AKS and Rancher.

## Authentication you already have

The part security teams will care about is that kconnect plugs into existing identity rather than inventing its own. It supports SAML (building on the saml2aws project), Azure Active Directory through the Microsoft Authentication Library for Go, AWS IAM credentials or roles, and Rancher token-based auth. An organisation can also ship company-wide configuration defaults so everyone authenticates the same way.

Sai's team uses it beyond humans at a terminal: it handles role-based cluster authentication for platforms like Jenkins and SonarQube, and runs behind their application deployment tooling to switch contexts across clusters.

## Aliases and history are the quality-of-life win

Every connection is saved to a history. Give a cluster an alias when you connect, and next time you reconnect by alias without repeating discovery. Nobody should have to remember a full EKS cluster ARN at 3 a.m.

The demo shows the full loop: apply a config file, connect to EKS using SAML with Google Apps as the identity provider (the prompt also offers Azure AD, ADFS and Ping, among others), choose an account, set the alias "dev", and run kubectl against pods that had been up for 27 hours. Then a reconnect by alias, a password prompt, and done.

It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, installs via a package manager or from GitHub, and has the usual open-source contribution path: fork, change, PR, review.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers with more clusters than they can name, especially in mixed EKS, AKS and Rancher shops with SAML or Azure AD in front. Teams with one or two clusters and a working kubectx habit can skip it.

Title: Uplift modeling finds who actually needs the discount
Description: Dmitriy Zolotukhin, Chief Data Officer at START, at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on uplift models for subscription offers and the data splits that made them stable.
Body:
A discount sent to someone who would have subscribed anyway is just money handed back. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Dmitriy Zolotukhin, Chief Data Officer at START, explained how his team used uplift modeling to decide which users of a video streaming service should get a subscription offer, and then spent most of the talk on the less glamorous part: getting the model to give the same answer twice.

This is a classic ML talk, not an LLM one. No language models appear; what you get is a clear case study of causal targeting and an honest account of validation pain.

## The business problem: buy the subscriber, not the coupon

The service makes money two ways: monthly subscriptions, or ads for users who don't subscribe. A discount is worth it if it converts someone who would otherwise stay on the ad tier, because recurring payment beats ad revenue. It is wasted on someone who was going to pay full price. Uplift modeling predicts exactly that difference: how a user's likelihood to subscribe changes if they are targeted versus not.

Requirements beyond accuracy were stability and adaptability. User acquisition is expensive, so experiment data is precious, and demand for films and shows swings with every new release. The model must not overfit to whatever is popular this month.

## The experiment and the features

The training data came from an experiment: the test group was offered a free six-day trial extension, shown so it couldn't be missed, while the control group got nothing. After the bonus period they recorded who converted to paid. Features came from how each user interacted with the smart TV app, the player, search (including how many searches returned nothing) and project pages, selected by their Gini score against conversion.

The evaluation metric is a Gini-style uplift curve: rank users by predicted uplift, compute the conversion difference between test and control as you move down the list, and compare the area against random ranking.

## Random splits gave random results

Here is the part that makes the talk worth watching. With ordinary random train and test splits, model quality swung between extremes depending on the split, sometimes no better than random ranking. Fixing the validation set and bootstrapping the training set didn't calm it down even after hundreds of runs.

So they tried, in order: splitting by registration date (older users train, newest users test, which mirrors production where the model scores new arrivals); stratified sampling on active days, conversion and whether the offer was shown, adding 1,000-sample chunks only if train and test scores stayed within 5% of each other; and Thompson Sampling over clusters of the remaining data, with a Beta distribution per cluster updated on whether each training attempt succeeded. Each step reduced the scattered peaks in the score distribution, but none alone produced a clean cluster of high-uplift users at the top.

## The combination that converged

The final method combined both ideas: the oldest 50% of users as the initial training set, then Thompson Sampling to pull more data from the newer half cluster by cluster. Zolotukhin says this almost always converged and ranked users tightly enough at the top to pick a threshold. They chose the top 20% by predicted uplift for the offer, with small randomised no-discount and all-discount groups kept as a gold-standard control. Next on the list: testing discount sizes and lengths, and the timing of the offer after the trial.

## Who should watch

Data scientists working on retention, pricing or marketing offers, and anyone who has seen a model's validation score wobble with the random seed. The talk is short and the transcript is rough, but the sequence of fixes is a good playbook.

Title: Payment fraud AI now has to beat adversarial AI too
Description: Sandeep Katuri at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on AI fraud detection for digital payments, biometrics, federated learning, adversarial attacks and post-quantum crypto.
Body:
What happens when fraudsters train their own models to look normal to yours? Sandeep Katuri, a Lead React Developer, spent his Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 talk on AI-powered fraud detection in cloud-native digital payments, and the most interesting part comes late: defending against adversarial AI and preparing payment encryption for quantum computers.

This is a broad survey talk. It strings together market figures, techniques and anonymised case studies rather than one system in depth, so treat it as a tour of the field.

## The scale problem

Sandeep frames it with two projections he cites: digital payments passing 15 trillion dollars by 2027, and online fraud reaching 48 billion dollars a year by 2025. Contactless payments, e-wallets and blockchain-based systems grow the volume; fraud grows with it.

Static rules cannot keep up, he argues, because fraudsters study them. AI models trained on transaction history, deep learning that keeps learning new patterns, and anomaly detection over behavioural data are his answer, with real-time monitoring that lets legitimate payments through and stops the rest in milliseconds.

## Biometrics without the friction

The real-time section pairs monitoring with multi-factor biometric authentication: facial recognition, fingerprints and behavioural analysis combined. The design goal he stresses is that verification finishes fast enough that the paying customer barely notices, so security does not cost conversions.

## Privacy-preserving collaboration

Two ideas from the blockchain section are worth knowing even if you never touch a chain. Zero-knowledge proofs let a transaction be verified without revealing sensitive details. Federated learning trains models across distributed networks while data stays local, which lets financial institutions learn from each other's fraud patterns without sharing customer records.

The case studies that follow (a "leading bank", "Fintech B", "Company X") report double-digit drops in chargebacks and faster processing. They are unnamed, so they are illustrations, not benchmarks you can check.

## The attacker has a model too

Here is the sharp bit. Adversarial AI manipulates transaction data, such as purchase patterns or timestamps, so a fraudulent transaction looks normal to the detection model. Sandeep likens it to a blind spot in the system's vision. The defence is adversarial training: expose the model to simulated attacks during training so it builds resistance, which he compares to a vaccine. Explainable AI joins the list too, so each fraud decision is traceable for regulators.

## Encryption with an expiry date

The last threat is quantum computing, which could render today's encryption obsolete. He points to post-quantum approaches that financial institutions are exploring, including lattice-based, code-based and multivariate cryptography, and argues for adopting quantum-resistant methods before the threat becomes real. For payment data that must stay confidential for years, that timing argument holds up.

## Who should watch

Developers and product people new to payments security who want a map of what the fraud stack involves, from models to biometrics to cryptography. Fraud data scientists will find the adversarial and federated sections the most relevant and the rest familiar.

Title: Azure AI Foundry is the governance layer for picking LLMs
Description: Peter De Tender of Microsoft at Conf42 LLMs 2025 tours Azure AI Foundry hubs, projects, model catalog, playground, RAG on your data and content safety.
Body:
Most organisations don't run one model; Peter De Tender showed a survey slide where none of the respondents relied on a single LLM. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, De Tender, a Microsoft Technical Trainer presenting from Redmond, walked through Azure AI Foundry as the place to manage that sprawl: one portal and SDK where cloud admins set up governance once and developers pick from a catalog of well over a thousand models, OpenAI and otherwise.

This is a Microsoft product talk with long live demos in the Azure portal. If you already know Foundry it is a refresher; if you know Azure but not Foundry, it is a solid orientation.

## Hubs and projects split the cloud team from the developers

The governance model is the part most worth understanding. A hub sits at the top of the topology and holds the shared setup: identity and access, networking, encryption, compute, storage, quota and model access. Projects live inside a hub, and that is where developers work. Role-based access control comes prebuilt, from owner and contributor down to reader, AI developer and an inference deployment operator role.

De Tender's framing: the cloud team builds the hub and projects, and developers consume building blocks inside a project instead of each deploying a full architecture themselves. Connections extend that idea to resources like Key Vault, AI Search or OpenAI endpoints, so you grant a project access to a resource rather than giving every developer rights on the underlying Azure services. The usual Azure tenant, subscription and management-group governance still applies around all of it.

## The model catalog and the quota you forgot to check

In the demo he filters the catalog by vendor and by capability (chat completion, for instance) and finds OpenAI models alongside Microsoft's Phi, Mistral and Meta's Llama, with DeepSeek added only weeks before the recording. Deploying a model means picking a deployment type (global standard is pay per API call), a version and a tokens-per-minute limit. That limit draws from a per-region quota; in his subscription a GPT-4o deployment had 8,000 tokens per minute out of 450,000 available in the region. Running out of tokens is a very Azure way to discover your app got popular.

Each deployment comes with copy-paste starter code for Python or C#, and the Azure AI SDK covers the same ground from GitHub, Visual Studio and VS Code for people who would rather not live in a portal.

## The playground, system prompts and your own data

The chat playground is where you test a deployment. De Tender compares an older GPT-3.5 deployment with GPT-4 on a question about the UK Prime Minister to show that training cut-offs differ between models, then adds a system message that turns the assistant into a polite Azure trainer who declines questions about AWS and Google Cloud and offers a Belgian beer instead.

The RAG part is "add your data": point the playground at Azure Blob Storage, Cosmos DB, Elasticsearch, a website or uploaded files, choose an AI Search index and how often it refreshes, and the model answers from your content. One upload step failed live in the recording, which he handled with good grace.

## Content safety closes the loop

He ends with Microsoft's responsible AI commitments (your prompts and data aren't used to train the models) and Azure AI Content Safety, which filters hateful, sexual, violent and self-harm content with configurable thresholds, attachable per model deployment.

## Who should watch

Azure developers and cloud admins setting up an AI platform for several teams, especially the hub and project section. Anyone outside the Microsoft ecosystem can skim it for the governance pattern, which applies to any multi-team model platform.

Title: OpenTelemetry can bill your SaaS customers, not just debug it
Description: Brian Loomis of Progress at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on tiered OpenTelemetry collectors that drive consumption billing and cluster bursting in Chef 360.
Body:
Logs tell a developer why a request failed; they do not tell the business what a customer used. Brian Loomis, Director of Architecture at Progress, showed at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 how his team added OpenTelemetry to Chef 360, a multi-tenant SaaS on consumption billing, so the same telemetry that watches the clusters also meters usage, warns customers before they hit their licence limit and triggers new clusters when one fills up.

It is a vendor-architecture talk about Progress Chef's own system, built around a prototype and a sample implementation, and it is refreshingly specific.

## Your billing unit is not your cloud bill

The mismatch Brian describes is the heart of it. Progress pays its cloud provider for CPU minutes, disk and EKS containers. Customers buy something else: DevOps minutes, jobs, job nodes. Classic logs and events track API calls and infrastructure, which correlate with the implementation, not with what the customer is paying for.

That gap hurts both sides. Customers who cannot see their usage either overbuy and end up with something that looks like shelfware, or they cap themselves to avoid another round with procurement. Either way the conversation the vendor actually wants, pay for what you use, never happens.

Meanwhile, debug logging everywhere does not scale. With a hundred tenants in one cluster and ephemeral containers that live for minutes, finding one customer's operation is the proverbial needle in a haystack, and your developers quietly become tier three support. Brian has a name for trawling interleaved logs across services: "data dog diving".

## Two tiers of collectors, two feedback loops

The architecture uses tiered OpenTelemetry collectors. Each customer deployment runs local collectors that feed a local telemetry dashboard. From there, data is optionally anonymised and forwarded over OTLP to a global collector operated by Chef and Progress. The customer controls the local tier, so they decide whether the vendor sees none, some or all of it, and can dial it up during troubleshooting and back down afterwards. Tenant data stays separated, which logs alone make hard.

Two feedback loops are what make it more than dashboards. The local collector signals the tenant provisioner when a cluster nears capacity, and the provisioner spins up a new cluster and routes new workloads there. The global collector signals billing when a customer approaches their contractual limit, so they can be offered an upgrade before work stalls. A short animation in the talk shows a red and a blue customer filling one cluster, bursting into a second, and blue buying more jobs rather than waiting.

Collectors also aggregate: five or ten API calls become one billable business operation.

## Same chart everywhere

A design rule worth copying: the Helm chart and telemetry pattern are identical whether Chef 360 runs as hosted SaaS, in a customer's cloud, on-prem or air-gapped. Decoupling the business unit (a job node) from the physical cluster is also how they get past what Brian calls the horizontal pod autoscaling ceiling: if a customer needs 500 scale units and a cluster tops out at 100, the provisioner simply knows to place four more.

The production service is Go on AWS EKS in scratch containers; the public sample is in .NET. He is clear about what is not done yet: moving workloads between cloud and on-prem, pinning tenants to clusters for GDPR regions, and smarter ML-driven provisioning.

## Who should watch

Anyone running multi-tenant SaaS with usage-based pricing, and platform teams arguing about whether OpenTelemetry is worth the effort beyond tracing. Brian found it pretty approachable, which is a useful data point against its reputation.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Bruno Ferreira on optimising observability with the OpenTelemetry Collector](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Bruno_Ferreira_observability_opentelemetry_collector) goes deeper on collector pipelines.
- [Prathamesh Sonpatki's handbook to OpenTelemetry metrics](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Prathamesh_Sonpatki_handbook_opentelemetry_metrics) is the metrics primer this design leans on.
- [Narendra Reddy Sanikommu on OpenTelemetry's messy problems](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Narendra_Reddy_Sanikommu_opentelemetry_messy_problems) is the honest counterweight.
