Title: Fraud detection gets better by flagging fewer innocent customers
Description: Sandeep Jarugula of U.S. Bank at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on AI fraud detection with predictive analytics, behaviour models and real-time risk scoring.
Body:
A fraud system that blocks half your legitimate customers is not secure, it is just rude. Sandeep Jarugula, Senior Software Engineer Team Lead at U.S. Bank, used his talk at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 to explain how AI-driven fraud detection in cloud-native financial systems combines predictive analytics with behaviour-based models, and why cutting false positives matters as much as catching fraud.

It is a short overview talk, about 15 minutes, aimed at people who want the shape of a modern fraud pipeline rather than model code. The numbers in it are industry figures Sandeep presents, not U.S. Bank internals.

## False positives are the hidden cost

The figure that frames the talk: traditional rule-based systems, in Sandeep's comparison, can generate up to 50% false positives, while AI-powered detection brings that under 10%. Every false alert is an analyst's time and a customer whose card stopped working at the till. Fewer of them means security teams spend their hours on genuine threats.

Predictive analytics does the first pass. Models analyse huge transaction volumes, score each transaction in milliseconds, and keep learning as fraud patterns change. That last part is the real difference from static rules: fraudsters read the rulebook too, eventually.

## Your customer's habits are the baseline

The second half of the pipeline is behavioural. The system builds historical profiles of how each user transacts and compares live activity against them, in real time. Sandeep's examples of anomalies are the kind any bank would recognise: an unusual international wire transfer, a sudden change of transaction location, or abnormal purchasing across several platforms.

Since, as he puts it, most fraud starts as irregular behaviour, catching the deviation early is how losses get prevented rather than refunded. He cites institutions such as JPMorgan, Mastercard and Goldman Sachs as heavy investors in this kind of system.

## The pipeline, in three moves

Sandeep breaks anomaly detection into three steps: establish a baseline, monitor in real time, and generate alerts. Risk management gets its own three: analyse the transaction, score the risk, take automated action. The point of real-time scoring is that the protective action (hold, step-up verification, block) happens before the money leaves.

None of this works without the boring parts, and he names them: data governance, model validation and continuous monitoring. A fraud model that nobody validates is a liability with a confidence score.

## Who should watch

Engineers joining a payments or fraud team who want a quick vocabulary of the moving parts: predictive models, behavioural baselines, risk scoring, automated response. If you already build fraud models, expect a refresher rather than new technique; there is no architecture diagram of a specific stack or discussion of feature engineering.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu on graph databases for financial fraud detection](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Venkateswarlu_Boggavarapu_fraud_detection_db_graph) adds the relationship angle that per-user baselines miss.
- [Pavel Zapolskii on building a reliable anti-fraud system with machine learning](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Pavel_Zapolskii_machinelearning_antifraud_systems) is more hands-on about the modelling.
- [Sasidhar Reddy Somula on real-time fraud prevention at scale with SRE and ML](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Sasidhar_Reddy_Somula_real_time_fraud) covers keeping such a system up.

Title: For product managers, AI is step five, not step one
Description: Waqas Khan of Kwalee at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on using LLMs for market research, feedback analysis and feature prioritisation, after the problem is defined.
Body:
Waqas Khan, Lead Product at the games developer and publisher Kwalee, has a rule for product managers adopting LLMs: AI is not step one. In his Conf42 Large Language Models 2025 talk he places it at step five or six, after the problem is properly defined, and spends most of the session on where LLMs earn their keep once you get there: market research, customer feedback, feature prioritisation, A/B test interpretation and reporting.

Khan is upfront that he is still learning this himself and testing it inside his own company. That makes this a practitioner's field notes rather than a framework, and a short one at that.

## Data-driven means knowing which touchpoint moves the KPI

Before LLMs enter the picture, Khan defines data-driven product management in concrete terms. Pick the KPI a feature is meant to move (retention, conversion, engagement, revenue, orders), instrument the customer touchpoints that affect it, and use that data both for roadmap planning and after launch. LLMs, in his framing, are a way to bring much larger datasets to that loop, including a rough sense of how users might respond to a feature before it ships.

## Five places an LLM helps a PM

He walks through the use cases one by one. Market research and trend analysis: a PM working alone might map 50 competitors, while an LLM can scan competitor updates, industry reports and news. Customer feedback analysis: sentiment and recurring-issue detection across a user base far too large to read by hand. Feature prioritisation: putting data in front of the room when the CEO, COO and business analysts all have opinions about what ships next. A/B testing: automating interpretation of results, combined with historical data. Reporting: executive summaries and dashboards generated rather than assembled.

The feature prioritisation point is the most honest one in the talk. Every PM knows the loudest voice often wins; Khan's pitch is that data is the only thing that reliably outshouts a C-level hunch.

## Start with ChatGPT, not a custom model

On tooling he names OpenAI's GPT models, Google Bard, Claude and Hugging Face Transformers, and mentions custom LLM integration as the resource-heavy option. His advice is to start simple: try ChatGPT on prioritisation, see how it behaves with your data, and only then move on to predictive analysis and test interpretation.

## Garbage in, biased roadmap out

The challenges section is where the talk earns its place. Validate data quality and sources, or you are planning to fail. Make sure someone (an analyst, a data engineer, a data scientist) can explain what the data means, and let them cut the garbage before it reaches a stakeholder slide. Watch the cost; don't jump on the bandwagon if your current data already answers your questions. Have legal check where training data came from.

His best-practice list starts with problem definition, and his example sticks: "customers are not logging in" is an outcome, not a problem. He also insists AI should be treated as an assistant that suggests, not something that makes product decisions on its own.

## Who should watch

Product managers early in adopting LLMs who want a checklist of use cases and pitfalls. Engineers looking for implementation detail won't find architecture or code here; this is about the PM's workflow.

Title: Micro-segmentation means a hacked web server can't reach the database
Description: Venkata Nedunoori of dentsu international at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on micro-segmentation in the cloud and a phased rollout that won't break your apps.
Body:
Guarding the front door is not much use if every room inside is unlocked. That is the analogy Venkata Nedunoori, Associate Director of Software Engineering at dentsu international, built his Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 talk on: micro-segmentation splits a cloud network into small isolated segments with their own policies, so an attacker who gets in through one workload cannot move laterally to the rest.

The talk is pitched at both technical and non-technical listeners, and it is at its best in the second half, where Venkata explains how to roll segmentation out without taking production down.

## Flat networks are a gift to attackers

Traditional security trusted everything inside the perimeter. In a flat network, one exploited system gives an attacker unrestricted reach, and lateral movement is exactly how advanced persistent threats, ransomware and insider attacks spread. In the cloud the perimeter barely exists anyway, since workloads span data centres and providers and scale up and down by the minute.

Venkata's worked example is a three-tier e-commerce app. Without segmentation, a compromised web server can talk to the application tier and then to the database full of customer data. With it, the web tier may call the app tier and nothing else, and the database is out of reach even for an attacker who is already inside.

## Policies follow identity, not IP addresses

The key difference from classic VLAN and subnet segmentation is granularity and context. Policies attach to individual workloads, containers or even processes, and decisions use application type, user identity, workload tags and security posture instead of IP addresses alone. That is what lets policy follow a workload when it moves or scales, which static firewall rules cannot do.

He names the enforcement options: host-based firewalls, hypervisor controls, software-defined networking, and in cloud-native setups AWS security groups, Azure network security groups and Kubernetes network policies. On the commercial side he mentions VMware NSX and Cisco Tetration.

Three components hold it together: policy enforcement, visibility (flow monitoring, packet inspection, analytics, so you know the real traffic before you block any of it) and automation, because nobody can hand-maintain thousands of rules in an environment that changes hourly.

## Monitor first, enforce later

This is the advice worth the watch. Do not segment everything at once; that, in his words, can lead to a disaster. Instead:

1. Map application dependencies and network flows.
2. Define policies from the observed traffic patterns.
3. Deploy segmentation in monitoring mode and let it soak.
4. Enforce gradually, starting with non-critical workloads.

He also lists the pitfalls he has seen: over-segmentation that breaks applications, static rules that rot, performance overhead from inspection, operational load, and developers pushing back when policies slow them down. The fixes are dynamic policies, orchestration, regular audits and involving cross-functional teams in testing. Finance and healthcare, with PCI DSS, HIPAA and GDPR obligations, are his main use cases.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers about to introduce network policies on a cluster that never had them, and anyone who needs to explain lateral movement to a non-security stakeholder. Seasoned zero trust practitioners will know the concepts; the phased rollout checklist is still a good sanity check.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: If the silicon is compromised, every layer above it is too
Description: FNU Parshant of Arm at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on dual-state hardware security for AI systems, from address-space partitioning to secure boot and enclaves.
Body:
Most AI security talks stop at the API, the model weights or the prompt. FNU Parshant, a logic design engineer at Arm with more than a decade in the field, went several floors down at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025: his talk explains dual-state hardware security models, where the chip itself splits the world into secure and non-secure states, and why that split matters more as AI pushes hardware harder.

It is a clear, well-paced explainer for software people who rarely think about what happens below the kernel.

## Hardware is the bedrock, and it cracks quietly

Parshant's core argument is that AI is not just another application. High-speed accelerators, bigger data pipelines and complex algorithms all widen the attack surface, and hardware flaws are much harder to detect and fix than software ones. Once the hardware is compromised, the OS, the applications and the models on top are all exposed.

His cautionary tale is Spectre and Meltdown: speculative execution was a performance feature until it became a data leak. As AI workloads demand ever more from CPUs and GPUs, he warns, performance features can open security gaps in the same way.

## A vault behind several locked doors

The foundation is address-space partitioning. Memory is divided into secure and non-secure regions; cryptographic operations, key storage and critical code run only in the protected zone, while ordinary applications run in lower-privileged areas. Memory management units and security controllers act as the locked doors in his analogy of a vault inside an office building.

On top of that come boundary markers and isolated enclaves, with Arm TrustZone and Intel SGX as the examples he names. Critical operations, encryption keys and sensitive model parameters live in the enclave, so they stay protected even if the main operating environment falls. Least privilege, enforced in silicon.

## Trust starts at power-on and gets rechecked

Secure boot builds the chain of trust. Firmware anchored in hardware checks the signature of the bootloader before running it, the bootloader verifies the kernel the same way, and a broken link stops everything after it. That shuts out rootkits that try to load before the OS and hide from security tools.

Boot is not the end of it. Parshant describes continuous runtime integrity checks on memory access, execution flow and stack behaviour, increasingly driven by machine learning. AI workloads help here because training, inference and preprocessing are predictable, so a model can learn what normal looks like for each and flag, say, a privilege change without authorisation or a burst of reads in a secure region. Periodic self-tests then recompute hashes and re-verify signatures on systems that may run for weeks without a reboot.

## The threats beyond the chip

Put together, these pieces form the dual-state model, which he credits with three benefits: protecting AI models as intellectual property, keeping sensitive data compliant with regimes like GDPR and HIPAA, and containing breaches so critical operations keep running.

He is careful to call it not a catch-all, and spends the closing on what it does not cover: supply chain risk from counterfeit chips and tampered firmware (answered by secure device identifiers, tamper-evident packaging and attestation), quantum-resistant encryption for hardware meant to last a decade, new attack vectors in neuromorphic chips, and constrained edge AI devices.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers deploying AI on shared or edge hardware, and anyone who has nodded at the words "confidential computing" without being sure what the chip actually does. Hardware security specialists will find it introductory.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Srinivas Vallabhaneni on scaling secure enclaves and confidential computing in Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Vallabhaneni_enclaves_security_confidential) is the software side of enclaves.
- [Swapnil Shinde on blockchain for secure, immutable firmware updates](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Swapnil_Shinde_blockchain_immutable_firmware) tackles the firmware supply chain.
- [Jena Abraham on machine learning in hardware verification](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Jena_Abraham_hardware_verification_innovations) looks at catching chip problems before they ship.

Title: An incident log nobody can edit, built on blockchain
Description: Jugnu Misal at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on blockchain for incident management: tamper-proof records, smart contract responses and audit-ready compliance.
Body:
The worst argument in a post-incident review is about what actually happened. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Jugnu Misal, an incident management engineer, made the case for recording security and operational incidents on a blockchain, so the timeline is shared, tamper-proof and ready for auditors, with smart contracts kicking off the first response steps.

Jugnu opens with a clear disclaimer: the talk is his personal research, not his employer's position. It is a short, conceptual talk, closer to an argument for an approach than a build guide.

## Central incident databases fail at the worst moment

The problem he describes will be familiar to anyone who has run incidents across regions. More connected systems mean more events to track, and traditional tooling keeps them in central databases that can be altered, delayed or lost exactly when they matter. Spread an organisation over several locations and keeping one trustworthy record gets even harder.

Blockchain's pitch here is narrow and specific: a shared record that no single person or company can alter. Every action is appended in a way that keeps it honest, so the record of who did what during an incident can be proven later. That matters most in regulated industries such as finance and healthcare, where disputed records turn into compliance problems.

## Smart contracts as the first responder

The second idea is automation. Smart contracts, which Jugnu describes as self-running programs, trigger responses when conditions are met, cutting the delay and human error between detection and action. The same mechanism handles access: permissions are granted by rules encoded in contracts, data is encrypted throughout, and every action is checked before it is allowed.

Whether you would put your pager logic on a chain is a fair question to bring to the talk. The useful framing is that the incident record and the access policy live in the same verifiable place.

## Compliance becomes a by-product

Because every action is logged automatically and the log cannot change, compliance reporting stops being a manual export. Jugnu also outlines how such a system itself gets audited: continuous security updates against new threats, compliance verification, review of day-to-day operations for inefficiencies, and testing of the technology for weaknesses.

He points to finance (tracking transactions), healthcare (patient records) and security firms (real-time threat monitoring) as the early adopters, then walks through a case study of an unnamed large financial company. In his telling, resolving an issue used to take almost two days; after the switch that time dropped by 72%, and compliance reporting became 89% faster. The company is not named, so read it as an illustration rather than a reproducible benchmark.

## The honest part: cost and legacy

Jugnu does not pretend this is free. A new system needs investment, training and a cultural shift, and integrating a blockchain with older systems is hard. His advice is to start small and scale up. He closes by looking at blockchain alongside AI and connected devices to predict problems earlier.

## Who should watch

Incident and compliance folks in regulated industries who are tired of arguing about whose timeline is right, and architects curious whether immutable ledgers fit their audit story. If you want implementation detail (which chain, which consensus, what throughput), this talk will not give it; it is a 15-minute concept tour.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Sai Krishna Gurram on blockchain-cloud integration for incident response in payment networks](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Sai_Krishna_Gurram_blockchain_payments_cloud) applies the same idea to payments.
- [Tanya Janca on incident response for developers](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Tanya_Janca_incident_response_developers) covers the human process the record is meant to support.
- [Chinyere Chinekezi on incident response playbooks](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Chinyere_Chinekezi_12_incident_playbooks_response) pairs well with the smart-contract automation idea.

Title: Cloud security works in layers, so one miss is not a breach
Description: Chakradhar Sunkesula of Compass at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on a layered cloud defense: zero trust, risk-based auth, API checks, AI detection, recovery.
Body:
Any single security control will eventually let something through; the question is what stands behind it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Chakradhar Sunkesula, Engineering Manager at Compass, laid out a multi-layer defense for cloud infrastructure where network, identity, API, detection and recovery controls back each other up, so no one layer is a single point of failure.

This is an architecture overview, not a product pitch or a code walkthrough. It is a compact map of the layers, with a few concrete mechanisms per layer that are worth stealing.

## The perimeter was always a polite fiction

Chakradhar starts from the usual suspects behind cloud incidents: misconfiguration, weak identity management and missing monitoring. His argument is that patch-after-the-breach is too late when every new app, data store and endpoint widens the attack surface.

So the network layer goes zero trust. Every request, internal or external, is verified, and AI-driven traffic analysis watches for odd behaviour. His example is easy to picture: a user who suddenly gets busy at 3 a.m. from a country where the company has no operations gets flagged or blocked automatically. He also likes tripwires, thresholds such as an unusual data exfiltration rate or an unexpected touch on a sensitive resource, that raise an alarm before an attacker can wander far.

## Authentication should cost more when the risk is higher

The identity layer is where the talk gets most practical. Users and devices get a risk class. A low-risk user on a known location may pass with one factor; a privileged admin signing in from somewhere new gets one-time passwords or biometrics on top. Tokens are short-lived, and a suspected compromise triggers a kill switch that revokes sessions across the board.

Authorization follows least privilege, with dynamic access control layered on: privileges shrink in real time when location or request volume looks wrong, and continuous auditing feeds back into how roles are designed. If you have ever found a service account with admin rights "just for the migration" two years later, this section is for you.

## APIs are the glue, so they are the target

In a microservice architecture the API is where attackers knock. Chakradhar's framework validates requests at several points (headers, payloads, tokens), has each microservice trust only specific tokens or request patterns, and pulls in threat intelligence feeds to reject known-bad IPs and domains. His anomaly example: an endpoint that normally sees 100 requests an hour and suddenly sees 10,000 should be flagged or blocked by a machine, not by a human reading a dashboard the next morning.

Behind that sits analytics across logs plus external threat intel, with automated responses such as isolating containers or forcing updates when new exploit patterns appear. Comprehensive logging pays off after a breach, when you need to know which accounts, endpoints and data were touched.

## Recovery is a layer too

The last layer is resilience: redundancy across regions and providers, automatic failover when a region is under a DDoS attack, and runbooks that say who does what, when and how. Orchestration tools roll the system back to a known safe state. Adaptive controls then update models, firewall rules and access policies from each new threat pattern.

The cost argument closes the talk. Chakradhar cites industry figures for reduced incident response cost and faster recovery, and notes that a stronger posture can lower cyber insurance premiums. Treat those numbers as the industry estimates he presents, not as measurements from Compass.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers who need a one-page mental model of cloud defense in depth, or a checklist to compare their own setup against. If you already run zero trust with risk-based auth and API anomaly detection, you will mostly nod along; the kill switch and tripwire ideas are the bits to take home.

Title: Real-time analytics in the cloud, one layer at a time
Description: Prithvi Raju Rudraraju of IT America at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on the ingestion, processing and storage layers behind real-time cloud analytics.
Body:
Before an LLM can say anything useful about your business, somebody has to get the data to it fast and in one piece. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Prithvi Raju Rudraraju, SAP ABAP/BW/HANA consultant at IT America, gave a short tour of the architecture behind real-time analytics in the cloud: an ingestion layer, a processing layer and a storage layer, each with its own rules of thumb about how hard you can push it.

A note on scope: despite the LLM-flavoured title, the recorded talk is about the data platform underneath AI, not about language models themselves. Treat it as an architecture overview of the pipes.

## Three layers, three jobs

Rudraraju splits a real-time system into three parts that have to work in sync. The ingestion layer is the front door, pulling streams from IoT devices, applications and third-party sources while keeping data quality and format consistent. The processing layer runs distributed, in-memory computation for analytics, ML models and business logic. The storage layer combines in-memory caching with persistent storage so you get both speed and durability.

None of that is new, but the talk is useful for the way it attaches operating thresholds to each layer.

## Leave headroom, because utilisation is a cliff

The recurring theme is that every layer degrades sharply past a certain load, so you should plan to run below it. For ingestion on platforms like Apache Kafka, he recommends proactive monitoring and keeping utilisation under roughly 80% to absorb traffic spikes. For processing, the target in normal operation is 60 to 70% CPU, with the warning that performance falls off quickly beyond 85% and deadlines start to slip. Storage follows the same pattern: latency stays steady until about 85% of capacity and then climbs.

If you have ever watched a queue go from fine to on fire in five minutes, this is the section that explains why the dashboard lied to you at 79%.

## Micro-batches and tiers

Two design patterns get specific attention. First, event-driven architecture with small micro-batches; he cites 25-event batches as the balance point between throughput and latency in the testing he describes. Second, tiered storage, keeping hot recent data on fast storage and moving older data to cheaper tiers, which he says improves query response for recent data compared with a single tier. Partitioning strategy is called out as the main lever for write throughput on distributed storage.

## Security and observability are part of the design

The second half covers what usually gets bolted on later. AES encryption, he argues, costs little enough in processing time that there is no reason to skip it. Authentication, compliance monitoring and real-time rule enforcement are presented as streaming workloads in their own right. On observability, he recommends ML-based anomaly detection for system health over static thresholds, plus distributed tracing with sampling so you get statistically useful traces without paying full overhead.

The talk quotes a lot of percentages from slides without naming the studies behind them, so read them as indicative rather than as benchmarks for your own system.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects new to streaming analytics who want a checklist of the layers and the thresholds people commonly use. Experienced data engineers will find it familiar; it is a breadth talk, roughly 15 minutes, without demos or code.

Title: Let an LLM do the first pass of your Well-Architected review
Description: Shoeb Bustani of AWS at Conf42 LLMs 2025 demos a Bedrock RAG sample that reads your architecture doc and drafts a Well-Architected review.
Body:
Anyone who has sat through an AWS Well-Architected review knows the drill: six pillars, a long list of questions, and a reviewer who has to read your 40-page design doc first. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Shoeb Bustani, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, showed a sample application that does that first read for you. You upload the architecture document, and Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic's Claude drafts answers to the framework questions, with recommendations, risks and citations back to the official documentation.

This is an AWS talk about an AWS sample built on AWS services. The design choices behind it transfer well beyond the console, though.

## Why reviews stop scaling

Bustani sets up the problem quickly. The Well-Architected Framework has six pillars (operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability) plus lenses for specific domains such as data analytics or financial services, and you can define custom lenses for your own standards. As cloud footprints grow, manual reviews become slow and resource-hungry, different teams apply the principles inconsistently, and new services keep shifting what best practice means. A review is meant to be a continuous activity, which is exactly what humans with calendars are bad at.

## Prompting alone isn't enough, so it's RAG

The obvious first idea is to turn every framework question into a prompt and loop through them. Bustani walks through zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting and then explains why that falls short: limited context, poor memory, and no access to the actual framework documentation. So the sample uses retrieval-augmented generation. The Well-Architected documentation is downloaded from the public AWS site, chunked, embedded and stored in a Bedrock knowledge base backed by OpenSearch Serverless. For each question, relevant passages are retrieved and ranked, then combined with the content of your uploaded document in the prompt.

## Quick mode for authors, deep mode for reviewers

The demo used a fictitious payment-processing solution with a 37-page architecture document. The app offers two analysis types. Quick mode bundles all questions for a pillar into one prompt, which Bustani pitches as a way for an architect to mark their own homework before facing an architecture review board. Deep mode answers each question separately and integrates with the AWS Well-Architected Tool: it creates a workload, ticks the best-practice choices the model thinks apply, fills in the notes and saves a milestone. The tool then computes risks from those choices, giving the human reviewers a baseline to start from rather than a blank form.

A detail worth stealing: when the document lacks the information to answer a question, the prompts make the model say so instead of guessing. Every review starts with a generated solution summary, and a chat panel lets you ask follow-up questions against either the summary or the full document. In the demo, a question about EC2 instance types failed against the summary and succeeded against the document, which is a nice live example of why grounding matters.

## The plumbing

The whole stack deploys with AWS CDK: a Streamlit front end on EC2 behind an Application Load Balancer and CloudFront with WAF rules, Cognito for users, S3 for uploads, SQS to trigger a Lambda that starts a Step Functions workflow, Textract to extract document text, and DynamoDB for run state. Bustani points to a blog post he co-authored and the code in the AWS samples repository.

## Who should watch

Cloud architects and platform teams who run Well-Architected reviews at scale, and anyone building a RAG system that has to answer a fixed questionnaire against a long document. The architecture walkthrough at the end is the most reusable part.

Title: The real secret to dynamic secrets is developer enablement
Description: HashiCorp's Rosemary Wang at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on application-agnostic vs application-aware patterns for rotating secrets without restarts.
Body:
Moving secrets into a secrets manager is the easy part; teaching every application to cope when those secrets change is the job. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Rosemary Wang, Principal Developer Advocate at HashiCorp, showed the two patterns for handling secrets that rotate or expire (application-agnostic and application-aware), demoed both with HashiCorp Vault, Kubernetes and Spring Boot, and landed on a non-technical punchline: there is no magic tool, only developer enablement.

## Rotation is a dependency change

Rosemary's opening is a familiar escalation. Security says no more copy-pasted API tokens, so everything moves into a secrets manager. Now applications fetch secrets over the network. Then a requirement arrives to rotate every 30 days, and every application has to reload and pick up the new version before the old one is deleted. Fine for one app; painful when many share a token.

She sorts secrets into three kinds: **static** (created and deleted by hand), **rotated** (automation creates the new one, you retire the old), and **dynamic** (automation both generates and revokes). Design for dynamic and the same patterns cover the other two. Every flow has the same three steps: authenticate and get the secret, the secret changes, the application reloads. It's the dynamic configuration problem with higher stakes.

## Pattern one: the app never meets the secrets manager

In the application-agnostic pattern, a separate process authenticates to the secrets manager and injects secrets as environment variables or files. The app reads them as it always has. When the secret changes, that process fetches the new one and either the framework live-reloads (Spring Boot and .NET can reload properties from files) or something restarts the app for it.

The demo uses the Vault Secrets Operator on Kubernetes with a Spring Boot payments app. A VaultAuth resource authenticates with a Kubernetes service account. A static secret (a payments processor username and password) and a dynamic database credential are synced into Kubernetes secrets, injected as environment variables, with a rollout-restart target on the deployment. The database credential has a three-minute lease for demo purposes, and after rotation the pods restart with a fresh username and password. No code changes.

A practical tip from her: if you're new to leases, rotate at about two-thirds of the lifetime, leaving time to confirm the app works before the old credential expires.

## Pattern two: the app does it itself

Some teams can't accept even a rolling restart, or don't run in containers at all. In the application-aware pattern the code authenticates to the secrets manager, tracks expiry (a timer or an event subscription), gracefully closes connections using the old credential, opens new ones, and retries and caches the existing secret if the secrets manager is unreachable.

Her Spring demo uses Spring Vault and Spring Cloud Vault: scheduled context refreshes for the static secret, a lease-expired event listener for the dynamic one. The step teams forget is re-injecting the new credential into the objects that use it. Reloading properties isn't enough; the Java DataSource has to be rebuilt, or the app keeps connecting with the old password. Spring's refresh scope rebuilds it and restarts the Hikari pool.

## Choosing, and the actual secret

Agnostic suits many languages and maximises platform automation, and rolling restarts barely matter with several replicas. Aware suits organisations standardised on one framework who want control over performance and behaviour, at the cost of refactoring and testing every codebase. Most end up with both: one team she worked with went application-aware and still needed the agnostic route for about 20% of apps.

Before choosing, assess runtimes, frameworks, availability needs, and every secret type with its rotation frequency. Then enable developers: document the patterns, publish code examples, hold office hours, and do live refactors with real teams. Those surface the surprises, like a codebase that didn't use bean annotations, so refresh didn't work, or GraalVM native images where reflection wasn't available.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers rolling out a secrets manager, security teams writing rotation policies, and Java developers who've been told their database password now expires. The demos are Vault-specific, but the patterns apply to any secrets manager.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Michael Levan on Kubernetes secret management with Vault](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Michael_Levan_kubernetes_secret_management_vault), a closer look at the Kubernetes setup.
- [Venkata Velavarthipati on workload identity and secretless OIDC](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Venkata_Velavarthipati_workloadidentity_oidc_secretless), for removing some secrets altogether.
- [Alex Soto on the secret of Kubernetes secrets](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Alex_Soto_kubernetes_secrets_secret), what a native Kubernetes Secret does and doesn't protect.

Title: Data scientists have the same problem ops had before DevOps
Description: Graziano Casto of Mia-Platform at Conf42 LLMs 2025 maps ML pain to cloud native fixes: data catalogs, Kubeflow, AI gateways, drift monitoring.
Body:
Graziano Casto, DevRel Engineer at Mia-Platform, opened his Conf42 Large Language Models 2025 talk with a confession: he is not an ML person. His friend Leonardo, a data scientist, is. Over a drink, Leonardo complained that putting a model into production takes longer than building it, and Casto recognised the shape of the problem immediately. It is the wall between developers and operations that DevOps was invented to knock down, rebuilt between data scientists and the people who run their models.

The talk follows that idea through Leonardo's workflow (data preparation, training and tuning, deployment and monitoring, repeat) and, for each pain point, borrows a fix that already exists in the cloud native world.

## Bad data governance is a culture bug, not a tooling bug

Leonardo's first complaint was data: no lineage, no clear owners, no idea how sensitive a dataset is. Casto's diagnosis is that this is a missing data culture first. Tools help a culture grow, though, and the one he recommends is a data catalog: a hierarchical archive of metadata that holds both the technical side (types, storage location, lineage between datasets) and the business side (ownership, compliance level). The model is only as good as the data it was trained on, so making that data findable and traceable comes before anything clever.

## "Works on my notebook" is the new "works on my machine"

The biggest gap was between Leonardo's local Jupyter notebook, where everything runs, and the production environment the delivery team inherits. Casto's answer is Kubeflow, the collection of open source projects for running the ML lifecycle on Kubernetes. Kubeflow Notebooks run web-based development environments as containers inside the cluster, so admins can hand data scientists standard images with the right packages, and experimentation happens in the same place production does. The Kubeflow Training Operator handles distributed training and fine-tuning, letting a job scale from one machine to a cluster through Kubernetes APIs.

Anyone who lived through the move from hand-built servers to containers will find the argument familiar, which is the point.

## Put an AI gateway between your app and someone else's model

Not every team trains models. Many just call GPT, Mistral or Llama from an existing product, and then the app ends up owning authentication, authorisation, prompt management, caching and spend checks. Casto's fix mirrors the API gateway: an AI gateway as middleware between application and model. It centralises those concerns, decouples the app from a specific provider and makes switching models (or using several) a configuration change rather than a refactor.

## Monitor the inputs and outputs, not just CPU

For monitoring, CPU and RAM tell you the system is alive, not that the model is right. Casto argues for watching the inputs the model receives and the outputs it produces, to catch three kinds of drift: data drift (input statistics change), prediction drift (outputs change even when inputs don't) and concept drift (the relationship between inputs and target changes). His stack for this is the boring, proven one: Prometheus for metrics and alerts, Grafana for dashboards.

## Tools alone just add complexity

The wrap-up is the platform engineering pitch: an internal developer platform that exposes all of this through a self-service catalog, so Leonardo can pick a notebook environment or a training cluster without filing a ticket. He ends with conversational developer experience: RAG over the platform's own assets, so you can ask the platform questions in natural language. That part is presented as an early-stage idea with a repo to try, not a finished product.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers who have been asked to support the data science team and want a map of where their existing skills apply. It is an overview talk, not a Kubeflow tutorial, and it is honest about that.

Title: Cloud sanity is transparency, simplicity and no lock-in
Description: Qumulus developer relations engineer Denish Tomar at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on taming surprise cloud bills with transparent, predictable pricing.
Body:
The scariest cloud alert is the one that arrives at the end of the month as an invoice. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Denish Tomar, a developer relations engineer at Qumulus, told a short, personal story about cloud chaos, and argued that the fix is less about new tooling than about three properties you should demand from any cloud setup: transparency, simplicity and flexibility.

Honest scope up front: this is a brief, light talk from a vendor's DevRel, and the solution it presents is Qumulus's own pricing model. Watch it for the framing and the questions it gives you to ask your provider, not for implementation detail.

## The small update that wasn't

Denish opens with a scene most of us have lived. You push what you think is a tiny change, and within minutes your Slack lights up like New Year's Eve fireworks. Then the real damage turns up weeks later on the bill. His description of cloud billing as a mystery novel where you never know the ending will land with anyone who has tried to explain a spike to finance.

His conclusion from that morning is the useful sentence of the talk: the cloud itself isn't the problem, the way we manage it is.

## Three things to demand

From there he boils cloud sanity down to three requirements:

- **Transparency**: know exactly what you are paying for. His restaurant line is a good one; you wouldn't order from a menu with no prices, so why accept it from a cloud?
- **Simplicity**: cut configuration complexity. Complexity, he says, doesn't make you smarter, it just makes troubleshooting harder. Think flat-pack furniture without the manual.
- **Flexibility**: no vendor lock-in. No provider should own your infrastructure choices, so keep your options open.

None of these is new, but they make a decent checklist when you're evaluating a platform or reviewing your current one. If you can't say what a workload costs per month, or how you would move it, you're missing at least two of the three.

## Where Qumulus comes in

The case study is a Qumulus client struggling with unpredictable costs across several vendors, with a surprise bill every month. Qumulus moved them to a fixed-cost model without per-operation metering, priced in a simple unit-based system instead of a charge for every resource and call. Denish compares the result to moving from a pay-per-minute phone plan to unlimited data: the spend became predictable.

The talk doesn't go into how the units map to resources or what trade-offs fixed pricing brings, such as paying for headroom you don't use. Those are the questions to take to any vendor offering flat pricing, Qumulus included.

## Who should watch

Engineers and team leads who are tired of explaining cloud invoices and want a quick framing for the conversation, and anyone evaluating alternatives to metered hyperscaler pricing. If you want FinOps mechanics (tagging, allocation, rightsizing), pair it with something more technical.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: In serverless, the energy bill and the cloud bill move together
Description: UBS associate director Neetu Gangwani at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on energy-aware autoscaling, ARM hardware and carbon-aware pricing for serverless.
Body:
Serverless made idle servers someone else's problem; it didn't make their electricity disappear. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Neetu Gangwani, Associate Director at UBS, argued that energy efficiency and cost efficiency in serverless computing are the same optimisation seen from two sides, and surveyed the strategies, case studies and open problems where they meet.

Scope note: this is a survey talk built on industry figures and anonymised case studies rather than one system Neetu ran. Read the numbers as reported claims and the structure as the takeaway.

## Why serverless won, and what it hides

Neetu starts with the familiar case for serverless: platforms that scale from a few requests to millions within milliseconds, pay-per-use pricing down to the millisecond, and operations simple enough that developers deploy faster because nobody patches servers. The catch is that as serverless workloads grow, so does their energy footprint, and data centres already use a meaningful share of the world's electricity. Fine-grained billing makes cost visible; energy stays invisible unless you go looking.

## Three levers on the energy footprint

She groups the techniques into three:

- **Energy-aware autoscaling**: ML models that learn from historical workload patterns and real-time metrics to allocate resources, aiming to cut waste without hurting response times.
- **Hardware-software co-design**: ARM-based processors and specialised accelerators that do the same work on less power than traditional x86, plus firmware tuning.
- **Function chaining optimisation**: co-locating functions and caching data so chained functions stop shipping the same payloads back and forth, and removing redundant compute cycles.

The third one is the most actionable for application teams today. A chain of functions that each re-fetch and re-serialise the same data is paying twice, once in invocations and once in watts.

## Pricing that knows about carbon

The more speculative part is carbon-aware pricing: models that factor real-time energy cost and environmental impact into the price, nudging workloads toward times and regions where energy is cleaner or cheaper. Paired with AI-driven allocation and energy monitoring, Neetu presents it as a way to cut both power use and spend. It's an emerging idea rather than something every provider offers, so treat it as a direction to watch.

## Case studies and the hard parts

She describes three anonymised examples: a Fortune 500 retailer running Black Friday on serverless with lower server energy use, a national healthcare network processing real-time patient data, and a global investment firm moving its trading platform to serverless. Each comes with energy and cost reductions, but without names or methodology.

The challenges are where the talk is most useful. There are no standard energy benchmarks, so comparing providers is hard. Per-tenant energy attribution in shared environments is still unsolved, which matters because serverless is multi-tenant by design. And regulation is arriving, with the EU Green Deal and regional carbon reporting among the frameworks she mentions. Her future directions call for industry collaboration on green computing standards and for giving developers energy monitoring tools and practical guidelines, because you can't optimise what you can't see.

## Who should watch

Architects and FinOps practitioners who need to add a sustainability dimension to cloud decisions, and teams facing carbon reporting requirements. If you want a hands-on Lambda tuning session, look elsewhere; this is the strategic map.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Neel Shah on green and sustainable software](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Neel_Shah_green_sustainable_software), the broader practice beyond serverless.
- [Yan Cui on serverless cost-saving tips](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Yan_Cui_serverless_saving_tips), concrete moves on the cost side of the same equation.
- [Clifton Reddy on green code](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Clifton_Reddy_green_code_sustainable), efficiency at the level of the code itself.

Title: Where AI earns its keep in an ETL pipeline
Description: Gaurav Mittal of Nordstrom at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on using AI in each ETL step, from extracting unstructured data to predicting failures and right-sizing infrastructure.
Body:
ETL scripts are written once and fixed forever, usually at night after a source system changed a field. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Gaurav Mittal, a software engineer at Nordstrom, walked through where AI helps in a classic extract-transform-load pipeline: in each of the three steps, and in running the pipeline itself.

It's an introductory overview, a good map for data engineers starting to think about AI in their stack, with tools named but no code.

## Why traditional ETL keeps needing people

Mittal's diagnosis is familiar. Extraction pulls from scattered sources in shapes that aren't readily usable, often via hand-written scripts or visual tools that still need someone who understands both the tech and the business. Unstructured data has no efficient non-AI path at all, which means humans tagging it. Source schemas evolve, so scripts drift and break. And infrastructure needs move with data volume, which nobody predicts well in advance. All of it adds up to ongoing manual work.

## AI in each of the three letters

**Extract.** AI is a natural fit for unstructured and semi-structured data: pulling entities from documents, and working out the structure of a web page or PDF whose layout changes over time.

**Transform.** Build a model of what the data should look like, then let it flag values out of range, missing fields that are normally present, and data in non-standard formats it can map to the expected one. When something is too far outside the norm, the pipeline pulls in a human instead of guessing.

**Load.** AI can size the infrastructure for the load step, scaling up for a spike and down for a lull, and handle common errors such as a number stored as a string. Again, a human gets called when the load is going badly in ways it can't handle.

## Running the pipeline, not just building it

The second half covers operations. Feed logs, time-series and sensor data into a model of past failures, and the system can flag a likely failure before it happens instead of after. The same signals help find bottlenecks and right-size compute and storage, which is where the cost savings come from: neither over- nor under-provisioned. Proactive is the theme; traditional pipelines mostly learn about trouble retroactively.

For tooling, he points to AWS Glue if you are on AWS, and Airbyte for an open-source route that can also process unstructured data.

## Low-hanging fruit

His starter list is pragmatic: tag incoming unstructured or semi-structured data with sentiment so later steps can use it, fill gaps in incomplete records, and run anomaly detection for fraud, the familiar case of your card provider blocking a purchase that doesn't fit your pattern.

The caveats are the right ones. Don't just throw data at a model: build access controls so the right users see the right data. Teams need new skills. And he sees most future workflows as a hybrid of human steps, AI steps and plain imperative code, with AI also enabling real-time analytics that need far less pre-processing than a warehouse-and-report cycle.

## Who should watch

Title: k0rdent wraps Cluster API so one manifest builds a cluster anywhere
Description: Mirantis engineer Bharath Nallapeta at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 demos k0rdent, open source multi-cloud Kubernetes provisioning on Cluster API and Sveltos.
Body:
Cluster API is the right abstraction for provisioning Kubernetes everywhere, and also a lot of YAML. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Bharath Nallapeta, Senior Software Engineer in the open source program office at Mirantis, introduced k0rdent, an open source project from Mirantis that packages Cluster API, provider controllers, Sveltos and an observability stack so a platform team can describe a cluster in one resource and get it on AWS, Azure, OpenStack or vSphere.

To be clear about scope: this is a project introduction plus a live demo, given by one of the people building it. It's a good look at how the pieces fit, not a neutral comparison with other tools.

## Platform teams need self-service, not a bigger DevOps team

Bharath's framing is platform engineering. Kubernetes started simple, the ecosystem grew, and now even experienced people find it complex. Enterprises want developer self-service, operational simplicity, customisation without changing the core model, visibility and control for admins, and security and compliance. A DevOps team as big as the development team doesn't scale, so the platform has to do the work.

He then lays out the usual options: do nothing and watch the cloud bill grow, assemble open source tools yourself and pay the integration learning curve, or buy a proprietary product and discover the lock-in a few years later. k0rdent is pitched as the enterprise-grade open source fourth option.

## Three jobs, mostly upstream parts

The architecture has three parts:

- **Cluster management** uses upstream Cluster API controllers plus the cloud-specific providers (CAPA for AWS, CAPZ for Azure, CAPV for VMware and so on), with k0s and k0smotron at the core of the management cluster.
- **State management** uses Sveltos, which deploys applications and add-ons across clusters. Want cert-manager on every cluster? Add it to the configuration and Sveltos puts it there, with an agent in each child cluster talking back to the management cluster.
- **Observability** ships in the package, so you don't have to wire up a monitoring stack per cluster.

Three custom resources tie it together. A ClusterDeployment describes one cluster and references a ClusterTemplate (per cloud: AWS, EKS, Azure, AKS, OpenStack, vSphere) and any ServiceTemplates for the add-ons you want installed.

## The demo: four clouds, one shape of manifest

Installation is a Helm chart into any management cluster; Bharath uses kind on a laptop. After `helm install`, the controllers, k0smotron and the rest are running, and listing cluster templates shows the pre-packaged options.

He then walks through what you supply per provider: a secret with credentials, a credential object, and a cluster identity (an Azure service principal, AWS keys, OpenStack variables). The ClusterDeployments themselves are short: template, credential, and a config block for control plane and workers. One of his Azure clusters uses a GPU instance type and comes up with an NVIDIA Tesla T4 worker; changing that is a matter of picking a different instance size.

Underneath, ordinary Cluster API objects appear (AWSCluster, AzureCluster, OpenStackCluster and their machines), which is reassuring if you already know CAPI. Kubeconfigs for each child cluster land as secrets in the `kcm-system` namespace; export one and you're in.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who have looked at Cluster API and winced at the setup, and teams running Kubernetes across more than one cloud or on-prem. If you need a single cluster on one provider, a managed service is still the simpler answer.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Gianluca Mardente on managing Kubernetes add-ons across clusters](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Gianluca_Mardente_kubernetes_addons_multiple_cluster_runtime_state), from the author of Sveltos, the state layer k0rdent uses.

Title: Ports and adapters let you change your cloud mind later
Description: Asher Sterkin at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on using the Ports and Adapters pattern to keep cloud infrastructure choices reversible as a system grows.
Body:
Most cloud infrastructure decisions are made on taste and then defended as facts. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Asher Sterkin, a software technology expert with about 40 years in the industry, argued that you can't avoid deciding too early, but you can make those decisions cheap to reverse, by applying Alistair Cockburn's Ports and Adapters pattern systematically to cloud architecture.

## The problem with early decisions

Asher's opening is the dilemma every growing system meets. What suits a large, mature system is too expensive and complex at the start. Early-stage shortcuts block growth later. And cloud vendors ship new features constantly, so a custom solution built last year may now be obsolete, or a risk.

He then lists how many choices there are: which cloud (or whether Kubernetes counts as one), compute (VMs, Lambda, containers, Step Functions), storage (relational, non-relational, blob), internal messaging (queues, pub/sub, streaming), external interfaces (load balancer, API Gateway, AppSync for GraphQL), observability, deployment tooling (CloudFormation, CDK, Helm, Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi), and the language and runtime combinations on top. Rarely is there one clear-cut answer.

## How decisions really get made

We're supposed to decide on facts: workload, SLAs for latency and throughput, security, cost, time to market, brownfield constraints. In practice, Asher says, decisions come from faith, experience from the last project whether relevant or not, likes and dislikes, hype, and the opinion of the most senior person in the room.

His alternative is set-based engineering. Early on you know little about interfaces, load, security changes or even the target market, so evaluate several candidates and keep as many options open as possible. Converge gradually, usually to a few configurations matching your environments, and lock one for production. Then expect feedback and metrics to send you back to the start with new candidates.

## Isolate the core, plug in the cloud

Ports and Adapters (also called hexagonal architecture) is what makes that loop affordable. Application logic knows nothing about the infrastructure it runs on. It talks through ports, which Asher describes as slightly more than interfaces: a collection of interfaces sharing a technology choice and the data flowing through them. Each port can have several adapters on different infrastructure, plugged in by a configurator that can be static or dynamic.

He uses the BlueZone example from the book, a parking system where drivers buy tickets and inspectors check cars. Use cases give the primary ports: driving ports for the driver and the inspector, a driven port for the payment service. The event flow gives secondary ports: a database, and, nicely, the current time, which the ticket logic needs and which you really don't want hard-wired.

## Let requirements pick the adapter

From there, requirements choose adapters. Stable schema plus ad hoc queries points to Postgres; a flexible schema to a document store like MongoDB; very high throughput and low latency to Cassandra. Regulators, customers and legacy integrations usually pick the cloud. Time to market pushes toward that cloud's serverless options; on AWS he lists Lambda with API Gateway or AppSync, Amazon MQ, Aurora Serverless, DocumentDB, Keyspaces and CDK.

Then production feedback arrives: too expensive, too slow, a missing feature. Now the alternatives are real options (Neon instead of Aurora, MongoDB Atlas, DataStax for Cassandra, Kubernetes behind a load balancer when steady high load makes Lambda a poor fit, Helm or Pulumi for deployment), and because the core only knows ports, swapping is an adapter change rather than a rewrite.

## Who should watch

Architects and tech leads on young systems who already sense that today's serverless stack won't be tomorrow's, and teams stuck mid-migration because infrastructure calls are threaded through business logic. It's a pattern talk, short on code and long on reasoning; Asher calls it the tip of the iceberg.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Luca Mezzalira on hexagonal architecture with serverless](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Luca_Mezzalira_hexagonal_architecture_serverless), the same pattern applied to Lambda code.
- [Yan Cui on patterns for efficient serverless](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Yan_Cui_patterns_efficient_serverless), for when the serverless adapter is the one you keep.
- [Lawrence Finn on breaking out of the cloud with a sidecar](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Lawrence_Finn_multicloud_breaking_cloud_sidecar), another route to avoiding provider lock-in.

Title: Scaling generative AI means a portfolio, not one chatbot
Description: Meethun Panda, Associate Partner at Bain & Company, at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on design principles, a layered stack and team roles for scaling generative AI.
Body:
Building one chatbot is a project; running dozens of generative AI use cases across a company is an architecture. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Meethun Panda, Associate Partner at Bain & Company, laid out how executives and architects should think about that second problem: four design principles, a layered stack with security running through every layer, and the team you need to carry use cases from definition to support.

It's a consultant's framework talk, high level by design. Read it as a map for planning conversations, not a build guide.

## Four principles for a stack that won't freeze

With new models arriving every week, Panda's first principle is **flexibility**: don't lock the architecture to one model or vendor. Then **scalability**, which in practice means the cloud and elastic hosting. Then **security and privacy**, and finally **monitoring** of every use case in production. None of these is novel, but the reason behind the first one is worth repeating: the model you pick this quarter is unlikely to be the one you run next year.

## The layers, bottom to top

His reference stack has the layers most enterprise teams will recognise:

1. **Infrastructure.** Compute, storage, network and provisioning, with GPUs for training and serving, moving from on-prem toward cloud and multi-cloud.
2. **Data management and engineering.** Ingestion, batch and change data capture, transformation, data quality, governance, and for generative AI, the vector database.
3. **Analytics platform.** Where models are built, trained, tested and served, including LLM selection among open and closed models and inference sized to the latency each use case needs.
4. **Modern software platform.** Real-time, event-driven microservices that embed AI into business processes, whether fintech, healthcare or pharma.
5. **Digital channels.** Mobile, web and wearables, the last especially relevant in healthcare.

Security cuts vertically through all of them, and he insists it be designed in from the start rather than added at the end.

## Choices that matter

For each building block, Panda lists the decision criteria. For LLMs and embeddings: capability fit (no single model covers every use case), security, ease of use and multilingual support. For vector databases, with Pinecone and Weaviate among his examples: latency, performance and scalability, flexibility, availability in your cloud, and cost. For the platform: compliance with your security norms and room for new use cases.

He also makes a point that deserves more airtime. Unstructured data is the fuel of large language models, yet for decades organisations gave it far less care than structured data. Documents sitting in inboxes and on laptops won't feed anything. Centralise them, label them, and build governed pipelines for extraction. His RAG walkthrough (chunk, embed, load into a vector database, embed the query the same way, retrieve the top few chunks, feed them to the model) is a basic version, and he calls it that.

## The team and the lifecycle

The closing section is the most practical for anyone staffing a programme. Scaling requires a delivery process that runs use case definition (with KPIs and the value you expect), discovery of the data needed, setup of infrastructure, model and vector store, development with proper UI/UX and a modular backend, deployment and monitoring, and maintenance. The roles span data engineers, data scientists, ML or LLM ops engineers, ML engineers, product owners and managers, SREs and UX developers. Note the SREs on that list; generative AI in production is still production.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering managers who need a shared vocabulary with leadership before a generative AI programme starts. Practitioners already running several LLM services will find it familiar.

Title: Multi-tenant SaaS: share the building, never the apartment
Description: Expedia Group's Shinu Pushpan at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on multi-tenant SaaS design, from data isolation patterns to security layers and noisy neighbours.
Body:
Multi-tenancy is an apartment building: everyone shares the walls and the plumbing, and nobody should be able to walk into the neighbour's kitchen. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Shinu Pushpan, Principal Software Development Engineer at Expedia Group, used that analogy to frame a structured overview of multi-tenant SaaS: how to separate tenant data, how to secure the boundaries, and how to stop one busy customer slowing down everyone else.

It's an architecture primer, organised as a tour of decisions rather than a war story. Good for anyone about to build, or inherit, a SaaS backend.

## The trade you're making

Shinu sets multi-tenant against single-tenant on four axes. Isolation: single-tenant gets dedicated infrastructure, multi-tenant gets virtual isolation through data partitioning. Cost: shared infrastructure is cheaper. Customisation: single-tenant can do anything per customer, multi-tenant is limited because everyone runs the same software. Maintenance: one codebase means one update for everyone, instead of patching every instance separately.

That last point is the quiet win. Anyone who has run a fleet of per-customer deployments knows the pain of a security fix that has to be rolled out N times, each with its own quirks.

## Three ways to store tenant data

The core of the talk is the data layer, with three patterns:

- **Shared database, shared tables**: every row carries a tenant ID. The most cost-effective, and the one where a missing `WHERE tenant_id = ?` becomes an incident.
- **Shared database, separate tables or schemas**: one database, one schema per tenant.
- **Separate databases**: full isolation and maximum customisation, at higher infrastructure and maintenance cost.

He doesn't declare a winner, which is right; the choice depends on how much isolation your customers and regulators demand and what you can afford to operate.

## Security at every layer

On security Shinu describes a zero-trust model that verifies every request at each layer, JSON Web Tokens for stateless authentication, and authorisation that combines role-based and attribute-based rules so permissions can depend on context. Data privacy controls add classification and geographic controls for regional compliance. Cross-tenant measures include network segmentation, real-time threat detection and resource limits.

## Noisy neighbours and other residents

Performance gets its own section: autoscaling on real-time demand, caching with a separate cache per tenant, load balancing that considers capacity, response time and tenant priority, and handling peak periods with automated scaling and request prioritisation.

The challenges slide is the most honest part. Preventing data leaks across tenant boundaries, implementing row-level security and respecting data residency rules. The noisy-neighbour problem, where one high-usage tenant degrades everyone else, which needs fair scheduling and tenant-specific SLAs. And customisation, where supporting per-tenant configuration without forking the codebase means managing schema variations, custom workflows and feature toggles carefully.

He closes with trends he sees coming: ML-driven resource prediction, serverless multi-tenancy, edge deployment for lower latency, and security frameworks that pair zero trust with AI threat detection and prepare for post-quantum encryption. Treat the figures on that slide as forward-looking industry claims rather than results from his own systems.

## Who should watch

Engineers designing a new SaaS product, and teams deciding whether their shared-table schema can survive the next enterprise customer's security questionnaire. Seasoned SaaS architects will know most of the material; it's a well-organised map rather than a new route.

Title: Rebuilding a desktop-only loan application for phones
Description: Ravi Chandra Chinta of Temple View Capital at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on moving a desktop-only loan application to a mobile-first Salesforce portal.
Body:
If 40% of your borrowers can't finish a loan application on their phone, the problem isn't the borrowers. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Ravi Chandra Chinta, Principal Salesforce Developer and Architect at Temple View Capital, told the story of replacing a desktop-only loan application with a responsive borrower portal on Salesforce Experience Cloud, and the numbers the lender tracked before and after.

It's a product case study more than an architecture talk: what was broken, which features fixed it, and how the team kept measuring. Useful if you build customer-facing portals in a regulated industry, where every abandoned form is a lost customer.

## The desktop-only tax

Ravi opens with the before picture. The legacy system only worked on desktop, and 40% of borrowers couldn't complete applications on mobile. Timeouts and compatibility issues drove a 65% increase in support tickets and added two and a half hours to completing an application. And 58% of users abandoned midway, often in the middle of complex forms.

Anyone who has tried to upload a bank statement through a desktop form on a phone will recognise every one of those numbers.

## One portal, three screen sizes

The fix was a fully responsive portal for iOS and Android phones, tablets and desktop, each with a role. Phones got a touch-optimised interface for applying on the go. Tablets suited reviewing and filling out applications. Desktop kept the advanced tools for detailed reviews and document management. Built on Experience Cloud and the Lightning platform, it was one codebase serving all three.

Four features did most of the work: real-time document uploads with automatic validation so incomplete submissions get caught early, e-signature integration (which Ravi credits with cutting closing time by 80%), personalised dashboards showing loan status and outstanding tasks, and in-app messaging with loan officers to replace email and phone tag.

## What changed, by the numbers

Ravi reports a 30% gain in processing speed for the underwriting team, application time for borrowers dropping from 25 to 15 minutes, 95% fewer system errors through better error handling and automated testing, and a 60% increase in mobile completion rates. Support calls about technical issues fell 40%, freeing the support team for harder cases, and customer satisfaction rose 35%. Going paperless removed over 100,000 pages a year.

A couple of figures shift between slides (one gives the old application time as 45 minutes, another as 25), so read them as the direction of travel rather than audit-grade benchmarks. The direction is unambiguous.

## Ask, iterate, test on real devices

The lessons section is the most portable. Surveys and interviews showed 78% of users ranked mobile access as their priority, which settled arguments about scope. The team shipped five major UI revisions based on borrower feedback, and tested across many devices with thousands of users before calling it done. After launch they used Einstein Analytics in Salesforce to track completion patterns and navigation, find drop-off points (cutting abandonment by 45%) and watch load times. The mobile-first cycle (design for phones first, test across devices, optimise from real usage data) reflects that 76% of their borrowers arrive on mobile.

## Who should watch

Salesforce developers and architects building Experience Cloud portals, and product teams in lending or insurance whose funnels leak on mobile. If you're after cloud-native infrastructure detail, this isn't that talk; it's about the user journey and how to measure it.

Title: Where Spark bills hide on Databricks and AWS EMR
Description: Comcast's Seshendranath Balla Venkata at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on cutting Databricks and AWS EMR costs via EBS, autoscaling, instance choice and shuffles.
Body:
The expensive line on a Spark bill is often not the compute you asked for but the disks, config calls and idle clusters you didn't notice. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Seshendranath Balla Venkata, Senior Manager of Data Engineering at Comcast, shared how his team saved millions in operating costs on Databricks and AWS EMR, and most of the levers are settings you can check this afternoon.

## Check the disks you're already paying for

His first Databricks lever is EBS. When Spark spills or shuffles to disk, it uses the node's local storage, or EBS if there isn't any. Many instance types already ship with plenty of local disk; his example is the i3.4xlarge, with 3.6 TB of local storage. Teams still provision EBS volumes on top and pay storage, IO, snapshot and transfer costs for disks the job doesn't need. Each job's share looks small; across a large fleet it isn't. He puts the possible savings on that line at 50 to 80%.

## Autoscaling is not free

The second lever is counterintuitive for anyone raised to turn autoscaling on by default. Every upscale and downscale on Databricks calls out to AWS to change resources, and those calls cost money, repeatedly. If you know a job's history and its data volume is predictable, Seshendranath's advice is to keep the cluster static and simple, and save autoscaling for workloads that genuinely fluctuate. He cites savings of up to 28% from getting this right.

Instance choice comes next. M-family versus I-family nodes (M5.4xlarge versus i3.4xlarge in his example) have very different storage and cost profiles, and picking one because a template said so leaves money on the table. Then spot versus on-demand by SLA: high-SLA jobs on demand, lower-SLA jobs that can safely restart on spot, where an occasional reclaim costs less than the discount saves.

## Spark tuning is cost tuning

The engineering section will feel familiar to anyone who has stared at the Spark UI. Keep shuffle and disk IO minimal. Set shuffle partitions in proportion to your cores so aggregations, joins and `reduceByKey` spread across the cluster. Cache only where it stops Spark recomputing an expensive part of the DAG, not everywhere. And deal with keys that pile all the data onto one node: split the problem keys out, or salt them so the work distributes. Every one of these shortens runtime, and on a pay-per-minute cluster, runtime is the bill.

He adds lifecycle policies for datasets and alerts on job cost thresholds, so a job that suddenly runs long gets investigated instead of quietly renewed every night.

## Three flavours of EMR

On the AWS side, he compares EMR on EC2 (most control, most cluster management toil), EMR on EKS (complex to set up but scales well once running) and EMR Serverless (least control, fully automated scaling, pay for what you use). His team migrated workloads toward EMR Serverless because that's where they saw the biggest savings, and he recommends trying it, especially combined with Graviton instances, which he credits with about 20% lower cost.

The rest of the EMR list mirrors Databricks: right-size clusters to workload patterns, be stingy with autoscaling, tune Spark executors and parallelism, vacuum ACID table formats so versions don't pile up in S3, set retention on S3 objects, and automate cluster shutdowns. That last one sounds obvious until you find a cluster that has been up for weeks with nothing running on it. He has, which is why it's on the list.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and platform owners responsible for Spark spend, and FinOps folks who need to know which questions to ask a data team. It's a practitioner's checklist, not a vendor pitch, and it applies whether you run Databricks, EMR or both.

- [Sruthi Erra Hareram on Databricks analytics reliability](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Sruthi_Erra_Hareram_databricks_analytics_reliability), keeping the same platform dependable.
- [Pradeep Gaddamidi on cloud cost monitoring](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Pradeep_Gaddamidi_cloud_cost_monitoring), the alerting half of his advice.
