Title: Four jobs an LLM can do in an enterprise front end
Description: Poornakumar Rasiraju of Highspot at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on conversational UIs, semantic search, generated content and the latency, cost and security work behind them.
Body:
The interesting LLM work in enterprise apps is rarely the model; it's what the user sees and how fast it shows up. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Poornakumar Rasiraju, Senior Software Engineer at Highspot, gave a compact overview of where LLMs fit in front-end applications, from chat to search to generated content, and of the latency, cost, security and scaling work you sign up for when you put them there.

It's a short, high-level talk: a map of the territory rather than code. Useful as a checklist before a design review.

## From static screens to adaptive ones

Rasiraju's starting point is that interfaces are moving from static, rule-based screens to systems that respond to what the user means. He groups the LLM capabilities into four jobs:

- **Conversational AI.** Chatbots and assistants that let users ask in natural language instead of navigating rigid menus, handling enterprise workflows such as IT service requests, HR processes and customer inquiries.
- **Smart search.** Semantic search that understands meaning rather than keywords, intent recognition to sharpen results, and discovery across structured and unstructured enterprise data.
- **Generated content.** Summaries, reports and insights produced on demand, plus personalised recommendations, notifications and feeds.
- **Developer productivity.** Code completion, bug detection and generated documentation for the team building the app.

Search is the one he spends most time on, and it's the right call: it's where users feel the difference between a keyword match and an answer.

## The engineering bill

The second half lists what makes these features hold up in production. Latency, cost and real-time responsiveness come first; his remedies are efficient API request handling, on-demand inference so you don't compute what nobody asked for, caching and load balancing. Nothing kills an AI feature faster than a spinner.

Security and compliance follow: protect user interactions with the model, put access controls in place so generated insights reach only the right users, and keep governance transparent and accountable. For scale, he points to dynamic scaling, handling bursts when thousands of users hit the system at once, and hybrid setups that pair cloud models with edge inference to cut latency.

On cost, he cited reductions available from strategic deployment, around 30% overall, with up to 50% better API efficiency from trimming unnecessary calls and 40% resource savings from right-sized models and request batching. Treat these as his ballpark figures rather than measured results from a named system.

## What's next for AI front ends

His trend list: multimodal input mixing text, voice and images; adaptive interfaces that change with user behaviour; predictive UI that anticipates the next action; and federated approaches that keep data private while still personalising. A brief case study describes an enterprise software company that hit performance bottlenecks, security concerns and adoption problems, and addressed them by optimising models, handling API calls efficiently and securing data.

The best practices he closes with are the ones teams skip under deadline pressure: secure the data, optimise the API path, keep humans in the loop for critical decisions, and monitor AI interactions so accuracy improves over time.

## Who should watch

Title: Fine-tune for stable knowledge, retrieve for knowledge that moves
Description: Muddassar Sharif, CTO of Virtuans.ai, at Conf42 LLMs 2025 weighs prompting, RAG, fine-tuning and training from scratch on cost, data and accuracy.
Body:
Every LLM project hits the same fork: put your private data into the model's weights, or fetch it at query time. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Muddassar Sharif, co-founder and CTO of Virtuans.ai, gave a business-first answer: fine-tune when the knowledge is stable, voluminous and needs to be precise; use retrieval when it changes often or needs citations; and expect plenty of real systems to need both.

## Two questions before any technique

Sharif starts where stakeholders should. Can an off-the-shelf model from OpenAI or Anthropic do the job? Those are fast, affordable and need no tuning. If not, does the use case need private data the public models have never seen? Only then do you choose how to bring that data in.

## Four ways to add knowledge

He lays out a ladder by data size and need:

- **Prompt engineering.** A small, fixed amount of context goes into the system prompt. Done.
- **RAG.** Data that changes a lot is retrieved at query time and added to the context. His example is a trading agent reacting to news: fine-tuning on yesterday's headlines makes no sense when you need the latest ones in seconds.
- **Fine-tuning.** A decent amount of domain data, adapted into the model so it answers better in that niche, say health tech.
- **Training from scratch, or full retraining.** Terabytes of data, results that partial tuning can't reach, or a need to keep the model fully private.

He also explains why tuning changes behaviour: the latest training takes precedence, so a model tuned hard on medical data learns that domain and partly unlearns other things. That's a useful warning for anyone who expects tuning to be purely additive.

His preferred route is parameter-efficient fine-tuning, which he describes as updating a few layers toward the end of the model while the rest keeps its general language skills. It's cheaper, faster and needs far less hardware than updating every weight.

## The bill nobody puts on the slide

The compute is often the smallest cost. Hosted fine-tuning from providers like OpenAI needs no infrastructure, though tuned models cost more per token. The big costs are data collection and preparation, which take people and engineering time; retuning on a schedule as data changes every few months; the delay before anything ships; and maintaining a custom model. A fine-tuned model is a pet, not cattle.

On the benefit side, Sharif cited figures as his own estimates: roughly 15 to 30% better accuracy in a specialised domain, around 50 to 60% fewer hallucinations, and an overall cost premium of about 15 to 20% for a tuned model. His ROI rule is simple: if the gain beats the premium, tune. He adds a strategic argument too: a model tuned on proprietary data is IP, an asset you could license, and with an open-source base your sensitive data stays inside your systems, which matters in healthcare and government.

## How the two compare

His side-by-side: fine-tuning has a high upfront cost and periodic retraining; RAG is cheaper to start, stays current, can cite sources, but adds tokens and latency on every call and needs a vector database. Choose fine-tuning for stable knowledge, high query volume, large domain knowledge and fast, precise answers. Choose RAG for fast-changing data, citations, small datasets or no upfront budget.

The closing example shows the hybrid: tune a support model on past resolved tickets to learn how to resolve issues, and retrieve the live refund policy and stock data at query time.

## Who should watch

Engineering leads and founders who have to justify an approach to someone holding a budget. It's conceptual rather than hands-on, and the numbers are rules of thumb, but the decision framework is clear.

Title: Observability answers why, monitoring only says something's wrong
Description: Software engineer Muhammad Ahmad Saeed at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on building logs, metrics and traces into cloud-native apps in five steps.
Body:
Monitoring tells you the CPU is high; observability tells you why. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, software engineer Muhammad Ahmad Saeed gave a clear introduction to building observability into cloud-native applications: the three pillars, a five-step rollout, the tools for each step, and a worked example of chasing a periodic slowdown to its real cause.

This is a first talk on the subject, and says so by starting from definitions. If your team is new to distributed systems or still arguing about whether dashboards count as observability, it is a good one to watch together.

## Ephemeral infrastructure eats your evidence

Muhammad's case for observability in cloud-native systems rests on three properties. They're distributed, so microservices talk over a network that adds latency and failure points. They're dynamic, with Kubernetes spinning resources up and down as demand changes. And they're ephemeral: by the time you start investigating, the instance that misbehaved may no longer exist. Without telemetry collected while it was alive, you're flying blind.

## The wrong suspect problem

His best example is about misdiagnosis. An endpoint's response time climbs. Without traces, the team concludes the endpoint is slow and starts optimising its code. In reality the database got slower at that moment, and the endpoint was just waiting. Without metrics and traces, he argues, performance work becomes a guessing game, and you end up fixing the innocent service.

The other costs of missing observability follow from that: longer mean time to resolution, and reliability that gets harder to reason about as the number of services grows.

## Five steps, in order

The rollout he proposes is sequential, and the order matters:

1. **Instrument** the code for metrics, logs and traces, using libraries built for your language.
2. **Centralize** collection and storage: Prometheus for metrics, Elasticsearch or Loki for logs, Jaeger or Zipkin for traces.
3. **Visualize and alert**, typically with Grafana.
4. **Contextualize** by connecting metrics, logs and traces so events correlate across the system.
5. **Automate** the pipeline so nobody has to assemble data by hand when something breaks.

For teams that don't want to wire it all together, he surveys platforms: Datadog, New Relic, and Honeycomb, which he singles out for high-cardinality, event-level analysis (one login, one API call, one query).

## Practices worth pinning to the wall

Instrument early and often, because retrofitting is painful once things scale. Pick metrics that matter to the business and filter out the rest. Structure your logs with a consistent format (timestamp, system name, application ID) and use the same format across services, since they all end up in one place. Correlate the three signals. Automate the pipeline so the data is already on the dashboard when you open it. And manage cost with retention policies and tiered storage, because logging millions of events an hour is not free.

## The case study: three pillars, one slow query

The closing scenario ties it together. An e-commerce application slows down periodically. Logs show rising error rates in one microservice, metrics show high CPU on a node, and traces pinpoint a slow database query. Fix the query, scale the service, and latency drops. Each pillar alone would have given a partial story; together they name the culprit.

## Who should watch

Developers and new SREs who want the vocabulary and a sensible order of operations. Experienced observability folks will find it familiar, but it's a handy talk to send to the team before you introduce tracing.

Title: Your Dockerfile's line order decides how often you rebuild
Description: Backend engineer Eti Ijeoma at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on Docker layer caching, instruction order, BuildKit cache mounts and registry caches.
Body:
A one-line code change shouldn't reinstall every dependency you own, yet plenty of Dockerfiles make sure it does. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Eti Ijeoma, a backend engineer at Manufactured, explained how Docker's layer cache actually decides what to rebuild, which habits quietly break it, and the BuildKit features that make CI builds stop starting from zero.

It's a practical, beginner-friendly talk. If you already write multi-stage builds with cache mounts in your sleep, skim it; if your CI pipeline spends minutes on `pip install` for every commit, watch it.

## How a build actually runs

Eti walks through the mechanics first. Docker loads the build context (every file in the directory you build from), parses the Dockerfile, and runs each instruction in turn. Each instruction produces a new immutable layer. On the next build, Docker reuses any layer whose inputs haven't changed, and that reuse is the whole game.

The catch is that the cache is a chain. Once one layer is invalidated, every layer after it is rebuilt too. So the question for every line is: how often does its input change, and what sits below it?

## Copy the requirements before the code

Her example is a small Python image. Start from the base image, copy only `requirements.txt`, run `pip install`, and only then copy the rest of the application. Because the dependency file rarely changes, the install layer stays cached; editing your code invalidates only the final copy step.

Flip the order, copying everything first, and every code change busts the cache for the dependency install too. Same files, same commands, very different build times. Her rule of thumb: stable instructions first, frequently changing ones last.

## The quiet cache breakers

Eti lists the usual suspects. Instructions in the wrong order. Frequent dependency churn, which forces a full reinstall each time. A broad `COPY` early in the file, where any change in the directory breaks the cache. Copying more than you need instead of being explicit about which files go in. And big images, which take longer to build and to ship.

Her fixes are the standard toolkit, and worth hearing in one place: multi-stage builds so the final image keeps only what it needs, a `.dockerignore` to shrink the build context, prefer `COPY` over `ADD` unless you need archive extraction, and use build arguments (`ARG`) rather than environment variables for build-time values, since `ARG` only exists during the build and keeps the image cleaner.

## Cache that outlives the layer

The advanced section is the useful bit for CI. With BuildKit, a `RUN --mount=type=cache` lets package managers keep their download caches between builds without baking them into a layer, so even a busted layer reinstalls faster. And `docker buildx` can export the build cache to a registry, so a fresh CI runner pulls the cache instead of rebuilding everything from scratch. Ephemeral runners are exactly where layer caching usually goes to die, so this is the trick that pays off most.

## Measure before you celebrate

Finally, she shows how to check whether any of it worked: `--progress=plain` for detailed output that shows which layers were reused, `docker history` to inspect layers and their sizes, and plain `time docker build` to compare runs. If you don't measure, you're just reordering lines for luck.

## Who should watch

Developers who own their Dockerfiles, and platform engineers who want a short talk to send to teams with slow pipelines. It's a fundamentals talk with concrete Dockerfile patterns, not a BuildKit internals session.

- [Adam Gordon Bell on compiling containers](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Adam_Gordon_Bell_compiling_containers), a look at how BuildKit turns a Dockerfile into an image.
- [Haseeb Majid on using Nix for reproducible builds](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Haseeb_Majid_using_nix_reproducible), a different answer to "why did that rebuild".
- [Eugene Khabarov on building enough with Bazel](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Eugene_Khabarov_build_enough_bazel), for when caching has to work across a whole monorepo.

Title: Cloud-native observability, the short version, and why OpenTelemetry won
Description: Sai Prakash Narasingu of ServiceNow at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 gives a primer on metrics, logs and traces, the open-source stack, and OpenTelemetry.
Body:
Before OpenTelemetry, picking an observability vendor meant picking their agent, their schema and their backend, and leaving was a migration project. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Sai Prakash Narasingu, Senior Staff Engineer for Cloud Observability at ServiceNow, gives a compact primer on cloud-native observability: the three signals, the open-source tools most teams end up with, and why an open standard changed the economics of switching.

The talk is listed as "Resilience: Harnessing Chaos Engineering to Build Robust Systems". The session as recorded is about cloud-native observability rather than chaos engineering, and it works as a first map of the field.

## Three signals, one purpose

Sai starts from the textbook definition, observability as the ability to measure a system's internal state from its outputs, and makes it concrete. Metrics tell you how a system is performing. Logs are the running record of what it's doing. Traces show the flow of a request through the topology: where it came in and where it went.

Why it matters more in cloud-native systems is the usual microservices story told well. Services accumulate APIs and dependencies, and once a request crosses a dozen of them, finding the slow one without traces is guesswork. He ties observability to four outcomes: real-time monitoring, faster issue resolution, better autoscaling decisions (scale up under sustained load, ramp down when utilisation drops), and shorter mean time to identify and resolve problems.

## The open-source stack most teams converge on

The tools section is a quick tour of the default toolkit:

- **Prometheus** scrapes and stores metrics and handles monitoring on top of them.
- **Grafana** visualises metrics from backends such as Prometheus or InfluxDB, with a large plugin ecosystem and alerting on thresholds.
- **OpenTelemetry** standardises how telemetry is collected and how it's reported to a backend, including trace context across tiers.
- **Jaeger** is a common tracing backend for OpenTelemetry data, stitching spans from many services into an end-to-end picture with dependencies.
- **Elastic Stack** covers log aggregation and analytics.

The OpenTelemetry part is the sharpest bit of the talk. He describes the pre-standard world where every vendor shipped its own API and agent with a vendor-specific schema, and once an organisation adopted one, "They're pretty much married to that vendor". A shared collection and reporting standard is what makes vendor portability possible.

## Real-world use and the bill that follows

He cites three public examples: Netflix using OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing across its microservices, Uber using Jaeger for end-to-end transaction monitoring, and Airbnb using Prometheus and Grafana for real-time performance monitoring.

The challenges are honest ones. Telemetry volume grows every year, and cost grows with it. And while collection is now standardised, visualisation isn't: each cloud presents data and metrics its own way. His best practices are correspondingly simple: use the open standard, build Grafana dashboards, automate anomaly detection on metric trends, and keep the whole setup friendly to CI/CD and frequent releases.

## What comes next

He closes with three trends: AI-driven anomaly detection, which most observability vendors are now focused on; wider use of eBPF for deeper observability; and tighter integration between observability and security tooling, an area where visibility is still restricted.

## Who should watch

Developers and new platform or SRE hires who need the vocabulary and the open-source toolkit of observability in one sitting. Experienced observability engineers won't find new techniques here, and anyone looking for chaos engineering experiments should pick another session.

Title: Translating podcasts end to end with Whisper, GPT-4o and TTS
Description: Rustam Musin at Conf42 LLMs 2025 builds a Kotlin pipeline that turns English podcasts into Russian ones, and is candid about what still sounds off.
Body:
Turning an English podcast into a Russian one takes three OpenAI models, a pile of glue code and some patience with MP3 files. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, software engineer Rustam Musin walked through a Kotlin pipeline that downloads episodes, transcribes them with Whisper, cleans and translates the text with GPT-4o, voices it with the TTS model and publishes a new RSS feed, and he was refreshingly open about the parts that aren't done.

## The pipeline, one step at a time

The architecture is a straight line of independent stages, which is what makes it easy to fix one part without touching the rest:

1. **Download.** Podcast4j fetches episode metadata and MP3 files from podcastindex.org.
2. **Transcribe.** The MP3 goes to the Whisper API, which returns text.
3. **Clean up.** GPT-4o fixes grammar and punctuation, and finds where the podcast actually starts.
4. **Translate.** A second GPT-4o call translates to Russian, asked to keep tone and style close to the original.
5. **Speak.** The TTS model voices the Russian text.
6. **Assemble and publish.** Audio chunks are merged and an RSS feed, built with the Java XML APIs, tells podcast platforms a new episode exists, with titles and descriptions translated too.

The supporting cast is Kotlin, Ktor for HTTP and Jackson for JSON.

## The limits shape the design

Two API limits drive most of the engineering. Whisper only accepts files under 25 MB, so long episodes get split and transcribed in pieces. The TTS model takes about 4,000 characters at a time, so the translated text is chunked, voiced piece by piece and merged. Most podcasts they tried fit under the Whisper limit; the long ones are why the chunking exists.

Merging is where it gets messy. Right now the MP3 files are simply concatenated byte by byte. Played start to finish, that works. Jump into the middle and some players get confused, because each file carries its own metadata, including the track length. Different bitrates and volume levels between chunks are also an issue. The plan is FFmpeg to merge metadata properly and level the audio. Every engineer has shipped a "works if you don't seek" feature at least once.

## Prompts for messy, mixed-language speech

The prompt work is the most transferable part. The clean-up prompt tells GPT-4o it's looking at a podcast transcript, to fix grammar and punctuation, translate anything not in English into English, find where the podcast starts and cut unrelated content, and output only the text. Translating everything to English first, then from English to Russian, worked better than translating a mix directly.

His example is a speaker mixing "AI is cool" with the Russian word for cool, which Whisper renders in English letters; the two-step approach produces a natural Russian sentence that keeps the casual tone. Ads, intros and outros are translated as part of the episode for now.

## What still needs work

Musin plays a before-and-after sample and doesn't hide the flaw: the Russian voice carries a slight American accent. The translation is close and understandable, but it doesn't yet sound native. Quality checking is manual review today, which won't scale; the plan is automated scoring such as BLEU plus native-speaker evaluation. Next steps include automated episode splitting, FFmpeg merging and custom-trained TTS voices.

## Who should watch

Anyone building a multi-model media pipeline, especially speech in and speech out, who wants a realistic picture of the seams. The code snippets are simple; the value is in the limits and the prompt design.

Title: Five patterns for digital twins that survive the factory floor
Description: Vinoth Manamala of TIBCO Software at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on five patterns that keep AI digital twins useful in real factories.
Body:
Most digital twins die the same way: the model is lovely, and then the factory happens. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Vinoth Manamala, Senior Data Scientist at TIBCO Software, walked through five patterns that kept AI-powered twins working in semiconductor and process plants, and the operational plumbing (data retention, edge inference, model lifecycle) that keeps them alive after the demo.

## Why the twin breaks before the factory does

Vinoth's list of failure modes is refreshingly unglamorous. Twins can't handle the messy reality of a production line. They don't adapt when conditions change. They treat every sensor reading as truth. They try to model everything at once. And they fall over when the plant network does, which in a factory is often. Each of these shows up as stopped production or a quality drop, so the cost is measured in scrap, not in dashboards.

## Track events, compute state

The first pattern is an event-first architecture: instead of storing fixed states, record every event and derive the state when you need it. Anyone who has worked with event sourcing will recognise the trade. In a chip fab the payoff was wafer rework. Wafers that repeat process steps had confused an earlier twin, which simply lost track of them. With the full event history, problems trace back to their source instead of to a guess.

## Models that know what time it is

Pattern two is AI that understands time. Different processes care about different windows, so the system uses neural networks that learn which time periods matter for each process. Vinoth credits this with a 27% improvement in prediction accuracy and warnings that arrive hours or days earlier, early enough for operators to act before material becomes scrap.

Pattern three is about when to learn. The models adjust their learning rate to how stable production is, so they pick up subtle drift in calm periods without overreacting when things get turbulent. He reports 62% fewer false alarms and models that stayed accurate 3.4 times longer without manual retraining.

## Be honest about dirty sensors

The fourth pattern is the one most teams skip. Factory sensors get dirty, drift out of calibration and fail. Vinoth's twin attaches a confidence level to every prediction, tells operators when the input data looks suspicious, and falls back to physics-based rules when it can't trust the numbers. That alone cut false alarms by 45% while still catching real problems.

Pattern five tracks processes at several timescales at once. The example is a good one: morning temperature swings slowly degrading a catalyst over weeks, invisible to any single window. The system can tie a brief event from weeks ago to a quality problem happening now.

## The fab that stopped losing wafers

In the semiconductor case study the team combined the event-based system with computer vision for defect detection and a process relationship map across more than 1,200 parameters. The results Vinoth shared: 94% accuracy in predicting needed rework, a 12% yield improvement and $4.2 million in annual savings. Engineers could also ask what-if questions, such as the effect of a temperature change, before touching the line.

## The boring parts that keep it running

The second half is practical advice. Keep high-frequency data for 24 hours and hourly summaries for months, but detect and preserve anomalies before compressing the normal stretches; he reports 78% less storage for 95% of the analytical value. Push lightweight models to the edge so equipment keeps working through network outages and syncs back later (99.97% uptime in a chemical plant). Run new models in shadow mode before they take control. And constrain the AI with physics: mass and energy don't appear from nowhere, and enforcing that cut impossible predictions by 94%.

His closing advice is to measure success by business impact rather than technical metrics, and to start with one focused problem before expanding.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and platform engineers building ML for industrial or IoT settings, and anyone whose models meet sensors they don't control. It's a pattern overview with case-study numbers rather than a code walkthrough, so bring your own implementation.

Title: One monitoring view for AWS, Azure, GCP and the private cloud
Description: SRE Arun Pandiyan Perumal at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on a reference architecture for unified multi-cloud monitoring and the tools to build it.
Body:
Every cloud provider ships its own monitoring, which is great until you run on three of them and your incident timeline lives in three tabs. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Arun Pandiyan Perumal, a site reliability engineer, laid out what a unified multi-cloud monitoring system needs: a layered reference architecture, a sober comparison of open source and SaaS tooling, and the practices that stop it turning into a fourth silo.

## Multi-cloud breaks monitoring in four places

Arun starts with the operational bill that arrives with multi-cloud. Data silos, because each provider's logging and metrics stack only sees itself. Latency and performance bottlenecks when you gather real-time data from globally dispersed networks. Compliance and security gaps, since every provider has different controls and defaults, so enforcing one policy everywhere is harder than it sounds. And cost: log and metric volume grows every day, and storing and analysing it gets expensive.

The case for unifying is mostly about mean time to resolve. When logs, metrics and events sit in one place, the on-call engineer spends the incident fixing things instead of correlating timestamps across consoles.

## A reference architecture in six layers

The most reusable part of the talk is the sample architecture:

- **Data collection** from AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and private clouds.
- **Monitoring agents** deployed in each environment, agent-based or agentless.
- **Aggregation**, split into log collectors, metrics aggregators that normalise performance data, and event stream processors for real-time streams.
- **Centralized monitoring and analytics**, which correlates the signal types and looks for anomalies and patterns.
- **Observability and alerting**, with dashboards and alerts on anomalies, breaches and failures.
- **Incident management**, where alerts feed the ITSM and ticketing tools.

Nothing exotic, and that's the point: each layer has one job, so you can swap a tool without redesigning the rest. He pairs it with five core components (collection, processing and correlation, visualization, automated remediation, and security monitoring), where the remediation layer runs playbooks or self-healing when thresholds trip.

## Open source vs SaaS, without the sales pitch

Arun compares Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger and OpenTelemetry with SaaS platforms such as Datadog, New Relic, Grafana Cloud, Dynatrace and Splunk. Open source means manual setup and maintenance and scaling that needs capacity planning, but no licence; the cost moves into infrastructure, storage and people. SaaS deploys quickly and scales elastically, with the vendor doing capacity planning, but the subscription grows with ingestion and storage. Pick your poison knowingly.

## Practices that keep it unified

His best practices read like a checklist for a design review: define a centralized observability strategy first; collect telemetry across infrastructure, application and network layers; normalise formats so metrics, logs and traces from different clouds can be correlated; prefer a vendor-agnostic platform to avoid lock-in; and embed observability into CI/CD so critical deployments are watched as they ship.

He closes on trends: AI-driven anomaly detection, observability for serverless and edge workloads, eBPF for kernel-level visibility on Linux, shift-left observability for DevOps and SRE teams, and security folded into the observability pipeline.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams that inherited a second or third cloud through an acquisition or a "best tool for the job" decision, and architects sketching a monitoring platform for the first time. It's an architecture overview, not a tool demo, so it pairs well with something hands-on.

Title: People are the glue between apps, and agents want that job
Description: Manish Ballal, GenAI GTM lead at AWS, at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on agentic automation for invoices and claims, large action models, and why orchestration is the hard part.
Body:
In most large enterprises, the integration layer between dozens of applications that don't talk to each other is a person copying data from one screen to another. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Manish Ballal, Global GTM Lead for Generative AI at AWS, argued that agentic automation, combining LLMs, action-taking models and existing automation under one orchestration layer, is the realistic way to take that work off people. He framed the talk as his personal view, not his employer's.

## The problem is white-collar plumbing

Ballal is specific about scope. He is not talking about factories but about processes like invoice handling, sales order processing, and claims in healthcare and insurance. Enterprises run productivity apps, ERPs, off-the-shelf and custom software, and the glue is staff stuck in repetitive work with no time to improve the process or talk to customers. His example: banks where hundreds of people do nothing but anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer checks.

The existing tools each cover a slice. RPA handles simple rule-based flows but is fragile with unstructured data and needs real infrastructure. API integration stalls on legacy apps that expose no APIs. Document processing, low-code platforms, data integration and classic ML each solve a piece.

## Brain and brawn

His mental model is easy to remember. An agent is an LLM as the brain, an orchestration layer taking input from a web app, chat or mobile, and tools to act with: portals, applications, knowledge bases, SaaS platforms, even user interaction. Then come large action models, the brawn, trained to act through interfaces such as browsers; he cites Anthropic's computer use and OpenAI's Operator.

The catch he points out: an action model can book you an Italian dinner in New York and Broadway tickets in a handful of steps, maybe asking a follow-up question. Ask it to run a 70- or 80-step business process and it struggles. A dinner booking that goes wrong is an anecdote; a claims process that goes wrong is an audit.

## Orchestration is the secret sauce

So the answer is not one more model but orchestration: combining action models, LLMs, document processing, API integration and low-code tools into one managed process. The business user, he stresses, does not care which technology runs. They care about the outcome, transparency into where a work item is, and the right metrics.

To size the prize he cites McKinsey's estimate of $2.6 to $4.4 trillion in value from generative AI, and US healthcare spending of about $4 trillion, of which he puts around $1 trillion down to inefficient processes.

## The four non-negotiables

His closing challenges for developers are the useful checklist:

- **Orchestration** of many services into a transparent, measurable process.
- **Governance and guardrails.** Would you accept 90% accuracy on the process that computes your monthly paycheck? Deterministic processes need auditability and responsible AI built in.
- **Human in the loop** for edge cases, because LLMs hallucinate.
- **Change management.** Archaic governance and security policies won't fit, and organisations need to get used to working alongside digital employees.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leads being asked to "add agents" to back-office operations, and anyone who needs a clear vocabulary for the business side. It's a strategy talk with no code; it frames the problem rather than showing an implementation.

Title: Where AI fits in clinical trial statistical programming
Description: Vamsi Upputuri of Gilead Sciences at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on AI and ML across clinical trials, from recruitment to CDISC mapping and submissions.
Body:
Clinical trials are a data pipeline with a regulator at the end of it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Vamsi Upputuri, Senior Statistical Programmer at Gilead Sciences, walked through where AI and machine learning now sit in that pipeline, from finding eligible patients to mapping data onto regulatory standards and assembling submissions.

It is a domain talk rather than an infrastructure one, and a fast one: a tour of use cases, each paired with an improvement figure. For engineers outside life sciences, it is a rare look at what statistical programming in drug development actually involves.

## Recruitment and safety

Patient recruitment is one of the hardest parts of any trial. Vamsi describes predictive analytics and matching algorithms that read electronic health records and genetic data to find candidates who meet the protocol, citing a 37% reduction in screening failures and faster enrolment, with a cardiovascular trial as the example.

Safety is the second theme. Instead of manual review against fixed thresholds, models scan patient records, trial data and real-world evidence for hidden patterns such as drug interactions linked to adverse events. His example is again cardiovascular: models flagging patients at risk of arrhythmia from subtle ECG changes, so clinicians can adjust treatment before complications arise.

## Data quality and monitoring

The middle of the talk is about the unglamorous work: ML-based extraction from structured and unstructured source documents, automated quality control that flags inconsistencies in incoming data streams, and real-time detection of protocol deviations. Risk-based monitoring decides which trial sites need a visit and which can be monitored remotely, which he links to a 25% cut in site monitoring cost.

## Standards and submissions

For a statistical programmer, the regulatory section is the core. Vamsi describes automation that applies CDISC standards consistently across study data, deep learning models for mapping data to those standards, automated validation checks, and NLP that reviews regulatory text and clinical documents for gaps before they go out. He ties this to faster validation and shorter submission timelines.

## Reading the numbers

Almost every slide carries a percentage: 45% shorter trial durations, 83% accuracy predicting adverse events, 94% accuracy on compliance checks. The talk presents these as industry results without naming the studies, and a few metrics are quoted with different values on different slides. Treat them as indicators of where the field is pushing, and check the primary literature before quoting any of them in a planning document.

His closing advice is more durable than the figures: a roadmap covering infrastructure, workflow training and phased deployment; close collaboration between clinical, IT and regulatory teams; and continuous validation of models for accuracy and bias. He points to federated learning, real-world evidence integration and automated trial design as what comes next.

## Who should watch

Engineers building data platforms for pharma or biotech, and data scientists moving into regulated work who want to know where the compliance pressure points are. If you need implementation detail, pair it with the platform talks below.

Title: Fraud scoring with reinforcement learning and Bayesian networks
Description: Surendra Lakkaraju of Amazon at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on dynamic e-commerce fraud risk scoring with RL, Bayesian networks and real-time pipelines.
Body:
Static fraud rules lose to attackers who change tactics every week. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Surendra Lakkaraju, Senior Software Development Engineer at Amazon, presented a framework for dynamic risk scoring of e-commerce transactions that combines reinforcement learning, Bayesian networks and a real-time processing architecture, with the explicit goal of catching more fraud without adding friction for honest shoppers.

The talk is a dense architecture overview, around twenty minutes, packed with throughput and accuracy figures. It describes the framework in general terms and does not tie it to a named Amazon product.

## Why static scoring breaks

Surendra sets the scene with the scale of the problem: roughly 5.7 trillion dollars in global e-commerce volume in 2024, fraud attempts at 1.8% of online revenue, a 307% surge in account takeover attacks, and 6.4 billion dollars lost to card-not-present fraud. Static rule-based scoring cannot keep up, and every extra check risks hurting the checkout experience customers expect.

## Four ideas in the framework

- **Multi-layer validation.** Each transaction passes through a chain of gates that mix rule-based checks with ML analysis.
- **Rich real-time signals.** Thousands of signals per transaction, spanning transaction patterns, user behaviour and merchant risk profiles.
- **Behavioural analysis.** Device fingerprinting and network analysis to spot VPN use and bot activity within milliseconds.
- **Continuous evolution.** Self-optimising models and dynamic thresholds that adapt to new tactics and learn from transaction outcomes.

## The machinery

The architecture has three layers: data ingestion with tight latency targets, an AI/ML processing engine with load balancing across a distributed node network, and dynamic threshold management that adjusts hundreds of thresholds every hour. On top sit a reinforcement learning component, whose reward function balances false positives, detection, customer satisfaction and network performance, and a Bayesian network that models probabilistic relationships between risk indicators.

Two engineering details are worth stealing. Class imbalance is brutal in fraud, where only a small fraction of transactions are fraudulent, so the system uses Borderline-SMOTE combined with adaptive synthetic sampling to rebalance training data. And model drift gets dedicated monitoring across sliding windows from one hour to 90 days, with 12 parallel A/B evaluation groups before new detectors ship. Materialised views refreshed roughly every 200 milliseconds keep the feature queries fast.

## Reading the results

The headline outcomes are strong: false positive rates down from 2.4% to 1.42%, and customer satisfaction scores up from 30% to 75%. Be aware that throughput and latency figures shift between slides, from 42,000 transactions per second in one place to about 2,000 concurrent transactions in another, so treat individual numbers as illustrative and focus on the design.

## Who should watch

Engineers building risk, trust and safety, or payments systems who want a reference architecture that goes beyond a single classifier. The resampling and drift-monitoring sections apply to any ML problem with rare positives.

Title: SAP S/4HANA Cloud explained, RISE versus GROW
Description: Sravan Kumar Nendrambaka of Nike at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 compares RISE and GROW with SAP, private versus public S/4HANA Cloud, and SAP's AI features.
Body:
If your company runs on SAP, the cloud question is less whether than which edition. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Sravan Kumar Nendrambaka, SAP S/4HANA Cloud Architect and SAP Lead Engineer at Nike, compared SAP's two cloud ERP offerings, RISE with SAP for large enterprises and GROW with SAP for mid-sized companies, and the public and private editions of S/4HANA Cloud behind them.

Sravan has more than 15 years in IT, with SAP implementations across healthcare, retail and oil and gas. The talk is an overview of SAP's own product line rather than a Nike case study, and much of it describes the offerings in SAP's terms.

## Two front doors to the same ERP

The comparison is the most useful part, laid out feature by feature:

- **Target.** RISE is for global enterprises with complex, multi-market needs. GROW is for agile mid-sized companies ready to expand quickly.
- **ERP.** RISE gives the full S/4HANA Cloud with flexible deployment. GROW uses S/4HANA public cloud with ready-to-run processes.
- **Implementation.** RISE is a strategic business transformation. GROW aims for a fast go-live on industry-tested templates.
- **Customisation.** RISE allows deep customisation for complex business models. GROW favours standardisation with essential options.

## The architecture underneath

RISE supports hybrid, public and private cloud deployment, keeps enterprises in control of their infrastructure, and leans on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) for custom extensions. GROW runs multi-tenant on shared infrastructure, with a library of more than 200 APIs for integrations. Both sit on SAP HANA's in-memory database.

The architectural advice that will outlive any product name is about customisation. Instead of modifying the core, which raises cost, hurts stability and complicates upgrades, SAP recommends side-by-side extensions on BTP. Anyone who has lived through an ERP upgrade with years of custom code in the core will recognise why.

## AI features and industry examples

On AI, Sravan covers intelligent automation of tasks like invoice matching and inventory management, predictive analytics for cash flow and maintenance, and SAP's conversational assistant, which he calls SAP Copilot. Industry examples span healthcare workflow and supply monitoring, retail personalisation and inventory, and oil and gas logistics.

Most of these sections come with improvement percentages, from cost savings to forecast accuracy. They are presented without sources, read like vendor positioning, and are best taken as SAP's claims rather than measured outcomes.

## Migration challenges

The closing section is practical: legacy data with inconsistent formats, handled with SAP Data Intelligence for validation and cleansing; customisation needs, handled with BTP extensions; and change management, handled with role-specific training and digital adoption tools.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering managers in SAP shops weighing a move to S/4HANA Cloud, and cloud engineers who suddenly need to understand what the ERP team is talking about. Engineers looking for integration code or performance data will not find it here.

Title: One feedback app, four Bedrock upgrades, and the chunking fix
Description: Sandeep Kumar P of AntStack at Conf42 LLMs 2025 grows an internal peer-feedback app from one prompt to RAG, an agent and Bedrock flows.
Body:
Ask engineers to rate their peers from one to ten and everyone gets a ten. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Sandeep Kumar P, Principal Solutions Architect at AntStack and an AWS Community Builder, used that very human problem to walk through four stages of adding AI to one internal app on Amazon Bedrock: a prompt, a knowledge base, an agent, and a multi-step flow.

It's a practical, console-level tour. If the words RAG, embeddings and agents feel overloaded, this is the talk that explains them with one running example.

## Stage one: let the model do the rating

AntStack had built a feedback app so project managers on different sprint schedules could collect peer feedback in one place. The data was centralised, but the scores were useless. So the team asked a model to read the written feedback and rate it on three categories (productivity, positive energy and reliability) from one to five.

They used the Bedrock chat playground to try the same prompt across models side by side, with latency and token counts shown so cost is visible early. Then came consistency, via plain prompt-engineering rules: give the model a role (an evaluator), describe the action with positive and negative cases (unrelated comments score minus one), define the variables, and fix a JSON output format. Bedrock's prompt builder let them test variants, and one demo makes the point well: changing a single line from lenient to strict visibly shifts the scores from the same model.

## Stage two: a knowledge base, and the chunking surprise

After about three months they had roughly 500 pieces of feedback, so they pointed a Bedrock knowledge base at an S3 bucket of it. Sandeep explains vectors, dimensions, indexes and embeddings with a fruit example, then walks the setup: default parser, Titan embeddings, OpenSearch Serverless via quick create, hybrid search.

The lesson worth the price of admission is chunking. With default chunking, asking for one person's feedback returned a summary of everyone's. Switching to no chunking, with one file per person so each file became a single chunk, and retrieving one source chunk per query fixed it. Your chunking strategy is a data model decision, not a default.

## Stage three: an agent as the bouncer

The chatbot let anyone ask about anyone. The fix was a Bedrock agent whose instructions extract the requester's email and whether the question is about themselves or someone else, then call an action group: a Lambda function that checks an admin list. Admins may query others (useful for mentors preparing a session); regular users get a polite refusal. With that guard in place, the bot went out to everyone so people could ask about their own feedback any time.

## Stage four: divide and conquer with flows

The ambitious version answers "how can I improve my career?" by combining feedback, skill sheets, current role and next-role expectations. Rather than one giant prompt, he built it as a Bedrock flow, a step-function-like map of prompts, Lambdas, conditions and knowledge base calls: identify intent, check the role, end early if unauthorised, classify the question, query the knowledge base, enrich with role and skills data, then summarise. Splitting it up also means a small, cheap model can do the classification step instead of a large one.

On cost, he notes that knowledge bases and agents carry no separate charge; you pay for tokens and the underlying resources such as the vector store and Lambdas. On effort, he said rebuilding the whole thing takes him under 30 minutes, and his first attempt with flows took under two hours.

## Who should watch

Developers on AWS who want to see the Bedrock building blocks in one coherent story, and anyone who needs a clear explanation of RAG for their team. It's an AWS-specific walkthrough; the chunking and authorisation lessons apply anywhere.

Title: KitOps packages models, data and code as one OCI artifact
Description: Shivay Lamba of Couchbase at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 demos KitOps ModelKits: models, datasets and code in one OCI artifact for existing registries.
Body:
A machine learning project is not one artifact. The weights sit in one place, the dataset in a data lake, the code in Git and the hyperparameters somewhere else. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Shivay Lamba, Senior Developer Experience Engineer at Couchbase and a community member of the open source KitOps project, showed how KitOps bundles all of it into a single OCI-compliant artifact called a ModelKit, so the registries and CI/CD tools you already use for containers can carry models too.

Note the scope: this is a talk about one open source project, with a live CLI demo. At the time of the talk, Shivay said KitOps was being donated to the CNCF and applying for sandbox status.

## The packaging gap

Shivay's starting point is that there is no standard for packaging and versioning everything you need to reproduce an AI/ML project. The result is that teams build a separate MLOps pipeline beside their DevOps pipeline, with manual handoffs between data scientists and the people who deploy, and duplicated effort on both sides. He cites a figure that almost 80% of models written by researchers never reach production, largely because of that deployment friction.

His historical framing: we went from machine-centric to VM-centric to container-centric, and the next step is model-centric, where the model and all its dependencies are the unit you ship.

## Kitfile, ModelKit, kit CLI

The pieces map neatly onto Docker concepts:

- **Kitfile.** A YAML manifest, the Dockerfile equivalent, listing the package details, model, code, datasets, docs and where each lives.
- **ModelKit.** The packed artifact, OCI-compliant, so it can be pushed to Docker Hub, a cloud registry on AWS, Azure or Google, or a specialised registry.
- **kit CLI.** `kit pack`, `kit push`, `kit pull`, `kit unpack`, `kit list`, with signing support so consumers can verify what they pull.

## The demo

In the terminal, Shivay logs in to Jozu Hub, a registry built for ModelKits, and runs `kit unpack` on a public YOLOv10 ModelKit. It unpacks layer by layer, like a container image, into a Kitfile, a README and the model in safetensors format. He then repacks it under his own name with `kit pack -t`, creates a repository and runs `kit push`.

The detail that will matter to teams is selective unpacking: a filter flag lets a data scientist pull only the dataset, or only the model, instead of downloading every layer every time.

## Into CI/CD and Kubernetes

Because ModelKits are OCI artifacts, they slot into GitHub Actions, Jenkins or a Dagger pipeline that rebuilds and pushes on every Kitfile change. Tags give you versioned experiments you can compare. For inference, a ModelKit can run as a container, or in Kubernetes via an init container or a containerised kit CLI. He closes on the community effort, discussed in the CNCF Slack, to make AI models first-class citizens in the OCI spec.

## Who should watch

Platform and MLOps engineers tired of maintaining a parallel toolchain for models, and DevOps teams being handed notebooks to deploy. If your organisation already standardises on OCI registries, this is a short path to reusing them for ML.

Title: Adding AI to a cloud system is mostly a modernisation job
Description: Radu Vunvulea of Endava at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on the services around the model: scaling, data catalogs, events, gateways and FinOps on Azure.
Body:
The model is the easy part. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Radu Vunvulea, Vice President of Cloud Capabilities at Endava and a Microsoft Azure MVP, argued that putting AI into an existing cloud system is mostly an application modernisation exercise, and that the services around the model (scaling, data, events, gateways, cost control) decide whether it delivers value or just a bigger bill.

Radu works from Cluj-Napoca and uses Azure for his examples, while noting that each service has an AWS or Google Cloud counterpart. The talk is close to an hour and is an architect's talk: no model training, lots of diagrams of what surrounds the model.

## We have been here before, with analytics

His framing is an analogy. Around 2020, many teams lifted and shifted to the cloud with a data layer that was not ready for analytics. In 2025 he sees the same pattern with AI: systems migrated in a hurry, modernisation deferred, and now an AI workload putting pressure on all of it.

He also separates two ways of using AI on Azure. Azure OpenAI is for pre-trained models consumed through an API, no data scientists or MLOps required, and he reckons that covers most cases. Azure Machine Learning is for when you train, which makes the model its own project inside a bigger programme.

## Five areas to modernise

- **Scalability and bottlenecks.** The bottleneck often is not the AI but the flood of queries and events it sends to your APIs, which can knock over services downstream.
- **Data silos and governance.** If every factory has its own repository, decide how to build an AI-ready data lake, and catalog what you hold and who may see it. His example is the salary database: a chatbot must show managers only their own reports' data.
- **Innovation versus compliance.** Enough governance to be safe, enough freedom to experiment.
- **Cost.** He tells the story of switching on everything in Application Insights and finding, a few weeks later, that "Application Insights cost me almost as much as the computation and database."
- **Deployment agility.** Teams need to ship models and AI services to dev and test as often as they ship code.

## The services that make it work

His Azure shortlist: AKS with mixed node pools so GPU, memory-heavy and ARM workloads each land on the right nodes; serverless functions behind an event-driven design to absorb the triggers AI generates; Microsoft Fabric to keep data close to where the model runs; Application Gateway and load balancers to protect and balance AI endpoints; Event Hubs for streaming updates; and Purview for the data catalog and governance. FinOps (reservations, Azure Advisor, Azure Automation) rounds it off.

He shows Microsoft's own reference diagram, where Azure OpenAI is a small box surrounded by API Management, Key Vault, networking and access control. As he puts it, building a cloud solution is not only about building a virtual machine, and the same goes for AI.

## Who should watch

Cloud architects and platform leads asked to add AI to an existing estate, especially on Azure. The walk-through of an e-commerce monolith moving to microservices, modern data, DevOps, then AI and finally operations is a good template for a roadmap slide.

Title: Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025: break it on purpose, everywhere
Description: Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 roundup - socio-technical experiments, network faults on Fargate, chaos in platforms, mobile apps, AI monitoring and security.
Body:
Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 ran online on February 20, 2025, with 28 talks, and the theme was scope creep in the best sense. Chaos engineering started with killing instances; in this lineup it reached on-call rotations, internal developer platforms, mobile apps, AI model monitoring, and security controls. The common thread: if you have not watched it fail on purpose, you do not know how it fails.

The talks are all on the [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/ce2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDA4LX-Xal04LBJN52V6C1C).

## The system includes the people

[Benjamin Wilms](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Benjamin_Wilms_reliable_system_unpredictable), co-founder and CEO of gold sponsor Steadybit, gave the keynote-style talk of the day. His definition of a system includes the infrastructure, pipelines, people, and processes around the software, and his best demo tested all of it at once: inject latency into one backend service and take down the gateway, then check that Datadog alerts within 90 seconds, PagerDuty opens an incident, someone acknowledges it, the system recovers, and the incident is resolved. Before any experiment, he also found an availability-zone risk just by colouring Kubernetes deployments by zone. He is clear that the point is the organisation, not blaming whoever was on call.

[Pierluigi Meloni](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Pierluigi_Meloni_success_people_tech), co-founder and CEO of Utterskills, pushed the human angle further: coding alone no longer makes you stand out, and most project failures come from human factors rather than technology. [Mihaela-Roxana Ghidersa](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_MihaelaRoxana_Ghidersa_mindset_software_build) of Signant Health looked at how reasoning patterns shape design decisions, and [Vitali Shchur](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vitali_Shchur_qa_mindset_startup) of Check Point Software argued that QA engineers at startups need to think like business analysts and usability experts too.

## Fault injection, hands on

[Sunil Govindankutty](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sunil_Govindankutty_network_resilience_experiments), an Enterprise Support Lead at AWS, opened with Werner Vogels's line that everything fails all the time, then demoed AWS Fault Injection Service experiments on Amazon ECS with Fargate: latency, packet loss, and blackhole conditions against a sample containerised application, so you can see the behaviour before your users do.

[Sayan Mondal](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sayan_Mondal_cultural_mindset_platform), a Senior Software Engineer at Harness and a LitmusChaos maintainer, argued for a chaos-first mindset in platform engineering: make resilience testing part of the internal developer platform and the CI/CD path, with a demo deliberately built to break. [Muhammad Ahmad Saeed](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muhammad_Ahmad_Saeed_chaos_microservices_engineering) covered designing microservices that hold up under failure, and [Muhammad Rizwan](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muhammad_Rizwan_architecture_systems_event) of Procode showed failure isolation and self-healing with event-driven architecture on Azure Event Grid. [Somaning Turwale](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Somaning_Turwale_resilience_recovery_disaster) of Microsoft took the bigger blast radius, disaster recovery with Azure Site Recovery.

## Chaos beyond the backend

Two talks took controlled failure to places it rarely goes. [Jaspreet Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Jaspreet_Kumar_mobile_apps), Lead Software Engineer at Microsoft, asked the obvious question in his abstract: why not break your mobile app before your users do? [Muddassar Sharif](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muddassar_Sharif_ai_model_systems), co-founder and CTO of Virtuans.ai, applied failure simulation to AI model monitoring, starting from the questions executives and engineering managers ask about LLMs in production and the monitoring concepts the industry already uses.

[Prashanth Reddy Kora](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Prashanth_Reddy_Kora_chaos_cloud_systems) of Centene stress-tested cloud database systems, and [Shashank Reddy Beeravelly](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Shashank_Reddy_Beeravelly_ai_data_quality) of Walmart looked at keeping data quality intact when the data itself is chaotic.

## Security as a failure mode

The security track treated breaches as just another failure to rehearse. [Sandeep Batchu](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sandeep_Batchu_security_cloud_defense), a Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft, made the case for chaos principles in cloud security testing. [Chirag Gajiwala](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Chirag_Gajiwala_resilience_models_security) of Nutanix explored reinforcement learning for adaptive resilience and generative models to simulate vulnerabilities, and [Vamsi Anumolu](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vamsi_Anumolu_security_devsecops_operations) of iCrossing covered DevSecOps across multiple clouds. [Rinku Mohan](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Rinku_Mohan_signon_design_implementation) of bettercoach went deep on single sign-on design and its integration traps.

## The quiet case for fewer moving parts

A few talks argued that resilience starts with less. [Denis Ermakov](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Denis_Ermakov_library_fundamentals_need), front-end lead at Techflow (which builds portfolio management software for banks), greeted his "lovely chaotic people" and then made the case against reaching for a shiny auth library in Next.js when the fundamentals already do the job. [Vivek Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vivek_Kumar_apps_vps_docker) compared VPS hosting with Docker, and [Hari Yerramsetty](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Hari_Yerramsetty_cost_optimization_success) of Flexport covered right-sizing, autoscaling, and FinOps.

The rest of the lineup ran from enterprise systems to networks: [Gopikrishna Yeturi](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Gopikrishna_Yeturi_performance_migration_framework) of LTIMindtree and [Lurduma Reddy Thirumala Reddy](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Lurduma_Reddy_Thirumala_Reddy_operations_workloads_scalability) on SAP migrations and SAP on Azure, [Jaya Krishna Vemuri](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Jaya_Krishna_Vemuri_investment_banking_accuracy) of State Street on reconciliation, [Naveen Gowda](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Naveen_Gowda_financial_automation_ecosystems) of Couchbase on financial workflow automation, [Rao Marapatla](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Rao_Marapatla_analytics_marketing_insights) of BreakthroughT1D on nonprofit marketing APIs, [Vedant Agarwal](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vedant_Agarwal_personalization_ranking_systems) of Walmart Global Tech on neural ranking, [Sai Charan Madugula](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sai_Charan_Madugula_iot_networking_agility) on SDN for IoT and 5G, and [Dmitrii Nikitin](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Dmitrii_Nikitin_development_maintenance_applications) of Quadcode on white-label Android apps.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to gold sponsors [Steadybit](https://steadybit.com/), [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), and [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

The series continues with [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ce2026) on December 3, 2026. Schedule your next game day accordingly.

Title: LLMs in customer support work best wired into the product team
Description: Ed Fullman, CPO at Veritas Automata, at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on 30+ years of call centres and how product managers should bring LLMs into customer experience.
Body:
The cheapest support call is the one that never happens, and the second cheapest is the one where the agent already knows what broke. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Ed Fullman, Chief Product Officer at Veritas Automata, drew on a career that runs from 1990s telecom call centres through web self-help to AI to argue that LLMs pay off in customer experience when product management is wired into the support loop, not bolted on afterwards.

## Thirty years of avoiding calls

Fullman once led a BPO handling broadband technical support for a large telecom, with 4,000 agents across seven countries and multiple vendors. That's the vantage point for his history: call routing and scheduling first, then web self-help, which diverted huge volumes away from agents, then machine learning for targeting and personalisation, and now chatbots that replace the old flowchart with something that adapts to the person asking.

He's clear about what call centres do well (the personal touch, someone who can actually change your settings or reverse a payment) and what hurts: high cost, and attrition driven by mixing low-value avoidable calls with high-value ones. Nobody wants to spend a shift answering the same question a release note should have.

## The product manager's blind spot

The sharpest point in the talk is about releases. When a new feature ships, call centre satisfaction tends to dip while agents learn problems nobody documented. Fullman wants AI-driven support to be informed by what the product team is doing: which features just deployed, which got pulled back after an A/B test produced a cluster of failures. Feed that into the support system and it can weigh its answers accordingly. Run it the other way, and product managers should see in near real time what customers are hitting.

## Where AI helps, concretely

He breaks the opportunity into personalised interactions (chatbots for customers, and the same context for agents so they reach resolution faster), proactive issue resolution (spot patterns in incoming contacts, trace them back to a bad release or conflicting configuration, and reach out by text or email before the escalation), adaptive self-help that matches a user's technical skill, workload scheduling with more data points, and sentiment analysis across calls and chat.

One idea stands out: call centre staff as graders of proposed AI responses. They are the people who know how things should work, so letting them review and reinforce the model is a realistic role, and it pulls them off calls that never needed a human.

## Case studies and the metrics to watch

His examples include the broadband engagement, where call avoidance kept rising and agent tiers shrank while the remaining agents did more specialised work, proactive airline rebooking, and a bank whose first-line AI assistant he described handling over a billion interactions with a 30% reduction in inbound calls. On metrics, the new one is AI deflection rate, alongside first call resolution, CSAT, agent retention and agent satisfaction, which he argues tells you where release communication is failing.

## Start small, keep the exits open

His roadmap advice is unglamorous and right: begin with a small project with measurable value, and design human escalation paths so users can jump out of an automated flow. Where they jump out tells you where the process is weak, and those conversations are richer feedback than surveys. His bottom line is that AI enhances human support rather than replacing it, except where answers were already deterministic.

## Who should watch

Product managers and support leaders planning an LLM rollout, and engineers building support bots who want the operator's view. It's long on experience and short on code.

Title: When one agent chain runs out of context, hire a manager agent
Description: Aleksandr Khramogin of LogicBoost at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on manager-worker agent hierarchies, structured messages, context budgets and failure recovery.
Body:
A single agent, or a neat chain of them, works until the task needs more specialities than one context window can hold. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Aleksandr Khramogin, AI engineer at LogicBoost, laid out the hierarchical alternative: manager agents that only plan and coordinate, narrow worker agents that execute, and explicit rules for messages, context and failure, built with tools such as LangChain and CrewAI.

## Why sequential agents hit a wall

Khramogin lists the failure modes of linear chains, and they'll sound familiar to anyone who has stuffed one prompt too many. Context windows saturate, forcing a trade between focus and completeness. Generalist agents are mediocre at specialised subtasks. Performance degrades as complexity grows, any failed link breaks the chain, and work that could run in parallel runs in a line. He reported that in their benchmarks, sequential approaches lost 40 to 60% of their performance when task complexity doubled.

He is also fair about the alternatives. Centralised control is simple but a bottleneck, decentralised swarms are resilient but inconsistent, pipelines suit standard workflows but not open-ended decomposition, and fixed role-based teams are good for collaborative work like content creation. Hierarchies are his pick specifically for complex decomposition.

## Managers that refuse to do the work

The architecture borrows from org charts. Manager agents at the top analyse the task, decompose it, assign subtasks, manage dependencies and integrate results. Worker agents in the middle each get a narrow system prompt for one domain: research, writing, code, data analysis, reasoning, verification. Tool agents at the bottom talk to APIs and databases. The key design rule is that the manager never tries to solve the problem itself, only to split and coordinate it. It's the one manager everyone wants.

## Messages and context are the real engineering

Two sections carry most of the practical value. First, inter-agent communication: five message types (task assignment, status update, dependency request, verification request, integration summary), each with an explicit schema, standard metadata and declared dependencies. He reported that structured protocols cut error rates by 60 to 70% versus unstructured messages in their testing.

Second, context management, which he calls the hardest part. The three enemies are flooding (too much irrelevant context), starvation (missing what's needed) and fragmentation (related facts spread across agents). His four countermeasures: summarise at each level so managers see summaries and workers see detail, share on a need-to-know basis, push reference material into a vector store for retrieval, and keep a shared memory that agents query selectively.

## Design for failure, and know the break-even

Hierarchies fail in new ways: workers fail tasks, dependencies get mismanaged, instructions lose meaning between layers, and context or API rate limits run out. Khramogin's answer is recovery that adapts to the failure type instead of blindly retrying; he said this recovers 83% of failures without a human in their production systems.

The honest bit is the cost curve. For a task with one to three subtasks, a sequential chain is cheaper and faster. He put the crossover at roughly five to eight subtasks, past which the hierarchy wins on errors, time and cost. His worked example is a project-planning system where a manager splits a high-level objective, a marketing campaign for a Q3 product launch, into work streams for research, task breakdown, resourcing, timelines and documentation.

## Where to start

His roadmap: begin with one manager and two or three well-defined workers, add structured messages and dependency handling, then failure recovery, then tune context and tokens. Use a strong reasoning model for managers and cheaper models for routine workers, plus structured logging and semantic checks on output quality, not just uptime. Treat the specific percentages as the speaker's own measurements; the patterns stand on their own.

## Who should watch

Engineers whose single-agent prototype is getting stuck on long, multi-skill tasks. If your agent does one thing well, this talk mostly tells you to leave it alone.

Title: AI root cause analysis starts with humans labelling the logs
Description: Nikhil Ramashasthri of Turo at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 lays out an AI-powered RCA pipeline, from data collection and SHAP to a human feedback loop.
Body:
Before a model can find the root cause of your outage, someone has to sort your logs, metrics and old incident reports into something it can learn from. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Nikhil Ramashasthri, Staff Software Engineer at Turo, made that unglamorous step the centre of his talk on AI-powered root cause analysis, and then walked through the rest of the pipeline.

The motivation is personal. His first on-call shifts leaned heavily on senior engineers, and only with time did he learn the product well enough to guess where an investigation should start. AI-powered RCA, as he frames it, is giving a machine that same learning curve, so it can surface hidden patterns and suggest a likely cause before anyone opens a log viewer.

## Three core pieces

The building blocks are machine learning that correlates patterns across very large volumes of telemetry and improves with each investigation, anomaly detection that flags deviations once baselines exist, and natural language processing for unstructured inputs like logs, feedback and support tickets.

## The pipeline, step by step

- **Data collection and preprocessing.** Aggregate logs and metrics, establish baselines, collect event data from Kubernetes, microservices and cloud providers, build ETL pipelines and do feature engineering so each issue can be scoped. He stresses that this needs human effort to categorise structured and unstructured data, and calls it the step he cannot emphasise enough.
- **Model development.** Random forests, deep learning and NLP for log analysis, with causal inference and SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) so the model can explain why it blamed something.
- **Real-time detection.** Kafka, Prometheus or the ELK stack in the data path, supervised learning, and graph-based dependency mapping across services.
- **Remediation and feedback.** Integrations with ServiceNow and PagerDuty for auto-ticketing, suggested fixes and runbooks, and a human loop that marks whether a proposed root cause was right before feeding it back into training.

## The honest part: challenges

Nikhil lists five obstacles: a high initial investment in storage, compute and AI expertise; data quality, since incomplete or noisy data produces inaccurate models; false positives and negatives that need continuous human validation; integration with a diverse set of existing tools; and security and privacy compliance.

He then shows a comparison table of legacy versus AI-enhanced RCA, with diagnostic accuracy rising from 78 to 95 and incident resolution time halving from eight hours to four. On one row, a one-to-ten data processing score, he adds, "but I don't quote me on that", which is the right spirit for reading the whole table: directional, not a benchmark.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform teams curious about AIOps who want a realistic view of what it takes, rather than a vendor demo. The talk will not tell you which product to buy, but it will tell you which data you need to start collecting now.
