Title: Salesforce and Agentforce, read as a cloud-native application
Description: Pradeep Reddy Guttha of Vertex Pharmaceuticals at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 explains Salesforce's platform and Agentforce through cloud-native principles.
Body:
Most people meet Salesforce as a CRM screen, not as a distributed system. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Pradeep Reddy Guttha, Architecture & Strategy Associate Director at Vertex Pharmaceuticals, flipped that view: he walked through the Salesforce platform, and its Agentforce AI agents, as an example of a cloud-native application built on containers, Kubernetes, multi-cloud and metadata.

Pradeep speaks as an enterprise architect who works with Salesforce, not as a Salesforce employee, and the talk is a short overview, about fifteen minutes. It is useful as a mental model of what sits under a SaaS platform you probably already depend on.

## The cloud-native checklist, applied to a SaaS giant

He starts from the standard principles (containerisation, microservices, orchestration, provisioning and automation) and maps each onto Salesforce:

- **From monolith to microservices.** Salesforce moved to containerised microservices managed by Kubernetes, so individual components can scale independently.
- **Kubernetes everywhere.** Used across on-prem and public cloud deployments for consistent, automated delivery.
- **Hyperforce for multi-cloud.** The platform can be deployed on public clouds such as AWS, Google Cloud and Azure without major reconfiguration.
- **Metadata-driven design.** Much of the platform's behaviour is defined as metadata rather than hard-coded logic, which is what makes it so configurable and why integrations are relatively easy.

The metadata point is the one worth pausing on. It is the reason one multi-tenant platform can look completely different for each customer, and it is a design idea that transfers to internal platforms too. On scale, he credits distributed systems and scalable storage for letting the platform absorb large data volumes and user traffic, which is the same claim any multi-tenant platform team has to earn every day.

## Agentforce and the trust layer

The second half turns to AI. Salesforce's earlier Einstein work has been joined by Data Cloud and Agentforce, virtual agents for service, sales and marketing that work around the clock, whether as a chatbot or an on-demand support agent. Pradeep is explicit that he sees them as agents working alongside people rather than replacing their jobs.

He describes the LLM features as sitting on what Salesforce calls the Einstein Trust Layer, with data masking, dynamic grounding, an audit trail and demasking, all running on the same cloud-native infrastructure as the rest of the platform.

## Who should watch

Salesforce architects and admins who want to explain the platform's internals to infrastructure colleagues, and platform engineers curious how a large SaaS vendor maps onto the cloud-native playbook. Do not expect configuration examples or benchmarks; this is an orientation talk.

Title: Cloud-native building blocks for data and AI, ending in a RAG stack
Description: Meethun Panda of Bain & Company at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 maps microservices, serverless GPUs, MLOps and security onto a containerised RAG architecture.
Body:
Your CI/CD pipeline needs a third letter once models are in it: continuous evaluation. That is one of the sharper points in Meethun Panda's talk at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, where the Associate Partner at Bain & Company, who advises Fortune 500 companies on data and AI, mapped the standard cloud-native toolkit onto data and AI workloads and finished with a containerised RAG architecture.

It is a short survey talk, about fifteen minutes, aimed as much at decision makers as at engineers. The value is in the map: which cloud-native piece solves which data or AI problem.

## Foundations before use cases

Meethun opens with the consultant's view: transformations are judged on business value, and cloud adoption only delivers it if the foundation is right. His list includes a platform that makes analytics use cases fast to build, cloud-native architecture for elastic scaling and self-healing, FinOps so large AI workloads stay cost-efficient, and governed, reliable, accessible data. He is careful not to declare on-prem dead; the future he describes is a mix of multi-cloud, SaaS and on-prem.

## Each building block, applied to AI

- **Microservices and containers.** Scale inference separately from data ingestion, isolate failures, and deploy modular pieces faster. Spotify's recommendation engine and Netflix are his examples.
- **Serverless.** For generative AI he highlights serverless GPUs and inference as a service, mentioning Groq's LPUs for fast inference. Use cases: chatbots, model inference and serverless ETL.
- **Storage.** Data lakes on S3, ADLS Gen2 or Delta Lake; warehouses such as BigQuery, Snowflake and Synapse; vector databases like Pinecone and Weaviate for embeddings.
- **MLOps.** Feature stores, model versioning, deployment, and monitoring for drift and bias, with continuous retraining of fraud models in banking as the example. This is where CI/CD becomes CI/CD/CE.
- **Security.** Differential privacy, masking and pseudonymisation for PII, compliance with GDPR, HIPAA and CCPA, HSM-backed key management, zero trust with least privilege, and API protection with OAuth2, JWT and mutual TLS.

## A naive RAG stack, done the cloud-native way

The closing architecture is a plain retrieval-augmented generation setup, which Meethun calls naive himself. Documents are chunked, embedded and loaded into a vector database. User queries hit a load balancer or API gateway, get embedded with the same model, retrieve the top matches and go to the LLM with a prompt template.

The cloud-native part is how it runs: every component (front end, back end, vector store, prompt template, LLM service) in its own container, Kubernetes with Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, Istio as the service mesh, the vector database as a stateful service with persistent storage, GPU nodes or a managed service such as Azure ML or SageMaker for inference, and Grafana plus the ELK stack for monitoring.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leaders planning a data and AI platform who want a one-screen checklist of components and concerns. If you already run RAG in production, the architecture will be familiar; the security and FinOps checklists may still catch a gap.

- [Kosseila Haddalene on running vLLM inference on Kubernetes across clouds](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Kosseila_Haddalene_vllm_kubernetes_gpu) at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

Title: Introducing uncertainty before users feel it
Description: Confidence comes from testing
Body:
# Break things. On purpose. Calmly.

Chaos engineering sounds dramatic. Like you’re about to pull cables out of walls and see who panics first.

In reality, it’s much more thoughtful than that. Mostly.

Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 is all about building systems that keep working even when the universe decides to be uncooperative. Network hiccups, failing dependencies, cloud outages, bad configs, expired certificates, and that one service nobody remembers owning. You know the drill.

This conference digs into how teams actually test resilience. Fault injection, chaos experiments, failure scenarios, and learning what really happens under pressure. There are talks on microservices, event-driven architectures, cloud databases, APIs, and what breaks first when things scale faster than expected.

AI shows up here too, because of course it does. Expect sessions on AI model monitoring, AI-driven chaos experiments, and using machine learning to detect issues before users do. Some talks focus on reliability. Others focus on making sure automation doesn’t confidently lead you in the wrong direction.

But chaos isn’t just technical. A big part of the program looks at people, culture, and mindset. Platform teams, leadership, communication, and why throwing more tools at a problem doesn’t magically make systems resilient. Spoiler: humans are still involved.

You’ll also find real-world case studies across cloud, mobile, security, finance, healthcare, and enterprise platforms. From testing disaster recovery to breaking things safely in production, this is chaos engineering where the goal is learning, not drama.

If you like understanding how systems fail before they fail loudly, this one’s for you. Controlled chaos beats surprise chaos. Every time.

Title: A chaos experiment that tests your on-call, not just your pods
Description: Benjamin Wilms of Steadybit at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on testing socio-technical resilience, from pod redundancy to Datadog and PagerDuty response.
Body:
Your redundancy works on paper and your runbook exists in Confluence; neither tells you whether the on-call engineer gets paged within 90 seconds when the gateway falls over. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Benjamin Wilms, co-founder and CEO of Steadybit, argued that a system includes the people and processes around the software, and showed a chaos experiment that verifies both halves at once.

Benjamin has been doing chaos engineering for around nine years. This is a vendor talk: the demos run in Steadybit, wired to Datadog and PagerDuty. The method transfers to other tooling, though, and that is the reason to watch.

## A system is more than its services

The talk starts from a definition. Software runs on infrastructure, is built through a pipeline, and is operated by people inside an organisation with its own processes. Benjamin uses the term socio-technical system for the whole thing. Failures can come from any part of it: a misconfiguration, a human error, an unexpected interaction between services, or two teams with mismatched processes.

He is blunt about the goal. A 100% error-free system will never exist; servers crash, networks lag, dependencies break. What you can do is make the system better at handling failure, and check that it really is.

The demo system is an online shop, with services like a bestseller list, checkout, and a hot deals service, each owned by different teams. Even grouped by area, the dependency bubble chart stays busy, which is his point about complexity.

## Find the risk before you run anything

Steadybit's approach has three phases: uncover risk, understand impact, then increase systemic resilience.

The first phase needs no experiment at all. Benjamin groups the shop's Kubernetes deployments and colours them by availability zone. The cluster spans two zones, the bestseller and checkout services are spread across both, and the hot deals service is not. That is a risk found purely from configuration data. Steadybit's advice feature then flags orange items, such as a checkout deployment that should run more instances, with a snippet to fix it.

The second phase verifies the fix. The experiment does a pre-check that all pods are ready, deletes a pod, and expects it back within 60 seconds while the system keeps serving. Steadybit collects Kubernetes events and deployment readiness into one report. Benjamin stresses running these early, in a pre-production environment, rather than starting in production.

## The experiment that pages a human

The third phase is where the talk earns its title. Benjamin takes a scenario from a past incident: a latency spike in the hot deals backend, followed by a total outage of the central gateway. The hypothesis covers people as well as software:

- Monitoring recognises the problem within 90 seconds and alerts the on-call team via PagerDuty.
- The incident is opened and acknowledged within three minutes.
- The system recovers within three minutes and the incident is resolved within four.

The experiment encodes all of it. Steadybit checks with Datadog that the system is healthy first, injects the latency and the gateway outage, then expects Datadog to report an alert, PagerDuty to show a triggered incident, someone to acknowledge it, Datadog to return to OK, and the incident to be resolved. In the recorded run, every step passed, so the technical recovery and the human response both held up.

He adds a rule worth repeating to any team that runs game days: this is not about how fast one person fixes an outage. Benjamin says he does not like finger pointing; the test measures how well the organisation detects and fixes faults and how its processes are coordinated.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform teams who already run basic fault injection and want to extend it to alerting and incident response. The "colour by zone" trick is a nice five-minute audit for any Kubernetes cluster. If you have never run a chaos experiment, the talk is accessible, but you will get more from it once you have.

Title: An AI content toolkit for founders who would rather ship
Description: Personal brand expert Yelyzaveta Didenko at Conf42 LLMs 2025 maps the AI tools founders can use for posts, visuals, video, SEO and email, with a human editing.
Body:
Most technical founders know they should post more and don't, because every hour on marketing is an hour not spent on the product. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, personal brand expert Yelyzaveta Didenko gave a brisk tour of the AI tools that can carry most of that load, from drafting posts to voiceovers to email sequences, with one firm condition: a human still edits.

It's a short, non-technical talk, closer to a curated tool map than an engineering session. That's the point; the audience is the founder who has a product to build.

## The problem, stated plainly

Didenko names three issues: founders struggle with content creation, they lack time, expertise and consistency, and marketing feels like a distraction from building. The result is that content takes a back seat, and with it go brand growth, lead generation and product visibility. The challenge she sets is a steady content presence without stealing focus from development.

## The toolkit, by job

She walks through the categories in the order a founder would hit them:

- **Writing.** ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for blog posts, LinkedIn articles and newsletters, adjusted to your tone and voice.
- **Design.** Midjourney for images and graphics, DALL-E and Canva for creatives without design skills.
- **Video and voice.** Synthesia for video avatars that read your script in several languages, ElevenLabs for voiceovers, and a tool that makes video and podcast editing work like editing a text document.
- **Social.** Tools that suggest and schedule posts, pick posting times from engagement data, and repurpose one blog post into LinkedIn posts, tweets and Instagram captions.
- **SEO.** Surfer SEO and Clearscope to optimise for keywords and to spot gaps in competitor content.
- **Email.** Mailchimp's AI assistant, HubSpot AI and Copy.ai for sequences, personalised messages, subject lines and send times.

The repurposing idea is the one most engineers will actually use: write one solid piece, let a model split it into the formats each channel wants.

## What it looked like in practice

Didenko points to cases of founders scaling blogs with AI-generated content, including a case study of a site that went from zero to thousands of monthly visitors within 12 months, and to Supergrow, a LinkedIn personal-branding tool whose users reported a 50% productivity increase. Treat these as the examples she chose rather than benchmarks; the talk doesn't break down the methods behind them.

## The co-pilot rule

The line worth keeping is her caveat. AI is best used as a co-pilot that handles the repetitive tasks while you refine and personalise the output, and the best results come from automation plus strategic human oversight. In other words, a model can draft your launch post, but it doesn't know which customer story made you start the company. She ends on what's coming: deeper personalisation, real-time AI video, and marketing strategies that adapt on their own.

## Who should watch

Solo founders and small engineering teams without a marketing hire, who want a quick inventory of tools to try this week. If you already run a content operation, you'll recognise most of the list.

Title: Resilience from the ground up, from Spring Boot to Kubernetes
Description: Praful Konduru of Meta at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 walks through redundancy, loose coupling and graceful degradation with Spring Boot, Docker and Kubernetes.
Body:
Resilience is cheapest when it is designed in on day one, and most expensive when it is bolted on after the first outage. That is the thread through Praful Konduru's talk at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, where the Meta software engineer, drawing on a decade that also included Amazon and PayPal, walked from design principles to a running container in about half an hour.

This is a good first talk on cloud-native resilience. Praful shows code on most slides, keeps the examples deliberately small, and is upfront about it: the e-commerce case study near the end is, in his words, "super hypothetical".

## What resilience means here

His working definition: systems that scale efficiently and keep their performance and availability when things go wrong. He separates three properties that often get blurred. Scalability is handling more load by adding resources. Elasticity is adjusting resources up and down with demand, so you are not paying for a million-customer day on a quiet Tuesday. Resilience is recovering from failure gracefully.

## Four principles, each with a reason

- **Redundancy.** Run multiple copies of every important component, so traffic can move when one server dies.
- **Loose coupling.** Minimise dependencies so a failure in one area does not cascade.
- **Fail fast and degrade gracefully.** Do not keep the user waiting while a broken instance restarts; route around it, and never leave them staring at an error page.
- **Monitoring with automated recovery.** Detect trouble and scale or restart without a human in the loop.

## The code walk-through

The practical half builds a toy service step by step. A Spring Boot `GreetingController` with `@RestController` and an injected `GreetingService` shows why splitting controller and business logic helps both testing and fault isolation. A Dockerfile on an OpenJDK base image, exposing port 8080, packages it; `docker build` and `docker run` start the container. Kubernetes then takes over for self-healing and automatic scaling of the pods.

He follows with a CI/CD pipeline that runs unit and automated tests on every pull request, across Ubuntu, Windows and macOS runners, and closes the loop with Prometheus for metrics and alerts and Grafana for dashboards, plus the ELK stack for logs.

## Who should watch

Developers moving from writing services to owning them in production, and teams that want a shared vocabulary for resilience before arguing about tools. If you already run chaos experiments and tune pod disruption budgets, this is a refresher at best; the related talks go deeper on fault isolation and continuous resilience.

Title: A field guide to microservices principles for cloud-native teams
Description: Muhammad Rizwan of Procode at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 covers when to leave the monolith, the core components of microservices and how to start small.
Body:
The best advice in Muhammad Rizwan's talk fits on a sticky note: start small, migrate one service, and expand from there. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, the Procode software engineer gave a compact primer on microservices in cloud-native systems: when to leave a monolith, which principles keep services sane, and which components and tools a team needs before the first split.

This is an introduction, and a tidy one. It runs about fifteen minutes and is best as a checklist for a team about to start, or as the talk you send a new hire before their first architecture review.

## When the monolith stops paying for itself

Muhammad does not treat monoliths as a mistake. They work well for small projects; the trouble starts as they grow. A large codebase makes updates slow and risky, scaling means redeploying the whole application, and long release cycles slow every feature down.

His three signals that it is time to move: the application is becoming hard to manage, different components need to scale independently, and DevOps and continuous deployment are real team priorities. If none of those hold, the monolith may still be the right call.

## Four principles before any code moves

- **Single responsibility.** Each service does one thing well, which keeps it small and maintainable.
- **Loose coupling, high cohesion.** Services are independent but still work together efficiently.
- **API first.** All communication goes through well-defined APIs.
- **Domain-driven design.** Service boundaries follow business capabilities, not database tables.

## The components you will end up running

The core building blocks come next: synchronous communication over REST or gRPC for real-time calls, asynchronous messaging such as Kafka for decoupled work, service discovery so services can find each other, an API gateway for security, load balancing and routing, and a database per service to keep teams independent. Docker and Kubernetes handle packaging and orchestration, serverless functions cover on-demand work, and CI/CD pipelines automate testing and delivery.

He is honest about the hard parts: distributed transactions and data consistency, the performance cost of choosing between REST, gRPC and message brokers, and security, where he names authentication, authorisation and zero trust. Observability gets its own slide, with Prometheus and Grafana for metrics and OpenTelemetry as the standard for logs, traces and metrics.

## Design for failure

The closing advice is the useful part. Do not migrate everything at once. Automate CI/CD, testing and deployment fully. Design for failure with retries, circuit breakers and fallbacks. Then keep learning: monitor, collect feedback and refine. Netflix and Uber appear as the reference migrations, both moving off monoliths to handle scale and agility.

## Who should watch

Developers and team leads who are new to microservices and want the vocabulary in one place. Experienced teams will find nothing surprising here, but may find a clean slide deck to borrow for onboarding.

Title: Why LLMs that never write code still train on code
Description: Antara Raman Sahay of Helmerich and Payne at Conf42 LLMs 2025 walks through Cohere research on how code in pre-training lifts reasoning and knowledge tasks.
Body:
General-purpose models that were never meant to write code still eat a lot of it during training. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Antara Raman Sahay, a software engineer at Helmerich and Payne, walked through Cohere research that asks the obvious question, to code or not to code, and found that code in the pre-training mix helps with natural language reasoning and world knowledge too, not just code generation.

This is a paper walkthrough, and a friendly one. Sahay explains the research rather than presenting her own experiments, which makes it a good primer on how training data choices get tested.

## The phases, explained with a childhood

Before the results, Sahay lays out the stages of training: pre-training (learn the structure of language from vast text), fine-tuning (adapt to a task), continual pre-training (add knowledge without losing the old), a cool-down phase (the learning rate drops and high-quality data gets priority) and evaluation. Her analogy maps them to a life: parents and school as pre-training, college as continual pre-training, and a career as cool-down, where you learn more slowly but specialise. It's cute and it sticks.

## Four robots, three exams

The experiments train models with different recipes and test them on natural language reasoning, world knowledge and code generation. Sahay presents them as four robots: one trained on text only, one on an equal mix of code and text, one on the balanced mix and then continually pre-trained on text, and one trained on code first and then on text.

The results she reported: the code-initialised model did best at natural language reasoning, the balanced-then-text model at world knowledge, and the balanced-only model at code generation. Scaling from 470 million to 2.8 billion parameters made every robot better at everything, which is the least surprising result in machine learning and still nice to see confirmed.

## How much code, and what kind

Sweeping the code share from 0% to 100% in a 200-billion-token run showed different curves per task. Natural language reasoning peaked around 25% code and 75% text. World knowledge went the other way, dropping as code increased. Code generation rose with the code share, so the all-code model won there.

Code quality mattered as much as quantity. Sahay compared variants that add markup languages such as HTML and CSS, code-adjacent data such as GitHub issues, StackExchange and Jupyter notebooks, and synthetically generated code. The synthetic code variant gave the best performance. Adding code in the cool-down phase also beat cooling down without it.

The headline numbers she quoted from the study: code in pre-training boosted natural language reasoning by 8.2%, the cool-down with code was crucial for world knowledge, and code-heavy models beat text models by about 12 times on code tasks.

## The recipe

Her takeaways are a practical checklist for anyone building or choosing models: use a balanced mix of code and text from the start, add synthetic code to help both code and language tasks, and keep code in the cool-down phase. If your job is mostly code, pick a code-heavy model; for general tasks, a balanced one. Open questions she flagged: what happens when synthetic code goes past the shares tested, and more elaborate cool-down phases.

## Who should watch

Engineers who use LLMs daily and want a mental model of why training mixes look the way they do, and anyone choosing between general and code-specialised models. It's an accessible summary, not a reproduction; read the paper for the full method.

Title: The business case for microservices, told in deployment numbers
Description: Abdul Hameed Mohammed of 7-Eleven at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 makes the numbers case for microservices and a three-step audit, plan, migrate path.
Body:
Every 11.7 seconds, the talk says, Amazon and Google push another code update to production. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Abdul Hameed Mohammed, Software Engineer at 7-Eleven, used that figure as the opening hook for a short, numbers-first argument that microservices are the default architecture for teams that need to ship often, and offered a three-step route out of a monolith.

Abdul has nine years in full-stack development, IoT integration and cloud work, with stints at 7-Eleven, Deloitte and Resoltech. This is a compact talk, well under twenty minutes, pitched at people who need to make the case to a business audience rather than at architects arguing about service boundaries.

## The argument is made in adoption statistics

Most of the talk is a run of industry figures. Netflix runs over 900 microservices to serve 167 million streaming hours a day. 84% of enterprises have adopted cloud-native architectures. Teams that move report 23 times more frequent deployments, a 65% drop in production failures thanks to fault isolation, and a 92% improvement in mean time to recovery. On the maintainability side, bug fixes reach production 37 minutes after discovery instead of the 24 hours a monolithic release cycle imposes.

The slides do not cite where each figure comes from, so read them as the industry's sales pitch for microservices rather than as data you can audit. Still, a deck like this is exactly what a team lead needs when someone above asks why the team is spending a quarter on a rewrite

## Three steps out of the monolith

The practical core is short and sensible:

1. **Assess.** Run a thorough architecture audit, find bottlenecks and dependencies, and set performance benchmarks before you touch anything.
2. **Plan.** Design services around business goals, define service boundaries and API contracts up front, and write a migration plan that accounts for risk.
3. **Implement.** Start with services that are low risk and high impact, put monitoring, automated tests and CI/CD in place, and iterate on real feedback.

None of this is new, but the order matters. Benchmarks before migration means you can later prove the move paid off, and starting with low-risk services means your first outage on the new architecture is a small one.

## One before-and-after

The case study is an unnamed e-commerce platform. Before: a 48-hour deployment cycle, frequent system-wide outages, a ceiling of 1,000 concurrent users with three-second page loads, and 8 hours of monthly downtime from full-system updates. After: 15-minute deployments with zero-downtime updates, 50,000-plus concurrent users at 200 ms page loads, and 99.99% uptime. It is the clearest slide in the deck, because it ties architecture to things a customer actually feels.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers early in a monolith-to-microservices conversation, who want ready-made talking points and a simple migration sequence. If you already run hundreds of services and your real problems are distributed tracing and data consistency, this will be too high level; the related talks below go further into the trade-offs.

Title: Fleet management as a stack of AI, IoT sensors and Kubernetes
Description: Vamsi Anumolu of iCrossing at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on combining predictive AI, IoT telemetry and Kubernetes to run vehicle fleets.
Body:
A truck that tells you about its failing gearbox two weeks early is worth more than one that tells you on the hard shoulder. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Vamsi Anumolu, Senior DevOps Engineer at iCrossing, laid out how fleet operators combine three layers to get there: AI models for prediction, IoT sensors for live vehicle data, and Kubernetes as the platform that runs both.

Vamsi brings 15 years across fintech, digital marketing and automotive, with a focus on platform engineering, reliability and streaming data. The talk is a high-level tour rather than a build log, so expect architecture boxes and outcome figures, not YAML.

## Fleet management is a data problem first

He starts with the plain definition: managing a company's vehicles and assets through their life cycle, to cut cost and raise performance. Today that mostly means a fleet manager staring at dashboards for tyre pressure, fuel and maintenance status, then deciding when to service or replace a vehicle. Ambulances, delivery trucks, ride-hailing cars: same shape of problem.

The pitch is to move from looking at a dashboard and reacting to systems that predict. AI models read engine data and maintenance history to forecast failures, and IoT devices feed real-time location and condition data so routes and schedules can be adjusted while the vehicles are moving.

## Kubernetes is the boring backbone, on purpose

The most engineering-flavoured section is the one on infrastructure. Vamsi casts Kubernetes as the backbone that makes the AI and IoT parts operable:

- **Scaling** microservices that ingest large volumes of IoT data in real time.
- **Automated deployment**, so model and feature updates ship continuously.
- **Resource efficiency** for the compute that AI inference and telemetry processing need.
- **Isolation and security** through containers, plus the flexibility to run in cloud, on-prem or hybrid.

He also points at edge computing as essential for fleets, since vehicles generate data far from any data centre. A later slide extends the story to multi-cloud across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud with automatic failover.

## The case studies, and how to read them

Three success stories carry the second half. An AI system processing around 500,000 data points from vehicle sensors, engine diagnostics and maintenance records reached 90% success forecasting mechanical failures two weeks out, with an average of 2.3 million in annual savings. An IoT rollout improved fuel efficiency by 20%. A Kubernetes platform cut deployment time from days to minutes while holding 99.99% uptime and handling peaks of 10,000 concurrent vehicle connections.

The talk does not name the organisations behind these figures or show how they were measured, so treat them as the target shape of an outcome rather than a benchmark you can quote to your CFO. The underlying pattern is sound either way: sensor data in, prediction out, maintenance scheduled off-peak instead of in an emergency.

## A 90-day roadmap

Vamsi closes with a phased plan: assess the fleet and its pain points, pick a pilot project, deploy the technology in stages, then optimise continuously. He frames it as a 90-day programme with weekly milestones and measurable KPIs, which is a sensible antidote to the instinct to boil the ocean with every sensor at once.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers in logistics, mobility or field-service companies who want a map of how predictive maintenance, telemetry and container platforms fit together. If you already run Kafka pipelines off vehicle CAN bus data, this will be familiar ground; if your fleet still runs on spreadsheets and a phone tree, it is a useful first picture.

Title: Microservices survived the hype cycle; use them where they fit
Description: Chad Green of Jasper Engines & Transmissions at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 answers the five big critiques of microservices with patterns and managed services.
Body:
In a 2016 job interview, Chad Green was asked what he thought of microservices and answered: "I think they're overhyped and this enthusiasm will fade very soon." He did not get the job. In his next role he built microservices because they fit the project, and at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 the Senior Software Architect at Jasper Engines & Transmissions gave a careful defence of them, critiques included.

Chad has 35 years in software, with a soft spot for event-driven design, serverless and API-first work (and a Lego city at home). The talk runs close to an hour and is the most balanced microservices session at the event: it concedes most of what the critics say, then shows what he does about each point.

## From hype to intelligent maturity

He frames the last decade as four eras. The hype years, roughly 2014 to 2018, when microservices were the silver bullet and every conference agenda was full of them. Rising skepticism from 2018 to 2022, as teams met distributed-systems pain, API gateways and service registries they now had to run. Then losing faith, with "it's time to abandon microservices" think pieces and teams moving back to modular monoliths. And now what he calls intelligent maturity: better tooling, and a clearer sense of when the style actually pays off.

## Four styles, compared honestly

Before defending anything, Chad lays out the alternatives. The monolith is a block of marble: solid, but every change means chiselling the whole thing. N-tier is a layered cake, where a problem in one layer spoils the slice. Microservices are a fleet of small boats that need constant radio contact. The modular monolith is a well-organised toolbox, where you still carry the whole box to use one screwdriver. He recommends the modular monolith for many mid-sized cases, and as a stepping stone you can later split.

## Five critiques, five answers

- **Operational overhead.** True, he says. His answer is to hand it to the cloud: Azure Container Apps, AWS Fargate or Google Cloud Run instead of running Kubernetes yourself, Azure Functions or Lambda for event handlers, and the platform's own monitoring.
- **Distributed-systems pain.** Prefer asynchronous messaging (Azure Service Bus in his shop), retries, circuit breakers and timeouts. He has often found a service mesh unnecessary for serverless, event-driven systems.
- **Data consistency.** Accept eventual consistency and use the Saga pattern with compensating transactions, plus event sourcing for an authoritative log.
- **Testing.** End-to-end tests get harder, but unit tests get easier. Build the pyramid properly, with Pact for contract tests and Playwright or Selenium at the top.
- **Skills.** His first response to this one is "boo hoo". Learning is the job, and teams that refuse to learn have a bigger problem than their architecture.

## Who should watch

Architects and tech leads deciding between a monolith, a modular monolith and services for their next system, and anyone who has read one too many microservices-are-dead posts. Azure shops get the most concrete tooling advice, though he maps each service to its AWS and GCP equivalent.

Title: Evals turn prompt tweaking into a repeatable experiment
Description: Hilik Paz of Arato.ai at Conf42 LLMs 2025 builds a support bot eval suite from vector similarity, JSON schema checks and LLM judges, then iterates to green.
Body:
A prompt that looks fine in three manual tries is not a tested prompt. At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Hilik Paz, co-founder and CEO of Arato.ai, showed how to replace "looks good to me" with a small eval suite: define what good means per business requirement, mix cheap deterministic checks with model-based judges, run the prompt against a dataset, and only ship when the scores say so.

It's a vendor talk in the honest sense: the live demo runs in Arato's platform, which manages prompts, model configs, datasets and evals. The method travels well beyond it.

## Pass/fail stopped being enough

Paz starts with why software testing needs a new chapter. Traditional APIs have well-defined outputs and error formats. LLMs don't. In his words, "We are moving toward a non-deterministic world" where the same input may come back different on the next call. So the test stops being a boolean and becomes a set of measurements you score, with a target you are either hitting or not.

He gives evals three jobs: be measurable (accuracy, relevance, structure), be repeatable across iterations, and be actionable, meaning a failed score should tell you what to fix in the prompt.

## Three families of evals, two ways to run them

The running example is a technical support bot for a fictional product, which in its first version answers a real question with something polite and useless. To pin down "better", Paz sorts evals into three groups:

- **Content**: compare the actual reply to an expected one from the dataset using vector similarity, check that certain words appear, check that sensitive data doesn't.
- **Format**: the calling code expects a specific JSON schema, so validate the reply against it.
- **Qualities**: is the answer grounded in the documents passed as context, and is it polite (one of the bot's stated requirements)?

Then he splits the mechanics. Rule-based evals (text matching, regular expressions) are fast, cheap and rigid. Model-based evals (an LLM as judge, embeddings for similarity) can ask nearly any question but cost more and are themselves non-deterministic, so you have to read their verdicts with some suspicion. His rule of thumb: deterministic where you can, model-based where you must. Grading a nondeterministic system with another nondeterministic system is fine, as long as you remember you did it.

## The dataset is half the eval

Before the demo, Paz spends a moment on test data, and it's the part teams skip. A useful dataset holds realistic user inputs plus the edge cases and odd inputs real users will type. The prompt becomes a template with placeholders, the dataset fills them, and every eval runs over every row.

## Watching the scores move

The live run is the satisfying bit. Version one fails several evals, including the JSON schema, and the UI shows exactly which inputs failed and why. Paz then adds a detailed example of the expected response format and tightens the instructions, reruns, and also swaps in Claude as a second model. Both models now pass all evals, which tells you the prompt change did the work, not the model swap. A side-by-side of the three experiments shows similarity to the expected answers staying high while the pass rate climbs. Only then does the new prompt go to production, where the same question gets a detailed, multi-option answer.

## Who should watch

Engineers who own an LLM feature and still test it by eyeballing a few chats. It's short, concrete and demo-driven; if you already run eval suites in CI, it's a refresher plus a look at one tool's workflow.

Title: Generative AI does the chores; data scientists still make the calls
Description: IBM's Omer Ali Omer and Syeda Narmeen at Conf42 LLMs 2025 on synthetic personas, augmented images and contract clauses, and where humans stayed in charge.
Body:
Will generative AI replace data scientists? At Conf42 Large Language Models 2025, Omer Ali Omer, a platform engineer, and Syeda Narmeen, a data scientist, both in IBM's client engineering team, answered with four client projects rather than a forecast. In each one, the model took over a tedious step and a person still had to pick the model, check the output or overrule the suggestion.

## From predicting to generating

Omer opens with the workflow shift. The classic data science lifecycle runs business understanding, data mining and cleaning, feature engineering, predictive modelling, visualisation, all centred on structured data. The generative version keeps business understanding but frames problems as generation. Prompt engineering takes the slot of feature engineering, context and embeddings replace labelled datasets, fine-tuning adapts models to a domain, and evaluation means judging generated content for coherence, correctness and ethics.

He doesn't wave away the anxiety. Models now produce in minutes insights that took days, companies swap custom classifiers and sentiment models for general ones, and data cleaning and feature engineering keep getting automated. That's the case for worry, stated fairly, before Narmeen makes the case against it.

## Four projects, four places a human mattered

**Synthetic focus groups.** A finance client's marketing team struggled to recruit focus groups and had to rerun each strategy with several groups. The team used an IBM Granite model fed with real customer data to generate customer personas (the sample is a 28-year-old single mother working as a teaching assistant). Data scientists chose the model and then validated that the personas resembled real customers, so the client could test bolder strategies against simulated groups.

**Not enough images.** A heavy-machinery client wanted to use site lifts more efficiently and keep personnel safe, but the site photos weren't enough to train on. The team augmented them in IBM Maximo Visual Inspection, with data scientists choosing which augmentations made sense, then combined the new images with sensor data to simulate scenarios, flag risks and find a more efficient way to run the lifts.

**Learning a domain fast.** On a telecom project predicting cell tower congestion, Narmeen used a model to explain unfamiliar terms (QoS among them), summarise the client's congestion formula and do first-pass analysis. When it suggested a KPI, successful handshakes, that the supplied data couldn't support, she overruled it. The model got her to competent quickly; it didn't get to decide.

**Contract clauses.** A company wanted generated clauses on top of its contract templates, adding or dropping items such as an indemnity clause per client. The first outputs were too wordy and added information nobody asked for, and the fix was data scientists iterating on prompts across the project. Anyone who has asked a model for "a short clause" knows the feeling.

## What's next, and what to do about it

Omer closes on three trends: multimodal models for specific use cases (watsonx hosting models that read text and images, used on medical reports), reinforcement learning as a feedback loop for generative models, and open-source AI widening access. The call to action is plain: work with the tools, and keep investing in your own skills.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and team leads wondering what the job looks like with a model in the loop. It's a practitioner's overview with concrete project stories, not a technical deep cut; engineers after architecture details will want something else.

Title: SpinKube runs WebAssembly apps on Kubernetes like regular pods
Description: Mikkel Mork Hegnhoj of Fermyon at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 demos SpinKube, running Spin WebAssembly apps in Kubernetes via a containerd shim, with KEDA scaling.
Body:
The OCI image for his demo app was a 12 MB WebAssembly binary, a 534-byte manifest and a 209-byte config, and nothing else. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Mikkel Mork Hegnhoj, head of product and DevRel at Fermyon, introduced SpinKube, the open source project for running Spin WebAssembly applications inside Kubernetes, and showed it deploying, configuring and autoscaling like any other workload.

This is a vendor talk in the sense that Fermyon builds Spin and co-maintains SpinKube, but it stays on the open source projects. SpinKube is a collaboration between Microsoft, Liquid Reply, SUSE and Fermyon, and both Spin and SpinKube have been accepted into the CNCF sandbox.

## Four pieces under the hood

SpinKube has four parts:

- **Spin operator**: translates the Spin application model into Kubernetes deployments, pods and services through a SpinApp custom resource. Optional, but it adds cluster-wide settings such as an OpenTelemetry endpoint.
- **containerd-shim-spin**: the runtime. On each node, containerd hands Spin apps to this shim instead of the usual container runtime, which is part of how SpinKube gets higher density.
- **Runtime class manager**: configures containerd on nodes, including nodes added later by cluster autoscaling.
- **SpinKube plugin** for the Spin CLI: scaffolds the YAML and pushes apps to OCI registries.

Install is familiar: cert-manager, the runtime class manager, CRDs, then the operator from a Helm chart.

## The demo: TypeScript to pod in a few commands

Mikkel builds a TypeScript HTTP app from a Spin template on a local k3d cluster. `spin new`, `spin build` to compile to WebAssembly, `spin up` to test locally. Then `spin registry push` to the ephemeral ttl.sh registry, `spin kube scaffold` to generate a SpinApp YAML, and `kubectl apply`. Two replicas come up, a port-forward answers curl, and Jaeger shows a trace of the request executing the component.

He then adds a variable to the Spin manifest, overrides it locally with an environment variable, and sets it in the SpinApp YAML for the cluster. Config maps and secrets work as well, and the operator ends up injecting the value as an environment variable in the pod.

The last demo pairs SpinKube with KEDA. A scaled object watches a CPU-heavy SpinApp, scaling between one and 20 replicas at 50% CPU, and new pods appear as load arrives.

## Why WebAssembly in Kubernetes

Mikkel closes with four reasons:

- **Size.** Dependencies are compiled into the binary, and a Rust hello world can be a few hundred kilobytes.
- **Startup and density.** Components start in under a millisecond. Each request loads only the components it needs and unloads them after, so idle apps cost little more than the host runtime. That is where density comes from.
- **Sandboxing.** Components have no file system or outside memory access, and network endpoints must be granted explicitly in the manifest.
- **Portability.** One binary runs on x64 and ARM64, with no multi-arch images or separate pipelines, which helps when chasing cheap spot instances.

He also cited ZEISS running SpinKube on Azure Kubernetes Service in proofs of concept, cutting compute cost by 60% without trading away performance.

## Who should watch

Platform teams curious about WebAssembly workloads alongside containers, anyone running serverless-style HTTP functions on Kubernetes, and edge or ARM-heavy shops. If you want WebAssembly internals, Fermyon's own channel is where he points you.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Sohan Maheshwar's [Build a Serverless WebAssembly App in Python using Spin](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2024_Sohan_Maheshwar_serverless_webassembly_app_spin) covers the Spin developer side.
- Deepu K Sasidharan's [Go Containerless on Kubernetes with WebAssembly and Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Deepu_K_Sasidharan_kubernetes_containerless_webassembly) takes the Rust route to the same cluster.
- Alex Casalboni's [From Cloud to Edge computing with WebAssembly](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Alex_Casalboni_cloud_edge_webassembly) moves WebAssembly to the edge.

Title: Automating tax and reconciliation across Salesforce, NetSuite, Avalara
Description: Naveen Gowda of Couchbase at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on API-led iPaaS integration and an ETL reconciliation loop for Salesforce, NetSuite and Avalara.
Body:
Finance teams lose days to reconciliations that exist only because three systems don't talk to each other. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Naveen Gowda, director of data engineering and integrations at Couchbase, showed how API-led integration through an iPaaS, plus an ETL reconciliation loop, keeps Salesforce, NetSuite and Avalara in sync, and what that did for tax accuracy.

It's a pragmatic architecture talk from the person who owns the pipes. No vendor pitch, just the shape of the system and the metrics it was judged by.

## Manual tax data is error-prone by construction

Gowda opens with a show of hands for anyone who has fought tax errors, missed deadlines or overdue reconciliations. The cause is familiar: legacy financial systems were never built for integration, so tax data gets entered by hand from ERPs, accounting software and tax services, and finance spends hours or days checking it. When tax rates, product categories and exemptions live in different systems, every manual update is a chance for a discrepancy, a penalty or an audit.

## APIs as the glue, iPaaS as the router

The fix is to let systems update each other. His running example: an invoice processed in Salesforce triggers an API call to NetSuite to update the financials and another to Avalara to calculate the tax. Microservices each do one job; APIs bind them; an integration platform as a service (iPaaS) routes requests between them.

The enterprise blueprint he shows starts with a customer ordering through e-commerce. The order syncs to the iPaaS, which routes it to Salesforce. An invoice is generated with tax from Avalara, goes back through the iPaaS and lands in NetSuite. Running across the top, an ETL tool keeps extracting from every system into a data warehouse for analysis and reconciliation. Multi-cloud placement adds redundancy, so a failover workflow can switch providers if one has an outage.

## Plan for the sync that fails

The most useful part is admitting integrations break. When a sync fails, from bad data or anything else, the data warehouse is the safety net. The ETL pipeline pulls raw data from Salesforce and NetSuite into a central data lake, SQL and Python scripts compare the two and flag discrepancies, and the flagged records are pushed into the iPaaS automation to be fixed. He gives the example of resolving a backlog of over a thousand mismatched invoices in about two hours, against the 10 to 15 days it usually took.

## The scorecard and a 90-day plan

The outcomes Gowda reports: 50 percent less manual effort, 98 percent tax accuracy, 30 percent faster revenue recognition, and savings from fewer errors and faster dispute resolution. His roadmap is three 30-day phases: audit and deliver an integration blueprint; test real-time tax sync and reach data accuracy; then add multi-cloud resilience with a 99.99 percent uptime target.

## Who should watch

Data and integration engineers who support finance, and engineering leaders asked to connect billing, ERP and tax tools without a reconciliation team. The reconciliation-loop design transfers well beyond these three products.

Title: The best backend is the one nobody has to think about
Description: Rinku Mohan of bettercoach at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on low-maintenance backends built from events, stateless services, autoscaling and restraint.
Body:
The most resilient systems are the ones that run without anyone noticing. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Rinku Mohan, senior software engineer at bettercoach, laid out how to build backends that scale without constant firefighting: modular where it pays, event-driven between services, stateless at the edges, autoscaled and observable, and no more complex than the business needs.

It is a principles talk, not a demo. The value is in the restraint it recommends as much as in the patterns.

## Modularity, but only where it pays

Rinku traces the path from simple monoliths that were easy to understand and hard to scale, to distributed cloud-native systems that scale and then demand constant care. Microservices let teams build, deploy and scale independently, but the goal is not microservices for their own sake. Design around the business domains. His line on it is worth pinning above a whiteboard: "If your application doesn't need microservices, don't force it."

The same restraint applies to serverless. Managed services take over scaling, patching and backups, and serverless removes servers from view, but cold starts and time limits are real constraints. A hybrid approach often works best.

## Events let services move at their own pace

The longest section is on event-driven architecture. Instead of calling each other and waiting, services publish events that consumers process independently, through brokers such as Apache Kafka, AWS EventBridge and RabbitMQ. Producers and consumers don't need to know each other exist.

His e-commerce example: one order-placed event triggers payment, inventory, shipping and customer notification, each listening and acting on its own. Under load, the model supports backpressure, with consumer lag monitoring and rate limiting keeping consumers from being overwhelmed. During a flash sale, you add consumers to spread the load.

## Stateless services scale by copying

Horizontal scaling is easy only when instances hold no session state. Rinku's pattern is stateless services for authentication, orders and inventory, with session data in an external cache or database, or carried in a JWT. Then any instance can serve any request.

Load balancers distribute traffic with round robin, least connections or weighted strategies (AWS Elastic Load Balancer, Nginx, Cloudflare), and drop failed instances from the pool. Autoscaling groups watch CPU, memory, network and request rates and add or remove instances, so a streaming service with evening peaks scales back down overnight.

## You can't fix what you can't see

Observability gets its own section: logs, metrics and traces through the ELK stack and AWS CloudWatch, distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry to find bottlenecks across services, and alerting through PagerDuty before anomalies become outages.

## The pitfalls that create maintenance

Rinku names three: overengineering, ignoring legacy systems (migrate gradually or wrap them with APIs), and missing documentation. He adds database choice: MongoDB and Cassandra for large distributed write-heavy data, PostgreSQL with JSON support as a structured-plus-flexible middle ground, and a warning against picking a database because it's trendy. Feature flags, API versioning and continuous refactoring keep the system adaptable.

His closing idea is invisible infrastructure: modular parts, automation that heals and deploys without hands, and simplicity as a deliberate choice. Every on-call engineer's dream, in other words.

## Who should watch

Engineers designing a new backend or untangling an old one, and tech leads who need a checklist that argues against complexity. Seasoned distributed systems people will recognise every pattern; the talk is a good one to share with a team.

## Related Conf42 talks

- James Eastham's [So You Want To Build An Event Driven System?](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_James_Eastham_event_driven_system) goes further on events and their trade-offs.

- Rob Richardson's [Horizontal Autoscaling with Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2022_Rob_Richardson_horizontal_autoscaling) shows the scaling half in practice.

Title: Three API layers to connect hospital systems without replacing them
Description: Venugopal Reddy Depa at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 explains MuleSoft's system, process and experience APIs as a way to join fragmented healthcare systems.
Body:
Hospitals rarely get to throw away the systems they have, so the integration layer has to do the work. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Venugopal Reddy Depa, senior application and integration developer at CRH Americas Materials, walked through MuleSoft's API-led connectivity model, with its system, process and experience layers, as a way to connect EHRs, labs, pharmacies and patient portals while leaving the legacy platforms in place.

Honest scope first: this is a talk about one vendor's integration approach, MuleSoft, applied to healthcare. It is heavy on outcome figures and light on implementation detail.

## The problem: data in eighteen places

Venugopal frames healthcare's integration pain in three parts. Data fragmentation, with a single hospital coordinating patient records across many EHR systems, so doctors rarely see the full picture. Legacy infrastructure, much of it 10 to 15 years old, never designed for real-time data. And regulatory compliance, where privacy and security rules delay projects and breaches are expensive.

The consequence he keeps returning to is clinical: test results delayed by disconnected systems, repeated tests, and decisions made without the full history.

## Three layers, three jobs

The core of the talk is the three-layer architecture:

- **System APIs** sit on top of the legacy platforms and expose their data in a standard form, so records from different hospitals, labs and pharmacies arrive in one shape. This is where you avoid a rip-and-replace.
- **Process APIs** orchestrate clinical workflows: lab results, prescriptions and treatment plans updated across systems, plus automated insurance claims, scheduling and prescription renewals.
- **Experience APIs** serve the data to people, with provider interfaces and patient portals for records, medications and appointments.

The useful idea is separation. Legacy quirks stay behind system APIs, business logic lives in process APIs, and front ends change without touching either. That holds for any integration platform, not just MuleSoft.

## From integration to personalised care

The middle of the talk links integration to personalised medicine: real-time patient data, AI-assisted imaging and genetic analysis, and clinical decision support that matches treatments and flags adverse drug reactions. The argument is that none of those models help if the lab, imaging and genetic data can't reach the same screen.

## The case study and its numbers

The case study is an unnamed large US healthcare network of 920 facilities serving 13.8 million patients a year. By the talk's account, deploying a new system across the network went from about 210 days to 58 days after moving to MuleSoft, with return on investment reached within 18 months. The talk and its abstract carry many more percentages on accuracy, savings and security. The network isn't named and the figures aren't sourced in the talk, so read them as the vendor-side case being made rather than independent benchmarks.

On security, the talk lists end-to-end encryption, data governance, role-based access control, monitoring of security events and automated HIPAA compliance checks.

## Who should watch

Integration engineers in healthcare evaluating MuleSoft or the API-led pattern, and architects who need language for a layered integration proposal. If you want FHIR resource mappings or Mule flows, this talk stays at the architecture level.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Gunjan Desai Rajendrakumar's [Platform Engineering for Healthcare Interoperability](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Gunjan_Desai_Rajendrakumar_interoperability_exchange_fhir) covers FHIR-based data exchange.
- Geetha Sharanya Bolla's [Reimagining Healthcare Access with Data Integration and Microservices at Scale](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Geetha_Sharanya_Bolla_healthcare_integration_scalable) takes the microservices route.

Title: Precision medicine is a data engineering problem first
Description: Santhosh Kumar Rai of Xpress Global IT Solutions at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on the pipelines, data types and compliance work behind AI-driven diagnosis.
Body:
Personalised treatment needs one patient's genome, records, scans and vital signs in the same place at the same time. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Santhosh Kumar Rai, SAP lead consultant at Xpress Global IT Solutions, argued that getting there is mostly data engineering: collection, integration, processing and analysis, built on real-time ETL and cloud infrastructure that stays HIPAA compliant.

It is a short overview, around fifteen minutes, aimed at engineers wondering what healthcare data work actually involves. Expect a structured map rather than code.

## Four jobs for the data engineer

Santhosh breaks the role into four stages:

- **Collection**: automated gathering of structured and unstructured data from electronic health records and other sources.
- **Integration**: joining disparate systems and formats while keeping integrity, quality and HIPAA compliance.
- **Processing**: real-time transformation through ETL pipelines so data is ready for clinical use.
- **Analysis**: machine learning and statistical models that turn data into treatment decisions.

The techniques that support them are real-time ETL for continuous patient data streams, scalable cloud architecture for very large datasets, and AI-driven analytics that look for early disease indicators.

## Four data types, four different headaches

The talk names the sources a precision medicine platform has to handle. Genomic sequencing, which he puts at over 200 gigabytes of data per patient. Electronic health records with the longitudinal history of treatments and outcomes. Medical imaging from X-ray, MRI and CT. And IoT monitoring that streams vital signs from wearables and bedside devices.

Each has a different shape and arrival pattern, from large files to continuous streams, which is why the processing layer matters as much as the models.

## Three case studies, one pattern

The case studies follow the same flow from data to action. Early disease detection combines genomic, clinical and real-time monitoring data into a patient profile across 50-plus indicators, applies pattern recognition and predicts progression months ahead. AI-assisted drug discovery screens molecular compounds and protein targets. Real-time patient monitoring streams vital signs, flags anomalies and routes urgent alerts to the right clinician.

The talk attaches improvement figures to each (faster diagnosis, shorter drug timelines, quicker response to critical events), but the case studies are not tied to named organisations or published studies, so treat the numbers as illustrative.

## Compliance and standards are the real bottleneck

The most practical section is on what slows these projects down. Security needs encryption and access control. HIPAA and GDPR require documentation, audits and careful management of who reads what. Patient trust depends on transparent handling and ethical AI.

Then there is interoperability. Santhosh says healthcare uses over 40 different data standards, and connecting EHRs, lab systems and imaging databases is a large recurring cost. Harmonised formats are the precondition for every analytics promise earlier in the talk. Anyone who has mapped one hospital's lab codes onto another's knows the feeling.

His action list closes it out: build a scalable, compliant infrastructure with automated backups, use real-time pipelines and AI analytics, and tackle security and standardisation up front.

## Who should watch

Data engineers moving into healthcare, and SAP or enterprise integration folks who want the healthcare vocabulary. If you need FHIR mappings or pipeline code, look elsewhere; this is the overview.

Title: DevSecOps across AWS, Azure and GCP starts with policy as code
Description: Vamsi Anumolu of iCrossing at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on shift-left security, policy as code, CI/CD scanning, CSPM and container security for multi-cloud.
Body:
Finding a vulnerability a week before release is the most expensive way to find it. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Vamsi Anumolu, senior DevOps engineer at iCrossing with 16 years in cloud and platform engineering, argued that teams spread across AWS, Azure and GCP need security built into the pipeline from the first commit, and described the principles and tool categories that get them there.

He calls it an introductory session, and it is: a structured overview for teams starting DevSecOps in a multi-cloud setup, not a tool-by-tool tutorial.

## Shift left, because Friday is too late

Anumolu's opening story will be familiar. In the old SDLC, code moved up through environments and security testing happened just before production. Find a serious issue then and you have about a week before the release to fix it. Shift-left security moves those checks into development, so issues surface while the code is still fresh and cheap to change, and makes security everyone's job rather than the last gate.

The CI/CD half of the idea is to make the pipeline enforce it: security scans, compliance checks and vulnerability assessments run as stages before code deploys to any environment, so every deployment gets the same treatment.

## Three principles for multi-cloud

He reduces DevSecOps for multi-cloud to three principles:

- **Policy as code**: security requirements written as executable code, enforced automatically and identically on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and the rest, which removes the manual errors of configuring each console by hand.
- **Automated security testing** in the pipeline: SAST, DAST and container security checks that catch vulnerabilities before production.
- **Continuous monitoring and threat detection**, with AI-assisted tools that correlate security events across clouds and spot anomalies for a quick response.

He reports a 40 percent reduction in compliance violations from automated checks and standardised controls, and development cycles at least 25 percent faster when automation and shift-left work together.

## The multi-cloud tax

Running several clouds adds three problems of its own. Vendor lock-in is countered with platform-independent architecture and standardised APIs. Cross-platform discrepancies need one security framework and automated compliance checks so controls don't drift between clouds. Global regulation, GDPR and HIPAA among them, needs data governance that enforces requirements automatically and monitors them in real time.

## Two cases and a toolbox

The talk includes two anonymised case studies. A Fortune 500 retailer with $20 billion in annual revenue automated security scanning and compliance checks across AWS and Azure, with a 35 percent drop in compliance violations, incident response cut from days to hours and three times the deployment frequency. A bank processing over a million transactions a day added vulnerability scanning to CI/CD and found 40 percent more issues during development, with 60 percent fewer production incidents.

The tool categories to look at are cloud security posture management (CSPM) for continuous misconfiguration detection across clouds, cloud SIEM for correlating security data and keeping audit trails, and container security with scanning, runtime protection and policy enforcement for Docker and Kubernetes. His four first steps: audit your current posture across all clouds, write the policies and standards, wire the tools into CI/CD, and set up continuous monitoring with alerts and response procedures.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers starting DevSecOps on more than one cloud, and managers who need the vocabulary and an ordered plan. Teams already running policy as code in production will know the material.

Title: The NLP building blocks behind every cloud-native text feature
Description: Mohit Mittal of NASCO at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 tours NLP from the Turing test to GPT-4, covering tokenization, tagging, NER, sentiment and deployment.
Body:
Before you call an LLM API, it helps to know what happens to your text on the way in. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Mohit Mittal, lead system architect at NASCO, gave a tour of natural language processing from rule-based systems to GPT-4, focusing on the components every text feature still relies on: tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, preprocessing and sentiment analysis.

It is an overview talk, and a good one to send a colleague who joined from the backend side and keeps hearing "tokens" in standups.

## A short history in one slide

Mohit starts with why language is hard for machines: ambiguity, context, idioms and variation. The history runs from Alan Turing's 1950 test through brittle rule-based systems to the data, compute and machine learning that made NLP practical over the past two decades. The model lineage follows: Word2Vec in 2013 with vector word representations, transformer models such as BERT and GPT-3, then GPT-4 in 2023 with better contextual reasoning. Zero-shot and few-shot learning let models handle new tasks without retraining.

The talk also spends a slide on market growth and healthcare's share of it, with figures you can take or leave; the technical sections are the reason to watch.

## Four steps up the ladder

Mohit lays out the core pipeline as a ladder:

- **Tokenization** splits text into words, subwords or characters. Word-based splitting struggles with compound words; subword methods like byte pair encoding and WordPiece break words into meaningful pieces so unknown words still get handled; character-level splitting suits languages such as Chinese.
- **Part-of-speech tagging** labels nouns, verbs and adjectives. His example is "run": a noun in "a morning run", a verb in "I run every day".
- **Named entity recognition** finds people, places, organisations and dates. In a sentence saying Apple Inc. is headquartered in California, NER marks Apple Inc. as a company and California as a location.
- **Preprocessing** cleans text: stop-word removal, lowercasing, handling misspellings.

The choice of tokenizer affects both accuracy and efficiency, which is worth remembering the next time a token count looks bigger than the text.

## Sentiment grew up

Early sentiment analysis used word lists and fell over on sarcasm. Machine learning on labelled datasets improved it, and context-aware models like BERT handle nuance far better. Mohit adds multitask learning for overlapping emotions, multilingual consistency, and hybrid rule-plus-deep-learning systems for sarcasm, which remains the hard case for humans too.

## Generation and the cost of running it

On generation, attention keeps long passages coherent, and techniques such as teacher forcing in training and nucleus sampling at inference reduce repetition. For deployment he lists four concerns: compute and inference latency (optimised decoding helps), data quality, MLOps practices such as automated monitoring for model degradation, and bias detection. His open challenges are factual accuracy, domain specialisation for fields like healthcare and finance, and privacy, where federated learning helps.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to NLP who want the vocabulary in one pass, and architects deciding which parts of a text pipeline to own versus outsource. Experienced NLP practitioners will know most of it already.

Title: Smart city data is messy, and NiFi is how Tim Spann tames it
Description: Tim Spann of Snowflake at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 pipes transit, traffic and sensor feeds through Apache NiFi into Snowflake and Iceberg, with a live TRANSCOM demo.
Body:
A smart city is mostly a data integration problem with traffic lights attached. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Tim Spann, senior solutions engineer at Snowflake, showed how he pulls city feeds in every format imaginable (GTFS transit protobufs, XML RSS, JSON sensors, camera images) through Apache NiFi into Snowflake and Apache Iceberg tables, then queries them with Cortex AI.

If you have seen Tim at Conf42 before, you know the format: a fast tour of the stack, then a live NiFi demo recorded on a Sunday with a running bet on whether the demo survives. It does.

## Every format, all at once

The opening is a census of city data. Transit systems publish GTFS, a binary format built on Google protocol buffers, and the Mobility Data folks keep a consistent list of feeds worldwide, so you could automate grabbing every transit system on the planet. Air quality comes from OpenAQ. Traffic arrives as JSON, regulations as email and documents, and street cameras supply images and video that can answer questions like whether buses are late because of double parking.

Tim's point is that semi-structured and unstructured data has to land somewhere it can be queried. Snowflake's variant type takes the odd stuff raw; structured tables, hybrid tables for transactional work and Iceberg tables for sharing across systems take the rest. Data can arrive via Kafka into Snowpipe, through Snowpark in Python, Java or Scala, or straight from NiFi.

## Why NiFi does the boring parts

NiFi gets the longest section, and Tim is openly a fan. The features that matter for city feeds are guaranteed delivery, buffering with back pressure, prioritised queues, per-flow control of latency and throughput, and full data provenance: every flow file's history and metadata, viewable in the UI. He notes NiFi originated at the NSA and has been in mission-critical use for years, and that NiFi 2.0 improved Python support for writing processors.

His own Python processors are the fun part: one extracts company names from documents with spaCy, one captions images with Salesforce's BLIP model, one classifies images with ResNet-50, and one turns addresses into latitude and longitude with Nominatim. Location is everything in a city.

## The demo: TRANSCOM to a Streamlit map

The live demo uses TRANSCOM, the coalition that handles traffic events across New York, New Jersey and Connecticut. NiFi polls the HTTP feed, converts the XML RSS into JSON, splits it into records, adds a timestamp and a unique ID, parses a point field into separate latitude and longitude, and loads the result into Snowflake. A Streamlit app then maps problem spots (lots in Manhattan, no surprise), and Cortex AI answers questions over the event descriptions for RAG-style lookups.

A second flow handles Irish Rail transit data: a large file of zip archives, uncompressed, split, given primary keys and loaded into lookup tables, with no hard-coded schema beyond the keys.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who have to integrate many public feeds, anyone considering NiFi for ingestion, and teams building on Snowflake or Iceberg. If you need a deep look at Cortex internals, Tim covers it at the overview level. NiFi runs as a Java app or in Docker if you want to follow along.

- Tim's [Building Apache NiFi 2.0 Python Processors](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2024_Tim_Spann_apache_nifi_2_processors) shows how processors like his BLIP captioner are made.

Title: Cloud security after the perimeter - zero trust, MFA and AI detection
Description: Sandeep Batchu of Microsoft at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on zero trust, MFA, AI threat detection, micro-segmentation and compliance automation in the cloud.
Body:
Perimeter security assumed there was an inside worth defending. Cloud adoption removed the walls, and Sandeep Batchu, principal software engineer at Microsoft with more than a decade securing cloud and hybrid platforms, used his Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 session to lay out the strategies that replace them: zero trust, strong identity, AI-assisted detection, segmentation and automated compliance.

Scope note: the session title promises controlled failure, but the talk itself is a strategy overview of modern cloud security rather than a guide to security chaos experiments. As an overview, it's tidy and well ordered.

## Never trust, always verify

Batchu frames the problem with the scale of cloud adoption and an expanding attack surface, with sophisticated multi-vector attacks that cost companies millions per incident. His first answer is zero trust: continuous verification of every user, device and application regardless of location, with multi-factor authentication, real-time monitoring and granular access control on every resource. He reports that organisations implementing zero trust have seen a 60 percent reduction in security incidents.

## Identity is the new firewall

The identity section is the most actionable. Use granular role-based permissions, just-in-time access and automated privilege management so standing admin rights stop being the default. Layer multi-factor authentication that combines biometrics, hardware tokens or time-based codes. Organisations using MFA, he says, report 99 percent fewer account compromises. If you only take one thing from the talk to your next architecture review, it's this.

## Let machines read the logs

AI and machine learning appear as accelerators for detection: tools that analyse millions of data points in real time and spot breaches earlier, and behaviour analytics that cut false positives so the security team spends its attention on genuine threats. His figures here are a 50x speed-up over manual methods and a 76 percent reduction in false positives.

He then looks further out. Post-quantum cryptography, using lattice-based or hash-based schemes, protects data against both classical and quantum attackers. Blockchain-style ledgers give tamper-proof audit trails and remove single points of failure.

## Shrink the blast radius

Micro-segmentation brings zero trust to the network: isolated segments, policies at the workload level, and much less room for an attacker to move laterally after a breach. Serverless architectures help too, with function-level isolation and event-driven security controls that remove whole classes of infrastructure vulnerability. Continuous compliance automation scans, validates and documents requirements in real time, so audit preparation stops being a quarterly fire drill.

He closes on collaboration: shared threat intelligence and coordinated incident response between companies and security researchers make everyone harder to hit.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects who own cloud platforms and need a structured overview of the controls a modern security posture expects, or a checklist for a security review. Security specialists, and anyone looking for hands-on security chaos engineering, will want a more technical session.
