Title: Last-mile delivery is where cloud and IoT pay for themselves
Description: Maimoon Saleem, senior program manager at Amazon, at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on how cloud analytics and IoT cut last-mile delivery cost, and where drones fit.
Body:
The last leg of a parcel's trip is the most expensive one. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Maimoon Saleem, senior program manager at Amazon, explained why last-mile delivery accounts for 53% of total shipping costs by her figures, and how cloud computing and IoT attack that cost through real-time tracking, predictive analytics and smarter fleets.

It is a compact talk, under fifteen minutes, structured as what, so what and what next. Good for an overview; the speaker sticks to the business case rather than system internals.

## Why the last mile hurts

Maimoon defines the last mile plainly: the parcel left a vendor, passed through a warehouse, reached a final-mile station and was dispatched to you. That last hop is the part customers see, and the costs pile up there: driver wages, fuel, insurance, vehicle maintenance, traffic and failed deliveries.

She names three problems. Costs are high. Traditional logistics lacks real-time visibility, so accuracy suffers. And customers want deliveries fast, free and trackable, a bar she says Amazon same-day delivery set for everyone else. Her summary of the customer is the best line of the talk: "The customer is never happy."

## What the cloud does

The cloud's job is processing volume in real time. Route planning that weighs traffic, delivery windows and package sizes as they change, demand and delivery-time forecasts from machine learning, and infrastructure that stretches for Black Friday or Prime Day and shrinks after. That last point matters for smaller carriers that can't own peak capacity. Her example is AWS powering Amazon's own route and inventory optimisation.

## What IoT adds

IoT supplies the data the cloud needs. GPS trackers and RFID tags give location and condition, which matters for temperature-sensitive goods. Connected sensors and automated picking speed up warehouses, which shortens everything downstream. In vehicles, sensors track fuel use, driver behaviour and maintenance.

The industry examples come with numbers she cites: DHL vehicles cutting fuel costs by 15% with real-time route optimisation, Amazon reducing delivery times by 25% with AWS analytics and IoT, UPS's ORION routing system saving 10 million gallons of fuel a year, and Alibaba's Cainiao network using smart lockers for contactless delivery.

## The next five years: drones and driverless vans

Maimoon expects two technologies to reshape the last mile by 2030: drones and autonomous vehicles. Regulation has held both back, and she sees that easing, with growing FAA adoption in the US and EU work on drone fleet rules. Amazon is working on its MK30 drone and Alibaba has started drone delivery for selected products in Shanghai. Cloud and IoT, in her view, are the enablers for mass adoption, with lower cost per delivery, routes that skip congestion and a smaller carbon footprint.

## Who should watch

Engineers joining a logistics or e-commerce team who want the business context in one sitting, and product people building tracking or routing features. If you want the architecture of a routing engine, this talk names the systems rather than opening them up.

Title: Tree ensembles on big.LITTLE CPUs need a worker pool, not more threads
Description: Andrei Stroganov of Samsung Research at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 shows why random forests stall on heterogeneous CPUs and how a worker pool gave a 4x speedup.
Body:
Adding threads made inference slower, and the CPU was the reason. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Andrei Stroganov, lead software engineer at Samsung Research, showed how random forest and gradient boosting inference in ONNX Runtime hits a concurrency penalty on heterogeneous CPUs, and how a simple worker pool with small batches removed it and delivered a four to five times speedup.

It is short, focused and has charts. The kind of talk you watch once and then remember the next time `n_jobs` doesn't help.

## Heterogeneous CPUs break an old assumption

Heterogeneous CPUs, the big.LITTLE design from phones, mix high-performance cores with energy-efficient ones on one chip. Andrei notes they are making their way into servers, which is why this matters beyond mobile.

Tree ensembles run on CPUs because their branching structure doesn't suit GPUs or NPUs. A random forest trains many trees on random subsets of the data; a gradient boosting machine trains trees in sequence, each correcting the last. Libraries such as ONNX Runtime, XGBoost and LightGBM parallelise them by giving each thread a share of trees or a share of the dataset. Both strategies quietly assume all cores are equal.

## The experiment

The setup is concrete: a weather forecasting dataset with 21 numerical features, an octa-core CPU with one very fast core, three slower cores and four efficiency cores, models of up to 100 trees, all run in ONNX Runtime.

With stock multithreading, random forest gets faster up to six threads and then slower with seven and eight. Gradient boosting is worse: the best case was two threads, more threads carried a large penalty, and the gain over one thread was only 1.2 times. You can't tell in advance which thread count is right.

## Why equal slices waste fast cores

Andrei's diagram explains it. Give equal work to a fast core, a core half its speed and two slow cores, and the fast core finishes early and idles while everyone waits for the slowest. Even with work stealing, where finished cores take over unfinished parts, cores still sit idle.

## The fix: tiny batches and a queue

The worker pool pattern splits the dataset into many small batches. Each worker thread takes a batch, processes it and asks for the next. Fast cores simply take more batches. Andrei's batch size was around 400 to 800 samples: small enough for the slowest core to finish in reasonable time, large enough that queue handling doesn't eat the gains.

With the pool, both models scale cleanly with thread count. Random forest plateaus at six to eight threads when the hardware runs out, with no penalty, and gradient boosting is fastest at eight threads, about four times faster. His summary across both models is a four to five times boost, from a change in scheduling rather than in the model, delivered through a custom C++ wrapper.

## Who should watch

ML engineers serving tree models on CPU, anyone deploying to ARM servers with mixed cores, and engineers who like a clean before-and-after benchmark. The lesson generalises: when cores are unequal, schedule by pulling work, not by splitting it.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: A meta operating system for the cloud-to-edge continuum
Description: Pawel Skrzypek of 7bulls.com at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 presents NebulOuS, an open source EU project that places apps across Kubernetes clusters from cloud to edge.
Body:
Your app is probably already running on a cloud continuum, you just haven't called it that. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Pawel Skrzypek, software architect at 7bulls.com, gave an update on NebulOuS, a Horizon Europe research project building a meta operating system that decides where each part of an application should run across public clouds, private data centres and edge sites, then keeps moving it as conditions change.

The abstract promised to explain what the heck fog is. The talk delivers that, then gets specific about Kubernetes.

## The continuum you already use

Pawel defines the cloud continuum as the traditional cloud extended to every entity that stores, processes or generates data: public clouds, private clouds and data centres, fog, IoT devices, edge sites, multi-access edge computing (MEC) and micro data centres near users. Multi-cloud and hybrid cloud are subsets; the continuum is the mix-and-match of all of them.

His everyday example is the smartphone or smartwatch app. Input, output and some processing happen on the device, heavy lifting happens in a cloud. Placing each piece well cuts latency to the user and uses resources better.

## What "meta operating system" means here

A meta OS, in Pawel's terms, is an operating system that extends beyond one server or one cluster and spans devices and clouds. NebulOuS is a consortium of research organisations, industry partners and end users who supply real applications to test it.

The project covers several layers:

- **Modelling**: a unified way to describe the continuum's resources, application requirements and data streams, with quality of service attached.
- **Optimisation**: compare offerings across the continuum with multi-criteria decision methods, pick the best set of resources, and keep reconfiguring.
- **Security and SLAs**: with many providers involved, NebulOuS adds smart-contract-based service level agreements.

Execution is all Kubernetes. NebulOuS deploys the application to clusters that may sit in a public cloud, a private data centre or a MEC location, collects metrics on response time and processing, and redeploys when a utility function (the goal measure of deployment efficiency) says it can do better.

It is open source under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, and the project publishes research papers and training material alongside the code. Pawel also pointed to open calls, with 1.35 million euro across nine grants for outside organisations that want to adapt an existing continuum application to NebulOuS.

## The use case: a fund run by algorithms

The demo application is Omphalos Fund, an alternative investment fund registered in Luxembourg that has been run by AI algorithms since January 2022. Its infrastructure spans two public clouds, a private data centre and a direct connection to the broker, which makes it a real continuum workload rather than a lab toy. Pawel showed its performance against benchmarks, including a maximum drawdown he put at 3% against over 30% for the NASDAQ from January 2022. Those are the speaker's figures for his project's use case, so weigh them accordingly.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers juggling clusters in more than one place, researchers in edge and fog orchestration, and anyone curious whether cross-cloud placement can be automated end to end. If you want a hands-on deployment walkthrough, the project website and technical reports are where Pawel sends you.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: Why AI agents and blockchains might need each other
Description: Shubham Gupta of Noblesoft Solutions at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on pairing autonomous AI agents with blockchain for shared data, smart contracts and audit trails.
Body:
If an AI agent acts on its own, somebody will eventually ask it to explain itself. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Shubham Gupta, analytics and AI leader at Noblesoft Solutions, made the case that blockchain answers that question: an immutable, shared ledger where agent decisions get recorded, enforced through smart contracts and audited later by every party involved.

It is an architecture-and-concepts talk built on diagrams rather than a demo, so expect a map of the idea, not a repository to clone.

## From tool to co-worker

Shubham opens with two points from Sam Altman's "Three Observations" essay: model intelligence scales with the compute, data and inference you give it, and the cost of a given level of AI falls by roughly ten times a year. His conclusion is that AI is moving from a passive helper in decisions to a virtual co-worker, and software engineering is where that shows first.

He then separates three things that often get blurred:

- **AI automation** runs fixed scripts with fixed rules (his example: a Zapier email integration).
- **AI workflows** manage multi-step processes with defined decision points (Netflix recommendations).
- **AI agents** reason their way to a solution with minimal human input (automated inventory and supply chain management).

That distinction is the most reusable slide in the talk. Plenty of products sold as agents are the middle one.

## What an agent is made of

The agent anatomy has six parts: a learning system, a goal framework, a reasoning engine, memory (short and long term), an interaction layer for APIs and responses, and a safety protocol with ethical constraints and validated outputs. The runtime flow follows: input processing, knowledge base, task planning, reasoning, tool calls through APIs, an execution engine with fallbacks and state, response generation, monitoring and a security layer with authentication, authorisation and audit logs.

Notice that audit logs already appear in the agent's own security layer. The blockchain half of the talk is about making those logs something other parties can trust.

## Where the ledger earns its keep

Shubham's blockchain primer covers the basics: a distributed ledger replicated across peer nodes, public, private and consortium variants, and proof of work or proof of stake for consensus. The properties he cares about are no single point of failure, data that can't be changed once recorded, and every participant seeing the same records.

He lists four reasons to combine the two:

- **Data integrity for AI**, since models are only as reliable as their inputs.
- **Coordination without a central authority**, when many agents from different owners must cooperate.
- **Smart contracts to enforce decisions**, so an agent's choice executes automatically and is harder to tamper with.
- **Auditability**, with agent decisions stored on-chain for later review.

The worked example is supply chain management. IoT sensors and enterprise systems feed AI agents, which raise insights and alerts. A smart contract records the resulting payment on the ledger, and manufacturers, suppliers, retailers, transport providers and warehouses all read the same copy as their source of truth.

## Who should watch

Architects weighing agents for multi-party processes, and blockchain engineers wondering where AI fits. If you want consensus trade-offs or gas costs, this talk stays above that level. Shubham closes with edge AI and federated learning as next steps, and a prediction about 2035 that you can judge for yourself.

Title: A deep learning field guide with a cybersecurity lens
Description: Chirag Gajiwala of Nutanix at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 tours reinforcement learning, transformers, TimeGPT, VAEs and graph neural networks for threat detection.
Body:
Security teams keep hearing that AI will find the attacker before the SIEM does. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Chirag Gajiwala, member of technical staff at Nutanix with more than eight years in data engineering, machine learning and cybersecurity, gave a guided tour of the deep learning families behind that promise and where each one fits in security work.

Know what you're getting: despite the chaos engineering framing in the title, the recording is a survey of model architectures, not a talk about failure injection. It works best as a primer for an engineer who wants to understand the vocabulary before evaluating AI-powered security tools.

## Reward, attention, convolution

Gajiwala starts with **reinforcement learning**: reward-based learning where a system improves by trial and error, unlike supervised or unsupervised models. Then the **transformer**, explained through its encoder-decoder structure and multi-head attention using translation as the example. His point on why transformers won is practical: they work in parallel, so they use GPUs efficiently and scale faster than CNNs or RNNs.

**Convolutional neural networks** get a walk through their building blocks (convolution, pooling to reduce dimensionality, fully connected layers, activation functions) with image tasks and obstacle detection for self-driving as the use cases. **Recurrent networks**, he notes, show up more in anomaly and pattern detection, which is where security comes in.

## Time series in a few lines

The most hands-on moment is TimeGPT from Nixtla, a pretrained transformer for time series forecasting. He shows how little code it takes: create the client with an API key, load a data frame from a URL or CSV, call forecast. For anyone who has hand-tuned a forecasting model for capacity planning or log volumes, that brevity is the pitch.

## Anomaly detection is where security fits

Generative models get a security angle. Variational autoencoders are, in his framing, especially useful for anomaly detection in cybersecurity, and he pairs them with RNNs for spotting unusual patterns. The advice is grounded: start with the tools you already run, a SIEM and the rest, and layer these models on top.

The same goes for AI-based threat detection in general. Attackers are starting to use AI to plan attacks such as DDoS, so detection needs to keep up, and AI can improve accuracy and cut false positives. But you have to train the model on your security data and compare its results against existing tools, he names Splunk and Exabeam, before trusting it. **Graph neural networks**, which model relationships between entities, are the family he expects to matter most for security monitoring over the next five to ten years.

## Work with compliance before you deploy

He returns twice to ethics and governance, which is the part security teams will appreciate. Before putting a model near production, work with your compliance team, make sure it isn't taking customer data or changing anything in your environment, and check it against your data governance framework. Multimodal AI and edge AI, running on local devices for speed and privacy, round out his look ahead, along with applications in drug discovery and personalised medicine.

## Who should watch

Security engineers and SREs who want a one-session overview of deep learning architectures before they evaluate AI-driven detection, and data engineers moving into security analytics. If you're after chaos experiments with AI in the loop, or already work with these models daily, this one is a refresher.

Title: How peer-to-peer networks find, route and reach their peers
Description: Akim Mamedov of 1tab at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 breaks P2P networks into protocols, discovery, transports and NAT traversal, with IPFS, Fluence and libp2p.
Body:
A peer-to-peer network is four hard problems wearing one name. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Akim Mamedov, lead software engineer at 1tab, took P2P apart into application protocols, peer discovery, transports and NAT traversal, then showed how IPFS, the Fluence network and the libp2p toolkit put those pieces back together.

It is a foundations talk, about twenty minutes, aimed at engineers who have used BitTorrent but never had to think about how the swarm finds itself.

## Equal peers, direct connections

Akim starts with the contrast to client-server. A server sets the rules, the API and the permissions, and clients either comply or don't connect. In a P2P network every member is equal and any peer can connect to any other.

The second property is subtler: peers talk directly. If A knows B and B knows C, A can't use B as a proxy to reach C. A asks B for C's address, then opens its own connection. That one rule shapes everything that follows, because every peer now needs a way to learn addresses and a way to actually get packets through.

## Discovery and routing are the real work

A new peer is useless until it finds others. Akim describes two common approaches: broadcasting through the network that a new peer has appeared so others contact it, or connecting to a known bootstrap peer and asking for its list of closest participants.

Routing is the follow-on problem. Knowing that a peer exists isn't the same as knowing how to reach it, so implementations keep a routing table with a graph-like structure to find a path through intermediate peers.

Underneath sit the transports. TCP and UDP do most of the lifting, QUIC layers on UDP, and WebTransport and WebRTC matter when peers live in browsers and move video.

## NAT is why your laptop needs a relay

The most practical section is NAT traversal. Your laptop on home Wi-Fi sits behind a router, so public peers can't reach it. You could configure the router to accept inbound connections, but Akim notes that is difficult for many users. The common fix is a publicly reachable relay peer: the laptop keeps a long-lived connection to it, and other peers send traffic through the relay, which forwards packets without interacting with them. Anyone who has debugged a home-lab port forward will nod.

## Three systems, one toolkit

The examples make the theory concrete:

- **IPFS**, the InterPlanetary File System, stores and serves files, websites and data across peers. Content held by many peers can be downloaded from all of them at once, the same trick BitTorrent uses, and it gets around per-country limits that a single central provider might impose.
- **Fluence** distributes compute instead of storage. Providers offer compute power, clients submit work, and the Aqua language lets you specify the execution model and choose which peer runs which code. Akim's pitch is independence from a central provider that can change its terms, plus an open market of providers.
- **libp2p** is the foundation many modern protocols build on, with ready implementations of addressing, peer identity, discovery, routing, transports, secure channels and stream multiplexing. If you ever plan to build your own protocol, he recommends at least reading its introduction first.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers curious about how decentralised storage and compute actually connect, and anyone evaluating IPFS or libp2p for a project. If you already know Kademlia tables and hole punching by heart, this one is a refresher.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Daniel Moya's [Decentralized Automation and RESTful Integration with Dimensigon](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Daniel_Moya_automation_decentralization_orchestration), from the same event, applies decentralisation to orchestration.

Title: Building your own web server in C# teaches you what Nginx hides
Description: Lucas Girardin at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 builds a .NET web server from a TCP listener up: connection limits, middleware, an admin API and per-module logs.
Body:
A web server is basically an infinite loop, until you have to run one. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Lucas Girardin, a cloud specialist who moved from software engineering into SRE work, showed how he built his own web server in C# on .NET, and why each feature he added (connection limits, a middleware pipeline, an admin API, module-aware logging) is a small lesson in how production servers behave.

The motivation is honest. Software engineers mostly build applications and features, not systems. Once his job shifted to monitoring and automating services, the systems underneath became the interesting part, and a web server is the right size: far simpler than a database, but with enough real problems to stay educational.

## Start with a socket and plain text

Step one is a TCP listener on an address and a port. Step two is answering in HTTP, which is easy to read and easy to parse: a status line, headers and a body, separated by blank lines. A hard-coded "hello world" response is enough to see curl accept it. Then you parse the request line and start routing.

Lucas also picked .NET for a practical reason: he wanted the server to run on Windows as well as Linux, the way Apache in a WAMP stack once did, and .NET lets the same C# run on both. Paths, metrics and scripting still differ per platform, handled behind abstractions.

## Connections are a budget

Connections consume resources, so the server has two thresholds. Below the first, it serves requests normally. Above it, it still accepts the connection but answers immediately with a 500, the cheapest path that still tells the client what happened. Past the second threshold, it closes new connections without a response. Brutal for clients, necessary for survival. That three-tier shape is a nice mental model for load shedding in any service.

## Everything interesting is middleware

Each accepted request goes through a pipeline: a chain of middleware that each take an HTTP context, do one job and call the next. His chain runs logger, authentication, directory, routing and a terminal middleware, built back to front. The router finds `index.html` under the web root, sets the MIME type, content length and status, and attaches the response to the context instead of sending it, because later middleware may still want to change it. Because every request has to pass through the chain, authentication or rate limiting slot in at one place.

## Operate it over HTTP, not SSH

Lucas wanted to manage the server remotely through endpoints, not by logging in to the host. So the server runs two independent modules: the web module on 8080 and an admin module on 4040, each with its own pipeline. The admin middleware exposes status, reload, restart and logs, protected with basic authentication (which he flags as fine for a demo, not for production without HTTPS). A script endpoint lists scripts in a folder and runs one by name, so admins aren't limited to the endpoints he anticipated.

## AsyncLocal keeps logs honest

Both modules are instances of the same class and share the logger middleware, so how does a log line know which module wrote it? The answer is a static execution-context class holding an `AsyncLocal` logger. Each module sets its own logger in its start method, child tasks inherit it, and any code running under that module logs with the right name. It is the cleanest .NET-specific idea in the talk.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers who use Kestrel, Nginx or Apache daily and want to know what they do, SREs who want a weekend project, and .NET developers curious about `AsyncLocal`. He closes with the challenges left on the table: caching, multiplexing, HTTPS, better auth and metrics.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Kazuki Higashiguchi's [HTTP Server on random available port in Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2022_Kazuki_Higashiguchi_http_server_on_random_available_port) is a short look at one listener detail.
- Sandeep Bhat's [Developing custom Load Balancer using Envoy](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Sandeep_Bhat_custom_load_balancer_envoy) is the next layer out.
- Hamida Rebai's [Architecting .NET Microservices in a Docker Ecosystem](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Hamida_Rebai_net_microservices_docker_ecosystem) puts .NET services into containers.

Title: Picking IaaS, PaaS or SaaS for enterprise analytics, a primer
Description: Prithvi Raju Rudraraju of IT America at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on matching cloud service models to analytics needs, and keeping cost and compliance in check.
Body:
The service model you pick decides how much of your analytics stack you still have to babysit. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Prithvi Raju Rudraraju, SAP ABAP/BW/HANA consultant at IT America, walked through infrastructure, platform and software as a service as three different trades between control and convenience, and argued that governance is what keeps any of them from turning into a surprise bill.

This is an introductory talk, and it says so by its structure: definitions first, use cases second, challenges and governance last. If you already run a data platform on AWS or Azure, treat it as a checklist for the people you are trying to convince, not as new material for yourself.

## Three models, three levels of control

Prithvi frames the models by what you stop owning. With IaaS (his examples are Amazon EC2 and Google Compute Engine) you rent virtual machines and storage, keep full say over operating systems, security settings and performance tuning, and stop buying hardware up front. You pay for what you use, and you scale up for a busy period and back down when it ends.

PaaS takes the environment off your hands too. He points to Azure App Service and AWS Elastic Beanstalk: preconfigured runtimes and tools so the team ships the pipeline instead of building the platform under it. The talk ties PaaS to automation of data pipeline tasks and to collaboration across teams in different time zones.

SaaS is the far end, where the application itself arrives ready. Salesforce and Google Analytics are the examples, with built-in visualisation and AI-assisted insight for people who want answers rather than infrastructure.

The figures on the slides (PaaS cutting time to insight by up to 40%, SaaS lifting operational efficiency by 30% or more, 83% of enterprise data workloads in the cloud by 2025) come without much context in the talk, so read them as the direction of travel rather than benchmarks.

## Analytics is the reason, not the platform

The use cases are the familiar three: predictive modelling for demand and market trends, real-time pattern recognition for fraud detection, and behavioural segmentation for marketing. None of them needs a particular cloud. What they need is data in one place, compute on demand, and the ability to scale when the quarter-end report lands on the same night as the batch job.

That is the useful lens for an enterprise team: decide which of these workloads you actually run, then pick the service model per workload rather than one model for the whole company.

## Governance is where the money goes

The section most worth your time is the one on challenges. Prithvi names three: security of sensitive data, compliance across jurisdictions and data sovereignty rules, and cost. On cost he is blunt that without planning resources you may end up spending more budget on cloud services than you expected, a lesson most finance teams learn from an invoice.

His answer is a governance framework in layers: foundation policies and standards at the bottom, continuous monitoring and compliance tracking of usage patterns in the middle, cost and performance optimisation on top. Agility and control have to be balanced on purpose, with clear accountability for who owns which resources.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving an SAP or BI estate toward managed cloud services, managers who need vocabulary for a migration proposal, and anyone new to the IaaS/PaaS/SaaS split. Platform engineers who already run FinOps reviews can skip to the governance part.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Bhaskar Goyal's [Cloud-Native AI at Scale: Architectural Patterns for Enterprise Success](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Bhaskar_Goyal_enterprise_cloud_patterns) covers the architecture layer above the service models.

Title: Mobile app speed is a retention problem, so measure it like one
Description: Jaspreet Kumar of Microsoft at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on data-driven mobile performance with smaller apps, caching, APM, anomaly detection and A/B tests.
Body:
Users don't file bug reports about a slow launch screen; they uninstall. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Jaspreet Kumar, Lead Software Engineer at Microsoft, makes the case for treating mobile app performance as a data problem: measure launch times, latency, frame rates and crashes continuously, then optimise where the numbers say users are hurting.

The talk is listed as "Chaos Engineering in Mobile Apps: Building Resilient Systems Through Controlled Failure". The session as recorded covers data-driven mobile performance optimisation and monitoring rather than failure injection, so watch it for the performance playbook.

## Performance is a business metric

Jaspreet opens with the numbers that get performance work funded. He cites that "53 percent of users abandon apps that take over 3 seconds to load", that every 100 milliseconds of extra load time can cost around 7% in conversions, and that users who hit delays are far less likely to buy again. Ratings follow the same curve in his figures: well-performing apps average 4.5 stars or more, slower ones around 3.5. The recording doesn't name the studies behind these, so treat them as industry rules of thumb.

## Four optimisations before anything clever

The practical core is a short list most teams can start on this sprint:

- **Reduce app size.** Compress assets, optimise images and split code so the first download is smaller.
- **Lazy loading.** Defer non-critical resources and load progressively, aiming for sub-second first screens.
- **Data caching.** Cache on the client with service workers and local storage to cut API calls and keep the app usable offline.
- **Efficient storage.** Optimise database queries, compress data and index what's read often to keep the memory footprint down.

None of this is new, which is rather the point: the gains come from doing the boring things systematically, and knowing which one matters for your app.

## Measure first, with tools that already exist

For knowing which one matters, he points to application performance monitoring platforms such as Firebase Performance Monitoring and New Relic, tracking cold and warm launch times, API response latency, frame rates and crash frequency, with dashboards and automated alerts on top. The analysis layer applies statistics and machine learning to that telemetry to find patterns, predict bottlenecks and put a return on each optimisation.

From there the talk moves to predictive monitoring: models trained on historical performance data that flag anomalies across sessions, device types and network conditions, and alert when metrics drift from their baseline before users feel it. He quotes large reductions in incidents and crash rates for teams that adopt it; as with the opening figures, the recording presents them without naming where they come from.

## Ship it in small, testable steps

The closing advice is iterative: change one thing, A/B test two or three variations at once, and watch load time, memory use and engagement along with direct user feedback. Each cycle compounds on the last. The final slides tie it back to the business case with figures for monthly active users and revenue growth from better performance and fewer crashes.

## Who should watch

Mobile developers and engineering managers who need a structured checklist for performance work, or ammunition to get it prioritised. It's a high-level overview without code or a worked case study, and if you came for chaos experiments on mobile clients, this recording doesn't run any.

Title: From on-prem ETL to cloud-native data integration
Description: Srujan Reddy Anugu of ADM at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on how data integration moved from on-prem ETL to cloud-native platforms, and what to get right.
Body:
Every enterprise has a pipeline that started as a nightly ETL job and is now load-bearing. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Srujan Reddy Anugu, a technology manager at ADM with 20 years across SAP, cloud and integration work, traced how data integration moved from on-premises ETL to hybrid and then cloud-native platforms, and which practices make the move pay off.

The talk is a short, statistics-dense overview. Its value is the map: which tools belong to which era, what the cloud platforms changed, and where governance and real-time processing fit.

## Three eras, with names attached

Srujan anchors each stage in real products, which helps.

- **On-premises.** SAP Data Services, Informatica ETL, Dell Boomi and SnapLogic on your own hardware: reliable, but expensive up front and capped by the boxes you bought.
- **Hybrid.** A mix of local and cloud, which he says about 89.3% of Fortune 500 companies run, with tools such as Apache NiFi and AWS Glue supporting hybrid scenarios.
- **Cloud-native.** AWS Glue, Azure Data Factory, Google Cloud Dataflow, SAP Datasphere and SAP's BTP integration tooling.

He then sketches the market: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud together holding close to 80% of cloud integration, with Azure growing fastest over the last five years and Google Cloud strongest in AI and ML.

## What actually changes in the cloud

Three benefits carry the argument. Elastic scaling: on-premises, scaling up is a project with downtime, whereas in the cloud it can happen automatically under load. Global reach: provider regions put data closer to users and improve reliability. And cost, where he highlights security spend in particular, citing reductions of nearly 60% against on-premises equivalents.

The rest of the talk is about practice. Containerisation, orchestration and automated testing in the deployment pipeline, he says, cut deployment failures sharply and speed up recovery through automated rollback. Microservices break monolithic integration apps into independently scalable services.

## Governance is part of the architecture

Srujan treats data quality as a design concern, not an afterthought: automated validation to catch bad data before it spreads, compliance tooling to shorten audits, and metadata management to speed up discovery and lineage. The specific percentages he cites are from his slides and should be read as indicative, but the order is right. If you cannot say where a field came from, you cannot trust the dashboard built on it.

For real-time processing, he points to low-latency event processing, high-throughput streaming and edge processing as the reason OLTP and OLAP-capable systems are now built together.

## Common problems, named

The challenges section is short and useful: data silos (addressed with schema matching and mapping), performance (query optimisation frameworks), and security and compliance (multi-layer security frameworks). His look ahead covers AI-assisted integration development, automated metadata matching that turns weeks of mapping work into hours, and real-time data quality monitoring.

## Who should watch

Architects and integration leads, especially in SAP-heavy enterprises, planning a move from on-premises ETL to cloud services. Engineers wanting pipeline code or a reference architecture will need a more hands-on follow-up.

Title: Multi-tenancy, explained by a product manager who has to pay for it
Description: Waqas Khan of Kwalee at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on moving SaaS to multi-tenant, with shared instances, isolated data and feature flags.
Body:
Onboarding customer number 20,000 should not mean provisioning server number 20,000. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Waqas Khan, a lead technical product manager at Kwalee and a software engineer by training, made the product-side case for multi-tenant architecture: one shared code base and infrastructure, data isolated per tenant, and the cost and maintenance savings that follow.

It is a product management talk more than an engineering one, and Waqas says so: he deliberately skips database security internals. What you get is the business logic of multi-tenancy, a few case studies and a practical list of things that go wrong.

## One instance, many isolated tenants

The definition is simple. In single tenancy, each customer gets its own instances and its own database. In multi-tenancy, customers share instances and infrastructure while their data stays isolated. His worked example: an ERP product serving 20,000 customers with identical features but their own branding. Instead of a separate set of EC2 instances per customer, you keep one code base, scale it horizontally as load grows, and give each new customer its own isolated data space, which he notes AWS database services can provide.

The payoff he lists: lower costs, easier maintenance and updates, and faster scaling. A bug gets fixed once and rolls out to everyone.

## The case studies

Waqas cites Grandstream's migration from single to multi-tenant setup, where new tenant setup time went from 232 hours to 106, client migration took under 76 hours, and bug fix times dropped from five hours to between one and two and a half. He also points to Salesforce, Shopify and Uber as well-known examples of the model, noting Salesforce has not published figures. These are his reports of public material rather than Kwalee internals.

## What can bite

He is direct about the risks. Data isolation and security are the big one; he argues modern encryption and data security tooling have reduced that risk to the point where large players are comfortable with it, but it remains the thing no customer will compromise on. Performance management and noisy-neighbour resource allocation come next, then scaling. And balancing per-tenant customisation against simplicity is a constant tension, because there is only one instance to keep healthy. Without solid backups and a fallback plan, that one instance is a single point of failure.

## Feature flags become infrastructure

His best-practice list (security first, performance tuning, backups, role-based access) ends with the point most worth stealing: once hundreds of thousands of customers share one deployment, feature flags are how you give some tenants a feature and not others. They need to be properly implemented, managed and optimised in the code base, whether built in-house or bought from a third party, which he frames as a product decision.

## Who should watch

Product managers and engineering leads deciding whether, or when, to go multi-tenant, and founders who want the cost argument laid out. Engineers looking for tenant isolation patterns at the database or Kubernetes level should pair it with something more technical.

Title: Software-defined networking as the control plane for IoT and 5G
Description: Sai Charan Madugula of the University of Central Missouri at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on SDN, 5G network slicing, smart grids and deployment hurdles.
Body:
Configuring every switch, router and firewall by hand was tolerable when a network had dozens of boxes. With billions of IoT sensors and 5G slices, it isn't. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Sai Charan Madugula of the University of Central Missouri gave an overview of software-defined networking (SDN) and why separating the control plane from the data plane is what makes IoT and 5G networks manageable.

This is an introduction, suited to software engineers who meet networking from the application side. It explains the concepts and the use cases rather than walking through a controller configuration.

## Split the brain from the muscle

The key idea is old in software and still new to many networks. In traditional networking each device decides and forwards on its own, configured one at a time, which is slow and error-prone. SDN separates the control plane, which decides where traffic should go, from the data plane, which forwards packets according to those decisions. Centralised software controllers then manage, optimise and automate the whole network.

Madugula's list of benefits follows from that: central control that cuts manual configuration and human error, programmability so the network adjusts to real-time conditions, automation, and lower cost. Changes that take weeks on a traditional network become policy updates.

## Slices for different jobs

The 5G section is the most concrete. SDN enables network slicing, where an operator carves virtual networks with different guarantees out of one physical network. His three examples: a slice for autonomous vehicles tuned for ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC), a slice for enhanced mobile broadband serving 4K video and cloud gaming, and a slice for massive IoT such as smart meters and environmental sensors.

SDN also assigns spectrum and bandwidth to match real-time demand, from low-power sensors to AR/VR, and optimises paths to cut latency for remote surgery, smart factories and synchronised robotics. For IoT in general it prioritises critical flows and rebalances bandwidth so millions of devices can share a network.

## Where it shows up

He walks through smart cities (traffic management, air-quality sensing, emergency response), industrial IoT (predictive maintenance, monitoring 10,000-plus sensors on a factory floor), vehicle-to-everything communication, and smart grids, where telemetry, load balancing and anomaly detection isolate faults quickly. The talk attaches percentages to several of these (up to 30 percent less traffic congestion, for one) without naming the deployments behind them.

## The hard parts

The talk is honest that SDN has its own problems. Integrating with legacy hardware networks needs compatibility strategies. Controllers become a latency bottleneck if they can't process data in real time. And large deployments need distributed controllers and a hierarchical architecture to scale.

The proposed answers are edge computing to move processing closer to devices, open protocols such as OpenFlow for interoperability, and software-defined security that builds threat awareness into the network itself. Looking ahead, he expects AI-driven, self-healing networks that predict failures before users notice.

## Who should watch

Developers and SREs who work on IoT platforms, telecom-adjacent systems or edge deployments and want a primer on what SDN and slicing mean for their traffic. Network engineers who already run SDN will find it a high-level recap.

Title: Two-tier neural ranking for recommendations under 50 ms
Description: Vedant Agarwal of Walmart Global Tech at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on L1 embedding retrieval, L2 sequence re-ranking and the ops that keep it under 50 ms.
Body:
A recommendation that arrives after the user has scrolled past is a recommendation nobody sees. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Vedant Agarwal, senior software engineer in search at Walmart Global Tech, explained the two-tier neural ranking design behind real-time personalization and the operational work that keeps end-to-end responses under 50 milliseconds.

The talk is a clear architectural overview of the pattern, with the infrastructure around it, rather than a disclosure of a specific production system. The figures he quotes are framed as observed results and findings from studies, and that's how they're reported here.

## Why real time is hard

Agarwal names three problems. Clickstreams and transaction logs are noisy and inconsistent, which hurts model accuracy. Scale means millions of concurrent interactions without losing responsiveness. And model drift never stops: a seasonal shift changes behaviour faster than a quarterly retrain can follow.

## Split retrieval from precision

The core idea is decoupling. **L1, candidate generation**, projects user behaviour and item attributes into a shared embedding space and uses approximate nearest neighbour search to pull a broad candidate set fast. His example: a corpus of more than a million items filtered to candidates in under 10 milliseconds. The point of L1 is to be cheap enough that L2 only has to look at a short list.

**L2, precision re-ranking**, uses sequence models such as LSTMs or transformers to combine long-term history with the current session. Attention lets recent clicks weigh more than old ones, so the ranking follows what the user is doing right now. He cites an increase in click-through rate of about 20 percent from this kind of dynamic re-ranking.

It's the same reason search engines don't run the expensive model over the whole index: you spend the compute where the shortlist is.

## Latency is an engineering budget

Getting under 50 ms end to end means trading some model complexity for speed without losing quality. In the talk, optimised inference pipelines with asynchronous processing and caching take latency from around 70 ms down to 45 ms. Auto-scaling and load balancing, watched in real time, keep it there under load.

The surrounding stack is familiar to anyone who runs streaming systems: Kafka and Apache Flink to ingest clicks and purchases continuously, microservices in Docker on Kubernetes for modular scaling and fault isolation, live feature engineering on session attributes (normalisation, feature crosses, embeddings), and Prometheus and Grafana for alerting on anomalies.

## Shipping models without breaking the page

Deployment gets its own section. KPIs and automated anomaly alerts catch deviations early, scheduled retraining deals with drift, blue-green and rolling deployments avoid downtime, canary releases on Kubernetes test updates before a full rollout, and A/B tests tied into CI/CD measure each change's real impact. On the business side, he reports outcomes such as a 15 percent increase in conversion and a 25 percent improvement in CTR.

He ends with what's next: multimodal personalization that mixes product images with text, federated learning that keeps data local for privacy and latency, and hybrid systems that pair rules with models for better interpretability.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into recommendation or search ranking who want the standard two-stage architecture explained in one sitting, and platform engineers who will be asked to keep such a system fast. ML researchers will find the model section high level.

Title: From batch reports to real-time product insights, in five steps
Description: Nimit Bhardwaj of Booking.com at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on cloud-native real-time analytics with Kafka, Flink, data lakes and serverless compute.
Body:
A dashboard that refreshes overnight answers yesterday's question. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Nimit Bhardwaj of Booking.com gave a compact introduction to cloud-native analytics: why batch-based systems leave a gap between when data is generated and when anyone can act on it, which building blocks close that gap, and a five-step path for getting there without ripping out what you have.

This is a short talk, around ten minutes, pitched as an orientation. It suits product managers and engineers who are new to streaming, or anyone who needs a clean mental model to explain why the analytics stack should change.

## The gap is the problem

Nimit's starting point is scale: he cites roughly 328 million terabytes of data generated every day. Traditional analytics systems, built around batch processing, mean decisions get made on historical rather than live data. The cost of that gap shows up as delayed decisions, missed opportunities and inefficiency. His examples of why speed matters are familiar ones: recommendations at Netflix and Spotify, banks that must act on a suspicious transaction immediately rather than hours later, and product teams tuning features from live user feedback.

## Four building blocks

He names the stack plainly:

1. **Event streaming** with Kafka or AWS Kinesis to move large volumes of live data.
2. **Serverless compute** that scales automatically, so you pay for processing only when it runs.
3. **Data lakes and warehouses** as the storage foundation for structured and unstructured data.
4. **AI and ML** on top, turning raw events into forecasts, risk signals and personalisation.

Containers and microservices make the pieces modular; streaming is what makes them real-time.

## Uber as the worked example

The case study is Uber's dynamic pricing. When a big event ends and demand spikes, the pricing engine adjusts in real time to balance riders and drivers. Nimit describes Kafka streaming ride requests, Flink processing them as they arrive, and Databricks for deeper analysis, with the results being smarter driver allocation, shorter waits and better pricing. It is a well-known public example rather than Booking.com internals, but it shows the whole pipeline in one picture.

## A modernisation path, not a rewrite

The most reusable slide is the roadmap. Identify your data sources (customer interactions, IoT devices, transaction logs). Add real-time ingestion with Kafka or Kinesis. Land the data in a scalable cloud data lake. Process it with serverless compute and ML. Surface results through real-time dashboards and alerts so teams can act immediately. His framing is strategic modernisation, not rip-and-replace.

He is honest about what goes wrong: latency when pipelines are not tuned, costs that climb when real-time systems are poorly architected, and security and compliance in regulated sectors such as banking and healthcare. The trends he expects next are edge computing moving analytics closer to sensors, more autonomous decision-making, and multi-cloud as the default to avoid lock-in.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people taking their first look at streaming analytics, or anyone who needs a ten-minute framing before a bigger architecture discussion. Experienced streaming engineers will find it introductory.

Title: What a data lakehouse fixes, layer by layer
Description: Siddhartha Parimi of Dell Technologies at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on lakehouses with Iceberg, Delta Lake and Spark, ACID tables and schema evolution.
Body:
A data lake without governance becomes a data swamp, and a warehouse without flexibility becomes a bottleneck. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Siddhartha Parimi of Dell Technologies explained how the lakehouse architecture combines the two: open table formats such as Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake on cheap object storage, a metadata layer for schema and catalogue, and Apache Spark and SQL engines on top.

It is an explainer, clear and well-paced, aimed at engineers and data leads who need to understand why lakehouses are being adopted and what each layer does. There are no live demos.

## Two architectures, two failure modes

Siddhartha frames the problem with a retailer handling structured purchase records, semi-structured web logs and unstructured customer reviews. A traditional warehouse forces the data into a rigid schema before analysis, which delays insight and adds cost, and struggles with semi-structured and unstructured formats. A data lake takes everything raw and cheap, but without governance it becomes unmanageable and hard to query. Legacy systems on top of that slow down as volumes grow.

His library analogy is a good one to borrow: the lake is a warehouse full of unsorted books, the warehouse is a tidy reading room with limited shelves, and the lakehouse aims to be the whole library, catalogued.

## Four layers that make it work

- **Storage:** open formats, Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake, over scalable storage.
- **Metadata:** schema evolution, indexing and cataloguing, so data can be found and queried.
- **Processing:** Apache Spark and SQL engines for both batch and real-time work.
- **Governance and security:** role-based access, encryption and audit logging.

The point of the combination: lake economics and support for every data type, with warehouse properties such as performance, schema enforcement and ACID guarantees.

## ACID is the feature that matters

The section worth the price of admission is on transactions. Plain data lakes do not guarantee consistency; lakehouse table formats add atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. His example is an e-commerce system processing many orders per second, where ACID guarantees mean a failure does not lose or duplicate orders. Schema evolution gets the same treatment: plan, implement without downtime, validate compatibility, monitor. That is how new data sources arrive without breaking existing pipelines.

## In-place processing beats copying data around

He also argues that lakehouses shrink the ETL tax: ingest directly from sources, transform in place with SQL and Python, and make data available to analytics immediately. One example he gives is a healthcare company whose patient-data processing went from 24 hours to 30 minutes after removing redundant ETL steps. He cites cost reductions of up to 30% and much faster queries from indexing and caching, presented as typical results rather than a Dell benchmark.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects weighing a move from a classic warehouse or a sprawling lake, and managers who need the concepts before a platform decision. If you already run Iceberg in production, this will be familiar ground.

Title: Azure Site Recovery, from replication to runbooks
Description: Somaning Turwale of Microsoft at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on how Azure Site Recovery replicates VMs, hits low RTO and RPO targets, and how to plan DR.
Body:
Disaster recovery used to mean backup tapes and a second data centre you hoped you would never visit. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Somaning Turwale of Microsoft gave a compact tour of Azure Site Recovery (ASR): how it replicates workloads from Azure, VMware, Hyper-V and physical servers, what recovery objectives it targets, and what a sane DR plan around it looks like.

It is a short product-focused session from a Microsoft engineer about a Microsoft service, so expect the Azure view of the world. Within that scope it is well organised and quick.

## Three eras of DR in one slide

Somaning opens with history. In the early 2000s, recovery was manual (tapes, secondary data centres) and could take 24 hours or more. Virtualisation with Hyper-V and VMware cut that to hours and made testing easier. Cloud DR adds fast failover, recovery time objectives measured in minutes and orchestration, without running a second site yourself.

## How it plugs into what you run

ASR's architecture depends on the source. Azure VMs need no extra infrastructure: an agent on the VM replicates to the target region. VMware and physical servers need an on-premises appliance plus a mobility agent on each machine. Hyper-V uses the ASR provider. The point is that one service covers mixed estates.

Replication combines several techniques: real-time block replication to keep recovery point objectives near zero, compression and deduplication to cut network overhead, delta sync so only changed data moves, and VSS-integrated snapshots so applications such as SQL Server and SAP stay consistent when you fail over.

## The numbers, with the usual caveat

Somaning cites enterprise workloads achieving 15-minute RTOs and RPOs of around 30 seconds, customer deployments with a 76% reduction in downtime, DR cost reductions of 40 to 60% thanks to pay-as-you-go pricing and no secondary site, and protection scaling to 10,000 instances. These are vendor-reported figures and will depend heavily on your bandwidth, change rate and application design.

## The plan matters more than the product

The most transferable part is the planning framework, which applies to any DR tool:

- Assess workloads and decide what is truly mission-critical.
- Validate infrastructure: bandwidth, latency and initial sync.
- Test failover regularly: planned, unplanned and test failovers, so it works when it matters.
- Write recovery runbooks with step-by-step instructions for the team.
- Train people and wire alerts into monitoring (ASR integrates with Azure Monitor and Azure Automation).

A DR plan that has never been rehearsed is a theory. His recommendations amount to rehearsing it until it is boring.

He closes with where DR is heading: AI that predicts failures, post-quantum cryptography for protected data, edge-to-cloud recovery for IoT workloads, and deeper Kubernetes integration.

## Who should watch

Ops and infrastructure teams on Azure, or with VMware and Hyper-V estates considering Azure as a recovery target, who want a quick overview before reading the docs. Teams on other clouds can still take the planning checklist.

Title: AWS SES is simple until you send 500,000 emails a day
Description: Dmytro Hlotenko of APA-IT at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on SES domain setup, deliverability, rate limiting with Step Functions and using SES events.
Body:
Amazon Simple Email Service sends the email. Everything else (domain alignment, reputation, throttling, knowing whether the message arrived) is on you. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Dmytro Hlotenko, cloud engineer at APA-IT in Vienna and AWS Community Builder, shared what running SES for one of Austria's largest media groups taught him, at a volume of over 500,000 emails a day.

It is a long, practitioner-heavy session with real opinions, a few war stories and an architecture he built himself. If you have ever had a well-formed transactional email vanish into a spam folder, this is your talk.

## Verify the domain, and do it within 72 hours

Dmytro's setup advice is specific. Verify a domain rather than individual addresses. When you create the identity, the DKIM records you are given expire if not validated within 72 hours. Use Easy DKIM so Amazon manages and rotates the keys; at his scale, with verifications for hundreds of customers, bringing your own keys is not worth it. Set a custom MAIL FROM domain and SPF so Gmail and Microsoft 365 see aligned headers, and add DMARC, starting with a percentage of mail while you debug. Put the SES configuration on a subdomain to keep it isolated from the domain your employees send from, which many enterprise security policies require anyway.

Two smaller tips stood out. Test alignment with mail-tester.com before production. And Apple's private email relay bounces SES mail by default until you register your sending domain in the Apple developer console; if you missed it, the bounced relay addresses sit in your suppression list and need a Lambda to clean up.

Getting out of the sandbox is its own skill: explain the use case, show a sample email, include an unsubscribe link, and do not try to fool support.

## The shared pool is shared reputation

By default SES sends from shared IP pools, so you share reputation with other senders. Dmytro's rule of thumb is that below about 100,000 emails a day the shared pool is fine. Above that, dedicated IPs give you control, but you then own blocklist monitoring (SES does not do it for you) and IP warm-up, starting with a couple of thousand emails a week and climbing. For one customer he split sending across SES accounts per region, mixing shared and dedicated IPs.

## Never call SendEmail naked

The core of the talk is rate limiting. Calling the send API directly works until you grow and start hitting throttling, and then emails quietly go missing. His reading of the limit: it counts recipients per second, so with a limit of 32 you could send one email to 30 recipients and another to 2 in the same second.

He walks through three escalating patterns:

1. **Chunking in the app.** Split the limit across workers (two pods at 15 each for a limit of 30) and pace calls with a leaky bucket or Resilience4j. Fine for stable, single-recipient sending; fragile under autoscaling.
2. **SQS plus a dead-letter queue, with Lambda sending.** Sending moves out of every application into one cloud-level service, with retries for free.
3. **A Step Functions "heartbeat".** EventBridge triggers a state machine every second, which reads the queued recipients and adjusts Lambda concurrency so each second fills the send rate without exceeding it. A broadcast to about 900 customers that used to take minutes now takes seconds.

He credits published work from several AWS community members as inputs to that design, including an article by Dennis Traub on precisely timed Lambda triggering with Step Functions.

## Events are the product

Configuration sets publish delivery, bounce, complaint, open and click events. Dmytro routes them through SNS and a small Lambda into CloudWatch for alarms, metric filters and Logs Insights, stores message IDs so applications can track each email's status, and uses QuickSight dashboards so non-technical colleagues can see failing deliveries. One app even shows users a banner asking them to fix their address when their mail bounces.

## Who should watch

Cloud and backend engineers who own transactional or bulk email on AWS, and anyone about to request an SES production limit increase. The rate-limiting section alone is worth the time if your app calls SES directly.

Title: A production-ready AWS app for about $3 a month
Description: Maksymilian Kalek of Perelyn at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on a cheap AWS stack with S3, CloudFront, Cognito, Lambda Powertools and Postgres on EC2.
Body:
The cheapest AWS resource is the one that is not running. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Maksymilian Kalek, a full-stack AI software engineer at Perelyn, showed the stack his team uses to run real applications for pennies, and closed with an AWS bill for an app in its MVP phase that came to about $3 for the month.

It is a practical, opinionated talk for indie developers, startups, side projects and any cost-conscious team building an MVP. Maksymilian is clear that a multinational will not notice the savings; a two-person team will.

## The stack, from the browser down

The architecture is deliberately modular, and he contrasts it with AWS Amplify, which he finds locks you into a specific service rather than just a vendor.

- **Deploy:** GitHub Actions for pipelines and AWS CDK for infrastructure as code, so nobody clicks around the console.
- **Frontend:** a React build in an S3 bucket behind CloudFront, which gives you HTTPS and global caching without a custom domain, priced per traffic volume you are unlikely to hit.
- **Auth:** Cognito, called from the frontend with the Amplify JavaScript libraries (not the Amplify service, he is careful to point out).
- **API:** API Gateway as a proxy and authorisation layer in front of a single Lambda.
- **Data:** DynamoDB where it fits, and PostgreSQL on a small EC2 instance where you need SQL.

## Lambda Powertools beats a wall of if-statements

When API Gateway proxies every request to one Lambda, something has to route by method and path. Maksymilian admits he once did that with a long chain of if-else checks on path strings and regrets it. Running Flask or FastAPI inside Lambda through wrapper libraries works, but he calls it a messy workaround that drags in a framework built for long-running servers.

His answer is AWS Lambda Powertools for Python: Flask-style route decorators designed for Lambda's event model, plus logging, tracing, validation, parsing and typing. Event handling is his favourite feature, and the one that makes a single-Lambda API maintainable.

The trade-offs he lists are honest: cold starts of a couple of seconds for large functions that have been idle, stateless execution, and deployment size limits.

## Skip RDS, run Postgres yourself

The database advice is the spiciest. DynamoDB is his default: pay per request and storage, low latency, a flexible schema (keep the model in your application code; migrations become Python scripts). When you need relational data, RDS costs at least 15 to 20 a month even while idle. A small self-managed EC2 instance running PostgreSQL costs a few dollars a month and can host extras such as vector stores. The price is that backups and maintenance are your job, which he thinks is worth it for low-traffic apps once it is set up.

## The bill

The closing slide is an AWS bill for one of Perelyn's applications, totalling about $3 for the month. Maksymilian's caveat is fair: more traffic means a bigger bill, but nothing like a production RDS cluster unless you suddenly scale to hundreds of thousands of active users. His rule: use serverless services as much as possible, except the ones that charge you around the clock just for existing.

## Who should watch

Builders of MVPs, side projects and internal tools on AWS, and anyone whose RDS line item is larger than their traffic justifies. If you run at enterprise scale with strict operational requirements, the self-hosted Postgres advice will not apply to you.

Title: Following one packet through Amazon EKS, hop by hop
Description: Dumlu Timuralp of AWS at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 traces pod, Service, NLB and ALB traffic in EKS through routing tables, iptables and the VPC CNI.
Body:
When an outage sits between the network team and the platform team, the person who can draw the packet's path wins. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Dumlu Timuralp, a Solutions Architect at AWS with a networking background at Nortel, Brocade and VMware, walked a packet through Amazon EKS from pod to pod, through every Kubernetes Service type, and finally in from the internet via Route 53 and an Application Load Balancer.

This is a proper packet walk: routing tables, ARP entries, MAC rewrites, NAT at each hop. He states the views are his own, observed with public tools, and deliberately shows the least optimal paths to make the mechanics visible.

## The VPC CNI gives pods real VPC addresses

The Kubernetes network model requires every pod to have its own IP and to reach other pods without NAT. Kubernetes leaves the wiring to CNI plugins, and on EKS that is the Amazon VPC CNI. It assigns pod IPs from the VPC CIDR as secondary IPs (or prefixes) on the node's ENIs, adding ENIs as the node fills up, and connects each pod's network namespace to the host with a veth pair.

The detail that makes people squint: inside the pod, eth0 has a /32 address and a default gateway of 169.254.1.1, with a static ARP entry that resolves to the host-side veth's MAC address. That is how all pod traffic ends up in the node's routing stack.

## Secondary ENIs take the long way round

Dumlu's most useful packet walk is about policy-based routing. Traffic arriving for a pod goes through the main routing table to the right veth. Traffic leaving a pod whose IP lives on a secondary ENI matches a separate routing table with one entry: the default gateway out of that ENI. So the reply to a pod on the same subnet still goes via the VPC router. It works, but it is the kind of thing that surprises you during a packet capture at 2am.

## Services: iptables does not care where the pod is

For a ClusterIP Service, kube-proxy watches the API and programs a virtual IP and iptables rules on every node. Traffic to the VIP is destination-NATed to a backing pod picked round robin, and the flow is marked so the reply can be source-NATed back to the VIP. The key point he stresses: iptables does not prefer local pods, so a request can cross nodes even when a matching pod sits right next to the client. He notes kube-proxy can also run on IPVS or eBPF, and that Kubernetes DNS is itself just another ClusterIP Service.

NodePort builds on that with an extra port on every node, and adds source NAT so replies come back the same way. A LoadBalancer Service with an NLB in instance mode registers every node as healthy, including nodes without a backing pod, so traffic can trombone from the NLB to a node and then to another node. In the cloud, he points out, that can mean cross-AZ hops, added latency and data transfer charges.

## Two fixes, in increasing order of directness

The first is `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on the Service: an extra health check means the NLB only sends traffic to nodes with local pods, and the client IP survives because the node no longer source-NATs. The second is the AWS Load Balancer Controller with target type IP, where pods themselves become load balancer targets and neither NodePort nor iptables is involved. The trade-off he flags is ELB target group quotas for very large Services. For NLB, client IP preservation is a separate attribute.

## Ingress, end to end

The finale stitches it together: Route 53 answers an alias record with the ALB's public IPs, the internet gateway translates the chosen public IP to the ALB's private address in that AZ, and the ALB, which always source-NATs (use X-Forwarded-For for the client IP), forwards to a pod, possibly in another AZ because cross-zone load balancing is on by default. Outbound, the VPC CNI source-NATs pod traffic to the node's primary IP before the internet gateway maps it to a public one.

## Who should watch

Anyone who operates EKS and has ever said "it's the network" without being sure. Network engineers moving into Kubernetes will find the vocabulary maps cleanly onto what they know.

Title: The case for running mission-critical SAP on Microsoft Azure
Description: Lurduma Reddy Thirumala Reddy of Intone Networks at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on HANA M-series VMs, Entra ID SSO, Power Platform and TCO for SAP on Azure.
Body:
If your company's general ledger runs on SAP, moving it to the cloud is less a migration than a heart transplant. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Lurduma Reddy Thirumala Reddy, a senior SAP consultant at Intone Networks and an SAP Basis and HANA administrator with more than 17 years of experience, made the business case for running mission-critical SAP workloads on Microsoft Azure.

Set expectations accordingly: this is an overview of Azure's SAP offering and the benefits Microsoft and its customers report, not an engineering walkthrough of a specific migration. It's useful as a map of which Azure pieces matter for SAP and why.

## What runs where

The talk sorts SAP workloads into three groups. SAP HANA runs on Azure's M-series VMs, built for memory-intensive databases. SAP NetWeaver applications (ERP, SCM, CRM and the rest of the Business Suite) run on certified infrastructure. S/4HANA is positioned as the future-proof target with real-time analytics and automation, with a reduced total cost of ownership on Azure.

The availability story leans on redundant data centres, availability zones, automated failover and disaster recovery. One practical point that gets less airtime than it deserves: elastic scaling earns its keep during month-end and year-end close, when SAP suddenly wants far more CPU and memory than the other 28 days.

## The integrations are the real draw

For a team already on Microsoft, the strongest argument is the neighbourhood. Thirumala Reddy highlights three integrations:

- **Microsoft Entra ID** for single sign-on across the SAP estate and centralised identity governance.
- **Power Platform** for dashboards, workflow automation and mobile apps on top of SAP data without heavy coding.
- **Azure Integration Services**, with pre-built connectors to more than 1,000 enterprise applications for real-time data sync.

He also covers the compliance portfolio (more than 90 standards, including GDPR, HIPAA and SOC 2 Type 2), encryption and threat monitoring through Azure's security tooling, and the 25-plus-year partnership between Microsoft and SAP behind the certified reference architectures.

## The numbers, and how to read them

The talk is generous with figures: up to 60 percent lower infrastructure cost through pay-as-you-go, 30 to 40 percent savings on licensing with Azure Hybrid Benefit, about 30 percent lower operating expense through automation, an average 45 percent reduction in TCO, deployments 40 percent faster with pre-configured templates, 75 percent better system performance, and full ROI within 18 months. These are presented as typical customer outcomes rather than measurements from one project, so treat them as targets to test in your own business case.

His closing advice is the part to keep: start from a cloud roadmap tied to business outcomes and your existing SAP investments, then build a migration plan with milestones, risk mitigation, testing protocols and business-continuity measures for the cutover.

## Who should watch

SAP Basis teams, enterprise architects and IT leaders drafting the case for moving SAP to Azure, who want a list of the services and arguments in one place. Engineers looking for migration tooling detail will want a more hands-on session.

Title: APISIX, Kong, Tyk, KrakenD and Gloo Edge, side by side
Description: Roman Rastiehaiev of HiBob at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 compares five open-source API gateways on plugins, storage, hot reload and speed.
Body:
Choosing an API gateway usually starts with a benchmark chart and ends with finding out what the gateway needs to store its config. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Roman Rastiehaiev of HiBob compared five open-source gateways (Apache APISIX, Kong, Tyk, KrakenD and Gloo Edge) on the details that bite later: language, license, storage, plugin model, auth and observability support, hot reload, and raw performance.

It is a comparison talk, and a practical one. Each gateway gets the same checklist, with links to the official docs on the slides, which makes the deck itself a decent reference to keep.

## What a gateway is for

Roman starts with the basics for anyone arriving from a monolith: a gateway is a reverse proxy between clients and backend services that routes on paths, headers, query parameters or identity; handles L7 traffic for REST, gRPC, GraphQL and WebSockets; splits traffic for A/B tests, blue-green and canary releases; caches, compresses and transforms requests; centralises auth (OAuth2, JWT, OpenID Connect, mTLS); and exports metrics, logs and traces. His case for open source is cost, transparency and community speed.

## The checklist, gateway by gateway

The differences that stand out from his walk-through:

- **Apache APISIX** runs on OpenResty (NGINX plus Lua), Apache 2.0, stores config in etcd or files, takes plugins in Lua, Go, Python and WebAssembly, and hot-reloads through its admin API.
- **Kong** is also NGINX and OpenResty, Apache 2.0, runs DB-less or backed by Postgres, ships over 50 built-in plugins and hot-reloads via the admin API.
- **Tyk** is written in Go, licensed under MPL (less permissive than Apache 2.0, he flags), uses Redis for caching, rate limiting and state, and stands out for native GraphQL support.
- **KrakenD** is Go, Apache 2.0 and fully stateless, with no database at all, configured from files or environment variables. The catch he highlights: its hot reload is documented as for development only, not production.
- **Gloo Edge** is built on Envoy, configured declaratively through Kubernetes CRDs or Helm, and aimed squarely at Kubernetes-heavy deployments.

He also notes two feature gaps in KrakenD's open-source edition: no WebSocket support (enterprise only) and no gRPC.

## Who is fastest, and why

Roman ranks them from fastest to slowest based on published vendor benchmarks and other public data, while warning that those benchmarks use different machines and configurations. APISIX comes first thanks to LuaJIT compiling plugins, then KrakenD (pure Go, stateless, built for aggregating API calls), then Tyk, then Gloo Edge, with Kong last because of its plugin execution overhead and Postgres-backed persistence, though he notes DB-less mode helps. The architectural explanations are more useful than the ranking: they tell you which knobs move performance.

## Where gateways are heading

The closing trends: AI features (so far, he observes, mostly plugins that simplify calling LLM providers), the Kubernetes Gateway API replacing Ingress, with Gloo Edge and Kong's ingress controller among early adopters, native GraphQL and gRPC, and API monetisation with metering and developer portals.

## Who should watch

Platform and backend engineers shortlisting a gateway, especially on Kubernetes. If you have already standardised on one, the comparison still shows what you gave up. One note: the abstract mentions Traefik and Envoy, but the talk itself covers the five above, with Envoy appearing as Gloo Edge's foundation.
