Title: An SAP SRM migration to HANA in a single short downtime window
Description: Gopikrishna Yeturi of LTIMindtree at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on a homogeneous SAP SRM migration to HANA using backup and restore, SWPM and validation.
Body:
Enterprise migrations are judged on two numbers: how long the business was down and whether any data went missing. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Gopikrishna Yeturi, senior specialist for package implementation at LTIMindtree, walked through an SAP SRM migration that reports a downtime window of 3.5 hours, checksum-verified data, and a 30 percent performance improvement afterwards.

It's a compact, slide-driven case study rather than a hands-on demo. Its value is the shape of the plan: which components were touched, in which order, and how integrity was proven.

## Backup and restore, not export and import

The migration was homogeneous, using a backup-and-restore method for the HANA database: full system snapshots plus incremental backups. Yeturi credits it with 99.9 percent data integrity and a downtime window under four hours. The installation side used SAP's Software Provisioning Manager (SWPM 1.0) with automated validation and checks, which he says cut deployment time by 35 percent and avoided critical incidents during the transition.

The trade-off is worth naming: backup and restore keeps things simple when source and target share a database platform, which is why it suits a homogeneous move.

## Every tier got attention

The talk goes component by component:

- **HANA** in-memory, column-based storage and parallel processing, with Yeturi reporting complex queries running 5x faster and compression cutting storage needs by 60 percent.
- **Content Server 6.0 patch level 11** for document management, with better indexing for search across 10 million-plus documents and AES-256 encryption with role-based access and time-limited sharing tokens.
- **MaxDB 7.9** behind it, handling a 50 percent increase in daily transaction volume, with failover clusters and automated backups and a recovery time objective under 15 minutes.
- **IIS** for the web tier, where caching and thread tuning took average page load from 2.8 seconds to 0.9 seconds, and HTTP compression reduced bandwidth by 45 percent, with load balancing for 10,000-plus concurrent users.

## How integrity was proven

The migration ran in off-peak hours to limit impact across time zones. Validation relied on automated checksums across more than 2 million records and a complete audit trail through the transition, which is the part to copy if you're planning something similar. Testing after the cutover covered unit, integration and full-scale simulation.

His keys to success are unglamorous and correct: a roadmap with milestones, risk mitigation and measurable KPIs; a cross-functional team of SAP consultants, DBAs and project managers; and rigorous testing. After go-live, real-time monitoring and scheduled health checks keep the gains from eroding.

## Who should watch

SAP Basis teams and architects planning an SRM or other NetWeaver-era migration, and anyone who needs a checklist of the tiers that move along with the database. Engineers outside the SAP world will find it a brisk tour rather than a transferable technique.

Title: Why your ML platform should probably be the Kubernetes you already run
Description: Prashanth Josyula of Salesforce at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on running the ML lifecycle on Kubernetes with Kubeflow training, pipelines and KServe.
Body:
If your company already runs its microservices on Kubernetes, the cluster for your machine learning workloads may already exist. That is the core argument Prashanth Lakshmi Narayana Chaitanya Josyula, Principal Member of Technical Staff at Salesforce, made at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025: Kubernetes gives ML teams elastic GPUs, per-team quotas and portable YAML, and Kubeflow turns that into a full training-to-serving platform.

Prashanth says up front that the session is mostly concepts. It is a structured tour, starting from Kubernetes basics, which makes it a good first talk for data scientists who are about to be handed a cluster, and a decent refresher for platform engineers about to hand one over.

## The ML lifecycle has a load problem

He frames the ML lifecycle as data preparation, training, validation, deployment and monitoring, then repeat. Each stage stresses infrastructure differently. Data volume grows without warning, so you either over-provision storage and compute up front or get caught short. Deep learning needs GPUs, and buying enough for peak demand means paying for idle cards most of the time. Inference endpoints have their own peaks. Prashanth is careful here: Kubernetes does not make these problems disappear, but it gives you the levers to make the right decisions about them.

## Four levers: scale, quotas, portability, automation

The concrete Kubernetes features he leans on:

- **Scalability.** Horizontal and vertical autoscaling, plus KEDA for scaling on external events such as queue depth. On managed clusters you can keep GPU node pools available and pay only when jobs use them.
- **Resource management.** Namespaces with resource quotas let, say, finance and sales submit ML jobs to their own slice of the cluster without eating each other's CPUs. Taints, tolerations and node selectors keep GPU nodes for the jobs that need them.
- **Portability.** Everything is YAML and custom resources, so the same definitions run on-premises, in any cloud or in hybrid setups.
- **State.** Persistent volumes, claims and storage classes let long training runs checkpoint intermediate models and parameters.

His GPU advice is worth underlining: do not put every workload on GPUs. Use tolerations and node selectors so that only the jobs that need them, such as large deep learning models, land there.

## Kubeflow as the platform layer

Rather than building your own framework on top of Kubernetes, Prashanth points to Kubeflow, which he describes as a platform combining several tools. Three components get attention: the training operator, which lets you declare a framework training job, such as a TensorFlow job, as YAML and submit it with kubectl; Kubeflow Pipelines, a Python library for defining the whole ML workflow end to end; and KServe for model serving, where an InferenceService resource exposes a REST endpoint, with ModelMesh underneath for high-performance, scalable serving with intelligent routing. He also touches on Katib for AutoML.

The walk-through of a job's lifecycle is simple and useful: define a TensorFlow job, submit it, watch it in the Kubeflow UI, then deploy the trained model with KServe.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and ML engineers moving onto shared Kubernetes clusters, and platform teams deciding whether to support ML workloads alongside services. Experienced Kubeflow operators will find it introductory; Prashanth himself says a hands-on workshop would be the follow-up.

Title: Rule-based AI for dental claims, from a Delta Dental product manager
Description: Pravesh Nikhare of Delta Dental of California at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on encoding dental insurance policy as rules to automate claims.
Body:
Dental claims are a rules problem wearing a paperwork costume. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Pravesh Nikhare, Senior Benefits Configuration Product Manager at Delta Dental of California, made the case that most of a claim decision can be written down as machine-readable rules (policy terms, regulatory guidelines, clinical practice), and that doing so is what lets an insurer process standard claims without a human touching them.

It is a business-side talk, short and slide-driven, aimed at people who own claims operations rather than people who write the rules engine. Read it as a map of where automation pays off in a regulated, paper-heavy workflow.

## Rules first, models second

The framing is worth noticing because so much of the AI conversation skips it. Pravesh's "rule-based AI" mimics an adjuster by encoding the decision logic explicitly: a claim is cross-referenced against policy terms, historical patterns and clinical guidelines, and flagged when something does not line up, such as an eligibility mismatch or a fraud signal. Natural language processing sits in front of that to normalise the messy inputs: dental documentation, procedure codes, patient histories.

For engineers, this is the reassuring part. Rules are auditable. When a regulator or a provider asks why a claim was denied, you can point at the rule, which is a lot harder with a model that only offers a probability.

## The numbers he puts on it

The talk leans on outcome figures, presented as industry results rather than a breakdown of one system's internals. Pravesh cites approval times dropping from an average of seven days to two, around 85% of standard claims processed with no human intervention, administrative costs down roughly 30%, and fraudulent payouts cut by up to 45% through real-time anomaly checks. He also walks through a case study of a large dental insurer that started at seven to ten days per claim with a 35% churn rate and got processing under 48 hours after deploying rules-based validation, real-time fraud detection and reworked payment flows.

Treat those as the speaker's reported figures; the talk does not show the measurement method. The useful takeaway is the shape: the gains come from removing the queue between steps, not from making any single step clever.

## The unglamorous part: legacy integration

The section that will matter most to anyone who has migrated an insurance system is the rollout plan. Pravesh recommends starting with an assessment of the existing infrastructure to find integration points and constraints, then piloting on non-critical workflows before touching core claims, with explicit data mapping, validation rules and rollback procedures for migrating historical claims.

He is candid about the obstacles: data migration is slow and fiddly, the upfront investment is real, and HIPAA puts strict limits on how patient data moves. None of that is solved by the rules engine; it is solved by planning, which is the honest answer.

## What comes next

He closes with two technologies he expects to bolt onto rules-based processing: blockchain as a tamper-proof ledger for claim records and payment verification, and computer vision to check dental X-rays against the procedures claimed. Both are offered as direction rather than shipped work.

## Who should watch

Product managers, analysts and architects in insurance or healthcare payments who need a vocabulary for automating claims and a sensible order of operations. If you are looking for rules-engine internals, code or architecture diagrams, this one stays at the business level.

Title: Predictive scaling, placement and remediation across clouds
Description: Veda Swaroop Meduri of Labcorp at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on using AI to forecast demand, place workloads and fix incidents in multi-cloud setups.
Body:
Reactive autoscaling waits for the CPU graph to spike; predictive scaling bets on when it will. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Veda Swaroop Meduri of Labcorp gave an overview of how AI-driven prediction is being applied to multi-cloud management: forecasting resource demand, placing workloads, trimming cost and catching failures before they page someone.

Set expectations first: this is a high-level survey of about fifteen minutes, closer to a strategy briefing than an engineering session. There are no demos or configs. What it offers is a tidy taxonomy of where prediction fits into cloud operations, plus a sensible adoption path.

## Three layers where prediction helps

Veda splits the topic into three areas.

**Resource management.** Dynamic scaling uses historical patterns and real-time metrics to forecast demand and resize ahead of a spike; automated provisioning deploys resources across environments in minutes instead of hours and removes configuration drift. He cites prediction accuracy up to 95% and cost reductions of 30 to 40% during low-utilisation periods.

**Optimisation.** Three jobs here: workload placement (weighing resource needs, network latency and performance metrics when deciding where things run), cost optimisation (spotting under-used assets and recommending instance or pricing changes), and security optimisation (behavioural analysis to flag threats early).

**Operations.** Predictive maintenance forecasts hardware failure, anomaly detection catches deviations from normal behaviour before they escalate, and automated remediation diagnoses and fixes known issues without a human in the loop.

The figures throughout are presented as industry outcomes, not measurements from a named Labcorp system, so read them as direction rather than benchmarks.

## The providers are already doing the plumbing

A short section maps the big three onto this: Amazon SageMaker for building and deploying models at scale, Azure's services spanning language, vision and automated ML, and Google Cloud's pre-trained models and custom AI tooling. His point is that the providers have lowered the barrier enough that teams without deep data science benches can start using predictive analytics.

The rest of the talk widens out to business implications (cost savings at the base, operational excellence above it, competitive advantage on top) and to sector examples in healthcare, transportation and manufacturing.

## Where to start

The closing advice is the most practical bit. Audit your current cloud estate first, including utilisation patterns and performance metrics. Map critical business processes to find the highest-impact automation targets. Benchmark AI-powered tooling against your own needs, then roll out in phases that start with quick wins. That ordering is right: a prediction model fed by an estate you have not measured will mostly predict your own blind spots.

## Who should watch

Managers and architects who want a vocabulary for AI in cloud operations and a sensible order of adoption. Practitioners after implementation detail (which signals feed the forecaster, how remediation is gated) will want to pair it with something more hands-on.

Title: Where AI earns its keep in procurement, per an SAP data scientist
Description: Parameswara Rao Tatini of SAP at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on AI for supplier selection, contract review, demand forecasting and supply risk.
Body:
Procurement is the department that reads every contract nobody else wants to. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Parameswara Rao Tatini, a senior data scientist at SAP, laid out where AI changes that job: supplier selection, contract review, demand forecasting and early warning on supply chain risk, and why the hard part of adopting it is data and legacy ERP, not the models.

This is a short overview talk, about fifteen minutes, built around use cases and industry figures. There is no code or architecture walk-through; think of it as a briefing you could forward to a procurement lead who keeps asking what "AI in sourcing" actually means.

## Four jobs AI takes off the desk

Parameswara organises the talk around four concrete tasks.

- **Supplier selection.** Traditionally driven by relationships, past performance and manual research. AI adds market trends and historical performance data to the decision; he cites a 42% improvement in selection accuracy.
- **Contract management.** Teams juggling hundreds of contracts make manual review the bottleneck. Automated review that highlights risky clauses, he says, cuts processing time by 60%.
- **Demand forecasting.** Models that combine sales trends, supplier performance and external factors, with forecast accuracy he puts at rising from 70% to 95%. Better forecasts mean less excess inventory and fewer stockouts.
- **Risk early warning.** Systems that flag supply disruptions before they land, which he quotes at 85% accuracy.

As with most talks of this kind, the figures are the speaker's citations from industry studies rather than results from a specific SAP deployment shown on screen. The ordering is the useful part: each task is a place where a human currently reads documents or spreadsheets to make a repeatable judgment.

## The blockers are boring, and that is the point

The talk's most practical section is about adoption. Procurement data is sensitive (supplier pricing, financials), so GDPR and CCPA compliance and protection from attackers come first; he cites 78% of organisations naming data security as a barrier. Then there is integration: most companies run older ERP procurement systems, so AI arrives through middleware and phased rollouts, and he notes that 65% of enterprises struggle with that step.

His advice is plain and correct: do not buy off-the-shelf software and switch it on. Plan a structured, phased implementation.

## Smart contracts and sector notes

Parameswara also covers AI-assisted smart contracts that combine blockchain execution with AI validation for fraud prevention and policy enforcement, and runs through how the same ideas apply in manufacturing (predictive maintenance, production planning), retail (inventory replenishment), tech companies (software and cloud contract analysis) and sustainability, where he cites a 28% carbon reduction from supplier selection and logistics optimisation.

## Who should watch

Engineers and data people heading into procurement or supply chain projects who want the business framing in a quarter of an hour, and procurement leaders who want a checklist of use cases. If you want model architectures or an ERP integration pattern, look elsewhere.

Title: Uplift models and stream forecasts for spending music marketing money
Description: Maksim Kariagin of Metyis at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on uplift modelling and stream forecasting for music marketing, served by Streamlit and FastAPI.
Body:
The interesting question in music marketing isn't who will stream a track, it's who will stream it because you paid for the ad. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Maksim Kariagin](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Maksim_Kariagin_technology_media_analysis), Data Science Lead at Metyis, who previously led research and analysis at Warner Music Group, showed two applications that answer money questions for a label: uplift modelling for ad targeting and stream forecasting for budget planning.

It's a short, well-structured talk of about thirteen minutes. The two case studies are concrete, and the closing architecture is deliberately simple.

## The music business drowns in data

Kariagin maps the industry onto five pillars: A&R (finding talent), recording and production, promotion and marketing, release and distribution, and monetisation and royalties. Each throws off data. At Warner Music Group he cites over 2.5 trillion streaming data points, 15,000 tracked parameters, data shared by 180 companies and 10 billion transactions a day. His diagnosis is that labels and artists know AI could help but don't know where to apply it; having the data isn't the problem, making sense of it is.

The sources he names: streaming platforms like Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon and YouTube for plays, skips and playlist adds; Chartmetric for fan engagement across platforms; and Librosa, the Python library, for audio features like tempo, pitch and mood.

## Why uplift, not just propensity

Each streaming service keeps its own data, so a label can't follow a listener across platforms. That limits classic customer modelling, and it's why he focuses on uplift modelling and forecasting.

The uplift setup is the textbook two-model approach: one model predicts engagement for users who saw an ad, another for users who didn't, and the uplift is the difference. You spend on the people whose behaviour the ad changes, not on fans who would have listened anyway. Applied to campaigns on TikTok and Spotify, he reports a 30% reduction in the cost of getting a track added to a user's library compared with traditional segmentation.

## Forecasting streams, then reading the model

The second case is a three-month stream forecast built from historical streaming trends, track metadata and the data sources above, using around 700 features. He reports forecasting accuracy improving by 60%, which matters for a group of independent labels such as Atlantic allocating budgets.

The better idea is what happened after the forecast. To interpret the model they built partial dependence plots, which showed a plateau: past a point, more marketing budget doesn't buy more streams. Reallocating spend based on where the curve flattens saved 27% of marketing costs without losing performance, he says. Every marketing team suspects its spend has diminishing returns; a plot that shows where they start is far easier to defend in a budget meeting.

## The cloud native part is pleasantly small

The serving architecture is a Streamlit front end where business users enter a scenario, a FastAPI backend that receives the request, runs the model and returns the forecast, and the result shown back in Streamlit in real time. No platform sprawl, just the minimum to put a model in front of the people who decide the budget.

His closing line of thought: AI is there to amplify creativity, not replace it, and the goal is connecting music with the right audience.

## Who should watch

Data scientists in media, marketing or any business with ad spend, and engineers who want a compact example of model-to-business-user delivery. If you need causal inference rigour (how the control groups were built, how uplift was validated), the talk stays at overview level.

Title: 800 KB of auth library versus 9.5 KB of your own code
Description: Denis Ermakov of Techflow at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 replaces NextAuth.js with 9.5 KB of session code and asks what a dependency is really doing for you.
Body:
The most popular auth library for Next.js promises authentication in minutes. Denis Ermakov, lead software engineer at Techflow, took it at its word, kept score, and ended up replacing it with three files and 9.5 KB of code. His short, cheerful talk at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 is a worked example of a question every team should ask about every dependency: what is this library actually doing for us?

Ermakov leads front-end work at Techflow, which builds program, portfolio and project management software for banks. Serious users, serious money, and, as he insists, no obligation to be serious all the time.

## The setup is standard, which is the point

The stack is ordinary: a Next.js front end, a REST API on a Java backend, and a separate authentication service. Two tokens, a refresh token that lives a week and an access token that lives a day, packed into a JWT stored in cookies on the client and in the database on the server. Nothing exotic, which makes it a fair test.

Google "auth library for Next.js" and you land on NextAuth.js. Ermakov reads the stats aloud: a huge weekly download count, about 800 KB unpacked, around 500 files, and 86 open pull requests. Setup is genuinely quick: an API route, a provider around the client, a few sign-in components. Library 1, do-it-yourself 0.

## The score turns

Then the gaps. The team needs credential-based login against its own backend, and that isn't supported out of the box, so they write a credentials provider whose authorize function calls the auth service. That's about 5 KB of code. Then access tokens need refreshing in the background so users don't get logged out at random. The library doesn't handle that either, so they write a refresh function and wire it into the JWT callback. More custom code, and the scoreboard flips.

## Sunk cost versus alternative cost

The useful framing is his split of costs. Sunk cost is code you write regardless, library or not: here, the 5 KB of credentials setup. Alternative cost is what replacing the library would take. For that he tallies a session module with encrypt, decrypt, create, delete, refresh, update, getSession and a session-exists helper (about 6 KB), a session context provider for the client (1.3 KB) and middleware for early token validation and refresh (2.2 KB). Total: 9.5 KB in three files, against 800 KB and 500 files.

## When a library is worth it

He isn't anti-dependency. Use one when you're on the clock and need something running now, when the problem is truly complex (he names React and WebRTC as things you shouldn't rebuild), or when the alternative is far more expensive. But count the hidden costs: upgrades, breaking changes, and being locked into someone else's roadmap, bugs and API decisions.

His homework is concrete: find one library in your project, calculate the cost of the alternative, remove it if that makes sense, and repeat every month. He even pre-empts the obvious heckle; the Axios and query-string imports in his old code have since become plain fetch with a tiny wrapper.

## Who should watch

Front-end and full-stack engineers, especially on Next.js, and tech leads who review dependency additions. It's quick, has real file sizes rather than vibes, and ends on a line worth stealing for your next code review: "Syntactic sugar causes cancer of semicolons."

Title: What a Phase 3 UTI trial says about antibiotic resistance
Description: Karthik Akinapelli of Takeda at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 walks through a Phase 3 trial of oral sulopenem vs ciprofloxacin and the resistance data it surfaced.
Body:
Roughly a quarter of the bacteria in this trial already shrugged off one of the most prescribed antibiotics before treatment began. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, Karthik Akinapelli, Associate Director of Statistical Programming at Takeda, presents the findings of a Phase 3 study comparing oral sulopenem with ciprofloxacin for uncomplicated urinary tract infections, and what the resistance data says about where treatment is heading.

It's an unusual slot for a cloud event. The session as recorded is a results briefing on the trial itself: design, efficacy, resistance patterns and safety. The surveillance in the title is the trial's resistance analysis; the recording doesn't walk through the cloud or AI stack behind it, so come for the data rather than the architecture.

## A big, blinded comparison

The study was double-blind and multicenter, run across 142 sites in four countries, and enrolled 1,671 women with symptomatic uncomplicated UTIs, the group these infections hit hardest. Karthik frames the stakes with a US figure: uncomplicated UTIs account for roughly 30 million antibiotic prescriptions a year, which makes them one of the most common reasons anyone is handed antibiotics at all.

## Where the drugs actually separate

Across the whole study population, sulopenem was statistically non-inferior to ciprofloxacin, with clinical cure rates of 65.6% against 67.9%. That headline hides the interesting part, which is what happens when the bug is already resistant:

- About 27% of urinary pathogens in the study were resistant to ciprofloxacin.
- In those ciprofloxacin non-susceptible infections, sulopenem succeeded in 62.6% of cases against 26.6% for ciprofloxacin, a highly significant difference.
- In patients with extensively drug-resistant pathogens (resistant to beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones or Bactrim), sulopenem reached an 80% combined clinical and microbiological cure rate.

The argument for an oral option here is practical: if a pill works where older antibiotics fail, fewer patients end up hospitalised on intravenous last-resort drugs.

## Resistance is a moving target

For anyone who works with data, the resistance numbers are the most striking slides. Across all pathogen species, 32% of isolates were resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and 18% to nitrofurantoin. Then the uncomfortable one: 41% of isolates that started out susceptible to ciprofloxacin were resistant after treatment. Treatment itself shifted the susceptibility pattern, which is exactly why Karthik keeps returning to ongoing surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship.

The trial also found 63% of patients had beta-lactamase non-susceptible infections and 13.5% had ESBL-positive infections, the populations with the fewest oral options.

## Safety, and a finding about follow-up tests

The safety profile was mild. The one notable adverse event was transient diarrhoea, in about 12.4% of sulopenem patients against 2.5% on ciprofloxacin; no serious adverse events were attributed to the drug, and discontinuation stayed below 3%. A secondary analysis found 18% of patients had asymptomatic bacteriuria after treatment, with no difference between arms. His reading: routine follow-up urine cultures in patients without symptoms may not be clinically useful, and dropping them would cut unnecessary antibiotic exposure.

He ends on next steps: personalised treatment, more work on resistance mechanisms, broader studies in diverse populations, and getting the findings into clinical guidelines.

## Who should watch

Engineers and data people working in healthcare and life sciences who want to see what a Phase 3 readout looks like from the statistical programming side, and anyone curious about antimicrobial resistance in numbers. It's a short clinical briefing, not a technical build, and a summary of trial results rather than treatment advice.

Title: Conf42 Python 2025 roundup: dunders, concurrency, data and agents
Description: Conf42 Python 2025 in review, from dunder methods, asyncio vs threads and FireDucks to fsspec, FastAPI fraud systems, agentic Django and WebAuthn.
Body:
Iyanuoluwa Ajao introduced a talk at [Conf42 Python 2025](https://www.conf42.com/python2025) by calling Python "the 2nd best language for everything", which is about as honest a summary of the ecosystem as you'll get. The event, streamed online on February 6, 2025, had 51 talks covering both halves of that joke: the language features and libraries that make Python good at so many jobs, and the tricks people use when it isn't fast enough. Speakers came from IBM, Meta, Microsoft, Walmart, Snowflake, Mastercard, Wells Fargo, Qualcomm, NEC and Treeverse.

## The language, used properly

[Eti Ijeoma](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Eti_Ijeoma_python_dunder_methods) (Manufactured Networks) went past `__str__` and `__repr__` to show how dunder methods make APIs feel native and can carry small domain-specific languages. [Iyanuoluwa Ajao](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Iyanuoluwa_Ajao_python_concurrency_patterns) (Fyyne) compared threading, asyncio and multiprocessing, with a practical rule for I/O-bound work: if the libraries you need support async/await, start with asyncio, because threads cost memory and need protecting when they share data; otherwise use threads, and save processes for real parallelism.

[Dmitriy Volkov](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Dmitriy_Volkov_packaging_busy_people) (Palisade Research) covered Python's packaging oddities for people with no time for them, plus the move towards a GIL-free CPython. When Python itself is the bottleneck, [Hariharan Ragothaman](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Hariharan_Ragothaman_cpp_python_workloads) (athenahealth) offloaded compute-heavy work to C++, and [Sourav Saha](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sourav_Saha_firedricks_dataframe_jit) (NEC Corporation) introduced FireDucks, a multithreaded DataFrame library with JIT compilation that detects and optimises common pandas performance problems without code changes.

## Data tooling that hides the plumbing

[Guy Hardonag](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Guy_Hardonag_file_systems_python) (Treeverse) gave hands-on examples of fsspec, the library that lets Pandas, TensorFlow and PyArrow treat local and cloud storage the same way. Anyone who has written `if path.startswith("s3://")` will appreciate it. [Daniel Emakporuena](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Daniel_Emakporuena_data_analysis_streamlit) built an analysis and dashboard tool on Streamlit for people who outgrew Power BI and Tableau, and [Tim Spann](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Tim_Spann_vector_databases_python) (Snowflake) combined structured, semi-structured and unstructured sources with Python.

At larger scale, [Dileesh Chandra Bikkasani](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Dileesh_Chandra_Bikkasani_network_performance_automation) (AT&T Labs) used Apache Airflow for network performance automation, [Amarnath Immadisetty](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Amarnath_Immadisetty_python_analytics_realtime) (Lowe's) built real-time customer analytics engines, and [Shashank Reddy Beeravelly](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Shashank_Reddy_Beeravelly_data_quality_management) (Walmart) covered AI-assisted data quality checks.

## AI and agents, in plain Python

[Anna Gutowska](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Anna_Gutowska_ai_agents_customizing) (IBM) introduced AI agents that combine LLM reasoning with planning, current information and external tools. [Craig West](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Craig_West_agentic_ai_django) treated agents in Django as "AI as API", building agentic endpoints from scratch, and [Sourabh Gawande](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sourabh_Gawande_ai_applications_practical) (Kusho) shared the practical side of building LLM applications. [Shannon Lal](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Shannon_Lal_image_search_python) (Designstripe) combined text search with semantic search for images using Motor, MongoDB and OpenAI. The most fun entry was [Jan Van Wassenhove](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Jan_Van_Wassenhove_code_music_electronic) (Sopra Steria), whose MusicAgent uses generative AI, Python and Sonic Pi to compose and produce electronic music live, album art included.

Search and ranking had a strong showing too: neural ranking for real-time personalisation from [Vedant Agarwal](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Vedant_Agarwal_personalization_neural_ranking) (Walmart Global Tech), vector-based semantic search from [Siddharth Pratap Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Siddharth_Pratap_Singh_search_vector_semantic) (Walmart Labs), and context-aware evaluation metrics for search from [Aditya Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Aditya_Singh_precision_metrics_framework). [Parul Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Parul_Gupta_ai_ml_prototyping) (Meta) described the tooling behind fast ML prototyping, and [Shubham Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Shubham_Singh_ai_code_review) took AI code review beyond syntax checks.

## Services at scale, and catching fraud

[Aby M Joseph and Jayalekshmi K S](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Aby_M_Joseph_Jayalekshmi_K_S_graphql_microservices_fastapi) (UST) built GraphQL microservices on FastAPI, and [Sushil Prabhu Prabhakaran](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sushil_Prabhu_Prabhakaran_python_cloud_scaling) (TCS) orchestrated async workflows with asyncio and FastAPI. Fraud detection got two architecture talks with the same toolbox: [Narendra Bhargav Boggarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Narendra_Bhargav_Boggarapu_fraud_python_transactions) (Wells Fargo) with FastAPI, Ray and MLflow, and [Vinod Upputuri](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Vinod_Upputuri_fraud_ml_numpy) (Mastercard) with PyTorch, Ray and asyncio. [Ajay Krishnan Prabhakaran](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Ajay_Krishnan_Prabhakaran_sms_spam_python) (Meta) covered SMS spam detection with NLP.

## Security and operations

[Sairam Durgaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sairam_Durgaraju_fido2_webauthn) (Evernorth Health Services) implemented passwordless, phishing-resistant login in Python with FIDO2, WebAuthn and hardware security keys. [Sandeep Batchu](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sandeep_Batchu_secure_cloud_applications) (Microsoft) covered secure-by-design cloud applications, and [Mounika Ponugoti](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Mounika_Ponugoti_device_security_attack) (Qualcomm) cost-effective embedded device security, from secure boot to control-flow integrity. On the ops side, [Justin Dearing](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Justin_Dearing_docker_windows_devcontainers) (Neudesic) showed several free ways to run Windows and Linux containers and devcontainers on Windows without Docker Desktop, built on WSL, and [Lurduma Reddy Thirumala Reddy](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Lurduma_Reddy_Thirumala_Reddy_hana_availability_pacemaker) (Intone Networks) automated SAP HANA high availability with Pacemaker clusters.

## Python outside engineering

[Liv McFarlin](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Liv_McFarlin_python_ux_innovation) (Wheels) showed a UX team using Python for research, prototyping and collaboration, [Vamsi Upputuri](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Vamsi_Upputuri_drug_development_python) (Gilead Sciences) Python in clinical drug development under compliance constraints, and [Rao Marapatla](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Rao_Marapatla_data_warehouses_nonprofits) (BreakthroughT1D) data warehouses for nonprofits.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Arato AI](https://arato.ai/?utm_source=conf42&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Conf42_mail) and [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), the gold sponsors, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) as newsletter partner, [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and the media partners. Every talk is on the [Conf42 Python 2025 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBo176Is4wP2F6UCB0yEkWO) and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/python2025).

Python stayed the common language across the rest of the year's Conf42 events; [Conf42 MLOps 2025](https://www.conf42.com/mlops2025) is a good next stop.

Title: AI in insurance, from underwriting to fraud, and the legacy in between
Description: Bhaskara Beeraka of American Family Insurance at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 surveys AI in underwriting, claims and fraud, and the legacy data hurdles.
Body:
Insurance runs on paperwork, risk models and a lot of old systems, which makes it a natural target for machine learning and a hard place to deploy it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Bhaskara Beeraka](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Bhaskara_Beeraka_insurance_innovation_insights), Senior Developer at American Family Insurance, gave a survey of AI across the insurance value chain (underwriting, claims, fraud and analytics) and of the data and integration problems that stand in the way.

Scope note up front: this is a slide-driven overview, around thirteen minutes, heavy on headline percentages and light on how they were measured. Treat it as a map of where AI lands in an insurer, not as a case study.

## Underwriting: more signals per application

Beeraka's first stop is underwriting, which he calls one of the key modules of any insurer. The pitch is that machine learning models, he mentions neural networks and gradient boosting, can weigh a far wider set of inputs per application than a human underwriter: structured and unstructured data, medical records, credit histories, IoT sensor data. Natural language processing pulls the relevant fields out of documents, and parallel processing evaluates several applications at once. The outcome he describes is faster policy issuance, fewer human errors and more precise pricing.

## Claims: settlement time is the metric customers feel

For claims, the headline he gives is average settlement time falling from 30 days to 4.5 days with predictive analytics that check a claim against policy terms, history and risk factors. Computer vision does the damage assessment from photos and video, with assessment time quoted as dropping from 48 hours to 2.4 hours. He ties faster settlement and real-time status updates to customer satisfaction and renewals, which is the business case any claims team will recognise.

## Fraud: throughput and false positives

On fraud detection he describes a parallel-processing architecture analysing around 125,000 transactions per second with neural networks that adapt to new fraud tactics, and stresses the number that matters most to customers: false positives, quoted at 0.05%. The design idea underneath, feature engineering plus ensemble learning to keep legitimate transactions flowing, is sound regardless of the exact figure.

The talk doesn't say which of these numbers come from American Family Insurance, from vendors or from industry studies, so keep the shapes and check the figures before quoting them in your own deck.

## The hard part is the data and the mainframe

The more transferable section is the challenges. Legacy systems create data silos that keep customer information spread across departments, poor data quality and inconsistent formats lead models to misclassify risk, and security requirements demand strong encryption and access control because breaches in insurance are expensive.

His integration recipe is pragmatic: modern APIs as a secure gateway between traditional systems and AI applications, microservices to break integrations into components you can update independently, and middleware as a translator between legacy databases and new platforms. For processing he names Apache Spark for in-memory computation, Kafka for streaming between systems and Hadoop.

## Explainability is a regulatory requirement, not a nice-to-have

He closes on explainable AI: turning model decisions into step-by-step reasoning that customers and regulators can read, with audit trails documenting every factor behind an automated underwriting or claims decision. In a regulated industry this is the part that decides whether a model ships at all, and he links clear, jargon-free explanations to fewer disputes.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects new to insurance who want a tour of where AI shows up, and teams preparing an internal case for modernising claims or fraud. ML practitioners looking for model details, evaluation methods or a production post-mortem won't find them here.

Title: Food delivery at scale runs on AI, with humans kept in the loop
Description: Praveen Payili of Horizonsoft Solutions at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on chat safety, voice ordering and ML infrastructure for food delivery, humans in the loop.
Body:
A food order touches a chat between driver and customer, maybe a phone call to a restaurant, a route and a forecast, all inside the time it takes the fries to go cold. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Praveen Payili](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Praveen_Payili_food_delivery_operations), Senior Data Engineer at Horizonsoft Solutions, walked through how AI is integrated into a food delivery platform and argued for a hybrid model where machines handle the volume and people handle the exceptions.

It's a short overview (about eight minutes) built around four systems. The platform isn't named in the talk, and the numbers come without methodology, so read it as an architecture sketch with reported outcomes.

## Why the industry needs it

Payili frames the market first: around 190 billion dollars in size with projected growth of 10.8% a year through 2030, and a large share of orders now placed from mobile. Food delivery, in his words, went from convenience to cornerstone of urban life, and AI moved from enhancing the service to reshaping how platforms operate.

## SafeChat+: moderating driver-customer messages

The first system is SafeChat+, an NLP-based communication safety layer that screens messages for inappropriate content. The figures he gives are the engineering ones you'd want: 94.3% detection accuracy, about 1,400 messages per minute at under 50 milliseconds of latency, across five major languages. He links it to a faster incident response than human moderation and to better driver satisfaction with fewer communication disputes. A moderation model sitting inline on a chat path at that latency is a real design constraint, and it's the most concrete part of the talk.

## Voice ordering, with human oversight

The second system handles phone orders with speech recognition and order processing, combining machine learning with human oversight so restaurant staff spend less time on the phone and more on service. He presents it as cutting wait times and errors.

## The data platform underneath

The third piece is the ML and data infrastructure, which he says processes 15 petabytes of real-time data daily. It feeds search ranking, AI-driven suggestions and dynamic routing. The implementation strategy he describes is data-driven: tracking over 200 performance metrics in real time, running around 800 A/B tests a month to tune algorithms, and coordinating millions of daily human-AI interactions while keeping humans in charge of oversight.

## Scaling and handoffs are the hard engineering

His technical challenges section is the part SREs will relate to. Peak load means millions of concurrent transactions per hour and terabytes of data an hour through distributed computing, with load balancing and predictive scaling to keep uptime high at peak. Multilingual intent recognition across six languages is its own problem.

The detail worth stealing is the AI-to-human handoff. He describes tens of thousands of handoffs a day and measures a context retention rate, how much of the conversation survives when a human takes over. If you run any bot with an escalation path, that's a metric you probably don't track yet, and should.

## What comes next

He closes with trends: autonomous delivery by self-driving vehicles and drones, AR/VR previews of dishes and restaurants, and personalised nutrition recommendations based on health metrics and dietary preferences. These are directions, not things the platform is shown doing.

## Who should watch

Engineers working on marketplace or logistics platforms, and anyone designing a human-in-the-loop system who wants a list of the components involved. If you want model architectures or code, this overview won't provide them.

Title: Why investment banks are moving reconciliation off spreadsheets
Description: Jaya Krishna Vemuri of State Street at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on cloud reconciliation engines with automated matching, real-time sync and audit trails.
Body:
Reconciliation is the job of proving two systems agree about money, and in many banks it still involves a person, a spreadsheet and a deadline. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Jaya Krishna Vemuri, a vice president at State Street Bank and Trust Company with more than 14 years building trading and reporting systems, laid out what a cloud-based reconciliation platform changes, from ingestion to the audit trail.

This is an architecture-and-benefits talk aimed at people who know the back office. It doesn't demo a product; it explains the moving parts and why each one matters to compliance.

## What breaks in the legacy flow

Vemuri lists the familiar failures. Analysts prepare data in spreadsheets, load it, match source against target, chase exceptions and build reports, mostly by hand, so period close slips. Manual steps add errors: a missed transaction, a wrong match, a file that never got loaded. Systems are disjointed because accounting software, custodians and banking platforms come from different vendors. Batch updates mean nobody sees today's position until tomorrow. And with so much manual work, auditing each step is slow and expensive.

## Four layers of a cloud reconciliation engine

The architecture section is the core of the talk:

- **Ingestion** through APIs and connectors for trade confirmations, settlements and market feeds, with error handling and buffering so a peak-hour surge gets queued instead of breaking the system or forcing users back to small batches.
- **A matching engine** with configurable rules plus machine learning for matching across many sources. Routine matches are handled automatically and only exceptions reach a human, who can comment, annotate and push changes back.
- **Processing and validation**, an ETL layer with built-in validation rules and anomaly detection for data quality and completeness.
- **Resolution and reporting**, with workflow routing that sends each flagged issue to the right person, plus dashboards and regulatory reports.

Underpinning it all is the audit trail: who changed what, when, how, and what broke. For a regulated firm that's the feature that sells the rest.

## The numbers he cites

Vemuri shares three anonymised examples. An investment bank cut manual processing errors by 70 percent within six months, took reconciliation time from 44 hours to under 45 minutes, and lowered reconciliation operating cost by 40 percent. A $10 billion hedge fund automatically resolves 92 percent of position breaks within minutes. A $50 billion asset manager shortened its daily reporting cycle from six hours to 90 minutes, raised accuracy from 96 to 99.8 percent, and handles three times the transaction volume. The talk doesn't name the firms or detail the methods, so treat these as illustrations of the ceiling.

## Where it goes next

He closes with three directions: AI pattern recognition that predicts and resolves discrepancies from historical data, blockchain ledgers and smart contracts as a shared source of truth between counterparties, and predictive dashboards that forecast issues before they hit operations. His three takeaways are to automate away the spreadsheet work, back automation with strong data governance and validation, and treat reconciliation as a source of real-time insight rather than a back-office chore.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects joining a fintech or banking data team, and operations leaders making the case for modernising reconciliation. If you already run a streaming reconciliation platform, the architecture slides will feel familiar.

Title: A checklist for running Apache Spark on Kubernetes for ML
Description: Anant Kumar of Salesforce at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on Spark on Kubernetes for ML, covering the Spark Operator, autoscaling, Iceberg and spot instances.
Body:
Spark wants to own the cluster and Kubernetes wants to own the cluster, and ML teams have to make them share. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Anant Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Anant_Kumar_apache_spark_clusters), Tech Lead at Salesforce, walked through how to build production-grade Apache Spark clusters on Kubernetes for AI and ML workloads, covering resource management, scaling, storage, observability, security, cost and delivery.

It's a broad, well-organised checklist rather than a long look at one problem: about 25 minutes of slides, no live demo, with the occasional production detail that makes it worth the time.

## Spark's driver and executors become pods

Kumar's mental model is simple: the Spark driver is the master, the executors are workers, and each runs in its own pod. Persistent volumes keep data available when pods are rescheduled, which matters because pods in Kubernetes are ephemeral and can be evicted at any time. StatefulSets cover components that need stable identity and storage.

The glue is the Spark Operator, installed with a Helm chart. Once it's in, Spark jobs become custom resources, so you create, read, update and delete Spark applications declaratively like any other Kubernetes object, and they can go through GitOps like the rest of your manifests.

## Requests, quotas and taints keep the cluster fair

Resource management is where most Spark-on-Kubernetes pain lives, and he covers the three knobs. Requests and limits set the minimum and maximum each Spark pod gets. Resource quotas per namespace stop one application from eating the cluster. Node affinity and taints put GPU-hungry tasks on GPU nodes and keep everything else off them.

For scaling, dynamic resource allocation monitors consumption and scales up for peaks and bursty traffic, then back down. He prefers horizontal scaling where it fits, because many general-purpose instances are cheaper than a few big ones, and suggests triggering both horizontal and vertical scaling from thresholds on CPU, memory or application metrics.

## Performance: partition, shuffle, push down

The performance section has the most Spark-specific advice. Partition data to reduce movement between workers. Use an external shuffle service to make shuffles more efficient across the cluster. Cache hot data in memory. And lean on the optimiser: predicate pushdown sends filters down to the source, his example being a query over Avro files where Spark pushes the filter into the Avro reader instead of reading every record. Broadcast joins and the Catalyst optimiser, which turns a logical plan into an optimised one, round it out.

## Observability, security and cost, briefly

The rest of the checklist moves quickly:

- **Observability**: Prometheus and Grafana for metrics, with a sidecar exporting in Prometheus format; Fluentd and Elasticsearch for logs; Jaeger or Zipkin for tracing; PagerDuty alerts on top.
- **Security**: network policies, encryption at rest and in transit, Kubernetes RBAC with least privilege, OAuth with an external identity provider, certificates and mTLS between internal services.
- **Cost**: spot instances for non-critical work (pick the zone and time of day when they're cheapest, and expect them to be taken away), right-sized allocations, and scaling idle resources down. He mentions the familiar story of EC2 instances left running far longer than anyone intended.
- **Availability**: multiple control-plane nodes for a highly available API server, and redundant workers so an evicted executor's retried task usually succeeds.

## The case study: a lakehouse on S3

His real-world example is a pipeline processing terabytes of data: Spark on Kubernetes for distributed processing, Hive Metastore as the catalog, and Apache Iceberg as the table format over S3. That combination gives schema evolution when business needs change, and Iceberg's time travel for compliance queries. For CI/CD he notes Maven as the usual build tool and Bazel gaining ground in monorepos.

His closing advice: start with a minimal cluster, automate deployment, scaling and monitoring, and benchmark regularly as workloads change.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers moving Spark from YARN or a managed service onto Kubernetes, and ML platform teams sharing GPU nodes with data jobs. If you already run the Spark Operator in production, skim to the performance and Iceberg sections.

Title: Cloud cost is a team sport - FinOps basics from Flexport
Description: Hari Yerramsetty of Flexport at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on right-sizing, reserved vs spot, tagging and joint FinOps reviews to cut cloud spend.
Body:
Most cloud bills don't explode because of one bad decision; they creep because nobody owns them. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Hari Yerramsetty, software engineer at Flexport, made the case that cost efficiency is a shared habit between engineering, operations and finance, and showed the FinOps loop (optimise, govern, monitor) that turns it into routine work.

It's an introductory talk. If you already run a FinOps practice you'll recognise the framework; if your team still discovers the bill at the end of the month, this is a tidy map of where to start.

## The bill is confusing on purpose (or at least by design)

Yerramsetty opens with the pain points. Pricing options like pay-as-you-go, reserved plans and spot pricing make it hard to know what you'll actually pay. Teams buy more compute and storage than they need. Without process, each team spins up its own resources without talking to the others, which means duplicated work and missed chances to share. And without visibility, nobody can say where the money goes.

His fix is cultural before it's technical: finance, operations and engineering set joint cost targets and review spend together. When a spike happens, engineering and finance investigate it side by side while operations adds automated policies so it doesn't recur.

## Four pillars, one loop

The framework he presents starts with an assessment of current spend and usage, which gives a baseline and the quick wins. Then optimise: right-size resources to real need and buy reserved capacity for steady workloads. Then govern: set policies and tag everything so each resource maps to an engineering org or project, with a cross-functional team owning the process. Then monitor continuously with dashboards and adjust in near real time. Repeat.

## Match the instance to the workload

The practical section is the most useful. Look at CPU and memory for your containers or EC2 machines and compare idle time with busy time before resizing. Reserved instances suit things that must always run; his example is a Kafka cluster. Spot instances suit transient work such as lower-priority scheduled jobs in a distributed system. Serverless avoids paying for idle servers at all, and auto-scaling lets capacity follow demand.

Governance gets concrete too: enforce tagging and cost allocation with automation, and in AWS look at service control policies. For tooling he lists AWS Cost Explorer, Azure Cost Management and GCP cost dashboards for visibility, Cloud Custodian and Terraform for policy as code, and CloudHealth and Apptio for FinOps reporting.

## Two cases, one pattern

He shares two anonymised cases. A product team with over-provisioned VMs and a database server scaled far beyond its needs introduced right-sizing and regular FinOps reviews, and saw a 30 percent cost reduction. A business unit with resource sprawl, where teams deployed independently, centralised governance, enforced tagging and held cross-functional reviews; the talk reports significant savings and a sustainable model for managing cost, without a figure.

The roadmap that closes the talk is assessment, planning (goals, KPIs, the cross-functional team), implementation, then monitoring and iteration, with executive sponsorship to drive the culture shift. His lessons: build cost into the design phase, avoid one-size-fits-all policies because teams have different compute needs, and automate enforcement so it doesn't depend on someone remembering.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers starting a FinOps practice, or anyone who has to explain a cloud invoice to a finance partner. Seasoned FinOps practitioners can skip to the two case studies.

Title: Your customer data platform is your LLM's long-term memory
Description: Ankit Awasthi of Twilio at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on personalising LLM apps by retrieving the right slice of a customer data platform profile at runtime.
Body:
A support bot that knows the return policy but not that you ordered the shoes yesterday is still a bad support bot. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Ankit Awasthi](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Ankit_Awasthi_llm_data_performance), Director of Engineering at Twilio, where he leads predictive and generative AI products, argued that personalised LLM apps are a data infrastructure problem first, and that a customer data platform (CDP) is the right place to get that data.

It's a concise, architecture-level talk, about twelve minutes, with no code but one genuinely useful design comparison.

## RAG fixes staleness, not personalisation

Awasthi starts with what LLMs are good at (natural conversation, summarisation, code snippets, copywriting, increasingly reasoning) and what they aren't: they're trained on static data, they hallucinate, and without context they can't personalise. Retrieval-augmented generation is the standard answer, pulling current, domain-specific or proprietary knowledge into the prompt.

His point is that RAG over a generic knowledge base still misses the user. His example bot has access to the return policy document and still gives a poor answer, because it knows nothing about the customer asking.

## What a CDP brings

A CDP, traditionally a marketing tool, collects events from sources like your web app, chatbot, point-of-sale systems or warehouse, resolves identities across platforms, and builds a unified profile per customer that it sends on to downstream tools. As a user interacts with more apps, the profile gets richer and the next conversation gets better. He compares it to ChatGPT's memory feature, extended across every touchpoint, from email to the mobile app.

Why not just a key-value store? Three reasons: a CDP breaks down silos when web and mobile teams capture behaviour differently, it does real-time capture and identity resolution, and it applies data governance by sensitivity.

## Three ways to put a profile in a prompt

This is the section to watch. He compares three implementations:

1. **Embed the whole profile** in every prompt. Complete, but prompts get huge, cost and latency climb, and it doesn't scale.
2. **Fetch predetermined traits**, such as location for a restaurant recommendation. Smaller prompts, but you only use what the engineer knew existed. If another team stores each user's favourite cuisine, your feature never sees it.
3. **Retrieve dynamically**: compute semantic similarity between the user's natural-language prompt and the data elements on the profile at runtime, and inject only the relevant ones.

The third option keeps the context small and uses the whole profile without anyone needing prior knowledge of its schema. It's RAG, pointed at the user instead of the documentation.

## The takeaways

Building an LLM app for many use cases means solving data infrastructure, data quality and data governance first. CDPs make a strong personalisation engine, and they work as long-term memory by storing structured traits and events the model can draw on when needed. The abstract mentions an engagement figure; the talk itself sticks to architecture, so don't expect a benchmark.

## Who should watch

Engineers building customer-facing assistants who have RAG working and still get generic answers, and data teams asked to "make the bot personal". If you already do per-user retrieval over a feature store, the comparison of the three approaches is still a handy way to explain the design to others.

Title: AI in DevOps in five minutes, an overview for newcomers
Description: Lakshmi Supriya Namana of Web Creators UK at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 gives a short overview of AI in DevOps, from failure prediction to self-healing.
Body:
Systems got complex faster than runbooks could keep up, and that's the gap AI is being pitched to fill. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Lakshmi Supriya Namana](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Lakshmi_Supriya_Namana_devops_automation_efficiency), DevOps Engineer at Web Creators UK, gave a short overview of where AI fits into DevOps: predicting failures, scaling resources, automating repetitive work and watching for threats.

Scope first: this is a high-level introduction of about five minutes, a slide-by-slide tour with no demo, architecture or code. It works as an orientation for someone new to the topic, and as a checklist for a team writing its first AI-in-ops proposal.

## The argument: speed outgrew manual operations

Namana's starting point is that DevOps is about speed, automation and continuous delivery, and that traditional methods struggle once systems get complex. Her list of pain points is the familiar one: manual overload, complex cloud native systems and security. AI's role, in her framing, is to add intelligence to the pipeline: monitoring that predicts, security that's automated, and less downtime.

## Four capabilities worth naming

She groups the AI capabilities into four:

- **Predictive analytics** to detect system failures before they happen.
- **Self-healing systems** that detect and resolve an issue automatically.
- **Smart autoscaling** that adjusts resources to demand.
- **AI security and compliance** that spots threats proactively.

Behind those she lists the enabling technologies: machine learning for predictions, natural language processing, computer vision for visual monitoring data, robotic process automation for repetitive DevOps tasks, and deep learning. For real-world flavour she points at Netflix optimising cloud performance for streaming, Google's proactive threat detection, AWS automating infrastructure management and GitHub's AI-assisted coding.

## The challenges are the useful slide

The most practical part is the list of what gets in the way. AI needs high-quality data to predict anything accurately, which in ops means telemetry that's complete and consistent. Integrating AI into existing pipelines is difficult. AI systems themselves have to be secured and kept compliant. And there's a skills gap: teams need people who understand both AI and DevOps. Her prescription is careful planning, investment and upskilling. That's short, but it's the honest part of every AIOps pitch, and the part most vendor decks rush past.

## Where she sees it going

Her future section lists autonomous DevOps (systems that manage and heal themselves), hyperautomation aiming at zero manual intervention, AI-driven security operations and smarter CI/CD pipelines that tune the whole delivery lifecycle. Read it as a direction of travel; the talk doesn't go into how a team would get there, or how you'd trust a pipeline that changes itself.

## Who should watch

Students, junior engineers and managers who want the vocabulary in five minutes. Practitioners already running anomaly detection or auto-remediation won't find new technique here, and should go straight to the deeper talks below.

Title: AI fraud detection needs a roadmap, not just a model
Description: Vinod Upputuri of Mastercard at Conf42 Python 2025 on supervised, unsupervised and deep learning for fraud, real-time prevention and an implementation roadmap.
Body:
Fraudsters adapt faster than rule engines get updated, which is the whole argument for learning systems. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Vinod Upputuri](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Vinod_Upputuri_fraud_ml_numpy), Senior Software Engineer at Mastercard with 11 years in financial services, gave an overview of AI-powered fraud detection: the three families of models, the prevention techniques that work in real time, and a four-step roadmap for rolling it out.

Expectation management first. The session title and abstract promise code with NumPy, PyTorch, Ray and asyncio, but the recording is a strategy overview with no code or library walkthrough. Watch it for the problem framing and the rollout plan; bring your own PyTorch.

## Three ways to learn what fraud looks like

Upputuri splits the models into three approaches. Supervised learning learns from labelled historical transactions, much like an email spam filter learns from flagged messages. Unsupervised learning finds anomalies that match no known pattern, such as an unusual device or location, and is what catches new schemes early. Deep learning processes thousands of data points per transaction in real time and, in his framing, stops fraud while it is happening rather than flagging it afterwards.

## Prevention happens in milliseconds

The real-time section has three techniques. Transaction analysis scores each payment as it arrives; his example is a New York cardholder whose card suddenly appears in London, flagged on location and amount. Behavioural biometrics builds a profile from how a person types, swipes and presses on a screen, a fingerprint that is hard to fake even with stolen credentials. Synthetic identity detection cross-references data across systems to spot identities stitched together from several real people, which traditional checks tend to miss.

He applies these to four use cases: transaction monitoring, account takeover protection, synthetic identity fraud in applications such as loans, and phishing detection, where natural language processing scans emails, messages and calls for suspicious patterns and links.

## A four-step rollout

The roadmap is the most reusable part:

1. **Define objectives** tied to the organisation's risk management strategy.
2. **Assess the data** before training, because poor or biased data produces poor or biased models; his example is discovering that behavioural signals were never collected.
3. **Select and train models**, trying supervised, unsupervised and deep learning, and favouring ones that adapt and can be explained.
4. **Deploy in phases with monitoring**, for instance online payments first, then other regions or transaction types once the model is tuned.

As he puts it, fraud detection is not a set-and-forget job.

## The hard parts

Upputuri is upfront about challenges. Biased training data can wrongly flag legitimate customers from particular demographics. Black-box models are hard to defend when a customer asks why their payment was declined, so explainable AI matters for regulators and customers alike. Regulation on data privacy and algorithmic fairness keeps moving, and static models decay as fraud tactics change.

The talk cites many headline percentages for accuracy, reduction in false positives and investigation speed. They are presented as industry figures, not Mastercard measurements, so treat them as context rather than benchmarks.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people new to payments fraud who want the shape of the problem and a rollout plan to discuss with risk teams. Engineers looking for distributed ML pipeline code should pair it with a more hands-on session.

Title: When one Redis isn't enough: a primer on caching and queues
Description: Wisdom Matthew of NALA at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 explains distributed caching (sharding, replication, load balancing) and partitioned queues in the cloud.
Body:
The database becomes the bottleneck long before the code does. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Wisdom Matthew](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Wisdom_Matthew_distributed_caching_queueing), Senior Backend Engineer at NALA, gave a clear primer on the two tools most teams reach for next: a distributed cache to take reads off the database, and a distributed queue to take slow work off the request path.

It's a beginner-friendly talk and says so from the start ("for folks who are new to all of this"). Diagrams over code, and a good one to hand a junior engineer.

## Cache-aside, then scale the cache

Matthew starts from the plain setup: client, server, database. Under high traffic every request hits the database. A cache in front of it serves frequently accessed data from memory; on a miss, the server reads from the database, writes the result to the cache and returns it, so the next request is fast. Memory beats disk, which is the whole trick.

When one cache instance can't hold the load, you distribute it. He covers three strategies and skips consistent hashing for time, which is a fair trade in a short talk:

- **Sharding** splits data across nodes. His example is range-based: a cache router sends keys 1 to 1,000 to node A, 1,000 to 2,000 to node B. With a 5 GB limit per node, two extra nodes take you to 15 GB.
- **Replication** copies data across nodes for availability and read speed. His diagram is a geo setup: a primary takes writes and syncs to secondaries, and the router sends a reader in Africa to the African node and a reader in Europe to the European one.
- **Load balancing** spreads requests across synchronised nodes, typically round robin, so no single node is the hot spot.

His practical advice: use the strategy your caching system ships with rather than building it in the application. Redis Cluster does sharding and replication out of the box. Memcached is the simpler key-value option. Managed versions include Amazon ElastiCache, Google Cloud Memorystore and Azure Cache for Redis, and self-hosting is possible if you enjoy pager duty.

## Queues: say thanks now, send the receipt later

The queue example is an e-commerce order. You don't want the user waiting while a PDF receipt is compiled and emailed, so the order service publishes a message, a queue holds it, and an email service consumes it when it's ready. Consumers subscribe to the topics they care about. One honest detail worth keeping: most queues aim for first in, first out, but the ordering isn't always guaranteed, so don't build on it blindly.

## Partitions are how queues scale

A single queue becomes its own bottleneck. Distributed queuing puts a broker in front of several partitions; producers publish to the broker, which decides which partition gets each message and how consumers receive it. Need more throughput, add partitions. He names Apache Kafka for high-throughput streaming, RabbitMQ for mature, complex routing, and NATS as the lightweight, low-latency option popular in cloud native stacks, plus managed services in Amazon SQS, Google Cloud Pub/Sub and Azure Service Bus. Same advice as for caching: let the broker manage partitions unless it truly can't meet your needs.

## Who should watch

Backend developers who have used Redis as a single box and are about to need more, and anyone who wants a crisp mental model before reading the Kafka or Redis Cluster docs. Experienced distributed-systems engineers will find nothing new, by design.

- [NATS: The Cloud-Native Challenger to Kafka's Messaging Throne](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Mohamed_Moussaoui_nats_cloudnative_kafka) by Mohamed Moussaoui at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

Title: White-label Android apps - one codebase, many brands, sane releases
Description: Dmitrii Nikitin of Quadcode at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on modules, palette tokens, trunk-based on-demand releases and brand-only smoke tests.
Body:
Shipping one Android app is work. Shipping the same app under a dozen brands, each with its own colours, features and impatient client, is a different sport. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, Dmitrii Nikitin, Android team leader at Quadcode, walked through how his team keeps a white-label B2B product flexible without letting the codebase turn into the cluttered app on his first slide.

His answer has five parts: structure the code so features can be swapped, drive UI colour from a token system, release per brand from stable tags, test only what a brand can break, and automate the Play Store upload. Each could be its own talk, he admits, so this one sticks to the key ideas and the traps his team hit.

## Modules first, toggles second

There is no magic checkbox in Android Studio for this, Nikitin says; it comes down to architecture. A multi-module project lets you swap a module per application, even at runtime, as long as modules share a unified entry point. That can be an existing framework (he points to Decompose and to one from Uber) or your own.

On top of that sit feature toggles, set at build time or served dynamically, the same plumbing used for A/B tests. The useful nuance: highly brand-specific changes can stay local so they don't clutter the admin panel, and a feature that proves useful across brands can graduate from hard-coded config to server-side config. Keep experimental and operational toggles apart in the admin panel, and let the implementation not care which kind it is reading.

## Colour is a function, not a list

The design system is the most transferable idea in the talk. Tokens are grouped by context (surfaces at different Z levels and states, text by importance, icons, borders), and each group knows how it should behave for contrast. The algorithm takes a colour in HSL, keeps hue and saturation, and moves lightness until the element is visible enough on its background. That one rule gives you light and dark themes, and lets you recolour the whole app for a new client.

When a client wants one specific button to break the rules in dark mode, a second layer, the component palette, defines tokens per component that still point back at the contextual palette. Because Quadcode's design system spans Android, iOS, desktop and web, the solution had to be cross-platform; the admin panel shows a vector preview of core screens so whoever configures colours sees the result before a build exists. Vector icons use the same tokens, so they recolour for free.

## Release from tags, fix in trunk

Clients ask for changes at random times and few will wait for the next iteration. Full regression on every brand is too slow. The team's compromise is trunk-based development with on-demand releases: small, frequent merges to main backed by tests in CI, regular fully tested releases, and per-brand patch releases branched from a version tag (1.0.0 to 1.0.1 in his example).

The rule he stresses: every fix still lands in trunk first, however tempting it is to patch the release branch. Skip that and you will eventually forget to merge it back. Because the patch branches from a tested tag rather than the latest trunk, the set of unverified changes stays tiny, which makes impact analysis quick.

## Test the brand, not the whole app again

Running the full suite for every brand burns CI time and rarely finds anything, since core behaviour doesn't depend on branding. Instead, tests create users in the needed state through a dedicated test API rather than hard-coded credentials, brand parameters (registration countries, app name, icons) live in a config class, and a separate brand scope checks what does differ: app identity, social login (different Google and Facebook consoles), push notifications, terms and other brand settings. The first app in a release gets the full run; the rest get the brand smoke scope.

Publishing is automated through CI plugins for Google Play (he shows Jenkins), with mapping files uploaded so crash stack traces can be restored. One warning from experience: don't enable the internal or beta track on a test app you don't plan to keep using, because Google may keep demanding policy updates for it.

## Who should watch

Android leads and mobile platform teams running multi-brand or multi-product apps from one codebase. If you only ship one app, the design-token section is still worth twenty minutes. The talk ends with Ragnar, his cat, credited with one slide.
