Title: Five fixes for slow backend APIs, shown in Spring Boot
Description: Garima Agarwal of Bank of America at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on pagination, async logging, caching, compression and connection pooling for faster APIs.
Body:
Slow APIs are rarely slow for exotic reasons. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Garima Agarwal](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Garima_Agarwal_backend_api_performance), Application Programmer at Bank of America, walked through five well-worn fixes (pagination, asynchronous logging, caching, payload compression and connection pooling) with a Spring Boot snippet for each.

It's a compact, practical checklist of a talk, about thirteen minutes, aimed at Java backend developers. If you've tuned a few APIs already, most of it will be familiar; if you're new to it, it's a good map.

## Name the bottlenecks first

Agarwal lists the usual suspects before the cures. Database queries, which are often the most time-consuming part of an API. Synchronous logging, where the request waits until each log line is written to disk. Large uncompressed payloads. Excessive database connections, where a surprising amount of time goes into opening and closing them. Redundant client requests from poor client-side logic or a double-tapped button. And no caching, so every request starts from scratch.

## Pagination: three flavours

For large datasets, fetching everything at once costs memory and latency. She compares offset-and-limit pagination, cursor-based pagination (a token marks the position, and the client sends it back for the next page) and page-number pagination with metadata like total pages. In Spring Boot, a controller can take a `Pageable` and return a `Page`, so only a slice of rows is fetched per request.

## Logging off the request path

Every synchronous log entry is a disk write the user waits for. Moving logging off the main thread with Logback's async appender (configured in `logback.xml`) or Log4j's equivalent keeps log lines in memory and flushes them in the background. It's the cheapest fix on the list, and probably the one most people forget is a fix at all.

## Cache what you read often

Spring's `@Cacheable` annotation intercepts a method call, returns the cached result if one exists for the same arguments, and otherwise runs the method and stores the result. Her point is the layer it creates between the application and the database: fewer database hits and faster responses for frequently accessed data.

## Compress, but check the CPU bill

Gzip is the widely supported default for text, while Brotli usually compresses better but more slowly. Agarwal adds the trade-offs people skip: compression costs CPU on both ends, small payloads may not be worth it, client and server have to agree on the algorithm, failures need error handling, and compression is not encryption. Spring Boot can turn on response compression with a few lines of configuration.

## Pool your database connections

Opening a fresh connection per request is pure overhead. A pool keeps connections open, lends one out, and takes it back. She recommends HikariCP and tuning the pool size to your traffic pattern, rather than picking a big number and hoping.

## The takeaways

She closes with the habits around the fixes: monitor and profile with Prometheus and Grafana, optimise queries, test and scale proactively for peak load, and put an API gateway with rate limiting in front of high-traffic services.

## Who should watch

Java and Spring Boot developers who own an API that got slower as it grew, and anyone preparing a performance checklist for code review. Engineers looking for distributed-systems depth (cache invalidation strategies, tail latency) will want to pair it with something heavier.

Title: Chaos engineering won adoption, and its open source projects need help
Description: Prithvi Raj of Mirantis, ex-LitmusChaos community manager, at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on how the chaos community grew and why its projects need contributors.
Body:
Chaos engineering crossed the chasm, and then its open source projects started running short of people. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Prithvi Raj](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Prithvi_Raj_community_tales_future), Community Manager and Developer Advocate at Mirantis and the long-time community manager of LitmusChaos, told the story of how that community was built and gave a frank assessment of where it stands.

This is a culture talk, not a tooling tutorial. No experiments get run, but plenty of history and community-building tactics get shared.

## From Chaos Monkey to the enterprise era

Raj sketches the timeline in eras. The innovation era: Netflix's Chaos Monkey terminating instances, the Simian Army, Pumba for Docker. The early adoption era, which he lived through: former Netflix engineers founding Gremlin, and a wave of open source projects including Chaos Mesh, Litmus, Chaos Toolkit and ChaosBlade, followed by cloud offerings like AWS FIS and Azure Chaos Studio. And now what he calls the enterprise era, with Steadybit, Reliably, Harness and AWS Resilience Hub consolidating chaos as a practice large companies expect.

Along the way the practice changed shape. It's no longer one SRE terminating an instance in production. Several teams (SRE, platform, developers, QA) run their own experiments, so collaboration features, ready-made experiment libraries, CI/CD and staging runs, blast-radius control and metrics matter. He agrees with the growing habit of calling the whole loop of inject, observe, alert and manage the incident resilience engineering.

He gives Gremlin a lot of credit, a 9,000-plus member Slack, ChaosConf, years of evangelism, and says it plainly: without Gremlin you can't talk about chaos engineering.

## How the Litmus community was built

The middle of the talk is the LitmusChaos story, from a side project at MayaData through ChaosNative and Harness to a CNCF incubating project with almost 5,000 GitHub stars, and, per Scarf analytics, 500-plus enterprises running it in some form. The tactics are transferable to any open source project:

- **Slack as the front door**, with response and close times on threads tracked, because a newcomer to chaos needs answers fast.
- **Community meetings on the third Wednesday of the month**, plus an APAC-friendly slot once adoption grew in China, India, Singapore and Australia.
- **Three kinds of calls** once contributors arrived: community meetings for user stories and roadmap, contributor meetings for PRs and issues, maintainer calls for internal blockers.
- **Content as the engine**: tutorials, blogs, talks, meetups in Bangalore, KubeCon appearances, and mentorship through Hacktoberfest, GSoC and LFX. He names mentees who went on to lead.

He also thanks Conf42 for its chaos engineering events over the years, which we'll accept graciously.

## The uncomfortable part: who is going to maintain this?

The last section is the reason to watch. Raj shows Chaos Mesh with barely 100 commits in twelve months, mostly from one or two people, and says the same pattern of fading contributions affects Litmus, ChaosBlade and the rest. His list of causes: tight budgets, skepticism about breaking things in production, limited knowledge outside the SRE persona, fewer chaos talks at conferences, and a GenAI story for chaos that hasn't been told well. He sees AI as useful here, for recommending which experiments to run and when, and tying chaos to monitoring and incident management.

His ask is direct. End users who depend on these projects should give back: code, a couple of engineers' time, case studies, or just talking about it.

## Who should watch

Chaos engineering practitioners deciding which open source tools to bet on, and anyone running an open source community who wants a field-tested playbook. If you want to learn how to write your first experiment, look elsewhere.

- [When Gremlins Play with Cockroaches: A Chaos Experiment](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Rain_Leander_when_gremlins_play_with_cockroaches_a_chaos_experiment) by Rain Leander at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022.

Title: AWS SAM across the whole serverless lifecycle, not just templates
Description: Urmila Raju of AWS at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 builds an event-driven GenAI app with AWS SAM, from sam init and local invokes to sam sync and pipelines.
Body:
Infrastructure as code for serverless is awkward because the business logic lives inside the infrastructure: EventBridge rules, Step Functions workflows, Lambda runtimes. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Urmila Raju](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Urmila_Raju_deployment_automation_scalability), Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, showed how AWS SAM (the Serverless Application Model) covers that whole cycle, using a GenAI app that summarises Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 sessions as the running example.

It's an AWS talk about an AWS tool, and a long, hands-on one. Expect a terminal on screen for most of it.

## Start with your operating model, then pick the tool

Raju doesn't open with SAM. She opens with how your organisation runs the cloud: traditional ops with separate app and platform teams, then distributed and decentralised DevOps, which differ in how much autonomy application teams get versus how much control the platform team keeps. The tool should follow that. She lays out the options fairly: CloudFormation in YAML, SAM on top of it, the CDK if your teams want to write infrastructure in Python, and Terraform or the Serverless Framework if you need something platform-agnostic. Her one caveat on the open source tools is timing: new AWS features land in CloudFormation first, so SAM picks them up immediately, while third-party tools take a while to catch up.

## The demo app is a small event-driven system

The app asks an attendee for their name and a session, fetches that session's abstract from a DynamoDB table, and asks a model on Amazon Bedrock (an Anthropic Claude 3 model, in the Step Functions execution she opens) for a summary. Then it takes a rating and free-text feedback and writes a thank-you note that reflects the sentiment. She rates her own session as excellent, which is the most relatable moment in any demo.

Under the hood, API Gateway calls a Lambda that only publishes an event to EventBridge; responses go back to the front end asynchronously. EventBridge rules route each event type to a Step Functions state machine, and the architecture splits cleanly across teams: integration, business logic, GenAI, front end. She builds only the integration team's slice live.

## What SAM actually saves you

A SAM template is CloudFormation with a `Transform` line; at build time it expands into a full CloudFormation stack. The serverless shorthand (`AWS::Serverless::Function` and friends, nine resource types in all) lets a few lines create a Lambda, an API Gateway, a DynamoDB table and the IAM role between them. She points to 75+ ready-made policy templates that scope a function to, say, read-only access on one table, and 19+ event source types that can trigger a function.

## The CLI is the bigger half

The rest of the talk walks the SAM CLI through the development cycle:

- `sam init` scaffolds a project from a quick-start template.
- `sam local generate-event` produces sample payloads for a source like API Gateway, and `sam local invoke -e` runs the function in a local Lambda container, which is why Docker is a prerequisite.
- For a REST API with real response mappings, she exports an existing API as OpenAPI YAML and points the template's definition at it, then runs `sam validate` and `sam deploy --guided`.
- `sam sync` pushes code changes without a full stack deployment, which pairs well with Step Functions: design the workflow in the console's studio, paste the ASL JSON into the project, and sync.
- `sam pipeline init --bootstrap` creates the buckets and roles for a multi-stage pipeline on one of five supported CI/CD systems, giving a platform team control over who deploys what, where.

## Who should watch

Teams already on AWS Lambda who have only used SAM as a template format, and platform engineers deciding how much deployment freedom app teams should get. If you're committed to Terraform across clouds, the operating-model section is still worth the first ten minutes.

Title: In a startup, QA should test the requirements before the code
Description: Vitali Shchur of Check Point Software at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on startup QA ownership, from requirement analysis to shared quality.
Body:
The cheapest bug is the one you catch in the requirements doc. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Vitali Shchur](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vitali_Shchur_qa_mindset_startup), QA Engineer at Check Point Software, argued that a startup's QA engineer should act as part business analyst, testing the requirements before anyone writes code, while the whole team shares ownership of quality.

It's a short talk, more framework than war story, aimed at startups where one QA person faces a team of developers and a deadline.

## Two myths that cost startups

Shchur starts with the myths: testing slows us down, and QA is for finding bugs at the end. Both are expensive. Production bugs damage reputation, and a bad user experience drives churn, which is a heavier price for a startup than for a company with a brand to fall back on. The answer is shifting QA left: involve it from the start, so issues are caught when they're cheap.

## Quality is a team sport

The QA ownership mindset treats quality as a shared responsibility, not a role. Traditional QA sits in its own box at the end of the pipeline; ownership puts it into every role. His practical example: when a deadline is tight and test cases exist, developers can help run the full regression. Not every day, he notes, but sometimes it's the right call.

His three pillars are **collaboration** (all teams accountable for quality), **automation** (less manual testing, more efficiency) and **continuous improvement** (learning from failures and refining process).

## QA as a business analyst

This is the section worth your time. Poorly defined requirements lead to the wrong feature, built well. Shchur's checklist of what QA should catch before development:

- **Ambiguous language.** Words like fast or secure need a definition.
- **Conflicting requirements.** Business expectations that don't match technical feasibility or the system's design.
- **Missing edge cases.** Rare but critical user scenarios.
- **Incorrect business logic.** Assumptions that don't match real-world behaviour.

And the techniques for finding them: ask what if, map the user journeys to spot inconsistencies, compare with industry standards, and validate the logic with developers and product managers. A requirement that says the page must be fast is a bug report waiting for a date.

## Developers, automation and the pipeline

Developers own unit and integration tests, and pairing QA engineers with developers improves coverage. Automation should run at every stage of CI/CD for fast feedback, but he cautions that not everything should be automated. Tools he names: Postman for API tests, and Selenium, Cypress or Playwright for UI automation. Bugs are inevitable, so a strong tracking and triage process and real post-mortems matter as much as the tests.

## Measuring it

Three metrics close the talk: defect leakage rate (how many defects escape to production), test coverage of crucial scenarios, and deployment stability (do releases go smoothly or bring frequent bugs?).

## Who should watch

QA engineers at startups who want to move upstream into requirements, and founders or engineering leads deciding what their first QA hire should do. Experienced QA leads will find it familiar; the requirement-analysis checklist is the part to steal.

Title: What a mobile-first rebuild did for a lender's loan portal
Description: Ravi Chandra Chinta of Temple View Capital at Conf42 Python 2025 on replacing a legacy loan application flow with a mobile-first borrower portal.
Body:
When most of your mobile visitors quit a loan application halfway, the problem is not your marketing. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Ravi Chandra Chinta](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Ravi_Chandra_Chinta_loan_mobile_portal), Principal Salesforce Developer and Architect at Temple View Capital, told the story of rebuilding a lender's borrower experience as a responsive, mobile-first portal, and what changed in the numbers afterwards.

It is a short case study told from the product and architecture side. The stack is Salesforce-centred (MuleSoft and Agentforce come up by name), and Python is not discussed in the recording, so watch it for the transformation story rather than for code.

## The legacy portal was leaking borrowers

Chinta lists three pain points. Performance was inconsistent, which frustrated users and hurt conversion. Mobile accessibility was poor: he describes a 60 percent abandonment rate among mobile users, the digitally native customers the lender most wanted. And outdated infrastructure produced complex workflows that made applying harder than it needed to be.

## Three pillars of the rebuild

The new portal rests on three ideas:

- **An adaptive interface** that works equally well on phone, tablet and desktop.
- **A streamlined application** with intelligent document processing through MuleSoft's IDP tool and secure e-signatures, so borrowers stop emailing PDFs of payslips.
- **A loan management hub**: a real-time dashboard giving borrowers visibility and control over their loans after they apply.

Underneath, the design principles are mobile-first layout, user-centred design that adapts to preferences, and a backbone of cloud infrastructure, APIs and multi-factor authentication.

## What changed

The results section is where the talk earns its slot. Chinta reports that average application time fell from 25 minutes to under 15, support call volume dropped by 40 percent, and customer satisfaction scores rose by 35 percent. Later slides add larger figures for processing time, loan approvals and operating costs; the talk does not break down how each was measured, so the application-time and support-call numbers are the most concrete ones to take away.

## Lessons that travel

His lessons are the transferable part. Use data on real borrower behaviour to decide what to optimise. Communicate clearly, with real-time status updates, because confident borrowers make fewer application errors. Keep a continuous feedback loop so the portal follows borrower expectations instead of the original spec.

Looking ahead, he describes three directions the team was exploring: an AI chatbot for round-the-clock guidance through complex steps, voice-driven loan applications for accessibility, and blockchain-backed loan records for transparency and fraud reduction. He frames all three as future work, not shipped features. He also ties the work to financial inclusion: a simpler mobile flow reaches borrowers that a desktop-only process quietly excluded.

## Who should watch

Product engineers and architects at lenders or other regulated businesses who are planning a front-end modernisation and want a compact before-and-after story. Engineers looking for implementation detail will want his longer Cloud Native session on the same platform.

Title: Why industrial IoT outgrows the monolith, and where Kubernetes fits
Description: Gayathri Jeganmohan of Microsoft at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on moving industrial IoT from monoliths to Kubernetes, with Azure IoT Operations as the case study.
Body:
A factory can't wait for a monolith to restart. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Gayathri Jeganmohan](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Gayathri_Jeganmohan_kubernetes_uptime_reliability), Software Engineer at Microsoft, argued that industrial IoT systems have outgrown tightly coupled architectures, compared the three ways to run microservices, and walked through Azure IoT Operations as a Kubernetes-native example running in industry.

It's an architecture overview, not a hands-on session: good for orienting yourself, light on YAML.

## The monolith fails all at once

Jeganmohan describes the classic industrial stack as four layers deployed as one unit: a device layer close to the sensors, a data ingestion layer, business logic and a UI. Tightly coupled, so when the business logic breaks, everything waits for it. Adding a new capability, her example being an app that calls an AI model, means testing the whole thing and taking it down to ship. That works for a small operation. With many devices and many factories, and with latency that matters when a machine is overheating, she argues it simply fails.

## Kubernetes, serverless or plain VMs

Before picking Kubernetes she lays out the alternatives honestly. Serverless functions such as Azure Functions or AWS Lambda are event-driven and fully managed, a good fit for work that only runs when something changes. Traditional VMs give direct control of hardware and suit legacy constraints or security rules that keep software off the cloud. Kubernetes, which she compares to a conductor deciding whether the guitarist or the pianist goes first, is the choice when you need orchestration, autoscaling, self-healing and observability at scale.

## Five reasons it suits the plant floor

Her case for Kubernetes rests on five points:

- **Scalability and resilience**: horizontal and vertical pod scaling, self-healing restarts, and multi-node failover so another node picks up when one dies.
- **Edge, on-prem and cloud**: lightweight distributions like K3s and MicroK8s run on low-power industrial gateways, and multi-cloud means you don't have to go all in on one provider.
- **Security**: role-based access control for fine-grained permissions, plus network policies and audit logging.
- **Observability**: Prometheus and Grafana for metrics and alerting, so a hot machine gets attention in real time.
- **Delivery**: CI/CD, quick rollbacks to the previous version, and blue-green deployments to test before production.

The abstract puts numbers on the move: 40% faster deployments, 99.9% uptime, 30% cost reduction and 3x better fault isolation. In the talk these are presented as the benefits of the approach rather than measurements from one named system, so read them as targets, not a benchmark. The mechanisms behind them (rolling updates, workload rescheduling across nodes, scaling down when idle, namespace and pod isolation) are the useful part.

## The case study: Azure IoT Operations

The last section maps the ideas onto Microsoft's Azure IoT Operations. On the left of the diagram sits the factory: IP cameras and OPC UA devices. Those workloads run on Kubernetes, with an edge-native, highly available MQTT broker that makes the system event-driven as well as containerised, and data flows that convert formats before the data reaches the cloud. Azure Arc lets you manage the edge from the cloud, GitOps handles deployments and rolling updates, and the data lands in services like Event Hubs, Event Grid, Fabric, Data Explorer and Power BI. Since she works at Microsoft, treat it as the home-team example; the pattern of Kubernetes plus an MQTT broker at the edge travels to other stacks.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects in manufacturing or IIoT who are still running a monolith and need the vocabulary to argue for a change. Kubernetes veterans won't learn new mechanics here; they may find the edge-gateway framing useful when explaining the move to plant engineers.

Title: SMS spam detection with TF-IDF, Naive Bayes and honest metrics
Description: Ajay Krishnan Prabhakaran of Meta at Conf42 Python 2025 on building an SMS spam classifier in Python, from text cleaning to precision and recall.
Body:
A spam filter that blocks one real bank code is worse than one that lets an occasional prize scam through. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Ajay Krishnan Prabhakaran](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Ajay_Krishnan_Prabhakaran_sms_spam_python), Senior Data Engineer at Meta, walked through building an SMS spam classifier in Python, from labelling and cleaning messages to TF-IDF features, Naive Bayes and SVM models, and the metrics that keep false positives honest.

It is a clear end-to-end introduction to classical text classification, the right level for someone building a first NLP model or teaching one.

## Why SMS spam is a security problem

Prabhakaran sets up the stakes beyond annoyance. Spam texts carry phishing links and scams that lead to financial loss and identity theft, and the flood makes people distrust legitimate messages too. The goal he sets is to classify every message as spam or ham, keep false positives and negatives low, and process high volumes quickly.

## Data first: collect, label, clean

The pipeline starts with a diverse data set of SMS messages covering many kinds of spam and normal conversation, because a model only generalises as far as its examples. Each message is labelled spam or ham by hand; supervised learning is only as good as that ground truth.

Cleaning removes special characters, numbers and punctuation, and lowercases the text so FREE and free count as the same word. Tokenisation splits messages into words, and stop-word removal drops filler words like and, the and is that carries little signal. A spammer's exclamation marks, it turns out, are less informative than their vocabulary.

## Turning words into numbers

For features he covers both a count vectoriser and TF-IDF. Term frequency rewards words that appear often in a message; inverse document frequency discounts words that appear everywhere. Words common in one message but rare across the corpus get the highest weight, which is exactly the profile of spam vocabulary.

## Two classic classifiers

Naive Bayes is the first model: a probabilistic classifier built on Bayes' theorem with the simplifying assumption that features are independent. That assumption is wrong for language and works anyway, which is why Naive Bayes remains the fast, cheap baseline for text. Support vector machines are the second, finding the hyperplane that best separates classes and using kernels when the data is not linearly separable.

## Measure more than accuracy

Training uses cross-validation across multiple data splits to catch overfitting. For evaluation Prabhakaran is explicit that accuracy alone misleads on imbalanced data, which SMS data usually is. Precision tells you how many flagged messages really were spam; recall tells you how much spam you caught; F1 balances the two. His priority is reducing false positives, so important messages are never filtered.

He closes with ongoing work: tuning parameters, feeding user reports and new data back into training as spam tactics change, and exploring deep learning and real-time processing.

## Who should watch

Python developers and students building their first text classifier, and engineers who need to explain precision versus recall to a product team. If you already run transformer-based moderation, this is a refresher on the baseline you should still be comparing against.

Title: Test against the real cluster before you open the pull request
Description: Anita Ihuman of MetalBear at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025 on shifting cloud testing left with mirrord, which plugs a local process into a remote Kubernetes cluster.
Body:
Most Kubernetes bugs that matter only show up in the cluster, which is exactly where developers test last. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, [Anita Ihuman](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Anita_Ihuman_kubernetes_development_testing), Developer Advocate at MetalBear, made the case for moving cloud testing to the moment you write the code, and showed mirrord, MetalBear's open source tool that runs your local process as if it lived inside a remote cluster.

It's a vendor talk in the honest sense: the first half is the problem, the second half is a live demo of the company's own tool. Both halves are short and to the point.

## The build-push-test loop is the expensive part

Ihuman starts with the workflow everyone recognises. Writing the code is the quick bit. Then you build it, make sure it behaves in a container, get it into a cluster, check it plays nicely with the other containerised services, and only at the far end of the pipeline does it meet anything resembling production. When something breaks there, you go round the whole loop again, and with hundreds of microservices that can eat hours or days.

The usual workarounds each carry a bill. Mocks give you optimistic conditions and an implicit guess at what production looks like, and someone has to configure and maintain them. Per-developer remote environments are closer to the real thing, but a team of a hundred engineers with a hundred environments pays for all of them. She cites NIST research on the theme that the later a defect is found, the more it costs to fix.

## "Remocal": local process, remote context

Shifting cloud testing left, in her framing, means validating code against a real cloud environment during development, not waiting for staging. That's where mirrord comes in. It has two halves: a layer that sits in the memory of your local process, and an agent pod that mirrord starts in the same network namespace as the pod you target. The layer intercepts low-level calls and forwards them to the agent, so your local code sees the cluster's network traffic, file system and environment variables while still running in your own debugger.

By default mirrord mirrors traffic, so the deployed service keeps answering requests while you watch a copy. The configuration file lets you switch to stealing incoming traffic instead, and control outgoing traffic, environment and file access.

## The demo: a weather app, a purple header

The demo is deliberately small. A weather microservice runs on an AKS cluster. Ihuman changes the header text and the background colour (purple, for the record), enables mirrord from the VS Code extension, picks a configuration that targets the weather app deployment, and starts a debug session. A mirrord agent pod appears in the cluster, the same URL now shows her changed version, and the production version stays untouched for everyone else. End the session and the agent pod removes itself.

Her list of practical points: no root access needed, available for VS Code, IntelliJ and as a CLI, works regardless of language, and doesn't care whether your cluster runs a service mesh or sits behind a VPN. Several local processes can each attach to a different remote pod at once.

## Who should watch

Developers on teams with many microservices whose "works on my machine" keeps failing in staging, and platform teams weighing shared dev clusters against one environment per engineer. If you already run mirrord, this is an introduction you can skip; if you've only heard the name, it's a quick way to see the workflow end to end. The questions it leaves for you, such as how to stop two developers stealing the same traffic in a shared cluster, are the ones to take to the docs.

Title: Injecting network faults into ECS on Fargate with AWS FIS
Description: Sunil Govindankutty of AWS at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 demos latency, black hole and packet loss experiments on an ECS Fargate API with AWS FIS.
Body:
The most useful chaos experiment is the one that proves your hypothesis wrong. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Sunil Govindankutty](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sunil_Govindankutty_network_resilience_experiments), Enterprise Support Lead at AWS and a member of its resilience technical community, ran network fault experiments against a containerised API on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate using AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS), and the black hole experiment did exactly that: instead of a friendly error, the API returned 500s and the load generator timed out.

It's an AWS engineer demoing AWS tooling, and a very clean one, because the demo follows the chaos engineering method step by step.

## ECS, Fargate and the faults that matter

He opens with Werner Vogels' line that everything fails all the time, then a quick primer: ECS schedules, heals and scales containers; Fargate runs each task in its own kernel without servers to manage; tasks come from task definitions, services keep them running and registered with load balancers, clusters group them.

Then the three network faults FIS can now inject into Fargate tasks:

- **Latency**, the kind you get from congestion, route changes or slow DNS.
- **Black hole**, where packets are silently dropped, TCP connections hang and dependencies return nothing at all.
- **Packet loss**, partial drops that show up as odd patterns in monitoring.

FIS packages actions, targets and safeguards into an experiment template, and the safeguards matter: attach a CloudWatch alarm as a stop condition and FIS halts the experiment when it fires, keeping the blast radius small. It integrates with EventBridge for third-party monitoring, and the experiment report can double as testing evidence for compliance teams.

## Prerequisites before any fault

The demo app is a CRUD API on an ECS Fargate cluster backed by an RDS MySQL database, with each task running the app container alongside an SSM agent container (a prerequisite for network faults on Fargate). Before injecting anything, he puts the prerequisites in place: a CloudWatch dashboard (no monitoring means the tree-falls-in-the-forest problem), synthetic load from an Artillery script since lower environments lack real traffic, and a check that there are no existing errors, since known errors should be fixed before experimenting.

Then the steady state: API Gateway latency around 22 to 25 ms from the system's view, and end-user P90 around 75 to 150 ms.

## Experiment one: latency, as predicted

The hypothesis: adding 200 ms of latency between the compute layer and the database will raise overall latency, but it will stay within the healthy threshold. The template targets the ECS tasks by cluster and service name, runs for five minutes, and the dashboard shows end-user P90 climbing to about 262 ms. Whether that's acceptable, Govindankutty notes, is a decision for you and your stakeholders. If not, the remedy might be failing the database over to a standby. Metrics returned to normal after the experiment, which is its own small confidence boost.

## Experiment two: black hole, not as predicted

The second hypothesis was that if TCP traffic to the RDS port is black-holed, the app will detect it and return a user-friendly error. Instead, API Gateway threw 500 errors and Artillery saw timeouts. Back to the drawing board, which is the whole point.

He also shows the packet-loss template: a configurable loss percentage, and sources that can be literal service names like DynamoDB or S3 (FIS resolves the IPs) or the domain of an external dependency such as a SaaS API.

## Who should watch

Teams running containers on ECS and Fargate who want to start chaos engineering with managed tooling, and anyone who wants to see the steady-state, hypothesis, experiment, observe loop done properly. If you're on Kubernetes or another cloud, the method still transfers.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Cloud Chaos Engineering with AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS)](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2023_Samuel_Baruffi_cloud_aws_fault_injection_simulator_fis) by Samuel Baruffi at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023, the earlier FIS walkthrough.
- [Enhancing Hypothesis Development Through Resilience Modeling](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Gunnar_Grosch_hypothesis_development_resilience_modeling) by Gunnar Grosch at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, on writing hypotheses worth breaking.
- [Shifting left chaos testing](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2023_Pablo_Chacin_shifting_left_chaos_testing) by Pablo Chacin at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023.

Title: Cloud security in layers, from zero trust to post-quantum crypto
Description: Sandeep Batchu of Microsoft at Conf42 Python 2025 on zero trust, IAM, ML threat detection, micro-segmentation and compliance automation for cloud apps.
Body:
Once your workloads live in someone else's data centre, the network perimeter stops meaning much. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Sandeep Batchu](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sandeep_Batchu_secure_cloud_applications), Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft, made the case for treating cloud security as a stack of layers, starting with zero trust and identity and reaching out to quantum-resistant encryption and automated compliance.

Worth knowing before you start: this is an architecture-level overview. It does not show Python code or libraries, so come for the security model and the vocabulary, not for snippets.

## Trust nothing by default

Batchu frames the problem with the attack surface that cloud adoption brings: more sophisticated attacks and no traditional perimeter. He cites industry statistics that 94 percent of enterprises rely on cloud services and that most enterprise data is now created and processed in the cloud, which makes it the obvious target.

His answer starts with zero trust. Older models assumed anyone inside the network was trustworthy; zero trust assumes no user or device is trusted by default. The core principles he lists are continuous verification, least-privilege access for both users and applications, and micro-segmentation to stop attackers moving sideways once they are in.

## Identity is the new perimeter

The identity and access management section turns those principles into controls. Role-based access control assigns permissions by responsibility, so people and services touch only what they need. Adaptive authentication weighs risk signals such as device, location and behaviour before deciding how hard to challenge a login. Policy enforcement restricts access for compliance, and multi-factor authentication combines passwords, biometrics and one-time codes. None of this is new, which is exactly why it is still the place most breaches start.

## Let the models watch the logs

Manual threat detection, he argues, is slow and error-prone, and gets worse with scale. Machine learning helps in two ways: behaviour analytics learns what normal looks like for users and applications and flags deviations, and threat-intelligence models learn from large volumes of known attack patterns to predict new ones.

## Segment the network, prepare the crypto

Micro-segmentation divides the network into isolated segments with their own controls, limiting what an attacker can do after breaching one. Batchu points to software-defined network policies and VLAN controls as the implementation tools.

Two forward-looking items close the technology section. Quantum-resistant encryption prepares for a time when quantum computers could break today's public-key schemes; starting the transition early, he argues, makes it manageable. Blockchain-backed audit trails make logs immutable, so tampering is detectable, and decentralised verification removes a single point of failure.

## Serverless and compliance as code

The last layer is operational. Serverless platforms abstract the infrastructure and make security monitoring easier to automate; Batchu attributes faster incident response to that automation. Continuous compliance automation replaces manual audit preparation with ongoing checks against regulations such as GDPR, CCPA and HIPAA, cutting the human error that creeps into spreadsheet-driven audits. He quotes large reductions for both; as with the opening statistics, they are presented as industry figures rather than a single system's results.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects new to cloud security who want one map of the main defensive layers, or leads preparing a security roadmap who need a structured list. Security specialists will know each layer already.

Title: Start with an isolation forest before reaching for deep learning
Description: Chirag Gajiwala of Nutanix at Conf42 Python 2025 surveys deep learning for security, then flags risky CVEs with PySpark and an isolation forest.
Body:
Security teams are told AI will find the threats their SIEM misses; the practical question is which model to try first. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Chirag Gajiwala](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Chirag_Gajiwala_ai_python_cybersecurity), Member of Technical Staff at Nutanix, toured the deep learning families relevant to cybersecurity and then showed his own starting point: a PySpark ingestion job and an isolation forest flagging anomalies in vulnerability data.

Most of the talk is a survey, so expect breadth over depth. The concrete part comes near the end, and its advice is the most transferable: understand the use case, start with simpler models, then climb.

## A map of the model zoo

Gajiwala starts with reinforcement learning, pointing to DeepMind's AlphaGo as the classic example and to robotics as a growth area. He then contrasts two generative families. GANs currently lead on image generation quality, while variational autoencoders are probabilistic models with a practical edge for anomaly and threat detection on security data sets.

Graph neural networks get a section because security data is full of relationships: hosts, users, vulnerabilities and connections. He argues GNNs can surface anomalies that SIEM tools such as Splunk and AlienVault miss, and stresses integrating them with existing tools rather than replacing them. Recurrent neural networks, which he distinguishes from image-focused CNNs, are his pick for sequential anomaly detection, and he highlights TimeGPT, a transformer-based time-series model, for forecasting and anomaly work in finance, web traffic and IoT.

## Where AI fits in a security team

His framing is pragmatic. Existing security tools are good, but they fail occasionally, and that is where models trained in Python can help with threat detection, vulnerability assessment and fraud prevention. Automation can also take over basic security reporting so engineers spend time on harder problems. He adds a section on ethics: privacy, bias and job displacement, and the need to involve compliance, security and governance teams before deploying models on sensitive data.

## The concrete bit: PySpark plus isolation forest

The demo half is the reason to watch. First, a PySpark job pulls data from a REST API into a Spark DataFrame and writes it to a store; he notes Spark's connectors for Cassandra, MongoDB, Elasticsearch and Kafka make it a natural fit for ETL in distributed systems.

Then the security model. Starting from a vulnerability data set, he cleans it, encodes severity and complexity, and uses the CVSS score as a feature. He focuses on entries with high complexity, medium severity and CVSS above six, trains an isolation forest, and extracts the anomalies. He reports also trying XGBoost and plans to test RNNs and transformer models next. The order matters: an isolation forest trains in seconds and gives you a baseline to beat, which is more than most transformer prototypes can say in their first week.

## Who should watch

Security engineers curious about machine learning, and data engineers asked to build anomaly detection for a security team, will get a vocabulary map and a sensible first project. Practitioners already running ML in a SOC will find the survey material familiar.

Title: How Azure Site Recovery handles failover for Azure, Hyper-V and VMware
Description: Somaning Turwale of Microsoft at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on RPO, RTO and the components Azure Site Recovery needs for each disaster recovery scenario.
Body:
A disaster recovery plan you've never failed over is a hope, not a plan. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Somaning Turwale](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Somaning_Turwale_resilience_recovery_disaster), a Senior Tech Support Engineer at Microsoft who specialises in Azure Backup and Recovery Services, walked through Azure Site Recovery (ASR): what it replicates, the components each scenario needs, and the drill schedule that keeps a recovery plan honest.

Scope check: this is a Microsoft engineer explaining a Microsoft product, and the talk is a structured tour of ASR rather than a vendor-neutral DR comparison. If you run on Azure or are considering it for DR, that's exactly what you want.

## Why a second data centre is a hard sell

Turwale starts with the traditional problem. Business continuity means surviving hardware failure, cyberattacks and natural disasters, but a secondary site costs hardware, power, cooling and staff, adds compatibility and compliance overhead, and sits idle most of the time. ASR's pitch is to replace that site with Azure: pay for what you use, and let the service automate failover and failback across on-premises and cloud workloads.

## RPO and RTO, defined plainly

He grounds the talk in the two numbers that define DR readiness. **Recovery point objective** is how much data loss is acceptable: the maximum age of the data you can restore. Lower RPO means more frequent or continuous replication. **Recovery time objective** is how fast systems must come back: the maximum downtime the business can tolerate. ASR's continuous replication and automated failover are aimed at keeping both low.

## Three scenarios, three parts lists

The core of the talk is a parts list per scenario, which is handy as a pre-flight checklist.

**Azure to Azure.** VMs replicate from a primary region to a secondary (Microsoft provides paired regions). You need a Recovery Services vault for settings and metadata, a replication policy for frequency and recovery-point retention (this is where RPO is set), a target region, a VNet and subnet that mirror the primary, public IP planning for post-failover connectivity, recovery plans that order the failover of dependent apps (database before app tier), managed disks, and optionally an Azure Automation account for runbooks during failover or failback.

**Hyper-V to Azure.** Standalone Hyper-V hosts or clusters managed by System Center Virtual Machine Manager replicate to Azure, with the same vault, replication policy and Azure target resources. Once the site is restored, you fail back to Hyper-V.

**VMware or physical to Azure.** Turwale covers only the modernised architecture, noting the classic one is on its way out. On premises you install a replication appliance on Windows Server that talks to vCenter or a standalone ESXi host, plus a mobility agent on each protected machine. One gotcha worth knowing: physical servers can't fail back to physical. You stay in Azure or fail back to VMware.

## Drills or it didn't happen

The implementation advice is where the chaos engineering audience will nod. Assess first; for VMware and Hyper-V, Microsoft's Deployment Planner can run for about a week to profile workload dependencies, network performance and RPO/RTO needs. Plan bandwidth, compliance and a rollout roadmap, and train the IT team. Then test on a schedule: he recommends regular failover drills (monthly, in one slide) plus quarterly full-scale recovery simulations, and test failovers in ASR run without touching production. Feed what the drills teach you back into the recovery plans.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure and platform engineers responsible for DR on Azure or on Hyper-V and VMware estates moving toward it, and SREs who want to know what a recovery plan in ASR actually contains. The product-level figures on cost and speed are Microsoft's framing; the component lists are the reusable part.

Title: Passwordless login with FIDO2 and WebAuthn in a Flask app
Description: Sairam Durgaraju of Evernorth Health Services at Conf42 Python 2025 on building FIDO2 and WebAuthn passwordless authentication with Python.
Body:
The safest password is the one your server never stores. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Sairam Durgaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sairam_Durgaraju_fido2_webauthn), Architecture Senior Advisor at Evernorth Health Services, explained how FIDO2 and WebAuthn replace passwords with public-key cryptography and showed the shape of a Python backend that registers devices and authenticates users with them.

It is a compact introduction, about the length of a coffee break: the protocol first, then a Flask implementation, then testing, troubleshooting and best practices. A good first talk on the topic if you have been meaning to add passkey-style login and want the moving parts named.

## What FIDO2 actually is

FIDO2, short for Fast Identity Online 2, is an open standard from the FIDO Alliance. Durgaraju splits it into two pieces. WebAuthn is the browser API that lets a site request passwordless authentication. CTAP, the Client to Authenticator Protocol, defines how external authenticators such as security keys talk to the browser. Together they let a phone, laptop or hardware key prove who you are without a shared secret crossing the wire.

## Register once, sign challenges forever

The flow has two halves. During registration, the user's authenticator (a security key, a phone, a laptop with biometrics) generates a key pair. The public key goes to the server; the private key never leaves the device. During authentication, the server sends a challenge, the device signs it with the private key after a fingerprint, face or PIN check, and the server verifies the signature with the stored public key. Match, and the user is in.

The security win follows directly: there is nothing reusable to phish or leak from the database. A stolen public key is about as useful to an attacker as a stolen padlock.

## The Python side

The prerequisites he lists are modest: Python 3.7 or later, Flask or FastAPI for the backend, and the `fido2` library. The code he walks through imports Flask and the FIDO2 server classes, including the relying-party entity, then exposes a registration endpoint that captures the user's device information and public key and an authentication endpoint that verifies the signed challenge. He notes the same pattern works with the managed WebAuthn and FIDO2 offerings of the major cloud providers.

Testing is pleasantly low-tech: run the Flask server, hit the register and authenticate endpoints with curl or Postman, then try a real YubiKey or Titan key in Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari. WebAuthn also works with Windows Hello, Mac and Android biometrics, and with USB, NFC and Bluetooth keys. For debugging he points to webauthn.io, which shows the requests and responses.

## When it breaks, and how to run it well

His troubleshooting list covers the usual suspects. Security key not detected: check the device supports CTAP. Invalid credentials: the key may not have registered properly, so retry registration. Browser problems: confirm WebAuthn is enabled.

Best practices round it off: validate authenticators through attestation and the FIDO Metadata Service, log authentication failures, and ship those logs to your SIEM with alerts on unusual patterns. He also suggests combining WebAuthn with OTP as an extra factor for higher-risk flows. He ties the motivation to compliance as well, citing NIST, GDPR and HIPAA as pressures pushing organisations toward stronger authentication.

## Who should watch

Python web developers and security engineers planning a passwordless rollout who want the protocol and the server responsibilities explained in plain terms. Identity specialists who already run WebAuthn in production will not find new material.

Title: Moving SAP BW to AWS starts with an honest inventory
Description: Gopikrishna Yeturi of LTIMindtree at Conf42 Python 2025 on migrating SAP BW to AWS, from assessment and migration services to post-move testing.
Body:
An SAP BW system is rarely just a data warehouse; it is a web of extractors, ERP connections and reports that finance relies on at month end. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Gopikrishna Yeturi](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Gopikrishna_Yeturi_sap_migration_performance), Senior Specialist in package implementation at LTIMindtree, outlined a strategy for moving SAP BW from on-premises to AWS, built around a thorough assessment up front and three rounds of testing at the end.

Scope check: this is a short consultant-style overview of the migration plan. There is no Python and no code in it, despite the event; it is useful as a checklist for SAP and cloud teams, less so as an engineering deep cut.

## Measure the estate before you move it

Yeturi's first step is assessment. BW landscapes routinely hold terabytes and sometimes reach petabytes, and that volume drives the infrastructure you will need. Just as important is the dependency map: connections to ERP platforms, the various data sources feeding BW and the enterprise reporting tools reading from it. Document all of it before planning the cut-over, he argues, or the integration surprises arrive after go-live.

## The AWS toolbox for the move

He names three AWS services for the migration itself:

- **AWS Migration Hub** to track the whole programme in one place and give every team the same view of progress.
- **AWS Server Migration Service** to automate server moves and reduce manual steps and downtime.
- **AWS Database Migration Service** for the database, with ongoing replication to keep downtime low and data intact.

For getting large data sets across, he pairs Amazon S3 as durable object storage for BW data with AWS Direct Connect, a private dedicated link that avoids pushing a petabyte through the public internet. Anyone who has watched a multi-terabyte transfer crawl over a VPN will appreciate that line item.

## Tune for the cloud, not the old data centre

Once on AWS, performance comes from matching resources to BW's workload: provisioned-IOPS EBS volumes for consistent I/O, memory-optimised or compute-optimised EC2 instances chosen for the query profile, and Auto Scaling to follow demand rather than sizing for the peak all year. He also calls for BW parameters tuned for cloud-specific configuration and queries optimised to cut processing time, with cost reviewed alongside performance.

The abstract promises 40 percent shorter timelines and 30 percent better query performance. In the recording these are not tied to a specific named migration, so read them as the outcome the approach aims for.

## Three kinds of testing after cut-over

The section most teams underinvest in is post-migration testing, and Yeturi gives it three passes. Functional testing, run by the functional team, confirms data loads, reports and analysis behave as before. Performance testing puts the new system under realistic load scenarios, because BW is a high-volume, resource-hungry system and the first month-end close is a bad time to discover a bottleneck. Security testing matters because BW and ERP systems are audited; data integrity and confidentiality have to be demonstrable, not assumed.

## Who should watch

SAP basis and BW teams, and cloud architects asked to plan their company's first SAP move to AWS, will get a tidy sequence to adapt. Engineers looking for Python content or migration war stories should pick another session.

Title: Chaos engineering for microservices: what to break first
Description: Muhammad Ahmad Saeed at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on the failure types microservices face, the experiment loop, and tools from Chaos Monkey to Toxiproxy.
Body:
Every microservice has dependencies, and every dependency is a failure you haven't met yet. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, software engineer [Muhammad Ahmad Saeed](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muhammad_Ahmad_Saeed_chaos_microservices_engineering) gave a well-organised introduction to chaos engineering for microservices: which failures to simulate, the five-step experiment loop, the main tools, and how to start without taking down something important.

If you are new to chaos engineering, or need a talk to send to the team before your first game day, this is a good first one.

## Map the dependencies first

Saeed opens with a plain diagram: one service talks to its database and to a second service through a queue; that second service calls a third over direct HTTP. Every arrow is a dependency, and every dependency can fail. His three goals follow from that picture: uncover weaknesses such as single points of failure, keep performance within a defined range as conditions change, and handle the unexpected gracefully so one failure doesn't take the whole service down.

Microservices make this harder in four ways he spells out: many moving parts (APIs, databases, queues, third parties), network dependencies prone to latency, packet loss and outages, dynamic scaling in Kubernetes that makes failure modes harder to predict, and frequent deployments by different teams on different schedules.

## Seven failures worth simulating

His catalogue is a practical starting checklist:

1. **Service failure.** He singles out the authentication service, which tends to take everything else down with it when it goes.
2. **Network issues.** Latency, packet loss, partitions.
3. **Dependency failures.** Databases, message brokers, third-party APIs.
4. **Load and scalability.** Does the hot service autoscale, and what happens to its callers meanwhile?
5. **Data consistency.** Corruption or replication delay during a failure.
6. **Configuration changes.** Does a bad config propagate and topple things?
7. **Cascading failures.** One fault triggering a chain reaction.

## The loop

The method is the classic one, clearly put. Define a steady state with metrics (errors won't be zero; know your baseline). Form a hypothesis about what should happen. Introduce controlled chaos. Observe, measure and make sure the system recovers. Then automate the experiments into CI/CD, so resilience is tested continuously and not once a year.

## The toolbox

He covers four tools in a sentence or two each: Netflix's **Chaos Monkey**, which randomly terminates production instances; **Chaos Mesh**, open source and built for Kubernetes, with a web UI and diverse fault injection; **Gremlin**, a commercial platform with a wide range of attacks across Kubernetes, cloud providers and more; and **Toxiproxy**, an open-source TCP proxy focused on network conditions. For case studies he mentions Slack's regular chaos experiments and incident drills, and Microsoft's managed Azure Chaos Studio.

## Start small, keep an exit

The best-practices section is where beginners should pay attention. Start with non-critical services. Run experiments in a controlled way, with feature flags and a tested rollback to a stable state, because your hypothesis about one harmless dependency might be wrong. Monitor everything (Prometheus, Grafana, the ELK stack). Automate so it's routine. And make sure self-healing exists before you lean on it. Breaking things is the easy half; putting them back is the part that needs a plan.

## Who should watch

Developers and SREs at the start of their chaos engineering journey, and team leads drafting a first experiment backlog. Practitioners who already run game days will know the material; the failure checklist is still a handy review.

Title: Mobile app speed is a stack of small, boring wins
Description: Jaspreet Kumar of Microsoft at Conf42 Python 2025 on mobile app performance, from app size and lazy loading to caching, async UI and A/B tests.
Body:
Users rarely uninstall an app because of one big failure; they leave after a hundred small waits. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Jaspreet Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Jaspreet_Kumar_python_performance_optimization), Lead Software Engineer at Microsoft, walked through a layered checklist for mobile app performance: shrink the app, load less up front, cache aggressively, keep the UI thread free, and then measure, predict and test your way to the next improvement.

A note on scope before you press play. Despite the title and the event, the recording barely touches Python; it is a platform-neutral performance strategy talk, with most concrete examples drawn from Android tooling. Treat it as a structured checklist, not a code session.

## Smaller apps install faster and start faster

Kumar starts with app size, because every megabyte is a download, an install and a cold start. His toolkit: remove unused code paths, use vector drawables instead of bitmaps where possible, compress images as WebP, and run resource-shrinking tools. On the code side he recommends modular architecture, ProGuard for shrinking and obfuscation, dynamic feature modules so rarely used parts download on demand, and careful dependency management. If you have ever found three JSON libraries in one APK, you know why that last item is on the list.

## Load what the user sees, defer the rest

Lazy loading is the next lever. Heavy graphics, video and secondary features should wait until they are requested, so the core screen is usable immediately and the rest arrives in the background. Kumar frames this as perceived performance: the app feels fast when the first useful thing appears quickly, even if the full feature set takes longer.

Caching is the network-side twin. Store critical data locally, combining in-memory and persistent caches, to cut redundant requests and keep the app usable on weak connections. Pair that with a mobile-appropriate database, lightweight transactions and queries that avoid fetching the same data twice.

## Keep the UI thread for the UI

Asynchronous processing gets its own section: push heavy operations to background threads so the interface never freezes. It is the oldest rule in mobile development and still the one most often broken under deadline, which is probably why Kumar spends time on it.

## Measure, predict, experiment, listen

The second half is about the feedback loop. Real-time monitoring captures granular metrics on responsiveness, memory and resource use so bottlenecks can be found rather than guessed. Machine learning anomaly detection then flags subtle performance deviations before they become incidents, and predictive models suggest where the next bottleneck will appear.

A/B testing turns opinions into evidence. Kumar recommends trying several optimisation techniques, measuring their effect on user experience, and running that as a continuous cycle. User feedback closes the loop: in-app surveys, usage analytics and interviews, prioritised by impact.

The abstract cites 50 percent faster load times, 15 percent fewer crashes and a 7 percent retention gain, and the closing slide adds 10 percent revenue growth. The talk presents these as achievable outcomes of the strategy rather than results from one named app, so use them as a sense of scale, not a promise.

## Who should watch

Mobile engineers and leads who want a complete checklist to audit an app against, or a structure for a performance roadmap. Experienced Android performance engineers will recognise every item; Python developers expecting Python tooling should look elsewhere.

Title: Event-driven architecture as a fault-tolerance strategy
Description: Muhammad Rizwan of Procode at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on decoupling with events, .NET and Azure tooling, and taming ordering and consistency.
Body:
If services don't call each other directly, one of them going down can't take the others with it. That's the resilience pitch behind event-driven architecture, and at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 [Muhammad Rizwan](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muhammad_Rizwan_architecture_systems_event), Software Engineer at Procode, walked through its principles, its costs and the .NET and Azure tools he uses, drawing on a real-time vehicle tracking system he built.

It's a structured overview for engineers new to EDA, with a bias toward the Microsoft ecosystem.

## Producers, brokers, consumers

Rizwan starts with the three moving parts. Producers emit events when something happens, such as a user clicking Buy Now. Brokers route them: Apache Kafka, Azure Event Grid and other message queues. Consumers react, for example by sending an email or push notification.

Three principles follow. **Decoupling**: payment and order fulfilment can run independently, so a failure in one doesn't cascade. **Asynchronous communication**: nobody blocks waiting for a response. **Real-time responsiveness**: react to a back-in-stock event or a live dashboard update the moment it happens.

## Fault tolerance you can explain to a product manager

His airline example is the one to borrow. If the payment service has problems, users can still browse flights and fill their carts, because nothing upstream is synchronously waiting on payments. Add horizontal scaling (new consumer instances when load grows) and independent deploys per service, and you get the scalability and modularity arguments for free.

His vehicle tracking system shows the pattern end to end: vehicles send location updates as events, the broker processes them and routes them to the right consumers, and when critical conditions are met, alerts go out by SMS or phone call.

## The bill comes due in debugging

Rizwan is upfront about the costs, which is the most useful part of the talk:

- **Event ordering and dependencies.** Asynchronous events arrive whenever they like. Getting the sequence right needs choreography or saga patterns.
- **Debugging and tracing.** A request no longer has a single path to follow. He recommends distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry or Jaeger, plus logs and metrics integrated from the start.
- **Data consistency.** ACID transactions give way to eventual consistency, so design for temporary disagreement between services and use compensating transactions when things need undoing.

His mitigations: event choreography and event sourcing for workflows, distributed tracing, and idempotent handlers so a duplicated event doesn't charge a customer twice. That last one is the cheapest insurance in distributed systems.

## The .NET and Azure toolbox

For .NET teams he lists Azure Event Grid for event routing between Azure services and third parties, Azure Service Bus for reliable delivery with queues, topics and subscriptions, MassTransit as a .NET-specific distributed messaging framework, plus Kafka for high-throughput streaming and RabbitMQ as a lightweight broker for microservice chatter.

## Keeping it affordable

Cost tips close the technical part: batch non-critical events instead of processing each instantly, autoscale consumers with serverless platforms like Azure Functions or AWS Lambda, and filter unneeded events at the broker (Kafka topic partitioning, Event Grid filters) before they burn compute. He ends with trends: AI in event processing such as instant fraud flags, more serverless EDA, and governance (event catalogues, schema registries) to stop event sprawl.

## Who should watch

.NET and Azure developers evaluating EDA for a new system, and teams who've adopted queues without a plan for ordering, idempotency and tracing. Seasoned distributed-systems engineers will recognise every point; the value is the clear structure.

Title: A reference stack for real-time customer analytics in Python
Description: Amarnath Immadisetty of Lowe's at Conf42 Python 2025 on Kafka, Spark or Flink, feature stores and FastAPI for real-time customer analytics, and when to skip it.
Body:
Real-time personalisation is a pipeline problem before it is a machine learning problem. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Amarnath Immadisetty](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Amarnath_Immadisetty_python_analytics_realtime), Senior Manager of Software Engineering at Lowe's, laid out the layers a customer analytics engine needs, from ingestion to monitoring, with a concrete tool choice at each step and a refreshingly honest note at the end about when you do not need any of it.

## Why retailers chase milliseconds

Immadisetty opens with the customer side: a survey he cites says 82 percent of customers now expect real-time, personalised experiences. His use cases are familiar ones. Amazon-style recommendations from browsing and purchase history, card fraud flagged when you shop in an unusual state, patient vitals streamed from IoT devices, Netflix choosing what to show based on time and history, in-store offers tied to app activity, airline prices that move with search behaviour. The common shape is collect, clean, score with a pre-trained model, trigger an action, and feed the response back so the model keeps learning.

## Six layers, one tool choice each

The core of the talk is a reference architecture:

- **Ingestion**: Kafka (or Kinesis) receives events from web, mobile, IoT, payments and social. Partition by customer or event type to keep ordering where it matters, and turn on compression; he prefers Snappy for throughput.
- **Stream processing**: Spark or Flink, enriching events by joining customer profiles from Redis or DynamoDB, aggregating clicks, purchases and session length, and dropping noisy records with Python rule engines.
- **Storage**: hot data in DynamoDB or Elasticsearch, history in S3, HDFS or GCS for month-on-month comparisons; Cassandra, InfluxDB and Druid also make his list.
- **ML**: train offline on data-lake history with PyTorch, keep models in a central registry, and use a feature store such as Feast for real-time features.
- **Serving**: FastAPI, Flask or TensorFlow Serving behind REST or gRPC, with push or pull delivery depending on the consumer.
- **Monitoring**: Prometheus for Kafka consumer lag, Grafana for pipeline dashboards, the ELK stack for errors.

Nothing exotic, which is the point. Each layer is a well-trodden tool with a Python client, so one team can own the whole path.

## Performance patterns that survive load

For throughput he names Python multiprocessing or Ray for CPU-bound work, Redis caching for profiles that would otherwise hammer the database, Kafka consumer groups to absorb back pressure, and Kubernetes or Lambda autoscaling for compute. For correctness: exactly-once processing in Flink or Spark, retries, and dead-letter queues in Kafka. Sharded Redis handles low-latency lookups, and predictions that need to be fast should be served as close to the customer as possible. The dead-letter queue deserves its spot; it is where your 3am mystery events go to wait for you.

## The best slide is the one that says no

Near the end Immadisetty steps back. If a system receives ten transactions an hour, it does not need Kafka; it can write straight to a database. If the insight is not needed immediately, batch processing is fine. Understand the business use case and the data volumes first, then pick the architecture. Plenty of streaming platforms were built for a dashboard someone checks on Mondays.

He closes with business outcomes: revenue uplift from personalisation, lower churn, cheaper support. He presents those as industry ranges rather than Lowe's measurements, so take them as motivation, not a benchmark.

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads designing their first event-driven analytics platform, or inheriting one and wondering why each box exists. Teams already running Flink in production will find it a checklist rather than news.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: FireDucks speeds up the pandas code you already wrote
Description: Sourav Saha of NEC at Conf42 Python 2025 on FireDucks, a lazy, JIT-compiled, multithreaded DataFrame library that runs existing pandas code unchanged.
Body:
Most pandas performance advice boils down to "write it differently". At Conf42 Python 2025, [Sourav Saha](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sourav_Saha_firedricks_dataframe_jit), Senior Research Engineer at NEC Corporation, made the case for letting a compiler do the rewriting instead. His team's library, FireDucks, keeps the pandas API, executes lazily, optimises the query plan just in time and runs the result on multithreaded C kernels.

It is a talk from the people who build the library, so expect a pitch, but a technical one: the first half is a genuinely useful lesson in pandas performance whether or not you ever install FireDucks.

## Three quizzes about your pandas habits

Saha opens with code quizzes. First, chained expressions versus a sequence of named intermediates. With the step-by-step version, every intermediate DataFrame stays referenced until the function ends, so Python cannot garbage-collect it. Chain the calls and each intermediate can be freed as soon as the next step has consumed it.

Second, sorting a whole frame when you only need two columns. Every other column gets sorted too and is thrown away. Select the columns first and the sort does a fraction of the work: projection pushdown.

Third, joining employees to countries and then filtering for one category, versus filtering first and joining a smaller table. That is predicate pushdown. Put the two together (narrow the columns, then the rows, then do the expensive work) and you have the execution order Saha wants every data scientist to internalise. It is the kind of thing SQL engines have done for decades while pandas politely did exactly what you typed.

## Lazy execution makes the compiler possible

FireDucks does not run your operations when you call them. It records instructions in an intermediate representation (the "FIRE" in the name stands for Flexible IR Engine; the ducks are a nod to the animal-themed DataFrame libraries, with no link to DuckDB). Execution is triggered when you print, write to CSV or Parquet, or aggregate. At that point the compiler inserts projections, reorders filters ahead of sorts, eliminates common subexpressions (his example: the same string-to-datetime conversion computed twice in a Kaggle notebook) and drops dead code, such as a sort whose result is never used.

There is pandas-specific tuning too. A groupby sorts by key by default, which is wasted work if you sort by the aggregated value afterwards; FireDucks spots that and sets `sort=False` for you. Saha measured the manual version on 100 million rows with high cardinality: 50 seconds with the default, 30 with the flag off.

## The numbers he showed

On TPC-H query 3 at scale factor 10, written naively in pandas, he reported 203 seconds and about 60 GB of memory. Hand-optimising the pandas code brought it to 13 seconds and 5.5 GB. FireDucks ran both the naive and the optimised versions in about 4.24 seconds and 3.3 GB. A Bitcoin moving-average demo went from about 4 seconds to 275 milliseconds, with only the import line changed. He also showed DB-benchmark and TPC-H scaling comparisons against Polars, DuckDB and Modin; treat those as the vendor's own benchmarks.

Usage is deliberately boring: `pip install`, swap `import pandas` for `import fireducks.pandas`, or run `python -m fireducks.pandas script.py` to patch every import. At the time of the talk it supported Linux only (WSL works) and Python 3.9 to 3.12.

## Who should watch

Anyone with a slow pandas notebook and no appetite to port it to Polars. Even if you stay on plain pandas, the chaining and pushdown section will make your code faster tomorrow.

Title: Vector search finds the products your keywords never mention
Description: Siddharth Pratap Singh of Walmart Labs at Conf42 Python 2025 on how embedding-based search works, from document pipelines to nearest-neighbour indexes.
Body:
Type "birthday gift for a 10 year old who likes science" into a keyword search engine and it goes looking for products whose listings contain those words. Almost none do. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Siddharth Pratap Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Siddharth_Pratap_Singh_search_vector_semantic), Staff Data Scientist at Walmart Labs, used that query to explain why vector search beats token matching: sellers list astronomy kits and science kits, not gift ideas for curious ten-year-olds, and only a system that matches meaning connects the two.

It is a conceptual tour rather than a code walkthrough, aimed at people who have heard "embeddings" in every meeting and want the architecture laid out end to end.

## Three generations of search

Singh starts with a short history. Token-based search did plain word matching, fine until human language got ambiguous, which it does constantly. Early semantic search tried to understand intent and context, but the models of the time were not good enough. Vector search is what you get when modern machine learning and NLP finally make that idea work: text becomes high-dimensional vectors, and similar meanings land near each other in that space.

He touches on the network families that produce those representations (RNNs for sequences, CNNs for local patterns, transformers for long-range dependencies) and on the index structures that make lookups fast, naming KD-trees and locality-sensitive hashing. The trade-off he keeps returning to is the one every search engineer lives with: speed, memory and accuracy, pick a balance.

## The pipeline has three moving parts

The implementation section is the most useful for builders. First, a document pipeline cleans raw text, splits it into chunks such as sentences or paragraphs, and runs it through an embedding model; stemming, lemmatisation and stop-word removal can help. Second, the query goes through the same model so query and documents share one vector space with the same dimensionality. Third, the index runs nearest-neighbour search to find the closest documents.

Then comes the part demos usually skip: ranking. Singh points out that semantic closeness is only one signal. Production systems also weigh document quality, historical popularity with users on the platform and user preferences. In other words, the vector index gets you candidates, and the ranking layer still has to earn its keep.

## Same idea, many domains

The applications section ranges widely. In e-commerce, vague queries finally return relevant products. In healthcare, records and papers that use different terminology for the same thing become findable, under the privacy rules that field demands. Academic search can link papers that are semantically close even without shared citations. Media recommendation and legal precedent search get the same treatment. The common thread is that the user does not have to guess the exact words the author used.

## The hard parts are still being worked on

Singh is candid that scale is the open problem: ever-growing data, distributed environments where things still have to be fetched fast, and embedding models that keep improving and need re-evaluating. He also points at privacy-preserving search across decentralised databases as a direction, a theme he picked up again in a later Conf42 talk.

## Who should watch

Backend and data engineers about to add semantic search to a product, and product people who need the vocabulary to talk to them. If you already run a vector database in production, the talk will mostly confirm what you know; the ranking-signals point is still worth a slide in your next design review.
