Title: Statistical programming is the quiet engine of clinical trials
Description: Vamsi Upputuri of Gilead Sciences at Conf42 Python 2025 on how SAS, R and Python programmers turn trial data into regulator-ready evidence.
Body:
Bringing a drug from discovery to market takes somewhere between five and ten years, and a surprising share of that clock is spent on data. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Vamsi Upputuri](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Vamsi_Upputuri_drug_development_python), Senior Statistical Programmer at Gilead Sciences, explained where statistical programming sits in that pipeline and why it decides whether a trial's results ever reach a regulator on time.

Set expectations first: this is an overview of the discipline, not a Python coding session. Python appears as one of three tools in the kit, next to SAS and R. If you write software and have never seen how pharma turns patient records into a submission, that is exactly the gap the talk fills.

## Three languages, three jobs

Upputuri frames the tooling as a history. SAS laid the foundation with validated procedures, audit trails and documentation, which is why it became the regulatory gold standard. R brought flexible statistical modelling, strong visualisation and a big package ecosystem, ideal for exploratory analysis. Python added machine learning, automated workflows and heavier data processing, especially for real-world evidence work. The point is not that one replaces the others: each covers a different part of the risk profile.

## Every trial phase asks a different question

The talk walks through phases one to four. Phase one is about safety, adverse events and dose tolerability. Phase two looks at safety and early efficacy in a small population. Phase three confirms efficacy in large groups. Phase four keeps watching long-term safety and real-world effectiveness, pulling in real-world data to catch safety signals.

Underneath all of them sits the same deliverable chain. Programmers turn the protocol into precise specifications, build SDTM and ADaM datasets following CDISC standards, and produce the tables, listings and figures (TLFs) that the statistical analysis plan calls for. Adaptive designs add dynamic sample-size calculations and treatment allocation, and interim analyses decide whether a study continues, changes or stops early. Plenty of engineers have shipped code with less riding on a single output table.

## Compliance failures cost months

The sharpest part is a pair of contrasting case studies. On the success side, Upputuri credits adaptive designs, real-time analysis and rolling submissions for compressing COVID-19 vaccine timelines, including running phase two and three at the same time. On the failure side, he describes an oncology trial whose submission slipped by six months because of CDISC compliance failures: inconsistencies in derived variables and missing documentation.

That second story is the one to remember. The analysis was not wrong in some deep scientific way; the paperwork around the data did not hold up. Submission artefacts like define.xml and the reviewer's guides, plus conformance checks with tools such as Pinnacle 21, exist to stop exactly that.

## Where the field is heading

The closing section lists four directions: real-world evidence from health records, claims and registries; decentralised trials fed by wearables and patient-reported outcomes; open-source R and Python under strict validation; and traceability through automated documentation and versioned environments. That last one will sound familiar to anyone who has argued for pinned dependencies and reproducible builds. Regulators, he notes, are writing guidance for complex designs, master protocols and validating AI and ML algorithms.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and Python developers thinking about moving into life sciences, and anyone supporting a biostatistics team who wants to know why they keep asking for audit trails. Experienced statistical programmers will know most of it already; the case studies are still a useful reminder to show a manager.

Title: AI in healthcare predicts well on average; the gaps are the story
Description: Veda Swaroop Meduri of Labcorp at Conf42 Python 2025 on AI diagnostics, readmission prediction, medical imaging and the bias and transparency gaps.
Body:
A diagnostic model with excellent average accuracy can still be much worse for some patient groups than others, and clinicians often can't explain its output. At Conf42 Python 2025, Veda Swaroop Meduri, Full Stack SDET at Labcorp, surveys how AI and predictive analytics are used in patient care, then spends the most interesting part of the talk on the gaps: data breaches, accuracy disparities and transparency.

This is a short, high-level overview built on industry figures rather than a case study or a code walkthrough. No Python is shown. It works as a primer on where AI shows up in healthcare and what can go wrong.

## Where AI earns its place

Meduri groups the benefits into diagnostics and operations. On diagnostics, ML systems reach high sensitivity rates across medical specialties, and convolutional neural networks spot subtle abnormalities in medical images. On operations, NLP takes paperwork off hospital administration, cutting administrative cost.

## Predicting who is at risk, before they are readmitted

Predictive analytics is the centre of the talk. Models flag high-risk patients in advance so care teams can intervene early, and analysing patient data has been used to reduce hospital readmissions. Gradient boosting ensembles combine many patient variables to predict clinical outcomes, which supports personalised treatment plans. None of it works without the data layer: Meduri stresses that each patient generates many structured and unstructured data points, and the accuracy of that data is mission-critical for the algorithms built on it. Garbage in, misdiagnosis out.

## The gaps are where the work is

The implementation challenges are the section to watch. Healthcare data breaches keep rising, and many organisations report weaknesses in how they secure their AI systems. Diagnostic algorithms can vary in accuracy significantly across demographic groups, which he calls out as a systemic bias that undermines equitable care. And only a minority of providers feel prepared to explain the reasoning behind an AI-driven decision to a patient. A model nobody can explain is a model nobody should fully trust at the bedside.

## A collaborative path forward

The closing pyramid places precision medicine, predictive analytics and patient engagement at the top, and the next steps are organisational: dedicated AI infrastructure and specialist hiring, security and ethics frameworks that cover data protection and algorithmic transparency, structured collaboration between clinicians, AI researchers and policymakers, and patient education so the people affected understand what the tools do. His recurring theme is that AI should amplify healthcare professionals, not replace their judgement.

## Who should watch

Engineers and testers moving into healthcare or life sciences who want a quick orientation on AI use cases and their risks, and product people preparing to talk to clinical stakeholders about bias and explainability. If you want model architectures or evaluation code, the related talks below go further.

Title: VPS or Docker? How to choose, and what one migration saved
Description: Vivek Kumar at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 compares VPS hosting with Docker and Kubernetes, with the Swoo app's move from 85 to 67 EC2 instances.
Body:
Giving every service its own server feels tidy until you look at the CPU graphs. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Vivek Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vivek_Kumar_apps_vps_docker), a software engineer who lists his employer simply as FAANG, compared traditional VPS hosting with Docker containers and walked through the Swoo app's migration to Docker and Kubernetes, which took it from 85 EC2 instances to 67 and cut its AWS bill by 20 percent.

It's an introductory talk, a good fit for teams still running one app per VM who are weighing whether containers are worth the learning curve.

## Apartments and shipping containers

Kumar's analogies do the heavy lifting. A VPS is a rented apartment in a big building: your own space with dedicated CPU, RAM and storage, but you share the physical structure. Docker is your belongings packed in a container you can move anywhere: the app and its dependencies in one portable unit that runs the same on a laptop, a test server and production.

The comparison that follows is the standard one, stated clearly:

- **Isolation.** A VPS runs a full operating system, so one crashing or compromised server doesn't touch the others. Containers share the host kernel and get process-level isolation, which is lighter but less robust. Kumar is fair about this trade-off.
- **Resources.** A full OS per VPS is heavy; containers share the host OS and start fast because there's no OS to boot.
- **Portability and deployment.** Containers move between environments without reconfiguration; VPS setups tend to need manual configuration per server, which drifts.
- **Scaling.** VPS scaling often means provisioning another server by hand; containers plus an orchestrator scale out on demand.

## Productivity is the underrated win

The section on teams makes a point that cost discussions skip. With hand-configured VPS environments, developers burn time on setup and fight differences between dev and production. Standardised container images mean faster onboarding and smoother CI/CD, so more time on code and less on works-on-my-machine archaeology.

## The Swoo migration

The case study is the concrete part. Swoo ran on 85 EC2 instances, each dedicated to one service such as search, user management or authentication, each provisioned with fixed resources whether it used them or not. As the app grew, that meant idle CPU and RAM, high costs and awkward scaling. The team moved to Docker and Kubernetes, packed services onto 67 instances with the same performance, and saw a 20 percent drop in AWS costs. Kubernetes gets credit for the autoscaling and self-healing that make the denser packing safe.

## When a VPS is still fine

Kumar doesn't declare VPS dead. A simple application with stable traffic may be perfectly served by one. Dynamic scaling or a microservice architecture is where containers pay off. Weigh infrastructure cost, scaling cost and the complexity of running the platform you pick.

## Best practices, both sides

For VPS: use configuration management like Ansible or Puppet, and monitor resource use. For Docker: multi-stage builds for smaller images, regular image updates for security patches, and an orchestrator. His migration advice is incremental: assess and refactor services so they containerise cleanly, build a small prototype first, use Docker Compose to test multi-container setups, wire images into CI/CD, train the team, add monitoring (ELK, Prometheus), and migrate gradually with a hybrid period.

## Who should watch

Small teams and startups on VMs deciding whether to containerise, and engineers who need a clear explainer to share with a manager. If you already run Kubernetes in production, this is a refresher, though the Swoo numbers are a handy reference for a cost conversation.

Title: Healthcare data security is a patient safety problem
Description: Avinash Mavireddi of CareDx at Conf42 Python 2025 on healthcare data growth, ransomware, legacy systems, zero trust and federated learning.
Body:
When a hospital gets hit by ransomware, the choice is between paying criminals and risking patient care, which is why Avinash Mavireddi treats cybersecurity in healthcare as a patient safety issue first. At Conf42 Python 2025, the Software Engineering Manager at CareDx surveys how healthcare organisations manage exploding data volumes, compliance and attacks, and which architectures help.

This is an industry overview rather than a technical walkthrough. There is no Python and no reference implementation; the talk moves through market figures, threat statistics and solution categories, citing a lot of percentages along the way. Use it as a briefing on the problem space and follow the threads that matter to you.

## The data is growing faster than the storage

Mavireddi opens with scale. Healthcare organisations handle structured patient records, unstructured clinical notes, high-resolution imaging and real-time IoT monitoring data, and he cites figures in the hundreds of terabytes a year per organisation, with data generation outpacing storage growth. Cloud adoption is the industry's response, and he frames it as a change in how care is delivered (remote care, resilient infrastructure), not just where servers sit.

## Attacks, compliance and old systems compete for the same budget

Three pressures stack up. Attacks: frequent attempted intrusions, a sharp rise in ransomware, and breach costs he cites as the highest of any industry. Compliance: HIPAA in the US, GDPR in Europe and local laws, with a meaningful share of IT budgets going to training, audits and documentation. Legacy: many institutions run systems more than a decade old, and maintenance of those systems eats most of the IT budget, leaving little for modernisation. That last point explains the first two: old systems are both harder to secure and more expensive to keep compliant.

## Data lakes and federated learning change who moves the data

The modern-architecture section covers two ideas. Data lakes bring patient records and imaging into one queryable place, speeding up clinical decision support and complex queries. Federated learning flips the usual pattern: instead of shipping sensitive records to a central model, the model goes to each institution's data, so hospitals can collaborate on AI without transferring patient data. For anyone who has tried to get a data-sharing agreement signed between two hospitals, that is the most practical idea in the talk.

## Zero trust, masking and anonymisation

On security controls, he lists AI-driven anonymisation of patient records, dynamic data masking that protects sensitive fields in real time with low latency for both structured data and clinical notes, zero trust architecture to stop lateral movement and data exfiltration, and biometric authentication. Automated compliance monitoring and stronger data governance round it out, so breaches are detected in minutes rather than discovered in an audit.

## Phase it, train people, keep adapting

The forward-looking slides name edge computing at the point of care, blockchain for sharing medical records, quantum-safe encryption, AI diagnostics and 5G telemedicine. The implementation advice is the part to keep: phased rollouts succeed far more often than big-bang deployments, stakeholder engagement drives adoption, training reduces user-caused incidents, and the plan has to keep adapting as threats change.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers new to healthcare IT who want the problem space in one sitting, and security folks preparing a case for zero trust or federated approaches in a clinical setting. Practitioners looking for configuration or code should pair it with the related talks below.

Title: Zero-downtime SAP HANA starts with failover you have actually tested
Description: Lurduma Reddy Thirumala Reddy of Intone Networks at Conf42 Python 2025 on SAP HANA high availability with Pacemaker and system replication.
Body:
When the database behind an SAP system goes down, the business stops with it, so a failover that has never been rehearsed is a hope, not a plan. At Conf42 Python 2025, Lurduma Reddy Thirumala Reddy, Senior SAP Consultant at Intone Networks with 17 years in SAP Basis and HANA administration, explains how to build SAP HANA environments that survive node failures using Pacemaker clusters and HANA system replication.

A scope note: the title mentions Python, but the recording is about HANA high-availability architecture and practice; scripting and automation code don't come up. If you run or plan HANA clusters, that is fine. If you came for Python, adjust expectations.

## Three pillars: fault tolerance, DR and tenants

The talk frames HANA high availability as three pillars. Fault tolerance through system replication and automatic failover. Disaster recovery across geographically separate data centres, for when a whole site is the failure. And tenant-level handling, where multiple HANA tenants get independent failover so you can recover one without disturbing the rest.

## A warm secondary, ready to take over

System replication keeps a synchronised secondary instance ready to take over when the primary fails. The goal is sub-minute failover, and the trick is preloading: a secondary that already has its data in memory doesn't need a long warm-up before it can serve. Pacemaker orchestrates the cluster and decides when the takeover happens, across both scale-up and scale-out configurations.

## Make the standby earn its keep

Standby hardware that sits idle is the classic HA budget argument. Thirumala Reddy's answer is the active/read-enabled configuration: the secondary accepts read-only queries, so reporting and other read-heavy workloads move off the primary. The abstract's pitch is doubling resource utilisation; the mechanism is spreading reads across both nodes without giving up consistency.

He also points to HANA's time travel capability for a different kind of failure: data corruption or an accidental change, where failing over would just replicate the mistake and rolling back to an earlier point in time is the real fix.

## Takeover decisions need rules, not reflexes

The section on takeover frameworks is where operations experience shows. Health assessment should combine several signals (system performance, memory, network connectivity, response times) rather than a single heartbeat, so the cluster doesn't fail over on a blip or sit still during a real outage. He points to SAP Note 2063657 as the reference for configuring failover thresholds and decision logic, and argues for adaptive strategies that put workload continuity and minimal data loss first.

## Test the failover before it tests you

The real-world stories centre on testing. A rigorous HA test programme caught a potential data-loss scenario during planned maintenance before it hit production. His test matrix covers graceful failover, primary node crashes, secondary node crashes and maintenance windows, which is a reasonable minimum for anyone whose HA design currently lives only in a diagram.

## Secure it, watch it, keep it current

The closing recommendations are the operational basics done properly: strict access control on the cluster, encryption at rest and in transit, regular security audits, Prometheus and Grafana for real-time metrics such as CPU, memory, network latency and response times, and a risk-based maintenance plan with automated patching and scheduled reviews. Design for growth with a modular architecture and automated provisioning, so adding capacity doesn't mean redesigning the cluster.

## Who should watch

SAP Basis administrators, HANA DBAs and infrastructure engineers building or auditing HANA clusters. SREs outside the SAP world will find the takeover-decision and testing advice transferable to any primary/replica database.

Title: Own your marketing data by pulling it from platform APIs yourself
Description: Rao Marapatla of BreakthroughT1D at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on replacing paid connectors with scheduled API scripts for nonprofit marketing analytics.
Body:
Paying a yearly subscription to fetch your own data back from Facebook is a strange deal once you say it out loud. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Rao Marapatla](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Rao_Marapatla_analytics_marketing_insights), Director of Data Infrastructure and Reporting at BreakthroughT1D, showed how a nonprofit can pull marketing data from social and ad platforms with its own scheduled scripts, land it in a database, and run BI on top, without a third-party connector.

It's a practical, low-ceremony talk: C# or Node.js, Postman, Windows Task Scheduler or AWS Lambda, and a target table. Nothing exotic, which is the point for a small data team.

## The pipeline in one paragraph

The flow Marapatla describes is simple. A script holds the platform credentials and API endpoint details, calls the API on a schedule, writes the results to CSV in a secure location, and a second step loads the CSV into the database, where reporting tools pick it up. The trigger can be Windows Task Scheduler on a box you already have, or AWS Lambda, which he notes is relatively cheap for this kind of job.

Since the data is yours, so is the pipeline. That's the main argument: a one-time build instead of a recurring licence fee.

## Read the API docs before you write a line

Most of the talk is the checklist he runs per platform, whether it's Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X, TikTok, YouTube, Google Ads, Bing Ads or Meta Ads:

- **Is the KPI you want actually exposed by the API?** If it isn't, raise a support ticket with the platform instead of guessing.
- **Which parameters does the endpoint need?** IDs, fields, limits and so on, per platform. Meta's insights endpoints get a special mention for their many parameters, and Bing Ads for being a little tricky.
- **Test it in Postman first.** Check the response shape and confirm your numbers match what the platform's own UI shows before you script anything.
- **Get pagination right.** Miss a page and your totals are quietly wrong.
- **Mind the refresh time.** In his experience, most platforms refresh their data after about 9 AM US Eastern; schedule earlier and you load yesterday's numbers.
- **Check special cases.** If you need sentiment from X, confirm the API supports it.

## Scheduling and loading without surprises

For Windows Task Scheduler you need admin rights, a named task, the path to your packaged script and a schedule. Before turning it on, create the target table in the database (he mentions Oracle and Amazon Redshift as targets) with the same column order and data types as the script's output. Then do two or three test runs with small data before trusting it. It's the kind of advice that sounds obvious until a column swap puts donation totals in the date field.

## The bigger picture

The second half zooms out to AI-driven donor analytics on top of the unified data: 360-degree donor views, predictive models for retention and giving, and a Lambda-based architecture handling large volumes. Those slides are dense with figures and lighter on how they were measured; the scripting half is where the reusable engineering is.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and analysts at nonprofits and small organisations paying for social-media connectors, and anyone who has to integrate several marketing APIs on a budget. Teams already on a modern ELT stack will find the approach basic, though the per-platform gotchas still apply.

Title: Using AI to catch bad data before it reaches decisions
Description: Shashank Reddy Beeravelly of Walmart at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on predictive validation, automated cleansing and pilot-first AI data quality.
Body:
Bad data doesn't crash anything. It just makes every report, model and decision downstream a little bit wrong, quietly. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Shashank Reddy Beeravelly](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Shashank_Reddy_Beeravelly_ai_data_quality), Software Engineer at Walmart, made the business case for AI-driven data quality management: validate predictively, clean continuously, enrich automatically, and roll it out one business unit at a time.

It's a short, business-oriented talk, closer to a strategy briefing than an engineering walkthrough, so set expectations accordingly: no code, no model architecture diagrams, plenty of outcome figures.

## Three jobs for AI in the data pipeline

Beeravelly splits the work into three capabilities:

- **Predictive validation.** Models learn the patterns in your data and flag likely issues before they hit operations, instead of waiting for a broken dashboard to tell you.
- **Automated cleaning.** Continuous monitoring that removes duplicates, standardises formats and corrects inconsistencies as data flows, not in a quarterly clean-up sprint.
- **Real-time enrichment.** Adding context from trusted sources so a bare record becomes something analysts can use.

Under the hood he points to neural networks and ensemble learning for validation and correction, combined with predictive analytics on top. The talk doesn't go into which models, features or tooling, which is the main gap for an engineering audience.

## The numbers, and how to read them

A lot of the talk is impact figures: accuracy gains, cost reductions, processing speed, and three anonymised case studies (a Fortune 500 bank, an automotive manufacturer across 12 plants, a national healthcare network). The abstract headlines 42 percent better accuracy and 850K records per minute. These are presented without methodology, so read them as the size of the prize vendors and teams are chasing, not as a benchmark you can expect on day one. The more transferable content is the rollout advice.

## Roll out like a cautious engineer

His implementation practices are sound and fairly universal:

1. **Pilot in one critical business unit.** Validate results, then expand based on lessons learned and measured return, instead of a company-wide launch.
2. **Audit before you automate.** Find your most valuable and most vulnerable datasets, and point AI at the ones tied to revenue, compliance and customer experience first.
3. **Measure continuously.** Define KPIs for data quality and business impact, monitor them automatically, and adjust as needs change.

That last point is where the chaos engineering connection lives. A data quality system is itself a dependency; if it silently degrades, it fails the same quiet way bad data does. Monitoring the monitor is part of the job.

## What comes next

Looking ahead, Beeravelly expects more predictive analysis for spotting trends early, automated compliance monitoring that catches regulatory violations in real time, and continuously verified data feeding faster decisions. His closing advice is to start by assessing your current data quality problems and pick the high-impact datasets first.

## Who should watch

Data and analytics leads building a case for investment in data quality, and engineers who need the business vocabulary for that conversation. If you want implementation detail, his companion talk at Conf42 Python 2025 and the pipeline talks below go further.

Title: Your click-through rate is measuring position, not relevance
Description: Aditya Singh of UW-Madison at Conf42 Python 2025 on correcting position bias, attention decay and format effects in search and recommendation metrics.
Body:
The item in slot one gets the most clicks, and your ranking model learns that it must be the best item, which keeps it in slot one. At Conf42 Python 2025, Aditya Singh of UW-Madison presents a framework for evaluating search and recommendation systems that separates how good content is from where it happened to be shown.

Traditional engagement metrics like click-through rate and conversion miss three things, in Singh's framing: position bias, the messy ways people actually interact (scrolling past, hovering, partial views, coming back), and the way different content formats influence each other. Ignore them and the feedback loop does the rest.

## Discount the click by the slot it came from

The first model is a position bias model: the probability of a click at position i includes an attention discount factor for that position. Normalise raw CTR by it and the apparent star in the top slot often looks much closer to baseline. Singh gives one calibration from their data: position five needed roughly a 3x adjustment to reflect true engagement. The second model is temporal decay of attention, which he says isn't linear: users have bursts of renewed interest when they hit something highly relevant. The third is cross-item influence, how one item changes engagement with its neighbours.

## Layout beats rank more often than you'd think

The observations are the fun part. On a mobile screen that shows three items on load, the fourth position behaves differently from the first three, and the pattern repeats around position eight. In a tile layout, the item ranked fifth can outperform the one ranked fourth simply because it sits right below the top result while number four is pushed to the far right. He sees a left-side bias in horizontal layouts (likely tied to reading direction), sharp drops at folds he calls attention cliffs, and a threshold where users switch from systematic to exploratory browsing, like nobody going to page three of search results unless they are hunting for something specific.

## You can't correct what you don't log

All of this depends on a data collection layer most teams don't have, and Singh is blunt that you should build it. Viewport tracking for real visibility. Scroll depth, computed as the viewport bottom over page height. Visibility time, summed per item. An attention score, active time over total time. Session journeys and content format metadata on top. The relative attention score he plots combines viewport time, active engagements and scroll velocity near the item, and the gap between the theoretical curve and observed behaviour is exactly what the framework sets out to measure.

## Formats change each other's numbers

The cross-format matrix is the most surprising slide. Singh notes the numbers are adapted rather than exact because some can't be shared, but the patterns hold: short-form video creates what he calls an attention halo that lifts engagement with neighbouring content for a few positions, interactive elements build engagement momentum, and complementary pairs such as an infographic followed by detailed text boost each other. If you evaluate each item alone, you credit the text for the video's work.

## What changed, and what's next

Reported results include better prediction reliability, higher optimisation success, and one team shortening its A/B testing cycles. Next directions: personalised normalisation per user, metrics for immersive formats, models that adapt online as behaviour drifts, and privacy-first, federated analytics.

## Who should watch

Ranking and recommendation engineers, data scientists who own engagement dashboards, and anyone whose A/B tests keep crowning whatever was placed at the top. It is framework-level and math-light; the slides hold the formulas.

Title: A layered cloud security framework, from micro-segmentation to kill switch
Description: Chakradhar Sunkesula of Compass at Conf42 Python 2025 walks through a multi-layered cloud security framework with zero trust, ML detection and API defence.
Body:
Cloud security fails at the seams between layers, so defend every layer and assume one will break. At Conf42 Python 2025, Chakradhar Sunkesula, Engineering Manager at Compass, walks through a multi-layered cloud security framework built on network segmentation, authentication, authorisation, API validation and ML-driven detection, with a kill switch and fast recovery at the end of the chain.

Honest scope: Python doesn't appear on screen, and the talk is a framework overview rather than an implementation. It is also dense with performance figures: detection accuracy, request volumes, breach reductions, ROI. Those are presented as results of the framework without the methodology behind them, so read them as the speaker's claims and judge the architecture on its own merits.

## Contain the blast radius first

The network layer is zero trust built on micro-segmentation: every subnet gets its own security context and strict, granular access policies, so an attacker who lands in one segment is stuck there. On top sits AI/ML traffic analysis that looks for attack patterns, including zero-days, and tries to cut false positives so the security team spends time on real alerts. Then a tripwire system of distributed sensors aimed at shrinking how long an attacker can stay hidden; Sunkesula contrasts an industry average of 72 days with a goal of under 24 hours.

## Identity is a stream, not a gate

Authentication gets the same treatment. Behavioural analysis classifies logins to catch anomalies that static checks miss, token and certificate validation is layered against spoofing, and a kill switch terminates compromised sessions across every connected system and device in well under a second. The point of that last piece is speed: once you know a session is bad, the clock is the enemy.

## Least privilege that keeps itself honest

Authorisation follows least privilege across many access levels, with dynamic access control that detects excess privileges and revokes them automatically, continuous auditing of access events, and real-time risk assessment over a long list of factors to adjust privileges on the fly. It is the part most teams do once at onboarding and never again, which is why it's worth seeing done continuously.

## APIs are the front door now

Because APIs are the backbone of modern applications, the framework gives them their own layer: validating every request with low latency, ML anomaly detection trained on historical API traffic and many per-request parameters, and threat intelligence from multiple external feeds refreshed frequently. Threat detection and response sit on top, with automated containment and complete incident documentation for compliance.

## Resilience is part of security

The last layer is about surviving what gets through: high uptime targets, ransomware prevention, and fast recovery compared with industry averages measured in hours. The closing slides turn to business impact (incident costs, compliance spend, insurance premiums) and future work on quantum-resistant encryption, stronger zero trust and AI-based predictive threat modelling.

## Who should watch

Security architects and platform leads who want a checklist of layers to compare against their own setup, and managers who need the vocabulary for a security roadmap. Engineers looking for concrete Python tooling or config examples won't find them here.

Title: Moving databases to the cloud, and the trade-offs that come with it
Description: Prashanth Reddy Kora of Centene Corporation at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on cloud DBMS elasticity, migration risk, vendor lock-in and a pilot-first plan.
Body:
Moving a database to the cloud trades hardware problems for planning problems. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Prashanth Reddy Kora](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Prashanth_Reddy_Kora_chaos_cloud_systems), Cloud Database Engineer at Centene Corporation, gave a short tour of cloud database management systems: why organisations move, what breaks during the move, and a pilot-first plan for doing it without drama.

A note on scope before you press play. The title and abstract promise chaos engineering for cloud databases, with simulated failures and stress tests. The recording is a broader overview of cloud DBMS adoption, and failure injection doesn't come up. Judge it as an executive-level briefing on cloud databases, and it does that job briskly.

## Why teams move

Kora's case for the cloud rests on three properties. Elasticity: a cloud DBMS can scale from gigabytes to petabytes without downtime, so you stop provisioning for a peak you hit twice a year. Multi-tenancy and pay-per-use: you share infrastructure and pay for what you consume, with security patches and updates handled by the provider. Serverless options: backups, scaling and maintenance move to the platform, which shrinks the operational work your team carries.

He backs this with a series of industry figures on market growth, cost reduction and performance. Treat those as the motivation slide they are; your own bill and benchmarks are the numbers that matter.

## What goes wrong on the way

The more useful slide is the one on problems, because these are what usually derail a migration:

- **Migration complexity.** Data integrity issues, downtime risk and schema compatibility problems are the usual suspects. His answer is careful planning, robust testing and a staged execution strategy.
- **Vendor lock-in.** Once your data and your queries depend on one provider's features, leaving gets expensive. Kora recommends portable architectures and a written exit strategy from day one. Nobody plans the breakup at the wedding, but databases make it worth doing.

Security and availability round out the picture: providers invest in encryption, threat detection and compliance tooling, and managed offerings come with uptime commitments, but it is still your job to pick a configuration that meets your continuity needs.

## Where cloud databases are heading

Three trends get a mention: NoSQL databases for unstructured, high-volume workloads; hybrid approaches that mix relational and NoSQL stores for different jobs; and cloud native applications built on serverless and microservices from the start. He also notes the career angle: cloud database skills are in demand, so learning them is a sound bet for DBAs.

## A three-step migration plan

The closing advice is the bit to keep:

1. **Assess.** Analyse database workloads, compliance requirements and peak usage patterns before you talk to any vendor.
2. **Explore options.** Compare AWS, Azure and Google Cloud on cost, scalability and security features for *your* workload.
3. **Pilot, then migrate.** Start with a small slice of the data (he suggests 10 to 15 percent), and run old and new in parallel to keep downtime down.

That pilot is also where the chaos engineering promise in the title would naturally fit: fail over the replica, kill a connection pool, and see whether the new setup behaves before the full cutover.

## Who should watch

Managers and architects who need a quick briefing on cloud DBMS before a migration discussion, and DBAs planning their first move off premises. If you want failure injection against a live database, pair it with one of the talks below.

Title: Fraud detection moved from overnight batches to milliseconds
Description: Narendra Bhargav Boggarapu of Wells Fargo at Conf42 Python 2025 on cloud ML fraud detection, false positives and a 1.5M transactions/second case study.
Body:
A fraud check that runs in tomorrow's batch is a fraud check the fraudster has already beaten. At Conf42 Python 2025, Narendra Bhargav Boggarapu, Lead Software Engineer at Wells Fargo, explains how cloud-based machine learning moved fraud detection from rule-based batch jobs to scoring transactions in tens of milliseconds, and why cutting false positives matters as much as catching fraud.

What the talk is and isn't: the abstract promises the Python internals (FastAPI, Ray, MLflow), but the recording stays at the architecture and business-outcome level. There is no code and those frameworks don't come up. Watch it for the shape of the problem and the case study, not for an implementation.

## Rules and batches leave a window open

Boggarapu starts with the legacy picture. Traditional systems ran on hand-written rules and processed transactions in batches, taking anywhere from 30 minutes to hours to flag something, longer at peak. He puts their accuracy as low as 50% in some cases, with a high false positive rate. That delay is the vulnerability: the window between a transaction and its review is where fraud happens.

## Speed comes from real-time scoring, not just bigger batches

The modern version aggregates data in real time from transaction logs, customer history and external threat intelligence, then lets ML models find patterns that rules miss. The numbers he gives are 20 to 50 milliseconds per transaction using parallel processing, fast enough to block a payment before it completes, with detection accuracy above 90% and the ability to adapt to new fraud patterns without someone rewriting rules.

## False positives are a customer experience bug

The section most engineers will nod along to is about false alarms. Every legitimate card payment that gets declined is a support call and possibly a lost customer. Boggarapu reports that their system cut false fraud alerts by more than 70%, and frames it as the second half of the job: accuracy without precision just moves the pain from the fraud team to the customers.

## The 1.5M transactions per second case study

The centrepiece is a Fortune 100 credit card provider processing more than 1.5 million transactions per second, which he compares to more than the New York Stock Exchange, and handling holiday peaks without degradation. Moving to the cloud-based system brought what he describes as a 71% reduction in fraud losses. The talk doesn't go into how the system is partitioned or deployed, which is the part we'd have liked more of.

## Security, audits and a 30-day pilot

The rest covers the controls around the models: AES-256 encryption at rest and in transit, layered defences with intrusion detection and biometric access control, monthly penetration tests and quarterly third-party audits for SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO 27001. His practical next steps are sensible: evaluate platforms on detection accuracy, processing speed and integration; start with a 30-day pilot to tune before full rollout; put a data governance framework in place; and share threat intelligence across institutions, because fraud rings don't stop at one bank.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people new to payments fraud who want the problem framed end to end, and anyone building the business case for moving a rules engine to ML. If you need the Python architecture the abstract describes, the related talks below get more specific.

Title: Monitoring AI in production: watch what goes in and what comes out
Description: Muddassar Sharif of Virtuans.ai at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on data drift, concept drift and alerting for ML models and LLM apps in production.
Body:
Every AI system in production is a bet that tomorrow's inputs look like yesterday's. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Muddassar Sharif](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muddassar_Sharif_ai_model_systems), Co-Founder and CTO of Virtuans.ai, boiled model monitoring down to two buckets: track the data going into the model, track the predictions coming out, and alert when either drifts past a threshold your business can live with.

It's a high-level talk aimed as much at engineering managers and executives as at ML engineers. Sharif says up front that he skips the maths of drift metrics; the value is the mental model and the LLM-specific examples.

## Start from the KPI, not the tool

Monitoring begins at design time. You decide how the system should behave and which KPIs prove it, then check whether production meets them. His examples: a bank's card-fraud classifier is judged on how well it separates fraudulent from legitimate transactions; an LLM answering customer-support tickets is judged first on whether it gives accurate information. Everything else is a sub-KPI hanging off that main one.

## Two kinds of drift, one goal

The core of the talk is the input/output split that he says has held for the last decade of ML practice:

- **Data drift**: the inputs change. His LLM example is a support agent built for refund and change-of-address tickets that starts receiving complaints about product quality instead. Same model, different world.
- **Concept or prediction drift**: the outputs change. A model that always predicted above 50 now predicts between 30 and 60, or an LLM that averaged a few hundred output tokens suddenly doubles its answer length.

For LLM systems he adds concrete signals: the topic mix of incoming queries, the sentiment of incoming tickets, hallucination rates, and token counts on the output side. Each one is cheap to track and each one tells you something changed before a customer does.

The end goal goes beyond a dashboard: a system that detects the anomaly and triggers a fix, whether that's retraining a classical model or revising the prompt in an LLM pipeline.

## How much drift can you afford?

The best section is about thresholds, because there is no universal number. In healthcare or finance, regulation and the cost of a wrong answer keep the tolerance tight. In retail demand forecasting, teams already overstock as a buffer, so they can absorb a large swing in predictions without much pain. Sharif's point: the threshold is a business decision, and the monitoring system just enforces it.

## The tools he mentions

For LLM apps he mentions LangSmith as widely used, plus an evaluation platform he runs in his own companies; both log every inference so you can track token changes and build custom evaluations such as hallucination checks. For classical ML, he points to Evidently AI, the open-source library many teams use for drift reports.

The abstract pitches this through a chaos engineering lens (simulating failures to stress-test alerts); in the recording the focus is the monitoring design itself. That's still the right foundation, since you can't chaos-test an alert you never defined.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers putting their first LLM feature into production, and data scientists who need to explain drift to stakeholders. Experienced MLOps engineers will know the concepts and may want something with more statistics in it.

Title: AI coding assistants, RAG over your codebase, and the skills to match
Description: Kartheek Medhavi Penagamuri Shriram of Microsoft at Conf42 Python 2025 surveys AI-assisted development, from code embeddings and RAG to ethics and new skills.
Body:
AI assistance now reaches past autocomplete into dependency management, testing, CI/CD and code search, and developers who don't learn how it works will use it badly. That is the case Kartheek Medhavi Penagamuri Shriram, Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft, makes at Conf42 Python 2025 in a broad tour of AI-assisted development and the skills it asks of engineers.

Scope check: this is a big-picture overview rather than a demo. No Python is written on screen and no single tool is walked through. It moves quickly through a lot of territory and quotes plenty of headline percentages (GitHub Copilot speedups, bug reductions, deployment gains) without showing the studies behind them, so treat those as the industry claims they are and check the sources before you put them in a planning doc.

## Assistants are only as good as their context

The most technical and most useful part of the talk is about context. Code embeddings turn source into numeric vectors so a model can search by meaning instead of keywords. Shriram lists three payoffs: finding the right function in a million-line codebase, spotting recurring architectural patterns and redundant code across repositories, and better comprehension of how pieces relate.

Retrieval-augmented generation builds on that. Instead of generating code in isolation, a RAG setup pulls in your documentation, past commits and team coding standards, so suggestions follow your naming conventions and design patterns and need fewer manual fixes. He points out it applies beyond new code too: refactoring legacy systems, scaffolding features and generating tests. If your assistant keeps proposing a logging library you banned two years ago, this is the section for you.

## The pipeline is the other half

Beyond the editor, the talk covers AI in the surrounding machinery: package managers that resolve dependency conflicts and flag vulnerable packages, ML-driven test generation that hunts for edge cases, CI/CD systems that learn from historical builds to predict failures and trigger rollbacks, and monitoring that scans logs for anomalies before they escalate. It also mentions forecasting delivery timelines from project history. The framing is that the gains come when these pieces join up end to end, not from one tool in isolation.

## Prompting and feature depth are team skills

On getting value out of the tools, Shriram's advice is organisational. Write contextual, domain-specific prompts. Use the debugging, refactoring and testing features, not only completion. Run structured learning (hands-on workshops, documentation reviews, real exercises) so the team builds AI literacy: prompt engineering, RAG, what training data does, where models fail.

## Audit trails, bias checks and the developer as orchestrator

The ethics section is practical rather than philosophical. Keep audit trails of AI decisions, training data and deployment details. Run bias detection, including what he calls programming-paradigm bias alongside gender and ethnicity. Set up governance with regular audits and training.

He closes on the role change: developers moving from writing every line to orchestrating AI tools, which means learning LLM APIs, MLOps skills like model versioning and monitoring, and designing systems that stay interpretable. His last point is the one most people agree on: the tools speed up repetitive work, and judgement stays with the human.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and tech leads building a case for AI tooling, or planning team training, who want the whole map in one sitting. Hands-on developers looking for a Copilot or RAG implementation guide will want something more concrete; the related talks below are closer to that.

Title: What cloud AI and workflow orchestration promise military operations
Description: Sushil Prabhu Prabhakaran of Tata Consultancy Services at Conf42 Python 2025 surveys cloud AI and workflow orchestration in military operations.
Body:
Defence organisations have the same data problem as everyone else, only with higher stakes: too many sources, too little time, and decisions that can't wait for a nightly batch. At Conf42 Python 2025, Sushil Prabhu Prabhakaran, Full Stack Lead at Tata Consultancy Services, gives a strategic overview of how cloud computing, AI and workflow orchestration are being applied to military operations, from situational awareness to logistics and training.

The talk is listed as "Scaling Python Applications: Cloud-AI Integration and Async Workflow Orchestration". The session as recorded is titled military digital transformation and stays at the strategy level; it doesn't include Python code, asyncio or FastAPI, so watch it as a domain briefing rather than a programming talk.

## Faster sense-making, faster decisions

Sushil splits the core argument in two. First, situational awareness: cloud AI architectures let commanders combine multi-source data streams in real time, with machine learning and distributed computing producing more granular, predictive pictures of the field. Second, decision-making: predictive models process mission-critical information quickly enough to shorten decision cycles, which he puts at 67% faster, so threats are spotted and risks assessed earlier.

## Where it shows up in operations

He walks through three operational areas:

- **Targeting.** AI-assisted drone targeting with higher accuracy, which he credits with reducing unintended casualties by up to 50%.
- **Cyber defence.** Machine-learning security systems that detect threats proactively; his figures are 94% of potential breaches stopped and incident response 76% faster.
- **Logistics.** Workflow orchestration over real-time supply chain data, with a 71% improvement in resource allocation and lower costs from better-chosen resources.

Training gets its own section: adaptive AI-driven simulations and instant, targeted feedback, with figures of 64% better operational readiness and training timelines compressed by 59%.

## The numbers need their footnotes

The case studies are anonymous: a military unit reporting a 3.2 times jump in mission effectiveness with 38% lower deployment costs, a tactical unit at 91% threat detection accuracy, and a logistics unit that optimised its supply chain management. The closing slide adds 43% higher operational efficiency and a 4.1 times return on investment. The recording doesn't name the programmes, systems or studies behind these figures, so read them as the shape of the argument rather than benchmarks you can reuse.

What the talk is clearer on is how the pieces fit: aggregated data feeding a shared operational picture, orchestration taking manual bottlenecks out of workflows so personnel can focus on higher-value work, and models that keep learning from operational data.

## The hard parts are not technical

Two challenges get explicit time. Data security comes first, with strong encryption and access control for sensitive information as a baseline. Then ethics: AI in military operations raises questions about autonomous decision-making, and Sushil argues for clear ethical frameworks with human oversight and accountability built in. Given the targeting slide earlier, that section deserves more than its few minutes, and it's the part most worth discussing with your team.

His view of the future is a stack of enhanced human-machine collaboration, AI-driven strategic planning, autonomous systems, advanced cyber security and data-driven insight, with training and cross-branch information sharing as the next steps.

## Who should watch

Engineers and consultants working on public sector or defence programmes who want the vocabulary and the claims they're likely to meet in strategy documents. Python developers looking for async scaling patterns won't find them here; the first related talk below is closer to that.

Title: Conf42 DevOps 2025: caches, flaky tests, Terraform and culture
Description: Conf42 DevOps 2025 roundup - scaling Sofascore with caching, frugal serverless, flaky tests, Terraform supply chain risk, incident response and LLMs in CI/CD.
Body:
Conf42 DevOps 2025 ran online on January 23, 2025, with 58 talks, and it opened the year with a reassuringly practical mix. Yes, LLMs showed up in CI pipelines and Kubernetes troubleshooting. But the talks that stuck were about the fundamentals: caching done right, bills kept small, tests that stop flaking, supply chains that do not hand over your cloud, and people who still have to respond when the pager goes off.

Every session is on the [Conf42 DevOps 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/devops2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCdGhBCZtLYRLD9MT4ddCES).

## Scale is mostly boring, and that's good

[Josip Stuhli](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Josip_Stuhli_scaling_users_performance), CTO of Sofascore, gave the kind of scaling talk that makes you want to look at your own cache config. In the talk he puts Sofascore at more than 28 million monthly active users and 400 billion requests a month, with a peak of 1.6 million requests per second. The early fix for servers falling over at peaks was a full-page memcache, which then hit the classic cache stampede: a missing key, thousands of users asking for it at once, and every request going straight to the database. The talk walks through the fix and other low-hanging fruit that is often overlooked.

[Yan Cui](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Yan_Cui_serverless_saving_tips) of Lumigo, an AWS Serverless Hero who has worked on AWS since 2010, brought a fire hose of money-saving tips for serverless, starting with the one everyone should do on day one: set up billing alarms. They lag by a few hours, but finding out hours late beats finding out when the bill arrives.

Gold sponsor Rapydo tackled the database side. [Matan Nataf](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Matan_Nataf_db_ops_rapydo), co-founder and CEO of Rapydo, explained why per-instance tools fail for fleets of MySQL and Postgres databases, and demoed throttling a runaway query that kept coming back after it was killed.

## Tests you can trust

Testing got a lot of airtime. [Mike Morgan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mike_Morgan_testing_flaky_strategies) of Buildkite covered how to identify, isolate, and eliminate flaky tests before they erode trust in the pipeline. [Mesut Durukal](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mesut_Durukal_agile_automation_test) of Indeed asked whether test automation is a silver bullet (it isn't) and listed the common pitfalls. Analog Devices sent three DevOps engineers with hardware-flavoured problems: [Bianca Popu](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Bianca_Popu_github_infrastructure_testing) on securely wiring public GitHub repositories to private Jenkins test infrastructure, [Stefan Raus](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Stefan_Raus_arm_fpga_testing) on test harnesses for ARM and FPGA-based systems, and [Andreea Andrisan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Andreea_Andrisan_linux_distro_release) on the release strategy for a custom Linux distribution.

## Your supply chain has root access

[Uri Aronovici](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Uri_Aronovici_cloud_terraform_hack), co-founder and CTO of ZEST Security, showed how widely used open-source Terraform providers and modules can be abused to take full control of a cloud production environment, with two attack flows and mitigation practices. If your modules are pinned to whatever latest happened to be, watch this one first.

The security track continued with [Josh Hankins](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Josh_Hankins_devsecops_program_start) of CBTS on starting a DevSecOps program from scratch, [Krishna Chaitanya Rudraraju](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Krishna_Chaitanya_Rudraraju_threat_modeling_developers) of Microsoft on threat modelling inside DevOps pipelines, [Hariharan Ragothaman](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Hariharan_Ragothaman_deployments_governance_securely) of athenahealth on unifying deployments for governance, and [Sheshananda Reddy Kandula](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Sheshananda_Reddy_Kandula_mobile_security_automation) of Adobe on automating mobile security assessments with MobSF and Jenkins.

## When it breaks anyway

PagerDuty brought two talks on the human side of operations. [Daniel Afonso](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Daniel_Afonso_incident_response_effective) shared lessons for effective incident response under the banner "Don't Panic!", and [Mandi Walls](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mandi_Walls_culture_challenges_devops) argued that culture is still the challenge: when the only tool a team controls is its tooling, every problem looks like a tooling problem.

Observability had its say too. [Dave McAllister](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Dave_McAllister_nginx_metrics_monitor) of NGINX walked through 15 NGINX metrics from the application layer down to the host, [Amir Krayden](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Amir_Krayden_kubernetes_blind_spots) of Senser combined topology with existing observability to find Kubernetes blind spots, [Shyam Sreevalsan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Shyam_Sreevalsan_observability_future_years) of Netdata sketched the next ten years of observability, and [Pradeep Gaddamidi](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Pradeep_Gaddamidi_cloud_cost_monitoring) of Evernote shared how a budget-tight team built open-source monitoring and logging.

## LLMs join the pipeline

AI talks were plentiful and mostly grounded. [Rajeshwari Ganesan and Chidambaram Ganapathy Sundaram](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Rajeshwari_Ganesan_Chidambaram_Ganapathy_Sundaram_devsecops_automation_systems) of Infosys built a multi-agent LLM system to resolve build failures across more than 100 internal applications. [Kosseila Haddalene](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Kosseila_Haddalene_kubernetes_ai_troubleshooting) of cloudthrill demoed K8sGPT for troubleshooting managed clusters including Oracle OKE, with OpenAI, Cohere, or Ollama behind it. [Nirhoshan Sivaroopan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Nirhoshan_Sivaroopan_ai_accuracy_trust) of WSO2 covered accuracy evaluation for RAG systems, and [Praveen Payili](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Praveen_Payili_ai_data_enterprise) presented AskDataAI, an agent for enterprise data access.

## People, code and the rest

Some of the most-shared talks were not technical at all. [Pawel Zajaczkowski](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Pawel_Zajaczkowski_tech_impostor_syndrome) of Xebia tackled impostor syndrome, and [Tomasz Manugiewicz](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Tomasz_Manugiewicz_engineers_power_quiet) of evoke made the case for the quiet engineers whose contributions get missed in extrovert-dominated teams. [Muhammad Ahsan Ayaz](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Muhammad_Ahsan_Ayaz_angular_refactoring_projects) of Scania told the story of refactoring a sprawling estate of Angular projects and what went wrong, [Denis Ermakov](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Denis_Ermakov_coding_sustainable_development) of Techflow argued that less is more in code, [Tiago Barbosa](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Tiago_Barbosa_api_development_software) of Rely.io made the case for API-first development, and [Caio Medeiros Pinto](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Caio_Medeiros_Pinto_environment_products_innovation) of Citi pitched environments as a service.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to gold sponsor [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

The series continued with [Conf42 DevOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/devops2026) and returns as [Conf42 DevOps 2027](https://www.conf42.com/devops2027) on January 21, 2027.

Title: Put chaos experiments inside your internal developer platform
Description: Sayan Mondal of Harness at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 shows a chaos-first mindset for IDPs, with a LitmusChaos plugin demo running in Backstage.
Body:
If your internal developer platform is the place developers go for everything, it should also be the place they go to break things on purpose. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Sayan Mondal](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sayan_Mondal_cultural_mindset_platform), Senior Software Engineer at Harness and a maintainer and community manager of LitmusChaos, made the case for a chaos-first mindset in platform engineering, then demoed the Litmus plugin for Backstage.

## IDPs are great until something breaks

Mondal's framing: internal developer platforms are self-service portals for infrastructure, deployments and governance, and they work beautifully on a sunny day. Cloud native systems, though, are hundreds of small services across clusters, talking over networks to APIs and data stores. His example is an authentication service going down and taking payments, dashboards and notifications with it, the classic cascading failure.

So the chaos-first principle: treat failure as inevitable, inject it early and often, and make resilience part of the platform instead of a fire drill after an outage. He's clear that this is one more layer on top of what platform teams already think about.

## Four pillars for chaos in a platform

The plan he lays out is a sensible order of operations:

1. **Define and execute experiments** that fit your stack, whether cloud native, legacy, Linux, Windows or mainframe. Manual at first, to learn where things break.
2. **Chaos as a service**, so application teams can switch experiments on and off themselves without a ticket.
3. **Chaos in CI/CD**, so every release gets tested against failure before production.
4. **Observability and automated evaluation**, so the impact of each experiment is measured rather than eyeballed.

## The demo: Litmus inside Backstage

The demo is the part platform engineers will want to copy. Setup is two config edits. In Backstage's `app-config.yaml` you point at your Litmus URL and supply a Litmus auth token, created in the ChaosCenter account settings under API tokens (with a TTL of your choice) and exported as an environment variable. In the entity YAML you add an annotation with your Litmus project ID.

Once installed, a component page in Backstage gets a Litmus tab: experiment and API docs, the ChaosHub with its catalogue of faults (node power-off, Docker faults, pod memory hog, pod delete and so on), the chaos infrastructure and the experiment runs. Mondal shows the execution plane running in a `backstage` namespace with cluster-wide access, targets the Podtato Head demo app in a `demo` namespace, and re-runs a pod-delete experiment with an HTTP health probe, watching the new run appear in Backstage. Add Prometheus and Grafana and you'd see the impact there too.

The punchline is less about the plugin than the pattern: the developer portal becomes the single place where services, their owners and their resilience tests live together. Fewer tabs, fewer excuses.

## Where he wants the field to go

He ends with three asks for the chaos engineering community: a maturity model so organisations can see where they stand, chaos budgets and guardrails that define acceptable disruption per component, and better automated evaluation wired into existing monitoring.

## Who should watch

Platform teams running Backstage who want resilience testing in the golden path, and Litmus users who haven't tried the plugin yet. It's an intro-plus-demo talk; the first half covers ground that chaos engineers know well, so experienced practitioners can jump to the demo. It's also a talk by a Litmus maintainer showing Litmus, which is exactly why the setup steps are precise.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Chaos Validation Made Easy: Plug & Play with Resilience Probes](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Neelanjan_Manna_Sayan_Mondal_chaos_validation_resilience_probes) by Neelanjan Manna and Sayan Mondal at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, the probe side of the same toolkit.
- [Embracing Resilience: Unleashing the Power of Chaos Engineering in CD Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Saranya_Jena_Sarthak_Jain_embracing_resilience_power_cd_pipelines) by Saranya Jena and Sarthak Jain at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, for pillar three.
- [3 Practices to Ensure a Smooth Platform Engineering Adoption](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Caio_Medeiros_Pinto_smooth_platform_engineering_adoption) by Caio Medeiros Pinto at Conf42 DevOps 2024.

[Watch Sayan Mondal's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Sayan_Mondal_cultural_mindset_platform) or the [YouTube recording](https://youtu.be/6dOWiZqjy2g).

Title: A data warehouse playbook for nonprofits, from governance to SCD2
Description: Rao Marapatla of BreakthroughT1D at Conf42 Python 2025 lays out how a nonprofit builds an enterprise data warehouse for donor, fundraising and finance data.
Body:
A nonprofit's donor data usually lives in the CRM, its fundraising data in another platform and its money in the finance system, which means nobody can answer a question that spans all three. At Conf42 Python 2025, Rao Marapatla, Director of Data Infrastructure and Reporting at BreakthroughT1D, walks through how to build an enterprise data warehouse that puts them in one place, and the unglamorous decisions that make or break it.

Honest scope first: despite the event, this is an architecture and process talk, not a Python one. You won't see code or a specific tool stack; Marapatla deliberately stays vendor-neutral and tells you to pick whatever fits your budget. What you get is a checklist from someone who has run this inside a nonprofit.

## Siloed systems give siloed answers

The core argument is simple. If only CRM data reaches your reporting database, every analysis is a CRM analysis. The moment leadership asks how giving patterns relate to financial performance, or wants one summary across business units, a siloed setup can't answer. Integration also pays off in maintenance: one team, one platform, one set of templates instead of several people pulling the same data from the same system for slightly different reports.

## Four capabilities, and the one people forget

Marapatla's core technical list is cloud infrastructure, ETL processing, an analytics engine and a data governance framework. On infrastructure, the item he flags as most often missed is the disaster recovery plan, and keeping it current with the schedule your production system actually runs on. On analytics, his point is the one every ML team learns the hard way: put AI on top of bad data and you get confident nonsense.

Governance gets the best example in the talk. One source says United States, another US, a third USA. All valid, all different, and every department has its own terminology. A governance group decides on one form with the stakeholders, explains why, and from then on the warehouse speaks one language. Multiply that by every field and you see why he puts governance next to the technology rather than after it.

## Sync times are a business conversation

A detail worth stealing: when the business asks for fresh data every morning at 6am, check when the source system updates. If the source refreshes at 9, a 6am sync delivers yesterday's numbers on schedule. The fix is talking it through with the business, with the pros and cons on the table, rather than just setting the cron.

The same thinking applies to reports. Marapatla splits them into operational reports, which need near real-time data, and analytical reports, where you agree a T-minus-one or T-minus-two day freshness. Real-time is only real if the source, the ETL jobs and the reporting tool line up, and live connections behave differently from extracts.

## Write the model down, keep the history

Two documents he treats as non-negotiable: a logical data model (tables, relationships, dependencies, reviewed by the respective teams) and a physical data model (what each table holds, primary and foreign keys). They become the master reference for everything after. For history, he recommends slowly changing dimension type 2, so you keep both the current and past state of a record.

## Plan for the systems you don't have yet

The challenges section is pragmatic. Today you integrate four systems; tomorrow the organisation onboards a fifth. Today the warehouse is one terabyte; plan, with some forecasting, for where it lands in five years. Sensitive data across jurisdictions needs masking rules per environment. And once it ships, train the staff, because an unused warehouse is an expensive archive.

## Who should watch

Data leads at nonprofits or small organisations starting their first warehouse, and engineers who keep being asked for one cross-system report that can't be built. If you want PySpark code or a tool comparison, look elsewhere; this is the planning layer.

Title: A Python library map for IoT data, from sensor to dashboard
Description: Gokul Balaguruswamy Naidu of Amazon at Conf42 Python 2025 maps Python libraries onto every layer of an IoT data system, with smart city and factory examples.
Body:
Every layer of an IoT data system, from the GPIO pin to the city dashboard, has a Python library that fits it. That is the organising idea of Gokul Balaguruswamy Naidu's talk at Conf42 Python 2025: the Amazon Software Development Manager walks the stack layer by layer and names the tool for each, then ties it together in smart city, factory and farm examples.

Set expectations: this is a broad survey, not a build log. There is no live code and no single system dissected. Its value is as a map, especially if you are a Python developer looking at IoT for the first time and wondering where your existing skills plug in.

## Ingest, stream, store

The data path comes first. Real-time processing is framed with a traffic system that retimes signals as sensors report congestion. Apache Kafka and Azure Stream Analytics handle the streams; on the Python side he points to pandas and PyKafka for cleaning and filtering incoming data, for example catching an unexpected jam. Apache Airflow orchestrates the pipelines. For storage, MongoDB for unstructured data like images, PostgreSQL for structured sensor logs, with pymongo and psycopg2 as the drivers. On the device side, Raspberry Pi GPIO and Adafruit Blinka talk to sensors, Paho MQTT moves messages, and PySerial talks to industrial hardware.

## Security is a library choice too

The security section is where IoT stops being a hobby: medical devices sending patient metrics, systems controlling power grids. Naidu covers TLS for transport (a home camera streaming to the cloud is his example), the cryptography and PyCryptodome libraries for encrypting streams, OAuth2 and JWT via Authlib so that only authorised devices reach the hub, and intrusion detection with scikit-learn or PyTorch models that flag anomalies such as one device suddenly flooding the network with requests.

One footnote from us, not the talk: he also names pycrypto for quantum-safe experimentation. The original PyCrypto package has been unmaintained for years; PyCryptodome and cryptography are the ones to install.

## Intelligence at the edge

The AI section is the most concrete. TensorFlow Lite and OpenCV let a drone detect obstacles on-device instead of waiting for a round trip to the cloud. Predictive maintenance uses scikit-learn, XGBoost or H2O.ai on vibration data: if a machine keeps crossing a vibration threshold, the model predicts a failing bearing before it fails. spaCy and NLTK cover voice control for home automation, and Matplotlib, Seaborn and Plotly build the dashboards, such as energy use by neighbourhood.

## Start small, then scale

The closing section is the most useful for beginners. Learn the hardware libraries and MQTT, then build a proof of concept: his example is a smart irrigation system with soil moisture and temperature sensors, a Python script that analyses trends, Flask for a small web UI, Matplotlib for charts and SQLite for history. Only then scale: move storage to DynamoDB or BigQuery via boto3 or the Google Cloud libraries, add TLS and OAuth2 as the user base grows, use asyncio to handle many devices concurrently, and lean on AWS IoT Core or Azure IoT Hub rather than building device management yourself.

## Who should watch

Python developers curious about IoT who want to know which libraries to look up first, and students choosing a first hardware project. Engineers already running fleets of devices will find it introductory; for them, the related talks below go deeper on specific layers.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Marie Cruz on monitoring plants with IoT sensors and Grafana Cloud](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Marie_Cruz_sensors_gardening_analytics) (Conf42 IoT 2025), a small real build in the spirit of Naidu's proof-of-concept advice
- [Madhu Niranjan Reddy Puduru on edge AI for smart cameras](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Madhu_Niranjan_Reddy_Puduru_vision_edge_processing) (Conf42 IoT 2025)
