Title: From commit to customer at speed
Description: Reliability is the goal
Body:
# DevOps is still a thing (and somehow bigger than ever)

Every year someone declares DevOps “done”, “dead”, or “just how things are now”.

And every year, DevOps quietly adds five more responsibilities, a few new tools, and at least one AI-powered opinion about how you should be doing your job.

Conf42 DevOps 2025 embraces that reality.

This conference is packed. Fifty plus talks across culture, cloud, data, security, testing, observability, incidents, scaling, performance, AI, LLMs, and whatever category your current problem accidentally falls into. If it touches delivery, operations, or keeping systems alive, it’s probably here.

AI shows up everywhere. From generative AI in cloud-native DevOps to AI-assisted monitoring, fraud detection, data pipelines, testing, and even build failure automation. Some talks focus on the promise. Others focus on trust, accuracy, and what happens when AI confidently gives you the wrong answer at scale.

But it’s not all machines. There are plenty of sessions on culture, leadership, impostor syndrome, quiet engineers, and the human side of running complex systems. Because no amount of automation fixes burnout, unclear ownership, or “we’ll just ship it and see”.

You’ll also find deep dives into Kubernetes, serverless, observability, security, incident response, healthcare platforms, and large-scale migrations. From zero to millions of users. From flaky tests to resilient systems. From “why is this slow” to “oh… that’s why”.

If DevOps is your job, your background, or your current identity crisis, this one’s for you. It’s messy, evolving, and still very much not finished.

See you there.

Title: Your app autoscales a thousandfold, your database does not
Description: Matan Nataf of Rapydo at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on managing fleets of MySQL and Postgres databases, with a live demo of throttling a runaway query.
Body:
Kubernetes and autoscaling groups let your application scale out on demand, but the relational database behind it is still one shared-everything box. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Matan Nataf, co-founder and CEO of Rapydo, argued that the tooling for running relational databases in the cloud has not kept up with microservices and multi-tenant architectures, and demoed how Rapydo tackles it.

Rapydo was a gold sponsor of the event, and this is a product talk: roughly half framing, half live demo of the Rapydo console. The framing is useful for anyone running more than a handful of MySQL or Postgres instances.

## From a few databases to thousands

Matan's history lesson is short. On-prem, a company ran a small fleet of databases for a few monolithic apps, with a full DBA team watching them. Load changed by modest percentages, so sizing for the peak was neither hard nor expensive.

Microservices changed that. Teams ship features daily, often on open-source MySQL and Postgres, and the fleet can grow to thousands of instances. Per-instance tools such as Amazon RDS Performance Insights show one database at a time, and with a fleet of 5,000 databases, he points out, looking at one instance at a time makes you reactive by definition.

He also names the uncomfortable part of the ops job: even when you find the bad query, the fix usually lives in legacy code owned by a development team, so all you can do is file it with them and wait.

## Three pillars: observability, resiliency, sane costs

Matan's spec for a modern database management tool has three legs, and he says missing any one of them fails:

- **Fleet-wide observability.** The slowest queries, top CPU and IO consumers, connection shortages, and locks and deadlocks across all instances in one view, with alerts on thresholds.
- **Resiliency without code changes.** Guardrails that protect the database from CPU spikes, runaway queries, repeated identical queries from buggy code, and idle connections eating the pool.
- **Sane costs.** Capacity planning that does not have to assume the worst spike, since he notes managed databases are often the second or third line on a cloud bill.

Rapydo maps onto that with two parts deployed in your own VPC: Scout for observability across Postgres and MySQL, and Cortex, an automation layer that works through a proxy and managed connections to apply caching, throttling, and query rewrites.

## The demo: a query that keeps coming back

The live demo is the best part. The master dashboard shows a 48-hour view of slow queries, top CPU consumers, and locks across the fleet. Grouping the lock view shows the single Postgres instance suffering most, and that two statements, one update and one select, generate most of the locks.

Then the real-time view: a MySQL 8 demo database at 100% CPU with all 250 of its 250 connections in use. Going back 15 minutes shows the same `SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS` query running four times in parallel, then 112, then 230, and 237 when he returns to the live view.

Matan kills the query, and the application immediately sends it again, which is the honest moment of the talk: killing queries is a fire extinguisher, not a fix. He considers a cache rule with table-based invalidation, which keeps cached data consistent with the table, then rejects it because the query uses the current date. Instead he applies a throttling rule, with a wildcard on the `LIMIT` clause, that lets that query run only two at a time. The parallel count falls from 75 to 46 to 2, and the database recovers while the app keeps sending the query.

## Who should watch

DevOps and SRE teams who own a large fleet of MySQL or Postgres databases but not the application code hitting them. The framing helps you argue for fleet-level tooling; the demo shows what intervening at the proxy layer looks like. If you run three databases and a DBA, it will feel like someone else's problem, for now.

Title: Hybrid image search in MongoDB: when keywords miss the Porsche
Description: Shannon Lal of Designstripe at Conf42 Python 2025 combines MongoDB text search, OpenAI embeddings and reciprocal rank fusion for image search.
Body:
Search a library of image descriptions for *automobile* and keyword search returns nothing, even though there is a red Ferrari and a black Porsche in there. At Conf42 Python 2025, Shannon Lal, VP Technology and Engineering at Designstripe, shows how his team combined MongoDB text search with OpenAI vector embeddings into one hybrid query, and what they still haven't solved.

Designstripe generates ready-to-publish social media posts from a scraped *brand DNA* (industry, tone, fonts, colours, logos). Each post needs an image, and the goal is to pull in the user's own uploaded or generated images when they fit the topic. That means matching a post about SVG illustrations to a picture whose description says *a woman with a dog working at her desk*.

## Text search finds words, vector search finds meaning

The demo makes the gap obvious. Plain text search for *car* returns the Ferrari, whose description contains the word, but not the Porsche, whose description doesn't. *Automobile* returns nothing at all. Keyword search is doing its job; the job is the wrong one.

The fix starts at upload time. When an image is stored in Google Cloud Storage, its description goes to the OpenAI embeddings API, and the resulting vector is saved in the same MongoDB document as the text, user ID and metadata. A vector search index on that field (Lal shows 512 dimensions, cosine similarity, and a filter path on user ID because images are per user) then lets *automobile* find both sports cars. Bigger dimensions tend to give better results and cost more storage, a trade he returns to later.

## One aggregation, two searches

Vector search has its own blind spot: ask for *black automobile* and you want the keyword *black* to count. Hybrid search runs both. In MongoDB that is one aggregation pipeline: a `$vectorSearch` stage, then a `$unionWith` on the same collection whose sub-pipeline runs a text search with a compound query and the same user filter. One round trip, two result sets.

Merging them is the interesting part. Lal follows MongoDB's reciprocal rank fusion recipe: each result gets a score based on its position in its own list rather than its raw search score (the constant in his example is 60), the vector and text ranks are combined per document, and the merged list is sorted. Weights let you favour text or vector results.

## Thresholds keep the hockey scene out

Rank fusion alone still surfaced a picture of kids playing hockey on a pond for *black automobile*, because similarity search always returns its nearest neighbours, relevant or not. The team added a match stage before the rank calculation that drops anything under a minimum vector score and a minimum text score. He suggests starting around 0.6 to 0.7 and tuning.

## The hard part is relevance, not setup

The candid ending is the best section. Setup is relatively easy; most of the time goes into making results good. User libraries are small, and MongoDB told the team its vector search is optimised for larger data sets, so four or five candidates don't always rank well. They are experimenting with giving vectors more weight for longer queries, with text boosting, and with larger embedding models (they moved from Ada to the newer text-embedding-3 models and saw better results with bigger vectors). The next idea is a final LLM pass that reorders the top 20 results and discards irrelevant ones, accepting extra cost and latency.

## Who should watch

Python developers already on MongoDB who want semantic search without adding a separate vector database, and anyone about to discover that *just add embeddings* is step one of ten. It is a walkthrough of the aggregation stages, not a FastAPI or ORM tutorial; Lal deliberately cut that.

Title: Why engineers need skills beyond code to get heard
Description: Pierluigi Meloni of Utterskills at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on the soft-skill hacks that turn a capable engineer into the go-to expert.
Body:
Being right about the architecture doesn't help if nobody in the room listens. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Pierluigi Meloni](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Pierluigi_Meloni_success_people_tech), Co-Founder and CEO of Utterskills, argued that the skills that get an engineer heard are learnable, and that they look a lot like algorithms: small, repeatable playbooks you can run without changing who you are.

Honest scope first: Meloni runs an e-learning company built around these "skills beyond code", and the talk closes with an offer for his course. The useful part is the stories and frameworks before that, which stand on their own.

## The consultant who didn't buzzword

Meloni spent 20-plus years in engineering roles and describes a familiar frustration: technical debt grows, nobody listened when you warned them, and now it's your problem because you built it. Meanwhile the loudest person in the room, the one he nicknames a sellosopher, climbs the ladder.

The turning point was a consultant called Steven at a clinical research company. Calm, nerdy, a real tech expert, and somehow influential in management meetings. When Meloni was about to pitch a big refactoring to management, Steven told him to postpone it, because as written it would land like giving a presentation in Chinese to an Italian audience.

Steven's three fixes are worth writing on a sticky note:

1. Know your audience: their KPIs, what they expect, what will bore them.
2. Use their language, with analogies from their domain.
3. Don't sell the solution. Make them understand the problem and the benefit, and let the how stay your black box.

The rewritten pitch went through, and Meloni realised there was no magic involved, just a bucket of clever hacks he could copy.

## COIN: feedback without the fireworks

The most practical framework in the talk is COIN, for when a colleague's code makes you want to swear in a review. Context (what you looked at), Observation (what you noticed, for example a module processing large amounts of data at once), Impact (slower responses, higher resource use) and Next steps (perhaps process in smaller chunks; would you be open to discussing it together?). Same message, no casualties. He notes, with a grin, that you can still say the rude version in your head.

## Three false beliefs

He then takes apart three objections he hears from engineers:

- My skills are great, my coworkers are the problem. He points at the Dunning-Kruger effect and at the gap between knowing what good communication looks like and doing it consistently. He cites the Standish CHAOS report, with roughly 30 percent of IT projects classed as successful for decades, and people and communication as the recurring cause.
- I don't want to go into management. Soft skills drive promotion to senior too, and engineers spend a big slice of their week in meetings anyway.
- Management just doesn't listen. That one, he says, is about expert status.

## Own the how, get in early on the what

The expert-status section is the sharpest. A surgeon or a car mechanic would refuse a customer's request to skip two thirds of the steps; software engineers routinely accept requests to just add an if, or to skip the tests because it is only the MVP. His rule: you own the *how*, so shield it. Then influence the *what* and the *why* as early as possible, before the point of no return where requirements are sealed. After that, the planners are forgotten and everyone remembers who built it.

## Who should watch

Mid-level and senior engineers who feel unheard, and tech leads who want language for coaching their team. It's a long, story-driven talk with a commercial ending; if you only want frameworks, skim for Steven, COIN and the how/what/why section.

Title: Threads, asyncio or processes? A short Python concurrency primer
Description: Iyanuoluwa Ajao of Fyyne at Conf42 Python 2025 explains when to use threading, asyncio or multiprocessing, with a two-YouTube-videos analogy.
Body:
Python gives you three standard-library ways to do more than one thing at once, and picking the wrong one is how a *faster* script ends up slower. At Conf42 Python 2025, Iyanuoluwa Ajao, Senior Software Engineer at Fyyne, gives a compact primer on threading, asyncio and multiprocessing, and a decision rule for choosing between them.

This is an intro talk, and a short one. If you already reach for `asyncio.gather` without thinking, you can skip it. If you are the person on the team who keeps getting asked *why didn't threads make this faster?*, it is a tidy fifteen minutes to send around.

## Two YouTube videos explain the whole thing

Ajao's analogy carries the talk. Open two YouTube videos. If you play one while the other is paused and buffering, then swap, you are doing concurrency: tasks overlap in time, but only one runs at any moment, and the switching happens because something is waiting on the network. If both videos play at the same time, that is parallelism, and it only works because you have more than one CPU.

That framing lines up with the rule the talk ends on. I/O-bound work (network calls, the buffering video) wants concurrency. CPU-bound work (maths, number crunching) wants parallelism across cores.

## Synchronous first, then threads

He starts from the plain synchronous version: a loop using the `requests` library that finishes one download before starting the next, like watching video one to the end before even opening video two.

The threaded version swaps that loop for a `ThreadPoolExecutor`, which creates a pool of threads and an executor to manage them. In the analogy each video is a thread and you are the executor. The catch he points out: the operating system decides when a thread pauses and another runs, so any data the threads share has to be protected to stay thread-safe. Threads also cost memory, which matters once you have a lot of them.

## asyncio is faster, if your libraries cooperate

The asyncio version uses `async` and `await`, and that is the whole trade-off. Ajao's claim is that asyncio is faster and lighter on resources than threading, but it needs libraries that speak `async`/`await`. `requests` doesn't, so the asyncio example switches to `aiohttp`. Use a blocking library inside a coroutine and the benefit disappears.

His decision rule for I/O-bound work is refreshingly short:

1. Is there an async library for the thing you need to call? Use asyncio.
2. No async library? Use threading. He mentions boto3, AWS's Python SDK, as the kind of case where you may end up there.

## multiprocessing is for when the CPU is the bottleneck

For CPU-bound tasks the talk moves to `multiprocessing` and a process pool. By default the pool size matches the number of CPUs on the machine, which is exactly the *both videos play at once* case. Separate processes sidestep the problem threads have with CPU-heavy Python code, at the cost of heavier workers.

The summary slide is the one to screenshot: I/O-bound means asyncio or threading, CPU-bound means multiprocessing.

## Who should watch

Python developers early in their concurrency journey, and anyone onboarding juniors onto a codebase full of `async def`. It won't cover the GIL internals, free-threaded builds or structured concurrency with task groups; treat it as the map, then go read the docs for the terrain.

Title: One UX architect learned Python, and her whole team got faster
Description: Liv McFarlin of Wheels at Conf42 Python 2025 on fake prototype data, a Streamlit style guide and local LLMs for qualitative research.
Body:
One person on a UX team learning Python can change what the whole team is able to do. That is the argument Liv McFarlin, Principal UX Architect at Wheels, makes at Conf42 Python 2025, walking through what she built since 2021 for design, research and collaboration at a fleet management company.

She says up front that this is not a technical talk: little code, no implementation walkthroughs. What you get instead is a working map of where Python pays off for people who are not software engineers, and an honest list of where the constraints (time, IT support, colleagues who don't want to learn Python) bent the plans.

## Fake data is the cheapest prototyping speedup

The first win was boring in the best way. Prototypes at Wheels need anywhere between 50 and 300 data points to feel real: names, phone numbers, postal codes, but also VINs, licence plates and company IDs. Before Python, designers either copied ten hand-made rows over and over or hopped between VIN and plate generator websites, then cleaned the results. McFarlin puts it at 30 minutes to an hour per prototype, before debugging why a filter now catches too many rows.

Her answer is a small package called Data Generator: Python scripts plus text files that emit fake core data points as Excel or PDF, with care taken not to accidentally produce a real VIN. Excel won, because it drops into both Axure and Figma. The first version had a UI built with MLJAR Studio; access problems killed the UI, and it now runs from the command line or a Jupyter notebook. Anyone who has watched an internal tool die in the access-request queue will recognise that move.

## A style guide that lives where the other team lives

The second story is about a partner team building data products in Streamlit, outside the UX team's corner of the org and without access to its design system assets. Pointing them at a style guide and walking away felt wrong, so McFarlin rebuilt a substantial part of the guide as a Streamlit app: colour pages for light and dark mode with CSS variable names and hex codes, an icon library with snippets and file paths, a style sheet with the web fonts.

The trick she highlights is that Streamlit lets you write Python functions that generate chunks of HTML and treat them like components. Not everything ports. Buttons, radio buttons, tabs, inputs, notifications and modals had to be rebuilt from scratch using a React template, and at the time of the talk only buttons and input fields were done. That kind of detail is why the talk is worth watching: it reports the half-finished state, not a press release.

## Research is where Python shines

The longest section covers qualitative analysis, which is most of the team's data: user tests, interviews, surveys. Tagging comments by hand can take a week or more. Her progression ran from sentiment analysis (VADER on a survey of roughly 3,000 responses) and basic text metrics, through topic modelling, to Hugging Face models and spaCy, where custom NER tags let the team spot which products and features a comment mentions.

Then came LLMs: scikit-llm with OpenAI for zero-shot and few-shot classification, results reviewed by two people, and team guidelines that pair every LLM analysis with a UXer who knows the domain. Safety concerns pushed the work to Ollama and Meta's Llama running locally, and McFarlin reports no drop in classification quality after the switch. On the quantitative side, Python moved the team past Excel into cluster analysis, association mining and network analysis.

## Know when to park the idea

Not everything shipped. A LangChain SQL chain over a PostgreSQL database was parked because nobody could guarantee the right queries came back, and the database design work was beyond a small team. A ChromaDB plus LangChain plus Ollama tool that generates summaries, topics and metadata for a library of 100+ external PDFs is in progress, with LlamaIndex and a RAG design as the next step. Her closing advice is practical: automate the repetitive and draining work, don't assume colleagues can or want to do what you do, step back when an idea costs more than you have, and don't wait for support before building a small version.

## Who should watch

Designers and researchers who suspect a little Python would help, and engineers who support a UX team and wonder what it actually needs. If you want code-heavy Streamlit or RAG internals, this is the wrong talk; it is a field report from someone doing it alone.

Title: Bad data is the BI problem, and AI can clean it at scale
Description: Shashank Reddy Beeravelly of Walmart at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on using AI to find, fix and fill data quality gaps in finance and manufacturing.
Body:
Every dashboard is only as honest as the table behind it, and most tables are less honest than we'd like. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Shashank Reddy Beeravelly, Software Engineer at Walmart, made the case that data quality is the real bottleneck in business intelligence and that AI (anomaly detection, NLP standardisation and ML-based gap filling) can fix it at a scale manual cleansing never reaches, with examples from financial services and manufacturing and a phased plan for rolling it out.

It's an overview with a lot of figures. The talk presents them as industry and case study results without naming the organisations or methods behind them, so read them as directional.

## Four ways data goes bad

Shashank names four problems most data engineers will recognise. Data teams spend a large share of their time, he says around 40 percent, firefighting quality issues. Enterprise systems are often incomplete, so insights hide in missing fields. A sizeable fraction of customer and vendor records are duplicates, which wastes effort and gives customers inconsistent treatment. And data decays: corporate data goes stale year by year, with B2B data degrading fastest. Each one quietly skews decisions made on top of it.

## What AI does about it

The solutions map onto the problems:

- **Detection and correction**: algorithms that find and fix inconsistencies automatically and much faster than rule-by-rule cleaning.
- **Standardisation**: NLP models normalising data across languages so a global dataset reads consistently.
- **Gap filling**: ML models inferring missing values so nobody has to key them in by hand.
- **Real-time validation**: systems checking records as they arrive, so errors are caught before they reach a decision rather than after.

The last point matters most for BI. Cleaning data after a report has gone to the board is an apology, not a control.

## Finance and manufacturing

In financial services, he describes machine learning accelerating transaction validation and fraud detection, pattern recognition cutting data-related errors and the regulatory risk that comes with them, and automated collection and validation shortening regulatory reporting. In manufacturing supply chains, AI validation watches production data in real time to catch defects, automated harmonisation keeps data consistent across global suppliers, supplier matching and verification drops from weeks of manual work to minutes, and models trained on history predict delivery times more accurately.

He then extends the same story to forecasting and inventory planning, customer segmentation and marketing, and operational overhead, the business outcomes that clean data feeds.

## Roll it out in phases

The practical section is the one to keep:

1. **Baseline first**: assess where your data stands today, then set quantifiable goals for customer, financial and operational data.
2. **Size the platform for growth**: plan for data volumes to keep climbing year on year, so you aren't re-platforming in three years.
3. **Pilot**: a 10 to 14 week pilot to test and refine before going wide.
4. **Validate in layers**: automated testing, business process validation and user acceptance testing.

None of this is AI-specific, which is the point. The model is the easy part; the baseline and the validation layers are what make the numbers believable.

## Who should watch

BI and analytics leads building the case for investing in data quality, and data engineers who want a quick outline of where ML fits in a cleansing pipeline. Engineers looking for specific tools, model choices or code won't find them here. Shashank also gave data-quality talks at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 and Conf42 Python 2025.

Title: Single sign-on that is secure, fast and invisible to users
Description: Rinku Mohan of bettercoach at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on OAuth 2.0 vs SAML, token risks, SSO performance and bridging legacy apps.
Body:
Single sign-on concentrates every login into one place, which is great for users and great for attackers. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Rinku Mohan](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Rinku_Mohan_signon_design_implementation), Senior Software Engineer at bettercoach, laid out how to design SSO that balances three things at once: security, performance and user experience. Drop any one, he argued, and adoption falls while risk climbs.

It's a compact talk, a solid primer for engineers who are about to own an identity integration and want the trade-offs in one place.

## Two protocols, two jobs

Mohan starts with the protocols. OAuth 2.0 is the token-based framework behind "log in with Google": the client app redirects to an authorization server, the user authenticates there, the app swaps an authorization code for an access token, and that token opens APIs on resource servers. The user never hands their password to the app.

SAML, the older XML-based standard, is the enterprise favourite. A service provider such as AWS or Salesforce sends the user to an identity provider (he names Okta and Azure), which issues a signed SAML assertion the service provider trusts. Log in once, reach everything. The rough rule from the talk: OAuth for cloud, mobile and API access; SAML where legacy enterprise apps live.

## Centralising auth centralises the blast radius

The risk section is the part worth rewinding. If the identity provider is compromised, every connected application is exposed, because whoever controls the IdP controls the front door to all of them. Tokens become high-value targets: a stolen access token opens sensitive resources, and replay attacks let an attacker reuse a valid token to hijack a session. Man-in-the-middle attacks on the token exchange round out the list.

His countermeasures are the ones every security review should check for:

- Short-lived access tokens, with refresh tokens to extend sessions, so a stolen token expires quickly.
- Multi-factor authentication (push, one-time password or biometric) so a stolen password isn't enough.
- Token scoping on least privilege: a token that reads user data should not be able to change system settings.
- Logging and monitoring of auth attempts, with blocking or step-up verification on odd patterns such as repeated failures or unusual locations.

For a chaos engineering crowd, there's an obvious experiment hiding in here: what happens to your fleet of apps when the IdP is slow or gone?

## Fast logins are a security feature

Mohan makes the case that performance belongs in the security conversation, because a slow, nagging login is what pushes users to work around SSO. His three levers: cache valid tokens so users don't re-authenticate for every system, load-balance identity providers so one busy server isn't a bottleneck, and validate tokens asynchronously so auth checks don't block API responses.

On the experience side, "A great SSO experience should feel invisible." That means one login per session, branded login pages that match the app so users trust where they are, and session persistence across services.

## Legacy apps get a translator, not a big bang

Plenty of enterprise software speaks neither OAuth 2.0 nor SAML. His answer is an SSO gateway that translates modern auth into whatever the old system understands, a gradual phase-in alongside existing logins, and backward-compatibility testing before a full rollout. He ends with the direction of travel: zero trust with continuous authentication, AI-assisted anomaly detection on login patterns, and decentralised identity.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers starting an SSO project, or inheriting one. It's an overview, not a protocol deep-end: no code, no token-validation internals. Identity specialists will know the material; everyone else gets a tidy checklist.

Title: How Nx generators and migrations tamed 150 Angular projects
Description: Muhammad Ahsan Ayaz of Scania at Conf42 DevOps 2025: moving a book's Angular projects into Nx, then using a migration to fix all of them at once.
Body:
Angular ships a major release every six months, which is fine for one app and a problem for a book with more than 150 example projects pinned to Angular 12. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Muhammad Ahsan Ayaz, Software Architect at Scania and Google Developer Expert in Angular, told the story of updating his Angular Cookbook's projects for the second edition: consolidating them into Nx workspaces, writing his own Nx plugin, and then discovering the problem generators can't solve, which Nx migrations can.

It's a story talk with code, and the "what went wrong" in the title is honest. He tried things, some of them were wrong, and the fixes are the useful part.

## One repo, two workspaces, lots of cats

Muhammad compares the job to walking 150 cats at once. The book is a cookbook, so every recipe has a starting state and a solution, and his structure reflects that: one GitHub repository with two Nx workspaces, `start` and `final`, each holding chapter folders with one project per recipe, migrating the projects from Angular 12 to 16 as he moved them in.

The first snag was developer experience, for readers and for himself. Nx derives project names from the folder hierarchy, so running a recipe meant changing into a folder and typing a long name made of chapter and recipe. His goals: run everything from the repo root with `npm run serve`, and drop the chapter from the name since every recipe name is unique in each workspace. A script handled the first. The second needed a plugin.

## Generators create, executors rename

Using Nx's plugin package, he built a plugin with two halves. A generator creates the Angular application and writes a rename executor into its project configuration, recording the chapter number and app name. The executor then reads that information and renames the project with a bit of regex. Wrapped in a bash script behind `npm run create`, adding a recipe became one command with the chapter, recipe name and header title, and serving it became `npm run serve` plus the recipe name. He admits he picked creating then renaming over naming it right at creation without a strong reason, which is the kind of honesty that makes the talk worth watching.

## Consistency, then the logo changed

Next he wanted every app to look the same: a header with the title, Angular logo and info button, and a dynamic content area below. He put fonts and Material icons in the generator's `index.html` template, the layout in the `app.component.html` template, and created a shared Nx library, `ngcb-ui`, with global SCSS wired into both workspaces. Two workspaces to configure, not 150 projects.

Then Angular changed its logo. Every project had the old one hard-coded as an SVG in its template. Fixing the generator doesn't help, because generators only run when a project is created, and all 150 already existed.

## Migrations are generators for code you already have

His fix was two steps. First, a header component in the shared library, so the header lives in one place from now on. Second, an Nx migration, which runs a generator across an entire workspace after the fact and is versioned against the plugin, so it fires on upgrade. His `replace-app-toolbar` migration walks every project, finds the existing toolbar and title, swaps in the library header, and adds the import to the TypeScript file, handling both standalone components and NgModule-based apps. Run once in `start` and once in `final`, it updated every recipe in two commits.

His lessons: managing 150-plus projects is possible, no solution is perfect the first time, and it's never too late to learn the tool you were avoiding. For him that was Angular schematics, the machinery under Nx generators and executors.

## Who should watch

Anyone maintaining many similar Angular or front-end apps in one org, such as internal tools, white-label builds or training material, and teams considering Nx who want to see generators, executors and migrations used on a real problem. If you're happy with a single-app repo, it's still a good look at codemods done safely.

Title: How banks structure a data warehouse for financial reporting
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Bharath Gaddam of Campbellsville University maps financial data warehouse architecture, from staging and star schemas to compliance.
Body:
Financial reporting lives or dies on whether every number can be traced back to its source. At Conf42 Python 2025, Bharath Gaddam, a senior database developer, walked through how financial institutions build data warehouses around that requirement: layered architecture from source systems to staging to a dimensional core, BI on top, and lineage and governance running through all of it.

One thing to know before you press play: despite the Python in the title, the talk is an architecture overview delivered from slides. There is no code on screen, so it is best for people who want the shape of the system rather than an implementation.

## Thirty years in three steps

Bharath frames the history in three eras. In the 1990s, warehouses were batch-oriented stores of historical statements, transactions and reconciliation data, mainly for regulatory reporting. In the 2000s, BI tools turned them into engines for risk modelling, portfolio analysis and automated compliance monitoring, with data mining feeding fraud detection and customer segmentation. Today, cloud and hybrid warehouses add real-time analytics and distributed processing of very large data sets.

## The layers, and why staging matters

The architecture is the classic one, explained clearly. Sources include transaction processing systems, external market data feeds and regulatory reporting platforms. Data lands in staging, where it is validated, cleansed and standardised before it reaches the core warehouse. The core holds history in dimensional models, typically star or snowflake schemas, as the single source of truth.

Staging is the step to take seriously. It is where format differences between systems get flattened and errors get caught before anyone builds a report on them.

## Design details that matter in finance

The implementation framework goes from requirements (stakeholder interviews, technical workshops, mapping reporting needs to specs) to schema design with fact and dimension tables, slowly changing dimensions to keep history, a chosen grain and clear hierarchies for drill-down. Performance comes from query optimisation, indexing and partitioning. Integration means robust ETL, APIs between systems and real-time synchronisation where needed.

BI sits on top in three modes: real-time dashboards for KPIs, risk metrics and market positions; ad hoc self-service reporting that drills down to transaction level; and predictive analytics for risk and investment decisions.

## Compliance is architecture, not paperwork

The strongest section treats regulation as a design input. End-to-end data lineage gives auditors a trail from report back to source. Governance enforces quality, role-based access, encryption and regular audits. Access has to balance fast retrieval for reporting against strict security. And automated monitoring checks data against frameworks such as the Basel capital rules, Dodd-Frank reporting, GDPR and SOX.

## Benefits, costs and the hard parts

Bharath cites reports produced 40 to 60% faster and reconciliation effort cut by about 30%, and he doesn't hide the cost side: initial deployments ranging from $5 million to $50 million depending on scale, plus ongoing maintenance. Lineage across many systems and unstructured inputs such as scanned documents remain hard problems. He closes with trends: cloud-native multi-cloud designs, AI for cleansing and validation, edge processing for latency-sensitive trading, and blockchain for tamper-evident records.

## Who should watch

Engineers joining a finance data team, or anyone who needs to explain why the warehouse has a staging layer and a lineage tool, will get a clear overview. Experienced data warehouse architects won't find new ground.

Title: Mental models that make you a better software designer
Description: Mihaela-Roxana Ghidersa of Signant Health at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025 on circle of competence, second-order thinking and inversion for developers.
Body:
Most bad software decisions are thinking errors before they are code errors. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, [Mihaela-Roxana Ghidersa](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_MihaelaRoxana_Ghidersa_mindset_software_build), Technical Lead at Signant Health, borrowed a handful of mental models (circle of competence, the map is not the territory, second-order thinking, inversion, Occam's razor) and showed what each one looks like on a real software team.

There are no YAML files or dashboards in this one. It's a talk about how developers reason, and it sits on a chaos engineering lineup for a good reason: the failures chaos experiments find were usually designed in by someone who didn't see them coming.

## Breaking stones or building a castle

She opens with an old story. A traveller asks workers on a hill what they're doing. Most say they're breaking stones; the last one says he is building a castle. Ghidersa's point is that developers switch between both modes. Some days you close the ticket and nothing more. Other days you try to understand the business and the system around the ticket. She is honest about why people get stuck in stone-breaking: the organisation, missing information, fear, burnout, or simply the wrong job.

The fix she proposes starts with a growth mindset. Telling yourself you're just not good at algorithms is a fixed statement; admitting you don't understand it *yet* leaves room to learn.

## Your circle of competence has a blind-spot ring

The circle of competence gets the most airtime. The inner circle is what you understand deeply, so deliver there with confidence. The next ring is what you know you don't know, so set goals and take projects just outside your comfort. Then come the dangerous zones: things you think you know (she brings in the Dunning-Kruger effect) and things you don't know you don't know.

A practical aside: don't identify as a .NET developer or a Java developer. Identify as a developer who uses .NET today. Technologies change; a label that welds you to one of them is a cage you built yourself.

For the blind spots she leans on Shane Parrish's *The Great Mental Models*: get more perspectives, keep ego out of it, and stay close to the consequences of your decisions. Teams that never live with the fallout of their choices end up with broken windows: small unrepaired issues in code and process that invite more damage.

## The spec is a map, production is the territory

The map is not the territory: that model may be the most useful model for anyone who has shipped something that passed every requirement and still broke. A specification, a diagram, a model: all simplifications. The running system has edge cases the document never mentioned, which is why she argues for testing the real behaviour and not just the paper version.

## Ask what happens next, then what happens after that

Second-order thinking gets the cobra effect as its cautionary tale: a bounty on dead cobras led people to breed cobras, and ending the bounty released them, leaving more snakes than before. Her software example is an e-commerce build where the first-order goals (search, checkout, payment, speed) are obvious, and the consequences of those choices further down the line are where the real design work hides.

## Invert the deadline

Inversion is the most immediately usable trick. Facing an aggressive deadline, skip the ten-steps-to-productivity listicle and ask what made you miss the last deadline, then avoid doing that. You've already validated the failure modes; start there. Occam's razor rounds it off: begin with the simplest solution unless the problem explicitly demands more, and watch for complexity chosen to look clever.

She closes with a line from Christopher Alexander: "When you build a thing, you cannot merely build that thing in isolation. You must repair the world around it."

## Who should watch

Engineers moving from senior to lead, and anyone mentoring juniors who need vocabulary for slowing down and thinking about the whole system. If you've already read Parrish or Munger, this is a well-applied refresher with software examples; if you want hands-on chaos tooling, look elsewhere on the lineup.

Title: Why data quality is a budget problem, and where AI helps
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Walmart software engineer Shashank Reddy Beeravelly surveys AI-driven data quality management, from deduplication to validation at scale.
Body:
Bad data is expensive before it is ever wrong in a dashboard. Shashank Reddy Beeravelly, a software engineer at Walmart, opened his Conf42 Python 2025 talk with the cost: data teams spend about 40% of their time on quality issues, which can eat up to a quarter of operating budgets. The rest of the talk surveys how AI techniques attack those issues and what a rollout plan should look like.

Calibrate before watching: this is a business-oriented survey, short and slide-driven, with no Python code and no named tools. The figures are presented as industry and case-study results without sources or methodology, so treat them as the speaker's framing rather than benchmarks.

## Four ways data goes bad

Shashank's problem list is a good checklist for any data platform:

- Incompleteness: many enterprise systems run at only 75 to 80% completeness.
- Duplicates: 25 to 30% of customer and vendor records, wasting effort and producing inconsistent customer contact.
- Decay: corporate data goes stale at roughly 23% a year, and B2B data at 36%.
- The time sink above, which turns all of this into lost engineering hours.

The decay numbers are the ones to remember. A perfectly clean table is a snapshot, and it starts rotting on the day you load it.

## Where AI fits in the pipeline

He groups the AI techniques by job. Anomaly and inconsistency detection fixes errors automatically, which he credits with a 67% lower error rate at 50 times the speed of traditional methods. NLP models standardise records across languages (94% accuracy in his figures). ML models fill gaps in incomplete records, and real-time validation systems check records in flight, at up to 850,000 records per minute.

He then applies this to two sectors. In financial services, ML speeds up transaction validation and fraud checks and cuts the time spent on regulatory reporting. In manufacturing supply chains, real-time validation catches production defects early, and automated supplier data matching turns weeks of manual reconciliation into minutes.

## The rollout plan is the most reusable part

The implementation advice is concrete enough to borrow:

1. Start with a baseline assessment of where your data stands, and set measurable targets for customer, financial and operational data.
2. Size the platform for growth. He suggests planning for 42% annual data volume growth.
3. Run a 10 to 14 week pilot before full rollout.
4. Validate in layers: automated tests, business process validation and user acceptance testing.

## Why it matters downstream

The last section ties quality to outcomes: better demand forecasts and inventory planning, tighter customer segmentation and retention, and less data-management overhead. The argument is the right one even if you discount the percentages: every forecast, model and segment inherits the quality of the rows underneath it.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and data leads building a case for investment in data quality will find the problem framing and pilot plan useful. Engineers looking for implementation detail, libraries or code should pair it with something more hands-on.

Title: Sensors, actuators, gateways, cloud: a quick tour of IoT's moving parts
Description: Abdul Hameed Mohammed of 7-Eleven at Conf42 DevOps 2025 breaks IoT into four components and gives a four-step roadmap for adopting it.
Body:
Strip the buzzwords off IoT and you get four kinds of things: something that senses, something that acts, something in the middle that filters and secures, and somewhere the data ends up. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Abdul Hameed Mohammed, Software Engineer at 7-Eleven with over nine years in IoT integration, cloud and full-stack work, used exactly that breakdown to explain how connected devices are changing healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing and homes, then finished with a short roadmap for businesses adopting it.

This is an introductory talk, fast and stat-heavy, and a decent first watch if IoT is new to you or your stakeholders.

## The scale argument

Abdul opens with market size and device counts: a market he puts at 1.39 trillion dollars, growing around 25 percent, and connections roughly doubling to 29.4 billion by 2030, carried by 5G and cloud computing. The point behind the numbers is that the devices don't just connect, they work together, which he calls intelligent connectivity, the "Internet of Everything" of his title slide.

## Four components, four jobs

The core of the talk is the anatomy:

- **Sensors** are the eyes and ears, collecting real-time data from environmental changes to operational metrics. Miniaturisation and falling prices are why they now turn up everywhere from wearables to factory machines.
- **Actuators** are the hands: adjusting a machine, dimming the lights, driving precision robotics on assembly lines and smart thermostats at home.
- **Gateways** are what Abdul calls the unsung heroes. They process data at the edge for real-time decisions, encrypt it, block unauthorised access, and filter and compress traffic so less of it has to travel to the cloud.
- **Cloud platforms** do the heavy lifting: scaling from hundreds to millions of devices and running the analytics and machine learning that produce predictive insights.

If you take one thing from the talk, take the gateway section. Most IoT architecture conversations jump from device to cloud, and the edge tier in between is where latency, cost and a lot of the security get decided. Skipping it is how you end up paying to ship every temperature reading across an ocean.

## Where it shows up

The industry examples are short: wearables in healthcare that alert a doctor before a complication, soil sensors and automated irrigation in agriculture, smart homes adapting lighting, heating and cooling to your preferences. Abdul attaches percentages to each, from lower monitoring costs to higher crop yields and energy savings; the talk doesn't cite sources for them, so treat them as the speaker's summary.

## A four-step adoption roadmap

For businesses, his roadmap is refreshingly plain:

1. **Assess needs**: find the inefficiencies IoT can fix and where automation or data insights create value.
2. **Choose components**: reliable, scalable devices that fit the goal.
3. **Implement security**: robust protocols to protect sensitive data, from the start.
4. **Analyse data**: turn raw readings into actionable insights and keep improving.

The order matters. Starting from the problem rather than the device catalogue is the difference between a pilot that ships and a drawer full of sensors.

## Who should watch

People new to IoT, product managers and business stakeholders who need the vocabulary, and engineers moving into an IoT team who want a quick mental model before the deep material. Practitioners who already run device fleets will find it high-level; the related talks below go further.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: What cloud and AI change in military operations, by the numbers
Description: Sushil Prabhu Prabhakaran of Tata Consultancy Services at Conf42 DevOps 2025: how cloud-AI integration and workflow orchestration reshape defence operations.
Body:
Defence is one of the few domains where "latency" can mean a decision on a battlefield rather than a slow page load. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Sushil Prabhu Prabhakaran, Full Stack Lead at Tata Consultancy Services, gave a short, metrics-heavy overview of how cloud computing, AI and smart workflow orchestration are being applied to military operations, from battlefield data processing and logistics to training and cyber defence.

Treat it as a briefing deck. It is built around headline percentages and covers a lot of ground quickly, and it doesn't go into specific systems, programmes or architectures.

## The pitch is decision speed

Sushil opens with the strategic case: improvements in operational efficiency, decision speed, real-time situational awareness and predictive analytics. The thread running through all of it is that commanders get better information sooner. Cloud-AI systems process battlefield data faster and cut critical mission response times, so decisions in high-stakes situations rest on more current data.

He presents the decision support side as a pyramid. At the top is threat detection accuracy, the 91 percent figure that also appears in the abstract, covering threats arriving online or in the field. Below it sit enhanced situational awareness, faster decision making and improved resource allocation, the layer that reduces overall cost.

## Logistics is where the cloud quietly earns its keep

The section most relevant to engineers outside defence is logistics. Through predictive analysis and intelligent workflows, Sushil says military supply chains became markedly more efficient, getting vital resources to frontline units faster and more precisely. Swap "frontline units" for "regional warehouses" and this is the same orchestration problem civilian DevOps and data teams solve every day, with considerably higher stakes for a missed delivery.

## Training and cyber defence

Two more areas get their own slides. For training, he describes AI-powered simulations that adapt to each individual, shorten learning curves by focusing on the main objectives, and generate realistic scenarios. For cyber defence, he talks about AI systems that block potential breaches, speed up incident response through AI-driven threat analysis, and keep learning as new threats emerge.

## The hard parts he names

The implementation challenges slide is the most practically useful part. Sushil lists three:

- **Data security**, with very high availability expectations met through advanced protocols.
- **An ethical framework**, so AI in military operations is deployed responsibly and not misused.
- **Integration** with existing systems, which needs to be smooth rather than an extra obstacle.

He then frames the return on investment (a 4.1x figure, also in the abstract), long-term cost savings and future-proofing against evolving threats, before closing on AI robotics and drones already in development.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects working on or near government and defence programmes who want a short overview of where cloud and AI are being applied, and anyone curious how the integration and ethics problems look in a domain where mistakes are measured differently. If you want sourced studies, named systems or reference architectures, the talk doesn't provide them; the figures are presented without methodology, so read them as the speaker's summary rather than benchmarks.

Title: IoT data belongs at the edge first, and its crypto needs a quantum plan
Description: Gokul Balaguruswamy Naidu of Amazon at Conf42 DevOps 2025 maps IoT data from sensor to cloud and argues lightweight post-quantum crypto is next.
Body:
An IoT fleet is a distributed system where most of the nodes run on a battery and speak a different protocol. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Gokul Balaguruswamy Naidu, Software Development Manager at Amazon, walked through how IoT data is collected, moved, stored and processed across edge and cloud, and ended on the problem most IoT architectures haven't started on: cryptography that survives quantum computers on devices with almost no compute to spare.

It's a structured survey rather than a case study, closer to a well-organised lecture than a war story, and a good one to hand to someone joining an IoT team.

## Four layers, one data path

Gokul uses the standard layered model. The perception layer is sensors, RFID readers and smart devices capturing temperature, motion and environmental readings. The network layer moves that data with lightweight protocols such as MQTT and CoAP, designed for constrained devices. The processing layer mixes edge and cloud to analyse it in time to matter, and the application layer turns it into dashboards and decisions. His smart city example: traffic sensors feeding central dashboards that steer traffic management in real time.

## Process close, archive far

The core architectural point is that centralised designs don't fit IoT. Combining edge and cloud cuts bandwidth and latency, which matters in industrial automation. Fog computing adds an intermediate tier where local gateways preprocess data before it goes to the cloud, useful in manufacturing where milliseconds count. Microservices let teams update one function without redeploying the whole system; his example is smart agriculture, where edge microservices watch soil conditions and pull weather predictions from the cloud.

Storage follows the same split. Cloud storage brings petabyte scale with geographic replication and tiering. Edge storage brings the very low latency autonomous vehicles need. Hybrid setups decide placement, sometimes with ML optimising for cost and access time, so a smart home keeps fresh security camera footage locally and ships history to the cloud. Processing is both batch, for historical trends, and streaming, using in-memory systems for continuous flows, with ML on top for predictive maintenance and anomaly detection.

## The usual suspects, honestly listed

Gokul doesn't pretend it's easy. Integration is hard because of diverse protocols, platforms and legacy systems. Latency is hard because network conditions in distributed deployments fluctuate a lot. Devices are short on CPU, memory and battery. The emerging fixes he points to are 5G for latency, containers and microservices for integration and scaling, energy harvesting and better batteries for longevity, and edge intelligence, such as drones analysing data locally to navigate terrain.

## Quantum-safe crypto is the pivotal research area

The closing section is the most forward-looking. RSA and ECC rest on factorisation and discrete logarithm problems that quantum computers can solve efficiently. Post-quantum cryptography uses problems believed hard for both classical and quantum attackers: lattice-based schemes (finding short vectors in lattices), hash-based schemes and code-based cryptography.

The IoT twist is that these algorithms need to be lightweight and energy efficient enough for constrained devices without hurting performance or battery life. Gokul argues research should focus on efficient implementations for IoT and on protocols to migrate existing fleets to quantum-safe infrastructure. Devices deployed in the field today may still be running long after the cryptography protecting them stops being safe, which is the real reason to start early.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to IoT who want the whole data path in one sitting, architects deciding what to process at the edge versus the cloud, and security folks who haven't yet considered what post-quantum migration means for a fleet of constrained devices. If you already run a production IoT pipeline, the quantum section is the part to jump to.

Title: Binding C++ to Python with pybind11, Boost.Python and cppyy
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Hariharan Ragothaman compares pybind11, Boost.Python and cppyy for moving compute-heavy Python code into C++ and back.
Body:
Hariharan Ragothaman, a lead software engineer at athenahealth, gave Conf42 Python 2025 a practical guide to splitting an application between Python and C++. He compares two static binding libraries, pybind11 and Boost.Python, with dynamic binding through cppyy, and his rule of thumb is simple: move only the code that needs the speed, because every crossing between the languages has a cost.

The talk is aimed at developers who know some C++ and have never wired it to Python. It walks through real CMake projects side by side.

## Two reasons to bind: speed and teams

Performance is the obvious reason. Newer Python versions bring options such as a free-threaded build and a JIT compiler, but heavy numerical work still ends up in libraries like NumPy, scikit-learn and PyTorch, whose cores are C or C++.

The second reason is organisational and more interesting. In embedded work he has seen developers write C++ while the test team writes Python, and the two code bases need to talk. Binding is how the testers call the product code directly.

He also opens with a short reminder that the languages have drifted closer: Python type hints, `typing.List` and `TypeVar`/`Generic` look a lot like C++ signatures, vectors and templates.

## Static binding, side by side

The setup needs a C++11 compiler, Python 3 and CMake, with pybind11 and Boost.Python from a package manager or fetched by CMake. pybind11 can even be vendored as headers.

The minimal example is an `add` function. In pybind11 you declare a module with a macro, attach a docstring and expose the function; CMake builds a shared library, you add it to the Python path and `import` it. The Boost.Python version differs in syntax and setup but does the same thing. A second example exposes a `Person` class with a constructor, getters and setters, so Python code can create one and call its methods.

Both libraries go further: mapping C++ exceptions to Python exceptions, passing STL containers and iterators, and NumPy support (a NumPy header in pybind11, a submodule in Boost.Python).

## Bindings are not free

Data has to be converted between C++ objects and Python objects at every call. Hariharan notes an implementation difference: pybind11 leans heavily on smart pointers, which he says makes it slower, and he cites benchmarks he found that put Boost.Python slightly ahead. Countermeasures include using the libraries' own types directly, typed arrays such as `array_t<double>` instead of generic conversions, and smart pointers to avoid dangling references. His choice: Boost.Python if you're already in the Boost ecosystem, pybind11 if you want a light dependency.

## Packaging, and the no-compile option

For anything bigger than a demo, package the module so others can `pip install` it, using setup.py or scikit-build, and publish to PyPI or your own registry.

The last option skips compilation. cppyy, built on the Cling C++ interpreter, lets you write C++ inside a Python script and call it from the global namespace. Hariharan likes its support for templates, inheritance, callbacks and lambdas, and its zero-setup workflow. All the code is in his GitHub repository.

## Who should watch

Python developers hitting a CPU wall, and teams where C++ and Python code have to meet, will get a working starting point. If you already maintain pybind11 extensions, the cppyy section is the new part.

Title: Every sensor in your supply chain is also a way in
Description: Nathalie Takpah of ParcelP at Conf42 DevOps 2025: IoT made supply chains visible and efficient, and widened the attack surface. How to balance the two.
Body:
The RFID tag that tells you where a pallet is can also tell an attacker where your network is. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Nathalie Takpah, Supply Chain Analyst at ParcelP, gave a short talk on how the Internet of Things transformed supply chain operations and what it costs in security: a much larger attack surface, devices without common standards, and sensitive data moving through every stage from raw material to doorstep.

It's a brief, accessible talk from the operations side rather than the security engineering side, which is exactly why it's useful to engineers: it shows how the business sees these devices.

## Why supply chains filled up with devices

Nathalie defines the supply chain broadly: acquiring raw materials, storage, distribution and transport until the product reaches the end user. IoT changed each stage. Shipping companies track consignments with RFID, GPS and barcoded pallets. Warehouse shelves with sensors record the type, colour and quantity of each item removed, which drives restocking decisions; she cites Amazon's shelf-stocking robots. Pharmaceutical companies log storage temperatures. Automotive plants put sensors on machines to call for maintenance before they fail.

To show what companies say they gained, she quotes a Morgan Stanley AlphaWise survey with Automation World, where improved operational efficiency tops the list, followed by productivity, new business opportunities and reduced downtime. The business case for more devices is settled. The security case is the open question.

## The dark side, with real incidents

She groups the weaknesses into three: a lack of standardisation across IoT devices, an attack surface that grows with billions of connected things, and exposure of sensitive data. Her examples are the ones every supply chain security person keeps on a slide: the SolarWinds breach in 2020, where a backdoor in software updates reached thousands of customers including government agencies and Fortune 500 companies; leaked data on over 3,000 Airbus suppliers; and the Mirai botnet's 2016 attack built from compromised cameras and routers. That last one is worth remembering because none of those devices were the target. They were the weapon.

## Security budget should track innovation budget

Her central argument is balance: every investment in connected innovation should come with a matching thought about protecting it, built into every layer instead of bolted on later. The strategies she lists:

- **Zero trust architecture**, assuming any device or network may already be compromised and enforcing strict access control.
- **Endpoint security**: encryption on IoT devices and regular updates.
- **Vendor collaboration** on secure design, so the platforms you buy are built for this.
- **Visibility**, using AI to spot anomalies and blockchain to secure records.
- **Shared standards and threat intelligence** across industry players, so everyone learns about the latest attack at the same time.

The last one is the most underrated. A supply chain is many companies, and an attacker only needs the weakest one.

## Where it goes next

Nathalie closes with a look ahead: autonomous vehicles and self-healing logistics networks, predictive risk management combining AI and IoT, and collaborative cybersecurity frameworks. Her call to action is to prioritise security alongside innovation and to work with government agencies, industry players and tech leaders rather than alone.

## Who should watch

Engineers who build or secure systems for logistics, retail or manufacturing and want to understand how operations teams think about connected devices, and anyone who needs a quick primer to share with non-security colleagues. Security specialists looking for attack techniques or tooling won't find them here; it's a strategy-level overview.

Title: fsspec makes cloud storage feel local, and lakeFS adds transactions
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Guy Hardonag of Treeverse shows how fsspec unifies storage for Pandas and PyArrow, and how lakefs-spec turns branches into transactions.
Body:
Pandas already speaks S3, and the reason is a library most people never import directly. At Conf42 Python 2025, Guy Hardonag, a founding engineer at Treeverse (the company behind lakeFS), explained fsspec, the filesystem interface that lets Pandas, PyArrow and TensorFlow treat local disks and object stores the same way. Then he showed the payoff of implementing it for lakeFS: multi-step writes that land on main as one atomic merge.

Guy works on lakeFS, so the second half is a lakeFS demo. The fsspec explanation stands on its own.

## Local files were easy; the cloud made everyone write connectors

Locally, everything just works: point `pd.read_csv` or a TensorFlow loader at a path. Moving to the cloud brings redundancy, scale, sharing and security, and also friction. Guy lists the usual workarounds. Syncing files up and down with the AWS CLI or boto3 works until it becomes error-prone and hard to maintain. Library-specific connectors help, but each library supports a different set of object stores, maintains its own implementation, and configures it differently.

## One interface, many backends

fsspec replaces that with a single filesystem abstraction for local and remote storage, plus shared features such as caching, transactions and concurrency, implemented once. For users, swapping S3 for another provider means changing the filesystem initialisation and the paths. Often you don't initialise anything: call `open` with a URL and fsspec picks up credentials from your environment the way the AWS CLI does. For library authors, integration comes free: Pandas uses fsspec under the hood, so any backend that implements it works with Pandas.

For storage providers, the job is to subclass `AbstractFileSystem`. It defines the methods a backend should supply and builds default behaviour on top of them. Read-only backends can leave write methods such as `put`, `touch` and `rm` unimplemented, and backends with async support can implement `AsyncFileSystem` instead. You register a new protocol through a setuptools entry point, register it manually, or send a pull request to fsspec's list of known implementations.

## lakeFS branches turn out to be transactions

lakeFS sits on top of an object store and adds Git-style commit, branch, merge, revert and tag, without copying data: a commit is a set of pointers, so a new branch over terabytes of data is instant. The lakefs-spec package, contributed by a company from the community rather than by Treeverse, implements fsspec for it. Most methods map straight to lakeFS SDK calls.

The elegant part is transactions. Starting one creates an ephemeral branch; your writes and commits happen there in isolation; finishing it merges back with a regular lakeFS merge, so everything appears on the target branch at once. Guy's take is that fsspec's transaction interface and lakeFS's commit model simply line up.

## The demo

Guy creates a lakeFS repository with sample data on lakeFS Cloud, then reads a file with plain Pandas using a `lakefs://` URI. Then he opens a transaction against the repo's main branch, filters the lakes data set down to Canadian lakes, writes them as Parquet and commits, does the same for Germany, and closes the transaction. In the UI, the ephemeral branch held two commits and then vanished; main has both files and a merge commit, with blame showing which commit added what.

## Who should watch

Data engineers juggling Pandas or PyArrow across local and cloud storage should watch the first half. Anyone who has wanted atomic multi-file writes on object storage, or who maintains a storage backend, should watch the second.

- [Milecia McGregor: Using Reproducible Experiments To Create Better Machine Learning Models](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2022_Milecia_McGregor_reproducible_experiments_better_ml_models), where data versioning earns its keep.

Title: A map of AI developer tools, from package managers to RAG
Description: Kartheek Medhavi Penagamuri Shriram of Microsoft at Conf42 DevOps 2025 surveys AI across the dev lifecycle and why human judgement stays in charge.
Body:
If you want one talk that lays out where AI already shows up in the software lifecycle, this is a compact one. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Kartheek Medhavi Penagamuri Shriram, Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft, toured AI coding assistants, AI-aware package managers, test generation, embeddings, retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering, with one through-line: the tools are collaborators, and human expertise stays at the centre of the project.

It's an overview, not a demo talk, so set expectations accordingly. What it does well is connect pieces that are usually discussed separately.

## Assistants are a second opinion, not an author

Kartheek starts with assistants like GitHub Copilot: real-time suggestions for function outlines, variable names and whole algorithms based on project context. The benefit he emphasises is reduced cognitive load. You no longer have to keep every detail in your head, and the assistant can help with documentation and tests too, which chips away at technical debt. He frames it as a reliable second opinion that lowers the odds of bugs slipping through.

## Your package manager is an underrated AI surface

The less obvious section is about npm, Yarn, Maven and NuGet. Dependency conflicts and version chains are tedious puzzles, and an AI that understands your project's exact dependency set can suggest compatible combinations and code that uses what's already installed. The security angle matters more: scanning for vulnerabilities, tracking signed packages and warning you before you import a risky library. Anyone who has untangled a peer-dependency error at 2am will see the appeal.

## Embeddings and RAG make the advice yours

The most technical stretch explains why AI can understand code at all. Embeddings turn code into numeric representations that capture meaning and structure, so a tool can find similar functions across a large codebase where keyword search would miss them. That helps reuse and consistency and cuts down on near-duplicate implementations.

Retrieval-augmented generation goes further by giving the model your team's documentation, codebase history and style guides, so suggestions follow your naming conventions and architecture instead of generic patterns. Kartheek argues this pays off across a project's whole life, from scaffolding new modules to refactoring legacy ones, because the AI keeps reinforcing patterns your team already approved.

## Prompts decide the quality

Vague prompts get vague or hallucinated code. Specific prompts with project context, the desired outcome and the coding style get much closer to production-ready output, and iterating on prompts is a skill worth building. He recommends teams run short workshops so developers get comfortable prompting, evaluating and iterating, and learn enough about how models are trained to know when to trust a suggestion and when to question it. In DevOps terms, he also points at AI generating infrastructure-as-code configs and watching logs and user behaviour for trouble.

## The responsible part

Kartheek mentions speed gains of up to 60 percent that some teams report, then spends as long on the costs: job displacement, data privacy and bias. For coding assistants, bias can mean quietly favouring certain frameworks or excluding certain patterns, so he suggests periodic audits with varied input styles, documentation of model training data and version history, and review boards or ethics communities to catch problems early. The developer's job shifts toward architecture, critical thinking and cross-team collaboration, and away from boilerplate.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and team leads building a shared vocabulary before rolling out assistants, and developers who use Copilot daily but haven't thought about where embeddings and RAG fit. If you already run retrieval over your own repos, you'll know most of this.

Title: Apache Airflow as the scheduler for network automation in Python
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Dileesh Chandra Bikkasani of AT&T Labs uses Apache Airflow DAGs to orchestrate network provisioning, speed tests and config jobs.
Body:
Network operations already run on Python scripts. Dileesh Chandra Bikkasani, Lead Software Engineer at AT&T Labs, argued at Conf42 Python 2025 that the missing piece is an orchestrator, and that Apache Airflow fits: DAGs for provisioning, telemetry and configuration jobs, retries and alerts built in, and a UI that shows where a run broke.

The talk is half slides, half a local Airflow demo, and works as an introduction to Airflow for people who know networks better than data pipelines.

## Networks outgrew hand-run scripts

Dileesh frames the problem in three parts. Complexity: layered architectures mixing legacy and modern systems, with many device types and protocols in one network. Scale: connected devices from watches to industrial IoT keep multiplying and getting denser per area. Latency and allocation: bandwidth, compute and storage have to be shared without creating bottlenecks, and something like an AR/VR stream won't tolerate lag.

Python is already the language of the fixes. He lists Netmiko and Paramiko for SSH-based device configuration, NAPALM and PySNMP, Ansible, NetworkX for topology analysis and simulation, and Pandas and NumPy for telemetry and logs. Software-defined networking and network function virtualisation controllers expose Python interfaces too.

## What Airflow adds

Airflow is open source, written in Python, and organises work as directed acyclic graphs: you define the tasks, their order and dependencies, and a schedule written like a cron expression. Operators and hooks connect to AWS, Azure and many other systems, and you can write your own.

Scaling is an executor choice. Start with the local executor on one machine, move to Celery to parallelise across workers, and use the Kubernetes executor to run tasks as pods. Failed tasks retry according to rules you set, and alerts go to Slack, email, Teams or Discord. His point about maintenance lands well: a thousand-line script tells you nothing when it fails at line 700, while a DAG shows which task failed and keeps its logs.

## The telecom use cases

The concrete examples come from his work with clients. SIM provisioning automates physical and virtual SIMs and IMSI range management, talking to each downstream system over whatever it speaks (SSH, Telnet or LDAP), validating the result and notifying someone at the end. He mentions using it for provisioning against the HSS for FirstNet, the US first-responder network, where it ran much faster than the legacy process. Other DAGs gather telemetry for speed tests and KPI anomaly checks, push configuration to routers and switches, and chain ETL into ML models for failure prediction.

## The demo

He starts Airflow locally with `docker compose up`, which brings up the web server, scheduler and a Postgres 13 metadata database. The tour covers pausing and activating DAGs, user and role management, stored connections with a test button, an example DAG with a graph view and per-task logs, and the REST API through Swagger. Secrets in connections are encrypted with a Fernet key.

## Who should watch

Network engineers who already script with Netmiko or Ansible and want scheduling, retries and visibility should watch. If you run Airflow in production already, the demo will be familiar; the telecom examples are the new part.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Tamara Janina Fingerlin: How to use common Python frameworks to test Apache Airflow data pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2024_Tamara_Janina_Fingerlin_frameworks_apache_airflow_pipelines), the next thing you'll need once DAGs carry production work.
- [Jason Belk: Introduction to Ansible for Network Engineers](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Jason_Belk_ansible_network_engineers), the configuration tool Airflow would schedule.
- [Sruthi Erra Hareram on optimising PySpark and Airflow workflows in cloud-native environments](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Sruthi_Erra_Hareram_etl_airflow_optimization), Airflow at scale on Kubernetes.
