Title: API-first is mostly about ending the frontend-backend waiting game
Description: Tiago Barbosa of Rely.io at Conf42 DevOps 2025: agree the API contract first, treat the API as a product, and new integrations come cheap.
Body:
The usual way a feature gets built has a hidden queue in the middle: the frontend team mocks the data it needs, files a ticket, and waits for the backend team to get to it. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Tiago Barbosa, Head of Developer Relations at Rely.io (an internal developer portal company), argued that API-first development removes that queue by moving the hardest decision, the API contract, to the very start, and showed how it let Rely.io ship integrations it never planned for.

## Code-first puts the contract in the middle

Tiago walks through the familiar sequence. The frontend builds screens on fake requests, asks the backend for an endpoint, and keeps adding complexity while the ticket waits for hours, days, or a few weeks. When the backend finally picks it up, the data the frontend assumed may not exist, or there is a security limit nobody considered. The two teams then agree a contract, the backend publishes a mock, and the frontend refactors to match it. The most important decision of the project got made after half the code was written.

Waiting engineers are expensive, so managers move them onto other work, and now you also pay for context switching. Nobody ends the sprint happy.

## Agree first, then build in parallel

In the API-first version the frontend, backend and product owner (plus design or UX if they are involved) start together and agree the contract up front. That first step takes longer, Tiago admits, possibly days or weeks. After it, the backend publishes a mock straight away, the frontend builds against it, and both sides write production code concurrently. There is still back and forth, but it happens between people who agreed on the same thing, which takes most of the frustration out.

He names three principles: design first (anything left unresolved resurfaces later as rework), collaboration from the start (so no team feels like a ticket queue for another), and user-centric design (talk to the developers who will consume the API, not just your own assumptions). The product owner is in the room because an API is a product, even when nobody outside the company calls it.

## The payoff is integrations you didn't plan

The strongest part of the talk is Rely.io's own experience. Because the platform was built on its REST API, the team could add a Kubernetes operator that populates the software catalog from GitOps definitions, a Visual Studio Code integration, Terraform provisioning, a Raycast extension for checking services from any screen, and AI agents, all on the existing API. Tiago stresses they never changed the API just to support an integration.

Customers did the same. One already had a Kubernetes operator with blueprints for teams, systems and domains, and pointed it at Rely.io's API in a couple of hours. Another wanted a security tool Rely.io had no plugin for, so they routed its violations through Logstash into the API in a couple of days instead of waiting for the roadmap. That operator pattern then became something Rely.io uses to onboard other customers.

## The boring practices that make it work

His checklist is deliberately unglamorous: clear, concise specs that follow existing standards for naming, methods and status codes; simple APIs, because complicated ones don't get adopted; documentation, even if it's only the OpenAPI spec; automated tests that check behaviour; and monitoring of both latency and usage. Usage data matters because it shows you the integrations people are building, such as calls from Azure DevOps pipelines, which tells you where to invest next. His view is that most of the design work has already been done by the industry, so read the standards before inventing tricks.

## Who should watch

Tech leads whose teams keep blocking each other across the frontend-backend line, and platform teams building anything other teams will integrate with. The talk is slides only and high-level, so if you already run contract-first with shared OpenAPI specs, the Rely.io customer stories are the part to watch.

- [Barkatul Mujauddin on API testing](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Barkatul_Mujauddin_api_testing), for the automated-testing part of the checklist.

Title: ML in the data center, from failure prediction to PUE
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Ashok Jonnalagadda of Hilmar reports results from ML-driven data center ops across maintenance, cooling, security and capacity.
Body:
Ashok Jonnalagadda, Principal Infrastructure Engineer at Hilmar, gave a short, number-dense talk at Conf42 Python 2025 on applying machine learning to data center operations. His headline figures: a 47% cut in unexpected equipment failures from predictive maintenance and a 31% improvement in resource utilisation from dynamic, workload-aware allocation.

Set expectations first. This is a rapid slide summary of about ten minutes, with no code, no model architecture beyond names, and no methodology for how the numbers were measured. It is useful as a map of where ML pays off in a facility, less so as a how-to.

## Predictive maintenance: warnings measured in days

The first area is equipment failure. ML models read real-time sensor data on temperature, vibration and power patterns and raise alerts up to 72 hours before a likely problem. Ashok cites 96% prediction accuracy and an average of 127 hours of downtime prevented per quarter.

The pattern is familiar from any reliability work: the value isn't the model, it is the lead time it buys the people who swap the fan.

## Utilisation and latency come from smarter placement

On compute, the system allocates resources dynamically from real-time workload analysis. Beyond the 31% utilisation gain, he reports server latency down 38% through intelligent load balancing and predictive traffic management, and application response 42% faster.

## Cooling is where the money is

Energy management gets the biggest numbers. A deep learning model tuned cooling through real-time temperature optimisation and airflow management, which he credits with a 42% improvement in cooling efficiency and 3.2 million kWh saved a year across the facilities. AI-driven thermal mapping and load distribution took power usage effectiveness from roughly 1.6 to 1.7 down to below 1.25 within six months.

If you have ever watched a CRAC unit fight a hot aisle it can't see, this section will feel very plausible.

## Security and capacity planning

For security, he describes threat detection at 98.5% accuracy across more than a million security events per second, a false-positive rate he puts below 0.01%, and critical incidents handled within 45 seconds.

Capacity planning uses LSTM neural networks over historical data across 2,000 performance metrics to forecast demand up to 18 months ahead, with scaling triggered 72 hours before predicted spikes. Across these programmes he cites average annual savings of $2.4 million for enterprise-scale deployments.

## The honest part: data quality and MLOps

The integration section is brief but worth noting. The hard parts are the ones every ML team knows: validation and cleansing pipelines so training data is consistent and labelled, balancing training cost against model complexity, and continuous integration plus monitoring so models keep behaving in production.

Two case studies close it out: a regional cloud provider's 800 kW facility saving 35% on energy with AI cooling, and a Fortune 500 deployment above six megawatts cutting equipment failures by 40% with predictive maintenance.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure and facilities engineers who need a quick inventory of ML use cases to pitch internally will get value in ten minutes. If you want to build one of these systems, you'll need to look elsewhere for the details.

Title: K8sGPT turns cluster errors into fixes, and your LLM can stay local
Description: Kosseila Haddalene of cloudthrill at Conf42 DevOps 2025: K8sGPT's analyzers, AI backends, anonymisation and operator mode on a managed OCI cluster.
Body:
K8sGPT is less magic than its name suggests, and that is the good news. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Kosseila Haddalene, founder and principal consultant at cloudthrill, showed that the real value of the CNCF project sits in its built-in analyzers, which encode SRE knowledge about what to check on each Kubernetes resource, while the LLM only turns those findings into readable suggestions. He then ran it against a managed Oracle OKE cluster with both OpenAI and a local Ollama model.

## The problem: every layer can break your PVC

Kosseila's example is a StatefulSet with a failing PersistentVolumeClaim on a managed cloud cluster. The cause could be the wrong storage class, a block volume formatted ext4 where XFS was expected, or someone changing a parameter in the cloud console on a volume the CSI plugin created. Correlating that across the stack takes deep knowledge of every layer, and the people who have it rarely write it down. Day zero feels great; day ninety, with a new Helm chart or operator landing from another team every week, does not.

His observation is that the jobs SREs struggle with (spotting patterns, translating noise into signal, predicting what fails next) are exactly the jobs language models are good at. So codify the repeatable failure modes and let a model explain them.

## The analyzers do the work, the model does the talking

K8sGPT ships with 19 analyzers, also called filters, covering pods, deployments, ReplicaSets, services, ingress, StatefulSets, nodes, network policies, PVCs and more. Each one pulls the relevant primitives from the API server and packages the result. `k8sgpt analyze` alone lists the problems and costs nothing. Add `--explain` and that package goes to an AI backend for a suggested fix, which is the moment, as Kosseila puts it, the counter starts running.

The flags he leans on most are `--filter` and `--namespace`, so a team responsible for one namespace in a busy multi-tenant cluster gets a short answer quickly instead of five pages. `--with-doc` attaches the Kubernetes docs for the resource, and the newer `--stats` flag shows how long each analyzer took. Backends are swappable with `--backend`: OpenAI is the default, and the list he showed includes Cohere, Hugging Face, Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex and OCI Generative AI. Running two backends on the same issue doubles as a second opinion and a homemade benchmark.

## Mind what leaves the cluster

There is an `--anonymize` flag that masks resource names before the payload goes out and restores them in the answer. Kosseila is candid that not every analyzer masks everything; he lists events, ReplicaSets, pods and PVCs among the gaps. He also points out that the CLI stores your backend API key in plain text in `~/.config/k8sgpt/k8sgpt.yaml`. His fix for both is the same: run inference privately in your own data centre, so there is nothing sensitive to leak and no key to sprawl.

Integrations extend the analyzers. `k8sgpt integration activate trivy` adds vulnerability and config audit reports, and in the demo the LLM summarised a Log4j CVE into an upgrade recommendation. Prometheus and Kyverno are supported too.

## Operator mode makes results a resource

The CLI runs on your machine. The operator, installed with Helm plus a secret for the API key and a K8sGPTConfig manifest, runs the analysis inside the cluster on its own and writes the suggestions into Result custom resources, which can feed a Grafana dashboard, a remote cache in S3 or Azure Blob, or Slack. Upgrading is a version bump in the manifest.

## The demo

On version 0.3.48, Kosseila adds an Ollama backend running a quantised Llama 3 on his laptop, then deploys a pod with a bad image name into a namespace called `broken`. OpenAI answers almost instantly; the local model takes its time and returns a broadly similar fix. His takeaway: pay for the hosted model where quality matters and keep routine or sensitive work local. He closes with K8sGPT's sibling project, a scheduler that uses K8sGPT insights to place workloads.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams onboarding juniors to on-call, anyone running managed Kubernetes on OCI, EKS, AKS or GKE, and teams that want AI-assisted triage without shipping cluster details to a third party. Skip the first ten minutes if you already know your transformer history.

Title: Python processors in Apache NiFi, with Iceberg and Snowflake behind
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Snowflake's Tim Spann runs Python inside Apache NiFi flows, explains Apache Iceberg and pushes live transit and flight data to Snowflake.
Body:
Tim Spann, a solutions engineer at Snowflake, used his Conf42 Python 2025 talk to show Python doing real work inside data pipelines: as custom processors in Apache NiFi, as Snowpark code pushed into Snowflake, and as the glue around Apache Iceberg tables. The demo pulls live Boston transit data and nearby aircraft positions, converts and enriches them, and ships them to Snowflake, Slack and S3.

Tim works for Snowflake and says so, so Snowflake features get airtime. Most of the talk, though, is about open-source tools: NiFi, Iceberg, Polaris and Streamlit.

## Three kinds of data, three kinds of pain

He sorts data the way most pipelines meet it. Semi-structured data, such as OpenAQ air-quality feeds in JSON, XML, Avro, Parquet, ORC or, in his demo, Protobuf, has hierarchy and arrays that are a pain in SQL. Unstructured data (PDFs, Word documents, images, audio, email) used to be parked next to a search engine; now Python libraries can extract text, turn a document into Markdown and feed it to RAG or other AI work. Structured data sits in tables and flat files and is the easy part.

## Why Iceberg keeps coming up

His pitch for Apache Iceberg is a list of things that used to hurt. Schema evolution as data changes. Time travel, for when you deleted something you shouldn't have. Hidden partitioning managed through metadata instead of Hive-era directory trees. Rollback, and compaction to fix the sparse small files that appending to object storage creates, which he compares to defragging an old hard drive.

Many engines read it, including Flink, PyIceberg, Trino and Snowflake, and catalogs include the newer Apache Polaris and the longer-running Nessie. You can write to Iceberg from NiFi processors or by saving a Snowpark DataFrame as a table.

## NiFi now runs your Python inside the flow

The headline for Python developers is that NiFi 2 runs Python as first-class processors, not as a shelled-out script. Tim has written a batch of them: extracting company names from text with spaCy, Hugging Face models and PyTorch; captioning images with Salesforce BLIP; classifying images with ResNet-50; scoring uploaded images for safety; detecting facial emotions; and geocoding addresses with Nominatim from OpenStreetMap, which he rates the best of the free options he tried.

Around that Python, NiFi supplies the boring guarantees: buffering with back pressure so a slow sink doesn't lose data, and provenance that records what happened to every record.

## The demo: buses and planes

A custom Python processor fetches GTFS real-time data, which is Protobuf, from the Boston transit system, validates it and returns JSON. NiFi splits it into records, routes the odd multi-carriage entries separately, extracts fields with JSONPath, adds timestamps and uses a QueryRecord processor with SQL to reshape it, then joins route details from a database.

A second flow reads ADS-B transponder data for planes near his house, filters it, pushes it to Snowflake, posts updates to Slack until the free Slack plan complains, and lands copies in S3. His cat, Mr. Splunk, makes a cameo.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who know Python but think of NiFi as a Java GUI tool should watch the processor section. Teams weighing Iceberg get a quick feature tour. If you already run NiFi 2 with Python processors, this is a tour of familiar ground.

Title: A checklist architecture for moving on-premises workloads to Azure
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Microsoft's Harikrishna Madathala walks through planning, tools and SAP-specific HA choices for on-premises to Azure migrations.
Body:
Harikrishna Madathala, Senior Customer Engineer at Microsoft, spent his Conf42 Python 2025 talk on the unglamorous part of cloud migration: deciding what you're moving, why, and with which Azure tool, before anything moves. His thread throughout is the Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF), with a strong SAP flavour, since SAP HANA workloads are where migrations get hardest.

It is an overview talk, delivered from slides, with no Python on screen. Treat it as a structured checklist from someone who does this with customers.

## Assess first, and pick goals that change the plan

Before migrating, take stock of hardware, software, network and applications, and find what is outdated or will need re-platforming. Then set objectives, because they change which tools you lead with. His example: if disaster recovery is the goal, you prioritise Azure Site Recovery to keep downtime minimal.

SAP workloads, especially SAP HANA and S/4HANA, get their own category. High availability, performance tuning and storage management all need more care than a typical web app.

## Three migration approaches, many tools

He uses the standard three: rehost (lift and shift, minimal changes), re-platform (adjust some components to suit Azure) and re-architect (redesign for cloud-native services such as Azure Kubernetes Service).

The tool list maps to the stages:

- Azure Migrate as the central hub for discovering and moving workloads.
- Azure Site Recovery for disaster recovery and failover during the move.
- Azure Database Migration Service for databases with minimal downtime, and Azure Data Box, a physical appliance, for very large data sets.
- Azure Data Factory to keep data synchronised across environments while both sides run.
- Azure Automation and Azure DevOps for repeatable, infrastructure-as-code deployments, plus Logic Apps to stitch workflows together.

After cutover, Azure Monitor, Azure Security Center and Azure Backup cover the operate phase. SAP systems need ongoing performance tuning and HANA storage optimisation even then.

## CAF gives the order of operations

The Cloud Adoption Framework phases are strategy (align with business goals), plan (readiness assessment), ready (governance and security baselines), adopt (execute while limiting disruption), govern (compliance and cost) and manage (monitoring, optimisation, scaling). On top sits the Azure Well-Architected Framework with its five pillars: cost optimisation, operational excellence, performance efficiency, reliability and security.

## High availability for SAP is a two-sided problem

The most concrete section is on SAP failover. On the Azure side, he cites availability zones with a 99.99% SLA and availability sets with 99.95%. On the SAP side, clustering tools such as Pacemaker, SIOS and Veritas InfoScale automate failover of the HANA database or application servers, so users don't notice when a primary system goes down.

## Who should watch

Engineers or architects about to plan their first Azure migration, particularly with SAP in the estate, get a tidy map of phases and tool names. If you have already run a CAF-led migration, you'll recognise everything here.

Title: Five ways to stop mashing retry on flaky tests
Description: Mike Morgan of Buildkite at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on finding, fixing and quarantining flaky tests, from atomic test design to clean CI environments.
Body:
If a test result can be changed by spamming the retry button, what is the test for? At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Mike Morgan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mike_Morgan_testing_flaky_strategies) of Buildkite, who heads its technical account management team, drew on four years of working with Buildkite's enterprise customers to lay out five strategies for flaky tests: identify them, design them out, stabilise the environment, use proper test tooling, and build a culture that fixes them.

It's a vendor talk in the honest sense. Morgan mentions Buildkite's ephemeral runners and its Test Engine product where they fit, says plainly that it isn't meant as a sales pitch, and keeps the advice tool-agnostic.

## Flaky costs confidence, time and money

His definition is the classic one: a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no change to the code. In his anecdotal experience, order dependency, environment issues and resource constraints are the most common causes. The cost comes in three flavours. Developers stop trusting results, and the worst case is shipping something broken because a real failure looked like noise. Retries slow CI, and since he sees most build time spent running tests, flakiness makes the biggest time sink bigger. And every retry burns compute and engineer salary.

## Strategy one and two: find them, then design them out

To find flaky tests, look for intermittent failures without code changes, tests that pass locally and fail in CI, and results that depend on something non-deterministic like time of day. Rerun suspects many times on purpose. At scale, use tooling that aggregates results across builds, because your own CI runs give a blinkered view.

Design is where most flakiness is fixed. Morgan's atomic test has four properties: independent of other tests, tightly scoped, deterministic with static inputs and clean state, and fast. Integration and end-to-end tests can't be fully atomic but can borrow the principles: one integration point or one user journey each, clean state, mocks for third-party APIs. Respect the test pyramid, so that when something flaps there's little noise around it.

## Strategy three: a clean environment every time

A polluted workspace from a previous job, half-managed dependencies and under-resourced hosts all produce flaky behaviour. Ephemeral runners that are torn down after each job remove contamination, though they are only as good as their original configuration. His aside on Macs will resonate with anyone who has babysat a closet of Mac minis: great desktops, hard work as long-running headless CI runners.

Docker helps everywhere. He describes a well-known grocery delivery customer that runs every job in a fresh container built from the same base image it uses in production, and scans failed-job logs for known infrastructure error strings to route the failure either to the developer experience team or back to the app team. Tag infrastructure metrics by job ID so spikes can be correlated with failures.

## Strategy four and five: tooling and culture

Good test tooling integrates with CI so you can click from a failed build log to the test's history, shows reliability and duration trends, detects flaky tests, assigns them to an owner, and quarantines them so they stop blocking builds.

Culture closes the loop. Make unblocking others a priority: if you see a flaky test, say something. Treat quarantine as temporary, because a quarantined test leaves its feature untested. Swarm when everything goes red, but only as a break-glass move. And avoid knowledge silos by writing up and mobbing on hard debugging sessions. He admits Buildkite has flaky tests too, which is the most reassuring line in the talk.

## Who should watch

Developer experience and platform teams, CI owners, and any engineer who has configured an auto-retry and felt bad about it.

Title: How Analog Devices runs CI on real ARM and FPGA boards
Description: Stefan Raus of Analog Devices at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on a hardware test harness with Jenkins, Artifactory, NetBox, golden boot files and results on GitHub PRs.
Body:
Software CI gets to throw away a broken container. Hardware CI has a board stuck mid-boot on a desk somewhere. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Stefan Raus](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Stefan_Raus_arm_fpga_testing), DevOps Engineer at Analog Devices, walked through the Hardware Test Harness his team built to test software on ARM and FPGA platforms automatically, including how it recovers boards from bad states without a human.

This is a real system description with architecture and lessons learned, not a vendor pitch.

## The thing under test: Kuiper Linux

The target is Analog Devices Kuiper, a free, open-source Linux distribution customised for Analog Devices signal chains, shipping device drivers, prebuilt boot files for FPGA and Raspberry Pi-based solutions, libraries and examples. It runs on AMD and Intel FPGA platforms, Raspberry Pi and NXP, and has its own package repository. Commercial test frameworks were either built for application-level testing or tied to a single hardware platform, so the team wrote their own.

## From pull request to physical board

The flow starts with a push or pull request to one of many monitored repositories (HDL, Linux, libraries, applications). After the build, binaries go to JFrog Artifactory, and a main Jenkins job downloads them, writes them to the boards attached to each agent, and runs tests in parallel. Tests are mostly Python, tagged by hardware compatibility.

Two design choices are explained well. Artifactory sits in the middle because the harness spans multiple physical locations, it buffers concurrency across many repos, and it versions binaries. Jenkins agents are physical machines because they control the hardware directly: power, UART, Ethernet and sometimes JTAG. Some build servers are physical too, for compute or paid licences like Xilinx and MATLAB.

## Nebula, NetBox and shared libraries

The supporting tools are where it gets interesting. Nebula, built in-house, is a set of Python scripts that manage hardware connections: UART commands, Ethernet IPs, file transfers over SSH, plus power distribution units and USB SD card muxes for physical reboots. NetBox, originally for documenting network racks, tracks every device under test and generates Nebula's YAML configuration (platform, attached board, addresses, PDU outlet, USB). Jenkins shared libraries hold common Groovy steps reused across pipelines.

Behind the combined diagram are over 100 CI pipelines in Azure, GitHub Actions or Jenkins and about 15 physical build servers.

## Closing the loop on GitHub

Results visualisation went through stages: raw Jenkins status, Blue Ocean, JUnit XML, then Logstash, Elasticsearch and Kibana dashboards. Each still needed a developer to go and look. The fix was posting hardware results back to the GitHub pull request without leaking internal IPs or Jenkins links, using result parsing, SSH tunnelling and summaries via Gist. That let them enable required status checks, so only changes that build and pass tests can merge. His colleague [Bianca Popu covered that integration in her own talk](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Bianca_Popu_github_infrastructure_testing), and [Andreea Andrisan covered the Kuiper release strategy](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Andreea_Andrisan_linux_distro_release), both at the same event.

## Golden files bring boards back

The final piece is recovery. Faulty boot files from CI can hang a board during boot. The harness detects that and restores a set of golden files, the last boot files that passed, so the board is ready for the next run. Only physical damage still needs a person. Agents run in Docker so one machine can host several setups, and boards are locked only while tests run, leaving them available for remote debugging the rest of the time.

## Who should watch

Embedded, FPGA and silicon teams trying to move beyond a bench of manually flashed boards, and DevOps engineers asked to bring CI to hardware for the first time.

Title: DataSense, a free Streamlit app for analysis without a Power BI login
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, data scientist Daniel Emakporuena demos DataSense, a Streamlit and Plotly tool that gives beginners EDA and dashboards without an account.
Body:
Daniel Emakporuena, a data scientist who mentors people starting out in data and programming, built his own analysis tool because his students couldn't get into Power BI without an organisation email. At Conf42 Python 2025 he demoed DataSense, a Streamlit app written entirely in Python and hosted for free on Streamlit Cloud: upload a file, get descriptive statistics, click through exploratory charts and assemble a dashboard, no account needed.

It is a beginner-focused talk and a live demo of one app, which is exactly what it says on the tin.

## The problem is friction, not features

Daniel's complaint about the big BI tools is less about what they can do and more about how they treat newcomers. You need a work login to start. You drag a column onto an axis and get an error without being told why it was the wrong column. You often end up on a course just to learn the interface.

DataSense is his answer: a short path from data in to chart out, with guard rails.

## What the app does

The data page takes CSV, JSON or Excel uploads, or offers sample data sets: a set of fire incident records by region of England and an employee data set. Loading one shows the equivalent of `df.head()`, the column types and null counts from `df.info()`, the row and column counts (44 rows and 8 columns for the fire data) and `df.describe()` output with mean, standard deviation and percentiles.

From there you choose between an automated exploratory analysis page and a dashboard builder.

## Guard rails beat error messages

The dashboard builder is where the design thinking shows. Charts are built with Plotly, which Daniel prefers for its interactivity over Matplotlib, and each chart type only offers columns that make sense for it. An area chart won't let you pick two text columns, and scatter plots ask for two numeric ones. Non-numeric fields simply aren't in the dropdowns where they'd break the chart.

He walks through area, pie, scatter, bar and histogram charts. The histogram lets you change the bin count and add a KDE line, which he uses to show how outliers in the burnt-area column skew the distribution compared with the incident counts. Every chart can be zoomed, inspected point by point and downloaded as an image for slides. The number of charts on the dashboard is a parameter you can raise or lower.

## How it's built

The code tour is short and readable: a `data.py` for upload and summaries, an exploratory analysis module, an error handler so users don't hit raw tracebacks, and `visualization.py` for the charts. The EDA side uses Matplotlib with Seaborn for styling; the dashboard uses Plotly Express and Plotly graph objects. A bit of custom CSS styles the pages, and he admits CSS isn't his strong point. The repo is public and he invites forks and pull requests.

One honest trade-off he mentions: because it runs on free Streamlit hosting, the app can take a few seconds to load.

## Who should watch

Mentors and teachers looking for a free, login-free tool for students, and Python developers who want to see how far Streamlit plus Pandas plus Plotly goes for a self-serve analytics app. Experienced analysts won't find new techniques, but the column-filtering idea is worth stealing for any internal tool.

Title: Test automation is the baseline, not a bug-free guarantee
Description: Mesut Durukal of Indeed at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on the pitfalls of test automation, from A/B instability and testability to slow suites and duplication.
Body:
A team bug bash can find plenty of issues in a product with a large automated suite, and that's the right outcome, not an embarrassment. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Mesut Durukal](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Mesut_Durukal_agile_automation_test), Senior Quality Assurance Automation Engineer at Indeed, catalogued the ways test automation falls short in continuous delivery, and what to do about each one. His bottom line: automation is the baseline you can't ship without, and it still won't give you bug-free software.

It's a structured, experience-based talk from a QA practitioner. No single tool is pushed; the value is in the taxonomy of problems.

## Why automation, and why it isn't enough

Durukal starts with the case for automation that every team already makes. With commits landing almost daily, manual testing alone can't cover the scope. Automation saves time through parallel runs across machines, extends coverage with data-driven positive and negative cases, and makes possible what humans can't do at all, like load testing with many concurrent requests.

Then he turns it around: if a test passes, is the result reliable? And if every designed case is automated, does that mean you're catching every bug?

## Problems that come from the product

His first category is the nature of agile delivery. Features change after customer feedback, so tests written once need continuous maintenance, and he wants QA involved early to keep up. Instability comes from A/B testing and canary deployments: you can't know in advance which instance your test will hit, so assertions need to cope with more than one valid result.

Testability is the subtle one. His example is a subsystem that syncs when an object is created elsewhere, in a part of the system the tests can't touch. You can mock or fake the other side, but the better move is to ask developers for test-only interfaces that let you trigger the condition directly. Hardware modules and AI components make things harder again, since functional automation alone can't establish how well an ML model performs.

## Non-functional quality and the bug bash

Performance, responsiveness under load and usability matter as much as functionality, and automation doesn't cover them on its own. He's direct that infinite testing isn't possible and bug-free software doesn't exist, so the goal is to reduce escaped bugs and prioritise by severity. His team's bug bash, a dogfooding session where everyone used the product, surfaced several issues automation had not, which is exactly why manual and exploratory testing stay in the mix. He also suggests chaos testing to see how the rest of the system reacts when parts go down.

## Problems in the test code itself

The implementation section has the best war story. A tenant-creation feature had to send a notification email, and checking it on every run meant unique addresses and credentials. The team built an email relay that caught messages to a known address pattern and forwarded them to one inbox they controlled. It worked, and it took real effort to set up, which is his point about test environments being engineering work.

Maintenance gets the rest: slow suites that leave developers waiting hours on merge requests (fix with parallel runs and by cutting redundant steps), duplicated steps that should live in shared helper classes so a fix lands in one place, and bug reports that need solid evidence to separate false alarms from real defects.

His call to action is simple: list the problems in your own framework, because there is always room to improve.

## Who should watch

QA engineers, SDETs and developers who own test suites in a CI/CD pipeline, plus managers who think 100 percent automation is the finish line.

Title: How SAP S/4HANA Cloud and SAP BTP fit together
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, SAP consultant Sravan Kumar Nendrambaka maps how S/4HANA Cloud, SAP BTP and SAP AI services combine in enterprise ERP projects.
Body:
Sravan Kumar Nendrambaka, an SAP S/4HANA and SAP Cloud consultant with over 15 years in healthcare, retail, oil and gas and manufacturing projects, used his Conf42 Python 2025 slot to explain how SAP S/4HANA Cloud and the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) work as one stack. The core idea: S/4HANA is the in-memory ERP core, and BTP is where integration, extensions and AI sit around it.

A note on scope before you press play. This is an architecture overview of the SAP ecosystem, delivered from slides, and it contains no Python. It suits engineers who have been told they'll be integrating with SAP and want the vocabulary first.

## From R/3 batch jobs to an in-memory core

Sravan starts with history, because it explains the design. SAP R/3 in the 1990s set the client-server pattern for enterprise computing, but with rigid data structures and batch processing. HANA arrived in 2010 with in-memory, columnar storage, and S/4HANA rebuilt the ERP core on top of it.

The architecture has three layers: the HANA database, the application layer with the business logic, and the presentation layer for the user experience. The big change is dropping the traditional aggregates and redundant tables. He cites storage reductions of up to 80% from the simplified data model, with analytics embedded straight into operational processes instead of copied out to a separate warehouse.

## BTP is the integration and extension layer

Integration between S/4HANA and BTP runs through the cloud integration suite, API management and an integration advisor, supporting both synchronous and asynchronous patterns: application-to-application, business-to-business and API-based scenarios.

For building things, BTP offers two tracks. SAP Build Apps is the low-code route for business users. SAP Business Application Studio is a cloud IDE for professional developers in several languages. On the AI side, SAP AI business services provide pre-trained models and APIs for jobs such as document information extraction, conversational AI and robotic process automation, with growing support for generative use cases like code generation and automated testing.

## Deployment is a choice, and hybrid is the common path

S/4HANA comes on-premises (maximum control, good for heavy legacy integration), in the cloud (faster rollout, automatic updates, less maintenance) or hybrid. Sravan frames hybrid as the practical middle road for phased migrations: keep some components on-premises while moving others, without stopping the business.

## What it looks like by industry

The industry section is the most concrete part. Retail uses real-time point-of-sale volume for inventory, pricing and promotions. Life sciences and healthcare need validated systems that meet GxP requirements and support FDA compliance. Manufacturing ties shop-floor systems and IoT into production monitoring and predictive maintenance.

He also covers commercial models (consumption-based through the Cloud Platform Enterprise Agreement, pay-as-you-go and subscriptions) and closes with SAP's roadmap themes: more AI and ML, natural-language interfaces and sustainability features.

## Who should watch

Developers and architects about to work near an SAP estate, or Python teams asked to build integrations against BTP, will get a compact map of the product names and how they relate. If you want code, APIs in action or hands-on migration lessons, this isn't that talk.

Title: The best code is no code, and other rules for a calm codebase
Description: Denis Ermakov of Techflow at Conf42 DevOps 2025 treats coding as communication and argues for less code, fewer libraries and a definition of done in CI.
Body:
A copyright year in a footer can grow into a bug you wrote yourself. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Denis Ermakov](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Denis_Ermakov_coding_sustainable_development), Lead Software Engineer at Techflow, built a whole talk on one premise: coding is communication, communication causes problems, so the most sustainable code is the code you never write. Then he live-coded the proof.

It's a funny, opinionated talk with demos rather than slides full of principles. Engineers who have argued about the testing pyramid will enjoy it most.

## Coding is a relentless choice between bad and worse

Ermakov's framing is that every day is thousands of small trade-offs: microservices or monolith, server or client rendering, time or space complexity. If code is just words translating business requirements for a machine, then all the usual failures of communication apply. Hence his first corollary: the best code is no code.

The footer demo makes it concrete. Hard-code the year. A newbie engineer worries about New Year, so the year becomes dynamic. Then someone wants a start year, which produces "2025–2025" and needs a fix. Finally you notice there was no problem to begin with. Nobody loses anything if the footer says less.

The GitHub Actions demo goes further. A simple lint-build-deploy workflow posts to Telegram. Then it gains a revert on failure. Then, since the previous commit might also be broken, a loop that reverts and rebuilds until it finds a healthy commit. His advice on betting against a possibly infinite loop in CI: he's played that game and lost. Just fix the commit.

## The best library is no library

Second corollary. His example formats a duration in milliseconds into days, hours, minutes or seconds. The tempting move is to pull in Moment.js because dates are awkward. His rewrite uses plain division with well-named variables, the same number of lines, and drops roughly 145 KB of dependency. The lesson isn't to ban libraries. Good naming often solves what a library was imported for.

## If you need words, code them

Third and fourth corollaries: style agreements belong in linters and formatters committed to the repo, not in a Confluence page about tab widths. And foster a team dictionary in the README, starting with what "done" means. His sample definition of done for a user story lists unit, integration and end-to-end test coverage targets, generated documentation (he uses TypeDoc with Copilot-written comments), a video link for the product owner, and the product owner's approval. Then wire those checks into GitHub Actions so done is something CI verifies.

He also takes a swing at the testing pyramid, suggesting one end-to-end test is worth more than a mountain of unit tests and mocks. Expect disagreement in the comments.

## Short feedback loops and boring routines

The last section is about people. Replace a once-a-day review by the smartest person in the room with daily pair or mob sessions. Pick a system of principles (Agile, Scrum, Kanban, anything) and follow it entirely, not selectively. Build small routines and stick to them. His homework: remove one library from your app today, drop one backlog item next sprint, and automate your definition of done.

## Who should watch

Developers and tech leads drowning in incidental complexity, and anyone who needs ammunition for deleting code in review.

Title: MusicAgent turns a team of LLM agents into a Sonic Pi band
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Jan Van Wassenhove of Sopra Steria shows MusicAgent, a Python multi-agent system that writes, codes and records songs in Sonic Pi.
Body:
Jan Van Wassenhove, lead architect at Sopra Steria Benelux, can't play an instrument, but he can code. At Conf42 Python 2025 he showed MusicAgent, his open-source Python project in which a set of cooperating LLM agents writes a song, codes it in Sonic Pi, reviews the code, records a WAV and even produces the album cover and a booklet.

It is the most cheerful talk at the event, and underneath the bananas it is a clear case study in how to split a creative job across agents.

## A song is a pipeline, so model it as one

Jan starts by listing what making a track actually involves: songwriting, structure, playing and arranging instruments, recording, mixing and mastering (trimming silences, adding a fade), then packaging. MusicAgent maps those onto a multi-agent system, where each agent has one narrow mission and they hand work along to reach the shared goal.

The phases are explicit. Design produces the concept, lyrics, arrangement (verses, chorus, bridge, solo, outro, which instruments play where) and a choice of samples from your own library. Creation has a Sonic Pi coder agent write a first version, which reviewer agents critique and the coder revises, for as many cycles as you configure. Mastering polishes. Publishing writes the WAV, the cover and a README booklet with the lyrics, the original input and the concept the agents came up with.

He points out the obvious parallel himself: requirements, design, implementation, review, test and deploy. MusicAgent is a software development life cycle with a beat.

## Configuration does the orchestration

The orchestration lives in config files rather than code. An artist config defines the style, the album look and which assistants take part, such as a concept artist or a Sonic Pi coder. A phase config says who does what, in what order, and how outputs flow forward. Agents call OpenAI or Anthropic through LangChain, and the app talks to Sonic Pi over Open Sound Control so you can hear a draft while the agents are still working.

You can drive it from a CLI or a web UI that shows the timeline of phases, the agent-to-agent conversation, logs and the generated code with a play button.

## The hard parts are context, tokens and model choice

Jan is candid about the hurdles. Sonic Pi has a limited set of synths and samples, so the agents need workarounds. Long multi-phase chains build up large contexts and bump into token and character limits, so passing the right outcome to the next agent takes care. And models differ by task: he started on GPT-3.5 and now uses models such as GPT-4o mini and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, finding one better at images and another better at code.

## The banana song, and its limits

The live demo asks for an electro track about bananas at the beach drinking cocktails, inspired by late-90s music, using the default setup with two code-review cycles and no human review to keep it quick. Out comes a folder with the Sonic Pi file, a cover of cocktail-drinking bananas and the booklet.

He doesn't oversell it. Sometimes the result is eclectic or breaks the Sonic Pi code, and the fix is more iterations, more detailed prompts and human feedback in the loop. He closes on Nick Cave's reply to fans sending him AI-written lyrics: the human still sets the direction.

## Who should watch

Anyone designing multi-agent pipelines will find the phase-and-review structure easy to borrow, and the demo makes it concrete. Sonic Pi fans get a new toy. If you want benchmarks or production lessons, this is a hobby project shared with enthusiasm.

Title: The numbers behind cloud-powered open banking, in ten minutes
Description: Narendra Bhargav Boggarapu of Wells Fargo at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on how cloud platforms and APIs drive open banking engagement, access and security.
Body:
Open banking is mostly an API problem with a trust problem attached. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Narendra Bhargav Boggarapu](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Narendra_Bhargav_Boggarapu_cloud_banking_security), Lead Software Engineer at Wells Fargo, gave a brief, statistics-heavy overview of how cloud platforms are reshaping open banking, from customer engagement to security and regulation.

Be clear on what this is: a short executive-style briefing of only a few minutes. It's built around industry figures rather than architecture, and it doesn't name the sources for those figures, so treat them as the speaker's summary rather than benchmarks to quote in your next design review.

## The headline claims

Boggarapu opens with adoption. He says 87 percent of financial institutions are implementing or planning open banking initiatives, and he credits the shift with a 71 percent increase in customer engagement and a 43 percent drop in customer acquisition costs. The talk title leans on the engagement number, so this is the claim to weigh most carefully.

The cloud's role, in his telling, is plumbing at scale. He describes 2 billion monthly API calls handled securely between banks and third parties, and links that to better customer satisfaction and wider access to financial products for underserved populations. Further figures cover personal financial management tool adoption, financial literacy and competition among providers.

## Security and consent are the product

For a DevOps audience the more useful thread is what has to be true for any of this to work. He emphasises robust encryption of customer data, transparent consent protocols that customers actually understand, and compliance with regulation such as PSD2, which he calls non-negotiable. Trust, in this framing, is a feature you ship and measure, not a disclaimer at the bottom of a page.

He also names three persistent challenges and how they are handled: data privacy, through advanced encryption and strict access controls; integration with legacy core systems, through middleware; and keeping up with evolving global regulatory standards, through frameworks that are continuously updated. That legacy-integration point is where most of the real engineering lives, and anyone who has wrapped a mainframe in a REST API will nod along.

## Success stories and what's next

He cites a few anonymised examples: a fintech startup growing through lending products built on open banking APIs, a traditional bank growing its senior customer base with user-friendly tools, and a major bank lifting engagement with an AI-powered financial advisor. Looking ahead, he expects AI and blockchain to add predictive analytics and transaction transparency, and pushes for global standardisation of APIs to make cross-border financial services easier.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to fintech who want the business context for why their bank keeps shipping APIs, and product people who need a quick framing of open banking's promises. Engineers looking for API gateway designs, consent flows or PSD2 implementation details will want a more technical session alongside it.

Title: Secure IoT devices from the design stage, then keep patching
Description: Victor Oriakhi, design engineer at SONAE, at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on applying DevOps habits to embedded IoT security, from secure boot to remote patches.
Body:
An IoT camera can be compromised with a screwdriver and a circuit board, not just a packet. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Victor Oriakhi](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Victor_Oriakhi_iot_embedded_devops), design engineer at SONAE, gave a compact introduction to securing embedded IoT systems with a DevOps approach: build security in from the design stage, test it in the pipeline, and keep monitoring and patching after the device ships.

It's an overview for people new to embedded security or new to applying DevOps practice to hardware. Expect principles and examples rather than toolchains.

## Embedded devices are the quiet brains

Oriakhi frames embedded devices as the brain behind modern robotics and IoT, doing specific jobs silently inside larger systems. His examples range widely: healthcare monitoring that tracks a patient's health, supply chain systems following goods between production stages, home thermostats, and critical infrastructure like railway systems and smart grids. The breadth is the point. The same class of small, connected, long-lived computer sits in all of them, and every one is a target.

## Three layers of risk

He sorts the threats into three levels, which is a handy mental model:

- **Hardware**: physical tampering, such as plugging a circuit into an IoT camera to pull sensitive data from it.
- **Firmware and software**: outdated firmware, unpatched software and weak encryption, all of which attackers will find if nobody updates them.
- **Communication protocols**: devices lean heavily on Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and unsecured links can be intercepted.

The hardware layer is the one web-focused DevOps teams tend to forget. Your pipeline can't fix a debug port left open on the board.

## What DevOps adds to embedded work

His argument for DevOps here is about speed and repetition. Continuous monitoring catches vulnerabilities in real time. Automated security testing in the CI/CD pipeline can simulate attacks on IoT devices to find weaknesses before deployment. And because detection and response are automated, issues get resolved faster.

## Design-time controls, post-deployment habits

The practical core is two lists. At design time: encrypt communications with TLS, use secure boot so the device only starts trusted software, and use trusted platform modules to protect hardware integrity, validating security at every stage from design through deployment to maintenance.

After deployment: log and alert on unusual activity so a breach raises an automated alert, and run patch management with regular firmware and software updates delivered remotely, so fixing a fleet doesn't need someone physically visiting each device.

He ties it back to business value too. Devices that aren't easily exploited earn user trust, get adopted, and open new markets, which is a useful line to have ready when someone asks why the security work is on the roadmap.

## Best practices and takeaways

His closing checklist: embed security at each stage of the lifecycle, run threat modeling and risk assessments regularly, use secure protocols like HTTPS and TLS, integrate security testing into CI/CD, monitor and patch after deployment, and write clear, actionable protocols for responding to incidents before you need them.

## Who should watch

Designers, systems engineers and DevOps engineers starting on connected hardware, or software teams inheriting a device fleet. Embedded security veterans will find it familiar ground.

Title: Four ways to run containers on Windows without Docker Desktop
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Justin Dearing of Neudesic shows free ways to run Linux and Windows containers on Windows 10/11 without a Docker Desktop licence.
Body:
If your company is too big to use Docker Desktop for free, you can still run containers on Windows. In a lightning talk at Conf42 Python 2025, Justin Dearing, Principal Consultant at Neudesic, walks through the free routes: Dev Containers on WSL, the Docker engine binaries for Windows containers, Podman, Rancher Desktop and containerd with nerdctl.

His motivation is practical. Neudesic gives him a Docker licence, but consultants often work on a client's laptop or virtual desktop where nobody bought one.

## The easiest path: let Dev Containers set up WSL for you

For a Python developer in Visual Studio Code, the shortest route is the Dev Containers extension. Create a dev container (he picks a Python image with zsh) and, if there is no Docker yet, VS Code offers to install a WSL distribution, installs Ubuntu, puts Docker inside it and wires VS Code up to use it.

The catch: that Docker lives inside the WSL distribution. Without extra socket configuration you can't reach it from Windows itself. For playing with Linux containers, Justin says, just open the Ubuntu shell and use it there.

Prerequisites matter here. You need WSL, Hyper-V and the Windows containers feature enabled, which needs an admin if you aren't one. After that, an unprivileged user can install WSL distributions freely.

## Windows containers: two binaries and some registry work

For Windows containers, Docker publishes the engine as a free download (the static binaries, which he finds by searching for Docker Community Edition). It is a zip with two files, `docker.exe` and `dockerd.exe`; version 27.5.1 at recording time. Justin unzips it from plain `cmd`, because Windows now ships curl and BSD tar, and BSD tar can extract zip files.

Then you add the folder to PATH, either per user under `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Environment` or machine-wide under the session manager environment key, and run `dockerd --register-service`. Now Docker is a Windows service you can start and stop like IIS.

Two configuration notes in `ProgramData\docker\config\daemon.json` save pain. Create a `docker-users` group and set it there, because with UAC on even an admin can't run the docker command by default. And if you need older 2019-based Windows containers on a newer host, look at Hyper-V isolation instead of process isolation. Installing this route needs local admin rights.

## Podman, Rancher Desktop, containerd

Podman is the daemonless, open-source reimplementation sponsored by IBM (Neudesic is an IBM company, though he stresses he doesn't know the Podman team). It runs rootless, its CLI matches Docker's, and it comes with a desktop GUI. It only does Linux containers, and his caution is that Dev Containers with Podman can be awkward: renaming the binary to `docker` mostly works, except when it doesn't. He also runs his kid's Minecraft server on it, which he counts as "pretty close to production".

Rancher Desktop from SUSE wraps similar tools in a GUI and adds Kubernetes options; he has used it but doesn't demo it. Finally, containerd with nerdctl is a fully open-source pairing whose Windows container support is less mature. He suggests it mainly if containerd is already part of your Kubernetes setup.

## Who should watch

Windows developers and consultants who need containers without a licence conversation will get a working recipe in a few minutes. If you're on macOS or Linux, skip it.

Title: Zero trust, post-quantum crypto and compliance as code in one map
Description: Sandeep Batchu of Microsoft at Conf42 DevOps 2025 surveys cloud security beyond the perimeter, from zero trust and AI detection to post-quantum keys.
Body:
The network perimeter was a nice idea while everything lived behind it. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Sandeep Batchu](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Sandeep_Batchu_cloud_security_threats), Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft (speaking for himself, not his employer, as he notes up front), laid out a broad map of what replaces it: zero trust, AI-assisted detection, quantum-resistant encryption, serverless controls and continuous compliance.

Set expectations accordingly. This is a survey across a lot of ground, delivered as principles rather than demos or configs. It works best as a checklist for spotting which parts of your own cloud estate you haven't thought about lately.

## Zero trust means verifying after login too

Batchu's definition is the standard one: assume every user and device is untrusted by default, inside or outside the network, and verify continuously. What he adds is emphasis on the "continuously" part. Continuous authentication watches user behaviour, device health and location after the login, adapting as conditions change, so a stolen session doesn't get a free pass.

Around that he stacks the usual building blocks: MFA, adaptive access policies that change requirements based on context, biometric and passwordless methods, and micro-segmentation with VLANs, software-defined networks and network access controls so that one breached segment doesn't hand over the rest.

## Plan for quantum now, quietly

The section that will be newest to many DevOps audiences is post-quantum cryptography. He points to NIST-approved algorithms built on problems quantum systems can't solve easily, such as lattice-based cryptography, and recommends a hybrid model that pairs classical RSA or ECC with lattice-based schemes. The appeal is backward compatibility: you start the migration without breaking legacy encryption. Add hardware security modules for key storage, automated key rotation, and cryptographic agility, meaning the ability to swap algorithms quickly when the threat model shifts.

## Serverless moves the perimeter to every function

For serverless, the attack surface is the functions, APIs and triggers themselves. His controls are concrete: granular IAM and least privilege per function, input validation and output encoding, function isolation so one compromise doesn't spread. Treat the API gateway as the front door with strong authentication, rate limiting and a WAF in front. Monitor event triggers for unrecognised sources. And scan third-party dependencies continuously, because a function is only as trustworthy as the libraries it imports.

## Compliance as machine-readable rules

The last theme is continuous compliance. Translate regulations into machine-readable rules, bake them into infrastructure as code templates and cloud configurations, monitor for drift in real time, and let automated remediation revert a bad configuration before an auditor finds it. The reports then become audit-ready on demand instead of a quarterly scramble.

He also covers AI-driven threat detection, behaviour analytics and blockchain-backed immutable logs; the talk cites some big percentage improvements for these, so check the recording for the figures and their context.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects building a cloud security roadmap who want one session that names every major area. If you need hands-on implementation for any single piece, pair it with something narrower.

Title: Your Terraform providers and modules are an unscanned attack path
Description: Uri Aronovici, co-founder of ZEST Security, at Conf42 DevOps 2025 shows how a vulnerable provider or malicious module can hand over a cloud account.
Body:
Terraform's own documentation warns that it cannot stop a malicious provider or module from exfiltrating sensitive data. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Uri Aronovici](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Uri_Aronovici_cloud_terraform_hack), co-founder of ZEST Security and a former lead security architect, took that sentence seriously and showed two attack flows, both of which he says he ran into in his career, that turn third-party Terraform code into full control of a cloud environment.

## Providers run with the keys to everything

The setup is quick and clear. Providers are the plugins (written in Go, talking to Terraform core over RPC and to cloud APIs over HTTPS) without which Terraform manages nothing. Modules are directories of `.tf` files you reuse. Both come from three tiers: official (HashiCorp), partner and community, all stored in public GitHub repos. That openness is great for review and equally great for an attacker hunting bugs or slipping in a malicious pull request.

His team analysed ten of the most widely used providers and modules across those tiers and found critical vulnerabilities in every tier, with community components carrying the largest share. Community providers see millions of downloads a month, and in his experience they sit outside the loop: not scanned as part of the SDLC or application security, and IaC scanners catch misconfigurations rather than vulnerabilities in the third-party code itself.

He asks three questions worth answering about your own setup: are you using Terraform in production, do you know which providers and modules you use, and are you scanning them?

## Attack one: an official provider that dropped a label

The first flow uses a 2021 CVE in the official Terraform Vault provider, which he met in production about two years before the talk. The provider failed to configure bound labels for Vault's GCP auth method correctly. The user's code was right; the provider mapped it wrong and left the label empty. An attacker holding a read-only JWT (the kind that leaks into public repos all the time) could authenticate with the admin role, then escalate through the gcloud API to lateral movement, exfiltration or disruption. Official tier, still exploitable.

He adds a quieter point: providers sometimes expose secrets or tokens by mistake, and many of those issues have no CVE at all. You only find them by reading the provider's issue tracker.

## Attack two: a module that brings a backdoor

The second flow is social engineering plus a tiny module. It creates an EC2 instance as advertised, and also passes Base64-encoded user data that installs a backdoor on boot. The trick works because DevOps teams routinely Base64-encode legitimate user data scripts, so nothing looks odd. Run `terraform apply` without reviewing the module, and you've deployed the attacker's access yourself.

## The defensive checklist

His mitigations are practical and mostly free:

- read the docs and the code of every provider and module you adopt, and check other users' feedback
- keep scanning those repos, if only to see how the owners handle vulnerabilities
- pin provider versions and commit the `.terraform.lock.hcl` file
- enable state locking, and audit plans and state files for misconfigurations
- use IaC security scanners early
- restrict CI/CD and log access with IAM, prefer temporary credentials, put VPCs, load balancers and WAFs in the way
- use CWPP tooling to catch malicious traffic, and alert in CloudWatch on any read or write to the state file

## Who should watch

Anyone with Terraform in a production pipeline, and security engineers who treat IaC as configuration rather than code with dependencies. It's short and concrete.

Title: AI agents are plain Python plus one very magical REST call
Description: At Conf42 Python 2025, Craig West builds AI agents from scratch with requests and OpenAI to show they are ordinary Python around one LLM endpoint.
Body:
Craig West, a self-described backend Pythonista from Brighton, spent his Conf42 Python 2025 talk taking the mystery out of AI agents. His claim: an agent is everyday Python wrapped around a single POST request, and once you see that, the rest is design patterns you already know. In his words, "AI agents are Python code with REST API calls to an LLM, admittedly a very magical REST API."

The talk is a code walkthrough rather than a framework pitch. Craig deliberately avoids agent libraries, because there are hundreds of them, and builds each pattern by hand from a public repo of numbered example files.

## Start with requests, not a framework

The first file calls the OpenAI chat completions endpoint with nothing but the `requests` library: a model (GPT-4o mini), an API key in the headers, a payload with a system prompt, the user message and a temperature. The response is a JSON string you drill through via `choices`, `message` and `content`.

The detail he wants you to notice is that there is only ever one endpoint. You never get a `/rate-joke` or `/route-ticket` route from the provider. Every different behaviour comes from what you send.

## The prompt is the route you write on the client

That leads to his central metaphor: agentic code is the same mouse turned 180 degrees. Instead of building endpoints on a server, you write them on the client in plain English and ship them with each request.

The second example asks for a joke for Pythonistas, plus a rating, plus a next-step field: publish if the rating clears 8.5, retry otherwise. A one-shot JSON example in the prompt keeps the output parseable. What happens next is ordinary Python. You read the `next` field and hand control to whatever your app uses, whether that is pub/sub, an actor model or a finite state machine. The LLM decided the branch; your code took it. That is the autonomy part of agentic AI, within bounds you set.

## Memory is just the history you resend

The FAQ example builds a small Gradio chatbot for a shoe store, with shop facts appended to the system prompt as a stand-in for retrieved data. The lesson is about state: every request is stateless, so the app passes the full conversation history back each time. That one list of messages is the agent's entire memory.

## Tools, reflection and ReAct are loops you can read

From there the patterns stack up. A tool prompt describes a calculator and a joke tool in Markdown, and the model answers with the function name and arguments to call. Your machine runs the function, not the LLM, and you feed the result back.

Reflection chains requests: generate code, ask for a critique as an experienced Pythonista, then ask for a final summary, appending each answer to the history. The planning example runs a reason-and-act loop over two small functions: it looks up a product price, calculates the total with VAT and returns the answer (360 for the laptop, 240 for the TV once the 200 base price gets VAT added). Craig steps through the loop by hand in a notebook first, then shows the same thing as a Python loop.

His wrap-up is the useful part. Look for where the AI actually lives in all of this and it is one function, the call to the LLM. Everything else is string parsing and control flow.

## Who should watch

Python developers who have used ChatGPT but find agent frameworks opaque will get the most out of this. If you already write your own tool-calling loops, it is a refresher. Craig himself says you need not grasp every line on the first viewing; the high-level shape is what matters.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Darya Petrashka on building a HuggingFace agent](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2024_Darya_Petrashka_unlock_power_llm_build_huggingface_agent), the framework version of some of the same ideas.
- [Michael Haim: Orchestrating AI Agents with Pattern Matching](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Michael_Haim_orchestration_patterns_determinism), for when the control flow around the LLM needs to be deterministic.
- [Elizabeth Fuentes Leone: Reduce AI Agents Costs and Mistakes with Semantic Tool Selection](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_tools_semantic_cost), the next problem once your tool list grows past two.

[Watch Craig West's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Craig_West_agentic_ai_django)

[Watch the talk on YouTube](https://youtu.be/BaWTWtKP7nE).

Title: The Python toolbox Kusho AI uses to keep LLM apps from falling over
Description: Sourabh Gawande of Kusho AI at Conf42 Python 2025 on Tenacity, Pydantic, server-sent events, RQ and promptfoo, plus how he picks a model provider.
Body:
An LLM call fails far more often than the REST APIs you're used to, so the first feature of any LLM app is surviving its own model. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Sourabh Gawande](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sourabh_Gawande_ai_applications_practical), co-founder and CTO of Kusho AI, shared the concrete Python stack his team settled on after about 18 months of building AI agents: Tenacity for retries, Pydantic for schemas, server-sent events for streaming, RQ for background jobs and promptfoo for evals, followed by a candid tour of model providers.

The speaker builds a commercial AI agent for API testing, but the talk is about plumbing, not the product. Most of the libraries are open source and none are his.

## Retries and timeouts from day one

Gawande's starting point is that LLMs are statistical machines producing token after token, so the same input won't always give the same output. In his experience a stable API fails around 0.1 percent of the time, while even mature LLMs land around one to five percent depending on the task, and chaining calls compounds the error rate. You can't wait for the models to fix that; the application has to.

So retries and timeouts go in from the first commit, not after the first outage. He recommends not writing them yourself. In Python his team uses Tenacity in production: a decorator on the function, with stop conditions such as three attempts, fixed or random waits, and timeout decorators. For JavaScript he names a similar npm library, and for LangChain users the retry output parser, which resends the prompt along with the failed output so the model knows what not to repeat.

## Validate every structured output

When you ask a model for JSON, XML, CSV or a list, sometimes a field goes missing, an extra one appears, or a bracket wanders off. His answer is a schema library. On Python that's Pydantic: describe the response as a class, validate the model's output against it, and retry on failure, since a couple of retries usually fixes it. On npm he suggests Yup.

Two refinements make this better than brute force. If the same failure keeps recurring, say single quotes instead of double quotes in JSON, put an explicit instruction in the prompt, because every retry turns a five-second call into fifteen or twenty. And although OpenAI's structured outputs can enforce a Pydantic class, he prefers validating in the application so switching to another provider doesn't lose the guarantee.

## Stream with SSE, queue with RQ

Users won't wait ten seconds staring at a spinner, and most LLM calls take five to ten seconds even for simple prompts. Streaming tokens as they arrive solves the perception problem. WebSockets work but need a separate implementation, and he argues Python isn't the most efficient place for them. Server-sent events reuse plain HTTP: in Flask or FastAPI it's roughly a generator and a couple of headers.

Streaming stops making sense when a job takes minutes, like generating a hundred essays at once, because the backend gets tied up and everyone else's requests suffer. Log the task, process it in the background and notify the user by email or Slack, since they've probably left the tab. Start with a cron job polling a pending-tasks table; when you need several workers, move to a task queue. His pick is RQ (Redis Queue), which he says takes about fifteen minutes to set up. Celery does the same job, but for Kusho it carried more than they needed.

## Evals are unit tests for prompts

Gawande treats evals like unit tests: run a prompt template against many inputs, assert on the outputs, compare models and costs, and wire it into CI so every build checks that the prompts still behave. His favourite tool is promptfoo, an open source CLI driven by YAML files, with a hosted version if you don't want to run it yourself.

## A provider tour with opinions

The closing section is a quick map of model APIs. OpenAI as the versatile, reliable default, with the GPT-4o versus 4o mini trade-off between accuracy and cost or latency. Anthropic's Claude as his choice for coding tasks. Groq for latency on hosted open models like Llama, Mixtral and Gemma. AWS Bedrock if sensitive data must stay inside your AWS account. Azure for OpenAI models with somewhat better latency in his tests, after some forms. GCP and DeepSeek as the ones he hadn't tried yet. Provider lists age fast, so treat this part as a snapshot of when the talk was given.

## Who should watch

Python developers shipping a first LLM feature into an existing product, who want named libraries rather than principles. If you've already seen his talk at Conf42 LLMs 2025, this one covers similar ground with the same Python-first picks.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Practical tips for building AI applications using LLMs](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Sourabh_Gawande_applications_practices_tradeoffs) by Sourabh Gawande at Conf42 LLMs 2025, the companion talk.
- [To build a production-ready distributed task queue system with celery](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Vishrut_Kohli_productionready_distributed_task_queue_system_celery_django_queing) by Vishrut Kohli of Grofers at Conf42 Python 2021, for when you outgrow RQ.
- [The Retry Storm That Ate My Budget](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Yamini_Rathamsetty_Karthik_Akula_cost_loops_tokens) by Yamini Rathamsetty and Karthik Akula at Conf42 AI Agents 2026, on what retries cost when agents loop.

[Watch Sourabh Gawande's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sourabh_Gawande_ai_applications_practical) or the [YouTube recording](https://youtu.be/vI1-ATx7tls).

Title: Threat modeling for developers starts with three questions
Description: Krishna Chaitanya Rudraraju of Microsoft at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on fitting threat modeling and STRIDE into DevOps pipelines without slowing delivery.
Body:
Threat modeling has a reputation as a week-long workshop with a whiteboard and a security architect. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Krishna Chaitanya Rudraraju](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Krishna_Chaitanya_Rudraraju_threat_modeling_developers), Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft, made the case that it belongs inside the normal DevOps loop instead: a repeating cycle, driven by three plain questions, with the mitigations wired into CI/CD.

It's a short, practical introduction aimed at developers. If you have never drawn a trust boundary, this is a good first talk; if you run a threat modeling program already, it will mostly confirm what you do.

## A cycle, not a document

Rudraraju describes threat modeling as a structured process that looks a lot like an agile iteration. Define the security requirements first: does the product need data encryption, or data kept in a particular region? Then diagram the system with its boundaries, meaning which components sit on the internet, which on-prem and which in the cloud. From the diagram, identify risks such as SQL injection or session hijacking. Pick mitigations, then test that the mitigations actually hold. Repeat as the system changes.

The engine of all this, he says, is asking the right questions. His three are worth pinning above the desk: what are we building, what can go wrong, and what are we going to do about it?

## STRIDE as a question generator

To make those questions concrete he leans on STRIDE, one letter at a time:

- **Spoofing**: are we using MFA, OAuth2?
- **Tampering**: can someone make unauthorised changes to persisted data?
- **Repudiation**: can a user deny a change they made, and what stops that?
- **Information disclosure**: can a user see data they shouldn't?
- **Denial of service**: are load balancers and cloud protections in place?
- **Elevation of privilege**: can anyone gain access they weren't given?

The framework is old, but presented this way it reads less like a compliance form and more like a code review checklist.

## Worked example: a small e-commerce app

The most useful part is a walk-through on a typical stack: React front end, Node.js back end, a database, and GitHub Actions for CI/CD. Spoofing shows up as fake tokens and session hijacking, mitigated with OAuth2. Tampering shows up as someone altering Docker images or deployed code, mitigated by signing both the code and the images. Denial of service shows up as API flooding against an internet-facing app, mitigated with rate limiting, throttling and autoscaling. Three letters, three concrete controls, all of which a team can verify in the pipeline.

## Tools, then habits

For modelling he points to the Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, which visualises components, data flows and boundaries, and the open-source OWASP Threat Dragon. For mitigation he names code analysis tools such as Snyk and Checkmarx, plugged into both local and CI builds, or your own feeds built on open vulnerability data. For runtime, Azure Monitor and Microsoft Sentinel.

His best-practice list is short: collaborate with security researchers, automate wherever possible so new developers inherit the protections, update the model as new threats emerge, keep learning, and monitor. Above all, start small with the critical areas and widen the boundary as you succeed.

## Who should watch

Developers who've been told to "shift left" and want to know what that means on a Tuesday afternoon, and tech leads who want a lightweight way to start before buying anything.
