Title: Start DevSecOps with performance goals, training money and nicer words
Description: Josh Hankins, Consulting CISO at CBTS, at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on launching DevSecOps with goals, training budget, champions and evaluation points.
Body:
The hardest part of a DevSecOps program isn't the scanner, it's getting developers to care before the deadline does. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Josh Hankins](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Josh_Hankins_devsecops_program_start), Consulting CISO at CBTS, told the story of standing up a DevSecOps program from scratch in an enterprise, and his playbook is mostly organisational: get security into managers' goals, pay for the training yourself, and rename the tollgates.

This is a leadership talk from someone with nearly 30 years in the field. There's very little tooling, and that is the point.

## Make security part of the performance review

Hankins framed the whole program around one line he repeated everywhere: secure coding is a form of code quality. Developers weren't being handed a new way of working, just asked to ship fewer defects.

Then he removed the standard excuses one by one. The no-time excuse went away when he worked with the VPs of software development to cascade security into annual goals and objectives, and even supplied sample SMART goals such as how many insecure code findings a team fixed before production. The no-money excuse went away when he went to finance and secured a separate training budget, so it came out of neither his team's budget nor engineering's. His observation about calibration meetings is dry and true: nobody ever got a failing review for fixing insecure code before it shipped.

## Training that developers actually finish

The education track evolved over three years, and he's candid about what didn't work. A two-day, on-site web app pen-testing class for 40 to 50 developers had solid content, but asking developers to think like pen testers suits only one or two people per room. A remote version split into four-hour afternoons went down better. The winner was an asynchronous Application Security Foundations course written by a developer for developers, followed by a secure coding principles class, with the author later brought in for a virtual fireside chat.

Around that he ran a monthly Hack Club lunch-and-learn on the OWASP Top 10, weekly DevSecOps office hours, and eventually handed both to people on his team as leadership practice.

## The star chamber and the Grafana dial

The secret sauce, he says, was matrix teams. A cross-functional group he called the star chamber (engineering, developer services, SREs, platform and IT security) drove the program behind the scenes. A security champions program spread the message through dev workstreams. And instead of building new paths, he folded secure coding principles into the existing developer services team's paved roads.

The measurable bits: in year one, all revenue-generating applications were compliant with the SAST tool's build-breaker by July. Exceptions became an automated, time-limited process inside the ticketing system, which also told his team where to tighten firewall, WAF or SIEM controls. A simple Grafana dashboard (green good, yellow not so good, red bad) let teams click through to the finding and to the colleague who had fixed a similar one. Announcing the dashboard with a countdown to the executives did the rest.

## Word marketing is a real control

His favourite lesson: call them evaluation points, not tollgates, because nobody likes paying a toll. Same check, less resistance. He closes on SBOMs and the 2021 executive order as the next maturity step, using libcurl CVEs to show how an SBOM turns a hunt for affected systems into a lookup.

## Who should watch

Security leaders and engineering managers about to launch a program, or rescuing one that developers ignore. If you want tool comparisons, look elsewhere.

Title: Real-time personalisation is a retrieve, rank and cache problem
Description: Vedant Agarwal of Walmart Global Tech at Conf42 Python 2025 on multi-tower ranking, semantic search, vector databases and caching for fast, accurate recommendations.
Body:
A recommendation that arrives after the shopper has scrolled past is just a wasted GPU cycle. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Vedant Agarwal](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Vedant_Agarwal_personalization_neural_ranking), Senior Software Engineer in machine learning at Walmart Global Tech, broke real-time personalisation into the parts that decide whether it works: a two-stage retrieve-then-rank architecture, semantic search with transformers, and the vector databases and caches that keep it fast.

It is an architecture survey with e-commerce examples rather than a code walkthrough, and it doesn't disclose Walmart-specific numbers. It is a good map of the moving parts for anyone about to build or inherit a ranking system.

## The four ways personalisation fails

Agarwal starts with the failure modes. High latency, because shoppers expect instant responses and slow recommendations break the session. Inaccurate suggestions, which erode trust. Poor relevance, which shows up directly as missed sales and fewer repeat customers. And scale, because the data grows with the business and the system has to stay quick anyway. Every later section is aimed at one of these four.

## Retrieve wide, then rank narrow

His main accuracy tool is the multi-tower architecture, which splits the work in two. Tower one does retrieval: narrow a huge catalogue to a manageable set by general relevance, his example being 100 products. Tower two ranks that set using the user's browsing history and other context. The split is what makes it scalable: the expensive model only sees a hundred candidates, not millions.

Semantic search improves the retrieval side. Embeddings and vector similarity match intent instead of keywords, so a search for affordable running shoes also finds what the catalogue calls budget-friendly or economical, and one for comfortable office chairs surfaces ergonomic and memory-foam models. Transformer models such as BERT and T5 handle the long, layered queries, like budget laptops with good battery life, because self-attention relates every part of the query to every other part and knows that affordable applies to the headphones while noise cancelling is a feature. For production he points to smaller distilled transformers plus pruning and quantisation to keep the compute bill sane.

## Speed comes from four boring tricks

The latency section is the most practical:

- **Vector databases** such as Pinecone, using approximate nearest neighbour search and indexes like HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) so similarity search stays fast across millions of items, with ranking models refining the results.
- **Model optimisation**: quantisation, pruning and knowledge distillation, so a recommender can predict quickly even on constrained devices.
- **Caching** of embeddings, user profiles and popular query results, with smart invalidation so trending items during a flash sale stay fresh, layered from in-memory stores through message queues to distributed caches, and edge computing to serve users from nearby servers.
- **Batch inference** that groups queries for GPUs or TPUs during busy periods.

None of these is novel on its own, which is his point: personalisation at scale is mostly the discipline of applying all four together.

## From relevance to conversions

The conversion section covers behavioural embeddings built from clicks, purchases and browsing (a sports-gear browser gets gym equipment and running shoes), neural networks that enrich catalogue data with tags such as summer wear or low sodium, and hybrid retrieval that combines keyword and semantic search. He closes the loop with dynamic feature pipelines that update session and trending features on the fly, plus A/B testing and monitoring of latency and conversion to keep tuning.

## Who should watch

ML and backend engineers building search or recommendations in e-commerce, especially those moving from keyword search to embeddings. Teams already running two-tower retrieval with a vector store will recognise the blueprint and may want the Chaos Engineering version below, which leans on operations.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Real-Time Personalization at Scale: Neural Ranking Systems and Operational Breakthroughs](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vedant_Agarwal_personalization_ranking_systems) by Vedant Agarwal at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2025, his follow-up on running these systems.
- [ML-Powered Search & Recommendation 101](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sergey_Polyashov_recommendation_search_scalable) by Sergey Polyashov at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025, the fundamentals from first principles.
- [Vector Databases 101 - How do they work?](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Stephen_Batifol_vector_databases_work) by Stephen Batifol of Zilliz at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, for what happens inside the index.

[Watch Vedant Agarwal's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Vedant_Agarwal_personalization_neural_ranking) or the [YouTube recording](https://youtu.be/ATKLVC9FncM).

Title: One deployment path, with an OPA gate and an SBOM per artifact
Description: Hariharan Ragothaman at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on unifying team-by-team deployments into one pipeline with Xray scans, SBOMs, OPA rules and GitOps.
Body:
If every team deploys its own way, nobody can say which artifacts are running or whether they passed the rules. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Hariharan Ragothaman](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Hariharan_Ragothaman_deployments_governance_securely) (athenahealth on the Conf42 program, AMD by the time he recorded the talk) walked through the unified deployment pipeline his team built to fix that: one path to Kubernetes, with security scans, an SBOM and a policy check before anything ships.

## Where it started: EKS, ECS and homegrown scripts

The starting point will look familiar. Some teams deployed to EKS, some to ECS, some ran their own homegrown strategies. Monitoring could count deployments, but there was no single place to set rules, track vulnerabilities or govern what went out. That fragmentation pushed them into DevSecOps and a push to get everyone onto Kubernetes-style deployments.

## The threats arrive through dependencies

Ragothaman spends a good chunk of the talk on why the pipeline is where security has to live. Modern applications pull third-party components at every stage, so threats split into source threats (unauthorised changes, a compromised repo, building from a modified fork), dependency threats and build threats. He notes that many reported critical CVEs aren't actually exploitable, which is part of why teams drown in findings.

Two newer examples stand out. Machine learning models on public hubs can carry code that runs when the model loads; his slide used a model named, with some irony, totally harmless model. And generative AI tools can hallucinate package names that attackers then register, so the next developer who asks the same question installs the malicious one. Even asking a chatbot explicitly for a secure file endpoint, he showed, still produced code open to path traversal.

## The pipeline, box by box

The architecture is the heart of the talk:

1. A developer writes code with the JFrog Xray plugin in the IDE (he used it in PyCharm and CLion), catching vulnerable dependencies before commit.
2. Jenkins picks up the push to GitHub or Bitbucket via webhook and builds.
3. The artifact lands in Artifactory, where Xray scans it against rules set per target environment, and an SBOM is generated.
4. A deployment orchestrator, which he calls the choreographer of all deployments, asks a compliance advisor service (Open Policy Agent with Rego rules) whether this artifact may go to this environment.
5. If yes, the orchestrator commits the Helm release or Kubernetes manifest to a GitOps repo, and Argo CD or Flux CD applies it.

Underneath, Artifactory folders map to environments with RBAC on each and IAM-restricted access. The point he keeps returning to: this is the zoomed-out view, and every box has its own layer of policy.

## Governance you can audit

The second half maps that pipeline onto governance: auditability (deployment logs in versioned S3), compliance with frameworks like GDPR and HIPAA via tools such as HashiCorp Sentinel or AWS Config rules, clear ownership through RBAC and namespaces (developers in staging, operations in production), policy enforcement with OPA and admission controllers, centralised logging, and continuous monitoring with feedback loops. Governance, he says, is an ongoing process, not a one-time activity.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevSecOps engineers consolidating several deployment styles into one, especially in regulated industries like healthcare. The diagram is the thing to steal; the governance section is a handy checklist for your next audit conversation.

Title: Reinforcement learning, LSTMs and sentiment in AI trading, plus the catch
Description: Sunny Guntuka at Conf42 Python 2025 on reinforcement learning, LSTMs and sentiment analysis in algorithmic trading, and the bias and black-box problems.
Body:
Markets run on numbers and on nerves, and an AI trading system has to read both. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Sunny Guntuka](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sunny_Guntuka_trading_algorithmic_python), a senior data analyst, gave a quick tour of the three AI techniques doing the work in algorithmic trading (reinforcement learning, LSTM networks and sentiment analysis) and of the problems that keep them from being a money printer.

It is a short talk, under seven minutes, pitched as a briefing for developers curious about finance. There is no code, so the Python in the title is implied rather than shown.

## Reinforcement learning adapts when the regime shifts

Guntuka's first technique is reinforcement learning: a model that learns by trying strategies, observing the outcome and improving. His argument for it is the weakness of traditional models, which struggle when market conditions shift. An RL agent keeps adjusting its strategy, and he pictures a trading bot that learns from past trades, adapts to market shifts and manages risk without human intervention. He claims AI-driven strategies improve risk-adjusted returns by up to 25 percent; the talk does not say where that figure comes from, so read it as the optimistic end.

## LSTMs remember what simpler models forget

Next come long short-term memory networks for price prediction. Their selling point, in his telling, is that they capture long-term dependencies in historical prices that simpler models miss and surface hidden trends, with a predictive accuracy gain of 15 percent over standard techniques. The relevance for high-frequency trading is anticipating movements slightly earlier than everyone else.

## Sentiment is a data feed too

The third leg is sentiment analysis, scanning news, earnings reports and social media in real time. His line is that markets run on emotion as well as numbers, because investor psychology drives prices. He says traders using sentiment have seen a 10 percent increase in intraday performance, most of all in small-cap stocks, where one headline can move the price.

## The catch, in four parts

The section worth more of your time is the list of problems:

- **Data overload.** Too much data can overwhelm models; he goes as far as linking it to hallucination.
- **Bias.** Models trained on biased historical data make biased decisions.
- **Regulatory compliance.** Financial AI has to meet strict legal and transparency standards.
- **Black boxes.** Many models can't explain why a decision was made, which is awkward when a regulator or a risk committee asks.

His conclusion is that AI in trading has to be implemented ethically and responsibly, with infrastructure to match: high-performance computing, millisecond execution, and compliance built into the system rather than bolted on.

## What comes next, and what developers need

He looks ahead to quantum computing for portfolio optimisation and risk (with a very large speed-up figure that is best taken as a forecast, not a spec) and federated learning, where institutions train models without the data leaving the building, for privacy and shared intelligence.

For developers, his advice is that financial acumen (market dynamics, risk management, regulation) matters as much as reinforcement learning and model optimisation, and that transparency and fairness are part of the job, not an afterthought.

## Who should watch

Python and data engineers wondering what ML work in trading looks like at the concept level, in under seven minutes. Quants and anyone who has shipped a trading model will find it introductory.

Title: Where AI earns its place in unified communications, from routing to transcripts
Description: Naga Praneeth Yerram of Informatica and Vaishnav Yerram at Conf42 Python 2025 on predictive call routing, live transcription and assistants in UC, and how to pilot them.
Body:
The most expensive call in a support centre is the one that gets transferred three times. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Naga Praneeth Yerram](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Naga_Praneeth_Yerram_Vaishnav_Yerram_communications_ai_automation), Unified Communications Engineer at Informatica, with Vaishnav Yerram, Senior Operations Manager at KIK IT, walked through where AI pays off in unified communications: predictive call routing, real-time transcription, virtual assistants, and a 90-day pilot as the sensible way to start.

It is a brief overview, under seven minutes, and despite the title it doesn't show any Python. Think of it as a map of the use cases, with the numbers presented as the industry's claims rather than results from a named deployment.

## Routing that knows who should pick up

The first and most concrete idea is AI-powered call routing. Instead of a static queue, a predictive model looks at historical call patterns, agent performance and past customer interactions, then matches each call with the right expert. Fewer transfers, better first-call resolution, and workloads balanced across agents by skill in real time. The talk credits this with support teams handling thousands of additional calls a day and with noticeably higher satisfaction scores, because customers reach someone who can actually fix the problem.

## Transcripts become the system of record

Second is speech recognition. The talk puts AI speech recognition at up to 95 percent accuracy even with background noise or several speakers, good enough to produce live transcripts that are searchable and shareable. The payoff is twofold: compliance gets a record of what was said, and nobody has to transcribe meetings by hand, which frees time for work that needs a person.

## Assistants take the calendar admin

Third are AI virtual assistants that schedule meetings, manage email and organise calendars. The claimed productivity boost is 30 to 40 percent, along with round-the-clock personalised support. More broadly, the speakers argue AI pulls voice, video and messaging into one place, reducing silos between teams, and that cloud-based systems let this scale as communication needs grow.

## Industry snapshots

The use-case slide gives three quick examples:

- **Healthcare.** Transcription and translation that the talk says halve documentation time.
- **Finance.** Chatbots handling up to 90 percent of inquiries, with machine learning watching for fraud patterns in real time.
- **Retail.** Personalised recommendations and faster query resolution, which means less load on support.

## Start with a 90-day proof of concept

The implementation advice is the part a team can act on. Evaluate the current communication systems first and identify where AI would help. Pick specific use cases with a real upside; the talk suggests aiming for efficiency gains or cost reductions above 30 percent. Run a 90-day proof of concept with clear KPIs to show return on investment. Then roll out in phases, with training and change management, rather than switching everything on at once.

The future section points at natural language processing that reads context, tone and intent across many languages, predictive scheduling, personalised communication styles and stronger security and compliance.

## Who should watch

IT and operations leads who own a UC or contact-centre platform and need a quick list of AI use cases to evaluate. Engineers looking for implementation detail, or for the Python, will want to pair it with a hands-on talk.

Title: Wire MobSF into Jenkins and every mobile build gets a security scan
Description: Sheshananda Reddy Kandula of Adobe at Conf42 DevOps 2025 demos automating mobile app security scans with open source MobSF and a Jenkins pipeline.
Body:
Mobile teams now ship monthly, and security reviews didn't speed up to match. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Sheshananda Reddy Kandula, senior security engineer at Adobe with 15 years in application security, showed a pragmatic fix: run the open source Mobile Security Framework (MobSF) in Docker and drive it from a Jenkins pipeline, so every APK or IPA gets a static scan, a scorecard and a PDF report without a human starting it.

It's a hands-on demo with a short intro to mobile risks. The goal, in his framing, is catching the low-hanging fruit early, not replacing a full manual assessment.

## Why mobile needs its own pipeline step

Sheshananda's context is familiar. Users carry 80 to 100 or more apps and actively use maybe half of them in a month, often without updates. Features used to launch on the web first and reach mobile once proven; now they must land on web, Android and iOS at once, with releases every month. And unlike a web app, a mobile app ships part of its logic to the device, where anyone can unpack the binary and read it.

He points to the OWASP Mobile Top 10 for 2024, highlighting improper credential usage and inadequate supply chain security. The supply chain point lands: app binaries that used to be 30 to 40 MB can now reach 300 to 400 MB, and most of that is bundled dependencies you didn't write.

## SAST, DAST and where MobSF fits

The two testing approaches get a quick definition. SAST analyses source or binary; DAST runs the app, exercises features and watches how it talks to the server and where it stores files, local storage or an external SD card. MobSF does static analysis out of the box and dynamic analysis if you set up a real device or emulator, which he leaves out of this demo.

The setup advice is simple: use the Docker image. Installing from source used to mean fighting Python and Java versions; the image comes ready. There's also a hosted MobSF Live if you're fine uploading your binary to someone else's server.

## The demo, step by step

Sheshananda uploads a sample Android APK in the MobSF web UI and follows the terminal as it hashes, extracts, parses and analyses the file. The report shows findings like an exported activity and a manifest explorer, and can be printed or downloaded.

The automation uses MobSF's REST API, and the Jenkins pipeline is short:

1. Store the MobSF API key in Jenkins credentials and set the MobSF URL as an environment variable.
2. Download the APK or IPA into the Jenkins workspace from wherever your builds land.
3. Upload it to MobSF and capture the hash in the response, which identifies the file.
4. Start the scan with that hash.
5. Fetch the scorecard, then download the PDF report.

The first run in the demo fails, for a reason anyone who has run a live demo will appreciate: the server hosting the APK hadn't been started. Once it was, the pipeline went green. Emailing the report is a configuration step he left for viewers to finish, and the script is attached to his slides.

## Where to take it next

From there, the pipeline can trigger on every new build, fail the job when results breach a policy you define, and notify the right people automatically. That's the DevSecOps payoff: efficiency and scale across many apps, and issues found before release instead of after.

## Who should watch

Mobile and DevOps engineers who own a Jenkins pipeline and have no mobile security step yet, and AppSec engineers who need to cover more apps than they have hours. If you already run MobSF in CI, the intro will be familiar.

- Ashwin Kumar's [Securing Real Time Mobile Analytics: Identity Binding and Low Latency Authorization for Distributed Enterprise Data](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Ashwin_Kumar_mobile_authorization_identity) looks at mobile security from the identity side.

Title: An environment is more than a VM, so ship it as a product
Description: Caio Medeiros Pinto of Citi at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on environment as a service: infra, secrets, rights, docs and costs delivered in minutes, not months.
Body:
Your CI/CD pipeline can be beautiful and your team can still wait three months to deploy its first proof of concept. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, [Caio Medeiros Pinto](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Caio_Medeiros_Pinto_environment_products_innovation), DevOps Human and Evangelist at Citi, argued that the gap sits before the first commit: getting an environment at all. His fix is environment as a service, run by a platform team as an internal product.

It's a framing talk built on years of working with teams, not a step-by-step build. The value is in the definition and the checklist.

## The holes your DORA dashboard can't see

Pinto walks through the three "endless adoption journeys" he sees in companies: Agile for customer focus, DevOps for throughput and reliability, and platform engineering for the experience of the engineers doing both. Each brings its metrics (cycle time, the DORA four, onboarding time), and each can look green while developers burn out.

The reason, in his telling, is that most automation starts after commit and push. Before that, a team migrating to the cloud may get compute from one group, then file a ticket with another for network configuration and a third for certificates. He lists the root causes plainly: lack of knowledge, capacity and budget, "if it works, don't touch it" habits, standards nobody has read, and bureaucracy. From his own experience, teams took 3 to 24 months to really adopt a new technology, and some waited three to six months for an environment to start a small POC. His verdict on that: "It's crazy."

## Define the environment, then productise it

The useful move in the talk is a definition. An environment, for Pinto, is everything a team needs to put its software somewhere and make it run. That means far more than a virtual machine or a Kubernetes namespace:

- resources: infrastructure and configuration
- secrets and credentials for databases, brokers and third parties
- processes and standards for promoting to production, including authentication, authorization and non-functional requirements
- rights and permissions for the team and support groups
- reusable assets so nobody reinvents the wheel
- documentation, which he calls the Achilles heel of platform teams

Because every organisation's list differs, he wants the platform team to treat environment delivery as a product exposed through APIs, with a clear SLA and delivery lead time as the cornerstone metric.

## Costs, training and trial plans

Three takeaways make the idea survivable. Make costs visible so teams share responsibility for the money. Offer trial plans, so a team can grab an environment for a day or two to try a technology. And invest in training plus observability, so the people consuming the platform can understand its logs and messages without opening a ticket.

## Crossplane, Testkube and OpenCost

For tooling he picks three CNCF projects. Crossplane as the control plane that defines environments as APIs and orchestrates providers. Testkube to run tests on demand across the lifecycle, including continuous testing after production deploys. OpenCost for real-time cost visibility across vendors. His proposed shape: a platform team owning an "environment as a service platform" that hands out certificates, network configuration and the rest along with the namespace, not after it.

He closes with three habits for platform teams: know your customer, use your own platform so you feel the same pains, and grow a T-shaped team of champions instead of one person who knows everything.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers drafting a roadmap, and engineering managers whose teams complain about ticket queues more than about code. If you already run golden-path templates, the checklist of what an environment contains is still a good audit.

Title: Workflow automation moves from hard-coded rules to models that adapt
Description: Kowsick Venkatachalapathi of BNY at Conf42 Python 2025 on replacing script-driven workflows with ML, NLP and reinforcement learning, and how to roll it out.
Body:
Every time the standard operating procedure changes, somebody opens the code, edits the workflow stages, and ships a new release. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Kowsick Venkatachalapathi](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Kowsick_Venkatachalapathi_workflow_automation_ml), Vice President of Software Development at BNY, argued that this cycle is the real cost of traditional automation, and that AI-driven workflows, where data rather than configuration decides the next step, are the way out.

It is a strategy talk, not an implementation session: no code, no Python, and a lot of headline percentages. Watch it for the framing and the rollout advice; look elsewhere for architecture.

## The problem with rule-based automation

Venkatachalapathi's description of traditional automation will be familiar to anyone who has maintained a BPM system. Workflows are written as rigid, script-driven processes in Java or .NET, with manual configuration, predefined stages and static rules that have little sense of context. When the business process changes, a developer has to rewrite the workflow and go through a full release, which is slow and expensive over the long run.

His alternative is a workflow whose stages are driven by data. In the BPMN and DMN world he works in, that means tasks and approvals generated from the data and the changing business process, with models that learn from history instead of a developer hand-editing branches.

## What the models are supposed to do

The talk lists where ML earns its keep, with numbers presented as industry figures rather than BNY results:

- **Fewer manual touches.** He claims AI-driven workflows can cut manual intervention by 50 percent and bring decision accuracy to 90 percent, by turning historical data into predictive models.
- **Finance.** Fraud detection models flagging fraudulent transactions with 95 percent accuracy.
- **Healthcare and manufacturing.** Predictive diagnostics spotting risks up to 18 months ahead, and predictive maintenance cutting unexpected equipment failures by up to 70 percent.
- **NLP.** Email that is parsed, prioritised and answered automatically, and chatbots that understand context and intent.

None of these is tied to a named system in the talk, so treat them as the upside case rather than a benchmark.

## Reinforcement learning for workflows that keep changing

The most technical idea is reinforcement learning. A reward-based agent learns from each interaction, refines its decisions and adapts to a changing environment. His example is supply chain management, where routing, inventory and logistics rules can be recalibrated as conditions shift, rather than re-coded.

He stacks the future of automation in four layers: robotics at the bottom for physical tasks, cloud computing for elastic infrastructure, IoT for real-time sensor data, and AI/ML at the top doing the learning and decision-making.

## Start with an audit, not a model

The rollout advice is the most reusable part. First, a process assessment to find the specific bottlenecks where ML would help. Second, data infrastructure, because models need clean, high-quality, diverse data before they are any use. Third, iterative implementation: targeted pilot projects with clear metrics, then progressive scaling. He closes on human and AI collaboration, with automation taking routine work so people spend more time on judgement and customers.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and architects responsible for BPM or approval-heavy systems who need a framing for an ML roadmap. Engineers looking for code or model choices will want a more hands-on talk.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: AI code review works as the co-pilot, with a human still flying
Description: Shubham Singh at Conf42 Python 2025 on how AI code review combines static and dynamic analysis, rules and LLMs, and why it still needs human context.
Body:
Everyone who has opened a pull request knows the ritual: submit, cross your fingers, hope the reviewer is in a good mood. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Shubham Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Shubham_Singh_ai_code_review), a freelance developer who has sat on both sides of open source review, explained how AI review tools work under the hood, what they are good at, and why his rule is that AI is the co-pilot and the human is the pilot.

It is an overview for developers starting to use AI reviewers, not a tool benchmark, and it is refreshingly frank about false positives.

## Review is detective work, and detectives get tired

Singh's framing of the problem comes from experience as both contributor and maintainer. Traditional review means scanning hundreds of lines for hidden bugs, bad logic and security issues. It is slow, human reviewers get tired, and tired reviewers give inconsistent feedback. Waiting for that feedback also stalls development: you submit, wait, fix, wait again.

AI review promises instant first-pass feedback that goes beyond syntax, judging whether code will run efficiently in the context of the legacy code around it, so humans spend their attention on the parts that matter.

## Four engines behind one comment

The most useful section breaks an AI reviewer into four components:

- **Static analysis**: checking code without running it, for style errors, security flaws and performance issues. The aim is to catch problems before they become disasters.
- **Dynamic analysis**: running the code to catch memory leaks, performance bottlenecks and security exploits that only show up at runtime.
- **Rule-based systems**: the organisation's or maintainers' coding guidelines, enforced consistently, like a strict teacher for your pull requests.
- **LLMs and NLP**: the layer that reads code the way a human would, recognises patterns, suggests improvements and sometimes rewrites code. His shorthand is a senior engineer who is available around the clock and never gets tired.

The point of separating them is that each fails differently, which matters when you decide how much to trust a given comment.

## Where it goes wrong

Singh is specific about the limits. AI lacks human judgement on design and creativity. His own example: he wrote a SQL query purely for testing and the AI reviewer flagged it as a security flaw, because it had no idea the code would never reach production. That is the classic false positive, and false negatives exist too. The fix he recommends is context: tell the tool what the code is for, through prompts or files, because it doesn't understand business logic on its own.

He also points out that AI is trained on code people have already written, so its suggestions can be monotonous, while humans can come up with solutions that are more maintainable and more creative. Humans should validate AI suggestions, and re-check anything the tool flagged unnecessarily.

## Co-pilot, pilot, and a short tool list

The division of labour he proposes: AI handles scalable first-pass review, common bugs and refactoring suggestions; humans own business logic, history (why this code was written this way and has stayed so long) and company policy. Tools he mentions as favourites include GitHub Copilot and CodeRabbit, a GitHub plugin that reviews code before it merges, and he suggests integrating them into existing development workflows rather than treating them as a separate step.

## Who should watch

Developers and maintainers about to add an AI reviewer to their repositories, and team leads writing the policy for how those comments should be treated. People already tuning review bots across many repos will want something deeper.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [From Prompts to Review Harnesses: Scaling AI Code Reviews Across 70+ Software Projects](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Guido_Scheffler_code_review_harness) by Guido Scheffler of CGI at Conf42 AI Agents 2026, the same question at fleet scale.
- [AI-Driven Code Review and Quality Assurance](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Prakash_Raj_Ojha_33_code_review_automation) by Prakash Raj Ojha of BNY at Conf42 Incident Management 2024.

Title: Sofascore scaled to 25 million users on Varnish and bare metal
Description: Josip Stuhli, CTO of Sofascore, at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on scaling a live-score app with layered Varnish caching, Postgres, queues and a move off the cloud.
Body:
Before Sofascore had autoscaling, it had a CTO saving the El Clásico page as static HTML and editing it by hand every time someone scored. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Josip Stuhli, CTO of the live-score app, told the story of scaling from that to more than 28 million monthly active users, 400 billion requests a month and a peak of 1.6 million requests per second, with infrastructure costing 0.6 percent of revenue.

This is one of the most practical scaling talks in the Conf42 archive: real numbers, real mistakes and a clear rule at the end of each chapter.

## Know when your users show up

The early lesson came from a cache stampede. With a full-page memcache, a missing key sent every concurrent request to the database at once. Sofascore's first fix relied on knowing its users: a worker that pre-cached every match being played in the surrounding hours, because those are the pages people open. Traffic could quadruple in the 15 minutes before a big game, so the system had to be ready before the whistle.

The static HTML trick bought time on two servers. Moving to AWS in 2013 bought elasticity. Then they found Varnish.

## Varnish is the one thing to remember

Josip says it outright: if you remember one thing from the talk, it's Varnish, a reverse HTTP caching proxy written in C that respects cache-control headers. Crucially, it does request coalescing: on a cache miss, only one request goes to the origin and the rest wait for its response, which solves the stampede.

The caching layer evolved. Baked into each autoscaled instance, the cache got worse as they scaled, because every machine missed separately. So they split caching from the backend, then sharded it: a first Varnish layer with plenty of CPU and bandwidth, using consistent hashing to route each URL to one machine in a second layer. The hit rate is high enough that the backend can go down for half an hour of database work and nobody notices.

Invalidation is handled by an internal PHP library (open sourced) that maps endpoints to the entities they depend on, so a change purges only the right URLs. He's also a fan of stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error, which together give you an always-on site.

## Pick the right tool, then change it

Sofascore moved from MySQL to MongoDB (because, in his words, web scale) and regretted it: replication issues, data type errors, collection-level locking, and no foreign keys for a product built on connecting data. They migrated to Postgres live, by timestamping every collection and replicating changes in iterations until the two were in sync. Elsewhere, slow work goes on a Beanstalkd queue with workers scaled independently. Microservices, Josip suggests, you probably don't need without a big team or a complex app.

## Why they left the cloud

The cloud bill eventually had more traffic than compute in it. Moving only the Varnish layer to rented bare metal, where bandwidth is included, cut bandwidth costs tenfold. Their back-of-the-envelope maths said they could over-provision everything twice and still pay a fifth, so they moved the rest. Good caching flattened their peaks: the cache layer sees 20x spikes, the backends about 2x. A team of five now runs infrastructure part-time alongside backend work.

Off the cloud they rebuilt cloud-like capabilities: Kubernetes across multiple data centres after the OVH fire, Longhorn for replicated volumes, NATS for pub/sub at over 800,000 peak connections, and ClickHouse with Apache Superset for 2 petabytes of analytics compressed into 50 terabytes. Geo-distributed caches dropped Australian latency from half a second to 80 milliseconds. Push notifications once looked enough like a DDoS that Cloudflare's protection blocked real users until they visited Cloudflare's engineers.

Josip still says cloud should be the default. Keep your options open if the bill is high.

## Who should watch

Anyone running read-heavy traffic with sharp peaks, and teams looking at a cloud bill that grows faster than their user base.

Title: Faster mobile apps start with smaller bundles and better telemetry
Description: Jaspreet Kumar of Microsoft at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on mobile app performance, from app size and lazy loading to caching, telemetry, A/B tests and AI monitoring.
Body:
Most users won't wait three seconds for your app to load, and they won't file a bug report either; they just leave. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Jaspreet Kumar, lead software engineer at Microsoft, gave a short, structured playbook for data-driven mobile performance: shrink the app, load what matters first, cache aggressively, instrument everything, and let A/B tests and AI-driven monitoring decide what to fix next.

At around 15 minutes, it's a checklist talk. The value is in the order of operations, from build-time wins to runtime ones, rather than in deep implementation detail.

## Two goals to aim at

Jaspreet opens with research showing more than half of users are likely to abandon an app that takes over three seconds to load, then sets two targets: about 30 percent smaller app size through resource compression and asset management, and 50 percent or more speed improvement through lazy loading and progressive rendering.

## Shrink before you speed up

App size is the easiest win, and it's not only about download speed: large apps eat device storage and become uninstall candidates. His three levers:

- **Resource optimisation**: compress images, video and other assets while keeping quality.
- **Code minification**: strip comments, whitespace, unused variables and files you don't need.
- **Dependency management**: audit and drop redundant libraries, and use tree shaking to remove unused code.

## Load what the user sees first

Lazy loading is about perceived performance. Critical UI should render within the first second for a good first contentful paint; everything else waits. IntersectionObserver-style APIs can pull in images and scripts as the user scrolls. Skeleton screens show the layout while content loads, and blur-up effects soften image transitions. None of this makes the network faster, but users judge the wait, not the bytes.

## Cache, and keep the UI thread free

On data handling, Jaspreet recommends caching with both memory and disk layers; in his example it cuts server requests by up to 40 percent and average load times from 2.5 to 1.5 seconds. Background threads and event-driven processing keep UI updates independent so the app holds 60 FPS during heavy data work, and debouncing and throttling keep scrolling and animations smooth.

## Telemetry in three dimensions

You can't optimise what you can't see. Firebase Performance Monitoring tracks startup time, HTTP requests, frame rates and network slowness; New Relic adds distributed tracing and code-level diagnostics; custom dashboards set thresholds and fire real-time alerts.

Jaspreet splits telemetry into three views that are worth keeping separate: technical (API response time, memory, battery drain), behavioural (which features people use, and where they get stuck) and operational (crashes, errors, anomalies). The combination is what tells you whether a slow screen is also a screen anyone cares about.

## Let the data pick the fix

A/B testing closes the loop: form a hypothesis from the telemetry, roll variants to user segments, compare load times, interaction rates and feedback over a set period, then ship the winner. AI-driven monitoring then adds anomaly detection and prediction on top, aiming to flag a regression before users feel it and to trace bottlenecks to their source faster.

The talk closes with business impact figures for retention, revenue and satisfaction. They're presented as typical potential gains rather than results from a specific Microsoft app, so treat them as a pitch for prioritising performance, not a forecast.

## Who should watch

Mobile engineers and product-minded leads who need a prioritised checklist to bring to a planning meeting, and DevOps engineers who own mobile release pipelines and want to know which metrics the app team should be watching.

Title: Python packaging for busy people: use uv, and maybe pixi for Conda
Description: Dmitriy Volkov of Palisade Research at Conf42 Python 2025 on the pain points of pip, Poetry and conda-lock, and why his one-line advice is to use uv.
Body:
Some talks bury the lede. [Dmitriy Volkov](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Dmitriy_Volkov_packaging_busy_people) of Palisade Research puts his in the first two minutes at Conf42 Python 2025: if you take one thing away, use uv. The rest of the talk earns that advice by walking through what goes wrong with pip, Poetry and conda-lock when you want an environment that still builds a year from now.

He is upfront that the talk includes opinions, and it is short, under ten minutes. Note that the abstract mentions the GIL-free future and AI speeding up CPython; the recording sticks to packaging tools.

## Where he is coming from

Volkov used to do build engineering on large polyglot projects, among them TON and KasperskyOS, the kind of codebase where C, Go and Rust submodules all have to build together and developers are unhappy when they don't. His goal there was to let people ship faster, and this talk applies that to Python projects.

## Specifying dependencies is solved; tools are not

His map of the space has two halves. The way to declare dependencies has converged: you can always use `pyproject.toml` and be fine. The tooling around it has not: there are about ten competing tools, and pip still works, which is part of the confusion.

He then climbs the ladder of needs. Install a library: `pip install`. Share with friends: `requirements.txt`. Still working in six months when NumPy updates: write down the version. Keep the environment synced automatically: a virtualenv manager. And then reproducibility, where it gets subtle. A pinned version is only guaranteed on PyPI, which won't let you replace a version once uploaded. Practitioners pull packages from elsewhere too, such as PyTorch from its own index, so if you want the project to behave the same in a year you should pin a hash.

## The grievances, tool by tool

- **pip and pip-tools.** Old pip could install incompatible packages and leave you with a broken environment (fixed in newer versions). The endorsed way to lock is to generate a lock file on each platform separately, so macOS, Windows and Linux each need their own build box committing lock files. And the documented secure way to use pip relies on a flag that disables pip's own dependency resolution, because you are supposed to have resolved and locked everything beforehand.
- **Poetry.** He wanted to love it. No built-in command to upgrade dependencies; differences from pip in how `pyproject.toml` is implemented that will bite you; and for about a year in 2022, interrupting `poetry install` or running two in parallel corrupted the cache. That was when he quit Poetry.
- **conda and conda-lock.** Conda's slowness is a meme (he cites two million Google hits for "conda slow"), which the libmamba solver improves. conda-lock also ships a vendored Poetry to handle pip requirements, which can lag years behind, doesn't behave like pip, and has been known to interfere with a global Poetry install.

## The praise: uv is fast enough to disappear

uv solves several of these problems through its design choices, and it is very fast, fast enough that he runs it from direnv on every directory change, something he couldn't do with pip and would never try with Conda. The caveat: uv has been iterating on its format without a stable API, so things occasionally break. He finds the time spent on those breaks trivial next to the time he lost to everything above.

His summary fits on a sticky note: instead of pip, uv. Instead of Conda, consider pixi, which he says the conda-lock developers are considering recommending in its place.

## Who should watch

Anyone maintaining a Python project with more than one contributor or more than one platform, and especially people still choosing between Poetry and pip-tools. It is eight minutes that may save you an afternoon.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Security considerations in Python Packaging](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2022_Gajendra_Deshpande_security_considerations_packaging) by Gajendra Deshpande at Conf42 Python 2022, on why hash pinning matters beyond reproducibility.
- [Your trusty Python package: TTPs of attacks on OSS in Python](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Leonid_Akinin_trusty_package_ttps_oss_python) by Leonid Akinin of EPAM Systems at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.
- [Oops, there's somebody in my package manager!](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Thomas_Chauchefoin_Paul_Gerste_somebody_in_my_package_manager) by Thomas Chauchefoin and Paul Gerste of SonarSource at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022.

Title: Observability's next decade runs on data, context and AI agents
Description: Shyam Sreevalsan of Netdata at Conf42 DevOps 2025 proposes a new observability equation of data, context and intelligence, and argues for decentralised stacks.
Body:
Metrics, logs and traces were the answer for a decade; Shyam Sreevalsan thinks they are now just the first term. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Netdata's VP of strategy, partnerships and product proposed a new observability equation, data plus context plus intelligence, and argued that the next ten years will reward stacks that collect everything at per-second resolution, attach business meaning to it, and let AI agents act on it.

Shyam says early on that this isn't a Netdata pitch, though he does explain some of Netdata's design decisions along the way. It's a talk about direction, so expect forecasts, not benchmarks.

## Too little, too complex, too expensive

His diagnosis of today sorts the pain into three overlapping buckets. Too little observability: a few dashboards that give false confidence, and sampling intervals so coarse that micro-spikes vanish. Too complex: the Prometheus and Grafana stack that was easy for the MVP and became a part-time job once services multiplied across on-prem and multiple clouds. Too expensive: powerful commercial platforms that startups can't afford, which pushes them back into one of the first two buckets.

## Context is the term most stacks skip

Data is the foundation, and Shyam's rules for it are blunt: collect everything and filter later, sample as often as you can, reject limits that come from the tool rather than your workload, and keep history as long as it's meaningful. Per-second data catches what ten- or sixty-second sampling hides, and it gives machine learning dense enough patterns to learn from.

Context is the part most stacks under-invest in. A CPU at 90 percent means one thing if it's normal for that component and another if it's never happened before. Shyam's layers of metadata include business context (revenue impact, SLOs), operational context (deployments, config changes, dependencies) and environmental context, like a third-party outage announced on someone else's status page. His before-and-after is the clearest slide: a raw CPU threshold alert versus a story that a revenue-critical service is seeing an anomalous slowdown during peak shopping hours, probably because of a recent deployment. Netdata's own move here is running anomaly detection on every metric it collects, not as an option.

## Agents with a job description

Intelligence means AI, and Shyam expects specialised agents rather than one big chatbot: reasoning agents for causal analysis across services, memory-augmented agents for matching historical patterns (you can't fit all your telemetry into a context window), planning agents for capacity and cost, and RAG-enabled agents that read your runbooks and Jira and execute playbooks. His example workflow: an agent detects a memory leak, runs git blame to find the commit, rolls it back and adjusts autoscaling, and you get a report. He suggests a new KPI to match: the percentage of routine incidents resolved without a human.

## Why centralised storage breaks first

The architecture argument is Netdata's thesis, stated plainly. Modern systems are distributed, so why force observability into one central data lake? Centralisation brings a single point of failure, egress and storage bills that climb with data volume, access control and data sovereignty headaches, and query performance that degrades at scale until you start throwing data away. Distributed storage with queries that fetch in real time avoids that, and keeps processing close to where a metric originates, where its context is.

## Who should watch

Observability owners planning the next platform choice, and SREs wondering which skills to build. Shyam's list for individuals: causal analysis, policy-as-code and security-as-code, multi-cloud and edge, and learning where AI agents fail. He sums it up with a prediction of his own: future SREs managing a hundred times more services with ten times less manual intervention.

- Indika Wimalasuriya's [Observability Maturity Model for AWS – From Reactive to Autonomous](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Indika_Wimalasuriya_observability_maturity_model) charts the same path towards autonomy.

Title: AWS Step Functions done right starts with standard vs express
Description: Bharat Vishal Tiwary of Amazon at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on orchestration vs choreography and Step Functions practices for timeouts, retries, payloads and cost.
Body:
A state machine that waits forever doesn't fail, it just never finishes, and nobody gets paged. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Bharat Vishal Tiwary, a software development engineer at Amazon, walked through serverless workflow orchestration with AWS Step Functions, and the best practices section, from timeouts to payload size, is where the talk earns its slot.

The first half is introductory: what serverless is, what a workflow is (making coffee, in his example), and how microservices talk to each other. If you've shipped Step Functions before, skip ahead to the second half.

## Orchestration or choreography

Bharat frames the choice with an order flow: when a customer places an order, something has to notify them, prepare the order and record metrics. In orchestration, a central service calls each of those in turn, like a conductor in front of an orchestra. In choreography, each service reacts independently to events from a broker. Orchestration gives explicit control, simpler workflow definitions and centralised error handling, at the cost of flexibility. Choreography gives service autonomy but needs distributed error handling and more complex monitoring. When you need a clear view of what happened and when, orchestration wins, which is the case the talk is about.

He also lists the field: Apache Airflow, Google Workflows, Microsoft Power Automate, Dagster and Argo, alongside Step Functions.

## The building blocks

A Step Functions workflow is a state machine built from a handful of components: request-response calls, choice states for branching, retries with backoff, human-in-the-loop approvals, parallel branches and map states for dynamic fan-out. You can drag them together in Workflow Studio in the console, or write Amazon States Language, a JSON-like definition, for version control. AWS CDK can lint the infrastructure code and generate validated CloudFormation templates before deployment.

## Pick the workflow type first

The most important design decision comes first. Standard workflows run up to a year, guarantee exactly-once execution, are billed per state transition and suit long-running or non-idempotent work, like an approval that might take three days or a payment you must never run twice. Express workflows are capped at five minutes, give at-least-once semantics for async and at-most-once for sync, cost far less, and handle high-volume, idempotent work. You can also combine them: a standard parent can invoke express children synchronously, though not the reverse.

## Timeouts, retries and the 15-minute rule

The practical list is worth a screenshot:

- Amazon States Language has no default timeout on a state, so a task can wait indefinitely without failing. Set timeouts, and use heartbeats on callback tasks that use a task token.
- Split exceptions into retriable (a dependency exception from SQS) and non-retriable (a null pointer), and retry only the first kind.
- Lambda for parallel, short tasks; Fargate for anything over 15 minutes; ECS or EKS when you need container control.
- Make every Lambda idempotent, don't hard-code Lambda function names (CloudFormation may prefix them), and version both functions and state machine definitions.
- For DynamoDB, use optimistic locking, transactions or conditional writes to avoid race conditions.
- Pass large payloads as S3 ARNs instead of inline.
- Watch the event history quota; start a new execution before you hit it.

For operations, the CloudWatch metrics to watch are state transitions, throttled transitions, execution duration, throttled execution starts and task failures. Add IAM roles per task, encryption at rest and in transit, CloudTrail and resource-level permissions. For cost, choose the workflow type deliberately and tag resources.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers about to build their first non-trivial state machine on AWS, and reviewers who want a checklist for a Step Functions design review.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Oskar Neumann's [One Step Ahead: Modern Application Architecture with AWS Step Functions](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Oskar_Neumann_modern_application_architecture_aws_step_functions) goes deeper on architecture.
- Md Mostafa Al Mahmud's [Event-Driven Architectures: Orchestrating Cloud Native Workflows](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Md_Mostafa_Al_Mahmud_eventdriven_architectures_orchestrating) takes the choreography side.
- Mohammed Fazalullah's [Build and orchestrate serverless generative AI applications](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Mohammed_Fazalullah_build_orchestrate_serverless) applies orchestration to GenAI.

Title: Layered security for embedded devices that can't afford much
Description: Mounika Ponugoti of Qualcomm at Conf42 Python 2025 on secure boot, CFI, ASLR, sanitizers and threat models for embedded devices with tight power and cost budgets.
Body:
Embedded devices skip security for the same three reasons every time: cost, power and performance. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Mounika Ponugoti](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Mounika_Ponugoti_device_security_attack), Staff Engineer at Qualcomm, laid out the defences that still fit inside those budgets, from secure boot and control flow integrity to sanitizers and dedicated crypto hardware, and argued for picking them with a threat model rather than a wish list.

Fair warning for the Python track: there is no Python in this one. It is a compact survey of embedded hardening, useful to anyone whose code eventually lands on firmware, and it stays at the checklist level rather than showing implementations.

## Attackers start with what is already known

Ponugoti's picture of the threat is unglamorous. Embedded systems sit in flight controls, healthcare devices, gas pipelines, cars and home automation, and attackers usually begin with the easy doors: default passwords and outdated firmware with buffer or stack overflows that are already public. She cites a study claiming 83 percent of embedded systems lack security features, and notes that breaches cost organisations heavily in damage and recovery. The talk doesn't name the study, so read the figure as context rather than a measurement.

## The baseline: code, boot, network, binary

The first layer is what most teams can do without new hardware:

- **Secure coding practices** to remove buffer overflows and memory corruption at the source.
- **Secure boot**, validating that the firmware being executed is authentic, so nobody injects code during boot or takes over after the OS comes up.
- **Intrusion detection** on the network, alerting an administrator or triggering automated action on suspicious activity.
- **Obfuscation**, randomising symbol names and function calls so reverse engineering a targeted attack takes longer.

## The advanced layer, one mechanism each

Then come the measures that need more care to roll out. Control flow integrity allows only validated execution paths, so an attacker can't jump from one part of the code to another. Address space layout randomisation loads the image at a different place in RAM on every boot, which breaks attacks that depend on fixed addresses. Stack canaries, code encryption and authentication of dynamically loaded modules close other doors. On multi-component systems-on-chip she stresses strict memory access control between components, because one compromised block can otherwise be the path into its neighbours.

Proactive habits round it out: patch regularly, since known issues are what attackers try first, and enable address sanitization and undefined-behaviour sanitization at runtime so crafted inputs can't push the system into undefined behaviour and corrupt memory.

## Budget security with a threat model

The core argument is about trade-offs. You don't have to apply everything. Run a threat model, identify the vulnerabilities that matter for this device, and restrict the risk profile to what fits its constraints. Where performance hurts, she suggests faster implementations of the security algorithms, dedicated hardware accelerators for cryptography, lightweight algorithms to spare the core, and trusted execution environments where the hardware already has them.

Her closing numbers again come from an unnamed study: 80 percent of critical vulnerabilities reduced by regular updates and scanning, and 90 percent of attempted breaches blocked by enhanced protocols. The takeaways are sensible regardless: design security in from day one, layer the defences, keep monitoring, and stay current on emerging threats.

## Who should watch

Firmware and IoT engineers who need a checklist to argue for in a design review, and application developers curious about what "secure by design" means below the operating system. Embedded security specialists will know every item.

- [Securing Embedded Systems in IoT: A Practical DevOps Approach](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Victor_Oriakhi_iot_embedded_devops) by Victor Oriakhi of SONAE at Conf42 DevOps 2025, the pipeline side of the same problem.
- [Leveraging Blockchain for Secure and Immutable Firmware Updates](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Swapnil_Shinde_blockchain_immutable_firmware) by Swapnil Shinde of OWASP at Conf42 IoT 2023, on the update path she says attackers love.
- [Building the Edge AI Revolution with Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Anushree_Nagvekar_edge_memory_safety) by Anushree Nagvekar at Conf42 Rustlang 2025, on Rust for AI at the edge, where the same hardware limits apply.

Title: Elastic cloud plus the right API protocol is how you survive the spike
Description: Himaja Sabbineni of Expedia Group at Conf42 Python 2025 on distributed computing, elasticity, gRPC, GraphQL and why REST still carries most integrations.
Body:
Black Friday doesn't care how your servers feel. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Himaja Sabbineni](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Himaja_Sabbineni_performance_cloud_architecture), Senior Software Engineer at Expedia Group, made the case that surviving traffic spikes takes two things working together: cloud architectures that scale elastically, and APIs chosen for the job, with gRPC and GraphQL where they fit and REST still doing most of the work.

Set expectations: this is a high-level overview aimed at architects and decision makers, with no code and no Python despite the track. It works best as a framing talk for a team about to modernise.

## Spread the load, then package it

Sabbineni starts with distributed computing: spread workloads across many servers so no single machine becomes the bottleneck and uptime doesn't depend on one box. Her example is Netflix redistributing load across its global servers during big releases. Containerisation is the second pillar. Docker and Kubernetes put code, dependencies and configuration into portable containers so the same thing deploys the same way everywhere, which kills a whole category of "works on staging" bugs.

## Elasticity is where the savings are

The more interesting section is on elasticity, which she defines as allocating resources dynamically to meet changing demand. Dynamic scaling brings servers online during a flash sale and takes them away when it ends. A streaming platform scales up in the evening peak and down in the early morning. Her point is that elasticity cuts both failure modes at once: without it you either go down under load or over-provision and pay for idle machines the rest of the year. The abstract claims costs can drop by 30 percent; the talk treats that as an industry-level figure rather than a measurement from one system.

## Pick the protocol, and don't retire REST yet

On APIs she sets out the modern options. gRPC is a high-performance framework for low-latency communication, common between microservices. GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need, so an e-commerce app fetches product details without dragging unrelated data along. Then comes the honest bit: despite both, she says over 80 percent of enterprise software systems still integrate over REST, for its simplicity and compatibility. Choosing an API style is a fit question, not a fashion one.

## What it looks like in practice

The industry examples are familiar but useful as a checklist. E-commerce platforms facing Black Friday need autoscaling to hold 99.9 percent uptime, and APIs for personalised recommendations, real-time inventory and payments. She cites the often-quoted finding that a one-second page delay can reduce conversions by up to 7 percent. Streaming services lean on scalable delivery and on APIs that analyse viewing preferences. In healthcare, APIs give secure access to patient records and automate scheduling and billing.

She also argues for a unified data ecosystem: APIs pulling purchase history, web analytics and supply chain data into one view so a retailer can predict trends and manage inventory. Her claim is that real-time data sharing lets businesses respond 40 percent faster to market changes; again, no source is given in the talk.

## The action list

Her closing steps are practical: audit the current infrastructure for bottlenecks, move dynamic workloads to scalable platforms (she names AWS, Azure and Google Cloud), use GraphQL or gRPC where performance matters, encourage teams to experiment, and keep cloud and API work within security standards and privacy regulation.

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads preparing a modernisation pitch who want the vocabulary in one place, and anyone new to cloud architecture. Engineers who already run autoscaling microservices won't find new mechanics.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Navigating the World of API Gateways](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Roman_Rastiehaiev_api_gateways_comparison) by Roman Rastiehaiev at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, a comparison of open source gateways for the API layer.
- [Horizontal Autoscaling with Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2022_Rob_Richardson_horizontal_autoscaling) by Rob Richardson at Conf42 Kube Native 2022, the elasticity part made concrete.
- [Service Engine: Auto-provisioned REST, GraphQL & gRPC Services](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Joe_Wingard_Autoprovisioned_REST_GraphQL_gRPC) by Joe Wingard at Conf42 JavaScript 2021, all three protocols from one service.

Title: The NGINX metrics worth graphing, and what their spikes mean
Description: Dave McAllister of NGINX at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on the core NGINX metrics, how to read spikes in connections and blocked requests, and native OpenTelemetry tracing.
Body:
A graph of active connections tells you nothing until you know what its shape means. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Dave McAllister, senior open source technologist at NGINX (part of F5), went through the core metrics for NGINX, from connections and request rate to cache hit ratio, and then did the more useful part: reading what spikes, slow climbs and jitter in them usually mean.

It's an NGINX talk from NGINX, and Dave is upfront that NGINX Plus, the commercial product, is less his area. Most of it applies to the open source core.

## Getting the numbers out

Open source NGINX exposes its metrics through the stub status module: one line in nginx.conf gets you eight metrics plus a health check. NGINX Plus adds an API endpoint with around 130. Both can scrape logs for more. For dashboards, NGINX uses Grafana heavily internally.

Dave repeats one caveat throughout: your mileage may vary. The list is a starting point for a general-purpose NGINX deployment, not a mandate.

## The list, grouped by question

The metrics fall into a few groups:

- **Load**: active connections and request rate. Request rate is usually a daily sawtooth; a sudden spike is a marketing promotion nobody told you about, or a DDoS.
- **Latency**: request time and upstream response time together, which in a microservices setup act as endpoint measurements for both NGINX and whatever sits behind it.
- **Errors**: the status variable, mostly 4xx and 5xx. When the error rate jumps, check for an attack first, then application bugs, then misconfiguration.
- **Resources**: CPU and memory, via top, htop or vmstat for open source, or Plus endpoints.
- **TLS**: SSL handshake time. Long handshakes point at configuration, or slow hardware.
- **Throughput**: bytes sent, which is what you size for at peak. Dave borrows John Mashey here: latency lives forever, throughput costs money.
- **Security**: blocked requests.
- **Caching**: cache hit ratio, via upstream cache status, if NGINX is a reverse proxy. Higher is faster for users and lighter on the backend.

## Reading the shape

The scenarios are the best part. For active connections at a baseline of about 500, Dave walks three patterns. A spike to 1,500 is a traffic surge (or you got Slashdotted, for those who remember), a DDoS, or a load balancer funnelling traffic to one system. A gradual climb is probably growth, so capacity planning is due, unless something is saturating or your scaling isn't keeping up. Wild bouncing points to periodic jobs, a report hammering a database, or a load balancer that needs its configuration checked. In Kubernetes, he adds, a noisy neighbour on the node can make your perfectly correct app look like the culprit.

Blocked requests follow the same three shapes. Normal is a handful per minute; a sudden tenfold jump is an attack or a recent firewall or WAF change producing false positives; a slow climb means you've appeared on someone's radar; erratic bursts usually mean probing. Blocks still cost resources, so a rising block count can show up as slower responses.

## Tracing without halving throughput

Dave closes with two open source projects. The NGINX OpenTelemetry module came about because existing modules, NGINX found, cost about 50 percent of request performance; the native one costs about 10 percent. It supports W3C trace context and OTLP over gRPC, is configured inside NGINX itself, and tracing can be toggled with cookies, tokens or variables without a restart. The NGINX Prometheus exporter turns stub status or Plus API data into Prometheus metrics and also covers NGINX's Kubernetes Ingress Controller and NGINX Gateway Fabric.

His closing line borrows an old observation: careful thought plus well-placed print statements is still the best debugging tool. Today, those print statements are metrics, traces and logs.

## Who should watch

Anyone running NGINX as a web server, reverse proxy or load balancer without a clear answer to which five graphs to open first during an incident.

- Prathamesh Sonpatki's [The Complete Handbook to OpenTelemetry Metrics](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Prathamesh_Sonpatki_handbook_opentelemetry_metrics) goes deeper on the metrics model.
- Nicolas Frankel's [Practical introduction to OpenTelemetry tracing](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Nicolas_Frankel_opentelemetry_tracing) covers the tracing side.
- Sandeep Bhat's [Developing custom Load Balancer using Envoy](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Sandeep_Bhat_custom_load_balancer_envoy) looks at the proxy layer from the Envoy side.

Title: Real-time topology turns Kubernetes logs and metrics into a map
Description: Amir Krayden of Senser at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on why logs, metrics and traces miss Kubernetes failures, and how eBPF-built topology adds the missing context.
Body:
The problem with logs, Amir Krayden likes to say, is that they require more logs, and rarely in the same place. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, the co-founder and CPO of Senser argued that Kubernetes troubleshooting fails less for lack of telemetry than for lack of context, and that a continuously updated, eBPF-built topology of the cluster is the cheapest way to add it.

Senser sells in this space, but the talk is about the concept, not the product: Amir closes with tips that apply whether you use a commercial tool or open source.

## Why Kubernetes is hard to debug

Amir's list of reasons will be familiar to anyone who has held a pager for a cluster. The system is distributed, so a monolith's closed, debuggable box is gone. The line between application and infrastructure issue is blurred, because Kubernetes is itself a software layer. Pods come and go, and CI/CD pipelines keep changing config and code, so you're aiming at a moving target. Networking stacks abstraction on abstraction (DNS, proxies, CNI plugins) until sniffing packets tells you little. Noisy neighbours on a shared node make your metrics lie. Third-party containers are black boxes.

## Three pillars, built for monoliths

The classic toolkit, he argues, grew up in a world where you could see the whole application. Metrics are just numbers until something tells you whether a CPU spike is worrying or normal. Logs are fragmented, and only an engineer can tell whether a lost database connection logged in a client pod relates to an entry in the database pod. Traces show service interactions, but full instrumentation is like full code coverage: everyone wants it, and the gap between wanting and having is large, especially for legacy code.

## Topology is how engineers already think

The core idea is that troubleshooting is backtracing. An API returns an error; you check its logs and metrics, then step back to the database transaction behind it, and so on. You're walking a path on a graph whether or not you have one drawn. A static architecture diagram goes stale; a dependency map refreshed every few minutes is better; real-time topology updates continuously with new services, deployments and interactions, down to which APIs and transactions flow between elements, plus the infrastructure underneath.

Amir walks three scenarios. A pod failing readiness probes due to slow storage becomes obvious once the map shows what it depends on. Horizontal pod autoscaling under high traffic that ends in throttling becomes recognisable as an infrastructure issue when you can see the nodes and node groups behind the new pods, and knowing that, he says, is already half the solution. A misconfigured network policy shows up as a connection you expected to see but don't.

## Why eBPF is the enabler

You can derive topology from distributed traces if you're fully instrumented. The approach Amir focuses on is eBPF: small, safe programs running in the Linux kernel that hook networking, kernel calls and application calls. That gives you API-level visibility, including encrypted HTTP/2 streams, without changing application code, with low overhead if implemented well, and on every node by default because it's native to Linux.

On top of the raw data you need a data model, so the topology recognises a new pod, a node group or a database as the same kind of thing every time, without manual updates.

## The pitfalls

His warnings are useful: a map is only as good as its data, so incomplete instrumentation produces a map nobody trusts. Stale maps mean deciding today on yesterday's data. And topology is rarely a smoking gun; it points you towards the root cause rather than naming it. Start small, apply the Pareto rule, lean on Kubernetes metadata like labels, config maps and events, and grow the model as you go.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who spend incidents correlating dashboards by hand, and teams evaluating eBPF-based observability who want the reasoning before the vendor demos.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Amir Krayden's [Bridging the Gap: Real-Time Topology as the Connective Tissue Between Platform Engineering and SRE](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Amir_Krayden_topology_engineering_sre) applies the same idea to platform teams.
- Shahar Azulay's [True Kubernetes Observability with eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Shahar_Azulay_kubernetes_observability_ebpf) covers the instrumentation layer.
- Nikolay Sivko's [Zero-instrumentation observability based on eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2024_Nikolay_Sivko_zeroinstrumentation_observability_ebpf) shows what you get without touching code.
