Title: How Meta speeds up ML prototyping with Bento notebooks and Conda
Description: Parul Gupta of Meta at Conf42 Python 2025 on Bento, Meta's internal Jupyter, plus Conda environments as notebook kernels to shorten research-to-prod.
Body:
The slow part of shipping a model is often the loop before production: massaging data, trying a hypothesis, losing the kernel when the laptop sleeps, starting again. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Parul Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Parul_Gupta_ai_ml_prototyping), a production engineer on Meta's Python Language Foundation team, described how Meta attacks that loop with Bento, its internal Jupyter distribution, and with Conda environments that escape the monorepo's one-version rule.

It is a short talk and a tour of ideas rather than a how-to. Nothing here is downloadable; the value is seeing which annoyances a company of Meta's size decided were worth engineering away.

## The AI lifecycle is a loop with lots of back-arrows

Gupta opens with a confession: when she started, she thought the AI lifecycle was linear. Collect data, train, test, deploy, done. It turned out to be a cycle full of revisions: product scoping, data engineering, model development, deployment, monitoring, business analysis, with arrows going backwards between most of them. She calls the data engineering and model development stages ML prototyping, and argues that making them faster speeds up the whole delivery of AI.

The standard tools for that stage are Jupyter notebooks (language-agnostic, backend-agnostic, good for feature work and hacky experiments) and Conda (isolated environments with pinned packages). Meta's work is about bending both to its scale.

## Bento: notebooks that survive Wi-Fi

Bento is Meta's internal Jupyter, tuned to the internal codebase and able to run code on different servers inside the company. The improvements she lists:

- **Scheduled notebooks.** Inspired by Papermill, Bento can rerun a notebook at any cadence on any server, privacy-aware, for recurring reports and model checks.
- **Persistent sessions.** Lose the network or close the laptop and a long-running execution keeps going; reopen the session later, possibly from another server, and the computed data is still there. Anyone who has watched a four-hour cell die with the Wi-Fi will understand why this one exists.
- **Cross-platform debugging.** One click on a Python file in VS Code at Meta drops you into a debugging session or a notebook with the dependencies you need, and notebooks also run inside VS Code, so moving in and out of the IDE is cheap.

She also mentions data privacy and security review integrations, serverless support, better SQL cells, multi-language kernels and autosuggestions from internally developed GenAI agents, without going into each.

## Conda versus the monorepo

The second half is about versions. Meta is a large monorepo with one version of each dependency across all projects. That is great for consistency and painful for a researcher who wants to try a different library version before committing to it. Conda sits at the other end: full control of dependencies, packaged as a portable, self-contained environment the user can reach from anywhere. Meta's Conda setup also adds telemetry on errors, package usage and vulnerability checks, so freedom doesn't mean flying blind. Gupta presents it as a newer addition meant to bring the open source experience inside in a controlled way, so researchers onboard faster and can work with their GitHub projects more freely.

## The combination is the point

Her last idea is the one to take home: run a Conda environment as the Jupyter kernel behind a notebook. Researchers get the notebook's interactivity and the environment's version freedom at once, which she says brought research and production development much closer together and reduced cost. She does not give numbers, so take it as a design pattern rather than a benchmark.

## Who should watch

Platform and developer-experience engineers who support data scientists, especially in monorepo shops wrestling with the same version tension. Individual data scientists will mostly get ideas to ask their platform team for.

- [Affordable ML Platform](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Zhiya_Zang_affordable_platform) by Zhiya Zang of TikTok at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, another big-company view of ML tooling.

[Watch Parul Gupta's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Parul_Gupta_ai_ml_prototyping) or the [YouTube recording](https://youtu.be/GqIgy_wVNfA).

Title: A ReAct agent in Python with LangGraph, Granite and three tools
Description: Anna Gutowska of IBM at Conf42 Python 2025 on what AI agents add to LLMs, then a live LangGraph ReAct agent on Granite 3.1 with three tools.
Body:
Ask an LLM today's date and it can't tell you; give it a tool and it can. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Anna Gutowska](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Anna_Gutowska_ai_agents_customizing), a data scientist in developer advocacy at IBM, used that gap to explain what an AI agent actually adds to a model, then built one live: a ReAct agent in LangGraph on IBM's Granite 3.1 8B Instruct, with tools for weather, YouTube search and online shopping.

It is an introduction with a working demo, and since the speaker works at IBM, the demo runs on watsonx.ai. The LangChain and LangGraph parts carry over to other model providers.

## Agents are LLMs that plan, call tools and check themselves

Gutowska's definition: a system that autonomously performs tasks for a user by designing its own workflow and using available tools. She breaks it into three stages. Goal initialisation and planning: extract the main goal from the query and split it into subtasks. Tool calling: fill the gaps in the model's training data with external datasets, web search, APIs or even other agents, updating the plan as results come in. Learning and reflection: feedback from other agents or a human in the loop, plus a store of past solutions so the same mistakes aren't repeated.

Her running example is mundane on purpose. "How many vacation days do I have left?" An LLM alone either hallucinates or admits it can't know. The same LLM with a tool that queries an HR database answers correctly. Nothing about the model changed; the system around it did.

## ReAct, not the JavaScript one

The reasoning pattern she uses is ReAct, short for reasoning and action, and "not to be confused with the JS framework", as she has learned once before. The agent extracts subtasks, picks tools, executes, then judges whether the output is good enough and loops if not. She also covers multi-agent systems: centralised designs are easy to coordinate but fail if the central unit fails; decentralised ones are robust but harder to coordinate. Either way, more agents means more chances of malfunction, infinite feedback loops and unpredictable behaviour, so she recommends ways to interrupt the system, human supervision and thorough testing before trusting agents with anything sensitive.

## The demo: tool binding versus a real agent

The notebook (published on GitHub and IBM.com) sets up watsonx.ai credentials, loads Granite 3.1 8B Instruct through LangChain's ChatWatsonx wrapper with temperature set to zero to limit hallucination, and defines three tools: OpenWeatherMap, YouTube search and Ionic, an e-commerce search tool.

The useful moment comes before the agent exists. With only `bind_tools`, asking for YouTube videos about Greece makes the model pick the right tool and extract "Greece" as the argument, but no tool actually runs and no answer comes back. Then `create_react_agent` from LangGraph wraps the same model and tools, and the message trace shows the human message, the AI's tool choice, the tool message with real results, and a synthesised answer with video titles and links. That contrast is the cleanest explanation of the difference between tool calling and an agent you'll find in half an hour.

Two more queries test tool selection: the weather in Athens, which comes back with temperature, wind, humidity and cloud cover, and suitcases under 10,000 cents. That last one is a gotcha worth remembering: Ionic prices are in US cents, so 10,000 means 100 dollars.

## Who should watch

Python developers who have used an LLM API and want to see the step from a model that merely suggests a function call to a system that runs it and answers. People already shipping LangGraph agents will find it basic.

- [Building a Production-Ready Voice AI Agent with LangGraph, RAG and Evaluation](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Arjun_Thakur_voice_langgraph_rag) by Arjun Thakur at Conf42 MLOps 2026, LangGraph taken to production.
- [From 150K to 22K Tokens: Context Engineering for MCP Tool-Calling](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2026_Nishant_Kumar_Thakur_Sonam_Raj_mcp_tokens_context) by Nishant Kumar Thakur and Sonam Raj at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, on what happens when the tool list gets long.

Title: Where LLMs fit in each stage of the DevOps lifecycle
Description: Ajay Krishnan Prabhakaran of Meta at Conf42 DevOps 2025 maps LLM uses across DevOps: code generation, reviews, IaC templates, chatops and docs.
Body:
Imagine a teammate who never sleeps, has read every line of the codebase and writes scripts faster than you. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Ajay Krishnan Prabhakaran, a data engineer at Meta, used that pitch to open a guided tour of where large language models plug into DevOps work: planning, coding, testing, deployment, infrastructure and team knowledge.

Set expectations correctly: this is an introductory map, not a case study. There are no benchmarks or production numbers, and Ajay doesn't claim any. What you get is a structured checklist of places to try an LLM, which is useful if your team is still arguing about where to start.

## A map, stage by stage

Ajay walks the lifecycle in order. In planning, an LLM can look at historical data and trends to suggest improvements and realistic goals. In coding, it offers generation, suggestions and debugging help. In testing and deployment, it can automate repetitive work like running suites and deploying applications, and flag likely problems before they hit production.

That framing is the talk's main contribution. Instead of a pile of use cases, you get a pipeline with an LLM-shaped slot at each step, which makes it easier to ask which slot your team actually has a problem in.

## More than autocomplete

The code generation section goes wider than writing functions. Ajay lists boilerplate for common patterns, translating code between languages (handy during migrations), producing unit and integration tests, and tailoring output to project constraints. On the editor side: suggestions that match your style, errors flagged as you type, and refactoring for readability.

LLMs also help with code review, spotting potential issues and suggesting fixes so best practices hold across the team. That's the cheapest experiment on the list, because a reviewer bot that's wrong costs a dismissed comment, not an outage.

## Terraform templates and the cloud bill

For infrastructure as code, Ajay points to LLMs generating Terraform and Ansible templates for AWS, Azure and GCP, so provisioning becomes consistent and repeatable across environments. He also suggests exploring LLMs for cost: analysing usage patterns and resource allocation to recommend where you're over-provisioned.

That second idea is phrased as something to explore rather than a solved problem, which is the honest framing. Generated IaC still needs the same review as hand-written IaC; the talk's benefit list assumes you keep that gate.

## Chatops and docs that stay current

The collaboration section may matter most day to day. Ajay describes LLMs in chat platforms answering debugging and troubleshooting questions, acting as a central knowledge base, answering questions about code and systems, and keeping documentation current, which matters for onboarding. He frames this as closing the gap between development and operations teams. He also mentions predictive maintenance: reading logs and metrics to anticipate problems before they occur.

His outlook is more specialised models for specific DevOps tasks and deeper integration with existing tools, so teams don't have to change their toolchain to benefit.

## Who should watch

Engineering leads drafting an AI adoption plan who want a complete list of candidate use cases, and DevOps engineers new to LLMs who want the vocabulary. If you already run AI review bots and agentic remediation in production, you'll find little new; pair it with one of the case studies below instead.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Niraj Katkamwar's [Prompt-Driven Microservice & Database Evolution: Using LLMs for Automated Schema Migration and DevOps Delivery](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Niraj_Katkamwar_llm_agents_delivery) applies the idea to schema changes.
- Deepanshu Kukreja's [AI Agents for DevSecOps: Automating Secure Infrastructure, Delivery, and Incident Response](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Deepanshu_Kukreja_agents_automation_incidentresponse) brings agents into the security side.

Title: Payment fraud defence needs three kinds of model, plus biometrics
Description: Vinod Upputuri of Mastercard at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on layered fraud detection: supervised, unsupervised and deep models, biometrics, synthetic IDs and NLP.
Body:
Fraud teams fight two errors at once: the stolen card that gets through, and the honest customer whose dinner payment gets declined. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Vinod Upputuri, a senior software engineer at Mastercard with more than 11 years in the financial domain, laid out how a layered AI system attacks both, from detection models to behavioural signals to phishing filters.

It's a compact talk, about a quarter of an hour, built as a tour of techniques with headline results for each. It's an architecture overview, not a code walkthrough.

## Why false positives are half the problem

Vinod's framing is that false positives deserve as much attention as missed fraud. Declined legitimate transactions disrupt customers, while missed fraud costs money; both erode trust, which he calls the essential asset in finance. The abstract sums up the headline results: 97% accuracy in real-time threat detection and false positives down by 63%.

## Three model families, three jobs

The detection section splits the work by what each model family is good at:

- **Supervised learning** trains on labelled historic transactions to recognise known fraud patterns and works in real time, stopping a fraudulent transaction before it completes.
- **Unsupervised learning** finds irregularities in unlabelled data, which is how you catch tactics nobody has labelled yet. Vinod credits it with a 42 percent improvement in fraud identification rate.
- **Deep neural networks** examine over 10,000 data points per transaction within milliseconds, and he credits them with a 76 percent reduction in card-present fraud.

The useful takeaway is the division of labour. Supervised models know yesterday's fraud, unsupervised ones flag today's oddities, and deep models find patterns too subtle for either.

## The latency budget is the product

All of that has to run inside a payment flow. Vinod describes a real-time system handling 100,000 transactions per second with analysis under 50 milliseconds, running around the clock with constant monitoring and instant alerts. For a DevOps audience, that's the interesting constraint: a fraud model that needs a second is a fraud model nobody can deploy in the authorisation path.

## Watching how you type, not just what you buy

Prevention adds signals beyond the transaction itself. Behavioural biometrics look at typing rhythm, mouse movement and scrolling habits to keep authenticating a user throughout a session; a sudden change in typing pattern mid-transaction is a flag. Device fingerprinting checks the operating system, hardware and IP address for unfamiliar devices. Together, he says, they cut account takeover attempts by 89 percent.

Two more layers round it out. Synthetic identity detection cross-checks data like social security numbers and credit history across sources to catch fabricated identities, with a 94 percent success rate cited. NLP scans over a million daily interactions for phishing signals such as urgent calls to action, blocking 98 percent of attempts per the talk.

## Implementation is compliance plus teamwork

The closing section is about rollout: regulatory compliance and transparency first, user experience protected, continuous learning so models keep up with new tactics, and cross-functional work between IT, security and business units. Reported outcomes include 91 percent customer satisfaction and fraud investigations down 73 percent.

## Who should watch

Engineers joining a payments or risk team who want a one-sitting map of the fraud stack, and platform engineers who will have to host these models under tight latency budgets. The figures are the speaker's headline results, presented without methodology, so treat them as orientation rather than benchmarks.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Sandeep Katuri's [AI-Powered Fraud Detection in Cloud-Native Digital Payments: Real-Time Security and Future Innovations](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Sandeep_Katuri_fraud_detection_digital_payments_security) covers the cloud-native deployment side.
- Sridhar Muthineni's [AI-Driven Fraud Detection & Personalization in Scalable Go Fintech Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sridhar_Muthineni_driven_fraud_detection) builds it in Go.
- Ndubuisi Obirije's [Impact of AI in detecting and monitoring fraudulent payments from social engineering](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Ndubuisi_Obirije_30_ai_fraudulent_payments) focuses on the social engineering angle.

Title: GraphQL on FastAPI, from the first schema to federation
Description: Aby M Joseph and Jayalekshmi K S of UST at Conf42 Python 2025 on pairing GraphQL with FastAPI and Graphene, then federating microservices behind one graph.
Body:
REST gives every client the same plate of food, whether it wanted the whole meal or one chip. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Aby M Joseph and Jayalekshmi K S](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Aby_M_Joseph_Jayalekshmi_K_S_graphql_microservices_fastapi), both Product Engineers at UST, showed how GraphQL fixes that mismatch, how FastAPI hosts it with a few lines of Graphene, and how GraphQL Federation lets several Python services answer as one graph.

The pair build Strollby, a travel platform, on GraphQL microservices in Python, and they are part of a Python community in Kerala. This is an introduction: if you have never written a GraphQL schema, it is a tidy first half hour. If you run Apollo Federation in production, skip to the last section of the video.

## Overfetching and underfetching are the real bill

The talk starts with the two classic REST failures. Underfetching: you need a user and their posts, so you call `/users` and then `/posts`, paying for two round trips. Overfetching: you need a first name, and `/users` hands you the address, the email and everything else, which hurts most on a phone with a weak signal. Add a web app, a mobile app and a dashboard that each want different fields, and teams end up versioning the API just to avoid breaking old clients.

GraphQL answers with a single `/graphql` endpoint and a schema that acts as the contract between front end and back end. The client asks for exactly the fields it wants; the server resolves them from whatever sits behind it (a user database, an order service, a third-party transaction API) and returns one JSON response.

## Queries, mutations, subscriptions, and a burger

Joseph walks through the three operations: queries to read, mutations to change data and get the new values back in the same response, and subscriptions that hold an open connection so the server pushes updates (notifications, dashboards) instead of the client polling.

The memorable bit is the restaurant analogy. REST is the fixed menu: you get the whole classic burger with lettuce, tomato and cheese. GraphQL is the place where you name your toppings. The waiter is the schema, telling you what toppings exist; the chef is the resolver, cooking only what you ordered. It is a good analogy to steal for the next time a product manager asks why the mobile team wants GraphQL.

On the Python side he splits libraries into code-first (Graphene, Strawberry: types and resolvers are Python classes) and schema-first (write SDL, implement resolvers in Python), the latter for teams that want the schema separate from the business logic.

## FastAPI does the plumbing

Jayalekshmi K S takes the FastAPI half. The stack she describes: Starlette underneath for routing, middleware and concurrency; Pydantic driven by type hints for validation and serialisation; Uvicorn with uvloop as the ASGI server. On top come OpenAPI and JSON Schema generation, Swagger UI docs, async support, dependency injection and middleware.

The demo is deliberately small. Import Graphene, FastAPI, Uvicorn and starlette-graphene3; define a `Post` type with an ID, a title and a summary; add a `Query` class whose resolver returns a hardcoded post; mount the GraphQL app at `/graphql`. Running a query for id, title and summary returns exactly those fields. The hardcoded resolver is where your database call would go.

## Federation: each service owns its fields

The closing section is the one microservice people should watch. With GraphQL Federation, a router sits in front of several GraphQL services and presents a single graph. Her example `Post` type gets its title from a post service, its reviews from a review service and its author from a user service. Each service defines only what it owns, and the federation layer stitches the response together, so the client never writes join logic. The speakers say plainly that there is much more to learn here; treat it as the map, not the territory.

## Who should watch

Python backend developers weighing GraphQL for a new service, and REST teams tired of versioning endpoints for each new client. Engineers already running federated graphs will find the basics familiar.

Title: Dunder methods make your classes feel built in, if you show restraint
Description: Eti Ijeoma of Manufactured Networks at Conf42 Python 2025 on using __add__, __eq__, __iter__ and friends to make custom classes intuitive, and when not to.
Body:
Add two of your own objects in Python and you get a `TypeError`. Add two NumPy arrays and it just works. At Conf42 Python 2025, [Eti Ijeoma](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Eti_Ijeoma_python_dunder_methods), a software engineer at Manufactured Networks, explained that the difference is a handful of double-underscore methods, built a small `Point` class to prove it, and then spent a welcome chunk of the talk on when you should leave them alone.

It is a beginner-to-intermediate talk. If you already write `__getitem__` without thinking, the value is in the list of things not to do at the end.

## The interpreter is calling your methods all along

Ijeoma's framing is that dunder (or "magic") methods are not magic at all. They are hooks the interpreter calls at defined moments. `len(x)` calls `x.__len__()`. `print(x)` asks `__str__` or `__repr__` what to show. `a + b` looks for `__add__`. Once you see that, the libraries you use every day look different: NumPy makes array addition read like arithmetic through `__add__`, and SQLAlchemy lets you write filters with `==` because its column objects implement `__eq__` to build SQL instead of returning a boolean.

One rule she stresses early: you can't invent your own. Writing `__custom__` on a class does nothing, because Python only calls the names it already knows. The full list lives in the Python data model documentation.

## A Point class, one operator at a time

The demo grows a `Point` step by step, and each step fixes a visible annoyance:

- `__init__` stores x and y, as usual.
- Printing shows the default type and memory address, which helps nobody, so `__repr__` returns something like a point at 2 and 3.
- Adding two points raises "unsupported operand types", so `__add__` adds the coordinates and returns a new `Point`.
- Two points with the same coordinates compare as not equal until `__eq__` compares x and y.
- `__mul__` scales a point by a number.
- `__iter__` makes the point iterable, so you can loop over its coordinates like a native collection.

Nothing here is exotic, and that is the point: six short methods and the class behaves like it shipped with the language.

## The don't list is the best part

Ijeoma argues that dunders make code clearer only when the operator means what readers expect. Her anti-patterns:

- A `Calculator` whose `__add__` multiplies. Technically legal, practically a trap.
- Implementing `__call__` because you can, especially when calling the object quietly adds numbers.
- Making up dunder names, which Python will never call and colleagues will puzzle over. Use a regular method.
- Implementing every dunder on one class until nobody can predict what an operator does.
- Trading readability for cleverness. It may look cool; it will be hard to maintain.

Her examples of good fits are domain ones: `__add__` in a graphics library where adding vectors is natural, `__eq__` in a game library for collision checks. Operator overloading is a promise about meaning, and the talk is really about keeping that promise.

## Who should watch

Python developers who write libraries or internal SDKs and want their objects to read like the standard library, and anyone who has met a surprising `+` in a codebase and wants vocabulary for the code review. Seasoned library authors can skim to the anti-patterns.

- [The Enters and Exits of Context Managers](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Mason_Egger_context_managers) by Mason Egger of DigitalOcean at Conf42 Python 2021, on `__enter__` and `__exit__`.
- [How Decorators Function](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2022_Andrew_Knight_how_decorators_function) by Andrew Knight of Applitools at Conf42 Python 2022, another piece of Python that looks like magic until you see the mechanism.

Title: Infosys mined five years of build logs to let agents fix CI failures
Description: Rajeshwari Ganesan and Chidambaram Ganapathy Sundaram of Infosys at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on a multi-agent LLM system for build failures across 100 apps.
Body:
A red build is cheap once and expensive a thousand times a month. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Rajeshwari Ganesan, distinguished technologist for ML/AI at Infosys, presented the multi-agent LLM system she and architect Chidambaram Ganapathy Sundaram built to diagnose and resolve build failures across roughly 100 internal enterprise applications. Measured from January to September 2024, average mean time to resolve dropped from four hours to 2.2.

It is an enterprise case study with real architecture diagrams, and the most transferable lesson is about evaluation, not agents.

## The goldmine was the logs

Before any model, the team had five years of build logs, about 500,000 of them, from applications running across 56 countries. They filtered out about 10,000 failure logs, stripped PII, studied the error distribution and turned the cleaned set into an evaluation dataset.

The analysis alone is worth hearing. Failure rates climbed once commits passed a certain size, and failures clustered late in the working day and on weekends. Finance applications had the highest failure rates among internal platforms, followed by developer productivity and HR tooling; by stack, Java led. The estate was deliberately messy: on-prem, cloud-native and hybrid, legacy and new, COTS products and containers.

## Prompts are perishable

The system evolved in steps. First, prompts over the logs with Azure OpenAI GPT-3.5. Then RAG for domain knowledge. Then GPT-4 and Anthropic's Claude, which forced a hard requirement: model swappability. The lesson Rajeshwari stresses is that a model change, even within the same family, can break your prompts. Their accuracy was 82 percent on GPT-3.5, improved on GPT-4, and dropped when they moved to the cheaper GPT-4o mini because the prompts no longer worked.

So they built three supporting pieces: an LLM hub to select and swap models (including your own fine-tuned small model, since frontier models can't be fine-tuned), prompt management with evaluations on every model change, and an evaluation chassis that runs automatically against the benchmark built from historic logs.

## Why agents, and which ones

Rajeshwari is careful about cost: agentic systems run several LLM calls where one used to do, so you need a reason. Hers is that DevOps is a partially observable domain, where you decide under uncertainty with incomplete data, and that calls for reasoning. Falling model prices and longer context windows made it viable.

The design has an orchestrator over four agents. The build agent has its own sub-agents: log analysis to extract failures, diagnosis to classify them (performance, security and so on), resolution to propose the fix from logs and artifacts, and notification. The agents call ordinary tools: SonarQube for static analysis, Git commit insights, Jira and Confluence for past fixes, and privacy masking for anything with PII.

## A judge is only as good as a solver

For evaluation they use LLM as a judge: a second model scores the first model's output and must give supporting evidence, not just a number. Citing a benchmark paper, she shows the same Claude model scoring differently as solver and as judge on a coding task, with the takeaway that a model's ability to judge solutions tracks its ability to solve the problem.

## The results, human ones included

Besides the MTTR drop, the team reports resolution quality up by about 30 percent and operating cost down 25 percent. The metric she calls out first, though, is team satisfaction: DevOps engineers who used to absorb repetitive escalations over Christmas and Thanksgiving were noticeably happier.

## Who should watch

Platform teams with a large, heterogeneous CI estate and a pile of historical logs they've never looked at, and anyone building agentic tooling who hasn't yet budgeted for prompt regression testing.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Chinmay Gaikwad's [Building Enterprise-ready CI/CD Pipelines using Agentic AI](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Chinmay_Gaikwad_cicd_agentic_ai) takes agents further into the pipeline.
- Liran Yushinsky's [Who Judges the AI Agent? LLM-as-Judge for Testing Non-Deterministic Code Generation](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Liran_Yushinsky_testing_judge_codegen) expands the judge idea.
- Hilik Paz's [How to evaluate your Evals?](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Hilik_Paz_evaluate_evals) asks whether your evaluation chassis can be trusted.

Title: In most large orgs, SRE and DevOps are one job wearing two badges
Description: Nagarjuna Malladi of Oracle at Conf42 DevOps 2025 maps where SRE and DevOps meet: observability, capacity planning, automation and AI-assisted remediation.
Body:
If you build the pipeline, you will probably end up watching what it deploys. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Nagarjuna Malladi, principal SRE at Oracle, argued that in large organisations the DevOps and SRE roles have already merged in practice, and that resilience comes from treating them as one loop: deploy, observe, plan capacity, automate the fix, repeat.

This is an overview talk. It covers a lot of ground at survey depth, and its value is in the war stories Nagarjuna hangs on each slide rather than in any single technique.

## One engineer, both halves of the loop

His starting example is his own time at Cisco on the DNA Center networking side. He wrote the Jenkins pipelines, deployed to virtual machines and AWS, and then had to go back and check CPU, memory and disk to see how the deployment was behaving. For internal customers in a big company, he estimates, you end up doing both the DevOps side and the SRE side in nearly every case.

The glue between those halves is ticketing and chat-driven alerting. Nobody can log into a thousand servers to look for an error, so the system has to raise the ticket and post to Slack or Webex, and changes move from lower to higher environments in a controlled way.

## Prometheus finds it, Grafana tells someone

The observability section is the most hands-on part. Nagarjuna's pitch for Prometheus is its exporters: URL checks, certificate expiry dates, system and network performance, Linux and Windows services, all through the same model. Grafana then visualises it and sends alerts straight to Slack, Webex, email or a ticketing system.

He ties the same stack to the question every finance team asks: why is storage growing, why is CPU scaling, what does it cost, and can anything be reused? Capacity planning, in his framing, is cost management with graphs. For logs he lists the ELK stack, Splunk and OpenSearch, whatever your company already runs.

## Restart the database before you page the human

The AI and automation slides are where the examples get concrete. One is a hypothetical retailer with a hundred stores in Texas, all monitored from a Dallas hub. If a router in Houston drops, someone drives or flies there while the store is closed, or a monitored, automated fleet lets the operator push a firmware update remotely with no downtime.

Another is a full database taking down healthcare trials. His suggested first response is automated: restart the database, capture the error messages into a separate log for later debugging, or tune it and trim unwanted logs before it fills up. That is the shape of most good auto-remediation: a safe first step, plus enough evidence for a human to find the real cause later.

## Every industry has its own definition of down

Nagarjuna spends time on why requirements differ by sector. Healthcare has strict protocols. Banking lives and dies by security. Retail has Black Friday, and his MacBook test: if checkout takes five or ten minutes, would you still buy it? The SLO you pick has to come from that context, not from a template.

His closing advice is cultural more than technical: whatever your role, from developer to sales, think like an SRE and chase the root cause instead of the quick fix.

## Who should watch

Developers and ops engineers moving into an SRE role who want a map of the territory, and managers who need a vocabulary for why the two teams keep overlapping. Experienced SREs will know the material; the Cisco and retail examples are the parts worth hearing.

Title: Incident response borrowed from wildfire crews, minus the panic
Description: Daniel Afonso of PagerDuty at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on incident command roles, clear severity definitions, checklists and the executive swoop.
Body:
The fastest way to make an outage longer is to have nobody in charge of it. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Daniel Afonso, senior developer advocate at PagerDuty, walked through the incident response process PagerDuty runs on itself. It is built on the Incident Command System that firefighters created after the 1970s Southern California wildfires, and his point is that the structure, more than heroics, is what turns chaos into calm.

The talk is a practical tour of process, with no product demo. If your team already has an incident commander rota and a postmortem habit, it's a good calibration check. If it doesn't, it's a starter kit.

## Define "incident" before production defines it for you

Daniel's first step sounds almost too obvious: agree on what an incident is. Ask around and different companies, and often different teams, give different answers. PagerDuty's version is any unplanned disruption or degradation of service that is actively affecting customers' ability to use the product. A major incident is any incident that needs a coordinated response between multiple teams.

The useful advice is to tie both to business metrics, not host metrics. A high CPU reading tells you how a piece of equipment is doing. PagerDuty watches outbound notifications per second; he suggests orders per second as the Amazon-style equivalent and stream starts for Netflix. A threshold such as more than 100 errors per minute, or more than 5 percent of customers affected, ends the argument over whether this is really a major incident before it starts, which matters, because nobody wants that debate while the house is on fire.

Crossing that line also changes the rules. Practices that would be unacceptable in normal operations, like shipping a fix without tests, can become the right call during a major incident. And a wrong decision beats no decision: it at least gives you new information.

## Make triggering cheap, then follow the same loop

PagerDuty triggers automatically where reliable business metrics exist, and also lets any human trigger a response with a chat command. Lowering that barrier, Daniel says, speeds up resolution dramatically; if customer support is suddenly flooded, nobody should wait for the alarm. Flashing lights or a mariachi band are also acceptable, he notes, as long as the mechanism is fast and available to everyone.

From there the loop is fixed: triage, mobilize, resolve, prevent.

## The incident commander outranks the CEO

The roles are where ICS earns its keep. The incident commander is the single source of truth and approves every action, and they don't need deep technical knowledge, only command of the process. A scribe keeps the timeline in a dedicated Slack channel so anyone can read status without joining the call. A deputy is the commander's right hand, not a spectator. Internal and customer liaisons handle communication, including the status page. Subject matter experts, paged first, do the fixing.

Preparation is drill work. PagerDuty runs Failure Fridays, treats some low-severity incidents as major ones for practice, and keeps checklists the way pilots do, because stressed people forget steps. Then comes the post-incident review, which Daniel credits for how the process improved over the years.

## The executive swoop

The most fun section covers pitfalls, led by the executive swoop. An executive drops in asking for a fix within 10 minutes, or a list of impacted customers right now, or tells responders to do something big. None of it is malicious, and all of it pulls people off the fix. The commander's counter is polite and effective: ask whether they wish to take command. Most don't. The prevention is boring and works: regular stakeholder updates, internally every 30 minutes or right after a change.

Other traps on his list: red herrings (everyone blames the network, nobody checks the recent deploy), debating severity mid-call, all-hands-on-deck calls, keeping people on the bridge at 3am when they're no longer contributing, and reading silence as a lack of progress.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers setting up a first on-call process, SREs who keep ending up as the accidental incident commander, and anyone who has watched an executive join a bridge and felt the temperature rise. Teams with a mature ICS-style process will recognise most of it; the pitfalls section is still worth the time. Daniel also points to PagerDuty's open incident response guide at response.pagerduty.com for the full version.

Title: Open-source monitoring and logging on a startup budget
Description: Pradeep Gaddamidi at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on building logging and monitoring with Elasticsearch, Prometheus and Grafana when money is tight.
Body:
The free tier of Elasticsearch will not send your alerts to Slack. Pradeep Gaddamidi, a DevOps engineer at Evernote, found that out while building logging and monitoring for a budget-tight startup, and his Conf42 DevOps 2025 talk is a field report from that job: choosing open-source tools, sizing hardware, automating everything, picking the first SLIs, and handling incidents and workload when you are the whole team.

## Check every requirement before you choose free

His first lesson is to research before committing to open source and tick off every requirement your organisation actually has. The Slack alerting gap is his example. The workaround was a Python script that filtered alerts from the Kibana server log and posted them through a Slack webhook. It worked, but he calls it a backdoor, and the next missing feature might matter more.

Hardware is the second lever. Reading the Elasticsearch docs showed that not every node needs the same resources: master nodes are light and went on small VMs, while data nodes do the indexing and searching and got high-CPU machines. Paying for what each role needs is the cheapest optimisation there is.

## Automate even when it feels slower

For monitoring he used Grafana, Prometheus, Mimir and InfluxDB on a Kubernetes cluster, deployed with Helm charts. Infrastructure went through Terraform, and Ansible configured the Elasticsearch instances. Grafana dashboards live in Git and are deployed by CI/CD, so if someone breaks a dashboard he can recreate it by rerunning the pipeline. The payoff showed when logs grew: adding data nodes meant a few new entries in Terraform and a run, and the nodes were up within minutes. Click-ops is quicker on day one and slower forever after.

## Start with saturation

On SLIs his advice is to begin with basic alerts rather than fancy dashboards. Availability, latency, error rate, throughput and traffic all matter eventually, but for a startup he would watch saturation first: CPU load, memory, network bandwidth. Knowing how full the system is tells you whether it can handle the load before you tune anything else.

## Toil causes the incidents you inflict on yourself

He splits incidents into self-inflicted and natural. His self-inflicted one is honest: short on time, he never set up disk alerts on Elasticsearch and kept cleaning a full `/tmp` by hand, until the day it caused an incident. That is toil, and he suggests treating it as real work with its own tickets and team time. For the natural incidents, he wants proper root cause analysis and blameless postmortems, using the five whys. His chain goes from a failed disk to missing scaling to no time for the DevOps engineer, which lands on a planning problem, not a person.

## Say no, or say what is fragile

The last section is about workload. Commit only to what you can deliver. When he was given a week or two to build a complete logging and monitoring system, he built one with a single point of failure and told the team and management exactly that, so a failure would not be a surprise. Track work in tickets so it is visible, and document everything so you can hand over before a holiday.

## Who should watch

Solo DevOps and SRE engineers at small companies, and anyone asked to build observability with no budget. Teams on a paid observability platform can skip the tooling and still use the parts on toil and expectations.

Title: A phase 3 trial of sulopenem against resistant UTIs, explained
Description: Karthik Akinapelli of Takeda at Conf42 DevOps 2025 walks through a phase 3 trial of oral sulopenem versus ciprofloxacin in uncomplicated UTIs.
Body:
This one is not about pipelines. Karthik Akinapelli, Associate Director of Statistical Programming at Takeda, used his slot in the healthcare track at Conf42 DevOps 2025 to present the results of a phase 3 trial comparing sulopenem, an oral antibiotic, with ciprofloxacin for uncomplicated urinary tract infections in adult women. The headline: sulopenem was clearly better against pathogens resistant to ciprofloxacin, not as good against susceptible ones, and comparable overall.

For engineers, the appeal is watching how a clinical statistician reads a result: endpoints, populations, and why a "worse" number can turn out to be a good sign. It is not medical advice, and neither is this post.

## Why a new oral antibiotic

The background is fluoroquinolone resistance. When a first-line drug like ciprofloxacin stops working in outpatient settings, patients end up in hospital. Sulopenem is, as Karthik describes it, the first oral penem developed specifically for multi-drug resistant gram-negative uropathogens.

The trial was double blind: five days of sulopenem versus the standard three days of ciprofloxacin. The primary endpoint is composite, requiring both clinical symptom resolution and microbiological eradication at the test-of-cure visit on day 12.

## Who was in the numbers

1,672 women were enrolled; 1,660 made the safety population (at least one dose) and 1,072 the microbiological intent-to-treat population where the primary endpoint was measured. E. coli caused about 85 percent of infections, and 27 percent of those were not susceptible to ciprofloxacin. Around 13.5 percent of isolates produced extended-spectrum beta-lactamase, a marker of multi-drug resistance.

## Three results, three different stories

Against non-susceptible pathogens, sulopenem was superior, with a treatment difference of 26.6 percent. Against susceptible pathogens it did not reach non-inferiority: 66.8 percent response versus 78.6 for ciprofloxacin. Across the whole population it did reach non-inferiority, 65.6 versus 67.9.

The explanation is the interesting part. Clinical response at day 12 was similar (81.1 versus 84.1 percent overall, and 83 versus 62.6 in the resistant group). The gap came from asymptomatic bacteriuria: patients who feel cured but still have a positive culture, which the composite endpoint counts as failure. That was 15.2 percent with sulopenem versus 7.8 with ciprofloxacin, yet outcomes at the day-28 follow-up were equivalent. The trial's conclusion is that this likely reflects normal flora returning, not persistent infection. A metric that punishes the right behaviour is a problem engineers will recognise from their own dashboards.

## Resistance and side effects

After ciprofloxacin, 41.7 percent of initially susceptible pathogens developed resistance, and some picked up ESBL genes. Sulopenem's MIC distribution stayed stable. On safety, sulopenem had more adverse events (25 versus 14 percent), mainly diarrhoea (12.4 versus 2.5 percent), most of which resolved on its own. No deaths occurred.

Karthik is upfront about limitations: the trial predates updated treatment guidelines, including asymptomatic bacteriuria in the endpoint may not match clinical practice, and follow-up was too short to judge long-term resistance. His takeaway is that empiric ciprofloxacin should be avoided where resistance exceeds 10 percent, and that local resistance data belongs in prescribing decisions.

## Who should watch

Engineers building software for clinical research or healthcare data, and anyone curious how trial results are argued. If you came to Conf42 DevOps for Kubernetes, this is the scenic route.

- [Cloud-Native Data Engineering in Healthcare](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Santhosh_Kumar_Rai_data_engineering_healthcare_precision) by Santhosh Kumar Rai looks at the data side of precision medicine.

Title: What a Salesforce Health Cloud rollout changed for care teams
Description: Anirudh Peri of Lookout at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on a 2022-2024 study of Salesforce Health Cloud rollouts and the factors behind them.
Body:
Care coordination that used to take 48 hours took 12. That is one of the figures Anirudh Peri, Director of GTM Applications at Lookout, presents at Conf42 DevOps 2025 from a study of Salesforce Health Cloud implementations across multiple healthcare facilities between 2022 and 2024. The talk covers what improved, what made the rollouts work, and how another organisation could repeat it.

Honest scope: this is a talk about one vendor's CRM platform in healthcare, focused on outcomes and rollout strategy. There is little pipeline or infrastructure content despite the DevOps framing in the title, so watch it for the implementation lessons.

## The problems on the table

Anirudh lists the usual healthcare pain: patient data fragmented across systems, slow care coordination, delayed responses, and care gaps that turn into complications. Add operational inefficiency, poor resource allocation and strict regulation, and both patients and providers pay for it.

## The numbers he reports

From the study, he reports patient satisfaction scores rising from 78 to 91 in the first year, time spent on care coordination dropping by 75 percent (48 hours to 12), and response times between provider offices and patients falling by 83 percent. He partly credits AI chat for routine queries, so patients do not always need a person to get an answer. Care gap identification improved too, giving providers room for preventive action. On the operations side, he cites a 32 percent reduction in operational overhead from automation and better resource allocation.

These are figures from the study he presents; the talk does not break down how each was measured, so treat them as reported results.

## What made the rollouts work

The part most transferable to any large platform rollout is the list of success factors. Comprehensive staff training, which he says drove adoption up by 85 percent within six months. A phased deployment starting with pilots, which he says cut disruptions by 75 percent compared with traditional big-bang methods. And cross-functional collaboration between IT, clinical and administrative teams, so that people who had used different systems ended up working under one platform and could get answers across teams.

On the platform side, he points to a 360-degree patient view that consolidates records, automated alerts and reminders that keep patients on their care plans, secure messaging between care team members, and analytics dashboards so clinicians do not have to read every note. For compliance he names HIPAA-compliant data management, role-based access control and regular compliance training.

## How to repeat it

His closing advice is plain: assess current workflows and their inefficiencies, involve clinical, administrative and IT stakeholders early, tailor the implementation to the organisation instead of copying a template, and keep gathering feedback and metrics after go-live. Anyone who has run a migration will nod at the advice to phase the rollout through pilots; it is good to see it backed by numbers from a regulated industry.

Title: Shard the mutex when your cache is write-heavy
Description: Aleksander Iskhakov, CTO of Tools for Brokers, at Conf42 DevOps 2025 benchmarks sharded locking against mutexes and shared mutexes in C++.
Body:
A reader-writer lock is a great fix for read-heavy code and does nothing for write-heavy code. Aleksander Iskhakov, CTO at Tools for Brokers, uses that gap to frame his Conf42 DevOps 2025 talk on sharded synchronization: split a shared container into a fixed number of independently locked shards, and threads stop queueing behind one mutex. He shows it in C++, benchmarks it, and then warns you not to reach for it too early.

## The example: a transactional cache

The running example is concrete. A `std::map` keyed by user ID, each value a vector of transactions, with three operations: read a user's transactions, write a new one, and pop the accumulated transactions for processing. Access it from a thread pool without synchronisation and you get data races, plus nastier bugs, like writing through an address that went stale when the tree rebalanced after a pop.

Step one is a plain mutex with `lock_guard`. Correct, but under load the threads spend more and more time waiting, and transactions get processed late.

## Shared mutexes help only when reads dominate

Step two is a reader-writer lock: `std::shared_mutex`, with `shared_lock` for reads and a unique lock for writes. If most operations just check transactions, readers run in parallel and the occasional writer waits briefly. Aleksander says it works like a charm in read-heavy settings.

Then he flips the workload. Remove reads entirely, keep only write and pop (a cache bombarded with transactions from many threads, drained now and then for processing), and both operations modify the container. The shared mutex is now pointless and you are back to one operation at a time.

## Partition by key, lock per partition

The insight comes from the data: every operation touches one user. One mutex per user would work, but you would need a synchronised container of caches, which puts you back where you started. Sharding is the middle ground. Pick a fixed number of shards, route each user ID by `user_id % N` (modulo instead of ID ranges, because newer users with higher IDs are likely more active), and give each shard its own mutex. The vector holding the shards needs no lock, because the shards never move: their addresses stay fixed no matter how many writes and pops happen.

## What the benchmark showed

His test ran on a machine with a concurrency of eight, with about 2,000 writes and 300 pops per second. Sharding nearly eliminated time spent waiting for the lock compared with a single mutex. More shards did not help much beyond four. His hypothesis, flagged as a hypothesis, is that the useful shard count is tied to hardware concurrency, so bigger servers may benefit from more. At 100,000 shards, effectively one mutex per user since IDs were generated in that range, he saw no speed gain and a much larger memory bill.

At a lower load (500 writes and under 100 pops per second) the advantage shrinks. Sharding only wins when a queue of waiting operations actually builds up. Absent that, the simple mutex is fine, and the extra code is a cost with no payoff.

## Who should watch

Backend and systems engineers working on multi-threaded services, especially in trading or payments where write bursts are normal. The C++ is light and the principles carry to any language. He published the cache implementations and benchmark code on GitHub and invites people to rerun the tests.

Title: AI in data pipelines: start with the pain points, then scale
Description: Srinivas Murri at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on using ML to catch data anomalies, scale pipelines and fix records, and how to adopt it in small steps.
Body:
Every data engineer has lost a night to one field with the wrong type. Srinivas Murri, who brings 18 years of data engineering experience, opens his Conf42 DevOps 2025 talk with exactly those late-night debugging sessions, then argues that machine learning can take over much of that firefighting: flagging anomalies as data flows, adjusting resources under load, and repairing records. His practical advice is to adopt it slowly, starting from your worst pain points.

Scope check: this is a big-picture talk. Several examples are explicitly hypothetical, and there is no code or tool walkthrough. It is best taken as a framing for where ML fits in a pipeline.

## The old way was throwing hardware at it

Srinivas describes early pipelines as a factory line: move a few files, clean them, run a report. As data grew larger, more varied and less structured, the line kept breaking. A source went offline, a transformation failed on a type mismatch, and the fix took hours. The standard responses were more hardware or more custom scripts, and neither was sustainable.

## Where ML helps

He names four places. Data quality checks that flag anomalies in real time instead of someone checking by hand, and that learn from the manual corrections engineers make. Resource scaling that adjusts to load, his example being a flash sale such as Black Friday when traffic spikes with no warning. Bottleneck prediction based on past performance, so a pipeline running slower than usual triggers an adjustment before it breaks. And real-time fraud detection, where models trained on transaction history spot suspicious patterns as they happen.

The most tangible example is record repair. He points to NLP-style techniques for unstructured data like logs and text, and for fixing records: inferring a missing city from a postcode, or correcting a misspelled name (he uses his own name, typed without one letter) based on what the model has learned.

He also describes a client whose daily sales forecasts were delayed by slow processing, which matters when decisions are due before 8 a.m. After moving to AI-driven pipeline management, he says, they generated forecasts in hours instead of days.

## Start small and earn trust

The adoption plan is the most useful part. Assess the current pipeline and list every pain point in a backlog. Pick tools that fit your architecture. Apply a model to one problem on a limited scale, measure whether it helped, and only then expand across the data platform. He places fully self-healing pipelines as a long-term north star, not something to expect on day two. The role he sees for engineers is working alongside these systems, which he calls augmented engineering.

## Who should watch

Data engineering leads looking for a way to explain to stakeholders where ML belongs in the pipeline, and engineers early in that journey. If you already run anomaly detection in production, you will want a more hands-on talk.

Title: Breaking a Linux distro release into packages that ship alone
Description: Andreea Andrisan of Analog Devices at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on splitting Kuiper Linux releases into Debian packages, stable branches and GitHub Actions.
Body:
When one bug in one driver can hold up an entire operating system release, the release process is the bug. Andreea Andrisan, a DevOps engineer at Analog Devices, shows at Conf42 DevOps 2025 how her team reworked releases for ADI Kuiper Linux, the custom distribution that ships on the company's product evaluation boards with reference designs, device drivers and development utilities. The short version: they broke the monolith into independently released Debian packages and let users assemble the image they need.

## Why the old process was slow

In the old flow, every software component was built during image creation, which made builds long. Components were released only through the Kuiper image itself, so there was no modularity: a bug found in one component delayed all of them. Anyone who has watched a release train wait on its slowest carriage knows the feeling.

## A stabilisation branch per release

The first change was branching. Each core component now gets a next-stable branch cut from master. Master keeps taking features while next-stable is tested and hardened. Fixes often land in both. When next-stable is ready, a release branch or tag is created from it; bugs found in release testing produce a release patch. After the release, next-stable is overwritten from master to start the next cycle. Nothing exotic, but it separates ongoing development from shipping the release, which is exactly what the monolith could not do.

## Components as Debian packages

The bigger change was decomposition. Libraries, user-space tools, boot files and other components are now developed, tested and released on their own schedules. Each one produces a Debian package as its release artefact, uploaded to Analog Devices' Linux package repository. Using standard Debian tooling makes installing and rolling back individual pieces ordinary work for users instead of a reimage.

On top of that sits a modular configuration file. Users pick which tools go into their custom image and can pin component versions, so a project that needs a specific library version can declare it before the build. An extra script lets them add other compatible tools. The result is a lighter image with nothing in it the user did not ask for.

## Testing in a lookalike environment

Testing works at two levels. Each component is tested on its own. Then components are tested against the full system, with a twist: instead of the whole image, the team builds lighter Docker images derived from a Kuiper build image, carrying just the dependencies each component needs. That catches integration problems during development rather than at release time. Andreea points to two colleagues' talks at the same conference for the details of that infrastructure.

## CI moved to GitHub Actions

The team moved CI from Jenkins to GitHub Actions. Build logs are now public, and fresh images are generated and published on GitHub as soon as a commit merges into the Kuiper repository, so users do not wait for an official release. Build configurations grew too: from a single 32-bit full image to 64-bit support and both basic and full variants for each architecture. A pull request template and the CODEOWNERS feature round it out, so the right reviewers are assigned automatically.

## Who should watch

Anyone releasing embedded Linux, board support packages or any product that bundles many components into one artefact. It is a short, concrete talk with no vendor pitch.

Title: DataOps on a lakehouse starts with one copy of the data
Description: Jorge Loaiciga-Rodriguez of Perelyn at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on pairing DataOps with a lakehouse, and the technical and people problems you will hit.
Body:
An incident that takes three hours to fix can take three months to win back the trust of the person staring at the dashboard. Jorge Loaiciga-Rodriguez, a senior platform engineer and consultant at Perelyn, makes that point at Conf42 DevOps 2025 in a talk on combining DataOps with a data lakehouse. His case is that the pairing addresses data quality, slow insight delivery and stakeholder misalignment at the root, and he is just as candid about where it goes wrong.

## The pipeline that looks fine on paper

Jorge tells the story through Ficsit, a fictional interplanetary megacorporation with half a million employees, a brand-new chief data officer, and departments that each grew their own tools. The example workflow is sentiment analysis on customer support reviews. Data starts in a relational database owned by customer success, gets copied hourly into a data lake by data engineering, gets modelled by data science, and ends in a BI report with its own cache.

Looked at closely, it has problems: at least one hard copy of the data, no central orchestration (a failure at step two is invisible at step four), and three or more formats along the way. The CDO's survey makes it worse. Pipelines are cyclically dependent, new data scientists still need training after six months because of obscure column names, permissions are a maze, the bill is unpredictable, and the manager just wants to know whether the dashboard can be trusted, because last time it looked funny.

## One lake, open formats, small stages

The target state is a single lake holding one copy of the data, in an open format such as Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake with ACID operations, so concurrent reads and writes do not collide. Storage is cheap compared with the pre-cloud era, which is why this trade works.

On top of that come staging schemas in small, well-defined steps. A staging layer only translates column and table names and fixes types. An intermediate layer enforces the file format, partitioning and compression, and adds data quality and freshness tests. A curated layer builds business objects. Because each step is small, you know where to look when something breaks. He recommends dbt to orchestrate the dependencies between models, mostly because it is open source with a big community.

The interesting twist: there is no dev, test and prod for tables. Everything is production, and changes ship as new versions of a model (a V2 next to V1), with consumers told to migrate before the old one is deprecated.

## Bring the warehouse to the lake, carefully

A warehouse sits on top for heavy, time-critical queries, incremental models and fancier transformations. His warning is that not every warehouse can read and write the lake directly, and picking one that cannot just builds a new silo. Wide tables are his final layer, because analysts find them intuitive and BI tools often want them. The cost is duplicated metrics across tables, which is why catalog, glossary and lineage metadata matter so much. He calls metadata the key to removing silos.

## Where it breaks

Technical traps: long enterprise licence contracts, lots of trivial tests that give false confidence, versioned models released without telling anyone (hard to estimate the blast radius), and skipping the mock-up, even an Excel sheet with dummy data, that aligns you with stakeholders. People traps: two teams reporting different conversion numbers, business users who think DataOps is the engineers' problem, and engineers attached to the tool they have used for years. His answer is to adapt DataOps to your organisation and iterate in small, quick steps.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers planning a lakehouse, and leads who need the vocabulary to sell it. He closes with reading: the DataOps Manifesto, dbt's best-practice docs, and the free book Cloud Data Management: Four Stages for Informed Companies.

Title: How banks build data warehouses that regulators can audit
Description: Bharath Gaddam at Conf42 DevOps 2025 walks through banking data warehouse architecture, from staging and dimensional models to lineage and compliance.
Body:
In banking, a report is only as good as your ability to prove where every number came from. Bharath Gaddam, a senior database developer, spends his Conf42 DevOps 2025 talk on the architecture behind financial data warehouses: how data moves from source systems to dashboards, how it is modelled, and how lineage and governance keep regulators satisfied.

Scope check: this is a structured overview of the architecture and its trade-offs, not a case study of one named bank. It works well as a map for engineers new to financial data.

## Three decades in one slide

Bharath starts with history. In the 1990s, warehouses were batch systems for basic regulatory reporting and a consolidated view of financial statements. The 2000s added business intelligence tools for risk modelling, portfolio analysis, automated compliance monitoring and data mining for fraud detection and customer segmentation. Today's systems are cloud-based or hybrid, with real-time analytics and AI-driven insights layered on top.

## The layers and why each exists

The architecture he lays out has four parts. Data sources include transaction processing systems, external market data feeds and regulatory reporting platforms. A staging area validates, cleanses and standardises data before anything reaches the core. The core warehouse holds history and dimensional models, organised as star or snowflake schemas for fast analytical queries. Business intelligence sits on top: real-time dashboards for KPIs and risk metrics, ad hoc reporting with drill-down to transaction level, and predictive analytics.

His implementation framework is a sensible order of work: requirements first (stakeholder interviews, technical workshops, a review of existing architecture), then schema design (fact and dimension tables, slowly changing dimensions, grain and hierarchies), then performance (indexing, partitioning, query optimisation), then integration with existing systems through ETL pipelines, APIs and synchronisation.

## Compliance is a design input, not an afterthought

The part most relevant to DevOps engineers is regulation. Bharath treats data lineage as essential: end-to-end tracking of origin, transformations and movement, so auditors get a trail and discrepancies can be traced quickly. Governance adds role-based access control, encryption and regular audits. He names the frameworks banks build around: Basel capital adequacy rules, Dodd-Frank reporting, GDPR and SOX. The design challenge he highlights is balancing fast retrieval with tight security, which is why multi-layered authentication shows up next to query tuning.

## The bill and the payoff

He gives numbers for both sides. On benefits, he says organised warehouses let organisations generate reports 40 to 60 percent faster and cut reconciliation effort by about 30 percent. On cost, he puts initial deployment between 5 and 50 million depending on scale, before ongoing maintenance. Maintaining lineage at growing volume and handling unstructured sources like scanned documents remain the hard problems. His future list covers cloud-native multi-cloud setups, AI for data cleansing and validation, edge computing for latency-sensitive trading, and blockchain for immutable record keeping, which he frames as emerging rather than established.

## Who should watch

Engineers joining a financial services data team, platform people asked to support a warehouse they did not design, and anyone who needs to explain to a stakeholder why lineage costs money. Seasoned warehouse architects will recognise most of it.

Title: Introversion is a spectrum, and quiet engineers can use it
Description: Tomasz Manugiewicz of evoke at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on the strengths quiet engineers bring and the tactics that help them and their leads.
Body:
Tomasz Manugiewicz, General Manager for Poland at evoke, opens his Conf42 DevOps 2025 talk by introducing himself as an introvert, then corrects it to "quiet engineer". The talk argues that introversion is a position on a spectrum that shifts with the situation, and that quiet engineers bring specific strengths that extrovert-shaped workplaces tend to miss. It ends with a toolkit for both the quiet professionals and the people who lead them.

## You are not a type, you are a setting

Tomasz starts with Carl Jung, who described introversion and extroversion as attitudes, not as kinds of people. Everyone has both, with one dominant. He admits that early in his career he wanted the tests to call him an extrovert, because he believed introverts did not get promoted. Learning that it is a continuum was a relief, and so was the word ambivert.

He then adds a second axis from psychologist Jonathan Cheek: four kinds of introversion. Social (fine in a crowd, recharges alone afterwards), thinking (deep solo focus, which is how Tomasz prepares talks), restrained (some days you just do not have the energy), and anxious (the nervous system says no before you do). His model suggests moving step by step, from anxious towards restrained and then social, rather than jumping straight to the conference afterparty. He is clear it is a model, not a law, which engineers will appreciate.

## The strengths are concrete

The middle section lists what quiet engineers bring: deep technical expertise, methodical problem solving, attention to detail, persistence on the bug that keeps you awake. As leaders, they tend to give autonomy instead of micromanaging, think before acting, and mediate conflict well. They also love a retrospective.

There is a sharp observation about executives. Tomasz says every CEO or CTO he has worked with has one trusted engineer they go to for critical missions: the proof of concept for the board, the deep research, the analysis that has to be right. That person is often quiet, rarely has it in their job title, and is very expensive to lose.

He also names a failure mode. He once watched two engineers sitting desk to desk exchange about 100 comments on one pull request in a week, because talking felt harder than typing. Good reviewers, but sometimes you need to turn your chair around.

## Tactics for meetings and events

The practical list is short and usable. Save mental energy before important meetings instead of filling every calendar gap. Arrive early so people come to you one at a time. At big gatherings, give yourself a job, like helping set up the microphone. Decide your exit time in advance and say it out loud so you hold yourself to it. A few minutes of music before a stressful talk helps him; coffee before intense meetings does not. Prepare an opening question, cultivate a few deeper relationships instead of many shallow ones, and remember that people enjoy talking about themselves, so ask what they are proud of lately.

For leads: do not assume, ask. Speak up about your quiet people's strengths in calibration. Allow private working space, judge on quality over speed, and offer more than one channel, from Slack to pull requests to email. One small swap he recommends to everyone is replacing an apology with a thank-you for someone's patience.

## Who should watch

Engineers who recognise themselves in the title, and every manager running a team where the loudest voice in planning wins by default. He closes on Susan Cain's book Quiet, which he credits for much of the framing.

Title: A real-time analytics pipeline in five stages, from click to cart
Description: Amarnath Immadisetty of Lowe's at Conf42 DevOps 2025 lays out collection, processing, storage, delivery and monitoring for real-time analytics.
Body:
Buy a washer online and the next recommendation should be a dryer, not something random from the garden aisle. Amarnath Immadisetty, a senior manager of software engineering at Lowe's, uses that example at Conf42 DevOps 2025 to frame a talk about building real-time analytics pipelines that respond within milliseconds. He splits the pipeline into five stages and names the tools that usually fill each one.

Scope check: this is an architecture overview built on public examples from Amazon, Netflix and Uber, not a tour of Lowe's internal systems. If you want a map of the moving parts and their usual tools, it delivers that.

## Collection is continuous, not a batch job

The first stage is collecting events from wherever they happen: websites (views, clicks, form submits), mobile apps, IoT devices, server and application logs, social media, and payment systems. Amarnath stresses that real-time means acting as each event arrives, via APIs, event trackers or streaming frameworks. He also points out that which sources matter depends on the business. A retailer cares about social sentiment and competitor sales; a healthcare system cares less about some of those.

One detail worth keeping: users move between the mobile app and the website, so the session has to follow them. Search on the app, see the recommendation on the web.

## Processing turns raw events into something you can act on

Processing is where events get cleaned, deduplicated, transformed and analysed. His examples are practical: the same purchase arriving from two sources should be kept once, and raw clickstream should become something like the most-clicked product in the last ten minutes. For tools he names Apache Flink and Apache Spark for open-source streaming, AWS Lambda for small tasks on new data, and Google Dataflow. He says he has seen Flink and Spark handle use cases above a million records per second without trouble.

He also makes a point teams forget: real-time decisions need history. Forecasting tomorrow's revenue or spotting a fraud pattern depends on a continuous record of past behaviour, so day one of a new pipeline will not be very smart.

## Pick storage by access pattern

The storage section sorts options into four groups. In-memory stores (Redis, Memcached) for instant recommendation lookups. NoSQL (MongoDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB) for high-scale reads and writes, with DynamoDB holding inventory so customers only see what is in stock. Time-series databases (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Druid) for metrics and forecasting. Data lakes (Amazon S3, HDFS) for the long history that machine learning models train on. Whatever you choose, his checklist is low latency, scalability, fault tolerance and flexible access.

## Delivery and monitoring close the loop

Delivery pushes insights to where they are used: dashboards in tools like Looker, APIs and microservices, Kafka topics, WebSockets, and alerts in Grafana that can, for example, block a suspicious card transaction. Monitoring and resilience run through every stage rather than sitting at the end.

His end-to-end example ties it together: a search event on an e-commerce site goes to a Kafka topic, Apache Flink processes it, results land in DynamoDB, the recommendation appears on screen, and Prometheus watches the whole path. He also cites industry figures for customer support sentiment analysis and return on investment; treat those as figures from articles he read rather than results from his own team.

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads starting a streaming project who want a vocabulary and a reference layout, or backend developers moving into data work. Experienced Flink operators will find it introductory.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Real-Time Personalization at Scale: Neural Ranking Systems and Operational Breakthroughs](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Vedant_Agarwal_personalization_ranking_systems) by Vedant Agarwal goes further into the recommendation end.
