Title: What HPC hardware teaches cloud infrastructure about watts
Description: FNU Parshant of Arm at Conf42 DevOps 2025 tours HPC interconnects, low-power SoCs and chiplets, and why the cloud inherits them.
Body:
Most DevOps talks start at the YAML. FNU Parshant, a staff RTL design engineer at Arm with 12 years in VLSI design, starts at the silicon. At Conf42 DevOps 2025 he walks through how high-performance computing got faster without melting the power budget (faster interconnects, low-power system-on-chip designs, 3D stacking and chiplets) and why those same ideas end up in the cloud instances your pipelines run on.

Honest scope first: this is a hardware survey, not a hands-on infrastructure talk. There is no Terraform here. What you get is a chip designer's map of where performance per watt actually comes from, which is useful context the next time someone asks why the Graviton bill looks different.

## The network between the chips is the computer

Parshant opens with interconnects, and he frames them as the backbone of an HPC system. The older generation he describes topped out around 100 Gbps; today's run at up to 400 Gbps with sub-microsecond latency. His point is less the headline speed and more what it enables: workloads that used to stall on data transfer, like localised weather simulation or training a large model, become feasible because nodes stop waiting on each other.

If you have ever profiled a distributed job and found it spending its life in all-reduce, this section will feel familiar. The fix at this scale is physical, not a config flag.

## Power is the constraint that shapes everything

The middle of the talk is about low-power SoC design. Parshant cites up to 75% power savings for modern designs over traditional architectures, and names concrete examples: AWS Graviton as a custom SoC in the cloud, NVIDIA SoC-based GPUs in autonomous driving, AMD EPYC consolidating compute and memory bandwidth. The thread tying them together is integration. CPUs, GPUs and FPGAs on one chip means fewer hops, less wasted energy and a smaller server footprint.

He then gets into packaging: 3D stacking (high-bandwidth memory on NVIDIA GPUs is the example) and chiplets (AMD Ryzen). Stacking shortens interconnect distances; chiplets improve yield and let vendors scale core counts without betting the wafer on one giant die.

## The next bottlenecks are heat and software

The closing section lists what still hurts. Thermal management comes first: dense chips run hot, and he points to liquid immersion cooling as one answer data centres are adopting. Interconnect scaling past one terabit per second is next, with silicon photonics as the candidate. Third, and most relevant for software people, is the tooling needed to actually use heterogeneous hardware: he names NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm as the frameworks that decide whether all that silicon gets used or sits idle.

That last point is the bridge to DevOps. Hardware keeps getting more specialised, and the teams that schedule work onto it well get the efficiency the spec sheet promised.

## Who should watch

Platform and infrastructure engineers who pick instance types, run GPU fleets or care about the energy line on the cloud invoice will get the most out of it. If you want a deployment walkthrough, skip it; if you want to know what is under the hypervisor, it is a compact tour. Frontier and Fugaku, the exascale and Arm-based supercomputers, make cameo appearances.

Title: Impostor syndrome runs in a loop, and you can break the loop
Description: Pawel Zajaczkowski of Xebia at Conf42 DevOps 2025 maps the impostor cycle, the biases that feed it, and practical ways to step out of it.
Body:
Impostor syndrome is a feedback loop that discards its own evidence. That is the core of Pawel Zajaczkowski's talk at Conf42 DevOps 2025. Pawel, a former Java developer who now manages several DevOps and development teams at Xebia Poland, explains why the feeling is so common in tech, how it keeps itself alive, and which small habits weaken it.

The abstract cites research putting impostor syndrome at almost 90% of people in IT. In the talk he is careful with the range, saying studies land somewhere between 50 and 90 percent depending on which one you read. Either way, the person next to you on the stand-up call probably has it too.

## The cycle that eats your successes

The centrepiece is the impostor cycle. A task arrives, anxiety follows, and you pick one of two routes: over-prepare (the unlogged extra hours, the countless self-reviews) or procrastinate. Because you are competent, the task succeeds anyway. Then the filter kicks in. Success gets attributed to the extra effort or to luck, never to skill, and the belief that you are a fraud grows a little with every lap.

This is the useful bit for engineers: it is a system with a bug in the feedback path. Positive signal comes in and gets dropped before it updates state.

## Why our industry makes it worse

Pawel gives three reasons tech is fertile ground. The work is intangible: a blacksmith can hand you a sword to judge, but try explaining low cyclomatic complexity to your grandmother. The field grows fast, so there is always more to know than anyone can learn. And social media success stories set a bar nobody actually clears.

He adds a few cognitive traps. The generic developer in your head merges what you learned from many different colleagues into one person who seems to know everything. Dunning-Kruger means the confident person on Mount Stupid can look more competent than you in the valley of despair. The spotlight effect makes you think others are watching your mistakes far more than they are.

## Small tools that work

The practical section is the best part. Everyone looks things up; Pawel admits he no longer remembers how to read a file into memory in Java after 12-plus years. Compare yourself only with your earlier self, because you see your own internals but only other people's public interface (he uses the object-oriented analogy, and it lands). Keep a written list of achievements, ideally on paper. Treat job ads as wish lists. When fear spikes mid-task, get up and walk, because panic is not when you do your best thinking.

For team leads, he suggests being a little vulnerable about your own failures so imperfection becomes normal, and building up goodwill before hard conversations. He also says plainly that therapy is fine and that many companies now fund it.

## Who should watch

Anyone early in their career, anyone who just switched roles, and every team lead. It is a culture talk with a structure an engineer can follow, and yes, the abstract warns it may contain traces of rubber ducks. He ends by naming the Clance IP scale if you want to test yourself.

- [Health Checks for Systems. What About Your Team?](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Sylvain_Kalache_burnout_oncall_sre) by Sylvain Kalache covers burnout, one of the dark places Pawel warns the cycle leads to.

Title: Four layers of an AI-powered cloud architecture, and a factory case
Description: Babita Kumari of Microsoft at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on AI-driven resource management, hybrid multi-cloud layers and a manufacturer that cut downtime by 47%.
Body:
Cloud cost and reliability work usually starts with a spreadsheet and ends with someone turning things off. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Babita Kumari, Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft, made the case for letting AI do more of that work inside the architecture itself: predicting resource needs, scaling automatically, and watching for threats, with a global manufacturing case study as the proof point.

It is a compact, executive-level talk: a framework and a set of results rather than configuration or code. Go in expecting the shape of the system, not the YAML.

## Three advancements that set the agenda

Babita opens with the shifts she sees in enterprise cloud architecture. Predictive resource management, with AI allocating resources dynamically at up to 91% accuracy and cutting waste. Automated scaling, where ML adjusts capacity during peaks for a 67% efficiency gain. And intelligent security, with AI threat detection preventing up to 99.7% of potential breaches. The abstract adds cost cuts of up to 42% and efficiency gains of 53% as the headline promise.

## Hybrid multi-cloud is the default now

Most enterprises, she says, now mix clouds: public platforms such as Azure and AWS host the bulk of workloads for scale and uptime, while private clouds hold sensitive data, such as credit data, for compliance and control. The hybrid model trades flexibility, performance and cost against each other rather than picking one.

## The four layers

The architecture section is the part to keep:

1. **Data processing**, sized for up to 100,000 transactions per second for real-time insight.
2. **AI and ML integration**, running more than 1.5 million intelligent operations a day for automated decisions.
3. **Security framework**, built on zero trust to protect sensitive data and meet compliance.
4. **Monitoring and analytics**, real-time and predictive, so problems are caught before they cost uptime.

Each depends on the one before; there is no useful AI layer without the data layer feeding it, and none of it is trustworthy without the last two.

## The manufacturer that was losing millions

The case study is a global manufacturer whose supply chain inefficiencies cost around $12.3 million a year. The fix combined AI-driven predictive analytics with real-time monitoring, to make better decisions earlier and cut downtime. The reported outcome: a 47% reduction in downtime, $4.2 million in annual savings, and a 52% improvement in supply chain reliability. The customer is not named, and the talk does not go into the models or data sources, so treat it as a direction of travel rather than a recipe.

## Best practices that are mostly about discipline

Babita's three practices are refreshingly unglamorous:

- **Assess the infrastructure regularly**, because needs evolve and a setup that was right last year may be oversized or undersized now.
- **Migrate gradually**, moving workloads incrementally to limit risk and keep the business running, which she calls the best approach for very large enterprises.
- **Define success metrics** up front, such as cost reduction, reliability and uptime, and keep measuring progress against them.

For integration, she adds dynamic parameter tuning across low and high demand, robust real-time monitoring with predictive analytics for proactive issue resolution, and continuous performance optimisation as requirements change.

## Looking ahead

Her outlook covers quantum-assisted ML models, multi-cloud orchestration that works as one platform, and edge computing for real-time processing close to the data. These are forward-looking claims, and the percentages attached to them in the talk are projections, not measurements.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leaders building a case for AI-assisted operations in a hybrid cloud, who want a layered reference model and a set of target outcomes to discuss. Hands-on engineers will want to pair it with something more technical.

Title: Where serverless AWS bills leak, from CloudWatch logs to 10 GB Lambdas
Description: Yan Cui, AWS Serverless Hero at Lumigo, at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on billing alarms, CloudWatch log costs, right-sizing Lambda memory and Lambda-to-Lambda calls.
Body:
On many serverless AWS accounts, CloudWatch costs more than the application it is watching, sometimes several times more. That was one of the first findings in Yan Cui's talk at Conf42 DevOps 2025. Yan, AWS Serverless Hero, Developer Advocate at Lumigo and independent consultant, has been on AWS since 2010 and collects money-saving tips the way some people collect stamps. He warned the audience to get ready to drink from the fire hose, and he was not exaggerating.

## Set billing alarms before anything else

Tip one is the first thing he does in any new account. Billing alarms lag by a few hours, but a few hours beats finding out when the invoice lands. His example is the team at PostNL, the Dutch national delivery service, experienced serverless users who shipped a one-line change that broke secret caching. Lambda functions started calling Secrets Manager on every invocation instead of once at cold start, across hundreds of millions of requests a day, and the billing alarm caught it within days. The damage was a few thousand dollars; hearing about it from the finance team weeks later would have been far worse.

## CloudWatch Logs is the usual top line

Yan's log advice is the most immediately actionable part:

- **Structured logging with deliberate log levels**: in production, record info and above, and sample a small share of debug logs (he suggests something like 5 to 10% of invocations) so you have debug data for every code path without redeploying when things break.
- **Set log retention**: the default is never expire. Logs lose value fast, so seven, 14 or 30 days is usually plenty.
- **Stop paying twice**: if you ship logs to another vendor, you still pay CloudWatch ingestion first. Lambda extensions with the Telemetry API can send logs straight to a third party, and an IAM tweak stops the function writing to CloudWatch at all.
- **Trim system messages**: with the log format set to JSON, Lambda's system log level setting controls the per-invocation start, end and report lines. At billions of invocations a month, those add up. Yan worked out by experiment which messages appear at which level, since the docs do not say.

He also plugs Lumigo's log management, which treats each log line as an event you can build metrics and alerts on; a disclosure worth noting, since he works there.

## More memory is a dial you can turn the wrong way

Lambda's one performance lever is memory, and cost scales with it. A client rendering hand-drawn style videos gave a function the full 10 GB to speed it up, and found it costing around $10,000 a month. The catch: past 1.8 GB you get a second CPU core, and at 10 GB you have six, but their Node.js renderer ran on a single event loop with no workers or child processes. They paid for six cores and used one. Dropping memory to 1.8 GB fixed it. That one function accounted for over 99% of their serverless spend, which is Knuth's critical 3% in action. Yan points to Alex Casalboni's Lambda Power Tuning state machine for finding the sweet spot.

ARM is about 25% cheaper per millisecond than x86, but some of his workloads ran 60% slower on it, which makes ARM more expensive overall. Where it shines is IO-bound functions that mostly wait on slow third-party services.

## Lambda-to-Lambda calls are usually a design smell

Synchronous Lambda-to-Lambda invocation means paying for the caller to sit and wait while the callee runs. Inside one service boundary, merge them and keep modularity in the code, not the infrastructure. Across services it is worse: you couple consumers to your function name, region and runtime choice. Give them an HTTP API instead, so you can move to Fargate later without anyone noticing. Async invocations within a service are fine for secondary work like analytics, with built-in retries and a dead-letter queue.

The rest of the talk keeps going: removing an SQS hop and a second function cut cost and latency for one team, caching at every layer, knowing that ALB gets pricier than API Gateway with large payloads, Werner Vogels's Frugal Architect laws about aligning cost with revenue, and when Lambda function URLs beat API Gateway.

## Who should watch

Anyone with an AWS bill that has a serverless line on it. It is dense, practical and full of real client stories; take notes.

Title: AskDataAI, a chat interface to enterprise data with RBAC built in
Description: Praveen Payili of Horizonsoft Solutions at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on AskDataAI, which pairs Qdrant hybrid search and GPT-4 agents with role-based data access.
Body:
Every company wants anyone to be able to ask the data a question, and every security team flinches at what "anyone" means. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Praveen Payili, Senior Data Engineer at Horizonsoft Solutions, presented AskDataAI, an AI platform that answers natural-language data questions through context-aware agents, and spent as much time on role-based access and caching as on the model.

That balance is what makes the talk worth a look. Data democratisation without security is a breach with a chat window; security without usability is the status quo.

## The tension it is built around

Praveen opens on the conflict: teams need fast, accurate data to make decisions, and access is fragmented across tools, while every expansion of access widens the risk to sensitive information and compliance. AskDataAI's answer has three parts: a conversational interface for technical and non-technical users alike, agents specialised for different data contexts (an "ask finance" agent that only searches finance datasets, for instance), and enterprise access control underneath.

## The retrieval stack

The technical section is the meat:

- **Qdrant** as the vector search engine, with hybrid and multistage searches and JSON payload filtering through its query language, so each agent and team only searches the collections it should.
- **A hybrid search model** combining vector and traditional search, which Praveen credits with a 20% accuracy gain across agents.
- **Reciprocal rank fusion re-ranking** using signals like page popularity and certification status, which he says improved relevance by 40%. Certified, trusted tables float to the top; popular ones too.
- **GPT-4**, customised for their data contexts, with a reported 35% cut in query latency.
- **Semantic dataset collections** that group tables by relevance, popularity and certification, so any agent can suggest the right tables.

## The unglamorous engineering that makes it usable

The list of plumbing is long and real. A back-end chatbot service with a batch mode and gRPC integration, a backend-for-frontend layer for faster development, and integrations with Slack and Kafka; the Slack bot lets people ask in plain English where they already work. Logging was rebuilt to be thread-safe with user ID propagation, so every request is traceable to a person, which matters for both debugging and audits.

Cost and latency get attention too. Prompt and response caching, including an evaluated semantic cache, cut latency and LLM spend on repeat questions. A guardrail caps the chat history passed to the agent at eight conversation turns or the token limit, whichever comes first, which keeps prompts small and bills smaller. Automated evaluation is part of the loop, and the UI sits at more than 75% unit test coverage.

## Access control is the feature

The RBAC section is where the platform earns enterprise trust: granular permissions per application, dynamic role assignment based on user activity and context, audit logs and compliance reporting, and integration with external identity providers such as SAML. Praveen reports a 99% reduction in unauthorised access, alongside a 60% boost in data discovery efficiency, a 20% gain in query accuracy and 35% faster responses, for a system sized for more than 15,000 concurrent users.

## Lessons and next steps

His three lessons are crisp: balance is the key between access and security; context matters, because agents must understand enterprise-specific data to be accurate; and continuous improvement through model updates and feedback loops. He adds that intuitive UI and clear documentation drive adoption. Next on the roadmap: multimodal data (images, video, audio), more enterprise tool integrations, forecasting and trend analysis, and multiple languages.

## Who should watch

Data platform teams building a "chat with your warehouse" tool, and security engineers asked to approve one. The specific mix of hybrid search, rank fusion on trust signals and per-team collection filtering is a useful reference design.

Title: Gate every RAG pull request on accuracy, with Ragas in CI
Description: Nirhoshan Sivaroopan of WSO2 at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on scoring RAG retrievers and generators with Ragas metrics and failing PRs that drop below thresholds.
Body:
Unit tests tell you the code runs; they do not tell you the chatbot still answers correctly. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Nirhoshan Sivaroopan, Software Engineer in WSO2's AI team, showed how to treat answer quality like any other regression: compute accuracy metrics for a retrieval-augmented generation feature on every pull request, and block the merge when they fall below agreed thresholds.

It is one of the more directly usable AI talks of the event, because it ends in a GitHub Actions workflow and a CSV you can actually read.

## Test the two halves separately

Nirhoshan starts with why context matters. A plain LLM answers from its pre-training, which makes answers generic and imprecise for your use case. RAG adds a retriever that searches a knowledge base for relevant documents and stuffs them into the prompt, and a generator that answers from that context. Each half fails differently, so each gets its own metrics, all from the Ragas library. The vocabulary: the question, the retrieved context, the generated answer, and the ground truth, a human-written reference answer.

## Retriever metrics: did we fetch it, and is it on top?

- **Context recall** checks whether every claim in the ground truth can be found in the retrieved context: ground-truth sentences attributable to the context divided by all ground-truth sentences.
- **Context precision** checks ranking: is the most relevant document near the top? Nirhoshan's point is practical. Hand an LLM a hundred documents with the key one buried in the middle and it may miss it and hallucinate from the wrong context.

The two pull against each other. Retrieve more documents and recall rises while precision can drop. The metrics tell you which knob to turn: the number of documents retrieved, the indexing strategy, the distance measure (cosine or Euclidean), or adding a re-ranker.

## Generator metrics: is it faithful, and does it mean the same thing?

- **Faithfulness** measures factual consistency with the context: claims in the answer that can be inferred from the context divided by all claims in the answer. Hallucinated sentences drag it down.
- **Answer semantic similarity** embeds the answer and the ground truth and compares them with cosine similarity.

These guide decisions such as which model to use and what temperature to run it at.

## The dataset is the real work

Nirhoshan is emphatic that dataset preparation is the key step. Questions must span easy, medium, hard and combined cases that resemble production; test only easy ones and you will be confident about the wrong thing. Ground truth must be written carefully, because most metrics are computed against it; sloppy ground truth makes the score meaningless.

## The pipeline

The code walks through it end to end. Run each question through the AI feature to collect answers and contexts, combine them with questions and ground truth into a dataset, evaluate with the chosen Ragas metrics, write everything to an accuracy results CSV, compute the mean per metric, and compare each against its own threshold, since each metric measures something different.

That script runs in a GitHub Actions workflow on every PR, with environment variables and secrets configured, and publishes the CSV as an artifact. Pass, and the change can merge. Fail, and you open the CSV to see which question regressed on which metric. His example: if the most relevant document is not ranked first, context precision falls, and introducing a re-ranker brings it back up.

## The costs nobody puts on the slide

He is candid about the downsides. Several metrics use an LLM as the judge, so scores vary slightly between runs and you want a highly accurate model doing the judging. Good ground truth is slow and expensive to write. LLM API costs add up at scale, and evaluation takes time in the pipeline. Budget for all three.

## Who should watch

Teams shipping RAG features into products who still review accuracy by eyeballing a few answers. If your PR checks are all green while users report wrong answers, this is the missing check.

Title: Where generative AI fits in a cloud-native DevOps pipeline
Description: Sai Sandeep Ogety, PeopleCert DevOps Institute Ambassador, at Conf42 DevOps 2025 maps generative AI onto code, CI/CD, security, scaling and monitoring.
Body:
The quickest way to judge an AI-in-DevOps pitch is to ask which stage of the pipeline it touches and what a human stops doing. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Sai Sandeep Ogety, DevOps Institute Ambassador at PeopleCert, answered that stage by stage for cloud-native teams, from code generation through CI/CD, security, resource scaling, observability and testing, and closed on the governance questions that come with it.

This is an introductory talk: a structured map rather than a case study, which makes it a good first watch for teams just starting the conversation.

## The pressures it is meant to relieve

Sai frames generative AI with familiar examples: ChatGPT for language tasks, GitHub Copilot for code, DALL-E for images. Then he lists four pressures in modern delivery that it can help with. Technology moves faster than developers can keep up, so contextual assistance helps. Applications keep getting more complex, so automation and error reduction matter. Cycles keep getting shorter, so faster testing and deployment give teams breathing room. And security and compliance demands keep growing.

He defines cloud-native DevOps as applications designed for the cloud, scalable, resilient and built on microservices, with planning, coding, testing, deployment and monitoring folded into one automated pipeline. AI's job is to make that pipeline adaptive as well as effective.

## Code and pipelines

The first two stages are the obvious ones. In code, Copilot-style assistants complete lines, generate whole functions from prompts and suggest refactors, which Sai argues reduces technical debt and frees developers to focus on business logic rather than wrestling with pipeline configuration.

In CI/CD he sees three gains: AI-generated tests for broader coverage and faster bug detection, deployment tooling that reads performance data to recommend scaling and rollout strategies, and predictive maintenance that flags issues before they become incidents.

## Security, scaling and observability

Security gets a section of its own: detecting unusual patterns in network traffic for faster threat response, vulnerability tools that scan code and suggest patches, and policy enforcement that catches risky configurations automatically.

On resources, AI predicts demand from an application's history, drives dynamic scaling to match real-time load, and surfaces cost insights.

The observability example is the one engineers will relate to most. After a production outage, instead of sitting down to write the whole root cause analysis by hand, a tool that has been watching the application can draft it from what it saw. Add anomaly detection that alerts teams before an issue lands and bottleneck detection with suggested fixes, and the on-call engineer has fewer blank pages to fill.

Testing closes the tour: generated test cases for coverage, automated execution for faster feedback, and predictive quality analysis to catch problems before production.

## The governance checklist

Sai ends on the part vendor decks usually skip: data privacy and regulatory compliance in how data is handled, mitigating bias so models do not produce discriminatory outcomes, and transparency in how AI models are built so teams can trust them and hold them accountable. None of it is optional once AI starts writing code and drafting incident reports.

## Who should watch

Teams and managers early in adopting AI across their delivery pipeline who want a stage-by-stage frame for the discussion, and anyone preparing a proposal that needs to cover security and governance as well as speed. Practitioners already running these tools will find it a high-level recap rather than new technique.

Title: Human-in-the-loop AI that learns when to stop asking humans
Description: Hemang Shah of Amazon at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on IP and logo monitoring that pairs ML models with expert reviewers, then routes only the hard cases to people.
Body:
A model trained on the whole internet knows the Nike swoosh, but it has never seen the logo your startup designed last Tuesday. That gap is the starting point of Hemang Shah's talk at Conf42 DevOps 2025. Hemang, a Software Developer at Amazon who works on ML models that detect logos, copyrights and trademarks at around 20,000 transactions per second, argued for human-assisted AI in intellectual property monitoring, and for a design where the humans gradually make themselves less necessary.

## The problem got bigger with generative AI

Hemang frames the stakes with an estimate of a trillion dollars a year lost globally to counterfeits and copyright infringement, a number he says has been rising sharply. One driver is generative AI itself: bad actors can now produce infringing content quickly and spread it across the web. Companies need systems that watch actively for misuse of their IP and act on it.

## The model toolbox

He walks through the families of models that do the detection:

- **Embedding search** with models like CLIP: turn images and text into vectors and run similarity searches, which beats keyword search because it is semantic rather than string matching.
- **NLP models** like BERT and RoBERTa for text, for example telling whether "apple" in a sentence means the fruit or the company.
- **Vision models** such as the YOLO family (v5, v7) and vision transformers for spotting unauthorised logos and trademarks in images.
- **Large language models**, which bring enough context to check a paper for plagiarism or judge whether an image misuses a brand.

Then the limits. Models are good at known patterns and statistical anomalies and bad at the unknown, which is the new-logo problem. LLMs also hallucinate and can give different answers to the same request. Humans bring context and judgement the models lack.

## Active learning: every review is training data

The basic loop is simple. Let the model make inferences, but do not take automated action on them alone. A domain expert reviews the output, actions are taken on the human decision, and the reviewed data becomes a golden set for fine-tuning the next model version.

Hemang splits the payoff into two kinds. Precision improves when the model stops making the false positives reviewers corrected in areas it was already decent at. Recall improves when it learns patterns it could not see before: brand X detected, brand Y missed, reviewers annotate brand Y, the next version catches both. In his experience a human-plus-AI setup tends to reach around 20% higher precision and about 25% better recall than the model alone over time, and keeps improving with each iteration.

## Scaling both halves of the system

The AI half scales the usual cloud way: containerised ML workloads on autoscaling compute on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud, with review data stored in cloud NoSQL databases that feed straight into training pipelines.

The human half is the clever part. As versions improve, the model becomes reliable in some categories before others; his example is a logo model that is great on shoes and shaky on bags. So you let it act automatically on shoes and park bag decisions for review, then prioritise the review queue by what matters most to the business. Humans see fewer, harder cases, and those cases are exactly the training data the model needs. Hemang reports that offloading about 40% of the human workload this way still keeps around 95% precision in most cases.

## A rollout plan in a few steps

His mental model for building one: assess the current IP evaluation pipeline, find which parts can be trusted to decide alone and which have high false positive rates, design where and how humans review (a UI, plus an output format the training pipeline can consume directly), train the reviewers, train the models, and keep monitoring so human touchpoints can be removed wherever accuracy is good enough.

## Who should watch

Anyone running ML classification where mistakes are expensive: trust and safety, brand protection, fraud, content moderation. The pattern of routing by per-category confidence applies well beyond logos. It is an architecture talk without code.

Title: AI in the machine room, measured in failures, cooling and PUE
Description: Ashok Jonnalagadda of Hilmar Cheese Company at Conf42 DevOps 2025 reports what AI changed in data center maintenance, capacity, cooling and security.
Body:
Most AI-for-ops talks stop at dashboards. Ashok Jonnalagadda, Principal Infrastructure Engineer at Hilmar Cheese Company, went down to the physical layer at Conf42 DevOps 2025: fans, chillers, power and the servers they keep alive. His talk is a scorecard of what AI and ML changed in data center operations across four domains, with critical failures down 47% and resource utilisation up 31% as the headline results.

Be clear about the format before you press play. It is a short, results-first talk: slide after slide of outcomes, with little on the models, the data plumbing or the sensors behind them. Treat it as a target list for your own facility, not a build guide.

## Predictive maintenance is the anchor

The first domain is equipment failure. Through real-time monitoring and predictive analysis, Ashok reports a 47% reduction in critical failures, warnings arriving 72 hours ahead, and 96% prediction accuracy. Three days of notice is the interesting number here: that is enough time to order a part and schedule a window, which is the difference between maintenance and an incident.

## More workload on the same hardware

The second domain is resource optimisation. AI-driven placement lifted utilisation by 31%, which he says let the data center absorb 40% more workload with no extra hardware purchase. Load balancing work cut latency by 38%, to response times under 10 milliseconds.

## Cooling is where the money hides

Energy management gets its own section. Smart thermal management that tunes airflow in real time gave a 42% gain in cooling efficiency and 23% savings on cooling cost, with deep learning models reading environmental sensors across the floor. Ashok also reports power usage effectiveness below 1.25. Anyone who has paid a data center power bill knows why the cheese company cares about keeping things cool.

## Security and capacity planning

On security, the claims are a 98.5% threat detection accuracy, response time cut from five minutes to 45 seconds, and a false positive rate of 0.08% while watching more than a million security events a day.

Capacity planning is the one section with a method attached, in four steps: collect real-time server metrics, workload patterns and utilisation data across data centers; push more than 500 million data points through ML pipelines to find usage patterns and growth trends; produce 12-month capacity forecasts with neural networks and time-series analysis, at 96% accuracy; then act on them with automated scaling recommendations.

## The money and the hard parts

The financial summary: $2.4 million in annual savings from cooling, hardware and maintenance, a return on investment reached within the first 18 months, and $3.2 million in savings for large facilities above five megawatts. The abstract pitches the approach for anything from 1 MW to 50 MW.

Ashok names the integration challenges briefly: legacy systems, data quality across more than 50 enterprise databases that needed validation and standardisation, a skills gap, and the cultural shift from traditional to AI-driven operations. His roadmap points at edge AI processing, quantum-assisted optimisation, self-managing autonomous data centers and AI-driven sustainability.

## Who should watch

Infrastructure and facilities engineers building a business case for AI in their own machine room, who want a set of benchmark numbers to aim at. If you want the how (feature engineering for sensor data, model choice, rollout), you will need to follow up with Ashok directly; the talk does not go there.

Title: AI at every stage of the DevOps loop, plus a Kubernetes Alexa skill
Description: Alejandro Mercado of KMMX at Conf42 DevOps 2025 tours AI tools across plan, code, test and operate, and demos an Alexa skill that manages Kubernetes.
Body:
Somewhere between AI replacing engineers and AI as glorified autocomplete sits the practical view: there is now an AI-assisted tool for every box on the DevOps infinity loop, and the job is picking where it actually helps. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Alejandro Mercado, Sales and DevOps Engineer at KMMX, walked that loop phase by phase and showed a side project of his own: an Alexa skill that manages a Kubernetes cluster by voice.

This is an overview talk, and Alejandro is upfront about it. He prefers "perspective" to "prediction", since he does not own a crystal ball.

## The loop, with an assistant at each step

The frame is the classic cycle: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor, repeat. Alejandro's argument is that systems have outgrown human attention. Cloud, on-premises, hybrid and multi-cloud, microservices next to monoliths, containers and several databases: there is not enough human power to watch all of it, so engineers need help to do more with less.

His examples per phase:

- **Planning**: Jira, Asana and Notion adding AI features to project management.
- **Code**: assistants such as GitHub Copilot, which he compares to pair programming, replacing the trip to Google or Stack Overflow for a forgotten method. You keep the steering wheel.
- **Testing and quality**: static analysis, unit testing, code coverage and mutation testing with tools from JetBrains, Snyk and SonarQube.
- **Infrastructure as code**: Terraform-style tooling that uses AI to catch inconsistencies at provisioning time, and Ansible for automated provisioning.
- **Incident response and monitoring**: Splunk, Datadog and ServiceNow, plus log-based root cause analysis on platforms like CloudWatch.

## AIOps is about failing before the user notices

The operations section is the most useful. Alejandro frames AIOps as moving from monitoring to observability: correlate patterns in resource use, latency and duration to spot a failure in the making, find the root cause before anything breaks, and ideally before a user notices. Logs are the raw material, which is why he insists you need good ones before any AI tooling can do root cause work for you. He ties it back to SRE practice too: service level objectives remain the measurable way to define and improve service quality, and AI tooling should move those numbers.

## Hey Alexa, how is my cluster?

The fun part is his experiment, built on Alexa because, in his words, he has an Alexa. Say "open Kubernetes manager" and the skill can create or destroy a cluster, ask for help, report a failing node, or raise an alarm when something goes down. It is a work in progress, and he pitches the idea rather than the code: hands-free operations while driving, better accessibility, and voice as one more input next to the keyboard. Whether you want `kubectl delete` to be one misheard sentence away is a question the talk leaves to you.

## Honest about the numbers and the hurdles

Alejandro quotes Gartner-attributed figures of mean time to recovery down 25% and deployment frequency up 30%, and then admits he does not know how they were calculated, which is more candour than most AI slides offer. He also notes that the impact is hard to measure because AI is often built into tools you already use.

The challenges list is realistic: hallucinated or misleading answers, data quality, integration that takes time and experimentation. His closing point is the right one for a DevOps audience: automation is a consequence of DevOps rather than its purpose, maturity is an ongoing journey, and the metrics to watch are still deployment frequency, response time, change failure rate and customer satisfaction.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers who want a map of where AI tooling plugs into each DevOps phase, or a starting point for a team discussion. If you already run AIOps in production, the Alexa skill is the new bit.

Title: Three test plans and a risk-based strategy for DevOps QA
Description: QA consultant Clara Ramos Gonzalez at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on test plans at company, project and SDLC level, plus shift-left and risk-based testing together.
Body:
DevOps teams like to say the pipeline is the test plan. Clara Ramos Gonzalez, a QA consultant with more than 14 years in the field, disagreed politely at Conf42 DevOps 2025: keep the continuous tests, but write test plans at three levels (organisation, project and SDLC) and run shift-left and risk-based testing side by side on top of them.

It is a structured, methodical talk about classic test management, applied to a world that ships every day. Her guiding line from the QA trade: for every development activity, there is a corresponding testing activity.

## Minimal documentation is still some documentation

Clara starts by placing QA inside the DevOps loop: continuous testing automates and validates every change, giving fast feedback and lower risk. Then she makes the case most agile teams avoid. DevOps relegates documentation to second place, she says, but minimal does not mean none, and the test plan is one of the documents you need. She walks through the 16 parts of a good one, from objectives and scope through risk assessment and mitigation, roles, schedule, defect tracking, environments, entry and exit criteria, automation, estimation, resources and deliverables.

## Three levels, one of them reusable everywhere

The core of the talk is splitting the plan into levels:

- **Organisational**: the overarching quality goals and standards, the industry and legal compliance you live under, the recommended methodologies and the tools in use across the company (JMeter for performance work, for example). If you have never written one, she says, start, because it becomes the baseline for every project.
- **Project**: the familiar one and the longest, with approach, entry and exit criteria, timeline, estimation, test cases and suites, risk analysis and responsibilities. Unique per project, built on the organisational standards.
- **SDLC**: tied to the delivery model (Scrum, Agile or here DevOps), written with project managers and developers, covering what testing happens at each CI/CD phase, automation strategy, acceptance criteria per iteration and non-functional testing. Shareable across every project that uses the same lifecycle.

The useful insight is that two of the three plans are written once and reused, which answers the usual objection that test plans slow DevOps down.

## Shift left until you hit static testing

On top of the continuous baseline, Clara runs two strategies. Shift-left means starting QA as early as possible, because the cheapest defect is the one caught in the phase that introduced it. She cites the industry figure that fixing a defect in development is 15 times cheaper than in production, and points out that projects do die of budget burned on late bugs. The earliest testing is static: tools such as SonarQube on code, and peer reviews of requirements, user stories, test scripts and code. Bring testers into design, and start performance and security testing early too.

## Then let risk decide the order

The second strategy is risk-based testing, and this is the section most worth stealing. Risk identification needs every relevant stakeholder in the room; Clara's favourite format is the risk workshop, with interviews, retrospectives and checklists as alternatives. Miss a risk or flag a non-risk and the whole strategy goes unused. Each risk then gets a level from likelihood and impact: a likely but low-impact risk is medium, an unlikely but critical one is still high.

Execution is ordered by that level, in one of two modes. Depth-first runs every test in strict descending risk order, robust but slow. Breadth-first runs the single highest-risk test for each feature first, giving stakeholders a quick read on the health of the whole product. Her teams start depth-first and switch to breadth-first as time and budget run down, which is honest about how projects actually end. Risk monitoring never stops, so you can always report residual risk for a go or no-go decision.

## Who should watch

QA leads and test managers building or defending a strategy in a DevOps shop, and engineering managers who want a vocabulary for "what did we test and why". It is a process talk with no tooling demo, so automation engineers looking for code will want something else.

Title: Wiring a private Jenkins to public GitHub repos without exposing it
Description: Bianca Popu of Analog Devices at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on triggering a firewalled Jenkins from GitHub webhooks via ngrok and publishing sanitised results as Gists.
Body:
Your open-source repo lives on GitHub, but your build needs licensed tools, huge artifacts and real hardware, so it runs on a Jenkins box behind the corporate firewall. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Bianca Popu, DevOps Software Engineer at Analog Devices, showed how her team connects the two: GitHub events trigger the private Jenkins through a tunnel, and results come back to every pull request without anyone outside ever touching the server.

It is a short, focused talk with a clear goal and two concrete problems, which is exactly how a CI design talk should be.

## Why not just use GitHub Actions?

Bianca answers the obvious question first. Cloud CI services are integrated and secure, but the product under test can rule them out: artifacts too big for the storage limits, third-party build or test tools that are large or need a paid licence, or builds too resource-hungry for hosted runners. Some teams simply prefer a self-hosted open-source platform, and she cites a 2023 JetBrains study naming Jenkins the most widely used CI system, which is why the talk centres on it.

The goal is to tie every build to a commit. Each push to main or a release branch, and each pull request, should trigger the pipelines for that exact commit, and the results should be visible to contributors and non-contributors alike.

## Problem one: GitHub cannot reach in

The firewall lets traffic out of the private network but not in, so a GitHub webhook pointed at the Jenkins server just disappears. Turning off the firewall is not an option, since it is the thing keeping private infrastructure private.

The fix is a web tunnel, and Bianca uses ngrok. The client runs on the Jenkins host and opens an encrypted tunnel from a local port to ngrok's servers, which forward webhook traffic to it, with end-to-end encryption so ngrok cannot read the payloads.

On the Jenkins side, three plugins do the interpreting:

- the **GitHub plugin**, endpoint `github-webhook`, for push events, so new commits;
- the **GitHub Pull Request Builder**, endpoint `ghprbhook`, for pull request and issue comment events (Bianca warns it has known vulnerabilities, so configure it carefully);
- the **Generic Webhook Trigger**, which accepts any HTTP request, more flexible but less GitHub-aware.

## Problem two: showing results without leaking the server

Posting a commit status from Jenkins is easy with the GitHub plugin. The catch is the reference URL behind the Details link on the check, which defaults to the Jenkins server's own address. That exposes your private IP to anyone browsing the repo. Pointing it at the ngrok URL instead forces visitors to either log in to Jenkins or get anonymous read access, and neither is acceptable.

Bianca's answer is pleasantly low-tech: process the results and publish them as a GitHub Gist. Gists render Markdown, so a post-build stage can turn console output into something readable by people who have never seen Jenkins, and the GitHub CLI can create them from a pipeline script. The essential step is sanitising the output first, so no credentials or secrets end up in a public Gist. The status check then links to the Gist, not the server.

Her example builds a repository with many projects and generates a Markdown table of per-project status, errors and warnings. One column even merges results from a second pipeline that runs each project on real hardware on a remote server, which is the subject of her colleague Stefan Raus's talk at the same event. She also recommends a dedicated bot account with read and write rights to post the statuses.

## What it buys you

Every commit carries its full test history, so finding the commit that broke things is a lookup, not an investigation. Every pull request is tested in the same controlled environment, which retires the "works on my computer" class of review argument, and reviewers and contributors see the same results.

## Who should watch

Teams with hardware-in-the-loop testing, licensed toolchains or oversized artifacts who still want a GitHub-native contributor experience. If your builds fit on hosted runners, this is still a useful lesson in how much a default URL can leak.

Title: Fifteen years in, culture is still the hard part of DevOps
Description: Mandi Walls of PagerDuty at Conf42 DevOps 2025 on why the C in CALMS stays hardest, and how Schein, Westrum and microcultures help teams fix what they can.
Body:
Technical teams fix what they control, and what they control is mostly tooling, which is why so many DevOps transformations bought a new CI server and kept the old culture. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Mandi Walls, DevOps Advocate at PagerDuty, argued that culture is still the part of CALMS that trips people up, and showed which levers an individual contributor can actually pull without waiting for a director to make a speech.

Mandi has been at this a while: she wrote the O'Reilly white paper Building a DevOps Culture in 2012. She also says up front that the talk is not about PagerDuty. It is a talk about people, with a medieval battle in the middle.

## The French knights did not have a tooling problem

The centrepiece is the Battle of Crécy in the Hundred Years' War. A French army that outnumbered the English marched into the field expecting the hand-to-hand fight that battles had always been, and met the Welsh longbow. The knights had no framework for changing their minds mid-battle, and a culture in which dying with honour beat retreating. They were mown down.

The point is not that you should bring archers to your next architecture review. It is that culture is the scaffolding an organisation uses to make decisions, and when the circumstances change faster than the scaffolding, people keep charging. Mandi borrows the old fish joke too: the young fish asking what water is. You rarely notice the culture you swim in.

## Change projects mostly die of culture

Mandi brings in McKinsey's research: organisations with healthier cultures post better returns, products are easy to copy while culture is not, and roughly 70% of change initiatives fail, about 70% of those for cultural reasons. Her arithmetic: about half of all change initiatives fail because of culture. Anyone who has lived through a stalled migration will recognise the pattern, where some strongly held value quietly outvoted the plan.

## Three models worth keeping in your head

The talk is a tour of models, and it picks useful ones.

- **Edgar Schein's three levels**: basic assumptions (the water), espoused values (what the company says about itself) and artifacts (mission statements, dress codes, the Walmart cheer). Mandi's own example is moving from Chef, with its famously sweary culture, to PagerDuty and having to ask whether swearing on stage was fine. Nobody had noticed it was a rule until someone new asked.
- **Occupational culture**: Schein's work on chemists showed practitioners often have more in common with their peers at other companies than with other departments in their own. Software engineers are the same, which is part of why DevOps, an attempt to change an occupational culture, takes something closer to a generational shift.
- **The Westrum model**: pathological, bureaucratic, generative. Messengers get shot, ignored or trained; failure leads to scapegoating, justice or inquiry. Mandi likes it because so much of the generative column is open to individual contributors: talk to the team next door, publish what you learned from an incident, put it on the wiki.

## Fix the microculture you are standing in

The most practical idea is microcultures. Early research on them was done on Slashdot, an opt-in community, and that is the useful property: a group that chose to be together can change its norms faster than a whole company. Your team and the half-dozen other Python teams on the same platform can agree how you deploy, review and write post-incident reviews, whatever the org chart says.

Mandi is honest about the limits. Changing a large organisation's culture is slow, sometimes it needs turnover, and sometimes the easiest fix is a new employer. Her homework list is solid: Tim Harford's Cautionary Tales episode on the French knights, McKinsey's culture paper, the Westrum summary from IT Revolution and the original paper at the NIH library. Start with Westrum, she says; it is the easiest one to grok.

## Who should watch

Engineers and team leads who suspect their DevOps problem is not a tooling problem, and anyone about to propose one more change initiative. It is a thoughtful, well-read talk, not a playbook with steps, and it ends with a Slack emoji joke that is truer than it should be.

Title: An SDET's checklist for testing cloud and serverless systems
Description: Saili Maliye at Conf42 DevOps 2025 maps what SDETs should automate in the cloud, from IaC checks, API contracts and cold starts to fault injection and cleanup.
Body:
Testing a serverless app means testing the infrastructure too, because half of what can break lives in a Terraform file rather than in your code. At Conf42 DevOps 2025, Saili Maliye, a Tools and Automation Engineer with close to ten years as an SDET, laid out the areas a test engineer has to own in cloud and serverless environments, with the tools for each and the traps she has seen along the way.

It is a broad survey rather than a single war story: eight areas, each with a why, a toolbox and a short how-to. Think of it as a checklist you can hold your current test strategy against.

## Test the infrastructure before it exists

Saili starts with infrastructure as code, because misconfigured templates turn into security holes, surprise bills and bottlenecks. Her advice: validate Terraform, CloudFormation or Azure Resource Manager templates before deploying, using a tool like Terratest; lint them against security and performance standards with a tool like Checkov; wire up automated rollbacks; and check regularly for drift between what the code says and what is running.

## APIs are the backbone, so test them in layers

In a serverless system the API is where services meet, and a bug there ripples. Saili's layering is sensible: functional tests for status codes and payloads first, then integration tests across APIs, contract tests to pin down dependencies between services, fault injection for error handling, security tests for authentication, authorisation and input sanitisation, and schema validation against an OpenAPI spec. Rest Assured, Postman, Newman and Karate all get a mention; the talk's demos lean on Java.

## Cold starts are a performance bug you can test for

Serverless brings its own performance quirks: cold starts, concurrency limits and scaling behaviour under spikes. Saili suggests generating traffic specifically to expose cold-start and concurrency effects, watching latency and throughput under different loads, and running distributed load tests with Gatling, JMeter or Artillery, with AWS X-Ray to see where the time goes. Then put it in the CI/CD pipeline so it runs every time, not once before launch. For the cold starts themselves, her fixes are warm-up scripts and caching on the critical paths.

## Break it on purpose, then clean up after yourself

Two sections stand out because they are the easiest to postpone. Fault injection with Chaos Monkey, Gremlin, AWS Fault Injection Simulator or LitmusChaos lets you rehearse latency, timeouts and dead dependencies, including cascading failures between microservices, before a user does it for you.

The other is environment cleanup, which Saili calls often overlooked. Test runs leave resources behind, and in the cloud forgotten resources bill by the hour. Her fixes: scripts that find and remove unused resources, lifecycle policies for old snapshots and objects, cleanup jobs scheduled after deployments and test runs, and tagging so you know what belongs to whom. Every team has a mystery load balancer; this is how you stop growing more.

## Start small, keep tests modular

The closing advice is practical. Automate one area first, such as API tests, then expand. Fail fast by testing early. Keep tests small, reusable and independent so debugging stays cheap. Treat security as part of the automation rather than a separate phase, watch the cost of running tests in the cloud, and resist tool sprawl: pick a set of tools that work together and document the workflow. For growth, she recommends cloud certifications, getting hands-on with Lambda, Azure Functions or Google Cloud Functions, mastering one language, and sitting closer to the DevOps team.

## Who should watch

SDETs and QA engineers moving from web or mobile testing into cloud-native work, and leads who want a map of what "testing the platform" should cover. It is an overview; if you already run contract tests and chaos experiments in CI, you will mostly be ticking boxes.

Title: Conf42 IoT 2024: Postgres on 63 Raspberry Pis, and other edge truths
Description: The Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 roundup - 39 talks on databases at the edge, vehicles and robots, IoT security, telemetry and AI on device data.
Body:
[Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024](https://www.conf42.com/iot2024) went out on December 19 with 39 talks, and the most memorable thing in it was a Pelican case holding 63 Raspberry Pi 3Bs running a PostgreSQL cluster on Kubernetes. That talk set the tone: IoT in 2024 was less about clever sensors and more about where the data lives, who can touch it, and how you debug a device strapped to a diver.

Speakers came from AWS, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Salesforce, AT&T Labs, Cisco, Oracle, UBS, FedEx and a long list of smaller teams. The talks split into five fairly clean threads.

## Where does IoT data actually live?

[Guillermo Ruiz](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Guillermo_Ruiz_raspberrypi_kubernetes_postgresql) of AWS opened the data thread with the hardware story: eight months of borrowed Raspberry Pis (not the latest ones), StackGres for Postgres on Kubernetes, and the honest admission that a cluster of cheap boards is still not cheap. It's a talk about distributed systems learned the hard way, with a cluster you can carry to a meetup.

[Chris Engelbert](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Chris_Engelbert_kubernetes_postgresql_cluster) of simplyblock covered the same pairing from the operator's chair. His title, PostgreSQL on Kubernetes: Dos and Don'ts, gets misread as a warning, and he corrects it early: "from my perspective, Postgres really loves Kubernetes," Chris Engelbert said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. The rest is about storage, latency and why an operator is a start, not the finish.

[Javier Ramirez](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Javier_Ramirez_database_architecture_traditional) of QuestDB argued for what he calls the Type III architecture, where databases store data in open formats like Apache Parquet and Arrow so your data lake and ML pipeline can read it without an export job. [Tim Spann](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Tim_Spann_opensource_build) of Zilliz toured the open source stack for building IoT applications, [Prashanth Reddy Kora](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Prashanth_Reddy_Kora_cloud_database) of Centene Corporation looked at cloud database systems for scale and cost, and [MK Sirajuddin](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_MK_Sirajuddin_kubernetes_container) of Five9 made the case for containers and Kubernetes as the way to ship and manage IoT workloads from edge to cloud.

## Robots, cars and chips

The physical-world talks were the most varied. [Chiara Civardi and Petr Aubrecht](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Chiara_Civardi_Petr_Aubrecht_robotics_applications_edge) of Payara Services looked at edge computing for robotic applications, where latency and flaky networks decide what runs on the robot and what runs elsewhere. [Rajesh Kamisetty](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Rajesh_Kamisetty_ai_safety_autonomous) of S&P Global covered sensor fusion and V2X in autonomous vehicle safety, [Maksim Lykov](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Maksim_Lykov_it_automotive_business) of Google traced how IT reshaped the automotive business, and [Maksim Kariagin](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Maksim_Kariagin_data_road_emergency) of Metyis used sensor data and ML to predict and mitigate road emergencies.

Industry got its turn too. [Akshat Kapoor](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Akshat_Kapoor_analytics_iiot) of Alcatel-Lucent Enterprise walked through real-time analytics in IIoT, from predictive maintenance to production tuning. [Dileesh Chandra Bikkasani](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Dileesh_Chandra_Bikkasani_twin_network) of AT&T Labs showed digital twins as a way to rehearse network failures before they happen. [Rajesh Guggilla](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Rajesh_Guggilla_oil_logistics) of Energy Transfer brought SAP IS-Oil TSW to bulk oil and gas logistics, and [Ramalinga Reddy Kotapati](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Ramalinga_Reddy_Kotapati_chip_technology) of Infineon Technologies went all the way down to silicon with the move from FinFET to gate-all-around transistors.

## Securing a billion small attack surfaces

Every connected device is a door, and four talks discussed the locks. [Amod Darshane](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Amod_Darshane_cybersecurity_network) of CDW paired network segmentation with zero trust architecture. [Chakradhar Sunkesula](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Chakradhar_Sunkesula_security_ai) of Compass laid out an AI-driven, multi-layered defence covering network, authentication, authorisation and API security. [Mahesh Vankayala](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Mahesh_Vankayala_identity_federation) of Oracle explained identity federation for devices and services, and [Neetu Gangwani](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Neetu_Gangwani_security_blockchain) of UBS combined blockchain with federated learning for privacy and trust across clouds.

## Debugging things you can't plug in

[Matteo Crippa](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Matteo_Crippa_mobile_telemetry) of Intent gave the most relatable talk of the day for anyone who builds companion apps. When the device is strapped to a climber or a diver, you can't attach a debugger, so telemetry becomes your only witness. His team built internal telemetry tooling for both developers and QA, and he walks through why.

[Parth Menon](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Parth_Menon_crisis_management) of Meta told a crisis story from his time at SAP Labs India: replacing a paper sign-up sheet for office visits with an automated contact tracing system during COVID, where notifying exposed employees used to take a couple of days. [Sai Krishna Paladugu](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Sai_Krishna_Paladugu_kiosk_ios) of FedEx covered iOS-powered self-service kiosks, [Karthik Vallamsetla](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Karthik_Vallamsetla_web_api) of Cisco showed modern Web APIs for data-driven IoT interfaces, [Gunjan Agarwal](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Gunjan_Agarwal_ar_vr_scalable) of Meta discussed designing AR-VR systems that scale, and [Amanda Hunter](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Amanda_Hunter_product_web) of Salesforce looked at targeted web experiences as a lever for IoT product adoption.

## AI on top of device data

The largest group asked what models can do with all those readings. [Natalia Drazhnik](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Natalia_Drazhnik_sata_decisions_smarter_system) of YCH Blue Digital Limited and [Babita Kumari](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Babita_Kumari_cloud_ai) of Microsoft covered AI-driven architectures for IoT systems, [Nandakumar Ramachandran Pezhery](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Nandakumar_Ramachandran_Pezhery_ai_multicloud) of Xoriant used IoT data to tune multi-cloud infrastructure in real time, and [Shradha Kohli](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Shradha_Kohli_ai_interface) of Salesforce made the case for explainable AI in conversational interfaces. [Kartheek Medhavi Penagamuri Shriram](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Kartheek_Medhavi_Penagamuri_Shriram_ai_development) of Microsoft showed AI coding assistants like GitHub Copilot applied to IoT development.

Domain talks filled in the rest: unified communications from [Naga Praneeth Yerram and Vaishnav Yerram](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Naga_Praneeth_Yerram_Vaishnav_Yerram_ai_communication), healthcare chatbots fed by wearables from [Abhishek Vajpayee and Rathish Mohan](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Abhishek_Vajpayee_Rathish_Mohan_ai_healthcare), fintech from [Sudeep Meduri](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Sudeep_Meduri_ai_fintech) of Google and [Andrei Alekseev](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Andrei_Alekseev_ai_fintech_financial) of Weltrade, workflow automation from [Kowsick Venkatachalapathi](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Kowsick_Venkatachalapathi_ai_ml_workflow) of BNY, and deep learning's reach into reinforcement learning, generative models and security from [Chirag Gajiwala](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Chirag_Gajiwala_ai_deep_cybersecurity) of Nutanix.

## The product side

A handful of talks remembered that someone has to want the device. [Daria Novosad](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Daria_Novosad_product_growth) of Tele2 covered where to find ideas for new IoT products, [Elena Budnik](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Elena_Budnik_crm_service) of PapaFinance tied IoT to CRM for proactive service at small companies, [Aliaksandr Zhastkou](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Aliaksandr_Zhastkou_technology_product_communication) of Yandex looked at new technology in product communications, and [Robin Sarkar](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Robin_Sarkar_data_analytics_portal) of Enstall made the case for self-service data portals.

## Thanks to the partners

[StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) joined as newsletter partner and [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, with media partners including [Manning](https://www.manning.com), [Packt](https://www.packtpub.com/), [CodeCrafters](https://codecrafters.io/?r=2qF) and [Infosec Conferences](https://infosec-conferences.com).

Every talk is on the [Conf42 IoT 2024 page](https://www.conf42.com/iot2024) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrA0In7SJnv39Fva-tU5fA9u). The series came back a year later as [Conf42 IoT 2025](https://www.conf42.com/iot2025).

Title: Where the physical world joins the internet
Description: And starts responding
Body:
# Everything is connected (and somehow it’s your problem)

Once upon a time, the internet lived safely inside computers.

Now it’s in cars, factories, medical devices, oil pipelines, kiosks, fridges, traffic systems, and that one sensor nobody remembers installing but everyone is afraid to touch. Welcome to IoT.

Conf42 Internet of Things 2024 is here to make sense of that world.

This conference covers the full IoT stack, from edge devices and connectivity to cloud platforms, analytics, security, and automation. You’ll find talks on robotics, industrial IoT, real-time analytics, digital twins, Kubernetes at the edge, and what happens when AI meets thousands of devices that never sleep.

AI is everywhere, obviously. Expect sessions on explainable AI for IoT, AI-driven cloud architectures, predictive analytics, automation, and using machine learning to turn massive streams of device data into something resembling a decision. There’s also plenty on observability, telemetry, and figuring out what’s actually going on when things stop behaving.

The use cases go wide. Healthcare, fintech, automotive, logistics, energy, retail, and smart infrastructure all show up. From contact tracing and crisis management to autonomous vehicles and supply chain optimization, this is IoT in the real world, not just diagrams on slides.

Security and reliability get their share of attention too. Identity federation, zero trust, blockchain, multi-layered defenses, and securing connected ecosystems where failure is not an option and “just reboot it” is rarely acceptable.

If your job involves devices, data, clouds, or explaining to someone why a sensor stopped reporting at 3 AM, this one’s for you. IoT is messy, powerful, and very much alive. Let’s talk about it.

Title: When the printer starts calling an external DNS server
Description: Amod Darshane (CDW) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on combining network segmentation with zero trust to contain IoT threats
Body:
A printer should talk to its print server and the monitoring system, and nothing else. When it starts querying an external DNS server, that's your red flag. Amod Darshane, Senior Consulting Engineer at CDW, used that example at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 to make his case: network segmentation contains IoT devices, zero trust keeps checking who they are, and you need both.

Darshane has about 16 years in networking, from route-and-switch work through network access control to SD-WAN and SASE projects, and the talk reads like it: a practitioner's tour of the building blocks, with the vocabulary explained along the way.

## Why are IoT devices such easy targets?

His list is familiar to anyone who has put sensors on a corporate network. Many IoT devices lack robust security protocols. Limited processing power and storage rule out heavyweight security agents. There are a lot of them, and they are prone to malware, DDoS and data breaches.

The wider threats compound it. Advanced persistent threats can sit undetected for around nine to twelve months while they quietly collect data. Insider threats come from employees, contractors and third-party vendors with legitimate access. And workloads are spread across data centres, cloud and multi-cloud, so the area to monitor keeps growing. Attackers, he notes, use AI to become more productive too.

## Segmentation, from VLANs to air gaps

Network segmentation splits the network into smaller isolated parts so a breach in one doesn't spread. Darshane covers the range: VLANs as logical broadcast domains (guest separate from corporate, printers with their own access), VRFs to separate guest, corporate and IoT traffic, fully air-gapped physical networks for IoT, and DMZs for applications exposed to the internet, with only the necessary ports open.

Next-generation firewalls get their own section: application-aware rules, deep packet inspection, intrusion prevention, geolocation filtering, multi-tenancy, and VRF and SD-WAN features on the same box. Software-defined networking adds zero-touch provisioning, where a device gets a DHCP address, calls home for its certificates and configuration, and configures itself.

## Zero trust, where identity expires

Zero trust is never trust, always verify. A device or user identity doesn't stay valid indefinitely; it is re-authenticated over time, and authorisation follows authentication with least-privilege access. The components he lists are identity and access management with MFA, micro-segmentation at the application or workload level, continuous monitoring with anomaly detection, SSO integrated with Active Directory, and role- or attribute-based access control.

His favourite example comes from network access control. A device authenticates with a certificate issued by the enterprise root CA and is placed in the right VLAN dynamically. When that certificate expires, it doesn't lose the network; it drops into a restricted VLAN where it can only fix its certificate.

## Why one without the other falls short

The synergy section is the argument of the talk. "the segmentation alone doesn't solve the problem of identity verification," Amod Darshane said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. Segmentation limits where an attacker can go; zero trust verifies every device and user even inside a trusted segment, with policies that change as a device's compliance changes. Together they stop lateral movement, east-west as well as north-south, and make anomalies like the chatty printer visible.

He sketches two deployments: smart manufacturing plants, where IoT sensors go into their own VLANs under zero-trust access policies so malware can't spread through them, and healthcare facilities, where medical IoT devices are segmented and authenticated to prevent unauthorised access.

## Where do you start?

His practical advice is unglamorous: identify your critical assets and group them logically, keep a single source of truth for inventory, audit it annually, then run a network assessment, apply zero-trust principles to critical applications first, and keep monitoring with behavioural analytics.

## Who should watch

Network and security engineers bringing IoT devices onto enterprise networks, and developers who want the networking vocabulary (VLAN, VRF, NAC, DMZ, ZTP) explained in one sitting. It is an overview, not a configuration walkthrough.

Title: One identity, many providers, and fewer than a hundred passwords
Description: Mahesh Vankayala (Oracle) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on industry-wide identity federation built on SSO and extended OAuth 2.0 scopes
Body:
The average user juggles about a hundred passwords, and 61% of data breaches involve credentials. Mahesh Vankayala of Oracle opened his Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 talk with those figures and proposed the fix: identity federation across a whole industry, where a person verified once can move between banks, hospitals or universities, and the devices that serve them, without starting from scratch each time.

It is a short proposal talk: a model, its technical building blocks, the sectors that would gain, and the obstacles.

## What is broken today?

Vankayala lists four problems. Password fatigue, with users reusing and weakening passwords. Security, with credentials in 61% of breaches and the human element in 85% of those. User experience, with 55% of consumers abandoning online purchases over password issues. And onboarding, where every provider repeats the same identity checks and pays for it.

## The model in four steps

His identity federation model has four parts:

1. **Single sign-on** across providers in an industry.
2. **Standardised identity attributes**, the verified, industry-specific information everyone agrees on.
3. **Consent management**, so the user controls what is shared and for what.
4. **An industry trust framework** with the rules and standards for taking part.

## How would you build it?

The technical layer reuses existing standards rather than inventing new ones. Extend OAuth 2.0 with industry-specific scopes for fine-grained access control. Federate the identity providers so each institution acts as both identity provider and service provider. Define an attribute exchange protocol to share user attributes securely between members. And run a federation registry, a central record of participating institutions and their metadata.

"we need to have a federation registry A centralized place where the registration for participating institutions And metadata are maintained," Mahesh Vankayala said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

## Who gains, by his figures?

The sector examples carry the talk's numbers, which come from industry estimates rather than a deployment he ran:

- **Banking**: onboarding time down 80%, cross-selling opportunities up 30%, customer retention up 25%, and identity fraud down by up to 90%.
- **Healthcare**: interoperable health IT could save the US healthcare system 30 billion dollars a year; shared, verified patient information could cut readmissions by 20% and save up to 30 minutes of administration per patient encounter.
- **Education**: transcript verification time down 90%, adult learner enrolment up 25%, and hiring times down 40% when credentials can be shared securely with employers.

## What stands in the way?

Regulation first: implementations must satisfy sector rules and data protection law, and he points to GDPR fines totalling 1.3 billion euros in 2021, a sevenfold rise on the year before. Security second, with 45% of organisations reporting more cyber attacks in the previous 12 months, so MFA and biometrics are table stakes. Privacy third, with 43% of respondents very or extremely concerned.

His remedies: align with regulations at a global level, since connected devices cross borders; privacy by design with granular consent; industry collaboration on interoperable standards; and education so organisations actually adopt them.

## Who should watch

Identity and security architects thinking about cross-organisation SSO, and IoT teams who need devices and users to authenticate across partners. The IoT angle is light; this is mostly an identity talk with an industry-consortium shape.
