Title: A four-layer security framework, measured in milliseconds
Description: Chakradhar Sunkesula (Compass) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on a zero-trust framework across network, authentication, authorization and APIs
Body:
Cutting the time to detect unauthorised access from 127 hours to under 3 minutes is the kind of number that makes a security team sit up. Chakradhar Sunkesula, Engineering Manager at Compass, quoted it at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 while walking through a multi-layered security framework with four pillars: network security, authentication, authorization and API security, all built on zero-trust principles.

The talk title promises IoT ecosystems; the talk itself is about securing cloud platforms, which is where most IoT data and device APIs end up. Expect a framework with a lot of metrics, not device firmware.

## Why perimeter security stops working

Sunkesula sets the scene with figures: worldwide public cloud spending of 545.8 billion dollars in 2023, an average of 43 cloud security incidents a month per organisation, 75% of them preventable, and a global shortage of about 4 million cybersecurity professionals. Perimeter models, built for on-premises networks, assume that whatever is inside can be trusted. In a distributed cloud, that assumption is the vulnerability.

## Layer 1: never trust the network

Zero trust means every request is authenticated and authorised regardless of where it comes from. In practice: front-end services, back-end services and databases sit in separate subnets, so a compromised segment doesn't hand over the rest. He reports an 85% reduction in lateral movement attacks from that isolation, and 99.97% of password spray and encryption key theft attempts thwarted with dynamic access control.

On top sits detection. ML-driven traffic analysis cut false positives by 92% while keeping 99.2% accuracy on real threats. Digital tripwires brought threat dwell time under 24 hours, with automated responses neutralising threats within milliseconds of detection.

## Layer 2: authentication that profiles behaviour

Instead of trusting a username and password, the system classifies each login attempt by location, device type, usage pattern and time of access. It handles 1.2 million authentication requests a day with response times under 200 milliseconds, and he credits it with blocking 99.7% of credential abuse attempts. AI-driven attack simulations keep testing it.

Token security uses risk-based lifetimes: a token's validity shrinks or grows with the user's behaviour and environment. Compared with fixed lifetimes, successful token exploitation dropped 91%. The kill switch is the memorable piece: it watches more than 30 behavioural patterns and revokes access across all contexts in under 100 milliseconds when something looks wrong.

"The ability to revoke access so quickly prevents attacker from maintaining a foothold in the system," Chakradhar Sunkesula said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

## Layer 3: least privilege, continuously

Authorization processes about 1.5 million decisions a day and automatically revokes excess permissions, which is how it fights privilege creep. Continuous permission auditing and dynamic privilege adjustments (3 million modifications a day, by his figure) are behind the 127-hours-to-3-minutes detection improvement, and they cut the time to revoke compromised privileges from 12 hours to milliseconds.

## Layer 4: APIs as the front door

The API layer validates 2.3 billion requests a day with response times under 50 milliseconds, using schema enforcement, rate limiting against denial of service, and input sanitisation against SQL injection and cross-site scripting. An anomaly detection model trained on more than 500 billion API requests evaluates 235 parameters per transaction and learns dynamic baselines across 89 usage patterns; he reports a 94% drop in false positives.

## How much of this transfers?

The headline outcomes he gives are a 99.97% detection rate for sophisticated attacks, 94% faster detection than traditional systems and a 76% lower cost per incident. The talk doesn't explain how these were measured or on which systems, so treat them as the speaker's reported results. The structure is the reusable part: four layers, each with a prevention control and a detection control, each with a latency budget.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers designing zero trust for cloud backends, including the ones behind IoT fleets. If you want a checklist of controls per layer with target numbers to argue about, this is it.

- Vaibhav Anil Vora on [zero trust from perimeter defence to continuous verification](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Vaibhav_Anil_Vora_zero_trust_security) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.
- Syed Rehan on [zero trust security with IoT](https://www.conf42.com/Web_30_2022_Syed_Rehan_zero_trust_security_iot) at Conf42 Web 3.0 2022.

Title: Federated learning keeps the data home, blockchain keeps the receipts
Description: Neetu Gangwani (UBS) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on pairing federated learning with blockchain for private, auditable AI across clouds
Body:
Federated learning lets several organisations train one model without pooling their data; blockchain gives them a tamper-proof record of who changed the model and how. Neetu Gangwani, Associate Director at UBS, argued at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 that the two together, run on cloud AI platforms, answer the trust problem in distributed AI: everyone keeps their data, and nobody has to take anyone's word for the model updates.

It is a framework talk: what each piece contributes, how they fit, and where the open problems are, rather than a production case with metrics.

## What problem is this solving?

Gangwani lists four pressures on distributed AI. Data sensitivity: personal and organisational data that cannot be shared or centralised. Security threats: adversarial attacks such as model poisoning and Sybil attacks. A trust deficit: when organisations or cloud providers collaborate, nobody can see what the others did, so the outputs are hard to trust. And regulation: GDPR and HIPAA demand privacy and accountability.

## Three parts, one job each

- **Federated learning**, which she credits to Google in 2017, trains local models on each party's own data. Only the model updates go to a central server, which aggregates them into a global model and sends it back for the next round.
- **Blockchain** supplies a decentralised, immutable ledger for those updates.
- **Cloud AI** provides the scalable training and serving infrastructure, from pre-trained models and APIs to managed ML platforms.

## What does the blockchain actually record?

This is the part worth the watch. Each model update is treated as a transaction, so every change to the shared model is traceable to who made it and how. Smart contracts automate validation and consensus on updates before they are accepted. Incentive mechanisms reward high-quality data contributions and discourage gaming the system. Cryptographic identity management restricts participation to authorised parties. And the ledger becomes the audit trail compliance teams ask for.

"these transactions should be immutable so that user don't have the rights to remove it, updated or do any modification," Neetu Gangwani said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

For privacy beyond keeping raw data local, she adds differential privacy and homomorphic encryption, so even the shared updates leak less. For throughput, layer 2 blockchain solutions to absorb the transaction volume of frequent updates.

## Where would you use it?

Her application list covers healthcare (hospitals collaborating on drug discovery and personalised treatment without exchanging patient records), finance (fraud detection models trained across institutions without exposing transaction data), smart cities, supply chain forecasting, and edge computing, where IoT devices train a shared model while their data stays on the device.

The healthcare case study ties it together: hospitals train on local data, the blockchain secures and records the model updates, and the expected outcomes are better diagnostics, faster drug discovery and GDPR and HIPAA compliance.

## What is still unsolved?

She is upfront that the framework has costs. Scalability needs efficient algorithms such as sharding. Aggregated updates still need protection through secure computation. Incentives have to reward contribution without introducing bias. Blockchain adds computational overhead to every training round. And governance is open; she suggests DAOs for decentralised model and version control.

## Who should watch

Architects in regulated industries looking at cross-organisation ML, and IoT teams wondering how to train on device data without collecting it. It is conceptual, so come for the component map and the list of open problems; there are no benchmarks or code.

Title: Gate-all-around fixes the transistor and hands the problems to layout
Description: Ramalinga Reddy Kotapati (Infineon Technologies) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on what the move from FinFET to GAA means for chip physical design
Body:
Gate-all-around transistors buy roughly 20% better power, 15% better performance and 30% better area than FinFET at advanced nodes, according to Ramalinga Reddy Kotapati of Infineon Technologies at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. His talk is about the bill that comes with those gains: denser, rule-heavy layouts that push more of the work onto physical design and EDA tools.

It is an unusual talk for an IoT event, one level below the device: what happens inside the chips that every sensor, gateway and accelerator runs on.

## Why did the industry move past FinFET?

Kotapati walks the lineage. In a planar transistor the gate sits on top of the channel and has limited control over it. FinFET raised the channel into a fin and wrapped the gate around three sides, which brought faster switching, higher current density and lower leakage, and you can put multiple fins under one gate for more drive strength.

At 3 nm and 2 nm, FinFET scaling runs out of road; the slides name channel width variation as one of the issues. Gate-all-around (GAA) surrounds the channel completely, and stacks planar channels vertically, which raises the effective channel width. More drive current, less leakage, lower power.

His summary of the shift is blunt. "So we have to adopt like advanced EDA tools," Ramalinga Reddy Kotapati said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, and the rest of the talk explains why.

## What gets harder for physical design?

This is the core of the talk. GAA moves complexity from the device to the layout:

- **Layout complexity**: many more design rules, and more of them interacting.
- **Interconnect**: reduced metal pitches need smarter routing, and via optimisation (multi-cut vias) becomes critical for performance and yield.
- **Power distribution**: with thinner metals, IR drop and electromigration need planning up front, or the design ends up burning power it shouldn't.
- **Multi-patterning**: metal layers and even standard cell pins are multi-patterned, so placement legalisation and routing have to respect those rules or you get shorts, DRC violations and congestion.

## Which tools and techniques does he lean on?

His answer is better EDA. AI-powered tools that predict layout issues early and speed up convergence. Multi-patterning-aware placement and routing. Support for 3D-IC design, including through-silicon vias and die-to-die interfaces.

On the design side he lists standard cell optimisation for GAA (track height reduction, pin access), careful clock tree synthesis with multi-point CTS to control latency and skew, shielding and buffer insertion for signal integrity as nets get more dominant, and design-for-manufacturing rules so the chip after fabrication matches the chip in the tool. For high-density designs he adds thermal management, statistical on-chip variation analysis (POCV) for process variation, non-default routing rules on higher metals for crosstalk, planning which clocks really need a full tree, and Network-on-Chip architectures for on-chip data movement.

## Where is it heading?

His outlook: 3D integration, stacking dies built on different technologies in one package; EDA tools for quantum designs; and tighter integration of analog and mixed-signal blocks. And more AI-driven methodology throughout, to keep design and manufacturing correlated as scaling continues.

## Who should watch

Physical design and backend engineers who want a compact checklist of what GAA changes, and software or IoT engineers curious about why chip schedules and costs keep climbing at the leading edge. The delivery is dense with acronyms and light on worked examples; treat it as a map of the problem areas.

Title: Three browser APIs, and the conversion numbers each one moved
Description: Karthik Vallamsetla (Cisco) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on Geolocation, Web Notifications and Intersection Observer in real projects
Body:
Lazy-loading product images with the Intersection Observer API cut page load times by 35% for a fashion retailer and lifted mobile conversions by 12%. That is one of several project results Karthik Vallamsetla, Software Engineer at Cisco, shared at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, in a short, practical talk on three browser APIs that let a web app behave more like a native one: Geolocation, Web Notifications and Intersection Observer.

The examples come from e-commerce work rather than IoT devices, but the lesson travels: the browser already ships the sensors and hooks, and the craft is in asking for them politely.

## Why these three?

Vallamsetla frames the talk around how far web APIs have come. Early APIs updated text or hid an element. Modern ones reach device features, handle real-time interaction and work offline, which is what lets progressive web apps compete with native apps. One project he mentions let shoppers browse previously viewed products without a connection, which paid off during Black Friday traffic.

## Geolocation, with a plan B

For an outdoor gear retailer, his team used the user's location and local weather to recommend hiking gear suited to where they were. He reports a 20% increase in conversions.

The more interesting detail is what happened when people said no. A fallback that let users type in a zip code kept 15% of the users who had denied location access. "Always explain why you are requesting location data and ensure it's handled securely," Karthik Vallamsetla said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

## Notifications people don't hate

The Web Notifications API reaches users when they are not on the site. For an e-commerce client, price-drop alerts on wishlist items drove a 25% increase in click-through rates during the holiday season.

He is just as clear about the failure mode: too many notifications and users switch them off. His fixes are letting users set their own preferences and timing messages well. Sending reminders during lunch breaks or evenings doubled engagement in one campaign.

## The unglamorous one that pays for itself

Intersection Observer tracks when elements enter or leave the viewport, which makes it the tool for lazy loading and scroll-triggered animation without hand-rolled scroll listeners. Beyond the 35% load-time cut, he stresses that it matters most on mobile, where bandwidth and CPU are tight.

## What happens when you combine them?

For a home goods retailer, his team stacked all three: Geolocation to find users near stores, Web Notifications for in-store promotions, and Intersection Observer to animate banners as users scrolled. He reports foot traffic up 30% and local sales up 20%. In another campaign, Geolocation paired with flash-sale notifications for nearby stores raised user engagement by 30%.

## The fine print

His challenges section is short and sensible: be transparent about data and comply with regulations such as GDPR, avoid notification fatigue, and treat mobile performance as a requirement. He closes by pointing at AR, VR and AI-powered APIs as the next wave.

The numbers are reported outcomes from his projects, without the experimental setup behind them, so read them as indications of what each API can do rather than benchmarks.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers building dashboards or companion web apps for connected products, and anyone who has shipped a location prompt that everyone declined. It is a quick talk with code-free explanations; the MDN pages will give you the syntax afterwards.

Title: Your database is a gatekeeper. Type III architecture fires it
Description: Javier Ramirez (QuestDB) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on Type III databases that store Parquet, speak Arrow and get data out as fast as in
Body:
When was the last time you wished your database used a more proprietary data format? Javier Ramirez, Developer Advocate at QuestDB, opened his Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 talk with that question, and the rest of it is the answer: a Type III database stores data in open formats such as Apache Parquet, speaks Apache Arrow on the way out, and gets data out as fast as it lets data in.

He is candid that QuestDB, an open source time series database, used its own binary format for years. The talk is about why they are changing that, with live demos, and why he sees other databases moving the same way.

## Why are databases gatekeepers?

Getting data into a traditional database is easy. Getting all of it out, say to train a machine learning model, means a slow export, moving data between servers and converting formats. "in a way, the database, It's acting as the gatekeeper to your data," Javier Ramirez said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

He traces it back to history. Databases were designed when a successful application stored a few million rows in its whole lifetime. IoT systems now produce thousands, sometimes millions, of rows per second. NoSQL answered with fast inserts and simple queries; OLAP answered with big batch analytics, separated storage from compute and invented the data lake. But OLAP formats on object storage were built for immutable, append-only data, which is a poor fit for streams.

## Streaming data is rude

His list of what makes streaming data hard is the part IoT engineers will nod along to. It gets very big and never stops. It bursts and lags. Sensors in factories around the world sit behind networks of different speeds, devices run out of battery, restart and disconnect, so data arrives late and out of order, often after you have already emitted results. Individual points lose value as they age while long-term aggregates stay valuable. And some queries feed alerts where seconds of latency are not acceptable.

That is the niche of what he calls fast databases, with time series databases as the IoT favourite: fast ingestion, fast queries on recent data, downsampling and tiering for the old stuff.

## QuestDB in numbers

The demo box at demo.questdb.io holds 1.6 billion New York taxi trips. An average trip distance across the whole set (2.8 miles) came back in about 200 milliseconds; limited to 2018, about 110 million rows, in 19 milliseconds. QuestDB's time-bucketing extension sampled the same average into 15-day or 22-day intervals in around 140 milliseconds.

Under the hood: columnar storage partitioned by time, a parallel SQL engine with a JIT compiler, almost no indexes, a parallel write-ahead log, and ingestion separated from reads so query load doesn't throttle writes. He mentions up to 5 million events per second on a single instance for the open source version.

## The three parts of a Type III database

Ramirez defines it with three components:

1. **Distributed computing**: storage separated from compute, possibly on object storage such as Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage.
2. **Open formats**: Parquet (Iceberg-compatible), compressed, with room for semi-structured data, so other tools can read the storage directly and skip the database.
3. **Egress as fast as ingress**: Apache Arrow as a columnar in-memory format, and ADBC, the Arrow equivalent of JDBC, so clients such as pandas or Polars receive columnar data with zero-copy and no row-by-row deserialisation.

QuestDB's twist is the first mile: the newest partition stays in its fast binary format, older partitions go to Parquet, and anything older still can tier off to object storage. Queries span all three without the user caring where the data lives.

The closing demo made it concrete. Chicago beach water sensor data in QuestDB, queried directly from the Parquet partitions with DuckDB. DuckDB returned slightly fewer rows for one date range than QuestDB, which turned out to be the point: the active September 2023 partition was still binary. Restrict the query to the Parquet partitions and the counts matched exactly at 5,478.

At the time of the talk, the Parquet support was in beta, with general availability planned for the following year.

## Who should watch

Anyone running time series or IoT data who also feeds a data lake or ML pipeline and is tired of nightly exports. Database people will enjoy the history section. It is a QuestDB talk in its demos, but the architecture argument stands on its own.

Title: Self-driving safety by the numbers, from 1,500 ms humans to 300 ms cars
Description: Rajesh Kamisetty (S&P Global) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on how sensor fusion and neural networks make autonomous vehicles safer
Body:
A human driver needs about 1,500 milliseconds to react; an autonomous vehicle, by the figures Rajesh Kamisetty quotes, needs about 300. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, the Lead Software Engineer at S&P Global gave a guided tour of how self-driving cars see, decide and fail safely, and why he thinks reaction time is the whole safety argument in one number.

Kamisetty comes at the topic as a data engineer with 14 years in the field, not as someone who builds cars, and the talk is pitched accordingly: an overview of the stack and the metrics that matter, for people who want to know how the pieces fit together.

## What does an autonomous vehicle actually sense?

The talk starts with the perception hardware and the numbers attached to each piece. Sensor fusion is the umbrella: sensors placed around the vehicle build a 360-degree picture that the software maps and acts on. Under it sit three families of sensors:

- **LiDAR** (Light Detection and Ranging) emits laser light to measure distance and depth, does 128-layer scanning across 360 degrees and reaches about 250 metres.
- **Cameras** capture more than 120 frames per second, with infrared for low light, and feed neural networks that interpret the images.
- **Radar** detects vehicles at around 300 metres, with accuracy he puts at plus or minus 0.1 metre.

He also cites the data rate: about 1.5 terabytes of sensor data per hour, processed alongside other inputs by the on-board models.

## Tesla bets on cameras, Waymo on everything

The most useful comparison in the talk is the split between the two best-known approaches. Tesla's Full Self-Driving is vision-only: better pictures, more of them, processed faster. Kamisetty points to two reasons for that bet. Tesla's large fleet gives it a much bigger data set than its rivals, and cameras are cheaper than LiDAR.

Waymo combines LiDAR, radar and cameras into one perception system, builds a high-definition map and pinpoints the vehicle's position within it. More hardware on the roof, more redundancy in what the car knows about its surroundings.

## Pedestrians are harder than cars

The neural networks behind these vehicles, he says, process almost 250,000 scenarios per iteration. Vehicle detection sits at 98% accuracy and pedestrian detection at 95%. The gap has a plain explanation: pedestrians step off the kerb without signalling.

"pedestrians are moving objects like moving people. So they come, they may suddenly cross the street or they suddenly pop in between," Rajesh Kamisetty said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

Reaction time is where the safety case lives. He cites a 37% reduction in collisions compared with human drivers, while being careful to call it a statistic rather than proof that autonomous vehicles are better. Mean time between failures is quoted at 50,000 hours.

## Where the numbers need to go next

The forward-looking part of the talk sets targets. Neural processing units are approaching 1,000 TOPS (tera operations per second). Communication latency between sensors and the rest of the system is heading for 5 milliseconds or less. Reaction latency, today around 300 milliseconds, is being pushed towards 100. Reliability needs to sit at 99.99% or better, because, as he puts it, you cannot get stuck in the middle of the road.

On the regulatory side he names ISO 26262 for functional safety and SOTIF (safety of the intended functionality), plus the validation regime: real-world miles driven, simulation runs, and edge cases such as snow, fog, rain and hail. He deliberately sets aside the ethics questions (who the car protects in an unavoidable collision) to stay on the technology.

## Who should watch

Engineers outside the automotive world who want a quick map of the autonomous vehicle stack: which sensors do what, how Tesla and Waymo differ, and which metrics the industry tracks. If you already work on perception systems, this is a primer, not new material, and the figures are industry-level claims, not results from a system the speaker built.

Title: Your next IoT product is hiding in your users' complaints
Description: Daria Novosad (Tele2) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on finding IoT product ideas in behavioural data, complaints and community feedback
Body:
Two thirds of IoT revenue comes from services, not hardware. Daria Novosad, Senior Product Manager at Tele2, used that figure at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 to make a product manager's point: an IoT company lives on ongoing engagement, so its best product ideas come from watching what users do with the devices they already own, and from listening to what annoys them.

It is a product talk, not an engineering one. No architecture diagrams; instead a method for going from device data to a feature people will pay for.

## Why is IoT growth so messy?

Novosad opens with the market numbers: 24.1 billion connected devices and 1.5 trillion dollars in revenue expected by 2030. The catch is fragmentation. Devices sit in smart grids, connected vehicles, lighting, media and healthcare, each with its own requirements, and the leading regions (China, North America and Europe) each bring their own compliance and localisation work. Scaling one product across that is hard, so she argues the numbers matter less than knowing exactly whose problem you solve.

## Three audiences, one pyramid

She splits IoT users into three groups: families who want simplicity and safety (smart home, energy savings), businesses who want efficiency and scale (industrial IoT), and industries such as healthcare that care about workflow integration.

Then she stacks them as a pyramid for micro-targeting. At the base, general users who want basic functionality and an easy setup. In the middle, segments such as energy-conscious users who want tailored saving features. At the top, micro-segments such as frequent travellers who need remote device management. Her thermostat example: basic features for everyone, AI-driven energy tools for the niche that will use them.

## Complaints are a roadmap

The sharpest section treats every user frustration as a product brief. Her case study is the Nest thermostat. Users found adjusting the temperature by hand tedious, so Nest built auto-scheduling, which learns preferences and adjusts on its own. The result she cites is around 12% savings on heating costs.

"Every frustration users face is a chance to innovate, is a chance to create something new," Daria Novosad said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

Behavioural data does the same job quietly. A smart thermostat records when people change the temperature, and that pattern is the raw material for predictive features. Her innovation loop is short: collect interactions and find patterns, turn them into insights, brainstorm against those insights, then prototype and iterate on user feedback.

## Start with one problem

On getting from idea to market she is firmly in the MVP camp: build something that solves one core problem, just one, test it with real users and refine. Communities help here. Surveys, beta programmes and forums turn customers into co-creators, and people who tested a prototype tend to stay loyal to the product.

She also looks outward at other sectors for gaps worth filling: Medtronic connecting insulin pumps, John Deere's smart farming equipment, Tesla's over-the-air updates. And she argues for partnerships, startups for agility, large companies such as Amazon for scale, universities for research, open source for fast prototyping.

## Who should watch

Product managers and founders working on connected devices, and engineers who want to understand how their device telemetry turns into roadmap decisions. If you want implementation detail on analytics pipelines, look elsewhere; this one is about what to build and how to find out.

Title: From web to headset - what XR development asks of software engineers
Description: Gunjan Agarwal (Meta) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on the tools, constraints and AI shortcuts of building scalable AR/VR products
Body:
Moving from mobile or web to a headset means a frame budget, a physics engine and users who get motion sick if you miss either. Gunjan Agarwal, an engineering leader at Meta who previously worked at Nutanix and Amazon, gave software engineers a field guide to XR development at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024: how it differs from 2D platforms, the tools that carry it, the challenges unique to it, and where AI shortens the work. She is explicit that the talk reflects her personal experience and independent research, not Meta's practices.

It is a foundations talk by design, broad rather than deep, and much of it transfers to 2D game and app development too.

## What changes when the screen is on your face?

XR is the umbrella for augmented reality (overlays like IKEA Place or Snapchat filters), virtual reality (full immersion on devices like Meta Quest or PlayStation VR) and mixed reality, where virtual objects behave as if they were part of the room (HoloLens, Meta Quest 3). She cites a projected market of over $250 billion by 2027.

"Unlike mobile and web, XR requires real time 3d environments," Gunjan Agarwal said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, which brings 3D modelling, rendering and physics into a software engineer's day. Spatial awareness and low latency are non-negotiable, refresh rates typically 90 Hz or more, and shared spaces bring their own privacy concerns.

## The toolbox: game engines first

Her headset anatomy covers lenses and screens, tracking sensors and cameras, spatial audio and microphones, haptic controllers and the CPU/GPU, with realism coming from stereoscopic depth, spatial audio and a wide, tracked field of view.

On the software side, the core skill is a game engine such as Unity or Unreal, which provides 3D rendering, physics, real-time processing, spatial audio, animation scripting (C# in Unity), input from controllers, hand tracking and voice, scene management, asset stores and cross-platform builds. Engineers also need the artists' vocabulary: meshes, materials and shaders, render pipelines such as URP and HDRP, baked versus real-time lighting, VFX, animation, post-processing. For AR there are SDKs like Apple's ARKit, Google's ARCore and Vuforia, with 8th Wall, Wikitude, MAXST and DeepAR as alternatives.

## Challenges unique to XR

Creating a successful AR/VR product "is no small feat," she says, and her list explains why:

- **Hardware limits**: processing power, battery life (foveated rendering, which draws only where the user looks in full detail, saves both), weight and comfort, and displays where higher refresh rates cost heat and power.
- **Latency and motion sickness**: tracking of head, eyes and position must be real time, and predictive algorithms that anticipate the user's next move hide the remaining lag.
- **Tracking through multiple sensors**: fusing cameras, gyroscopes and accelerometers reliably.
- **Content**: detailed 3D models that still run on modest hardware, helped by level of detail and texture compression.
- **Testing**: a mix of simulated environments and real-world tests, plus automated stress tests of the rendering pipeline and sensor inputs.
- **User safety**: eye strain, discomfort and real-world hazards, handled with prompts to take breaks and boundary systems like Guardian.

## What makes an XR product scale

Her three levers: user experience design (spatial design, AR that works in bright sun and dim rooms, UI that adapts when users sit, stand or move outdoors), performance (low-latency architecture such as edge computing, optimised 3D content, adaptive streaming and compression to save bandwidth), and interoperability, building on standards and popular tools like Unity so apps run across devices and third-party developers can join.

## Where AI helps

The closing section sorts AI into three jobs. For developers: generating 3D models and textures (she names Midjourney and Leonardo.ai), procedural environments (Runway), AI-assisted physics and animation, and automated testing that finds edge cases humans miss. For users: personalised content, NLP-driven conversations with virtual characters (ElevenLabs), personalised spatial audio and emotion-aware adaptation in training, therapy and games. For creators: AI animation (DeepMotion), help drafting branching stories, real-time translation, and low-code platforms such as Unity Muse that lower the barrier to entry.

## Who should watch

Web, mobile and backend engineers considering a move into AR/VR, and technical leads scoping their first XR product. Experienced Unity developers will know most of the toolbox but may find the challenge checklist handy for onboarding.

Title: When the chatbot reads your glucose monitor - AI-driven IoT in healthcare
Description: Abhishek Vajpayee (Metropolis Technologies) and Rathish Mohan at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on IoT-fed healthcare chatbots and scaling them
Body:
A healthcare chatbot that only reads what you type knows less than your smartwatch. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Abhishek Vajpayee (Metropolis Technologies) and Rathish Mohan (Lore | Contagious Health) explained how IoT-based chatbots take sensor and device data as input, why that makes round-the-clock, personalised care possible, and what infrastructure it takes to keep those systems fast as the patient base grows.

It is a two-speaker overview that moves from chatbot architecture to recommender systems to ML infrastructure best practice. Expect a map of the territory rather than a system they built.

## How is an IoT chatbot different from a regular one?

Mohan starts with the classic architecture. A user sends input (text, voice, an image, a button click) through some interface; a processing module, anything from a rule-based engine to a stack of ML submodules, works out a response; back-end services call knowledge bases and other models to build the final answer.

An IoT chatbot keeps that shape but adds a new input layer: signals from sensors, smart devices and IoT gateways, pushed to the cloud and handed to an NLP engine, a voice engine or a full dialogue manager. The result is a bot whose answers are context-aware because they draw on what the devices report, not just on what the patient remembers to say.

## Accessibility first, then personalisation

The first payoff is availability. Device-driven systems work around the clock, past office hours and geography, and voice-enabled devices make care easier to reach for elderly and disabled patients: a voice assistant can remind someone to take medication or talk them through managing a chronic condition. The detection side can be automated so events trigger the right care.

Personalisation comes from recommendation algorithms. Mohan walks through collaborative filtering (learning from behaviour), content-based filtering (matching item attributes to preferences) and hybrid or ensemble models that combine both. His example is a wearable tracking sleep patterns that recommends lifestyle changes or signals a physician when it spots irregularities.

## Personalisation at scale is an infrastructure problem

"Personalization at scale introduces challenges," Abhishek Vajpayee said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. As users and data grow, the system still has to answer with low latency. He points to Netflix, which processes billions of recommendations a day, as proof the pattern works at scale and can carry over to analysing patient data.

The building blocks he names are the familiar ones: cloud platforms such as AWS, Google Cloud and Azure, with managed ML services like SageMaker, Vertex AI and Azure ML; containers and Kubernetes; streaming ingestion with Apache Kafka or Google Pub/Sub; Hadoop and Spark for distributed processing; and serverless compute for bursty load.

His best practices are short and sensible:

- store structured and unstructured data in a data lake, on distributed storage such as HDFS or Amazon S3
- tune hyperparameters at scale and train across GPUs or TPUs
- automate model deployment and testing with CI/CD
- monitor model performance with tools like Prometheus and Grafana

He also frames shared infrastructure as a team accelerator: pre-built platforms shorten time to value and let teams scale without overhauls.

## Real-world cases and the open problems

Two examples anchor the talk: AI chatbots that handled millions of COVID-19 queries during the pandemic and took load off health systems, and IoT glucose monitors that send real-time alerts to doctors and patients to prevent diabetic emergencies.

The closing is candid about what still needs work: data privacy (HIPAA compliance for sensitive health information), integration between many devices and healthcare systems, and reliability for functions where downtime is not an option.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product owners starting on health-tech chatbots or remote monitoring who want the architecture and the infrastructure checklist in one place. Teams already running ML in production will recognise most of the stack.

Title: The kiosk is an iPhone now - NFC, Bluetooth and QR for touch-free service
Description: Sai Krishna Paladugu (FedEx) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on building contactless self-service kiosks on iOS with NFC, Bluetooth, QR and Apple Pay
Body:
The self-service kiosk you scanned a return label at was probably an iPad. Sai Krishna Paladugu, iOS Mobile Specialist at FedEx, used his Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 talk to map out how iOS devices become contactless kiosks: NFC for tap-to-pay and tickets, Bluetooth for proximity, the camera for QR and barcodes, Apple Pay for payments, and a custom app tying it to the back office.

It is a broad survey of building blocks and use cases across retail, healthcare, transport and hospitality, not an architecture walkthrough. One note for readers of the abstract: the 30% cut in transaction times it mentions doesn't come up in the talk itself.

## The three ways a phone talks to a kiosk

**NFC** handles the moments that need a tap. Customers pay by holding an iPhone to the kiosk, present digital tickets for validation and access control at a cinema or an airport, and authenticate securely for personalised services.

**Bluetooth** gives proximity. A kiosk can check a user in automatically as they approach (a doctor's appointment, for instance), greet them by name based on their preferences, and push location-based offers. His example is a shopping mall where a shopper's iOS app surfaces promotions from the stores around them.

**QR and barcode scanning** follows a three-step flow he calls scan, process, respond: the camera reads the code, the kiosk software looks up the customer's data in the back end, and the kiosk shows information or completes the transaction. The example closest to his day job is a return shipment: a customer arrives with the retailer's QR code from an email, scans it, and the kiosk prints the label. "they don't need to print at their home," Sai Krishna Paladugu said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

## Payments and the custom app

Apple Pay is the payment layer he recommends, for three reasons: transactions are encrypted and tokenised, which protects card data and limits fraud; Face ID and Touch ID add biometric authentication; and Apple Pay is widely accepted across industries.

Around that sits a custom iOS app with a brand-specific interface, back-end integration with CRM and ERP systems for real-time data synchronisation, and multi-language support, such as switching to Spanish for a store whose customers mostly speak it. The point of a custom build, he argues, is that retail, shipping and air travel each want a different flow.

## Where the kiosks earn their keep

- **Retail**: product search against store inventory, barcode price and availability checks, and self-checkout with Apple Pay. With 150 customers and two or three staff in a store, he notes, kiosks take the questions people would otherwise queue to ask.
- **Healthcare**: digital check-in, appointment scheduling and bill payments, which cut waiting and paper. He points to the pandemic as the moment touch-free interactions became expected in clinics and labs.
- **Transportation**: check-in with a QR code, digital boarding passes stored on the device, real-time gate and departure changes, and self-service bag tags paid with Apple Pay.
- **Hospitality**: room keys issued to the wallet, a digital concierge for restaurant recommendations and bookings, and express checkout.

## What comes next

His outlook has three parts: AI for personalised and predictive interactions, which he says needs more research into what customers want and where the limits are; augmented reality for product demos and navigation; and deeper IoT integration, with kiosks and iOS devices tied into smart sensors, HVAC, lights and cameras.

## Who should watch

iOS developers asked to build a kiosk or point-of-service app, and product teams scoping contactless flows who want the menu of Apple technologies in one place. Engineers looking for kiosk hardening, offline modes or device management will need to look elsewhere.

Title: Telemetry beats logging when your BLE device is at the bottom of a pool
Description: Matteo Crippa (Intent) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on using the phone as a telemetry proxy to debug BLE devices from the office
Body:
Your logs only contain what you remembered to log, and the user is halfway up a mountain. Matteo Crippa, mobile team lead at Intent, a company that builds companion apps for connected devices, argued at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 that automated telemetry, captured by the phone as it talks to a Bluetooth Low Energy peripheral, turns days of field debugging into hours at your desk.

Crippa has been building iOS apps since the first public iOS SDK beta, more than 15 years, and since 2019 a lot of Flutter companion apps for IoT products. The talk ends with a pitch for his team's help, but the core is a practical argument any mobile or firmware engineer can use.

## Why isn't logging enough?

"Automation is the key," he says, and that is the whole difference. Logging depends on a developer deciding in advance where to put log lines. Miss one condition and you find out when the device is in the field, and if the app is being used to climb a mountain, swim or drive a fast car, shipping a debug build and asking the user to repeat the climb isn't an option.

Telemetry, in his framing, is an automated, continuous stream of data that lets you replay what happened second by second. It behaves like a transparent proxy: it captures everything, stores it locally on the phone when there is no connection, and syncs to a back end once there is.

## A drone makes the case

His warm-up example is a hobby of his: building custom drones. Motors, propellers, antenna, GPS and battery all have to work together, or the drone ends up splashed on the floor. Open-source flight firmware exposes the data, but you can't plug in a cable mid-flight. Telemetry gives you motor speeds, battery temperature and millivolts, GPS position and the camera feed in real time, which answers whether you can make it home before the battery dies and where to look if you don't.

## What goes into a BLE telemetry timeline

Devices with their own connectivity (Wi-Fi, NB-IoT, a SIM) can send telemetry directly. BLE devices can't, so either a physical gateway or the phone has to relay. For the phone-as-gateway case, his list of what to capture:

- connection status and RSSI (signal strength)
- battery levels, for every battery the peripheral has
- the full flow of commands sent and received
- BLE error codes
- the firmware version

Put on one timeline, that is close to a replay of the session.

## Telemetry in action: the swimming pool

The scenario is a BLE tracker used in a pool, with a trainer on the side waiting for a swimmer to finish a lap, and a complaint that training data is missing. Behavioural debugging tells you only that. Logs show a battery update at 55% and then a peripheral disconnect, which is interesting and not much more. Telemetry shows the GATT notification, firmware 0.2, the battery dropping suddenly to 5% after a specific command, then the disconnect. The sync is intermittent because the battery collapses, which points at the firmware, not the app.

"the developer doesn't have to start swimming or learn swimming," Matteo Crippa said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. The bug was found in hours from the office, and the same data could be shared with the QA and firmware teams to reproduce it.

## How it fits into an app

The tool he describes is built on the native layers, Objective-C on iOS and a low-level implementation on Android, so Flutter and React Native apps can import it without trouble. Data is stored locally, synced when there is internet, and browsable remotely by developers, QA and firmware engineers alike. His advice is to collect almost everything and filter later.

His business case is three lines: shorter time to market, lower debugging and testing costs, and more reliable products with fewer returns. If you doubt it, he suggests reading the app store reviews of BLE apps that launched without that groundwork.

## Who should watch

Mobile developers building companion apps, firmware engineers tired of irreproducible field bugs, and QA teams testing connected products outdoors.

Title: Break the twin, not the network - digital twins for IoT resiliency
Description: Dileesh Chandra Bikkasani (AT&T Labs) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on using digital twins to rehearse IoT network failures before they happen
Body:
You can't take down a production firewall to see what happens, but you can take down its copy. Dileesh Chandra Bikkasani, Lead Software Engineer at AT&T Labs, argued at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 that digital twins give IoT operators a safe place to rehearse outages, congestion and disasters, and a feedback loop that pushes the lessons back into the physical network.

It is a conceptual talk: definitions, a lifecycle, use cases and challenges, without a production case study or benchmark numbers. As a structured introduction to why network teams keep mentioning twins, it does the job.

## What is a digital twin, exactly?

"digital twins are nothing but a virtual replica of the actual physical system," Dileesh Chandra Bikkasani said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. The important word is replica, not snapshot: a twin is fed near-real-time data from the physical system, so its state tracks reality. That is what separates it from the traditional approach he describes, where sensor data lands in a data lake, gets cleaned, and feeds machine-learning models that predict failures. That gives you a big table of data, not a model of the system you can poke.

Twins come at several levels: a single asset (a car, an aeroplane, a smart device), a process such as a manufacturing line from point A to point B, a whole system, or a network of systems. Anywhere you can get data out of IoT devices, he says, you can build one.

## The loop is the point

His lifecycle has four steps: collect the data (store and transmit it), evaluate and analyse it, simulate with different parameters, and link back to the physical system to apply the change. The car example makes it concrete: you can't crash a real car a hundred times, but you can run a hundred simulated crashes with different parameters and keep the setting that works. Once the data links are in place, that loop can be automated.

## Resiliency vs fault tolerance

He separates the two goals the twin serves. Network resiliency is the ability to withstand disruptions and recover quickly: less downtime, fewer service interruptions, data protected during outages. Fault tolerance is the ability to keep working when part of the system fails, rather than collapsing into a full outage.

IoT makes both harder: more interconnected devices, mixed protocols and standards, applications that need real-time data, latency and packet loss, security exposure and scale. With a hundred thousand connected devices, he notes, nobody can reproduce every failure in the physical world.

## What a twin lets you rehearse

The concrete wins he lists:

- **Proactive failure detection**: simulate device errors or congestion, such as 100,000 users hitting the network at once, and have systems ready.
- **Security drills**: simulate a firewall going down without touching real users.
- **Predictive maintenance**: forecast equipment failures and schedule maintenance with no impact on the live system.
- **Disaster recovery**: model an earthquake or a flood across interconnected systems, which is impossible to test physically.

Use cases span smart cities (energy grids that predict blackouts and fold in renewables, traffic and public transport flows), industrial IoT (machine health, lean manufacturing) and healthcare (remote patient monitoring through a digital replica of a patient's health).

## The hard parts

Twins inherit every data problem in the building. Integrating data from millions of sensors across databases and APIs while keeping it consistent and accurate is the first challenge. Scaling is the second: simulating a million devices is feasible, closing an automated feedback loop for all of them is much harder. The third is synchronisation, keeping the virtual model a faithful reflection of the current physical state, starting with setting it up exactly like the real world.

Looking ahead, he expects AI-driven twins that make autonomous decisions, 6G networks and ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) to speed up the data exchange, and twins that span industries.

## Who should watch

Network and IoT engineers new to digital twins who want the vocabulary and a mental model. Practitioners already running twins in production will find it familiar ground.

Title: The taxi ride is the targeting signal - Yandex Go's segmentation lessons
Description: Aliaksandr Zhastkou (Yandex) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on ML and location segmentation that turns product messages from spam into service
Body:
Product messages only work when they reach the person who needs them right now. Aliaksandr Zhastkou, Product Owner at Yandex working on the Yandex Delivery service, showed at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 how ML scoring and location-based segmentation in the Yandex Go super app turned a hard sell (getting taxi riders to use delivery) into a 14% lift in orders.

The talk is a tour of modern product communications for people who build or buy them: what CRM communications are, where AI tools now help, and how to segment without spamming. The Yandex Go case is the part worth the time.

## What counts as product communications?

Zhastkou defines them as everything that connects customers with the value of the product: emails, SMS, push notifications, chatbots, product recommendations, social media and, increasingly, notifications on IoT devices. His first thesis is that CRM communications are communications built on customer data, so you decide what to offer, to whom, when and through which channel from real information rather than hypotheses.

He brings credentials: more than seven years in product communications, a part in growing Yandex Delivery to over 18 million users in four years, and a service that now operates in 22 countries. He also opens with a stack of third-party figures, such as McKinsey's estimate that 35% of Amazon's revenue comes from AI-based recommendations and that 80% of customers expect personalised experiences.

## Where AI tools already do the CRM marketer's job

The process he describes runs from data collection and segmentation through strategy and creative work to testing and performance analysis, and large CRM vendors now automate chunks of it. He walks through Salesforce Einstein (lead prioritisation, segmentation, predicting customer needs) and HubSpot's AI features (content generation, automated workflows, predictive lead scoring, NLP chatbots). Two chatbot cases follow: Sephora's Virtual Artist on Facebook Messenger and Kik, with an 11% increase in makeover bookings, and Luxury Escapes, which reported a 3x conversion rate with an AI chatbot built with Master of Code.

## Segment for a business goal, not for its own sake

"There can be a million of segmentations. The main thing is the business goal," he says. His three example goals: personalise to raise the effect of a message, cut acquisition cost by keeping expensive channels like SMS for the right people, and reduce spam when a service has more products than any one user cares about.

The toolbox covers demographic, geographic, psychographic, technographic, behavioural, interest-based and value-based segmentation, plus two multi-vector models Yandex uses: RFM (recency, frequency, monetary) and NPS combined with customer value.

## The Yandex Go case: riders who might need a courier

The business task is converting taxi users into delivery users, and it has two problems. Delivery shares the super app with Yandex Food and Yandex Market, so nobody can message every user without spamming them. And most people need a courier only occasionally, when they forgot something at work or want to send a friend a book.

Step one is ML scoring to pick users most likely to need delivery soon; such scores can also forecast the next order, churn or the best time to send. Step two is location: if you take a taxi to a hardware store, the app suggests a cargo service for heavy purchases during the ride, and five minutes after arrival a push notification repeats the offer. That segmentation increased orders by 14%, he reports.

IoT shows up in the same role, as a source of usage data: smart speakers such as Amazon Echo and Google Nest and fitness trackers such as Garmin and Fitbit, which he credits with up to 50% higher email open rates and 25% better retention respectively.

"Every segmentation strategy should align with a clear business goal," Aliaksandr Zhastkou said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. His homework list for the year ahead: generative AI, voice search, omnichannel personalisation and AR-powered products.

## Who should watch

Product managers, growth and CRM teams, and engineers building notification systems who want the reasoning behind a targeting rule.

Title: Fix it before the customer calls - IoT data as a CRM input for SMEs
Description: Elena Budnik (PapaFinance) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on feeding device data into CRM so small businesses can serve customers proactively
Body:
Most customer service starts with a complaint. Elena Budnik, CEO of PapaFinance, a learning platform for small and medium-sized businesses, used her Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 talk to argue that SMEs can flip that order: let connected devices report the problem, let the CRM open the ticket, and reach the customer before they notice anything is wrong.

It is a short, business-level overview rather than an engineering walkthrough, aimed at SME owners and the people who advise them on where IoT pays off.

## How do IoT and CRM fit together?

Budnik's model has two halves. IoT supplies real-time data from devices, which shows how customers actually use a product and how it behaves. The CRM turns that data into actions: automated alerts, scheduled maintenance, an issue resolved before it escalates. Her example is the cleanest version of the idea: "smart home devices triggering service calls before users notice an issue," as Elena Budnik put it at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

## What SMEs get out of it

She lists four benefits. Cost savings, because predictive maintenance prevents expensive downtime. Customer retention, because proactive service raises satisfaction. Personalisation, because device data lets offers and messages fit individual needs. Efficiency, because automated workflows cut manual intervention.

The use cases cover three sectors. Retail: connected shelves that track inventory and reorder automatically. Healthcare: wearables sending real-time health data that alert physicians. Manufacturing: predictive maintenance on equipment to reduce downtime.

## The stack she points to

On the IoT side, the usual cloud platforms: AWS IoT, Azure IoT Hub and Google Cloud IoT. On the CRM side, Salesforce IoT Cloud, HubSpot and Microsoft Dynamics 365 with its IoT integration. The talk doesn't go into how the two are wired together; the point is that an SME doesn't need to build either half from scratch.

## Where it gets hard

Budnik is direct about the obstacles. Data privacy, meaning compliance with regulations such as GDPR. Security, since every connected device is a possible way in. Infrastructure cost for devices, networks and software. And data management: IoT produces large datasets, and getting them into a CRM in a usable shape is its own project.

Her best practices follow from that list. Start with scalable, modular solutions that can grow with the business. Put robust security around both the devices and the CRM data. Train staff to manage and interpret IoT-CRM workflows. Audit data privacy and compliance regularly, because trust is the asset proactive service depends on.

## What comes next

She sees three trends: AI-powered CRM that uses machine learning on IoT data to predict customer needs, real-time data streaming for faster decisions, and predictive analytics that catch customer issues before they escalate.

## Who should watch

SME founders and consultants deciding whether connected products can earn their keep through service rather than hardware margin. Engineers looking for integration patterns will want to pair it with something more technical.

Title: Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: secrets, supply chains and the race you lose
Description: The Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 roundup - 43 talks on secrets management, supply chain and policy, Kubernetes security, edge defence and AIOps.
Body:
[Conf42 DevSecOps 2024](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2024) went out on December 5 with 43 sessions, and if one word ran through the day it was secrets: the API keys that end up in Git, the config values nobody tracks, and the question of what happens to all of that once generative AI makes stealing it cheaper. Around that core sat the usual DevSecOps furniture, done well: SBOMs, policy as code, Kubernetes hardening, DDoS at the edge, and a few honest stories about what broke.

Speakers came from Harness, Doppler, Gcore, Okta, Microsoft, Google, Oracle, Salesforce, GM Financial, Turo and a long list of smaller teams.

## Why do secrets keep leaking?

The Doppler team opened the theme with the [panel discussion](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024__panel_discussion), AI Is Coming For Our Secrets, with Chandler Mayo, Amber Britton, Adam Meehan and Nic Manoogian on why credentials are the soft target of 2024. [Nic Manoogian](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Nic_Manoogian_secretops_automation_workflows) then gave the framework talk. Every app, he argues, has code, compute and secrets, and only the first two have Git-like automation around them. SecretOps is his layered model for fixing the third, and he was upfront about the vendor angle: "I am not trying to sell you on the product. I want to sell you on the framework," Nic Manoogian said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024.

[Dewan Ahmed](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Dewan_Ahmed_securing_gitleaks_repos_secret) of Harness took the problem to the commit. Collaborative repos, a stray env file with a database credential, too many repositories for anyone to watch: his talk shows Gitleaks and Harness Open Source catching the secret before it lands, with a live demo. [Deepu K Sasidharan](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Deepu_K_Sasidharan_kubernetes_security_containers) of Okta closed the loop in Kubernetes with OAuth for access and secret management inside the cluster.

## Supply chain, policy and shifting left

[Safeer C M](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Safeer_C_M_software_bill_materials) gave a clean primer on the software bill of materials and where it fits in a DevSecOps pipeline. [Anthony Laiuppa](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Anthony_Laiuppa_vulnerability_management_developers) of Morning Consult asked whether every critical vulnerability is truly critical and how to consolidate scanning, triage and ticketing so developers stop hating the process. [Graziano Casto](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Graziano_Casto_policy_rbac_authorization) of Mia-Platform implemented RBAC authorisation as policy as code with Rönd and Open Policy Agent.

[Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Peter_De_Tender_devsecops_applications_shifting) of Microsoft toured security tools that plug into Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions, for teams whose security currently starts when the data centre is on fire. [Joshua Arvin Lat and Raphael Joseph Rosario](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Joshua_Arvin_Lat_Raphael_Joseph_Rosario_devsecops_roadmap_integration) of NuWorks Interactive Labs drew a roadmap for rolling security into DevOps at scale. The delivery side came from [Megha Kadur](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Megha_Kadur_gitops_devops_navigation) of Barracuda on GitOps workflows, [Madhu Kumar Yeluri](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Madhu_Kumar_Yeluri_infrastructure_code_terraform) of Fortune Technologies on Terraform practices, [Hoang Dinh Nguyen](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Hoang_Dinh_Nguyen_developer_platform_kusion) of Viettel Group on an internal developer platform built with Kusion, and [Julio Arruda](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Julio_Arruda_devops_workflows_genai) on GenAI tools across the SDLC. [Victor Onyenagubom](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Victor_Onyenagubom_security_soft_skills) reminded everyone that the soft skills are what make any of it stick.

## Kubernetes and the cloud underneath

[Abdul Karim Memon](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Abdul_Karim_Memon_kubernetes_networking) of ReLambda delivered a beginner-friendly walk through Kubernetes networking, following a packet from pod to pod. [Thiyagarajan Aramudhan](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Thiyagarajan_Aramudhan_kubernetes_framework_security) of GM Financial stacked security level by level, from infrastructure and Calico at the cluster to image scanning, Istio and OPA. [Carlos Solis Salazar](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Carlos_Solis_Salazar_azure_management_security) of OZ showed Azure Arc extending management and security to hybrid and multi-cloud estates, [Daniil Koshelev](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Daniil_Koshelev_monolith_microservices_transitions) of Tinkoff covered the move from monolith to microservices, [Praveen Valaboju](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Praveen_Valaboju_advanced_cloud_integration) of Landauer brought cloud integration to healthcare, and [Prashanth Reddy Kora](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Prashanth_Reddy_Kora_data_security_cloud) of Centene Corporation looked at the security case for cloud database systems.

## The edge, the API and the race condition

[Lukasz Karwacki](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Lukasz_Karwacki_protection_Infra_web_apps) of Gcore explained why web application and API protection is not enough without DDoS protection underneath, drawing on a network of more than 180 points of presence. [Paul Edward](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Paul_Edward_race_financial_transactions) of Compado told the day's best war story: a race condition in a financial system, explained with two kids and one cookie jar, and what it took to close it. It's a short talk that will make you reread every balance update you've written.

APIs got three talks: [Nikhil Bharadwaj Ramashasthri](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Nikhil_Bharadwaj_Ramashasthri_api_development_scalable) of Turo on API-first development, [Anirudha Karandikar](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Anirudha_Karandikar_api_security) on generative AI for API governance and sprawl, and [Karthik Vallamsetla](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Karthik_Vallamsetla_web_api_uiux) of Cisco on modern Web APIs for secure UI. [Mahesh Vankayala](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Mahesh_Vankayala_identity_federation_security) of Oracle covered identity federation and single sign-on with OAuth 2.0.

## When the pager goes off

[Birol Yildiz](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Birol_Yildiz_aiops_alert_noise) of ilert went after alert floods with AI: grouping alerts by content similarity and tuning thresholds so duplicates collapse without hiding real problems. [Indika Wimalasuriya](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Indika_Wimalasuriya_aiops_resilience_aws) of Virtusa showed AIOps for operational resilience on AWS, [Nagarjuna Malladi](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Nagarjuna_Malladi_reliability_sre_practices) of Oracle joined SRE practice with DevSecOps, and [Abhishek Vajarekar](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Abhishek_Vajarekar_resilient_alwayson_services) covered redundancy, failover, chaos engineering and automated recovery. [Ilan Finkelstein and Pieter VanIperen](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Ilan_Finkelstein_Pieter_VanIperen_ciso_dead_what) of Owndata argued for simulating the bad day before it arrives, [Ramon Izaguirre Bilbao](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Ramon_Izaguirre_Bilbao_rating_cybersecurity_power) of Internet2.ai pitched rating as a cybersecurity tool, and [Clifton Reddy](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Clifton_Reddy_green_code_sustainable) of American National made the case for greener code.

## AI and regulated industries

Explainable AI for chatbots came from [Shradha Kohli](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Shradha_Kohli_conversational_ai_trust) of Salesforce and, for healthcare, from [Abhishek Vajpayee and Rathish Mohan](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Abhishek_Vajpayee_Rathish_Mohan_healthcare_chatbot_transparency). Title: When security stops being a checkpoint
Description: And becomes part of the workflow
Body:
# Security wants to be your friend (promise)

DevSecOps is that thing everyone agrees is important and then quietly argues about in pull requests.

Should security shift left? Should it shift everywhere? Should it maybe stop breaking the build five minutes before a release? Big questions. Strong feelings.

Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 is here to unpack all of that.

This one goes wide and deep. There are talks on securing infrastructure, web applications, APIs, and Kubernetes clusters that absolutely did not ask to be exposed to the internet. You’ll hear about secrets management, Git leaks, identity federation, policy as code, and why credentials have a habit of showing up where they really shouldn’t.

AI is very much in the mix. Expect sessions on AIOps, alert noise reduction, AI-driven security assessments, explainable AI, and the slightly terrifying reality of AI being very interested in your secrets. There’s even a panel dedicated to that exact concern, because of course there is.

Beyond tools, the conference also digs into culture, governance, and the human side of security. Soft skills, leadership, compliance, resilience, and what DevSecOps looks like in healthcare, finance, supply chains, and other environments where mistakes are extra expensive.

You’ll find practical talks on Terraform, GitOps, cloud databases, internal developer platforms, and shifting from monoliths to microservices without everything catching fire. There’s also room for bigger conversations about trust, accountability, and what “secure by default” actually means in real teams.

If your job lives somewhere between shipping fast and sleeping at night, this one’s worth your time. DevSecOps isn’t getting simpler, but at least you don’t have to figure it out alone.

Title: Where the barrels go - SAP IS-Oil TSW for bulk oil and gas logistics
Description: Rajesh Guggilla (Energy Transfer) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on how IS-Oil TSW automates nominations, tickets and inventory reconciliation
Body:
Moving crude and refined product by pipeline, rail and ship generates paperwork at a scale most software engineers never see. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Rajesh Guggilla, Principal Specialist for IT SAP IS-Oil at Energy Transfer, walks through IS-Oil TSW, the Traders and Scheduler's Workbench, and argues that automating nominations, ticketing and inventory reconciliation is where bulk oil and gas logistics saves real money.

Honest scope first: despite the IoT in the title, this is a functional tour of an enterprise logistics module, not a talk about sensors or device fleets. Think of it as a briefing for the people whose systems receive the data that pipeline meters and terminals produce.

## Why logistics errors are expensive in this industry

Guggilla sets the stakes with the size of the market: the global oil and gas industry was valued at $3.3 trillion as of 2023. "Inefficiency in logistics can lead to substantial financial losses," Rajesh Guggilla said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, and his reference point is a mid-sized refinery processing 250,000 barrels a day, product worth about $20 million daily. At that volume a scheduling slip or a wrong ticket is not a rounding error, and the industry is leaning harder on automation and integration to keep multimodal logistics under control.

## What TSW actually does

TSW is the scheduling and documentation layer for bulk product movement: purchases, sales and transfers. He breaks it into four functions:

- **Nomination management**: scheduling bulk refined and crude movements, with real-time updates and coordination across stakeholders, built to handle high transaction volumes.
- **Electronic ticketing**: the documentation of each movement. He puts the effect at a 95% reduction in documentation errors and capacity for up to 10,000 tickets a day.
- **Multimodal support**: one logistics view for rail, pipeline and marine.
- **Inventory reconciliation**: matching what the books say against what the tanks hold, with a claimed 99% reduction in inventory discrepancies.

It also integrates with terminal invoicing, which is where the downstream finance savings come from.

## The numbers he puts on it

The quantitative section is the core of the talk. Beyond the 95% error reduction, Guggilla cites a 60% cut in reconciliation time, a 70% cut in invoice processing time, and the rule of thumb that a 1% improvement in inventory accuracy is worth about $1 million a year to a mid-sized refinery. Real-time visibility, he says, can lower inventory holding costs by up to 15%, and better compliance can reduce compliance-related costs by 30-50%.

His case study returns to the 250,000-barrel-a-day refinery: inventory reconciliation down to 30 minutes, and $10 saved per ticket by moving to electronic ticketing. The figures are presented as outcomes rather than with a measurement method, so treat them as the vendor-side picture of what good looks like, not a benchmark.

## Where it fits in the bigger trend

He frames TSW within two market trends: automation technologies (projected to reach $22.1 billion by 2027, with productivity gains of up to 25%) and cloud integration (a cloud applications market expected to reach $10.9 billion by 2027). The forward-looking claim is that digital transformation could be worth $2.5 trillion for the industry by 2030, with AI, cloud and sustainability-focused solutions doing the heavy lifting. TSW's role in that story is the plumbing: it sits between existing inventory and invoicing systems and shortens the loop from a physical movement to a reconciled, invoiced record.

## Who should watch

SAP consultants and IT teams in oil and gas midstream, and engineers building the integration between field measurement systems and ERP who want to know what the business side of the pipeline expects. Readers looking for IoT device architecture won't find it here; the talk is short and squarely about the logistics software.

Title: 63 Raspberry Pis, one Postgres cluster, and a 300 Mbps bottleneck
Description: Guillermo Ruiz (AWS) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on building a 63-node Raspberry Pi K3s and StackGres cluster, and what broke on the way
Body:
What happens when you run sharded PostgreSQL on 63 borrowed Raspberry Pi 3B boards in a Pelican case? At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Guillermo Ruiz, Senior Developer Advocate at AWS, tells the story of an eight-month side project with the team behind StackGres: K3s, network boot, Citus sharding and a home-made metrics pipeline, all squeezed through one shared 300 Mbps link. The takeaway is refreshingly honest. The Postgres part was the easy bit; power, network and observability were where the weeks went.

It is the most hands-on talk of the event, and the one to watch if you have ever thought a Pi cluster would be a cheap weekend.

## What went into the case?

The hardware was a friends-and-favours effort: Raspberry Pi 3B boards lent by OnGres and others, UniFi switches and a gateway, two 40-port USB chargers (so a hard ceiling of 80 Pis), fans, and a borrowed Prusa 3D printer that produced more than 84 pieces for the bays and the fan mounts. The final build has three rows of 21 Pis cooled by 15 fans: 63 nodes, quad-core ARM at 1.2 GHz each, roughly 250 cores and 63 GB of RAM in total.

The software stack is Ubuntu 24.04, K3s for lightweight Kubernetes, StackGres for Postgres on Kubernetes, and PXE boot instead of SD cards. "We run out of money, so we couldn't have SD cards for every single Raspberry Pi in the cluster," Guillermo Ruiz said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

## Network boot is a lesson in naming things

Two 48-port switches carry the cluster. Each Pi's name matches its switch port and the last octet of its static IP (172.16.5.105 is the bottom switch, port 5), which turns troubleshooting into reading a label. Infrastructure sits at the end of the switch, partly from old scar tissue: Ruiz recalls a Cisco design with the reset button by port 1, so plugging in a cable could reboot the switch. His better advice is to learn how many ASICs your switch has and spread the heavy talkers across them.

The PXE flow is DHCP for a fixed address, TFTP for the bootloader, NFS for the OS image, with overlay file systems so 63 nodes share one image but keep their writes separate. Older Pis need network boot enabled by hand, 63 times. The PXE script they started from targets Raspberry Pi OS, so on Ubuntu they fell back to the legacy Debian-based image and patched the script to run non-interactively. MAC addresses came from the switch's MAC table; serial numbers came from grepping and awking the dnsmasq logs.

## StackGres was the easy part

The surprise is where the pain wasn't. Deploying Postgres with Citus sharding by hand would take about two weeks, he estimates, and automating it with Ansible about two months; with StackGres it is 20 to 30 lines of YAML and a Helm chart. The demo shows the Patroni topology: 20 workers, each with its own replica.

Everything around it fought back. K3s needed cgroups enabled, and etcd ran as a single external instance on the NAS (he flags the missing redundancy). A Pi 3B+ has around 910 MB of usable memory, so the control plane and the NAS moved to two AMD64 desktops. Nodes flapped from out-of-memory errors, storage disconnects and congestion; one root cause was a faulty USB charger. Envoy had to be recompiled for ARM (now public in StackGres), Cilium failed, and the iSCSI targets moved from TGT to LIO. That took about a month and a half of trial and error.

## Can 63 Pis report their own metrics?

Not the usual way. There was no room for Prometheus node exporters, and sending metrics from every node straight to AWS cost bandwidth and money. The workaround: a small Python script using psutil collects CPU, memory, disk and network, gzips them and posts them to a gateway every 120 seconds; the gateway aggregates every five minutes and pushes to Amazon CloudWatch through boto3, with Grafana on top.

It still didn't hold up. Frequent transmission from 63 nodes saturated the shared link, compression cost more CPU than it saved, and the single gateway became a bottleneck with gaps in the data. Ruiz's verdict is that classic exporters don't scale on 3B+ boards, and newer Pis would fare better.

## Who should watch

Anyone planning an ARM or edge Kubernetes cluster, Postgres-on-Kubernetes users curious about StackGres and Citus, and homelabbers who want to know where the hours will really go. Next on the team's list: other Linux distributions, newer boards such as the Orange Pi, a real application on top, and a chatbot trained on the cluster's own errors for StackGres incident support.

- Chris Engelbert (simplyblock) on [PostgreSQL on Kubernetes: dos and don'ts](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Chris_Engelbert_kubernetes_postgresql_cluster).
- MK Sirajuddin (Five9) on [containers and Kubernetes for IoT](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_MK_Sirajuddin_kubernetes_container), the theory behind this build.
- Javier Ramirez (QuestDB) on [the Type III database architecture](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Javier_Ramirez_database_architecture_traditional) for time-series data.
