Title: Twenty WAFs in a row won't save a server that is down at layer 4
Description: Lukasz Karwacki (Gcore) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on why web app protection and L3/L4 DDoS protection only work together
Body:
A perfect web application firewall is no help when the box behind it has been flooded off the network. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, [Lukasz Karwacki](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Lukasz_Karwacki_protection_Infra_web_apps), Security Solution Architect (Edge Network) at Gcore, argued that web application and API protection (WAAP) and infrastructure DDoS protection are two halves of one job, and that attackers will probe both until they find the half you skipped.

This is a vendor talk: it explains the attack types and the reasoning first, then shows how Gcore puts the pieces together. The examples lean heavily on game servers, which makes it more fun than the usual e-commerce slide deck.

## What kinds of DDoS attack are we talking about?

He sorts them into three families:

- **Volumetric attacks** swamp bandwidth with UDP and ICMP floods, IPSec floods and amplification. Near-zero good traffic, a whole ocean of junk.
- **Connection attacks** open connections and never close them. His webshop example is 10,000 fake shoppers who add something to the cart and then sit there; his game server example is one fake player opening 20,000 connections. SYN, ACK and RST floods live here, along with Slowloris.
- **Application attacks** at layer 7 use little volume and a lot of cleverness: requests that send the server into expensive loops until CPU and memory run out. HTTP GET/POST floods and game-server-specific attacks sit in this group.

The trend line is the usual one, pointing up. His slides cite 7.9 million DDoS attacks in the first half of 2023, a 31% year-on-year increase.

## Why is mitigation within a minute too late?

The sharpest argument in the talk is about timing. Compare a service that filters all traffic from the first packet with one that catches 100% of an attack but only after a minute. Sixty seconds of a terabit per second is enough to take any single server down, and a web app might shrug off a restart while a game server full of players will not. His conclusion is that traffic has to arrive at the origin already clean, which means always-on filtering, as close to the attack source as possible so the latency penalty stays small.

## Why do you need both layers?

His scenario: a Minecraft server with an in-game shop on the same machine and the same network. Protect the shop with a WAF and leave the game server bare, and the attacker takes the whole host down through the game port. Protect only the game server, and the shop becomes the way in. Attackers, he said, will hit both and keep hammering whichever one falls over.

Even a flawless WAF that only lets valid HTTP requests through cannot help once the network layer is saturated. Lukasz Karwacki said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "layer seven will have nothing to do with it because there will be no server to, to proceed the layer seven requests."

The WAAP side, in his list, means a WAF for the OWASP Top 10 and zero-days, bot management that lets search indexers in and keeps scrapers and automated pen-testers out, layer 7 DDoS protection for HTTP floods, and API security.

## Which controls did he show?

The infrastructure side came down to a handful of concrete controls, each tied to an attack type from earlier:

- **Geo access control**: a US game server only accepts US traffic, a European one only European, which blocks most of the world by default.
- **Rate limits per user**: if a normal Minecraft player opens at most five connections, cap it at six. The connection attack stops being interesting.
- **Packet validation**: drop malformed packets, whether they come from an attacker or from a misbehaving router at some ISP.
- **Behaviour analysis**: nobody legitimate adds 10,000 items to a cart, so the WAF can block that session on behaviour alone.

He also showed side-by-side gameplay of Counter-Strike on an unprotected server under attack and on a Gcore-protected one. The unprotected server stayed up, but lagged so badly that nobody could play. A server that responds but stutters loses players just as surely as one that is down.

## Where does the CDN fit?

The last piece is putting the CDN, the WAF and DDoS protection with one provider. On the network side his slides note that Gcore's infrastructure carries 80-85% outbound and 15-20% inbound traffic as a CDN, so there is plenty of inbound headroom to absorb attack traffic. The numbers in the slides for the network itself: 180+ points of presence, 50+ cloud locations, 14,000+ peering partners and 200+ Tbps of capacity.

## Who should watch?

Anyone running game servers, or a web app and its backend on the same network, who has bought a WAF and assumed the DDoS problem was solved. It is an introduction rather than a tour of mitigation internals, and the second half is a Gcore product walkthrough.

- Andrey Slastenov on [DDoS threats from IoT and 5G devices](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Andrey_Slastenov_iot_5g_devices_ddos_threat_landscape) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

## From Gcore

Gcore runs a global edge network with CDN, infrastructure DDoS protection and web application and API protection, the stack this talk walked through.

Title: Containers and Kubernetes for IoT, explained from the sealed box up
Description: MK Sirajuddin (Five9) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on why containers and Kubernetes suit IoT fleets, and what they cost you
Body:
IoT fleets have the same problem as any distributed system, only with more devices and worse network links. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, MK Sirajuddin, Senior Cloud Engineer at Five9, makes the case that containers and Kubernetes are the foundation for managing that sprawl, from the gateway at the edge to the analytics in the cloud, and he is just as clear about the bill: complexity, observability, security and cost.

This is an introductory talk. If you already run k3s on a rack of gateways, you know most of it. If you are an IoT team still deploying firmware-adjacent services by hand, it is a compact map of why the cloud-native crowd keeps telling you to containerise.

## What does a container buy an IoT team?

Sirajuddin starts with the basics. A container packages the application code, its libraries and every dependency, so it behaves the same in development, testing and production. "Think of container as a sealed box that includes everything your app needs to function," MK Sirajuddin said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

For IoT, that means software for an edge device or a gateway can be built and tested on a laptop and then shipped to the field without the classic library mismatch that makes something work on one machine and nowhere else. He names Docker, Podman and CRI-O as the usual tools, and lists four benefits: portability (on-premises to cloud to edge), consistency, a light footprint (a typical container starts in milliseconds, far faster than a virtual machine boots) and scalability, as in spinning up more containers when sensor traffic spikes during a festival or a sporting event in a smart city.

## Why Kubernetes once the containers multiply

More applications means more containers, and at some point somebody has to manage them. "Imagine trying to manage thousands of containers by hand. It's error prone and time consuming," he said. Kubernetes is his answer: it schedules containers across servers, restarts failed ones, scales horizontally on CPU, memory or custom metrics, and handles service discovery and load balancing.

The IoT angle is coordination. Kubernetes can run the whole chain, from data ingestion at the edge to centralised analytics, and replace a component when it dies. Because it runs on AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and on-premises, the same IoT data pipeline can run analytics in different regions or clouds, which he pitches as protection against vendor lock-in once deployments go global.

## Microservices, rolling updates and the edge

The architecture he recommends splits a monolith into small services: one for ingestion, one for pre-processing, one for machine-learning inference. Several services share the same hardware without conflicts, which matters on resource-constrained edge boxes, and CI/CD pipelines keep the software patched. New features such as anomaly detection on sensor data can be tested and shipped without hand-building an environment each time.

For IoT deployments specifically, he lists what Kubernetes brings: autoscaling as device counts grow, processing pushed closer to the edge for latency-sensitive jobs like traffic control, rolling updates across thousands of devices at once, and hybrid or multi-cloud placement so data is processed where it makes most sense. His case study is Spotify, which moved from a monolith to microservices on Kubernetes to handle peak streaming load, with faster deployments and lower infrastructure costs. He says himself that it is not strictly IoT; the point is that the same scaling story applies when device counts climb.

## The bill: four things that will hurt

The most useful part for a team weighing the move is the challenges list:

- **Complexity**: Kubernetes has a steep learning curve and engineers need training.
- **Monitoring and debugging**: seeing what is happening across edge devices and cloud needs real tooling; he names Prometheus and Grafana.
- **Security**: containers, clusters and APIs need constant patching and hardening.
- **Cost**: scaling too aggressively or leaving unused containers running inflates the cloud bill.

His advice is to start small: pick one modest IoT application, containerise it, scale gradually, train the team, bring in experts if Kubernetes is new to you, and build in security hardening, monitoring and cost optimisation from the start.

## Who should watch

IoT engineers and engineering managers who haven't containerised yet and want the argument in one sitting. Kubernetes veterans can skip to the challenges section, or watch the talk this one pairs with, where the hard parts get very concrete.

Title: Kubernetes secrets are just base64 - and the rest of the hardening list
Description: Deepu K Sasidharan (Okta) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on Kubernetes hardening - RBAC with OIDC, real secret management, network policies, non-root containers
Body:
A stock Kubernetes Secret is a plain-text resource holding base64 strings, and base64 is not encryption. Deepu K Sasidharan, Senior Developer Advocate at Okta, co-lead of JHipster and author of the KDash dashboard, made that the centrepiece of his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk: a tour of Kubernetes security best practices for the cluster, the infrastructure underneath it and the containers on top, most of which are not enabled by default.

It is a practical checklist talk with commands and manifests, the kind you finish with a list of tickets.

## What does Kubernetes give you out of the box?

Four layers: TLS for all API communication, a pluggable authentication layer, authorisation through one or more models, and admission control modules that validate every authorised request except reads. The point he makes up front is that the defaults stop there. "Most of the security best practices, are not enabled by default," Deepu K Sasidharan said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024.

## RBAC plus OIDC is the access story

Of the authorisation models (ABAC, RBAC, Node, Webhook), RBAC is the one he recommends: the most widely used, flexible enough to mirror your organisation's access rules. Check it with `kubectl cluster-info dump | grep authorization-mode`, and enable it with `--authorization-mode=RBAC,Node` on the API server. Then Roles, ClusterRoles and their bindings, scoped to namespaces or resources.

For authentication, OpenID Connect beats client certificates, basic auth and static tokens. Nothing sensitive sits on the user's laptop, onboarding and offboarding happen in the identity provider, and you inherit MFA, passkeys and hardware keys like YubiKeys. The flow: `kubectl` calls kubelogin, which opens a browser to the OIDC provider (Okta or Auth0 in his example), swaps the response for an access token, and hands it back to `kubectl` for API calls. Bind RBAC to groups from the provider and user management leaves the cluster entirely.

## So what do you use instead of Secrets?

Three options, in increasing order of security and setup effort:

- **Sealed Secrets.** A controller in the cluster holds a key pair; developers encrypt with the public key using the `kubeseal` CLI and commit the result to Git. The controller decrypts it into a normal Secret. Simple, GitOps-friendly, best for small teams.
- **External Secrets Operator.** A SecretStore describes how to reach HashiCorp Vault, AWS or Google Secrets Manager or Azure; an ExternalSecret manifest names what to fetch and contains nothing sensitive, so it can be committed. The operator syncs values into Kubernetes Secrets. Better for bigger teams.
- **Secrets Store CSI driver.** A SecretProviderClass is referenced in the pod's volume spec, and the secret is mounted into a tmpfs volume for that pod only, removed when the pod goes. No Kubernetes Secret is created, so even someone allowed to read Secrets sees nothing. Most secure, most tedious.

With the first two you still need RBAC on the resulting Secrets, since they are base64 again once inside the cluster.

## The rest of the list

For the cluster: keep Kubernetes and `kubectl` current (check the Kubernetes security and disclosure page; kOps and kubeadm help on-prem), lock down kubelet HTTP endpoints, API and SSH for non-admins, use network policies so a compromised pod can't chain into its neighbours, keep workloads out of the default namespace, and set resource quotas, limit ranges and container limits so one rogue library can't take down the node. Audit logging plus Prometheus and Grafana alerts on ingress, egress and unknown IPs round it out.

For infrastructure: TLS everywhere, etcd behind TLS, a firewall, encryption and strong credentials, IAM policies on EKS, GKE or AKS, frequent credential rotation, and restricted access to the cloud metadata API.

For containers: never run as root (use a least-privileged user and `--chown` on Docker copies), use minimal official images with deterministic tags (`node:14.2.0-alpine3.11`, not `node:14-alpine`), block unneeded kernel modules, scan images in CI with Clair, Anchore or Snyk and fail the build on findings, audit with Docker Bench for Security, and use Pod Security Admission to limit host access. His reason for the last one: more than a million Docker images have been found carrying malware at different times.

## Who should watch

Anyone running a production cluster who hasn't audited it against a list like this, and teams still committing base64 Secrets to a private repo and hoping. Platform engineers who've done all of it can skim to the secrets comparison.

Title: Let the edge decide, let the cloud think - IoT and AI across multi-cloud
Description: Nandakumar Ramachandran Pezhery (Xoriant) at Conf42 IoT 2024 on IoT plus AI for real-time multi-cloud optimisation, edge-first, with Kubernetes in the middle
Body:
Every hyperscaler sells a tool to manage your multi-cloud estate, and each one works best inside its own cloud. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Nandakumar Ramachandran Pezhery, Vice President - Cloud Solutions at Xoriant, argued that AI fed with IoT data is what fills the gap: local, latency-sensitive decisions at the edge, heavy analytics in whichever cloud suits, and Kubernetes keeping the workloads portable between them.

The abstract promised 15 minutes and the talk comes in under ten: a quick, vendor-heavy tour of the services involved, one customer result, and a pitch for agentic AI at the edge. No code or architecture deep-cuts, but a useful map of which managed service does what.

## Why isn't each cloud's own tool enough?

Organisations go multi-cloud for flexibility, to avoid lock-in and to put each application where it runs best, across AWS, Azure and GCP. The cost is managing workloads, security and spend across all of them. The hyperscalers do offer answers, AWS Control Tower, Azure Arc and Google Anthos, but each is designed around its own ecosystem. Hybrid options such as AWS Outposts and Azure Stack bring cloud on premises, but for edge use cases he sees them as bolt-ons rather than purpose-built. That gap, in his framing, is the opening for AI.

## Who does what between edge and cloud?

His split is the useful part of the talk. IoT devices produce a continuous stream; protocols such as MQTT and CoAP carry it with low latency. Edge platforms like AWS IoT Greengrass and Azure IoT Edge preprocess and run local inference on latency-sensitive data (the slides call this data gravity), while the cloud does long-term analytics and model training with SageMaker, Azure Machine Learning or Vertex AI. AWS IoT Core handles edge-to-cloud transfer and Azure IoT Hub device management.

Kubernetes, with a service mesh such as Istio, is the glue. Because containerised applications don't carry a whole operating system, they can be moved between providers based on cost and performance, and data can go to the nearest server for processing. AI-driven orchestration then scales pods up or down from runbook automation triggered by alerts: data volume at the edge, processing demand at the centre, or plain cost.

## What does agentic AI add?

His definition is pragmatic: AI that makes decisions autonomously from real-time IoT data, at the edge or in the cloud as needed. Greengrass running SageMaker-trained models lets devices act locally while syncing with the cloud for broader insights. "That's how it is supposed to be designed," Nandakumar Ramachandran Pezhery said at Conf42 IoT 2024.

Use cases on his list: predictive maintenance across a multi-cloud estate, real-time supply chain rerouting over MQTT, building management (HVAC, lighting, energy), personalised customer experiences and coordinating autonomous vehicles. Smart cities combine LoRaWAN sensors with Azure Digital Twins for traffic and infrastructure; OPC UA shows up for industrial IoT and DDS for deterministic communication in smart grids.

## Does it pay off?

His one hard number comes from a large manufacturing customer he worked with: vibration sensors over MQTT, failure patterns detected by agentic AI, and proactive alerts. The result was about 84% less downtime, nearly 12% cost savings and 8% additional production. At the scale of a big production line, as he points out, that is a lot. Other examples, such as sharing patient data across clouds or AI route optimisation with live traffic data, are described without figures.

## Who should watch

Architects deciding where IoT workloads should run across clouds and the edge, who want a quick inventory of the managed services and protocols in play. If you already run Greengrass or IoT Edge in production, expect a summary rather than new tricks.

Title: Postgres loves Kubernetes, as long as storage and huge pages are right
Description: Chris Engelbert (simplyblock) at Conf42 IoT 2024 on running PostgreSQL on Kubernetes - storage, backups, huge pages, pooling and operators
Body:
People keep reading his title slide as "Postgres: don't do Kubernetes", and Chris Engelbert keeps correcting them. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, the Chief Developer Advocate at simplyblock (with Ubisoft, Hazelcast, Instana and Timescale on his CV) argued that running PostgreSQL on Kubernetes is a good idea today, then spent the rest of the talk on what you have to get right: storage, backups, huge pages, connection pooling, an operator, and dedicated nodes.

"From my perspective, Postgres really loves Kubernetes," Chris Engelbert said at Conf42 IoT 2024. It's a dense, opinionated, practical talk with links to go deeper, and one of the strongest of the event.

## What does the internet think is wrong with it?

He opens with a Family Feud round sourced from X ("always ask for a friend"). Kubernetes wasn't designed for databases: true ten years ago, when it was stateless-only, but stateful support arrived years ago. Persistent storage is too slow: depends on what you plug in; a USB stick behind a persistent volume will indeed be slow. Nobody understands Kubernetes: partly fair, and if you understand none of it, don't run anything on it. Databases and applications should be separated: agreed, and not an argument against Kubernetes. The one he concedes is extra indirection, which is lovely until something breaks and you have to find where.

## Why bother at all?

His reasons: avoiding cloud vendor lock-in (managed services like RDS serve the mainstream, and the moment you need a less common extension, Timescale for instance, you may get an old or limited version), faster time to market and lower cost through automation, one deployment model for apps and databases, and easy read replicas. At his own IoT startup, clevabit, metrics arrived every 10 seconds but were averaged per minute anyway, so replica lag didn't matter: writes went to the primary and queries were spread across all nodes.

## The boring parts that aren't optional

- **Encrypt everything.** TLS in transit, encryption at rest, secrets in Kubernetes Secrets, cert-manager or your cloud's credential management.
- **Real backups.** Not pg_dump, which isn't a backup tool, and no home-grown scripts. Continuous backup of the write-ahead log plus snapshots with pgBackRest or Barman, stored on object storage, never on your own nodes (a MinIO in the same cluster doesn't count).
- **Test the backups regularly.** His team did it weekly by scaling the Patroni cluster up by one replica: it restored from backup, streamed the rest via replication and joined. Once it served requests they knew the backups worked, then scaled back down.
- **Plan upgrades.** A major Postgres upgrade with pg_upgrade needs both versions in the image and double the storage for a while. Managed Kubernetes supports only recent versions, so expect a cluster upgrade roughly once a year.

## What's actually different on Kubernetes?

Postgres configuration itself barely changes; just size shared_buffers, work_mem and friends to the container limits, and hire a consultant if you don't know them. The real differences:

**Storage.** Use a CSI driver that supports encryption at rest, high IOPS and low latency (SSD or NVMe, so probably not NFS). He favours disaggregated storage, since databases grow in data faster than in compute, and snapshots and clones let you run heavy reports on a throwaway copy. He found around 150 CSI drivers and catalogued their features at storageclass.info.

**Resources and huge pages.** Requests, limits and quotas take a while to understand. Huge pages have to be configured three times: on the worker node's kernel (ideally reserving memory at boot), in the pod spec, and in Postgres.

**HA and pooling.** Use a cluster manager for automatic failover; he recommends Patroni, from Zalando. "I would claim never run Postgres without connection pooling at all," he said, since opening connections is expensive in Postgres and serverless makes it worse. He prefers Pgpool-II over PgBouncer; watch out for writes hiding behind SELECT, such as Timescale's create_hypertable.

**Guard rails.** Network policies, RBAC, and policy managers like OPA or Kyverno to stop random containers mounting database volumes. Be careful with deny-all defaults, though: he heard of a Kyverno setup that locked itself out of the Kubernetes API. Observability with Prometheus plus a proper log pipeline.

## Pick an operator, then give it its own nodes

Helm charts handle day one; operators handle day two. His shortlist: CloudNativePG and StackGres from OnGres, with Crunchy Postgres for Kubernetes, the Zalando operator, and KubeDB if you're still on 9.6. StackGres ticked every box in his comparison, including loading extensions into images on the fly. For a database of any size, use a dedicated node pool, pin and taint, and use Kubernetes for automation, not overprovisioning. His closing borrows Kelsey Hightower: Kubernetes won't magically turn Postgres into Cloud SQL.

## Who should watch

Anyone running, or being told to run, Postgres on Kubernetes. Bring a notebook.

Title: Contact tracing over BLE, and the iOS background quirk that shaped it
Description: Parth Menon (Meta) at Conf42 IoT 2024 on a BLE contact tracing app built at SAP Labs India that worked around Android and iOS GATT limits for 7,000+ staff
Body:
The hard part of Bluetooth contact tracing isn't the epidemiology, it's that Android and iOS each break a different half of the protocol. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Parth Menon, who leads Mobile Storage Infra on Android for Meta's products, told the story of the COVID-era contact tracing app he helped build in the R&D department at SAP Labs India, and the cross-platform Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) architecture that got around both operating systems' limits.

It's a short talk, under ten minutes, and one of the more concretely technical sessions of the event: a real problem, real platform constraints and the design that resolved them, with 7,000+ employees as the outcome.

## What problem did SAP need solved?

During 2020 and early 2021, as offices reopened, SAP tracked visitors on a manual sign-up sheet. When someone reported sick, staff went through the sheet and phoned everyone who might have been in contact. It took a couple of days, during which the infection could keep spreading, and it was full of false positives: people on opposite sides of the campus landed on the same sheet.

The business wanted automation, less delay and, since COVID looked temporary, minimal hardware spend. The answer was the device everyone already carried and nobody shares at the office: their phone.

## Why Bluetooth Low Energy?

BLE uses little power, has a short range (a feature for contact tracing) and can move small amounts of data. Both Android and iOS support the Generic Attribute Profile (GATT): a device advertises a service ID in its scan record, nearby scanners find it, connect, and read a scan response or characteristic that identifies the device or user.

The team also ruled out the alternatives. Wi-Fi drained the battery more and was more complicated, especially on iOS. RFID meant hardware investment. NFC's range was too low. Classic Bluetooth now broadcasts temporary MAC addresses, precisely so malls and advertisers can't track people, which also made it useless for identifying colleagues.

## Where do Android and iOS each fall short?

This is the meat of the talk. On Android, multiple clients can connect to one server, but when a client connects to a second server the first connection drops, and connections are asynchronous, so you have to queue them yourself and risk missing nearby devices. On the plus side, Android can broadcast two IDs in the scan record and its scan response keeps working with the app backgrounded or the screen locked.

iOS is the mirror image. Its scanner API queues connections for you, but it can broadcast only a single ID per service. "When the app is backgrounded, the scan response will return a null value, making it impossible to identify the device," Parth Menon said at Conf42 IoT 2024.

## Three tracing paths, one contact graph

Every phone reports who it saw to SAP's internal servers at regular intervals, building a graph of employee contacts. The architecture runs three independent methods:

- **Android to Android**: the advertiser broadcasts two IDs, one for the service and one for the user; the scanner records the second as an edge.
- **iOS to iOS**: every device advertises the same service ID, scanners pick up the temporary MAC address of each GATT server, connect, and read a characteristic holding the device identifier.
- **Cross-platform**: every Android device also runs a GATT server, and the iOS device does the work, connecting and reading the Android ID, and reporting the edge in both directions.

Putting the iOS phone in charge of mixed pairs sidesteps both problems at once: the null background scan response on iOS and the queueing limits of Android GATT clients. It's a nice example of designing around the platform instead of fighting it.

## Did it work, and what about privacy?

More than 7,000 employees installed the app and used it to visit the office. Geofencing kept it from running in the background when employees weren't at work, so it wasn't tracking people's private lives. SAP holds a patent on the approach.

## Who should watch

Mobile engineers who have fought BLE background behaviour, IoT developers designing proximity features across Android and iOS, and anyone who likes a talk where the constraint table explains the architecture.

Title: Rate the ISP, not the IP - moving the perimeter to the attacker's side
Description: Ramon Izaguirre Bilbao (Internet2.ai) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on rating the ISPs that originate traffic, so defence starts at the attacker's network
Body:
An IP blocklist forgets: once a phishing server is cleaned up, its address goes back to being a good address. Ramon Izaguirre Bilbao, Founder and CEO of Internet2.ai, argued at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 that the unit worth rating is the ISP network the traffic comes from, because a network keeps a history. His pitch is to add a second perimeter at the origin of the traffic, scored like a restaurant on a review site, on top of the defences at your own front door.

Honest scope first: this is a founder presenting his company's approach, and the ISP rating it describes is Internet2.ai's product. The idea is worth hearing on its own merits, and he keeps the commercials out of it.

## Why does defence at the destination keep losing?

Ramon Izaguirre Bilbao said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 that "if that was a race, we are not winning," pointing at well-funded organisations that still get breached. His framing: today we defend where the traffic lands, with firewalls and everything behind them. That is good, and not enough. Millions of attacks a day from every angle are like millions of people trying your doors and windows around the clock, so a breach becomes a matter of when. He quotes a CIO of a large organisation who now designs defences on the assumption that the enemy is already inside, which, as he puts it, "Really sounds a little bit Too much."

The root cause he names is cyber impunity. Attacks are close to free, attackers are anonymous, and cross-border law enforcement is so slow that consequences are rare. That is how script kiddies end up breaching organisations with millions in revenue: the return on attacking is very high because the cost is near zero.

## What does rating an ISP actually involve?

The comparison is eBay and Amazon: nobody would buy from a stranger online without seller ratings. Apply the same to the networks sending you traffic and you can say that traffic from this network is usually malicious and traffic from that one usually isn't.

The inputs he describes: probes distributed around the world that see malicious traffic, third-party reports on bad IP addresses mapped back to the ISP that owns them, and proprietary algorithms, all collected in real time. The key difference from IP reputation is memory. An ISP rating keeps the history of how a network behaved yesterday as well as today, and how many times it has been rated, which is the restaurant point: four stars from 1,542 reviews means more than five stars from two. The rating policy itself is set by AI with minimal human oversight, and the technique was patent pending at the time of the talk.

## And the obvious objection about proxies and chained hops?

He raises it himself: attackers chain through servers in several countries. His answer is that the chain can be followed back the same way it was built. The deterrence argument is that if the ISP an attacker connects to is watching and can raise a complaint in the attacker's own country, prosecution stops being an international legal puzzle, and a script kiddie "will think it twice" before going after a big target.

## How would you use it on Monday?

Three use cases:

- **Traffic monitoring**: ingest the ratings into your SIEM; he mentions a direct integration with Microsoft Sentinel that doesn't require changing the ingestion layer.
- **Operational limits**: a bank with a low risk appetite could let a user check a balance from a poorly rated ISP but restrict money transfers from it.
- **Risk assessment**: profile how many customers and employees connect from well or poorly rated ISPs, and decide what that exposure is worth.

He adds that the company works with the rated ISPs to help low-scoring networks improve, rather than just publishing a bad score. The football analogy closes it: nobody puts all eleven players on the goal line and waits; you defend in layers, starting in the other half. The stakes have moved past electrons and circuits: he recalls an NHS blood donation appeal in the UK, driven partly by a cyber attack on the health service.

## Who should watch

Security architects and SOC leads interested in threat intelligence beyond per-IP blocklists, and fraud teams thinking about network-level risk scoring. Expect a strategy argument and a product overview, not a technical deep look at the scoring model.

Title: APIs are like teenagers - a stage-by-stage API security checklist
Description: Anirudha Karandikar at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on building API security into design, development, testing, release, operations and monitoring
Body:
"APIs are like teenagers. They need constant supervision or they will break the rules in ways you never imagined." That is how Anirudha Karandikar, a Principal Engineer at a Fortune 500 company with around 18 years in API management, opened his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk, and the rest is the supervision plan: security practices for every stage of an API's life, from design through development, testing, release, operations and monitoring.

One note on scope: the abstract frames the session around generative AI for API governance, and the talk itself doesn't go there. What it delivers is a dense, well-ordered API security checklist, which is arguably more useful.

## Why start at design?

His numbers set the stakes. Over 80% of web traffic was expected to pass through APIs by 2025; 91% of organisations had an API security incident in the previous year; fixing a vulnerability in production costs 30 times more than in design; nearly 80% of API vulnerabilities come from misconfigurations or coding mistakes; and only 40% of organisations test APIs for vulnerabilities during development. APIs, he says, have taken over from web applications as the most targeted attack vector. The message: catch them early, catch them often.

## What belongs in the design review?

The longest section and the one to bookmark. Highlights:

- **AuthN and AuthZ** via OAuth, with identity providers such as Okta or Azure implementing it.
- **Classify every API** by data (restricted, confidential, internal, public) and as internal or public. Many breaches started with an internal API exposed to the internet with internal-grade guardrails.
- **Encrypt in transit beyond TLS.** HTTPS with TLS 1.2 is a given; he argues for explicit payload encryption too, hybrid or AES, and if performance rules out the whole payload, at least the sensitive attributes.
- **Return only what is needed**, mask anything sensitive you must log, and keep error messages generic while logging specifics securely.
- **Short-lived tokens** with a secure refresh. "Many attacks have happened due to the long lived tokens," Anirudha Karandikar said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024.
- **Version APIs and retire old ones**, keeping track of which consumers use which version; outdated APIs left running are a classic back door.
- **Lock down private API docs** to authenticated users, since exposed documentation is a ready-made attack manual.
- **Cap request and response sizes**, against resource exhaustion attacks that wrap garbage in otherwise valid requests.

Plus rate limiting, input validation and least privilege, which he treats as table stakes.

## And after the design?

**Development**: reserve sprint capacity for library and framework upgrades; automate dependency updates with Renovate (Log4j is the cautionary tale); keep secrets in HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager and stop them reaching Git with ggshield; run static and dynamic analysis in CI; make peer reviews look at security too, ideally against a checklist tailored to your codebase. His infrastructure-as-code example is a good one: set up an S3 bucket by hand across ten environments and one of them will miss an access policy. SonarQube in CI and SonarLint or Checkmarx in the IDE shift feedback left.

**Testing**: SAST, DAST, container image scanning (base images carry vulnerabilities too), performance tests that check what leaks when timeouts grow or backends stall, and negative access tests plus penetration tests as a major chunk of the test plan.

**Release**: canary deployments to limit the blast radius of a bad build, and automated security sanity tests on every deployment.

**Operations**: a WAF against SQL injection and XSS, bot detection that tells your own bots from crawlers, and an API gateway doing five jobs - access policy, request translation, routing, rate limiting and throttling, and schema compliance that rejects malformed requests before they reach the backend. A SIEM such as Splunk, IBM QRadar or Microsoft Sentinel correlates events across the mesh of services.

**Monitoring**: RED metrics (rate, errors, duration), regular checks of security headers and access controls at the gateway, sampled tracing with Jaeger or AppDynamics as an x-ray of the system, and monitoring dashboards open to developers, not just ops.

## Who should watch

API owners, backend leads and platform teams who want a single checklist to run a new API against, or to audit an old one. Security specialists will know every item; the value is in having all of them in order on one page.

Title: How the car turned into a connected computer, from ECUs to Android Auto
Description: Maksim Lykov (Google) at Conf42 IoT 2024 on how IT turned cars into connected devices, from 1980s ECUs to OTA updates, V2X and mobility as a service
Body:
Your car's first computer was there to keep it inside emissions limits; its latest one wants to read your messages aloud. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Maksim Lykov, Software Engineer at Google working on Android Auto (smartphone projection onto supported vehicle displays), traced how IT reshaped the automotive business across three pillars: smart connected vehicles, infotainment, and the trends that may make owning a car optional.

It's a history-and-outlook talk for a general technical audience, not an Android Auto internals session. If you want a coherent timeline of how cars became IoT devices, with the tensions spelled out, it does the job well.

## How did cars get their first computers?

Lykov's timeline starts in the 1980s with electronic control units (ECUs), introduced to improve engine performance and efficiency as emission rules tightened, which marked the shift from mechanical to electronically controlled systems. The 1990s added anti-lock brakes and airbag controllers built on sensors and microprocessors, plus CD changers and early navigation. The 2000s brought GPS, Bluetooth hands-free calling and telematics such as GM's OnStar, the first time cars talked to external systems. In-car entertainment itself goes back to the AM radios of the 1930s.

## Smartphones moved into the dashboard

The real break came in the 2010s. Apple CarPlay launched in 2014, with Android Auto shortly after, and the first carmakers to adopt CarPlay included Ferrari and Mercedes-Benz, followed by brands like Hyundai and Chevrolet. Phones brought navigation, music, messaging and voice assistants with them, and reset what drivers expect from a dashboard.

Lykov, who builds one of these platforms, is candid about the cost. Infotainment has become complicated, and touchscreens and voice commands can distract. "Drivers can easily become overwhelmed by too many options," Maksim Lykov said at Conf42 IoT 2024. His bar for in-car AI: it has to add real value without complicating the driving.

## OTA updates and V2X make the car a node

The IoT section covers two ideas. Over-the-air updates let vehicles receive navigation and infotainment upgrades, bug fixes and critical safety patches remotely, with Tesla as the benchmark that ships features like battery efficiency improvements without a service visit. Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication splits into V2V (other vehicles), V2P (pedestrians), V2I (infrastructure such as traffic lights) and V2C (the cloud), so a car can warn the one behind about sudden braking, and signals can tune traffic flow. He calls V2X early-stage but a cornerstone for coordinating autonomous vehicles.

## Why isn't autonomy here yet?

Autonomy is described on the usual five levels, from driver assistance to no human at all, and Lykov lists four blockers: technology reliability (he notes Waymo only operates autonomously in certain cities), regulatory approval (Tesla's Autopilot under legal scrutiny), safety in unpredictable situations, and public trust. Automation also lives in the factory, where he points to Tesla's robotics in battery assembly and painting.

## Will you still own a car?

Mobility as a service (MaaS) is the business model shift: ride-hailing such as Uber and Lyft, and subscriptions from Volvo and Porsche, where you can switch from a weekend sports car to something practical during the week. Lykov expects platforms that bundle ride sharing, public transport and bike rentals, and automakers such as BMW and Ford pivoting from selling cars to selling services.

The risks get a proper section. The 2015 Jeep Cherokee remote takeover is his reminder that connected cars are attack surface, and V2X widens it. Cars also collect a lot of data about drivers, habits and locations, which brings GDPR-style obligations. His closing trends are personalisation, blockchain for vehicle history and supply chains, quantum computing for real-time route optimisation, and VR (Audi's virtual showrooms, BMW's training). He cites McKinsey's projection of an automotive software and electronics market of about $462 billion by 2030.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into automotive or connected-vehicle work who want the big picture, and IoT folks curious how the car industry thinks about software. If you already work on V2X or in-vehicle platforms, it's a refresher.

Title: An SRE field guide, from Terraform to HIPAA, in one sitting
Description: Nagarjuna Malladi (Oracle) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on the building blocks of SRE - cloud, networking, databases, observability, automation and industry rules
Body:
Site reliability engineering is not one skill but about seven, and most job descriptions quietly expect all of them. Nagarjuna Malladi, Principal Software Engineer SRE at Oracle, used his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk to lay those skills out in order: cloud-native infrastructure, networking, databases, observability, automation, the advanced practices like chaos engineering and error budgets, and what changes when the system belongs to a bank, a retailer or a hospital.

Set expectations by the talk, not the abstract. The abstract leans on AI-driven security and chaos engineering; the talk is a survey of the SRE discipline with security woven in as one concern per layer. It is a good map for someone moving into SRE, less so for someone already on call.

## What is SRE for, in one paragraph?

He starts with the Google origin story and three goals: keep services available and reliable, automate operational tasks so manual errors go away, and manage failures so recovery time, and therefore disruption, shrinks. The framing he stresses is proactive: SRE is as much about preventing failures as reacting to them.

## The stack, layer by layer

**Cloud-native infrastructure.** AWS, Azure, GCP and OCI as the platforms; Terraform, CloudFormation and ARM templates for infrastructure as code; Lambda, Azure Functions and Cloud Functions for serverless; Kubernetes, ECS and AKS for containers; IAM, VPCs, security groups and encryption for cloud-native security.

**Networking.** Redundant, low-latency topologies; latency, throughput and jitter monitoring with machine learning for anomaly detection; firewalls, IDS/IPS, VPNs and zero-trust architectures; DNS and CDNs to cut latency. "Networking is the backbone of any distributed system," Nagarjuna Malladi said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024.

**Databases.** Replication for high availability, backups and geographic distribution for disaster recovery, query optimisation, indexing and caching with Redis or Memcached, sharding and partitioning for horizontal scale, and encryption, fine-grained access control and data masking for security. He admits this one deserved a talk of its own.

**Observability.** Metrics for utilisation, latency and error rates; centralised logging with the ELK Stack or Splunk (and the clouds' own OpenSearch offerings); tracing with Jaeger, Zipkin and AWS X-Ray; alerting on dynamic thresholds and anomalies. His aside on machine learning is practical: it can tell you at what time of day the system runs hot on CPU or load. Underneath it all, SLIs, SLOs and SLAs.

**Automation.** His favourite topic: CI/CD with Jenkins, GitLab CI and GitHub Actions; Ansible, Puppet and Chef for configuration; Python, Bash and PowerShell for the scripts; self-healing and auto-scaling to cut MTTR.

## Where do chaos engineering and error budgets fit?

As the advanced tier. Chaos engineering with Chaos Monkey or Gremlin, controlled failure to find the limits before production does, which he concedes "might seem counterintuitive." Error budgets let a team spend reliability risk deliberately, trading stability against shipping speed. Capacity planning uses machine learning and trend analysis to forecast resource needs.

## Does the industry change the job?

This is the section with the most colour. In financial services the weight is on security, regulatory compliance such as GDPR and SOX, and high-frequency transactions that cannot stop; he names JPMorgan, Capital One and Citibank. In e-commerce it is scale at peak, Black Friday at Amazon or Walmart, and fraud, because the attackers show up exactly when the load does. In healthcare it is HIPAA, interoperability and life-critical systems, where even doctors don't get to see every part of a patient's record.

The security point running through the whole talk is that reliability work and security work share the same controls: access control, encryption, monitoring and automated response.

## Who should watch

Developers and ops engineers moving into SRE who want the whole territory and a reading list of tools in one place, and managers writing an SRE job description. Experienced SREs will recognise every slide; send it to the new hire instead.

Title: Workflow automation that learns instead of following a rulebook
Description: Kowsick Venkatachalapathi (BNY) at Conf42 IoT 2024 on moving workflow automation from fixed rules to ML, NLP triage and reinforcement learning
Body:
Rule-based automation is great until the first case nobody wrote a rule for, and then a human gets paged. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Kowsick Venkatachalapathi, Vice President of Software Development at BNY, laid out how AI and machine learning turn workflow automation from a fixed set of rules into a system that learns from data, triages its own inbox and improves its policy over time.

It's a broad, conceptual talk: a pipeline, a set of industry examples and a closing look at ethics, rather than a build log of one system. Its value is the structure, which is a reasonable blueprint for anyone planning to put ML into business process automation.

## What's wrong with rule-based workflows?

Traditional workflow automation, in his framing, covers business process automation, case management and decision management, all driven by a preset of rules. It follows predefined paths and needs extensive human oversight for exceptions and complex scenarios. It works for basic processes but lacks adaptability. The ML version adds pattern recognition and prediction, so the system can prioritise tasks, spot bottlenecks and forecast problems before they land.

## How does an AI decision pipeline fit together?

Four steps, in order:

1. **Data collection and cleaning** from many structured and unstructured sources. He flags noise and outliers as the usual pain, and preprocessing as the most important task in any machine learning work.
2. **Pattern recognition** on historical data to find trends and correlations.
3. **Model building**: predictive models that forecast outcomes and recommend actions, retrained as data accumulates.
4. **Automated decision execution** within predefined criteria, taking humans out of the routine loop.

His industry examples follow the standard map: fraud detection that adapts to new tactics in finance, predictive diagnostics in healthcare, demand forecasting and supply chain optimisation in manufacturing, personalised recommendations in retail.

## Let NLP read the inbox

The most practical section is on natural language processing. Customer support teams drown in email, and NLP can categorise and prioritise messages by content and urgency, route them to the right team, run sentiment analysis on feedback and support tickets, and back chatbots for routine queries. He breaks NLP-driven task management into its own four steps:

- **Content analysis**: entity recognition, topic modelling and intent classification on each message.
- **Task extraction**: pulling out the meeting request, the report deadline, the support need.
- **Prioritisation and assignment**: by urgency, importance, workload and expertise.
- **Automated follow-ups**: reminders, escalations and status reports to stakeholders.

## Reinforcement learning closes the loop

"Nothing is perfect in the first place," Kowsick Venkatachalapathi said at Conf42 IoT 2024, which is his cue for reinforcement learning. An adaptive workflow starts with basic rules and limited knowledge, explores different actions, learns which ones lead to better outcomes, refines its policy, and keeps adapting as the business changes. Examples: rescheduling production lines around equipment failures in smart manufacturing, adapting high-frequency trading strategies to market conditions, routing telecom traffic to prevent congestion, and balancing supply and demand on smart energy grids.

## What results does he cite?

He closes with success stories by sector, without naming the organisations behind them: an AI fraud detection system in banking that cut false positives by 60% and saved $50 million a year, an ML diagnostic tool with 30% better early disease detection, an AI-optimised supply chain with 25% lower inventory cost and 15% faster delivery, and NLP support automation that cut ticket resolution time by 40%. Read them as illustrations of the potential, not benchmarks.

The IoT link comes at the end: sensors and connected devices provide the real-time inputs that let these systems automate physical processes, not only digital ones. Cloud AI services, he expects, will bring the same tools to small and medium businesses. The ethics checklist covers data privacy and GDPR, bias audits, explainability for regulators, and reskilling for people whose jobs change.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and architects scoping where ML belongs in an existing business process automation stack, especially support and ticket triage. If you want code, model choices or a production war story, this is not that talk.

Title: AIOps for AWS security - baseline, correlate, then let it heal itself
Description: Indika Wimalasuriya (Virtusa) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on using CloudWatch, DevOps Guru and GuardDuty AIOps to detect, correlate and auto-fix AWS security incidents
Body:
Security teams are rarely short of alerts; they are short of alerts worth reading. Indika Wimalasuriya, Associate Director and Senior Systems Engineering Manager at Virtusa, spent his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk on how AIOps on AWS turns that noise into something actionable: baseline normal behaviour, correlate events across services, forecast what is coming, and automate the response with CloudWatch, Lambda and Systems Manager.

It is a broad map of AWS services and seven security use cases rather than a single implementation story, from an AWS Community Builder in cloud operations who clearly lives in this console.

## Why is cloud security operations so hard?

He opens with the Cost of a Data Breach Report 2024: an average breach costs $4.48 million, and 46% of breaches involve customer personal data. Then he walks the lifecycle - identify, protect, detect, respond, recover, govern - and names the cloud-specific pain in each: inconsistent telemetry across multi-cloud, misconfigured cloud-native services, false positives from fragmented detection, playbooks not automated across regions, slow restores of distributed systems, and audit readiness in an estate that scales itself.

The amplifiers are familiar: on-prem to cloud elasticity, monoliths to microservices, and telemetry volume. He calls the last one a data paradox: more data, with less information in it.

## Who owns what?

Before any AI, the shared responsibility model. AWS secures the cloud itself: regions, availability zones, edge locations and the foundation services for compute, storage, database and networking. You secure what you put in it: your content, platforms and applications, IAM, operating systems, network and firewall configuration, client- and server-side encryption, and traffic protection. Then the service tour by lifecycle phase: Security Hub, Organizations, Control Tower, Config and Trusted Advisor to identify; VPC, Shield, WAF, IAM, Cognito and Firewall Manager to protect; GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie to detect; and CloudWatch triggering Step Functions, Lambda or Systems Manager to respond.

His advice on that wall of logos is sensible: AWS offers loads of tools, which doesn't mean you have to use all of them. Pick by need.

## Where does the AI actually help?

The AIOps goal comes in three steps: eliminate incidents with predictive maintenance, detect the rest fast with intelligent alerting, and resolve them with self-healing. CloudWatch supplies metric and log anomaly detection, natural-language query generation and insights for containers, Lambda and EC2. Amazon DevOps Guru, one of his favourite services, baselines the whole account and adds anomaly detection, root cause analysis by correlating data sources, proactive recommendations and cross-service correlation.

The seven use cases are the practical core, each with examples:

- **Anomaly detection in logs and metrics**: API call spikes tied to a possible DDoS, calls from unknown IPs, bursts of failed logins.
- **Event correlation**: failed logins next to outbound traffic, S3 bucket access linked to an unusual IAM role, simultaneous logins from distant regions.
- **Noise reduction**: fewer GuardDuty false positives, duplicate alerts suppressed during maintenance windows, high-risk vulnerabilities first.
- **Forecasting**: DDoS predicted from traffic patterns, IAM role misuse anticipated from past behaviour, patching needs.
- **Automated incident response**: isolate compromised instances, block malicious IPs via firewall updates, revoke compromised credentials.
- **Threat intelligence integration**: block known bad IPs and phishing URLs, enrich logs with threat feeds.
- **Behavioural analytics**: access attempts outside working hours, unusual data transfers by specific users.

On correlation he is blunt about why it matters: "noise is sometimes one of the greatest challenges we face these days," Indika Wimalasuriya said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024. Detection has improved; finding the real problem underneath it is what costs the time.

## How do you measure whether it worked?

Set goals first (reduce MTTR, shrink blast radius), integrate CloudTrail and GuardDuty data with the AIOps layer, and get security, DevOps and ITIL teams working together. The KPIs he proposes mix security and delivery: MTTD, MTTR, MTBF of customer-impacting incidents, percentage of incidents self-healed, system availability, NPS, and the DORA trio of change frequency, lead time and change failure rate. The closing point: baseline these before you start, or you won't know if you are improving.

## Who should watch

Cloud security and SRE teams on AWS deciding which managed AI features to switch on, and leads who need a structured list of use cases to pitch AIOps internally. If you already run GuardDuty with automated Lambda remediation, the use-case list doubles as a gap check.

Title: Multi-cloud or hybrid cloud for your data? A short field guide
Description: Prashanth Reddy Kora (Centene Corporation) at Conf42 IoT 2024 on when multi-cloud and hybrid cloud help data management, and the costs they add
Body:
Spreading your data across clouds buys you resilience and leverage, and charges you in complexity. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Prashanth Reddy Kora, Cloud Database Engineer at Centene Corporation, gave a compact overview of multi-cloud and hybrid cloud architectures for data management: what each model is for, what each costs you, and the four practices that keep them sane.

A note on scope before you press play. The abstract promises IoT case studies; the talk itself is a short, general primer on cloud architecture strategy, with industry statistics and no case studies or demos. It is a good ten-minute orientation for someone new to the trade-offs, and not much more.

## Why is everyone suddenly in more than one cloud?

Kora's numbers, all from industry surveys he names: Gartner expects 95% of new digital workloads to be deployed on cloud-native platforms by 2025, IDC puts the global datasphere at 175 zettabytes by 2025, and Flexera's 2023 survey found 87% of enterprises with a multi-cloud strategy and 72% embracing hybrid cloud. A HashiCorp survey he quotes has 76% of organisations using multiple clouds.

The two models solve different problems, and the talk is clearest when it separates them.

## Multi-cloud: a hedge against one vendor

Multi-cloud means using services from several providers. The benefits he lists are redundancy (better disaster recovery and less downtime risk), vendor flexibility (pick the best service from each), cost optimisation through pricing competition, and performance from distributing workloads. In the HashiCorp numbers, 63% cite improved disaster recovery and 45% cost savings.

The bill comes as operational complexity. Security policies have to stay consistent across providers, integrating data between clouds is hard, cost monitoring has to span every provider, and you need people who know all of them. Anyone who has tried to keep IAM roles equivalent across two clouds will nod along.

## Hybrid cloud: keep the crown jewels at home

Hybrid cloud combines on-premises infrastructure with private and public cloud. For data management, he argues, it's the more interesting model, because it lets you:

- **Keep data sovereign.** Sensitive data stays on premises or in a private cloud to meet regulatory requirements.
- **Burst for peaks.** Public cloud capacity takes the spikes.
- **Migrate legacy gradually.** Move old systems over time without breaking operations.
- **Archive cheaply.** Push rarely accessed data to lower-cost public storage tiers.

He cites Nutanix's 2023 survey: 87% of IT decision-makers consider hybrid cloud the ideal IT model, with adoption expected to grow 39% over the next five years. The challenges mirror multi-cloud: integrating on-prem with cloud services, security and compliance across environments, cost monitoring and skills.

## What keeps either model from becoming a mess?

Four practices, the closest the talk gets to a checklist:

1. **Data governance**: clear frameworks for managing data across every platform.
2. **Integration tools** that work between providers.
3. **Cloud-agnostic technologies**, so you are not just swapping one lock-in for another.
4. **Continuous optimisation**: keep monitoring performance and cost, because the right placement changes as needs do.

"Overcoming these challenges requires a careful planning," Prashanth Reddy Kora said at Conf42 IoT 2024, and the talk's main message is that skilled people and tooling decide whether these architectures pay off. He closes with a market projection of $44.6 billion for multi-cloud by 2027.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers about to move from a single cloud to a multi-cloud or hybrid setup who want the vocabulary and the standard trade-offs in one place. If you already run databases across clouds, you will want the deeper talks below.

Title: A data portal is Marie Kondo for your company's scattered data
Description: Robin Sarkar (Enstall) at Conf42 IoT 2024 on data portals for self-service analytics, and the security, literacy and quality traps that stall them
Body:
Most companies don't lack data, they lack the one place where anyone can find it without filing a ticket. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Robin Sarkar, Director of Analytics & Digital at Enstall, made the case for data portals: a central, governed, searchable home for an organisation's data with self-service analytics on top, so the product manager, the HR lead and the junior support agent can answer their own questions.

It's a business-facing overview, not an architecture walkthrough: no vendor, no stack, plenty of analogies. Sarkar opens by apologising for the topic, then spends the talk proving it deserves better.

## Why do we need a portal at all?

His framing: the global datasphere was projected to grow from 33 zettabytes in 2018 to 175 zettabytes by 2025, and most organisations still can't find the shirt in their own closet. "Think of data portal as your super organized friend, Marie Kondo," Robin Sarkar said at Conf42 IoT 2024. His retail example: sales, inventory, customer support and marketing live in separate systems, so every cross-team insight is a manual, inconsistent stitching job.

## What does a data portal actually include?

Five features, each with a concrete example:

- **A centralised repository.** In healthcare, patient records, lab results and billing sit in different systems; one place means up-to-date information for the people treating patients.
- **Self-service analytics.** Dashboards that non-technical users can drive without asking the data team for every report.
- **Data governance.** Access controls and compliance built in, so growth doesn't mean sensitive data in the wrong hands.
- **Search and discovery.** The analyst who needs last quarter's sales for one region types it and gets the dataset.
- **Collaboration tools.** Share an insight, tag the sales team and work on it in the portal instead of 50 emails.

## What's the payoff?

Sarkar leans on a stack of industry statistics, and it's worth being clear these are figures he quotes, not results from a portal he ran: a 33% increase in decision-making speed, 24% higher data literacy among non-technical staff, 16% higher productivity, up to 20% less time spent searching for data. On the business side he cites data-driven companies being 23 times more likely to acquire customers, six times more likely to retain them and 19 times more likely to be profitable. Treat them as directional; the talk gives no methodology.

The more convincing points are the small stories. A junior customer-service employee spots a recurring complaint pattern in the portal, it reaches a strategy meeting, and suddenly they're the office hero. A fitness company sees which classes fill up and moves the timetable. That's the actual mechanism: more people can look at the same single source of truth, so fewer insights die in someone's spreadsheet.

## Where do data portals fail?

The best section is the honest one. Sarkar lists four ways rollouts go wrong, each with a fix:

- **Security**: 67% of organisations name it a primary concern, and the IBM 2021 figure for an average breach is $4.24M. His answer is a zero-trust model, where every user and device is verified, plus encryption and regular audits.
- **User adoption**: only 20% of professionals feel confident in their data literacy. Train by role, so HR learns engagement trends and marketing learns campaign dashboards, and keep it from being boring.
- **Data quality**: garbage in, garbage out. Automated cleansing before data hits the portal, plus clear governance policies.
- **Scalability**: data grows faster than infrastructure, so go cloud or hybrid.

## Who should watch

Analytics leads trying to sell a data portal or self-service BI initiative to leadership, and engineers who will have to build one and want the business vocabulary. If you want reference architectures, catalogue tools or lineage design, look elsewhere; this is the why, not the how.

Title: Three browser APIs an e-commerce site should already be using
Description: Karthik Vallamsetla (Cisco) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on Geolocation, Web Notifications and Intersection Observer for e-commerce, with consent done right
Body:
Telling users why you want their location is worth a 30% bump in opt-ins, according to Karthik Vallamsetla, Software Engineer at Cisco. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 he walked through three browser APIs - Geolocation, Web Notifications and Intersection Observer - with the e-commerce results he has seen from each, and the consent and fatigue rules that keep them from becoming creepy.

A note on scope: the abstract mentions Explainable AI and a 50% engagement boost; neither appears in the talk. What you get is a practical frontend talk drawn from his e-commerce work, where the security angle is user consent, encryption and data retention.

## Why browser APIs, and why now?

His framing is the arc from DOM manipulation (update some text, hide an element) to APIs that reach device hardware, location and offline storage, which is what made progressive web apps viable. The opening example sets the tone: real-time inventory updates for a major retailer kept availability accurate through Black Friday traffic, with a 15% reduction in cart abandonment and a 10% boost in revenue.

## Geolocation: ask nicely, and have a plan B

Use cases are the obvious ones: nearby stores with the product in stock, location-based promotions, regional recommendations. For an outdoor gear retailer, recommending hiking gear by location and local weather lifted conversion by 20%.

The best practices are the part to copy:

- Explain the ask up front. "We use your location to show nearby store inventory" is his example wording, and it is the one credited with the 30% opt-in lift.
- Use encrypted connections and don't keep location data longer than you need.
- Offer a manual fallback such as a zip code field. In one project that kept 15% of users who had denied location access.

## Web Notifications: three a day, tops

Notifications reach users when they are not on the site: price drops on wishlist items, flash sales, abandoned carts. Technically that means a permission request plus a registered service worker for the background work. A holiday wishlist sale campaign got a 25% click-through rate.

The difference between useful and uninstall-worthy is control. Let users pick the type and frequency, send at the times analytics say they engage, and cap the volume. "Limit notifications to three per day to prevent fatigue," Karthik Vallamsetla said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024. Frequency caps cut opt-out rates by 15% in one project, and an abandoned-cart nudge sent 24 hours after browsing recovered 18% of carts.

## Intersection Observer: stop listening to scroll events

Intersection Observer tells you when an element enters or leaves the viewport, so you can lazy-load images and start animations only when something is visible, without a pile of scroll listeners burning CPU. For a fashion retailer, lazy loading through it cut page load times by 35% and lifted mobile conversion by 12%.

## Do they work better together?

That is his closing case: Geolocation spots users near a physical store, a notification tells them about an in-store promotion, and Intersection Observer animates the banner when it scrolls into view. He reports a 30% increase in foot traffic and a 20% rise in local sales.

The challenges are the usual browser ones. Use feature detection, ship fallbacks for unsupported features, and keep API calls and caching efficient; a modular architecture handled this in a global e-commerce project. On the horizon he points at WebXR for virtual showrooms, the Web Neural Network API for in-browser personalisation, and WebUSB for things like label printing.

## Who should watch

Frontend engineers and product teams in e-commerce, and anyone who has to argue for a permission prompt with legal in the room. The numbers are his own project results, presented without methodology, so treat them as directions rather than benchmarks.

Title: At Turo, the API contract comes before the code
Description: Nikhil Bharadwaj Ramashasthri (Turo) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on API-first development with OpenAPI 3.0, stakeholders in the design room and strict versioning
Body:
Most API scope arguments happen after the endpoint ships, when the mobile team discovers what the backend meant. Nikhil Bharadwaj Ramashasthri, Staff Software Engineer at Turo, used his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk to explain how Turo moved that argument to the start: define the API contract with the people who will consume it, then implement, then test and deploy. His teams report 29% higher developer satisfaction and a 35% higher API adoption rate since.

It is a short talk, under ten minutes, and works best as a field report on adopting API-first rather than a tutorial. The abstract's promise of real-world examples from Uber and GitHub amounts to a mention in the use cases and the conclusion.

## What problem pushed Turo to API-first?

Scope. He describes Turo struggling with the explicit versus implicit scope of an API when the backend team didn't understand what third-party clients, frontend developers or mobile developers actually needed. The lesson they took: the stakeholders using an API define its scope.

So the backend team started inviting those stakeholders into API design brainstorming, which closed a lot of loose ends. The pattern that came out of it is three steps: define the API contract, implement it, test and deploy.

He also cites a 2023 Postman survey in which 67% of developers expected to spend more time on API work, which is the economic case for getting the contract right early.

## What goes into the contract?

The producer side defines the endpoints and the request and response structures together with stakeholders, sometimes with mocked data so consumers can start before the implementation exists. The principles on top: loose coupling and modularity so components scale and change independently, abstraction and encapsulation so internals can change without consumers noticing, and consumer-driven design.

For the format, Turo uses OpenAPI 3.0. He compares it with RAML 1.0 and the Markdown-based API Blueprint: OpenAPI supports both YAML and JSON and has extensive code generation, where the others are limited. The tools around it are Stoplight, SwaggerHub and Postman for design, Postman, SoapUI and Prism for testing and mocking, and Swagger UI for documentation. Swagger UI is where his teams explicitly agreed on things like HTTP error code responses, which is exactly the detail that otherwise gets decided by whoever writes the handler.

## Where does security come in?

Mostly through process. The challenges he lists are a steep learning curve, version management with backward compatibility, and API vulnerabilities. Turo handled the first with breakout sessions and training on Swagger and OpenAPI, the second by following versioning policies strictly (URL versioning is the example strategy), and the third with API gateways and regular audits.

The best practices round it out:

- Design APIs with the intention of future-proofing them, for reuse and extension.
- Implement robust error handling and validation; it improves both reliability and security.
- Keep documentation current (Stripe is his example of doing it well).
- Involve stakeholders early and gather feedback.
- Version effectively so transitions are smooth.

## Did the developers like it?

That is the most telling line in the talk: after a few projects, "our developers are never going back to code first approach," Nikhil Bharadwaj Ramashasthri said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024. Beyond the satisfaction and adoption figures, he credits API-first with parallel development (frontend and backend working against the same contract at once) and shorter time to market. Use cases he sees for it include independently scaling microservices, headless CMSs, integration platforms, mobile apps like Turo's, and IoT ecosystems such as Philips Hue.

## Who should watch

Backend leads whose frontend and mobile teams keep discovering API changes in production, and anyone making the case for OpenAPI-first to a team that writes the spec after the code. Ten minutes is a cheap price for the Turo story.

Title: Predicting freight car derailments with SMOTE, a random forest and one decision tree
Description: Maksim Kariagin (Metyis) at Conf42 IoT 2024 on a derailment model for a big European railway that cut accidents 80% and saved $12M a year
Body:
Derailments are rare, which is great for the railway and terrible for your training set. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Maksim Kariagin, Data Science Lead at Metyis, told the story of a model built for one of the largest railway companies in Europe that predicts which freight cars are likely to derail, and the trick that made it useful to the business: turning a random forest's probabilities into readable risk profiles with a decision tree.

The talk title says roads; the case study is rails. Nobody should complain, since the numbers he reports are an 80% reduction in accidents and $12M a year in savings on repair costs.

## What data goes into a derailment model?

The team started with historical derailments as the target and 78 key parameters pulled from a long list of railway systems, covering January 2016 to July 2019: wagon location by station and track, wagon characteristics and repair history, track incidents and defects, repair schedules, train manifests with cargo weight, wagon technical passports, speed restrictions, weather station data and station coordinates. On top of that came sensor data from the track and the wagons, so the model saw near real-time readings and not only daily records.

They also engineered 30 calculated indicators, such as average cargo weight and time between repairs. Quantitative variables were standardised and categorical ones one-hot encoded.

## How do you train on a 1% event rate?

Here was the first real problem: only 1% of the records were derailments, 99% were non-events. Undersampling the non-events throws away information. A model with no rebalancing at all, Kariagin said, gave poor results. The answer was SMOTE, which generates synthetic minority-class samples from the patterns in the independent variables instead of just duplicating rows at random.

For the algorithm they picked a random forest: strong on lots of tabular data, interpretable through variable importance, and less prone to overfitting than the other models they tried on imbalanced data. It reached a ROC AUC of 0.91, with true positive and false positive rates around the 80% mark in his telling. He makes the point that ROC AUC alone is not enough with this much imbalance, so the team also checked PR AUC, which focuses on how well the model finds the minority class.

## A threshold sized to your inspection crews

The output is a derailment probability per wagon, and the cutoff threshold becomes a business dial. Few inspectors: set it high and look only at the riskiest freight cars. More capacity: lower it and catch wagons with lower, but still meaningful, risk. It's a nice reminder that the threshold is an operations decision, not a modelling one.

## Feature importance is not a risk profile

Gini-based variable importance showed what mattered: concrete track sections, winter, tanker wagons, cargo weight, average speed, gravel ballast, train length, even engineer overtime and work experience. Some of that you can't change (winter keeps arriving). Some you can, like wagon type, cargo weight and track material.

But a ranked list of variables doesn't tell a maintenance team which combination is dangerous. So they fed the random forest's probabilities into a decision tree, trading a little sophistication for rules a human can act on. One profile: fewer than 38.5 wagons, under 51.5 years since issue, and a ratio of speed on the last section to average speed below 1.0385, which carries a 94.5% probability of derailment and covers 21% of cases.

"So not only probability, but clear actionable patterns," Maksim Kariagin said at Conf42 IoT 2024, summing up what the company actually needed.

## Who should watch

Data scientists working on rare-event prediction (fraud, outages, failures), and anyone who has shipped an accurate model that the business then ignored because nobody could explain it. It's a short talk, and the random-forest-into-decision-tree step is the part worth stealing.
