Title: DevSecOps explained as a coffee shop, then the six things that go wrong
Description: Joshua Arvin Lat and Raphael Joseph Rosario (NuWorks Interactive Labs) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on six realities of rolling out DevSecOps and their fixes
Body:
A coffee shop can open without CCTV. It just won't stay open long once someone notices. Joshua Arvin Lat, CTO of NuWorks Interactive Labs, and his colleague Raphael Joseph Rosario, IT Supervisor there, used that picture at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 to introduce DevSecOps, then spent the second half on the six realities teams hit when they actually roll it out, each with a reality, a challenge and a fix.

This is an introductory talk, delivered as a two-hander (they call each other "Sir Arvs" and "RJ"). It suits people starting a DevSecOps programme more than people three years into one.

## What does a coffee shop have to do with a pipeline?

The analogy maps cleanly. Developers are the interior designers: they lay out the bar, tables and chairs for a smooth customer experience, and can leave blind spots if nobody thinks about security. Security is the CCTV, watching for theft and suspicious activity. Operations is the shop manager who makes sure the cameras actually record and the footage is stored.

The extensions are the useful part. Automation is motion detection: nobody watches every hour of footage, the system flags unusual activity, the way automated tests flag vulnerabilities before they get serious. Monitoring is reviewing the footage for patterns, like a door that keeps being left open. And a tight budget is the shop that can only afford basic cameras, which is the honest version of most security tool selection.

The pipeline section is a quick tour: CI builds and tests every push, CD packages and ships, security scanning checks for vulnerabilities, insecure dependencies and policy compliance along the way, and operations monitoring tracks health and alerts after deploy.

## The six realities, and what to do about each

Joshua Arvin Lat takes the second half, and it's the reason to watch. Each item follows the same pattern.

**1. Resistance to change.** Breaking down silos is hard. "Developers may view security as a blocker," he said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, while security teams are used to working alone. Fix: cross-team communication, training, shared responsibility, and small early wins you can celebrate, with key stakeholders involved from the start.

**2. Speed versus security.** The perception that security slows delivery is not entirely wrong: the early stages do feel slower while checks are embedded. Fix: lightweight automated checks that run in the background and give fast feedback.

**3. Integration challenges.** CI/CD, scanning and monitoring mean many tools, and legacy systems make tool overload worse. Fix: start with a few key tools and automate the critical security checks first.

**4. Developers without security expertise.** And security teams who don't know development workflows. Fix: secure coding training, and security champions inside the development team.

**5. Legacy systems.** Many have no APIs and no automated tests, so they don't drop into a modern pipeline. Fix: modernise gradually, adding APIs or wrapping them in automation where you can.

**6. Budget and resources.** New tools, training and maybe staff cost money. Fix: start with open source tools, scale up gradually, and justify further spend with the cost savings from fewer vulnerabilities and faster releases.

## Is the advice new?

Not really, and it doesn't try to be. The value is the structure: six named failure modes, each with a concrete first move, which is roughly the slide you need when someone asks why the DevSecOps rollout stalled. The pattern of fixing culture with small wins and champions before buying more scanners is the right order.

## Who should watch

Team leads and engineering managers starting a DevSecOps rollout, and developers who want a gentle introduction to why the security team keeps adding pipeline steps. Practitioners after tooling depth can skip it.

Title: Real-time IIoT analytics needs a real-time network first
Description: Akshat Kapoor (Alcatel-Lucent Enterprise) at Conf42 IoT 2024 on why best-effort networks can't carry real-time IIoT analytics, and what TSN, 5G and edge fix
Body:
Predictive maintenance gets the conference slides, but a vibration sensor's reading is useless if it arrives after the bearing has seized. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Akshat Kapoor, Director Product Management at Alcatel-Lucent Enterprise, walked through the three layers of an industrial IoT (IIoT) analytics system, sensing, communication and analytics, and argued that the middle one, the network, is where real-time ambitions usually fall over.

He knows the plumbing: at Alcatel-Lucent Enterprise he is responsible for the full range of Ethernet switching products, from campus LAN and industrial Ethernet to data centre switches. The talk is an architectural survey, no live demo, but a well-organised one.

## What does "real time" mean in a factory?

Kapoor defines real-time analytics by its deadline: the system has to analyse data and respond within a set window, which ranges from nanoseconds in network communications to milliseconds in medical diagnosis. Real-time IIoT analytics comes in two flavours, predictive and prescriptive, and that deadline is what separates them from descriptive dashboards.

The payoff is the familiar one. Instead of swapping a part as it nears its mean time to failure (MTTF), machine learning on live telemetry plus the part's history spots early warning signs before the failure age. Downtime is expensive, he notes, and costs climb fast once production deviates or stops.

## Sensors are the easy part, until you prepare the data

The sensing layer is vibration, temperature, pressure and current or power-consumption sensors, chosen for the machine and the parameter that best predicts its failures, and placed where they capture the most informative data. The pain is data preparation: sensors from different parts of a line produce wildly different data (some geotagged, some not), and Kapoor reminded the audience that data preparation takes up to 80% of the time and resources of a data analysis operation.

## Why can't the plant network just be IP?

This is the heart of the talk. "The current package switch network, which is based on best effort, is not sufficient to meet the requirements of real time analytics in IIoT," Akshat Kapoor said at Conf42 IoT 2024 (packet-switched, the transcript mishears it).

Different workloads want different things. Robots and drones need predictability. Safety systems and electrical utilities need low latency. Sensor aggregation needs bandwidth. Wearables need wireless. Everyone needs security and, crucially, a shared sense of time. His toolbox, with no one-size-fits-all:

- **SDN** to manage heterogeneous networks and prioritise real-time tasks.
- **Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)**, the IEEE Ethernet standards for bounded latency, low jitter and minimal packet loss at the data link layer, increasingly paired with OPC UA for interoperability.
- **Real-time-aware wireless**, carrying TSN methods over to Wi-Fi.
- **Private 5G with network slicing**, logically separate virtual networks on one physical network.
- **Device-layer tricks** such as priority-aware packet processing and MAC-layer filtering, so best-effort traffic doesn't starve real-time tasks.

## Cloud, edge, or a digital twin?

For the analytics layer he compares three architectures. Pure cloud gives you compute but brings latency, bandwidth limits and flaky connections. Edge-cloud collaboration processes near the devices and sends heavy analytics and storage to the cloud. The newcomer is the digital twin, a virtual replica continuously updated with real-time data, paired with discrete-event or hybrid simulation; in the hybrid case the twin runs as another node of the physical system and provides adaptive control.

## Which models actually get used?

A compact cheat sheet: SVMs and decision trees for supervised failure classification; k-means and PCA when you have little labelled failure data and want anomaly detection; CNNs for vibration and acoustic signatures; LSTMs trained on sensor history plus failure timestamps to predict remaining useful life (RUL); and CNN-LSTM hybrids that combine feature extraction with time-series modelling.

He closes with the unsolved bits: volume, velocity and variety of data, the lack of standardisation between wired and wireless networks for things like TSN and quality of service, and security, with GDPR and ISO 27001 as the compliance anchors.

## Who should watch

Data and ML engineers moving into industrial settings who have never had to think about the network, and OT engineers who want a map of where analytics architectures are heading. If you already run TSN in production, the networking section is a refresher.

Title: Kubernetes security as five layers, from firewall to code review
Description: Thiyagarajan Aramudhan (GM Financial) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on securing Kubernetes in five layers - infrastructure, cluster, container, application, code
Body:
A Kubernetes cluster with no RBAC, no pod security and no network policy lets any pod talk to anything, which is also the default. Thiyagarajan Aramudhan, Cloud Services Manager at GM Financial, spent his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk taking one such architecture and hardening it layer by layer: infrastructure, cluster, container, application and code, with a tool for each on Azure, AWS and open source.

It is an overview talk rather than an internals one: a map of which control belongs where, and a reasonable checklist to hold your own cluster against.

## Why bother with a framework at all?

He opens with Red Hat's Kubernetes security report: 67% of organisations delayed deployments because of Kubernetes security concerns, and 46% lost revenue to a Kubernetes security incident. "Wait, no need to be panic. Let's stay alert," he said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, which is the right tone for a slide of scary percentages.

The starting point is a typical API and web app: a UI going through API management to two services on Kubernetes, talking to a database, a service bus, a key vault and external services. Requests reach API management with no controls in front, and pods have no restrictions on who they talk to. He calls it what it is: very high risk.

## Level by level, what goes where?

The approach is the onion: each layer assumes the one outside it can fail.

| Level | What he adds | Example tools |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Infrastructure | Firewall in front of API management, subnets, NSGs, patching | Azure Security Center, NSGs, Azure Firewall; AWS Security Hub, security groups, WAF; OS hardening |
| 2. Cluster | RBAC, network policy, encrypted pod traffic | Azure RBAC and Policy, AWS IAM roles, Calico, Istio |
| 3. Container | Minimal base images, image scanning, signed images, runtime monitoring | Azure Container Registry, Amazon ECR and Inspector, Trivy, Clair, security contexts |
| 4. Application | Secure coding, secrets out of the code | Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Sealed Secrets |
| 5. Code | Code reviews, static and dynamic analysis, automated compliance checks | Azure DevOps and AWS CodePipeline security features, SonarQube, Open Policy Agent |

He scores each layer as 20% of the way to a secured system, so finishing level five gets you to 100%. Read that as a progress bar for the talk rather than a measurement; nobody's cluster is ever 100% secure.

## Default deny first, then open what you need

The most actionable step sits at level two. Set a Calico global policy of default deny for all incoming traffic, then add network policies that allow each pod to reach only its corresponding services. Istio (available as an add-on on AKS) handles encrypting the pod-to-pod communication through its sidecar. That one pattern turns any-pod-can-call-the-key-vault into an explicit allow list.

At the container level the advice is the boring kind that works: small base images, scan them in the registry, sign them, and watch them at runtime. At the application level, secrets live in Key Vault, Secrets Manager or Vault, not in the repo.

## What comes after level five?

Two extras: AIOps for proactive threat detection and automated remediation, and zero trust, "never trust, but always verify", applied as granular access control. Observability tools such as Grafana sit across all five layers to catch vulnerability alerts in real time.

His closing line is the one to keep: "securing Kubernetes is not a one size fits all solution." You pick the tools by cloud provider or go open source; the point is that every layer has an owner.

## Who should watch

Teams putting their first services on AKS or EKS, and managers who need a one-page picture of where Kubernetes security controls live and which product covers each. If you already run default-deny network policies and signed images, you will find it a familiar checklist.

Title: AI coding assistants are only as good as the context you feed them
Description: Kartheek Medhavi Penagamuri Shriram (Microsoft) at Conf42 IoT 2024 on getting more out of AI coding assistants by sharing repo and package context
Body:
An AI coding assistant that can't see your dependencies is guessing which version of your framework you run. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Kartheek Medhavi Penagamuri Shriram, Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft, made the case that tools like GitHub Copilot and Cursor pay off once you give them your repository, your packages and clean code to read, and that the developer still owns every line they accept.

Fair warning on scope: despite the IoT conference, this is a general talk on AI-assisted development, and an overview rather than a hands-on demo. It is a tidy map of where these tools help, where they bite, and which skills shift as a result.

## Where does a developer's week actually go?

The starting point is a familiar one. Frameworks multiply, budgets and headcount don't, and a big slice of the day goes to cleaning up rather than building. Kartheek put that slice at nearly 30% of developer time spent on debugging, tech debt and fixing errors. Manual code reviews help, but they miss subtle edge cases and need people to line up their calendars, and without real-time help you are back in the documentation tabs.

His list of assistants is the usual cast: GitHub Copilot, IntelliCode, Tabnine, Kite and, most recently, Cursor. What they offer is completions, early bug and code-smell detection while you type, and refactoring suggestions such as a newer library call that replaces a hand-rolled loop. On the payoff he cited a GitHub Copilot pilot where productivity rose by up to 50%.

## Why does context matter more than the model?

This is the most practical part of the talk. Modern assistants can share repository context with the underlying large language model, and that changes the quality of what comes back. Kartheek's concrete advice:

- **Hook the assistant into your package manager.** With NuGet or npm dependencies visible, suggestions match the libraries and versions you actually use, not whatever was most common in the training data.
- **Know what's under the hood.** Embeddings let the model work on the meaning of your code, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pulls in your own classes, functions and docs, so suggestions follow project patterns.
- **Write code a model can read.** Clear comments, clean code and a consistent style are context too. Share relevant files with the assistant, inside your privacy and security rules.

"Optimizing AI coding tools is not just about using them, it's about integrating them thoughtfully into our development process to maximize their benefits," Kartheek Medhavi Penagamuri Shriram said at Conf42 IoT 2024.

## What do the tools do outside the IDE demo?

He walks through examples by industry: generating boilerplate such as REST endpoints and authentication flows, suggesting faster SQL and data pipelines, fast iteration on rule-based fraud detection in fintech, HIPAA-compliant data integrations in healthcare, and quicker prototyping of game mechanics and rendering optimisations in gaming.

Looking ahead, he expects AI to generate test cases for edge cases, run CI/CD pipelines from historical build data (predicting failures, triggering rollbacks), estimate task timelines, and assist human code reviewers rather than replace them.

## What can go wrong?

The ethics section is more grounded than most. Models learn from existing code, so they can suggest less secure practices or non-inclusive naming; the fix is diverse training data plus regular audits of the output. Developers may merge generated code they don't understand, which is how vulnerabilities sneak in, so review it like any other pull request. And sending proprietary code to an AI service is a data-privacy question: on-premises options and strict access controls are part of the answer.

## Which skills change?

Kartheek's list: learn the tools properly (configuring them, sharing project context, knowing when to reject a suggestion), get good at prompting, and move your time from boilerplate to architecture, algorithms and user experience. He frames the assistant as a collaborator, not a replacement.

## Who should watch

Teams starting to roll out Copilot-style tools who want a checklist of benefits, context tricks and risks to brief their developers with. If you already run RAG over your monorepo and audit generated code, you will recognise most of it.

Title: Self-driving cars react in 10 ms, regulation and security take years
Description: Spandana Sagam (General Motors) and Govardhan Reddy Kothinti (Aptiv) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on what autonomous vehicles promise and what blocks them
Body:
A human driver needs about 250 milliseconds to react; an autonomous vehicle needs about 10. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Spandana Sagam, Senior HIL Development Engineer for autonomous and automated driving at General Motors, and Govardhan Reddy Kothinti, Functional Safety Manager at Aptiv, give a two-part overview of autonomous vehicles (AVs): what they could do for safety, cities and logistics, and the regulatory, cybersecurity and social problems that decide how fast any of it arrives.

It is a short, high-level talk for a general audience, not an engineering deep look at sensor fusion or safety cases. Sagam covers the benefits, Kothinti the challenges.

## What makes the safety case?

Sagam starts with the technology: AI, machine learning and sensor fusion giving the vehicle a 360-degree view and real-time decisions. The sensor stack lists LIDAR for 3D mapping, radar for detection in any weather, cameras for object recognition and ultrasonic sensors for close range, with automation graded from level 0 (none) to level 5 (full).

The safety argument rests on one figure: human error contributes to 94% of serious traffic crashes, by NHTSA's count. A machine that brakes or steers around an obstacle in milliseconds, keeps watching all the time and follows traffic rules consistently removes much of that. The 10 ms versus 250 ms comparison is the headline number.

## What would it do to cities and freight?

The urban argument is about ownership. Spandana Sagam said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "AV can be used as a shared fleet, reducing the number of cars on the roads." Fewer private cars means less parking, and she cites a potential drop in parking from 14% to 5% of urban land, space that could become parks and pedestrian zones. She also lists less congestion, better links with public transport and more independence for elderly and disabled people.

For logistics, the point is hours. Autonomous trucks can run 24/7, where human drivers are limited by regulation. Add fewer human errors, better fuel efficiency and AI route optimisation for predictable delivery times, plus drones for last-mile deliveries.

## What stands in the way?

Kothinti, who has spent more than 18 years on safety-critical embedded, avionics and autonomous systems, takes the second half, and it is the part closest to this conference's subject.

**Regulation.** Testing rules are currently state by state. He argues for global frameworks that settle safety, liability and insurance, and that evolve with the technology.

**Cybersecurity.** Govardhan Reddy Kothinti said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "These vehicles are interconnected with cloud based systems and communicate with the surrounding infrastructure." Every one of those links is an attack surface, and an attack on an AV can reach vehicle control. His minimum: strong encryption and intrusion detection. A security engineer would want threat models and update chains here, and the talk stays at the level of naming the risk.

**Infrastructure.** Smart roads, high-precision GPS and 5G networks all need significant investment before AVs can run safely at scale.

**Environment.** Electric autonomous vehicles have no tailpipe emissions, and optimised driving and less congestion could cut energy use by up to 60%. The slides also list the counterweights: more vehicle miles travelled and the energy demand of the AV technology itself.

**Ethics and society.** The trolley problem, how an AV chooses in an unavoidable crash, is still open. The vehicles collect large amounts of location, behaviour and environment data, which must be protected to keep public trust. Benefits should reach underserved and rural communities, not only rich city centres. And jobs that depend on human drivers will shrink, so he calls for retraining programmes.

## Who should watch?

Engineers curious about AVs who want the whole picture in one sitting, and security folks looking for a reminder of how connected vehicles widen the attack surface. If you want the details of an automotive security architecture or a functional safety process, this talk only sets the scene.

Title: Two withdrawals, one balance - the race condition that drained a wallet
Description: Paul Edward (Compado) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on the wallet race condition that let attackers withdraw the same money twice, and the locks that stop it
Body:
A wallet endpoint can check the balance, check the wallet exists, deduct, save and still hand out money it doesn't have. Paul Edward, Senior Fullstack Engineer at Compado, used his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk to tell the story of a race condition in a financial app's withdrawal flow that attackers turned into a loss of over 70 million, then reproduced the bug live and fixed it with a database transaction and a row lock.

It is a short, practical talk with a live demo. If you have ever written read-balance, check, subtract, save without a lock, it is aimed at you.

## What actually went wrong?

The setup is the classic one. A user has 1,000 in their wallet. An attacker fires two withdrawal requests at exactly the same moment. Each request reads the balance, sees 1,000, passes the sufficiency check and writes its deduction. Both are approved, and the same money leaves twice. Multiply by hundreds of transactions and you have the incident.

"So it is like your code is running just too fast for his own good," Paul Edward said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024. His point is that this is not a language problem: Java, Python and SQL databases are all just as exposed if nobody serialises access to the record.

He puts it next to some expensive company: Knight Capital losing $440 million in 45 minutes in 2012, the $40 million-plus NASDAQ paid out after the Facebook IPO glitches, and GTBank's October 2024 upgrade that brought two weeks of transaction failures.

## The demo: ten requests, a thousand out of five hundred

The best part is the live reproduction. A Laravel (PHP) wallet controller has a `withdraw` method that does everything a code reviewer would nod at: find the wallet, throw if it is missing, throw on insufficient balance, deduct, update the record, return success.

A single request from a small Python script behaves: 600 becomes 500. Then the script sends ten concurrent requests for 100 each against that 500 balance. All ten succeed, a thousand goes out, and the endpoint still reports a balance of 100. As he summed it up: "I have cheated the system."

His suggestion is blunt and worth taking: run a script like that against your own withdrawal or redemption endpoints. The results "might be very shocking to you."

## How do you fix a race condition in a wallet?

The second method, `withdrawFix`, takes the same payload and changes three things:

- It opens a database transaction (Laravel has this built in), so any failure rolls back everything before it.
- It reads the wallet with a lock for update, so a second request waits until the first one is done with the row.
- It checks the balance inside the transaction, rolls back on insufficient funds, and commits only after the deduction.

Same ten concurrent requests against 500: the balance steps down 400, 300, 200, 100, 0, and the rest get "insufficient balance".

The wider list from the incident response: disable the vulnerable feature and patch first, then redesign the transaction flow, add locking (distributed locks where you have more than one database), make API operations idempotent, add monitoring and anomaly detection so small irregularities alert, and bring in double-entry accounting so every debit has a matching credit. The investigation itself was log review plus reproducing the bug in a controlled environment; the key finding was missing synchronisation in database transactions.

## Treat every bug like a breach

The lessons slide is short. Small flaws have big consequences. Test concurrency under load, not just the happy path, and review code asking what happens when two people press the same button at once. Monitoring would have caught it earlier, and they hadn't built it yet. "Treat every bug like it could be your next big breach," he said, and repeated it for the people in the back.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers on payments, wallets, credits, coupons or inventory, and anyone reviewing that code. Seniors who already reach for `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` by reflex can skip to the demo; it is still a good one to send a junior.

Title: AI fraud detection cuts false positives by 60%, and regulators are catching up
Description: Sudeep Meduri (Google) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on AI across fintech, from fraud detection and robo-advisors to compliance and bias
Body:
Rules-based fraud detection is rigid, slow to adapt, and wrong often enough to annoy the customers it protects. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Sudeep Meduri, Senior Software Engineer at Google, surveys how AI has changed financial services, starting with fraud detection, where he cites a 60% drop in false positives and a 50% rise in true positives, then moving through personalisation, algorithmic trading, compliance, and the regulation that is coming for all of it.

It is a broad survey talk with well-known industry examples, not a system walkthrough. Despite the title, IoT barely appears; the subject is AI in fintech.

## Why does fraud detection come first?

Because it is where AI made the clearest gains. Traditional systems relied on fixed rules; ML models find anomalies in huge volumes of transactions and keep learning as fraudsters change tactics. His slides add that models track over 100 behavioural patterns in real time. The result he reports: false positives down by over 60%, true positives up by almost 50%. Fewer false alarms means fewer legitimate customers getting their card blocked at the till, which is what builds trust in digital finance.

His best-known example is about documents rather than fraud: JPMorgan's COiN system reviews 12,000 commercial loan agreements in seconds, work that had taken 360,000 hours.

## Personal finance at robo-advisor prices

The personalisation section is about scale. By analysing spending habits, income patterns and financial goals, AI tailors banking advice to each customer. Robo-advisors such as Wealthfront and Betterment offer portfolio management that used to be reserved for high-net-worth clients at a much lower cost, and ML can build portfolios around individual risk appetite and ESG preferences. Bank of America's Erica is his example of a digital assistant that guides users through complex tasks.

## Trading in milliseconds

In markets "where even milliseconds matter," as Meduri says, deep learning models forecast trends from historical prices, volumes and news feeds, and execution algorithms read liquidity and the order book to minimise cost and market impact. Citadel is his example of a firm that invested heavily in AI for its edge.

## Compliance is the sleeper use case

The section most relevant to engineering teams is RegTech. "AI powered compliance tech solutions can automate a lot of the data collection, processing, and analysis tasks, reducing manual effort and also errors," Sudeep Meduri said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. ML models track rule changes across jurisdictions and interpret what they mean, and predictive analytics flags compliance risks before they turn into findings. Back-office NLP pulls key fields out of unstructured financial documents, and chatbots take the 24/7 queries.

## What could go wrong?

Meduri gives the risks real space:

- **Privacy and security**: GDPR and similar rules, plus the cybersecurity needed to keep customer trust.
- **Algorithmic bias**: unfair outcomes in credit approvals and loan decisions, which need diverse training data and regular audits.
- **Explainability**: models have to justify decisions to users and to regulators.

On regulation he expects algorithmic accountability to become a mandate, so institutions must explain how AI decided; stricter data privacy rules for financial data; tighter data localisation laws that keep data inside national borders; and ethical guidelines on top. Regulators, he notes, face the hard job of keeping pace with the technology without killing innovation.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into fintech who want a one-sitting map of where AI is used and which regulatory pressures will shape their designs. People already building fraud or trading systems will know the examples; the regulatory outlook is the part worth their time.

Title: A quick map of deep learning's three frontiers, from AlphaGo to anomaly detection
Description: Chirag Gajiwala (Nutanix) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on deep reinforcement learning, GANs, VAEs and what they mean for security
Body:
Deep learning moved on three fronts at once: agents that learn by trial and error, models that generate data, and detectors that spot what doesn't fit. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Chirag Gajiwala, Member of Technical Staff at Nutanix, who works on AI/ML in cybersecurity, gives a fast primer on all three, deep reinforcement learning, GANs and VAEs, and on where they point for security teams.

It is an overview for people who know the acronyms and want the map: short, conceptual, and with no code or demo. The figures below come from the literature he cites, not from his own systems.

## What is deep reinforcement learning, in one paragraph?

An agent interacts with an environment, makes mistakes, and adjusts to maximise reward. Pair that with deep neural networks and it can handle huge state spaces. Gajiwala's milestones make the progress concrete: AlphaGo beating Lee Sedol in 2016, UC Berkeley's robotic grasping reaching a 43% success rate after 800 attempts in 2018, and Waymo's self-driving cars logging 35 billion simulated and 20 million real-world miles by 2023.

The technique he singles out is transfer learning: an agent reuses knowledge from one task on another, which cuts training time and the amount of data needed. That is how a driving model takes what it learnt in simulation onto real roads, how a robot generalises grasping across object shapes, and how game AI carries strategy from one game to the next. "So this is where reinforcement learning is a boon," Chirag Gajiwala said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

## GANs versus VAEs: which does what?

The clearest part of the talk separates the two generative families.

**GANs** pit a generator against a discriminator until the fakes are good enough to fool it. The applications he lists, with the cited figures:

- Image generation: StyleGAN2 producing photorealistic images at an FID of 2.84.
- Video synthesis: NVIDIA's vid2vid at 2048x1024 and 30 fps.
- Medical data augmentation: a 7% improvement in imaging classification accuracy.
- Drug discovery: generated drug-like molecules with a 39% success rate.

**VAEs** encode data into a latent space and reconstruct it, learning compact representations on the way. Their best uses are less flashy and more useful to an operator:

- Dimensionality reduction: gene data compressed by 98% while keeping 95% of the information.
- Anomaly detection: 96% accuracy in cybersecurity tasks at a 0.1% false positive rate.
- Music generation: coherent 16-bar melodies, with 75% of listeners satisfied.

The distinction he draws is worth keeping: GANs are for making realistic data, VAEs are for understanding the shape of normal data, which is exactly what you need to notice abnormal data.

## Where does this land in cybersecurity?

Gajiwala's own field gets the forward-looking treatment. AI for real-time threat detection and anomaly analysis, automated vulnerability assessment and patching, and fraud detection through pattern recognition. His view is that current tools miss a lot of threats, and that models built on GANs and VAEs will increasingly carry detection, threat modelling and risk identification, including DDoS detection. The flip side, noted on his slides: attackers use AI too, so adversarial AI is the challenge that comes with the territory.

## What comes next?

His trend list: graph neural networks for graph-shaped data such as social networks, recommendation systems (the Netflix and Amazon Prime kind) and drug discovery; multimodal models that handle text, images, audio and video together; AI on edge devices for IoT and autonomous systems, the one nod to the event's theme; and more focus on explainable, accountable AI.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers who need a fast refresher on how RL, GANs and VAEs differ before a security or ML planning conversation. Practitioners already working with these models will find nothing new; there is no implementation detail or evaluation of a real system.

Title: Design your outages like a dimmer, not a light switch
Description: Abhishek Vajarekar at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on designing for failure, from failover and fail-open choices to graceful shutdown and circuit breakers
Body:
It's Black Friday, and the payment component goes down. Does the whole store go with it, or do shoppers keep browsing while payments retry in the background? At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Abhishek Vajarekar, Software Development Manager, works through the seven patterns that decide which of those two headlines you get: redundancy, failover, graceful degradation, graceful shutdown, chaos engineering, circuit breakers and automated recovery.

His starting point: "The question is not if your system will fail, but when, how, and what happens next." The talk is a well-organised survey rather than one company's war story, with each pattern paired with the trap that comes with it.

## Redundancy and failover, the expensive basics

Redundancy comes in three layers: infrastructure (multiple data centres or availability zones), data (replication, synchronous for consistency-critical writes, asynchronous where a little lag is acceptable) and service (several instances behind a load balancer with health checks). It costs money, and he is frank that the job is matching it to risk tolerance, for example hot backups for systems that must take over instantly and cheaper cold backups for those that can wait.

Failover is the switch to those backups. Automatic failover, such as promoting a database replica when the primary dies, is fast but needs careful configuration and testing. Manual failover gives control but is slower and error-prone under pressure. DNS failover can be either, and he flags its catch: propagation delays, which you reduce with low TTLs. Other traps on his list: data inconsistency during the switch, false positives that fail over a healthy primary, and failover paths nobody has tested.

## Fail open or fail closed?

This is the most useful section. Abhishek Vajarekar said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "Think of it as a dimmer switch rather than an on off button." Graceful degradation keeps core functions running and turns off the extras: a streaming service drops to standard definition, a shop shows the catalogue without personalised recommendations.

Then the decision every component needs before the incident, not during it. Fail open, and the system carries on degraded: a ride-sharing app keeps booking rides with default or cached prices when the pricing engine is down. Fail closed, and the system stops: a bank halts payments when fraud detection fails. Non-critical features should usually fail open, sensitive ones closed. He adds that users accept limits when you tell them clearly what is broken and what still works, and that degraded modes need their own testing because they are rarely exercised.

## Shutting down without dropping anything

Graceful shutdown gets more attention than usual here. The techniques are connection draining (finish active requests, refuse new ones), health check signalling (in Kubernetes, fail the readiness probe so the load balancer stops sending traffic to the pod), state persistence (a messaging service writes unsent messages to a queue before exiting), and timeouts and grace periods set from real request durations. His payment example shows why: a sloppy shutdown can charge customers twice, or not at all.

## Chaos engineering and circuit breakers

Chaos engineering is the fire drill: inject failures on purpose (terminate services, partition the network, exhaust CPU or memory) in controlled experiments, and measure mean time to recovery, error rate and user impact. Start in staging or on non-critical components, limit the blast radius in production, invest in observability first, and use tools such as Chaos Mesh to scale it.

Circuit breakers stop one slow dependency from taking everything down. Closed lets traffic through while counting failures; open blocks calls after a threshold; half-open lets a few test requests through after a cooldown. His practical notes: set thresholds from historical data, use rolling windows so a short spike doesn't trip the breaker, pair breakers with retries and exponential backoff, and always have a fallback, because a breaker with no fallback leaves users with nothing.

## Letting the system heal itself

Automated recovery covers autoscaling (which also replaces unhealthy instances), self-healing through Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes, and automatic rollback when a release pushes error rates up. Two failure modes to design against: health checks so sensitive they restart healthy pods, and recovery loops that restart the same component forever. Check whether the service actually processes requests rather than just CPU, and limit restarts before escalating to a human.

## Who should watch?

Engineers who want a single, structured checklist of resilience patterns, and leads preparing a design review. Seasoned SREs will know the patterns; the fail-open versus fail-closed framing and the shutdown section are the ones to share with the team.

Title: A fintech support team went from 14 people to 3, and the bot works nights
Description: Andrei Alekseev (Weltrade) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on where AI already runs fintech, from support and fraud to trading signals
Body:
When AI arrived in one fintech support department, the team went from 14 people to 3. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Andrei Alekseev, CMO at Weltrade, tours the places AI already does real work at brokers and crypto companies: support bots, fraud and AML checks, AI-generated marketing, and trading signals for nervous first-time traders. His examples come from companies he has worked at or talked to, which makes this a field report rather than a forecast.

It is a marketer's view of fintech, with 20 years in marketing, 14 of them in the industry. There is nothing on IoT despite the event, and no code, but plenty of specifics.

## What happened to the support team?

At a crypto startup, his team was among the first to try Intercom's built-in AI feature, in two ways. First, a bot in the online chat that solved the most common problems rather than just answering questions: finding a transaction on the blockchain, or checking verification status at the KYC stage. That cut incoming requests straight away.

Second, they connected the AI agent to the live support conversations so it could learn from them. After a couple of weeks they let it run on its own, but only on night shifts, when live agents were short. It did well, and the department now has three people instead of 14. His case for it is blunt: faster, more accurate, not subject to moods, and it "can work 24 seven without salary," Andrei Alekseev said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

A smaller idea worth copying: a Telegram bot that collected the last 24 hours of reviews from Trustpilot, the App Store and Google Play, translated them, and sent him a summary at 9 a.m. every day.

## Fraud, AML and the dealing desk

The infrastructure section is the most interesting for engineers. Sanctions screening and transaction checks, including crypto wallet addresses, used to be bought from vendors at several thousand dollars a month; he says you can now build it yourself. At his current company, AI watches the dealing side for suspicious trading, price manipulation and bonus fraud, for example very similar trades from the same location and IP address on different devices. It also helps dealers manage liquidity and the order book, and deal with price slippage.

## Content made by machines

He reports that eToro's marketing director told him almost all of the site's text, images and translations are made with AI, and that the brand's Olympic Games campaign was 95% AI-made. Rootstocklab's website content and its campaign for Bitcoin's birthday are his second example.

## Trading signals for first-timers

At Libertex, where he worked for six and a half years, a trading academy of 12 people produced ideas, strategies, digests and quarterly reports. After training a model for a long time, the academy became Libertex Lab, and two people remain, working with prompts. The new-user problem it solves is fear of the first trade: which direction to open, long or short. Trading signals let a newcomer open several deals in one click.

His favourite example is Walbi, a trading platform built around AI from the start. Traders pick one of five AI assistants, called buddies, matched to assets, risk tolerance and strategy. Each buddy watches news, social media and charts, and pushes a signal you can accept in one click. If Elon Musk posts something nice about Dogecoin, the buddy says buy.

He finishes with Bloomberg and Reuters using AI to scan weather and disaster news for threats to crops such as coffee, cocoa and wheat, and drafting analysis for a human to act on.

## Who should watch

Product and growth people at brokers, exchanges and payment companies who want concrete examples of where AI has taken over real jobs. Engineers will get the most from the fraud and dealing section. Treat the forecast accuracy claims as anecdotes; no data is shown.

Title: Take authorization out of your services and put it in a sidecar
Description: Graziano Casto (Mia-Platform) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on policy-as-code RBAC with Open Policy Agent, Rego and the Rönd sidecar
Body:
Every microservice that carries its own copy of the permission check is a future inconsistency. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Graziano Casto, Developer Relations Engineer at Mia-Platform, shows how to pull authorization out of service code in two steps: first into Open Policy Agent and Rego, then into Rönd, an open-source Kubernetes sidecar created at Mia-Platform that enforces Rego policies in front of your APIs without touching the services themselves.

Rönd is his company's project, and he says so up front. The access-control half of the talk is useful on its own.

## Roles or attributes?

He starts by widening the word policy. A policy is a set of rules that describe what must hold in a system, and authorization is just one kind. Graziano Casto said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 that "even rules like the age limit for purchasing alcohol can, in a way, be considered a policy."

His running example is an internal developer platform. Senior developers can read project configuration, commit and deploy. Junior developers can read and commit but not deploy. Platform administrators can do all of that and create projects. Assigning those permissions user by user gets messy fast, so you group them into roles: role-based access control (RBAC). The alternative, attribute-based access control (ABAC), decides on attributes of the user and the resource. RBAC is simple but coarse, and teams that need detail end up adding roles until they have hundreds. ABAC is granular but takes time and expertise to set up correctly.

His recommendation is a hybrid: roles for the high-level rules, attributes for the exceptions. Give users project and environment attributes, and a senior developer can deploy, but only to their own projects. A junior developer has no deploy permission in their role, yet an environment attribute for non-production lets them deploy to dev for their own projects. Plain RBAC cannot express that without inventing a new role.

## Why not keep the checks in the code?

Because it only works while the system is small. Enforcement code next to business logic is fast to write and easy to find. But the same rule gets copied into every service that needs it, a rule change means a code change even when the business logic didn't change, and at scale nobody can see all the rules in one place.

Policy-as-code moves the rules into their own repository, written in code, and puts an agent between users and APIs to enforce them. You get transparency, fewer manual configuration mistakes and policies you can test automatically. The agent is Open Policy Agent (OPA), a CNCF graduated project, with policies written in Rego. His sample policy allows a POST to an order route only when the store in the request body matches the store assigned to the user. The user's role comes from decoding the JWT in the request header, and the request is authorized if any of the policy's `allow` blocks returns true.

## Where does Rönd come in?

OPA still runs as a service your application calls over REST or through an SDK, so a little coupling remains. Rönd removes it. It is a lightweight sidecar container that uses OPA and Rego underneath and adds roles, permissions and user groups as building blocks, so RBAC comes out of the box.

Configuration lives in your OpenAPI files. You add an `x-rond` property to each route and HTTP verb you want to protect, with the name of the Rego policy to apply. Two further features go beyond allow or deny:

- **Query generation**: a policy filters the response dataset before it reaches the client.
- **Response policies**: a policy runs after the API call and changes the response schema, so power users get the full customer payload from the same endpoint where less privileged users get it without sensitive fields.

## Does it hold up at scale?

Mia-Platform built Rönd to handle authorization for its own IDP, and also offers it for customer workloads on the platform. The figures he shows: more than 30 microservices, more than 500 policies, more than 300 routes. Because it is a sidecar configured from OpenAPI specs, it can be added to an existing application without changing the services. It also exposes metrics for how often each policy runs, how long evaluation takes, and the sidecar's resource use.

## Who should watch?

Backend and platform engineers with authorization logic scattered across services, and anyone choosing between RBAC and ABAC. If you already run OPA, the Rönd section shows a way to stop calling it from your code.

Title: DevOps is 60% culture, so security has to ride along at every step
Description: Peter De Tender (Microsoft) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on shifting security left in Azure DevOps and GitHub, from branch policies to Key Vault
Body:
A learner once screen-recorded one of Peter De Tender's DevOps workshops, spotted the Azure DevOps personal access token he created on screen, and pushed it to their own GitHub repo. GitHub flagged it within minutes. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, De Tender, Azure Technical Trainer at Microsoft, uses stories like that to walk through shifting security left across the whole DevOps cycle, with demos in Azure DevOps, GitHub, Azure Key Vault and Microsoft Defender for Cloud.

It is a Microsoft-stack talk by design, but most of the advice ports to any platform.

## What does he mean by DevOps?

He gives the Microsoft definition (the union of people, process and products to deliver value continuously to end users) and then his own: integrating the culture of delivering value to the end user, relying on team collaboration and workload automation. The split matters to him. Peter De Tender said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "DevOps is 60 percent related to the culture." The other 40% is tooling, and teams that install every tool without collaborating are, in his words, not really doing DevOps.

His cycle is develop, validate, package, run and operate. DevSecOps keeps the same cycle and squeezes security into every stage, instead of the traditional pattern of securing only the runtime, which is where attacks land and where fixing them is slowest and most expensive. Shifting left, for him, does not mean only at the start: security comes back at every step.

## What changes at each stage?

- **Develop**: threat modelling, linting and code scanning, credentials kept out of source code, and peer review.
- **Validate**: code analysis again, secret management, pull requests with required approvals, unit tests and container vulnerability scanning.
- **Package and release**: secure infrastructure as code (Bicep, ARM, Terraform, CloudFormation), container scanning and release quality gates.
- **Run and operate**: role-based access control on the platform, secrets in Key Vault rather than app settings, and a security posture view with Defender for Cloud, plus a SIEM such as Microsoft Sentinel for incidents.

## What do the demos cover?

**Permissions and repos.** Azure DevOps projects have their own permission model, so a project manager sees boards without code access. He prefers a multi-repo layout, with application code in one repository and the ARM-to-Bicep infrastructure in another, so a web developer gets access to the app repo and never sees the infrastructure, and vice versa.

**Branch policies.** Editing `main` directly works and is exactly the problem. Branch policies require a minimum number of reviewers, from a named group, before a pull request can merge.

**Scanning.** An Azure DevOps pipeline with a scanning task reports outdated packages and known vulnerabilities. The Visual Studio Marketplace lists third-party options; he names Aqua, Snyk and the built-in scanner, and later Sonar in the build with SonarCloud results checked again as a pre-deployment quality gate. On GitHub, code scanning is built in for public and private repos, and Dependabot can open the version bump that fixes a vulnerable dependency.

**Secret scanning.** That is where the leaked-token story fits. GitHub recognised the token as belonging to an Azure DevOps organisation and notified him, and he stresses this came from GitHub's standard secret detection, not his Microsoft badge.

**Key Vault.** Pipeline variable groups can encrypt secrets, or link to Key Vault, with a catch: enabling the link clears the existing variables, so you need a separate library for Key Vault secrets. For apps, he shows the progression from secrets in code, to secrets in Azure app settings, to app settings that only reference a Key Vault secret, with access policies giving the function app get rights only. Key rotation, manual or scripted through Azure Automation, closes the loop, because the app points at the Key Vault object rather than its content.

**Defender for Cloud.** Even the free tier gives a secure score and recommendations: scan this container image, disable public access on this storage account. Its DevOps security view pulls in the state of Azure DevOps and GitHub repos, so the security team sees the same Dependabot and CodeQL findings the developers do.

## Who should watch?

Teams on Azure DevOps or GitHub who want a tour of what is already in the box before buying more tools, and trainers looking for a sensible order to teach DevSecOps in. At about 45 minutes, most of it demos, it rewards watching with a browser tab open on your own project.

Title: AI call routing takes first-contact resolution from 45% to 80%
Description: Naga Praneeth Yerram (Informatica) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on AI in unified communications, from call routing to transcription
Body:
The fastest way to make a support call worse is to send it to the wrong person. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Naga Praneeth Yerram, Unified Communications Engineer at Informatica, walks through what AI adds to unified communications (UC): routing calls by customer data, real-time speech recognition and automated transcription. The comparison he shows has first-contact resolution rising from 45% to 80% once the routing gets smart.

The talk is co-authored with Vaishnav Yerram, Senior Operations Manager at KIK IT; Naga Praneeth Yerram presents it. It is a short overview, more of a map of the territory than a build guide, and the IoT link in the title stays at the level of remote equipment monitoring.

## What does AI add to UC?

UC is the stack that puts voice, video, messaging and collaboration on one platform. "AI takes UC to the next level by introducing intelligent automation, real time analytics, and data driven decision making," Naga Praneeth Yerram said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

He names three features that carry most of the value:

- **Intelligent call routing**: use what you know about the customer to match them with the best available agent, which is what moves first-contact resolution.
- **Speech recognition and transcription**: deep learning models that keep up with complex, real conversations and turn them into documentation without anyone typing.
- **Predictive analytics**: anticipate what the user needs and automate the response before they ask.

Together he credits these with a 40% improvement in system efficiency and a 60% increase in customer satisfaction.

## The before-and-after table

The most concrete part of the talk is a comparison of traditional and AI-enhanced UC systems:

| Metric | Traditional | AI-enhanced |
|---|---|---|
| First-contact resolution | 45% | 80% |
| Average response time | 15 min | 9 min |
| Customer satisfaction | 65% | 85% |
| Call routing accuracy | 70% | 95% |

Transcription accuracy goes from 85% to 98%. The talk doesn't say where the figures come from, so read them as the case for the technology rather than a benchmark you can reproduce.

## Where does it apply?

Per sector: HIPAA-compliant transcription for patient documentation in healthcare, compliance monitoring and secure communication in financial services, supply chain communication and remote equipment monitoring in manufacturing, and AI-driven call management for customer engagement in retail.

## What gets in the way, and how to roll it out

The challenges are the familiar three: integrating AI with legacy communication infrastructure, users resisting new tools, and finding time and budget for implementation, training and maintenance.

His deployment advice is sensible and transferable:

1. **Phased implementation**: start with a pilot and scale on feedback and performance.
2. **Training**: role-specific modules, plus ongoing support and refresher sessions.
3. **Data management**: a structured data governance framework and privacy-first design, which matters when every call becomes a transcript.
4. **Change management**: involve stakeholders early, communicate clearly and measure success.

Looking ahead, he expects virtual assistants with emotional intelligence that handle scheduling and project coordination, and cites a 38.4% CAGR for AI-enhanced UC through 2028, driven by hybrid and remote work.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers who run a contact centre or a collaboration platform and want a quick checklist of where AI fits and how to introduce it without a revolt. If you need architecture or vendor comparisons, look elsewhere.

Title: The fastest language is not the greenest, and idle servers are the reason
Description: Clifton Reddy (American National) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on measuring software carbon with SCI and cutting idle waste with serverless, Wasm and GraalVM
Body:
Rewriting everything in C will not save the planet if the server spends the rest of the hour idling at 60% of peak power. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Clifton Reddy, Web Consultant and Manager at American National, argues for treating carbon like any other architectural concern, next to performance, security and cost, and walks through how to measure it with the Green Software Foundation's Software Carbon Intensity specification and where the real waste sits.

His framing device: code red means a security problem, so code green should mean a carbon one.

## How do you put a number on software carbon?

Reddy starts with a map of grid carbon intensity, the greenhouse gas emitted per unit of electricity, and points at Electricity Maps for real-time data. If you run workloads in several clouds and regions, he suggests a pet project: check how much the same job emits depending on where and when it runs.

For the software itself he uses SCI, the Green Software Foundation's Software Carbon Intensity specification, which is also an ISO standard. SCI is carbon per functional unit: ((E × L) + M) / R, where E is the energy the software consumes, L the location-based marginal carbon intensity of the grid, M the embodied emissions of the hardware, and R the functional unit, such as one API call or one batch job. The functional unit is the useful bit. It turns a vague claim of being green into a number you can track per request, and compare between releases.

He is in the leadership group of a Green Software Foundation chapter, and lists the foundation's Impact Framework and Carbon Aware SDK among the tools to measure with.

## Is the fastest language the most efficient?

He leans on a research paper that ran the same benchmarks across many languages on the same hardware and measured energy with Intel's RAPL (Running Average Power Limit). He picks two benchmarks: binary-trees, where C used the least energy, and regex-redux, where TypeScript did. No single language wins everything.

Then the twist: even fast code doesn't help if the machine idles afterwards. He cites the PowerNap research, which found typical server utilisation below 30% while idle servers still draw 60% of their peak power. Containers don't automatically fix it either; a CAST AI study found that only 13% of provisioned CPUs and 20% of memory are actually used in cloud computing. Clifton Reddy said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "The fastest language is not always the most energy efficient."

## So where does the waste go?

Into idle capacity. His answer is resource density, packing more useful compute into the same power and cooling, and he walks through three ways to get it:

- **Serverless**: functions scale with demand, terminate when done and run in micro VMs or containers packed densely on shared hardware. The catch is cold starts, functions that are rarely invoked but kept running, vendor lock-in and weak local development and CI/CD support.
- **WebAssembly with WASI**: a portable binary format that runs at near-native speed in a sandbox, with WASI giving it standard access to files, network and time outside the browser. He compares a Wasm app starting in 52 milliseconds with 250 milliseconds for an AWS serverless function, says Wasm has no concept of a cold start, and quotes Docker founder Solomon Hykes saying that Docker would not have been needed if Wasm and WASI had existed in 2008.
- **GraalVM**: ahead-of-time compilation of Java into native executables that start instantly, skip JIT warm-up and use less CPU and memory.

## What can a DevOps team change on Monday?

The operations list is practical. Monitor resource use constantly. Schedule builds and deploys for the hours when your cloud provider's grid is greener. Track and report emissions automatically. Use autoscaling and load balancing to stop over-provisioning. Consider a provider with renewable energy and efficient data centres. And his best idea: check the SCI score during build and deploy and suggest changes when it rises, the same way a pipeline fails on a test coverage drop.

He closes honestly: no language, runtime or operational style gets you to zero carbon. A combination of them gets the number down.

## Who should watch?

Engineers and managers who want a starting point on green software that goes beyond turning off unused instances, and anyone looking for a measurement model to put in a pipeline. The SCI formula and the idle-power numbers are the parts to take away.

Title: From a $70 Raspberry Pi AI Kit to Iceberg tables, all on open source
Description: Tim Spann (Zilliz) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on building IoT apps with Raspberry Pi, MQTT, Kafka, Apache NiFi 2 and Flink SQL
Body:
A Raspberry Pi with a 13 TOPS AI accelerator costs about $70 now, which makes edge AI a hobby budget item. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Tim Spann, Principal Developer Advocate at Zilliz, tours the open source stack he uses to get IoT data from that kind of device into a cloud data lake: MQTT and Kafka for transport, Apache NiFi 2 for routing and provenance, Flink SQL for streaming analytics, and Apache Iceberg at the end. Then he runs it live, waving at a pose-estimation camera.

It is a sampler, as Spann says up front: lots of devices, lots of options, links to his back catalogue for depth. If you have seen his earlier Conf42 talks, this is the 2024 hardware refresh.

## How much compute fits at the edge now?

The device section is a quick benchmark tour. The Raspberry Pi 5 with 8 GB of RAM plus the AI Kit's Hailo-8L module gives you 13 TOPS; the newer AI Kit+ doubles that to 26. Spann remembers when a powerful NVIDIA device gave you 10. At the top end, NVIDIA's Jetson AGX Orin offers 275 TOPS, 2,048 cores and 64 GB of RAM; his old Jetson Xavier NX manages 21.

His conclusion is the useful bit: an edge device is now a server. With 64-bit CPUs, containers, lots of RAM and fast Wi-Fi, it can sit in a vehicle or a robot and aggregate data from a mesh of tiny, low-power sensors before shipping it on over Kafka, MQTT or Pulsar.

On the AI side he demos Hailo's pose estimation, which tracks 17 keypoints per person (eyes, ears, shoulders, joints), and points at small language models such as Hugging Face's SmolLM, at 1.7 billion parameters, for local decisions where a round trip to the cloud takes too long.

## What does the pipeline look like?

Two small devices feed the demo. An Adafruit FunHouse, with a 240 MHz processor and a few MB of RAM, reads its sensors and publishes JSON over MQTT. A Raspberry Pi with breakout sensors sends richer records. Spann's habit is worth copying: every raw message carries a timestamp, a unique ID, the host, its MAC address and remaining disk, alongside the sensor readings, so you can debug a device from its data.

From there the options branch: MQTT into a Pulsar or Kafka server, Kafka Connect or Snowpipe into Snowflake, files dropped into S3, JDBC straight into a warehouse, or Flink SQL aggregating the stream into Iceberg. He also shows a table built automatically from a single sample JSON file, then used as the schema to validate incoming data.

## Why NiFi sits in the middle

Apache NiFi gets the most airtime. IoT data is sparse, bursty, sometimes broken and often in odd formats, and NiFi handles guaranteed delivery, buffering, back pressure and prioritised queues, so an overheating alert can jump ahead of the routine readings. NiFi 2 adds Python processors and runs on JDK 21+. "Java is back," as Spann puts it.

The feature he calls the killer is provenance and lineage: when data arrived, its size, what touched it, the Kafka offset and partition. Push that into tables and keep it in Iceberg in cold storage, and when someone asks where the training data for a model came from, you have the answer.

He shows two custom Python processors: one that converts an address into latitude and longitude with geopy and OpenStreetMap, because sensors exist somewhere and location drives joins; and one that turns a GTFS transit feed, Boston's buses in the demo, into JSON.

## The live demo

Sensor readings flow into Kafka and on to a notebook; NiFi consumes the same topic and shows each record with its provenance; the pose-estimation Pi samples frames to a separate Kafka topic and posts them to Slack. He learnt the hard way to sample: sending every frame was too much. As he signs off, "as long as we have enough cats involved, we'll be in a good place," Tim Spann said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who have been handed an IoT project, and makers who want their Raspberry Pi data in something sturdier than a CSV. It is a breadth-first tour; for depth on any one piece, follow his links or the related talks below.

Title: An AI cloud blueprint that promises 42% lower costs, with a factory to prove it
Description: Babita Kumari (Microsoft) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on AI-enhanced hybrid cloud architecture for enterprise and IoT operations
Body:
Enterprises overspend on cloud by an average of 45%, and most of the waste comes from managing resources by hand. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Babita Kumari, Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft, presents an AI-enhanced cloud architecture that predicts resource needs, scales and secures workloads automatically, and spans public clouds, private infrastructure and the edge. She backs it with a Fortune 500 manufacturing case that reports $4.2M a year in maintenance savings.

Set expectations: this is an executive-level blueprint delivered as a run of figures, not an engineering walkthrough. There is no code, and the numbers come without methodology. Useful if you need the business case; thin if you need the how.

## What problem is it solving?

Kumari opens with four pain points and a number for each:

- **Cost**: an average of 45% overspending, driven by inefficient resource use and manual optimization.
- **Resource management**: 38% average resource wastage, inconsistent workload distribution and poor capacity planning.
- **Security**: more than 12,000 cloud security incidents a year, with 4.5 hours average detection time.
- **Prediction**: 37 hours of unplanned downtime a month from reactive management.

"These aren't just technical problems, they are everyday business problems," Babita Kumari said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. That framing explains the rest of the talk, which is pitched at the people who sign off budgets.

The market slide supplies urgency: a $263.4B AI-cloud market by 2027, growing at a 42.8% CAGR, with 89% of enterprises said to prioritise cloud-AI integration.

## What is in the architecture?

Four building blocks:

1. **Predictive resource management**: ML on historical usage, seasonal variation and growth trends, quoted at 91% prediction accuracy.
2. **Intelligent security**: zero-trust architecture, real-time monitoring and automated compliance checks, with 99.7% threat detection accuracy claimed.
3. **Dynamic scaling**: automatic workload balancing and multi-region optimization, credited with a 67% reduction in overprovisioning.
4. **Multi-cloud integration**: a unified management interface and vendor-agnostic deployment.

The deployment shape is hybrid. Public cloud does about 65% of the work, split across Azure for ML training, AWS for data lake operations and Google Cloud for specialised AI services. The remaining 35% runs on private infrastructure for sensitive data and on edge computing across 150 global locations. For an IoT audience, that split is the most transferable idea: keep the sensitive and latency-bound work close, and rent the heavy training.

The aggregate results claimed: 42% lower operational costs, 53% higher process efficiency and 89% fewer security incidents.

## The factory case study

The concrete part is a Fortune 500 manufacturer. Reported savings: $4.2M a year in maintenance, $2.1M less on emergency repairs and $1.3M from inventory optimization. Operationally, 52% better resource allocation and 47% less downtime. The system handles 850,000 data points per minute at 99.9% uptime, and the plant gains 17.4 production days a year. Those extra days are the number a plant manager will remember, since downtime is what the predictive maintenance pitch is really about.

## The roadmap

The forward look runs from advanced orchestration (94% workload-balancing efficiency, 67% lower latency) through fully automated, self-healing resource management by 2025-2026, to zero-touch autonomous operations later. It also leans on quantum computing integration and quantum-safe protocols. Treat this section as a vision statement rather than a delivery plan.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering managers who need to make the case for AI-driven cloud operations to leadership, and who want a reference shape for a hybrid public-private-edge deployment. Engineers looking for model details, failure stories or how the 91% was measured won't find them here.

Title: Let the pull request write its own tests, docs and description
Description: Julio Arruda at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on GenAI in DevOps workflows, from context-rich prompts to a pull request that adds its own tests and docs
Body:
Nobody reads the pull request description because nobody writes one. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Julio Arruda, Microsoft MVP and GitHub Star, shows two places generative AI earns its keep in a DevOps workflow: inside the IDE, where GitHub Copilot fixes a SQL injection and explains unfamiliar code, and inside the pipeline, where opening a pull request triggers a GitHub Actions job that writes the unit tests, the documentation and the review summary.

Half the talk is a practical primer on prompting; the other half is demos.

## Why does the same question get two different answers?

Arruda calls prompt engineering an art rather than a recipe, and his reason is the one everyone learns the hard way. Julio Arruda said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "If you change one thing, one small thing, if you include a comma in your prompt, your answer can be changed, entirely changed".

His demo makes the point with Copilot Chat. The first prompt asks how to structure an app that displays electric vehicle data, and gets a generic menu: MVC, MVVM, microservices, serverless, monolith. The second prompt says it is Express and TypeScript, a large project with more than 1,000 users online, Keycloak for authentication, deployed on Azure Kubernetes Service. Now the answer has a project layout, Keycloak integration code, routes for the vehicle data and container configuration. His summary: "Basically, good things in the prompting, good things out in the answer."

He also explains the system prompt, the set of rules a tool like Copilot adds before your question (be a code assistant, don't write vulnerable code, don't discuss politics), which is why your request and the tool's answer are never just your words in and the model's words out.

## Where does GenAI help across the SDLC?

He gives four reasons to use it: developer experience, productivity, learning, and more time for the business logic. The learning one comes with a personal story. He needed a VS Code extension in TypeScript, a language he had never written, and with Copilot explaining and suggesting code he shipped a working extension in two days.

Then he lists where it fits in the workflow:

- **Code creation**: the assistant in the IDE, the use everyone already knows.
- **Code review**: generating a detailed description of what a change does, change by change, so the approver doesn't have to read every line or call the author.
- **Documentation**: regenerating Markdown docs from the code on every change, so docs stop rotting after version one.
- **Test generation**: unit tests that follow your standards, and functional tests written in natural language that find the page fields themselves, so a renamed component doesn't break the suite.
- **Code correction**: fixing bugs and vulnerabilities, by hand in chat or in batch.

He adds modernisation, from COBOL to Java or from Java 8 to Java 21, as the next frontier.

## What does the IDE demo show?

A SAST tool has flagged a SQL injection in `User.java` in a project he doesn't know. He asks Copilot to explain the class, then to refactor it and fix the injection. Copilot swaps the statement for a prepared statement and explains each change. He notes that Copilot lets you switch models, with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1-mini and o1-preview in the picker. Then an SDLC assistant extension he helps build generates Markdown documentation for the class and a unit test file with mocks, asking whether to include existing tests as extra context.

## What happens when the pull request opens?

The second demo is the one to watch. He commits the fixed `User.java` to a new branch and opens a pull request on GitHub. That triggers a GitHub Actions pipeline that calls the assistant three times: update the unit tests for the changed implementation (some tests removed, others added), generate fresh documentation including a section on the vulnerabilities still present (password storage, exception handling), and post a review. The review is a summary of the change, a file-by-file explanation, recommendations specific to this change, and an explanation of the vulnerabilities, with examples.

It is a vendor-neutral idea even though he shows his own tools: any CI system that triggers on pull requests can do this.

## Who should watch?

Teams that use Copilot as autocomplete and want to see it in code review and documentation, and platform engineers thinking about AI steps in CI. Prompting experts can skip to the demos.

Title: Explain the chatbot's reasoning and users forgive its mistakes 40% more
Description: Shradha Kohli (Salesforce) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on a 150-user study of LIME, SHAP and counterfactuals for chatbot transparency
Body:
A chatbot that shows its reasoning gets forgiven for its mistakes. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Shradha Kohli, Engineering Management at Salesforce, presents a study that applied three explainable AI techniques, LIME, SHAP and counterfactual explanations, to three chatbot architectures and tested them on around 150 users. With explanations, comprehension rose 48% and error tolerance 40%.

It is a compact research summary. The IoT angle in the title is light; the substance is chatbot transparency, which applies to any conversational interface, smart speakers included.

## Why do chatbots need explaining at all?

Kohli traces the arc from 1960s pattern-matching bots to machine learning and NLP systems that understand context and generate human-like replies. The more capable they get, the more they behave as black boxes, and that opacity hurts trust, accountability, and the team's ability to improve the system. Unexpected answers and biased decisions are hard to fix when nobody can see why the model chose them.

## Three ways to open the box

The study used three well-known methods:

- **LIME** (local interpretable model-agnostic explanations) builds a local linear approximation of the model's behaviour by perturbing inputs and watching outputs. It explains one response at a time.
- **SHAP** (Shapley additive explanations) uses game theory to give a unified measure of feature importance, both globally and locally, so it shows patterns across many interactions.
- **Counterfactual explanations** find the smallest change to the input that would produce a different output, which tells users which words actually drove the decision.

Each was applied to three models: a retrieval-based model, a generative transformer model and a hybrid. The evaluation used faithfulness, stability and comprehensibility, in three stages: model selection, applying one XAI method, then evaluating the results.

## What changed for users?

The headline numbers, as Kohli reported them: comprehension up 48%, error tolerance up 40%, use of chatbots for complex tasks such as healthcare or finance up 27%, overall trust up 35% and engagement up 31%.

The qualitative finding is the more interesting one. Participants felt more confident in the bot and were more likely to forgive occasional errors once they could see the reasoning. "This whole black box sort of became a white box to them," Shradha Kohli said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. Without explanations, users had little idea why the bot answered the way it did and little patience when it got things wrong.

Each technique earned its place. LIME was good at explaining individual responses, SHAP at showing feature importance across conversations, and counterfactuals at revealing how sensitive a response was to small input changes.

## The catches

Kohli doesn't oversell it. Generating thorough explanations in real time adds latency, which a chat interface can't hide. Explanations have to be pitched at the user: too technical and non-technical people learn nothing. And not every technique suits every architecture, so model choice and XAI method go together.

There is an ethics trade-off as well: transparency must not leak sensitive details of the model or its training data, and explanations themselves must not reinforce stereotypes. For developers, the benefit is practical: XAI insights help find biases, improve response accuracy and make debugging cheaper over the life of the system.

Her pointer for future work is transformer-scale models, where she suggests hierarchical explanations, from individual attention weights up to higher-level semantic representations.

## Who should watch

Teams shipping a conversational interface in a domain where users need to trust the answer, such as finance, healthcare or support. It is a good quick primer if you know the names LIME and SHAP but haven't seen them compared on chatbots. The study details beyond the metrics are thin, so treat the numbers as directional.
