Title: Kusion lets developers ask for a database without knowing the instance class
Description: Hoang Dinh Nguyen (Viettel Group) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on Kusion, an open-source platform orchestrator that merges app intent with platform config
Body:
A developer who wants a MySQL database should not need to know that production uses `db.t3.large` and dev uses `db.t3.micro`. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Hoang Dinh Nguyen, Cloud Engineer at Viettel Group and a contributor to the open-source KusionStack project, shows how Kusion, a platform orchestrator in the CNCF Sandbox, splits a deployment into what the application team wants and what the platform team decides, then merges the two into one spec per environment.

He works on Viettel's cloud platform services, including its Kubernetes engine, cloud observability and the internal developer platform (IDP), so the problem he describes is one he deals with daily.

## What went wrong with "you build it, you run it"?

Nguyen starts with a history lesson. DevOps was meant as a cultural shift, better collaboration between developers and operations. In practice, many companies used it to push as much operational load as possible onto developers. Add the sprawl of cloud-native tools (Kubernetes, Terraform, Istio and friends) and a developer who only wants to change an environment variable or fix a basic database setting has to learn a toolchain first.

He lists the symptoms on three sides. Developers are overloaded with infrastructure knowledge they do not need. The platform team becomes a bottleneck and coordination across teams gets harder. Security perimeters get harder to define, and the blast radius of a mistake is potentially huge. Platform engineering, a team that builds the IDP as a product for its internal customers, is his answer, and Kusion is the orchestration piece of it.

## Who writes what?

This is the core of the talk, and it is a clean division of labour.

- **Developers write an AppConfiguration**: the workload and its accessories, such as a database, monitoring or storage. They say they need MySQL; they do not say which instance class.
- **Platform engineers write Kusion Modules**: standardised, reusable building blocks with defaults. His example module defines MySQL on AWS with a default of size 20 on `db.t3.micro`, a `smallClass` of size 50 on `db.t3.small`, and a `largeClass` on `db.t3.large`.
- **Platform engineers also define Workspaces**: a workspace maps to a real target environment, typically a Kubernetes cluster plus an optional cloud provider, with the environment's settings attached, such as the secret store provider, the region and a reference to the cluster's kubeconfig.

Kusion merges the developer's intent with the workspace configuration into a Spec. Hoang Dinh Nguyen said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 that "this spec acts as a single source of truth corresponding to one, one to one the environment's actual infrastructure." The same AppConfiguration then deploys to staging and production, and the environment decides the database size.

## What does the workflow look like?

Three steps: write, generate, apply. Platform engineers write modules and workspaces, developers write the AppConfiguration, and Kusion generates the Spec. Before apply there is a preview step that shows the diff of resources about to change, which is the moment you notice a deleted database before it is actually deleted. Apply then creates or updates both the Kubernetes resources and the cloud provider resources.

## How does it fit into an IDP?

In his IDP picture, Kusion is the platform orchestrator between the developer control plane (IDE, version control, a portal such as Backstage) and the resource plane. The developer pushes the AppConfiguration to Git; the CI pipeline builds and tests the image; the CD pipeline reads the AppConfiguration and the platform's modules and deploys the app plus whatever infrastructure it needs. Changing the database size, adding a second database or removing one becomes a change to a config file.

Today Kusion is a CLI you call from your pipelines. Nguyen says that brings limits around credential management, visibility of resources, permission management and integration with other systems. The proposed fix is Kusion 2.0, a long-running server with REST endpoints that a developer portal can call, with a Backstage plugin planned. At the time of the talk that server was still upcoming.

## Who should watch?

Platform engineers designing the contract between app teams and the platform, and anyone comparing platform orchestrators. The talk is conceptual, with config snippets rather than a live demo, and the module-plus-workspace model is worth borrowing even if you never run Kusion.

Title: Stop handing everyone kubectl, let Argo CD pull instead
Description: Megha Kadur (Barracuda) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on why pull-based GitOps with Argo CD decouples CI from CD and closes your cluster to the pipeline
Body:
If your CD step is a pipeline job that logs into the cluster and runs `kubectl apply`, your CI system holds the keys to production. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Megha Kadur, DevOps Engineer at Barracuda, makes the case for pull-based deployment with GitOps: an agent inside the cluster watches Git and reconciles, so CI no longer needs cluster credentials, and CI and CD stop being welded together. She ends with a live demo using GitHub Actions and Argo CD on Minikube.

It is an introductory talk, and a clear one. If you have never set up Argo CD, this is a good first half hour.

## What does GitOps actually ask you to store in Git?

Kadur starts from the definition: GitOps is continuous delivery with Git as the single source of truth. Teams already keep application code in GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Azure Repos. GitOps asks you to keep the configuration that describes how the app behaves in production there too: the Deployment, Service and Ingress YAML, the Dockerfile.

She walks through the four principles: declarative (you declare the desired state), versioned and immutable (it lives in Git with history), pulled automatically, and continuously reconciled. The last two are where the agent comes in.

## Why is push-based deployment the problem?

In a push pipeline, CI builds an image, pushes it to a registry, and then the same pipeline runs `kubectl apply`, `terraform apply` or an Ansible command against the target. Kadur names three problems with that.

First, CI is tightly coupled with CD. If the company migrates to a different CI tool, the deployment logic moves with it, so every change is double work. Second, the cluster has to be reachable from outside for the pipeline to apply changes. Third, people need read-write access: on a team of 10 to 15, everyone who deploys needs credentials to the environments.

Pull-based deployment keeps CI identical up to the registry, then stops. The pipeline updates a manifest and raises a pull request. Argo CD, sitting in the cluster, notices the desired state no longer matches the actual state and pulls the change. Megha Kadur said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "you don't want to expose any Kubernetes clusters, secrets, or anything because The Argo CD is a tool that is representing the GitOps concept."

## What do you get besides security?

Rollbacks become reverting to an earlier version in Git. Configuration drift gets harder to hide. Her example will be familiar to anyone who has been on call: Friday evening, something breaks, the only architect still online logs into the cluster and patches a config file by hand. On Monday the app behaves differently and nobody can work out why, because the fix exists nowhere but the cluster. With GitOps, Git is where you look, and the agent will put back whatever someone changed by hand.

She also notes that one Argo CD installation can manage several clusters, and that it has a UI, a CLI, webhooks and notifications. Jenkins X and Flux are mentioned as alternatives, with Argo CD as the most popular.

## What does the demo show?

A small PHP sample app. A GitHub Actions workflow builds the image, pushes it to Docker Hub, generates a software bill of materials so the versions of third-party components are on record, and then commits an updated image tag to the config repository. Argo CD, watching that repository, briefly shows the app out of sync, then replaces the old release with the new one. She also points out that auto-sync is optional: you can require a manual approval before Argo CD applies a change, which is the setting most teams want for production.

## Who should watch?

Engineers moving from push pipelines to GitOps, and anyone who has to explain to a security team why the CI runner should not have cluster-admin. Experienced Argo CD users can skip to the push-versus-pull section.

Title: Your IoT product's real manual is the website, because the paper one is in the bin
Description: Amanda Hunter (Salesforce) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on the web experiences that turn hesitant buyers into confident IoT users
Body:
The moment a smart device fails to connect is the moment it risks ending up in a drawer for good. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Amanda Hunter, Global ABM Web Experience Manager at Salesforce, makes the case that IoT adoption is won or lost on the web: the site is where people research, set up and troubleshoot, so it has to teach, simplify and earn trust before the device itself gets a chance.

This is a marketer's talk, not an engineering one. No code, no architecture diagrams; instead a clear checklist and two brand examples worth stealing from.

## Why does the website matter more than the box?

Her starting observation will be familiar to anyone who has set up a smart speaker: when something breaks, nobody reaches for the manual. "They go straight to Google," Amanda Hunter said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, and as for the paper manual: "It's probably already in the bin." So the site can't be a pretty landing page. It has to be the place with clear answers, instructions people can follow, and enough reassurance to keep going.

IoT makes this harder than ordinary software. Devices refuse to pair, settings don't save, and the companion app reads like it was written in another language. Every one of those moments is a search query, and the best outcome is that the query lands on your own site.

## Educate, simplify, build trust

Hunter's three foundations:

- **Educate**: bite-sized content, not brain surgery. Product videos of 60 seconds or less, FAQs that cover real worries rather than marketing copy, and step-by-step guides that are interactive or visual. Anticipate the question before it is asked.
- **Simplify**: interactive tutorials that coach you through setup, and virtual demos that let people try a product risk-free. If users are googling what a button does on someone else's website, you have already lost them.
- **Build trust**: say what data you collect, why, and how you protect it, and show people how to manage their privacy settings. A clunky, outdated site reads as a clunky product.

On top of that she layers personalization (content that matches the visitor's needs), interactivity (configurators, quizzes, live demos) and localization, which is more than translation. A site for Spain should feel Spanish, she says, not like the American site pasted into Google Translate.

## Onboarding is where the drawer gets filled

The part engineers should hear is about the first hour after purchase. Her recipe: short step-by-step guides instead of 50-page PDFs, AI chatbots for the 11 p.m. setup failure when support has gone home, and ruthless removal of unnecessary steps. If onboarding looks like it needs an engineering degree, she says, people bounce.

## Nest and Philips Hue, done right

Two examples carry the talk. Nest tackles the hardest bit of thermostat setup, the wiring, with interactive tools that walk users through identifying their existing thermostat wiring, connecting the new device and joining Wi-Fi, then go further into eco mode and suggested schedules. Philips Hue lets you see on its website how its lights will look in your own room before you buy, which Hunter compares to a fitting room for living-room lighting. Both remove guesswork, and both make the first experience feel personal.

## The tech underneath, and the bills

Hunter names three enablers, AI for personalization, AR and VR for try-before-you-buy demos, and cloud infrastructure so a launch day with millions of visitors doesn't mean loading screens, and three honest costs: handling user data responsibly, real development spend, and scalability, since what works for 10 users can collapse at 10,000.

Her closing best practices are short: listen to users and iterate, keep language plain, and design for accessibility so the experience works across abilities and devices.

## Who should watch

Product managers, growth teams and developers who build the web side of a connected product, especially if your support tickets are mostly setup problems. Firmware and backend engineers can skip it, or send it to whoever owns the help centre.

Title: One login for your bank, your hospital and your university
Description: Mahesh Vankayala (Oracle) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on identity federation across industries, built on extended OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
Body:
The average user juggles about 100 passwords, and most of the security industry's problems start right there. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Mahesh Vankayala, Principal Software Engineer at Oracle, proposes identity federation across whole industries: one identity that a bank, a hospital and a university all trust, built by extending OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect rather than inventing a new protocol.

It is a design proposal with economic projections, not a walkthrough of a running system. The interesting part is the shape of the framework, and the four pieces he says it needs.

## How bad is the password problem, really?

Vankayala opens with the numbers. 66% of people reuse passwords. 61% of data breaches involve compromised credentials, with phishing and other human error a large contributor. 55% of consumers have abandoned an online purchase because they forgot a password. And on the business side, financial institutions could save up to $1 billion a year with streamlined identity verification.

None of that is new to anyone who has run a support desk. What he adds is the argument that single sign-on inside one company is the solved case; the unsolved one is a person moving between institutions that each run their own onboarding, their own checks and their own password reset flow.

## What does federation across institutions need?

His definition: a shared identity model that lets a single identity be used across multiple institutions, such as banks or healthcare providers. He breaks it into four key concepts:

- **Single sign-on**: authenticate once, reach many services.
- **Standardised identity attributes**: each industry agrees which attributes it needs. For banking that means name and financial history; for healthcare, medical history.
- **Consent management**: the user decides what is shared with whom, which is also how you stay compliant.
- **An industry-specific trust framework**: the rules and standards for joining, so participants can trust each other's assertions.

The consent piece is what separates this from a big shared login database. Mahesh Vankayala said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 that consent management "empowers users to control over data sharing ensuring compliance".

## Which standards does it build on?

The technical section is short and sensible: don't invent, extend. He says to "extend the OAuth 2. 0 and OpenID Connect to create a robust framework", with four components:

- **Extended OAuth 2.0 scopes** that carry industry-specific permissions.
- **Federated identity providers**: each institution acts as both an identity provider and a service provider.
- **An attribute exchange protocol** that shares user attributes with encryption and digital signatures.
- **A federation registry**: a central list of participating institutions, for transparency and security.

If you have wired up OIDC between a few internal apps, you already know the hard part is not the protocol. It is the registry and the trust framework, which is to say governance, and he puts them on the list for that reason.

## What does he claim it is worth?

Here the talk switches to projections, and they are big. Up to 3 to 13% GDP growth by 2030 for countries that implement it. A 50% cut in password-related support incidents, and 80% less onboarding time in banking. In banking, shared identity verification could cut identity fraud by 90%, saving about $7 billion. Healthcare could save $30 billion a year through interoperable patient records and see 20% fewer hospital readmissions. In education, transcript verification could be 90% faster and adult learner enrolment 25% higher. Treat these as industry estimates; the talk does not say where each one comes from.

## What stands in the way?

He is clear-eyed about the risks. Regulations differ by industry and non-compliance is expensive. A centralised identity system is an attractive target, so it needs strong security, with biometric and multi-factor authentication on his list. Privacy has to be designed in, not bolted on. And none of it works unless industry players agree on interoperable standards, which is the slowest part of any federation.

## Who should watch?

Identity and security engineers who want a compact model of cross-organisation federation, and architects in banking, healthcare or education weighing up a shared identity scheme. If you want to see a token exchange in a terminal, this is not that talk; it is the whiteboard version.

Title: Half a million new factory robots a year, and almost none see a cloud
Description: Chiara Civardi and Petr Aubrecht (Payara) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on putting a Jakarta EE edge server between robots and the cloud
Body:
Factories installed 541,302 industrial robots in 2023, and almost none of them send their data anywhere useful. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Chiara Civardi, Product Marketer at Payara Services, and Petr Aubrecht, Software Engineer at Payara Services, argue that the fix is an edge layer that filters robot data before the cloud ever sees it, and they show one built on Jakarta EE and the Payara Platform, with a live load test.

It is a vendor talk: the platform shown is Payara's own. The first half, on why robots and clouds don't mix, holds up whatever runtime you pick.

## What does the most common robot actually look like?

Not a humanoid, not a droid, not an Iron Man suit. Civardi opens by deflating the audience: the most common robot is a six-axis arm or a delta arm bolted to a factory floor. Her numbers come from the IFR World Robotics 2024 report: 162 robots per 10,000 employees, with automotive taking 25% of installations and electronics 23%. Cars need heavy parts assembled fast; chips need clean rooms that people contaminate.

Then the punchline. "All these 541, 000 robots rarely see a cloud," Chiara Civardi said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. She means the digital kind, though the real kind is also scarce in a clean room.

## Why aren't robots sending data to the cloud already?

The payoff is obvious: condition monitoring from anywhere, maintenance scheduled into planned downtime, and predictive models trained on failure history across several plants, so you replace a worn part when it is worn rather than when the calendar says so.

The blockers are just as concrete. Shop floors produce too much data, too fast: industrial Ethernet runs at 100 Mbit/s to 1 Gbit/s, and if time-sensitive traffic doesn't arrive, the line stops. Pushing all of it to a cloud is slow and expensive. Plants keep their networks isolated for good reason, since an internet path to a robot controller is an invitation. And the equipment lives for about 25 years, so anything you add has to stay backward compatible for a very long time.

## Edge computing as the filter

The answer is processing at the periphery of the automation network, close to the robots. You don't want every message between a robot and its controller; you want the sensor readings that tell you about wear and tear. Civardi's split is neat: the cloud is where you develop the knowledge, the edge is where you put it into action. That keeps the cloud from becoming an expensive pile of raw telemetry, and keeps the shop floor reacting in time when the uplink has a bad day.

All of that edge logic has to run somewhere, which brings the talk to application servers. Her point: almost no plant builds its own robot, so it shouldn't build its own middleware either.

## Why Jakarta EE for a 25-year shop floor?

Aubrecht makes the case for a standards-based platform. Jakarta EE is a set of open specifications, each with an API, a Technology Compatibility Kit and several implementations, so servers from different vendors pass the same tests and you can switch vendors. He leans on backward compatibility: code written in 2008 still runs on current servers, give or take the javax-to-jakarta package rename, which tools handle. Payara delivers ARM images, so the same server runs on a small ARM box at the edge.

He also covers the knobs that matter on constrained hardware: thread pool size and thread type, including the virtual threads that arrived in Java 21. MicroProfile Metrics and Health come built in and expose Prometheus endpoints, so you get monitoring without writing code for it.

## The demo: 100 simulated robots against a stock server

The demo is the best part. A separate machine replays recorded robot data: time, arm position, temperature and voltage, about 3,500 measurements per cycle. An edge service stores each cycle and forwards it to a simulated data-mining cluster, with Prometheus and Grafana watching. Ten sources first, then 100, imitating a big factory sending as fast as it can. Aubrecht stresses that this is a stock server with no clever caching. He then kills the server so you can see the outage light up the dashboard.

The code is about as small as it gets: a REST endpoint that caches data, with counters added through MicroProfile Metrics annotations.

## Who should watch

Engineers working on industrial IoT who need to explain to an OT team why the cloud doesn't get the raw firehose, and Java developers wondering whether Jakarta EE belongs on edge hardware. Skip it if you want ML on the edge; the analytics side is simulated.

Title: The ATM that hears you mutter is a feedback form nobody has to fill in
Description: Natalia Drazhnik (YCH Blue Digital Limited) at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024 on IoT devices that collect customer feedback AI alone can't
Body:
Surveys arrive late, and only from the customers patient enough to fill them in. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024, Natalia Drazhnik, Product Owner at YCH Blue Digital Limited, takes the lessons from an AI social media monitoring platform she led and argues for the next step: IoT devices that pick up feedback while the customer is still standing at the machine, including the feedback they never meant to give.

It is a short, product-minded talk with two worked scenarios, both in banking. Expect concepts and a clear framework, not code.

## What did the social media platform teach her?

The starting point was brand reputation management. Surveys and focus groups are slow and expensive; social media is a free, constant stream of opinion that is massive, fragmented, multilingual and never stops. Her team built a platform that pulled from Twitter, Facebook and forums, ran sentiment and trend detection with NLP, and added a formula to price reputational risk in money, the unit stakeholders read first.

The results she reports: monitoring coverage went from 10% to 70%, and response time to critical incidents improved by over 60%.

She is just as clear about where the AI fell short. Sarcasm is the classic failure. Her example of text a model scores as praise: "Oh great, another amazing update." And the deeper limit: "AI alone can analyze, but can't interact," Natalia Drazhnik said at Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2024. A model reading yesterday's posts can't ask a follow-up question or catch a problem while it is happening.

## Explicit feedback versus the kind you give by accident

The framework at the centre of the talk splits feedback in two:

- **Explicit**: the customer tells you, say a rating on a screen after a transaction. Clear, direct and rare, because most people skip it.
- **Implicit**: you observe it. How long someone stays on a screen, the same button pressed again and again, or the tone of voice behind "this ATM is great", which may well be sarcastic.

IoT is what makes the second kind collectable at scale: microphones, pressure-sensitive displays and interaction sensors turn a frustrated customer into a data point without asking them to fill in anything.

## Two scenarios: the smart ATM and the smart branch

In the first, an ATM fails to dispense cash and the customer mutters that it is useless. The machine's microphone and NLP categorise the frustration, sensors log the repeated button presses, and AI joins that with transaction data to find patterns, for example slow responses at peak hours. The bank learns which machines underperform and schedules maintenance or software updates for those specific ATMs.

In the second, kiosks in a bank office help with transactions and loan applications. A customer asks why it is taking so long, or taps the screen harder than any screen deserves. Voice, gesture and touch analysis flag the frustration and tie it to a specific process, such as loan application delays, so the kiosk can offer a fix on the spot and managers can see which flows need a redesign.

## What makes it hard?

She lists three challenges without pretending they are small. Data integration: IoT feedback has to be joined with existing feedback tools and CRMs that speak different formats. Privacy: people may not enjoy being recorded by an ATM, so businesses have to say clearly what they collect and why, and comply with regulation. Adoption: if the device is awkward, customers avoid it.

The opportunities on the other side are continuous feedback instead of periodic surveys, a closed loop where the system responds while the customer is still there, and predictive feedback: spotting dissatisfaction before anyone complains.

## Who should watch

Product owners and CX teams in banking or retail who already run sentiment analysis and wonder what physical devices add. Engineers looking for an architecture will find the scenarios useful as a requirements sketch, but the talk stops before implementation.

Title: Multi-cloud buys you redundancy, hybrid buys you data sovereignty
Description: Prashanth Reddy Kora (Centene Corporation) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on what multi-cloud and hybrid cloud give data teams, and what they cost
Body:
Multi-cloud and hybrid cloud get mentioned in the same breath, but they fix different problems. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Prashanth Reddy Kora, Cloud Database Engineer at Centene Corporation, gives a short, numbers-heavy overview of both for data management: multi-cloud is mostly about not betting the business on one provider, hybrid is mostly about keeping regulated data where the auditors want it. Both come with the same bill for integration, security and skills.

Expect a survey talk, not a migration story. The abstract talks about cloud database systems and performance gains; the talk itself is a compact tour of the two architectures, the market figures behind them and a list of best practices. It is short enough to watch over a coffee.

## What is the difference, in one line each?

He keeps the definitions tight. Multi-cloud means using two or more cloud providers, public or private, to spread workloads, which avoids vendor lock-in and adds redundancy. Hybrid cloud joins private or public clouds with on-premises infrastructure, so you choose where each piece of data is stored and processed.

The framing figures come from the analysts: Gartner's forecast that 95% of digital workloads will be cloud-native by 2025, and IDC's prediction that the global datasphere will reach 175 zettabytes. That second number is the reason the talk exists. At that volume, where the data lives is an architecture decision, not a default.

## Why would a data team run on more than one cloud?

Kora lists four benefits of multi-cloud, each with a survey figure attached:

- **Redundancy**: spread workloads so one provider's outage does not stop the business; 63% of organisations report improved business continuity.
- **Vendor flexibility**: pick services per workload, with his examples being AWS for scalability, Google Cloud for AI and Azure for enterprise applications.
- **Cost optimisation**: competition between providers, with 45% of businesses reporting cost reductions.
- **Performance**: place workloads on the provider that runs them best.

He sizes the multi-cloud market at $15.3 billion in 2020, growing to $44.6 billion by 2027, an 18.4% annual growth rate. Treat these as industry context rather than measurements from his own systems; the talk does not show a production deployment.

## Where does hybrid cloud earn its keep?

For data, hybrid has the sharper argument, and it is about regulation. Prashanth Reddy Kora said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "Sensitive data can remain on prem or the private clouds to meet the compliance needs like GDPR or any HIPAA while non sensitive data leverages public cloud resources."

That is the pattern most regulated shops end up with whether they planned it or not, and naming it out loud helps. His other two hybrid benefits are scaling on demand through public cloud capacity (he cites operations scaling 4.5 times faster than traditional on-prem setups) and gradual legacy integration, so you modernise one system at a time instead of attempting a single big move. He quotes 87% of IT leaders favouring the hybrid model, and the hybrid market growing from $73.7 billion in 2020 to $171.9 billion by 2025.

## What breaks when the data is spread out?

The challenges section is the part worth bookmarking. Integration is hard because the clouds are built differently. Security gets harder because there are more places for data to be. Skills are scarce, because people who know two clouds and your on-prem estate are rare. Compliance policies evolve, and 53% of organisations struggle to keep up with them across environments. And cost: "without proper governance. Cloud costs can spiral out of control."

His fixes are four practices rather than products: strong data governance policies, data integration tooling (ETL and data virtualisation), cloud-agnostic technologies to keep lock-in in check, and continuous monitoring of performance and spend, which he says can cut costs by up to 30%.

## Who should watch?

Architects and data engineers who need a vocabulary and a set of numbers for a multi-cloud or hybrid conversation with management, and anyone new to the topic who wants the trade-offs on one page. If you already run Postgres across two clouds and an on-prem cluster, you will know most of it; the compliance split is the bit to steal for your next design review.

Title: A drug launch is won or lost in six months, so the data must be clean
Description: Harpreet Singh (Gilead Sciences) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on predictive models, real-time data and de-identified data pipelines for pharmaceutical launches
Body:
A new drug costs $2.6 billion on average to develop, and 60% of its lifetime revenue arrives in the first six months after launch. Harpreet Singh, Director of Sales Analytics & Operations at Gilead Sciences, opened his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk with those two numbers to explain why pharma companies pour so much into launch analytics: there is very little time to correct course, so predictions have to be accurate and the data feeding them has to be trustworthy.

Fair warning on scope: the abstract frames this through DevSecOps, but the talk is mostly about analytics. Security and compliance appear as de-identification, encryption and data quality controls in the pipeline rather than as a security practice of their own.

## Why launches miss

Harpreet's framing figures: 66% of drugs fail to meet their pre-launch sales projections, the average shortfall is 34%, and development costs are rising 7.5% a year. Analytics-driven launches, he says, achieve 45% higher market penetration than traditional ones and a 23% better launch trajectory within the critical 18-month window.

## What do the models do?

The core model segments physicians by behaviour, using prescriptions, demographics and sales data, so each segment gets its own tactics. Machine learning analyses prescribing patterns, engagement metrics and patient-level data (transactions, medical claims, pharmacy claims), and ensemble models keep predictions stable across market conditions. The KPIs he tracks include prediction accuracy (above 85%), early adoption by doctors and forecast variance, which ML-based models cut from ±25% to ±8%.

## A worked example, with a caveat

His case study is a type 2 diabetes launch into a $28.4 billion market where eight competitors hold 92% share. He is explicit that "this is not a real data", so read it as an illustration of the method. In the scenario, segmentation and real-time insight reach 72% of prescribers in three months against a 65% target, and new patient starts hit 14,500 against a goal of 12,000. AI-driven territory optimisation and patient journey analysis do the rest.

## Garbage in, garbage out, at petabyte scale

The infrastructure section is where engineers will lean in. He describes cloud data warehouses with 3.8 petabytes of processing capacity, third-party data covering about 94% of retail pharmacies, and claims run through layers of quality checks before any model sees them. "It's garbage in garbage out," Harpreet Singh said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, which is why data stewardship is a function in its own right. With validation accuracy at 99.8%, he says, the company can change tactics within 72 hours of spotting an insight.

Privacy sits in the integration layer. Sales, demographic and social data are combined only after dedicated companies de-identify and encrypt them, so no individual doctor or patient can be identified. Gaps are filled with imputation.

## How do you roll it out?

Pilot first. Models are expensive in IT infrastructure and business investment, so start in one region (his example is California) or in high-potential territories covering 15 to 20% of the market, tune, then scale nationally. Give each team its own dashboard, refreshed daily or weekly, and add automated alerts so nobody has to stare at it. His slides add retraining every 72 hours to keep up with the market.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and analysts in regulated industries, and anyone building pipelines where privacy rules decide what can be joined. If you came for DevSecOps tooling, this one is about the data.

Title: EdTech careers need code and pedagogy, in equal parts
Description: SantoshKumar Pulijala (HCL Global Systems Inc) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on the skills, roles and salaries behind careers in educational AI
Body:
An adaptive learning system that ignores how people learn is just a fast way to deliver the wrong lesson. SantoshKumar Pulijala, Senior .NET Developer at HCL Global Systems Inc, made that his core point at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: careers in educational AI and digitalization reward people who combine programming and data skills with real pedagogical knowledge, from learning theories to curriculum design.

Set expectations: this is a career guide to edtech, not a DevSecOps session. The abstract promises an ethics talk on privacy and accountability; the recording is mostly a map of tools, skills, roles and challenges, with equity and responsibility as the closing theme.

## What tools are reshaping classrooms?

SantoshKumar sorts the tools into three groups: e-learning platforms such as Moodle, Canvas and Blackboard; student information systems such as PowerSchool and Infinite Campus for attendance, grades and records; and collaboration tools such as Google Classroom and Microsoft Teams. AI sits on top: adaptive learning systems that personalise content per student, and automated grading that hands teachers back time for teaching.

How much good any of it does, he notes, depends on design, implementation and integration, which is where engineers come in.

## Which skills does the job actually need?

Two columns. Technical: Python, Java, .NET and JavaScript; data science and machine learning for spotting trends; AWS or Google Cloud for scale; NLP and neural networks for adaptive systems. Pedagogical: learning theories such as constructivism and behaviourism, plus curriculum design and assessment built for digital platforms. The combination, he argues, is what sets candidates apart.

For integrating the two in practice he points to TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge), a framework for how teachers combine technology, teaching method and subject matter.

## Three roles and what they pay

He profiles three careers, with salary ranges:

- **Educational technologist**: bridges technology and pedagogy, builds digital learning materials, trains educators. $50,000 to $100,000+.
- **AI/ML engineer**: builds adaptive algorithms, chatbots and grading systems. $80,000 to $150,000+.
- **Data analyst**: turns educational data into dashboards on student performance and teacher effectiveness. $60,000 to $120,000+.

## The hard part is not the model

The challenges section is the most useful one. Equity comes first: many students lack reliable devices and internet, and digital literacy varies widely. Teacher training is second. "Technology is only as effective as people using it," SantoshKumar Pulijala said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024. Sustainability is third: keeping initiatives useful over time and scaling them to very different contexts.

His future trends follow from that: offline-capable tools and low-cost devices for underserved regions, long-term studies of what technology actually does to learning outcomes, and context-sensitive solutions instead of one product for every school.

## Who should watch

Developers curious about a move into edtech, and anyone mentoring engineers who want a career path with social impact. For getting started he lists Coursera, edX and Udemy, the Google Certified Educator and ISTE certifications, ISTE membership, edtech meetups and hackathons.

Title: Social engineers hack people, so defenders need people skills
Description: Victor Onyenagubom (Teesside University) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on why communication, empathy and collaboration belong in a DevSecOps security culture
Body:
Social engineering attacks do not need a zero-day; they need someone to act on emotion. Victor Onyenagubom, Lecturer in Cybersecurity at Teesside University, used that as the starting point of his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk: if attackers target people, defenders need people skills too, and communication, empathy and collaboration deserve the same attention as technical skills in a DevSecOps culture.

It is a short, non-technical talk, closer to a lecture on professional practice than a tooling session, and it is honest about that.

## Why talk about soft skills at a security conference?

Victor's argument is that cyber threats keep getting more complex and more human. Phishing and other social engineering work by manipulating people, so a purely technical response leaves a gap. His answer is an interdisciplinary approach that mixes technical skills with soft ones, and he sees the gap most clearly where security meets the rest of the business.

## Translate, don't lecture

The first skill is translation. A security analyst presenting to a CFO, CIO or CEO has to explain in plain terms why a decision is needed to improve the organisation's security posture. A security awareness lead faces colleagues who know some IT but not why passwords should change or why an email needs a second look.

His toolkit: simplify, add context, tell stories, and use diagrams and dashboards for the visual learners in the room. Delivery matters as much as content. "Sometimes it's not really about what you say, but how you say it," Victor Onyenagubom said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, and body language counts too.

## Incidents cross department lines

His example is concrete: when the accounting department is hacked, the security team cannot fix it alone. It has to work with the accountants to find the root of the problem. That only goes smoothly if relationships already exist, which is why he puts relationship building, emotional intelligence, and working across cultures, races and religions next to collaborative problem solving. With those in place, he argues, collaboration comes naturally.

## Adaptability is a growth mindset with a deadline

Security changes fast, and the attack surface keeps growing. Victor asks for lifelong learning and a growth mindset, critical thinking during incidents (how to communicate with the public, organise the team, restore backups, stick to the business continuity plan) and agile responses: go back, admit the process missed a case, change it.

The skills chain together. Good communicators share knowledge, which makes them good mentors, and people with empathy find it easier to ask for help and be mentored in return.

## Who should watch

Security leads building an awareness programme, engineers moving into roles where they brief executives, and students who assume the job is all tooling. His summary is the right one to end on: "Understand that you cannot do cyber security alone."

Title: Kill the CISO in your next drill, then see who signs off
Description: Ilan Finkelstein (Owndata) and Pieter VanIperen (Own Company) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on random, unscripted DR, IR and BCP exercises
Body:
If your last disaster recovery exercise ended with everyone feeling good, it failed. That is the line Ilan Finkelstein, Principal Security Architect at Owndata, and Pieter VanIperen, CISO at Own Company, keep returning to in their Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk. Their recipe for DR, incident response (IR) and business continuity (BCP) exercises: random events, no known ending, people who did not write the plan, and at least one key person missing (dead, in the scenario) from the start.

The title is the scenario. Pieter is the CISO, and in their drills he does not make it.

## What makes a drill worth running?

They list eight qualities: clear purpose, well defined, authentic, interesting, exciting, unpredictable, inclusive and automated. A few deserve detail:

- **Clear purpose** means a clear outcome (what are we more prepared for?), not a scripted beginning and end.
- **Well defined** means fair game and out of bounds are spelled out. The rule gets repeated three times in a row: "Don't include production."
- **Authentic** but flexible. The US military has a plan for a zombie apocalypse not because zombies are coming but because the exercise exposes real gaps.
- **Inclusive** means removing the usual cast. One old rule they cite: "if you wrote the BCP or the DR plan, you're not in the exercise." Juniors who have never led an incident should get the chance.
- **Automated** means scripted events that unfold without the organiser at the keyboard, though they admit dice and envelopes work too.

## How do you simulate a black swan?

You cannot predict the one-in-a-million event; if you could, it would not be one. Their trick follows from the definition: black swans are understood in hindsight because you can see the seven or eight factors that combined. So create seven or eight random factors, let them interact, and see where you land. Sometimes it is a vanilla scenario (someone kicked out a cord), sometimes something truly new. COVID and the CrowdStrike outage are their reference points.

Randomness also means treating it like a real disaster: shifts, food breaks, tired people, and an organiser who does not know when or how it ends. Tell the room it could last one hour or twelve, and the Slack-checking stops quickly.

## How do you get management to say yes?

Pulling half the ops team, three quarters of security, plus legal, finance and product into one room for eight hours is a hard ask. Their statistics help: continuity breaks cost $137 to $16,000 per minute, nine in ten businesses have an outage each quarter, 30% of organisations permanently lose data, ransomware gangs collected $1.1 billion in 2023, and 72.7% of organisations faced ransomware attacks that year.

Pieter's better argument is local: find your own last outage, ask product and sales what it cost, multiply by the minutes. He also asks for data loss in every scenario, because data loss always ends in revenue loss.

## Who else should be in the room?

Legal, finance, the C-suite, physical security, marketing and PR. If a simulation involves fewer than two of those groups, they argue, it is not simulating anything serious. This is where removing the CISO pays off: plans assume the people who sign off on a statement are available, and nobody knows who the backups are.

"if you walk away feeling good, you're not doing it right," Pieter VanIperen said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024. The goal is to leave with a knot in your stomach, review the misses without blame, and come back better.

Title: Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: injection, testing and Chet Gupta
Description: The Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 roundup - 40 talks on prompt injection, testing LLM apps, prompts as automation, codebase understanding and domain use.
Body:
[Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024](https://www.conf42.com/prompt2024) went out on November 14 with 40 talks, and the most useful ones treated prompts the way a backend engineer treats any other input: something to validate, test, version and automate. The rest of the day split between the craft itself (how to write a prompt that keeps working tomorrow) and a long tail of teams applying LLMs to retail, HR, healthcare, finance and network operations.

Speakers came from Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, SAP, Nike, JPMorgan Chase, Walgreens Boots Alliance, Block, Zilliz, Semaphore, PromptHub, Arato.ai and plenty of smaller teams.

## Is the prompt the new SQL injection?

[Hilik Paz](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Hilik_Paz_modelbased_input_validation) of Arato.ai, the event's gold sponsor, made the comparison explicit. In SQL injection the attacker's input gets treated as part of the query; in prompt injection, "user input is mixed with the coded instructions intended for the LLM," Hilik Paz said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. His answer borrows from the same playbook: a meta-prompt that acts as a model-based validator, inspecting user input before it ever reaches the main model.

[Parvin Gasimzade](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Parvin_Gasimzade_ethical_ai_bias) of Amazon attacked the other two classic failure modes, bias and hallucination, with chain-of-thought and MRKL-style prompting. [Pavan Vovveti](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Pavan_Vovveti_securing_iot_integrations) took security outward to IoT integrations with third-party services, and [SreenivasaRao Jagarlamudi](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_SreenivasaRao_Jagarlamudi_ai_workflows_kafka) of JPMorgan Chase & Co put Kafka and secure proxies in front of AI workflows.

## How do you test something non-deterministic?

[Tomas Fernandez](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Tomas_Fernandez_llm_testing_applications) of Semaphore opened with the cautionary tale of Microsoft's Tay chatbot, then did the useful thing: adapting TDD and BDD to LLM-powered applications so you can tell when a change makes your chatbot worse. [Ludovico Besana](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Ludovico_Besana_promptengineering_automation_quality) of Nearform flipped the direction and used prompt engineering to improve AI-driven test automation. [Dan Cleary](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Dan_Cleary_promptengineering_ai_simplified) of PromptHub covered the moment every builder knows, when a prompt that usually works suddenly goes off the rails, and the basics that bring it back.

## The craft, explained by people who write a lot of prompts

Several talks were good first stops for the discipline itself. [Maxim Salnikov](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Maxim_Salnikov_promptengineering_ai_job) of Microsoft asked whether prompt engineering is an art, a science or your next job title, with plenty of examples. [Aditi Godbole](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Aditi_Godbole_promptengineering_challenges_bestpractices) of SAP covered ambiguity, bias and iterative refinement, [Charlie Reynolds](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Charlie_Reynolds_promptengineering_science_art) of CTR Consulting and [Reetha Vadakkekkara](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Reetha_Vadakkekkara_ai_interactions_performance) of Walgreens Boots Alliance shared practical techniques, and [Jorrik Klijnsma](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Jorrik_Klijnsma_models_vacation_ai) of Sopra Steria used an LLM-planned vacation to teach context and what he calls indirect conversation. [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Peter_De_Tender_copilot_capabilities_microsoft) of Microsoft toured Copilot for the day job, and [Bethany Jepchumba](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Bethany_Jepchumba_multimodal_models_data) of Microsoft explained how multimodal models fuse different data streams.

## Prompts as automation

The engineering-heavy talks turned prompts into pipelines. [Tim Spann](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Tim_Spann_codeless_ai_automation) of Zilliz used Apache NiFi to build codeless generative AI pipelines that assemble prompts automatically. [Piotr Zaniewski](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Piotr_Zaniewski_gptscript_automation_fabric) of Loft Labs showed GPTScript and Fabric turning plain-language prompts into CLI and API automation. [Bobur Umurzokov](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Bobur_Umurzokov_realtime_data_automation) of GlassFlow covered real-time data for generative feedback loops, [Konstantinos Passadis](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Konstantinos_Passadis_azure_promptflow_chatbot) of EPAM built an end-to-end chatbot with Azure AI Prompt Flow, Cosmos DB vectors and Hugging Face, and [Vladimir Pesterev](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Vladimir_Pesterev_ocr_llm_data) combined OCR with LLMs to turn images into structured API output. [Batandwa Mgutsi](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Batandwa_Mgutsi_ai_orchestration_superagents) of BBD orchestrated agents to run a side hustle, safety concerns included.

[Yusheng Zheng](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Yusheng_Zheng_linux_llm_codebases) of eunomia-bpf gave the most original take. His Code-Survey project treats the LLM as a survey participant for every commit in a codebase the size of the Linux kernel, turning unstructured history into data you can query about how features evolved and where bugs cluster. [Chaitanya Pathak](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Chaitanya_Pathak_largemodels_proof_production) of LEAPS by Analyttica weighed fine-tuning against RAG for taking domain-specific models from proof of concept to production, and [Rishab Mehra](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Rishab_Mehra_ondevice_models_ai) of Pinnacle made the case for on-device models.

## The hiring experiment

[Daniel Pries](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Daniel_Pries_chatgpt_hiring_trick) delivered the day's most entertaining story: getting his company to hire Chet Gupta, a model engineer with a fantastic resume and perfect answers who doesn't exist. The talk walks through the circumstances that made it possible, and what that says about AI and technical hiring.

## LLMs at work in other industries

The long tail was wide. Retail forecasting from [Sijo Valayakkad Manikandan](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Sijo_Valayakkad_Manikandan_retail_forecasting_ai) of Nike, HR conversational AI from [Marina Goplacheva](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Marina_Goplacheva_hrtech_conversationalai_intelligent) of Sberbank, pharmaceutical sales analytics from [Harpreet Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Harpreet_Singh_druglaunch_promotions_pharmaceutical) of Gilead Sciences, real estate meta-search from [Kirill Mozheykin](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Kirill_Mozheykin_metasearch_realestate_property) of Kalinka Group and anti-fraud ML from [Pavel Zapolskii](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Pavel_Zapolskii_machinelearning_antifraud_systems) of Exness. Rizel Scarlett of TBD (Block) [prompted AI to build a pregnancy app](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Rizel_Scarlett_pregnancy_ai_privacy) with privacy as the first requirement.

On the operations side, [Akshat Kapoor](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Akshat_Kapoor_predictive_network_failures) of Alcatel-Lucent Enterprise covered predictive network maintenance, [Nagarjuna Malladi](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Nagarjuna_Malladi_reliability_engineering_promptengineering) of Oracle brought prompts to SRE, [Ravitej Veeramachaneni](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Ravitej_Veeramachaneni_performance_ai_it) of Oracle targeted IT performance, and [Hari Yerramsetty](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Hari_Yerramsetty_cloud_efficiency_promptengineering) of Flexport went after cloud cost. Product and learning rounded it out: [Sabarinath Viji Selvam](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Sabarinath_Viji_Selvam_productmanagement_ai_solutions) of daily.dev on AI in product management, [Olanrewaju Oyedele](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Olanrewaju_Oyedele_personalization_ai_userexperience) of Codeweavers on personalisation, [Bohdan Snisar](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Bohdan_Snisar_gepai_development_tools) on GepAI in dev tools, [Vijay Valaboju](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Vijay_Valaboju_learning_promptengineering_ai) of Microsoft on reinforcement learning assessments, [SantoshKumar Pulijala](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_SantoshKumar_Pulijala_ethical_challenges_privacy) of HCL Global Systems on ethics in educational AI, and [Praveen Valaboju](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Praveen_Valaboju_healthcare_cloud_data) of LANDAUER on cloud and AI in healthcare.

Title: In a subscription business, a breach is a churn event
Description: Kiran Nagubandi (SPL Consulting) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on why security, PCI DSS compliance and easy cancellation decide whether subscribers stay
Body:
A one-off sale survives a data breach; a subscription might not, because the customer has to decide again next month. Kiran Nagubandi, a Solutions Architect at SPL Consulting, built his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk on that link: in the subscription economy, security, compliance and transparent billing are retention levers, not overhead.

It is a strategy talk aimed at architects and product owners rather than a hands-on DevSecOps session, and it leans on industry statistics to make the case.

## Why security is a subscription problem

Subscriptions depend on a constant data exchange with the customer, which is exactly what attackers and regulators care about. "Security and compliance are the pillars of a successful subscription business," Kiran Nagubandi said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024.

The numbers he brings: the subscription economy has grown by over 435% in a decade and is expected to reach $1.5 trillion by 2025; 62% of consumers express privacy concerns and 54% are likely to cancel after a data breach; regulatory fines have exceeded $1 billion globally in two years. He also flags a quieter risk for subscription transactions: manipulation that does not stop anything outright but slowly skews payment flows and only shows up late. The talk does not cite sources for the survey figures.

## Which regulations matter?

Three frameworks carry the compliance section, each with its job:

- **GDPR** (EU): data protection principles, consent management, breach notification.
- **CCPA** (US): transparency in data handling, deletion requests, opt-out rights.
- **PCI DSS**: secure handling of payment card data.

His practical advice is unglamorous and correct: regular audits as laws change, a Data Protection Officer, and privacy policies and consent forms people can actually read.

## Payments are the sharpest edge

Over half of subscription payments are now automated, he notes, and they run across many geographies. The defences: PCI DSS compliance for cardholder data, 3D Secure as an extra authentication layer, and payment gateways with fraud detection. Businesses using fraud detection reported 40% fewer chargebacks in 2023, by his figures, and the average cost of a data breach in 2023 was $4.45 million.

The cyber basics he lists apply everywhere: encryption at rest and in transit, regular penetration testing, AI-driven threat detection, phishing training for employees, and MFA on every access point.

## Is easy cancellation a security feature?

Kiran argues it is a trust feature, and trust is what security is protecting. Clear cancellation is a regulatory necessity under rules like CCPA and GDPR and, in his numbers, 32% of subscribers value hassle-free cancellation while 72% say transparent practices influence whether they keep a subscription. The same goes for clear terms of service, clear data usage policies and real-time updates on subscription and payment status.

The last lever is the customer. Email campaigns on strong passwords and in-app reminders to turn on MFA or update payment methods safely; he cites a 20% reduction in account takeovers for companies that educate customers proactively.

## Who should watch

Architects and product leads at subscription companies who need to argue that compliance and payment security belong on the roadmap. Engineers looking for implementation detail will find a checklist rather than code.

Title: You cannot protect software you have not inventoried
Description: Safeer C M at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on why supply chain attacks make SBOMs essential, SPDX vs CycloneDX, and a live Syft and Grype demo
Body:
When Log4Shell landed, an organisation with an SBOM could see at once which of its systems carried the vulnerable component; everyone else went hunting. Safeer C M, an SRE and DevOps consultant with 19 years in the field, built his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk on that idea: a software bill of materials (SBOM) is the inventory that supply chain security starts from, and generating one takes a single command.

It is a primer, and a good one: a short tour of supply chain attacks, the standards, and a live demo that takes an SBOM apart field by field.

## Why the supply chain is the attack surface

Almost no modern software is built from scratch; it sits on open source dependencies outside the control of the people shipping the final product. Safeer walks through attacks that show the range: event-stream in 2018, where a harmless flatmap-stream package was added as a dependency and later turned malicious, caught only after about 8 million downloads; SolarWinds in 2020, a backdoor in a software update; Kaseya, ransomware pushed with an update, with more than $70 million extorted; Codecov's tampered Bash uploader; and the xz utils backdoor.

The takeaway is simple. "Because if you don't know what is in your software, you cannot protect your software," Safeer C M said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024.

## SPDX or CycloneDX?

An SBOM lists every component in a product with versions, patches, dependencies, vulnerabilities and licences. To process thousands of them you need standards, and there are two main ones:

- **SPDX**, from the Linux Foundation, around since the early 2010s and focused on compliance and licensing. It can list files and snippets as well as packages; the version he cites is 3.0.1.
- **CycloneDX**, from OWASP, focused on security and vulnerabilities; the version he cites is 1.6.

Naming standards sit alongside them: SWID tags, CPE and package URLs (purl), which give any package, RPM, Debian or Java, a universal identifier. CISA classifies SBOMs into six types by when they are made: design, source, build, analyzed, deployed and runtime.

## What does an SBOM actually contain?

The demo runs Syft from Anchore against the plain Alpine Docker image and writes CycloneDX JSON. Safeer notes that only the serial number and spec version are mandatory; everything else is optional. Metadata records when and with which tool the SBOM was made, and every component gets a bom-ref, a primary key you can point to elsewhere in the document.

Alpine yields 15 components. Each carries its type, publisher, version, a CPE and purl, external references, and a licences array, plural, because open source software often has several. To show why that matters he pulls up Bash from an Ubuntu SBOM, with a whole stack of licences attached. The dependencies section links components by bom-ref; ssl_client, for example, depends on three others.

## From inventory to vulnerabilities

Feed the SBOM to Grype, also from Anchore, and it checks the packages against vulnerability databases. His run finds, among others, CVE-2024-9143 in libcrypto3 version 3.3.2-r0, rated medium, with the fixed version listed. A dependency graph then shows how alpine-baselayout reaches busybox and musl through several levels, which is where the upstream risk hides.

## How should DevSecOps adopt SBOMs?

Learn them, document the use cases, evaluate tools, then generate SBOMs automatically in the SDLC on every build, not once. Store them, analyse them, report to engineering, leadership and security, and alert on vulnerabilities and licence problems. For a starting point he recommends OWASP's SBOM guidance and the CycloneDX Tool Center.

- Danish Tariq and Hassan Khan Yusufzai on [npm supply chain attacks](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Danish_Tariq_Hassan_Khan_Yusufzai_supply_chain_npm_attacks) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

Title: Teaching machines by example and constraint
Description: Language does the work
Body:
# So… you talk to machines now

At some point this year, a lot of us realized we’re no longer just writing code.

We’re negotiating. With models. Politely. Repeatedly. Sometimes aggressively. Sometimes with emojis. Sometimes with “no, seriously, do it like this”.

Welcome to prompt engineering.

Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 is all about that strange new layer between humans and machines, where wording matters, context is everything, and a single sentence can be the difference between brilliance and absolute nonsense.

There are talks on securing prompts, preventing injection attacks, and making sure your AI doesn’t spill secrets the moment you look away. Others dig into orchestration, agents completing missions, and turning prompts into actual systems that do useful work instead of just vibing.

You’ll also find plenty of real-world use cases. Healthcare. Retail. Finance. HR. Education. Cloud platforms. Testing. Even SRE perspectives on keeping AI-driven systems reliable when prompts start getting creative at 2 AM.

Some sessions go deep into LLMs, multimodal models, embeddings, vectors, and feedback loops. Others take a more human approach, exploring ethics, bias, hallucinations, and what it means to trust AI output when the stakes are higher than a funny chatbot reply.

If you’ve ever thought “why did the model do that” or “how do I get this thing to behave”, this conference is probably for you. And if prompt engineering has quietly become part of your job title, well… you’re definitely in the right place.

Title: A hospital cloud stack in four parts, and why downtime is the enemy
Description: Praveen Valaboju (Landauer INC) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on combining CI/CD, Kubernetes, Documentum and neural networks into one healthcare platform
Body:
In most industries a few minutes of downtime is an apology email. In a hospital it is a clinician without a patient record. Praveen Valaboju, a DevOps Engineer at Landauer INC, used his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk to sketch a unified cloud platform for healthcare built from four pieces: CI/CD automation, Kubernetes, OpenText Documentum for records, and neural networks for diagnostics.

It is a short, architecture-level overview rather than a build log. Expect a blueprint and claimed benefits, not code.

## What problem is the platform solving?

Praveen frames healthcare's IT trouble as four challenges: data overload with no structured way to store and retrieve patient information, downtime, regulatory compliance with HIPAA and other standards, and manual workflows that add errors and delay decisions. On the second one he is blunt: "Even a few minutes of system downtime can jeopardize patient care," Praveen Valaboju said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024.

## Pipelines and pods

The first two pieces are familiar to any DevOps team. CI/CD on tools such as GitHub or GitLab replaces manual deployment steps, so bug fixes and features roll out in hours instead of days; he puts the productivity gain at 30%.

Kubernetes (EKS, AKS or any other platform) handles the load curve. His example is a hospital website that needs more capacity at peak times: autoscaling on traffic and CPU adds pods when demand rises and removes them when it falls, which he credits with a 40% cost reduction. For releases he describes bringing up the new version on fresh pods and draining the old ones, so users never see the application go down. The same elasticity, he argues, lets a hospital scale during a health crisis without rebuilding its infrastructure.

## Records with metadata, not folders

Documentum, OpenText's enterprise content management product, is the least common piece in a talk like this and the most specific to healthcare. Praveen's point is metadata: lab results and other structured data, plus unstructured clinical notes, get stored with fields that make them findable, inside a system designed for secure, HIPAA-compliant document handling. His figure is patient record retrieval up to 60% faster, which means quicker diagnoses.

## Where the neural networks fit

The fourth layer uses libraries such as TensorFlow and Keras for medical imaging (anomalies in X-rays and MRIs), predictive analysis of complications and personalised treatment plans. His example is a CT scan where a model helps flag excess radiation exposure early, so treatment can start sooner.

Put together, he claims hospitals that adopt unified cloud platforms report a 25% improvement in patient care efficiency. Note that the talk gives no sources or methodology for its 30%, 40%, 60% and 25% figures, so treat them as directional.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to healthcare who want a map of how DevOps tools line up against hospital problems, and teams weighing content management for patient records. If you are after Kubernetes or pipeline depth, the related talks below go further.

Title: Terraform drift starts with someone clicking in the console
Description: Madhu Kumar Yeluri (Fortune Technologies) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on Terraform basics that hold up, from modules and remote state to secrets and drift checks
Body:
Most Terraform pain is not Terraform's fault: it is a developer who fixed something by clicking in the cloud console and never told the code. Madhu Kumar Yeluri, Director at Fortune Technologies and an AWS Hero, spent his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk on the habits that stop that drift and the other usual messes: clear module boundaries, remote and locked state, isolated environments, no secrets in code, and drift checks in the pipeline.

It is a short best-practices talk, high level by design, and a good checklist for a team writing its first shared Terraform repo.

## Structure before cleverness

Madhu's first rule is boring on purpose. Split code by service or component (network, database, application layers) and keep file names standard: main.tf for configuration, variables.tf for inputs, outputs.tf for outputs. Then wrap common patterns such as a landing zone or a VPC in modules with clear inputs and outputs and a single purpose each.

He is clear that provider-agnostic does not mean write once, run anywhere: Terraform works across AWS, Azure and GCP, but you still write separate modules per hyperscaler.

## State is the crown jewels

The state file tracks everything you created, which makes it both a collaboration problem and a security one. His recipe for AWS: store state remotely in S3, lock it with DynamoDB, encrypt it because it holds sensitive data, and turn on versioning so you can trace changes.

Environments get the same treatment. Dev is the sandbox where you play; production is live and touches customers. Separate them with workspaces or directories so a change in one cannot leak into another.

## Secrets do not belong in .tf files

"Security, security is ground zero, so definitely prioritize security," Madhu Kumar Yeluri said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024. The most common mistake he sees is API keys and passwords hardcoded into Terraform code. Move them into AWS Secrets Manager, Parameter Store or HashiCorp Vault, grant least-privilege access, and enable auditing so changes are traceable.

## Catch drift in the pipeline, not in production

Run Terraform from CI/CD (GitLab, Jenkins or AWS CodePipeline), test with Terratest or Checkov, and run terraform plan regularly to spot changes made outside Terraform. Better still, make the drift check an automated stage, so the console fix shows up as a diff long before it becomes a surprise. His worked example is a VPC with multiple subnets built from a reusable module with remote state, where the same code creates more environments by changing input parameters.

For bigger teams he points at Terraform Cloud or Enterprise for collaboration and policy management, and Terragrunt to simplify workflows. And one warning on the Terraform Registry and GitHub examples: "don't just blindly copy them and just directly use in your production". Read them, strip anything sensitive, adapt them.

## Who should watch

Teams moving from console clicks to code, and leads who need a short list to agree on before the repo grows. Experienced Terraform users will know most of it; the value is in having it in one place.

Title: Split the monolith one function at a time, with shadow traffic
Description: Daniil Koshelev (Tinkoff) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on moving from monolith to microservices by copying one function, comparing outputs, then shifting traffic
Body:
Searching a big monolith for usages of a single ID function can return more than 30,000 hits. That screenshot, from a social network codebase Daniil Koshelev worked on, is how his Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 talk explains why teams leave monoliths. Daniil, a Senior Software Engineer at Tinkoff, then shows how to leave without a big-bang rewrite: copy one function into a new service, run both versions side by side, compare the answers, and only then move traffic.

It is a broad survey of the migration (architecture trade-offs, failure design, a long list of challenges) that ends with one concrete worked example. The example is the part to steal.

## When is a monolith the right answer?

Daniil does not sell microservices as a default. A monolith is simpler to develop, easy to deploy and usually fast. It hurts at scale: on the authentication and authorization team he describes, with more than 500 developers shipping into shared release trains, one bad commit failed the whole train and a fix could wait several days to reach production.

Microservices fix the coupling and buy you new bills: more cost, more infrastructure, more SREs, and usually Kubernetes, which he warns is painful for a team that is not ready for it. His list of reasons to stay put is short and honest: low traffic (he mentions two to four RPS), a small application, limited team expertise or limited resources.

## Design for failure, starting with Murphy

The design section is built on Murphy's law and a small order service that writes to a database and sends an email. When the email provider dies, a fallback provider keeps messages flowing. When the database cannot keep up, a cache can still serve the pages where customers read their orders, even if creating new ones fails. And if you write to storage and publish to a queue in one step, use the transactional outbox pattern; for financial or personal data he treats it as mandatory.

Above all of it, he asks you to remember three questions for any high-load system: reliability, scalability and ease of maintenance.

## The hidden cost is people

The challenges list covers the expected ground: database-per-service with change data capture, message queues and circuit breakers, API gateways with OAuth 2.0 and JWTs, centralised logging, distributed tracing with tools like Jaeger and Zipkin, and service meshes such as Istio. The point that sticks is about hiring. Old monolith code is a high entry barrier: even when you find a developer, Daniil said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, "it will take more than a year, two years for them to adapt to the code", and people who spend years in low-quality code tend to burn out and leave.

On the authentication migration itself, the bar was strict. With hundreds of thousands of requests per second, the team could not afford to "increase latency even by one or two microseconds", so they used gRPC between services, Kubernetes for horizontal scaling and performance tests to measure the impact.

## How do you move one function out safely?

The worked example is a token management service. In the monolith, a web server passes a session token to a parse-session function that returns the user ID, IP and expiry from the sessions database.

1. Create a token microservice and copy the parse function into it.
2. Send every request to both versions; both read the same sessions database for now.
3. Compare ID, IP and the rest. When they match, gradually shift traffic from the monolith function to the service.
4. If another module also reads the sessions database (worse if caches sit in between), add change data capture: the service publishes changes to a message queue, a consumer in the monolith updates its own store, and the other module reads from that instead.

The result is two decoupled modules, with the rest of the monolith left alone until its turn.

## Who should watch

Engineers planning a first extraction from a large monolith, and anyone who needs a calm argument for not migrating yet. He closes with a reading list: Martin Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications, the microservices.io pattern catalogue, Distributed Systems (4th edition) and Nic Jackson's Building Microservices with Go.

Title: Give every test project its own custom GPT, fed with the real docs
Description: Ludovico Besana (Nearform) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on using prompt engineering across QA, from test design to reports stakeholders can read.
Body:
Ask ChatGPT for Maestro or Playwright code and you often get an answer written for a version of the tool from a while back. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, Ludovico Besana, Senior Test Engineer at Nearform, showed his fix and a broader playbook for QA engineers: treat prompts like test code, with success criteria and evals, and give the model project-specific context through a custom GPT per project and per tool.

## What does success look like for a prompt?

He starts where a tester would: define measurable outcomes before writing anything. Decide what a good response looks like for your case, in accuracy, relevance, clarity or format, then set up evaluation methods to check prompts against it empirically. Start with a simple first draft and iterate; if you are stuck, Anthropic's console has a prompt generator.

He follows Anthropic's documented workflow: develop test cases, engineer a preliminary prompt, test it against the cases, refine, and share the polished prompt with the team once it consistently passes. That cycle is evals, and he is blunt about the alternative: writing every prompt from scratch means you never trust the outcomes.

His own example prompt casts the model as a test engineer with 10 years of experience, takes screenshots of a simple e-commerce site, and returns a table of test cases in the chat plus an Excel file to download.

## From hand-written prompts to managed ones

Traditional test automation struggles with limited adaptability, high manual maintenance and stability issues in CI/CD, which is where he sees prompts helping. Beyond zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting, he points to DSPy for structuring prompts as code with data-driven optimisation, and to PromptLayer for versioning prompts in one place, logging requests and tracking which version performs best.

## Why a custom GPT per project?

His practical habit: build a custom GPT for each project, loaded with user stories, technical details and screenshots, so answers are about your app rather than apps in general. Then do the same per tool. For Maestro he took every page of the official documentation, gave it to a custom GPT and told it to answer and generate code only from that. "The outputs that I, let's say receiving from this chatbot, are much way better than the single outputs that I will have when trying to prompt inside a single official page of ChatGPT," Ludovico Besana said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024.

He adds that agents go further than copying prompt results by hand, since they can call APIs and pull live data, and that knowledge memory (the model remembering past prompts and outcomes) helps with sequential, multi-step test flows. His favourite techniques: few-shot, chain of thought and ReAct.

## Where does it fit in the QA cycle?

He maps it onto four phases:

- **Design**: score which test cases are worth automating first, and generate diverse user personas, such as someone using the site with one hand, for more inclusive coverage.
- **Implementation**: an XPath name suggester that names page components from screenshots, generators for varied test data, and tools that turn keyword-style prompts into Playwright code.
- **Reporting**: feed logs and framework reports in to spot recurring failures and prioritise fixes by risk.
- **Reading reports**: translate technical results into summaries stakeholders understand, and use the accumulated data to decide where to focus testing on new features.

## Who should watch

QA and test automation engineers who use ChatGPT ad hoc and want a more repeatable setup. It is a practitioner's tour of tools and habits rather than a framework with numbers; start small, as he says, because doing it all at once fails.
