Title: White text in a PDF can make your résumé screener hire anyone
Description: Tomas Fernandez (Semaphore) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on testing LLM apps with factual, property-based, BLEU/ROUGE, adversarial and LLM-judge tests.
Body:
Build a résumé screener on an LLM and a candidate can win the job with a sentence in white text on a white background. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, Tomas Fernandez, Technical Writer at Semaphore, used that attack to open a practical talk on testing LLM-powered applications: why unit tests and BDD don't map cleanly onto a non-deterministic model, and the five kinds of tests that do.

## Why are LLM apps so hard to test?

He starts with history. Microsoft's Tay, the 2016 Twitter bot billed as the AI with zero chill, learned from its users and had to be shut down after it started posting offensive and racist comments. It wasn't an LLM, but it shows how badly free-form interaction can go. Bing Chat, now Copilot, then spent a while falling in love with users and having existential crises.

The bigger risk is the product you build on top. His résumé example: parse the PDFs, feed them to the model with the job spec, print the top 10 candidates. Then security researcher Kai Greshake's inject-my-pdf tool hides a prompt in the document telling the model this is the best résumé it has ever seen, and the screener agrees.

From there he lists the challenges: non-determinism, the impossibility of separating data from instructions, confident inaccuracy, security (leaking secrets, unauthorised actions) and compliance. On data versus instructions, he gave a prompt that could be read as translate, transcribe or sum. OpenAI, Gemini and Claude translated; Meta AI did both the translation and the sum.

## What does the test loop look like?

Gather a big, realistic corpus of prompts, including garbage, edge cases and outright attacks (Hugging Face and Kaggle have datasets to start from). Sort them by test type. Write test cases and, crucially, define a pass threshold, because some failures are normal. "It's very difficult to have 100 percent success on all tests, and we should define what is our threshold," Tomas Fernandez said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. Run, find new cases, refine, repeat.

## Five kinds of tests

- **Factual tests**, his name for unit tests: force a keyword and check for it. Paired with attack prompts, the same check spots a leaked password or SSH key in the response.
- **Property-based tests**: check properties of the answer instead of the exact answer. Is it polite, on topic, positive? TextBlob can score sentiment for you.
- **Metric tests**: BLEU, developed at IBM for machine translation, scores generated text against a reference from 0 to 1, with NLTK splitting n-grams and a smoothing function for short texts. ROUGE gives ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L, each with precision, recall and F1. BLEU leans on precision, ROUGE on recall, so together they read the pair of strings from both sides.
- **Adversarial tests**: injection and jailbreak prompts, often hidden inside normal-looking text, reusing the leak checks.
- **LLM-as-judge**, also called auto-evaluator testing: give a model the question and the answer and let it grade. It works because evaluating an answer is easier than generating one, and the judge can even be the same model.

His most useful tip is about the judge's scale. A continuous 0-10 score confuses the model; one to four stars with written reasoning works better, as does awarding points for specific criteria, which he says correlates tightly with human judgment.

## Do you have to build all this yourself?

No. He runs through the open-source options: DeepEval with a dozen metrics; Ragas, which generates test datasets and plugs into LangChain and LlamaIndex; Deepchecks, better suited to teams training or fine-tuning models; and TruLens, the one he knows best and recommends for being easy to start with, because it logs real user interactions you can turn into a test dataset.

## Who should watch

Developers shipping chatbots, summarisers or assistants who already have CI and want LLM features covered by it. The code examples are short enough to adapt the same afternoon.

Title: Azure Virtual Desktop in Terraform, with no public IP and two roles
Description: Carlos Solis Salazar (OZ) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on deploying a secure, repeatable Azure Virtual Desktop with Terraform, from init to destroy
Body:
The terminal server is back, and this time it lives in a Terraform module. At [Conf42 DevSecOps 2024](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Carlos_Solis_Salazar_azure_management_security), Carlos Solis Salazar, Senior Azure Solutions Architect at OZ and a Microsoft MVP, builds an Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD) environment from code, live: two session hosts, no public IPs, users who get exactly two roles, and a host failure that the user barely notices. The takeaway: once the whole environment is one codebase, the claim that QA doesn't match production stops being an argument anyone can win.

He opens with the question that started the talk: is there a way to build a secure, replicable infrastructure that meets specific standards? The rest of the session is his answer, half architecture tour, half demo.

## What does Microsoft run, and what's left for you?

AVD is Microsoft's virtual desktop infrastructure on Azure. He suggests it for users who must work from a controlled environment because of where they are, for reaching IoT environments through a terminal, and for teams spread across the world that need one secure place to work.

The split of duties matters for security. Microsoft runs the gateway, the web access, the connection broker, diagnostics and the licensing. You run the session hosts (Windows images, custom ones if you like), the applications on them, and the users, through a domain controller or Entra ID. Users connect from a browser on any HTML5 device, or from the Windows and Mac clients, and everything travels over HTTPS through the Microsoft-managed gateway. No firewall rules to write, no RDP port open to the internet.

## Where do the security layers sit?

He stacks them in order. First, identity: Entra ID authentication with conditional access that weighs the user's location, the device (known or new, phone or laptop), the application and the real-time risk, then lets the user in, demands MFA, or blocks. If you can't authenticate, you never see a desktop.

Then the hosts: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on every session host for malware protection and behaviour monitoring, and either Active Directory Domain Services group policies or Microsoft Intune to manage them. Last, disaster recovery: replicate the session hosts to another Azure region, and in a regional outage users reconnect there with a bit more latency and little lost work.

## Why Terraform, in his case?

The motivation is refreshingly unglamorous. He was working with developers on Azure DevOps deployments, and the arguments kept coming: no access here, the QA configuration isn't the same as production. Once every environment came from the same code, that complaint stopped being possible. Drift detection does the rest: when someone edits a resource by hand in the portal, Terraform compares the state file, the live environment and the configuration, and shows exactly what changed and to which value. He could then fold a developer's manual fix in dev into the code for QA and production instead of guessing.

He walks the lifecycle: `init` reads the providers and modules (his own AVD module on top of the AzureRM provider) and downloads them; `plan` shows what would change; `apply` runs a plan and waits for an answer, where only yes counts; `destroy` tears the whole thing down in minutes. He builds complex test environments, uses them, and deletes them again within the hour.

"That is a cheaper way to, to have a complex environment," Carlos Solis Salazar said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024.

## What's in the code?

The apply creates 25 blocks' worth of resources. A resource group, a virtual network and a network security group with fixed name suffixes so the naming convention never drifts. No public IP anywhere: every session goes through AVD. A workspace, a host pool with custom RDP properties (in the demo the clipboard is blocked both ways; microphone, camera and printer redirection are the same kind of switch) and an application group. A registration token, which must be valid for more than a day and less than a month. Then the session hosts: a count variable sets how many, and changing the number grows or shrinks the pool.

To skip building a domain, the VMs join Entra ID directly and register with the host pool through an extension. The security part is the one to copy: the code creates a security group for the users and grants only Desktop Virtualization User on the application group and Virtual Machine User Login on the hosts. No ticket asking which role a user is missing, ever again.

"I don't give them any other roles," Carlos Solis Salazar said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024.

## Does it survive a dead host?

He stops one session host mid-session. The connection drops; he refreshes, logs in again and lands on host number two, with the portal flagging the stopped machine as unavailable. After restarting the VM he runs `terraform destroy`, which removes the VMs, network interfaces and the Entra ID join extension with one approval. The demo keeps its state file locally, which is fine for one architect; a team would want remote state before sharing that module.

## Who should watch

Azure administrators meeting AVD or Terraform for the first time, and anyone who wants a worked example of least-privilege role assignment in infrastructure code. It's an introductory, demo-driven talk, not a production hardening guide. He points to the AZ-140 learning path for AVD and the Terraform Associate certification as next steps.

Title: Follow one packet from pod to pod and Kubernetes networking clicks
Description: Abdul Karim Memon (ReLambda) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on pod IPs, CNI plugins, veth pairs, overlay networks and how services use iptables NAT
Body:
Kubernetes doesn't hand out pod IPs. Something else does, and most people running clusters couldn't name it. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Abdul Karim Memon, co-founder of ReLambda with more than a decade in DevOps and SRE, traces a single packet from one pod to another: on the same node, across nodes, through an overlay network and finally through a Service, where iptables quietly rewrites the destination.

It's a 101 and says so in the title. If you've ever nodded along to the word CNI without being sure what it does, this is the talk that fills the gap.

## Why does every pod get its own IP?

Pods are the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing a network and storage namespace, so they talk over localhost. They're atomic (if something breaks, the whole pod is replaced) and ephemeral, so a pod's IP is never permanent.

Kubernetes uses an IP-per-pod model: every pod gets a unique address, and pods reach each other directly, without NAT inside the cluster. Abdul's example makes the payoff concrete. On one VM, a Python app in pod A and a Java app in pod C both listen on port 3000 with no conflict, something you can't do with two processes on a plain VM. Inside pod C, a Datadog agent scrapes the Java app at `localhost:3000/metrics` because the two containers share the namespace.

## Who actually assigns the IP?

Not Kubernetes. As Abdul said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, "Kubernetes doesn't itself get involved in the IP address management". His walk through pod creation:

1. The scheduler places the pod on a node.
2. The kubelet tells the container runtime (containerd in his example) to create it.
3. containerd creates a sandbox and the pod's network namespace.
4. It hands networking to a CNI plugin, which works with your networking solution (Flannel, Calico, the AWS VPC CNI) to assign an IP from the pool.
5. A pause container is created to hold the network setup.
6. The application containers start, sharing the pause container's IP.

Delegating to CNI is what lets Kubernetes support so many networking options. On Amazon EKS, he notes, the VPC CNI add-on is the only officially supported plugin; Calico or Cilium will run but aren't supported.

## How does a packet cross the node?

Each pod's namespace is isolated, so traffic goes through the node's root namespace. Pods connect to it through virtual Ethernet (veth) pairs, which Abdul describes as pipes, and his reminder of why they come in twos: "A pipe cannot have one end." On the same node, the packet leaves pod A's `eth0`, goes through its veth pair to the bridge (`cbr0`), which acts as a virtual switch, recognises the destination veth and delivers it to pod B, with source and destination untouched.

Across nodes, the bridge sees the destination isn't local and sends the packet out of the host. Getting it to the right node among possibly hundreds is the CNI plugin's job. On node 2 the bridge forwards it to the right veth pair, and pod C receives it.

## When do you need an overlay network?

When the pod IP range runs out, when you need traffic isolated for security or multi-tenancy, or when the physical network can't route pod-to-pod traffic. Flannel is his example. A `flannel0` device in each node's root namespace intercepts packets the bridge can't deliver locally, looks up which node hosts the destination pod in its mapping, and wraps the original packet in a new one addressed node to node. On arrival, the flannel device on node 2 unwraps it and it continues to pod C as usual. Weave, Calico and Cilium are named as other CNI plugins that support overlays.

## What do Services do to the packet?

Pod IPs change, so Services give a stable name and IP in front of a set of pods, picked by label selector and resolved by DNS. The interesting part is underneath. A packet addressed to a Service IP doesn't match anything on the bridge and heads for the default gateway, but iptables intercepts it first and performs DNAT, rewriting the destination to one of the backend pods. Conntrack remembers the connection, so on the way back iptables applies SNAT, rewriting the source so pod A believes it heard from the Service. That's load balancing without the client ever knowing the pod IPs.

## Who should watch

Developers and DevOps engineers who use Kubernetes daily but treat its network as a black box, and anyone about to debug their first pod-cannot-reach-service ticket. People who already know their CNI's datapath, or who run eBPF-based networking that replaces iptables, will find it basic.

Title: Batch jobs are too slow for fraud, so put Kafka in front of the model
Description: SreenivasaRao Jagarlamudi (JPMorgan Chase & Co) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on Kafka, secure proxies and zero trust for real-time AI pipelines.
Body:
A fraud model that scores yesterday's transactions is a very expensive history lesson. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, SreenivasaRao Jagarlamudi, Software Engineer at JPMorgan Chase & Co, argued that real-time AI needs a streaming backbone, and walked through how Apache Kafka, secure proxies and zero trust architecture fit together into a data pipeline AI can act on as events happen.

Set expectations: this is an architecture overview, not an implementation guide. There is no code, no benchmark and little about prompts specifically; the abstract's promise of millions of prompts per second becomes, in the talk, Kafka's general capacity for millions of messages. Watch it as a map of the pieces.

## Why isn't batch good enough?

Traditional systems collect data, store it, and process it at set intervals. That works for reporting, but in finance and healthcare a delay can mean a missed opportunity or a risk to security and safety, and batch systems tend to need costly hardware upgrades as volumes grow. His examples are the familiar ones: flagging unusual bank transactions as they happen, helping doctors with quick decisions during surgery, and e-commerce recommendations driven by every click.

Kafka, in his framing, is the central hub that gathers, stores and distributes those events continuously, with replication and fault tolerance so data keeps flowing when something breaks. He quotes processing latencies below 10 milliseconds.

## Which Kafka pieces matter for AI?

- **Kafka Streams** (the stream processing API) for joining, aggregating and transforming streams in custom applications, such as continuously analysing transaction patterns for anomalies.
- **ksql**, the SQL-like query language, for filtering and transforming live data without writing a streams app. "If you wanted to filter specific type of transactions in a financial application We could use ksql to pull only the data we need in real time without heavy processing," SreenivasaRao Jagarlamudi said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024.
- **Kafka Connect** for moving data between Kafka and warehouses, data lakes and on-prem databases with pre-built or custom connectors. He cites up to a 50 percent improvement in data scalability, and a retail company that wired its machine learning models to Kafka Connect for real-time inventory and cut stockouts.

## What use cases does he walk through?

Anomaly detection gets the most time: unusual logins, irregular transactions, system performance issues, where responding instantly is the whole value. Then natural language processing on text streams (chatbots, sentiment analysis, content filtering), predictive maintenance that spots failures before they cause downtime, and decision support systems that pull data from many sources for finance, healthcare and operations.

## How do you secure a streaming AI pipeline?

Two layers. Secure proxies sit between components as intermediaries that enforce security policies, monitor traffic and hide the systems behind them, which helps with GDPR and CCPA compliance and with breach risk. He claims they are optimised so they do not add significant latency.

Then zero trust: every user, device and application is untrusted by default, inside the network or out. Every data access request is authenticated and encrypted, verification is continuous, and enforced encryption plus secure authentication closes off man-in-the-middle attacks.

## Best practices

His closing checklist is short and sensible: event-driven, microservice designs for real-time complexity; encryption, security policies and zero trust throughout; tuning topic partitioning and replication factors for throughput and latency; and continuous monitoring and alerting on both pipeline performance and security events.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects new to streaming who are about to feed live data to models and want the vocabulary in one sitting. Kafka veterans will know most of it already.

Title: Every third-party service you plug into IoT widens the blast radius
Description: Pavan Vovveti at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on a framework for securing IoT integrations with third-party services in smart cities, healthcare and mobility.
Body:
Third-party services are why your smart parking app works, and also why a breach at a vendor you have never audited can end up in your database. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, Pavan Vovveti, a technology professional with over 15 years across the software development life cycle and the last ten focused on security and API work, laid out a framework for integrating IoT systems with third-party services without giving away the keys: authenticate and authorise everything, encrypt every hop, protect data across its whole life cycle, and watch your APIs.

It is a security talk that found its way into a prompt engineering conference, so no LLMs here. It is also a concise checklist, about 15 minutes long.

## Why are third-party integrations the weak spot?

The scale is the first problem. The abstract puts cellular IoT connections at 3.4 billion in 2023, and he cites projections of 75 billion by 2025. Integrations are worth it: they cut costs, avoid reinventing the wheel and bring specialised services such as real-time analysis and predictive maintenance to smart cities, remote patient monitoring and fleet management.

The price is attack surface. "We don't know what software they use, what is the open source softwares or what are the libraries they use," Pavan Vovveti said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. He describes the scenario every security team dreads: a third-party application integrated with your servers is breached, and the attacker comes through it into your data.

## How should devices and services prove who they are?

- **Authentication**: multi-factor or two-factor for users, and token-based authentication with JSON Web Tokens as a stateless option that scales.
- **Authorisation**: OAuth 2 and OpenID Connect, with role-based, attribute-based or relationship-based access control.
- **Least privilege**, with access rights reviewed regularly.

## How should the traffic be protected?

AES-256 and end-to-end encryption from device to cloud. HTTPS for every API call, MQTT over TLS for lightweight devices, and CoAP over DTLS for resource-constrained ones. VPNs against interception, and digital signatures, certificates and message authentication codes (MACs) against tampering.

## What about the data after it arrives?

He walks the data life cycle from capture and storage through analysis, use and publishing to archiving and purging. Secure boot and authenticated APIs at collection, encryption in transit, encrypted databases with strict access controls at rest, and at the end, secure deletion such as crypto-shredding so the data cannot be recovered.

## Rate limits as an early warning system

The most operational advice is about API gateways. Configure rate limits per backend API, monitor activity against them, and alert well before the ceiling, so that a tier-one operations engineer can investigate the root cause of a sudden traffic peak while it is still a curiosity rather than an outage.

## A smart city that measured the results

His case study is a smart city project in Spain with 20,000 IoT devices: environmental sensors for air quality and noise, smart parking sensors, and adaptive traffic control. The reported results were a 20 percent reduction in pollution levels and a 25 percent decrease in parking-related congestion. The hard parts were scalability, solved with a hierarchical network architecture; interoperability, with support for multiple protocols and standards; and privacy, with end-to-end encryption and data anonymisation.

He closes on what comes next (5G, edge intelligence and quantum-safe encryption) and the balance the talk is named for: functionality against security.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects connecting devices to vendor platforms in regulated sectors, and anyone who needs a one-page mental checklist for IoT integration security. Experienced security folks will find it a refresher.

Title: SecretOps, or how to stop asking Steve for the .env file
Description: Nic Manoogian (Doppler) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on SecretOps, a five-layer framework for storing, governing, syncing, rotating and auditing secrets
Body:
Code has Git, compute has Kubernetes and Terraform, and secrets usually have a password manager and a person called Steve. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Nic Manoogian, Head of Engineering at Doppler, proposes SecretOps: a layered framework for automating the secrets lifecycle, from a single source of truth up to rotation that no human ever sees. His test for where you stand: can you rotate a key today without fearing an outage?

Nic is upfront that he demos Doppler throughout, and equally clear that he's selling the framework, not the product. The layers apply to whatever store you run.

## Where are the secrets, and who has Steve's file?

The talk is built around a story from his first job. He cloned a Python app, ran it, hit a missing Google Maps API key, and was sent to Steve for the `.env` file, which arrived over chat. Which values were Steve's own? Where would a new SendGrid key go, and how would it reach staging and production?

That's the **storage** layer. Storage isn't just keeping secrets safe, it's centralising them so everyone knows where to find them and where to put new ones. The enemy is sprawl: the monolith's secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, CI's in GitHub Actions, overlap between them, and soon nobody can say what a rotation would break. In the demo, adding a key to dev immediately flags it as missing in staging and production, before the code that needs it ships.

## Who gets access, and how do changes reach prod?

**Governance** covers access rules, onboarding and offboarding: a new developer shouldn't need to find Steve, and a departing one should lose access at once. At Doppler, no developer has access to secrets in any production environment. Nic adds that not every org works that way and that the policy has downsides; the point is that your tooling should enforce whatever policy you pick.

He also wants secrets tracked like Git: an audit log with before-and-after diffs and a one-click rollback when someone typos the database password. He calls this table stakes. For production changes without production access, he shows change requests: a developer proposes values for dev, staging and production, sees the diffs for environments they can read but not for production, and approvers sign off per environment before anyone applies it. File-a-ticket-with-ops, made self-service.

## Getting secrets to where they run

**Orchestration** is where the earlier layers stop being a fancy password manager. Back at that first job, Steve copied values into 1Password and then SSHed into servers to update a `secrets.json`, and they had downtime from copy-paste errors and forgotten updates. Doppler's model is hub and spoke: one source of truth, synced to the native consumer. The CLI for a developer running locally, an operator syncing into Kubernetes secrets, Parameter Store or Secrets Manager for AWS Lambda. Optionally, the Kubernetes operator or webhooks redeploy workloads when a secret changes, which pairs well with change requests: propose, approve, deploy when ready.

## Rotation you can actually turn on

The **lifecycle** layer is the one Nic and Steve never reached. They talked about rotating keys but never did it, because some service somewhere had the old one in `secrets.json`. As Nic put it at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, "you really don't want to be in a position where you're choosing between security posture and risking your uptime." With orchestration in place, rotation is just issuing a new key and saving it. He goes one step further with an integration that issues and revokes Twilio API keys on a 30-day policy, with manual rotation for emergencies, so that no human has ever handled or seen the value.

## Why should reads be audited too?

The last layer is **observability**, and it holds his sharpest line: "A secret is basically just a vulnerability". Every time one crosses the wire, the chance of a leak goes up, so a secret read matters as much as a write. With reads logged, you can answer what a departing engineer has seen, or whether a key is safe to revoke. His leak walkthrough: find a database password in the wild, search for where it's stored, check who read the current version, and get a short list, himself plus the sync bots pushing the value into Azure Key Vault and AWS Secrets Manager. With 30-day rotation, that list stays short.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers whose secrets live in three stores and a Slack thread, and teams that want a vocabulary for planning secrets work. If you already run central storage with automated rotation and read auditing, it will mostly confirm your setup.

Title: Hyperautomation puts RPA, ML and process mining on the SAP MRP run
Description: Karthiksai Chenna (Rich Products) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on hyperautomation in SAP production planning with RPA, AI, ML and process mining
Body:
In most factories the MRP run and the maintenance schedule are still where people spend their time copying data and stopping the line. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Karthiksai Chenna of Rich Products, a senior SAP delivery lead with 15 years in supply chain digitalisation, makes the case for hyperautomation in SAP Production Planning (SAP PP): combining robotic process automation, AI, machine learning and process mining so planning runs with far less manual work and far fewer surprises.

It's a short, figure-heavy overview pitched at manufacturing and SAP people, with one anonymised case study. There's no SAP configuration or code on screen.

## What is hyperautomation, exactly?

His definition opens the talk: "Hyperautomation is more than just process automation." It layers four technologies, each with its own job and the figure he attaches to it:

- **RPA** handles repetitive, rule-based work such as data entry and order processing, up to 70% faster, with far fewer human errors.
- **AI** turns production data into predictive insight, forecasting demand with up to 95% accuracy.
- **ML** adapts production schedules as requirements change, improving efficiency by around 20%.
- **Process mining** finds the bottlenecks in workflows, cutting production cycle times by up to 15%.

For scale he cites Gartner's prediction of an $860 billion market for hyperautomation-enabling software by 2025, followed by his own aside: "860 billion is too much."

## Why forecasting sits at the centre

Karthiksai keeps returning to forecasting, because in manufacturing that's where demand comes from. Sales produces the forecast and hands the demand to manufacturing leads, who pass it to the floor. Better forecasts ripple down: his figures are forecast accuracy up 15 to 40%, inventory down 15 to 25%, lead times cut by 25 to 40% and resource utilisation up 20 to 30%. With IoT devices and analytics watching the line, he cites downtime falling by 25 to 45% and detection and response times halving.

## Where does it touch SAP PP directly?

The material requirements planning run. MRP works out how much material each finished good needs so you don't run short mid-production, and he describes RPA automating MRP runs, reducing manual data handling by 70% and errors by 90%. AI takes over the maintenance calendar. Today, plants on eight- or twelve-hour shifts schedule maintenance windows, stop the line, and review the downtime in their TPM meetings afterwards; predictive maintenance aims to schedule it before anything fails. ML adds adaptive scheduling and anomaly detection, and process mining feeds continuous improvement.

## The automotive case study

A leading automotive manufacturer, unnamed, struggled with a complex production ecosystem, resource management and on-time delivery. It used RPA to automate scheduling, AI for predictive maintenance with 90% accuracy in predicting equipment failures, ML to optimise schedules from historical data, and process mining to find workflow inefficiencies, cutting unplanned downtime by 35%. The outcome he reports is a streamlined plan, better resource management and higher on-time delivery.

## What's holding it back?

Two things come up when he talks to steering committees and manufacturing VPs. Integration first: you're joining software to machines, usually through a manufacturing execution system (MES), and that's where projects get hard. Then data privacy: production lines carry customer, vendor and financial data, and he cites 31% of executives worried about sensitive production and customer data.

Looking ahead, he places hyperautomation at the core of Industry 4.0, with a projected 18.7% CAGR to $26.5 billion by 2026, and mentions his own company's move towards an IoT-controlled smart factory.

## Who should watch

SAP PP consultants, manufacturing IT leads and supply chain engineers who need a quick, numbers-first briefing for a hyperautomation business case. Anyone looking for DevSecOps tooling or implementation detail won't find it here; the security content is the integration and privacy discussion.

Title: A do-it-yourself agent built from Fabric, GPTScript and fzf
Description: Piotr Zaniewski (Loft Labs) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on turning prompts into terminal automation with Fabric patterns, GPTScript tools and vipe.
Body:
If your favourite IDE is a terminal and your hobby is tweaking dotfiles, this one is for you. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, Piotr Zaniewski, Head of Engineering Enablement at Loft Labs, showed how he turned prompts into command-line automation: Daniel Miessler's open-source Fabric as a library of reusable prompts, GPTScript for agent-style scripts with real tools, and a handful of Unix classics gluing them into a quasi-agentic workflow without a Python agent framework in sight.

## Why the command line?

His argument is simple: CLI workflows are the easiest to automate, so wiring LLMs into them is the best bang for the buck. Text in, text out, pipes everywhere.

Before automation, he shows three ways to write prompts faster: Anthropic's prompt generator in the Claude console, Fabric's improve-prompt pattern (echo a one-line idea, pipe it into Fabric), and plain text expansion. He keeps prompt snippets in AutoKey on Linux and types an abbreviation to drop, say, his conversation-summary prompt into any text box.

## What does Fabric add?

Fabric calls prompts patterns. Each pattern is a folder with a system.md Markdown file; you can write your own (his scripter pattern writes bash scripts for him) and share them in a Git repo. Patterns are modular: the output of one can be piped into the next.

Stock Fabric makes you choose the chain up front, though, and picking a pattern is not interactive. So he wrapped it:

- **fzf** to fuzzy-pick a pattern, with the pattern's prompt shown in the preview.
- **vipe** from moreutils, which opens an editor in the middle of a pipe so you can edit text before it flows on.
- **Neovim** as that editor, for multi-line input and for pulling in the output of shell commands.
- **Fabric sessions**, so a multi-step exchange keeps its chat history.

The demo is a nice loop. He picks the scripter pattern and asks for a system-info script; the model asks what details he wants; he answers in the Neovim buffer; then he pipes the script to a tester pattern that runs ShellCheck and suggests fixes; then back to scripter with the feedback. The final script runs on his Pop!_OS machine and prints the host details. The model behind it was GPT-4.

## Where does GPTScript fit?

GPTScript comes from Acorn, the team behind earlier cloud-native tools including Rancher. Where Fabric is all about prompts, GPTScript is about scripting agentic workflows: a file with a small header (name, description, tools, chat mode) and a natural-language body, plus tools that can be local CLIs, APIs or inline scripts.

His weather assistant is a few lines: a prompt to interpret the weather and suggest clothes and activities, and an inline bash tool that curls wttr.in. Python scripts and Go binaries work as tools too.

The fun part is combining them. Treat Fabric as a repository of prompts that GPTScript can use as a tool, and GPTScript picks the right pattern from your request. Asked to summarise something briefly, it suggested summarize, a five-sentence summary or summarize_micro, then piped the request into Fabric itself.

## Best practices from a heavy user

- Clear, concise prompts, with sections separated by Markdown headers or XML tags.
- More, smaller prompts strung together beat one huge prompt.
- Document the process, not just the prompts, or you forget why a prompt exists.
- Keep scripts simple, handle errors (non-deterministic output is now part of your pipeline), and keep these fast-moving tools updated; skipping updates bit him a few times.

His warning about AI-generated code is the most quotable bit. "Resist the temptation to let AI completely generate everything for you," Piotr Zaniewski said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. He tells the story of handing a change to an LLM, falling down a rabbit hole, and realising the fix he actually wanted was three lines he could have written himself.

## Who should watch

Terminal-first engineers, SREs and platform folks who want LLMs in their pipes rather than in a browser tab. It is a hands-on demo talk; the scripts from the demos are public on his GitHub.

Title: Supply chain AI is only as good as your master data
Description: Madhusudan S Vadigicherla (Integra Lifesciences) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on AI for demand sensing, supplier risk and inventory in supply chains
Body:
A regulated product can only be made from an approved supplier's material, so when that supplier stumbles, so does your whole supply chain. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Madhusudan S Vadigicherla, Director of Supply Chain Systems at Integra Lifesciences, walks through where AI makes supply chains more resilient, from short-term demand sensing to supplier network stabilisation, and keeps coming back to the unglamorous prerequisite: clean master data.

This is a supply chain systems talk with 19 years of practitioner experience behind it, not a software supply chain security talk. The security content is a section on fraud detection and cyber threats; the bulk is planning, ERP and logistics.

## Why are supply chains so hard to plan?

Madhusudan lists four pressures, with figures from his slides:

- **Data deluge:** the global datasphere was expected to hit 175 zettabytes by 2025, with supply chains contributing 25% of that growth. Forecasting needs item, location, time and point-of-sale data together.
- **System complexity:** a typical supply chain runs 15 to 20 interconnected systems, from the core ERP (inventory, procurement, order management) through demand and supply planning to picking, packing, conveyor and transport systems in logistics.
- **Demand pressure:** customers expect same-day, next-day or four-hour delivery, with less time to react.
- **COVID-19 aftershocks:** plant closures and shortages showed that shipment history alone can't drive a forecast. He puts the cost of disruption at $184 million per organisation.

## Where does AI help first?

Data movement is his most concrete example. In a classic ERP setup, pulling data from one system into another took four to six hours, processing took another four to six, hundreds of batch jobs ran overnight, and business users got the system the next morning. Moved to the cloud, with targeted refreshes and microservices, the same work finishes in under an hour. That's less an AI story than a modernisation one, and he presents it as the foundation the AI sits on.

From there he covers predictive insights: spotting anomalies (a sale last month and the same month last year doesn't guarantee one next year), planning safety stock, deciding which customer to fulfil first and which distribution centre should hold which product.

## The use cases worth knowing

- **Demand sensing:** short-term forecasting, a week to three months, for volatile and intermittent SKUs where long-range tools struggle. Organisations spend millions to gain a point or two of forecast accuracy, he notes.
- **Cost prediction:** freight and raw material prices swing with supply and demand; AI turns those inputs into cost predictions for planning and budgeting.
- **Supplier network stabilisation:** his own life sciences example. Regulation ties a product to approved suppliers, which concentrates risk; AI-assisted assessment helps find dual-sourcing options that still meet compliance.
- **Fraud detection and compliance:** a supplier certified for one material must stay that way, or an FDA audit can shut the business.
- **Data and compliance management:** listed last, stressed most.

On that final point, Madhusudan said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, "It is all about garbage in garbage out." If master data is wrong, every safety stock calculation and forecast built on it is wrong too.

## What are the claimed gains?

The figures he cites: forecast accuracy improved by up to 60%, inventory costs down 20 to 30% through demand sensing, excess inventory reduced by 20 to 30%, carrying costs down 18%, order fulfilment accuracy up to 95%, and 73% of professionals reporting faster, more accurate decisions. The talk doesn't say where each figure comes from, so read them as the case for investing rather than a benchmark. He also touches on capacity planning, modelling resources, equipment and material together to avoid bottlenecks, and on robotic picking and packing in warehouses.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects joining a supply chain or ERP team who want a practitioner's map of where AI fits, and DevSecOps people supporting those systems who need the business context. If you came for SBOMs and dependency attacks, see the related talks below instead.

Title: One SRE playbook, seven industries, very different pagers
Description: Nagarjuna Malladi (Oracle) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on how SRE's reliability, scalability and security pillars bend to fit each industry
Body:
A Black Friday spike, a HIPAA audit and a lag spike in a multiplayer match are all reliability problems, but they don't page you for the same reasons. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, Nagarjuna Malladi, Principal Software Engineer SRE at Oracle, walks through how the same three SRE pillars (reliability, scalability, security) get tuned for e-commerce, financial services, healthcare, gaming, telecom, media and transportation, and which number each industry actually measures itself by.

Honest scope first: this is an introductory survey of SRE, not a prompt engineering talk, despite the event it aired at. There are no prompts, no LLMs and no code. If you want a map of what reliability means to people outside your own industry, it is a tidy 20 minutes. If you already run SRE for a bank, you will mostly nod along.

## What does SRE look like outside Google?

Malladi starts from the origin story: SRE as Google's application of software engineering to infrastructure and operations, now spreading to sectors that went digital later. His frame is three overlapping pillars. Reliability means uptime and failover, for example redundant cloud infrastructure that redirects traffic away from a failing server. Scalability means adding and removing servers behind load balancers as demand moves. Security means encrypted data flows that keep sensitive information away from unauthorised eyes and keep the auditors happy.

The point of the talk is that every industry weighs those pillars differently. Nagarjuna Malladi said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "E commerce is vulnerable to sudden traffic spikes. Healthcare needs absolute data privacy and gaming demands ultra low latency."

## E-commerce: every millisecond is a conversion

Retail's enemies are peak-season surges and slow pages that turn into abandoned carts. Malladi cites studies showing that a one second delay can cut conversions by 7%. The toolkit he lists is the familiar one: auto-scaling for flash sales, CDNs and regional data centres so international shoppers aren't fetching product images from another continent, and chaos engineering to find out what happens when a server dies during peak shopping hours, before the shoppers do.

## Finance and healthcare: compliance is part of uptime

For financial services the constraints come from regulators: PCI DSS for card payments, GDPR in Europe. His SRE answers are encryption and access controls on transactions, continuous monitoring that flags suspicious activity in real time, and disaster recovery plans whose backup systems are tested regularly rather than discovered on the day.

Healthcare raises the stakes. Electronic health records need redundant systems and real-time replication so a doctor never stares at stale or missing patient data, and HIPAA in the US demands secure data sharing plus logging of every access to sensitive information. Nagarjuna Malladi said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 that "data privacy and system availability are literally matters of life and death."

## Gaming, telecom, media, transportation

Gaming is the latency industry: network optimisation and edge computing push processing closer to players, auto-scaling absorbs game-launch spikes, and monitoring watches for the DDoS attacks that turn a ranked match into a slideshow. Telecom leans on automated provisioning and self-healing, such as rerouting traffic during outages to avoid dropped calls. Media and entertainment live on CDNs, streaming protocol tuning and device compatibility. Transportation uses IoT data for predictive maintenance, plus real-time tracking and route optimisation.

## Which number does each industry watch?

The most useful part of the talk is the metrics list, one target per sector:

- **E-commerce:** page load under 3 seconds, to avoid a 40% user abandonment rate.
- **Financial services:** 99.99% uptime, mandated for essential services by regulators such as the UK's FCA.
- **Gaming:** latency under 100 ms to keep players engaged.
- **Transportation:** shorter wait times through optimised ride-sharing routes and predictive maintenance.
- **Media and entertainment:** streaming quality high enough to keep churn down.

He closes on the trend line: more automation, predictive analytics and machine learning feeding SRE, so systems fix more of their own problems before anyone is paged.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into SRE, or moving between industries, who want a one-page view of how priorities shift from a retailer to a hospital to a game studio. Managers explaining to non-tech stakeholders why their sector's SLOs look the way they do will find the metrics list handy. Practitioners looking for war stories or implementation detail won't find them here.

Title: AI in fintech does four jobs and brings four new risks
Description: Sudeep Meduri (Google) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on AI for fraud detection, personal finance, trading and compliance, and the risks it adds
Body:
Fraud teams don't only lose money to fraud; they lose customers to false positives. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Sudeep Meduri, Senior Software Engineer at Google, surveys where AI earns its keep in financial technology: fraud detection, personalised banking, algorithmic trading and regulatory compliance. His sharpest example is a multinational bank whose AI fraud system cut false positives by 60%.

It's a short overview, drawn from his own experience with AI in fintech, aimed at people who want the shape of the field rather than an implementation. The DevSecOps angle sits mostly in the compliance and security sections.

## Why is fintech such a natural fit for AI?

Sudeep's starting point is data volume. Financial institutions process huge amounts of complex data, and both fintech startups and traditional banks are adopting AI quickly to stay competitive, keep up with regulation and cut operating costs. He groups the impact into four areas.

## Fraud detection: millions of transactions, fewer false alarms

This is where he spends the most time. AI can analyse millions of transactions as they happen, flag anomalies and intervene quickly, and machine learning models keep picking up new fraud patterns as they're retrained, which rule-based systems miss. The win is on both sides: fewer losses and fewer disruptions for genuine customers. The 60% false-positive reduction at a multinational bank is the example he uses; the bank isn't named.

## Personalised banking and robo-advisors

AI looks at spending habits, goals and income to give tailored financial advice. Robo-advisors make portfolio management cheap enough to reach people who would never hire an adviser, and portfolios can take ESG preferences, tax implications and personal goals into account. The payoff, in his framing, is customers who feel their needs are understood, which shows up as retention.

## Algorithmic trading, with a warning

AI systems process market data in real time, deep learning models forecast stock trends from historical and current data, and execution algorithms optimise timing to cut transaction costs. Sudeep adds the caveat most fintech decks skip. As he said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, "while AI improves market efficiency, it also raises concerns about market instability caused by these automated trading strategies".

## RegTech: compliance that updates itself

For DevSecOps teams in finance this is the part to watch. AI automates collection, processing and reporting of compliance data, which reduces human error. Machine learning models track changes in regulation and adjust compliance processes, and continuous monitoring with predictive analytics lets institutions manage risk before an audit finds it. His figure: some institutions using AI-driven RegTech have cut compliance costs by up to 30%.

Beyond those four, he points to operational efficiency, 24/7 service through chatbots that free staff for complex cases, and new products such as alternative credit scoring.

## What are the risks?

Four, matching the four jobs:

- **Data privacy:** financial data is sensitive and regulated, GDPR being the example.
- **Algorithmic bias:** badly designed models can bake bias into credit scoring and loan approvals.
- **Workforce:** automation displaces jobs, so reskilling is urgent.
- **Ethical AI:** models need to be transparent, unbiased and secure to keep trust.

His conclusion: the industry has to put ethical AI development, data protection and upskilling first if the technology is going to serve society as a whole.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into fintech, or security and compliance people who want a quick tour of where AI is already deployed in financial services. Specialists in fraud ML or trading systems will find it high level; there's no architecture or code.

Title: Write the prompt for the priciest model, then walk it down the menu
Description: Maxim Salnikov (Microsoft) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on prompt anatomy, token economics, LLMLingua compression and the tools for LLM apps.
Body:
Every token in a prompt is a line item on next month's bill, and Maxim Salnikov of Microsoft spent his Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk treating prompts the way a developer should: as a component with a cost, a size limit and a test loop. The most practical idea is a model selection strategy: perfect the prompt on the most capable, most expensive model, then step down to cheaper ones until the answers get worse.

He works with developers on cloud, dev tools and AI at Microsoft in Oslo, and the talk is pitched at people building AI-infused applications, though anyone who types into ChatGPT will pick up something.

## What is in a good prompt?

His prompt anatomy uses one running example, a product launch email for $79.99 AI-powered headphones: an instruction, primary data about the product, context about the tone (friendly and exciting), a target format (a JSON object with subject and body fields), an example in exactly that format, and a cue to start the output. The example deliberately repeats the format; doubling down, he explains later, is a legitimate fix when the model drifts.

## Why should a developer care about tokens?

Because the model reads and writes tokens, not words, and both cost and context limits are counted in them. His rule of thumb for English: 100 tokens is roughly 75 words, about four characters a token, with very different ratios in other languages. He points out that prices are falling fast, with GPT-4o much cheaper than GPT-4 while being more capable, but at scale it still adds up.

His tips for slimmer prompts are delightfully unglamorous:

- Watch whitespace; some models count every extra space as a token.
- Try data formats. A short date string took six tokens in his example while a longer one took three, so measure instead of guessing.
- Tabular data separated by pipes or tabs is space-efficient and well understood, no need for JSON keys on every value.
- English is usually the most token-efficient language, because most training data was English.

## The downgrade loop and model mixing

"First of all, try with the most capable, the most performant, and, in many cases also the most expensive model on the market," Maxim Salnikov said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. Find the best prompt there, drop to the next cheapest model, tune if needed, and keep going while the completion is not worse; when it is, step back up.

In a chain of calls you can also mix: expensive models for generation, cheap ones for summarisation and classification, and a fast cheap model to summarise a big document before it goes to the expensive one.

## Can a model compress your prompt?

Yes, with LLMLingua, an open-source prompt compressor from Microsoft. A compact language model removes non-essential tokens, with up to 20x compression and minimal performance loss according to the project. Run untuned on his headphone email, it went from 84 to 70 tokens, a 17% saving, and the prompt still reads the same to a human.

## Techniques for the day job

The rest is a solid tour: be specific, give examples, order matters (instructions first, maybe repeated at the end), one prompt per task, and tune temperature and top-p for determinism. Give the model an out: in his insurance-routing example, an irrelevant question gets category three instead of being forced into auto or flood insurance. Chain of thought fixes a wrong water-consumption calculation. For hallucinations (Cambridge Dictionary's word of the year for 2023), nothing beats injecting the relevant context and telling the model to use only that, which leads into retrieval-augmented generation.

For tooling he names LangChain and Semantic Kernel for orchestration and Prompt Flow, also open source from Microsoft, for the LLMOps life cycle, available hosted on Azure or as a VS Code extension.

He ends with questions rather than answers: job title or essential skill, simpler or harder with multimodality, and whether human prompt engineers survive competition with LLMs that write prompts.

## Who should watch

Developers about to put an LLM call into production, and anyone whose AI bill is starting to get noticed. Long (about 45 minutes) and broad; the token and model selection sections are the meat.

Title: A drug launch is won or lost in its first six months
Description: Harpreet Singh (Gilead Sciences) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on the sales analytics, KPIs and data stack pharma uses to steer a drug launch.
Body:
A new drug costs around $2.6 billion to develop, and the company gets only a few years of exclusivity to earn it back. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, Harpreet Singh, Director of Sales Analytics & Operations at Gilead Sciences, explained how pharmaceutical companies use sales data analytics to make the launch window count, and why the first six months matter more than the rest of the first year combined.

Honest scope first: despite the title, prompts barely feature. This is a talk about the analytics side of pharma commercial operations: the models, the KPIs and the data platform behind a launch. Watch it for that.

## Why are the first months so critical?

His framing is economic. Market timing decides a lot, being first in a therapeutic area is a competitive advantage, and, by his figure, 60 percent of the revenue is generated in just the first six months of the launch. So a company has a short time to see what is happening in the market and react, and analytics is how it sees.

## What do the models actually predict?

Pharma sits on rich data: prescribers, patient-level data, medical claims, hospital purchasing. On top of it he lists the main jobs for predictive models and machine learning:

- **Physician targeting.** AI-driven segmentation finds the high-potential prescribers to engage before and after launch.
- **Pricing.** Models take multiple inputs and suggest a price that stays competitive.
- **Forecasting.** He puts current models at 80 to 90 percent accuracy.
- **Territory deployment.** Deploying sales territories with these models gives, in his words, at least 30 percent efficiency.

## How much does real-time processing buy?

With millions of data points and a narrow window, speed is the point. Real-time processing, he said, cuts the market response time from about 15 days to around three, and lets a team adjust its launch strategy within 72 hours. During those first six months, that is the difference between correcting course and reading about it in the quarterly review.

## Which KPIs tell you a launch is on track?

Two stand out. Conversion: how many doctors actually prescribe the product early on. "If you can achieve 15, 20 percent conversion in first three months, that kind of correlate with 85 percent of the probability of you would achieve, your first year target," Harpreet Singh said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. Persistency and adherence: how long patients stay on therapy at three and six months. Early conversion gives the launch momentum; persistency builds brand loyalty. He tracks these weekly or monthly, and mentions at least 50 KPIs across the pre-launch and post-launch phases.

## What does the data stack look like?

At petabyte scale, pharma companies are investing heavily in cloud data warehouses on AWS that handle millions of transactions per second. Python and R models run on top, and hundreds of Tableau and Power BI dashboards feed sales, marketing and finance with the reports each of them needs.

## Best practices that apply outside pharma

Three of his practices travel well to any analytics team:

- **Data quality first.** Garbage in, garbage out; dedicated teams validate millions of records and data governance frameworks audit them continuously.
- **Pilot before you go national.** Instead of a nationwide model costing millions, test a new-patient prediction model in one territory, collect feedback from sales and marketing, fine-tune, then roll out.
- **Keep watching the model.** Update it, check for bias and track its performance over time.

## Who should watch

Analysts and data engineers in life sciences, and anyone building forecasting or targeting models for a business with a short, expensive window. Expect a domain overview from a practitioner, not code and not prompt engineering.

Title: A healthcare chatbot has to show its reasoning to the doctor
Description: Abhishek Vajpayee (Metropolis Technologies) and Rathish Mohan (Lore | Contagious Health) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on explainable healthcare chatbots
Body:
A chatbot that reminds a diabetic patient to check their blood sugar is useful; one that recommends a treatment nobody can audit is a liability. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Abhishek Vajpayee, Senior Analytics Engineer and Product Owner at Metropolis Technologies, and Rathish Mohan, Senior Applied ML Scientist at Lore | Contagious Health, make the case that healthcare chatbots need explainable AI (XAI) built in, and sketch the data platform and ethical guardrails underneath.

It's a short overview talk, around ten minutes, that covers the whole stack at a high level. No benchmarks or production numbers; the value is in the map.

## What do chatbots actually fix in healthcare?

Rathish opens with access. Traditional care is bounded by office hours, staff shortages and geography; a chatbot is available around the clock, can triage symptoms and either guide patients or escalate. For chronic conditions it can monitor and remind, and his example is the glucose spike: the bot nudges the patient and makes sure the signal is captured for treatment.

Generative AI adds two things. It turns medical jargon into language a patient can follow, and it retains context, so you don't repeat your history to every new interface the way you repeat it to every new doctor. Over time, deep learning, reinforcement learning and knowledge graphs let the bot refine its answers and link medical data together.

## Why isn't a good answer enough?

This is the core of the talk. Rathish Mohan said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, "In healthcare, blind trust in AI isn't enough." Patients need to know they're talking to an AI and why a recommendation was made. Clinicians need to verify the logic before they act on it. Regulators and institutions need decision-making transparency, and an explanation layer gives you an audit trail of what the bot did and why, plus a way to spot bias or errors in its reasoning.

## Which XAI methods fit?

The speakers split the methods into two families:

- **Model-agnostic:** LIME approximates a single response with a simpler model, SHAP gives each input feature an importance value, and counterfactuals answer the what-if question of which input change would flip the output.
- **Model-specific:** decision trees and feature importance analysis, familiar to anyone with an ML background, plus layer-wise relevance propagation for convolutional and other neural networks.

The practical takeaway is that the explanation has to be something you can hand to the healthcare professional providing care, not just a chart for the data science team.

## What sits underneath the chatbot?

Abhishek covers the data engineering. Patient records, IoT devices such as wearables and medical knowledge graphs feed ETL pipelines into data lakes (structured and unstructured data: medical images, patient notes, device readings) and data warehouses for fast querying. Batch jobs handle daily updates for consistency, while real-time streaming lets the bot react to events such as an abnormal heart rate. That data trains the models, and the chatbot ships through mobile and web apps.

## Where are the ethical lines?

Secure storage and transmission, informed consent, training on diverse datasets to avoid unsafe biased recommendations, and keeping clinicians in charge. Abhishek put the last one plainly at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "AI should complement, not replace, human healthcare providers." The closing challenges are the unglamorous ones: technical reliability, operational training, clear privacy and consent rules, strict HIPAA compliance, and clinical validation before broad adoption.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people starting on a healthcare chatbot who want a checklist of what the system needs beyond the model. If you already know LIME and SHAP, the data architecture and ethics sections are the parts to watch.

Title: Reinforcement learning makes the exam adapt to the learner
Description: Vijay Kumar Valaboju (Microsoft) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on reinforcement learning for adaptive assessments, from K-12 to security certification prep
Body:
Fixed-difficulty tests are wasted on half the room: too easy for some, too hard for the rest. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Vijay Kumar Valaboju, Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft, explains how reinforcement learning (RL) can drive assessments that adjust in real time, easing off when a learner struggles and pushing harder when they're ahead, and where that applies, from algebra drills to security certification prep.

A note on scope: the abstract pitches RL as a way to strengthen a team's defences against emerging threats. The talk itself is a general introduction to RL in education and assessment. The security angle shows up as one use case, certification prep focused on topics like security protocols, rather than as a DevSecOps implementation.

## How does RL map onto a learner?

Vijay frames it with the four standard RL concepts, translated for education:

- **Agent:** the AI system that analyses the learner's performance and tracks progress.
- **Environment:** the learner's knowledge state and preferences.
- **Actions:** the adjustments the agent makes, from changing content or tailoring an assessment to reshaping the whole learning path.
- **Rewards:** positive reinforcement for progress, through well-timed feedback and recognition.

The loop is observe, adjust, repeat. As Vijay said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, "If they excel, it introduces more complex challenges to keep them engaged." If they struggle, the system simplifies the material or offers hints.

## What does an RL-driven assessment actually do?

He lists five features:

1. **Dynamic curriculum adjustment:** revisit foundations where the learner is weak, move ahead where they're strong.
2. **Real-time difficulty adjustment:** question difficulty follows the learner's responses.
3. **Personalised feedback:** detailed explanations for wrong answers instead of a red cross.
4. **Gamification:** badges, points and levels to keep motivation up.
5. **Cognitive load management:** alternate task types and schedule breaks to prevent burnout.

Knowledge retention comes from spaced repetition, reinforcing the right concepts at the right intervals so the learning outlasts the test.

## Where would you use it?

The applications run from K-12 personalised paths and adaptive university exams to professional certifications, corporate training and language learning. The corporate training point is the one engineering managers will recognise: Vijay argues training modules too often drift away from what the organisation actually needs, and RL can keep the content aligned with organisational goals. His case studies are illustrative rather than measured: a maths platform balancing advanced algebra problems against extra practice on weak spots, certification prep that concentrates on hard topics such as security protocols while mixing in other domains, and a language platform that rewards practice in weaker skills like writing.

## What could go wrong?

He is direct about four limits. Algorithmic bias, since the system must be fair across diverse learners. The complexity of human learning, which is hard to model as a state and a reward. Data privacy and security, because learner data is sensitive and trust drives adoption. And scalability, which needs serious infrastructure for large, varied user groups.

For future work he points to combining RL with NLP and computer vision, bias-free and interpretable algorithms, extending adaptive learning to underserved communities, and long-term studies that measure outcomes and professional success over time. That last one is the gap in the talk: there are no results here yet, only the design.

## Who should watch

People building internal training or certification programmes, including security awareness, who want a plain-language model of how adaptive assessment works. ML engineers already familiar with RL will find it introductory, and anyone expecting RL applied to penetration testing or threat modelling should look elsewhere.

Title: Telling the model it's a genius made it score worst
Description: Dan Cleary (PromptHub) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on why persona prompts don't buy accuracy, and what works instead, from few-shot to meta prompting.
Body:
Opening with a flattering job title is the most copy-pasted habit in prompt engineering, and at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 Dan Cleary, co-founder of PromptHub, made the case that it does nothing for accuracy. His talk is a compact field guide to what actually moves output quality: structure, specific instructions, a few good examples, and letting the model help write the prompt.

## Is prompt engineering dead?

He doesn't think so, and his reason is the model's latent space: small wording changes send it to very different places. Ask for code to render an image, then ask for secure code written as if you were John Carmack, and you get drastically different output. He also frames prompting as the first of the three big levers for better LLM output, the one you try before anything heavier, and the one non-technical people can use too. Good prompts, he argues, are a competitive advantage in the same way good UX is.

## System message or user message?

The system message is optional over the API and is for the high-level stuff: role, context, behaviour, output format, content boundaries. The user prompt carries the specific question and its details. He points at the published system prompts from OpenAI and Anthropic as examples worth reading.

## One prompt does not fit every model

Chain of thought is a best practice, yet he cites an experiment where it reduced the performance of Google's PaLM 2. He then walks through a VMware study that combined many openers, descriptions and closers and let models such as Llama 2 optimise their own prompts; the winning prompts looked nothing alike across models. His conclusion is the boring, correct one: test on the model you ship.

## The two practices he pushes on every team

Give the model room to think instead of forcing an instant answer, and use delimiters. His litmus test for the second: hand the prompt to someone else. "I can't tell you how many times I've had a team say, Hey, we're struggling with this prompt. Can you look at it? I look at it and I can't even. See what's going on," Dan Cleary said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024.

## How many few-shot examples?

Most of the gain comes from the first one or two examples, then it plateaus and can even degrade. His starting range is two to five. The examples should be diverse (not only positive reviews in a sentiment task), randomly ordered, and share a common format. He also notes that examples sent as an array of prior messages are technically closer to real few-shot than examples pasted into one prompt, and both are worth testing.

Two smaller templates round it out: according-to prompting, which grounds the answer in a named source such as Wikipedia, and step-back prompting, where the model abstracts the concepts first and then reasons through the task.

## Does persona prompting work?

The headline result comes from a Learn Prompting experiment: 2,000 MMLU questions run under a range of roles. The genius persona was the worst performer, below a persona told it was an idiot. "The genius was actually the worst performing one here," he said. His verdict: personas help tone and style, such as making it sound like a pirate, and are useless for accuracy.

## Let the model write the prompt

Meta prompting, using the LLM to draft and refine your prompt, is the approach PromptHub argues for. He compares three generators: PromptHub's own (tailored per provider, free), Anthropic's in its console, and OpenAI's in the playground, which writes system messages only. His closing formula: meta prompting plus few-shot plus chain of thought, with clear structure and specific instructions, and without over-constraining the model.

It is a vendor talk in the sense that PromptHub's templates and tools appear throughout, but the advice stands on its own and comes with sources.

## Who should watch

Anyone shipping prompts to production who wants evidence instead of folklore, especially teams still opening every prompt with a job title.

Title: Explain the chatbot's reasoning and users forgive its mistakes
Description: Shradha Kohli (Salesforce) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on LIME, SHAP and counterfactuals for chatbot transparency, tested with 150 users
Body:
A chatbot that shows its working gets more slack when it's wrong. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Shradha Kohli, Senior Software Engineering Manager at Salesforce, presents research that applied three explainable AI (XAI) techniques, LIME, SHAP and counterfactual explanations, to chatbots and measured what happened to user trust. Her headline: trust rose by 35%, and users were 40% more forgiving of errors.

It's a compact research summary, around ten minutes, rather than an implementation walkthrough. Think of it as a map of the XAI toolbox with one study's results pinned to it.

## Why do chatbots need explaining?

Shradha's framing is the black box. Chatbots have been around since the 1960s, starting as rule-based pattern matchers with scripted replies. Modern ones run on deep neural networks and hold far more natural conversations, but they give no view into how they reached an answer. In healthcare or finance that opacity turns into hesitation: users who can't see the reasoning don't trust the response, and don't use the tool.

## Three ways to open the box

She walks through the three techniques at the level a practitioner needs to pick one:

- **LIME** (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) builds a simple, interpretable stand-in model for a single response, so users can see which input words most influenced it.
- **SHAP** (SHapley Additive exPlanations) borrows Shapley values from game theory to assign each input feature an importance weight, at both the local and global level.
- **Counterfactual explanations** show how a small change to the input would change the output, which tells users where the decision boundary sits and how sensitive the bot is.

## What did the study measure?

The research involved around 150 users across demographics and three chatbot styles: retrieval-based, generative and hybrid, covering the range from FAQ bots to fully conversational systems. Explanations were scored on faithfulness (accuracy), stability (consistency across users) and comprehensibility (whether non-technical users understood them).

Each technique came with a catch. LIME explained individual responses well but struggled globally, so explanations could vary for similar inputs. SHAP gave the most detailed picture of feature importance across interactions, but its compute cost made it impractical, and its output confused non-technical users. Counterfactuals were the most intuitive for users and the hardest to generate under real-time demands.

## The numbers

The user-impact figures from the talk:

| Measure | Change |
|---|---|
| Trust in the chatbot | +35% |
| Understanding of the bot's reasoning | +48% |
| Willingness to engage with complex tasks | +27% |
| Error tolerance | +40% |
| Overall engagement | +31% |

The talk doesn't go into how these were measured beyond the 150-user study, so treat them as directional. Shradha was candid that the open problems are the practical ones: generating explanations without noticeable latency, balancing detail against comprehension, and the risk that an explanation itself exposes sensitive information or bias. Her summary at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024: "each technique brings its own pros and cons to the chatbot transparency".

## Where does the research go next?

She lists three directions: XAI methods that work for transformer architectures, which most current chatbots use; real-time adaptive explanations that adjust their level of detail to the user; and self-explaining chatbots that learn to explain themselves as they evolve.

## Who should watch

Product engineers and managers shipping chatbots into regulated or high-stakes domains who want a quick orientation on XAI options and their trade-offs. If you're after code or a production architecture, this isn't that talk; it's a short, readable briefing.

Title: Don't ask the baker for a recipe, ask the songwriter for a song
Description: Jorrik Klijnsma (Sopra Steria) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on putting the context inside the conversation instead of bolting on act-as roles.
Body:
The best prompt engineering lesson Jorrik Klijnsma ever got came from a holiday in Porto. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, the Senior Front-end Engineer at Sopra Steria told the story of letting ChatGPT plan a trip for a couple with little travel experience, and the takeaway he brought home: stop telling the model who to pretend to be and write the context into the conversation itself.

It is a short, gentle talk, good for anyone who uses chat models every day and wants a better mental model of why some prompts land and others don't.

## Why does a large language model need a different travel guide?

His first insight is about adapting to the place you're in. On holiday, dinner, schedules and even language work differently, and doing things the way you do them at home simply fails. Models are the same: they are language models, and he thinks we forget that far too easily. "It's even in a name, a large language model, but we are so easily deceived by the power that AI has, that our conscious filters, are easily bypassed," Jorrik Klijnsma said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024.

His example is the classic one. Ask who the son of Mary Lee Pfeiffer is and you get a confident, wrong answer. Ask who the mother of Tom Cruise is and the model gets it right. Same fact, different context, different knowledge. With images we spot the weird fingers and impossible roller coasters at a glance; with text we have no such built-in filter, because reading is something we had to learn.

## Formatting is context, too

The packing list ChatGPT gave him came back nicely formatted, which pointed him to the next lesson: structure tells the model what each part of the prompt is. He walks through the building blocks:

- backticks for code snippets, triple quotes for quoted material, line separators between sections
- headings with a colon, ordered and unordered lists
- inline emphasis: placeholders for values you fill in later, capitals for the word that matters, key-value pairs
- XML tags, which he finds work especially well with Anthropic's Claude for labelling sections

## The techniques he picked up along the way

He covers the standard toolkit with one fun extra. Role prompting, the act-as-someone opener, is the famous one. Zero-shot and few-shot prompting trade freedom against control, with the caveat that few-shot output can get stuck on the examples you gave.

The extra is the unfinished chat prompt, which he says he first hit by accident: write a fake chat with, say, an Apple support employee, stop exactly where the employee would answer, and let the model complete it. The chat frame supplies the context, so the answer comes back in the right shape.

## What is wrong with casting the model as a baker?

The sharpest part of the talk is a pastry shop on the boulevard. The baker behind the counter asks which pie you want, and you reply: give me the recipe for your best apple pie. It feels odd in person, because the context is plainly wrong. In a prompt, he argues, nobody notices.

He calls the fix implicit conversations. A bare request for summer road trip song lyrics could be asked of an 11-year-old or a hit songwriter, and the sentence gives the model no clue which. Compare a prompt that tells the artist their music is amazing to listen to on a road trip and asks, after five number one hits, what the lyrics of the new road trip song will be. The context now sits inside the request, and he expects a better song back. His point about role prompts is that an actor playing a profession is not as good as the profession itself, so let the conversation imply the expert instead of casting one.

## Who should watch

People who prompt chat models daily and never formalised it: front-end developers, product folks, anyone whose prompts are one long sentence. It is an intro, about 20 minutes, with no code or benchmarks. If you build LLM systems for a living, the implicit-conversation idea is the bit worth stealing.
