Title: A full disk and storage at 90% are the same page
Description: Birol Yildiz (ilert) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on grouping duplicate alerts by meaning, using text embeddings and a tunable similarity threshold
Body:
Two alerts can share zero words and still be the same incident. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Birol Yildiz, co-founder and CEO of ilert, shows how his team groups alerts by meaning rather than by text: turn each alert into a vector embedding, compare it with recent alerts, and fold anything close enough into one page. He then explains the pipeline well enough that you could build it yourself.

It is a vendor talk, demoed in ilert, but the second half is a recipe that works with any alerting stack.

## Why bother with alert grouping?

Alert floods drive up MTTA and MTTR and add stress at exactly the wrong moment, the major incident at 3am. Birol opens with a customer result: after two weeks of intelligent alert grouping, alert volume dropped by 93%, and response time improved by more than four hours.

He also tours the other places ilert uses AI across the incident lifecycle: a chat assistant that builds on-call schedules (a follow-the-sun rotation described in plain language), drafting status page updates from a few words, and post-mortems reconstructed from the war-room chat and monitoring data. On that last one, Birol said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, "it almost feels irresponsible not to use, not to leverage AI", with the model producing an 80% draft so the team spends its time on the learning part.

## Can a model tell a coffee machine from a water cooler?

The demo starts light. Using Postman to fire events into ilert, Birol sends an alert about the coffee machine on floor two, then the same problem reworded as the machine taking a coffee break, then a Java pun. All three land in one alert with a counter. Then the water cooler on floor two breaks: same floor, overlapping words, different thing, so it gets its own alert. That distinction matters, he points out, because the water cooler might belong to another team, and wrongly merging it means nobody gets paged.

The sharper test is technical. "The hard drive is full" followed by a storage alert about reaching a 90% limit share no words, and they still group. Then he replays 31 real Prometheus alerts from a production flood. With grouping off, that is 31 alerts. With grouping on, the blackbox HTTP probe failures collapse together while genuinely separate problems, a RabbitMQ node down, a hardware status warning, a firewall subnet running out of IPs, stay separate.

## How does the pipeline work?

Four steps, per his slides:

1. **Preprocess.** Normalise alerts into one format (ilert already does this across 100+ integrations), then clean them: drop unique IDs and timestamps, strip JSON and markdown down to plain text. That cuts tokens and stops the format from influencing the match.
2. **Vectorise.** Run the text through an embedding model. ilert self-hosts a general-purpose model from Hugging Face, trained on data that includes Stack Overflow, so it handles technical text. With millions of events a day, an external API call per alert was a performance and stability risk they didn't want. BERT, Sentence-BERT or OpenAI's embeddings are named as options.
3. **Deduplicate.** Store vectors in a vector database and, for each new alert, query for close neighbours within the grouping window (five minutes by default) using a similarity function such as cosine similarity. Above the threshold, it merges. An optional step has a generative model summarise the cluster.
4. **Feedback.** Thumbs up or down on each grouping, with the metrics exposed so you can tune.

## Is 0.75 the right threshold?

The default similarity threshold is 0.75 on a scale from 0 to 1: closer to 1 groups fewer alerts, lower groups almost everything. Birol is clear that the number has no meaning in isolation; 0.75 can suit one domain while another needs 0.9. ilert's answer is a preview slider that replays past alerts as you move it. He also flags model choice: a model trained mostly on English may behave differently if your alerts aren't in English.

## Who should watch

On-call engineers drowning in duplicate pages, and anyone building alert routing who wants a concrete, small-scale use of embeddings that isn't a chatbot. The demo is ilert; the design is portable.

Title: Git never forgets, so stop the secret at the push
Description: Dewan Ahmed (Harness) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024 on blocking secret commits with Gitleaks rules and Harness Open Source secret scanning
Body:
A revert commit does not un-leak an API key: the key is still sitting in the history for anyone who clones the repo. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, Dewan Ahmed, Principal Developer Advocate at Harness, shows how to catch secrets before they ever land, using the open-source scanner Gitleaks and the secret scanning built into Harness Open Source, and demos a push being rejected live.

It is a short, practical talk: a few minutes of why, a look inside a Gitleaks rule, then a demo you can repeat on a laptop with Docker.

## Why do Git repositories leak secrets so easily?

Dewan gives three reasons. Repositories are collaborative, so more hands means more chances for someone to commit the wrong file. Accidental commits are easy: you stage everything you touched locally, including the `.env` file you were testing with a database credential in it. And the number of repositories keeps growing, with public, private and open-source repos multiplied by microservices, which makes access control harder to keep tight.

His branch diagram makes the core point. A developer commits an API key on a feature branch, someone spots it and adds a commit to remove it, then another branch picks up a database credential, an SSH key and an access token, and another fix reverts them. Every one of those secrets is still in the history. Erasing Git history is hard, so the only cheap fix is the one that happens before the commit lands. That is his case for shifting left: less exposure time, less remediation work.

## What does a Gitleaks rule look like?

Gitleaks scans Git repositories, files and directories against predefined and customisable secret patterns. It is lightweight and runs locally, as a pre-commit hook or in CI/CD pipelines.

The best detail in the talk is a rule Dewan wrote himself. He contributed a Gitleaks rule for Harness personal access tokens and service account tokens, and the pull request was merged upstream. He walks through the regex: the token starts with `pat` or `sat`, then a dot, a 22-character alphanumeric segment (dashes and underscores allowed), a dot, a 24-character segment, a dot and a 20-character segment. His aside that most of us would ask ChatGPT to get the brackets right is the most honest thing anyone has said about regex. If your organisation's tokens aren't covered yet, his point is that the contribution process is straightforward, so write the rule.

## How does Harness Open Source fit in?

Harness Open Source is a single lightweight Go binary that runs locally or on a small cloud VM. It bundles a code repository, CI, CD, an artifact registry and Gitspaces, pre-configured dev environments based on dev containers (think GitHub Codespaces). Projects map roughly to GitHub orgs, each holding repositories with their own pipelines. Dewan positions it for individual developers and small teams, with the commercial Harness platform as the upgrade for governance and scale.

The demo is the payoff. He starts it with Docker on localhost port 3000, creates a project, imports the public PodInfo repository from GitHub, clones it into VS Code and adds a `config.yaml` containing a fake Harness personal access token from the harness-community lab repo. Then he flips the secret scanning toggle under the repository's security settings, which blocks commits containing passwords, API keys and tokens and is based on Gitleaks. The push fails. The log names the file, the commit ID and the detection: a generic API key.

## What doesn't it do?

Dewan is upfront about the limit. The push-time check stops new secrets; it does not go back through history. As he said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024, "if you already have existing secrets in the repository, it doesn't scan and find and detect those." So you still need a one-off history scan, and rotation for anything already exposed.

## Who should watch

Developers and platform engineers who want a five-minute setup for push-time secret blocking, and anyone curious about how Gitleaks rules are written. Security teams who already run history scanning and vault-based workflows will find it introductory. It is a Harness developer advocate showing Harness Open Source, and the Gitleaks part works without it.

Title: Meet the product alchemist, the PM who also designs and ships with AI
Description: Sabarinath Viji Selvam (daily.dev) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on how AI reshapes product management, from PRDs and market research to churn analysis
Body:
The churn analysis a product manager files with the analytics team and waits a week or two for can be roughed out in one ChatGPT session, if you know which segments to ask about. Sabarinath Viji Selvam, on the product management leadership team at daily.dev, argued at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 that this is only the start: within three to five years one AI-assisted person will cover what a PM, designer and analyst do today, and product orgs will get 40 to 50% leaner.

Engineers will recognise the half of the talk about prompting techniques; the rest is a PM's view of where AI takes work off the plate and where it can't.

## Is product management dead?

He opens with the bold version of the claim, "product management is dead or is it?", and then softens it: the job will look very different. Sabarinath Viji Selvam said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "We are already entering what I call the age of the product alchemist."

To get there he sorts PM work into three buckets (ideation, execution, and alignment or leading with influence) and rates AI's impact on each task, drawing on sources including Lenny's Newsletter:

- **Strategy and vision:** highly impacted, with tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity.
- **Specifications:** highly impacted. AI gets a PRD to perhaps 75%, and the PM polishes the last 25% before it goes to engineering. ChatPRD and WriteMyPRD are on his list.
- **User research:** moderately impacted. Feed processed interviews to a GPT and it extracts insights, but talking to customers stays human.
- **Roadmaps:** AI drafts an outline; the final version still comes out of sessions with design and engineering.
- **QA:** highly impacted, as AI-driven testing tools improve.
- **Stakeholder alignment:** moderate at most. Convincing people and building a case for a product remain people work.

## What happens to the org chart?

Today's trifecta of engineer, designer and PM (plus an analyst) collapses into a hands-on product alchemist who generates wireframes and mockups, writes code and launches. He also expects the group PM layer to flatten while senior individual contributors grow in importance. His sketch takes a 12-person product org with a VP, directors, senior PMs and junior PMs, and claims at least a 40 to 50% reduction in typical team size because the tools free up so much time. It's a prediction, not a measurement, and he presents it as one.

## Which prompting techniques does a PM need?

The toolkit is the standard one, well explained: assign a persona (imagine you are Christopher Nolan and pitch me a storyline), zero-shot, few-shot, meta prompting with explicit rules, and chain-of-thought. His few-shot example feeds a GPT pairs of client brief and content so it matches tone and brand guidelines on the next brief. The chain-of-thought example is the classic: asked how many apples a cafeteria has after starting with 23, using 20 and buying 6, the model says 27; shown one worked example step by step, it gets 9.

## What do the demos show?

Two case studies, both in ChatGPT.

**Market research for a sports management app.** Told to act as a market researcher, the model estimates TAM, describes the market's growth and lists segments such as amateur sports clubs and educational institutions. Asked for features for amateur clubs, it proposes member management, events and scheduling, notifications and rosters. Then he asks it to prioritise with ICE (impact, confidence, effort) or MoSCoW. The model fills in scores, and he's clear that this is where the PM's real work begins: talk to users, judge the business impact, then feed that back in.

**Churn analysis.** He uploads a public churn dataset of a fictitious finance company (credit score, demographics, balance, tenure, card ownership, activity, salary). ChatGPT lays out an approach, categorises the fields, builds a correlation matrix and finds satisfaction score negatively correlated with leaving. It ignores age and salary until he asks, then reports that older customers churn slightly more, with little difference by salary. Without AI, he says, that analysis request might take a few days to a week or two in an analytics backlog. With it, the PM does the preliminary pass and hands the analysts something to build on. The lesson in the demo: you still need to know which segments matter, because the model didn't think of age on its own.

## Who should watch

Product managers and engineering leads curious how far ChatGPT gets in PM work today, and anyone hiring for product roles. Engineers already fluent in prompting can skip the techniques section and jump to the demos.

Title: Personalisation wins the Spotify switch, but only if users trust the data deal
Description: Olanrewaju Oyedele (Codeweavers) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on AI-powered personalisation, the models behind it and the privacy rules it has to follow
Body:
One good weekly playlist can move a customer for years. Olanrewaju Oyedele, Senior Digital Product Owner at Codeweavers, made that case at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 with his own switch to Spotify, then walked through how AI personalisation moved from static segments to real-time profiles, the models that power it, and why consent and audits decide whether users stay or leave.

Set expectations: this is a product-level overview of the field, not a case study of a system he built. The abstract talks about his own work; the talk itself stays general, with Amazon, Spotify and Netflix as the examples. It's a good primer for product owners and a quick refresher for engineers.

## Why does personalisation matter?

He defines AI personalisation as machine learning and predictive analytics that use browsing history, purchases and cross-device interactions to predict what a user wants next, and then serve individual content, product suggestions or even dynamic interfaces.

The numbers he cites are big ones: McKinsey's 2023 report, he says, links tailored experiences to a 50% rise in user interaction and up to a 200% rise in conversion rates, and users are 60% more likely to return when interactions feel personalised. The anecdote is more convincing than the statistics. Olanrewaju Oyedele said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "I switched to Spotify from another music app due to how highly relatable the mix I get on Spotify is." He's been there for more than three years.

## What changed from segments to real time?

Older personalisation was static: broad groups by demographics (everyone aged 20 to 30 with similar interests) or purchase history (you bought this, so here is something like it). It works up to a point and ignores the individual. AI makes it adaptive. Dynamic user profiles update continuously with current behaviour and context, such as the time of day someone is active, so recommendations shift as tastes do. If a user suddenly starts on a new music genre, Netflix- and Spotify-scale engines adjust quickly, and that responsiveness is what keeps retention up.

## Which models do the work?

Two families carry most of it:

- **Collaborative filtering:** if two users engaged with similar content, recommend to one what the other liked. It uses individual and collective behaviour, so it works even when a user's own activity on an item is thin. Spotify's Discover Weekly is his headline example.
- **Neural networks:** they combine clicks, dwell time and purchase patterns into a detailed preference profile and predict what will engage.

The data comes from web interactions, app usage and purchase history, processed in real time. For teams that would rather buy than build, he names Adobe Experience Cloud, Google AI and Salesforce Einstein. On the payoff, he cites the figure that Amazon's recommendations account for 35% of its sales.

## What can go wrong?

Three things. Privacy, under regimes such as GDPR in Europe and CCPA in California, where getting it wrong means penalties and lost trust. Bias: a model trained on skewed data can favour some groups and narrow the diversity of recommendations. And infrastructure, which is complex and resource-hungry at scale.

His fixes are practical: publish clear data usage policies, make personalisation opt-in, and audit algorithms for bias regularly. On the UX side, don't bombard users with suggestions; a subtle, contextual recommendation feels curated rather than pushy.

## How do you start?

His four-step plan: map the user data you have (web, app, purchases), set specific goals such as engagement or retention, train on diverse datasets to limit bias, and keep refining based on metrics and feedback, because personalisation is never a one-off project. Looking ahead, he expects AR and VR try-ons (clothes, furniture in your living room) and predictive personalisation that suggests the trip or the meal before the user asks.

## Who should watch

Product owners and managers building a personalisation roadmap, and engineers who want the business framing before they pick a recommender architecture. If you want implementation detail, pair it with the more technical talks below.

Title: Fraud adapts faster than your neural net trains, so stack boosting and humans
Description: Pavel Zapolskii (Exness) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on building fintech anti-fraud with gradient boosting, market data and independent human filters
Body:
A payment system that quotes a fixed EUR/USD rate and lets the customer decide later whether to pay has just sold a free currency option. Pavel Zapolskii, Senior Quantitative Researcher at Exness, opened his Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk with that bug and spent the rest of it on how to catch the people who exploit it. His advice is deliberately unfashionable: skip the neural networks, build an ensemble of boring models on the right data, and put analysts and an operations team around the model, because independent filters multiply.

The abstract promises a framework that gets 80% of the result for 20% of the effort, and the talk delivers it as a design walk-through from a simple model to a full platform.

## What counts as fraud?

His definition is metric-first: fraud is customer action the company didn't intend that degrades a key metric. If the customer exploits the company's own inefficiencies, it's endogenous; otherwise exogenous. Framing it that way lets you measure each fraudster by the drop they cause in money, retention or whatever the metric is.

Two examples set the range. In free-to-play games, cheaters use software to bypass paywall levels meant for very skilled players or paying ones, which also ruins online competition; the tell is attempts per level and how fast a hard level falls. In fintech, the currency case: the billing system fixes the rate when the application is submitted, the customer watches the market, and pays only if the euro moved their way. The insurance on that option costs the customer nothing, so the strategy has a positive expected value.

## Why not neural networks?

Probability and ML work when the same event repeats under similar conditions. Fraud doesn't oblige. Zapolskii compares anti-fraud to a gladiator arena where you never know what happens next: the same scheme comes in many variations and adapts to your defences. Pavel Zapolskii said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 that because of this, "neural networks go bad faster than you set it up."

His list of what works: quantile regression on enriched data, Monte Carlo probability estimates, tree-based models (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), automatic ARIMA-GARCH, and plain trend-and-variance detection. What he'd avoid: deep learning, RNNs, Temporal Fusion Transformers and Lag-Llama.

The starting model is simple. Build a payment cost metric (money in one currency, money out in another, commissions, normalisation), use gradient boosting with autoregression to predict it and its confidence interval, and check whether actual values fall inside. Drill into segments, a country such as India for instance, and a hypothesis appears: something odd is going on with rupee and dollar payments.

## What breaks when you take it to production?

Deployment looks easy: train offline on the data lake, run the model in a persistent Kubernetes pod reading user data from Kafka, reload it on a cooldown. Then three problems show up.

- **User data isn't enough.** This fraud is defined by market moves, so the model needs currency quotes, which means engineers building an efficient market-data reader, a market provider and an aggregator, data-quality checks, and time-based joins with correct timestamps. All without slowing the product.
- **The target is too broad.** Payment cost splits into commission costs, market arbitrage, timing, and payment-system and counterparty costs. Each fraud type needs its own metrics, and the result is a stack of models plus a decision rule that matches your risk appetite. He describes supervised gradient boosting as a set of smart ifs, with the smartest if still yours to set.
- **Load is uneven.** Spark on CPU fell short; his team moved to Trino, which handles memory better (GPU Spark is an option but fiddly). At peak times the product's core functions get the resources, so the anti-fraud block either runs a cheap version that catches the biggest fraudsters, or recalculates a few minutes after load settles.

## Where do the people come in?

This is the part he calls the most important. Treat the ML model, the analysts' filters and the operations team as independent catchers with probabilities P1, P2 and P3. The chance a fraudster slips past all three is the product of their misses, so overall detection is 1 - (1-P1)(1-P2)(1-P3).

The worked example: analysts notice a metric drop in India tied to one payment system. ML engineers predict the metric and isolate the quantiles with odd behaviour; the clear cases get blocked immediately, while borderline ones, where the model is near average accuracy, go to the operations team to judge by hand.

Monitoring closes the loop. Online, track the potential business cost of fraud and how it behaves, as an early warning. Offline, use PR-AUC given the class imbalance, watch the false positive rate to protect honest users, and retrain when the model degrades.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and data scientists in payments, trading or gaming who are tempted by a shiny model for fraud. It's light on code and strong on system design.

Title: One flat, five listings, three square footages, and the ML that merges them
Description: Kirill Mozheykin (Kalinka Group) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on how ML-driven metasearch merges, dedupes and ranks real estate listings
Body:
Anyone who has hunted for a flat knows the routine: the same property on three sites, with three prices and two different ideas of how big the kitchen is. Kirill Mozheykin, a private broker and former Chief Product Officer at Kalinka Group, gave Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 a guided tour of real estate metasearch: the machine learning that pulls listings from many platforms into one feed, merges the duplicates, fills the gaps and ranks what's left.

It's an industry overview rather than a build log. There's no architecture of his own on show; instead he maps the problems, the standard techniques and the companies using them, which makes it a useful orientation for engineers about to work on property or marketplace search.

## Why is property search so messy?

Kirill Mozheykin said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 that across platforms like Zillow, Redfin and Realtor, "Listings are inconsistent, data isn't standardized, and you often find yourself jumping between sites". He breaks that into three problems:

- **A fragmented market.** Listings are spread over many platforms, so buyers and sellers miss opportunities unless they check every source.
- **Inconsistent data structures.** One site lists square footage, another highlights amenities; formats and terminology differ, so comparing is hard.
- **Weak personalisation.** Users get bombarded with irrelevant listings or miss good matches.

Metasearch answers by aggregating from MLS databases and brokerage websites, normalising terms and formats, removing duplicates and presenting one list. His flagship example is Flatfy, which aggregates listings from more than 10,000 websites in 30 countries and uses machine learning to filter duplicates, fill in missing details such as addresses and prices, predict prices for thin listings, and run convolutional neural networks over photos to spot watermarks and judge renovation quality.

## What makes metasearch hard to build?

Four engineering challenges, in his order:

1. **Data collection.** Most real estate sites impose strict API limits, so real-time access is hard and listings go stale, which costs user trust. Integration then means normalising formats and terminology, and deduplicating postings made several times by users or agencies, which matters for SEO as well as for users.
2. **Recommendations.** Collaborative filtering learns from clicks, previous searches and interactions; content-based filtering matches preferences against price, size, location and amenities. Platforms use both.
3. **Images.** CNNs detect interior styles, kitchens, layouts and swimming pools, so users can search by what a place looks like; image deduplication removes repeated photos within a listing.
4. **Scale.** Distributed search engines such as Elasticsearch or Apache Solr handle indexing and real-time queries over large volumes.

## How does the ranking work?

The search layer is classic information retrieval plus language models. BM25 ranks listings against a query using term frequency and document length; vector space models represent listings and queries as vectors to measure similarity. BERT-style models handle intent and jargon, for instance whether condo and apartment mean the same thing in a given context, and let users describe what they want in natural language rather than keywords.

On top of that he lists the ML jobs that keep the feed clean: matching duplicates across sites by pattern recognition and key identifiers, predicting missing values from similar listings, normalising location names, and spotting fraudulent listings as anomalies. Automated valuation models combine price history, location and image data; he cites error margins as low as 4% for homes and 6% for commercial properties.

## Who is doing this already?

The case studies cover Zillow (its Zestimate draws on millions of property photos and data points), Trulia (recommendations from browsing behaviour), Redfin (personalised recommendations and real-time market data), CBRE (predictive analytics for commercial investment and ML-backed virtual tours) and Itransition (ML systems that gather data from public databases and social media). On the agent side, Lofty, an AI-powered real estate CRM, automates follow-ups, while chatbots provide round-the-clock answers and tools such as VEED.IO help produce video tours.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product managers starting on marketplace or listings search, in property or any domain where the same item shows up in many feeds with different data. If you already run entity resolution and learning-to-rank in production, the talk's breadth will be familiar; its value is the map of the domain and its players.

Title: OCR reads the receipt, the LLM files it into JSON
Description: Vladimir Pesterev at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on building a receipt-scanner API with Tesseract.js, Deno and OpenAI function calling in JSON mode
Body:
OCR gives you every word on a receipt in one undifferentiated heap; your API needs line items, a subtotal and a total. Vladimir Pesterev showed at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 how a software engineer closes that gap in a few dozen lines of TypeScript: Tesseract.js pulls the text out of the image, and an OpenAI model with function calling and JSON mode maps it onto a JSON schema you control.

He's upfront that this is a software engineer's view, not a data scientist's, and the talk is a live-coding demo from an empty folder to a working endpoint. Think of it as the receipt-scanner hello world you can adapt to invoices, forms or anything else with text in a picture.

## Why isn't OCR enough on its own?

Optical character recognition turns images of typed text into machine-readable text, and there's no shortage of it as a service: Amazon Textract and the Google Cloud Vision API are the obvious ones. The catch, as Pesterev puts it, is that OCR alone is not enough: it returns unstructured text, while most APIs speak JSON or another serialisable structure. You still need something that knows which number is the unit price and which is the total.

That's the job he gives the LLM. OpenAI's API offers function calling, which he calls one of its most useful features, and a JSON mode. Vladimir Pesterev said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "The model's output is guaranteed to be valid JSON when JSON mode is enabled."

## What does the pipeline look like?

The flow is short:

1. The client sends a request with the URL of a receipt image.
2. Tesseract.js (free and open source, which is why it wins over Textract here) downloads the image and extracts the text.
3. The text goes to the OpenAI chat completions API with a prompt and a function definition.
4. The model calls the function, and its arguments, already shaped as JSON, go straight back to the client.

The server runs on Deno, which he pitches as Node.js, but better. `deno init` scaffolds the project, `Deno.serve` provides the built-in HTTP server, and a quick echo server tested with curl proves the plumbing before any AI shows up. Tesseract.js comes from npm: create a worker once, then call its recognise function on each request.

## Where does the prompt engineering happen?

In two places. The chat completion carries two messages: a system message that tells the model to act as a helpful receipt analysis tool, and a user message with the prompt, which has the OCR output concatenated in. He calls writing that prompt the most creative part of the job and expects you to tailor it to your own documents.

The heavier lifting is in the function tool. Its JSON schema defines the receipt: an array of items, each with a description, unit price and amount as required properties, plus subtotal and total as numbers. The handler takes the first choice, looks for the tool call by name, returns a server error if it's missing, and otherwise sends the arguments back as the response body. The demo uses GPT-3.5 with one choice and JSON mode on.

## Does it actually work?

Mostly. The result has every field he asked for, and one amount comes back slightly wrong when he compares the JSON with the original receipt. That's the honest lesson of the demo: the schema guarantees the shape of the answer, not its correctness. He also points out what he skipped for time and what a real service needs: argument validation and token optimisation.

## Who should watch

Backend and full-stack developers who have been handed a document-extraction feature and want the shortest path to a working prototype, especially in TypeScript. If you already run structured outputs in production, this is a refresher; if you've never wired OCR to an LLM, it's a clear twenty-minute start.

- Bethany Jepchumba on [how multimodal models work](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Bethany_Jepchumba_multimodal_models_data) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, where GPT-4o reads the image itself.
- Harsha Vardhan Reddy Yeddula on [document management with Azure Machine Learning](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Harsha_Vardhan_Reddy_Yeddula_azure_document_management) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.

Title: Make the LLM fill in a survey for every Linux kernel commit
Description: Yusheng Zheng (eunomia-bpf) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on Code-Survey, which has LLMs answer surveys about commits to map how the eBPF subsystem evolved
Body:
You can't paste the Linux kernel into a context window, and RAG is far better at finding a function than at explaining why a subsystem keeps breaking. Yusheng Zheng, founder of eunomia-bpf, presented Code-Survey at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: treat the LLM as a survey participant, hand it a structured questionnaire about each commit, and turn years of patches and mailing-list prose into a dataset you can query. His team pointed it at the kernel's eBPF subsystem and got answers about feature history, coupling between components and where verifier bugs come from.

## What kind of understanding is missing?

LLMs already find bugs and write functions, so they understand code at some level. Zheng is after higher-level questions: how new features affect stability or performance, whether components have lifecycle stages, how a feature changed over time, which files attract bugs and which components depend on each other. The answers help with software design, bug studies, root-cause analysis, code review, new debugging and CI tools, and onboarding newcomers to open source projects.

Traditional methods (static analysis, manual review) are slow and incomplete, and they miss the context buried in commit messages, emails and discussions. The usual LLM tricks don't fit either. In-context learning hits the context limit. RAG depends on accurate retrieval, so it's best at small, precise questions about specific snippets. Fine-tuning is costly and risks overfitting on limited data. None of them handles design questions that span many files and a long history.

## How does Code-Survey work?

The premise, as Zheng put it: "what if we could ask every developer to take a survey about everything they contribute during the development process?" Asking the humans isn't practical, so the LLM stands in for them, on the grounds that "software development is a social activity", Yusheng Zheng said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, and its records can be surveyed.

The pipeline:

1. Human experts and LLM agents agree on the high-level questions.
2. They identify the data types and sources needed to answer them.
3. They design survey questions, for example the main type of a commit, with fixed choices such as bug fix or new feature, plus a description and hints for context.
4. Each survey definition becomes a form containing the commit details and the questions, and the LLM fills one in per commit, across thousands or hundreds of thousands of commits.
5. Humans or more LLM agents check the results, and the questions get refined where needed.

The output is a tagged, structured dataset you can query, analyse quantitatively and chart.

## What did it find in eBPF?

They chose eBPF because they know it well enough to verify the findings (eunomia-bpf works on it), because it evolves fast and is complex, and because Linux is developed through emails and patches, which is exactly the unstructured record the method needs. The early results:

- **Feature history.** The attach events show how use cases shifted: eBPF began with networking and has grown into tracing, profiling, security hooks, struct_ops and more.
- **Coupling.** The syscall interface and the libbpf library change together; new helpers and kfuncs usually mean updating the eBPF verifier too; runtime features such as BPF links touch several components at once.
- **Bugs.** Adding new eBPF instructions tends to bring more bugs into the verifier, with a clear overlap between instruction additions and verifier bug counts.

The full report is on GitHub and in the arXiv paper ([2410.01837](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01837)), and the tool is at [github.com/eunomia-bpf/code-survey](https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/code-survey).

## How do you stop the survey-taker from making things up?

The best practices carry over to any LLM tagging job: predefined tags and categories so answers are standardised, agent workflows that review and refine their own answers, an explicit not-sure option so the model doesn't invent an answer when information is missing, pilot testing with iterative refinement of the questions, consistency checks for contradictory answers, and running the survey several times to average the results.

He's frank about the limits. LLMs still misread and hallucinate, incomplete data leaves gaps, and human experts are still needed to design the survey and validate it. Next on the list: more automation with agents, a robust evaluation framework, stronger models such as o1, and the same treatment for LLVM, Kubernetes and Apache projects.

## Who should watch

Kernel and eBPF people curious about their subsystem's history, researchers doing empirical software engineering, and anyone who has to tag a mountain of unstructured text with an LLM and wants the answers to hold up. It's short and to the point.

- Anais Dotis on [how kernel programming escaped the kernel](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Anais_Dotis_ebpf_linux_networking) at Conf42 Observability 2026.

Title: Conf42 JavaScript 2024: heap limits, local variables and AI in the browser
Description: The Conf42 JavaScript 2024 roundup - 36 talks on Node.js performance and security, AI in the browser, TypeScript, React, tooling and JavaScript in industry.
Body:
[Conf42 JavaScript 2024](https://www.conf42.com/js2024) went out on October 31 with 36 talks, and the best of them were about what happens to JavaScript after it ships: heaps that hit their limit, stack traces that don't say enough, event loops that a single bad regex can stall. Around that production core, the day covered AI running inside the browser, TypeScript's type system doing more work than it gets credit for, and a lot of React.

Speakers came from Sentry, Mattermost, Intel, Black Duck, Esri, ING, Walmart Global Tech, Bit.dev, Gatling, DragonflyDB, Block and a long list of smaller teams.

## What does Node.js look like under load?

[Gabriel Schulhof](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Gabriel_Schulhof_25_travails_memory_inmemory) of Intel told the most satisfying debugging story of the day. The Node.js process behind the Auction.com graph service, the GraphQL layer that handles about 85% of client requests, kept reaching its heap limit of roughly two gigabytes. The talk follows heap profile diffs, flame graphs and async_hooks until the subscription resolvers behave.

[Abhijeet Prasad](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Abhijeet_Prasad_1_superchargedproduction_stacktraces_localvariables) of Sentry showed how the Sentry SDKs use the Node.js inspector API to attach local variables to production stack traces, so an error report looks more like a paused debugger. [Muhammad Yasir Rafique](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Muhammad_Yasir_Rafique_42_memoryleaks_nodejs_diagnostics) of Find My Facility covered the full memory-leak toolkit, from Chrome DevTools to the inspect flag and profilers. [Mohammed Zubair Ahmed](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Mohammed_Zubair_Ahmed_41_realtimechat_performance_100kusers) of Mattermost walked through measuring and improving a React, Redux and WebSocket web app for 100,000 active users.

## How do you knock a Node.js app over?

[Allon Mureinik](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Allon_Mureinik_4_dosattacks_nodejs_prevention) of Black Duck answered with the event loop. Node.js is single-threaded, so the denial of service you should worry about is often not a flood of requests but one request that keeps the loop busy. His talk catalogues the common mistakes that make that possible and the habits that prevent it. He also gets the obligatory MS-DOS joke out of the way early.

Security came up in a few other places too: [Manpreet Singh Sachdeva](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Manpreet_Singh_Sachdeva_37_kubernetes_bestpractices_security) of Walmart Global Tech on Kubernetes security for JavaScript applications, [Ammar Khan](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Ammar_Khan_zero_trust_security) of Auxin on zero trust for containers, and [Rizel Scarlett](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Rizel_Scarlett_56_jsonwebtokens_mobile_security) of TBD (Block) on verifiable credentials as JSON Web Tokens, the technology behind mobile driver's licences. [Fabien Vauchelles](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Fabien_Vauchelles_23_livecoding_antiban_webscraping), creator of Scrapoxy, live-coded anti-ban web scraping techniques.

## Can the browser run the model?

Two talks said yes. [Danielle Maxwell](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Danielle_Maxwell_19_ai_browser) of Rotational Labs showed Transformers.js and TensorFlow.js running machine learning in the browser, so JavaScript developers don't have to switch to Python. [Mohamad Shiralizadeh](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Mohamad_Shiralizadeh_40_aibrowsers_builtin_future) of ING explored the built-in AI APIs arriving in browsers, with live demos and live coding.

AI also showed up on the developer side. [Sharon Barr](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Sharon_Barr_63_genaidevtools_unittesting_automation) of Early let GenAI tools write the unit tests, and [Prakash Ojha](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Prakash_Ojha_49_aicodereview_automation) of BNY covered AI-assisted code review and quality assurance.

## Types, hooks and the front end

TypeScript had two strong talks. [Kacper Szewczyk](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Kacper_Szewczyk_31_typescript_developerexperience_improvement) of RST Software Master asked how much you can trust static type analysis on greenfield and legacy projects alike, and [Joe Zhou](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Joe_Zhou_76_typesafety_fullstack) of DragonflyDB achieved end-to-end type safety across client and backend without GraphQL or Swagger.

React got the most sessions. [Daniel Espino Garcia](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Daniel_Espino_Garcia_18_reacthooks_improvement_development) of Mattermost explained how hooks work on the inside, [Raihan Nismara](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Raihan_Nismara_52_react_accessibility_frontend) of Telkom Indonesia covered accessibility essentials, [Courtney Yatteau](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Courtney_Yatteau_15_react_gamification_frontend) of Esri added scoring, badges and challenges with gamification, and [Alok Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Alok_Kumar_5_3dwebsite_r3f_webdevelopment) of UtkalLabs built 3D scenes with React Three Fiber. [Aleksandr Guzenko](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Aleksandr_Guzenko_3_architecturaldebt_featuresliceddesign_cleancode) of IT_ONE made the case for Feature-Sliced Design as a guard against architectural debt, [Abhinav Chunchu](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Abhinav_Chunchu_2_adaptiveinterfaces_datadrivenux) of Lowes covered adaptive user interfaces, and [Francisca Beatriz Medina Concha](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Francisca_Beatriz_Medina_Concha_24_algorithmicart_creativity) of LATAM Airlines made algorithmic art with p5.js.

## Tools that change the build and the test

[Konstantinos Leimonis](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Konstantinos_Leimonis_34_rspack_bundling_webdevelopment) of Bit.dev explained Rspack, the Rust-based bundler, and its architecture. [Iniubong Obonguko](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Iniubong_Obonguko_27_serversidejavascript_nitrojs_supercharging) introduced Nitro for server-side JavaScript that deploys anywhere. [Gil Zilberfeld](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Gil_Zilberfeld_26_playwright_automation_testing) of TestinGil fit Playwright into an hour, [Samir Akarioh](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Samir_Akarioh_61_loadtesting_optimization_gatling) of Gatling went past web performance into load testing, and [Jubin Thomas](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Jubin_Thomas_30_scalablebackend_microservices_ecommerce) of Signet Jewelers built an e-commerce backend from Node.js, Express, MongoDB and AMQP microservices.

## JavaScript in other industries

A strand of talks applied JavaScript and AI to specific sectors: dialysis care from [Ram Meka](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Ram_Meka_54_ai_healthcareinnovation), healthcare IT from [VijayaAshwin Jagadeesan](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_VijayaAshwin_Jagadeesan_72_healthcareit_emergingtechnologies), life and annuities claims from [Praveen Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Praveen_Kumar_50_ai_claimsprocessing) of AllianzLife, utility operations from [Rajesh Kolli](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Rajesh_Kolli_53_ai_utilityoperations) of ykunt inc, retail promotions from [Anandakumar Kumaravelu](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Anandakumar_Kumaravelu_6_aipersonalization_customerretention) of Sada Systems, self-service kiosks from [Sai Krishna Paladugu](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Sai_Krishna_Paladugu_59_selfservicekiosks_ios) of FedEx, SAP HR self-service with SAPUI5 from [Lakshmi Gogula](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Lakshmi_Gogula_ess_sap_hr_sapui5), and AEM content work from [Bhanu Gogula](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Bhanu_Gogula_aem_performance_single_page_app). [Crystal Yang](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Crystal_Yang_16_socialimpact_programming) of Audemy closed the theme with JavaScript for social impact.

## Thanks to the partners

[StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) joined as newsletter partner and [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, with media partners including [Manning](https://www.manning.com), [Packt](https://www.packtpub.com/), [CodeCrafters](https://codecrafters.io/?r=2qF) and [No Fluff Jobs](https://nofluffjobs.com/).

Every talk is on the [Conf42 JavaScript 2024 page](https://www.conf42.com/js2024) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDgexCF_ygfCwh9KuWgldj2). The series returned a year later as [Conf42 JavaScript 2025](https://www.conf42.com/js2025).

Title: A RAG copilot's road to production starts with eyeballing and an eval set
Description: Chaitanya Pathak (LEAPS by Analyttica) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on taking a RAG copilot from POC to production with metrics-driven development
Body:
Every RAG proof of concept is evaluated the same way: someone reads the answers and nods. Chaitanya Pathak, Chief Product and Technology Officer at LEAPS by Analyttica, told Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 how his team turned that habit into an asset. They used the eyeballing phase to start a human-labelled gold-standard dataset, moved to supervised, reference-based evaluation, and only then started on LLM-as-a-judge. The rest of the talk is a tour of the retrieval choices that survived a year in production.

A note on scope: the abstract promises fine-tuning versus RAG with LLaMA 2 and GPT-4. The talk itself is a case study of one RAG system, with fine-tuning as one component of it.

## What is being built?

LEAPS is a low-code, no-code data science platform for non-technical users, covering pre-modelling, modelling, deployment and serving. The system in the talk is its copilot, a RAG-based inference engine made of a parent pipeline that orchestrates several child pipelines. It answers three umbrella questions: what can I do next (a recommendation engine), what else can I do (a scenarios engine that agrees on intent with the user, then builds the scenario in the backend), and do it for me (a processing engine that generates models, pre-processing steps, charts and dashboards from a few inputs).

## How do you evaluate a RAG system you can't eyeball forever?

Pathak calls their approach metrics-driven development, and the evaluation work "takes a lot of our time". It rests on three pillars:

- **Approach:** reference-based, so everything depends on ground truth, which needs gold-standard eval data labelled and annotated by humans.
- **Scope:** end to end, plus component-level metrics for retrieval and generation. Retrieval is scored with F1 (a balance of precision and recall); generation with faithfulness and answer relevancy, using the Ragas framework.
- **Design considerations:** how many components are non-deterministic (two use LLMs), how many conversation turns are allowed (they moved from single-turn to bounded multi-turn), and which prompt flows each ability needs.

The journey went in three stages. Chaitanya Pathak said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 that throughout the POC "all that the teams were doing was eyeballing", but the analytics team collected those query, context and response triples into eval data from day one, topped up with synthetic generators. That fed structured supervised evaluation, and now an early move to LLM-as-a-judge, which he warns needs sophisticated prompt engineering of its own.

## Which retrieval choices held up?

On data preprocessing, they compared fixed-size, content-based and semantic chunking and settled on semantic, while noting a hybrid strategy can win for other data. Sparse retrieval (TF-IDF and BM25) served them well until vocabulary mismatch started to bite, so dense retrievers are the next POC. Metadata was there from day one: on documents, chunks and prompt versions, but also on the user's business context, captured as an organisational business map and KPIs, which drives routing across three databases (product docs, user history, business context).

Query enhancement arrived once conversations loosened up: LLM-based query decomposition with chain-of-thought prompting, and HyDE to generate hypothetical documents for chunk classification. Every added layer is weighed against latency, which is why DevOps sits in the RAG work. The product runs on AWS, sometimes behind customer firewalls, so concurrency and cost shape the architecture.

For retrieval and re-ranking: filtered vector search since day one, cross-encoders over bi-encoders (they use Cohere's reranker; the bi-encoders are being phased out), hierarchical indexing with parent and child nodes, and corrective RAG (CRAG) in POC as a lightweight retriever that scores its own retrieved documents. Fine-tuning is standard for each LLM component, on synthetic data where real data is missing.

## Where does prompt engineering fit in RAG?

His takeaway: a simple RAG uses prompts only for augmentation, but every component you hand to an LLM needs its own carefully engineered prompt. In his words, "sophisticated prompt engineering is absolutely bedrock" once LLMs spread through the pipeline. Next on the list: a modular RAG architecture with dockerised microservices to support subscription pricing, end-to-end prompt versioning (an open problem for them), unit tests with Promptfoo, and agentic tools in the orchestrator, which today runs on custom rules.

## Who should watch

Teams with a RAG demo that works and a production date that worries them. It's a dense checklist delivered at speed, light on numbers but heavy on what one team actually chose and why.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Ofer Mendelevitch on [measuring hallucinations in RAG](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Ofer_Mendelevitch_rag_measuring_hallucinations) at Conf42 Large Language Models 2024.
- Srinivas Chennupati on [production-ready RAG systems](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Srinivas_Chennupati_knowledge_rag_strategies) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025.
- Varun Joshi on [why metadata is the missing piece of RAG](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Varun_Joshi_rag_metadata) at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026.

Title: JavaScript: small script, big universe
Description: One more dependency, one more galaxy
Body:
# JavaScript is doing everything now

Once upon a time, JavaScript was just there to make buttons clickable. Cute. Simple. Innocent.

Fast forward a bit and now it’s running in browsers, on servers, inside kiosks, across healthcare systems, helping with AI workloads, securing containers, and probably judging your variable names. Growth, right?

Conf42 JavaScript 2024 is here to embrace that chaos.

This one covers the whole JavaScript universe. AI in the browser. Built-in AI features. JavaScript in healthcare, utilities, finance, and retail. Unit tests generated for you while you quietly sip your coffee. Server-side performance, memory leaks, security, and what happens when your Node.js app decides to go rogue.

There’s React. Obviously. Hooks, accessibility, gamification, and UX that actually adapts to users instead of annoying them. TypeScript gets plenty of love too, from developer experience to end-to-end type safety. And yes, there are deep dives for when you’re feeling brave.

If you’re more of a backend person, we’ve got Node.js talks on scalability, DoS protection, stack traces that actually make sense, and production debugging without losing your sanity. If frontend is your thing, expect bundlers, performance, web APIs, and creative uses of JavaScript that go well beyond forms and modals.

Basically, if JavaScript is part of your job description (or your personality at this point), you’ll find something here. Or several things. Possibly too many things.

You’ve been warned.

Title: On-device LLMs fix privacy today, but need 30B parameters to beat the cloud
Description: Rishab Mehra (Pinnacle) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on why on-device LLMs are safer and greener, and what it takes to reach GPT-4o quality locally
Body:
A 7-billion-parameter coding model beat an 8-billion general-purpose one at writing Minesweeper, on a laptop, with no internet. Rishab Mehra, Founder and CTO of Pinnacle and previously on on-device machine learning at Apple, used that kind of side-by-side at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 to argue that LLMs belong on the device: it removes the privacy problem by design, cuts the energy bill, and the remaining quality gap closes through specialisation, adapters and hardware that can hold around 30 billion parameters.

## What problems do on-device models solve?

Mehra lists three problems with today's LLMs and tackles two. The first is privacy: the most useful assistants need personal data, often your screen, and you end up trusting both the model provider and the startup in between. The second is carbon. He cites published estimates that training GPT-4 emitted as much as driving 18 million miles in a gasoline car, and that a single GPT-4 query can equal charging a phone 60 times. (The third, models that mimic humans well enough for voice-clone fraud, he leaves for another talk.)

Moving the model onto the device answers both. No network connection, no middleman, and Rishab Mehra said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "So there's no privacy risk anymore." The models also have to be small to fit, so they are greener by construction.

## How good are local models right now?

The demos run through Ollama on a MacBook. Llama 3.1 8B writes a passable one-line opener for his own talk; a much larger Llama fails to load at all, eating 32 GB of memory before giving up, which puts the practical ceiling for that machine at roughly 7 to 10 billion parameters. GPT-4o, in the cloud, nails the opener as a baseline.

The coding test is the fun part. Asked for Minesweeper in Python, Llama 3.1 8B produces sensible-looking code that doesn't run; it took Mehra 15 to 20 minutes to fix. GPT-4o's version works first time, and he promptly loses on turn one. CodeQwen 7B from Alibaba, a model tuned for code, produces a game that runs but shows you where the mines are and doesn't end when you hit one. He got it fully working in under five minutes.

The benchmark numbers on his slides back that up:

| Model | Chat / reasoning (MMLU) | Coding (MBPP EvalPlus) |
|---|---|---|
| Llama 3.1 8B | 73.0 | 72.8 |
| Llama 3.1 70B | 86.0 | 86.0 |
| GPT-4o | 88.7 | 87.8 |
| CodeQwen1.5 7B | n/a | 78.7 |

The smaller, specialised model beats the general one of similar size by about six points on coding.

## What already works offline?

He walks through Apple Intelligence on an iPhone in airplane mode. Style transfer (rewrite an email in a friendly tone) works well; proofreading and rewriting are hit and miss, with one rewrite confusing who signed the email. Dictation works flawlessly offline, as does translation once you download the language pack, and notification summaries. Summarising a long email, though, needed the internet. His scorecard: speech-to-text is about as good as the server side, summarisation gets you around 80% of the value, translation is almost there.

## What would make on-device the default?

His bar for the minimum viable product is GPT-4o-level accuracy on the device, and he names the levers:

- **About 30 billion parameters on device.** He thinks 8 to 10 billion is too small to hold enough knowledge, while 60 to 70 billion models already score well and could be compressed down.
- **Deeper specialisation.** "Models need to be more specialized", he says: not just a coding model but a Python model.
- **Adapters** such as LoRA, adding a layer like "games in Python" without training a new model.
- **Better compression** on the software side, plus processing units built for LLMs and faster memory architecture on the hardware side.

If that lands, he expects private, local models for augmented work (your whole work context, nothing sent to a server), therapy, legal help and medical diagnosis, all areas where people hold back data today because they don't trust where it goes.

## Who should watch

Engineers deciding between a cloud API and a local model, and anyone curious how far a MacBook gets with Ollama. The demos are honest about the failures, which makes the benchmark table more convincing.

Title: Let Apache NiFi build the prompt, and let Milvus skip the LLM call
Description: Tim Spann (Zilliz) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on automating prompt building with Apache NiFi 2.0 pipelines and Milvus vector search
Body:
Most prompts arrive half-built: a user types the laziest possible question and expects the system to fill in the rest. Tim Spann, Principal Developer Advocate at Zilliz, used his Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk to argue that the filling-in is a data engineering job, and that a streaming tool such as Apache NiFi can do it without anyone hand-writing glue code. Add a vector database such as Milvus with cached answers, and some prompts never need to reach the LLM at all.

It is a short, brisk talk, and Spann says up front that he had been in hospital that week. The source code and slides are linked from the talk.

## What does prompt automation actually mean?

Tim Spann said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 that "prompt automation is really about making prompts as powerful and as easy as possible", which in practice means removing the drudgery between the question and the model. His pipeline starts with unstructured data (documents, images, logs, email, social posts, PDFs) turned into embeddings and stored in a vector database. When a query comes in, an approximate nearest neighbour search pulls back the closest matches, and those results become the context the LLM sees.

The automation happens around that query. The pipeline can pre-parse the user's input, pick or fill a prompt template, apply whatever decision logic you've set, and augment it with retrieved context before anything is sent to a model.

## Why cache prompts in the vector database?

This is the idea worth stealing. Spann suggests keeping the most popular questions in their own Milvus collection and matching new queries against them, using scalar filtering alongside vector search to catch ones that are the same or nearly the same. A hit means you already have the answer. As he puts it: "often you may not even need to call the LLM if we've got things cached."

He pairs that with the usual RAG benefits: better accuracy, fewer hallucinations, answers grounded in your own domain data, and no lock-in to one model or platform, since whatever sits in the vector database works with any model. You also keep ownership of the data. Libraries such as LangChain and LlamaIndex can build some of these prompts for you, and prompt templates cover the rest.

Milvus itself gets a quick pitch: open source, over 30,000 GitHub stars at the time, pip-installable in a notebook, and the same code runs in Docker, a big cluster or Zilliz Cloud. It supports dense and sparse embeddings, filtering and re-ranking.

## Where does NiFi fit?

A Python app is fine for many cases. For real-time workloads, Spann reaches for dataflow pipelines, with Apache NiFi as his main example (Apache Flink and other streaming tools get a mention). The pipeline does the unglamorous parts: ingest, route, clean, enrich, transform, parse, chunk and vectorise, then craft the prompt from templates or logic, call out for context, and round-trip the result to Discord, Slack, a REST interface, Kafka or SQL.

NiFi 2.0 is the version to use, he says, because it runs on recent Java and can run Python. That means the Python libraries you'd already written become pipeline steps: one of his extracts company names from a prompt before anything else happens, others caption images, filter out problematic images with a classification model, or detect facial emotions. Apache Kafka sits in the middle as the hub that distributes work to Flink, Ray, Spark or straight into Milvus. (He also notes that Prague has a good Kafka museum, the other kind.)

## What does the demo show?

Two things. A Milvus collection of live aircraft data he captures in flight, with images, latitude and metadata next to the vectors, ready for conversational queries over it. Then a small RAG example where LangChain builds the prompt from a query like "what's in this image" and returns the answer. His GitHub examples also include street-camera streaming you can chat with from Slack, and an edge use case on a Raspberry Pi.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who already run NiFi or Kafka and are being asked to make an LLM feature work, and anyone building RAG who hasn't yet thought about caching popular questions. It's an overview with a quick demo, not a long build-along, so pair it with the longer talks below.

Title: Computers finally meet us halfway, with eyes, ears and text at once
Description: Bethany Jepchumba (Microsoft) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on how multimodal models such as CLIP, DALL-E and GPT-4o work, with demos
Body:
For decades people learned to speak computer, because computers couldn't take in more than one kind of input at a time. Bethany Jepchumba, Cloud Advocate at Microsoft, used her Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk to explain what changes when a model can read, see and hear in one go: how attention and transformers make multimodality work, how CLIP and DALL-E are built, and a set of GPT-4o demos that range from a dashboard explainer to a cookie review.

It's an introduction, and a good one if multimodal is still a buzzword on your team's roadmap rather than something you've shipped.

## Why multimodal, and why now?

Her framing is simple. Most generative AI so far has worked in one modality: chat in natural language, or vision only, or speech only. Bethany Jepchumba said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 that "we as humans interact with the real world using multiple senses", and because computers couldn't, "us human beings have had to learn how to interact with computers versus the other way around."

She sets the scene with three figures: private investment in AI doubled, 50% of organisations have adopted AI in at least one business area, and 70% of employees are ready to embrace it. Then she lays out the single-modality models most people already know: GPT models for language, Whisper for speech, DALL-E for generating images from text. A multimodal model reasons across text, images and audio in the same conversation.

## How does a model handle several modalities at once?

Two building blocks carry the explanation. The attention mechanism lets a model weigh which parts of its input matter for the question at hand, and it can build those relationships within one modality or across several. The transformer architecture builds on attention: you can give each modality its own encoder and feed them all into a shared transformer layer, where the cross-modal work happens.

## What CLIP and DALL-E actually do

CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) takes a large set of image and caption pairs, encodes each side with its own encoder, and puts both embeddings in the same vector space. Training pulls matching pairs together and pushes non-matching ones apart, which is what makes it useful for classifying images or steering image generation from a caption.

DALL-E goes the other way: a text prompt in, an image out. Jepchumba credits the scale of its training data, image and text pairs that teach the association between words and visuals, and the transformer's attention for decoding the prompt. More data means better performance, she notes, up to a point.

## What can you do with GPT-4o today?

The demos run on GPT-4o through Azure OpenAI, which also hosts GPT-4, Whisper and DALL-E for the single-modality jobs. The use cases are deliberately everyday:

- **Describe an image.** A tray of home-baked cookies gets an accurate description (golden brown, uneven, homemade), then a follow-up on how to bake better. The model's advice starts with reading the recipe, which is fair.
- **Spot anomalies.** She uploads a cake generated by DALL-E and asks what's wrong with it. Nothing, it turns out. The serious version of the same idea: compare images from areas hit by droughts or floods.
- **Explain a dashboard.** A Power BI retail sales report gets broken down section by section, followed by suggestions for extra metrics and step-by-step instructions for a multi-year sales trend analysis. A chart you like can also be turned into code.
- **Translate what you see.** Photograph a poster or label in a language you don't read and ask for a translation.
- **Feedback on drawings and handwriting**, which is how she uses it personally.

She closes with Microsoft's Responsible AI principles (fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, accountability), plus pointers to the Azure AI community on Discord and Microsoft's Generative AI for Beginners course.

## Who should watch

Developers and product people who need a clear mental model of multimodal AI before building with it, and anyone who wants a quick tour of what GPT-4o handles well with images. Engineers already running vision-language models in production will know the material; the follow-ups below go further.

Title: Load-test the chat server, then measure the browser
Description: Mohammed Zubair Ahmed (Mattermost) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on load-testing a React and Redux chat client and comparing builds, not absolute metrics
Body:
Server load tests tell you how many users a chat backend can hold. They say nothing about whether the browser tab of the next user to log in is freezing. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Mohammed Zubair Ahmed, Software Design Engineer at Mattermost, explained how the team points a real browser at a server under synthetic load, measures the client, and compares builds to find performance regressions in the Mattermost web app.

The talk is about the client only; the server side, as he puts it, needs its own talk. And despite the 100k users in the title, the talk is about method rather than a scaling war story with headline numbers.

## Why is a real-time client hard to keep fast?

Mattermost's web app is a single-page React app with Redux and Redux Thunk for state and the WebSocket API for real-time updates. The trouble starts with the volume of incoming WebSocket events at elevated usage. Many of them trigger more requests: a new post arrives with a user ID, and if that user isn't already in the Redux store, the client goes back to the server to fetch them. Add the constant trade-off between over-fetching and under-fetching, and a UI that still has to respond to clicks.

## How do you simulate thousands of users?

With Mattermost's in-house load testing tool, mattermost-load-test-ng. A user controller drives each simulated user in a loop (posting, switching channels and teams, opening threads, reacting), and a coordinator manages the cluster of load-test agents. The coordinator keeps adding users while reading server metrics from Prometheus, then backs off until it reaches equilibrium, the point where no more active users can be added.

The client-side extension connects a real browser to one of the app nodes while that load runs, drives it with an automated test suite, and pipes browser metrics into the same Prometheus, with Grafana on top. To compare versions, they run build A in an environment, wait for equilibrium, run the client automation and record the metrics; then repeat with identical settings for build B.

## Which metrics matter?

Because client numbers depend on hardware, browser and whatever else the user has open, Mohammed Zubair Ahmed said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 that "comparison is the key over here, not the absolute values". The toolkit:

- **Memory profiles** in Chrome DevTools, to find leaks and wasteful allocation before they crash the tab.
- **CPU profiles**, because a hot client slows down every other app on the machine too.
- **Frames per second** during interaction, to catch choppy re-renders.
- **HTTP archives (HAR)**, to find long-pending requests nobody knew about. The request itself is cheap; processing the response into the store is the heavy part.
- **Web Vitals** via Google's library and **Lighthouse** for FCP, LCP, CLS, Interaction to Next Paint, total blocking time and speed index.
- **Custom Mattermost metrics** such as channel switch and team switch time.

## What did they actually fix?

He walks through pull requests, each backed by before-and-after comparisons that also serve as a record of why the change was made. One reducer accounted for 34% of memory usage in a profiled interaction because objects were left dangling and never garbage collected, and browser GC pauses are expensive. A third-party profile popover library leaked memory and was replaced by a newer, supported one. User status updates, which aren't sent over WebSocket because of server cost, were being polled and hammering the Redux store until the app froze; a small data manager now queues status requests and flushes them at a configurable interval. Another fix stopped the client fetching full threads for channels the user wasn't viewing.

## What are the caveats?

Network latency first: "network latency will eat away all your hard work", so 30 ms shaved off the client disappears behind a slow server. Then perception: a slow first load makes users decide the app is bad, so reports like "channel switching is slow" have to be reproduced with the load tool rather than taken at face value. And gains aren't linear; some fixes pay a lot, most pay a little.

## Who should watch

Anyone running a React and Redux app with live updates (chat, dashboards, collaboration tools) who suspects the browser is the bottleneck and wants a repeatable way to prove it. It is a process talk with real PRs, not a code walkthrough.

Title: Write the LLM's output back to the vector DB, and keep it fresh in real time
Description: Bobur Umurzokov (GlassFlow) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on generative feedback loops that stream Supabase changes into Weaviate
Body:
Most RAG demos treat the vector database as a snapshot you load once. Bobur Umurzokov, Developer Relations Manager at GlassFlow and a Microsoft MVP for Azure AI services, used his Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk to argue for the opposite: a generative feedback loop, where the model's output is embedded and written back to the vector store, and every change in the source database flows through the loop within milliseconds.

It is a concept-plus-demo talk built on his employer's product, GlassFlow, with Supabase as the source and Weaviate as the destination. The pattern stands on its own; the tooling is one way to build it.

## What is a generative feedback loop?

A feedback loop uses current outputs to improve future results. A generative feedback loop (GFL) applies that to generative AI: take what the LLM generated, vectorise it, save it back to the vector database, and use it for future processing. Bobur Umurzokov said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "the outputs become the inputs for the loop cycle."

He separates it from plain generative AI, which runs one way: input in, content out. A GFL keeps improving the output over time, which also makes it more complex, because you need a way to collect feedback and adjust. A code generator that loops with tests until the code improves is his short example.

## Where would you use one?

His use cases are all about data that changes:

- **Recommendations** that refine themselves as users click, browse and buy.
- **Real estate listings**, where price, availability and features (add a sofa, remove the fridge) change constantly and descriptions should stay current for search.
- **Job listings** that emphasise remote work or flexible hours when that is what candidates search for.
- **Travel itineraries** shaped by a user's past searches, and personalised viewing in the style of Netflix.

## Why does real time matter?

The architecture is a pipeline in the middle of the loop. Detect a change in a source (an API, files, a database), for example a new Airbnb listing. Ask OpenAI or another model to generate a description from the listing's attributes. Calculate embeddings for that generated text. Store them in the vector database. A user searching in plain language for a cozy apartment in Paris then gets current options, because the query is embedded and compared against a corpus that never went stale.

He positions GlassFlow as the pipeline layer: a serverless, Python-first platform where you write a transformation function and it scales without you running Kafka plus Flink. Sources include PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Google Pub/Sub and Amazon SQS, with destinations such as databases, BI tools and vector stores.

## The demo: Airbnb listings from Supabase to Weaviate

The demo uses Airbnb listing data for New York City and builds the pipeline in about 15 minutes:

1. **Weaviate Cloud**: create a cluster and an `AirbnbNYC`-style collection with OpenAI's text2vec vectoriser and `text-embedding-3-small`.
2. **GlassFlow**: create a pipeline with a webhook source, and a Python transformation whose `handler` function takes the Supabase row, asks OpenAI for a listing description, and builds the embeddings. Add the OpenAI dependency, then set a webhook sink pointing at the Weaviate cluster URL with the API key in the header.
3. **Supabase**: on the listings table, create a database webhook on insert events, with the GlassFlow pipeline access token in the header, and enable real-time on the table.

A Python script inserts 20 new listings in a batch. Each insert fires the webhook, GlassFlow enriches it, and the results land in Weaviate. In Weaviate's GraphQL console he runs a structured query (the five most-reviewed listings in Brooklyn), then a natural-language one, luxury apartment with a nice view, which returns matching listings with AI-generated summaries that were not in the original data. Change a listing's price in Supabase and the vector store reflects it immediately.

His sample questions show what the pattern is for: popular listings by area, budget-friendly places in Brooklyn under 100 US dollars with positive reviews, or a free-text search for a great view.

## Who should watch

Python developers and data engineers with a Supabase or PostgreSQL source of truth who want their vector store to keep up with it, and anyone whose RAG index goes stale between nightly reloads. Teams already doing change data capture into a vector store will mostly see a GlassFlow walkthrough.
