Title: Load tests in JavaScript, from npx to a GitHub Action
Description: Samir Akarioh (Gatling) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on writing Gatling load tests in JavaScript, reading the report and running them from CI
Body:
Your Lighthouse score says nothing about what happens when a few thousand people click Buy at once. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Samir Akarioh, Developer Advocate at Gatling, made the case for load testing next to front-end performance work and demoed a Gatling simulation written in JavaScript against a small CRUD API, from `npx gatling run` to a GitHub Actions workflow on Gatling Enterprise.

It is a vendor talk, and it says so: the product is Gatling, the open source load testing tool, with its paid Enterprise edition in the second half.

## Why bother if the pages are already fast?

Because traffic spikes are when sites fall over, and he lists the usual suspects: Ticketmaster during big ticket sales such as Taylor Swift's, and e-commerce sites on launch day. Two figures carry the business argument: the highest e-commerce conversion rates occur on pages that load in 0 to 2 seconds (Portent, 2019), and bounce probability increases by 32% when page load time goes from 1 second to 3 seconds (Google, 2017). Make an Amazon shopper wait five seconds and they are on eBay.

His one-line definition: "load testing is typically, you will send a lot of users and see when the application will crash." He illustrates it with a photo of a packed French train, which any French commuter will recognise as a load test in production.

## Which load test do you need?

He places load testing under non-functional performance testing, beside web performance, with an APM such as Datadog or Dynatrace watching while it runs. Then three shapes:

- **Capacity test**: ramp up, say 5 users every 10 seconds, to find the breaking point and maximum capacity.
- **Stress test**: a sudden spike, like a million users arriving after a TV appearance.
- **Soak test**: sustained high load for a long time, to surface memory leaks and slow degradation.

## What does a Gatling script in JavaScript look like?

The demo API manages users. The script imports from Gatling's core and HTTP modules and defines a simulation, which he describes as the recipe Gatling follows. Each step checks its status: list users and expect 200, create one with a random UUID name and expect 201, then fetch, edit and delete it. Every virtual user gets its own session, so the script stores the new user's ID and name and reuses them in later requests.

The setup block sets the injection profile (in the demo, a minute of nothing, a burst, a capacity ramp, then a soak) and can carry assertions, such as failing the run if more than 20% of requests error. Running it is `npx gatling run`.

## What does the report tell you?

Minimum, maximum, mean and percentile response times per request, error counts, and drill-downs by endpoint. His own run is honest about the API: one request took around a second, some calls returned 404 where 200 was expected, and the checks failed under parallel users. "I don't trust concurrency in my API, so I need to implement this." Finding that before your users do is the whole point.

## Can it run on every pull request?

That is the Enterprise half. You package the simulation, upload it, create a simulation in Gatling Enterprise and copy its ID; a short GitHub Actions workflow then triggers the run through Gatling's action. He mentions integrations with Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Dynatrace, Slack and Microsoft Teams. The Enterprise report adds a summary for business readers (error ratio, total requests, peak concurrent virtual users) plus timelines and filtering by status. It can also generate load from several AWS regions at once, say Sydney, Paris and the US, which open source users would have to build themselves.

## Who should watch

Front-end and full-stack developers who have never written a load test and would rather do it in JavaScript than learn another language. It is a short intro with a live demo, not a capacity-planning masterclass.

Title: One balanced diet prompt, refined until it fits a 10-year-old's eyesight
Description: Reetha Vadakkekkara (Walgreens Boots Alliance) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on refining one prompt with specifics, context, format and examples
Body:
Give me a balanced diet for a day gets you a diet for nobody in particular. Reetha Vadakkekkara, Azure Solutions Architect at Walgreens Boots Alliance, built her Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk around that one request, rewriting it step by step in ChatGPT until it described a 10-year-old boy with an eyesight problem, and showing how each change reshaped the answer.

It is a beginner-friendly talk of about 20 minutes. The single running example is its strength: you watch the same question get better, rather than read a list of tips.

## What kinds of prompts are there?

She sorts prompts into three types. Instructional prompts ask for a format or style: a poem of ten lines, an essay, a cover letter. Contextual prompts supply background, such as business growth strategies based on current economic trends. Interactive prompts treat the model as a discussion partner, asking follow-up after follow-up, the way you might talk through an election.

Her optimisation rules are four: be specific, use examples, set the context, and set the tone or level of formality. The theory is brief; the case study does the work.

## How does the answer change as the prompt sharpens?

Step one is the general prompt. ChatGPT returns a long, generic answer with an explanation of what a balanced diet is and several options for breakfast and mid-morning snacks.

Step two adds specifics: a balanced diet for a six-year-old girl. The options change to suit a child.

Step three adds context: a balanced diet for a 10-year-old boy with an issue in eyesight. The model treats eyesight as a possible nutritional question and tailors the plan.

Step four is instructional. She asks for bullet points with a maximum of ten lines, and the explanations shrink while the points stay.

Step five goes interactive. She asks what causes eyesight issues in a 10-year-old boy, in a paragraph of five sentences, and gets screen time, genetics, nutrition, bright light and UV exposure. Then she follows up with only the new question, which vitamins are needed, and the model keeps the earlier context. Reetha Vadakkekkara said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "For the further questions, we don't need to ask the same question again, we just need to ask about what are all the vitamins required."

Finally she sets an example of the shape she wants (genetic factors as a heading with an explanation, excessive screen time as a heading with an explanation) and the model reformats the whole answer to match.

## Few-shot, chain of thought and tree of thoughts

The advanced section is brief. Few-shot learning extends the format example: the more examples you give, the better the model generalises the output you want. Chain of thought, in her framing, is asking the model to explain its reasoning step by step and then questioning that reasoning, for instance why a family history of myopia raises the child's risk, and by how much. Tree of thoughts asks for several perspectives on the response so you can pick the one to pursue. Purists will note her chain of thought leans more on follow-up questioning than on the classic worked-example prompt, but the instinct, make the model show its work, is the right one.

## Can you trust the answer?

Her evaluation section is the part to keep. No response should be taken as 100% right, because every model is limited by its training data. If the model was trained on data up to 2023, it will not know 2024 figures, so a company's latest financials need another source. She checks three things: relevance (does it answer this prompt), coherence (is it logically structured and easy to follow) and accuracy (are the facts right). Then iterate: test the same prompt in different wordings, compare the outputs, and adjust phrasing, context and examples based on what you see. A model that gives different answers to the same question in different words is telling you something.

## Who should watch

People starting with ChatGPT or Copilot at work who want to see, in one example, why detail and context matter. Experienced prompt engineers can skip it, or send it to the colleague who still types three-word prompts.

Title: A spinning box to a flying bird in one React Three Fiber session
Description: Alok Kumar (UtkalLabs) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on building a 3D scene with React Three Fiber and Drei, from mesh basics to models and Netlify deploys
Body:
Three.js has a reputation for boilerplate, and React Three Fiber is the argument that most of it can go. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Alok Kumar, Software Engineer at UtkalLabs, live-coded a 3D scene in a Vite and React project, from a single mesh through lights, shadows, animation and an imported glTF model, and then deployed it like any other static site.

It is a beginner-friendly, hands-on session. If you know React and have never touched WebGL, this is the on-ramp.

## What sits under R3F?

He builds the stack bottom-up. WebGL is the JavaScript API that gives the browser low-level GPU access for 2D and 3D graphics. Three.js abstracts it into a scene graph with geometries, materials, textures, lighting and animation. React Three Fiber (R3F) then brings React's declarative model to Three.js: JSX and hooks to manage the scene, reusable components for 3D objects, and easy integration into existing React apps. Drei, a community collection of ready-made helpers for R3F, covers the rest.

For motivation he shows NASA's interactive solar system, where you can zoom to a satellite and orbit it, and his own portfolio: a laptop model with his résumé scrolling on its screen.

## How much code does R3F save?

The vocabulary comes first: a scene is the stage, objects are the actors, a camera is the point of view, and a renderer draws the scene from that camera. An object is a mesh, which combines a geometry (shape) with a material (look).

The native Three.js version needs a canvas element, a `querySelector`, a scene, a `BoxGeometry`, a `MeshBasicMaterial`, a mesh added to the scene, a `PerspectiveCamera` and a `WebGLRenderer`. The R3F version is a `<Canvas>` wrapping a `<mesh>` with a geometry and a material inside. Alok Kumar said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 that "Canvas comes prebuilt with camera, renderer, and everything." Defaults you can override when you need to.

## From flat to 3D

A torus knot with a basic material looks like a 2D sticker. Swapping in a normal material, which maps normal vectors to RGB colours, makes the curvature visible. Then come two Drei helpers: an axes helper to show X (red), Y (green) and Z (blue), and `OrbitControls`, which lets you rotate and zoom the camera instead of staring at the front of the object. Position, rotation and scale props handle transformations.

## Why animate with delta?

Animation runs through the `useFrame` hook, which fires on every rendered frame and passes the scene state and `delta`, the time since the last frame. Attach a ref to the mesh and change its position or rotation per frame. Add a fixed amount per frame, he points out, and the object travels twice as far per second on a 60 FPS screen as on a 30 FPS one. So "instead of going with plain units, we'll be using Delta for our animations": the motion is smoother on the faster screen, but both objects end up in the same place after a second.

## Lights, shadows, backgrounds

Standard materials react to light, so his purple box turns black until he adds one. He walks through ambient light (everything lit equally), directional light (sun-like), point light and spotlight. Shadows need three opt-ins: `shadows` on the canvas, `castShadow` on the light and the box, and `receiveShadow` on a ground plane. His performance warning is worth keeping: a moving object's shadow is recomputed every frame, so only add shadows to objects that actually need them. A Drei `Environment` component turns a photo into a background, with visible seams if the image wasn't shot for 360 degrees.

## Models and deployment

Real scenes use models, typically made in Blender and exported as glTF or GLB (Three.js also supports OBJ and FBX). He loads a licensed bird model with Drei's `useGLTF`, renders it through a `primitive` component, scales it down to 0.03 after some trial and error, and reuses the same ref and `useFrame` code to make it fly. Deployment is anticlimactic in the best way: `npm run build`, then ship the `dist` folder to Netlify, Vercel or GitHub Pages like any static site.

## Who should watch

React developers who want a first 3D scene on a page, and anyone who bounced off raw Three.js. People already shipping production R3F won't learn much new, though the shadow-cost reminder is a good one.

Title: EdTech grew fast, now it owes students privacy, access and an explanation
Description: SantoshKumar Pulijala (HCL Global Systems Inc) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on the ethics of AI in EdTech, from student data to grading algorithms
Body:
The cautionary tale every EdTech team should know is the UK's A-level grading algorithm, which downgraded students from disadvantaged backgrounds. SantoshKumar Pulijala, Senior .NET Developer at HCL Global Systems Inc, used his Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk to map the ethics of AI in education around four concerns (privacy, equity, transparency and digital well-being) and to assign each one to the people who can fix it: policymakers, educators and developers.

It is a policy and ethics overview of about 20 minutes, packed with statistics, and light on engineering. Prompt engineering does not come up; the AI here is adaptive learning, tutoring and automated assessment.

## How big did EdTech get, and how fast?

He sets the scale first. By his figures the sector was valued at nearly 90 billion in 2020 and is projected to reach about 285 billion by 2027, a shift accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, when over 94% of countries implemented remote learning and about 60% adopted online platforms.

The innovations are the familiar trio. AI and machine learning bring adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring and automated grading, and he cites a 2.5 times increase in maths skills from adaptive learning. VR and AR make abstract concepts tangible, with a 7% improvement in test scores. Data analytics in learning management systems let teachers track progress in real time. His caveat comes immediately: AI-driven systems should be transparent and unbiased, and VR must be accessible and not intrusive.

## Student data is a security problem first

Compliance is the floor, not the goal. He names FERPA, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act in the US, and GDPR in Europe, and points out that EdTech tools collect academic records, attendance and even behavioural information, in some countries with weak or no data protection law. The threat is not hypothetical: 408 cyber incidents were reported in US schools in 2020, up 18% on the previous year. His conclusion is that schools need real security investment and clear privacy policies, because trust is the product.

## Who gets left out?

The equity figures are stark. Only 25% of students in low-income countries have access to digital resources, against 96% in high-income countries. In the US, he says about 43% of households earning under 30,000 a year lack home broadband. Students with disabilities hit barriers when platforms lack accommodations, and biased algorithms can reinforce the inequalities EdTech was supposed to reduce.

## Why must grading algorithms explain themselves?

Transparency is where AI ethics bites hardest, because AI now touches evaluations and learning paths. He cites 63% of parents worried about algorithmic decisions affecting their children's assessments, and 86% of teachers who believe AI systems need a human element to guide decisions and catch bias. SantoshKumar Pulijala said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "The black box nature of AI, where complex algorithms make decisions without clear reasoning can be a problematic leading to issues with fairness and accountability." The A-level case is his proof: explainability and human oversight are requirements for any system that grades children.

## Screen time is an engineering concern too

The fourth concern gets less attention in tech circles. He cites studies linking more than two hours of screen time a day to lower scores on language and thinking tests, plus eye strain, posture and mental fatigue. On the positive side, schools that teach digital literacy and screen time management report a 40% reduction in cyberbullying incidents.

## Responsible implementation, by role

His strategy section turns the concerns into practice: data governance with clear policies, regular audits and dedicated privacy staff; infrastructure investment for equity; explainable algorithms and regular bias audits; balanced screen time with mental health support and digital citizenship programmes. Then the division of labour: policymakers write comprehensive privacy law, educators get ongoing training and evaluate tools ethically, and developers adopt privacy by design. For engineers in the audience, that last line is the job description.

## Who should watch

Developers and product managers building for schools or universities, and anyone writing an AI policy for an education product who wants the main risks and figures in one place. Note that the statistics are presented without sources on screen, so look up the originals before quoting them in a board deck.

Title: Retraining is the expensive fix for bias, prompts are the cheap one
Description: Parvin Gasimzade (Amazon) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on few-shot, chain of thought and MRKL as low-cost fixes for bias and hallucination
Body:
Most advice on AI bias ends with retrain the model on better data, which is sound and expensive. Parvin Gasimzade, Tech Lead at Amazon, used his Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk to lay out both sides: what causes bias and hallucination, the data-level fixes, and then three prompt techniques (few-shot examples, chain of thought and MRKL) you can try the same afternoon.

It is a clear, paper-referenced introduction of about 20 minutes. If you know the Attention Is All You Need lineage and the chain of thought paper, the value is in how he connects them to ethics, not in new research.

## Where do bias and hallucination come from?

He starts by asking ChatGPT to define an LLM, and asks you to remember two phrases from its answer: generate human-like text, and trained on vast amounts of data. Both explain the trouble. Models from the 2017 transformer paper to GPT-3, with its 175 billion parameters, learn from books, websites, Wikipedia and forums like Reddit, which are not reliable sources and carry their own misinformation and bias.

Bias he defines as systematic errors that treat some groups unfairly, with the well-known face recognition example: trained mostly on lighter-skinned faces, a model has higher error rates on darker skin tones. The sources are imbalanced training data, model design and feature selection, subjective labelling by annotators, and biased user input that ends up in retraining data. The cost is unfair treatment and lost trust.

Hallucination is the model producing incorrect or fabricated information. Low-quality data, missing context, and language the model struggles with, such as sarcasm, idioms and cultural references, all push it to fill the gaps by making things up.

## The data-level fixes, and their price tag

For bias: diverse datasets that cover the demographics you serve (a medical assistant needs data from diverse patients and conditions), fine-tuning and debiasing, bias audits, algorithm transparency, and regular updates as social norms shift. For hallucination: high-quality data, contextual training on domain language, fine-tuning on verified domain data, external knowledge sources such as a database to check facts, and continuous learning from user interaction.

Then the pivot of the talk. Parvin Gasimzade said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "all the previous methods we discussed for both minimizing the bias and reducing hallucinations is not scalable and cost efficient as they require retraining, fine tuning". Prompt techniques, by contrast, are quick to implement and quick to try.

## Three prompt techniques he recommends

**Zero-shot and few-shot.** Zero-shot relies purely on what the model already knows. One-shot adds a single example, few-shot several, and his illustration is the English-to-French translation from the GPT-3 paper. He suggests few-shot wherever labelled data is scarce, for example classifying emails with a handful of examples.

**Chain of thought.** From the Google research paper: show the model a worked example with step-by-step reasoning instead of just the answer. His walk-through uses the paper's maths problem: with standard prompting the model gets the new problem wrong; with a reasoning example it gets it right. Asking the model to think step by step reduces hallucination on multi-step tasks.

**MRKL.** Modular Reasoning, Knowledge and Language, from AI21 Labs, connects the model to external tools and knowledge sources. Real-time weather, live stock prices and a calculator are his examples: the model parses the user's input and passes parameters to a calculator through an API, instead of guessing at complex arithmetic it handles badly. If that sounds like tool calling, it is, and this paper is one of its ancestors.

## What should teams take away?

His takeaways are principles more than recipes: ethical AI means fairness, transparency and accountability; prompting is a practical lever against bias and hallucination; the work is continuous, with ongoing evaluation and diverse perspectives; and organisations have to commit to it. The reference list, five arXiv and OpenAI papers, is a decent reading list on its own.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people who need a grounded explanation of where bias and hallucination come from, and a starting set of techniques with sources. Practitioners already running evals and retrieval in production will find it introductory.

Title: Eight levels of anti-bot, beaten one header at a time
Description: Fabien Vauchelles (Scrapoxy) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 live-codes past user-agent checks, rate limits, ASN blocks, fingerprints and obfuscated JS
Body:
Every anti-bot defence is a question about whether you look like a real browser, and each answer costs you more effort than the last. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Fabien Vauchelles, creator and main contributor of Scrapoxy, live-coded his way through a deliberately hostile demo site, level by level, from a fake user agent to reverse-engineering obfuscated JavaScript that RSA-encrypts a browser fingerprint.

Fair warning on the event name: the spiders are Python, written with Scrapy. The JavaScript is on the other side of the fight, in the detection scripts, in Babel used to unpick them, and in Scrapoxy itself. Fabien Vauchelles said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 that "Scrapoxy is a free and open source proxy manager", written in Node.js and Angular. Since version 4 shipped in February 2024, he says over 650 users have installed it, exchanging one petabyte of data across 55 billion requests and 6 million proxies.

## The setup

The story follows Isabella, a student who wants hotel reviews to train a travel-planning model. She stays on the legal side as he frames it: public data only, no personal details, no accepted terms and conditions, and no hammering the site. The target is his own practice site of accommodation listings and reviews, with protections stacked like levels in a video game.

## Levels 1 and 2: look like Chrome

Level 1 is a plain Scrapy spider: start requests, parse with CSS selectors, follow pagination, 50 items. Level 2 rejects the default Scrapy user agent, so he copies Chrome's. Then the site complains about a missing client hint header, the `sec-ch-ua` family that real Chrome sends to confirm the user agent, including the platform. Claim Windows in one header and the other headers had better agree.

## Levels 3 and 4: IP addresses have a résumé

Level 3 answers with HTTP 429, too many requests, which means one IP is not enough. Enter proxies, and a tidy taxonomy:

- **Datacenter proxies** on AWS, Azure or GCP: fast, cheap, reliable, and easy to spot, because the IP range maps to an autonomous system number named after the cloud.
- **ISP proxies**: hosted in datacenters but using IP addresses rented from clean ASNs such as mobile carriers or broadband providers.
- **Residential proxies**: real laptops and phones, often from apps that share the device's bandwidth, with the user's agreement, as an alternative to ads or subscriptions.

He starts Scrapoxy in Docker, adds an AWS connector, and ten instances in Dublin appear in the console within seconds. A Scrapy middleware routes traffic through Scrapoxy, which spreads requests round-robin for a 100% success rate. Level 4 then spots the Amazon ASN, so he swaps the connector for ten US ISP proxies from a commercial vendor without touching the spider. Scrapoxy also scales the instances down when the scraping session ends, which he calls a huge cost saver.

## Levels 6 and 7: the fingerprint is the test

Level 6 sees POST requests leaving the browser at intervals, carrying platform, time zone and the real user agent gathered by JavaScript. In his words: "So I cannot rely anymore on only HTTP request. Now I need real browsers." Scrapy hands the downloads to Playwright, ten Chrome sessions execute the site's JavaScript, and the items come back, slower but intact.

Level 7 checks the fingerprint for consistency: a browser in Europe/Paris coming from a US IP is a lie. Rather than change the IP, he sets the Playwright browser's time zone to America/New_York.

## Level 8: read their code

The last level encrypts the fingerprint payload and obfuscates the script that builds it. Before deobfuscating, he shows how obfuscation is done: base64-encoded strings behind a decoder function, constants to unfold, strings split into pieces, and bracket notation hiding `window.screen`. A Babel-based script reverses those steps. The cleaned output still has meaningless function names, but it shows an RSA public key and a POST of the WebGL vendor and renderer. He forges that payload in the spider, encrypts it with the key, and collects all 50 items.

His verdict on when to bother is the most useful line in the talk: deobfuscation pays off only when you need millions of requests fast. Otherwise use Playwright, "Because deobfuscating source code can take a lot of time and take a lot of energy." That is the defender's whole strategy.

## Who should watch

Anyone building scrapers, and anyone defending a site against them, since the talk doubles as a tour of what bot detection checks. It is a live-coding session, so expect terminal output and Chrome DevTools rather than slides.

Title: Every Microsoft Copilot in one sitting, and a system prompt that serves beer
Description: Peter De Tender (Microsoft) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on prompting across Microsoft 365 Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Copilot Studio and Azure AI Studio
Body:
Ask an Azure-only assistant who the UK prime minister is and, if Peter De Tender wrote its system prompt, it apologises and recommends a Chimay Blue. Peter De Tender, Business Program Manager and Azure Technical Trainer at Microsoft, used his 45-minute Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 session to walk through the whole Copilot family, demo by demo, and to show that the same prompt habits carry from Word to VS Code to a custom model.

It is a vendor tour by a trainer, and it says so: the goal is to show what each Copilot does and how prompting changes between them, not to compare them with other tools.

## Is prompt engineering really engineering?

His first move is to rename it. Engineering sounds hard, so inside Microsoft they prefer the art of the prompt, or as he puts it, prompt artistry. He illustrates it with his own trainer bio picture: list what is in the photo (spiky hair, glasses, grey hoodie, Microsoft logo, Surface laptop, Seattle skyline, Belgian flag), turn that list into a prompt, then keep 99% of it and swap only the style from Pixar to Simpsons to Marvel comic.

For business prompts he uses four building blocks: the goal (what Copilot should do), the context (why, and who is involved), the source (web or work) and the expectations. His example asks for the latest Microsoft financial report, for a meeting with executives next week, from web or work data, as a summary in seven bullet points. His line for what changes: "You're switching from searching into finding."

## Web versus work in Microsoft 365

The first demos run on copilot.microsoft.com. Signed in with a personal account, he asks for beef stew recipes with beer in them, because Belgium. Signed in with a work account, the same entry point becomes BizChat, and the important toggle is web or work. Web answers come from what the model was trained on, with public sources linked. Work answers come from Microsoft Graph, meaning OneDrive, email, Teams and SharePoint, scoped to files the user can already access.

He describes Microsoft 365 Copilot as GPT-4 behind Graph, running in the user's own security context, with prompts and content not used to train the model. He puts the licence at roughly 30 per user per month, and tells you to check with your account team.

Inside the apps, the demos show drafting in Word (turn this text into a table, then keep or refine it), asking for key takeaways from a financial report with sources pointing to paragraphs, and the PowerPoint narrative builder turning one prompt into an outline, slides, images and speaker notes in a couple of minutes. Copilot Lab, at aka.ms/copilotlab, supplies vetted sample prompts per application.

## GitHub Copilot on a real repo

The developer section uses his own YouTube summarizer app, which calls Azure OpenAI to turn a video summary into three to five bullet points. With `@workspace` he asks GitHub Copilot to explain a selection in the context of the whole project, then to add Azure Key Vault integration (it lists the NuGet packages and new code as a draft to accept), to document a settings snippet, and to rewrite the C# into Python. The point he repeats: everything is a draft, and you are still the pilot.

## Building your own: Copilot Studio and Azure AI Studio

For custom assistants he shows two routes. Copilot Studio is the low-code one, with templates such as a safe travels bot, website Q&A, store operations and an IT helpdesk, plus connectors to third-party services like Google Drive, DocuSign and Slack. Azure AI Studio is for development teams: a model catalogue beyond OpenAI (Llama, Phi, Mistral, Cohere), a chat playground to compare models, and fine-tuning and custom apps.

The playground demo makes the knowledge cut-off visible: GPT-3.5 Turbo answers the UK prime minister question as of September 2021, GPT-4o with later data. Then comes the system prompt. Peter De Tender said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "You are a Microsoft technical trainer and expert on Azure platform. You can only answer Azure questions. If any other domains come up. In the question, apologize and offer the user a Belgian beer suggestion." The model refuses the politics and suggests a Trappist instead, which is a cheerful way to show how much a scoped persona controls.

## Who should watch

Teams on Microsoft 365 deciding what Copilot is worth, developers new to GitHub Copilot, and anyone who wants to see the full Microsoft Copilot range in one place. If you want prompt research or benchmarks, look elsewhere.

Title: Your mobile driver's license is a JWT with a better lawyer
Description: Rizel Scarlett (TBD, Block) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on how verifiable credentials, signed as JSON Web Tokens, power mobile driver's licenses
Body:
The token in your app's `Authorization: Bearer` header and the driver's license in a phone wallet are closer relatives than they look. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Rizel Scarlett, Staff Developer Advocate at TBD (a Block company), explained verifiable credentials, the W3C standard behind mobile driver's licenses, and showed that many of them are simply signed JSON Web Tokens, then built one live with TBD's Web5 credentials SDK.

The framing device is buying wine online and forgetting your ID while the delivery driver waits. Her boss, Angie Jones, actually did the grown-up version: she bought alcohol online by showing a mobile driver's license on her phone, and the technology behind that license is a verifiable credential.

## What is a JWT, and can you tamper with it?

A quick refresher first. Rizel Scarlett said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 that "JWT or JSON Web Token is a secure way to share information between two parties online." Three dot-separated parts: a header (token type and algorithm), a payload (the data), and a signature that verifies the data wasn't changed on the way.

Then the quiz: tamper proof or tamper evident? She pastes an EdDSA-signed token into JWT.io, Auth0's decoder, and starts editing the payload to rename "Alice Smith". The decoded data turns into garbage characters. You can change a JWT; you just can't do it without it telling on you. Tamper evident, which is exactly the property an ID needs.

## Verifiable credentials are digital paper

The W3C, the standards body Sir Tim Berners-Lee helped form, has working groups on digital identity, and one of their outputs is verifiable credentials: digital proofs of specific facts about people, organisations or entities. Think digital versions of an ID, a degree, a driver's license or a health insurance card, stored in the same phone wallet as your boarding pass. In her words, "many of them are just cryptographically signed JSON web tokens"; others use CBOR, depending on the issuer and purpose.

The flow has three roles. The issuer is a trusted organisation (the DMV, a passport office, a university) that creates and signs the credential. The holder is who it's about. The verifier is whoever asks for proof. In the bar example, the DMV issues a credential saying you're over 21, signs it into a JWT, you store it on your phone, and the bartender scans it while programmatic checks run: expired? trusted issuer? over 21? The bartender might only see a check mark.

## Why not just show the plastic card?

Selective disclosure. Her illustration is Joe from Netflix's You working as a bouncer and memorising your home address. The bar doesn't need your address or even your full name. "They just need to know that we are truly over the age of 21." A verifiable credential can reveal only the fields the verifier asks for; her example passport credential shares name, date of birth and gender, and withholds the rest.

There is a durability argument too. If your university shuts down after a natural disaster, a signed diploma credential on your phone still proves you graduated, with nobody left to phone.

## Where else is this showing up?

Beyond booze: pharmacies trading stock with each other and proving the medicine, the pharmacist and the pharmacy are legitimate; the Content Authenticity Initiative (Adobe, Nikon, Sony, Microsoft and others) attaching provenance to images in an age of AI-generated content; a native tribe establishing identity for businesses in special economic zones; and the European Digital Identity Wallet, which aims to let every resident, citizen and business store documents on their phone by 2026. The challenges she names are standardisation and interoperability, and educating the public on why any of this is better.

## The live build

The demo creates a decentralised identifier, calls `VerifiableCredential.create` with a type, issuer, subject, expiry and data (a self-signed workshop attendee credential for Conf42 JavaScript 2024), signs it with the DID to get a JWT, decodes it on JWT.io to prove the data is really in there, and presents it. Her closing point: "None of this is something new." The pieces are JWTs and public-key signatures you already use; the experience is what's new.

## Who should watch

Web developers who know JWTs from auth and want the identity-wallet side of the story, and anyone curious what actually happens when a phone gets scanned at a counter. It is an introduction with a short demo, not a tour of DID methods or the cryptography underneath.

Title: Ship the rough MVP, then let teachers tell you what to build
Description: Crystal Yang (Audemy) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on turning a small JavaScript project into games for 1,000+ blind students with MVPs, volunteers and users
Body:
Good intentions and a code editor don't add up to social impact on their own. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Crystal Yang, Founder and CEO of Audemy, told the story of how a small JavaScript project became an educational games platform for blind and visually impaired students, and argued that the missing piece for most technical people is business discipline: build a minimum viable product, put it in front of users, and iterate.

It is a short, non-technical talk. There is no code on screen. What it offers instead is a founder's playbook with real numbers: Audemy has reached over 1,000 blind students, partnered with seven schools for the blind around the world, and runs on a team of over 30 volunteers.

## Why technology, and why JavaScript?

Yang gives four reasons technology suits social impact: it scales without the geographic limits other approaches have, it is accessible to anyone with an internet connection, it automates work so resources go further, and it is a breeding ground for experiments on old problems.

JavaScript gets its own case at the end. It runs on the web, so anyone who can open a website can use your product. It is interactive and can be customised for users with different abilities. And it plugs into everything else, from a natural language API to hardware talking to a JavaScript backend.

## How rough can the first version be?

Rougher than you think. Audemy's first MVP, by her own account, was "pretty much just a program that regurgitated basic math problems", wrapped in text to speech and automatic speech recognition. She didn't polish it. She took it to teachers who work with blind students, and their feedback shaped both the educational value and the accessibility of what came next.

Her loop is the classic one: build the essential features for the core problem, launch to a small audience, gather feedback, implement, repeat. The point she adds is that software makes the loop unusually cheap. A teacher asked for screen reader support or keyboard interaction, and, as Crystal Yang said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024, "in at most a week, I would be able to implement their suggestions." Try that turnaround with a hardware prototype.

## How do you staff a project with no budget?

With volunteers, recruited on purpose. Her first rule is to know exactly which roles you need (developers, designers, outreach, social media) and recruit only for those. The cautionary example is memorable: "I've seen like an hr manager at a 10 person like volunteer venture".

Her second rule is to go where volunteers already look. Platforms such as VolunteerMatch and Idealist list nonprofits that need help, and they attract people learning to code who want real-world experience. Being a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit, she says, makes it much easier to recruit people who share your values.

## Who are you building for?

Know your users and how to reach them. For Audemy that meant blind students and their teachers, reached through schools for the blind, with teachers integrated into development. Because the product solved problems teachers actually had, rather than assumed ones, getting users became much easier.

## Who should watch

Developers with a side project they suspect could help people, students thinking about a nonprofit, and anyone who needs a reminder that the first version is supposed to be embarrassing. If you want React or Node.js internals, this is not that talk; it is about everything around the code.

Title: A pregnancy app whose data lives in your own node, built by an agent
Description: Rizel Scarlett (TBD, Block) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on using the Goose agent to build a pregnancy app on decentralized web nodes
Body:
Download a fertility app and, before anything else has happened, every feed you own starts selling you baby products. Rizel Scarlett, Staff Developer Advocate at TBD (Block), recorded her Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk at 35 weeks pregnant, and used it to build the alternative live: a pregnancy app whose data sits in a user-owned decentralized web node, written mostly by the Goose developer agent.

It is a short, cheerful demo talk, about 20 minutes, with a real point about privacy and a practical one about giving an agent context it cannot have learned.

## Who should own pregnancy data?

Her opening is personal. She decided to start a family, downloaded an app, and TikTok, Instagram Reels, Facebook, Target and YouTube all switched to motherhood ads. She notes how cruel that is for someone who has had a miscarriage and keeps being reminded by every app. Her answer to the question of who should own the data is simple: you.

Rizel Scarlett said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "they don't really care that much for my privacy. this is nice to track, but it's also sharing my data with a ton of different, platforms."

## What is a decentralized web node?

Decentralized web nodes (DWNs) are open source personal data stores. Her mental model is an encrypted Dropbox the user owns. Access is controlled through protocols, JSON objects that declare who can create, read, write or query each type of record. In a chat example anyone can create a message but only the author and recipient can read it. For a pregnancy app that means the user decides whether a provider, a partner, parents or only herself can see each record.

## Goose is an agent, not a model

The building tool is Goose, Block's open source developer agent, running in the terminal and also in VS Code and IntelliJ. She is careful with definitions. Goose is not an LLM: you bring your own, whether that is GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet or Gemini. Goose sends your goal to the model, gets a plan back, shows you the plan, and executes it through shell commands.

She calls it semi-autonomous, and likes that. It pauses to check in before some commands, and that matters because models hallucinate. When a command fails, Goose asks the model for an updated plan (forgot to pin the React Testing Library version, say), tells you when something runs too long, and hands back commands that need your password. Her distinction between agents and automation is crisp: automation responds to a known situation with a predetermined recipe; an agent is given a goal and decides the actions.

## How do you prompt an agent about tech it has never seen?

The first demo is a warm-up: a collaborative real-time drawing app in Next.js. Goose plans canvas setup and a WebSocket backend and creates the files; she then shows a pre-made version, cooking-show style.

The interesting part is the second demo. DWNs are new, so neither the model nor Goose knows much about them. Her fix is a `.goosehints` file, into which she pasted the relevant parts of the DWN documentation, so the agent has the context in every session. Then she writes her own plan in a `plan.yaml`: a kickoff message (build a Next.js pregnancy due date calculator), and tasks such as creating the directory, installing Next, React and the Web5 API, and building a form for the first day of the last cycle. She starts the session with that plan and Goose works through it.

The result is plain but works. Enter April 4, 2024, and the app reports 30 weeks with a due date of Wednesday, January 8, 2025, and prints the record it wrote to the DWN, encoded data and record ID included, which is the proof that mattered. A more detailed version, styled with Vercel's v0, lets you sign in as self, provider or partner and track cycle dates and flow.

Her slides add the configuration side for those who want to try it: Goose profiles in `~/.config/goose/profiles.yaml` with a provider, a heavier processor model, a lighter accelerator model and a moderator setting, plus toolkits for files and shell, screenshots and GitHub.

## Who should watch

Developers curious about agentic coding tools who want to see the plan and hints workflow rather than a single chat prompt, and anyone building health or other sensitive apps who wants a different data ownership model. Expect a demo, not a security review of DWNs.

Title: Write the validator once, infer every type from client to database
Description: Joe Zhou (DragonflyDB) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on end-to-end TypeScript type safety with Zod, Drizzle and Hono, no GraphQL or Swagger DSL needed
Body:
The fastest way to make TypeScript types lie is to write them by hand next to a validator that says something slightly different. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Joe Zhou, Developer Advocate at DragonflyDB, shows the alternative: define the shape once as a runtime validator, infer the types from it, and chain that from the database table through the HTTP handler to a typed client. The stack is Zod, Drizzle and Hono, with no GraphQL schema, no Swagger file and no code generation.

The running example is a bookstore API, "maybe like the next Amazon", and it's built up one layer at a time.

## Why bother with runtime validation in TypeScript?

Because types vanish at runtime and JSON from a client doesn't care what you declared. He's a backend developer by history, across JavaScript, TypeScript, Go and Rust, with a strong preference for statically typed languages: knowing the payload has the right shape and every field is valid is what lets him sleep at night.

He starts with the built-in utility types as a warm-up. `Omit<BookRecord, 'id'>` gives a `BookRequest` without the server-generated ID, `Pick<BookRecord, 'title'>` a `BookPreview`, and `Readonly<BookRecord>` an immutable record. Angle brackets operate on types; round brackets on values. Useful, but none of it checks that an ISBN is actually an ISBN.

## Zod: the validator is the source of truth

With Zod, `bookRecord` is a value: `z.object({ id: z.string().uuid(), ISBN: z.string().regex(...), ... })`. Call `bookRecord.parse()` on an object missing fields or with a non-UUID author ID and it fails. Then `z.infer<typeof bookRecord>` hands you the TypeScript type, and `bookRecord.omit({ id: true })` gives you a request validator and, by inference, its type. One definition, no drift.

He's candid about the ISBN regex: an LLM wrote it, probably not the strictest one, but good enough for the demo.

## Drizzle: start at the table

Drizzle defines the `books` table in code (primary key, non-null columns, a date mode for the timestamp), and its Zod integration derives an insert schema from the table. On top go the rules a database column doesn't express easily: default the ID to a UUIDv7 if missing, require a title of at least one character, accept only books published after 2000 (arbitrary, he admits), match the ISBN regex, and keep stock at zero or above.

The request schema is then derived from the insert schema: drop the ID, and swap the publication date for a string that's parsed into a date, since JSON doesn't carry dates. Two layers of validators, request and pre-insert, each with an inferred type nobody typed by hand. Is that too much validation? "I do validation everywhere when necessary," Joe Zhou said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. It costs some compute; how much you want depends on how paranoid your system requirements are.

## Hono: typed server, typed client

Hono runs on standard web APIs, so the same app runs on Node.js, Deno and Bun. The `POST /books` handler uses Hono's Zod validator middleware with the request schema, so bad payloads are rejected before your code runs, and `c.req.valid('json')` comes back typed as the inferred `BookRequest`. Before insertion, parsing again with the insert schema fills in the UUID.

The trick that closes the loop is exporting `typeof` the route. On the frontend, Hono's client takes that server type and the base URL and returns a strongly typed client: it knows `/books` exists, that it accepts POST, and what the JSON body must look like. Use GET by mistake or misspell a field and the compiler tells you before you run anything.

## What about the cache, GraphQL and tRPC?

For the cache layer, Redis OM works with Dragonfly too, since Dragonfly is Redis-compatible, but there's no Zod integration yet. His pragmatic take: if you're caching blobs rather than editing individual fields, a plain string value is fine. In the vendor part, he says Dragonfly's multi-threaded architecture handles 25 times more throughput on a single multi-core instance, where mostly single-threaded Redis uses one core, with JSON and search built in rather than added as modules.

On alternatives: GraphQL and Swagger are great when several languages consume your API, but they bring their own DSL and usually code generation. tRPC gives client-server type safety too, but doesn't expose a standard HTTP API. If you're the only consumer, tRPC may suit you better; if others will call your API, Hono keeps plain HTTP and you still get full type safety on your own client.

## Who should watch

TypeScript developers who maintain types and validation separately and are tired of the two disagreeing. The code is small and incremental, so it's easy to lift into a real project.

Title: IT performance is a boulder you push forever, and why that is fine
Description: Ravitej Veeramachaneni (Oracle) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on why IT performance problems never stay solved, and what to do about it
Body:
Every engineer has restarted a database, watched the slowness disappear, and closed the ticket without ever learning why. Ravitej Veeramachaneni, Principal Software Engineer at Oracle, built his Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk around that experience: performance is a Sisyphean task, and the job is to manage it well rather than to finish it.

He presents the talk as a Sisyphean struggle with performance issues, a reflective tour of why they persist. The AI and prompt engineering angle in the title shows up only as machine-learning monitoring and future research, so expect a conceptual talk, not prompts or code.

## Why doesn't performance ever stay fixed?

His opening claim is about users, not systems. Ravitej Veeramachaneni said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "There's no such thing as, as users being completely satisfied with performance." Even an unchanged system loses ground, because a competitor ships something faster, or because what counted as acceptable a year ago now feels slow. His example is the phone: each generation is only marginally faster than the last, yet a ten-year-old handset cannot run today's apps. Real-time video at 4K and 8K raises the bar again for compute.

Then there is business impact. For a Google or an X, a few minutes of downtime costs millions of dollars, which is why performance work never runs out of budget justification.

## Complexity hides the root cause

The technical core is the complexity conundrum. Modern systems mix cloud infrastructure, microservices and IoT devices, and every integration is a new place for a bottleneck. A delay in one microservice's data processing cascades through the whole application; a slow database drags down every report built on it.

The restart problem is the honest bit. You restart, the issue goes away, the logs tell you little, and the bug is hard to reproduce. With every component bringing its own performance characteristics, isolating the root cause becomes the expensive part of the job. Anyone who has been on call recognises this, and few talks admit it so plainly.

## Humans, budgets and trade-offs

Three non-technical forces get their own sections. Code and configuration: inefficient algorithms and misconfigurations are still a leading cause, and skill levels vary across teams, so product quality varies with them. User behaviour: a launch or a promotional event sends traffic a system was never designed for, and unexpected data growth creates strain nobody planned. His YouTube view counter example, outgrown by a handful of videos, illustrates how growth breaks assumptions even when it is not strictly a performance bug.

Budgets come next: limited hardware, licences and skilled people force choices such as upgrading server capacity versus funding cyber security. And fixes have side effects. He has seen this often: "You fix one area of the code and break something else." His example is a new database connector that an integrated system does not support, so a performance upgrade becomes an integration outage. Speed versus data consistency, and extra authentication layers that add response time, are the trade-offs he names.

## Where does AI fit?

The solutions section lists machine-learning anomaly detection that warns before users notice, AI-driven root cause analysis, distributed tracing, chaos engineering, autoscaling and DevOps practices. His future-research list goes further: context-aware predictive models on big data, autonomous systems that configure and allocate resources in real time (he notes we do not have that today), human and AI collaboration in troubleshooting, and standardised metrics, such as industry-wide latency benchmarks, so environments can be compared.

## What it means for the people doing the work

The most practical advice is about skills. Move from reactive troubleshooting to predictive management. Developers should understand the DevOps side, and DevOps engineers should be able to read code and tell bad from good. Above all, explain performance in business terms to non-technical stakeholders: an oil and gas company will fund IT work once it sees what slowness costs the business.

## Who should watch

Early and mid-career engineers who want a framework for why performance work keeps coming back, and leads who need words for budget conversations. Skip it if you want benchmarks, tooling demos or prompt engineering.

Title: Write emergency evacuation instructions is not a prompt, it is a wish
Description: Aditi Godbole (SAP) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on structuring prompts as context, task, format, examples and constraints, then testing them
Body:
Ask a model to write emergency evacuation instructions and you get a poster for no building in particular. Aditi Godbole, who works in data science, AI and ML at SAP, used her Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk to show the fix: a five-part prompt structure, a before-and-after rewrite for a 1,000-seat concert venue, and a checklist for validating prompts once they work.

This is a compact, well-organised introduction, around twenty minutes. If your team writes prompts by trial, error and vibes, it is a good shared vocabulary to hand them.

## Why bother engineering a prompt at all?

She gives four reasons: more accurate and relevant answers, less time and compute spent, lower cost on commercial AI services, and less risk from bias and hallucination. Her framing of the discipline is the line worth keeping. Aditi Godbole said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "Think of it as learning to speak the language that bridges human intent and AI capability."

The challenges are the familiar five: ambiguity, bias steered by wording and training data, context dependency (a small change in phrasing changes the answer), token and character limits, and inconsistency across similar queries.

## Context, task, format, examples, constraints

Before writing anything, she asks five questions: what is the purpose and who is the audience, what context does the model need, what are the constraints and the model's limits, what format should the answer take, and what safety considerations apply.

The structure that follows is the core of the talk. Start with relevant context, state the task, specify the format, add examples when they help, and finish with constraints. Her best practices are short: clear and direct instructions, iterative refinement, testing for bias and sensitivity, and context that narrows the scope.

## The online store rewrite

The first worked example starts with a store owner asking how to improve customer satisfaction. She points out what is missing: which areas matter, how many suggestions, quick tips or deep strategies, and what size of store. The improved prompt, from her slides:

> Provide 5 actionable strategies to improve customer satisfaction for a small online retail business. Focus on areas such as customer service, website usability, and post-purchase follow-up. Keep recommendations concise and achievable for a small team.

Every phrase does a job. Small retail business tells the model the team has limited resources; five concise strategies sets the shape of the answer; the three focus areas stop it wandering into pricing or branding.

## Same model, much better evacuation plan

The second example is the memorable one. The vague version produces generic text that ignores emergency types, languages and accessibility. The improved prompt specifies a 1,000-seat concert venue with three floors and six exits, fire, medical and security scenarios, instructions for disabled patrons, staff roles, a digital display format with at most three bullet points per section, universal emergency symbols, multiple language indicators, assembly points and an authoritative but calm tone.

The result has separate instructions per emergency type, assembly points, mobility assistance and a staff breakdown. The lesson is not that long prompts win; it is that the prompt should carry the facts the model cannot guess.

## When the prompt works, test it anyway

The second half covers technique and verification. The advanced toolbox: chain of thought for multi-step reasoning, role assignment, few-shot examples, system instructions, if-then conditional prompts, and temperature to trade creativity for factual answers.

Her pitfalls cut both ways. Overcomplication dilutes the main point as surely as vagueness does, and assuming the model has background knowledge you never provided is the classic trap. Ignored constraints, from character limits to ethical boundaries, round out the list.

Then validation: an accuracy check, a task completion check, relevance, a bias review, consistency testing (repeat the prompt and see whether quality holds), and testing with real users. That last step is where most internal prompt libraries never go, and it is the one that tells you whether the prompt works for the people using it.

## Who should watch

People new to prompt engineering, and leads who want a structure their team can agree on. Experienced practitioners will know the techniques but may still borrow the validation checklist.

Title: TypeScript changes nothing at runtime, which is exactly the point
Description: Kacper Szewczyk (RST Software Master) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on TypeScript developer experience - Omit vs Pick, template literal types, type guards, DeepNullable
Body:
Most new languages promise faster code, better memory use or nicer concurrency. TypeScript promises none of that: compile it away and you get the same JavaScript, the same memory, the same app. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Kacper Szewczyk, React Native Developer at RST Software Master, argues that this is the whole point. TypeScript exists for developer experience, and he proves it by typing a scientific grant application system with `Omit`, `Pick`, template literal types, type guards and a four-line `DeepNullable`.

## Why did TypeScript happen at all?

He opens with a story from Microsoft in 2008. A team of C# developers is told their new project needs JavaScript in the browser. Their answer: we'll do it, without writing a line of JavaScript. Enter Script#, which translated C# classes into JavaScript functions.

It worked, sort of. Their tests covered C# code that never ran in production; what shipped was whatever the translator produced, so every release needed manual testing of the generated JavaScript, and bugs were safer to patch in the output than in the translator. The team's real complaint about JavaScript turned out to be narrow: they couldn't be sure what a function would accept or return, something the C# compiler checks before anything runs. Add that to JavaScript and they could live with it. TypeScript 0.8 went public in 2012.

"The type itself was created to improve developer experience," Kacper Szewczyk said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024, adding that it was made for the love of developers, or for the hate of JavaScript.

## Base types are dummies; derive from the real one

The demo domain is a grant application: an applicant, an application number, attachments and approval steps (in Europe, at least a formal review and a final review). Applicants come in three shapes: a private person with a social security number, a private person without one who gives a birth date instead, and a company with a name and a tax ID.

Making every field optional loses the rule that at least one of them must be filled. Three explicit types repeat five fields. The classic DRY fix, a `BaseApplicant` intersected into each, bothers him: it's a type that doesn't exist in the business, and unlike an abstract class in C# or Java, nothing stops someone from creating one except not exporting it.

His alternative treats the common case, `PrivateApplicant` with an SSN, as the source of truth:

- `PrivateApplicantWithoutSSN = Omit<PrivateApplicant, 'SSN'> & { birthDate: Date }`: follows the base type automatically, which is what you want for a near-twin.
- `CompanyApplicant = Pick<PrivateApplicant, 'firstName' | 'lastName' | 'email' | 'phoneNumber' | 'address'> & { companyName; taxId }`: an explicit list, so when `firstName` and `lastName` become `fullName`, the compiler stops you here and you decide by hand.

`Omit` where change should flow through, `Pick` where you want control. That's the most reusable idea in the talk.

## Regex in the type system

Application numbers look like `AB123456/2021`. A template literal type, `${ApplicationTypeCodes}${number}/${ApplicationYear}`, with unions for the codes and the years 2020-2024, turns the format into a compile-time validator: write 2025 or drop the digits and the editor flags it. "TypeScript has regex included in their language, and that's beautiful," he said. He then generates the years with a recursive `ComputeRange<N>` type that builds a tuple until its length hits N, and warns it has limits: push the range too high and the compiler errors out.

## Upload versus download shapes

Attachments are different on the way in (a `File` in a multipart request) and out (a `fileUrl`). One payload type plus `Pick` derives the other. Template literals name the keys (`Attachment 0` to `Attachment 4`), `Record` turns the list into an object you can look up by name instead of iterating an array, and `Partial` handles applications that don't need every attachment.

## Guards, readonly and drafts

- **Type guards**: `isObjectWithKey` checks for a non-null object, `isPrivateApplicant` checks for the `SSN` property, and TypeScript narrows the type inside the `if` and in the `else`. Run guards on API responses locally and a renamed backend field shows up as an error in minutes.
- **`Readonly`** for a submitted application, so a reviewer's function can only touch verification date, status and verifier.
- **Drafts**: grant forms take days, so users save half-finished ones. `Nullable<T> = T | null` and a recursive `DeepNullable` make every field in the tree optional in four lines. Swap `null` for `undefined` to avoid writing out all the nulls.

## Who should watch

Developers who use TypeScript daily but stop at interfaces and unions. The grant domain is concrete enough that every utility type earns its place. His two takeaways: use the advanced types the language already ships, and use type guards for safe, fast checks.

Title: A healthcare platform blueprint, from GitHub Actions to Documentum
Description: Praveen Valaboju (LANDAUER) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on one healthcare cloud platform with CI/CD, Kubernetes, Documentum and neural networks
Body:
Healthcare IT has a fragmentation problem before it has an AI problem: patient demographics in one system, clinical notes in another, imaging somewhere else, and HIPAA watching all of them. Praveen Valaboju, DevOps Engineer at LANDAUER, used his Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk to sketch one platform that pulls those pieces together: GitHub Actions and Docker for delivery, Kubernetes for capacity, Documentum for content, and neural networks for the workflow on top.

It is a short, high-level architecture talk, about fifteen minutes of a reference stack rather than a case study with dashboards. Prompt engineering itself barely appears, so come for the platform shape.

## What problem is the stack solving?

His problem statement has three parts. Medical information keeps growing in volume and complexity. Traditional systems are fragmented, which makes them inefficient and hard to scale. And regulation such as HIPAA puts strict requirements on how any of that data is handled. The goal he sets is better patient outcomes with lower operating cost and stronger compliance, on a platform that is efficient, scalable and secure.

## Delivery first: fewer hands on the deploy button

The first layer is CI/CD. GitHub Actions automates the path from development to deployment, and Docker keeps environments consistent from a laptop to production, so the classic works-on-my-machine discrepancy goes away. The argument for a hospital IT team is release frequency: applications have to keep up with changing medical needs, and a manual release process does not.

The one number in the talk sits here. Praveen Valaboju said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "Reducing manual intervention in deployment minimizes human error leading to 50 percent drop in deployment issue". He does not say where it was measured, so treat it as a target rather than a benchmark.

## Kubernetes for the surge, not just the steady state

Kubernetes earns its place with two properties. Autoscaling handles demand spikes, and his examples are public health emergencies and large data processing jobs. High availability matters more here than in most industries, because orchestrating workloads across nodes with failover keeps clinical applications reachable, and he links downtime directly to patient safety. That framing is worth borrowing when you need to justify redundancy to a budget holder.

## Documentum as the system of record

The least common choice in the stack is OpenText Documentum for content management. In his design it stores structured and unstructured data together, from demographics to clinical notes to medical imaging, which simplifies retrieval and interoperability. The compliance features do the heavy lifting: tracking document access and modification gives detailed audit trails for HIPAA. The productivity claim is time: clinicians spend less of it hunting for records.

## Where does the AI come in?

Neural networks sit on top in three roles. Convolutional neural networks for pattern recognition in radiology images, which he says can potentially diagnose some conditions more accurately than human radiologists. Predictive models that use historical data to flag patients for early intervention, with diabetes and heart disease as examples. And plain workflow automation, such as sorting medical records or prioritising patients.

The integration point between Documentum and the models is metadata. New information arriving for a patient triggers a workflow, such as updating the EHR or raising an alert when something is missing, and the AI layer suggests diagnostic tests or treatments based on patterns in that patient's data. His unified platform closes with the operational wins: insurance claims, appointments and record updates automated, and information silos removed across departments, with room later for wearables, genomic data and precision medicine.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers starting work in a regulated healthcare environment who want a map of the moving parts. If you want implementation detail, evaluation numbers for the clinical models or a prompt in sight, this is not that talk.

Title: Zero trust for containers, mapped from build to runtime
Description: Ammar Khan (Auxin) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on zero trust for containers - image scanning, microsegmentation, least-privilege IAM, mTLS and runtime policy
Body:
Inside the cluster is not the same as trusted. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Ammar Khan, DevOps Engineer at Auxin, applies zero trust to containerised environments: five principles (segmentation, runtime security, network security, IAM and image security), mapped onto the build, test, staging and production stages of a pipeline, with before-and-after examples for each.

A note for the JavaScript crowd: there's no JavaScript in this one. It's a platform security talk, useful to anyone whose Node.js services end up in containers, which is most of them.

## What does zero trust actually change?

The old model trusted anything inside the corporate network. That stopped matching reality once workloads spread across microservices, clouds and regions, people started working from home and coffee shops, and every application grew a web of internal and external integrations, plus an open source supply chain where one vulnerable library can hit countless applications.

His one-line summary: "trust is neither binary nor permanent," Ammar Khan said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. It has to be continuously earned and verified. The process has four steps: establish trust through authentication and authorization, enforce policy across the environment, continuously verify whether that trust still holds, and respond to threats in real time with automated incident response.

For containers specifically, the threats he lists are a compromised host taking its containers with it, vulnerable images sitting in the registry, attacks on running containers, and flaws arriving through third-party images. Zero trust answers with fine-grained access control, least privilege, blocked lateral movement and real-time monitoring, and it also helps with standards such as SOC 2 and GDPR.

## Five principles, five fixes

- **Image security.** Before: images deployed without consistent verification. After: every application, whatever its version, is scanned before deployment, images are signed and checked for tampering, and verification happens at deploy time as an ongoing step in the pipeline.
- **Segmentation.** Before: every container can talk to every other one, which is ideal for lateral movement. After: microsegmentation into isolated groups with their own policies. His example isolates backend containers and allows ingress only from a namespace selector matching backend services.
- **IAM.** Before: containers with broad access. After: least privilege per container, with access revoked when it's no longer needed. In his Harness pipeline example, an IAM role is what allows pulling the image from AWS Elastic Container Registry, so only authorised users and processes get to it.
- **Network security.** All service-to-service traffic encrypted and authenticated, whether containers share a host or not. He shows mutual TLS enforced across a namespace as part of a service mesh.
- **Runtime security.** Containers must behave as designed once deployed. Policies as code replace manual enforcement: if a shell starts as root inside a container, an alert fires for immediate action.

## Where does each control sit in the pipeline?

His lifecycle map is the slide worth screenshotting:

1. **Build**: vulnerability scanning on every build, security policies as code from the start.
2. **Test**: registry scanning, security automation, and admission controls so only trusted components get through.
3. **Staging**: compliance against CIS benchmarks and a container firewall as an extra layer.
4. **Production**: compliance with frameworks such as PCI and NIST, workload protection, runtime scanning and real-time alerts.

The thread through all four is the same idea as the definition: security is a continuous activity in the pipeline, not a one-time gate.

## Who should watch

Developers and DevOps engineers who ship containers and want a vocabulary and a checklist for zero trust, and teams preparing a security roadmap who need the controls laid out by stage. It's a concise overview; the examples are short manifests and pipeline snippets rather than a full lab.

Title: Your cloud bill is mostly housekeeping, then ask a FinOps expert prompt
Description: Hari Yerramsetty (Flexport) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on cutting cloud waste with FinOps basics, role prompts and cost-watching AI agents
Body:
Most cloud waste is not exotic. It is the EBS volume nobody deleted, the hackathon instance still running in the other cloud, the S3 bucket full of logs with no lifecycle policy. Hari Yerramsetty, Software Engineer on the infrastructure team at Flexport, spent his Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 talk on that unglamorous list, then showed where an LLM fits: as a role-prompted FinOps expert reading your invoice, and later as an agent that shuts down idle resources for you.

Honest scope: this is a broad FinOps primer with a prompt engineering chapter at the end, not a benchmark of AI cost tools. If you already run Karpenter, tag everything and get budget alerts, the first two thirds will feel familiar.

## Where does the money actually go?

He opens with a figure from his slides: studies show up to 30% of cloud spending is wasted through resource mismanagement. The cause he describes is human, not technical. Teams spin up instances and test databases, build features the business later drops, and nobody decommissions them.

His tour of cost drivers is practical:

- **Compute**: bigger instance families get expensive fast, and serverless stops being cheap when you call the same function 100,000 times.
- **Storage**: bucket sprawl in S3, EBS volumes left behind after the VM is deleted (detached, still billed), and RDS databases provisioned with IOPS for traffic that may arrive someday.
- **Data transfer**: NAT gateways, transit gateways, VPC peering and cross-AZ traffic across ten accounts, a charge that creeps up quietly.
- **Third-party services**: licences bought through the cloud provider, such as Red Hat on EC2.

The best anecdote is his own. Engineers on a hackathon project three years earlier forgot to turn off instances in a Google Cloud account, because almost all the company's work lived in one provider. Multi-cloud is mostly a way to have more places to forget things.

## The boring techniques still carry the weight

Right-sizing comes first, with AWS Trusted Advisor flagging idle instances, unattached volumes and databases with no recent connections. In Kubernetes, that means setting requests and limits from what observability says the app uses, rather than handing a service five vCPUs out of caution. His slides put autoscaling at savings of up to 30% compared with static provisioning, with the reminder that scaling down after the Thanksgiving promotion matters as much as scaling up.

He walks the instance menu too: spot for CI/CD and batch work that can survive termination, reserved for the baseline you need 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, on-demand for the rest. Container density, node autoscaling with Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler, watching for jobs stuck in restart loops, S3 lifecycle tiers, compression and regular data audits round it out.

## Unit economics, in one sentence

Cost allocation tags get the clearest argument in the talk. Hari Yerramsetty said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: "if you're making a hundred dollars in a transaction and you're spending eighty dollars on a cloud cost That's not a viable business model". Tags tell you which team and which project those eighty dollars belong to, and FinOps is the cultural part: engineers see the cost of a provisioning decision close to when they make it, not when the bill lands at the end of the month.

## What does the LLM do here?

The prompt engineering section is short and concrete. He uses role prompting, giving the model the role of a FinOps expert plus context, and shows two prompts. One asks the model to explain unblended and amortised costs on an AWS bill, which is genuinely useful if you are new to cloud billing. The other hands over an AWS invoice and asks why the bill was higher than usual and how to reduce spend. He notes it works with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Llama.

The forward-looking part is agents built with LangChain or CrewAI: a simple agent that notices a database taking no connections, tells the infrastructure team, and stops it. He presents this as the direction he is excited about rather than something shown running, and the abstract's promise of up to 35% savings is not backed by a worked example in the talk itself.

## Who should watch

Engineers who have just inherited an AWS bill, and teams starting a FinOps practice who want a checklist with names attached. Skip it if you came for prompt techniques in depth.
