Title: Where JavaScript sits in an SAP HR self-service app
Description: Lakshmi Gogula at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on building SAP HR employee self-service with SAPUI5, OData services, a Java backend and async JavaScript
Body:
Every leave request an employee files without emailing HR is a small win for the HR team's inbox. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Lakshmi Gogula, an SAP specialist with experience across ABAP, SAP BTP and SAP Fiori, lays out the stack behind that win: SAP HR as the system of record, SAPUI5 for the front end, a Java backend for business logic, OData services in between, and asynchronous JavaScript keeping the UI responsive while it all talks.

Set expectations before you press play. This is a short architecture overview, not a case study. The abstract mentions engagement, error and accessibility gains from a Fiori-based upgrade; the recorded talk doesn't present those figures or walk through a specific migration, so treat it as a map of the moving parts.

## Why employee self-service at all?

Her framing is the business one. "Employee self service has become a vital tool in empowering employees and streamlining HR process," Lakshmi Gogula said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. Employees update personal details and file leave requests themselves, HR stops being a data-entry desk, and administrative overhead drops.

Behind the self-service screens sits SAP HR's usual scope, which she summarises module by module: employee records (personal data, job history, qualifications, contracts), time and attendance (working hours, overtime, leave, absences, feeding payroll), payroll (salaries, tax deductions, bonuses, benefits) and benefits administration (health insurance, retirement plans, paid time off, enrolment and compliance with local rules).

## What does SAPUI5 bring?

SAPUI5 is SAP's UI toolkit built on HTML5, CSS and JavaScript, and the framework behind Fiori apps. The selling points she lists are responsive layouts that adapt to screen size and orientation, and a library of ready-made controls (tables, forms, charts, buttons) that can be customised to an organisation's branding and support accessibility standards. For an HR app that employees open on a phone between meetings, responsive by default matters.

## How do the pieces fit?

Her integration architecture splits the work three ways:

- **Java** for backend business logic, data processing and services.
- **SAPUI5** for the front end, with JavaScript handling real-time interactions in the browser.
- **OData services** as the contract between SAP HR and the UI, retrieving and updating employee data.

The JavaScript section is aimed at SAP developers more at home in ABAP than in the browser: `var` versus block-scoped `let` and `const`, DOM manipulation, event listeners, and promises with `async`/`await`. The point of the last one is the practical core of the talk. Submitting a leave request or updating an address goes out as an AJAX call, the server answers in JSON or XML, and only the affected part of the page updates. Keep those calls asynchronous and the UI doesn't freeze during long-running backend operations.

## Where is it heading?

She closes on modular development (Java, JavaScript and SAPUI5 each owning a layer, which makes the system easier to scale to more features and users) and on a future outlook: frameworks like React or Angular entering HR front ends, and AI and machine learning for more personalised employee experiences.

## Who should watch

SAP functional and ABAP developers who need a quick orientation in how a SAPUI5 front end, OData and a Java backend fit together for HR self-service. JavaScript developers new to the SAP world get a vocabulary list. If you want migration numbers or production lessons, this isn't that talk.

Title: Chet Gupta, the ChatGPT candidate who beat the interview rubric
Description: Daniel Pries at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on running interview questions through ChatGPT, and what fraud-proof technical hiring needs instead.
Body:
Somewhere in the middle of a technical screen, the candidate's audio dropped, he typed "I can't hear you", and Daniel Pries heard the keyboard clicks through the microphone that supposedly wasn't working. The person on camera was mouthing someone else's answers. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, [Daniel Pries](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Daniel_Pries_chatgpt_hiring_trick), an engineering manager with 20+ years in engineering, told how that interview led him to build a fake candidate out of ChatGPT, run it through his own hiring process, and discover the model sometimes knew the material better than the answer key.

It's the most entertaining talk of the event, and the lessons apply to any process built on questions with a right answer.

## Why was hiring broken before AI arrived?

He sets the scene with data. From February 2019 to February 2020, before the US shut down for COVID-19, applications across all industries fell 47%: the Great Resignation. At the same time Microsoft, Apple and Alphabet grew by thousands or tens of thousands of staff between 2019 and 2022, all from the same talent pool. Recruiting had been digitised to cope: automated resume screening, scheduling, chatbots and automated coding tests.

Then add fraud: stand-in voices, candidates reading questions off screen, and new hires who on day one are not the person who interviewed. "If you're not cheating, you're not trying," Daniel Pries said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, describing how plenty of job seekers saw it.

## How did Chet Gupta come about?

Pries had already been arguing that the automated code assessments tested puzzle-solving (Mensa-level puzzles you could crack with for loops) rather than code quality, maintainability or complexity. In 2022 he asked whether anyone had tried the questions on Copilot or ChatGPT. Crickets. Once GPT-3.5 went public in late 2022, he ran them himself, and a bunch could be solved easily, which meant retiring them and writing new ones.

The candidate was born over a late-night drink at a conference in snowy Ohio, sketched on a napkin with a fellow speaker: Chet Gupta, a play on ChatGPT. A fake LinkedIn profile turned out to be frowned upon, so they stuck to DALL-E headshots (which came back full of stubble, glasses and assumptions about who engineers are, an unplanned lesson in model bias), the coding tests, the technical screen and the competency-based interview. Crucially, they brought talent acquisition in early rather than ambushing them.

## How well did ChatGPT interview?

Uncomfortably well:

- **Competency questions.** Asked about a team facing challenges, Chet produced a textbook situation-task-action-result answer: communication across time zones, a poorly documented third-party API, then daily stand-ups, Jira or Trello, and pairing. You can read it as excellent or as Chet inventing Agile; either way it scores.
- **Algorithms.** A retired question, checking whether a string's parentheses are balanced in Java, got a stack-based solution. The rubric used an integer counter instead, cheaper on memory, but both are good enough answers.
- **Data structures.** Explaining Java's ConcurrentHashMap, Chet covered per-bucket locking and then volunteered the performance trade-off of the locking, the kind of judgement interviewers look for. Its answer clashed with the rubric on locking, so Pries researched it, and the model was closer to right than the rubric.

"Our candidates were better at development and being a better gatekeeper than we were for engineers," he said. Several questions took longer to type than for ChatGPT to answer, leaving a candidate time to add the ums and pauses that make a read-out answer sound human.

## What changed afterwards?

The organisation trained interviewers to spot cheating, cut ties with a sourcing vendor that turned out to be sending fraudulent candidates, and confronted the testing vendor. Their advice was to proctor the tests, which nobody can do at hundreds of interviews a year without pulling the best engineers off real work. His verdict on the toolchain: "Our adaptive testing is no longer an effective litmus because you're just one prompt away from being able to get a well reasoned answer."

The fixes are social rather than technical: cameras on, and his favourite trick, holding up a Post-it with an instruction for the candidate to read and act on, or asking them to look left or right, to check who is really seeing the screen. Hiring managers can also drop a test when it doesn't fit the role.

His closing rules are humane: assume positive intent, remember that just because it can be automated doesn't mean it should be, lead with empathy for the people who spent years rolling out those tools, bring talent acquisition along, and seek a win for everyone. The person you hire will spend about 1,800 hours a year with your team.

## Who should watch

Every engineering manager who interviews, and the recruiters they work with. Bring your own question bank and plan to retire some of it.

Title: From a folder of PDFs to a cited chatbot with Azure Prompt Flow
Description: Konstantinos Passadis (EPAM) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on a no-code RAG chatbot with Azure AI Studio, AI Search, Prompt Flow and a Flask web app.
Body:
Most chat-with-your-documents tutorials start with a vector database install. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, [Konstantinos Passadis](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Konstantinos_Passadis_azure_promptflow_chatbot), Cloud Solutions Architect at EPAM and a Microsoft Azure MVP, built one entirely through Azure's portals: upload PDFs, let Azure AI Search vectorise them, clone a Prompt Flow template, deploy it as an endpoint and paste the generated client code into a small Flask app, which answers with citations to the source PDF.

It's a beginner-friendly workshop and he says so. One note: the abstract mentions Cosmos DB, Hugging Face and React, but the demo uses Azure AI Search, Azure OpenAI and Flask.

## What do you need before you start?

An Azure subscription (the free trial gives around $200 of credit for 30 days), Azure AI Search at the Basic tier for the vector index, Azure OpenAI with a chat model and an embeddings deployment, App Service to host the web app, and VS Code or any IDE.

Creating an Azure AI Hub in AI Studio (ai.azure.com) provisions most of the rest for you: storage, Key Vault for secrets, a container registry (every deployed flow becomes a container) and a machine learning workspace. Projects live under the hub, so one hub can hold separate prompt-flow and chat-completion projects with shared networking and IAM.

## How does the data get in?

His dataset is a set of one- or two-page PDFs explaining Microsoft licensing options, Windows 10 and Office 2019 among them. In AI Studio you create a new index, upload the files, point it at the AI Search service and the OpenAI embeddings connection, and leave the compute on auto-select. The job, which runs in the machine learning workspace (ml.azure.com), cracks the documents, chunks them, generates embeddings and registers the vector index.

## What's inside the flow?

He clones the "Q&A on your data" template rather than starting from scratch, and the graph is already wired: inputs, a lookup step against the registered index (hybrid vector plus keyword search, default top-k), prompt generation, and an LLM step. Each node carries an activate config, a condition that decides whether it runs; the template needs all of them, so he leaves those alone.

The system message does the grounding work: answer only from the given context, be as precise as possible, and add a citation after each sentence. Prompt Flow lets you keep variants of that node (he shows three) for testing different system prompts side by side. He runs the flow with GPT-4 on a serverless compute session and gets a licensing answer for Windows 10 with links to the source PDFs.

## How does it become a web app?

Deploy creates a managed online endpoint with key-based authentication on a VM you size yourself (he picked a 10-core one and a single instance) and routes 100% of traffic to the deployment, though you can split traffic between flows to send a slice of users to a test version. The endpoint's identity comes with five roles assigned for you: writing to the workspace, reading secrets, reading storage, pulling the image from the registry and logging to storage. Autoscale rules can add instances on load, for example when traffic stays at 85% for five minutes.

The Consume tab hands you client snippets in C#, Python and JavaScript. He drops the Python one into a Flask app, moves the API key and endpoint into App Service environment variables instead of code, and deploys from VS Code.

## What will bite you?

Quotas. Free and trial subscriptions cap things like CPUs per region, and experiments pile up resources fast. "So when you are experimenting, remember to delete everything after you finished your experiments," Konstantinos Passadis said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. Stopping an idle web app also saves money, since you pay mostly for storage; the trade-off, visible in the demo, is a slow first response after it restarts.

## Who should watch

Developers and cloud engineers new to RAG who want to see the whole Azure path once, end to end, with the portal clicks shown. If you already run retrieval pipelines in code, this is a tour of the managed route rather than new technique; his code is on his GitHub and blog.

Title: Most React hook fixes are about having fewer dependencies
Description: Daniel Espino Garcia (Mattermost) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on React hooks - what useCallback costs, when to memo, and when useState is the wrong tool
Body:
Plenty of `useCallback`s in real React codebases are protecting a function that never needed to live inside the component. That's one of the habits Daniel Espino Garcia, Software Design Engineer at Mattermost, goes after at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. His talk opens up how hooks work inside React, argues that their overhead is rarely your bottleneck, and then gives a set of concrete rewrites whose common thread is fewer, clearer dependencies.

The examples come from real life: Mattermost, the open source alternative to Slack and Microsoft Teams, has a mobile app written entirely in functional components and a web app migrating to them, and it takes outside contributions. He has seen a lot of hooks, "some of them pretty smart uses some of them not so much."

## What is a hook, under the hood?

"Hooks are the future, or at least they are since 2019 when React added them," Daniel Espino Garcia said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. In `ReactFiberHooks.js`, each hook is an object with a `memoizedState` and a `next` pointer to the following hook: a linked list. That's the whole reason for the rule against calling hooks conditionally. Change the call order and the list no longer lines up.

He walks through `useCallback`'s two halves. `mountCallback` stores the callback and its dependencies on first render; `updateCallback` compares the new dependencies with the stored ones and returns the old callback if they match. Yes, that costs memory, a dependency-comparison loop and some garbage collector stress. No, it probably doesn't matter: by Amdahl's Law, speeding up a part of the run only saves you that part's time, and your bottleneck is almost certainly not too many `useCallback`s. Readability comes first, because the code is written once and read many times.

## Move things out of the component

The cheapest dependency is the one you don't have. A constant or a callback that doesn't touch props or state belongs at module scope:

- It never changes between renders, so nothing needs to list it as a dependency.
- It isn't recreated each render, so less garbage collection.
- Nobody can quietly make it depend on something tomorrow.

The same principle covers what goes in the array. If an effect calls `handleAndroidKeyboard`, which calls `blur`, depend on `handleAndroidKeyboard` (wrapped in `useCallback` with `[blur]`), not on `blur` directly. List what the function actually uses, so the next person doesn't delete a dependency that looks unused.

## When is useState the wrong tool?

This section is the most useful. His rules:

- **Intermediate variables over raw props.** Compute `canPost = !isArchived && hasPermissions` and depend on `canPost`. One clearer name, one dependency, and the callback only changes when the result changes.
- **Lazy initialisers.** `useState(() => getOptionFromValue(options, defaultValue))` runs the loop over options once, not on every render.
- **Refs for values that don't affect rendering.** An infinite scroll's page counter is never displayed, so it goes in `useRef`, not state.
- **Functional updates.** `setElements(prev => [...prev, ...newElements])` drops `elements` from the dependency array and the re-renders that came with it.
- **The effect smell.** `setState` inside a `useEffect` with no `await` before it means the component renders twice for nothing. An aspect ratio computed from `width` and `height` is just `const aspectRatio = width / height`.

His summary: state for values that affect rendering and must persist independently of props; refs for component references and values that don't affect rendering; plain computed values for everything derivable from props and state.

## What should you memoize?

Only reference types. Memoizing a string buys nothing, since strings compare equal between renders anyway. Memoizing an object you immediately spread into props is equally pointless. `useMemo` is for objects and lists passed as props or used as dependencies, and for genuinely heavy calculations. `useCallback` is for functions passed as props or used as dependencies, not for a function you call during render to compute a prop's value.

## Custom hooks should be stable

Repeated boilerplate, like registering a navigation listener that checks for the back button, calls a callback and removes itself, becomes `useBackNavigation(onPressClose)`. Less repetition, one place to fix it. The catch: a custom hook that returns a new function on every call is a trap for its callers. Wrap the return value in `useCallback` so the same inputs give the same output, which is what anyone using a hook expects.

## Who should watch

React developers past the basics who want rules they can apply in code review tomorrow, and anyone tired of arguing about whether to wrap everything in `useCallback`. Short, code-heavy and opinionated in the right places.

Title: Screen readers never see your React components, only the accessibility tree
Description: Raihan Nismara (Telkom Indonesia) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on React accessibility - WCAG basics, semantic HTML, WAI-ARIA, auditing tools and getByRole tests
Body:
Your screen-reader users don't experience your React components, your CSS or even your DOM. They get the accessibility tree the browser builds from it, and every `div` pretending to be a button shows up there as exactly what it is. That's the thread running through Raihan Nismara's talk at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. The Frontend Developer at Telkom Indonesia gives a complete first course in React accessibility: who struggles with the web and why, the four WCAG principles, the React fixes, how to audit, and how to write tests that query by role.

It's an essentials talk, and says so in the title. If you're the person on your team who already runs axe in CI, this is the talk to send to everyone else.

## Who gets locked out, and by what?

He starts from the users rather than the spec. People with physical disabilities often rely on the keyboard or on assistive hardware such as sip-and-puff devices, and run into missing keyboard support, invisible focus and a focus order that jumps somewhere unexpected. Blind users hit missing alt text and unclear structure. Low-vision users fight small fonts, poor contrast, information conveyed only by colour, and fast animation. Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and people with cognitive and learning disabilities, lose out when there are no captions, subtitles, transcripts or sign language.

The motivation comes from a line by Mary Pat Radabaugh of IBM, from 1988: for people without disabilities technology makes things easier, for people with disabilities it makes things possible. He adds the curb cut effect: the ramps cut into pavements for wheelchair users turned out to help everyone with a stroller or a bike.

## What do the WCAG principles mean in practice?

Perceivable, operable, understandable, robust. His translation: provide text alternatives and captions; make every function work from a keyboard and give people enough time with carousels and sliders; tone down animation that can trigger seizures; show users where they are (mark the current page in the nav); keep layout predictable so the header doesn't wander between pages; help people fill in forms with clear input hints and error messages; and make sure the markup works across browsers, devices and assistive technology.

## The React fixes

- **Use the real element.** A link is an `<a>`. "If you want to try to provide some link, use anchor tag," Raihan Nismara said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. You get keyboard support, the browser's links list and bookmarking for free; a styled `span` gives you none of them.
- **Semantic structure.** `header`, `nav`, `section`, `footer` instead of a stack of `div`s, with `div`s nested inside them where you need wrappers for layout.
- **Keyboard and focus.** `tabIndex={0}` puts an element into the natural tab order; `-1` keeps it focusable from code but out of the tab order, which suits dialogs and modals. Give focus a visible style, and use `autoFocus` or a `useRef` plus `useEffect` to move focus where the user needs it.
- **Labels.** Wrap inputs in a `label` or use `htmlFor`, so a checkbox is announced with its label, its type and its state instead of a bare state.
- **Page titles in SPAs.** Update the document title on route changes; he uses React Helmet.
- **WAI-ARIA for custom widgets.** A `div`-based toggle needs `role="checkbox"` and `aria-checked` to be announced as one. `aria-labelledby` joins related text, such as a product name and its Shop now button, into one announcement, and `aria-describedby` attaches hints and errors to an input.
- **The `as` prop pattern** for components that must render different elements by context, such as a heading component that can be an `h1`, an `h2` or a `span`.

To see the tree yourself, open the Accessibility pane in Chrome DevTools.

## How do you audit and test it?

Manual checks first: Lighthouse, WAVE, the ChromeVox screen reader, Accessibility Insights for Web and the axe DevTools extension. Then automation. An accessibility linter in the editor, `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` for JSX, and Cypress with axe-core injected to scan whole pages.

For unit tests with React Testing Library and Jest (or Vitest), he swaps `getByTestId`-style queries for `getByRole`: find the button named Dark mode and expect `aria-pressed` to be true, or find the level-2 heading by role. Tests written that way break when accessibility breaks, not when copy changes.

Short on time or budget? Start from a component library that already handles this, such as Chakra UI, Material UI, Bootstrap, Adobe's React Spectrum or Radix. His demo CRUD app uses React Spectrum, and the ChromeVox run over it announces every control correctly.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers who know accessibility matters but have never opened the accessibility tree, and teams wanting a checklist to bring to their next sprint. The business case is in there too: a bigger audience, better UX and SEO, and in some countries legal exposure if you skip it.

Title: Prompt like a film director, not like a search box
Description: Charlie Reynolds (CTR Consulting) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on clarity, imagination, orchestrating specialised AIs and iterating on prompts.
Body:
Ask an LLM "what's the weather?" and you get what you deserve. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, [Charlie Reynolds](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Charlie_Reynolds_promptengineering_science_art), founder of CTR Consulting and a fractional CTO, gave a short, upbeat primer arguing that good prompts need two things engineers tend to undervalue: precision about what you want, and the imagination to ask for something you don't already know.

This is a short first talk on prompting, aimed at people early in their AI use. Seasoned prompt engineers can skip it.

## Why does a specific prompt get more than you asked for?

His running example is the weather. "What's the weather?" is vague. "What's the weather in Paris next Tuesday morning for my business trip?" gets a forecast, and often a bonus: because you said why you're asking, the model may suggest what to do in Paris given the conditions. Context is a cue the model will use, and you can feed its extras back in to refine the next prompt.

The content-generation version: not "generate an article about AI" but a 500-word article on AI's impact on healthcare using statistics from the last five years.

## What does he mean by orchestration?

Chaining specialised AIs, each with its own prompt, so one's output becomes the next one's input. A text generator, then a sentiment analyser, then a summariser. Or a pipeline that summarises a pile of articles, passes the summaries to a model specialised in spotting bias, then hands everything to a third that assembles a final output with the bias removed.

The customer service example is the most practical: a chatbot talks to the customer while a separate model tuned for sentiment watches for frustration and decides when a human should step in. The catch he flags is that each component needs real clarity about what it is expected to produce, or the pieces won't fit together.

## How should you approach writing prompts?

His three parts:

- **Clarity and imagination.** Think of yourself as a director guiding actors: picture the final performance, then write prompts that lead there.
- **Context and orchestration.** Complex tasks need contextual prompts per model and a clear contract between them.
- **Iteration and refinement.** As in software, each pass gets closer.

He frames the whole thing around Einstein's line that imagination is more important than knowledge. Asking an AI about what you already know wastes most of it. "The next time you interact with AI, don't just ask it for an answer, imagine the possibilities," Charlie Reynolds said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. His last tip is cheap and underused: ask the model itself what is suboptimal about your prompt and how to improve it.

## Who should watch

Managers, product people and developers new to prompting who want a quick mental model, and anyone who needs to explain orchestration to a non-technical team. There is no code or tooling; for depth, pair it with the more technical talks below.

Title: GAMES, a five-letter checklist for gamifying a React app
Description: Courtney Yatteau (Esri) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on gamifying React apps with XP bars, Context API, memoization, Suspense and social sharing
Body:
Gamification is half psychology and half plumbing, and Courtney Yatteau's talk at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 is honest about the plumbing. The Developer Advocate at Esri, a former high school maths and computer science teacher, packs her approach into an acronym, GAMES, then builds a small gamified map app in React that picks up one letter at a time: an XP bar, a context-backed store, memoization, lazy loading and a Share on X button.

The pitch is that React's component model suits this kind of feature well: progress bars, badges and leaderboards are reusable interactive components, and the hard part is keeping state and rendering sane as you add more of them.

## What does GAMES stand for?

- **G, Gamified components**: XP points, badges, progress bars, weekly targets. Her example is Codecademy, which combines all four.
- **A, Advanced state control**: React's Context API for state many components need. She cites Headspace managing UI theming through a context provider.
- **M, Memoization**, which evolves into modern optimization: `React.memo` and `useMemo` to skip re-renders, with the React Compiler (in beta at the time) set to automate most of it. Grammarly's suggestions panel is her example of a memoized component that re-renders only when the typed input changes.
- **E, Efficient rendering**: `React.lazy` and Suspense, so heavy components and animations load when needed. Duolingo's character animations are the case study.
- **S, Social interaction**: leaderboards, following friends, sharing milestones. Duolingo again.

Starbucks gets the full five-letter treatment: a stars progress bar, bonus challenges for visiting several days in a row, Context for locale and currency, memoized prices and formats, and gift cards for the social part. Treat the architecture claims about other companies' apps as her reading of them; for Starbucks she says the app likely uses lazy loading and Suspense, rather than claiming it.

## Why is gamification more than badges?

Her framing: "It's really about how we create these applications to make users want to come back for more," Courtney Yatteau said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. The apps people can't put down take routine or hard tasks (ordering coffee, learning a language, managing anxiety) and attach achievement to them. The teacher background shows here: she has watched it work on students before writing it in React.

## The demo: XP on a map of Washington, D.C.

The live-coding half starts with a Vite project and a map component that renders Washington, D.C. through Esri Leaflet and the ArcGIS community basemap, with the API key read from `import.meta.env`. A `useRef` holds the map instance so it initialises once, not on every render, and she drops in the classic reminder that Leaflet wants latitude first while other mapping libraries want longitude first.

Then the letters:

1. **G**: a `ProgressBar` component takes the current XP, fills to a max of 100 and resets on level-up. A Gain XP button adds 10 per click. She suggests the real version should award XP for places the user discovers on the map.
2. **A**: the local `useState` moves into a `GameContext` with `useReducer`, handling an increment-XP action (payload 10) and a reset-XP action, and a `GameProvider` wraps the app in `main.jsx`.
3. **M**: the progress bar gets wrapped in `React.memo` so it re-renders only when XP changes. She admits it barely matters in an app this size and matters a lot once leaderboards and multiplayer arrive.
4. **E**: the progress bar is loaded with `React.lazy` inside a Suspense boundary with a loading fallback, to show the mechanics of code splitting.
5. **S**: a `SocialShare` component builds a pre-filled X post with the user's XP and opens it in a new window.

The starter and final code are at [github.com/cyatteau/gamified-demo-conf42js-2024](https://github.com/cyatteau/gamified-demo-conf42js-2024).

## Who should watch

React developers who've been asked to make a product stickier and want a structure for it, and anyone who wants a gentle, working example of Context plus `useReducer`, `React.memo` and Suspense in one small app. Seasoned React engineers will know the hooks; the value is in how they map onto game mechanics.

Title: An HR assistant that interrupts the workflow won't get used
Description: Marina Goplacheva (Sberbank) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on designing conversational AI for HR, from micro UIs to how human the bot should seem.
Body:
Employees don't live in HR systems, so an HR assistant that makes them open one is dead on arrival. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, [Marina Goplacheva](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Marina_Goplacheva_hrtech_conversationalai_intelligent), product owner for conversational AI in Sberbank's HR transformation department, shared lessons from building chat and voice assistants for HR since 2019, including the skill that failed precisely because it asked people to step out of their day to use it.

This is a product and design talk rather than a prompting one, and it's better for it.

## Why does conversational AI suit HR so well?

Because HR and employees don't share a vocabulary. People don't know what a service is called or which app it lives in; letting them ask in their own words removes that gap. In a big enterprise with a sprawl of tools, one conversational entry point (the "interfaceless UI") replaces several. It also skips much of the change management that comes with rolling out a new HR platform, since it can sit on top of existing systems without re-engineering them, and it can live in the messaging apps people already use.

She has designed skills for nearly every HR area, from onboarding and leave to compensation and performance management. Oracle, Workday, SAP SuccessFactors and ADP have since moved the same way.

## What do teams get wrong when they build one?

They let the technology outrun the design. If the design isn't up to the level of the technology, that alone blocks adoption. She points to a knowledge and cultural gap between UX designers and ML engineers, and argues designers now need a much better grasp of what happens in the back end. Design also has to account for how human conversation actually works, and for models degrading over time.

User research still matters. Designing voice skills for an internal assistant, she found herself structuring voice flows like a UI's logic tree, while users who talked to Amazon Alexa at home spoke to the skill as if it were a person. Two mental models, two very different products.

For personalisation at scale, fix the data, and not only its quality: build a layer of codified descriptions and dictionaries of employee data, because the LLM has to query that context. For complex decision-making, consider putting human experts into the development process to see what the ideal process looks like.

## How human should the assistant be?

Less than you'd think. Back in 2019 she spent hours a week debating how to make interfaces sound like people. Then the usage data from the internal assistant showed employees using it for utilitarian goals, with wording to match: it was a tool. "And frankly, I don't think people should make emotional connections with things," Marina Goplacheva said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. Heavy anthropomorphism mostly sets expectations the product can't meet.

## Does it have to be pure natural language?

No. Her team got good results embedding micro UIs inside conversational skills, mixing natural language with small graphical components. Some HR tasks are simply better in a content-rich interface, and a hybrid lets you have both.

## Why did that one skill fail?

It solved a real, tedious task employees disliked. But using it meant interrupting their workflow to open the assistant on another device, and that interruption wasn't worth it to them. Nobody used it. The context in which the interaction happens shapes whether it feels useful at all, especially for blue-collar workers who spend little time in any system.

Her last point is that AI doesn't need to run end to end. In a regulated domain like HR, payroll issues may need direct controls and more rigid technology outside the AI components. Align the assistant with a business objective, and weigh your HR data, tech stack and risk tolerance before building.

## Who should watch

Product managers and designers building internal assistants, in HR or any enterprise domain. No code or architecture here; the value is in the failure story and the anthropomorphism argument.

Title: The Node.js memory leak was an event listener, as usual
Description: Muhammad Yasir Rafique (Find My Facility) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on finding Node.js memory leaks with heap snapshots, --inspect and clinic.js
Body:
Servers restarting again and again under heavy traffic, and nobody sure whether to blame the server, a controller or a single function: that's the production story at the centre of Muhammad Yasir Rafique's talk at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. The Node.js Backend Developer at Find My Facility traces the leak back to the usual suspect, an event listener holding references to objects nobody needed, and lays out the toolkit that found it: heap snapshots in Chrome DevTools, Node's `--inspect` flag, clinic.js and `process.memoryUsage()`.

It's an introductory talk. If you've never opened a heap snapshot, it gives you the map; if you live in the Memory tab already, it will mostly confirm what you know.

## Why do leaks hurt more in Node.js?

Node's event-driven model keeps a lot of callbacks and functions in flight at once, which is why it shines for I/O-heavy work. It also means anything those callbacks forget to release piles up in one long-running process. The symptoms he lists are the ones to watch on your dashboards: memory usage that climbs over time, response times that get slower, and frequent garbage collection pauses. Left alone, it ends in crashes and restarts.

## How did the team find it?

At first, by flailing. He is candid that the team didn't know where to start, and the leak only showed up under heavy load. What worked was comparison over time. "With the help of the memory snapshots and profiling tools, our team was able to pinpoint the exact issue which causes the memory leaks," Muhammad Yasir Rafique said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024.

The method is simple and worth stealing: take a heap snapshot before a suspect operation and another after it, then look at what survived that should have been garbage collected. Run the process with `--inspect`, attach Chrome DevTools, and you get the same snapshot and heap comparison tooling you'd use in a browser, pointed at your server.

## The fix was boring, which is the point

The culprit was an event listener that kept references to unused objects alive after each run. The fix: remove listeners once their work is finished and clean up properly after every execution. Hard to spot, easy to repair, like most leaks.

He groups the common causes into three:

- **Accidental globals**, which live for the whole lifetime of the process (a beginner favourite).
- **Closures** that capture variables from an outer function and keep them around longer than intended.
- **Event listeners and callbacks** that are never removed, especially in long-running apps.

## Which tools for which stage?

His layering goes from manual to continuous:

- **Chrome DevTools and `--inspect`** for snapshot-by-snapshot investigation during development.
- **clinic.js** for broader diagnosis: memory leaks, but also CPU bottlenecks and slow queries.
- **`process.memoryUsage()`** logged from the app itself, tracking heap and RSS (resident set size) so growth shows up in your logs before it shows up as an outage.
- **New Relic or Datadog** for real-time memory monitoring in production, so you see the climb after a release instead of after the third restart.

He also gives the V8 garbage collector its due: it frees what's unreachable, and understanding what keeps an object reachable is most of the job.

## Who should watch

Backend developers who suspect a memory leak and don't yet have a routine for proving it. Real-time and high-concurrency systems get a short section at the end on why continuous operation makes leaks harder to catch.

Title: Conf42 Incident Management 2024: vendors, networks and who watches the monitor
Description: The Conf42 Incident Management 2024 roundup - 35 talks on vendor outages, network incidents, monitoring the monitoring, AI for on-call and security response.
Body:
[Conf42 Incident Management 2024](https://www.conf42.com/im2024) went out on October 17 with 35 sessions, and the strongest talks shared an uncomfortable premise: the incident that wakes you up is often not in your code. It's in your vendor, your network, or the monitoring system that was supposed to tell you about the first two. Around that core, the day covered AI for on-call teams, security incident response, and a broad set of industry case studies.

Speakers came from PagerDuty, Meta, Mattermost, VictoriaMetrics, Caber Systems, Microsoft, Walmart Global Tech, Caterpillar, Workday, BNY, Nike and a long list of smaller teams.

## Whose outage is it anyway?

[Mandi Walls](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Mandi_Walls_25_vendor_incidents_management) of PagerDuty opened the theme with vendor incidents, the ones where your service is down and it isn't your fault, but your customers don't care. She grounds it in an old cloud idea credited to John Allspaw: "One of the first key tenets or mantras of cloud computing was you own your own availability," Mandi Walls said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. The talk is about what to do before and during somebody else's outage so your team still looks in control.

[Maksim Kupriianov](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Maksim_Kupriianov_solving_network_incidents) of Meta took the incidents with the widest blast radius: DNS, DHCP, routing, VPN, directory services, load balancers. When those fail, everything above them fails with them, and his talk covers what to know before that day. [Ravi Theja Kambhampati](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Ravi_Theja_Kambhampati_38_network_resilience_scalability) laid the foundations underneath with routing, switching, VLANs, OSPF and BGP.

## Who monitors the monitoring?

[Mathias Palmersheim](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Mathias_Palmersheim_27_monitoring_monitoring_how) of VictoriaMetrics asked the question most teams skip: if your monitoring falls over in the middle of the night, does anyone get paged? He offers cheap ways to get started and tips for teams that already watch their watchers. He also admits to talking about observability on his first date with his wife, which his office had a betting pool on.

[Zuodong Xiang](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Zuodong_Xiang_52_resilient_systems_amazon) walked through real outage scenarios and what they taught, starting with a traffic flood where autoscaling keeps adding hosts that fail their health checks as fast as they arrive. It's a good talk for anyone who has watched a fix make the outage worse.

## Can AI take the 3am call?

[Spiros Economakis](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Spiros_Economakis_44_sre_ai_empowering) of Mattermost, who leads infrastructure and customer reliability engineering there, showed where GenAI helps SRE teams during a high-severity incident: finding the root cause while also updating internal teams and customers. [Rob Quiros](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Rob_Quiros_39_architecture_false_positives) of Caber Systems argued that security tools protect the conduit and hope the data inside is safe, and proposed an architecture that avoids that correlation to cut the false positives burning out SOC teams. The Performanta team (Guy Golan, Brendan Kotze, Stephen Kreusch and Elad Sherf) held the [panel discussion](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024__panel_discussion) on what happens when the IT tools themselves stop working, and how to keep incident management in control.

[Chinyere Chinekezi](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Chinyere_Chinekezi_12_incident_playbooks_response) of Sapphire made the case for playbooks in incident response, [Samikya Reddy Balguri](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Samikya_Reddy_Balguri_41_zero_trust_cyber) of Caterpillar brought zero trust architecture to incident management, and [Victor Onyenagubom](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Victor_Onyenagubom_47_incident_cyber_awareness) argued for cyber-awareness across the team. Title: Use prompts to write the forecasting scaffolding, not the forecast
Description: Sijo Valayakkad Manikandan (Nike) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on chain-of-thought, tree-of-thought and self-refine prompts for retail forecasting code.
Body:
Nobody asks ChatGPT for next quarter's T-shirt demand and ships the number. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, [Sijo Valayakkad Manikandan](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Sijo_Valayakkad_Manikandan_retail_forecasting_ai) of Nike, a data scientist focused on forecasting at scale, showed the useful version: tightly specified prompts that make an LLM write the SARIMA baseline, the feature pipeline and the EDA plots, so the data scientist spends the time on judgement instead of pandas boilerplate.

The abstract promises lessons from Amazon and Kroger; the talk itself is a practitioner's prompt cookbook, which is arguably more useful.

## Why is retail forecasting hard in the first place?

He starts with the value chain. A T-shirt might travel from a plant in China by road to a port, by ship to Europe, by truck to a distribution centre, through another warehouse and on to a store or your doorstep. Every hop adds uncertainty, and the product has to be designed and manufactured long before anyone knows whether grey with an abstract print is still trending.

Then the horizon changes the question entirely:

- **24+ months**: product design, contracts, strategy.
- **3 to 24 months**: assortment planning, space optimisation, sales and operations planning.
- **3 to 12 weeks**: workforce, capacity, inventory allocation, distribution centre replenishment.
- **1 to 3 weeks**: allocation, clear-outs, discounts.

Add granularity (one product in one store is far noisier than a region), fragmented data from IoT and payment devices, and COVID-19, which he calls an eye-opening moment that pushed retailers towards real-time forecasting.

## Which prompting techniques fit forecasting?

Three, each with a worked prompt:

- **Chain of thought** breaks the job into steps: prepare the data, explore and evaluate models, finish with evaluation on the test set, and list the key considerations at each step.
- **Tree of thought**, his favourite, asks for three approaches (traditional, machine learning, hybrid), each with steps, advantages and limitations, and a recommendation. The model's answer for large seasonal retail data was a hybrid: ARIMA for trend and seasonality, XGBoost on the residuals.
- **Self-refine** asks it to build a SARIMA model, score it with MAPE, critique it and fix it. The expected critique is the one every retail forecaster has written: seasonality captured, holiday peaks underestimated. The fix is adjusting seasonal parameters or adding an exogenous holiday indicator.

That last loop is just how data scientists work anyway: baseline, experiment, evaluate, repeat. The prompt makes the model walk it.

## What does a good forecasting prompt look like?

Closed, not open-ended. His proof-of-concept prompt names everything: time-based indexing, missing values, outlier detection, parameter search by grid search or AIC minimisation, an 80/20 train/test split, MSE and MAPE, actual-versus-forecast plots, residual diagnostics, a report on stationarity and autocorrelation, and the libraries (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib). His data transformation prompt gives the exact column names of his dataset so the output pastes straight in. The EDA prompt asks for Plotly charts, STL decomposition and Z-score anomaly flags.

The point of all that detail is keeping the model on rails. "There is a lot of information that's given to the AI model So that it doesn't hallucinate," Sijo Valayakkad Manikandan said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, adding that "it is still your job to provide these specific instructions so that AI models can easily generate them."

The most forward-looking example extracts sentiment from news headlines with spaCy or Transformers and runs Granger causality tests against stock prices, a stand-in for the retail version: a social media sentiment index feeding demand sensing.

## Where does it go wrong?

Vague prompts produce models that ignore seasonality or intervals. Generated deep learning models can be hard to interpret and debug. No model trained on limited data anticipates a pandemic. And the generated code won't handle missing values, irregular intervals or outliers unless you ask it to, so data problems slip through silently. His practical advice is to lean on LLMs hardest for exploratory analysis and visualisation, where mistakes are easy to spot.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and analysts building forecasting pipelines who want reusable prompts for the tedious parts. Experienced forecasters won't learn new statistics here; the value is the prompt patterns, which transfer to any time-series work.

- [Piotr Stepinski](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Piotr_Stepinski_forecasting_timeseries) on time-series forecasting at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.
- [Harpreet Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Harpreet_Singh_druglaunch_promotions_pharmaceutical) of Gilead Sciences on pharmaceutical launch analytics, from the same event.

Title: Treat the learner as the state and the next question as the action
Description: Vijay Valaboju (Microsoft) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on reinforcement learning for adaptive assessments, learning paths and gamified feedback.
Body:
A fixed exam measures what you knew on the day; an adaptive one decides what to ask next. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, [Vijay Valaboju](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Vijay_Valaboju_learning_promptengineering_ai), senior software engineer at Microsoft, framed AI-driven assessment as a reinforcement learning problem: the learner's knowledge is the state, the system's choice of content or question is the action, and performance feedback is the reward.

It's a short conceptual talk. Despite the title, prompt engineering barely appears; what you get is a clean map of where RL fits in a learning platform.

## How does the RL framing work?

He starts from the textbook definition: RL is "a branch of machine learning focused on how agents should take actions in an environment to maximize cumulative rewards through trial and error method," Vijay Valaboju said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. Map that onto education and the agent is the learner or the adaptive system, the environment is the content and assessments, the state is the learner's knowledge level, actions are the choices the agent makes, and rewards are feedback on performance.

Once you see it that way, most of the features of a modern learning product fall out as policies.

## What does an adaptive system change?

- **The curriculum.** Performance is analysed in real time, so a learner who excels at maths gets advanced topics now, without the usual waiting period.
- **The difficulty.** Accuracy and response time decide how hard the next challenge is, high enough to teach and low enough to avoid frustration. His example is a software developer preparing for a cloud computing certification, getting targeted questions on their weak spots.
- **The feedback.** Instead of a score at the end, the system explains mistakes and misconceptions immediately, then adjusts the path: new content where the learner is ready, foundations revisited where not.
- **The rewards.** Badges, points or virtual currency tuned to the individual, with achievements set at the learner's skill level so they stay challenged but not overwhelmed. A language platform that sees heavy engagement with speaking exercises can incentivise writing tasks to balance the two skills.

He also covers continuity across laptop, phone and watch, and anytime-anywhere assessments for working professionals and remote learners.

## Can it plan ahead?

That's the most ambitious section. Using historical data and industry trends, an RL system could predict which skills a learner will need, introduce those topics early, and optimise the long-term trajectory by modelling how skills interact, so the path builds competence rather than a pile of badges.

## What's still hard?

He names two challenges: algorithmic bias, which matters for fairness and transparency in educational technology, and the sheer complexity of human learning. Future work, in his view, is better interpretability and combining RL with NLP.

## Who should watch

Product people and engineers in edtech or internal training platforms who want a vocabulary for adaptive learning. If you already build RL systems, there's no reward design, algorithm or result here to dig into; it's an overview.

Title: An e-commerce backend split by business capability, not by tech stack
Description: Jubin Thomas (Signet Jewelers) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on sizing e-commerce microservices by business domain and building them with Node.js, Express and MongoDB
Body:
How big should a microservice be? Jubin Thomas, Technical Architect at Signet Jewelers, answers that at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 by refusing the question: size follows the business function, not a line count. His talk is a first tour of an e-commerce backend built as microservices, from domain boundaries through testing, Docker and Kubernetes, to a small order service in Node.js, Express and MongoDB.

Set expectations accordingly. This is a primer that covers a lot of ground quickly, aimed at developers who are about to break up their first monolith rather than teams already running a hundred services. The AMQP part of the title gets a mention as a prerequisite (RabbitMQ, if you use a message broker) rather than a section of its own.

## What is the right size for a microservice?

He defines a microservice as "an approach to engineering focused on building single function modules with well defined interfaces and operations," Jubin Thomas said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. His sizing rule follows from that: the business function a service performs matters more than its scale. One service might hold a dozen entities, another a couple of dozen; what matters is that each maps to a bounded context from domain-driven design. User stories are the tool he recommends for finding where one business domain ends and the next begins.

That also changes how teams are drawn. In a monolith shop, teams tend to split by technology or skill set. In a capability-centric design, each product team owns a business capability end to end.

## The four services every shop needs

His minimal e-commerce split is shopping cart, order, customer and inventory. In the monolith they share one database behind one business-logic layer. In the microservice version each owns its own store, and he deliberately shows them mismatched: customer in Redis, order in MongoDB, shopping cart in Microsoft SQL Server, inventory in Oracle 12c. Polyglot persistence is the point, not an accident.

Inside the order service he uses an aggregate root: the order ties together customer, shipping address and a payment strategy, which in turn can be a credit card, cash or a bank transfer. Adapters wrap database access and APIs, and converters handle chores like mapping enums to integers in the database. He also flags the classic CRUD trap for shared models: read and write representations drift apart, records get locked under contention, and permissions get messy because every entity is both read and written.

## Testing, containers, orchestration

The testing section walks the usual pyramid for distributed systems: unit, component, integration, contract and end-to-end tests, the contract layer being the one that catches two services disagreeing about an interface. Docker gets the build, ship and run summary, and Kubernetes the pods, services, scheduling, scaling and self-healing tour. If you already run containers, this is the part to skim.

## A tiny order service in Express and MongoDB

The code half is a five-file Node.js app for ordering a product: `db.js` opens the MongoDB connection through Mongoose; a product model (description, name, ID, brand) with an Express server on port 3000 exposing POST, GET-by-ID and DELETE routes; and an order model (product ID, initial date, delivery date) with its own server that saves new orders and fetches them, all or by ID. It is small on purpose: two services, two schemas, two servers, each changeable without touching the other, which is the conclusion he lands on.

He picks Express for the demo and names NestJS as the other popular option for Node.js microservices.

## Who should watch

Developers and students who want the whole microservices vocabulary in one pass, with a concrete e-commerce split to hang it on. If you're after messaging patterns, sagas or scaling numbers, look at the related talks below.

- Mohammed Zubair Ahmed on [a real-time chat for 100k users](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Mohammed_Zubair_Ahmed_41_realtimechat_performance_100kusers) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024.

Title: Red alerts happen
Description: Good crews bring everyone home
Body:
# When things break (because of course they do)

Let’s be honest. Nobody wakes up excited about incident management.

You don’t pour your morning coffee thinking, “Ah yes, today I would love a surprise outage, a flood of alerts, and a Slack channel named incident-sev-1-final-final-v3.” And yet… here we are.

The good news is, you don’t have to suffer alone.

Conf42 Incident Management 2024 is bringing together a whole lineup of people who spend an impressive amount of time dealing with things going sideways. On purpose. There are talks on AI, automation, cloud, security, data, monitoring, and all the fun stuff that usually shows up right when you were about to log off.

You’ll hear about AIOps, SRE tooling, chatbots that might actually be helpful, debugging ML systems, handling vendor incidents, and figuring out why the network decided to have feelings today. There’s also plenty on architecture, resilience, zero trust, and reducing false positives, because nothing builds character like being paged for something that wasn’t broken.

Some sessions dive into regulated worlds like healthcare, finance, and utilities, where incidents are extra spicy and “just restart it” is not a valid strategy. Others focus on cloud migrations, Kubernetes security, and the quiet art of keeping systems upright while everyone else is asking what went wrong.

If incidents are part of your job (or your life, at this point), this one’s for you. Bring your curiosity, your scars, and maybe a sense of humor. You’ll probably need it.

See you there!

Title: LLMs are great at tests and terrible at refactoring
Description: Bohdan Snisar (ex-Revolut) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on where generative AI helps the SDLC (tests, requirements, search) and where it breeds tech debt.
Body:
The autonomous AI software engineer is still a dream; an LLM that writes your edge-case tests is already here. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, [Bohdan Snisar](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Bohdan_Snisar_gepai_development_tools), a senior software engineer formerly at Revolut, walked through the software development lifecycle phase by phase, naming the tools he actually uses, and ended on the uncomfortable bit: unsupervised AI code ages into legacy faster than the human kind.

## Where does AI fit in the SDLC?

He sorts projects into four boxes: conventional systems built the conventional way, conventional systems built with AI-augmented tooling, AI products built the old way, and AI products built with AI tooling. The talk lives in the second box, which is where most teams with a Copilot licence are.

He points to a recent survey paper of research on LLMs in software engineering: most work targets development itself, followed by maintenance, requirements, design and management, and most tasks are about generation, then recommendation and classification. He suspects maintenance is the bigger prize, given how much software already exists.

As for fully autonomous engineers, Devin and the open-source SWE-agent exist, and by the benchmarks they don't work that well yet. Splitting the job into functions and automating pieces is the practical path.

## Can LLMs help before anyone writes code?

Yes, and this is the underrated part. People are bad at saying what they want, and LLMs are good at turning unstructured requirements into specifications or user stories. Because they carry generic knowledge, they can point at gaps in the requirements you didn't know were there, feeding follow-up questions. They can also classify functional and non-functional requirements out of sources like app-store reviews and turn them into half-refined tickets for grooming.

## Which tools earn their keep?

His honest field notes:

- **Replit** for prototyping: authentication, database access and the rest of the standard scaffolding come fast, but it's Python and JavaScript territory, weak on rarer or harder languages like Rust and on anything non-standard.
- **Cursor**, the VS Code fork, for code completion and targeted edits, though it struggles with big projects, so he copy-pastes code into it and back into his IDE.
- **GitHub Copilot Workspace** for search across specs, code and docs, good at merging information, shakier when it loses the wider context.
- **CodeRabbit** for pull request review, where he finds what it missed and it finds what he missed: a good combo.
- **Dosu** for answering and resolving GitHub issues from the codebase, sometimes without a human.

He also wants LLMs placing log statements with context, since developers tend to log wherever the last bug was.

## Why are tests the sweet spot?

Because the model imagines more edge cases than you do. He sees proven value in unit tests, Selenium end-to-end specs and synthetic test data. The worked example is Meta's paper on automated unit test improvement with LLMs (arXiv 2402.09171): generate candidate tests, pre-process, check they build, check they pass, then keep the ones that raise coverage and open a pull request.

His scorecard: good for boilerplate, small changes that don't touch many classes, tests and test data, unfamiliar tasks (CSS for backend developers) and integrated search over a data lake. Bad at changing complex code, refactoring and generating code across multiple classes. He is sceptical of the headline Java migration savings too, since Java's backward compatibility makes version upgrades mostly minor edits.

## What does it do to code quality?

He cites GitClear's analysis showing code churn rising since the LLM boom. Experienced developers can judge and fix what the model produces; newcomers often can't. If you follow the model without supervision, "It creates a legacy code quicker than people usually do," Bohdan Snisar said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024. Generation is cheap; the maintenance bill arrives later.

## Who should watch

Engineering leads deciding where to spend AI tooling budget, and developers who want a practitioner's map rather than a vendor's. It's an overview with opinions, no deep demo; the test-generation and tech-debt sections are the ones to keep.

Title: One request is enough to stall a Node.js app
Description: Allon Mureinik (Black Duck) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on how JSON, XML bombs, ReDoS and sync I/O let a single request block the Node.js event loop
Body:
You don't need a botnet to take a Node.js service down. A 36-character query string can do it. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Allon Mureinik, Senior Engineering Manager at Black Duck, walked through four everyday patterns (JSON parsing, XML and YAML entity expansion, backtracking regexes and synchronous storage calls) that let one request tie up the event loop, and the cheap fixes for each.

He is explicit about scope: no DDoS, no rate limiters, no load balancers. Those belong to the deployment layer. This talk is about what the application itself can do so that a single malicious request can't deny service to everyone else.

## Why is Node.js so exposed to this?

Because of the same design that makes it fast. Node runs user requests on a single main thread, the event loop, and hands slow work (usually I/O) to a small worker pool. That works as long as every tick on the loop is tiny. Anything that hogs the loop blocks every other request in the queue.

That reframes the problem. "If a malicious request takes two hours to fulfill, that might be okay," Allon Mureinik said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024. What matters is whether legitimate users get served during those two hours. DoS defence here is about not blocking others, not raw speed.

## JSON: linear, boring, still worth a limit

`express.json()` ends up calling `JSON.parse` on the event loop, and his benchmark shows parse time growing roughly linearly with body size. An attacker gets a linear lever, which is the least scary case, but it is also the easiest to close. His real-world example: a customer login form with 8-character usernames and 12-character passwords whose backend happily parsed a 2 MB JSON body. The fix is one option, `express.json({limit: '40kb'})`, or whatever your real payloads need plus a buffer. Where big JSON is part of the protocol, parse it off the loop with a streaming library such as JSONStream or BFJ. BFJ is slower than `JSON.parse` by its own documentation, and that's fine: slow in a worker beats fast on the loop.

## XML and YAML: a billion laughs in 650 bytes

The classic billion laughs attack nests entity definitions ten deep, each expanding to ten of the previous one. His graph is the punchline: at seven levels the XML is about 650 bytes and expands to roughly 29 MB in memory; eight levels heads towards a gigabyte.

The defences come in order of preference: don't use XML, don't let tainted input reach your XML parser, and if you must parse it, switch entity expansion off (for the libxml wrappers, `noent: false` or `huge: false`). In 24 years as an engineer and manager he recalls one system that genuinely needed on-the-fly entity definitions. Then sanitise before parsing, not after. And for anyone feeling smug about never touching XML: YAML supports the same recursive references, so YAML bombs exist too, and the same tactics apply.

## ReDoS: 35 characters, five minutes

The regex demo uses the deliberately silly pattern `/(a+)+/` against strings of a's followed by a single b, forcing the engine to backtrack through every grouping. Up to about 30 characters it stays bearable. Then it falls off a cliff: around 35 a's took about 300,000 ms, roughly five minutes, and at 36 the benchmark ate enough CPU that the music he was playing started lagging and he killed it.

The mitigations:

- Check hard-coded regexes for nested quantifiers; SAST tools are good at this.
- Don't accept raw regexes from users. If you need wildcard search, accept a simplified syntax and build the regex server-side.
- Put length limits on any tainted input that a risky regex evaluates.
- Use [RE2](https://github.com/google/re2), which has no backtracking and so isn't vulnerable to ReDoS, or a vetted library such as validator.js instead of hand-rolled patterns for emails and URLs.

## Sync storage calls are the wrong way, full stop

`fs.readFileSync` and every other `*Sync` API, in core or in fs-extra or adm-zip, tells you it will do its work on the event loop. Fine at startup, never inside a request handler. Your laptop's NVMe hides the cost; the cloud provider's storage, which you don't control, won't. His summary of the two options: there's the async way, and there's the wrong way.

## Who should watch

Node.js backend developers who think about SQL injection and XSS but have never benchmarked their parsers. His closing argument is that DoS bugs take far less skill to exploit than injection: nothing gets stolen, but the business stops. Review the defaults of every library you ship, because they are rarely tuned for production, let alone security.

Title: Predictive network maintenance should tolerate misses, not false alarms
Description: Akshat Kapoor (Alcatel-Lucent Enterprise) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024 on building ML models that predict network faults, and why false positives hurt most.
Body:
Networks have been fixed the same way since the early internet: something breaks, you detect it, you reroute. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024, [Akshat Kapoor](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Akshat_Kapoor_predictive_network_failures), Director of Product Line Management at Alcatel-Lucent Enterprise, laid out how to build a model that predicts network failures instead, and made one counter-intuitive call: tune it to accept missed faults before you accept false alarms.

Despite the event name, this isn't a prompting talk. It's a clear, practical overview of machine learning for network operations.

## What actually breaks networks?

He opens with the failure mix from a study he cites: link failures (a fibre cut or a misconfigured link) at about 32%, operating system failures and software bugs around 18%, human misconfiguration another 18%, then hardware reaching end of life, and cyber attacks. The price tag is the Gartner figure of $5,600 per minute of downtime, and for telecom operators globally the annual cost can exceed $60 billion.

The case study is the 2022 Rogers outage in Canada: a day-long outage that left about 12 million people, a quarter of the population, without internet, emergency and payment services included. The root cause, a software update that took the routers down, took far too long to find. Then there are the wholesale SLAs: every extra minute of downtime is money owed to the smaller networks riding on the big operator.

## Why isn't reactive good enough any more?

Two reasons. Gray failures: a path that is technically up but can't meet the quality-of-experience requirements still looks healthy to reactive routing, so traffic keeps going down it and users get jittery video. And complexity: IoT devices onboarding every day, multi-cloud, and OT networks (factory automation, train networks) merging with IT networks. Reactive systems also have, in his words, "zero ability to learn from the faults or errors that have happened in a network."

He cites studies putting predictive fault detection accuracy at up to 95%.

## How do you build a fault-prediction model?

The steps are the familiar ML pipeline, with the network-specific choices spelled out:

- **Define the problem first.** Gray faults or black faults (a total link outage)? Hardware or software? Short-term forecasting within a month, or a longer horizon?
- **Collect data.** Historical fault records with the network state at the time (public datasets exist, but mostly outdated), plus real-time monitoring from routers, switches, servers and applications: packet logs, alarms, flow telemetry, packet traces, device configuration, topology.
- **Engineer features against the KPI.** For fault detection that means alarms, packet loss spikes, jitter, packet errors, latency and degrading user experience, plus seasonality.
- **Train.** A 70/30 train/test split with spatial and temporal diversity. No single best algorithm, but long short-term memory networks, decision trees and random forests cover most use cases. Supervised learning on labelled faults, unsupervised for unusual patterns, and usually a hybrid wins.

## Why minimise false positives?

Because a predicted failure that never happens still triggers action, such as rerouting traffic that was fine. Every forecaster makes errors, so you choose which ones. "In short, accept imperfections," Akshat Kapoor said at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024: aim for minimum or zero false positives, even if that means not catching every fault.

That works because predictive and reactive aren't rivals. Reactive mechanisms still catch what the model misses or gets wrong; if traffic is rerouted in anticipation of a fault, the networking gear can detect the bad prediction and revert to the original route.

## What's the payoff?

He quotes studies showing predictive maintenance reduces downtime by about 50% and cuts maintenance costs by around 30 to 40% in some cases, with root-cause hints that let teams fix the underlying issue rather than the symptom. The hard parts are messy, inconsistent data, knowing which features actually correlate with faults, picking a technique per problem, and getting models to learn across networks that are not built uniformly. Further out he sees autonomic self-healing networks reacting to faults in seconds.

## Who should watch

Network engineers and SREs who own infrastructure and want a structured way to think about ML for fault prediction. There is no demo or code, and the numbers come from cited studies rather than his own deployments, but the problem-definition checklist and the false-positive argument are worth the time.

Title: Node.js stack traces can carry local variables, via the inspector
Description: Abhijeet Prasad (sentry.io) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on attaching local variables to Node.js production stack traces with the inspector API
Body:
A production stack trace tells you which line threw. It doesn't tell you what `userId` was at the time, and that is usually the question. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Abhijeet Prasad, a software engineer who maintains Sentry's open source JavaScript SDKs, showed how the team made local variables appear next to Node.js stack frames by turning the built-in `inspector` module, the same machinery debuggers use, into a production tool.

It is a short talk about how Sentry built the feature, so the product is front and centre, but the technique and the list of things that went wrong apply to anyone curious about the Node.js inspector.

## Why couldn't Node.js do this before?

Sentry already attached local variables to stack frames for Python, PHP and Ruby, where the language exposes the data. JavaScript doesn't: no standard library API hands you the variables in scope when an error is thrown, and the feature request stayed open for a long time because the answer was always that the runtime couldn't do it. Then the team realised the `node:inspector` module, built on the V8 inspector protocol, could. A debugger attached to a process can see every frame's scope, so a debugger you attach to yourself can too.

## How does it work?

The SDK opens an inspector session and starts a worker thread whose job is to watch it. The worker tells the debugger to pause on exceptions, caught or uncaught. When an error is thrown in the main thread:

1. The debugger pauses the main process.
2. The worker checks the pause reason is a real exception, then walks every frame of the stack, not just the top one.
3. For each frame it collects the local variables through `Runtime.getProperties`, flattening objects and arrays into something serialisable.
4. It calls a function in the paused process that writes the frames and their variables to a global, releases the inspector objects to avoid leaking memory, and resumes.

When the SDK turns the error into an event, it looks up that global and attaches the variables to the matching frames. "although it can be weird, you're actually pausing the process, it's actually not that expensive to do this," Abhijeet Prasad said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024.

For users, all of this sits behind one option in the SDK's init call, `includeLocalVariables: true`. His demo is an Express app that throws with a few variables in scope, which then show up in the event beside each frame.

## What went wrong along the way?

The challenges list is the most useful part for anyone thinking of doing this themselves:

- **Worker overhead and memory pressure.** A worker and an inspector session per process have a CPU and memory cost that needed keeping in check.
- **Handled versus unhandled exceptions.** Pausing behaves differently for an error you catch than for one that bubbles up to the global handlers.
- **ESM versus CommonJS.** At the time of the talk, a Node.js bug kept the feature from working fully under ESM (tracked in [nodejs/node#38439](https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/38439)).
- **Minified code.** Variables renamed by a TypeScript-plus-minifier build, say for a Lambda deploy, can't be mapped back yet; that waits on the source map spec adding support for minified variable names.
- **One inspector at a time.** With local variables on, you can't attach your own debugger to the same process.
- **Node.js only.** It relies on the V8 inspector and Node's standard library, so browsers, Bun and Deno are out for now.

The implementation, edge cases included, is in the open source [sentry-javascript](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript) repository.

## Who should watch?

Node.js developers who debug production errors from stack traces alone, and anyone who wants to see the inspector module used for something other than breakpoints. It is brief and concrete.
