Title: A stockout is an incident, and forecasting is its early warning
Description: Sijo Valayakkad Manikandan (Nike) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on demand forecasting that moves retail incident response from reactive to proactive
Body:
In retail, the outage is an empty shelf, and by the time someone notices, the fix is an expensive emergency truck. Sijo Valayakkad Manikandan, a data scientist at Nike who works on forecasting at the scale of millions of time series, argued at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 that demand forecasting is incident prevention: if you can see the stockout coming weeks out, the supply chain team stops firefighting.

The talk is broad, covering the retail value chain, why forecasting is hard, three families of models and two anonymised case studies, and his practical tips for building forecasters are the part most engineers will keep.

## Why does retail need to guess so far ahead?

Goods flow from manufacturer to distribution centre to store to consumer, often across continents and several modes of transport, while customers now expect same-day or even ten-minute delivery. A jacket that needs to be in a city next winter needs to be ordered long before anyone knows how many people want it. Customers are fickle too: a celebrity in the right jacket and demand spikes. Omnichannel retail breaks the old proxy of foot traffic, because a visit to the store may end in an online order, or none.

## One forecast does not fit every team

His clearest framing is the forecast horizon, because each horizon serves different people:

| Horizon | Decisions it feeds |
|---|---|
| 1 to 3 weeks | Store and distribution centre replenishment, inventory allocation, end-of-season clearance |
| 3 to 12 weeks | Workforce optimisation, capacity management |
| 3 to 24 months | Assortment planning, space optimisation, long-lead-time purchasing, S&OP |
| Beyond 24 months | Strategic planning, product design, contractual obligations |

Short-horizon users want high accuracy at the SKU and store level; strategic planners want gallons of milk for a whole region. On top of that come hierarchy (store forecasts must add up to state, region and country forecasts), data fragmentation across POS, e-commerce and payment types, demand volatility, and the trade-off between accuracy and the compute to get it. COVID-19 made all of it worse at once: buying moved online, factories in Wuhan shut, and retailers had to rebuild forecasting to be flexible and resilient.

## Statistics, machine learning or deep learning?

He walks through the three classes with honest trade-offs. Statistical models such as ARIMA and exponential smoothing (including Holt-Winters for seasonality) are simple, interpretable and good for stable demand, but struggle when patterns shift fast. Machine learning (decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting) handles non-linear relationships and external inputs such as weather, promotions and social media buzz, at the cost of more data, compute and explainability. Deep learning (RNNs, LSTMs) captures long-range dependencies for volatile, large-scale forecasting, but needs lots of data and is the hardest to explain to the planners who must trust it.

## How should you start?

This is the section to bookmark. Start with exploratory data analysis to check you are solving the right problem and to find quality issues. Check for gaps and stationarity in the series. Pick metrics that fit the goal, MAPE or WMAPE for example, and always set a naive baseline. "If your advanced models can't beat this, there is something wrong, right?" Sijo Valayakkad Manikandan said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. Start simple, and skip deep learning when data is thin: with 50 data points, he notes, a naive model may well win. And be able to explain why you chose your model; if you cannot, something is off.

## Did it work anywhere?

He offers two case studies and says up front that he does not have all the details. A global retailer with over 1,000 stores, stuck in reactive last-minute replenishment, moved to an ML demand forecast using weather and regional events and saw 30% fewer stockouts and 25% fewer emergency replenishments. A quick-service restaurant chain with 2,000+ locations, where missing lettuce means missing menu items, used AI-driven forecasting to get 20% fewer ingredient shortages and 15% less food waste. In both, incident management went from reacting to warnings ahead of time.

Looking ahead, he expects more IoT data for real-time inventory, social media and event data for demand sensing, privacy rules shaping what can be collected, and LLMs turning forum and social text into features for demand models.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and engineers new to retail forecasting, and SREs who want to see how incident thinking applies to supply chains. Forecasting veterans will know the material; the implementation tips are still a good checklist for juniors.

Title: A routing and switching refresher for whoever gets the network page
Description: Ravi Theja Kambhampati (Texas A&M University) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on the L2/L3 basics, VLANs, STP, OSPF and BGP, behind resilient networks
Body:
When an incident turns out to be the network, the person holding the pager often knows Kubernetes far better than spanning tree. Ravi Theja Kambhampati, Engineering Manager at Texas A&M University, aimed his Conf42 Incident Management 2024 talk squarely at that gap: a compact tour of Layer 2 switching, Layer 3 routing, the protocols that hold both together and the design features (QoS, IPsec, route redistribution) that keep a network up and scaling.

Set your expectations: this is a 101. There are no outage stories, packet captures or troubleshooting walkthroughs. It is a clean refresher of vocabulary and concepts, which is exactly what you want before you try to read a network engineer's incident notes.

## Why should incident responders care about L2 versus L3?

Because they fail differently. Switching works at Layer 2 of the OSI model and moves frames inside a LAN by MAC address; routing works at Layer 3 and moves packets between networks by IP address. "Understanding these concepts is really crucial for incident management where quick troubleshooting and scalability are often required," Ravi Theja Kambhampati said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. Knowing which layer a symptom lives on is half the diagnosis.

## What keeps a LAN from drowning in its own traffic?

He covers four switching building blocks:

- **MAC learning and forwarding.** Switches keep a MAC address table so frames go only to the port that needs them, instead of everywhere.
- **VLANs.** One physical network split into logical ones, by department or function. Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain, so broadcasts stay local, which cuts the risk of a broadcast storm and helps security.
- **Trunking.** A single link carries many VLANs, tagged according to IEEE 802.1Q, so you do not need a cable per VLAN.
- **Spanning Tree Protocol.** Redundant links are good for resilience and terrible if frames loop forever. STP blocks the loops so the redundancy does not take the network down.

## Which routing protocol does what?

The routing half is a short comparison of four names you will meet in any network postmortem:

- **OSPF** (Open Shortest Path First): a link-state protocol for large enterprise and service provider networks, with fast convergence and good scalability.
- **EIGRP**: Cisco's protocol, known for quick convergence and efficient use of bandwidth.
- **BGP**: routes between autonomous systems. "BGP is a backbone of the internet," as he put it. It is highly scalable, supports policy-based routing, and needs careful configuration.
- **MPLS**: not a routing protocol but a label-based forwarding technique that service providers use for traffic engineering and VPN services.

Choosing among them is about strengths and weaknesses, not fashion, and he leaves it at that level.

## What turns a working network into a resilient one?

Three design concepts. Route redistribution lets OSPF, EIGRP and BGP share routes so mixed environments stay connected, with the warning that it needs planning to avoid routing loops. Quality of Service prioritises voice, video and critical applications over traffic that can wait, which matters most when links are congested in the middle of an incident. IPsec encrypts at the network layer and builds the tunnels behind most VPNs.

He maps all of this to enterprise networks in finance, retail and manufacturing, 5G in telecoms, hybrid cloud and SD-WAN, and IoT and edge, then ends on what is coming: software-defined networking, network function virtualisation and intent-based networking automating much of what is configured by hand today.

## Who should watch

SREs, platform engineers and incident commanders who need the network vocabulary and a mental model of where L2 ends and L3 begins. Network engineers already fluent in OSPF areas and BGP communities will not find anything new.

Title: Adaptive user interfaces work best with an off switch
Description: Abhinav Chunchu (Lowes) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on adaptive user interfaces that learn from behaviour and context, and where they go wrong
Body:
Google Maps changes its interface depending on whether you are walking, driving or on a bus, and nobody had to file a settings ticket for it. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Abhinav Chunchu, Senior Software Engineer at Lowes, surveyed adaptive user interfaces (AUIs): the techniques behind them, the results he attributes to them across industries, and the tension between adapting to users and leaving them in control.

This is a concept tour rather than an implementation talk; there is no framework, library or JavaScript code on screen. It works as a vocabulary and a checklist for product and front-end teams thinking about personalisation.

## What counts as an adaptive interface?

Chunchu defines AUIs as systems that change their behaviour and appearance in real time to fit an individual user, based on their interactions, learned patterns and environment. Static interfaces are one-size-fits-all; adaptive ones aim for three things: personalised experiences, lower cognitive load and better accessibility for users of varying abilities. The idea dates from the 1990s; machine learning and data analytics made it practical.

## Five techniques, five famous examples

He maps each technique to a product most people have used:

- **Personalisation** from user profiles: Amazon recommending products from browsing and purchase history.
- **Context awareness**: Google Maps adjusting to travel mode, location, device and even time of day.
- **Machine learning**: Spotify's personalised playlists built from listening habits.
- **User feedback loops**, both implicit (time spent on a feature) and explicit (ratings): Duolingo adjusting exercises to a learner's level.
- **Modular design** that lets interfaces rearrange around usage: Tableau dashboards tailored to each analyst.

## What do the numbers say?

He attaches an engagement and efficiency gain to each technique: personalisation +25% engagement and +20% efficiency, context awareness +30% and +35%, machine learning +40% and +30%, feedback loops +35% and +25%, modular design +20% and +40%. By industry: adaptive EHR systems that tailor screens for doctors and nurses cut task completion time by 35%; adaptive learning platforms such as Smart Sparrow brought a 15% improvement in test scores and 22% more course completions; Amazon and Alibaba saw 35% higher click-through and 28% better conversion from adaptive recommendations; and learning thermostats such as Nest save 15 to 30% of energy.

None of these come with a named study, and percentages for a technique in general are hard to pin down, so read them as illustrations of direction rather than benchmarks for your roadmap.

## Where do adaptive interfaces go wrong?

The challenges section is the most practical part. Data privacy comes first: adaptation runs on behavioural data, so it needs encryption, clear data usage policies and compliance with rules such as GDPR. Development complexity is next, because good adaptation needs solid algorithms and a lot of testing, which stretches timelines. The third is the one designers tend to skip: users like adaptive features but also want control. As Abhinav Chunchu said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024: "Providing the customization options or the ability to disable adaptive behaviors can enhance the user satisfaction."

Anyone who has had a menu reorder itself under their cursor will agree. Adaptation that can't be overridden turns into a guessing game.

## Where is it heading?

More capable AI predicting needs more accurately, expansion into AR, VR and IoT, and an ethics layer covering consent, data security and the balance between automation and user control. On accessibility, his examples are concrete: interfaces that raise font sizes or switch on high-contrast mode for users with visual impairments.

## Who should watch

Product engineers and designers starting on personalisation who want a structured overview and a list of pitfalls. If you need implementation patterns for a React or vanilla JavaScript app, use this to frame the problem, then look for a hands-on talk.

Title: If your monitoring dies at 2am, does anyone get paged?
Description: Mathias Palmersheim (VictoriaMetrics) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on monitoring your monitoring, from heartbeats to a second isolated system
Body:
The quietest night on call might be the one where the alerting stack is down. Mathias Palmersheim, a solutions engineer at VictoriaMetrics, used his Conf42 Incident Management 2024 talk on that philosophical question and its practical answer: a second monitoring system that watches only the first, isolated from it in every way you can manage, plus cheap stopgaps if you cannot get one approved.

It is a short, opinionated talk from a self-described observability nerd (his office ran a betting pool on whether he would talk about observability for an entire first date). He works for a monitoring vendor, and the top option in his list is a paid service his company sells, but most of the talk is vendor-neutral.

## How did he get here?

His first IT job was IT manager at a factory with no monitoring. The alerting system was users walking into his office to say an application was down and the outage was costing the company tens of thousands of dollars an hour. Monitoring fixed that, but alerts arrived by email next to notes about which car park to use, so every message carried the same jolt of stress.

The fix was a dedicated noisy notification channel allowed to override Do Not Disturb, with a named person responsible for each incident instead of a shout into the room. His bar for what earns that channel: life, liberty or property. Physical harm, compliance trouble that brings in the government, or losses above a cost threshold. Anything else can wait for morning.

## Why is two monitoring systems the sweet spot?

Then came the question in the title. A monitoring of monitoring system (MoM, in his slides) watches only the primary, and the primary treats the MoM as just another application. Of course the MoM can fail too, and adding a third and fourth buys more nines along with more cost and more knowledge to maintain. "So usually the sweet spot is two," Mathias Palmersheim said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024.

The catch is isolation. Two copies of the same tool, same version, same region and same infrastructure-as-code inventory will fail together. His checklist:

- Different notification services, because notification services are apps and apps fail.
- Different infrastructure providers, or at least different regions and separate deployments.
- Different humans. Not because your team is careless, but because different groups of people rarely make the same mistake at the same time.
- Change management that forbids upgrading or reconfiguring both systems at once, since upgrades and config changes are a frequent cause of outages.

The minimum the MoM must do is health checks: cheap to store, easy to set up. The cost is context. With only up/down checks, the outage itself is your first signal, and mean time to resolution grows because you diagnose and fix at once. His recommendation is to treat the MoM like any other important application, with dashboards, runbooks and preventive alerts.

## What if you cannot get a second system approved?

He ranks the options from quick and dirty upwards.

**Heartbeats.** One system pings another and an alert fires when the pings stop. Examples are ANag with Nagios, and self-hosted Grafana OnCall reporting to a Grafana Cloud account. Simple, but there is little context, a phone losing LTE produces false positives, and it does not always assign a person to the incident.

**Vendor status pages.** If your monitoring is a cloud service, subscribe to the vendor's status page, and hope they do not host it themselves. Easy to set up, but the notifications are usually quiet ones like email, and it does nothing for self-hosted stacks.

**Health check services.** Self-hosted Uptime Kuma or a cloud service. These do hook into noisy notifications, but you either expose your monitoring to the outside (a conversation with security) or run an agent to beacon out. Configure them to look for a string in the response, because a 200 with a valid certificate can still say unhealthy in the body.

**Two independent systems**, done properly, then **buying a cloud service** to watch your self-hosted stack (or an on-prem system to watch the cloud one), which gets you different humans and different upstream vendors almost for free. He points out that a cloud bill for monitoring one application is small, especially when observability people who know relabeling rules and streaming aggregation run it. Top of the list is a **dedicated MoM service** with humans who reach out alongside the alert. VictoriaMetrics offers one in some enterprise plans, and he is upfront that it is the most expensive option.

Whatever you build, test it: break the MoM on purpose, check that the primary pages you, and have someone watch the primary's dashboards during the test to find hidden dependencies between the two.

## Who should watch

Anyone running a self-hosted Prometheus-style stack who has never asked what pages them when it dies, and platform teams writing the case for a second system to their manager. It is short, and the isolation checklist alone is worth the time.

Title: Healthcare IT by the numbers - AI, FHIR, cloud and blockchain
Description: VijayaAshwin Jagadeesan at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on the trends reshaping healthcare IT, from AI diagnostics and FHIR APIs to blockchain records
Body:
Poor data quality costs healthcare systems $342 billion a year, and the average healthcare breach runs $7.13 million. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, VijayaAshwin Jagadeesan, a Technical Architect, surveyed the four trends he expects to reshape healthcare IT (AI and machine learning, advanced analytics, interoperability with cloud migration, and blockchain for data security) and what institutions must invest in to keep up.

Scope check: this is an industry briefing, dense with market figures, and despite the event and the title it doesn't get into JavaScript or code. Treat it as context for building software in healthcare, not a how-to.

## Why is healthcare going digital so fast?

The market numbers set the scene. The global digital health market was worth $96.5 billion in 2020, with a projected compound annual growth rate of 15.1% to 2028, driven by telehealth, electronic health records and better diagnostics. COVID-19 pushed it hard: telehealth use grew 154% in 2020. As VijayaAshwin Jagadeesan said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024: "The shift is not temporary." Patients and providers both found digital care convenient enough to keep.

## What does AI add to diagnosis and treatment?

He frames AI and ML in three roles: spotting patterns in imaging and patient data that humans miss, recommending treatment tailored to a patient's history and genetics, and predicting complications before they happen. The figures he cites: AI breast cancer screening that cut false positives by 5.7% and false negatives by 9.4%, AI-guided depression treatment with 6% higher remission rates, and models that predict acute kidney injury 48 hours before onset at 92% accuracy.

Analytics work at the population and hospital level. Predictive models flag patients at high risk of type 2 diabetes with 84.4% accuracy. Workflow analytics cut emergency department boarding by 20% and raised early discharges by 21%. In research, big data helped identify a novel antibiotic from 1.5 billion compounds. The individual studies behind these numbers are not named in the talk.

## Is interoperability the real bottleneck?

For developers this is the most relevant section. Hospitals run legacy systems that have to talk to new ones, and integrating them is a top priority for 19% of hospital executives. His answer is standards-based APIs: FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) solutions cut data integration time by 75%. Cloud migration brings scalable storage and easier access to patient data, with the healthcare cloud computing market projected at $64.7 billion by 2025.

## What does blockchain bring to patient data?

He spends the most time here. The pitch: a decentralised ledger has no single point of failure, written data is immutable without network consensus, SHA-256 hashing makes tampering evident, and smart contracts can enforce access rules so only authorised people see protected health information. Every transaction leaves an audit trail useful for HIPAA and GDPR compliance, and a compromised node doesn't expose the whole database.

His real-world example is Estonia, which uses a blockchain-based system to secure citizens' health records, keeps them tamper-proof and lets patients control who sees them. The supporting figures (breaches reduced by up to 80%, potential industry savings of $100 to 150 billion by 2025, a pilot that halved administrative costs) come without sources, so weigh them accordingly.

## What should healthcare organisations do now?

Five recommendations: invest in digital infrastructure that scales and integrates, set real data governance (that $342 billion quality bill), upskill staff in data literacy and analytics, partner with technology firms, and prioritise cybersecurity given the $7.13 million average breach. The benefits he lists in return are better outcomes from earlier diagnosis, precision medicine, smoother data sharing through FHIR, remote patient monitoring that reduces readmissions, easier regulatory reporting and stronger clinical decision support.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects joining a healthcare IT team who want a fast briefing on where the money and the attention are going. If you want to see FHIR or blockchain implemented, this talk sets the context and you'll need a second, hands-on one.

Title: When the customer authorises the fraud, the model has to notice
Description: Ndubuisi Obirije (Afriex) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on AI that flags social-engineering-driven payments in remittance fintech
Body:
The hardest payment fraud to stop is the one the real account holder approves. Ndubuisi Obirije, co-founder and CTO of the remittance app Afriex, used his Conf42 Incident Management 2024 talk to explain how social engineering turns customers into the delivery mechanism for fraud, and what happened when his team put AI on the problem: about 80% accuracy flagging social-engineering-driven transactions and more than $1 million in fraud stopped within a short deployment.

It is a short, broad talk. The first half sets out the threat and the industry numbers; the Afriex results come in one tight section, without much on the model itself.

## How does a social engineering payment fraud unfold?

He describes a four-stage cycle. Information gathering: phishing emails, data bought online about potential victims. Establishing a relationship: contact and trust-building, so nothing feels suspicious later. Exploitation: by now the victim is in the net without knowing it. Execution: the victim authorises the payment, to the fraudster's account or through a marketplace purchase.

For a remittance company, that last step is the problem. Credentials are correct, the device may be the customer's own, and the customer clicked approve. Rules built for stolen cards do not see it.

## Why the industry is betting on AI

The stats slide is a quick tour, with sources: the global fintech market at $340.1 billion with the AI segment at $44.08 billion (Fortune Business Insights, Statista); 72% of companies using AI in at least one business function (McKinsey); AI identity verification projected to save banks $900 million and 29 million hours of digital onboarding (Accenture); chatbots cutting the cost of user inquiries by up to 80% (Juniper Research). The scale of the problem is larger: $800 billion to $2 trillion is laundered globally each year.

## Which fraud types can AI help with?

Phishing and identity theft are the two he treats as the usual first steps. For phishing, machine learning looks at communication patterns, such as suspicious subject lines and content, and warns the user or the employer. For identity theft, AI-powered identity verification is the line of defence, and he thinks there is still a lot of room to improve it.

Beyond those come money muling (people, often unwitting, moving illicit funds through their own accounts), document forgery, account takeover and deepfake fraud with synthesised faces and voices. His point on deepfakes is that the same generative tools making fraud easier are also what will catch it.

## What did Afriex actually measure?

This is the section worth the click. Within less than three months of deploying AI detection for fraudulent activity, especially social engineering, Afriex saw roughly 80% accuracy in flagging such transactions and identified and prevented over $1 million in fraudulent transactions. "We've seen over 80 percent accuracy in flagging social engineering attempts, in our platform," Ndubuisi Obirije said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024.

The less flashy win is operational: fewer false positives and shorter investigations, because the compliance team now starts from transactions the system has already flagged, rather than from a raw queue. He frames the approach plainly: the team had already seen the patterns, and AI automates spotting them.

## Who gets targeted?

Everyone, he insists. Older adults (70+) are trusting and less familiar with technology; in the US they account for the highest losses from reported cybercrime. Younger adults have a bigger digital footprint. He cites a September 2023 survey of American adults in which three in ten had experienced financial fraud or cybercrime, with 35 to 54 year olds the most targeted at 36% and 18 to 34 year olds at 22%.

His takeaways: no one is immune, vulnerabilities differ by age group, awareness and education matter, and protection should be age-specific. Detection works best paired with customers who know what a scam looks like.

## Who should watch

Fintech engineers and fraud and compliance teams who want a framing for social engineering as an incident type, and a real-world data point from a remittance platform. If you want feature engineering or model details, the talk does not go there.

Title: Moving from Webpack to Rspack starts with renaming one file
Description: Konstantinos Leimonis (Bit.dev) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on Rspack, the Rust bundler that speaks Webpack config, and how to migrate to it
Body:
If your Webpack build is slow enough to have its own coffee break, Rspack is the low-drama way out: a Rust-based bundler that keeps Webpack's configuration and most of its loaders and plugins. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Konstantinos Leimonis, Software Engineering Tech Lead at Bit.dev, walked through why Rspack exists, how to migrate, and the one CSS modules trap that will greet you on day one.

## How did we get from concatenation to Rspack?

Leimonis starts with a short history. The first bundlers did little more than concatenate scripts. Browserify (2013) let Node.js developers reuse code in the browser by crawling the CommonJS dependency tree into one file and polyfilling Node built-ins such as process, buffer and crypto. Webpack went further and built a dependency graph of every asset: CSS, images, SVGs, even HTML, all requirable from JavaScript. That gave us components as reusable bundles of assets, natural hot module replacement (HMR) and a huge loader and plugin ecosystem. Webpack reached 120 million downloads a month, and searching npm for webpack returns about 6,000 packages.

Success brought the bill: large bundles, slow HMR, long production builds, and a cottage industry of blog posts on making Webpack faster. Rspack came out of ByteDance, the company behind TikTok and CapCut, which runs many large monolithic applications with complex bundling needs. Production builds there had grown to as long as half an hour, and dev server cold starts could take several minutes.

## Why is it so much faster?

Rust, and parallelism. JavaScript has weak support for multithreading; Rspack's native code uses every core of a modern CPU. It ships as precompiled native code through NAPI-RS, a framework for building Node.js add-ons in Rust, with a JavaScript library on top that your build talks to like an SDK.

The headline features: fast startup, fast HMR, Webpack compatibility, framework agnosticism (React, Vue, Svelte), built-in CSS and asset handling, JSON and web workers, code splitting and tree shaking on by default, and Module Federation v2. In benchmarks it beats Webpack with Babel by a wide margin and holds up against Vite. Re.Pack, which bundles React Native with Webpack, reported five times faster builds and HMR after switching.

## What does a migration look like?

The happy path is three steps: add `@rspack/core` and `@rspack/cli` as dev dependencies and remove `webpack`, `webpack-cli` and `webpack-dev-server`; swap `webpack serve` and `webpack build` for `rspack serve` and `rspack build` in your npm scripts; rename `webpack.config.js` to `rspack.config.js`. He then pretends the talk is over. As Konstantinos Leimonis said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024: "That's actually a joke, a really bad joke, sorry for that."

The joke is only half a joke; for simple setups that is enough. To get the full speed you go further:

- **Loaders**: existing Webpack loaders work, but replace `babel-loader` with the Rust-based `builtin:swc-loader`, which handles TypeScript and JSX and avoids constant JavaScript-to-Rust round trips.
- **Asset loaders**: `file-loader` becomes `asset/resource`, `url-loader` becomes `asset/inline` (Base64 data URIs only for now), `raw-loader` becomes `asset/source`.
- **Plugins**: most Webpack built-ins exist under the same name and options, so `webpack.DefinePlugin` becomes `rspack.DefinePlugin`. `html-webpack-plugin` still works, but `rspack.HtmlRspackPlugin` is the Rust implementation and builds much faster.

## The CSS modules trap

The caveat he spends real time on: in a React project that imports `styles` from an SCSS module as a default export, Rspack compiles with only a warning and the app renders with no styles at all. You can change every import to `import * as styles`, but he'd rather not rewrite source code to switch tools. The alternative is config: enable the experimental `experiments.css`, set the CSS generator to `esModule: false` and the parser to `namedExports: false`, keep `sass-loader` with the rule type set to `css/auto` so Rspack decides between plain CSS and CSS modules, and drop `css-loader`. He has asked the Rspack team to make that the default.

## What has Bit seen in practice?

At Bit, Leimonis says customers who migrated saw builds at least three times faster, five times in some cases. Bit's Config Mutator wraps Rspack configuration in a descriptive API (set the mode, add TypeScript, React, CSS modules or SCSS) without knowing the generator and parser internals, and can adjust a config you already have.

He closes with the family built on Rspack: Rsbuild for an out-of-the-box dev setup, Rspress for static sites, Rsdoctor for analysing builds and Rslib for library authors.

## Who should watch

Anyone maintaining a large Webpack setup who wants faster builds without a rewrite. If you are already happy on Vite, this is a useful look at the other path.

Title: Feature-Sliced Design puts every front-end file in one of six layers
Description: Aleksandr Guzenko (IT_ONE) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on Feature-Sliced Design as an off-the-shelf architecture that keeps front ends maintainable
Body:
Every front end reaches the day when adding a button means touching nine files and nobody remembers why. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Aleksandr Guzenko, Tech Lead at IT_ONE, argued that most teams should stop inventing architecture per project and adopt a ready-made methodology, and made the case for his favourite: Feature-Sliced Design (FSD), which sorts an application into six layers from shared UI kit up to the app shell.

It's a compact introduction, aimed at developers who have never used a named front-end architecture. Guzenko says plainly that FSD is not the only answer, just the one he likes best.

## What makes a front end good or bad?

He names three qualities. Business efficiency, how well the app helps the business earn money, is mostly about business decisions and outside the developer's hands. That leaves two for engineers. Scalability is how fast you can add a feature or module. Maintainability is how easy the app is to change over years; when it's high, development costs grow slowly, and when it's low, you eventually reach the point where rewriting is cheaper than changing anything.

## Why can't we just write good apps?

Because the balance between scalability, maintainability and delivery speed is set under bad conditions. The future is unclear at the start. As Aleksandr Guzenko said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024: "the most important decisions we had to, we have to make at the beginning when we have the least information." Requirements change mid-build, usually when a manager arrives with a new concept and half the code goes. Time is limited. And every application is different, so the best solution for one doesn't carry over to the next.

## Three ways out

Guzenko lists three universal options. Become an architecture master: the longest and hardest path, many patterns and many mistakes, and even then your team may not share the knowledge. Use a few well-known practices everywhere: easier and better than nothing, though with the risk that every problem starts to look like a nail. Or use an out-of-the-box solution, which he calls the most efficient, because the rules and the docs already exist.

## What is Feature-Sliced Design?

FSD is a set of rules and conventions for organising code, built on four foundations: SOLID principles, public APIs for modules, low coupling with high cohesion, and FSD's own rules. The core rule is the layering. An application is split into up to six layers:

- **Shared**: the most abstract layer, with no business knowledge, such as buttons, selects, inputs and layouts.
- **Entities**: business objects such as user, post and comment, with their UI and data fetching.
- **Features**: user actions, such as liking or reposting a comment, deleting a post or updating a profile.
- **Widgets**: compositions of entities and features, such as a post card with its repost, comment and download actions.
- **Pages**: high-level composition of a whole page.
- **App**: global styles, types, providers such as routing and theming, and the exported application object.

Layers below App can hold slices (user, post, comment in Entities), and slices split into segments such as UI, model and API. One version note he flags: diagrams from the first version of FSD show a Processes layer, which is deprecated in version 2. The FSD team also publishes a decomposition cheat sheet for working out which layer a piece of a feature belongs to.

## Why FSD rather than something home-grown?

His five reasons: it combines time-tested patterns with rules aimed at modern front ends, having been released in 2020; it has a community and a documentation site, so onboarding a newcomer means sending a link; it bundles the experience of many experienced developers, with a core team contributing almost every week; it fits projects from a to-do list to dashboards with very large codebases; and once learned, it applies everywhere, so you stop reinventing.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers and leads on a growing React or similar codebase who want a vocabulary for structure and a starting point. Architects who already run a layered or modular front end will find it familiar; the useful part is the layer-by-layer breakdown. The talk stays at the level of concepts, so follow up with the FSD website at feature-sliced.design for import rules and examples.

Title: Stop sending pineapple coupons in winter, says the ML
Description: Anandakumar Kumaravelu (SADA, An Insight company) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on machine learning that personalises retail coupons per customer
Body:
Every weekly flyer is a broadcast to an audience that mostly does not care. Anandakumar Kumaravelu, a senior cloud engineer at SADA, An Insight company, used his Conf42 Incident Management 2024 talk to make the case for replacing it with coupons built per customer from purchase history, browsing behaviour and context, and to walk through the four model families that do the work.

Honest scope first: despite the event, this is a retail marketing talk, not an incident management one. It is also high level, light on architecture and heavy on examples, several of them from his own shopping trips.

## What is wrong with the flyer?

His examples are relatable. A buy-two-get-one deal on pineapples in winter exists because the store is overstocked, not because you want pineapple. A shampoo-and-conditioner bundle is useless if you buy one brand of each, or buy herbal shampoo online. Generic offers serve the store's inventory, so shoppers learn to ignore them.

The alternative uses data the store already has. Loyalty numbers, phone numbers and app sign-ups tie every receipt to a person. Six months or a year of receipts says which wine you buy every month, so the offer can be a discount on that wine, or on the chips that usually go home with it. "So rather than a very generalized discounts and offers, we want that customer to take leverage on what he has purchased on his history," Anandakumar Kumaravelu said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. He says he has built this for a retailer himself and calls the project a success, without naming the client.

## Which data goes in?

Five kinds: purchase history and frequency (he would collect at least three years), browsing behaviour on the site and app, demographics such as age, gender and location, contextual data like time of day, device and nearest store, and social media activity. Age matters for more than targeting: an under-18 or under-21 shopper should never be offered alcohol, whatever they search for.

## Four model families do the work

- **Collaborative filtering** suggests items liked by similar customers, for example people in the same age band.
- **Content-based filtering** recommends products similar to what this customer already bought.
- **Deep learning** finds non-obvious patterns. His example is seasonal: customers who buy groceries also buy cold medicine in winter, which he connects to supermarkets opening in-store pharmacies, and tired shoppers to the sandwich counter inside the store.
- **Natural language processing** reads reviews and feedback for sentiment and preferences.

## What does it buy you?

He cites a 37% increase in coupon redemption, a 22% boost in customer retention, and conversion rates up to 150% higher in some cases, plus cheaper marketing because offers go only where they are relevant. No source or methodology comes with those figures, so read them as directional. The industry examples are the familiar ones: Amazon's recommendation engine, which he says drives 35% of its sales, Netflix's personalised recommendations, credited with saving it $1 billion a year in churn, and Sephora's Virtual Artist app, where users try 50 looks per session on average.

The best anecdote is his own. After a $50 shop, the receipt offered a free slice of pizza at the food counter just as he was planning to go and buy lunch. That is the real-time offer he expects to become normal: tied to what you just did, not mailed for next week.

## Where does it go wrong?

He spends real time on the risks. Personalisation needs sensitive data, and a diabetic customer who tells the app should get no cake coupons, and should never have that fact leak. GDPR and CCPA compliance is the floor. Models carry bias: a vegan professor friend of his gets meat offers and is offended every time. Over-personalised offers feel invasive, so customers need transparency and control over their data. And the infrastructure, data cleaning and skilled people cost real money before the first coupon prints.

## Who should watch

Engineers and data people starting on a recommendation or loyalty project who want a plain-language overview of the moving parts. If you came to Conf42 Incident Management for outages, skip this one.

Title: In utilities, AI predicts the transformer failure and humans decide
Description: Rajesh Kolli (ykunt inc) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on pairing AI with human expertise for predictive maintenance, smart meter data and customer service
Body:
Nobody wants a neighbourhood outage because a transformer quietly wore out. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Rajesh Kolli of ykunt inc made the case that utilities get the most from AI when it does the forecasting and data crunching (failing equipment, odd consumption, 2am billing questions) while people keep the judgment calls.

It's an overview talk about the utility sector rather than a coding session; JavaScript appears mainly as the layer behind dashboards and customer apps. The recording also cuts off a little before the end.

## Why are utilities moving now?

Kolli's observation is that utilities usually adopt technology late, long after other industries, and that this has changed because customers changed. People expect to see their bill, their consumption and their rates on a phone in real time, and they are signing up for rebate, time-of-use and net metering programmes as they move to clean energy. Add the pressure for reliability and sustainability, and the sector needs both faster data processing and better customer service.

His mention of JavaScript is concrete in one place: business intelligence dashboards, with WebFOCUS as the example of a tool where JavaScript carries the user experience.

## Where does AI pay off first?

**Predictive maintenance.** Machine learning models predict transformer failures and optimise maintenance schedules, so the outage never happens. The same approach catches meters that stopped sending reads, which otherwise leaves customers staring at stale usage data.

**Customer service.** Chatbots provide 24/7 support for routine questions such as how to find a bill or usage history, suggest energy-saving tips and point customers at programmes like net metering or time-of-use. Humans take the complex cases. Kolli is enthusiastic here, suggesting a chatbot could largely replace a phone team and quoting near-perfect accuracy without a source; treat that as opinion.

**Data management.** Smart meters and sensors produce large volumes of data in real time. Cloud and AI let a utility scale storage and compute on demand instead of growing its on-premises infrastructure, then use the data to optimise distribution, decide when to shift loads, integrate renewables and spot anomalies. Water is his favourite example: unusual consumption from a commercial customer, or a diversion, can be caught before the bill turns into a dispute ticket. He also mentions monitoring for grid security when buying power from markets such as the Southwest Power Pool.

## What is the human for?

This is the thread that holds the talk together. AI processes and suggests; people validate. As Rajesh Kolli said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024: "Human professionals validate AI recommendations, ensuring that critical judgments and ethical concerns are addressed." Human experts also supply context when something unexpected happens, which in a utility is most days with weather in them.

The economics follow: analysts and service staff stop hunting anomalies by hand and make faster decisions on AI recommendations. The catch is skills. He expects continuous training in data literacy and in interpreting AI output to become part of the job.

## What did the Catapult Project show?

His case study is the Catapult Project with a public utility in Kansas: AI-driven edge computing processes smart meter and sensor data in real time so anomalies get an immediate response, and AI-enhanced customer service brings proactive, personalised interactions. The reported outcome is higher customer satisfaction; no figures are given.

## What comes next?

Three trends: edge computing for real-time grid decisions, deep learning and reinforcement learning for better load forecasting and failure prediction, and autonomous systems such as drones and self-healing grids that keep crews out of dangerous work during outages. He uses the 2021 Texas grid failure as the motivating example for forecasting demand before it overwhelms supply.

## Who should watch

Developers starting work for a utility, or building dashboards and customer apps on top of meter data, who want a tour of where AI is being applied in the sector. Engineers looking for model architectures or measured results will want a more technical talk.

Title: In a dialysis clinic, the incident is a patient's blood pressure
Description: Ram Meka at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on using predictive maintenance, real-time sensors and automated reports to cut incidents in dialysis care
Body:
Most incident management talks measure damage in error budgets. Ram Meka, a principal systems developer with over ten years of building kidney care products, spent his Conf42 Incident Management 2024 talk on a setting where an incident can be a dialysis machine failing mid-session or a patient's blood pressure sliding toward a crash. His argument: the same three AI tools SREs know, prediction, continuous monitoring and automated reporting, map directly onto dialysis care.

It is an overview, not a production case study. The talk spends its first third on the clinical background and the incident process, then sketches how AI fits each step.

## Why does dialysis need incident management at all?

Scale and strain. "The World Health Organization estimates that over 2 million people globally are on dialysis," Ram Meka said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024, and the number grows with diabetes and hypertension. Hemodialysis sessions run about three to five hours, several times a week, mostly in clinics; peritoneal dialysis can run at home.

The pressure points he lists will sound familiar to anyone who has run a busy system. Overcrowded centres stretch wait times. Patients arrive with several conditions at once, so each needs a tailored plan. Machines, infusion pumps and monitors wear out faster under heavy use, and maintenance gets deferred when the schedule is full. Deferred maintenance means more breakdowns, and rushed procedures mean more infections, vascular access problems and electrolyte imbalances.

## The incident process is one SREs already run

Meka walks through the healthcare incident cycle, and it is close to a postmortem process: detect and report (with non-punitive reporting so near misses actually get logged), assess and prioritise by severity, investigate with root cause techniques such as five whys or a fishbone diagram, implement corrective actions, monitor whether they worked, and share the lessons through meetings, training and newsletters.

## Where does AI fit?

He splits it into three applications.

**Predictive analytics** uses historical and real-time data to forecast incidents before they happen. The pipeline is the usual one, data collection, feature selection, model training, validation, deployment, and he lists models already used in hospitals for readmission risk, sepsis, chronic disease progression, medication adherence and emergency department use.

**Real-time monitoring** is where dialysis gets specific: bioimpedance and weight sensors for fluid balance, plus conductivity, pH and temperature sensors on the dialysate. Watching those continuously catches rapid fluid shifts, blood pressure changes and electrolyte imbalances while there is still time to act. His example: an AI system detects subtle changes in a patient's blood pressure trend during a session and alerts staff, who adjust the fluid removal rate before a hypotensive episode.

**Automated reporting** captures device readings and conditions at the moment of an incident, then uses natural language processing to turn staff voice notes into a filled-in standardised report. Less paperwork, fewer details forgotten by the time someone writes it up.

## What does it look like in one clinic?

To make it concrete he describes an illustrative centre, SmartCare Dialysis Center: a medium-sized facility with 30 machines serving about 120 patients, plagued by recurring equipment failures. The plan is IoT sensors on every machine reporting operating temperature, fluid flow, pressure, filter status and component vibration, combined with historical maintenance records and past failures to train a predictive maintenance model. The talk names the expected benefits, fewer failures and fewer interrupted treatments, but gives no measured results, so treat it as a design sketch.

The same thinking extends to scheduling: a patient who reliably needs longer sessions gets booked into a quieter slot, which shortens waits for everyone.

## The constraints are the hard part

Meka does not skip the unglamorous parts. HIPAA compliance, end-to-end encryption in transit and at rest, and role-based access control come first. Legacy clinical systems speak different data formats, so integration needs real APIs. Patients should be told when AI is monitoring their sessions and offered an opt-out where appropriate, and training data has to cover different ethnicities, ages and socioeconomic backgrounds or the predictions will be wrong for the patients least able to absorb the error. He also recommends mixed teams, nephrologists, nurses, technicians, data scientists and ethicists, with something like a monthly seminar where each side explains its field.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into health tech who want the domain vocabulary, and SREs curious how their incident playbook translates when the system under watch is a person. If you want model architectures or production numbers, this is not that talk.

Title: A four-phase plan for AI in life insurance claims
Description: Praveen Kumar (AllianzLife) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on using AI and ML to automate life and annuities claims and predict what policyholders want
Body:
A life insurance claim arrives as a stack of documents that someone has to read, check for accuracy, check for fraud and push through state-specific deadlines. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Praveen Kumar, Practice Lead at AllianzLife, walked through where AI and machine learning take that work over in the life and annuities (L&A) business, and how a carrier should roll them out: assess, pilot, scale, then keep retraining.

Know what you're getting: this is a business-level talk for people building systems in insurance, not a JavaScript talk despite the event. There's no code and no stack, and the abstract's 90% prediction accuracy figure doesn't come up on screen. What it does give you is a clear map of the domain and a sensible adoption plan.

## What makes life and annuities different?

Kumar starts with the basics for outsiders. L&A carriers sell long-term risk management and investment products: customers put money into policies or indexes tied to them and plan for retirement, college tuition or other goals over decades. Two areas decide whether a carrier keeps its customers: claims processing and customer experience. Both suffer from heavy manual workloads, exposure to fraud and rising demand for personalised service.

The shift he argues for is from reactive to proactive: instead of responding to a claim or a complaint, predict it.

## Which parts of a claim can a model take over?

He breaks claims processing into steps that each map to an AI or ML job:

- **Document handling**: AI extracts and processes information from claims documents, cutting manual data entry.
- **Anomaly detection**: ML models flag patterns that suggest a fraudulent claim, so the carrier intervenes before the money leaves the building.
- **Predictive analytics**: models predict resolution times and resource needs, which matters because each US state sets its own processing requirements.

The payoff is faster resolution, lower overhead, less fraud and happier customers. On the consumer side, ML on large datasets finds preferences and behaviour patterns, which feed tailored products and outreach that reaches a customer before an issue escalates. The results he lists are retention, satisfaction and conversion on personalised offers.

## What do the numbers say?

The case studies are anonymised as Company A, B and C. Company A's AI claims processing cut processing time by 60% and fraud losses by 30%. Company B used ML on customer data to personalise offerings and saw a 20% rise in policy renewals. Company C applied predictive analytics to resource allocation for a 40% cut in operational costs. No methodology comes with the figures, so read them as directional. He also claims chatbots answer 95% of customer questions, again without a source.

## How should a carrier roll it out?

The roadmap is the most reusable part:

1. **Assessment and strategy**: pick AI/ML use cases that line up with business goals.
2. **Pilot projects**: a couple of use cases, built and deployed small. As Praveen Kumar said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024, "So the phase two for me is more of a proof of concept model".
3. **Full-scale implementation**: roll out across the organisation, integrate with the core insurance systems and train people.
4. **Continuous optimisation**: retrain and refine models as data accumulates.

He stresses training more than technology. As Praveen Kumar said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024: "If the people or the resources who are using the systems are not skilled enough, are not trained enough, then I think we can't really get the efficiencies out of these systems."

The challenges are the expected three: data privacy and state and federal regulation, integration with large legacy systems that already move huge volumes of data, and a shortage of people who can build and run AI/ML in production. Looking ahead, he points to conversational AI for 24/7 service, real-time risk assessment, AI-driven underwriting to shorten time to issue a policy, dynamic pricing and sentiment analysis.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects new to insurance who need the vocabulary and a sense of where models fit in a claims pipeline, and managers drafting an AI adoption plan. If you came to a JavaScript conference for JavaScript, this one is outside that brief.

Title: Six sevs that page you at 3am, and the fix each one taught
Description: Zuodong Xiang at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on six real outage patterns, from retry storms to untested runbook scripts, and how to stop them
Body:
Most outages are reruns. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Zuodong Xiang (who goes by Shawn) walked through six incident patterns he has seen in production, from a traffic flood that kills its own autoscaling to a runbook script that takes availability to zero, and pulled one durable lesson out of each. The second half turns those lessons into a checklist for prevention, detection, mitigation and the review afterwards.

It is a practical talk with no product in it. If you carry a pager, most of it will feel familiar, which is exactly the point.

## How does more capacity make a traffic flood worse?

The first sev starts with CPU near 100% on every host after a site-wide traffic spike. Autoscaling kicks in, but a host pinned at 100% CPU cannot answer its health check, so the autoscaler marks it dead and replaces it. The replacement gets the same flood and dies the same way. More hosts, same outage.

The mitigation was to cap max connections per host so a box only accepts the traffic it can serve, and let the fleet come back. The long-term lesson: load test for the maximum number of connections a host can actually handle, before a busy day finds that number for you.

## Why is a retry storm multiplication, not addition?

His retry example is worth drawing on a whiteboard. A client calls service 1, which calls service 2, which calls the database. The database is down. Service 2 retries twice, fails, and reports back. Service 1 then retries twice, and each of those attempts triggers service 2's two retries again. That is six retries from one request, and every extra layer multiplies it. The bottom of the stack gets flattened by its own callers.

During a big shopping event the fix was blunt: drop most of the traffic, stop retrying, add hosts. The lasting fix is to standardise retry logic with exponential backoff, respect HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, and put a circuit breaker on each dependency so a struggling service stops getting hammered.

## Plan B can take down someone else's plan A

The third pattern is the circuit breaker's evil twin. Dependency A fails, so traffic fails over to dependency B, which was never sized for it and falls over too, breaking every other service that relies on B. His advice is uncomfortable but sound: in day-to-day operation, focus on fixing dependency A, and do not introduce a backup dependency unless it has been prepared properly, for example as a lever for a planned high-traffic event.

## A bad commit is a process bug

When a commit takes server availability down 100%, Xiang argues the commit owner is the wrong place to look. Code review, unit and end-to-end tests, manual QA, feature gating, change management and risk assessment all had a chance to stop it. "So every bad commit actually carries some positive lesson for you to reflect what was missing in the release process," Zuodong Xiang said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024.

The remaining two patterns are smaller but nastier. Code orphaned by a reorg gets escalated to a team that has never heard of the feature (fix: ownership annotations in code, tooling or the wiki, plus a real handover process). And a script referenced in a runbook, never tested, takes the system to 0% availability. Production-impacting scripts deserve the same testing, QA and review as production commits.

## What goes on the checklist?

The prevention list is defensive coding: gate features and ramp them gradually, log exceptions with the context you will need at 3am, fail fast instead of leaning on backups, handle errors gracefully, be null-safe (he name-checks Kotlin), set timeouts on every dependency call, and retry sparingly with exponential backoff.

For detection, alerts should come from an operational goal such as an availability target or an SLA, use historical data to sit between noisy and missed, and always link a runbook. "3am stuff shouldn't be needing any thinking," he said. Dashboards cover trends and correlation, and load and chaos testing tell you your system's real limits.

Mitigation is the emergency room: follow the runbook, then ask whether the problem lines up with a time, a commit, an app version or a gating change, and whether other teams see the same thing. For known high-traffic events and big launches, prepare a risk plan, dedicated dashboards and levers for the worst case, and re-run your load and chaos tests first. The sev review stays blameless: a timeline to shorten time to detect and mitigate, a five-whys root cause, and tracked action items with dates, because untracked lessons are just stories.

## Who should watch

On-call engineers early in their pager career will get the most out of this, and team leads can lift the checklist straight into an onboarding doc. Seasoned SREs will recognise every pattern, but the retry arithmetic and the Plan B warning are good to have in someone else's words.

Title: Let AI write your unit tests, then let mutants check them
Description: Sharon Barr (Early) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on generating unit tests with an AI assistant versus an AI agent, and mutation testing the result
Body:
Most developers would rather write the feature than the test for it, and generative AI tools are now good enough to take that second job off their plate. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Sharon Barr, co-founder and CEO of Early, generated Jest unit tests for the same user service twice, once with the Cursor assistant and once with Early's own test-generation agent, then used Stryker mutation testing to show that 100% coverage is not the finish line.

Honest scope: Barr is a founder demoing the company's own product next to a general-purpose competitor. The comparison is useful anyway, and the mutation-testing section stands on its own whatever tool wrote the tests.

## Why bother with unit tests at all?

Barr opens with the CrowdStrike outage: an array out-of-bounds read, a null pointer exception, a blue screen of death, and $5.4bn in losses by one report, with Delta Air Lines alone losing $500M. The cost of a bug climbs steeply the further it travels from the keyboard, and unit tests are the cheapest place to catch it.

The time split Barr cites from developer studies makes the same point from the other side: roughly 38% of developer time goes on test code and testing-related work, from writing tests to maintaining them to debugging. People are already paying for testing; the question is whether they spend that time well.

Henry Ford's faster-horses line frames the pitch. Writing tests by hand is the horse; generating them automatically is the car, and the interesting question is what you can do with a car that you couldn't with a horse.

## Assistant or agent: what is the difference in practice?

The demo method is small: `checkMaxNumberOfUsers` throws if a user count exceeds a configured maximum. Ask Cursor to generate happy-path and edge-case tests, apply them to a new file, and the suggestions don't compile at first. Wrong object properties, a `number` where a `bigint` belongs, a missing decimal import. Each error gets a quick fix with AI, one at a time, and some tests still fail on dependencies.

Early runs as an IDE extension that lists files, classes and methods with coverage at the method level. Generate tests for the same method and it adds mocks, groups happy-path and edge-case tests, and suggests documentation and a code improvement (cache the max-users value to save database calls) along the way. Three methods reach 100% coverage. A few tests come back red, and Barr points out that a red generated test is sometimes a broken test and sometimes a real bug.

The framing: an assistant answers question by question until you're satisfied, while an agent takes over a whole task, loops with the LLM on its own and hands back a working result. As Sharon Barr said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 about finishing an agent's output with an assistant: "It's trying to complete something that started at 90%, not 50%."

## Where does generation fit in the workflow?

Four use cases: continuous testing during development, testing a pull request thoroughly before submitting it, testing private methods (make one public, generate tests, make it private again) and test-driven development done differently. In the TDD flow Barr starts from a bare method signature, generates basic red tests, writes fuller documentation so the next round gets specific (return 404 if the project is not found), then implements happy path and edge cases until four tests go green at full coverage.

## Who tests the tests?

The best part of the talk. As Sharon Barr said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024: "high coverage does not necessarily mean high quality." Mutation testing injects small changes into your code and expects your tests to fail; every mutant that survives marks code your tests don't really check.

Barr runs Stryker on the user service. With the full generated suite (100% coverage) the mutation score is 96.55%, with only one mutant surviving. Then three tests get deleted. Coverage still looks respectable at 84%, but the mutation score falls to 51.72%. That gap is the argument for running mutation testing on any suite, generated or not. One practical catch from the demo: red tests have to be fixed or skipped before Stryker will run.

## Who should watch

Teams weighing AI test generation who want to see the rough edges of a general assistant next to a dedicated agent, and anyone who still treats a coverage percentage as proof. Skip the middle if you have seen Cursor before; don't skip the Stryker part.

Title: When the network goes, it takes your monitoring with it
Description: Maksim Kupriianov (Meta) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on why network incidents cascade, and the out-of-band prep that keeps you able to respond
Body:
The worst part of a network incident is not the outage, it is that your dashboards, your SSH and your team chat all ride on the network that just broke. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Maksim Kupriianov, Production Engineer at Meta and a former SRE and long-time system administrator, explains why network incidents were the most devastating ones he has seen, and what to build before one hits: redundancy, an out-of-band management network, monitoring and playbooks you can reach from outside, and regular drills.

It is a practical, experience-driven talk that sits squarely in the incident management track, with as much on human behaviour during the chaos as on routers.

## What counts as a network incident?

His definition: an unexpected event that disrupts or degrades critical network services, hurting their availability, integrity or performance. The interesting part is the list of what counts as critical: DNS, DHCP, routing, VPN and NTP/PTP; firewalls, IDS/IPS, certificate centres and physical access control; directory services for authentication and authorisation; cloud and container orchestration; and the load balancers, web servers and CDNs that deliver traffic.

These incidents almost always cascade. When a DNS server fails, everything that depends on DNS starts to misbehave. "By the way, please never depend on DNS," Kupriianov said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024, adding the realistic caveat that plenty of services still do. Then you lose access to your monitoring and diagnostics, usually fast, while everybody in the company asks what is going on.

He backs it with a list of big-name outages: Cloudflare in July 2020 (20 minutes, a router misconfiguration), Google Cloud in December 2020 (authentication, about 50 minutes), Microsoft Azure and Teams in March 2021 (3 hours, Active Directory), Fastly in June 2021 (1 hour, a bug triggered by a customer configuration), Facebook in October 2021 (6 hours) and AWS in December 2021 (6 hours 30 minutes). His conclusion: "In the IT world, network incidents are as certain as sunrise."

## How does one actually unfold?

The triggers are varied: failing power supplies or line cards, a CPU that silently corrupts data, software bugs and unsupported scenarios, misconfiguration, attacks, fibre cuts, and in one case from his own career, an animal that got into a transformer and caused a fire and a power outage. From his marketplace years he adds Black Friday, when you are only as safe as your capacity planning.

Then comes the cascade. Interdependent systems fail, such as everything behind authentication. Applications retry, the callers of those applications retry too, and the wave of requests finishes off whatever was still standing: a server built for a hundred requests a minute does not survive a million. Links saturate. Monitoring goes dark or floods you with alerts, remote access disappears, and the chat tool you would coordinate in may be down too.

He flags a security trap: the temptation to open a firewall hole or disable it to get things working. Attackers wait for exactly that. Lowering the security level during an incident is, in his words, very bad practice.

## What should exist before it happens?

- **Redundancy**, including geographic, for the external events no router config can fix.
- **An out-of-band management network**, so the alternative is not driving to the data centre with a console cable.
- **Backups and failover**, with backups stored away from the systems they protect.
- **Continuous audits and health checks**: network assessments, hardware maintenance, capacity planning. Not a PDF of green ticks.
- **A subset of monitoring reachable out of band**, for example general health metrics exported to a rented service elsewhere.
- **Playbooks and network docs kept outside your network**, and checked regularly, because people forget the alternative password and where they stored it.
- **Drills**: turn off DNS in one location and watch what happens.

## How do you behave when everything goes dark?

Stay calm first; panic makes everything slower. Gather information from logs, out-of-band access and user reports, and determine the scope. Appoint an incident manager as the single point of contact who tracks state and talks to stakeholders while engineers dig. Have a secondary communication channel that everyone already knows how to join; he has seen incidents where people could not even find a colleague's phone number. Tell stakeholders plainly, without jargon. Prioritise critical services, decide what can wait, find the root cause, make a plan and stick to it.

His pitfalls are the usual suspects, and still common: rushing without a plan, poor communication, skipping procedures that exist for security or legal reasons, fixing symptoms instead of the root cause, and burning out the team on a long incident instead of rotating people. Afterwards, run a post-incident review and update the runbooks, or wait for history to repeat itself.

## Who should watch

SREs and network engineers, and incident commanders who have never had to run an incident without their usual tools. If your playbooks live only on the wiki inside your network, start here.

Title: Where JavaScript and AI fit into dialysis care
Description: Ram Meka at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on mapping predictive analytics, personalised treatment and JavaScript dashboards onto dialysis care
Body:
Dialysis patients usually spend three sessions a week hooked up to a machine, and every one of those sessions produces data that mostly goes unused. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Ram Meka, a Principal Systems Developer with more than a decade in kidney care products, laid out where AI-driven predictive analytics and JavaScript applications can help: spotting high-risk patients early, tailoring treatment, and planning clinic capacity.

Set expectations before you press play: this is a structured overview of the domain and the opportunities, not a code walkthrough or a case study with figures. The abstract's promises of cut hospitalisations and real-time wearables show up in the talk as directions, not measured results.

## Why is dialysis a hard problem for software?

Meka starts with the clinical picture. Dialysis replaces the function of failing kidneys for people with end-stage renal disease (ESRD), a condition that affects millions worldwide. It comes in two main forms, haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis, each with different implications for how patients are managed.

He groups the challenges into three. Complex treatment protocols: as Ram Meka said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024, "Patients typically undergo dialysis sessions three times per week." That is logistics and time for the patient and scheduling for the clinic. Complications, including cardiovascular problems, infections and anaemia. And cost: equipment, medication and staff add up to a heavy burden on patients and health systems.

## What does JavaScript actually do here?

The JavaScript part is the plumbing and the glass. He names D3.js and Chart.js for interactive dashboards that make patient data readable for clinicians, Node.js for collecting and monitoring data from many sources in real time, and front-end work for interfaces that patients actually use, which matters when the goal is adherence to a demanding schedule.

The same stack shows up in his real-world list: telehealth applications that let patients consult nephrologists remotely, and dashboards that clinics use to track key performance indicators for dialysis care.

## Where does the AI earn its keep?

Predictive analytics on historical data covers three jobs in his framing:

- **Risk assessment**: combine demographics, treatment history and lab results to flag patients at elevated risk of complications, so the care team intervenes before an emergency.
- **Treatment optimisation**: machine learning models that forecast how an individual patient will respond to a given protocol, so therapy fits the patient.
- **Resource allocation**: forecast demand for dialysis services to plan staff, schedules and machine use.

Personalisation builds on that. JavaScript applications pull data from many sources into one patient profile, AI models monitor health parameters continuously so the treatment plan can change as the patient does, and patient-facing apps add education, reminders and self-management tools. He cites research on machine learning models that predict hospitalisations and adverse events among dialysis patients with high accuracy, without naming a specific study or figure.

## What gets in the way?

Three barriers, all familiar to anyone who has shipped software into a hospital. Data privacy and security, with HIPAA compliance as the baseline. Resistance from both clinicians and patients, which he answers with training and education rather than a better UI. And data quality: as Ram Meka said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024, "the efficacy of AI models is contingent upon the quality and comprehensiveness of the data utilized for training."

Looking ahead, he expects more capable real-time models, wider telehealth reaching remote and underserved areas, and closer work between clinicians, data scientists and developers.

## Who should watch

Developers new to healthcare who want a map of the dialysis domain and the vocabulary their clinical colleagues will use. If you want architecture diagrams, model choices or numbers, this talk won't supply them; pair it with something hands-on.
