Title: Your vendor is down, and your customers still blame you
Description: Mandi Walls (PagerDuty) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on tiering vendors, writing vendor runbooks and running post-incident reviews on their outages
Body:
The 500s are coming from your payment provider, the status page is all green, and 80 people are on the bridge call waiting. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Mandi Walls, DevOps Advocate at PagerDuty, makes the case that a vendor's outage is still your incident, and that almost everything that decides how it goes for your customers happens before it starts: tiering your vendors, naming an owner for each, writing vendor runbooks, and reviewing their incidents as seriously as your own.

It is a vendor-neutral talk despite the employer (she says up front that the opening is as much PagerDuty as she is going to talk about), and full of detail you only learn on those bridge calls.

## Why is a vendor outage your problem?

Walls starts from the old cloud mantra that you own your own availability, pointing to John Allspaw's Kitchen Soap post from around 2013. Your providers don't know your KPIs. "Your vendors, Whether it's your cloud provider, another SaaS provider, they're just your landlord on the internet," Walls said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. So you need your own insurance for when the landlord has a bad day. Her extreme example is the OVHcloud data centre in Strasbourg that burned down in 2021. The common case is smaller: configuration errors, DDoS, a subsystem quietly misbehaving.

## Sort vendors into tiers

Most companies have dozens of SaaS tiles in their SSO portal, so she sorts them:

- **Tier 1**: customer-facing or in support of production. IaaS, shopping cart and payments, search, and the metrics, monitoring and alerting you need when things break. An outage here can mean a revenue hit; if you know the cost per minute, write it down.
- **Tier 2**: the build and test path. QA tools, CI/CD, infrastructure as code, source control, maybe user docs. Customers may not notice, but you cannot ship the fix.
- **Tier 3**: everything outside the path to production, such as experiments and internal reporting. Should never block production work.
- **Other**: the tools your own incident response runs on: video calls, team chat, wikis. PagerDuty's own backup plan is knowing where to go if Zoom or Slack is down, with accounts already set up there.

Then put the vendors on your service diagrams instead of the usual cloud shape drifting off the edge, so responders know exactly which customer flows go through which third party.

## Buy support for the relationship, not the help

The most counter-intuitive advice: for Tier 1 vendors, consider a premium support package even if you never need implementation help. "You buy up to support, not because you need help with the implementation, but because you want a closer relationship with the vendor," she said. Run the numbers; ten minutes of their outage may pay for the whole contract. Then take the regular check-in calls, file good bug reports, and become a customer they know by name. That gets you a direct line and a place on the first-notified list.

## Who owns the vendor at 3am?

Ownership drifts from procurement and legal to project managers to whoever runs the thing day to day. Her rule: whoever relies on the vendor in production, ideally a team already on call, is the internal contact. The team that built the shopping cart integration owns the cart vendor. If tech writers chose the docs platform, they need an on-call responsibility for it too, because engineering cannot fix it.

Each Tier 1 and 2 vendor gets a runbook, available to everyone: account numbers and user IDs, where the keys live in the vault, what features you actually bought (so support does not tell you that you never paid for that), your support level (the reason nobody answered in 30 minutes may be that you bought two-hour support), contacts and shared Slack channels, renewal date, and how they want errors reported. It also helps when you caused the problem yourself, say by hammering their API until they locked you out.

## During and after the incident

Contact or wait? Big outages make the news; small subsystem failures often do not even reach the status page, so call your account team, which also helps them scope it by region or database segment. If you wait, release the bridge, appoint one person to watch vendor updates, and keep stakeholders and the support team informed. On public status pages, no trash talk: you chose the vendor, so it is still your problem.

Then run a post-incident review, even though it is not your bug. Over time it replaces "your vibes and your feelings about this vendor with actual data," which is exactly what you want at contract renewal. Invite the vendor; they may send an executive. Decide on switching vendors only after things calm down, never mid-outage, unless the data centre has actually burned down.

## Who should watch

Incident commanders, SREs and platform teams who depend on SaaS (everyone), and especially anyone who owns vendor contracts without realising they also own the incidents.

Title: What makes a chatbot adaptive - the feedback loop, explained
Description: Abhi Ram Reddy Salammagari ([24]7.ai) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on how adaptive chatbots learn from feedback where rule-based bots stall
Body:
A rule-based bot is a decision tree with a chat window on it, and it falls over the moment a user types something nobody scripted. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Abhi Ram Reddy Salammagari, Senior Software Engineer at [24]7.ai, explains what replaces it: adaptive chatbots that run a loop of understand, respond, collect feedback and refine, so every conversation makes the next one a little better.

Scope check: despite the title, the talk is a general introduction to adaptive chatbots rather than an incident management talk, and the abstract's figures (30% faster responses, 25% better interactions) do not come up in the session itself. Read it as a primer on how the technology works, from someone who builds conversational systems for a living.

## Why do rule-based bots hit a wall?

"Traditional chatbots are rule based systems," Salammagari said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. They rely on predefined scripts with a limited set of responses, which is fine for narrow jobs such as answering FAQs. The limits show in dynamic, complex conversations: no flexibility, and no graceful way to handle input the script did not expect.

Adaptive chatbots differ in three ways, in his framing. Continuous learning, where machine learning grows the knowledge base automatically instead of someone hand-editing a fixed database. User feedback integration, so behaviour changes as needs change. And dynamic responses, adjusted and refined per interaction rather than pulled from a static table.

## What is under the hood?

Three technologies. Natural language processing to interpret and generate language and handle complex queries. Machine learning to predict user intent better with each interaction. And reinforcement learning, which he contrasts with supervised learning on labelled data: the bot learns by trial and error from feedback and adjusts its strategy.

Recent progress, he says, comes from transformer models such as BERT and GPT for understanding context and nuance, reinforcement learning for adjusting strategy in real time, and sentiment analysis so the bot can change tone when a user is clearly annoyed.

## The four-step loop

The core of the talk is a simple cycle:

1. **Understand.** NLP extracts intent and context from the user's input.
2. **Respond.** The bot consults its ML models to generate a reply informed by earlier interactions.
3. **Collect feedback.** Explicitly, through ratings, or implicitly, from how the conversation flows.
4. **Refine.** That feedback goes back into the system and shapes future responses.

For anyone who has run a support or incident bot, the implicit-feedback step is the interesting one: a user who rephrases the same question three times is telling you something no thumbs-up button will.

## Where does it get hard?

His applications are personalised education (lessons that adapt to a student's progress), customer support (faster, accurate answers that need fewer human agents) and digital assistants (scheduling and complex questions, learning preferences over time).

The challenges are honest ones. Privacy, because these bots collect a lot of user data; encryption and anonymisation are his remedies. The complexity of human language: ambiguity, sarcasm and emotion. And balance. "Automation boosts efficiency, but can feel impersonal," he said, and the answer he proposes is building empathy and emotional intelligence into the bot. He closes on the open research problem of more robust unsupervised learning.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people who are about to replace a scripted support bot and want the vocabulary and the architecture in outline. If you already ship LLM-based assistants with feedback loops and evals, this one covers ground you know.

Title: Two lines of JavaScript to prompt an LLM that lives in Chrome
Description: Mohamad Shiralizadeh (ING) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on prompting Chrome's built-in Gemini Nano model from JavaScript, no ML skills needed
Body:
What if the LLM was already installed, sitting inside the browser your users have open anyway? At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Mohamad Shiralizadeh, Software Engineer at ING, demoed Chrome's experimental built-in AI: a Prompt API backed by the on-device Gemini Nano model. Create a session, call `prompt`, and get an answer without a network call, an API key or a single line of machine learning code.

It is a short, upbeat talk with a live-coding segment that goes wrong in the instructive way live coding usually does. Note that it covers an early preview: the API shape he shows (`window.ai.assistant.create`) is the one from Chrome's 2024 developer preview.

## Local or cloud LLM?

He opens with the trade-off. A local LLM runs on your machine, so you are capped by its hardware, but you get privacy (the data stays put), low latency (no network) and low cost (no subscription). A cloud LLM brings the bigger, better-trained model, and with it network latency and the bill from your cloud provider. Put a local model in the browser, which is already on every machine your web app reaches, and you get the first column for free.

## What does the API look like?

His disclaimer: no machine learning and no AI expertise required. You `await` a session from the `ai` object on `window`, then call `session.prompt()` with a question such as where Amsterdam is. His test returned "Amsterdam is the capital city of Netherlands." As Mohamad Shiralizadeh said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024: "So with two lines of code, I could ask LLM something."

The second call is `promptStreaming`, which returns a standard browser stream so you can render tokens as the model predicts them instead of waiting for the full response.

Prompt engineering still pays off. He shows N-shot prompting: a session created with `temperature` and `topK`, a system prompt that casts the model as a tour guide, and two examples (Netherlands gets the Rijksmuseum, Italy the Colosseum). Ask about Iran and the model picks up the pattern and suggests the Grand Bazaar.

## The live demo: tags for a blog post

The demo is a blog post form that suggests tags as you type. On every input event it prompts the local model to act as an author helping people find tags and to return JSON, with the text wrapped in XML-style tags because, in his experience, models parse that better.

The real-world wrinkles show up fast. The model returns its JSON wrapped in a Markdown code fence, so he strips the backticks with a regex before `JSON.parse`. The result is an object with a `tags` property rather than a bare array, which costs a round of debugging on stage. And prompting on every keystroke floods the model, which is your laptop, so he adds Lodash `debounce` at a few hundred milliseconds. For a sentence saying AI is awesome and he is presenting at a conference, the suggestions came back as conference, technology and artificial intelligence. The whole feature took about 30 lines.

## How to switch it on

The setup at the time: Chrome Canary or Dev, `chrome://flags/#prompt-api-for-gemini-nano` set to Enabled, `chrome://flags/#optimization-guide-on-device-model` set to Enabled BypassPrefRequirement, then `chrome://components` and Check for Update on Optimization Guide On Device Model to download the model. The internet connection is needed once, for that download. He also urges joining Google's built-in AI early preview program, because the API is not stable and he still hits issues himself.

His list of use cases: classification, tagging and keyword extraction, helping users compose text, summarising articles and chat logs, generating headlines, answering questions over the unstructured content of a page, translation and proofreading.

## Who should watch

Web developers curious about on-device LLMs who want to see the smallest possible working feature, warts included. If you need production guarantees today, treat this as a preview of where browsers are heading, not a dependency.

Title: You don't need Python to ship ML in the browser
Description: Danielle Maxwell (Rotational Labs) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024 on running pretrained models client-side with TensorFlow.js and Transformers.js
Body:
A JavaScript developer who wants object detection or image captioning in an app does not have to detour through a Python course first. At Conf42 JavaScript 2024, Danielle Maxwell, Junior Distributed Systems Engineer at Rotational Labs, showed two open source libraries that run pretrained models on the client: TensorFlow.js from Google and Transformers.js from Hugging Face, each with a small demo you could rebuild in an afternoon.

She is upfront about the angle: she works next to machine learning experts and does not count herself as one. That makes this a good first talk on browser ML, pitched at people who know JavaScript and would rather not clean a dataset before lunch.

## Why run the model in the browser at all?

Maxwell lists four wins. User data never leaves the device, which matters a lot for privacy-sensitive apps. Latency drops because there is no round trip to an API. The model keeps working offline, which suits progressive web apps. And deployment gets simpler: the whole thing ships as a static site, no inference server to build.

The bill comes in four parts too. The first load downloads the model, which can take minutes on a slow device or network. A model sitting in the browser can be extracted or copied, which is a non-issue with open models and a real one with custom ones. Large models bring performance trouble. And you now own the problem of updating and versioning models that live on other people's machines. Both libraries install from a CDN or npm, and both also run server-side inference on Node.js if the trade-offs go the other way.

## TensorFlow.js: start pretrained, retrain later

TensorFlow.js gives you three levels: use an existing model, retrain one with your own data through transfer learning, or build and train your own. Its model catalogue covers image classification, object detection, pose and hand detection, question answering, a text toxicity detector and speech command recognition, with more on the Kaggle model hub.

The demo is plain HTML and vanilla JavaScript loading the COCO-SSD object detection model. Upload an image, call `detect`, and draw the returned class, confidence score and bounding box over the picture. She fed it a photo of Lionel Messi holding a trophy. It found a person at roughly 66% confidence and ignored the trophy entirely, because the training data was mostly about people. Her fix is the retraining path: a dataset with trophies, or with footballers, so the model could say more than person.

## Transformers.js: the pipeline does the boring parts

Transformers.js also runs pretrained models, and it can load custom models converted from the Python side. Its tasks span NLP (text classification, translation), vision (classification, object detection), audio (speech recognition, audio classification) and multimodal work such as zero-shot image classification, which could have caught the trophy the COCO model missed.

Her pick for beginners is the pipeline API, which wraps a model together with the preprocessing of inputs and the postprocessing of outputs. Three lines of sentiment analysis on a sentence calling Conf42 JavaScript a great conference returned POSITIVE with a score of 0.9998. If you don't name a model, the library picks a default for the task.

The second demo, hosted on a Hugging Face Space, does image-to-text: upload a photo and get a caption under it. A shot of Alex Morgan celebrating a goal came back as "two women are playing soccer on the field", basic but accurate. The Hugging Face model hub filters by library, so you can list only models known to work with Transformers.js.

Her closing line is the thesis of the talk. As Danielle Maxwell said at Conf42 JavaScript 2024: "remember, you don't have to be an expert to get started with working with AI in the browser."

## Who should watch

Front-end and full-stack developers who have never touched a model and want a working mental map of what runs client-side, plus the trade-offs to raise before shipping it. ML engineers will find nothing new about the models; the value is in seeing how little glue code the browser side needs.

Title: In healthcare IT, the legacy integration is the bottleneck
Description: VijayaAshwin Jagadeesan at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on AI, analytics, FHIR and cloud in healthcare IT, and why legacy integration gates all of it
Body:
An AI model that predicts kidney injury two days early is only useful if the patient data reaches it from a twenty-year-old hospital system on time. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, VijayaAshwin Jagadeesan, a Technical Architect, surveys where AI, data analytics, cloud and blockchain are taking healthcare IT, and the thread running through it is the unglamorous one: none of it works until the legacy systems are integrated.

Scope check: the abstract frames the talk around incident management, but what he delivers is a market and trends overview of healthcare technology, dense with cited industry figures. The incident angle is indirect, through failure prevention, data quality and integration. Go in expecting a briefing, not a runbook.

## How fast is digital health growing?

Jagadeesan opens with the market. Digital health was worth $96.5 billion in 2020 with a projected 15.1% compound annual growth rate from 2021 to 2028, and the CDC reported a 154% jump in telehealth use in 2020 over the previous year. COVID was the catalyst; telemedicine stayed. AI in healthcare specifically was valued at $6.7 billion in 2020, with a projected 41.8% CAGR through 2028.

## What does AI actually do in a hospital?

The clinical examples carry the most concrete numbers. AI image recognition in breast cancer screening cut false positives by 5.7% and false negatives by 9.4%. At the Mayo Clinic, AI-guided treatment improved remission rates for depression by 6%. Predictive models can flag acute kidney injury in hospitalised patients up to 48 hours before onset with 92% accuracy, which is the difference between intervening and reacting. He also covers sepsis early warning, chronic disease monitoring from wearables, clinical decision support, NLP over electronic health records, and AI-assisted triage in emergency rooms.

On the operations side, healthcare data grows by 48% a year. His analytics example: at Johns Hopkins Hospital, predictive analytics cut emergency department boarding hours by 20% and raised early discharges by 21%. Supply chain forecasting for critical medicines gets a mention too, an outage of a different kind.

## Why is legacy integration the real problem?

This is the section incident responders should watch. New tools such as EHRs, telehealth platforms and AI diagnostics have to plug into infrastructure that, in his words, is often fragmented. "These legacy systems are often outdated, fragmented, and incompatible with the modern technologies," Jagadeesan said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. The result is data that cannot be accessed in real time and clinical workflows that slow down. He cites 19% of hospital executives naming legacy integration as their top IT priority.

His answer is standards first. FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) gives systems a uniform protocol for exchanging data, and he cites FHIR-based solutions cutting data integration time by 75%. Cloud migration is the second lever, with the healthcare cloud market projected at $64.7 billion by 2025; his deck cites Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center cutting IT costs by 30% after migrating. Blockchain is the third, for tamper-resistant data sharing: a provider-data pilot by Humana and UnitedHealthcare reportedly halved administrative costs by removing data discrepancies.

Most figures come without methodology, so treat them as signposts, not benchmarks.

## What should organisations do next?

His closing advice is four items: invest in digital infrastructure (linked to 2.5% higher hospital profit margins), fix data governance (poor data quality costs US healthcare billions a year, and better data management can cut errors by 30%), train staff on the tools (23% higher productivity and 18% better patient outcomes in hospitals that invested in digital training), and partner with technology companies rather than building everything in-house.

## Who should watch

Architects and IT leads new to healthcare who want the big picture and its numbers in one sitting. Engineers looking for implementation detail on FHIR or clinical AI will want something more hands-on.

Title: Copy-paste documentation is a bug - moving Salesforce articles to DITA
Description: Bhanu Gogula at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on a six-step automated pipeline that moves Salesforce articles into DITA topics in AEM Guides
Body:
If the same paragraph about a product feature lives in 400 knowledge base articles, the 401st edit is the one somebody forgets. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Bhanu Gogula, a full stack web engineer with more than 10 years of experience, walks through a six-step, mostly automated pipeline for moving articles out of Salesforce and into Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) Guides as structured DITA content, with validation at the end so the migration itself does not become the incident.

It is a practical, tool-by-tool talk with small Python snippets for each stage. Nobody is getting paged for a documentation migration, but the incident angle is real: broken links, missing images and lost metadata are what users report the week after a careless one.

## Why leave Salesforce for AEM Guides?

Salesforce is a strong CRM, Gogula says, but it lacks the tooling for complex content management. AEM Guides brings DITA support, structured authoring and multi-channel delivery.

The real argument is the content model. In linear documentation, "When the same content is needed in the other document or sections, it has to be copied again and again," Gogula said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. Document A and document B both describe the same product feature, so every change has to be made twice, and twice becomes dozens as the library grows. A component content management system (CCMS) breaks content into topics, links them into documents through maps, and keeps each chunk in exactly one place. Update the topic, and every document that links it changes. It is DRY, applied to prose.

## The six steps

1. **Extract.** Selenium Wire drives the Salesforce articles pages and pulls the title, body and metadata of each article. In his words, it acts like a robot collecting the data, so nobody copy-pastes thousands of articles by hand.
2. **Create HTML pages.** Each article becomes its own small HTML file with title, content and metadata, an intermediate format before DITA.
3. **Clean and fix paths.** Rewrite relative paths so images and links resolve inside AEM, then run JTidy to fix malformed markup. Skip this and the conversion step chokes on someone's unclosed tag from years ago.
4. **Convert HTML to DITA.** Articles become DITA XML topics and maps.
5. **Upload.** The ACS Commons Asset Importer moves titles, body text, images and metadata into AEM Guides.
6. **Validate.** Check every article in AEM: does it render, do the links work, did the metadata land where it should. Anything broken gets fixed before the migration is declared done.

The snippets in the deck are deliberately minimal (a Selenium Wire loop, an f-string HTML template, a string-replace for paths, a DITA topic wrapper), more a sketch of the pipeline shape than production code. Fine for understanding; expect to add error handling and retries before you point it at a real org.

## What does DITA buy you afterwards?

Gogula spends a good part of the talk on the after-migration payoff. DITA content is typed (concept, task, reference topics, organised by maps), which keeps it findable and reusable. The DITA Open Toolkit publishes the same source to web pages, PDFs and mobile-friendly formats without rewriting anything.

His favourite benefit is rebranding. Change a logo or design style once and it applies everywhere. Rename a product mentioned in thousands of articles by changing one central variable in a key map instead of editing each article. Anyone who has grepped a docs repo for an old product name will feel this one.

## Who should watch

Teams moving a knowledge base off Salesforce, technical writers evaluating a CCMS, and engineers asked to script a content migration who want a sensible order of operations. If you already run DITA at scale, it will be familiar ground.

Title: An NLP primer for incident people - sentiment, generation and NER
Description: Vishal Khadake (HYR Global source Inc) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on three NLP techniques - sentiment analysis, language generation and NER
Body:
Most of what happens in an incident is text: alerts, tickets, chat threads, angry customer emails, the postmortem nobody wants to write. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Vishal Khadake, NLP data scientist at HYR Global source Inc, gives a compact primer on the three natural language processing techniques that do most of the work on that text: sentiment analysis, language generation and named entity recognition.

Honest scope first. The abstract pitches NLP for faster, more accurate incident response; the talk itself is a general introduction to NLP and does not walk through an incident workflow. Treat it as the vocabulary lesson you need before evaluating any AI-for-incidents tool, not as a blueprint.

## What is NLP, in one breath?

Khadake places NLP at the intersection of artificial intelligence, linguistics and cognitive psychology, with one aim: getting computers to understand, interpret and generate human language in a useful way. The task list runs from speech recognition and text analysis to sentiment analysis and translation. The everyday examples are the ones you would expect: virtual assistants and automated customer support.

## How does sentiment analysis actually work?

"Sentiment analysis is also known as opinion mining, determines the emotional tone behind a piece of text," Khadake said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. The pipeline he describes is the classic one: preprocess the text (clean and standardise it), extract features that capture the important linguistic traits, then classify as positive, negative or neutral. The classifiers range from traditional algorithms such as Support Vector Machines up to deep learning models like BERT.

His applications are customer feedback, brand monitoring and social media tracking. The incident-shaped reading is yours to make: the same classifier that tracks brand mood can flag the support ticket that is quietly turning into an escalation.

## Language generation and NER

Language generation is the transformer part of the talk. Models such as GPT-3 and GPT-4 learn patterns from large amounts of text and predict word sequences from context, which is what powers chatbots, automated reports and summaries. Automated reporting and summarising are the two that matter to an on-call team.

Named entity recognition finds and labels people, places, organisations and dates in text. Khadake covers three ways to build it: rule-based approaches, machine learning models (his deck names CRFs and Bi-LSTMs), and hybrids. His example is search: recognising the entities in a query improves the answer. In incident terms, that is the step that pulls the service name, region and timestamp out of a free-text report.

## What still goes wrong?

He lists three hard problems. Ambiguity: the meaning of a word shifts with context, which trips up machine interpretation. Multilingual processing, especially low-resource languages without big training sets. And ethics: bias in language models and privacy, which matters most in sensitive domains such as healthcare.

Looking forward, he points at smaller and faster models that keep their accuracy (the Green AI push), multimodal models that combine text, images and audio, commonsense reasoning, and more explainable models.

## Who should watch

Incident managers and SREs who keep hearing NLP terms in vendor pitches and want the basics in one sitting. Data scientists will find nothing new here; it is a primer, and a tidy one.

Title: Terraform builds the box, Chef locks it down
Description: Karthik Jataprole (Workday Inc) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on pairing Terraform and Chef so security config ships with every deployment
Body:
A security group someone clicked together in a console at 2am is a future incident with a timestamp already on it. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Karthik Jataprole of Workday Inc makes the case for taking humans out of that loop: provision cloud infrastructure with Terraform, configure and harden it with Chef, and run both from the CI/CD pipeline so every environment gets the same security settings on every deploy.

It is a short, introductory talk: a clean explanation of how the two tools divide the work, not a live demo. If you have written a Terraform module that triggers a Chef run, you already know the shape. If you are still choosing how to combine provisioning and configuration management, it is a quick orientation.

## Why automate security infrastructure at all?

Jataprole starts with the Cloud Security Alliance figure that 93% of organisations have significant concerns about cloud security. His argument is the boring, correct one: manual deployment and management of security infrastructure is slow and error-prone, and the error rate grows with the estate. "As cloud environments grow, automation and tools like Terraform and Chef offer a scalable solution," Jataprole said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024.

Automation also earns its keep with compliance. His deck ties it to HIPAA and PCI DSS: when the policy is code, applying it consistently and proving you did both get easier.

## Who does what: Terraform or Chef?

The division of labour is the heart of the talk:

- **Terraform**, HashiCorp's open source infrastructure-as-code tool, provisions the resources: VMs, networks, storage, databases, security groups. The infrastructure is defined in code, version controlled and repeatable.
- **Chef** configures what Terraform built. Cookbooks and recipes describe the desired state, the Chef Server stores them, the Chef Client runs on each node to make it match, and developers write and test cookbooks on the Chef Workstation. That covers security patches, firewall rules and access policies.

He outlines three ways to wire them together. The plain one: Terraform provisions, then Chef configures. The reusable one: Terraform modules that call Chef cookbooks, so creating a VM and giving it the security baseline become one reusable building block. And Terraform's remote-exec provisioner running Chef commands on newly created instances. On top sits the CI/CD integration, so each deployment provisions and configures with the same standards applied.

## What does it buy you during an incident?

The incident management payoff is speed of remediation. When a vulnerability turns up, you change the cookbook or the module and push the fix across the fleet with Chef, while Terraform handles any infrastructure change such as a modified security group. No ticket queue of servers to patch by hand, no drift between production and staging because someone fixed only one.

The other benefits follow from the same idea: identical configurations across development, testing and production, fewer misconfigurations because nobody is applying policies from memory, and the ability to scale without loosening security to keep up.

## Where does it get hard?

His two case studies are short and come without numbers: a financial institution automating PCI DSS compliance across its cloud environment, which cut the time spent on compliance audits and manual configuration errors, and a healthcare organisation using the pair to keep HIPAA compliance with encryption and access controls deployed automatically.

The challenges slide is the part worth pinning to the wall: growing infrastructure complexity, secrets management (passwords and API keys must not end up in the code you just version controlled), compliance in dynamic environments, and the skills IaC demands. His remedies: modular design, automated compliance checks, and training the team.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to infrastructure as code, and security or compliance teams wondering how provisioning and configuration management fit together. Practitioners who run either tool in anger will want something more advanced.

Title: Conf42 Kube Native 2024: frugal clusters, VMs in pods, business dashboards
Description: The Conf42 Kube Native 2024 roundup - 31 talks on EKS cost, KubeVirt, GitOps at scale, schema migrations, business-driven monitoring and runtime security.
Body:
[Conf42 Kube Native 2024](https://www.conf42.com/kubenative2024) went out on September 26 with 31 talks, and it was a pragmatic one. Few speakers argued about whether to run Kubernetes; most were busy making it cheaper, moving the last virtual machines onto it, deploying across many clusters without losing track, and checking that the green dashboard means the business is actually working.

Speakers came from AWS, Wix, Netflix, CircleCI, Sysdig, Kubermatic, Kasten by Veeam, WSO2, Zilliz, Amadeus, The Trevor Project and a long list of smaller teams.

## How do you run Kubernetes without burning money?

[Piyush Mattoo and Dariush Azimi](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Piyush_Mattoo_Dariush_Azimi_karpenter_kubernetes_optimization) of AWS took Werner Vogels' Frugal Architect ideas to Amazon EKS: find underused resources, autoscale properly, mix Spot and Reserved Instances, and watch storage and network costs. [Chakkree Tipsupa](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Chakkree_Tipsupa_karpenter_kubernetes_scaling) of AWS went deeper on Karpenter for scaling, optimisation and upgrades, and [Yuriy Bezsonov](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Yuriy_Bezsonov_multicluster_kubernetes_gitops) of AWS showed GitOps patterns for production deployments across many clusters.

[Eddie Webbinaro and Moo Olaniyan](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Eddie_Webbinaro_Moo_Olaniyan_terraform_kubernetes_enterprise_demos) of CircleCI gave the best applied example. Their field engineering team deploys a full customer reference architecture to three AWS regions from scratch with custom Terraform modules and EKS, so a tailored enterprise demo can be requested across all clusters in under 15 minutes.

## What about everything that isn't a container yet?

[Koray Oksay and Batuhan Apaydin](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Koray_Oksay_Batuhan_Apaydin_kubevirt_vms_kubernetes_workloads) of Kubermatic opened with a CNCF survey figure: only 39% of respondents ran containers for most or all production applications. KubeVirt is their answer for the rest, running virtual machines alongside containers on one platform, with a getting-started path. [Daniil Fedotov](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Daniil_Fedotov_cloud_native_data_protection_organization) of Kasten by Veeam used Kubernetes tools to organise data protection across the many data services modern apps accumulate, and [Victor Onyenagubom](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Victor_Onyenagubom_data_security_encryption_kubernetes) covered encryption for data at rest and in transit.

[Rotem Tamir](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Rotem_Tamir_database_schema_reliable_migrations) of Ariga told a developer horror story, set on a sunny day in Tel Aviv, where a product manager asks for one new status on a user entity and the ORM migration goes wrong. His fix is database schema-as-code with Atlas, which detects risky migrations before they run.

## Is the dashboard lying to you?

[Or Rozenzweig](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Or_Rozenzweig_business_monitoring_pods_monitoring) of Wix argued that pod-level monitoring misses the failures users feel. "The way I see it, monitoring is the gift wrapper you put on before you ship the feature to production," Or Rozenzweig said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024. His talk builds a business-driven Grafana dashboard step by step, tracking KPIs instead of only latency and errors.

[Amir Krayden](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Amir_Krayden_decoding_incidents_troubleshooting) of Senser dissected a real Kubernetes failure to show why logs mislead without application and infrastructure metrics beside them. [Erwin de Keijzer](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Erwin_de_Keijzer_gitops_perses_dashboard_visualization) of TrueFullstaq demoed Perses, the GitOps-native dashboard tool for Prometheus, and [Siri Varma Vegiraju](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Siri_Varma_Vegiraju_multicloud_observability_simplification) of Microsoft argued for standard schemas and open source tools in multi-cloud observability.

## Securing the runtime

[Aleksandra Drobnjak](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Aleksandra_Drobnjak_kubernetes_security_falcosidekick_threat_detection) of Sysdig ran a hands-on threat detection session with Falcosidekick on a pre-built Kali Purple VM. [Venukumar Chirlawar](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Venukumar_Chirlawar_cloud_security_threat_detection_multilayered) of Amazon layered encryption, next-generation firewalls, WAFs, IDPS and SIEM for cloud security, and [Ravi Theja Kambhampati](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Ravi_Theja_Kambhampati_routing_switching_network_infrastructures) of Reailize covered routing and switching for resilient networks. [Pubudu Gunatilaka](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Pubudu_Gunatilaka_api_governance_kubernetes_api_management) of WSO2 used the Kubernetes Gateway API for API management.

## Developer experience on Kubernetes

[Anita Ihuman](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Anita_Ihuman_local_machine_mirror_dev_environment) of MetalBear showed remocal development, running local code against a real cluster without the rebuild-and-redeploy loop. [Leigh Capili](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Leigh_Capili_cloud_native_nix_development) of Flox gave a Nix primer for cloud-native nerds, with live demos and what he promised would be some performance art. [Anupama Pathirage](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Anupama_Pathirage_kubernetes_ballerina_deployments) of WSO2 used Ballerina to generate Dockerfiles and Kubernetes YAML from code, and [Abhinav Chunchu](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Abhinav_Chunchu_golang_k8s_development) of Lowes covered why Go and Kubernetes fit together.

Streaming had two contenders: [Mohamed Moussaoui](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Mohamed_Moussaoui_nats_cloudnative_kafka) of Amadeus pitched NATS against Kafka, and [Bobur Umurzokov](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Bobur_Umurzokov_jvm_kafka_streaming_data) of GlassFlow built streaming pipelines without the JVM or Kafka. [Tim Spann](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Tim_Spann_cloud_native_open_source_vector_databases) of Zilliz ran open source vector databases the cloud-native way for RAG and semantic search, and [Jubin Thomas](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Jubin_Thomas_order_management_scalable_microservices) of Signet Jewelers built order management from microservices.

## Kubernetes with a mission

[Paul Pham and Jesus Alfredo Pizana Espinosa](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Paul_Pham_Jesus_Alfredo_Pizana_Espinosa_argocd_kubernetes_crisis_intervention) of The Trevor Project gave the talk with the highest stakes. The nonprofit runs crisis services for LGBTQ+ young people by text, SMS and web chat, and used Argo CD, Kubernetes and Redis to expand those services to Mexico. Healthcare talks came from [Deepak Talasila](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Deepak_Talasila_ai_platforms_cost_transparency) of Google on cost transparency, [Shiva Kumar Chinnam](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Shiva_Kumar_Chinnam_healthcare_kubernetes_data_processing) of Rialtic on data processing and [Ram Meka](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Ram_Meka_artificial_intelligence_dialysis_healthcare) of Fresenius Medical Care on AI in dialysis care, with [Vishal Khadake](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Vishal_Khadake_nlp_kubernetes_applications) of HYR Global Source on NLP in Kubernetes-native apps.

Two talks stepped back from the cluster entirely. [Ramneet Bhatia](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Ramneet_Bhatia_engineering_launches_highimpact_leadership) of Netflix shared lessons from captaining the launch of paid sharing, and [Chris Gallivan](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Chris_Gallivan_flow_process_optimization) of Planview argued that the efficiency obsession has us looking for flow in all the wrong places.

Title: There is no smooth Azure migration, only a mitigated one
Description: Mahesh Thoutam (FM Global) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on picking an Azure migration strategy and moving in phases to keep incidents small
Body:
Every migration plan has a slide promising a smooth migration, and every engineer who has run one knows it is fiction. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Mahesh Thoutam, Senior Business Intelligence Developer at FM Global, says it out loud and builds his Azure migration advice around it: choose the right strategy per workload, migrate in phases, and validate at every step so the problems you will hit stay small.

"there is no term called smooth migration. We would be facing issues while doing this, but we can mitigate them," Thoutam said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024.

It is an introductory talk, a good map for a team about to start, not a war story. The abstract promises a 50% cost cut; the talk does not back that figure, so take the abstract with a grain of salt.

## Which of the five Rs fits your workload?

Thoutam opens with a Flexera figure: 83% of enterprise workloads expected in the cloud by the end of 2024, and plenty of organisations hitting unexpected costs, performance degradation and incompatibilities between legacy systems and the cloud on the way. His frame is the familiar set of strategies, with honest trade-offs:

- **Rehosting** (lift and shift): minimal changes, quick and low risk, a fast exit from the data centre. In his experience this suits smaller organisations with less data. The catch: you skip most of what the cloud offers.
- **Refactoring**: small changes to make an app cloud-ready, picking up platform services like Azure PaaS. Medium complexity.
- **Rearchitecting**: real rework, breaking monoliths into microservices. This is where cloud advantages start, and where the time and effort go up.
- **Rebuilding**: a new app from scratch on cloud-native services. Greatest benefit, greatest cost.
- **Replacing**: swapping a legacy app for a SaaS product on Azure. Good for non-core business apps.

The choice, he says, depends on application complexity, business criticality and how mature the organisation is in the cloud. Mixing strategies across a portfolio is the normal case.

## Plan before you lift anything

His planning phase has three parts. Workload evaluation: map dependencies, assess criticality, assign a strategy per workload. Skill assessment: find the gaps in the team's Azure knowledge and train or bring in an expert. Cost analysis: compare the current infrastructure bill with projected Azure costs and estimate ROI over the short and long term, which is also how you get stakeholders to sign off.

He refuses to put a timeline on the phases (plan and assess, design and prototype, reverse engineering, migration, testing, release), because it depends entirely on the organisation and its data. That is the honest answer, even if no project manager wants to hear it.

## Where do the incidents come from?

The incident management angle lives in the best practices. Phased migration first: move workloads in waves, test and validate each one before the next, so a failure hits one wave rather than the whole estate. Then security and compliance, assessing both on-premises and cloud environments, with Azure Security Center for monitoring. Then data integrity: audit and validate data before, during and after the move, with Azure Data Box for large transfers. His deck adds Azure Migrate for mapping application dependencies, so interconnected apps move together instead of one ending up on the wrong side of a slow network link.

Beyond the technical risks, the deck lists the human ones: teams afraid of change (answer with clear talk about reskilling and job security) and skill gaps (certifications or hiring). After the move come Azure Monitor and Application Insights with dashboards and alerts, auto-scaling, rightsizing and Reserved Instances, and regular Azure Advisor reviews. His case study, a Fortune 500 company that rehosted first and refactored gradually, reports a 20% cut in infrastructure costs and 35% better application response times.

## Who should watch

Teams early in an Azure migration who want a vocabulary and a checklist, and managers who need to explain why rehosting everything is not the end of the road. Seasoned cloud architects can skip it.

Title: Getting SAP HR off the office desktop and onto Fiori
Description: Lakshmi Gogula at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on moving legacy SAP HR to Fiori for security, mobile access and forms that guide the user
Body:
Legacy SAP HR screens were built for a clerk at a desk in a world that still had Internet Explorer. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Lakshmi Gogula, an SAP specialist working across ABAP, Gateway OData, SAPUI5, Fiori and BTP, walks through migrating those HR processes to SAP Fiori: a responsive UI, tighter security, and forms that steer people away from the mistakes that end up as support tickets.

Set expectations: this is a structured overview of the migration's goals and building blocks, not a case study with metrics. The abstract mentions a 40% engagement boost and 35% fewer errors; the talk itself does not come back to those numbers, so treat them as the abstract's claim.

## What is actually wrong with legacy SAP HR?

Gogula lists four problems and then the bill they run up. Interfaces designed decades ago with little thought for the user, so people get lost and make errors. Slow processing in recruitment, onboarding and performance reviews. Security built for an era when it mattered less. And no mobile access. "HR systems that can be accessed only from an office desktop are no longer sufficient," Gogula said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024.

The business cost follows: lower employee engagement, slow hiring that pushes good candidates away, breach risk, and HR staff spending their days working around the system instead of with it. That last one, she notes, does not scale as the company grows.

## What does the migration aim for?

Three goals: security and compliance with industry standards, a modern responsive UI, and self-explanatory forms that cut training time.

On security she covers encryption of data in transit and at rest, multi-factor authentication, and role-based access control, so that only authorised staff can read or change a given type of HR data. Her reasoning for RBAC is blunt: not everyone needs to see the same level of information. That is also the hook for GDPR compliance, which she treats as non-negotiable for anyone holding personal data.

The responsive part is the obvious win: the same Fiori app on desktop, tablet and phone, so a manager in an off-site meeting can approve a leave request from their phone and an employee on the road can apply for leave without waiting to be back at a desk.

## Forms that ask only what matters

The most practical thread is form design. Fiori forms guide users through multi-step processes and only ask for what is relevant given earlier answers; her example is a benefits application that adapts to previous selections. Fewer fields, fewer wrong formats, fewer calls to HR.

Onboarding is the worked use case. HR starts the process in a few clicks, the new hire gets a welcome email pointing to a mobile-friendly portal, and documents, signed forms and training modules all happen there, without a visit to the office.

## What sits under the hood?

On the back end, Gogula names the tooling: object-oriented ABAP, dialog programming and remote function calls (RFCs) to speed up key HR processes and cut resource use; service-oriented architecture and web services to exchange data in real time with time management, benefits administration and external vendors, replacing manual re-keying.

Two smaller items close it out. Internet Explorer's end is a forcing function: Fiori runs in Chrome, Firefox and Microsoft Edge, which also future-proofs the HR front end. And with SAP Floor Plan Manager and Adobe Forms, her team built dynamic forms that adapt to input, plus a custom utility that automatically delegates workflow tasks when the primary department admin is away, so approvals do not stall because one person is on holiday. For the incident management crowd, that small utility is the most relatable idea in the talk: a single point of failure, removed.

## Who should watch

SAP teams planning a move off SAP GUI-era HR transactions, and IT leads who need a checklist of what a Fiori migration should cover. If you already run Fiori in production, you will know most of this.

Title: Nix packages as container layers, and the 127-layer wall in between
Description: Leigh Capili (Flox) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on using Nix through Flox for reproducible dev environments, then as container layers
Body:
Containers turned a virtualization technology into our packaging format, and Leigh Capili thinks Nix can give it the packaging discipline it never had. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, the Senior DevRel Engineer at Flox (and long-time Kubernetes and Flux contributor) walks from workflow to artifact to runtime: reproducible dev environments with Flox, Nix-built container images, and a containerd snapshotter that bind-mounts Nix store paths instead of stacking overlay layers.

It opens with a rap about a broken `npm build` on a Tuesday after lunch, which is the most honest description of dependency drift you will hear at a conference.

## Why does Nix fix what package managers break?

Most package managers spread a package across the standard Unix hierarchy, so environments are hard to namespace: two versions of MySQL means two binaries fighting over `/usr/bin`. Nix hashes every package and stores it in its own folder in the Nix store, much like a container layer, then does the clever part of assembling those folders into a working environment by managing paths and the loader. The cost is a functional language that is notoriously hard to use. Capili is candid about it: Nix is "fully declarative", but "hard to get into and honestly, pretty academic", and the stack traces are "super gnarly".

Flox is the open-source answer (GPLv2, written in Rust, `github.com/flox/flox`): a package manager on top of Nix with friendlier verbs, installable from Brew, apt, RPM or a plain Nix install. Windows users get it through WSL, since Nix itself does not run on Windows.

## Imperative commands, declarative manifest

The first demo looks ordinary: `flox list`, `flox remove go`, `flox install go`. The point is underneath. Every imperative command edits a manifest, which immediately produces a lock file with everything needed for a bit-for-bit reproducible package, an idea he says Flox "pretty much stole" from language package managers. Commit the `.flox/` folder and a teammate, a CI runner or a systemd unit gets the same environment.

He shows it with a Terraform repo whose commit adds OpenTofu, plus a hook that runs `tofu init` on `flox activate`. On his Apple Silicon Mac it activates OpenTofu 1.8.2 on Darwin ARM64; then he SSHes into an ROG Ally running WSL and gets the same version, natively built for Linux AMD64. No containers, just subshells, environment variables and read-only folders. The demo also hits a `PATH` ordering surprise live, which makes it more convincing, not less.

His favourite metaphor: a globally installed Google Cloud SDK is a table saw left plugged in next to your soldering bench. Put it in an environment, and when you `exit`, you can no longer spend money.

## Docker Compose without the containers

The best demo is a RAG app from `flox/floxenvs`: Python, a Weaviate vector database, Ollama and the Verba UI, declared as services in the TOML manifest. Capili said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 that it feels "a lot like Docker Compose, but with no containers". The trick Compose does not have: open several shells into the environment, and when the last one closes, the services stop. No idle databases eating your battery, and the processes run natively on the Mac's own chip instead of a pretend Linux box.

## Where do containers come back in?

`flox containerize` (Linux only for now) turns an environment into an OCI image with each Nix dependency as its own layer. Both container layers and Nix store paths are content-addressed, so in theory every Nix package could live in an OCI registry once, fully deduplicated, with no thirty copies of bash across thirty images.

Then the kernel says no. OverlayFS tops out around 127 layers, so Flox caps at 99 to leave room for your own layers, and past that it has to heuristically merge packages, which wrecks the cache-hit ratio.

The fix he demos comes from PDT Partners: nix-snapshotter, a containerd plugin. On a NixOS box, `nerdctl info` lists Nix next to native and overlayfs storage. containerd then asks the Nix daemon for store paths and bind-mounts them into the container. Bind-mounts are cheap, and by his rough research recent kernels allow around a hundred thousand of them.

## The bigger bet

The closing argument is speculative and clearly labelled as such: Nix packages stored natively in OCI registries, builds that push a tagged manifest of a few kilobytes, a hundred Kubernetes nodes with deduplicated access and no pull delay, maybe a non-conflicting layer snapshotter that does not need a Nix daemon everywhere. He talks about deduplicating your Elastic Container Registry account or shrinking your Harbor disks. `flox build` with pure builds and private catalogs were still under construction at the time.

## Who should watch

Platform and Kubernetes engineers tired of "works on my machine", and anyone curious about Nix who bounced off the language. It is a Flox talk from a Flox engineer, heavy on live demos, and honest about what was not finished yet.

Title: Your false positives start with trusting the label on the API
Description: Rob Quiros (Caber Systems) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on tracing data lineage through API payloads to make access control deterministic
Body:
A SOC that sees 95 false alarms out of every 100 is not doing detection, it is doing triage for a living. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Rob Quiros, CEO and co-founder of Caber Systems, argues the root cause is architectural: we guard the APIs and hope that tells us something about the data inside them. His fix is to identify the data itself, byte sequence by byte sequence, so that a breach shows up as a plain authorization failure instead of a chain of indicators.

Fair warning on scope: this is a founder presenting the approach his company built. It is also one of the clearer explanations of why data-in-use access control is hard, and the first half stands on its own.

## Why are there so many false positives?

Quiros opens with the SANS 2023 incident response survey: a 95% false positive rate, up 20% since 2019, while teams still missed about a fifth of real incidents. Companies collectively spend around $60 billion on tools that raise indicators of compromise, and an indicator is not a compromise. A real incident is a hit to the confidentiality, integrity or availability of data, so why not watch the data directly?

Because, he says, we only can at rest. On a storage system, data, owner and permissions sit together. The moment an API copies that data into a service, the ownership and permissions stay behind. From then on we control access to the API and treat it as a proxy for the data.

His metaphor is a bag labelled sand. The gateway checks the label; nobody checks the bag. "There's no correlation between API parameters and what the data is inside, who owns that data, and who can access it," Quiros said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. His verdict on zero trust network access: "It's infinite trust zero access, because that's what we're doing." DLP gets no better marks: it tells you a payload looks like PII, never whether it is your PII or mine.

## Three problems that make this hard

He names three, and they are worth stealing for any architecture review:

1. **APIs don't carry permissions.** Data gets copied service to service and its ownership is dropped on the first hop.
2. **Service accounts hide the end user.** The front end authenticates the user, then calls the back end with its own broad credentials. Storage never learns who will finally see the data: the confused deputy problem.
3. **APIs move chunks, not objects.** The same byte sequence lives in many documents with different policies, so you cannot tell from the bytes which policy applies.

Generative AI gets all three at once. Documents go into a vector database without their permissions, chunks from different owners get mixed into one RAG response, and even copying permissions fails because a deduplicated chunk ends up carrying the policy of whichever document it was seen in last.

## eDRM, BeyondProd, or lineage tracing?

Quiros compares three architectures. Enterprise digital rights management encrypts per object, which works until a service extracts a chunk and every chunk needs its own re-encryption and key distribution. Google's BeyondProd plus Zanzibar passes data permissions down and user credentials up through every microservice, so each hop can authorise. It is the right design, he says, but it meant re-engineering Google's services, and most enterprises running hundreds of open source and third-party services cannot do that.

Caber's option is data lineage tracing without code changes. It runs content-defined chunking over API payloads in a time window, finds payloads and stored objects that share chunks, and builds a map of which sequence came from which source. Time-series analysis, event ordering and pruning of impossible paths narrow that map down to the sequences whose permissions are known. It needs two or more observation points, since one place alone tells you only what data looks like.

## What did the demo show?

An alert: user Bob accessed data owned by Amy, matched on 7 byte sequences out of about 10,000 in her document. The call graph then showed the path: Amy uploads through a Nextcloud-style service into an S3 bucket, another service extracts text and writes it into a shared bucket, and Bob sees a preview. Every step was individually authorised. End to end, it was a leak, and the graph points at the service to stop.

The second demo applies the same idea to RAG over Apple 10-Q filings, treating 2024 as material non-public information. Most of the text overlaps across years, so only the sequences unique to 2024 get redacted before they reach the LLM for an ordinary user, while the CFO gets the full answer.

He is upfront that this rests on hashes, so collisions are possible, at a probability he puts around 0.00001%, against 95% false positives today.

## Who should watch

Security engineers and incident responders drowning in alerts, and anyone building RAG over documents with real permissions. The framing of the three hard problems is useful on its own; the product half shows one way through them.

Title: Zero trust means the breach stays in one room
Description: Samikya Reddy Balguri (Caterpillar) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on zero trust - continuous verification, microsegmentation, least privilege
Body:
The perimeter model has one job and one failure mode: once someone is inside, they can walk anywhere. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Samikya Reddy Balguri, Principal Application Security Engineer at Caterpillar, gave a structured introduction to zero trust architecture: why the perimeter stopped making sense, the principles that replace it (never trust, always verify; microsegmentation; least privilege), the tools that implement it, and what makes rollouts hard.

It is a primer rather than a war story, a good first talk on zero trust for engineers and incident responders who want the vocabulary and the moving parts in one place.

## Why did the perimeter stop working?

Remote workforces, SaaS applications and IoT devices connect and disconnect constantly, so the network is no longer a neatly defined space. Attackers get in through weak VPN configurations, poorly secured APIs or a single compromised IoT device, and in a traditional setup one compromised system can cost you the whole network through lateral movement.

Zero trust flips the basis of trust from network location to identity, device posture and context. "Zero trust is not just about keeping the bad guys out, it's about constantly questioning who and what is allowed in and why," Samikya Reddy Balguri said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024.

## What does never trust, always verify mean in practice?

Every access request is evaluated on multiple factors wherever it comes from, and verification doesn't stop at login. The session is checked continuously against device health, location and behaviour: is the device jailbroken, is it patched and on a current OS, is the request coming from an unusual location, does the user's access pattern match their normal one? She calls this a risk-based access control model.

Microsegmentation breaks the network into small isolated zones with traffic inspected between them, virtual firewalls inside the environment. If a threat gets into one segment, it stays there. Least privilege, which she calls non-negotiable, limits what an attacker can do with any access they do gain. For incident responders, those two together are the difference between containing an intrusion and rebuilding the network.

## What are the building blocks?

Her four components:

- **Identity and access management**: MFA tied to a central identity provider, and SSO with continuous re-evaluation throughout the session.
- **Microsegmentation**: software-defined networking (SDN) or network access control (NAC) to put micro-perimeters around databases, applications and individual workloads instead of one flat network.
- **Behavioural analytics**: machine learning watching how users and devices access resources, not just who, to raise alerts before a breach.
- **Policy enforcement points**: checkpoints at the network, application and user layers where traffic is validated against policy, using next-gen firewalls, IDS/IPS and secure web gateways.

## How do you roll it out?

Start with identity, because passwords alone aren't enough and MFA is the cheapest big win. Then segment, with tools such as VMware NSX or Cisco Application Centric Infrastructure for software-defined policies on which workloads may talk to each other. Her example: finance has no business talking to the HR system unless it is absolutely necessary. Then enforce policy at every layer, using orchestration from vendors such as Palo Alto Networks or Fortinet so policies update automatically as threats emerge.

## What makes it hard?

She is direct about the friction. Users and IT staff push back on continuous authentication because it feels cumbersome, so education matters. Legacy systems were not designed for zero trust and may need upgrades or workarounds like virtual patching and network-level access controls. Continuous verification adds latency if the infrastructure isn't built for the extra checks. And the cost covers technology, training, processes and sometimes a network redesign.

Looking further out, she expects AI to adjust policies dynamically as threats emerge, blockchain-based decentralised identity to remove single points of failure, quantum-resistant encryption to become necessary, and zero trust to stretch to cloud and edge. Her adoption examples are general: US government agencies using it against insider threats, and finance and healthcare companies reporting fewer breaches, with GDPR and HIPAA pushing in the same direction. The talk doesn't put numbers on those results, so take it as the conceptual map rather than a business case.

## Who should watch

Engineers and incident responders new to zero trust, and teams about to start an IAM or segmentation project who want the full picture first. Security architects already running a zero trust programme will know the material.

Title: A class should be fireable by exactly one executive
Description: Arpit Gaur (Microsoft) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on SOLID principles as loose-coupling rules for any code, not just OOP, with C# examples
Body:
How small is a single responsibility, exactly? Arpit Gaur, Principal Engineer at Microsoft, has a test you won't forget: a class should only be fireable by one C-level executive. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024 he walked through all five SOLID principles with C# examples, argued that they are general loose-coupling rules rather than an object-oriented thing, and showed an anonymised e-commerce refactor where adopting them cut the bug count by 40%.

It is a classic, well-paced refresher with memorable analogies, aimed at engineers who know the acronym and want it to stick.

## Who is the code for?

His starting point: machines have become fast and efficient, so readability is the real constraint. "We are not writing the code for machines," Arpit Gaur said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. We are writing it for teammates and for our future selves two to six months from now, so a change in one component must not break something five steps down the control flow.

He credits the principles to Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob) and the acronym to Michael Feathers, and repeats throughout that they apply to functions, modules, classes and services alike.

## S and O - one boss, and new shapes without surgery

The single responsibility example is an Employee class that calculates pay, saves to the database and generates reports. Pay belongs to the CFO, persistence to the CTO, reporting to the CEO or COO: three executives who could fire you over one class. The fix splits it into Employee, EmployeeRepository and ReportGenerator, each doing one job well. The hard part, he admits, is choosing the granularity, and the executive test is his heuristic.

For open/closed, an AreaCalculator with overloads for rectangle and circle has to be modified for every new shape, because a triangle's base and height mean nothing to it. Put a calculate-area method on an IShape interface and a triangle becomes a new class, with the risk of breaking existing features close to zero.

## L - the square is not a rectangle, at least not in code

The Liskov example is the classic square that overrides a rectangle's width and height setters, which quietly breaks any code expecting a rectangle. His analogy is the best line in the talk: when a couple divorces, their lawyers are not getting divorced themselves. Classes are representatives of real-world things, and the relationship between a real square and a real rectangle doesn't have to hold between their classes. Make both implement IShape with their own dimensions, and swapping one for the other returns the right area instead of a surprise.

## I and D - robots don't eat, and engines don't weld to chassis

Interface segregation: a robot worker forced to implement a human IWorker interface with work, eat and sleep ends up with not-implemented exceptions and awkward tests. Split into Workable, Eatable and Sleepable, and the robot implements only what it does. He points out that Java has spent roughly the last decade splitting its own big interfaces into smaller ones.

Dependency inversion: a CustomerService that depends directly on a SqlCustomerRepository has to be opened up the day you move to DynamoDB, MongoDB or Cassandra. Depend on an ICustomerRepository instead and the new database is a new class. His analogies are an IDE that shouldn't crash because one small vendor's plugin has a bug, and an engine connected to the chassis through standard cables rather than welded in.

## Does it pay off in production?

His case study is an e-commerce platform that started as a small monolith selling books on the internet, anonymised from his decade at Amazon. Tight coupling made changes risky and caused outages, and developers stopped refactoring for fear of breaking things. The refactor applied each principle: SRP to split product catalog, order management and payment processing, OCP for pluggable payment gateways (cards, bank transfers, one-time cards, cash on delivery, per country), DIP to decouple business logic from the move from Oracle SQL to in-house SQL and NoSQL stores. The slides give the results: bug count down 40%, new feature development time down 30%, and better developer morale.

He then maps SOLID onto the cloud: small Lambda or Azure Functions doing one job, easier unit tests, a better fit for TDD and safer CI/CD.

## When not to use it

His pitfalls section is worth the price of admission. Don't force SOLID into everything, and if a simple codebase gives you no trouble, leave it alone. "Don't fix what isn't broken," he says, and don't build ten interfaces for ten classes around a function that will never change. Tech debt can't be avoided, only kept low.

## Who should watch

Mid-level engineers who want SOLID explained with examples they can repeat in a code review, and seniors looking for better analogies for their juniors. Those who already teach SOLID will mostly come away with the CXO test and the divorce lawyers.

Title: Run one service on your laptop and let the cluster think it is home
Description: Anita Ihuman (MetalBear) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on remote-to-local Kubernetes development with mirrord, cutting the build-push-deploy loop
Body:
The slowest part of Kubernetes development is usually not the code but the containerise, push, deploy and wait that follows every one-line change. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Anita Ihuman, Developer Advocate at MetalBear, makes the case for remote-to-local development, which she calls remocal, where the one service you are editing runs on your laptop while everything it depends on stays in the cluster, and demos it with MetalBear's open source mirrord.

It is a vendor talk in the sense that MetalBear builds mirrord, but the tool is open source and the first half is a fair comparison of the development setups most teams already use.

## Why is the inner loop so long?

"We all know that developers hate bugs, right? But there is something developers hate more than bugs, and that is slow development cycles," Anita Ihuman said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024. For a cloud application, a change has to be built, containerised, run in a cluster, checked against every other component and then deployed, with the risk of breaking production at the end. With tens to hundreds of microservices, many dependencies and several developers working in parallel, that loop repeats across services until the errors stop.

She lists the costs: lengthy rebuilds and redeployments, suboptimal testing with mocks that only approximate production and miss compatibility, performance and security problems, and growing dependence on DevOps teams, who end up fixing a shared staging environment that everyone deploys untested code to.

## What is wrong with all-local or all-remote?

Fully local environments are fast and keep your favourite debugging tools, but they run on limited laptop resources, need constant upkeep of API scripts and mock data, and bring the classic works-on-my-machine problem when libraries depend on a specific processor architecture.

Fully remote development environments take load off laptops and push workflow logic into CI/CD, but every change still means containerising, pushing to a registry and deploying to the cluster before you see the effect. Debugging gets frustrating, and a cloud environment per developer drives up cloud costs.

Remocal is the hybrid: run the microservice you are working on locally, keep services, databases and dependencies remote. You get production-like conditions, your own IDE and fast feedback, and the team can share one environment instead of paying for one each.

## How does mirrord pull it off?

mirrord comes as a CLI and as an IDE plugin, and has two parts. The mirrord agent runs as a pod in the cluster, in the same network namespace as the pod you target, so it can reach that pod's network, file system and databases. The mirrord layer sits in the memory of your local process, intercepts low-level functions and redirects them to the agent. Your local code behaves as if it were running in the cluster, against real data.

The practical claims she makes: no root access needed on your machine, the agent only lives for the session and removes itself afterwards, startup takes a couple of seconds, you can run several local processes each attached to a different remote pod, and it does not care whether the cluster uses a service mesh or a VPN.

## The demo: a weather app, edited live

The demo is a small Python weather app that calls an API for the city you type. Ihuman changes the page title to Anita's weather application and the prompt text, then opens a `mirrord.json` that targets the weather-app deployment and sets mirrord to steal its traffic rather than mirror it. She starts a debug session from the IDE, mirrord creates the agent, and a fresh browser tab on the cluster's address shows the new title, still fetching real weather for Texas and a city in Nigeria. Nothing was built or pushed, and anyone hitting that URL sees the local change.

`kubectl get pods` shows the mirrord agent running next to the deployment; stopping the debugger makes the agent terminate itself. Her proposed loop: code and test on staging with mirrord, open a PR once it looks good, then let automated tests, staging and end-to-end checks take over, with less time spent on mocks and a lower chance of failure late.

One thing worth thinking through before you copy it: stealing traffic on a shared environment means everyone on that URL sees your work in progress, which is great for a demo and a team conversation in real life.

## Who should watch

Developers on microservice teams whose inner loop runs through a CI pipeline, platform teams building golden paths and arguing about per-developer environments, and anyone who has spent a lunch break waiting for an image push. Teams already using a similar tool will get a clear comparison of the trade-offs.
