Title: AI can pay a life insurance claim faster, never fully alone
Description: Praveen Kumar (AllianzLife) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on AI and ML for life and annuities claims processing and consumer behaviour analysis
Body:
A life insurance claim arrives at the worst possible moment for the family filing it, and then waits in a queue of manual reviews. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Praveen Kumar, Practice Lead at AllianzLife, gave an industry overview of where AI and machine learning cut that wait in the life and annuities business, and where they help predict what customers want next. His case study: AI document automation cut claims resolution time by 40%, from weeks to days.

It is a business-side talk, framed for people who know the insurance value chain, with no architecture or model details.

## What are life insurers struggling with?

He names three pressures. Claims processing involves manual tasks, paper documentation and multiple layers of review before anything is paid, which brings delays, errors and unhappy beneficiaries. Consumer expectations are shifting quickly, and insurers struggle to gather and analyse enough data to personalise their offers. And the cost of insurance, which he describes as what it costs a company to acquire a customer and issue a policy, is squeezed by administrative costs, regulation and competition; those overheads should not end up loaded onto the policyholder.

## Where does AI fit in a claim?

In his description, the path from claim receipt to approval can be automated: extract data from the claim documents, validate it and route it for approval. Machine learning looks for patterns in claims data to detect inconsistencies and potential fraud, and predictive models use historical data, such as the policyholder's medical history, to anticipate claim outcomes.

The important caveat is human review. "There is never a complete 100 percent automation, but there is always a human factor involved," Praveen Kumar said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. Suspicious cases are flagged for a person, not denied by a model. In a business where a wrong decision lands on a grieving family or a regulator's desk, that is the only sane design.

The operational effects he lists follow from that: less manual data entry, document classification and claim assessment, fewer errors and faster processing, lower claims-handling costs, and fraud caught in real time early in the process rather than at the end.

## What does AI tell insurers about customers?

The consumer side rests on three ideas. Pattern recognition: ML sifts through customer data to find trends in buying behaviour, payment patterns and product preferences, and how those move between two points in time. Personalisation: customised product recommendations, policy terms and pricing, which also reduce what insurers spend on marketing to acquire customers. Proactive engagement: predicting future needs so insurers can offer services before the customer asks.

On the service side, he points to round-the-clock chatbots and virtual assistants, so a customer with a question at night doesn't wait for the next business day, and to retention as the payoff of more relevant service.

## Do the case studies hold up?

He presents two anonymised examples. A large life insurer implemented AI-powered document automation for claims, automating extraction, validation and classification, and reduced claims resolution times by 40%, with operational costs down 30% and processing cut from several weeks to a few days. A second company used machine learning on payment history, demographics and purchase patterns to personalise product offerings and saw a 20% increase in customer retention. No company names or methodology are given, and the percentage figures in the abstract on claims accuracy go beyond what the talk itself presents.

## Where should an insurer start?

His adoption roadmap has four steps. Start where the impact is highest, which he says is claims processing and customer analytics. Build a data strategy first, because any AI or machine learning model is only as good as its data, and collect and manage that data in a compliant and ethical way. Build capabilities in-house or with vendors. Then monitor, test and tune the systems continuously so they stay aligned with business goals.

## Who should watch

Product, operations and IT people in insurance looking for a structured overview to frame an AI programme, and engineers new to the domain who want to understand the claims and annuities value chain. Engineers looking for implementation detail or model evaluation will not find it here.

Title: Ballerina writes the Dockerfile and the Kubernetes YAML for you
Description: Anupama Pathirage (WSO2) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on Ballerina generating Docker and Kubernetes artifacts straight from integration code
Body:
What if the compiler that already knows your service's ports and resource paths also wrote its Dockerfile and Kubernetes manifests, and refused to build when your readiness probe pointed at the wrong path? At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Anupama Pathirage, Director of Engineering at WSO2, where she leads Ballerina development and developer relations, shows how the open source Ballerina language takes an integration service from code to a running Kubernetes deployment without anyone hand-writing YAML.

It is a tour of a language her team builds, so expect a product tour: the first half covers Ballerina's development tooling, the second half is a live demo from VS Code to Rancher Desktop.

## Why should the application developer care about deployment?

Pathirage's opening argument is that development and deployment are no longer separate jobs. Cloud integration means many services and APIs working together, highly dynamic environments with containers and autoscaling, configuration overhead for scaling and monitoring, and security and compliance across all of it. If the developer has to think about all that anyway, the language may as well help.

## What makes Ballerina different from another general-purpose language?

Ballerina, developed by WSO2 since 2016 and first released in February 2022, is optimised for integration. Its syntax sits in the C, Java and Go family, but its abstractions target three things integrations always fight with: data (shape, manipulation, communication), network (clients and services over different protocols) and concurrency. "The compiler itself can detect some data races during the compile time," Anupama Pathirage said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024, which matters because integration applications are inherently concurrent.

The tooling list is long. Every program gets an automatic, editable sequence diagram in the VS Code plugin, so a service that reads from GitHub and writes to Google Sheets shows both endpoints at a glance. There are graphical designers for REST and GraphQL services, a visual data mapper over Ballerina's record type (the canonical representation for JSON, XML and the rest), documentation generated from code comments, a persist module that works like an ORM over databases, Redis, Google Sheets or in-memory stores, and more than 600 connectors, with an OpenAPI tool to generate new ones from a spec. AI features include GitHub Copilot awareness of the syntax, an assistant that generates unit tests and documentation, and an automap feature for the data mapper.

## From `bal build` to a running pod

The deployment story is the point of the talk. `bal build` produces a self-contained JAR. Add `--cloud=docker` and you get a Dockerfile and image with the required dependencies; add `--cloud=k8s` and you get Kubernetes artifacts too. A `Cloud.toml` file adjusts what is generated at build time, and because the compiler understands resources, configurable variables and service definitions in the code, the output matches the application.

Observability comes along without extra code: every Ballerina program is observable by OpenTelemetry tools, with metrics in Prometheus and Grafana, tracing in Jaeger or Zipkin, and logging through the Elastic Stack.

## The demo: a hotel booking service

The demo is a hotel reservation backend that takes booking requests from a web portal, checks room availability with a room service, transforms the data (first and last name merged in the data mapper) and returns confirmed reservations. `bal run` starts it locally on port 9090, and curl and the built-in Try It view hit the rooms and bookings resources.

Then the useful bit. Pathirage adds a readiness resource, declares a readiness probe in `Cloud.toml` with the base path `/hotel`, and runs the Kubernetes build. It fails: the probe path in the config does not match the resource function name, and the compiler catches it. One fix later, the target directory holds a Dockerfile and a Kubernetes YAML with the service, replicas, image name and the readiness probe with a 30-second initial delay. Applied to Rancher Desktop, the service comes up behind a NodePort, and the same requests now succeed through the cluster. No YAML typed by hand.

## Who should watch

Integration developers tired of maintaining manifests next to their code, platform teams weighing how much deployment knowledge to push onto application developers, and anyone curious about a language that treats services and network clients as first-class syntax. If your stack is settled on Java or Go with Helm charts, watch for the idea of compiler-checked deployment config rather than the language itself.

Title: The billing system is the heart of a utility, so replace it carefully
Description: Rajesh Kolli (ykunt inc) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on modernising a utility's customer information system, with Kansas City BPU's Catapult project
Body:
When a utility's billing system misbehaves, thousands of households find out on the same day. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Rajesh Kolli (ykunt inc) walked through why utilities replace their legacy customer information systems (CIS), what a modern one has to connect to, and how the Board of Public Utilities in Kansas City ran its Catapult project, which moved head-end, meter data management, CIS and asset management systems off legacy software in one programme.

One note on scope: the abstract promises an AI-driven case study and efficiency forecasts, but the talk itself is mainly about CIS modernisation. AI and analytics show up as things a modern platform makes possible (demand forecasting, predictive maintenance), not as models the speaker built. Watch it for how a utility's core systems fit together.

## What does a CIS actually do?

The CIS is the system that runs customer interactions, billing and services, and it centralises customer data so the rest of the utility can work from one source. In a modern setup, smart meters feed usage data through meter data management into billing with no human in the loop. "So everything is automated from the grid to the billing system," Rajesh Kolli said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. Customers, meanwhile, expect to check usage, see their bill and pay from their phones.

He also explains a constraint most software engineers never think about: US public utilities answer to regulators who approve their rate structures, so any change that adds a financial burden on customers goes through a formal process, and the CIS has to implement whatever rate structure is approved.

## Why do legacy systems hold utilities back?

His list of legacy problems is familiar from any old enterprise platform: scalability limits as data and customer base grow, siloed systems without real-time communication, inefficient workflows (he describes ten clicks to reach the information needed to answer a customer), rising maintenance costs, and security weaknesses against modern threats. Many still run on-premises with in-house server, admin and DevOps staff handling every installation and upgrade, and long response times during high-demand periods hurt customer satisfaction.

## The CIS sits in the middle of everything

The architectural point is integration. A modern CIS connects to meter data management (MDM), which collects and processes the meter readings first, to GIS and CRM, and to asset management such as IBM Maximo for meters, inventory and crews during outages. Smart meters and IoT devices generate enough data that some checks, such as meter voltage tests, no longer need a technician sent out from the depot.

Real-time analytics on top of that data supports peak demand management. His example is a big NFL game when everyone is home at once; with forecasting from smart device data, a utility can reward customers for using less energy during peak times. The same platform handles net metering, where customers with their own solar panels feed surplus into the grid and draw from it when they need more.

## How do you replace it without a blackout in billing?

The upgrade process he describes is deliberately unglamorous:

- **Assessment**: evaluate weaknesses and bottlenecks, collect pain points from end users, find regulatory and compliance gaps.
- **Planning**: a technology roadmap, resource allocation, and goals aligned with the board's strategic priorities.
- **Implementation**: phased, functionality moved over piece by piece before the final cutover, with data migration planned so nothing is lost or corrupted.
- **Training and support**: billing clerks, MDM analysts and business users trained, with regression test cases run before go-live.
- **Risk mitigation**: a separate team identifying risks and their operational impact during the transition.

## What changed after Catapult?

The outcomes he reports are mostly qualitative: reduced processing times through automated workflows, faster query resolution with customer data at hand, data-driven demand forecasting, cost savings from modern infrastructure, better collaboration between departments and faster onboarding. The one number he gives is billing: issues from the daily billing cycles dropped by more than 50 to 60 percent with the new system, which he credits to data availability, accuracy and dashboards.

Looking ahead, he expects the modern CIS to absorb EV charging stations, more renewable sources and new regulations through incremental upgrades rather than another big-bang replacement.

## Who should watch

Engineers and IT leaders in utilities or other regulated industries planning a core-system replacement, and anyone curious how meter data actually becomes a bill. Those looking for AI architecture should pick a different talk.

Title: Hack your own minikube and watch Falcosidekick catch you doing it
Description: Aleksandra Drobnjak (Sysdig) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on runtime Kubernetes threat detection with Falco and Falcosidekick in a ready-made Kali Purple lab
Body:
The quickest way to believe in runtime detection is to attack a cluster yourself and see the alert appear seconds later. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Aleksandra Drobnjak, Customer Solutions Engineer at Sysdig, hands viewers a pre-built Kali Purple virtual machine with minikube, Kubernetes Goat and Falcosidekick installed, and walks through a few attacks, from a simple exec into a pod to a Metasploit-made root shell, with Falco flagging each step.

It is a hands-on lab more than a lecture: a short slide intro to Falco, then a live session in the VM. Drobnjak works for Sysdig, whose commercial threat detection engine is built on Falco, but everything in the lab is open source.

## Why runtime detection, if you already scan for CVEs?

Her point is that not every attacker needs a CVE. Some exploit identities that ignore least privilege, some exploit compliance drift that a point-in-time report misses, and some are insiders, like a candidate who looks good on paper, interviews well and has a malicious intent. Traditional event management tooling was not built for Kubernetes events and short-lived container logs, so you need eyes on what containers actually do at runtime.

## How Falco and Falcosidekick fit together

Falco, a CNCF graduated project, hooks into the Linux kernel through a kernel module or an eBPF probe, collects system calls, and applies rules (filters for the behaviour you care about) in user space. Each event is tagged with container attributes (ID, name, image repository, tags) and Kubernetes attributes such as namespace and pod name. The rules catch early signs of an attack across the MITRE ATT&CK framework: reconnaissance scripts, privilege escalation, log and shell history deletion, binaries downloaded into containers, exfiltration attempts, and the mass file renaming of ransomware campaigns.

Falco on its own ships only a handful of output destinations. "It can fan out Falco's output to over 60 destinations," Aleksandra Drobnjak said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 of Falcosidekick, across web, chat ops, logging, streaming, alerting and observability platforms. The lab uses Falcosidekick UI, a web view of events by rule, severity and tag, with Swagger docs for API queries.

## What is in the lab VM?

The VM runs Kali Purple, the defensive Kali project structured around the NIST framework's identify, protect, detect, respond and recover. On top: tools for a local Kubernetes cluster, Kubernetes Goat (an intentionally misconfigured learning platform), Kubenomicon (offensive and defensive Kubernetes techniques with practical commands, building on Microsoft's Kubernetes threat matrix), Nmap and Metasploit, and Atomic Red Team tests to simulate ATT&CK-style attacks.

Her setup tips save time: start minikube with about 2 GB less RAM than the VM has (16 GB on her 20+ GB VM, try not to go below 8 GB) and at least two vCPUs, and if Kubernetes Goat pods land in error state, run its teardown and setup scripts again.

## Three attacks, three alerts

First, the Kubenomicon exec-inside-container technique: `kubectl exec` into a pod in the secure-middleware namespace, and Falcosidekick UI reports a terminal shell in a container with the default rules.

Second, the Kubernetes Goat RBAC least-privilege misconfiguration scenario, the classic case of a team granting more than it needs. From inside a pod, the API server address comes out of environment variables, a service account token turns up, and Falco reports that the Kubernetes API server was contacted from a container. Feeding the token to Metasploit's Kubernetes modules shows one token limited to get, list and watch in a single namespace; a second token allows every action on every resource across all namespaces. The exec exploit module then creates a new pod and drops her into a root shell, and the pod creation shows up in the UI.

Third, an Atomic Red Team rootkit test from a pod triggers another default rule. The lesson across all three is that the default Falco ruleset already covers a lot of the noisy first steps attackers take.

## Where to go after the lab

Her next step is Falco Talon, the response engine for Falco detections, which can invoke an AWS Lambda function, enforce a Kubernetes network policy, or label a suspicious pod or terminate it. She also points to Sysdig's free Falco training for writing your own rules, and the Falco Slack community.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers and SREs who run Kubernetes and have never seen what their cluster looks like to an attacker, security engineers new to containers, and anyone preparing for a Kubernetes security certification. Bring a machine that can spare a lot of RAM if you want to follow along.

Title: Three ways to build AIOps on AWS, from flip-a-switch to DIY
Description: Indika Wimalasuriya (Virtusa) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 compares CloudWatch, a data lake with SageMaker, and DevOps Guru for AIOps on AWS
Body:
Static thresholds assume your system behaves the same at 3am on a Sunday as at noon on Black Friday. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Indika Wimalasuriya, Associate Director and Senior Systems Engineering Manager at Virtusa and an AWS Community Builder in cloud operations, laid out three ways to replace them with AIOps on AWS: lean on CloudWatch's built-in anomaly detection, build your own data lake with SageMaker models on top, or switch on DevOps Guru and let it baseline the account. Each trades effort for control in a different place.

## Why are incidents going up, not down?

He opens with a puzzle. The State of Digital Operations study for 2024 found a 13% year-over-year increase in customer-facing incidents, despite everything the industry has learned. His explanation is the shift from monoliths to microservices, on-prem to cloud, servers to serverless: more data sources, more data, and an exponential rise in failure scenarios through dependencies.

The OpsRamp AIOps study he cites says what enterprises want from AIOps: 58% see anomaly detection as a key benefit, about 60% want less noise and more accurate data, around 51% want better root cause analysis and a similar share better dependency understanding, and half want lower MTTR. Thresholds, he argues, are never static; what you need is a baseline and an alert when it is breached.

## Eliminate, detect, resolve

His model of AIOps has three jobs. First, predictive maintenance: catch the small, not-yet-impactful behaviour changes before they snowball into an outage. "There's nothing great about picking something after it has happened," Indika Wimalasuriya said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. Second, being realistic that some incidents will get through, detect them fast with intelligent alerting. Third, resolve them quickly, ideally with self-healing.

## Approach one - use what CloudWatch already does

The observability-based approach is the easiest. Instrument with the CloudWatch agent and OpenTelemetry for metrics, logs and traces, then build on CloudWatch's stack: dashboards, SLOs, Container Insights, Lambda Insights, Logs Insights, Application Signals, CloudWatch RUM and synthetic tests. The AIOps payload is metric anomaly detection (most alerting is metric-based), log anomaly detection for new errors and spikes, Application Signals using ML to spot behaviour changes, and natural-language query generation. If you have built observability properly, he says, these native features give a solid AIOps platform without much extra work.

## Approach two - your own data lake and models

The data lake approach is the opposite end. Land all telemetry in Amazon S3 (logs, metrics, traces, events, plus ITSM data), stream it with Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose or move it with AWS Glue, govern it with AWS Lake Formation, process it on Amazon EMR or Glue, and train anomaly detection and forecasting models in Amazon SageMaker. Amazon Lookout for Metrics can help, and results go to QuickSight and back to CloudWatch.

He is frank about the trade. You get control over what data you ship, strong governance and models tuned to your domain. You also need subject matter experts and time. This is the option for teams whose needs outgrow the defaults, not a weekend project.

## Approach three - turn on DevOps Guru

Amazon DevOps Guru is the managed middle: pick the coverage, connect sources such as CloudWatch, AWS Config and X-Ray, and it baselines normal behaviour across the account and raises insights when something deviates. He lists anomaly detection across metrics and logs, root cause analysis that correlates related problems to cut noise, resource optimisation suggestions, database monitoring, capacity forecasting, cross-service correlation, Lambda coverage, and security and compliance support, with remediation built on top. The heavy lifting is AWS's, which is precisely its appeal.

## How do you know AIOps worked?

His closing strategies are practical: set a clear goal (often the missing piece), feed in observability, ITSM, wiki and Confluence knowledge, bring operations and other teams to the table, automate the actions behind intelligent alerts, and train people so AIOps fits the team. Measure success in customer terms first (NPS, availability, reliability), then MTTD, MTTR, MTBF and the percentage of incidents that self-heal, and finally in DORA terms: shorter lead time for change and a lower change failure rate, because teams stop firefighting.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform teams running on AWS who need to choose between built-in, managed and custom AIOps, and managers who want a success-metrics checklist before funding one. It is an architecture comparison without a live demo.

Title: Five layers of cloud defence, and the misconfigured firewall that beat them
Description: Venukumar Chirlawar (Amazon) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on layered cloud security - network, app, encryption, IAM, endpoints - plus threat detection
Body:
Defence in depth only works if every layer is actually configured, and the most famous cloud breach in the talk came down to one that was not. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Venukumar Chirlawar, Senior Software Development Engineer at Amazon, lays out a multi-layered model for securing cloud environments (network, application, data encryption, identity and access management, endpoints), then adds advanced threat detection and proactive measures on top.

It is a structured overview rather than a hands-on session: no demo, no Kubernetes manifests, and no product walkthrough. Think of it as a checklist with explanations, good for building a mental model or sanity-checking a security programme. The abstract also mentions WAFs, SIEM and a 79% cut in breach response time; those do not feature in the recording, which sticks to the five layers.

## Why layers, and not a better wall?

Chirlawar frames the stakes with the cloud market heading for $1.3 trillion by 2025 and a familiar list of threats: data breaches from poor access controls or vulnerable applications, insecure APIs, insider threats that bypass perimeter defences, and the compliance load of GDPR and HIPAA. The layered approach answers all of them with redundancy. "This holistic strategy ensures that if one layer of security is compromised, others remain intact to protect the system," Venukumar Chirlawar said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

He walks data through the stack in order: the network layer filters traffic, the application layer relies on secure code and vulnerability management, encryption protects data at rest and in transit, IAM decides who gets in under what conditions, and endpoint protection covers the laptops and phones that are a common attack vector.

## What goes in each layer?

**Network.** Firewalls with predefined rules to protect virtual networks, next-generation firewalls adding deep packet inspection and application awareness, IDS to spot deviations and raise alerts, IPS to drop or reroute malicious traffic, DDoS protection that is usually built into the cloud provider's infrastructure, and VPNs for encrypted tunnels from user devices.

**Application.** Defences against SQL injection and cross-site scripting through secure coding and a secure SDLC, automated patch management, penetration testing and vulnerability scanning.

**Encryption.** AES-256 for data at rest so a compromised storage system still yields nothing readable, TLS in transit, and key management covering secure generation, storage and rotation.

**IAM.** Role-based access with least privilege, plus multi-factor authentication so stolen credentials alone are not enough.

**Endpoints.** Endpoint protection against malware and ransomware, mobile device management to enforce policy on phones, and EDR for real-time monitoring of endpoint behaviour.

## Detecting what the layers miss

For threats such as zero-day attacks, he points to behavioural analytics, machine learning and AI that look for patterns and anomalies in real time. Behavioural analytics is singled out for insider threats and account takeovers, because it flags users acting unlike themselves. Automated real-time response can block activity and isolate compromised accounts, cutting response time. Around all of it sit continuous audits, monitoring and vulnerability management, so configurations stay current and compliant.

## Two case studies, one lesson

Netflix is the positive example: a multi-layered strategy with custom tools such as Security Monkey to monitor its cloud environment, regular security testing, and automation to detect and respond faster. Capital One is the cautionary one. In 2019 its breach exposed the personal information of over 100 million people, and he attributes it to a misconfigured firewall and weak access controls. That is the real argument for the whole talk: the layers exist on paper in most organisations, and the breach happens in the one that drifted.

The best practices follow from there: regular audits, vulnerability assessments and pen tests, patch management, a zero trust model with strong access controls and MFA, continuous monitoring, and keeping up with new threats. The look ahead covers AI-driven threat detection and the need for quantum-resistant encryption such as lattice-based cryptography.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into cloud security, developers who want to see how their part (secure code, secrets, IAM roles) fits the bigger picture, and managers drafting a security roadmap. Security practitioners will find it familiar; the runtime detection talk below is the deeper, hands-on companion for Kubernetes.

Title: Where AI personalisation tips over into manipulation
Description: Sravan Yella (Hewlett Packard) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on the ethics of AI marketing - manipulation, privacy, disinformation and bias
Body:
The same model that recommends the right running shoes can also learn exactly when you are tired enough to buy the expensive ones. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Sravan Yella, CRM Engineering Leader at Hewlett Packard, gave a short, statistics-heavy briefing on that tension: what AI personalisation does for marketing, the three ethical failures it invites (manipulation, privacy breaches, disinformation), and the guardrails he thinks companies need - transparency, bias mitigation and human oversight.

One note on scope: despite the title, the talk is about AI in marketing; incident management doesn't come up. Read it as an ethics primer for people who build CRM and marketing automation systems.

## Why do marketers want AI so badly?

He opens with the upside. Machine learning, natural language processing and predictive analytics deliver personalised experiences at scale, and he cites the Marketing AI Institute figure that 84% of marketing leaders expect AI to change marketing fundamentally within five years. His retail case study: AI-powered recommendations brought a 40% increase in conversion rates and a 30% cut in customer acquisition costs. Personalised recommendations, he adds, can lift click-through rates by 35% and conversions by 18%, and 91% of consumers say they are more likely to shop with brands that personalise offers.

## When does a nudge become manipulation?

The first ethical problem is the flip side of those numbers. Algorithms can exploit psychological vulnerabilities to nudge people into purchases or engagement without them noticing the influence. His framing is consumer autonomy: if people don't understand what is shaping their decisions, the principle that they are choosing freely gets shaky. That is the uncomfortable line every recommendation engine product meeting should have on the whiteboard.

## How much does the model know about you?

Privacy is the second. AI marketing runs on browsing behaviour, purchase patterns and personal preferences, and the inferences go further than the inputs: he cites research in which algorithms predicted political affiliation with 87% accuracy from social media activity alone. 78% of consumers, in a study he quotes, worry about how AI-powered marketing affects their privacy. Large data stores also make large breaches, and he points to a 2023 incident at a major social media platform that exposed the biometric data of over 150 million users.

## Engagement-optimised systems spread whatever engages

The third problem is disinformation. Algorithms that rank for engagement amplify false content unintentionally, and he cites a study finding AI-generated fake news 70% more likely to be shared than accurate stories. From Pew Research Center he quotes that 38% of Americans encountered AI-generated political content in the 2024 US presidential election, with 62% of them believing it was real. Fact-checking AI helps but lags: his example is Facebook's system labelling 85% of false content within 24 hours, and a lot can go viral in 24 hours.

## What does responsible practice look like?

His guardrails are three. Transparency: 82% of consumers in one study want companies to say how AI drives decisions on personalised pricing, recommendations and targeted ads, so marketers should explain how their systems decide. Bias mitigation: ad targeting, pricing and personalisation can bake in bias, and he cites a mitigation method that reduced targeting disparities by 45% on a major advertising platform. Human oversight: automated systems decide fast, and "human oversight is definitely needed until an AI system is mature enough," Sravan Yella said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024.

On social media he names echo chambers and filter bubbles, and proposes algorithmic diversity and user-controlled content curation as the fix.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product owners working on CRM, recommendation or ad-targeting systems who want a compact list of the ethical risks and the figures commonly cited about them. The talk is a survey: most statistics come with short source attributions on screen rather than discussion of methodology, and there is no implementation detail on, for example, how to run a bias audit.

Title: Below every Kubernetes network sits a VLAN, a spanning tree and BGP
Description: Ravi Theja Kambhampati (Reailize, a B-Yond company) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on Layer 2 and Layer 3 basics for resilient, scalable networks
Body:
Your pods talk over a CNI, your CNI talks over somebody's switches, and those switches still run on ideas from decades ago. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Ravi Theja Kambhampati, Engineering Manager at Reailize, a B-Yond company, gives a guided tour of the routing and switching foundations underneath: Layer 2 segmentation, Layer 3 routing, how the two work together, and the security and automation layered on top.

This is a fundamentals talk, and it says so in its title. There are no configs, packet captures or numbers. What it offers is a clean, ordered refresher, useful for platform and cloud engineers who grew up on VPCs and never had to touch a physical switch.

## Layer 2: keep traffic local, and keep it from looping

Kambhampati starts at Layer 2 of the OSI model, which handles transmission within a network segment. VLANs segment a network logically rather than physically, so accounting and HR can share the same hardware while their traffic stays apart. That segmentation improves security by isolating sensitive data and improves performance by cutting unnecessary traffic. Trunking lets multiple VLANs share one physical link while keeping their boundaries.

The Spanning Tree Protocol gets the drama it deserves: in a large network, a loop lets frames circulate endlessly and clog everything. STP prevents loops while keeping a primary path and a backup, so the redundancy you cabled in does not turn into a broadcast storm.

## Layer 3: OSPF inside, BGP between, MPLS for speed

Routing is where traffic crosses networks. OSPF is the dynamic protocol that keeps recalculating the best path and scales well inside large enterprises. BGP routes between autonomous systems run by different organisations. "Think of BGP as a backbone of the internet," Ravi Theja Kambhampati said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024. MPLS forwards on short labels instead of long network addresses, which speeds things up in high-traffic networks.

## Why the two layers only make sense together

The central point is synergy. VLANs at Layer 2 give isolation; routing at Layer 3 connects the isolated segments so marketing, finance and HR can exchange what they must without exposing everything else. Done properly, the integration reduces latency and maximises throughput by avoiding unnecessary hops. Anyone who has designed Kubernetes namespaces plus network policies will recognise the same balancing act between segmentation and connectivity, one layer down.

## Redistribution, QoS and the security layer

Three advanced concepts follow. Route redistribution lets several routing protocols coexist in one network by sharing route information. Quality of service prioritises traffic, for example the audio and video of a call over a background download, so performance holds up under congestion. And security: ACLs filter on IP address, protocol or port, such as letting only the finance team reach a financial database, while IPsec authenticates and encrypts each IP packet, typically for VPNs connecting remote staff to the corporate network.

## Where it is heading: automation, ML and zero trust

The closing section looks forward. Manual configuration and monitoring stop being feasible at scale, so automation applies consistent configuration across many devices at once and can apply pre-configured fixes when monitoring spots a known problem. Machine learning adds predictive analysis from historical data and anomaly detection that can flag a breach or a malfunction. On security, he describes the shift to zero trust, where every user, device and data flow is authenticated, authorised and continuously validated, with threats assumed to come from inside as well as outside. The industry examples are short sketches: high-availability networks in financial services, BGP in 5G telecom networks, and IoT connectivity for smart cities.

## Who should watch

Cloud and platform engineers who want the vocabulary to talk to their network team, students preparing for networking fundamentals, and developers curious what actually happens below the overlay. Network engineers will know every slide; for them, the Kubernetes networking talks below go further.

Title: At 2am, let the AI write the status update
Description: Spiros Economakis (Mattermost) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on using GenAI to triage, write updates and draft postmortems so SREs can fix
Body:
Half of a bad incident is not fixing anything: it is writing the same update three ways for three audiences while the database burns. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Spiros Economakis, Director of Product Operations at Mattermost, who leads its infrastructure and customer reliability engineering teams, walked through a single 2am page and showed where generative AI takes that busywork off the on-call engineer: severity triage, internal and customer updates, log analysis and the postmortem draft.

The demo runs on Mattermost's own Playbooks and Copilot, so it is partly a product tour, but the workflow maps onto any incident tooling.

## Why is on-call so draining?

He starts where every on-call engineer lives: a page in the middle of the night that wrecks sleep and focus, then a burst of multitasking. Find the root cause, update internal teams, write customer updates, and do all of it while checking dashboards, logs and metrics, with support and customer success asking what is going on. His point is that incidents don't just stress people out; constant firefighting also slows innovation, because nobody is building.

## Walk through one incident

The scenario is a database CPU alert above 90% at 2am, delivered by PagerDuty, Opsgenie or whatever wakes you. His slides add his wife wondering which will crash first, the servers or him.

Step one is process, not AI. A predefined incident playbook in Mattermost opens a dedicated channel as the war room and loads a checklist, because communication is where incidents usually leak time.

Step two is severity. He feeds Mattermost Copilot the observability graphs, dashboard screenshots and data, and the model classifies the incident as severity 2 because of severe database performance problems, with a summary of the nature of the issue. That multimodal input, screenshots included, is the part worth noticing: the model works with what the responder already has on screen.

Steps three and four are updates. The same context produces an internal status update posted with a few clicks, then a customer-facing update generated from the team's own template. Writing both by hand, he notes, took time and left room for errors.

## Feed it more context as you investigate

As the investigation goes on, he adds service logs plus input from support and customer success. The AI combines it with the context it already has and highlights patterns a responder might miss in the first rush. "We were under stress, we were sleepy, right? We just woke up from our REM sleep," Spiros Economakis said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024, which is a fair summary of why a second pair of eyes that never sleeps helps.

## The postmortem starts as a draft, not a document

Once the issue is resolved, the AI generates a postmortem with a timeline of events, the evidence, how it was resolved and suggested action items. With many people talking in a thread, that summary saves hours of manual stitching. He is explicit about its limits: without human context, the postmortem is just an AI-generated summary, and in practice a lot more happened during the incident than the thread shows. It is a starting point for the team to edit together.

## Not an artificial SRE

His closing caveat is the most useful line in the talk. AI makes mistakes, and it is not an artificial SRE that does the work for you. What it does well is automate repetitive tasks in teams that, as he points out, often have no separate incident commander or communications lead. Engineers refine the suggestions and make the final decisions.

The takeaways come down to three: understand the problem faster through combined data and summaries, less multitasking because updates and summaries are automated, and less time managing the incident and more time fixing it.

## Who should watch

On-call SREs and incident leads at small teams where one person plays every role, and anyone designing an incident workflow in ChatOps tooling. It is short and concrete; those looking for evaluation data on AI triage accuracy will not find it here.

Title: Carving an order management system into microservices, one capability at a time
Description: Jubin Thomas (Signet Jewelers) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on splitting order management into capability-sized microservices on Docker and Kubernetes
Body:
A shopping cart, an order, a customer and an inventory record do not have to share a database, a deploy or a release date. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Jubin Thomas, Technical Architect at Signet Jewelers with 14+ years in supply chain and retail, walks through how to split an order management system into microservices sized by business capability, and how Docker and Kubernetes carry them to production.

Honest scope first: this is a primer. It covers the vocabulary and the reference diagrams of microservice design for a retail order system in about twenty minutes. The abstract also promises resilience and integration techniques; the talk itself spends its time on decomposition, testing layers and the Docker and Kubernetes basics. If you are new to the topic it is a tidy map. If you already run microservices, skim it for the order-domain example.

## How big should a microservice be?

Thomas's answer is that the business function or domain decides, not the scale. In an order management system, payments and checkout are separate modules because they are separate capabilities. One service might hold a dozen entities and another just one; what matters is which business domain it owns. "Emphasizing user stories will enable us to precisely outline the limits of the business domain," Jubin Thomas said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

The comparison with the monolith is the familiar one, made concrete. The monolith bundles the RDBMS, a Java backend and a JSP or ASP front end into one unit: every feature redeploys the lot, and scaling means running more copies of the entire application. His microservice version breaks out shopping cart, order, customer and inventory, each with its own store: Redis for customers, MongoDB for orders, SQL Server for the cart and Oracle for inventory. He describes the result as loosely coupled services with bounded contexts, a natural consequence of applying the single responsibility principle at the architecture level.

## Capability-centric design and the aggregate root

In his capability-centric design each capability gets its own front end, back end and database, plus a product team that runs it. The domain-driven design part centres on the aggregate root: any reference from outside an aggregate goes only to its root, so the root can guard the integrity of the whole. Order is the root in his example, linked to a customer, to line items, to a shipping address and to a payment strategy that can be credit card, cash or bank transfer.

The shopping cart example then lays the order service out as ports and adapters: domain entities (order, item, shipping address, payment), ports such as an order repository, order service and order query web service, adapters holding the real database and API implementations, and converters. The detail that makes it real is the status converter: an order status of complete is stored as the integer 100 in the database.

## Where plain CRUD starts to hurt

He also lists the problems with a single CRUD model in a busy order domain: the read and write representations of the data drift apart, records can clash when multiple actors work on the same data in parallel, the risk grows with complexity and throughput, and security gets harder because every entity is exposed to both reads and writes. That list is the usual argument for separating reads from writes, although the talk stops at the diagnosis.

## Testing the pieces and the whole

The testing section is the classic pyramid applied to services: unit tests, component tests, integration tests for the communication paths between components, contract tests at the boundary of an external system to check it meets what the consuming service expects, and end-to-end tests of the entire system. Tools named: Cucumber, JUnit and Mockito for mocking the responses of neighbouring services.

## Docker and Kubernetes, in brief

The deployment part is an introduction: Docker's build, ship and run, with images built on a laptop or in CI, pushed to a registry and run on cloud or on-prem; then Kubernetes as the orchestrator focused on scheduling, scaling and self-healing, with pods (one or more containers and volumes, a shared namespace, one IP per pod) and services (a stable network endpoint with a label selector and load balancing).

## Who should watch

Developers and architects in retail or e-commerce who are about to break up an order monolith and want a shared vocabulary for the first design meeting, and students looking for one example carried from domain model to Kubernetes. Teams already deep into service meshes and event sourcing will find little new here.

Title: AI code review, by the numbers it claims
Description: Prakash Raj Ojha (BNY) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on how AI code review and AI-driven testing change speed, coverage and quality
Body:
Manual code review scales roughly as well as one senior engineer's patience. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Prakash Raj Ojha, Software Architect and Technical Lead at BNY, gave a compact overview of how AI tools such as Amazon CodeGuru and DeepCode take over the repetitive part of review and QA, and put a scorecard on it: up to 75% less review time, 35.7% better bug detection and development cycles a third shorter.

It is a short, high-level talk aimed at teams deciding whether to bring AI into review and testing, not a hands-on tool comparison.

## Why does manual review stop working?

His framing is about scale. Developers checking each other's code for bugs, performance bottlenecks and security holes works on a small codebase and gets inefficient as it grows. Human review is slow by nature, error-prone and resource-hungry, and the backlog of pull requests waiting for a reviewer is where delivery speed quietly goes to die.

AI review tools, in his description, scan thousands of lines in minutes and flag memory leaks, inefficient algorithms, improper error handling and security vulnerabilities, with feedback during development rather than after. They also learn from past reviews. "As the time goes, they get better and better," Prakash Raj Ojha said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024.

## What changes in testing?

The QA section is the more interesting half. He lists four things AI brings to testing:

- **Test case generation**, including diverse cases that cover edge cases and rare user behaviour, which predefined test suites tend to miss.
- **Test prioritisation** based on recent code changes, so the tests most likely to fail run first.
- **Self-healing tests** that adapt when the UI or code structure changes, instead of breaking on every renamed selector.
- **Defect prediction** from historical test data, pointing QA at the parts of the code most likely to hold bugs.

Predictive analytics shows up on the review side too: historical data used to predict bottlenecks and bugs before they ship, so developers can act before the incident rather than during it.

## What does the scorecard say?

His metrics of success, as presented in the talk:

| Metric | Figure he quoted |
|---|---|
| Bug detection rate | +35.7% |
| Development cycle time | -33.3% |
| Code review time | -75% |
| Test case generation time | -75% |

He adds that developers can write up to 50% more lines of code per day with AI support, and cites Amazon CodeGuru identifying 90% of critical issues in code, leading to a 50% reduction in downtime. The talk does not give sources or methodology for these figures, so treat them as the case for trying the tools rather than a benchmark you can hold a vendor to. Lines of code per day is also a metric any reviewer would raise an eyebrow at: more code is only good news if the review keeps up.

## The catch

He is honest about the costs. Teams have to invest in training and infrastructure to integrate AI tools into existing environments. A tool that learns from your unique codebase needs continuous maintenance, and the models need regular updates as they meet new coding patterns. None of that is free, and none of it happens by itself after the procurement meeting.

His outlook: AI embedded across the whole lifecycle, including CI/CD, predictive maintenance and automated code standardisation, with developers moving to the creative problem-solving that tools can't do.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and tech leads building the case for AI review or test tooling, and QA leads curious about self-healing tests and test prioritisation. Engineers who already run AI review bots in their pipelines will find it familiar ground.

Title: Your sprint is fast. The 120 days before it are the problem
Description: Chris Gallivan (Planview) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on why flow dies in the seams between teams, not in Scrum or productivity dashboards
Body:
Agile and DevOps made the build-and-release part of software delivery fast, and then everyone kept staring at it. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Chris Gallivan, Principal Flow Advisor at Planview, argues that most organisations look for flow in the wrong places (feature roadmaps, developer productivity dashboards, Scrum metrics) when it is actually lost in the seams between people and teams.

It is a no-Kubernetes, no-code talk about how work moves through a company, delivered by someone who clearly enjoys a music metaphor.

## Which flow are we talking about?

Gallivan starts by asking ChatGPT, and gets two definitions: flow as a personal state of being, where you can do no wrong, and flow as bringing valuable software to users sooner. His answer is that you need both. A person in flow tends to produce value, and an organisation will not deliver value faster unless its people actually feel that state.

## Frederick Taylor is still in the building

The history section explains where today's instincts came from. Frederick Taylor's 1909 principles of scientific management (find the most efficient way to do tasks, divide responsibilities, pay for performance, rigid hierarchy and surveillance) gave us, in Gallivan's telling, managers, consultants and RACI charts. Taylor's line that one type of person plans and another executes produced the two-box organisation: management in the tower, workers below.

Then the experiment. Gallivan asked managers why work is delayed and got inefficient processes, unproductive people, people not following the process, and people taking on too much WIP, which maps almost one-to-one onto Taylor. Workers blamed working on the wrong things, too many disparate demands, scope creep and too many number ones. Each side points at the other. His reply to the workers, "poor babies", is affectionate and pointed: no business stakeholder will dial back demand because engineering asked nicely.

## The streetlight is on the wrong 70 days

The streetlight effect is the core image: the man looks for his keys under the lamp because the light is better there. Agile and DevOps lit up one piece of the value stream and filled it with metrics. In his example a request spends 120 days in ideation, 50 in creation and 20 in release, so IT optimised the last 70 days and left the longest stretch in the dark.

## Features, productivity dashboards and Scrum are dead ends

Feature obsession runs into the debt spiral, a diagram he adapts from Gene Kim: push features year after year, debt, risk, toil and defects pile up, and feature work slows to a crawl. He says this is what killed Nokia. The way out is pausing feature work to pay down debt for months or years, which is hard because the people feeding features in get promoted for it. One of his clients made debt work and modernisation its strategy for two to three years.

Productivity dashboards get similar treatment. If 90% of software cost is maintenance and 70% of coding effort is understanding the code, making code easier to understand beats measuring keystrokes. And agency matters: "Humans feel the most energized when they feel some sense of agency over the work they're doing," Chris Gallivan said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024. Rigid Scrum delivers stories to an artificial cadence while, as one customer told him, the delivery of value looks the same as it did 20 years ago.

## Where flow actually goes to die

His better picture overlaps demand generation and demand fulfilment instead of separating them. A real delivery path runs through sales, marketing, business owners, product managers, product owners, designers, front-end and back-end engineers, release and support engineers, and every handoff is a seam. "If you don't manage the seams, that's where flow goes to die." The costly causes live there: nobody can schedule for fastest value alone, product-to-engineering handoffs are poor, unplanned work comes from both sides, and quality is everyone's problem.

He leans on Repenning and Sterman's 2001 paper, "Nobody Ever Gets Credit for Fixing Problems That Never Happened": the working-harder loop closes the gap with competitors quickly but not for long, while the working-smarter loop pays off only after a long feedback delay that impatient organisations cut short. Then the jazz: first-graders play their own part, a good Detroit club band listens to each other, and the value is in the space between the notes.

## The tips worth keeping

Measure value as the customer sees it, at the feature level rather than stories. Put your best engineers on design, since most of development is thinking. Track dependencies even though it is hard. Sequence work for fastest value first and finish before starting. Measure unplanned work and remove it. Be suspicious of averages such as average flow time. And choose working smarter, then be patient enough to wait for it.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, product leads and anyone whose team ships fast and still hears that delivery is slow. Developers get a vocabulary for why their dashboards look green while customers wait. There is no tool walkthrough.

Title: Catch the duplicate API at commit time, not three years later
Description: Anirudha Karandikar (Fortune 500 Company) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on taming API sprawl with a central contract repo, CI gates and an LLM
Body:
Every large company has at least four address-management APIs, and nobody remembers who owns three of them. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024, Anirudha Karandikar, Principal Engineer at a Fortune 500 company who works across the whole API lifecycle, laid out a blueprint for fixing that: put every API contract in one repository, enforce standards in CI, and then let an LLM do the boring parts - spotting near-duplicates, answering which API returns user details, and writing the documentation nobody keeps up to date.

It is an architecture proposal, not a product demo, and the interesting bits are in how the pieces line up.

## How did we end up with tens of thousands of APIs?

He starts with a quick history: Netflix and Amazon pioneered microservices around 2011-2013, the term went mainstream in 2014-2015, and Docker plus Kubernetes did the rest. Distributed development gave teams autonomy, and autonomy gave everyone their own repos, standards and release timelines. The bill came due as enterprises scaled, and he names four line items: duplication (every team solved location, address or user management on its own), weaker security control (non-standard APIs open different attack vectors, and more APIs mean a bigger attack surface), operational inefficiency, and documentation that drifts away from the real API.

## Centralise the contracts, not the code

The key move is narrower than it sounds. Teams keep their implementations in their own repositories; only the API definitions move into a central monorepo that becomes the single source of truth. On top of that sit business rules and standards: naming conventions for base paths and paths, OpenAPI as the spec, and custom tags for domains such as payments or supply chain.

Then come starter kits. Code generators can already turn a contract into a skeleton, and he wants teams to go one level down and bake the cross-cutting concerns in: logging format, observability, authn and authz, error handling, even the container images. Change the logging standard once and everyone using the kit inherits it. The developer, in his words, only has to care about the functional code.

## A similarity check as a quality gate

The governance model is a CI/CD pipeline on the contract repo. A new or changed contract runs through compliance policies, a linter that can produce a score, and a quality gate with a threshold; below it, the build fails and the developer gets feedback. The last gate is the one that targets sprawl directly: an LLM similarity check against existing APIs, comparing request and response shapes, descriptions or the downstream domains being called.

The goal is to "check whether you really need a net new API or what are what you are trying to achieve can be achieved by extending any of the existing APIs", Anirudha Karandikar said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024. Cheaper to have that argument with a pipeline at review time than with an incident at 2am.

## The discovery tool is a RAG system over your Swagger files

His API discovery tool has four building blocks: an LLM (ChatGPT, Claude, Llama or similar), a vector database such as Pinecone or FAISS, an OpenAPI/Swagger parser, and a web interface. The contracts are flattened into structured JSON (endpoints, methods, parameters, responses, descriptions), embedded, and mapped to natural-language intents, so "how do I get user details?" lands on the right endpoint. Responses quote the relevant part of the original Swagger definition, which he calls contextual augmentation, and he is upfront that the first answer usually needs a few rounds of follow-up prompts.

## Documentation that follows the contract

The same setup writes docs. Define a structure (overview, endpoints, inputs and outputs, examples, error handling), template the prompt so only endpoint details change, and run it either in bulk for a backlog of a thousand undocumented APIs or on every contract check-in. The pipeline styles the LLM output as Markdown or HTML and opens a merge request against the developer portal, where a human reviews and adds context. The review step matters: the generated text is a draft, not gospel.

## What about the sprawl you already have?

For companies already sitting on thousands of APIs he suggests four steps: move definitions to the central repo gradually rather than in a big bang, feed live gateway usage data to the LLM to find unused versions and decommission them, run the similarity check across the whole estate to form cohorts for consolidation, and tag APIs (public versus internal, deployment platform) so a query like "all public-facing APIs" returns a list in seconds when a new security policy lands.

One note on scope: the abstract quotes percentage improvements for duplication, quality and productivity, but the talk itself doesn't present measured results. Watch it for the design.

## Who should watch

Platform and API teams who own a developer portal, architects arguing for a contract-first monorepo, and anyone who has been asked to find out how many APIs the company actually has. Expect diagrams and pipelines, not code.

Title: A custom GPT briefed like a whole quant team
Description: Arsalan Sheikh (ex-Oracle) at Conf42 Incident Management 2024 on prototyping an algorithmic trading system with a custom GPT-4o and GitHub Copilot
Body:
Most people prompt an LLM like a vending machine. Arsalan Sheikh, who works in treasury and capital markets (ex-Oracle), briefs his like a project kickoff. At Conf42 Incident Management 2024 he showed how he built QuantLab, a custom GPT on GPT-4o, fed it a delivery methodology, a team structure, a system architecture and a research paper, and used it with GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code to prototype an algorithmic trading system in Python without waiting for a team to free up.

It is a practitioner's workflow talk with a live walkthrough, and explicitly not financial advice: he calls the trading strategy educational.

## Why does a domain expert need to prototype at all?

His pitch is personal. He comes from business, program management and technology, and generative AI means someone who understands the business problem can iterate on a solution directly. He is careful not to oversell the tool: "an AI tool is just a tool," Arsalan Sheikh said at Conf42 Incident Management 2024, and the secret sauce is still the person with the skills. His list is long: math and statistics, software engineering, data science, cloud and big data, problem solving, ethics, domain knowledge, and the collaboration skills to build anything at scale.

He frames the domain as time series analysis, which reaches well beyond finance: patient monitoring, predictive maintenance, demand forecasting, energy load forecasting, weather, network traffic and fraud detection. The trading system is his worked example, but the method is meant to carry over to any timestamped data.

## Give the model a process before you give it a task

The most transferable idea is how much structure he loads into the GPT before asking for a single line of code. He mapped CRISP-DM, the data science methodology, onto lean development and trained QuantLab to follow that flow, so the model works through business understanding, data preparation, modelling, evaluation and deployment in order instead of wandering off. The stated reason is hallucination: give a precise context of how things should get done, and the output stays on track.

Then he gives it an org chart. QuantLab is told it represents software developers, data scientists, data analysts, domain experts, QA, security specialists, DevOps and data engineers, who should question each other and validate the prototype. "Why reinvent the wheel when we know a structure works like this?" was his justification. A one-person project with a simulated stand-up, essentially.

## The architecture and the inputs

The model also gets the target architecture: data ingestion from a broker source, preprocessing, strategy implementation, a backtesting agent, risk management, trade execution, parameter optimisation, and monitoring and logging so he can debug the result. He lists the modules, their functions and candidate design patterns, and leaves room for the design to evolve through the conversation.

The context inputs are three: historical time series data so the model works with real data points, a published research paper describing a trading strategy he found promising, and starter code from earlier projects he knew to be bug-free, so the generated code matches the way he likes to write and read Python. Building QuantLab took about a week of prompting back and forth before he was happy with the output.

## From QuantLab to Copilot and back

The toolchain loop goes like this. QuantLab handles research, requirements, solution architecture and boilerplate, much of it in a Jupyter notebook. The code moves into Visual Studio Code, where GitHub Copilot refactors it, suggests a project structure and helps debug and test. Processed market data goes back into QuantLab for exploratory analysis and charts, the insights drive a parameter-tuning run in VS Code, and the cycle repeats until the output is good enough to call a prototype. One nice engineering touch: strategy and user parameters live in a separate JSON configuration, so a future front end could change the strategy without touching code.

The demo shows the real chat history with QuantLab, including the custom GPT's instructions and knowledge files (tables and diagrams), and the notebook in VS Code. QuantLab is public, so viewers with a ChatGPT subscription can try it.

## Who should watch

Analysts and domain experts who code a bit and want a disciplined way to use ChatGPT and Copilot for prototypes, and engineers curious how much up-front context changes the quality of generated code. Quants looking for a strategy or performance numbers will not find them here; the talk is about the method.

Title: Every critical launch needs a captain, and the captain needs a runbook
Description: Ramneet Bhatia (Netflix) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on the launch captain role behind Netflix paid sharing - readiness checks, runbooks and launch rooms
Body:
When a launch touches most of your users and a lot of revenue, the most dangerous assumption in the room is that someone else is watching the dashboard. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Ramneet Bhatia, Senior Software Engineer at Netflix, distils the lessons from captaining the launch of paid sharing into a playbook: name one launch captain, give them a runbook that holds everything, and run the day off it.

This is a process talk, not a Kubernetes one, and it is all the more useful for that. Any engineer who has been on a big launch call will recognise the failure modes this playbook is designed against.

## Why one person, and not a committee?

Bhatia defines a critical launch by three traits: large-scale user and revenue impact, high visibility with senior leadership tracking it closely, and a huge cross-functional effort. Spreading ownership across a few key stakeholders sounds safe, but the talk warns it invites diffusion of responsibility, the bystander effect, where people are less likely to act because others are around.

The fix is a dedicated launch captain with two jobs: launch readiness and smooth execution, and being the focal point of communication for every partner team and leadership. At Netflix that is usually a senior engineer, but Bhatia says it can be anyone close to the solution who understands the feature, the business impact and the systems involved, and who can picture the launch from the seat of a user, a customer service agent, an engineer and a data scientist.

## Decide what good looks like before the traffic arrives

The captain starts weeks ahead, while the rest of the team is heads down on building and testing. The work rests on three pillars: strategy, collaboration and communication. Strategy means a launch plan, the metrics that signal progress, and a mental model of what those metrics should look like on a good day, so the strange trend stands out on launch day instead of being argued about.

Pre-launch, that turns into concrete steps. Weekly readiness checks can be as light as an async Slack check-in where every team reports on-track or names the blocker. A launch accountability matrix lists the engineering and product point of contact for each domain. Launch dashboards get a high-level view plus troubleshooting views, and should answer the obvious questions (how many users signed up, how many bought) before anyone asks. Collaboration covers the unglamorous dependencies, such as getting customer service knowledge base articles and FAQs updated in time.

## The runbook is the source of truth

The runbook template is worth stealing: the feature overview, the teams and their contacts, the accountability matrix, a pre-launch checklist (go/no-go from every stakeholder, configurations to enable, systems to pre-scale, teams to notify), launch day steps with a validation for each one, the monitoring dashboards, mitigation and rollback scenarios, and a post-launch section for metrics, open issues, tech debt and learnings.

The rule behind it is blunt. "Critical launches get intense. So always assume you will likely not recall all the minor details at the right time," Ramneet Bhatia said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024. Writing rollback scenarios down in advance means nobody brainstorms a rollback at the worst possible moment. The final runbook gets reviewed with the extended team, and calendar invites mark who must be present and which metrics they own.

## Running the launch room

High-impact launches ramp: a small percentage of users first, widening over hours or days. Early on, with little traffic, the captain spot-checks the first successes and failures, records them, and computes success and failure rates as a baseline, since those percentages should hold roughly steady as traffic grows.

When an anomaly appears, the captain pulls in the relevant teams to judge severity and impact, then tells the wider group whether it is a launch blocker, critical or major. Critical and major issues go into the runbook as under investigation with an owner. A blocker gets a smaller group in a separate war room, so the main room keeps its focus. When opinions conflict, Bhatia wants the captain to hear dissent and, without consensus, make the call while stating the risks and trade-offs. The day ends with a status update, an agreed support model for the late hours, and a thank-you note telling people to rest.

Post-launch, the team moves from active watching to automated alerts, tunes the pageable and email alerts, follows up on open issues and runs a retrospective.

## Who should watch

Senior engineers about to own their first big rollout, tech leads who keep ending up as the de facto coordinator, and SREs who want launch days to look more like a rehearsed procedure than an incident. It is short on Netflix-specific numbers and long on a checklist you can use next week.

Title: NATS in one CLI session - subjects, wildcards and free load balancing
Description: Mohamed Moussaoui (Amadeus) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on NATS and JetStream as a simpler cloud-native messaging layer, shown live from the NATS CLI
Body:
NATS gets you publish-subscribe, request-reply and load balancing out of a single binary you can start with one command. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Mohamed Moussaoui, Java Software Developer at Amadeus, makes the case for NATS as the cloud-native challenger to Kafka, tours what NATS Core and JetStream offer, and then demos the core patterns live from the NATS CLI.

Set expectations right: this is a compact introduction, and despite the title there is no head-to-head benchmark against Kafka. What you get is a clear map of NATS features and a demo that makes subject-based messaging click in a few minutes.

## Why look past Kafka at all?

Moussaoui opens with a smart city: a weather station reports 30 degrees in the city centre, a weather app pushes sunscreen reminders, and smart thermostats ask about the power grid before cranking up the cooling. Kafka, RabbitMQ and Apache Pulsar all handle this kind of traffic. His argument is about what they cost to run: infrastructure complexity that grows with scale, resource-hungry scaling, and the work of keeping delivery reliable through network failures and node outages.

NATS is pitched as the answer to those three: easy to deploy, with authentication and encryption built in, and able to handle millions of messages per second. It is designed for cloud-native apps, IoT and microservices, and to run from the cloud out to the edge.

## Subjects are a tree, and wildcards do the routing

Everything in NATS builds on pub-sub over subjects, which are hierarchical names separated by dots: `time`, `time.eu`, `time.eu.paris`. A publisher sends to exactly one subject. Subscribers get the flexibility through two wildcards: `*` matches a single token (`time.eu.*` catches Paris and Madrid), and `>` matches one or more tokens (`time.>` catches everything under `time`).

On top of pub-sub sit request-reply, queue groups for load balancing across subscribers, and clustering that uses a gossip protocol for server discovery and Raft for leader election.

## What does JetStream add?

JetStream is the persistence layer, and Moussaoui shows it is a flag away: start the server with JetStream enabled or switch it on in the config file. It brings stored and replayable messages, replay policies (a consumer can receive stored messages at their original publication rate instead of as fast as possible), retention by time, message count or size, and work-queue streams for distributing tasks.

Two features make NATS more than a broker. A key-value store on top of streams, with expiry and atomic compare-and-swap, which he says can replace Redis in many scenarios: configuration, distributed locks, simple caches. And an object store for large files, with metadata and versioning. Security covers TLS, NKey authentication, JWT authorisation and multi-tenancy through accounts that each get their own subject space.

The feature he singles out is decoupled flow control. "If you have a slow consumer, it doesn't impact your producers or other consumers," Mohamed Moussaoui said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024. That lets a consumer replay history and then switch to live processing without anyone else noticing.

## The demo: smart city over the CLI

The demo keeps to NATS Core. `nats server run` starts a local server. A subscriber listens on a Casablanca zone-one temperature subject, a publish of `26` arrives, then a second subscriber uses `*` to hear every zone in Casablanca and a third uses `>` to hear every city. Publishing to Rabat, then to Casablanca, shows exactly which subscribers wake up for which message.

Queue groups are the satisfying bit. Three subscribers join the same queue, a publisher sends a message every second, and the messages spread evenly across the three. Kill one and the other two pick up the rest, with no consumer group rebalancing to wait for. The request-reply demo then shows that a request is just a publish with a reply-to inbox subject, visible to anyone subscribed to everything.

## Who should watch

Developers who have only seen Kafka and want a quick feel for subject-based messaging, and teams choosing a messaging layer for microservices, IoT or edge deployments. Kafka veterans looking for throughput numbers or a migration story will need to look elsewhere; the official NATS docs are the next stop after this.
