Title: A Python engineer, a price recommender, and no Kafka cluster to babysit
Description: Bobur Umurzokov (GlassFlow) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on building real-time Python data pipelines on serverless infra, skipping Kafka and the JVM
Body:
Plenty of data teams want real-time pipelines and very few want to run Kafka to get them. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Bobur Umurzokov, Developer Relations Manager at GlassFlow, tells the story of Bob, a Python data engineer who wants an AI price recommender for a used-car site, and argues that a Python-native, serverless stream processor gets Bob to production without a JVM, a broker or a Kubernetes crash course.

It is a vendor talk: the second half is a demo of GlassFlow, his company's product. The first half is a fair tour of why the classic Debezium-plus-Kafka stack scares small teams.

## What was wrong with the obvious design?

Bob's first sketch is the textbook one: Debezium captures changes from the primary database, Kafka carries the events, and a Python prediction service calls the OpenAI API and pushes a suggested price to the website and an analytics tool. Then the constraints arrive. Bob has no Kafka experience, no DevOps background and no time to learn Kubernetes. He wants everything in Python, he wants several engineers working on one pipeline, and the prediction service has to notify the web app in real time.

The war stories he collects are the useful part. Umurzokov describes users "taking nine months to implement production ready Kafka based data pipelines if they are self managed", and companies where 50 teams lean on a single Kafka cluster that one person understands. The open questions of self-managed Kafka get a list of their own: who owns it, what the right configuration is, one cluster or several, how to upgrade brokers, how to size storage per topic, and how to monitor any of it.

## Does managed Kafka fix it?

Partly. He names Redpanda, Aiven for Apache Kafka, Confluent and WarpStream, and points out what they leave on your plate: someone still has to design the setup, watch for over-provisioning and fluctuating bills, and run transformations somewhere else. His example is Amazon MSK, where transformation logic means paying for Lambda functions on the side. The data engineer is still waiting on a DevOps ticket to get a proof of concept running.

## Why a Python stream processor?

His pitch for Python stream processing frameworks is that they fold the streaming platform and the stream processor into your application code. "No JVM, no wrapper, no orchestrator or server side engine you need," Bobur Umurzokov said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024. You keep pandas and whatever libraries you already use, you can try a pipeline from a Jupyter notebook, and the original data stays in the primary database while the framework runs a transformation layer on top. He also nods at alternatives that are not Python frameworks at all: cloud-native queues from Azure, Google and Amazon, and NATS.

## What does the GlassFlow demo show?

The second version of Bob's architecture swaps Debezium and Kafka for Supabase and GlassFlow. A Supabase webhook fires on every insert, update or delete in the car price table, GlassFlow receives the event, a Python transformation function calls OpenAI's chat completion endpoint to predict the price, and the result goes to a webhook destination (webhook.site in the demo).

The walkthrough in the GlassFlow web app is five steps: name the pipeline, pick a webhook source, paste the transformation function, set the destination, create. The Supabase side needs the pipeline ID and an access token in an HTTP header. The demo also has the most honest moment of the session: the first run fails because the function imports OpenAI and the pipeline does not list it as a dependency. Add it to the requirements, insert four rows again, and four transformed events land at the webhook.

Under the hood, he says, GlassFlow runs on Docker, NATS and Kubernetes, so the cluster is still there; it just belongs to someone else. Other example pipelines he mentions: clickstream analytics with Streamlit or Plotly dashboards, classified ads enriched with LangChain or OpenAI and stored in Redis, Airbnb listings feeding a Weaviate vector database, and log anomaly detection.

## Who should watch

Python data engineers and data scientists who need a real-time proof of concept and have been told the first step is a Kafka cluster. Platform teams can watch it too, as a reminder of how the Kafka ownership question looks from the other side of the ticket queue. If you already run Kafka happily, the first half will feel familiar and the second half is a product demo.

Title: CircleCI built its sales demos like production, and customers asked in
Description: Eddie Webbinaro and Moo Olaniyan (CircleCI) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on a Terraform and EKS demo platform in three regions that customers now run.
Body:
Most sales demos are one-off snowflakes held together by a field engineer's memory. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Eddie Webbinaro, Senior Director and Head of Field Engineering at CircleCI, and Moo Olaniyan, Senior Field Engineer, showed the alternative they built: a fully infrastructure-as-code enterprise reference environment on Terraform and Amazon EKS, spread across North America, EMEA and Japan, good enough that customers started asking to run it themselves.

It is a CircleCI talk and the demo shows CircleCI's release features, but the architecture and the lessons apply to any team that keeps rebuilding the same environment by hand.

## Why start with the finished cake?

Eddie credited a former solutions engineer with the rule: "you always got to start the conversation with a finished cake". So the talk opens with the demo. A CircleCI pipeline builds and deploys a sample app, nicknamed Doctor Demo, to EKS clusters in North America and EMEA, and the app's colour shows which version is live. The CircleCI releases dashboard tracks the progressive rollout as traffic shifts to the new version. Eddie then drags the EMEA error rate up to 200%; the release agent spots that the error limit is exceeded, stops shifting traffic and rolls back, while North America carries on. No developer touches a credential, and nobody has to intervene.

## What problem were they solving?

Moo put it bluntly: "Each demo needed to be unique, which meant we were constantly reinventing the wheel." Demos used different tech stacks and different stories, did not reflect enterprise environments, lacked separation of duties and consistent controls, and needed significant prep and cleanup. Customers could not see themselves in them, wanted hands-on access, and sales cycles ran longer as a result.

The team set two goals: cut the effort to deliver a clean, consistent demo with a highly available, reusable environment, and raise the level of conversation with a platform that mirrors real enterprise infrastructure for development, security and operations teams alike. Getting there took technology chats across North America, EMEA and Japan/APAC time zones, then vision chats about the story to tell, while the team kept closing deals the old way.

## How is the platform built?

Two early decisions shaped it. Multi-tenant won over an environment per field engineer: isolation was attractive, but the cost was not justified, and enterprise teams work in shared spaces anyway. Build won over buy: the demo automation tools they found covered only part of the need and lacked the control to mirror customer environments.

The architecture has three layers:

- **Global**: DNS and IAM policies shared by every region.
- **Region core**: EKS clusters, networking, routing and certificates, identical in each region.
- **Region platform**: HashiCorp Vault for secrets, Nexus for artifacts, and namespaces for demo apps.

Everything is code except two one-time manual steps, buying the domain and the initial IAM role setup. Istio is the service mesh and ingress, with Kiali, Grafana and Prometheus for visibility. Secrets get serious treatment: SSO for operator access to AWS, OIDC web identity so pipelines provision the stack without stored credentials, Vault's root key in AWS KMS so Vault auto-unseals, operators restricted to narrow roles outside the pipeline, and pipelines loading further credentials from Vault through predefined policies.

## What happened after launch?

Adoption was slow at first. The environment worked but lacked the wow factor, and the architecture was too tangled for easy contributions. Better demo apps (modular microservices, firmware testing, mobile releases) and visual deploy tracking changed that, and each new field engineer cleaned up a bit more. It became the go-to demo platform, used by teams outside field engineering too.

Then a customer asked: "How do we get our own access to your sandbox environment?" Making that possible meant removing hard-coded IDs and paths, parameterising the setup and finishing the provisioning documentation, which was already about 80% done. The result is portable enough for customer POCs, sandboxes and full trials, and some customers have deployed it locally for testing.

## Who should watch

Field and solutions engineers tired of hand-built demo environments, and platform teams that want a compact reference for layered Terraform on EKS with Vault and passwordless pipelines. The release-dashboard demo is CircleCI-specific; the rest is portable.

Title: A first look at sentiment analysis and language generation
Description: Vishal Khadake (HYR Global Source Inc) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 with a beginner tour of NLP: sentiment analysis, language generation and their uses.
Body:
"This product is the worst thing I ever loved" is the kind of sentence that breaks a naive sentiment model, and the reason NLP got interesting. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Vishal Khadake, Data Scientist at HYR Global Source Inc, gave a beginner's tour of natural language processing built around two applications, sentiment analysis and language generation, and where businesses put them to work.

Set expectations before you press play: despite the event and the abstract's Kubernetes-native framing, the talk itself does not cover Kubernetes, deployment or serving at all. It is a non-technical NLP primer, and judged as one it is clear and well organised.

## What is NLP, in one breath?

Vishal's definition: "Natural Language Processing or NLP is a branch of AI that enables computers to understand and generate human language." He traced the field from ELIZA in the 1960s, which mimicked simple conversation, to BERT, GPT-3 and GPT-4, which write articles and hold conversations. Everyday examples do the rest: Alexa and Siri parsing voice commands, Google Translate keeping meaning intact across whole pages, Grammarly suggesting fixes to your writing.

## How does sentiment analysis work, and where does it fail?

Sentiment analysis labels text as positive, negative or neutral using models trained on large datasets that learn which words and phrases signal which tone. The easy cases are easy: a phrase built on love reads positive, one built on hate reads negative. Context is the hard part, which is where the sarcastic review from the opening comes in; Vishal said modern models handle sarcasm, irony and mixed emotions in one sentence far better than older ones.

His examples of where it pays off: a retailer with thousands of reviews that wants a spike in negative feedback about one product flagged before it becomes a crisis, and financial institutions reading social media chatter about stocks to gauge market sentiment.

## What is language generation actually doing?

Language generation is a model predicting the next word or phrase, trained on huge amounts of text, which is why more and better training data produces more coherent and relevant answers. Ask a virtual assistant about the weather and you get a contextual reply, not just a grammatical one. GPT-class models stretch that to essays and code.

The applications he listed are the familiar ones: chatbots that take common customer queries so human agents handle the complex ones, generated product descriptions, personalised marketing emails and social posts, and dialogue for video game characters. Beyond those two techniques, he pointed at healthcare (analysing patient data for diagnosis and treatment plans), finance (fraud detection in transactions and communications) and retail (recommendations and service automation).

## What numbers come with it?

The supporting material quotes a 20% rise in customer satisfaction from sentiment analysis, and virtual assistants that respond 30% faster and 25% more accurately with language generation. No sources or methodology are given, so treat them as illustrative rather than as benchmarks for your own project.

## Where does he think it goes next?

Faster real-time processing, more specialised models for specific industries and tasks, and ethical frameworks that keep AI interactions transparent, fair and unbiased. The closing advice is to keep learning as the field moves.

## Who should watch

Managers, analysts and engineers from outside machine learning who want a short, plain-language map of what NLP does before a deeper project. ML practitioners, and anyone hoping for model serving on Kubernetes, should pick one of the talks below instead.

Title: For EKS fleets, Git should be the source of truth, not of hope
Description: Yuriy Bezsonov (AWS) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on the GitOps Bridge: Terraform builds EKS clusters, Argo CD runs add-ons and apps across a hub and spokes.
Body:
One cluster with one pipeline is fine. Twelve clusters on seven Kubernetes versions with twelve pipelines is how you lose track of what is running where. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Yuriy Bezsonov, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, laid out a pattern for running EKS fleets with GitOps: Terraform creates the clusters and the cloud resources, then hands Kubernetes over to Argo CD through what AWS calls the GitOps Bridge, with a hub cluster managing dev, staging and production spokes.

It is an architecture talk built on EKS Blueprints, so it is AWS-flavoured throughout, but the split of responsibilities between Terraform and Argo CD applies to any cloud.

## Why does the push model break at scale?

Yuriy started where most teams start: Git, an infrastructure-as-code tool such as Terraform, CloudFormation, CDK or Pulumi, a state file in S3, and a pipeline that tests, enforces policy and deploys. Add environments and it stays manageable. Keep growing, across lines of business, legacy apps, stateful workloads and machine learning training and inference, and it does not: too many clusters, versions and pipelines, plus add-ons, team access and per-environment configuration on top.

The push model also has no clear answer to which component holds the truth: Git, the Terraform state, the pipeline or etcd. His verdict: "It is not source of truth anymore, and it's more, I would say, source of hope." Even integrating a new service, his example was Amazon Bedrock, needs someone to wire it into every pipeline, and with many business units it may never happen.

GitOps fixes that with four principles: declarative desired state, stored versioned and immutable in Git, pulled by an agent in the cluster, and continuously reconciled. The payoff is consistency, lower complexity, auditability and better security.

## What is the GitOps Bridge?

The worked example is the AWS Load Balancer Controller. It needs an IAM role and policy that let it manage AWS resources. Installing its Helm chart with Terraform works, but it is push again, and only runs when someone applies.

The bridge splits the job. Terraform creates the IAM role, then writes a Kubernetes secret for the cluster with the role referenced in its annotations. An Argo CD ApplicationSet reads that secret's metadata and generates an Application that installs the add-on with the right configuration. Terraform keeps doing what it is good at, AWS resources and clusters, and Argo CD owns everything inside Kubernetes. The pattern is integrated with EKS Blueprints and works for workloads as well as add-ons, wherever configuration can come from Terraform-generated metadata.

## How does it scale to a fleet?

Generic ApplicationSets live in one add-ons repository and act as templates; Argo CD renders them into different Applications with per-cluster values. In the hub-and-spoke model, a central Argo CD in a hub cluster manages dev, staging and production clusters, each represented by a secret in the hub. Terraform workspaces reuse the same code for each cluster's configuration, and label matching lets different clusters get different add-on versions from the same repository. Argo CD also creates namespaces and enforces RBAC and policies for teams.

Some customers go further and have Argo CD drive AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK) or Crossplane to create the VPC, the EKS cluster, S3 buckets and Amazon RDS databases. At that point, he said, Kubernetes is less a container orchestrator and more a platform framework. Application configuration follows the same layout: one repo with base, staging and prod directories, so production can run different replica counts and secrets from staging.

## How do you keep it secure?

Store Git credentials in AWS Secrets Manager and let the External Secrets Operator create the Argo CD repository secret. Use Kyverno to allow only SSH credentials, and only for approved Git servers. Never let Argo CD reach remote clusters with service account tokens that never expire; configure its application controller, API server and repo server with IAM roles via IRSA or EKS Pod Identity, specify the role when adding a cluster, and have a Kyverno policy reject cluster secrets that carry a kubeconfig token instead of a role.

## Who should watch

Platform teams that have outgrown a pipeline per cluster, and anyone managing Kubernetes add-ons with Terraform's Helm provider and feeling the pain. The talk points to an Argo CD on EKS workshop and the EKS Blueprints GitOps patterns for hands-on follow-up.

Title: Kubernetes Gateway API will make your API gateway boring, on purpose
Description: Pubudu Gunatilaka (WSO2) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on how the Gateway API moves security and traffic policy out of services and commoditises API gateways.
Body:
Remember when you cared whether a disk was FAT32 or NTFS? At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Pubudu Gunatilaka, Senior Technical Lead at WSO2, argued that API gateways are heading the same way: the Kubernetes Gateway API standardises them into a commodity, and the real work moves up to API management and governance. On the way there he showed exactly where plain Ingress runs out and how HTTPRoute, custom backends and a single control plane pick up the slack.

The talk ends with WSO2 APK, WSO2's Gateway API implementation, but most of it is a clear, vendor-neutral explainer of Ingress versus the Gateway API.

## Where does Ingress run out?

Pubudu's running example is a movie ticketing system with order, payment, movie and theatre services behind an Ingress controller. Because Ingress does not provide security or rate limiting, every service implements them itself. Ingress handles host- and path-based routing; anything more, such as path rewrites, CORS, sessions or timeouts, goes into controller-specific annotations, which do not scale as the configuration grows.

His list of Ingress limits:

- HTTP and HTTPS only, with no native TCP, UDP or WebSocket support.
- Basic routing, with no traffic splitting or header-based routing.
- Not easily extensible without custom controllers.
- Minimal security, so mutual TLS needs extra configuration.
- No built-in metrics or traffic monitoring.
- No granular control over retries, timeouts or rate limiting.

## What does the Gateway API change?

The Gateway API, introduced by the Kubernetes community in 2019, splits responsibility across role-oriented custom resources. Infrastructure providers own the GatewayClass, cluster administrators own the Gateway, and application developers write HTTPRoutes for their APIs.

The side-by-side comparison makes the case. The Ingress for the order service needs an nginx annotation to rewrite /orders to /orderList. The equivalent HTTPRoute declares a hostname, a rule matching POST on /orders, a URLRewrite filter, a RequestHeaderModifier filter adding an x-order-id header, and a backendRef to the order service on port 9090. Filters are attached per rule, which is what lets them act as API policies: rate limiting, authentication, authorisation.

Extensibility was in the design from the start. When a backendRef is not enough, an implementation can define its own resource, such as a Backend with protocol, base path and a 20-second timeout, and the HTTPRoute simply references it. The same goes for filters. WSO2 APK uses this to add custom resources for backends, rate limiting, authentication and scopes. The net effect, in his framing, is that the gateway takes over security and traffic control and service developers get back to business logic.

## Why Envoy, and why a control plane?

After a short history of gateways, from protocol converters through hardware load balancers, application delivery controllers, SOAP and REST gateways to micro gateways and cloud gateways, Pubudu explained why Envoy became the default runtime for re-architected API gateways: it was built for cloud native environments, is open source, already powers many Ingress controllers, ships authentication, authorisation, rate limiting and response caching, supports REST and gRPC, and is extensible with native filters, Lua and Wasm.

The gateway is still only the data plane. A control plane holds the API management portals and sends instructions to data planes that can run in different clouds, regions or on-premises. Developers configure their gateways with Kubernetes custom resources, but subscriptions, applications and policies still come from the control plane, which is where governance is enforced. Because every implementation follows the same specification, one control plane can govern several different gateway implementations.

## Gateways become infrastructure

That leads to the closing claim. "You were worried about the file format of your file system that is FAT32 or NTFS", Pubudu said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024, and he expects API gateways to fade into the background the same way. What is left to compete on is API management proper: lifecycle, governance, marketplaces, versioning, productisation and insights, much of which, he noted, has to be redesigned to fit the cloud native ecosystem.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers still stacking Ingress annotations, and API product owners wondering where governance lives once routing is declared in Kubernetes. It is an architecture talk with YAML, not a hands-on demo.

Title: Karpenter skips the node group and asks EC2 directly
Description: Chakkree Tipsupa (AWS) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on Karpenter v1: right-sized nodes, consolidation, Spot, Graviton and AMI drift upgrades, demoed on EKS.
Body:
Cluster Autoscaler scales node groups; Karpenter scales pods' actual needs. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Chakkree Tipsupa, Solutions Architect at AWS, explained what changes when you remove the Auto Scaling group from the scaling path on Amazon EKS, then spent most of the talk in a live demo of Karpenter v1: right-sized instances in seconds, a CPU limit that stops the fleet, Spot and Graviton swaps, consolidation, taints and zone spreading.

It is an AWS talk about an AWS-originated project, and a practical one. If you run EKS with Cluster Autoscaler, the demo alone is a good half hour.

## What's wrong with Cluster Autoscaler plus Auto Scaling groups?

Chakkree opened with a party: you do not know how many guests will turn up, so you either reserve too many tables or scramble for more. Fixed capacity on Kubernetes works the same way. He then named three concrete problems.

First, speed. Pending pods trigger Cluster Autoscaler, which talks to the Auto Scaling group, which calls the EC2 API: several hops before a node exists. Second, waste. The node group adds another m5.large for one leftover pod and leaves 1.5 vCPU idle. Third, rigidity. A new deployment that needs GPUs cannot schedule on the existing group, so the platform team has to create a separate GPU node group first.

## How does Karpenter change the path?

Karpenter replaces both Cluster Autoscaler and the Auto Scaling group. It watches pending pods, works out what they need and calls EC2 Fleet itself, picking an instance that fits and, within your constraints, the cheapest one. Node groups as a concept go away.

What you configure instead is a NodePool. The example in the talk allows the c5, m5 and r5 families, excludes nano, micro and small sizes, restricts zones to us-west-2a and us-west-2b, allows both amd64 and arm64 (Graviton), allows Spot and On-Demand (Spot is preferred when both are allowed), and caps the pool at 100 CPUs. You can run a single NodePool for everything, several to isolate expensive hardware, teams, AMIs or noisy tenants, or weighted pools, for example to use Reserved Instances and Savings Plans first before falling back to Spot or On-Demand.

Consolidation handles the waste problem: with the policy set to WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized, Karpenter bin-packs pods onto fewer nodes, or moves two pods sitting on separate m5.xlarge nodes onto one new m5.large. Upgrades ride on drift: an EC2NodeClass that selects the latest AMI alias makes Karpenter roll nodes onto each new EKS-optimised AMI and drain pods as it goes, or you pin a version and bump it when you choose.

## What does the demo show?

The demo starts with two nodes and an inflate deployment that requests one CPU per pod. Scale it to five replicas and a c6a.2xlarge appears; Chakkree's comment was that "it's super fast to detect and this one is faster than auto scaling group and cluster auto scaling". The Karpenter logs show the reasoning: five pods requesting five CPUs, seven pods once kubelet and kube-proxy daemons are counted, and an instance type chosen from the allowed families.

Scale to 20 and twelve pods stay pending, because the NodePool's 10-CPU limit has been reached. Raise it to 1,000 and a c6a.4xlarge arrives for them. Allow arm64 and Spot and Karpenter replaces the On-Demand node with a Graviton Spot instance, which he said can be up to 70% cheaper. Switch consolidation to WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized, scale down, and underutilised nodes are replaced and deleted. A taint on the NodePool keeps pods off new nodes until the deployment gets a matching toleration, and a topology spread constraint makes Karpenter launch nodes across three availability zones.

## What should you know before onboarding?

Install Karpenter from its Helm chart, and do not run the Karpenter controller on nodes it manages, or it can delete the node it is running on. Put it on Fargate or a small dedicated node group. AWS publishes a step-by-step guide to migrating from Cluster Autoscaler, and an existing custom AMI pipeline can be reused.

## Who should watch

EKS operators still on Cluster Autoscaler, and anyone sizing GPU or mixed-architecture workloads who is tired of managing a node group per instance type. As Chakkree warned, Spot only suits workloads that tolerate interruption.

Title: How The Trevor Project took crisis services to Mexico on Argo CD
Description: Paul Pham and Alfredo Pizana (The Trevor Project) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on moving crisis services to Kubernetes and Argo CD to launch in Mexico.
Body:
Some launch dates are set by the business; this one was set by the calendar. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Paul Pham, Engineering Manager, and Jesus Alfredo Pizana Espinosa, Technical Lead, both at The Trevor Project, explained how the LGBTQ+ suicide prevention nonprofit moved its crisis services off a managed Salesforce platform onto an open source stack of Kubernetes, Argo CD and Terraform, and went live in Mexico on National Coming Out Day, October 11, 2022. Since then the platform has supported more than 20,000 young people in Mexico.

It is a rare Kubernetes talk where the SLO has a human on the other end, and the lessons are the ones any small team learns when it adopts GitOps under a hard deadline.

## Why leave Salesforce?

The Trevor Project took its first phone call on August 11, 1998, and has since added SMS and web chat. Its US crisis services ran on a managed Salesforce service that connected young people with counselors and kept case records. That works for one country. For a global expansion, Paul said, it would take too long to scale and to maintain separate instances per country.

Choosing where to go first was its own project: the team started from 194 countries and used five criteria (safety, scale, equity, language and learning) to narrow the list to Mexico and the Philippines. Mexico went first as a neighbouring country where operations could be set up safely. The result was the global platform, also called CSM (crisis services management), built to be scalable, highly available, multi-language and multi-channel.

## What does the stack look like?

Alfredo walked through the architecture:

- **GCP** for infrastructure, **GitHub** for source and GitHub Actions for CI/CD.
- **Terraform** for infrastructure as code, with templated cluster definitions driven by variables for environment and region.
- **Kubernetes**, with one cluster for the UI and one for the backend, per environment (QA, dev, staging, production).
- **Argo CD** for continuous delivery into those clusters.
- **Twilio** as the contact centre platform, handling SMS, WhatsApp and web chat in real time.
- **MongoDB** for persistence and **Redis** for caching.

Application manifests are built with Kustomize: a base plus per-application overlays, rendered into real manifests with config maps, deployments and external secrets. Before Argo CD, the team generated those files with scripts, which was tedious and error-prone. Argo CD follows the GitOps pattern of treating the repository as the source of truth, so branches and tags map to versions per environment, and its UI shows at a glance which services are healthy, out of sync or crash-looping during a release.

## What went wrong along the way?

Three challenges, honestly stated. A strict launch date meant defining an MVP and choosing tools that cut delivery time. The team lacked experience with the open source stack and learned it while building. And during the migration they maintained up to 10 repositories, carrying data from the old platform to the new one, before consolidating into monorepos.

The lessons follow directly. Paul was candid about cutting corners: "we were deploying manually instead of, sometimes going through the whole pipeline." So: upskill engineers, product managers and the rest of the team on new technology before the project, not during it. Add observability as part of the launch rather than after the first outages, since knowing whether pods are up, and for how long, is what speeds up root cause analysis across several clusters. And track costs. As a nonprofit, they want to autoscale pods with traffic, scaling down when it is quiet, to keep service quality without paying for idle compute.

## What did it achieve?

Two numbers: more than 20,000 young people in Mexico supported with the help of specialised counselors, and a platform that sustainably scales to more than 1,500 chats per month.

## Who should watch

Small platform teams adopting Argo CD and Kustomize on a deadline, and nonprofit engineers weighing a managed SaaS platform against an open source stack. The architecture is conventional; the context and the candour are what make it worth the time.

Title: The Kubernetes log that errors first is rarely the one to blame
Description: Amir Krayden (Senser) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on enriching Kubernetes logs with topology, metrics and deploy history to find the root cause next door.
Body:
In a distributed system, the service that throws the error is usually a victim, not the culprit. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Amir Krayden, Co-founder and CEO of Senser, took one real Kubernetes failure, a frontend returning server errors, and showed why logs alone send you scrubbing through the wrong node, and how topology, metrics and deployment history get you to the actual fault (a lost Redis connection one hop away) much faster.

The investigation runs in Senser's own product, so this is a vendor talk. The method, though, is tool-agnostic, and Amir says as much: the same steps work in whatever observability stack you run.

## Why aren't logs enough on their own?

The talk's thesis fits in one line: "the problem with logs is that usually they require more logs." In Kubernetes, the other logs you need sit on another node, in another pod, behind another service.

Amir gave a few reasons individual logs lack context. A human wrote them, and humans are bad at predicting the future: each log line encodes the author's past experience and assumptions about which corner cases matter. Teams review code changes carefully but rarely review what their logs will mean later. A log captures one moment of one event while other things happen in parallel. And a log knows nothing about topology: which services, nodes and infrastructure it is connected to. He listed what that costs: MTTR, total investigation time, and SRE sanity.

## What does context mean in practice?

Three things enrich a log:

- **Topology**: a live, high-level map of nodes, services and infrastructure and how they connect. Holding that in your head is hard when the system autoscales and pods are ephemeral.
- **Metrics**: CPU, memory, network latency and error rates around the moment of the log, to tell a resource problem from an application one.
- **Deployment history**: what the CI/CD pipeline shipped recently, new images or configuration changes, since a lot of errors correlate with a recent deploy.

Getting all three is hard either way. Commercial tools such as Dynatrace, Datadog and New Relic cost money for full coverage and still need dashboards built and maintained. An open source stack of OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Grafana often means manual instrumentation, with coverage gaps, overhead and production impact. His spoiler: eBPF plus automated topology.

## How did the investigation actually go?

The log-only path is the one most of us know. The frontend log points at a gRPC connection failure to the cart service in an e-commerce app. You assume the issue is local, scrub through the logs just before and just after the event, and work up the layers from infrastructure to application, eliminating causes one by one. It works, slowly, and as Amir put it, the first thing you see "is not the source of the problem, but it's already stage two".

The enriched path starts with the map. Filtering the APIs the frontend is a client of shows the cart service, and those APIs are erroring too, which clears the frontend and moves the investigation one hop. Because the topology carries live connectivity status, the next step is visible immediately: the cart service has lost its connection to its Redis store. At that point, he said, you are about 90% of the way to the fix.

## Which pitfalls should you avoid?

- **Incomplete instrumentation.** Amir called OpenTelemetry and distributed tracing a very important part of the toolset, but most environments are partially instrumented, and the blind spots hurt. eBPF can auto-instrument without touching code.
- **Tribal knowledge.** Codify deployment history and past incidents, but leave room for situations nobody has seen.
- **Incorrect heuristics.** Without system-wide context, you fixate on the node or service where the error showed up. Assume the root cause is next door, possibly in a third-party or cloud service.

His tips: use topology, metrics and deployments together; go top-down from high-level views before drilling into logs; and consider eBPF, automated topology and AIOps for root cause analysis.

## Who should watch

On-call engineers and SREs who live in kubectl logs during incidents, and teams weighing eBPF-based observability. Expect a methodology and a product walkthrough, not a tutorial on building the map yourself.

Title: Perses wants to be Prometheus's Grafana, with dashboards in Git
Description: Erwin de Keijzer (TrueFullstaq) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on Perses, the GitOps-native CNCF dashboard tool: live demo, CUE and Go, and honest gotchas.
Body:
Most dashboards are ClickOps that someone later regrets. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Erwin de Keijzer, DevOps Engineer at TrueFullstaq, walked through Perses, the dashboard tool that went into the CNCF sandbox with the explicit goal of being GitOps-native: dashboards defined as data, applied with a CLI, diffed in Git and generated from CUE or Go. His verdict is enthusiastic but fair. Perses already looks good and versions cleanly; Grafana still wins on features.

He is upfront that he has no affiliation with the project, just a fondness for it, which makes the list of gotchas at the end more useful than a maintainer's pitch would be.

## What is Perses trying to be?

Erwin read out the project's goals and was careful to call them goals, not achieved milestones. Perses wants to be the standard dashboard tool for Prometheus, GitOps-compatible from the start, and Kubernetes-native, adopting the Kubernetes data model and eventually shipping CRDs, so you could deploy a dashboard right next to the ServiceMonitor that feeds it. It wants static validation of the dashboard format, so a CI pipeline can reject a broken dashboard before it ships, and plugin support. The odd one out is publishing npm packages, which turns out to be about sharing its visualisations with the wider ecosystem, the Prometheus UI included.

## What does the demo show?

The first demo runs Prometheus and Perses from a Docker Compose file, with Perses on the latest tag "because YOLO". Variables, data sources and secrets exist at a global level and at a project level. Erwin creates a project called ClickOps, adds a Prometheus data source, and builds a time series panel of goroutines that, in his words, looks good by default. Every dashboard can show the JSON behind it.

The second half is the part GitOps people came for: percli, the Perses CLI. Erwin admits he is not sure how to say it and settles on "Berkeley", because that's funnier. He applies a numbered set of files (project first, since everything depends on it, then data source, then dashboard), opens a blackbox-exporter dashboard with variables populated from Prometheus label values, edits a panel group in the UI, pulls it back with the CLI and shows the Git diff. The first diff is noisy with whitespace changes; after a second round trip it shrinks to the width and alignment he actually changed.

## How does it compare with Grafana?

His scorecard: customisation goes to Grafana by a distance, and he misses the Explore tab most. Style goes to Perses, whose defaults he thinks look better. Ease of use is a draw; after ten years on Grafana he found Perses quick to learn. GitOps-friendliness goes clearly to Perses. The future is bright but, as he put it, still a bit murky.

## Dashboards as code, in CUE or Go

Perses pushes dashboards-as-code (DaC) with two options: CUE or the Go SDK. Erwin's description of CUE is the best line of the talk: "It's like YAML and toml and Python and Go had a four way and this is the very odd baby". The practical value is the logic. CUE types are generated from Perses's Go types, so definitions stay aligned with the code, and if statements and for loops let one definition produce consistent dashboards for development, acceptance and production even when labels or naming conventions differ. Both CUE and the Go SDK export the YAML that percli applies.

## What will bite you today?

The gotchas list is why this talk is worth watching before you adopt Perses:

- "Dashboards and panels don't save unless you click save." It is not obvious that you are in edit mode, and a refresh throws away your work.
- Names created in the UI do not match the CLI: spaces and special characters turn into underscores.
- Units are cloud-native only (bytes, time, rates). No currencies, no SI units, so his power usage dashboard cannot show kilowatt-hours.
- The Kubernetes integration does not exist yet; the operator repository has activity but nothing usable.
- Ephemeral dashboards with a TTL sound great for CI/CD, but do not work with percli yet.
- Documentation is limited, and the percli DaC setup fails on macOS because of fixable permission issues.

He closes with an invitation to contribute, and a promise of a personal thank-you note to anyone who does.

## Who should watch

Platform and observability engineers who keep Grafana dashboards in Git with a lot of glue, and anyone curious whether Perses is ready for them. The demo is hands-on and the caveats are specific.

Title: Multi-cloud observability is an SDK problem before it's a dashboard one
Description: Siri Varma Vegiraju (Microsoft) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on replacing per-cloud monitoring SDKs with OpenTelemetry plus one exporter per provider.
Body:
Run on three clouds and you end up with three monitoring SDKs, three dashboards and an on-call engineer who has to debug the dashboards before they can debug the outage. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Siri Varma Vegiraju, Software Development Engineer at Microsoft, argued that the fix starts in the code: emit everything through the OpenTelemetry SDK once, let a per-provider exporter do the translation, and put Grafana on top for a single view.

It is an introductory talk, clear and well paced, aimed at teams that have drifted into multi-cloud and are now paying for it in instrumentation sprawl.

## Why do teams end up on several clouds?

Siri opened with the survey figure that 98% of enterprises use or plan to use multiple clouds, then gave three reasons. Data sovereignty: serve customers in many countries and each set of privacy and data protection laws can push you to a provider that fits. Vendor lock-in: a provider can raise a price, change a service or deprecate it, and the business should survive that. Cost: providers differ on egress, compute, network and storage pricing, and a team that can mix them pays less.

None of that is controversial. The interesting part is what it does to observability.

## What breaks when every cloud brings its own SDK?

With one cloud, the code is simple: one monitoring SDK emits metrics to one provider dashboard. With two or three, you import two or three SDKs, each with its own versioning, deprecations and semantics, and you maintain all of them. The dashboards differ too, down to how they aggregate: some sample at five minutes, some at one, and someone has to document which is which.

Siri's sharpest point was about who pays for that: "The on calls In addition to be debugging the service outages are also debugging the dashboards now." Add the cost of hiring and training engineers who know every provider's tooling, and the observability bill grows faster than the infrastructure.

## How does OpenTelemetry flatten it?

The goal he set was a single pane of glass, which in turn requires being provider-agnostic. OpenTelemetry, a CNCF project supported by AWS, Azure, GCP and Oracle, provides that through five pieces:

- **Specification**: matters when someone implements OpenTelemetry for a language; most teams never touch it.
- **Semantics**: the shared schema that makes a unified view possible.
- **SDK**: what your service calls to emit metrics, logs and traces, available in C#, Java, Go, Ruby and more.
- **Exporter**: translates OpenTelemetry data into what a given backend understands. Azure Monitor, AWS and Google Cloud each have one.
- **Backend**: the provider itself, or Prometheus and Jaeger.

The before-and-after architecture is the practical heart of the talk. Before: a VM, a service and the Azure Monitor SDK, welded to Azure. After: the same service calls the OpenTelemetry SDK, and the Azure exporter ships the data. He stressed that the exporter is not a sidecar, just another package or Maven dependency imported into the service. Adding a second cloud means adding a second exporter to the list of extensions; the namespace and the code that emits metrics do not change.

## One dashboard, then the rest of the toolbox

For the single view, Siri pointed at Grafana pulling in data from all the providers, so developers debug in one place. He closed with the wider open source set that plugs into the same SDK: Prometheus for metrics, Loki for logs in Grafana alongside metrics, and Zipkin and Jaeger for traces. His summary: "As multi cloud architecture keeps growing it is very important that organizations make vendor agnostic strategy part of their architecture and part of their culture."

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads whose services emit telemetry through a cloud vendor's SDK and who suspect a second provider is coming. If you already run the OpenTelemetry Collector in production, this is a refresher; there is no collector topology or sampling discussion.

Title: Why Kubernetes tooling keeps getting written in Go
Description: Abhinav Chunchu (Lowes) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on why Go's small binaries and 2 KB goroutines make it the default language for Kubernetes tooling.
Body:
Kubernetes is written in Go, and so is most of what plugs into it. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Abhinav Chunchu, Senior Software Engineer at Lowes, made the case that this is no accident: Go's small static binaries, fast startup and cheap goroutines line up with what a container orchestrator rewards, which is why he expects Go to stay the default language for controllers, operators and the next wave of Kubernetes projects.

It is a short, high-level talk, closer to a well-argued briefing than a tutorial. If you already write operators in Go, you will nod along; if you are choosing a language for your first Kubernetes-native service, it is a tidy summary of the arguments.

## What does Go give you inside a container?

The argument starts with startup time. Containers get killed, rescheduled and scaled out constantly, so a service that takes a long time to boot pays that cost on every pod. Abhinav contrasted Go with heavier stacks: "The currently services like in Java or Spring Boot or other, PySpark, other features from the other frameworks are very heavy loaded and heavy duty, applications where they have the more startup time and scaling those high microservices is much harder compared to the Go."

A compiled Go service ships as one small binary, starts almost immediately and keeps a modest memory footprint. He listed networking, file I/O and memory-intensive work as areas where Go does well with little overhead, and argued that its native concurrency lets it outperform many other languages in multi-container setups where tasks run in parallel.

## Why goroutines matter to an orchestrator

The most concrete number in the talk is about memory. Goroutines start at roughly 2 KB each, against the 512 KB to 1 MB a thread typically costs in other languages. That difference is what lets a controller watch thousands of objects, or a service hold thousands of concurrent connections, without the resource bill that would make Kubernetes' own autoscaling pointless.

Channels are the other half of the story. They give goroutines a safe way to pass data, which in a distributed Kubernetes setup means fewer data races and fewer bugs that only appear under load. Kubernetes itself leans on the same model to manage large numbers of microservices without excessive resource consumption.

## How much of the ecosystem is Go?

Abhinav cited CNCF survey data from 2023 claiming that 70% of Kubernetes controllers and operators are written in Go, and said organisations pick it because it shortens development time without giving up performance. He also showed two anonymised case studies: one company that moved to Go-based controllers and saw 30% faster scaling, another that reached 99.99% uptime with Go-based operators. Neither came with methodology, so treat them as illustrations rather than benchmarks.

## Where it goes next

The closing section looks at where Kubernetes is heading: edge computing and multi-cluster management, with projects such as KubeEdge and Cluster API named as the places Go will keep doing the heavy lifting. His summary of the pairing was short: "Go's performance, scalability, lightweight nature make it ideal for the modern cloud native systems."

## Who should watch

Developers and team leads deciding what to write their first operator or Kubernetes-native microservice in, and anyone who has to explain to management why the platform team keeps asking for Go. Experienced Go and operator authors will not find new material here; there is no code and no live demo.

Title: Green pod dashboards, broken checkout, and how Wix monitors the funnel
Description: Or Rozenzweig (Wix) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on business-driven monitoring with Prometheus, Loki and Grafana, tracking funnel KPIs instead of pods
Body:
Every pod can be healthy while buyers cannot pick a delivery option at checkout. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Or Rozenzweig, Backend Developer on the Wix e-commerce platform, argues for business-driven monitoring: map the product funnel, put metrics on every step, and alert on business KPIs such as delivery-step conversion instead of only latency and errors. Then he builds the dashboard live in Grafana.

## Why aren't pod metrics enough?

Wix has excellent out-of-the-box monitoring, and Or's point is that it is scoped to a single microservice or even a single pod. The scale makes the problem obvious: Wix powers over 10 million sites, 1 million of them e-commerce, and its microservices expose over 150 million unique metrics per hour and half a trillion logs a day. Latency and error rates for one service tell you nothing about whether a buyer got through checkout.

He is clear this is not developers doing analysts' work. Analysts measure KPIs monthly for growth; this is end-to-end monitoring of product funnels to catch user-facing bugs before users report them.

## Three steps and three open source tools

The toolbox is Loki for logs, Prometheus for metrics and Grafana for visualisation and alerts. All open source; at a low-budget startup Or ran them on premises with Docker Compose, so no big-company platform is required.

The method:

1. **Map the funnels and define KPIs.** Identify the crucial flows, break them into steps, and bring product and business analysts in. Every funnel needs at least one KPI. For Wix e-commerce the big one is checkout conversion, with per-step KPIs inside it.
2. **Light up the dark spots with metrics.** Instrument not just error paths but the paths that mean the product is working. Be generous; with Prometheus and Grafana wired up, a new metric is one line of code and one line in Grafana.
3. **Visualise it in Grafana**, picking the panel type that fits each step.

## Labels are power, and a footgun

The real-world example is Wix's delivery system, which calls carriers such as USPS for live delivery options and costs during checkout. A single success metric gave a blurry picture: something succeeded, something failed, but which carrier? Adding the carrier ID as a label turned one metric into dozens of monitored flows, one per carrier, with a `by (carrier)` at the end of the query.

The catch is cardinality. Every new label value is a new metric series, and an unbounded label can push a service into spending all its effort on being monitored until it stops being monitored, and then stops working. Wix even alerts on how many metrics each service exposes.

"Wix actually exposes a monitoring alert on the number of metrics we use for monitoring, which is a monitoring cannibalism, if you ask me," Or Rozenzweig said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

## The demo: four panels for one funnel

Starting from an empty dashboard on top of Prometheus, Or builds the delivery funnel in four steps, using `sum` to aggregate across pods (the business does not care which pod) and Wix's m1_rate, a one-minute average, for smoother graphs:

- Calls to the delivery system's entry point, as the count of buyers who want delivery.
- Active delivery carriers per request, switched from a time series to a stat panel showing the mean.
- Successful carrier API calls, then failed ones, broken down by carrier label. One app shows up failing frequently, which is exactly the kind of thing he can go and fix.
- Delivery step conversion, using the analysts' metrics: delivery method completion divided by the contact details step before it.

He then adds an alert routed to the on-call channel, because in a week or two everyone forgets the dashboard exists, and recommends a linked investigation dashboard with filters, ready-made queries and latest logs to go from business symptom to root cause fast.

## Who should watch

Backend developers who own features end to end, SREs whose dashboards are all green during incidents, and anyone about to add a label with user IDs in it. His closing line is that monitoring is how you become the owner of a product rather than only its developer.

Title: The best fix for money-moving race conditions is no concurrency at all
Description: Nikita Melnikov (Atlantic Money) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on replacing row locks and distributed locks with Kafka-backed actors in Go
Body:
A transfer that is cancelled by compliance and marked as paid in the same second is not an edge case in fintech; it is a Tuesday. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Nikita Melnikov, VP of Engineering at Atlantic Money (and formerly of Tinkoff Bank and Tinkoff Investments, where he worked on systems handling 300,000 requests per second), walks through why database locks and distributed locks struggle with this, and how his team models each transfer as an actor fed by Kafka instead.

The thesis is in the abstract: "the best concurrency is no concurrency." Rather than coordinating many writers, make sure each transfer only ever has one.

## Where does the lost update come from?

The example is Atlantic Money's own flow. A customer sends $100 to have €90 delivered. Between "wait for dollars" and "send euros" sit a stack of steps: record payment details, screen sanction lists, run anti-fraud, check limits, calculate fees, exchange currencies.

Meanwhile, the compliance service decides to cancel the transfer. Two transactions both select the transfer with status `CREATED`, one sets `CANCELLED`, the other sets `PAYMENT_RECEIVED`, both commit. Read the row afterwards and the status is whichever write landed last. For a payments company, undefined status is not an acceptable answer.

## Why not just SELECT FOR UPDATE?

It works, and it is simple: no new tools, no new abstractions, Postgres blocks the second transaction until the first commits. The problem is arithmetic. With an average processing time of five seconds and 100 operations a second, you have 500 active transactions, most of them idle while calling external services or writing audit data.

That costs resources and, worse, eats connection pools. With a pool of 16 connections and concurrent work on the same transfer, each request grabs a connection and waits on the lock until the pool is empty and nothing else, including unrelated customers, can be served.

## And locks?

A Go `sync.Mutex` per transfer works until you run more than one node. Then a pay request on node 1 and a cancel request on node 2 each hold their own perfectly valid lock, which is to say no lock at all.

Distributed locks via Hazelcast, ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul or Redis fix that and bring a new list of problems: ordering (nodes in different zones reach the lock manager at different speeds, so who gets the lock is hard to reason about), acquisition timeouts, holding timeouts, what to do when you lose the lock mid-process or crash holding it with partial state, and deadlocks when you need locks on the transfer, the customer and the recipient in different orders. Melnikov is candid that he knows no way to guarantee freedom from deadlocks other than testing, "but testing is super complex in distributed systems," he said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

## Treat the transfer as a state machine

The pivot is modelling. A transfer is a finite state machine: `created`, `payment_received`, `checks_sent`, `checks_pending`, then approved or rejected. State transitions happen only through commands (`ReceivePayment`, `SendChecksForProcessing`, `ApplyCheckResult`), each state allows only certain commands, and a command can trigger effects such as sending the next command. You cannot jump from payment received back to waiting for payment because the domain does not allow it.

That gives three requirements: communication through messages, durable message storage, and one-at-a-time handling per transfer.

## How Kafka and actors deliver that

Kafka covers the first two. Using the transfer ID as the message key routes every command for a transfer to the same partition, and `acks=all` buys durability at the cost of latency. Consumer groups cover the third: each partition is consumed by exactly one instance, so each transfer is processed sequentially, while consumers still scale horizontally.

On top sits the actor model, explicitly as a concept rather than a full Erlang or Akka implementation (no supervision trees, no location transparency). The Go interfaces are small: a `Storage` to get and put state by key, an `Actor` with `Receive(state, command)`, a mailbox and a command producer. The Kafka consumer loads state, calls the actor and saves the new state.

Two production details stop it from being a toy:

- **The double-write problem.** Write to Postgres and then crash before producing to Kafka, and you are inconsistent. The fix is the outbox pattern: save new state and outgoing effects in one Postgres transaction, then let Debezium stream the outbox table into topics like `compliance.commands`, `payments.commands` and `transfer.events`.
- **Toxic messages.** A bad format, wrong version, logic error or unexpected state should not block a partition forever. Those go to a dead-letter topic.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers building anything with money, inventory or bookings, where two writers on one record is a correctness bug, and Go developers curious about actors without adopting a framework. The first half is a clear tour of why the usual fixes break; the Kafka and actor design is the payoff.

Title: Milvus splits a vector database into pods so it can scale like one
Description: Tim Spann (Zilliz) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on Milvus, the open source vector database built cloud native, from pip install to billions of vectors
Body:
A vector search library is fine until you need durability, replication, deletes and a thousand people querying at once. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Tim Spann, Principal Developer Advocate at Zilliz, makes the case for Milvus, the open source vector database whose architecture looks a lot like any other well-behaved Kubernetes application: stateless proxies, separate workers for querying, data and indexing, a message log in the middle and object storage underneath.

Tim works for the company behind Milvus and its managed version, Zilliz Cloud, and says so. The talk is half architecture, half live demos, with plenty of cats.

## Why not just bolt a library onto Postgres?

Tim is fair to the alternatives. Libraries such as FAISS, Annoy and HNSW are great for prototyping and, per his slides, comfortable up to around a million vectors; Milvus uses some of them under the covers. Existing databases with an approximate nearest neighbour plug-in, such as PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch or MongoDB, cover the middle ground. A purpose-built vector database earns its place when you need billion-plus scale, full CRUD, real-time search, top-k, range and hybrid search, multi-vector queries and a distributed deployment.

The motivating data is unstructured: images, video, audio, PDFs, logs. His slides cite IDC estimates that 80% of new data will be unstructured, and that 90% of unstructured data is never analysed. Embedding models turn it into vectors; the database makes those vectors durable and searchable.

## What does Milvus look like on Kubernetes?

The architecture slide will look familiar. Proxies sit behind a load balancer as the access layer. Coordinators handle the root, query, data and index work. Worker nodes for query, data and index scale out independently, so a burst of searches does not starve ingestion. Kafka or Pulsar serves as the log broker, so data is not lost and nothing waits on anything else, etcd holds metadata and coordination, and MinIO, S3 or Azure Blob stores logs, snapshots and index files. Compute and storage are decoupled, so the cluster can shrink as easily as it grows.

On scale, his slides claim 10 billion vectors of 1,536 dimensions in a single Milvus or Zilliz Cloud instance and around 100 billion vectors in one of the largest deployments. Milvus supports 15 index types, including HNSW, IVF variants with quantisation, DiskANN for datasets that should not live in RAM, and GPU indexes such as CAGRA, which came from NVIDIA.

The same code runs at every size. Start with `pip install pymilvus` and Milvus Lite in a notebook, move to Docker, then to a Kubernetes cluster with the Helm charts, or to the managed service.

"If you didn't know, it's also a bird, but we're talking about the database," Tim Spann said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

## The demos

Tim opens with public demos: a chatbot over open source project documentation, a reverse image search, and a multimodal search for ceiling cats where an image vector and a text vector are searched together and reranked into one result. Then he moves to his own code: a Zilliz Cloud free-tier cluster browsed with Attu, the open source GUI, showing JSON metadata filters, partition keys, tunable consistency, vector search from an uploaded image and generated query code. A Python job pulls Medium RSS feeds, embeds them with a Hugging Face Sentence Transformers model on his laptop CPU, and inserts them into Milvus; a LangChain RAG loop answers questions over the collection and posts the results to Slack.

His argument for RAG is practical: better and more relevant answers, fewer hallucinations, and with local models through Ollama, data that never leaves your hands.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers asked to run a vector database for an AI team, and developers choosing between a plug-in and a dedicated store. The architecture section is the part to study; the demos show how little code the happy path takes.

Title: Run the postmortem before launch, and ban the engineers from fixing anything
Description: Laurent Parenteau (Grow Great) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on running a pre-mortem that finds project risks without becoming a fix-it session
Body:
Postmortems are excellent, and they all share one flaw: they happen after the outage. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Laurent Parenteau, software engineering coach and mentor at Grow Great, makes the case for the pre-mortem, a group exercise where you pretend the project has already failed and work backwards to why, while there is still time to do something about it.

It is a short, practical talk with no tooling, and the most useful part is the list of ways to run one badly.

## Why bother?

Parenteau opens with a sobering figure from the Standish Group: 74% of all IT projects fail. He is careful about the definition. Most failures do not end in flames; they are delays, missing features, or a rough launch followed by a few weeks of firefighting. All of it is cheaper to prevent than to fix.

## What is a pre-mortem, exactly?

A risk discovery technique in two steps:

1. **Set up a hypothetical future.** If the project launches on May 4th, the group declares it is now the week after May 4th, and the launch was a complete wreck.
2. **Ask what went wrong.** Then brainstorm, as in a postmortem, but before anything has broken.

The framing is the trick. The slides cite University of Colorado research finding this kind of prospective hindsight increases the ability to identify reasons for future outcomes by 30%, compared with simply asking what could go wrong.

## How do you run one well?

Parenteau's dos and don'ts come from his own sessions:

- **Keep the group small.** As with any brainstorm, bigger groups mean fewer people speak and less airtime for each.
- **Mix perspectives.** Three DevOps engineers will produce one DevOps engineer's worth of risks. Bring a project manager, someone from sales, engineers from different parts of the stack, anyone relevant.
- **Do not problem solve.** This is the one engineers break first. Someone names a risk, and an engineer immediately starts designing the fix. Stop them. "So you keep note of the problem, but you prevent people from solving it," Parenteau said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. The goal at this stage is volume.
- **Do not reject anything yet.** Tell people an idea is stupid and they go quiet. His example from a past session: the CEO dies before launch. Not much an engineer can do about it, but it goes on the list.
- **Keep asking why.** Vague risks hide several specific ones. "The server crashed" could mean overload, a hardware fault, an application failure, or a spike in logins or account creation at launch. Dig until you get the specific ones.
- **Remind everyone of the goal.** A room listing every way a project can burn down gets gloomy. Repeat that listing a risk does not mean it will happen, and that naming it now is how you stop it.

## Then what?

The output is a long, messy list, so the follow-up matters as much as the session:

1. **Group and clean up.** Merge items that describe the same problem in different words, and group different causes that end in the same failure. Go back to whoever raised an unclear item.
2. **Assess the risk.** Use judgement on likelihood and impact. Mitigating everything would take forever, so address the most likely ones and park the rest.
3. **Share the mitigation plan**, above all with the people who took part. Close the loop: here is what we found, here is who owns what.

That last step has a benefit beyond risk reduction. A team that sees its fears written down with an owner and a plan next to each one is more confident and more motivated, and Parenteau argues that morale alone improves the odds of success.

## Who should watch

Tech leads, engineering managers and platform teams about to launch something with a date attached. If you already run pre-mortems, the dos and don'ts are a quick sanity check; if you only run postmortems, this is a low-cost habit to add.

Title: Every multiplayer cursor is pub/sub plus a WebSocket
Description: Vitor Norton (SuperViz) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on the code behind live cursors and presence: rooms, channels, pub/sub and WebSockets
Body:
Those little coloured cursors gliding across a Figma or Miro board look like magic, and the code underneath is surprisingly small. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Vitor Norton, Developer Advocate at SuperViz and a ten-time Microsoft MVP, takes a mouse-pointer component apart layer by layer: a room, a channel, a pub/sub event broker, and finally the WebSocket that makes it work across machines.

It is a beginner-friendly, code-on-screen talk. Norton says plainly that the snippets are for demonstration, not the source of Miro or Figma, which is the right framing: you come away knowing how the pattern works, not with a production library.

## What counts as a collaboration component?

Norton, who admits his whole brain lives in his productivity tools ("If I lose my account on notion, I'm dead," he said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024), starts with four examples:

- **Form elements** synced as people type, handy when a support agent fills a form with a customer on the phone.
- **Who-is-online** presence indicators.
- **Mouse pointers**, including following a colleague's cursor.
- **Contextual comments** pinned to any element of a page, even a 3D scene.

His bet is that any application shipped to the world without features like these is missing something.

## Rooms first, then pointers

The top-level API is a room: a group of participants sharing an ID, such as a meeting URL or a document. A room does nothing on its own. You construct a mouse-pointer component and add it to the room, optionally with conditions (the host might not see pointers, say). In React you would typically wrap the room as a provider.

Inside the pointer, there are three jobs:

1. **See when someone else moves.** Subscribe to a `mouse-moved` event on a channel, and in the callback set the stored x and y. It works much like `addEventListener` on an HTML element.
2. **Tell everyone where you are.** Listen to the document's own mouse-move event, wrap `clientX` and `clientY` in a position object, and publish it to the channel.
3. **Keep it smooth without flooding the wire.** Throttle with the browser's `requestAnimationFrame`, around 30 frames per second, so the pointer does not look laggy and you do not blow through rate limits by sending more data than needed.

## What is the channel, really?

This is where the talk earns its title. The channel is a real-time event broker added to the room, and you can open as many as you like: one for pointers, one for typing indicators, one for live locations.

Stripped down, it is a pub/sub with two methods over an events object. `subscribe(event, callback)` creates an empty array for the event name if it does not exist and pushes the callback onto it. `publish(event, data)` loops over that event's callbacks and calls each with the data. Norton relates it to the observer pattern, the same family of ideas behind Redux.

The catch: everything so far only works inside one browser tab. Pub/sub on its own has no idea there are other devices in the room.

## Why WebSockets and not HTTP?

The missing piece is a WebSocket, a persistent, bidirectional channel between client and server. With plain HTTP, every update means opening a connection, sending a request, reading the response and closing it. Doing that about 30 times a second per user is the kind of design that eventually takes your server down. A WebSocket opens once, carries messages both ways for the life of the page, and closes when you leave, giving the low latency that games, live updates and stock tickers need.

## Where you have already seen it

The examples are everyday: Uber and WhatsApp live location (the driver publishes, you subscribe and redraw the map), Microsoft Teams meeting status and attendee presence, typing indicators in chat apps (only a true/false flag travels, not your keystrokes), collaborative whiteboards like Miro, and Gather's virtual office where audio and video fade in as avatars get close.

## Who should watch

Front-end and full-stack developers who have used real-time features but never built one, and platform engineers who need a quick mental model before choosing a real-time backend. If you have already implemented pub/sub over WebSockets, this is a refresher. For further reading Norton recommends Addy Osmani's Learning JavaScript Design Patterns.

Title: Health insurance claims run in nightly batches, and Kubernetes fits that shape
Description: Shiva Kumar Chinnam (Rialtic) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on moving healthcare claims processing from Ansible on bare metal to EKS and Argo CD
Body:
Health insurers collect claims all day and process them in one big batch overnight, which means infrastructure that sits idle for most of the day. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Shiva Kumar Chinnam, Senior Cloud Engineer at the insurance technology startup Rialtic, walks through how a large health insurer moved its claims processing from Ansible scripts on bare metal to Amazon EKS with Argo CD, and halved its downtime in the process.

The case study comes from a conversation with a colleague at a large health insurance company rather than from Shiva's own employer, and the talk is a gentle introduction, so expect the migration story and the reasoning rather than configs.

## How does a claim actually move?

Shiva's explanation of the domain is the most useful part for outsiders. A patient gets care; the provider, a doctor or a hospital, files a claim with the insurer, which the industry calls the payer. The payer checks each claim against healthcare policies, from simple rules (nobody gets three knee replacements, there are only two knees) to multi-step rules that vary by state and by programme, such as Medicare or Medicaid. Payers also send claims to specialist processing companies, which is where Rialtic works: claims come in, get processed, and go back.

The scale is the reason it matters. His slides put US healthcare at a $4.5 trillion economy in 2022, with the highest healthcare spend per person in the world.

## What did the old setup look like?

Two on-premises data centres, Java binaries built in GitHub CI, pulled from a registry and deployed straight onto bare-metal machines by a patchwork of Ansible and shell scripts. With a microservices architecture, that was a lot of code to maintain. Ansible ran from engineers' laptops, local changes did not always get committed, and deployments happened once a week inside maintenance windows that took a data centre down.

## What changed on Kubernetes?

The new stack is EKS with GitOps: manifests and Helm charts in Git, Argo CD deploying from the registry to the cluster. That alone fixed the uncommitted-change problem and gave a clear change control trail.

The gains Shiva reports:

- **50% reduction in downtime**, mostly from rolling updates replacing maintenance windows, plus self-healing when an instance fails.
- **Canary deployments** to test a new version on a slice of traffic before full rollout.
- **Cost savings on the nightly batch**, by scaling the infrastructure up once a day for processing and back down afterwards with EKS autoscaling.
- **Spark jobs via Airflow**, using its Kubernetes operators so DAGs run jobs inside the cluster.
- Easier Datadog integration for real-time monitoring, and RBAC for security and compliance.

## Should every healthcare company do this?

Refreshingly, no. "Kubernetes is not really useful in all the use cases," Shiva Kumar Chinnam said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024. For a small application without a microservices architecture, he points to plain EC2 instances, Elastic Beanstalk or AWS Lambda instead.

For those who do go ahead, his order is assessment first, then planning (containerise, build pipelines, write Helm charts, automate with GitOps), a pilot with one microservice in a non-critical system, gradual scaling to the critical ones, and monitoring throughout. His outlook ties it to AI and ML: healthcare runs on data, and teams that build Kubernetes expertise now will be better placed for those workloads.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to healthcare who need the claims pipeline explained in ten minutes, and teams still deploying with Ansible from laptops who want a sober case for GitOps without hype.
