Title: A private team GenAI assistant on AWS serverless for $19 a month
Description: Samuel Baruffi (AWS) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on an open-source, serverless Bedrock assistant with shared prompt templates for platform teams
Body:
Fifty engineers, five prompts a day each, Claude 3 Haiku behind it: $19.32 a month, everything included. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Samuel Baruffi, Principal Global Solutions Architect at AWS, walks through an open-source GenAI assistant that runs entirely in your own AWS account on serverless services and Amazon Bedrock, and shows why the interesting feature is not the chat box but shared prompt templates.

He is upfront that this is an AWS sample, not a product to deploy and forget: "It's not a full fledged solution," Baruffi said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Treat it as an architecture pattern to fork.

## Why would a platform team build its own?

Baruffi's pitch is aimed at platform engineers specifically. Developer self-service, navigating a stack where AWS alone has more than 200 services, and consistent security and compliance all benefit from GenAI. The argument for hosting it yourself rather than buying a subscription is control: authentication, authorisation, data retention and encryption all live in your account, under your policies.

The solution is called Improve Employee Productivity with a GenAI Assistant, in the aws-samples GitHub organisation.

## What can users actually do?

- **Playground:** pick a model, send a prompt, get a streamed answer. Nothing new, as he says himself.
- **Templates:** the real value. A template stores a model choice, a system prompt and user data with a `${variable}` placeholder. Templates are private (creator only) or public, which here means visible to every authenticated user of your deployment, not the internet. A team can curate a product-naming or Python bug-fix template once and everyone reuses it, with advanced users able to inspect the system prompt and tweak temperature, top-k and top-p.
- **Multimodal input:** all the Claude 3 models used support images, so a template can take a photo alongside text.
- **Chat with templates:** conversations keep context, so you can fix buggy Python, ask for a Node.js rewrite, then a summary.
- **History:** every interaction is stored in a database you own.

The demo also shows code-aware formatting with copy buttons, generating a CloudFormation template for an EC2 instance and a VPC.

## How is it built?

Everything is pay-as-you-go; nothing is provisioned for months ahead. The nine services and their jobs:

- **CloudFront + S3 + AWS WAF:** host the React UI, terminate HTTPS, and filter DDoS, SQL injection, XSS or whole countries.
- **Amazon Cognito:** sign-in, integrated with both APIs so unauthenticated calls are denied by API Gateway.
- **API Gateway REST + Lambda:** templates, history and the rest of CRUD, with functions in Python and JavaScript.
- **API Gateway WebSocket + Lambda:** the streaming path. The browser holds a WebSocket, a Lambda calls Bedrock, and the gateway routes tokens back to the right connection.
- **DynamoDB:** chats, templates and history, encrypted by default, with retention you control.
- **S3** again for uploaded images, which the streaming Lambda fetches at inference time.
- **Amazon Bedrock:** one API to the models, billed per input and output token. Baruffi states that Bedrock does not store prompts or use them to train models.

Deployment uses AWS SAM (CloudFormation underneath) driven by a single `deploy.sh` that takes a region and an admin email, deploys back end, front end and default templates, and creates the first user. CloudShell or Cloud9 work if you would rather not install Python, SAM, Node.js and jq locally.

## What does it cost?

The estimate in the talk, for us-east-1, 50 users, five uses a day, 500 input and 200 output tokens per request, with $16.51 of non-Bedrock services in every row:

- Claude 3 Haiku: $19.32 a month
- Claude 3 Sonnet or Claude 3.5 Sonnet: $50.26
- Claude 3 Opus: $185.26

He compares Haiku's total with a single person's $20-plus chat subscription. The caveat he gives himself is fair: prices change, regions differ, and Bedrock was not in the AWS pricing calculator at the time, so check the numbers for your own setup. The talk was recorded in August 2024, so the model line-up has moved on since.

## Who should watch

Platform teams asked to provide a sanctioned internal AI assistant, and anyone who wants a worked example of streaming LLM responses through API Gateway WebSockets. It is an AWS-centric talk by an AWS architect, so expect AWS services throughout.

Title: One YAML claim, 285 lines of Crossplane, zero tickets
Description: Piotr Zaniewski (Loft Labs) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on designing a platform as an API, demoed with Port, Argo CD, Crossplane and vCluster
Body:
The complexity of cloud infrastructure never disappears; a good platform just decides who gets to look at it. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Piotr Zaniewski, Head of Engineering Enablement at Loft Labs, argues that the way to build an internal infrastructure platform is to design it as an API, and then proves it with a live demo where a developer clicks one button and gets an app, an Azure storage account, a Grafana dashboard and a private virtual Kubernetes cluster.

The talk is roughly half principles, half demo, and the demo is the reason to watch.

## Which kind of platform is this about?

Zaniewski separates three kinds. Business platforms like Uber or DoorDash connect consumers and vendors. Domain-specific platforms wrap cross-cutting business functions, such as a mapping service handling geofencing and address translation. Domain-agnostic platforms are the building blocks underneath, infrastructure or security, and that is his subject.

Why build one if you already have AWS or Azure? Because the cloud is built for every customer at once, so it exposes far more than your developers need. A platform isolates the useful parts so developers do not have to learn Kubernetes or a catalogue of cloud services before shipping.

His six building blocks: a self-service portal (which can be a web UI, a script or a bare API), an abstraction layer of programmatic APIs over existing ones, automated GitOps-style workflows, monitoring and observability with rollbacks and canaries, security and governance including tenant isolation and audit trails, and a product organisation that keeps the platform evolving.

## Why Kubernetes as the contract?

The key principle is API-driven design, the way every successful cloud exposes itself. Zaniewski frames an API as a pipeline: developers on one end with whatever interface they like, outbound processes on the other talking to Argo, Kubernetes or a cloud.

In the demo, platform and developers agree on the Kubernetes-style API. Kubernetes already exists, has a strong ecosystem, and lends itself to custom APIs via CRDs. The developer's entire request is a small YAML file, an app claim custom resource, with a spec holding three parameters (a connection string name, an image, a port) and a namespace hard-coded for the team.

## What happens after the click?

The flow, step by step:

1. The developer picks an action in Port, a developer portal similar to Backstage, and accepts the defaults.
2. Port kicks off a CI pipeline that opens a pull request with the claim against an apps-deployment repository.
3. The platform team reviews and merges (optional, but shown).
4. Argo CD picks up the change and applies it to the cluster.
5. Crossplane, with its Azure provider and functions for Kubernetes, Helm and HTTP, reconciles everything: an Azure resource group and storage account, the app's three replicas, an ingress, a vCluster and a Grafana dashboard scoped to the team's namespace.
6. A Slack notification tells the developer the app is up and how to connect to their vCluster.

The developer then creates a blob with `kubectl apply` on another tiny YAML, refreshes, and the Node.js app reads it. Deleting is the mirror image: another Port action, another PR, and Argo CD and Crossplane remove both the Kubernetes resources and the cloud infrastructure.

The best detail: the whole thing ran on a local kind cluster on his laptop. AKS, EKS or GKE would work the same way.

## Where did the complexity go?

Into a Crossplane composition of 285 lines of YAML, owned by the platform team. That is the honest trade: developers write ten lines, platform engineers maintain the composition that turns them into an account, a service, an ingress, a deployment, a namespace, a vCluster and a container.

He calls out two wins beyond speed. Ticket waits vanish because the vCluster gives developers admin-level freedom in a sandbox, so they stop asking for ingress controllers to try out. And it follows zero-trust thinking: developers never needed Azure access at all. Pull requests double as the messaging system between teams: actionable messages that developers send and the platform team reviews.

His closing quip lands well for 2024: "we didn't even mention AI once," Zaniewski said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers choosing between a portal-first and an API-first design, and anyone who wants to see Crossplane, Argo CD, Port and vCluster wired end to end without slides doing the heavy lifting. If you already run Crossplane compositions in production, the principles section will be familiar; the demo is still a tidy reference.

Title: A one-line enum change, a locked table, and five ways to avoid both
Description: Rotem Tamir (Ariga) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on reliable database schema migrations with schema-as-code, tests and migration linting in Atlas
Body:
The pull request was ten lines of migration and one line of model change. It passed CI, the tech lead approved it, and it took production down. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Rotem Tamir, Co-Founder and CTO of Ariga and co-maintainer of the open source projects Ent and Atlas, uses that story to argue that schema migrations need the same automation and testing we already give application code, and demos five strategies to get there with Atlas.

It is a vendor talk in the sense that every demo uses Atlas, Ariga's database schema management tool. The strategies themselves are portable.

## What went wrong with the enum?

"It is a developer horror story," Rotem Tamir said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024, and he tells it like one. A developer using the Sequelize ORM in Node.js adds an invited value to a user status enum. On MySQL, changing enum values the wrong way makes the database rewrite the entire table, and the table stays locked for the duration. On a small table that is milliseconds. On a busy production table it is hours: CPU to the roof, 100% error rate on critical endpoints, and no way to stop it, because a rollback only starts after the change completes.

His five whys land on the uncomfortable root cause: there was no automation to verify the change, only human reviewers, and humans approved it.

## Why should teams care beyond one outage?

Because fear of schema changes slows everyone down. Teams that have been burned stop refactoring, batch changes together and move slowly. Rotem's pitch is that reliability and velocity stop being a trade-off once migrations are verified by machines.

## Strategy zero: automate the migration at all

Before the five, a baseline he finds missing in a surprising number of companies: someone connects to production by hand and applies the change before a deploy. It is error prone, slow, unrepeatable, has no audit log, and is unfair to whoever has to do it. In his words, making a manual change on a production database is one of the most stressful things you can do as an engineer.

## The five strategies

1. **Schema as code.** Like Terraform for databases: declare the desired state, let the tool compute the diff and plan the migration. The demo runs `atlas schema apply` against a local SQLite file, approves the plan, reruns it to show there is nothing left to do, then adds an email column and gets a planned ALTER TABLE.
2. **Unit-test database logic.** Constraints, triggers, functions and stored procedures are code, so test them. The demo defines a Postgres function in Atlas's HCL dialect and asserts on its output, breaking and fixing the test to show it bites.
3. **Test data migrations.** Backfills and column splits have no undo button in most relational databases. Atlas tests migrate to the version before, seed data with INSERTs, run the migration under test, and assert on the result.
4. **Lint migrations in CI.** Atlas's analysis engine classifies planned changes by risk. Dropping a table is flagged as a destructive change; renaming a column is flagged as backward incompatible, which breaks the data contract between your backend and your database. Rotem cites a published postmortem from February of that year in which a migration accidentally dropped production tables and the team spent the next 24 hours recovering.
5. **Pre-migration checks.** Some failures depend on production data, such as adding a unique constraint to a column that already has duplicates, which passes on every empty dev and CI database. Atlas migration files in txtar format can carry a checks section that runs before the migration, for example asserting a table is empty before dropping it.

## Who should watch

Backend developers who own their migrations, platform teams wiring databases into CD pipelines, and anyone who has watched an ALTER TABLE pass in staging and stall in production. The lock-on-enum story alone is worth the time.

Title: Your developer portal knows the plan, not what production did
Description: Amir Krayden (Senser) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on feeding real-time runtime topology back into the IDP so platform and SRE share one view
Body:
An internal developer portal is a beautifully maintained record of intent: the schema, the service catalog, the requests and limits someone typed in. Production rarely reads it. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Amir Krayden, co-founder and CEO of Senser, argues that the missing half of every IDP is the runtime, and that a continuously discovered, real-time topology is the shared language that closes the loop between platform engineers and SREs.

Senser is an AIOps company built on eBPF and machine learning, and the talk includes views from its product. The argument, though, stands without it, and the closing advice is tool-agnostic.

## What does the IDP miss?

Krayden's list is specific. Resources behave differently at runtime than their requests and limits suggest, because the node has its own ideas about what it can give. APIs and the interactions between services are hard to model statically. Third-party dependencies, from public APIs to payment gateways, often never make it into the schema at all. And runtime misconfiguration happens, such as someone changing the cloud console directly and bypassing the IDP, leaving it confidently describing a world that no longer exists.

The reason this is hard is structural. Static configuration is a tree you can traverse. "The runtime environment is a live, moving, changing graph," Krayden said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, fed by infrastructure events, application behaviour and the deployment pipeline all at once.

## Security already solved this once

The best part of the talk is the analogy. Application security went through the same split: a static catalog (vulnerabilities, open-source components, secrets, auth and encryption frameworks) on one side, and the runtime questions on the other. Is it actually deployed? Is it internet-exposed? Is it behind a WAF? Is it misconfigured at runtime?

Joining those two views is what made shift-left workable. It gave an accurate attack surface, let teams prioritise real risk instead of drowning in every CVE, and allowed guardrails to move earlier in the SDLC. Krayden's claim is that platform engineering needs the same join, and the runtime half comes from topology.

## Three places runtime context pays off

He structures the payoff around three use cases:

- **Anticipating reliability impact.** Topology turns tribal knowledge about past deployments into data points: which services were affected, what happened to downstream SLOs and SLAs, and what a service really costs to spin up in CPU and memory. His example is a service deployed for high-volume transactions that, at peak hours, overloads memory and takes down downstream services like a customer account dashboard and transaction confirmations.
- **Verifying deployments in real time.** IDP guardrails such as memory, CPU, latency and bandwidth limits are usually set during development, often on intuition. Runtime data shows whether they are too low or too high and flags deviations, such as a new service suddenly burning excessive CPU, with the context of who is talking to whom.
- **Investigating issues.** The service catalog is a fine starting point for root cause analysis, but it only extends through provisioning and orchestration. Matching it against the runtime catalog is how a team finds out whether a degrading service is its own fault or a third party's.

## Pitfalls and a sane way to start

The pitfalls are honest. Closing the loop is a first step, and maintaining it needs real resourcing. Runtime context must be complete across resources, APIs and third parties, which costs both time and tooling; eBPF-based auto-discovery reduces the toil of wiring a million dashboards. And a static snapshot of topology is just documentation with better graphics: it must be discovered and updated continuously.

To get started: build the topology (observability tools help but need extensive configuration; some platforms auto-discover with eBPF), integrate it with the IDP through the observability and incident integrations most portals already have, prioritise quick wins such as real-time deployment verification on your most failure-prone services, then scale step by step to prove value internally.

## Who should watch

Platform teams whose IDP is drifting from reality, and SREs tired of being the only people who know what production looks like. Expect a conceptual talk with some product screens, not a build-it-yourself tutorial.

Title: Kanister turns your backup scripts into Kubernetes custom resources
Description: Daniil Fedotov (Kasten by Veeam) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on Kanister, the CNCF project that runs application-consistent backup and restore as CRDs
Body:
Every team has a backup script that only one person understands. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Daniil Fedotov, Senior Open Source Engineer at Kasten by Veeam, shows how Kanister, a CNCF sandbox project, moves that script into Kubernetes: Blueprints describe what to do, ActionSets run it and keep a log, and Profiles say where the data goes. The demo backs up an Amazon RDS Postgres database to S3, drops a table, and brings it back.

## Why back up Kubernetes at all?

Daniil starts by knocking down four myths. Everything is stateless: no, the cluster and its configuration have state (secrets, RBAC, DNS), and his slides cite a CNCF study from 2020 with 55% of respondents running stateful workloads. GitOps will recreate everything: it recreates the application, not the data, and audits, forensics and point-in-time recovery still need copies. My cloud provider backs it up: providers explicitly tell you to set up your own disaster recovery and export your data, and accounts do get lost. And etcd backups protect you: in his words, restoring etcd almost never gets applications back into the desired state.

Add the 3-2-1 rule (multiple copies, different media, one off-site) and you have to move data out of the cluster it lives in, which is harder than it sounds.

## What makes it harder than backing up a VM?

Cloud native applications span many domains and moving parts. Data might sit in a managed cloud database, in a separate namespace, or right next to the application code. Backups come in flavours: storage snapshots that are only crash-consistent, snapshots with freeze hooks, data-service dumps with pg_dump or mongodump, and application-centric backups that coordinate all of the above, including scaling workloads down and back up. Most cloud tools do exactly one of those things, such as an RDS snapshot or a volume snapshot.

## Blueprints, ActionSets and Profiles

Kanister, created by Kasten and launched at KubeCon NA in 2017, was accepted into the CNCF sandbox in September 2023. Installed by a Helm chart, its controller adds three custom resources:

- **Blueprint**: the template for actions such as backup, restore and delete. Each action has phases that run sequentially, and each phase executes a function, for example scaling a workload or creating an RDS snapshot.
- **ActionSet**: a command to run an action. It references a Blueprint, fills its template values, points at an object (a ConfigMap, StatefulSet or Deployment) and a Profile, and records the status of every phase plus the artifacts produced.
- **Profile**: the destination, such as an S3 bucket, S3-compatible storage, Azure Blob or Google Cloud Storage.

The neat consequence is that ActionSets become your log of operations, stored in the cluster: what ran, against which Blueprint, where the data went, which artifacts came out and when.

## The demo: drop a table, restore it

The setup is an RDS Postgres database, a cluster with a database client and a ConfigMap pointing at RDS, Kanister with access to an S3 bucket. Daniil seeds a table, installs Kanister with Helm, applies the RDS Postgres Blueprint from the Kanister repository, creates a Profile, and uses the kanctl helper to create a backup ActionSet. The artifact lands in S3.

Then he drops the table, which he argues is a more realistic disaster than disk corruption.

"In the real world people drop tables all the time," Daniil Fedotov said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

The restore is one kanctl command that creates a new ActionSet from the backup one, inheriting its Blueprint, Profile and artifacts. The table comes back. Everything ran on Kubernetes runners, with no extra machines and nothing executed locally.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers running stateful services on Kubernetes, anyone with databases outside the cluster but applications inside it, and teams whose backup story today is a cron job and hope. Kanister functions also cover KubeExec and KubeTask for arbitrary commands, PVC data, volume snapshots and Amazon RDS.

Title: Five security layers, four breach stories, one misconfigured firewall
Description: Venukumar Chirlawar (Amazon) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on layered cloud defence, threat intelligence, IDS choices and breach lessons
Body:
The Capital One breach did not need a zero-day. A misconfigured web application firewall and weak access controls were enough to expose data on more than 100 million customers from Amazon S3. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Venukumar Chirlawar, Senior Software Development Engineer at Amazon, uses that story and three others to make the case for multi-layered cloud protection plus advanced threat detection, and to show where each layer earns its keep.

Set expectations correctly: this is a structured survey of cloud security, not a close look at any one tool. If you want a map of the territory, with the jargon unpacked, it does that job well.

## Why layers instead of one big wall?

The premise is defence in depth. "This approach ensures that even if one layer is compromised, others remain intact to protect the system," Chirlawar said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. With cloud spending expected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2025, he argues, traditional perimeter models no longer cover environments that are dynamic and distributed by design.

His step-by-step build has five layers:

1. **Network:** firewalls, intrusion detection and prevention, secure protocols.
2. **Application:** secure coding, regular vulnerability assessments, patch management.
3. **Data:** encryption at rest and in transit with strong, current algorithms. AES-256 leads usage in cloud environments, ahead of RSA and TLS.
4. **Identity and access:** IAM, role-based access control, multi-factor authentication.
5. **Endpoint:** antivirus and EDR on laptops, phones and servers, which he calls the last line of defence.

The pitfalls list is short and familiar: overlooking endpoints, skipping employee training, and letting protocols go stale. He also stresses understanding the shared responsibility model with your cloud provider, which is exactly where the Capital One story went wrong.

## What does advanced threat detection add?

Layers stop known attacks; advanced persistent threats, zero-days and targeted attacks are designed to slip past them. Chirlawar walks through the stages of an APT from reconnaissance onward, with the point that early detection is what limits the damage.

Two tool families get the most time. A threat intelligence platform (TIP) aggregates feeds from open source, commercial vendors and internal logs, analyses them with correlation engines and machine learning, and turns the result into actionable intelligence: updated policies, IDS configuration, automated responses.

The intrusion detection section is the most useful for anyone choosing a product. Network-based IDS watches traffic across the infrastructure; host-based IDS watches individual machines and is better for insider threats. Signature-based detection catches known threats and misses novel ones; anomaly-based detection finds the unknown and pays for it in false positives. Passive IDS alerts a human; active IDS, better known as an IPS, blocks automatically. A hybrid that combines both detection methods and integrates with TIPs, SIEMs and firewalls gives the broadest coverage. Performance matters too: an IDS that adds latency under high traffic is a cost, not a control.

The architecture ties it together: IDS feeds the TIP, the TIP feeds intelligence back, the SIEM stores and correlates logs from both, and SOAR tools trigger predefined responses.

## What do the case studies teach?

- **Capital One, 2019:** more than 100 million customers exposed, an $80 million fine from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Lesson: audit cloud configurations and tighten access controls.
- **Netflix:** fully on AWS, multi-layered security with continuous monitoring, internal tools Security Monkey and Lemur, and chaos engineering that simulates failures and breaches.
- **Sony PlayStation Network, 2011:** 77 million accounts including card details, 23 days offline, losses estimated at $171 million. Lesson: patch software and encrypt sensitive data.
- **Dropbox:** two-factor authentication, encryption at rest and in transit, regular audits, penetration testing and a bug bounty programme.

## What comes next?

Chirlawar names container escapes, misconfigured serverless permissions and supply chain attacks as the emerging threats, with zero trust, frequent audits and vendor risk management as the mitigations. Looking further out: AI-driven threat detection, and quantum-resistant encryption, since quantum computers could break RSA and ECC. His advice is to inventory current encryption now and plan the transition, including key management, before it is urgent.

## Who should watch

Platform and application engineers who own a slice of cloud security without being security specialists, and anyone who needs a vocabulary refresher before an IDS or TIP procurement. Seasoned security engineers will find little new.

Title: The safest email attachment is the one you never attach
Description: Gaurav Mittal (ThermoFisher Scientific) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on replacing PII attachments with zipped, password-locked, expiring S3 links
Body:
Every company that emails customers their insurance documents, medical receipts or e-visas is one wrong forward away from leaking someone's PII. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Gaurav Mittal, a data science manager at ThermoFisher Scientific, shows a small, all-AWS pattern that takes the attachment out of the email entirely: password-protect the file, park it in S3, and send a pre-signed link that expires.

It is a short, practical talk with one architecture and one piece of code. No new product, no framework, just four building blocks most teams already have access to.

## What goes wrong with a plain attachment?

Mittal's scenario is the everyday one: an insurer sending a renter's insurance document, a hospital sending receipts, a country sending an e-visa that carries passport details. The risks he lists are man-in-the-middle interception, insecure email servers, and missing or inadequate encryption that lets anyone with access to the transmission read the attachment.

User education and antivirus help on the receiving end. His focus is the sender's side: what an organisation can do so that a misdirected email is useless to whoever receives it.

## Layer one: a password the customer already knows

The first layer is a password-protected zip built with pyminizip, an open-source Python library. Its compress call takes the source file, the destination, a password and a compression level.

The neat bit is the choice of password. Mittal suggests something only the recipient knows, such as their date of birth or the last four digits of their phone number. The fraudster who receives a mis-forwarded email cannot open it, and the legitimate customer is not emailing support for a password reset.

To run it in AWS Lambda, install the library locally with `pip install pyminizip -t .`, zip it, and upload it as a Lambda layer so the function's code can import it.

## Layer two: links that die on schedule

The second layer is access control through S3 pre-signed URLs, which grant time-limited access to an object without touching the bucket policy or handing out AWS credentials. How long a URL can live depends on what signed it:

- an IAM instance profile: up to 6 hours
- AWS Security Token Service: up to 36 hours
- an IAM user (Signature Version 4): up to 7 days

After that, the link simply stops working. Mittal's demo uses an IAM user to get the full seven days.

## Sending it with SES, politely

The email goes out through Amazon SES, which needs a verified sender identity and can send to verified or unverified recipients. The constraint he calls out is a sending rate of 40 emails per second, so his final code puts a one-second `time.sleep` between sends to stay clear of throttling. He notes that the right pacing depends on your own implementation.

The full flow fits in one Lambda: generate the CSV, compress it with a password, store it in S3, generate the pre-signed URL, send the email through SES.

## Why it beats attaching the file

Three wins, in his words and order. A wrong recipient lacks the password. The link has a time limit. And the email itself carries nothing: "if you look in the emails, there is no attachment," Mittal said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. That last one also has a cost angle: attaching files from Lambda takes time, sending a URL does not, and Lambda bills for duration.

A fair caveat the talk does not dwell on: a password built from a birth date is guessable for anyone who knows the customer, and zip encryption strength varies by tool. Treat it as a strong improvement over a bare attachment, not as end-to-end encryption.

## Who should watch

Engineers at insurers, healthcare providers or any business that emails documents with PII, especially if those emails come out of a Lambda today. It is a quick watch and the pattern can be shipped in an afternoon.

Title: The frugal EKS playbook is see the spend with Kubecost, then let Karpenter act
Description: Piyush Mattoo and Dariush Azimi (AWS) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on cutting Amazon EKS costs with Kubecost visibility and Karpenter autoscaling
Body:
The Amazon EKS control plane costs the same whether you run three nodes or three thousand; it is everything else that sneaks up on you. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Piyush Mattoo and Dariush Azimi, both Senior Solutions Architects at AWS, take Werner Vogels' Frugal Architect keynote from re:Invent 2023 and apply it to Kubernetes: get granular visibility into where the money goes with Kubecost, then act on it with Karpenter.

It is a conversational, two-person session with two live demos, and the speakers cheerfully admit it is not scripted. That works in its favour: the questions one asks the other are the ones you would ask.

## Where does EKS money actually go?

Piyush starts with the bill. The control plane is fixed at 10 cents an hour, with no extra control plane cost as you scale. The real spend is the data plane: workload cost (pods, containers, autoscaling settings), network cost (data transfer, Elastic Container Registry, load balancers, NAT gateways), and logging and monitoring.

They lean on a CNCF study on Kubernetes costs from December 2023: costs are rising for many organisations, over-provisioning is by far the most common cause, followed by failing to deactivate unused resources and technical debt in workloads not built for cloud native environments. On tooling, the same survey had cloud providers' own tools such as AWS Cost Explorer first and Kubecost first among Kubernetes-specific tools. The pattern they see with customers is both: Cost Explorer for the whole cloud bill, Kubecost hyper-focused on the cluster.

## Kubecost answers who spent it

Dariush demos the Kubecost dashboard, breaking spend down by namespace, pod, controller and any team or environment labels you have set, plus saved reports and a savings page with recommendations such as right-sizing cluster nodes. Kubecost comes in a free and an enterprise tier.

When Dariush is asked what the recommendations are based on, Piyush looks it up live: Kubecost queries metrics from Prometheus (installed by default with it), pulls public AWS pricing through APIs, and can integrate AWS Cost and Usage Reports for account-specific accuracy. Pair it with AWS split cost allocation data, which attributes the cost of a shared EC2 instance, storage and networking to individual workloads based on actual usage, and a node full of pods stops being one opaque line item.

## Karpenter turns the insight into fewer nodes

Cluster Autoscaler adjusts node counts based on pod scheduling, but can be slow and inflexible about instance types, a real limitation when AWS has hundreds of them. Karpenter, built by AWS and donated to the Kubernetes autoscaling special interest group, provisions nodes for unschedulable pods within seconds, picks instance types on the fly, and supports consolidation and bin packing. It is Kubernetes native in the sense that it respects your scheduling constraints: node selectors, affinity, taints and tolerations, topology spread.

The demo uses eks-node-viewer for a live view of nodes, pods and estimated cost per hour and per month. Dariush scales a deliberately named CPU- and memory-hungry app from 7 replicas to 125 and the pods go from pending to running in seconds. Two of the three starting nodes are on-demand and one is spot, because the NodePool allows both capacity types, and a weight parameter favours high-priority workloads.

Piyush explains why Karpenter does not simply grab the cheapest spot instance: the cheapest pool is often tiny and close to interruption, so Karpenter uses the EC2 Fleet API's price-capacity-optimized strategy.

"It gives you the cheapest instance type, but then it doesn't give you the one which is about to be interrupted," Piyush Mattoo said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

## Cost optimisation is a habit, not a migration step

The takeaway is visibility plus action. Do not treat cost work as a one-off at migration or cutover; review utilisation continuously, right-size workloads, clean up unused resources and establish cost governance so the savings stick.

## Who should watch

EKS operators who have Cluster Autoscaler running and a bill that keeps growing, and FinOps folks who need to explain where Kubernetes spend lands. It is an intro to both tools, not a deep tuning session.

Title: The million-dollar platform is a spreadsheet before it's a portal
Description: Krzysztof Halasa (BlueSoft) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on why a platform is an org change, and the $1.44M a year it saves
Body:
Every developer team that spends release week begging another team for a Kafka topic is burning money nobody budgeted for. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Krzysztof Halasa, IT Management Advisor at BlueSoft, puts a number on it: for a company spending about $5 million a year on IT, the lack of a platform costs roughly $1.44 million annually, and a well-built platform gets most of that back.

It is a short talk aimed at managers more than at people writing Terraform, and it says so up front: platform engineering is mostly an organisational change with some technology attached.

## Why call it an organisational change?

Halasa draws on four years of building internal developer platforms, as a manager of several and an advisor to teams doing it for the first time. His definition is refreshingly unglamorous. "If you treat your developers as you normally treat your clients," Halasa said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, and design services around their needs, you have become a platform engineer.

The preconditions he lists are about authority, not tooling. Responsibilities must be clearly defined for the platform team and every other team. The platform team needs the mandate to implement those responsibilities across the DevOps toolset, so the same job is not done three times by three teams. Only then come orchestrators and SecOps tooling. His summary: platform engineers focus on developers' needs, not on DevOps tools.

The process is plain product development. Analyse the users (developers), plan the architecture, define services, choose an interface, then deploy by changing team structures, setting business metrics and agreeing SLAs. The analysis phase is where he puts the weight, and the one line worth pinning above the planning board: "You shouldn't tailor organization to fit the platform."

## What does a good platform feel like on day one?

The example is the strongest part. A new stream-aligned team posts a request through the platform's channel: a Java application, a data store, exposure to the public network, integrations with a core banking system and a regulatory system, about a thousand transactions a day, mostly from Polish locations.

Minutes later, with no platform engineer in the loop, the team has a repository containing a demo service in their language. The demo service already has CI/CD pipelines deploying into their own Kubernetes space (a namespace, a dedicated cluster, or occasionally a VM), is wired into logging, monitoring and tracing, talks to a database, exposes an API, and publishes and consumes topics. Instructions come attached. The team can ship to end users on the first day instead of spending week one collecting network requirements.

## Three layers, and the portal is optional

On the technology side Halasa describes three layers. At the bottom is the DevSecOps layer most large companies already have, though rarely organised, deduplicated or automated. Platform engineering adds an orchestration layer, the definitions of platform services plus the scripts that change each underlying tool (create the namespace, the database, the observability index, the repository, copy in the demo service). On top sits the interface layer.

He is pragmatic about that top layer: it does not have to be a Backstage instance or even a portal. Simple APIs or Jira tickets work, though dedicated tools pay off as the platform matures. He also expects AI and chatbots to show up in the interface layer soon.

## Where the $1.44 million comes from

The closing calculation is simple enough to redo with your own numbers, which is the point:

- 10 application teams, about six developers each
- an average rate of $50 an hour
- one release per team per month, 12 a year
- one week of team effort per release on non-feature work: environments, observability hookups, security, network integration, and chasing the people who create databases and topics

That is 10 × 6 × $50 × 40 hours × 12 releases, or $1,440,000 a year. Halasa puts it at 15 to 20 percent of the IT budget in such a company, and argues the saving scales with size. Long-lived applications need less than a week per release and new teams need far more; the week is his blended figure.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and heads of platform who need to justify a platform team to someone holding a budget. If you already run a mature IDP, the content is familiar, but the cost model is a handy template for the next budget meeting. Halasa also mentions his online course on platform engineering for managers, so expect a brief plug.

Title: Secure LLM apps like data routers, with the pipelines you already own
Description: Omer Farooq (Auxin) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on securing LLM apps by reusing DevSecOps pipelines and treating prompt logs as privileged
Body:
The fastest way to make a GenAI feature expensive is to build a brand-new security programme for it. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Omer Farooq, founder and security engineer at Auxin Security, argues the opposite: an LLM application is a cloud-native app that happens to route a lot of data, so secure it with the SAST, DAST, SCA and threat-detection tooling you already run, plus a few LLM-specific additions.

His formula is on the label: LLM SecOps is LLM applications plus LLMOps plus LLM security. The goal is to add GenAI to existing products without raising operating costs or re-engineering delivery, integration and security.

## What does an LLM application actually look like?

Farooq walks through a common reference architecture rather than a product. A query becomes an embedding, the embedding is looked up in a vector database, the retrieved data is injected into a prompt, the prompt is optimised and sent to a model API (sometimes via a cache), and the response passes a content filter before it goes back to a user or a machine.

His framing is that these apps are data routers. They pull from near-real-time systems, IoT and OT equipment, search engines and catalogues, and that is exactly what makes them both useful and risky. Every integration needs a secure network path, delegated access, and a check that the user asking the question is entitled to the data the semantic search is about to fetch.

## One secured backend, many front ends

The architectural advice that carries the most weight is decoupling. Keep the UI or machine interface separate from the LLM backend, and build one multi-tenant backend with detailed rights management for data and assets. Bots, translation services, summarisation and middleware can all sit in front of it.

The security payoff is that front ends get secured with the non-LLM models you already use, while the new LLM-specific controls are built once, in the backend. Front ends can even be low-code; the slides name Streamlit and Gradio, alongside data-router frameworks such as LangChain, Semantic Kernel and LlamaIndex.

He also flags model choice as a security decision: an open-source model pulled from the public internet comes with different consequences than a managed, curated one.

## What changes in the pipeline?

Less than you might fear. The backend is still cloud native, so secrets, tokens and service accounts should be injected and rotated the way they are today. The differences Farooq calls out:

- **Model APIs are metered services.** Use delegated access and the end user's identity where possible, rather than one shared credential at department level, and keep token and metered usage tracking outside the service.
- **New detections in your existing SecOps tools.** A user repeatedly attempting prompt injection is a threat scenario you need to write, and threat-intelligence feeds should cover LLM application types.
- **The vector database is a database.** Protect it as you would a relational or NoSQL store, even though its purpose differs.

## Why your prompt logs are the crown jewels

The point most teams miss is about logging. Users type personal details, PII and company-sensitive material into prompts, so the logged questions and answers need encryption at rest, in transit and in use, with column-level or double encryption on the prompt and response columns and tight access to audit trails. "This can be considered equally privileged as two people's conversation," Farooq said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

He maps the main threats to existing controls: content filtering for ethical concerns, data rights management and column encryption for data leakage, SecOps and threat intelligence for adversarial attacks (including attacks that try to induce hallucination), and input validation, throttling and content filtering for prompt injection and model poisoning.

## The tactical checklist

The closing list is practical: run LLM code, including config-heavy serverless functions, through the same secure coding practices and SAST/SCA scans as everything else, focusing on the chains; filter content in both directions; make sure data ingested into the model is classified, labelled and tagged; test rights management with DAST; and log end to end, correlating AI service logs with compute, storage and network logs, so you can trace abuse, illegal data use, hallucinations or injection after the fact.

## Who should watch

Security and platform engineers who have been told to "add AI" to an existing product and want a mental model that fits their current pipelines. It is a strategic overview with architecture talk, not a demo, and there is no tool-by-tool walkthrough of the scanners.

Title: KubeVirt runs your stubborn VMs as pods, and Flux can ship them
Description: Koray Oksay (Kubermatic) and Batuhan Apaydin at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on KubeVirt, running VMs as Kubernetes workloads and deploying them with GitOps
Body:
Every container migration has that one app that refuses to move. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Koray Oksay, Kubernetes Consultant and trainer at Kubermatic, and Batuhan Apaydin, organiser of KCD Istanbul, show how KubeVirt lets that app stay a virtual machine while living in the same cluster, under the same tools, as everything else, then deploy a Fedora VM end to end with Flux and a Helm chart.

The abstract sets the stakes with the CNCF Annual Survey 2023: only 39% of respondents said they run containers for most or all production applications. The rest have a lot of VMs.

## Why put a VM inside Kubernetes at all?

Batuhan lays out the trade-off. Containers share the host kernel and are light; VMs carry a whole operating system and a hypervisor, which costs overhead but buys full isolation and compatibility with older workloads. Some applications need the VM model because of dependencies or architecture, yet teams still want the operational benefits of the container platform.

KubeVirt's answer is one platform instead of two. You manage VMs like any other Kubernetes resource, scale and restart them with familiar tooling, run legacy applications next to new microservices, and live-migrate running VMs between nodes without downtime during maintenance.

## How does a VM become a pod?

Koray walks the architecture. The virt-operator installs and manages the other KubeVirt components. The virt-controller watches VM resources and creates virtual machine instances (VMIs). Each VM runs inside its own virt-launcher pod on a node, and virt-handler, a DaemonSet on every node, handles lifecycle operations and migrations. Under the hood KubeVirt uses libvirt to talk to a hypervisor such as QEMU.

The important design choice: scheduling, networking and storage are delegated to Kubernetes. KubeVirt adds the virtualisation, the cluster does the rest, so VMs follow the same scheduling and resource management as containers.

## The demo: a Fedora VM, delivered by GitOps

The demo runs on bare-metal Kubernetes from metal-stack cloud, which matters: on a public cloud you need nested virtualisation, and on AWS a metal instance type. The demo repo (github.com/koksay/kubevirt-demo) covers both Flux and Argo CD; the talk uses Flux.

The flow is pleasingly boring. Commit the KubeVirt operator and custom resource manifests, let Flux reconcile, and watch virt-operator, virt-api, virt-controller and virt-handler come up. Then add a HelmRelease that points at a chart in the GitHub container registry, with values for memory, hostname, a Fedora container disk and cloud-init user data. The chart also generates SSH keys as a secret. Push, reconcile, and a virt-launcher pod appears in a new namespace with the VM running inside it.

Koray connects with `kubectl virt ssh` using the generated key, runs `uname -a` to show the VM's own kernel, then calls the Kubernetes API service from inside the VM to prove the point of the whole exercise.

"So the application you have running here, whatever that is, it can connect to other services inside your Kubernetes clusters so that your virtualized application can just connect to your containerized applications," Koray Oksay said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

You will need virtctl, or the `kubectl virt` plugin, to interact with the VMs.

## Where it goes next

The pair point to vendors building on KubeVirt, including Kubermatic, which can create Kubernetes clusters out of KubeVirt VMs running on a KubeVirt cluster. The closing argument is that you do not have to choose between VMs and containers while you modernise, and that consolidating both onto one platform is a migration strategy in itself.

## Who should watch

Platform teams carrying a VM estate next to a Kubernetes one, and anyone planning a lift-and-shift that cannot be fully containerised yet. The demo is a ready-made GitOps template for running VMs as code.

Title: Your platform became a monolith, so break it up like one
Description: Robert Kelly (Liatrio) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on why enterprise platforms must feel small, whatever their size, built as a platform of platforms
Body:
The enterprise platform was supposed to be the easy button, and in many companies it has turned into the thing developers route around. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Robert Kelly, VP of Technology Enablement at Liatrio, argues in a tight 15 minutes that platforms grew into monoliths by Conway's Law, and that the fix is the one we already use for monolithic applications: split it into a platform of platforms that, to its users, still feels small.

## What is a platform supposed to be?

He doesn't redefine the word, he borrows two definitions. The CNCF platforms white paper: an integrated collection of capabilities defined and presented according to the needs of the platform's users. Martin Fowler's: a foundation of self-service APIs, tools, services, knowledge and support arranged as a compelling internal product. Both boil down to abstraction, hiding the complexity underneath behind a simpler interface.

Then the uncomfortable test: if you called your platform's customers and asked whether it is easy, what would they say? If the platform, or the team behind it, makes something harder than it would otherwise be, it isn't helping.

## Platforms are disruptive, in the wrong way

Kelly leans on Clayton Christensen's The Innovator's Dilemma: products based on disruptive technologies are typically cheaper, simpler, smaller and more convenient to use. Internal platforms aren't trying to disrupt AWS or Azure. They are meant to disrupt enterprise processes: the toil, the ticket queues, the painful approvals between a team and production. That's where most of a platform's value lives.

Few platform teams would describe their platform as cheaper, simpler and smaller, and his explanation is history. The platform was usually built by a DevOps team, shaped by the organisation around it, and grew to keep up. It now spans hundreds of tools across dozens of automation paths, and "platforms have become synonymous with the term tool sprawl," Robert Kelly said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Platform engineers spend their days integrating the latest tools instead of solving business problems with the teams they serve. The snowball has become a monolith, like other enterprise applications before it.

## A platform of platforms

Look at the platform from above and it is really a sum of capabilities: the internal developer portal, CI/CD, security tooling, observability, cloud infrastructure, FinOps, governance, and fast-growing AI/ML. Some are bought, some are built, each is complex in its own way, and together they are too much for one team to support well.

So stop treating them as one thing. Each capability may be its own platform with its own team and product roadmap. The rule that keeps this from fragmenting the developer experience: how users interact with all of them shouldn't be distinctly different, and the platform just shouldn't feel large. (He also counts, with some self-awareness, how many times he has said the word platform.)

## Where do you start? The thinnest viable platform

Like breaking up any monolith, start small. Kelly points to the thinnest viable platform from Team Topologies by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais: the smallest set of APIs, documentation and tools that accelerates the teams using it. Sometimes version 1.0 of a platform is a wiki page.

The Team Topologies interaction model matters more than the size. If the platform team provides capabilities as a service, behind self-service portals and APIs, then new features don't force consuming teams to change how they work. Adoption costs little, and the platform feels small no matter how much automation sits behind it.

## What changes for the platform team?

Breaking up the monolith needs a strategy, and he lists the tools: value stream mapping and domain-driven design to find the boundaries and how many platforms you really have; investing in the platform as a product even if nobody did before; raising the bar on standards and treating everything as code; leaning on APIs and self-service; real user feedback and usage metrics; and inner sourcing with pull requests so the internal community can contribute alongside the platform teams.

He closes with his own punchline: a big change, a lot of lift, and a lot to take on at once. Easy, right?

## Who should watch

Heads of platform or DevOps in large organisations where one team owns hundreds of tools, and anyone making the case to split a platform team. It's short and opinionated, a conversation starter rather than a playbook.

Title: Kubernetes data security is encryption plus the person on the train
Description: Victor Onyenagubom (Teesside University) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on encrypting Kubernetes data at rest and in transit, and training the humans around it
Body:
Most Kubernetes security checklists stop at the cluster boundary. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Victor Onyenagubom, Lecturer in Cybersecurity at Teesside University, walks the layers of data protection in Kubernetes, from disk encryption up through mutual TLS between pods, and then past the cluster to the part teams skip: the employees who can leak it all on a bus.

It is an introductory, conceptual talk, a good first map of the territory for developers who have just been handed responsibility for a cluster's data. There is no demo and no YAML.

## Why does Kubernetes data security deserve its own talk?

Victor's case is the cost of getting it wrong: financial loss from a breach, downtime, broken customer trust, and legal exposure under data privacy laws that differ from continent to continent. Organisations that store personal or customer data in a cluster without adequate technical measures can be fined. And clusters increasingly do hold sensitive data, from API keys and database credentials to customer records.

## Pick your encryption before you pick your tools

He starts with the three families. Symmetric encryption uses one key to encrypt and decrypt, which makes it fast. Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair and is more secure but slower. Homomorphic encryption lets you compute on data without decrypting it first, which is the interesting one for privacy-sensitive processing.

## Data at rest is three layers deep

For stored data Victor stacks three protections. Disk encryption covers the case where physical security fails and someone walks off with, or gets access to, the disk. File system encryption means that even with the disk in hand, the files are unreadable. Encryption in the storage layer covers databases, API keys and other stored secrets. Around that sit secrets management tools for credentials, encrypted volumes, and the storage services of the major cloud providers.

## Data in transit: TLS, then mutual TLS, then walls

Pods and services talking to each other are exposed to eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle attacks and interception. TLS encrypts that traffic. Mutual TLS goes a step further: both client and server present certificates, which is where zero trust starts, treating all traffic as untrusted until it authenticates.

Network segmentation is the third layer. Split the system into front end, back end and database, allow only the front end to talk to the back end and only the back end to talk to the database, and an attack on one segment does not take everything down.

## The cluster is only as safe as the people with access

His five fortification steps are least-privilege access control with regular audits of who can reach what, strong passwords and multi-factor authentication, prompt patching, security monitoring with tools such as StackRox, Clair and Anchore, and security training. The last one gets the most passion.

"Most organizations are guilty of Only having technical security measures, but ignoring the human security factor of actually training their employees around human security," Victor Onyenagubom said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

His examples are refreshingly concrete: don't post details about your Kubernetes setup on social media, shred sensitive documents, and when working remotely, check who is reading over your shoulder on the train. His closing point is that data security in Kubernetes is never finished; it is a process you keep adapting.

## Who should watch

Developers and students new to Kubernetes security who want the vocabulary and the layers in one sitting. Seasoned platform security engineers will know the material, but may want to borrow the framing for their next internal training.

Title: An ex-iOS developer on replacing two native apps with Flutter
Description: Dmitry Taraev (Quadcode) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on moving from native iOS to Flutter, and two real migrations to a single codebase
Body:
Cross-platform debates usually happen between people who have only shipped one side. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Dmitry Taraev, Flutter Developer at Quadcode, brings a rarer view: six years of native iOS work (including VK Music) before switching to Flutter in 2019, and two projects where a Flutter app replaced an existing native one in the stores. His verdict is positive, with a precise list of where Flutter still hurts.

## Why go cross-platform at all?

His pitch is honest about the arithmetic. One codebase is "not two times faster because you're making one app, but still significantly faster than two separate apps," Dmitry Taraev said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. It needs fewer developers, though Flutter developers are a little harder to find. The quality is reliable, but the app can look different from a native one, especially on iOS.

For product owners the bigger win is one codebase: both platforms release at the same time on the same version, instead of two teams drifting apart.

## What does a native developer gain?

- **Hot reload and hot restart.** Change a colour, a font or a layout, save, and see it almost instantly; bigger changes need a hot restart that takes seconds rather than a full rebuild.
- **Declarative UI.** He compares a Flutter `Text` widget with the imperative style iOS used before SwiftUI, and the declarative version wins on readability.
- **Modularity.** Features split cleanly into modules you can reuse across the app or across projects.
- **Everything is a widget**, Dart runs on a single thread with isolates for parallel work, and `async`/`await` makes network calls easy, with the widget rebuilt when the result lands.

## Where does Flutter still hurt?

You learn a new framework and a new language, and the job market for Flutter is smaller. You can't escape the platforms either: the bigger and older the project, the more native code you'll write. His example is App Tracking Transparency, which exists only on iOS, so you write a plugin. Expect strange bugs whenever a new iOS, Android or Xcode version ships, and SDKs with no Flutter plugin yet, although many already exist. On the product side, scrolling and some UI feel different from what iOS users expect, and he hit animation lags that he says can be worked around.

When to use it: quick MVPs, apps meant to look the same on both platforms, and the free web (and desktop) build. When to think twice: when you already have one native app and native developers, or when the app must follow Apple's Human Interface Guidelines exactly, which he considers very hard or even impossible in Flutter.

## The big migration: Yandex Pro

Yandex Pro is the app drivers and couriers use for Yandex Taxi. He joined in 2019 when a new team was hired to build the iOS app on a tight timeline. They tried React Native first, but the security department said no, so they tried Flutter, and the team liked it enough to aim at replacing the native Android app too.

The basic iOS release came in 2020. The native Android app couldn't pause, since thousands of users relied on it, so new features were built twice while the Flutter app caught up. Along the way they wrote plugins for the SDKs they needed: the Yandex Map SDK, the centre of the main screen with routing, points and layers, plus camera, audio and Bluetooth. In 2022 they reached a single codebase, and the Flutter Android build replaced the native app on Google Play. "For the users, it was just like update, but for us, it was a huge change," he said. The team grew to about 40 developers.

## The small one: Blush

The second project went the other way. Blush, an AI dating simulator, had a native iOS app and no Android app, and a three-person team. They shipped Flutter on Android first in 2023, kept building features for both the native iOS app and the Flutter app, and moved iOS users to the Flutter build in early 2024. The hard part was data: the native app used Firebase and stored a lot locally, with no backend of its own.

## What about the alternatives?

He sees Flutter as the most popular option, with React Native close behind. React Native wraps native widgets and runs JavaScript in a virtual machine, while Flutter renders with Skia and compiles to binary; JavaScript developers are plentiful, but he flags potential performance and security concerns, especially on iOS. Cordova and Ionic use HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Kotlin Multiplatform looks promising, and Xamarin has become .NET MAUI.

## Who should watch

Mobile leads deciding whether to merge two native codebases, and iOS developers wondering what they'd lose by switching.

Title: Centralise the expertise, hand the innovation back to app teams
Description: Marina Burkhardt and Martin Sakowski (AWS) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on decentralised platforms built from blueprints, not one central bottleneck
Body:
The usual internal platform turns its own team into the bottleneck: every app team's feature request lands in one queue. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Marina Burkhardt, Solutions Architect at AWS, and Martin Sakowski, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, argue for redrawing what counts as the platform: a mix of central services and shared blueprints that app teams pick from, adapt and own, so the expertise stays central while the innovation moves to the teams closest to customers.

## Do standards kill creativity?

Sakowski opens with a sheet of paper. DIN A4 is exactly 210 by 297 millimetres, one sixteenth of a square metre, and because nobody argues about it, envelopes, folders, drawers and printers all fit. You do have to break your long sentence onto a new line, but nobody claims A4 has stopped anyone writing or drawing. HTTP is the same story: a fixed standard that made the web possible instead of limiting it.

"Standards actually enable innovation," Martin Sakowski said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. The platform's job is to provide the abstractions and standards that remove cognitive load, so teams get speed and still meet their requirements.

## What makes a platform worth using?

Burkhardt gives three characteristics:

- **Enabling, with transparent, shared components.** "A platform shouldn't be a black box," Marina Burkhardt said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Document it, open-source the code at least internally, and share components so nobody reinvents the wheel. Transparency builds a sense of shared responsibility.
- **Extensible and scalable.** You can't predict every team's needs, so stay flexible about tools and architectural patterns, and automate (she names AWS CDK) so onboarding keeps pace as teams arrive.
- **Evolutionary.** Treat the platform as a product: it should lower total cost of ownership and get easier to use over time.

Good intentions don't scale without mechanisms, so she adds four: abstractions that hide complexity, sane defaults that minimise mistakes, automation that raises velocity, and controls that enforce compliance.

## Why does the central model break?

Sakowski quotes Peter Gillard-Moss of Thoughtworks: platforms are a way of centralising expertise while decentralising innovation to the customer or user. Innovative teams are small and self-sufficient, and they make most decisions on their own.

In the centralised model, the platform team owns and operates everything, and app teams request features. That moves cognitive load from app teams to the platform team, and with enough app teams the platform team becomes the bottleneck. You've centralised the innovation along with the expertise.

In the decentralised model, the platform team publishes blueprints, and app teams own the whole lifecycle of what they build from them. They don't drown in cognitive load because the blueprints carry the platform team's abstractions; they still meet central requirements, and they can evolve the stack themselves or with the platform team.

## Three ownership patterns, and you don't have to pick one

Burkhardt walks through the patterns she sees most with AWS customers:

1. **AWS accounts as the platform.** An account vending machine, owned by the platform team, hands out accounts with networking (VPCs, subnets, routing), observability (logs, metrics, CloudWatch dashboards) and security pre-built, using AWS Organizations, AWS Config, CloudWatch and IAM. High flexibility, lower abstraction.
2. **Managed clusters as the platform.** For teams who just want to run containers, the platform team runs multi-tenant clusters with CI/CD, ingress control, access management and health checks. Less flexibility, more abstraction.
3. **Deployable application patterns.** Ready-made blueprints such as CDK constructs that teams customise, often best suited to high-performing teams already comfortable with their own accounts.

The punchline is freedom of choice. In their four-team example, one team builds everything on a vended account, one uses a managed cluster plus a Helm-chart pattern, one uses the cluster alone, and the serverless team uses templated serverless patterns. All of it is the platform.

## Golden path, paved road, floating platform

They frame the blueprints as the golden path on a paved road: the opinionated, supported way, with room to step left or right inside the guardrails. Sometimes the detour becomes the next golden path. To run it, borrow from open source: version components, give each its own lifecycle to shrink the blast radius, make them usable with docs, scaffolding and a CLI, customisable with parameters, escape hatches and forks, transparent, and self-service through APIs.

Their last image is the best one. The base you build on, such as the AWS cloud, keeps evolving. If your platform doesn't, it becomes a sinking platform that makes things harder than going native. Keep adapting and you have a floating platform that stays ahead of the base.

## Who should watch

Platform leads whose team has become a ticket queue, and architects deciding how much of the stack app teams should own. It is a conceptual talk with AWS examples, not a product demo.

Title: Where AI earns its keep in dialysis care, from risk scores to machines
Description: Ram Meka (Fresenius Medical Care) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on AI in dialysis care, from hospitalisation risk to predictive machine maintenance
Body:
Dialysis is a lifeline with a waiting list. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Ram Meka, Principal Systems Developer at Fresenius Medical Care with over a decade of building kidney care products, mapped where AI already helps dialysis care: predicting which patients are heading for hospital, tailoring treatment, squeezing more capacity out of clinics and keeping the machines themselves from failing mid-shift.

Fair warning on scope: this is a domain overview, not a Kubernetes talk. There is no cluster, no code and no architecture diagram. What you get is a clear map of the problem space from someone who works in it, which is exactly what an engineer joining a healthcare team needs on day one.

## Why does dialysis need help at all?

Ram opens with the numbers. Chronic kidney disease affects over 700 million people worldwide, and for patients who progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), dialysis takes over the job the kidneys can no longer do. It works, but it is expensive, there are regional shortages of machines and trained staff, and outcomes vary even when protocols are followed. Longer waits for treatment mean worse health, so every efficiency gain is measured in patients, not dashboards.

## Predicting the hospital visit before it happens

The headline figure is predictive analytics: models that predict hospitalisation risk with over 80% accuracy. The point is not the score but what it buys, a window for early intervention. Ram describes these systems pulling together lab results, treatment responses and patient history so care teams can act before a complication turns into an admission.

"By anticipating potential complications, we can initialize timely medical interventions, significantly reducing the likelihood of severe health issues," Ram Meka said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

Personalised treatment protocols follow the same logic: models analyse each patient's data and adjust the plan as new results arrive, with the goal of better biochemical markers and fewer uremic symptoms.

## Capacity is the quiet win

The operational section is the most interesting part for anyone who builds systems. Ram cites studies suggesting AI-integrated clinics can raise patient capacity by up to 20% without lowering care quality, mainly through workflow automation (less paperwork and fewer scheduling delays) and resource allocation that matches staff and equipment to real patient flow. In a field where the bottleneck is chairs, machines and nurses, that is a bigger deal than any model accuracy number.

Remote monitoring and telehealth extend the same idea outside the clinic: continuous tracking of patient data with real-time alerts when something drifts, so problems surface between visits rather than at the next one.

## The machines get a pager too

The part SREs will recognise is predictive maintenance for the dialysis machines themselves. Models forecast failures and maintenance needs so a machine is serviced before it breaks during treatment. It is the same playbook as disk failure prediction in a data centre, except the outage has a patient attached to it.

## What could go wrong

Ram closes with four challenges: data privacy (HIPAA compliance and breach protection), algorithmic bias (models need diverse training data or they will deliver unequal care), implementation cost against long-term return, and regulatory compliance. None of them is solved in the talk; they are flagged as the work that has to happen before any of the benefits are real.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into healthtech, product people scoping AI features for clinical settings, and anyone who wants a quick tour of the dialysis domain. If you came for Kubernetes internals, this one is a context-setter rather than a how-to.

Title: LLMs that read hospital chargemasters so patients don't have to
Description: Deepak Talasila (Google) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024 on an AI platform that turns chargemasters and claims into personal US healthcare cost estimates
Body:
You can compare the price of a USB cable across ten shops in a minute, but not the price of a knee scan across two hospitals. At Conf42 Kube Native 2024, Deepak Talasila, Staff Software Engineer at Google, presented an AI platform for US healthcare cost transparency: large language models parse hospital chargemasters, insurance claims and user-reported bills into a pricing database, and machine learning models turn that into personal cost estimates, provider comparisons and help negotiating the bill.

Scope note: despite the Kube-native framing in the title, the talk is about the product and its data pipeline, not about Kubernetes. Expect the problem, the architecture in words and the results, not manifests.

## Why is a medical bill such a surprise?

Deepak's framing is that US healthcare pricing is opaque to everyone, doctors included. The same procedure costs different amounts at different providers, in different zip codes, and depending on what insurance decides to cover. He tells the story of a friend who, without good insurance as a student, put off treating a leg injury until he had a job, and the delay made the injury and the eventual costs worse. Delayed or avoided care is the expensive side effect of not knowing the price.

## How does the platform build a price?

There are three steps. Data collection pulls from hospital chargemasters, insurance claims and costs that users report themselves. Models are trained on that data with features such as regional variation, provider-specific pricing and the user's insurance coverage. Real-time estimation then answers a specific question for a specific person in seconds, with validation and user feedback feeding back into the data.

The enabling piece is the LLM stage. Pricing data lives in long, inconsistent documents, and Deepak credits the last two to three years of language models for making it tractable.

"This would not have been possible to do with with the previous with the previous textual understanding," Deepak Talasila said at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

## How accurate is accurate enough?

This is the most honest part of the talk. Estimates come with a stated variance of plus or minus 50% for common procedures and plus or minus 30% for complex ones. Deepak acknowledges the range looks wide, and argues it is still a large step up from having no number at all. For freshness, models weight recent data more heavily, so a 2024 estimate leans on 2023 and 2024 prices rather than 2016 ones, while older data still helps the model generalise.

## What did users get out of it?

Beyond estimates, the platform compares prices and quality ratings across providers and generates negotiation support: letters with billing and comparison data attached. Deepak reports that users of the negotiation feature saw an 18% reduction in their medical bills, and a 20% reduction in avoided or delayed care among users once they could budget for treatment.

## Privacy and fairness, by leaving data out

The privacy design is mostly subtraction. Deepak describes encryption and secure computation, differential privacy, federated learning, and not keeping individual data after training. On fairness, the model deliberately takes no personal identifying features, so two people with the same condition, area and coverage get the same estimate.

Next on the list: integration with electronic health records and predictive health spending models, for example estimating what a person with diabetes should expect to spend in one, five and ten years.

## Who should watch

Engineers working on healthcare data, anyone building LLM-based document extraction into a structured database, and product people who want a worked example of where an estimate with honest error bars is still worth shipping.
