Title: Customise Oracle EBS the supported way or redo it after every patch
Description: Harikrishna Reddy (Medical College of Wisconsin) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on customising Oracle EBS with reports, interfaces, conversions, extensions
Body:
Every company that buys Oracle E-Business Suite ends up bending it to fit, and the bending has a name: RICE. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Harikrishna Reddy, Senior Enterprise Applications Engineer at the Medical College of Wisconsin, gives a practical survey of the four RICE components (reports, interfaces, conversions and extensions) and the one rule that ties them together: customise inside Oracle's guidelines, or your work disappears at the next patch.

One note before you press play: the talk is entirely about Oracle EBS. The abstract's mention of Microsoft Fabric doesn't come up, so come for the ERP content.

## What is RICE, and why should a platform engineer care?

RICE stands for Reports, Interfaces, Conversions and Extensions, the framework for customising Oracle EBS. Reddy's framing for this audience is that the modular approach lets a platform team adapt a large ERP to changing business demands without forking it, and slot it into a platform-centric architecture. His slides cite that 78% of Oracle EBS users implement RICE customisations within two years of deployment.

## Reports: standard, custom, ad hoc

Standard reports ship with whichever EBS modules you license. Custom reports exist because every company has its own requirements. Ad hoc reports cover real-time analysis. When designing them, think about data sources, formatting and what the users actually need.

On tooling, his slides put Oracle Report Builder at 45% usage, BI Publisher at 35% and Oracle Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition at 20%. His own recommendation in the talk is BI Publisher, with OBIEE rarely used.

## Interfaces: where the security questions live

Interfaces connect EBS to everything else, and come in three shapes: API-based (web services and REST), file-based, and messaging through queues or topics. The design checklist is data formats, security and error handling. He stresses security because an interface is literally someone getting into your system, or you getting into theirs, often across firewalls. Oracle Integration Cloud and Oracle SOA Suite are the integration tools he sees in use.

## Conversions: the data is the system

Conversions cover migration, transformation and loading, for data migration, warehousing and archiving. Plan for data quality, formatting and validation, and use Oracle's loaders such as Data Pump and SQL*Loader, typically when a legacy application is shut down and its data moves into Oracle. The slides add the steps that save projects: cleansing and validation, mapping source to target structures, testing conversion scripts, and mock conversions.

His reasoning for taking it seriously is blunt: a system is its data, and corrupted data damages everything that runs on top of it.

## Extensions: the patch cycle is the real constraint

Extensions are where companies add custom tables, custom forms, and custom workflows, such as an approval chain with three levels at one company and fifteen at another. Build them with Oracle's own tools like Oracle Application Extension or JDeveloper, and follow Oracle's customisation guidelines strictly.

The reason is the upgrade cycle. Oracle patches twice a year, and "if you don't follow the correct process, aligned by Oracle, all your changes, the custom changes will be wiped out," Harikrishna Reddy said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. You then rebuild them by hand.

## Do the case studies hold up?

He closes with case-study figures: a manufacturing company saving $75 million through improved reporting, a retail chain saving $12 million through supply chain interfaces, a financial institution reaching 99.98% data accuracy after migration, and a pharmaceutical company saving $15 million through extensions. He describes them as gathered from a small survey and online sources, with no companies named, so treat them as illustrations rather than benchmarks.

The best practices are the durable part: a clear strategy, iterative development and testing including mock conversions, balancing customisation against maintainability and future upgrades, and the Oracle community at support.oracle.com.

## Who should watch

Engineers who have just landed on an Oracle EBS team and need the vocabulary, or platform engineers who suddenly own an ERP integration. It is an overview, without code or demos.

Title: At a billion rows, ALTER TABLE and mysqldump become your enemies
Description: Lukas Vileikis at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on running MySQL and MariaDB with billions of rows, from bulk loads and schema changes to backups
Body:
Most MySQL advice assumes your table fits comfortably on the disk twice. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Lukas Vileikis, author of the book Hacking MySQL: Breaking, Optimizing, and Securing MySQL for Your Use Case, shares what he learned running MySQL and MariaDB with billions of records behind a data breach search engine: bulk loading beats `INSERT`, `ALTER TABLE` can eat your free space, and `mysqldump` stops being a backup strategy long before you'd like.

## Why does one query return in 0.01s and its twin time out?

He opens with two full-text searches using `MATCH ... AGAINST`, one plain and one in Boolean mode with an `@` sign. The first finishes in 0.01 seconds; the second times out. It is a bug he found while building his breach search engine and reported (MySQL bug #104263), and his best guess is the query takes a different path inside the database. The lesson for the rest of the talk: full-text indexes are prone to behaviour you wouldn't expect, so test the exact queries you plan to run.

## The basics still do most of the work

Before anything clever: configure the server in `my.cnf` with the InnoDB parameters that matter (`innodb_buffer_pool_size`, `innodb_log_file_size`, `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit`), and only ask for what you need, so a `LIMIT 1` query doesn't scan 20,000 books to return one.

Use InnoDB (or XtraDB on Percona Server). If someone switched a table to MyISAM, switch it back. The one thing MyISAM does better is report an exact row count, because it keeps it in metadata and InnoDB doesn't.

For schema, his rule is to keep things simple, avoid inventing things, and lean on the documentation: simple data types, indexes, normalisation, partitioning. Avoid `TEXT` where you can, remember `VARCHAR` costs its length plus one or two bytes, and use `utf8mb4_unicode_ci`, because MySQL's `utf8` only stores three bytes per character and some queries will error out. He also mentions disabling `STRICT_TRANS_TABLES` and `STRICT_ALL_TABLES` so over-long values are truncated instead of rejected, a trade-off he says doesn't fit every use case. Silently shortened data is still shortened data.

## Load data, don't insert it

For bulk loading, skip `INSERT` and use `LOAD DATA INFILE` with its options for character set, field and line terminators and escaping. Each `INSERT` goes through locking, integrity checks and preparing for the next row; loading raw data skips most of that overhead.

Partitioning (his example is `PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS` over three columns with nearly 30 partitions) lets queries treat the table as smaller pieces while the database still sees one table.

## ALTER TABLE copies the whole table

This is the trap that catches people with big data. `ALTER TABLE` makes a copy of the table on disk, changes the copy and swaps it in. A 200 GB table on a disk with 57 GB free simply runs out of space.

His workarounds:

- Use a column `DEFAULT` instead of a mass `UPDATE` where the value is known in advance.
- When adding a column at the end of the table, `SET SESSION alter_algorithm='INSTANT'` adds it without rewriting anything (MariaDB 10.3.2 and later).
- Instead of adding a `UNIQUE` index to deduplicate a huge column, export the data, run `sort -u` on it, and load the clean file back.
- `INSERT IGNORE` to skip errors, `DELETE ... FOR PORTION OF` to delete by time period, and `TRUNCATE` when the whole table goes.

## How do you back up a billion rows?

Not with `mysqldump`. It works, but the file gets huge and a restore can take weeks or time out. His approach is raw data: `SELECT * INTO OUTFILE` to export, `LOAD DATA INFILE` to restore, with far less overhead than a logical dump full of `CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT` statements.

And when someone fires 10 million queries at once because you forgot the rate limiter, `SHOW PROCESSLIST` gives you the IDs and `KILL` gets rid of them while you add the rate limiting.

## What tools does he actually reach for?

Mostly himself: "nobody knows your database better than you," Lukas Vileikis said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. After that: `mariadb-secure-installation`, the slow query log, MySQL Enterprise Edition if you need its firewall and audit features, and clients and monitors such as DbVisualizer, Arctype, Redgate Monitor and ClusterControl.

He ends with the Schrödinger's table: lose power mid-load and you can be left with a `.frm` definition file whose data file is gone. The database sees the table but won't drop it until you put a data file back in place.

## Who should watch

DBAs and backend engineers whose MySQL or MariaDB tables have crossed into hundreds of millions of rows, and anyone about to run `ALTER TABLE` on one.

Title: Your Istio mesh is already emitting the metrics you need
Description: Siddhartha Khare (New Relic) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on the Envoy metrics every Istio mesh exposes and how to chart them
Body:
The nice thing about a service mesh is that every request already passes through a proxy that counts it. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Siddhartha Khare, Senior Technical Account Manager at New Relic, gives a compact introduction to Istio and its observability: what the control and data planes do, which metrics the Envoy sidecars expose for free, and a short demo charting them for a Kubernetes cluster in New Relic.

Set expectations: this is a short, introductory talk. If you've never looked at what an Istio mesh reports, it is a quick orientation; mesh veterans will know most of it.

## Why do microservices need a mesh at all?

He starts from the microservices definition: independently deployable, loosely coupled services organised around business capabilities, each usually owned by one small team. The autonomy is the point, and also the problem, because the traffic between all those services needs managing somewhere.

Istio is that somewhere: a dedicated infrastructure layer added transparently to your applications. It handles load balancing for HTTP traffic, routing rules, failovers, and fault injection rules you can use to run chaos experiments against your own services.

## Control plane and data plane, briefly

The control plane he describes is the classic component split:

- **Pilot** configures the proxies at runtime and propagates new configuration to them.
- **Citadel** issues certificates and rotates them, effectively the mesh's internal certificate authority.
- **Galley** validates configuration and hands it to Pilot for distribution.

(Recent Istio releases ship these together as a single `istiod`, but the responsibilities are the same.)

The data plane is Envoy, injected as a sidecar next to each application container in the pod. Make sure sidecar injection is enabled, because Envoy carries all traffic between services and out to external ones. Without it, as he puts it, nothing will work.

## Which metrics should you watch?

This is the useful part. "Istio's envoy proxies automatically collect and report the detailed metrics" through a Prometheus endpoint, Siddhartha Khare said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, so the data is there before you install anything. The ones he highlights:

- `istio_requests_total`, a counter of requests handled by the proxy, which you can break down by destination service.
- `istio_request_duration_milliseconds`, a distribution of how long the proxy takes to process HTTP requests.
- `istio_request_bytes` and `istio_response_bytes`, the sizes of HTTP request and response bodies.
- `istio_tcp_connections_opened_total` for TCP traffic.

Beyond those there is a long tail: certificate expiry metrics for the agent, Go runtime metrics for routines and threads, and the full set of Envoy metrics.

## What does it look like in a real cluster?

The demo connects a cluster named after the conference through New Relic's Kubernetes integration, then drills from the cluster overview to the Istio ingress pod: CPU utilisation, throttling, memory, and the ingress logs over a wider time window.

From there he builds the views most teams want, using NRQL, New Relic's query language: request volume per minute by pod and app, request duration, traffic into the front end and the back end with its source (in his setup a sleep pod and the front end generating database traffic), outbound requests split by response code so the 200s and 404s are visible, a histogram of client request latency, and a percentage breakdown of response codes.

It's a New Relic demo, and he says plainly that any tool scraping the Prometheus endpoint will do the same job.

## Who should watch

Engineers who just inherited an Istio mesh and want to know what it can already tell them, or teams choosing between mesh dashboards. If you want sidecar-less meshes or deep Envoy tuning, try the related talks.

Title: Platform teams can't right-size what they can't see
Description: Neel Shah (Middleware) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on why observability is the platform team's tool for scaling, cost, troubleshooting and developer experience
Body:
A platform nobody can see into is a platform you scale by guesswork and debug by rumour. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Neel Shah, Developer Advocate at Middleware, gives a short, introductory tour of why observability belongs at the centre of a platform team's work: correlated logs, metrics and traces are what let you scale ahead of demand, stop paying for idle resources, find root causes and give developers something better than a guess.

It is a 101 talk and a brisk one. If you already run OpenTelemetry in production, this is a refresher; if you're the person trying to convince a new platform team to invest in telemetry, it is a tidy list of arguments.

## What are the three signals for?

He frames the core objectives in the usual three parts. Log management collects application and service logs to understand behaviour and performance impact. Metrics give the graphable view of performance over time, which is how you catch problems before users do. Traces follow a request across services and show where the bottleneck actually lives, rather than where you assumed it was.

## Five things a platform gets out of it

The bulk of the talk walks through the benefits, each with a concrete scenario:

- **Resource allocation.** Correlate usage data with demand and you know when to scale up, when to scale down and when the peaks are, instead of reacting after the fact.
- **Cost.** If monitoring shows only 10-20% of a resource is used while you pay for all of it, you have found your downsizing target. His point is that over-provisioning is invisible without the metrics.
- **Troubleshooting.** Trace an issue back to its origin, whether that is a misconfiguration or code, and get real-time alerts to Slack, email or Teams so the outage window shrinks.
- **Developer experience.** Developers see how their changes behave in production, which means less time troubleshooting and more time shipping features.
- **Data-driven decisions.** His example is a Black Friday sale: if you monitored the last one, you know how far traffic and purchases rose compared to a normal day, and you can plan capacity for the next.

## Where does it go wrong?

He names three challenges. Data overload: collecting everything is not a strategy, and he argues for selective collection tied to business objectives, with rules, flags and alerts on the logs that actually matter, such as security events and performance-impacting errors. Integration complexity: multi-cloud estates scatter logs, traces and metrics across different tools. And skill gaps, especially around applying AI and ML to operations.

His answer to the second problem is consolidation. "We need a single platform where logs, traces, monitoring, everything could be possible," Neel Shah said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. This is where his employer's product appears: he uses Middleware as the example of one platform connecting databases and cloud providers. It is a brief mention, not a demo.

## What's next for observability?

The closing section points at three trends: AI and ML for anomaly detection and troubleshooting, observability moving out to edge computing, and the steady growth of OpenTelemetry as the open standard that keeps instrumentation portable. The best-practice list is short and sensible: start with clear objectives, implement end-to-end tracing, automate, keep improving, and make observability a shared habit across the company rather than one team's dashboard.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to platform work, or managers building the case for telemetry spend. Practitioners looking for implementation detail, sampling strategies or OpenTelemetry Collector configuration will want one of the talks below instead; this one is about the why.

Title: Ship your SLOs to staging before production does it for you
Description: Indika Wimalasuriya (Virtusa) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on managing Datadog monitors, dashboards and SLOs for AWS as Terraform code
Body:
If your dashboards and SLOs only exist in production, your developers meet them for the first time during an incident. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Indika Wimalasuriya, Associate Director and Senior Systems Engineering Manager at Virtusa, argues for treating the whole Datadog setup for AWS workloads (integrations, log pipelines, monitors, synthetics, SLOs, access control, maintenance windows) as Terraform code that moves through every pre-live environment on its way to production.

## Why do platform teams need this?

He opens with two figures from the Catchpoint SRE Report 2024: 66% of organisations use between two and five monitoring or observability tools, and 24% breached a contractual SLA in the previous 12 months. More tools, still missing commitments.

His platform engineering picture is familiar to anyone in a large company: three lines of business, many application teams, each picking its own alerting, logging and dashboard tooling. Over time there is no single source of truth, onboarding a new service is a project, and nobody can compare one team's reliability with another's. The platform team's job is a unified observability strategy with self-service access for developers, and code is how you make it repeatable.

## What goes into the repo?

The talk walks through a Terraform layout with a `main.tf`, the Datadog provider configuration, variables, and YAML definitions for monitors, SLOs, dashboards and maintenance windows. The modules he lists:

- **Integration.** The AWS-Datadog integration automated end to end, agents for EC2 and containers, the Lambda library for serverless. Datadog and AWS keys read from AWS Secrets Manager rather than sitting in the code.
- **Log shipping.** CloudWatch logs forwarded to Datadog with filters by level and regex. His warning is practical: Datadog is paid and log volume gets expensive, so filter before you ship.
- **Synthetic monitors** that mimic real user journeys, with retries configured.
- **Alerts** correlated with SLOs, layered across caching, middleware, service and end-to-end journeys, using fixed thresholds or Datadog's anomaly and forecast monitors with team routing and tags.
- **Common metrics and dashboards.** EC2, container and Lambda services tend to need the same views, so build them once and give a new team a Git repo to plug into instead of a blank Datadog account.
- **APM, RBAC and accounts**, including read-write privileges and cost views.

## SLOs written by developers, not by the ops team at go-live

This is the sharpest part of the talk. Datadog supports SLOs as good events over total, monitor-based uptime, or time slices, and all of them can be code. Instead of defining SLOs after launch, "we want our developer community to think about SLOs, service level objectives, when they're designing, developing, testing," Indika Wimalasuriya said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

Ship them with the service and they exist in pre-live environments too. Then the performance, soak and stress tests you already run tell you how the SLOs behave under spike traffic, before real users do it for you.

## Maintenance windows from the pipeline

A small idea that saves a lot of pages: define Datadog maintenance windows as code and have the CI/CD pipeline open one for the deployment, suppress the relevant alerts, and close it afterwards. He also mentions Datadog webhooks calling remediation code in Lambda as a route to self-healing.

## How do you know it worked?

He wants the programme measured: MTTD, MTTR, MTBF, SLO trends, and the DORA metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate). His best practices are the unglamorous ones: protect the API keys, version everything in Git, modularise instead of a big-bang rollout, run it through the pipeline, keep it centralised, and use Datadog's direct integrations where they save time.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams running Datadog on AWS with many application teams, especially if every team's dashboards look different. It is an architecture and practices talk with snippets, not a step-by-step Terraform tutorial.

Title: Your infrastructure has an API but no Terraform provider? Write one
Description: Harel Safra (Riskified) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on building a Terraform provider in Go, from scaffolding to a published registry release
Body:
Infrastructure as code works right up to the resource nobody wrote a provider for, and then it's back to a manual script and a Confluence page. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Harel Safra, Data Platform Engineering Team Lead at Riskified, shows that the fix is within reach of any platform engineer: if the thing has a public API, you can write the Terraform provider yourself, and he walks from an empty repo to a provider published on the Terraform Registry.

That is exactly what his team did. They used Terraform everywhere except one database, which was still managed by hand. So he learned the plugin framework, wrote a provider, and his team now runs it.

## Who is allowed to write a provider?

Anyone. Terraform core knows how to plan, create and diff, but has no idea how any particular piece of infrastructure works; providers are the plugins that bridge core and the infrastructure API, talking to core over RPC. There were already 4,400+ providers at the time of the talk, and Safra's point is that you don't need to work for the vendor to add one. "Anyone can create more providers," Harel Safra said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. "You don't have to be part of the infrastructure team."

The stack he draws is simple: Terraform core, then your provider in Go, then a client library, then whatever native protocol the infrastructure speaks (HTTP, gRPC, SQL, system calls). His practical advice: if one version of the target API already has a Go client, pick that one, because it makes the rest of the work much easier.

## Do I need to know Go first?

Enough to read and write it, not to be an expert. He learned from the Go tour at go.dev and liked that the compiler catches errors before runtime. The gotcha he flags for newcomers: Go has no exceptions, "meaning you need to explicitly check for error conditions for function calls." Skip those checks and the code panics instead. Then read HashiCorp's developer documentation for how the pieces fit together.

## A provider that manages lines in a text file

The demo is deliberately tiny so the plumbing stays visible: a provider whose `file` resource has a file name and a list of lines, backed by a toy API that can only read, write and count lines. The code lives in his GitHub repo `terraform-provider-file`, and it starts the recommended way, by cloning HashiCorp's provider scaffolding for the plugin framework, which handles the RPC side so you only write business logic.

From there the walkthrough covers what every provider needs:

- **CRUD methods.** Create, read, update and delete map onto what core asks for. Attributes the API can't change in place get handled by core as delete plus create.
- **Schemas and attributes.** Each attribute has a type (string, int, list, map, object), properties such as required, optional or sensitive, and optional validators. His example forces the file name to match a regex and the lines list to have at least two entries.
- **Descriptions do double duty.** The attribute descriptions are copied into the generated documentation that ends up on the registry, so write them properly.
- **Framework types are not Go types.** They carry null and unknown states; you call methods like `ValueString()` or `ElementsAs` to get native values out.

## How do you debug it without publishing?

Two ways. Point Terraform at your local build with a `dev_overrides` block in the CLI config, or run the provider's main with the debug flag, copy the environment variable it prints, and run `terraform plan` in another terminal. The live demo does the second: Terraform pauses, the debugger stops at a breakpoint in the read method, and you step through the call for `file2` like any other program.

Then acceptance tests: `_test.go` files with steps that apply a config, check attributes, update the lines and check again, run with `make test`.

## Shipping to the registry

Create a GPG key, store the private key and passphrase as GitHub secrets, and push a semver tag like `v0.1.0`. The tag triggers the GitHub Action that comes with the scaffolding, which builds the executables and notifies the registry through a webhook; the registry uses the GPG key to check the code is really yours. Add the repo in the Terraform Registry, authenticate with GitHub, wait a few minutes. One warning worth repeating: the registry is public, so nothing proprietary goes in.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers with a homegrown tool, a SaaS database or an internal service that everyone still clicks through by hand. If you've never opened a provider's source, this is a calm, demo-driven first tour.

- Andrew Kirkpatrick on [self-service, PR-based Terraform](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Andrew_Kirkpatrick_selfservice_PRbased_Terraform).

Title: Crashlytics is green and your iOS users are still stuck
Description: Siarhei Misko (Rakuten Viber) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on building observability into iOS apps with cheap logs, bitmask metrics and coordinators
Body:
A crash reporter only tells you about crashes, and most of the ways a mobile app fails don't crash. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Siarhei Misko, iOS Team Lead at Rakuten Viber, makes the case that iOS teams should design observability into the app the way backend teams already do, and shows the specific patterns he uses: tiered logging, a bitmask that survives a killed extension, and navigation data harvested from coordinators.

## Why isn't crash reporting enough?

He starts with a team that shipped an app with no analytics, no logging, no Crashlytics. Users complain the second screen crashes, QA can't reproduce it, and the team ships a new build and hopes. Adding Apple's built-in crash reports or Firebase Crashlytics fixes that particular blindness, and he counts it as a first step towards observability.

The harder failures produce no crash at all. A product manager mistypes a field in a feature-flag config that nothing validates, and a slice of users silently loses a feature. A release that passed every test makes registration fail on one phone model and iOS version. "It's important to understand that traces, metrics, and logs by themselves are not observability," Siarhei Misko said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. The property comes from aggregating them where you can chart, break down and alert.

His starting list for what to measure: critical user stories (registration, login, payments, sending messages, search), including how fast they complete; flows that depend on frequently changing configuration; and flows that depend on external systems, including another team's internal API.

## Logs are the heaviest tool you have

Every observability tool costs the device something, and logs cost the most. So he splits the problem into delivery and collection.

Delivery can be live (fine on the backend, wasteful on a phone, since you get logs when everything works), on demand (a flag the app receives at login, a push notification, or a menu item the user taps), or triggered by an event such as a crash or a critical error.

Collection can be continuous or switched on later. Continuous logging needs buffered writes rather than open-write-close per line, file rotation with a size cap (his example is 20 MB), and no debug level in release builds. On-demand collection misses the first occurrence, because recording only starts after someone notices. His answer is a combination: error, warning and critical always on; info and notice switched on by a flag, a push or a user request.

## Where should iOS logs go?

- **OSLog** is fast and privacy-aware, but awkward to get at: connect the phone to a Mac, pull a sysdiagnose (up to 15 minutes and more than 200 MB), or read it programmatically, which only gives you the current process, not extensions or previous launches.
- **A text file**, starting with an open-source framework like SwiftyBeaver and adapting it once you know what you need.
- **Firebase Crashlytics** custom logs and non-fatal events, attached to crash reports. Good for a start, but sampled, limited in log lines, and with no custom queries.

Two Swift tricks keep the overhead down: wrap the body of the debug log function in `#if` so the compiler drops those calls from release builds, and take the message as an `@autoclosure` so expensive descriptions are never evaluated when the level is off.

## How do you observe a process iOS kills without warning?

The best example in the talk is the notification service extension. "iOS strictly enforces a 24MB RAM limit" for it, and exceeding it kills the process with no crash report and no log line. His fix is an option set where each bit marks one completed step, plus a final bit for reaching the end, persisted to disk after every change. On the next launch the app checks the last value and sends a metric if the run stopped early. You learn which step dies, at almost no memory cost.

## Architecture makes metrics cheap

Clean structure does most of the work. With the coordinator pattern the app always knows the user's path, which compresses into a short string of screen codes. The active coordinator at termination time gives a last screen metric: if many users close the app on the same screen, something on it is broken. The same coordinators time app start and key flows like payments, and a clearly defined API layer records which requests ran during startup. His favourite small metric is the annoyed tap: the same UI element tapped again and again, usually because it isn't doing anything.

## Who should watch

iOS and mobile platform engineers with Crashlytics wired in and nothing else, and backend observability people curious what the client side looks like under a 24 MB budget.

- Frank Courville on [state machines in Swift](https://www.conf42.com/Mobile_2022_Frank_Courville_swift_power_of_state_machines).

Title: An oven sold once costs cloud money forever, so Electrolux put cost next to latency
Description: Long Zhang and Vladimir Shcherbinin (Electrolux) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on a Backstage IDP for infrastructure and open source cost tools
Body:
Electrolux sells a connected oven at a fixed price, and from then on the oven and its app keep talking to the cloud on Electrolux's bill. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Senior SREs Long Zhang and Vladimir Shcherbinin of Electrolux show how their platform team turned a stream of support DMs into a Backstage-based internal developer platform, then made cloud cost visible on the same dashboards as service metrics, with tools they have open sourced.

It is a practitioner talk from a team running services for appliances in three categories, taste, care and wellbeing, on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, which the abstract puts at more than 10 million connected appliances worldwide.

## From DM queue to self-service

Shcherbinin describes where they started, about three years earlier: an SRE team fielding access requests, infrastructure issues and requests for data from production databases all day, while developers waited. "It feels every day that you are the most important person in the world," Vladimir Shcherbinin said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, and he did not mean it as a compliment.

A Python script that automated their Terraform made them faster but did not remove them from the loop. Meanwhile the organisation grew from about 20 developers to more than 300, and the platform team did not grow with it. So they built a platform: first a home-made one, then Backstage, initially just its UI, later its authentication and catalogue too.

## What does the platform actually do?

- **Onboarding**: a user onboarding plugin with access policies pre-defined from the org structure, so engineering leads grant every access a new joiner needs on one page and never message the SREs.
- **Infrastructure from templates**: production-ready Terraform modules behind a UI. Pick the EKS template and the platform creates the VPC and cluster, then installs the autoscaler, ingress controller, Datadog agent and their own cost exporter, so logs, metrics and cost show up without the developer configuring anything.
- **An escape hatch**: teams that need something without a template, such as a proof of concept with a new IoT technology or a rarely used DNS setup, write their own Terraform modules, which still run through the platform so everything is tracked in one place.
- **Versioned templates**: improve a template and running infrastructure is updated automatically, with approval flows, auditing and cloud data sync.
- **Service management**: CI/CD status, secrets, registry images, pod restarts and manual deploys of a chosen version, all from one page with no direct cluster access.

The payoff Shcherbinin quotes is a backend developer telling him that infrastructure used to be a black box, abstract and scary, and that once it was visualised and safe to use he started doing things on his own. Because the original platform was heavily customised and AWS-only while teams asked for Google Cloud and Azure, they started an open source rewrite intended to replace it, beginning with infrastructure management.

## Why don't developers care about cost?

Zhang takes the cost half. Management asks what project X costs, what the trend is and how to cut it, questions that need aggregation across clouds. Developers, when asked, often answered that they simply don't care. Then a cost spike arrives, management asks why, the platform team cannot tell what the resources are used for, and the ball goes back to the developers anyway.

Their answer comes in two parts:

- **Cost metric exporters**: services that pull cost data from a provider (the AWS one uses the Cost Explorer APIs) and expose it as Prometheus metrics, so cost lands in Grafana or Datadog next to the service's own metrics. Vendor-neutral, extensible and listed on the Prometheus exporters page.
- **InfraWallet**: a Backstage plugin that aggregates cost from AWS accounts, Azure subscriptions and Google Cloud into the standard FOCUS categories, with grouping, filters and caching.

## Cost without context is just a bigger number

InfraWallet's business metrics feature puts unit economics on the cost graph: monthly active users, transactions, connected devices. If active users double and cost rises a little, the cost per user just fell. Zhang's real story: the IoT category's daily cost jumped while connected appliances barely moved, and the IoT team quickly traced it to air conditioners misconfigured to send unnecessary messages to AWS IoT.

Tools are only the start, he says. Electrolux runs regular cost optimisation programmes, run like a competition, in which developers use the platform's cost views to propose savings across databases, messaging, storage, logs, APM, metrics and CI/CD. The last round saved $32,101 a month. His summary for everyone: "cost engineering is not only about techniques. But also about culture."

## Who should watch

Platform teams drowning in Slack requests, and anyone trying to get developers to look at cloud cost without nagging. It is concrete, and the cost tools are on GitHub under electrolux-oss to try.

Title: If your platform only serves runtimes, you have rebuilt the ops wall
Description: Graziano Casto (Mia-Platform) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on why platforms must also serve data, APIs and composable business logic
Body:
Platform engineering was supposed to tear down the wall between developers and operations, and a platform that only orchestrates infrastructure risks putting up a new one. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Graziano Casto, Developer Relations Engineer at Mia-Platform, argues that a modern internal developer platform has to treat data, APIs and reusable business logic as first-class building blocks next to clusters and pipelines.

He is clear that the infrastructure-centred view is not wrong, only incomplete. The talk extends it.

## Why do we need platforms at all?

Casto opens with a deliberately provocative line: "Platform engineering is the natural evolution of DevOps." Not a replacement. DevOps is alive and well, and platform engineering industrialises its practices so more teams can use them.

The reason is cognitive load. When Werner Vogels coined "you build it, you run it" at Amazon in 2006, developers ran virtual machines. Today the CNCF map of cloud native tooling counts 119 projects and more than 1,800 code repositories, by his figures. His hiking analogy captures it: a straight trail with the odd fork is a walk, a junction with a hundred paths is how you get lost. Platform engineering, in a Gartner phrase he quotes, shifts that burden from the platform's users onto the platform.

His supermarket version of the same idea: with a platform, you know what you need, take it off the shelf and use the self-checkout. Without one, you know exactly what you need and still queue for someone else to let you pay.

## Creators, composers and curators

The most useful part of the talk is a vocabulary for who does what on a platform:

- **Creators** build things from scratch, such as infrastructure, pipelines and libraries, which become building blocks. They are often the early adopters of new tools.
- **Composers** combine those blocks into digital products. Today's composition becomes tomorrow's building block, so composers turn into creators.
- **Curators** make the cooperation work by providing tools, publishing building blocks and sharing practices. They are the platform engineers.

His analogy is a woodworking shop. The curators keep the tools working and bring in new ones; one carpenter makes a drawer; another uses drawers to build a chest of drawers, which someone else builds into a kitchen. In software, a building block might be a fully configured Kubernetes cluster, a Crossplane CRD, a Kafka topic, a payments API or a whole application, and the shop's facilities are a catalogue, monitoring and log tooling. Casto calls the result a circular economy of software: resources keep getting reused and repurposed.

## The usual anatomy, and what it leaves out

The common picture, close to the CNCF platforms white paper he recommends, puts the platform between product teams and their dependencies: interfaces (web UI, APIs, CLI), a control plane orchestrating everything, and integrations that give developers on-demand environments and pre-built pipelines, tracing, secrets management and testing tools. Cloud engineers automate the infrastructure providers, developers build products, platform engineers own the golden paths, docs and platform-as-a-product work.

The gap is everything a product needs besides a runtime: data, ML, APIs, security and privacy. Leave those out, he warns, and "We run the risk of creating the new barriers between platform engineers and developers similar to the barriers that exist in the past between operations and developers," Graziano Casto said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

## Composability and data join the platform

His extended platform adds two layers. Composability: API gateways and portals that make applications reachable and documented, orchestrators that handle sagas in a standard way, micro-frontends, and an internal marketplace of building blocks. Data: a data catalogue for discoverability, a control plane that watches data flows from source to destination in real time and can stop, resume and analyse them, and an approach to building a data fabric inside the platform.

On AI, his angle is the interface rather than the workload: a conversational assistant that knows your data models and their lineage, the pipelines, the golden paths and the marketplace, and can tell you how other teams integrated a block. Troubleshooting a production issue or running a proof of concept with that context, he suggests, would look very different.

## Who should watch

Platform teams whose roadmap is all clusters and pipelines, and data or API teams wondering where they fit in the platform conversation. Casto works for a vendor of a platform builder and says so; the talk itself stays conceptual, and he credits his CTO with first formulating the ideas, which were also taken to the CNCF platforms working group.

Title: Your platform is generic; RAG is where the banking knowledge goes in
Description: Ajay Chankramath (Brillio) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on augmenting domain-specific platforms with LLMs and RAG, with a banking case study
Body:
Most of an internal developer platform looks the same whether you build payments software or hospital systems; the domain knowledge is the part nobody can buy off the shelf. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Ajay Chankramath, CTO and Managing Director for Platforms and Products at Brillio, argues that retrieval-augmented generation is how that domain knowledge gets into an AI-augmented platform, and walks through an eight-step blueprint for banking and financial services (BFSI) developers.

His most quotable claim is also the one he is most careful with: that platform engineering plus RAG could push developers' productive time far beyond where it sits today.

## Why bother with AI on the platform at all?

Chankramath anchors it in the reasons platforms exist: time to market, cost and developer productivity. None of those, he stresses, have anything to do with GenAI. The metrics stay the same; LLMs are a way to move them, through code and test generation, smoother CI/CD, better ephemeral environments, less repetitive work and less cognitive load.

He also gives a working definition of platform engineering as eight or nine axes: application runtime (containers, Kubernetes), service mesh (Istio), pipelines with compliance and governance built in, service catalogues, observability strategy as well as tooling, data infrastructure, and developer experience reporting, all tied together by internal developer platforms and their orchestrators. In his picture DevOps is the cultural paradigm, platform engineering enables it, developer experience requires it and SRE is supported by it.

## Which models for which job?

He sorts AI into predictive (forecasting, trend analysis, incident management, predictive observability) and generative (code, tests, documentation, automated decisions), then maps models to platform work: GPT-4 for code generation and DevOps assistance, Codex for autocompletion, infrastructure as code and API integration, BERT for log analysis and doc retrieval, T5 for data transformation and config management, RoBERTa for semantic search across repos, Llama for chatbots and code review.

If you train or fine-tune, epochs matter: too few and the model underfits, too many and it overfits, and the training loop is about finding convergence. His conclusion, though, is that training LLMs is still hard and costly, and RAG is where most teams will see the difference: it bridges the gaps in what a model learned by adding domain and organisation data to each query.

## The eight-step BFSI blueprint

The case study's problem statement is improving the developer experience for BFSI engineers by combining traditional platform work with RAG:

1. **Identify the critical domain APIs**: account creation, balances and transactions, payment processing, loan and investment management, reporting, trading, customer management. Bring product management in, because two banks doing similar things can still have different priorities.
2. **Build domain-specific RAG sources**: internal docs, regulatory guidelines, ontologies and taxonomies, open banking APIs, market data, research publications, vendor APIs, financial data lakes, community forums and SDKs, plus models and knowledge graphs.
3. **A platform abstraction layer** that exposes APIs for the common banking tasks alongside APIs for RAG usage, such as document retrieval and augmented query responses.
4. **A self-service portal** with documentation and a sandbox.
5. **Ephemeral environments** as dev containers with the banking tools and RAG integrations preinstalled.
6. **End-to-end observability**: logging, monitoring dashboards, distributed tracing, exposed to developers.
7. **CI/CD pipelines** published as templates, with security, compliance and automated testing stages.
8. **Automated security and compliance** checks that alert developers.

His point about the list is that only the first two steps are domain-specific. Steps three to eight are the same for any platform, which is exactly why a team can reuse its platform playbook and concentrate the domain effort on APIs and retrieval sources.

## The 70:30 claim, with an asterisk

The pitch for the whole exercise is a ratio. In a typical organisation without much platform investment, he says, "it's only about 30 percent of your developers time is productive" and the remaining 70% is overhead and duplicated work. Platform engineering, by the data he cites, moves that to 60% value-add. With GenAI and RAG he suggests it could reach 90%, and he is upfront that this last number is a hope, not a measurement: "I haven't seen a lot of data yet," Ajay Chankramath said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, adding that what he is seeing looks promising and asking anyone with data to get in touch. He also sees leverage beyond coding and testing, in solution architecture, requirements analysis and user research.

## Who should watch

Platform leads in regulated industries who are being asked what GenAI means for their roadmap, and want a structured answer that does not start with buying a chatbot. The case study is pseudocode and architecture, not a running system.

Title: DevOps started in a 1980s factory novel, not at DevOpsDays 2009
Description: Justin Reock (Cortex) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on how the theory of constraints, open source and 12-factor led to platform engineering
Body:
The word DevOps dates to Patrick Debois and DevOpsDays Belgium in 2009, but the thinking behind it is older than most of the people who practise it. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Justin Reock, Head of DevRel at Cortex, traces platform engineering back through the 12-factor app and open source to Eliyahu Goldratt's theory of constraints, and arrives at a blunt economic claim: in a software business the only thing worth optimising is the time from keyboard to revenue.

This is the third version of a talk that used to be called DevOps, 12-factor and open source. The history is the fun part; the argument underneath it is what makes it useful.

## Why does a physicist's business novel matter to DevOps?

Reock starts with the rallying cry: "it's no longer the big beating the small. But the fast beating the slow." That is a statement about throughput, and throughput is the vocabulary of Goldratt, the physicist who mapped the mechanics of machines onto how organisations flow. His vehicle was The Goal, a page-turning novel about a manufacturing VP rescued by a change agent who teaches the theory of constraints. If that plot sounds familiar, it should: Reock notes that Gene Kim will be the first to tell you The Phoenix Project is The Goal retold through DevOps.

The theory describes any machine with three parts: cost, inventory and throughput. Map them onto software and, in Reock's words at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, "cost is still cost. Inventory is code and throughput is money."

## Throughput beats cost cutting

The shift Goldratt asked for is to stop treating cost as the thing to optimise. Reock applies that directly to the layoffs of recent years: cost cuts without a plan to protect throughput tend to fail over the long run, through brain drain and the rehiring that follows when a company has cut too deep.

If code is inventory, then everything between writing it and shipping it is waste. Reock remembers copying a jar onto a disk and walking it to another department, which tested it on a system that matched production by luck, if at all, with weeks between commit and market. And inventory rots while it waits. Dependencies age and vulnerabilities land, pulling engineers off the work in flight. Continuous improvement is how you outrun that entropy, and it matters less what you improve than that you keep improving something. The DevOps conveyor belt and the deployment-frequency DORA metric fall straight out of it.

## Pythagoras versus Newton

Why is so much of the modern platform open source? Reock answers with a parable. Pythagoras taught geometry, the knowledge behind water and housing, to a closed inner circle in Croton; outsiders were shut out, a nobleman called Cylon turned on the school, Pythagoras died in exile and we still cannot say which work was his. Newton published the Principia for anyone to use. Florentine workshops and Parisian salons ran on the same openness. Imagine running a cloud on a closed, licensed TCP, he says, and nothing we have would work.

## The 12 factors are friction reduction

Portable infrastructure asks you to write code differently, and the 12-factor app from the Heroku folks is his framework for it. He does not claim every successful deployment is fully 12-factor, only that the relationship is inverse: "the less 12 factor it is, the more friction, the more tech debt, the more toil you should expect."

He walks the list with the reasoning attached: one codebase, many deploys, so it can trigger any pipeline; explicit, isolated dependencies; config in environment variables because every POSIX system has them; backing services as attached resources; separate build and run; stateless processes; port binding because TCP is universal; scale through the process model; disposable services with fast start and graceful shutdown; dev/prod parity, the problem Docker quietly solved; logs as event streams pushed to an aggregator, so admins never log into five layers of abstraction; and admin tasks as one-off processes.

## Then the freedom turned into sprawl

All that portability over-indexed on velocity. Most companies, he says, now track monoliths and microservices across silos in spreadsheets and Confluence pages, lagging systems of record that nobody updates, so nobody knows who owns what or what depends on what. His proposed next layer is the internal developer portal, as Cortex and Backstage build it: a real-time, continuously updated system of record that every engineer can reach and that aligns standards, ownership and service quality. He frames it as moving a platform from orchestration to choreography.

## Who should watch

Anyone who has to explain to leadership why platform work pays, since the cost-inventory-throughput mapping is a ready-made slide. Note that Reock works for an internal developer portal vendor, and the last few minutes make that pitch, ending with an invitation to Cortex's in-person conference on developer portals. The history and the 12-factor walkthrough stand on their own.

Title: Before you share a GenAI model, assume someone will poison or invert it
Description: Akshay Sekar Chandrasekaran (Intuit) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on securing GenAI model sharing and deployment, from zero trust to TEEs
Body:
A model trained on poisoned data will cheerfully tell you one plus one is four, and a model that leaks its training data can put a patient's health record on the internet for good. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Akshay Sekar Chandrasekaran, Senior Technical Compliance Manager at Intuit, lays out a security checklist for sharing and deploying GenAI models inside a company: the two attacks to plan for, zero trust and API hygiene, signed models, trusted execution environments and automated scanning in the pipeline.

One note before you press play: the talk page carries the title and abstract of a talk on GenAI for governance, risk and compliance. The recorded session is a different angle on the same subject, titled Secure AI Model Sharing and Deployment, and it is about securing the models themselves rather than using them for GRC. The abstract's percentages do not appear in it.

## Which attacks should you plan for?

He picks two and gives each a risk, a detection method and a mitigation.

**Data poisoning.** Someone tampers with the training data and the outputs drift. Detect it with data validation and provenance checks before training, and by examining outputs for hallucinations and bias. Mitigate by regularly retraining on cleansed, validated data so any early tampering gets diluted.

**Model inversion.** An attacker uses a model's outputs to infer sensitive details from its training data: personal or healthcare information, which in the US means a HIPAA violation, reputational damage and fines. Detect and limit it with privacy controls and output scrubbing that add randomness, and policies applied before and after training. Mitigate with strict access controls and an audit trail of who built the model and who fed it suspicious input. The stakes are permanent, he points out: once the data is out, nobody can scrub it off the internet again.

## Zero trust, applied to models

The security principles start with zero trust, never trust, always verify, even for a request coming from inside the corporate network. For GenAI he breaks it into three:

- **Continuous verification** of data inputs, because input and output interact in near real time.
- **Fewer insider threats** through need-to-know access, so nobody can quietly corrupt training data or walk off with model configurations.
- **Adaptability** to changing cloud environments, for instance logging every access through an API gateway and keeping the logs for compliance.

Most teams build on vendor APIs (he names OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face), so API security gets its own list: OAuth2 or OpenID for identity, fine-grained authorisation, privileged access management or just-in-time access that expires on its own, rate limiting and a CDN such as Cloudflare or AWS against denial of service, TLS in transit, and gateways adding IP allow-listing and forensic logging.

## Computing on data you can't see

Two techniques carry the privacy-heavy cases. Homomorphic encryption lets a model compute on ciphertext, with results that decrypt to what the plaintext computation would have produced, so a model can train on an encrypted dataset, or on data pooled from several sources, without anyone touching the raw records. Trusted execution environments isolate sensitive processing inside the processor, out of reach of the main operating system and even of administrators. His everyday example is the phone, where sensitive assistant and messaging data is processed in such an enclave.

For deployment he adds digital signatures to prove a model has not been altered, secure key management and version control, real-time anomaly detection on model behaviour, and automated response with feedback loops. In operations: vulnerability scanning of models and data pipelines in CI/CD, behavioural analytics and code analysis, and security assessments run continuously so bugs are fixed before a model ships.

## The healthcare case study

It all comes together in a HIPAA-bound healthcare company training a diagnostic model on anonymised patient images: homomorphic encryption so the model processes encrypted images directly, a signature check of the model before each use, and a TEE so the confidential data exists only inside the computation. His forward look covers post-quantum cryptography from standards bodies such as NIST and GenAI-driven predictive security models.

The conclusion is the one security teams always want heard: build it in at the start of the product lifecycle, as part of "a proactive approach where security is not an afterthought, but a foundational component of all AI initiatives," Akshay Sekar Chandrasekaran said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers being asked to host or share internal models, who want a structured checklist to compare their setup against. It is a survey of controls, without a demo or tool walkthrough.

Title: Kubernetes DR is easy until ExternalDNS and cert-manager meet a second cluster
Description: Lev Andelman (TeraSky) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on why self-service DNS and certificates make Kubernetes disaster recovery tricky
Body:
Search for Kubernetes disaster recovery and the recipe looks like a lullaby: two clusters in two regions, a DNS record in front, copy some data across. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Lev Andelman, CTO of the solution integrator TeraSky, shows where that recipe breaks: the moment developers get self-service DNS and certificates through ExternalDNS and cert-manager, the second cluster starts fighting the first one.

His verdict from years of DR work with startups and large enterprises: "nothing is simple in doing a DR for Kubernetes and it's actually pretty tricky," Lev Andelman said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

## Why did DR get harder?

Because Kubernetes moved infrastructure into developers' hands. In the old world one infrastructure person created servers, disks and load balancers, configured DNS and issued certificates, and that same person knew exactly what a failover required. Now a developer gets a load balancer from an Ingress, a disk from a PV and PVC, and a certificate from an annotation. Convenient, and nobody holds the whole failover picture any more.

His stage for the talk: two AWS regions, one EKS cluster in each. He deliberately skips the RTO and RPO philosophy; you decide what those mean for you.

## The easy cases really are easy

A stateless deployment with no inbound traffic: apply the same YAML to both regions, run it active-active or deploy on demand. Add inbound traffic with manual DNS and it is still fine: a service, an Ingress, and a CNAME or weighted DNS record you flip in an emergency.

Persistent volumes are the part every search result covers. Velero backs a cluster up to object storage and restores it into another. Portworx runs continuously, shipping data through object storage to a second cluster that keeps restoring it, and gives you commands to fail the workload over. The data, in other words, is a solved problem with tooling. That is not where his customers get hurt.

## Problem one: ExternalDNS fights over the record

With ExternalDNS installed, an Ingress creates its own A record in Route 53, and cert-manager reads the TLS block and fetches a Let's Encrypt certificate into a secret. Great self-service. Andelman's line on it: "Great power comes great responsibility, as we know."

Deploy the same Ingress in both clusters and ExternalDNS in each one claims the same record. His fix is three hostnames:

- a **primary** Ingress in cluster one and a **dr** Ingress in cluster two, each letting ExternalDNS create its own record automatically;
- a **main** hostname, the one customers use, served by an Ingress in each cluster whose ExternalDNS hostname annotation is set to empty, so it never touches Route 53;
- a CNAME for main that you own by hand, pointing at primary or dr, with a very short TTL so a failover moves traffic quickly.

Without the main Ingress, the CNAME would deliver requests with a Host header no Ingress listens for, and nobody answers.

## Problem two: the certificate doesn't match the name

Customers hit main, but cert-manager issued certificates for primary and dr. Andelman's trick: put several hosts in the TLS section of the primary (or dr) Ingress so cert-manager issues one certificate with both names as subject alternative names, then have the main Ingress reuse that same secret instead of requesting its own. The browser sees a certificate that matches, and only one Ingress per cluster talks to Let's Encrypt. The end state: self-service DNS, self-service certificates, and a failover you control with one record.

## What do teams forget?

His closing list is the practical part, in his words a true Pandora box:

- Not everything should be replicated. You cannot copy the same Ingress into both clusters once ExternalDNS and cert-manager are in play, and restored resources often need their labels adjusted.
- Dependencies outside the cluster fail too: the manifest repository holding your YAML and Helm charts, the image registry, monitoring, CI/CD and authentication all have to be reachable from the second site.
- Teams fixate on copying data and ignore connectivity, which is usually what breaks.
- Drill the DR plan and run chaos experiments against it, or you are trusting a diagram.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers running EKS (or any multi-cluster Kubernetes) with ExternalDNS and cert-manager who have a DR requirement on paper. It is short, YAML-level and aimed at intermediate Kubernetes users, as the abstract promises.

Title: VK couldn't rewrite millions of lines of PHP, so it compiled them to C++
Description: Alexandr Kolobov (V Kontakte LLC) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on how VK scaled with custom storage engines, KPHP and heavy caching
Body:
When your PHP codebase is too slow and too big to rewrite, you can stop treating the language as fixed and compile it instead. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Alexandr Kolobov, a team lead at VK (V Kontakte), walks through how one of the world's largest social networks outgrew off-the-shelf tools: around 800 custom storage engine clusters, a PHP-to-C++ compiler called KPHP, caching everywhere, and a microservice that resizes images on the fly.

The lesson he draws is less about VK's specific stack than about the order of operations: find the biggest bottleneck, fix that, repeat.

## When is a system actually high-load?

Kolobov gives the checklist (millions of daily requests and concurrent users, terabytes to petabytes of data, three nines or better, geographic distribution) and then a one-line definition that is more useful than the list. "High Load is it when usual methods for processing requests, storing data, and managing infrastructure are no longer enough, and there is a need to create custom solutions," Alexandr Kolobov said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

His rough thresholds: over 10,000 requests per second, latency around 300 ms, availability above 99.99% and resource utilisation above 50%. VK, by the figures he shows, sits well past them: 100 million monthly users, 100 million posts and 9 billion post views a day, about 20,000 servers, 3 million requests per second at 120 ms latency and 99.94% availability.

## Why off-the-shelf tools stop fitting

His case against external solutions at this scale is specific. They are built for broad market applicability, which costs performance. They are well tested, but when you find a bug you cannot fix it quickly unless you are a committer, and upgrading to the fixed version can break compatibility. They need constant tuning and may not scale the way you need. Meanwhile user expectations have moved: maintenance windows used to be acceptable, five nines now means roughly five minutes of downtime a year, and growth can be explosive enough that scaling has to be linear at any moment.

## 800 tiny databases, each with one job

VK's first big break with convention came in 2009, when relational databases could no longer keep up. The team started writing its own storage engines: microservices with embedded databases written in C and C++, each built around one data structure and one kind of query. Messages, recommendations, photos, hints, lists, logs and news each get their own. By his count there are now about 800 engine clusters, and a task that needs an unusual structure or query gets a new engine.

The engines store data in simple, low-level structures, sometimes close to bare indexes, so reads need minimal processing. Master-slave replication and strict data-level sharding give horizontal scaling. Everything is cached heavily, often pre-computed, with sharded caches behind custom wrappers. At VK's size, he notes, caching stops being a performance trick and becomes the main way to keep load off the backend.

## The compiler that saved a rewrite

The code was the next bottleneck. Millions of lines of PHP were too slow, and rewriting them in another language was out of the question. VK's answer was KPHP, which translates PHP into C++. He reports it as about 10 times faster in production, and 2 to 40 times faster in synthetic tests. It now supports PHP 7 and 8 features and adds strict typing, shared memory, parallelism, coroutines, inlining and NUMA support. Alongside it the team built NoVerify, a PHP linter for large codebases that checks git diffs before push, indexing about a million lines of code per second and analysing about 100,000.

Only after the storage and the code were fixed did VK move parts of the application to microservices in Go and Java over gRPC, mainly for time to market and the freedom to pick a language per service.

## Images: stop storing every size

The last bottleneck was content. Every image had to exist in several sizes for retina and non-retina mobile, web and other interfaces, and the pre-resized copies ate storage. VK dropped them and built ImageProcessor, a microservice that generates sizes on the fly, and moved delivery from JPEG to WebP. The results he quotes: photos 40% smaller and delivery 15% faster, a 50 to 100 ms improvement.

He closes by pointing out that the big players converge on the same moves: Netflix with EVCache and its own storage, Yandex with ClickHouse, LinkedIn with Espresso and Kafka, Twitter with Manhattan. And with a caveat: "there are no fixed rules for creating high load applications. It's always an experimental process."

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers whose systems are starting to outgrow their database or their language runtime, and anyone curious how a PHP shop reached millions of requests per second without a rewrite. It is a tour of decisions rather than a code walkthrough.

Title: Developers are the root cause, so build tools for the scary changes
Description: Elliott Clark (Batteries Included) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on turning incidents into platform tools and UI that keeps developers safe
Body:
The hardware will add one plus one more or less forever; it is the humans changing the software who cause the outages. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Elliott Clark, founder and CEO of Batteries Included, argues that when a change type keeps biting you, the platform answer is a tool that makes that change hard to get wrong, not one more unit test.

Clark has spent his career building systems for other engineers: C# tools and WPF at Microsoft, Apache HBase as an open source committer at Cloudera, then ads, developer efficiency and distributed data stores at Facebook. The talk distils what that taught him about where platforms let failures through.

## Who causes the incidents?

Platform goals pull against each other. You want software that stays maintainable, a short path from idea to production, reliability, and fast recovery when things break, and every metric or check you add to protect reliability feels like it slows the idea-to-production clock. Clark suggests settling the argument by looking at what actually goes wrong. "Developers are the root cause," Elliott Clark said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. We are the ones who change the software.

He sorts what slips through into two buckets. Not understanding: you never fully grasped the business problem, the distributed system or the edge cases, or that an easier path existed ten choices ago. Not testing: no integration test, no proof that backups restore, no recent failover drill. The two feed each other, but he warns against reaching for "one more test" by reflex. If you are holding the tool upside down, unit tests written after the fact will not help.

## Anatomy of a green-checkmark outage

His worked example will feel familiar to anyone who has read a postmortem. A product team needs to write new data to an existing database. A junior-to-mid DevOps engineer helpfully adds a user to the database permissions and, thinking ahead, bumps production storage too, with the wrong units: a few trillion gigabytes instead of a few million bytes. Every test environment passes, because only production has that size setting. A reviewer sees green checks and approves. The deploy either jams the pipeline for everyone until someone reverts, or takes pods down.

Clark lists what went wrong, and almost none of it is the engineer's fault:

- Two unrelated changes rode in one PR, because paying the test-and-deploy toll once is easier than twice.
- The schema's units were not obvious: when one is needed, which one, when it applies.
- CI tested production-like environments, not production.
- Green checks were trusted over reading the diff, and reviewers were not YAML or platform experts, nor should they be.
- After the failure, nobody could tell which change to roll back.

## Build the tool, not the test

His fix: both changes were hard and scary, so make them neither. Build a UI that loads the YAML, knows the schema, validates the input and tests size changes in the right environment, and that class of incident cannot recur. Repeat for each scary change and you accumulate a set of tools shaped by real failures.

Not everything deserves a guardrail, and his mental model for where to draw the line is rock climbing. Bouldering a metre or three over a padded floor needs no harness; it would only slow you down. On a mountain face, which is to say in production, you want the harness even though every move gets more controlled.

## Four UI patterns that make platforms safer

He closes with patterns he has seen work:

1. **No modals where accuracy matters.** "When you see a pop up, your initial reaction is to try and make it go away." An "are you sure you want to delete this database?" dialog trains people to click through it. Use a full page and make them read and scroll.
2. **Move validation earlier.** A linter at edit time gets heeded; an error after the commit hook gets skipped, and skipped errors become tech debt.
3. **Show who changed what, when.** A combined change history speeds up debugging and teaches new developers how the platform behaves.
4. **Expose enough of the inner workings** that users trust the abstraction and never need to break through it.

## Who should watch

Platform teams deciding what to build next. Clark's habit of mining incidents for tool ideas is a ready-made backlog method. The talk ends with a short note that Batteries Included, a source-available infrastructure platform on Kubernetes, was about to come out of stealth; the rest is product-neutral. The abstract's promise of deployment pipelines and orchestration frameworks is covered mostly through this one incident story rather than a tour of tools.

Title: Microservices won't buy your nines alone; availability is a six-layer cake
Description: Ilya Kaznacheev (Capgemini) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on why high availability spans application, platform, data, infra and hardware
Body:
The popular recipe for high availability has three steps: migrate to microservices, question marks, profit. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Ilya Kaznacheev, Lead Cloud and Applications Architect at Capgemini and a former Google Developer Expert on Cloud, fills in the question marks: availability is a stack of layers, from application code down to the cable under the street, and your nines depend on every one of them cooperating.

He earned the view the hard way. One of his recent projects was building a public cloud provider from scratch, with Kubernetes as a service at its core, which put him on the side of the layers most application teams never get to see.

## Why aren't microservices enough?

Because the application is only the top layer. Kaznacheev compares microservices to sagas: fine in theory, often poor in practice, because the real world is more complicated than the books. Splitting a spaghetti monolith into "separated spaghetti balls" does limit the blast radius when one part fails. But an elegant service mesh on a platform that falls over still falls over.

At the application layer his checklist is the familiar one, said plainly:

- **Avoid single points of failure** and keep modules independent.
- **Redundancy**: run more replicas, scale them up for Black Friday and down for the summer lull so the AWS bill shrinks with traffic.
- **Load balancing**, from round robin to CPU-aware routing, plus dynamic scaling.
- **Reduce dependencies**: talk over APIs, never a shared database; be careful with shared libraries and magic variables; keep one domain's features in one service, or you build a distributed monolith.
- **Go asynchronous** where chains of synchronous calls would cascade, using message-based or fire-and-forget event-based communication.

On redundancy he is refreshingly blunt. "This is our main tool, achieving higher availability and higher reliability. It's that simple. Humanity still not invented something better," Ilya Kaznacheev said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

## What do the lower layers give you for free?

The middle of the talk walks down the stack, and the point of each stop is the same: know the features the layer under you already offers, so you can lean on them instead of reinventing them.

**Platform.** Clustered systems such as Kubernetes, Kafka and Hadoop redistribute load when a node dies. Every Kubernetes worker node acts as a gateway into the cluster network, so losing node one doesn't lose the route to your pod on node two. Orchestration adds lifecycle control, autoscaling on CPU, requests or consumed messages, anti-affinity to keep replicas off the same node, and self-healing through health checks.

**Data.** Database replicas, broker replicas, backups for the day the data centre burns, and four kinds of caching: in-application, in-database, standalone (a Redis instance) and CDN. His CDN example will be familiar to anyone who has launched on social media: a thousand people hit your index page at once, and cached copies are what keep it up.

**Infrastructure.** Hot migration moves a VM with its memory and state to another host when the first one fails, which is great, and surprising if you didn't know it happens. Instance groups, software-defined networks, redundant software load balancers, replicated block storage and network-attached disks, which is how Kubernetes can remount a volume on another node after a failure.

**Hardware.** RAID, servers spread across racks, and more than one internet provider per data centre. Kafka's rack awareness is his example of layers working together: tell Kafka which brokers sit in which rack and it keeps replicas of a partition off the same rack. And on the network uplink: "A single physical cable is a single point of failure, that can be an angry excavator or something like that." It happens, he notes, again and again.

## The icing is global availability

On top of the cake sit the options for when a whole site goes away: a standby disaster-recovery data centre with constantly replicated data (plus a lot of rehearsal), cloud regions with three or more zones so a Kubernetes cluster spread across them loses only capacity, and global server load balancing over BGP anycast for businesses that cannot afford a city or country outage. A user in Japan lands on the nearest regional installation, a user in Mexico on another, and the same mechanism spreads heavy load across regions. YouTube is his example of an application built this way.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers and architects who own an availability target and want a checklist that goes below the application layer. It is a survey that stays broad rather than going deep on any single layer, and the three-line summary is the takeaway: availability is made of many levels, each level must cooperate with the others, and you design for all of them.
