Title: Your analytics are clean, and stuck upstream of everything that needs them
Description: Hubert Dulay (StarTree) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on the streaming plane, the layer that bridges operational and analytical data
Body:
Your data warehouse holds the cleanest, best-governed copy of your data, and your applications can barely touch it. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Hubert Dulay, Developer Advocate at StarTree and author of the O'Reilly books Streaming Data Mesh and Streaming Databases, argues for a third data plane, the streaming plane, that sits between operational and analytical systems and serves real-time data products to both.

It is a conceptual talk: a vocabulary and an architecture, not a demo. If you build data platforms, the vocabulary is worth having.

## What is the data divide?

Dulay starts with the two planes everyone already runs. The operational plane is microservices on row-based OLTP databases, built for inserts, updates, deletes and single-row lookups. The analytical plane is data lakes, warehouses and lakehouses on columnar OLAP stores, built for aggregations and joins. Data flows left to right through ETL or ELT, getting cleansed, enriched and obfuscated on the way.

The insights are supposed to flow back to the applications, to make revenue or stop losing it. That return trip is the problem. "Moving data from analytical to operational is hard. It's an upstream path," Hubert Dulay said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Columnar stores and Parquet files are great for scanning a few columns over billions of rows and miserable at handing back complete records. In his words, "OLAPs don't like to return all rows and columns." Reverse ETL and data activation tools exist precisely to paddle against that current.

## Data gravity is why the warehouse keeps getting heavier

His second concept borrows from astronomy. Accumulated data behaves like a planet: its mass pulls in services and applications the way a planet pulls in moons. In a classic architecture every operational system feeds the one analytical planet, which grows heavier with history and slower to answer. The streaming plane works like a ring of satellites, processing data closer to its source so not everything has to fall into the warehouse before anyone can use it.

## What actually lives in the streaming plane?

Five kinds of system, by his inventory:

- **Connectors** moving data between sources and sinks.
- **Streaming platforms** such as Kafka, Redpanda and Pulsar, the backbone that distributes and routes streams.
- **Stream processing frameworks** transforming data in motion.
- **Streaming databases** storing and serving streams.
- **Real-time OLAP stores** answering analytical queries on fresh data with low latency and high concurrency, the category StarTree's Apache Pinot plays in.

Serving comes in two flavours. Synchronous: a client queries a streaming database or real-time OLAP store and waits for the answer. Asynchronous: a client subscribes to a Kafka topic and reacts to changes as they arrive, so no update is missed.

## Materialized views are the dial between latency and flexibility

The most useful idea in the talk is how push and pull queries share the work. In batch databases a materialized view is a cached query result refreshed on a schedule. In stream processing it is updated continuously and incrementally as events arrive. A push query does the heavy lifting of building the view; clients then either subscribe to its changes or run pull queries against it.

Dulay draws this as a spectrum. Lean on push queries and pre-computed views and you get low latency but rigid queries, the right trade for user-facing features that need instant updates. Lean on pull queries and you get ad hoc flexibility at the cost of latency, because the serving engine does more work per request. The materialized view sits in the middle, and where you put the dial is a product decision, not a database one.

## Replicate globally, consume locally

The last piece is geography. If the operational data lives in EMEA and the consumers sit in APAC, you do not want APAC services reaching across the planet for every read. Replicate the Kafka topics between regions instead, and local applications consume a stream that is still a stream, bounded only by the speed of light. Combine that with a streaming data catalog (table definitions, validation rules, data types, lineage) and you get virtual data products: discoverable, subscribable, served locally even when the source is remote. His summary also makes a bet worth noting: SQL as the universal language of the streaming plane.

## Who should watch

Platform and data engineers who own both a Kafka cluster and a warehouse and keep building one-off pipes between them. Dulay's framing gives you words for a design review. Skip it if you want benchmarks or code; there are none.

Title: A developer roadmap starts with sticky notes and a severity vote
Description: Ruby Kaur (Best Egg) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on building a developer roadmap from engineers' pain points, from journey map to backlog
Body:
Plenty of platform roadmaps are a list of tools someone wanted to try. Ruby Kaur, Senior Director Product Manager at Best Egg, walked through the opposite approach at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024: start from a business problem, map the engineers' journey, collect their pain points, vote on severity, plot impact against effort, and only then write epics, a now-next-later roadmap and finally backlog stories. Her case study asks one question: how might we deliver an email communication in under an hour?

It is a product-management framework talk with a made-up case study, short and methodical, with no tooling beyond a Miro board.

## Why tie the roadmap to the company strategy?

A roadmap, in her framing, is a communication tool as much as a plan: it aligns stakeholders and developers on what is being built and why. Her example: if the company aims to grow revenue 20% in a year, the product strategy should favour work that drives cross-sell, upsell (showing customers premium plans) and renewals. That way every feature can be traced to a business goal, and the engineering work gets recognised as a contribution to it.

## The case study: emails that take too long

The fictional company is marketing-led, and email is a big revenue driver, but getting a campaign from a marketer's idea to customers' inboxes takes too long, so the content is stale on arrival. Faster email means faster revenue and more monthly active users.

The current-state assessment interviews the personas in the workflow (marketers, engineers, customer support) using the Jobs to be Done framework: what each is trying to achieve, what blocks them, what outcome they want. The team then picks engineers as the focus, because they build and deploy the systems that send the emails. The vision follows: the engineering team delivers email communications in under an hour. Candidate success criteria include cutting delivery time from days or weeks to under an hour, engineering productivity, system reliability and stakeholder satisfaction.

## Map the journey, then vote

Engineers list pain points on stickies across five stages of their journey:

- **Requirements:** unclear requirements, shifting priorities, misaligned stakeholders.
- **Development:** poor tooling, tech debt, integration issues.
- **UAT:** too few test environments, bad test data, slow feedback.
- **Deployment:** complex processes, manual steps, configuration errors.
- **Monitoring:** weak tools, no real-time alerts, missing metrics.

Each sticky gets a high, medium or low severity vote against the goal, always tied back to the one-hour target. Unclear requirements, for example, rate high because they hurt several stages.

## Quick wins, major wins and money pits

The team then estimates effort and plots pain points on an impact-effort grid: major wins (high impact, high effort), quick wins (high impact, low effort), fill-ins (low, low) and money pits (low impact, high effort). "You'd be surprised at how many organizations have money pit items in their backlog and end the year with very low value delivered," Ruby Kaur said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

## From discovery to backlog

Product discovery stays high level: brainstorm with engineering, product and business analysts; group ideas into epics (lack of a dev test environment becomes an epic to establish one, with fewer post-deployment bugs as its acceptance criterion); prioritise by impact and feasibility; lay them out as a roadmap. She recommends now, next and later as the first format, until estimates firm up. Then the PM and engineers scope an MVP, write product requirement documents, and turn them into backlog user stories.

## Who should watch

Platform product managers and engineering leads who need a repeatable way to turn developer complaints into a defensible plan. If you already run journey mapping and impact-effort sessions, you'll recognise the steps.

Title: Golden path templates that hand developers a VM or an AI app
Description: Cedric Clyburn and Valentina Rodriguez Sosa (Red Hat) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on platform as a product, Backstage and golden paths
Body:
Building an app used to mean opening an editor. Now it means Podman or Docker, a registry, somewhere to run containers, CI/CD, and a lot of YAML. Cedric Clyburn, Senior Developer Advocate at Red Hat, and Valentina Rodriguez Sosa, Principal Technical Marketing Manager at Red Hat, used their Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 talk to show the platform-as-a-product answer: an internal developer portal built on Backstage whose golden path templates provision a virtual machine or scaffold an AI app with the organisation's practices baked in.

It is a Red Hat talk, and the demos run on Red Hat Developer Hub and OpenShift; the principles and the Backstage parts apply to any portal.

## Where does the developer's time go?

The opening is a two-hander. Cedric lists the stack he has to learn before shipping an internal tool; Valentina adds Tekton pipelines, Argo CD, Helm charts, Grafana, Istio and Kafka. "I'm starting to feel a little bit overwhelmed," Cedric Clyburn said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, and the CNCF project map makes the point for him.

The numbers on the slides come from a Salesforce productivity survey: more than three-quarters (76%) of organisations say cognitive load is high enough to hurt productivity, and 39% point to rising workload and demands from other teams. The traditional model doesn't help: requirements up front, requests by ticket, problems fixed after the fact. Valentina has seen worse: "a customer had sometimes months waiting just to have access to a cluster".

## Platform as a product, defined

They borrow Evan Bottcher's 2018 definition: a digital platform is a foundation of self-service APIs, tools, services, knowledge and support, arranged as a compelling internal product. The product operating model swaps tickets for on-demand automation and fixed requirements for continuous review of user needs. The slides quote Gartner naming platform engineering a top 10 strategic technology trend for 2024, and an IDC prediction that by 2027 70% of enterprises will adopt a composable, internal-facing app platform.

The iceberg slide is the useful mental model: under the portal sit identity and RBAC, compute, network and storage, source control, artifact and image builders, CI, artifact storage, observability, CD, security scanning, and services such as DBaaS or Kafka-as-a-Service. The portal's job is to hide that weight. The pillars of the internal platform: onboarding, code time (a fast inner loop), build time (consistent promotion) and run time (monitoring and logging).

## What Backstage brings

Backstage, created at Spotify and now a CNCF project, has five parts: the software catalog (ownership and metadata for services, sites, libraries, pipelines), plugins (190-plus from the community), software templates (the golden paths), TechDocs, and search.

Valentina's demo walks Red Hat Developer Hub: a customisable home page, the catalog with tags and filters, RBAC so teams only see their own components, API contracts, learning paths and a tech radar. Then a template provisions a medium RHEL virtual machine through OpenShift Virtualization; as the developer she can only pick its name, while the platform team fixes storage, size, cluster and namespace. The VM then shows up with its topology and a VNC console.

Cedric's demo scaffolds a Python Flask app that calls a model served on the cluster with KServe, with source repo, GitOps manifests and pipelines generated from a template.yaml. The app produces photos of Teddy on the beach, which is as good a smoke test as any.

## Security, shifted left

The security slide is a shopping list of open source: Keycloak for SSO, Sigstore for signing, KubeLinter for Kubernetes YAML, Tekton Chains and Konflux, Project Quay and Clair for image scanning, Argo CD for drift, Open Policy Agent, Falco at runtime, StackRox, and GUAC for security metadata. Their best practices: shift security left, find your personas and champions, start small with TechDocs and evolve into templates, and keep one portal.

## Who should watch

Teams about to stand up Backstage or evaluating Red Hat Developer Hub, and anyone who needs a clear pitch for platform as a product. The principles section is short; most of the value is in seeing templates work end to end.

Title: Build the thinnest viable platform, and measure it by the team
Description: Cansu Kavili Ornek (Red Hat) and Val Yonchev (Team Topologies) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on Team Topologies principles for platforms
Body:
A Kubernetes cluster is not a platform, and a department with platform in its name is not a platform team. Cansu Kavili Ornek, Associate Principal Specialist Solution Architect at Red Hat, and Val Yonchev, Head of Customer Success at Team Topologies, spent their Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 talk on eight principles from Team Topologies that separate platforms people use from platforms people route around. The short version: a platform exists to speed up flow, cut cognitive load and give teams autonomy, and if it doesn't, decommission it.

The two have built platforms together for about seven years across very different domains, and the talk is full of field stories rather than theory. It assumes you have at least skimmed the book.

## What is a platform for?

Three jobs, all at once: accelerate the flow of value, reduce cognitive load across the whole socio-technical system, and enable substantial autonomy for the teams consuming it. A platform team, in Team Topologies terms, is a grouping of teams (stream-aligned, complicated-subsystem and others) producing a compelling internal product, not one team and not an org chart box.

## The team is the unit, so say development experience

Val's first principle is about language. Leaders talk about developer productivity and developer experience, and the words push them to measure individuals. The team is the smallest unit of delivery, so measure productivity, experience and platform value per team: development productivity, development experience.

## Should this platform exist at all?

Cansu tells of an organisation whose new platform team, with good intentions, collected common services and became the bottleneck, raising cognitive load instead of cutting it. Money already spent is no argument for continuing; re-evaluate or even start over.

The Team Topologies answer is the thinnest viable platform. Product owners build magnificent castles when developers need a skateboard or a tent, and the minimum can be as small as a wiki page. To decide what goes in, they use event storming from domain-driven design to draw boundaries between platform teams, and Wardley mapping to decide build versus buy. Val's verdict on one client that wrote its own service mesh: "For Christ's sake, why?"

## Treat the platform as a product, for several kinds of customer

A government agency engagement gave them three developer personas: default path users who want the golden path and nothing else, adaptive users who want to tweak parts (say, testing) through configurable services, and innovative users who experiment and should be able to contribute back. One size fits none.

Build for one representative team first. In a Finnish insurance engagement in 2018, a stream-aligned team, an enabling team and platform team members worked in one room; the platform team built only what that application needed to reach production, and new ideas went to the team at the next table for a yes or no. They also argue for making platform services optional where security allows, because internal competition improves products the way Android and iPhone push each other.

## Platforms have layers, and teams need APIs

Platform engineers are developers too, so the infrastructure under the platform should be just as easy to consume. Between teams, a team API (published as a template on the Team Topologies GitHub) says what a team offers and plans, so consumers don't need a meeting. And since no platform is ever intuitive enough, time-boxed enabling teams help consumers adopt it and feed what they learn back.

"Team topology is a verb," Val Yonchev said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Like sourdough, it is continuous practice, never a big bang, and not always great results.

Their closing definition: platform engineering is a culture of building platform services that are easy to consume, reduce cognitive load, keep evolving, and are economically viable.

## Who should watch

Platform leads who were handed a mandate and a headcount, and managers deciding how to measure a platform team. Pair it with the book.

Title: Containers on AWS, picked by where the responsibility line sits
Description: Chakkree Tipsupa (AWS) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on choosing between App Runner, ECS, EKS, Fargate and EC2 by shared responsibility
Body:
AWS has a lot of ways to run a container, and Chakkree Tipsupa, Solutions Architect at AWS, admits as much: his slides count 34. His way through them at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 is the shared responsibility model: each service from ECS to App Runner moved the line between what AWS runs and what you run a bit higher. His rule of thumb comes at the end: start with the most managed option and only drop down a layer when you have a reason.

This is an AWS speaker explaining AWS services, with a live App Runner demo; it is an orientation talk for teams new to containers on AWS, not an in-depth look at any one service.

## Three layers: registry, orchestrator, compute

He sorts the options into layers. Amazon ECR holds images, with scan-on-push or scheduled scans and version tracking. The orchestrator is Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS or AWS App Runner (third-party options such as Red Hat's exist, but are out of scope). Compute is AWS Fargate, the serverless option, or EC2 instances.

The opening statistic is AWS's own: nearly 80% of all cloud containers run on AWS.

## How the responsibility line moved, 2013 to 2021

The history section is the clearest part of the talk:

- **2013:** customers installed Docker on EC2 and ran their own Kubernetes or Mesos control planes on more EC2. Running instances to manage your instances "just felt so wrong," as he puts it.
- **2015, ECS:** AWS takes the orchestrator. You still own load balancers, auto scaling, CI/CD for both images and application, and patching of the OS, runtime and agent.
- **2017, Fargate:** no instances to launch or patch. Load balancing, scaling and pipelines are still yours.
- **2018, EKS:** a managed Kubernetes control plane, on EC2 or Fargate, for customers already running self-managed Kubernetes.
- **2021, App Runner:** AWS takes the load balancer, auto scaling and CI/CD too. You bring source code from GitHub or an image in ECR.

## What does App Runner look like in practice?

The demo pushes a tagged Docker image of a small hotel room management app to a private ECR repository, then creates an App Runner service from it: an IAM role so App Runner can pull the image, CPU and memory size, the port, auto scaling from one instance up to 25, public or private endpoint, and outbound networking to an RDS database in another VPC. Creation takes 7 to 10 minutes in his case, and the result is a URL. No instances, no Fargate tasks in sight. He adds room four on the fourth floor through the web UI and it lands in the database.

## How do you choose?

His comparison has three axes. Operational complexity and flexibility rise together: low for App Runner, medium for ECS, high for EKS, which can run anything in the CNCF ecosystem. Scaling is automatic on request count for App Runner, while ECS and EKS scale on CPU, memory, load balancer request count or custom metrics. Cost optimisation is limited for App Runner, since AWS runs it on ECS with Fargate under the hood, but high for ECS and EKS with Reserved Instances, Savings Plans and Graviton.

Portability is the tiebreaker: ECS is proprietary, so workloads that must move between clouds or on-prem lean to EKS. Otherwise, "always start your experiment with the highest abstraction first," Chakkree Tipsupa said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Need control over scaling? Move to ECS. Need the CNCF toolbox? EKS.

## Who should watch

Developers and small platform teams deploying their first containers on AWS, and anyone who has to explain to a manager why Kubernetes is not the only answer. Experienced EKS operators will know all of it.

Title: Trust is a line item, and losing ten engineers costs $3.5 million
Description: Leslie Martinich (Competitive Focus) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on trust, ethics and engaged leadership as the fix for disengaged teams
Body:
Leslie Martinich opens her Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 talk with a confession: "I hate waste." Wasted work, cancelled projects, wasted careers. The Founder and President of Competitive Focus, who has led product teams in software, argues that the fix is leadership built on trust rather than control, and she puts a price on getting it wrong: replacing ten engineers can cost $3.5 million a year.

It is a leadership talk with no technology in it, built around one hard case study (Challenger) and a handful of sentences you can use in your next one-to-one.

## Why are teams disengaged?

Her slides cite the numbers: 65% of employees are not engaged, 20% are actively disengaged, and only 20% are actively engaged. For remote workplaces the number one challenge is trust, which she credits with boosting productivity by up to 50%, retention by up to 65%, and speed of decision making by up to 35%.

Trust also has economics: when it goes up, speed goes up and cost goes down. Her examples are the airport security lines after 11 September 2001, the cost of low trust at planetary scale, and Warren Buffett buying McLane Distribution from Walmart after a two-hour meeting, with the deal closing in a month.

The problem, she says, is that people want choices while leaders want control, and most leadership training is about management of something (meetings, performance, projects, risk). All useful, all about control.

## Three questions for ethical decisions

Trust requires ethical behaviour, and she compresses a history of ethics into three questions worth writing down:

- **Can I sleep at night?** Aristotle, virtue and character.
- **What if everybody did this?** Kant's categorical imperative.
- **What is the greatest good for the greatest number?** Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism.

She applies them to the Challenger launch in 1986: the coldest launch ever, a previous low of 53°F, a forecast of 28°F. Morton Thiokol engineers recommended against launching because the O-rings hadn't been tested that cold; after a recess, Morton Thiokol called the evidence inconclusive and the launch went ahead.

## Say the risk in the other person's terms

Her lesson from Challenger is about communication, and she says it is everyone's job, because the individual contributor usually sees the risk first. Don't be Chicken Little about every risk, and don't be the person who says I told you so afterwards. Know what your audience cares about and frame the warning in their terms; her rewrite for the night before the launch starts with wanting the launch to go smoothly and ends with waiting for warmer weather.

## What does an engaged leader actually do?

Be present (devices away, no glancing down the hall for someone more important). Be respectful: instead of "you worry too much," she suggests "I see that's a concern to you. Tell me more about that." Listen to ideas you think are wacko and ask how they could fit the schedule. And enlist the team in architecture, breakdown and estimates instead of handing out chunks; her example is an engineer who asked for five days, was given eight, and now owns the work.

The retention arithmetic: ten people at $175,000 in salary and benefits, times two to replace each one, is $3.5 million a year. Halve the attrition and you save $1.75 million, before counting easier recruiting from a team that tells friends it likes its boss.

## Who should watch

New engineering managers and tech leads, and senior ICs who need to raise a risk without being ignored. Engineers looking for a technical talk should pick another session from the event.

Title: Hybrid DNS on AWS without running your own DNS servers
Description: Atif Siddiqui (Silicon Valley Bank) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on multi-account hybrid DNS with Route 53 Resolver endpoints and RAM
Body:
"Nobody cares about DNS until it stops working," reads the abstract of Atif Siddiqui's Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 talk, and the job of a platform engineer is to keep it that way. Atif, Senior Principal Software Engineer at Silicon Valley Bank, walks through a multi-account hybrid DNS design on AWS: Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints in a shared network account, forwarding rules shared to spoke accounts through Resource Access Manager, and two security services that belong next to it.

It is a dense 20 minutes for people who already know VPCs; expect a reference design rather than a demo.

## What did hybrid DNS look like before Resolver?

Before Route 53 Resolver arrived in November 2018, you either bought a marketplace product or ran DNS servers on EC2 to forward corporate domains on-prem, and owned their resiliency and scaling yourself. Atif calls it a classic case of a customer doing unappreciated heavy lifting.

The building block was always there: every VPC reserves the .2 address of its primary CIDR (10.0.0.2 for 10.0.0.0/23) as the resolver, which is why it is still called the +2 resolver. Resolver endpoints extend it across the hybrid boundary.

## Inbound, outbound, and which way is which

The direction is from AWS's point of view:

- **Inbound endpoints** take queries from the on-prem network and resolve VPC resources and private hosted zone records. On-prem DNS must send recursive queries to them, not iterative ones.
- **Outbound endpoints** send queries from AWS to on-prem DNS, through forwarding rules that point at the on-prem servers (10.50.50.50 in his example) for the corporate domain.

Endpoints are ENIs, so provision them in every Availability Zone the VPC spans and give them security groups: inbound rules open on port 53 TCP and UDP for the inbound endpoint (from the on-prem range, a 10.0.0.0/8 in his example), outbound rules on 53 for the outbound one. Resolver is regional and a VPC resource, so it lives in a shared services account such as Core Network.

## How do spoke accounts share it?

Two pieces make it multi-account. Resource Access Manager shares the resolver rules with spoke VPCs across the AWS Organization. And every spoke account's private hosted zones are associated with the Core Network VPC where the endpoints live, so an on-prem lookup arriving at the inbound endpoint can resolve an EC2 record in any spoke.

He stresses what DNS doesn't do: it resolves names but VPCs stay isolated. Packets still need Transit Gateway between VPCs and a VPN or Direct Connect to on-prem.

## Two security tools to switch on

GuardDuty, which Atif clearly likes as a model of how security products should ship: one click to enable, and it analyzes VPC flow logs, CloudTrail and DNS logs for threats such as data exfiltration over DNS. And Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, announced in early 2021, which filters outbound DNS from VPCs against AWS managed or custom domain lists with allow, block and alert actions, optionally per record type. The slides recommend AWS Firewall Manager to roll it out across the organization.

## Route 53 Profiles

The newest piece, released in April 2024, bundles private hosted zone associations, forwarding rules and DNS Firewall rule groups into a profile you share through RAM. He says plainly that he hasn't tried it yet, but expects it to make the design simpler. "There is no escaping DNS and everyone just expects it to work," Atif Siddiqui said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

## Who should watch

Cloud network and platform engineers setting up a landing zone with an on-prem data centre still attached. Skip it if your estate is single-account and cloud-only.

Title: Privacy is a policy layer your infrastructure has to carry
Description: Natalia Grybovska (Meta) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on building infrastructure that knows which data is sensitive and enforces privacy policy
Body:
Ask an engineer what privacy work looks like and you'll hear end-to-end encryption and Signal. Natalia Grybovska, Software Engineer at Meta with three years in big-tech privacy, used her Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 talk to correct that: most privacy engineering is making infrastructure know which data is sensitive, which policies apply to it, and where it travels. Her closing advice is a roadmap by company size, from context propagation at a startup to data lineage and automated breach detection at big tech.

It is a high-level map of the domain rather than a build guide, and a very clear one.

## Why is privacy bigger than security?

"privacy is so much more than security," Natalia Grybovska said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Encryption is one part. The rest comes from regulation, and GDPR is her reference point: most newer data protection laws borrow from it, so being GDPR compliant gets you most of the way, with exceptions such as the US Federal Trade Commission.

She runs through the principles quickly: data protection, transparency (those privacy notices everyone clicks past are a legal requirement), user control including the right to be forgotten, deletion, data minimisation, purpose limitation (emails collected for registration can't be reused for marketing without consent), retention, and accountability, meaning you can prove compliance when asked.

## Policies, data and code

Her model has three parts that have to meet:

- **Regulations and commitments become policies.** A commitment is something a company promises without being required to, and is then held to; her example is WhatsApp and end-to-end encryption. Each policy has a scope, enforcement logic and a way to attach to data. Two examples: email can't be used for marketing without consent in the EU; bank statements can't be kept longer than seven years in the US.
- **Data understanding.** Categorise and register sensitive data centrally, then annotate it wherever it lives: APIs, DTOs, database and data sink schemas. The advanced step is data lineage, a graph of where an email address enters, what it passes through and where it ends up. You can buy lineage or build it from production sampling, dynamic analysis, instrumentation, probing and static analysis.
- **Infrastructure and code.** Code associates sensitive data with its policies, propagates that policy context along the call tree, and enforces the policy where the data lands.

Lineage pays for itself twice: it powers continuous checks that data isn't ending up or lingering where it shouldn't, and it generates evidence for regulators.

## Which practices prevent incidents?

Access control and encryption you probably have. Add anonymisation before data reaches third parties or analytics (swap user IDs for replacement IDs, keep the mapping on a separate security layer) and data coarsening, such as approximate rather than precise location. On the organisational side: documented privacy policies, employee training, privacy reviews on feature launches, risk assessments and audits. Staying compliant is harder than launching compliant, which is where automated breach detection comes in: scheduled verification jobs that raise an incident, whether an email or a filed task, when data drifts out of policy.

## What should you build at your size?

- **Startup:** context propagation and distributed tracing (useful for debugging anyway), a basic consent implementation, encryption and access control.
- **Growing company:** established privacy policies, training, data categorisation and annotation, policy propagation and the first enforcement logic.
- **Big tech:** data lineage, continuous compliance with automated breach detection and evidence generation, regular risk assessments and audits, because regulators are more likely to knock.

The talk has one unscripted moment near the end, "sorry, this is my cat making noise," and the cat does not derail the roadmap.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who keep getting privacy tickets without the context behind them, and startup tech leads deciding what to put in place now so a later GDPR audit isn't a rewrite.

Title: Move the buttons for 99% of users before you build your own LLM
Description: Roman Shmyhelskyi (Hitachi Vantara) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on why engineers need business acumen and five ways to build it
Body:
Two tickets in your backlog: build your own LLM for 1% of users, or move some buttons for the 99% who use that screen daily. You can only do one. Roman Shmyhelskyi, Software Engineering Manager at Hitachi Vantara, opened his Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 talk with that choice, and spent the rest of it explaining why the boring ticket is usually right and how engineers learn to see it.

This is a career talk, not a technical one. It is aimed at strong individual contributors who watch less brilliant colleagues get promoted.

## Why aren't hard skills enough?

"But today, hard skills are not enough," Roman Shmyhelskyi said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. He describes an engineer he worked with who could out-argue anyone on React versus Angular or JavaScript internals, whose code he reviewed just to learn from it, and whom promotion kept passing by. Not an isolated case, he says, and the job market makes it worse: every posting attracts hundreds of applicants.

His slide puts the reason in type-system terms: hard skills are like booleans, soft skills are like floats. To a non-technical manager you either can deliver a feature or you can't. Communication, collaboration and critical thinking sit on a spectrum that anyone in the room can see and rank.

## What is business acumen, practically?

His definition: several soft skills (problem solving, communication, critical thinking, leadership or proactivity) applied to the right context. Treat each feature like a small business.

He is blunt about the context. Business is about earning money, even non-profits need income, and that is why we're employed. "That's a sad capitalist reality." In a software company that means more clients, which means understanding their needs quickly, solving their problems quickly, and iterating quickly.

This doesn't make you a product owner. Business analysts and PMs know what needs doing; you know the cost of doing it. His example: a PM says a change is small because a similar one shipped on another project, and you know it needs architectural work. That gap is where an engineer with business sense proposes a better route.

## Five habits that build it

1. **Learn your company's industry**: its vocabulary and its regulations, through articles or courses.
2. **Learn where the money comes from**: who the customers are (consumers, businesses, government) and the revenue model. Sales and leadership are usually happy to explain.
3. **Listen proactively** at town halls: take notes, ask follow-ups, instead of leaving them on in the background.
4. **Ask why** for every feature. It feels awkward at first, then becomes instinct, and sometimes reveals that a small change to an existing project solves the problem. As a self-described lazy engineer he finds that the most satisfying outcome.
5. **Find a mentor outside engineering**, or outside the company.

## Who wants what

His shortcuts list what each context needs: startups want speed, innovation, adaptability and tolerate tech debt; corporations want stability, scalability, optimisation and to avoid loss of trust; product companies want value, innovation and quality; service companies want delivery on time, within budget, meeting expectations, efficiently. PMs want the smallest resource spend for a requirement; leadership wants strategic vision, profitability and long-term growth.

The payoff he lists: company success that can flow into pay, a wider network of advocates outside tech, better behavioural interviews, and a risk-free rehearsal for running your own business one day.

## Who should watch

Senior engineers stuck at the same level, and new managers who need a script for coaching them. If you already sit in planning meetings and ask why, it will mostly confirm what you do.

Title: Microfrontends work best when one team owns the slice top to bottom
Description: Venkata Sai Manoj Pasupuleti at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on splitting monolithic web apps into microfrontends owned by vertical teams
Body:
A one-line UI fix should not need a full regression run of the payment service. Venkata Sai Manoj Pasupuleti, a lead software developer at a FAANG company, made the case for microfrontends at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024: split a monolithic web application into independently built, tested and deployed pieces, and give each piece to a team that owns both its UI and its API. His preferred cut is vertical (home page, cart, payments), not horizontal (one UI team, one API team).

It is a conceptual introduction, with an e-commerce site as the running example and no code, so it suits teams deciding whether to split rather than teams already mid-migration.

## What breaks in a monolithic web app?

He lists five problems, in an order most frontend leads will recognise from their own retros:

- **Tightly coupled code and scaling.** Frontend, integration layer (GraphQL in his diagram) and services (Node.js, Spring Boot, Python, Rust) ship as one unit. If the API layer needs more instances, you scale and redeploy everything.
- **Slow cycles.** A new hire has to understand the whole application before contributing, and a small UI change still needs testing across the frontend, integration and backend layers.
- **Cascading failures.** A minor bug in authentication can surface in the user dashboard, and the root cause is hard to find.
- **Technology lock-in.** One framework, one version of each library, everywhere.
- **Team coordination.** As teams grow they step on each other in shared CI/CD pipelines.

## What do you get from splitting?

Independent deployability is the headline. Each microfrontend is developed, tested and deployed on its own, so one team can release without waiting on the others. He described the ideal as "a very well choreographed dance where each team moves in sync with other without stepping on each other's toes," Venkata Sai Manoj Pasupuleti said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

Fault isolation is the one that matters most at 2am. In his e-commerce example, if payments has a problem, customers can still browse and add items to the cart; only checkout is down. And technology choice moves to the team: the home page team might pick React for its rendering needs while payments uses Vue.js, because that is what the team knows best.

The scaling argument extends to people. New teams take new microfrontends instead of piling onto one codebase.

## Where do microfrontends go wrong?

The best-practices section is where the talk earns its time:

- **Pick the split.** Vertical means one team owns a business capability end to end (the cart UI and the cart API). Horizontal means one team owns all UI, another all APIs. He says vertical is the more common choice and points to IKEA and Spotify as examples.
- **Define contracts.** Well-defined APIs between microfrontends, and no shared state coupling, so teams can iterate as long as they honour the contract.
- **Plan cross-app communication.** In a monolith, components just call each other; across microfrontends you need event-driven patterns, event buses or a global state manager.
- **Keep one look.** A design system and shared component libraries so the site feels like one product, not four apps stitched onto one page.
- **Keep one security model.** Consistent authentication, authorization and secure communication across every team's piece.

The closing list of companies using the approach includes Spotify, Amazon, IKEA and DAZN.

## Who should watch

Frontend and platform engineers weighing a split of a large web app, or managers who need the trade-offs in one place. If you want module federation configs or a migration story with numbers, this one stays at the whiteboard level.

- For the counter-argument, Maksim Zemskov on [scaling an application without microfrontends](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Maksim_Zemskov_glorious_monolith_scaling_application_microfrontends).

Title: Your VM flow logs are a security platform waiting to happen
Description: Siri Varma Vegiraju (Microsoft) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on building a network telemetry platform that checks traffic against security baselines
Body:
Most teams collect network traffic data for one incident and then forget it exists. Siri Varma Vegiraju, Technical Leader at Microsoft, argued at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 that the same packets should feed a shared platform: collect every VM's ingress and egress, enrich it, store it once, and let security, compliance and capacity teams all build on top. His security example is the useful part: a traffic analyzer that checks every flow against a baseline rule and pages the security team when something talks to a database it shouldn't.

It is a compact architecture talk, about 20 minutes, with no code but a clear blueprint.

## Why build a platform instead of a tool?

He gives three reasons to want network telemetry in the first place. Zero Trust asks for network segmentation, and you can't segment a topology you can't see. Threat and anomaly detection needs the data: an unknown or malicious IP, or one identity touching a lot of resources in a short window. And compliance: if you serve government agencies or run in national security regions, network telemetry is part of your audit.

The platform framing is about not building that pipeline three times. One store, one schema, one contract, and a service team with a new scenario just comes to the platform, takes the data and runs with it.

## Collect, enrich, store, and fix the schema first

The building blocks are deliberately boring. An agent on each VM snapshots traffic every minute or two (tcpdump on Linux, WinDump on Windows) and writes it to disk; a shipping agent such as Fluentd sends it to a data sink. A streaming or batch job then enriches billions of events a day with VM metadata (name, owning account, SKU) and maps source and destination IPs to known ranges, before landing everything in the final store that consumers read.

His one warning is about the contract, not the plumbing. "it is better to think about the schema design from the beginning itself," Siri Varma Vegiraju said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, plus the VM ID you attach yourself: get that right before a dozen teams depend on it.

If you are on a public cloud, skip the agents. AWS, Azure and Oracle all offer flow logs; drop them into S3 or Azure Storage and start at the enrichment step.

## What does a security baseline look like?

Baselines are the minimum policies every team must follow, from secret scanners in the build to blocking high-risk ports like 22, where SSH brute force happens. The network version reads the telemetry store and evaluates each flow:

- A simple rule: ingress to this SQL server may only come from one known source. Anything else is non-conformant and alerts security.
- A scalable rule: tag IP ranges by role, say a range of data stores and a range of VMs, and allow ingress to the data store tag only from the VM tag.
- The strict version: if either side of a flow isn't a known service tag, mark it non-compliant.

Tags are what turn a pile of IP allowlists into rules a human can still read, which is the difference between a baseline and a spreadsheet nobody trusts.

## The same data answers other questions

Once the store exists, extensions are cheap. Security recommendations: if segmentation shows teams talking across segments, tell them how to cut that cross-traffic. Capacity: if links between VMs and a data store sit at 60 to 70 percent bandwidth, provision more before it hurts.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers who already have flow logs and no plan for them, and anyone designing segmentation for Zero Trust. Expect architecture diagrams and rules of thumb, not a product demo.

Title: Security is everybody's job, including the people who build the platform
Description: Victor Onyenagubom (Teesside University) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on building a security-aware culture in platform development teams
Body:
Your fridge has an IP address, and so does the attack surface it adds. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Victor Onyenagubom, Lecturer in Computing at Teesside University, makes the case that platform development teams need security awareness built into how they work, not bolted on by a separate team. His core message: "cyber security is everybody's business, not just the security team's business," Victor Onyenagubom said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

It is a broad, practical checklist, delivered like a lecture, and it covers both the technical controls and the culture that keeps people using them.

## Why now?

Attack vectors keep multiplying, from IoT cameras to smart fridge freezers, while businesses lean ever harder on technology. He points to the CrowdStrike outage, when a single failure grounded airport operations, as a reminder of how much now runs on software.

## What does secure by design mean for a platform team?

Security first, however fancy the thing you are building. Then testing before anything reaches production: a proper QA process, automated security tools, penetration testing where someone attacks your system to find where it is vulnerable, and static code analysis to catch bugs such as openings for SQL injection. He suggests getting penetration testers in regularly, for example every three months.

## Which technical controls does he list?

- **Input validation and password rules**: his example is a minimum of 15 characters with upper case, lower case and symbols for access to sensitive files.
- **Authentication and authorisation**: multi-factor authentication, so the person logging in is the person who should have access.
- **Encryption and least privilege**: confidentiality and integrity from the CIA triad, with access on a need-to-know basis.
- **Secure logging and monitoring**: who accessed what, and when. After an attack, those logs are your investigation.
- **Network security and segmentation**: firewalls are non-negotiable, inside the network as well as at the edge, plus a secure VPN so remote workers connect without exposing core systems. For detection and threat intelligence he mentions tools such as IBM QRadar, Qualys, Darktrace and Microsoft Defender, and says to pick what fits your budget.
- **Physical security and backups**: barriers and cameras for data centres, and backups that survive a fire.

Continuous monitoring matters because attackers do not sleep. Tools throw false positives, so check the logs before dismissing an alert, and escalate anything unusual to your line manager.

## How do you make people care?

This is the culture half of the talk. Awareness training should be regular, not a one-off at onboarding, and should cover the everyday habits that stop staff becoming the attack vector through social engineering: a clean desk policy, regular password changes, keeping work details off personal social media. Encourage openness so people speak up when something looks wrong; "It could be the difference between you being cyber safe and you being cyber attacked." Reward the team's security champions, with recognition or a gift, so everyone sees good behaviour noticed.

Have a written incident response plan covering before, during and after an incident, with a dedicated team, in-house or outsourced, so the same attack does not land twice. And make practice fun: threat modelling, simulations of real-world scenarios, quizzes and security games.

## Who should watch

Platform and development team leads who want a one-stop checklist to compare against what their team actually does. Security engineers will know the material; the value is in the framing for people who do not think of security as their job.

Title: Frugal image pipelines start with the file format
Description: Anna Heng Chi (Amazon) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on cutting image pipeline cost with formats, adaptive compression, serverless and parallelism
Body:
The cheapest byte to process is the one you never stored. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Anna Heng Chi, Software Engineer at Amazon, walks through how to build image data pipelines that are fast without being expensive, drawing on her work at Amazon. The order of her advice is the useful part: pick formats and compression before you reach for more compute, then go serverless and parallel, then measure everything.

## Why are image pipelines expensive?

Images now feed medical imaging, object recognition for autonomous vehicles, product search in e-commerce, social media, and increasingly multimodal AI training. At that scale four things bite: storage cost, intensive computation, long processing times that can bottleneck real-time applications, and network bandwidth for moving the data around. Her goals for a frugal pipeline follow directly: minimise processing time, optimise resource use, reduce storage costs.

## Which format, and how much compression?

The first decision is the format. JPEG is lossy with adjustable compression, a good balance for photographs and complex colour gradients, and supported everywhere. PNG is lossless, keeps quality through repeated edits and handles transparency, so it suits logos, icons and graphics. The next generation squeezes harder: WebP from Google (lossy and lossless), HEIC from Apple (built on HEVC), and AVIF, based on the AV1 codec, which promises better compression than both but is still early in adoption.

The rule underneath is the size-versus-fidelity trade-off. Lossy fits where minor quality loss is acceptable; lossless is for cases where fidelity is critical, such as medical imaging and archives. She recommends established compression libraries over custom code, for their optimised algorithms and hardware acceleration.

The smartest idea in the talk is adaptive compression: analyse the image, then compress regions differently, "such as smooth background can be compressed more, while faces and edges need to compress less to preserve the visual quality," Anna Heng Chi said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Smaller files, same perceived quality, lower storage and bandwidth bills.

## What does the cloud side look like?

Object storage (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage) for scalable, durable, pay-as-you-go storage. Serverless functions, mostly AWS Lambda in her case, for on-demand resizing, thumbnail generation and format conversion. Managed vision APIs, mainly Amazon Rekognition (Google Cloud Vision and Azure offer the same), for object detection, classification, facial recognition and content moderation, which saves building and maintaining your own models.

For cost: spot instances for spare capacity, right-sizing, reserved instances for steady load, usage analysis, and budget alerts for when spend crosses a limit, "which can happen quite often," she adds.

## How do you scale the processing?

Two kinds of parallelism. Data parallelism splits the image set into chunks processed across many nodes. Task parallelism splits the work itself, resizing, filtering and feature extraction, into independent subtasks that run concurrently and are synchronised at the end if needed. The frameworks she names are Apache Spark, Dask for parallel Python, and Ray for parallelising Python and ML workloads, with Docker and Kubernetes for packaging and running the pipeline reliably across machines.

Then keep optimising: profile each stage to find bottlenecks, improve algorithms, move heavy work to GPUs or accelerators, tune parameters, and cache results of expensive transformations and feature extractions that run repeatedly on the same images, plus memoisation of function calls. Her team tracks usage and cost with Amazon CloudWatch, and the numbers end up in leadership meetings.

She closes on ethics: privacy, bias and transparency in image processing, which her team weighs case by case against the benefit to the customers of those images.

## Who should watch

Engineers starting out on a large image dataset, or inheriting a pipeline whose bill is growing faster than its throughput. It is a broad survey of options rather than one architecture with benchmarks, and a good checklist.

Title: Map the value stream first, then let AI float on a platform
Description: Romano Roth (Zuhlke Group) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on value stream mapping, floating platforms and AI as a platform capability
Body:
When the CIO says "we need to have AI", Romano Roth asks why, and then gets out the sticky notes. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Roth, Global Chief of DevOps and partner at Zühlke, argues that AI-augmented DevOps only works on two foundations: a value stream map that shows where the real bottleneck is, and a platform built so that AI becomes one more self-service capability. He then demos what that looks like on the platform Zühlke built with LGT, a bank in Liechtenstein.

Roth has been at Zühlke for 22 years, organises the DevOps Meetup Zürich and DevOpsDays Zürich, and has more than 250 videos on his YouTube channel, so this is a practitioner's talk with a working system behind it.

## Where should AI go in your delivery process?

Wherever value stream mapping says it hurts. Get everyone who touches a product from idea to production into a room, list the steps, name who owns each, then measure process time (actual work), lead time (including waiting), and percent complete and accurate (how often work bounces back). In his example, testing has 8 hours of process time against 336 hours of lead time, and only 50% of its output is right first time. Across the whole stream: 161 hours of work inside 2,160 hours of lead time, an activity ratio of 7%.

That map tells you where to aim. Roth's caveat is the important bit: a process change may fix the bottleneck better than any model, so think of AI last. Where AI does fit, he lists options per stage, adapted from Gartner: risk and delivery prediction in planning, Copilot-style help in code, auto-remediation of vulnerabilities in build, change impact analysis and intelligent test selection in test, deployment health checks with automatic rollback, configuration drift fixes in operate, and AIOps pattern recognition and root-cause analysis in monitor.

## Why does a platform matter for AI?

Because AI only scales on standardisation. Many teams with their own local tooling become small product teams on a self-service platform run by a platform team that treats the platform as a product. Product teams create value for customers; the platform team creates value for product teams.

His architecture has the internal developer portal, often Backstage, as a thin top layer, which he says is why some companies are disappointed with Backstage: the provisioning, automation and integration layers below it are the real work. Tools are integrated through adapters, so replacing one is cheap. "I even don't know how long GitLab will be on the market," Romano Roth said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, hence a GitLab adapter under a unified repository block.

## What is a floating platform?

His key principle. Plug in tools and vendor platforms (GitHub, GitLab, cloud providers) and build developer experience on top, but "What you never, ever should do is duplicate a feature from one of the tools or from one of the platforms below." Integrate, and the platform floats up as the tools ship new features. Hide, abstract or duplicate, and "your platform will start to sink."

Inside that platform AI is one capability, though a large one: apps such as chatbots and coding assistants, tooling such as prompt engineering, RAG and vector databases, a model hub, and the GenAI infrastructure APIs at the bottom.

## What does the demo show?

A governed internal chat at Zühlke where employees do not need to know which LLM is behind it, so the provider can be swapped. A container registry with an analyse button that sends image layers to a model tuned for container image analysis, built because the platform team was too small to help every team with its images. Namespace log analysis on Kubernetes. A service catalog offering Azure OpenAI and an LLM platform, on which developers built a project reference finder for bids and a set of agents with tuned system prompts, including a company analyser. Next up: a fix-it button that turns a log finding into a pull request, and a coding assistant on the platform's AI services to avoid per-seat subscriptions.

## Who should watch

Platform leads under pressure to add AI to the SDLC who want a method instead of a shopping list. The value stream section alone is worth the time.

Title: A self-service GenAI platform where anyone ships a bot in five minutes
Description: Murali Mallina (Softrams) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on a serverless GenAI platform for chatbots, agents, AI for BI and agent crews
Body:
If plain English is now a programming language, the platform's users stop being only developers. That is the premise of Murali Mallina's talk at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Mallina, CTO of Softrams, a civic digital services firm working with US federal agencies, describes the serverless GenAI platform his team built so that anyone in the company, technical or not, can create a grounded chatbot in about five minutes and share it once it is good.

## Why build a platform at all?

Federal customers come with unusual constraints, and Softrams needed something it could deploy in its entirety into a customer's own environment. Mallina's goal was to get from experiment to production in days to weeks, where classic ML experiences used to take weeks to months.

The bigger reason is who is building now. "LLMs made this natural language as a new programming language," Murali Mallina said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, so business teams can create assistants from instructions and their own documents. A platform is how you give them that without each one reinventing infrastructure, access control and guardrails, or leaking data.

## What can people build on it?

Softrams sorted the use cases into four groups, each with its own infrastructure, workflows and observability:

- **Chatbots**: answers grounded in a private knowledge base, loaded through connectors such as SharePoint or by uploading documents.
- **Agents**: chatbots that decide their own flow, call tools, APIs and functions, and can act for the user, such as creating a task or updating a status in Jira.
- **AI for BI**: business users ask questions of company data in natural language; an orchestrator picks the data sources, fetches and processes the data, and explains how it got the answer. Mallina says their fastest answers come back in about 30-35 seconds to three minutes, against days to weeks for the old request-to-analyst loop, with charts, reports and even slide decks as output.
- **Agent crews**: teams of self-organising agents with different roles for multi-step work such as reports, analysis, automated security testing or documentation.

## What is under the hood?

The first version is a single AWS CDK project: infrastructure, vector stores, orchestration, pipelines and access control, deployable into any AWS account. Versions for Azure, Google Cloud and on-premises Kubernetes followed. It connects to models on Amazon Bedrock, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI and Google Vertex, or to self-hosted models, on AWS through SageMaker.

His simplified architecture is short on purpose: a front end of your choice, Amazon Cognito with single sign-on, API Gateway, a vector database, data sources, and an orchestrator. The orchestrator, a container or set of microservices, is the crux: a plain chatbot calls Bedrock directly, a RAG bot fetches context first, and agents, AI for BI and crews all run their loops there. Everything stays inside the customer's security boundary.

## What did a year of running it teach them?

Education is the secret sauce, in his words. People are excited and scared at the same time, worried about leaking data or causing a security incident, so everyone, not only developers, gets training in prompting and threat modelling; his playbook lists a Week of AI. Experimentation comes next: private sandboxes, immediate feedback on cost, latency and retrieval quality per query, GitHub Copilot for engineers, and hackathons. Then the platform itself: application types, threat models, model validation, guardrails and generous observability.

His summary slide carries two warnings worth repeating: GenAI applications are naturally non-deterministic, and traditional testing strategies do not work on them. His advice is to "try to optimize your experiences for the non typical users first", the people who are not engineers, and to treat the platform as a product: MVP, user feedback, iterate.

## Who should watch

Platform teams asked to give everyone GenAI safely, particularly in regulated or government environments. You get a reference architecture and an operating playbook, not code.

Title: From days to minutes by making Kubernetes your infrastructure API
Description: Yuriy Bezsonov (AWS) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on infrastructure controllers and compositions with ACK, Crossplane and GitOps
Body:
Your pod deploys in minutes, then waits days for the database ticket. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Yuriy Bezsonov, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, traces why application delivery on Kubernetes stalls on backing services, and shows how infrastructure controllers and compositions put both the runtime and its cloud resources behind one Kubernetes API.

## Why do some deployments take minutes and others days?

Bezsonov uses the retail sample app from the Amazon EKS workshop: UI, orders, checkout, carts, catalog and assets, backed by MySQL, Amazon DynamoDB, ElastiCache for Redis and Amazon MQ. Some of that lives in the cluster, some outside it. He then sorts delivery into three streams:

- **Kubernetes only**: manifests plus things Kubernetes already knows how to create, such as load balancers via Services and Ingress and EBS volumes via persistent volumes. Minutes.
- **Infrastructure as code with a handover**: a separate infrastructure monorepo where a platform or DevOps team approves the pull request that creates DynamoDB or S3. Hours.
- **Ticketing**: the developer files a ticket and the database team gets to it when it gets to it. Days.

Platform teams want consistent, secure, compliant, observable deployments. Developers want full ownership of their app including its backing services, fast. Both are reasonable.

## Step one: put infrastructure next to the code

He cites the AWS CDK best-practices guide: whoever owns the runtime should own the infrastructure, so both live in the same repository. Merge once, and two pipelines fire, one to the cluster and one to CDK, CloudFormation or Terraform. "Applying this practice reduces the deployment time from hours to minutes," Yuriy Bezsonov said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

## Step two: let Kubernetes manage the cloud

You could write an operator to manage external resources, but "writing your own operator, it is rather complex and what I would call undifferentiated heavy lifting." Pre-built infrastructure controllers do that job instead, exposing cloud services through the Kubernetes API with declarative configuration. The two he names are AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK), built and supported by AWS, and Crossplane, the CNCF project with an extensible framework and a broad community.

## Do developers now need to be cloud experts?

No, and this is the best idea in the talk. With compositions the developer asks for a database instance and owns its configuration and lifecycle. The platform team decides what that means: on premises, PostgreSQL with Prometheus; on AWS, Amazon RDS with IAM and Amazon CloudWatch. Bezsonov notes IaC tools already do this, quoting the CDK docs on composition as the key pattern for higher-level abstractions and Terraform's modules. On Kubernetes, the CNCF platforms white paper points to KubeVela, built on the Open Application Model, and Crossplane.

The bonus of going through the Kubernetes API is the ecosystem: Helm or cdk8s for packaging, Argo CD or Flux for GitOps, Kyverno or Open Policy Agent for policy, applied to infrastructure the same way as to deployments.

## What does the reference solution do?

AWS's reference solution, published as a blog series with sample code, uses compositions and controllers to provision EKS clusters themselves from a management cluster via GitOps. Onboarding an app: the developer commits runtime and infrastructure config to an app repo, opens a PR to a central repo, the platform team approves, Flux reconciles, and Crossplane creates the RDS instance. One flow from line of code to running app.

## Who should watch

Platform teams building an internal developer platform on EKS, or anyone stuck between developers who want ownership and a ticket queue that will not give it to them. It is AWS-flavoured but the patterns transfer.

Title: Teaching robots to take products apart for the circular economy
Description: Lav Kumar (Salesforce) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on AI-guided robotic disassembly to recover metals and cut e-waste
Body:
Shredding a phone is the fastest way to recycle it and the worst way to get its gold back. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Lav Kumar, Lead Member of Technical Staff at Salesforce, makes the case for the opposite approach: AI that works out how a product was put together, and robots that take it apart precisely enough to recover what is inside.

It is a sustainability talk on a platform engineering stage, so expect manufacturing and materials rather than Kubernetes. Kumar gave a version of it at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 too.

## Why is disassembly the bottleneck?

Because modern products are dense. Kumar points out that "a single smartphone contains over 60 different elements," Lav Kumar said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, including gold, silver and rare earths, all packed tightly with plastics and other metals. Laptops, batteries and cars follow the same pattern. At end of life that density means valuable components get discarded, which is both an economic loss and more waste.

He also cites research that "up to 80 percent of a product's environment impact is determined at the stage of design." Good design helps, but whatever is already in circulation still has to be taken apart efficiently to be reclaimed.

## What do AI and robots actually do here?

Two jobs. The AI analyses a product's structure and material composition, identifies the screws, fasteners and adhesives, and decides the order in which components should come off so nothing valuable is missed or contaminated. The robots execute that plan, with sensors that tell them what material they are holding so they can adjust grip or cutting technique rather than crush a circuit board.

Traditional recycling, by contrast, often shreds first and sorts later, which mixes metals and plastics and lowers the value of everything recovered. Glued-together products make it worse.

## What are the numbers?

Kumar quotes several figures from industry adopters, without naming the companies:

- a 30% increase in usable components retrieved by firms using AI-driven disassembly;
- up to a 50% improvement in material recovery rates;
- a 40% increase in recovered valuable materials in one e-waste case, where robots with vision systems and machine learning pulled out processors, memory chips and batteries for resale to manufacturers;
- recycled aluminium saving up to 95% of the energy needed to make new aluminium from bauxite.

A second case covers electric vehicle batteries, where an AI-guided system separated lithium, cobalt and nickel with minimal contamination, pure enough to go back into new batteries. That closed loop is the circular economy in one sentence. AI also helps sorting downstream, separating plastics by chemical composition so the recycled material is clean enough for automotive or construction use.

## What comes next?

He expects AI to analyse material composition in real time during disassembly, which matters most in electronics where designs change fast, and new robotic tools to handle products that are currently too complex or labour-intensive to recycle at all.

## Who should watch

Engineers curious about where AI meets physical-world sustainability, and anyone building software for manufacturing or recycling operations. It is a conceptual overview with industry statistics rather than an implementation walkthrough, and the figures are presented without their original sources.

Title: Personalised offers start with integrated systems, not better copy
Description: Vamsi Srivangipuram (DIRECTV) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on how enterprise application integration feeds offer management
Body:
The salesperson calls a hot lead, only to learn the customer bought last week. Vamsi Srivangipuram, Principal Software Engineer at DIRECTV, has been that salesperson, and at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 he uses moments like that to make the case for enterprise application integration (EAI) as the foundation of offer management. The takeaway: personalised offers fail on stale, siloed data long before they fail on creative.

Srivangipuram brings 18 years across solution design, business analysis and product management, the last ten at DIRECTV driving solutions in the offers and decisioning space. This is a business-architecture talk, aimed at the people who have to explain to leadership why integration is worth funding.

## When does a business need to care?

He starts with a startup: an accounting program, a CRM, an email tool, none of them talking. Marketing wants a prospect list, so someone walks over to sales, who exports it from the CRM by hand. Fine at ten people. As the company scales it adds HR, a CMS, billing, analytics, supply chain, messaging, and customers start expecting the website, the app and the store to know who they are. He cites Accenture: 91% of consumers prefer brands that recognise them and provide relevant offers. "customer loyalty isn't just granted. It must be earned," Vamsi Srivangipuram said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024.

Without integration, he argues, every team works from outdated or conflicting data. Manual segmentation goes stale before the campaign launches. McKinsey's estimate, on his slides, is that companies lose 20-30% of revenue to poor integration.

## What is EAI, in his words?

The textbook definition is the connection and coordination of software applications across an organisation. His shorter one: "it addresses lack of communication." He walks through four integration types:

- **Presentation integration**: merging apps at the UI level, sometimes screen scraping. Unified view, but outdated and shallow.
- **Business process integration**: an order in order management triggers the invoice and books the installation technician. Efficient, but each touchpoint is a security surface and a failure can ripple system-wide.
- **Data integration**: transforming data so other systems can interpret it. Raises quality, and spreads bad data just as fast if nobody maintains it.
- **Communication integration**: APIs, microservices and middleware. Flexible, scalable and asynchronous, at the cost of complexity and exposed APIs to secure.

On methodology he goes from point-to-point (does not scale), through hub-and-spoke, bus and middleware (logic abstracted so a vendor can be swapped later), to microservices, which he calls the most widely used today.

## Does it pay off?

His case studies: Sephora joined in-store and app data so staff can recognise a customer who browsed a product on the app, and consolidated its regional affiliate programmes; his slides credit the loyalty integration with a 27% increase in conversion and an 11% rise in average order value. Shell unified loyalty programmes across regions so pricing analysts can tell whether a station's customers are passing through or live nearby. He also quotes Epsilon's 29% lift in open rates for personalised emails and McKinsey's figure of up to 50% lower acquisition costs.

The implementation roadmap is four phases: planning, modelling, implementation and maintenance, with the last one covering monitoring and feeding changing business needs back in. Best practices are clear objectives, planning with every stakeholder from legal to sales, standards so vendors stay swappable, data quality as a daily job, and agile delivery.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects in retail, telecom or any business with a loyalty programme and a dozen systems that do not talk to each other. Expect frameworks and industry statistics, not code.

Title: The chatbot as the platform's front door, layer by layer
Description: Nagarajan Madhavan (Intuit) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on AI chatbots for self-service provisioning, CI/CD and incidents, and how to build one
Body:
Every platform team has a queue of requests that are really one sentence long: spin up a test environment, roll back that deploy, where is the runbook. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Nagarajan Madhavan, Mobile Platform Lead at Intuit, argues that an AI chatbot is the natural interface for that queue, and spends most of his talk on the architecture you need behind it.

Madhavan has worked on front-end teams and developer platforms, shipping tools, SDKs and self-serve kiosks, and frames the talk around a wish every platform engineer has had: an assistant that takes the repetitive work off your plate.

## What gaps does a chatbot fill?

He lists four. It simplifies complexity by putting a natural-language interface over infrastructure that is overwhelming to drive directly. It automates the repetitive: "Chatbots can handle routine operations like deployments, monitoring, and scaling, significantly reducing the manual workload for the engineers," Nagarajan Madhavan said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. It lives where teams already talk, Slack or Microsoft Teams, so decisions happen in the conversation. And it lets developers self-serve without waiting for a central team, which in turn frees that team from answering the same question for every group it supports.

Unlike a form or a portal, a bot can also start the conversation: triggered by an event, available around the clock.

## What would you actually use it for?

Five use cases:

- **Infrastructure provisioning**: ask for a testing environment with two EC2 instances and let the bot do the rest.
- **CI/CD**: trigger builds, deployments and rollbacks with chat commands.
- **Monitoring and alerts**: alerts land in the chat, and engineers run diagnostics or recovery from the same thread.
- **Incident management**: escalation, real-time updates and coordinated actions during an outage.
- **Knowledge access**: documentation, FAQs and troubleshooting steps on demand, instead of digging through manuals.

## What sits behind the chat window?

This is the meat of the talk. His layered architecture:

- **User interaction layer**: the chat surface (Slack, Teams, web, mobile) with session handling.
- **NLP layer**: intent recognition (what the user wants done) and entity recognition (what it should be done to), plus sentiment and context.
- **Core AI layer**: dialogue management holding the conversation's context and memory, knowledge-base integration over your docs, and the LLM.
- **Integration layer**: APIs and middleware into Jenkins, Kubernetes or cloud management systems, where the actual work happens.
- **Response generation**: template-based answers, dynamic responses, or multimedia such as a generated report dropped into the thread.
- **Security**: identity and access management deciding who may run which command.
- **Continuous learning**: models improved over time from past interactions.

Privacy and regulatory compliance run across all of them.

## What goes wrong?

Ambiguous commands are the first risk: a bot that misreads a request near production is worse than no bot, so natural language understanding needs care. Security is the second, because the bot holds keys to sensitive systems; he calls for role-based access control and multi-factor authentication. Integration across a heterogeneous toolchain is hard. And adoption is not automatic: an unfriendly or untrustworthy bot simply does not get used.

He closes on two trends: multimodal input (voice, documents, gestures, not just text) and deep integration, where the bot picks up context from what the user was doing in the surrounding UI before they opened the chat.

## Who should watch

Platform teams weighing a ChatOps or AI assistant layer and wanting a checklist of the components and the risks. It is an architecture overview without a live demo, so pair it with a hands-on talk if you want code.
