Title: Three specialists, one RAG bot for the EB-1A green card maze
Description: Ankit Virmani at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on grounding an EB-1A guidance chatbot with RAG, and halving its response time with backoff
Body:
Anyone who has tried to research the US EB-1A extraordinary ability green card knows the problem: the information is everywhere, some of it right, most of it a time sink. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Ankit Virmani, an ethical AI and data engineering specialist, teamed up with mobile developer [Namaswi Chandarana](https://www.linkedin.com/in/namaswi-chandarana/) and UX designer [Tina Gada](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tina-gada/) to show how they built the EB1A Xpert bot, an iOS chatbot grounded with retrieval augmented generation (RAG). The takeaway: the hard parts were hallucinations and rate limits, and both had boring, effective fixes.

It is a three-person, three-discipline talk: AI backend, mobile client and user experience, each presenter covering their slice.

## Why not just ask a general-purpose LLM?

Because it made things up. Virmani describes early testing where answers to EB-1A questions were simply wrong, which is not what you want from a tool people use to plan an immigration case. The fix was grounding. The team scouted good-quality documentation on the various aspects of EB-1A, fed it into a retrieval system, and built the classic four-box flow: the user asks, the retrieval system fetches the relevant passages, those passages augment the prompt, and the LLM answers from them.

"the model is not using its own intelligence, but it's using the intelligence from the retrieved information that we have given to the model using a document," Ankit Virmani said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. That is the whole point of RAG in a domain where accuracy matters more than eloquence: you choose the corpus, so you can predict what kind of answers come back.

The team deliberately stayed neutral on which LLM sits behind it. Chandarana says they experimented with several and picked a popular one on ease of integration, response quality and accuracy.

## What does the stack look like?

The client is native iOS: Swift, SwiftUI and The Composable Architecture (TCA). The server is Node.js, handling authentication, receiving chat requests, doing prompt engineering so the RAG output comes back in the format the app expects, polling the model while it works, then cleaning up the response before it goes to the phone.

The most useful engineering detail is about rate limits. Requests to the model kept failing because the API tier had per-minute token limits, and repeated requests blew through them. Chandarana's fix was the one every SRE will nod at: "we added an exponential backoff to our backend," Namaswi Chandarana said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Response times dropped from 10-15 seconds to around five to seven, and the error rate went down with them. She is candid that two to three seconds is the real target and they are not there yet.

## Can UX make a slow model feel faster?

Gada's part covers what a designer does when the backend has a five-second floor. She started with user interviews with prospective applicants, did competitive analysis of ChatGPT and custom GPT apps to borrow familiar UI patterns, and worked with development on how to show response time in the interface. First-time users land on a dashboard of the questions research said people ask most; answers come back as a summary plus bulleted next steps. She also built the brand guidelines and design system from scratch, with colour contrast and accessibility checked throughout.

## What is still missing?

The team lists its own gaps: no in-app way for users to give detailed feedback, iOS only for now (Android and web are planned), and US-only release even though applicants can be anywhere. Next on the list are auto-generated action items, voice input, and reminders tied to those to-dos.

## Who should watch

Small teams building a domain-specific RAG chatbot on a mobile client, especially if you are about to hit your first token-per-minute wall. It is an overview of approach rather than a code walkthrough; the presenters say outright they kept the specific model and tooling out of it.

Title: AI finds the molecule, platform engineering carries the data
Description: Amit Taneja (UMB Bank) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024 on why AI drug discovery depends on pipelines, scalable compute and observability
Body:
A new drug costs more than $2.6 billion and takes over 12 years to reach patients. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024, Amit Taneja, Engineering Lead at UMB Bank, walks through how AI is cutting into both numbers, and argues that the models are only half the story: the other half is the platform underneath them.

It is a short, high-level tour, structured as a series of pairs. Each AI idea is followed by the platform engineering practice that makes it workable at scale.

## What is broken in traditional drug discovery?

Taneja names three problems: high cost, long timelines, and inefficiency, because traditional methods lean on experimental screening that is slow and expensive. His first platform answer is automation. Automated pipelines move data from one phase to the next without someone shepherding files between teams, which cuts manual intervention and the waiting that comes with it.

## Which AI methods does he cover?

Four, each in a sentence or two:

- **Deep learning**: CNNs and RNNs analysing chemical and bioactivity data.
- **Virtual screening**: evaluating large chemical libraries to find high-potential compounds.
- **Molecular docking**: simulating how a drug will bind to its target.
- **Generative models**: designing novel molecules for a specific therapeutic purpose.

He also cites AI models predicting success rates above 80%. The platform pairing here is scalable cloud infrastructure that grows with the dataset, plus CI/CD for models, so every improvement is tested and deployed quickly instead of sitting between training and production.

## What do the case studies show?

Two well-known ones. Exscientia and Sumitomo Dainippon Pharma used AI to create an immuno-oncology molecule in eight months, against a typical four to five years, and took it into clinical trials faster than traditional timelines. The second is Halicin, an antibiotic effective against drug-resistant bacteria, found after AI screened over 6,000 compounds.

Taneja reads both through a platform lens. For the Exscientia molecule, automated processes, large-dataset handling and integrated research tools shortened the timeline. For Halicin, he points to a data-oriented architecture with centralised data pipelines that let the models screen compounds efficiently.

## Where does it get hard?

The challenges list is honest: data quality (the models are only as good as large, accurate, comprehensive datasets), model interpretability, and the fact that AI predictions still have to survive rigorous lab validation. On the platform side, he adds observability and monitoring of data flow and model performance, so problems in the models show up before they contaminate results, and resource optimisation that scales compute and storage with demand without the bill running away.

His closing line is the thesis of the talk: "the success of AI in drug discovery is heavily dependent on robust platform engineering," Amit Taneja said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024. Looking ahead, he expects platforms to become collaboration environments where data scientists, biologists and chemists work on the same data.

One note on scope: the abstract promises AI slashing development costs by 70%. That figure does not come up in the talk itself, which sticks to the numbers above.

## Who should watch

Platform and data engineers who have been asked to support a research or life-sciences team and want the vocabulary: virtual screening, docking, generative chemistry, and where pipelines and CI/CD fit around them. It is a primer, not a detailed architecture session, and it is about 15 minutes well spent if the domain is new to you.

Title: qc2 glues classic quantum chemistry codes to Qiskit and PennyLane
Description: Carlos Murilo Romero Rocha (Netherlands eScience Center) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on qc2, open-source glue for VQE chemistry on quantum SDKs
Body:
Every variational quantum chemistry run starts with a classical one: before a quantum circuit can estimate a molecule's energy, a traditional chemistry code has to supply the reference state, the integrals and the orbitals. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024, Carlos Murilo Romero Rocha, research software engineer at the Netherlands eScience Center, presents qc2, an open-source Python package that does that handover for you, feeding classical chemistry output into Qiskit Nature and PennyLane, and shows a full VQE calculation on water in a few lines.

## Where does qc2 come from?

The Netherlands eScience Center builds open-source research software with Dutch researchers and runs training from basic Python to CUDA. qc2 is the result of one of its projects, QC for QC, a collaboration that includes SURF. The goal, in the project's own words, is to make traditional computational chemistry codes interoperable with quantum computing frameworks, so chemists can run their calculations on quantum computers without writing the plumbing.

## Why is chemistry a natural quantum workload?

Rocha's framing is the clearest short version of the argument you'll hear. Atoms and molecules have discrete energy levels, which are the spectrum of the molecular Hamiltonian, so finding them means solving the Schrödinger equation as an eigenvalue problem. The catch, as Carlos Murilo Romero Rocha said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024: "this equation can only be solved exactly for one electron systems", hydrogen and not much else.

Everything else is approximation. The usual route is the variational principle: write the unknown wave function as a combination of known basis functions and tune the coefficients to minimise the ground-state energy. On a classical computer that becomes diagonalising very large matrices, and the most accurate method, full configuration interaction, scales exponentially with the number of electrons and orbitals. That is the bottleneck quantum hardware is supposed to relieve, and qc2 targets small molecules, where the most accurate methods can still be tested.

## How does VQE fit in?

In today's noisy intermediate-scale quantum era, the workhorse is the variational quantum eigensolver, a hybrid algorithm. Prepare qubits in a reference state, apply a parameterised circuit (the ansatz), measure the energy of the molecular Hamiltonian, and let a classical optimiser pick new parameters until the energy converges.

The algorithm needs five ingredients: a reference state, a variational form, initial parameters, a qubit Hamiltonian and an optimiser. The first and fourth only come from a classical chemistry code, as the Hartree-Fock wave function, the one- and two-electron integrals and the molecular orbital coefficients. Chemists traditionally choose physically motivated ansätze from coupled-cluster theory.

## What does a qc2 run look like?

qc2 follows four design rules: reuse existing open-source chemistry tools and standard data schemas, integrate with Qiskit and PennyLane, stay modular with a built-in algorithms package, and keep the interface simple. Under the hood it uses custom calculators for the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE), which drive your chemistry program behind the scenes and write its results to formatted data files. qc2 reads those to build the reference circuit and the qubit Hamiltonian, then hands them to algorithm classes that run on Qiskit Nature or PennyLane.

The water example has three steps after the imports:

1. Create a qc2 data object with the molecule and an output file name. That file stores the results and can restart a later calculation.
2. Attach and run a qc2 ASE calculator for your chemistry code; the demo uses PySCF.
3. Instantiate the algorithm class and run it.

"Very simple and very straightforward," as Rocha put it. The modularity shows in the second example: orbital-optimised VQE (oo-VQE), which relaxes the molecular orbitals along with the circuit parameters, uses the same input with a different algorithm class. In his benchmark on water at its equilibrium geometry, oo-VQE converges below plain VQE, as expected, and lands almost exactly on the energy from a traditional quantum chemistry reference method.

## Who should watch

Computational chemists curious about quantum hardware, and quantum developers who need real chemistry inputs without becoming chemists. The code lives at [github.com/qc2nl/qc2](https://github.com/qc2nl/qc2), and the team welcomes contributions, from new ideas to forks.

Title: Quantum computers need new materials, and new materials need quantum computers
Description: Baran Ozdemir (OZFengineering) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on how quantum computing and materials science feed each other, from drug crystals to 2D photonics
Body:
Materials science and quantum computing are stuck in a loop: you need better materials to build better qubits, and you need better quantum computers to design those materials. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024, Baran Ozdemir, independent entrepreneur at OZFengineering, looks at both directions of that loop, with the pharmaceutical industry as his main example on one side and photonic 2D materials on the other.

It is an overview talk for people coming from the materials or engineering side, light on algorithms and heavy on the parameters a materials engineer worries about.

## Why throw a quantum computer at materials?

Ozdemir's case starts with the size of the search space. Designing a material means juggling structure, properties, processing and characterisation at once: atomic structure, molecular arrangement, alloying elements, the kinetics and thermodynamics of how polymer chains move. Every one of those is a parameter, and simulating the combinations classically is where you run out of road.

Quantum hardware is his answer because of the exponential scaling of qubits, two to the power of n states for n qubits. "This parallelism allows a quantum computer to work on a million computations at once," Baran Ozdemir said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024. He uses the classic comparison that a 30-qubit machine would match a conventional computer running at teraflops, against the gigaflops of a typical desktop, and points to IBM's processors passing a thousand qubits as the sign that the capacity is arriving.

## Why pharma first?

Pharma is where he sees the clearest fit, and he brings numbers. Pharmaceutical companies have spent about 19% of net revenue on R&D over the past two decades, against about 15% for software and semiconductors, two other research-heavy industries. Global pharmaceutical revenue reached an estimated 1,482 billion US dollars in 2022, according to IQVIA figures he cites.

The quantum value for pharma, in his framing, sits in research and development: understanding disease, finding targets, and the materials questions that decide whether a drug works as a product. Crystallinity ratio, solubility optimisation and formulation all generate huge amounts of test data that has to be analysed fast, and COVID-19 showed how fast that has to be. Semiconductors get a similar treatment: growing crystalline structures where electron stability and band gap depend on billions of parameters.

## What does a quantum computer want from its materials?

The second half flips the direction. For photonic quantum technology, the electrical and optical properties of the material decide whether you get usable photons at all, and two-dimensional materials are central to getting stable ones. He compares several transition-metal compounds, including molybdenum disulfide and molybdenum diselenide, across the parameters that matter:

- **Photon lifetime**: too short and there is no time to process the photon, which limits what algorithms you can run.
- **Emission wavelength range**: each material emits in its own band, and the system has to be designed around it.
- **Photon purity**: cleaner photons carry clearer information.
- **Band gap**: the energy spacing between the n-type and p-type sides, which shapes how photons are produced.
- **Operating temperature**: the one he keeps coming back to. Cooling is energy, and "the cryogenic temperature is waste of time and waste of energy," as he put it. Materials that work at warmer temperatures make the technology usable outside a lab.

He also places quantum dots and broadband technologies as two routes that both lean on 2D materials for stability, designed at the nanometre scale.

## Who should watch

Materials scientists, chemical engineers and semiconductor people who want a map of where their field meets quantum computing. Ozdemir says himself that he keeps the technical detail of each parameter short, so expect the shape of the problem rather than worked simulations or a specific algorithm.

Title: Quantum theory still has no clean phase operator, and Dirac knew it in 1927
Description: Pranav Srikanth (QuGain Quantum Technologies) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on why nobody has defined a proper quantum phase operator since Dirac
Body:
Position and momentum get tidy operators in quantum mechanics. Phase, the thing every oscillator and every light wave obviously has, still does not. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024, Pranav Srikanth, co-founder of QuGain Quantum Technologies, walks through almost a century of attempts to define a phase operator for the quantum harmonic oscillator, starting with Paul Dirac in 1927, and shows that each fix trades one problem for another.

It is a short, maths-forward history talk: a good fit if you remember your bra-kets and want to know why this corner of the theory is still open.

## Why does phase need its own operator?

The quantum harmonic oscillator is the standard model of a particle oscillating around an equilibrium point, and it doubles as the model for a mode of the electromagnetic field. Classically, phase is just where you are in the cycle. In quantum theory an observable needs an operator, and that is where it breaks. Srikanth is clear that this matters beyond the blackboard. "Understanding the phase operator is not just an academic exercise," Pranav Srikanth said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024: quantum optics and quantum information both depend on precise phase.

## What went wrong with Dirac's version?

Dirac's 1927 idea was the natural one: split the annihilation operator into a phase part and an amplitude part, writing it as e^(iφ) times the square root of the number operator. The trouble is that the exponential piece is not unitary, so it does not preserve the inner product of the Hilbert space, a basic requirement. Its expectation values were also ambiguous, which makes the result hard to read physically.

## A run of near misses

The rest of the talk is a tour of the repairs, each a step forward with a catch:

- **Louisell, 1963.** Work with cosine and sine phase operators and their commutation relations with the number operator instead. That gets you unitarity, but still no Hermitian phase operator, and Hermitian is what guarantees real eigenvalues you can measure.
- **Susskind and Glogower, 1964.** Decompose the annihilation operator differently, using a one-sided unitary shift operator, to define cosine and sine operators. Clever, but those operators do not commute, so they are not a complete set of phase variables.
- **Carruthers and Nieto.** They studied the Susskind-Glogower operators further and found continuous eigenvalue spectra on the interval from -1 to 1. Their commutator turns out to be proportional to the vacuum projector, the zero-photon state, so the non-commutation never goes away.
- **Pegg and Barnett.** Define the phase operator on a finite-dimensional subspace of the Hilbert space and the maths becomes consistent. It gets awkward again as the dimension goes to infinity, which is the full space you wanted in the first place.

Srikanth points out that the Pegg-Barnett exponential looks a lot like Dirac's original, adding "just see how the world is very cyclic in nature." Sixty years of work, and the formula comes back round to where it started.

## What would a good phase operator need?

He ends the history with a checklist. A valid phase operator should be Hermitian, so its eigenvalues correspond to measurements. The classical identity should hold, cos² φ + sin² φ equal to the identity. And it should evolve in time the way phase should, starting value plus the oscillator frequency times elapsed time. Nothing so far ticks all three without caveats. Recent models address Hermiticity and time dependence, and the open questions now sit in extending these ideas to more complex quantum systems.

## Who should watch

Physics students, quantum optics people and quantum software engineers who like knowing where the foundations are still soft. It moves fast through the operators and skips the derivations, so treat it as a map of the literature rather than a lecture course.

Title: Einstein's spooky action, Bohr's comeback and why it matters for AI
Description: Rich Niemiec (Viscosity) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on entanglement, from the 1927 Solvay debates to quantum-accelerated AI and robots
Body:
Rich Niemiec, Chief Innovation Officer at Viscosity, opens his Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 talk at the 1927 Solvay conference and ends it with Boston Dynamics' robot dog. In between he argues that entanglement, the effect Einstein refused to accept, is about to become the engine under generative AI. It is a wide-angle keynote, part physics history lesson and part tour of where AI and robotics are heading, rather than a technical walkthrough.

## Who was arguing with whom?

The story starts with the photo everyone has seen: Einstein, Schrödinger, Pauli, Bohr and Born in one room. Niemiec retells the famous exchange, with Einstein insisting God does not play dice and Bohr answering, as Niemiec quoted him at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024, "Einstein, stop telling God what to do."

Einstein's objection became the EPR paper (Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen), which called quantum theory incomplete. Bell later turned the argument into something you could test, and John Clauser ran that test in 1972 with polarised photons from calcium atoms. Clauser got the Nobel Prize for it in 2022. Entanglement turned out to be real. Einstein was wrong, just very late in finding out.

## What is entanglement, in plain words?

Niemiec keeps the definitions short. Two particles interact so that neither can be described on its own any more: measure one electron as spin up and its partner comes out spin down. A qubit sits in a superposition of 0 and 1 until it is measured. When that fragile state breaks you get decoherence, which is where most quantum computer errors come from. He gives a sense of how fast that is improving: superposition lasted 1.75 seconds in 2008 and 3 hours by 2013, once researchers learned to run colder.

His red-and-white-ball analogy does the rest. Entangle two balls, move them a galaxy apart, look at one, and the other is already the opposite colour. Then the punchline physicists settled on: "Now, what physicists have said is these particles aren't communicating across this large distance." No signal, just correlation, so relativity survives. His summary line, said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024: "With quantum entanglement, it's no longer spooky action at a distance, it's correlation at a distance."

One caution if you watch it: the talk goes further and describes quantum teleportation as a way to move ones and zeros instantly across the world. Standard teleportation protocols also need an ordinary classical message, so no useful data travels faster than light. Take that section as a picture of the idea, not a networking design.

## Why should an AI engineer care?

Here the talk turns to the algorithms. Shor's algorithm for factoring, which underpins internet security, and Grover's algorithm for unstructured search both run far faster on quantum hardware than the best classical alternatives. Niemiec adds k-nearest-neighbour search, the workhorse behind vector indexes in AI apps, and the variational quantum eigensolver as candidates for quantum speed-ups, plus a possible boost for reinforcement learning.

His scale argument goes through address spaces: 8-bit gave us 256 directly addressable values, 32-bit gave us 4 GB, 64-bit gives 16 exabytes. Then the quantum jump: just 512 qubits span 2^512 states, well past a googol. Three qubits already cover all eight 3-bit states at once until measured. He cites Google's claim that a calculation estimated at 47 years on classical hardware ran in 6 seconds on its quantum machine.

The timing is the point. Uber took 70 months to reach 100 million monthly users, Instagram 30, TikTok 9, ChatGPT 2. Niemiec's bet is that quantum hardware arrives just as AI demand is exploding.

## Where does it go from there?

The second half is a futurist's tour: robots with faces and expressions doing dangerous jobs, AI recreations of historical figures, vector embeddings in Oracle's database (find a house like this one, in another city, under a certain price), virtual reality replays of past conferences, implants, and the Black Mirror version of all of it, from ransomware on connected appliances to hacked pacemakers. He closes on ethics, sentience and the Sophia robot, and with a call to use the moment well.

## Who should watch

Anyone who wants the entanglement story told with history and humour, and leaders looking for a broad view of how quantum, AI and robotics might meet. If you want circuits, error-correction maths or benchmarks, this is not that talk; the physics is there to set up the bigger picture.

Title: Responsive components start on the smallest screen
Description: Nitish Mehrotra (Meta) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on adaptive web components built mobile first, with SSR, accessibility and design systems
Body:
A web component that only looks right on your monitor is half finished. At [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Nitish_Mehrotra_quantum_systems_future), Nitish Mehrotra, a software engineer at Meta, makes the case for building adaptive user experiences from the smallest viewport up, with responsive layout, performance, accessibility and server-rendered delivery treated as one discipline rather than four.

Expectations first: the title says quantum computing, but the talk is entirely about responsive web design, from Flexbox to progressive web apps. Come for frontend craft and you'll be well served; come for qubits and you won't.

## Why does responsiveness still matter?

Because the devices keep multiplying: phones, tablets, desktops, smart TVs, embedded screens. Early web teams built a separate site per device, which stopped scaling as device types grew; responsive design replaced that with one codebase that adapts. Mehrotra's point is that this isn't about shrinking images or fonts, it's about rethinking how content is delivered and used in each context.

He cites the figures that make the business case. Mobile accounted for 67% of global online traffic by 2021. "Nearly 60% of developer teams now prioritize responsive design to boost revenue and retention," Nitish Mehrotra said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024.

## What are the building blocks?

The fundamentals, explained cleanly:

- **Visual hierarchy and information density.** Larger headline type, contrast and white space steer the eye to what matters.
- **Layout APIs.** Flexbox and CSS Grid for flexible layouts, fluid grids in relative units instead of fixed pixels.
- **Media queries.** One stylesheet that adapts by width, height, orientation and resolution, instead of one per device.
- **Mobile first.** Design for the smallest screen and touch first, then progressively enhance. It forces you to decide what's essential, which helps users on slow connections most.

## How do performance and accessibility fit in?

As requirements, not polish. He cites case studies where responsive modules loaded 37% faster than non-responsive versions. The techniques are the familiar list: image optimisation, WebP, lazy loading, minified CSS and JavaScript, fewer HTTP requests, code splitting, and regular audits with Lighthouse or WebPageTest.

Accessibility gets the same treatment: semantic HTML for screen readers, sufficient colour contrast, ARIA attributes for dynamic content, keyboard navigation for every button and link, and WCAG as the benchmark.

## Where does architecture come in?

Responsive at scale needs a shift from client-side scripting to universal delivery. Server-side rendering builds HTML per request for faster loads and better SEO; static site generation builds it once and serves it from a CDN. Both reduce reliance on client-side JavaScript, often the real bottleneck. Frameworks such as React, Vue and Angular, with meta-frameworks like Next.js, let the same components render on the server or at build time.

Then the process layer: user research (interviews, surveys, usability testing) plus analytics tools such as Google Analytics, Hotjar and Crazy Egg to find where people drop out, a design system like Google's Material Design or IBM's Carbon for consistency, and cross-browser testing with tools like BrowserStack. Progressive web apps round it off with offline access and push notifications.

The talk illustrates each section with an unnamed case study: a mobile-first e-commerce redesign with 20% more mobile conversions, a news site whose SSR switch brought 25% more organic traffic, a travel site with 40% more completed bookings, a financial services design system that cut development time by 30%, and a retailer's PWA with 50% better retention. None of the companies are named, so treat the numbers as illustrations.

## Who should watch

Frontend engineers and designers who want a well-organised refresher, or a checklist to hand to a team new to responsive work. Seasoned frontend folks will recognise every item.

Title: Four ways to break a GenAI model, and what GRC can do about it
Description: Akshay Sekar (Intuit) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on poisoning, inversion, adversarial and backdoor attacks on GenAI, and AI in governance and compliance
Body:
A model is only as trustworthy as the data it learned from and the inputs it is fed, and attackers know it. At [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Akshay_Sekar_revolutionizing_cybersecurity_ai), Akshay Sekar, Senior Technical Compliance Manager at Intuit, sorts the threats into four attack classes, walks through three real-world-style incidents, and then flips the view: how GenAI itself is being used in governance, risk management and compliance (GRC).

It's an overview, aimed at people who own risk rather than people who train models. One note on scope: the abstract quotes efficiency, threat-prediction and compliance percentages, but the talk itself doesn't present those figures. What it does deliver is a clear taxonomy and a compliance lens.

## What are the four attacks?

Each one comes with how it works, an example and the defence:

- **Data poisoning.** Corrupt or crafted records slipped into training data skew the model. Alter the street-sign images an autonomous car learns from and it may misread stop signs. Defences: validate data before training, use only trusted sources, run anomaly detection during training.
- **Model inversion.** Carefully crafted queries let an attacker reconstruct or infer the private records a model was trained on, which is a serious problem for anything trained on medical data or personal identifiers. Defences: limit how much information the model outputs, and apply privacy techniques to obscure training data.
- **Adversarial inputs.** Noise humans can't see makes a model misclassify, such as a facial recognition system tagging an innocent person as a criminal. Defences: adversarial training on such examples, plus input validation that filters manipulated inputs.
- **Backdoors.** A trigger planted during training makes the model misbehave on cue, for example a surveillance system that conveniently ignores specific people. Defences: inspect training data rigorously, monitor model behaviour, detect anomalies in responses.

## What do the incidents look like?

Three case studies. A deepfake news anchor spreading geopolitical messaging, which undermines trust in media; mitigations include watching for lips and audio out of sync, deepfake detection tools and public awareness. A cloned CEO voice instructing a subordinate to transfer funds to an unauthorised account, which is the argument for MFA and auditable approval processes over voice authentication. And a trading algorithm whose training data was poisoned with tiny changes, so it traded at a loss while the attackers profited: the case for continuous auditing and anomaly detection on any model that moves money.

## How does GenAI help GRC?

The second half is where Sekar's day job shows:

- **Governance.** AI analyses corporate data to spot trends and forecast governance issues, monitors compliance with policies and regulation, and records decision paths so they can be audited.
- **Risk.** Banks already flag transactions that cross thresholds; models predict credit risk from transaction patterns and detect fraud and cyber attacks from network traffic.
- **Compliance.** Tools track regulatory changes, and in healthcare enforce HIPAA by encrypting patient data and controlling access by role, reducing human error and simplifying audits.

## What should a team actually do?

Start with threat modelling, vulnerability assessments and security audits before training, not after. Then real-time monitoring, encryption and access controls, patch management, an incident response plan, and adversarial examples in the training set. On the legal side he names GDPR, the California Consumer Privacy Act, BIPA for biometric data and the then-new EU AI Act, plus the open questions on AI-generated IP and liability when an autonomous system causes harm.

His closing line is the thesis: "the security of generative AI is not a technical issue, but rather a broad concern that impacts public trust and ethical deployment of technology," Akshay Sekar said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024.

## Who should watch

Compliance, risk and security leads who need a vocabulary for AI threats, and engineers who will be on the receiving end of their questions. ML security specialists will know the taxonomy already.

- Eugene Neelou's [gentle introduction to LLM security](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Eugene_Neelou_gentle_introduction_llm_security).
- Manuel Heinkel and Puria Izady on [securing your generative AI application](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Manuel_Heinkel_Puria_Izady_generative_ai_security).

Title: Stop placing quantum gates by hand; describe the function instead
Description: Vincent van Wingerden (Classiq) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on high-level quantum programming that synthesises hardware-aware circuits for you
Body:
Quantum programming today looks a lot like writing assembly with a pencil. At [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Vincent_van_Wingerden_programming_quantum_circuits), Vincent van Wingerden, Director of Commercial Partnerships at Classiq, argues that gate-level design doesn't scale to the circuits people actually want to run, and shows the alternative: write what the program should do, and let a synthesis engine decide how, for the specific machine you target.

This is a vendor talk: a short pitch for the Classiq platform with a live demo. It's also a clear explanation of why quantum software needs the jump that classical software made from assembly to compilers.

## Why doesn't gate-level design scale?

If you've seen a quantum circuit diagram, you know the picture: horizontal lines for qubits, boxes for the operations applied to them. A handful of qubits and a few gates is easy. A medium circuit takes much longer and much more thought about efficient construction. The big ones, the circuits behind quantum chemistry and other interesting use cases, are where hand-placement breaks down.

And it gets worse. A circuit that runs well on one machine can run badly on another, so you end up maintaining two versions. When a bigger machine with more qubits arrives, you reprogram to use them. All of it is manual.

## What does high-level synthesis change?

You describe the functionality, not the gates. That matters because "the same functionality can be achieved in various ways on a quantum computer," Vincent van Wingerden said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024, and a wrong implementation choice produces a less efficient circuit. Classiq's compiler, or synthesis engine, makes that choice for you.

The detail that makes it interesting is the second input: the target hardware. The compiler optimises for that specific machine, so moving to a new architecture or a bigger chip is a configuration change. In his words, "if you want to target a new machine with a different architecture or you have more qubit available, you do not need to reprogram anything." You can then inspect the synthesised circuit in an analyser, run it on providers such as Amazon, Azure and IBM from the platform, or export it as QASM and run it anywhere.

## What does the demo show?

Grover's algorithm, the unstructured search that beats a classical scan, set up to find integer values of a, b and c that satisfy a small arithmetic equation. In the web IDE you type the expression, choose the variable types (integer or float, decimal places, signed or unsigned), and pick the optimisation goal: the shallowest circuit or the fewest qubits.

He constrains the synthesis to 25 qubits, because the simulator he wants to run on tops out there, and optimises for depth. The engine produces the full Grover circuit, from variable initialisation through the oracle and the diffuser. Execution on the simulator gives a histogram whose peaks are the valid solutions. Start to finish took him about five minutes, which is the whole argument in one number.

## Has it been used on anything bigger?

Three examples. With Rolls-Royce, an HHL-based computational fluid dynamics study, billed as the largest simulation ever run on NVIDIA's cuQuantum: 39 qubits and 10 million gates. With an Italian bank, a new way of pricing rainbow options, implemented quickly enough to test whether the method worked. With another bank, research on which QAOA parameters give the best circuit for portfolio optimisation.

For context, Classiq describes itself as a team of about 65 with $63 million in funding, serving both enterprises and academia.

## Who should watch

Quantum developers tired of hand-tuning circuits per backend, and classical engineers who want to see what a compiler-first approach to quantum looks like. It's a product talk, so weigh it the way you'd weigh any vendor demo.

Title: The worst observability anti-pattern is not having a plan
Description: Indika Wimalasuriya (Virtusa) at Conf42 Observability 2024 maps log, metric and trace anti-patterns to AWS services, and names the missing plan as the worst
Body:
Two thirds of organisations run between two and five monitoring or observability tools, and almost a quarter still breached a contractual SLA in the last year. Indika Wimalasuriya, Associate Director and Senior Systems Engineering Manager at Virtusa, opens his Conf42 Observability 2024 talk with those Catchpoint SRE Report 2024 numbers, then walks pillar by pillar through the anti-patterns that make more tools fail to buy more reliability, and the AWS service he would reach for against each one.

Honest scope: this is a talk by an AWS Community Builder about why AWS is "your ally or the best friend" in observability. It is a catalogue and a mapping, not a demo.

## Why do more tools not mean fewer breaches?

The survey slide sets the puzzle. 64% of organisations say they should monitor endpoints even outside their physical control, 44% say learning from incidents has the most room for improvement, 24% breached a contractual SLA in the last 12 months, and 66% already use two to five tools. His reading: everyone agrees observability matters and failures are normal, yet the tooling keeps piling up without the results. "So something is not working," as he puts it.

The cause, in his telling, is the usual trio of microservices, cloud and the shift from predefined monitoring to observing unknowns. More data sources, more data, more failure points, and the unknowns surface "in the most unexpected times".

## Logs: too many, not structured

The first anti-pattern is excessive, unstructured logging that turns into noise. His answer is centralising in Amazon CloudWatch (with CloudTrail), and leaning on newer CloudWatch features he names in the talk: log anomaly detection and natural language search, which help when you are stuck with messy logs you can't rewrite this quarter.

## Metrics: plenty of numbers, wrong ones

Three metric anti-patterns get their own rows. Unclear and misaligned SLIs and SLOs that don't match business or user expectations. Bad sampling intervals, which leave you either without data when you need it or drowning in it. And monitoring piles of metrics unrelated to customer experience, which he describes as a false sense of comfort. The AWS side: CloudWatch custom metrics and alarms built around SLIs and SLOs, configurable resolution, and AWS Compute Optimizer for steering towards the metrics that matter.

## Traces: the pillar nobody prioritises

Tracing has the longest list: traces not given priority, inconsistent trace IDs, code that isn't instrumented properly, over-instrumentation, long spans that cover a whole request lifecycle, and real user monitoring data never joined to APM data. AWS X-Ray carries most of these (consistent trace IDs across services, sampling rates, X-Ray SDKs), with OpenTelemetry as the option if you prefer it, and AWS Step Functions for breaking up long spans. His favourite detail is how cheap the first step is: with AWS Lambda, "enabling x ray is probably a one click."

## End to end: alert floods and blind spots

The big-picture anti-patterns are the ones on-call engineers recognise: alert overload and fatigue (CloudWatch Alarms with anomaly detection, Amazon SNS), disjointed tools with too many dashboards, ignored non-functional requirements (managed services such as Lambda and RDS), not understanding upstream and downstream dependencies (CloudFormation, Systems Manager), and environments that drift between prod, staging and test (Elastic Beanstalk, CodePipeline).

## Why is the missing plan the biggest one?

The closing section is the part worth the video. Teams jump straight into tooling. What he asks for instead is an observability maturity model with an end game: from reactive to proactive, to predictive, to autonomous, applied to logs, metrics and traces as well as infrastructure, networking and security. He is explicit that his model is not meant to be copied as is; build one that suits you, so that "observability is not just a destination, it's a journey," Indika Wimalasuriya said at Conf42 Observability 2024.

Progress gets measured in business terms: MTTD, MTTR, mean time between failures, availability, user experience, resource use, developer velocity and alignment with SLOs. If the business can't see the value, he warns, the business won't fund it.

## Who should watch

Teams on AWS who suspect they have the tools but not the results, and anyone who wants a checklist of observability anti-patterns to audit against. If you run multi-cloud or don't use AWS, the anti-pattern list still holds; the service mapping won't.

Title: Open source Kubernetes monitoring still sends you a bill
Description: Michael Levan at Conf42 Observability 2024 installs kube-prometheus and Datadog on EKS, and argues open source monitoring is never actually free
Body:
Every team picking a Kubernetes monitoring stack ends up having the same argument: run it yourself for free, or pay a vendor. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Michael Levan, trainer, consultant and content creator, settles it with a demo of both on the same EKS cluster and one blunt point: the free option has a bill too, it just arrives as salaries and nodes.

It is a short, hands-on session. No architecture diagrams, mostly a terminal, Helm and two browser tabs.

## What counts as monitoring and what counts as observability?

Levan draws the line quickly. Monitoring is graphs, alerting and "seeing everything on a screen". Observability, in his framing, is "more around the idea of taking action". Then he gets to the part he cares about: two realms, homegrown open source and enterprise SaaS, installed side by side so you can judge the difference yourself.

## Why install kube-prometheus instead of Prometheus and Grafana?

The first half runs on an EKS cluster, though he notes the steps are close to identical on AKS, GKE or on-prem. Everything goes in through Helm, because he would rather manage one chart than a pile of separate Kubernetes manifests.

The choice of kube-prometheus over a plain Prometheus plus Grafana install is about dashboards. Install the two separately and you start with an empty Grafana. Install kube-prometheus and you get a set of Kubernetes dashboards out of the box: API server, compute resources, CPU, memory. He port-forwards to Grafana, logs in with the chart's default admin credentials (change those before anyone else finds them) and then imports a community Argo CD dashboard by its ID in a few clicks. His advice on custom dashboards: "don't reinvent the wheel if you don't have to."

He is also clear about the gap. kube-prometheus gives you the monitoring piece. For the full logs, traces and metrics picture you add Tempo for traces and Loki for logs on top of Prometheus.

## Where does the cost hide in a self-hosted stack?

This is the sharpest part of the talk. The open source stack costs nothing to download, and Levan immediately takes that back: you pay for the engineers who run it and for the infrastructure it runs on. He puts it in startup terms, too. If everyone is already working 13 hours a day, adding another tool to babysit may not be the smart move, or it might be, depending on how the team is set up.

## What does the Datadog side look like?

The second half installs Datadog on the same cluster. Create an API key, export it with the cluster name, add the Datadog Helm chart and run what he calls a "fairly large helm installation" configured for high availability: multiple replicas, kube-state-metrics, container log collection. He says it takes two to three minutes for data to appear.

Then the tour: the Kubernetes overview and explorer, every namespace (including the monitoring namespace that kube-prometheus just created, a nice touch), and the drill-down on a single pod showing its cluster, service, host, deployment, replica set, IPs, metadata, related resources, logs and metrics, all in one place. Signing up is free, and he says he has been demoing Datadog for a long time without a bill because he deletes everything straight after.

He does not pretend the SaaS side is cheap. "Now, Datadog is expensive, don't get me wrong," Michael Levan said at Conf42 Observability 2024. He even refuses to call it the more enterprise-grade option, since the Grafana and Prometheus stack can give the same feel. What you buy is a stack someone else runs, with support behind it.

## So which one should you pick?

His closing line is the takeaway of the whole session: "Either way you're paying. You're either paying engineers to manage it and the infrastructure to run it on, or you're paying a SaaS solution." The right answer depends on your organisation, not on the licence.

## Who should watch

Engineers standing up monitoring for a first production Kubernetes cluster, and leads who need a quick, vendor-neutral way to frame the build versus buy conversation. If you already run a tuned Prometheus, Loki and Tempo setup, this is a 101 and you can skip it.

Title: The quantum computer is more than the golden chandelier
Description: Archit Srivastava (o9 Solutions) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on the full quantum hardware stack, the qubit architectures and India's quantum mission
Body:
Search for a picture of a quantum computer and you get the golden chandelier: a dilution refrigerator hanging from the ceiling. At [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Archit_Srivastava_principium_hardware_ecosystem), Archit Srivastava, Senior Technical Consultant in data engineering at o9 Solutions and founder of the quantum hardware community AiQyaM, argues that the fridge is only the bottom of the stack, and that a country without people who understand the rest of it won't get useful quantum software either.

The talk is called Principium, Latin for the beginning, and it's pitched that way: an introduction to quantum hardware, the global market, and where India stands. Expect a guided tour rather than physics derivations.

## What is actually in a quantum computer?

Start at the bottom of the fridge. The qubits sit at around ten millikelvin, under layers of cryogenic shields, quantum amplifiers, superconducting coil lines and input microwave lines, with the temperature dropping at every stage on the way down. "It is not just the dilution refrigerator or the picture that we generally see of a quantum computer," Archit Srivastava said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024.

Above the qubits sits a whole classical machine. Control and readout electronics span room temperature down to the cold stages: readout transceivers built on FPGAs, DACs and ADCs that read many qubits at once, and cryogenic CMOS chips to ease the input/output bottleneck. Above that come firmware for hardware error mitigation, error correction, circuit and hardware optimisation, logic-level compilation, and finally the algorithms and user interfaces. If you come from classical systems, it's a familiar layer cake with a very cold bottom layer.

## Which qubit architecture wins?

None yet, which is the point of the section. Srivastava walks through three:

- **Superconducting qubits**, coupled through resonators, the route behind IBM's Condor chip with more than a thousand qubits.
- **Trapped ions**, controlled with laser beams that can entangle any two ions in the chain. He points to a compact trapped-ion demonstrator that fits into standard equipment racks, with modules for optics, readout, electronics and fibre routing.
- **Photonic qubits**, which use photons as the building blocks and, he argues, are easier to realise than superconducting machines.

The architecture matters for more than performance: which one a country can build depends on the materials and suppliers it has access to.

## How big is the market?

He quotes the market forecasts: the global quantum computing market was about $500 million in 2021 and is expected to reach $1.76 billion by 2026, a 30.2% CAGR, rising to $2.5 billion by 2030. Hardware alone was valued at $300 million in 2021, projected to hit $1.3 billion by 2027, dominated by IBM, D-Wave, Rigetti and IonQ with startups closing in. He counts 102 companies shaping the field and notes that the number grows constantly.

## Where is India in all this?

The National Quantum Mission plans to invest about INR 8,000 crore over five years in quantum computing, communication and sensing, skilled people, labs and testbeds. Srivastava lists the Indian ecosystem he's part of, from Quantum Computing India and BosonQ Psi to academic groups such as IIT Madras and TIFR, and expects India to become a significant contributor by 2030, with a focus on cryptography, simulation and AI applications. His theme throughout: quantum programmes need academia, industry and government working together.

Use cases get a quick roll call at the end: protein folding, quantum chemistry, design optimisation, supply chains, disease risk prediction and portfolio optimisation, on a 50 to 100 year horizon.

## Who should watch

Software people who have only ever seen quantum through an SDK and want a picture of the hardware underneath, and anyone tracking India's quantum ecosystem. Hardware engineers will find it introductory.

Title: Your open source download count is mostly bots, and other lessons from Scarf
Description: Avi Press (Scarf) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on what a billion open source downloads reveal - 100 downloads per user, bots, and nobody upgrading
Body:
A million downloads might be a million users, or one Watchtower instance with an itchy trigger finger. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Avi Press, founder and CEO of Scarf, shares what his company learned from analyzing more than a billion downloads of about 2,500 open source packages: on average there are roughly 100 downloads per unique user, much of the volume comes from automated systems, and most users never download a second version.

It is observability pointed at an unusual target, the adoption of the software rather than its runtime, and the numbers will change how you read every download badge.

## Where does the data come from?

Scarf runs a gateway in front of package and container registries. Maintainers publish through it, Scarf redirects the request to Docker Hub, PyPI, npm, GitHub releases or wherever the artifact lives, and passively records the metadata on the way. The IP address is enriched with metadata from providers such as Clearbit and 6sense (plus plain WHOIS) and then deleted along with other PII. The dataset mixes commercial and non-commercial projects, single-vendor and foundation-hosted ones (Apache, Linux Foundation, CNCF), and it skews American because Scarf's customers do.

The scale at analysis time: about 19 million anonymized origin IDs and 670 million downloads in the first quarter of the year alone.

## What counts as a user?

There is no login, so nobody knows exactly. Scarf uses two estimates that err in opposite directions. An endpoint ID is a hashed IP address, which undercounts: a corporate VPN puts thousands of people behind one egress IP. An origin ID hashes IP, user agent and other headers, which overcounts: one developer downloads from home, a café and the office. The real number sits between them.

About 2% of downloads come through detectable VPNs, he estimates at least 2.2%, so they don't wreck the analysis.

## Why are download graphs unreliable?

Because the ratio of total downloads to unique users averages about 100 to one, and swings from around 15 to one for some projects to far higher for others. CI pipelines, artifact mirrors, web crawlers, Renovate bot, Skopeo, Diun and Uptime Robot all show up as high-volume, low-signal clients. LinuxServer.io, which repackages popular apps as containers and was approaching 20 billion downloads, found in Scarf data that about half the pulls of its WireGuard image came from 20 users, probably misconfigured or overly eager update tools.

Avi doesn't soften the implication for investors who funded projects on their charts. He said at Conf42 Observability 2024 that "these download graphs are not reliable in any way, shape or form."

## What else shows up in a billion downloads?

- **Open source is everywhere.** Every country except a couple of near-empty territories, including points close to both poles. Government networks download it across most of the world, with the US, Brazil and Australia leading, even though governments rarely file GitHub issues.
- **Big business uses it.** About 1.2 million distinct businesses appear, covering 95% of the Fortune 500, measured from live traffic with no self-reporting.
- **Clouds and registries.** AWS dominates hosting traffic, with Hetzner third. Docker Hub leads container registries and was taking share back from GitHub Container Registry, with Quay a distant third.
- **User agents vary wildly.** Pip earns praise for sending a readable JSON blob with CPU architecture, a CI flag and system details. Homebrew and Docker do well too. Go's HTTP client, used under the hood by Helm, Kubernetes and plenty else, tells the server almost nothing.
- **Nobody upgrades.** `latest` is the top version for more than three quarters of packages, and most users who download a specific version never come back for another. Shipping a security patch is not the same as anyone running it.

## Why should maintainers care?

Avi's argument goes beyond vanity metrics. The registries already hold this data and mostly don't share it with the people who arguably own it. Companies that can't see how their open source is used struggle to commercialize it, hit a growth wall, and reach for license changes. Better, responsibly collected usage data is, in his view, part of keeping open source businesses on open source licenses.

His takeaways: pair raw downloads with a uniqueness measure, put rich information in your package manager's user agent if you maintain one, be pessimistic about upgrade adoption, and remember that your software is probably used far more widely than your issue tracker suggests.

## Who should watch

Open source maintainers, DevRel and product people at commercial open source companies, and anyone who has quoted a download number in a pitch deck. It is a vendor talk in that Scarf collects this data, but the findings stand on their own.

Title: Quantum warfare: QKD works, quantum radar is still a prototype
Description: Komal Pandya (Indian Institute of Technology, Patna) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on which military quantum tech works today, from QKD to radar
Body:
Most quantum hype collapses into one question: what works now? At [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Komal_Pandya_quantum_warfare_advancements), Komal Pandya, a doctoral researcher in computer science at the Indian Institute of Technology, Patna, answers it for defence, technology by technology, with a status line for each: quantum key distribution is commercially available, quantum clocks are lab prototypes being miniaturised, and quantum radar is still proof of concept.

It's the most thorough survey of the event, a long and structured walk through quantum computing, communication and sensing, what each would do on a battlefield and what's blocking it. If you want one talk that maps the whole field with honest maturity labels, this is it.

## Where does quantum computing help a military first?

Not on a soldier's laptop. "Due to their size and need for cryogenics, quantum computers are unlikely to be personal devices in the near future," Komal Pandya said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024. They run as cloud-accessed subroutines inside classical programs.

Two areas get the attention. Quantum machine learning for threat classification, big-data intelligence processing and combat simulation is still research, held back by error correction, encoding classical data into quantum states and the lack of stable quantum memory. Quantum optimisation (QAOA, QUBO on annealers, and quantum-inspired classical algorithms) is further along, with proof-of-concept results in logistics, traffic and finance, and obvious military uses in mission planning, resource allocation and supply chains. Her timeline: better error correction within five years, machines with hundreds to thousands of qubits in five to ten, and fault-tolerant systems in ten to twenty.

## Is quantum communication ready?

Partly. QKD, with the BB84 and E91 protocols, uses the no-cloning theorem so any eavesdropper disturbs the key and gets noticed. Products are on the market, and China's quantum science satellite has shown entanglement-based secure links over hundreds of kilometres.

The catch is engineering: point-to-point links, no efficient quantum repeaters yet, expensive single-photon hardware, fibre ranges of tens to hundreds of kilometres, and side-channel attacks on real implementations. Post-quantum cryptography is the parallel track. Shor's algorithm threatens RSA, Diffie-Hellman and ECC (ECC's shorter keys make it the easier target), while symmetric ciphers and hashes mostly survive with bigger keys. Her advice: prioritise PQC and build crypto-agility now.

## What can quantum sensors do?

This is the most concrete section. Chip-scale atomic clocks reach an uncertainty of 2 × 10⁻¹², quantum-logic single-ion clocks about 9 × 10⁻¹⁸, precise enough to measure height differences on Earth to a centimetre. That matters for GPS-free navigation, missile guidance and synchronising operations.

Quantum radar could spot stealth aircraft and resist jamming, but "quantum radar systems currently have limitations in range and power," as she puts it, and entanglement doesn't survive real-world noise well. Quantum imaging (ghost imaging, SPAD arrays) promises seeing around corners and in low light. Underwater, SQUID magnetometers could detect submarines from up to 6 km, against a few hundred metres for classical magnetic anomaly detectors.

## Who is spending what?

The US and China lead. US quantum investment went from $500 million in 2015 to about $2.1 billion in 2021; China's grew from $300 million to an estimated $13 billion over the same period. The quantum warfare market was valued at $134.66 million in 2022 and is forecast to reach $540.91 million by 2031, a 16.8% CAGR.

She closes on the non-technical blockers: ethics and the laws of war, a possible new arms race, standards and interoperability across nations, training military personnel, and funding sustainably.

## Who should watch

Security engineers deciding how urgent PQC is, and anyone who wants a status board for quantum tech that separates shipped from speculative. It's long and dense; keep the video's chapters handy.

Title: Where did the account-opening event go? Observing event-driven apps on AWS
Description: Urmila Raju (AWS) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on observing event-driven apps on AWS - business SLAs first, then CloudWatch metrics, logs and X-Ray traces
Body:
A bank promises that a savings account opened in the mobile app will be live in two hours. A day later the customer calls: still nothing. The mobile team sees the request placed successfully; the core banking team never got it. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Urmila Raju, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, uses that story to show how to make an event-driven application observable on AWS, starting from the business SLA and working down to CloudWatch metrics, logs and X-Ray traces.

It is an AWS-native talk, and it says so: the tools are CloudWatch, X-Ray and Lambda Powertools. The method, SLA first and telemetry second, carries over to any stack.

## Why is event-driven architecture hard to observe?

Urmila is a fan of EDA: loosely coupled teams ship independently, failures stay contained, async processing scales, and designing around business events brings business and technology people to the same table. But it is hard to get right, for three reasons: eventual consistency, end-to-end performance that suffers from one slow component, and business SLAs that span synchronous, near-real-time and batch steps.

Her opening question is the whole talk in one line: "So what happened to the account opening request? Or should I say, what happened to the account opening event?"

## Start with the SLAs, not the dashboards

The example workflow comes from event storming: the customer logs in, picks a product, eligibility gets checked, the request is placed, the account is opened, then interest schedules, push notifications, a welcome email and a survey follow, each from its own domain. The SLAs are explicit. Requests 24/7. Eligibility in real time, defined as 100 milliseconds. Account operational within two hours. Mobile notification within two hours. Welcome email within a day.

The architecture behind it uses API Gateway and Lambda for the synchronous eligibility check, EventBridge and SQS to carry the request to an on-premises core banking system, and EventBridge again to fan out the account-opened event. With serverless, the lower monitoring layers are AWS's job, so you can focus on application and business observability. The questions to answer: what if eligibility takes more than 100 ms, the account service is down, or the push notification fails?

## Which metrics catch a lost event?

Urmila walks up the AWS observability maturity model: foundational monitoring, intermediate insights, advanced correlation and anomaly detection, proactive root-cause identification. By her estimate, the built-in CloudWatch metrics cover about 70% of observability needs. The ones that matter here:

- **SQS** is pull-based, so `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage` rising means the consumer isn't keeping up. Alarm on it well before the two-hour SLA runs out.
- **EventBridge** is push-based, so the broker owns retries. Configure retries and a dead-letter queue based on the business SLA, then watch `DeadLetterQueueInvocations`: anything landing there is a failed event.
- **Lambda** invocations, duration, memory and concurrency, and **API Gateway** counts, latency, errors and throttling, which can be a deliberate defense rather than a problem.

Organize them with a namespace per application and dimensions per function, queue or event bus. For business metrics like sign-ups or revenue, emit custom metrics from the Lambda code, preferably through the Embedded Metric Format, which writes them asynchronously, instead of the synchronous PutMetric API that adds to execution time.

## Logs, insights and traces

Lambda Insights splits a function's time into cold start, bootstrap and execution, and finds memory leaks, costly functions and regressions after a new version; if eligibility alone runs longer than 100 ms, you know where the SLA went. API Gateway logs at ERROR or INFO level, and metric filters turn log patterns, such as a count of 403s, into metrics. CloudWatch Logs Insights queries find the 100 most expensive executions or the last 100 errors, and a natural-language query generator (in preview at the time) writes the query syntax for you.

For proactive work: threshold alarms routed to SNS or an incident tool, anomaly detection alarms that learn daily patterns (hundreds of account requests at midnight might be an attack, not a marketing win), and log pattern analysis that flags log shapes it has never seen. AWS X-Ray traces requests through API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB, and through EventBridge if the producer propagates the trace header, building a service map that shows where the 100 ms went. CloudWatch ServiceLens puts it all in one view.

## The eight-step checklist

Observe what matters to the business, measure against SLAs, identify telemetry sources, plan an alerting strategy with severities and actions, design dashboards for specific audiences, pick tools (OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Grafana are valid choices on AWS too), make observability part of operational readiness, and iterate.

## Who should watch

Teams building serverless or event-driven systems on AWS, especially anyone who has lost an event between two queues. If you are not on AWS, the SLA-first method and the broker metrics still translate.

Title: Breeding better security scanners with genetic algorithms
Description: Pratik Thantharate (Paycor) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on AI/ML for DevSecOps - evolved vulnerability detectors, LSTM monitoring and generated playbooks
Body:
Most security scanners are tuned by hand, one threshold at a time, until the false positives stop annoying people or the false negatives start. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Pratik Thantharate, Principal Software Engineer in Test at Paycor and a researcher in DevOps, ML and security, proposes letting evolution do the tuning: treat the scanner's parameters as genes, breed them against known vulnerable samples, and keep the fittest. He reports 30% fewer false positives and 25% better detection of novel vulnerabilities than the previous tooling.

The talk is a research overview of AI/ML across observability and DevSecOps, delivered fast and at a high level. The genetic algorithm section is the one with the most substance.

## Why traditional DevOps practices strain

Pratik's setup is familiar. DevOps broke down silos and sped up deployment, but environments now span microservices, serverless functions, containers and cloud services, and the logs, metrics and traces they emit arrive faster than people can read them. Rule-based anomaly detection struggles with that dynamism; ML models can learn what normal looks like across many metrics and flag multidimensional anomalies, such as an unusual pattern of API calls that might mean a breach rather than a simple CPU spike.

For root-cause analysis he points to causal inference and graph analysis, with an example worth keeping: a database slowdown traced back to a network misconfiguration three hops away.

## Can ML keep pace with continuous deployment?

"So in DevOps, speed cannot come at the cost of safety," Pratik said at Conf42 Observability 2024, and his answer is ML as a security multiplier. Threat detection models analyze network traffic, logs and user behavior to spot subtle, evolving attack patterns that signature-based tools miss. Vulnerability management becomes continuous scanning plus predictive analysis of which parts of an ever-changing attack surface are likeliest to be targeted, so defenses get prioritized. Threat modeling, traditionally a slow manual exercise, can be automated: map the architecture, find the data flows, flag the attack vectors and suggest mitigations.

## How do you evolve a vulnerability detector?

Genetic algorithms show up in two places in his work. First, generating test cases: variation produces unusual API call sequences and race conditions that a predefined suite wouldn't think of.

Second, and more interesting, tuning the detectors themselves. Each parameter, a pattern-matching rule or an anomaly threshold, is a gene. Candidate configurations run against a dataset of known vulnerable code; those that find real vulnerabilities while raising few false alarms count as fit. Selection, crossover and mutation run over thousands of generations. The result he reports is the 30% drop in false positives and 25% gain on novel vulnerabilities, which in practice means a security team that spends less time triaging noise. The talk doesn't detail the dataset or baseline, so read the numbers as his team's result rather than a general benchmark.

## What is an intelligent monitor?

Pratik describes a cognitive ops engine built on LSTM networks, which are good at sequences, trained on the stream of logs, metrics and traces from tools like New Relic and AppDynamics and on past incidents. When new telemetry arrives, the model reads it as a narrative rather than isolated data points. A generative model, GPT-3 in his description, then writes a playbook in plain language: for a looming database deadlock, something like a note that the pattern resembles a past incident, a suggestion to raise the connection limit and retry, and the exact command. Experience replay, borrowed from reinforcement learning, lets the engine revisit past incidents and learn which actions worked.

## What can go wrong?

He is clear about the risks. Models are only as good as their training data, and biased or incomplete datasets mean missed threats or false positives. Deep learning is opaque, which is a problem when the decision is security-critical, so interpretable techniques matter for trust. Analyzing user behavior raises privacy concerns, for which he suggests differential privacy, and autonomous decisions in a pipeline need governance. The people side matters too: DevOps engineers need ML basics, data scientists need to understand DevOps workflows, and security experts should steer the ethics.

## Who should watch

Security and platform engineers looking for ideas on where ML fits in a DevSecOps pipeline, especially the genetic tuning idea, which you could try on your own scanner rules. Expect concepts and results, not code.

Title: Terraform builds the box, Chef locks it down
Description: Karthik Jataprole (Workday) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on splitting cloud security automation between Terraform provisioning and Chef config
Body:
Hand-configured security drifts, and drift is where the breaches live. At [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Karthik_Jataprole_cloud_security_automation), Karthik Jataprole of Workday makes the case for a clean division of labour: Terraform provisions the cloud resources, Chef configures and hardens what runs on them, and both live in version control so every security change has an audit trail.

It's a short practitioner talk from someone who has used Terraform for about eight years, across AWS, Google Chronicle and Splunk Cloud. It's an overview with one worked example, not a code walkthrough, and the event name aside, there's no quantum in it.

## Why automate security infrastructure at all?

Because people make mistakes in consoles. Manual security configuration is prone to human error and inconsistency, and inconsistency multiplies when your footprint spans Asia Pacific, Europe and the Americas. Jataprole lists the payoffs: consistent configuration in every environment, fewer misconfigurations, better compliance with security best practices, faster deployment and scaling of security infrastructure, and more productive IT teams.

He also points out who benefits beyond the platform team: CERT teams, SOC teams, security compliance and global compliance teams all need to see and trust the same configuration, and a repo gives them one place to look.

## Who does what: Terraform or Chef?

The split is the useful bit:

- **Terraform** provisions: virtual machines, VPNs, VPCs, transit gateways, networks, storage and EBS volumes. You declare an EC2 instance with its volumes and sizes in the code and Terraform makes it so.
- **Chef** configures: installing security software, configuring firewalls, pushing configs, managing LDAP roles and AD groups, using its cookbook repositories.

Together they cover the security infrastructure lifecycle, including automated hardening and patching. On speed, he's a fan: with Terraform "you can scale up, expand, destroy, deploy configurations, everything in a matter of less than two minutes," Karthik Jataprole said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024.

## What does it look like in a hybrid estate?

The case study is a large enterprise with a hybrid cloud spanning the US, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and Asia. On-premises servers get their configuration from Chef. Anything in the cloud (AWS, Chronicle, Splunk Cloud) is Terraform, with network security groups and resources described in files like `main.tf` and `networking.tf`, and Chef configuring the security controls on top.

The result: better security posture, less manual effort and faster time to market. His example: once the networking team has the account ready, standing up a service in New Zealand, with VPC network, transit gateways and scaling, takes about an hour, and tearing it down is just as quick.

## What are the gotchas?

- **Learning curve.** Two tools, two languages.
- **Repo hygiene.** Every change checked in, peer reviewed, approved and merged; always work off a fresh pull.
- **Integration.** Existing on-prem security tools need a path into the pipeline.
- **Access to the repo itself.** Keep the Terraform repo restricted to the team that owns it, not open across the company, for compliance reasons. Your infrastructure code is a map of your infrastructure.

Looking ahead, he expects integration with cloud security posture management (CSPM) and cloud workload protection platforms (CWPP), a shift towards policy as code and compliance as code, and more automated security testing and remediation.

## Who should watch

Teams running both cloud and on-prem fleets who are deciding where provisioning stops and configuration management starts. If you already have Terraform and Chef in one pipeline, this will confirm your choices rather than change them.
