Title: AI fraud detection in banking - the numbers, and the questions to ask
Description: Giriprasad Manoharan (Atyeti) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on AI and data engineering for bank fraud detection - up to 90% accuracy, 25% fewer false positives
Body:
Rule-based fraud systems in banks catch too little and flag too much. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Giriprasad Manoharan, Senior Data Engineer at Atyeti, makes the case that real-time data pipelines plus careful feature engineering let AI models do better on both counts, citing detection accuracy of up to 90% and up to 25% fewer false positives.

Set expectations first: this is a five-minute overview, a run through the headline results and principles rather than an architecture or a code walkthrough. It is worth a watch for the framing and the numbers, as long as you bring your own follow-up questions, and we suggest a few below.

## Why do traditional systems fall short?

The starting point is the baseline. According to the talk, traditional fraud detection catches only 50-70% of fraud, while around 30% of what it flags turns out to be legitimate. Both numbers hurt. Missed fraud is direct loss; false positives are blocked cards, angry customers and analysts burning hours on cases that were never fraud. Giriprasad's point is that these limits strain resources and erode customer trust at the same time.

## Where does data engineering come in?

His argument is that the model is only as good as the pipeline in front of it. Two pieces carry the load:

- **Real-time pipelines** that process and analyze large transactional datasets as they arrive, rather than in overnight batches.
- **Feature engineering** that reduces dimensionality and turns raw transactions into a cleaner, more informative input, which he credits for detection accuracy reaching up to 90%.

On top of that, optimized models cut false positives by up to 25% while keeping detection sensitivity high, and case studies from financial institutions show fraud occurrences down by up to 40% along with operational efficiency gains.

## Why does interpretability matter more in a bank?

This is the most practical point in the talk. Giriprasad said at Conf42 Observability 2024 that models "need to be interpretable and scalable, particularly in dynamic banking environments". Regulators expect to see why a transaction was blocked, and transaction volumes only grow, so a model that is accurate but opaque, or accurate but can't scale, doesn't ship.

He also links fraud detection to customer trust: a system that catches more and bothers fewer honest customers is a security feature customers notice.

## What the talk leaves for you to ask

Because the format is short, the figures arrive without methodology, and that is where a practitioner should dig. Before trusting any vendor or paper with similar numbers, it is worth asking:

- Is the 25% a relative cut in false positives (30% becoming about 22.5%) or a drop of 25 points?
- Is "accuracy" measured on a balanced set? Fraud is rare, so accuracy on raw transaction data can look excellent while recall stays poor; precision and recall tell you more.
- Which features did the work, and how fresh do they need to be for real-time scoring?
- How is explainability delivered to analysts and regulators, per decision or per model?

None of these are criticisms of the talk; they are what turns a headline into something you can benchmark against.

## Who should watch

Data engineers moving into fraud or risk teams who want the shape of the problem in one sitting, and engineering managers who need the business case for a feature pipeline. If you want model architectures and evaluation detail, look elsewhere.

Title: Behind every ChatGPT prompt is a stack of cloud abstractions
Description: Karan Khanna (Coupang) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on how IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless shape private, hybrid and SaaS GenAI deployments
Body:
Type a prompt into ChatGPT and the model is the smallest part of what answers you. At [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Karan_Khanna_cloud_ai_scalability), Karan Khanna, an engineer at Coupang, maps the rest: the GenAI building blocks, the cloud abstractions that host them, and the three ways organisations deploy the lot, from fully in-house to SaaS.

It's an introductory talk, presented as his personal views, and a good one if you need a clean mental model of where GenAI sits on top of cloud infrastructure. Despite the event, no quantum is involved.

## What actually has to run for a GenAI app?

Khanna lists the building blocks: foundation models (FMs), large language models as a subset of them trained on language, the trained model with its learned weights, inference code that bridges model and application, data pipelines for preprocessing and formatting, and an API or web layer to send prompts and receive output.

Then the parts nobody demos: monitoring and alerting, auto-scaling groups, load balancers, API gateways, integration services, CI/CD and regulatory and security gates. "When you go to chat GPT, for example, when you enter any text prompt, it doesn't give you the answer by itself," Karan Khanna said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024. It has a lot of moving pieces, and every one of them needs a home.

## Which cloud abstraction is which, in house-hunting terms?

His analogy works. IaaS (EC2, Azure VMs) is buying the land from a builder: you skip the regulatory pain but build the house yourself. PaaS (Heroku, Cloud Foundry) is getting the house without wiring the subnets and firewalls. SaaS (HubSpot, Salesforce, Shopify) is moving into a finished place you can customise but don't build. FaaS, or serverless (AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions), is renting a room: you bring a function, someone else owns the building.

## In-house, hybrid or SaaS?

This is the core of the talk:

- **In-house or private.** End-to-end control and end-to-end responsibility. Models, LLMs, app and service layer all in your own data centres, typically with an orchestrator such as Kubernetes, Borg, Tupperware or Mesos. Think autonomous driving teams training on NVIDIA hardware, or a healthcare provider keeping patient data entirely inside its walls. Defence fits here too.
- **Hybrid.** Bring third-party or open models (from Google's Model Garden, Vertex AI or SageMaker) and keep application and inference code in your own data centre. Khanna says this applies to most use cases.
- **SaaS.** Everything in the cloud with the right controls (GDPR and the like), as in Google's AI Studio. Low-code and no-code app builders are the newest extension: drag, drop, ship a chatbot.

## What do the abstractions buy you?

Efficient resource allocation (serverless and auto-scaling absorb spikes), streamlined CI/CD and integrations, and scalability. The industry section is brief. In healthcare, the GenAI tool Klara cut phone-based patient interactions by 50% and raised patient satisfaction by 30%. In creative work, DALL-E and Adobe Firefly put image generation in more people's hands.

Title: An OpenTelemetry Collector component does nothing until a pipeline names it
Description: Steve Flanders and Curtis Robert (Splunk) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on configuring the OpenTelemetry Collector, from host metrics to the OTel demo
Body:
The OpenTelemetry Collector's YAML looks friendly until you add a processor and nothing changes. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Steve Flanders, Engineering Leader at Splunk, and Curtis Robert, Software Engineer at Splunk and an approver on the Collector's contrib repository, explain how Collector configuration actually works, then build one live from an empty file to a filtered Prometheus feed, and finish on the full OpenTelemetry demo in Kubernetes.

Steve has been on OpenCensus and OpenTelemetry since the start and was writing a book on the project at the time; Curtis does the typing, typos included, which makes the demo more useful, not less.

## What is the Collector, and where does it run?

A single Go binary that ingests, processes and exports traces, metrics and logs. Two placements are common. As an agent, a sidecar or a Kubernetes DaemonSet, one per host, it takes buffering and retry work off the application. As a gateway, a clustered standalone tier, it aggregates and filters; tail-based sampling or a one-off scrape of the Kubernetes API belong there. Instrumentation can send to an agent, the agent to a gateway, the gateway to one or more backends, or you can skip the Collector entirely.

Distributions matter more than people expect. Core (`opentelemetry-collector`) holds what a pure OpenTelemetry setup needs, OTLP in and out. Contrib (`opentelemetry-collector-contrib`) holds the vendor and community receivers, processors and exporters. There is a Kubernetes distribution with a Helm chart and an operator, and a builder for custom distributions, which Steve recommends for mature production setups that want a smaller attack surface.

## How is configuration put together?

Components come in five types: receivers (push or pull), processors, exporters, extensions such as health checks, authentication and service discovery, and the newer connectors, which act as an exporter in one pipeline and a receiver in another.

The key idea is that configuration takes two steps. You define and configure components at the top of the file, then you enable them in signal-specific service pipelines. Curtis put it plainly: "you can define as many components as you want, receivers, processors, exporters, connectors, but if they're not a pipeline, they will not be used."

Inside a pipeline, receiver and exporter order doesn't matter, but processor order does; whether you sample before you filter or filter before you sample is a business decision the YAML makes for you. A pipeline can receive OTLP and export Zipkin, which is what makes the Collector vendor-neutral. Docs for each component live in its README in the GitHub repos rather than on opentelemetry.io. You can also set config via command-line flags or environment variables expanded inside the YAML, and the OpenTelemetry Transformation Language (OTTL) was in development as a standard way to express transformations.

## The live build, step by step

Curtis starts with a binary from the releases page and a config of one receiver and one exporter: the host metrics receiver every 10 seconds with only the memory scraper (CPU and disk scrapers don't work on macOS), and the debug exporter at detailed verbosity. `system.memory.usage` appears with used, free and inactive data points.

Then he adds the resource detection processor with the system detector to stamp host name and OS type (first attempt: invalid key, the field is plural). Next a Prometheus exporter on localhost:8889 with resource-to-telemetry conversion turned on, so host attributes become labels; the metric shows up as `system_memory_usage_bytes` because Prometheus naming differs. Last, a filter processor drops data points where state is inactive, using the OpenTelemetry metric name, not the Prometheus one, since conversion happens in the exporter. After one more fix (inactive has to be a string), the inactive series stops in Prometheus.

## What does the OpenTelemetry demo show?

The official demo is a shop of microservices in .NET, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python and more, deployed to Kubernetes with Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger and OpenSearch behind the Collector. Curtis uses OTelBin to visualize the Collector config, then follows the traces pipeline into the spanmetrics connector, which turns spans into request count, error count and duration metrics that feed the metrics pipeline. After buying a few telescopes, Jaeger shows the checkout path across services written in different languages in one uniform view, and Grafana has dashboards for logs, the spanmetrics output and the Collector's own throughput and memory.

## Who should watch

Anyone who has copy-pasted a Collector config and hoped. If you are about to run the Collector in production, the agent-versus-gateway and distribution sections are worth the time alone.

Title: If it can send an HTTP request, it can send a trace
Description: Justin Scherer and Justin Snyder (Northwestern Mutual) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on a REST service turning CI jobs and human steps into OTel traces
Body:
OpenTelemetry is easy if you write code in a language with an SDK. It is a lot less easy for an ActionScript app, a no-code prototype, a GitLab pipeline or a four-eyes approval step. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Justin Scherer, Lead Software Engineer, and Justin Snyder, Manager DevOps Engineering, both at Northwestern Mutual, show the OTel rest-trace service they built: a small API that hides OpenTelemetry behind a few REST endpoints, so anything that can make an HTTP call can start a trace, add spans and close it.

It's a short talk, two code walkthroughs and a clear idea, and that idea travels well beyond insurance.

## What gap does it fill?

Scherer lists three. OpenTelemetry is simple for developers who live in code and arcane for everyone else. Legacy integration is sparse; mainframe users have the Open Mainframe Project, but plenty of other legacy tech has nothing, and he names ActionScript, which Adobe stopped supporting while companies kept running it. And manual human processes, like a request that one person approves and then a manager signs off, don't fit any instrumentation library.

You could call the OpenTelemetry ingestion API directly, but Snyder explains why few processes can: requests are protocol buffers with complicated formatting and responses, and you have to keep a copy of OpenTelemetry's schemas in your own code base and update it as they change. Put that behind a service, and the instrumentation and the connection to the observability backend become one point of ingestion that everything else talks to over plain HTTP.

They credit the open source TracePusher project as the starting point; the rest-trace service grew from using and extending it.

## Which use cases does that open up?

Four, in their list: technologies with no SDK, including in-house tools nobody else uses; manual processes such as deliveries or phone support; no-code platforms whose built-in APM isn't the one you use; and CI/CD systems like Jenkins, GitLab, GitHub and CircleCI. Justin Scherer said at Conf42 Observability 2024: "You now don't just have your DevOps loaded into APM, you also have bizops loaded in."

## What does it look like in code?

The first demo extends an Express app that already has standard OpenTelemetry instrumentation. The API handler calls the service to start a trace and gets back a trace ID, and that ID is the one thing you must carry everywhere, passing it into each function. Each business sub-process starts a span (getting a span ID back), adds a name and properties that show up as attributes, does its work and closes the span. A final call ends the trace and the service ships it to the backend. In Dynatrace, which the team uses day to day, you see one trace with two spans, their timings and the attributes you can query and alert on.

The second demo is a GitLab CI pipeline. The first stage starts a trace and writes the trace ID to a file passed between jobs; build and test each open and close a span; the last stage closes the trace. The span closure can carry the test result, so success or failure becomes part of the trace rather than a log line somewhere else. Since every context shares IDs, traces from the API, the pipeline and a human process can be linked into one end-to-end picture.

## What is still missing?

They are candid that it was early days. Teams inside the company were each creating traces their own way, so the first job is standardizing what deserves a trace and what goes into APM. The REST bodies map one-to-one to OpenTelemetry keys, which helps nobody who doesn't already know OpenTelemetry, and leads to a pile of near-duplicate attributes. And they planned to open source the tool.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers who want pipelines, legacy systems or business processes on the same trace view as their services. If you already emit spans from CI with a native integration, the design discussion is still worth the 20 minutes.

Title: AI runs the network today; quantum is the optimiser still on order
Description: Chaitanya Kadiyala (Arm) and Sadha Chilukoori (Meta) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on AI-run networks and where quantum optimisation fits next
Body:
Networks have outgrown the people who configure them by hand. At [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Chaitanya_Kadiyala_Sadha_Chilukoori_quantum_network_management), Chaitanya Kadiyala, Director of Product Marketing at Arm, and Sadha Chilukoori, a data engineer at Meta, split network management into two eras: AI, which already predicts failures and tunes traffic, and quantum computing, which they pitch as the optimiser and the security layer that comes after.

It is a short, high-level talk, closer to a strategy briefing than an engineering session. No architecture, no code, no named deployments. What it does well is put the AI and quantum claims in the right order: one is shipping, the other is a roadmap item.

## Why can't humans keep running the network?

Kadiyala opens with scale. Demands on networks are growing exponentially, and "the traditional manual methods of network management are no longer sufficient to cope with the complexity and the scale of modern networks," Chaitanya Kadiyala said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024. Anyone who has diffed two router configs at 2am will not argue.

## What does AI already do for the network?

Chilukoori takes the middle section and walks through three wins, each with a figure. The talk doesn't say where the figures come from, so read them as the speakers' estimates:

- **Predictive maintenance.** Models predict disruptions with accuracy often up to 90%, so issues get fixed before users notice.
- **Self-optimisation.** Systems adjust to traffic loads in real time, the way a self-driving car adjusts to the road, with efficiency gains of over 30% compared with traditional methods.
- **Automation of routine work.** Cutting manual tasks reduces operational cost by roughly 25% and frees engineers for work that isn't toil.

The examples come from outside networking as well: streaming recommendations, cars that adapt to the road and predictive maintenance in factories. Every section ends with the same move: quantum computing could take this further, by analysing bigger datasets or by searching solution spaces classical machines can't cover.

## Where does quantum actually fit?

The second half is the quantum case, and it is more careful than the abstract suggests. Two applications stand out.

**Optimisation.** Routing, resource allocation and traffic management are combinatorial problems. Quantum algorithms could, for example, route data packets to minimise latency and maximise throughput. That's the honest version of the promise: a better solver for problems network engineers already have.

**Security.** Quantum cryptography offers the prospect of encryption that can't be broken by computation, and quantum-resistant algorithms are being developed because quantum computers could break today's encryption standards. For networks, that second point is the one with a deadline.

The talk is also clear about the limits: quantum computers are early, there are hard technical problems before wide adoption, and there's a shortage of skilled quantum engineers and quantum-specific software.

## What should a team do first?

Their roadmap is sensible and has nothing quantum about it: assess your current infrastructure, find the areas to improve, roll AI in by phases rather than in one go, and work with experienced providers. Keep quantum on the roadmap, not in the change window.

## Who should watch

Managers and architects who need a quick framing of AI and quantum in network operations for a planning conversation. Network engineers looking for implementation detail won't find it here; the related talks below go deeper on the quantum side.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Sam Samuel on [quantum communication challenges in scaling quantum computers](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2022_Sam_Samuel_communication_challenges_scaling_quantum), the networking problem inside the machine.
- Robert Slade on [what quantum computing means for security](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2022_Robert_Slade_implications_for_security).
- Gayathri Jeganmohan on [quantum-powered IoT security](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Gayathri_Jeganmohan_quantum_iot_security).

Title: Instrumenting a Node.js service with OpenTelemetry without touching its code
Description: Zameer Fouzan (New Relic) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on wiring traces, metrics and logs into a Koa app with a wrapper file and the OTel Collector
Body:
The fastest way to start with OpenTelemetry is to leave your application alone. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Zameer Fouzan, Senior Developer Relations Engineer at New Relic, instruments a small Node.js service built on Koa for traces, metrics and logs using a single wrapper file loaded before the app starts, then routes everything through the OpenTelemetry Collector to a backend, with the source code untouched.

It is billed as a 101 and it is one, but a hands-on one: you watch the spans, metric histograms and log records appear in the console and then in New Relic, which plays the backend in the demo.

## What is OpenTelemetry, briefly?

A CNCF project formed in 2019 by merging OpenTracing and OpenCensus. It is a specification first: language SDKs implement a common API for traces, metrics and logs, with shared semantic conventions so attributes look the same whether you instrument Java today or something else tomorrow. Data leaves over OTLP, on HTTP or gRPC, to whichever backend you choose. Zameer opens with the familiar standoff between developers and ops, updated for the container era: "Today I've even heard people complaining that it's my container is working fine, you're just not deploying my container correctly."

## How do you instrument without changing the app?

The OpenTelemetry recommendation for Node.js is a separate wrapper file that Node loads before `index.js`, so instrumentation is in place from the first line. Inside it:

- **Traces**: a tracer provider with a resource carrying the service name, a batch span processor (the recommended one, to keep export overhead down) pointing at a local Collector, and W3C trace context and baggage propagators so requests can be stitched across services. `getNodeAutoInstrumentations` patches HTTP and Koa; he switches off the file-system instrumentation as noise.
- **Metrics**: a meter provider with a periodic exporting reader. The default flush is 60 seconds; you can go down to one, but he warns that an aggressive meter burns CPU, so tune it.
- **Logs**: a logger provider with simple and batch processors and the Bunyan instrumentation, which patches the existing logger so every record gains trace ID, span ID and severity. A log hook adds custom attributes such as the service name.

Exporters default to localhost on 4317 (gRPC) or 4318 (HTTP), so with a local Collector there is very little to configure. Always set a service name; otherwise everything arrives as an unknown service.

## Where does it pay off?

The demo calls a weather endpoint that hits an instrumented service on AWS, which in turn calls OpenWeatherMap. The trace map shows every hop, including the uninstrumented external one, and which service is slow. A request with a bad parameter returns a 404, and both services show red on the error view.

The good part is the join. Because log records carry trace and span IDs, you go from a failed trace to its log lines without leaving the screen, or from an error log straight to its trace. That cycle, he says, is what stops the dev-versus-ops blame game. Automatic instrumentation gives sparse error detail for external calls; that is the moment to add manual spans and custom error messages where you now know you need them.

## What does the Collector add?

Receivers, processors and exporters, wired together in service pipelines in a YAML file. He adds a host metrics receiver for memory, file system and network data, attaches an environment attribute to logs in a processor, and shows that dropping an exporter from a pipeline still lets the Collector process the data. Run it in Docker with the `contrib` image, which carries most community receivers, processors and exporters, and open ports 4317 and 4318.

On sampling, head-based gives an overall statistical view, tail-based keeps the actionable traces and cuts Collector CPU and span volume noticeably, and probabilistic sampling at a fixed percentage is his suggested starting point for new projects before refining tail-based policies.

His closing warning is the one to tape to the monitor: "Just having a form of automatic instrumentation and collecting telemetry is not observability." Zameer said at Conf42 Observability 2024 that OpenTelemetry "helps engineers work based on data and not opinion."

## Who should watch

Node.js developers who have never instrumented a service, and anyone who wants to see logs-to-traces correlation actually work end to end. If you already run the Collector in production, the sampling section is the part worth skimming.

Title: Real-time AI has a half-second budget, and the network eats it first
Description: Michele Taroni (Gcore) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on serving models at the edge to keep end-to-end inference under half a second
Body:
A well-optimised model can still feel slow if the request has to cross an ocean first. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, [Michele Taroni](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Michele_Taroni_global_pipeline_edge) of Gcore explained how the company built inference at the edge: shrink the model's compute time, route each request to the nearest GPU region over a CDN backbone, and keep the whole round trip under the half second humans perceive as instant.

It is a sponsor talk about Gcore's own platform, but the latency arithmetic in the middle applies to anyone serving models to users spread across continents.

## Why does serving location matter more than training location?

His framing: as AI moves from pilots into production, the main compute workload moves from training to inference, and inference has an end user waiting on it. Training wants raw throughput. Gcore's training side is NVIDIA A100 and H100 clusters with NVLink inside a node and InfiniBand between nodes. Serving wants low latency wherever the user happens to be.

His example uses Mistral 7B run locally: a prompt of about 200 tokens and an answer of about 20 took around 250 milliseconds. That feels real-time. Put the user in Tokyo and the model in a US data centre, and network latency alone can double or treble that, so the end-to-end time creeps towards a second.

Michele Taroni said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024: "around half a second is around about the time which as a human we perceive that to be in real time." Any slower and people notice the lag. Chatbots are the familiar case, but he also listed autonomous driving, live streaming and quality inspection in mining and manufacturing. Some of those also need data processed locally for regulatory or privacy reasons.

## What has to be true to hit real time?

He named three requirements: distributed compute close to users, a low-latency backbone connecting it, and runtime deployment that can be reconfigured without drama.

### Make the model cheaper to run

For the compute side, focused on LLMs, Gcore used four families of optimisation:

- **Operator fusion**, merging operators to cut overhead per step.
- **Quantization**, storing weights and activations in fewer bits.
- **Compression**: sparsity to trim unnecessary connections, and distillation to train a smaller model that mimics a larger one.
- **Parallelism**: tensor parallelism across devices and pipeline parallelism for larger models.

He noted the obvious catch: each of these trades some accuracy for speed, and you have to check you have not traded away too much.

### Make the trip shorter

The network side borrows the logic of 5G and CDNs. With 180 CDN points of presence, a request reaches Gcore's network and back in about 30 milliseconds on average, and gets to an inference node in about 50, compared with a few hundred milliseconds in a typical public cloud setup, by his estimate. If the optimised model takes 100 to 400 milliseconds, the total stays under half a second. He put automatic speech recognition, object detection and text-to-speech in the same bucket.

### One endpoint, many regions

Deployment is container as a service behind a single anycast endpoint. A user in Kyoto hits a local CDN node, and smart routing sends the request to the nearest inference region, Tokyo; a user in Rio de Janeiro is served in Brazil. The data and the model stay in-region, which also means you could run a different model per region, such as one trained only on Japanese user data in Japan. Each region autoscales, so compute follows demand both up and down.

## What did the demos show?

Three demos. A face avatar that changes as prompts are typed (Elon Musk, Bill Gates, Madonna, a Jeff Bezos from his hair era). An English-to-Luxembourgish voice-to-text translation that came back in under half a second, which is handy since, as he admitted, he does not speak Luxembourgish despite the head office being in Luxembourg. And a generated video from a customer's generative platform that trains on Gcore's H100 infrastructure and serves its models through Gcore's inference services.

At the time of the talk the edge inference product was entering beta, with a model catalogue including Mistral and Stable Diffusion alongside bring-your-own models, and DDoS protection on the endpoint. He said the team was working to bring latency down to a few tens of milliseconds.

## Who should watch?

ML engineers moving a model from a notebook to users in several regions, and anyone who has optimised inference down to 200 milliseconds and still gets complaints from Asia. Expect architecture and demos, not code.

Title: Your output swings like Serena Williams' form, and data can show why
Description: Alex Harris (Adadot) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on treating developer performance like sports analytics, with causal AI finding what speeds teams up
Body:
Ask a developer how consistent their output is and they'll say pretty steady. At [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Alex_Harris_strokes_keystrokes), Alex Harris, co-founder and CEO of Adadot, argues that the data says otherwise: developer performance has the same violent ups and downs as an elite athlete's, and it should be coached the same way, with data the developer owns.

This is a founder talk with a product demo of Adadot in the second half, and despite the event name there is no quantum in it. It is a Moneyball argument for engineering teams.

## Do nerds and jocks really have the same performance curve?

Harris starts with the 90s movie trope: the jocks and the nerds sit at different tables. Then he turns to the data. Most people imagine athletic progress as a smooth curve from beginner to advanced. The real record, even for Serena Williams, is a jagged sequence of peaks and drops.

Developers look the same once you chart how much code they commit and how much of it reaches production error free. The gap between a good month and a bad one, he says, can be ten times. "If you ask most developers, they will assume they have a very kind of steady flow, but in reality they have massive ups and downs," Alex Harris said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024.

## Why are engineering teams flying blind?

Sports figured this out a while ago. Harris quotes coaching surveys: over 50% of coaches use performance analysis tools to share video clips with other coaches and staff, about 68% collate quantitative game data, just under half use live coding analysis during games and roughly 40% get a written match report with statistics.

Engineering, by comparison, runs retros on impressions. Marketing has Google Analytics, sales has Salesforce; engineers ask what made them faster or slower and answer from memory. He puts the cost at about $60 billion of engineering productivity wasted in the US every year.

## Why hasn't anyone solved this already?

Three reasons, and they are the most transferable part of the talk:

- **Breadth.** Coding is a small slice of the job. Scoping, planning and requirements work is mostly invisible to data capture.
- **Framework sprawl.** There are about 21 broad engineering frameworks (agile, scrum, Kanban and friends), and no team runs any of them in pure form.
- **Adoption.** If developers don't love the tool, it's dead. A monitoring tool for managers is the fastest route to that.

## How does Adadot turn signals into advice?

It pulls from GitHub and GitLab, Jira, Google Workspace or Outlook calendars, and Slack, because many causes of bad code aren't code: no focus time, poor scoping, review queues. For each developer it runs seven models of what drives positive momentum, averages the best three, and repeats that daily to produce personal recommendations. Teams turn those into missions with three difficulty levels and earn badges for completing them.

The privacy design is the bit to note. Individuals see their own data; managers see only the team aggregate. Harris pitches it as ammunition for the developer, for promotion conversations or checking whether a new hire is ramping up, and explicitly not as a way for a boss to check who's slacking.

The demo shows the three pillars (work, collaboration, well-being), sprint re-scoping, ticket distribution, review bottlenecks and focus-time tracking. It ends on a lead-time feature that builds a per-team causal AI model of what actually shortens lead time, meetings and review pickup included.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers who suspect their retros run on vibes, and developers who want numbers for their next promotion conversation. If you want an independent study of developer productivity metrics, this isn't it: it's one vendor's approach, presented by its CEO.

Title: Model monitoring tells you the accuracy dropped; observability asks why
Description: Omotayo Alimi (Ceedees Investments) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on observing ML, LLM and vision models - drift, hallucinations, SHAP and Grad-CAM
Body:
A model that passed every offline test can still embarrass you in production, and the dashboard showing its accuracy won't say why. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Omotayo Alimi, Senior Software Engineer at Ceedees Investments, surveys model observability across three families of systems, classic ML, large language models and computer vision, and lays out what goes wrong in each and which techniques tell you why.

It is a survey talk: broad, well organized, light on war stories. Think of it as a checklist you can hold your own ML platform against.

## How is model observability different from model monitoring?

Omotayo draws the line clearly. Monitoring collects metrics over time, detects anomalies and trends, checks the model stays within thresholds and focuses on system health. Observability gives real-time insight, diagnoses issues inside the process, reveals the dependencies underneath and explains why the anomaly happened. On root-cause analysis he said at Conf42 Observability 2024: "It helps engineers to go down into the root cause and helps them understand the specifics behind any specific issue."

His cautionary tale is Bard's launch campaign, which claimed the James Webb Space Telescope took the first ever image of an exoplanet. It didn't, and in his words "Google reportedly lost $100 billion in market value because of this blunder." The point is that users often can't tell when a model is wrong, so somebody upstream has to.

The building blocks he lists are event logging, tracing data through each stage, model profiling, bias detection and anomaly identification.

## What breaks in classic ML?

Three things, mostly. Data drift: the statistical properties of the data move away from the training set, as covariate shift (input distributions change) or model drift (the relationship between inputs and target changes), driven by customer behavior, the external environment, demographics or your own product updates. Performance degradation as usage grows, from overfitting, outliers, adversarial attacks or shifting patterns. And data quality: missing data, labeling errors, disparate sources, privacy constraints, inconsistent formats and samples that don't represent reality.

The metrics are the familiar ones: precision, recall, F1, AUC ROC and MAE. For explaining decisions he covers SHAP, which computes the Shapley value of each feature for global and local importance, and LIME, which perturbs inputs and trains a simpler model on the results to estimate which features mattered.

## Why are LLMs harder to observe?

Because there is often no single right answer. Omotayo's list of LLM-specific problems: hallucinations, no single ground truth, answers that are correct but irrelevant or badly toned, jailbreaks that slip past safety, and the cost of retraining to keep answers current.

The evaluation toolkit he proposes is user feedback on bias and misinformation, embedding visualization to compare prompt and response embeddings for relevance, prompt testing, checking that retrieval systems fetch from the right sources, and fine-tuning on domain data instead of full retraining. Automated scores include BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR and CIDEr, alongside human feedback, custom metrics and RLHF. For explanation, attention-based techniques show which tokens a transformer weighted most, and saliency methods compute gradients against the input or mask features to see what changes.

## And computer vision?

Images drift too: lighting and backgrounds change. Occlusion hides the object you care about and causes misclassification, labeled training images are scarce, and some use cases, medical diagnosis and self-driving cars among them, make every error expensive. The remedies are image-quality and performance metrics, domain experts in the labeling loop, real-time monitoring of cameras and sensors at the edge, label reviews, and fine-tuning when the data diverges. Metrics: mAP, IoU and panoptic quality. For explanation, he compares Integrated Gradients, XRAI (which scores regions rather than single pixels) and Grad-CAM's heatmaps.

He closes with where the field is heading: explanations ordinary users can read, explainable AI used to spot bias, explainability methods borrowing from psychology and philosophy, and causal AI.

## Who should watch

Software and platform engineers who have inherited models in production and need a vocabulary for what to measure. ML specialists will know most of it, but the side-by-side of classic ML, LLM and vision failure modes is a handy reference.

Title: Observability 2.0 starts with one database and ends with a full-disk forecast
Description: Swapnil Kulkarni (Kloudfuse) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on a unified, context-rich signal store that makes forecasts and dynamic alerts possible
Body:
Plenty of teams took their old monitoring setup, bolted on a few dashboards and declared themselves observable. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Swapnil Kulkarni, Customer Success Engineer at Kloudfuse, explains why that doesn't hold up, and what he calls observability 2.0: one store for every signal, enriched with context, so alerts and forecasts can reason about the data instead of comparing it with a fixed number.

This is a short, high-level talk, closer to a map of the territory than a tutorial. Its best moment is a concrete Kubernetes use case near the end.

## What is wrong with monitoring plus dashboards?

Swapnil starts from the textbook definition: observability is the ability to determine a system's internal state by examining its outputs. The usual pipeline collects metrics, events, logs and traces, aggregates them in a time-series store, then visualizes and alerts on thresholds.

He lists what strains that pipeline. Cloud-native components appear with a click and immediately start emitting metrics and logs nobody has modeled. Users expect end-to-end visibility of every request, not just errors. Downtime is expensive, and so is the observability platform itself if nobody knows how much data is being ingested. Security and compliance add their own questions; his example is a TLS certificate and who renews it before it expires. As he put it, "the observability stack needs to understand the increasing complexity of your systems."

## Why one database for every agent?

The heart of the proposal is a poly agent and a unified database. Data arrives from Datadog and New Relic agents, from Prometheus, from OpenTelemetry, each in its own format. Grafana can put many data sources side by side, but mixing them in one panel gets awkward because the shapes differ.

Normalize it all into one store and you can attach context to every signal: for a log line, the Kubernetes cluster, namespace and pod, or the host name, cloud and AWS region. Where the application doesn't send that context, the agent or platform enriches it. Then a question like which services are failing in one availability zone becomes a query.

He is firm on one constraint. Swapnil said at Conf42 Observability 2024 that "we should not go into the same space where we were while trying to solve the problem", meaning the new platform has to sit on open standards such as Prometheus and OpenTelemetry so the data can leave if you do.

## Dynamic thresholds, and a volume that never fills up

With correlated data, alerts can watch rates of change instead of static lines. His example: a utilization metric that climbs 20% within five minutes triggers an alert, whatever its absolute level.

The use case that makes the talk worth the time is predictive maintenance for stateful sets. Kubernetes volumes don't grow themselves, and the cloud provider won't resize them for you. Kloudfuse applied a forecasting algorithm to volume usage to predict when each volume will fill, three or five days ahead, so the volume gets resized before the application starts throwing errors. The same approach extends to capacity planning for nodes, replicas and hosts beyond what the autoscaler covers, plus automated incident routing to PagerDuty or Jira.

## It needs developers too

Swapnil closes on observability-driven development: new applications and infrastructure designed to emit the right signals with the right context, development and operations working on instrumentation together, and continuous improvement because nobody gets it right in the first pass.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers new to the monitoring versus observability debate, or anyone who needs a framework for explaining it upward. Experienced practitioners will find little new beyond the volume-forecast example.

Title: Recycling fails at the screwdriver, and AI robots aim to fix that step
Description: Lav Kumar (Salesforce) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on AI-guided robots that take products apart so more materials can be recovered for a circular economy
Body:
The weak link in recycling is often not the furnace or the sorting line but the step before: taking the product apart without wrecking what is inside. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Lav Kumar, Lead Member of Technical Staff at Salesforce, argued that AI-guided robots doing that disassembly are what make a circular economy practical, and put the gain at up to 50% better material recovery.

It is a short overview talk on an industrial problem, unusual for an ML conference, and it is more vision than engineering detail.

## Why is disassembly the hard part?

Modern products are dense, glued and mixed. Lav Kumar said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024: "For instance, an average smartphone contains over 60 different elements". Many of them, rare earth metals included, are essential and hard to recover. When components are difficult to separate, they get discarded, which loses revenue and sends more to landfill.

The traditional answer makes it worse. Shredding an old laptop mixes metals and plastics, contaminates the recyclable fractions and lowers the quality of what comes out. And many products are designed with no thought for how they will come apart, which matters because, as he puts it: "Research indicates that up to 80% of a product's environmental impact is determined at the design stage."

## What do the robots actually do?

He describes robots driven by GPT-based systems combined with vision and haptic sensors. Concretely:

- Machine learning models trained to recognise the different screws and fasteners in electronics, so they can be removed without damaging components.
- AI that optimises the disassembly sequence of a complex product to minimise damage and maximise recovery.
- Sorting gold, silver and palladium from old circuit boards in e-waste facilities, then sending them for refining and reuse.
- Sorting plastic types for higher purity in recycled plastic.

Electric vehicle batteries are his clearest example of the stakes: lithium, cobalt and nickel recovered from an old pack is material that does not need to be mined.

## What do the numbers say?

He cites three figures. Industries using AI in disassembly report a 30% increase in the retrieval of usable components. Companies implementing these technologies report up to a 50% improvement in material recovery rates. And in one case study, AI-driven robots disassembling electronic devices raised material recovery by 40%, with the recovered metals sold back to manufacturers in a closed loop. A second case study, an AI-guided disassembly system for automotive parts at a manufacturing company, cut time and cost and produced refurbished parts for new vehicles.

The companies and studies behind these figures are not named, so read them as the direction of travel rather than benchmarks you can reproduce. Anyone wanting to build such a system will need to go to the robotics literature for the how.

## Who should watch

Engineers curious about where ML meets physical manufacturing, sustainability teams looking for a quick framing of AI-assisted disassembly, and product designers, since the 80% design-stage figure puts much of the responsibility on them. If you want model architectures or robot control details, this is not that talk. Lav Kumar gave a version of it at [Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Lav_Kumar_revolutionizing_sustainability_economy) too.

Title: AI drug discovery in six minutes, and why the quantum part can wait
Description: Amit Taneja at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024 on how machine learning trained on ChEMBL and PubChem cuts the decade and $2.6B behind a new drug
Body:
Bringing a new drug to market takes more than ten years and, by the industry's own count, upwards of $2.6 billion. At [Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Amit_Taneja_quantum_advances_pharma), Amit Taneja, an engineering lead, gives a short, brisk primer on where machine learning attacks that bill: the screening and candidate-picking stage, before anyone pipettes anything.

Honest scope first. The title promises quantum computing and pharma; the talk itself is about AI. Quantum does not come up once. What you get is a compact map of AI-assisted drug discovery, a case study and a list of the problems that still stand in the way, all in about six minutes. Treat it as an overview for someone who hasn't followed the field, not as a methods talk.

## What is so expensive about finding a drug?

Time and failure. Taneja opens with the two numbers that frame the whole field. The process often takes "over a decade from initial discovery to market launch", and the money is worse: "the costs associated with bringing a new drug to the market are staggering, frequently exceeding over $2.6 billion per drug," Amit Taneja said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2024.

Most of that cost is spent on candidates that never make it. Pick better candidates earlier and the whole pipeline gets cheaper. That is the entire pitch for machine learning here.

## Where does the training data come from?

From the big public chemistry and bioactivity databases: ChEMBL and PubChem. They are the reason this works at all. Decades of measured molecular interactions sit in them, which is exactly the labelled data that deep learning and reinforcement learning models need to predict how a molecule will bind to a target.

With models trained on that data you can do virtual screening and molecular docking at a scale no wet lab could match, ranking huge candidate libraries and only sending the promising ones to experiments. If you've ever tuned a search ranking, the shape is familiar: cheap model filters, expensive check confirms.

## Did the models find anything?

The case study is about cancer. A deep learning model applied to ChEMBL looked for inhibitors of key enzymes involved in cancer progression and flagged several that were previously unknown. Follow-up experimental assays confirmed high efficacy and favourable safety profiles, and the compounds are described as candidates for further clinical trials. The talk doesn't name the paper or the team behind the study, so take it as an illustration of the workflow rather than a result you can check from the video.

The headline claim is that AI can cut R&D costs dramatically: "AI can actually slash research and development costs by up to 70%," as Taneja puts it. He also lists faster time to market, quicker response to pandemics and new outbreaks, and a path to personalised medicine built around individual patient characteristics.

## What could go wrong?

The closing section is the most useful for engineers, because it is the part that stays true whatever the model architecture:

- **Data quality and standardisation.** Garbage in, plausible-looking molecules out.
- **Bias.** Models trained on skewed data produce skewed discovery.
- **Domain experts in the loop.** AI-generated insights need chemists and pharmacologists to validate them.
- **Regulation.** Approval processes were not designed with AI-discovered drugs in mind, and that is a new problem in its own right.

## Who should watch

Engineers and data people curious about pharma who want the vocabulary (ChEMBL, PubChem, virtual screening, docking) in one sitting. If you already work in computational chemistry, you can skip it. If you came for qubits, go to the related talks below.

Title: Watch technology, customers and regulators, then act on what you see
Description: Shishir Jayant (Remitly) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on how tech companies stay competitive by tracking market trends and building a culture of adaptability
Body:
What is new in tech today can be obsolete tomorrow, and the companies that survive are the ones built to change. That is the thesis Shishir Jayant, Director of Strategic Partnerships at Remitly, brought to Conf42 Machine Learning 2024: watch three kinds of market signal, turn them into action through four habits, and the payoff is resilience as much as growth.

It is a short, non-technical strategy talk, closer to a leadership framework than an engineering session, and that is the right expectation to bring to it. The abstract promises case studies of companies that thrived amid change; the talk itself stays at the level of principles.

## Which signals should a tech company track?

He names three areas he would double down on from his professional experience:

- **Emerging technologies**: artificial intelligence, blockchain and the Internet of Things, which can disrupt whole industries and reward early adopters.
- **Consumer behaviour**: growing demand for cloud-based solutions, a focus on data privacy, the rise of the experience economy.
- **Regulation**: the area engineers most often treat as someone else's problem.

The regulatory point is the most interesting one, coming from someone who runs partnerships at a cross-border payments company. Many new technologies have no precedent, so regulators are learning as they go, and the rules around data security and privacy keep moving. Staying informed keeps you compliant and avoids disruption, but he goes further. Shishir Jayant said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024: "A lot of times, having a seat in the table with the regulators will also provide a platform to voice your opinion and actually help regulators in forming laws which are right for the business, right for the consumers, and right for the market."

He also stresses that market intelligence only helps if it is shared across teams and businesses, not kept in one strategy deck.

## How do you turn trends into action?

Four strategies, each with a concrete edge:

- **Agility**: rigid business models adapt slowly. Break down silos between departments, encourage cross-functional work and let employees make decisions. Alongside the top-down view he wants a ground-up channel, so people closest to the market can say what they are seeing.
- **Data-driven decisions**: analyse consumer behaviour, track competitors' strategies and measure the effectiveness of your own programmes, so strategy rests on evidence.
- **Continuous learning**: his critique here is pointed. Companies that fixate on top-line or bottom-line numbers often drop training and upskilling first. He argues for professional development programmes, workshops and conferences as the thing that keeps a team able to change.
- **A culture of innovation**: let people take calculated risks, and let them fail and learn, treated as seriously as shipping successes.

## What does adaptability buy you?

He lists four benefits: increased market share from responding to customer needs first, higher customer satisfaction and loyalty from products that fit evolving preferences, more innovation from a learning culture, and resilience. The last one is the argument that matters in a downturn: the tech industry is volatile, and businesses that adapt quickly can absorb unexpected disruption and come out stronger.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, staff engineers moving toward strategy, and anyone making the case internally for a training budget or for engaging early with regulators. Engineers looking for ML techniques will find none here, and the talk is light on examples, so treat it as a checklist to compare against your own organisation rather than a playbook with numbers.

Title: Centralized monitoring builds in low fidelity by design
Description: Shyam Sreevalsan (Netdata) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on the seven sins of centralized monitoring and why the data should stay on the node
Body:
Your infrastructure is spread across clouds, clusters and data centers, yet almost every monitoring tool you run funnels everything into one big bucket. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Shyam Sreevalsan, Senior Technical Product Manager at Netdata, argues that this one design choice is why observability gets expensive and blurry at the same time, and that the fix is to keep the data on the node that produced it.

It is a Netdata talk, and the second half shows Netdata's architecture. The first half, a list of what centralization costs you, holds up whatever you run.

## Why does centralizing make data worse?

Shyam defines fidelity as granularity plus cardinality. Low granularity (one sample every 60 seconds) gives you blurry data; low cardinality (ten hand-picked Postgres metrics out of the hundreds available) gives you blind spots. Combine the two and you have an abstract picture that feels like observability without being it.

The trap is that a central server ties fidelity to cost. Going from one sample a minute to one a second is 60 times the data on the wire and in storage; going from ten metrics to 1,000 is 100 times. So teams trim, and as Shyam put it, "we're building in low fidelity by design."

The trimming is where it hurts. Teams cherry-pick what to collect, then discover the gap during the postmortem and add the missing metric to the dashboard, one incident too late. Shyam said at Conf42 Observability 2024 that "nobody, no matter how much of an expert you are, can anticipate what metric would be useful while you're troubleshooting an outage at 03:00 a.m. in the morning."

## The other six sins

Fidelity is the first of seven. The rest, briefly:

- **Scalability**: the central server is the bottleneck, and scaling your own Prometheus can eat time that should go to the product.
- **Cost**: central storage, central compute and egress, with bills that grow faster than the infrastructure. He cites the press stories about seven-figure observability bills.
- **Accuracy**: generic thresholds applied centrally miss local anomalies, and central anomaly detection needs to know whether a metric came from a Raspberry Pi or an Nvidia H100 rig.
- **Resilience**: one server down means no monitoring at all. He points to the Datadog outage of the previous year that left customers blind for hours.
- **Efficiency**: processing delays, resource overload and the energy cost of the monitoring itself.
- **Data privacy**: one repository concentrates the risk, raises GDPR-style compliance questions, and makes it hard to keep some networks off the grid entirely.

## What does decentralized look like in practice?

The design has three rules: keep the data at the edge, where compute and disk are already spare; replicate it across the network so ephemeral nodes don't take their history with them; and unify everything at query time rather than at ingest.

Netdata's version has three parts. The agent collects every metric per second, stores it in its own time-series database, and runs alerts and anomaly detection locally. Parents are ordinary agents that receive streams from children, so a fragile production box can offload storage, alerting and ML to a neighbor. Netdata Cloud stores no observability data at all; it keeps a map of which node holds what and fans queries out to the parents in real time.

The numbers come from Netdata's own benchmark, so treat them as the vendor's figures: on an empty VM the agent finds 2,000+ time series and 50+ preconfigured alerts, and 3 GiB of disk holds two weeks of per-second, three months of per-minute and two years of per-hour data. In the comparison table, the Netdata agent uses 181 MB of memory against Dynatrace's 1,400 MB, and sends 0.01 GB of egress a month against 11.4 GB.

## The objections, answered

Shyam takes on the usual worries. Heavy agents: see the table. Load on production: each agent serves only its own small dataset, and a parent can shield sensitive nodes from queries entirely. Slow queries: many tiny parallel queries beat one big one. Bandwidth: only the charts on screen get queried, not all 2,000 series.

He is candid about why few vendors do this. Edge resource use has to be minimal, aggregation has to happen invisibly, deployment has to stay simple, and the vendor has to give up control of the data, which is a hard sell if your business model is storing it.

## Who should watch

SREs staring at an observability bill, and anyone running a DIY Prometheus stack who wants principles to steal even without switching tools. Skip it if you want a hands-on demo; the dashboard tour is short.

Title: AI agents are LLMs given the tricks humans use to cover their flaws
Description: Jonathan Harel (Fine) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on why planning, reflection, tools and memory turn eager, hallucinating LLMs into useful agents
Body:
Humans are bad at mental arithmetic, have a knowledge cutoff and confidently make things up, and we still get work done because we plan, check our work, use calculators and ask colleagues. That is the whole pitch of AI agents, according to Jonathan Harel, co-founder and VP R&D at Fine, at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. Give a large language model the same crutches and it stops looking like a gifted child and starts looking like a junior colleague.

He is upfront that the field has more questions than answers, and that the talk draws on public material from well-known researchers. What he adds is the view of someone building coding agents every day.

## Why do LLMs need help at all?

His tour of failures is the funniest part of the talk, and each joke maps to a real limitation. ChatGPT identifies random ASCII art as the Mona Lisa (eagerness to answer). It invents a world record for crossing the English Channel on foot (hallucination). It answers that 100 machines take 100 minutes to make 100 devices (weak logic). It agrees that two plus five is eight once the user's wife insists, and blames its 2021 training data (knowledge cutoff, plus a spine made of jelly). Then the built-in guardrails, and the users who route around them: asking which piracy sites to avoid, or asking it to play a grandma who reads out Windows 10 product keys at bedtime.

His point: these are human failure modes too, and humans developed planning, reflection, tool use and collaboration to work around them.

## What exactly is an agent?

He uses a definition worth keeping. Jonathan Harel said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024: "AI agents are LLMs set up to run iteratively with some tools, skills and goals or tasks defined." Iteratively is the key word: after every step the LLM is called again to look at what happened and decide the next action.

The building blocks:

- **Tools**: calculator, calendar, code interpreter, web search, including tools the user does not understand (an accounting agent using accounting software you have never opened).
- **Memory**: short-term for the current flow, long-term in vector databases accessed with RAG, procedural memory for how a task should be done, and personal memory for how a specific user likes it done.
- **Planning**: breaking a task into sub-goals, chain of thought, self-critique and reflection. He calls this the most interesting part.

Agents are not new, he notes: reinforcement learning had them, including OpenAI's hide-and-seek agents that learned to block doors and steal the ramp. OpenAI's attempt to train agents to use computers by randomly pressing keys and clicking did not really work. LLMs are what finally made general agents practical.

## Free-form loop or fixed plan?

Reflection is easiest to see with code. Ask an LLM to write a function, then ask a second LLM to review it for bugs, feed the review back, repeat, maybe run tests along the way. Automate that chat and you have an agent.

The design question is how much freedom to give it. A free-form loop lets the agent decide each next action, which can end in a very short loop or a very long one, with little control. A fixed plan (outline, research, draft, critique, revise) is predictable but rigid. The papers he cites land in the middle, and he points to AlphaCodium for code: a deterministic preprocessing phase, then iterations where the AI decides when it is done.

## Does it work?

On HumanEval, he shows GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 zero-shot scoring between 48% and 67%, while agentic workflows with reflection, tool use and planning push results toward 100%. GPT-3.5 inside an agentic workflow beats GPT-4 zero-shot, which matters to anyone paying for tokens.

Then the counterweight: an agent asked to book appointments on someone's calendar fills it so densely no human would accept it. Agents lack the common-sense context we take for granted. He compares the whole field to autonomous vehicles: easy to imagine, slow to build.

## What should we expect from agents?

Three predictions. We will wait: delegating a task and getting the answer after 30 minutes or an hour, the way we delegate to people. Interfaces are unsolved: chat, GUI, CLI, everywhere or one place. And infrastructure will feel it: if coding agents pick up every open ticket and finish each in half an hour to two hours, a CI/CD pipeline with 10,000 tests gets hammered. That last one is the kind of second-order problem platform teams should be thinking about now.

He also notes that individuals and small companies, not the model giants, publish much of the agent research, which makes it an open field to work in.

## Who should watch

Engineers who use ChatGPT daily but have not built an agent, and anyone who needs a clear mental model of tools, memory and planning before reading the papers. It is a conceptual talk with no code, and a good first one on the topic.

Title: The 3am log line you need was written months earlier, or never
Description: Shyamkumar Kalariya (Zenduty) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on the logging mistakes that hide incidents, and structured logs with trace IDs that don't
Body:
Whether a 3am incident takes ten minutes or three hours is mostly decided weeks earlier, by whoever wrote the log lines. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Shyamkumar Kalariya, Software Engineer at Zenduty, an incident management platform, catalogues the everyday logging mistakes that leave on-call engineers blind (missing context, wrong levels, inconsistent fields, mismatched types) and the habits that fix them: structured logs, a trace ID on every line, and alerts built on the logs themselves.

It's a practical talk aimed at application developers, with examples in Python-style code. Seasoned SREs will know most of it; the team members who write the logs you read at 3am may not.

## Why log at all?

Shyamkumar's four reasons: troubleshooting production issues, where logs are often the only record of what a request actually did; monitoring health and performance, down to timing a code block between a start and end timestamp; security auditing and compliance (who logged in from which IP, who did what); and understanding how users move through the application. Under the hood, most logging frameworks have the same four parts: loggers that capture events, handlers that send them to a file or stream, filters that drop or enrich events, and formatters that shape the output, such as JSON.

## Which mistakes hide the incident?

- **No context.** Operation failed feels self-explanatory to the person who just wrote the function. Two weeks later nobody knows which request, which user, which input. Without context the line just takes up storage.
- **Wrong log level.** Everything logged as error means you can't filter for real errors; a genuine error logged as warning gets missed.
- **Inconsistent structure.** One line carries the function name, user ID and IP; the next only a file name and line number. Search by user ID and the second operation vanishes from your results.
- **Type mismatch for the same key.** A field that is the integer 15 in one record and the string 15 in another, or a JSON object in one place and a string in the next. Many log backends reject the mismatched records, and you conclude the request never reached that code. It did.

## What does a good log line carry?

A message someone else can understand, plus metadata: function, line number, the exact error, user, IP. Above all a trace ID or correlation ID on every log line in the request cycle, so one search returns everything the request touched, across microservices, and links logs with metrics and traces. Leave out PII such as card numbers and passwords. Decide the structure once and stick to it.

He also warns against the blanket exception handler. Catching every error as request failed tells you nothing. Think through what can go wrong in the block and catch each case with its own message; if you don't know what can fail, don't catch it at all. Let it fail and let monitoring raise an incident, rather than swallowing a bug that could hurt the company technically or financially.

## Logs as an alerting source

Structured logs make the rest possible: charts and heatmaps of events over time, alerts on event frequency, abnormal durations and specific status codes, and anomaly rules. His example: traffic normally runs at 30 to 40 requests per second, so a jump to 100 or more is worth a page, and as the product grows to a normal 50 to 60, the threshold should move with it, or you train everyone to ignore the alert. Storage matters too: centralise, set retention to what you actually need, move older logs to cold storage, index the fields you search by, and back it all up.

## What does it look like at 3am?

With good charts, most anticipated failures show up in the visualisation before you touch a log search. For the rest, take the request ID from the alert or stack trace and pull every event of that request. His example is Zenduty's phone number verification: each check (already verified, block list, telecom provider, allowed country) is logged, so when a customer says the OTP never arrived, the failing check is one search away.

Big teams, he notes, often run two parallel streams: info (info, warning, error and critical) for developers, and debug for whoever runs operations, handed out when info isn't enough. As he put it at Conf42 Observability 2024, "be careful you don't get lost in the logs". For tooling he lists ELK, EFK (Fluentd in place of Logstash) and Grafana Loki with Promtail, plus Alertmanager for the alerts.

## Who should watch

Developers who write logs but rarely read them under pressure, and team leads writing a logging guideline. If your platform already enforces structured logs with trace IDs, this is a checklist to confirm you're covered.

Title: Ask an image model for a disabled person and you get a wheelchair
Description: Emmanuelle Aboaf (SHODO) and Thanh Lan Doublier at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on how AI helps disabled people daily and where its biases shut them out
Body:
Ask an image generator for a disabled person in a realistic environment and you get a wheelchair, almost every time. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Emmanuelle Aboaf, a .NET developer at SHODO, and Thanh Lan Doublier, a machine learning engineer, explained why that default is wrong, where it comes from in an ordinary data science project, and which AI tools genuinely change their days. Both speakers are deaf, and Thanh Lan uses a wheelchair, so this is a talk from users, not about them.

Their answer to the title question is both: AI is already part of how they work, and the same statistics that make it useful push minorities to the edge of the distribution.

## How common is disability, and how visible?

Their overview starts with scale: about 1 billion people, roughly 15% of the world population. Then the part most teams get wrong. Emmanuelle Aboaf said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024: "Did you know that 80% of disabilities are not immediately visible." She fact-checks her own figure on stage (another common claim is 50%), and the conclusion holds either way: most disabilities are invisible, deafness included. Their families of disability cover physical, sensory, cognitive, intellectual and disabling illnesses such as endometriosis or multiple sclerosis.

## Where does the wheelchair bias come from?

Thanh Lan walks through a realistic project: generate advertising images of disabled people, with no in-house dataset, so scrape a search engine. The search results are mostly wheelchairs, and so is the model trained on them. Their slides put wheelchair users at about 3% of the disabled population. The images from Microsoft Designer they show also skew toward one type of person, and a test by Jeremy Andrew Davis of AI images of autistic people produced faces that all looked alike, and sad.

She calls it a cognitive bias with two costs: the wheelchair becomes the definition of disability, and everyone else gets erased from the data.

## Which steps of an ML project let bias in?

The useful part for practitioners is a walk through the pipeline, one step at a time:

- **Framing and metrics**: decide which error hurts more. In disease detection a false negative is worse than a false positive; for a marketing email it barely matters.
- **Exploratory data analysis**: outliers get treated as noise. In a dataset of typical software engineers, two deaf women developers, one in a wheelchair, look like outliers, and a recruitment model that drops them does real harm.
- **Evaluation**: a sign language model trained and tested on American Sign Language scores well, then fails in France, where people use French Sign Language. Good validation numbers, wrong context.
- **Production**: drift means retraining, and interaction with users can make a model more biased over time, so the exploratory phase has to be redone on production data.

## Which AI tools actually help?

Emmanuelle uses automatic captions every day and is clear about their limits: in a video call she still lip-reads, listens through her implants and reasons from context to repair the errors, which is exhausting. Uploaded videos should get captions checked by a human. Other tools they cite: Microsoft Seeing AI, which describes the surroundings like a talking camera; Be My Eyes and its GPT-4-based Virtual Volunteer, with the open question of whether blind users can blindly trust it; Signer.ai and Signapse for sign language; Oticon hearing aids that reduce ambient noise; Mintt fall detection; and Rango, a smart white cane.

They also cover the failures. The Eliza chatbot case, in which a man in Belgium took his own life after conversations with it, is the darkest example. The everyday ones: sound recognition with so many false positives it gets switched off, and asking ChatGPT to make a site accessible, which did not work well. Overlay tools do not fix accessibility either; you have to work on the code yourself.

Their closing principle is "nothing about us without us": design and evaluate with disabled people, and hire them. As they put it: "Your users are varied, so it's important that the diversity exists."

## Who should watch

ML engineers who build datasets or evaluation suites, product teams shipping captioning or vision features, and anyone who has never tested their product with a deaf or blind user. The transcript is rough in places (two deaf speakers on automatic captioning, which proves their point), but the argument is clear and the examples are specific.

Title: An ML platform on three PCs comes down to GPU sharing
Description: Zhiya Zang (TikTok) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on building an affordable ML platform where GPU sharing, not more hardware, does the heavy lifting
Body:
Most ML platform talks assume a rack of A100s and a budget line to match. Zhiya Zang, Senior Software Engineer at TikTok, went the other way at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024: what does a usable ML platform look like when you have one PC, or three, and a handful of consumer GPUs? His answer fits in one sentence. Zhiya Zang said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024: "So the key point of affordability is GPU sharing."

The proof at the end is a platform he built a few years earlier that ran on three PCs with three 1060-class cards.

## Why is an idle GPU the real cost problem?

He lists four ways a GPU wastes money. It is expensive to begin with. It sits idle outside working hours. It is also idle during working hours, because most workloads spend time on CPU and IO between kernel launches, so a model that runs "solely on the GPU" rarely hits 100% utilisation. And GPUs keep getting more powerful while experiments often use small hyperparameters and a fraction of the memory. One job per card leaves most of the card unused.

The audience he has in mind is the one priced out of the usual platform: startups and small businesses that need to scale later rather than buy now, universities and labs teaching end-to-end ML on a single machine, non-profits, and freelancers working on one PC with one GPU.

## What can you leave out?

He splits a typical platform into an application layer, infrastructure and hardware. The application layer has an ML side (data engineering, experiments, training, inference) and a data side (feature store, model management, data lake). His affordable version drops the data side entirely for now. The target users handle small datasets, and because the data platform and the ML platform can be decoupled, a dedicated data platform can be built separately once the business grows. A useful bit of discipline: the cheapest component is the one you postpone.

## How do you run Kubernetes on one PC?

The platform needs separate container environments for experiments, training and inference, which means Kubernetes. He notes Kubernetes wants at least three nodes, and the hardware may be a single box. His fix is OpenStack underneath: it has a single-machine deployment path, handles a mix of VMs, containers and bare metal, scales from one machine to a multi-node cluster, and can later be removed when the platform moves to a self-hosted or public cloud, without disrupting the Kubernetes cluster above it. OpenStack as a stepping stone rather than a destination is not a common take, and it is the most reusable idea in the talk.

## Which GPU sharing option fits which job?

This is the core of the talk, a tour of four options:

- **NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG)**: partitions a card into up to seven isolated instances with dedicated compute, memory and bandwidth. The strongest isolation, good for inference and small training jobs, and ruled out here because only high-end professional GPUs support it; the cheapest he points to is the A30.
- **GPU time-slicing**: each process gets the whole GPU for a time slice. Flexible, but no memory or fault isolation. One process hogging VRAM or crashing hurts everyone else, and the context switching stretches total task time, so he places it with training rather than latency-sensitive inference.
- **NVIDIA MPS**: merges processes into one shared GPU context and one command queue, which cuts context-switching overhead and works on all current GPUs. The catch: if one task fails, all tasks sharing the context fail, so he keeps it for experiments.
- **Tencent TKE GaiaGPU**: an open-source, third-party approach based on CUDA hijacking. It intercepts CUDA memory allocation and release calls to enforce per-container memory limits, and monitors utilisation to cap compute with hard or soft limits. Because the compute limit is enforced by monitoring and adjusting, it guarantees fairness over the long run, not over short bursts, so very short tasks such as inference are a poor fit.

The mapping is the takeaway: MIG for isolation if you can afford the card, time-slicing for training, MPS for experiments, GaiaGPU when you need isolation on consumer hardware.

## Who should watch

Anyone running ML on a teaching lab machine, a startup's spare workstations or a single home GPU, and platform engineers who want a compact comparison of GPU sharing modes. It is an architecture overview, not a step-by-step build, and the GaiaGPU section rewards a follow-up read of the 2018 paper he cites.
