Title: Autoscaling halves the bill only with a ceiling and a cooldown
Description: Preetham Vemasani (Uber) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on predictive vs reactive autoscaling, the thresholds that keep it cheap, and where research goes next
Body:
Autoscaling's pitch is that you pay for capacity only when traffic needs it. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Preetham Vemasani, Senior Software Engineer at Uber, walks through the two families of dynamic resource allocation, predictive and reactive, an AWS Auto Scaling example where halving the instance count halved the bill, and the configuration rules (upper bounds, cooldowns, monitoring) that decide whether autoscaling saves money or quietly multiplies it.

Set expectations: this is a short, high-level overview rather than an engineering teardown. The abstract mentions success stories from AWS, Netflix and Airbnb; in the talk they get a few sentences each. It works best as a first map of the topic.

## Predictive or reactive?

Preetham frames dynamic resource allocation through an e-commerce shop. It needs moderate capacity during business hours, peak capacity during a flash sale, and very little when the store is closed. Allocate by need and you get both better service and a smaller bill.

Most techniques fall into two buckets. Predictive scaling forecasts load from historical data and provisions ahead of time: you know the sale is coming, so the capacity is there before the customers arrive. Netflix is his main example, scheduling capacity on AWS from the viewing patterns in its user data. Reactive scaling responds to what is happening now: a sudden rush arrives, the system adds resources instead of falling over. AWS, Google Cloud and Azure all offer both. He calls predictive scaling the more cost-efficient of the two, provided it is watched closely.

## Does it actually save money?

The AWS Auto Scaling example is simple arithmetic: instance count went from 10 to 5, daily cost from $9.98 to $4.99 and monthly cost from $299.52 to $149.76, a 50% reduction on both. It's a toy-sized case, but it shows the mechanism.

## How do you keep autoscaling from running away?

This is the most useful part. Three rules:

- **Observability first.** Predictive scaling in particular needs solid monitoring and alerting, because when the forecast is wrong you want to know before your users do.
- **Upper and lower bounds.** Without a ceiling, a scaling policy can keep adding resources and the bill grows with it. Set the maximum from what the business is willing to pay, not from what the cloud will give you.
- **Cooldown periods.** After a spike, don't scale straight back down. A cooldown avoids flapping and protects transactions that are still in flight.

The theme is balance: optimise for performance, but with a budget you have agreed on in advance. And capacity isn't automatically useful. As Preetham said at Conf42 Observability 2024, "adding more resources doesn't automatically work for most of the services": each application has to be able to consume what it is given, and each team needs to evaluate how scaling actually affects its service.

## Where is it heading?

He sees machine learning as the next step for predictive scaling, with models trained on years of usage data producing near-perfect schedules, and reinforcement learning as a promising way to tune scaling policies continuously. Serverless makes autoscaling even more central: when no service is tied to a particular server, the platform has to place and replicate work on demand. IoT and edge computing push the same ideas toward real-time, time-sensitive workloads.

His pick for the biggest research opportunity is multi-cloud and hybrid cloud. If one microservice runs on AWS, another on Google Cloud and the database on Azure, scaling one side without the others invites rate limiting and degraded performance. Cross-cloud autoscaling, multi-objective optimisation, security, data privacy and regulatory compliance round out his list of open problems, along with a call for closer collaboration between industry and academia.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers new to autoscaling who want the vocabulary and the guardrails in one sitting. If you already tune Kubernetes autoscalers for a living, pick one of the deeper talks below.

Title: When a threshold can't see the fault, an LSTM autoencoder can
Description: Anais Dotis-Georgiou (InfluxData) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on IIoT anomaly detection with HiveMQ, Quix, Hugging Face and InfluxDB 3.0
Body:
A failing machine that spikes is easy; a failing machine that keeps its rhythm and stays inside the usual standard deviation is the one that ruins your week. Anais Dotis-Georgiou, Developer Advocate at InfluxData, used her [Conf42 Machine Learning 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Anais_DotisGeorgiou_quix_hugging_face) talk to build an end-to-end industrial IoT pipeline for exactly that case: robot sensor data over MQTT through HiveMQ, streamed by Quix into InfluxDB 3.0, scored by a Keras LSTM autoencoder served from Hugging Face, and alerted on in Grafana.

It is a vendor DevRel talk, and it says so, but the architecture is mix-and-match and the whole thing is a containerised example on GitHub you can run on free tiers. One note on scope: the abstract promises Holt-Winters forecasting too, but the talk itself covers only the anomaly detection half.

## What does a time series database need to do?

She grounds the talk in time series basics. Metrics arrive at regular intervals; events, like a machine fault or a heart attack, do not, though aggregation turns any event into a metric (faults per day). A time series database must store timestamped data queryable in time order, absorb high write throughput (an industrial vibration sensor can produce 10,000 points a second), query efficiently over long ranges, and scale horizontally.

InfluxDB 3.0 is a rewrite of the storage engine on the Apache stack: DataFusion for query execution, Arrow in memory, Parquet on disk. The two motivations she names are near-unlimited cardinality, so you stop agonising over tags versus fields, and interoperability with ML and BI tools, Tableau included, through Arrow Flight and ODBC/JDBC drivers.

## How does the data get from robot to database?

The scenario is a fictional Packing Co with three packaging robots, one of which periodically fails and needs a manual reset. A simulator spins up a thread per robot, each with its own HiveMQ connection, and publishes JSON with metadata (machine ID, barcode, provider) and readings for temperature, load, power and vibration to topics like machine/machine1. She covers the Python paho client, including a tip: HiveMQ's public broker accepts insecure connections, handy for testing, while HiveMQ Cloud requires TLS and credentials.

Quix, which runs Kafka under the hood behind Python plugins and a UI, subscribes with the machine/# wildcard, parses the payload onto a stream, and writes raw data to a machine_data table in InfluxDB. A source plugin reads it back, runs it through the model, and writes scores to an ml_results table for Grafana.

## Why an autoencoder and not a threshold?

Because in the real world anomalous data can be seasonal too. An autoencoder learns normal patterns without labels; "auto encoders were actually originally used for image compression, but it was found out that they work great for time series anomaly detection," Anais Dotis-Georgiou said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

She explains the Keras architecture with a robot-learning-a-dance analogy (she's a dancer). An LSTM layer with 16 units memorises the broad moves, a 4-unit layer keeps the key moments, a repeat vector and mirrored LSTM layers rebuild the sequence, and a time-distributed dense layer sharpens each step. Score new data by reconstruction error: the model rebuilds normal data well, so high mean squared error means something is off.

## How do you get the model out of the notebook?

Her framing of the real bottleneck: data scientists live in Jupyter and Keras, production lives elsewhere, and great models take forever to ship. Hugging Face acts as the model repository, Quix has a native Hugging Face plugin, so data scientists push models and data engineers wire them in with incremental testing. In the demo you can inject anomalies live and watch them come out tagged, with an MSE percentage, and Grafana alerting fires when enough anomalous points land in a window.

Next steps she sketches include labelling the anomaly type (bad bearings, shaky belts, unexpected load), LLMs for protocol conversion and natural language interfaces, encoding expert troubleshooting knowledge, and self-defined digital twins.

## Who should watch

IIoT and data engineers building their first streaming ML pipeline, and data scientists who want a clear mental model of LSTM autoencoders for time series. If you already run model serving in production, the architecture walk-through is the part worth your time.

Title: Four Spark jobs that adaptive query execution still won't save
Description: Marcin Szymaniuk (TantusData) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on debugging skew, exploding self-joins and lazy evaluation traps in Spark 3
Body:
Spark 3's adaptive query execution fixes a lot, but a perfectly correct SQL query can still run for an hour and never finish. Marcin Szymaniuk, CEO of TantusData, used his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Marcin_Szymaniuk_apache_spark_sql) talk to walk through four simplified production cases where you still have to tune by hand, reading each one from the Spark UI the way you would on a real incident.

The schemas and SQL are deliberately tiny; the debugging method is the real thing.

## Why bother tuning Spark 3 at all?

His short history: Spark 1 was unstable and you kept asking ops to restart services. Spark 2 was stable, but correct SQL could still fail because of data distribution or size, and without knowing why you were left guessing at parameters. Spark 3 with AQE resolves many common problems, skewed left joins included, but not all of them. Knowing how to debug saves your time, your team's time and your cloud bill.

## How do you spot skew in the Spark UI?

Case one is a window function: for each user's app events, use lead() over a partition by user ID, ordered by timestamp, to get the next event's timestamp and see where users get stuck. Simple and correct.

The UI tells a different story. After 23 minutes, 126 tasks have finished and one is still running, on its fourth attempt. The stage shows only 5 GB of output but 150 GB of memory spill and 80 GB of disk spill. The event timeline is a wall of tiny green tasks finishing in about 10 seconds and one long bar that keeps failing.

The SQL tab is where he looks next, and the box to watch is Exchange. "Shuffle is something expensive in general, because it involves disk, network and so on," Marcin Szymaniuk said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. Hovering it shows hash partitioning by user ID, which maps the box back to your code. The input is 100 GB and a billion records, and the shuffle write side looks harmless with a top partition of 45 MB. The shuffle read side is where it breaks: one partition holds gigabytes, because one user produces far too many events and a single partition is always processed by a single task.

## How do you fix it?

First, confirm skew is the cause, and check whether it's a data bug or whether you can filter the problem users out. Upgrade to Spark 3 if you haven't, since many skew cases are handled for you there. If you still need a manual fix, change the grain: partition by user and day, not just user, then patch up the last event of each day, which now has no next timestamp, and union the pieces back. The result is an even task distribution, and a job that never finished now completes in about a minute.

He adds a caveat worth framing: decide what you are optimising for (wall clock time, cloud spend, your own time, or code simplicity) before you go further.

## What about a job that reads almost nothing and never ends?

Case two looks the same in the timeline, but the shuffle read is only 20 MB. The SQL tab gives it away: a sort-merge join already emitting more than 4 billion rows and climbing. It's a self-join of a products table on order ID for basket analysis, a Cartesian product per order, all handled by one task because the join key is the order ID.

The fix is salting: add a random salt to one side, duplicate the other across every salt value, and join on order ID plus salt. The row count doesn't shrink, but the work spreads across many tasks. In his run the top task drops to eleven minutes, with a salt range of around 180.

## Why does my loop get slower every iteration?

Cases three and four are lazy evaluation, taught on day one of every Spark course and forgotten by day two. Run a complex transformation in a loop and Spark just keeps appending to the plan: the first iteration takes 23 seconds, later ones a minute, then nine. He calls loops suspicious, "somewhat like doing a batch within a batch system". Checkpoint or materialise intermediate results, which also nudges you into splitting a huge DAG into maintainable modules.

The nasty one is non-determinism. Split a DataFrame into train and test by a random column, write both, and the random values are regenerated for each write, so the sets overlap and records go missing. A friend of his lost a lot of time to exactly that overfitting bug. Use the standard library split, or materialise first.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who own Spark jobs, and data scientists who run them and want to know when they're blocked. His closing advice applies to the second group: "You don't want to be a PhD in spark," but you should know when to ask for help, and who to ask.

Title: Your PromQL query is slow because it reads 16 million samples
Description: Roman Khavronenko (VictoriaMetrics) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on measuring PromQL and MetricsQL query cost by series and samples, then cutting it
Body:
Two PromQL queries that differ only in their metric name: one returns in 3.5 seconds, the other in 50 milliseconds. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Roman Khavronenko, co-founder of VictoriaMetrics, explains the gap with two numbers you can measure yourself, series selected and samples selected, and turns that into a short list of fixes for Prometheus and VictoriaMetrics alike. The one-line version, as he said at Conf42 Observability 2024: "selecting less data is the most effective way to optimize the query performance."

PromQL and MetricsQL share the same syntax, so the first half applies to any Prometheus user. The second half shows what VictoriaMetrics adds on top.

## Why SQL tuning tricks don't transfer

Roman asks ChatGPT how to speed up a `SELECT *` and gets the usual list: indexes (but not too many), select only the columns you need, filter early, rethink the schema, partition by time. In a time-series database almost none of that is yours to change. The data model is fixed (metric name plus labels identify a series, values and timestamps live in separate compressed columns), indexes are created automatically and blocks are already partitioned by time. The one lever you hold is filtering.

## How do you measure a query's cost?

Count the series with `count(last_over_time(<selector>[5m]))` and the samples with `sum(count_over_time(<selector>[5m]))`, using the query's range for range queries. Applied to his opening pair: the slow query selects about 1,000 series and 16 million samples, the fast one a single series and 17,000 samples. No mystery left.

There's a catch for Grafana users: selected samples are not processed samples. A range query runs the expression once per step. `max_over_time(...[1h])` over a one-hour range at a one-second step is evaluated 3,600 times, each time over an hour of data. Raise the step to 30 minutes and the same panel becomes cheap.

## Which functions cost the most?

From cheapest to most expensive: label manipulation (`label_replace`, `label_join`), transforms (`abs`, `round`), aggregations (`sum`, `avg`, `max`), and rollups that look back over a window (`rate`, `increase`, `min_over_time`). Rate and increase are probably on most of your dashboards. Then, in a size of their own, subqueries: the inner query runs many times and feeds the outer one, and they are hard to read too. His advice is blunt: "If you want queries to be fast, don't use subqueries."

## Four fixes for Prometheus

- **Caching front ends.** Prometheus has no built-in query cache, so put a reverse proxy such as Promxy or the Thanos query frontend in front. Re-running a range query 30 minutes later reuses the cached points and fetches only the new ones.
- **Filter pushdown.** Dividing a filtered expression by an unfiltered one makes Prometheus select everything in the denominator before throwing most of it away. Repeat the filter on both sides: in his example, 3 seconds became 70 milliseconds with the same result.
- **Recording rules.** Precompute dashboard queries. The cost is constant evaluation load on the database, extra series to store, and rules nobody remembers to update when the metric changes.
- **Sane steps and windows.** Not too small a step, not too long a lookbehind.

## What does VictoriaMetrics add?

The VictoriaMetrics-specific part is a set of tools aimed at the same problem. A cardinality explorer in the UI lists the metric names, labels and label values with the most series, so you can decide whether that expensive metric is worth keeping. It also works against a Prometheus URL. Query tracing works like PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN ANALYZE: a tree of every execution stage with timings, series and samples selected (his example: 500 series and 66,000 samples), memory used, and how much came from cache. Caching of range and instant queries is built in, and filter pushdown happens automatically and shows up in the trace.

Instead of recording rules there is stream aggregation in vmagent: aggregate before the data reaches the database and optionally drop the raw samples, which can cut storage and load many times over. vmagent can sit in front of Prometheus or any other remote-write target.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose Grafana dashboard takes a minute to load mid-incident, and anyone writing alert rules with subqueries. The `count` and `count_over_time` checks are worth adopting before you change a single query.

Title: The data that makes an LLM capable is the data that makes it leak
Description: Pratik Thantharate (Paycor) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on the LLM privacy paradox and why governance plus DevSecOps has to share the fix
Body:
The indiscriminate scraping that gives large language models their range is the same thing that lets them repeat a credit card number or a private message word for word. Pratik Thantharate, Principal Software Engineer in Test at Paycor, frames that tension as a privacy paradox in his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Pratik_Thantharate_privacy_predicament_datahungry) talk, and argues there is no purely technical way out: it takes technique, DevSecOps practice and governance together, plus accepting some trade-offs.

Set expectations: this is a short position talk, a structured argument rather than a demo. There's no code, no benchmark and no case study, which makes it a quick listen for leads and policy-minded engineers and a skip for anyone wanting implementation detail.

## What exactly is the paradox?

Training an LLM means ingesting a mind-boggling amount of web pages, books and personal communication with little filtering. That lets the model memorise and regurgitate sensitive material verbatim: credit card numbers, private messages, copyrighted text, defamatory content. And the harm doesn't stop at leaks. The same data carries societal biases, stereotypes and misinformation, which the model absorbs and spreads at scale.

So the data driving the capabilities is also the source of the privacy and human rights risk. Constrain training data too hard and you undermine the model's broad knowledge; leave ingestion unchecked and the risk is unacceptable.

## Can't we just filter the data?

Partly. Thantharate lists data filtering, differential privacy and synthetic data as the main technical mitigations, and is realistic about them: at the scale of modern language models they are computationally and logistically hard to apply. "We may also need to accept that some calculated privacy trade offs are unavoidable, at least with this current method," Pratik Thantharate said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. His answer is a governance framework that assesses and manages risk per use case, rather than one rule for every deployment.

## Why can't we audit what a model learned?

Because even with cleaner training data, an LLM is an opaque black box. Its complexity makes it impossible to trace which data influenced a given output, and without that you can't show the system is safe and unbiased or hold anyone accountable when it goes wrong. Monitoring and better visibility into model behaviour help, but his argument is that transparency and auditability have to be designed in from the ground up, not bolted on after release.

## Where does DevSecOps come in?

This is his practical anchor. Treat privacy and ethical AI principles the way DevSecOps treats security: integrated into every phase of the development cycle for LLM systems, owned by cross-functional teams rather than a review at the end. Alongside that, he calls for continued research into privacy-preserving training and secure ML techniques, and for governance frameworks built jointly by companies, policymakers and representatives of the communities the models affect.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, QA and security engineers starting to own LLM features, who need a concise vocabulary for the privacy risks to bring to a design review. Practitioners already doing differential privacy or red-teaming won't learn new methods here; the related talks below go deeper.

Title: An actionable alert can roll back the deploy before anyone wakes up
Description: Leonid Yankulin (Google) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on designing alerts by when, what and how, then automating the response with Pub/Sub
Body:
The oldest playbook in operations is restart it, and it rarely needs a human at 3am. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Leonid Yankulin, Senior Developer Relations Engineer at Google Cloud, takes alerts apart into three components (when, what and how), shows which alerts are good enough to automate, and finishes with a live demo where an error-rate alert on a Cloud Function triggers its own rollback through Pub/Sub and Cloud Build.

The title is Latin for forewarned is forearmed. The talk is a practical one about alert design, and the demo is Google Cloud, though he notes most providers can do the same.

## Why do alerts stop working?

Leonid's starting point is alert overload. Teams flooded with alerts respond slower and burn out, so they lower priorities, auto-open tickets, and many of those tickets end up abandoned, adding to the team's technical debt. An alert that cries wolf too often ends up like the shepherd boy.

He wants alerts to be efficient, which for him means three components each done well.

## When: alert on what users feel

Start from the end: what problem does this alert discover, and does it affect users? Prefer metrics that reflect user experience over resource metrics, and when unsure, reach for the golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Consider the rate of deterioration rather than only a threshold. And always require the condition to hold for a period. Latency touching 10 seconds once fires on harmless one-off delays; average latency at 10 seconds over two minutes says the system really is slow.

## What: ship the context with the page

An alert saying CPU is above 90% for five minutes is hard to act on. The same alert with a link to a dashboard of the processes eating that CPU is much faster to fix. Capture as much context and metadata as you can, and attach playbooks and team chats. His key point: "information that is easy to obtain during the alert is often very hard or even impossible to discover when it is time to respond to the notification", Leonid said at Conf42 Observability 2024. An alert with enough information for an efficient response is what he calls actionable.

## How: delivery you can audit

The notification method has to deliver reliably despite delays, support an escalation path when a notification fails or nobody responds in time, carry all the alert data, and keep an audit trail for the postmortem. One alert can use several channels with a format suited to each.

## When can the response be automated?

Raising an alert is already automated, and a notification that opens a ticket is already an automated response. With an actionable alert, the on-call steps of identify the cause, find the playbook and execute it collapse into one, because the playbook travels with the alert. So the only question left is whether a machine could execute it.

His test has three parts: the alert is actionable, the cause is deterministic from the captured information, and the response needs no human decision. An ambiguous cause or a judgement call means no. Arguments like high-priority alerts deserve a human shouldn't decide it. For automation the components tighten: alert on individual resources rather than whole services, capture all resource metadata and the condition details, and use a resilient, asynchronous channel with a parseable format like JSON.

## The demo: a Cloud Function that rolls itself back

The app is a small Go Cloud Function that answers `/ping` with 200 and anything else with 204. The alert condition, shown in Monitoring Query Language and then in PromQL, which Cloud Monitoring also supports, tracks the ratio of non-ok executions to all executions over one-minute windows and fires above 20%. Assume the alert is enabled on every deploy, so the fastest mitigation is rolling back to the previous version.

Run through the test: the app and the resource are the same thing, the cause (the new version throws too many errors) is deterministic, and rollback needs no human. So Leonid adds a Pub/Sub notification channel next to the email one, creates a Cloud Build trigger subscribed to that topic, and deploys a version that answers every request with 400. The incident opens once the aggregated metrics catch up, the Cloud Build job redeploys the previous version, and when the error ratio drops back under the threshold Cloud Monitoring closes the incident itself. You only need the cause of the alert to mitigate, he notes, not the root cause.

## Who should watch

On-call engineers drowning in pages, and platform teams deciding which alerts could become runbooks a machine executes. The Google Cloud demo translates to any provider with alert webhooks or a message queue.

Title: Give data scientists encrypted production data, keep the key in prod
Description: Antonio Murgia and Francesco Valentini (Agile Lab) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on GDPR-safe ML data sharing with format-preserving encryption
Body:
Every ML team has the same quiet sin: the model works on dev data, falls over in production, so someone copies a sample of production into a lower environment. Antonio Murgia and Francesco Valentini, data architects at Agile Lab, an Italian data management consultancy, used their [Conf42 Machine Learning 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Antonio_Murgia_Francesco_Valentini_gdpr_beyond_data) talk to compare the GDPR-friendly alternatives, rate each one honestly, and propose a recipe that hands data scientists realistic data with only the sensitive columns encrypted, and never the key.

Antonio covers the regulation; Francesco covers the techniques and the architecture.

## Why does data minimisation keep clashing with ML?

Antonio opens with the data-is-the-new-oil metaphor and follows it through to the bad parts. "For example, data breaches are very similar to oil spills," Antonio Murgia said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, alongside privacy violations as pollution and regulatory fines as environmental fines. The numbers behind it: the 50 biggest breaches from 2004 to 2020 compromised 117 billion records, with Yahoo's 2013 breach at 3 billion and Facebook's 2019 exposure at 530 million.

He walks through GDPR's principles (lawfulness, purpose limitation, accuracy, storage limitation and the rest) and its obligations, such as impact assessments, breach notifications and a data protection officer, then picks one to focus on: data minimisation, Article 5(1)(c), collect and process only what is necessary. The trouble is that people building models need real data, and that clashes with the principle almost every time.

## Which anonymisation technique wins?

None, which is the useful finding. Francesco runs through generalisation (ages become a 20-30 band, birth dates become the year), randomisation by noise addition or shuffling, and suppression or redaction. Each has a cost: suppress the age column in a study about age and illness and the dataset is useless; redact an integer into 2* and you've silently turned it into a string and broken every downstream contract.

Their comparison matrix rates each method on secrecy, privacy and utility. Suppression and noise addition score best on secrecy and privacy but poor on utility; generalisation is good on utility but poor on secrecy. It depends on the use case.

## Where do encryption techniques fit?

Two get serious treatment:

- **Format-preserving encryption (FPE)**, a NIST-standardised symmetric scheme with several modes of operation, keeps the length and format of a credit card number, SSN or phone number while encrypting it. It is weaker than AES, but existing applications and schemas keep working. Implementations include Bouncy Castle and Google Cloud's DLP library.
- **Homomorphic encryption** lets you compute on ciphertext, in partial, somewhat and fully homomorphic flavours (Microsoft SEAL and others implement it). It sounds like magic, he admits, and it is computationally heavy, slow and hard to implement.

Tokenisation and synthetic data (Faker, Mockaroo) round out the menu. The recap is a fair pros-and-cons table: sampled production data is realistic but a compliance and breach risk and goes stale; synthetic data is safe but may miss real-world nuance and is hard to validate; encrypted data complicates key management and testing; anonymised data risks re-identification when joined with other datasets.

## What does the recommended setup look like?

On a cloud data lake with a medallion architecture (bronze, silver, gold), in their example on AWS:

1. In the production account, encryption with FPE becomes a mandatory step in the pipeline, from ingestion through normalisation to delivery, owned by the data teams.
2. A read-only cross-account policy lets the non-production account read the encrypted layer. "The minor environment never writes to prod," Francesco Valentini said, and the encryption key never leaves production.

Because FPE preserves format, referential integrity holds, schemas don't change and business logic runs without code changes. Data engineers prototype new silver datasets from encrypted bronze, analysts build new models and reports, ML engineers train on realistic data with only sensitive columns scrambled, and CI/CD from dev to QA to production keeps working.

## How do you forget someone across five copies?

The add-on is crypto-shredding for the right to be forgotten: encrypt the data, then delete or overwrite the key, and every copy across every medallion layer and environment becomes unreadable at once. Combined with FPE from day one of a new data platform, it solves both safe sharing and multi-copy deletion. Both speakers stress that none of it works without knowing where PII lives and its lineage.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers and architects who own the line between production and dev, and ML leads tired of asking for production extracts. Lawyers won't learn new GDPR here; engineers will get a concrete design to argue about.

Title: Reading a team's mood from 35,000 commit messages
Description: Pavel Perfilov at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on mining Git commit messages with NLTK, TextBlob and Hugging Face models for team insight
Body:
Developers rarely read the git log unless they need to travel back in time, and managers never do. Pavel Perfilov, who has spent 15+ years in fintech as developer, engineer, project manager and product manager, argued at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Pavel_Perfilov_code_insight_pattern) that commit messages are an overlooked data source on how a project and its people are doing, and he runs a full NLP pipeline over the pandas repository in a Jupyter notebook to prove it.

The use cases are theoretical and the data is open source, as he says up front; the code is a notebook you can rerun on your own repos. The abstract mentions Apache Tika, which doesn't feature in the talk.

## Why would a manager care about commit messages?

His scenario: a new project manager inherits five long-running projects. Requirements, plans and documentation tell you what should be happening; learning how people actually feel and work can take months or a year. Classic management theory (planning, organising, leading, controlling) is missing context, emotions and sentiment. Commit messages are noisy and low level, which is exactly why nobody mines them, and exactly what NLP is for.

## What does cleaning a git log involve?

More regex than you'd hope. He pulls messages, timestamps and author emails from pandas into a DataFrame, then strips Git and CI keywords, emails, links and merge messages, and pulls out abbreviations. Descriptive stats come first: contributions and unique contributors per year trace a classic product life cycle curve, summer is quieter, and a handful of top contributors carry the project.

Word counts are useless until stop words go, then tokenising and lemmatising with NLTK's WordNet lemmatizer leaves a vocabulary that reads like a developer's. A few lemmas are enough to classify messages as features or bugs and chart both over time.

## Can you trust sentiment scores on dev slang?

Partly, and he is blunt about the catch. The fastest negative-sentiment detector turns out to be a swear-word search (some developers use them more than others; he hopes your company has a policy). WordNet-based scores flag words like error and problem as negative and improving and refinement as positive, so you can track scores per person and per period. TextBlob adds polarity and subjectivity with almost no code; polarity over the years swings like a sinusoid, and feature commits skew more positive than bug fixes.

"The most of the words of the dev slang are having the negative sentiments, so don't be surprised if you get the horrible scores," Pavel Perfilov said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. His advice: always check the original commits behind a score.

## What do transformer models add?

Emotions instead of a single polarity number. A pre-trained emotion classifier from Hugging Face, run on a sample of 2,000 commits (about five minutes on his laptop), tags messages with labels such as annoyance, disapproval, confusion and anger. Neutral and approval dominate; drop them and annoyance and disapproval track the project's busiest periods, topping the chart in 2020, one of the busiest years for contributions. Positive emotions are scarce. Some labels are clearly triggered by single words or capital letters, so he says the model would need fine-tuning on commit text.

## Can it summarise what someone has been doing?

Yes, with a trick. Summarise each of a contributor's last ten messages with a news-trained Facebook summarisation model, then summarise the combined summaries, because one pass over mixed-context text gets messy. The ChatGPT API does better, and lets him change the prompt to get a shorter, emotional, or what-was-good-and-what-was-bad version. His closing advice: "NLP programming is very iterative so be ready."

## Who should watch

Team leads and engineering managers curious about what their repos say beyond DORA metrics, and data folks who want a ready notebook for practising NLP on text they already have. Anyone uneasy about per-developer sentiment dashboards should watch too: the talk shows how easily the scores mislead, which is an argument for treating them as prompts for a conversation, not a performance review.

Title: GoFr hands a Go service metrics, logs and traces before you write any
Description: Srijan Rastogi (gofr.dev) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on how the GoFr framework gives Go services metrics, logs and tracing by default
Body:
Most Go services earn their observability one library at a time: a Prometheus client here, a logger there, an OpenTelemetry setup that someone copied from the last project. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Srijan Rastogi, a Go developer on the GoFr team, shows the alternative: an opinionated open-source framework where a hello-world handler already ships with Prometheus-format metrics, structured logs, a health endpoint and distributed traces, and a two-service demo where those defaults point straight at a 4.5-second database call.

It's a framework talk by one of its developers, so the focus is what GoFr gives you, with a short refresher on observability at the start.

## The three pillars, in plain words

Srijan's refresher is brief and friendly to newcomers. Observability is understanding a system's internal state from its external output. Metrics are the gauges on your car's dashboard: speed, fuel, warning lights. Traces follow a request across services. And "think of logs as your application diary", he said at Conf42 Observability 2024: they record what happened inside the code at each point in time, the detail that metrics summarise away.

## What does a hello-world GoFr app give you?

The live build takes a couple of minutes. Create a module, `go get gofr.dev`, add a `configs/.env` file for the HTTP server, databases and a trace exporter, then in `main.go` create the app with `gofr.New()` and register a handler. GoFr handlers return an `interface{}` and an `error`, so the hello handler returns its string and nil.

Start it and the server listens on port 9000, while a separate metrics server comes up on 2121 without any extra code. That endpoint already has memory and goroutine metrics plus HTTP response metrics per route, status code and duration, all in Prometheus format. A health check answers at `/.well-known/alive`. The terminal logs are neatly formatted and can switch to structured JSON for filtering by key, with configurable log levels. Every request gets a correlation ID that doubles as its trace ID, and pasting it into GoFr's hosted tracer UI shows the span for the GET on `/hello` through the GoFr router with its timing.

On tracing, GoFr can export to Zipkin and Jaeger as well as its own tracer, and you can register custom metrics for your own use case on top of the defaults.

## Finding the slow call in two microservices

The second demo is the useful one. Two services, an order service that calls a downstream order-data service, which owns a migrations-created orders table in its database. Srijan drives traffic at both with JMeter and puts the default metrics on a Grafana dashboard (the dashboard JSON is in his repo): goroutines, memory, request counts by path, method and status code, response time heatmaps and p90, p95 and p99.9 latencies, plus database response times, query types and open connections for the data service.

A spike on the p99.9 latency in the front service leads to the data service, where POST requests are the culprit and the database took around 4.5 seconds to respond. Switching the trace exporter config to GoFr's own tracer and restarting both services gives every request a trace, which shows the path a request took across both services with method, scheme and status code. The health endpoint of the front service even reports whether its downstream service is up.

## Who should watch

Go developers starting a new microservice who'd rather not assemble an observability stack by hand, and teams evaluating GoFr. If you already run a mature OpenTelemetry setup, the conceptual part will be familiar; the demo of default metrics is the part to watch.

Title: Catching the grant application that came back with a few words changed
Description: Akshay Jain (Innovate) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on spaCy, TF-IDF similarity and clustering to triage funding applications
Body:
Reject a funding application and some applicants will reword a few paragraphs and send it straight back. Akshay Jain, Data Engineering Manager at Innovate, a government funder that backs companies' projects, used his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Akshay_Jain_topic_modelling_text) talk to show how his team triages a flood of long-form applications with classic NLP: spaCy for named entities, TF-IDF style similarity to spot near-duplicates, and clustering to map which sectors the money is flowing into.

It is a practitioner's progress report on a real pipeline, part shipped and part still in the lab, and it uses plain Python libraries rather than large language models.

## What is the team actually trying to find?

Four things, in his framing:

- **Entities.** Which people, organisations and countries appear in an application, so public money doesn't go to a sanctioned company or person.
- **Similarity.** Whether two applications are near-copies, either resubmissions after a rejection or the same bid sent to several categories.
- **Sectors.** Which industry each application really belongs to, to read market trends and plan reviewer capacity.
- **Hierarchy.** Which sub-categories under each industry attract the most applications and funding.

## How much code does entity extraction take?

Very little, which is his point. Load a spaCy model (he demos en_core_web_lg), pass in text, and read back the entities. His sample is a news extract about Andy Murray's 500th hard-court win in Dubai: spaCy tags the players as people, Dubai as a location, the Qatar Open as an event, plus dates and cardinal numbers. Built-in types cover persons, organisations, geopolitical entities, products, laws, dates and more. Store the output and you have a queryable index for compliance checks.

## How do you catch a lightly edited resubmission?

Two routes. The quick one uses a library's built-in document similarity, which handles tokenisation and lemmatisation internally and returns a score; his toy example compares a sentence about salty fries and hamburgers with one about fast food tasting good. Above a threshold, the pair is flagged, and if an earlier rejected application resembles a new one, the new one gets a closer look.

For anything more custom (TF-IDF, n-grams, cosine similarity over vectors) the text needs cleaning first: lowercasing, stripping punctuation and stop words, tokenising and lemmatising so related word forms land on the same root. NLTK does most of that.

## Which clustering worked?

They started with k-means on vectorised text, which separated applications into sector clusters well enough. Fuzzy c-means did better on their data, which he puts down to how the words in these applications connect in vector space. That matters because a company registered in one sector often applies for innovation in another, and soft cluster membership captures that overlap. On top of the clusters they extract the most frequent bigrams and trigrams to label what each cluster is about. The pipelines run in Python on AWS, using SageMaker notebooks.

## What isn't solved yet?

The topic hierarchy. They are experimenting with agglomerative clustering to build a tree from category down to sub-topics and tags, and he is candid about it. "Right now, the results which we are seeing on this particular technique using algorithm clustering is not that much satisfactory," Akshay Jain said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

One more finding runs against fashion: they tried keyword-extraction libraries, which gave reasonable results, but for their domain the basic Python approach of n-grams plus term frequency and inverse document frequency gave better ones.

## Who should watch

Engineers facing a pile of long, similar documents (grants, tenders, claims, support tickets) who want a cheap, explainable baseline before reaching for embeddings or an LLM. The talk's own abstract is about streaming data pipelines and doesn't describe it, so go by this summary instead. Researchers looking for new topic modelling methods can skip it.

Title: Your SLA lives on a diesel generator - a data center tour for developers
Description: Egor Karitskiy (Wildberries) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on why developers of critical systems need to know power, cooling and connectivity
Body:
Plenty of architecture diagrams end at three instances behind a load balancer. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Egor Karitskiy, Head of IT Infrastructure at Wildberries, takes developers one floor further down, into the data center itself, and argues that how much of it you need to understand depends on how critical your system is. "The more critical system is, the deeper infrastructure awareness should be", he said at Conf42 Observability 2024.

It's a short, deliberately introductory tour from someone who has run critical infrastructure for more than 15 years, including an infrastructure transformation at a large European bank before the marketplace job. If you have never stood in a data hall, it fills a real gap. If you have racked servers yourself, you'll mostly enjoy the free-cooling enthusiasm.

## What is infrastructure awareness?

His analogy: picking where to host a system is like picking a daycare for your child. You could choose the cheapest or the closest, but a responsible parent checks. Egor's team calls the equivalent infrastructure awareness: understanding the engineering and IT systems under the product layer.

How deep you go scales with criticality. A pet project on your laptop can fail at no cost but your evening. A back-office lunch-ordering app down for a week is inconvenient. A customer-facing marketplace going down can put the business itself at risk. For anything in the last category, stopping at several instances where the rest take the load isn't enough. You need to know where the servers and virtual servers actually run, which cloud provider is involved, how old the hardware is, what quality of data center hosts it, and in which country and region. Many root causes of critical failures, he points out, live at that level: racks, servers, connectivity.

## Data centers are measured in kettles

The three pillars are electricity, cooling and connectivity. Fire suppression, physical access control and automation matter, but in his framing they're optional; without the three pillars a data center is useless.

Capacity is measured in power, not floor space or rack count, which Egor likes to put in kettles. Small data centers go up to 3 MW, medium ones 3 to 10 MW, large ones beyond 10. One megawatt powers about 200 homes. Hyperscalers such as Amazon, Google and Meta build at gigawatt scale.

Power flows like a tree: high-voltage lines from the grid, transformers down to medium and then low voltage, a primary distribution panel, UPS units that carry the load during grid failures, busbars over the racks with hanging outlets, and diesel generators that take over in a long outage and can run for months if fuelled.

## Every watt becomes heat

His trick question for the audience is what all that electricity is used for. The answer: "Electricity is 100% transformed into heat and to nothing else." So the cooling plant is the other half of the bill.

He walks through the options. Air conditioning, the most common, works like the units at home, only bigger. Chillers move heat out with water and are more efficient but harder to install and maintain. Adiabatic cooling evaporates water in chambers or mats, usually as a supplement. The exotic end includes Peltier elements and underwater data centers like Microsoft's Project Natick.

His favourite is free cooling: push outside air through the IT equipment and do nothing else. Warm day? Move more air. It needs only fans and the outdoors, which makes it one of the most energy-efficient methods there is.

## Can PUE go below 1?

Free cooling also gives some of the best power usage effectiveness (PUE), the ratio of total facility energy to the energy that reaches IT equipment, ideally 1.0 and never quite reached. You can measure it instantaneously or as an annual average, and many companies, in Egor's words, "worship pue as a sacred animal".

Below 1? Only if you switch from energy to money. A few data centers in the US and Europe sell their waste heat as hot water to nearby towns, and in money terms their PUE drops under 1.

He ends in the data hall: racks, units, ports and drive slots on the front for the engineers. And GPUs. A GPU node is physically small but draws a lot of power and produces just as much heat, so AI capacity forces data centers to upgrade both electrical and cooling infrastructure.

## Who should watch

Developers and architects of critical systems who have never asked where their servers physically sit, and SREs who want the vocabulary to question a hosting provider. It's a primer, not a design guide.

Title: Your notebook is a spreadsheet; DVC turns it into a pipeline
Description: Tomas Fernandez (Semaphore) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on taking a cats-vs-dogs model from Jupyter to Hugging Face with DVC and CI/CD
Body:
Git can't hold 800 MB of training images, but it can hold a hash of them, and that one trick is most of MLOps. Tomas Fernandez, Technical Editor at Semaphore, used his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Tomas_Fernandez_mlops_jupyter_production) talk to take a ResNet-34 cats-or-dogs classifier out of a Kaggle notebook and into an automatically deployed Streamlit app on Hugging Face, using DVC for data and pipelines, an S3 bucket as shared cache, and CI/CD for the rest. Everything is open source or free.

It is a hands-on demo, based on a workshop his team ran in Belgrade, and it assumes you already know the machine learning part.

## What's wrong with shipping from Jupyter?

Nothing, until you try. "The main problem I think Jupyter notebook have is that they work like Excel, they work great in your machine," Tomas Fernandez said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. Great for exploration, unworkable as a deployment artefact. So step one is moving the notebook's code into plain Python scripts with small changes, and step two is dealing with the data.

His four reasons for bothering: less manual work, the ability to scale onto bigger machines, consistency, and traceability, meaning you know exactly which data and parameters produced which model.

## How does DVC track data without storing it in Git?

The Oxford-IIIT Pets subset he uses is about 800 MB as a tarball, enough to hit Git limits quickly even with large file support. Running dvc add on it writes a small .dvc pointer file holding the hash, size and path, adds the original to .gitignore, and moves the real file into a local cache, linking it back into the working directory (reflinks on macOS, so nothing is duplicated). You commit the pointer, not the data. Different branches can point at different datasets, and dvc checkout swaps the right files in from the cache.

## Why treat ML pipelines like Makefiles?

Because that's what they are. "Pipelines are like make files for machine learning," as he put it. Each stage in dvc.yaml declares its dependencies, outputs, metrics and plots, and the command to run. He builds three:

- **prepare** unpacks the tarball into individual images.
- **train** fine-tunes the pretrained network and outputs the model plus a confusion matrix, top losses and fine-tuning plots, declared as plots so DVC can compare them across runs.
- **test** loads the model, runs predictions on images from Wikipedia and passes or fails on its exit code.

dvc repro runs only what changed, and dvc.lock records the hashes of inputs, outputs and scripts. Delete a model file or a plot and the next repro restores it from the cache instead of retraining. Training on his laptop took about 15 minutes, a cost you pay once rather than on every run. The slides show the split: 1,293 training images and 554 for validation.

## How do teammates share the cache?

Add a DVC remote, here an S3 bucket created for the demo, set it as the default, and dvc push uploads the cache. The team workflow then becomes: git pull, dvc pull, dvc repro, commit dvc.lock and dvc.yaml, git push, dvc push. Everyone shares one cache with every iteration anyone has run.

## What does CI/CD add?

Automation all the way out. In Semaphore (he works there and says so, while pointing out any CI tool will do), the shared setup installs DVC and pulls the cache; a train job runs repro and pushes new models back to the remote; a test job runs the test stage. Two delivery pipelines follow: one builds a Docker image (non-root user, models plus Streamlit app) and pushes it to Docker Hub, the other deploys to a Hugging Face Space over SSH, since Spaces are Git plus LFS underneath.

The local Streamlit app was 99% sure his freshly woken cat was a cat. The Hugging Face version, deployed only by a push, agreed.

## Who should watch

Data scientists whose models live in notebooks and who want the shortest credible path to reproducible, automated deployment, and DevOps engineers asked to support ML teams. Experienced MLOps folks won't find surprises, but the DVC cache explanation is one of the clearest around.

Title: Database monitoring should end in a fix, not another graph
Description: Divine Odazie (Severalnines) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on swapping graph overload for advisors, alarms and auto-recovery in ClusterControl
Body:
Dashboards full of database graphs help the DBA who built them and few others. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Divine Odazie, Technology Evangelist at Severalnines, argues that developers who now own most of their environment need fewer charts and more answers: what broke, why, and a button to fix it. His vehicle for the argument is Severalnines' own ClusterControl, shown in a live demo where a primary PostgreSQL node goes down and the report afterwards shows zero minutes of downtime.

It is a product talk, and it says so. The value for non-users is the checklist of what a database observability tool should do beyond drawing lines.

## What's wrong with legacy database monitoring?

Divine names three limitations. Graph overload: tools capture everything and visualise it beautifully, but "most developers don't understand most of the metrics", he said at Conf42 Observability 2024. Limited database support: organisations run PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis and more, and a tool per engine means a pile of tabs and more cognitive load. And visibility without action: the tool tells you a replica is broken, then you go elsewhere to repair it.

## What should the tool cover?

His list, mapped onto ClusterControl's features:

- **Holistic dashboards**: a cluster overview plus database-specific views (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE rates, active and idle sessions) and server metrics like load, disk IOPS, network and uptime.
- **Load balancer monitoring**: traffic distribution, response time, health checks, latency and error rates for the proxy in front of the database, which he says many tools skip.
- **Performance monitoring**: advisors that come with a status and a justification, daily database and table growth, configuration variables, long-running transactions and deadlocks.
- **Query monitoring**: top queries by occurrence or execution time, outliers that run longer than normal, current connections.
- **Fault detection and response**: alarms with recommendations, automatic failover, self-healing and scaling from the same console.
- **Activity center and reports**: alarms, jobs and audit logs of who did what, plus scheduled availability, backup, schema change, capacity and incident reports you can email to yourself before a Monday morning.

ClusterControl is self-hosted, has a free community edition, uses Prometheus under the hood (with Grafana available for custom dashboards) and can be driven with Terraform, Ansible or Puppet.

## What does the demo show?

The demo environment runs two imported clusters, a MySQL Galera cluster and a PostgreSQL primary-replica pair, 17 nodes in all, including ProxySQL and Prometheus nodes. Zooming one graph zooms the rest to the same window, and the ProxySQL view shows one writer node and two backup nodes.

The advisors are the most hands-on part. One flags table access without an index on a test database with around 7,000 I/O operations. Advisors are scripts in ClusterControl's own JavaScript-like language, so Divine opens the CPU advisor, changes its threshold, recompiles, and watches the excessive-CPU warning appear, then sets it back to 90.

Then come the failures. He SSHes into the Galera primary straight from the console, runs a sleep query, and a long-running query alarm appears within seconds with the query text and a tuning recommendation. On the PostgreSQL cluster he stops the primary with auto-recovery on: a critical cluster failure alarm fires, the replica is promoted, the old primary comes back as replica, and the alarm clears. The availability report he generates afterwards shows 99.98% availability and zero minutes of downtime for the period.

## Who uses it?

He closes with two case studies: Westpay, a Swedish fintech whose team spent hours manually tweaking systems and worried about key-person dependence, and HolidayPirates, for whom managing, monitoring and scaling databases took too much time. Severalnines puts ClusterControl at 200+ organisations.

## Who should watch

Teams running several open-source database engines who are tired of stitching monitoring and repair together, and developers who inherited a database and its dashboards without inheriting a DBA. If you want a vendor-neutral survey, this isn't it.

Title: The LLM never calls your API; it tells you to
Description: Ricardo Covo (Centrilogic) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on wiring existing web APIs into Azure OpenAI chat with function calling, in C#
Body:
Years of REST endpoints become a natural language interface the moment you describe them to a model as tools. That's the pitch Ricardo Covo, Principal Consultant in the app dev and modernization practice at Centrilogic, makes at [Conf42 Machine Learning 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Ricardo_Covo_unlocking_llm_potential), and he proves it with a timesheet API, a Blazor chat app and a GPT-3.5 Turbo deployment on Azure OpenAI, live in Visual Studio with breakpoints.

It is a demo-heavy, C#-first walkthrough of chat completion with tools, aimed at developers who have APIs and want to know what the plumbing actually looks like.

## What does the model actually see?

Covo starts with the basics, and they are worth hearing said plainly. A chat is a list of messages with roles: system (the set-up), user, assistant, and tool. The service has no memory of its own, so every request carries the whole conversation. His warm-up demo sets a system prompt of a helpful assistant obsessed with cookies, and the bot dutifully steers a plain hello toward cookies, which is the clearest possible demonstration that the system message is in charge.

## Who executes the function?

You do. This is the bit most newcomers get backwards. You send the model tool definitions (a name, a description, a JSON schema for parameters) alongside the messages. When the model decides a tool is needed, the response's finish reason flips from stop to tool calls, with an ID for each call. Your code runs the function, sends the result back tagged with that ID, and only then does the model write a human answer.

"The service is not going to call your APIs or your functions on its own. It's going to tell you to call it, and then you perform the actual function calling," Ricardo Covo said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. That also means the execution path is yours to choose: an inline method, a DLL, or an HTTP call to a web API, which is where his demo ends up.

## How smart is the argument filling?

Smart enough to be useful. His timesheet API, running in Azure Container Apps (scaled to zero, so the first call is slow and he says so), has two endpoints: GET projects and POST hours. He defines a get-projects tool with no parameters and an add-hours tool requiring hours, description and entry date.

Ask which projects are available and the model calls get-projects, which returns Phoenix, Griffin and Kraken. Then ask it to add 2 hours to Project Phoenix for today and the model fills in project ID 1 from the earlier result in the conversation, invents a placeholder description, and picks today's date. An hour on Kraken for yesterday correctly resolves to project 3 and yesterday's date.

There is a catch he flags: the model only knows today's date if you put it in the system prompt. Leave it out and he says you get a weird 2022-ish date.

## What happens when the API says no?

His API rejects a second entry for the same day. The error goes back to the model as the tool result, and the model apologises politely in natural language. His takeaway is practical: the model can only explain an error as well as your API describes it, so a vague 400 gets you a vague apology.

## What did he learn the hard way?

Four lessons close the talk:

- APIs and SDKs were changing very quickly, and SDK and model versions make a difference when something mysteriously doesn't work.
- Tool descriptions are prompts, and they cost tokens on every call. "Optimizing system prompts and function definition is crucial, and also it will save you money," he said.
- As a C# developer he found the .NET SDK solid, but admits "it does seem like Python is a first class citizen on all of this". Learn to read Python, at least.
- Azure OpenAI Assistants, then in preview, move the system prompt and tool definitions server-side under an assistant ID, so you stop resending them with every call. He bets that is where this is heading.

## Who should watch

.NET developers and API owners who have used ChatGPT but never seen the tool-call round trip in a debugger. If you already ship agents, it's a refresher; if you're about to, the breakpoint-by-breakpoint flow is the clearest 30-minute explanation of function calling you'll find.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Shadi Elyafi on [MCP for B2B workflows](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Shadi_Elyafi_mcp_b2b_workflow) at Conf42 Golang 2026, where the tool idea grew a protocol.

Title: Swapping containers for WebAssembly when every sensor needs its own model
Description: Piotr Stepinski (infinitii ai) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on running Rust and Polars forecasting models as WASM in Deno instead of containers
Body:
When every sensor site needs its own refitted model, the container start-up cost starts to dominate the actual maths. Piotr Stepinski, CTO of infinitii ai, used his [Conf42 Machine Learning 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Piotr_Stepinski_forecasting_timeseries) talk to test whether WebAssembly can replace containers as the runner for time series forecasting jobs, using a Rust model built on Polars and executed by Deno. His verdict is a qualified yes: promising, not production-ready.

It is a short, honest experiment report, including the parts that went badly.

## Why do containers stop scaling here?

His story starts with water engineering in York, Canada: sensors in pipes measuring level, velocity and temperature, with the usual data quality mess of dead batteries, malfunctions and spikes. Even if the ideal outlier model were a simple linear fit, time series data brings autocorrelation and seasonality, and every location needs its own slope. So instead of one model deployed once, you get one model per site, refitted over and over.

His team's current pipeline is a sensible one: Kubernetes, Cassandra for time series storage, Kafka feeding jobs to worker services. It is fine at hundreds of sites. At hundreds of thousands, the per-job process overhead of spinning up a container environment becomes the latency problem. WebAssembly modules are smaller and faster to start than containers, and WASI lets them run outside the browser, which makes them an interesting candidate for exactly this kind of fan-out.

## What model did he use?

Deliberately a simple one: a daily pattern. Average the signal into five-minute buckets across the day and you get a profile of a typical day. His team uses it as a baseline, and he says it is surprisingly hard to beat when predicting the signal. He implemented it in Rust with Polars, which he pitches as a faster pandas thanks to the Arrow data model and lazy evaluation.

## What went wrong on the way?

Plenty, and this is the most useful part of the talk. Getting Python into WASM failed. The lack of sockets in WASM makes something as basic as an HTTP request a project. Embedding Wasmtime in Rust meant manual memory allocation and, in his words, dependency hell.

"At some point I even thought that what I'm gonna show during this talk, so I'm gonna show lessons learned, my failure," Piotr Stepinski said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

The rescue was Deno, which runs WASM binaries natively. He compiled the Rust daily pattern with wasm-pack, wrote a small JavaScript runner that executes it over randomly chosen CSV files, and compared it against the same daily pattern written in NumPy and called from JavaScript. In the demo the Rust/WASM version gets through almost 150 MB of files in about a second, and the Python version is slower to start and slower to finish.

## So can you use it in production?

Not yet, by his own account. Three gaps remain:

- **Python.** You can't really compile Python data science code to WASM, and most of the field writes Python.
- **Sockets.** Still missing, which blocks normal I/O.
- **Parallel processing.** Deno handled it for his experiment, but in general you have to solve it yourself, in Rust or otherwise.

He doesn't see WASM and Docker as rivals, either, pointing at early WASM-based workloads on Kubernetes. He hopes to come back with a part two on actually running it in production.

## Who should watch

MLOps engineers running many small models where orchestration costs more than inference, and Rust-curious data scientists. If you want a production recipe, this isn't it; if you want to know which walls you'll hit before you start, it is time well spent.

Title: Four small models for the four big headaches of omnichannel retail
Description: Jubin Thomas (Signet Jewelers) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on using ARIMA, random forests, KNN and Q-learning for order fulfillment
Body:
A product gathering dust on one store's shelf while the same item is sold out two towns over is an inventory visibility problem, and Jubin Thomas, Technical Architect at Signet Jewelers, thinks a handful of classic machine learning models can fix a good chunk of it. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Jubin_Thomas_ecommerce_omni_channel_optimization) he walks through four omnichannel fulfillment problems and attaches a model to each: ARIMA for sales forecasting, a random forest plus k-nearest neighbours for sourcing and delivery dates, another random forest for stock levels, and Q-learning for routing.

Fair warning on scope: this is a tour with toy data. Every use case runs on a made-up Company A with about 10,000 records, and he says so up front.

## What problem is an order management system failing to solve?

Thomas has 14 years in supply chain and retail, mostly on IBM Sterling Commerce, one of the two big order management vendors alongside Manhattan. These systems take an order from a store, website, mobile app, kiosk or call centre and deliver it wherever the customer chose, governed by piles of fulfillment and orchestration rules. What they don't give you is a live picture of where stock actually sits.

"In a non AI world, it is very hard for a retailer to have that kind of inventory visibility," Jubin Thomas said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. The second problem is suboptimal sourcing: shipping from the wrong node, which costs money, carbon and customers.

## Can ARIMA still win a forecasting bake-off?

On his small dataset, yes. He builds a sales forecast from transaction date, quantity and price, and compares three Python time series models: ARIMA, SARIMAX and exponential smoothing. Auto ARIMA picks the (p, d, q) parameters for him and lands on (5, 0, 1). On the 20-row test set ARIMA came out ahead with a mean absolute error of 1.8 units, with the other two higher. The broader point he stresses is the loop: feed the model daily sales, refit, adjust parameters, repeat, because a forecast that stops learning starts lying.

He is also clear that real retail training data runs into the millions of records, so treat the numbers as a worked example rather than a benchmark.

## Why does the estimated delivery date matter so much?

The delivery date on a product page is usually a stack of lead-time buffers: store to carrier, carrier to door. Pad it too much and people leave; he cites an e-commerce article claiming 47% of shoppers abandon a cart when that date misses their expectations.

His fix trains a random forest regressor (100 estimators, random state 42) and a k-nearest-neighbours classifier (five neighbours) on historical delivery data: customer zip, store zip, shipping option and whether fulfillment succeeded. Ask for 100 units with standard shipping and it finds a store holding 110 and predicts a date about six days out; switch to overnight and the date becomes the next day; drop the quantity to ten and it picks a store 2.4 miles away. Ask for more than any store holds and it says there is no available inventory nearby, which is the correct answer and more honest than many storefronts.

## How do you decide how much stock to keep?

The third demo is a small Flask app over a random forest trained on product data: product ID, unit cost, revenue, day of week, holiday flag, expected delivery days. Feed it a known product and it predicts an inventory level close to the training value; bump revenue and the recommended stock rises from 23 to 41. Running the same input twice gives the same answer, which he uses to explain what that random state of 42 is for.

## Is Q-learning overkill for warehouse routing?

For the finale he uses Q-learning, which he calls "one of the simplest reinforcement learning algorithm", to find a route from North Carolina to New York across a graph of East Coast states, tuning gamma, alpha and epsilon and letting the reward matrix do the work. The path it finds runs up the coast through Virginia, Washington DC, Delaware, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, which matches what a map would tell you. Scaled up, the same idea picks fulfillment centres.

## Who should watch

Retail and supply chain engineers who know their order management system inside out and want a first map of where ML could plug in. Data scientists who already ship demand forecasts won't find new techniques here; the value is in seeing which retail pain maps to which model.

Title: Netdata's bet - keep every per-second metric at the edge
Description: Costa Tsaousis (Netdata) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on a distributed design that collects everything per second and queries it where it lives
Body:
Most monitoring stacks get expensive for one reason: everything flows to one central database, so you end up sampling less often and collecting fewer things to keep it alive. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Costa Tsaousis, founder and CEO of Netdata, explains the opposite design: collect every metric, every second, store it on the node that produced it, and fan the queries out at read time.

It is the founder telling the story of his own open-source project, so expect Netdata front and centre, along with the engineering reasons behind each choice.

## Why does a central database force low fidelity?

Costa breaks fidelity into granularity (how often you sample) and cardinality (how many sources you collect). Low on both and you get an abstract, blurry view. A centralised design has to cut both to scale and to control cost, and it stays expensive anyway. His comparison: Netdata collects around 3,000 metrics per second on an empty VM, where a typical setup takes about 100 metrics every 15 seconds, which works out to roughly 450 times more data.

He also argues with four common practices: monitor only what you understand (no, monitor everything), sample every 10 to 60 seconds (not enough on virtualised infrastructure, and per-second data makes correlations obvious), build dashboards in advance (data has infinite correlations, so dashboards should be generated and explorable), and ML can't help observability (it can, if every time series gets its own model).

## What does a single agent actually cost?

On a fresh cloud VM with nothing else installed, the agent comes up with more than 150 charts, more than 2,000 unique time series, more than 50 alerts, a systemd logs explorer, a network connections explorer and unsupervised anomaly detection on every metric. Two years of retention fit in 3 GB of disk, at about 1% of one CPU core and 120 MB of RAM, with disk I/O close to zero. The custom time-series database stores half a byte per sample on its high-resolution tier.

Fan-out queries are faster, not slower, because a thousand servers each answer a tiny query. Bandwidth isn't the worry either, since streaming collected data dominates and query traffic is small by comparison. As Costa put it at Conf42 Observability 2024, "most of the time most of the data are never queried."

Need centralisation for ephemeral nodes or a sensitive database server? The same agent acts as a parent: children stream to it, replication backfills gaps after a broken connection, and Netdata Cloud stitches parents and agents into one view without storing the metrics itself. In their stress test, a Netdata parent beat Prometheus with a third less CPU, half the memory and 10% less bandwidth. He also cites a December 2023 University of Amsterdam study that rated Netdata the most efficient agent for Docker systems.

## Dashboards without a query language

Automatic dashboards work because infrastructures share components: the same databases, web servers, disks and network interfaces. Netdata describes metrics with its NIDL model (nodes, instances, dimensions, labels), so every metric gets a chart and alerts attach to component types (all disks, all web servers) without hand work.

Costa calls the query language the biggest problem of monitoring tools, because it turns every new view into a development task. Each Netdata chart instead carries point-and-click controls: per-node, per-application and per-label breakdowns with their volume share, anomaly rate and min/avg/max, plus on-the-fly grouping. Gaps are shown on purpose. Netdata runs at the lowest priority, so a missing per-second sample means the box was too overloaded to collect it.

## 18 models per metric

Each time series gets 18 ML models trained on its own history, and a sample is flagged only if all 18 agree it's anomalous. The anomaly bit is stored next to the value, so you can query anomaly rates of the past. On top sits a scoring engine: highlight a spike or a dip, and it ranks every metric on every server by anomaly rate or rate of change in that window. The host anomaly rate, the share of a node's metrics that are anomalous at the same moment, shows anomalies arriving in clusters across nodes.

## Logs stay in systemd-journald

For logs Netdata uses the same edge approach: leave them in the systemd journal, which indexes every field and value without splitting words, a middle ground between Loki's few labels and Elasticsearch's full-text index. Netdata samples a million or more entries for its field statistics and contributed patches to systemd that made journal queries 14 times faster. For apps that write plain files, log2journal parses text, JSON or logfmt with regular expressions and feeds it via systemd-cat-native, on Linux, FreeBSD, macOS and Windows.

The last piece is functions: plugins expose live data, such as PostgreSQL's running slow queries, routed to whichever browser asked. Netdata stays open source and earns through Netdata Cloud.

## Who should watch

Anyone paying for a central metrics store who suspects they are sampling too little, and anyone curious how per-metric anomaly detection runs on a tiny CPU budget. Bonus: the microphone died five minutes from the end, so Costa recorded the finale from a Greek island on his way to a wedding.
