Title: Self-hosting an LLM means the model is a fifth of the work
Description: Joshua Arvin Lat (NuWorks Interactive Labs) and Sophie Soliven (edamama) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on running self-hosted LLMs without surprises
Body:
Calling a paid LLM API takes a credit card and a hello world; running your own open-source model takes a server bill from day one and everything around it. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Joshua Arvin Lat, CTO of NuWorks Interactive Labs and an AWS Machine Learning Hero, and Sophie Soliven, Director of Operations at edamama, compared the two paths and listed the practices that keep a self-hosted LLM setup affordable and safe: right-sized environments, a mostly serverless shell around the model, security from the attacker's chair, debugging, monitoring, setup versioning, async deployment and gradual automation.

Soliven opens with the concepts (AI, ML, deep learning, generative AI; narrow, general and super intelligence) and hands over to Lat for the practices. It's an overview with an AWS SageMaker flavour, not a hands-on demo.

## API or self-hosted?

They compare three dimensions. **Barrier to entry**: the API wins easily, less code, no infrastructure. **Infrastructure cost**: simple prompts make APIs look cheap, but complex queries, longer token lengths and repeated attempts add up quietly, and once you're locked in, migrating gets hard. Self-hosting is a higher but fixed cost, and unlike small ML models, LLMs generally don't get a serverless option on the cloud platforms, so you pay the hourly rate of a very large server. **Flexibility and control**: self-hosting wins: fine-tune, change the flow, swap in a model the paid APIs don't offer yet.

## How do you keep the bill sane?

Split the environments. The always-on data science environment (SageMaker Studio or a notebook instance, in their reference setup) should be a small instance type, because it runs all day. Training runs on large instances billed per second, deleted when the job ends, so a 30-second job costs 30 seconds. Inference endpoints often need smaller instances than training. Picking instance types per task is the cost strategy.

Then remember that the model isn't the application. In Lat's words, the deployed model is "probably one fourth or one fifth or even one 6th of the overall application": you still need a front end, a back end and a database. When you're in a rush, wrap the non-serverless model endpoint in serverless pieces. Their reference architecture is about 70% managed and serverless: an S3 static website front end, API Gateway invoking an AWS Lambda function, which passes inputs to the SageMaker inference endpoint. The cloud provider takes the sysadmin work, and the team spends its time on the model.

## What can go wrong when you own the whole stack?

Security first, and from the attacker's point of view. "No amount of best practices can really replace an actual attacker," Joshua Arvin Lat said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. Self-hosting puts prompt injection and data poisoning in your lap: if an attacker alters the storage bucket feeding an automated tuning pipeline, the next model version carries the poison without the attacker ever touching the endpoint.

The rest of the list:

- **Debugger**: with distributed training and parallel experiments, use a dedicated debugger with breakpoints and alerts, so you find the problem early instead of five or six hours into a failed training job.
- **Model monitoring**: capture requests and responses, or you can't judge whether answers are acceptable. You can't analyse data you never collected.
- **Setup versioning**: the whole system changes, not one component. Version one has no RAG; version two adds a vector database and maybe a weaker model. Are those even comparable?
- **Deployment options**: some models answer in half a second, some take several minutes. With no serverless and no guarantee of a 30-second answer, asynchronous, event-driven invocation is often the right deployment type.
- **Automation**: not everything in one go. Start with small scripts for data processing and cleaning, then turn the steps that won't change into formal processing jobs.

## Who should watch

Teams deciding whether to move off a paid LLM API, and ML engineers on AWS planning a first self-hosted deployment. If you already run LLM endpoints in production, the setup-versioning point is the one most likely to make you rethink your experiment tracking.

Title: Deepfake detectors alone won't save us, says Block's Raj Kollimarla
Description: Raj Kollimarla (Block) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on why fighting deepfakes takes detection, provenance, regulation and media literacy working together
Body:
A classifier that spots fake videos is a fine thing, until the next model generation makes its training data obsolete. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Raj Kollimarla, Lead Machine Learning Engineer at Block, argues that deepfakes are a problem no single discipline can solve: detection models, content provenance, regulation and media literacy each cover a gap the others leave open, and they only work when they are built together.

It is a conceptual talk, not a code walkthrough. Expect a framework and a tour of approaches, aimed at engineers who want the shape of the problem before picking tools.

## Where does generative AI fit?

Raj starts by placing generative AI in the wider field. You can slice AI by technique (classic machine learning versus deep learning), by data dependency (supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised) or by goal: discriminative models that tell groups of data apart, and generative models that make new data. LLMs and image, video and 3D generators sit in the second bucket, built as transformer-based foundation models that learn the statistics of their training data and generate from prompts.

He then picks three industries where the impact is already concrete. In drug discovery, models narrow the huge space of candidate molecules so scientists synthesise and test far fewer. In architecture and design, a model fed a building's constraints proposes candidate designs in seconds rather than months. And in media, an AI-generated image won a Sony photography award before its origin came out.

## Why are deepfakes harder now than in 2018?

He defines deepfakes as hyper-realistic fabrications: content that looks human-made at first glance, with inconsistencies that get harder to spot every release. The risks run from the personal (a cloned voice calling your bank to move money) to the societal (misinformation, fake news, copyright disputes over voices used without consent).

His demo is the well-known Jordan Peele and Barack Obama video, about six years old at the time. It still convinces, and that is the point: "six years in the field of generative AI is almost like a lifetime", Raj said at Conf42 Observability 2024. Producing something like it today needs a reasonably fast computer and a browser, no special hardware and no Jordan Peele.

## What can the technology itself do?

Detection is the first line. Supervised detectors need large human-labelled sets of real versus generated content, which is expensive and increasingly unreliable when humans themselves can't tell the difference. Raj describes methods that lean on the context around a piece of content instead, such as the title and metadata a video is posted with, rather than hand-made labels. And there are dedicated architectures: he names XceptionNet, a convolutional network variant, combined with vision transformers for feature extraction.

## Provenance versus verification

The most useful distinction in the talk is between two questions. Provenance is about origin: who created this, when, how, and who owns it. Verification is about the content itself: is it original or modified, authentic or fake, internally consistent or not. Industry efforts such as C2PA, the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, define a common metadata format attached to content, checked with open tooling.

The weakness is obvious to anyone who has handled signed artefacts: "someone who is motivated enough can actually mess with the cryptographic signatures", he said. His proposal is to anchor that provenance metadata in a blockchain or other distributed ledger, so the record of origin rests on consensus rather than on one central authority that can be tampered with.

## Media, consumers and lawmakers

The non-technical pillars get equal weight. Media outlets should do first-party verification, checking a viral clip's origin before publishing it. Consumers should give social media content less weight than authenticated sources. And regulation is moving: Raj counts 14 US states that had introduced some form of deepfake legislation by early 2024, with elections driving the pace. Most of those frameworks assume a way to track content authenticity exists, which loops back to provenance.

His conclusion is that these approaches fail in silos. Regulators need the ledger, the ledger needs standards, standards need detection research, and all of it needs funding incentives so security keeps pace with generation.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people new to deepfake defence who want a map of the options, and anyone building trust and safety tooling who needs the provenance-versus-verification vocabulary. If you are after benchmark numbers for detectors, this isn't that talk.

Title: A Slack bot that asks five LLMs at once, built on a NiFi stream
Description: Tim Spann (Cloudera) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on turning streaming events into prompts with Apache NiFi 2.0, Kafka and the Milvus vector database
Body:
Batch-load your documents into a vector store once; everything after that should arrive as a stream. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Tim Spann, Principal Developer Advocate at Cloudera, built that idea live: Apache NiFi 2.0 reads his Medium RSS feed, chunks new articles into the Milvus vector database and announces them on Kafka and Slack, while a second flow listens to an open Slack channel, cleans up incoming questions and fans each one out to several open models at once.

Expect a demo-heavy talk in Spann's usual style, light on slides and generous with cat photos. The abstract's promise, streaming events converted into prompts and LLM results processed downstream, is exactly what he shows.

## Why stream into a vector store at all?

The slides quote IDC's estimate of 175 zettabytes of data globally by 2025, 80% of it unstructured: text, images, video, logs, emails, 3D models, chemical structures. Spann's split is pragmatic. The first load of existing documents and websites is a batch job and should be done carefully, double-checked. After that, a new article on Medium or a new message in Slack needs to be indexed or answered right away, so a prompt built a minute later already has the context.

He also argues for not calling the model at all when you can avoid it: put a semantic cache like GPTCache in front, because the question may have been answered already. "Let's save energy, let's save money, time, network bandwidth, don't call out if you don't need to," Tim Spann said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. Sometimes the vector search result is the final answer.

## What does Milvus bring?

A quick tour of the open-source vector database he uses throughout: pip-install it in a notebook, integrate with OpenAI, LangChain and LlamaIndex, dense and sparse embeddings, filtering and many index types, because one index stops being enough once data types and search patterns multiply. Multi-tenancy through collections and partitions matters in production when, for performance or legal reasons, some data shouldn't sit with other data. The architecture will look familiar to anyone who saw his Apache Pulsar talks: compute scaled separately from storage, query and index workers, an object store (MinIO for small setups), etcd for metadata and Kafka or Pulsar between components. The slides put the project at 27K+ GitHub stars and 25M+ downloads. Molecular similarity search gets a mention as a use case people don't expect.

## What changed in NiFi 2.0?

Python is now a first-class citizen: you can write full processors in Python (3.10 or newer, which he says you should be on anyway for security) and make them available to the whole NiFi cluster. His example is a geocoding processor that turns an address into latitude and longitude using an OpenStreetMap-based library, so the pipeline can tell whether a question is about a place before it goes to a model.

## How do the two demo flows work?

**Medium to Milvus**: NiFi pulls the Atom feed (ten latest articles per fetch, with older ones bulk-loaded separately), converts it to JSON, splits the items, parses the HTML into small chunks ("optimizing those chunks is always a fun exercise") and writes them to Milvus, inspected with the Attu GUI. The text also goes to Kafka, where any consumer can post to Slack, Discord, email or, in his words, a fax.

**Slack to many models**: a universal Slack listener on his open Slack group filters messages (only one channel, skip his own bots), runs prompts through a Hugging Face model to catch unsafe text (it flags a lot of safe text too, he admits) and sends each cleaned question to several models at once: Mixtral, TinyLlama, Mistral 7B, Phi-3 and Llama 3, plus a model that translates into Spanish. Answers that aren't junk get posted back. Some questions skip the LLMs: a stock price comes from a stock API, and a weather question about Wildwood, a New Jersey beach town, gets geocoded and answered by a weather service, the most useful reply in the bunch. Images posted to Slack go through the Towhee library; his cat on a purple bean bag chair is described accurately.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who already run NiFi or Kafka and want to plug LLMs into existing flows, and anyone building RAG who has only ever thought about the initial load. If you want a polished architecture review, this isn't it; if you want to see the moving parts actually move, it is.

Title: An LLM primer that ends in Amazon's 2-billion-document counterfeit hunt
Description: Satyanand Kale and Gayathri Shivaraj (Amazon) at Conf42 Observability 2024 on using LLMs, RAG and cheap hosting tricks to cut infringement audits by 80%
Body:
Most LLM 101 talks stop at the transformer diagram. At Conf42 Observability 2024, Satyanand Kale, Senior Software Development Engineer in Amazon's brand protection organisation, and Gayathri Shivaraj, Senior Program Manager at Amazon, go from attention heads all the way to the bill: what it costs to run models and a retrieval index at Amazon scale, and how his team uses LLMs to cut human audits for infringement detection by 80% for famous brands.

It is a broad primer first and a case study second. If you already know what self-attention is, skip ahead to the hosting, RAG and cost sections, which are where the talk earns its slot.

## What ground does the primer cover?

Gayathri opens with the basics: LLMs as models trained on huge datasets to understand and generate language, built from three pieces (the transformer architecture, pre-trained parameters, fine-tuning), and good at generation, translation, summarisation, sentiment analysis, classification and named entity recognition. Satya then walks the transformer from the 2017 "Attention Is All You Need" paper by Vaswani et al.: self-attention, positional encoding, feed-forward layers, encoder and decoder, multi-head attention, layer normalisation and residual connections. His example is the classic one, where "cat" in "the cat sat on the mat" pays most attention to "sat" and "mat".

On fine-tuning he lists three approaches: hyperparameter tuning (learning rate, batch size, epochs), one- or few-shot learning in the prompt, and domain adaptation for a single well-defined task.

## Playground, managed endpoint or your own box?

The practical middle section is a ladder of hosting options. At the bottom: playgrounds and APIs, with AWS Bedrock (Jurassic-2, Titan, Claude, Command, Llama, Mistral, Stable Diffusion, plus embedding models) and a live tour of the Hugging Face hub with Mistral 7B Instruct. The free serverless inference there is throttled per API key, which is why he warns it is for experiments only. Next rung: Hugging Face dedicated endpoints billed by the hour, or deploying the same model into your own SageMaker account with the code Hugging Face generates. Top rung: fine-tuned models on Bedrock, Bedrock's Custom Model Import (Mistral, Flan and Llama architectures at the time), or your own inference code and model tarball on a SageMaker endpoint.

## RAG, and what the index really costs

The limitations list is the familiar one: hallucinations, a training cut-off, weak domain knowledge, bias, expensive fine-tuning and sensitive data. Their fix for the first three is retrieval-augmented generation in four steps: pick a knowledge base, clean and index it (AWS OpenSearch, a vector database on the FAISS engine, Pinecone), build a fast retrieval layer (k-NN, semantic or keyword search), then stitch the results into the prompt.

Then come the numbers. An ml.g5.12xlarge with four NVIDIA A10G GPUs runs about $7 an hour; an ml.p4d.24xlarge with eight A100s about $37. And the retrieval side is no cheaper: Satya's team keeps an infringement knowledge base of "2 billion documents that costs us around million dollars a year", he said at Conf42 Observability 2024. His advice is to index with IVF-Flat or IVF-PQ rather than HNSW to cut memory, and to treat the index as a cost line in its own right.

The cost playbook beyond that: per-request APIs when you don't need a fine-tuned model, distillation, quantisation from FP32 to FP16, pruning, autoscaling, async invocation and batching, reserved and spot instances, response caching, and model cascading, where a small cheap model filters traffic and only the hard cases reach the big one.

## How does Amazon brand protection use it?

The case study is short but concrete. The team detects trademark and copyright violations by analysing brand names, logos and other IP on product listings against a corpus covering trademarks for around 100,000 brands and copyrights and logos for another 50,000. LLMs also spot counterfeits through subtle listing differences, catch obfuscations such as N1ke for Nike, and help analyse seller behaviour.

The headline figures: "we reduce the human audits for detecting infringements by 80% for famous brands like Apple", Satya said at Conf42 Observability 2024. For hard-to-find copyright violations the LLM runs on around 1 million products a day and flags about 20% of them, around 200,000, for a deeper look. He also points to public Amazon features built on LLMs: review highlights, generated listing content for sellers and Amazon Pharmacy answering questions from internal wikis.

## Who should watch

Engineers who need a single map of the LLM stack on AWS, from playground to self-hosted endpoint, and anyone pricing a RAG system who has only priced the model. Practitioners deep in LLM ops will find the first half familiar.

Title: Your simple GPT-4 Turbo chatbot costs $50k a month
Description: Michal Mikolajczak (datarabbit) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on GenAI's real costs, privacy, jailbreaks, small models and the AI Act
Body:
A chatbot with 1,000 daily users sounds modest until the invoice arrives. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Michal Mikolajczak, Founder and CEO of the ML software house datarabbit, ran the numbers: about $3,000 a month on GPT-3.5, and beyond $50,000 a month for the same bot on GPT-4 Turbo, the model inexperienced teams tend to start with. His talk is a field report on the challenges his team hits shipping LLM applications, and the trends that are slowly fixing them.

A broad survey, at its best when specific: the cost model, the self-hosting maths, the jailbreak gallery.

## Why can't LLMs just answer the question?

He opens with the basics for newcomers: a foundation model is still a machine learning model, trained on roughly internet-scale data, adapted through fine-tuning or in-context learning. Then the failure modes. Tokens mean a model can't reliably reverse his name. Ask for a random number and you mostly get 42. And ask why Conf42 is "always happening in China instead of France" and you get several plausible, entirely invented reasons. The serious versions: the lawyer who filed ChatGPT's fabricated case law and, he says, lost his licence, and DPD's chatbot, released without guardrails, writing poems about why DPD is the worst delivery company in the world.

His test for all of it is the one for any ML model: errors are a given, so is it useful enough for the product?

## Where does the business value come from?

Not from chatting. The use cases are broad (code support, content generation, game quest writing, Bash-to-PowerShell translation, chatbots that book meetings) but the value comes from connecting the model to private company data and tools. His team's internal assistant answers who handles reimbursements and what the company's encryption standard is, which no model was trained on. Hence the reference architecture: an agent orchestrator with tools like calculators, code interpreters, web search and knowledge bases.

## API or self-hosted?

Commercial APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic's Claude, Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini) are easy and pay-per-use, but you don't control the model: an update can quietly break your use case, fine-tuning is limited, and data privacy worries block projects. Open-source models such as Llama and Mistral give you full control and privacy, and leave you running the infrastructure. A consumer GPU like the RTX 3090 or 4090 has 24 GB of memory, not enough to load Llama 2 even in its smallest 7-billion-parameter version at full precision.

Quantization is the standard way out, from 32-bit floats down to 16-bit, int8, int4 or lower, with less memory and faster arithmetic. Push too far and quality falls off a cliff: they tried going below int4 on one project, and "It was very cool before, now it became a drooling dummy," Michal Mikolajczak said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

The cost model behind the headline: 1,000 users a day, 25 interactions each, 22 working days a month, 7,000 input tokens per call (the whole conversation kept in context) and 1,000 output tokens.

## Is the privacy problem going away?

Partly. Providers such as Microsoft with OpenAI and Amazon now promise no storage or logging of prompts and outputs and private network connections inside AWS; two of his medical clients, after analysis, were fine sending data to an LLM on Amazon. Banks and hospitals that still won't are why small language models are a trend: under roughly seven or eight billion parameters, cheap to fine-tune, and small enough for laptops and phones. He demos Microsoft's Phi-3 running locally in about 3.5 to 4 GB.

## Why are hackers excited about GenAI?

He cites a survey where over 40% of hackers expect GenAI to increase vulnerabilities and more than half expect GenAI tools to become major targets. The gallery: the grandma napalm jailbreak, a Chevrolet dealer's chatbot agreeing to sell a car for one dollar as a legally binding offer, an airline chatbot whose hallucinated discount a tribunal held the company to, hidden white text on a web page turning Bing into an Amazon gift voucher scam, and an image with an invisible message telling a vision model to advertise a 10% sale at Sephora. Security for LLM apps, he says, is still very green.

## What's coming?

Better and cheaper models, longer context windows (from 2,000 tokens to several Harry Potter books, sometimes replacing RAG at a higher price), agents and tools as the default, multimodal models in both directions, and regulation catching up: the US executive order of late 2023 and the EU AI Act, with its prohibited practices, risk management, documentation and watermarking duties. His advice: talk to a lawyer before you deploy.

## Who should watch

Tech leads and CTOs scoping their first LLM product and needing a reality check on cost, privacy and security. Practitioners who already run LLMs in production will know most of it, but the cost model is worth stealing for your next budget meeting.

Title: An Airflow pipeline that fine-tunes GPT only if it fits a $20 budget
Description: Tamara Janina Fingerlin (Astronomer) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on a RAG plus fine-tuning content pipeline built on Apache Airflow 2.9 features
Body:
Anyone can wrap an LLM API in an afternoon; keeping the data fresh, the costs capped and the pipeline alive when the API rate-limits you is the actual job. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Tamara Janina Fingerlin, Developer Advocate at Astronomer, toured an open-source Apache Airflow project that writes LinkedIn posts about Airflow: a RAG pipeline into Weaviate, a GPT-3.5 Turbo fine-tuning pipeline with a budget gate, a champion-versus-challenger model pick, and a Streamlit front end.

Astronomer is the company behind much of Airflow's development and sells a managed version, Astro, but everything in the demo runs on open-source Airflow, and the code is on GitHub at astronomer/gen-ai-fine-tune-rag-use-case. The talk assumes you can already write a DAG.

## Why orchestrate GenAI with Airflow at all?

Her list of what breaks between a Jupyter prototype and production: API outages and rate limits, training and augmentation data that goes stale, tools and models that change every month, complex pipelines where you must know which data went into training (GDPR is a good reason), and scale. Airflow's answers are retries, being tool-agnostic because every task is Python, datasets, dynamic task mapping and branching for the structure, OpenLineage for lineage, and CI/CD on pipeline code. Her framing: "it's not just your data that sets you apart from your competitors, it's also the quality of your orchestration."

Some numbers she cites: Airflow is downloaded 22 million times a month, the Airflow Slack has 46,000 members, and 28% of the almost 800 respondents to the Apache Airflow survey already use it to train or serve ML models.

## Which Airflow features matter for GenAI pipelines?

A fast run through the basics first:

- **TaskFlow API**: put `@task` on a Python function instead of writing a PythonOperator. She has switched to decorators wherever possible, and you can mix them with traditional operators.
- **Retries**: she rate-limited herself while building the demo. Set a default (say three) in the config, then crank it up with exponential backoff on the finicky API tasks.
- **Branching**: `@task.branch` returns the task id to run next. Watch the trigger rules downstream, because a skipped branch blocks tasks that wait for all upstreams to succeed; `one_success` is the usual fix.
- **Deferrable operators**: a long fine-tuning job hands its wait to the triggerer and frees the worker slot.

Then the two features that got big updates in Airflow 2.9. Dataset scheduling, her favourite, now supports logical AND/OR expressions, a DatasetOrTimeSchedule that runs on a cron and on dataset updates, and a REST API endpoint so a dataset update can come from another deployment, a curl command or a button on a website. Dynamic task mapping (`partial` for fixed arguments, `expand` for the ones that vary, plus `expand_kwargs` and `.map`) gains custom map index templates, so a mapped test task can be labelled with its accuracy instead of 0, 1, 2.

## What does the demo pipeline actually do?

The ingest DAG runs daily at midnight or when its datasets update, creates the Weaviate class on the first run via a branch, extracts guides and text files through modular per-source functions, splits them with LangChain and ingests 14 chunks through a dynamically mapped WeaviateIngestOperator, each mapped instance labelled with its guide and chunk. It also uses two small 2.9 touches: a display name with emojis, and max consecutive failed DAG runs set to five, so a DAG that fails every night of your vacation pauses itself.

The fine-tuning side is a chain of DAGs linked by datasets: new training examples trigger formatting, then validation, where the pipeline counts the tokens and estimates the cost before anything is sent to OpenAI. "So this is one way that you can use branching to protect yourself from accidentally incurring a lot of cost," Tamara Janina Fingerlin said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024; her budget was set at $20. The fine-tune itself runs as a deferrable operator, and a champion-versus-challenger DAG keeps whichever model scores better. The Streamlit app augments the prompt with Weaviate results, calls the current champion, and sends the post to DALL-E for an illustration, mostly because the Airflow pictures it makes are funny.

## Who should watch

Data and ML engineers who already run Airflow and want a working GenAI reference to fork, and anyone curious what Airflow 2.9 added. Swap the Airflow guides for your own corpus and the LinkedIn examples for your own posts, and it writes about whatever you like.

Title: Five internal AI projects at Aviatrix, from sales briefs to Copilot
Description: Tabraiz Feham (Aviatrix) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on five in-house AI projects, the tool stack behind each and the numbers reported
Body:
Most enterprise AI talks are about strategy. This one is a show-and-tell. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Tabraiz Feham, who works on SaaS product development at Aviatrix, walked through five AI projects the multi-cloud networking company runs internally: customer briefs for sales, lead scoring, a support chatbot, GitHub Copilot and AI-generated presentations, each with its tool stack and the results the team reports.

The talk is short, roughly ten minutes, and it's an inventory rather than a teardown: no architecture diagrams, no prompts, no evaluation method behind the percentages. What it does give you is a realistic picture of where a mid-size B2B company actually put AI first: sales, support and developer productivity, with off-the-shelf tools glued together rather than models trained in house.

For context, Aviatrix sells networking and security across AWS, Azure, GCP and Alibaba Cloud and, in his words, is "Trusted by over 500 enterprises worldwide."

## What does a sales team get from AI first?

Two of the five projects point at sales.

**Network mission briefs** pull real-time customer insights from several sources into one 360-degree view of each customer, so a salesperson walks into a call knowing the account. The stack: Coda for document generation, Copy.ai for the AI-written narrative, and a data lake for storage. The team has generated over 500 briefs and reports a 30% shorter sales cycle, data access twice as fast and 95% accuracy in insights.

**The lead scoring app** matches leads against the ideal customer profile (ICP), pulls data from various sources automatically and assigns a score from multiple factors, so the team works the most promising prospects first. It runs on Copy.ai for content, Coda for workflow automation and Salesforce as the CRM, scores over 5,000 leads a month, and is credited with a 25% lift in lead conversion and a 15% boost in sales productivity.

Both are the same pattern: gather scattered customer data, let a model write the summary or the score, put it where sales already works.

## Can a chatbot really cut support tickets in half?

That's the claim. The AI support chatbot answers common questions on the Aviatrix support portal on its own and escalates the hard ones, creating tickets in Zendesk and routing them to the right support tier. Intercom handles the live chat and Copy.ai the content. Reported results: 80% of common inquiries automated, response time down 60%, support tickets down 50%. The escalation path is the part worth copying; a support bot that can't hand off is just a polite wall.

## What did GitHub Copilot do for the developers?

Aviatrix rolled out GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code, tied into the CI/CD pipeline. The numbers here are the most eye-catching and the least explained: development speed up 50%, developer productivity up 40%, and 30,000 lines of code contributed. Lines of code as a success metric will make some engineers twitch, and the talk doesn't say how speed or productivity were measured, so read these as the team's own estimates.

## And the slide decks?

The fifth project is an AI presentation platform that builds slides automatically, keeps them on brand and helps with visual storytelling. The team reports a 70% reduction in presentation preparation time, twice the engagement and 30% more content personalisation. Given how many hours a sales org spends nudging boxes on slides, this one may have the shortest payback of the lot.

## Who should watch

Ops, sales engineering and IT leads looking for a concrete list of where to start with AI inside a company, and a sense of which off-the-shelf tools tend to show up in the stack. If you want to know how to build any of these, the talk won't tell you; if you need a slide of plausible first projects for your own leadership, it's ten well-spent minutes.

Title: A product manager's checklist before shipping a GenAI feature
Description: Pramod Nammi (Meta) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on top-line vs bottom-line GenAI, its three risks, and the guardrails enterprise customers expect
Body:
Every enterprise roadmap in 2024 had a GenAI line on it, usually without a plan for when the model makes things up. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Pramod Nammi, Product Manager at Meta, laid out how a PM should think about it: sort use cases into revenue (top line) and cost (bottom line), know the three risks, pick a deployment model, and ship with disclaimers, reporting, fallbacks and admin controls that B2B customers will ask for anyway.

The abstract promises lessons from his work at Microsoft and Meta; the talk itself is a structured overview rather than war stories. Treat it as a framework for PMs new to the space, not a case study.

## Is GenAI a hype cycle or a trend?

He starts with the tech (GANs with their generator and discriminator, variational autoencoders for filling gaps in limited data, and LLMs, where it all reaches regular users through natural language) and three reasons for the surge: better algorithms, Nvidia-class hardware, and decades of human-made content online to train on.

Then the Gartner view at the time: generative AI at the peak of inflated expectations, five to ten years from the plateau of productivity. The predictions he quotes are aggressive: 40% of enterprise applications with embedded conversational AI by the end of 2024, 30% of enterprises using AI-augmented development and testing in 2025, 60% putting GenAI in their websites and mobile apps by 2026, at least 100 million people working with robo-colleagues by 2026, and around 15% of new applications generated by AI without a human by 2027. Grade those yourself with hindsight.

## Where does GenAI earn money, and where does it save it?

His industry tour runs from drug discovery and clinical trial design in pharma to vehicle design, flight simulation and medical imaging. The useful part for PMs is the split:

- **Top line**: GenAI inside external products, either enhancing an existing product or as a new offering whose main value is GenAI, which can carry a premium. Features: summarisation, content generation, customer case summaries, natural-language search instead of a hand-built index, and, further out, automated actions.
- **Bottom line**: GenAI in internal processes such as business reporting, internal communications, knowledge management, feedback processing and customer support, where the payoff is cost.

## What can go wrong?

Three risks: accuracy (hallucinations in business-critical flows), bias in the training data, and intellectual property, including prompts and customer data leaking into a third-party model's training. His next steps for a PM who has picked an LLM: evaluate it against what the product actually needs (language understanding, content generation, automation, accuracy, bias), document use cases and user journeys so the team knows where GenAI touches the experience, write a responsible AI strategy, and set up governance with dashboards on model performance and user feedback.

## What does responsible GenAI look like in the UI?

"Deploy Genei in a responsible fashion in a way that ensures transparency, accountability and user control," is how the talk summary puts it, and Pramod Nammi said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 that "the goal here is to establish trust." In practice:

- Disclaimers that AI output can be wrong.
- Reporting tools for harmful results, with a reason field, and someone reading the reports.
- Fallbacks, so a user who doesn't want AI can still finish the job they pay for.
- Transparency that the user is talking to AI, plus citations and explanations where possible.

## Off the shelf, fine-tuned or in-house?

Three deployment models: off-the-shelf LLMs (fast to integrate, no business context, and your prompts may train someone else's model), fine-tuned or bespoke models (much better output from enterprise data) and instance-based LLMs, fine-tuned and run entirely in house, so the data never leaves your instance.

For enterprise and B2B, the policies customers will expect: blur faces in uploaded images, warn users off sensitive data and detect it, turn off logging on the LLM side so prompts aren't stored or trained on, keep PII such as names, location and IP addresses away from the model, and give customer admins controls to switch GenAI off or scope who can use it and what they can share.

## Who should watch

PMs and engineering leads writing their first GenAI product spec, and anyone selling AI features into enterprises who needs the admin-controls checklist. Engineers looking for evaluation methods or architecture will want something deeper.

Title: Scale the stateless half, queue the writes, guard the race
Description: Mike Malyi (Youhodler) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on splitting services into stateless and stateful parts, CQRS, idempotency and queues
Body:
Not every service can be stateless, but most of a service can be. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Mike Malyi, Senior Software Engineer at Youhodler, made the case for hybrid microservices: split each service into stateless components you can run in any number of instances and a few stateful ones that own the data, route reads and writes with CQRS, and move the conversation between them onto a message queue.

It's a backend architecture talk at an ML conference, and the ML link is light: pre-trained model services that take an image and return a classification are one of his examples of things that are naturally stateless. The rest applies to any system that has to survive more requests tomorrow than today.

## What do you get from stateless services?

Nothing is kept between requests, so every request carries what it needs. That buys horizontal scaling (add or remove instances with the load, which Kubernetes makes easy), failover without losing state, simpler deploys, load balancers that can send any request anywhere, and authentication that verifies each request on its own. His examples: API gateways, auth servers that mint tokens from the credentials in each request, load balancers, notification services sending SMS and email, and pre-trained model services.

## What do you do with the stateful part?

Split it out. Stateless components take incoming requests and do computation, data processing and validation; stateful components store and change state with whatever specialised storage they need. Both can live in one repository and be started from different entry points, and you run many more stateless instances than stateful ones, because the stateful side needs synchronisation and doesn't scale horizontally as easily.

CQRS (command query responsibility segregation) is the routing rule. Commands, which change state, go to stateful components; queries, which read, go to stateless ones. Reads and writes then scale independently and can use different data models.

## Why are synchronous calls a trap under load?

The stateless component calls the stateful one over HTTP or RPC and waits. It's easy to build, the client gets an immediate answer and the data flow is easy to trace. The price: if the stateful component is down, the request fails; under high load it becomes the bottleneck; and complex stateful work adds latency to every call. His mitigations are load balancers in front of stateful instances where you can run more than one, RPC over a broker like RabbitMQ, and timeouts with retries, with the catch that you can't blindly retry a request whose first attempt has an unknown outcome.

## How do you stop the race condition?

Race conditions are, in his words, the "source of my daily headache": several stateless instances updating the same state in one stateful component at once. Three defences:

- **Locks and transactions**: a database that supports transactions, operations grouped so they run all or nothing.
- **Idempotency**: operations that can be repeated safely, through unique request identifiers, conditional requests and the right response codes. He notes that fintech companies love it because it stops them spending money twice.
- **Data versioning**: a version field checked before every update; if it changed since the read, reject and retry.

## Why go async?

The bigger fix is to stop waiting. The stateless component validates the request, builds a command (say, create order) and puts it on RabbitMQ or Kafka; the stateful component picks it up and writes to the database. Because most requests succeed, the stateless side can send an optimistic response without waiting for the stateful side. Event-driven architecture goes one step further: the stateless side publishes events, and the stateful component, the notification system and analytics all subscribe, so adding a new consumer doesn't touch the producer.

Then watch the queues. "Pay particular attention to the number of unprocessed messages in the queue. If this number grows, something may be wrong," Mike Malyi said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. He also asks for clear contracts and documented events and commands, so new components can plug in without archaeology.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers whose service has outgrown one instance, and ML engineers putting model inference behind an API who want the surrounding system to scale with it. If you already run CQRS with an outbox and idempotency keys, this is a recap; if those words are new, it's a compact map.

Title: Your card tap is four processes, and the last one is the hard part
Description: Michael A Johnson (Meta) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on authorization, capture, settlement and reconciliation, and where ML fits in card payments
Body:
You tap, the terminal beeps, you walk off with your coffee. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Michael A Johnson, Software Engineer at Meta, unpacked what happens after the beep: authorization, capture, settlement and reconciliation, five or six parties passing messages around, and a reconciliation step he rates as the most daunting part of the whole thing. Then he shows where machine learning earns its keep.

Johnson has worked in payments since 2014, at Meta, Adyen and Wise among others, starting at a company embedding EMV data into card chips. This is a clear explainer for engineers who are moving into payments or already in it and never got the full picture.

## Why should an ML engineer care about payments plumbing?

The numbers he opens with, for 2022: over 600 billion card transactions a year, $4.2 trillion in spending, and a $30 billion annual loss to fraud. That last figure is where most ML budgets in payments come from.

## Who is actually involved in a card payment?

The cast list: the payment card (physical or virtual, with its 16 to 18 digit primary account number, the PAN), the cardholder, the issuing bank, the card scheme or network (Visa, Mastercard, American Express, China UnionPay), the merchant, the acquiring bank that processes payments for the merchant and usually supplies the terminals, and an optional payment gateway or processor, mostly for online payments.

## What happens between the tap and the money?

From the customer's side it's tap, maybe a PIN or 3DS, approved or declined. Behind it:

- **Authorization**: the merchant sends the request to the acquirer, which routes it to the right network from the leading PAN digits. The network uses the first six digits, the BIN (or IIN), to find the issuer. The issuer checks balance, fraud and limits, freezes the funds and the approval travels back the same way.
- **Capture**: no money has moved yet. Usually once a day, sometimes two or three days later, the merchant sends a batch to the acquirer, which splits it per network; the network splits it again per issuer, and each issuer matches every capture record to a transaction it authorized. This is why your banking app shows pending versus completed, or an available balance below the booked one.
- **Settlement**: the issuer moves the actual money, via the scheme or directly to the acquirer, which then pays the merchant.
- **Reconciliation**: making the money in and the money out agree, across authorizations, reversals, chargebacks, fees and multi-currency transactions settled in another currency.

"Reconciliation, as far as I'm concerned, is, like, the most difficult, the most daunting part of this whole process," Michael A Johnson said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. Authorization needs speed; everything after it is back-end work that can be computationally heavy.

## Why does a fuel pump make reconciliation hard?

Pre-authorization. In countries where you tap before you fill up, the pump authorizes, say, 100 pounds, you buy 60 pounds of fuel, and the capture arrives for 60. The issuer has to know it's the same transaction. Hotels do the same with damage deposits. And the clock is running: capture too late, within the seven to 15 day window he cites for pre-authorizations and authorizations, and the transaction is reversed and the money goes back, even if the guest already slept in the bed.

## Where does machine learning come in?

Four places:

- **Fraud detection and prevention**: issuers, networks and acquirers all run fraud systems, and models that keep learning new tactics make them more effective.
- **Discrepancy detection**: not fraud, just the many things that go wrong across authorization, capture, settlement and reconciliation, flagged for a human before a human would have found them.
- **Predictive analysis for treasury**: a global issuer settles in pounds, dollars, Swedish krona and more, and has to hold liquidity in each. Models can narrow down how much to hold per currency, given rates and volatility.
- **Customer experience**: personalised authentication methods, rewards and promotions, plus credit scoring and risk management.

The challenges are the ones you'd expect in a regulated industry: data privacy and security ("where there's money, there's tendency for fraud"), compliance with GDPR and PCI, and models that introduce bias against certain groups, which need monitoring.

## Who should watch

Engineers joining a payments team, ML engineers about to build fraud or reconciliation models without knowing the flow underneath, and anyone who has wondered why a hotel charge sits pending for days. The ML section is a survey; the payment lifecycle walkthrough is the reason to press play.

Title: Stop being a hammer looking for generative AI nails
Description: Arushi Srivastava (NTT Data) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on bolting AI checks onto Stanford's five design thinking modes before you build
Body:
Most AI products that flop are technically fine and solve nobody's problem. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Arushi Srivastava, Senior Director at NTT Data, argued that the trust and adoption problems haunting AI apps are largely design problems, and showed how to take the five-mode Stanford d.school design thinking process and add AI-specific checks to each step instead of learning a whole new framework.

Srivastava has 20 years in software consulting, from Java EE through big data, IoT and blockchain to AI, and now leads designers, developers and architects shipping AI for enterprise customers. This is a process talk with no code, and it knows it.

## Why don't users trust AI products?

She lists the usual suspects: bias, accuracy that decays as data drifts, explainability, security plus copyright and IP, quality (parroting, outdated answers) and hallucinations. Her favourite example of the last one, heard on NPR, is a product review writer where an AI asked about gym belts drifted into waist belts and fashion belts.

The root cause she names is tunnel vision. Teams built the algorithm first and thought about the end user later. She adds that data is now a fourth participant next to people, process and technology, and nobody designs from its point of view. And it is all new: nobody has lived in an AI world before, so nobody knows what to expect from it, users included.

Design thinking doesn't fix the talent gap or the energy bill of large models, she concedes. It goes after the adoption and trust part: the user at the centre, cross-functional teams to catch bias, and iterations that get the thing back in front of users early.

## When is design thinking the wrong tool?

This is the most useful section, because it saves you from the workshop nobody needed. It is not a band-aid for a production trust crisis you need fixed within a week. It is not a quick response to a competitor. And it is not for teams who have the technology and are shopping for a problem. "So there again, hammer looking for nails," Arushi Srivastava said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, about the enterprise rush to put generative AI into insurance and everything else. Use it when you have a user group, a wicked problem with no obvious answer and a new experience to create.

Her running example is AI-recommended treatment plans from electronic health records. Done through design thinking, the first finding may be that patients shouldn't be the user group at all. Physicians or nurse practitioners might be, with different recommendations per role and a confidence score that tells a doctor how much weight to give the output.

## What changes in each mode for AI?

Rather than adopt IBM's Design for AI framework (shown as the alternative, with a steeper learning curve), she keeps the five Stanford modes and adds AI considerations:

- **Empathize**: observe users in the non-AI world, in context. Sit with the patient when the diagnosis lands, not on a video call. Pick data sources for authenticity and accuracy, and fit general-purpose AI to the user's context.
- **Define**: write the problem statement and the how-might-we questions, then pull in security, privacy, infrastructure and technology teams for the non-functional side. Write down the values each phase is tested against: target accuracy, acceptable drift, the continuous learning approach, privacy guidelines.
- **Ideate**: seek out alternative and even conflicting data and points of view, which she argues makes models less biased and harder to manipulate. List the AI pitfalls, and borrow from parallel universes: a healthcare team looks at retail and finance.
- **Prototype**: prototypes need more technology than wireframes now. Set test goals from the values in the define mode, split the problem into modules and test each, and expect users to colour outside the lines.
- **Test**: show something users can actually poke, not a verbal idea, record their reactions and keep asking why, even if the answer is a pivot.

## Who should watch

Product managers and tech leads about to start an AI product, and engineers who keep being handed "add GenAI to it" tickets. If you already run discovery with real users, the AI-specific checklist in the define and prototype modes is the part to steal.

Title: A baby-on-board sticker turns a fish into a dog, 90% of the time
Description: Anmol Agarwal (Nokia) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on the five attacks every ML team should know, and three open-source tools that fight back
Body:
Paste a small "baby on board" square into the corner of half the fish photos in your training set, and your image classifier will start calling fish dogs. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Anmol Agarwal, Senior Security Researcher at Nokia, walked through exactly that backdoor attack with the open-source Adversarial Robustness Toolbox, and it worked 90% of the time. The point: machine learning is software, it has an attack surface, and both training and inference are on it.

The talk is billed as a beginner's guide, and it is one: a tour of the main attack families with real incidents attached, then mitigations, then three open-source tools. If adversarial ML is a phrase you nod along to without being able to name the attacks, this is your 30 minutes.

## What can an attacker actually do to a model?

Agarwal splits the attacks across the two phases of model development, learning and inference, and covers five of them:

- **Poisoning**: tamper with the training data or labels. Against availability (flip cat and dog labels until the model is useless) or against integrity (plant a backdoor, like the stop sign with a yellow square that the model learns to read as a speed limit).
- **Property inference**: learn things about the training set the model never used as features, because it stores more than it needs to.
- **Membership inference**: query the model to work out whether a given sample was in training. Harmless with dog breeds, ugly with hospital records.
- **Model extraction**: hammer a victim model with queries, nonsense passages included, and train a copy that behaves the same. Both an IP and a privacy problem.
- **Evasion**: feed the deployed model an adversarial example, such as the classic panda with a sprinkle of noise that the model reads as a gibbon.

## The incidents are the memorable part

Each attack comes with a story. Microsoft's Tay chatbot, built to chat with 18 to 24 year olds and learning from Twitter, was taken offline within 24 hours after users fed it offensive tweets: poisoning in the wild. PoisonGPT used rank-one model editing (ROME) to change one answer in an open-source model, so it claims Yuri Gagarin walked on the moon while behaving perfectly on every other prompt. Meta's Llama leaked on 4chan about a week after it was announced, which serves to illustrate extraction, with the fair caveat that some people argue open models help safety research.

The evasion examples are the ones you'll repeat at lunch. A University of Maryland and Facebook AI sweater that makes its wearer invisible to an object detector. The 2019 Tesla Autopilot research, where an adversarial image that looks like a clear day gets a high rain score and switches the wipers on, and noise on lane markings makes the car lose the left lane. And a satellite object detector that is about 94% sure of a car until stickers and tape go on the roof.

## So how do you defend a model?

The mitigations are mostly security hygiene applied to ML: secure by design, confidentiality, integrity and availability for the data, least privilege for people and for the third parties calling your APIs. On the ML side, outlier detection to catch poisoned points, storing only the data you need to blunt property inference, and anonymisation, which healthcare already does. GenAI folks get pointed at the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, where training data poisoning and prompt injection map straight onto the attacks above.

"There are many open source tools that exist to help defend against adversarial machine learning attacks," Anmol Agarwal said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, and the last third of the talk shows three:

- **Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART)**: a Python library covering evasion, poisoning, inference and extraction. The demo poisons 50 training images with the baby-on-board trigger, loads a Hugging Face model in PyTorch and gets the 90% attack success rate.
- **ModelScan** from Protect AI: scans saved models for serialization attacks and reports unsafe operators by severity before you load anything.
- **MITRE ATLAS**: the ATT&CK-style matrix for ML, with tactics from reconnaissance to model access. The walkthrough covers the Cylance malware detection case study, where researchers reverse-engineered the model and hand-crafted malware it scored as benign.

## Who should watch

Engineers shipping models who have never threat-modelled one, and security people who want the ML vocabulary. If you already run red-team exercises against your models, you'll know the material; the ART demo is still a handy reference.

Title: Business outcomes lag, so discover with product outcomes
Description: Quoc Cuong Nguyen (Spotify) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on data-driven product discovery that starts from product outcomes, not a pile of metrics
Body:
Large products collect millions of data attributes and billions of data points a day, which makes picking the ones that matter for discovery the hard part. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Quoc Cuong Nguyen, Product Manager at Spotify, explains how to cut through it: start from a desired outcome, translate business outcomes into product outcomes, pick metrics by product life cycle stage, and add qualitative data for the why.

His starting definition: "product discovery is essentially a decision making process," Quoc Cuong Nguyen said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, which means it needs data as input. The trick is knowing which data.

## Business outcomes vs product outcomes

He defines discovery as identifying key problems and their best solutions to achieve a desired outcome, and leans on Teresa Torres, author of Continuous Discovery Habits: good discovery starts with a clear desired outcome.

The catch is that teams are usually handed business outcomes: grow users, revenue, profit, retention. Those are lagging indicators; by the time you can measure them, it's too late to act. So the team's job is to turn them into product outcomes. If the business outcome is revenue growth, product outcomes might be existing customers buying more, paying more for the same product, or new customers from new countries or segments starting to buy. Product outcomes are leading indicators, give fast feedback loops, and are largely within the team's control.

## Pick metrics by life cycle stage

Then translate product outcomes into metrics, chosen by where the product is:

- **Early stage**: retention, because users must see value before anything else matters. Track churn, DAU/WAU ratio and engagement.
- **After product-market fit**: scaling. Sign-ups, conversion and customer acquisition cost show whether acquisition works and whether new users become engaged ones.
- **Established**: revenue and profitability. Average revenue per user, customer lifetime value and free-to-paid conversion.

Quantitative data tells you what users do; it doesn't tell you why. User interviews, usability tests and customer support conversations supply the motivations, frustrations and emotions that complete the picture.

## Netflix and Spotify as proof

Netflix personalises recommendations, layouts and thumbnails per user to improve engagement and retention, an effort estimated to have created a $1 billion revenue uplift. It also uses viewing data to spot gaps in its catalogue and decide what to produce or acquire, which is how House of Cards, Stranger Things and Orange Is the New Black came about.

Spotify's Discover Weekly drops a new personalised playlist every Monday. The data also shapes strategy: noticing that users built playlists by hand for activities like working out, Spotify started generating them automatically. And it shares insights back through Spotify for Artists, helping artists with targeted marketing and tour planning.

## The two classic mistakes

The first is focusing on the wrong metrics, ones that don't align with the desired outcome. The second is relying on data so heavily that "data becomes a blocker instead of a leverage," as he put it, which bites early-stage products hardest, because data is scarce there. Product teams have to be comfortable deciding with imperfect information. Watch data quality too: inaccurate data leads to misleading measurements and worse decisions.

## What it takes to do this well

His five factors: clear goals and success metrics from a sharp product vision; the right tool set (BI platforms, user research tools, an A/B testing framework); a data-driven culture across the organisation, not just the product team; experimentation, so you can quantify impact and validate assumptions; and data hygiene, with robust collection and validation behind every insight.

## Who should watch

Product managers who feel buried in dashboards, and engineers who want to understand why their PM keeps asking about leading indicators. It's a compact framework talk with no Spotify internals beyond the public examples.

Title: Four ML workers per GPU cut the bill by 4x
Description: Chinmay Naik (One2N) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on scaling eKYC ML models to 2 million+ requests a day on Nomad, GPUs and a cloud-agnostic stack
Body:
A GPU running one ML worker at 20% utilisation is an expensive space heater. At Conf42 SRE 2024, Chinmay Naik, founder of One2N, walked through scaling a set of eKYC machine learning APIs to more than 2 million requests a day, and the best moments are the two production incidents, one of which cut GPU cost by four times.

The first few minutes map MLOps onto the DevOps loop (data preparation, training, model registry, serving, monitoring, with continuous training added to CI/CD). Then it turns into a case study, which is where the value is.

## What was being scaled?

The client sold eKYC APIs to B2B customers in sectors such as insurance and telecom, called through a mobile SDK: face matching between two images with a score from 0 to 1, face liveness detection, and OCR that pulls name, date of birth and address from an ID card photo. Requests went through a load balancer to an API layer, onto RabbitMQ, to GPU-backed ML workers, with results in Postgres and Redis and images in object storage.

The targets: 99% availability during business hours, under 3 seconds latency at the 95th percentile, and costs kept under control.

## Why cloud-agnostic, and why Nomad?

Every component had a portable option: S3, GCS or MinIO for images; self-hosted Redis or ElastiCache; RabbitMQ rather than SQS; Postgres on RDS or Cloud SQL. The point was to run the same code on any cloud, on premises, at a customer site or air-gapped. Chinmay Naik said at Conf42 SRE 2024 that "we could package the same wine in a different bottle". HashiCorp Nomad was the orchestrator, not Kubernetes, because the team needed something simple to run on premises and had Nomad experience, not self-hosted Kubernetes experience.

## Removing single points of failure

RabbitMQ ran as a three-node cluster with queue replication across availability zones. ML workers were spread across zones too, except the cloud provider offered GPUs in only two of the three, so autoscaling and deployment automation had to learn about a two-zone exception. Redis and Postgres went to managed services: stateless is easy, stateful is hard, and the ML side was hard enough.

## Autoscaling with linear regression and a manual override

Capacity planning started at the bottleneck, the ML workers, with long load tests per model to find how many requests one GPU node sustains. The autoscaler is refreshingly simple. A capacity predictor runs every 20 minutes, takes the request rate, its growth and the current node count, and uses linear regression to predict the desired node count. The autoscaler updates Nomad and posts the change to Slack. Time-based rules pre-warm the fleet before stores open, and a manual override covers marketing campaigns. He says it has run for years without trouble.

## Incident one: the 20% GPU

With Nomad's Docker driver they ran one ML worker per GPU and saw about 20% utilisation. After digging through Nomad GitHub issues (#6708 is still open, he notes), they switched to the raw_exec driver running Docker Compose, which fit four workers on one GPU at about 80% utilisation. "It straight away brought our cost down by four x." The price is that Nomad no longer handles graceful shutdown for you, so they wrote scripts to tear the containers down properly.

## Incident two: 25-second responses with idle workers

During a rollout to new stores, response times went above 25 seconds against a 3-second target. Workers had no queue depth and no processing lag. The culprit was on the API side: only 5 goroutines consumed result messages from RabbitMQ. Raising that to 30 brought responses back under 3 seconds. The lesson in his words: "our preconceived notion and the first response was to look at workers as a problem". They added cross-service latency tracking afterwards.

## Who should watch

SREs inheriting ML workloads, and anyone paying for GPUs that sit mostly idle. His other lessons: data quality matters most, operations work is a first-class citizen, and collaboration with data scientists shrank the model image from about 10 GB to under 3 GB, which made new nodes ready much faster.

Title: Your data project failed before you picked Snowflake
Description: Jesse Anderson (Big Data Institute) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on why 85% of data projects fail, and the who, what, when, where and how that prevent it
Body:
Social media will tell you a data project failed because someone picked Snowflake over Databricks, or Python over Rust. Jesse Anderson, Managing Director of Big Data Institute and author of the book Data Teams, disagrees. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 he starts from Gartner's figure that 85% of data projects fail, which matches his own experience, and argues that technology is only one small, if important, piece. The rest is who, what, when, where and how.

## Who: three teams, in the right ratio

Hiring a bunch of data scientists and hoping for the best doesn't work. You need data scientists, data engineers and operations engineers, and you need more data engineers than data scientists. Asked which team matters most, his answer is all three. Without data engineering you lack software engineering and distributed systems skills; without operations nobody keeps things running; without data science, why bother at all?

## What: AI is not a strategy

"AI is not a business value," Jesse Anderson said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. Applying data and AI to something specific can create value, but there must be a clear, attainable path to it. A board-level data strategy that says "we're going to use our customer data to understand our customers better" has no plan, no execution and nothing to measure.

## When: neither yesterday nor whenever

Two failure modes. Unattainable deadlines, often from executives who read a vendor's claim that data is easy, set the team up to fail on day one. "When it's ready" teams never ship. And with the economy as it is, projects that take too long to generate value get cancelled, whatever the board said about having all the time in the world.

## Where: don't trust the vendor diagram

Novice teams copy a vendor's or cloud provider's reference architecture, and that architecture says to use the vendor's technology for everything, because marketing wrote it. Get an architecture review from someone who has done it before.

The same goes for conference architectures. Uber's big data platform went through three generations, each a response to a limit they hit. Copying the third generation means building for someone else's problems. Don't over-engineer, don't copy, and move only when necessary.

## How: one to three things, not ten

Teams that try ten things at once finish none of them, and the context switching makes the total take two or three times longer. His advice when mentoring: a singular focus of one to three things, ideally one or two.

## Bonus: why is the data valuable?

Eventually an accountant will ask why you cost so much. "I look for a ten x Roi in this investment," he said: spend €100,000, aim for €1 million. The number comes from the business customer, so ask them. The target gets business people's attention, and it leaves a cushion: hit only 5x and you are still at €500,000.

## The gaps aren't all technical

AI projects are rarely just new technology; they are organisational, people and skill changes. A data warehouse team renamed to data engineers without programming skills is a gap no tool fixes. These problems don't fix themselves, so get help: outsourcing, technical or management consulting.

He also likes to invert: imagine the project failed and ask why. Ask how good a data engineer is at data science, and vice versa. Ask what the business would say if the cluster were turned off; "What cluster?" is a bad sign.

## What the survey showed

His 2023 Data Teams survey got 81 responses from companies of all sizes. The highest and lowest value creators faced similar challenges. The difference: high-value teams used more methodologies, had two to three teams rather than one or two, and followed far more best practices.

## Who should watch

Data team leads, engineering managers and anyone writing a data strategy slide. If you are mid-project and can't answer one of his questions, he says, answer it now.

Title: Vector databases, from the second-to-last layer to HNSW
Description: Stephen Batifol (Zilliz) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on how vector databases work, from embeddings and distance metrics to FLAT, IVF, PQ and HNSW
Body:
Plenty of teams run a vector database; far fewer can explain what an index actually does with their embeddings. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Stephen Batifol, Developer Advocate at Zilliz (the maintainer of the open-source Milvus vector database), opens the box: where vectors come from, how similarity is measured, and how FLAT, IVF, quantisation and HNSW trade accuracy for speed and memory.

It's a 101 in name, but it goes deeper than most: by the end you can reason about index choice instead of copying a default.

## Can't I just use NumPy?

Technically yes, he says, at a thousand embeddings. At scale you hit the questions libraries don't answer: hybrid search and filtering, billions of vectors, multi-tenancy, whether data lives in memory, on disk or in S3, security, and updating embeddings. SQL and NoSQL databases struggle too: they're inefficient in high-dimensional spaces and lack vector indexes. His reason for a dedicated database: unstructured data is about 80% of the world's data, and vector operations are too computationally heavy for traditional database infrastructure.

## Where does a vector come from?

Run your data through a deep learning model trained on the right kind of data, then cut off the last layer, because you want what the model learned, not its prediction. "And the second to last layer contains all the semantic information without doing the prediction," Stephen Batifol said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

Embedding model choice matters. He lives in Germany and works with German documents, so OpenAI's embeddings aren't always enough; he uses Jina AI and points people at the Hugging Face leaderboards. Similar things land close together in vector space, which is what makes search work. Use cases go well beyond RAG: recommendations, semantic, image, video and audio search, molecular similarity, anomaly detection for fraud, and multimodal RAG.

## Which distance metric?

Rule of thumb: match the metric used to train your embedding model. Euclidean (L2) measures straight-line distance and is sensitive to magnitude, so it suits simpler encodings like locality-sensitive hashing. Inner product captures both orientation and magnitude. Cosine measures only the angle, is the NLP default, and is just a normalised inner product, but it is a poor fit when magnitude carries meaning, such as image embeddings based on pixel intensity.

## The index zoo

"There's not one index that is absolutely the best for everything," he said. The walk-through:

- **FLAT**: exhaustive k-nearest-neighbour. Perfectly accurate, linear in the number of vectors, doesn't scale.
- **IVF-FLAT**: partition embeddings around centroids, compare the query with centroids first, then search the closest partition. Much faster; tune `nprobe` to search more partitions so you don't miss a neighbour sitting just across a boundary.
- **IVF-SQ8**: scalar quantisation maps each float dimension to integers using per-dimension min, max and a step size.
- **IVF-PQ**: product quantisation splits vectors into sub-vectors, clusters each, and stores the nearest centroid's ID, for much stronger memory compression.
- **HNSW**: a skip list crossed with a navigable small-world graph. Search enters at the sparse top layer and descends layer by layer toward the nearest neighbour.

His index-picking guide: FLAT if you need 100% recall; standard IVF for indexes between 10 MB and 2 GB; consider PQ or HNSW between 2 GB and 20 GB; composite indexes such as IVF_PQ or HNSW_SQ from 20 GB to 200 GB; and disk-based indexes beyond that. Milvus also offers GPU indexes for workloads that need high accuracy at high speed.

## How Milvus scales

He closes with the Milvus architecture: object storage (MinIO, S3, Azure Blob) at the bottom, independent query, data and index worker nodes above it, coordinators and proxies on top. Because the workers are separate, each scales up and down on its own, which is how it reaches billions of vectors.

## Who should watch

Engineers building RAG or search who picked HNSW because a tutorial did. It's a vendor talk from Zilliz, but the first two-thirds are vendor-neutral fundamentals.

Title: Uptime is the wrong SLO for event-driven systems
Description: Ricardo Castro (FanDuel) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on SLOs for event-driven systems built on freshness, availability and correctness, checked by synthetics
Body:
In an event-driven system every service can be up while the data is late, missing or wrong. At Conf42 SRE 2024, Ricardo Castro, Principal Engineer, SRE at FanDuel, proposed three SLO dimensions for event-based architectures (freshness, availability and correctness) and synthetic monitoring as the way to measure the ones you cannot observe directly.

It is a short, high-level talk; Castro says outright that the implementation details are for later talks. What it gives you is a clean mental model for SLOs on asynchronous flows.

## Freshness: how old is this event when it arrives?

Think of a stock trading system with delayed price updates, or a self-driving car reading a stale sensor. Ricardo Castro said at Conf42 SRE 2024 that "Freshness is measured by the time an event creation takes to be consumed." Real time is relative: the acceptable threshold depends on the use case.

With two services exchanging events, freshness is the time from service one to service two, self-reported by the consumer as a histogram. When one event triggers a cascade of others, you measure the same way at several points, each with its own threshold.

## Availability: did the event actually get there?

Uptime does not cut it here. In his words, "Availability is not just about if a system is online or offline, it centers on whether core functionality is accessible within acceptable time frames." A consumer can fail and processing can slow while every component reports healthy.

In the two-service case, availability means the event emitted by service one arrived at service two, which is easy to check. In a cascade, it has to be measured at several points, and doing that online may not be feasible. His answer is synthetic monitoring: "Think of it as using a robot to continuously test your system like a real event would." Scheduled synthetic events give predictable, controlled tests; real user monitoring gives messier truth. He recommends both together.

## Correctness: garbage in, garbage out, at scale

An event can arrive on time and still be wrong. A bad sensor reading or an invalid transaction propagates silently and can end in inaccurate reports or irreversible actions. Correctness means the event reached service two in the right format, and, in a cascade, that correlated but different downstream events are right too.

Synthetic tests help again, because they can assert on outputs, not just responses: send specific event data and check that the calculation came out right or the database update actually happened. The catch is overhead. Validation costs latency, so the rigour has to be balanced against the system's speed requirements.

## SLOs are a conversation, not a number

He closes on process. Start with the most impactful metric for each of the three dimensions and refine it over time so it tracks real user experience and business goals, in close dialogue between engineers and the people who understand what the system is for.

## Who should watch

Engineers running Kafka-style pipelines or event-driven microservices who have SLOs on their HTTP endpoints and nothing on their queues. It is a short overview, so pair it with something hands-on.
