Title: Insights nobody acts on are worth nothing, so tell a story
Description: Ambili T (Rittman Mead) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on turning data into stories, with a live Oracle Analytics demo from raw table to storyboard
Body:
Self-service BI gave everyone the power to find insights, and most of those insights now sit unread. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Ambili T, Principal Consultant for Analytics at Rittman Mead, argues the missing step is communication: frame the data as a story, or watch the insight-to-value conversion rate drop. She then builds one live in Oracle Analytics, from a raw dataset to a storyboard for management.

Honest scope: Rittman Mead is an Oracle data and analytics consultancy and the demo is Oracle's product, so half the talk is a product walkthrough. The storytelling half applies to any tool.

## Why do insights go to waste?

Her diagnosis: data volume, variety and velocity keep growing, and the pool of people generating insights has expanded beyond analysts and data scientists. That's good, but "not an ounce of value can be created unless the insights are uncovered and also translated into actions or business outcomes," Ambili T said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

Her historical proof is Florence Nightingale in the Crimean War. Her rose chart of deaths in 1855 helped convince the British army to put sanitation before guns, and deaths fell sharply after a sanitation committee cleaned up hospital drinking water and ventilation in March 1855. Add the parable of the blind men and the elephant (context matters) and a USC study of people with damage to the brain's emotion centres who struggled to make basic decisions, and you have her case: decisions run on emotion, so data needs a narrative.

## Same numbers, better story

A small example makes the point. A plain table compares traditional and flexible schedules: productivity 70 versus 85 out of 100, satisfaction 60% versus 90%. Shown raw, the audience has to work out what matters. Shown as a visual with the key message stated and red and green colour coding, it lands at a glance.

## The demo, step by step

Working in Oracle Analytics Cloud (OAC, on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure; Oracle Analytics Server is the on-premises option), she:

- **Connects** to data, including REST endpoints, or drags in a spreadsheet.
- **Explores** a Sample Superstore sales dataset, where auto insights generated by machine learning suggest visualisations before you've asked anything.
- **Prepares** the data in a transform editor that records each step and can undo it, with one-click ML-suggested enrichments. Clicking a city column offers to add population, and a new column appears.
- **Visualises** by dragging fields onto the canvas; the tool picks a chart type, and any visualisation can filter the others. She cites more than 45 built-in visualisation types plus extensions, and one-click trend lines.

## The story the data told

Then the narrative: a map of sales by state with headline tiles and conditional formatting, sales over time from February 2017 to December 2020 with average and trend lines, products ranked by sales, and finally profit by category. Furniture tables lost around $18,000. Brushing across visualisations showed tables sold reasonably well, so the inference was that discounts above approval limits caused the losses. That became the story's tagline, presented as a storyboard with a hidden working canvas and notes left in for management.

## What makes a great data story?

Her closing checklist: know your audience, keep it relevant to their knowledge and goals, outline a story arc with a beginning, middle and an end that is a specific call to action (the thing that separates a data story from a report), and use intentional, legible, well-labelled visuals that don't mislead, with attention to colour, accessibility and diversity.

## Who should watch

Analysts and BI developers who present to executives, and teams evaluating Oracle Analytics. If you use another BI tool, the first and last third still apply.

Title: Carbon intensity should be the fifth golden signal
Description: Pini Reznik (re:cinq) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on adding Software Carbon Intensity to the golden signals and running carbon budgets like error budgets
Body:
Latency, traffic, errors and saturation tell you whether a service is healthy. None of them tells you what it costs the planet. At Conf42 SRE 2024, Pini Reznik, co-founder and CEO of re:cinq, argued that SREs are the people best placed to fix that: add Software Carbon Intensity as a fifth golden signal and treat emissions with the same SLO machinery that already governs reliability.

## Why should an SRE care about carbon?

Reznik builds the case quickly. The world emits about 56 billion tons of carbon equivalent a year. COVID cut that by about 5% in 2020, and a year later it was as if it never happened. The IT industry emits roughly 3 to 5% of the total, more than aviation, and on current trends that could reach 14% by 2040 as AI and cloud grow.

Regulation is catching up. The EU's Fit for 55 commits member states to cut emissions by 55% by 2030, and CSRD reporting is now required of large enterprises. Reporting is only the first step: his expectation is fines and carbon taxes on whoever does not reduce. And because your cloud provider's scope 1 and 2 emissions become your scope 3, you will need detailed, near real-time numbers from your suppliers, more like a nutrition label than an annual report.

## What does not work

He names three traps. Greenwashing, now under a new EU directive that requires companies to prove their claims. Carbon offsets, most of which, he says, are not real. And follow the sun, chasing greener grids across regions, which sounds good but needs spare capacity in each region, ignores embodied carbon and idle energy, and gets worse if everyone moves to Norway at once.

## SCI, measured like an SLI

The core proposal uses the Green Software Foundation's Software Carbon Intensity specification: energy consumed by the software, times the carbon intensity of the grid (Poland runs about 80% on coal, Norway and Sweden almost entirely on green energy), plus embodied hardware emissions, per functional unit such as an API call. Pini Reznik said at Conf42 SRE 2024 that we should "start using the fifth golden signal", and then run it like an SLO: measure today's emissions and set that as the initial target, eliminate the obvious waste, lower the target step by step, and nudge teams when they break it. An error budget, only the budget is carbon.

Measurement is the hard part, and he is honest about the tooling. Kepler exports Kubernetes energy consumption to Prometheus using eBPF; Scaphandre works at the bare-metal and kernel level. re:cinq's own open source Aether converts energy and embodied carbon in cloud and on-prem systems into emissions using the live grid mix. Below that, profilers can attribute energy down to the line of code.

## Where are the cheap wins?

His advice is to "kill the zombies, descale your clusters", right-size everything, autoscale, and consider ARM over x86. Running stable services and spiky batch jobs in the same cluster over-provisions it; splitting them can shrink a cluster sometimes by 50%. Do not spin up an environment for every commit nobody tests. Do not buy availability the business does not need: more nines mean more redundancy and more emissions. Ask whether you need Cassandra when a small Postgres would do.

Hardware lifespan matters too, because embodied carbon is spent before the server is switched on. He cites Amazon extending server life to six years and saving $900 million along with the emissions. His rule of thumb from re:cinq's work: about 50% off by removing infrastructure waste, then another 20 to 30% from optimising software.

And the bananas from his opening question? About 110 grams of CO2 each. Not that bad. Air-freighted asparagus is the real villain.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who will be asked for carbon numbers before long, and anyone who wants a reason to delete idle clusters that finance will also like. His closing homework: read Building Green Software and start measuring.

Title: The best model changed three times while he wrote the talk
Description: Richard Finlay Tweed (Thought Machine) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on rolling out LLM tools without overcommitting, from local models to RAG
Body:
If your company is about to sign a three-year contract with one LLM vendor, Richard Finlay Tweed would like a word. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, the Senior Site Reliability Engineer at Thought Machine shares the system patterns he has seen work for rolling out LLM tools inside a business: don't overcommit, build a small library of working examples, let teams self-serve, make the right thing easy, and respect the limits.

He opens with a tl;dl list and the evidence for his first point: between starting the script and recording it, "The best model changed three times," Richard Finlay Tweed said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

## Why not pick one model and standardise?

Because things are moving too fast, and because different use cases benefit from different models. Tweed's advice is to focus on the style of problem and the building blocks, not a vendor. Enforcing a single LLM wastes opportunities; teams will need different tools for different jobs, and that's fine. The same logic applies to contracts: avoid large up-front or long-term commitments, since nobody knows who will be the top performer in six months.

## Examples beat policy documents

Not everyone knows what LLMs are good for. A library of real examples from your own business lets teams copy and improve on something that already works. Pair it with a library of non-examples: data sources you are forbidden by law or contract to use, listed plainly so nobody misuses them by accident.

On policy, he is a realist. Your high performers are already using these tools whatever the rules say. "Just saying no isn't going to stop folks," he said. Give them approved paths, the tools they actually want plus data they're allowed to use with them.

The biggest winners, he argues, are less technical teams. Support teams have user manuals, runbooks and example tickets, exactly the context that makes off-the-shelf models shine, and they shouldn't have to learn to program to use it.

## Architecture one: keep it on the laptop

Tools such as Jan and Ollama run models locally on a modern MacBook or a Windows machine with a dedicated GPU. With remote APIs switched off and only approved models loaded, documents, prompts and results never leave the machine, which suits strict data residency rules. Local clients can also call your approved central services instead of a third-party vendor. It's slower than dedicated hardware, but it's a nearly free way for people to find out whether this style of tool helps them at all.

## Architecture two: RAG with personas

Instead of spending tens of millions training your own model, use an off-the-shelf one with retrieval augmented generation. The user's query goes to your server, which searches a vector database of chunks from your wikis, runbooks and PDFs, builds a prompt (his example: "you are a helpful service desk employee. Help the users as much as you can based on only the information that is provided in the context"), adds the context and question, and sends it for generation.

The middle server is where self-service lives: let teams register personas, each with its own prompt, model and document set. Teams bring the documentation and the use case; the platform team doesn't reinvent middleware each time.

## The limits, stated plainly

LLMs make things up; they generate plausible text with no concept of truth, so keep a human over the loop reviewing output. Their knowledge is outdated, so expect old library APIs. They're better at skeletons than detail: good for a pitch deck's broad strokes, or, as he admits, "make me a bash for loop, for example. I can never get that right." And they get expensive: GPUs have long waitlists, and per-token billing adds up fast once you stuff large documents into every prompt. Estimate costs first.

## Who should watch

Platform, SRE and IT teams asked to provide LLM tooling for the rest of the company. It's vendor-neutral on purpose and short on code, long on sensible defaults.

Title: Every platform feature you ship is a support ticket you'll answer
Description: Adam Gardner (CNCF) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on platform engineering for 1,000 developers at Dynatrace, treated as a product and kept small on purpose
Body:
Platform teams rarely fail for lack of features; they drown in them. At Conf42 SRE 2024, Adam Gardner, CNCF Ambassador, told the story of a nine-month platform engineering effort at Dynatrace that started as a hands-on training demo and grew into a testing ground for 1,000 developers, and his main lesson is to build less.

## How does a conference workshop become a company platform?

It began when Andreas Grabner asked Gardner for an observable platform engineering hands-on session at Perform, Dynatrace's yearly conference in Las Vegas. The instructors played the platform team; each attendee played an application team. They ran six of these sessions, and the whole thing is public: it spins up in a GitHub Codespace.

The stack reads like a CNCF project list. GitLab on the cluster as the source of truth, so attendees needed no outside accounts. Argo CD, Argo Workflows and Argo Rollouts for the GitOps side. Backstage as the platform UI. Keptn watching what Argo deploys and generating DORA metrics. OpenTelemetry and the collector, cert-manager, OpenFeature for feature flags, CloudEvents, NGINX ingress, and security scanners such as kube-hunter and kube-bench. Observability starts at boot: the platform emits an OpenTelemetry trace of its own startup to show it came up healthy.

The platform offered exactly two things: onboard a new application (name, version, DORA metrics, security scans, dashboards, next, next, deploy), and a feedback form that packaged answers as a CloudEvent, so the platform team saw feedback in real time.

The surprise came on day two. Sales engineering, post-sales, R&D and support all came to ask about it. Sales engineers wanted disposable demo environments. New hires wanted templates, a Spring Boot app or a Dynatrace app. Everyone wanted infrastructure on demand. And support wanted a reproducible environment per ticket, thrown away once the ticket closes.

## Platforms are products, and time is money

Gardner's first lesson: even with no money changing hands, someone has to fund a team, so treat the platform like a product. That means a roadmap, a product manager and an outreach programme, because other teams have finite attention. Platforms are abstractions that turn the complex into a commodity, and they are a place to nudge. His onboarding form shows a yes or no box for security scans, pre-selected to yes. You do not need to understand the scanner to accept a sensible default.

## Bloat is a security problem, not just a taste problem

Bloat leads to security, performance, compliance and maintenance issues. As Adam Gardner said at Conf42 SRE 2024, "A feature today that you implement is a support ticket tomorrow."

He admits he fell for it himself. After the first version shipped, he filed issues for feature flagging, Kyverno, chaos tools and compliance tooling. The response: "And actually, there were no comments. Nobody wanted this stuff." He closed every issue. No demand is a signal.

## MVP or MVSP?

He recommends the Minimum Viable Secure Product checklist, backed by Salesforce, Google, CISA and Okta among others. His exception: something temporary, throwaway and kept away from customer or production data can stay a plain MVP, because you can assume a breach and lose nothing real. For reading, he points to the CNCF App Delivery TAG's platforms white paper and its platform engineering maturity model.

## Where Dynatrace went next

The work produced a supported OpenTelemetry Collector distribution from Dynatrace, a new Backstage plugin, work on cloud native standards for pipeline observability (pipeline started, finished, errored), a look at Crossplane or operators to replace the Monaco tooling for configuration as code, and dev containers as the standard for disposable environments.

## Who should watch

Anyone about to start a platform team, or running one that keeps growing features nobody asked for. The demo repo alone is worth the visit if you want a working Backstage plus Argo plus OpenTelemetry setup to poke at.

Title: In fintech, AI should be the answer to a question
Description: Adhikar Babu (Worldpay) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on where AI pays off in financial services and why it must start from a real problem
Body:
An AI toothbrush is a good sign the hype train has left the station. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Adhikar Babu, Senior Product Manager at Worldpay, gives a product manager's map of AI in financial services: where it already works, where it is heading, and the four ways it goes wrong. His core rule: "AI is a means to a problem and not the opposite way," Adhikar Babu said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

It's a short strategy talk, aimed at people deciding what to build rather than how to build it.

## Three kinds of AI

Babu opens with a quick AI 101 in three generations. Predictive ML is what most financial services run today: rules, text analysis, data extraction and predictions. Generative AI, the GPT era, is multimodal and adds summarisation, code generation and contextual conversation. The future he calls general intelligence: deeper context, persistent memory, System 2 reasoning, and proactive rather than reactive behaviour.

Why now? Capable LLMs from players like OpenAI, Hugging Face and Google's Gemini; traction, with ChatGPT one of the fastest products to reach 10 million users; real potential across industries; and plenty of hype, such as AI toothbrushes and AI PCs.

## Who benefits?

He sees three archetypes that can get real value from AI: companies that are data-rich, with network effects and large datasets; compliance-driven organisations focused on monitoring and governance; and product-led companies that can test ideas quickly and drop what doesn't work.

## Where AI shows up in finance

Today, he sees generative AI mostly in personal finance (spend management and budgeting apps such as Monarch acting as an AI money buddy) and customer support, where almost every bank and fintech has an AI bot. "Klarna recently claimed that their AI is able to do a work of 700 agents," he said.

Next, he expects three deeper areas:

- **Risk and compliance**: real-time credit decisions for the unbanked and underbanked. BNPL providers already do this in B2C; he sees the bigger untapped opportunity in B2B trade financing.
- **Internal processes**: companies such as Stripe and HighRadius let staff ask for data in plain language ("find me the transactions for the past 30 days") instead of waiting on a report, a big deal for large organisations where finding data is often the hardest part.
- **Developer tools**: Stripe again as an early leader, and a future where a developer asks for a payment service with a given provider and acquirer and the AI wires up the connections.

## Four ways it goes wrong

Babu's word of caution has four parts. Hallucinations are real: models make nonsensical assumptions or invent data. Garbage in, garbage out: biased or dirty training data means a biased model. Governance controls: decide what AI may and may not do, especially where tasks are mission-critical or regulated. And over-engineering: putting AI in a product doesn't solve a problem by itself, which is how you end up with a solution looking for a problem.

## How should financial institutions respond?

His playbook is four steps: find critical, manually intensive problems AI can actually solve; assess the options, build, buy or partner, and know each one's limits; reorganise, building the culture and talent to adopt AI; and experiment, with iterative proofs of concept to check whether AI is fit for purpose.

## Who should watch

Product managers and engineering leads in payments, banking or fintech who need a quick framework for AI investment discussions. Don't expect architectures or numbers from Worldpay's own systems; this is a market view.

Title: Put Kafka between your OpenTelemetry collectors and scale on lag
Description: Pranay Prateek (SigNoz) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on putting Kafka between OpenTelemetry collectors so ingestion spikes queue up instead of dropping data
Body:
An OpenTelemetry Collector that receives a 10x traffic spike has two options: scale up in time or drop data. At Conf42 SRE 2024, Pranay Prateek, co-founder of SigNoz, explained how SigNoz Cloud stopped betting on the first option by putting Kafka between its gateway collectors and each tenant's collector, then scaling the tenants on consumer lag.

It is a production architecture walkthrough from people who run an observability backend for paying customers, which makes it more useful than the usual forum thread on whether to use Kafka with OpenTelemetry at all.

## What is wrong with collectors talking straight to collectors?

Prateek recaps the OpenTelemetry Collector as a pipeline of receivers (more than 90 of them, from host metrics to Kafka), processors (attribute changes, filtering) and exporters (ClickHouse, Kafka, a vendor backend). SigNoz, an open source observability platform with 17K+ GitHub stars, has been OpenTelemetry-native since it started in 2021.

In the original single-tenant design of SigNoz Cloud, a load balancer sent each customer's data straight to that tenant's collector. Two failure modes followed. If the tenant or its database went down, agents got 5xx responses and data was lost after a few minutes. And if a customer's ingestion jumped 10x within minutes, the tenant could not scale fast enough and rejected data until its database caught up.

## Kafka as a six-hour shock absorber

The fix: customers hit a fleet of gateway collectors, which use the Kafka exporter to write into Kafka; each tenant's collector reads with the Kafka receiver. A spike lands in the queue, and the tenant keeps consuming at its own pace while it scales. The setup he showed has a 6-hour retention period, a replication factor of 3 and a 10 MB maximum message size.

There is a bonus he clearly enjoys. Collectors are stateless and horizontally scaled, so the spans of one trace can land on different instances, which makes tail-based sampling awkward. With Kafka you can use the trace ID as the partition key, so all spans of a trace go to one partition and the sampling decision gets easy. Dropping every health-check trace becomes a filter, not a distributed systems problem.

## Consumer lag is the scaling signal

SigNoz monitors SigNoz with SigNoz (the monitor monitoring itself): records produced and consumed per tenant, producer-to-consumer latency, and consumer lag. Pranay Prateek said at Conf42 SRE 2024 that "consumer lag is like one of the pointers which helps you decide what to and when to scale the tenants". When lag on a partition crosses a threshold, they get alerted and scripts add consumers. The ceiling is partition count, since partitions are Kafka's unit of parallelism, so more tenant collectors also means more partitions.

Batching pays off too: because collectors send data in batches, they see a compression factor of 10 to 15 before it enters Kafka.

## What is still unfinished?

He is candid about the gaps. Partitions are not yet added automatically as a topic's ingestion grows. A tenant collector that hits a permanent failure can leave a partition stuck; the plan is to drop after a few retries or send the message to a dead letter queue. They want the tenant pipeline (Kafka receiver, processors, exporter) to be synchronous, so offsets are committed only after the write to the database succeeds. And exactly-once delivery across the whole write path stays on the wish list, which anyone who has tried it will recognise.

## Who should watch

Teams running OpenTelemetry Collectors at a scale where a single customer can flood a pipeline, and anyone designing a multi-tenant telemetry backend. A short talk with a real configuration.

Title: Stop drawing home icons and ship the design system
Description: Elena Shabanova (PolyAI) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on building a design system on a startup clock with prioritisation and AI Figma plugins
Body:
Startups need a design system most when they have the least time to build one. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Elena Shabanova, Senior Product Designer at PolyAI with nine-plus years in product design and design system work at SberTech, Gett and SpatialChat, lays out how to build one under a dense roadmap: prioritise ruthlessly, buy what you can, and let Figma plugins and AI do the tedious parts.

Her framing is economic. "Using design system is all about saving time and money," Elena Shabanova said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, and she cites industry figures such as design systems reducing time on design tasks by 30-50% and allowing reuse of up to 70% of code.

## Why is it harder in a startup?

All teams face consistency, stakeholder alignment, communication gaps, technical constraints and adoption. Startups add speed, a dense roadmap, no assigned design system team, budget limits and prioritisation conflicts with the roadmap.

Her first escape hatch is the happy path: a brand-new product can just buy an existing design system. Marketplaces such as UI8 and Design Systems Repo offer everything from hundreds of components to tiny starter kits, usually with a Figma file and code.

## What do you build first?

Existing products can't take the happy path, so they need a strategy: a roadmap, a long-term vision, real users (designers, engineers, QA, marketing), metrics such as user satisfaction, and an adoption plan. Then prioritisation, with three options:

- **MoSCoW**: must, should, could, won't-have-right-now. Colour palette, grids, icons and fonts are must-haves; an early startup can park combo boxes and date pickers.
- **Atomic design**: start from sub-atomic pieces (colour, typography, spacing), then atoms (icons, buttons, labels, inputs), then molecules, organisms, templates and pages.
- **Roadmap-based**: build a component only when a planned feature needs it. Lots of work early, then a mostly complete system by mid-roadmap.

She usually mixes atomic and roadmap-based: colours first, then components feature by feature. The process mirrors feature work, discovery, design, development and release, with audits, user testing, documentation and an announcement so users know what changed.

## Let plugins do the boring parts

Colour palettes can take hours or weeks, so generate them: Color Scale Generator, Magic Color Palettes and an AI Color Palette Generator that builds styles from images or brand guidelines. Typography: Typography Style Guide Generator, Text Styles Generator and Typescales, some of which collect the styles already scattered across your mockups.

Icons get her best line: designers "already designed like thousands of different versions of home icon," so buy a set or use Material Symbols and the libraries on Toools.design. Newer beta plugins such as Generate Design Systems and Atomic Design System Generator promise a whole system from a prompt; so far they produce styles, fonts and a few simple components.

For handoff, Figma's Dev Mode generates code to paste into the repository, and Storybook (or an alternative) shows engineers states and patterns. Documentation gets DS-GPT inside Figma, EightShapes Specs for component anatomy and spacing, and zeroheight as the single source of truth.

## Scale and adoption are people problems

A system that can't scale ends up with many near-duplicate components and documentation for each. Her fixes: collaboration between builders and users, modular and flexible components, thorough documentation and version control so people know which button is current. Adoption needs education, feedback loops, visible impact, and recognition for the people building the system.

## Who should watch

Designers and frontend engineers at startups who keep postponing a design system. It's a Figma-only talk, a practical checklist with named tools rather than theory.

Title: Ten review comments will hurt even a ten-year veteran
Description: German Urikh at Conf42 SRE 2024 on code review that catches bugs without wrecking morale, from comment tone to arguments
Body:
Code review is the one place where engineers grade each other in public, and most teams never discuss how to do it well. In a lightning talk at Conf42 SRE 2024, German Urikh, a Senior Software Engineer, argues that a review has two jobs, catching bugs and keeping the author productive, and that the second fails far more often than the first.

It is short and practical: no tooling pitch, just habits you can adopt on your next merge request.

## Why bother reviewing at all?

Urikh starts with the sceptic's question: reviewers could be writing features instead. His answer comes in three parts. More eyes on code means more chances to catch bugs, privacy and security issues before they turn into production downtime, regulator problems or lost customer trust. Review spreads best practices and code style across a project, and juniors learn approaches they did not know. And review stops unintended workflows: one developer should not be able to push to production and verify their own change, so review doubles as a security layer.

## Deep review or syntax pass: say which one you did

For a thorough review he checks out the author's branch locally, so the editor flags syntax errors and he can jump between files to keep the context. When it matters he books a calendar slot and puts on headphones.

The opposite mode is legitimate too. With several merge requests a day, a pass over syntax and obvious bugs may be all you have time for. The rule is to tell the author you skipped the business logic, so nobody mistakes your approval for a deep review.

## Adapt the comment to the person

His favourite tip. For a junior colleague, someone new to the project or a more sensitive person, he writes a polite request with the full reason: why the code was needed once and why it is not needed now. For a senior colleague who already has the context, a bare two-word note that it is not needed is enough, and they will ask if they want more. Same change, two comments, both correct for their reader.

## Too many comments trip the ego, even a seasoned one

Urikh has more than ten years of experience and still reacts badly to a wall of feedback. Receiving ten or more comments, he admits, "my first reaction is to, I don't know, to try to protect myself". His fix: keep only the most significant comments and move the rest offline.

He also asks reviewers to say when they like something. A one-line thank-you costs nothing. As German Urikh said at Conf42 SRE 2024, "happy developer means, after all, more productive developer, right?"

## Stop the comment ping-pong

A review thread is a public space, so a disagreement there feels like a public attack. Two rounds of replies in, the goal is no longer the code: "it eventually becomes a battle of egos, like whose comment is going to be the last?" Move it to Slack or a call, then leave a note on the thread, saying it was discussed offline, so later readers know a decision was made and whom to ask.

## Who should watch

Tech leads and senior engineers who review a lot, and anyone who has ever opened a merge request to find thirty comments. It is a lightning talk, so expect five minutes of habits, not a review framework.

Title: Your battery icon was the first dynamic UI
Description: Yashwanth Kotha (SHL) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on AI-driven interfaces that personalise and adapt to how users feel, plus the ethics
Body:
Interfaces that change based on who you are and how you feel sound like science fiction, until you notice you've been using one for years. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Yashwanth Kotha, Senior UX Designer at SHL, walks through how AI and machine learning are turning static screens into dynamic, personalised and emotion-aware experiences, and what designers owe users in return.

It's a designer's tour of the idea, from the command line to brain-computer interfaces, with case studies along the way.

## Dynamic UI is older than you think

"Technically, the battery meter on your smartphone is a type of dynamic UI," Yashwanth Kotha said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. It changes colour as the charge drops. What's new is how much more nuanced these adaptations have become.

His main example is Apple. The iPhone's Dynamic Island turned the notch into an interactive element. macOS switches between dark and light modes by time of day. iOS 16 tied custom lock screens, wallpapers and widgets to Focus modes, which can switch on by location, though you have to set that up yourself the first time. His hypothesis: even Apple, famous for strict design, is bending toward the customisation Gen Z users expect.

## Where personalisation comes from

The familiar version is recommendations. Kotha uses Netflix: stream a few Marvel films and a week later your Saturday-night home screen is full of things tailored to you. Amazon's product suggestions work the same way.

The pipeline behind it is straightforward to describe: collect interaction data (clicks, browsing history), train models to predict preferences and emotions, then adapt the interface in real time. He names the three model families doing the work, supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, and the infrastructure cost: you need serious compute, and you have to keep the data safe and private.

For product teams outside wearables, his advice is practical: adapt the core functionality people use most, surface specific data points at key moments, make intuitive changes based on location and time, and give power users manual customisation.

## Reading the room

Emotion-aware systems add another input. Facial recognition estimates whether you look happy or sad, voice analysis reads mood from tone, and text analysis infers feelings from what you type. The payoff, he argues, is more engaging interactions, higher satisfaction and greater loyalty.

Two case studies make it concrete. Personalised learning platforms tailor lessons to each student's history; he cites the Southern Nevada Urban Micro Academy, and reports schools seeing higher engagement and better completion rates. Emotion-aware games lower the difficulty when the player is frustrated and ramp it up when they're bored.

## The part designers can't skip

Kotha's closing section is ethics: data privacy and security first, transparency in how AI makes decisions, accountability for those decisions, bias prevention, and informed consent. An interface that reads your face needs to tell you it is doing so. He looks ahead to AR and VR, brain-computer interfaces and multimodal input mixing voice, touch and gesture, including a new screenless AI device that works entirely through voice and a camera.

## Who should watch

UX designers and product managers looking for a vocabulary and a set of examples for adaptive interfaces. It's a high-level, upbeat overview; engineers wanting model architectures or implementation detail won't find them here.

Title: Protein folding went from supercomputers to transformers
Description: Iaroslav Geraskin (TikTok) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on how deep learning replaced slow physics simulation in protein structure prediction
Body:
Predicting how a protein folds used to mean renting time on a supercomputer and waiting. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, Iaroslav Geraskin, a machine learning engineer at TikTok with a master's in computational biology and a year spent on antibody structure prediction for drug discovery, traces how the field moved from physics simulation to statistics to end-to-end deep learning, and why the physics never quite went away.

It's a compact history lesson with a clear argument: each generation of methods used more evolutionary information, ran faster, and borrowed more from image and text models.

## Why predict structure at all?

A protein is a chain of amino acids, and its function depends on the 3D shape that chain folds into. Getting the sequence is cheap; getting the structure experimentally is hard. So if you want to run computer experiments, say designing an enzyme that speeds up plastic breakdown, or understanding how antibodies bind to the coronavirus spike protein, you first need a predicted structure.

The key extra signal is the multiple sequence alignment (MSA): line up similar proteins from a database and look at which positions change together. If one position flips its charge and a distant position flips too, they are probably close in 3D space, even if they are far apart in the sequence.

## Physics is a three-body problem with thousands of bodies

Geraskin explains why molecular dynamics is so expensive by pointing at the three-body problem: even three interacting particles have no closed-form solution, and the system is chaotic. Simulating a protein means taking lots of small steps under forces that depend on atom coordinates, on high-performance hardware. The upside is trajectory analysis: you see how the protein moves, not just where it ends up.

The workarounds came in two flavours. Homology modeling stitches fragments of known structures with similar sequences into a good first guess, so the simulation starts closer to the answer. Statistical potentials use observed structures to penalise unlikely positions, but those statistics only hold within a protein family.

## Where deep learning took over

"And that's where deep learning comes in," Iaroslav Geraskin said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. AlphaFold 1 used convolutional networks on MSA features, encoded like a 2D picture, to predict a distribution over distances between pairs of residues. Physics-based folding then ran much faster because it knew which positions were likely.

AlphaFold 2 went further: templates plus MSA in, transformers in the middle, and a structure module that predicts angles and distances directly, end to end, with no iterative simulation. Protein language models do something similar with a single sequence, compressing evolutionary knowledge from a large database into an LLM and training a small network to predict geometry. AlphaFold 3, released the month he recorded the talk, adds a diffusion module and handles ligands, DNA and other molecules that proteins bind to.

## The physics still earns its keep

"Physics based methods are not dead still," Iaroslav Geraskin said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. Deep learning models don't know physics, so their output can be locally wrong; a few iterations of physics-based refinement relax the structure into something more natural. And if you need trajectories, simulation is still the only option.

His conclusion: the hard problem now is getting more data sources into a single model, and the tools keep arriving from elsewhere, with transformers, diffusion and convolutional networks all trickling down from images and text into biology.

## Who should watch

ML engineers curious about what AlphaFold actually does, and anyone who wants the bridge between classic computational biology and modern architectures in under half an hour. It's an overview talk: no code, no benchmarks, just a clean map of the methods.

Title: AI design tools are a big book of answers, not a new story
Description: Kirill Sidorets (The Open Platform) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024 on why AI design tools speed designers up but still need human creativity
Body:
Every designer has asked whether Midjourney is coming for their job. Kirill Sidorets, Senior Product Designer at The Open Platform, gives his answer at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024: not yet, and probably not in the way you fear. AI is a fast assistant that learns from what already exists; the creative leap still comes from people. The best results, he argues, come from combining the two.

It's a short, opinionated overview for designers, with a tour of tools and one real campaign as evidence.

## What does AI lack that designers have?

Sidorets starts by defining creativity: thinking outside the box, connecting unrelated things, taking risks and embracing failure. AI can produce novel combinations from data and algorithms, but it has no emotions, experiences or culture to draw on, and that is where human work gets its depth.

His metaphor is the line worth remembering. "To be honest, it's like having a really big book of answers, but it doesn't know how to write a new story," Kirill Sidorets said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024. AI is great at learning from what has been done before and much weaker at something totally fresh, so for now it is "a reliable assistant" that still needs human guidance for originality.

## The toolbox

The middle of the talk is a quick tour of tools he thinks belong in a designer's kit:

- **Uizard** scans paper sketches and turns them into editable digital prototypes using machine vision. For anyone who starts interface work with a pen, this is the one to try.
- **Midjourney** generates high-quality images from short text prompts in seconds, in the browser.
- **DALL-E 2**, OpenAI's text-to-image model, the successor to the original DALL-E from early 2021.
- **Visual Electric**, an image generator built for creatives, with a canvas that feels closer to Figma than to a chat box.
- **Adobe Firefly**, a standalone web app pitched as safe for commercial use.
- **Magician**, an AI plugin for Figma that handles copywriting and generates icons from text.

The pattern across them: they take the repetitive part (resizing, basic layouts, first drafts of imagery) so the designer spends the time on the artistic decisions.

## The campaign that saved 90% of the hours

His case study is a pet insurance company that wanted a cheerful illustration style for internal communications. A single creative team of illustrators, designers and copywriters used AI to produce over 750 images of household pets, then put them on internal products and merchandise such as coffee coasters. He reports that the approach saved 90% of the designers' work hours. The point he draws is not that AI did the work, but how powerful it is in the hands of a talented team.

## The ethics questions he leaves open

Sidorets ends with questions rather than answers: will AI replace human intuition in design, and can algorithms avoid violating morality and law? His position is that AI has no sense of what is fair, so it needs strong rules, ongoing checks and humans keeping an eye on it. Machine learning can analyse trends and user preferences to inform decisions, but keeping the balance between efficiency and the human touch is the designer's job.

## Who should watch

Product and UI designers deciding which AI tools to try first, and engineering leads wondering where AI fits in their design team's workflow. It's an inspirational overview rather than a technical session; expect a tool list and a viewpoint, not workflows or benchmarks.

Title: Six resilience patterns a fintech team uses to sleep at night
Description: Dmitrii Pakhomov (Tinkoff) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on bulkheads, in-memory caches, reloadable config, fallbacks, retries and circuit breakers in Scala
Body:
One slow backend can exhaust a shared connection pool and take every feature down with it. Dmitrii Pakhomov, Architect and Scala Tech Lead at Tinkoff, opened his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk with that scenario, then worked through the six patterns his team relies on for high-load systems that move user money: bulkhead, in-memory cache, reloadable config, fallback, retry and circuit breaker.

"Resilience patterns are practices that help software survive when things go wrong," Pakhomov said at Conf42 SRE 2024. None of the patterns is new; the value is in his recipes for when each pays off and where it bites back.

## Why does one slow backend break everything?

His example app calls three backends through HTTP clients that share one connection pool, plus CPU and RAM. If backend one turns slow, its requests sit waiting and fill the pool, so calls to healthy backends two and three can't go out. One failure becomes a total outage.

The bulkhead, named after a ship's watertight compartments, gives each HTTP client its own limit on concurrent requests, so only features tied to the slow backend degrade. The same idea isolates any resource: cap background jobs, or cap incoming requests so a traffic surge (say, from an upstream service losing its caches) gets errors instead of crashing your app with out-of-memory. In Scala he builds it from two semaphores, one limiting concurrency and one forming a queue of pending requests to absorb short spikes.

## Can a cache make you more reliable than your backends?

Yes, he argues, and the reasoning is neat. If an operation needs several backends and each fails independently, your error rate is higher than any one of theirs. An in-memory cache takes the network out of the path: "Caches stored in memory have zero chance of error." Fewer network calls and lower latency come along for free, and your app can end up with a lower error rate than its dependencies.

That is easy for non-personalised data like news feeds. For per-user data, you need requests from a user to land on the same instance, and he says you don't need a heavy sticky-session system for it: a stable load-balancing algorithm such as consistent hashing on user ID is enough, and when a node fails only that node's users get rebalanced.

For data every request needs, like access policies or subscription plans, even a cached source is a critical dependency. If it's small, replicate it fully: load a snapshot at startup and stream updates from a topic. Every read then comes from memory.

## What about the twelve-factor fast-startup rule?

Replicating data at startup breaks the twelve-factor disposability principle of fast startup. Pakhomov's view is that fast startup mostly exists so platforms can move workloads, and Kubernetes already copes with slow starters via startup probes. The real cost is slow rolling updates when you need to change a timeout or cache TTL in a hurry.

His fix is reloadable config: keep configuration in a concurrent variable refreshed by a background thread, so changes apply without restarts. The hard part is that HTTP or database clients may need reinitialising for new timeouts to apply, though some, like the Cassandra Java driver, already reload their configuration on the fly. As a bonus, the same mechanism gives you feature flags.

## Fallbacks, retries and the circuit breaker

A fallback serves a lower-quality backup instead of an error, often a fallback cache holding the last successful response. A stale balance with a delayed-update note beats a big red error box, and it buys the owning team time to fix the backend.

Retries cut error rates too, and they're simpler than caches because there is no cache invalidation, one of the famously hard problems. But retrying against a failing backend multiplies its traffic and makes things worse, so retries must come with a circuit breaker: when the error rate passes a threshold, block calls for a while, then let a few through to test recovery.

His last point is the most opinionated. Retries and circuit breakers often live in load balancers, but infrastructure lacks error context: it can't always tell whether an error is retryable, or whether it should count towards the breaker's threshold. So sometimes they belong inside the application. And don't skip telemetry, since good logs and metrics make all of this tunable.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers on high-availability services, Scala or not, who want a practical refresher on resilience patterns with trade-offs attached. It's short and focused, and pairs well with a longer distributed systems talk.

Title: Before you trust your SLO, price your risks in bad minutes
Description: Jaiprakash Pherwani (Tata Consultancy Services) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on testing SLOs against a risk catalog of bad minutes per year
Body:
An SLO is a promise, and most teams never check whether their architecture can keep it. Jaiprakash Pherwani, Offerings Lead at Tata Consultancy Services, used his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk to show how to answer that with a risk catalog: list what can go wrong, estimate how long it takes to detect and repair, convert each risk into bad minutes per year, and compare the total against your error budget.

"Risks are very, very vital for any SRE," Pherwani said at Conf42 SRE 2024. The talk is short and practical, built around the risk analysis approach from Google's SRE material, which is the right place to start if your SLOs were picked by gut feel.

## Are your SLOs realistic?

He opens with an application made of services, each with sub-services, and a list of uncomfortable questions. Is detection and alerting in place? Can the architecture deliver the response times and user experience you promised? What happens when the underlying cloud infrastructure disappears for a moment? Is there auto-healing? If a release breaks something, can you roll back?

Risk analysis is how you answer them. It covers dependencies, capacity, monitoring, operations and release processes, and measures each risk by mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to repair (MTTR), the percentage of users affected, and how often it happens (MTBF).

## What goes into a risk catalog?

A risk catalog is a structured list of every risk per service, built by brainstorming across teams: developers, system engineers and cloud architects. It should span infrastructure and software and include SLIs, MTTD, MTTR and MTBF. Two inputs matter most. Map the customer journey (in a retail example: browse the catalogue, pick a product, add to cart, check out, ship) and note which services each step touches. And mine your history: "Past incidents give you a lot of data to define and include it in your risk catalog."

The sample catalog he walks through, credited to Google's SRE playbook, shows how concrete it gets:

| Risk | MTTD | MTTR | Bad mins/year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config mishap reduces capacity, causing overload | 30 min | 120 min | 91 |
| New release breaks a small set of requests, unnoticed for a day | 1,440 min | 40 min | 120 |
| Operator accidentally deletes the database, restore from backup | 5 min | 510 min | 129 |
| Cloud provider regional VM/network outage | 2 min | 30 min | 16 |

Each row also carries the share of users affected (20% for the config mishap, 100% for the database deletion) and the time between failures, which gives incidents per year. The database deletion is rare, about once every four years, but its 510-minute restore makes it the most expensive risk on the list. The numbers start as estimates and get refined as production incidents add real data.

## Which risks can you accept?

Rank the risks by bad minutes and compare them against the error budget. The slides use three bands. Red risks cannot be accepted: a single occurrence would exceed the error budget for one risk. Amber risks should not be accepted, since they are major consumers of the budget, though you might live with a hard-to-fix amber risk by fixing some cheaper green ones to buy budget back. Green risks are acceptable: in aggregate they don't push you over budget, though fixing them adds headroom for the unexpected.

The output is a decision list: is the SLO achievable given these risks, how will you reach it, and which engineering work goes first because it removes an unacceptable risk. That last part is where product management may need to approve the extra engineering effort.

Rating also points at the levers. Better observability, log ingestion and log management shrink time to detect; automation shrinks time to repair; more stable releases stretch the time between failures.

## Where does chaos engineering fit?

As the calibration tool. Estimates of MTTD and MTTR are guesses until you inject faults (infrastructure, application, network) and measure how long detection and recovery actually take. Chaos experiments also surface blind spots: risks nobody would have written down. Feed those back into the catalog, re-rank, and adjust the SLOs and the engineering plan.

## Who should watch

SREs and service owners setting their first SLOs, or inheriting ones nobody can justify. It is a brisk walkthrough of a method rather than a deep case study, and the slides make a good template to copy into a spreadsheet.

Title: Your platform team is a product team whose customers can just leave
Description: Marco Pierobon (Thoughtworks) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on the challenges platform teams face and how product thinking, MVPs and team topologies fix them
Body:
Developers rarely file a bug against an internal tool they dislike; they quietly stop using it. Marco Pierobon, Lead Developer at Thoughtworks, built his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk around that kind of problem: the specific challenges platform teams face across developer experience, business, technology and their own way of working, and the practices that address each, with the overall prescription of running the platform as a product.

It is a structured, consultant's-eye view rather than a single case study, and a useful checklist for platform leads.

## What makes platform work hard?

Pierobon groups the challenges into four buckets.

**Developer experience.** Developers must be at the centre, with a consistent experience across services, so they barely notice moving from one to another. Feedback is scarce: when a tool doesn't fit, developers drop it and look elsewhere. Simplicity and usability pull against each other, and "whenever there's a trade off between the two, we should always favor usability," Pierobon said at Conf42 SRE 2024, meaning easy to use with extra power for advanced users, not bare-bones.

**Business.** Platform teams often lack insight into organisational strategy and product roadmaps, so features arrive late or untested. Senior stakeholders may distrust platform technologies, which slows cloud moves and initiatives like carbon footprint measurement. And many organisations misread the operating model, treating the platform team as a support desk or a CI/CD squad.

**Technology.** Cognitive load is high, with CI/CD, monitoring, instrumentation and database tooling all needing experts. The roadmap gets eaten by firefighting, escalations, business requests and acting as the point of contact for third-party vendors. Sitting at least two levels away from the business, the team can feel disconnected from the outcome.

**Platform teams themselves.** They support many stacks (Java, Kotlin, .NET, Go, Python) and many vendors, must keep up with fast-moving tools for security and to catch new features, sometimes have to plug gaps where a chosen service isn't enterprise grade or doesn't meet the company's SLAs and SLOs, and live with vendor lock-in from choices made years ago.

## How do you overcome them?

The fixes mirror the buckets. For developer experience: research and segment your internal users, build Personas, ship the smallest feature that meets the need and iterate, offer an internal developer portal with documentation and fast service creation, write troubleshooting docs so teams need less help, and collect continuous feedback, including scoring how useful the platform team's help was.

For business alignment: attend business all-hands, align the platform roadmap with product roadmaps on timelines as well as features, and provide a strong foundation of governance, security by default, SRE practices, FinOps and carbon reduction.

For technology: treat the platform as one integrated ecosystem even when it's built from several vendors; adopt evaluation techniques the organisation approves, scoring enterprise readiness, SLAs, extensibility, industry adoption and the vendor's reputation; give each platform product a lifecycle with criteria for creation, maintenance and retirement; and prefer vendor-agnostic tools. His example is Terraform over CloudFormation or Bicep, since the same tool can also manage something like Okta configuration.

For the team: tie the roadmap to business strategy, showcase delivered value, and make product teams independent with self-service, onboarding and playgrounds. His aspirational North Star: a developer who joins a team can commit and deploy to production on their first day.

## What does product thinking look like inside a platform team?

The final section is the meatiest. Define who the client is (usually internal development teams) and how those teams differ. Work towards MVPs and balance competing priorities. Measure success both qualitatively and with numbers: faster paths to production, fewer production accidents, smoother onboarding.

Give the platform a real SDLC. "It shouldn't be an excuse that infrastructure is harder to test," he argued, pointing to Terraform's frameworks for unit, integration and end-to-end tests and a test pyramid like any codebase. Use feature toggles to ship to production early and expose features to specific users. Pick the right level of abstraction, since leaky ones force users to understand the layer below anyway. And define done: is a feature finished when merged, deployed, released as a library, or when every team has upgraded? Track who runs which version and give teams a reason to update.

From Team Topologies he takes the enabler role, used case by case and with an agreed end date so the development team becomes self-sufficient, plus core building blocks, DDD-style platform domains to cut context switching, and independent dev streams. From portfolio management: only build abstractions over third-party products when they add value, encode organisational rules as strong defaults, and track each platform product's cost, adoption, usage and ROI, ready to pivot if the return doesn't materialise.

## Who should watch

Platform engineering managers and leads who want a framework to explain their team's problems upward, and engineers moving from a support-style ops team to a product-style platform team.

Title: Too much data for one chart? Sample it, shrink it, then nest it
Description: Serter Kazim Solak (Yapı Kredi) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on visualising large, complex datasets with sampling, dimensionality reduction and interactive charts
Body:
A chart of ten million points shows you a blob. Serter Kazim Solak, Head of Data Warehouse and Data Mining Development at Yapı Kredi, used his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk to cover how to make large, complex datasets readable: pick the right chart type, make it interactive, and shrink the data first with sampling, aggregation, dimensionality reduction and clustering, then show structure with hierarchical views.

It is an introductory survey rather than a tooling demo: no specific library or product appears, and the abstract's promise of pipelines and model tuning doesn't really feature. What it does offer is a compact checklist for anyone whose dashboards have outgrown a single line chart.

## Why visualise at all?

Solak lists five benefits: complex information becomes easier to understand, visuals are more engaging and memorable than raw tables, they cross language and expertise barriers, interactive views give faster insight than traditional analysis, and they tell a story. That last one he ranks as the most important. "Visualization helps convey the story behind the data," Solak said at Conf42 SRE 2024.

The chart menu is the familiar one: pie charts and histograms, line and area charts, scatter plots and bubble charts, Gantt charts and heat maps, network and tree diagrams.

## What does interactivity buy you?

His case for interactive visualisation is that it lets people explore rather than just read. In practice that means:

- **Highlighting** key points by changing colour, size, shape or opacity, and adding annotations, labels and tooltips for context.
- **Focus** by zooming, panning and filtering out noise.
- **Filtering and selecting** categories, data points or time windows.
- **Drill-down and drill-up** between detailed records and higher-level summaries.
- **Sorting and ranking** by value, frequency or name to spot top performers and outliers.
- **Exploratory analysis**, where users change the view and parameters to test hypotheses and find hidden patterns.

For SRE readers, that list doubles as a decent spec for an incident dashboard.

## How do you visualise a dataset that's too big?

This is the core of the talk, a multi-phase approach in four parts.

**Sampling and aggregation.** Random sampling works when the population is homogeneous; stratified sampling splits the population into groups (by age or location, say) and samples each so every subgroup is represented. Then aggregate the sample into summary statistics such as averages and counts, which cuts the computational cost while keeping the trends.

**Data reduction and summarisation.** Reduce the number of variables with dimensionality reduction (principal component analysis is his example) or with feature selection, which can be supervised or unsupervised depending on whether it uses a target variable. Then summarise with medians, standard deviations, percentiles, histograms and box plots, which also expose outliers.

**Clustering and dimensionality reduction.** Clustering groups similar points, such as customers with similar buying behaviour, with k-means, hierarchical or density-based algorithms depending on the data. Projecting high-dimensional data down to two or three dimensions makes it plottable.

**Hierarchical and nested visualisations.** Treemaps, dendrograms, nested pie and bar charts show data at several levels of granularity and support drilling down through the hierarchy.

## Best practices, in order

His four rules: know your audience and match their expertise; choose the visualisation that carries your message, considering data type and what the audience already understands; tell a story with a clear narrative flow; and simplify, with clear labels and annotations and nothing extra. His closing takeaways compress it further: clear data for good information, storytelling, a goal behind every function, and the right visual metaphor.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and analysts building their first dashboards over large tables, and SREs who want a quick refresher on why their 400-series time-series panel is unreadable. Experienced visualisation practitioners will find it basic.

Title: No Terraform provider for your database? Write one, it's mostly CRUD
Description: Harel Safra (Riskified) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on writing a Terraform provider from zero, learning Go, the Plugin Framework, debugging and publishing
Body:
When infrastructure as code stops at the edge of your database, the fix is a Terraform provider you write yourself. Harel Safra, Data Platform Engineering Team Lead at Riskified, used his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk to walk from zero (no provider, manual scripts, a lot of Confluence pages) to a published provider in the Terraform Registry, with a toy provider and a live debugging demo along the way.

There were more than 4,100 published providers at the time of recording, and Safra's point is that you don't need to be the vendor to add one. "The main point is that anyone can create more providers," Safra said at Conf42 SRE 2024. All you need is an API you can talk to.

## How does a provider fit into Terraform?

After a quick refresher (declarative tools like Terraform versus imperative ones like Pulumi), he lays out the architecture. Terraform core, the binary you run with `terraform plan`, talks to the provider over RPC. The provider uses a client library in-process to speak the infrastructure's native protocol, which might be HTTP, but just as well gRPC, SQL or system calls. So step one is understanding your infrastructure's API and finding a Go client for it. Without one, you are reverse engineering the protocol, which he describes as a bit annoying.

## Do you need to know Go?

Some. Providers are written in Go, and Safra learned it via the step-by-step Tour of Go: control structures, interfaces, enough to be productive. He likes that it's simple and compiled, so problems surface before production. The one trap for anyone coming from languages with exceptions is that Go has none: check every returned error or your provider will fail in confusing ways. For Terraform specifics he used HashiCorp's plugin documentation in the developer portal, reading the overview first and the rest on demand.

## What does the code actually look like?

His demo provider manages lines in text files under a base path set in the provider configuration. One resource type, a file with a name and a list of lines, deliberately limited because real APIs are limited too. You start by cloning the terraform-provider-scaffolding-framework repo and build on the Plugin Framework, the recommended way, which hides most of the protocol with Terraform core.

Each managed resource implements four operations: create, read, update and delete. Each one changes the infrastructure and also tells core how to amend the state. Read fetches the real current state; update changes only mutable attributes; for immutable ones, core destroys and recreates. Every method follows the same shape: take what core sent, do the work through the API, return a response so state is updated correctly.

Schemas map configuration to code. Attributes have types (primitives, or lists, maps and objects), properties such as required, optional or sensitive, and optional validators: his filename attribute is checked with a regex, and the lines list must hold at least two elements. Write descriptions everywhere, because the documentation generator copies them straight into the provider's docs. One more gotcha: framework types aren't native Go types, since they carry null and unknown states, so you call methods like `IsNull`, `ValueString` or `ElementsAs` to get at the values.

## How do you debug and test it?

Locally, a dev overrides block in the Terraform CLI config points the registry address at your build, so nothing needs publishing. Logs do for simple cases; for the rest, run the provider under a debugger with the debug flag, export the environment variable it prints, and run `terraform plan`. The demo breaks inside the read method once per file while Terraform waits for the provider's answer.

Acceptance tests sit next to each resource in a `_test` file, run with `make testacc` locally and in GitHub Actions on deploy. State changes are checked for you; anything on the infrastructure side you validate yourself, as in his checks of a file's name and first line.

## How do you publish?

Create a GPG key and add the private key and passphrase as repo secrets. Then the detail that cost him time: tags must be named like `v0.1.0` for the release automation to pick them up. Add the repo in the Terraform Registry once; webhooks and a default GitHub Action handle each new tag after that.

His real-world result was a provider managing users in Aerospike, which didn't exist before, and which people appear to be using.

## Who should watch

Platform and database engineers with a system Terraform can't manage, who have been putting off the Go learning curve. Expect a practical walkthrough with code, not a Terraform intro.

Title: A field guide to the ways distributed systems lie to you
Description: Aleksei Popov (Stenn Technologies) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on distributed systems failure modes and a fix for each, from idempotency keys to fencing tokens
Body:
Networks drop requests, clocks drift, garbage collectors freeze the world, and followers serve yesterday's data. Aleksei Popov, Software Engineering Manager at Stenn Technologies, used his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk to catalogue those failure modes one by one and pair each with a concrete pattern, then zoomed out to cybernetics, service types and SRE principles for keeping a growing microservice estate under control.

It is a dense, wide survey, closer to a guided tour of *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* than a war story, and useful precisely because it puts so many patterns side by side.

## Why go distributed at all?

Popov starts with the case for leaving the monolith: you can't scale modules independently, complexity is harder to contain, every change means redeploying everything, one huge codebase lacks enforced rules, and you're locked into one runtime. Microservices buy horizontal scalability, high availability, geographic distribution, technology choice and easier architecture control. The price is a list of troubles: unreliable networks, unreliable clocks, process pauses, eventual consistency, observability and evolvability.

## What do you do when the network loses your request?

A request can be lost, queued, hit a crashed or paused node, or be processed while the response is lost or delayed. You can't tell which. His sequence of fixes:

- **Timeouts** on the caller side, which is often fine for back-office tools.
- **Retries**, since most network issues are temporary.
- **Idempotency keys**, because a retry of a request the server already processed can create duplicate orders or payments. The server checks the key and returns the previous response.
- **Circuit breakers**, to fail fast instead of hammering a service that is already struggling and triggering cascading failures.

## How do you stop concurrent writes eating each other?

"Concurrency is one of the most intricate challenges in distributed systems," Popov said at Conf42 SRE 2024. Two operations updating the same account balance without protection means the last write wins and money goes missing. In ACID databases the practical answer is snapshot isolation, built on MVCC, which most popular SQL databases offer and which detects lost writes. Many NoSQL stores trade ACID for BASE, so he shows compare-and-set, using Cassandra's lightweight transactions with `IF NOT EXISTS` and `IF` conditions. For exclusive access to a resource there's the lease, which expires automatically if its holder dies.

## The dual write problem

Write to the database, then publish to Kafka, and one of the two can fail. Publish first and commit second, and other systems react to a transaction that never happened, which, as he dryly notes, leads to interesting conversations with the legal team. The fix is the transactional outbox: write events to an outbox table in the same transaction and let a relay poll and publish them, giving at-least-once delivery (consumers must be idempotent anyway). The alternative is log tailing, reading changes from the database's transaction log with connectors: less application code, more coupling to the database.

## Clocks, leaders and pauses

"Unreliable clocks is one of the most tricky problems in distributed systems," he said. Time-of-day clocks drift with NTP; monotonic clocks are fine for durations but can't be compared across machines. Precision Time Protocol exists for regulated or real-time cases, at significant cost.

When a leader dies, followers need consensus to elect a new one. He walks through Raft: heartbeats, elections, log replication, and commits once half the followers acknowledge. Read-after-write surprises from eventual consistency get the simple fix of reading from the leader for the user who just wrote. Matters like sanctions checks can't tolerate the lag at all.

Process pauses (GC stop-the-world, VM suspension, context switches, I/O delays) break leases: a paused client wakes up still believing it holds a lease that has already gone to someone else. Fencing fixes it with a monotonically increasing token that the data store checks, rejecting writes with a stale one.

## Keeping it evolvable

Observability gets distributed tracing with Jaeger, plus a preference for orchestration over choreography for visibility (with the orchestrator made highly available, since it is otherwise a single point of failure). Then cybernetics: systems thinking, feedback loops, adaptability, goal-oriented design via domain-driven design, and hierarchy. He argues the fallacy is that all microservices are the same, and proposes service types: public apps and APIs, backend-for-frontend, product workflows, reusable domain components such as KYC or payments, gateways and adapters, and platform components, grouped behind macro-domain APIs at scale.

The SRE section covers embracing risk, SLAs/SLOs/SLIs, automating toil, monitoring everything and simplifying, plus infrastructure as code and Jepsen-style fault injection. He closes with Gall's Law and three ways to measure complexity: cyclomatic complexity, time to train a new engineer, and explanation time.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers moving from a monolith to services, and SREs who want a vocabulary for the failure modes their developers keep rediscovering. Each pattern gets a slide's worth of time, so treat it as a map and go deeper on the ones that bite you.

Title: On-call for Kubernetes clusters is a runbook and automation problem
Description: Pravar Agrawal (IBM) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on debugging common Kubernetes cluster issues on call, with runbooks, ChatOps bots and in-cluster scripts
Body:
SSH-ing into worker nodes one by one is not an on-call strategy. Pravar Agrawal, Senior DevOps Engineer at IBM working on the IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service, used his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk to walk through the cluster issues that keep paging Kubernetes SREs, a debugging order for them, and the automation that turns a long investigation into a single command.

It is a compact talk, pitched at engineers who are new to on-call or about to join a rotation, and it says so.

## What does being on call actually involve?

Agrawal defines on-call plainly: for a set period you are available to respond to production incidents with urgency, and every company implements it differently. The rules are the same everywhere: acknowledge and verify the alert, analyse the impact, communicate with the teams involved through the proper channels, then apply a corrective action or a fix. He lists PagerDuty, Jira, Opsgenie and ServiceNow as the usual incident management tools, and frames the whole cycle as deploy, troubleshoot, alert, escalate and track it all in tickets.

## Which cluster issues keep coming back?

His list will look familiar to anyone who has run Kubernetes in production, on one cluster or many:

- Problems with services running on the node itself, where manually SSH-ing in to check isn't always possible.
- Pods stuck in Pending (poor schedulability onto nodes) or Terminating (often when the application stops responding after a delete).
- API endpoints down or slow, either at the application level or in Kubernetes core components.
- One or two etcd pods unavailable out of an HA set.
- Worker node reloads that are impractical to do by hand.
- Disks hitting capacity, with alerts around the 90% mark.
- Failing health checks, including readiness and liveness probes.

## How should you approach the debugging?

There's no golden rule, he says, but there are right ways. Start with the error message and work out the blast radius: how many services and components are affected. The smaller it is, the easier the diagnosis. Use monitoring tools such as Prometheus and LogDNA to see the last recorded healthy state, from both application and cluster logs. If it's a Kubernetes problem, get cluster access fast and check the master components, etcd and the other core pieces: pod logs if they run as pods, service logs if they run under systemd. If the issue is wide, isolate the service by restricting its usage.

## Where does automation help most?

The goal is cutting the time to respond and to get infrastructure statistics. Agrawal wants automation that fetches cluster stats, runs real-time commands, handles node reboots and core service restarts, queries historical data for recurring patterns, and runs scheduled clean-up jobs so you don't hit a resource crunch at the worst moment.

His shades of automation, roughly from simplest to most ambitious:

- **Runbooks** that are well documented and point the on-call engineer to the relevant Jenkins job or a GitHub issue from a similar past incident.
- **ChatOps bots** in Slack, Teams or Mattermost that gather live cluster statistics, run kubectl commands and, if authorised, reboot or reload worker nodes. He names the open source Botkube as an example.
- **In-cluster scripts** deployed as DaemonSets, sidecars or custom resources that trigger on a condition, such as cleaning a disk when it fills up.
- **AI-based analysers** to pull more detailed information from the cluster.
- **Curated dashboards** built on your existing monitoring tools for both a holistic and a detailed view.

## Advice for new on-call engineers

The closing section is aimed at beginners: exposure is what seasons you, so learn the whole architecture well enough to connect components during an incident, keep runbooks close, and study recent outages and the alerts that preceded them. His last line is the one worth pinning above the pager. Agrawal said at Conf42 SRE 2024 that "if the alert auto resolves, it doesn't always mean that there is nothing wrong, so it's better to look anyways."

## Who should watch

Engineers about to start their first Kubernetes on-call rotation, and team leads writing an onboarding checklist for one. Seasoned cluster operators will recognise everything here; the value is a tidy map of the territory.
