Title: Nix dev shells end the half-day yak shave on old Go projects
Description: Haseeb Majid (Curve) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on Nix flakes, dev shells and direnv for Go tooling that matches on every laptop and in CI
Body:
Reopen a Go project you last touched six months ago and the first afternoon goes on reinstalling the right golangci-lint. At [Conf42 Golang 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Haseeb_Majid_using_nix_reproducible), Haseeb Majid, Backend Software Engineer at Curve, showed how a Nix flake plus a dev shell gives every developer and every CI job the same tool versions, loaded when you `cd` into the repo and gone when you leave. His GitLab pipeline went from about 22 minutes to eleven and a half along the way.

It's a practical intro: the first half builds a working dev environment, the second half opens the hood on derivations and flakes, and it ends on Docker.

## What's wrong with tools.go?

Go teams already have a trick for this, and Majid shows the one Curve uses on some projects: a `tools.go` file behind a `tools` build tag, importing golangci-lint, GoReleaser and Cobra with blank imports so `go mod tidy` keeps them, plus a make target that `go install`s the lot into `GOPATH/bin`.

It works until it doesn't. Two projects pinning different versions of the same linter overwrite each other's binary, so you have to remember to reinstall when you switch. And it only covers Go tools: GNU Make, GNU Parallel or the CLI tools your bash scripts expect are out of scope. Snap, Flatpak, asdf and virtualenv each fix part of the problem; he wants one tool that fixes all of it.

## What does a Go dev shell look like?

The entry point is `flake.nix` - he compares it to `main.go` for your Nix config. Inputs are git repositories: nixpkgs (with its 80,000 packages) and numtide's flake-utils, which saves the boilerplate of building for each architecture (x86_64 Linux, Apple Silicon and friends). The output is a `devShells.default` made with `pkgs.mkShell`, listing the packages: Go 1.22, golangci-lint, gotools.

`nix develop` drops you into the shell; golangci-lint (1.56.2 in the demo) now resolves to a path in the Nix store. Add direnv with a one-line `.envrc` containing `use flake`, approve it once with `direnv allow`, and the environment loads itself when you enter the folder and unloads when you leave. Onboarding becomes clone, allow, start coding.

The same flake can install pre-commit hooks through the shell hook, with the built-in Go hooks for linting and tests that only touch the files you're committing. As Majid said at Conf42 Golang 2024, it "saves us time waiting for CI and save some credits as well". He flags the trade-off: pre-commit is normally configured in YAML, and some people dislike hiding a tool's native config behind Nix.

## Why is it reproducible and not just repeatable?

The deep-dive section is the part worth the full watch if Nix has always felt like magic. Everything is an expression; nixpkgs' golangci-lint entry calls `buildGoModule`, which wraps the `derivation` built-in. Building is two steps: evaluation turns expressions into a `.drv` file (a recipe), then build time turns the recipe into a package in the Nix store.

The store path is a cryptographic hash of every input, so changing one environment variable gives a different package. That's what lets two versions live side by side, makes the dependency tree explicit (Go depends on bash, bash on glibc), and lets Nix fetch pre-built binaries from the official cache instead of compiling. Timestamps are pinned to epoch 1 - 1 January 1970 - because a build date baked into a binary would break determinism. Packaging something missing from nixpkgs yourself is usually a one-package job, he found, since its dependencies are already there.

Flakes add the lock: `flake.lock` pins nixpkgs to a specific revision, so a laptop and a CI runner resolve the same versions until someone bumps the lock (a scheduled CI job can do it, Dependabot-style). He uses flakes in all his projects, with one warning: they're still an experimental feature and can ship breaking changes.

## Does it pay off in CI?

On GitLab CI he includes a community Nix job template that copies the Nix store to and from the GitLab cache before and after each job, so dependencies installed in a `pre` stage are shared by later stages, which then run `nix develop -c golangci-lint run`. Total runtime: eleven and a half minutes, against roughly 22 before. He calls the number anecdotal himself, the right amount of humility for one pipeline. GitHub Actions users get similar caching from Determinate Systems' actions.

## Why not Docker?

He keeps Docker for building and shipping images. As a dev environment, he points to the old line that "it's repeatable, not reproducible": build the same Dockerfile six months apart and you likely get a different image. Dev containers also make personal tooling (fzf, zoxide, your shell) awkward - you either bloat the image or run a slower startup script. His verdict is mild: give both a go, though he found Nix easier.

## Who should watch

Go developers who have lost a morning to a CI-only linter failure, and anyone who has bounced off Nix's docs and wants a guided path that starts with something useful.

Title: Run your incident call like a ward round with three columns in a doc
Description: Dan Slimmon (D2E) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on clinical troubleshooting, a symptoms-hypotheses-actions loop for faster collaborative diagnosis
Body:
The fix for a chaotic incident call is a shared doc with three headings. Dan Slimmon, Managing Partner at D2E, spent his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk on clinical troubleshooting, the method he built over 16 years and thousands of production issues (previously at HashiCorp and Etsy): list the symptoms, brainstorm hypotheses, pick actions that rule hypotheses out, repeat. His promise is shorter and less stressful incidents, and the demo makes a good case for it.

"Clinical troubleshooting is a scientific procedure for collaborative diagnosis," Slimmon said at Conf42 SRE 2024. As the name suggests, it borrows from how a team of doctors works a difficult case.

## What does a bad incident call look like?

Slimmon tells it as two timelines of the same outage. The flower service's throughput drops by 40% mid business day, from about 1,000 to about 600 pollen tokens per second. Barb, an SRE who knows a little about the service, gets paged and starts building a house of cards in her head: graphs, error messages, source code, half-baked theories.

Alice from another team joins and offers help. Barb, not ready to explain things she hasn't explained to herself, asks her to sit tight. Then the honeybee service starts erroring, Alice wanders off to look at that, and the call splits into two independent investigations. Seth, their grand-boss, arrives firing questions about customer impact and the plan. Support joins with customer reports. Two more developers join and need context. Twenty minutes in, there is still no plan, and everyone who arrives has to interrupt Barb to find out what's going on. Anyone who has carried a pager will recognise every beat.

## The same outage, with a structured diagnosis

In the second timeline, Barb answers Alice by opening a shared doc with headings for symptoms, hypotheses and actions, and putting it on screen. Two symptoms go in: throughput dropped, and latency dropped at the same moment. Barb's first hypothesis is that flower crashes on certain slow requests that then never get logged, which would explain both. Two actions get explicit owners: check the kernel logs for crashes, and read the flower service's readme.

The readme gives Alice a second hypothesis: an upstream client is sending less traffic, so the over-provisioned service answers the rest faster. The honeybee page becomes a symptom rather than a distraction and suggests a third: connections being dropped at the TCP level, perhaps by the Nginx proxy in front of flower. Then a rule-out action pays off. Comparing graphs shows honeybee's error rate growing linearly before flower's throughput fell, so honeybee is earlier in the causal chain, and hypotheses one and three are dead.

When Seth arrives this time, most of his answers are already on screen, so he lurks. Support's customer reports go on the symptom list, and they go back to updating the status page. The call's bandwidth stays with the people diagnosing.

## What makes a good symptom, and a good hypothesis?

The tips section is where the talk earns its keep.

**Symptoms** are statements of fact about observed behaviour, as quantitative as possible, with no supposition. The flower service throughput dropped by about 40% at a given time is a good symptom: numbers on two dimensions and no theory attached. The flower service is dropping requests is a bad one, because it smuggles in a hypothesis; in the example, flower wasn't dropping anything.

**Hypotheses** must explain one or more symptoms and be falsifiable: you should be able to imagine an action that would prove them wrong. A downstream service is bottlenecked, so less traffic reaches flower qualifies. The flower service is crashing doesn't: depending on your stack you may never be able to prove it isn't, and it doesn't say why throughput and latency would fall. "It's really all about ruling things out, not proving things," he said, and he admits that is a mental shift.

**Actions** come in three kinds. Rule-out actions eliminate hypotheses and move you towards a diagnosis. Research actions, like reading the readme, rule nothing out but generate new symptoms and hypotheses. The best are diagnostic interventions: clearing honeybee's cache when you suspect a bad cached object either fixes the incident or kills that hypothesis, so you win both ways.

He adds two facilitation habits. Assemble the most diverse group you can (specialists from different parts of the stack, support, solutions engineers), because more perspectives produce more hypotheses. And keep pulling the conversation back to the doc, filing what people say under the right heading.

## Who should watch

Every on-call engineer and incident commander, especially on teams where incidents become a single hero's monologue. It's a short, story-driven talk, and you can use the method on your next page without asking anyone's permission.

Title: go build compiles your code; Bazel builds the rest of the pipeline
Description: Eugene Khabarov (Arctic Wolf) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on Bazel for Go, with hermetic, cached builds of generators, binaries, images and manifests
Body:
`go build` turns Go files into a binary. A real build also runs code generators, pins a compiler, builds container images, renders Kubernetes manifests and publishes it all, and most teams glue that together with a Makefile and good intentions. At Conf42 Golang 2024, Eugene Khabarov, Lead Developer and DevX at Arctic Wolf, makes the case for Bazel as the orchestrator, then builds and deploys a small gRPC microservice stack to Kubernetes with a single `bazel run`.

## What counts as a dependency?

His answer: anything that can change the output. He sorts them into three groups.

- **Code and tools**: Go packages (pinned by `go.mod` and `go.sum`), the Go compiler itself (whatever happens to be installed, or a version baked into a CI image), and generators, because `//go:generate` can call any arbitrary binary or script before the compiler even sees a file.
- **Environment**: the host machine you build on, the target you build for (macOS or Linux, amd64 or arm64), the CI runner, and environment variables.
- **Publishing**: Docker for images, tar or zip archives for AWS Lambda, Kustomize, ytt or Helm for manifests, the AWS CLI, and usually Make to tie it together.

Go has a good answer for the first item and shrugs at the rest. Is the build reproducible? Hermetic, beyond wrapping it in a Docker image? Can it restart from the failed step instead of from scratch? His conclusion is that `go build` is one step, and what you need is build orchestration: one command that fetches every pinned dependency, builds artifacts, and publishes them to ECR or S3, without deploying them.

## What does Bazel bring?

Bazel is Google's open source build and test tool, aimed at very large codebases and multi-language, multi-platform builds. You describe builds declaratively in Starlark, a strict subset of Python meant for configuration rather than applications. It builds in parallel across every core it finds, locally or on remote runners, caches downloaded dependencies and intermediate results, and rebuilds only what changed.

The principles that make it trustworthy are hermeticity (same inputs, same output, regardless of what is installed on the host), source identity (checksums on every input), and sandboxing. Eugene Khabarov said at Conf42 Golang 2024 that "we need to define all the inputs explicitly, and if we don't define them, build will not see them."

## How does a go:generate pipeline look in Bazel?

His first demo is a toy generator that prints a hello world Go program. The plain Go flow takes four steps: build the generator, `go generate` with it, build the generated file, run it. With Bazel it is `bazel run //go:hello-world`.

The project has no Go files of its own, only a `WORKSPACE` and `BUILD.bazel` files. The `WORKSPACE` loads the rules_go ruleset by SHA-256, registers Go 1.20.3 as a toolchain for Bazel to download, and pulls the generator with `go_repository` pinned by version and sum. The `BUILD.bazel` declares a `genrule` that runs the generator to produce `hello.go`, a `go_library` over it, and a `go_binary` embedding the library. Run the binary target and Bazel works the chain backwards: generate, compile the library, link, run.

Labels are worth learning early. Eugene Khabarov said at Conf42 Golang 2024: "Label is a unique name for a build target." `//` is the workspace root, `//go` a package, `:hello-world` a target; `//...` builds everything, and `@hw_generator//...` builds an external dependency.

## Does it scale past hello world?

The second demo builds two gRPC services, Docker images for them and for an Envoy proxy that translates HTTP into gRPC, and deploys everything to a local minikube cluster driven by Tilt, from one command. A request with a valid token goes through the auth service; an invalid one is refused.

Nobody wants to hand-write a `BUILD` file per package, and you mostly don't have to: Gazelle generates them, keeps them current, formats them and manages Go dependencies. Image and publishing targets you still write yourself. `bazel query` answers questions such as which packages use package X, or where a transitive dependency came from, and can emit a graph for Graphviz. Rulesets such as rules_oci and rules_proto cover other jobs, catalogued on awesomebazel.com.

## Who should watch

Go teams whose Makefile has grown its own folklore, polyglot monorepos, and anyone who has been burnt by a build that only works on one laptop. It is an introduction: it shows what Bazel buys you, not the migration pain or the learning curve, which you should budget for separately.

Title: Agile sprints ship code; reliability lives in everything else
Description: David Argent (Salesforce) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on how Agile's short-term focus hurts online services, and what to lock in before the first sprint
Body:
A control plane that can replace one host at a time is fine, right up until it runs a 10,000-node database. David Argent, Senior SRE at Salesforce and a veteran of Microsoft and Amazon, opened his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk with that war story, then spent half an hour on why Agile's short planning cycles quietly produce exactly this kind of design, and how to keep the benefits without becoming what he calls an Agile victim.

His core point: Agile is a set of principles, not a methodology, and favouring working software over documentation or change over plans does not mean ignoring architecture, failure modes or everything that isn't code.

## How do Agile teams set themselves up to fail?

Argent builds it as a failure curriculum. Failure 101 is having no definition of success: if you can't measure what makes people use the product, or what would make you stop building it, you can't tell whether you delivered. Failure 201 is not planning for success. Features rarely live in a vacuum, and behind them sits a long list of invisible requirements: data integrity, security, a zero-downtime deployment profile, performance and scalability floors, monitoring, incident management, disaster recovery.

Failure 301 is not planning for Murphy. "There is no such thing as a safe change," Argent said at Conf42 SRE 2024, and he has the scars to show it: a change aimed at non-production, carrying a default config value that filtered through to production and took it down. Partners, networks, hardware, power and cooling will all fail you at some point. Planning for failure is not enough either; he wants teams to know how to recover from a complete outage, because coming up cold with empty caches while live traffic keeps arriving is a different beast from a partial outage. He cites Prime Day 2018, carrying the pager for a database service, as the place he learned that.

## What should you decide before writing code?

The cheapest place to change something is before the first line exists. His design checklist has three parts.

**Anticipate failure.** Define what is acceptable and stop there: "Each nine is somewhere in the ballpark of an order of magnitude more expensive than the one that came before it." If you need four nines, don't build five; if the target is 200 ms, don't engineer for 25. Design for fast recovery, measure everything, automate responses (cranky, sleep-deprived SREs help nobody), plan for being 100% hard down, and build degraded modes, because serving some traffic beats serving none. Layer your security so attackers face more than one hurdle.

**Anticipate success.** He argues "the most dangerous thing for an online service is being embarrassingly successful." Leave the hooks to scale by a couple of orders of magnitude, prefer architectures that scale components independently, avoid processes that scale linearly with people (manual customer onboarding is his example), and know which traffic is high-value enough to protect when resources are tight.

**Anticipate change.** Put APIs and abstractions between business logic and its callers, assume zero-downtime upgrades must be possible, and prefer loose coupling wherever you can afford the asynchrony.

## One-way doors versus two-way doors

The tactics section pairs two rules that look contradictory. Delay non-critical decisions as long as possible, so you learn more about the problem before committing. But get the critical architecture right the first time: scalability, availability, performance, security and data integrity are expensive or impossible to retrofit, and security is the poster child for being bolted on at the last second. If your architecture can't support your customer scenarios, he says, you don't have an architecture yet.

The bridge is the two-way door: make decisions reversible wherever possible, so taking one step back to go three forward is cheap. He also wants SREs and product owners in design reviews, not only coders and architects, since SREs know how services actually run in production.

## Is code really the only deliverable?

No, and this is the section most teams should steal. Service code is the easy part: a dedicated team writes it and it gets engineers promoted. Monitoring, alerting, runbooks, customer documentation, security testing, deployment tools, SLAs, OLAs and SLOs, admin tools and reporting are deliverables too. Put them in the backlog, since the backlog is king in most Agile shops. Consider a release sprint where non-blocking code waits while the team fixes bugs, finishes non-code collateral, runs game days that break non-production to test runbooks and incident response, rehearses deployments and trains operations staff. And reward the engineers who do that work.

## Who should watch

Tech leads, TPMs and SREs who sit in sprint planning and keep losing the argument for reliability work. It is a principles talk with good war stories, not a tooling walkthrough.

Title: Your startup doesn't need an SRE team yet, it needs SRE habits
Description: Evgenii Korneev (MyGig) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on running SRE without an SRE team, and the five questions that tell you when to hire one
Body:
Most small teams think of SRE as a headcount question. Evgenii Korneev, CTO at MyGig, spent his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk arguing the opposite: SRE is a set of habits you can adopt on day one, a weekly developer on-call rotation carries you a long way, and a dedicated SRE hire only makes sense once a short checklist of pressures says so.

"SRE is not about creating a team of on call engineers who will save your service day and night from crashes," Korneev said at Conf42 SRE 2024. He is clear the talk is aimed at engineering leads rather than individual engineers, and it is short: a CTO's operating manual, not a deep technical dive.

## What should a small team do first?

Define what down means for your product before you buy any tooling. Korneev's starting list is SLIs first, then SLAs and SLOs, then an error budget. His example SLIs are refreshingly specific: successful user auths at 95% a month, successful payments at 99%, articles posted at 99.5%, front-end availability at 99.8%. The matching availability criteria read like alert rules: more than 50 users an hour failing to authenticate, more than 10 payments an hour failing for internal reasons, the web app unreachable from more than one location for over 10 minutes.

After that come the unglamorous fundamentals:

- Monitoring and alerts wired to those targets, with the team told which metrics matter to the business.
- Automated builds and deploys from the start. Fewer manual steps, fewer mistakes.
- Tests, even when launch pressure says skip them, because they speed up later development as well as stabilising it.
- Restricted production access. Ideally no developer touches the production database; only operations does.
- Internal tools for running the service: dashboards, admin panels, feature toggles. These are what make the previous point survivable.

His claim is that these principles are enough until the product turns into a sprawling multi-component system.

## How do you run on-call without burning people out?

As the system grows, time to find and fix failures grows with it, and the obvious move is putting developers on call. Korneev describes the dilemma neatly. If the on-call person only answers availability alerts, quiet weeks breed complacency (his example is someone deciding they can pop to the pool at lunch, which is of course exactly when it breaks). Load them up with every production bug instead and each rotation becomes a grind that ends in burnout.

He picks the lighter option and hedges it with a roster. If this week's on-call engineer is unavailable, the next name on the list responds, then the next, and anyone who gets pulled in out of turn moves to the end of the list as a small reward. His team tried daily rotations and went back to weekly: handing over incident analysis mid-failure to the next person was too awkward. The rule that keeps a week bearable is simple: the on-call person responds only to the alerts you defined as significant, and everything else goes through the normal workflow.

## When is it time to hire an SRE?

There is no strict threshold, but he gives five questions:

1. How strict are your availability requirements? A fintech holding user funds sits higher than most.
2. How heavy is the load, and how popular is the service? Outages at scale cost more reputation.
3. How well is the development team performing, in productivity and quality? On-call eating everyone's time is a signal.
4. How complex is the system? Past a point, developers know too little of it to handle incidents alone.
5. What does the budget allow? Can you afford someone whose peak activity is during major outages?

If at least three point to yes, you probably need SRE. Even then, he suggests checking whether better test coverage or refactoring away complexity would fix the problem first. And watch the budget: the first SRE is usually a developer from the same team, whose seat still needs filling.

## Why communication counts as reliability work

The last third is about people. Work talk belongs in shared team chats rather than private messages, so everyone sees the issues, the decisions and their impact. All-team meetups cover how big tasks were solved; team-lead meetings cover cross-team design. Document at least the hardest parts of the system, put it into onboarding, and check new hires actually understood it after probation. In his summary, he puts it plainly: "there is no room for secrets in an engineering team."

He also argues for spending scarce budget on one engineer well above the market's average senior rather than two ordinary hires. Someone with ten-plus years has already met most of the failures your incident plan is guessing at.

## Who should watch

Founders, CTOs and engineering managers at small and mid-sized teams deciding whether to start an on-call rotation or open an SRE role. Experienced SREs will find little new, but may enjoy a crisp checklist to hand to their leadership.

Title: Build your own L7 load balancer from Envoy, a Go control plane and cloud-init
Description: Sandeep Bhat (Harness) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on a cloud-agnostic L7 load balancer from Envoy, a Go xDS control plane and cloud-init
Body:
A managed cloud load balancer is convenient right up until you need the same thing on three clouds, or notice what it costs at idle. At Conf42 Golang 2024, Sandeep Bhat, Staff Software Engineer at Harness, shows how to assemble a layer 7 load balancer from parts: Envoy as the data plane, a small Go control plane that feeds it configuration over gRPC, and a cloud-init script that boots both on any VM. The demo ends with a backend killed mid-traffic and the balancer quietly routing around it.

## What does the load balancer need to do?

He starts from first principles. Load balancing spreads incoming traffic across application servers so none is overwhelmed, gives you high availability when one dies, and lets you scale horizontally. Round robin, weighted round robin and least connections are the usual algorithms. The cloud versions (AWS ALB, Azure Application Gateway, GCP's offering) all boil down to incoming traffic, rules, and target groups. The talk deals with layer 7 only.

His requirements list: spread traffic over multiple backends, serve multiple domains from one balancer, health-check targets out of rotation, run on any cloud, and scale by picking a bigger or smaller VM.

## Why Envoy, and which parts of it?

Envoy is a CNCF graduated project that came out of Lyft, written in C++, with about 19k commits and 22k GitHub stars on his slides. It is a layer 7 reverse proxy whose behaviour is built from chained filters, much like middleware in an API server, and it already does service discovery, load balancing, health checks, rate limiting and observability.

The pieces he uses: listeners (ports 80 and 443), filter chains (domain matching and anything else that should act on the request), clusters (logical groups of upstreams for a domain or path), upstreams (individual VMs) and secrets (certificates). A static config with a round-robin cluster and an HTTP health check every 5 seconds with a 2-second timeout is enough for one service. It does not scale to adding domains without restarts.

## The Go control plane is the interesting bit

Instead of a static file, Envoy boots with dynamic resources: Listener Discovery Service and Cluster Discovery Service, both pointed over gRPC at an `xds_cluster` on 127.0.0.1:18000. That cluster is the Go control plane, running on the same VM as a systemd service next to Envoy.

The control plane is small. One goroutine runs the xDS gRPC server backed by a snapshot cache; another runs a sync loop, a `time.Ticker` in a `for`/`select`, that polls an API server for the latest configuration and pushes a new snapshot into the cache. He notes websockets would beat polling. The API server sits outside the VM and reads from a database (a Postgres JSONB column works) where each row describes a host, its target IPs, incoming and outgoing ports, and health-check settings.

Add a domain to the database, and on the next sync Envoy picks it up without a restart or downtime.

## Cloud-init makes it cloud-agnostic

Packaging is a cloud-init user-data script that installs Envoy as a service, downloads the control plane binary and starts both. Setting `scripts-user` to `always` in `cloud_final_modules` makes the script run on every boot, not just the first, which doubles as an upgrade path for new control plane versions. The same script works on AWS, GCP and Azure.

## Is it actually cheaper?

His comparison uses Ohio (US East) prices: an ALB at $0.0225 per hour comes to about $16.20 a month before any Load Balancer Capacity Unit charges for connections, bytes and rules, while a t2.micro at $0.0116 per hour is about $8.30 a month plus traffic. He counts only the base components on both sides, so treat it as a floor rather than a full TCO; your own LB is also yours to patch, monitor and keep highly available, which the talk doesn't cost out.

## The demo

Three terminals (Envoy, the API server, the control plane), an `/etc/hosts` entry pointing his test domain at localhost, and two Nginx VMs on AWS that print their own IP. Sandeep Bhat said at Conf42 Golang 2024 as requests alternated between the two: "So as you can see here, it's routing traffic evenly across both of them." He stops one VM, the health check fails it out, and every request lands on the survivor.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who need the same edge on several clouds or on-prem, and Go developers who have heard of xDS and want to see how small a working control plane can be. It is an architecture walkthrough with code snippets rather than a production-hardened design: TLS, HA for the balancer itself and the control plane's failure modes are left as exercises.

Title: Your SRE skills gap is a people problem, so build a community
Description: Jorge Luis Castro Toribio (NTT DATA) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on growing SRE skills across a 600-person delivery org with a community of practice, OKRs and a game
Body:
A handful of people who really know SRE, spread across a delivery organisation of hundreds, is a reliability risk no tool can fix. Jorge Luis Castro Toribio, Lead of Transformation Strategy at NTT DATA, tells at Conf42 SRE 2024 how his team turned that into an SRE community of practice at a large IT enterprise, and how they kept it alive past the point where earlier communities had quietly died.

This is a talk about organisational design, not tooling. You won't see a dashboard. What you will get is a reusable template: a canvas, sample OKRs, metrics and a gamification trick.

## What was broken?

The setting: more than 600 people across Latin America, Europe and elsewhere, working on mobile, web and in-house products, with different cultures, time zones, skills and roles. The symptoms were familiar. Services that weren't reliable after go-live, low availability, low organisational resilience, only a few engineers with strong SRE skills, and very little collaboration. In his words, it looked like people worked for different companies.

He grounds the fix in SRE's own principles: SLOs with consequences, time to make tomorrow better, teams that can regulate their workload (he links this to cognitive load), and failure as an opportunity to improve, which he ties to psychological safety. A community of practice, borrowing Etienne and Beverly Wenger-Trayner's definition, is a group that shares a concern for something they do and learns to do it better as they interact regularly.

## Learning by doing, not by slide deck

The community follows the experiential learning cycle: share a concrete experience, reflect on it (context, metrics, people), conclude what to try, then experiment actively, small first, scaling what works. Psychological safety is what makes that last step happen.

The structure is simple. A CoP lead deals with stakeholders and keeps the community focused on value. A core team organises the first sessions and then rotates, so anyone can run one. A backlog captures the gaps between business needs and current SRE capabilities. And the whole thing is treated as an investment of time and talent, aligned to business strategy.

Sample OKRs he shares (the targets are left as X on purpose; pick your own):

- Improve reliability and availability: an X% reduction in incidents impacting production.
- Improve team collaboration: X cross-functional workshops or hackathons with global groups.
- Increase SRE capabilities: X% more participation in SRE training or certifications.

## A canvas for the minimum viable community

The design tool is a minimum viable community canvas with nine fields: purpose, audience, values, goal, expectations, roles, rules, rituals for prioritising the backlog, and communication channels. Their purpose statement: bring experts and enthusiasts together to improve the reliability and performance of digital services, and build a doers culture.

The expectations field is where they learned the most. Community member experience, he says, is a function of reality and expectation, so they asked first. The feedback was blunt: fewer slides and talks, more hands-on work, mob programming, and real stories of SRE failures and wins.

For metrics he suggests three: shares and collaboration, number of experiments (kaizen), and outcomes in quality, speed, savings and reliability.

## How do you stop a community from fading out?

Previous communities at the company started strong and disappeared after a few iterations. This time they added a minimum enjoyable game, built with the Octalysis game design framework: the Reliability League. Experienced SREs play Batman, each paired with sidekicks, the developers and juniors building SRE skills, and the Batmans' job is to turn sidekicks into heroes. It sounds silly. It's meant to, and it worked well enough that they had plenty of both.

He reports more experiments, better service availability, lower turnover and strong NPS on community sessions, without figures. His lessons: rotate the core team, remember that the community becomes what it practises, and treat developer experience as an outcome. Jorge Luis Castro Toribio said at Conf42 SRE 2024: "Your business grows as your communities and people grow."

SRE leads, engineering managers and transformation people trying to spread SRE beyond a small expert team in a large, distributed organisation. Engineers after technical depth won't find it here.

Title: Secure, fast, robust: an SRE's checklist for Go APIs
Description: Prabesh Thapa (Capsule) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on a checklist for Go APIs, from auth, passwords and rate limits to caching, health checks and retries
Body:
Most API incidents trace back to something on a checklist nobody ran. Prabesh Thapa, Senior SRE at Capsule and a Docker Captain, turns his Conf42 Golang 2024 talk into exactly that checklist: what a Go API needs to be secure, fast and robust, each item with a short Go snippet. None of it is exotic. All of it is the stuff that shows up in postmortems.

## What does secure mean for an API?

The longest section, and the most opinionated.

- **Tokens, chosen on purpose.** Know whether you need an access token or an ID token. If you use JWTs, sign them with a strong algorithm and secret, and know that misconfiguration is their usual failure; he points to PASETO as a more opinionated alternative with less room for error. OAuth 2.0 with the right flow for SSO, access plus refresh tokens for microservices.
- **CORS and cookies.** Don't leave CORS on defaults. Cookies get `Secure` and `HttpOnly`, an HMAC with a strong secret, and a SameSite policy that doesn't stay on the relaxed local-development setting in production.
- **Re-authenticate before critical changes**: email, password, profile, even for a logged-in user, checking both that they are authenticated and that they are authorised.
- **Validate and sanitise everything** with go-playground's validator and bluemonday rather than home-made helpers, against SQL, NoSQL and XSS injection.
- **Audit trails with a baseline**: define what each role should do and alert on activity outside it, such as a customer account poking at the admin portal.
- **Boring error messages.** A response that says the user does not exist is an enumeration oracle. Return one generic message instead.
- **Passwords**: bcrypt; reject passwords containing runs of characters from the user's email or username; reject anything on a common-passwords list (his slide links the SecLists top 10k); check length and complexity.

His least conventional advice is about secrets. Prabesh Thapa said at Conf42 Golang 2024: "Personally I don't like using environment variables." Any code in the process can read them with `os.Getenv`. He prefers a config file protected by filesystem permissions, loaded once and passed explicitly into a server struct, so secrets reach only the code that needs them.

The section closes with masking or tokenising sensitive fields, rate limiting with per-endpoint policies (a password reset endpoint should not share a budget with list-orders) and limit, remaining and reset time in the response, native TLS support for when no proxy terminates it, and Snyk, Dependabot and Wiz to keep dependencies patched.

## What makes it fast?

The usual suspects, done properly. Stop writing `SELECT *` and fetch only the columns you need; index the columns you filter on; cut redundant queries. Cache repeated reads in memory or Redis, send `ETag` and `Cache-Control` so clients can cache too, and put static content on a CDN. Paginate (offset or cursor) because it reduces data transfer and latency, not just to make the UI tidy. Reuse connections with a pooled HTTP client.

On microservices he is refreshingly blunt: they are a double-edged sword, and only warranted when separate teams own separate business domains like payments or fulfilment.

## What makes it robust?

- **Fail early, fail fast**: check config and dependencies at startup and exit with a clear error rather than failing later on the first request.
- **Status codes that mean something**: 403 Forbidden when the user is logged in but not allowed, 401 when they aren't authenticated, balanced against not leaking too much.
- **Errors with context.** In his words, "don't just check errors, handle them gracefully": wrap with `fmt.Errorf`, return them up the stack, and only panic in `main`.
- **A request ID on everything**, for log correlation, Sentry and Jaeger, and idempotency: a retried POST with an ID you have already processed can be ignored.
- **Transactions** for multi-step writes (his example is a MongoDB session with snapshot reads and majority writes), so a failed checkout rolls back the charge.
- **Structured JSON logs**, split into transport logs and application logs, ready for Loki.
- **Liveness and readiness endpoints**, the first returning commit, branch and tag, the second checking the database and Redis.
- **Retries without storms**: exponential backoff on the client, 429 or 503 plus a `Retry-After` header from the server.
- **Metrics and versioning**: time series for baselines, anomaly detection and capacity planning, and versioned endpoints for clients that won't upgrade.

He closes by comparing API tuning to fiddling with an old nineties TV until brightness, picture and sound are all acceptable at once.

## Who should watch

Developers building or reviewing their first production Go API, and leads who want a list to hold a code review against. Each item gets only a minute or two, so treat it as an index of what to look up next rather than a tutorial on any one topic.

Title: Kubernetes is an HTTP API with a reconciliation loop attached
Description: Alex Dejanu (Systematic) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on why Kubernetes is a platform for building platforms, shown with a live log-draining operator and its CRD
Body:
Every Kubernetes talk opens with the same architecture diagram: control plane, etcd, workers. Alex Dejanu, SRE at Systematic, points out at Conf42 SRE 2024 that other orchestrators have the same diagram, so that can't be what makes Kubernetes special. What does is underneath the YAML: an HTTP API you can extend, and a watch loop that keeps reality matching what you declared. He proves it with a small operator, built and deployed live, that drains logs from any pod carrying a label.

It's an explainer for people early in their Kubernetes journey, or anyone who uses it daily without ever having looked behind `kubectl`. It does that job well, in about half an hour.

## Where did it come from?

A quick history: Kubernetes grew out of Google's internal Borg cluster manager and its successor Omega, whose papers he recommends reading. The first prototype was written in Java, effectively a Borg cell on a local machine, before the rewrite in Go. The first public commit came in 2014, and a year later it was donated as the seed technology of the CNCF, which now hosts almost 200 projects. Google's announcement called it an open source cluster scheduler, not an orchestrator, and that wording matters.

He illustrates the lingo with a story from his early meetings: someone asked for a solution that supports automatic resource bin packing for workloads, and he assumed they weren't talking about Kubernetes. They were. Bin packing is the Borg scheduling heritage, and it is the textbook definition.

## Everything is an API endpoint

The first demo makes Kubernetes look like a computer. On a laptop you run `top` and sort by CPU. In a cluster, `kubectl top pods` sorted by CPU across all namespaces gives you the same view, and `kubectl top nodes` does it per node. Turn up the verbosity and you can see the request to the metrics API. Send the same request raw, pipe it to `jq`, and the JSON is the same, just in nanocores instead of millicores. `kubectl api-resources` lists every kind as what it really is: an endpoint in an API group with a version.

`kubectl explain pod` shows the two halves the controller cares about: `spec`, the desired state, and `status`, the most recently observed one, with phases such as Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown.

## A controller observes, analyses and corrects drift

The controller pattern is a generic watch loop: observe the desired state, compare it with the current one, correct the drift. An operator is just a custom controller, usually paired with a custom resource that configures it. Run `kubectl get crds` on any real cluster and you'll find Harbor, Jaeger or Keycloak resources sitting there already.

## The demo: an operator in a few steps

1. Apply a CRD that adds a new API group with one kind, `LogDrain`, whose only spec field is a string called `target`. `kubectl explain` immediately documents it.
2. Build the operator, a small binary, into a Docker image. Give it a service account and cluster role bindings, because it has to talk to the API, then deploy it. Its logs show it watching for LogDrain objects and finding none.
3. Create a LogDrain named `demo-ld` with target `kcd`. The operator picks it up at once.
4. Start a bare Nginx pod with the matching label. As soon as it's ready, its logs appear in the operator's output. A second pod, a small Flask app, gets the same treatment.

The whole thing is small enough to read in one go, which is the point.

## Should you build an operator?

His advice is short and worth repeating: extending the Kubernetes API with custom resources and controllers is easy, which is exactly why you should think twice. Something can work and still lack a proper developer experience or a real use case. Kubernetes is a platform for building platforms, and that is how platform engineering grew on top of it, but every custom resource is another abstraction someone has to maintain.

The closing line is the one to tape to the monitor. Alex Dejanu said at Conf42 SRE 2024: "Kubernetes is only as good as the infrastructure it runs on top of". The many-small-nodes versus few-large-nodes debate continues, and an under-provisioned cluster gets no magic.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to Kubernetes, and developers who use it every day through YAML and want the mental model behind it. If you have already written a controller with kubebuilder, you can skip this one.

Title: Observability from the kernel, and why the tool shouldn't touch your traffic
Description: Nikolay Sivko (Coroot) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on zero-instrumentation observability, mapping eBPF tracepoints to metrics, spans and profiles with no code changes
Body:
Every team that instruments by hand starts with its most critical services and, a year later, still has only those. Nikolay Sivko, Founder and CEO of Coroot, makes the case at Conf42 SRE 2024 for collecting metrics, logs, spans and CPU profiles from the kernel with eBPF instead, with no SDKs and no redeploys, and he names the exact tracepoints his open source agent hooks to do it.

It is a founder talking about his own product, Coroot, which is open source under Apache 2.0. The eBPF explanations are general enough to be useful whatever you run.

## Why not just instrument everything with OpenTelemetry?

He doesn't say don't. He says it's slow, it never reaches 100%, and it never finishes. Third-party and legacy services can't be modified. Teams instrument the critical paths first and stop there. Every new service has to remember to integrate the SDK. And with hundreds or thousands of services on dynamic Kubernetes nodes, the blind spots are exactly where the next incident hides.

Before the how, he lists the what, which is a good checklist on its own: SLIs (requests, errors, latency) per service; the same for every outbound call to services and databases; CPU, memory and disk; network latency, connectivity and packet loss; node metrics; runtime internals such as GC, thread pools, connection pools and locks; orchestrator state like unschedulable pods; logs; and profiles to explain CPU spikes.

## Which hooks does the agent use?

This is the part worth pausing the video for. He explains the three ways to attach: kprobes on any kernel function (powerful, but functions get renamed between kernel versions), tracepoints (statically defined and relatively stable, which is what Coroot prefers) and uprobes on user-space functions. Maps keep state between calls; perf maps, a ring buffer, move data to user space.

The coroot-node-agent then uses:

- `task_newtask` to see new processes by PID, with container metadata resolved from `/proc`.
- `oom/mark_victim` plus `sched_process_exit`, so a terminated process is tagged as killed by the OOM killer rather than just gone.
- `sys_enter_open` to find each container's log files and disk partitions.
- `sys_enter_connect`, `inet_sock_set_state` and `tcp_retransmit_skb` to track every TCP connection, failed handshakes and retransmissions, the latter being a decent proxy for packet loss.
- Read and write syscalls on sockets for layer 7 data, parsed in two phases: fast protocol detection in the kernel, where the verifier forbids loops and complex logic, then full parsing in user space.

For TLS, the agent reads data before encryption and after decryption: uprobes on `SSL_read` and `SSL_write` for OpenSSL users, and on Go's crypto/tls functions for Go binaries. The protocol list covers HTTP, gRPC, Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, Memcached, Cassandra, Kafka, RabbitMQ and NATS.

## Is running code in the kernel safe for production?

Two guarantees make it reasonable. The verifier checks every program for finite complexity before it runs. And kernel-to-user communication goes through a bounded ring buffer: if the user-space side falls behind, data is overwritten, not blocked. You might lose some telemetry, but you don't slow the system. For an observability tool, he argues, that is the right trade.

## What can't eBPF tracing do?

He is upfront about it: eBPF gives you spans, not traces. OpenTelemetry SDKs generate a trace ID and propagate it; from the kernel there is no trace ID to stitch requests together. One open source tool works around this by rewriting requests to inject trace headers. He doesn't like that. Nikolay Sivko said at Conf42 SRE 2024: "I believe that observability tools should observe. They shouldn't change your data".

His answer is to support both: eBPF spans everywhere from minute one, OpenTelemetry traces where teams add the SDK. Coroot can act as an OpenTelemetry backend for logs and traces, with Prometheus for metrics and ClickHouse for logs, traces and profiles.

## What does it look like in practice?

A service map shows up a few minutes after install, with request rates, errors and latency per link. It is per instance, not per service, so you can see a Postgres primary and its two replicas and the network round-trip time between each pair. eBPF CPU profiling, at 60-second resolution by default, turns a spike on a CPU chart into a flame graph, and a comparison mode diffs it against the previous period. His example drills from a Kubernetes component's CPU chart down to the individual function calls burning it.

## Who should watch

SREs with a large estate of services they can't or won't instrument, and anyone who wants a concrete map from eBPF hooks to the signals they produce. If you already run an eBPF-based tool, the tracepoint list and the spans-versus-traces discussion are the reason to watch.

- Sooter Saalu on [writing your own eBPF programs](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Sooter_Saalu_writing_programs_ebpf) at Conf42 Observability 2025.

Title: gosec found nothing, SonarCloud found 206 things, and neither found the XSS
Description: Munawar Hafiz (OpenRefactory) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on the gaps in Go static analysis, tested with gosec, SonarCloud and OpenRefactory's iCR
Body:
Static analysis has two failure modes: it misses the bug that matters, or it buries it under hundreds that don't. Munawar Hafiz, CEO of OpenRefactory, spends his Conf42 Golang 2024 talk on both, then runs three tools against a Go codebase with two known security holes: Google's gosec, SonarCloud, and his own company's Intelligent Code Repair (iCR). This is a vendor talk, and the head-to-head is the vendor's own demo, but the setup is a useful template for evaluating any SAST tool.

## Why are static analysis tools struggling?

His opening numbers set the scene. Over 150 vulnerabilities land in the National Vulnerability Database every week. Munawar Hafiz said at Conf42 Golang 2024 that "research data has shown that existing static analysis tools detect only about 14% of all the bugs detected," and added: "The remaining 86% of the bugs are detected by pure luck." He puts typical false-positive rates at 50% to 90%, which means someone on the team triages nine non-bugs for every real one.

The third gap is fixing. Tools report; humans patch, and humans get it wrong under pressure. His example is Log4Shell: four fixes released in four days, the earlier ones not fully closing the hole.

## What iCR claims to do differently

iCR runs as a set of Docker containers: a web navigator that connects to GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, one analysis engine per language (Java, Python and Go), and a reviewer where you accept or reject findings and push accepted fixes to a temporary branch. He describes three building blocks: deep path-based static analysis, machine learning and generative AI (summarisation to understand context and cut false positives, generation to improve fixes), and code refactoring tech from his 20-plus years building rewriting tools.

The claims, all his: as low as 3% false positives on benchmarks, synthesised fixes for about half the detected bugs, and around 11% more developer productivity. The talk does not show the benchmark behind these, so treat them as vendor figures.

## The test: two known bugs in a real Go project

The interesting part is the experiment design. He takes Red Hat's Service Provider Integration Operator, about 20,000 lines of Go, and checks out an old version that still had two critical bugs later fixed upstream: a cross-site scripting issue and an open redirect. Any tool's job is to find those two.

- **gosec**, run with all rules, reports nothing. No triage burden, but no protection either: both holes stay open.
- **SonarCloud** reports 33 security bugs, 6 reliability bugs and 257 maintainability issues across the repo. Filtered to the Go code, that becomes 206 issues, none of them security: duplicated string literals, high cyclomatic complexity, empty functions.
- **iCR** reports two issues, the open redirect and the XSS, each with a taint trace from where untrusted input enters to where it is used. For the open redirect it has no fix. For the XSS it synthesises one that sanitises the input with the bluemonday library, import included.

His triage arithmetic: at ten minutes per finding, 200-odd reports cost a developer roughly 2,000 minutes before anyone fixes anything. He concedes these particular findings were benign enough to triage faster, but the point stands for noisier codebases.

## How much should you read into it?

One application, two bugs, chosen by the vendor, is a demo rather than a benchmark. It does show something real about Go tooling: a linter-style scanner and a code-quality platform answer different questions than a taint-tracking analyser, and a zero from gosec is not the same as zero vulnerabilities. If you evaluate tools yourself, his method is worth stealing: go back to a commit with known, later-fixed CVEs and see who finds them.

## Who should watch

Go teams choosing a security scanner, or living with one whose findings nobody reads any more. Expect a product walkthrough in the middle (a recorded demo of the iCR workflow on a Python project) and the Go comparison at the end.

Title: Autoscaling is too slow for a spike, so rate limit and shed load
Description: Ivan Lemeshev (Unity) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on surviving traffic spikes with five rate limiting algorithms and load shedding, built in Go
Body:
Autoscaling handles load that grows gradually. It does nothing for a burst that arrives faster than new instances can start, or for one client eating every core you have. At Conf42 Golang 2024, Ivan Lemeshev, Senior Software Engineer at Unity, overloads a small Go HTTP service on purpose, then walks through the two defences that work in that window: rate limiting and load shedding, with a Go implementation of each and the honest caveat that both cost something.

## What does overload actually look like?

A server can only run so many concurrent requests before it spends more time context switching and collecting garbage than doing work. Past that threshold latency climbs steeply, clients time out, and availability falls even though the process is technically still up. In the worst case it runs out of memory and dies.

His spike sources come in two kinds. The predictable ones are launches, sales, seasonal peaks and the daily rhythm of your audience. The unpredictable ones are viral posts, a competitor's outage sending users your way, DoS attacks, scraping bots, and slow external dependencies whose users retry their way into your service.

To make it concrete he builds a password-generator service in Go and runs it in a distroless container limited to one CPU and 300 MB of memory, with swap pinned to the same value so the container can't cheat. Grafana k6 ramps from 0 to 1,000 virtual users over two minutes, holds, then ramps to 2,000 and holds, each user sleeping 100 ms between requests (about ten requests per second each). At 1,000 users latency stays low. At 2,000 the container runs out of headroom and the latency percentiles shoot up.

## Which rate limiting algorithm should you pick?

He covers five, each with a trade-off:

- **Fixed window counter**: one counter per time window. Cheap and simple, but a burst straddling two windows can let through twice the limit.
- **Sliding window log**: stores a timestamp per request and counts those inside the window. Accurate, but memory grows with request volume.
- **Sliding window counter**: weights the previous window's count by how much the sliding window overlaps it. A middle ground: nearly as accurate, far cheaper.
- **Token bucket**: tokens refill at a steady rate, each request spends one. Low memory and smooth, but allows bursts up to the bucket size.
- **Leaky bucket**: requests drain at a fixed rate. Smoothest output, but a quick burst gets dropped even when the user is under their average rate.

His demo implements a token bucket keyed by client IP, behind a mutex, wrapped in middleware that answers 429 when `IsAllowed` says no, configured at a bucket size of one and a refill of one token per second. The k6 run shows lower average load and less extreme latency, but no miracle.

The reason matters more than the chart. Ivan Lemeshev said at Conf42 Golang 2024: "Using a rate limiter has its overhead and costs as well." An in-process limiter burns the same CPU it is trying to protect, and with several instances it needs shared state, such as counters in Redis, or a distributed limiter in an API gateway. His slides list Go packages to borrow rather than write: `golang.org/x/time/rate`, `uber-go/ratelimit`, `juju/ratelimit`, `mennanov/limiters`, `tollbooth` and others.

## Load shedding: fail some requests on purpose

Rate limiting is about fairness per client. Load shedding is about the server itself: when it detects that it is overloaded, it rejects random or non-critical requests, slows down background work, or redirects traffic, so the critical paths still answer in time. In his words, "A controlled slowdown is better than a complete system breakdown in this situation." The cost is explicit: some users get errors or delays, and some processing may be delayed or lost.

His detector is deliberately crude, and he says not to ship it: a ticker fires every 10 ms, and if the gap between ticks exceeds 11 ms the runtime is assumed to be starved, so an atomic flag flips and middleware returns errors until things recover. Under the same k6 profile it also lowered the average load. For the real thing he points to the Amazon Builders' Library article on using load shedding to avoid overload.

## Who should watch

Backend developers who have a vague sense that they should rate limit but have never compared the algorithms, and anyone who wants a reproducible overload test with Docker resource limits and k6. The Go code is small enough to read in the video; the production lessons are in the caveats.

Title: A WAF is chicken wire around a wall with holes in it
Description: Joshua Fox (DoiT International) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on why a web application firewall breeds complacency, and the few cases where you should still deploy one
Body:
The CISO is shouting, the app is full of holes, and someone says: get a WAF. Joshua Fox, Senior Cloud Architect at DoiT International, argues at Conf42 SRE 2024 that this is usually the wrong move: a web application firewall blocks your own users, misses the attacks that matter, and lets the team skip learning security. Then, to be fair, he lists the cases where you should get one anyway. The examples run on Google Cloud Armor, though the argument applies to any WAF.

His comparison sticks: a jewellery store with giant holes in its concrete walls puts up a chicken wire fence and says that at least it has a fence.

## Why do teams buy a WAF in the first place?

He names the drivers, roughly from least to most dangerous. A live attack fire drill. A penetration test, which is an attack you paid for. He tells the story of a pen tester who declined the offered password; Joshua Fox said at Conf42 SRE 2024: "Within ten minutes he was tap dancing through the database." Then outside requirements: an audit, a government regulation, a customer's RFP, a cloud partner programme. That is compliance, not security, but you can't argue with it.

The most dangerous driver is the security blanket, the thing that lets leadership feel warm and cosy. All of these come with urgency, and the problem with urgency is that quick and dirty fixes stay that way. The team never builds the expertise it needs.

## What does a WAF actually do?

He demos it on a deliberately broken Scrabble app, reachable through two load balancers on two subdomains, one with Cloud Armor and one without. Pick a player name of `<script>alert("HACKED YOU")</script>` and, on the unprotected route, the victim's browser runs it. Through Cloud Armor the request comes back forbidden. It works, but it's a crude weapon.

The mechanics: Cloud Armor attaches to the load balancer, which has to decrypt HTTPS to inspect it. Policies hold rules ordered by priority (lower number wins), and each rule has a match condition and an action of deny, allow or log. Matches can be IP allow and deny lists enforced at the edge, whole geographies, or content scans with regular expressions. His advice is to use the preconfigured rule sets for SQL injection, cross-site scripting and friends, built from OWASP signatures, and to tune their sensitivity rather than write your own rules. He shows one real signature regex to make the point that you won't write a better one.

## Why won't it protect you?

**False positives.** He once tried to file a cross-site scripting bug in a bug tracker, and the report vanished because it contained the attack string. Software forums, apps that pass JavaScript around on purpose, apps with hundreds of unvetted text fields: all get blocked. DDoS protection can block the Australian Open, the one traffic spike a tennis site exists for. Shared IPs behind NAT mean blocking a hacker can block your best B2B customer.

**Preview mode is no cure.** Dry-run mode logs what would have been denied, but he has seen teams sit in preview for months, paying, because they don't know their own app well enough to decide.

**False negatives.** Regexes have limits, they must be fast, and only the first few kilobytes of a request get scanned, so anything after that goes through. Attackers change IPs, countries and strings. And the worst class of bug, broken access control, is invisible to a WAF: it can't know which pages you meant to protect. Search pages are a classic, because who checks that every snippet in the results is authorised for the user searching?

**New risk.** The WAF reads every decrypted request, so its bugs are your bugs. Every rule costs latency. And pricing per rule, per policy and per request is negligible until you go big, at which point an enterprise commitment that your product manager makes you back out of is expensive.

His real answer is *job zero*: a secure application, someone on the team owning security, everyone trained. Escape strings, and treat React's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` as the warning label it is.

## When should you use one anyway?

- External requirements: it's a compliance choice, so go ahead.
- Third-party or commercial apps whose code you can't fix.
- Central supervision in a large company, where a security team blocks a fresh CVE such as Log4j while it chases the product team, using the WAF as a monitoring and temporary control tool.
- When you know exactly what to block: a specific attacker IP, or an allowlist for a business partner.
- Advanced features you can't build: managed DDoS protection, machine-learning adaptive protection, threat intelligence lists such as Tor exit nodes, or a vendor's human response team.

Do it before the fire drill, and prefer your cloud provider's WAF (Cloud Armor, AWS Shield) because TLS is already terminated at its load balancer, and pay-as-you-go suits a ramp-up that will take longer than you expect.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who get handed a WAF as a security strategy, and the managers who hand it to them. It's opinionated, practical and short on vendor gloss.

Title: Profile-guided optimization in Go: 2% faster, zero lines changed
Description: Yashvardhan Kukreja (Red Hat) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on Go PGO, using production CPU profiles so the compiler inlines only the hot functions
Body:
The Go compiler makes its inlining decisions blind: it sees your code, not your traffic. Profile-guided optimization (PGO) fixes that by feeding it a CPU profile from the running program. At Conf42 Golang 2024, Yashvardhan Kukreja, Software Engineer (SRE) at Red Hat, explains why inlining is the optimization that benefits most, and demonstrates PGO on a small markdown-rendering server, with a gain of about 2% from a rebuild alone.

## Why does the compiler need help at all?

He starts from the compiler pipeline (lexer, abstract syntax tree, semantic analysis, intermediate representation, optimization, code generation) and a few classic optimizations: constant folding, loop unrolling, dead-store elimination. Then he narrows in on inlining.

Calling a function costs something every time: a new stack frame, parameters pushed, a jump, a return. Inlining pastes the function body at the call site, which removes that cost and often enables more optimization. His `sum(1, 2)` example becomes `1 + 2` and then simply `3` at compile time.

The catch is that inlining everything bloats the binary. More static instructions means more instruction cache misses, more page faults, and on something the size of a Raspberry Pi, possibly thrashing. Too little inlining and you pay call overhead; too much and you pay for the size. What you want is to inline the hot functions and leave the cold ones alone, and the source code alone cannot tell the compiler which is which.

## Why not instrumentation and benchmarks?

Feedback-driven optimization is not new. The early approach was instrumentation: the compiler injects timers and call counters, you run benchmarks, and the collected data steers the next build. He lists three problems: the instrumented code is bloated, the extra benchmark step makes builds slow, and the benchmarks may not resemble production at all, so the compiler can optimize for the wrong hot path and make things worse.

His one-liner on the alternative: "If you hate benchmarks, don't use them." Sample-based profiling of the real workload needs no extra code in the binary: the kernel interrupts the process at intervals and records the instruction pointer and call stack. PGO is exactly that loop: run in production, collect a CPU profile, rebuild with it.

## What did PGO actually change in the demo?

The demo app is a server with a POST `/render` endpoint that turns markdown into HTML. Building with the `-m` gcflag prints the compiler's inlining decisions, and two calls on the hot path are not inlined, among them `io.ReadAll`, which runs on every single request. Non-leaf functions are often skipped by the default heuristics.

He then runs the PGO-free binary under a load generator, captures a 30-second CPU profile, saves it as `default.pgo`, and rebuilds with `-pgo=auto`. This time the compiler inlines `io.ReadAll`, plus whatever else the profile marks hot inside the libraries. The cost shows up in the binary: the original was roughly 8.5 MB, and the PGO build came out about 0.2 MB larger.

## How big is the win?

Benchmarking both binaries and comparing with benchstat, his slides show a 1.88% improvement, with no change to the code. In the live run the average went from 309 to 301 microseconds per operation. Yashvardhan Kukreja said at Conf42 Golang 2024: "I did not have to change a single line of code and I got this benefit out of the box."

He is upfront that 2% on a toy server under light load is modest, and expects bigger gains on real services with real traffic; that part is his expectation rather than something the talk measures. The more durable lesson is the workflow: profile under realistic load, commit the profile, rebuild, and verify with benchmarks before believing anything.

## Who should watch

Go developers who have heard of PGO and want the reasoning behind it, not just the flag. The first third is a compiler refresher; skip ahead to the demo if you already know what inlining costs. The code is on his GitHub, linked from the slides.

- Nishant Roy on [heap optimizations in Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2023_Nishant_Roy_heap_optimizations).
- Jesus Espino on [squeezing performance out of Go functions](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2023_Jesus_Espino_squeezing_function).

Title: Every cloud, every boot mode, fully tested in three hours worst case
Description: Ederson Brilhante (Cisco) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on a staged GitHub Actions, Packer, Terraform and Ansible pipeline that builds multi-cloud, multi-boot images
Body:
Shipping one VM image is easy. Shipping it to AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, VMware and OpenStack, with and without Secure Boot, from a hardened base nobody wants to copy-paste, is where pipelines go to die. Ederson Brilhante, SRE Technical Leader at Cisco, shows at Conf42 SRE 2024 how his team builds images for Cisco's Resource Connector this way, and why a change to the hardened base image is fully tested across every cloud and boot mode within three hours.

Ederson Brilhante said at Conf42 SRE 2024: "The worst case scenario that we identified was 3 hours."

## What is being built, and why is it hard?

The Resource Connector is part of Cisco's zero trust network access suite: a tunnel-like component deployed in the customer's subnet, next to the private app users want to reach. Customers live in different clouds and data centers, so the image has to be wherever they are. Some clouds support TPM and Secure Boot, and the product should use them; internally, the team also needs images with Secure Boot disabled for troubleshooting and debugging.

The images come out of three stages. A hardened image starts from Canonical's Ubuntu and adds the security checks and mandatory configuration; the team uses it for internal runners and services too. A product base image adds partitions, OS upgrades and current CVE fixes. The product image installs Cisco's proprietary software and selects the boot mode.

The trap is shared code. One build script per cloud with common logic is easy to maintain until a one-line change for AWS breaks Azure. Every new cloud or boot mode adds to that pain.

## One repo per stage, GitHub Actions as functions

The fix is structural. Each stage gets its own repo, plus a fourth tester repo with integration, performance and vulnerability tests. All repos share the same folder layout, so knowing one means knowing them all.

The building blocks:

- **GitHub Actions composite actions, one per cloud**, treated as functions with a contract: these inputs, these outputs, and cloud-specific details (VPCs and subnets on AWS, resource groups on Azure, the lab on VMware) stay inside.
- **Reusable workflows** that call those actions.
- **Packer** to build images in parallel across clouds and boot modes.
- **Terraform** to deploy test environments. Its state file is the reason it was chosen: build, test and teardown run as separate jobs, sometimes days apart for longevity tests, and teardown needs to know exactly what was created, including after a half-failed deploy.
- **Ansible**, agentless over SSH, both for building and for tests. Test tasks ignore errors so every check runs, then a callback plugin tallies results and fails the pipeline if anything failed.
- **A pinned-versions file** in every repo, so each change is reviewed in a PR and any bug can be traced to the commit that pulled in a new version.

Reproducibility is a hard requirement: the same commit must produce the same image, over and over.

## How does a change to the hardened image get tested?

Say someone changes a shared Ansible task in the hardened suite. The PR builds a temporary hardened image for every cloud, then temporary base images from it, then temporary product images per boot mode, deploys VMs, runs sanity tests and tears down. Only if all of that passes does it merge.

Merging triggers a chain of PRs: a final hardened image, then a PR bumping it in the base repo, which runs regression again because the base stage does OS upgrades that can't be pinned. The product stage pins everything, so its PRs skip full regression. A script diffs the dependency file against main and builds a matrix of only the affected clouds and boot modes. Merged images then go through vulnerability scans, performance and soak tests, and a few days in staging before they are ready for GA and the marketplaces.

A detail practitioners will appreciate: GitHub's dynamic matrix doesn't render chained pipelines well in the graph view, so the team hard-codes those blocks to keep the flow visible.

## The developer experience bits

Two workflow-dispatch pipelines remove most of the toil. Dev builds let an engineer pass custom versions and get an image without merging anything. The debug VM pipeline deploys a chosen image with ephemeral SSH access for as long as requested, say one hour, using GitHub environment rules to wait before an automatic teardown. In between, the engineer runs Ansible playbooks from their laptop: fix the typo, rerun, no commit-push-wait loop.

Because clouds build in parallel and differences are self-contained, adding a cloud doesn't lengthen the build or the test time.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams who ship VM images or appliances to more than one cloud, and anyone whose GitHub Actions setup has grown into one enormous YAML file. The repo layouts and composite action samples are the reusable part.

Title: Chaos engineering is for the outputs your tests can't predict
Description: Hareesh Iyer (AWS) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on why tests miss the outages that matter, and a four-step loop for running chaos experiments safely
Body:
Your tests know the input and the expected output. The outages that make the news don't. That is the core argument of Hareesh Iyer, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, at Conf42 SRE 2024: a short, clear introduction that explains why chaos engineering exists, how it differs from testing, and the observe, hypothesise, experiment, verify loop for doing it without taking production down yourself.

He says up front that it's a high-level introduction for people new to the topic, and it is. If you're sending a colleague one talk before their first game day, this is a good candidate.

## Why do big companies still have big outages?

He opens with three incidents:

- **Southwest Airlines, December 2022.** A windstorm forced cancellations, but the crew scheduling system couldn't handle the volume of changes and went down. Between December 21 and 30 the airline cancelled around 15,000 flights, on some days around 60% of its schedule, during peak holiday travel. He puts the reported cost at around 1.2 billion dollars, plus a PR disaster.
- **Meta, October 2021.** Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp were down for more than five hours after an engineer doing routine maintenance accidentally disconnected Meta's data centers from the internet. Hareesh Iyer said at Conf42 SRE 2024: "I personally think this was a good thing for humanity." Meta's ad revenue felt differently.
- **Amazon S3, February 2017.** Again human error: an engineer running commands typed something incorrect, and because so many customers build on S3, many big ones were hit directly.

The figures on why this matters come from IDC and the Ponemon Institute: $1.25B to $2.5B in annual application downtime costs for the Fortune 1,000, $500K to $1M per hour for a critical application failure, $474K as the average cost per hour of downtime and $100K per hour for an infrastructure failure.

## Tests live in one quadrant

None of these companies skips testing, so why did testing miss it? His answer is the known/unknown grid. Unit, integration and regression tests sit in the quadrant where you know both the input and the expected output. Southwest knew the input (weather) but not the output. Meta and AWS couldn't predict the exact human error or its blast radius. Those are the known unknowns and unknown unknowns, and you need a different tool for them.

That tool is the experiment. A test checks actual output against expected output. An experiment starts with a hypothesis because the output is unknown. He borrows the vaccine analogy: inject a small, controlled dose of harm to build immunity. The important correction: chaos engineering isn't about creating chaos; it's about uncovering the chaos already inherent in the system.

He also covers the origin: Netflix moving to AWS in 2008, Chaos Monkey randomly terminating EC2 instances in production (unpopular at first, which was the point), then the Simian Army simulating availability zone and region failures, and finally the Principles of Chaos Engineering manifesto.

## The loop: observe, hypothesise, experiment, verify

1. **Observe steady state.** You need logs, metrics and traces, and you need them correlated, before you can say what normal looks like.
2. **Hypothesise.** Fill in the blank: under these circumstances, customers still have a good time. Or, for security: under these circumstances, the security team gets paged.
3. **Run experiments.** Pick common failure modes first: single points of failure, excessive load, artificial latency between components, misconfiguration and bugs, and shared fate where fault isolation doesn't hold.
4. **Verify and act.** Rank findings by business impact. Security and resilience findings should outrank new features, and his slides suggest finding an executive sponsor to make that stick.

## Start small and keep it running

The blast-radius advice is the practical core. Production is the end goal, but don't start there. Begin in a lower environment with a limited scope you understand, add guardrails that stop the experiment and roll back if something unexpected happens, then move to production as confidence grows and widen the scope. And automate: systems change, so a hypothesis that held last quarter needs checking again.

## Which tools does he point to?

AWS Fault Injection Service, with native integration into many AWS services; Azure Chaos Studio; Gremlin as a commercial option; and Litmus if you want open source.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers new to chaos engineering, and anyone who has to explain to a sceptical director why passing tests didn't prevent the last incident. Practitioners who already run game days won't find new techniques here.
