Title: Why goroutines are cheap, and how benchstat and pprof catch slow code
Description: Marco Marino (ION) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on the Go scheduler, goroutine stacks, and finding slow code with benchmarks, benchstat and pprof
Body:
Two pipelines with the same shape, one of them 40% faster, and the reason turns out to be a hand-written loop doing what `strings.ToLower` already does. Marco Marino, a software engineer at ION, uses that example at Conf42 Golang 2024 to walk the full loop of Go performance work: why the runtime makes concurrency cheap, how to write a benchmark that means something, how to compare two runs with benchstat, and how to open the result in pprof until the guilty line is obvious.

It was his first conference talk, and it is pitched at Gophers who have written Go for a while but never sat down with the profiler.

## Why is Go fast at concurrency in the first place?

He starts with a contrast to Java's classic threading, where each Java thread maps to a kernel thread and the OS scheduler decides who runs. In his Java experiment, with 100 threads about 51% of CPU time went into the actual work function; with thousands of threads that share fell to about 27%, the rest lost to context switches. A thousand sleeping Java threads showed up as 1,000 OS threads plus 18 for the JVM. The equivalent Go program needed two.

The difference is Go's M:N scheduler: many goroutines multiplexed onto `GOMAXPROCS` OS threads through per-processor contexts with their own run queues. A context that runs out of goroutines steals work from another, so threads stay busy without the kernel getting involved. On top of that sits CSP: goroutines talking over buffered or unbuffered channels instead of sharing memory behind mutexes, which is why he likes building programs as pipelines.

Memory matters too. OS threads get a fixed-size stack, wasteful for one thread and too rigid for hundreds of thousands. A goroutine starts with roughly 2 KB of stack that grows and shrinks as needed, so there is less state to save on every switch.

A note on scope: the memory model in the title means goroutine stacks here, not the happens-before rules of the Go memory model document.

## How do you write a benchmark worth comparing?

Same machine, a stable environment, and the code under test isolated from everything else. Benchmarks live in `_test.go` files as `BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B)` functions, and `b.N` is not yours to set: the runtime decides how many iterations it needs.

His trick for comparing two implementations with benchstat is to keep the benchmark function name identical: run it against `RunPipeline1` and save the output as the before file, then swap the call to `RunPipeline2` and save the after file. Run with `-run=x` so no unit tests tag along, and with `-benchmem` so you get bytes and allocations per operation next to nanoseconds per operation.

The benchstat comparison is what started the hunt: the second pipeline was about 40% faster, used about 40% less memory, and made around 86% fewer allocations.

## What does pprof show that benchstat can't?

Benchstat tells you that one version is slower; pprof tells you where. Marco Marino said at Conf42 Golang 2024: "Profiling is the process of keeping track of all the inner functions that your main function runs." Add `-cpuprofile` and `-memprofile` to the benchmark run, open the CPU profile with `go tool pprof`, and `top` lists the most expensive functions. Every stage near the top belonged to the first pipeline.

Then `list` on the slow lowercasing stage shows the culprit line by line: a loop lowering the string one character at a time, around 17 seconds of samples. The fast pipeline calls `strings.ToLower` directly. That still has a cost, but overall it saved almost 5 seconds. The memory profile tells the same story in allocations.

## The fine print he adds at the end

- Store the result of the function under test, or the compiler may optimise the call away and flatter your benchmark.
- pprof samples at a fixed frequency, so short runs can mislead. Raise `-benchtime` (and use `-count`) to collect more samples.
- Watch memory: allocations wake the garbage collector, and GC time is time your code isn't running.
- Design for pipelines of goroutines, and benchmark on a machine without load spikes.

## Who should watch

Go developers who know `go test` but have never compared benchmarks properly or opened pprof. If you already profile weekly, the first half on the scheduler will be familiar, but the benchstat workflow is a neat habit to borrow.

Title: Azure Chaos Studio, from resource provider to 99% CPU in one sitting
Description: Peter De Tender (Microsoft) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on Azure Chaos Studio, a portal walkthrough from enabling targets to CPU pressure and AKS pod chaos
Body:
Peter De Tender, Business Program Manager and Azure Technical Trainer at Microsoft, spends his Conf42 SRE 2024 session building chaos experiments in Azure Chaos Studio live in the portal: register the resource provider, onboard a VM and an AKS cluster as targets, hammer two VMs with 99% CPU for ten minutes, kill a process, then let Chaos Mesh restart pods. If you run on Azure and have been meaning to try chaos engineering, this is the half hour that gets you to a first experiment.

It is a product walkthrough by a Microsoft trainer, and it is honest about that. It is also funny, which helps.

## Why break things on purpose?

He starts with the definition from the Principles of Chaos: experimenting on a system to build confidence in its ability to withstand turbulent conditions in production. Peter De Tender said at Conf42 SRE 2024 that it is "the official definition coming from the principles of chaos, which if you ask me could be the name of a rock band."

His running example is the curious case of CPU pressure. A workload runs fine for months, then the CPU spikes and the database or web app falls over. The CPU is rarely the root cause: latency in a database update or a network path that stops writes can be what pins it. And the system is never one VM. It is scale sets, AKS, Cosmos DB, Service Bus and serverless, sometimes across Azure, AWS, Google Cloud and on-prem at once. He also puts the DevOps engineer on the list of failure sources, with the Friday-afternoon release as evidence.

He is clear that chaos engineering is not new. Netflix engineers started it around 2008 while moving from their own data centers to the public cloud. In his view it is not DevOps 3.0, just a tool every DevOps team should carry.

## How is a Chaos Studio experiment built?

Chaos Studio is chaos engineering as a service: you inject faults into Azure workloads. There are two kinds of fault:

- **Service-direct** faults need no agent. Cosmos DB, Key Vault, network security groups and AKS work this way.
- **Agent-based** faults run inside Windows or Linux virtual machines through an installed agent.

An experiment is itself an Azure resource, so you can deploy it with ARM templates or Bicep. Inside it, steps run sequentially; each step holds branches that run in parallel; each branch holds actions such as a fault or a wait. Targets are grouped into selectors. That is the whole model, and he says as much: deploy resources, create experiments, run them.

## What does the demo actually show?

The setup steps are the part most tutorials gloss over, and he does them all:

1. Register the Chaos provider under the subscription's resource providers.
2. Enable targets: an Ubuntu VM (agent-based) and an AKS cluster, with Cosmos DB enabled service-direct.
3. Create a managed identity for Chaos Studio, not for the target VM, and connect Application Insights for the metrics.
4. Build the experiment: CPU pressure at 99% for ten minutes on two VMs (a web server and a database box), then a second step that kills a process.

Why 99 and not 100? His answer: "once it reaches 100% cpu, it's typically crashing the server."

The fault library is broad: VM and scale set shutdown, Cosmos DB failover and request unit throttling, Key Vault access denial, memory pressure, service stops and a set of AKS faults that come from the open source Chaos Mesh. For the AKS ones you translate the Chaos Mesh YAML into JSON for the experiment.

Then the demo does what demos do. The experiment fails because the role assignment didn't save, which turns into the best lesson of the session: the experiment's identity needs permission on the target, and Reader is all it needs. He switches to an earlier run that ran from 4:46 to 4:56, exactly ten minutes, and completed. The AKS experiment then stops and restarts pods while `kubectl get pods` shows them cycling.

One practical gotcha from the preview he used: the portal didn't show the JSON of a Chaos Mesh fault in edit mode, so keep your fault snippets somewhere else.

## Who should watch

Azure engineers and SREs who want to get from zero to a running chaos experiment without reading the whole docs set first. If you already run Chaos Mesh or Litmus on AKS, the value is in seeing how Chaos Studio wraps them in Azure resources and RBAC. The talk doesn't cover experiment design or steady-state hypotheses in depth.

Title: Seven system design mistakes that look fine until traffic shows up
Description: Kirill Parasotchenko (Delivery Hero) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on idempotency keys, outbox queues, jitter, rate and body limits, and retries with backoff
Body:
Most outages in distributed systems are not exotic. Kirill Parasotchenko, Senior Software Engineer at Delivery Hero, spends his Conf42 Golang 2024 talk on seven mistakes that every service team makes at least once: missing idempotency keys, network calls inside database transactions, clients that all wake up at the same minute, no rate limiter, no request size limit, no retries, and retries without backoff. Each one gets a small diagram, the failure mode, and the fix.

It is a short, brisk talk, closer to a checklist with worked examples than a lecture, and that is its appeal.

## Why does a retried request count twice?

The first example is an advertisement service that records ad impressions and forwards them to an external ad service, which increments a counter. Latency spikes between that service and its database, the user's client gives up after the counter was already incremented, and retries. The second attempt succeeds too. One impression, a counter of two.

The fix is an event ID: a unique ID per impression, separate from the ad ID, passed all the way downstream so the database can deduplicate. The ad ID says what was shown; the event ID says which showing this is.

## Don't hold a database connection while you wait on someone else's API

Mistake two is a transaction that inserts an ad campaign and then makes a POST to an external service before committing. It works in testing. Under load, with a slow external dependency, every in-flight request pins a pooled connection until the remote call returns, and the pool runs dry.

His fix is a queue, and the simplest one is a table in the same database: insert the campaign and create a job row in one transaction (two SQL statements against one database, so the transaction is safe again), then let a worker pick up the job and call the external service. You trade immediate consistency for eventual consistency and get your connection pool back.

## Two million clients and one cron expression

The third case is a client app that checks for new plugin versions. Organically, that load spreads over the day. Hardcode the check to a fixed time, and all 2 million clients in his example hit the service in the same instant, which is a load test nobody scheduled. The fix: each client picks a random time.

Because you don't always control the clients, the fourth mistake is having no rate limiter in front of the service: a global cap on requests per second, plus per-user limits so one noisy client can't starve the rest, whether the cause is a DDoS or bad client design.

## Rate limits don't stop a 5 GB request body

Limiting the number of requests says nothing about their size. His Go example is a POST handler that reads the whole body into memory; send it 5 GB and the likely outcome is an out-of-memory crash. A single line of Go that caps the body at 500 KB fixes it, and the oversized client gets an error instead of taking the process down.

## Retries need backoff, and backoff wants jitter

Requests to external services fail for boring reasons, so no retries means a high error rate and a poor user experience. But hammering a struggling dependency is worse. Kirill Parasotchenko said at Conf42 Golang 2024 that retrying without backoff against an overloaded service means "we are making things worse, not better, because we don't let the service recover."

He closes with four backoff strategies: linear (a constant wait, say one second), linear with jitter (one second plus a few random milliseconds), exponential (1, 2, 4, 8 seconds), and exponential with jitter. The jitter variants exist for the same reason as the random check-in time earlier: to stop many clients retrying in lockstep.

## Who should watch

Engineers early in their backend careers, and anyone preparing for a system design interview, will get the most from it. Seasoned SREs will recognise every incident and can use it as a ten-minute refresher to send to a new teammate. Apart from the body-limit snippet, it is language-agnostic.

Title: SRE 2.0 is GenAI use cases sorted by feasibility, pillar by pillar
Description: Indika Wimalasuriya (Virtusa) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on SRE 2.0, a feasibility-versus-value map of GenAI use cases across seven SRE pillars
Body:
Indika Wimalasuriya, Associate Director and Senior Systems Engineering Manager at Virtusa, uses his Conf42 SRE 2024 talk to name a thing: SRE 2.0, site reliability engineering with generative AI built into every pillar. The useful part is not the label but the method. For each of seven SRE pillars he lists GenAI use cases, sorts them on a feasibility-versus-business-value grid, and walks one high-value case through its inputs, outputs and feedback loop.

Indika Wimalasuriya said at Conf42 SRE 2024: "I firmly believe SRE 2.0, which is adapting generative AI, will amplify your reliability."

## Why bother now?

He opens with the KPMG Generative AI Survey 2023: 77% of participants expect GenAI to have the largest impact on their business of all emerging technologies, 73% believe it will increase workforce productivity, 71% plan to ship their first GenAI solution within two years, and 64% expect a competitive advantage from it. IT, tech and operations came out as the function where respondents expected the most benefit, ahead of marketing, sales or R&D.

His second argument is about code. A survey he cites predicts that by 2026 half the code in our systems will come from generative models. If operations is a software problem, as SREs like to say, better-structured code means fewer things to page about, and SREs should use the same tools on their side of the fence.

## The complexity problem, briefly

Monoliths became microservices, monitoring became observability, on-prem became cloud, poly-cloud or hybrid. Each move added data sources, data volume and, in his words, an exponential rise in failure scenarios. That is the gap GenAI is supposed to fill.

## How do you make an LLM useful for operations?

Before the use cases he spends time on LLM risks (bias, misinformation, hallucinations, privacy, IP) and the three standard mitigations:

- **RAG with a knowledge base.** Load observability data, design documents, architecture diagrams, ITSM data and the CMDB into a vector database so the model answers from your estate, not its training set. His example: a remediation engine that already has hundreds of scripts your teams wrote should be in the context.
- **LLM agents.** He shows the AWS Bedrock pattern, where an agent breaks a task into steps and calls APIs at each one. If a remediation script needs the exact IP address of the target server, the agent fetches it from the CMDB instead of guessing.
- **Prompt engineering.** Clear objectives, relevant context, continuous evaluation, iterative refinement, plus the knobs: temperature, top-p, top-k, stop tokens, repetition and presence penalties.

## Seven pillars, one grid each

The core of the talk runs through observability; SLIs, SLOs and error budgets; system architecture and recovery objectives; release and incident engineering; automation; resilience engineering; and blameless postmortems. A few of the high-feasibility, high-value picks:

- **Observability:** generate anomaly detection models, predict bottlenecks and resource trends, and analyse logs to find root causes of performance issues.
- **SLOs:** recommend error budget allocations from business priorities and user expectations, and predict SLO violations before they happen. He admits picking the right SLO target is always a challenge; here the LLM proposes and stakeholders review.
- **Architecture and recovery:** predict the impact of failure scenarios on availability, estimate recovery times from incident history, and spot single points of failure in architecture diagrams.
- **Release and incident engineering:** generate runbooks, predict incident severity from incoming alerts, recommend real-time responses, write release notes.
- **Resilience engineering:** pick and run chaos experiments from identified risk factors.
- **Postmortems:** mine historical postmortems for recurring patterns. Teams write postmortems well; few ever compare fifty of them.

Every worked example has the same shape: inputs, LLM, output, then a human validation and feedback loop. That repetition is the real message.

## What should improve, and what can go wrong?

He measures success with the usual suspects: SLO alignment, change frequency, change failure rate, lead time, MTTD, MTTR and MTBF. He offers no figures of his own, so treat this as a framework, not a result.

The pitfalls list is short and correct: skipping validation, ignoring user feedback, ignoring ethics, and treating a model as a static solution. On ethics he passes on a meme: "don't ask a lady their age, gentlemen about the salary and LLM about their training data set."

## Who should watch

SRE managers building a GenAI roadmap who want a long list of candidate use cases with a prioritisation method attached. Engineers looking for an implementation or a benchmark should look elsewhere: there is no demo and no production data.

Title: A field guide to where AI fits in an SRE's week
Description: Asutosh Mourya (Trilitech) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on mapping AI tools onto five SRE jobs, from alert filtering to toil, and the six reasons adoption stalls
Body:
If you have been asked to add AI to your SRE practice and don't know where to start, Asutosh Mourya, in engineering management at Trilitech, gives you the map at Conf42 SRE 2024. His short talk takes five things SREs do every week (alerting, anomaly detection, incident analysis, capacity planning and toil) and names the technique and the tools that apply to each, then lists what makes adoption fail.

It is a survey, not a war story. There are no before-and-after numbers and no demo. What you get is a well-organised checklist you can hold your own stack against in under half an hour.

## What is the SRE job AI is supposed to help with?

He starts from the classic definition: reliability, scalability, performance and response time, at lower cost. Asutosh Mourya said at Conf42 SRE 2024: "A good SRE generally automates themselves out of a job". AI, in this framing, is the next layer of that automation, not a replacement for the engineer.

## Train on your own past incidents to cut alert noise

The first and most practical idea is supervised learning on historical incident data. A model that has seen which alerts turned into real incidents can learn to tell genuine alerts from false ones and to estimate severity from patterns that correlate with major disruptions. Fewer pages, and the loud ones are the right ones.

Next to that sit dynamic thresholds. Static thresholds flood you at peak load and miss early warning signs in quiet periods. A forecasting model that predicts load lets alert sensitivity move with it. His example of the next step: an AI system notices a service's response time climbing and triggers auto-scaling or a restart without waiting for a human. Grafana's dynamic alerting and metric forecasts are his tool of choice here.

## Anomaly detection starts with boring statistics

Before any machine learning, establish a baseline with plain statistics (mean, median and friends) and flag numeric outliers. Only then reach for heavier tools: principal component analysis to reduce high-dimensional metrics to the variations that matter, and DBSCAN clustering to group similar behaviour and isolate the points that belong to no cluster. The tools he lists are the Splunk Machine Learning Toolkit, Grafana Machine Learning outlier detection, Davis AI in Dynatrace and Datadog's Bits AI.

The order is the useful part. Teams that skip the baseline end up with a clever model nobody can explain at 3am.

## GenAI earns its keep during the incident

Generative AI shows up where humans are slowest under pressure: reading. Models that condense logs, metrics and user reports into a short incident summary help a team grasp scope and impact quickly, and the same summaries feed post-mortems and keep stakeholders informed. He points to Amazon DevOps Guru for automated root cause analysis and Grafana's Incident auto-summary for the write-up.

## Capacity planning and toil

For capacity, he describes machine-learning-assisted performance and capacity planning: combine ML with load testing, simulate load scenarios from past performance data and see where capacity runs out before production does. Seasonal spikes and promotions are the obvious use. Splunk's ML toolkit, Dynatrace baselining and Datadog's predictive monitoring all cover parts of it.

For toil: Pulumi's AI assistant for infrastructure as code, Mabl and Testim for tests that maintain themselves as the application changes, and Sonar and CodeClimate in CI to stop technical debt piling up.

## Why do AI rollouts in SRE stall?

The closing section is the one to bookmark. His list of blockers: missing skills on the team, poor data quality, resistance to change, integration with existing systems, high costs, and compliance and security concerns. The remedies are unglamorous and correct: train people, fix data governance first, roll out gradually, pick tools with flexible APIs, and calculate ROI before buying. Start small and scale the spend as the value shows up.

## Who should watch

SRE leads who need a structured overview to plan an AI roadmap, or to sanity-check a vendor pitch against the categories that matter. Engineers who already run anomaly detection in production will find it introductory.

Title: Your Go test suite already knows which syscalls your app needs
Description: Alessio Greggi at Conf42 Golang 2024 on generating seccomp profiles from Go unit and integration tests with Harpoon, an eBPF syscall tracer
Body:
If your tests exercise most of your code, they also exercise most of the system calls your binary will ever make. Alessio Greggi, a software engineer, used his Conf42 Golang 2024 talk to turn that observation into a pipeline: trace the syscalls your Go tests trigger, and ship a seccomp profile as a build artifact next to the binary. The word almost in the title is there for a reason, and the honest part about where the approach breaks is the most useful bit of the talk.

## What is a seccomp profile, and why build it in CI?

Seccomp is a Linux kernel feature that restricts which system calls a process may make. A profile is the list of allowed (or denied) syscalls attached to a program. Alessio Greggi said at Conf42 Golang 2024: "So it works as a firewall for system calls." Kubernetes uses it heavily, including a default profile that blocks the most dangerous calls.

Hand-writing a tight profile for your own service is tedious and easy to get wrong. His idea is to generate it at the end of the test pipeline, and to treat its quality as a function of coverage: if your tests cover 70% of the code, the extracted syscall list is reliable for that 70%. Go helps here. Coverage for unit tests arrived in Go 1.2, and Go 1.20 added coverage for integration tests, which pushes the measured percentage up considerably.

Deployment is the easy half. An init container downloads the profile from the artifact registry, drops it on the node under the kubelet's seccomp directory, and the application container references it with a `Localhost` seccomp profile in its security context.

## Integration tests are easy, unit tests are noisy

For integration tests you build the binary, run it under `strace` or `perf` with scripts that check the expected results, and collect what it calls. Done.

Unit tests are where it gets awkward. You cannot `strace go test`, because `go test` compiles and runs the test binary in one go, and you would trace the toolchain along with your code. Building the test binary separately with `go test -c` and tracing that is better, but still noisy: test setup that reads fixtures from disk shows up as file opens and reads your function never makes.

## Harpoon: trace only while the function runs

His answer is Harpoon, a small eBPF tool. You build the test binary, find the mangled symbol of the function you care about with `objdump --syms`, and run `harpoon -fn <symbol> ./binary.test`. Harpoon attaches a uprobe at the function's entry and a uretprobe at its return, and only records syscalls between the two. In his demo, tracing an `InterfaceExists` function from one of his own iptables-related projects yields just the syscalls that function makes.

## Where does it break?

Uretprobes and Go do not get along. A uretprobe works by overwriting the probed function's return address with the address of a trampoline into the eBPF program. Go stacks move around at runtime, which he attributes to the garbage collector, so the restored instruction pointer can be wrong and the program can be corrupted, or the return is simply never reported.

The workaround, from a long-standing bcc issue, is to skip uretprobes entirely: uprobes can be attached at arbitrary offsets, so Harpoon places one uprobe on every `RET` instruction in the function to simulate the return probe.

That workaround forced a library change. Harpoon started on iovisor's gobpf, which sits on bcc and could not attach uprobes at offsets. Moving to Aqua Security's libbpfgo, a wrapper over libbpf, made offsets possible and brought CO-RE (compile once, run everywhere), so the eBPF program no longer needs GCC at runtime and can be built once in a pipeline and distributed.

## Who should watch

Go developers running workloads on Kubernetes who keep meaning to tighten seccomp but never get past the default profile, and anyone curious about the practical friction of uprobes on Go binaries. It is a short talk about an experiment, not a finished product: the profile is only as good as your coverage, and branches your tests skip are syscalls your profile will block in production.

Title: An eBPF honeypot and a GenAI copilot as a deployment gate
Description: Michele Dodic (Accenture) at Conf42 SRE 2024 on a five-stage AIOps journey ending in zero-touch ops, with eBPF and a GenAI copilot guarding deploys
Body:
Most AIOps talks stop at a maturity diagram. Michele Dodic, SRE Associate Manager at Accenture, and his colleague Anastasia (Nastia) Archangelskaya, Cloud Advisory Manager at Accenture, keep going at Conf42 SRE 2024: after the roadmap from reactive monitoring to zero-touch operations, they run a GitLab pipeline where an eBPF experiment catches a container reading `/etc/passwd` and an OpenAI-backed SRE copilot tells you not to ship it.

The takeaway is modest on purpose. Michele Dodic said at Conf42 SRE 2024: "start simple and scale fast."

## Why would an SRE want AIOps at all?

The problems on the list are familiar to anyone on call: siloed multi-cloud estates nobody sees end to end, incidents that spread before anyone has fixed them, and alert fatigue from monitoring that fires without correlating anything. Michele frames the answer in SRE terms: measure everything, learn from failure, automate what makes sense. Better MTTD and MTTR need end-to-end insight first, which is why observability is the prerequisite for AIOps and not an optional extra.

## What does the journey look like, stage by stage?

Nastia walks through it as a ship at sea, which works better than it sounds:

- **Monitoring** (the vigilant lookout): metrics on speed, fuel and engine health, someone shouting when a number goes red. Is it working or not?
- **Observability**: add the captain's journal (logs) and follow the crew (traces). Metrics, logs and traces together tell you why, not just what.
- **Full-stack contextual observability**: the business context. Sailing from Italy to Spain needs one amount of fuel; Italy to Spain via Alexandria needs another. Topology-based correlation and root-cause analysis live here.
- **Intelligent or predictive observability**: machine learning on historical data, so you see the failure before it happens. Resolution is still manual.
- **Autonomous, zero-touch AIOps**: the ship steers itself and heals itself.

She is clear that this is iterative, that different parts of one organisation sit at different stages, and that not every team needs to reach the last one. Knowing where you are is the point of the exercise.

## Where does eBPF fit?

Michele gives a short eBPF refresher: sandboxed programs in a privileged context, extending the kernel without changing its source or rebooting. Programs are event-driven, firing on syscalls such as `execve`, so the kernel sees everything your containers do. In his words, "the kernel becomes a sort of big brother as it is able to see everything."

That visibility is the answer to the black-box container. The talk covers three use cases:

1. **Risk assessment in containerized applications.** eBPF watches container creation, file access and networking per node, and scales from one pod to a large microservice estate, feeding a mission control dashboard that can trigger remediation.
2. **Blocking deploys to an unstable production.** A pipeline stage filters eBPF events; an AI model using context and topology data detects that prod is unhealthy and blocks any deployment until it recovers. Several teams shipping features concurrently is exactly when you want that gate.
3. **An SRE copilot on GenAI.** When response time rises and the error budget burns, one process pages the SRE team while another asks OpenAI for a draft post-mortem and suggested remediation, shown on the mission control dashboard.

## What does the demo show?

The demo is a DevSecOps pipeline in GitLab: deploy the app to Kubernetes, deploy a honeypot, run an eBPF experiment with Cilium's Tetragon, then pass the Tetragon output to the OpenAI copilot. Tetragon logs show `/etc/passwd` exposed in the container; the copilot flags it as a security risk before anything reaches production. A cleanup stage tears it down. Mission control is built on Dynatrace, first as a classic dashboard of eBPF attack events and honeypot heartbeat, then as a custom AppEngine app tracking each pipeline stage, failure ratio and the copilot's suggestions.

It is a demo, not a production case study: no fleet numbers, no false-positive rates. The pattern is the useful part, and it is easy to copy with open-source parts.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who want a vocabulary for where their team sits on the AIOps curve, and anyone curious how eBPF security events and an LLM can sit together as a pipeline gate. If you already run Tetragon or Falco in CI, the maturity model is the new material; if you don't, the demo is.

- Nikolay Sivko on [zero-instrumentation observability with eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2024_Nikolay_Sivko_zeroinstrumentation_observability_ebpf), also at Conf42 SRE 2024.

Title: One Go codebase, desktop and phone apps, and no 40 GB SDK first
Description: Andrew Williams (Fyne Labs) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on building native GUI apps for desktop, mobile and web from one Go codebase with Fyne
Body:
Go already made command line tools pleasant to build and ship; Andrew Williams wants it to do the same for graphical apps. At Conf42 Golang 2024, the founder of the Fyne project and CEO of Fyne Labs walks from an empty directory to a markdown editor that runs on a Mac and in the iPhone simulator, gets unit tested without opening a window, and is packaged for the app stores, all with one codebase and the `fyne` command line tool.

## Why is GUI development still so painful?

Williams starts with a short history. Most of today's widget toolkits carry a heavy C heritage: manual memory management, thread handling, and string types designed before Unicode and multibyte runes mattered. The modern alternatives in Go, Rust and JavaScript are often bindings over that same old technology, so they never feel idiomatic. The polished platform toolkits from Apple and Google are large and assume a lot of prior knowledge. His favourite example is a hello world for an unnamed toolkit that needed a 10 GB download and took 40 GB of disk before the first line of code.

The other catch: the vendors with modern toolkits want you building for their platform, not everyone's.

## What does Go bring to the table?

Write once, compile for every target, ship a single binary with no runtime dependencies, and get native performance because the compiler does the work. Andrew Williams said at Conf42 Golang 2024 that Go offers "a great way to lower the barrier of entry to building graphical applications, just like it does command line applications."

Fyne is his attempt to cash that in: an open source toolkit, roughly six years old at the time of the talk, with 23,180 GitHub stars on his slides. It targets Windows, macOS, Linux and the BSDs, iOS and Android, the browser through WASM (nearly complete, with the next release meant to finish it), and embedded devices such as Raspberry Pi kiosks.

## From go mod init to a markdown editor

The setup is honest about its one wart: you need Go 1.17 or newer plus a C compiler, because Fyne talks to the graphics stack natively. Linux usually has gcc already, macOS gets it through Xcode, Windows needs MSYS2 and mingw. Then it is `go get fyne.io/fyne/v2@latest`, an `app.New()`, a window, a label, and `ShowAndRun()`. He warns that some editors auto-import the wrong major version, so check for `v2` in the import path.

The more interesting demo is a markdown editor in a handful of lines: a multi-line entry and a rich text widget side by side in an adaptive grid, with the entry's change callback wired straight into the rich text's markdown parser. The same code then runs in the iPhone simulator, switches to light mode because that is the iOS default, and flips the grid's orientation when the device rotates.

## GUI tests that don't grab your keyboard

Unit testing graphical apps is usually where good intentions go to die. Fyne ships a test package that simulates typing and double-taps on a widget, so a test can type "hello" into an entry, double-tap to select the word, and assert on the selection and cursor column. The test runner executes the app in memory, without real input or output devices, so no windows pop up and the tests are fast.

## Packaging and the stores

The `fyne` CLI fills the gap between `go build` and what each platform expects: `fyne package` builds an `.app` bundle on macOS or an `.exe` with icon and metadata on Windows, `fyne install` puts the app in your launcher, and `-os android` or `-os ios` with an app ID cross-compiles for phones. If the C toolchains get in the way, `fyne-cross` does the builds inside containers. `fyne release` handles signing with Apple profiles and certificates or an Android keystore, and a `FyneApp.toml` file keeps all those flags in source control.

## The rest of the toolkit

The second half is a tour of the `fyne_demo` app: canvas primitives drawn with OpenGL acceleration, bundled icons and light and dark themes, basic and input widgets, forms, and collection widgets (list, table, tree, grid wrap) built on three callbacks so only visible rows get rendered. That is how you scroll through hundreds of thousands of items. The file dialog hands you a URI reader rather than a file path, which is why the same code can stream a document out of iCloud or Dropbox on iOS. Community packages in fyne-x add map and terminal widgets, and FyshOS goes all the way to a Linux desktop where every app is a Fyne app.

## Who should watch

Go developers who have only ever shipped servers and CLIs and wondered what a desktop or mobile app would cost them. It is an introduction with plenty of code, from the toolkit's author, so expect enthusiasm for Fyne rather than a comparison with other toolkits.

Title: From a twelve-step BERT deployment to three lines of LangChain
Description: Deepak Karunanidhi (Novartis) at Conf42 LLMs 2024 on how LLM productionization differs from classic MLOps, and why prompting beats fine-tuning by default
Body:
Deploying a fine-tuned BERT model the classic way takes a twelve-step checklist. Calling a foundation model through LangChain takes three lines of Python. At Conf42 LLMs 2024, Deepak Karunanidhi, Associate Director of Data Science and Machine Learning at Novartis, put the two side by side to show how much of the productionization burden moves when you switch from training task-specific models to prompting a foundation model, and what LangChain offers for the part that is left.

Despite the title, this is less a forecast than an introduction: a tour of traditional MLOps, a primer on in-context learning, and a short LangChain demo. Karunanidhi brings more than 15 years in data science and machine learning, three of them mainly in generative AI.

## What did productionizing a model use to look like?

His baseline is BERT, the model that made transformers the default for NLP tasks. The checklist: train or fine-tune on a large dataset, usually on GPUs; tune hyperparameters such as learning rate and epochs; optimise, for example with quantisation; serialise to TensorFlow's SavedModel or PyTorch's TorchScript; serve with TensorFlow Serving or TorchServe; design an API; add load balancing and auto-scaling; monitor latency, throughput and error rates; secure it; build CI/CD; version for rollback; keep optimising.

He spends time on the serving layer. TorchServe exposes inference and management APIs, can host several models in one container, keeps them in a model store on EBS, and serves them over HTTP. The container goes to Amazon ECS or Azure Container Apps behind a load balancer, provisioned with CloudFormation. A CI/CD pipeline retrains and redeploys when production data drifts from the training data, with A/B variants and rollbacks on top.

None of that is wrong, and teams still run it. His point is the sheer amount of process, for a model that does one task.

## What changes with a foundation model?

A foundation model like GPT-4, Claude or Mistral can do many tasks without fine-tuning. You describe the task in the prompt, in context, alongside the input. The pipeline shrinks to cleaning the input, writing the prompt, calling the model, and orchestrating it with a framework such as LangChain or LlamaIndex. That saves the GPU time and the retraining loop.

He doesn't rule fine-tuning out. Some domain-specific tasks need it. But as Karunanidhi said at Conf42 LLMs 2024, "most of the problem can be solved well enough by using the right amount of prompting technique", naming chain of thought, self-consistency and tree of thoughts as the techniques to try first. His prompt example sets a role, an unbiased professor scoring answers from zero to ten, before passing in the input.

## What does LangChain add?

Structure for the part after the prototype. LangChain, in Python or JavaScript, breaks an app into steps (pre-processing, model call, post-processing) that can be chained in sequence or in parallel, and the LangChain Expression Language cuts the glue code. Around it: LangServe turns a chain into a REST API, LangSmith handles debugging, testing, evaluation and monitoring, and templates give deployable reference architectures. He mentions Azure's prompt flow as a similar idea, with each step plug-and-play.

For production he lists scalability for concurrent requests, testing support, monitoring, API-based deployment, and prompt versioning, where prompts are evaluated and refined before release like any other artefact.

## How short is the demo?

Short. After `pip install langchain langchain-openai` and an API key, it is `ChatOpenAI()` plus `llm.invoke()` with a question about how LangSmith helps with testing. Step two adds a `ChatPromptTemplate` with a system message casting the model as a world-class technical documentation writer, piped into the model. Step three appends a `StrOutputParser`, so the chain reads `prompt | llm | output_parser`. That is the whole demo. Deployment, monitoring and evaluation get named rather than shown.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and ML engineers who know the classic MLOps stack and want a map of what carries over to LLM apps, or managers who need to explain why the GenAI project doesn't need a GPU cluster. If you already ship LangChain apps, there is little new here.

Title: Semantic search is easy until you have 1.5 million records
Description: Ben Fistein (Semantee.ai) at Conf42 LLMs 2024 on the pitfalls of semantic search in production, from embedding cost to keyword fallback and SQL
Body:
Type *cheap car suitable for my dog* into a catalogue of about 100 BMWs and you get three Active Tourers with roomy boots. At Conf42 LLMs 2024, Ben Fistein, co-founder of Semantee.ai, showed that demo at the end of a short talk on semantic search, and spent most of it on the part vector database marketing skips: everything between we have vectors and users get good results.

It is a founder's talk about his own product, and it is brief. The useful bit is a list of production problems his team hit, which applies whatever stack you pick.

## What is a vector database, in two dimensions?

Fistein's primer uses the old king, queen, man, woman example with toy coordinates: king at (1, 1), man at (1, 1.5), queen at (2, 2), woman at (2, 2.5). Man sits closer to king than to queen because the words are semantically linked. Real systems store text, images or audio as vectors, compare them with cosine, Euclidean or Jaccard distance, and use an approximate nearest neighbour index (HNSW in Semantee's case) to find the closest matches.

The technology is not new. He dates it back to around 2005, with MonetDB, but LLMs made it practical, and he quotes Gartner's prediction that about 30% of enterprises will have adopted vector databases by 2026.

## Where does it break in production?

Most vendors give you one piece, either the vector model or the LLM, and leave the plumbing to you. His list of questions you will have to answer:

- **Which LLM?** GPT-4 is neither the cheapest nor always the best. He notes it effectively works through English, so results can differ by query language; for truly multilingual search you want a language-agnostic embedding model.
- **Which similarity algorithm?** Each has trade-offs; pick for the use case.
- **What about large datasets?** This is the big one. Their first customer had 1.5 million records, and Fistein said at Conf42 LLMs 2024 that "1.5 million records using GPT four would have taken several years just to get vectors from", at a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars. Optimising embedding generation was where the work went.
- **How to curb cost?** Use a big model for generation and a much smaller one for search.
- **Re-indexing.** Catalogues change daily, and every change means re-embedding.
- **Integration.** It has to plug into the customer's existing systems, which for them meant exposing everything as REST endpoints.

## When should you not use semantic search at all?

The hybrid section is the most practical part. A query for a red house between 200 and 400 square metres with a garage is mostly structured filters, and Fistein reckons almost no model besides GPT-4 parses it correctly anyway. Hand the parameters to keyword or SQL search and use semantics for the fuzzy bits. As for someone typing red car: "Probably overkill to use semantic search for that."

Since nearly every e-shop has a SQL database underneath, you also need a way to translate a semantic query into SQL. He doesn't say how they did it, only that it took a lot of tuning.

## What else is it good for?

Beyond search: routing support tickets or incidents by category, similar-image search, retrieval for chatbots, recommendations by meaning (nose drops suggest tissues and allergy relief), anomaly detection for banks hunting out-of-pattern behaviour, and matching long documents to similar ones. Semantee also renders results on an interactive 3D map of semantic proximity, which is optional but fun.

The demo closes it out. A query for extravagant cars for successful managers returns the XM, BMW's most expensive SUV, plus two fully specced models in loud colours. The model got extravagant right.

## Who should watch

Product engineers about to add semantic search to a catalogue or knowledge base, who want the list of traps before they start. If you need implementation detail on how Semantee solved them, the talk names the problems more than the solutions.

Title: Go gotchas that compile fine, from leaky time.After to non-nil nils
Description: Dmitry Korolev (Avito) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on common Go mistakes with slices, strings, channels, time.After, WaitGroup, mutex copies, defer and interfaces
Body:
Go is friendly until a nil interface is not nil. At Conf42 Golang 2024, Dmitry Korolev, Senior Software Engineer at Avito, goes through the mistakes that compile cleanly, pass review and then bite in production: slices that share memory, a time.After that leaks about 200 MB, a WaitGroup used wrong, a copied mutex, a defer that logs zero and an interface that is nil and not nil at once. Each one comes with the reason from the language internals or the docs, and the fix.

It is a dense checklist talk. Mid-level Go developers will recognise at least two of these from their own git history.

## Why does append inside a function not change my slice?

A slice is a small struct, a pointer to an array plus length and capacity, and Go passes it by value. Writing to index zero inside a function changes the shared array, so the caller sees it. But if the slice is full (length equals capacity), append allocates a new array and the slice inside the function now points there; later writes never reach the caller. The same sharing bites when you reslice and append into the original's spare capacity. The built-in copy gives you an independent slice.

The memory version is sneakier. A news scraper keeps the first 100 runes of every article as a preview. The preview slice is 100 elements long, but its capacity, and the whole article behind it, stays alive in the cache. Hello, memory leak.

Why runes at all? Strings are UTF-8 bytes, so slicing and len work on bytes, and the first two bytes of a Chinese greeting are not two characters. Converting to runes fixes that, at the cost of keeping two copies of the text.

## Who should close a channel, and when?

Reading from a closed channel is fine; writing to it or closing it twice panics. So the writer closes. And only close when the reader needs to know, for example a for-range loop over the channel, which otherwise waits forever. "There is nothing wrong with leaving the channel unclosed," Dmitry Korolev said at Conf42 Golang 2024; the garbage collector takes care of it.

## Why does time.After leak memory in a select loop?

The classic: select on an event channel, with a time.After of 15 minutes to warn when nothing arrives. Every loop iteration creates a new timer channel, and per the docs the underlying timer is not recovered by the garbage collector until it fires. With about a million events, at roughly 200 bytes per channel, that is about 200 MB held for 15 minutes. The docs' fix: use NewTimer and Stop it when it is no longer needed.

## The goroutine bugs hiding in one example

The goroutine example starts five goroutines that add 1 to 5 into a sum, expecting 15. The closure captures the loop variable, not its value, so the goroutines often see the last one. Go 1.21 shipped an experiment and Go 1.22 changed loop-variable semantics so it no longer happens, but older code still has it. The same code has a second bug: wg.Add is called inside the goroutine, so Wait can return before some goroutines have even started.

Then a counter struct with a mutex and a map, with methods on a value receiver. Each call copies the struct, mutex included, the copies stop protecting anything and the program dies with fatal error: concurrent map writes. sync types carry a noCopy marker so go vet can flag the copy. Atomics have their own trap: "Operations with atomics are atomic individually, but not atomic collectively," as Dmitry put it. Check that a number is even, print it, and you can print 287.

## Defer, nil interfaces and vendoring

A deferred log of a named return value prints zero, because deferred arguments are evaluated when the defer statement runs, not when the function returns. Wrap it in a closure and it reads the final value.

An interface is a type plus a data pointer, and it equals nil only when both are empty. Return a typed nil pointer as an interface and you get a value that prints nil but fails the nil check.

Last, go mod vendor copies only the packages needed to build and test your module, not the whole library. Dmitry reads that as a hint: a library that hides the calls to an external service inside itself takes control away from the services consuming it.

## Who should watch?

Go developers past the tutorial stage, reviewers who want a list of things to look for, and anyone whose service eats more RAM than it should. Seniors can treat it as a quiz.

Title: RAG cuts hallucinations, and a small open model checks what is left
Description: Ofer Mendelevitch (Vectara) at Conf42 LLMs 2024 on why RAG reduces hallucinations and how the open HHEM model scores answers against their sources
Body:
Ask GPT-3.5 whether Will Smith ever hit anyone and it will tell you, with great confidence, that there is no record of it. At Conf42 LLMs 2024, Ofer Mendelevitch, head of developer relations at Vectara, used that answer to open a talk on hallucinations in retrieval augmented generation: why RAG reduces them, what it takes to build RAG yourself, and how Vectara's open source hallucination evaluation model, HHEM, scores a response against the facts it was given.

A fair warning on scope: despite the title, measurement is a short section. Most of the talk is the case for RAG, the do-it-yourself architecture, and a walkthrough of Vectara's RAG-as-a-service with three demos. It is a vendor talk, but the architecture part is vendor-neutral and worth the time.

## What is a hallucination, exactly?

Mendelevitch's definition is the useful one. As he put it at Conf42 LLMs 2024, "hallucination is when the LLM can actually give you a good response that looks very authentic and looks very convincing, but it's actually wrong." The Will Smith answer is wrong for a reason everyone watching the Oscars two years earlier knew.

RAG attacks this by not making the model rely on memory. Before answering, the system asks a retrieval engine for relevant chunks of your data and puts them in the prompt as facts. In enterprises that data is usually private, so the model could not know it anyway.

## What does do-it-yourself RAG involve?

More than one box on a diagram. On the ingest side: pull documents from databases, SaaS tools such as Jira or Notion, or files on S3 and Dropbox; extract text from PDFs and slides; chunk it (a page, three paragraphs, two sentences, and the choice affects quality more than people expect); run each chunk through an embedding model that turns text into a vector of roughly 1,000 floats; and store the vectors in a vector database.

On the query side: embed the user's question, retrieve the closest chunks, build a prompt along the lines of here is the question, here are the facts, and send it to an LLM such as GPT-4, Claude or Llama 2. Optionally validate the answer with a guardrails product before it reaches the user, and optionally take an action, like opening a Jira ticket.

Each step is a system to run and pay for, with DevOps and ML engineers to maintain it. Mendelevitch's point is that it gets much harder when you go from ten documents to a million.

## Why RAG beyond fewer hallucinations?

His list: answers come with citations, so users can check them; no training step, so your data does not leak into a future model; it is cheaper than retraining; and his favourite, per-person access control. If HR documents sit in the corpus, the retrieval engine can leave them out of the facts unless the person asking is allowed to see them.

## How do you measure what is left?

This is HHEM. Give it a set of facts and the LLM's response, and it tells you whether the response is consistent with those facts. It is open source on Hugging Face, and Vectara uses it to run a public leaderboard ranking LLMs by hallucination rate, which shows that models differ, and by how much.

The demos make it concrete. AskNews crawls BBC, NPR, CNN and other sources daily and answers questions such as whether AI should be regulated, with clickable citations, and can answer in German from English sources. The same app with HHEM adds a confidence check after generation, here run through Hugging Face inference, and labels the answer high confidence. A third demo is a chatbot over 100 to 150 crawled IRS pages that handles follow-ups such as which conditions make tuition deductible. Mendelevitch adds the obligatory warning to use a tax advisor, not his demo.

## Who should watch

Developers about to build their first RAG app who want the full pipeline in one diagram, and teams weighing build versus buy. If you came for evaluation methodology, the HHEM section is a pointer to the model and leaderboard rather than a how-to.

Title: GoFr, a Go framework that ships metrics and traces before your first route
Description: Aryan Mehrotra (GoFr.dev) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on GoFr, an opinionated Go microservice framework with built-in metrics, tracing, logging and data sources
Body:
Most Go services spend their first week wiring the same things: config, logging, a database pool, Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry. At Conf42 Golang 2024, Aryan Mehrotra, Software Developer at GoFr.dev, demos GoFr, an opinionated open source framework that does that wiring for you, so a hello-world service already logs every request with a correlation ID, exposes metrics and can export traces.

Honest scope: Aryan works on GoFr, so this is a maintainer showing his framework. It is also a well-paced live demo that shows exactly what you get out of the box.

## What does GoFr include?

The feature list: built-in observability (traces and metrics, plus custom ones), authentication with OAuth, basic auth and API keys, fine-grained log levels that can change on the fly without a restart or redeploy, REST and gRPC APIs, configuration management, database integrations and migrations, and a circuit breaker for calls between services, so a dead dependency does not get hammered with retries. For data, it supports MySQL, Postgres and other SQL databases, Redis and MongoDB, and pub/sub over Kafka, Google Cloud Pub/Sub and MQTT.

## What does hello world look like?

Two lines are in every GoFr app: gofr.New, which initialises logging, metrics and data sources from configuration, and app.Run, which starts the HTTP server with health-check and metrics routes already registered. "By default, it starts the server on the port 8000, which we can override using the configs," Aryan Mehrotra said at Conf42 Golang 2024.

A route is a path plus a handler that takes GoFr's context and returns a value and an error. Return hello world and the response comes back as JSON wrapped in a data field, with a 200 status set by the framework according to REST conventions. That wrapper is deliberate: every service built with GoFr answers in the same shape. Every request also gets a log line with a correlation ID, the status code and how long it took.

## How much work is a database?

Config, mostly. Aryan starts MySQL in Docker, copies the connection settings from the docs into the .env file in the configs directory, and on the next start the app is connected. The handler reaches the database through the context and runs show databases. Moving to Postgres means changing the dialect in config, not the code. Turn the log level to debug and the executed queries show up in the logs, handy for tuning.

## What do you get for observability?

Metrics on a separate port, 2121 by default and configurable, with the basics already there: SQL connections in use and open, and request duration histograms by path, method and status. You can add your own counters, up-down counters, histograms and gauges from the context.

Tracing uses OpenTelemetry. Point the config at a Zipkin exporter and every request shows up as a trace from router to handler, findable by its correlation ID. With two services, one using Redis, the trace follows the call from the first service to the second and back. The demo ends on GoFr's public Grafana dashboards, imported into a local Grafana and fed by one of the repo's example servers under generated load: request counts, latencies, status codes, outbound SQL queries and Redis commands.

His closing argument is that by taking care of database connections and tracing, the framework leaves developers to focus on core functionality, which means less time to production, easier debugging and more productive developers.

## Who should watch?

Teams starting several Go microservices who want them to look and behave the same, and developers who are tired of copying observability boilerplate from the last project. If you prefer assembling your own stack from the standard library, this shows what you would be signing up for in exchange for convention.

Title: Before you fine-tune on Bedrock, check whether RAG already does the job
Description: Suraj Muraleedharan (AWS) at Conf42 LLMs 2024 on running LLMs on Amazon Bedrock like any workload: RAG first, invocation logs, metrics, NeMo Guardrails
Body:
Everyone wants to fine-tune, and most of them don't need to. At Conf42 LLMs 2024, Suraj Muraleedharan, Principal Architect for Platform Engineering in Global Financial Services at AWS, took the operational excellence pillar of the AWS Well-Architected Framework and applied it to large language models on Amazon Bedrock: choose models on speed, precision and cost, reach for RAG before fine-tuning, and turn on invocation logging, metrics and guardrails before anyone calls it production.

It is an AWS architect talking about an AWS service, so expect Bedrock throughout. The operational advice travels well beyond it.

## What changes from MLOps to LLMOps?

Less than the acronyms suggest. Muraleedharan runs through the design principles first: operations as code, frequent small reversible changes, refining procedures, anticipating failure, learning from it, and observability for actionable insights. A Bedrock API is still a dependency you version, deploy and watch.

The real difference is the model lifecycle. Classic MLOps trains one model per task and retrains it when new data arrives. A foundation model is trained once on everything, then reused across projects through prompting, RAG or fine-tuning. People still matter more than tooling, and as Muraleedharan said at Conf42 LLMs 2024, "Conway's law doesn't change much when it comes to deploying a software".

He splits users into providers who build models from scratch, tuners who adapt them with domain data, and consumers who only prompt. The roles are transferable, and each needs different skills.

## How should you pick and customise a model?

Model selection comes down to three trade-offs he sees in the field: speed, precision and cost. Some customers will give up a little precision for a much cheaper model when the token volume is large.

Customisation is a ladder: prompt engineering, then retrieval augmented generation, then fine-tuning, then continued pre-training, with complexity, cost and time rising at each step. His field observation is the line to remember: "What has been observed is in majority of the cases, rag is good enough." Fine-tuning needs far more compute and expertise, raises harder questions about proprietary data, and risks under- or overfitting on a thin dataset. His advice is to benchmark prompting against RAG before going further, with a clear business reason for each extra rung.

On Bedrock, Knowledge Bases provide managed RAG, covering ingestion, retrieval and augmentation, with session context for multi-turn chats and automatic citations. Fine-tuning takes labelled data from S3 and produces a private copy of the base model. At the time of the talk that covered Llama 2, Cohere Command and Amazon Titan models, with Anthropic's Claude not yet supported, and continued pre-training was for Titan Text with unlabelled data.

## How do you call it?

The workhorse pattern is API Gateway to Lambda to Bedrock, the same serverless pattern teams used before Bedrock existed. Lambda can be swapped for EC2, ECS or EKS. The code is a `bedrock-runtime` client in boto3, a body with the prompt, max tokens and temperature, and `invoke_model` with a model ID. The catch he flags: the request and response payload shape differs per model, so switching from Claude to Titan or Llama is not just a new ID. Outside Lambda, use temporary credentials, and if no AWS SDK is available, sign the request with SigV4 yourself.

## What can you observe out of the box?

Invocation logging, switched on at the Bedrock level, writes each prompt and response to S3, CloudWatch or both. His sample asked Claude to explain the three-body problem with a 300-token cap and got 296 output tokens back, a good reminder to check how close you run to the limit. CloudWatch gets invocations, invocation latency, client and server errors, throttles, and input and output token counts without extra work. Model evaluation, then in preview, scores models for accuracy, toxicity and robustness on built-in or your own prompt datasets.

## Where do guardrails sit?

For safety he uses NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails as a shim between the caller and the Bedrock model. Its config defines five kinds of rails: input rails that can reject a user message, dialog rails that steer how the model is prompted, retrieval rails that can drop a RAG chunk, execution rails, and output rails. That is how you keep a bot on topic and enforce standard operating procedures. Examples are in the aws-samples amazon-bedrock-workshop repository on GitHub.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams who own a Bedrock account and need the operating checklist, and architects about to approve a fine-tuning project who should first ask for the RAG benchmark.

Title: LangChainGo, from one prompt to a RAG pipeline on Qdrant
Description: Alexandre Evangelista de Souza (Indev Web) at Conf42 Golang 2024 on LangChainGo, a Go port of LangChain, from simple prompts to RAG over a PDF with Qdrant
Body:
LangChain is usually a Python or JavaScript conversation. At Conf42 Golang 2024, Alexandre Evangelista de Souza, CEO and Founder of Indev Web, shows its Go port, LangChainGo, in a short code-first session: call a model, swap providers by changing three options, stream a response, and then build a small retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline that answers questions about a PDF stored in Qdrant.

It is a quick tour from a developer based in Brazil, and it reflects the library as it stood in early 2024. Treat it as a map of what LangChainGo covers, not a reference.

## What is LangChainGo?

A port of LangChain to Go. Alexandre's first warning is that the documentation was new and incomplete at the time, so the GitHub repo is where the real picture lives. The building blocks are familiar if you know the Python version: models, vector stores, document loaders, agents, memory and chains. The integration list he reads out is long, including OpenAI, Ollama, Mistral, Google AI, llama.cpp, llamafile, NVIDIA and Perplexity, plus a model from Brazil, with Whisper on the way.

## How little code does a first call take?

Import the packages, create an OpenAI LLM instance and call it with a context and a prompt. Options include temperature and stop words. His test prompt is the start of a sentence about the first man to walk on the moon, so the model only has to finish it.

The useful trick is that anything with an OpenAI-compatible API plugs into the same client. For Groq he sets the model, the token and the base URL, and the rest of the code stays the same. NVIDIA's endpoint works the same way, with a catch he points out: used like that, it could not give him embeddings, so it is no good for the RAG half. He also shows message-based calls with a system message and a human message, a max-tokens setting and a streaming function that prints tokens as they arrive.

## How does the RAG demo work?

The classic pipeline: load a document (a PDF here, though it could be a text file or a database), split it into chunks, embed and save the chunks in a vector store, retrieve the relevant ones for a question, and send them with the prompt to the model.

His vector store is Qdrant Cloud, configured with a URL, an API key and a collection name, though other vector stores would do the job. A helper loads the PDF and splits it into documents, and a second function sends them to Qdrant. Then the lesson every first RAG demo teaches: run the ingest twice and you have stored everything twice. So he splits the program into ingest, which runs once, and query, which only grabs the existing vector store and runs a similarity search.

The query side sets an explicit model (in that version, he warns, do not rely on the defaults), creates an OpenAI embedder, retrieves the matching chunks, adds them to the context and answers through a conversational ReAct agent wrapped in a chain, with a low temperature. Asked about the book in the PDF, it answers with the number it found there. "Very simple, very easy. Thank you for watching," Alexandre Evangelista de Souza said at Conf42 Golang 2024, and for a working RAG loop in Go that is a fair summary.

## Who should watch?

Go developers who want to see whether they can build LLM features without adding a Python service next to their Go one. It is short and moves fast, so keep the LangChainGo repo open alongside it; APIs have moved since.

Title: Assume the model is vulnerable and design around it
Description: Eugene Neelou (OWASP Foundation) at Conf42 LLMs 2024 on ten LLM security risks, from jailbreaks and denial of wallet to model theft and poisoned supply chains
Body:
Researchers cloned a high-value ChatGPT model for a few hundred dollars, against the tens of millions it took to train. That is one of ten risks Eugene Neelou packs into a short talk at Conf42 LLMs 2024. Neelou, who co-authored the OWASP Top 10 for LLM security and coined the term MLSecOps, gives a fast tour of how LLMs widen the attack surface, and ends with one piece of advice that covers all ten: treat the model as vulnerable and build the controls around it.

He calls it a gentle introduction and means it. Each risk gets a scenario and the business consequence, not a mitigation playbook, and he says plainly that the format leaves no room for solutions.

## What can attackers do to the model itself?

**Jailbreaks** get past the safety filters vendors put on chat apps, using techniques from language switching to data format tricks to persuasive negotiation with the model. For a general chatbot that means bad press. In regulated or mission-critical use, worse.

**Prompt injection** goes after the system prompt, the instructions users never see. Extract it and a competitor gets the brains of your app: business processes, confidential documents, pricing. If the model reads external files or web pages, the instructions can be planted there. His example is a good one: "Imagine a resume that tricks a recruiting LLM into giving the highest possible rating to this resume."

**Data poisoning** is easier than it sounds. Tampering with an internet-scale dataset is hard without internal access, but creating thousands of fake accounts that send millions of chat messages, benign one at a time and malicious together, can shape a model trained on chat history. The result ranges from worse quality to backdoors that bypass content filters.

## What about availability and IP?

**Denial of service** can come from a single crafted file that triggers expensive processing. Its cousin, **denial of wallet**, simply floods the app with API calls, and Neelou says it can exhaust a budget in minutes or hours.

**Model theft** turns that traffic into an asset: send millions of carefully chosen prompts, collect the answers, train a near-identical copy. The cheap ChatGPT clone came out of exactly that. **Data leakage** uses the same interrogation to pull out memorised secrets, such as IP or customer details, and he notes companies rank it as their top worry.

## Where does the model hurt the rest of the system?

**Insecure output** is the risk that doesn't need an attacker. Copilots generate vulnerable code and insecure configs, and models hallucinate package names. Attackers already register the frequently hallucinated names and fill them with malicious code.

**Insecure plugins** extend the attack surface: a sales-analytics plugin with loose database permissions leaks customers' financial details, and a plugin that fetches URLs can be used much like a classic SSRF to pivot into the infrastructure. **Insecure agents** are worse, because they act. An email-triage agent that auto-replies can be told to send attackers sensitive data, leak the contact list or mail phishing to everyone. The same goes for coding copilots with repo access and DevOps agents holding cloud permissions, and the damage scales automatically.

Finally the **supply chain**: public models, datasets and libraries that can be compromised so the app looks normal while someone else steers it. He calls it one of the most critical and stealthy risks.

## The one piece of advice

Since LLMs, like other ML models, are inherently open to adversarial attacks, the fix is architectural. As Neelou said at Conf42 LLMs 2024: "It is crucial to assume LLM vulnerability and design applications with this in mind, implementing safety guardrails and security controls around vulnerable but useful models." Look at the whole system, not only the model or the dataset.

## Who should watch

Anyone who needs the LLM threat model in one short sitting: engineering managers, product owners, security people new to ML. Practitioners who already know the OWASP list will want the talks below for the hands-on side.

Title: Base64 walked a stock chatbot past its own guardrails
Description: Pranav Shikarpur (Pangea) at Conf42 LLMs 2024 on prompt injection, insecure output handling, PII leaks and jailbreaks, with a defence for each
Body:
The guardrails held until Pranav Shikarpur asked the model to decode a Base64 string. At Conf42 LLMs 2024, Shikarpur, Developer Advocate at Pangea and an early contributor to learnprompting.org, showed how he got a public demo chatbot built to buy stocks to tell users to short Nvidia and buy GameStop and call it financial advice, then walked through the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications with an attack and a defence for each item he covered.

It is a vendor talk, and it says so: the defences end in a demo of Pangea's redaction and audit log APIs. But most of the talk is attack technique, and that part is worth the time on its own.

## How does a prompt injection actually play out?

Shikarpur's starting rule is the old application security one. In his words at Conf42 LLMs 2024, you should assume "user inputs are always going to be malicious". The classic demo is a translate-to-French prompt in the OpenAI playground that abandons its few-shot examples the moment a user types an instruction to ignore all previous instructions and print a pwned message.

The more interesting case is real. Vercel's AI chat playground, a generative UI demo that buys shares and checks stock prices, carries a disclaimer that nothing in it is financial advice. Shikarpur first ran a prompt-leaking attack, asking what was written at the top of the document, because apps typically put their prompt first and the user's text below it. That leaked a large chunk of the system prompt, which he compares to reconnaissance in a red team engagement. With the prompt in hand he injected the Nvidia and GameStop advice. The guardrails blocked the phrase about financial advice, so he appended it as a Base64 string, which the model decoded and printed.

Why it matters: Air Canada lost a case after its chatbot promised a customer a discount the airline's policy never offered.

The defences he shows are cheap: instruction defence (warn the model that users may try to change its instructions), sandwich defence (repeat the original task after the user input, since the last text is what the model weighs most), and input filtering with block lists or redaction APIs.

## What happens when generated code gets executed?

Insecure output handling is next. An app that turns English into Python and runs it with `os.system` works fine until the prompt asks for a script that forks forever. Shikarpur's fork bomb took one injected instruction. The real-world example is the MathGPT case documented in MITRE ATLAS, where an attacker used prompt injection to make generated code pull the app's OpenAI API key out of the host process.

His rules: don't execute code that you've never seen before; if you must, run it in an isolated environment with no internet access; and scan generated files and binaries first with something like Pangea File Intel or VirusTotal.

## Where does PII leak?

Into training data, mostly. He cites the Google C4 dataset containing records from the Colorado and Florida voter registration databases, Samsung banning ChatGPT after staff pasted internal source code into it, and a Cyberhaven study of employees pasting company data into chatbots. The defence is redaction at both points where data enters, fine-tuning and inference, before it reaches the model.

The OWASP list he set out to cover included training data poisoning, but the talk spends that slot on jailbreaking instead. He shows the DAN (do anything now) prompt getting Mistral's chat to explain how to hot-wire a car, and admits the only defence he has seen work is training a second model to classify user inputs.

## Log everything, then prove it wasn't touched

The closing best practice is tamper-proof audit logging: of data used to fine-tune a model, so you can retrain from a clean point after an accidental PII upload, and of every chat input and output. The demo summarises a patient record with names, locations, phone numbers and emails redacted before the model sees them, and the summary still holds up. The open source app is at git.new/chatgpt.

## Who should watch

Developers shipping their first LLM feature who have not yet thought like an attacker, and security engineers who want concrete, reproducible examples to show their product teams. The tax day joke at the start ages well too: don't let an LLM do your taxes.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Eugene Neelou's [gentle introduction to LLM security](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Eugene_Neelou_gentle_introduction_llm_security), the OWASP risk map in one sitting.
