Title: Your cloud SIEM caught 30 secret reads and missed the batch call
Description: Kennedy Torkura (Mitigant) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on testing cloud threat detections by emulating real attacker techniques
Body:
The best moment in this talk is a detection that works 30 times and then misses the one call that matters. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, [Kennedy Torkura](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Kennedy_Torkura_threat_informed_defense), Co-Founder and CTO of Mitigant, made the case for threat-informed defense: pick the attacker techniques relevant to you, build detections for them, then emulate those techniques in your own cloud to prove the detections fire. His AWS example found a gap that a single new API call walked straight through.

It is a sponsor talk with a demo of Mitigant's cloud attack emulation product at the end, but the method in the middle needs nothing more than CloudTrail, a detection rule and an afternoon.

## What is threat-informed defense?

The definition comes from MITRE Engenuity: the systematic application of a deep understanding of adversary tradecraft and technology to improve defenses. He frames it as a signal-to-noise problem: most security news is not about your organisation.

It rests on three pillars that feed each other:

- **Defensive measures**, anchored on MITRE ATT&CK. The Enterprise matrix, version 14 at the time, has 14 tactics and 234 techniques. Nobody covers all of them, and his point is that you should not try. Pick the slice an attacker would actually walk through your infrastructure.
- **Cyber threat intelligence**, which narrows that slice further. His example is Scattered Spider, the group behind the MGM Resorts ransomware attack, which targets sectors such as entertainment, telecoms and technology. The free ATT&CK Navigator maps the group to the techniques it uses, and filtering to infrastructure as a service leaves a short list.
- **Testing and evaluation**, the pillar he says gets talked about least. MITRE recommends adversary emulation: mimicking real threat actors in a way that is safe and, crucially, repeatable, so you can rerun it after hardening and see whether anything improved.

## Why emulate instead of pen-test?

He walks through MITRE Engenuity's five questions for deciding whether you need adversary emulation. The one that lands for engineers is about data: are you collecting the right data and running the right queries to detect a given technique? Most cloud detection is a query over log events, and either half can be wrong. Get them wrong and you pay in false positives and alert fatigue, or worse, silence.

For a real-world model he points to GitLab, whose security team publishes its stealth red and purple team process. Emulation only starts at step six, after brainstorming, logistics, adversary profiling, tabletop exercises and capability development. Step seven, validating detection and response, is detection engineering under another name.

Detection engineering itself he describes as a young discipline that grew up once the perimeter collapsed. Firewalls, WAFs and IAM sit at the front door; SIEM, XDR, NDR and cloud detection and response deal with attackers already inside. Detection engineers write rules much like software, often as Sigma rules in YAML, such as one that fires when AWS CloudTrail is stopped, updated or deleted.

## How does one API call slip past?

The worked example ties the three pillars together. Threat intelligence says Scattered Spider harvests credentials from cloud secrets stores, ATT&CK technique T1555.006. You have a detection for it. So you emulate it against AWS Secrets Manager, with logs flowing from CloudTrail into Datadog Cloud SIEM.

Mitigant ran two variants. One reads secrets one at a time with GetSecretValue. The other uses BatchGetSecretValue, which AWS released in November 2023, to fetch about ten secrets in a single call. CloudTrail recorded both. Datadog flagged the 30 single GetSecretValue calls and missed the batch call entirely.

The cause was the query. The example rule he showed matched on GetSecretValue only, so the newer API was invisible to it, and the fix is one more event name. Kennedy Torkura said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "the threat detection systems might miss some detections, either because the cloud service provider kind of had new APIs or they released new features".

## What did the demo show?

The demo runs Mitigant's attack actions against an AWS account: make a private S3 bucket public (mapped to ATT&CK discovery), create a new IAM user with API keys and full S3 access, and disable logging on an S3 bucket. It connects over the AWS API, and as he put it, "we don't install agents at all." Resources can be exempted with tags, CloudTrail evidence lands in the report after about ten minutes, and everything is rolled back automatically about five minutes after the attack. The report has fields for the objective and your observations of what your detection system did.

## Who should watch?

Detection engineers and cloud security teams who have written rules but never proved they fire, and SREs curious how the chaos engineering habit carries over to security. He is, after all, one of the people who pioneered security chaos engineering.

Title: Paraphrasing turns AI text detectors into a coin flip
Description: Aldan Creo (Accenture) at Conf42 LLMs 2024 on how AI text detectors work, from GLTR to Binoculars and watermarks, and why paraphrasing beats them.
Body:
The tools that promise to spot ChatGPT homework are weaker than their marketing suggests, and the reason is in how they work. At Conf42 LLMs 2024, Aldan Creo, Technology Research Specialist at Accenture, walks through the main families of AI text detectors from scratch and then shows why a good paraphrase drops their accuracy towards chance.

The title is a provocation, and the talk mostly delivers a clear explainer of detection. The evasion section only makes sense once you know what the detectors are measuring, which is why he asks viewers to sit through the first twenty minutes.

## What is a detector actually looking at?

His starting point is that an LLM is a text predictor, the same idea as your phone keyboard guessing the next word, just bigger. Every detector in the talk exploits that.

**Classifiers** are trained on labelled human and machine text and answer yes or no. OpenAI launched one in January 2023 and later retired it because it was not reliable. He points to Ghostbuster as the current state of the art if you want a classifier.

**White-box analysis** looks at the probability of each token. GLTR colours every word by how likely GPT-2 was to pick it: a wall of green means the model would have written this itself, while human text is full of words the model finds surprising. DetectGPT adds a twist: perturb the text and compare scores. If the original looks far more model-like than its rewrites, a model probably wrote it.

**Watermarking** splits the vocabulary into a red list and a green list and bans the red words during generation. Weak watermarking skips the rule when two tokens almost always go together, so *Barack* can still be followed by *Obama*. A text with lots of red words is human; one with none came from a watermarked model.

## The capybara problem

The most fun section is about context. Ask ChatGPT for a few sentences about a capybara who is an astrophysicist and you get exactly that, which is very likely given your prompt. A teacher reading the result never sees the prompt, so the text looks surprising, and surprise reads as human.

Binoculars tackles this by separating two sources of surprise: the text being unusual, and the text being human. It normalises perplexity by the expected surprise of an LLM on that text, and compares the result with a threshold of 0.85: above is human, below is AI.

## Why paraphrasing wins

Once you know detectors measure token statistics, the attack is obvious: change the tokens. Rewriting has to go deeper than swapping five words, but done properly it works. The figures he shows, from the paper *Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?*, track a watermark detector: 97% accuracy on the original text, 80% after a PEGASUS paraphrase, 64% with T5 and 57% with a fine-tuned T5.

"If we like paraphrase the text, we make the detector behave as the flip of a coin," Aldan Creo said at Conf42 LLMs 2024.

His tool list includes Quillbot, Grammarly, DIPPER and T5 on Hugging Face, a round trip through another language with DeepL, and his favourite, DeepL Write, because you pick each rewrite yourself.

The manual tricks follow from the detection mechanics. Tell the model who you are and how you write. Ask for active voice. Feed it very specific facts. Outline the structure, or write the opening yourself so it copies your style. Try other models and other languages, since detectors lose accuracy outside English. Avoid famous quotes and boilerplate legal text, which look machine-made to a detector because every token is predictable. And spend your rewriting effort on the opening, since many detectors only scan the first paragraph or two to save compute.

## Humans are no better

Reading for clues helps a little: a teenager writing like a PhD, the wrong dialect, a hallucinated fact or bad maths. But he is blunt about human judgment, saying that "human annotators are horrible, are really bad at detecting generated text". He closes with the view that detection will only get harder as models improve, and leaves the ethics for another talk.

## Who should watch

Teachers, trust-and-safety teams and anyone asked to buy an AI detector should watch it to understand what those tools can and cannot do. It is beginner-friendly: no maths beyond the idea of probability.

Title: 5,000 serverless apps on one Kubernetes node is a WebAssembly argument
Description: Sohan Maheshwar (Fermyon) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on why serverless WebAssembly beats containers and microVMs on density and cold starts
Body:
Cold starts and idle containers are both density problems, and WebAssembly attacks both. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, [Sohan Maheshwar](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Sohan_Maheshwar_future_cloud_webassembly), Developer Relations Lead at Fermyon and formerly at AWS, argued that the next wave of cloud compute is serverless WebAssembly: functions that start in under a millisecond, pack thousands to a node, and run on any architecture, built with the open-source Spin framework.

The talk is a good first look at Wasm on the server, with a live Spin demo and a comparison against Firecracker microVMs, and it ends on Fermyon's SpinKube and its commercial Kubernetes platform.

## What is wrong with containers and serverless today?

He names three problems. Containers are provisioned for peak load, so they mostly sit idle, burning money and electricity; he cited an Andreessen Horowitz estimate of about 100 billion dollars of market value lost to this. Configuration keeps growing with every dependency. And serverless has cold starts, which teams pay to work around by keeping instances warm.

For an outside opinion he quotes Docker founder Solomon Hykes, who tweeted that if Wasm and WASI had existed in 2008, there would have been no need to create Docker.

## What is WebAssembly, minus the hype?

The boring answer, as he puts it, is that it is just another bytecode format: a portable compilation target, built in the mid-2010s by browser vendors including Mozilla. Compile from many languages to a Wasm module and run it in any Wasm runtime (Wasmtime is the most popular) on any OS or architecture, from Kubernetes to a Raspberry Pi. Think JVM, minus the single language.

Two properties matter for servers. Wasm is sandboxed by default, so a module gets nothing until you grant it, the reverse of how most code runs. And WASI, the WebAssembly System Interface, adds files, clocks, random numbers and networking outside the browser while keeping that sandbox around I/O.

## How fast is the Spin workflow?

Spin is Fermyon's open-source framework for serverless Wasm apps, with 15+ languages and 4.6K GitHub stars at the time. The demo was four commands: `spin new` (picking an HTTP or Redis trigger, with community triggers for MQTT and SQS, then a language, Rust here), `spin build`, `spin up` to test locally with curl, and `spin deploy` to push to Fermyon Cloud.

The application manifest is TOML and maps routes to components, and each component can be written in a different language, so one route of a calculator in Python and another in JavaScript works. The manifest is also where capabilities live: a module may only call an HTTP host listed in its allowed outbound hosts.

## Why does it suit serverless so well?

He gave four reasons, with numbers from his slides:

- **Binary size**: a Rust hello world is about 2 MB, about 300 KB compiled ahead of time; the demo's HTTP API was about 2.3 MB JIT and 1.1 MB AOT.
- **Startup time**: comparable to native code, only 2.3x slower in the benchmark he cited.
- **Portability**: the same build runs across operating systems and architectures.
- **Security**: a capability-based sandbox.

The bigger argument is multitenancy. Borrowing from Marc Brooker, a system's value is set by long-term average traffic and its cost by short-term peak traffic, so the more tenants you can safely pack onto the hardware, the closer cost gets to value. VMs packed a few apps, containers more, Wasm functions far more. His analogy: gas, liquid, solid.

## How does it compare with Firecracker?

He uses the characteristics of an ideal serverless unit from the Firecracker paper (Agache et al., 2020), the microVM behind AWS Lambda. Isolation and performance come out even: both are sandboxed and near-native. Wasm wins in two places. Density: thousands of functions per node needed a 48-core, 382 GB RAM, 3,360 GB disk machine for microVMs, against 8 cores, 32 GB RAM and 100 GB disk for Wasm. And fast switching: about 125 ms from startup to cleanup for a microVM, under 1 ms for Wasm. He was candid that soft allocation (overcommitting resources, which Lambda does at up to 10x) is still untested for Wasm.

## What about Kubernetes?

SpinKube, launched just before the talk, is an open-source project with contributions from Microsoft, Liquid Reply, SUSE and Fermyon. It combines a containerd shim for Spin, a runtime class manager, a Spin operator that manages Spin apps as custom resources, and a Spin plugin that scaffolds the deployment YAML.

Fermyon's enterprise Fermyon Platform for Kubernetes pushes density further. Sohan Maheshwar said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "You can actually run 5000 serverless apps in one Kubernetes node." A prerecorded demo showed 5,000 apps on an Azure Kubernetes cluster answering with sub-millisecond cold starts, which his slides put at 50x workload density.

When will this go mainstream? His answer was "gradually and then suddenly", noting that 2023 was the year of WebAssembly that didn't quite happen.

## Who should watch?

Platform and serverless engineers tired of paying for warm instances or idle pods who want the case for server-side Wasm with real numbers.

Title: An internal developer platform where a git push buys you a database
Description: George Hantzaras and Dan Mckean (MongoDB) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on Kubernetes operators as the engine of an internal developer platform
Body:
The cheapest way to add a capability to an internal developer platform is to teach Kubernetes about it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, [George Hantzaras](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_George_Hantzaras_Dan_Mckean_internal_developer_kubernetes), Director of Engineering for Kubernetes at MongoDB, and Dan Mckean, Senior Product Manager at MongoDB, showed how operators turn Kubernetes into the platform of platforms, then built a database-as-a-service golden path where developers get a MongoDB Atlas cluster and its credentials from a git push.

The first two thirds are a clear refresher on how Kubernetes extends itself, from the control loop to operators. The last third is a demo using MongoDB's own Atlas Kubernetes Operator, so you know whose product shows up.

## What is an internal developer platform supposed to do?

The talk starts from the CNCF definition. A platform is a foundation of tools and services for building, deploying and managing applications; an internal developer platform goes further by cutting developers' cognitive load, giving them a consistent experience through golden paths, and being designed around its users. Platform engineering is the work of building and running that thing.

Two terms carry the rest of the talk. Platform capabilities are what users get, such as observability, managed databases or secrets management. Platform interfaces are how they get them: a CLI, a GitOps workflow with Argo CD or Flux, or a portal like Backstage.

## Why is Kubernetes the default foundation?

The speakers are honest that no hard data proves most IDPs run on Kubernetes, only industry consensus, analyst coverage and vendor case studies. The reasons given are the familiar ones: containerisation, autoscaling, orchestration, running on any cloud or on premises, and declarative management. Kubernetes earned the platform of platforms role through extensibility, the CNCF ecosystem, standardisation, and the CSI, CRI and CNI interfaces for storage, runtimes and networking. He also flags the counter-argument that Kubernetes is getting too complex, and suggest abstraction may be the fix.

## From control loop to operator

This section is the best part for anyone who has used operators without thinking hard about what they are. The controller manager runs built-in controllers (replication, endpoints, namespace), and each one runs the same loop: get the desired state from the API server, get the current state, reconcile. That loop is where self-healing, scaling and consistency come from.

A custom controller, typically written in Go, runs that same loop against a custom resource whose schema you define in a CRD. An operator packages one or more custom controllers with the rest of what an application needs: CRDs, deployment and service manifests, Helm charts, documentation and monitoring tools. The useful distinction is between internal operators, which manage resources inside the cluster (deployments, stateful sets, persistent volumes), and external operators, which manage things outside it, a hyperscaler service or a SaaS such as Atlas, through their APIs.

## What did the demo build?

George Hantzaras ran the demo, focused on one IDP capability: database as a service.

- **Install the operator** with the Atlas CLI, which also creates API keys in Atlas and stores them as Kubernetes secrets.
- **Create an Atlas project** and then a cluster from short YAML files describing the cloud provider, instance type and region. `kubectl apply` creates the custom resources; the operator calls the Atlas Admin API to create the real things.
- **Add the interface**: install Argo CD, point an Argo CD application at the infrastructure-as-code repository, and repeat the same files with a `git push` instead of `kubectl apply`. No team needs direct access to the cluster any more.
- **Connect an app**: an AtlasDatabaseUser resource references a password secret; the operator writes back a secret with the connection string, and a pod running the Mongo shell reads it from an environment variable and connects.

The demo is undramatic, and he took that as the point. George Hantzaras said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "when it comes to managing infrastructure in critical production environments, not having fireworks is a good thing."

## Who should watch?

Platform engineers deciding how to expose managed services to developers, and anyone who wants the clean version of the controller, custom controller, operator story. If you already write operators, skip to the demo for the external-operator plus Argo CD pattern.

Title: Building a RAG super-doctor, four upgrades past naive retrieval
Description: Zain Hasan (Weaviate) at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024 on query rewriting, hybrid search, autocut and re-ranking for RAG chatbots
Body:
A doctor sees about 100,000 patients in a career; a retrieval system can read 167,000 case reports before you finish describing your shoulder pain. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, Zain Hasan, Senior Developer Advocate at Weaviate, used an AI diagnostic assistant he calls a super-doctor to walk through a full RAG stack and four techniques that make its retrieval good enough to trust: query rewriting, hybrid search, autocut and re-ranking.

The medical framing is a teaching device, not a clinical product, and the stack is entirely open source. The techniques transfer to any chatbot over a large document collection.

## What the assistant has to do

Hasan sets five requirements. Access to more patient cases than any doctor sees. Search over them, because no model can reason over hundreds of thousands of cases at once, so it needs the top five or ten. Citations for every proposed diagnosis, since an unexplainable system will not be used in medicine. Reasoning over technical medical text. And all of it in real time, within seconds of the patient finishing.

Pasting symptoms into a chat model is the baseline. A model fine-tuned on medical data does better, and so does good prompting. RAG does better still and adds the citations: retrieve similar cases and articles, hand them to the model with the new patient, and let it propose diagnoses grounded in the sources it read.

## The open-source stack

- **Data**: the open PMC-Patients dataset, 167,000 patient summaries extracted from case reports in PubMed Central, plus 1.4 million PubMed article abstracts.
- **Vector database**: Weaviate, storing a vector per case and article and returning the most similar ones to a query such as "My left shoulder hurts and I have numbness in my thumb and index finger."
- **Embeddings**: MedCPT, with a query encoder for short patient descriptions and an article encoder for long abstracts and case histories.
- **LLM**: he used ChatGPT and GPT-4 in his experiments, and offers Meditron-70B as the open alternative. It is Llama 2 70B further trained on 48.1 billion tokens of medical text and then supervised fine-tuned, and it outperforms Llama 2 70B and GPT-3.5 on medical reasoning tasks.

## Four upgrades

**Query rewriting.** We are bad at writing queries and at writing prompts, so let a model do both. A language model rewrites the patient's sentence into something like "Pain left shoulder. Numbness thumb. Numbness index finger.", which reads worse to a human and retrieves better. DSPy, also open source, searches iteratively for the prompt that gets the best diagnoses out of the LLM.

**Hybrid search.** Medicine is full of exact terms (disease names, drugs, compounds) where semantic similarity is the wrong tool and a keyword match is enough. Run vector search and keyword search together and merge the results. In Weaviate it is one changed line.

**Autocut.** Results come back with similarity scores. If the top four are close together and the fifth and sixth sit after a big jump, drop the tail before it reaches the model. Fewer irrelevant cases mean less confusion and less hallucination. Also one line.

**Re-ranking.** Over-fetch, say 20 to 40 candidates, then let a heavier model compare each one with the patient description and reorder them. The new scores are more reliable because a more powerful model produced them, and only the top five or six go to the LLM. One more line in Weaviate.

## Fast enough for the consulting room

The vector search takes milliseconds and the generation maybe half a second to a second, so the whole loop runs while the patient is still in the room. The doctor forms a view, the assistant proposes diagnoses with citations, and the two together are better informed than either. "Everything that I've talked about in this entire talk is open source," Zain Hasan said at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, from the language model and vector database to the re-ranker and autocut.

## Who should watch

Engineers whose RAG prototype works on the demo questions and falls apart on real ones. The four techniques are in rough order of effort, and three of them are single-line changes if your vector database supports them. Domain-specific teams (legal, finance, science) will recognise the hybrid search argument.

Title: Just don't do it, says the title. Then he tells you to do it
Description: Jan Karremans (CYBERTEC) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on why Postgres belongs in Kubernetes once an operator plays the DBA
Body:
The title is a dare. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, [Jan Karremans](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Jan_Karremans_databases_kubernetes), Sales Leader at CYBERTEC and a self-described techie in sales, opened with "just don't do it" and spent the session arguing the opposite: running Postgres in Kubernetes is where data management is heading for the next decade, provided an operator such as CloudNativePG does the database administrator's job.

Set expectations accordingly. This is a short talk about mindset and history more than a hands-on guide: no YAML, no benchmarks, no failover demo. What it gives you is the case for why a database person should stop treating Kubernetes as the enemy.

## Why would a database person come round to Kubernetes?

His own route explains a lot of the framing. He spent decades in proprietary databases, Oracle in his case, migrated himself to Postgres, and got into Kubernetes about three years before the talk, working with the team that figured out how to put the elephant in a box.

His big-picture claim borrows a line from Marc Linster, PostgreSQL Fellow: Postgres is the most transformative technology since Linux. The first wave of open source replaced the easier layers, tools and then operating systems (VMS, Solaris and proprietary Unix all lost to Linux). The second wave is reaching the parts most deeply woven into an organisation: data processing, with community-governed projects like Postgres and Kubernetes. A quick tour from System R and the great debate of 1974 to Ingres, Postgres and today's multi-model Postgres, relational plus JSON documents, supports the point.

## What does cloud native actually change?

Most of the middle is about how applications are built now, and why the database cannot sit it out. The traditional model is a steam train: requirements, technical design, architecture, code, and a first testable build two years later, by which time the requirements have moved. The model he prefers is a flock of birds, where each microservice reacts to its neighbours and the whole shape shifts smoothly.

He picked four buzzwords that he thinks have now earned their keep: agile, microservices, DevOps and CI/CD. The DevOps point is the classic one: you do not fix a server, you change the Ansible playbook and rerun it, and in the container world you throw the container away and start a new one. On CI/CD he admitted a change of mind. He had assumed continuous delivery was the hard part, until he realised continuous integration is harder, because it means the application in the repository must be deployable at every moment. For a database person that drags in continuous testing and test data management.

Measurement comes from DORA: deployment frequency, how fast you restore a service, going from a release every year to one every couple of hours. And his warning about hype applies to the AI wave too: cloud took 10 to 15 years before people really understood how it changed day-to-day IT, so start from your own requirements, not the vendor's buzzword.

## What does the operator do?

The Postgres part arrives near the end. CloudNativePG, created by Gabriele Bartolini and team and now a CNCF project, runs Postgres the Kubernetes way. Jan Karremans said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "rather than bringing Kubernetes to postgres, what we did is take postgres and actually bring it to Kubernetes". The operator covers day one and day two operations, including high availability, switchover and load balancing, so the user deploys and uses it. In his words, "it captures a database administrator, puts it in a box, right?"

At the time of the talk the project had just passed 3,000 GitHub stars. His closing point is that both projects are community governed, so the people using them decide where they go next.

## Who should watch?

DBAs and data people who still think of Kubernetes as infrastructure that is built to break, and platform teams who need an argument for why stateful workloads are no longer off-limits. If you already run CloudNativePG in production, this one is the why, not the how.

Title: Test serverless code locally against the real cloud, then throw the stack away
Description: Yan Cui (Lumigo) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on remocal tests, plain zip deployments and ephemeral environments for faster serverless work
Body:
Mocks tell you whether your code does what you expected, not whether it works. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, [Yan Cui](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Yan_Cui_patterns_efficient_serverless), Developer Advocate at Lumigo and an AWS user since 2010, laid out three habits for an efficient serverless workflow: test Lambda code locally against real AWS services, keep deployments boringly simple, and give every feature its own short-lived environment.

He also consults, and most of the advice comes from watching client teams hurt themselves. It is framework-agnostic, though the demo uses the Serverless Framework.

## Why are mocks not enough?

Local tests against mocks are fast, debuggable and need no deployment. The catch, in his framing, is that they check your code against your assumptions, and you used the same assumptions to write both the code and the test. He has seen plenty of applications pass every test and fail the first time they run in AWS.

Mocks also skip everything that is not your code: IAM permissions, API Gateway authentication, AppSync resolver templates, EventBridge event patterns, direct service integrations. Yan Cui said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "Customers are not going to care if the problem is with your configuration and not your code."

Testing in the cloud covers all of that, but a full deployment after every small change makes the feedback loop painful.

## What is remocal testing?

His answer is remocal testing: run the code locally, so breakpoints and fast iteration still work, but point it at real AWS resources such as DynamoDB tables, SNS topics and queues. Around it sit unit tests for domain logic and end-to-end tests for what only exists after deployment, such as API Gateway request validation, transforms and Cognito or IAM auth.

The demo makes this concrete. The same test cases switch between modes with a test-mode environment variable. In remocal mode a helper requires the Lambda handler locally and calls it with a stubbed event and context; in end-to-end mode the test creates a Cognito user, gets an ID token and calls the deployed API Gateway endpoint. One schema test, checking that a POST body needs a string `name`, can only run end to end, because that validation lives in API Gateway.

There is a nice unplanned moment, too: he commented out the database write and the test stayed green. A breakpoint showed the bug was in the test, a neat accidental argument for stepping through tests.

## Why avoid Lambda layers?

His deployment advice is to use the simplest option that works. Lambda layers, container images, custom runtimes and provisioned concurrency all have their uses, but in his words, "for 90% of use cases you shouldn't use any of these options."

He saves his strongest words for layers as a way to share code, with a long list of reasons:

- No semantic versioning.
- Security scanners don't know about them, so they can't check them for known vulnerabilities.
- A limit of five layers per function, and they still count towards Lambda's 250 MB unzipped size limit.
- They make local and remocal testing harder, because the dependency only exists in AWS.
- They don't really work for compiled languages like Java or .NET, which need dependencies at compile time.
- Publishing an update is more work than with npm, and you lose bundling and tree shaking.

Instead: shared code within a project goes in a folder and gets bundled with each function, which SAM, the Serverless Framework and CDK all support; shared code across projects goes into a private npm registry. Stick to zip files and managed runtimes so the platform owns the runtime, and use container images only when you outgrow the 250 MB limit.

## How should environments be organised?

At minimum one AWS account per stage (dev, test, staging, production) to contain both throughput problems and breaches. Large organisations should go to one account per team per stage, and business-critical or high-throughput workloads get their own set.

Inside those accounts, ephemeral environments are what he calls easily the most impactful practice to come out of serverless. The loop is four steps: `npx sls deploy -s dev-my-feature`, iterate with remocal tests against it, open a PR so CI runs everything, then `npx sls remove -s dev-my-feature`. CI does the same with an environment per commit SHA. Nobody steps on anyone else's toes and shared stages stay free of test data. With usage-based pricing, idle environments cost nothing; serverful pieces such as RDS or OpenSearch should be shared across ephemeral environments rather than recreated.

Two rules stop the environments colliding: don't name resources explicitly unless you must, so CloudFormation adds a random suffix, and when you must, as with EventBridge buses, put the environment name in it.

## Who should watch?

Teams on AWS Lambda whose tests pass locally and fail in the cloud, or who share a single dev stage and keep tripping over each other. Veterans will know the ideas; the layers list is still handy for design reviews.

Title: An LLM cannot forget, but its RAG index can, in seconds
Description: Olivier Ruas (Pathway) at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024 on real-time vector indexes that make a RAG chatbot forget deleted documents
Body:
Delete a confidential PDF from the folder and the chatbot stops quoting it on the very next question, with no nightly reindex. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, Olivier Ruas, R&D Engineer at Pathway, argued that the answer to models that cannot unlearn is not more fine-tuning but a retrieval index that reacts to every insert and every deletion as it happens.

It is a short, focused talk: the problem, why fine-tuning does not solve it, and a live demo of a RAG pipeline built with Pathway, the company's Python data-processing framework.

## Two things LLMs are bad at

Ruas starts with the familiar gap: models only know what they were trained on, so they cannot answer about events after their cut-off or about your non-public documents. The second problem gets less attention. What a model learned stays learned. If the training data held something outdated (his example is Pluto's status, which keeps changing), deliberate misinformation, copyrighted text or personal data, the model has no way to drop it, and it treats the last version it saw as the truth.

## Why fine-tuning is the wrong tool for this

Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained model on your data. It is batch training, so you need all the data at once in a suitable schema, and preprocessing can be costly. More importantly, the result is still an LLM, so it still cannot forget. When a document changes, you start again from the base model. That makes fine-tuning unsuited to data that changes in real time.

Prompt engineering, putting the latest Pluto articles straight into the question, works but is tedious by hand. RAG automates it: embed the query, find the most similar documents in a vector index, and build the prompt from them. And the context can be forgotten: remove a document from the index and it no longer shows up in any answer.

## Reactivity is the requirement

The catch is how fast the index follows your data. If a document must be removed for legal reasons, a system that reflects the removal a month later invites lawsuits. Batch reindexing every hour or every 20 minutes leaves windows where answers are inconsistent with the source. "As we say, garbage in, garbage out, so you need to update your index as soon as possible," Olivier Ruas said at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024. His one-line version: reactivity is key. His prescription is an event-driven, real-time vector index that indexes documents when they arrive and drops them when they are deleted.

## The demo

The pipeline is pure Python on Pathway, which wraps a scalable engine underneath and handles the calls to the OpenAI API for both embeddings and chat completion. The model choice is not fixed; he notes Meta or Mistral models, or a self-hosted one, would work the same way. The code reads like a recipe: a connector watches a folder of PDFs (Pathway also has connectors for Kafka topics, Google Drive and SharePoint), you configure the embedder, the chat model and the splitter, initialise a vector store over the documents, expose a REST endpoint for queries, retrieve the most similar document per query (one in the demo, 10 to 30 in real use), build the prompt and return the completion.

The folder holds two documents, one of them Alphabet's financial report. Asked for Alphabet's 2022 revenue in millions of dollars, the bot answers with the figure he then checks against the report's revenue page. He deletes the file. Asked again, the bot says it has no information. Nothing was restarted.

## Who should watch

Teams running RAG over documents that change or must be removable on request: legal, compliance, HR and anyone handling personal data. It is also a tidy argument to bring to the meeting where someone proposes fine-tuning to fix stale answers. It is a vendor talk in the sense that the demo uses Pathway, but the reasoning applies to any index.

Title: A 101 tour of three clouds, and why serverless bills by the call
Description: Artem Lebedev (Microsoft) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on AWS, Azure and GCP basics, serverless pay-per-use, and lock-in, security and cost traps
Body:
Serverless boils down to one billing rule: you pay for function calls, not for servers sitting around waiting for them. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Artem Lebedev, Software Engineer at Microsoft with more than ten years in the trade, gave a compact overview of the three big cloud platforms, what serverless buys you, and the three problems that follow you there: data protection, vendor lock-in and cost.

This is a first talk, and it says so. If you already run Lambda in production, you know the material. If you are a developer, student or manager who wants the map before the territory, it is a tidy half hour.

## What do the three clouds actually offer?

Lebedev walks through Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform with a top five for each. For AWS: EC2, RDS, S3, Lambda and CloudFront, with AWS described as having customers in 190 countries, more than 200 services and over half of the global public cloud share. For Azure: Virtual Machines, Blob Storage, Azure Kubernetes Service, Azure Functions and Azure Active Directory, plus the OpenAI models Azure exposes to application developers. For GCP: Compute Engine, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Google Kubernetes Engine and its AI and machine learning suite.

The useful part of the comparison is how much the lists rhyme. Every vendor has rentable VMs, durable object storage, managed Kubernetes and a function runtime. The names change; the shapes don't. That symmetry matters later, when he gets to lock-in.

## What does serverless buy you?

His definition is the plain one: serverless is a way of getting on-demand backend services where you pay for code execution rather than for maintaining infrastructure. The three benefits he lists are scalability (automatically adapting to changing workloads, riding through traffic spikes), cost-effectiveness and performance tooling. The cost argument is the one that lands best on low-traffic workloads. As Artem Lebedev said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, "We just don't pay if we don't use".

## Who runs on this, at what scale?

Three case studies anchor the abstractions:

- **Amazon** uses its own cloud, including Lambda, EC2 and S3, to absorb traffic spikes on Prime Day and Black Friday.
- **Kaiser Permanente** uses Microsoft Azure to collect and analyse data from medical devices and to run telemedicine, for a patient base of 12.4 million.
- **Supercell**, the studio behind Clash of Clans, built its entire game infrastructure on AWS. Each player starting a game needs a server-side session, so server count has to grow with players. It runs EC2 across multiple availability zones and stores up to ten terabytes of game event data per day, scaling down during quiet periods.

Note that the Supercell example is classic elastic EC2 rather than functions. The talk uses it to show elasticity in general, which is fair, but don't expect a serverless architecture walkthrough here.

## What goes wrong once you move?

Three challenges, each with a short prescription:

- **Security and compliance.** When the provider manages the servers, protecting health records or financial data gets harder, and HIPAA and GDPR still apply. His fix: follow the provider's security guidelines, run regular security audits, and enforce strong identity and access management.
- **Vendor lock-in.** Vendor-specific logic makes switching from AWS to Azure or GCP expensive. His answer is cloud-agnostic building blocks, containerisation and microservices, so moving stays possible.
- **Cost management.** Pay-per-use is only cheap if you watch it. He points to AWS Cost Explorer and Azure Cost Management, plus resource cleanup, budget alerts and regular reviews of usage patterns to rightsize. A function that costs nothing at idle can still cost plenty when someone forgets it in a loop.

## Where is it heading?

The closing trends are edge computing (lightweight serverless functions running on edge devices, close to the IoT data), AI and machine learning integrated into cloud platforms (Azure's access to GPT-4 and DALL-E being his example), and hybrid and multi-cloud. On multi-cloud his summary is the honest pitch for it: "In other words, you use the best each cloud provider can offer you."

## Who should watch

Newcomers to cloud, people choosing between AWS, Azure and GCP for the first time, and anyone who needs a vocabulary refresher before a migration meeting. Experienced serverless engineers can skip it; there is no code, no architecture walkthrough and no benchmark.

- Lawrence Finn on [breaking out of a single cloud](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Lawrence_Finn_multicloud_breaking_cloud_sidecar), for the lock-in question in practice.
- Sam Williams on [building a serverless-first SaaS startup in 30 days](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Sam_Williams_serverless_first_saas_startup_in_30_days).

Title: A bank onboarding chatbot that is mostly not a chatbot
Description: Denis Skokov at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024 on shipping GenAI for bank business onboarding with scripted dialogue, OCR and LLM extraction
Body:
Opening a business bank account takes about seven days and costs the bank around £400 per customer, and most of that time is spent emailing for a contract that has not expired. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, Denis Skokov, chief product officer at a generative AI startup, explained how his team built an assistant that collects and checks onboarding documents for banks, and why the winning design keeps the LLM on a short leash.

It is a product and go-to-market talk with a clear architecture section: useful to anyone selling GenAI into a regulated, risk-averse customer.

## Where the seven days go

Skokov splits know-your-business (KYB) onboarding into six steps: verifying company data in registers, working out the ownership structure from documents, identity verification, sanctions and adverse-media checks, verifying business activity from contracts and invoices, and checking the source of funds from bank statements. Several of those already take minutes thanks to automation. The days hide in two places: back-and-forth clarification (managers go back to clients with questions about three times, and each round can take two days) and manual review of 20+ pages of documents, sometimes contracts of 50 or 100 pages. He puts the serviceable market for this kind of compliance software at $4.3 billion.

## Scripted dialogue, small LLM tasks

The product talks to the customer in a chat, collects documents, extracts their data, runs the checks and writes a compliance report listing discrepancies and the customer's explanations. The compliance officer reads the report and decides, in about ten minutes rather than seven days. The example report flags an invoice paying the client for a supply of pipes while its registered industry is consulting (the client's answer: they are pipe industry consultants) and an office rent that looks suspiciously low.

The interesting part is what the LLM is not allowed to do. An LLM left to run a structured conversation on its own is hard to control, so the dialogue is a hard-coded scenario. The LLM gets small, single tasks: answer this one question about invoice requirements from the knowledge base, or extract these fields from this text. OCR is a separate service, not the LLM, because the quality is higher. Register APIs supply data to compare against what was extracted. "It is mix of chat and hard coded logic," Denis Skokov said at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, and quick buttons skip the chat entirely where typing adds nothing.

## Integration in a week, not a quarter

Banks have old, complicated architectures, and a proper API integration takes months. For proofs of concept the team embeds its chat in an iframe on the bank's authorised website and emails the finished report and documents to the compliance manager. Rolling that out takes about a week. For the longer term they integrate with the CRM and case-management systems banks already use, such as Salesforce, so the assistant becomes one more step in a flow the bank trusts.

## Answering the four objections

Skokov's table of bank concerns is the most reusable slide in the talk:

- **OpenAI trains on our data.** Not on the corporate API, where data ownership stays with the bank; they bring the policy documents to prove it.
- **Chatbots are unreliable.** True, which is why the dialogue is rigid and answers come only from a checked internal knowledge base. One banker liked the checks but asked for a form instead of a chat.
- **Extraction quality will be low.** Banks remember when reading a new document type meant training on thousands of samples. Show test results and let them try their own documents.
- **Integration is hard.** Offer the instant PoC integration, and plug into the big CRMs for the strategic version.

## The team it takes

Three roles he calls mission-critical. Data scientists, whose job has shifted towards prompt engineering and extraction but who still own dataset quality, labelling and testing. A QA engineer with prompt engineering experience, a role he had not heard of before this project, who tests LLM responses at volume and writes the tools to automate it. And a backend developer combined with DevOps, because a bank will judge the infrastructure as hard as the model.

## Who should watch

Founders and product managers selling LLM features to banks or other regulated buyers, and engineers designing LLM workflows where the model must not improvise. The architecture applies equally to lending, credit and legal due diligence, which he names as the next document-heavy processes.

Title: A first Google Cloud Function, from use cases to hello world
Description: Neel Shah (Internauts Infotech) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 with a beginner's tour of serverless on Google Cloud Functions and its best practices
Body:
Neel Shah, Product Manager at Internauts Infotech, gave Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 a starter talk on serverless with Google Cloud Functions: what the model is, where event-driven functions earn their keep, the habits that keep them cheap and safe, and a console demo that ends in a working hello world. If you have deployed a function before, you can skip it; if you haven't, it is a gentle on-ramp.

His definition is the plain one. "Serverless computing in a layman language is execution model where your infrastructure will be scaled and maintained by the service provider," Neel Shah said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. You write the code; the provider handles scaling up when traffic arrives and down when it leaves.

## Why go serverless at all?

He lists the usual advantages: cost that follows consumption (low traffic, low bill), automatic scaling, and time spent on code instead of infrastructure. He places it at the end of a timeline that runs from physical machines through virtualisation, cloud computing and containers to microservices, with every big provider now offering a serverless service. The key concepts are event-driven execution, automatic scaling and pay-per-execution.

Cloud Functions is Google Cloud Platform's offering, and he stresses that it is language-agnostic: Node.js, Python, Java and .NET among others.

## Where do functions fit?

His use cases, each with a small scenario:

- **Webhooks and API glue.** A failed Jenkins deploy raises an alert that triggers a function to redeploy. A GitHub push fires a webhook into a function that posts to Slack: two third-party services joined by a function.
- **Real-time data processing.** Polls during a live cricket or football match, with results that change what the app shows next.
- **Image and video processing.** Resize every uploaded photo to around 2 MB before storage, and keep the storage bill down.
- **Microservices**, mobile backends, and **IoT** home automation, where a function connects sensors from different vendors.

## Which habits keep functions healthy?

His best practices are the right ones to learn early:

- **Design stateless functions.** Chains where one function waits on another break when the first one fails.
- **Keep dependencies lean.** Lightweight libraries mean faster starts and a smaller attack surface.
- **Set up monitoring and logging**, so you know when usage crosses the limits you planned for.
- **Plan for cold starts.** A function that idles for a month and then meets a big sale needs a warm-up strategy, or the first wave of users pays for it.
- **Measure execution time** and tune timeouts from real test runs rather than guesses.
- **Lock down security.** Least-privilege IAM roles, security scans on third-party libraries, and no passwords or keys in function code: use the provider's key management or HashiCorp Vault.

## What does the demo show?

A walk through the Google Cloud console: create a function, name it, pick a region (the console flags low-carbon regions), choose a trigger (HTTP, Cloud Storage, Firestore, Pub/Sub), set the autoscaling instance limits, pick Python, edit the code inline, deploy, test. A minute or two later the hello world greets him by name.

## Who should watch?

Students and developers who have never deployed a function and want the vocabulary plus a click-by-click first run. It stays at the introductory level throughout; there is no architecture, cost modelling or production story here.

Title: Dirty reads, phantom reads and half-dead clusters, a primer
Description: Santosh Nikhil Kumar (ByteDance) at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024 on isolation levels and replication against partial failures
Body:
A single machine either works or it does not; a distributed system can be mostly up and partly lying to you. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, Santosh Nikhil Kumar, Senior Software Engineer at ByteDance, gave a primer on the two non-functional problems that bite every large backend: how transaction isolation levels trade consistency against concurrency, and how replication keeps a system serving through partial failures.

One note on scope before you press play: despite the title, LLMs do not appear in the talk. It is a clear, beginner-friendly refresher on database isolation and replication, useful to anyone building the platforms that LLM services run on, but there is no model-specific material.

## The shop where everyone touches the same row

His example is an e-commerce platform. Two buyers view and purchase the same pair of gym gloves, a third buys a motorcycle helmet and an office chair, and the seller changes a price while all of this happens. Every action is a read or a write, run as a transaction, and the isolation level decides what locks are taken, how long read locks are held, and whether a reader blocks on a row being changed or sees the last committed version. In his definition, isolation is the degree to which a transaction must be isolated from data modifications made by other transactions.

## Three levels, three anomalies

He builds the levels up by the anomaly each one removes:

- **Read committed** stops dirty reads: transaction two cannot read the row transaction one changed until it commits, so it never sees data that is later rolled back. Locks are released as soon as the data is read, which keeps concurrency high and performance good. Non-repeatable and phantom reads remain.
- **Repeatable read** stops non-repeatable reads: if a transaction reads a row twice, nobody can change it in between, because the transaction holds locks on every row it references for its whole duration. Stronger consistency, at the price of contention, lower concurrency and more deadlock risk. Phantoms can still appear.
- **Snapshot isolation** stops phantom reads, where a range query (all players earning more than some amount) returns new rows the second time because another transaction inserted them. Committed versions are copied aside with version numbers, copy-on-write, and each transaction reads the snapshot as of its start. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers. The cost is storage for all those versions.

His slides rank snapshot isolation as the strongest of the three he covers; serializable isolation and the write-skew anomaly that snapshot isolation still allows are outside the talk, so treat it as a starting point rather than the full map.

## Partial failure is the distributed-systems tax

The second half covers partial failures: a subset of nodes fails while the rest carry on. On one computer, as he puts it, "It's zero or 100. There is nothing in between if it is a single computer." In a cluster you get node failures from hardware or software, and network partitions that split nodes into segments that cannot reach each other, with inconsistency, degraded performance or temporary unavailability as the symptoms.

His answer is replication, in six flavours:

- **Full replication**: every node has the whole dataset. High availability, expensive in storage and bandwidth.
- **Partial replication**: only the important or hot subsets are replicated, which demands careful partitioning.
- **Sharding**: horizontal partitions spread across nodes, so a node failure only affects its shard.
- **Replication chains**: each node replicates to its successor, which adds fault tolerance but also latency and complexity.
- **Primary-backup**: a primary serves requests and replicates asynchronously, so writes are not blocked, and a backup is promoted when the primary fails.
- **Quorum-based**: reads and writes coordinate across a quorum, giving strong consistency while tolerating some failed nodes.

## Who should watch

Developers moving from single-database apps to distributed backends, and anyone who wants the read-anomaly vocabulary straight before a design review. Experienced database engineers can skip it, and anyone looking for LLM-specific distributed-systems material will not find it here.

Title: Four ways to ship safely, four ways to fail gracefully
Description: Ricardo Castro (FanDuel / Blip) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on the deployment and runtime patterns that keep cloud native apps up
Body:
Microservices, external APIs and managed infrastructure buy you speed and scale, and they also give you many more places to break. Ricardo Castro, Principal Engineer and SRE at FanDuel / Blip, used his Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 talk to lay out the two toolkits for that fragility: four deployment patterns for changing a live system safely, and four runtime patterns for surviving its dependencies. His premise: resilience has to be a foundational principle, not a feature added later.

It is a compact, well-organised reference talk: each pattern gets a definition, an analogy and a diagram. Good for onboarding, or for settling an argument about what a dark launch actually is.

## How do you deploy without taking the app offline?

**Blue-green.** Two identical production environments. Blue serves users; green gets the new version and is tested. Flip the load balancer to green; if anything goes wrong, flip back. The rollback is instant, which makes this the safety net for big updates.

**Rolling updates.** Replace instances gradually, one at a time or a percentage at a time, watching errors as you go, and pause or reverse if something looks off. "This is like changing the tires of a moving car one at a time," Ricardo Castro said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. Kubernetes does this for you, which is why it fits containerised environments so well.

**Canary deployments.** Named after the birds miners took underground. Shift a small slice of users to v2, watch the key metrics, widen the slice step by step until 100% are on it, and switch back if the numbers turn.

**Dark launches.** Ship the code fully hidden, test it live, collect real performance data and feedback from selected groups, then turn on the switch for everyone. Gate it with feature flags per user, or with a special header only certain users send.

The four differ mainly in what gets exposed: blue-green swaps everything at once with an instant escape route, rolling and canary limit the blast radius by instances or by users, and dark launches separate deploying from releasing.

## What keeps a live system standing when its dependencies wobble?

**Timeouts and retries.** Without a timeout, service A waits as long as service B takes, five seconds in his example. If five seconds is unacceptable, set three and treat anything slower as a failure. Retries give the call a second, third or fourth chance, with growing intervals so you don't flatten a service that's already struggling. Together they stop one slow dependency from stalling everything upstream.

**Rate limiting.** A traffic cop, or the queue outside a popular club. It caps incoming requests so a spike can't overwhelm a service, keeps one noisy client from hogging resources, and blunts deliberate floods. Over the limit, the client gets a too-many-requests response instead of everyone else's capacity.

**Bulkheads.** From ship design: compartments, so one flooded section doesn't sink the vessel. Limit concurrent connections to a backend, give components fixed memory, or split a service into instances so an overwhelmed replica only hurts its own clients. The same idea scales up to whole features: one broken feature shouldn't stop the others.

**Circuit breakers.** Like the ones in your fuse box. When calls to a service keep failing, the breaker opens and rejects calls immediately, so pointless retries stop clogging the network and the failing service gets room to recover. After a set period it lets a few requests through; if they succeed, it closes again.

His last diagram makes the point worth remembering: these combine. A circuit breaker wraps calls that also carry timeouts and retries, and each layer decides whether a request is OK or not.

## Who should watch?

Developers moving into their first distributed system, and teams picking a rollout strategy who want the options side by side. Experienced SREs won't find new patterns here; they will find a clean explainer to send to the next person who asks why retries need backoff.

Title: Malicious packages phone home, so firewall the CI runner with eBPF
Description: Mert Coskuner (Yahoo) and Cenk Kalpakoglu (Kondukto) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on kntrl, an eBPF agent blocking rogue egress from CI runners
Body:
Most malicious packages that land in a pipeline need to talk to the network: to send stolen credentials out, or to pull the next stage in. Mert Coskuner, Principal Product Security Engineer at Yahoo, and Cenk Kalpakoglu, CEO and co-founder of Kondukto, turned that into a defence at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: kntrl, an open source eBPF agent that runs on the CI runner, watches every outbound TCP and UDP connection and blocks the ones your policy doesn't allow.

It is a short talk in three parts: why (the threat), how (eBPF), and a demo on a GitHub Actions runner.

## How bad is the package problem?

The slides cite Sonatype detecting 245,032 malicious packages in 2023 alone, twice as many software supply chain attacks as in 2019 to 2022 combined. Mert Coskuner groups the attack vectors into three: vulnerable or typosquatted packages, compromised or look-alike pipeline tools, and broken artifact integrity, where code or a container image is swapped to deploy a crypto miner or a backdoor.

His worked example is an npm package, execution-time-async, posing as the code profiler execution-time and reported by Phylum. It steals login credentials and passwords from browsers, then downloads a Python script to control the compromised machine remotely, and its author keeps changing the IP addresses to stay hidden. It was tied to a North Korean threat group. When the team analysed attacks like this one, including the Lazarus group's, the common pattern was the network layer.

## Why eBPF?

Cenk Kalpakoglu explains the choice. They wanted to monitor and prevent at runtime, and eBPF lets you "write kernel level applications without literally writing or compiling anything in the kernel," Cenk Kalpakoglu said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. Thanks to compile once, run everywhere, one binary works on any recent Linux kernel, which covers most CI runners.

The options they explored for future sensors include egress control, DNS queries, file reads and writes, the process tree and spawned processes with their arguments. They started with traffic control.

## How does kntrl work?

The playbook, from the slides:

- Probe TCP events with kprobes on `tcp_v4_connect` and `tcp_close`.
- Probe UDP with a kprobe on `ip4_datagram_connect`.
- Filter egress traffic with a `cgroup_skb/egress` program.
- Decide pass or block in a Go application in user space, which acts as the policy engine.

So the kernel side observes and enforces; the user-space side decides. Events from the pipeline flow up through dedicated channels, and a verdict flows back down to the filter.

## What did the demo show?

First locally: with kntrl running, HTTP calls to Google and Amazon were blocked while the allowed call that downloaded the artifact went through. Then in GitHub Actions, with a deliberately simple workflow: one step simulating a malicious exfiltration call, one uploading an artifact. The malicious step got network unreachable, the legitimate step worked, and a report at the end listed what happened. It ships as a single binary and as a Docker image, depending on your runner.

## What was next for the tool?

The newer version added UDP support and detection of GitHub's meta IP ranges, so traffic to GitHub itself can be allowed or blocked by configuration. In progress at the time: a rule engine based on Open Policy Agent, then a process monitor sensor to track which files a job touches and flag file system anomalies. They asked for contributors from the security and eBPF communities.

## Who should watch?

Platform and security engineers responsible for self-hosted or GitHub-hosted runners, and anyone who has wondered what a poisoned dependency could reach from inside a build. It is a project introduction, not a production case study: no performance numbers, no rollout story. The repository is kondukto-io/kntrl on GitHub.

Title: Business chatbots, where vector search alone falls short
Description: Marcin Szymaniuk (TantusData) at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024 on RAG, hallucination checks, LLM costs and privacy in business chatbots
Body:
Embed four holiday-rental descriptions and they land right next to each other in vector space, nowhere near the word banana and of no help telling a cheap Cornwall cottage from a pricey London flat. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, Marcin Szymaniuk, CEO of TantusData, drew on several client chatbot projects to list what goes wrong when you integrate an LLM chat into a business, from retrieval to hallucinations, cost and licences.

The talk is deliberately tool-agnostic (he warns that some libraries will have died by the time you watch it) and leans on lessons rather than a product pitch.

## Why naive vector search disappoints

His running example is a travel assistant on a vacation rental site: "I need an apartment with elevator in London." The textbook answer is to embed the listings, embed the query, and hope the listing that mentions an elevator wins. In practice, listings are long, similar in wording, and general-purpose embeddings are good at general language, not your domain. "But magic does not exist," Marcin Szymaniuk said at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024. You may need fine-tuned embeddings, and you will certainly need to split documents, because embedding models accept limited input and longer is not automatically better.

## The secret ingredients

His list of what actually moves quality:

- **Splitting with care**: chunk size (very big chunks lose information in a fixed-size vector) and context, so a PDF chunk keeps track of which chapter or section it came from, as part of the chunk or its metadata.
- **Self-query retrieval**: LangChain's self-query retriever turns a question into a structured query over attributes you define, such as price or offer name, when chunks are too similar to rank by vector distance alone.
- **Better sources than PDF**: sometimes the fix is a better parser; sometimes the same data exists somewhere structured.
- **Hybrid search and other sources**: Elasticsearch or an internal search API is a fine retriever, most vector databases also do BM25 keyword search, and backend databases, data lakes, warehouses and external APIs can all feed the chat.
- **Re-ranking**: query aggressively across all of them, then re-rank and keep the most promising candidates.
- **Preprocessing with an LLM**: if users ask about elevators but your metadata has no elevator field, batch the descriptions through an LLM, extract the attribute, and store it. Classification is something LLMs do well out of the box.

## Checking for hallucinations costs something

Relevant context still does not guarantee a correct answer. His demo uses NVIDIA's NeMo Guardrails with an older OpenAI model. When did the Roman Empire collapse passes. How many goals were scored in a given season of Poland's Ekstraklasa gets flagged: the tool asks the same question three times, gets three different answers, then asks the model whether the first answer agrees with the other two. It does not. The catch, as he puts it, is that there is no free lunch: extra API calls cost money and latency, and false positives happen.

His broader conclusion is that you are partly back to square one. "Tools like llms are impressive, but you still have to do your homework." Data quality and careful engineering remain the job. Tools like NeMo Guardrails, MemGPT and Weaviate help but are young and change fast; he shows LangChain's commit history as evidence. So test retrieval, which is deterministic and under your control; test LLM behaviour where you can, knowing that temperature zero does not make the output deterministic; and collect data from real users from day one.

## Privacy, licences and the price list

Every call sends your data to a provider. If that is not allowed, you need a private LLM, a private embedding model and a private vector database, which is manageable but adds a lot to maintain. Read the licence: open source does not always let you use the model's outputs to train another model.

On cost, his slide is a useful snapshot from the time: GPT-3.5 at $0.5 per million input tokens and $1.5 per million output, GPT-4 at $30 and $60, Claude 3 Opus at $15 and $75, and Gemini at $0.125 and $0.375 per million characters. Tokenizers differ, so the same text costs a different number of tokens per model. Self-hosting turns per-request cost into hardware plus maintenance divided by traffic, which at low traffic is painful. Open-source models were behind commercial ones, so start with RAG before fine-tuning, and when you do tune, know that P-Tuning, LoRA, IA3 and SFT differ in data needs and latency. Keep the business goal in view: most teams are not research labs.

## Who should watch

Engineers about to build their first customer-facing RAG chatbot, and the product owner who has to approve its budget. It is a checklist talk, and a good one.

Title: The disk that filled too slowly to trip an alert
Description: Israel Heringer (Meta) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on metrics, dashboards and alerts that are actionable, plus learning from failures
Body:
The best story in Israel Heringer's Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 talk is a database disk that filled up too slowly for the sudden-change alerts and too fast for anyone to notice before the weekend. Israel Heringer, Software Engineer at Meta, uses it to make his main point about monitoring: alert on dangerous trends, not just on outages, and make every dashboard and alert tell you what to do next.

It is a fundamentals talk in four parts: choosing metrics, building dashboards, setting alerts, and learning from failures. The test he sets for all of it is simple: can I sleep in peace, or go on holiday, and trust I'll be told if something goes wrong?

## Which metrics should you watch?

Two kinds, not detached from each other. Business metrics: KPIs, goals, user behaviour. Technical metrics: response time, error rate, machine constraints such as CPU, memory, I/O and network. His examples lean technical, but the same dashboards and alerts work for both.

## What makes a dashboard useful?

A dashboard is all you need to know at a glance, over a time window. He uses a New Relic APM screen as the example (not sponsored, he notes): error rate, throughput, transaction time, Apdex. Two habits stand out:

- **Pick the period to match the seasonality.** Thirty minutes is fine for a deploy; a weekly view shows whether today's daily swing is the normal one.
- **Start with two chart types.** Time series for trends and spikes: an error rate that sits at 0.1% and jumps to 1% after a rollout is a tenfold jump, and maybe the moment to stop the rollout. Stacked area charts for share of a total: if Android's slice of users suddenly shrinks, you probably shipped a critical Android bug.

There are bar charts, heat maps, histograms and waterfalls too, but a chart you can't interpret is useless. Draw guidelines for expected values and soft limits (if the error rate should sit between 0.1% and 0.2%, draw both lines), add filters by platform or service, and make it drillable: error rate up, which errors, show me the stack trace. And don't build a wall of widgets so dense that the important thing stops jumping out at you.

## What makes an alert worth waking up for?

We all deserve peace of mind, as he puts it. Alerts are automated notifications on predefined conditions, aimed at specific people or teams, and they demand immediate attention, which is why noise kills them. "If the alerts are too noisy" and fire every few minutes or every day, "you will probably end up ignoring them," Israel Heringer said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024.

So: alert only on critical metrics, with clear severity levels (a main page returning 404 is not the same as a slow endpoint), and add early-trend alerts. That is where the disk comes in. The database storage was growing at a pace that never tripped the sudden-movement alerts, yet fast enough to run out over a weekend; people only found out on the Friday. An alert warning that storage will be full in X days would have saved the headache.

Every alert should say what it means and what to do: which dashboard to open, and whether there's an escalation path. The flip side matters too: with a good setup, no open alerts should be a fair signal that everything is fine.

## How do you learn from the failures anyway?

Ask why, then ask again. His example leaves the cloud on purpose: a server in a data centre shuts down because it was unplugged. Plugging it back in fixes it for now, but why was it unplugged? Someone passing by, a panicked reaction, or a cleaner who unplugged it and forgot. Keep asking until you reach the root cause, then ask what could have caught it earlier and which dashboard or alert was missing. Every significant failure should end with a plan, for the system and for its monitoring.

## Who should watch?

Title: Self-hosting Llama 2 for a marketplace assistant, and the GPU bill
Description: Bongani Shongwe (Adevinta / eBay) at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024 on what self-hosting Falcon and Llama 2 costs next to a paid LLM API
Body:
Self-hosting an open LLM sounds like the way out of API bills and vendor lock-in, until you try to rent a GPU in Europe. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, Bongani Shongwe, Senior Data Engineer at Adevinta / eBay, reported his team's experiment replacing GPT-3.5-turbo with self-hosted Falcon and Llama 2 for a conversational search assistant, and why the honest conclusion was to start small and offload gradually.

It is an experience report with real numbers, which makes it more useful than most build-versus-buy slides.

## The product behind the experiment

Adevinta runs classified marketplaces such as Leboncoin in France, Kleinanzeigen in Germany, Marktplaats in the Netherlands and Kijiji in Canada: 25+ marketplaces, 2.5 billion monthly visits, around 5,700 employees. The team was building a conversational search assistant, headed for A/B testing on Leboncoin, that helps a user go from "ford focus or fiesta" to a narrowed search by asking about model year, fuel type and transmission. Behind it, two GPT-3.5-turbo calls: a conversation LLM that talks to the user, and an extraction LLM that summarises the preferences from the history and feeds them to the search API.

The paid API had downsides: slow onboarding while providers rationed access, a new line item in the budget, and extra latency from calling outside Adevinta's infrastructure. Self-hosting promised privacy and compliance, customisation, control over quality of service, and no lock-in.

## Hugging Face, TGI and a GPU hunt

They started with Falcon 7B to learn the deployment, found it lacked depth for the assistant, and moved on to the chat-tuned Falcon 40B and Llama 2 70B, both with the multilingual support a multi-country marketplace needs. Serving was Hugging Face's Text Generation Inference (TGI): a Docker image that downloads the weights and serves them, with tensor parallelism, continuous batching, token streaming, bitsandbytes quantisation, and OpenTelemetry and Prometheus for tracing.

The hard part was hardware. On Google Cloud they could not get GPUs in European or North American regions and found spot capacity only in East Asia and the Middle East. The A100 80GB was the card everyone wanted and almost nobody could get, so they settled on the A100 40GB. GKE looked attractive for autoscaling, but deployments took long or never came up, and the largest GPU node they could get was 12 GB. They fell back to VMs.

## What the experiments showed

A VM with one GPU gave short latency and quick deployment but capped the maximum tokens at the GPU's memory. Several GPUs gave more memory and longer outputs, but slower start-up and higher latency, which the team put down to I/O between the GPUs. Longer, more complex prompts are slower; shorter, vaguer ones invite hallucination.

Max output tokens mattered most. At 256 both models were adequate, though Llama 2 sometimes cut off mid-sentence. With more tokens, Falcon's responses grew and it "started to hallucinate, appearing to have a conversation with itself." Llama 2 gave fuller answers but latency rose sharply. Both coped with French when the system prompt asked for it; mixed English and French conversations stuck to French, and Falcon hallucinated more in French. And the prompts from the GPT-3.5 version did not transfer. "We found out there's no one to one switch between using different models," Bongani Shongwe said at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024.

## The bill

One A100 40GB VM (12 vCPU, 85 GB memory, 500 GB disk) came to US$2,791.02 a month. The A100 80GB setup the tests pointed towards was US$4,129.07 a month, for a single instance, before networking, people and maintenance. Scaling out multiplies that. Meanwhile OpenAI cut GPT-3.5-turbo prices, and fine-tuning the hosted model sped up its responses, which removed two of the original reasons to leave.

His recommendation: a lightweight model such as Falcon 7B is fine for internal use. Keep the enterprise API, move functionality to your own model piece by piece, and stop when you reach the balance that suits you.

## Who should watch

Teams writing a build-versus-buy memo for LLM serving, and anyone who assumes open weights mean cheap inference. The GPU availability story is the part most people learn the hard way.

- Michael Yuan on [self-hosted LLMs across devices and GPUs](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Michael_Yuan_Selfhost_LLMs_on_Macacross_devices_Fast_and_Efficient) at the same event.
