Title: The OpenTelemetry Collector stores nothing, so export it or lose it
Description: Siddhant Khisty (SigLens) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 with a first tour of OpenTelemetry, from the three pillars to the collector pipeline
Body:
The OpenTelemetry Collector keeps none of your data. It receives, enriches and forwards, and if no exporter points at a backend, the telemetry is simply gone. Siddhant Khisty, Developer Advocate at SigLens, built his Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 talk around that pipeline: a first tour of observability's three pillars, why OpenTelemetry became the standard, and what a collector config actually does.

This is a beginner's talk and says so by its pace. If you have never written a collector YAML, it is a tidy twenty minutes.

## Why bother, if the server is fine?

He opens with the familiar 3am story: a server in your own data centre goes down, from a power failure or too much load, and the failure cascades into the applications and databases on top. Data goes missing, customers leave, the ops team gets a flood of calls and has no idea what is wrong, because nobody gave them any visibility into the box.

His analogy is the car you maintain yourself. Without the right tools you won't know a tyre is low until it's flat. Observability is the tyre gauge for servers, and it also helps you predict, not just debug: an e-commerce site that knows its daily spikes can provision ahead of them.

## What are the three pillars, briefly?

- **Logs**: timestamped records of events, such as a warning at 2:15am that nobody was awake to read, which is why they get shipped to a backend.
- **Metrics**: CPU and memory over time, HTTP requests accepted and dropped.
- **Traces**: function A calls B in 50 milliseconds, B calls C, and so on. Each hop is a span; the whole journey is the trace.

## Why did OpenTelemetry win?

Before it, there were around 14 or 15 competing observability standards, in his count. "If you come from the web development world, you know how much of a pain this can be, having multiple standards for the exact same thing," Siddhant Khisty said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. OpenTelemetry set out to unify them, absorbed most of them, and is now the de facto standard.

Developers instrument code with the OTel APIs and SDKs, or try auto-instrumentation, which he has seen working with Node.js and which covers a handful of languages. Ops people point it at infrastructure: system logs, memory and syscalls on a VM, or Kubernetes through the OpenTelemetry Operator, installable with a Helm chart.

## What does the collector actually do?

His example source is Argo CD, which already has built-in telemetry; you only tell it where the collector lives. Then the pipeline:

1. **Receiver** accepts whatever is sent, over gRPC or HTTP. In his sample config the HTTP receiver listens on localhost port 4318.
2. **Processor** adds context or reshapes data. A failed-deployment warning from Argo can be enriched with CPU and memory readings or a background batch job's details. His sample uses the batch processor.
3. **Exporter** sends the result, in OTLP format, to an observability backend. Almost every backend speaks OTLP now; he names Grafana, Loki and SigLens.

The `service.pipelines` section ties it together per signal: for traces, which receivers feed it, which processors run and in what order, which exporter ships it. Order matters; list the CPU enrichment before the batch step and that is the sequence the data takes.

To install, ops folks get two routes: Docker Compose on a plain VM, or Helm on Kubernetes. The Operator and its finer points are out of scope here.

## Who should watch?

Engineers new to observability who keep hearing OTel and want the moving parts named in order. People already running collectors in production will find nothing new. The closing pitch for SigLens as a backend is brief and clearly labelled.

- Siddhartha Khare on [tracing CI/CD pipelines with OpenTelemetry](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Siddhartha_Khare_tracing_triumph_o11y), also at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024.

Title: Put the fire out before you rebuild the stairs
Description: Richard Finlay Tweed at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on incident habits from hundreds of incidents, starting with mitigate, don't fix
Body:
When something breaks, an engineer's first instinct is to open the source code and find the bug. Richard Finlay Tweed, Senior Site Reliability Engineer, spent his Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 talk arguing that this instinct is wrong, at least at the start of an incident: stop the damage, restore service, and save the fix for later. The talk is short, built on lessons from hundreds of software incidents, and every point is mapped onto a house fire.

He says up front what it is not: a guide to incident management process. It is about how people behave during incidents, and where that behaviour goes wrong.

## What counts as an incident?

His own definition: "An incident is a coordinated response to mitigate an issue." The key word is coordinated. In the burning house, declaring the incident means putting the fire out and getting everyone out safely, not choosing new wallpaper.

## Why shouldn't you fix the bug?

Because it takes too long and can make things worse. "Sorry to break it to you, but this is a complete waste of your time in these situations, especially at the start of an incident," Richard Finlay Tweed said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. However fast your CI and however solid your tests, building a fix and testing it to your team's standard won't beat a rollback, a feature flag or traffic shifted away. An incident is no excuse to skip safe coding practices either. And if you need another team, page them.

The analogy: you don't install a replacement wooden stairwell while the house is still on fire.

Panic belongs in the same section. Take a moment to see what is actually happening before acting, the way you'd check how far a fire has spread and what kind of extinguisher is nearby before putting water on an oil fire.

## Who is in charge?

Without clear ownership, incidents fail in one of two ways. Either the bystander effect sets in (surely someone else is on it), or everyone tries to be the hero and gets in each other's way. The fix is roles:

- An **incident manager** coordinates, keeps track of who is doing what, and does not touch the fix.
- An **operations lead** is hands-on-keyboard for the mitigation.

Ask for specific things with a specific time for updates. Hand over explicitly: "will you take over as incident manager?", then confirm it out loud. In the house fire, whoever finds the fire is incident manager until the firefighters arrive, and then briefs them: how many people are inside, how far it has spread.

Against decision paralysis he has a neat trick: don't ask "what should we do?" State what you're going to do and ask whether anyone disagrees. Engineers love correcting someone who's wrong; his slide credits the idea to Ward Cunningham. And write everything down: who thought what, what was done and why. Latecomers get up to speed faster, and the write-up becomes much easier.

## What should you learn afterwards?

More than the bug. Incidents show how your systems, your processes and your people really behave, which is often not how they behave nine to five. His examples: the silence and escalate buttons sit too close together for a 4am brain, and now a director is awake. Or the runbooks only use the service's old name, and half an hour goes to working out what it is. Expect most of your preparation to be forgotten in the heat of the moment; what matters is getting back on track.

## Should you declare an incident?

If you're wondering, yes. Wondering at all means it deserves investigation. If it turns out unnecessary, ask the five whys about that too; dashboards that are always red because of a bad threshold are a bug in their own right. A smoke alarm that goes off for burnt toast beats one that stays quiet during a real electrical fire.

He points to the Google SRE book's incident management guide and the US National Incident Management System for the process side.

## Who should watch?

New on-call engineers before their first big incident, and teams whose incidents keep turning into group debugging sessions. It is brief and non-technical, and that's the point.

Title: Six AWS vector stores and one API call for RAG
Description: Samuel Baruffi (AWS) at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024 on choosing an AWS vector store and letting Bedrock knowledge bases run the RAG loop
Body:
Ask Claude Instant how many features AWS launched in 2022 and it says it does not know. Point the same question at four Amazon shareholder letters through a Bedrock knowledge base and it answers over 3,300, with a citation. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, Samuel Baruffi, Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, used that demo to close a tour of the vector databases AWS offers and the managed service that wires them into retrieval-augmented generation.

This is an AWS talk about AWS services, and it says so. Its value is the side-by-side of six vector options, which is hard to find in one place, and a demo that shows what a managed RAG pipeline actually stores.

## What RAG is fixing

Baruffi lists four limitations of LLMs: limited contextual understanding, no domain-specific knowledge (your private documentation was never in the training set), weak explainability, and confident inaccuracy, which is the polite name for hallucination. Embeddings are the bridge. An embedding model turns a chunk of text into an array of floats that carries its meaning; you chunk documents (embedding models have input limits), store dense or sparse vectors, retrieve the nearest ones with k-NN or approximate search at query time, and hand the text back to the model as context.

## Pick the vector store you already run

His guidance is to pick the database your team already knows, not a new one:

- **Aurora PostgreSQL and RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector**: for existing Postgres users or anyone who prefers relational. No driver changes, ACID and point-in-time recovery stay, HNSW and IVFFlat indexes, L2, inner product and cosine distance. Over a billion vectors and up to 16,000 dimensions (2,000 indexed).
- **Amazon OpenSearch Service and OpenSearch Serverless**: for NoSQL and hybrid search, keyword and vector in one query. The k-NN plugin, configurable recall, over a billion vectors, a Neural Search plugin that calls the embedding model for you, and zero-ETL from DynamoDB.
- **Amazon DocumentDB**: for teams on DocumentDB or the MongoDB API with JSON-heavy data.
- **Amazon MemoryDB for Redis**: vector search in preview at recording time, up to 32,000 dimensions, for chatbots that need single-digit millisecond latency.
- **Amazon Neptune Analytics**: vectors inside graph traversals and graph neural network use cases, up to 65,000 dimensions.

## Bedrock does the plumbing

Amazon Bedrock is the managed, pay-per-token way to call foundation models; as of 30 March 2024 he counted seven providers: AI21 Labs, Amazon, Anthropic, Cohere, Meta, Mistral and Stability AI, covering text, embeddings and image generation. Bedrock does not use your data to train those models. Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock is the part he wants you to remember. "It can be very cumbersome to build this completely rag solution," Samuel Baruffi said at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, so the service does ingestion and retrieval for you. You drop files in S3, choose an embedding model and a vector store (at the time: OpenSearch Serverless, Aurora, Pinecone and Redis Enterprise Cloud, with MongoDB coming), sync, and query. A single RetrieveAndGenerate API call does the retrieval, adds the chunks to the prompt, calls the model you selected and returns the answer with citations. A retrieve-only mode gives you just the chunks.

## The demo, and what is inside the index

The demo is worth watching for one detail. After the plain model fails the question, Baruffi opens the OpenSearch Serverless dashboard and shows what Bedrock wrote: one document per chunk, with an id, a sequence number for where the chunk sat in the source file, the Titan embedding vector, and the raw text in a separate field ready for hybrid search. Then the knowledge base answers the same question correctly, cites the exact chunk, and he repeats it through the API with a knowledge base id, model id and session id. No magic, just a well-organised index.

## Who should watch

Teams on AWS choosing between pgvector, OpenSearch and the rest, and anyone who wants to see a managed RAG pipeline end to end before deciding whether to build their own. Engineers off AWS can still take the comparison criteria (existing skills, hybrid search, latency, graph needs) to any vendor.

- Akanksha Sheoran on [why data decides GenAI success](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Akanksha_Sheoran_growth_Innovation_data), the data-strategy view from AWS at the same event.
- Suraj Muraleedharan on [operational excellence for LLMs on Amazon Bedrock](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Suraj_Muraleedharan_amazon_bedrock_operational), also at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024.

Title: Are you working for the machines, or are they working for you?
Description: Indika Wimalasuriya (Virtusa) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on a four-level AWS observability maturity model, from reactive to autonomous
Body:
If a page at 3am means you open the laptop and start digging, you are working for the machine. Indika Wimalasuriya, Senior Systems Engineering Manager at Virtusa, opened his Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 talk with that question and answered it with a four-level observability maturity model for AWS: reactive, proactive, predictive, autonomous. His most useful line is the one that limits it: not every system needs to reach the top.

## Why a maturity model at all?

Cloud native removed a lot of overhead and added its own complexity: microservices with long upstream and downstream chains, autoscaling that makes everything dynamic, CI/CD that raised production velocity. Traditional monitoring falls apart here, in his view, and observability without a direction drifts.

A model gives you a north star: where you are, where you're heading, and how you compare with the rest of the industry. He is explicit that his version is a template to customise, not a standard. And every step should be measured against business outcomes, or "your business partners will not see the expected benefits," as Indika Wimalasuriya said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024.

## What are the four levels?

- **Reactive** (keeping the lights on): some logs, limited metrics, no traces. You find out the app is down from process and infrastructure alerts, or from customers.
- **Proactive**: logs, metrics and traces are all there. Exceptions in logs raise alerts, thresholds fire, and you often know about an incident before customers report it.
- **Predictive**: anomaly detection and forecasting on the same telemetry, so you spot symptoms that drift outside business-as-usual and fix them before they reach users.
- **Autonomous**: the system reads its own telemetry, judges its internal state and runs self-healing remediation without a human in the loop.

He then crosses the levels with the pillars: logs, metrics, traces, alarms, dashboards, canaries (synthetic tests of key journeys), real user monitoring, infrastructure, network and security, and cost. Traces barely exist at the reactive level and become topology-aware, context-propagating distributed traces at the predictive one. RUM starts at proactive. AI and ML appear from predictive upwards.

## Does every system need to be autonomous?

No. It depends on complexity and how mission-critical the system is. "For most of the systems between proactive and predictive will do the job," he said, balancing operations against cost. Mission-critical systems, where any bad customer experience costs money, are the ones that justify predictive and autonomous. Cost goes up as you climb, he notes, but the higher levels take out human effort, so the bill can come down by the end of the journey.

## What does it look like on AWS?

His reference setup is an app with a front end, microservices and a database, wired up in this order:

1. **Real user monitoring first** (CloudWatch RUM, a snippet in the front-end code), because front-end performance is what users see.
2. **APM with distributed tracing**, via OpenTelemetry, to get a service map and follow a request from the browser through API Gateway to the SQL. This is where he spends the most time: without trace context, a DBA who spots a slow query can't tell which journey or which user triggered it.
3. **Logs into CloudWatch** through the CloudWatch agent, with log anomaly detection on, so a new error class alerts the day it appears, not when someone asks how long it has been going on.
4. **Metrics with CloudWatch anomaly detection**, which learns upper and lower bands instead of fixed thresholds.
5. **Amazon CodeGuru** for application profiling and **Amazon DevOps Guru** for account-wide ML anomaly detection.
6. SLIs, SLOs and error budgets, plus infrastructure monitoring.

KPIs to track the climb: mean time to detect, mean time to resolve, mean time between failures, and SLO achievement.

## Which pitfalls does he call out?

Mind log retention, or the logs are gone when you need them a week later. Keep granular metrics and traces; high-level views hide the ground-level detail. Don't forget systems that don't feel critical but are. Centralise telemetry instead of building tool or data silos. And enable detailed monitoring and anomaly features knowingly, because on AWS they cost money.

His outlook: near term, OpenTelemetry adoption for full-stack tracing; mid term, built-in AI/ML in observability tools; long term, the machines working for you. He closed with a bet that AWS, on the strength of CloudWatch Application Signals and log anomaly detection from re:Invent, would move into the leaders' quadrant of Gartner's observability rankings.

## Who should watch?

Engineering managers and SREs who need a vocabulary for where their observability stands and a sequence for improving it on AWS. It is a framework talk with service names, not a hands-on demo.

Title: A growth marketer's tour of LLMs, from conversion rates to PartyRock
Description: Venkata Sai Chaitanya Gatreddi at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024 on using LLM tools to measure, segment and personalise marketing
Body:
Most LLM talks are about building the model; this one is about the person who has to hit a revenue number with it. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, London-based growth and go-to-market advisor Venkata Sai Chaitanya Gatreddi walked through how he uses LLM-powered tools to answer marketing questions faster: conversion rates, ROI, customer segments, and the spreadsheets nobody wants to write formulas for.

Set expectations accordingly. It is a practitioner's overview with short demos in BigML and Amazon PartyRock, not an engineering talk, and it is most useful to marketers and growth people who have not yet wired an LLM into their weekly reporting.

## The stack, seen from marketing

He starts with the four layers of generative AI: applications, fine-tuning, foundation models and infrastructure. Applications are where most marketers meet LLMs, through APIs and features embedded in tools they already use. Fine-tuning is for when the output is not what you expected and you need it more relevant; he expects demand for people who can do it. The foundation model market, he argues, will mature and diversify quickly, and infrastructure will need serious retrofitting. He also flags the cost side: the compute needed to train the largest models has been doubling every 3.4 to 10 months, which makes cost and carbon emissions part of any adoption decision.

## Asking the analytics tool instead of clicking through it

The shift he describes is from filtering dashboards to asking questions. Before, you opened Google Analytics, picked a date range and read off a conversion rate. With LLM features in product analytics tools, you ask what the conversion rate of a campaign was between two dates. He organises the marketing side around three measures:

- **Conversion rate**: use data to see what works and what does not.
- **ROI**: framed as payback period. If you spend 100 dollars, how long do campaigns have to run before you get it back, and when does profitability start?
- **Customer segmentation**: separate messaging for prospects in the US, India and the UK, down to personalised images and GIFs.

## Three use cases worth stealing

His use cases are refreshingly mundane. First, searching data and crunching numbers. "I hate Excel," he admits, and AI spreadsheet helpers now write the formulas and calculations for him. Second, sales intelligence: call-analysis tools such as Gong turn a sales call into sentiment, word clouds and comparisons with teammates' calls, showing where a pitch goes well and where it falls apart. Third, analytics that move from what customers do to why, connecting a change shipped last week to a conversion bump today.

## The demos

In BigML he loads ad campaign data (ad name, campaign, placement, CPA, video views, CPM, CPC) and shows models, topic models that group campaign keywords with their probabilities, and a quick view of which ads drove repeat followers. It is a whirlwind rather than a tutorial, and he cuts it short for time. The agenda's other demo is an SEO assistant he built in Amazon PartyRock, AWS's no-code playground for LLM apps, which is a reasonable first project for a marketing team that wants to try building rather than buying.

## Where it gets hard

Two challenges close the talk. Adoption: getting stakeholders to buy in, training staff, and integrating LLM systems, plus the recurring questions of whether it is safe, whether data leaks, and what the model is trained on. And privacy. "Navigating the privacy regulations in the customer trust is key," Venkata Sai Chaitanya Gatreddi said at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, and his answer is education: show people how privacy is maintained before asking them to trust the tool.

## Who should watch

Marketing and growth leads looking for a starting list of LLM-assisted workflows, and engineers who support a marketing team and want to know what that team is likely to ask for next. If you want architecture, prompts or evaluation, look elsewhere.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Udipta Basumatari on [ML and GenAI for vibe marketing](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Udipta_Basumatari_vibe_marketing_genai) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.

Title: Your Jenkins pipeline is a distributed system, so trace it
Description: Siddhartha Khare (New Relic) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on tracing Jenkins builds with the OpenTelemetry plugin, stage by stage
Body:
A failed build usually means scrolling through console output until something red appears. Siddhartha Khare, Technical Account Manager at New Relic, showed a shorter route at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: install the Jenkins OpenTelemetry plugin, point it at an OTLP endpoint, and every pipeline run becomes a trace, with each stage as a span you can time, compare and click into.

It is a short talk: a quick recap of OpenTelemetry and CI/CD, the case for watching the pipeline itself, and a demo on New Relic as the backend. Any OTLP-compatible backend would take the same data.

## Why watch the pipeline and not just the app?

His argument is that the CI/CD pipeline is mission-critical infrastructure, and nobody runs mission-critical infrastructure blind. With observability on the pipeline you catch problems before they escalate, spot anomalies, performance regressions and misconfigurations, and get the data to make decisions about resource allocation or tool consolidation.

The benefits he lists are the classic ones applied to the build system: fault isolation (limit the blast radius of a failure), faster MTTR on broken builds, faster release rates, and more transparency and accountability across teams that would otherwise work in silos.

## How much setup does it take?

Very little, which is the point of the demo. His Jenkins job is a typical one: clean the workspace, check out the code, build a Docker image, push it to Docker Hub, delete local images, update a Kubernetes deployment file and deploy. To instrument it:

1. In Manage Jenkins, install the OpenTelemetry plugin.
2. In the system configuration, set the OpenTelemetry endpoint to your backend. His was New Relic's OTLP endpoint on port 4317.
3. Authenticate with a header carrying the ingest license key, then save.

Jenkins then shows up as a service in New Relic's APM view with response time, throughput and error rate, plus a service map of what it talks to. Each job appears as a transaction; in his demo one section took 93% of the time, which is the kind of thing you want to know before buying faster runners.

## What does a build look like as a trace?

Open a trace and the stages unfold as spans: the agent initialising, the checkout at 1.65 seconds, the Docker build at 3 seconds, the push. The anomaly detection flagged one span as 3.79 seconds slower than its average, without anyone writing an alert rule.

Then he filtered for errors. The red trace pointed at the first failure, a clone from the wrong repository, and the exception opened with its full stack trace. "These are the information which you will start getting once you instrument it right," Siddhartha Khare said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. Logs come along too, including which build changed and its Jenkins URL.

For the days you don't want to open traces, there are out-of-the-box dashboards: number of builds and failures, executed jobs, average job duration, the longest and most-failing steps, the most common errors and queue time.

## Who should watch?

Teams running Jenkins who already have an OpenTelemetry backend and have never pointed their build server at it. It is a vendor demo and an introduction, not an advanced session: no custom spans, no sampling discussion, no cost talk. As a ten-minute proof that pipeline tracing is a plugin and a header away, it does the job.

Title: How a 512-neuron layer hides over 100,000 features
Description: Boluwatife Ben-Adeola at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024 on superposition, the reason LLMs represent more features than they have neurons
Body:
If every feature a language model knows needed its own neuron, GPT-2 small would run out of room long before it ran out of English. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, independent AI researcher Boluwatife Ben-Adeola explained superposition, the hypothesis that networks pack far more features than they have dimensions by betting that most features are rarely active at the same time, and how sparse autoencoders pull those features back out.

It is a conceptual walkthrough of mechanistic interpretability, built on Anthropic's published work, with no code and a lot of careful definitions. A good first talk on the topic if calling the model a black box has started to feel like an excuse.

## Three claims about what is inside

Mechanistic interpretability, as he frames it, pushes back on the idea that neural networks are inscrutable magic with linear algebra. It looks at representations: what a model has learned to look for in its inputs, and how that information is carried through the layers. The school of thought he presents makes three claims. Representations are decomposable into discrete features, those features combine linearly, and the *feature* is the unit worth studying.

Decomposability is the weak claim; any network that generalises to a purple triangle it never saw is composing things it learned. Linearity is the strong one. "Linearity is a very particular statement about how different entities interact," Boluwatife Ben-Adeola said at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024. Being a vector of numbers does not make a representation linear. His counterexample packs a red value and a blue value into one number by abusing decimal places and a floor operation: perfectly valid, perfectly nonlinear, and miserable to reverse-engineer. The evidence for linearity starts with the well-known 2013 result on word vectors, where the offset between uncle and aunt matches the one between man and woman, and extends to work showing that even abstract functions, such as noticing that the prompt is a game of words and opposites, show up as directions.

Why care? Linear composition narrows an enormous space of possible encodings down to one we understand very well. That helps diagnostics, and he does not shy away from where it leads: from reading a model's state to steering it.

## The puzzle: too few neurons

Lossless linear encoding wants one orthogonal direction per feature. Redness, blueness, squareness and triangle-ness need four. But GPT-2 small has on the order of 100,000 neurons and almost certainly encodes more than 100,000 features, because it is modelling language. Something has to give.

## Superposition trades noise for capacity

The superposition hypothesis says networks give up perfectly orthogonal directions and squeeze in more features than dimensions, accepting a little interference. It works because of sparsity: of all the features worth knowing, only a few show up in any one input. In the toy models he walks through, a network with no sparsity sticks to representing two features in two dimensions, while at 80% and 90% sparsity it starts packing in more. When a single feature is active, the small leakage onto other directions gets switched off by the nonlinearities. When two features fire together, the interference can add up to look like a third feature that is not there at all. Relative importance matters too: given one spare direction, a model would rather know which language the text is in than whether it is in the past tense.

## Getting the features back out

The 2023 paper he covers takes a one-layer transformer and trains a sparse overcomplete autoencoder on its 512-dimensional MLP layer. Overcomplete means the hidden layer is much wider than the input, so the model's compressed features have room to spread out. Sparse means each feature is pushed to light up a single unit, which is purely for our benefit as readers. The largest runs went up to about 131,000 features. "They were able to extract way over 100,000 reasonable features," he said, from a layer that would have 512 if nothing strange were going on. Examples include a feature that fires on Arabic script and one that fires on DNA sequences. Along the way he offers a working definition: a feature is a property a model would give its own neuron if it had enough neurons.

The next step, as he sees it, is scaling these autoencoders to much larger models.

## Who should watch

ML engineers who use LLMs every day and want a mental model of what the activations mean, and anyone about to read Anthropic's interpretability papers who wants the vocabulary first. Skip it if you want benchmarks or tooling; this is the theory.

Title: Keep the EC2s, fix everything around them
Description: Dmytro Hlotenko (APA-IT Informations Technologie) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on modernising a working AWS app without rearchitecting it
Body:
You inherit an AWS workload that works. The tempting move is a rewrite onto containers-as-a-service; Dmytro Hlotenko, Cloud Engineer at APA-IT Informations Technologie in Vienna, priced that option for his app at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 and found Fargate would cost 473% of the plain EC2 baseline. So he kept the EC2s and rebuilt everything around them: spot fleets, a baked-image pipeline, GP3 drives and Aurora Serverless v2, with no developer time spent on the database move.

The app is MediaContact-Plus, the press-release distribution service of the Austrian press agency's tech arm: 50,000 journalist and blogger contacts, over 750,000 sends a month through Amazon SES, a 97% delivery rate. It was the company's first cloud deployment, running since 2021, and he took it over rather than built it.

## What did the inherited setup look like?

A vanilla deployment, in his words. Docker containers on on-demand EC2, a single RDS instance, no automation, health checks that only hit the load balancer, no secrets management, no WAF, and redeploys by ClickOps. His slide caption for the single RDS: a single point of failure. A new node took about 500 seconds to boot and join service.

His rule for changing it was social before technical: don't scare the developers. The baseline they knew (Docker on hosts) stayed; the improvements happened on the cloud side, transparently. Before touching anything he talked to the solutions architect who built it, read CloudWatch metrics and Insights, load-tested with Apache JMeter, Selenium and Robot Framework, and broke things on purpose with AWS Fault Injection Service to find the monitoring blind spots.

## Why not ECS, EKS or Fargate?

He likes ECS on Fargate and recommends it as a first choice for new apps. The numbers for this one, relative to bare on-demand EC2 in an auto scaling group at 100%: a Savings Plan brings it to 62%, a spot fleet to 51%, EKS with EC2 workers to 140%, and Fargate with the same vCPU and memory to 473%. "If I would take the fargate for our application my product owner would kill me," Dmytro Hlotenko said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024.

There were non-price reasons too: the team wanted control of the host for data processing rules, wanted to stay portable back to their own data centres, and the workload was memory, I/O and network heavy while the CPU idled. Graviton got a fair hearing and a pass for now: dependencies, AVX instructions, monitoring agents and a Jenkins pipeline that would all need reworking mid-project.

## How do you make spot instances boring?

One on-demand instance (covered by a Savings Plan) always serves traffic; the extra business-hours capacity comes from spot instances in separate auto scaling groups behind the same load balancer. The application knows where it runs: database migrations and long batch jobs go to the on-demand node, short interruptible work goes to spot. The two-minute interruption notice is enough to finish or checkpoint. Scheduled scaling adds nodes before the morning peak, and a warm pool keeps pre-baked instances ready.

The boot time fix was EC2 Image Builder in a pipeline of EventBridge, Step Functions, Lambda, SNS and SQS. A new release, a critical Amazon Inspector finding (that one skips the change process) or a fresh Red Hat image triggers a rebuild with updated dependencies, automated tests, then a change request; on approval a Lambda swaps the launch template, respecting business hours. Docker images are cached on the AMI and hot shared data sits on EFS. ClickOps became CDK.

## Which database settings bite first?

The RDS console wizard can hand you a GP2 volume, and a small GP2 drive running out of burst credits shows up as huge I/O waits and an app that is simply down. GP3 gives consistent performance on small drives and costs less. Check encryption while you're there, and watch swap: on GP2, swapping burns the same credits the database needs.

RDS Proxy cut multi-AZ failover by 79% in his test (five minutes to one) but does nothing for read-write performance. Read replicas meant asking developers to re-engineer, and they had no budget. Aurora Serverless v2 gave the same performance for about 35% less, because it stops paying for an idle database overnight. A provisioned instance, he said, is "basically like to have the heating switched on when nobody is living for the months in the apartment." The migration was a snapshot plus an endpoint change, made painless by a Route 53 private hosted zone so nobody's connection strings moved.

## Who should watch?

Cloud engineers handed someone else's working AWS account, and anyone about to propose Kubernetes for a three-container app. It is AWS-specific and dense with service names; the transferable part is the order of operations: observe, talk to people, price the options, then change what the developers won't notice.

Title: GraalVM native image takes 6.6 seconds down to 0.8, at a price
Description: Gregorio Palama (Lutech) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on compiling a Spring Boot service with GraalVM native image, and the reflection traps
Body:
A Spring Boot app with one endpoint started in 6.6 seconds on the JVM and in 0.8 seconds as a GraalVM native executable. Gregorio Palama, Senior Cloud Engineer and DevOps at Lutech, ran that comparison live at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, then spent the second half on what the speedup costs you: slow builds, a closed-world assumption that hates reflection, and libraries that aren't ready.

The framing is Sergio Leone's The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, with each character delivering a line about memory footprints. It works better than it has any right to.

## Why would a microservice care about startup time?

He starts from the cloud native pitch the big three providers all publish: scalability, lower cost, higher availability. For JVM services that boils down to three targets: a smaller memory footprint, less CPU and faster startup. Less memory means more replicas per node. Faster startup means a new replica serves users almost immediately, so you can run fewer of them and still scale out under load.

The demo is deliberately tiny: Spring Boot, one controller, one GET endpoint returning a greeting. No services, no repositories. Even that took six-odd seconds to come up on HotSpot, most of it Spring building its bean definitions at startup.

## What does native image actually do differently?

A good chunk of the talk is a clear tour of the JVM's tiered compilation: the interpreter (slow, collects profiling data), the C1 JIT (kicks in for frequently executed code, fast warmup), and C2 (optimises hot code past certain thresholds for peak performance). GraalVM swaps C2 for the Graal compiler, written in Java and plugged in through JVMCI, with extra optimisations such as removing unnecessary heap allocations.

Native image is the other path: ahead-of-time compilation. Your code, its libraries and the JDK go through a loop of points-to analysis, running initialisations and heap snapshotting until a pass adds nothing new. Substrate VM, also written in Java, gets compiled in to provide garbage collection and thread management. The output is a platform executable with the code in its text section and a pre-built image heap in its data section. Spring's AOT plugin pre-generates the bean definitions that would otherwise eat those 6.6 seconds, so the snapshot already contains an initialised application.

Result: 0.8 seconds to start, and a smaller resident set (modest on a hello-world, as he admits).

## Where does it bite?

The closed-world assumption. The compiler never runs your app, so anything it can't prove reachable by static analysis is left out of the binary. Reflection and dynamic proxies are the usual victims. The build succeeds; the error comes at runtime, when the code reaches a class nobody told the compiler about.

He showed the metadata that saves you: a second demo with a record DTO and a POST endpoint, and the generated reflect config telling native image to keep the DTO's declared fields, constructor and accessor. Libraries ship their own reachability metadata, and where they don't, the GraalVM team works with library authors to add it.

The other drawbacks on his list:

- Native builds take far longer and need more resources than generating bytecode. He paused the recording for the build; the JVM build didn't need it.
- Some dependencies drag in things you must exclude by hand, such as two logging implementations fighting behind one facade.
- AspectJ's load-time weaving relies on agents, which native image doesn't support.
- Shaded libraries, with their renamed packages, don't play well; use the unshaded ones.

## What is the advice?

Use the tracing agent: run the app on the JVM with the agent attached, drive it with end-to-end tests, and it writes the config files for you. "Just use the tracing agent because it does all the job for us," Gregorio Palama said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. Then test the native executable itself, because a binary that compiled is not a binary that has every class it needs.

Spring Boot is only the example. "Everything that we've seen with the demo application using spring is exactly the same and is valid for every microservices framework built with a language on the JVM," he said, pointing at Quarkus's native guide as well.

## Who should watch?

Java developers who have heard native image is fast and want the mental model before trying it, and platform teams wondering why their JVM pods need so much headroom. It is an introduction with a live demo, not a production migration story; the Leone quotes are a bonus.

Title: Your GenAI app is still an app, and it still needs a database
Description: Akanksha Sheoran (AWS) at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024 on why business data, not the foundation model, decides whether GenAI pays off
Body:
Everyone has access to roughly the same foundation models, so the model is not your moat. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024, Akanksha Sheoran, Principal Data Lead at AWS for the UK public sector, argued that the part of a GenAI project that decides whether it is useful sits below the waterline: storage, operational databases, pipelines and governance.

It is an introductory, architecture-level talk with an AWS flavour, aimed at teams that have picked an LLM and are only now asking where the context is supposed to come from.

## Why is the model the easy part?

Sheoran uses an iceberg: the GenAI application is the visible tip, and underneath sit a storage layer, purpose-built databases (document, graph, vector-enabled), data integration in batch or streaming, and governance for quality, privacy and security. Most customers she meets focus on the tip. "Genai applications are still applications, and like any other application, you need a database underneath it," Akanksha Sheoran said at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2024.

Her point about differentiation is blunt. Off-the-shelf models are on marketplaces and GitHub for anyone to download. "So data is the difference between the generic genai application and those that know your business and your customer deeply." She has watched teams bolt a foundation model onto nothing and see little benefit, while teams that worked backwards from their own data got applications that actually served customers. Using your data does not mean training your own model either: most organisations will fine-tune or, more often, retrieve.

## The numbers she leans on

She cites Goldman Sachs forecasting a 7 trillion dollar increase in global GDP from generative AI, and a McKinsey report warning that companies which cannot harmonise and give access to their data will not be able to fine-tune or fully use GenAI. From a survey of chief data officers: 93% said data strategy is crucial to making generative AI custom to their business, and 37% named the lack of the right data foundation as one of their top challenges. Her checklist for that foundation is short: data that is up to date, complete, accurate, discoverable and available.

## A RAG request, step by step

The most useful section walks the end-user critical path of a retrieval-augmented generation request in nine steps:

1. The user asks the application a question.
2. The application loads the relevant prompt template.
3. It checks the conversation history store so the user can pick up where they left off.
4. It queries profile or situational data, for example the order a customer wants to return.
5. It turns the question into embeddings with the model.
6. It runs a nearest-neighbour search over the vector store.
7. It sends the assembled prompt to the LLM.
8. It updates the conversation state and history.
9. It returns the answer.

Off the critical path sit ingestion, batch and stream processing, and the pipelines that keep the vector store and the warehouses fresh. Count the steps that are a database call: most of them. Her travel example makes the same point. A personalised itinerary joins customer profile data (past trips, hotel preferences, family members' ages) with flights, hotel inventory and promotions, and how fast you can reach and secure those datasets decides how good the answer is.

## Keep the vectors next to the data

After a gentle primer on embeddings (cat sits near kitten, dog near puppy; semantic search turning "bright colour golf shoes" into a precise query), she makes the architectural case. Customers told AWS they wanted vector search inside the databases they already run, so it is available in Amazon OpenSearch, Aurora PostgreSQL, RDS for PostgreSQL, Neptune and DocumentDB, with DynamoDB reachable through zero-ETL. Storing vectors with the business data means no sync jobs and no extra silo. She closes with AWS's unify, modernise, innovate flywheel, which she says you can enter at any point, plus pointers to the Generative AI Innovation Center and hands-on workshops.

## Who should watch

Architects and data leads who need to explain to a steering committee why the GenAI budget includes database work. Engineers who already run RAG in production will find the material familiar; the nine-step walkthrough is still a handy checklist for where latency and stale data come from.

Title: E-commerce won't kill the shop, but a slow website might kill your sale
Description: Dmitry Bardysh (Yandex Delivery) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on why in-store retail survives the e-commerce boom, and why omnichannel wins
Body:
Online shopping keeps growing, and physical stores still take most of the money. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Dmitry Bardysh, Head of B2B Operations at Yandex Delivery, with a career running operations at Uber and Yandex, lays out the numbers on both sides and lands on a clear answer: neither channel wins alone, and the retailers doing well are the ones blending them.

This is a business and market talk, not an engineering one. The part engineers will care about most is short, and it's about page load times.

## How big is e-commerce, and how big isn't it?

Dmitry's figures (sources on his slides): global e-commerce sales passed $5.7 trillion in 2022, and its share of retail reached 18%, projected to hit 21.8% by 2024, with an estimated 2.71 billion online shoppers in 2024. The pandemic pushed adoption along during lockdowns.

The other side is bigger. In-store retail bounced back in 2021 with 8.2% growth to about $21 trillion, above pre-pandemic levels, and a 2023 survey found 43% of consumers still prefer the tangible experience of shopping in person. His hypothesis follows from that. Dmitry Bardysh said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 that "the future of commerce is a dynamic interplay between the digital and traditional retail realms."

## Why can't we resist shopping online?

The list of reasons is long and familiar: global reach and 24/7 opening, convenience, a wider product range, cost savings on rent and staff, no queues, personalised recommendations, easy price comparison, user reviews. For businesses, there's more: small sellers can compete with big ones, digital marketing costs less, customer data comes for free, inventory tracking is tighter, and dynamic pricing and chatbots become possible.

The trends he picks out:

- **Mobile commerce**: mobile went from 67.2% of e-commerce sales in 2019 to 72.9% in 2021, citing Statista.
- **Social commerce**: 55% of American consumers bought something online right after discovering it on social media in 2022.
- **User experience**: 88% of online consumers are less likely to return to a site after a bad experience.

## Your page load is part of the shop

That third trend is the one with an engineering bill attached. Citing a Kissmetrics study, Dmitry says 47% of consumers expect a page to load in 2 seconds or less, and 40% will abandon a site that takes more than 3. In a physical store, nobody walks out because the door took three seconds to open. Online, they do, and the competing shop is one tab away. His conclusion: invest in fast, responsive sites, intuitive navigation and interfaces people can use.

## Why do people still shop in real life?

Four reasons, each with a number from his slides: the tangible experience, avoiding online risks (a Retail Dive survey found 62% prefer to examine products physically and 49% want to dodge shipping costs), face-to-face service (74% of global consumers want more human interaction while shopping, per PwC), and the overall appeal of music, scents and visuals, with 90% more likely to buy when they enjoy the store's environment.

## Who is getting the blend right?

His examples of the omnichannel approach: Starbucks with 31 million monthly app users and 41% of US sales from its rewards programme, Walmart with 268 million customers and 63.5% e-commerce sales growth in 2021, and Sephora with 31 million loyalty members. For what comes next he points to personalised mobile shopping (Shopify's 1.75 million merchants and 86% revenue growth in 2020), sustainability (Patagonia giving 1% of sales to environmental causes) and AR, VR and AI, with IKEA's AR app placing furniture in customers' homes.

His answer to the title's question is yes: traditional retail has a future if brands adapt, rework physical spaces, and let consumers decide the balance between in-person and digital.

## Who should watch

Product and business people in retail and delivery, and engineers on e-commerce teams who want the market context for their roadmap. If you want architecture, look elsewhere in the Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 lineup.

Title: Argo Rollouts gives Kubernetes the two strategies it doesn't ship with
Description: Karan Jagtiani (Storylane) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on blue-green and canary deployments in Kubernetes with Argo Rollouts, demoed on kind
Body:
Kubernetes gives you two deployment strategies out of the box, Recreate and RollingUpdate, and neither lets you hold a new version in front of 20% of users while you look at the graphs. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Karan Jagtiani, Software Engineer at Storylane, compares four strategies and their trade-offs, then demos blue-green and canary releases with Argo Rollouts on a local kind cluster, manual promote button included.

It's a clear, well-paced introduction: half concepts, half terminal. The demo project is on his GitHub.

## Why bother with zero downtime?

His four reasons: downtime costs revenue, it damages user experience, it erodes customer trust, and many companies have SLA obligations to their customers. The setup he builds on is the standard path: DNS to load balancer to Kubernetes ingress, then service, then deployment.

## What do the built-in strategies give you?

**Recreate** deletes the current deployment, then creates the new one. It's simple, needs no extra resources, and avoids two versions writing to the same data source, which makes it fine for non-production environments and single-tenant databases. It also means downtime during every rollout, a slow rollout when there are hundreds of pods, and real trouble if the new version fails after the old one is already gone.

**Rolling** brings up new pods and only removes old ones once the new ones are running. It's resource-efficient and has no downtime, which makes it a good default for dev and staging, but rollbacks get complex, stateful apps get awkward, and spotting problems mid-rollout is tedious.

## Canary or blue-green?

**Canary** sends a subset of traffic, say 20%, to a canary group while the rest stays on the original deployment. It looks like a rolling update, but you control the group and the pace: real-user feedback, gradual resource use and a quick rollback. The price is complex traffic routing, monitoring overhead, users seeing different versions, and a limited testing scope.

**Blue-green**, his favourite, keeps two full copies: one serving production, one taking the new release for testing, UAT or load tests before the two are swapped. You get no downtime and an immediate rollback, and you pay with double the resources, an idle copy for long stretches and harder data management.

## What does the Argo Rollouts demo show?

Argo Rollouts is an open source Kubernetes controller with a Rollout custom resource for blue-green and canary releases, plus rollbacks, traffic shifting and a dashboard. Karan runs it on a kind cluster with nginx:

- **Blue-green**: two Services with the same selector, wired into the Rollout as the active service (live traffic) and the preview service (the test bed). With auto-promotion disabled, changing the image tag to latest creates a new revision that sits alongside the old one until someone clicks Promote in the dashboard (`kubectl argo rollouts dashboard`, on port 3100) or runs the CLI. After the swap, the old ReplicaSet scales down after a configurable delay of 30 seconds.
- **Canary**: one Service, and a Rollout with steps, each a weight and a pause. With five pods, each 20% step adds one pod to the canary group. The first pause is indefinite, so the rollout waits for a manual promote; later pauses last 10 seconds and promote themselves.

The step list is the useful bit: weights, pause durations and the number of steps are all yours to set in YAML.

## What usually goes wrong?

His best practices are rigorous testing in a live environment, real-time monitoring, graceful degradation and traffic control. The pitfalls list is more pointed: inadequate rollback procedures, overlooked dependencies, insufficient load testing, neglected user experience during rollouts, complex monitoring setups, and database migrations. Karan Jagtiani said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "Ignoring database migrations, this is something that is very common." With two environments sharing a database, a migration applied for the new version can take down the one still running the old code. Blue-green doubles your pods; it doesn't double your database.

On rollbacks he speaks from experience: "I have seen this multiple times where there are no rollback procedures and when something goes down then it gets very scary and difficult to roll back to the previous working deployment."

## Who should watch

Engineers whose Kubernetes deployments are still plain RollingUpdate and who want a concrete next step, and anyone choosing between canary and blue-green. If you already run Argo Rollouts with analysis templates and metric-driven promotion, this talk stops before that.

Title: From fine-tuned BERT to an ECS endpoint, without SageMaker
Description: Deepak Karunanidhi (Novartis) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on fine-tuning BERT, tracking runs in MLflow and serving it with TorchServe on AWS ECS
Body:
Training the model is the part data scientists like. Knowing which run produced the good numbers, and getting that model behind an API, is the part that decides whether it ships. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Deepak Karunanidhi, Associate Director for Data Science and Machine Learning at Novartis, walks the full path for a text classifier: a pretrained BERT from Hugging Face, fine-tuned on a GPU, every experiment logged in MLflow, packaged for TorchServe and deployed on Amazon ECS instead of SageMaker endpoints to save cost.

It's an end-to-end overview rather than a deep technical session. Each stage gets a few minutes, which makes it a good map for someone moving from notebooks to production.

## What comes before any training?

Deepak starts with the lifecycle he follows on every project: define the problem (image classification, translation, summarisation, question answering and so on), collect the data, pick performance metrics before training anything, decide the evaluation procedure, clean the data, build a baseline, fine-tune, then deploy.

For text the cleaning steps are the classic NLP ones: strip ASCII noise and special characters, remove stop words, then stemming and lemmatisation, with part-of-speech tags or embeddings where needed. The split is train, test and validation, in ratios such as 70/15/15. The metrics come from the confusion matrix, and he makes the useful point that the problem decides which one matters: if you can't afford to miss a positive, you optimise for recall and accept more false positives.

## Why fine-tune instead of train?

The demo task is binary sentiment classification: "this is an amazing model" should come out positive. Rather than building from scratch, he takes a pretrained transformer from Hugging Face, which offers per-task model families: BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT and XLM-RoBERTa for classification, Marian, BART and T5 for translation, GPT-2 and later for chat. BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers, trained with masked language modelling and next-sentence prediction) is the general model; fine-tuning makes it specific to your task and domain.

The code uses AutoTokenizer and AutoModelForSequenceClassification, so swapping BERT for RoBERTa, BioBERT or another model is a command-line argument. Training runs on GPUs with CUDA, split across devices, and the hyperparameters he tunes are mostly learning rate and number of epochs, with batch size alongside. You keep going until recall and precision hit the benchmark the problem needs, which he puts at 85% or 95% depending on the case.

## Which run was that, again?

The best moment is the slide of plain training code: load data, extract n-gram features, train, compute accuracy. Then the question every ML engineer has asked. Deepak Karunanidhi said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "Now, what version of my code was this result from? No idea."

MLflow is the fix. Wrap training in a run, log parameters and metrics, store everything in a backing store (S3 in his setup), and use the built-in UI to compare runs by timestamp, features, accuracy, precision and recall. When you fine-tune dozens of times with different seeds and parameters, it is the only way to know which one to promote.

## How does the model get to production?

Serving is TorchServe. A trained, evaluated model is converted to a MAR file and placed in a model store; TorchServe exposes an inference API and a management API, and one instance can serve several models.

The AWS layout:

1. Train on a GPU machine and push the MAR file to S3 with a script.
2. Build a Docker image and push it to ECR.
3. A Jenkins CI/CD pipeline deploys it to ECS, on EC2 in his case (Fargate also works), with a load balancer in front.
4. Applications call the TorchServe inference API.

He chose this over SageMaker endpoints for cost. The trade-off isn't explored in detail, but the reason is stated plainly, which is more than many architecture talks manage.

## Who should watch

Data scientists who have fine-tuned a transformer and now need to track and serve it, and engineers asked to host a PyTorch model on AWS without SageMaker. MLOps veterans won't find much new.

Title: Cold-starting a social marketplace means supply first, one submarket at a time
Description: Igor Sedachev (Avito) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on beating the marketplace cold start with incentives, stacked growth loops and dense submarkets
Body:
Most marketplaces die before they have a market. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Igor Sedachev, Head of Seller Experience Product at Avito, gives a product strategy talk on the cold start problem in social marketplaces, the platforms that blend e-commerce with social media, and his recipe fits on one slide: find the right incentives, use them to start a flywheel, and grow density one submarket at a time.

Fair warning: there's no Kubernetes here. It's a product talk at a cloud conference, and a useful one for engineers who build platforms and want to know what the product side is worrying about.

## What is the cold start problem?

Igor uses the standard three maturity levels. Cold start: no supply, no demand, a chicken and egg problem and no liquidity. Growth: balancing your value proposition and incentive budget to outcompete other players. Dominance: more than 50% market share, capturing the remaining demand until saturation. You can't skip the first stage, and it's where most startups, new products and new features die.

## Why blend media and commerce at all?

His history lesson is short. Before the internet, a seller selling a microphone paid offline media for marketing and offline stores for distribution, and neither knew much about the audience. The internet swapped these for social media and online stores, and both started collecting preferences: what you like, what you bought, what you abandoned in the cart. A social marketplace combines both sets of preferences and both budgets: the seller's marketing spend and distribution spend can go to one company. Hence everyone drifting towards the middle, with media moving to performance-based pricing and e-commerce adding ratings, reviews and user content.

So a social marketplace has to be a good media product and a good marketplace at the same time.

## The media side: authors, content, distribution, audience

Four questions, each to be stated as a hypothesis and then tested:

- **Authors**: who produces the content and why they'd do it with you, for money, audience, fame, or just a place to keep what they already make.
- **Content**: text, pictures, video, stories. This one shapes the technical strategy too, because video costs far more to store than text, and AR or VR content would cost more again.
- **Distribution**: subscriptions, or a recommendation system that pushes content by interest. Recommendations need data you don't have during a cold start.
- **Audience**: why anyone should come, and what they get from it.

## Where do you find your first sellers?

Incentives come first: map the potential user's customer journey, find the moment your product fits into their life, and build a value proposition relative to the competition, which for a content product is anything that eats time, from a book to a walk with the kids. Then pick a segment that current players underserve. Calling a big YouTube creator to ask them to move to an unknown startup goes about as well as you'd expect. Someone not on any big platform, who grows with you, sticks with you emotionally and economically.

## Why does supply come before demand?

Supply sticks around longer, and a piece of content can be reused, recut and tested across distribution methods. Igor Sedachev said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "If you somewhere create a demand but you have zero supply, you just burn your money and your efforts." If you insist on starting with demand, he wants you to have a good explanation for your team and a test first.

The flywheel is several growth loops stacked on top of each other: authors share their first video outside the platform and bring friends; then a second loop, such as challenges where viewers recreate a video with tools you make easy. The more loops you stack, the more network effects you get, and every free user still adds value through recommendations and search.

## Density, not averages

The last idea is the most transferable. A marketplace is a set of isolated submarkets, split by language and by theme. A new creator making chemistry videos in Japanese does nothing for the density of English chemistry videos, so you can't measure density on average. In a cold start, pick a few submarkets, test mechanics there, then scale what works to the neighbours. The product can stay universal; marketing and partnerships are where you focus by submarket.

## Who should watch

Product managers and founders building two-sided platforms, and engineers on marketplace teams who want the reasoning behind the roadmap. If you came to Conf42 Cloud Native for infrastructure, this one is a detour.

Title: Amazon SES won't tell you who bounced unless you wire it up
Description: Marcos Henrique (Welbe Care) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on tracking Amazon SES bounces, complaints and opens with CDK, CloudWatch and SNS alarms
Body:
Amazon SES will happily send your email and say very little about what happened next. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Marcos Henrique, Senior Cloud Engineer at Welbe Care, shows how to fix that with a small AWS CDK stack in TypeScript: a configuration set that publishes sending events to SNS and CloudWatch, plus alarms that page a human when bounces or rejects cross a threshold.

It was his debut talk, and it's a compact one: a quick tour of how SES works, the metrics worth caring about, then the code.

## Why does SES need extra observability?

He names two common problems. The first is deliverability: getting into the inbox rather than the spam folder depends on sender reputation, so you need to watch the numbers that drive it. The second is the lack of monitoring and reporting out of the box. The story behind the talk: his team needed to know how many people had received an email about safety regulations, didn't have the visibility, and had to build it.

He opens with Charity Majors' line that observability is about being able to ask any question of your systems at any time, and closes on the same note. Marcos Henrique said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "We need to know the whys of our system."

## Which SES metrics matter?

The two SES building blocks are verified identities (a domain, subdomain or address that proves you're allowed to send) and configuration sets, the rules applied to those identities, which is where tracking lives. The metrics he walks through:

- **Delivery rate and delay**: did it arrive, and how late.
- **Open rate and click-through rate**: whether anyone cared. His sample dashboard showed healthy delivery peaks but few opens, a hint that the emails' calls to action needed work.
- **Bounce rate**, split into hard bounces (the address doesn't exist) and soft bounces (full mailbox, temporary trouble).
- **Complaint rate**: recipients marking you as spam, which hurts reputation fast.
- **Rendering failure**: a template sent without one of its parameters.

## What does the CDK stack do?

The hands-on part is a single stack class. Step by step:

1. **Create a configuration set** with sending enabled and reputation metrics turned on.
2. **Add an SNS event destination**, so every send, reject and bounce lands on a topic. That's the upstream feed: hang a Lambda off it, ship it to Datadog, or write it to CloudWatch Logs.
3. **Add a CloudWatch event destination** with dimensions, so the metrics can be sliced by sending rate, bounce rate and the rest.
4. **Create alarms** from a map of event types to thresholds. Each alarm sets the metric namespace and name, the statistic (sum, average, min, max, p99), evaluation periods, comparison operator, and how to treat missing data, so silence doesn't wake anyone up.
5. **Send alarms to a separate SNS topic**, the one that notifies people. In his example it's imported from a core infrastructure project and routed to Slack, and a single reject is enough to raise an alarm.

The split between the two topics is the useful design detail: one feeds machines downstream, the other wakes up the DevOps person. Mixing them is how you end up paging someone for every delivered newsletter.

## Who should watch

Anyone sending transactional or campaign email through SES who has been asked whether people got the email and had no answer. CDK beginners also get a readable example of a stack that does one real job. If you already pipe SES events into your observability stack, you can skip it.

Title: A shared staging queue can't keep up with your pull requests
Description: Natalie Lunbeck (Shipyard) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on replacing the shared staging queue with an ephemeral, production-like environment per pull request
Body:
Production deployment got containers, GitOps and autoscaling; pre-production mostly kept its four long-lived environments and a queue. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Natalie Lunbeck, Software Engineer at Shipyard and primary author of the open source guide ephemeralenvironments.io, makes the case for a full-stack, production-like environment per pull request, and walks through the six properties such an environment needs to be worth having.

It is a 101, as the title says, and it comes from a company that sells ephemeral environments. The product barely appears, though; the talk is about the workflow.

## What's wrong with staging?

Her picture of the usual setup will be familiar: a handful of static environments for the whole team, coupled together and sharing dependencies, so that breaking staging can take the others down with it. Against that, the daily volume of pull requests. You open a PR, wait for review, merge to main, deploy to staging alongside the other fifteen branches that landed that day, and run end-to-end tests against the pile. Something breaks. You guess which change did it, open a fix, and go round the loop again. Days pass between a bug and its confirmed fix.

## What is an ephemeral environment?

The definition she uses, from the community guide: a short-lived, encapsulated deployment of an application, created automatically on every code change through GitOps. In practice: open a PR, the CI workflow spins up an environment, hands its URL to your end-to-end and integration tests (which need a real database, so the stack has to be full), and you learn about bugs within the time it takes the tests to run.

Natalie Lunbeck said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "So instead of context switching, you can just kind of sit back, relax, wait for your test to fail and then go right back." Staging then only has to find conflicts between branches that were already tested on their own. She says Shipyard sees people deploying around 50% faster, and testing sometimes 40 times more often, which she admits sounds fake.

## The six pillars

The checklist is the most reusable part of the talk, useful whether you build or buy:

- **Dev workflow**: no overhead. Hook it to the Git provider, open a PR, get a link; every later commit on the PR updates the same environment.
- **Collaboration**: developers review against a running app, and product managers click through a feature instead of judging a screen share. QA can check out a single branch early instead of testing features in a bundle.
- **Testing**: point the existing CI/CD pipeline at the environment's URL for both automated and user testing, per feature and on every merge.
- **On demand**: GitOps first, no manual steps. Environments appear on significant changes and disappear on their own, so a colleague in a later time zone can spin one back up hours after you've shut it down.
- **Security**: isolated environments are safer, but still sanitise data (no PII in test data) and put SSO in front, through GitHub or Google, rather than writing your own auth.
- **Cost control**: a few static environments run 24/7 and sit idle most of that time. Environments that live a few hours each mean you can have many more at once and still spend less.

## Who should watch

Teams living with a staging queue who want the argument for moving off it, and platform engineers drafting requirements for a preview environment system. If you already run environments per PR, the pillars make a decent audit list, but there's little here you won't know.

Title: An enterprise data platform, built up one component at a time
Description: Raja Chattopadhyay (Capital One) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on growing a data lake into a platform with writers, pipelines, a catalog and a portal
Body:
Every data platform starts as an S3 bucket and a promise. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Raja Chattopadhyay, Engineering Manager at Capital One, starts from exactly that and adds one component per problem until he has a full enterprise data ecosystem: a data writer, a governed pipeline, a catalog with access control, a transformation platform, a portal and a path for machine learning. Each piece is justified by the specific mess the previous version leaves behind.

It is a reference architecture talk. The diagrams are marked as illustrations, not an actual implementation, so expect a design walkthrough rather than a tour of Capital One's production stack.

## What goes wrong with a plain data lake?

In its simplest form a data lake is storage where structured and unstructured data is written and read. Raja lists three problems that show up immediately: publishers write in disparate formats (Parquet here, CSV there), consumers don't know where to read from, and data arriving at intervals makes a comprehensive view hard.

The first fix is a standard way in. A **data writer** gives each sub-organisation its own area of the lake, authenticates the publisher and the dataset it writes to, and organises data as delta files plus aggregates, partitioned and stored as Parquet, with Iceberg or Hudi where you need transactions. A matching **data reader** serves consumers based on their identity and the datasets they may see.

## Who reads the data, and from where?

Consumers come in four kinds: data analysts, data scientists, applications, and the ones you don't know about yet. Raja keeps a bucket for that last group on purpose, because somebody always invents a new way to use the data. Batch consumers read from the lake, real-time ones from a database or low-latency store, and the unknowns need custom sinks. Tools differ too: APIs for real-time access, notebooks for data scientists, dashboards and SQL for analysts.

That brings three new problems: keeping data consistent across sinks, duplicated effort to write to each of them, and stopping unauthorised access.

## The pipeline is where governance lives

The answer is a **data pipeline** between first-class storage (the lake and the stream) and everything downstream. Its jobs, orchestrated by something like Airflow:

- **Governance**: schema checks, quality checks and scans for sensitive data.
- **Routing** to the right sinks, with mechanisms to make sure data is eventually written.
- **Light transformation**, such as data type changes.

Batch data goes to the lake first and is also routed to the streaming platform; real-time data goes to the stream first and is batched before landing in the lake. The steps are plug and play, so new governance checks can be added later without every platform implementing its own. A **catalog** (DCAT is the suggested model) makes data discoverable and stores routing rules, and tag-based access control decides who can read what.

## Shared compute, a portal and a feature store

Left alone, every team builds its own compute, capacity goes unused, everyone maintains their own infrastructure and nobody does DataOps the same way. A **data transformation platform** takes scripts through CI/CD, runs them on on-demand compute, grants data access based on the job's context, and hands results back to the data writer.

The **data portal** ties it together for humans, with tiered onboarding so publishing isn't blocked on paperwork: tier 1 just publishes, tier 2 adds basic governance like schema, tier 3 adds data quality. Machine learning reuses the same pieces: raw data in the lake, a transformation job that extracts features into a feature platform (lake storage plus a serving API, perhaps with a low-latency cache), a training job, and offline predictions written back to the lake. Real-time prediction is explicitly out of scope.

## The cloud-specific bits

The closing section lists AWS challenges with options rather than prescriptions: one central account for data versus an account per sub-line of business, scanning sensitive data and encrypting, masking or deleting it so a breach yields little, keeping historical data on premise versus migrating it, tagging every service with its sub-LOB for billing, and CDMC as a governance standard. The last item is the one teams forget. Raja Chattopadhyay said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "Cloud is someone else data center." Each account has soft and hard limits, so capacity still needs planning.

## Who should watch

Architects and data platform leads at large organisations who need a vocabulary and a component map for the platform they are building. If you want code or a migration story with numbers, this is not that talk.
