Title: Streaming is batch plus the question of what to do with late data
Description: Ankit Virmani (Forbes Technology Council) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on watermarks, triggers and the scaling settings that keep streaming pipelines healthy
Body:
An event that happened at 8am shows up in your pipeline after 11am. Do you count it? At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Ankit Virmani, a member of the Forbes Technology Council with about ten years in big data engineering, explains why that question is the whole difference between batch and streaming, and then lists the infrastructure and code settings that stop streaming pipelines from hanging, skewing or falling over.

The first half is a compact primer on the streaming vocabulary, with Apache Beam examples. The second half is a field-notes list. Both are short and dense.

## Why is streaming harder than batch?

Batch works on bounded data: a table or a file with a beginning and an end. Correctness means your business logic gives the right output for that input. Completion means you processed all 10,000 records, or you know that 4,000 failed on a schema issue.

Streaming has neither boundary. Data arrives out of order and late, because of network trouble or bandwidth between the source and the processor. So correctness becomes the business logic plus a policy for out-of-order data, and completion becomes a judgment call: is data that is 30 minutes late still worth processing? 40? Ankit calls this the dilemma between correctness and completion, and the rest of the vocabulary exists to manage it.

## Watermarks, triggers and accumulation, briefly

- **Event time** is when the thing happened (you pressed pause); **processing time** is when the pipeline saw it.
- **Windows** chop the stream into temporal chunks so you can group and aggregate, as you would in batch. Fixed, sliding and session windows are the usual shapes.
- **A watermark** is the notion of completeness: all input with event time below X has been processed. It is not perfect, so you still need a strategy for late arrivals.
- **Triggers** decide when a window's results are emitted: on event time, processing time or data.
- **Accumulation** decides whether successive results for a window build up (a running total) or replace each other.

His Beam example pulls it together: a fixed 60-second window, a trigger 60 seconds after processing time so late arrivals get a minute's grace, and discarding accumulation so you get the final result rather than a running sum. Three questions organise the whole design: what results are calculated, when in event time, and when in processing time they are materialised.

## Scaling a stream you can't pause

The considerations section is where the field experience shows. The point that sets the tone is vertical autoscaling in flight: a stream sometimes needs more memory on one machine rather than more machines, and you cannot stop the flow to resize. "It's running water, it's running data," as he put it.

The rest of the list:

- **Dynamic work rebalancing**, so idle workers take load off stragglers instead of letting skew build up.
- **Decouple window processing** from the other stream operations so each can scale on its own.
- **Resource hints**: tell the pipeline which steps need how much memory or GPU instead of leaning on autoscaling to guess.
- **Combine instead of group by** where you can, because group by shuffles far more data.
- **Right-size files** to between 100 MB and 1 GB per shard, depending on output size.
- **Keep sources and sinks in the same region** where possible.
- **Use type hints**, so Beam raises errors at pipeline construction instead of hours into a run.

## Never retry forever

The most quotable item comes with a customer story: a team whose default was to retry forever, and whose pipelines kept hanging as a result. Ankit Virmani said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "Always have a time period or a retry count which returns an error and ideally sends the element to a dead letter queue after a particular number of retries, and you can always reprocess those dead letter queues later." It's the streaming version of a lesson every on-call engineer learns once: an operation without a timeout is an outage with a delayed start.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving from batch to streaming who want the vocabulary straight, and Beam or Dataflow users who want a checklist of settings to review. Seasoned stream processing people will know the concepts but may still pick up a setting or two.

Title: 950 million events a day through Kinesis without hot shards
Description: Akshay Jain (Innovate UK) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on running a 950M-events-a-day Kinesis pipeline, shard distribution, big records and canary events
Body:
A streaming pipeline that copes with the average day is easy. The hard part is the hour a batch job rewrites half your DynamoDB table. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Akshay Jain, Data Engineering Manager at Innovate UK, shares what his team learned pushing 950 million added or updated events a day from DynamoDB Streams through AWS Lambda into Amazon Kinesis, and the lessons boil down to this: spread records evenly across shards, keep records small, agree the schema first, and send fake events through the pipe to prove it works.

## What did the pipeline look like?

The upstream system was DynamoDB, updated both by APIs and by batch jobs. An ECS cluster ran a KCL application that read the DynamoDB stream and wrote to SQS. A Lambda function picked up the SQS messages, enriched them according to the data contract agreed with consumers, and wrote them to a Kinesis stream. Downstream, consumers stored the data in Elasticsearch and showed metrics in a web app. The goal: data visible in the web app as soon as possible after it landed in DynamoDB.

The tricky bit was the shape of the load, not just its size. API updates trickle in; batch jobs arrive as a flood, and the system had to absorb both.

## How many shards, and how fast can you write to them?

Kinesis makes you pick shard counts, on demand or provisioned. Akshay warns that on-demand capacity at this scale gets costly, and that provisioned capacity needs care too. On the producer side, the Lambda has to write fast enough to keep latency down but not so fast that it hits shard throttling. The team started at around 200 shards and tuned the Lambda concurrency against that.

His practical lever for the throttling side: Lambda's concurrent execution setting. Capping concurrency slows writes to the shards, which buys you time while you work out the right shard count.

## Are your shards actually evenly loaded?

Uneven partition keys give you hot shards drowning in records next to cold ones doing nothing, and you pay for both. To see it, turn on shard-level metrics with the EnableEnhancedMonitoring API (IncomingBytes, IncomingRecords, WriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded, IteratorAgeMilliseconds and friends). They cost extra. The free alternatives are counting per-shard records in the consumer, or logging the PutRecord responses, which tell you which shard each record landed in. Akshay's advice is to start with the built-in metrics.

If the distribution is skewed, he shows two fixes:

- **Hashed partition keys**: pass a hash of the record, or of a random number, as the partition key so records spread uniformly.
- **Explicit hash keys**: list the stream's shards and their hash key ranges, then assign an ExplicitHashKey to each record in round robin. When both are set, the explicit hash key wins over the partition key.

## What happens when the schema keeps growing?

The data contract kept gaining descriptive columns, comments and descriptions mostly, and every one made records bigger. A shard takes up to 1 MB per second of writes, so fatter records mean either more shards or more throttling. The fixes: compress records (GZIP, Snappy, LZ4) or use a compact format like Avro, at the price of extra CPU on both ends. The better fix, which he admits his team did not get to implement, is to keep bulky descriptive data in S3 or a database and pass a reference through the stream instead.

Which leads to his strongest opinion. Akshay Jain said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "So what I generally recommend is to go for the schema registry first before even implementing streaming solutions." On AWS that means the AWS Glue Schema Registry, with versioning so producers and consumers can follow the schema as it changes. Without a registry, a shared code base holding the schema definitions does the job.

## Canary events: test the pipe with fake parcels

The best idea of the talk is the validation trick. The team published dummy events into the stream that walked through the same lifecycle as real products (open, in review, in progress, closed), recording CloudWatch metrics for each on the producer side. Consumers read the same dummy events and published their own metrics. Comparing the two on a schedule, with an acceptable deviation range, told them whether the pipeline was lagging, overloaded or broken, and alerts fired when the gap grew too wide. It's a canary for data: a cheap way to know the pipe is flowing before a user notices the dashboard is stale.

## Who should watch

Data engineers running Kinesis, or about to, especially anyone whose load arrives in batch-shaped spikes. It is a focused, AWS-specific experience report, light on theory and heavy on knobs.

Title: Cloud security starts with what you made public by accident
Description: Sena Yakut (Lyrebird Studio) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on cloud security basics, from no public resources to alerts with a plan
Body:
Most cloud breaches don't need a zero-day. They need a bucket somebody made public in 2019 and a CloudTrail nobody switched on. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Sena Yakut, Senior Cloud Security Engineer at Lyrebird Studio and an AWS Security Hero, walks through a short, opinionated to-do list for keeping attackers out of an AWS or Azure estate, and the first item is the boring one that matters most: stop exposing things you don't have to.

It is a practitioner's checklist rather than a tour of one service, and it is honest about that. If you run cloud accounts and nobody has ever owned security for them, this is a good half hour.

## Why is cloud security such a mess?

Sena lists six sources of pain: too many providers, product requirements that change faster than threat models, a shared responsibility model that companies don't fully read, a sprawl of resources (used and unused), a matching sprawl of attack surfaces (endpoints, networks, databases, AI and IoT services), and tools that get bought, installed and forgotten.

Her one-line summary of the threat: "So we love the cloud, so attackers do." The numbers she brings come from the Orca Security 2024 State of Cloud Security Report: 91% of organisations have at least one vulnerability older than ten years, and 46% have one more than 20 years old. Containers, storage buckets and virtual machines are the asset types malware hits most, which is also a fair description of what most of us run.

## Public by default is the expensive default

The top recommendation is blunt: do not use public resources unless you really, really need them. A static website with public photos in S3 is fine. A bucket an attacker can write to, or wipe, is not. Neither is a publicly reachable database, a container registry that leaks credentials, or an exposed Amazon SageMaker notebook someone else gets to run models in on your bill.

She also flags the denial of wallet amplification attack: large files sitting publicly in S3 that someone downloads on repeat until your invoice becomes the outage.

## Know what you have, then read the manual

The second item is inventory: which resources, where, why, with which vulnerabilities, misconfigurations (unused access keys, public buckets, CloudTrail not enabled) and endpoints (load balancers, Lambda functions, API Gateway). Cloud security posture management tooling and CIS benchmark scores are, in her words on the slides, not enough but a good start.

Then the item developers love least: read the documentation. Her argument is practical. Many security features are only off because nobody knew they existed, and reading the docs cuts dependence on outside help.

## An alert without a plan is just noise

Sena calls alerting the most important thing in the cloud: anomalies, threats against resources, and configuration changes, like an attacker quietly creating a new IAM user for themselves. But getting alerts is half of it. Each one, false positives included, needs analysing, and the team needs a plan for what happens next. Monitoring rounds it out, with a useful side effect: the same visibility catches cost anomalies.

Encryption gets the best line of the talk. Sena Yakut said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: "We need to dance like no one is watching. Encrypt like everyone is." In transit and at rest, current TLS versions, and keeping up as old protocols get retired.

## The human items are the hard ones

The last three are about people. Be open to change: she quotes what she calls "the most dangerous phrase in English languages. We always done it this way." Don't isolate teams, because developers, architects and security engineers each see different parts of the risk, and siloed teams end up analysing the same vulnerability twice. And think "what if": what if these credentials leak, what does the attacker do next, and what do we do after that.

## Who should watch

Developers and DevOps engineers who have inherited cloud accounts and need a priority order, and small teams without a dedicated security function. Seasoned cloud security engineers will recognise every item; it may still be useful as a talk to send to the rest of the org.

Title: In an event-driven system, the event schema is your API
Description: James Eastham (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on business events, sparse vs fat events, versioning with CloudEvents and embracing eventual consistency
Body:
Swapping HTTP calls for a message bus does not make a system event-driven, and it can leave you more coupled than before. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, James Eastham, Senior Cloud Consultant at AWS, walks through building an event-driven architecture for a fictional company, Plant Based Pizza, sharing the mistakes he made on real systems along the way. His central point: events are a business language, and their schema is the contract everything else depends on.

He says up front that this is not a talk about AWS services, just boxes and lines. It is one of the clearest introductions to event-driven design you will find, with enough intermediate patterns to keep experienced engineers awake.

## Why move off HTTP at all?

Plant Based Pizza already runs microservices, with an order processing service that has to know where the kitchen, pickup, delivery and new loyalty point services live. Each new service means changing the order service, and a failure in loyalty points, nowhere near the critical path, can stop the business taking orders.

He frames this through types of coupling (technology, location, temporal, data format, data type, semantic) and Gregor Hohpe's rule: "The appropriate level of coupling depends on the level of control you have over the endpoints." Tight coupling among three services your team owns is fine. Across team or company boundaries, reduce it. Event-driven architecture, in Martin Fowler's framing, reverses the dependencies: the order service no longer knows who listens.

## Business events, not button clicks

An event is an immutable fact, like a light switched on (no un-switching it, only a new light switched off event). But a Windows Forms button click or an S3 object created notification is a technical event. Event-driven systems run on business events: order confirmed, pizza boxed, staff member clocked in. Two pizza companies would have different events because they speak different languages, and that is the point.

That makes events first-class citizens with event-first design. "Your event schema is your API in event driven systems," James Eastham said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024.

## Sparse or fat events?

His first implementation published a sparse notification event, order confirmed with just an ID, and had the kitchen call back for details. He has done this for real: it works until there are five, then ten subscribers all hammering the producer, at which point the order service catches fire. Producers should be unaware of their consumers.

Event-carried state transfer, a fat event with the order inside, removes the callback but couples everyone to the schema. His multi-currency story shows the cost: change the order value from a number to a value-and-currency object for the kitchen, and you discover an analytics service depending on the old shape. In his words, "you've just broken a system that you didn't even know existed."

His answer is a mix of process and structure:

- **Governance without bureaucracy**: breaking changes go through a lightweight, asynchronous RFC.
- **The metadata/data pattern**, or the CloudEvents specification, giving each event a type, source, unique ID (so consumers can be idempotent), time and, crucially, a version.
- **Parallel versions**: publish v1 and v2 side by side, ask consumers to move, then switch off v1.

Where does he land on fat versus sparse? It depends, and he admits he keeps changing his mind. One option he is exploring is events carrying a wider set of identifiers, order ID plus customer ID and delivery address ID, so each service still owns its data but knows what to look up.

## Subscribers own their load

With HTTP, callers worry about the callee's rate limits and auth. With pub/sub, that responsibility moves to the subscriber. A queue at the subscriber's boundary absorbs a sudden 100x burst and acts like an anti-corruption layer where incoming schemas can be validated.

## Async all the way, except at the edges

Asynchrony brings eventual consistency, explained with paying for pizza in cash (strongly consistent) versus by card (the charge shows up eventually). You cannot solve it, only architect for it. Observability needs a trace ID and span ID (OpenTelemetry) or at least a correlation ID in every event to reconstruct cause and effect.

At the boundary, thin synchronous APIs accept commands, validate, store and publish. Events drive the business logic, and queries read views the order service keeps updated from the same events, so the furious refresh of the order status page returns fast. His final advice: start small, and if you have an HTTP estate, simply begin publishing events alongside it.

## Who should watch

Developers starting their first event-driven service, and teams whose event bus has quietly become a distributed monolith. Bring a pizza.

Title: An Amazon product manager's playbook, from idea to sunsetting
Description: Tanvi Mishra (Amazon) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on product leadership, from seven development phases and data-driven roadmaps to retiring products
Body:
Engineers spend a lot of time on the receiving end of roadmaps and rarely see how they are made. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Tanvi Mishra, Product & Strategy Head at Amazon, lays out product leadership as she has practised it in nearly seven years at the company, from Amazon's launches in the Netherlands, Sweden and Poland to her later work: seven phases of product development, four traits that make a product leader, and the techniques Amazon uses to manage a product long after launch.

Honest scope: this is an introduction to product management, not a cloud native talk. It suits engineers moving towards product or tech lead roles, and anyone who wants to know what their PM is optimising for.

## What does a product manager actually own?

She names four responsibilities. Strategy, aligning the product with business goals. Vision, the long-term picture that keeps a team building things that last. Roadmap planning, the plan of enhancements and milestones over time. And stakeholder management, which she calls the key part of delivering any product, because success comes from partnerships across development teams, leadership and cross-functional groups.

## Seven phases, and the last one never ends

Her product development cycle runs: idea generation, market research (validating needs and pain points, assessing competition), conceptualisation (a concrete concept grounded in that research), design and planning (features, architecture and roadmap), prototyping (alpha or beta versions to catch problems early), testing and refinement with user feedback, and finally launch with post-launch monitoring.

She stresses that last step. Shipping is the start of the measurement, not the end of the work.

## Four traits for Leadership 2.0

- **Visionary thinking**: anticipating market shifts and adjusting the roadmap before they arrive.
- **Adaptability**: products go obsolete and customer requirements change, so strategy has to change with them.
- **Communication**: the vision cannot live only in your head; it has to be shared and documented for everyone on the journey.
- **Empathy**: her personal favourite, because it makes customer pain points easier to see and team dynamics easier to manage.

## How do you run the team and the roadmap?

Her three recurring challenges are communication gaps across many stakeholders, timeline pressure (balancing speed against quality, and asking whether customers need the thing at all), and resource allocation with conflicting priorities. Her countermeasures: collaborative tools (Jira, Slack, Confluence) with clear owners and timelines, agile methods such as Scrum or Kanban, and a culture where people feel safe sharing ideas. She also brings up Amazon's two-pizza teams: small, autonomous groups with enough people to deliver and few enough to avoid bureaucracy.

For prioritisation she uses business impact assessment, strategic alignment with long-term company goals, and user feedback to sort features into must-haves and items that can wait six to twelve months. At Amazon, she notes, user experience often wins over short-term profitability when the two conflict.

"As a product manager, data is the coolest tool and absolutely it is a non negotiable tool for developing great products," Tanvi Mishra said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. Her core metrics are user engagement (time in app, feature usage, click-through), conversion, customer satisfaction measured by NPS, and retention.

## What happens after launch?

Three lifecycle techniques, each with an Amazon example:

- **Sunsetting**: retiring what no longer fits, like the Kindle Voyage, discontinued as customer preferences and Kindle technology moved on.
- **Pivoting**: Amazon Echo started as a voice-activated assistant and grew into a smart home hub.
- **Continuous iteration**: Prime keeps adding benefits and features based on feedback.

Engineers will recognise the sunsetting point from their own world. Deprecating a service is a product decision too, and it goes better when someone owns it.

## Who should watch

Engineers stepping into product, tech lead or engineering manager roles, and teams who want a shared vocabulary with their PMs. Experienced product managers will mostly find a tidy recap; her reading list starts with Marty Cagan's Inspired.

Title: Turning every plant worker into a risk hunter, with points and seasons
Description: Ruslan Zaripov (KRiT) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on RiskHunter, a gamified app that crowdsources industrial safety hazards from every employee
Body:
A metallurgical plant or refinery can cover more than ten square kilometres, and one safety officer with a checklist will not see every loose guard or leaking steam pipe. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Ruslan Zaripov, CEO of KRiT, presents RiskHunter, his company's mobile app that turns hazard spotting into a game for every employee, and argues that bottom-up safety crowdsourcing beats top-down compliance.

It is a product talk about KRiT's own system, short and practical. It is also one of the rare talks where gamification is about keeping people alive rather than shipping more commits.

## What is wrong with conventional risk management?

He starts with a number: 5,486 fatal work injuries in the United States in 2022, up 5.7% from 5,190 in 2021, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Then four reasons the usual approach plateaus:

- **Static policies and procedures** that emphasise compliance over building a safety culture.
- **Periodic inspections** that are time-consuming and miss emerging or unforeseen risks.
- **Learning from the past**: analysing incidents after they happen rather than finding hazards before they hurt someone.
- **Limited employee engagement**: workers follow the rules but aren't part of the strategy.

The alternative he calls safety crowdsourcing, where every employee is a sensor. "So the focus safety is first and productivity is second," Ruslan Zaripov said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024.

## How does the app work?

The loop is simple. Spot a risk, take a photo, add a comment and a category, and send it to the risk manager for that area. The manager validates it, creates a work order, and after the fix attaches a photo to the report. The reporter gets a notification and points. His examples include rotating equipment that got a guard and a damaged steam pipe that was repaired.

He insists the feedback step is the heart of the system: "Because if there is no feedback, then the employees, they quickly lose the interest in this application." Anyone who has filed a ticket into a void will agree.

## Which motivation works better?

RiskHunter runs two models. Material motivation trades points for prizes: vouchers, online cinema subscriptions, sports gear, gift certificates. Personal motivation uses badges and levels inspired by fitness apps, for example a medal for reporting five or more risks in a month. He says intangible rewards work better in the long term, so that is where KRiT now puts its focus.

## Hunting seasons, quests and geofenced briefs

The gamification layer has a few clever mechanics:

- **Hunting seasons** award extra points for one hazard type at a time, such as falls from height, electrical or equipment safety, so a plant can spend two weeks on electrical issues, or focus on slips after rain.
- **Competitions** between plants and between teams within a plant. He reports people getting genuinely keen to finish first.
- **Tasks** that earn points for safety training, exams and surveys, integrated with the corporate learning management system.
- **A morning safety quest** pushed as a notification: a tip, a short video or a quiz of the day, while people are fresh.
- **Location-based safety briefs**: walk into a warehouse zone and get its safety information, with a read confirmation.

Managers get dashboards of elimination ratios and trending risk types, such as slips and trips or exposure to harmful substances, and work high-priority risks first.

## Does it work?

KRiT's case figures, from one large industrial enterprise in 2021-2022: more than 22,000 users, more than 180,000 potential risks identified, more than 150,000 eliminated, and 583 risks of possible fatal injury found and removed. He claims a 25% reduction in injuries and a 50% reduction in fatal injuries. These are the vendor's own numbers, presented without a control group or methodology, so treat them as a promising case rather than a study.

## Who should watch

Anyone building internal tools that depend on voluntary participation, from incident reporting to blameless postmortems, and especially teams in manufacturing, energy or logistics. The lessons on close-the-loop feedback and rotating focus transfer neatly to software.

Title: One External Secrets Operator for the whole cluster fleet, not one per cluster
Description: Gianluca Mardente (Cisco Systems) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on syncing secrets once into a management cluster and fanning them out to a fleet with Sveltos
Body:
The External Secrets Operator works beautifully on one Kubernetes cluster. Install it on fifty and you have fifty copies of the credentials it uses to reach your secrets manager, and fifty places to update when they rotate. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Gianluca Mardente, Principal Engineer at Cisco Systems, shows a tidier pattern: run the operator once in a management cluster, and let Sveltos, a Kubernetes add-on controller, distribute the resulting secrets to every managed cluster.

It is a short, focused talk: one problem, two open source tools, one architecture. Good value if you run a fleet.

## Why use a secrets manager at all?

He covers the basics quickly. A secret is anything you want kept confidential: API keys, passwords, certificates, SSH keys. A secrets management system gives you strong encryption (never plaintext, authorised users only), one place to create, rotate and delete secrets, and audit logs of who accessed what and when. That last one matters for compliance and is where any incident investigation starts.

The catch is that the secrets manager does not live in your cluster, so something inside the cluster has to bridge the gap.

## How does External Secrets Operator do it?

The External Secrets Operator is an open source operator that integrates with AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, IBM Cloud Secrets Manager and more. Given credentials for, say, Google Cloud Secret Manager, it creates a native Kubernetes Secret with matching content, and when you update the value in the secrets manager (the only place you should edit it) it notices the drift and updates the Kubernetes Secret.

## What breaks with a fleet?

The obvious move is one operator per cluster. "But that is the wrong approach. It's not scalable and error prone," Gianluca Mardente said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. You configure it N times, and a credential change means N updates.

## Sveltos does the fan-out

Sveltos runs in a management cluster. It has built-in support for Cluster API clusters, which it discovers on its own, and other clusters (GKE, Civo, Rancher and more) can be registered. Its only requirement is network connectivity from the management cluster to the managed ones.

What gets deployed where is declared in a ClusterProfile custom resource:

- **clusterSelector**, a label selector picking target clusters, for example every cluster carrying a given environment label.
- **helmCharts**, deployed to every matching cluster (his example installs Kyverno 2.6.0).
- **kustomizationRefs**, directories of Kustomize files that Sveltos renders and applies.
- **policyRefs**, ConfigMaps or Secrets whose data holds Kubernetes resources in YAML or JSON.

Anything can also be a template, instantiated at deploy time from resources in the management cluster. The slides note that Sveltos needs the right RBAC to fetch those resources.

## The combined flow

Put both tools in the management cluster. External Secrets Operator syncs a secret from Google Cloud Secret Manager into the management cluster; Sveltos watches that Secret and copies it into every managed cluster, in his demo a GKE cluster and a Cluster API one. Update the value in Secret Manager and the change ripples through: the operator updates the management copy, Sveltos sees the change and updates every managed cluster.

One source of truth, one set of credentials for the secrets manager, and a fleet that stays in sync. The trade-off, which the talk doesn't dwell on, is that the management cluster now holds every secret the fleet needs, so it deserves the strictest protection you have.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers running more than a handful of clusters, especially with Cluster API. If you have one cluster, the External Secrets Operator half is a fine primer and you can stop there.

Title: Your Spark driver on Kubernetes is a naked pod, and Incorta wrapped it
Description: Ahmed Gaber and Nadine Khaled (Incorta) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on Spark-on-Kubernetes pain points and Chidori, their cluster manager for Spark jobs
Body:
Run Spark on Kubernetes in cluster mode and your driver becomes a pod that no Deployment, StatefulSet or ReplicaSet owns. If it dies, the job dies, and nothing brings it back. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Ahmed Gaber, Cloud Engineering Manager at Incorta, and Nadine Khaled, Software Engineer at Incorta, walk through that and six other problems with Spark on Kubernetes, then show Chidori, the AI/ML cluster management platform Incorta built to host drivers, queue jobs and make them observable.

It is a vendor talk in the useful sense: half of it is a clear list of pitfalls that apply whether or not you ever touch Chidori.

## What does Kubernetes give Spark?

Ahmed Gaber starts with the mechanics. A client submits a job; in cluster mode the driver runs as a pod and asks Kubernetes for executor pods, which the scheduler places as capacity allows. The wins are real: cluster autoscaling so nodes aren't idling, dynamic allocation so executors scale in and out within an application, spot nodes for big savings, and fast local SSDs for Spark's scratch space.

"Also we notice most of spark bottlenecks come from the shuffling issues," Ahmed Gaber said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, which is why the scratch-space tip matters more than it sounds.

## Seven ways it hurts

The challenges section is the part worth bookmarking:

1. **The naked pod.** The driver is a single point of failure with no controller to restart it.
2. **Driver pod scatter.** Drivers end up spread across nodes, and those leftover pods stop the autoscaler from scaling nodes down, which eats the cost savings.
3. **Startup overhead.** Waiting for a new node, then for a driver pod to install heavy Python libraries and configuration before the job starts.
4. **The default scheduler.** kube-scheduler was designed for scale-out microservices. It lacks batch scheduling, multiple queues and gang scheduling, which distributed AI and ML workloads need.
5. **Dependency management.** Wheels, eggs, JARs and frameworks pile into ever-larger container images that deploy slowly and need constant compatibility tracking.
6. **Topology awareness.** The scheduler places pods on resource requests and affinities, but node conditions such as disk pressure or throttling also matter, so node and pod affinities have to be combined carefully.
7. **Integration and monitoring.** The Spark UI and history server see jobs, stages and tasks, but not how the cluster behaved around them, and spark-submit is a CLI that third-party tools struggle to drive.

## How does Chidori address them?

Chidori's server is itself a Kubernetes Deployment that hosts Spark drivers, so the platform's availability guarantees cover the driver. An API server exposes create, delete, list and get-logs operations to spark-submit and to third-party tools. Jobs land in a queue, with interfaces for RabbitMQ, Google Cloud Pub/Sub and Azure, and admins cap how many drivers run at once and how much memory and CPU they may consume. A scheduler pulls jobs when capacity allows and starts a goroutine for each, while a core engine tracks the lifecycle and stores metadata for monitoring and auditing.

It submits to several Spark back ends: Incorta, plain Kubernetes and Databricks. A Spark Connect layer serves clients, and it fits alongside MLflow and Kubeflow. The pitch is that data scientists focus on models while Chidori handles the infrastructure.

## What does the demo show?

Nadine Khaled installs it with Helm charts and checks the pieces: the Chidori server Deployment, a RabbitMQ StatefulSet for the queue, and the Chidori core Deployment for monitoring. Python packages such as TensorFlow are managed by the platform rather than installed per job, and driver memory is chosen per job. The monitoring UI filters jobs by status, date, schema and table, shows a job's history as a chart of load durations, downloads driver logs, opens the Spark history server, and generates signed shareable links so a colleague can see a job's history without credentials.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers running Spark on Kubernetes, especially the ones who have watched an autoscaler refuse to drain a node because of one lonely driver. The challenge list is general; the solution is Incorta's.

Title: Your platform team's job is DevEx, not running Kubernetes
Description: Christian Denich and Robert Hoffmann (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on working backwards from developers with DevEx, then GenAI development companions
Body:
Platform teams love to name themselves after what they run: the Kafka team, the Kubernetes team. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Robert Hoffmann, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, and Christian Denich, Customer Solutions at AWS, argue that this identity is where platform engineering starts to go wrong. Their alternative: compose cloud and SaaS, build only what you must, and spend the freed-up capacity measuring and improving developer experience, with GenAI development companions as one of the tools.

Robert Hoffmann takes the first half (platforms and the DevEx framework), Christian Denich the second (GenAI). Both work at AWS, and the demos show an AWS assistant, Amazon Q, so calibrate accordingly. The first half stands on its own regardless of vendor.

## How do platform teams end up in a downward spiral?

The starting point is Werner Vogels' 2006 rule, you build it, you run it, and the cognitive load it put on developers facing the sprawl of the CNCF ecosystem. Platforms fix that by centralising expertise while decentralising innovation, as Peter Gillard-Moss of ThoughtWorks put it. But Robert Hoffmann lists six steps of what he calls the downward spiral of platform engineering:

1. Prioritising the wrong work streams and features, because you are not close enough to your developers.
2. Reinventing the wheel with undifferentiated services.
3. Spending most of your resources operating them: your own Kubernetes clusters, your own Kafka clusters.
4. Clinging to those services when they should be deprecated, because the team's identity is attached to them.
5. Believing you are good at building abstractions, without designing for the moment they fail and dump the full stack trace on someone.
6. Only measuring the services you already have, which builds an echo chamber.

On identity he is blunt: "That's our job. It's not our job to run a Kubernetes cluster per se," Robert Hoffmann said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, the job being developer productivity. He also points viewers to Charity Majors' talk on the perils, pitfalls and pratfalls of platform engineering, and her line that a platform org should wrap and package infrastructure needs while running as little infra as possible.

## What does working backwards with DevEx look like?

The DevEx framework, from Abi Noda, Margaret-Anne Storey, Nicole Forsgren and Michaela Greiler (the people behind DORA and SPACE), models developers along three dimensions: feedback loops, cognitive load and flow state. Combine it with Amazon's working-backwards process (five customer questions, a press release and FAQ written before anything is built) and you get a concrete plan:

- **Perceptions first**, through surveys or interviews. Are you satisfied with how long it takes to validate a local change? How easy is it to debug production? What keeps you out of flow?
- **Workflow metrics** to ground those answers, such as code review turnaround and time to get a change to production, which catch teams that have settled into their misery.
- **KPIs** as north-star measures, such as the perceived ease of delivering software, to check that each change moves things the right way.

The output is a minimum lovable product, and it may be much cheaper than expected: a wiki page, a few well documented infrastructure as code templates, or room to try GenAI companions.

## Why a coding companion is not enough

Christian Denich brings the numbers. Citing McKinsey, he notes that about 75% of the estimated annual impact of GenAI comes from four functions, software engineering among them. Coding companions help (the slides quote 27% more likely to complete a task and 57% faster on average), yet he guesses adoption in German enterprises is below 20%.

Then the statistic that reframes the talk: "The typical developer only spends 4 hours and 21 minutes coding, and that's per week," Christian Denich said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. That is 52 minutes a day, and Gartner puts 73% of developer time on running and maintaining applications against 27% on innovation.

So the target is a development companion across the whole lifecycle. His demos show it summarising an app from internal documentation, drafting a Jira user story, checking whether services are allow-listed under the company's service control policies, planning and implementing a feature with tests, explaining a failed test as a permissions problem and generating the CLI command to fix it, and upgrading old Java code through a managed transformation job. He also introduces knowledge discovery efficiency, a 0 to 100 score for how much a developer still has to learn to finish a task.

The closing line ties both halves together: spend less time building the perfect abstraction, and let a companion explain the imperfect one.

## Who should watch

Platform leads deciding what to build next, and anyone who suspects their internal platform is measured by how many services it runs. The GenAI half is a product tour; the DevEx half is the keeper.

Title: Your platform team is building Atlas when it should build dark matter
Description: Asanka Abeysinghe (WSO2) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on platformless engineering, where the internal developer platform fades from developers' focus
Body:
Enterprise application teams spend their time on Kubernetes, service meshes and microservice resiliency instead of the applications the business asked for. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Asanka Abeysinghe, CTO of WSO2, argues for platformless: the platform still exists, but like dark matter it holds everything together without anyone having to look at it, so developers can get back to shipping digital experiences.

It is a 20-minute concept talk from a vendor. The ideas are general, and the last stretch shows where WSO2's own product, Choreo, fits. Worth knowing going in.

## What is the problem with platforms?

He opens with Atlas holding up the world, which is how the platform looks inside most enterprises: everything an IT team does depends on it. The trouble is who carries it. In the CTO clubs he joins in the Bay Area, the talk is about teams consumed by infrastructure.

"The problem is application development teams are focusing on building a platform rather than delivering applications," Asanka Abeysinghe said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024.

His layering explains why that matters. On top sit digital experiences, owned by product owners. Below is the business platform, owned by the chief architect and application architects. At the bottom is the internal developer platform (or portal), the domain of platform engineering teams. Competitive advantage comes from the top two. The internal developer platform is technical plumbing that looks much the same in every company, so investing your best engineers there buys little differentiation.

## The delivery pipeline is not the whole platform

He splits the internal developer platform into an infrastructure and delivery layer and an enterprise software engineering layer. Most platform teams build the first and neglect the second. When developers aren't productive on the platform, they drift back to shadow IT and build outside it.

The engineering layer covers both development time and runtime. At development time there is API design and a marketplace where services are published for discovery and consumption, with domain-driven design grouping workloads. At runtime the same grouping shows up as cells, his cell-based architecture: components inside a cell talk over a mesh, and authentication, authorization and entitlements around each cell build a zero trust environment.

## What makes an experience platformless?

Four ingredients, with platform engineering as the foundation:

- **API-first** everywhere: data, domain and edge APIs, exposed, secured and published without the application team hand-crafting the plumbing.
- **Cloud native middleware**: the old word still matters, but the capabilities (security, service mesh, message brokers, API gateways) are now disappearing into code and infrastructure, and the platform should provide them.
- **Developer experience**: self-service, wired into the organisation's approved pipelines by default, and open to developers' own tools, whether that's VS Code, a CLI or system APIs for extending the platform.
- **Platform engineering** that covers the full lifecycle (create, run, manage, deprecate) with observability and debugging, and that includes people who understand application development, not only DevOps and SRE skills.

His best analogy is email. Companies used to run their own mail, chat and calendar servers, with LDAP, spam filters and backups. Now they sign up for Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 and just collaborate. Platformless aims for the same shift for developers: just add developers.

## Build or buy?

Building means a dedicated platform team that treats the platform as a product and keeps maintaining it; handing it over and walking away does not work. A framework such as Backstage is one starting point, with API gateways, marketplaces, cells and a service mesh added on top. Buying means a SaaS internal developer platform; his examples include hosted Backstage providers, Harness, Red Hat Developer Hub and WSO2 Choreo. Whichever you choose, check it against the four ingredients.

He closes with the Platformless manifesto, written with Sanjiva Weerawarana and Paul Fremantle and published on GitHub under CC BY 4.0, with pull requests welcome.

## Who should watch

CTOs, architects and platform leads who suspect their platform team has become the product. Engineers looking for implementation detail will find a framework and a vocabulary rather than code.

Title: Scalability is the art of spending money on purpose
Description: Gaurav Raje (MoneyLion) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on scalability vs efficiency on AWS and picking fixed, auto scaling or serverless by demand shape
Body:
Scalability and efficiency both get you more requests per second, and teams mix them up all the time. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Gaurav Raje, Engineering Manager at MoneyLion and author of the O'Reilly book Security and Microservice Architecture on AWS, draws the line cleanly: efficiency gets more out of the resources you have, scalability means adding resources, and on AWS the real question is which kind of scaling your demand curve deserves.

He labels it a beginner talk, and it is: a well-organised tour for engineers who are about to make their first architecture trade-offs on AWS, built around one running example, an e-commerce site that sells sunglasses.

## You can't have all six

He judges every system on six dimensions: efficiency, scalability, availability, security, cost and simplicity. His rule of thumb is that you get at most four, often three, and sometimes one or two. Choosing which to give up is, by his definition, the architect's job.

The AWS shared responsibility model is the main lever. He uses Albert Barron's pizza-as-a-service analogy: cook at home and you control the gluten-free base and the buffalo mozzarella but also wash the dishes; eat out and you control nothing but worry about nothing; takeout sits in between. Managed and serverless services sit on the same spectrum, trading flexibility for responsibility.

## Is it scalability or efficiency?

When the e-commerce site has its overnight success and RAM is through the roof, you can add memory or servers (scalability), or make the code handle more with the same hardware, for example by adding caching (efficiency). You want efficiency first, but it hits diminishing returns, and the last thing a growing business wants is to turn away customers when the extra resources were one API call away.

Scaling has a price beyond the bill. The first casualty is simplicity: you scaled, and now you have a Frankenstein application with cables going everywhere that somebody has to tame.

## Vertical first, horizontal when it runs out

Vertical scaling means a bigger box: more RAM, CPU or throughput, a switch to a memory or compute optimised instance at a similar cost, or moving a database off a shared cluster onto dedicated hardware. No code changes, and in the cloud it takes minutes. But instance sizes have ceilings and the returns flatten fast.

A small pricing aside is the most useful minute of the talk. Walking through on-demand prices for the t4g family, he shows that each tier step tracks the extra gigabytes of memory, while the jump from two to four vCPUs between t4g.large and t4g.xlarge does not appear to cost anything extra. Memory is what AWS charges for, so memory is what to optimise when projecting costs.

Horizontal scaling needs an application built for it. "A fun joke one of my old boss used to tell me was nine couples can't have one baby in one month," Gaurav Raje said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. Adding a server only helps if the work can actually be split.

## Fixed capacity, auto scaling or serverless?

Over-provisioning wastes money on day one and still runs out on day one hundred. Auto scaling teaches AWS when to add a server, say at 90% average CPU or 85% RAM, but it is still stepwise, it can lag or overshoot, and the logic itself adds complexity. Serverless (Lambda, Aurora Serverless, DynamoDB) hands scaling to Amazon, within limits, as long as your workload fits its shape.

His closing case study puts Aurora's three modes against three demand curves:

- **Flat, sustained demand**: a fixed-capacity cluster. Cheapest and simplest; serverless would mean paying a premium for scaling you never use.
- **Steady with a predictable lunchtime spike**: time-based auto scaling, up at 11:00 and down at 13:30, rather than paying the serverless premium all day.
- **Bursty and unpredictable**: serverless, so you don't build and maintain complicated scaling logic yourself.

Same database, three right answers. That is the talk's real lesson.

## Who should watch

Developers and new architects on AWS who want a clear vocabulary for scaling conversations, and anyone who has to explain to finance why the serverless option is not always the cheap one. Seasoned AWS architects will find little new.

Title: Your logistic regression has opinions. Bayes makes it show its doubts
Description: Salman Saeed Khan (Afiniti Europe Technologies) at Conf42 Python 2024 on probabilistic programming and why coefficients should be distributions
Body:
A logistic regression hands you one number per coefficient and no hint of how sure it is. At Conf42 Python 2024, Salman Saeed Khan, Associate Director at Afiniti Europe Technologies, gives a compact introduction to probabilistic programming: treat unknown parameters as random variables, sample their posterior with MCMC, and get predictions that come with their own uncertainty. The demo fits the same small model twice, once the classic way and once in Stan from Python.

It is a short, theory-first talk. One note on scope: the abstract promises PyMC3, but the demo in the recording is built with Stan.

## What is wrong with point estimates?

Salman lists four gaps in conventional machine learning. As Salman Saeed Khan said at Conf42 Python 2024, "the fundamental challenge in conventional machine learning and AI techniques is the lack of uncertainty quantification." Models give a single answer without saying how reliable it is. They are data hungry and want correctly labelled data. They have no framework for encoding expert domain knowledge or prior beliefs. And they keep getting more opaque while the public asks for more accountability on decisions derived from data and AI.

What he wants instead is a framework that encodes expert knowledge, copes with limited data, returns predictions with their uncertainty and stays explainable.

## Frequentist versus Bayesian, in one paragraph

In the frequentist view, parameters are fixed unknown constants, and uncertainty lives in the data-generation process, handled through confidence intervals and p-values about long-run frequencies. In the Bayesian view, parameters are random variables with probability distributions, so the uncertainty sits in the parameter itself. Bayes' theorem does the bookkeeping: start from a prior, multiply by the likelihood of the observed data, and divide by the marginal likelihood, which is the normalising constant that keeps the posterior a proper distribution.

The difference shows up at prediction time. Non-Bayesian inference picks the parameter value that maximises the likelihood and predicts with that single value. Bayesian inference predicts by averaging over the whole posterior distribution.

## Why do you need MCMC?

Because the normalising integral is usually intractable. In a high-dimensional parameter space there is no closed-form posterior, and numerical integration is too expensive. The workaround is to stop computing the posterior and start sampling from it: "So if we are able to sample from this posterior distribution, we effectively have its posterior distribution," he said. With N samples, a prediction is just the average of the predictions under each sample.

Markov chain Monte Carlo does the sampling: build a Markov chain whose equilibrium distribution is the posterior and record its states. The talk lists the usual samplers: Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, the No-U-Turn Sampler and Sequential Monte Carlo.

That leads to his definition. In his words, "probabilistic programming is merely a programming framework for bayesian statistics." The workflow has three steps: identify the unknown parameters and give them priors (that is where expert knowledge goes in), specify the likelihood of the observed data as a function of those parameters, then run a suitable sampler to get chains that approximate the posterior.

## The demo: height, weight and a binary label

The dataset holds height, weight and a binary is-female flag for a population sample. First comes a standard logistic regression, which returns a coefficient each for height and weight and nothing about their range.

Then the same problem in Stan. Salman walks through the program's blocks (data, transformed data, parameters, transformed parameters, model, generated quantities), of which a simple model needs only a few. The model block sets priors on the intercept and the two coefficients, then a Bernoulli-logit likelihood on the binary target. From Python he compiles the model, passes the data as a dictionary, runs the MCMC sampler and gets a series of samples for every parameter. From those you can read the mean, median and spread of each coefficient, and predictions can use the full distribution instead of a single number, so each prediction carries its own uncertainty.

## Who should watch

Python developers and data scientists who know scikit-learn and have heard Bayesian methods are worth the bother but never saw the bridge from Bayes' theorem to working code. Experienced Stan or PyMC users won't find new material; it is an introduction, and the Stan documentation is where he sends you for more complex models.

For more on uncertainty, try [Andrei Stroganov and Andrei Visochan on fast confidence estimation for classification and regression models](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Andrei_Stroganov_Andrei_Visochan_estimation_regression_confidence) and [Jose Manuel Ortega's tips and tricks for data science projects with Python](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2023_Jose_Manuel_Ortega_tips_tricks_data_science_projects).

Title: Stop inner-joining your evidence away in Spark
Description: Gokul Prabagaren (CapitalOne) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on swapping Spark inner joins for left outer joins so every dropped row can explain itself
Body:
If a Spark pipeline decides a credit card transaction does not earn rewards, somebody in a regulated bank will eventually ask why. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Gokul Prabagaren, Engineering Manager in Card Loyalty at CapitalOne, explains how his team's rewards job could not answer that question, and the small change that fixed it: stop filtering rows with inner joins and start enriching them with left outer joins.

It is a short, focused talk about one design pattern, told through a production system that processes millions of credit card transactions a day.

## What does the rewards pipeline do?

The platform behind CapitalOne card rewards reads daily transactions, applies account-specific eligibility rules (is this account allowed to earn right now?), then transaction-specific rules (is this a purchase, or a payment that earns nothing?), computes the earn and persists it. It runs on Apache Spark, and every rewards product flows through it.

## The filtering approach, and why it bit them

The first version did what most Spark code does. Each stage was an inner join against the rules data, so non-matching rows simply vanished. In his ten-transaction example, five survive the account rules, two survive the transaction rules, and those two get their points.

Fast, tidy and impossible to debug. Everything happened in memory, so once the job ran there was no trace of what happened to the eight rows that dropped out, or at which stage. For a bank, that is not an academic gap.

"Being in a regulated industry, we really need to know mainly what has happened to the transactions which we really did not provide earned," Gokul Prabagaren said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024.

The usual reply from Spark people is to add counts after each stage. He takes that apart in two lines. Counts are expensive actions that a job working on millions or billions of rows may not afford at every stage. And a count tells you how many rows disappeared, never why.

## Enrich instead of filter

The pivot is a left outer join at each stage. Instead of dropping the rows that fail a rule, the pipeline pulls the context the rule needs into new columns: the account status from the accounts data, the category from the transaction data, then a boolean flag per stage saying whether the row is eligible for the next step. As he puts it, the rows are not changing, the columns are growing.

The final computation selects rows where the flags are true and lands on exactly the same result as the filtering version. The difference is that the rejected rows are still there, carrying the status and category that explain their fate. That gives you:

- the state of each record at every stage, preserved in the original data set for later analysis,
- per-stage flags that say why a row was dropped, not just that it was,
- no need for costly count actions to reconstruct what happened.

It is a small idea, and that is its appeal. You trade some width in your DataFrames for a pipeline that can testify about itself, which is a bargain any on-call engineer who has been asked where a customer's points went will take.

## Is it in production?

Yes. The team shipped the first version with filtering, then switched to enriching early on. The enriching job is the one now processing millions of credit card transactions daily and awarding millions of miles, cash and points to CapitalOne customers.

## Who should watch

Data engineers running multi-stage Spark jobs where someone, sooner or later, will ask why a record did not make it through: finance, compliance, billing, loyalty. It is an intermediate pattern talk with worked examples rather than a wall of code. If you already keep audit columns in your pipelines, you will mostly be nodding along.

Title: Cloud agnostic by running everything in Kubernetes is a worse data center
Description: Abhay Dutt Paroha (Schlumberger) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on strategic lock-in, facades and tenant context for cloud-agnostic multi-tenant SaaS
Body:
The popular recipe for avoiding cloud lock-in is to put everything in containers on Kubernetes and walk away. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Abhay Dutt Paroha, Software Team Leader at Schlumberger, explains why that recipe quietly turns your team into the operators of a home-made data center, and what he does instead when building cloud-agnostic, multi-tenant SaaS: strategic lock-in, a facade layer, and a tenant ID that travels through every request, log line and metric.

He speaks from building a few of these systems for real-time upstream operational data in the oilfield, so the advice is shaped by teams that had to keep them running.

## Why is running everything on Kubernetes not enough?

He sets up the straw man and then knocks it over. Need messaging? RabbitMQ or Kafka in a container. Cache? A Redis cluster in containers. A database, object storage, monitoring? PostgreSQL, MinIO and the ELK stack, all in containers. Every one of them now needs patching, upgrading and babysitting.

"Simple answer. Use Kubernetes and you are done," Abhay Dutt Paroha said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, before pointing out that one of the reasons companies moved to the cloud in the first place was to cut engineering effort. Running your own copies of managed services reverses that. In his words, instead of using what the provider offers, "we are creating an often worse data center or infrastructure."

He adds the less obvious leaks in the abstraction:

- **Stateful workloads** on StatefulSets bring their own storage, networking, security and monitoring headaches.
- **Data residency**: a system for a bank has GDPR to satisfy, so the provider's actual data center map matters, and so do failover and latency.
- **Networking differences**: Google Cloud's VPC is a global resource, unlike AWS and Azure. Ingress is free, egress is not, and each provider prices it differently.
- **Infrastructure as code** bakes the provider in. Moving Terraform from GCP to Azure, he compares to porting an application from Java to Go: the concepts survive, the code does not.

## Strategic lock-in plus a facade

His fix has two halves. First, accept lock-in where it is cheap to undo: use managed products that have a counterpart on the other clouds (Cloud SQL and Azure Database for PostgreSQL, GKE and EKS, Bigtable and DynamoDB, Knative for serverless), and keep Kubernetes for running your own services rather than your databases and brokers.

Second, keep your own code ignorant of the provider. A cloud-agnostic microservice talks to a messaging facade, and the facade talks to a provider adapter for Pub/Sub, Azure Service Bus or SNS. Switching clouds means writing a new adapter while the service stays untouched. It is the classic Gang of Four facade, applied at the infrastructure seam.

## What changes when the app is multi-tenant?

The second half of the talk walks through the SaaS fundamentals: onboarding, authentication and authorization, data partitioning, tenant isolation, metering and billing, and tenant-aware operations. Tenancy touches every layer, from feature flags in the front end and throttling at the API gateway down to partitioning in the data layer.

The code difference is small and important. A plain API reads a key and queries DynamoDB; the SaaS version also reads a tenant ID from the request, because without it you cannot isolate data, meter usage or bill anyone. Options for carrying that tenant context include a JWT claim, a query string parameter, a custom header such as an x-tenant-id, or a separate lookup service, which he warns becomes a single point of failure.

Two practical habits follow. Put the code that reads the authorization header, gets the token and extracts the tenant ID in a shared library so every service does it the same way. And push the tenant context into structured logs and into metrics via an OpenTelemetry collector, so per-tenant behaviour is visible.

## Silo, pool or bridge?

For data partitioning he compares three models: a database per tenant (silo), a shared schema with an indexed tenant ID column (pool), and one database with a schema per tenant (bridge). He personally went with the bridge for the isolation it gives, while stressing it is a per-microservice decision driven by compliance, performance, data distribution and noisy neighbours. Isolation is a separate question: either every tenant gets its own environment, or a shared environment enforces isolation through runtime policies fetched from a tenant access manager before touching any resource.

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads designing a SaaS product that must run on more than one cloud, or that has just signed its second big customer with its own compliance rules. It is an architecture talk with diagrams and illustrative code, not a live demo.

Title: Your scanner found the bug a year ago. Codemodder writes the fix
Description: Dan D'Avella (Pixee) at Conf42 Python 2024 on Codemodder, an open-source framework that turns security tool findings into mergeable Python fixes
Body:
Most teams already run a security scanner. Far fewer act on what it finds. At Conf42 Python 2024, Dan D'Avella, Principal Engineer at Pixee and lead maintainer of the open-source Codemodder framework, argues that the fix itself has to be automated, and shows how Codemodder glues Semgrep-style detection to LibCST-based rewriting so the result lands as a diff a developer will actually merge.

## Why aren't security findings getting fixed?

Dan opens with two figures from Veracode's State of Software Security 2024 report: roughly 63% of applications have flaws in first-party code, and 42% of all applications have flaws that persist unremediated for longer than one year. Veracode calls that second number security debt. His point about the first one is that years of attention on third-party dependencies (Log4Shell and friends) let us forget the code we wrote ourselves.

Detection is not the bottleneck. There is no shortage of open-source and commercial scanners, and most people in the audience would admit to running at least one. Some smaller teams run none at all, and senior developers often believe they mostly write secure code already. Either way the backlog stays put, which is why Dan wants fixes applied automatically: merge fixes for the old findings, and catch new problems before they get merged in the first place.

## What makes a codemod different from a refactoring tool?

A codemod is code plus modification. As Dan D'Avella said at Conf42 Python 2024, "a code mod is code that is capable of changing or updating other code." The prior art is real: Facebook's codemod for large refactors with a human in the loop (no longer actively maintained), jscodeshift for JavaScript and TypeScript migrations, and Instagram's LibCST for parsing and transforming Python. None of them were built around security.

Codemodder's philosophy has three parts: fix problems found by other tools, tell a story that teaches the developer why the new code is safer, and keep changes small enough to approve at a glance. "So it doesn't really matter if we propose changes that nobody wants," he said. A fix nobody merges is just a more polite alert.

There are two flavours. Fix-only codemods consume results from tools such as Sonar, CodeQL or Semgrep, usually in SARIF. Find-and-fix codemods run Semgrep with Pixee's own rules, which gives teams without a security practice both halves in one tool. You install it with `pip install codemodder`, point it at a project, and it edits files on disk and writes a CodeTF file describing what changed.

## Which fixes does it ship?

The catalogue was at roughly 40 to 50 codemods. Dan walks through five:

- **Unsafe PyYAML loader** swapped for the safe loader, closing an arbitrary code execution path.
- **defusedxml** in place of the standard library XML parsers, which the Python docs themselves warn against for untrusted data. His personal favourite.
- **Unclosed resources** rewritten as context managers.
- **SQL built with f-strings** turned into parameterised queries.
- **List comprehensions** rewritten as generator expressions where possible, a memory win with a side of denial-of-service protection.

The last three look like trivial diffs and are not: he notes that the logic behind the resource-closing and SQL codemods is far more sophisticated than the change they produce.

## Detector, transformer, metadata

Each codemod has three parts. The detector finds the problem (a parser for external results, or Semgrep run directly). The transformer pipeline, built on LibCST, changes the code. The metadata tells the story: a name like `pixee:python/use-defusedxml`, a one-line summary, and a long-form description kept in a separate Markdown file so it doesn't clutter the code.

The defusedxml codemod exposes the hard part: the fix needs a new dependency. Requirements files are easy, but dependencies can live in `pyproject.toml`, `setup.cfg` or `setup.py`, and Codemodder has to pick the right one. "It's actually a bit harder to solve than the problem that dependabot has because they can just identify existing dependencies and update them," he said.

## Writing your own

The worked example is a secure-random codemod that replaces the `random` module with `secrets.SystemRandom`, using a Semgrep pattern that excludes code already on `SystemRandom`. The `on_result_found` callback calls `update_call_target`, adds the `secrets` import and removes the now unused `random` import. Run against pygoat, a deliberately vulnerable Python web application, the diff looks like a reviewer's suggestion. A simpler API squeezes the same codemod into 20-25 lines, while the lower-level path exposes LibCST's `leave_Call` for harder cases such as flipping `subprocess` calls to `shell=False`. Custom codemods load as plugins from a cookiecutter template.

He closes on open questions, not a roadmap: would developers trust an LLM to make security changes, and would the transparency of open-source rules survive the switch?

## Who should watch

Python developers with a pile of unresolved scanner findings, AppSec engineers tired of filing tickets, and anyone who has written a LibCST transformer and wondered how to make it reusable. It pairs well with [Ukanah Dean on Python security best practices](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2024_Ukanah_Dean_python_security_best_practices_protecting_common_vulnerabilities) from the same event, [Safeer C M on SAST foundations with open-source Semgrep](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Safeer_C_M_sast_open_source_semgrep) and [Joseph Hejderup on static analysis for dependency tools](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Joseph_Hejderup_going_beyond_metadata_adopting_static_analysis_dependency_tools).

Title: Build the Azure landing zone before the first workload lands
Description: Atif Siddiqui (Silicon Valley Bank) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on the Cloud Adoption Framework, landing zone design areas and Terraform rollout
Body:
Atif Siddiqui opens with an uncomfortable number: per HFS Research, which surveyed over 500 senior executives at some of the world's largest companies, only a third of enterprises are realising their cloud ambitions. In his Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 talk, the Senior Principal Software Engineer at Silicon Valley Bank argues that the fix starts before any workload moves: follow Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework, and build an Azure landing zone as the foundation for security and governance.

It is a short, condensed talk, by his own description a flavour of a very large topic, but it packs the framework, the design areas and a deployment recommendation into a few minutes.

## Why start with the Cloud Adoption Framework?

The Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) is Microsoft's lifecycle framework for cloud programs, and Atif walks its phases in order:

- **Strategy** asks why you are moving at all. Motivations fall into three groups: critical business events (exiting a data centre, a merger or acquisition), migration (cost savings, agility) and innovation (scaling to new markets or regions). They must tie to business outcomes.
- **Plan** turns that into action: assess the application portfolio for migration or modernization, align the people, and check skills, closing gaps with training.
- **Ready** picks an operating model (decentralized, centralized or distributed) and builds the landing zone.
- **Migrate** chooses between rehost (lift and shift), refactor and replatform per workload.
- **Innovate**, **Secure**, **Manage** and **Govern** follow: define business value with stakeholders and ship an MVP, protect data and IP, run each workload by its business criticality on cost and SLAs, and keep checking compliance iteratively.

His favourite part is the least technical. "Alignment, in my mind, is one of the most underrated elements of the framework," Atif Siddiqui said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, because the program only succeeds if every stakeholder shares the vision.

## Eight design areas, one foundation

A landing zone is his answer to the enterprise double bind of moving fast while keeping a strong security posture. It is an environment that follows key principles across eight design areas:

1. Azure billing and Microsoft Entra tenant, the top two levels of alignment.
2. Identity and access management, including separation of duties.
3. Network topology and connectivity, since most enterprises still have a data centre and need hybrid links.
4. Resource organization: consistent naming, tagging and subscription design.
5. Security, across network and workloads, with NIST and Microsoft's own benchmarks.
6. Management, led by cloud ops, where SLAs such as RTO and RPO get agreed with the business.
7. Governance, enforcing compliance and security requirements.
8. Platform automation and DevOps, where the platform team leads with infrastructure as code.

## Platform versus application landing zones

There are two kinds. The platform landing zone centralises shared foundations: identity, management and connectivity, often in a hub-and-spoke network. Application landing zones hold the subscriptions for workloads, split into online for internet-facing and corp for internal ones. Microsoft's reference layout adds two more management groups: decommissioned, for subscriptions on their way out, and sandbox, isolated from everything else so experiments can't leak into production.

## Portal, Bicep or Terraform?

Microsoft's landing zone accelerator can be deployed through the Azure portal, Bicep or HashiCorp Terraform. Atif picks Terraform because it has a huge presence in enterprises and suits a multi-cloud strategy. Microsoft publishes the modules in the Terraform registry and on GitHub, with examples tiered from level 100 to 400 (level 300 adds the hub-and-spoke topology). His advice from the slides: consume and configure the modules rather than customising them.

## Who should watch

Cloud platform teams and architects starting an Azure program in a regulated or large organisation, and anyone who has inherited a subscription sprawl and wants the target shape. It is a map, not a walkthrough: there is no live deployment, so follow up with Microsoft's CAF docs and the Terraform examples.
