Title: Stock ticks from Python to Kafka to Iceberg on a laptop
Description: Karin Wolok (Project Elevate) and Tim Spann (Cloudera) at Conf42 Python 2024 on stream processing with RisingWave, Kafka, NiFi and Iceberg
Body:
Getting stock prices into Kafka from Python takes a producer, a key and a send. Getting them into an Apache Iceberg table takes PyIceberg and a SQLite catalog on your laptop. At Conf42 Python 2024, Karin Wolok of Project Elevate and Tim Spann, Principal Developer Advocate at Cloudera, split a talk in two: a primer on stream processing with RisingWave, then a demo of Python feeding Kafka, Iceberg and Apache NiFi with live market data.

Honest scope: the title promises an LLM generating predictions, and the talk does not get there. What it delivers is the plumbing that would feed one, plus a good conceptual overview for anyone new to streaming.

## What is stream processing, and what can you query?

Karin Wolok starts from first principles. Streaming ingestion (Kafka, Redpanda, Pulsar, Amazon Kinesis) brings events in as they happen instead of in batches; stream processing transforms and computes on that data while it is in flight, before it is stored. The query types she walks through, each with an example:

- **Filtering**: pick log entries with errors that need immediate attention.
- **Aggregation**: average temperature over the last ten minutes of a sensor stream.
- **Joining streams**: combine click data with product data to understand behaviour.
- **Windowing**: total sales for each hour of the day over a week.
- **Pattern recognition**: a series of failed logins flagged as a possible breach.
- **Stateful processing**: track user sessions and detect when one goes idle.

Her point about why it matters is the one most streaming intros skip. As Karin Wolok said at Conf42 Python 2024: "The capabilities of what you can do with real time analytics go way beyond dashboards." Her example is LinkedIn telling you who viewed your profile so you can act on it: real-time insight handed to the end user, sometimes as a premium feature.

## Where does RisingWave fit?

RisingWave is an open source, distributed SQL stream processing database written in Rust. It reads from streaming sources, runs incremental computations, keeps materialized views updated as data arrives, and can store results itself or send them downstream. Storage and compute are separate and scale independently. Its pitch for newcomers is the learning curve: it speaks SQL and is Postgres compatible, so you do not need to learn a big new framework first. The architecture has a serving layer that parses and plans SQL, a processing layer, a metadata service coordinating the nodes, and a storage layer on object storage such as S3. Use cases: streaming ETL, real-time analytics and event-driven applications.

## How much Python does the pipeline need?

Tim Spann's half answers that with code. His framing for generative AI: models, large or small, need a lot of data, and Python plus NiFi gets that data cleaned and into the pipeline, whether it lands in a model, a vector store or a Kafka topic that RisingWave then reads. As Tim Spann said at Conf42 Python 2024, "a lot of it's enabled by Python."

The demos, with code in his GitHub repositories (PaK-Stocks and FLaNK-Py-Stocks):

- Pull quotes with the `yfinance` library, send each record to Kafka with a simple producer pointed at a broker running in Docker, and every 1,000 records append a batch to an Iceberg table through PyIceberg with a SQLite-backed catalog. Not for production, he notes, but you can learn the whole stack on a laptop without paying for S3.
- Inspect the resulting Parquet files with the Parquet command-line tools, no query engine needed.
- Stream trades from the Finnhub WebSocket API straight into Kafka, which he calls amazingly fast.

Iceberg is the part he is most enthusiastic about: a table format usually on Parquet whose metadata lets any engine read the same tables, and supports appends, schema changes and time travel, so you can ask what the data looked like two days ago.

## NiFi as the glue

The last demo is a NiFi flow driven from Slack. Ask for the current IBM stock price in a channel; a listener pushes the message to Kafka, a Python processor extracts the company name, Alpha Vantage turns it into a ticker symbol, Twelve Data returns the price, another Python processor fetches the company's Wikipedia page, and the answer goes back to Slack. NiFi, which started at the NSA in 2006 and became a top-level Apache project in 2015, contributes provenance (you can always show how a record got loaded) and prebuilt components for the boilerplate, leaving Python for the complex parts. His deeper look at NiFi's Python processors is a separate talk at the same event.

## Who should watch

Python developers who keep hearing Kafka, Iceberg and stream processing in the same sentence and want one session that shows how they connect. Skip it if you came for LLM-driven stock predictions.

Title: Write the handler once, move it from Lambda to Workers with Hono
Description: Nikolay Pryanishnikov (Station Labs) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on Hono, a TypeScript web framework built on web standard APIs that runs on any JS runtime
Body:
Moving an API from AWS Lambda to Cloudflare Workers, or from Node.js to Deno, usually means rewriting every handler, because each runtime invented its own request and response shapes. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Nikolay Pryanishnikov, Full Stack TypeScript Developer at Station Labs, shows why that is changing: runtimes are converging on the `Request` and `Response` objects from `fetch`, and Hono, a small web framework built only on those web standard APIs, runs the same code on Node.js, Deno, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, Vercel, Netlify, Lambda and Lambda@Edge.

The talk is in two halves: why JavaScript runtimes disagree, then a tour of Hono's features, with code for each.

## Why does the same handler not run everywhere?

He starts with the distinction people blur: an engine executes code (V8 in Chrome, Node.js and Deno; JavaScriptCore in Safari and Bun; SpiderMonkey in Firefox), while a runtime adds the event loop, libraries and APIs around it. Runtimes disagree on all of the latter. Reading a file is `readFile` from `fs/promises` with an encoding in Node.js and `Deno.readTextFile` in Deno. A Lambda handler receives `event` and `context` and returns a value; a Vercel Node.js handler receives `req` and `res` and calls `res.send`.

Worse, one provider can mean two runtimes. Vercel's Node.js and Edge runtimes need different code, and the Edge one accepts only ESM packages, not CommonJS. Serverless runtimes in general may limit npm packages, expose only web standard APIs, or block direct database connections.

The way out is WinterCG, a community group of Cloudflare, Vercel, Deno, Node.js and others working on runtime interoperability through shared web standard APIs. With `fetch`'s `Request` and `Response`, a handler takes a request and returns a new response, and the code moves.

## The forgotten return

His argument for the new API shape comes from production pain. With the `res.status(); res.send()` style, forget the `return` and execution carries on, sometimes writing a second response, and you find out from errors in production. Returning a `Response` makes that bug impossible. "If you are returning, you must return something," Nikolay Pryanishnikov said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, and once you return, execution stops.

## What Hono gives you on top

Hono, Japanese for flame, was created by Yusuke Wada, a developer advocate at Cloudflare. Nikolay's tour of it:

- **Portability.** Server to serverless and back, between runtimes and between hosts. On Node.js you need an adapter, one dependency and a line or two of code. You can also embed Hono in a Next.js project's API folder and later lift that folder out to stand alone without changes.
- **Speed.** Nikolay says it has the fastest router for Cloudflare Workers and for Deno, and even with the Node.js adapter it is three times faster than Express. There are five routers: RegExpRouter (the fastest), TrieRouter (supports all patterns), SmartRouter (the default, picks between those two), LinearRouter for one-shot environments like Fastly Compute, and PatternRouter, the smallest, for constrained environments.
- **Type safety and a generated client.** Export `typeof app` as a type, pass it to `hc` from `hono/client`, and you get a fully typed client for every endpoint's inputs and outputs. Nikolay calls it the killer feature: in a monorepo the frontend stays in sync with the API, and a public API can ship its client as an npm package.
- **Middleware.** `app.use(logger())`, CORS on a path, basic auth on POST only; built-ins for JWT, caching, compression, CSRF, ETag and secure headers, third-party ones for Sentry, tRPC and more. A custom middleware is one async function of `c` and `next`.
- **Validation and docs.** `zValidator` from `@hono/zod-validator` checks the query, body or params and hands you typed values via `c.req.valid()`. `OpenAPIHono` from `@hono/zod-openapi` records every route and serves OpenAPI docs at an endpoint like `/doc`, no generation step.

## Who should watch

TypeScript developers building APIs on serverless or edge platforms, and anyone who has been bitten by a platform's custom handler signature. The runtime half is a clear primer even if you never adopt Hono; the second half is a feature tour by an enthusiastic user, not the maintainer, so expect advocacy rather than trade-offs.

Title: Retiring the Jenkins box? A first AWS CodePipeline, click by click
Description: Prithvish Kovelamudi (Marqeta) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on why AWS-heavy teams can swap Jenkins for CodePipeline, with a live S3-to-EC2 pipeline
Body:
Somewhere in most AWS shops there is a Jenkins server that someone has to patch, back up and keep its plugins compatible. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Prithvish Kovelamudi, Software Engineer at Marqeta, makes the case that teams already invested in AWS can hand that job to AWS CodePipeline, and then builds a working pipeline from an S3 artifact to EC2 instances in the console.

This is a short, beginner-friendly session: about half comparison, half demo. If you have never opened CodePipeline, it gets you from an empty console to a running pipeline with no detours.

## What do you stop doing if you leave Jenkins?

Prithvish compares the two on five axes, Jenkins as the incumbent throughout:

- **Integration.** CodePipeline talks natively to Lambda, EC2, S3 and CloudFormation. Jenkins can reach the same services, but usually through third-party plugins and extra setup, which he counts as more points of failure.
- **Scaling.** CodePipeline scales with the demand on the pipeline. Jenkins needs someone to add agent nodes or reallocate resources.
- **Maintenance.** "Jenkins, on the other hand, requires periodic manual updates, backups and patching," Prithvish Kovelamudi said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, and plugins can bring compatibility issues and vulnerabilities with them. With a managed service, AWS handles updates, patches and backups.
- **Security.** IAM roles, service roles, AWS Secrets Manager and fine-grained access controls tie directly into the pipeline; matching that on Jenkins takes more plugins and configuration.
- **Cost.** Pay as you go suits variable workloads. Jenkins is free software, but the servers, patching and people's time keep costing money.

The comparison is one-sided by design, and the honest framing is in his own pitch: this is for organisations already heavily invested in the AWS ecosystem. Multi-cloud teams or those with deep Jenkins pipelines will want to weigh portability, which the talk doesn't cover.

## Three stages, one of them optional

The model is the one every CI/CD tool shares. A **source** stage supplies the code or artifact (S3, AWS CodeCommit or Amazon ECR). An optional **build** stage compiles and packages, typically with AWS CodeBuild. A **deploy** stage ships the result through AWS CodeDeploy, Amazon ECS, or ECS blue/green deployments. The sample architecture he shows pushes a CodeCommit repository to ECS through a CodeDeploy blue/green action.

## The demo: S3 to EC2 via CodeDeploy

The live part skips the build stage, since the artifact needs no compilation, and spends its time on CodeDeploy, which is where newcomers get stuck:

1. Create a CodeDeploy application (a sample Java app, compute platform EC2).
2. Create a deployment group, the piece that decides which EC2 instances receive the deployment. Instances are picked by tag, for example every host tagged as prod, and advanced settings control how many instances update at once and what counts as failure.
3. Give it a service role with CodeDeploy access, tightened to your own security needs.
4. Create the pipeline with S3 as the source (bucket plus object key), skip build, and point deploy at the application and deployment group.

One real-world snag shows up on camera: pipeline creation clashes with a service role left over from an earlier run, and he deletes it in IAM before retrying. Then the pipeline triggers from the source artifact and deploys.

## Who should watch

Engineers on AWS who have only used Jenkins or GitHub Actions and want to see CodePipeline's moving parts once, end to end. If you already run CodePipeline in production, this is a refresher at most; the session stops before blue/green, approvals or multi-account setups.

Title: Same Python app, three base images, from 1 CVE to about 1,700
Description: Marco Verleun (i-share) at Conf42 Python 2024 on SBOMs as food labels for software, and how the base image decides your CVE count
Body:
A small Python worker app has exactly one medium CVE. Put it in the `python:latest` container image and it ships with about 1,700. At Conf42 Python 2024, Marco Verleun, Linux, DevOps and Kubernetes engineer at i-share, used that one app to argue for software bills of materials (SBOMs): a way to show people your software is safe without showing them your code, the way a food label tells you what is in the jar without giving away the recipe.

## Why a food label?

Would you eat from an unlabelled jar? It might be delicious, it might be dog food. A label lists the ingredients and where the product came from, so people with allergies or diets can decide, but it does not tell you how it tastes or how it was made. As Marco Verleun said at Conf42 Python 2024: "A bill of material tells you what is inside, just like a food label does."

An SBOM, usually JSON or XML (CycloneDX publishes examples), lists package names, types, locations and checksums. Like a label it does not know about your allergies, here CVEs. Every security scanner does the same trick internally: inventory the packages, match them against databases of known vulnerabilities. The advantage of keeping the SBOM is that you can re-run the matching whenever a new CVE drops. When the next curl advisory lands, the question of which of your apps are affected becomes a database query rather than an afternoon.

## What does the base image do to a clean app?

The demo app is `worker.py`, written by Jérôme Petazzoni for Kubernetes demos. Same Dockerfile, only the `FROM` line changes, and the app runs fine in all three images. He generated SBOMs with Syft and scanned them with Grype (chosen for tidy slide output, not as an endorsement). The results, valid when he wrote the talk and likely worse since:

| Source | Critical | High | Medium |
|---|---|---|---|
| worker.py | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| python:latest | 21 | 359 | 519 |
| python:3.9.18-slim | 1 | 11 | 28 |
| python:alpine | 0 | 1 | 18 |

Size tells the same story: the Alpine build is roughly 110 MB, the `python:latest` build almost 1.5 GB, so more than 1.3 GB of software the app never uses. Yes, it is a container and isolated, he says, but anyone who compromises the app finds a well-stocked toolbox inside, and with that many vulnerabilities getting in is not hard either. Switching the base image needs no code change at all. Even the Alpine image was a bit stale, with fixes already available for nine of its known vulnerabilities.

## Keep the SBOM, let a tool watch it

Being, in his words, a bit lazy, he lets tools do the re-evaluation. Dependency-Track stores SBOMs, pulls fresh vulnerability data from several sources about every 24 hours, and opens tickets or sends notifications when a new match appears. Renovate can automate the upgrades.

SBOMs also travel. The US federal government expects vendors to provide them before it buys software, projects publish them on GitHub so you can analyse before you install, and container registries can now store them next to images (Docker's build attestations, sbom-oci), so a Kubernetes cluster can check an image before it deploys rather than after.

One caveat he is careful to make: a clean CVE report says the components are not known to be vulnerable. It does not prove the code is free of malicious logic.

## Which tools?

His starter list: Syft, Microsoft's sbom-tool, Kubernetes' bom and the sbom-operator for generating; sbom-oci and Docker attestations for storing; Dependency-Track, Trivy and KubeClarity for analysis. Trivy fits pipelines well because it generates and scans in one go and can fail a build on a critical CVE. His warning: "there are many scanners, but there are not all good." Some only understand Java, some read `requirements.txt`, some only scan Debian or RPM packages, so benchmark a few against your own stack.

## Who should watch

Python developers who ship containers and have never looked at what their base image brings along, and anyone asked by a customer or procurement team to prove their software is safe. It is an awareness talk with one memorable demo, not a deep supply-chain security course.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: Choreograph between bounded contexts, orchestrate inside them
Description: Md. Mostafa Al Mahmud (Brain Station 23) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on mixing EventBridge choreography and Step Functions orchestration in EDA
Body:
The choreography-versus-orchestration debate has a tidy answer, and Md. Mostafa Al Mahmud, Software Engineer at Brain Station 23 and an AWS Community Builder in the serverless category, gives it at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: use events on a bus between bounded contexts, and a workflow engine inside a context where order, state and retries matter. On AWS that means Amazon EventBridge for the first and AWS Step Functions for the second.

It is a broad introduction to event-driven architecture (EDA) on AWS, from the vocabulary up to a Step Functions error-handling demo, with a best-practices list that borrows heavily from domain-driven design.

## The building blocks, and the one property that matters

He starts with the vocabulary: events are immutable records that something happened (an order created, a payment received); producers publish them; consumers react, possibly many per event; brokers sit in between, either as routers that push to subscribers or as stores that consumers pull from. The payoff is loose coupling: in his e-commerce example, orders, billing, shipping and inventory chained by synchronous calls fail together, while services that only know event formats can change independently.

The property he singles out is idempotency, because EDA retries by design. A Lambda triggered by an order-placed event fails on a network blip, the service retries, and without a guard you have a duplicate order. The fix is an idempotency key inside each event so a consumer can tell it has already processed it.

## Five patterns, mapped to services

- **Point-to-point**: a queue as a mailbox, one consumer. Amazon SQS or Amazon MQ.
- **Publish-subscribe**: one message, many subscribers. SNS topics for simple fan-out, EventBridge buses for routing on message attributes.
- **Event streaming**: consumers pull and track their own position. Kinesis Data Streams or Amazon MSK.
- **Choreography**: no central controller; each service reacts on its own.
- **Orchestration**: a coordinator controls order and state. Step Functions or Amazon MWAA.

"While choreography promotes decentralized and flexibility, orchestration provides centralized control and coordination," Md. Mostafa Al Mahmud said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. The useful part is where he puts the line. Between bounded contexts, say sales and support, or an order service and an inventory service, choreography over EventBridge keeps each side ignorant of the other's internals. Inside one context, such as insurance-claim document processing, where an orchestrator classifies an upload as a driver's licence or a car photo, routes it to the right extractor and writes the result, orchestration gives you order, state and error handling. A producer can do both at once: emit events on the bus for others while running its own Step Functions workflow internally.

## A KYC workflow as the worked example

The example to remember is know-your-customer onboarding. An account system publishes a new-account-request event; a Step Functions workflow in a dedicated KYC service runs identity verification and a risk assessment; depending on the outcome it publishes account-approved or account-rejected; EventBridge rules route those to the account domain and the customer service domain. Loose coupling between domains, a readable sequence inside one, little custom code.

On Step Functions he covers the standard-versus-express choice: standard workflows run up to a year with exactly-once execution, priced per state transition, suited to long-running, auditable processes; express workflows run up to five minutes with at-least-once execution, priced by number and duration, suited to high-rate streaming and IoT ingestion. The demo then shows Retry and Catch states sending a custom Lambda error and a timeout to fallback steps.

## Best practices worth stealing

The closing list is a good checklist: event storming workshops to find the business events with every stakeholder in the room; notification events versus event-carried state transfer (thin pings versus rich payloads); the conformist pattern, an anti-corruption layer and an open host service for contracts between contexts; revisiting event design regularly; and deciding which events need ordering. "Not all events need to arrive in the specific sequence," he notes, but when an order-updated event must follow order-created, use a service that guarantees it: Kinesis preserves order within a shard, SQS FIFO within a message group ID.

## Who should watch

Developers new to EDA on AWS who want the service map and the DDD vocabulary in one sitting. Experienced event-driven folks will find the choreography-plus-orchestration framing and the KYC example the parts worth their time.

Title: A Python sandbox for business rules, and the import that ate the disk
Description: Zhiya Zang (TikTok) at Conf42 Python 2024 on a custom Python sandbox for rule execution, using resource limits, AST blocklists and interpreter pools
Body:
A rule engine runs thousands of tiny pieces of user-written Python, each a few milliseconds long. Wrap every one in a Docker container and the startup time is the workload. At Conf42 Python 2024, Zhiya Zang, Senior Software Engineer at TikTok, described the custom sandbox the team built instead: Linux resource limits for isolation, AST analysis for security, and an interpreter pool after they found that `import requests` alone could saturate a disk.

It is a short, focused talk that packs one design into three pillars: isolation, security and performance.

## Why not just use a VM or Docker?

The rules express business logic, written in Python because it is powerful and easy to read. Without isolation, rules for different purposes can interfere with each other or do things nobody intended, which threatens the engine's stability and security.

Virtual machines give strong isolation at a high cost in performance and resources. Docker is lighter, sharing the host kernel, and attractive for many workloads. But this engine executes numerous small tasks at high frequency, so container startup adds unacceptable latency, and even Docker's smaller overhead adds up at that scale. Hence a sandbox built for the job.

## Isolation: ulimit from the standard library

The first pillar uses Python's built-in `resource` module, a wrapper over the Linux `setrlimit` API, to cap CPU time, memory, stack size and file-system quota for the process. Two details make it more than a config file:

- Limits are set per rule execution and can change at runtime, so each rule gets the budget its business scenario needs rather than one global setting.
- A time guard watches the run time of each execution, so an infinite loop in someone's rule gets killed instead of holding a worker forever.

## Security: read the code before you run it

Resource limits are reactive; they fire while the code runs. The proactive layer parses each rule with Python's `ast` module, walks the tree to find every imported module and called function, and checks them against a blocklist at both module and function level. Malicious code is rejected without ever executing, which saves resources and avoids damage that no execution control could undo.

The other half is error handling. Rules run isolated from the core service, so an exception in a rule cannot crash it. Instead of failing silently, the sandbox captures the traceback and returns it to the rule's author so they can see which line broke.

## Performance: the import that ate the disk

The first design spawned a fresh sandbox process per request. Perfect isolation, terrible throughput: each new interpreter re-imports its packages from disk. As Zhiya Zang said at Conf42 Python 2024: "We found that with only 20 to 30 requests per second, the sandbox will exhaust the disk bandwidth and the time consumption for each request will increase from few milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds or even several seconds."

The reproduction is small enough to remember: a rule that only does `import requests`, 16 processes on an 8-core machine with an SSD, and execution time climbs to 300 milliseconds for a rule that normally needs a few.

The fix has two parts. A pool of Python interpreters that get reused across executions, and preloading of the common libraries when each interpreter starts, so later rules find them already in memory. Library import time drops to almost zero and the disk I/O pressure goes away.

## Who should watch

Engineers building rule engines, plugin systems or any feature that runs user-supplied Python, and anyone weighing containers against process-level isolation for short-lived tasks. It is a design overview rather than a code walkthrough, and it does not go into how complete a blocklist can be in a language as dynamic as Python, so treat it as the skeleton to build your own threat model on.

Title: Pick the data structure first, the database second
Description: Santosh Nikhil Kumar (ByteDance) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on B-trees vs LSM trees, quadtrees, secondary indexes and CRDTs as design trade-offs
Body:
Choosing between Postgres, RocksDB and Elasticsearch is really choosing between B-trees, LSM trees and inverted indexes. That is the thesis of Santosh Nikhil Kumar, Senior Software Engineer at ByteDance, at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024: you don't build storage engines from scratch, but you do need to know what is inside one to pick the right engine and tune it for your workload.

The talk is a tour of four design decisions: storage data structures, local versus global secondary indexes, conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), and inside-out versus outside-in system design. The abstract also promises security, pagination, caching and error handling; the session itself sticks to those four topics, so come for storage trade-offs rather than an API checklist.

## Which data structure fits which workload?

Each structure gets a real-world service to anchor it:

- **B-trees for email.** Mail services (on PostgreSQL in his example) need fast lookups and range queries, such as every email from one sender between two dates. A B-tree prunes everything outside the range, keeps disk I/O low on cheap disks, and gives O(log n) lookups, inserts and deletes.
- **Quadtrees for proximity.** Yelp-style "what's near me" search uses spatial indexing (MongoDB and PostGIS are his examples). Each node is a region split into four quadrants, dense areas subdivide further and sparse ones stay coarse.
- **LSM trees for write-heavy systems.** A digital wallet, HDFS and Kafka absorb heavy writes. RocksDB buffers writes in memory, flushes immutable sorted SSTables to disk, and compacts them in the background with a merge sort so reads don't have to scan every table. Buffer size, flush frequency and compaction thresholds are the tuning knobs.
- **Inverted indexes for search.** Map each word to the documents that contain it, so a query becomes a lookup rather than a scan.

## Local or global secondary index?

The second part is the most practical. His example: a book store partitioned by genre across Virginia, Seattle and Europe, and a query for all books by one author. With a local secondary index (partitioned by document), each partition indexes its own rows, so the query fans out to every partition and a microservice aggregates the results: scatter and gather, paid for in network calls and compute.

A global secondary index (partitioned by term) answers the cross-partition query directly, at the cost of maintaining a separate index across a large distributed system. "After all, everything in life is a trade off," Santosh Nikhil Kumar said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. His rule of thumb comes with two cases: a shopper browsing Sony products inside the electronics partition wants a local index; HR listing every manager in a company sharded by country wants a global one.

## CRDTs for multi-leader conflicts

Multi-leader replication buys availability, fault tolerance, write scalability and data close to users. It also buys conflicts. Two users rename the same Google Doc from A to B and from A to C on different leaders; when the leaders sync asynchronously, each finds a title it didn't expect. CRDTs, data types that merge concurrent edits deterministically, resolve that.

His code sample is a Java counter with an `AtomicInteger` and a merge method. Read it critically: the merge takes the maximum of the two values, so two leaders that each increment once merge to 1, not the 2 the printed comment expects. A correct grow-only counter keeps one count per leader and sums them. A small slip, and a good reminder that the merge function is the whole CRDT.

## Inside-out or outside-in?

The last section frames end-to-end design. Inside-out starts from the data model and pushes outward through data access classes, microservices and APIs to the UI: engineering-driven work like a monolith-to-microservices decomposition or a banking system built around accounts and transactions. Outside-in starts from user interactions and pulls inward: product-driven work like an e-commerce checkout.

## Who should watch

Engineers preparing for system design interviews or their first data-heavy architecture decisions. If you have read *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, much of it will be familiar, and the secondary index section is the part worth your time.

Title: A Python security checklist that starts with salting your hashes
Description: Ukanah Dean (Khalide) at Conf42 Python 2024 on Python security basics, from input validation and file uploads to hashing, Fernet and bcrypt
Body:
In 2012, LinkedIn lost the passwords of about 6.5 million accounts, and security experts said they were easy to unscramble because the hashes were not salted. At Conf42 Python 2024, Ukanah Dean, Fullstack Developer at Khalide, opened his tour of Python application security with that story and ended it with a live demo that shows the difference between a bare SHA-256 digest and a bcrypt hash. His closing advice, as Ukanah Dean said at Conf42 Python 2024: "one big encouragement is try not to get hacked."

Honest scope: this is a broad, checklist-style survey of web application security for Python developers, not a close study of one attack. It works best as a map of what to look up next, and as a reminder list for a team about to ship a Django or Flask app.

## Why do Python apps get targeted?

His argument is that popularity is the attack surface. Python comes preinstalled on many Unix systems, so a compromised box with a vulnerable Python app is an easy target. The risks he lists: weak input handling (the root of SQL injection, XSS and command injection), vulnerable third-party libraries, framework-specific pitfalls, a preinstalled Python nobody updates, and sloppy file permissions. Past breaches he uses as cautionary tales include Reddit in 2018, with passwords hashed with SHA-1, already considered weak at the time.

The threats get a short explainer each: SQL injection, cross-site scripting, cross-site request forgery, and command injection, which he calls less common because it takes more effort to pull off, and more dangerous because it can mean full remote code execution and lateral movement across the network.

## Input validation is the first line of defence

The secure-coding section is the most practical part:

- Trim inputs, validate formats with regular expressions (`re`, or regex validators in Django forms), enforce numeric ranges, and prefer dropdowns where the set of valid values is fixed.
- Enforce password policies (length, character classes, no dictionary words), with libraries like passlib for generating and hashing.
- Treat file uploads as hostile: validate on the server, never only on the client, check the MIME type and extension against an allow-list, cap upload sizes per file and per user, scan for malware, use Pillow to check that images are what they claim to be, and park uploads in temporary storage until they pass.
- For file handling in general: sanitise file names to block path traversal, lock down permissions with chmod and chown, encrypt sensitive files at rest and use `with open(...)` so files get closed.
- Manage dependencies deliberately; he recommends Poetry, and pipdeptree to see what you actually pull in.

## Authentication, authorisation, sessions

The checklist here is familiar but complete: HTTPS everywhere, MFA, secure unique session tokens stored server side with timeouts, rate limiting against brute force, no hard-coded credentials (environment variables or config files instead), established libraries like Flask-Login or Django's auth system, safe password-reset flows, logging every login attempt, successful or failed, and role-based access control for who can do what.

## Encryption or hashing?

He draws the line cleanly. Encryption is reversible with a key and protects confidentiality (AES, RSA, ChaCha20). Hashing is one-way and protects integrity (SHA-256, SHA-3, bcrypt). Need the original back? Encrypt. Need to check it has not changed, or store a password? Hash, with a salt.

The live demo makes it concrete. With the `cryptography` package he generates a Fernet key, encrypts a message and decrypts it back. Then `hashlib` for a plain SHA-256 digest, a salted SHA-256, and `bcrypt.hashpw` with `bcrypt.gensalt()`. The bcrypt output, full of dollar signs, dots and slashes, carries its own salt and cost, which is why it is his personal favourite for passwords.

## Tools beyond your own code

For security work in Python he points to cryptography (symmetric and asymmetric encryption, HMAC, signatures), Nmap for network discovery, Scapy for crafting and sniffing packets, and Impacket for SMB, RPC and Active Directory work in Windows penetration tests. Static analysis with Bandit, Flake8 and pylint, central logging with the ELK Stack or Graylog, and regular penetration tests with Metasploit or Kali Linux round out the list.

## Who should watch

Junior and mid-level Python web developers who want one talk that names every area they should be checking. Seasoned AppSec engineers will know the material; the demo is the part to skip to.

Title: An Envoy in front of every registry, and no restarts for policy
Description: Manik Kashikar (Thoughtworks) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on an Envoy-based service mesh securing data exchange between government building blocks
Body:
The hard part of a government's digital services is rarely one system. It is the birth registry, the ID card office and the patient records all needing to swap data securely and consistently. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Manik Kashikar, Google Cloud Practice Lead at Thoughtworks, walks through a service mesh built on the Envoy proxy for exactly that case: an Envoy "security server" in front of every building block, fed access rules by a control plane at runtime.

It is a short talk: a primer on service mesh and Envoy, then one architecture for a European government initiative.

## What a service mesh takes off your services

The setup is the standard argument, made clearly. Without a mesh, every microservice has to know whom it calls, how, and at which endpoint, and every team rebuilds tracing, retries and authentication from scratch. With a mesh, a proxy next to each service handles routing and filtering from configuration. Manik lists what you get: distributed tracing across chains of internal and external calls, traffic management (load balancing, routing, retries), encryption, authentication and authorization, service discovery, circuit breaking and fault injection, and policy enforcement such as rate limiting and access control.

The slides add a fair caveat: Envoy is not the only option, and proxies such as NGINX and Traefik can do the job too.

## Envoy in four nouns

Envoy, originally built at Lyft and now part of the CNCF, works at layer 4 and layer 7. Its key selling point in the talk is that configuration changes don't need a restart, where traditional proxies would force one and cause downtime. To understand it, Manik says, you need four configuration concepts:

- **Listeners**: an IP and port waiting for HTTP, HTTPS or TCP traffic.
- **Routes**: a routing table that matches on path, headers and metadata to pick a cluster.
- **Clusters**: groups of upstream services, with a load-balancing algorithm across them.
- **Endpoints**: the individual instances, updated dynamically as they come and go.

Inbound traffic hits a listener, runs through the filter chain, gets routed to a cluster and lands on an endpoint. That model is worth having in your head before you read any Envoy YAML.

## The government use case

The problem: an initiative to give governments a reusable framework of interoperable digital components, so nobody rebuilds the same pieces for each country. The technical ask was a gateway for secure data exchange between building blocks over OpenAPI-based interfaces, with standardised data-sharing policies.

The design puts an Envoy proxy in front of each building block. "There will be one envoy proxy which we are calling as a security server," Manik Kashikar said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. It intercepts requests, evaluates access policy and returns a go or no-go. A control plane receives policy changes from a policy admin service, generates access rules and pushes them to the relevant proxies over the xDS protocol, so policies take effect at runtime with no restart. A separate authentication service sits in the data path and authenticates upstream and downstream services.

The proxies come in three deployment modes: an Envoy in front of classic applications on VMs, with routing forcing all traffic through it; a sidecar next to applications on Kubernetes; and an external-facing proxy for traffic to and from other security servers.

## Why this design

His justification is practical. Access rules are encoded in local proxy configuration, so enforcement saves network calls. Dynamic config means no restarts and higher availability. The same approach covers cloud-native workloads and VMs, supports HTTP/2 and gRPC, and brings logging, metrics and tracing for free.

## Who should watch

Architects weighing a mesh for a mixed estate of VMs and Kubernetes, especially in regulated or public-sector settings, and engineers who want a quick mental model of Envoy's configuration. It stays at the architecture level, with no configuration walkthrough or benchmarks.

Title: Your GenAI app is a workflow, so stop writing it as Lambda glue
Description: Mohammed Fazalullah (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on orchestrating Bedrock, Hugging Face and human review with AWS Step Functions instead of code
Body:
Calling a model is one line. Calling a model, retrying it, waiting for a transcription job, asking a human to pick a title and then generating an image is a distributed system. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Mohammed Fazalullah, Senior Developer Advocate at AWS, argues that this part belongs in AWS Step Functions rather than in Lambda glue code, and builds a video-titling pipeline out of Amazon Transcribe, Amazon Bedrock, Hugging Face and a human reviewer to prove it.

It is an AWS developer advocate showing AWS services, with working demos and a public sample repository at the end.

## Why not just write the code?

He starts where most serverless apps start: Lambda one calls Lambda two. Then Lambda one also needs Lambda seven, a step fails halfway, and you add a database to track state. Then some steps must run in parallel, some branch on input, and one needs a human to approve a credit limit above the auto-approve threshold. Each of those is doable in code, and each is more code to own. "One thing you have to understand is code is also a liability," Mohammed Fazalullah said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024.

His small example: a Lambda function that fetches one item from DynamoDB needs the SDK import, parameters, a query wrapped in try/catch, a handler with another try/catch and some serialisation. In Step Functions it is one `GetItem` task with retry, catch and a dead-letter queue configured on the state.

Step Functions in his summary: serverless, pay per use, scales to zero, a drag-and-drop Workflow Studio on top of the JSON-based Amazon States Language (ASL) that you can commit and review in pull requests. It integrates with over 220 AWS services, and the SDK integrations alone expose over 10,000 API actions without custom integration code.

## Three call patterns do most of the work

The talk leans on the three ways a task can wait:

- **Request-response**: call and move on.
- **Job run (`.sync`)**: wait for a long job to finish. Bedrock's create model customization job integration uses it, which suits fine-tuning in data pipelines.
- **Callback (`.waitForTaskToken`)**: pause until someone returns a token. This is how the human gets into the loop, for minutes or months.

Bedrock's optimized integrations, invoke model and create model customization job, are the GenAI hooks. One limit worth knowing: Step Functions carries at most 256 KB of state, so large prompts and outputs go through S3 as input and output locations.

## Prompt chaining, with every step visible

The first demo invokes Llama 2 on Bedrock to summarise a transcript of a 2012 interview between Werner Vogels and Jeff Bezos, with token counts and per-state timings in the execution view. The second is a three-step prompt chain on Cohere Command: name a random city in Southeast Asia, then describe it, then describe it some more, each step appending the previous answer to the context. It picked Ho Chi Minh City. He also shows its failure mode honestly: on another run the third prompt drifted off the city, and the fix is to pass the city explicitly as a field in later prompts rather than trusting the model to keep track.

## The full pipeline: titles, a human, an avatar

The final architecture: API Gateway puts a request on SQS, a Lambda starts the workflow, Amazon Transcribe runs in a wait loop until the transcript lands in S3, then a parallel state asks Bedrock and a Hugging Face model for title suggestions at the same time. Hugging Face is reached through the HTTPS endpoint integration, which uses an Amazon EventBridge connection for auth (OAuth, basic or API key) and a test state to check one step before deploying.

Failures get two treatments. Transient ones retry with backoff so you don't hammer the third party. Hard ones stop the execution, and Redrive restarts it from the failed step once you've fixed the cause, with a redrive count in the event history. The chosen title comes back from the reviewer's page via the task token over AWS IoT Core WebSockets, and Stability AI on Bedrock generates the avatar, returned as an S3 presigned URL. The code is in the `amazon-bedrock-serverless-prompt-chaining` sample on GitHub.

## Who should watch

Serverless developers adding GenAI features to existing apps, and anyone whose LLM prototype has started sprouting retry loops. If you already know Step Functions well, the Bedrock integrations, HTTPS endpoints and Redrive are the new parts.

Title: Your slow model is probably slow before it reaches the model
Description: Ivan Popov (Abound) at Conf42 Python 2024 on balancing ML speed and accuracy, profiling preprocessing with yappi and picking XGBoost or LightGBM
Body:
A loan aggregator gives a lender a few seconds to return a quote, or the offer is not shown at all. A diagnostic model can take its time, because a doctor will. At Conf42 Python 2024, Ivan Popov, Data Scientist at Abound in London, argued that commercial ML is a trade between speed and accuracy set by the business, and that when a decent model is too slow, the first place to look is the data preprocessing code, not the GPU budget.

It is a practical, generalist talk for working data scientists: how to decide which side of the trade you are on, then a toolbox of fixes in plain Python.

## Who decides between speed and accuracy?

The business does. He uses accuracy as an umbrella for every quality metric (F1, ROC AUC, IoU) and names three levers that move both it and latency: model architecture complexity, the amount and quality of input data, and hardware. His examples sit on a spectrum:

- **Loans**: speed first. The quote is rarely final; underwriters review it later.
- **E-commerce recommendations**: a strict balance. Too slow and the customer leaves; too wrong and you lose the sale. As Ivan Popov said at Conf42 Python 2024: "Imagine a heavy metal fan getting Taylor Swift tickets as a recommendation."
- **Medical diagnosis**: accuracy first.

To place your own model, ask what it is for, whether it is internal or customer facing, which outcome and KPIs it serves, and what its users expect. As a rule of thumb, customer-facing models (recommenders, chatbots) lean toward speed, while internal analytics such as financial forecasting or supply-chain predictions can run overnight and should be right. He adds that the rule bends: some internal tools need speed too.

## Can money fix it?

Partly. Better CPUs and GPUs speed up inference without touching accuracy, but large spending can buy a small gain, and budgets are finite. And hardware does not fix bad data, poor feature selection, or an architecture that overfits or underfits. His example of a bad architecture choice: a fully connected network for image segmentation, where every pixel is a feature and every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer.

## Start with the data

The first fix is a good dataset with clean labels. For a handwritten digit classifier, that means many writers and styles and a balanced distribution of digits; one writer's handwriting, or missing digits, produces a model that cannot generalise. Smaller and clean beats larger and dirty, since augmentation can grow a good dataset later.

## Find the bottleneck with a profiler

Preprocessing is where most of the code gets written, and he calls it one of the biggest sources of inefficiency. Training-time preprocessing does not slow inference, but inference data has to go through the same steps. Wrapping functions in `time()` stops working once the pipeline spans many classes and files, so he reaches for a profiler: cProfile, or his choice, yappi, which is written in C, fast, and profiles asynchronous code. His reading guide: use wall time for async code, watch `ncall` for functions called far more often than expected, `tsub` for time spent in a function excluding its sub-calls, and `ttot` for the total.

The usual suspects it finds:

- **pandas `.apply()`**, which does not vectorise and returns new objects. For one column, use a built-in vectorised operation, such as multiplying the column by two directly. For several columns, avoid `apply(axis=1)`: write a function over NumPy arrays and call it on the series' `.values`.
- **Repeated calculations**: if a value depends on metadata like city or car type, compute it once per group, not once per row.
- **pandas where NumPy would do.** NumPy is written in C and wins on efficiency.

## Fewer features, simpler models

Feature selection is the last preprocessing step and affects both speed and accuracy: more data points is good, more columns per data point often is not. He uses SHAP values, a game-theoretic, model-agnostic measure of each feature's contribution, ranked by magnitude rather than sign, to drop the weak features. The `shap` package does the maths and the plots; they are cheapest to compute on simpler models like gradient-boosted trees.

That leads to his last point: most business problems do not need an LLM or a transformer. XGBoost (around since 2014, flexible, sparse-data friendly, with its DMatrix structure and regularisation) grows trees level by level, which can be slower on large datasets. LightGBM grows leaf-wise, is often much faster on large data and handles categorical features natively, at the cost of more memory. There is no universal winner. Both train quickly, so test both and let the results decide.

## Who should watch

Data scientists shipping their first customer-facing model, and engineers inheriting a pandas-heavy inference path that is mysteriously slow. If you already profile your pipelines, the business-framing half is the new part.

Title: AWS generative AI in one sitting, from Trainium to a boto3 call
Description: Samuel Baruffi (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on the AWS GenAI stack, from chips and SageMaker JumpStart to Amazon Bedrock and live Python calls
Body:
If you want the whole AWS generative AI stack explained bottom to top in under an hour, this is the map. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Samuel Baruffi, Senior Global Solutions Architect at AWS, walks from GPUs and custom silicon through Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to Amazon Bedrock, then finishes in a terminal calling Claude 3 Sonnet and Amazon Titan with a few lines of Python.

It is a survey talk by an AWS architect about AWS services, recorded in early March 2024, days after Anthropic released Claude 3. Treat the model list as a snapshot; the architecture choices it explains have aged better than the version numbers.

## The real decision: pay for the instance or pay per token?

The most useful distinction in the talk is about billing, not models. SageMaker JumpStart is a hub of pretrained models you deploy with a click, onto instances in your own account. You pay for that instance every minute it runs, busy or idle. Samuel spells it out: you are not paying per token, you are paying for the whole instance, which can get expensive depending on the model.

Bedrock is the other end: one API, foundation models as a service, priced on demand per input and output token, with no GPUs to manage. That makes it the cheap place to iterate. JumpStart (and fine-tuning big models like Falcon 180B there) is for when you need control over the hosting.

Under both sits the hardware. The slides trace the NVIDIA lineage on EC2 from the CG1 instance's Fermi GPUs to P5 with H100s, and AWS's own chips: Trainium for training, which he puts at up to 40% better price performance than comparable GPUs, and Inferentia for inference.

## What Bedrock actually gives you

At recording time Bedrock had seven model providers: AI21 Labs (Jurassic-2), Anthropic (Claude), Cohere (Command and Embed), Meta (Llama 2), Mistral AI (Mistral 7B and Mixtral 8x7B), Stability AI (Stable Diffusion XL 1.0) and Amazon's own Titan models. Claude 3 Sonnet was live, with Opus and Haiku coming soon, all multimodal with 200K context.

On top of the models he goes feature by feature:

- **Customization**: drop labeled data in a private S3 bucket and Bedrock fine-tunes Titan, Cohere or Llama 2 models for you. He calls it a last resort, after prompt engineering and RAG.
- **Knowledge bases**: managed RAG. Documents in S3, embeddings from Titan or Cohere, vectors stored in a database such as OpenSearch Serverless, then semantic search feeds the right chunks to the model.
- **Agents**: give a model instructions and an OpenAPI spec, and it calls Lambda to hit your API, for questions such as a live stock price that a model alone would hallucinate.
- **Guardrails** (preview): deny topics like investment advice on input and output.
- **Batch mode** and **model evaluation** (both preview): bulk inference from S3, and automatic or blind human evaluation across models.

Data sent to Bedrock is not used to train the base models and is encrypted by default, with VPC endpoints if you want traffic to stay off the public internet.

He also lists six AWS databases with vector support (OpenSearch, DocumentDB, MemoryDB for Redis, RDS and Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector, and Neptune) and Amazon CodeWhisperer, free for individuals with a Builder ID.

## The demo is the part to steal

The demo starts in the Bedrock console's playground: a poem about AWS from Claude 3 Sonnet, a side-by-side comparison of Claude 3 against Claude 2.1, Stable Diffusion images of a cat on the moon. The good trick is the menu that shows the exact API request behind each playground run, so you can copy the payload instead of guessing it.

Then Python with boto3: `invoke_model` for a plain request to Claude 3 Sonnet, the same call pointed at Titan Text with a different body format, `invoke_model_with_response_stream` for chat-style streaming, and a multimodal call that sends a base64-encoded cat photo and gets back an accurate description. "All what I've done here is probably less than a penny because it's all on demand," Samuel Baruffi said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. The code is based on the public Amazon Bedrock samples repository on GitHub.

One practical tip: enable model access in the Bedrock console first. It costs nothing, and nothing works until you do.

## Who should watch

Developers and architects starting with generative AI on AWS who want the service map and a working first API call. If you already ship on Bedrock, skip to the demo or pick a talk on running it in production.

Title: Can you copy the idea of opposite out of an LLM and paste it elsewhere?
Description: Boluwatife Ben-Adeola at Conf42 Python 2024 on mechanistic interpretability with NNsight, reproducing function vectors with causal interventions
Body:
Feed a language model `old: young, awake: sleep, dark:` and it knows you are playing opposites. Now take the activation it built for that game, average it, and add it to a model that has only been told `encode:`. Does it say `decode`? At Conf42 Python 2024, independent AI researcher Boluwatife Ben-Adeola walked through exactly that experiment, from the function vectors paper, using the NNsight library, and showed what the Python actually looks like when you poke at a large model's insides.

It is a research talk with code, aimed at Python developers curious about mechanistic interpretability rather than at people who already do it.

## Why look inside at all?

He starts with two premises: neural networks solve an increasing number of important tasks, and it would be at least interesting, and probably important, to know how. Interesting because, as Boluwatife Ben-Adeola said at Conf42 Python 2024, "these models arrive at solutions that no person could write a program for." Important because anything powerful enough to sit in strategic places in society needs some transparency before people can trust it.

Mechanistic interpretability (mech interp) is the branch that goes granular: build a causal model of how discrete components, an attention head, an MLP layer, an embedding, produce an observed behaviour. The tool he picks from the kit is the causal intervention. Treat the network as a computational graph of unknown nodes, settle on a behaviour you care about, perturb one node, and watch whether the output changes. If it does, the node is on the critical path and worth drilling into. If not, ignore it.

## The function vectors hypothesis

The worked example is the function vectors paper (arXiv 2310.15213) from Northeastern University. The question: is there a portable component for an operation like opposite?

The intuition he builds is that the vector at the final colon token, layer after layer, accumulates more than the fact that it is a colon. By the end it knows the next token is new, and somewhere along the way it must also hold something like an instruction to apply opposite to the previous word. If that representation is roughly linear, you can run many opposite prompts, grab the vector at the last token of each, average them into one vector `h`, and add `h` to a zero-shot prompt that has no idea which game is being played.

## What NNsight adds

Running a 70-billion-parameter model several times with surgery in the middle is not an M1 MacBook job. NNsight is the interface to NDIF, a remote inference cluster made available to researchers who cannot afford to run very large models themselves (inference only, not training). It also runs models locally if you have the RAM. He mentions TransformerLens as the other popular open source option.

The design leans on Python context managers. Inside a `runner` context, each `invoker` context builds one sub-graph of reads and writes: read a layer's input, set layer 11's MLP output to zero, and so on. Nothing runs while you write it. When the outermost context exits, the whole intervention graph is sent to the cluster, the model runs with your edits, and results come back. The gotcha that follows: "we have to explicitly tell the model to save any value that we want to read outside of the context." Values you only need for computation inside the graph stay remote, which matters when each one is hundreds of thousands of numbers. Do the averaging remotely, send back only the condensed vector.

## Did it work?

The experiment has two parts in one runner. First, for layer 8 (the real study sweeps every layer and plots which ones matter), take the hidden state at sequence position -1 across a batch of opposite prompts and `.mean()` over the batch dimension, saving only the result. Second, two invokers: a clean zero-shot baseline, and a run that does `+= h` at the same layer.

The baseline mostly parrots: minimum is minimum, arrogant is arrogant, inside is inside, with the odd surprise (on gives I, answer gives yes). With `h` added, some examples tilt toward the opposite. He is upfront that the effect is modest. The paper goes further by isolating the contributions of the top attention heads instead of averaging a whole layer's output, which removes noise and makes the effect much clearer; he left that step out of the talk.

## Who should watch

Python developers who have heard of mechanistic interpretability and want to see what an intervention actually is in code, and ML engineers weighing NNsight or remote inference for research. The code snippets come from the ARENA curriculum, which he recommends as the place to learn mech interp properly.

Title: One anomaly is noise, a hundred at once is an incident
Description: Costa Tsaousis (Netdata) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on unsupervised per-metric ML that ranks what was anomalous instead of paging on it
Body:
Machine learning in monitoring has a reputation problem, and Costa Tsaousis, founder and CEO of Netdata, starts his Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 talk by agreeing with it. His answer is narrow and practical: train small models per metric on every node, never page anyone on a single anomaly, and use anomalies that fire together across many metrics to rank where to look during an incident.

The talk opens with Todd Underwood's SREcon19 session from Google, "All of Our ML Ideas Are Bad (and We Should Feel Bad)", in which Google asked SREs what they wanted from ML and found that none of their ideas would work. Costa's pitch is a few ideas that survive contact with production.

## Why can't you train on server A and run on server B?

The core argument is about what a model actually learns. Take two database servers on identical hardware, same OS, same Postgres version, same data. Train a model on A and apply it to B, and you get false positives, because the model has absorbed A's workload: a reporting query B doesn't run, a load balancer that splits traffic slightly unevenly. So shared, pre-trained anomaly models are out.

What is left is modest and useful. "Machine learning is the simplest solution for learning the behavior of metrics," Costa Tsaousis said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. Given enough history, a model can say whether the sample you just collected is an outlier: a single bit, true or false.

## Noisy bits become a signal when they line up

A single model is noisy. Netdata reduces the noise by keeping 18 models per metric: per its defaults, one trained every 3 hours on the last 6 hours of data, together covering about 57 hours. A sample counts as anomalous only when all of them agree. That still produces false positives, which is why Costa is blunt that "an anomaly should not be something to wake up at 03:00 a.m."

The useful part comes next. When those imperfect anomaly bits fire together across many metrics over a short window, it is no longer random: something at the system, service or application level is behaving in a way not seen recently. Netdata stores the anomaly bit next to every sample, computes an anomaly rate for any query, and a host-level anomaly score, the share of a host's metrics that are anomalous at the same moment. In the demo, servers spike to around 10% of their metrics anomalous at once, clustered within a short delta of each other.

## From speculating to reading a sorted list

The workflow change is the bit to steal. In most stacks, a latency spike starts a round of guessing: is it the database, the storage, the network? In Netdata you highlight the time window, and the scoring engine walks every metric on the node, scores it for that window and returns a list sorted by anomaly rate, with the aim that your "aha moment" sits in the first twenty or thirty entries. A metric correlation mode does the same by similarity of change, so highlighting a spike can surface the dive that caused it.

Each chart also carries an anomaly ribbon, and the NIDL controls (nodes, instances, dimensions, labels) show which nodes and instances contribute to a chart, their share of the volume and their anomaly rates.

## How heavy is ML on every node?

Netdata's pitch is that the agent runs everywhere, collects per second from 800+ integrations with zero configuration, and keeps data on your servers, with parents (or Netdata Cloud) as optional centralization points. Logs stay in systemd-journal rather than a separate log database. On cost, Costa cites a stress test of a Netdata parent against Prometheus with 500 servers, 40,000 containers and 2.7 million metrics per second: 35% less CPU, 49% less peak memory, 12% less bandwidth and 98% less disk I/O, at about 0.6 bytes per sample on disk for per-second data. The detection is unsupervised and starts flagging within 10 to 15 minutes of installation, before all 18 models exist.

Next on the list are ML profiles (sensitivity, purpose such as security or troubleshooting) and time segmentation, so Monday mornings are judged against Monday mornings.

## Who should watch

SREs burned by anomaly alerts that page on noise, and anyone deciding where ML belongs in an observability stack. It is the founder presenting his own open-source product, so expect Netdata throughout, but the train-locally, alert-never, rank-on-demand argument travels to any tool.

Title: Containerize the monolith first, let Amazon Q refactor it second
Description: Richard Lees and Jorge Alvarez (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024 on moving a Tomcat monolith to ECS with App2Container, then upgrading it with Amazon Q
Body:
Every company has one: the Java app on a server nobody remembers configuring, with zero documentation and a team that would rather ship features than touch it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2024, Richard Lees, who runs application modernization go-to-market for AWS in EMEA, and Jorge Alvarez, a Senior Specialist Modernization Architect at AWS, showed a two-step way out: lift it into containers on Amazon ECS with AWS App2Container, then use Amazon Q to start refactoring the code once it lives on AWS.

It is an AWS talk showing AWS tools, and it says so. The value is in watching both tools run end to end on a real Tomcat app rather than on marketing slides.

## Why containerize before you refactor?

Richard sets up the scenario as one many teams will recognise: an application "developed years ago with zero proper documentation", a team not comfortable with containers or AWS deployment practices, and new business requirements waiting in the queue. Rewriting it into microservices on day one is the expensive path. Instead, step one is to get the monolith into a container for quick wins in cost, resilience and a standard deployment process. Step two is the refactor, because, in his words, applications are easier to refactor once they're already on AWS.

He walks through the familiar trade-off first. Monoliths are simple to start, deploy and test; they get painful as the app and team grow, when a small change means redeploying everything and a memory leak in one module can take down the whole application. Microservices fix independent deployment and scaling, at the cost of a distributed system.

He frames all of it inside four AWS modernization pathways: move to cloud native, move to managed, move to managed databases and move to open source.

## App2Container works without the source code

The detail that makes App2Container interesting is what it does not need. Jorge explains that it is a command-line tool for Java and .NET applications that runs on the server itself, on premises or on EC2, and scans what is running there. "One important caveat is Appto container doesn't need the source code," Jorge Alvarez said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024. It finds the processes, dependencies and web root, then generates the Dockerfile, the image and the deployment artifacts.

The demo follows the CLI's own sequence:

- `init` configures the instance profile, the region (us-west-2 in the demo) and an S3 bucket for artifacts and logs.
- `inventory` detects the Java application running in Tomcat and gives it an ID.
- `analyze` writes an `analysis.json` with container parameters. Jorge bumps the base image from Ubuntu 18 to Ubuntu 20 there, and App2Container warns him about the change during containerization.
- `containerize` builds the Dockerfile and image and validates them.
- A `deployment.json` picks the target: ECS on Fargate in the demo, with a switch for EKS artifacts if you prefer Kubernetes. The one thing you have to give it is the target VPC ID.
- `generate app-deployment` produces the CloudFormation that stands up the ECS cluster and a load balancer, and the app answers on its public DNS name.

Richard's estimate afterwards: containerized and deployed on ECS in less than 45 minutes, even the first time.

## What Amazon Q did with the Java 11 code

Part two runs inside VS Code with the AWS Toolkit and Amazon Q. The headline is Amazon Q Code Transformation upgrading the project from Java 11 to Java 17 (Maven only at the time of recording). It needs the current version and the path to the JDK, builds a transformation plan, and returns the proposed changes plus a log, which flags the Maven version changes to watch.

While that runs, Jorge uses the chat to explain an unfamiliar `OrderManager` class, suggest refactors and optimisations for a long method (pull the authorization logic into its own method, consider parallel streams, tighten validation and error handling), and answer how to add Amazon Cognito. In the dev tab he asks for security issues in the POM file, which he seeded on purpose, and in `OrderManager`, then has Q generate the fix as a diff with a unit test.

The case for the effort comes from a figure Jorge quotes: developers spend 73% of their time running and maintaining applications, and about 27% on the work they actually want to do.

## Who should watch

Teams sitting on Java or .NET apps on VMs who want a concrete first move, and anyone curious what an AI assistant does with a real version upgrade. The abstract mentions the Strangler Fig pattern, but the session itself spends its time on the two demos rather than on decomposition patterns, so pair it with a talk that covers how to carve the services out.

Title: A Hugging Face agent is an LLM that writes three lines of Python
Description: Darya Petrashka (SLB) at Conf42 Python 2024 on building a Hugging Face Transformers agent, chaining its curated tools and adding a custom one
Body:
An LLM is bad at writing a whole script and good at writing three or four lines of code. Hand it a box of well-described tools and those few lines are enough to caption an image, translate the caption and read it out loud. At Conf42 Python 2024, Darya Petrashka, Data Scientist at SLB, built a Hugging Face Transformers agent live in a Colab notebook, chained its predefined tools, ran into a Spanish voice that did not sound Spanish, and fixed it by writing her own tool.

It is a hands-on introduction to the agents API that shipped in Hugging Face Transformers, with the notebook, slides and links in her GitHub repository, dashapetr/hf_agents.

## What is an agent, and what is a tool?

In her framing, an agent is an LLM you prompt to perform a set of tasks, with access to a toolbox. A tool is deliberately small: a single function with a name and a description, each dedicated to one very simple task, like a hammer that is for nails. Ask the agent to read the content of an image out loud and it works out that it needs the image captioner first and the text-to-speech tool second, writes the code, and runs it in a Python interpreter.

Why care? Prompting instead of coding, and chained output: generate an image, edit it, caption it, translate the caption, voice it, with each output saved as a variable and passed to the next step.

## Setup is a token and a few lines

Prerequisites: a Hugging Face token (a free read token is enough), and in her case an OpenAI API key, because she drives the toolbox with the OpenAI agent. Install the latest transformers, log in, initialise the agent, and `agent.run()` takes a natural-language prompt plus variables such as an image.

Her first demo captioned a breakfast photo as a plate of food with eggs, bread and a cup of coffee. The agent prints its reasoning, the tool it picked and the code it generated before running it, which makes it easy to see what it actually did.

## The curated toolbox

The predefined tools built on transformers models:

- Document question answering (Donut) and text question answering (Flan-T5)
- Image question answering (BLIP) and image segmentation (CLIPSeg)
- Speech to text (Whisper), zero-shot text classification and summarisation (BART)
- Translation via Meta's No Language Left Behind model

The transformers-agnostic ones include a text downloader that is just a Python script fetching a URL, plus Stable Diffusion flavours for text to image, image transformation (her example: add a rock to the picture) and text to video.

One practical warning from testing: NLLB claims around 200 languages, but through the agent not all of them worked, some threw errors, so she kept a list of roughly 80 that did. Check your language before you build on it.

## When the built-in voice fails, grow another leg

Her translated Spanish caption, voiced by the default text-to-speech tool, came out as English pronunciation of Spanish words. She tried running translation and voicing separately; no better. So she wrote a custom tool.

She pictures the agent as an octopus whose legs are tools, and you can keep adding legs. The recipe: write a plain function around the Google text-to-speech library (gTTS) that takes text and a language code, then subclass the `Tool` class from transformers with a name, a description the agent reads to decide when to use it, input and output descriptions, and a `__call__`. She used the langcodes library to turn the language name Spanish into the code gTTS expects, re-initialised the agent with the new tool, and the same caption finally sounded Spanish. Custom tools can also be pushed to the Hub for others to use.

## Is it production-ready?

Her own verdict is honest. As Darya Petrashka said at Conf42 Python 2024: "Agents are still experimental, they still a little bit brittle for many use cases, especially when it comes to some complex prompting with different steps." Expect unexpected output, practise your prompts, and try other LLMs (including open source ones) as the agent. For broader agent frameworks she points to LangChain and Amazon Bedrock.

## Who should watch

Python developers who want a gentle, practical first look at tool-using agents, with every step visible in a notebook. If you already build agents with function calling, the custom-tool section is the part worth your time.

Title: Boomers, millennials and Gen Z all want to row. They ask different questions
Description: Pawel Zajaczkowski (Xebia) at Conf42 Python 2024 on generational differences in tech teams, and why they are a delicate tool, not a hammer
Body:
Tell a crew of boomers to row and they row. Tell Gen X and they ask for the target, the speed and the deadline. Millennials point at the engine. Gen Z asks whether the island called profit is the right one. At Conf42 Python 2024, Pawel Zajaczkowski, Software Development Manager at Xebia and a former developer who "moved to the dark side", gave a talk about generations in tech that lands between the two usual camps: the differences are real enough to be useful, and too weak to be a management system.

There is no Python in it. It is a people talk for the person who leads a team of developers and DevOps engineers spanning four generations, told with memes that, by his own description, try to bash everyone equally.

## Are generational differences real or a myth?

Search for generational differences and you get manuals for handling boomers and millennials. Search for generational differences myths and you get articles saying it is all nonsense. His answer is in between, and he backs it with three observations:

- **Every older generation complains about the younger one.** A Babylonian clay tablet from 1000 BC already calls the youth rotten, evil, godless and lazy. He calls it generational narcissism: our cohort is the best, the young are immature, the old block progress.
- **The labels slide.** Research usually sees four generations at work, two seen as immature and two as adult. Today Gen X is described as the last adult generation; 20 years ago it was the boomers, and Gen X was the one without respect for its elders.
- **Age changes people too.** From roughly 20 to 50, conscientiousness and agreeableness go up while openness, extraversion and neuroticism go down. Some of what looks like a generation is just people getting older.

On top of that, cultural differences and, above all, individual differences outweigh the generational ones. Hence the line that sums up the talk, as Pawel Zajaczkowski said at Conf42 Python 2024: "Don't use it as a hammer labeled millennial or boomer and just use it on everyone." He suggests treating it as "a delicate tool in your people skills arsenal" instead.

## Who actually works in IT?

Mostly millennials. In the Polish software house he showed, roughly 80% of staff are Generation Y, with a little Gen Z and Gen X on either side. A Dutch consulting company has more Gen X and a few boomers, because the industry there started earlier and consultancies hire more senior people. So whatever your team looks like, the median colleague probably remembers dial-up.

## A field guide, one generation at a time

The second act walks through each cohort with its formative events, a short manual and a roster of famous tech people (Knuth, Liskov and Ken Thompson for the Silent Generation; Stroustrup, Gosling and Guido van Rossum for the boomers; Torvalds and Carmack for Gen X; Ryan Dahl and Melanie Perkins for the millennials):

- **Baby boomers** (roughly 58 to 77): face to face, high power distance, hierarchy, loyalty, hard skills. Make them happy with a formal title and a chance to mentor.
- **Gen X** (42 to 58): the latchkey kids. Autonomous, results-focused, career-driven, prone to burnout, so a good lead watches for the symptoms.
- **Millennials** (27 to 42): the Y stands for why, and the reason had better be sensible. Team players, the first to insist on life-work balance, low power distance (the boss is more a buddy than a superior), flexible, often freelancers.
- **Gen Z** (10 to 26): online natives shaped by the pandemic and remote schooling. They want a cause beyond profit, a quick feedback loop rather than a yearly review, gamification that helps, and a flat hierarchy where respect is earned rather than granted by title.

For Gen Z he could not name eight famous tech people yet. Plenty run successful startups; it is too early to say which ones change the world.

## What does everyone want?

The boat story closes on the point that matters for managers: the list of what every generation wants is the same list. Stability, a leader who knows the direction, some independence, visible results, a life outside work, flexibility, feedback, good atmosphere, a just cause and respect. The generations differ in emphasis, not in kind, and each one invented a piece of the modern workplace the others now enjoy. He points to Frederic Laloux's Reinventing Organizations for the longer version.

## Who should watch

New team leads and engineering managers, especially anyone managing people older than them for the first time. Developers can watch it as a forty-minute explanation of why their manager keeps asking how they feel about the roadmap.
