Title: The best SDK is the one you stop owning
Description: Adam Furmanek (Metis) at Conf42 Python 2024 on three SDK rewrites and why handing instrumentation to OpenTelemetry beat per-stack libraries
Body:
Every SDK starts as a small library and ends as a support contract with every ORM release on the planet. At Conf42 Python 2024, Adam Furmanek, Head of Engineering at Metis, walked through three generations of the Metis SDK and the lesson they paid for: the less code you own, the less breaks on you. His summary, as Adam Furmanek said at Conf42 Python 2024: "the best thingy is the thingy that you don't own."

## What the SDK had to do

Metis does database observability aimed at developers, before production. The pitch: your query was fast locally because the table had 100 rows, but it scans the whole table, and in production that hurts. To say that, Metis needs three things per request: which REST endpoint was called, which SQL ran while handling it (with parameters), and the execution plan, which it fetches itself with `EXPLAIN`. Alert the developer before commit, or at the latest in CI/CD.

The tenets for the SDK were strict: easy to use, a one-time integration for the whole team, ideally no code changes, and ideally zero dependencies.

## Version one: an SDK per tech stack

Python with FastAPI and SQLAlchemy is one stack. JavaScript with the pg driver and Sequelize is another. Java with JDBC, Spring and Hibernate is a third. The first approach shipped a library for each, hooking into the web framework and the ORM, enabled with `pip install` plus one line at the entry point.

Users liked it. Maintaining it was another story. Flask instead of FastAPI is a new stack. A different SQLAlchemy version is a new stack. A different driver under SQLAlchemy is a new stack. Almost nothing beyond the code that sends data to Metis could be reused, even JSON encoding differed between libraries and Python versions, and some ORMs ran the REST handler and the query on different threads with no shared identifier to correlate them.

## Version two: read it from the database

The second design stamped each SQL query with the trace id in a comment, and a Metis collector container read the database logs, matched the stamps and pulled the plans. Less ORM integration, new problems:

- The database had to be reconfigured to log execution plans for every query, which is hard on ephemeral databases spun up with Testcontainers and often needs a restart.
- All those logs cost money to store and process.
- Some ORMs refuse comments, comments can break monitoring integrations, and one ORM call can fan out into several SQL statements of which only one gets stamped.

## Version three: move the ownership

The current approach drops the SDK. Applications use OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation, switched on from outside the process with environment variables, and send traces to a local Metis collector, which extracts the SQL, runs `EXPLAIN` and forwards the result. No application code changes in Python, JavaScript, Java or .NET (C++ and Go still need manual setup), no database changes, and when a new ORM version breaks its instrumentation, fixing it is the ORM authors' job. Metis maintains only the collector.

It is not perfect: not every library supports auto-instrumentation, some emit `$1` placeholders instead of parameter values, so Metis has to parse logs to rebuild the query, and correlating REST with SQL is still not always possible.

## The cross-language lessons

The second half is advice for anyone shipping one SDK in several languages:

- **Keep the feature set primitive.** Generics, macros, prototypes versus classes and `eval` do not port. Uniform functionality and one set of docs mean giving up language-specific tricks.
- **Prefer gRPC over hand-rolled JSON** when every target language has it: one schema definition, generated code, fewer encoding surprises. Prefer open standards over a proprietary protocol you will own forever, even if you have to squeeze your structures into them.
- **Treat all the SDKs as one SDK.** One shared test set across languages, every change tested in every language, a bug found in Python hunted in the JavaScript and Java versions too, isolated environments with Docker, Testcontainers or Nix, a monorepo with tooling such as Lerna, and explicit, minimal dependencies.
- **Appoint a language champion.** Nobody knows every ecosystem, so each language gets one person who tracks ORM, driver and build-system changes and reports in weekly meetings.

## Who should watch

Anyone maintaining a client library in more than one language, or about to start one. The Python content is the context, not the subject; the lessons apply to any SDK team. It is a case study told from experience, without code on screen.

Title: Your Airflow DAGs are Python, so test them like Python
Description: Tamara Janina Fingerlin (Astronomer) at Conf42 Python 2024 on testing Airflow DAGs locally and in CI with dag.test(), astro dev pytest and DAG rules
Body:
The worst way to learn a data pipeline broke is a Slack message from someone senior asking where their dashboard went. At Conf42 Python 2024, Tamara Janina Fingerlin, Developer Advocate at Astronomer, made the case that Airflow pipelines are just Python code, so every testing and CI/CD habit you apply to application code applies to them too, and then showed the full route from a laptop to production with every test on the way.

It is a practical, demo-heavy talk: the code lives in a public repository (astronomer/external-talk-demos, branch 2024-conf42-python-airflow-testing-prod), and everything she shows works with open source tools. You do not need to be an Astronomer customer.

## Why bother testing a DAG?

Her numbers set the stakes. Airflow has 12M+ monthly downloads, 2,800+ contributors and 1,600+ building blocks, and in an Astronomer survey of 806 users, 81% said Airflow is important or very important to their business. As Tamara Janina Fingerlin said at Conf42 Python 2024, "Airflow is the orchestrator to your data symphony", which means a wrong note lands on a dashboard a director is staring at.

Testing will not stop every failure, she says, but when something does go wrong, a tested pipeline tells you which parts you can trust while debugging.

## Local first: CLI commands and a debugger

Locally she uses the open source Astro CLI: `brew install astro`, `astro dev init` in an empty folder, `astro dev start`, and a minute or two later Airflow runs in Docker on localhost:8080 with two example DAGs. From there the testing toolkit is:

- `airflow dags test` runs one full DAG run; `airflow tasks test` runs a single task, handy for the one task in the middle of a long DAG you keep iterating on.
- `astro dev parse` catches import errors, duplicate task ids and accidental cycles (it is a directed acyclic graph, after all).
- `astro dev pytest` runs everything in the tests folder, with any Python framework, not just pytest.
- `astro dev upgrade-test` checks your DAGs against a newer Airflow or Astro Runtime version and diffs the pinned packages. In the demo it flagged a major pytest bump between runtime 10.2 and 10.3.

Her favourite lesser-known trick is `dag.test()`. Add an `if __name__ == "__main__"` block that calls `.test()` on the DAG object, and the DAG runs under the VS Code or PyCharm debugger like any script. You can pick an execution date (useful if you worry about date logic on 1 January), inject connections from a YAML file, swap variables and pass DAG conf. In the demo she flipped a variable from multiply to minus and got 14 - 23 instead of a product. Her verdict on the alternative: as a junior developer she had a lot of print statements in her code.

## Three kinds of tests, one command

In CI, a PR from a dev branch to staging runs `astro dev pytest`, which covers three test types:

- **DAG validation tests**, the Airflow-specific ones: is the DAG valid, plus custom rules that enforce architecture. Her examples: allow only approved schedules (so nobody ships a cron string that runs every five minutes instead of daily), require tags, allow only specific operators, and the classic one, assert `catchup=False` so a forgotten flag does not trigger a pile of backfills.
- **Unit tests** for your own code: custom hooks and operators, and functions inside `@task` tasks. Operators from provider packages are already tested upstream.
- **Integration tests** for real API calls, with a warning that they can cost money and time, "especially nowadays with llms."

The demo uses unittest, plain `assert` and pytest side by side to prove the point that the framework is your choice. Twelve tests pass; then she sets `catchup=True` and watches the validation test fail, which is exactly the job.

## From staging to production

The GitHub Actions workflow runs the same `astro dev pytest` command as her laptop, then deploys. She recommends letting code run a few days in a staging deployment as an end-to-end test, because some edge cases only show up with real data on certain days, then bundling PRs into a staging-to-production PR that runs the tests again. And one confession from experience: wait for the checks before you merge, even when you are 100% sure it is just a small change.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who already write DAGs but test them by clicking the trigger button and hoping. If you have never touched Airflow, the opening 101 on DAGs, tasks, decorators and operators gets you far enough to follow along.

Title: Multi-party computation lets two banks score a client without sharing data
Description: Petr Emelianov (Bloomtech) at Conf42 Python 2024 on secure multi-party computation, from secret-shared addition to private credit scoring.
Body:
Encryption keeps thieves out; it does nothing about the well-meaning company that just wants your data. At Conf42 Python 2024, Petr Emelianov, CEO of Bloomtech, introduced secure multi-party computation (MPC), the family of protocols that lets several parties compute a result together while each one learns nothing but that result, and worked through the arithmetic with numbers small enough to check in your head.

It's an introduction with real maths, not a product pitch: secret sharing, addition, multiplication, and the security caveats that separate a classroom protocol from one you'd ship.

## Security and privacy are not the same problem

Petr Emelianov said at Conf42 Python 2024: "The point is that the security measures protect your data from being stolen. It protects you from bad guys." Privacy is wider, because most of the people who want your data are not bad guys; they want to build better services.

He makes it concrete with Bob. A stolen credit card is a classic security incident with a clear playbook: block the card in the banking app, done within ten minutes. Bob's annual income leaking is milder but stickier, because the targeted promotions and ads don't stop even after his income changes. His face is the worst case, since it logs him into his phone, pays for his coffee and gets him through airport gates. "Bob can easily block his bank card. He can even change his annual income. But it's really hard to change one's face."

The IBM Cost of a Data Breach figures on his slides show the trend: the average cost of a breach rose from $3.62 million in 2017 to $4.45 million in 2023, and the cost per record from $141 to $165. His diagnosis: "We have created a lot of brilliant security measures, but ended up with data security without data privacy."

## How do you add numbers nobody can see?

MPC rests on secret sharing. Split a secret into random numbers that sum to it; any single share is meaningless, and even all shares but one reveal nothing.

Bob holds 3, Alice 6, Mallory 1, and they want the total. Bob splits his 3 into 2, minus 5 and 6, keeps the 2 and sends one share to each friend; Alice and Mallory do the same with theirs. Each person adds up the shares they hold (Bob gets 0, Alice minus 3, Mallory 13), they swap those partial sums, and everyone arrives at 10. Nobody learns anyone else's input.

## Multiplication takes three servers and a rectangle

Multiplying is harder. He uses replicated secret sharing with three servers that are assumed not to collude, possibly run by different organisations or cloud providers. Bob splits 3 into 1, 4 and minus 2 and gives each server two of the three shares, so no single server can reconstruct the secret but any two could. Alice does the same with 6.

The intuition is geometric: the area of an a-by-b rectangle equals the sum of the nine smaller rectangles you get by cutting each side into three. Each server computes the pieces it can, and the pieces add up to 18. Because some pieces could be computed by more than one server, simply exchanging them could leak data, so each server's result is treated as a private input and fed back through the addition protocol. Chain enough additions and multiplications and you get real functions without ever revealing an intermediate value.

## From toy arithmetic to credit scores

A linear regression is just additions and multiplications. Picture two banks whose client data is protected by banking secrecy laws, and a third party holding trained regression weights. Run the regression under MPC across three servers and the banks get an accurate credit score while neither reveals its data and the model owner keeps the weights private. He calls the example a bit toyish, but says Bloomtech solves similar tasks every day.

## What does MPC cost you?

The price is infrastructure beyond what ordinary computing needs, protocol complexity (real protocols are much harder than these examples), and overhead: one arithmetic operation turns into many messages over comparatively slow networks. Then there are the four security considerations on his list:

- **Randomness**: cryptography needs cryptographically secure random number generators, and he warns that "using simple generators like one from the Python standard library can be completely insecure."
- **Modular arithmetic**: real protocols work over finite algebraic structures such as cyclic groups, not unbounded integers.
- **Malicious parties**: the protocol must hold up even if someone deliberately deviates from it.
- **Collusion**: two servers in the multiplication example could combine shares and recover every secret; more complex protocols reduce that risk.

To experiment, he recommends Meta's CrypTen library, as a playground rather than for production. His conclusion compares MPC with the alternatives: it reveals only the final result, unlike federated learning; it is less resource-hungry than homomorphic encryption, more practical than differential privacy, and runs in software on commodity hardware rather than depending on enclaves like Intel SGX.

Title: If you copy-paste the same field 1,000 times, write a Python bot
Description: Andre Santos (Bookeepers Solutions) at Conf42 Python 2024 on RPA with Python, with a live bot that looks up codes in a desktop app and fills Excel.
Body:
Somewhere in your company, someone is copying a code from a spreadsheet into a desktop app, copying the answer back, and doing it again. At Conf42 Python 2024, Andre Santos, Python Developer at Bookeepers Solutions, gave a short introduction to robotic process automation (RPA) with Python and then let a bot do exactly that job on screen, one row at a time, while nobody touched the keyboard.

He has been writing Python for more than five years and RPA for more than two, at a Brazilian company that provides accounting and tax services. Andre Santos said at Conf42 Python 2024: "My job here is to help my colleagues to reduce their time spent on repetitive tasks." That is the whole talk in one sentence, and a job description more engineers could borrow.

Set expectations accordingly: this is a brief, beginner-level talk, half slides and half demo. If you've already scripted a GUI with PyAutoGUI, you know the territory; if you haven't, it's a quick way to see what's possible.

## What is RPA, and why Python?

RPA is the use of software to handle repetitive tasks so people can spend their time on more complex work. It works against whatever systems a company already has, whether that's an ERP such as SAP, an internal tool or a web application. His case for Python is the usual trio: a simple syntax, a broad set of libraries, and a large community that has probably already solved your problem.

The benefits he lists are time, fewer human errors and lower operating costs, delivered three ways: automated end-to-end workflows, automatic extraction and entry of data, and faster, consistent execution. His examples by industry: transaction processing, report generation and compliance tasks in finance; patient records, appointment scheduling and billing in healthcare; inventory, order processing and customer data validation in retail.

## A worked example: invoices that arrive by email

The case study is familiar to anyone near an accounts payable team. Invoices arrive by email every day. Someone opens each PDF, pulls out the invoice number, the date and the total, and types them into the accounting system or a spreadsheet. A Python bot can watch the inbox, open the PDF attachment from the right sender, run OCR to extract the fields and save them wherever they need to go.

For building such bots he points to PyAutoGUI, Selenium, Keyboard, NumPy and pandas, among others: PyAutoGUI and Keyboard for driving desktop interfaces, Selenium for browsers, and the data libraries for whatever comes back.

## The demo: a desktop app, an Excel file and a bot

The live task is deliberately mundane. A spreadsheet holds a list of codes. For each one, he has to open a search screen in a desktop application, paste the code, run the search, copy the description that comes back and paste it into the spreadsheet next to the code. He does the first two by hand so you feel it. "So here I have five codes but imagine if I have 100 codes, 1000 codes, and to do this again and again and again and again," he said.

Then the Python version: it imports the Excel file, opens the desktop application, queries one code at a time, extracts the description and writes it back into the workbook. You watch the cursor search, copy and save, row after row, until every description is filled in. "That's saving my time. That's the real benefit," he said, which is the RPA business case without a slide.

## What comes next for Python RPA?

His closing slide looks ahead to deeper AI integration for more intelligent automation, and back to the people: bots take over the repetitive work so employees can focus on the initiatives that grow the business.

## Who should watch

People in finance, operations or back-office teams who know a little Python and suspect half their week could be scripted, and developers who get asked to help them. Experienced automation engineers can skip it; the value here is seeing how little code a useful bot needs.

Title: A stats API with a few dozen requests a day doesn't need a message bus
Description: Alex Sharypov (Playrix) at Conf42 Python 2024 on avoiding overengineering with task refinement, small increments, tests and planned refactoring.
Body:
Most overengineered systems start with one unasked-for requirement. At Conf42 Python 2024, Alex Sharypov, Python Software Developer at Playrix, traced how a statistics endpoint worth a few days of FastAPI work turns into a weeks-long, message-bus-driven project nobody can change cheaply, and set out six habits that stop it from happening.

It's a short, process-focused talk with no code on screen, aimed at teams and tech leads more than at individual Python tricks.

## What counts as overengineering?

His definition: using more complex and advanced technologies than the task actually needs. He blames three forces. Developers like building something impressive. Managers bring tasks with an unclear scope. And there's an endless supply of fashionable architectures and algorithms, while most business problems are solved by popular frameworks and boring code that won't look good on a CV. Alex Sharypov said at Conf42 Python 2024: "As a metaphor, we could make a spacecraft to travel between two points in the same city. Cool, expensive, but useless."

## How does a few days of work become several weeks?

The worked example is a front end that needs statistics, aggregated from other services' APIs. Context matters, and here the context is modest: no high load, no response-time requirement. "There will be several dozen requests per day," he said. The sufficient solution is a FastAPI (or Django, or Flask) app that queries the sources asynchronously in real time, processes the results and returns JSON, scaling with more workers behind a gateway if it ever has to.

But nobody pinned that context down, and someone insists the API must be very fast and survive heavy traffic. Architecture invention begins: separate workers fetch from the sources over message queues, store everything in a local repository and serve from there, and the source services must change to publish on the bus. Some source teams refuse. A few days of estimated work becomes several weeks. The team falls behind, cuts corners, and moves the tests to the technical-debt pile. The code ships, sort of, and the first change request means touching several nodes of a system that never needed to exist. Everyone is satisfied except the client, who paid for it.

## Six habits that keep it simple

His fixes are mostly organisational:

1. **An experienced developer** who can judge the task and its architecture honestly.
2. **Task refinement**: analyse the business requirements and clarify every detail before design starts.
3. **Architecture review**: decide where change will happen and how the code is organised, and weigh load, processing time, correctness, validation and error handling. If the design starts collecting parts that may be useful one day, split them into later iterations.
4. **An iterative process**: break the work into increments, each one shippable to production on its own.
5. **Refactoring and optimisation**, planned rather than improvised.
6. **Tests** covering the business scenarios during development, so later refactoring can't silently break working interfaces.

## Small increments, shipped separately

His example is changing the sort field of a query, which needs a new index. Ship the index first. Then switch the code to sort by the new field. Then, if nothing else uses it, drop the old index. You could release all three at once, but in bigger cases release assembly and merge conflicts become the bottleneck, so you hide unfinished features and deliver in parts. Smaller increments are easier to review, conflict less and are less likely to hide a mistake. After each increment, get it to the consumer and collect feedback; sometimes a partial feature is enough, and sometimes the client cancels the rest.

## Refactoring is not optimisation

He is strict about the difference. Refactoring improves code without adding features: hunt the dirty spots (duplicated code, long methods, large classes, long parameter lists, redundant temporary variables, data classes, ungrouped data, leftover debug output) and simplify, without rewriting the service from scratch, which is re-engineering. Query tuning, speed, memory and leak fixes are optimisation, which matters but often makes code harder to read and creates new refactoring work. Both cost money without adding features, so tell the client upfront that development doesn't end when the service first works. In his experience, most clients accept that when they hear it before the work begins.

The last ingredient is shared ownership. Decisions should be made by the whole team, knowledge spread across it, and code documented. "When responsibility is shared among everyone, the quality will be good," he said, while a single owner tends to produce subjective, suboptimal designs.

Title: Python 3.12 in one sitting, from type statements to a GIL per interpreter
Description: Dmitrii Ivashchenko (MY.GAMES) at Conf42 Python 2024 on Python 3.12's typing syntax, freed-up f-strings, faster asyncio and the new monitoring API.
Body:
Python 3.12 is the release where `TypeVar` boilerplate and f-string quote juggling went away. At Conf42 Python 2024, Dmitrii Ivashchenko, Software Engineer at MY.GAMES, toured the release in four areas (typing, syntax, performance and debugging), PEP by PEP, with a before-and-after code sample for nearly every change.

It's a brisk changelog talk rather than an exploration of internals, and that is the point: half an hour of it beats reading What's New end to end.

## Typing finally gets its own syntax

PEP 695 is the headline. Instead of declaring `T = TypeVar('T')` and inheriting from `Generic[T]`, you write the type parameter in square brackets: `def max[T](args: Iterable[T]) -> T` and `class List[T]`. The same PEP adds the `type` statement for aliases, so `type Point[T] = tuple[T, T]` replaces the `TypeVar` dance, and the parameters can be a `ParamSpec`, a `TypeVarTuple`, a bounded type variable (a sequence of hashables) or a constrained one (a sequence of ints or strings).

Aliases are also lazily evaluated. His example sets `type Alias = 1/0`, and the `ZeroDivisionError` only fires when you touch `__value__`. That laziness is what makes mutually recursive aliases practical.

Two smaller ones you'll use often: PEP 692 lets `**kwargs` be typed precisely with `Unpack` on a `TypedDict`, instead of a vague union, and PEP 698 adds `@override`, so a type checker flags the child class that thought it was overriding `get_color` but actually defined `get_colour`.

## f-strings stop fighting you

PEP 701 rebuilt f-string parsing, and the result is mostly the removal of annoyances. You can reuse the same quote type inside the braces, nest f-strings as deep as you like, spread expressions over multiple lines with comments, and use backslashes and Unicode escapes such as joining a list with a newline or a black heart suit. Error messages now point at the exact spot in the f-string and even suggest the missing comma. Separately, `itertools.batched` arrives, so you can stop pasting your own chunking helper into every project.

## Where did the speed come from?

His figures, from the release notes and benchmarks he cites:

- **asyncio**: up to 75% faster in benchmarks, with faster socket writes, faster task creation and `current_task` reimplemented in C, which he says is four to six times faster on its own.
- **inspect and typing**: `inspect.getattr_static` is 2 to 6 times faster and `isinstance` checks against protocols 2 to 20 times faster, though protocols with 14 or more members can get slower.
- **Comprehension inlining** (PEP 709): list, dict and set comprehensions no longer create a throwaway function object and run up to twice as fast, with a small catch around iterating `locals()`.
- **Other**: experimental BOLT optimizer support, regex substitutions 2 to 3 times faster, and faster `super()` calls.

Then the one that made headlines. Dmitrii Ivashchenko said at Conf42 Python 2024: "Each Python interpreter now gets its own global interpreter lock." PEP 684 lets sub-interpreters run in parallel across cores, but in 3.12 only through the C API; he expected a Python API in 3.13, and it eventually shipped in 3.14 as `concurrent.interpreters`.

He is refreshingly frank about the niche items. PEP 683's immortal objects skip reference counting for objects such as `None`, which helps very large applications like Django deployments with lots of users, but "Still, this cool feature is only useful for a few Python projects." PEP 688 exposes the buffer protocol to Python with `__buffer__` and `__release_buffer__`, great for sharing memory with C extensions and something most Python users will never touch.

## Better errors, cheaper debuggers

The debugging section is where 3.12 is kindest to beginners. A `NameError` inside a method now suggests `self.blech`, a forgotten standard library import gets a hint, `import a.y.z from b.y.z` asks whether you meant `from ... import ...`, and importing `chainmap` from `collections` suggests `ChainMap`.

For tool authors, PEP 669 adds `sys.monitoring`, a low-impact API where profilers, debuggers and coverage tools register callbacks only for the events they care about. "Debugging and coverage can now be nearly overhead free," he said.

## Who should watch

Anyone still on 3.11 or older planning an upgrade, and library authors who want the typing changes in their heads before they meet them in a pull request. If you already read the release notes line by line, this is a fast recap.

Title: Functors in Python, explained with dots, arrows and no maths degree
Description: Chaur Wu at Conf42 Python 2024 on functors in Python, from fmap over lists to profunctor pipelines, using the funclift package and simple diagrams.
Body:
Category theory has a reputation for scaring off working programmers. At Conf42 Python 2024, Chaur Wu, a software developer based in the San Francisco Bay Area, gave a guided tour of the functor family (covariant, contravariant, applicative, bifunctors and profunctors) for Python programmers with no category theory background, using an open-source package called funclift and a lot of very simple diagrams.

He says upfront that he trades mathematical rigour for ease of understanding. The result is the gentlest route to `fmap` and its relatives you're likely to find in Python, and a dense one: eight concepts in under half an hour.

## Start with dots and arrows

The motivating example is two functions: `get_price` takes an item and returns an int, `is_pricy` takes an int and returns a bool. Chaur Wu said at Conf42 Python 2024: "To visualize the code, we can draw types as dots and functions as arrows." Composing the two functions into `is_item_pricy` is just following two arrows in a row. Dots, arrows and rules for composing arrows: that is a category, and this one, with Python types as dots and Python functions as arrows, he calls the category of types.

## A functor lifts a function into a box

Mapping `is_even` over a list is usually a comprehension. With funclift's `CList` you call `fmap(is_even)` instead, which lifts a function from int to bool into a function from a list of ints to a list of bools. Anything that maps dots to dots and arrows to arrows this way, with the right properties, is a functor. Two practical boxes follow:

- **IO** wraps a side effect, such as reading a number from the console, into a value. You can `fmap` `is_even` over a number that hasn't been read yet, and nothing happens until you call `unsafe_run`. Side effects get pushed to the boundary of the program and the core stays referentially transparent.
- **Option** fixes partial functions. `ten_mod_by` blows up on zero; returning `None` instead makes it total but forces if/else wherever you compose it. Returning `Nothing` or `Some` keeps it total and composable, since `fmap` skips the missing case for you.

Functors compose too. A list of options needs `Compose` to reach the numbers inside, and once you see that functors can be chained like arrows, you get the category whose dots are categories and whose arrows are functors.

## Contravariant and applicative functors

A covariant functor keeps the arrow's direction; a contravariant one flips it. His example is `Predicate`: `cmap(str_to_int)` turns a predicate on ints into a predicate on strings, so you can ask whether the string six is even.

Applicative functors need one more idea, a closed category, where function types are themselves dots. Skipping the formal route via lax closed functors, the practical payoff is `ap`: take a curried `sum`, `fmap` it over `Some(20)` to get an option holding a function, then `ap` it to `Some(30)` and get `Some(50)`. Multi-argument functions now work inside the box.

## Bifunctors and profunctors: where pipelines appear

A bifunctor maps over two type arguments at once. funclift's `Either` holds a `Left` or a `Right`; `bimap(negate, add1)` on `Right(5)` gives `Right(6)` and leaves the other side alone.

A profunctor is contravariant in its first argument and covariant in its second, which is easiest to picture as a box that takes an A and outputs a C. `dimap(f, g)` adds a function on the way in and another on the way out. He mentions `Forget`, `Star` and `Costar`, then builds a `Star` around `ten_mod_by`: three gives `Some(1)`, zero gives `Nothing`. Then `dimap(str_to_int, is_even)` turns it into something that takes a string and returns an option of bool. "As you can see, the code example we have starts to look like some sort of data pipelines that can be chained and compose in flexible ways," he said, which is the honest sales pitch for the whole zoo.

## Who should watch

Python developers who keep running into Haskell or Scala vocabulary and want the intuition without the textbook, and anyone who has used `Optional` and wondered what else sits in that family. You'll want the slides open next to the video: the code examples are short, but each one builds on the last.

Title: The Unix shell ignored cursor movement in 1975 and never caught up
Description: Ilya Sher (Beame) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on why the shell still works like a telegraph, and an interactive, semantic UI to replace it
Body:
Your terminal can put the cursor anywhere on the screen, and has been able to since the VT52. Your shell still uses one line of it. Ilya Sher, CTO at Beame and author of Next Generation Shell (NGS), argued at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 that the Unix shell's user interface is stuck in a send-text, receive-text paradigm inherited from the telegraph, and sketched what a shell that understands its own output could do instead.

Sher has used bash since around 1996 and got fed up enough with it in 2013 to start writing his own shell. This short talk is the design argument behind NGS's planned UI.

## What's actually wrong with the shell?

He splits the shell into two things: a programming language and a user interface. The language problems (arcane syntax, error handling as an afterthought, no structured data) are widely understood, and several modern shell projects are working on them. The UI is the part nobody is fixing, so that's the talk.

"The user interface is basically the same as a telegraph," Ilya Sher said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. You send text, you receive text, and that is the whole conversation.

## How did we end up typing into a telegraph?

The history is a chain of incremental improvements with no rethink. The telegraph became the teleprinter (keyboard plus printer, two of them cross-connected, the TTY). The teleprinter got wired to computers to replace punched cards. Then the video display unit replaced the paper, but behaved exactly like paper: new text at the bottom, everything else scrolls up.

The real breakthrough was the VT52 in 1974 or 1975, which supported cursor movement. Bill Joy responded with vi in 1976, and text editing moved from typing commands such as add text or delete text to editing anywhere on a full screen. The shell's response, per Sher, was nothing, pretty much to this day: "most of the screen is not actually interactive. It's treated like paper." The interactive part is the command line, plus a few lines when completion pops up.

## What would an interactive shell look like?

Text on the screen becomes a representation of objects, a bit like links on the web. The shell tracks which text maps to which object, each with a type, an id and a display name: a file, or an AWS CodePipeline pipeline. Interacting with an object asks every plugin which of them handles that type, and the menu is assembled from their answers, with a default action for a click or Enter.

The bonus material extends this to objects of interest: the shell shows CI/CD runs of pipelines you created or runs triggered by your commit, the way a mail client shows new mail, with editable rules explaining why each item appeared.

## Why does recording have to be semantic?

The usual complaint about web UIs is that you have no record of what you did, and nobody accepts that for serious work. So every interaction must be recorded and shown to the user immediately, at the highest semantic level possible. If you clicked the failed pipeline, the recording should capture the pipeline with status failed, so replaying it tomorrow opens whichever pipeline failed tomorrow. Same for instances: i-123 is meaningless and will be gone soon; you picked it because of a name tag, a VPC or a security group, and that is what should be captured. That's more powerful than shell history.

## Isn't that too much work for a shell?

Sher has a rebuttal for the two usual objections, that a shell has no business doing semantics and that it is too much work: it already does. Shells understand exit codes for basic error handling, and command line completion needs a per-program plugin that understands arguments. That work got done, and understanding output is the same order of magnitude. His comparison is Notepad versus a JetBrains IDE, with vi plus language plugins in between: the more a program understands its data, the more powerful it is.

## Who should watch

Anyone who lives in a terminal and has copy-pasted an instance id from one command's output into the next. It's a vision talk, short and opinionated, not a demo: the UI described is still work in progress in NGS (ngs-lang.org). It sits a little outside chaos engineering, which is part of the fun.

Title: Put a hexagon inside your Lambda and swapping DynamoDB stops hurting
Description: Hazel Andrea Saenz Giron (Cognits) at Conf42 Python 2024 on hexagonal architecture inside AWS Lambda, so storage and email become swappable adapters.
Body:
Serverless splits your system into functions; hexagonal architecture splits each function into a business core and replaceable edges. At Conf42 Python 2024, Hazel Andrea Saenz Giron, Software Architect at Cognits and an AWS Community Builder in the serverless category, argued the two belong together, and showed a Python Lambda where moving from DynamoDB to Aurora, or from email to SMS, touches one adapter and nothing else.

It's an introductory, story-led talk with a small working demo: a good first look at ports and adapters for anyone writing Lambdas, less so for people who already run the pattern.

## How she got here

Her design history is a familiar one. First monoliths, everything on one server. Then layers: web server, application server, database server. Then MVC and microservices. Moving to the cloud showed the old habits still work but cost more than they used to, and in serverless projects she found the code harder to maintain. Her conclusion: the change can't stop at the server level, it has to reach how the code inside each function is organised.

## What is hexagonal architecture, in one picture?

It is a pattern that separates an application's core logic from its interactions with the outside world. At the centre sits the domain, where all the business logic lives. Around it are ports, the interfaces the domain talks through. On the outside are adapters, the concrete pieces: an API, a database, an email service. Because the domain only knows about ports, you can plug a new input or output in, take an old one away, and the business logic stays put.

Her three benefits:

- **Testability**: the business logic is decoupled from external components, so unit tests can feed mock adapters into the ports and test the domain alone.
- **Flexibility**: changing the database, the user interface (mobile to web) or the transport is an adapter change.
- **Maintainability as you grow**: when the business rules change, you know exactly where to go.

## Why serverless and hexagons fit

Serverless already treats an application as a collection of functions responding to events, with no servers to patch and scaling handled for you. Both ideas push towards separation of concerns, and she lists what the mix gives you: interchangeability, simplicity despite the intimidating name, separation of concerns, event-driven entry points (each event comes in through an adapter) and decoupling. Lambda decouples your code from the infrastructure; the hexagon decouples it further inside the function.

Then the warning, with a Spider-Man slide. Hazel Andrea Saenz Giron said at Conf42 Python 2024: "With a great power comes a greater responsibility." The pattern only works if the team actually designs the split before typing, and holds that line across many developers and many change requests. Skip that step and you get spaghetti in hexagonal clothing.

## The demo: a signup Lambda with two adapters

The example is a basic API: API Gateway invokes a Lambda that creates a user, stores it in DynamoDB and sends a welcome email through Amazon SES. Inside the function:

- the **handler is the domain**: it receives the payload and calls a save-user port and a send-email port, with no database or email code in sight;
- a **DynamoDB adapter** holds the table name and the insert, and returns the new user id;
- an **SES adapter** holds the sender, recipient and message body.

She runs a test event with a name and an email address, and the welcome message arrives in her inbox. Then the point of the whole exercise: "If I'm going to change that, the only thing that I need to change is the adapter and I don't have to change any logic into the business side." Moving to Aurora is a new storage adapter; switching the welcome email to an SMS is a new notification adapter. Testing also splits cleanly: unit tests aim at the domain, integration tests at the adapters.

The code is in her article on implementing hexagonal architecture for serverless apps in under ten minutes, linked from the talk. Her parting advice is to design a function before writing it, because the time spent comes back during maintenance and when onboarding new developers.

Title: Your vendor's Kafka benchmark is marketing, so run your own
Description: Elad Leev (Dojo) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on benchmarking Kafka or Pulsar yourself with OpenMessaging Benchmark, at peak traffic plus a buffer
Body:
Every streaming vendor has a chart showing their broker beating everyone else's. Elad Leev, Senior Data Platform Engineer at Dojo, argued at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 that those charts tell you nothing about your own cluster, and showed how to find its real limits with the Linux Foundation's OpenMessaging Benchmark (OMB). The takeaway: benchmark on production-identical hardware, aim at your peak traffic plus a buffer, and use the results for capacity planning, alert thresholds and config advice for your developers.

Dojo has a reason to care. It enables 130,000 businesses to take card payments from 4 million consumers a day, mostly in pubs, bars and restaurants across the UK, so a lot of data moves through its streaming platform.

## Why not trust the published numbers?

Leev opens with Jim Gray's 1991 benchmark handbook: no single metric can measure a system's performance across all applications. The same Kafka cluster behaves very differently depending on message size, traffic pattern and producer and consumer configuration. Vendor benchmarks, in his view, are a marketing job with few engineers anywhere near them. As a data-driven team you have to run the test yourself.

Knowing the limits pays off three ways: more accurate capacity planning, preventive maintenance, and less toil. And the limiting factor is almost always one of four things: disk, memory, CPU or network.

## What makes a benchmark worth trusting?

His criteria, in order:

- **Mock your environment, no tricks.** Same machine types, same JVM, same number of nodes as production, even if it costs more. "It's not a game. We are not trying to aim for a better result or getting better numbers or anything like that. We actually aim for an accurate result in the benchmarks," Elad Leev said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024.
- **Aim for the peak.** Collect system and application metrics first, know your SLAs and SLOs, decide whether a latency spike counts as downtime, then test at peak traffic with headroom. He cites Werner Vogels' 2016 line that failures are a given, and suggests testing for N minus one: you should still serve peak load after losing a machine or two.
- **Scalable and portable.** Today it's Kafka or Redpanda, tomorrow it might be RabbitMQ, Pulsar or NATS. The benchmark should move with you and scale its workers up and down like your services do.
- **Simplicity.** If others can't understand and reproduce the test, it loses credibility. Document the process and the key results.

## What should you measure while it runs?

Brendan Gregg's USE method: for every resource, check utilization, saturation and errors. Gregg pitches it as finding 80% of server issues with 5% of the effort, and Leev compares it to a flight attendant's emergency checklist. Concretely: CPU system, user and idle time plus load average; memory buffers, cache and, for JVM systems, heap and GC time; network bytes in and out and dropped packets; disk io-wait and queue length.

## Why OpenMessaging Benchmark instead of kafka-producer-perf-test?

Kafka ships its own performance scripts, RabbitMQ has tools, NATS has its bench utility, and JMeter still works for JVM systems. All of them lock the benchmark to one product. OMB is vendor neutral and has two parts: a driver that assigns tasks, creates topics and orchestrates, and workers that execute the load against the cluster. It installs with a Helm chart on Kubernetes (or runs outside it), and you scale workers to match the pod count of your biggest or most critical service.

A test is a driver config (connection string, IO threads, request timeout, then producer settings such as acks, linger.ms and batch size, then consumers) plus a workload file with message size, randomized payloads and producer rate. Leev's advice is to survey your biggest producers and consumers first and copy their real configurations into the tests, then add edge cases. Results print to the screen, save to a file and can be charted with the project's Python script.

## What do you get out of it?

Five things: end-to-end latency (and which knobs, like a lower linger or batch size, improve it for latency-critical services); a stress test of your Grafana or Datadog dashboards, which should not break exactly when the cluster is overloaded; your bottleneck, so you can lower an alert threshold before a disk hits I/O starvation; a scale-up ballpark from adding brokers mid-test and watching latency; and, with enough runs, a configuration suggestion tool where developers can see the latency cost of a bigger batch size without paying to test it themselves.

## Who should watch

Platform and data engineers who own a Kafka, Pulsar or RabbitMQ cluster and plan capacity by gut feeling. It's a practical method talk, not a tour of results: no Dojo numbers from their own runs, but a clear recipe for producing yours.

Title: Polars lets you run plain SQL on a CSV bigger than your RAM
Description: Tom Levy (Own Company) at Conf42 Python 2024 on Polars SQLContext with lazy frames, streaming sinks and CTEs over a 200-million-row CSV.
Body:
If you think in SQL but your data lives in CSV files too big to load, Polars has a shortcut. At Conf42 Python 2024, Tom Levy, Software Engineer at Own Company, showed how Polars' SQL context runs ordinary SQL queries, common table expressions included, over lazy frames, using a 200-million-row Pokémon dataset that won't fit in memory on most laptops.

It's a short, hands-on talk: four sections, all code, built on one running example with a Pokémon theme that does more teaching than you'd expect.

## What is Polars, and why reach for it?

Tom Levy said at Conf42 Python 2024: "Polars is a data frame interface on top of an online analytical processing query engine." It is written in Rust with Apache Arrow as the memory model, which gives it memory management without a garbage collector.

His list of reasons: speed (he points to the published Polars benchmarks against pandas and others), memory efficiency, I/O against local and cloud storage, lazy evaluation, an API that is friendly to people coming from other dataframe libraries, the SQL context, the usual filter, sort, join, group and aggregate operations, interoperability with pandas, and an open-source licence the maintainers say will stay that way.

## SQL on a dataframe in five lines

The warm-up is a three-row dataframe of trainers with an id, a name and a badge count. You create an SQL context, register the dataframe under a table name, and run a query selecting the trainers with eight badges. Passing `eager=True` returns a ready dataframe instead of the default lazy frame, which is fine when the result is small. One trainer comes back.

## How do you query a file that doesn't fit in memory?

This is the core of the talk. The Pokémon file has 200 million rows and four columns: id, name, type and trainer. Instead of reading it, `scan_csv` returns a lazy frame that only references the file, so nothing is processed until a query runs.

Two schema strategies sit side by side. For the Pokémon file, `infer_schema_length` tells Polars how many rows to sample to guess column types (more rows, slower inference). For the trainers file he spells the schema out: integer id, string name, integer badges. `register_many` registers both tables at once, and a quick `SHOW TABLES` confirms the context sees them.

Then the actual question: the id and trainer of every Charizard. Why Charizard? "Because everyone loves charizard," he said. Since the query returns a lazy frame, he doesn't collect it at all: `sink_csv` evaluates the query in streaming mode and writes straight to a result file, so neither the input nor the output has to fit in memory.

## CTEs work too, so long queries stay readable

Common table expressions let you name a temporary result and build on it. His example defines `champions`, the trainers with eight badges (anyone who has finished a Pokémon game knows that's what it takes to beat the league), then joins it to the Pokémon table on trainer name with an alias, capped with `LIMIT 6`. This time he collects with streaming enabled, so results arrive in pieces rather than all at once, and converts the rows to dictionaries. The dataset has a single champion, so six rows come back.

His closing caveat matters: Polars' SQL does not support every SQL operation, and the user guide lists what is covered. The API on screen is from early 2024, and Polars moves fast, so check the current docs before copying it.

## Who should watch

Analysts and engineers fluent in SQL who keep hitting memory limits with pandas, and anyone curious what lazy evaluation buys you in practice. If you already know Polars inside out, this is a quick refresher on the SQL side rather than new ground.

Title: Four API habits that keep data-heavy systems from paying twice
Description: Santosh Nikhil Kumar (ByteDance) at Conf42 Python 2024 on REST vs Thrift, async callbacks over queues, gateway rate limits and idempotency keys.
Body:
Double-click the pay button and the only acceptable outcome is one charge. At Conf42 Python 2024, Santosh Nikhil Kumar, Senior Software Engineer at ByteDance, laid out four API design decisions that data-intensive systems (Netflix, Amazon, TikTok, Instagram, Google Maps) depend on: REST for HTTP and Thrift for RPC, asynchronous calls with callbacks, rate limiting, and idempotency.

It's a fundamentals talk built around one simple architecture diagram and a payment example that keeps coming back, so it suits engineers who are moving from building endpoints to designing systems. One note for this audience: the code samples are Java and Spring Boot, though the patterns are language-neutral.

His framing of an API is the client's view of an abstraction. Santosh Nikhil Kumar said at Conf42 Python 2024: "API is like a steering in a car where the driver doesn't need to know how the engine works."

## Why REST at the edge and Thrift inside?

In his reference diagram, users reach the system through a load balancer, a gateway fans out to microservices, and some calls leave for external partners such as Visa, Stripe or PayPal. The calls from the outside world are HTTP; the calls between services inside the backend are RPC.

REST earns the edge for three reasons. It is stateless, so every request carries everything the server needs and no strings tie request one to request two, which keeps scaling simple. It is resource-oriented, so a path like users, then a user id, then posts maps cleanly to what the backend retrieves. And it is where the non-core concerns live: authentication, authorisation, rate limiting, caching, logging, monitoring. Keeping those at the HTTP layer leaves the RPC calls to do pure business logic.

Inside, Apache Thrift (originally from Facebook) wins on three things. Code generation: describe the request, response and service once in a Thrift file, then generate client and server code for Java, Python or Go, which removes most of the hand-written compatibility glue between services in different languages. A binary protocol that is cheaper to serialise and send than JSON or XML. And generated servers that handle concurrent requests and support asynchronous communication.

## Don't make the user wait for Visa

A synchronous payment chain, from service one to service two to service three to the card network, is a poor experience and does not scale. His alternative: service one drops the pay request onto a distributed queue (Kafka or RocketMQ) and immediately tells the user it's processing. Consumers move the work along through a second queue to the external call, and the request carries a callback URL. When the partner finishes, it POSTs to that URL.

The resilient part is the third queue. The callback lands in a queue rather than straight in the handler. If saving state or the follow-up RPC fails, the consumer doesn't acknowledge the message, so it stays queued and gets retried until the handler completes.

## Callbacks and webhooks are cousins, not twins

A callback starts with a request: the caller hands the callee a URL to answer on. A webhook starts with an event on the sender's side. His example is GitHub notifying Slack about a pull request being opened, merged or commented on, by calling a URL Slack registered. Webhooks are always asynchronous; callbacks can sometimes be synchronous.

## Rate limits belong at the gateway, mostly

Rate limiting caps requests per client per time window, which prevents abuse, keeps access fair for everyone sharing the endpoint and protects stability. Over the limit, the client gets a 429. His Spring Boot example is a single annotation allowing five calls per 60 seconds. Where the logic lives is a trade-off, but he has a default: "I personally always designed where the systems do the rate limiting at the gateway layer."

## Idempotency keys make retries boring

Back to the double-tap. "Do you want your money to be deducted twice or what?" he asked. Each request carries an idempotency key, a UUID tied to the client, which can be assigned by the gateway or a dedicated service rather than the client. The backend looks the key up in a key-value store (a map, Redis, whatever fits). Found: return the stored response without doing the work again. Not found: process, then record the key.

He closes by listing what he left for another session: pagination, filtering, security and error contracts for systems where lots of requests also mean lots of errors.

Title: Chaos engineering starts at the module, not the game day
Description: Dhiraj Kumar Jain (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on why developers should build failure models and chaos tests while they write the code
Body:
The usual order is: build the whole thing, then run a game day before launch and fix what breaks. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, Dhiraj Kumar Jain, Software Engineer at AWS, argues for the reverse. Developers should think chaos while designing and coding even small modules: inject failures as each piece is built, so that resilience accumulates bottom-up into more nines for the whole system.

He works on the storage layer of Aurora, a multi-tenant, distributed, auto-scaling storage platform, and maintains tooling for running OpenSearch on Kubernetes, so the advice comes from someone who builds distributed systems for a living.

## What separates chaos engineering from chaos testing?

His distinction: chaos testing is injecting failures. Add observability (a hypothesis, proactive monitoring, and fixing what you find) and it becomes chaos engineering. The cycle starts from the steady state, makes hypotheses about how the system behaves after, say, a power, cloud service or database outage, runs the experiment, validates the hypotheses and improves the system.

One detail matters: "There should be some randomness in your experiments," Dhiraj Kumar Jain said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. Without it, a chaos experiment is just another integration test asserting known outcomes, when the point is to observe and find unknowns. His example is a data-centre fire: it does not take everything down at once, it spreads rack by rack until the whole availability zone is gone. Intermittent, uneven failure injection is closer to reality than a clean 30-minute shutdown.

## Why should developers care?

He leads with a Gremlin survey of companies that practise chaos engineering as a habit: 47% saw increased availability, MTTR fell by 45% and MTTD by 41%. His reading is that those organisation-wide results only come when chaos is plugged into every part of the software development lifecycle.

The obstacles, from the same survey: lack of awareness and experience first, closely followed by other priorities, and more than 10% of engineers saying they fear something might go wrong. His answer to the last is that nobody should start in production. Begin in pre-prod, move to a prod-like environment and the beta stage, and get to production later in the journey.

## How do you run a controlled experiment on your own code?

He gives five steps that work for a module, a service or a whole product, with the boundary widening each time:

1. Identify the boundary and scope of the experiment.
2. Build the failure model: if service A depends on service B and database D, what happens when either fails, or both, simultaneously or in sequence?
3. Think through dependency failures, external (a managed cloud service, a self-hosted MongoDB) and internal (sister systems).
4. Inject failures and monitor.
5. Validate the results.

His worked example is a microservice doing CRUD operations and some computation on a VM with a SQL database. Thinking chaos at design time leads to replicating the database across availability zones and regions; then a cache so that, if even that fails, users get stale data instead of errors. For the compute, surviving AZ+1 (a whole availability zone down plus one more instance) means at least three instances, one per AZ. Then the experiments: shut the database down, add network latency until you find the point where the customer experience degrades, and kill two of the three instances to see if the last can carry the load.

## How does this become routine?

Manual experiments (ad hoc runs and game days, such as taking a database down for six to eight hours) are the start. The goal is automated experiments in CI/CD, canary releases and continuous experimentation, so every check-in produces a resilience score. His example: alarms generated from CloudFormation or Terraform templates, with a pipeline step that injects a failure and checks the alarms fire, which catches a bug in the alarm-creation code before release.

His best practices: know the steady state, build a failure model, control the blast radius, add randomness, test in real-world conditions, monitor and log extensively, run a post-incident analysis after every experiment, and start today. He quotes Jesse Robbins, Amazon's former Master of Disaster, to the effect that every dollar spent on failure buys a dollar's worth of lessons.

## What does the ecosystem look like?

Numbers he cites: 63% of 400+ IT professionals have performed chaos experiments and 30% run them in production; GitHub has over 200 chaos engineering projects with 16k+ stars; and teams that experiment frequently are more likely to exceed 99.9% availability. The open source tools he names include LitmusChaos, Chaos Monkey, ChaosBlade, Chaos Mesh (strong for Kubernetes) and Chaos Toolkit, with managed services from the major clouds. No single tool suits everyone, because every service has its own failure model and success metrics.

## Who should watch?

Application developers who think chaos is the SRE team's job, and tech leads looking for a lightweight way to put failure thinking into design reviews and tests. It is a clear introduction with one worked design example, not a tool demo.

Title: Sketching algorithms trade a little accuracy for a lot of speed
Description: Tun Shwe (Quix) at Conf42 Python 2024 on data sketches, the kilobyte-sized structures that answer big-data queries in one pass with known error bounds.
Body:
Your slow `GROUP BY` on a billion high-cardinality rows has a cheaper cousin: answer approximately, with an error bound you can prove. At Conf42 Python 2024, Tun Shwe, VP of Data and DevRel at Quix, gave a tour of sketching algorithms, the small, single-pass data structures that turn big-data questions into small-data ones, and showed how to use them from Python with Apache DataSketches.

## What counts as a sketch?

His working definition: sketches are small, stateful, streaming programs that deal with huge volumes of data and return approximate answers orders of magnitude faster than exact techniques. Four properties carry the idea:

- **Small**: usually a few kilobytes, growing sublinearly as the input grows.
- **Streaming**: each item is seen exactly once.
- **Stateful**: a compact summary of what has been observed, never the raw items.
- **Fast and mergeable**: results combine without losing accuracy.

Tun Shwe said at Conf42 Python 2024: "It's grounded in the truth that when it comes to big data, approximate solutions are favorable over exact solutions, because they're a good tradeoff for memory resources and time."

He contrasts that with ChatGPT, which also hands you a best guess but won't tell you how wrong it might be. A sketch's estimator comes with mathematically provable error bounds, so you know how much to trust the answer.

## Why is the exact answer so slow?

He walks through the MapReduce word count from the Hadoop docs. After splitting and mapping, each node holds local counts that can't simply be added, because the same word shows up on several nodes. So the data gets shuffled until identical keys sit together, and only then reduced. Hadoop, Spark, Snowflake and most distributed databases work this way, and Jeff Dean's latency numbers make the cost plain: a datacenter round trip is thousands of times slower than a memory reference. "And the take home message here is that shuffling is slow," he said.

## Mergeability is the superpower

The retail example makes it concrete. Quix, in his hypothetical, opens four stores in the world's fashion capitals, London, Paris and Tokyo among them. Annual sales are additive, so you sum them. Unique products per store are not, because the London and Paris shelves overlap, and the identities are gone once you've aggregated. Store a sketch per store per day instead, union the days into a monthly sketch per store, then merge the European stores' sketches for a regional distinct count, in near real time and without a batch job that hauls raw data across stores.

## A tour of the sketch zoo

He groups the families he likes best:

- **Counting uniques and duplicates**: HyperLogLog and Compressed Probabilistic Counting for cardinality.
- **Frequent items**: heavy hitters or top-k, such as the most viewed talks at a conference.
- **Quantiles**: the 25th, 95th or 99th percentile of time spent on a page, with well-defined error bounds.
- **Sampling**: reservoir sampling keeps k samples from n items.

## How Count-Min works, with burgers

The worked example counts food orders. The naive version is a hash map from item to count, which grows with every new item and stops scaling as cardinality explodes. Truncating keys to three letters saves space until a burrito collides with a burger.

Count-Min runs each item through several hash functions instead, each pointing to a column in a small 2D array of counters. A burger hashes to positions 1 and 6, and both counters go up by one. To query, look up the item's positions and take the minimum, hence the name. With ten items it mostly matches the exact counts, but the taco shows the failure mode: one of its counters reached 4 from collisions while the true answer was 1. The fix is to make the array wider or add hash functions, the two knobs every sketch exposes.

## Getting started in Python

Apache DataSketches, which he says became an Apache top-level project in 2021, ships Java, C++ and Python implementations that are cross-language compatible, so a Java stream processor can feed a Python query side. His Jupyter demo loads Spotify artist data with pandas, asks for 90% confidence and 1% relative error, lets the library suggest the number of hashes and buckets, then estimates counts for popular artists. In production you'd feed it from Kafka, or from a change-data-capture stream with Debezium. And you may already have sketches: Druid, Postgres and Hive have supported them for years, with Apache Pinot and Spark adding them recently.

## Who should watch

Data engineers staring at expensive distinct counts and percentile dashboards, and anyone who has heard of HyperLogLog but never seen inside one. It's an approachable introduction: no proofs, plenty of pictures, one clean worked example.

Title: Don't roll back the release, turn the flag off
Description: Matthew Schillerstrom (Harness / LitmusChaos / OpenFeature) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on pairing chaos engineering with feature flags
Body:
With plain continuous delivery, one bad feature in a release of fifteen means rolling back all fifteen. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, Matthew Schillerstrom (Harness / LitmusChaos / OpenFeature), a product manager for feature flags at Harness who previously ran chaos engineering product work at Gremlin and built the chaos engineering programme at Target, argues that two practices fix complementary halves of the problem: chaos engineering tells you how the system fails, and feature flags let you stop a failing change without redeploying.

He also worked at a nuclear power plant on keeping things safe and reliable, which explains the tone: calm, and very interested in knowing how things work before they break.

## What happens when a release turns into an incident?

He describes an exercise with his team that needed no chaos tooling at all, just a Miro board. Draw the happy path: developers ship, customers use and give feedback, the business tests new ideas. Then add the incident column (network outage, disk failure, whatever) and fill in everything the team must do before it gets back on the happy path: the page or the customer report, dashboards, responding, fixing, testing, troubleshooting. Support, ops, several development teams, security and database people all pile in. The feature that was meant to make customers happy has become an incident, and teams get so used to it that they normalise it.

## Why is CI/CD not enough?

Because it ends at the production deployment. His slide lists the problems: one bad feature means a full rollback, deploy and release are the same event, you cannot control who gets a feature, production issues hit every user, and you cannot isolate a change. The result is reduced velocity, increased risk and a poor developer experience, with developers babysitting deployments because releasing to prod also means releasing to every customer.

The business side gets numbers. Cloud infrastructure spending rose 23% in 2023, his slide says, citing Canalys, and Gartner forecasts public cloud end-user spending of $678.8 billion in 2024, up 20.4%, with generative AI services adding pressure. Incidents drive part of that cost, as teams over-provision to recover. He also counts churn, onboarding, training, risk and, interestingly, being too reliable: you do not need five nines, just enough for the customer experience you are after.

## What questions does chaos engineering answer?

Kubernetes is meant to self-heal, yet the common failure modes remain (system instability, resource exhaustion, resource contention, configuration errors, scaling issues), and the applications on top may not survive them. Resiliency patterns in code and infrastructure exist to degrade gracefully, but he sees a lack of testing, and people still laugh when chaos engineering comes up. His comparison is child car seats: what seemed fine decades ago looks absurd now, and in a few years skipping proactive testing may look the same.

The questions he puts to teams: what are my single points of failure, where does my system tip over, what happens when a Kubernetes pod restarts, does it scale at peak, are my dashboards configured correctly, does my paging work? Without chaos experiments, you will not know.

## What does the combined workflow look like?

His four-step release workflow:

1. **Developers write code, with every change behind a feature flag.** Code ships on time and features can be tested for impact.
2. **DevOps releases to production and tests there, with nothing changed for users.** Deploys stay on time, the process stays the same, and failure can be tested safely.
3. **Product managers decide who gets the feature.** Release variations are controlled, and "you don't roll back, you just turn the flag off," Matthew Schillerstrom said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024.
4. **Product and development decide what to iterate on**, faster and more collaboratively with flags.

The open source pieces he points to are both CNCF projects: LitmusChaos for chaos experiments and OpenFeature for vendor-neutral feature flagging.

## Who should watch?

Teams who ship big, coupled releases and dread rollbacks, product managers curious about controlled releases, and chaos practitioners looking for a way to make experiments part of everyday delivery. It is a conceptual talk with no demo.

Title: Stream processing for Python developers, minus the JVM and the jar files
Description: Tomas Neubauer (Quix) at Conf42 Python 2024 on Quix Streams: Pandas-style streaming DataFrames on Kafka, with no Flink or JVM in the loop.
Body:
Stateful stream processing has mostly meant Java, and Python teams have paid for it in jar files and socket hops. At Conf42 Python 2024, Tomas Neubauer, Founder and CTO of Quix, made the case for Quix Streams, an open-source library that puts a Pandas-like DataFrame API on top of Kafka, then live-coded a crash detector from his phone's accelerometer to show it.

## Where the idea came from

Before Quix, Neubauer led the team at McLaren that connected Formula 1 cars at the track to the factory. Each car produced roughly 20 million numerical values per minute, far too much to persist and query through a database in the middle, so the team moved to Kafka. That fixed the transport. The harder problem was people: the engineers who needed the data worked in Python and MATLAB, and the streaming world did not.

Tomas Neubauer said at Conf42 Python 2024: "streaming is traditionally Java based ecosystem and all the tools and frameworks and engines are built in Java, and as a result it's quite hostile to Python engineers."

## When do you need stream processing at all?

His test has two questions. Do you have a lot of data, so you want to filter, normalise, join or downsample before it lands in storage? Or do you need to react in seconds rather than minutes, hours or days, like an overheating reactor core or a food delivery two minutes out? One yes is enough. With five messages a day, he notes, you probably don't care.

## Two architectures, both with a catch

The first option is a broker client library, such as Confluent's Kafka client, plus your own orchestration on Kubernetes. It is elegant while you process one message at a time with no memory of the previous one. The moment you need state, you are solving one of the hardest problems in computing: keeping that state correct at scale and through hardware failures.

The second option is a full framework like Flink or Spark. Neubauer walks through a Flink job that counts words per chat room per hour. You hunt down the right connector jar (and the jar that jar depends on), you connect Flink to Kafka rather than your own code, and your Python word-count function gets registered with Flink, so every message travels between Java and Python over sockets. You also can't set a breakpoint in it, because it runs on some Flink node, not your laptop. He shows the exception he got from a correct Flink connector paired with the wrong Kafka client jar, which will look familiar to anyone who has lost an afternoon to classpaths.

The same job in Quix Streams fits on one page and runs in a single Python runtime. "I can just put a breakpoint in that method and debug it, see what's happening," he said.

## How Quix Streams is put together

The design is Python plus Kafka plus Kubernetes. Kafka handles replication and horizontal scale of the data. Your Python service runs as a Kubernetes StatefulSet backed by a persistent volume, with its state backed up to a changelog topic. More compute means more replicas; more throughput means more broker nodes. The library is built to behave in containers, including graceful shutdowns, and the API copies Pandas DataFrames on purpose, so batch muscle memory carries over to streams.

## The live demo: a crash detector in a few lines

The pipeline in Quix Cloud takes phone telemetry through a web gateway, converts the raw JSON into tabular rows, and hands them to a features service that Neubauer writes on screen in VS Code, inside a dev container that mirrors the deployed environment. Step by step he:

- filters to rows that carry accelerometer readings,
- converts the nanosecond epoch timestamp into a readable string,
- adds a column with the absolute acceleration across all three axes, so the phone's orientation stops mattering,
- and, because a single pothole on a bike shouldn't count as a crash, adds a hopping window of 2 seconds that emits every 250 milliseconds, summing the forces and keeping only the final row of each window.

Shaking the phone pushes the sum up four times a second, and the result goes to an output topic for a front end or API to consume.

## Who should watch

Python developers who have been told their streaming job must be written in Java or Flink SQL, and data teams who want windowed, stateful processing without a second runtime. It's a product talk from the company that builds the library, with a real demo rather than slides about one.

Title: If the profile won't load, hide the Follow button
Description: Olumide Akinremi (Sabi) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on chaos for the frontend - map what each view depends on and decide how it should fail
Body:
Users never see your backend. They see a blank page, a button that does nothing, a request that times out on a bad connection, and then they leave. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, Olumide Akinremi, Technical Team Lead at Sabi, brings chaos engineering to the side of the stack where users actually live: deliberately break what the frontend depends on, and decide in advance how each part of the page should fail.

The abstract leans on serverless; the talk itself is mostly about the frontend and the services behind it, and is a good first talk on frontend chaos rather than a serverless architecture session.

## Why is the frontend the hardest place to be resilient?

Most of what breaks a frontend is outside the frontend engineer's control. The backend that returns the data for a page goes down and nothing renders. Customer support, the CTO or the app store reviews let you know. On top of the backend, the frontend has its own list: JavaScript engines, plugins, accessibility, styling, latency, viewports, internationalisation and multi-tenancy. A feature that works end to end in Chrome can fail in another browser because of one unsupported function or style.

New features do not help. Akinremi's point is that every feature adds surface for users to hit, and the feature they relied on yesterday can break while they try the new one.

His analogy is a road trip: you check the car, carry a spare tyre and know what you will do if you run out of fuel, before you set off, not on the hard shoulder.

## Which failures should you plan for?

His worked example is a streaming platform built from microservices: an authentication service, a movie service, a recommendation service and a watch-history service, with a cache in front of some of them and a database that feeds them all, and React, Angular or mobile clients on top.

Walk through each failure. If the database goes down, nothing reaches the frontend. If authentication fails, users cannot log in, but should people who are already in still be able to stream and see recommendations? That depends on how much your application really relies on the service, and the answer decides how you build. Simulate each service failing, watch how the whole system reacts, and design the reaction.

## How should a page fail gracefully?

The LinkedIn profile page makes the idea concrete. It is many small views: the profile section, a feed, recent activity, posts, and suggestions of people to follow, each driven by different data and a lot of personalisation.

Two rules come out of it. First, do not show a control without its context. If the suggestion card cannot load the person's picture and name, showing a Follow button is pointless and confusing: follow whom? Second, know the dependency order. On this page, the user profile is the piece everything else hangs off, because recommendations, suggested posts and recent activity all derive from it. No profile, no point showing the rest; fail the page cleanly. Profile loaded but suggestions missing? Show what you have, because the most important thing is on screen.

"So I said focus on what to fail and how it should fail," Olumide Akinremi said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. That sentence is the talk.

## Which tools did he suggest?

He closes with a short list for creating the failures: Chaos Monkey, Azure Fault Analysis Service, Gremlin and Chaos Mesh. There is no demo of them, so treat it as a starting list.

## Who should watch?

Frontend and full-stack engineers who have never run a chaos experiment, and backend teams who want a reminder of what their outage looks like from the browser. It is an introduction: the value is the habit of mapping each view's dependencies and agreeing on its failure behaviour before an outage does it for you.
