Title: Python to a deployed Wasm function in four Spin commands
Description: Sohan Maheshwar (Fermyon) at Conf42 Python 2024 on building serverless WebAssembly apps in Python with Spin, and why Wasm could fix cold starts
Body:
Sohan Maheshwar opens with a bold bet: the next wave of cloud computing will run on WebAssembly. At Conf42 Python 2024, the Developer Relations Lead at Fermyon backs it with a beginner-friendly explanation of how Wasm works, two live demos with Fermyon's open source framework Spin (a Python hello world deployed to the cloud in four commands, then a serverless Llama 2 call), and a look at the component model, which lets one app mix modules written in different languages.

It is an introductory talk on the speaker's company's tooling, aimed at people who have heard of neither Wasm nor serverless. If you already ship Spin apps, skip to the component model at the end.

## What is WebAssembly, minus the hype?

"The boring answer is it's just another bytecode format," as Sohan puts it. Wasm started in the browser, where Adobe, Figma and Shopify use it, as a portable compilation target. Think JVM, but for many languages: Rust, C++, JavaScript, TypeScript, Zig, Go and Python all compile to Wasm modules that run wherever a Wasm runtime does, on ARM or x86, Windows, Mac, Linux, a Raspberry Pi or Kubernetes.

Modules are sandboxed by default. His analogy: the module is a hotel guest, the runtime is the hotel; you get your room, shared facilities only if they are granted. WASI, the WebAssembly System Interface, is what made server-side Wasm practical, adding files, clocks and random numbers while keeping that sandbox and dropping any dependency on a browser or JavaScript.

## How does Python, an interpreted language, become Wasm?

Compiled languages like Rust go straight to a Wasm module. Interpreted ones need the interpreter itself compiled to Wasm: CPython in Wasm form gets bundled with your program. The good news is that you never touch that step. In the demo, the app manifest (`spin.toml`) simply calls `py2wasm` to build the module.

## What does the demo show?

`spin new` offers templates by trigger (HTTP, or Redis, since serverless is event driven) and language. He picks HTTP with Python, writes a handler that returns a 200 with a greeting, then `spin build`, `spin up` to test locally with curl, and a fourth command to deploy to Fermyon Cloud. The resulting `app.wasm` is a couple of megabytes.

The second demo calls Llama 2 through Spin's LLM interface in about ten lines of Python, with the model named in `spin.toml` so it can be swapped later. Running inference on a MacBook would take around ten minutes, so a plugin sends the local app's model calls to the cloud. The result is cat jokes. "Well, I didn't say the jokes are good, but well, it is a joke," Sohan Maheshwar said at Conf42 Python 2024.

## Why would Wasm change serverless?

His four reasons, with the figures he cites:

- **Binary size**: a Rust hello world is about 2 MB, about 300 KB compiled ahead of time; a basic Spin HTTP API is about 2.3 MB JIT and 1.1 MB AOT.
- **Startup time**: comparable to native code, around 2.3 times slower than native in the benchmark he cites.
- **Portability**: the same build runs across operating systems and architectures.
- **Security**: a capability-based model, where every inbound or outbound request and file access has to be granted.

The serverless argument is cold starts. He puts typical public cloud cold starts at around 500 milliseconds and up to two to three seconds on AWS Lambda, which teams work around by pinging functions to keep them warm and paying for the privilege. With Wasm, Fermyon cold starts a module on every execution in about two milliseconds and scales back to zero. The containers argument is utilisation: teams provision for the monthly peak, and lightweight Wasm apps scale fast and pack far more densely.

## What is the component model?

The part he is most excited about. If every language compiles to Wasm, and modules agree on interfaces, a JavaScript app can use a Rust YAML parser and a Python date formatter without caring what they are written in. For Python, componentize-py, from the Bytecode Alliance, turns an application into a component from a WIT file, the name of a WIT world, the Python module targeting it, and the directories holding its dependencies.

## Who should watch?

Python developers curious about Wasm on the server, and anyone tired of cold-start workarounds. Spin's docs live at developer.fermyon.com/spin.

Title: A digital twin for a six-axis robot arm, from Three.js to C#
Description: Ivan Chiou (PAIA) at Conf42 Python 2024 on syncing a browser-based Three.js robot arm with a physical one through ROS, rosbridge, Python and WebRTC
Body:
Robot arms are expensive to share among a class of students, and expensive to crash. At Conf42 Python 2024, Ivan Chiou, Senior Technical Manager at PAIA, walks through DigitalTwins, an educational system built so university students can manipulate a six-axis robotic arm from a web page, with a Three.js model in the browser and the real arm moving in sync, watched through an IP camera. "It's really helpful to decrease the cost in the physical environment," Ivan Chiou said at Conf42 Python 2024.

This is a full-stack tour rather than a single deep idea: design, frontend, 3D, video, ROS, Python, C# and deployment, each with the code that glues it to the next layer.

## What does the system look like?

The UI has three parts. An information display shows the virtual 3D arm, the physical arm on the IP camera feed, the six axis coordinates and error messages. A control panel has a reset button, a control for each of the six axis angles, motor movement speed, and action recording, so a sequence of moves can be saved and replayed. A sidebar holds the editable device list and user login. The frontend is Vite, Vue, Vue Router, Pinia, Tailwind and SCSS; the mockup was designed in Figma with help from a generative AI image tool, prompted towards a cyberpunk look of neon on black.

## Why ROS, and how does the browser talk to it?

ROS, the Robot Operating System, is not really an operating system but a framework installed on top of one. Ivan explains its building blocks: nodes as the basic unit, packages that hold them, and stacks as collections of packages (he compares that to how a conda install pulls in many packages at once). Nodes communicate through topics, which work like channels any node can subscribe to, plus services and actionlib for longer-running actions.

The browser joins the ROS cluster via rosbridge, with the ROS JavaScript library subscribing to a topic so the Three.js components change angle and position as messages arrive. On the backend, a Python node uses `create_subscription` on the same topic. Its listener callback parses the JSON message, records alarm codes to the device through the API, and reads joint angles, positions, RPMs and torque values.

## How do virtual and physical stay in sync?

Changing the six axis angles, from a control or a recorded action, sends the same data to both arms in the standard ROS message format. A ROS Cloud API stores device state and actions in a cloud database, with endpoints for devices, a single device, and a device's actions; a `move` action carries the angle and speed for each axis.

The Python side only calls the API when the angle list has actually changed, then passes messages over a websocket to C#, where the vendor SDK drives the physical arm: run each axis to position, report current angles, positions, RPMs and motor torque.

## Three.js basics, with clipping planes

A good chunk of the talk is a Three.js primer: scene, camera, objects, light, renderer. The useful detail is the perspective camera's four parameters, field of view, aspect ratio, and the near and far clipping planes. Only objects between the two planes are rendered, so cubes outside them vanish until you move a plane. Directional light placed above the arm gives the model its shading.

## What broke with the camera?

The video path has the most war stories. A TP-Link Tapo C320WS camera speaks RTSP; the open source webrtc-streamer project, available as a Docker image, turns that into WebRTC for the page. Locally that just works. In production, the DigitalTwins dashboard and the webrtc-streamer API server had to be deployed together, solved with docker-compose. The page showed a black screen until the camera connection was switched from UDP to TCP. And since the camera had no external IP, port forwarding with `socat` exposed it.

Deployment is Jenkins: build the Vite app, bake the API and camera URLs into `.env`, build a Docker image, push it to Amazon ECR, then SSH to EC2, pull and run docker-compose, both in the cloud and on premises.

## Who should watch?

Engineers building teleoperation or digital-twin dashboards who want to see one complete working chain from a browser slider to a motor. If you only need the Three.js basics, the primer section stands on its own.

Title: A resilience score of 66 should roll back your deploy
Description: Saranya Jena and Sarthak Jain (Harness) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on adding a chaos step with a resilience-score gate to CD pipelines
Body:
Most CD pipelines check that a deployment came up. Fewer check that it can take a hit. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, Saranya Jena and Sarthak Jain, senior software developers at Harness and maintainers of the open source LitmusChaos project, show how to add a chaos step to a deployment pipeline: inject a fault after rollout, score how the application held up, and roll back automatically when the score falls below what you expected.

The talk is half argument, half demo, and the demo is the reason to watch: you see the gate fail and the rollback fire.

## Why put chaos in the pipeline at all?

Sarthak Jain opens with the numbers on his slides: the Gartner IT Key Metrics Data report puts the average cost of downtime at around $5,600 per minute, and according to Zendesk, 39% of customers avoid a product or service after a bad experience. The fixes are a more resilient system and a better MTTR, and chaos in CD automates the work towards both.

He gives five reasons for a pipeline chaos step: early issue detection (a component that goes unresponsive under load is cheaper to fix in QA), enhanced resilience, improved incident response, continuous validation, and wider adoption of chaos in teams that are still nervous about it.

Continuous validation is his favourite, with the line of the talk: "practicing chaos engineering once or twice and thinking your application is resilient is like hitting the gym on a new year and thinking that you will be fit for the rest of the year," Sarthak Jain said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. For teams that still fear chaos will disrupt things, his advice is to start with simple experiments in the pipeline and let the results do the convincing.

## What does the pipeline look like?

Saranya Jena's demo uses a microservices shopping app with cart, checkout and currency converter services. The Harness CD pipeline has four parts:

1. **Rollout deployment.**
2. **Observe deployment**: check the app is healthy, or roll back. (In the demo it is just a short sleep; in real life, your own commands.)
3. **Chaos step**: a pod CPU hog experiment that loads the CPU in the target cluster and namespace where the app runs.
4. **Failure strategy**: what happens when the chaos step fails.

## How is the expected resilience score chosen?

The chaos step carries an expected resilience score, the minimum the application must reach for the step to pass. It is the pipeline version of the steady-state hypothesis: define healthy, inject a fault, check the SLOs. To pick the number, look at the last resilience scores of previous runs (in her list, one experiment scored 100 and a Lambda function timeout experiment 50%) and refine it as more runs come in.

The score comes from probes. In the passing run she opens, three probes (a cart service availability check, a website latency check and a pod status check) all pass, for a score of 100 against an expected 90.

## What happens when it fails?

The failing run is the good bit: expected score 90, actual 66. The chaos step fails, the failure strategy kicks in, the rollback runs, and a post-rollback health check confirms the previous deployment is healthy.

Rollback is one option in the step's advanced settings. Others include manual intervention after a timeout, ignore, abort, retry and mark as success. Her guidance: in QA you might just ignore or mark as success; in production, roll back to a safe deployment. Steps can also run in parallel or in series, so you can stack several chaos experiments.

## Does it only work in Harness?

The demo uses Harness Chaos Engineering with Harness CD natively, but the APIs are available for external pipelines, and she shows the same deploy, chaos step and rollback sequence running in GitLab. Pipelines can also be triggered by a webhook instead of by hand; her example fires on a cart service deployment change.

## Who should watch?

DevOps and platform engineers who own a CD pipeline and want a first, low-risk place to put chaos, and teams already using LitmusChaos or Harness who want to see the resilience-score gate in practice. It is a vendor demo, presented by maintainers of the open source project underneath it.

Title: Tune your AWS autoscaling in a notebook, not in production
Description: Gustavo Amigo (Amazon Prime Video) at Conf42 Python 2024 on simulating AWS autoscaling with pandas to pick scaling parameters that hold up in production
Body:
The usual way to fix autoscaling that is too slow is to bump the scale-up increment, watch the next traffic spike, and hope. At Conf42 Python 2024, Gustavo Amigo, Senior Software Development Engineer at Amazon Prime Video, does it the other way round: load test one host, fit a line, write a small autoscaling simulator in Python, brute-force the parameters, and only then touch production. The parameters it picked worked on the first real load test.

The machine learning in the title is a linear regression, and that is the point: ordinary data science tooling (pandas, Jupyter, Locust, boto3) goes a long way on infrastructure problems.

## What is the problem?

A service on AWS Elastic Beanstalk behind an Application Load Balancer, running on t3.micro EC2 instances in an autoscaling group, with very standard settings: add or remove one host at a time, scale up when average CPU is above 25%, down below 15%, the threshold has to be breached for five minutes, and a new host takes three to four minutes to come up.

The traffic shape is the nasty one: ramp to 30,000 requests per minute over ten minutes, then surge to close to 150,000 within eight minutes. Gustavo notes this happens in real life, with Black Friday, promotions, or a marketing email nobody told the team about. Too conservative and you pay for idle hosts; too aggressive, or rather too slow, and the service falls over.

## How do you find one host's limits?

Load test a single host with Locust, then pull the CloudWatch metrics into pandas with boto3. A practical tip: save them to CSV straight away, because CloudWatch drops high-resolution data after a while (he cites around 24 hours for 10-second granularity).

Two findings come out of the notebook. CPU against requests per minute is linear, which he checks rather than assumes, and the regression gives about 35% CPU at 40k RPM for one host. And latency is fine until CPU passes 50%, then it falls apart. That 50% becomes the hard limit: keep every host below it, while using as much CPU as possible so the fleet is not paying for idle capacity.

## Why simulate instead of testing in production?

Changing scaling parameters in production is risky and slow: you change something, often overnight, wait, then run a load test that must not cause the outage you are trying to prevent. So he writes a simulator that models the AWS policy (five minutes over threshold, trigger a scale-up, wait three to four minutes for a healthy host, spread the load) and a traffic shape generator producing the surge as a dataframe.

With the default settings, the simulated CPU stays well above 50% for around 15 minutes, because the surge arrives while the fleet is still one or two hosts. The first instinct, scale up two hosts at a time instead of one, does not fix it either. That is exactly what teams do in production, he says, and some give up on dynamic scaling and just run ten hosts all the time.

## What did the search find?

Two loops: scale-up increments from 1 to 10 and upper thresholds from 11% to 35%. Keep only runs whose maximum CPU stays under 50%, then rank by average CPU utilisation. The winner: scale up two hosts at a time at a 15% upper threshold, with a predicted average CPU of about 16% and a peak of 39%.

Then production. A 40-minute Locust run with a ramping user count peaked at around 120k RPM rather than the planned 150k, but hosts were added two at a time, CPU peaked at roughly 26 to 27%, and response times stayed stable. "I ran the load testing in production, and it just worked," Gustavo Amigo said at Conf42 Python 2024. Comparing the two runs also improved the model: real AWS started adding hosts earlier than the simulator but added them more slowly.

## Who should watch?

SREs and DevOps engineers who own an autoscaling group and have never quite trusted its numbers. The technique, he argues, carries over to capacity planning, alarms, caching and troubleshooting, because observability tools alone hit their limits fast. The abstract mentions alarms and caches; the talk only works through autoscaling, but the method is the takeaway. The code is in his conf42-python-24 repository on GitHub.

Title: A chaos finding nobody can price will not win the budget
Description: Tejendra Bhandari (Nokia) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on turning chaos experiments into reusable pools and putting a revenue figure on what they find
Body:
Plenty of teams run chaos experiments and collect insights. Far fewer turn those insights into a number a business owner cares about. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, Tejendra Bhandari, Cloud Security Architect at Nokia, talks to the presales engineers, architects and champions who have to sell chaos engineering inside organisations new to it, and his answer is to build a pool of reusable experiments, automate them, and translate every finding into money or effort saved.

It is a strategy talk with no demo, drawing on his work across media, medical and delivery domains. The ideas are general; the value is in the order he puts them in.

## Where should a chaos programme start?

Start from business requirements, even when the business does not know them yet. Is the goal resilience, fewer outages, something else? Then find the team with the widest view: not necessarily one with the whole organisational picture, but one that works with many other teams and can act as a platform owner. Ask them for the most painful area, because there always is one, and point your first experiments there.

When you have no access to the business or no information about the platform, start in whatever environment the organisation allows, with the most common and easiest experiments, to learn how the infrastructure and network behave.

## How do experiments cross domains?

Bhandari's multi-domain idea is grouping by platform. If you ran experiments on AWS and got insights, multiply them across everything else that runs on AWS, treat similar platforms as one bucket, and build a strategy for that bucket. Experiments should be agile enough that another team can make a small change and run them against their own service, even in a different domain of the same organisation.

Visibility is part of the work. Write up the impact of each run as an artifact, publish it across the organisation, and publish it more than once. Teams using the same platform every day may not know the failures they are exposed to until they read about someone else's.

## How do you get teams to adopt them?

Make them generic, then make them easy. Hand out experiments to run on services manually at first, then turn them into automation-pipeline use cases so nobody has to edit anything; they just run it and read the output. The easier it is, the fewer conflicts and the more teams join in, until the pool of use cases feeds itself.

From there, depth: chain experiments that hit infrastructure, then the network layer, then the API or application layer, and you get an end-to-end result instead of three isolated ones.

## How does a chaos finding become a revenue number?

"Then the most important part is conversion of these use cases into revenue," Tejendra Bhandari said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. His illustration: an application behind a load balancer that looks perfectly healthy. A chaos run on the load balancer shows that transactions are being rejected during a high-availability switchover, something the team had not spotted. Report it as a share of rejected transactions during failover, translate that into dollars at risk on a peak sales day, and add the person-days it would take to fix the problem during a production outage. That number gets mapped to the use case and its outcome, and that is what wins the next business conversation.

Once the use cases run automatically in a CI/CD pipeline, every run produces outcomes you can keep mapping to effort or revenue.

## Open source or a licensed tool?

He gets this question often, and his answer is that it depends on your experiments. Begin manually, using open source tools and communities to find experiments others have already tried, then curate your own. Once you have a pool of experiments, decide whether a licensed tool is worth it, based on your business requirements and the technology you have already invested in.

## Who should watch?

Engineers and presales people who need to justify a chaos programme to a business audience, and champions in organisations where nobody has run an experiment yet. If you want tooling detail or a worked architecture, look elsewhere; this is about framing and rollout.

Title: NiFi 2.0 finally lets Python into the flow, properly
Description: Tim Spann (Cloudera) at Conf42 Python 2024 on writing Apache NiFi 2.0 Python processors that feed LLMs, vector stores and transit feeds
Body:
Apache NiFi has always been a Java tool, and calling Python from it used to mean shelling out and hoping. At Conf42 Python 2024, Tim Spann, Principal Developer Advocate at Cloudera, shows what changed in NiFi 2.0: Python processors are now first-class, and that is how a streaming pipeline gets at the Hugging Face, LangChain and vector database libraries that only really exist in Python. He walks through the anatomy of a processor, a shelf of ones he wrote himself, and a live demo on his laptop.

Expect a Cloudera-flavoured talk, with a stack overview up front, but the bulk is processors and code you can copy from his GitHub.

## Why does a streaming tool need Python?

Because that is where the AI libraries are. Tim's pipelines ingest unstructured files, enterprise APIs and streams, then chunk, vectorise and push the data to models and vector stores. Doing that from Java was difficult; earlier Python support in NiFi was, in his word, kludgy: the script ran on its own outside the flow. NiFi 2.0 brings proper Python integration alongside JDK 21 support, which he describes as faster and leaner with better use of threads. The release goals also list JSON flow serialisation, a rules engine for development assistance, and running a process group as stateless.

The minimum for writing your own: Python 3.10 and JDK 21.

## What does a processor look like?

A boilerplate Python class. You import the NiFi API bits, point at the Java interface that bridges the two worlds, and declare processor details (version, description, tags) and property descriptors, which become the fields a user fills in the NiFi UI. His example wraps the IBM watsonx.ai SDK, so the properties are the prompt, the API key and the project ID.

The work happens in `transform(self, context, flowfile)`. The context gives access to properties and the environment; the flow file is whatever data arrived. You return a result with a relationship (success or failure), the contents, and any attributes.

His design tip is the most reusable idea in the talk: often you should not change the contents at all. Pass the flow file through untouched and add what you computed as attributes. It is fast, it keeps the pipeline's data intact, and you can decide later whether anything needs rewriting.

## Which processors did he build?

- **Extract company names** from text using Hugging Face, spaCy and PyTorch, returning all companies plus the first one in its own attribute. He chains it to a REST call for the stock symbol, then the stock price.
- **GTFS readers** for transit data (trip updates, vehicle positions, alerts), including a compound reader for feeds that return more than one type. In the demo it pulls vehicle positions for Halifax, Canada, and splits them into JSON rows.
- **WebVTT to text**, stripping timestamps and cue numbers from video captions before they go into a prompt or a vector store.
- **watsonx.ai inference** through IBM's official SDK.
- **System monitoring** with psutil, output as attributes.
- **Synthetic records** with Faker for demos and tests.
- **Wikipedia pages** as HTML or text, picked dynamically, for example for the company the extractor just found.

NiFi 2.0 also ships Python processors: Pinecone, ParseDocument and ChunkDocument, ConvertCSVtoExcel, DetectObjectInImage, PromptChatGPT, and PutChroma and QueryChroma.

## What does the demo pipeline do?

His Medium feed comes in through regular NiFi processors, then ParseDocument and ChunkDocument split the articles so they fit a vector store, and PutChroma stores them. A Slack-driven flow cleans incoming messages, queries the vector store, builds the prompt, calls the model through PromptChatGPT and posts the answer back to Slack and Kafka.

He adds a sensible caution about routing everything to an LLM. Some Slack questions are a database lookup or a REST call for the current stock price. "You got to be smart about how you use these models. Don't use them for things they're not designed for," Tim Spann said at Conf42 Python 2024.

## Who should watch?

Data engineers running NiFi who want AI steps in the flow without a sidecar service, and Python developers who would like their library to show up as a drag-and-drop box. He calls it the early days of Python processors and invites people to write and share their own.

Title: To get chaos engineering funded, stop calling it chaos
Description: Andrew Benoit at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on winning budget for fault injection - court the skeptics, drop the chaos buzz, tie it to business value
Body:
A team of brilliant engineers ran a proof of concept that found tons of bugs before they reached production. They loved the word chaos so much they had T-shirts. Their executives did not, and the funding was delayed by six months. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, Andrew Benoit, a sales leader and go-to-market advisor with three years of selling chaos engineering behind him, uses stories like that to teach the people who lead chaos initiatives how to get them bought.

It is a talk from the other side of the table, and that is what makes it valuable. Engineers rarely get told how an enterprise purchase is really decided.

## How do you get value out of your sales rep?

Benoit's sales rep owner's manual starts with a reassurance: enterprise reps are not trained to never take no for an answer. They have limited time, dozens of demo requests a month, and weekly forecast calls where they must explain the technical fit, the competition, who is involved and the timeline. A rep who drags out deals that cannot close gets no help from leadership. A rep with a real project, a timeline and budget gets carte blanche, and so do you: roadmap sessions, technical one-on-ones, access to their executives.

His practical asks: never take your own meeting notes; have the rep send a recap after every meeting with attendees and mutually agreed next steps, and object right away if it is wrong. And meet in person when you can, which brings us to the politics.

## Why are purchases more like elections?

Decisions are seldom top-down any more. Executives lean on the opinions of the people below them, so an enterprise purchase becomes an election with dozens of constituents and several personas. Benoit's framework marks three as mobilizers, the people who can actually push an initiative through:

- **Go-getters**, enthusiastic about change and persuasive with colleagues. (The climber looks similar but cares more about their own advancement, so takes fewer risks.)
- **Teachers**, experienced, respected, and keen to share what they are looking into.
- **Skeptics**, the surprise entry. Unlike blockers, who are dogmatic and may work against you, skeptics are cautious but open to persuasion, and once won over they bring almost everyone else with them.

Friends are nice but lack the influence, so time spent with them is a distraction. The most common mistake he sees is avoiding the skeptic and hoping they go away; he has watched months of proven value go down the drain when a sidelined skeptic delayed the deal at the last minute. "Do not avoid the skeptic," Andrew Benoit said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024.

## What should the goal be, if not chaos engineering?

Not to build a chaos engineering practice. You can have one and still do things badly. The goal is measurable outcomes such as availability, downtime or mean time to resolution, using fault injection as the means. He recommends dropping the word chaos entirely: "In fact, even Netflix doesn't use the term chaos engineering anymore for this reason."

Better still, attach fault injection to initiatives that already have priority and budget:

- **Cloud migration**, usually the most visible project in an enterprise. His slide puts 2024 global public cloud spend at $678.8 billion, growing 20.4%. Validate resilience, scalability and recovery before the embarrassing outage.
- **Observability**: game days regularly show that teams were not collecting enough metrics to know when things would go haywire, often metrics that are free and just need configuring.
- **Disaster recovery**, which many banks he worked with were not testing to their own standards.
- **Education**: he sold an almost six-figure deal to a customer who only wanted it to teach hundreds of summer interns how their systems fit together.

## How do you build the business case?

Quantify what an extra nine is worth. His table assumes $5,000 per minute of downtime: at 99% availability that is 5,256 minutes and $26.28 million a year, at 99.9% it is 526 minutes and $2.63 million. He deliberately uses a conservative figure, because an aggressive estimate hands the skeptic an easy win. Add the cost of missed SLAs, triage hours per year and past incidents the plan would have prevented.

Then write an implementation plan, because leaders fear shelfware: which applications first and why, which metrics prove success, what internal resources and executive support you need. Knowing your usage also helps you negotiate pricing that fits it.

## Who should watch?

Engineers who have been volunteered to lead a chaos (or any tooling) initiative, and anyone who has watched a good proof of concept die in procurement. Benoit also points out that leading the initiative is an audition for future leadership roles.

Title: Three Python ways to pull Arrow tables out of InfluxDB 3
Description: Anais Dotis-Georgiou (InfluxData) at Conf42 Python 2024 on querying InfluxDB 3 over Apache Arrow Flight from Python, and why columnar storage suits time series
Body:
InfluxDB 3 speaks Apache Arrow end to end, which means any Python code that can talk Arrow Flight can query it and get a columnar table back. At Conf42 Python 2024, Anais Dotis-Georgiou, Developer Advocate at InfluxData, compares the three clients you can use to do that, explains why the FDAP stack (Flight, DataFusion, Arrow, Parquet) sits under the database, and shows three open source projects built on top.

It is a vendor talk about the speaker's own company's database, and a friendly one: the point is interoperability, so much of it applies to any Arrow Flight data store.

## What makes time series data different?

Anais starts with the basics. A single stock price means little; the trend over time is what you act on. Time series comes in two kinds: metrics, measured at regular intervals (a vibration reading every second), and events, which are unpredictable but can be aggregated into metrics, such as machine faults per day.

A time series database, in her framing, needs four things: time-ordered data, high write throughput (an industrial vibration sensor writes around 10,000 points per second), efficient queries and aggregations over time ranges, and horizontal scalability. Her benchmark figure for InfluxDB v3: at a dimensionality of 160,000, around 329 million rows per hour, or 4 million values per second.

## Why columnar, and why Arrow?

Arrow is the in-memory columnar format, Arrow Flight moves large Arrow datasets over the network, Parquet is the durable columnar file format on disk, and DataFusion is the query engine that lets you use SQL or InfluxQL. Her sidebar on columnar storage is the clearest explanation in the talk. To find the max of one field in row storage, you walk every row and every column. Store by column and you scan one block. Neighbouring values share a type and, in time series, often the same value: a room's temperature sampled every minute barely moves. That makes compression cheap and lets scans use SIMD instructions.

The open stack is also an ecosystem play. Dremio uses Arrow and Flight; many ML tools read Parquet. "When you contribute to these upstream projects, then so many other tools benefit from it," Anais Dotis-Georgiou said at Conf42 Python 2024.

## Which client should you use?

The three options, all in the talk with code:

- **The plain Arrow Flight client** (`pip install pyarrow`): create a `FlightClient` with a gRPC TLS URL, build a JSON ticket holding the namespace, the SQL query and the query type, call `do_get`, `read_all()`, and convert to pandas. The query type can be switched to InfluxQL, and the boilerplate is database agnostic.
- **The Arrow Flight SQL client** (`pip install flightsql-dbapi`): wraps the Flight client. Execute a query to get flight info, take the ticket from the first endpoint, request the Arrow stream, read it into a PyArrow table. The catch she flags: Flight SQL returns streams, and how streams come back differs a good deal between languages, which makes reusable boilerplate across databases harder.
- **The InfluxDB v3 Python client** (`influxdb_client_3`): also a wrapper over Flight, with `InfluxDBClient3` and a `query` method where you pick `sql` or `influxql` and a return mode, including pandas and Polars dataframes, ready for forecasting or anomaly detection libraries.

The abstract also promises building a CLI; the talk does not get to that.

## What can you build with it?

Three projects from the InfluxCommunity GitHub organisation:

- **Grafana**: InfluxData contributed a Flight SQL plugin, so any Arrow Flight data store can feed Grafana dashboards. The InfluxDB 3 Quick Starts repo shows it alongside the InfluxDB-specific plugin.
- **Mage**: an open source data pipeline tool she describes as an alternative to Apache Airflow, used here for anomaly detection on machine data with half-space trees, including a small interface to inject anomalies and trigger alerts.
- **Quix**: Python-controlled event streaming on Kafka. Robot arms publish over MQTT to a HiveMQ broker, data lands in InfluxDB, Quix runs an autoencoder model stored on Hugging Face for anomaly detection, and Grafana shows the results.

## Who should watch?

Python developers moving to InfluxDB 3 who want to know which client to install, and data engineers curious what Arrow Flight looks like in practice. If you already query Flight endpoints daily, the sidebar on columnar storage is the part to send your colleagues.

Title: Diffusion models still can't serve ramen without chopsticks
Description: Jayram Palamadai (University of Chicago) at Conf42 Python 2024 on how diffusion models work, where they still fail, and how C2PA could tag AI media
Body:
Ask DALL-E for a bowl of ramen without chopsticks and you will get chopsticks, every time. At Conf42 Python 2024, Jayram Palamadai, an AI researcher at the University of Chicago, uses that failure to explain what diffusion models really learn, after a tour of how they work, the research pushing them into video and 3D, and the provenance standards meant to keep photorealistic fakes in check.

Honest scope: the abstract mentions his own text-to-3D research, but the talk is a broad survey of visual generative AI rather than a walkthrough of it. It is also a snapshot of early 2024, recorded just after OpenAI showed Sora, which forced him to rewrite part of the deck.

## How does diffusion actually work?

Two processes. The forward process adds noise to an image step by step (x0, x1, x2...) until only noise is left, with a schedule controlling how much noise each step adds. A linear schedule adds the same amount every time; he points to OpenAI researchers using a non-linear schedule that preserved image quality for longer. Each step depends only on the previous one, which makes it a Markov chain.

The reverse process is where the model earns its keep. It takes a noisy image, predicts the noise separating it from the original, subtracts it, then, counterintuitively, adds some noise back to land on an intermediate step, and predicts again. Repeat, and the approximation keeps improving. Combined with text encoders, this is the basis of DALL-E 3, Stable Diffusion and Imagen.

## What is the research doing with it?

He picks a handful of recent projects:

- **NVIDIA Picasso**, for enterprises training custom visual models on their own libraries through the Edify platform, with Shutterstock, Getty Images and Adobe among the early adopters.
- **Live Portrait 3D**, an NVIDIA project that turns a single face portrait into a neural radiance field (NeRF) in real time, at 24 frames per second on consumer hardware. A NeRF maps a 5D input (x, y, z plus two viewing-direction coordinates) to colour and opacity.
- **Simulated tennis** learned from broadcast video, using hierarchical policy networks that chain shots into rallies with realistic physics and no annotations of stroke types.
- **Diffusion for 3D models** from Tsinghua University researchers, producing objects you can manipulate in six degrees of freedom.

## Where do the models still fall over?

The ramen test is the memorable one: the training data seems to have chopsticks in every ramen photo, so the model cannot imagine the bowl without them. That raises his real question, whether AI can be creative or only reflects the creativity of its training data, which matters in the fight between AI companies and artists.

He also ran Winograd schemas, sentences that need context to resolve, through DALL-E. A bowling ball breaking a table worked. A trophy too large for a suitcase worked. The prompt "the large ball crashed right through the table because it was made of styrofoam" failed: everything in the room came out as styrofoam. Physics and object interaction remain weak in video too; in Sora clips he points out a chair that floats and morphs, a flame that ignores the wind, and wax that melts the wrong way.

Then a twist: one clip he shows as AI footage is a real drone flight over Chicago, and it does not look out of place.

## How do we tell what is real?

He expects fakes to become impossible to spot with the naked eye within a couple of years, and lists the risks: tampered security footage and evidence, ads for products that do not exist, propaganda dressed up as educational video. His optimism rests on C2PA, a proposed specification recording the origin and edit history of media, from camera to Photoshop to YouTube. "This would ensure that every pixel edited would leave a footprint," Jayram Palamadai said at Conf42 Python 2024. He notes that OpenAI pledged to adhere to C2PA once Sora is released.

The second safeguard is, in his words, "the solution turns out to be more AI": TikTok requires users to tag AI-generated content, which builds a labelled dataset for training media classifiers.

## Who should watch?

Developers who use image models but never looked under the hood, and anyone who wants a quick map of the provenance debate. If you want code or the text-to-3D work from the abstract, this is not that talk.

Title: Citi runs production on one data centre for a day, every month
Description: Charles Akl (Citi Bank) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on monthly production game days, Wheels of Misfortune and the tools Citi's SRE team uses
Body:
Banks are not known for breaking things on purpose. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, Charles Akl, Head of NA SRE and NAM Core Production Management at Citi Bank, gives a quick tour of how his team does it anyway: a monthly production game day that fails over and runs the day out of a single data centre, a role-playing incident drill called Wheels of Misfortune, and a mix of Gremlin, Chaos Monkey and an in-house tool for the lower environments.

It is a short talk, an overview rather than a detailed walkthrough, and useful precisely because it shows what a regulated enterprise actually schedules, rather than what a conference slide says it should.

## Why is a bank doing chaos engineering at all?

Akl's team is turning its level 2 production support into an SRE team, and he treats chaos engineering as one of the core principles of that move. He uses the principlesofchaos.org definition, the discipline of experimenting on a system to build confidence that it can withstand turbulent conditions in production, and lists the payoff as promoting innovation, better partnership, better incident response, generated knowledge, and higher reliability and resilience as the customer experiences it.

## What does a production game day look like?

Once a month, on the Monday and Tuesday after the monthly release weekend, the team runs a production stress test of the NAM core ecosystem. They have written plenty of Ansible playbooks that, through an in-house tool, do a one-touch failover, and the business then runs the whole day out of a single data centre. The point is to find the threshold the ecosystem can tolerate. Results are measured automatically, and the team is working on automating the return to normal too.

A chaos backlog feeds the experiments: top incidents, new components being deployed, big design changes, and requests from teams.

## What is a Wheel of Misfortune?

"Wheels of misfortune is a very fun exercise," Charles Akl said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. It is a role-play of an emergency with nothing touching production. People from incident management, problem management, product, SRE and performance meet every couple of weeks for 30 minutes to pick topics (usually past major outages, sometimes cybersecurity), and once a quarter they run and record a full exercise.

The roles are borrowed from tabletop games. A game master, an experienced engineer who knows how the services interact, describes how the player learns about the breakage: an alert, or a message from the contact centre or a manager. The volunteer player says what they would do, which dashboards to open, which diagnostic commands to run, which playbooks to read. Non-player characters interact with the player as the scenario unfolds, the audience stays quiet unless called in, and hints come out if the player gets stuck. The debrief explains the backstory. The payoff is practice at elevated stress levels, a check on whether architecture diagrams are up to date, and a shorter mean time to mitigate.

## Which tools does Citi use below production?

- **Gremlin**, the SaaS platform, on legacy physical JVMs on Linux servers. A typical run: 100 transactions per second over a 30-minute window, measure average response time, then launch a high CPU attack at the ten-minute mark and watch what happens to I/O and everything else. This runs quarterly, and the team is integrating Gremlin with OpenShift to attack pods.
- **Chaos Monkey**, which he calls one of his favourite tools, to terminate instances at random, for example in OpenShift namespaces, and measure what happens to other layers and to the customer.
- **Ape Army**, an in-house platform that brings down random services, pods and network links while load is injected, then checks that no messages or trades were lost.
- **Manual tests**: edit a YAML file, change a Java service's configuration to disable a component, or restart a service and watch.

The attack menu is the familiar one: resource attacks (CPU, memory, I/O), state attacks (shutdown, process killer, time travel) and network attacks (latency, packet loss, black-holing connectivity). Outside production the team also shuts down core services, a major database or a core mainframe component, and asks the questions that matter in banking: did the user get the right message, and was their data still there?

## Who should watch?

SRE leads in financial services or any regulated shop looking for a realistic chaos calendar, and anyone who wants to borrow the Wheel of Misfortune format for incident training. Expect a fast overview with no demos.

Title: SuperDuperDB wants your models to live next to your rows
Description: Duncan Blythe (SuperDuperDB) at Conf42 Python 2024 on running AI models, listeners and vector search inside your existing database, without moving data
Body:
Most AI architectures start with a database and then copy its contents into a pipeline, a feature store and a vector database, each with its own sync job. At Conf42 Python 2024, Duncan Blythe, Founder and CTO of SuperDuperDB, pitches the opposite: wrap the database you already have, install models into it, and let the outputs and the vector index live alongside the data. The talk closes with a demo that makes a video searchable in plain English from a Jupyter notebook.

It is a talk about the speaker's own open source project (Apache 2.0 on GitHub), so expect a product walkthrough, but a code-heavy one.

## What problem is it attacking?

Duncan's diagnosis is that data and AI live in separate silos. Getting AI into production means duplicating data across locations, building ETL and MLOps pipelines, and bolting on specialised vector databases, which in his view only make the graph of tools worse. "With super Duper DB, you're able to build AI without moving data," Duncan Blythe said at Conf42 Python 2024. "AI" here covers LLMs and generative models, classic machine learning, and custom workflows combining them.

## How is it built?

SuperDuperDB is a Python package and a deployment system at the same time. Under the `db` object you get three stores: the data backend (your existing database), a metadata store and an artifact store for model data. Work runs on a scalable scheduler built on Ray, fed either by developer requests or by a change data capture daemon listening for new data. An optional vector search component plugs into the query API.

## What does the code look like?

The API is small and consistent:

- **Connect** by wrapping your database URI; queries against MongoDB look like ordinary PyMongo queries, and SQL backends work through the Ibis library once you define a schema and table.
- **Encoders** define custom data types; his example is an MP3 type that pickles bytes.
- **Models** are generalised computations, not only PyTorch or Hugging Face models: a regex that extracts URLs counts, so does a spaCy pipeline for named entity recognition, so does custom API request logic. No pre-built integration is needed; you bring the library.
- **predict_in_db** runs a model over a selected key, saves the outputs back into the database.
- **Listeners** make that automatic: wrap a model in a listener on a query, and new data matching the query gets processed as it arrives.
- **Vector indexes** wrap a listener, which keeps them up to date, and make the selected data searchable.
- **Stacks** combine components, can be parameterised into a higher-level app with free variables, and export to a JSON-serialised format with references to artifacts.

Models are declared with the dataclass decorator, which also gives a tidy path to exposing them over a REST API.

## Can it really search a video in a few lines?

The demo is the convincing part. Duncan inserts a video into a MongoDB collection by its URI; the system downloads and caches it. A custom model built with OpenCV subsamples frames and saves them back to the database. Two components of OpenAI's self-hostable CLIP model, one visual and one textual, are wrapped in a multimodal vector index, so frames can be searched by text or by image. A query for elephants in the woods returns documents with timestamps, which point straight to the elephant. A search for a playing monkey works too, proving the first result was not a fluke.

The use case he picks is telling: sensitive recordings you would rather not send to an externally hosted API. Everything in the demo runs in your own deployment.

## Who should watch?

Python developers who keep writing glue code between a database and a model server, and teams weighing whether a separate vector database is worth another moving part. If you need a managed, battle-tested platform, judge the project by its current state on GitHub, not by a demo. The pattern of listeners on queries and indexes on listeners is worth knowing either way.

Title: When SREs lose shell access, chaos becomes a self-service platform
Description: Jay Hankins (Salesforce) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on moving chaos from central game days to a self-service platform for service owners
Body:
In 2015, a Salesforce game day meant an SRE with privileged shell access logging into a server and killing processes while someone wrote down what happened. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, Jay Hankins, Lead Member of Technical Staff and a chaos engineer on Salesforce's chaos platform team, explains why that model died when Salesforce moved to the public cloud, and what replaced it: a platform that lets service owners run their own chaos experiments safely, whenever they like.

It is a short, dense talk and one of the clearest descriptions around of what self-service chaos needs at enterprise scale.

## What broke the old game day model?

Back then, Salesforce ran its own data centres, SRE owned the availability of pretty much everything, and SREs had wide shell access. Chaos meant rebooting hosts, killing processes, or asking network and data-centre engineers to switch off ports or pull power.

Then came Hyperforce, the public cloud infrastructure. It brought shared foundational services (PKI, secrets, ingress and egress proxies) and removed most interactive shell access. Salesforce also fully embraced service ownership: service owners became responsible for the end-to-end operational health of their services, with no more throwing it over the fence to SRE.

Three problems followed. SRE was less central; a central game day team could not learn the architecture and edge cases of every new or redesigned service; and the old shell-based approach was ruled out by the new privileged-access constraints.

## Why hand chaos to service owners?

The reframe is simple. "Service owners know their service better than anybody else," Jay Hankins said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, so they are best placed to name failure points and fixes. Shifting chaos left in the development cycle shortens the time from finding a problem to fixing it, instead of waiting for a customer to find it in production.

## What does a self-service chaos platform need?

Hankins lists four scale challenges, each turned into a requirement:

- **The AWS footprint.** The core CRM product is hundreds of services across 78 AWS accounts, and one service might keep its containers in one account and its database, cache and S3 buckets in others. Humans logging into each account is infeasible, so the platform must attack many accounts at once.
- **Multi-tenant Kubernetes.** Services spread over many namespaces times many clusters. Owners must be able to attack their own service everywhere it runs, but never shared services or the worker nodes, and without knowing much about Kubernetes or deploying workflows and configmaps themselves.
- **Inventory and access.** The platform has to discover and group every resource type a team owns (deployments, S3 buckets, RDS databases), tie into SSO to match owners to services, and lean on Hyperforce's opinionated tagging and labelling to keep the blast radius to what you own.
- **Safety and outcomes.** It integrates with the change and incident management database and refuses to attack during an incident or maintenance. Owners measure experiments with the same SLOs and monitors they use in production.

That last point creates a feedback loop. Any disagreement between a chaos experiment's outcome and the SLO, he says, is a chance to improve the SLO's definition.

## What should you look for in tooling?

His five recommendations: pick tooling that is multi-substrate (Hyperforce is designed for other clouds too, and acquisitions bring surprises); use RBAC plus tags and labels so it is never unclear who can attack what; prioritise extensibility such as webhooks and custom integrations; get a toolbox that covers both large game-day-style experiments and precise attacks on one service; and put SLOs in your hypotheses.

## So are game days dead?

No. They get optimised for purpose and expertise. Service owners take the concrete technical fixes. Game day teams, with their wide view of the infrastructure, take compliance exercises such as SOC 2 and data RPO/RTO, people and process chaos (page the incident response chain while the first responder is unavailable), shared IT service chaos (what if the wiki with all the runbooks is down?), and tabletop sessions that help owners scope attacks using what has hurt other services before.

## Who should watch?

Platform and SRE teams in large organisations moving from a central chaos team to service ownership, and anyone designing guardrails for multi-account AWS or shared Kubernetes clusters. It is architecture and requirements rather than a product demo.

Title: Finding adverse drug events in tweets, from BERT ensembles to prompts
Description: Deepak Karunanidhi (Novartis) at Conf42 Python 2024 on detecting adverse events in social posts with BERT ensembles, and why prompts may replace the training
Body:
A patient tweets that they got a headache after taking a new medicine. In pharma, that tweet may be an adverse event that has to reach the FDA, and someone has to find it among millions of posts. At Conf42 Python 2024, Deepak Karunanidhi, Associate Director of Data Science and Machine Learning at Novartis, walks through how his team built that detector with fine-tuned transformer ensembles, and argues that generative AI with prompt engineering can now skip most of the training phase.

It is a use-case talk rather than a coding one: the problem, the pipeline, the model framework, and the trade-off between fine-tuning BERT and prompting a foundation model.

## Why is this a machine learning problem at all?

Before social media, adverse events came to physicians by email or phone and were passed on to the FDA. Now pharmaceutical companies advertise new products on Twitter, Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn, and patients report side effects in the same places. Reviewing all of it by hand is, in Deepak's words, a humongous task. The pipeline he describes pulls posts and emails through data connectors, preprocesses them, runs them through an ML platform, and sends only the flagged records to skilled technical reviewers. The junk never reaches a human.

The constraints make it harder than ordinary text classification: informal channel-specific language, anomalies that are rare (the talk frames it as perhaps one in a thousand), the need to mimic a practitioner's medical understanding, GxP compliance, and almost no tolerance for false negatives.

## Why a false positive is cheap and a false negative is not

That last constraint drives every design choice. "We should not miss any anomaly in our real data," Deepak Karunanidhi said at Conf42 Python 2024. The team accepts a skew towards false positives, since a human reviewer will clear them, and only promotes a model once it reaches around 98 to 99% recall on operational and production quality test data.

Repeatability matters too. The same text must get the same verdict on every inference, because the system sits inside a risk management framework. The talk recommends checking that the chosen framework and compute support reproducibility for safety-critical work.

## What does the anomaly identification framework look like?

- **Labelled data first.** Fine-tuning needs roughly 20,000 to 30,000 labelled records. Skilled annotators are interviewed, trained on guidelines, and work in pairs; a reviewer validates their labels, and disagreements go to a further annotator, with final labels decided by majority vote.
- **An ensemble, not a model.** Multiple BERT and BioBERT models trained with different random seeds run side by side. If any of them flags the text as an adverse event, it goes to human review.
- **A rule engine as a guardrail.** Heuristic rules based on products and medical events catch edge cases the models miss.
- **Sampling the rest.** Unflagged records are sub-sampled for business review so the team notices if the algorithm's performance degrades.
- **Pluggable models.** The framework accepts BERT today and XLM-RoBERTa, GPT or Llama 2 tomorrow, with a Chinese RoBERTa variant for Chinese text. It is built on PyTorch and Hugging Face Transformers, trained on 8 Tesla K80 GPUs in data-parallel mode, with MLflow for experiment tracking and the model registry. Hyperparameter optimisation tunes learning rate and epochs, and the best three or four models form the ensemble.

## Is BERT still worth the trouble?

Deepak is candid about the cost: long training times, a big labelled dataset, a separate PyTorch serving setup in production, a tendency to overfit on smaller datasets, and predictions that are hard to explain. His alternative is to treat a foundation model such as GPT-4, Claude or Llama 2 as a classifier, steered with in-context examples, instruction tuning and chain-of-thought prompts, and to fine-tune only if prompting cannot do the job. In his view, prompt engineering will solve the problem in most cases, which moves the team out of the model training phase entirely.

The talk does not show measured results for the prompted approach against the BERT ensemble, so treat that part as direction rather than evidence. The ensemble-plus-rules-plus-humans pattern is the transferable bit.

## Who should watch?

Data scientists in regulated industries, and anyone building a classifier where missing one positive costs far more than reviewing ten false alarms. The talk is light on code and heavy on process, which for this kind of system is where the risk lives.

Title: Your security stack is untested until you run the experiment
Description: David Lavezzo (Capital One) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on proving security controls work with experiments, not vendor claims or incidents
Body:
Security teams buy a tool, tick the box and assume the box stays ticked. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, David Lavezzo, Director of Security Chaos Engineering at Capital One, makes the case for proving it instead: run safe, repeatable attack experiments against your own defences, record which layer saw what, and turn the result into a baseline you can measure drift against.

He has done security chaos engineering since 2017 and is a contributing author on the Security Chaos Engineering report and the book Security Chaos Engineering: Sustaining Resilience in Software and Systems. The talk is as funny as it is practical. He is also clear about what it is not: not red teaming and not a penetration test, but the groundwork you do before paying offensive teams to steal your lunch money.

## Why doesn't buying the tool answer the question?

Leadership hears about the next terrifying threat and asks: are we safe? The usual reply is that signatures and configurations are in place. That, Lavezzo says, does not answer the question. The answer should be that you modelled it, here are the results, and here is how gaps are tracked.

He points to the Verizon DBIR, which keeps naming misconfigurations rather than vulnerabilities as the leading cause of breaches, and to how hard the so-called basics really are: asset inventory, access control, backups you have actually restored, native controls such as Windows Defender Application Control that few teams manage well. "If you need to be certified to use a product or go through 40 plus hours of training, it's probably not well designed," David Lavezzo said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. Badly designed things fail, so you need to know how your tools work, whether they work, and whether they keep working.

Incidents are a poor way to find out. People are stressed, the bad thing has already happened, and a bad retrospective turns into blaming the human. His line on phishing is worth stealing: if one click ruins everything, the problem is the system, not the person who clicked.

## How does a security chaos experiment work?

Secure today does not mean secure tomorrow. Tuning, patching, reassigned people and changed priorities all alter how a system behaves after it was signed off. So the experiment has a familiar shape: a hypothesis (when X happens, the system responds with Y), an experiment with a stated purpose, evidence collection, and repeat, forever.

He distinguishes this from testing: "Testing implies a right or wrong answer, and we're not looking for right or wrong." The goal is new information for better decisions.

Practical advice for building experiments:

- Break down a real attack; The DFIR Report is a good source of adversary actions. Most adversaries end up looking alike: untrusted code executing.
- Start with what you control. The endpoint is usually easiest.
- Never use real malware. Use non-destructive stand-ins such as EICAR or Mimikatz. Please don't actually ransomware yourself.
- Expect layers. A single file download should leave two to four pieces of telemetry across the stack.

The output is a scorecard: attack stages mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques (staged download T1105, system discovery T1082, a modified scheduled task T1053, a POST beacon T1102) against firewall, IPS, IDS, web proxy, HIDS, app control, AV and EDR, each cell marked blocked, logged, alerted or missed. A payload blocked at the endpoint is not a win. It means every earlier layer let it through. Automate the experiment, and the baseline becomes a drift detector for every patch, tune or platform replacement.

## What about the friends?

The second half explains the title. The same data helps hunt teams validate analytics, architecture teams find duplicated tooling, operations check that critical alerts still fire, and product owners decide on renewals with evidence rather than a vendor's MITRE evaluation slide. It also makes you popular with audit, which he presents as a mixed blessing.

The compliance payoff is his best line: "It enables you to be compliant because you're secure, not secure because you're compliant." Instead of asking for the best AV money can buy, ask how to reduce the impact of a malicious actor in your environment.

His getting-started list: start small, target business goals, accept that not every miss is a gap to fix, be nice (nobody helps a mean person trace why something broke), and know that success means more work.

## Who should watch?

Security engineers, detection engineers and SREs who keep getting asked whether the security tools actually work. Anyone who has to defend a tooling budget will get a ready-made way to show value. The tone is irreverent throughout, half-human, half-ravioli AI art included.

Title: Your image pipeline is a delivery URL with opinions
Description: Sharon Yelenik (Cloudinary) at Conf42 Python 2024 on analysing images at upload with AI, then personalising each one through its delivery URL
Body:
Once a site has more images than a designer can eyeball, or any user-generated content at all, someone has to make crop, caption and moderation decisions without looking. At Conf42 Python 2024, Sharon Yelenik, API and DevX Content Writer at Cloudinary, [shows a small Python app](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2024_Sharon_Yelenik_personalizing_images_aipowered_features) that runs AI analysis on every upload and then uses the results to transform each image automatically. The headline trick: put sunglasses on every detected face, and only on faces.

It is a vendor talk with Cloudinary doing the heavy lifting, and it is short and practical: one demo, then the code behind it.

## What can AI tell you about an image before you show it?

Sharon walks through the analysis types that let a program make decisions an art director would otherwise make by hand:

- **Moderation**, essential for user uploads, so nothing inappropriate reaches the page.
- **Object detection**, with bounding-box coordinates for each object (car, lady, jacket, bag in her example).
- **Auto tagging**, the twin of detection: it stores what was found as tags you can query later.
- **Face detection**, including the count and coordinates of each face.
- **Colour detection**, the predominant colours of the picture.
- **OCR**, any text in the image.

## How does the demo use all that?

Users upload a batch of photos through an upload widget. The app then sorts them into People and Shoes based on the detected objects, titles each one from its auto tags, prints what it found underneath (detected text, face count and coordinates, orientation, predominant colour), adds a border in the predominant colour, and makes every image a square. Then the sunglasses go on. As Sharon dryly notes, "None of the shoes are wearing sunglasses."

The squaring is the part worth noticing. Forcing tall and wide shots into a square usually means cropping off something important or squashing the image. Instead the demo uses generative outpainting to extend each picture so it fills the frame without distortion.

## Where does the analysis switch on?

In an upload preset, created once from Python with `cloudinary.api.create_upload_preset`. The preset is unsigned, so the browser widget can upload without exposing the API key and secret, and its parameters do the work: colour tracking for the predominant colour, face detection, Google auto tagging at a 0.7 threshold (objects detected with 70% confidence become tags), OCR for text, and moderation via the Amazon Rekognition add-on. Credentials come from an environment variable loaded from a `.env` file.

The output function lists every asset carrying the demo's tag, pulls each one's analysis JSON through the API, and skips anything whose moderation status is not approved. Orientation is just width divided by height.

## Why is the delivery URL the interesting part?

Because the transformations are not a separate processing job. Every edit is a parameter appended to the image's delivery URL. "All I have to do is programmatically change its delivery URL and voila, you'll see it affecting how the image actually is displayed," Sharon Yelenik said at Conf42 Python 2024.

So the app builds a URL per image: width and height 600, a generative-fill pad for the background, a sunglasses overlay anchored to the faces, a border in the detected colour, and `quality=auto` plus `fetch_format=auto` to pick the compression and format each requesting browser handles best. The original asset never changes; the personalisation lives in the string.

## Who should watch?

Python and web developers building catalogues, marketplaces or anything with user uploads, who want to see what a hosted image pipeline looks like from the code side. If you want to train your own vision models, this is not that talk: the AI here is called, not built. The demo code is on GitHub, linked from the talk.

Title: An LLM app in 24 hours, yes. A RAG app, give it longer
Description: Joshua Arvin Lat (NuWorks Interactive Labs) and Sophie Soliven (Edamama) at Conf42 Python 2024 on why RAG beats fine-tuning for company knowledge
Body:
Can you build a generative AI application in a day? At Conf42 Python 2024, Joshua Arvin Lat, CTO of NuWorks Interactive Labs and AWS Machine Learning Hero, and Sophie Soliven, Director of Operations at Edamama, answer yes for a self-hosted LLM and "it may take a bit more time" once you want it to answer from your own documents. Their talk is an on-ramp to retrieval augmented generation (RAG): what it is, why it is usually a better first move than fine-tuning, and what the AWS plumbing looks like.

Set expectations: this is an introductory talk. Roughly two thirds is concepts, from the AI family tree down to RAG variants, and the build is shown as architecture and a few lines of SDK code rather than a full live coding session. If you have already shipped a RAG pipeline, you can skip it. If you are about to pitch one, it is a tidy 30 minutes.

## Why not just fine-tune the model?

Sophie lays out the customisation ladder by difficulty: prompt engineering at the bottom, then RAG, then fine-tuning, then building your own foundation model at the top. RAG's selling point is that it adds knowledge "without changing pretrained model weights": the model stays as it is, and you fetch context from an external source, typically internal company knowledge bases, and pass it in with the query.

"You don't need to fine tune all the time to get the output you require," Sophie Soliven said at Conf42 Python 2024. Her examples are grounded in e-commerce, which is her day job: a model that knows the catalogue, a customer service assistant that follows the company's own policies, personalised search that knows purchase behaviour.

She also earns the RAG pitch by listing five LLM limitations first: fairness and bias inherited from the training corpus, hallucination, speed and cost, security and misuse (deep fakes, phishing, propaganda), and interpretability, which matters most in healthcare, finance and legal applications. RAG with up-to-date internal sources is offered as a direct answer to the hallucination problem.

## Naive, advanced, modular: which RAG are you building?

The talk splits RAG into three types:

- **Naive RAG**: indexing (chunk the data and embed it into vectors), retrieval, generation. Easy, and it shows: low precision gives misaligned chunks and hallucinations, low recall misses relevant chunks, stale data gives wrong answers, and responses can get repetitive.
- **Advanced RAG**: pre- and post-retrieval strategies to lift retrieval quality, such as sliding windows, fine-grained segmentation and metadata.
- **Modular RAG**: modules you can substitute and rearrange to fit your requirements.

That list of naive RAG failure modes is the most useful checklist in the talk. Each one maps to something you will debug in production.

## What does the AWS version look like?

Joshua takes over for the build. A model is deployed to its own Amazon SageMaker inference endpoint from a notebook or SageMaker Studio using the SageMaker Python SDK: call `deploy` with an initial instance count and an instance type sized to the model. The endpoint is essentially a web server hosting the model. In front of it sit API Gateway and AWS Lambda as the backend, a static frontend on S3, and a database if the application needs one.

The RAG part starts with a folder of PDFs synced to an S3 bucket. Amazon Textract extracts the content, FAISS holds the vectors, and LangChain builds a chain over the endpoint that uses the document context. The difference shows when you ask questions: the answers come from the PDFs, not just the model's training data. As Joshua Arvin Lat put it at Conf42 Python 2024, "we're now no longer limited to what the large language model has to offer."

## So, 24 hours?

Their verdict: a generative AI app in a day is doable. The RAG version takes longer because the time goes into setting up the resources and services, and into getting the data and files right. Anyone who has watched a chunking strategy eat a sprint will nod.

## Who should watch?

Developers and product people new to generative AI who want the vocabulary and one concrete AWS reference architecture in a single sitting. Engineers already tuning retrievers should head to the talks below instead.

Title: Your gas compressor is a planning bug worth millions a year
Description: Eugene Lykov (Visionis) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on why rotary equipment breaks simulation tools and what flat fuel-gas estimates cost
Body:
Most oil and gas companies plan 20 years of production with a fudge factor: take a fixed percentage off the top for the gas the plant burns itself, and move on. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, Eugene Lykov, Senior Software Engineer at Visionis, argues that this flat percentage is a slow, cumulative modelling error, and that the culprit is the hardest machine in the plant to simulate: the rotary compressor.

It is an unusual talk for a chaos engineering conference. There are no fault injections and no Kubernetes. The chaos here is physical: a machine whose operating point never sits still, and software that pretends it does.

## What do engineers model well, and where does it fall apart?

Lykov starts with the engineering idea of a process: a chain of tasks that turns inputs into an output, whether that is a car plant, a brewery or an oil refinery. Any of them can be written down as a mathematical model. His ladder of difficulty is a useful one:

- **Modelled best:** single physical parameters (temperature, pressure, flow rate, energy). Excel handles these when the relationships are simple and linear.
- **Modelled well:** well-described combinations such as thermodynamics, hydrodynamics and chemical reactions.
- **Modelled not so well:** machines where many parameters move together, above all industrial rotary equipment such as compressors (for gases) and pumps (for liquids).

## Why is a compressor so hard to simulate?

A compressor's job sounds trivial: raise the pressure of a gas. The problem, in Lykov's word, is variation. Every model of machine has its own performance curves, a fingerprint that ties pressure ratio, flow rate and power together for a specific impeller at a specific rotation speed. Change the speed and the whole map shifts. Multiply that by every hardware design on the market, then run machines in parallel or in series so they influence each other.

"So literally it is almost impossible to do universal software solution," Eugene Lykov said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024.

Commercial process simulators exist, and he names Aspen, ProSim and SimTech among the powerful ones. His complaint is flexibility: they are mostly proprietary and closed, they simplify, and they tend to skip rotary complexity. If your machine does not fit, you can file a support request and wait for the next version, sometimes for years, or build your own.

## What did the home-grown model actually do?

Lykov's own example comes from a company with a full simulation model of a project's assets, where everything simulated fine except the compressors: a series of 16 MW machines driven by gas turbines, with various impellers installed. He built separate Python models for each part of the chain (compressor, shaft, turbine, fuel gas), passing values along from pressure, flow rate and RPM through mechanical power and losses to heat power, calorific value and gas composition. By approximating the performance curves, the combined model calculated fuel gas consumption per machine across the whole operating range.

The neat trick was integration. The Python code plugged into Petroleum Experts software through its OpenServer interface, driven from Python via pywin32, an interface that was originally used to pull out reports. Nobody had to replace the existing modelling stack; the precise compressor model just slotted in beside it.

## Why does the precision matter?

Fuel gas burned by compressors is product the company never sells. On a typical 20-year production profile, Lykov compares three lines: raw production, production minus a fixed own-use percentage, and the simulated figure. The gap between the last two looks small in any one year, but it compounds, and he puts the scale at up to hundreds of millions of dollars per year on big projects. The divergence is visible by the middle of the project's life.

The sharper point is the abandonment phase, when production can no longer be profitable and decommissioning should start. A wrong own-use estimate moves that date. In his example the two estimates land almost a year apart, a year in which costs exceed profits. His summary is blunt: take the conservative average and probably lose millions later, or invest in modelling software now.

## Who should watch?

Engineers who build software for industrial operators, anyone curious how digital twins of physical plant get made, and SREs who like seeing capacity planning in a domain where the hardware is the size of a house. It is a short talk, a problem statement plus one worked example, closing with a call for more open-source work between industry and the software world. Do not expect code on screen.
