Title: A pod delete, three resilience probes and a score of 75
Description: Neelanjan Manna and Sayan Mondal (Harness) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on resilience probes that check a chaos experiment's impact for you
Body:
Injecting a fault is the easy half of chaos engineering; deciding automatically whether the system survived it is the hard half. Neelanjan Manna, Software Engineer at Harness, and Sayan Mondal, Senior Software Engineer at Harness, both LitmusChaos maintainers, used their [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Neelanjan_Manna_Sayan_Mondal_chaos_validation_resilience_probes) to show resilience probes: reusable checks you attach to any fault, which turn a chaos run into pass, fail and a resilience score.

It is a product talk, demoed in Harness Chaos Engineering, but Sayan points out the same probe features exist in open source LitmusChaos.

## Why measuring impact is the bottleneck

Neelanjan opens with the cost of downtime: Slack's SLA payouts, a smoke-triggered power shutdown in a Wells Fargo data center, and British Airways stranding 75,000 passengers. His point is that cloud-native apps sit on a stack of dependencies, cloud services, Kubernetes and platform, and ship weekly or faster into many environments, so nobody can predict every failure. Running chaos in CI/CD at that pace only works if you can measure the impact of each fault automatically.

He is also clear about ownership. "Chaos engineering is a culture oriented approach which finds its place as part of the DevOps practices and hence developers and SRE should work together for the best efforts," Neelanjan Manna said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. Developers start early and small, and SREs scale it into pipelines, staging and then production.

## What is a resilience probe?

Sayan's definition: a pluggable check you configure once and reuse across experiments. "It's basically a write once, use anywhere kind of a paradigm," he said. You create it globally, attach it to faults, and read the results.

The probe types for Kubernetes infrastructure are HTTP, command, Kubernetes, Prometheus, Datadog, Dynatrace and SLO; Linux infrastructure gets HTTP, command, Datadog and Dynatrace. Uses range from hitting health or downstream URIs and running your own health-check functions, to CRUD on Kubernetes custom resources, PromQL assertions, and checking an SLO's error budget.

What makes them useful is the run mode:

- **SOT**, start of test: assert before chaos begins.
- **EOT**, end of test: assert after it ends.
- **OnChaos**: assert while the fault is active.
- **Continuous**: poll throughout the run.
- **Edge**: assert before and after.

## The demo: delete the cart service

The setup is a GKE cluster with Prometheus and Grafana, running the Online Boutique microservices demo. The target is the cart service, and the fault is a plain pod delete picked from the chaos hub. Three probes go on it:

- An **HTTP probe** in SOT mode, checking that the front end's URL returns a 200.
- A **command probe** in Edge mode, running kubectl get pod in the boutique namespace and asserting that more than zero cart service pods are running.
- A **Prometheus probe** in Continuous mode, asserting that probe success percentage stays at or above 90.

The cart QPS drops in Grafana as the pod dies. The HTTP probe passes with a 200. The command probe passes: the expected value was greater than zero and the actual value was one. The Prometheus probe fails at 88.33% against the 90 target. The experiment's resilience score comes out at 75, which Sayan sums up as okay, but worth looking into.

That failure is the useful bit. Without the probe, the pod came back in seconds and the shop looked fine, so a human watching the UI would have called it resilient. The probe caught the dip.

## Who should watch

Teams already running LitmusChaos or Harness Chaos Engineering who still check experiment results by eye, and anyone designing pass/fail criteria for chaos in CI/CD. Expect a vendor demo, but the probe modes and the SLO-style thresholds carry over to whatever tooling you use.

Title: Put tech debt at the top of every sprint, and stop over-analysing the rest
Description: Ewald Verhoeven (TestCoders) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on why teams slow down, paying tech debt every sprint, and scoring decisions with AHP and Pugh
Body:
If you have ever held a dedicated bug sprint, or cancelled a retro to finish work that was almost done, this one is about your team. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, [Ewald Verhoeven](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Ewald_Verhoeven_software_delivery_team), Quality Advocate Lead at TestCoders, argued that teams slow down for the same three reasons everywhere (bugs, legacy and technical debt) and offered two fixes: pay down tech debt first thing every sprint, and make big decisions with a scoring matrix instead of gut feeling.

It is a process talk from a test automation consultant, with examples from client teams and a personal closing story.

## What does a slowing team look like?

His symptoms: bug sprints, backlog items older than twelve months, cards piling up in the testing column, cancelled retros, product owners doing the testing. Such teams typically finish less than 90% of what they planned.

His definitions are pragmatic. A bug is something that was delivered, tested and worked, and now doesn't. Legacy has no crisp definition, but the signals are clear: the system outlives the team or the tech stack, people are afraid to touch it (some won't even clone the repo), and there are no tests, which means no way to learn what it is supposed to do.

## How should a team treat technical debt?

He uses the deliberate/accidental, prudent/reckless quadrant. Deliberate and prudent is fine: you know you are taking on debt and plan to pay it back. Deliberate and reckless means no plan at all. Accidental and prudent means you find out later and fix how you work. The one to avoid is finding out and ignoring it.

The money analogy makes the point stick. A €6,000 trip, €2,400 saved at €200 a month, and €3,600 borrowed to repay within a year leaves you €1,200 short, or €100 a month you have to find somewhere: rent, insurance, utilities, the car or food. Skip that planning and the debt decides for you; in software, that means more bugs and dirty fixes left in production.

His rule is blunt. Ewald Verhoeven said at Conf42 DevOps 2024: "You put technical debt on the top of your backlog every sprint, and you finish it first."

His example of the vicious cycle comes from test automation. A flaky end-to-end test blocks the pipeline, someone disables it to get the build green, coverage drops, bugs follow, a hotfix ships, nobody re-enables the test, and the loop starts again.

## Why are DevOps teams better at it?

In his experience, real DevOps teams with developers and operations engineers working together handle tech debt better because everyone feels the pain across the whole lifecycle, not just in their own phase. The first way of DevOps is flow, small changes moving from dev to ops without waiting, and that needs automation everywhere: tests, CI, deployment and release.

You don't need a DevOps team to start. His suggestion is to look at your definition of done. It lists the chores nobody likes (release notes, manual tests, quality gates, peer reviews), a ready-made automation backlog.

## How do you make a team decision without a week of opinions?

The second slowdown is decision making. DevOps favours data over gut feeling, but every decision is emotional underneath, so the trick is to quantify it. He uses two complementary tools, walked through with a real case: a team choosing a contract testing tool.

- **AHP matrix** (Analytic Hierarchy Process): list the criteria (pricing, collaboration and source control, OpenAPI 3.0 support, learning curve, a mock server, future GraphQL support) and compare them in pairs only, scoring how much more important one is with Fibonacci numbers (1, 2, 3, 5, 8). The output is a weight per criterion. That team ranked collaboration and source control and OpenAPI 3.0 highest.
- **Pugh matrix**: take the weights, pick one candidate as the baseline (here Pact), and score the others against it per criterion from -2 to +2. Postman and PactFlow were the alternatives; the numbers in his demo were made up on the spot to show the mechanics.

The argument stops being about who liked which tool at a previous job and becomes about the criteria this team agreed on.

## Why is good enough good enough?

His last point is the one he asked people to remember: Ewald Verhoeven said at Conf42 DevOps 2024, "So please make informed decisions, but stop overanalyzing. Good is good enough."

He learned it the hard way. About ten years before the talk, while serving in the Royal Netherlands Army, he was attacked by a man with a knife outside his home. He survived with minor injuries and was treated for PTSD, but the case was never solved and none of the facts made sense, and he kept analysing it. What helped was accepting that no new facts were coming, and moving on.

## Who should watch?

Scrum teams with a growing backlog of old items, team leads tired of tool debates, and test automation engineers who have watched a disabled test turn into a bug farm.

Title: How a $5M test environment sold chaos engineering to a cautious boss
Description: Kyle Shelton (Toyota) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on selling chaos engineering to risk-averse leaders with TCO, small pilots and hard data
Body:
Asking your leadership for permission to break production is a hard sell, so don't lead with breaking things. Kyle Shelton, Senior DevOps Engineer at Toyota, used his [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Kyle_Shelton_risk_averse_culture) to explain how to pitch chaos engineering to conservative, bottom-line-first leaders: talk total cost of ownership, ask for small pilots, bring the data. His case study is a $5 million request for a duplicate environment that, by his account, turned into a $20 million swing.

## Why do modern systems need this at all?

Kyle started at Verizon on the VoLTE rollout. Deployments took six weeks, four of them on site racking servers, and every data center was built to 40% capacity so a failover would only push the surviving side to 80%. Today you can get a simple MVP to customers in about 45 minutes on a public cloud. That speed comes with more abstractions, more dependencies and a shared responsibility model in which a data center you don't own can hurt you.

His summary of the practice is the classic one: define steady state, write a hypothesis, inject chaos in a controlled way, observe, evaluate. He stresses that observability comes first. If you cannot put metrics and a score on your system, chaos engineering will not get you far. He also points to principlesofchaos.org and to your cloud provider's published service events as a ready-made list of real failures to test.

## Spotting the conservative mindset

Three signs to look for. A risk-averse, bottom-line-first view, where failure is framed only as lost money. Outage fatigue: at Splunk, during a move from an overseas NOC to an in-house team, he was paged at 2 am every other night, and the older engineers were worn out. And slowness: two weeks for a change board, two more for a maintenance window, six weeks before three lines of code run. "I personally hate going slow, but slow is steady sometimes," Kyle Shelton said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. Your job is to speed it up without ignoring why it is slow.

## Selling it: speak TCO

Kyle calls sales the skill he is always trying to grow, and tells how he once got an executive to fund an office soccer team by pitching it as a fix for support, sales and SRE never talking. It worked, and he met his wife through it.

For technology, the argument is total cost of ownership. His example: a managed tool at $100,000 a year looks expensive until you count the $400,000 of engineering time spent running the open source alternative. Reliability goes into the same sentence: happy customers mean happy engineers mean happy bosses, and fragility costs revenue, talent and SLAs.

His buy-in playbook:

- Do a cost-benefit analysis and bring charts, graphs and developer surveys. An old VP of his said that without charts and graphs, it didn't happen.
- Ask for a small pilot in a sandbox, win, and build on the win.
- Show you can control the blast radius.
- Speak the listener's language: business value for executives, failure types and backout plans for a CTO.
- Iterate. New errors mean new improvements.

As he put it, "you are literally asking to break things, but you're asking to break things to make them better." Lead with the second half.

## The $5 million ask

At Splunk, Kyle worked on moving the whole fleet of about 15,000 instances from Ansible and Chef to Puppet and Terraform, onto Graviton and from D-series to I-series instances, in roughly eight and a half months. He had the biggest, most customised customer, the first to pay a million dollars, with half their stack already leaving. Failure would have cost serious revenue.

He asked the chief cloud officer for $5 million to duplicate the customer's environment for three months: replicate four petabytes of data, run the migration two or three times, break things on purpose and document everything. The early runs did hit catastrophic failures, in the practice environment. The real migration went through flawlessly. He says the move to about 80 I-series instances in place of roughly 400 D-series ones gave a tenfold margin on the investment, and he does not think the migration would have happened without those tests.

## Who should watch

Engineers who already believe in chaos engineering and keep losing the argument with management. It is a persuasion talk, light on tooling, with Chaos Monkey, Harness and its open source LitmusChaos, Gremlin and Chaos Mesh named at the end as places to start.

Title: How Kong made its gateway faster, and how it proves it every day
Description: Wenchao Xiang (Kong) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on Kong Gateway's Rust router, LMDB config store, plugin fixes and daily performance tests
Body:
At 10,000 routes, the router stops being a detail and becomes the gateway. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, [Wenchao Xiang](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Wenchao_Xiang_kong_gateway_performance_enhancement), Senior Software Engineer at Kong, walked through the performance work behind recent Kong Gateway releases: a router rewritten in Rust, configuration moved to LMDB, a new event library for NGINX workers, plugin fixes for Prometheus and rate limiting, and the bare-metal test rig that catches regressions daily.

Every benchmark here is Kong measuring Kong, but the methods are worth copying.

## What changed in the plugins?

**Prometheus.** The plugin did fine with a few routes and slowed as route counts grew. The 3.4 release sped up metric scraping and cut high-cardinality metrics, and the slides credit three fixes: a table pool so scraping stops creating temporary Lua tables all the time, yields inside long loops so one scrape does not hog the CPU and stall request processing, and replacing functions LuaJIT could not compile (the NYI ones) so the plugin runs on the JIT. The talk showed a clear p99 latency drop from 3.3 to 3.4.

**Rate limiting.** With counters in external storage such as Redis, the old plugin talked to the store on every request. The new batch queue in 3.4 lets the plugin write counters to an in-memory queue and flush them asynchronously, with a new `sync_rate` setting to control how often. In Kong's comparison against an unnamed Go-based open-source gateway, p99 and RPS came out nearly twice as good.

## Why rewrite the router in Rust?

Almost every request passes through the router, so it is the hottest code in a gateway. Since version 3.0 Kong has shipped the ATC router, a DSL-based design where routes are written as expressions, which he says gives more flexibility and better performance without losing readability on large configurations. It is written in Rust for C-like speed with safer memory handling, which was not easy given that Rust is not natively supported in OpenResty.

He reported p99 latency in testing with 10,000 routes dropping from 1.5 seconds to 0.1 seconds. Two more changes help: a cheaper router rebuild, which per the slides cut worst-case rebuild latency from 20 seconds to 5 with 10,000 routes, and conditional rebuilds from 3.0 that only rebuild when routes have actually changed.

## What replaced shared memory?

Kong runs on NGINX and OpenResty, with a master process forking isolated workers. Two things used to live in NGINX shared memory, and both changed.

- **Configuration** moved to LMDB in 3.0. Shared memory used too much memory and was not transactional, so keeping data consistent meant extra code. LMDB, a transactional embedded key-value store, cut memory use and improved RPS while configuration was being pushed constantly, with a further 50% to 70% drop in rebuild time, especially with many workers.
- **Events between workers**, used for things like router rebuilds and health checks, moved to lua-resty-events, a publish-subscribe library in pure Lua. The old shared-memory version needed a lock for every access and a size fixed at startup. In tests posting 1,000 events every 5 ms and 10,000 events every 100 ms, the two libraries tied at low load and the new one won as load increased.

## How does Kong catch performance regressions?

This is the section to steal. The rig is two bare-metal machines on a private network, one generating load with wrk and one running Kong. Upstream and gateway sit on the loopback so wrk gets the network bandwidth, the NIC interrupts, upstream and gateway are pinned to separate CPU cores, and turbo boost is disabled so numbers stay stable.

Each test suite collects at least 100 samples, and RPS, latency and memory are compared by mean, median and standard deviation and by their PDF and CDF. Results from release tests and daily runs go into the same storage, and the daily run is compared against the baseline. Wenchao Xiang said at Conf42 DevOps 2024: "We do the test every day and if the difference happens the test is considered a failure and we will get a notification about it." When that happens, the team runs perf, reads the flame graph to find the guilty function, fixes it and reruns perf to confirm.

## What can you tune yourself?

Large payloads are the common exception to Kong's out-of-the-box tuning. A request body bigger than the buffer spills to disk, and disk I/O can block the NGINX event loop. Raising the request buffer size above the default helps, and so does the response buffer for large upstream responses. Do not turn buffering on for real-time traffic, long-lived or streaming connections, line-by-line processing, or memory-limited environments.

## Who should watch?

Teams running Kong at scale, and anyone building a performance regression pipeline for a proxy or gateway. The tuning section is short; the methodology is the reason to watch.

Title: Chaos war games at Vodafone UK start by pulling a cable
Description: Gabor Gerencser (Vodafone UK) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on running chaos war games, from tabletop exercises to full environment drills
Body:
A chaos war game is a fire drill for your software and the people who run it, and the first one should be boringly simple. Gabor Gerencser, Tech Lead in the performance and chaos engineering team at Vodafone UK, used his [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Gabor_Gerencser_war_games) to share how Vodafone runs them: tabletop exercises first, environment-based games later, and a pile of lessons on participants, goals and reporting.

## Why war games, and how do you sell them?

Gabor frames chaos in terms of knowns and unknowns. Known knowns you can plan for, resilience patterns such as circuit breakers cover some of the uncertainty, and the unknown unknowns are the ones that catch you completely off guard. Like firefighters training in purpose-built buildings, teams practise simulated incidents to find weak spots in communication, processes and knowledge before a real incident does it for them.

First you need to know your current state, with observability and metrics such as MTTR, incident counts, defect numbers and code quality. Then you need stakeholders on board, and they care about revenue and customer satisfaction. His back-of-envelope example: 100 users each generating £1,000 an hour is £100,000 an hour at risk; make it 1,000 users and you are at a million. War games cost preparation time, environments and sometimes licences, and he argues the benefit outweighs it.

## Tabletop or environment-based?

**Tabletop war games** are the cheap way in: people around a table, in person or online, going through scenarios. The slides put them at one to two hours, no environment needed, six to 30 participants. Vodafone's largest had about 15 and it worked well. They expose gaps in process, knowledge, communication, documentation and architecture. Gabor suggests not recording them, so people speak openly; have a scribe take notes instead. Vodafone uses a PowerPoint deck, warms up with simple puzzles such as guessing a missing word in an acronym like MTTR, and builds up to TV show formats.

**Environment-based war games** cost more: dedicated environments, longer preparation, a briefing and a longer retrospective. The slides give six to eight hours. They range from focused games with a few teams to full end-to-end ones with 20 to 30 people. Production war games need maturity: if your incident numbers are not already low, stay in a test environment. Vodafone mostly uses Chaos Toolkit plus manual steps, so it is far from fully automated. Simulate the outside world too: before one game they analysed how they talk to third-party suppliers and wrote response templates to play the supplier's part.

## Make it fun, keep it safe

Gamification does a lot of work. Time limits, people against people or teams against teams, a leaderboard, prizes, and random event cards in the style of a board game: the CI/CD pipeline is broken while you have a P1 to fix, or the chat tool is down, so how do you coordinate now? Just keep it safe, keep it blameless, make clear it is a simulation, and have a rollback plan for whatever the game breaks.

## Lessons from Vodafone's games

The headline lesson fits on a sticker. "Keep it simple, just pull a cable," Gabor Gerencser said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. Kill an ECS instance in the AWS console; you do not need automation to start. Vodafone once planned an ambitious scenario, ran late on preparation and had to scale back to make the deadline, because complexity is not your friend.

More from the list:

- Start with common scenarios such as a slow API response, which works for almost any system and naturally leads to circuit breakers.
- Do not test known issues. Fix them first.
- Make it production-like, ideally with production-like traffic, but do not let missing load block you; a database failover needs none.
- Train people before the game, never put people without production knowledge into a production game, and name backup participants because people get ill and go on holiday.
- Every game needs a host and a scribe. Swap roles: let a developer play SRE.

## Delivering and publicising results

Findings only count if they get fixed. Vodafone writes a report for every game (TLDR, summary, description and improvement areas with impact, probability and recommended actions), tracks each item until it ships, and retests so a fix stays fixed. Credit the participants by name, and share results beyond the team.

## Who should watch

Anyone asked to start game days or war games with no budget and a sceptical audience. It is practical and process-heavy, with no tooling demo, and full of details you can reuse in your first session.

Title: Most Kubernetes misconfigurations are one-line fixes nobody made
Description: Joe Pelletier (Fairwinds) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on what 330,000 scanned workloads say about Kubernetes cost, reliability and security hygiene
Body:
Developers guess their resource requests, and they guess high. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, [Joe Pelletier](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Joe_Pelletier_kubernetes_benchmark_report), Vice President of Product Strategy at Fairwinds, walked through the 2024 Kubernetes Benchmark Report, built from more than 330,000 workloads scanned by Fairwinds Insights. The pattern across cost, reliability and security: many of the worst findings are one-line fixes that never got made, often because a bad manifest got copied from one team to the next.

It is the third year of the report and the largest sample so far, with more than a dozen policy types. The talk covers about a quarter of the full report, by his estimate, and finishes with a short pitch for Fairwinds Insights.

## How do you read the charts?

Every chart plots the share of an organisation's workloads affected by a check against the share of organisations at that level. The useful reading tip: when the group of organisations with fewer than 10% of workloads affected shrinks year over year, the problem is getting harder to control, even if the average looks similar.

## Where is the money going?

The headline finding, measured for the first time this year: 37% of organisations need to right-size 50% or more of their containers. Without tooling or feedback loops telling them what to set, developers over-provision memory and CPU, and nobody notices until the bill arrives. The other end of the chart is encouraging, with 57% of organisations at 10% or fewer workloads affected, so some teams do get it right.

Missing requests are the bigger trend. 78% of organisations have at least 10% of their workloads missing CPU requests, up from about 50% the year before. Kubernetes treats requests as optional, but the scheduler cannot place a workload well without them. His view is that this is one of the easiest problems to fix with guardrails: flag it at pull request or at admission, and use the moment to teach.

## Which reliability basics are being skipped?

- **Image pull policy**: about 24% of organisations rely on a cached image for 90% of their images because the pull policy is not set to Always, which risks inconsistency and stale, unpatched images.
- **Health checks**: about 66% of liveness probes and 69% of readiness probes are missing. These need some application-specific input, which may explain why teams skip them.
- **Replicas**: 30% of organisations have fewer than 10% of deployments missing replicas, better than in 2023, but many still have far more.

He calls the replicas case the copy and paste problem: one team's manifest without replicas becomes the starting point for the next team, and the misconfiguration spreads. Joe Pelletier said at Conf42 DevOps 2024: "this is usually a very quick fix, like a one line change to your infrastructure as code."

## Is security getting better or worse?

Both, depending on the check. About 28% of organisations run 90% of their workloads with insecure capabilities such as NET_ADMIN, sometimes needed, often copied in by accident. Running as root is the good-news story: 30% of organisations run 70% or more of their containers as root, down from 44% in the previous report. It is also a one-line change, and he guesses its fame as the textbook Kubernetes misconfiguration helped.

Image vulnerabilities improved too. 26% of organisations have fewer than 10% of workloads affected, up from 12% in 2023, which he reads as teams upgrading third-party images and scanning more. Almost 84% of organisations now have near-complete scan coverage of running containers, up from 64%.

Fairwinds added checks from the NSA's Kubernetes hardening guidance, including one for network policies. The picture is split: 37% of organisations have fewer than 10% of workloads without a network policy, while a majority have more than half their workloads without one, which means those pods can talk to anything in the cluster.

## What does he suggest doing about it?

Guardrails at two points in the pipeline: at pull request, when infrastructure-as-code changes are made, and at admission, when workloads are deployed. Give developers the feedback and an easy way to fix it, and keep configurations consistent. This is where the Fairwinds pitch comes in: Insights covers configuration checks against standards such as the NSA guide, SOC 2 and ISO 27001, image scanning, Kubernetes cost allocation and right-sizing recommendations.

## Who should watch?

Platform teams who own a multi-tenant cluster and want numbers to bring to the next argument about whether admission policies are worth it. It is a short, data-driven talk; download the full report for the breakdowns.

Title: Electrolux turned chaos engineering into capture the flag
Description: Long Zhang and Kristina Kondrashevich (Electrolux) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on a capture-the-flag chaos game day and chaos built into a Backstage IDP
Body:
The best way to get developers into an observability tool is to hide something in it and award points for finding it. Long Zhang, Senior SRE at Electrolux, and Kristina Kondrashevich, Product Manager for SRE products, showed at [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Long_Zhang_Kristina_Kondrashevich_organization_fun_continuous) how they ran a capture-the-flag chaos game day for 41 developers, and how they then built chaos experiments into their internal developer platform so it does not depend on one big event.

## What problem were they solving?

Electrolux makes connected ovens, fridges, vacuum cleaners and dishwashers, launched in over 60 countries. A new developer meets two connectivity clouds, mostly on AWS but with services on Azure, IBM and Google Cloud, and every team had its own monitoring tool. During incidents the SRE team had to dig through all of them to find a root cause.

Kristina's first step was not chaos at all: move every team onto one observability platform, Datadog, for end-to-end tracing from appliance to cloud to app. Teams onboarded one by one, and usage varied wildly; some only ever searched logs. A scoreboard of which teams used which features turned out to be the first piece of gamification, as people started asking how to earn all the stars. Kristina notes that when you change something in an organisation, you cannot expect everyone to adapt quickly.

## How do you run a chaos game day as capture the flag?

Long, who holds a PhD in software reliability and was speaking at Conf42 for the third time, took the idea from security. The game ran in staging, because the first one was about learning, not production resilience. "We think everything can be a flag, for example, the piece of logs, name of metrics or the method that raises exception, et cetera," Long Zhang said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024.

Each experiment follows the same flow. The SRE team plants the flag by injecting a fault, releases instructions written as an end-user complaint, later releases a hint (finding the flag before the hint scores higher), then closes it. One example: a user tries to load an appliance profile by its ID and gets a 404; find the name of the method that raised the error in the trace.

His experiment design tips:

- Start from the goal. Here it was infrastructure knowledge and troubleshooting on one platform, so every experiment produced something observable: error logs, odd metrics, broken traces.
- Inject at any level, report from the user's side. Database latency or a microservice exception both arrive as a ticket that says the app cannot change the fridge temperature, just like a real support escalation.
- Don't write your own tooling. AWS Fault Injection Simulator and LitmusChaos already exist.

## Did it work?

The numbers: 41 developers from 12 teams in four countries, seven experiments and 181 submissions, which was more than the team could comfortably review by hand. The game also turned up real resilience issues nobody had injected. One developer whose team lost because their mobile app sent no logs or metrics went back and set up real user monitoring in Datadog; other teams added monitors and alerts.

Incidents dropped by 33% afterwards. Long is careful that the game days are not the only cause, since they also reworked incident management, but the SRE team now sees game days as a way to hand operational responsibilities to developers.

## From game day to platform feature

The catch was effort: manual experiment design, manual review of flags, internal trials and event logistics. So the next step puts chaos into the platform. Electrolux's internal developer platform, built about two years earlier, runs on Backstage with Terraform templates the SRE team defines for EKS, databases and other resources. The first version added a chaos button to resources such as a microservice on Kubernetes: pick a fault model, set the latency or error type, choose an environment, and write down your hypothesis to compare against what the observability platform shows.

To scale, they adopted the LitmusChaos Backstage plugin with LitmusChaos 3.0, which brings multi-tenancy and fault models at the cloud provider and Kubernetes levels. Next on the list: multi-level, automated experiments and a closed feedback loop between the platform and observability.

## Who should watch

SRE and platform teams who have bought an observability tool nobody uses well, and anyone planning their first game day. The capture-the-flag format and the hint-for-points trick are easy to copy.

Title: Your CTO knows 4% of the problems, and DevOps needs the other 96%
Description: Tomasz Manugiewicz (Grand Parade / William Hill) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on how CTOs think during a DevOps transformation and how engineers can earn their trust
Body:
Engineers going through a DevOps transformation want their CTO's support, and the CTO, it turns out, wants theirs. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Tomasz Manugiewicz, General Manager at Grand Parade / William Hill, explains how the transformation looks from the C-level seat: what executives need, which cognitive biases they fall into, and how an engineer can become the person a CTO turns to.

There is no code and no tooling in this one. It is a talk about organisations, aimed squarely at engineers who would rather understand the people above them than complain about them.

## Is DevOps a mindset or a tool chain?

Both, he says. The tool chain (Puppet, Chef, Docker, Jenkins, build pipelines) is the easy part: engineers are curious and learn it. The hard part is who uses which tool, which standards apply, and how development and operations work together in the middle zone of infrastructure as code, containers, orchestration and CI/CD that could belong to either team. Moving from a monolith run by a monolithic org chart to microservices is a change in how people work, not only a change in the stack.

His model for that change is Kurt Lewin's three steps: unfreeze, change, freeze. Unfreeze by creating a climate for change and showing why it matters to the business and to each person. Enable the organisation in the middle, with tools, training and plenty of one-on-ones, which he calls the most critical stage. Then freeze, so people do not drift back to the old tool or the old line that pipelines are not an operations job. The goal between the silos is shared responsibility, and shared responsibility only works once trust removes the blame game.

## Why does the CTO see so little?

Engineers are specialists with deep knowledge and a narrow view; executives trade depth for breadth. Manugiewicz maps the whole organisation onto a computer: organisational behaviour, strategy and structure feed a mindset bus and a technology bus, structure works as organisational memory, and collaboration is the collective CPU. Both buses run on trust, cognitive (this person can deliver) and emotional (this person is open and honest with me).

The number that sticks is the iceberg of ignorance: executives know only about 4% of the problems in an organisation, while the teams know all of them. The gap, he argues, comes from eroded trust, because people hide problems from managers they expect to be blamed by. Fixing it means making it safe for problems to bubble up.

## Which biases should you expect?

Using Marshall Rosenberg's work on needs and a catalogue of over 100 cognitive biases, he groups executive needs and pitfalls into four areas. Behaviour: executives need your presence and support, and can fall for choice-supportive bias, like a new CTO replaying what worked at the last company, plus conservatism and confirmation bias. Strategy: they are achievers who want a roadmap and can overestimate impact, ignore bad news (the ostrich effect) or be overconfident about moving to AWS in a year. Structure: they want consistency, stability and clarity, which can produce clustering illusions; his example is a leader who wanted to merge two unrelated departments because both had strategic projects in their name. Collaboration: they want inspiration and belonging, which is why they ask you to the office for a workshop, and they are exposed to groupthink, false consensus and the halo effect.

## How do you show up for your CTO?

The closing tips come wrapped in shipping metaphors. Be a container that carries information to your CTO. Be the go-to person for special tasks. Build trust between your crew and the skipper rather than joining a narrative about the bad CTO. Know your coordinates, keep a roadmap and alternatives. Ask for meetings and propose solutions. Be a tugboat that helps normalise the tech stack, and be honest about a technology's limits instead of choosing AWS because it is AWS. Above all, look beyond the horizon of the business. As Tomasz Manugiewicz said at Conf42 DevOps 2024, "We are not just here to code, we are just here to grow the organization."

## Who should watch

Senior engineers and tech leads who keep losing arguments with leadership and want to know why, and anyone about to pitch a DevOps change upward. Engineers looking for pipeline techniques should pick another talk.

Title: From quarterly to weekly releases, with synthetic monitoring as the safety net
Description: Daniel Paulus (Checkly) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on moving a 40-engineer startup from quarterly to weekly deploys, guided by DORA metrics
Body:
Daniel Paulus, who leads engineering at Checkly, once took a startup of roughly 40 engineers from manual, error-prone monthly-to-quarterly releases to stable weekly deploys in weeks rather than months, and a program manager measured a 70% increase in engineering velocity from Jira and GitHub data along the way. At Conf42 DevOps 2024 he turns that experience into a blueprint, ordered by difficulty, with one load-bearing idea: put synthetic monitoring in place first, so every later change has a safety net.

The story is from a previous company, not Checkly, which he describes as already a DORA elite performer. Checkly sells synthetic monitoring, and he is open that seeing its value in that transformation is part of why he joined.

## Why DORA, and why all four?

Paulus uses the four DORA metrics as his compass: lead time for changes, deployment frequency, time to restore service and change failure rate. His reason for using all four is that any single one is easy to game. Deploy frequency alone can be pumped up with dependency bumps and says nothing about how long a Jira ticket takes to reach production, or whether every deploy ships a new bug.

He also names the political reality early. DevOps work is opportunity cost, and some business-minded manager will ask why two weeks went by with no features and no bug fixes. You need numbers to answer that.

## The retro you have probably sat in

The starting point will be familiar: the system is too complex and brittle, manual QA is slowing everyone down, deploys take days and need a Slack channel to coordinate, the DevOps team is a bottleneck. And the usual action items: rewrite the service in a new language, deploy quarterly instead of monthly because deploys are expensive, add a meeting for cross-team dependencies. He guarantees none of them will get you out.

Before the steps, a word on change management, which he clearly cares about most. Understand why things are the way they are before judging, listen to concerns, and explain the purpose as often as people need to hear it. Some people will leave. You win most of the rest by being successful.

## Easy: CI, simplification and synthetic checks

Step one is CI on GitHub Actions or whatever is lying around, even an unused company Jenkins. Building the software and simply starting it in CI beats nothing. Step two is a refrain that comes back at every level. As Daniel Paulus said at Conf42 DevOps 2024, "Carelessly introduced complexity is the root of all evil." Reduce branches, delete dead code, drop unused dependencies.

Step three is the hinge of the talk: synthetic monitoring. Take end-to-end tests that log in and exercise the critical flows (create a document, buy something, open a list of users) and run them on a schedule. It can be set up in days, covers the whole application, and gives you an immediate, unambiguous signal: the login is broken, roll back.

## Medium and hard: automate, merge, shrink the diff

Medium: automate deployments so they are repeatable, make the services that must always be up zero-downtime deployable, and keep simplifying by removing redundant libraries, stale configuration and dead feature flags. Hard: merge the 15 repositories that need 15 PRs for one change, remove services nobody uses, be a little more monolithic, and strip DevOps over-engineering, for example S3 instead of a mounted block volume, or a hosted database instead of running your own.

On the process side, move to trunk-based development with small PRs and fast rollbacks. Small changes are easy to review, and when they break you know what broke. His line on the alternative: "if you have the diff created by three teams over one month deployed to production and it breaks, good luck figuring out what the hell went wrong."

## What did the first weekly deploy look like?

Painful, which is the honest part. The first weekly deploy took a full day because it exposed manual steps everyone thought were automated. After a retrospective and a round of fixes, the next one took a couple of hours, and later less than that. Weekly is not elite, he concedes, but it is far better than quarterly and shrinks the diff dramatically.

The final level, marked emotional damage, is organisational: cross-functional, stream-aligned teams that build and run their own services, no permanent standalone DevOps team, and no manual QA as a release gate. QA moves to exploratory testing, catching the broken chart or the FAQ typo that a synthetic suite of core flows should never try to cover.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and tech leads stuck in a low-maturity org who need an order of operations and an argument for leadership. Teams already deploying daily will recognise every step.

Title: Your cloud still burns carbon, it just burns it somewhere else
Description: Neel Shah (Internauts Infotech) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on green DevOps - measuring cloud carbon and cutting it with right-sizing and carbon-aware scheduling
Body:
Moving to the cloud does not make your carbon footprint disappear; it moves it into someone else's data centre. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Neel Shah, Product Manager at Internauts Infotech and an organiser of local Google Cloud, Docker, CNCF and HashiCorp communities, gives a short introduction to green DevOps: how emissions from software are counted, which tools measure them, and a checklist of changes that cut carbon and the cloud bill at the same time.

It is a first talk on the topic, compact and checklist-shaped, and a good one to hand to a team that has never looked at the emissions side of its infrastructure.

## Is hosting on the cloud carbon-free?

He opens with the misconception and answers it straight away: "I have all my data on cloud so I don't emit carbon dioxide. Is that true? No." Every site and application hosted in a data centre emits indirectly, because the data centre does. Green DevOps, as he defines it, puts environmental impact up front alongside speed and functionality, and the pitch is that it pays twice: less energy means less CO2 and lower cost.

## How is software carbon counted?

Shah walks through the Greenhouse Gas Protocol's three scopes. Scope 1 is fuel you burn directly. Scope 2 is indirect emissions from the electricity you buy. Scope 3 is everything else, from business travel to purchased materials. For DevOps teams, he explains, hosting in a private cloud lands in scope 2, while hosting on public or hybrid cloud lands in scope 3.

To compare workloads and regions he points to the Green Software Foundation's carbon intensity formula, which accounts for the energy consumed and the emissions embodied in the hardware. For measurement, the big three each have their own tooling: the AWS carbon footprint tool, Google Cloud Carbon Footprint and Microsoft's sustainability calculator for Azure, and Google's console flags low-CO2 regions when you pick one. The open source option he recommends is Cloud Carbon Footprint, which takes your cloud billing data and turns it into an emissions dashboard.

## What actually cuts emissions?

The practical list is the part to screenshot:

- Cache static data so repeat visits do not recompute or refetch it.
- Delete unused storage and keep infrastructure at the bare minimum.
- Prefer stateless designs and queue non-urgent requests instead of processing everything at once.
- Scale down when not in use, and use serverless services that scale to zero.
- Right-size instances, use spot instances where they fit, and cap autoscaling groups and containers.
- Choose regions or zones the cloud provider marks as lower carbon.

None of it needs a big programme, and he suggests rolling it in gradually.

## Carbon-aware computing in three moves

The more interesting section covers carbon awareness. Temporal shifting means scheduling non-urgent work for when the grid's carbon intensity is low. Demand shaping means degrading gracefully when it is high: serve lower-resolution images or video, or run a Jenkins-style CI farm on fewer worker nodes and queue the rest instead of running everything in parallel. Spatial shifting means routing requests to the region with the lower carbon intensity rather than simply the nearest one, which he describes Google doing on top of its load balancing.

His closing example ties it to FinOps: a service running five nodes by day, when solar power keeps carbon intensity low, can drop to two or three at night. Same scale-down, two wins.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers new to sustainable software who want the vocabulary and the tool names in one sitting. Teams already reporting scope 3 emissions will not find new methods here.

Title: One pod in one Availability Zone fails exactly how you would fear
Description: Bent Krause and Oliver Steenbuck (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on chaos at the cloud layer, with an FIS Availability Zone disruption on EKS
Body:
Does Kubernetes move your only pod to another Availability Zone when the zone goes dark? No, and Bent Krause, Associate Solutions Architect at AWS, shows it live. In their [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Bent_Krause_Oliver_Steenbuck_chaos_cloud), Bent and fellow AWS Solutions Architect Oliver Steenbuck argue that chaos engineering belongs at the cloud infrastructure layer too, explain how AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) works, and run an AZ disruption against a single-pod app on Amazon EKS, before and after a fix.

## Why move chaos from the JVM to the cloud?

Oliver opens with Werner Vogels, Amazon's CTO: failures are a given, and everything will eventually fail over time. He does not knock application-level chaos. In Java, fault injection runs inside the JVM, as an agent next to it, or in the service mesh, and it is a fine way to test your code.

The cloud layer adds things the JVM cannot see: a more holistic monitoring view, cloud-specific limits and scaling failure points, cross-account interactions, and disaster recovery validation, such as checking that a switch to another region happens inside the time you promised.

The unit of resilience is the Availability Zone. Zones in a region have independent network providers and power, and are placed with geography in mind, so a river through the city does not flood every zone at once. Spread a web tier and a primary/standby database across zones, and losing one zone means the load balancer routes around it and the standby takes over.

## How does FIS keep the blast radius in check?

FIS is AWS's managed chaos service. Start in the console, then move to the CLI and JSON or YAML templates you can version and code-review. Experiments can run in sequence (gradual degradation, such as rising latency) or in parallel (several issues at once, which is how most real outages happen). Oliver is blunt about what that means: "It's not faking something with metric manipulation, but it's actually impacting how things work at the control plane level," Oliver Steenbuck said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. Instances really terminate and APIs really throttle.

So the safeguards matter: stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms, rollback, and IAM controls over which fault types and resources an experiment may touch, including tag-based rules such as only EC2 instances tagged for the test environment. Results flow into CloudWatch or your own monitoring, and EventBridge can stop an experiment or start the next one.

Bent adds two scenarios that had just launched at re:Invent: cross-region connectivity disruption, for active-active or active-passive setups where replication (a DynamoDB table, say) suddenly stops, and AZ power interruption, where instances and containers just stop.

## The demo: ping, pong, nothing

The app is a tiny API that answers every request with pong, one pod on one node pinned to us-east-1a with a node selector, exposed through the AWS Load Balancer Controller. "I personally am not the most Kubernetes experienced guy," Bent said, so he wants to know whether Kubernetes will rescue a single pod.

Locust drives about 240 requests per second at a steady 120 ms response time. The FIS template has one action, disrupt connectivity, which blocks packets in and out of the targeted subnets for two minutes, with a filter limiting the target to subnets in us-east-1a. Start it and successful requests drop to zero. They do not even fail cleanly: connections just hang with no error code until the experiment ends.

The fix is two replicas and an affinity rule that spreads them across nodes in different zones. Same load, same experiment: this time there is only a very short gap, because the load balancer health check runs every 5 seconds and needs one more check to drop the dead target.

## Best practices to take home

Start with small templates, one action each, so you learn what each does. Test in an environment shaped like production (Docker Compose in staging tells you little about an EKS cluster in production). Shrink the blast radius with least-privilege IAM and use stop conditions as the emergency brake, especially in production.

## Who should watch

Engineers running workloads on AWS who have done chaos at the application layer and want a clear picture of what infrastructure-level faults look like. The demo is short, honest and reproducible.

Title: Your unit tests are a requirements document, so don't let AI write them
Description: Joe Skeen (World-Class Engineers) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on intuitive unit testing in PowerShell and Pester, from plain sentences to one-line asserts
Body:
Most developers agree unit tests matter and quietly hate writing them. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Joe Skeen, Owner and Mentor at World-Class Engineers, argues the hate comes from writing them backwards, and walks through a pattern he calls intuitive unit testing: write the requirements as plain sentences first, turn the sentences into nested test blocks, and push all setup into before-each hooks until every test is a single assertion.

His examples are in PowerShell and Pester because it is a DevOps conference, but the principles carry to any language and framework.

## What is a unit test actually for?

Skeen starts with the testing pyramid and a point that is easy to forget: the higher you go, the more tests you need to cover every combination of use cases. End-to-end tests have to walk through every permutation of every feature; unit tests isolate each component, mock its dependencies and cover the edge cases with far less code. So unit tests should be the base of the strategy, and end-to-end tests used to dodge them are a problem.

His own definition does the heavy lifting for the rest of the talk. As Joe Skeen said at Conf42 DevOps 2024, "unit testing is the process of aligning requirements with reality." Done his way, a test suite reads like a list of requirements you can take to a non-technical stakeholder and ask: is this what you meant?

## Why not let ChatGPT write them?

This is where the AI argument comes in, and it is sharper than the usual hand-wringing. To get good code out of ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot you have to describe the requirements precisely. "Well, if you take all of the time to do that, you have already done about 90% of unit testing." The thinking is the job; the typing is the cheap part.

He is happy to let AI turn the sentences into test scaffolding, as long as it never touches the sentences themselves. His second reason is the training data: most unit tests in the wild are duplicated, badly named, called something like test one, and that is what the models learned from. Until that changes, he would not trust them to produce a maintainable suite.

## A privacy doorknob, specified

To separate the method from any particular codebase, he specifies something everyone has used: a privacy doorknob with an outside knob, an inside knob, a push button and a latch bolt. The requirements are sentences of the form what, when, should. A privacy doorknob, when the push button is not pressed and the user turns the inside knob clockwise, should turn the outside knob counterclockwise and should retract the latch bolt.

The list grows fast: both directions, both knobs, the locked state, what happens when someone closes an open door that is locked and the latch bolt meets the frame, and what happens if someone simply applies too much force. He does not insist every exceptional case has a graceful answer. It is fine to decide the knob breaks, as long as you know that is the decision. When the list gets overwhelming, apply DRY to the sentences: hoist the shared when clauses, and accept that some outcomes repeat.

## From sentences to Pester, one assert per test

The sentences map directly onto Pester's describe, context and it blocks, nested as deep as the conditions go, with the it statements as the leaves of the requirements tree. Each test starts out as a standard arrange, act, assert: source the file, create the doorknob, press the button, turn the outside knob clockwise, check the result.

Then the refactor that gives the pattern its name. Every describe and context gets a before-each that sets up exactly what its own sentence claims, so the arrange steps move up the tree. The action becomes a script block defined where the action is named and invoked in the innermost context. Tests shrink from roughly eight to twelve lines to a single assertion each. He also names the variables in testing vocabulary, a subject under test and an action, with a useful sanity check: if your action does not call anything on the subject under test, you may be testing your own mocks.

Run Pester with detailed verbosity, which he wishes were the default, and the output prints the original sentences back, each one ticked off.

## How many tests is enough?

His closing example is a remove-vowels function. Test classes of input, not every input: empty, null and whitespace-only strings, a short string with some vowels, only vowels, no vowels, a very long string for performance, and Unicode such as emoji or other scripts. Every combination of letters is neither feasible nor useful.

## Who should watch

Developers who write tests out of obligation, and team leads looking for a test style that juniors can follow and stakeholders can read. If your team already writes BDD-style specs with one assert per test, the PowerShell scoping tips are the new part.

Title: Inside MightyMeld, a visual React editor that writes to your code
Description: Opemipo Disu (Fermyon Technologies) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on how MightyMeld's studio, scribe and envoy turn drag and drop into React code
Body:
Not every talk at a chaos engineering conference is about breaking things. Opemipo Disu, Developer Advocate at Fermyon Technologies, used his [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Opemipo_Disu_mightymeld_architecture_frontend) to explain how MightyMeld, a visual development tool for React applications, is put together: a studio you drag components around in, a scribe that writes the changes into your local code, and an envoy that connects the two through a plugin in your build.

It is a short architecture 101 rather than an in-depth tour or a live build. The value is in the mental model of the three parts, so you know which one is misbehaving when a visual edit does not show up in your code.

## What is MightyMeld for?

Opemipo describes it as a way to build React applications by dragging, dropping and editing components. "In this context you don't have to write code, it's what you build is what you get," Opemipo Disu said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. He pitches it at React developers and at people with little React experience, with one caveat: you still need to understand the framework you are working in, or you will make mistakes faster.

The prerequisites he gives are basic JavaScript, some React, and a CSS library you like. Chakra UI, Tailwind and Bulma all get a mention, and the point is that MightyMeld does not tie you to one.

He is also keen to correct one misreading: MightyMeld is not mainly a code generation tool. "If you want to use it as a code generation too, you can, but that's not the aim," he said. The aim is visual editing of a real code base.

## The three parts

**The studio** is the visual development environment and the only part you touch. It shows your running app in a browser view with its layout, lets you drag, drop and edit, and sends each change to the scribe. Edits go through requests to an LLM that updates the code.

**The scribe** is, in his words, the heart of the architecture. It is in charge of code generation and updates: when you edit a component in the studio, the scribe makes the change in your local code base. It also handles communication with the envoy and passes results back to the studio. Opemipo ranks it as the most important of the three.

**The envoy** is lightweight on purpose, because it carries a lot of responsibility. It provides the MightyMeld plugin and the browser API the studio relies on, and without it the application does not launch at all. The scribe talks to the envoy over HTTPS and sockets.

## The plugin does the plumbing

The MightyMeld plugin hangs off the envoy and goes into your existing tooling. The talk lists SWC, Remix, React and Next.js as places it fits. If the studio shows nothing, the plugin and envoy are where to look first: no plugin, no browser view, no running app.

## Who should watch

React developers who have seen visual builders before and want to know how this one keeps the code base the source of truth, or anyone sizing up MightyMeld for a team that mixes developers and designers. Chaos engineers can safely skip this one, or treat it as a palate cleanser between fault injection talks. It is a short session of concepts, with no failure modes in sight.

Title: Run your end-to-end tests before the merge, not after staging
Description: Natalie Lunbeck (Shipyard) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on running Cypress end-to-end tests against an ephemeral environment on every pull request
Body:
Most teams run their end-to-end tests after merging, against a staging environment that already holds five other people's branches. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Natalie Lunbeck, Software Engineer at Shipyard, makes the case for moving those tests in front of the merge: give every pull request its own full-stack ephemeral environment and point the end-to-end suite at it, so the bug lands on the desk of the developer who wrote it, the same day.

It is a short, practical talk: one diagram of the usual workflow, one of the better one, then a live demo with Cypress, GitHub Actions and Shipyard. Shipyard is her employer's product, and the demo uses it; the pattern itself is tool-agnostic.

## Why do end-to-end tests end up on staging?

Her framing of the three test types is the familiar one. Unit tests take an input and assert on the output, cheap enough to run on every commit. Integration tests check a function against its neighbours. End-to-end tests exercise whole application workflows, which means they need a production-like copy of the latest code, and most companies do not have the infrastructure to spin one up per branch. So the end-to-end suite waits for staging.

The result is the loop everyone has lived in. You open a PR, a peer reviews it, it merges, it deploys to staging, and some time later the end-to-end run happens, possibly against several merged branches at once, because a team might only be testing twice a week. QA sifts through the failures, sends you back to the drawing board, and you open a new PR and start the loop again. Lunbeck points out the second-order cost: QA cannot estimate a release date when nobody knows what staging will uncover, and there are often several days between a merged pull request and a test run.

## What changes when every PR gets an environment?

The proposal: attach a full-stack ephemeral environment to every pull request, built from that branch, infrastructure-identical to production including the database, with less data but realistic. Run unit, integration and end-to-end tests against it, and do code review with the running app open next to the diff. Because the environments are GitOps-driven, they shut themselves down on merge.

The ordering detail is the part worth stealing. Tests run first, review second. As she put it, "it's important to loop in your peer after the tests have run, because it really shouldn't be their job to uncover any bugs in your code. They're just really checking for best practices." Staging still runs the suite once more, but by then the only failures left should be features colliding with other features.

## The demo: a Venmo clone with a deliberately broken button

The application is the Cypress team's Venmo clone, a front end and back end defined in a Docker Compose file, with the back end attached to a database. Her Cypress tests are deliberately simple: create a user, sign in, open user settings, fill in an email and phone number, and check that the save button is of type submit.

She first runs the suite from her terminal against the environment URL, then moves it into a GitHub Actions workflow in a fork of the Cypress repo. The Shipyard GitHub Action takes an API token and a bypass token from the repository secrets, authenticates into the ephemeral environment and runs the same Cypress command against it, on every commit and pull request.

Then the fun bit. She opens a PR that changes the submit button to a reset button, pretending it is a cool new feature. The PR gets its own environment, separate from the base one, the end-to-end run fails on exactly that assertion, and staging never sees the breakage. Before pushing the fix she loads a database snapshot from the base environment into the PR environment, so the next run starts from an identical database rather than one littered with the test user from the previous run. Small step, and the one that keeps end-to-end suites from becoming flaky.

## Who should watch

Teams whose QA stage is a weekly queue of surprises, and anyone arguing internally for preview environments who needs a concrete before-and-after workflow to show. If you already run a per-PR environment and gate merges on it, this is a quick confirmation rather than new ground.

Title: Break AWS on your laptop before AWS breaks it for you
Description: Harsh Mishra (LocalStack) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on shifting cloud chaos testing left with LocalStack and fault injection running locally
Body:
Chaos testing cloud components usually means doing it in staging or production, because the managed services are proprietary and there is nowhere else to run them. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Harsh Mishra, Software Engineer at LocalStack, shows the alternative: run an AWS emulator in a Docker container on your laptop, point the AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) at it, and watch a whole region go dark without paying for a single real resource.

This is a vendor engineer demoing his company's open source emulator, and he says so up front. The method, though, applies to whatever emulation layer you use.

## Why not just chaos test in the cloud?

Mishra's argument is about the gaps unit and integration tests leave: missing error handlers, missing health checks, missing fallbacks, the failures that come from your provider rather than your code. Testing those on real cloud has two costs. Deploying the full set of databases, message queues, Kafka and Kubernetes clusters costs real money, and some of these experiments take hours, days or weeks to run reliably, which kills the agility DevOps is meant to buy.

He name-checks the established tools (Chaos Monkey, LitmusChaos with its Chaos Center, Chaos Mesh, ChaosBlade, Chaos Toolkit) and points viewers to Pablo Chacin's earlier Conf42 Chaos Engineering keynote on shifting chaos testing left with Grafana k6.

## Mocks, service emulators, cloud emulators

The most useful part of the talk is the testability pyramid for cloud code. At the top, mock libraries such as Moto, which redirects AWS API calls from your tests to fake resources via decorators. Below them, single-service emulators such as DynamoDB Local. Then full cloud emulation, where many services run locally and talk to each other. At the bottom, real staging.

His DynamoDB example draws the line neatly. A mock returns a parsable API response with random attributes and no state; an emulator actually stores and retrieves what you wrote. Single-service emulators still fall short: you cannot hook DynamoDB Local up to AppSync or Lambda, and they lag behind the real APIs. Mocks are fine for scoping a unit test, but a chaos suite built on them diverges from production behaviour, which defeats the point.

## An RDS failover in under two minutes

The first demo is a Python script using boto3 that creates a global RDS cluster with primary and secondary clusters across regions, triggers a global cluster failover and asserts that the standby was promoted. LocalStack installs via pip, starts with one command, and listens on localhost port 4566; the SDK just gets a different endpoint URL. On real AWS, Mishra says, setting this up takes more than an hour. Locally the assertions pass in a minute or two, and stopping the container removes everything, ephemeral by design.

## Taking Lambda and a region offline

The second demo is a serverless image resizer: Lambda functions, an S3-hosted website, SSM parameters and SNS topics, deployed locally with one script. Upload a photo, get a resized copy. Then he opens a chaos dashboard with predefined FIS experiment templates and makes Lambda unavailable. The next upload produces no resized image, and the container logs show the Lambda invocation failing per the FIS configuration. Next experiment: take all of us-east-1 down to simulate a regional outage, and the S3-served site itself starts throwing exceptions. Stop the experiment, refresh, and the app is back.

He notes FIS locally can also add latency to every API call and inject faults into DynamoDB or Kinesis, which is where most real-world surprises live.

## How should you structure the suite?

The closing advice is classic chaos engineering method, applied to a laptop. Establish a steady state first, measured by throughput, error rate or latency. Write a hypothesis that matches real-world events. Sort experiments into knowns and unknowns, start with the knowns because they are the low-hanging fruit, then go looking for the unknowns. Then put the experiments in CI so every infrastructure change is checked against them. In his words, cloud emulators "can always help you around with some of the low impact risks, like a missing failover, a missing handler, or things that might just fall under your radar during your usual unit testing or integration testing setup."

## Who should watch

Developers building on AWS who have never chaos tested because staging is too expensive or too shared to break on purpose. Seasoned chaos engineers will find the method familiar; the value is in seeing FIS experiments run against emulated services in seconds.

Title: One EC2 instance, one FIS experiment, one obvious lesson
Description: Kiranpreet Chawla (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on tying chaos engineering to AWS Well-Architected with a first Fault Injection Simulator experiment
Body:
The quickest way to learn that a single instance is a single point of failure is to stop it on purpose. Kiranpreet Chawla, Solutions Architect at AWS, did exactly that in her [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Kiranpreet_Chawla_resilient_apps): she ties chaos engineering to the AWS Well-Architected Framework, then walks through a first AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) experiment in the console, fixes what it exposes, and runs it again.

It is a beginner's talk, and a tidy one. If you have never clicked through FIS, this is the short version.

## Where does chaos engineering sit in Well-Architected?

Well-Architected has six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. Kiranpreet focuses on three of them, operational excellence, reliability and performance efficiency. The link to chaos is explicit: the reliability pillar recommends running tests that inject failures regularly into pre-production and production. That practice is chaos engineering, which she defines as stressing an application with disruptive events, watching how it responds and making improvements.

The point is control, not vandalism. "It is about breaking things in a controlled environment through well planned experiments," Kiranpreet Chawla said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. Run it during working hours, not as a surprise at the weekend.

## The phases, and the questions after the experiment

She covers the loop: steady state, hypothesis, run experiment, verify, improve. Start in staging, earn trust, then move toward production. The verify step comes with a good list of questions to take into any review: what happened, what was the customer impact, did the notification carry enough to investigate, what could have reduced our time to detect or time to remediate by 50%, can this apply to similar systems, and how could incident response improve.

## FIS in four nouns

FIS is AWS's managed chaos service, built around safeguards that watch the blast radius and stop an experiment when alarms fire. Four components: an **action** (the fault), a **target** (a resource, or resources matched by criteria such as tags), an **experiment template** (actions, targets and stop conditions) and the **experiment** you start from a template. One template can run across several environments.

## The demo: an internal app goes public

The scenario: management decides an internal messaging app, never built to best practice, should go public. It runs on one EC2 instance and one RDS instance in a single Availability Zone, behind an Application Load Balancer, inside an Auto Scaling group. The load balancer is there even for one instance, for health checks and to make adding instances easy later.

Hypothesis one: if the only instance is stopped and started, the app stops accepting requests but recovers quickly. In the console she creates a template with the EC2 stop-instances action, targets the instance, and starts it. The site goes down, the instance comes back, the site comes back. She notes you would not normally run an experiment you know will cause an outage; this one is non-production and deliberate.

Two findings come out. There was no alarm telling anyone the app had stopped answering, so she adds a CloudWatch Synthetics canary. And one instance is a liability, so the Auto Scaling group now runs several. Hypothesis two: if one instance in the group is stopped and started, the app keeps serving clients, because the load balancer sends traffic to the healthy ones. Next steps she suggests: spread across Availability Zones, make RDS highly available, add CI/CD.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to chaos engineering on AWS, or anyone who needs a short internal explainer of how FIS templates, actions and targets fit together. If you already run FIS in pipelines, the other AWS talks at this event go deeper.

Title: Your unit tests check the rows, not the query plan
Description: Adam Furmanek (Metis) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on database guardrails - query plans via OpenTelemetry from laptop to production, so slow SQL never ships
Body:
A query that fetched one user read nearly 300,000 rows and ran for 25 seconds, and every test in the suite was green. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Adam Furmanek, DevRel at Metis, argues that automated tests can't catch database performance problems because they only check what comes back, and makes the case for database guardrails: capture execution plans from the developer's laptop, CI and production, and tell developers about the slow query before it ships.

The last part of the talk demos Metis, his employer's product. The first two thirds, on what breaks in SQL databases and why tests miss it, stand on their own for any Postgres or MySQL shop.

## Why does this need a new approach?

His framing is organisational. Microservices moved complexity from deployment into operations: everything talks to everything, logs are scattered, and the order of events is unclear. Conway's law says teams mirror architecture, cross-team communication is the slow part, and so a good DevOps culture minimises the reasons to communicate. For databases that means developers can't keep waiting on DBAs. They need to own their databases and self-serve the troubleshooting, which requires tools that tell a story instead of dashboards that present lots of data but lack any information.

## What breaks in SQL databases?

Three areas, he says: code changes, schema changes, and the one teams miss, the same query being executed differently over time because statistics, indexes or configuration changed.

- **Joins that explode.** The 25-second query joined many tables for one user, multiplying rows the ORM then discarded to build a single entity. Splitting it into eight small queries and joining in application code brought it down to milliseconds.
- **Readable rewrites that cost you.** On a boarding passes table of about 8 million rows, the same logic ran in 8 seconds with plain joins and 13 seconds as a CTE. Same results, so every test stays green.
- **Schema migrations** that rewrite a table and take it offline in production, are hard to stop midway, and are never exercised by unit tests, which run against the database before or after the migration, never during.
- **Indexes** that speed reads and slow every insert, update and delete, or that a query quietly stops using six months later.
- **ORMs**, with N+1 queries in lazy mode, the giant join in eager mode, and hidden choices about transactions, caching, pooling and migrations. Some ORMs have even dropped a production table when they couldn't reconcile the schema.

The root problem, in his words at Conf42 DevOps 2024: "We do assertions on the content that we extracted from the database, but we do not assert the way the data was extracted." Locally you have a few hundred rows, so nothing looks slow.

## Aren't load tests for this?

They help, but too late and at a cost. A meaningful load test takes hours, needs its own fleet, and needs production-like data you have to anonymise under GDPR. It runs at the end of the pipeline, so a failure sends you back to the whiteboard, code review and pre-prod. Then there is configuration: trigram or JSONB indexes, pgvector or a separate vector database, vacuuming, fragmentation, noisy tenants, old database editions.

## Database guardrails, stage by stage

His solution starts from the planner. Prefix a query with EXPLAIN and the engine returns its plan: each row an operation (scan, join, sort, filter) with a cost, an arbitrary measure of how hard it is. That tells you whether an index is used.

Then wire it into the lifecycle with OpenTelemetry, which you can enable without changing code by dropping in the libraries and setting environment variables:

1. **Locally**, the app sends traces to a collector, which asks the database for the plan of each query it ran and forwards it to a central platform that flags inefficient queries.
2. **In CI**, the same capture runs during tests, plus analysis of schema migrations, with a warning on the pull request.
3. **In production**, a tool pulls metrics, configuration, extensions, schemas, data shape and plans, so the platform can say the query was fine on your laptop but will not fly against the production row count.

He separates monitoring (alerts, raw data, thresholds set by hand) from observability (what happened and why). His example of the story you want: you deployed a change on Wednesday, the query stopped using an index, and Saturday's peak traffic made the database slow.

The Metis demo shows that loop: an API call mapped to its SQL, table scans flagged with a fix, and a pull request warning not to drop an index that production used over 6,000 times in the last seven days.

## Who should watch

Backend developers who own their schema and ORM code, and platform engineers deciding how much database knowledge to push into product teams. If you already gate PRs on EXPLAIN output, the first half is a good list of failure modes to check against.
