Title: Secure code is not enough when 114 dependencies ride along
Description: Melissa McKay (JFrog) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on why supply chain security goes past your own code - dependencies, base images, pinned versions, least privilege
Body:
Melissa McKay took the secure coding courses, learned SQL injection and CSRF, and thought she was set. Then she ran a Maven dependency tree on one microservice and found 114 direct and indirect dependencies, seven layers deep, in an application of seven microservices. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, the Developer Advocate at JFrog (also a Java Champion and Docker Captain) walks the software supply chain from the developer's laptop to production and shows how many attacks never touch the code you wrote.

The talk grew out of a JFrog and NGINX discussion series she ran with Damien Curry of F5, following an application's journey episode by episode. This is the security episode, told from a developer's point of view.

## Why should a developer care beyond their own code?

The stakes first. Equifax, March to July 2017, was an Apache Struts vulnerability that was known but not patched in time: $1.4 billion in cleanup costs, $1.38 billion in consumer claims, 143 million customers. Log4Shell had every Java developer cringing; she cites Stephen Magill of Sonatype estimating about 70,000 open source projects using log4j directly and about 174,000 transitively. The MOVEit Transfer hacks of 2023 hit Zellis, British Airways, the BBC, PokerStars (110,000 users) and IBM-managed systems holding data on 4.1 million Colorado patients. IBM put the global average cost of a breach in 2023 at $4.45 million, up 15% over three years.

Writing secure code is still your job. She recommends OWASP's sarcastic essay on how to write insecure code (default deny means denying your code can ever be broken; mix as many languages as possible so nobody can learn all the security rules). But SolarWinds is the counterexample: 18,000 customers received a digitally signed update with a backdoor, which suggests the binary was swapped after compilation, likely in the build or distribution pipeline. No amount of careful coding prevents that.

## Where can an attacker get in?

Everywhere an artifact or dependency moves, which is why she points to SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) as a way to measure progress. Two developer-controllable examples get the most time.

**Dependency confusion.** Alex Birsan showed that internal package names leak (npm requests reveal them) and version requirements accept the specified version or anything greater. Publish a public package with the same name and a higher version, and a misconfigured package manager pulls it instead of the internal one. His bug bounties for this came to $130,000. The fix is to configure your artifact manager so internal package requests resolve only from internal repositories, because that is not the default.

**Left-pad.** After a naming dispute with the messaging company kik, npm sided with the company, and the developer unpublished his kik package along with 272 others, including left-pad. A short padding function, depended on transitively by half the JavaScript world, vanished. Cameron Westland republished an identical version as 1.0.0, but projects pinned to 0.0.3 stayed broken. No malicious code involved: just the trap of relying solely on public repositories.

## The Dockerfile that has every problem

Her contrived Dockerfile is a checklist in nine lines. An untrusted parent image pulled from Docker Hub by default, with no tag or SHA. Even a tag is not enough, she argues, because it is "more of a pointer than anything" and can be overwritten. Packages installed with no version, or with an old, possibly vulnerable one, which bites hardest when a new developer builds from a fresh cache. A `curl | bash` of an external script, which in her own team broke builds twice when the vendor first changed it to an incompatible version and then moved it. And running as root: Sysdig's 2022 report found 76% of 3 million containers ran as root, and its 2023 report found 83% of 7 million. We are getting worse.

## Is there any hope?

Her list of fixes:

- **Educate yourselves** and mix seniors with juniors so mentorship happens. OWASP cheat sheets and the OpenSSF trio of free secure software development courses on edX are her picks.
- **Don't rely solely on public repos.** Save every artifact your builds need in a local artifact management system. She works for JFrog and mentions Artifactory, but says open source options exist and the point is to have one.
- **Pin explicit versions**, with SHAs for Docker images and where appropriate for npm.
- **Manage permissions.** Sysdig found 90% of granted permissions are not used.
- **Scan regularly, keep systems maintained, and have a plan** for the production security incident, because it will happen.

Melissa McKay said at Conf42 DevOps 2024: "Make sure that you're keeping track of your dependencies so that you don't have broken builds for unknown reasons."

## Who should watch

Developers who think security is the security team's job, and anyone writing Dockerfiles from copied examples. Security engineers will know the incidents; the Dockerfile walk-through is still a good thing to show a team.

Title: Of 932 vulnerable dependencies, only 12 were reachable
Description: Kyle Kelly (Semgrep) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on triaging open source vulnerabilities with reachability, semver easy wins, and ignoring most transitive CVEs
Body:
Your dependency scanner says 2,500 vulnerabilities. Kyle Kelly, Security Researcher at Semgrep and founder of the CramHacks supply chain security newsletter, argues at Conf42 DevOps 2024 that almost all of them are noise: code-scanning reachability cuts hundreds of version-matched alerts down to the tens your code can actually hit, and semantic versioning turns much of what is left into an upgrade button.

He works on Semgrep's supply chain product and says so, so the reachability section is partly a product explanation. The research numbers and the remediation advice stand on their own.

## How big is the open source pile?

Over 90% of organisations use open source, GitHub recorded 52 million new open source projects in 2022, and 70-90% of an application's stack is said to be open source. He adds a caveat to that last figure: counting code that actually executes, the share is far smaller, since for any imported dependency you are likely using about 10% of its functionality.

Vulnerabilities: just over 28,000 CVEs in 2023, though many are for commercial products, and the GitHub Security Advisory database is the more useful source for open source. Coverage is uneven by ecosystem: his slide counts 4,445 advisories for Maven and 3,277 for npm, against 33 for Swift, 24 for Erlang/Elixir and 8 for Dart and Flutter. If you live in the small ones, an SCA tool has little to tell you. In his experience, anything below high severity can usually wait while highs and criticals exist. EPSS and CISA's KEV catalogue help less than you would hope, because both lean towards commercial products.

## What does reachability actually mean?

The word means different things in different tools. CycloneDX's cdxgen calls a dependency reachable if your code uses it at all; others call a vulnerability reachable if it hits a direct dependency or a public-facing app. Semgrep's version scans your code for the specific vulnerable usage described in the advisory, using Semgrep rules researchers write per vulnerability.

The funnel on his slide: thousands of new vulnerabilities, hundreds that match your dependency versions, tens that result in actual vulnerable usage. The evidence:

- An NC State study comparing SCA tools found only 2.1% of roughly 2,500 alerts were reachable through static analysis.
- Semgrep's internal study of 1,100 open source projects found 932 vulnerable packages by version, and only 12 were reachable.

Results vary by language: JavaScript and Python benefit most because of their modularity, C# less so. Why static over dynamic analysis? Build reproducibility is often a nightmare, static analysis does not need your code to run, and it scales to thousands of projects without per-project tuning.

He has a favourite category of wasted effort too: "it's a regular expression denial of service vulnerability, and it's on an internal application." His verdict on that kind of finding, as he said at Conf42 DevOps 2024: "Don't spend valuable security engineering time fixing these ridiculous vulnerabilities."

## Fixes exist, people just don't take them

Sonatype's 2023 report found 96% of known vulnerable downloads had a fixed version available. Log4j is the sharpest example: over 300 million vulnerable downloads since December 2021, and roughly 25% of downloads in the last seven days he checked were still vulnerable versions.

So the easy wins:

- **Use semver.** Of 200 vulnerabilities, maybe 100 are patch upgrades (hit the button) and 50 minor (look a little closer). Read the changelog for majors. Semver is not enforced: a Maven Central study found roughly 20% of non-major releases were breaking, so 80% were safe.
- **Keep the manifest honest.** Exact versions, `~` for patches, `^` for minor and patch, `*` for anything. Give broad ranges to well-maintained packages you use lightly, and tight ones to load-bearing ones. A large-scale npm study found over 87% of dependencies were set to receive updates automatically, but they only arrive if you regenerate the lock file.

## The spicy take: ignore transitive vulnerabilities

GitHub's 2020 Octoverse report put the average JavaScript project with ten direct dependencies at 683 transitive ones, and more than 90% of vulnerable dependencies are transitive. His position: usually ignore them. You cannot realistically patch five levels down, static reachability does not follow the one function you imported, and respectable packages issue their own advisory when a transitive vulnerability affects them, which turns it into a direct one. If one direct dependency drags in a mass of transitive vulnerabilities, that tells you something about its maintenance.

His three takeaways: reachability can reduce false positives by up to 98%, build reproducibility and semver solve many headaches, and transitive vulnerabilities can usually be ignored.

## Who should watch

AppSec engineers drowning in Dependabot alerts and developers asked to fix them, especially in JavaScript and Python. Those running strict compliance regimes may find the transitive take too spicy, which is a good reason to watch and argue.

Title: Hand an LLM the architecture diagram and it drafts your chaos plan
Description: Indika Wimalasuriya (Virtusa) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on generative AI for each stage of chaos engineering, from dependencies to blast radius
Body:
Testers test what they know, and outages come from what nobody knew. Indika Wimalasuriya, Senior Systems Engineering Manager at Virtusa, used his [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Indika_Wimalasuriya_smart_chaos_generative_AI) to show generative AI filling in the stages of chaos engineering that people still do by hand: give a model the architecture diagram and it lists dependencies, steady state, hypotheses, test cases and blast radius. He calls the end-to-end version Smart Chaos.

It is a walkthrough of prompts and their outputs on one example system, built in AWS PartyRock, plus a proposed pipeline. Not a production story.

## Why are distributed systems still falling over?

Indika's framing: layered architectures mean a bug in one layer ripples into the others, and bugs can show up a week after the deploy that caused them. He points to the 2021 Facebook outage (around five hours, Instagram and WhatsApp down with it), the Fastly outage that took Amazon, eBay, Reddit, Twitch and UK government sites with it, and a large Datadog outage. These companies have the money, tools and people, and still fail.

His explanation is that QA teams build test cases from requirements, so they test the knowns. Chaos engineering exists to probe the unknowns, but done properly: "there's nothing like doing a chaos engineering a chaos way, and that will not give you any value," Indika Wimalasuriya said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. He recommends starting outside production, and measuring everything (observability, SLOs, the four golden signals) while you do it.

## Ten stages, mostly manual today

He lists ten steps of a chaos workflow and marks where people do the work today: discovery, dependency identification, steady state definition, hypothesis, experiment design, blast radius, the Rumsfeld matrix of knowns and unknowns, monitoring and analysis, documentation and reporting, and iteration. Each needs a subject matter expert, and he argues each is something a model can draft.

## The EV charging demo

The example is an electric vehicle charging system on AWS, taken from an Amazon case study: Route 53, a Network Load Balancer, Fargate, IoT components, Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, DynamoDB and S3. With PartyRock apps he feeds the diagram to a model and asks, stage by stage:

- **Dependencies.** The model names the charging station, the OCPP protocol handler, the charging station management system, payment provider, notifications, telemetry ingestion, billing and authentication. His pro tip: try different models, as one gave a clearly better list than another.
- **Steady state.** For example, the API gateway is available and returns a 200 for OCPP requests, and the payment gateway processes charging-session payments.
- **Hypotheses.** If the OCPP handler goes down, stations cannot start or stop sessions. If billing goes down, new sessions cannot be authorised or paid for. The slides name Claude as the model here.
- **Experiments and blast radius.** Test cases such as powering off the OCPP handler or stopping the database, then the services and users each one would hit.
- **Known knowns and known unknowns** from the Rumsfeld matrix, as separate prompts.

Diagrams go stale, so he suggests adding a live service map, such as the one CloudWatch with X-Ray generates, so the model can compare the design with what actually runs.

## Smart Chaos as a pipeline step

The end state plugs into CI/CD. After a deploy, the workflow pulls service maps, logs, metrics and traces, defines steady state and dependencies, writes hypotheses, assembles experiments from a library of small templates (API failure, instance termination, resource exhaustion), runs them with a small blast radius, watches SLOs and error budgets, and widens the radius on later runs.

His best practices are sensible: clean, relevant data in; a big library of small experiment templates; gradual expansion, no big bang; feedback loops. The pitfalls: data bias (a model that only ever targets critical workflows), uncontrolled expansion, and dropping the humans. "Don't eliminate your human completely, still roping him in," he said.

## Who should watch

Chaos and SRE leads wondering which parts of experiment planning an LLM can draft today. Expect prompts and generated lists rather than a running system; the autonomous pipeline is a design.

- Soumen Chatterjee and Nathalie Rauschmayr on [chaos engineering in the age of AI and ML](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Soumen_Chatterjee_Nathalie_Rauschmayr_at_the_age_of_ai_and_ml) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022.

Title: Your fish tank thermometer needs prevention, not a detection alert
Description: Antoinette Hodes (Check Point Software Technologies) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on why IoT devices need preventive, zero tolerance security built into the device
Body:
By the time a detective control spots the compromised doorbell, it is already a jump host into your network. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Antoinette Hodes, Security Evangelist at Check Point Software Technologies, argues that IoT and OT devices need a zero tolerance security architecture: preventive controls hardened into the device itself, so it keeps working as intended against today's attacks and tomorrow's zero-days.

It is a vendor evangelist's talk and a strategic one: a tour of the 2023 threat timeline, the regulations arriving, and the business case, rather than an implementation guide.

## Why prevention over detection?

"IoT devices require prevention, preventative security controls rather than detective security controls," Antoinette Hodes said at Conf42 DevOps 2024. Her reasons are the things compromised IoT devices actually do: act as a stepping stone into the network (HVAC administrators connecting straight in from the internet), get ransomed (OT devices included, in the context of Russia and Ukraine), spread laterally through propagation attacks where an infected device hunts for others, steal data, and kick off the cyber kill chain.

The example that sticks is the casino whose smart fish tank thermometer was used as a jump host to extract sensitive data. Nobody threat-modelled the fish.

She frames zero tolerance as three verbs: protecting with preventive controls, ensuring the device is safe (no misuse, no accident, mitigated physical risk) and preserving its intended behaviour. A Ring doorbell and an infusion pump need different postures, but both hold sensitive information.

She also opens with history: the first cyber attack, in 1834, when François and Joseph Blanc manipulated data on France's telegraph system, the equivalent of an internet stock fraud.

## What did 2023 look like?

Her IoT and OT threat timeline for the year:

- **January**: Ghostsec claims the first ransomware encryption of a remote terminal unit (RTU), the kind used by energy companies.
- **March**: Sandworm's CaddyWiper disrupts the Ukrainian power grid, erasing data and causing a massive blackout.
- **June**: the RSOCKS proxy botnet, 350,000 compromised assets from doorbells and garage doors to industrial IoT and phones, built on known vulnerabilities and weak credentials and sold as high-quality proxies.
- **October**: a Wyze Cam vulnerability allowing a reverse shell and takeover.
- **November**: Cybernews researchers hijack 27,044 printers and make them print a five-step guide to securing a printer, the most polite breach of the year. Also November: an attack on Danish critical infrastructure through vulnerable Zyxel devices, with remote code execution and buffer overflows.

The Colonial Pipeline attack is on the list too, and she is careful about it: it was not an IoT attack but an unpatched VPN that shut down operations. Her warning on credentials is practical: default-password lists for IoT, IIoT and OT devices are public, and combined with Shodan or Google dorks, attackers automate the rest.

## Why is IoT so hard to secure?

Complex interconnection, a massive attack surface, devices spanning smart homes to industrial plants, tiny hardware budgets and no standardisation at all. Then there is the data: at rest on the device (the doorbell recording, ideally encrypted), in transit (the video on its way to the cloud) and in use, which she calls the most vulnerable, open to memory manipulation and remote code execution.

Manufacturers are squeezed from both sides. The factory has source repos, build and release management and device security (secure debug lock, root of trust, secure key storage, secure identity). The market has competition, cost against functionality, scaling and supply chain disruptions.

## Regulation is coming, and it says the same three things

Her slide lists the EU Cyber Security Act, Cyber Resilience Act, Radio Equipment Directive, DORA, NIS2, ETSI EN 303 645, the UK PSTI regime and the US Cyber Trust Mark. Their common key elements: secure access and access control, authentication and authorisation (including brute-force protection), and data protection. Security embedded on the device covers all three.

The numbers behind the urgency, from 2022: 26,448 vulnerabilities in total, 4,135 of them critical, which works out to 72 a day with 11 critical ones every day. Twenty-five years ago, she recalls, a 7 or 8 severity put her team in panic mode.

She closes with the Robert Mueller line: "There are only two companies, those that have been hacked and those that will be hacked". Check Point, she adds, has a third category: those that have been hacked and still don't know.

## Who should watch

Security architects and DevOps teams shipping connected devices or running fleets of them, and anyone who needs the regulatory map for IoT in one place. Engineers wanting firmware hardening recipes will find the why here and need to look elsewhere for the how.

Title: With eBPF in the kernel, your chaos experiment has nowhere to hide
Description: Francesco Sbaraglia and Michele Dodic (Accenture) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on eBPF and GenAI to observe, design and seed chaos experiments
Body:
A chaos experiment you cannot observe is just an outage you scheduled. Francesco Sbaraglia, SRE Tech Lead at Accenture, and his colleague Michele Dodic used their [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Francesco_Sbaraglia_Michele_Dodic_accelerating_resilience_ebpf) to argue that eBPF fixes the observing part: it watches every system call on a Kubernetes node, which lets you see the experiment, stop it, and even replay a real incident as a new one. A GenAI copilot then turns that data into the next hypothesis.

They are upfront about the angle: the focus is security observability, not security itself.

## What does eBPF actually add to chaos engineering?

Michele walks through the basics. eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) runs sandboxed programs in a privileged context, which makes the kernel programmable. It started in networking and is used by Meta, Google and Netflix among others. It extends the kernel without changing the kernel source or rebooting. A process makes a system call such as execve, the call fires the eBPF program you attached, and you see it. A short Python snippet with the BCC library shows the hello-world version: attach a function to execve and every new program on the machine triggers it.

That is the hook for chaos work. With eBPF on every node, "the kernel becomes a sort of big brother because from this point onwards it is able to see basically everything," Michele Dodic said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. One deployment or a sprawling microservice estate, the eBPF view scales with it, and it needs no application or configuration changes.

## Four problems, one kernel hook

The talk is built around four challenges the pair keep meeting, each with an answer:

- **Connectivity troubleshooting across distributed Kubernetes clusters.** eBPF shows what is really happening inside containers, including the ones doing things they should not.
- **Visibility and control during experiments.** eBPF events and metrics feed the Big Red Stop Button, the abort switch borrowed from factory machinery, and become input for AI prediction.
- **Security chaos experiments.** Using Cilium's eBPF network policies, they isolate pods and run network, service mesh, multi-cluster and resource exhaustion experiments without killing pods or deploying new tools. The slides list the top three Kubernetes attack routes as misconfigured containers, unintentional cluster misconfiguration and malicious container images; the talk focuses on the second.
- **The very first experiment.** A Chaos Engineering Copilot built on generative AI, fed with postmortems, incident data, architecture documents, eBPF behaviour data and live observability data.

## The copilot is a prompt, and that is fine

Francesco shows the copilot as a small script against the OpenAI service, run from the CI/CD pipeline on every deployment. A system role makes the model a chaos experiment expert, a second step adds context (past incidents, postmortem reports, live data), and the last asks for a step-by-step hypothesis and experiment for one service. Each finished experiment feeds the next run. The advice is the right kind of cautious: "We always need to validate before we run."

## The demo: Tetragon watching a boutique shop

The live part runs the Online Boutique microservices demo, with Hubble UI showing traffic between services and the checkout service as the target. Tetragon listens for eBPF events. Francesco applies tracing policies one by one (loaded libraries, capability use, every process, then all TCP connections) and plays the bad guy inside a container, listing users and probing for privilege escalation. Every step lands as an event. A CPU stress experiment shows up too, as a process event, so you can confirm the experiment does what you meant it to do.

The TCP policy is the clever bit. It logs Locust, the load generator, opening connections to the front end, plus some calls that are not normal ones. Capture that from a real production incident, hand it to AI, and you can rebuild the incident as a controlled experiment. Running experiments directly in kernel space is next, and he admits it is a bit dangerous, so it stayed out of this demo.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers and SREs running chaos on Kubernetes who want better proof of what an experiment did, and anyone curious where eBPF tools such as Cilium, Hubble and Tetragon fit in a resilience practice. Michele's closing advice: "Start simple and scale fast."

Title: A passing test can be the most dangerous result in your pipeline
Description: Mesut Durukal (Indeed) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on QA in DevOps - fast, reliable, maintainable tests, plus test design that catches the bugs coverage misses
Body:
Everyone complains about the red test that shouldn't be red. Mesut Durukal, QA Lead at Indeed, spends part of his Conf42 DevOps 2024 talk on the opposite case: the green test sitting on top of a real bug. His frame for QA in DevOps is two axes, speed and quality, and he shows how test execution time, flakiness and maintainability decide the first, while test design and learning from escaped bugs decide the second.

It is a broad, practitioner-level tour of what a QA lead measures and fixes, aimed at teams moving from seasonal releases to continuous delivery.

## Why does QA belong inside DevOps rather than after it?

His picture of QA is a bridge between the customer, product owners and developers: find out what users actually expect, find out what the developers actually built, and get both on the same page. Continuous delivery raises the stakes. Every release candidate needs checking for performance, usability and maintainability, not only functional correctness, and that only scales with automation and early QA involvement. Leave QA out of the process and those quality dimensions go unchecked until production.

He ties QA metrics to the DORA view of the product: speed of delivery and quality of delivery. On the speed side his slides list features waiting for test, average execution duration and flaky test retries. On the reliability side: escaped bugs, customer feedback and incidents from production.

## Speed: slow, flaky and fragile tests all stop the pipeline

- **Execution time.** "So execution of test cases is directly affecting the delivery time," Mesut Durukal said at Conf42 DevOps 2024. Profile the slow tests, delete unnecessary waits, and make tests independent so the suite can be split and run in parallel.
- **Reliability.** Flaky tests mean retries, and retries mean a longer run. Every failing test also halts the pipeline while someone decides whether it is a real bug or a false alarm.
- **Maintainability.** While a broken test is being fixed, delivery waits. His example is UI automation: when a page layout changes, locators kept outside the spec files (his slide shows a `data-test-id` selector) get updated in one place. Remove duplication so every fix has a single source of truth.

## The four boxes of a test report

His reliability grid is worth keeping on a sticky note. The feature is fine and the test passes: no problem. The feature is broken and the test fails: real bug. The feature is fine and the test fails: false alarm. The feature is broken and the test passes: what he calls a silent horror, the case that ships the bug to production and costs more later.

Both bad boxes usually trace back to test smells, the test-code equivalent of code smells, around coverage and maintainability. His fix is quality gates for test code as well as product code: static analysis and peer review before a new test is merged into the framework.

## Quality: coverage numbers don't catch escaped bugs

You can have fast tests and 100% coverage and still get bugs reported from production. His explanation is the verification versus validation gap: checking what was implemented is not the same as checking what was supposed to be implemented. The remedies he lists:

- Keep test scope current after every feature and every refactor.
- Vary test data: not only integers and strings but doubles, not only positive values but negative ones, and run on the browsers, devices and operating systems users actually have.
- Use test design techniques such as equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis for the corner cases.
- Try persona-based testing. His slide has three: an 83-year-old in APAC using a voice assistant (accessibility tests), a 34-year-old gamer in the EU who hates slow pages (functionality and performance), and a 19-year-old in the Americas juggling several browsers on mobile (cross-browser tests).

## Listen to your bugs

The last section is about monitoring. Chart bugs by severity and by component on dashboards, because raw data is hard to read. Then run postmortems on them: a bug carries information about a weakness in the process, and QA's job is not only to find bugs but to stop the next batch from being written.

## Who should watch

QA engineers and SDETs making the case for test-code quality, and DevOps engineers whose pipelines spend more time on retries than on deploys. It is a survey rather than a case study with numbers, so treat it as a checklist for your own suite.

Title: Fault tolerance starts with deciding what is allowed to break
Description: Maria Rogova (Meta) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on fault-tolerant systems - rank features first, then test your tools, degrade gracefully and add redundancy
Body:
You cannot protect everything, so the first design decision in a fault-tolerant system is which parts are allowed to fail. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Maria Rogova, Software Engineer at Meta, walks through resilience in two halves: the system design (modularity, graceful degradation, redundancy) and the tooling and process needed to keep that design honest once it ships, because a well-designed system with poor maintenance still falls over.

It is a compact checklist talk, a good refresher or a first map of the territory rather than a war story from Meta's infrastructure.

## Do you really need fault tolerance everywhere?

She starts with the failure types: hardware, network, human error (which she notes happens quite often), environmental disasters such as floods or lightning, and security breaches. Then comes the question most teams skip. With unlimited engineers, time and money you could build the perfect system; in the real world you prioritise, and you ask whether each protection is worth it from a business perspective.

Her exercise: list every feature and rank them against each other. In a food delivery shop, a broken checkout stops the business. Broken search suggestions do not. That ranking tells you which parts to duplicate and which to leave alone.

## Test the tools you will lean on during the outage

The process half has a few points that are easy to nod along to and rarely done:

- **Monitoring with automatic detection**: thresholds, false positives and all, because nobody can watch dashboards day and night.
- **A test environment as close to production as possible**, such as a small copy of the cluster, plus stress tests for your Black Friday.
- **Test your tools.** Maria Rogova said at Conf42 DevOps 2024: "Test that your monitoring system is actually monitoring, test that your recovery script is actually working."
- **Automate recovery and write runbooks**, so that mid-incident nobody is guessing a command's parameters and a new joiner can still act.
- **Chaos engineering**, run as a controlled process you can roll back. Her example: a system spread across three data centres but designed to run on two, so disconnect one and check.
- **Incremental rollout**: ship to a small percentage of users, wait, watch metrics, expand. A critical bug then hits a few people instead of everybody.

## Ask what happens when each box goes down

On design, she wants systems modular, distributed and scalable, and then she proposes an exercise for the finished draft: go component by component and ask what happens if this one goes down. The database, this service, that process. The answer should be that the system is okay. If it is that everything goes down, you have found a single point of failure. External dependencies count too: if a third-party API starts returning errors, does your system still work?

Graceful degradation is the part she finds most interesting. Under memory pressure, return a simplified response instead of failing. And think about the UI: if the "find similar" feature behind a product button is down, decide in advance whether you grey the button out or hide it.

## Diversity and redundancy, with their costs

Diversity means more maintenance, she admits, but it protects you. If the company chat runs on the same internal infrastructure that just went down, engineers cannot coordinate the recovery, so keep a backup channel. Likewise consider a second cloud provider, not only a second data centre.

Then the redundancy catalogue: hardware (RAID, hot standby), software (process replication, and N-version programming, where a critical function is implemented several times and the outputs compared), multiple network paths, data mirroring and backups, and geographic spread across data centres or countries.

## The improbable happens

She closes with reminders that low-probability failures are not zero-probability: four successive lightning strikes on a Google data centre on 13 August 2015, and Twitter and Instagram both having problems on 14 July 2022 for unrelated reasons. Her most recent example, from January 2024, involved external APIs again: Amazon product descriptions replaced with an LLM's "I apologize but I can't fulfill this request" because sellers had automated them with ChatGPT.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving into system design or on-call ownership who want a structured checklist, and team leads who need a vocabulary for arguing that the checkout path deserves more redundancy than search. Experienced SREs will know most of it; the feature-ranking and test-your-tools points are still worth stealing.

Title: Your chaos hypothesis should come out of a resilience model
Description: Gunnar Grosch (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 on building a resilience model first, so every chaos experiment tests a hypothesis worth testing
Body:
Most chaos engineering talks are about the fun part: picking a tool, injecting a fault, watching the graphs. Gunnar Grosch, Principal Developer Advocate at AWS, spent his [Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Gunnar_Grosch_hypothesis_development_resilience_modeling) on the step before that: building a resilience model, so the hypothesis you test is one that actually matters. His takeaway is simple. Time spent anticipating failure before the experiment makes the experiment worth far more.

## Why bother modelling before you break things?

Gunnar starts with an AWS story. In 2012, an operator ran a routine maintenance procedure on the Elastic Load Balancing control plane exactly as instructed, and it deleted configuration data. Calls to modify existing load balancers started failing, and the team found it had no recovery procedure for that data. They had to invent one on the spot. A resilience model would have shown the missing recovery control long before the incident, and that gap would have turned into a hypothesis to test.

AWS has run the practice with customers in North America, Latin America, Europe and Asia. "These customers, they've shared that they have probably avoided over 65 incidents if they had created a resilience model prior to go live," Gunnar Grosch said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024. He adds a softer benefit: the model gives a team a shared picture of how its system works.

## The system is bigger than the architecture diagram

The first step is to define the system honestly. The usual diagram of a container-based e-commerce app shows the tech stack and leaves out half of what keeps it running: the version control for the infrastructure as code, the monitoring platform, the automated controls (autoscaling groups, circuit breakers, RDS failover logic) and the human operators with their dashboards and restart buttons. Both the automation and the people can change the stack, so both can cause or prevent downtime, and both belong in the model.

To keep the scope sane, you then cut the system into user journeys or system functions (authentication, ordering, delivery) and pick one critical path. Modelling everything at once, he warns, turns into an infinite engagement.

## Five ways a function can fail

For each function, Gunnar uses a five-part template: no function, over function, under function, intermittent function and unintentional function. For a user login, that reads: login fails, users get admin rights, users get read-only access, only some users can log in, the wrong user gets logged in. Each failure mode then gets a business cost (lost sales, customer trust, even fines), so the team can weigh the cost of a control against what it protects.

The phrasing matters. "Failure modes, they should be written from the perspective of the business or the business process the system supports, and it shouldn't call out the cause of the actual failure mode," he said. Causes come next, as failure scenarios, and one failure mode usually has several.

## Four kinds of controls, and the hypothesis writes itself

Every scenario is mapped to four control types: detective (alarms on error responses, a drop in orders per second), preventive (circuit breakers, redundancy), corrective or recovery (the procedure that clears the impairment) and testing (anything that checks whether you are exposed). Gaps are findings in their own right.

From there the hypothesis is an if-then sentence built from a scenario and its controls. His worked example is an online storefront on Amazon EKS with DynamoDB, Aurora MySQL, ElastiCache for Redis and RabbitMQ, and the failure mode is order submission failing. Three scenarios come out of it:

- The TLS certificate on the Application Load Balancer expires. Alarms exist and certificates rotate annually, but nothing tests it. Hypothesis: operators are notified and troubleshooting starts.
- The storefront cannot find user sessions in the cache. No detection and no prevention, but users are redirected to log in with the basket kept, and an automated test covers it.
- Under high load the cache evicts recent sessions. An alarm fires on non-zero evictions and the cache was sized through load testing, but there is no test. Hypothesis: operators are notified and the cache is right-sized.

Each one is specific, testable and tied to a real business loss, which is a long way from killing a random pod to see what happens.

## Who should watch

Teams that already run chaos experiments and suspect they are testing whatever was easiest to break. It is a method talk, not a tool demo: no fault injection on screen, just a repeatable way to decide what to inject. Bring a whiteboard.

Title: The CEO wanted his own VMs, so Bitovi turned GitHub into the platform
Description: Leo Diaz Longhi (Bitovi) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on wrapping Terraform and Ansible in GitHub Actions so any developer can deploy infrastructure from a workflow
Body:
It started with the CEO asking the infrastructure team to set up a VM for him, and then asking why he had to ask. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Leo Diaz Longhi, Platform Engineer at Bitovi, tells how that request turned into a catalogue of open source GitHub Actions that let a developer deploy anything from a static site to an EKS cluster by adding a workflow and a few inputs.

The point is not Bitovi's tooling in particular. It is that GitHub Actions, used with a bit of discipline, already gives you the pieces of a platform: an interface (inputs and outputs), an implementation you can hide (the action's steps), and an audit trail (the repository).

## How did they get from scripts to a platform?

He walks the evolution in three steps. No DevOps: sysadmins with Bash or Python scripts, config files and documentation, plus a lot of clicking in cloud consoles. Slow and easy to get wrong. DevOps: Terraform and Ansible brought standards and automation, but every environment still needed variables set and settings tweaked by hand, and someone from DevOps had to step in.

Bitovi's first answer was BitOps, an open source tool that bakes the IaC tools, automation scripts and pre/post hooks into a Docker container, so nothing needs installing. That still left config files to write, a repository layout to follow, and a Docker engine to run it on. GitHub Actions closed the gap: the scripts that generate what BitOps needs moved into the actions, and the configuration moved into workflow inputs.

He is clear that BitOps is not required. Some of their most popular actions don't use it at all.

## An action is a Terraform module with a nicer front door

From the DevOps engineer's side, `action.yaml` declares inputs and outputs and lists the steps: a command, a script or a call to another action. It wraps the IaC tools and isolates the developer from them, exposing only what you choose. He makes the comparison himself: if you know Terraform, it looks a lot like handling inputs and outputs in a module.

From the developer's side, deploying to an EC2 instance is one more workflow next to the lint and test ones. Deploying Storybook to GitHub Pages collapses to a single step. And each action offers an input variable to download an artifact with the generated Ansible and Terraform code, so the curious can see exactly what ran, while the repository itself stays free of scripts and Terraform files.

## Sensible defaults from the repo itself

The trick that made reuse bearable: instead of setting a dozen Terraform variables per deployment, the actions derive them from repository specifics such as the repo name or the branch, and fall back to sane defaults for the rest. Need a bigger instance, a database proxy or an exposed port? Change one input.

"That way you can get your resource up and running with little to no intervention in just a few minutes," Leo Diaz Longhi said at Conf42 DevOps 2024.

Building one action per need got slow, so they pulled the shared code into a common layer for all actions. That is the Commons framework his colleague Karamveer Kaur Sangha demos in her talk at the same event.

## What does the platform engineer see?

Environments as repositories. His example has three infrastructure repos, dev, QA and prod, each with a workflow per resource: an EFS volume, an RDS database, Docker on EC2. Copy the dev repo, change the variables, and you have QA in minutes. Workflows can run on manual triggers or schedules, and the repo history doubles as a record of what was deployed when.

The catalogue they built in a few months includes React and Storybook to GitHub Pages, static sites to S3 with a CDN and Route 53, Docker build-tag-publish, Prometheus and Grafana, ECS and EKS clusters, Aurora, RDS and Redis, EFS and self-hosted GitHub runners.

## Who should watch

Small platform teams, or DevOps engineers who keep getting the same infrastructure request, and anyone weighing whether they need a developer portal before they need a good set of reusable workflows. It is short and conceptual; pair it with Karamveer Kaur Sangha's demo to see the moving parts.

Title: Kafka or RabbitMQ? Apache Pulsar's pitch is both, in one broker
Description: Julien Jakubowski (StreamNative) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on Apache Pulsar as one platform for both work queues and data streaming, scaled by layer
Body:
Most event-driven stacks end up with two brokers: Kafka for the ordered, replayable streams and RabbitMQ for the work queues. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Julien Jakubowski, developer advocate at StreamNative, makes the case for Apache Pulsar as one platform that covers both semantics, and spends most of the talk on why its split compute-and-storage architecture scales without partition rebalances.

Honest scope: StreamNative was founded by Pulsar's original creators and sells a managed Pulsar service, so this is an advocate's tour of Pulsar's features rather than a neutral bake-off. It is still a clear explanation of when you need a queue and when you need a stream.

## Queue or stream: what is the actual difference?

He separates the two cleanly. Data streaming means events processed in order, large ingestion volumes, retention, and big catch-up reads; think real-time analytics, fraud detection, ingestion. Kafka and Amazon Kinesis live here.

Message queuing is about decoupling task execution. His example is push notifications to Alice's and Bob's iPhones: nobody cares who gets theirs first. What you need is adding and removing workers on the fly, not blocking the queue when one consumer is busy or fails, redelivering failed messages later, and a dead letter queue for the undeliverable ones. That is RabbitMQ and Amazon SQS territory, and a streaming platform is not built for it.

Pulsar implements both. As he said at Conf42 DevOps 2024: "So you have only one SDK to learn as a developer and you have only one broker to manage in production."

## Scale by the bottleneck you actually have

The core of the talk is three levels of elasticity, each tied to a bottleneck:

- **Messages piling up in a topic** (the most common one): add consumers to a shared or key_shared subscription. With Kafka, adding an active consumer to a group means adding a partition on the broker side and rebalancing data, which he warns can cost performance or even cause downtime. Pulsar has no partitions to add, and key_shared keeps the ordering guarantee.
- **Too many producers, consumers or topics**: add broker nodes. Brokers are stateless; a new one takes load migrated from the others, connections move transparently, and no data moves.
- **Storage capacity**: add bookies, the Apache BookKeeper storage nodes. A new bookie gets new messages right away, with no rebalance to wait for.

All three scale back down too, which is where the infrastructure savings come from. For Kubernetes, StreamNative's operators define clusters as manifests, under a free-to-use community license.

## Durability, offload and geo-replication

Topics are made of segments spread across bookies, a different storage model from Kafka's partitions. With a replication factor of three, every segment sits on three bookies, so killing one loses nothing. Old segments can be offloaded to cheaper cloud storage; a consumer replaying a topic reads some messages from object storage and some from bookies without noticing. Geo-replication between regions is built in and bidirectional, mostly a matter of configuration.

## Can I keep my Kafka and RabbitMQ clients?

Multi-tenancy is native: tenants and namespaces let several teams share one cluster with isolated data. His line: "This is a built in feature." For existing estates, protocol handlers let Kafka, RabbitMQ and MQTT clients talk to Pulsar, so you do not rewrite thousands of lines of microservices to migrate.

The community numbers he quotes: more than 600 contributors, 10,000 Slack members and 1,000+ organisations using it. Pulsar started at Yahoo in 2012 as its cloud messaging service, went open source in 2016 and became a top-level Apache project in 2018.

## Who should watch

Teams running both Kafka and RabbitMQ and wondering whether they need two, and anyone who has scheduled a partition rebalance for a quiet Sunday. If you want benchmarks or failure stories from production, this talk points you to StreamNative's resources rather than showing them.

Title: Platform teams fail when they don't use their own platform
Description: Caio Medeiros Pinto (Citi) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on three practices for platform team adoption - customer-centric leads, dogfooding and home-grown champions
Body:
A platform team that doesn't run its own workloads on its own platform is guessing. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Caio Medeiros Pinto, DevOps & EE Lead at Citi, argues that platform engineering adoption comes down to three practices: a lead who treats stream-aligned teams as customers, a team that eats its own cooking, and champions grown in-house instead of hired at market rates.

It is a people-and-process talk, not a tooling one. He draws on leading a platform team that ran a DevOps toolchain (versioning, builds, deploys, scanning, test automation) for the product teams around it.

## Why do DevOps adoptions need a platform team at all?

He opens with the first line of *The DevOps Handbook* (Gene Kim, John Willis, Patrick Debois, Nicole Forsgren): product owners, developers, QA, IT ops and infosec working together without silos. The catch is that each of those roles brings its own tools. Without aligned management, teams pick different platforms for the same job. He has seen one company where one team built on Jenkins and another on Travis CI, so neither could share fixes or lessons.

Platform engineering, as Team Topologies by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais frames it, puts an internal team in charge of that toolchain as a product: templates, golden paths, and platforms kept reliable and stable. He lists three payoffs: standardisation with boundaries rather than removed freedom, lower cognitive load (you no longer need to hire product engineers who can also babysit a CI server), and fewer blockers in the delivery lifecycle. Without it, someone on the product team ends up restarting the Jenkins instance or tending the Kubernetes and Grafana stack instead of building the product.

## Why is the adoption hard?

Three challenges. Lack of time against rising demand: everyone is busy, and the moment one team succeeds with the platform, every manager wants it, which means more users, more doubts and more requests. Ways of working: teams arrive with their own habits and toolchains from previous jobs, plus compliance flows, overly specific requirements and, in globally distributed teams, language barriers. And keeping the platform team engaged, because cognitive load and burnout hit them too.

## Practice 1: lead like the stream-aligned teams are customers

Each platform team needs a lead with a design thinking mindset who identifies the internal customers, learns their real objectives and lets those set priorities. Two companies building the same kind of platform will find different needs. His concrete tools: empathy maps, proto-personas and user personas, made visible to the whole team.

## Practice 2: practice what you preach

This is the one with teeth. He has seen platform teams that did not use their own platform, and it was a mess because they did not know what was really happening in production. His fix: shared metrics to track whether the team actually uses the platform, internal and external usability testing before a release, showcases and demo days, and lightning talks to spread the knowledge.

## Practice 3: don't search for experts, form them

A platform is never one tool. His slide shows Kibana, Kubernetes and Grafana, each owned by someone. Everyone on the team is T-shaped: general knowledge across the whole toolbox, plus one platform they own, with its documentation, configuration and bugs. Experts on the market are expensive; formed ones stay. Career paths aligned to team needs, certification and training paths, game days and chaos engineering sessions where the team breaks the platform on purpose, and a calendar of tech talks led by the champions.

"So the knowledge needed to manage all these platforms is crazy, right?" Caio Medeiros Pinto said at Conf42 DevOps 2024, which is as honest a job description for a platform team as any.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and leads about to stand up a platform team, or running one that adoption has stalled on. If you want Backstage plugins or Terraform modules, this is the wrong talk; it is about the team. His own further reading: Manuel Pais on platform as a product, Mallory Haigh's *DevOps ain't dead but... we gotta talk*, Puppet's State of DevOps Report 2023, Lucas Galante's nine steps to platform engineering hell, and Nicki Watt on people, process and platform.

Title: Prometheus and Grafana on EC2 from one GitHub Action call
Description: Karamveer Kaur Sangha (Bitovi) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on hiding Terraform and Ansible behind a GitHub Action so a workflow file is the whole platform
Body:
What if the developer-facing side of your platform was a single workflow file, and everything with Terraform in it lived somewhere else? At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Karamveer Kaur Sangha, DevOps Consultant at Bitovi, deploys Prometheus and Grafana to an AWS EC2 instance by committing one change to a repository that calls Bitovi's open source "Deploy Prometheus" GitHub Action, then opens up the action to show where the infrastructure as code went.

It is a short, demo-led talk. The takeaway is the layering: the user writes a workflow, the action holds the opinions, and a framework underneath, Bitovi's Commons, runs the IaC tools so nobody has to install them.

## What does the user actually write?

Very little. The deployment repository holds an observability folder with the Prometheus scrape targets and a Grafana data source, plus a workflow that calls the action. The required inputs are an AWS access key ID and secret access key. Optional ones set the AWS region and the EC2 instance type, and one input points the action at the config folder.

For the demo she comments out a line in the workflow and commits straight to main. That commit is the deployment. By the end of the talk the run is green, Prometheus answers on port 9090 at the instance's IP, and the scrape target shows up and healthy.

## Three repositories, three jobs

While the workflow runs, she walks the stack from the top:

- **Deployment repo**: owned by the user. Workflow plus config, nothing else.
- **Action repo**: Bitovi's Deploy Prometheus action. Its action file exposes the inputs developers may set and defines the steps, such as copying the Prometheus and Grafana configuration to the right destination before calling Commons.
- **Commons repo**: Bitovi's open source framework, a wrapper around BitOps, which has Terraform and Ansible baked in as containers. It merges the deployment and action repositories into the order BitOps expects, runs the tools, and exposes outputs so they can be reused.

The action tells Commons where its Ansible code lives through an input parameter, and the same pattern exists for Terraform and Helm. As she put it, Commons "would make sure that your deployments are ready without you to concern about deploying or installing terraform, ansible or any IAC tools."

That is the platform engineering idea in its smallest form: the golden path is a `uses:` line, and the IaC complexity sits in two repositories the platform team owns.

## Is it only Prometheus?

No. Prometheus is the example; the same structure backs a catalogue of Bitovi actions on the GitHub Actions Marketplace. The ones she lists include deploying Docker to EC2, an EKS or ECS cluster, Helm to EKS, Aurora and RDS databases, a Redis cluster, EFS, a self-hosted GitHub runner, StackStorm on a single VM, and static sites to S3 with a CDN and Route 53.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers who want a concrete picture of what self-service can look like without building a portal first, and anyone already living in GitHub Actions who wonders how far `with:` inputs can stretch. It is a quick demo plus a repo tour, not a line-by-line read of Commons, so expect to read the repositories afterwards.

Title: Many clients, many IPs, one GitHub Actions matrix of Gatling runs
Description: Kaye Alvarado (Asurion) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on load testing from many client IPs by running Gatling in parallel GitHub Actions runners
Body:
A load test from one machine tells you how your platform treats one very enthusiastic client. Real traffic comes from many clients with many IP addresses. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Kaye Alvarado, DevOps Engineer at Asurion, showed [the low-ceremony fix her team used](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Kaye_Alvarado_loadtesting_pipeline): write the load test as code in Gatling, then trigger the same workflow in parallel on several GitHub Actions runners, each with its own IP.

It's a short talk, and that's the point. The closing advice is to keep things simple, and the talk takes its own medicine.

## Why load test at all here?

Her team had migrated their platform to a more modern architecture and needed proof that the new sizing kept the availability of the old one. So they simulated real production traffic against an isolated non-production environment, pushing towards the system's upper limits.

## Why Gatling?

The selection criteria are the ones any DevOps team would write down: open source, ease of use and community, programming language, triggering from the command line, and reports. JMeter, Locust and Gatling all tick most boxes, so she's candid that it often comes down to what your developers already know. For them it was Gatling.

## What goes into the Gatling code?

A quick walk through the project layout:

- **`gatling.conf`** in the `conf` directory, where you point Gatling at your simulations and resources directories.
- **Resources**: feeder files with the values your scenarios use, such as credentials or sample data.
- **Simulations**: the tests themselves, traditionally Scala and now also Java. Variables fed from a map, an HTTP protocol config with common headers like `Accept` and `Content-Type`, a scenario that feeds credentials, calls the API and asserts the expected result, and a setup that injects users with open or closed injection profiles.

A shell script launches the Java program, and the run ends in Gatling's HTML report: successes versus failures, per-request response times, users over time against responses per second. Enough to tell whether the infrastructure needs tweaking.

## How do you get many IPs?

Put it in a pipeline. The code lives in GitHub; triggering the workflow in parallel spins up multiple GitHub runners, each with its own server IP, all sending traffic to the platform at once. "And that's it. That's the solution," Kaye Alvarado said at Conf42 DevOps 2024.

Four small problems needed solving to make it reusable:

1. **Pick a simulation without the interactive prompt**: set it in the Gatling config file, replaced in a workflow step.
2. **Reuse across environments**: the environment lives in the API domain, so a `sed` command rewrites it in the simulation code.
3. **Override auth headers** and 4. **override injection rates**: both become workflow inputs written into the load test code.

The workflow installs Java, runs the shell script, and uploads the HTML report as a GitHub artifact. Push it to a server, an email or a Slack message if you prefer.

## What should you watch out for?

Design tests to reach the breaking point, or close to it; start from a baseline scenario built on production data and adjust load between runs. Consider scheduled runs, with heavier traffic at peak times of day and lighter traffic off hours. And her personal preference: serverless wherever possible, to skip maintaining your own load generators.

## Who should watch

Teams who want a believable multi-client load test without standing up a distributed load-testing cluster, and anyone already on GitHub Actions. If you need tens of thousands of distinct source IPs or coordinated ramp-ups across runners, this approach won't stretch that far, and the talk doesn't claim it does. Her blog post on load test as code for non-coders, on Asurion's dev community, fills in the Gatling details.

Title: Four ways to stop hand-writing near-identical Airflow DAGs
Description: Aliaksandr Sheliutsin at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on Airflow DAG factories fed by CSV, Google Sheets or Airflow connections, plus event-triggered DAGs
Body:
If your Airflow repo has thirty DAG files that differ only by an ID and a start date, this talk is your intervention. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, freelance data engineer Aliaksandr Sheliutsin shared [four tricks from client work](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Aliaksandr_Sheliutsin_leverage_airflow_pipelines): three ways to generate DAGs from configuration, from a CSV file to Airflow's own metadata database, and one way to make a scheduler-first tool react to events.

The abstract promises more fireworks than the talk delivers; what you get is calmer and more useful: four patterns, each with honest pros and cons from a real project.

## Trick 1: one CSV, one DAG factory

The starting case: a client pulling data from many decentralised organisations through the same API, each with its own ID and its own start date. Instead of a DAG file per organisation, one CSV lists them all and a DAG factory creates a DAG per row.

The upsides he lists: adding an entity is one line of config, which the scheduler picks up; less code; a per-DAG start date, so no runs crawling empty history; and isolation. He chose separate DAGs over one big one on purpose, because a single DAG would hit the API for empty dates on younger entities and force a re-run of everything whenever one changed. A separate data validation pipeline reads the same config, so every new row is validated for free.

The downsides: it takes more Airflow understanding, there are more ways to break the scheduler, and pipelines that look similar often aren't. Keep bolting on special cases and the factory turns into a spaghetti bowl of if conditions. "So sometimes it's really better to create separate pipelines for this kind of similar pipelines," Aliaksandr Sheliutsin said at Conf42 DevOps 2024.

## Trick 2: let the client edit a Google Sheet

The upgrade: his client wanted to add pipelines without him. So the config moved to a shared Google Sheet, read through the Google Sheets API. Others can now add DAGs, and changes skip the commit-and-deploy step entirely.

The price is validation, and he's emphatic about it. DAG files are parsed by the scheduler, so an API that takes two or three seconds to answer can crash it. Users will ignore even good documentation. His fix is to fetch the sheet, validate the rows, write them to a local file, and have the DAG factory read only that file, so garbage never reaches the scheduler. And because you'll miss something too, add error notifications.

## Trick 3: generate DAGs from Airflow connections

A client kept creating and dropping MySQL databases, each needing its own pipeline, and credentials don't belong in a config file. So each database becomes an Airflow connection with a fixed name prefix. The DAG code queries the metadata database through SQLAlchemy, lists the connections, filters by prefix and builds a DAG for each.

No external API calls, no separate config to maintain, and the extra query is a rounding error next to what the scheduler already does. The risk: lose the metadata database, or migrate Airflow to a new server, and your connections and therefore your pipeline config go with it. Back it up.

## Trick 4: make Airflow event-driven

Airflow is for schedules, until it isn't. His case had low event volume, a few an hour, but results needed as soon as possible. The application, which they didn't control, published to Google Cloud Pub/Sub; a Cloud Function on that topic triggered an unscheduled DAG through the Airflow API.

He rejects the obvious alternative, a DAG that polls the queue every minute, because it fills the metadata database with a mountain of empty one-minute runs and slows the whole installation. The limit is volume: thousands of events an hour won't work, and he puts the practical ceiling at about one event every five minutes. Often that's enough.

## Who should watch

Data engineers maintaining many lookalike Airflow pipelines, and anyone asked to let non-engineers add pipelines. Platform folks get a useful reminder that DAG parsing is part of the scheduler's hot path.

Title: Code review is not a stamp competition
Description: Israel Heringer (Meta) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on efficient code reviews that fit the team, code and goals, automate the trivia and skip the gatekeeper
Body:
Send a ten-line pull request and get ten comments; send 500 lines and get "looks good to me". At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Israel Heringer, Software Engineer at Meta, used that familiar joke to open [a talk on efficient code reviews](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Israel_Heringer_efficient_code_reviews_codebase), and his answer is less about reviewer heroics and more about shaping the process around the team, the code and what you want reviews to achieve.

It's a short, process-level talk with no tooling pitch. Think of it as the checklist you wish someone had handed the team before the first review war.

## What is a code review for, and what isn't it?

He starts with the reasons everyone lists (finding bugs earlier, code quality, security, sharing knowledge, mentoring newer engineers, compliance) and then the ones nobody admits to. A code review is not for blaming or shaming someone's code, not a stage for showing off your engineering skills, and not about executing the code. It's reading, analysing and commenting so the change gets better.

There are three common approaches: pair programming, over-the-shoulder reviews and tool-assisted reviews (the pull request). Most of his advice targets the last, though nearly all of it transfers.

## Look inward before writing any rules

Before setting up a process, he asks three sets of questions.

- **The team**: seniority, familiarity with the code, whether people work alone or together, communication style, time zones.
- **The code**: coding standards, testability, the riskiest paths (his example is a bank's core banking feature that can't break in any way), legacy versus new.
- **The goals**: catching bugs, improving quality or test coverage, onboarding newcomers.

Goals shift over time, and he's fine with the review focus moving with them. What doesn't change, in his view, is that the practice is here to stay, not a temporary fix.

## Efficient is not the same as fast

"We are not trying to be fast. We are trying to be efficient," Israel Heringer said at Conf42 DevOps 2024. That means actually reading the code instead of skimming it, and treating reviews as something other than a stamp competition; the reviewer who did 200 reviews this month has proved nothing about whether the team got better.

Comments should be clear and actionable. "This doesn't look good" with no alternative or pointer to a practice doesn't improve the code, it just creates friction. Focus on what matters for the context: functionality first, then design and complexity (is it over-engineered?), tests and evidence, then style, consistency and naming. Be explicit when nitpicking: prefix with `nit` so the author knows it's optional and the back-and-forth stays short.

And automate whatever can be automated. Auto-formatters, linters and CI warnings exist for almost every language. He recalls a project years ago where pull requests went back for tabs instead of spaces, which is not a good use of a human.

## The author has homework too

Code review is a team effort, not a solo duty for the reviewer. Write code for the people who will read it, since code is read more often than written. Split big changes into smaller, meaningful ones, because a large change is slower to review and harder to iterate on. Attach the test runs or other evidence. And reviewers: drop the bossy tone. "Have you considered..." lands better than "you should have".

## How do you introduce reviews without killing autonomy?

The closing section is the most practical. Avoid the gatekeeper, the one person who, intentionally or not, has to approve everything; it's bad for them and for the team. Map the exceptions before you need them: if every change needs an approval, what does the on-call engineer do at night with nobody around to approve the fix? Reviews should be part of shipping, not a high-friction checkpoint.

Encourage open discussion with no finger-pointing, review the pain points, iterate, and recognise people who give good reviews. If the team can't absorb it all at once, start small: selected projects, only the critical code paths, randomly sampled reviews, or even non-blocking reviews where a change may land after a few days without one.

## Who should watch

Tech leads setting up or repairing a review process, and anyone whose team argues more about reviews than about the code. Senior engineers won't hear much new, but the context questions and the unblocking ideas are a good template for a team retro.

Title: ElastiCache Serverless ends the cache capacity guessing game
Description: Indika Wimalasuriya (Virtusa) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on AWS ElastiCache Serverless replacing cache capacity planning, plus the traps of easy caching
Body:
Every cache cluster you have ever sized was either too big (you paid for it) or too small (your users paid for it). At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Indika Wimalasuriya, Associate Director of Managed Services at Virtusa, walked through [AWS ElastiCache Serverless](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Indika_Wimalasuriya_aws_elastic_cache_serverless), announced at re:Invent 2023, as the way out of that trade-off, and then spent his closing minutes on the new mistakes a one-minute cache makes easy.

It's an overview for engineers deciding whether to try it, not a benchmark or a migration story.

## Why does a few milliseconds matter?

He opens with the familiar argument that speed is revenue, backed by the usual industry figures: Walmart saw conversions rise 2% for every second shaved off page load, COOK gained 7% by cutting load time by 0.85 seconds, and Mobify measured a 1.11% conversion lift per 100 ms on its homepage. Caching frequently accessed, rarely changing data is the decades-old answer, buying low latency, high throughput and a layer you can scale separately from the database.

## Which AWS cache, then?

AWS had three in-memory options before serverless, and his comparison is useful on its own:

- **ElastiCache for Memcached**: simple, non-persistent, no replicas or automatic failover.
- **ElastiCache for Redis**: adds persistence, replication, backups, failover, sharding and Global Datastore.
- **MemoryDB for Redis**: durable, and the only one of the three tuned for ultra-low sub-millisecond latency.

## What actually hurts with server-based caches?

His list: capacity management, scaling (on which metric?), operational load (patching, backups, security), manual high availability, the cost of a separate high-spec cluster, and slower development because every feature now has a cache design to think about. If he had to pick one, it's capacity, because capacity is cost.

Anyone who has done a capacity plan and shipped it to production lands in one of two groups. Over-provision and you bleed money on headroom you never touch. Under-provision and every traffic spike above the line becomes a customer-facing incident. That is the gap he expects serverless caching to close.

## What does serverless change?

The numbers he gives for ElastiCache Serverless:

- A cache created in under a minute, with no capacity to manage.
- 700 microseconds at p50 and 1.3 milliseconds at p99.
- Up to 5 TB of storage.
- A 99.99% availability SLA and a single endpoint.
- PCI-DSS and SOC compliance, HIPAA eligibility.

Pricing comes in two parts: data stored in GB-hours (each cache is metered for at least 1 GB), and ElastiCache Processing Units (ECPUs), where each read or write consumes 1 ECPU per kilobyte transferred and extra vCPU time or data scales it up. He quotes about $0.125 per GB-hour in US East at the time, and reminds you it varies by region.

The setup is three clicks: choose serverless, name it, create. Connect with `openssl s_client` to the endpoint, `set` a key, `get` it back. He skips a live demo because, honestly, there isn't much to watch.

## The new trap: caching because you can

This is the best part of the talk. When standing up Memcached or Redis took real effort, teams asked whether they needed a cache at all. "But here, now that we can make a cache within less than 1 minute, I would say someone would just go and create a cache and rely on that," Indika Wimalasuriya said at Conf42 DevOps 2024. His anti-patterns:

- **Over-reliance on caching**: critical data must still be retrievable from the primary source, with fallbacks in place.
- **Ignoring cache misses**: handle them gracefully and detect them quickly.
- **Neglecting security**: AWS runs the infrastructure, but the data in the cache is yours to authenticate, authorise and encrypt.

And the best practices to pair them with: pick an access pattern (read-through, write-through, write-behind, cache-aside, refresh-ahead), use efficient serialisation such as MessagePack, Protocol Buffers or Avro, design cache keys like `user_profile:{user_id}`, and monitor hit and miss rates, latency, evictions, transfer volume and size.

## Who should watch

Teams on AWS running ElastiCache clusters sized by guesswork, or about to add a cache to a service for the first time. If you want load tests or a cost comparison against a provisioned cluster, the talk doesn't have them; it's a capability tour with a sensible checklist at the end.

Title: OpenTelemetry metrics into Prometheus, and every gotcha on the way
Description: Prathamesh Sonpatki (Last9) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on shipping OpenTelemetry metrics to Prometheus, from collector tricks to temporality and naming traps
Body:
OpenTelemetry has no storage backend, and Prometheus is the natural place to put its metrics, which is exactly where the friction starts. At Conf42 DevOps 2024, Prathamesh Sonpatki, Developer Evangelist at Last9, gave [a handbook-style tour of OpenTelemetry metrics](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Prathamesh_Sonpatki_handbook_opentelemetry_metrics): how the data model differs from Prometheus, what the OpenTelemetry Collector can do before anything is stored, and the conversion traps between the two.

It's a reference talk, best watched with your collector config open in the next window. Last9 builds Levitate, a time series database that accepts both formats, and it gets a mention at either end; the middle is vendor-neutral.

## Why look at OpenTelemetry metrics at all?

He opens with the case for: OpenTelemetry is the second most popular CNCF project after Kubernetes, it brings vendor neutrality through a standard API and spec, and semantic conventions plus shared metadata promise correlation across metrics, logs and traces. The metrics project had three stated goals: connect metrics to the other signals, give OpenCensus users a migration path (you can still see OpenCensus in the design), and interoperate with existing standards such as Prometheus and StatsD.

Prometheus, for contrast: pull-based scraping of `/metrics`, the text exposition and OpenMetrics formats, float values, a label-based data model, and cumulative reporting. A counter that reads 1, 4, 7, 9 reports exactly that.

## The collector is where the work moves

The OpenTelemetry Collector sits between source and backend with receivers, processors and exporters. The Prometheus receiver is, in his words, a drop-in replacement for a Prometheus doing the scraping: paste your existing scrape config, service discovery included, into the collector config.

Processors are the interesting layer. Batch and memory limiter are the defaults, the latter refusing data and forcing GC when the collector nears its limits, so a metrics flood doesn't take it down. Beyond those you can redact, change attributes, and generate new metrics with arithmetic, such as pod CPU utilisation from pod CPU usage divided by the CPU limit. Transformation processors rename, drop and aggregate, which means high-cardinality series can be rolled up before they ever hit storage. "Your recording rules use cases probably will not be needed anymore because you can just create or transform the metrics in the collector itself," Prathamesh Sonpatki said at Conf42 DevOps 2024.

On the way out there are three options: let Prometheus scrape the collector's own `/metrics`, remote write to long-term storage, or use the then-experimental OTLP push into Prometheus.

## So why isn't it just plug and play?

Because the two models disagree in several places:

- **Metric types.** OpenTelemetry has counters, asynchronous counters, up-down counters (sync and async), gauges and histograms; Prometheus has counters, gauges, summaries, histograms and sparse histograms. One-to-one matches convert; the rest are not supported on the way to Prometheus.
- **Temporality.** Cumulative reports the running total, delta reports the change since last time (3 instead of 4 in his example). Cumulative needs client-side state; delta is stateless. Prometheus only does cumulative, while Datadog recommends delta for performance. The catch with delta: drop a sample and that data is gone, whereas with cumulative, rate and similar functions absorb the gap.
- **Naming.** OpenTelemetry uses dots and a mandatory unit, like `http.requests.duration` in milliseconds; Prometheus uses underscores and often puts the unit in the name, as in `http_requests_duration_milliseconds_count`. Receivers and exporters normalise names in both directions, but never convert units. And renamed metrics can quietly break dashboards built on the old names.
- **Out-of-order data.** OpenTelemetry pushes in batches, and Prometheus historically rejected out-of-order samples.

## What is Prometheus changing?

The roadmap he walks through: better out-of-order support, UTF-8 in metric and label names (which would end the dots-to-underscores dance), delta temporality support, handling OpenTelemetry resource attributes, storing metric metadata, and performance work. Some of it was slated for Prometheus 3.0, according to the dev summit discussion he cites.

## Who should watch

Teams already on Prometheus who are being nudged towards OpenTelemetry SDKs, and anyone who has watched a Grafana dashboard go blank after putting a collector in the path. The temporality and naming sections alone will save you an afternoon. If you want hands-on config, look elsewhere; this is the map, not the walkthrough.
