Title: Stop copying pipeline YAML; SPS Commerce runs 2,000 pipelines off templates
Description: Travis Gosselin (SPS Commerce) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on reusable Azure Pipelines templates, from parameters and extends to versioning and guardrails
Body:
Travis Gosselin, Distinguished Software Engineer for developer experience at SPS Commerce, makes the case at Conf42 DevOps 2024 that copy-pasted CI/CD YAML is a tax you pay on every change, and that Azure Pipelines templates are the way out. His team uses them to roll out more than 2,000 pipeline definitions across 40 teams, and the talk is a tour of the template features that make that possible, including the one most people miss: templates can restrict what a pipeline is allowed to do, not just insert content.

It is a hands-on talk with lots of YAML. If you live in GitHub Actions, the concepts transfer; the syntax does not.

## Why does copy-paste stop working?

Gosselin frames developer experience as studying, improving and optimising how developers get work to production, and he opens with a line that should be on every platform team's wall: developers work in rainforests, not planned gardens. Tools accrete over years, and lead developers end up inventing their own workflows.

CI/CD sits at the centre of all of that. Look at what a build does: shared context and variables, security constraints, versioning, private package feeds, build and unit tests, pushing artifacts, tagging the repo, notifications. Only how you build and verify the thing is unique to each pipeline. Deployment is the same story: organisation, security, change management and artifact promotion barely differ. Copying that YAML into every repo means one fix becomes a hundred pull requests.

Azure DevOps, he notes, is cloud agnostic despite the name: SPS Commerce deploys about 80% of its services into AWS through it.

## Includes, parameters and three variable syntaxes

The anatomy is trigger, pipeline, stages, jobs, steps; stages run in sequence by default and jobs in parallel, and deployment jobs are a distinct type tied to environments. A file becomes a template when it declares parameters: typed (string, number, boolean), required unless they have a default, optionally restricted to an enumeration such as dev or prod. Complex parameters go further: objects, lists of environments with metadata like whether approval is required, and the special stepList, jobList, stageList and deploymentList types, so callers can pass in their own steps for you to wrap. Template expressions can loop over those lists and branch on them.

Variable templates hold only variables, so a deployment template can import dev or prod variables dynamically by environment. Then the part that trips everyone up: three variable syntaxes evaluated at different times. Template expressions render first, at compile time, and can even change keys, not just values. Runtime expressions come in the middle, useful for conditions. Macro syntax resolves last, at task execution.

The limits are generous: 20 levels of nesting, 100 separate YAML files and 10 MB of memory parsing, which he has not hit yet.

## Remote templates and how to version them

The real win is a shared templates repository referenced as a resource, so every repo uses the same logic. Gosselin is blunt about the risk: "in one line change, in one character change, you could actually blow up every pipeline in your organization," Travis Gosselin said at Conf42 DevOps 2024. Lock that repo down, require approvals, and add validation and PR checks.

On versioning he compares three strategies: branch-based (v1 and v2 branches, which couples all template versions together), commit or tag based (immutable, which is not always what you want), and his preference, the version in the template name. That works like a major API version: a v1 deploy template can sit beside a v2 while the build template stays at v1, teams need no explicit ref, maintainers can still patch v1, and the repo stays trunk-based.

## Extends turns templates into guardrails

Includes are composition; extends is inheritance, and a pipeline can extend only one template. That base template can wrap whatever stage list the team provides: pick the agent pool, add standard variables, prepend a context job. With advanced template expressions it can loop over each job and inject steps, such as downloading artifacts or authenticating to private feeds like JFrog, or reject certain tasks outright, for example erroring if anyone adds a raw Bash script step. That is how you codify security and best practice in CI/CD, with the caveat that such templates are hard to validate, so automate their tests.

## What it looks like at SPS Commerce

The numbers from his slides: 60 projects, 40 teams, 430 users, 500 daily pipelines, 15,000 pipeline runs and 1,300 production deploys a month, and 2,000 pipeline definitions on templates. The composition is a versioned base template with a context job (who is building, cost attribution, Slack channels), GitHub Advanced Security code scanning stages in a couple of lines, standard build stages including one for UI static assets and CDNs, a layered deploy workflow, and a documentation deploy stage. Teams use only the top-level templates; the rest are internal.

His advice: do not start with the great pyramid. Ship a few small composable templates, let engineers notice they can drop one in, then build the base. Open questions he is still working on include how far to abstract and how to retire old template versions.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers running Azure DevOps at any scale, and anyone designing shared CI/CD for an internal developer platform. Bring your YAML goggles.

Title: Your microservices ship like a monolith until deploy stops meaning release
Description: Naresh Waswani (Simpplr) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on escaping the distributed monolith by deploying one service at a time behind feature flags
Body:
Naresh Waswani, Senior Architect at Simpplr, describes at Conf42 DevOps 2024 a team that thought it was doing microservices and was actually running a distributed monolith: many services shipped together on release day, by checklist, with everyone on a bridge call. The fix he lays out is one idea with a lot of governance attached: a deployment of a service into production is not the same as a feature release, so put every feature behind a flag and deploy each service the moment its work is done.

The abstract pitches this for beginners to intermediates, and that is accurate. If you already run trunk-based development with flags, the challenges section is the part to watch.

## How do you know you built a distributed monolith?

The tell is the deployment pattern. Each service has its own artifact in the repository, but shipping one feature means deploying several services to production together. Waswani lists the technical causes: service boundaries drawn wrong (or a domain split so finely that one requirement touches many services), a shared data store where one schema change cascades everywhere, and too many shared libraries, so a single library change forces every consumer to redeploy.

Then there is the cause that is not technical at all: a predefined release cadence, common in SaaS. Features finished in week one wait for the monthly train. The reasons can be legitimate: marketing wants a launch with some buzz, customers cannot absorb features faster, compliance means a penetration test report goes out with each release, support needs training and user guides.

## What does release day cost?

Three things. High risk, because when a bundle of changes fails you do not know which one broke it. Long deployments, which hurt the near-zero-downtime promise of microservices. And burnout. He describes the ritual: one person per service on a bridge, deploying A, then B, then C, in a fixed order, handing over to the automation team for sanity checks, and then praying to the release god. If it fails, you often roll back everything. The team's productivity that day, he says, goes to literally zero.

## Deployment is not a feature release

The solution sounds almost too simple: deploy the service as soon as a feature is developed. Two objections follow immediately: what about the release cadence, and what about the half-finished feature Y sitting in the same branch as finished feature X?

"A deployment of a service into production is not equal to a feature release," Naresh Waswani said at Conf42 DevOps 2024. Both objections are answered by feature toggles, which at heart are the humble if condition we all already trust. Every feature goes behind a flag, off by default. With trunk-based development, half-built code can reach production safely because nobody can reach it, and turning a feature on does not need a redeploy.

The benefits he lists: low risk, since a failure points at one service you can flag off or roll back alone; flexibility to ship early when a customer is about to churn rather than waiting for the cadence; dark and beta launches to one or two friendly customers who become your live testers before wider rollout; testing in production behind a flag for a test user, when a lower environment lacks the licences or integrations; and, because you deploy daily, mastering the art of deployment.

## What does it cost you?

He is clear that nothing comes for free:

- **Low fault tolerance**: the flag service, homegrown or third party, is now on every request path. If it goes down, your entire product goes for a toss.
- **Testing explodes**: hundreds of on/off flags make full combinations impossible, so pick core use cases and services and test those combinations; add more if you have the CPU and time.
- **Governance**: naming that shows which service owns a flag, a cap on how many you keep, and a declared lifetime (two weeks, two months) enforced by fitness functions that flag expired toggles.
- **Operational ownership**: in production, product owners should own flags, because they know which customer gets what and when; in lower environments, leads, architects or QA.
- **Tech debt and learning curve**: every flag must eventually be removed, so use patterns that make flags easy to remove, not just easy to add.
- **Observability and resiliency from day zero**: you want to spot a flag flipped by mistake before a customer tells you.

## Who should watch

Teams that have split a monolith and are still deploying on a monthly train with a bridge call, and architects who need a structured argument for trunk-based development and flags. Pair it with Travis Gosselin's earlier feature flag talk for the velocity side.

Title: Containers slow the inner loop by 45%, and shared preprod makes it worse
Description: Debosmit Ray (DevZero) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on GitOps-backed, production-like ephemeral environments for every stage of the SDLC
Body:
Debosmit Ray, founder of DevZero, argues at Conf42 DevOps 2024 that most developer friction comes from environments that differ at every stage of the software lifecycle, and that the fix is declarative: keep the environment configuration next to the code and let GitOps spin up a production-like, isolated environment for each change. His back-of-envelope maths makes the case: going from a plain build to a containerised microservice loop can cut a developer's daily iterations from 72 to 40.

It is a conceptual talk with diagrams rather than a demo; DevZero, which builds in this space, gets a single mention at the end.

## Inner loop, outer loop and where the time goes

Ray splits the SDLC the usual way. The inner loop is the developer's read-eval-print loop: code in the IDE, local checks, push a branch somewhere for end-to-end testing, repeat. The outer loop starts at code review and runs through CI/CD, preproduction, staging and production. Any failure in the outer loop sends you back to the start of the inner one.

He then walks through a ticket the slow way: pull main, create a branch, set up the local dev environment, wait for the IDE to index, code, find somewhere to test end to end, write unit and integration tests, get a review (a diligent reviewer also tries it in a preview environment), merge, and push through preprod and staging. Almost every step that is not writing code is a candidate for automation, from environment setup to provisioning a test environment from whatever branch you are on.

## What does the container tax look like?

This is the number to remember. Assume six focused hours a day, 360 minutes. A classic code, build, run, inspect loop takes about five minutes, so you get 72 iterations. Add container builds and the rest of the container ergonomics and the same loop takes about nine minutes: 40 iterations. "On the left hand side, I could do 72 iterations. On the right, I can only do 40, which is actually a 45% degradation," Debosmit Ray said at Conf42 DevOps 2024. Strictly, 72 to 40 is closer to 44%, but nobody needs to argue over the last point.

The point is not that containers are bad but that their cost lands in the loop developers repeat most often, so that is where an environment that is ready the moment you start pays off.

## Why shared preprod hurts

His preprod example will be familiar to anyone who has used a shared staging cluster. You push a front-end change. Bob is updating the API gateway. Sally is running a database migration. Your logs suddenly fill with migration errors that have nothing to do with you, and now you are debugging someone else's afternoon.

The GitOps answer is ephemeral preproduction environments: each change tested in isolation, then the same tests run again once everything lands on main. If you did not change the environment config in source, you got the golden path, so every failure is caused by your change and not the infrastructure. Review gets the same benefit, and when the change merges, the infrastructure that was spun up for it is deleted automatically, which also cuts cost.

## What counts as an environment, and what is testing for?

Ray's definition of an environment is a useful checklist: the application runtime, relevant dev or test data, access to downstream services, reachability from upstream services, access for a human, isolation from production unless it is production, source code and build tools, and shared or dedicated tenancy.

Testing, in his framing, exists for three reasons: functionality (does it meet the acceptance criteria), interoperability (am I calling downstream APIs correctly, are latency and response shapes acceptable) and confidence (will this make future deployments more error-prone or page the on-call more often). Docker Compose is fine for basic functional testing in dev, but production-symmetric infrastructure gets more valuable closer to CI, where it shows real latencies.

The most interesting idea comes near the end: running your service inside a real call chain while it sits in your IDE with the debugger attached, so upstream callers hit the code you are editing. That moves the discovery of integration bugs back into the inner loop, where fixing them is cheapest.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers designing preview or ephemeral environments, and engineering leads trying to explain to finance why a staging cluster per change is cheaper than it sounds. If you already run per-PR environments on Kubernetes, the inner-loop maths and the environment checklist are the parts worth stealing.

Title: Grenade testing finds the platform versions that don't blow up together
Description: Jonathan Mounty (Cisco) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on grenade testing, a cheap automated check of which Kubernetes platform tool versions work together
Body:
Jonathan Mounty, a cloud engineer and engineering leader at Cisco, shares a testing technique his team built for a Kubernetes-based multi-cloud platform with hundreds of clusters at Conf42 DevOps 2024. They call it grenade testing: whenever a core platform tool ships a new version, a pipeline builds a real minimal cluster with the latest of everything else and records whether the combination works. It cut the time to detect version incompatibilities from weeks to hours.

"Grenade testing itself actually involves no actual grenades, but it does provide an output of compatible versions that don't blow up when they're used together," Jonathan Mounty said at Conf42 DevOps 2024.

## Why isn't unit plus integration testing enough?

His team owns everything from the data centre to the application layer: environment definitions, the machines, the control plane, metrics and observability, and the deployment pipelines. The stack is mostly CNCF: a manifest of sizes, instance types and core versions turned into Terraform by two tightly coupled in-house tools, infractl and federated-infra; a control plane provisioned with Ansible and Kubespray (in his words, lots of relatively horrible Ansible); Helm for application deploys; and a command-and-control cluster running the automation, all stitched together by pipelines in a workflow engine such as Argo.

At that scale, configuration and version combinations become the critical point of failure. The slide-ware pipeline always looks green. The real one has a misconfigured cluster breaking Terraform rendering, a fix you thought was backward compatible that was not, and the engineer who pushed at 4:47 on a Friday before a week of PTO, found by everyone else at 9:24 on Monday.

Combinatorial testing of every version is intractable. Unit tests stop at the component boundary. Full integration environments get expensive fast, especially when every use case of the platform wants its own environment and nobody wants theirs changed often. And semantic versioning, he notes, is not respected as much as we might like.

## How does a grenade test run?

They split failures into two kinds: before a control plane exists (broken config, Terraform or Ansible) and after (application incompatibility, bad networking, misconfigured base images). Then:

1. Identify the core tools most likely to break the control plane: infractl, federated-infra, the Kubernetes provisioning step and the base image.
2. When any of them releases, a monitoring pull request triggers a pipeline that pulls the latest versions of the others and brings up minimal clusters in several places, for example the private data centre, AWS and a Cluster API cluster.
3. Check the control plane is healthy, install base applications, run minimal tests.
4. Record the version combination as passed or failed in a log committed to the main branch; on failure, identify the faulting component and notify the engineer via blame.

Because it always pulls latest, it also nudges teams towards current versions. It runs in a mimic of production with the production pipelines, without paging, and it is not a chaos monkey.

## The cluster that stays up

The clever extension: the latest successful grenade cluster is left running as a permanent test target, and the previous one is destroyed. New Helm chart versions are deployed against it automatically and can optionally be merged straight into the integration environment if they work, which shrinks drift between development and production. Teams can plug in their own tests, for example networking expectations.

## Where it sits, and what it does not do

On his comprehensive-versus-maintainable chart, grenade testing sits between stubbed integration tests and full integration and system tests: broad brush, mostly automated, low cost. Manual acceptance testing stays at the far end, "which may well be the worst job maybe ever".

He is candid about the limits. Figuring out who to blame is hard when one version bump carries several pull requests, or a flaky API or capacity shortage fails the run. It does not validate application behaviour, only that things deploy. Platform apps like a CNI can break clusters in creative ways unrelated to base images. AWS can fail where the private data centre passes because the Terraform differs. And it needs engineering time to maintain.

The wins: more confidence in releases, automatically generated compatibility information, build success data to judge platform quality, and no per-application test environments to keep current. His favourite before-and-after: the first challenge for a new platform engineer is still building your first cluster, but now at least the versions are known to have worked once.

It is a concept rather than an open-source project, and Mounty credits colleagues Jon-Paul Sullivan and Lorne Hyde for the build.

## Who should watch

Platform teams running many clusters with in-house provisioning tools, and anyone whose integration environment has become a political negotiation. It is a short talk with a reusable idea.

Title: The best automation is the one you can hand to the next team
Description: Mandi Walls (PagerDuty) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on reducing toil by turning siloed expertise into safe, auditable self-service automation
Body:
Mandi Walls, DevOps Advocate at PagerDuty, makes a sharp point at Conf42 DevOps 2024: the automation that pays off most is not the script you run for yourself but the one you design so another team can run it safely without you. Write automation for delegation, treat it as an internal product with users, and toil starts moving off the expert's plate instead of piling up in a ticket queue.

It is a vendor-light talk; PagerDuty and its Rundeck-based automation platform get a mention only in the last minute.

## Why is Alice stuck in a ticket queue for a sandbox?

Walls builds the talk around one painfully familiar example. Alice, a developer on a microservice, needs a sanity-check environment in the development cloud account before pushing to the main pipeline. Compliance rules mean she cannot create it herself, so she files a ticket. FinOps reviews it first and bounces it if her team is over budget or has too many old environments. If it passes, it joins the cloud ops queue and gets done eventually.

Nobody in the story is doing anything wrong. Each team has real expertise: developers know libraries and runtimes, FinOps knows spend and budgets, cloud ops knows access, security and how it all fits together. As organisations grow, that expertise silos naturally and is hard to cross-train. The result is that "a lot of the work that goes into getting software from idea to production has nothing to do with the application code itself," Mandi Walls said at Conf42 DevOps 2024.

## Is automation AI?

A short side quest, because people ask. AI can help you write automation, with more luck if your stack is open source and well documented online, and less if it is homegrown or hidden behind a support portal. But automation is not AI: it does not learn and grow with your systems, and you still invest people hours in maintaining it. No margarita while the scripts run themselves.

She is equally frank about the drawbacks: loss of expertise (keep newer engineers in the workflow so they can handle what the automation cannot), brittleness (automation must change when the services and dependencies change), and the bad-management mirror image of the margarita dream, the boss asking why anyone is still employed.

## What makes automation safe to delegate?

Borrowing from Lee Atchison's book Architecting for Scale, she lists the properties automation should share with good software: testable, flexible rather than hard-coded, reviewable, in version control, applicable to related systems rather than a one-off, and repeatable and auditable. Her rant on the shared-systems point is worth the price of admission: two teams on either side of a cubicle wall running the same platform but compiled separately, so binary incompatible that they cannot share a single script.

Delegation adds user-facing requirements, which is where she draws the line to platform engineering:

- **Support how users work**: some want a CLI, some a web button, some a Backstage module.
- **Helpful results**: not just an error, but that you are over budget or already have six environments and should clean one up.
- **Consistency**: the same naming, options and error style everywhere; no jargon or inside jokes.
- **Documentation in context**, so people do not come back to you on Slack.

In the finished version of the Alice story, she logs into the automation platform, sees the jobs for her team, clicks provision, the budget check runs without a human, and every run is logged. When her colleague Ben finds the account full on Friday, he can see Alice's environment from Thursday and ask whether she is done with it.

## What should you automate first?

Two lenses. The first plots tasks on simple-to-sophisticated against no-impact-to-high-impact; for incident response that runs from read-only info gathering and performance checks, through restarts and diagnostics, up to multi-service rolling restarts, rollback and redeploy, and failover. The second is the classic XKCD frequency-times-duration chart: if cloud ops provisions environments 40 times a week, the hours add up fast. Even quarterly jobs are worth automating, she adds, precisely because nobody remembers how to do them.

Then there is the maturity path: automation opportunities in the backlog, human-initiated automation (where most of it lives), automation with oversight on a trigger, automation with a fallback to a human when it fails, and finally tasks that are just monitored as metrics instead of tickets.

## Who should watch

SREs and ops engineers drowning in request tickets, and anyone starting a platform team who wants a framework for deciding what to turn into self-service. It pairs well with Dylan Etkin's developer-side take on toil from the same event.

Title: AI that writes the Terraform and the IAM policy, so you design the system
Description: Saurav Panda (Cloud Code AI) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on AI for DevOps resource management, from natural-language IaC to least-privilege IAM and self-healing
Body:
Saurav Panda, founder and CEO of Cloud Code AI, makes a big-picture case at Conf42 DevOps 2024: DevOps has become a pile of automation with a steep learning curve, and AI's best job is to flatten that curve by writing the infrastructure code, the IAM policies and the first round of fixes. His two case studies, a serverless API and an AWS IAM policy generated from plain English, are the concrete bits; the rest is a map of where AI could fit in the pipeline.

Honest scope: this is a short overview talk from someone building a product in this space, with demos of Cloud Code AI's own tools. Go in expecting a tour, not a manual.

## Why does DevOps need an AI layer at all?

Panda opens with a quick history: DevOps as an idea in 2007, the #DevOps hashtag debates by 2010, adoption into the Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) in 2015, high performers treating it as the norm by 2016, and security, privacy, policy and data folded into DevOps culture by 2019. Every step added tools, and every tool added something to learn. His closing argument is that the community's real goal should be to bring that learning curve down, so engineers spend their time designing infrastructure rather than doing manual grunt work.

## Infrastructure as code, written from a sentence

The traditional route to IaC is writing it by hand or adapting predefined templates, which he calls time-consuming and repetitive. The alternative he shows: describe the serverless API you want in natural language, and the tool picks the resources (a DynamoDB table, Lambda functions, API Gateway), wires up the IAM permissions between them, and produces a Terraform file on deploy.

"This is like a 400 line long terraform file generated in minutes," Saurav Panda said at Conf42 DevOps 2024. The slides also point to GitHub Copilot as a head start for writing IaC. Beyond generation, he lists proactive assistance: AI reviewing an infrastructure design for cost savings and efficiency, and acting as an overseer of pipeline quality and security for SREs.

## Least privilege without the guesswork

The second case study is the one worth pausing on, because anyone who has written an AWS policy by trial and error knows the pain. You ask for the services and the permissions you need, in plain language, and the generator returns a least-privilege policy to paste in. Panda calls it the tip of the iceberg: with access to how services actually connect, AI could generate dynamic IAM policies from usage patterns and behaviour, for services as well as people.

The same security section covers AI scanning code for vulnerabilities and suggesting fixes, and automating both standard and user-defined compliance checks.

## Optimisation, testing and self-healing

The rest of the talk sketches the operations side:

- **Infrastructure and resource optimisation**: use historical data, usage patterns and performance metrics to anticipate demand and allocate resources with less human intervention.
- **Automated testing**: generate test cases and push them through the pipeline.
- **Self-healing**: detect and resolve issues as they arise, before they escalate.
- **Predictive analytics**: notify teams before problems occur.
- **Anomaly detection**: scan code and data for irregularities and start corrective action.

He frames all of it with an aviation analogy: automation is an autopilot, which does not replace the pilot but lets them fly with more precision. His bolder predictions are that software will get cheaper to build, and that one day a cloud provider will handle IPs, domains and wiring on its own, which he admits is a little bit in the future.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers who want a quick map of where AI tooling was heading in DevOps at the start of 2024, especially IaC generation and IAM. If you want benchmarks, failure modes or how to review AI-written Terraform safely, this talk does not go there; pair it with something more hands-on.

Title: Oracle's Autonomous Database is a robot DBA that never asks for a raise
Description: Rich Niemiec (Viscosity North America) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on Oracle ADW and ATP, in-database machine learning and why the DBA job changes rather than ends
Body:
Rich Niemiec, Chief Innovation Officer at Viscosity North America and a long-time Oracle author, spends his Conf42 DevOps 2024 talk asking the question every DBA has asked about automation: will the robot take my job? His answer, after a fast tour of Oracle Autonomous Data Warehouse (ADW) and Autonomous Transaction Processing (ATP): it takes the patching, tuning and provisioning, and leaves you the work that is closer to the business.

Fair warning on scope: this is an Oracle-centric talk with a lot of ground covered, from database provisioning to support vector machines to Gartner hype cycles and Twilight Zone clips. It works best as a tour of what autonomous Oracle could do at the start of 2024.

## Why a self-driving database?

Niemiec frames autonomy against DBA workload: 78% of DBAs report unplanned downtime, automation is lacking, and two out of three struggle to give full security protection. Oracle's answer, first shipped with the 18c database, is a database that is self-driving, self-securing and self-repairing: it applies patches before you know there was a risk, tunes itself, and recovers on its own. Viewed that way, the autonomous database "is really a robot. It just doesn't get up and walk around," Rich Niemiec said at Conf42 DevOps 2024. Like Alexa and Siri, it works 24/7 and never asks for a raise.

He also slips in practical advice for Oracle shops: be on at least 19c, the long-term release, with 23 next and innovation releases in between.

## ADW or ATP?

The two flavours are tuned for opposite query shapes:

- **ADW** stores data in columnar format with in-memory column storage and data summaries. Good for analytics: summing a column, computing all the salaries.
- **ATP** stores rows and caches individual records in memory, with automatic indexing. Good for response time: finding one salary.

Where a workload sits in between, he leans towards ATP. ATP's automatic indexing is the interesting part: machine learning watches the SQL on the system, proposes candidate indexes and execution plan changes, and applies them after testing and validation. Under both sits Exadata with Real Application Clusters for node failover and Active Data Guard for regional failover, which he says gives an SLA of 99.995%.

## How long does it take to stand one up?

This is where the demo earns its keep, because the numbers are refreshingly small. Provisioning an ATP database took two minutes; ADW took a minute and 20 seconds. Stopping took 25 seconds, restarting 30, and scaling from one CPU to two was a menu click. You can also set an auto start-stop schedule, take full clones or refreshable clones, and use a performance hub to see which SQL is eating database time, I/O or CPU.

He points to the free tier at oracle.com/cloud/free and its 30-day trial of everything else, and compares the always-free allowance with AWS: two databases instead of one, four instances instead of one, 200 GB of block volume instead of 30. He also reminds the audience who still has to watch the bill, shut idle databases down and write the security policies: the DBA or the DevOps engineer.

## Machine learning without leaving the database

The second half moves to Oracle Machine Learning notebooks (Zeppelin-based, with Jupyter available), SQL, PL/SQL, Python or R. His method is the classic one: start from the business problem, pick the function (classification, clustering, anomaly detection, regression, association rules, time series), then the algorithm, train on 60% of the data and test on the other 40%.

The examples are memorable: a one-class support vector machine to flag anomalous customers, a decision tree telling a lawyer to take a $30,000 settlement because proceeding loses $2,500 on average, a classifier picking who will buy a Chicago Bears credit card. AutoML is the punchline: a notebook that took him two or three days by hand was rebuilt, with every algorithm tried and scored, in four minutes.

He closes with generative AI: the transformer as the leap past RNNs, hallucinations as the catch, grounding on your own data (via Oracle's Cohere partnership), and Oracle's new vector search, illustrated with a house-hunting app that finds a home like yours in another state.

## Who should watch

Oracle DBAs and DevOps engineers running Oracle who want a quick picture of what ADW, ATP and in-database ML can take off their plate. If you do not run Oracle, the job-security argument and the AutoML anecdote are the transferable bits.

Title: ChatGPT and Copilot are good pair programmers, but they don't read minds
Description: Mihaela-Roxana Ghidersa (Signant Health) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on bringing ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot into daily dev work, one prompt and one project at a time
Body:
Mihaela-Roxana Ghidersa, Technical Lead at Signant Health and a Microsoft MVP, gives a practical first tour of ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot at Conf42 DevOps 2024. Her main point is simple and still the one most teams skip: both tools are only as good as the context and instructions you hand them, so treat prompting as a skill and roll the tools out gradually.

This is an intro talk, recorded when GPT-4 was the new thing and Copilot Chat had just landed in the editor. If you already live in an AI-assisted editor, the demos will feel familiar. If your team is still deciding whether to let these tools near the codebase, the integration checklist at the end is the useful part.

## Two tools, two jobs

Ghidersa splits the pair cleanly. ChatGPT is the generalist: natural language in and out, it remembers earlier turns of a conversation, writes and explains code in many languages, and adapts tone and format to what you ask. She uses it well beyond code, from day-by-day holiday plans to getting the tone right in a feedback email.

Copilot is the specialist that sits in the editor. Trained on a large body of source code, it reads your existing code and comments and suggests completions, whole functions, refactorings and tests in real time, and it adapts once you correct it. She pushes back on the idea that it is a crutch for juniors: in her view it is a learning and exploration tool for everyone, because it surfaces patterns and practices as the code grows.

## Prompting is a communication skill

The talk's best line comes before the demos. "As amazing as these tools might be, they don't read minds," Mihaela-Roxana Ghidersa said at Conf42 DevOps 2024. Her prompting advice is compact:

- Give clear, precise instructions, with the details and criteria that matter.
- Know what the tool is built for: text, images or data analysis are different tools.
- Expect to iterate. Read the response, see what was missing (format, language, formality, JSON), and refine.
- Set a persona when it helps, for example asking for an answer as an experienced software architect would give it.

She adds a wry observation: we will patiently rephrase a question five times for a chatbot, then get annoyed when a colleague does not understand us the first time. Learning to prompt might make us better at talking to people too.

## What the demos show

In ChatGPT-4 she asks for the SOLID principles, gets a long answer, then narrows it: real-world examples, short explanations. Then she asks for a presentation outline for "the first principle" without restating which list she means, to show the model keeping context, and finally asks for a shorter version aimed at a twelve-year-old.

In her editor she opens Copilot Chat on an old training project, asks it to explain a selected block of router code, and writes a comment asking for a function that calculates the time between two dates. The suggestions arrive, but generic ones, and she says that was deliberate: a thin project with little context gets thin answers, and a first session in a repo has not yet picked up its patterns.

## How should a team roll this out?

Her integration process reads like a sensible adoption plan:

- Understand the tool's capabilities and set realistic expectations.
- Pick tools that fit the project, the team's skills and existing systems, and that you can configure.
- Integrate gradually: try it on small projects before your product.
- Put quality control on every output you use, and keep giving feedback.
- Mind data privacy, security and bias; use the tools to enhance people, not replace them.

She closes on ethics and long-term impact, including the environmental cost of scaling AI infrastructure, and with a list of starting points: GitHub's Copilot docs, OpenAI's text generation guide, Microsoft Learn on Copilot and building a private ChatGPT with Azure OpenAI, and DeepLearning.AI.

## Who should watch

Developers and team leads who have not yet used Copilot or ChatGPT seriously and want a calm, hype-light introduction, or someone preparing an internal brown-bag on the subject. Experienced users can skip to the integration checklist.

Title: Treat every toil automation as a cheap experiment
Description: Dylan Etkin (Sleuth) at Conf42 DevOps 2024 on killing developer toil with low-lift automations you can try, measure and throw away
Body:
Dylan Etkin, co-founder and CEO of Sleuth, argues at Conf42 DevOps 2024 that the best fix for developer toil is not one heroic automation but a stream of small, low-lift ones you can treat like experiments: switch one on, measure it, keep it or bin it. If an automation takes a week to build, you get one shot at it; if it takes a click, you get dozens.

It is a short talk with a clear vendor angle (he says so himself near the end), but the framework holds up without the product.

## What counts as toil?

Etkin, who worked at Atlassian in the days when tests still ran on his laptop, defines developer-experience toil as the repetitive tasks that matter but deliver nothing to customers. He gives three tells: things "our team always does" by hand (move the ticket, ping the PM), manual steps in a workflow (find everyone involved in a change and ask in Slack before a deploy), and syncing state between systems. His verdict on that last one: Jira is the place that is never in touch with reality.

He frames automation as a staircase: automated unit and synthetic tests around 2001, infrastructure as code from Puppet and Chef to Terraform around 2005, then pipelines with no manual steps. Each step made the next possible, and the cloud tools most teams now share (Git hosting with code review, an issue tracker, CI/CD, PagerDuty) are what make cross-tool automations practical today.

## Why does the automation have to be low lift?

This is the heart of the talk. Every engineer knows the trap of the side quest that ate the sprint. "What happens almost nine times out of ten is that I start working on the automation. It's far more complicated than I thought," Dylan Etkin said at Conf42 DevOps 2024.

Low-lift automations change the economics. A context switch that costs a minute is never worth a week of tooling, but twelve of them are worth a few clicks each. And cheap automations become a continuous-improvement loop: hypothesis, experiment, measure, repeat. His second trait is cultural: tooling defines culture, because an automation enforces what the team already agreed. Requiring an issue key in every pull request title is a team norm; the bot just gets to be the bad guy instead of a colleague.

## Four kinds of automation worth having

Etkin sorts what teams do today into four buckets, with one example each:

- **Guardrails**: the we-always and we-never rules. Never merge during an incident. Cap pull requests at a number of changed files, since DORA-style deploy frequency rises as batch size falls. When you reformat the whole codebase, you skip the check, and the exceptions tell you whether the rule fits.
- **Notifications**: context-sensitive nudges, not red dots. A draft PR open for eight days of an agreed ten gets a reminder; a review goal of ten hours gets a ping at hour seven.
- **Actions**: if this, then that across systems. A PagerDuty incident locks pull requests in GitHub; a production deploy moves the Jira issue to deployed, so support can tell a customer the fix is live rather than guessing from a merge date.
- **Workflows**: the combination of the above that carries work from idea to launch.

## The incident lock, and the deploy that made it worse

His favourite workflow is locking merges while production is in an incident. He had done it for years by posting a do-not-deploy warning in Slack, which fails for the obvious reason: someone does not read Slack and hits merge. Worse, a deploy mid-incident can replace the infrastructure and turn CPUs at 90% into a hard-down outage. Using PagerDuty as the source of truth and putting the merge block in GitHub, where developers actually click, makes the rule enforce itself and lift itself when the incident resolves.

Sleuth's own pre-production smoke test flow shows the experiment loop in practice. They started with plain Slack approvals before promotion to production, then auto-promoted small changes after 10 minutes of healthy monitoring, then let a quick-fix label on a pull request skip the gate entirely. Each change was cheap, so they could see how it fit the way they worked.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and platform folks who keep hearing "devex" and want a concrete list of things to switch on next sprint. Etkin closes with a plug for Sleuth's automations marketplace and is candid that most of any catalogue will not fit your team: maybe three to five will, and 25 will not. Either way, the four buckets are a useful audit checklist on their own.

Title: Conf42 IoT 2023: devices that touch the physical world
Description: The Conf42 IoT 2023 roundup - 13 talks on IoT testing and protocols, device security, the carbon cost of connected things, and edge data tooling.
Body:
[Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2023](https://www.conf42.com/iot2023) went out on December 14 with 13 talks, and the thread that tied them together was a plain one: IoT is the part of software that touches physical things. Water meters leak, robots move, firmware lands on devices nobody can reach, and every connected sensor draws power. The talks split cleanly into four tracks (deep dives, security, sustainability and tools), with speakers from AWS, Cloudera, StreamNative, StarTree, Signify (Philips Lighting), Energy Vault, OWASP and a handful of smaller engineering shops.

## How do you test and wire a system made of layers?

[Vipin Jain](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Vipin_Jain_endtoend_testing_strategy) of Metacube Software opened the deep-dive track with an end-to-end testing strategy for IoT. His argument: testing each component is not enough when many applications work in tandem, so deconstruct the system into layers, build small automation around each, and blend unit, integration and end-to-end tests. The more complex the solution, the more the unit tests matter. His summary of the field is fair: IoT testing is challenging, not difficult.

[Samarth Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Samarth_Gupta_communication_protocols) of Think Future Technologies took the layer below that, the protocols. Wired first (UART, I2C, SPI between sensors and microcontrollers, Modbus on the factory floor), then the wireless options that seem to multiply every other week. It's a useful map for anyone who knows HTTP well and has never had to pick a bus.

[Mayank Aggarwal](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Mayank_Aggarwal_accelerate_enterprise_technology) of CG Infinity covered the enterprise angle, showing with live demos how companies can add IoT to their processes while keeping existing systems intact.

## What can a few devices and a model actually do?

Two talks put machine learning on real hardware. [Vishwajeetsingh Desurkar](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Vishwajeetsingh_Desurkar_dots_magic_ruby) of SimplySmart Technologies, which builds end-to-end water management, showed anomaly detection for maintenance problems and abnormal usage, written in Ruby. Yes, Ruby, and he spends a section answering exactly that objection.

[Youhana Hana](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Youhana_Hana_build_smart_robot_aws) of AWS went bigger: robot fleets. With an estimate of 20 million robots by 2030, he walked through AWS IoT RoboRunner for mixed fleets, a CI/CD pipeline that tests new behaviour in RoboMaker simulation before the container images reach real robots, and IoT Greengrass for over-the-air updates at the edge.

## Why does IoT security hurt more?

The security track started from the stakes. [Susie Su](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Susie_Su_ai_revolution_security_workforce) of Signify (Philips Lighting) mapped where AI and IoT meet, walked five real AIoT use cases and made the case that IoT security has to come first, because a compromised device acts on the physical world rather than just leaking a database.

[Swapnil Shinde](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Swapnil_Shinde_blockchain_immutable_firmware) of OWASP looked at firmware distribution across the 15 billion connected devices he cited from a 2023 report. His design records update hashes on a blockchain (public, or private with Hyperledger or Polkadot Substrate) with the binary on IPFS, so a tampered image fails verification, and he demoed it from a hackathon project. [Raed Ahsan](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Raed_Ahsan_steganography_hackers) of Rsecurity showed the attacker's side: steganography, hiding payloads and stolen data inside ordinary media files, as a way into individual IoT devices.

## Does a connected device have a carbon bill?

Yes, and two talks put numbers on it. [Dr. Anubha Jain](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Dr_Anubha_Jain_green_sustainability_smart_living) of IIS University projected IoT devices growing from 9.7 billion to 29.4 billion between 2020 and 2030 and argued for building hardware-, energy- and carbon-efficient applications from the start, through green coding, low-code development and automated quality monitoring.

[Olivier Bierlaire](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Olivier_Bierlaire_your_cloud_emits_co2) of Carbonifer moved the question to the backend those devices talk to. His talk explains the three emission scopes, the Green Software Foundation's SCI (software carbon intensity) formula, and how to estimate emissions when you run on a public cloud and can't put a probe on the hardware. If you think the cloud is someone else's chimney, this is the 30 minutes that changes your mind.

## The tools that move edge data

The tools track was all about getting data off devices and making sense of it fast. [Tim Spann](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Tim_Spann_David_Kjerrumgaard_flipn_stack_edge_ai_flink_nifi_pulsar) of Cloudera and David Kjerrumgaard of StreamNative presented the FLiPN stack: Apache NiFi (with MiNiFi agents on devices) to scoop data up, Apache Pulsar to carry it, including a topic per device at scale, and Apache Flink to process and join it. Everything is Apache, which is either a feature or a dependency diagram, depending on your mood.

[Madhumita Mantri and Suvodeep Pyne](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Madhumita_Mantri_Suvodeep_Pyne_business_metrics_startree_thirdeye) of StarTree tackled what happens after the data lands: troubleshooting real-time business metrics with StarTree ThirdEye, anomaly detection on large time series, and a live demo of drilling from an alert to its cause. [Tadeh Hakopian](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Tadeh_Hakopian_information_visualization_digital_twins) of Energy Vault closed the track with digital twins for buildings, built from IoT, cloud and data, and a sensible plea to start simple and agree on shared data standards before reaching for the 3D model.

Title: A digital twin is only as good as your sensor inventory
Description: Tadeh Hakopian (Energy Vault) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on digital twins for buildings: inventory the devices and agree the terms before the 3D model
Body:
The 3D model is the part of a digital twin everyone wants to demo, and the last part you should build. At Conf42 IoT 2023, Tadeh Hakopian, Program Manager at Energy Vault, gives a practical tour of digital twins for buildings and industrial sites, and his advice keeps coming back to the unglamorous order of work: know your devices, agree your vocabulary, get the data chain working, and only then pick a visualisation.

It is an overview talk, broad rather than deep, from someone with a construction and design background who has clearly sat in meetings where telecom, security and architecture people used the same word for three different things.

## What is a digital twin, minus the marketing?

A digital representation of a physical object or system, updated in real time. His ingredients are IoT, cloud and data. His use cases run from factory robot arms to vehicles, wearables, building energy use and a bridge tracked for displacement over time. The benefits are the ones facility managers care about: live status without sending someone out, maintenance history in one place instead of binders, and predictions from that history.

## Why start with standards?

Because there are too many of them, not too few. His point is that the gap is shared terminology, not technical specifications, and he points to the Digital Twin Consortium as the body trying to harmonise the language. Even a phrase like structured store of information can mean a SQL database, GIS, CAD, point clouds or IoT streams, so spell it out early.

## What does the stack look like?

Devices connect to a gateway (the device usually has none of its own, and a remote site with poor bandwidth makes that a real bottleneck), then middleware stores and processes the data, then applications present it. He uses Azure Digital Twins, IoT Hub and Cosmos DB as one worked reference, notes AWS and others have equivalents, and shows a Palantir Foundry ontology model on live flight data. His honest warning on tooling: "There isn't anything so far that I would really say you can rely on for the next couple of years, at least, maybe longer."

So: keep it simple and inventory first. "If you don't know what you got, you can't use it," Tadeh Hakopian said at Conf42 IoT 2023. A home already has thermostats, cameras and door cameras; an Arduino board stuck to a wall can report temperature. His best example is small hygrometers retrofitted to catch leaks, since leaks routinely cause damage in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, so a modest investment heads off a serious cost overrun. At the other end of the scale sits Ford's Dearborn plant, with its major equipment on IoT and mapped in 3D.

## Which visualisation should you pick?

The one your end user can read. He walks through 3D models (an Autodesk example with hourly temperature and lighting per room; most projects already have a model you can reuse, or you can scan one with Matterport or a phone), VR for remote equipment training, plain floor plans for occupancy and that one cold corner, and asset clusters, like a hospital locating its gurneys. That last one solves a real problem: when Gus from facilities is off for the day, nobody knows where anything is. Game engines handle the messy part, merging incompatible engineering formats through Datasmith into Unreal. Helsinki's city-scale twin is built on CityGML.

## How do you get one funded?

Owners pay, so build the business case: understand the RFP, run a pilot, describe the ROI so the accountants are happy too. Get on the leading edge of adoption, because joining late means a rushed kludge, and he has worked on many. Then treat it as a cycle: assess, plan, document, train, release, analyse, update, repeat.

## Who should watch

Engineers and project managers new to digital twins, especially in buildings and facilities, who want the map before the territory. If you already run a twin in production, this is a refresher, not new ground.

Title: Raspberry Pi to Flink SQL in one pipeline with the FLiPN stack
Description: Tim Spann (Cloudera) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on the FLiPN stack, Apache Flink, NiFi and Pulsar, carrying edge sensor data into streaming SQL
Body:
Getting sensor data off a device is the easy part; getting it somewhere a SQL query can join it is where edge projects stall. At Conf42 IoT 2023, Tim Spann, Principal Developer Advocate at Cloudera, and David Kjerrumgaard, Developer Advocate at StreamNative, show the FLiPN stack: Apache NiFi to collect, Apache Pulsar to buffer, Apache Flink to process, running end to end from a Raspberry Pi 400 to a live Flink SQL query.

The pitch is that everything is Apache and already wired together. David wrote the NiFi-to-Pulsar connector, and there is a mature Flink connector for Pulsar, so the pattern is mostly configuration rather than glue code.

## Where does each piece run?

Not all of it at the edge. "You're probably not running Flink on the edge," Tim Spann said at Conf42 IoT 2023. MiNiFi, the small NiFi agent, sits on the device; Pulsar may live a level up; Flink is usually downstream, taking billions of data points and running real-time SQL on them. Tim's point is that even with all three in one Docker container on a laptop, the code and SQL do not change when you move to a real cluster.

The slides back the scale claims with two production examples: Comcast using Flink on 3B+ data points a day from 25 million customers for real-time ML predictions, and Splunk ingesting 10 petabytes a day through Pulsar for cyber-security detection.

## Why Pulsar in the middle?

David's job in the talk is the case for Pulsar, and he does not undersell it: "Everything Kafka can do but better and more is how I describe it." His list: queuing and streaming semantics from day one, infinite retention with tiered storage, dead letter queues, scheduled delivery, rebalance-free scaling with no data movement, geo-replication (it was built at Yahoo in 2012 for exactly that), multi-tenancy and encryption. Pulsar also speaks Kafka, MQTT and RabbitMQ protocols besides its own.

The number that matters for IoT is topics. Tim cites more than a million; David corrects him live: "It's actually 10 million now, Tim, I've updated that 10 million." He adds that Oxia, the ZooKeeper replacement, should push that further. That makes a topic per device, or per sensor, a reasonable design rather than a dare. The pair then argue, pleasantly, about whether anyone wants to write a SQL join across 10 million topics. The answer is the usual one: it depends on your architecture, and Pulsar no longer decides it for you.

## Why NiFi instead of a logging agent?

Logging agents are simple and edge-only. NiFi brings guaranteed delivery, back pressure, prioritised queuing, data provenance, version control and hundreds of processors. In the demo the Raspberry Pi 400 runs a MiNiFi agent that calls a shell script, which runs Python to read the sensors (carbon dioxide and volatile chemicals), then posts JSON over HTTP to a NiFi 1.24 listener. NiFi cleans it up, pushes it into a Pulsar topic, and a Flink SQL query picks it up and feeds a materialised view exposed as a REST endpoint for a dashboard. Each new reading travels the whole chain while you watch.

## What was new in NiFi 2.0?

Tim also tours the NiFi 2.0 release candidate on JDK 21. It brings Python processors, including ones for chunking documents, calling ChatGPT and writing to vector stores such as Chroma and Pinecone. A new processor listens to Slack. Process groups can run stateless, as a start-to-finish job, and parameters can come from 1Password, a database, Azure Key Vault or AWS secrets. Flow analysis rules let admins steer new users away from deprecated components.

## Who should watch

Data engineers building IoT ingestion who want a working reference pipeline, and Kafka users curious what Pulsar adds. It is an advocates' overview with a short demo, not a tuning session, and the two hosts clearly enjoy it.

Title: An anomaly alert is half the job; ThirdEye goes after the why
Description: Madhumita Mantri (StarTree) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on real-time anomaly detection and root-cause drill-downs with StarTree ThirdEye on Apache Pinot
Body:
A dashboard that shows a spike tells you something broke. It does not tell you which city, which device or which holiday did it. At Conf42 IoT 2023, Madhumita Mantri, Product Lead at StarTree, and Suvodeep Pyne, Founding Engineer at StarTree, walk through StarTree ThirdEye, an anomaly detection and root-cause tool built on Apache Pinot, and spend most of the half hour on the part after the alert fires.

It is a vendor talk with a live demo of the product. It is also an honest one about the boring work underneath: if your data model is wrong, your real-time alerts will be slow and expensive.

## Why is monitoring real-time metrics hard in the first place?

Madhumita frames the problem with an IoT example: devices spread over many locations start heating up, and you want to know before they shut down. Her list of obstacles is the familiar one for anyone who has run streaming pipelines: data volume and velocity, data quality and consistency, integrating sources that are partly online and partly offline, and latency that gets worse as the data grows.

Her opening line sums up the talk's stance. "Don't wait for a problem to become a crisis before you take action," Madhumita Mantri said at Conf42 IoT 2023.

Anomalies, in her framing, come in more than one shape: a sudden spike or dip, or a gradual change over time that nobody catches by eye. And the metric underneath can be stable, seasonal, trending upward or spiking at regular intervals, which is why one threshold rule does not fit all of them. Building that yourself means stitching storage, algorithms and an investigation UI together, and that stitching is the pitch for ThirdEye.

## What does the demo actually show?

Suvodeep runs a demo instance on a simulated rideshare dataset (think cab rides, with wait time as the metric). He creates an alert on summed wait time, flips the granularity from daily to hourly to show the seasonality, and picks the Matrix Profile algorithm, which he describes as a StarTree algorithm for patch-level analysis. With default settings it flags the one odd spike.

The more useful part is the multidimensional alert. Instead of watching total wait time, he slices it by ride type and city, and ThirdEye works out which slices carry the most weight. New York dominates; San Francisco economy rides are about 16% of the traffic. One alert then watches every one of those time series.

## How does it get from anomaly to cause?

Clicking an anomaly opens the root-cause analysis view. The top contributors point at traffic conditions, and the heat map backs it up: moderate traffic up 161% in the window, heavy traffic roughly tripled. ThirdEye also overlays events, in this case public holidays (Armed Forces Day turns up as a candidate), and the investigation can be saved and shared with the team, with a note on what the analyst concluded.

The second use case is sensor data: a temperature alert per device ID rather than on the overall sum, where the drill-down suggests more devices simply became active. That is the IoT angle in one screen: per-device alerts without writing one alert per device.

## The part most teams skip: modelling the data

The under-the-hood section is worth the watch even if you never touch ThirdEye. An anomaly detector queries constantly, every minute or five, so schema choices turn into compute bills. Suvodeep's example: "if you have your timestamp as a string, for example, these are typically much more expensive in terms of compute power to parse rather than if you have something like a long". Pre-computed time buckets avoid runtime transforms, and the StarTree index pre-computes metrics across dimensions so a query over a high-cardinality dataset is not a table scan.

He closes on plumbing: notifications by email and Slack, with PagerDuty listed as coming soon at the time, webhooks for your own integrations, an API-first design, a Helm chart for Kubernetes, and a community edition on GitHub that covers most of what the demo showed.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers who already have metrics in a real-time store and are tired of alerts that only say something is wrong. Skip it if you want algorithm internals; this is a product walkthrough plus solid data modelling advice.

Title: An m4.large in Ireland emits about 5 grams of CO2 an hour
Description: Olivier Bierlaire (Carbonifer) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on measuring cloud carbon with the SCI formula, then cutting it by right-sizing and carbon-aware shifting
Body:
Moving to the cloud doesn't make emissions disappear, it moves them into your scope 3. At Conf42 IoT 2023, Olivier Bierlaire, founder of Carbonifer, shows how to estimate what your cloud infrastructure emits with the Green Software Foundation's Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) formula, which tools fill in the numbers you can't see, and how to cut the total with right-sizing, region choice and carbon-aware scheduling.

It is one of the more practical sustainability talks around: a worked calculation, a tool list, and a set of reductions you could start on Monday.

## How big is the problem?

His figures: data centres use 20 to 25% of the electricity consumed by the digital sector, which itself is about 1.3% of electricity worldwide, excluding crypto mining (IEA). Digital technology accounts for around 4% of greenhouse gas emissions and its energy use grows about 9% a year (The Shift Project). The cloud emits about 330 megatons of CO2 a year, comparable to France or the UK, and more than civil aviation.

Companies have reasons to care beyond conscience: ESG funds, hiring and retention, customer retention, cost, and regulation. He covers the EU's CSRD (large companies from 2024, listed SMEs from 2026, scopes 1, 2 and 3), the SFDR for financed emissions, and the SEC climate disclosure rule with scope 3 optional.

## Where does cloud fall in the GHG scopes?

Scope 1 is direct emissions (your diesel generator), scope 2 is purchased energy (your electricity bill), scope 3 is everything else in the value chain. On a private cloud, the electricity is scope 2 and the servers you bought are scope 3. On a public cloud, it is all scope 3. Where scope 3 ends is up to you: Mozilla's 2019 report counted people using Firefox and found 98% of its footprint came from product use.

## The SCI formula, worked through

SCI adds usage emissions (energy × PUE × grid carbon intensity) to a share of embodied emissions from manufacturing, delivery and disposal of the hardware. His example, from the slides:

- An AWS m4.large (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) at 50% use: about 10 Wh, or 0.01 kWh.
- PUE in AWS Ireland: 1.2.
- Grid intensity in Ireland: 316 gCO2/kWh.
- Usage: 0.01 × 1.2 × 316 = 3.8 gCO2eq per hour.
- Add 1.2 g of embodied emissions per hour and the SCI is 5 gCO2eq per hour.

The units are CO2 equivalent because generation also emits gases like methane, which he puts at 84 times more potent than CO2.

Grid intensity and PUE are easy to find (Electricity Maps shows live grid intensity). The hard parts on a public cloud are the hardware's energy profile, which CPU and memory you actually have, embodied emissions, and future energy mix. Estimates and coefficients help, but carefully: an energy-efficient Arm-based Graviton instance can come in under 1 on the coefficient scale while a legacy CPU climbs to 8.

## Which tools fill the gaps?

From one-click to fine-grained: the AWS Carbon Footprint Tool, Google Cloud Carbon Footprint and the Microsoft Azure Sustainability Calculator for monthly per-account totals; Cloud Carbon Footprint, open source, which reads your cloud bills and gives daily emissions; Scaphandre, which measures real CPU power if you have physical machines; the Climatiq and Boavizta APIs, which take an instance type and duration and return usage and embodied emissions; and his own open-source Carbonifer, which reads a Terraform project and estimates emissions before you apply it. The Green Software Foundation's awesome-green-software list has more.

## Cutting it: FinOps, then carbon awareness

The reductions start with the obvious: optimise the code so you don't buy bigger machines to hide it, pick the right instance type and the latest CPU generation, and right-size. A well-run hyperscaler beats a room of underused on-premises servers kept for traffic spikes. FinOps practices like night-time shutdowns and autoscaling groups save money and carbon together. One caveat: reserved instances save a lot of money, but you still run the same number of instances and emit the same CO2.

Region choice is the cheapest big lever: on Google Cloud's European regions he shows Paris at about 70 grams of CO2 per kWh and europe-central2 above 700.

Then the carbon-aware patterns:

- **Temporal shifting**: run batch work, video processing, model training, DB indexing, when the grid is cleaner, as Google does for its own workloads.
- **Demand shaping**: do less when the grid is dirty, such as dropping video quality or running fewer CI workers, so PRs build a little slower during a CO2 peak.
- **Spatial shifting**: route load to the greenest region. A HotCarbon'23 paper he cites added grid carbon intensity to a multi-cloud load balancer and cut emissions by 21% with no latency compromise, or 51% with acceptable latency.

Olivier Bierlaire said at Conf42 IoT 2023: "You cannot reduce what you cannot measure." Collect usage metrics, estimate kWh, estimate grams per hour, then reduce and schedule.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers and FinOps people asked to report cloud emissions, and anyone who'd like a defensible number instead of a vendor dashboard they can't explain.

Title: Green IoT has two halves, and your code is one of them
Description: Dr. Anubha Jain (IIS University) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on green IoT, from energy-efficient chips and code to sleeping sensors and carbon-aware testing
Body:
Tens of billions of connected devices mean tens of billions of batteries, chargers and future landfill entries. At Conf42 IoT 2023, Dr. Anubha Jain, Director of the School of Computer Science & IT at IIS University, splits the response into two jobs: greening of IoT, which makes the hardware and software themselves efficient, and greening by IoT, which uses devices to cut energy and waste elsewhere. Her point for engineers is that software counts: it doesn't burn energy directly, but it decides how hard the hardware works.

It is a broad survey, academic in tone, more a map of the field than a close study of any one technique. If you want a structured overview to hang your own reading on, it does that well.

## Why IoT has an environmental bill

She starts with growth: Statista's figures show connected devices tripling from 9.7 billion in 2020 to 29.4 billion by 2030, most of them consumer devices. IPv6 helps make that possible, taking the address pool from 4.3 billion to 3.4×10^38. Dr. Anubha Jain said at Conf42 IoT 2023: "So the growth of IoT does not come for free." More devices mean more energy use, more batteries, more electronics production, and so more e-waste and greenhouse gas emissions.

Her answer is not less technology but greener technology: renewable power, energy-efficient procedures, and judicious use of what's already there.

## Greening by IoT: devices that save more than they cost

The use cases cover a lot of ground:

- **Water and energy metering** for households, offices and industry, with real-time usage sent to phones.
- **Aquaculture**, where IoT tracks fish health and water conditions and predicts feeding needs to cut waste.
- **Smart buildings** with demand-driven heating, cooling and lighting, and thermostats that learn preferences. She cites a reduction of roughly 15% in New York City's overall energy consumption during the pandemic from smart lighting.
- **Telemedicine and remote health monitoring**, **smart waste routing**, **wildlife monitoring** with drones and acoustic sensors, and connected collars for livestock.
- **The Internet of Energy**, where real-time consumption data lets grid operators forecast peaks and adjust supply.

## Greening of IoT: the hardware, then the code

On the device side, she describes a lifecycle of green design, production, deployment and disposal, with recyclability planned from the start. Chip design matters most: integrating sensors and processing on a single chip, and splitting processors into low- and high-compute cores with a scheduler that puts each task on the cheaper one.

Software gets the most interesting section. Applications should be hardware-, carbon- and energy-efficient, reduce network distance and spread carbon awareness. Language choice is part of that: she cites research comparing 27 programming languages on ten problems for energy, speed and memory, where C came out as one of the most energy-efficient.

Testing is the part most teams never think of. Every test run burns CPU time, so a near-zero-defect suite has a carbon footprint. Her suggestions: run tests on demand in virtualised cloud environments instead of dedicated rigs, select tests smartly rather than running everything, and shift testing left so bugs get caught before they cost repeated runs.

## The rules that apply to any device you ship

Her list of principles reads like an embedded engineer's checklist with a sustainability label:

- Turn off what isn't needed: sleep scheduling for sensors.
- Send only the data that's needed: predictive data delivery.
- Shorten the data path with smarter routing.
- Trade processing for communication, with data fusion.
- Use advanced communication such as MIMO.
- Prefer renewable power: solar, wind.
- Raise awareness with smart metering and notifications.

She extends this to the enabling tech too: smaller RFID tags made of biodegradable material, battery-free wireless sensor networks with energy harvesting, M2M links at minimum transmit power, and virtualised, smaller data centres.

Her future-research list focuses on energy harvesting, low-power chipsets, better energy storage (including printed and polymer batteries) and energy-efficient routing.

## Who should watch

Students and engineers new to sustainable computing who want the whole field in one sitting, and teams building battery-powered fleets looking for a checklist. If you already know the green software literature, skip to the testing and principles sections.
