Title: Conf42 DevSecOps 2023: secrets in Git, poisoned packages and botnets of cameras
Description: The Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 roundup - 33 talks on secrets management, supply chain attacks, IoT botnets, Kubernetes security, observability and DevSecOps culture.
Body:
[Conf42 DevSecOps 2023](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2023) went out on November 30 with 33 talks, and the attackers in them were refreshingly unglamorous. They read old Git history, take over the npm account of a tired maintainer, log into cameras with the default password, and wait. The defensive talks matched: find the secret before it ships, know what your dependencies are, trap the intruder with a fake credential, and build a culture where security is part of the pipeline rather than a gate at the end.

Speakers came from Gcore, Red Hat, Dell Technologies, Deloitte, Thoughtworks, New Relic, GitGuardian, Aiven, Altinity, Cerbos, Sevco Security, Semaphore, SPS Commerce, Fleet Device Management, EPAM Systems, OWASP and many smaller security shops.

## Why do secrets keep ending up in Git?

Because deleting a file doesn't delete it, as [Daniel Oates-Lee](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Daniel_OatesLee_git_secrets_repos) of Punk Security reminded everyone. His talk covers what kinds of secrets leak, where they hide in history, and how Punk Security's SecretMagpie finds them across repos. [Alex Soto](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Alex_Soto_kubernetes_secrets_secret) of Red Hat started from an uncomfortable default, a Kubernetes Secret is not secret at all, and showed how to manage them in the GitOps era. [Sam Gabrail](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Sam_Gabrail_secrets_management_gitops_argocd_hashicorp_vault_injector) of TeKanAid Solutions demoed the full path with Argo CD and the HashiCorp Vault injector, from Kubernetes auth to a token to secrets in the pod.

[Dwayne McDaniel](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Dwayne_McDaniel_detecting_honeytokens) of GitGuardian flipped it: since attackers want your credentials, give them fake ones. Honeytokens turn a leaked credential into an alarm, and his horror stories explain why you want one. [Peleg Porat](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Peleg_Porat_configurations_weak_link_chain) of Configu widened the lens to configuration in general, the unencrypted files and scattered settings that make it the weak link.

## Who do you trust in your dependency tree?

[Danish Tariq and Hassan Khan Yusufzai](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Danish_Tariq_Hassan_Khan_Yusufzai_supply_chain_npm_attacks) researched account takeover of npm maintainers at scale, gathering packages from public sources to measure how many could be hijacked, and closed with prevention. [Leonid Akinin](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Leonid_Akinin_trusty_package_ttps_oss_python) of EPAM Systems did the same for Python with live demonstrations of attacker tactics, techniques and procedures against open source packages, including campaigns aimed at Windows developers in 2023.

[Marek Najmajer and Aleksander Baranowski](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Marek_Najmajer_Aleksander_Baranowski_beyond_sbom_risk_assessment) of Linux Polska and EuroLinux went beyond the SBOM: 96% of companies use open source, few assess its risk in a structured way, and signals such as popularity and the distribution of maintainer activity over time help. [Travis Gosselin](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Travis_Gosselin_fortifying_codebase_github) of SPS Commerce made the case for centralising on GitHub's own tooling, with a line worth repeating: over 90% of CVEs aren't present in the most recent dependency versions, so Dependabot and staying current is the single best habit.

## What happens when the devices fight back?

Gold sponsor Gcore sent its head of security, [Andrey Slastenov](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Andrey_Slastenov_iot_5g_devices_ddos_threat_landscape), to explain how poorly secured IoT and 5G devices become DDoS weapons, with an increase of over 300% in IoT-driven DDoS attacks in the first half of 2023 alone. [Brian Contos](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Brian_Contos_hacking_demos_secrets_asset_intelligence) of Sevco Security followed with an industrial robot hack and the numbers behind extended IoT: almost 5 million internet-accessible cameras, and about 50% of passwords on such devices still the default. [Susie Su](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Susie_Su_revolution_iot_workforce) of Signify (Philips Lighting) looked at how AI and AIoT reshape DevOps and InfoSec roles.

## Clusters, clouds, endpoints and code

[Gufran Mirza](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Gufran_Mirza_securing_kubernetes_istio_service_mesh) of TrustCore Systems secured Kubernetes service-to-service traffic with Istio: service accounts turned into certificate identities, mTLS between services and JWT for end users. [Fouad Mulla](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Fouad_Mulla_cloud_security_containers_infra_workloads) covered container security, from public base images to running as non-root. [Joshua Arvin Lat](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Joshua_Arvin_Lat_iac_security_best_practices) of NuWorks Interactive Labs went through infrastructure-as-code security, including what happens if the server running your IaC templates is the one that gets compromised. [Zach Wasserman](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Zach_Wasserman_securing_endpoint_open_software) of Fleet Device Management applied DevOps practice to endpoints with osquery and Fleet across macOS, Linux and Windows.

On application access, [Alex Olivier](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Alex_Olivier_modernizing_auth_decoupled_abac) of Cerbos moved authorization from hard-coded roles to decoupled ABAC, with GDPR- and CCPA-style regional rules as the case that breaks the if statements.

## Hunting the threats you already know about

[Fulvio Colombrino](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Fulvio_Colombrino_detect_known_unknowns) of Deloitte built detection analytics on MITRE's TTP-based hunting approach to catch known unknowns, explained with a wine metaphor. [Jagdsh Chand](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Jagdsh_Chand_iterative_threat_modelling_agile_development) of Thoughtworks fitted threat modelling into agile sprints in five steps, with tight scoping and evil brainstorming that wears the attacker's hat without falling down rabbit holes. [Timo Pagel](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Timo_Pagel_metricca_software_metrics_collection_analysis) of OWASP introduced MetricCA for automating security metrics from Jira and GitHub, and [Michal Davidson](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Michal_Davidson_cybersecurity_security_domains) of Dell Technologies argued that cybersecurity is too general a word to hire for, and should be split into domains.

## Observability as a security and design tool

[Roni Dover](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Roni_Dover_opentelemetry_code_prod) of Digma argued that OpenTelemetry should feed back into how developers write code, not just into dashboards. [Siddhartha Khare](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Siddhartha_Khare_opentelemetry_path_observability) of New Relic covered where OpenTelemetry and its collector were heading. [Robert Hodges](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Robert_Hodges_monitoring_open_source_analytics_visualization) of Altinity built fast, cheap monitoring on ClickHouse and Grafana, and [Muralidhar Basani](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Muralidhar_Basani_simplifying_kafka_governance) of Aiven showed Klaw for governing thousands of Kafka topics, ACLs and schemas with self-service.

## Culture eats pipelines

[Tanya Janca](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Tanya_Janca_more_than_pipelines) of We Hack Purple defined DevSecOps as AppSec plus DevOps and wove security through the three ways of DevOps, a reminder that there is much more to it than a pipeline. [Gene Gotimer](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Gene_Gotimer_doom_devsecops) of Praeses listed ten reliable ways to doom it, from slow onboarding and change advisory boards to measuring too many metrics at once. [Romano Roth](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Romano_Roth_architect_continuous_delivery) of Zuhlke covered architecting for continuous delivery, [Jhonnatan Gil Chaves](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Jhonnatan_Gil_Chaves_security_development_continuous_delivery) of Globant added security to container delivery, and [Grzegorz Sztandera](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Grzegorz_Sztandera_devopssup_extended_devops_one_team) of MakoLab told how his 24/7 DevOps-plus-support team grew from three people to ten.

The AI talks were career talks: [Rich Niemiec](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Rich_Niemiec_ai_machine_learning_101) of Viscosity North America gave an AI and machine learning 101, and [Tomas Fernandez](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Tomas_Fernandez_technical_writing_ai_career_path) of Semaphore argued technical writing survives LLMs because so much of it is interviewing people. And [Chester Santos](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Chester_Santos_instant_memory_training), a US memory champion, taught visualisation techniques for remembering anything, which is one way to stop writing passwords down.

## Thanks to the sponsors

[Gcore](https://gcore.com/) and [Teleport](https://goteleport.com/) were the gold sponsors, with [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), [Sysdig](https://sysdig.com/) and [Uptime Labs](https://uptimelabs.io/) at silver and [unpack.tech](https://www.unpack.tech/) as newsletter partner, alongside media partners including [Manning](https://www.manning.com), [Packt](https://www.packtpub.com/), [Infosec Conferences](https://infosec-conferences.com), [Kube Careers](https://kube.careers/) and [Kube Events](https://kube.events/).

Every talk is on the [Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 page](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2023) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrD0aOqoNsHslCreSCfgLC-s). The series returned a year later as [Conf42 DevSecOps 2024](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2024).

Title: A picture hides a password until someone runs steghide on it
Description: Raed Ahsan (Rsecurity) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on how attackers pull credentials out of images with steghide, then use them to get root
Body:
Hiding credentials inside a JPEG feels clever right up to the moment an attacker downloads the JPEG. At Conf42 IoT 2023, Raed Ahsan, founder of Rsecurity, runs a short live attack from a Kali Linux machine: find a web server, pull an innocent car photo off it, extract a hidden credentials file with steghide, log in, and climb to root through the victim's bash history.

It is a compact, beginner-friendly demo in the style of a capture-the-flag box. The abstract frames it around IoT devices; the target in the demo is a Linux web server, and the lessons apply to any box that stores secrets this way.

## What steganography is for, and why it fails here

Raed Ahsan said at Conf42 IoT 2023: "steganography is the art of embedding data behind media files". People use it to keep confidential data, bank details or server passwords, away from a third party in transit: anyone who opens the file just sees the picture.

He points out the first weakness straight away. If an attacker has both the original image and the one carrying data, the file sizes differ, because the embedded version is larger. Hiding is not the same as encrypting, and the talk is a tidy demonstration of the difference.

## The attack, step by step

The chain is short, which is the point:

1. **Scan.** Port 80 is open, so there is a web server.
2. **Bust directories.** With Gobuster, OWASP DirBuster or the DirBuster bundled with Kali, the attacker finds an image file and a secret text file.
3. **Check the image.** It is a valid JPEG of a Lamborghini, with intact headers. Nothing to see.
4. **Read the text file.** It mentions a `data.txt` that isn't on the server, plus a password. The missing file has to be hiding somewhere, and images are the usual place.
5. **Extract.** steghide pulls `data.txt` out of the JPEG with that passphrase. Inside: a username and password.

No cracking tools needed. As he put it, the passphrase was "just hosted on the web server in clear text", so John the Ripper never leaves its box.

## From user to root via bash history

With the extracted credentials he logs in as the user (they would work over SSH too), then goes looking for privilege escalation. His habit: read the bash history first, because people type passwords, logins and connection commands into their shells all the time.

The history holds a Perl one-liner that created a user named tom with root privileges in `/etc/passwd`, along with that user's password. Switch to tom, `id` returns 0, and the box is his. In his words, the confidentiality, integrity and availability triad is broken by one image and one careless text file.

## Where the next secret will hide

His closing note is about where things go next. Images are the traditional carrier, so any attacker who finds one on a target will scan it in depth with tools like steghide. Audio files, video files and documents get less scrutiny, which makes them both the more likely hiding place and the thing defenders should check.

The defensive takeaways write themselves: don't treat steganography as a secret store, never publish the passphrase next to the file, keep credentials out of shell history, and don't create root-equivalent users by hand with a command anyone can later read.

## Who should watch

Developers and IoT engineers who've never seen an attacker's workflow end to end, and anyone starting in security who wants a clean example of chaining small mistakes into root. Experienced pentesters will recognise every step.

- Andrey Slastenov on [IoT and 5G devices as DDoS weapons](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Andrey_Slastenov_iot_5g_devices_ddos_threat_landscape) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

- Amod Darshane on [cybersecurity for networks](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Amod_Darshane_cybersecurity_network) at Conf42 IoT 2024.

Title: Quarterly security assessments are too slow, so MetricCA automates them
Description: Timo Pagel (OWASP) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on MetricCA, which turns DevSecOps maturity activities into Grafana dashboards and alerts
Body:
A security assessment that lands once a quarter tells a product team how it did three months ago, which is roughly as motivating as a gym that only weighs you at Christmas. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, Timo Pagel, leader of the OWASP DevSecOps Maturity Model (DSOMM), introduced [MetricCA](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Timo_Pagel_metricca_software_metrics_collection_analysis), the Metric Collector and Analyzer: an open source tool that pulls evidence of security activities from YAML files and from tools such as Jira and Confluence, checks it against maturity thresholds, and pushes the result to Grafana dashboards with alerts.

It is a short talk about a project that was still in draft and implementation, so expect architecture and intent rather than a finished product demo.

## Why do teams need faster security feedback?

Timo frames maturity models as a way to prioritise when there are too many security options, and likes to split them into two DevOps strategies: harden your DevOps processes and technologies, and use the ones you already have (a build pipeline that runs security tests, a Prometheus and Grafana stack that can alert on security incidents).

The problem is the assessment cadence. He runs assessments quarterly, yearly or biannually, but teams want feedback on the activity they just finished. Timo Pagel said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023: "But as a product team I want fast feedback for my performed security activities to stay motivated." His example metric is mean time to respond to vulnerabilities: if a team did well, it should see that, and if it is slipping, it should hear about it.

## How does MetricCA work?

Two kinds of input. Manual assessments live in YAML: activities per team and per application, plus a configuration file with the maturity model definitions, levels and thresholds. Team activities are inherited by that team's applications, a one-to-many relationship, so having a security champion per team counts for every app the team owns.

Manual entries lag, though. A team that documents threat modelling in Confluence should not have to document it again in YAML. That is the collector's job: it reads sources such as Confluence, Jira, OWASP Dependency-Track and even Azure Active Directory. In his example, a Confluence page labelled threat modelling, carrying the date, the participants and the application ID, is picked up automatically.

The analyzer combines both sources, checks each team against its thresholds at a given level (mean time to patch, for example) and generates the Grafana security dashboard, with the thresholds baked in. If a team is supposed to threat-model every quarter and hasn't in three months, Grafana can warn it before the auditor does. The dashboards are generated from the Java application so the project is not tied to Grafana.

## Who changes the YAML?

Pull requests. A product owner edits the YAML in the repository or through a web UI (say, confirming the team has read the required security policies), opens a pull request, and a security architect approves or rejects it. A schema for the YAML is planned so mistakes surface in the pull request itself. The activity model is meant to be generic, with typed components behind an interface so organisations can define their own activities.

## What doesn't it fix?

Timo is upfront that it is not a silver bullet. Teams still have to perform the activities and record them, which is cultural work. His recommendation is to keep YAML for the static things you can't automate and push everything else through the collector. At the time of the talk the project was in draft, with implementation estimated for the end of 2023, and he invited ideas through the OWASP Slack DSOMM channel.

## Who should watch

AppSec and security champions leads who already use DSOMM or a similar model and are tired of spreadsheet assessments, and platform teams with a Grafana stack wondering what security data belongs on it. It is a compact architecture overview, not a hands-on demo.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Sandeep Panghal and Juan Antonio Conde on [automated DevSecOps maturity assessment](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Sandeep_Panghal_Juan_Antonio_Conde_automated_devsecops_maturity_assessment_nextgen).
- Jagdsh Chand on [iterative threat modelling in agile development](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Jagdsh_Chand_iterative_threat_modelling_agile_development), the activity MetricCA's collector picks up from Confluence.
- Darren Richardson on [threat modelling CI/CD environments](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Darren_Richardson_threat_modelling_cicd_environments).

[Watch the talk on YouTube](https://youtu.be/VQqepKa4Dis).

Title: A starjacked PyPI package, live, and the payloads Semgrep never saw
Description: Leonid Akinin (EPAM Systems) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on Python supply chain TTPs, demoed live, from starjacking to an ngrok-tunnelled RAT
Body:
A brand-new Python package can show almost 5,000 GitHub stars a minute after you publish it, and PyPI will happily display them. Leonid Akinin, Security Architect at EPAM Systems, did exactly that on Test PyPI at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, then spent the rest of the talk walking a set of intentionally malicious packages through the tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) attackers use against Python developers. The takeaway: static analysis catches the lazy payloads, and the rest is down to where you install from and what runs underneath.

[The talk](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Leonid_Akinin_trusty_package_ttps_oss_python) is a heavy live demo in a Kali Linux VM plus a Windows 10 sandbox, with a disclaimer up front that the code can be weaponised. His reason for teaching attacks at a defence conference is simple. Leonid Akinin said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023: "I always consider that to learn how to defend, you need to learn how to attack."

## Why is Python supply chain security still a problem?

He opens with 2023 alone: a well-known machine learning package compromised through a dependency in January, PyPI temporarily suspending new users and projects in May after a flood of malicious packages, six malicious packages aimed at Windows users in July, and the ongoing VMConnect campaign. Citing Sonatype's figures, he puts the average year-over-year growth of supply chain attacks between 2019 and 2022 at 742%.

The TTP framing comes from MITRE: tactics are the why (initial access, perimeter bypass, data exfiltration, ransomware), techniques the how (malicious uploads, typosquatting, starjacking, code injected through stolen developer credentials). The talk focuses on techniques.

## How does starjacking work?

The package metadata lets you point at any GitHub repository. Leonid bumps the version of a small CLI package that reports your public IP, builds it, uploads it with twine to Test PyPI (production PyPI is watched by security vendors, and he would rather keep his account), and the fresh project shows nearly 5,000 stars, nearly 2,000 forks and a respectable list of issues and PRs. The URL in `setup.py` points at the example project from the Python packaging docs. Same package, borrowed reputation, under five minutes.

Typosquatting gets a defensive tip worth stealing: big vendors such as Microsoft now register stub packages under likely typo names, and he recommends public projects do the same.

## What gets past static analysis?

Six obfuscation methods ship the same tiny infostealer (OS, version, host IP, username, sent as JSON to a listener): reversed base64, a list of Unicode code points, the two combined, an encrypted payload whose key comes from a Pastebin dropper, precompiled bytecode, and an embedded Go binary.

Semgrep flags the `exec` calls and the Go source he left in the repo for reference. It does not flag the bytecode or the compiled binary, because it reads syntax and does not decompile. Two of six walk straight through.

## Where does the payload run?

Three entry points: `__init__.py` on import, a custom install step in `setup.py`, and droppers that fetch the real payload from Discord, Pastebin or Telegram bots. All three fire in the demo, once on build, once on install, once on import. On Windows, the same CLI launches a bundled dropper that pulls a reverse shell. Microsoft Defender catches it through behaviour; with real-time protection off, the shell lands. Semgrep, run on the same package, sees the `exec` in `setup.py` and the utils module but misses the call to the bundled executable.

The finale is a package that claims to search package managers. It searches, and quietly installs its own dependencies, starts a Flask server from precompiled bytecode with endpoints for OS info, process list, username and a screen grabber, then exposes it through an ngrok tunnel so NAT and firewalls stop mattering. A separate package posing as a collection of database connectors harvests SSH keys and base64-obfuscated environment variable names such as AWS access keys on import. Leonid Akinin said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023: "Ngrok is super useful, but you have to be careful."

## What actually protects you?

He splits defences into pre-supply and post-supply. Before install: individual development sandboxes (no big shared dev servers), checking that the package name matches the repository and was not published five minutes ago, manual review (grep `setup.py` for base64, odd Unicode lists, precompiled files), pinned versions, package quarantine, private PyPI proxies instead of direct downloads, SCA in pre-commits (JFrog Xray CLI, Safety, Semgrep), and AV/EDR. After install: least privilege on build agents (no root Jenkins nodes), traffic monitoring, and Semgrep plus SCA plus SBOMs in CI/CD, where a changed hash for the same version is a red flag.

His best real example: two private PyPI mirrors, an interim one where new packages are scanned and a production one developers are forced to use. It added a delay on first download and caught about a dozen real malicious packages that developers had typosquatted.

## Who should watch

Python developers who `pip install` from a README, platform teams running build agents, and AppSec people who want to see why one scanner is not a strategy.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Danish Tariq and Hassan Khan Yusufzai on [npm supply chain attacks](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Danish_Tariq_Hassan_Khan_Yusufzai_supply_chain_npm_attacks), the JavaScript side of the same problem.
- Marek Najmajer and Aleksander Baranowski on [risk assessment beyond the SBOM](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Marek_Najmajer_Aleksander_Baranowski_beyond_sbom_risk_assessment).
- Ukanah Dean on [Python security best practices](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2024_Ukanah_Dean_python_security_best_practices_protecting_common_vulnerabilities).

Title: Put the firmware hash on a chain the attacker can't rewrite
Description: Swapnil Shinde (OWASP) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on securing OTA firmware updates by verifying update hashes against a private blockchain
Body:
Over-the-air updates have a single point of failure: the server that holds both the firmware and the hash the device checks it against. Compromise that server and the attacker signs their own homework. At Conf42 IoT 2023, Swapnil Shinde, an OWASP contributor, shows how to move the hash, and optionally the binary, onto a private blockchain, so a device verifies every update against a ledger nobody can quietly edit, then demos it on an ESP32.

It is a practical talk with a live demo, built on a hackathon project and published research. The demo shows the happy path; the attack results come from the papers he cites, which he says plainly.

## Why OTA is the soft spot

Shinde opens with the scale: 15.14 billion connected IoT devices in 2023, with 29.42 billion expected by 2030, and consumer devices making up 67.5% of them. The 2022 reports he cites show a 77% increase in malicious firmware update injection and a 60% surge in DDoS attacks targeting OTA updates.

Wired updates are safe and impractical, since nobody recalls a fleet to a service centre. Wireless updates expose ports and radio links. He lists three attacks: man-in-the-middle, where the device pulls a malicious image from a spoofed server; DDoS, which floods the update server until devices can't get updates (IP allowlisting helps); and the worst one, the compromised central server, from which an attacker can create or modify an update and push it to the whole fleet.

The normal flow makes that last case obvious. The vendor compiles C or embedded C into one binary, uploads it, gets a location back, sends an MQTT message telling devices where to pull it, and the device checks the hash it downloaded alongside the binary. Swapnil Shinde said at Conf42 IoT 2023: "But this is centralized, why not replace it with blockchain?"

## What the chain adds

He gives a quick primer for people who haven't touched blockchains: blocks hold data plus the previous block's hash, nodes add the network and consensus, and a tampered node gets re-synced from its peers. Three properties matter here. An immutable ledger keeps recorded update transactions unalterable. Smart contracts enforce update rules such as time constraints and cryptographic verification. Decentralisation means an attacker has to take on many nodes, not one server.

Public chains are out, because anything you write is public. For a private network he lists three routes: Ethereum's Geth with a custom genesis block, Hyperledger Fabric from the Linux Foundation, or Polkadot's Substrate in Rust. The consensus choice is a cost trade-off: proof of work is secure but resource hungry, and lighter mechanisms give up some security.

## Three functions do the work

The reference design on Hyperledger Fabric deploys a smart contract (chaincode) with three calls exposed as REST APIs:

- **push**: the vendor records update name, version and firmware hash, and gets a transaction ID.
- **verify**: the device sends the transaction ID and the SHA-1 hash it computed from the binary it received, and gets back valid or invalid.
- **query**: returns the verification status.

An invalid hash means the device rejects the update and stays on the old firmware. That requires modifying the device's OTA library so it can call the chain's RPC or HTTPS endpoints. The cited research ran man-in-the-middle and denial-of-service attacks against this design and couldn't get a malicious update installed: a spoofed image fails verification, and a DDoS that blows the update's time constraint just makes the update fail and roll back.

## The ESP32 demo

The hackathon build runs on HyperSDK from Ava Labs. The firmware binary goes to IPFS, so the file itself is immutable too, and the chain stores its IPFS URL with the hash. Devices can't hold a wallet, so a separate service handles signing and exposes HTTP endpoints the device can call, the same role Infura plays for Ethereum. On the device side, the team forked the ElegantOTA library to call the chain before installing.

The live run is satisfyingly small: change a dot to a plus in the firmware, rebuild, create a project and an update through the vendor service, trigger the update on the ESP32, watch it send its computed hash to the chain, get valid back, and start printing plus signs over serial. Attacks aren't demoed, because the project was still in development.

One thing worth doing if you build this for real: use a stronger hash than SHA-1 in the verify call.

## Who should watch

Embedded and IoT engineers responsible for OTA pipelines, and security folks curious whether blockchain earns its place anywhere in IoT. Here it has a narrow, defensible job, a tamper-evident notary for firmware hashes, rather than everything at once.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Gresshma Atluri on [IoT supply chain defence](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Gresshma_Atluri_security_supplychain_defense) at Conf42 IoT 2025.

Title: Threat modelling that fits in a 15-minute backlog refinement
Description: Jagdsh Chand (Thoughtworks) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on iterative threat modelling with STRIDE and DREAD inside agile ceremonies
Body:
Threat modelling has a reputation as a week-long workshop run by security specialists, ideally after the architecture can no longer change. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, [Jagdsh Chand](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Jagdsh_Chand_iterative_threat_modelling_agile_development), Lead Consultant at Thoughtworks, shows the five-step agile version his colleagues refined across Thoughtworks teams, worked through on OWASP Juice Shop, and argues it can run in roughly 15 minutes of every backlog refinement once the team has done it once.

## Why the traditional version fails

Classic threat modelling is done by security people with little developer involvement, which breeds three misconceptions. That pen tests and code reviews cover it: they find bugs, but "Threat modeling will uncover design flaws which cannot be identified by these techniques." That it can wait until after delivery, by which point a foundational flaw means rewriting the architecture. And that it is too complex and slow. Agile threat modelling answers with a defensive mindset inside the dev team, a collaborative approach each team can tailor, awareness of business impact beyond the team's bubble, and an exercise small enough to repeat any time.

## Five questions, one guinea pig

The steps are five questions: what do we want to accomplish, what are we building, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good job. Before step one, set a security objective built on the CIA triad. For Juice Shop (OWASP's deliberately insecure online juice store) that becomes four goals: protect the shop's reputation and sales, reduce breaches of customer PII, reduce malicious alteration leading to financial loss, and keep the shop available.

**Scope** small: a new security-sensitive feature like login or checkout, one microservice and its collaborators, a high-level pass for security tech debt, or the delivery pipeline itself. Too much scope means no findings in the time you have. The demo scopes one user story, customer login.

**Represent** it as a data flow diagram with entry points, assets and trust boundaries. Here: the front end redirects to an external identity provider, the Node.js backend validates the auth code and stores the token in the session.

## Evil brainstorming with STRIDE

Then everyone, product owners included, puts on the attacker's hat. Chand compares PASTA, attack trees and VAST, then picks timeboxed STRIDE as the developer-focused option: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege, each with key concepts and prompting questions. Can someone brute force the login or use a known-compromised password? Can an attacker delete logs? Do error messages leak your database version? The rule is to stay out of rabbit holes "and focus on quantity over quality."

On the login flow that yields no logging of unauthorised attempts, brute force, DDoS, input tampering, no strong password policy, unauthenticated APIs and customer details stored in a JWT.

## Prioritise with DREAD, then write tickets

Rank threats by DREAD (damage, reproducibility, exploitability, affected users, discoverability) against the security objective. DDoS comes first because it hits availability directly; weak password configuration second, because it is easily reproduced with off-the-shelf tools and leads to a PII breach.

Mitigations become backlog items, never spreadsheet rows or emails: a definition of done requiring all APIs to be authenticated, an acceptance criterion rejecting malicious IPs, a tech debt story for password strength, an epic for logging unauthorised entries, and a spike to check whether customer data in the JWT is a real problem. The other anti-pattern: picking the easy mitigation first. The riskiest threat goes first, even if its fix is hard.

## Making it iterative

Step five reflects on scope, tools and findings, and tweaks the next round. The first full session takes about an hour; after that it rides along in backlog refinement at roughly 15 minutes. In person, print the cue cards and use a whiteboard; remote, use any whiteboard tool, and save the artefacts digitally either way. The parting line: "You don't need to be a security engineer or expert to run a threat model."

## Who should watch

Agile teams with no dedicated security engineer, and AppSec people looking for a format developers will actually repeat. It is a clear, structured walkthrough with a realistic example, light on jokes but heavy on reusable checklists.

Title: From one engineer to ten, with DevOps and 24/7 support in one team
Description: Grzegorz Sztandera (MakoLab) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on growing one ops team that covers DevOps, operations and 24/7 support by hiring for personality
Body:
Grzegorz Sztandera's first month running MakoLab's operations team went like this: he inherited three people, two resigned, and he was left with one engineer and a production system on 24/7 support. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, [Grzegorz Sztandera](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Grzegorz_Sztandera_devopssup_extended_devops_one_team), Operations Manager at MakoLab, tells how that team grew to ten people in two years by combining DevOps, operations and ITIL-style support in one unit he calls DevOpsSup, and why he hired juniors for attitude rather than seniors for skills.

This is a management case study, not a security talk: no tooling deep dives, plenty of hard-won lessons for anyone building an ops team.

## What is DevOpsSup?

He splits the work into three parts. Dev is building: CI/CD, infrastructure as code, Python and Bash, service architecture. Ops is running what was built, or what the customer hands over, with monitoring, hypercare after deployments and predictive maintenance. Sup is ITIL processes: incidents, problems, change requests, log analysis and reports, around the clock on call.

The team sits between developers, QA and project management on one side and customers, third parties and end users on the other. On top of full engagements it offers a plug-in mode: join a project, do one job, switch off. His example is a customer with a hand-built AWS environment; the team optimised it, rewrote it in Terraform, deployed the new infrastructure and left.

## How do you grow a team from one to ten?

Mostly juniors and regular engineers, each with a different specialty (databases, IT processes, AWS, CI/CD), sharing common daily tasks. The database person is the ITIL person's expert and the other way round, so everyone learns from someone. The first year cost 1,162 overtime hours across the team, and he did over 100 a quarter himself.

The practices that made it work:

- **Onboarding by the newest joiner**: onboarding took three months, and the best guide turned out to be whoever joined last, since they remember what was confusing.
- **A DevOps bootcamp**: three months of AWS, Terraform, Jenkins and ITIL for people new to DevOps, then straight onto real production work.
- **Remote integration**: cameras on for every call, with no excuse, one-to-ones outside the office, and weekend trips to Polish cities.
- **Risk management**: of the risks he tracked, 20% were about people, 50% about quality and 30% about the customer or missing skills.

The reasoning behind hiring for personality: "we can learn everything, but we are not able to change our attitude as fast as we can learn the new technologies," Sztandera said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023. Need it done today? Hire a senior. Building something to last? Give people room to learn.

## What did it deliver?

From one customer and one project in 2021 to seven customers and twelve projects by the end of 2022, eight of them running. Revenue from the first project more than doubled within a year, and the team's revenue grew more than 300% in two years.

For one product over two years: more than 200,000 processes a week, over 500 deployments, more than 400 defects found in logs before end users noticed, and over 1,000 incidents handled with an SLA above 99.5%. The team raised more than 600 incidents with other vendors, who managed about 95%. Their own monitoring spots problems after about a minute, against 10 to 15 minutes for the customer's alerts. On a health sector project, cloud cost optimisation cut bills by over 50%.

## The manager's calendar is a warning

The funniest slide is his calendar from a year or so earlier: six or seven meetings in parallel, one on the laptop and one on the phone, fine until someone asked him to speak. The fix was delegating the technical lead to the engineers and acting as a people leader first, business leader second. His summary: for the customer the team can be a one man army, "but inside we are not one man but one team army."

## Who should watch

Engineering managers building a combined DevOps and support team, especially with juniors and remote staff. Skip it if you came for security tooling.

Title: When AI meets IoT, a hack stops being a website outage
Description: Susie Su (Signify (Philips Lighting)) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on why AIoT puts security first, because hacked devices act on the physical world
Body:
A compromised web app costs you uptime and money. A compromised device that controls heat, motion or a gas pipeline can cost lives. That asymmetry is the core of Susie Su's talk at Conf42 IoT 2023: Su, Global Software Operations Architect at Signify (Philips Lighting), maps where AI and IoT meet (AIoT) and argues that security has to come first, for the AI models and the devices alike.

It is a short, high-level overview, closer to a map of the territory than a how-to. The abstract also promises job-market impact; the talk itself sticks to use cases and security.

## What AIoT looks like in practice

Su defines AIoT simply as AI plus IoT and gives three arenas: automated vehicles (Tesla, Waymo, Mobileye, Cruise, Baidu), smart cities (lighting, which is Signify's business, plus video surveillance, traffic monitoring and smart buildings), and manufacturing, where deep neural networks do product quality checks on the production line.

She then picks five AI subfields and pins each to a real product:

- **Natural language processing**: smart speakers with Alexa, Google Assistant or Siri, using voice recognition so people can talk to a device.
- **Expert systems**: IBM Watson in hospitals for medical diagnosis.
- **Machine vision**: quality inspection on production lines.
- **Planning**: self-driving cars choosing routes.
- **Robotics**: Boston Dynamics' Spot, navigating terrain and joining rescue missions in places too dangerous for people.

## Why does a hacked device matter more than a hacked server?

This is the sharpest point in the talk. Susie Su said at Conf42 IoT 2023: "If our traditional software, if it has been hacked by AI, it will just cause your website downtime or your financial losses." A device is different. Her example is a smart home pushed to heat a bedroom past 100 degrees Celsius: that doesn't lose data, it kills someone.

Industrial control systems (ICS) raise the stakes again. She points to a timeline of ICS security incidents, including a 2012 cyber intrusion campaign against gas pipelines, and to the nuclear industry: attacks on that kind of infrastructure could damage a city or a country, not a handful of users.

## Where IoT security sits

Su places IoT security inside the familiar taxonomy: information security contains cybersecurity, which spans network, cloud, endpoint, application and IoT security. Under IoT security she lists 5G networks, the Internet of Vehicles and industrial IoT, with ICS inside that. The old classifications still apply; AI just widens the scope fast.

AIoT security then has three parts to protect: the AI model, the physical device, and the connection and data flowing between them.

## The AI security checklist

For the model side, she runs through a list worth pinning next to any AIoT design review: data security, privacy preservation, information security, explainability and transparency (a black-box model trained with malicious intent could take a device somewhere nobody expects), IoT security itself, human-AI interaction security, model security as more and more models ship, bias and fairness, lifecycle security, regulatory compliance and hybrid AI-human security.

For the device side, the advice is the unglamorous one that most fleets still get wrong: firmware and hardware have bugs like any software, so IoT products need regular updates that patch vulnerabilities.

## Who should watch

Product managers, architects and students who want a quick overview of AIoT and a checklist for its security risks. Security engineers will find the taxonomy familiar and no technical depth; this is a starting point.

Title: The box that runs your Terraform is the juiciest target in the account
Description: Joshua Arvin Lat (NuWorks Interactive Labs) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on IaC security, from insecure template defaults to poisoned pipelines
Body:
Infrastructure as code makes your cloud reproducible, and that includes reproducing a mistake in every environment at once. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, [Joshua Arvin Lat](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Joshua_Arvin_Lat_iac_security_best_practices), CTO of NuWorks Interactive Labs, AWS Machine Learning Hero and author of a book on building penetration testing labs in the cloud, runs through the IaC security practices that matter most, and keeps returning to one theme: the machine or pipeline that applies your templates usually holds the keys to everything.

## Why IaC changes the risk

He starts from the growth of a web app: front end, back end and database, then a CDN, load balancer, auto-scaling servers and firewalls bolted on. Templates turn that sprawl into text files, and one template plus different parameters gives you staging and production. Every resource should be tagged so you can count what exists, spot what is missing and see which resource needs which permissions, and each one gets its own scoped IAM role.

## Defaults rot

"The tricky part with using infrastructure as code is the templates and examples available online may already be outdated," Lat said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023. Copy an old example, or ask a generative AI tool for one, and you may inherit insecure settings. The classic is an S3 bucket opened to the world holding a database dump. Cloud providers on AWS, Azure and GCP regularly change defaults to safer ones, and your templates will not pick that up by themselves, so read the announcements.

## How one admin role becomes a full compromise

The section worth the time is the attack chain. The shortcut many teams take: a server in a public subnet runs the IaC CLI with a super-admin IAM role, which is very convenient. Compromise that server and the attacker can do anything in the account. Running the tooling in containers is no fix if the containers have excessive permissions: "a lot of people think that using containers would be a silver bullet," and container escape gets the attacker onto the host. From there, IAM privilege escalation (creating new IAM resources to gain more access) leads to deleting everything, spinning up expensive resources until the account is shut down, attacking other organisations, or reading the databases with sensitive data.

## Pipelines help, and are themselves a target

Keeping infrastructure in git gives you versions, testing in staging before production, and reusable layered templates. It also lets pipelines scan templates for vulnerabilities on every push. But pipeline runners carry IAM roles too, and a script or payload slipped into a template can run with those permissions: poisoned pipeline execution. Teams pour effort into production, Lat warns, while "the weak link could be any existing pipelines which are used by the development teams."

His last point is easy to forget: IaC deletes as readily as it creates. Know the settings that protect production databases and other critical resources from accidental modification or deletion before someone runs a destroy.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to Terraform or CloudFormation who want the security mental model before they hand a CI runner admin credentials. It is a short, concept-level talk without tool demos; experienced cloud security folks will know the material, but the attack chain is a good one to show a team.

Title: Endpoint detections as pull requests, with osquery and Fleet
Description: Zach Wasserman (Fleet Device Management) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on querying endpoints with SQL via osquery and shipping detections through GitOps
Body:
DevSecOps usually means pushing security onto developers; Zach Wasserman runs it the other way and brings developer habits to the security team. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, [Zach Wasserman](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Zach_Wasserman_securing_endpoint_open_software), CTO and co-founder of Fleet Device Management and co-creator of osquery, shows how to query laptops, servers and containers with SQL, and how to ship a new detection as a reviewed pull request that CI applies on merge.

## What counts as an endpoint?

Broadly, any computing device: macOS, Windows and Linux laptops and desktops, Chromebooks, but also servers, containers, factory control planes and Raspberry Pi class IoT devices. The same tooling can reach all of them.

## Why SQL for endpoints?

osquery is the agent. It runs on macOS, Linux and Windows, is MIT licensed, and was built for performance and reliability so it can sit on production servers as well as corporate laptops. Its trick is presenting wildly different sources as tables. `SELECT * FROM users;` returns user accounts on all three operating systems. Behind the same interface are flat files (/etc/hosts, crontab, SSH known_hosts), SQLite stores such as macOS Gatekeeper's configuration, system APIs (Apple System Log, Keychain), application APIs (Docker, Carbon Black), event streams (FSEvents, Linux BPF and audit, Windows events) for file integrity monitoring, file hashes and permissions, and plists.

The payoff is joins. His example joins `processes` and `process_open_sockets` on PID and filters for `sshd` listening on anything other than port 22: an SSH daemon on a nonstandard port, in five lines. The point he makes is that non-developers can ask questions like this without writing code.

## Fleet: osquery at scale, all of it via API

Fleet coordinates the agents across thousands to hundreds of thousands of machines. It runs live queries, inventories software and flags vulnerable versions (his screenshot shows Chrome installs with CVEs), tracks compliance with organisational policies, triggers automations, and ships scheduled query results as JSON logs to S3, Elastic, Splunk or Snowflake. An open source Chrome extension mimics osquery for ChromeOS. Fleet is open core, and "Everything that I'll talk about in this talk today is available on the fully open source MIT license portion of fleet," Wasserman said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

## The demo: a detection goes through code review

This is the section worth the video. A pull request adds a YAML file defining the nonstandard-SSH query, a ten-second interval and logging turned on. Alongside it is an alert definition for Matano, which fires whenever that query returns rows. A teammate reviews it, checking it will produce few false positives and few false negatives; the repo only allows approved PRs to merge. On merge, a GitHub Actions job installs the tools and applies the configuration to both Fleet and Matano.

You get the audit trail for free: who changed the detection, why, and who approved it. "It's the CI actions that enable this Gitops workflow that I think are the really powerful thing here."

## How hard is it to deploy?

Not very. Fleet needs MySQL, Redis and a Linux server binary, with Terraform provided for AWS (a SaaS version exists, but the talk sticks to open source). Whether to expose it to the internet depends on whether laptops off the VPN need to check in. The fleetctl CLI builds osquery packages as .msi, .pkg, .deb and .rpm, which you push with your usual tools, Chef for servers and MDM for workstations, or bake into VM and container images so new instances enroll themselves.

## Who should watch

Security engineers who still manage detections by clicking around a console, and platform teams curious what endpoint visibility looks like with open source tools. It is a compact introduction from the person who co-created osquery, so the SQL examples alone are worth the time.

Title: Robots are IoT devices with legs, and AWS wires them that way
Description: Youhana Hana (AWS) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on building connected robots with AWS IoT Core, Greengrass, RoboMaker and a simulation-first CI/CD pipeline
Body:
A modern robot is an IoT device that happens to move: it streams telemetry, takes over-the-air updates and runs ML models at the edge. At Conf42 IoT 2023, Youhana Hana, Solutions Architect at AWS, walks through the AWS reference architectures for exactly that, from device shadows in AWS IoT Core to a CI/CD pipeline that tests robot code in simulation before it touches real hardware, ending with a Boston Dynamics Spot reading valves on a factory floor.

Be clear about the scope: this is an AWS talk showing AWS services, one architecture per use case. The value is the patterns, most of which carry over to any cloud.

## Why connect a robot to the cloud at all?

Hana opens with an Oxford Economics estimate that the global stock of robots could reach 20 million by 2030, and a short history: first-generation robots, like the classic robotic arm, were pre-programmed or human-directed; the current generation does complex, autonomous work alongside people. Youhana Hana said at Conf42 IoT 2023: "We believe that connecting robots to the cloud and cross edges is powering the next evolution in robotics."

He frames the Internet of Robotic Things as four verbs: sense (sensors, LiDARs, cameras), connect (to the cloud and to other robots), learn (train models on fleet data, deploy them back), and actuate (act on the world safely around humans and other machines).

## Device shadows: tell the robot what you want, not what to do

The first architecture is telemetry plus control through AWS IoT Core. Sensor and log data flow up into databases and a data lake for dashboards. Control goes through the device shadow, a JSON document holding the robot's reported and desired state. An application writes the desired state; when the robot is online it fetches it and works towards it, then reports its new state back. That decoupling is what lets you command a robot that's currently in a dead zone.

IoT Core speaks MQTT, HTTPS, MQTT over WebSocket and LoRaWAN, uses mutual authentication and end-to-end encryption, and can filter and transform messages with rules on the way in.

## Thing groups make fleet A/B testing boring

For software deployment, he puts fleet A in one thing group and fleet B in another, then uses AWS IoT Greengrass, the open-source edge runtime, to ship different software versions to each group. That is A/B testing for robots, using the same grouping you'd use for any device fleet. Greengrass runs Java, Python, Node.js or containers, and filters and aggregates data locally so you choose what goes to the cloud.

The ML-at-the-edge variant uses the same runtime: train and optimise in Amazon SageMaker (or bring your own model), deploy to the robot through Greengrass, send the data it gathers back for labelling, and retrain.

Video gets its own path: Amazon Kinesis Video Streams for ingest, storage and playback, with WebRTC for real-time streaming and remote control from a browser or mobile app, and hooks into Amazon Rekognition, TensorFlow and OpenCV.

## Test in simulation, because the robot is expensive

The strongest section is on simulation with AWS RoboMaker. Hana gives three reasons customers use it: you can reproduce the exact scenario that triggered unexpected behaviour, including unsafe edge cases you would never stage with real hardware; "you can speed up the clock and run simulation faster than real time"; and you can multiply test coverage with parameterised, repeatable simulation worlds.

That feeds the CI/CD reference pipeline. A pull request merged to the integration branch triggers AWS CodePipeline; AWS CodeBuild runs the ROS and Docker builds and pushes images to Amazon ECR; AWS Step Functions drives batch tests in RoboMaker; results land in Amazon S3 for Amazon Athena and QuickSight. Only when the simulation passes do the images go, via Greengrass, to real robots in a test area, whose results join the simulation data. After that the code merges to main and goes over the air to the production fleet.

For mixed fleets from different vendors, AWS IoT RoboRunner provides a central data repository and SDKs for interoperability, such as a shared space with entry and exit points where robots wait until they are cleared.

## The Spot demo

The closer is a re:Invent demo: a Spot robot on an autowalk mission runs two inference models hosted on Greengrass, one locally to find a valve and one remotely to decide whether it is open or closed. Images go to S3, a Lambda function updates DynamoDB and CloudWatch through an AWS AppSync GraphQL API, and a dashboard shows each valve's state.

## Who should watch

Robotics teams starting to think about fleets rather than single robots, and IoT engineers who want to see how device shadows, OTA updates and simulation testing combine. If you're not on AWS, watch for the pipeline shape and skip the service names.

Title: Dependabot and CodeQL, or how to tame security tool sprawl in GitHub
Description: Travis Gosselin (SPS Commerce) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on consolidating supply chain and code security in GitHub with Dependabot and Advanced Security
Body:
Developers write code for about 52 minutes a day, so every security tool that drags them into yet another dashboard eats into very little time. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, [Travis Gosselin](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Travis_Gosselin_fortifying_codebase_github), Distinguished Software Engineer for Developer Experience at SPS Commerce, argues for pulling supply chain and code security into the place developers already live, GitHub, and spends most of the talk on the practical details of Dependabot and GitHub Advanced Security, pitfalls included.

## Why consolidate at all?

His framing comes from developer experience: "developers work in rainforests, not planned gardens." Tools sprouted over 20 years whenever someone had a need, and nobody curated the result. He cites the 52-minute figure from Software.com's code time report, a share of organisations consolidating security vendors for operational reasons that rose from 29% in 2020 to 75% in 2022, and Dynatrace's finding that 62% of organisations run four or more application security solutions. Meanwhile GitHub ships 60 to 70 feature releases a month, so knowing where to look is half the job.

## Dependabot: update constantly, and group the PRs

The case for Dependabot rests on one stat from Mend.io's 2021 report: over 90% of CVEs are not present in the most recent dependency versions. Gosselin's conclusion: "the single best security practice that you can do in terms of consuming external supply chain security is to just keep your packages up to date all the time." Mend's dentist analogy fits: go once every five years and it really hurts.

The pieces, in order:

- **Dependency graph**: free, gives you an SBOM per repo and across the org. He notes 83% of security teams lack an accurate real-time SBOM.
- **Alerts and security updates**: one click turns a CVE alert into a pull request, or dismiss it with a reason. His warning: switch on security updates for an organisation with 3,000 repos and each one may open a PR, which kicks off a build, which floods your CI queue.
- **Version updates**: configured in `.github/dependabot.yml`, covering Go, Maven, Gradle, npm, NuGet, pip, Docker, Terraform modules, git submodules and GitHub Actions, with private feeds via org-level secrets, schedules, PR limits and ignore rules (the AWS SDK, which seems to publish daily, gets weekly patch updates at most).

The feature that changed his mind is grouped pull requests. Ten separate PRs where updating one package breaks another means none of them pass checks without a human shuffling branches. Groups bundle test dependencies, interdependent core packages or all AWS SDK updates into one PR. If you wrote Dependabot off years ago as too noisy, he says, try it again. At SPS Commerce it also drives inner source: an `allow` filter on your own org's packages is how consuming apps actually pick up new library versions.

Pitfalls he lists: no built-in auto-merge, no way to wait until a release has aged a few days, and Renovate as the cross-platform alternative.

## Advanced Security: one interface, many scanners

GitHub Advanced Security is paid, licensed per active committer in the last 90 days. Secret scanning is the easy win: push protection blocked over 17,000 credentials in a year once it went generally available for public repos, it can check with providers whether a detected key is live, and custom patterns cover internal token formats. "Secret scanning is a no brainer," he said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

Code scanning is the more interesting design. It is a framework and UI, not a scanner: CodeQL (formerly Semmle) is the first-class tool, but anything that emits SARIF can upload results, from 42Crunch on OpenAPI specs to IaC scanners, 67 integrations when he took the screenshot. The developer payoff is on pull requests: annotations only on the lines you changed, a configurable status check that fails the PR, and code quality queries such as unused variables alongside security ones, so reviewers see clean code. He walks through the CodeQL CLI flow (database create, analyze with a query suite, upload the SARIF) and a custom query that finds an empty if statement.

His caveats are fair: CodeQL runs remotely and takes three to five minutes, so it is no replacement for a linter in the IDE; setup can be costly if your build is unusual; custom queries take onboarding; and he wants YAML and JSON support. On cost, he says SPS Commerce found it significantly lower than comparable tools.

## Who should watch

Platform and developer experience engineers on GitHub deciding what to switch on and in what order. It is a practitioner's tour with config snippets and rollout warnings, not a product launch.

Title: Your config permissions are all-or-nothing, and that's the bug
Description: Peleg Porat (Configu) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on why scattered, all-or-nothing configuration access is a security hole, and configuration-as-code
Body:
Most teams lock down their code and their infrastructure, then leave the configuration that glues them together spread over a dozen tools with permissions that are either everything or nothing. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, [Peleg Porat](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Peleg_Porat_configurations_weak_link_chain), Co-Founder and CEO of Configu, argues that application configuration is the weak link in the security chain and walks through five ways it breaks: permissions, unencrypted files, monitoring, automation and the defence layers around them.

## What counts as configuration?

Porat starts from the Twelve-Factor App: config is everything that varies between deploys. Code is the logic, configuration is the behaviour. In practice that means environment variables, secrets and feature flags, kept apart from the code and, in most companies, kept apart from each other too: in repos, folders, secret managers, feature flag services, infrastructure tools and cloud vendors. He compares it to having your shirt in one wardrobe and your trousers in another room.

## Why are permissions the first thing to break?

Two problems compound. Storage is fragmented, so nobody has one view of who can read what. And permissions in most of those systems are binary. "Either you have full access to all of your configuration files or you have none," Porat said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023. That forces a choice between over-permission (the junior developer who can reach the production database) and under-permission (the senior developer who cannot open the one file needed to fix a critical bug, and the downtime that follows).

His answer combines two models. RBAC works like GitHub repo access: a team gets an environment. ABAC works like sharing a single Google Doc: one person gets one value. Configu layers both, so developers and QA get dev and test, DevOps also gets prod, and one named developer can be granted just LOG_LEVEL in production without seeing the database connection string next to it. "In configuration, not everyone needs access to every piece of data."

## Secrets in Slack defeat the secret manager

The unencrypted-file section is the one most readers will recognise. He cites a Facebook breach where hundreds of millions of user records sat on servers without encryption, and blames convenience more than malice: developers keep config in plain text files and paste it to each other on Slack or email. HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager does not help if the value then travels as clear text, because everyone assumes it is safe. The fix he proposes is collaboration through one layer that orchestrates the existing stores, so nobody keeps a local plaintext copy.

## Monitoring and automation, briefly

Configuration changes are usually tracked in several tools that each tell part of the story, and alerts arrive after the damage. He wants the same visibility for config that Datadog, Splunk or Prometheus give for code, in one place. On automation, Ansible, Terraform and Puppet already handle infrastructure; application configuration deserves the same, from the developer's laptop to production, with humans still setting the rules and checks.

## Honest scope

This is a principles talk with a vendor close, and it leans heavily on metaphor (castles, mazes, orchestras, a smoke alarm that goes off after the fire). The abstract promises a demo of the open source implementation; the talk describes Configu's approach and points you to github.com/configu/configu rather than showing it running. The RBAC-plus-ABAC section is the part worth taking back to your team, whatever tool you use.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers who own environment variables and secrets across many services and suspect their access model is too coarse. Security leads looking for a short framing of configuration risk for developers will find it useful too.

Title: An SBOM tells you what you ship, not whether you should trust it
Description: Marek Najmajer (Linux Polska) and Aleksander Baranowski (EuroLinux) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on scoring open source risk beyond the SBOM
Body:
Knowing which open source components are in your build is step one; knowing which of them are about to rot, or come from somewhere you'd rather not depend on, is the hard part. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, [Marek Najmajer of Linux Polska and Aleksander Baranowski of EuroLinux](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Marek_Najmajer_Aleksander_Baranowski_beyond_sbom_risk_assessment) present SCARM (Software Composition Analysis - Risk Management), a model that scores every dependency, and the system built from them, on four dimensions: who writes it, how alive it is, how good the code is, and how its CVEs behave.

## Why isn't an SBOM enough?

"There is a big hole in security in every software made and installed due to opensource components," Najmajer said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023. He quotes 96% of companies using open source and doubts many of them have a structured approach to its risk. DevSecOps covers SAST, DAST and IAST on your own code, but not the components you never bought and never really chose. Their motto is KYCC: know your code and coder.

The SBOM gives you the inventory, including the libraries your libraries call. But "no third party component is risk free," so the goal is picking the less risky one, and swapping a component late can mean new architecture, new licences and lost customers.

## The four dimensions

Baranowski runs through the vectors, and argues the system score matters more than any single component's, the same way you patch systems, not CVEs.

- **Contributor profile**: project load, number of contributors, time zone and geopolitical risk. A repo with stars, open issues and no merged change in two years is abandoned, even if nobody said so. Time zone also predicts how fast a fix lands after an exploit drops at night.
- **Project dynamics**: an interest index (popular code gets more eyes, with the Heartbleed caveat), activity over time and the change in active contributors, since one maintainer means a bus factor of one. Low activity is not automatically bad: mature tools such as the Linux ACL utilities barely need commits.
- **Code quality**: size, style, sensitive code, dead code, documentation. They were surprised how much software fails today's standards, with unchecked buffers in C and volatile misused as thread safety in C++. Language trends count too: a project in a language with a shrinking pool of programmers is a long-term risk.
- **CVE dynamics**: CVSS v2, v3 and v4, and the CVE list for the last 90 days.

## The geopolitics part is blunt

Speaking from Poland, Baranowski does not dodge it: open source can be weaponised, and he would think twice before using software produced in a country threatening his own. "Weaponizing the open source put the whole movement of open and free software at risk," he said. Export controls on software get a mention too.

## CVE counts punish the honest

The CVE dimension is his least favourite. Filing a CVE is bureaucratic, often slower than the fix, and a reputation hit, so plenty of maintainers quietly ship the patch. Score projects by CVE count and you reward that silence. "We are punishing the good guys," he said, pointing to Daniel Stenberg's post on why curl's CVE count reflects honesty. They tried estimating missing CVEs statistically and gave up, because a score must rest on real data.

## Where it plugs into the pipeline

Najmajer names four touchpoints where component choices fail: architecture and design (picking a risky component), CI/CD build (a spoofed or compromised source), maintenance (taking new versions unchecked) and decommissioning (choosing the wrong replacement). SCARM sits in testing and production vulnerability checks. The research is co-financed by the EU through Poland's National Centre for Research and Development, and it surfaces in the SourceMation portal: scored, regularly rebuilt images for around twelve runtime platforms, and side-by-side scores to help choose between, say, MariaDB, MySQL and PostgreSQL, or Redis and RabbitMQ. The portal was about a month from launch when they recorded.

## Who should watch

Security architects and platform teams who already produce SBOMs and wonder what to do with them. It is a model and a product preview more than a how-to, but the four dimensions are a checklist you can apply by hand tomorrow.

Title: Catching water leaks with machine learning in plain Ruby
Description: Vishwajeetsingh Desurkar (SimplySmart Technologies) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on detecting water meter anomalies with native Ruby ML gems
Body:
When your whole product is written in Ruby, rewriting it in Python is a poor way to add machine learning. At Conf42 IoT 2023, Vishwajeetsingh Desurkar, Principal Engineer at SimplySmart Technologies, shows how his team stayed in Ruby to detect anomalies in water meter readings: Prophet for forecasting, Rover for data frames, and a simple rule that a reading far from the forecast means a leak or a broken meter.

SimplySmart builds end-to-end water management, from the meter hardware to the mobile app and admin tools for residential and commercial projects. The talk is short, practical and mostly code walkthroughs; the abstract mentions live demos of Ruby-powered devices, but what you get is notebooks and graphs rather than hardware on a desk.

## The problem: 80,000 meters and nobody to stare at them

Water meters produce time series, and at a small scale a person can spot a meter acting up. Desurkar describes the fleet growing from 1,000 meters to 10,000, then 40,000 and on towards 80,000, at which point manual maintenance stops working. The second problem is abnormal usage: a tap left open, a leak, water the company exists to save.

Both problems reduce to anomaly detection. The awkward part was the language. Vishwajeetsingh Desurkar said at Conf42 IoT 2023: "But is it really possible to perform machine learning sort of application using Ruby?" His first searches turned up nothing useful in the top results.

## The Ruby ML stack exists, mostly thanks to one person

The breakthrough was finding the work of Andrew Kane, who has written a long list of native Ruby libraries (including Blazer, for business intelligence). Desurkar's emphasis is on native: earlier Ruby ML options were often wrappers around Python libraries, which made customising them painful because underneath, everything was still Python.

The stack he walks through:

- **Numo::NArray** for NumPy-style matrix maths and scientific calculations.
- **IRuby** to run a Ruby kernel in Jupyter notebooks.
- **Rover** for data frames, the pandas role, and in his view the most optimised option, written in Ruby itself.
- **Rumale** for the scikit-learn role. His sample trains a transformer and a linear SVC classifier, dumps both to files, reloads them for prediction and reaches about 98% accuracy on a sample dataset, in ten to twelve lines.
- **Daru** for data analysis, plus fastText for text and Nyaplot and Vega for plotting. He notes, for Indian viewers, that daru is slang for liquor, which is an unfortunate name for a data analysis gem.

The model-dumping step is the useful habit here: train once on a lot of data, persist the model, load it at prediction time rather than retraining on every request.

## Two shapes of anomaly, two different repair crews

The part worth stealing for any IoT fleet is how he maps anomaly types to actions:

- **Point outliers**: a single junk reading, often from a power failure. If a site shows two or three of these a day, send someone to check the supporting electrical system, not the meter.
- **Subsequence anomalies**: a run of readings fluctuating up and down. That points at the meter hardware itself, so a hardware technician gets told proactively.

A Ruby port of the Prophet forecasting library detects these from a series loaded out of a CSV, returning the points with their timestamps and values, which then get plotted.

## Detection by forecasting catches the open tap

Abnormal usage is harder, because a water meter is a counter that only goes up, so a spike detector sees nothing. Instead, Prophet learns the consumption pattern and forecasts the next values. His example: a site uses around 1,000 litres between ten and twelve in the morning, 200 to 300 litres in the quiet afternoon, and rises again in the evening. If the afternoon suddenly shows 1,200 or 1,300 litres, that is a leak or a tap someone forgot to close, and the resident or facility owner gets an alert.

The code is short: load the CSV into a Rover data frame, fit the Prophet model, build future data frames at a fixed periodicity, predict, and flag the actual readings that sit well away from the forecast line.

## Who should watch

Ruby teams who've been told machine learning means a second stack, and anyone running a fleet of metering devices who wants a simple, explainable first pass at anomaly detection. Data scientists won't find new methods here; the value is in the mapping from anomaly shape to maintenance action, and in proof that the gems exist.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Piotr Stepinski on [time series forecasting](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Piotr_Stepinski_forecasting_timeseries) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

Title: A slimmer image is not a safer image, as PetClinic proves
Description: Jhonnatan Gil Chaves (Globant) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on scanning container images and hosts in the pipeline, with a Spring PetClinic demo
Body:
Shrinking a Docker image with a multi-stage build makes it lighter, not safer, if both versions sit on the same base. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, [Jhonnatan Gil Chaves](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Jhonnatan_Gil_Chaves_security_development_continuous_delivery), DevOps Engineer at Globant, walks through the four security problems of containerised apps and then scans Spring PetClinic twice to show it: two images of very different sizes, the same 40 issues.

## What goes wrong with containers?

Gil Chaves starts from the CNCF glossary definition of a container and the usual benefits: portability, isolation, resource efficiency, and teams moving faster from a laptop to lower environments to production. Then he lists the four challenges, mapped against the OWASP Docker Top 10:

- **Image vulnerabilities**: flaws in the three layers of any image, the operating system, the runtime and the application itself.
- **Misconfigurations**: exposed ports such as 22 for SSH, secrets left in the image, insecure files, and container registries with leaked credentials where an attacker can swap an image for an evil one under the same tag.
- **Supply chain attacks**: code modified somewhere in the lifecycle so the product you ship to customers carries a malicious package. The impact list is data breaches, disruption, privilege escalation and reputation damage.
- **Identity and access management**: what the container can reach, with access control lists, attribute-based access control and, on Kubernetes, RBAC.

For each one the answer sits in the pipeline: vulnerability detection, misconfiguration detection, supply chain checks and IAM enforcement, with the security and compliance section of the CNCF tool catalogue as the menu.

## The demo: two PetClinics, one base image

The repo (jthan24/conf42-2023devsecops on GitHub, with a sensible warning not to run it in production) builds Spring PetClinic two ways. The first Dockerfile compiles with Maven and keeps the whole source tree in the image. The second is multi-stage: build in one stage, copy only the JAR into the production stage. The mini image is clearly smaller.

He then runs Docker Bench for Security against his own Arch Linux host, mounting /etc, the Docker socket and friends read-only. It catches that his Docker daemon was listening on a port without TLS, which he admits he had opened for other proofs of concept.

Next come image scans. A misconfiguration and CVE scan flags the same low and medium findings on both images, because both build on Eclipse Temurin, which is based on Ubuntu. Snyk agrees: 40 issues on PetClinic, 40 on PetClinic mini. Multi-stage builds cut weight and attack surface from the source code, but the base image's vulnerabilities come along for the ride. Pick the base carefully, then scan it anyway.

## The tools are the easy part

The talk closes on people rather than scanners. Selling a DevSecOps culture inside a company is hard, he says, and "it's not easy to sell something like that." Tools are where you start, but the job is getting teams into security training and making security their habit too, "because not all dev teams are open to start for this journey."

## Who should watch

Developers and DevOps engineers taking their first steps with container security who want a concrete demo they can clone and rerun. It is an introductory talk: the scanning is the payoff, and experienced platform teams will know most of the material.
