Title: Hunt the attacker's habits, not their hashes
Description: Fulvio Colombrino (Deloitte) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on TTP-based threat hunting that catches what the EDR and SIEM miss by default
Body:
Hashes and IPs are cheap for an attacker to change; how they work is not. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, [Fulvio Colombrino](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Fulvio_Colombrino_detect_known_unknowns), Cyber Security Analyst at Deloitte and head of a threat hunting project for an international client, shows how his team built detections around tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), and caught a BITSAdmin abuse that neither the client's EDR nor its SIEM flagged out of the box.

## Why climb the pyramid of pain?

The talk is framed by David Bianco's pyramid of pain. At the bottom sit hashes and IP addresses, which Colombrino calls brittle: an attacker swaps them in minutes. At the top sit TTPs, which take more time to detect but force an adversary to change their whole approach once you can see their kill chain. He justifies the extra effort with a wine metaphor (he is Italian, so this is mandatory): a slightly better bottle, then cheese, then orange jam, each a small spend for a much better evening.

## Pandora sits between the tools and the infrastructure

The project, called Pandora (opening the box of known unknowns), was built with his colleague Niko Mkhatvari over roughly a year. It rests on three points: avoid a single point of failure by covering both the EDR and the SIEM, reduce dwell time, and assume breach so the hunting is proactive instead of only post-incident. Pandora does not replace EDR, SIEM, AV, proxy or PAM. It sits between them and the infrastructure, catching evasive techniques that slip past the commercial defaults.

## The workflow, borrowed from MITRE

The method follows MITRE's TTP-based hunting approach:

1. Build a threat model of the client, from several vendor reports rather than one, to reduce bias. Attackers have sector and technology preferences, so you start with the TTPs most likely to reach you.
2. Write abstract analytics: what would you need to see to raise an alert?
3. Check data requirements, then fill gaps: enable event logs, add sensors, fix misconfigurations that drop data you already have.
4. Write and baseline the rules, test them, deploy, hunt.

Baselining is the part he stresses most. Commercial EDRs and SIEMs are general by design, and every organisation has its own noise: GPO-driven daily routines, OS activity, short-lived outliers from new software, and admins doing things that look a lot like attacker behaviour. Tune for that up front or drown in false positives.

## A lab that looks like the victim

For testing they built three virtual machines: an EDR detonation box, a SIEM detonation box and a log collector, fenced off from the network. The detonation machines mimic the most common end-user device, because that is what gets infected first. "Because of course theory is something, but practice is another," Colombrino said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

## The BITSAdmin case

The worked example covers two techniques that share one tool, BITSAdmin: Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) and System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218). The analytics watch for the BITSAdmin process with flags like /addfile, /SetNotifyCmdLine or /Resume. The data source was Windows process creation, Event ID 4688, since the client did not run Sysmon, and even that needed a parsing fix in the SIEM before the queries worked. Replaying the techniques with Atomic Red Team, neither the EDR nor the SIEM detected them by default; with the custom rules, both did.

## What comes next?

His close: "techniques are not set in stone." Revisit rules as techniques evolve, work down the TTP list, and only start modelling whole APT kill chains once your defences are mature.

## Who should watch

SOC analysts and detection engineers starting a structured hunting programme. It is a short, methodical talk, light on tooling detail but with one concrete, reproducible example.

- Jagdsh Chand on [iterative threat modelling in agile teams](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Jagdsh_Chand_iterative_threat_modelling_agile_development) at the same event.
- Darren Richardson on [threat modelling CI/CD environments](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Darren_Richardson_threat_modelling_cicd_environments).

Title: Every real IoT system is wired and wireless at once
Description: Samarth Gupta (Think Future Technologies) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on picking IoT protocols, from UART and I2C to Zigbee, LoRaWAN and NB-IoT
Body:
The wired-versus-wireless debate in IoT has a boring answer, and Samarth Gupta, IoT Developer at Think Future Technologies, gives it at Conf42 IoT 2023: a complex IoT system always uses both. Sensors talk to the microcontroller over wires, the microcontroller talks to the gateway and the server over radio, and your job is to pick the right protocol for each hop based on power, range and how much data you actually send.

The talk is a guided tour of about a dozen protocols, with the trade-offs of each and a few opinions along the way. It is an introduction, and a good one if you came to IoT from the server side and the acronyms on a datasheet still look like line noise.

## Wired: reliable, secure, a bit dull

Gupta sells the wired side honestly. A cable gives a known path from point A to point B, so less interference, no eavesdropping from outside the enclosure, and better speed. He points out that Ethernet still beats Wi-Fi at home: on his 1 Gbps connection, Wi-Fi gets 400 to 600 Mbps while the cable gets the full gigabit.

Then the basics every embedded developer meets on day one:

- **UART**: the simplest serial protocol, in almost every appliance from smart TVs to cars, easy to implement and short-range.
- **I2C**: two wires, many devices, each with its own address. Most industrial-grade sensors sit on an I2C bus. Fewer devices on the bus buys you more range or speed.
- **SPI**: one master (usually the microcontroller), high speed, but four wires per slave, so the wiring grows fast. You find it in anything with an antenna, Wi-Fi routers included.

The industrial and automotive layer comes next. **Modbus** runs most manufacturing machinery. **OPC UA**, a standard from a consortium of IoT vendors, exists so a Samsung gateway can talk to a Siemens or Honeywell sensor; it is complex to implement, but SDKs hide most of that. **CAN** carries engine RPM, coolant temperature, speed and fuel level in every vehicle, and you can read part of it by plugging a reader into the OBD port.

His verdict on the wired world is that not much innovation happens there. Which is where the second half of the talk comes in. Samarth Gupta said at Conf42 IoT 2023: "wireless protocols are much more interesting than wired ones because wired ones is something very basic".

## Wireless: pick two of range, power and speed

Bluetooth is short range, roughly 20 to 25 metres, and BLE trades range for battery life, which suits a smartwatch that only needs two or three metres. Wi-Fi gives high data rates but draws too much power for battery devices, so it lives in things on mains power, like smart speakers.

**Zigbee** is the home-automation workhorse: low power, a gateway, mesh networking where devices relay each other's messages, and a range of about 100 metres. He has an opinion on the rivalry with Z-Wave too: "According to me, I think in the war between Zigbee and Zwave, Zigbee has already won that war".

## LoRaWAN, NB-IoT and a satellite twist

His favourite is **LoRaWAN**: a cheap gateway in your home gives you a private network over 5 to 8 km, and battery-powered sensors can run five to eight years. The price is speed, often a few kbps, which is plenty for a temperature reading. It runs on the unlicensed ISM band and shows up in smart cities and smart agriculture.

**NB-IoT** does a similar job on licensed spectrum, sold by mobile operators who reuse their existing 4G and 5G antennas. Gupta has used both, and his deciding factor is ownership: LoRaWAN lets you run your own infrastructure, NB-IoT means going through a network provider. **Sigfox**, in the same low-power wide-area space, he describes as slowly getting outdated.

The fun bit is Lacuna, a startup putting LoRaWAN receivers on satellites so that anything with a view of the sky, say a container ship, can send sensor data to your server.

## How to choose

His method is short. Start from the use case. Does the device have mains power, a battery or solar? How much data does it send? Temperature and humidity values fit a low-power wide-area protocol; a video stream needs Wi-Fi or Ethernet. A smart LED shows the mix in one product: wired from the microcontroller to the LED, Wi-Fi or Zigbee from the microcontroller to the internet. A smart factory runs its machines on Modbus and its environment sensors on LoRaWAN.

## Who should watch

Software engineers starting on hardware, product people who need to read an IoT architecture diagram, and anyone choosing between LoRaWAN and NB-IoT for a battery-powered fleet. Seasoned embedded engineers will know most of it.

Title: Honeytokens, or how to make the attacker's favourite loot snitch
Description: Dwayne McDaniel (GitGuardian) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on honeytokens, decoy credentials that alert you the moment an intruder tries them
Body:
Attackers who get inside go looking for hardcoded credentials, so give them some that only ring an alarm. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, [Dwayne McDaniel](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Dwayne_McDaniel_detecting_honeytokens), Developer Advocate at GitGuardian, makes the case for honeytokens: decoy keys that look real, grant nothing, and tell you who tried them. He opens the talk by pasting an AWS key pair into a public GitHub repo, and closes it by showing who came knocking.

## Why bet on credentials as bait?

Because that is what attackers want, and they are predictable about it. McDaniel walks through three breaches. At Uber in September 2022, an MFA-fatigued admin let an attacker in, who then found PowerShell scripts on a network share with hardcoded credentials, including admin access to the Thycotic PAM, and from there AWS, GCP, Slack and the HackerOne console. At AstraZeneca, test environment credentials sat on public GitHub for over a year while another developer had pushed real patient data into that same test environment. At CircleCI in January 2023, malware on a remote engineer's unpatched machine stole secrets from the internal network and customer applications.

The CircleCI one is the hook: an outside researcher noticed his honeytokens firing inside CircleCI and said so publicly before the official announcement. The scale numbers come from GitGuardian's own scanning of every public GitHub commit: 10 million secrets exposed in 2022, a 67% jump on the 6 million of 2021, and on average 5.5 commits out of every 1,000 leaking at least one secret.

## Deception is older than your threat model

There is a fun history detour, from the Trojan horse and the inflatable tanks of the WWII Ghost Army to Cliff Stoll chasing a 75-cent billing error at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in 1985 and inventing the honeypot along the way. Then Fred Cohen's Deception Toolkit in 1991, Augusto Paes de Barros coining the term honeytokens in 2003, Thinkst adding AWS keys to Canarytokens in 2016, and Kevin Mandia calling honeytokens early warning signs at RSA 2023. The arc is the useful bit: from fake systems to fake data to fake credentials that look exactly like the real thing.

"Honey token is a decoy credential that doesn't allow any real access," McDaniel said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023. It looks identical to a real one, and using it raises an alert with at least the caller's IP address.

## How do you build one?

The reference design is GitGuardian's open source ggcanary, built with Terraform on AWS: IAM users with no permissions at all, CloudTrail logging into an S3 bucket, a Lambda that matches access attempts against the list of decoy users, and a Slack message or an email via SES or SendGrid when one matches. He recommends deploying it in a region you use for nothing else. Other DIY routes are SpaceSiren (needs AWS know-how) and Thinkst's self-hosted canarytokens (needs Docker). Off the shelf there is the free canarytokens.org for one-off tokens (AWS keys, fake credit cards, PDFs), Thinkst Canary for scale, GitGuardian's Honeytoken module, and options inside Microsoft Sentinel, CrowdStrike and Proofpoint. It is a vendor talk with an honest vendor list, and he says plainly he is biased toward his employer.

## Where do they go, and where don't they?

The rules are short and sensible:

- **Private places only**: private repos, CI, Jira, Slack, Vault. Nobody has a legitimate reason to touch them, so any use means trouble.
- **Never public**: AWS, GitHub, GitLab, GitGuardian and plenty of bots scan public code constantly and will set them off.
- **One token per repo or environment**, so an alert points at exactly one place.
- **Automate it**, and treat it as a habit rather than a project: "If you added one new honey token per sprint, and your average sprint is three weeks, then you're going to get a lot of coverage in a year's time."
- **Think blue team**: use the IP and user agent to block and rotate, not to hunt people down.

## The demo pays off the opening

Remember that key he pasted into a public repo? Twenty-six minutes later it had been tried twelve times. First AWS itself, which scans for its own leaked keys, then GitGuardian, then two callers in the US and one in India with TruffleHog as the user agent, all calling get-caller-identity to see whether it worked. That is the best argument in the talk for keeping honeytokens out of public repos, and for how fast leaked keys get picked up.

His closing line is the thesis: "it's really hard to win if you only play defense." Cut the dwell time, break the attacker's playbook, and most of them move on.

## Who should watch

Security engineers and platform teams who own CI, repos or Vault and want a cheap tripwire. It is an introductory talk, well paced, with a live demo that lands. If you already run Canarytokens, skip to the best practices.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Daniel Oates-Lee on [secrets in git repos](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Daniel_OatesLee_git_secrets_repos) at the same event.
- Brian Contos on [hacking demos, secrets and asset intelligence](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Brian_Contos_hacking_demos_secrets_asset_intelligence).

Title: Expired maintainer domains left 2,843 npm packages exposed
Description: Danish Tariq and Hassan Khan Yusufzai at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on npm account takeover via expired email domains, and RubyGems dependency confusion
Body:
Security researchers Danish Tariq and Hassan Khan Yusufzai presented at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 a registry-wide study of one quiet npm weakness: maintainer accounts tied to email addresses on domains that have expired. Across more than 2.1 million packages they found 2,843 packages whose maintainers were exposed that way, with over 250,000 dependent repositories behind them.

The talk is a research report with defensive tooling, not a product pitch, and they open with a clear disclaimer that it is for awareness only. Tariq covers the supply chain background, Yusufzai the numbers.

## Why is the maintainer's email part of your supply chain?

Tariq's framing is a cake: the chef made it, but if the butter or the pistachios go bad, the customer still gets sick. Software is the same, built from dependencies of dependencies. He shows Express's own dependency web to make the point that you trust far more than you install directly. He lists the main attack families: vulnerable dependencies (Log4Shell), typosquatting, repojacking, dependency confusion, and the focus here, account takeover.

An npm package is only as safe as its maintainers' accounts, and each account recovers through an email address. When that address sits on a custom domain that lapses, whoever registers the domain next can receive the account's recovery email. Tariq points to a real case reported by The Register, where a package with 36,000 dependent projects was exposed this way. The defensive version is simple: list every package you use, look up its maintainers' email domains, and check them against WHOIS expiry. Doing it by hand doesn't scale, so they published a small scanner (npm-account-hijacking-scanner on GitHub) that takes a package or a list and can run from a cron job or pipeline.

## How big is the problem across npm?

Yusufzai's numbers, from a snapshot taken in late 2022:

- 2,118,539 packages collected, close to the whole registry.
- 6,789,211 maintainer email entries, 603,887 unique.
- 132,632 unique domains, of which 675 had expired.
- Those domains matched 845 unique email addresses.
- 2,843 packages confirmed exposed.

The headline number looks small next to 2.1 million, which is why they turn to impact. Those 2,843 packages had 93,007 dependent packages, 257,687 dependent repositories, 50,390 contributors and 413,839 forks. The concentration is the scary part: maintainers average more than 11 packages each, and some single addresses maintain thousands. "So just imagine the impact here, how much of impact one expired domain can have on NPM packages," Yusufzai said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

They also flag the gap their scan didn't cover: maintainer emails that appear in public breach dumps, where a reused password does the same job as an expired domain.

## And RubyGems?

A second study looked at dependency confusion in Ruby. Out of 160,953 gems, they scanned 1,700 openly disclosed dependencies scraped from GitHub, Bitbucket and GitLab, and found 285 vulnerable or claimable, about 16%. They released GemScanner, which reads a Gemfile.lock and flags any gem behind its latest version, not just ones with a published CVE.

## What should you do about it?

- **MFA everywhere.** npm and RubyGems started requiring MFA for top packages and have been extending it.
- **Treat updates as untrusted input.** Watch security bulletins, validate checksums, review code, and evaluate third parties' security posture.
- **Scan the dependency tree.** GitHub security alerts and Dependabot, GitLab scanning, npm audit and retire.js for Node, bundler-audit for Ruby, OWASP Dependency-Check for Java and .NET.
- **Keep an SBOM.** Their open source pick is CycloneDX with Dependency-Track, which gives you the inventory you need to answer "are we affected?" fast.

## Who should watch

AppSec and platform teams who own dependency policy, and open source maintainers still using a vanity-domain email for their registry account. Renew it, or move it.

Related Conf42 talks:

- Leonid Akinin on [trusting open source Python packages](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Leonid_Akinin_trusty_package_ttps_oss_python) at the same event.
- Marek Najmajer and Aleksander Baranowski on [risk assessment beyond the SBOM](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Marek_Najmajer_Aleksander_Baranowski_beyond_sbom_risk_assessment).
- Simon Gurney on [subdomain hijacking](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Simon_Gurney_subdomain_hijacking_vulnerable), the same expired-name problem one layer up.

Title: Conf42 JavaScript 2023: let the browser and the server do more
Description: The Conf42 JavaScript 2023 roundup - 32 talks on React Server Components, less JavaScript, monoliths vs micro frontends, Node.js, tooling and the web's carbon.
Body:
[Conf42 JavaScript 2023](https://www.conf42.com/js2023) went out on November 16 with 32 talks, and the most useful ones shared a suspicion of your bundle. React Server Components moved rendering back to the server, a whole talk argued for replacing JavaScript with HTML and CSS, and two talks on frontend architecture disagreed, politely, about whether the monolith has to be split. Around them sat Node.js internals, a solid tools track, a couple of blockchain clients and an honest look at what a page view costs in CO2.

Speakers came from LinkedIn, AWS, Akamai Technologies, Yandex, Playtech, NearForm, Mattermost, MY.GAMES, Polypane, Permit.io, Kadena, Metis, Configu, Push-Based.io and a long list of agencies and startups.

## Where should rendering happen?

[Tejas Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Tejas_Kumar_react_server_components) took React Server Components apart: how React looked ten years ago, how it works today, and why it is an architecture as much as a library, with the server present at every level of the tree and real gains for data fetching. [Ken Snyder](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Ken_Snyder_remix_philosophy) of Shoreline Health argued that the Remix philosophy (lean on the server, nested routes and outlets, web standards) is worth adopting even if you never install Remix. [Guilherme Dalla Rosa](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Guilherme_Dalla_Rosa_architecture_ecommerce_platform) of MerCloud showed what happened when a traditional React app had to be replicated per B2B customer, and how Next.js with server-side rendering and CDN caching turned it into one multi-tenant platform. [Juan Felipe Gomez](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Juan_Felipe_Gomez_cms_jamstack_innovation_web_dev) of Make it Real traced the path from WordPress to headless CMS and the JAMstack.

## Do you need JavaScript for that?

Often not, said [Kilian Valkhof](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Kilian_Valkhof_moving_features_css_html) of Polypane, walking through patterns that now have native HTML and CSS equivalents: styled form controls with appearance none, focus-visible for keyboard users, datalist for suggestions. The browser has more rights than your page, so its version often does more. [Francesco Sciuti](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Francesco_Sciuti_browsers_made_by_others) of devmy explained what the browser goes through to render a page, multi-process architecture and sandboxing included, and [Ankit Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Ankit_Gupta_shadow_dom) of Intelekt AI covered the Shadow DOM for encapsulated components.

[Julia Ziebinska](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Julia_Ziebinska_better_web_reducing_carbon_emissions) of Akamai Technologies put a number on the bloat: an average page view generates about 1.8 grams of CO2, and she showed how to measure your own site and cut it with simple frontend and resource changes. Every kilobyte you don't ship is a tiny tree.

## Split the monolith, or make it glorious?

[Aleksandr Guzenko](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Aleksandr_Guzenko_breaking_monolith_code_splitting_techniques) of IT_ONE gave six ways to split a frontend monolith, from NPM packages as a first step to Module Federation in webpack 5. [Maksim Zemskov](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Maksim_Zemskov_glorious_monolith_scaling_application_microfrontends) of Yandex took the other side with Yandex Direct, a codebase over 20 years old: micro frontends are not the only way to scale, and the real enemy is high coupling, which you can fight inside one app. [Vadim Tsaregorodtsev](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Vadim_Tsaregorodtsev_git_submodules_monorepo) of Emerging Travel Group shared code across projects with git submodules, a monorepo at home.

## Node.js, from the event loop up

[Lorenzo Pieri](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Lorenzo_Pieri_nodejs_eventloop_fairytale) of Birdie explained the event loop as a fairy tale, knights of the thread and all, and it is a good first talk on the subject. [Gabriel Liechtman Manor](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Gabriel_Liechtman_Manor_building_auth_nodejs) of Permit.io covered authorization done well: middleware instead of scattered if statements, a permission model first, and tools such as OPA, OPAL and Zanzibar-style systems. [Vladi Stevanovic](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Vladi_Stevanovic_nodejs_app_realtime_collaboration) of Multiplayer showed how to add Figma-style real-time collaboration with CRDTs or operational transformation, and [Anton Kalik](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Anton_Kalik_ai_nodejs_custom_sports_activity) of Amenitiz built a workout suggestion service on Node.js and OpenAI. [Daniele Fontani and Daniele Ciulli](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Daniele_Fontani_Daniele_Ciulli_frontend_unchained_develop_apis) of Sintra Digital Business went further and skipped the backend with their own CRUD framework.

## The tools that keep a big codebase honest

[Chris Ng](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Chris_Ng_zero_lint_failures_tackling_codequality_challenges) of LinkedIn told how a large app with thousands of lint failures got to zero: new rules must resolve their existing failures, owners are identified, incentives matter, and the whole road took almost a year, with the last 20% the hardest. [Julian Jandl](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Julian_Jandl_js_heap_memory_leaks) of Push-Based.io read heap snapshots and retainer lists in Chrome DevTools to find memory leaks, and [Steven Schkolne](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Steven_Schkolne_browser_dev_tools_code) of MightyMeld asked why browser devtools still don't understand your components.

[Taslan A. Graham](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Taslan_A_Graham_web_accessibility_testing_playwrightjs_axecore) of CradleApps automated accessibility testing with Playwright and axe-core. [Adam Furmanek](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Adam_Furmanek_database_guardrails) of Metis made the case for database guardrails that catch slow queries before production, [Peleg Porat](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Peleg_Porat_everythingascode) of Configu applied the as-code idea to configuration, [Gil Zilberfeld](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Gil_Zilberfeld_apis_refactoring_patterns) of TestinGil refactored ugly API code to patterns under end-to-end tests, and [Joshua Arvin Lat](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Joshua_Arvin_Lat_securing_applications) of NuWorks Interactive Labs covered securing JavaScript apps from day zero, in-browser ML models included. [Aleksandr Tkachenko](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Aleksandr_Tkachenko_skeleton_mammoth_reusable_loaders) of Playtech presented Skeleton Mammoth, his dependency-free CSS library for skeleton loaders.

## JavaScript in unusual places

[Alfonso Graziano](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Alfonso_Graziano_videos_react) of NearForm edited videos in React with Remotion and built a cloud rendering farm for them. [Dmitrii Ivashchenko](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Dmitrii_Ivashchenko_webgl_to_webgpu) of MY.GAMES walked the migration from WebGL to WebGPU for games, [Andrey Makarov](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Andrey_Makarov_battleship_game) of Islamic Coin built multiplayer Battleship with React and Socket.IO, and [Arundeep Nagaraj](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Arundeep_Nagaraj_easy_mode_fullstack_figma_aws_amplify) of AWS turned Figma designs into React components with Amplify Studio. On chain, [Albert Groothedde](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Albert_Groothedde_javascript_client_smart_contracts) of Kadena introduced a typesafe client for Pact smart contracts and [Cesar Cordero Rodriguez](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Cesar_Cordero_Rodriguez_develop_web3_webapp_python) of LatinChain built a Pi Network app with a JavaScript frontend and Python backend. [Daniel Espino Garcia](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Daniel_Espino_Garcia_magic_oss_project) of Mattermost closed the loop on where all those npm packages come from, and why free means freedom.

## Thanks to the sponsors

[QuadCode](https://quadcode.com/) was the silver sponsor, with [unpack.tech](https://www.unpack.tech/) as newsletter partner, alongside media partners including [Manning](https://www.manning.com), [Packt](https://www.packtpub.com/), [bpb online](https://bpbonline.com/), [Dev It Jobs](https://devitjobs.uk/), [CodeCrafters](https://codecrafters.io/?r=2qF) and [Vihat Technologies](https://vihattechnologies.com/).

Every talk is on the [Conf42 JavaScript 2023 page](https://www.conf42.com/js2023) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrAjSjOwtyUUZYTWZZfupwc1). The series returned a year later as [Conf42 JavaScript 2024](https://www.conf42.com/js2024).

Title: Security is six jobs, and most of them aren't hacking
Description: Michal Davidson (Dell Technologies) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on splitting security into domains for careers, hiring, diversity and holistic design
Body:
Michal Davidson, Software and Security Architect at Dell Technologies, argued at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 that "security" is too broad a word to build a career, a job ad or a secure system around. Split it into domains (compliance, network security, monitoring, cryptography, security architecture and hacking), she says, and you get clearer career paths, better hiring, and fewer systems with one door bolted shut and a window wide open.

Davidson leads public cloud security for Dell's PowerFlex software-defined storage, lectures on cyber security, and started her career as a developer who knew nothing about security. That background drives the talk.

## Why does the single blob hurt?

Her first motivation is diversity. Fewer women work in security than in tech overall, and she thinks part of the reason is the image of the security expert as a hacker: the teenager in a basement who types for two minutes and is inside the bank. If that's the bar, plenty of capable people decide the field isn't for them. Her counter, which is the talk's thesis: "it is possible to become a security expert without necessarily knowing hacking," Davidson said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

The second is hiring. Listings for "security engineer" or "security architect" share a title and describe entirely different skills. Naming the domain says what you actually need. The third is engineering: if a customer asks for federal compliance and all attention goes there, you get the padlocked door next to the open window. Holistic security means walking around the house and checking every domain.

She's explicit that her six are one way to cut it. Use five or ten if you like; the point is to cut it.

## What are the domains?

**Compliance.** FedRAMP, the US executive order, SOC 2/3, ISO 27001, DISA STIG, HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR. These are third-party standards, so they must be generic, which makes them process-heavy and unable to capture your system's specifics. Compliance usually makes a system more secure. It does not make it secure.

**Network security.** Classically perimeter, authentication (who?) and authorisation (what?). Cloud and zero trust added a constant third question: why is this identity doing this now? IAM, SSO and MFA now sit at the centre; data centre networks became VPCs and firewalls became security groups. Her caution: mutual TLS with the latest protocol is worthless if the private key behind the certificate can be stolen.

**Monitoring.** Anomaly detection, IDS and IPS, and much of what gets sold as cloud security (CNAPP, CSPM, CWPP). Unusually, the experts here often come from data science and machine learning, not security, which makes it a natural entry point for those backgrounds.

**Cryptography.** Her own way in, via smart cards. The maths behind it is accessible, and she recommends everyone in security learn the basics: symmetric vs asymmetric, encryption vs signing. Protocols like TLS make far more sense after that. Inside it sit embedded security (secure boot, trusted execution environments on phones under bring-your-own-device) and cryptanalysis, the fun cat-and-mouse part.

**Security architecture.** Security reviews and threat modelling, which she urges you to do as early as possible: a review at the end produces a list that gets postponed to the next release, while the same effort at the start changes the design. It also means designing security products from building blocks, and never rolling your own crypto.

**Hacking.** White-hat hacking, pen testing and reverse engineering. When she studied reverse engineering with tools like IDA and OllyDbg, the lesson was patience. She compares it to Sherlock piecing a shredded letter together: the film shows two minutes, the real job takes a week. The two-minute hack you see usually runs on someone else's long work.

## Who should watch

Engineers curious about moving into security who don't see themselves as hackers, and managers writing security job descriptions. She ends with free starting points: the Cryptography and Software Security courses on Coursera, Cybrary for pen testing, and the Medium blogs of Taimur Ijlal (Cloud Security Guy) and Prof. Bill Buchanan.

Title: Let the Vault agent fetch the secret so your app doesn't have to
Description: Sam Gabrail (TeKanAid Solutions) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on moving hard-coded MongoDB credentials into Vault with the agent injector and Argo CD
Body:
Sam Gabrail, President of TeKanAid Solutions, used his Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 talk to take a small app with hard-coded database credentials and fix it without touching the application code: deploy it with Argo CD, then let the HashiCorp Vault agent injector drop the MongoDB username and password into the pod as files. The app never learns Vault exists.

It's a hands-on demo talk. Gabrail runs a DevOps and platform engineering academy, and the demo app, the repo and the Codespaces setup come from his course material, so you can follow along step by step.

## What's the starting point?

The school app lets students enrol in courses: a Vue.js front end, a FastAPI back end and MongoDB, each a Kubernetes deployment with a ClusterIP service, installed with Helm on minikube inside GitHub Codespaces. The credentials are hard-coded, and the API logs say so. Anyone with access to the repo has the database password.

Step one is GitOps. Argo CD runs as a Kubernetes controller that compares the live state with the desired state in git and marks drift as OutOfSync; you can sync by hand or turn on auto-sync. Gabrail deletes the namespace, lets Argo CD recreate the app from a manifest pointing at the repo, and gets a real-life GitOps moment for free: a values file he forgot to change breaks the API pod, so he fixes it in git, pushes, and lets Argo CD reconcile.

## How does a pod prove who it is?

The awkward question with any secrets manager is secret zero: how do you authenticate to get the first secret? Here the answer is Vault's Kubernetes auth method. The Vault agent in the pod presents the service account's JWT, Vault checks it with the Kubernetes API, and if Kubernetes vouches for the pod, Vault returns a token with a policy attached that allows reads from specific paths only.

## What does the injector change?

The Vault agent injector is a mutating webhook. It watches pod create and update events for the annotation `vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"` and rewrites the pod spec to add Vault agent containers and a shared in-memory volume (at `/vault/secrets` by default; the demo uses `/app/secrets`). Two flavours:

- **Init container**: fills the volume before the app starts, which suits cron jobs such as backups.
- **Sidecar**: keeps authenticating and re-rendering as the pod runs, which suits long-lived services and matters once secrets change over time.

From there you choose. A Vault-aware app can read the token file the agent writes and call Vault itself, at the cost of code changes. A Vault-unaware app gets its secrets rendered by Vault agent templates, which use the Consul Template project and Go templating, so the agent writes `schoolapp-mongodb-username` and `schoolapp-mongodb-password` files and the app reads files. You configure rendering either with annotations or with a ConfigMap, never both.

## The demo, end to end

Vault goes in with Helm in its own namespace: init, unseal, log in with the root token, enable a KV v2 secrets engine, write the MongoDB credentials, add a policy for that path, and configure Kubernetes auth bound to the app's service account and namespace. On the root token he is blunt: "the root token is only for creating authentication methods and it is to be revoked in production environments," Gabrail said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

Then the GitOps payoff: flip the Helm values to the injector-with-templates mode, commit, push, and Argo CD's diff shows the new annotations before you sync. After the sync the API pod has two containers, the logs report credentials from Vault KV via the injector, and exec-ing into the pod shows the token and the two rendered files. He also points out that Vault doesn't have to run in the cluster; only the injector does.

## What's the next step?

Static KV secrets still mean long-lived credentials. Gabrail's recommendation is Vault's MongoDB dynamic secrets engine: the app gets just-in-time credentials with a TTL and asks for fresh ones when they expire, so nothing long-lived sits anywhere.

## Who should watch

Kubernetes teams with credentials in values files who can't rewrite every service to call Vault directly. If you've never set up Vault's Kubernetes auth, the walkthrough is a clear first pass.

Title: From LAMP to headless, a short history of the CMS
Description: Juan Felipe Gomez (Make it Real) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on how the CMS went from static pages to WordPress to headless and the Jamstack
Body:
The web started static, got dynamic with WordPress, and then went static again with an API behind it. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Juan Felipe Gomez, Full-stack Developer at Make it Real, traces that loop in a compact history of the content management system, ending with headless CMSs, the Jamstack and where to go to start building one.

It is a short talk and an introduction, not an advanced session. Gomez, speaking from Medellin, Colombia, flags it up front: "this is my first time as a speaker". If you already run Next.js on top of a headless CMS, this is the backstory; if you are a developer who keeps hearing about headless in meetings, it is a tidy short primer.

## Why did the CMS exist in the first place?

The early web was static pages with no database queries behind them, which made them cheap and fast. By the mid-1990s sites needed frequent updates and the first, proprietary and closed-source, CMS products appeared. The early 2000s brought open source alternatives such as WordPress, Drupal and Joomla, growing up alongside the LAMP stack (Linux, Apache, MySQL and PHP, Python or Perl). That pairing kicked off the era of monolithic web development: dynamic pages assembled from database queries per visitor, and static sites faded out.

The point of all of it, in Gomez's framing, was handing the keyboard to non-technical people. His example is an amateur food blogger: in the early web they would need HTML skills or a developer; with a CMS they publish in a few clicks from an admin panel. He credits that accessibility with a richer and more diverse web.

## What broke the monolith?

Phones. A monolithic CMS renders HTML for one kind of client, so mobile often meant a second, simplified version of the site. Smart TVs, gaming consoles, voice assistants like Alexa and IoT devices made it worse, and the need for omnichannel delivery became obvious.

The answer was the headless CMS: cut the presentation layer (the head) off the back end and serve content through an API, so a smartwatch and a website read the same source. To a visitor, nothing looks different. To a developer, content becomes a service you consume, and the front end is no longer tied to the CMS's templating, so React or Vue is fair game.

## So what is the Jamstack, exactly?

Gomez is careful here: Jamstack is not a specific set of technologies but a name for a set of widely used architectural practices. J is JavaScript, with your choice of React, Svelte, Angular or Vue. A is APIs, the services you call, such as Auth0, Cloudinary, Stripe, or WordPress itself, now demoted to one service among several. M is markup, prebuilt by a static site generator.

His sharpest observation is about where the effort went: for years it was all back end, and now there is a modular stack on the client side, moving away from the monolith towards something closer to microservices. He lists the claimed advantages as better performance, higher security, easier scaling and a better developer experience, though the talk asserts these rather than measuring them.

## Where should you start?

The closing section is a resource tour. Vercel's template gallery, filtered to CMS, gives deployed demos with their repositories, and Gomez is a fan of learning that way: "I'm one of the person that thinks that one of the better ways to learn is reading others people's code". Next.js Learn has a 16-chapter Next.js course plus a React foundations course and guides such as e-commerce with Next.js and Shopify and headless WordPress with Next.js. Netlify's integrations page rounds out the list.

## Who should watch

Junior developers and anyone who needs the CMS-to-Jamstack story in one sitting. Experienced Jamstack builders can skip it and pick one of the deeper talks below.

Title: Testing IoT end to end means mocking the probe, not the patient
Description: Vipin Jain (Metacube Software) at Conf42 IoT 2023 on testing IoT end to end by splitting the system into layers and mocking each one
Body:
Assembling the whole IoT system and then testing it feels like the honest way to do end-to-end testing. At Conf42 IoT 2023, Vipin Jain, QA Head and Project Delivery Manager at Metacube Software, argues it is mostly the slow way: break the system into layers, give each block a clean interface, and automate around the blocks with stubs and virtual assets, so you find the broken protocol before the whole rig is built.

It is a strategy talk built around one worked example, not a tool demo. If you test software and someone just handed you a device, it is a good map of where to start.

## Why not just test the assembled system?

Jain lists what goes wrong with the build-it-all-then-test habit most organisations follow. It does give a realistic simulation of the end user's experience, but the assembled system can't simulate every situation, building it is time-consuming and costly, and errors surface late, when a fix means reworking the setup and pushing back time to market.

IoT makes that worse for reasons he spells out: multi-layered systems, dissimilar technologies from low-level microcontrollers to server code, features that span layers, incompatible protocols between devices, and teams that sit far apart and write use cases that don't match. Then there's the deceptive simplicity of a device with almost no UI. Vipin Jain said at Conf42 IoT 2023: "I can write 100 test cases and can say that look, everything is working fine, but those 100 test cases are actually just testing the code which is written, which can be only 10% of the entire architecture".

He also walks through how IoT architecture grew from two layers to three to the seven-layer model in use today (physical devices, connectivity, edge computing, data accumulation, data abstraction, application, collaboration and process). Every one of those layers is a place to apply test logic, and that is the base of his strategy.

## A glucose monitor makes the stakes concrete

The running example is a blood glucose tracking system: a wearable sensor patch, an insulin injector, a smartphone acting as middleware, and a cloud healthcare system that compares readings against the patient's history, flags unwanted patterns, alerts medical staff, and can push a dosing change back to the injector. If the patient can't respond, the system can send GPS data so an ambulance finds them.

That one product covers sensors, wireless hops to the phone, cloud storage, bandwidth, a human consultation queue and an actuator that injects a drug. Asking whether it works end to end is a lot of questions in one sentence.

## Deconstruct, then isolate

His answer has two halves. First, deconstruct the system into perception, network, middleware, business and application layers, which only works if the system was designed to come apart into small blocks with well-defined interfaces. Testability is a design requirement, the same way automation has to be built into code before automation engineers can use it.

Second, isolate components and test early. For the glucose probe, dipping a sensor into a liquid with a known glucose level is neither practical nor scalable. Instead, intercept the `ReadProbe()` call and redirect it to a stub or mock that returns reasonable values, hard-coded or read from a test data store. The probe drops out of the test, and everything downstream becomes automatable.

The server side gets the same treatment. A Node.js stub covers simple responses; for richer cases he recommends service virtualization, which can answer by input pattern, record real traffic and replay it, and even switch between the real system and a virtual asset. The prioritised queue of medical consultants, humans in the loop, is exactly the part you replace with a virtual equivalent.

## Unit or functional tests? Both, on purpose

On the old argument, his recommendation is a blended approach. Unit tests matter more as complexity grows and pinpoint root causes quickly, but they are expensive, need an engineer to write them, and are brittle because they sit so close to the code. Functional tests break less often but make systemic bugs hard to trace. For the messaging layer, where MQTT or HTTP carry JSON or proprietary binary payloads over publish-subscribe or request-response, simple Python scripts work for a few scenarios but stop scaling once you go from a few hundred to a few thousand.

His closing line is the fair summary: "IoT testing is challenging, but it is not difficult."

## Who should watch

QA leads and test engineers moving from web or mobile into connected devices, and embedded teams who want a vocabulary for talking to them. It stays at strategy level: no framework recommendations by name, no code.

Title: A Kubernetes Secret is base64 in a trench coat
Description: Alex Soto (Red Hat) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on securing Kubernetes secrets in git, in etcd and at runtime, and why Vault dynamic secrets win
Body:
Alex Soto, Director of Developer Experience at Red Hat, walked Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 through the three places a Kubernetes secret can leak in a GitOps setup: in git, in etcd, and inside the running pod. His answer for each is another layer, ending with HashiCorp Vault dynamic secrets, where nobody knows the password at all.

"A Kubernetes secret is not a secret at all by default," Soto said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, and the rest of the talk is the follow-up. He co-authored a book on Kubernetes secrets management, and the talk feels like a guided tour of it with live demos.

## Why is GitOps the trigger?

Soto's GitOps model is two repositories: source code with CI that builds an image, and a config repo of manifests watched by Argo CD (or Flux). Promoting to production is a pull request from a staging branch to a production branch. Everything is code and everything is in git, which is lovely until the to-do app needs a PostgreSQL password and someone writes a Secret manifest. Its values are base64: encoding, not encryption. Anyone with repo access decodes them in one command.

His framing for the whole talk: there is no 100% secure system, only layers, so an attacker who breaks one meets the next.

## Phase one: secrets in git

Two projects, both Kubernetes controllers:

- **Sealed Secrets.** `kubeseal` fetches the controller's public key and turns a Secret into a SealedSecret with encrypted data. You delete the original, commit the sealed one, and only the controller in the cluster can decrypt it and materialise a normal Secret. Delete the SealedSecret and the Secret goes with it.
- **External Secrets.** Nothing secret goes into git, only configuration: a store pointing at Vault, and an ExternalSecret naming the path and key, refreshed on an interval (15 seconds in his example). The controller pulls the value and creates the native Secret.

His rule of thumb: Sealed Secrets if you live on Kubernetes Secrets, External Secrets if you already run a secrets manager. The Vault operator does the same and adds rolling updates when a secret changes.

## Phase two: secrets in etcd

The harder part. By default etcd stores secrets unencrypted, so anyone with etcd access, its logs or its backups has them. Kubernetes added an encryption configuration, but the decryption key sits in etcd next to the data, which Soto compares to not encrypting at all against a serious attacker. Moving etcd outside the cluster is possible and, in his words, nobody does it. His recommendation is the KMS plugin, which hands encryption to an external system such as Vault, so an attacker needs to compromise two systems instead of one.

## Phase three: secrets at runtime

Even with encrypted git and etcd, the pod gets plaintext. Environment variables are the worst option: `export` shows them, and some monitoring tools log them. Volumes are better, an in-memory file system, but his demo execs into a pod and simply cats the password file. Reading from the Kubernetes API is safer but means a lot of YAML.

His preferred route is direct: the app talks to the secrets manager over HTTPS and keeps the value in its own memory. The costs are real: a new tool to learn and operate, and code changes. The payoff is auditing, rotation and dynamic secrets. With dynamic secrets, Vault sets the PostgreSQL password itself, rotates it on a schedule (60 minutes in his example), and gives the same value to the app, so no human, operator or developer ever knows it. In the demo a Quarkus app's datasource config names Vault as its credentials provider and contains no password.

"Remember, no secrets is the best secrets," he said, before closing with rotation and threat-detection tools like Falco, StackRox and Snyk.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers adopting GitOps who haven't yet decided where secrets live, and anyone who encrypted etcd and assumed the job was done.

Title: Delete the script tag and see if your Remix app still works
Description: Ken Snyder (Shoreline Health) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on the Remix philosophy - web standards and forms that work before, or without, JavaScript
Body:
Ken Snyder, Principal Engineer at Shoreline Health and co-founder of the UtahJS meetup, spent his Conf42 JavaScript 2023 talk arguing that the best parts of Remix are not Remix-specific at all. Lean on `Request`, `Response`, `fetch`, `FormData` and plain HTML forms, and you get an app that paints on the first response, works before hydration, and keeps working with JavaScript switched off entirely.

His reason for caring is not academic. Shoreline sends cancer patients educational material, and those patients often open one or two pages on a slow cellular connection. Every extra round trip before the content appears is a round trip a worried person waits through.

## What does a Remix app actually look like?

Most of the talk is a live build of a shopping list, about as small as a CRUD demo gets. `npx create-remix` scaffolds the app (Snyder notes over 100 community templates), and each file in `routes/` becomes a URL. A `loader` returns data with Remix's `json` helper; the component reads it with `useLoaderData`, and passing `typeof loader` gives you typed data on the client without writing a schema or a shared types file.

Mutations are just forms. A POST form hits an exported `action`, which reads `await request.formData()`. Return from the action and Remix calls the loader again and re-renders. The neat trick is buttons: give a `<button>` a `name` and a `value`, and clicking it behaves as if the form had a hidden input. That is how one route handles delete, load-into-cart and unload with no `onClick` anywhere. He stretches the same idea to a sortable, paginated, filterable user table where every control is a submit button, and with a GET form the whole state lands in the URL for free.

## Why does the first render beat a single page app?

A classic SPA ships HTML, then fetches a bundle, then fetches data, then paints. Remix bundles the loader, component and action for the server, so the first response arrives already rendered with data; the client bundle only hydrates, intercepting forms and links to fetch just what changed. Snyder's framing: with Remix the page is fully painted first and fully interactive shortly after, while a SPA needs several waterfalls before it paints anything.

Because it all speaks `Request` and `Response`, Remix runs on a long list of adapters: Cloudflare Workers, Deno, Bun, Netlify, Vercel, AWS Lambda, Express, Fastify and more. He counted 116 community stack repositories at the time.

## The IE11 problem that made it click

Shoreline integrates with a popular electronic medical records vendor whose desktop app embeds web content through Internet Explorer 11. Auditing every dependency for polyfills sounded miserable. Remix's own docs said its module scripts would not load in old browsers, and then that the app could still work in any browser ever made, because forms and links are plain HTML.

He demonstrates it: comment out the `<Scripts />` component in `root.tsx`, and the network tab goes quiet while adding items still works. Deleting breaks, because the action returned `null`; in a no-JS world an action should redirect, like a 2005 multi-page app. Snyder said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 that "for the first several days that I use remix, I turned the script tags off completely just so I could kind of see and understand how these form mutations work". A good habit to steal.

## Future flags make upgrades boring

The last pillar is how Remix ships change: public RFCs on GitHub, and future flags. Snyder notes "There were six breaking changes between V one and V two", and each could be opted into one at a time (the error boundary syntax, for example) long before v2 shipped, so the major upgrade was mostly done before it arrived. He also previews the roadmap of the time: moving the build onto Vite as a plugin, loader and action middleware for auth checks, and better tools for optimistic UI.

## Who should watch

React developers who have only built SPAs, and anyone tired of a dependency per web API. The takeaway travels: learn the platform primitives, design forms that work before hydration, and think about the user on a bad network. Or, as he put it at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "when I write remix route, I don't have to worry where my code runs."

Title: Deleting the .env file doesn't delete the password
Description: Daniel Oates-Lee (Punk Security Limited) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on why leaked secrets live on in git history, and rotating, not rewriting
Body:
Daniel Oates-Lee, Director and DevSecOps Evangelist at Punk Security, showed at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 how a secret committed once stays in git for good, and why the fix is to scan in two places and rotate the secret, not to rewrite history. He closes with a live demo of secretMagpie, Punk Security's open source tool for finding secrets across every repo you own before you switch on scanning in CI.

He came to DevSecOps via development, systems operations and pen testing, and it shows: the talk is built on incidents, not checklists.

## What actually goes wrong?

The opening story is the one people remember. A consultancy pushed a web app with its AWS keys in it on the Friday before a bank holiday. An attacker found the keys, spun up a crypto-mining farm and ran up thousands. The team rotated the key but added no detection, and on the next bank holiday weekend did it again and got hit twice as hard.

Oates-Lee splits the problem into secrets that should be public but carry too many permissions, and secrets that should never be there at all: .env files, Terraform tfvars, database passwords in config, API keys, tokens, and private keys. He once saw an NGINX container's private TLS key pushed to a public repo. Even the managed ones can leak into logs and traces, be used to escalate privileges, or be borrowed by an insider. One investigation ended with a developer using a production database password to dump production data into a test environment.

## Why doesn't removing it work?

He walks the junior-developer scenario: admin/admin committed to main with the message `add creds`, spotted, replaced with a placeholder in a commit called `removed password`. The password was never rotated, so anyone who clones the repo goes back one commit and logs in. Doing it on a feature branch doesn't save you: a standard merge keeps the history, and even with a squash merge, the old commit can be pulled out if you know its hash.

To show how easy the attacker's side is, he searches GitHub commits for `remove aws keys` live and gets around 15,000 recent results. His estimate: "bad guys can on average probably find an AWS key that's been uploaded within five to ten minutes," Oates-Lee said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

## How should you defend?

- **Scan twice.** A pre-commit hook on the developer's machine, and the CI pipeline as backup, because developers can and do disable hooks. Scanning on every push is enough; rescanning on the pull request adds little.
- **Rotate, don't rewrite.** Once a secret is pushed, record what happened, rotate it, and check no other repo or app uses it.
- **Ticket every finding.** Raise it automatically into a security backlog so rotation is tracked. Not as punishment, he stresses, but as proof the team took it seriously.
- **Move secrets into a vault.** AWS SSM Parameter Store via assumed roles, or Argo CD pulling from a vault at deploy time. Vaults give you audit logs of who read what, alerts on unusual access, and make frequent rotation (even on every release) practical.

Tool options he lists include Gitleaks, TruffleHog, GitGuardian and the built-in scanning in GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps.

His best adoption story: a team building software for the NHS insisted it didn't write vulnerabilities and fought pipeline scanning. Two days after Gitleaks went in, they complained it was blocking deploys with false positives. It had caught a production AWS key in code headed for the development environment. The scanning stayed.

## secretMagpie in practice

secretMagpie runs Gitleaks and TruffleHog together, because they find different things, across a GitHub or Azure DevOps organisation, GitLab, Bitbucket or a local path. It defaults to scanning 20 branches per repo, configurable, and outputs CSV, JSON or a filterable HTML report where you mark findings as confirmed, rotated or false positive. Against OWASP's deliberately leaky WrongSecrets repo, the demo found 536 secrets, 200 unique, including private keys, AWS and GCP keys. He recommends using it as a one-off audit to tune your CI scanner, not as the CI scanner itself.

## Who should watch

Anyone about to roll out secret scanning across an existing estate, and anyone who still believes deleting the file fixed it.

Title: Untangling a messy Next.js API with four boring patterns
Description: Gil Zilberfeld (TestinGil) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on refactoring a tangled API into validators, repositories, adapters and factories to make it testable
Body:
The API that's impossible to test usually isn't wrong, just knotted: validation in the route, database calls in the domain object, a Kafka producer opened inside a method called `inviteParticipants`. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Gil Zilberfeld, CEO and CTO of TestinGil and author of Everyday Unit Testing, took exactly that kind of TypeScript endpoint and refactored it step by step into ports and adapters, without changing what it does, until each piece could be tested on its own.

It is a live-coding talk built around one endpoint, and the patterns are old friends.

## What's the goal of refactoring here?

His goal is the same in every codebase: code that works, over and over again, through every new feature and bug fix. That needs two properties. Easy to change, which means cohesion (code dealing with the same thing lives together) and separation of concerns (code dealing with different things doesn't). And easy to test, which means fewer dependencies and loosely coupled interfaces and events. The more setup a test needs, the more likely nobody writes it.

## The mess

The demo is a meeting scheduler: a Next.js app router API with a single `POST /meetings/schedule` taking emails, a date and time, a topic and a room. Mongoose talks to MongoDB, KafkaJS sends invitations. The route parses and validates the request, the calendar creates a meeting, the meeting saves itself through Mongoose, then opens a Kafka producer, changes each invitee's status and sends the messages.

The function returns nothing useful, so to check whether a meeting was scheduled you have to query the database or call another API. Every test means starting the server, the database and Kafka: a full end-to-end test for every scenario.

## Step by step, without changing behaviour

Each step just moves code; the functionality stays identical.

1. **Organise.** Split enums and interfaces from objects.
2. **Draw the domain boundary.** Borrowing from domain-driven design, entities (calendar, meeting, invitee) go inside; Mongoose schemas and the Kafka message shape move to a data file on the boundary. The code is still coupled to the database, just tidier.
3. **Pull out validation.** The route held the rules for a valid meeting: it has a topic, at least one invitee and a date in the future. Moved into a `MeetingValidator` class, it has no dependencies and is fully unit-testable. He frames it as DDD's anti-corruption layer: don't let bad data create invalid entities, or your logic grows code for every invalid case.
4. **Add a repository.** A `MeetingRepository` with `addMeeting` and `updateMeeting` takes over the Mongoose calls. An ORM speaks schemas, your app speaks meetings, and "Cleaner code speaks one language," Gil Zilberfeld said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023. Swapping MongoDB for something else no longer touches the meeting.
5. **Add an adapter for Kafka.** Broker config, connection, producer and message creation move into a Kafka adapter behind an invite-sender interface. The meeting now just loops over invitees and calls the sender.
6. **Introduce factories.** The meeting still creates its own repository and adapter, which is coupling. A factories file fixes that.

## Ports and adapters in practice

Steps four to six apply Alistair Cockburn's ports and adapters idea: keep application logic in the middle and talk to the UI, databases and queues through interfaces. The HTTP API is one of those interfaces too; as long as the contract holds, either side can change. The repository is one kind of adapter.

## Three ways to write a factory

The factories file shows three variations. A calendar factory with a private instance, the classic version, useful when you want to validate creation. A meeting repository factory with a public instance, so a test can swap in a mock repository or one backed by a JSON file. ("Is it risky? Yes, but yeah, Javascript is risky," he notes.) And an invite sender factory that creates the default Kafka adapter unless something was set from the outside first.

Tests can now set the factories up before creating a meeting. He prefers this, or a service locator, over passing everything as parameters, where something at the top of the tree has to build everything for the code below.

## What did it buy?

Nothing new was written, only wrappers with good names and moved code. But now you know where the next feature goes: validation rules into the validator, a new database into repositories, RabbitMQ instead of Kafka into an adapter, and the application logic, the part that carries the value, stays untouched. The validation cases that previously needed the whole stack become unit tests, so you need one end-to-end scheduling scenario instead of ten.

His homework: learn a handful of patterns, read up on domain-driven design (bounded contexts, entities, what goes in and out), and refactor in small steps, mostly by hand, since JavaScript tooling offers less automated refactoring than some languages.

## Who should watch

Node.js and TypeScript developers whose API handlers have grown into everything-functions, and teams who only have end-to-end tests because nothing smaller is possible.

Title: OpenTelemetry's collector is where the savings live
Description: Siddhartha Khare (New Relic) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on OpenTelemetry basics, the collector, tail-based sampling and who is adopting it
Body:
Siddhartha Khare, Technical Account Manager at New Relic, gave Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 a compact primer on OpenTelemetry: what it standardises, how instrumentation works, and why the collector, with tail-based sampling, is the piece that turns telemetry from a cost into something you can afford to keep.

It's an introductory talk, about 15 minutes, and it says so. If you have never configured an OTel pipeline, it's a good first stop. If you run one, the sampling section is the part to watch.

## Why does anyone need a standard?

He opens with a number: companies typically use four to six tools to collect telemetry. Monitoring tells you red or green, up or down; observability, built on metrics, logs and traces, lets you understand the internal state of a system from its outputs. He walks through who uses it: developers to debug and find bottlenecks, DevOps and SREs for health and reliability, product managers to see how users actually interact with features.

OpenTelemetry, then a CNCF incubating project, came from merging OpenCensus and OpenTracing. If you've used Jaeger or Zipkin, he notes, you've already tasted the OpenTracing side. He credits its rise to four traits: ubiquity across languages, vendor neutrality, interoperable SDKs built on the same specification, and configurability. He cites Gartner's prediction that by 2025, 70% of cloud-native application monitoring would use open source instrumentation, and CNCF activity data placing OpenTelemetry second only to Kubernetes.

## Start automatic, then add context

The building blocks are semantic conventions for common operations like HTTP calls and database queries, APIs and SDKs per signal, automatic instrumentation, and OTLP, the protocol that ships data to whichever backend you choose. His advice for teams starting out is automatic instrumentation first, since it takes far fewer lines than manual spans.

His closing caution is the line to keep. "Only collecting the telemetry data is not useful. The instrumentation should be including the contextual data to make more sense," Khare said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

## What does the collector actually do?

The collector runs as a standalone process and gives you one place to receive, process and export telemetry. It is built from three component types: receivers, processors and exporters, and the contrib repository already has many of each. Processors do the useful work: filtering, batching, adding attributes. It can also scrape infrastructure metrics, and his example pulls CPU, memory and network data from a host. Prometheus and Grafana integration was still experimental at the time.

## Head, tail or probabilistic sampling?

Head-based sampling decides at the root span, before anything interesting has happened. Tail-based sampling waits, groups spans by trace ID, checks error status and duration, and forwards only the high-value traces. His demo config keeps only traces slower than 5,000 milliseconds, and the throughput and ingestion graphs drop the moment that policy kicks in, which in a metered backend means real money. Probabilistic sampling, keeping a fixed percentage, rounds out the options.

Exports in the demo go to Zipkin, Prometheus and New Relic's OTLP endpoint, the vendor-neutral promise in practice.

## Who is adopting it?

His case study is Skyscanner, which paired open standards with observability and retired 12 internal and external systems, cut about 15 minutes from each merge request in its mobile build pipeline, and could build SLOs from any metric or event, back end or front end. He also lists AWS's distro (ADOT, usable as a Lambda layer), native support in .NET and on Azure, and Next.js shipping OpenTelemetry export out of the box.

## Who should watch

Engineers about to pick an observability stack, and anyone whose tracing bill grows faster than their traffic. The tail-sampling config alone is worth the quarter hour.

Title: How LinkedIn burned down 6,000 lint failures, and why the last 20% took a year
Description: Chris Ng (LinkedIn) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on getting a huge JS codebase to zero lint failures with file owners, scorecards and a no-new-errors rule
Body:
A lint rule with 7,000 open failures isn't a rule, it's a suggestion everyone has learned to ignore. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Chris Ng, senior staff software engineer at LinkedIn, told the story of how his team took a large JavaScript application from that peak to zero lint failures: removing close to 6,000 of them with 55 engineers between November 2021 and January 2023, and learning that most of the hard parts weren't software.

It is a process talk, and a good one, for anyone who owns developer experience in a big repo.

## Why lint rules in the first place?

Back in 2017 his team had a rule that a practice missing from the docs wasn't a real thing: you couldn't block a pull request on a best practice nobody had written down. Lint rules automate that. They run in the IDE, in pre-commit hooks via tools like Husky, and in GitHub Actions on changed files, so the error is caught as early as the developer's setup allows. Prettier handles formatting, ending the bikeshedding; lint rules handle consistency, bugs and migrations.

His bug example is a nice one. Code reads `paging?.start + paging?.count` to be safe when the API omits the paging object. If it comes back as an empty object, that's `undefined` plus a number, so NaN, and ESLint's `no-unsafe-optional-chaining` catches it.

## What does scale look like?

The application had been in production for eight years: over 24,000 application and test files, over 100,000 commits, lines of code growing 21% a year, around 67 human-written pull requests a day, and more than 800 contributors with at least five commits each. At that size, adding rules without fixing old failures just piles them up. At the peak the app had over 7,000 errors sitting there.

The campsite rule doesn't work when the campsite is already a landfill.

## What worked, and what didn't?

They tried three things first:

- **Blocking commits on files with lint failures.** Unpopular, overridable (but overriding emails everyone), and the one that actually stopped the bleeding.
- **Per-rule limits**, such as five allowed instances of `no-unused-vars`. Too much bookkeeping; they only cared that the number went down.
- **A platform review model** with a central group reviewing for standards. It worked sometimes, not reliably.

Blocking commits had a loophole: when a manager, or the manager's manager, wants it shipped today, people code around files full of failures or override. So they added a volunteer task force to own the lint framework, and a lint proposal process with one rule that changed everything: before a rule is enabled as an error, all its existing failures must be resolved. You can enable it as a warning to collect feedback; the exception is a rule that prevents something that has repeatedly taken production down.

Rule authors pushed back: what if there are 1,000 errors, what if I break production fixing them? His answer is that rule authors know best what needs fixing, so they're less likely to break things than a feature team stumbling over the failure mid-sprint. And the bigger lesson: "not all problems are software engineering," Chris Ng said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023. Talk to people, explain why, help them through it.

## Incentives, tooling and a weekly scorecard

His slogan for this part: "Incentives, incentives, incentives." The pieces:

- **One owner per file**, a team rather than a person, so nobody has to hunt down who's responsible.
- **A deliberately basic dashboard.** The first version was an unstyled HTML table, rebuilt nightly by a cron job on someone's VM, using LinkedIn's Checkup task runner to run ESLint and output SARIF, so each failure links straight to its line. It broke failures down by team, by rule, and both.
- **A weekly scorecard email**: green for a week-over-week decrease (or already at zero), yellow for no change, red for an increase. Red usually meant an ownership change or a config or dependency mistake, not a rogue engineer, which was still worth knowing early.
- **Personal shout-outs** to two or three engineers a week, with links to their PRs.

## Does the last 20% matter?

The 80/20 rule showed up on schedule: the first 80% went fast, the last 20% took about as long again, nearly a year. They finished with help from other teams and with task force volunteers fixing stragglers themselves. Zero, he argues, is self-sustaining. In a file full of failures, adding one more feels fine; in a clean file it stands out.

The results: close to 6,000 failures removed, 55 contributing engineers, a 30% increase in perceived code quality in their quarterly surveys, and the rules kept evolving throughout, with over 80 rule or dependency changes from more than 45 contributors in the past year. The 2017 motto got an update: a practice without a lint rule isn't a real thing.

## Who should watch

Platform and developer experience engineers inheriting a repo full of `eslint-disable` comments, and engineering managers who need a plan that doesn't rely on goodwill alone.

Title: Your code shipped. Do you know if it even ran?
Description: Roni Dover (Digma) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on continuous feedback, using OpenTelemetry traces in dev to catch N+1 queries and scaling problems
Body:
Roni Dover, Co-Founder and CTO of Digma, argued at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 that the DevOps loop has a hole in the middle: continuous feedback from running code back to the developer. His fix is to switch on OpenTelemetry during development, read the traces while you code, and let tooling surface the problems instead of waiting for production to do it.

He's been a developer for over 25 years. The talk is half argument, half demo in a modified Spring PetClinic, and everything in it is open source or free. The last part shows Digma, his own free IntelliJ plugin, so expect some product.

## What do developers actually know about their code?

Dover's first story sets the bar low on purpose. A developer refactored a data access layer, got it reviewed, wrote tests, shipped it, and a month later the team found it had never run because of a bad if statement. Asked why he hadn't checked, the developer answered: how?

"So in the spectrum of what do I know about my code? Sometimes it doesn't go even beyond do I know whether my code runs?" Dover said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

The second story is the opposite: a strong engineer who printed per-iteration timings of a batch job to the console and watched the numbers scroll past like the Matrix, spotting regressions by feel. Dover doesn't recommend the spam, but he admires the ownership. Debuggers show one instant, tests give pass or fail, and APM dashboards grew up serving SREs, so developers get very little feedback in between. One VP of engineering told him his engineers thought the team's observability dashboards were screenshots.

## Why OpenTelemetry changes the economics

OpenTelemetry merged OpenCensus and OpenTracing and, in Dover's words, is evolutionary rather than revolutionary. What's new is that everybody agrees on it, so Spring, FastAPI, ASP.NET, Kafka, RabbitMQ, Postgres and MongoDB libraries already emit it. In Java you attach the agent with an environment variable, no code changes, and you trade too little data for too much, which he calls the easier problem.

He focuses on tracing: a trace is the anatomy of a request, made of spans for each step.

## What did the traces find in a feature that passed its tests?

He added a vaccinations feature to PetClinic, with an external mock API, a new table, Testcontainers integration tests and a code review. By the usual standards it was done. Then Jaeger showed what adding one pet really did:

- 256 and 164 spans for single requests.
- A classic N+1 select pattern from lazy-loaded ORM relationships around visits and types.
- A pile of background HTTP calls from a leaky abstraction: touching the vaccine record silently called the external service.
- Queries fired during view rendering, the open-session-in-view anti-pattern.

All of it visible in a single trace, without changing the code. His team then had the tools and still didn't use them: one developer found too many issues that weren't his, another found nothing twice and stopped looking. Manual trace review behaves like manual testing did before CI, a chore nobody volunteers for.

## Making the feedback continuous

His conclusion is that analysis has to be automatic, the way tests became continuous. In the demo, Digma reads the same OpenTelemetry data in the IDE and flags excessive HTTP calls, the N+1 query with its affected endpoints, 133 ms of DB queries hiding behind more than 7 seconds of asynchronous HTTP client time, and, from CI performance-test traces, a scaling issue: a roughly 3-second degradation per execution at about 31 concurrent calls, traced to an external owner-validation function.

He also points to continuousfeedback.org, his collection of OpenTelemetry setup guides, an open-source stack and a draft continuous feedback manifesto.

## Who should watch

Backend developers who have OpenTelemetry in production but never open a trace locally, and team leads wondering why code review and green tests still let N+1 queries through. Java folks will get the most from the demo.
