Title: From one eval() to a reverse shell: securing JavaScript apps end to end
Description: Joshua Arvin Lat (NuWorks Interactive Labs) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on the attack chain from unsafe JS code to cloud IAM abuse and denial of wallet
Body:
Every developer knows `eval` is bad. Far fewer could show you why. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Joshua Arvin Lat, CTO of NuWorks Interactive Labs, AWS Machine Learning Hero and author of a book on building penetration testing labs in the cloud, did exactly that: he took a harmless-looking calculator, turned it into a reverse shell, and then followed the attack chain out into the cloud account behind it.

It is a broad, introductory security talk in three parts: the code, machine learning in the browser, and the infrastructure around your app. Expect a demo and a checklist, not a close study of any single tool.

## Why does security get skipped?

He starts with the honest bit. Organisations rank short- and long-term financial goals and customer happiness high, and compliance low. So teams ship features and push security checks down the backlog, with the familiar argument that there's nothing to secure without a business. His counter: security has to be there from day zero or day one, because bolting it onto a running app is far harder than adding a firewall.

There's a second gap. Developers know some security best practices, but most have never seen an attack work. Becoming a productive developer already takes months to a year; nobody budgets another two or three years to learn offensive security. That's why he frames everything around the cyber attack chain: knowing what an attacker does next tells you what to fix first.

## How does a calculator become a reverse shell?

The demo is a Node.js app that evaluates a maths expression. Type `1 + 1`, get `2`. Bare minimum met.

Then the input changes to `require('child_process').exec('touch hello.txt')`, and a file appears on the production server. Still a toy, so he escalates. On an attacker machine, `nc -nvl 14344` starts listening. The next input pipes `/bin/sh` through a named pipe into netcat pointed at the attacker's IP. The victim server connects out, and the attacker now runs commands on it as if over SSH. Once the attacker has that shell, in his words, "it's technically game over for that machine."

From there the chain continues: hunting for passwords, finding and downloading databases, and, if the server runs in the cloud, IAM privilege escalation. His fix at the code level is mundane and correct: code reviews, with someone in the room who can not just say that `eval` is dangerous but demonstrate it.

## What changes when the model runs in the browser?

Part two covers machine learning in JavaScript. The classic setup runs inference on a server: a mobile app uploads a cat photo, the backend model returns one for cat, zero for not. Now you can also ship the model to the browser and run inference there. The benefits he lists are real: it works offline, needs no inference servers, helps data privacy because the image never leaves the device, and cuts latency.

The catch is equally simple: anything you push to the browser can be downloaded by anyone who knows how. A competitor can lift your model and build their own site on it. His rule of thumb is to keep proprietary models server-side, and put models in the browser for demos, non-proprietary data, or when you're comfortable with the model being copied or know how to protect it.

## What about everything around the code?

Part three widens the frame:

- **Libraries and frameworks.** Know each one's vulnerabilities and configuration risks, such as forgetting to enable production mode, and watch for malicious packages with backdoors.
- **Automated vulnerability management.** A scanner that re-checks servers and container images whenever they change, as a second layer beside code review.
- **Network isolation.** Private and public subnets designed so one compromised machine doesn't hand over its neighbours.
- **Restrictive IAM permissions.** This is the one that turns a breach into a catastrophe. A server's IAM role lets scripts on it call cloud APIs, and an over-permissioned role can let an attacker who popped one box delete every resource in the account. "Never give too much power or permissions to a server," Joshua Arvin Lat said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023. Machines are principals now, so scope them like you'd scope a human, or give them nothing at all.
- **Denial of wallet.** A serverless API on AWS Lambda can autoscale happily under a flood of requests, and you pay for what you use. Plan for DDoS in the architecture before a bill arrives that is too big to pay.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers who have never seen an exploit run, and teams moving Node.js workloads or ML inference into the cloud without a security person on staff. Security engineers will find it familiar, but the `eval`-to-shell demo is a handy one to show a team that still thinks input validation is optional.

Title: A memory champion's pie fight beats your sticky notes
Description: Chester Santos (ChesterSantos.com) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on memory training: visualise, add senses, make it absurd, and four steps for names
Body:
Chester Santos, the 2008 USA National Memory Champion, ran an interactive memory session at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, and it is the one talk on the schedule with no pipelines in it. His claim: with three principles and a few minutes of practice you can memorise a random 15-word list forwards and backwards, and get much better at names.

Be clear about scope. This is a soft-skills workshop, not a security talk, and it ends by pointing at his paid online memory school. It is also genuinely fun, and the techniques work while you watch.

## What are the three principles?

Santos starts with a guided exercise: picture two politicians debating in your living room, then a pie fight between them. Then hear it, smell it, touch it, taste it. The three principles fall out of that scene.

1. **Turn information into pictures.** We remember faces and forget names because we see a face but never see a name. Make the abstract thing visual: Mike becomes a microphone, Alice becomes a white rabbit.
2. **Add senses.** Each extra sense brings more of the brain into the encoding, which means more connections to retrieve it by. He cites his appearance on PBS's NOVA, where he trained host David Pogue and neuroscientists explained the extra brain areas the techniques recruit.
3. **Make it strange.** We remember the absurd without effort. An elephant spraying water in the room you're sitting in would stay with you for life.

## Does the story method work on a real list?

The live test: monkey, iron, rope, kite, house, paper, shoe, worm, envelope, pencil, river, rock, tree, cheese, dollar. He turns it into one absurd chain (a monkey dancing with a giant iron, a rope catching the iron, a kite on the other end crashing into a paper-covered house, and so on down to a cheese tree firing dollars) and you replay the story to recall the words. Watching it, you'll probably get most of the list back, which is the uncomfortable part.

"My brain is not different from anyone else's. I've just learned powerful techniques and gone through a little bit of training," Santos said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

The second exercise shows it scales past random nouns. Giant machines smash gold and silver, vehicles rise out of the metal, medicine shoots from the windows, oil explodes from the medicine: you have just memorised the UK's top five exports (machinery, precious metals, vehicles, pharmaceuticals, oil). The images are cue cards, not exact copies. That is the bit worth stealing for presentations and customer meetings, where reciting the ten key facts without notes reads as expertise.

## Why does an engineer care?

Santos calls the problem digital dependency: people who no longer know their own phone number, ride-hail drivers who are lost when the app dies after years in the same city. Memory is use it or lose it, he argues, and the 30-to-40-year stretch of routine work after school is where most of us stop training it. His counter-examples: a Malaysian competitor in his late sixties at the World Memory Championship who had memorised an English-Chinese dictionary by page and row, and workshop attendees in their sixties and seventies outscoring professionals in their twenties.

## Four steps for names

The section most engineers will use on Monday:

1. Repeat the name immediately when introduced.
2. Ask one early question that uses the name.
3. Connect the name to anything you already know: a famous John, a friend with the same name.
4. Say goodbye using the name.

Combine that with the visual trick, anchored on something distinctive about the person's look (the microphone tangled in Mike's hair), and he reckons 80% recall of people you meet is realistic.

## Who should watch

Anyone who speaks at conferences, works with customers or has ever walked out of an onboarding week with nothing in their head. Skip it if you came to Conf42 DevSecOps strictly for supply chain security.

Title: Your browser has about ten milliseconds per frame. Stop wasting them
Description: Francesco Sciuti (devmy) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on browser processes, the critical rendering path and how to keep frames inside budget
Body:
Every janky animation you've ever closed in disgust was a browser that missed its deadline. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Francesco Sciuti, CEO of the Italian frontend consultancy devmy and a Google Developer Expert and Microsoft MVP, took a half-hour tour inside the browser: the processes it runs, the journey from bytes to pixels, and why each frame is a race against the clock that your code can help or sabotage.

It is a conceptual talk with diagrams rather than code, delivered with Sicilian hand gestures and Batman references. If the phrase critical rendering path makes you nod vaguely, this is your refresher.

## Why should a web developer care how browsers work?

Browsers, he points out, are the most widely used software there is, ready to run any kind of application, built from millions of lines of C++. You don't have to write one, but understanding some of its mechanics explains why things that seem absurd happen, and lets you make better decisions. His framing for the topic: users love to see pixels as quickly as possible, and browser makers have to deliver that against whatever you shipped.

## One browser, many processes

There is no standard for browser architecture, but the common design today is multi-process, and the talk follows Chromium's:

- **Browser process**: the UI (address bar, tabs, menus), coordination of the other processes, and creation and teardown of renderers.
- **Renderer processes**: roughly one per tab (iframes can get their own), parsing HTML, running JavaScript and owning the DOM.
- **Network process**: every request, isolated so a crash or a security issue doesn't take down everything.
- **GPU process**: hardware acceleration, working closely with the renderers.

They talk over IPC. The upside is sandboxing, hang detection for a runaway tab, privacy of sensitive data and site isolation; the downside is extra memory and a lot of chatter between processes. Typing a URL is a relay race: the browser process hands the request to the network process, then commits the response to a renderer, which takes over the navigation.

## What happens between bytes and pixels?

Inside the renderer the pipeline runs parsing, style, layout, paint and compositing:

- **Parsing**: raw bytes become characters, then tokens (an opening `div` tag becomes a start token), then DOM nodes. CSS goes through a similar process into the CSSOM.
- **Layout**: the main thread walks the DOM and styles to build the layout tree, with only visible elements, then computes the exact size and position of every one of them. This is reflow, and it is expensive.
- **Paint**: the browser works out z-order and turns the layout into paint records: what to draw, in what order, what overlaps.
- **Compositing**: the page is split into layers; the compositor thread, separate from the main thread, breaks them into tiles for the raster threads, assembles a compositor frame and sends it via the browser process to the GPU. Scrolling can be handled here without the main thread.

Input follows the same split. The browser process only knows where a touch happened, and passes it to the renderer. The compositor tracks the regions with event listeners attached, the non-fast-scrollable regions, and only waits for the main thread when input lands in one of them. Elsewhere it keeps producing frames.

## How tight is the frame budget?

"It's crucial for the browser to render about 60 frames per second to ensure smooth animation," Francesco Sciuti said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023. By his estimate that leaves the pipeline roughly ten milliseconds per frame, and missing it is what users see as jank.

The good news is that not every frame needs every step. Change only a text colour and layout can be skipped. Animate with `transform` and `opacity` and the browser can skip layout and paint, leaving the work to the compositor and GPU. And the event loop lives on the main thread, alternating between your tasks and the render steps, so a long task directly delays the next frame.

## So how do you make the browser's life easier?

His closing list of things to dig into:

- `requestAnimationFrame` for visual updates and `requestIdleCallback` for work that can wait.
- `will-change` to promote an element to its own layer, used with care.
- `async` and `defer` on scripts.
- Web Workers to move heavy work off the main thread entirely.
- `preload` to manage resource priority.
- Learning which CSS properties and JavaScript APIs force layout and paint, and avoiding them in hot paths.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers who know the event loop from interview prep but have never connected it to rendering, and anyone debugging scroll jank who wants the mental model before opening the Performance panel. Browser engineers can skip it, and he asks the Chrome team to be merciful anyway.

Title: Continuous delivery starts with products and ends with a platform
Description: Romano Roth (Zuhlke) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on architecting for continuous delivery: product mindset, built-in quality and security, platform teams
Body:
Romano Roth, Chief of DevOps and Partner at Zuhlke, used his Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 talk to argue that you can't architect for continuous delivery while still running projects. You need products, quality and security built in from the planning step, and eventually a platform team so product teams don't drown in their own toolchain.

Roth has spent 21 years at Zuhlke and is president of DevOpsDays Zürich. The talk is a broad map rather than a close-up: it walks the whole DevOps loop and picks four places where architecture decisions decide whether you can ship continuously.

## Why do projects break the value stream?

He opens with the familiar picture: business writes ideas into documents and Jira tickets, throws them over the wall to development, which throws code to testing, which throws something green to operations, which somehow gets it running, and the client looks at the result and says it isn't what they wanted. Each handover is a wall in the value stream.

His diagnosis is the project itself. A project has a start, an end, a fixed feature list and a budget, so it optimises output: features, stories, code. A product optimises outcome: did the customer's problem go away? Agile shrank the batches, he says, but teams kept doing projects. DevOps is the way to organise around a product's value stream instead.

## What does the science say to build?

Roth leans on Accelerate by Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim and its 24 capabilities in five groups: continuous delivery, architecture, product and process, lean management and monitoring, and culture. A few he singles out: trunk-based development, loosely coupled modules with clear inputs and outputs owned by teams of at most five people, and no change approval boards. He cites the State of DevOps Report 2021 gap between the highest and lowest performers: 973x more frequent deploys, 6570x faster lead time and time to restore, 3x lower change failure rate.

The Tesla full self-driving rollout serves as his worked example: a canary to drivers with high safety scores, a wider release, a rollback of a regulated car's software, then a fix forward within a day. That only works if deployment and release are separate things. "Deployment is bringing the code into production with the feature toggle off and releasing means we are going to switch on the feature toggle," Roth said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

## Quality and security are architecture, not phases

On built-in quality he quotes former Tesla agile coach Joe Justice: half of what a Musk company invests in a new product goes into automated testing. Roth's route there is behaviour-driven development for acceptance criteria in given-when-then form, test-driven development below that, and a test pyramid flipped from many manual end-to-end tests to many unit tests. The goal shifts from finding bugs to preventing them.

Built-in security follows the same shift left: threat modelling during planning, merge requests, then software composition analysis, license compliance, SAST, container scanning and secret detection in the build, DAST after deploy, and scheduled pipelines that rescan what is already in production, because new vulnerabilities keep arriving for old versions. He made a 25-video series comparing such pipelines on GitHub and GitLab.

Operability gets the same treatment. You build it, you run it means architecting for observability up front, application telemetry written by developers, infrastructure as code, rehearsed disaster recovery and incident post-mortems owned by the team, not by operations alone.

## Why does it end with platform engineering?

Add all of that up and every team is running its own cloud, Kubernetes, CI/CD, monitoring, security scanners, Jira and Confluence, cost management, and somewhere in there an application. Roth calls out the result: reinvented wheels, no synergies, people who can't move between teams and very high cognitive load.

His answer is a platform team that builds a product for the product teams: runtime, DevSecOps checks, identity, centralised security and the observability stack. The rule that keeps it from becoming another silo: product teams still build their own pipelines and run their own products. The platform enables; it doesn't operate.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and architects starting a DevOps transformation, and anyone who needs one talk that connects projects-vs-products, Accelerate and platform engineering into a single argument. If you already run a platform team, the first half will be review.

Title: You probably don't need microfrontends, you need module boundaries
Description: Maksim Zemskov (Yandex) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on scaling a 20-year-old frontend with isolated modules, linted boundaries and Feature-Sliced Design
Body:
Microfrontends solve one problem really well: keeping teams from tripping over each other's code. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Maksim Zemskov, lead software engineer at Yandex, argued that you can get almost all of that inside a single repository, and showed how the Yandex Direct advertising platform, whose frontend had several million lines of code when he joined, scaled without splitting into microfrontends at all.

He leads the infrastructure team for Yandex Direct, a codebase over 20 years old. The talk is the playbook his team ended up with.

## Why do monoliths stop scaling?

Not because of hard algorithms or complicated UIs, he says, but because of coupling. In the worst case, two modules that depend on each other have two connections; three can have six; four can have twelve. Keep going and you get a big ball of mud, where every task means reading half the codebase. A monolith makes this easy because nothing stops you importing anything from anywhere.

Microfrontends fix that by force: separate applications, often separate repositories, talking through public APIs or events. You also get independent teams, release cycles and rollbacks. The bill is real, though: complex integration infrastructure, a deep understanding of your bundler, SSR as a distributed system, backward-compatible contracts between apps, and shared dependency upgrades. Anyone who has tried to bump React across a fleet of microfrontends will recognise that last one.

## What makes a monolith glorious?

His answer: keep one repository, one release and easy code reuse, but enforce boundaries with tools. As Maksim Zemskov said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023, "Software architecture is mostly about rules and constraints that lead to the creation of flexible and scalable system." The difference between a regular monolith and a good one is that the rules exist and linters check them.

The building block is the module: a cash balance widget, a data filter, a sidebar or a whole page, each responsible for one product or technical feature, with bigger modules composed from smaller ones.

## Inside a module: segments with one-way imports

Every module follows the same internal layout, so engineers can move between them. He borrows segments from Feature-Sliced Design (UI, model, API and shared utility code, for example) and orders them like clean architecture layers: UI can use model and API; model can use API but nothing from UI. That settles arguments such as whether a state manager may show a toast after saving. It may not; that's the UI's job.

## Between modules: one door, kept small

Isolation is the part that keeps change safe:

- **No global side effects.** No patching globals or loading polyfills from a module, because other modules will quietly start depending on it.
- **A public API.** An `index` file at the module root is the only thing others may import, enforced with ESLint and plugins such as eslint-plugin-boundaries. Yandex Direct uses plain ES module re-exports of React components, Redux selectors and actions, which costs no extra infrastructure and works with code analysers, so the dependency graph can drive selective test runs.
- **Keep the API small.** Fewer exports, fewer props, simpler data structures. Every extra field is another dependency.
- **Isolated styles.** With CSS modules, select only by classes and pseudo-classes, never import another module's CSS, pass a class name as a prop if you must override, and don't define new custom properties inside modules, since they're global too. Stylelint enforces it.
- **Isolated data.** No single global store and no exposing a module's store wholesale. Each module owns its data and exposes CQRS-style read and write operations, with subscriptions for UI updates and read-only types (or `Object.freeze`, at a runtime cost) to stop mutation.

## A shared runtime, sized with care

Modules need common ground: bundler features, environment variables, browser and Node.js targets, and core libraries. The Yandex Direct runtime pins TypeScript, React and Redux, because the public APIs depend on them, plus conveniences like the HTTP client, router and component library. A bigger runtime is riskier to change, since every change hits all modules at once; a smaller one means reinventing things per module.

## Deciding where code goes

For decomposition he recommends Feature-Sliced Design, which Yandex Direct has used for over two years. Its six layers import in one direction only, from app down to shared, and modules on the same layer can't import each other. The downside he admits is a steep learning curve, so write documentation with examples from your own app.

"Developing a monolith like this requires some additional effort, but it's still a lot less effort compared to adapting a microfrontend architecture," he added. In his view there is only one objective reason to adopt microfrontends: you need teams fully isolated, with their own technologies, processes and releases.

## Who should watch

Frontend leads staring at a growing monolith and a microfrontends proposal, and teams already on Feature-Sliced Design who want the reasoning behind the rules. His starter kit: TypeScript, ESLint and Stylelint for the rules, and dependency-cruiser to police imports.

Title: A working monitoring stack in about 100 lines with ClickHouse and Grafana
Description: Robert Hodges (Altinity) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on building cheap DIY monitoring from vmstat, ClickHouse and Grafana in about 100 lines of code
Body:
You don't need a monitoring vendor to watch your hosts; you need a collector, an analytic database and a dashboard. Robert Hodges, CEO of Altinity, built exactly that live at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023: vmstat output turned into JSON, loaded into ClickHouse, charted in Grafana, about 100 lines of code in total. Then he hammered his own machines until the collector stopped reporting.

Honest scope: Altinity is a ClickHouse service provider, so the database choice is no surprise. The pattern, and the reasons ClickHouse fits time-series data, are worth knowing either way.

## Why build your own?

Monitoring exists to answer questions. Why are users seeing performance problems? When did it start? How many users are affected? Which service is at fault? Those need history, not a terminal running vmstat until the numbers blur. Off-the-shelf observability products can do it, but they can be costly, your needs may be specialised, or monitoring may be your business and you want to own the stack and the data.

The design has three parts: something to collect and ingest the data, an analytic database to hold it and answer fast, and a visualisation layer.

## Why ClickHouse for monitoring data?

Hodges compares the open source options: OpenSearch for full-text search over unstructured logs, Presto for federated queries over data lakes, and ClickHouse for real-time analytics, meaning answers almost instantly on very large data. His reasons:

- It is a SQL database with something like MySQL's simplicity, Apache 2.0 licensed, and it runs anywhere from a phone to clusters of hundreds of servers.
- Columns are stored separately as sorted, compressed arrays. "Particularly in observability cases, we can often get compression levels of 90 or even 95% on data," Robert Hodges said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.
- Vectorised query execution uses SIMD instructions and fits CPU caches well, with parallel queries across shards and replicas.
- Dozens of input formats (CSV, JSONEachRow, Protobuf, Parquet), so your collector's output is probably readable as is.
- Strong time support: DateTime and DateTime64 down to nanoseconds, plus functions to round timestamps to the hour or year.

Grafana is the natural partner: built for time series, easy to install, many data sources and panel plugins, good zoom in and out, and open source under AGPL 3.0.

## How does the pipeline work?

Four steps, each small:

1. **Collect.** A Python script of about 14 lines runs vmstat at one-second intervals and emits each sample as a JSON document with a timestamp, the host and the measurements, such as 98% idle.
2. **Model.** A ClickHouse table with timestamp, day and host as dimensions and the vmstat values as measurements, using the MergeTree engine, partitioned by day and ordered by host then timestamp. That sort order keeps neighbouring rows similar, which is why they compress so well.
3. **Load.** An INSERT in JSONEachRow format, posted with curl in about two lines, or a small Python loader.
4. **Show.** A Grafana dashboard with CPU, detailed CPU breakdown and memory panels, and a host selector. He uses Altinity's ClickHouse plugin for Grafana, which he says has around 12 million downloads.

The bonus is full SQL over your own data. His example query lists hosts that ran above 25% load for at least a minute in the last 24 hours, and counts those minutes.

## The demo: beating up the hosts

The live part runs on two machines in his home office. He zooms Grafana into a short window, then runs sysbench to load the CPUs, followed by stress with first four and then eight memory-hungry workers. ("You have to love any performance test program that calls its workers hogs.") CPU pegs at 100%, memory climbs, and then gaps appear in the charts: the machine is so loaded that the collector can't produce data. That gap is a monitoring lesson of its own.

The code, dashboard and loaders are published in Altinity's clickhouse-sql-examples repository, in the open source monitoring directory.

## Who should watch?

Engineers who want observability data they fully control, and anyone curious why column stores keep turning up under monitoring products. Hodges is clear that a production version also needs configuration management and operating ClickHouse and Grafana themselves; on Kubernetes he points to the Altinity operator for ClickHouse.

Title: Moving from WebGL to WebGPU, and why your textures come out upside down
Description: Dmitrii Ivashchenko (MY.GAMES) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on porting WebGL code to WebGPU pipelines, WGSL shaders and new coordinate conventions
Body:
Port a WebGL renderer to WebGPU and the first bug report is usually the same: everything is upside down, and half the scene vanishes too early. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Dmitrii Ivashchenko, lead Unity developer at MY.GAMES, walked through what actually changes between the two APIs (devices instead of contexts, pipelines instead of programs, WGSL instead of GLSL, uniform buffers only) and the convention differences that explain those two bugs.

It is a dense, code-first tour aimed at people who already know WebGL. If you've never bound a buffer, start elsewhere.

## Why move now?

WebGL 2.0 (2017) still sits on OpenGL ES 3.0, while native graphics moved on to Vulkan, Direct3D 12 and Metal, which give developers lower-level control, and those three are the foundation WebGPU is built on.

At the time of the talk, WebGPU had shipped in Chrome 113 and Edge 113, with Firefox and Safari in development. On the engine side Babylon.js had full support, Three.js experimental support, PlayCanvas was in development, Unity had announced early experimental support in the 2023.2 alpha and Cocos Creator officially supported it. His conclusion: it's a wise move to start migrating, or at least to prepare projects for it.

## What replaces the WebGL context?

In WebGL you get a context from a canvas, and it is tied to that canvas. WebGPU starts with an adapter from `navigator.gpu.requestAdapter()`, which represents a GPU (possibly a software one such as SwiftShader) and can be chosen by power preference. From the adapter you request a device, the main interface for creating textures, buffers and pipelines, then configure a canvas context against that device. One device can render to several canvases, or to none.

Features (such as `texture-compression-bc` or `timestamp-query`) and limits (such as `maxTextureDimension2D` or `maxBindGroups`) are the rough equivalent of WebGL extensions, with one catch: you only get what you ask for when requesting the device, otherwise you're on the baseline defaults.

Commands are recorded through a command encoder into render and compute passes, finished into a command buffer and submitted to the device's queue, which at the time was the only queue available.

## Programs out, pipelines in

The biggest conceptual shift is state. A WebGL program combines vertex and fragment shaders, and everything else (blending, vertex layout and so on) is global state you set before each draw call. That is flexible and, on large projects, error-prone.

A WebGPU render pipeline bundles the shaders with the rendering state into one object. Building one looks more verbose, but as Dmitrii Ivashchenko said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023, "WebGpu encapsulates more aspects of rendering into a single object," which makes rendering more predictable and harder to get wrong.

## Uniform buffers, and only uniform buffers

Plain WebGL sets uniforms one API call at a time. WebGL 2 added uniform buffers, with `bindBufferRange` to bind slices of a large one; WebGPU does the same with dynamic offsets passed to `setBindGroup`. The difference is that WebGPU has no individual uniforms at all. Modern GPUs prefer one big block of data over many small ones, so his advice is one large buffer, with different parts used for different draw calls, instead of recreating and rebinding small ones.

That also suggests the migration path: move to WebGL 2 and uniform buffers first, and the jump to WebGPU gets smaller.

## WGSL instead of GLSL

WGSL is more verbose than GLSL but recognisable, with stricter typing and explicit data sizes. Vertex and fragment entry points can live in the same shader module as long as their function names differ. For converting existing shaders he points to Naga, a Rust library that translates GLSL to WGSL and runs in the browser through WebAssembly.

## Why is everything flipped, and why is it clipped?

Two conventions bite almost everyone:

- **Texture origin.** OpenGL and WebGL put the first pixel at the bottom left; Direct3D and Metal use the top left, and WebGPU follows them. If your WebGL code reads pixels from the framebuffer, a `y = 1 - y` adjustment fixes the coordinates.
- **Clip-space depth.** WebGL uses -1 to 1; WebGPU uses 0 to 1, like Direct3D, Metal and Vulkan. Objects disappearing or clipping too soon is the symptom. Generate a 0-to-1 projection matrix (gl-matrix has `perspectiveZO`), or pre-multiply an existing projection matrix with one that remaps the range.

## Performance tips

Keep the number of pipelines small, since every extra pipeline is more state. Don't create a pipeline and use it immediately: creation finishes on another thread and the queue stalls waiting for it, causing visible jank. Leave time between creation and first use, or better, use `createRenderPipelineAsync`. And use render bundles, prerecorded reusable chunks of a render pass, to cut JavaScript overhead; GPU performance is the same either way.

## Who should watch

Graphics and game developers with a WebGL codebase deciding when to migrate, and engine contributors who want the conceptual map before diving into the spec.

Title: Every Kafka topic needs an owner and a second pair of eyes
Description: Muralidhar Basani (Aiven) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on governing thousands of Kafka topics, ACLs and schemas with self-service approvals in Klaw
Body:
Creating one Kafka topic, granting producer and consumer access and promoting it to a higher environment can take at least ten emails and two to three hours of command execution, not counting the time waiting for humans to reply. Muralidhar Basani, Staff Software Engineer at Aiven, opened his Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 talk with that and then showed the fix: Klaw, an open source toolkit that puts every topic, ACL, schema and connector behind a request, an approval and a named owning team.

Honest scope: Klaw is an Aiven open source project, Apache-licensed, and the talk is built around five demos of it. The governance problems he describes apply whatever tool you use.

## Why does Kafka get messy?

Kafka is easy to adopt for its scalability, retention and reliability, and the trouble only shows once the project grows. Large companies end up with hundreds or thousands of topics, and the questions pile up. Who is allowed to produce or consume on this topic? Who owns it, its connector, its schema? How do you promote tested configs from lower to higher environments? Is access control really enforced? How do you back up the configuration for disaster recovery?

When the answers live in email threads and spreadsheets, nobody knows who ran which command, and manual releases cause outages. Schemas are the sharpest example. Basani points out that many Kafka consumer clients run into deserialisation issues when a new schema version is released on a topic, unless the right compatibility is set.

His analogy is a library: a pile of books where you can't find anything, against shelves that are categorised and track who has rented which book, and for how long.

## Why weren't existing tools enough?

He credits CMAK (Kafka Manager from Yahoo) for its friendly UI, Julie GitOps for keeping metadata in Git with CI/CD, and Provectus's UI for Apache Kafka for observability and troubleshooting. The gap: a user can still create a topic or ACL directly on the cluster without approval, and nothing records ownership, so there is nobody to contact when something breaks.

## Governance, self-service, security, automation

Klaw is built on four principles:

- **Governance**: roles, ownership, audit, naming conventions, and Klaw as the single source of truth. It detects manual changes on the cluster, notifies admins and can sync them.
- **Self-service**: teams create, promote, edit and claim topics, request producer and consumer access, schemas and connectors, without waiting on an infrastructure team.
- **Security**: Kerberos and SSL to the clusters, login through Active Directory or SSO, and ACL details (IP addresses, principals) masked for teams that don't own the topic.
- **Automation**: provisioning, promotion across environments, metadata sync and notifications on every request.

Under the hood are two Spring applications and a React UI. Ownership metadata and configs live in a metastore (H2 by default, MySQL or another RDBMS for production), and it connects to any number of Kafka clusters.

## The four-eyes principle, demoed five times

Every change follows the same pattern: one user requests, another approves, only then does Klaw apply it to the cluster. The demos run it with two users, William and Jennifer: creating a topic, a consumer ACL on a topic owned by another team (the owning team decides), a schema request, and promoting a topic from dev to test.

Do you really need two people for this? Basani's answer is yes: topics and ACLs are infrastructure, and infrastructure as code gets peer-reviewed. Is ownership mandatory? Also yes. "Basically this ownership gives responsibility to them," Muralidhar Basani said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

## Disaster recovery is a sync away

The last demo is the most practical. A superadmin with sync permission pulls topic configuration from a cluster into Klaw; in the demo, 162 topics show as out of sync and get assigned to a team in one bulk action. It syncs in both directions, so after an outage Klaw can reinstate topics and ACLs on a new cluster. It syncs configuration only, never the messages on the topics.

## Who should watch?

Platform teams running shared Kafka clusters for many product teams, and anyone whose topic requests currently arrive as emails or Jira tickets. Schema registry support covers Aiven's Karapace and Confluent Schema Registry.

Title: Your node_modules folder is source code you're allowed to fix
Description: Daniel Espino Garcia (Mattermost) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on reading, debugging and patching open-source dependencies with patch-package
Body:
Most developers treat `node_modules` as a black hole you `rm -rf` when things get weird. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Daniel Espino Garcia, software design engineer at Mattermost, argued the opposite: it is the most useful folder in your repo, because every dependency in it is readable, debuggable and patchable, and he showed how the Mattermost mobile team uses that to track down bugs, ship fixes before upstream releases and bend libraries to their needs.

The first third is an open-source primer. The rest is practical, with real examples from a React Native app.

## What does open source actually promise?

He starts with misconceptions. Free means freedom, not cost: the Open Source Initiative definition centres on redistribution. The community is not free labour either: people only contribute to a product they've found, used and believe in, and you still have to review the pull requests. And it is not a niche, with around 90% of code out there using open source one way or another by the figures he cites.

He separates fully open source, open core and merely code-available software, and puts Mattermost in the open core camp with what he describes as more than 90% open code under a thin closed layer.

## Can you debug a dependency instead of filing a complaint?

The best story in the talk: the Mattermost app occasionally mixed up images, only on iOS, and only rarely. They narrowed it to a direct dependency, FastImage. With a closed binary, the only move would have been an email to the vendor. Instead they opened the library in `node_modules`, saw that the JavaScript side mostly delegates to a native component, followed the iOS code, and found that FastImage wraps `SDAnimatedImageView` from another library. The bug lived one layer further down.

They didn't fix it themselves, but they could report it precisely in the right repository, and a few versions later it was fixed.

## Is it worth calling flattenStyle yourself?

The same habit answers performance questions that documentation doesn't. Should you flatten styles before passing them to React Native components? Reading the source shows the basic components already call it, so doing it yourself buys you nothing.

What about the cost of `useMemo`? The bundled React code is minified and unreadable, so he takes the long route: find the package on npm, follow the repository link, check you're on the right branch, find `updateMemo`, then locate the corresponding code in your own `node_modules`. His verdict on the overhead is that, in general, it is not much.

## The fix is on main but not released. Now what?

He lists the options when a library bug is fixed upstream but not yet in a release:

- **Wait** for the release. Fine until the bug is time-sensitive or hits a critical path.
- **Install from main.** A bad idea: you want one commit, not every untested change on the branch.
- **Fork and cherry-pick.** Works, but you're now syncing a fork, switching back when the release lands, and switching to the fork again for the next fix.
- **Patch the package.** His favourite.

With `patch-package` you edit the files directly in `node_modules`, run `npx patch-package`, and get a patch file that's reapplied on every install. For the image bug, that let them pull the underlying library fix in without waiting for FastImage to bump its version.

## Patching to change behaviour, not just fix it

Patches also let you disagree with a library politely. `react-native-haptic-feedback` hard-codes its vibration types, and they needed one with a specific duration. Rebuilding the library, forking it or asking the maintainer to add something only Mattermost needs all felt wrong, so they patched it.

The sharper example is WatermelonDB, which Mattermost uses as an alternative to Redux for app state, backed by SQLite. It guards data integrity by refusing to batch records without changes and refusing to update rows with pending changes. Mattermost needed to go around those guards, while still warning the developer, and without loosening them for everyone else. A local patch keeps the dangerous path contained to their app.

His caveat is the one to remember: "remember that you have patched." Before you open an issue on someone's repository, make sure the bug isn't yours.

## Give something back

Openness pays Mattermost back beyond code: localisation contributions, security research through HackerOne bounties, auditable code for customers, community QA during Hacktoberfest, and peers answering each other on the community server. "Mattermost wouldn't be the same without you," Daniel Espino Garcia said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023, addressed to that community. His asks: open your libraries and tools if you can, upstream your fixes as pull requests, and donate to the projects you depend on.

## Who should watch

JavaScript and React Native developers who have never opened a dependency's source, and teams currently maintaining a fork just to carry one fix. Daily `patch-package` users can skip to the stories.

Title: Ten ways organisations sabotage their own DevSecOps
Description: Gene Gotimer (Praeses) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on ten organisational habits that doom a DevSecOps adoption, and the fix for each
Body:
DevSecOps transformations rarely die because of tooling. They die because the organisation gets in its own way. Gene Gotimer, DevOps Engineer at government contractor Praeses, has been through enough transformations to count the ways, and at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 he listed ten habits that virtually guarantee failure from the start, each with what to do instead.

It's a quick, dense talk with no fluff, and most viewers will recognise at least three of their own employers in it.

## Dooms one to three: fake speed

**Slow onboarding.** If it takes days, weeks or months before a new hire contributes, it bores them, sets a slow pace and tells them how little you thought about their arrival. Have the laptop ready, the tools installed and the permissions granted, then pair, mob or ensemble with them, and practise that ahead of time.

**The pretend cloud.** Running your data centre in the cloud is not using the cloud. Of NIST's five essential characteristics, the one Gotimer sees missing most often is on-demand self-service. Put cloud resources behind a long ticketing and approval process, and executives get frustrated that the cloud didn't make anything faster, while the organisation is the thing stopping it.

**Pretend agile.** A top-down, standardised process is not agile, which is driven by self-organising teams. His line about it lands: "But you say we have a stand up for an hour every day." The sign you aren't agile is status meetings, status reports, status roll-ups and monthly summaries of all of them. Invite stakeholders to stand-ups or reviews instead.

## Doom four: the change control board

"Every production change must be approved by a group that has no idea what we do," Gene Gotimer said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023, describing the change advisory board. You can't release several times a day if approval comes from a group that meets several times a month, and he cites the DORA research finding that such boards increase risk rather than reduce it.

The replacement is evidence. Show a disciplined process: pull request approvals, quality gates, least privilege, and infrastructure as code with immutable infrastructure, so it is always clear what is going to production.

## Dooms five to eight: culture

**Afraid to fail.** No failure means no learning. Protect psychological safety aggressively and ruthlessly, aim for a generative culture in Westrum's sense, constrain the blast radius of experiments, and be loud and public about what you learned, good or bad.

**Unchanging culture.** DevSecOps is a culture, not a set of tools, and it can't stop at the team boundary. Evangelise to other teams so they want what you have, and find a champion who keeps you out of trouble for doing things differently. His slide quote: "If you don't manage your culture, your culture will manage you."

**Unchanging policies.** Existing policies were usually written for monthly or yearly changes. Find out why a policy exists, then use automation to generate evidence that you meet its intent, instead of following it blindly or quietly ignoring it.

**Too many decision makers.** If many people are responsible for a decision, nobody is. Gotimer reaches for the Office Space scene with eight bosses, and notes this usually traces back to fear of failure. Find a champion and highlight early wins so someone wants to take the credit.

## Dooms nine and ten: numbers and hope

**Too many metrics.** Quoting Goodhart, a measure that becomes a target stops being a good measure. Too many metrics turn management into whack-a-mole. Pick one target metric, improve it, add process to protect it, then pick the next.

**Unrealistic expectations.** DevOps won't make problems vanish; it usually shines a light on them. You will need more discipline, not less, and you will fail more often, not less. Set realistic expectations and people can see steady progress.

## Who should watch?

Engineering managers, transformation leads and the engineers who keep explaining to them why the new pipeline didn't fix everything. It pairs well with any talk on tools, as the reason those tools stall.

Title: That feature you built in JavaScript may now be one line of CSS
Description: Kilian Valkhof (Polypane) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on replacing JS toggles, sliders, accordions, modals and scroll effects with native HTML and CSS
Body:
Once you've learned how to build a slider in JavaScript, you never learn it again, and that is the problem. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Kilian Valkhof, founder of Polypane, ran through a grab bag of features that used to need JavaScript and now ship in the browser as HTML and CSS: toggles, autosuggest, colour pickers, smooth scrolling, carousels, accordions, modals and container-aware components, plus a look at what was coming next.

He is no JavaScript hater. Polypane, his browser for developers, is built with web technologies, so he writes "a ton of javascript all day, every day." The talk is about checking your assumptions.

## Why prefer HTML and CSS at all?

His argument is the rule of least power: choose the least powerful language suitable for a given purpose, which on the web means HTML over CSS over JavaScript. JavaScript can throw, fail to load, cost resources to download and run, and lock out keyboard and assistive technology users. HTML and CSS are declarative: you tell the browser what you want and let it do the heavy lifting.

The takeaway he wants you to leave with: "just because you know that something needs Javascript, that doesn't necessarily mean that it's still true in modern browsers," Kilian Valkhof said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023. Check every now and then.

## Form controls the browser already wrote for you

- **Custom toggles.** A checkbox inside a label (clicking anywhere on the label toggles it, for free), `appearance: none` so the browser stops treating the input as replaced content and gives you back the `::before` pseudo-element for the nib, and `:checked` to slide it across. Accessibility comes along because it is still a checkbox.
- **Focus styles.** Use `:focus-visible` so the outline appears for keyboard users only. And instead of `outline: none`, use `outline-color: transparent`: it looks identical until someone turns on Windows forced colours mode, where the browser replaces the transparent colour with one they can actually see.
- **Autosuggest.** A `<datalist>` linked to an input through the `list` attribute filters options as you type and still accepts free text.
- **Colour picker.** `<input type="color">` comes with an eyedropper that can pick colours from anywhere on the screen, outside the browser too, something a web page is never allowed to do itself. Add `color-scheme: dark` (or `dark light`) and native controls follow the user's theme.

## Scrolling without a jQuery plugin

The old way was a jQuery snippet animating `scrollTop` to an anchor's offset. The new way is `scroll-behavior: smooth`, and every internal link is upgraded. The same option exists in `scrollTo` and `scrollBy` via `behavior: "smooth"`.

He makes a point of the accessibility catch: for people with vestibular disorders the smooth scroll is what makes them unwell. So the default should be no smooth scrolling, enabled only inside `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`.

Two finishing touches: `scroll-margin-top` so the target doesn't land under a fixed header, and the `:target` pseudo-class to highlight the section you just jumped to. Then scroll snap for carousels: `scroll-snap-type` on the parent, `scroll-snap-align` on the children. His demo centres randomly sized cards with one declaration, and he invites you to estimate the JavaScript you'd have written for that instead.

## Accordions and modals are just elements

`<details>` and `<summary>` give you an accordion, with the `open` attribute as the initial state that updates as the user clicks (unlike a JSX prop, it doesn't stay stuck open). His one gotcha: add a pointer cursor and hover state to `summary`, because it doesn't look clickable by default.

`<dialog>` needs a sliver of JavaScript, a call to `showModal()`. In return you get focus trapping, a `::backdrop` you can blur, closing through a form with `method="dialog"`, `returnValue` to tell which button was pressed, and placement in the top layer, so no z-index wars with the chat widget. Unlike `alert` and `confirm`, it doesn't block the main thread.

## Components that know their own size

Container queries let a component change layout based on its parent's width rather than the viewport's, with `cqw` and `cqh` units alongside `vw` and `vh`. It replaces the layout prop you pass depending on where a component lands.

## What was still on the horizon in late 2023

He closes with features that were partly shipped at the time: CSS masonry (behind a flag in Firefox, in Safari Technology Preview), `selectlist`, a fully stylable select that had been renamed from `selectmenu` less than a month earlier, the `:has()` selector (in Chrome and WebKit, in Firefox Nightly), which he uses to reveal a free-text Other field with zero listeners, and scroll-driven animations in Chromium as a replacement for scroll-linked JavaScript animation libraries. Check current browser support before copying those four.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers who learned their patterns before 2020 and haven't revisited them, and anyone reviewing a dependency list that includes a slider, a modal library and a scroll plugin. The accessibility notes alone justify the time.

Title: Your authorization if-statement will not survive the sales team
Description: Alex Olivier (Cerbos) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on moving authorization from if-else code to decoupled, policy-based ABAC as a company scales
Body:
Every product starts with one line of authorization: if the email ends in our domain, you're an admin. Alex Olivier, on the founding team (product) at Cerbos, spent his Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 talk scaling a fictional company through six stages until that line becomes an unmaintainable mess copied into several languages, then argued for pulling all of it out into a separate, policy-driven authorization service.

Honest scope: Cerbos is his company's open source project, and it is the example he uses. The six-stage story is the best part, and it applies whatever tool you end up picking.

## AuthN is not AuthZ

Olivier sets the vocabulary first. Authentication challenges a user for a credential and returns a verified identity. Authorization is the next question: what can this person actually do, on which resource? His slide adds a line to Benjamin Franklin's death and taxes, credited to every product manager: ever-changing authorization requirements.

## Six stages of authorization pain

The story, as he tells it:

1. **The blissful days of roles.** A boolean: is this person an employee? Maybe an OAuth scope.
2. **Sales changes the packaging.** Now it's admin OR premium package. Maybe feature flags.
3. **Selling into another region.** GDPR, CCPA and data locality mean a region check before every data fetch. Libraries like CASL and CanCanCan help a little.
4. **Enterprise customers.** A company with 70,000 employees won't fit into two roles; now you need groups, directory data from Active Directory or LDAP, and membership checks in every request handler.
5. **A new CISO wants ISO 27001 and SOC 2.** Every authorization decision now needs an audit log of inputs and outputs, in a strict format you can show an auditor.
6. **Engineering wants microservices.** The main app is Node and TypeScript, the ML work is in Python, there is a legacy .NET component. All that logic has to be rewritten and tested in every language.

"Can you confidently say that every service in every language is behaving as it should?" Alex Olivier asked at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023. Most teams that reach stage six can't.

## What a decoupled authorization service looks like

His answer borrows from authentication's maturity curve: few teams build their own login anymore, so why build your own authorization layer? The service takes three inputs, the principal (user ID, roles, attributes like team or region), the resource (type, ID, attributes like owner) and the action (not just CRUD but approve, flag, export, whatever your domain has), evaluates policies, and returns allow or deny.

The policies are YAML files in Cerbos's case, one per resource type. They cover RBAC (does the user have the role?) and ABAC, where the decision depends on attributes of the principal and the resource. His example: there can never be an owner role, because ownership depends on which user and which specific record. That has to be an attribute check.

In the application, the big if-else block becomes one SDK or API call. Policies live in Git with unit tests and branch-based deployment, and the decision points pull the new version after merge, so changing authorization logic doesn't mean redeploying the app.

## Why it has to run next to your app

One detail is easy to miss. Authentication can be done once and cached for half an hour; authorization can't. It sits in the blocking path of every request, so the service must be fast and local. Olivier recommends running it as a sidecar in the same Kubernetes pod, says Cerbos evaluates decisions in under a millisecond, and calls going out over the internet for authorization checks "just a terrible design decision".

## The trade-offs he admits

Advantages: logic defined centrally, policy evolving independently of code, language and framework agnostic, GitOps friendly, and one consistent audit trail because every decision happens in one place. Costs: another service to deploy and scale (pick a stateless one), a new policy language to learn (YAML, love it or hate it), and a new component in the critical path, so health checks matter.

## Who should watch?

Back-end engineers whose permission checks are spreading across services, and anyone heading into SOC 2 who hasn't thought about authorization audit logs yet. The stage-by-stage walkthrough is the bit to show your product manager.

Title: Shadow DOM in six minutes, and what closed mode really hides
Description: Ankit Gupta (Intelekt AI) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on Shadow DOM encapsulation, open vs closed roots, and using it in React, Angular and web components
Body:
Global CSS is a shared apartment: sooner or later somebody's `button { }` rule ends up in your kitchen. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Ankit Gupta, a founding member and tech lead at Intelekt AI, gave a short, demo-driven introduction to Shadow DOM, the browser feature that puts a wall around a component's markup and styles, and showed what the difference between open and closed shadow roots looks like in practice.

This is a lightning-length 101, around six minutes. Watch it if Shadow DOM is still on your someday list; skip it if you already ship web components.

## What is Shadow DOM for?

Ankit Gupta said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 that "it is a fundamental web technology that helps you encapsulate your web components and styles, making them immune to global scope." He calls it a protective shell: your component's code won't interfere with the rest of the page, and the rest of the page won't interfere with it.

He points to production users to show it isn't a toy: YouTube uses it for the video player so that custom page styles don't break the player's layout, Google Maps uses it to encapsulate the map component, and Material UI appears on the list too.

## Open or closed: who gets the key?

Shadow DOM comes in two modes, and the distinction, in his words, is how much each exposes to the outside world. You pick the mode when you call `attachShadow` on the host element.

The demo is where the talk earns its slot. He builds a page with a `custom-button` element, attaches a shadow root in closed mode, adds a style block and a single button inside it. Then he tries the obvious thing: a page-level style setting the button's background to green. Nothing happens.

The useful bit is the next step. He switches the mode to open and the page style still does nothing. Open mode doesn't let global CSS leak in; the encapsulation holds either way. What open mode gives you is a JavaScript handle. With a script that grabs the host by id, goes through its `shadowRoot`, runs `querySelector` on the button and sets the background colour, the button turns green.

Flip the mode back to closed and the button reverts to blue, and the console reports "cannot read properties of null": the `shadowRoot` property returns nothing to outside code. DevTools still shows the shadow root, labelled closed, with its styles and button visible to you as the developer. Closed hides the internals from other scripts on the page, not from the person with the inspector open.

That is the cleanest takeaway for anyone deciding between the two: both modes isolate styles, and the mode only decides whether outside JavaScript can reach in.

## Does it work with my framework?

He shows three routes:

- **React**: call `attachShadow` on the reference of a JSX element, via a ref.
- **Angular**: Shadow DOM sits at the core of Angular's component encapsulation, switched on with the `encapsulation` property in the component decorator.
- **Plain web components**: `attachShadow` inside the custom element, no framework needed.

The talk stays at the show-the-call level for each; it doesn't go into theming, slots, event retargeting or how form controls behave across the boundary. Treat it as the starting point, then read up on CSS custom properties and `::part` when you need to let consumers style your component on purpose.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers who have heard of Shadow DOM but never opened a shadow root in DevTools, and React or Angular developers curious about what the browser does natively. It is short enough to watch before your next stand-up, and the open-vs-closed demo clears up a common misunderstanding. The code is linked from his final slide.

Title: Most of DevSecOps happens outside the pipeline
Description: Tanya Janca (We Hack Purple) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on AppSec goals you can reach without touching CI/CD, from inventory to incident response
Body:
Ask an AppSec team what their DevSecOps program is and too many will say they bought $100,000 of tools and put them all in the pipeline. Tanya Janca, Founder of We Hack Purple and author of Alice and Bob Learn Application Security, used her Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 talk to argue that this is the smallest part of the job. Her definition: DevSecOps is AppSec plus DevOps, and most AppSec program goals can be met without touching the pipeline at all.

## What does DevSecOps mean to her?

Janca does a quick 101 on CI/CD first (integration, delivery, and the rarer continuous deployment), then frames everything around the three ways of DevOps: efficiency of the whole system, fast and accurate feedback to the right person, and continuous learning. She adds the accuracy part on purpose, because security tools get that part wrong a lot.

Pipelines serve the first two ways well. But she learned the limits the hard way on an open source project, where she planned to run 100 tools and a teammate asked whether he could please write some code. "But if you put every single thing into the pipeline, your developers will not want to be friends with you anymore," Tanya Janca said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

## Goal one: you can't protect what you don't know you have

Inventory comes first in most AppSec programs, and none of it needs CI/CD. Scrape domains, put network agents on servers, run Nmap and scan for open ports, look at your cloud's PaaS and IaaS, scrape your code repositories, or buy one of the newer tools that discover apps on-prem and in the cloud. If an app isn't in your inventory, it is unlikely to be in a pipeline either.

## Find bugs where they are cheapest

She wants bugs found in written code, running code and third-party code, and from as far left as possible. That means the IDE for some checks, scans the moment code is committed, weekly scheduled scans of dependencies, and dynamic scans that run overnight so they don't hog resources during the day.

Her rule for what does belong in the pipeline is practical. Tools with false positives shouldn't go there. Anything that takes six hours, or even 16 minutes, shouldn't go there. And continuous scanning catches what a pipeline misses when nobody runs it for weeks because the team is off touring the hostels of Europe.

## Knowledge, education and tools for developers

The third way of DevOps is learning, and Janca maps a lot of AppSec onto it: reference materials, an advocacy program, a security champions program with one person per dev team, lunch and learns, time reserved in calendars for learning. Then hand developers the tools directly: static analysis, secret scanning, linting, software composition analysis, IDE plugins and security unit tests, most of which work before the code even compiles.

## A secure SDLC, not a secure build step

The bit that frustrates her most is teams that stop at the build. What about standard security requirements for every API, web app or serverless project? A secure coding guideline, and teaching it? Threat modelling in design, pen tests in testing, an AppSec person assigned to the project team, a sprint dedicated only to security? Automated tools are notoriously bad at business logic flaws, and red teams, pen testers and chaos exercises have no business touching your pipeline.

## Incident response and metrics close the loop

Incident response should be a trained team that understands AppSec, with a process, access to the inventory from goal one, read-only access to repos, and post-mortems. Metrics should drive the program: review all tool output every three months, try new tools on one project before rolling them out, visit other AppSec shops and learn from them.

"Appsec is not a tool that you can buy. It's not a button you can press," she said, adding that there is no check you can write either, though she would accept one.

## Who should watch?

Security people building or rescuing an AppSec program, and DevOps engineers who are tired of being handed one more blocking scanner. Janca is funny and fast; expect a lot of ideas, no demo. She also runs a Monday mentoring-matching hashtag and points to her free We Hack Purple community at the end.

Title: Your website has a carbon bill, and a linter can read it
Description: Julia Ziebinska (Akamai Technologies) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on measuring a site's CO2 per view and cutting it with ec0lint and lighter assets
Body:
Every page view costs a few grams of CO2, and the heaviest offenders are the boring things: a PNG that should be a WebP, a moment.js import, a font served as TTF. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Julia Ziebinska, a software engineer at Akamai Technologies and main developer of the open-source ec0lint, showed how to measure a site's footprint and argued that most of it can be cut at the point you write the code, not after launch.

She says up front that it is a less technical talk. It is a good primer.

## How does a website emit CO2 at all?

She follows a data packet through its life: stored in a data centre ("clouds are not just shadows in the sky"), carried by network infrastructure that is always powered, and rendered on a device that also had to be manufactured. Her headline figures: about 4% of all greenhouse gases come from the digital world, and the cloud was heading for 100 zettabytes of stored data by 2025.

For websites specifically, she cites an average of 1.8 g of CO2 per page view. At 10,000 views a month that sums to 216 kg a year, roughly the same as driving 900 km in a petrol car.

She also ran her usual ritual of testing the conference's own site in the Website Carbon Calculator. The Conf42 page came out dirtier than 94% of the pages tested, at almost 4 g per view, with the consolation that it runs on sustainable energy. Fair cop.

## Where does the formula come from?

The estimate follows the Sustainable Web Design methodology, popularised by Tom Greenwood's book of the same name. It only models data transfer, because the data centre and device stages are too hard to estimate per site. The inputs are page size, an energy figure of 0.81 kWh per GB transferred, a grid intensity of 442 g CO2 per kWh, and a split between first visits (everything downloaded) and returning visits (only 2% of the data, the rest cached). Page weight is the lever you control.

## Which choices actually move the number?

This is the practical core, and it reads like a performance checklist with a different scoreboard:

- **Libraries.** moment.js weighs 4.23 MB and costs 1.48 g CO2 in her table; lodash 0.5 g; jQuery 0.47 g; axios 0.16 g. Much of lodash and jQuery can be plain JavaScript, and the built-in `fetch` covers most HTTP client needs.
- **API calls.** Fewer of them, only the data you need, and cache locally instead of asking again.
- **Images.** The same picture as SVG is 126 KB (0.26 g); as PNG 2,111 KB (6.05 g); as TIFF 6,329 KB (18.13 g). SVG and WebP win.
- **Video.** Her advice is to skip it if you can, and use WebM if you can't.
- **Fonts.** System fonts first, then self-hosted, and WOFF2 over WOFF over TTF.
- **Colours.** A dark theme saves energy on OLED screens.
- **Hosting.** Pick hosts on renewable energy with a good PUE; The Green Web Foundation keeps a directory, and she names Seravo, S4 Hosting, Strato and Krystal Hosting.
- **Tracking.** Her sharpest example: USA Today's GDPR-compliant European copy, built without user data collection, was 91% lighter and faster.

The side benefits are the ones your product manager already cares about: faster loads, better SEO, and fewer lost users, with 53% abandoning a site that takes longer than 3 seconds.

## What does ec0lint do differently from Lighthouse?

Lighthouse audits a page that already exists. ec0lint is an ESLint-based linter (with ecolint-style for Stylelint) that flags the problems while you write: heavy libraries, font format and source, image and video formats, video autoplay, missing lazy loading, image resolution, background colour and dark mode. A CO2 module, a CI/CD report, React, Angular and TypeScript plugins, and editor plugins were on the roadmap at the time of the talk.

Her team's analysis says applying the Sustainable Web Design techniques can cut page size by up to 88% with no visible change for users. Extrapolated to 250,000 websites, that takes the equivalent of 220 million km of petrol driving down to 26 million.

She is modest about the scale of it. "We are aware that our tool is only a drop in the ocean of needs," Julia Ziebinska said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023, and asked for contributors and GitHub stars instead.

## The non-website advice

The first half covers personal digital habits: email (sending one averages about 4 g of CO2), spam filters, smaller attachments, keeping laptops six years instead of four (190 kg of CO2 saved per person), deleting unused apps. Her line for developers is the most relatable one: "You can be a nontypical programmer and close your tabs."

## Who should watch

Frontend developers who want a carbon angle to put next to their performance budget, and anyone who needs ammunition to delete moment.js. The libraries and image tables alone are worth the time.

Title: Istio security in three demos - identity, strict mTLS, deny by default
Description: Gufran Mirza (TrustCore Systems) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on securing Kubernetes traffic with Istio identities, strict mTLS, gateways and deny-all policies
Body:
Inside a default Kubernetes cluster, any service can call any other. Gufran Mirza, Co-Founder of TrustCore Systems, used his Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 talk to show how Istio closes that gap in three steps: give every workload a cryptographic identity, require mutual TLS between them, then deny everything and open access one rule at a time. Each step comes with a live demo where you watch requests get dropped.

## What does the sidecar actually do?

Mirza starts with the service mesh basics. Without a mesh, routing, retries, circuit breakers and network policy live inside your application code. With Istio, that infrastructure logic moves into a sidecar proxy (Envoy, written in C++, named istio-proxy in the pod) that sits next to your container and intercepts all incoming and outgoing traffic. The proxy doesn't modify requests; it enforces policy, and when a request fails a policy, your application never sees it.

The practical win is independence. You can change network policy without rolling out the application, and vice versa. Sidecars can be injected by hand, automatically by labelling a namespace, or per deployment through annotations. He also notes that since Istio 1.5 the old separate components (Citadel for certificates, Mixer for telemetry, Galley for config validation) are consolidated into the single control plane.

## Identity comes before policy

You can't write a rule that lets service A call service B until A and B have identities. In most clusters that identity is the Kubernetes service account; GCP service accounts, AWS IAM roles or on-prem user accounts also work.

The flow is neat. When a pod starts, the istio-proxy creates a key pair and sends a certificate signing request to the control plane, which signs a certificate scoped to the service account and returns it over the SDS API. Certificates live in memory, so deleting the container deletes the certificate, and the control plane rotates them before they expire.

## Permissive, strict, disabled

Istio has two kinds of authentication: end-user authentication with JWTs, and service-to-service authentication with mTLS, which is the focus here. Mutual TLS has three modes: permissive (accept plain text and mTLS), strict (mTLS only) and disabled. You can set them mesh-wide, per namespace or per workload. "In general, we want mtls enabled within all of our service mesh applications," Gufran Mirza said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

The first demo makes it concrete. An httpbin service runs in namespace foo inside the mesh with strict mTLS; a sleep pod runs in namespace bar with no sidecar. The sleep pod's request gets a connection reset from httpbin's sidecar. Delete the policy and the same call goes straight through.

## The front door: ingress gateway modes

Exposing services to the outside world goes through the ingress gateway, a reverse proxy at the edge of the mesh that handles TLS. Mirza explains its three TLS modes:

- **PASSTHROUGH**: the gateway doesn't terminate TLS; the client and the application pod do mTLS directly.
- **SIMPLE**: server-side TLS terminated at the gateway, no client certificate needed.
- **MUTUAL**: two-way TLS between client and gateway, terminated at the gateway.

His second demo uses passthrough to an NGINX pod, accepting traffic only on port 443 for one hostname. A request with the client certificate works; port 80 fails with an SSL error, and a different hostname is dropped at the gateway. His advice on the gateway config is to be strict about what you accept, down to minimum TLS versions and cipher suites.

## Authorization: allow nothing, then open up

The third step answers whether service A can send this request to service B. Istio authorization policies support ALLOW, DENY and CUSTOM actions, enforced at runtime by each Envoy proxy. Mirza's recommended starting point is the allow-nothing policy, then incremental ALLOW rules: the database is reachable from the back end, never the front end.

The demo has three services in namespace auth: inventory, users and a third service. One policy lets only the inventory service account make GET requests to the third service; the users service has a policy with no rules, so everything to it is denied. GET from inventory succeeds, POST is forbidden, users is unreachable. Delete the policies and everything opens up again, which is exactly the point.

## Who should watch?

Kubernetes operators who installed Istio for traffic management and never turned on the security half, and anyone who needs a clear explanation of what mTLS modes and gateway TLS modes actually do. The YAML is on screen; this is a hands-on talk.
