Title: One wrong character in a connection string, and why config needs a schema
Description: Peleg Porat (Configu) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on configuration-as-code, with a schema file that validates and composes config values across environments
Body:
Infrastructure went as-code years ago; the environment variables your app reads at startup mostly didn't. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Peleg Porat, co-founder and CEO of Configu, makes the case for configuration-as-code and demos Configu, his company's open-source tool for it: a schema file that lives with your service code, validates every value, and exports per-environment config from wherever it is stored.

## Code is logic, config is behaviour

He starts from the Twelve-Factor App's config section: an app's config is everything likely to vary between deploys. Software is code (logic) plus configuration (behaviour), and the configuration includes environment variables, secrets, feature flags and other settings. Formats vary (`.env`, JSON, YAML and more), and he notes that Node.js added built-in `.env` file support in v20.6.0, a sign of how central the humble env file has become.

## What goes wrong today?

From conversations with developers and DevOps engineers at startups and large companies, Configu heard the same complaint: configuration is fragmented, stored as raw text across databases, files and third-party services. The results he lists are internal friction, governance gaps, distracted developers and data risk, and settings that are wrong or stale cause downtime.

His cautionary tale is short and painful. Peleg Porat said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 that a company told him about a developer who "accidentally changed a single character in their database connection string." Connection strings look human-readable but are full of special characters, so a typo is hard to tell from a valid component. The app failed critically, and finding the cause took far too long.

## What does configuration-as-code give you?

His list of benefits is long: consistency and reproducibility across environments, history of who changed what and when, automated deployments, reviewable and auditable changes, fewer manual errors. Most of these come from one move, treating configuration declarations as code that is versioned, reviewed and validated like the rest of the repo.

## Four nouns: Config, ConfigStore, ConfigSet, ConfigSchema

Configu models it with four concepts:

- **Config**: a single value, made of a key, a value and the set it belongs to, such as a debug level of `error` in production.
- **ConfigStore**: wherever values are saved and read, from text files and databases to secret managers and other configuration tools.
- **ConfigSet**: the context, often an environment like development or production, but also a region or a customer, and sets can be nested so a child inherits from its parent.
- **ConfigSchema**: the configuration-as-code part, a `.cfgu` file in your service repo that declares each key with its type, default and metadata such as description and test restrictions.

## The demo: hello world, validated

The app is a JavaScript one-liner that prints a message from an environment variable; run it plainly and you get `undefined`. `configu init` with the get-started flag generates a schema with three keys. The greeting is a regex-checked type with a default of `hello`, the subject a free string defaulting to `world`, and the message a template built from the other two, which he suggests for composing connection strings and endpoints.

With a JSON file configured as the store, `upsert` writes `hey` and `conf42` into the development set. Validation happens on write: trying `blah` as a greeting fails the regex. He then upserts a production greeting and a subject for a customer set nested under production, so the customer inherits production's values and overrides one.

Running the app with defaults only prints the hello world message. Exporting the development set as `.env` produces a file you can pipe to disk. Exporting the production customer set prints a welcome for that customer: one schema, several environments, nothing copied by hand.

## Who should watch

Teams juggling `.env` files across environments and customers, and anyone who has lost an afternoon to a typo in a secret. It is a short vendor talk by the tool's co-founder; the concepts are useful even if you never install Configu.

Title: Treat your container images like secrets, because they are
Description: Fouad Mulla at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on why containers are not secure by default, and the images, runtime and network fixes that make them so
Body:
Containers can make an application more secure, but only if you stop trusting the defaults. That is Fouad Mulla's message at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023. Mulla, a multi-cloud security architect, opens with two figures from an Aqua Security report: in 2021 about 40% of container images were pulled from public sources, and only 12% of containers ran as a non-root user.

Put those together and you get a lot of unvetted code running with more privilege than it needs. The rest of the talk is a checklist for fixing that, from the image to the network.

## Do you need containers to be secure?

No, and Mulla says so up front. Containers are not a prerequisite for application security. Used well, they help: runtime separation, a smaller attack surface because you only deploy what you need, a predefined setup that is easy to patch and consistent, and isolation that helps contain a breach. Used carelessly, they are the opposite. "Using containers without thinking about security is a recipe for a disaster," Fouad Mulla said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023.

## Where containers bite

His list of challenges is worth pinning to a wall:

- **The daemon attack surface.** Only trusted users should reach the API, it shouldn't be exposed unless needed, and the host needs patching.
- **Secrets management**, where images themselves count as sensitive material, not just passwords and keys.
- **Untrusted content**: compromised or vulnerable images from public registries.
- **Sprawl and ephemeral runtimes.** Containers spin up and die fast and share CPU and other host resources, which makes monitoring and forensics hard.
- **Lightweight isolation.** Containers separate workloads less strongly than VMs, so breakout scenarios matter.

The ephemeral point deserves a moment. An immutable, short-lived container may be replaced before anyone starts the investigation, so the incident plan has to account for logs and records being kept somewhere that outlives the container.

## Images are sensitive data

The takeaway he repeats most: treat container images as sensitive data. Apply strict access control, review them, scan their contents. Start from official, minimal base images, avoid unnecessary packages and tools, and scan regularly as part of the pipeline. Never hard-code secrets into an image.

For the AWS flavour of a secure pipeline, he walks through CodeCommit, CodeGuru to catch credentials embedded in code, AWS Secrets Manager, IAM and CloudWatch, and stresses that Azure or Google Cloud work just as well. For linting Dockerfiles he names Red Hat's dockerfile_lint and Hadolint, and for scanning images two open source tools: Anchore Engine, which plugs into CI/CD so only compliant images reach production, and Clair from CoreOS, which ranks findings by CVE. Cloud registry scanners, such as the one in AWS private registries, cover the same ground.

## Going beyond the defaults

"Docker is not secure by default" is on his takeaways slide, and the fixes are concrete:

- Least privilege, and isolation for sensitive workloads, with gVisor, Kata Containers or hypervisor-based containers where the data justifies it.
- Immutable containers: never patch a running one, replace it. Read-only filesystems cut down the places an attacker can persist.
- Resource limits so a single container can't exhaust the host or be used for a DoS.
- Kubernetes security contexts and pod security policies, or the equivalent in your orchestrator.
- Infrastructure as code to keep environments consistent while the team races to ship.

He frames all of this as a balance between developer flexibility and robust security, not as a gate.

## The network: default deny, then open up

On network segmentation Mulla is direct. Use micro-segmentation and Kubernetes namespaces as boundaries, apply network policies that block everything by default, and add only what each service needs. Isolate sensitive workloads first, which also helps with compliance. Encrypt container traffic with TLS, audit regularly, and consider a service mesh such as Istio or Linkerd for finer traffic control, feeding its logs into whatever WAF, IDS or IPS you already run.

## Who should watch?

Teams moving workloads into containers who want a structured checklist, and security folks who need the vocabulary to talk to platform teams. It is a survey of practices and tools rather than a hands-on demo.

Title: One CSS skeleton loader that borrows your component's layout
Description: Aleksandr Tkachenko (Playtech) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on Skeleton Mammoth, a pure-CSS skeleton loader driven by three classes and a data attribute
Body:
Most skeleton loader tutorials have you build a grey twin of every component, and then maintain both forever. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Aleksandr Tkachenko, senior software engineer at Playtech, shows Skeleton Mammoth, his open-source library that does it in pure CSS: three classes on your existing markup, and the skeleton inherits the component's own layout and dimensions.

## Why skeletons, and what's wrong with the existing ones?

A skeleton loader (also called a skeleton screen or content placeholder) mimics the page layout while data loads, the way YouTube and LinkedIn do. His case for them: better perceived performance, lower bounce rates, smoother transitions, and attention on progress rather than on waiting.

His survey of existing solutions found five recurring problems. Limited customisation, so the skeleton doesn't match the real design. Little support for screen reader users. Poor reusability: you either write a separate placeholder copy of each component or restructure the component itself, and both cost a lot of extra code. Maintenance burden as the content evolves. And framework lock-in: to use one skeleton from a big library such as MUI you still install its core.

He also weighs the alternatives and finds them wanting as replacements. Spinners are simple and universally understood but say nothing about what is loading and feel like the whole site is loading. Progress bars give precise feedback for uploads or full-page loads but lack context and are tricky to animate accurately. Showing nothing costs no effort and makes the site look slower.

## Pure CSS, no JavaScript, on purpose

His requirements were reusable across components and frameworks, configurable, feature-rich and dependency-free. That pushed him to plain CSS, written in SCSS for development but compiled to pure CSS with no runtime. The idea he keeps returning to: the skeleton should inherit the layout of whatever it is applied to.

The demo uses a React card (image, title, subtitle), though nothing is React-specific. Add `sm-loading` to the card while the data state is loading, `sm-item-primary` to the image wrapper and `sm-item-secondary` to the two text fields. That's it. The base styles hide the children's real content and visual extras like borders, and draw the skeleton in the space the element already occupies, so you never set a width or height. An empty element still renders, because the styles guarantee at least a non-breaking space. The base styles also include a part that tells screen reader users the content is loading. Remove `sm-loading` and the real card appears; the transition between the two is yours to design.

## How do you configure CSS without arguments?

CSS can't take parameters the way a JavaScript function does, and adding JavaScript would break the whole premise. His workaround is data attributes. Pass a JSON-stringified object such as `{ animation, theme, opacity }` to `data-sm-config` next to `sm-loading`, and attribute selectors match on its values and apply the right styles.

Aleksandr Tkachenko said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "Thus, using an attribute selection, we match elements that have an explicitly specified attribute and its values." A neat trick to steal for any CSS-only component.

## The extras that make it usable

- **Dark mode** through `prefers-color-scheme`, applied automatically unless you set a theme explicitly.
- **Reduced motion** through `prefers-reduced-motion`. Animation is on by default, but users with vestibular motion disorders who have that setting enabled get none.
- **Animations**: none, wave, wave-reverse and pulse.
- **Opacity**, so you can fit the default colours to your design without overriding them.
- **Custom properties**: every colour and animation value (duration, timing function and so on) lives in a variable on `:root`. Override the matching variables in your own stylesheet to restyle the primary item or slow the wave; the documentation lists them all.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers tired of maintaining placeholder twins of every card, and anyone building a small CSS-only library who wants to see how far classes, custom properties and attribute selectors can stretch. It is a short, focused talk about one library by its author, with a fair look at when a spinner or progress bar is the better tool.

Title: Writing is 20% of a technical writer's job, and that's the safe part
Description: Tomas Fernandez (Semaphore) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on why technical writing stays a worthy career next to LLMs, and how to use them
Body:
Forrester's 2023 forecast put technical writers in the corner of the chart nobody wants to be in: high exposure to generative AI. Tomas Fernandez, Technical Writer at Semaphore, answered the obvious question at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 with a short yes and a long "it depends". Writing is the part of the job language models can do; the other 80% is interviewing people, and that is where the career lives.

It is a short, opinionated talk built on five reasons, and it comes from someone who writes blogs, video content and ebooks for a living.

## Why is this leap different?

Fernandez doesn't hand-wave the threat. Every technological leap had people crying about lost jobs, and sometimes they were right (there are no typesetters left), but new technology usually made more jobs than it destroyed. Language models are a different class of thing, he argues, because they produce text at scale and feel like they can think. There are already products that take code and output documentation, and Synthesia that can deliver a talk with a virtual avatar.

## Five reasons not to panic (too much)

**1. The hype cycle.** Crypto has been through it; language models are just starting. In the early phase, the press prints the most extreme outcomes because fear sells.

**2. AI already failed to replace writers in a high-stakes business.** The 2023 Writers Guild of America strike ended with Hollywood settling with the guild. Back in tech, he points out that Google's State of DevOps 2023 report had AI as the lowest contributor to team performance.

**3. The limits are real.** Models trained on internet text inherit its misinformation, clutter and verbosity. Some companies can't use them at all for privacy or compliance reasons. Add context size limits and model updates shipped without notice.

**4. You can adapt.** This is the practical core (see below).

**5. Writing is 20% of the job.** "You have to interview people, you have to talk to SMEs, to developers, to product managers," Tomas Fernandez said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023. You have to put yourself in the users' shoes and prioritise information, which models struggle with.

## The uncanny valley of generated text

The biggest problem with AI text, in his view, is not hallucination. It is the uncanny valley, the aversion people feel towards things that try to look human and nearly make it. He shows it with roboticist Hiroshi Ishiguro and his robot twin, then argues text has the same problem in a quieter form. Read enough unedited model output and you notice nobody is at the wheel, and there is no "I-ness" in it. For documentation that sounds minor, until you remember the reader has to trust it.

## Cyborg, director or Swiss army writer?

His adoption spectrum is the most reusable idea in the talk. At one end, the cyborg publishes raw model output, usually under pressure to ship volume, and it shows: inaccurate, too long, slow to reach the point. At the other end, the classical writer can't or won't use AI, often for compliance reasons.

The middle has two roles:

- **The director** prompts paragraph by paragraph, rewrites, goes back and forth, and keeps the big picture coherent, like a film director coaching actors.
- **The Swiss army writer** (his own camp) uses the model where it beats him: outlining, writer's block, research, summarising, translation, editing, brainstorming, while still writing half or more of the text by hand.

The middle is where he wants writers to be, so they don't become over-dependent and don't lose their skills. His bar for worrying is clear: until a model can sit down with a developer and ask the right questions, writers are safe.

## Who should watch?

Technical writers, developer advocates and anyone who owns docs and has been asked whether a model could just do it. It is a short talk with no demo; the adoption spectrum is worth stealing for your own team discussion.

Title: The stair-step chart that means your components never die
Description: Julian Jandl (Push-Based.io) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on reading the JS heap, GPU layer memory, and hunting detached DOM nodes with browser dev tools
Body:
"Aw, Snap!" is usually not a bug in Chrome. It is the browser killing a tab that ate too much memory, and leaks are a common reason it got there. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Julian Jandl, performance engineer at Push-Based.io, explains what actually fills a tab's memory, how to read a heap snapshot, and a repeatable routine for finding leaks, ending with Microsoft Edge's Detached Elements tool pointing straight at the leaking line of code.

## What eats memory in a browser tab?

Three things, in his breakdown. Your JavaScript objects: `let movie = { title: 'Spiderman' }` lives in memory until it is nulled, and a spread copy for immutability doubles the cost. The DOM your templates produce: every node and its attributes and text take space. And composition layers from your CSS, which live in GPU memory, a resource low-end phones don't have much of.

## Reading the heap without drowning

For a quick look, Chrome's Performance Monitor charts JS heap size, DOM node count and event listeners over time, and the Task Manager (and, in newer Chrome, a tooltip on the tab itself) shows the footprint. For depth, there is the Memory tab and three terms worth learning. Shallow size is the object alone. Retained size is everything freed if the object goes, and it is the number to prioritise by. Distance is how far the garbage collector has to walk the graph to reach the node.

The routine: hit the collect-garbage icon first, then take a heap snapshot, then filter by class name. His `FindMe` demo object with a large array shows up in a 5 MB snapshot for a page with one title on it. Select a node and the retainers list shows who is still holding on to it, which is the thread you pull when hunting leaks.

## Layers cost real megabytes

`will-change: transform`, `translateZ(0)`, 3D transforms, `<video>`, `<canvas>`, animated opacity or transform and a few stacking situations each promote an element to its own layer. Chrome's Layers panel (hidden under More tools) shows them in a rotatable 3D view, with a memory estimate and the compositing reason for each. On the Observable landing page, one tile with an accelerated transform animation costs 10.5 MB; the outer document layer, 35 MB. Fine on a desktop GPU, less fine on a phone.

## What leaks, and how do you spot it?

A leak is memory your app allocated and no longer uses but can't release. Julian Jandl said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "So the worst case is when you repeatedly allocate memory without cleaning up." Mount and unmount a leaky component a few times and the Performance Monitor draws a staircase. His example run added 50 MB of heap, 70,000 DOM nodes and 400 event listeners. A healthy app climbs a little and drops back after garbage collection.

The usual culprits:

- **`console.log`**: the console keeps a reference to whatever you logged, even when DevTools is closed.
- **Globals**: anything on `window`, or a module-level const outside the component's class scope, never goes away.
- **Leftover subscriptions**: intervals, RxJS timers and event listeners that are never torn down keep their closures, and everything those reference, alive. He calls this the number one cause.
- **DOM references**: remove a button while a function still references it, and it becomes a detached element, gone from the page but not from memory.

## Edge's Detached Elements tool does the tracing

Since front-end code is mostly components tied to DOM nodes, detached elements are where leaks show up. Edge 93 added a Detached Elements tool. His order of operations (the buttons sit in the wrong order, he notes): collect garbage, read detached elements, then analyse the heap. Entries without an ID afterwards can be ignored. Clicking one opens the retainers list, where a `V8EventListener` entry links to the source line.

In the demo, toggling a list pushes the heap from 120 MB to 200 MB to 270 MB, and forced garbage collection doesn't help. The trail ends at an anonymous `change` listener on a bold toggle inside a plain JavaScript `ListItem` class. The fix is the one every framework does for you: store the handler as a named property, add a `destroy()` method that calls `removeEventListener` with it, and call it when the list is torn down. After that, a manual garbage collection takes the heap back to about 7 MB.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers with a single-page app that gets slower the longer it stays open, and anyone who has never opened the Memory tab on purpose. It is a practical tools tour; you can follow along with your own app.

Title: Git submodules, the monorepo you already have installed
Description: Vadim Tsaregorodtsev (Emerging Travel Group) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on sharing Next.js code across three travel products with Git submodules
Body:
You build feature X on project A. Months later you build it again on project B, by copying it. The third time, on project C, neither copy looks like the original. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Vadim Tsaregorodtsev, lead software engineer at Emerging Travel Group (ETG), tells this Groundhog Day story, with Bill Murray as the recurring guest, and explains why his team skipped both a monorepo and shared npm packages and went with plain Git submodules.

## Three products that look the same until they don't

ETG runs hotel booking brands in B2C and B2B, and Tsaregorodtsev leads the front end of the B2B transportation products: flight tickets, rail tickets and transfers. All three are Next.js apps with the same set of pages, a similar domain, similar services and similar supplier work. They are still not one app painted three colours. They have different backends in different languages, plenty of non-overlapping edge cases, and each needs its own release cycle and versioning, even for the same feature.

## Why not a monorepo?

It is the obvious answer, and he rejects it for this team. A single Git history across products that release independently is confusing. Monorepo tooling can scope history and releases per project, but that is one more technology for a small front-end team to learn and maintain, and he would end up as the bus factor of one. He is honest about the other side too. Vadim Tsaregorodtsev said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "It's much simpler to copy a feature from one project to another rather than continuously maintain an abstraction that's only beneficial in a couple of cases." He points to Dan Abramov's talk on the WET codebase for more on over-abstracting.

## Why not packages?

The company already runs a polyrepo with shared packages: a dedicated team owns the UI component library, and Yarn installs it straight from a Git URL, no private registry needed. The flow is intuitive: do the work, bump the version, set it in the app. It works well for components, which you can test in Storybook, and for helpers, which you can unit test. It falls apart for bigger pieces, like a custom Next.js `_app` that wires up the Apollo client and a generic `getInitialProps` for every page. To test that in a separate repo you'd need to rebuild half the project's infrastructure there. `yarn link` gets you through development, but at that point you are reinventing workspaces.

## How submodules fill the gap

A submodule is just a Git repository, referenced from the parent by a commit instead of a version in `package.json`. `git submodule add <url>` creates a `.gitmodules` file (name, path, URL) and an entry that `git diff` shows is a commit hash. `git submodule update --remote --init` fetches the files; ETG wraps it in a Yarn script for local work and CI. The result is an ordinary directory in the project.

The workflow needs teaching, even though it is good old Git. Change something inside the submodule, commit and push there, then commit the updated pointer in the parent repo too. Branching is where it gets clever. By default a submodule tracks the default branch, which would push every change onto every product. So ETG uses the shared repo's main branch as a sync point and gives each product its own core branch (Avia, railways, transfers). A feature branch is merged into, say, the Avia core branch, and the other products pull from main only when they need the feature. That inverts the package model, where one production line forces every app onto each update.

The side benefits are the selling point. IDE search covers the shared code like any other folder. The submodule holds plain TypeScript, imported without a build step, so there's no waiting for a library pipeline. Lint, tests and build run once for app and shared code together. You can share large chunks of application logic, not just components. And moving the copied features into the submodule turned up several typos that had been copy-pasted from project to project.

## Rules learned in a year

- Treat the submodule as a dependency: it must not import from the app, though it can rely on the app's other dependencies, the way a React state manager expects React.
- Share translations for shared text so translators don't do the work three times.
- Tag releases (his example is v1.0.17) so a production bug can be reproduced against the submodule code that shipped.
- Keep files small for tree shaking: if project C needs ten of a hundred helpers, split them.
- When two projects need the same feature at once, agree on the interface, let one team build the shared part and the other its own side, then swap.
- Document all of it; that becomes the onboarding guide.

## Who should watch

Small front-end teams running several similar apps that need independent releases, especially if a monorepo migration sounds like a quarter you don't have.

Title: When AI hacks IoT, the outage has a body count
Description: Susie Su (Signify (Philips Lighting)) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on AIoT, the DevOps skills AI can't copy, and an 11-part map of AI security
Body:
A hacked website goes down. A hacked pipeline, power grid or car can kill someone. That is the core of Susie Su's talk at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023: Su, Global Software Operations Architect at Signify (Philips Lighting), argues that once AI moves into connected devices (AIoT, AI plus IoT), security stops being about uptime and money and starts being about physical safety, so the security model has to grow to match.

It is a broad, framework-style talk in three parts: what AIoT is, what it does to DevOps jobs, and what AI security should cover.

## What does AIoT look like in practice?

Su starts from her own industry. Her examples of AIoT include automated vehicles (Tesla, Waymo, Mobileye, Cruise, Baidu), smart cities with lighting, video surveillance and traffic monitoring, and manufacturing lines that use deep neural networks for quality checks.

The demo idea is a nice one for anyone who has fiddled with smart bulbs. Take a photo of the Black Forest, turn the image into lighting parameters the hardware understands, send the command, and your bedroom gets the same ambience. She points to OpenAI's DALL-E 3 as the kind of model that can now handle the image-to-parameters step. It is a small, friendly example, but it shows the chain that matters later: model output turns into hardware commands.

## Which DevOps work can AI actually take?

The middle section is about jobs, and Su doesn't sugar-coat it. Her slide compares the roles predicted ten years ago to be automated (telemarketers, bookkeeping clerks, receptionists, proofreaders) with today's list, which now includes coders, software engineers and data analysts. She frames current AI as roughly a Google level 3 software engineer.

Then she lists what it can't do, and it reads like a job description for a senior DevOps engineer:

- Handle intricate, open-ended problems, such as a migration across many departments with zero downtime for the running business.
- Show the depth of thought of a professional engineer who sees the whole lifecycle, from communication to Linux and networking.
- Think critically.
- Collaborate across teams: interpersonal skills, leadership, teamwork, work ethic.

On that last point she is blunt. "It's not like if it's just a machine, just because of your test, can understand what you really mean," Susie Su said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023. Read that as: the hard part of DevOps was always people, and that is the part that stays.

## Why is IoT the scary part of AI security?

This is the section worth the watch. Su contrasts a software attack, which takes your website down or costs money, with an attack on IoT. "If AI hacked IoT industry is so horrible, it means it will kill someone," she said. Her slides place IoT security inside cybersecurity, next to network, cloud, endpoint and application security, and break it down into 5G networks, the Internet of Vehicles and industrial IoT, including industrial control systems. She walks through a timeline of real industrial control system incidents, with gas pipelines and nuclear facilities as the cases where one compromised device can hurt a whole city.

## What should AI security cover?

Drawing on ten years in cybersecurity and three in AI, Su proposes eleven areas. The useful bit is how each maps to a concrete technique:

- **Data security**: confidentiality, integrity, availability, encryption, access control, anonymised data.
- **Privacy preservation**: differential privacy (managed noise in the data) and federated learning (training spread over devices so raw data never leaves).
- **Information security**: the classic list, from application and cloud security to incident response, cryptography and disaster recovery.
- **Explainability and transparency**: transparent models are easier to audit and debug.
- **IoT security** and **human-AI interaction security**: preventing impersonation and the malicious use of AI output.
- **Model security**: adversarial perturbations, transfer attacks, white-box and black-box attacks.
- **Bias and fairness**: bias mitigation and fairness-aware learning.
- **Lifecycle security**: coding practices, regular updates and proper disposal of systems when a project ends.
- **Regulatory compliance**: GDPR, industry rules, ethical guidelines. Her point: relying on AI firms to be good-hearted is not a plan.
- **Hybrid AI-human security**: a human in the loop for threat detection and overall oversight.

The lifecycle item is the one most teams forget. Software gets switched off; a model that is still feeding devices needs to be retired on purpose.

## Who should watch?

Engineers in IoT, embedded and industrial settings who need a checklist for AI risk, and DevOps folks wondering where their job is heading. It is a taxonomy and a point of view, not a hands-on talk: no code and no tooling demo.

Title: Machine learning 101 starts with the business problem, not the model
Description: Rich Niemiec (Viscosity North America) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 on picking ML algorithms by business problem, from decision trees to RAG on Oracle
Body:
Most ML projects fail at the first question, not the last: nobody wrote down what they were trying to solve. Rich Niemiec, Chief Innovation Officer at Viscosity North America, spent his Conf42 DevSecOps 2023 talk on exactly that order of operations: business problem first, then the function, then the algorithm. The algorithms, explained in plain English, turn out to be the easy part.

Be clear about scope: this is a 101, and his abstract says outright that it is not for the experts. It is also a database person's tour, heavy on Oracle, with Twilight Zone episodes as the running gag.

## Problem, function, algorithm

His recipe for supervised learning is a three-step funnel. Name a specific business problem: not making more money, but finding which customers look like your best ones. Pick the function: classification, clustering, anomaly detection, regression, attribute importance, association rules, time series. Only then choose among the algorithms for that function. Train on about 60% of the data, test and score on the other 40%, compare algorithms, then run the winner against the big data.

The slides push for precise problem statements. Targeting the best customers is poorly defined; customers who spent $500 or more in the most recent 18 months is something a model can work with.

## A plain-English tour of the algorithms

This is the bulk of the talk and the most useful part for newcomers:

- **Decision trees**: a lawyer deciding whether to take a case, weighing the win, the loss and the costs. Niemiec uses one to predict who will buy a sports-logo credit card.
- **Random forest**: many decision trees, which smooths out the curvy line and keeps the model from fitting too closely.
- **Neural networks**: show it 1,000 cats and 1,000 dogs; the math under it is decades old, and backpropagation does the tuning. With deep learning, the model finds the features itself.
- **Anomaly detection**: what sits outside the sphere. Subtle-anomaly models are used in nuclear power plants, airliners and Oracle's Exadata hardware.
- **Clustering**: k-means by distance, and Oracle's O-Cluster by density.
- **Principal component analysis**: of 80 reasons a customer buys, maybe 20 matter. His aside on eigen (Dutch or German for your very own, so you go looking for your Eigen customer) is the best mnemonic in the talk.
- **Association rules**: the a priori algorithm and the classic bread, diapers and milk market basket.

His point is not that you should implement these. It is that the code is short. Attribute importance for "who buys insurance" is a few lines of SQL against a table, and Oracle's AutoML tried every classification algorithm and generated a Python notebook in about four minutes for work that took him days.

## The DBA is most of the ML job

One claim stands out for this audience. Data science is about 20% of an ML project, Niemiec argued; the rest is finding the right data, cleansing it and checking it for bias, which is DBA and developer work. "So we're moving from predictive to prescriptive right now," Rich Niemiec said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2023: the CFO doesn't want last quarter's numbers, but what to do to hit next quarter's.

## From transformers to RAG

The last third covers generative AI. He traces it to the "Attention Is All You Need" transformer paper from Google Brain and one of its authors, Aidan Gomez, who went on to start Cohere. Oracle partnered with Cohere instead of building its own LLM, and added a vector database so you can query by image or document alongside JSON, graph, spatial and relational data. On hallucinations, the answer he shows is retrieval augmented generation over a company's own protected data.

There is a handful of figures along the way: ChatGPT reached 100 million users in two months, against 70 months for Uber, 30 for Instagram and nine for TikTok. APEX, Oracle's low-code tool, has around 2 million apps with about 3,000 built a day, according to him, and now generates SQL from plain English prompts.

## Who should watch?

Developers and DBAs who want the vocabulary of ML before their first project, and managers who need to tell classification from clustering in a meeting. If you already ship models, skip it; if you run Oracle, there is a lot here for you.

Title: Your tests check what a query returns, never how it runs
Description: Adam Furmanek (Metis) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on database failures unit tests can't see, and catching them early with execution plans and OpenTelemetry
Body:
A query that reads 300,000 rows and runs for 25 seconds will pass every unit test you have, because your local database has a hundred rows and your tests only compare results. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Adam Furmanek, DevRel at Metis, catalogues the database problems that sail through CI and blow up in production, and argues for database guardrails: checking execution plans against production as early as the developer's laptop. The last part demos Metis, his company's product built on that idea.

## Why one DBA doesn't cut it any more

His starting point: a product used to mean one database behind a load balancer, and one DBA could keep it fast. Now every service has its own SQL and NoSQL stores, logs are spread across scaled-out microservices, and when something slows down you can't tell whether it started where you see it. Monitoring dashboards show that there is a fire. They don't say how it started or how to put it out.

He sorts what breaks into three buckets: code changes (your app queries differently), schema changes (columns, types, indexes) and what he calls query changes, where the exact same SQL starts executing differently because statistics went stale, configuration changed or the data distribution moved.

## The ways green tests lie

The examples are where the talk earns its slot.

- **The aggregate root.** An ORM call fetching a user with all its related data turned into one SQL statement over about eight tables. In his production case it read around 300,000 rows and ran for nearly 25 seconds. The fix was counter-intuitive: many small queries, joined in application code, ran in a split second.
- **The readable refactor.** On a boarding passes table of about 8 million rows, a version using a CTE to compute a double checksum ran in 13 seconds; the equivalent query without it ran in 8. Same rows, same green tests.
- **Schema migrations.** Adding a column bloats every `SELECT *` and can force a full table rewrite that takes minutes, hours or longer while the database is busy. Dropping a column is nearly never safe when other applications share the database, since their tests never knew it existed. Changing a column type can quietly change how numbers, dates or geolocation are represented.
- **Indexes.** They speed up reads and slow down every write. Hand a junior developer a slow query and the answer "add an index", and you may end up with indexes everywhere, some unused six months later, and no test will ever notice.
- **Engine differences.** Test against an in-memory database and production against another engine, and you test against different bugs. His history lesson is the Halloween problem, where an update to give everyone under 10,000 a 10% raise kept finding the same rows again because they moved as they were updated, until everyone earned at least 10,000.

## ORMs: helpful, and opaque

Lazy loading gives you the N+1 problem: one query for all aircraft, then one per aircraft for its seats. Switching to eager mode everywhere just brings back the giant join. Polymorphism patterns (table per hierarchy, per type, per concrete class) cost performance, and types don't map cleanly: JavaScript has no database collation and no decimal precision. Then the visibility questions most teams can't answer: what is your isolation level, who commits or rolls back, is there a connection pool, what happens on schema drift.

As Adam Furmanek said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "unit tests and integration tests are going to be green, but we will hit errors when we go to production." Load tests catch some of it, but they cost hours, hardware and anonymised production data, and they come at the very end, after review and merge.

## What does a database guardrail look like?

The core idea is the execution plan. Every query goes through parser, rewriter and planner; `EXPLAIN` shows the plan as nodes (sequential scans, index scans, nested loop or hash joins), each with an arbitrary cost, and the engine picks the cheapest. Capture the queries your code runs locally, through OpenTelemetry instrumentation of the web framework, ORM and SQL driver, and you can evaluate those plans with production statistics. A query that is instant on your hundred rows can be flagged before it ever ships.

His three pillars: prevent bad code from reaching production by shifting checks left, monitor with an understanding of what the database is doing rather than raw CPU charts, and troubleshoot automatically by connecting a slowdown to the deploy that caused it.

## The Metis part

The demo shows Metis tracing a REST endpoint to its SQL, the plan and table statistics, and flagging a scan of about 16 million rows with a suggested index. It also analyses pull requests, including schema migrations that lack indexes, and monitors production hosts, queries and indexes. It is a vendor demo; the first two thirds stand alone.

## Who should watch

Backend and full-stack JavaScript developers who lean on an ORM and have never read an execution plan. You'll come away knowing which green builds to distrust.

Title: Treat a smart contract like a database schema and generate the client
Description: Albert Groothedde (Kadena) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on parsing Pact smart contracts into TypeScript definitions for a typesafe transaction builder
Body:
Prisma reads your database tables and hands you a typesafe client. Albert Groothedde, architect on the developer experience squad at Kadena, wants the same thing for smart contracts. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023 he shows how `@kadena/client` parses contracts written in Pact and generates TypeScript definitions, so front-end code gets autocompletion and type checking for blockchain calls instead of hand-written JSON.

## What is a smart contract, for a JavaScript developer?

Groothedde's framing will feel familiar to anyone who has written a REST API: a smart contract is a piece of code stored on a decentralised platform, holding a schema plus the functions allowed to touch it. His short version is "a set of secure, serverless functions that can interact with a database on a decentralized platform".

The running example is a streaming subscription. A `subscribe(account, months)` function writes a record keyed by account, then calls `coin.transfer` in a different contract to pay for those months. The `coin` module keeps a key-value table where the key is the account name and the value holds a balance and a guard, a function that returns true or false when its conditions are met. Lookups are by key, never by a `where` clause, which keeps them fast.

## Why Pact gives up loops on purpose

Pact is the contract language on Kadena, and it is Turing incomplete by design. Albert Groothedde said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "Turing incomplete means that there's no way to do recursion or loops, which actually makes the language a lot more safe." No infinite loops, no stack overflows from runaway recursion; you map over the items you have and that's it.

The payoff is formal verification through model checking. His example is the `transfer` function's conserve-mass property: summed across the table, balances must net to zero, so no function can print money into the system or quietly remove it. If one could, the check fails.

Inside `transfer` the safety rails are visible. The sender can't also be the receiver, both accounts must be valid, and the amount must be above zero, since a negative transfer would mean receiving money. The actual debit and credit sit inside `with-capability`, which works a bit like a callback in JavaScript: the code only runs if the sender signed for that `TRANSFER` capability with exactly those arguments. The transaction itself is JSON with two parts: the code, such as `(coin.transfer "albert" "john" 133.7)`, and the signers, each with a public key and a list of capabilities they sign for, followed by the signatures.

## Why a JavaScript client at all?

Because getting a transaction onto the chain is a lot of plumbing. Build it (write the Pact code, add the right capabilities, set network ID, chain ID and who pays gas), sign it with a wallet, submit it, then wait for it to be validated. `@kadena/client` wraps all of that. With the generated types in place, typing `coin.` in the editor lists every function in the module with its arguments, and adding a signer for the transfer capability is type checked too.

## From Pact source to TypeScript definitions

The middle of the talk is a detour through the wormhole into parser grammars, built up live: a number as a run of digits, then whitespace, then repeated numbers, then `+` and `-` operators turned into objects with a left side, a right side and an operator. Once you have seen that, the Pact parser reads naturally. A method is a parenthesised block whose kind is `defun`, followed by an atom stored as the name, an optional type rule (a colon plus an atom) stored as the return type, and a block of atom-plus-type pairs stored as parameters. Capabilities used through `with-capability` are extracted too, so the generator knows what a signer has to sign.

The parser output for `coin.transfer` is plain JSON (module name, functions, typed parameters, extracted capabilities), and the TypeScript definition is, in his words, basically a big string concatenation over it. Missing types become `any`. The abstract adds the design choice that makes this maintainable: the library is entirely type definitions, with no runtime code generation, so the generator can improve without breaking changes.

The recap lists four pieces: an expression builder for typesafe Pact expressions, a transaction builder for signers and metadata, signing utilities for wallets such as Chainweaver and WalletConnect, and a client that submits a transaction and listens until it is verified.

## Who should watch

TypeScript developers curious how codegen from a foreign language actually works, and anyone building front ends for Kadena. The parser section is the most portable part: the same approach works for any DSL you'd like typed.

Title: Put axe-core in your Playwright suite and let the PR fail
Description: Taslan A. Graham (CradleApps) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on wiring axe-core into Playwright tests and running accessibility checks on every pull request
Body:
Most accessibility bugs are boring: an image without alt text, grey text on a grey button, a page with no title. Boring is exactly what a machine is good at catching. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Taslan A. Graham, web developer at CradleApps, walks through the case for accessibility, the WCAG principles behind it, and then a hands-on setup that runs axe-core inside Playwright tests and on every GitHub pull request.

## Why bother, beyond doing the right thing?

Graham's list is the one to send to a sceptical product manager. Accessible software is inclusive and works with assistive technologies such as screen readers. It widens your user base. Much of it improves things for everyone: alt text helps every user, not just those with visual impairments. It helps SEO, since practices like a title on every page and alt text on images are things search engines reward. And in some countries it is a legal requirement.

The standard behind all of it is the W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), built on four principles. Perceivable: text alternatives for non-text content, captions for multimedia, content that survives a screen reader. Operable: everything reachable from the keyboard, enough time to read, nothing that might trigger seizures. Understandable: readable text, predictable behaviour, help avoiding and correcting errors. Robust: compatibility with present and future tools, properly nested elements, a name, role and value for non-standard components.

## The usual suspects

The common failures are a checklist you can run against your own app tonight: missing alt text (he cites WebAIM's finding that 31.3% of home page banners lacked it), poor colour contrast, a heading hierarchy that jumps around and confuses screen reader navigation, missing ARIA attributes, form inputs without labels, pages you can't drive from a keyboard, and layouts that fall apart on mobile.

## Does automation replace manual testing?

No, and he is clear about it. Taslan A. Graham said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "It is important, though, to note that automated accessibility testing is not a replacement for manual test, but it should be used in conjunction with manual testing for a more holistic testing experience." Automation is for the tedious, common issues (ARIA attributes, alt text, contrast, landmark labels, page titles); humans catch the rest.

## The setup, step by step

The demo starts from a small website with deliberate problems. He installs `@axe-core/playwright`, the package that makes the axe-core engine available inside Playwright, then runs `npm init playwright@latest` (JavaScript, default test folder, no GitHub Action, browsers installed later in CI). The generated `playwright.config.js` gets switched to ESM, the HTML reporter is kept, and the default projects run the tests on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.

The test itself is short. Navigate to the home page, create an `AxeBuilder` with the current page, call `analyze()`, and expect the violations to be an empty array. `npx playwright test` prints the issues and opens the HTML report. Each violation carries a description, a rule ID you can look up in the axe-core rule list, an impact level and a help URL. The contrast finding shows the foreground and background colours, the required 4.5:1 ratio the page falls short of, and the exact anchor element that failed. A missing `<title>` comes back with an impact of serious.

## From local test to a PR check

The last step is a GitHub Actions workflow triggered on pull requests: Ubuntu, Node 18, install dependencies, start the server, run the tests. Push it, and the accessibility report shows up on the PR with the same rule IDs, impact levels, offending HTML and help links. Once the backlog of issues is fixed, he suggests making the check required so nothing merges with new violations. That bit isn't demoed, but it is one checkbox in the repository settings.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers who know they should test accessibility and haven't started, and teams already on Playwright who can add this in an afternoon. It is a beginner-friendly talk: the first half is the why and the WCAG basics, the second half is the code.

Title: JSX is the scene file the web never had
Description: Steven Schkolne (MightyMeld) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on why browser dev tools show the DOM, not your code, and how a JSX-aware tool closes the gap
Body:
Game developers in Unity drag a button onto a screen, wire its click handler to real C# code and pause the running game to inspect it. Web developers open Chrome DevTools and stare at a DOM that looks less like their code every year. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Steven Schkolne, founder of MightyMeld, asks why, and argues that JSX finally gives the web what Unity, Interface Builder and Flash always had: a visual part of the code that a tool can safely edit. The second half demos MightyMeld, his product built on that idea.

## Why don't we have this already?

Schkolne gives the history three answers. The first is the one every old-timer offers: we tried it, it was called Dreamweaver. He pushes back on the folklore. Steven Schkolne said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "Dreamweaver actually didn't fail. It was a really successful product in terms of as maybe the first no code tool". What it never managed was the round trip. The more you worked visually, the messier the code got, and hand-written JavaScript confused it, so the back-and-forth between design and code fell apart. Its descendants (Wix, Squarespace, Webflow) are great for people who don't code and still don't go the other direction.

The second answer: we had it, it was Flash. Flash really did unify visuals and code, but it took a shortcut, a single box on the page where everything lived, much like a canvas today. It never made the jump to the open, dynamically loaded document model of the web, and it didn't survive mobile.

## Every good visual tool has a scene file

The third answer is the heart of the talk. Unity has `.unity` files, Interface Builder has `.xib`, Flash had `.fla`: files that hold layout and geometry separate from behaviour, inside environments owned by one company. The web has neither a scene file nor an owner. Early HTML was close to one, which is why Dreamweaver worked on plain pages. Then CSS and JavaScript tangled visuals with function, and MVC template layers were too shallow to help. JSX, about ten years old at the time of the talk, is his candidate: a clean separation between what appears on screen and what doesn't, bundled into components. In his words, "the time is right for web devtools to start to understand your code and allow you to work visually with it."

## What does a code-aware dev tool look like?

The demo is a React app built with Chakra UI, with the MightyMeld runtime added as a Vite plugin and a config file holding the dev server command. `npx mightymeld` opens the app in an iframe inside MightyMeld Studio. In edit mode, clicking an element shows the JSX that drives it rather than the DOM: a `NavLink` inside a `map` is one node in the tree and four things on screen. Props show up and can be edited. From there he renames text, duplicates and deletes elements, drags one above a title, tweaks a gap, drops in a JSX snippet as a building block, and tries an AI prompt to make a background green. Each change lands as a small, targeted edit in the source on disk, which you can commit from the tool or from your usual git setup. He contrasts that with the big blobs of generated code older design-to-code tools produced.

## How the pieces talk

Three components make it work across Next.js, Vite and other setups without dictating how you run your app. The Envoy runs locally beside the app: it starts your dev server with your own command, instruments the build so DOM nodes know where they came from in code, and injects a browser API. The Scribe receives the front-end code you include in the config and builds representations of components, JSX and styles. The Studio combines the two: the browser API says what you clicked, the Scribe says what code that is. An edit goes Studio to Scribe, which computes the new code, sends it to the Envoy and hot reload refreshes the app. Git operations travel the same path, since the Envoy sits on the local disk.

His closing twist: hot module reloading means the web can beat Unity here, since Unity, at least when he used it, couldn't edit on the fly.

## Who should watch

React developers who spend their days mapping DOM nodes back to components, and anyone who remembers Dreamweaver and wants a fair account of why it stalled. It is a founder demoing his own product, but the history and the scene-file argument stand on their own.

Title: A video is just 30 screenshots a second, so React can edit one
Description: Alfonso Graziano (NearForm) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on building a JSON-driven video render engine with Remotion, and rendering it at scale on AWS Lambda
Body:
If a video is a sequence of images plus an audio track, then a browser viewport screenshotted 30 times a second is a video waiting to happen. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Alfonso Graziano, senior software developer at NearForm, shows how Remotion turns React components into MP4s, builds a small render engine driven by a JSON timeline on top of it, and pushes the rendering out to AWS Lambda.

He opens as a sceptic. Alfonso Graziano said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "The first time I heard someone saying, hey, you know you can create a video with react, my reaction was like, what is this useful?" The rest of the talk is his answer.

## How does Remotion actually make a video?

The pipeline is refreshingly unmagical. You write the video as React code. Puppeteer screenshots the viewport frame by frame, and FFmpeg stitches the frames together and lays the audio on top. Around that core, Remotion ships the library with its abstractions (compositions, sequences, audio and video components), a Player component that previews a video live without rendering it, Remotion Studio for scrubbing a timeline and tweaking props, and Remotion Lambda for rendering in the cloud. Getting started is `npm init video`.

The use cases he lists are the ones that make the idea click: parameterised videos where only a few inputs change, automated workflows (a GitHub Action renders a clip and posts it to Slack or YouTube), and video SaaS products built on top, such as trimming or subtitling tools.

## A timeline is just a JavaScript object

The interesting design choice is not using Remotion directly. Graziano adds a layer: a video editor (out of scope for the talk) produces a JSON video description, and a render engine built on Remotion turns that description into a video. The JSON looks like what anyone who has opened DaVinci Resolve or Adobe Premiere Pro would expect: project settings such as FPS and name, then a timeline holding multiple video and audio tracks, each holding assets.

In code, the composition renders a timeline component that loops over the tracks. Each track becomes a Remotion sequence, and each asset gets its own sequence with a start frame and a duration in frames. Audio tracks hold audio; video tracks can hold video, images, text and even a CSS container for your own styles. The whole description is validated by a Zod schema, which pays off in Remotion Studio: the props panel becomes a form. His example is a social media manager who types in the score and the scorer's name after each goal, clicks render and has a clip ready to post. The demo is a birthday video with animated text, an image slideshow and a fade, and the project is on GitHub as alfonsograziano/create-videos-with-react-talk.

## What about rendering thousands of videos?

Two options. Render locally, meaning on any machine you own or rent, and at volume that becomes a pool of workers pulling jobs with autoscaling. Or render on Lambda, which he clearly prefers: cheap, parallel enough to render a long video in minutes, and quick to set up: "If you have an AWS account, it just takes five minutes, more or less." The catch, per the docs at the time, is that Lambda only renders videos under 30 minutes, so his pattern is Lambda by default with a fallback to a local machine for long ones.

The Lambda demo is a short script: load the deployed function's name, call `renderMediaOnLambda` with the props (the same video, with Goku swapped in for SpongeBob), then poll the render ID in a loop until the render finishes, printing progress along the way, and then show the S3 URL of the finished file.

## Who should watch

React and Node.js developers who have ever been asked to produce the same video with different names on it a few hundred times, and anyone curious how far a component model stretches. It is an introductory, demo-led talk; the value is in seeing the JSON-to-timeline layer, which is the part you would build for a real product.

Title: Your ISR cache will happily serve tenant A's page to tenant B
Description: Guilherme Dalla Rosa (MerCloud) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on moving a B2B storefront from one stack per customer to one multi-tenant Next.js app
Body:
Multi-tenancy in Next.js is easy right up to the moment your cache serves one customer's prices to another. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Guilherme Dalla Rosa, co-founder and CTO of MerCloud, explains how his team collapsed a B2B e-commerce storefront from one AWS stack per customer into a single Next.js app on Vercel, and the routing trick that keeps incremental static regeneration from mixing tenants.

## Why B2B storefronts are their own beast

MerCloud sells a B2B e-commerce platform to manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers and importers. That is a different shape from the shop where you buy one television and never come back: customer-specific pricing by tier or region, product-dependent tax rates, bulk orders and multi-layered approval chains, all for buyers who restock every week.

The MVP was a plain React app on AWS: Fargate behind a load balancer, a CDN in front, static assets and product images on S3. It worked well enough to onboard the first customers. The catch was that every tenant got its own copy of the whole stack, each sized for that customer's demand. Costs grew with every signature, onboarding meant deploying and configuring a new stack, deployments crawled because there were so many stacks to update and invalidate, monitoring was painful and performance was poor.

## One app, many domains

The rebuild went multi-tenant: one instance serving every customer, with data isolation chosen per need (fully isolated, fully shared or a hybrid, driven by tenant requirements like GDPR as much as by MerCloud's own). The stack became Next.js for the React expertise the team already had, deployed on Vercel for the edge network, preview deployments per branch and a serverless-first model where idle nights and weekends cost nothing. The existing API stayed on AWS.

The usual SaaS move, parsing the tenant from a subdomain, didn't fit. MerCloud's customers expose the storefront to their own buyers on their own domains, sometimes several domains per tenant. So there is a mapping table of domain to tenant. When a tenant adds a custom domain in the admin app, a routine registers it through the Vercel Domains API, and the tenant proves ownership with a DNS entry.

At request time, Next.js middleware running at the edge reads the host header, asks a global tenant API for the match and injects the tenant into a request header. Fetching from middleware adds latency to every response, so his advice is to cache that lookup in an edge key-value store and only hit the real API on a miss.

## How does ISR leak data between tenants?

This is the part worth the half hour. Incremental static regeneration caches a rendered page per URL with a TTL; after expiry the stale page is served while a fresh one renders in the background. Now put two tenants on the same path. User one from tenant A triggers the regeneration, user two from tenant B requests the same URL, and, as Guilherme Dalla Rosa said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "The answer here is user two will be served the version of the page that was generated for user one that belongs to tenant a, a different tenant."

The fix is to make every route tenant-aware: a dynamic segment for the tenant at the very root of the router, so each tenant's pages are cached under their own path. That puts the tenant ID in the URL, which nobody wants on a custom domain, so a rewrite in the Next.js config adds the segment internally while the browser keeps showing the clean URL. It is the same answer the long-running Next.js GitHub discussion eventually landed on, and the Vercel Platforms Starter Kit, which arrived after MerCloud had shipped, does domain-based routing, middleware rewrites and the Domains API in nearly the same way. MerCloud does its rewrites in the config rather than middleware because the first version was built on Next.js 10, before middleware existed.

The demo shows it working with two local domains pointing at localhost, each tenant getting its own cached page with a 60-second TTL. The template is public on GitHub as guidr/nextjs-multi-tenant.

## What changed, and what he'd tell you

The outcomes are qualitative, with no benchmark numbers: lower latency from the edge, no infrastructure to babysit, faster feature delivery, and tenant onboarding reduced to adding a record in the admin system. The lessons are sharper. Be careful with server-side rendering, since anything re-executed on every request is hard to cache. Make observability tenant-aware with consumption metrics, so when one tenant is under a DDoS you can find the noisy neighbour fast. And the classic, in his words: "don't do early optimization. You probably get it wrong and you have to redo it later."

## Who should watch

Anyone building SaaS on Next.js that serves customers on their own domains, and anyone about to turn on ISR in an app where two users can see different data at the same URL. It is a practical architecture story with a small demo, not a full treatment of data isolation.

Title: Building Battleship with React, Socket.IO and an anti-cheat idea
Description: Andrey Makarov (Islamic Coin) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on building a Battleship game with React, Node.js and Socket.IO, AI opponent included
Body:
Battleship is a distributed systems problem in disguise: two players, hidden state, and a referee who must not leak it. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Andrey Makarov, Lead Software Engineer at Islamic Coin, builds the game in React with a Node.js and Socket.IO backend, shared game logic in between and an AI opponent on the server. It is a weekend-project talk with a clear goal. Andrey Makarov said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "purpose of this video is to inspire you to create your own games."

## The rules, as code

Each player has a 10 by 10 board. Ships go horizontally or vertically and must not touch, and the fleet is the variant he settled on: one carrier of five cells, two battleships of four, three cruisers of three and four destroyers of two. Hit a ship and you shoot again; miss and the turn passes.

The interesting design choice is the flow. A player's shot goes to the server, the server asks the opponent what is at that position, the opponent answers with the result and its new board state, and the server caches it and returns the result to the shooter. Neither client ever holds the other's board. Cells are unknown, missed, killed or filled, and an opponent's filled cells are reported back as unknown.

## Shared logic, three folders

The repo has client, server and a shared folder used by both sides (he admits a proper package would be cleaner, but this is a demo). The shared code does the heavy lifting:

- **Board generation.** For each ship, find every legal position, pick one at random, place it and mark its surroundings as missed so the next ship can't touch it. Once every ship is placed, clear those markers.
- **Firing.** A miss on an unknown cell marks it missed. A hit checks the neighbours in every direction; if the whole ship is down, the cells around it become missed automatically.
- **Sunken ships.** Scan the board for killed cells, follow each ship to its ends and confirm it is surrounded by misses, then sort from biggest to smallest.
- **Game over.** Check whether any filled cells remain.

## An AI that finishes what it starts

The server-side AI generates its own random board on a new game. On its turn it looks for wrecked ships, ones hit but not sunk, and fires next to them; otherwise it picks a random unknown cell. A game class caches both boards and switches the active player, and Socket.IO handlers cover new game against the AI, fire, and the catch event for answering an opponent's shot. He notes the class could later get observers so third parties can watch a match.

On the React side there are four scenes: setup (generate a board until you like it, then press ready), the game itself (your board and the opponent's side by side), and win and lose screens. In the live run the colours are off, the AI sinks one of his ships, and he wins anyway.

## What is missing, by his own account

Makarov is clear that many aspects aren't covered, real player-against-player multiplayer first among them. His two improvement ideas are the best part of the talk:

- **Stop cheating with a hash.** Each client hashes its board at generation (he suggests MD5 is enough here) and sends it to the backend, which stores both hashes; at the end of the game, a hash that doesn't match the final board exposes a player who moved ships mid-game.
- **A statistical AI.** After enough games, compute where players most often place ships and start shooting there.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers who want a small, complete Socket.IO project to learn from, and anyone who agrees with his point that react can be used not only for forms. Experienced game developers will find nothing new; it's a friendly build-along.

Title: React Server Components send objects, not HTML, and here is the proof
Description: Tejas Kumar at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on building React Server Components from scratch to show how they work
Body:
The most common thing people get wrong about React Server Components is what goes over the wire. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Tejas Kumar, a developer relations consultant, builds server components from scratch on Express and Vite, following Dan Abramov's RSC-from-scratch guide, to show that the server sends serialised React elements, then explains how to get a codebase ready for them.

Tejas Kumar said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "A lot of people say they send HTML to the client. They don't do that." The rest of the talk earns that line.

## React has always been an architecture

Kumar starts with history. React ten years ago meant JSX, view as a function of state, one-way flux data flow and a pile of hand-written webpack and Babel config. Today it is a Vite one-liner and the tooling is invisible. Server components, he argues, put us back in the some-assembly-required era: an architecture built on next-generation tooling that was still experimental and not production ready when he gave the talk, which brings the server in at every level of the tree. A single card or blog post can be a server component while its parent stays a client one, so bulky dependencies like a date formatter or a Markdown parser never ship to the browser.

## Building it, one error at a time

The demo app is a dog breed site with a rotating dog, a name field and full page reloads that wipe both. The build goes in steps, and each failure teaches something:

1. **Add a server.** Express, a dynamic import per path, renderToString of the layout. Now there is HTML, but with holes where the data should be.
2. **Make components async.** Delete the useState and useEffect plumbing and just await fetch inside the component. React crashes: objects are not valid as a React child, found a Promise.
3. **Turn JSX into a client object.** A recursive function handles null, strings, numbers, booleans and arrays; for objects it checks $$typeof against Symbol.for('react.element'). If the element's type is a string like div, it processes the props; if it is a function, it calls the component, awaits it and recurses into whatever it returned. The output is one big plain object tree. Render that to HTML on the server and the pages finally have data.
4. **Hydrate on the client.** Inline the tree into the page as a script so there is no extra network waterfall, then hydrate. It breaks worse, because symbols don't survive JSON.stringify. A replacer swaps the element symbol for a placeholder string on the server, and a reviver passed to JSON.parse swaps it back on the client.
5. **Client-side navigation.** Intercept link clicks, push history state, fetch the next page with a jsx=true query parameter that returns just the serialised tree, and call root.render with it. The typed name survives, the background colour fades instead of flashing, and the dog never stops spinning.

That is the whole mechanism: a JSX tree becomes an object, gets serialised, crosses the network and React picks it up on the other side. Kumar also widens the meaning of client: anything that consumes the server component output, including React on the server producing HTML.

## Should everything be a server component?

No. "Client components have their place, server components have their place," he says, and the job is to weave them together. His three tips for getting ready:

- **Fetch data early**, as high up as possible and before any state is set, ideally at the server level.
- **Move interaction boundaries down.** A card with a title, body and button is usually one file, but the onClick handler can't be serialised, so the button must be its own component. Keep interactive pieces in granular modules of their own.
- **Replace context with server-side cache.** React context is shared across clients on the server, so per-user data like preferences belongs in a cache namespaced by user.

He ends on the community itself, asking for kinder discourse after watching people like Dan Abramov burn out.

## Who should watch

React developers who use Next.js App Router and want to know what it is doing under the hood, and anyone who has nodded along to an RSC explanation without quite following it. It's a long one, mostly live coding; the from-scratch build is the payoff.

Title: A Node.js service that asks OpenAI for your next workout as JSON
Description: Anton Kalik (Amenitiz) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on a Node.js and Express service that turns user indicators into OpenAI workout suggestions
Body:
The interesting part of an LLM feature is rarely the API call; it is the contract you force the model to keep. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Anton Kalik, Senior Software Engineer at Amenitiz, builds a sports activity service in Node.js and Express that sends a user's indicators and last workout to OpenAI and gets back a structured JSON plan the client app can render. The prompt does most of the work, and the talk shows exactly how it is set up.

## What does the service do?

The loop is simple. A user has indicators (age, weight, height, lifestyle) and a history of activities. When the client asks for a suggestion, the service reads the indicators and the last activity, builds a prompt, calls OpenAI and returns a new activity with a plan. Accomplish it, ask again, and the next suggestion takes the last one into account. A timer on the client decides the cadence: daily, weekly or monthly.

To keep the model from inventing sports, Kalik gives it a fixed list of activity types and asks it to choose one that fits the indicators and the last session.

## The stack

Nothing exotic, which is the point:

- **Express** for routing and controllers, scaffolded with a Node.js app generator.
- **Postgres** with migrations for three tables: users (name, username, email), indicators (one row per user) and activities (type, duration, user, timestamp).
- A small base model class that the user, indicator and activity models extend, so controllers reuse find-by-user-id and update-by-user-id methods.
- **Redis** for sessions and **JWT** middleware, so Postman calls carry a bearer token after sign-up.
- The official **openai** npm package, version 4 at the time, configured with an API key from an environment file.

There are three routes that matter: auth, GET suggest and an endpoint to update indicators when your weight or lifestyle changes.

## The prompt is the API

The system prompt tells the model it must return JSON and spells out every field: activity type (from the sorted list of allowed activities), duration in minutes, a description, how much water to drink in millilitres, an explanation of why this activity, and a plan array covering how to start, continue and finish. The user message carries the indicators and, if one exists, the last activity.

One of his sample responses suggests 45 minutes of cycling, with an explanation tied to the previous session. Another proposes skiing after a CrossFit day, which prompts the obvious question he asks himself: what if it is summer where the user lives? His answer is that the suggestions are only as good as the prompt, so add region or weather to the context if you need it.

He also explains the request knobs in plain terms. Messages carry roles: system for instructions about how to behave, user for the person, assistant for the model's own replies. Anton Kalik said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "Messages are like the back and forth text between you and the AI." Temperature controls how surprising replies are, and he runs at 0.9 for variety; lower values give more predictable output. The model is GPT-3.5 Turbo, which he picks as the cheaper and stable option. Max tokens caps how long the response can be.

## The honest shortcut

The demo inserts the suggested activity into the history as soon as it is generated, as if the user had done it. Kalik flags that this is a presentation shortcut: a real app should record only accomplished activities, ideally confirmed from something like a watch, so the next suggestion is based on what actually happened.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers wiring an LLM into an ordinary CRUD backend for the first time, who want a concrete example of structured output prompts, roles and temperature in a working Express app. If you already validate model output against a schema and retry on failure, you will be ahead of the talk; it doesn't cover validating the JSON that comes back.
