Title: Take authorization out of your Node.js code and into a policy engine
Description: Gabriel Liechtman Manor (Permit.io) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on moving Node.js authorization out of middleware into policy as code with Cedar and OPAL
Body:
Your passport proves who you are once per trip; your boarding pass gets checked at every door. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Gabriel Liechtman Manor, Director of Growth and DevRel at Permit.io, uses that pair to separate authentication from authorization, then argues that authorization belongs in a dedicated, declarative service rather than in if statements and Express middleware. The demo runs AWS's Cedar policy language behind OPAL, the open-source policy administration layer his team maintains.

## Why is authorization still hand-rolled?

Authentication got easy. OAuth decoupled the auth server from applications, JWTs made tokens verifiable without a round trip, and a SaaS provider gives you MFA, social login, session management and the rest in a few lines of code. Authorization didn't get the same treatment, so most teams still write it themselves.

Manor walks through the usual evolution. First, `if (user.role === 'admin')` inside the handler. Then a rolesRequired middleware, cleaner but only as granular as a role. Then a permissionsRequired middleware next to it. Then the requirement that doesn't fit, such as checking a user's paid tier from another service halfway through the business logic. Add a staging environment where admin should behave like production's superadmin, a Python data app that needs the same rules, and an auditor asking why a decision was made, and the code gets dirtier with every sprint.

His wish list for an authorization service: declarative, generic across permission models, unified in one place, agnostic of language, decoupled from application code, and easy to audit.

## Five steps: model, author, analyze, enforce, audit

**Model.** Every decision has three parts: a principal, an action and a resource. Manor's version: "Is a monkey allowed to eat a banana?" The application only enforces; a separate service decides. Enforcement shows up at three levels: feature toggles in the UI or gateway, true-or-false checks in the application logic, and data filtering at the database.

Then pick a model. ACL he calls end of life: fine for firewalls, hard to scale for apps. RBAC is easy to define, use and audit, but it stops at the resource type, so a rule like only the owner may edit this document is out of reach. ABAC decides on attributes of users and resources and is the most granular, though configuration can get hard. ReBAC derives permissions from relationships, like Google Drive's account, folder, document chain, and suits consumer-scale apps.

**Author.** Policy languages, which he describes as more configuration than programming: Open Policy Agent's Rego, AWS's open-source Cedar, and OpenFGA for Zanzibar-style ReBAC. A Cedar rule reads like the model itself, a permit with principal, action and resource, plus a when clause such as the principal being one of the resource's editors.

**Analyze, enforce, audit.** A Cedar agent runs as a sidecar and answers is_authorized calls over HTTP. On the frontend, he points to CASL for feature toggling.

## The demo that changes a rule without a deploy

OPAL ties it together with one Docker Compose file: an OPAL server watching a Git repository of policies plus an external data source (mocked with Nginx, standing in for something like a CRM), and an OPAL client wrapping the Cedar agent next to the app. The Node.js blog API has one middleware that always does the same thing: send principal, action and resource to the agent.

Admins can do anything, plain users only GET, writers can POST and PUT. Then he tightens the rule so writers can publish only with more than 1,000 karma, commits it, and OPAL pushes the new policy to the agent. The 800-karma writer gets access denied; the senior writer creates the article. Gabriel Liechtman Manor said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "I haven't changed any kind of user data or any kind of application code". A Python app consumes the same service to make the point about language agnosticism.

Permit.io, the commercial layer on top of OPAL with a policy UI, gets a short mention; he says plainly that OPAL is enough to start.

## Who should watch

Backend developers whose Express routes are sprouting permission middleware, and anyone about to add a second service that needs the same rules. The talk is strongest on modelling; the demo shows the policy-as-code loop working in minutes.

Title: The Node.js event loop, told as a fairy tale with dragons
Description: Lorenzo Pieri (Birdie) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on the Node.js event loop as a fairy tale, and why four phases are all you need to reason about
Body:
Somewhere in a server far, far away, the Blocking Dragons roam. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Lorenzo Pieri, a full-stack engineer at Birdie (his own title is full stack wizard), explains the Node.js event loop as a fairy tale, then drops the metaphor and boils the loop down to the handful of phases you actually need to reason about. It is billed as an introductory talk, and it is a good first one.

## Once upon a time, threads

The story starts with the Knights of the Thread, who came from kingdoms such as Javadom and Pythonville to fight the dragons that block your code. Each kingdom had its own magic: POSIX threads in one kingdom, the NIO order in Javadom, a scroll called asyncio in Pythonville. Then word spread of the Lands of Promise (the pun is intended), where nothing blocks, because everything works out eventually. Pieri flags *eventually* as the important word.

The Lands of Promise have one rule above all, which Lorenzo Pieri said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 as "you shall not block the thread". The main thread is a single-thread castle at the centre of the land, home to Sir Call Stack, valiant knight of asynchrony who sorts every task into its queue, and the fairy who runs the event loop.

## Where does the heavy work go?

The loop is the heart of each village, the market square where tasks meet and do their synchronous business. A task carrying something heavy knows it can't just stand in the square and block it. It leaves through the Desert of Asynchrony to the Forest of libuv, where elves of the thread pool spawn threads (a limited number of them) to do the heavy work. With their callbacks done, tasks walk back to town and rejoin the queue, and Sir Call Stack applies their results.

The moral, aimed at anyone writing Node.js services: don't fear the dragons, but never underestimate them. One careless synchronous call in the wrong place and the whole village waits.

## The real phases, then the useful ones

Then the fairy tale gives way to the docs. The loop has six phases:

- **Timers**: callbacks from setTimeout and setInterval whose time has come.
- **Pending callbacks**: I/O callbacks deferred from the previous cycle.
- **Idle, prepare**: internal housekeeping only.
- **Poll**: retrieve new I/O events and run their callbacks. This is where the loop spends most of its time, waiting when there is nothing to do.
- **Check**: setImmediate callbacks.
- **Close callbacks**: for example a socket closed abruptly.

His practical advice is to ignore two of them. Idle and prepare are internal, and by the time close callbacks matter you are on your way out of the program. That leaves timers, callbacks, poll and check, and the picture he wants you to keep is not a neat circle but a back-and-forth: after each phase, process.nextTick callbacks and promise microtasks run before the loop moves on. Know which phase you are in, and you can predict ordering.

He skips the heap and call-stack diagrams on purpose. Picture a tavern: the heap is where the mead is stored, the call stack is the people at the bar, the calls are the orders. As long as everyone gets the mead they ordered, nobody cares about the cellar.

## The quiz

The talk closes with an exercise: setTimeout with zero delay, setInterval, process.nextTick, setImmediate and console.log are queued in a script. Which runs first? The boring one, console.log, because, in Pieri's words, "console log is a synchronous operation which never gets inside the loop whatsoever". Work out the order of the other four yourself; that is the point of the exercise.

## Who should watch

Juniors who have been told not to block the event loop and would like to know what that means, and anyone who has to explain it to them. Seniors will find no new facts, but they may steal the tavern analogy. The simplification is deliberate: the thread-pool story stands in for all async work, which is a fine mental model for a first pass.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Allon Mureinik on [preventing DoS attacks in your Node.js application](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Allon_Mureinik_4_dosattacks_nodejs_prevention) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024, where the event loop is the target.
- Muhammad Yasir Rafique on [taming memory leaks in Node.js](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Muhammad_Yasir_Rafique_42_memoryleaks_nodejs_diagnostics).
- Shai Almog on [debugging Node.js applications in production](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Shai_Almog_Debug_NodeJS_Lightrun) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.

Title: What Multiplayer learned adding real-time collaboration with Yjs
Description: Vladi Stevanovic (Multiplayer) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on building real-time collaboration with CRDTs and Yjs, and the four lessons it taught
Body:
Everyone has a folder with design_final_aj.psd and final_aj+tj_design.psd in it. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Vladi Stevanovic, Director of Community at Multiplayer, explains how the company built Figma-style real-time collaboration into its product with CRDTs and the open-source Yjs library, behind a central collaboration service, and the four things that turned out harder than the docs suggest.

Multiplayer, Stevanovic clarifies early, is not an MMORPG. It is a collaborative SaaS platform for teams designing and managing distributed systems, which is why collaboration was a core requirement rather than a feature request.

## What counts as real-time collaborative?

Vladi Stevanovic said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "Real time collaboration is now table stakes". The working definition has four parts: real-time updates that reach every user as near instantly as the network allows, live playback down to each collaborator's cursor, presence and status so you can see who is around, and data integrity, so concurrent changes never silently lose work. That last one is both a UX and a backend problem.

## Why not just broadcast over WebSockets?

The first idea is to take your REST API and broadcast every request and response to all connected clients. That works until two people change the same thing at once, at which point you get the classic symptom: words in the wrong order, characters in odd places. Merging conflicting changes sensibly requires the context of the data and the state of the client making the change, not just the new value.

Two families of technology solve this: operational transformation (what Google Docs uses, which may be too complex for a startup that wants to ship) and conflict-free replicated data types. "You could still use websockets, but it's just a lot more work and time," Stevanovic adds.

CRDTs give strong eventual consistency: even when clients drift because of a flaky connection or high latency, every replica ends up in the same state. Multiplayer chose Yjs because its docs, maps and arrays map onto ordinary JavaScript types, so the app needed no radical refactor. It also brings a big set of ready integrations (code editors, whiteboards, rich text), painless client reconnects, network agnosticism and awareness features out of the box.

## A central peer, on purpose

CRDTs can run peer to peer, but Multiplayer put a central peer in the middle: a collaboration service that serves the latest document to a joining client, shares edits across connected clients and saves snapshots. A directory service cluster decides where sessions run, tracks them and can move them, and collaboration services are deployed close to users to keep latency down. The talk is upfront about the cost: more CPU and memory on the server, and harder scaling, because the central peer must sit near its clients.

Not everything goes through Yjs either. Presence (avatar stacks) uses plain WebSockets because it spans multiple documents at project level. Comments have one owner and aren't temporary, so they are REST calls plus WebSocket notifications. Yjs is reserved for state that needs conflict resolution or temporary state belonging to the document: live updates, co-editing, undo and redo.

## Four lessons from production

1. **Order isn't free.** Yjs arrays don't maintain element order without some work. An integer order field means renumbering everything after each insert, which doesn't scale on long lists. Multiplayer used fractional indexing, the approach Figma uses, backed by an arbitrary-precision library, because JavaScript's built-in number type runs out of precision after enough inserts in the same spot.
2. **Architecture follows the business.** Snapshotting and keeping data in specific locations for security requirements such as GDPR needed the central service. If you need offline mode, peer to peer fits better.
3. **Scope the collaboration.** Multiplayer has branches and filtered views of documents, so cursors and avatars only show people on the same document, in the same branch, at the same time. Showing everyone everywhere would only confuse.
4. **Yjs won't wire dependent views for you.** Rename a component in one view and every document referencing it must update without a refresh, so the team built that propagation by listening for changes on the Yjs documents.

The closing advice: don't reinvent the wheel (Liveblocks gets a mention as a hosted option), and design for collaboration from the start, since bolting it on later is messier, though still far less work with Yjs than with raw WebSockets.

## Who should watch

Developers about to add live presence and co-editing to a Node.js app and wondering whether WebSockets alone will cut it. Expect architecture and lessons rather than a code walkthrough.

Title: Conf42 Incident Management 2023: runbooks, LLMs and people who stop being heroes
Description: The Conf42 Incident Management 2023 roundup - 10 talks on AI for runbooks and training, observability for LLM features, red teaming and on-call culture.
Body:
[Conf42 Incident Management 2023](https://www.conf42.com/im2023) went out on October 19 with 10 talks, and it landed right as generative AI was arriving in every on-call toolchain. Half the lineup asked what LLMs can do for incident response (write runbooks, train responders, pick what to automate) and one asked the reverse: how do you run an LLM feature in production without it becoming the incident? The other half was about people: who causes incidents, what developers should do during a breach, and why the on-call hero is a pattern to retire.

Speakers came from Honeycomb, Chronosphere, Shoreline.io, Uptime Labs, Payoneer, SimilarWeb, Strong Crypto Innovations, Sportingtech, NuWorks Interactive Labs, edamama and We Hack Purple.

## Can generative AI fix the runbook?

[Anurag Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Anurag_Gupta_generative_ai_fix_runbooks) of Shoreline.io started from the complaint every on-call engineer has made: runbooks go stale, so teams escalate far more often than they should. His core problem with runbooks is that they don't actually run. Shoreline's answer is runbook automation that gathers diagnostics before a human touches the machine, with generative AI drafting and editing runbooks copilot-style, and fine-grained access control once those runbooks execute in a controlled environment.

[Joshua Arvin Lat and Sophie Soliven](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Joshua_Arvin_Lat_Sophie_Soliven_automation_strategies) of NuWorks Interactive Labs and edamama took the strategy view: automate only the parts of a process that yield significant benefits, lean on existing tools rather than building from scratch, and use AI for automated remediation, simulation and training.

Training was the focus for gold sponsor Uptime Labs. [Mahdi Jelodari](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Mahdi_Jelodari_it_training_generative_ai) showed the company's simulation platform, a gamified environment where engineers and managers practise incidents, people skills included, and how AI helps responders form better hypotheses, with the step-by-step reasoning on screen.

## How do you keep an LLM feature on call?

[Christine Yen](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Christine_Yen_sre_observability_building_llms) of Honeycomb turned the question around. Building on LLMs feels like magic; maintaining the probabilistic code behind it is like building on any black box, so treat it with the tools you already trust: instrumentation, observability and SLOs, early in development. Her evidence is Honeycomb's own Query Assistant, released in May 2023 after about six weeks of development then another eight weeks of iteration, with SLOs setting a baseline at release to show whether each change moved the needle. The techniques are tool-agnostic, which makes this one of the more durable AI talks of 2023.

## What does the attacker know that your tools don't?

Silver sponsor Strong Crypto Innovations sent [Christopher Haller](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Christopher_Haller_atomic_red_team_threat_actors), its offensive security practice lead, with a question for anyone paying for MDR: will your detections fire when it matters? He walked through the MITRE ATT&CK framework and Red Canary's Atomic Red Team project, which runs small, known attacker techniques so you can find the gaps between threat actor activity and what your tools detect. His numbers set the urgency: an average breakout time of 79 minutes and a 312% rise in attackers' use of remote monitoring and management tools.

[Tanya Janca](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Tanya_Janca_incident_response_developers) of We Hack Purple covered the developer's role in a security incident: five things the security team needs from you, including not breaking the chain of custody, following need-to-know, spotting an incident in progress and not trying to be a hero. Security incidents, she argued, are the most expensive way to deal with a vulnerability.

## Who causes incidents, and what do you learn from them?

[Paige Cruz](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Paige_Cruz_no_place_like_production) of Chronosphere told the day's best war story: three years on the pager before she caused her first production incident, with a logging improvement she had tested extensively locally. The retro walks the translation from Helm template to Kubernetes manifest, and the lesson is in the title. Some things only production can show you.

[Andre Carvalho](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Andre_Carvalho_insights_through_reports) of Sportingtech, an incident team lead, showed incident reports as a source of decisions: severity, MTTR, time to resolve and SLOs, visualised, then used for platform improvements and resource allocation. [Dor Amram](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Dor_Amram_rise_crisis_growth_improvement) of SimilarWeb, a silver sponsor, made the team-growth case: a learning culture, guilds, reading your own system documentation, and design reviews before implementation as a way to spot the next storm early.

## Retire the on-call hero

[Einat Mahat](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Einat_Mahat_oncall_heroes_effective_practices) of Payoneer, on call since 2012 and a mentor to on-call engineers since 2016, closed with the culture talk. Good leadership gives engineers ownership of their services from inception to production; great leadership builds an on-call culture that supports them, with sidekicks, shared war stories and a team that works like a league rather than a single caped engineer. The superhero metaphor runs the whole talk, and it works better than it should.

## Thanks to the sponsors

[StormForge](https://www.stormforge.io/), [Teleport](https://goteleport.com/) and [Uptime Labs](https://uptimelabs.io/) were the gold sponsors, [Similarweb](https://www.similarweb.com/) and [Strong Crypto Innovations](https://www.strongcrypto.com/) silver, and [Steadybit](https://steadybit.com/) the startup sponsor, with [unpack.tech](https://www.unpack.tech/) as newsletter partner and media partners including [JetBrains](https://www.jetbrains.com), [Manning](https://www.manning.com), [Packt](https://www.packtpub.com/), [Infosec Conferences](https://infosec-conferences.com) and [GDPRwise](https://gdprwise.eu/).

Every talk is on the [Conf42 Incident Management 2023 page](https://www.conf42.com/im2023) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrB44Zc1LD3Yrp1Uv2opzokS&si=9WZppv3SU0nwCQPJ). The series returned a year later as [Conf42 Incident Management 2024](https://www.conf42.com/im2024).

Title: From a Figma card to a live React app with AWS Amplify Studio
Description: Arundeep Nagaraj (AWS) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on turning Figma designs into data-bound React components with AWS Amplify Studio
Body:
Pixel pushing is a real job description, just not one anyone wants. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Arundeep Nagaraj, Solutions Architect Manager at AWS who leads the developer experience team for AWS Amplify, shows how Amplify Studio turns a Figma component into a reusable React component, binds it to a GraphQL-backed data model and ships it in a Next.js app. The demo builds a cat reviews app end to end.

This is a vendor talk about AWS's own tooling, and it is honest about being one: the second half is a screen-by-screen build.

## Why does design-to-code keep breaking?

Nagaraj describes the handoff most teams know. Designer hands off to frontend, frontend waits on backend, changes bounce back and forth, some designs turn out to be impossible, and the process spirals. Developers spend months nudging UI until it looks pixel perfect, and the other side isn't happy either: according to AWS's own analysis, "about 50% of the designers are not satisfied with the implementation." His summary: "So designers are not happy and developers are frustrated."

Amplify Studio's answer is to make the Figma file the source of the component code.

## What is in the Amplify box?

He splits Amplify into five parts:

- **Amplify libraries**, use-case-centric client libraries for cloud-powered web and mobile apps.
- **Amplify Studio**, a visual environment for the app backend that also syncs Figma designs.
- **Amplify CLI**, the same capabilities as a command-line toolchain.
- **Amplify UI**, an open-source design system of themeable, responsive, accessible React components: connected ones like the authenticator (sign up, sign in) and primitives like buttons, text fields and cards.
- **Amplify Hosting**, managed CI/CD and hosting.

## The cat reviews build

The demo follows a clear sequence, and it is the reason to watch.

1. Create the app in the AWS console under Amplify; while the backend provisions, scaffold a Next.js app with create-next-app (the default had just moved to Next.js 14).
2. Install the Amplify packages, chiefly the Amplify UI React package, and define a Reviews data model in Studio: name, description, an image, and a rating stored as a float, because a cat can score 4.7. Save and deploy, and Studio creates the GraphQL API on AWS AppSync without you writing a schema by hand.
3. Open the prebuilt Amplify Figma template, take its review card, delete the price (cats are priceless), add a favourite button, round the corners, then paste the Figma file URL into Studio and sync. The card comes back looking exactly as edited.
4. Bind the card's fields to the data model (image, name, description, rating) in a point-and-click panel, and tweak the generated create form: the description becomes a text area, the rating a stepper field.
5. Run amplify pull to bring the generated components into the local project, render the create form, then a collection of review cards.
6. Subscribe to onCreateReviews, an AppSync subscription over WebSockets, so a new review shows up in the feed in real time.

His closing claim is that a workflow that would have taken hours, days or months comes down to potentially less than an hour. The demo supports that for a CRUD-shaped app built on Amplify's own templates; how it holds up for a heavily custom design system is a question the talk doesn't test.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers who want a full-stack app on AWS without hand-wiring AppSync, auth and hosting, and teams already designing in Figma who want to see the sync loop working. If you need full control of the generated component code or are not on AWS, watch it as a reference for the design-to-code idea rather than a recipe.

- Luca Mezzalira on [hexagonal architecture with serverless](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Luca_Mezzalira_hexagonal_architecture_serverless) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.

Title: Building a Pi Network web3 app with a JavaScript front and any backend
Description: Cesar Cordero Rodriguez (LatinChain) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on building Pi Network apps with a JavaScript frontend and a Python or PHP backend
Body:
Most web3 tutorials start with MetaMask and Ethereum. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Cesar Cordero Rodriguez, co-founder representative at LatinChain and a senior Odoo technical consultant, starts somewhere else: Pi Network, its own Pi Browser, and the Pi API Platform. The takeaway is an architecture you already know. The frontend catches the payment request in JavaScript, the backend talks to the Pi platform in whatever language you like, and the answer travels back to the user.

It is a short, practical talk, essentially a guided tour of an open-source repository and the official docs, so set expectations accordingly.

## What is the Pi stack?

Three pieces, as he lays them out:

- **Pi Network**, a cryptocurrency based on Stellar that you mine from your phone daily. The talk's abstract puts the network at more than 45 million users.
- **Pi Browser**, which he describes as something like MetaMask, but specifically for Pi Network. It is where Pi apps run.
- **Pi API Platform**, the API you build Pi apps against.

His own project, LatinChain, is a Pi app where people play games daily using crypto, and it won the Pi Hackathon 2021. The code is public under the pi-apps organisation on GitHub, in Python, JavaScript and HTML.

## How does a payment flow work?

The heart of the talk is the request loop. The frontend, written in JavaScript or TypeScript, captures the user's request to pay. That request goes to your backend. The backend makes the call to the Pi API Platform, gets the response and returns it to the frontend, so the user gets an answer to what they asked for.

The point he keeps returning to is that the backend is your choice. LatinChain's production backend is Python on Odoo 14, with the models for the games and the Pi integration in the repository. The simpler first-app example in the repo's docs folder pairs client-side JavaScript with a PHP server script, precisely to show, as Cesar Cordero Rodriguez said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023, that "you can use any backend". The one thing you must keep in sync is the authentication setup: the same configuration on the client side and the server side, plus your app key from the Pi Browser developer portal.

He separates the two payment directions. User-to-app payments, where an end user pays your app, are covered by the LatinChain examples. App-to-user payments, where the app pays out, are in Pi's official documentation, with examples in Ruby, Node.js, Python, Go, Blazor and C#.

## The licence has a fence around it

One detail worth reading twice before you fork. LatinChain is open source, and you can build new apps on top of it, but only inside Pi Network: the licence does not let you take the system to a competing platform. If you are evaluating it as a starting point, check that the terms fit what you want to build.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers curious about Pi Network specifically, who want a working reference repo and a map of where the official docs live. If you were hoping for smart-contract internals, chain mechanics or a security review, this isn't that talk; it is a pointer to code and documentation, delivered quickly. The recording ends with a look at Pi apps running inside Pi Browser, LatinChain among them.

Title: A 100 KB library that stands in for your whole backend
Description: Daniele Fontani and Daniele Ciulli (Sintra Digital Business) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on Crudit, a multi-tenant REST API over MongoDB in one edge function
Body:
Some apps don't deserve a backend team. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Daniele Fontani (CTO) and Daniele Ciulli (Software Developer) of Sintra Digital Business presented Crudit, an open-source JavaScript library of roughly 100 KB that turns an Express handler in a serverless function into a multi-tenant REST API over MongoDB Atlas. The pitch: a frontend developer ships a working app without writing, hosting or operating a backend.

## Who is the modern stack too expensive for?

Fontani opens with an honest accounting of the architecture most of us now default to: a single-page app talking to a fleet of microservices, message queues, a relational store, a cache. He likes it. Best-of-breed tools, teams working in parallel, specialists doing what they do best.

The bill shows up elsewhere. You need several teams or competencies, a single person can no longer do the job, and when something breaks it starts in the backend and surfaces in the frontend, so finding it takes a while. The people who feel this most are low-budget projects, small companies and startups: the quick-and-dirty app that used to take a weekend now needs an org chart. Crudit is the Daniele pair's answer to whether a web app can still be built with ease. Fontani's goals for it: run in the free tiers of Azure, AWS or Vercel, stay easy to customise, and as he put it, "we want to avoid license fees".

## What does Crudit actually do?

Ciulli then walks through the features, one config object at a time.

- **CRUD with tenancy built in.** Mount Crudit on an Express app inside a Vercel edge function, give it a database connection, and every request becomes a REST call: POST creates, GET reads, PUT updates, DELETE deletes. Each user writes to their own MongoDB database, and the request path picks the collection. User Daniele posting to a path called prova lands in Daniele's database, in the prova collection, and nobody else can read it.
- **Custom endpoints.** Override a route with your own handler and a login-required flag. That is how you add login and registration, with whatever auth method you trust.
- **Server-side validation.** Scope rules to a database and collection by name or by regex (for example, only the admin users' databases), with the schema written in validator.js syntax. Bad data never reaches the collection.
- **Hooks on events.** Functions that fire on database events and can block the write. His example is a before-save hook that could call a third-party service to check a customer's billing details and throw an error back to the client if they fail; the demo logs who wrote what, and when, into a logs database.
- **Mutations.** Register a migration once, then apply it to a single database, to one database with every mutation not yet run, or to all databases at once. A flag decides whether one failing mutation stops the run. For a multi-tenant app, that last mode is how you change a document shape across your whole customer base.

The DevOps story is that there isn't one. Crudit runs in any Node.js-compatible runtime: Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure Functions, edge functions. Daniele Ciulli said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023: "You don't need to think about scaling, you don't need to think about dimensioning your server because it's all handled by the cloud."

## When should you not use it?

This is the most useful slide in the talk, and plenty of library authors skip it. Crudit is the wrong tool for apps built around media assets (no asset support yet), strongly relational data (it is document-only), heavy business logic, a hard split between business logic and data, or anyone who needs a back-office UI, which you would have to build yourself. It fits frontend-driven full-stack JavaScript apps, Node.js plus MongoDB projects, and exploratory or hobby projects where staying inside the free tiers brings the cost to zero.

The roadmap at the time: configuration imported from YAML and JSON (handy for bulk-editing mutations), media assets stored in a bucket without a custom endpoint, and, of course, more GitHub stars. The package installs with `npm i crudit`.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers who keep writing the same thin Express-plus-Mongo layer for side projects, and anyone building a small multi-tenant tool on a startup budget. If your data model has joins in it, the talk will tell you so itself.

Title: Six ways to split a frontend monolith, from iframe to Module Federation
Description: Aleksandr Guzenko (IT_ONE) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023 on when a frontend monolith stops paying off and which of six splitting methods fits
Body:
The iframe shipped in 1997 and it is still a legitimate way to split a frontend. At Conf42 JavaScript 2023, Aleksandr Guzenko, Tech Lead at IT_ONE, who leads development of a large banking application, lays out six ways to break a frontend monolith, from that old tag to Webpack 5 Module Federation, and closes with a plain table of when each one is the right call.

It is a compact talk, and a refreshingly unideological one: he starts by defending the monolith.

## Is the monolith actually the problem?

Guzenko frames it with the familiar cost-per-line curve. A monolith is cheap early, because everything lives in one place. Micro-architecture costs more up front, for the setup each independent piece needs, but its cost climbs slowly as the codebase grows. The monolith's cost curve bends sharply upward, because every change touches the whole system.

His conclusion is two sentences long: the monolith is not bad, and, as Aleksandr Guzenko said at Conf42 JavaScript 2023, "monolith is not bad until a certain point". Spotting that point is subjective, so he gives four triggers:

- Long builds and CI pipelines (his example: a pipeline that needs six hours).
- Rapidly increasing codebase complexity.
- A rising entry threshold, where only senior developers can be onboarded efficiently.
- More than five people on the project, which he admits is the softest one; he knows a 15-person monolith that works well.

## The six options, in order of age

**iframe.** The original frontend micro-service. Still the right answer for embedding a module, such as a map on a landing page, or composing a few simple apps, like an independent sidebar of links.

**Nginx or another proxy server.** Some pages are served as a separate bundle behind a proxy. He calls it the most controversial and non-obvious option: you reload the whole bundle on navigation, lose the single-page-app benefits and duplicate code. It earns its place during a framework migration, where old pages stay on the old app and new pages go to the new one until only one remains.

**Web Components.** Native component encapsulation of styles and logic, browser support and framework independence, so one component can live inside React, Angular or Vue apps. Why didn't it take over? Because people choose React and Angular for their APIs (hooks, context, decorators) and their ecosystems, not only for components. Good for a company-wide UI kit.

**npm packages.** The most common method and, in most cases, the best one. Split the app into packages first; you can turn those packages into micro-frontends later. The costs are real: debugging means rebuild, substitute and rerun the host just to see a console line, and releases go package-first, then version bump, then host deploy. The payoffs are easy implementation, versioning and faster pipelines, because the host no longer runs every package's tests.

**single-spa.** A container that registers applications, gives them lifecycle methods (load, mount, unmount) and maps URLs to apps. Pick it when you must combine apps written in different frameworks.

**Webpack 5 Module Federation.** Only on Webpack 5; on version 4 the plugin is not an option. Each app declares an entry point listing what it exports, which he likes as a public-API pattern, and shared libraries are cached so ten React apps don't load React ten times. Unlike single-spa, you can consume a single module from another app, say just its selectors, rather than the whole application.

## The decision table

His closing slides are the part to screenshot. Proxy server: you are mid-migration, don't want micro-frontends, and can sacrifice performance for a while. npm: you want a smaller codebase and don't want micro-frontends at all. single-spa: mixed frameworks, lifecycle control or URL-based routing between apps. Module Federation: you want to optimise the bundle and you are on Webpack 5.

## Who should watch

Frontend leads arguing about micro-frontends who need a shared vocabulary, and teams who suspect they need them but would be fine with a few npm packages. If you already run Module Federation in production, this is a refresher, not new ground.

Title: In a security incident, the developer's job is to not be the hero
Description: Tanya Janca (We Hack Purple) at Conf42 Incident Management 2023 on the five things developers must do, and not do, during a security incident
Body:
The most helpful thing a developer can do in a security incident is often the least heroic: call the security team, stay reachable, and touch nothing. At Conf42 Incident Management 2023, Tanya Janca, Founder and CEO of We Hack Purple and known online as SheHacksPurple, boiled her incident response training for IT staff down to five rules, each illustrated with a story from her years responding to incidents.

The stakes are set early. "Security incidents are the most expensive way to deal with a vulnerability," Tanya Janca said at Conf42 Incident Management 2023. She adds that it's also the most time-consuming, scary and humiliating way.

## Why train developers in incident response at all?

Janca used to do AppSec full time, and she watched well-meaning people break things, destroy evidence and make investigations much harder. So she and her colleagues trained the whole IT department: help desk, system administrators and developers, on what an incident looks like and when to call. Afterwards, she says, incidents cost less, went more smoothly, did less damage to the organisation's reputation, and relations with other teams improved.

She separates two terms. A security event is when something strange is happening and you suspect a problem, so it needs triage. A security incident is when you're certain something bad has happened or is happening. Finding your company's data for sale on the dark web is an incident, no triage needed.

## The five rules

1. **If you see something, tell the security team.** A manager once called her in a panic because his sensitive USB drives had vanished from a locked drawer. A secure courier had collected them while he was at lunch. She praised him for following the policy: "I'd rather a false positive anytime over a false negative." Her developer-specific example is an API that keeps crashing or slowing down for no clear reason, which could be a bot or a brute-force attack. Call security; they can usually tell you quickly whether it's a security problem.
2. **Don't leave without telling us.** During one incident a developer's app had cross-site scripting and was being actively exploited. She left to brief her bosses, came back 45 minutes later, and he had gone to catch his bus. He wasn't on call, nobody had his number, nobody else had permission to push a fix, and there was no WAF or CDN in front of the app. It was attacked all night while she watched, unable to stop it.
3. **It's an emergency, so treat it as top priority.** No regular team meetings, no lunch, no other deadline first. If your boss objects, send them to the security team.
4. **Follow need to know.** Don't tell anyone who doesn't need the details, your boss included. They may know you're working on an incident; anything more comes from the security team.
5. **Don't try to manage it yourself.** This one gets two stories.

## The concrete building with malware

She arrived late after a dentist appointment to find the C-level executives in a meeting room, panicking. A help desk worker had decided to run the incident himself and told them the company's second building was infected with malware. "That building is made of concrete. It does not have malware," she told them. The real cause: the building's head had banned watching the Winter Olympics, so 80 to 90% of the staff were streaming figure skating at their desks and the internet connection gave up. Because the executives had told their admins, the rumour ran for months, people wanted to evacuate, and it took her three days to get the incident back under control.

## Chain of custody is not a detail

The second story comes with a trigger warning and no graphic detail. At an office where her mentor once worked, a help desk technician investigating on his own came across images of child abuse, deleted material and only then called security. He had broken the chain of custody, so none of it counted as legal evidence and the offender went free. Four years later the technician was still in therapy. Incident responders accept that risk and know how to collect evidence, when not to look and when to call the police. Developers never agreed to carry that.

## Who should watch

Every developer, sysadmin and help desk engineer who might be first to notice something odd, and every security team that wants a ready-made briefing for them. It's an accessible talk, and the stories will stick long after the list fades.

Title: The best on-call leaders know when to tell engineers to stand down
Description: Einat Mahat (Payoneer) at Conf42 Incident Management 2023 on on-call routines, triage, lessons learned and leaders who protect engineers from burnout
Body:
Putting developers on call only works if leadership protects them from it as much as it hands it to them. At Conf42 Incident Management 2023, Einat Mahat, R&D Group Leader at Payoneer, laid out a full on-call playbook, from routine and expectations through triage and lessons learned to culture, and saved her sharpest point for the leaders: your job is to keep the pager from burning your team out.

Mahat has carried the pager since 2012 and mentored on-call engineers since 2016, and the talk is told as a superhero story, complete with an Uncle Ben quote about great power and great responsibility.

## What does a healthy on-call routine look like?

The sidekicks come first. Incident management systems such as ServiceNow and PagerDuty, dashboards, and APM tools such as Datadog and New Relic do the watching, but she ranks teammates as the most valuable sidekick: nobody should face an incident alone. Rotations are set per team, by sprint, weekly or otherwise, usually run by a team leader, and tracked in anything from a shared document to PagerDuty or Zenduty.

The expectation is simple: guard the system's health, and when summoned, by a person or an alert, respond and acknowledge. Her favourite rule of etiquette is about the human on the other end. "If it's a person calling you in the middle of the night, be nice. Trust that he's not doing that for fun," Einat Mahat said at Conf42 Incident Management 2023.

## Restore first, investigate later

Her on-call odyssey moves from proactive to reactive. The good on-call engineer watches dashboards and alerts and checks recent deployments before anything breaks; the great one scouts for trouble and fixes it before it escalates. When something does fire, the order is triage, then mitigation, with the root cause investigation held until later.

Triage starts with gathering the basic facts and getting help. If the problem is in your area, mitigate or resolve it; if not, find the right specialist and do a warm handover. Either way, you own the scene and stay until the incident is over. The primary goal is restoring service and minimising customer impact through a workaround, a rollback or a direct fix, and only then digging into why.

## What goes into a lessons-learned document?

After the dust settles, every incident gets a lessons-learned review, whether you call it a postmortem or an incident review. Her checklist: summary, detection, triage, mitigation, timeline, root cause analysis (the five whys work here), and action items with owners and ETAs. The prevention work that follows is where the value lands: runbooks and documentation for faster triage next time, tests and automations that replicate the incident scenario, and better metrics and alerts. Each incident should leave the system a little harder to break the same way.

## Leaders own the schedule, and the stand-down

The leadership list is concrete: make sure managers schedule the rotations, write the guidelines and expectations, review the process now and then so it fits the company, define incident severities and SLAs, and build an escalation policy that matches them.

The part she clearly cares about most is burnout. Respect the team's time, keep late-night calls for real emergencies, and recognise that many issues can wait until morning. "Some of my proudest leadership moment come from identifying a situation as noncritical and telling my heroes to stand down," she said. Done right, that builds trust: engineers engage more when they know they'll only be woken for something that matters.

## The culture rules

Her do's and don'ts are short. Don't play the blame game or pass incidents around like a hot potato; a blame culture stops people from taking risks or owning mistakes. Don't wait passively for solutions; show urgency. Communicate clearly with the teammates on the incident, your manager and stakeholders. Take responsibility, and do it kindly.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers setting up or repairing an on-call rotation, and engineers about to take their first shift. It's a practices talk rather than a tooling one; experienced on-call teams will recognise most of it, but the lessons-learned checklist and the leadership section are worth stealing.

Title: Monthly incident reports are a roadmap, once the data is clean
Description: Andre Carvalho (Sportingtech) at Conf42 Incident Management 2023 on turning incident report data into priorities, staffing and prevention
Body:
The incident report most teams file and forget can tell you which service to fix first, how many engineers the fix needs, and whether last year's work paid off. That is the case Andre Carvalho, Incident Management Team Lead at Sportingtech, made at Conf42 Incident Management 2023: collect the same handful of metrics every month, clean and structure them, and the report becomes the input for platform priorities, resource allocation and prevention.

He calls it a light presentation, and it is: a short, practical walk through a reporting workflow by someone who writes weekly, monthly and stakeholder reports for a living and admits it's a personal passion.

## What should an incident management lead measure?

He starts with the incident cycle in five steps: detection, investigation, eradication (the fix, deployed and communicated), recovery while you watch the dashboards, and post-event activity. Data piles up through the first four; the fifth is where the incident management lead analyses it.

The role has four jobs: capture what happened each month, coordinate between teams so the next reaction is faster, document the process, and prevent repeats. The four metrics he considers essential are severity, MTTR, SLOs (the agreements with internal and external clients) and frequency, including how many incidents are repeats. He is clear that the exact set differs by company; some care more about financial figures, others about reporting.

## Clean, structure, then visualise

"Data per se doesn't say anything, it's just random numbers," Andre Carvalho said at Conf42 Incident Management 2023. His three steps are unglamorous on purpose. Clean: fix typos, check that fields match, make sure empty values are either filled or have a reason. Structure: relate the tables, Excel and pivot tables in his case. Visualise: the charts, his favourite part, where patterns start to show.

## Cross three metrics before you prioritise

His example dashboard, explicitly illustrative, crosses incident volume, MTTR and impact per service area. Transactional services were the most affected, and the rise in their incidents went with a 5% drop in revenue. Login and access incidents held steady quarter on quarter, and those teams resolved them fast, with low MTTR. DDoS attacks increased over the last two quarters but had little or no end-user impact.

To order the work he uses a prioritisation matrix of urgency against impact, where impact runs from a single user to multiple users to system-wide, and each cell is critical, high, moderate or low. Applied to the example, transactional services come first, then login and access, then DDoS. The same report a year later shows whether the effort worked: fewer incidents, better MTTR and SLOs, less customer impact.

## The report is also a staffing tool

The less obvious use is resource allocation. When a new project or a fix from an incident comes up, the plan runs: define objectives, plan, identify the technical resources, identify the workforce, implement, follow up. The reports supply the history: this many incidents of this type took this many developers and this many hours. Over months that gives a credible estimate of how many people a type of problem needs. The payoff he lists is better MTTR and SLOs, growth in GGR, and the one he likes best, engineers under less stress because the work is sized right.

He ends on prevention. "By leveraging our past, we can prevent or predict till an extent the future," he said: alerts and preventive actions built from the patterns in the reports, so the team spends less time reacting.

## Who should watch

New incident managers and team leads who have the data but no reporting routine, and anyone who has to explain to stakeholders why one service gets the engineering time. Engineers looking for tooling or statistics will find a spreadsheet-level method, which is rather the point.

Title: The one-line Helm change that deleted a security sidecar in prod
Description: Paige Cruz (Chronosphere) at Conf42 Incident Management 2023 on the config change that passed every environment except production
Body:
A one-line logging change sailed through local testing, a PR review, acceptance and an overnight bake in staging, then took the whole site down in production. At Conf42 Incident Management 2023, Paige Cruz, Senior Developer Advocate at Chronosphere, tells the story of the first production incident she caused as a senior SRE, how a diff of rendered manifests found the cause, and how she turned the outage into the best Kubernetes lesson her company ever got.

Her conclusion is the title: there's no place like production, however many environments come before it.

## How did a logging tweak take down a whole site?

The setting was a 13-year-old cannabis platform connecting consumers with dispensaries: a marketplace with live inventory, delivery, ads and point-of-sale systems. Cruz had held the pager for years without ever causing an incident, while closing out a Kubernetes migration, starting a CI/CD migration and watching about 80% of her department leave.

The target was Traefik, one of two proxies routing traffic. Its logs were unstructured, so they couldn't be indexed, queried or graphed. She wanted structured JSON logs she could filter by path, remote IP, referer or router name. The change lived in Helm configuration, though the team didn't run Helm itself: charts were rendered into raw Kubernetes YAML and handed to an Argo CD app of apps, which pointed at the individual Argo application that synced to the clusters.

The plan was careful. Local testing, a heads-up to developers, review from the most tenured engineer on the team, acceptance (monitored mostly by the scream test: if nobody screams, it's fine), staging overnight, and a quiet slot for production. The deploy went green. Minutes later the incident channel lit up with alerts from teams across the stack.

## Roll back first, believe later

She was sure it couldn't be her change, so she muted the channel; she wasn't primary on call. Then the primary, who had also reviewed her PR, sent a DM saying he thought it was her Traefik change and asking her to roll it back. She hit revert without needing to be convinced, joined the call, said so, and the graphs recovered quickly. Mitigation doesn't need a root cause.

Two details from the aftermath stand out. Several engineers messaged her to praise her bravery for owning the change, which she read as a sign of a cultural problem with on-call. And she didn't blame herself, crediting the learning-from-incidents community: she had taken every precaution, and anyone else making that change would have hit the same wall.

## Spot the difference, hard mode

The investigation came down to rendering the Helm charts into raw Kubernetes manifests for each environment and diffing them, which she calls face-palmingly simple in hindsight. Only production was missing a component: a security sidecar in the Traefik pod that vetted requests on their way in. Her one line, added to an environment-specific values YAML in the hierarchy, had overwritten the block defining that second container. Nothing warned her along the way.

None of the parts is hard on its own: YAML, Go templates, Kubernetes, application definitions, the Argo app of apps pattern. The trouble is how they are layered and point at each other.

## How to spend an outage's attention

The next morning everyone wanted to know what happened, and she treated that attention as a gift. The retro document traced every step from Helm template to manifest to Argo application to app of apps, written so anyone in the company could follow it. She took it, plus a life-of-a-request diagram, to the backend chapter, the frontend chapter and SRE study time. For a Ruby, Node and Elixir shop new to Kubernetes she spelled out Go templating quirks, the precedence of Helm values files and what actually happens when a PR merges. The diagram was the hit: some engineers were seeing the request path end to end for the first time.

For leaders, a metaphor answered what happened before anyone asked how. Her PR amounted to "taking out the front door of our house and replacing it with a brick wall," as Paige Cruz said at Conf42 Incident Management 2023: nobody could get in, while those already inside could still talk to each other.

## Who should watch

Anyone running GitOps on layered config, and anyone writing their first incident review after causing the incident. It's a story talk, funny and honest, with the technical lesson in the diff.

Title: Conf42 Kube Native 2023: ambient mesh, less YAML and kinder dev loops
Description: The Conf42 Kube Native 2023 roundup - 21 talks on sidecar-less meshes, zero trust, GitOps, developer experience, cost and a £34bn card data platform.
Body:
[Conf42 Kube Native 2023](https://www.conf42.com/kubenative2023) went out on September 28 with 21 talks, and three of them were about the same thing: Istio's ambient mode, which takes the sidecar out of the service mesh. That says a lot about where Kubernetes was in 2023. The cluster itself had become the boring part; the conversation had moved to the layers around it, meshes, zero trust, GitOps, the developer's inner loop, and the bill at the end of the month.

Speakers came from Google, AWS, Teleport, JFrog, VMware, Veeam, Sonar, Globant, WSO2, Hasura, Ambassador Labs, Kubeshop, Kubefirst, HackerRank, IMESH, CVS Health, Dojo and Dojo & Co.

## Is the sidecar-less mesh ready?

[Abdel Sghiouar](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Abdel_Sghiouar_ambient_mesh) of Google gave the introduction to ambient mesh: why sidecars were the default, what a per-node ztunnel and HBONE tunnelling (a single mTLS connection using HTTP CONNECT) change, and why it can beat sidecars on performance while staying compatible with existing sidecar-based meshes. [Md Azmal](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Md_Azmal_ambient_mesh_sidecar_zero_trust) of IMESH framed the same architecture as a zero trust story with smaller cloud bills: ztunnel for the secure overlay, waypoint proxies for layer 7, and no changes to existing workloads to adopt it.

[Rob Richardson](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Rob_Richardson_service_mess_service_mesh) of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints asked the question that should come first: do you need a mesh at all? His talk compares Linkerd and Istio with live demos and gives you the vocabulary to justify, or decline, the investment.

## Trust nothing, scan everything

[Jonathan Vila](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Jonathan_Vila_secure_microservices_zerotrust_approach) of Sonar opened with more than 4,000 data breaches in 2021 exposing 22 billion records, then demoed zero trust for Quarkus microservices with Istio on a local cluster, enforcing identity validation on every service without touching a line of Java. [Jacob Beasley](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Jacob_Beasley_m9sweeper_open_source_security_platform) showed M9sweeper, an open source platform that bundles CNCF-recommended tools for image scanning, cluster scanning, pen tests, policy and intrusion detection, with a blunt baseline: don't expose your API server on the internet and don't make everybody an administrator.

[Julia Furst Morgado](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Julia_Furst_Morgado_kubernetes_virtualization_admin) of Veeam translated Kubernetes for people who already run virtualisation: compute, storage and networking, mapped concept by concept, for teams heading into hybrid estates.

## How much YAML does one engineer need?

Less, said [Robert Hoffmann](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Robert_Hoffmann_yaml_software_cdk8s) of AWS, who introduced CDK8s for describing deployments in Python, TypeScript, Java or Go, turning CRDs into classes and getting real abstractions instead of copy-pasted manifests. [Frederic Harper](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Frederic_Harper_git_sht_done) of Kubefirst made the GitOps case with the repository structure that runs his own cluster, secrets in HashiCorp Vault and the pull-based CD that makes Git the source of truth. [Anuruddha Liyanarachchi](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Anuruddha_Liyanarachchi_network_services_realworld_ballerina) of WSO2 pitched Ballerina, a language with network primitives built in, for services that are mostly integration, and [Akshay Bhat](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Akshay_Bhat_graphql_efficiency_flexibility) of Hasura showed GraphQL with Hasura as the data layer for Kubernetes workloads.

## Why is the inner loop so slow?

[Edidiong Asikpo](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Edidiong_Asikpo_closing_developer_experience_gap) of Ambassador Labs named the gap: containers made the build, push and test cycle slower, and a slow inner dev loop hurts everyone. Telepresence bridges local machine and cluster through a two-way proxy, with global and personal intercepts. [Karan Jagtiani](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Karan_Jagtiani_devops_serverless_knative) of HackerRank built serverless on his own cluster with Knative and explained when that beats the cloud provider's offering.

Testing and debugging had their own track. [Ram Mohan Rao Chukka](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Ram_Mohan_Rao_Chukka_kuttl_improve_e2e_testing) of JFrog told how a move from waterfall to daily releases pushed his team to KUTTL for end-to-end tests developers actually run locally, so nobody has to ask who broke the build. [Maria Ashby](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Maria_Ashby_troubleshooting_demystified_workflow) of Kubeshop shared five troubleshooting practices with Botkube bringing cluster alerts and commands into Slack, Teams, Discord or Mattermost, and [Jhonnatan Gil Chaves](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Jhonnatan_Gil_Chaves_observability_metrics_open_source_tools) of Globant toured metrics, logs and traces with open source tools.

## What do platforms at scale look like?

Gold sponsor Teleport brought the most specific architecture of the day. [Stephen Levine](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Stephen_Levine_scaling_multi_cluster) described Teleport Cloud: a dedicated Teleport instance per customer on EKS clusters in six regions, more than 100,000 ultra-long-lived reverse tunnels, and why plain GitOps wasn't enough for coordinated upgrades, so the team built a narrow tool of its own, a sync controller.

[Sandeep Mehta](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Sandeep_Mehta_businesscritical_data_platform_process_card_transactions) of Dojo described the self-serve data platform behind more than £34bn in card transactions, on GKE, under PCI rules and strict SLAs, with autoscaling as a core part of the design. [Antoni Ivanov](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Antoni_Ivanov_devops_data_ml_engineering) of VMware argued that data applications are applications too, and need APIs and data contracts mapped onto the DevOps cycle.

## Metrics, money and the people using it

[Michael Levan](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Michael_Levan_cost_resource_optimization) covered cost and resource optimisation, with the sensible caveat that saving money stops being a win once performance degrades. [Joel Tosi](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Joel_Tosi_metrics_matter_easy_impactful) of Dojo & Co, tired of being the person who says all metrics are bad, moved organisations from simple to directional to economic metrics, with Shewhart's control charts to separate common-cause from special-cause variation. And [Erissa Duvall](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Erissa_Duvall_accessibility_testing_101) of CVS Health gave an accessibility testing 101 built on the W3C guidelines, a reminder that the people using what the cluster serves are the point.

## Thanks to the sponsors

[Gcore](https://gcore.com/) and [Teleport](https://goteleport.com/) were the gold sponsors, with [unpack.tech](https://www.unpack.tech/) as newsletter partner, alongside media partners including [Manning](https://www.manning.com), [Packt](https://www.packtpub.com/), [Kube Careers](https://kube.careers/), [Kube Events](https://kube.events/), [Infosec Conferences](https://infosec-conferences.com) and [CodeCrafters](https://codecrafters.io/?r=2qF).

Every talk is on the [Conf42 Kube Native 2023 page](https://www.conf42.com/kubenative2023) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrAsq4jEk8yDtEYUPWqyqZa5). The series returned a year later as [Conf42 Kube Native 2024](https://www.conf42.com/kubenative2024).

Title: The trouble with runbooks is that they don't run
Description: Anurag Gupta (Shoreline.io) at Conf42 Incident Management 2023 on generating runbooks with LLMs and turning them into executable, audited notebooks
Body:
Most teams that have runbooks have stale ones, and most of the rest have none. At Conf42 Incident Management 2023, Anurag Gupta, Founder and CEO of Shoreline.io, showed how his company uses LLMs to draft runbooks from real incident data, why every generated runbook still gets a human curator, and why the document should be something you execute rather than copy and paste from.

This is a vendor talk and a short one: a quick demo of Shoreline's product, not a general method. It is still a useful look at what LLM-assisted runbook tooling could do as early as 2023.

## Start from the incidents that cost the most

The demo opens on a top problem report fed continuously from PagerDuty. For each group of incidents it tracks MTTA, MTTR, the number of people involved, how long it took and how often it happened, so you can sort by aggregate MTTR and fix the most expensive problem first. In the example that was an Apache server being down.

The grouping is the interesting part. Lightweight clustering decides which tickets look alike, ignoring noise such as hostnames. On top of that an LLM adds semantic matching: a ticket about a full disk and one about a full persistent volume claim are the same issue, or at least respond to the same diagnostics and repair commands.

## A runbook drafted second by second

From the Apache group, Gupta generates a runbook on screen. It lays out diagnostics to check the VM's status, read the logs, confirm the deployment is running, check that the VM is reachable and that the needed ports are open. He then adds a prompt asking whether the process crashed and needs a restart, and gets a bash script back, followed by a restart remediation. The targets he lists are Kubernetes, VMs, Linux or Windows and the three major cloud providers. A finished runbook exports to Markdown, for example a Confluence wiki, or into Shoreline.

## Hallucinations are why a human curates the library

He doesn't pretend LLMs are reliable. Because they hallucinate, Shoreline manually curates the runbooks it creates and those its customers create; at the time of the talk the library held a little over 300, with a goal of about 1,000. The idea is that a team starts from a runbook that has already been tested, instead of waiting for the incident to write one. For MongoDB alone the library had eleven.

## Make the runbook executable

His core complaint is one every on-call engineer will recognise. "For me, the core problem with runbooks is that they don't actually run," Anurag Gupta said at Conf42 Incident Management 2023. Copying commands onto every node you need to fix is slow and error-prone, so Shoreline's runbooks are notebooks in the style of Jupyter: Markdown explanation and runnable actions side by side.

Two examples show the shape. One handles an application load balancer returning 500 errors: collect load balancer names across hosts, get their details, describe the ingress paths, and if needed take a heap dump and do a rolling restart. The other is a high-CPU run on a bookstore service. It checks the instance count and the release, waits a minute to see whether the CPU spike is real, lists the top processes and threads, finds a JVM thread, confirms allocation failures in the logs, then dumps, restarts and validates that the issue is gone.

## Access control and audit come with it

Once runbooks execute in a controlled environment, every run is recorded, including standard output and standard error. Access control can be fine-grained: who can run which actions on which resources and when, for example only while on call, plus approval workflows and integrations with Slack, Teams, observability tools and ticketing systems.

## Who should watch

SREs and incident managers whose runbook wiki is out of date, and anyone weighing LLM-generated remediation who wants to see one vendor's guard rails: clustering on real ticket data, human curation, audit logs and scoped permissions. Expect a product demo rather than a vendor-neutral framework.

- Einat Mahat on [creating on-call heroes](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Einat_Mahat_oncall_heroes_effective_practices), including turning each incident into runbooks and automation.

Title: Kubernetes cost optimisation starts with scaling down, not with a tool
Description: Michael Levan at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on Kubernetes cost and resource optimisation, why scale-down matters, and a self-hosted vs SaaS tool demo
Body:
If you run 20 worker nodes and have never needed more than six, the fix is not a dashboard. At Conf42 Kube Native 2023, Michael Levan, consultant, trainer and content creator, gives a short, practical take on cost and resource optimisation in Kubernetes: the money follows the resources, scaling down matters as much as scaling up, and saving money is never worth a slower cluster. He then installs two optimisation tools, one you run yourself and one SaaS, to show what the trade-off looks like.

It is a quick talk, roughly half principles and half demo, aimed at engineers who have been asked to cut the bill and aren't sure where to start.

## Why should engineers care about money?

Levan finds the FinOps wave a little ironic. Ten-plus years ago, as a sysadmin and even on the help desk, he worked closely with finance on budgets and specs, and he has seen IT directors report to the CFO. IT was always the department that spent money; what has changed is that the business now runs on technology.

His one hard rule: save money, but not at the cost of performance. Scaling three worker nodes down to one to save money is a mistake, because "it's going to mess up performance on the cluster." Cost work that breaks the environment is not optimisation.

## Isn't the cloud unlimited anyway?

No. On-prem, an extra server means a reseller, shipping, racking and configuration. In the cloud the limits are quieter but real: regional caps and quotas. He recalls an Azure region about a month before the talk where the storage account service ran out of capacity, so nobody could create new storage accounts there.

Resource optimisation, then, is making sure what runs is needed. In the 20-nodes-for-a-peak-of-six example, keep a couple spare for spikes to seven or eight and drop the rest. The same applies to applications, network and storage: over-allocating and under-allocating both cost you.

## Scaling down is half of autoscaling

Teams tend to think of scalability as scaling up. His example is an e-commerce site: Cyber Monday needs two or three extra worker nodes, but for six or eight months of the year those nodes sit idle and you are paying for them. Scaling back down is "arguably just as important as scaling up." His shortest summary of cost work: don't spend unless you absolutely have to. Get resources right and cost optimisation mostly takes care of itself in the background.

## Self-hosted or SaaS?

He lists the field: CAST AI, StormForge, plus the native tools in AWS, GCP and Azure. Then two installs on an AKS cluster with at least two nodes:

- **A self-hosted platform.** Download the installer for your OS, run it, pick the environment (AKS here), a cluster name and a domain suffix (set a real one in production), then `kubectl port-forward` and log in with the default admin credentials. Capable, he says, but you own running it.
- **StormForge, as SaaS.** Name the environment in the portal, copy the generated Helm values into a values.yaml, `helm install`, and the verify step passes in about 10 to 15 seconds. The portal shows current versus optimised requests and efficiency by cluster, namespace and workload, plus paid Optimize Pro features and performance testing for benchmarks. It is a paid product.

On a demo cluster there is nothing to optimise yet, so the dashboards are mostly empty. The point is the operating model: pay for SaaS and have it managed, or run it yourself.

## Who should watch

Engineers and team leads starting Kubernetes cost work who want the reasoning before the tooling. If you need deep rightsizing techniques or VPA tuning, pair it with the talks below.

- Prathamesh Sonpatki on [cost instrumentation](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Prathamesh_Sonpatki_cost_instrumentation).

Title: An API gateway is a traffic cop at the edge of town, not a service mesh
Description: Rob Richardson (The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on when a service mesh earns its cost, with Linkerd and Istio demos
Body:
Inside a Kubernetes cluster, by default, your services talk to each other over unencrypted HTTP, and nothing stops a rogue pod from calling them. At Conf42 Kube Native 2023, Rob Richardson, Portfolio Architect at The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, explains what a service mesh does about that, demos Linkerd and Istio side by side, and ends with the part most mesh talks skip: when the extra containers are not worth it.

It is an introductory talk, and a well-built one. If you have been told you need a mesh and want to know whether that is true, start here.

## Why isn't the API gateway enough?

His framing is a growing town. Traffic gets congested, so someone puts a traffic cop at the edge of town who penalises anyone too fast or too slow. Traffic flows, but "we optimized mediocrity." What you want is cars that coordinate with each other.

The API gateway is that cop. It is a great fence for north-south traffic: monitoring inbound calls, counting usage for billing. But it sees nothing of east-west traffic, the calls microservices make to each other and to each other's data stores. A service mesh covers both.

## How does a mesh work?

He walks a single call. Service A talks to a proxy in its own pod over localhost. The proxy asks the mesh control plane (separate from the cluster's) whether A may call B. B's proxy asks whether it may accept traffic from A. If both say yes, the proxies open a mutual TLS tunnel, with certificates bound to the mesh's trust chain and possibly your PKI. Neither service changes a line of code.

Everything else follows from routing all traffic through Envoy proxies. The talk groups the payoff into crawl, walk and run:

- **Crawl**: monitoring, logging of status codes and call chains, service health (500s and high latency).
- **Walk**: intelligent routing for A/B tests, beta channels and canaries, plus circuit breakers. Without one, every client retries a struggling service the moment it comes back, and it falls over again.
- **Run**: a live network topology built from real traffic, which you can compare with the architect's diagram to spot the feature flag someone forgot to turn back on, and distributed traces.

## Linkerd or Istio?

He compares philosophies rather than feature lists, since both move fast. Linkerd puts everything you need to start in the box, installs smoothly and contributed much of the Rust networking stack it runs on; go beyond its features and you reach for third parties. Istio assembles the best open-source projects and lets you switch features on and off by profile.

The Linkerd demo is the install path: CLI, `linkerd check --pre`, CRDs, install, `linkerd check` (which waits until everything is ready), the viz extension, then the dashboard with namespaces, deployments, success rates and who-calls-what, also available from `linkerd stat` and through Prometheus.

The Istio demo uses the Bookinfo sample with three versions of the reviews service: no stars, black stars, red stars. With VirtualService rules he sends 100% to v1, then 80/20 to v2, then all to v2, then a canary where user jason gets v3 while everyone else stays on v2, then all to v3. No downtime at any step. Then the dashboards: Prometheus for `istio_requests_total`, Grafana's control-plane dashboard, a Jaeger trace showing that the details service is not where time goes, and Kiali's graph with an unused v1 fading to grey.

## When is a mesh worth it?

It costs something. You run roughly twice the containers; Envoy is leaner than a Java Tomcat app, so maybe one and a third to one and a half times the workload, and you pay to host it. His case for paying:

- A mix of trusted and untrusted workloads: PKI or PCI services that need a virtual cage, multi-tenant clusters, code run on behalf of others.
- Hard boundaries between tenants, because "namespaces are an organizational boundary, not a security boundary," he said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023.
- Encryption in depth inside the cluster, not just at the front door. If mTLS is all you need, he suggests a lighter-weight option; with observability and control on top, a mesh fits.
- Routing features like A/B tests and beta channels, alongside the other needs.

If you have one microservice, he notes, a mesh might be overkill.

## Who should watch

Engineers deciding whether to adopt a mesh, and anyone who has to justify one to whoever pays the cloud bill. If you already know Istio well, the cost-and-fit section is the part to keep.
