Title: Automate the parts of incident response that pay off, not all of it
Description: Joshua Arvin Lat (NuWorks Interactive Labs) and Sophie Soliven (edamama) at Conf42 Incident Management 2023 on pragmatic, AI-assisted incident automation
Body:
Picture an e-commerce site that has run quietly for a year until customers can't get through checkout, and the fix lands five days later: five days of sales gone. That is the opening scenario of the Conf42 Incident Management 2023 talk by Joshua Arvin Lat, CTO of NuWorks Interactive Labs, and Sophie Soliven, Director of Operations at edamama. Their answer is pragmatic automation: automate the specific steps that clearly pay for themselves, use the tools you already have, and keep a human in the loop wherever automation can do real damage.

Lat is an AWS Machine Learning Hero and the author of Machine Learning with Amazon SageMaker Cookbook, Machine Learning Engineering on AWS and Building and Automating Penetration Testing Labs in the Cloud. Soliven brings nine years in e-commerce, fintech and retail in the Philippines, with a focus on process and risk management.

## What does pragmatic automation mean in practice?

The core principle is selectivity. While automation has real advantages, "not every aspect of a process needs to be or should be automated," as Joshua Arvin Lat and Sophie Soliven said at Conf42 Incident Management 2023. Their example is a cloud setup that alerts on traffic spikes, unauthorised access attempts and system failures. Auto-scaling during a traffic surge and blocking suspicious IP addresses after unauthorised access attempts are good candidates for automation. The rest of the alerts still go to the IT team for manual review.

The second principle is to build on established incident management tools rather than writing your own. Mature platforms come with community support and documentation, take less development time, and leave the team free to spend its effort on configuration that fits its own environment.

## Where AI fits, and where a human still signs off

The talk walks through a set of AI-assisted techniques, each with its limits stated:

- **Chatbots** handle common incidents and queries first: they gather the initial facts, guide users through basic troubleshooting and escalate to the right people.
- **Simulation and training**: AI-powered penetration testing tools can stage security incidents in a controlled environment, giving IT and security teams practice before the real thing.
- **AI-powered root cause analysis** sifts large volumes of data for patterns faster than a person can, but the speakers insist human experts review the output before anyone acts on it.
- **Automated remediation** ranges from basic notification and logging all the way to fixing issues without human intervention. The risk is that an automated fix causes the next outage, so they recommend a phased rollout from the basic levels up.
- **Automated tagging of corrupted records** flags inconsistent rows in databases so data administrators don't hunt for them by hand.
- **AI-powered monitoring and alerting** for network security, performance and anomaly detection, aiming to spot problems before they happen.
- **Incident report drafting**: generating the first version of the incident report document in a few minutes instead of hours, with more consistent results.

The thread through all of it is balance: speed from automation, judgment from people. Automation that nobody supervises is just a faster way to make the wrong change.

## Who should watch

Teams early in incident automation who want a map of where AI and automation can help and where they need guard rails. It is a conceptual overview with no product demos, benchmarks or architecture walkthroughs, so engineers who already run auto-remediation in production will find little new.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Anurag Gupta on [using generative AI to fix out-dated runbooks](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Anurag_Gupta_generative_ai_fix_runbooks) at the same event, for a concrete take on generated diagnostics and repairs.
- Birol Yildiz on [AIOps and alert noise](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Birol_Yildiz_aiops_alert_noise) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2024.
- Andre Carvalho on [what incident management reports reveal](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Andre_Carvalho_insights_through_reports), also at Conf42 Incident Management 2023.

Title: Dojo scales card-scheme file processing on queue depth divided by four
Description: Sandeep Mehta (Dojo) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on a self-serve, PCI-compliant file platform on GKE that scales pods on Pub/Sub backlog
Body:
Card payments look instant at the till, but settling them runs on files: Visa, Mastercard, Amex and Diners send XML, CSV, fixed-width and proprietary formats, from 2 KB to multiple gigabytes, often all at once. At Conf42 Kube Native 2023, Sandeep Mehta, Engineering Manager for Data Platforms at Dojo, explains how his team built a self-serve file processing platform on GKE for over £50bn in card transactions. The core trick fits on one line: unacknowledged Pub/Sub messages divided by four equals the number of pods to run.

## Why is this data problem hard?

Dojo powers face-to-face payments for around 15% of UK card transactions, he says, mostly bars, pubs, restaurants and corner shops. The constraints stack up:

- **Regulation.** An e-money licence from the FCA means customer funds must be safeguarded at all times; owning the full payment stack means PCI DSS Level 1, raw card numbers (PANs) in the data, and a yearly audit.
- **Complexity.** More than 1,000 schemas, many of them fragile proprietary formats that change often. One reconciliation, checking a merchant's net settlement against authorised transactions, alone needs a pile of CSV, XLS and XML files.
- **Scale.** Around 500,000 files a day, and source SLAs overlap so they arrive in bursts.
- **Criticality.** Internally they call it building a nuclear power station: it cannot fail.

Every format gets parsed into one: chunked Avro, picked for schema evolution, sized evenly so you don't end up with a 2 GB file next to a few-KB one. Downstream jobs then load it into the warehouse, Kafka, Snowflake or an MLOps platform.

## Why not a central data team?

He walks the three generations: enterprise warehouses, the Hadoop era, and today's centralised platforms on Kafka, Apache Beam and managed services. Centralised works for simple domains. With rich domains and many sources and consumers, the central team becomes the bottleneck for access, new sources and schema changes, owns data it doesn't understand, and ends up in a blame game. Engineering applied domain-driven design years ago; data mostly forgot to.

So Dojo moved to data mesh: domain ownership, data as a product, federated computational governance (payments sets encryption standards, marketing sets 28-day retention for GDPR) and a self-serve platform. "If you successfully build this, which means self serve data platform, you've got 80% things right," he said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023.

## How do files get in and get masked?

Source connectors pull from storage buckets, external APIs, webhooks, SFTP servers and, yes, Gmail attachments. Rclone, running as a Kubernetes CronJob, does most of the moving. Webhook events are batched into files to keep one shape. A serverless function parses one provider's data out of an email body, because of course there is one.

Encrypted files land in the PCI platform. There they are decrypted in memory on confidential computing nodes, re-encrypted with Dojo's own key and archived, unzipped on disk if needed, and any PANs are masked. Only masked files go on to the non-PCI platform, which takes them out of PCI scope.

## Scaling on queue depth

Each file landing in GCS emits an event into Pub/Sub. A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on an external metric sets pods to unacked messages divided by four, capped at a few hundred, since one file takes about a second. Cluster autoscaler adds nodes when pods go pending. At peak that is around 300 pods across 40 nodes working through a couple of hundred thousand files in about 30 minutes.

Two lessons cost them sleep. Getting requests and limits right took production trial and error (the slides show 200m/500m CPU and 128Mi/256Mi memory), and he mentions they "started hating pagerduty" along the way. And cluster autoscaler only reacts to pending pods: if a pod requested too little and then starves on a busy node, nothing scales. They misread the docs and lost a couple of days to slow processing before working that out.

## What makes it self-serve?

The non-PCI translate pods parse every file according to a schema registry, and each pipeline belongs to one domain. Through a web UI, a domain team adds a column or a new feed without filing a ticket with the data team. The registry doubles as a data contract and an SLA monitor: say your file must reach BigQuery by 09:00 and you get alerted if it doesn't.

A state store tracks each file through FILE_CREATED, TRANSLATE_TODO, TRANSLATE_STARTED, success, skip or error, and Avro upload. Pods check it before taking a file, which prevents duplicate processing from repeated queue events, and transient errors go back to TODO for another pod. The same events feed a file monitoring service, Slack alerts per stage with playbooks, and Grafana dashboards next to Prometheus infrastructure metrics. DataHub for the catalog was in progress.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers in regulated industries, and anyone autoscaling batch work on Kubernetes from a queue. The autoscaling section and the state machine are the reusable parts; the data mesh section is a clear argument for why the platform is shaped that way.

Title: Your 14-sale day was noise, and a process behavior chart can prove it
Description: Joel Tosi (Dojo & Co) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on moving from simple to impactful metrics, and using process behavior charts to tell signal from noise
Body:
A new release ships on day eleven, sales jump to 14, and everyone wants to celebrate. At Conf42 Kube Native 2023, Joel Tosi, co-founder of Dojo & Co, runs the numbers with a process behavior chart and shows that 14 sits comfortably inside the system's normal range. So does the 4 the next day. The release changed nothing. His talk is about getting past metrics that are easy to count, and about having the statistics to know when a change actually mattered.

It is a Kube Native talk with no Kubernetes in it, and that is fine: it is the talk to send your manager after someone asks for a cycle-time dashboard.

## Why measure at all?

Tosi admits he used to be the person who called every metric bad: cycle time alone, burndown charts, CPU percentages. Then he realised that is not a position. People want to know whether investments work, and as he put it, "When we can't measure what we should, we measure what we can. And then, of course, we optimize for the wrong thing."

He frames everything on a value stream from business hypothesis to customer. On the cheap left side, before code exists, exploit variability and try many ideas. Once you commit, minimise variability and deliver. And watch for suboptimising: making server deployment fast does not help if the rest of the stream is slow.

## Simple, directional, impactful

His three groupings work as a maturity ladder:

- **Simple**: easy to count, isolated. Number of defects, teams doing automated deployments, velocity. If you have nothing, start here.
- **Directional**: simple metrics over a time horizon. Is the defect rate falling? Did the infrastructure automation investment actually cut cycle time? Did better test automation reduce defects?
- **Impactful or economic**: these need intentionality. Cycle time for a delivery that mattered, systemic cost reductions, stopping bad ideas, shrinking queues and toil.

The catch with the top tier is agreement. Measuring a delivery that mattered requires the organisation to agree on what matters, what to do with bad ideas instead of falling for sunk costs, and why queues and toil are bad. He quotes Don Reinertsen's *Principles of Product Development Flow*: "When cycle times are long, innovation happens so late that it becomes imitation."

## How do you know a change made a difference?

With Walter Shewhart's charts, also called control charts or process behavior charts, which separate common-cause variation from special-cause variation. A stable system left alone keeps delivering within a range; the goal is not to react to noise.

The recipe from the talk: plot daily values and their average. Take the absolute difference between each consecutive pair of days, sum those, and divide by the number of differences (nine, in his ten-day example). Multiply by 2.67 and add and subtract that from the average to get the upper and lower limits. In his sales example the upper limit lands a little above 15 and the lower limit below zero, floored at zero. So anything from 0 to 15 is the system being itself, and day eleven's 14 earns no raises. Takeaways: be intentional about what you measure, get more frequent data points (weekly samples take a long time to say anything), and use it for product, process and tech changes alike.

## What he measures instead

The last third is where his attention had moved:

- **Predictability versus variability.** Organisations ask when things will be done but don't track how variable test setup, data, environments and dependencies are. Chain five steps that each work 80% of the time and the whole chain works about a third of the time. The fix is less variability, not more process. Variability also creates queues, and waiting is expensive.
- **Cognitive load.** Teams doing DevOps and DevSecOps juggle too many contexts, and it shows in big repos and bad coupling. Rearchitecting or replatforming is often the answer.
- **Information lead time.** How far up the org chart does a team go to get a decision? The fix is pushing context down to the people doing the work, which sounds easy and isn't.
- **Social learning and a diffusion index.** Team members self-assess skills; shrinking the gap between the highest and lowest self-assessed scores reduces reliance on single people and erodes silos.

His reading list: Mark Graban's *Measures of Success*, Donald Wheeler's *Understanding Variation* (where the multiplier is explained), and Reinertsen again.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, platform leads and anyone who has been asked to prove a tooling investment paid off. The chart section alone will save you from at least one premature victory lap.

Title: Istio ambient mesh, demoed: label a namespace, get mTLS, skip the sidecars
Description: Md Azmal (IMESH) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on Istio ambient mesh, ztunnel and waypoint proxies for zero-trust mTLS and L7 policy without sidecars
Body:
The best moment in this talk is a tcpdump. At Conf42 Kube Native 2023, Md Azmal, founding engineer at IMESH, curls an echo server across two nodes and the request body sits in plain text on the wire. He installs Istio with the ambient profile, labels the namespaces, curls again, and the same capture shows only encrypted traffic. No pod restarted, no sidecar injected. That is the pitch for Istio ambient mesh, and the rest of the talk is a full demo of what you still get without sidecars: L4 and L7 authorization, canary routing and the usual observability stack.

## What is wrong with sidecars?

He gives the classic Istio picture first: a control plane injects an Envoy sidecar into every pod of a labelled namespace, and that sidecar handles traffic management, observability and mTLS. The costs he lists:

- Injection modifies the pod spec and redirects traffic inside the pod.
- At 4,000 or 5,000 pods, even a lightweight sidecar adds up to massive resource use.
- Traffic capture and HTTP processing, which are computationally expensive, all happen in every sidecar, at both L4 and L7.
- Upgrading means restarting the application. "If you have to update the sidecar, then good luck," he said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023.
- Server-first protocols interfere with permissive mTLS, and non-conformant HTTP implementations can break.

## How does ambient mesh split the work?

By layer. A per-node ztunnel (zero trust tunnel), written in Rust, does only L4: mTLS, simple authorization, TCP metrics and routing. It never parses HTTP, which keeps it light. Waypoint proxies, which are plain Envoy pods deployed per namespace or per service account, handle L7: rich authorization, HTTP metrics, routing, retries and the rest. Waypoints are optional and scale like any other Deployment.

Between them, ztunnels speak HBONE (HTTP-Based Overlay Network Environment), an HTTP CONNECT tunnel that carries all traffic through a single port, 15008. One port means fewer connections to manage, cleaner interoperability with load balancers and better handling of server-first protocols such as MySQL.

On security, the ztunnel acts like a SPIFFE node agent: it assumes the identity of workloads on its node, sends a CSR per service account to istiod, and istiod, acting as the CA, signs an X.509 certificate. The SPIFFE ID in each request names the namespace and service account it came from, which is what policies match on.

## What does the demo cover?

The setup is an AKS cluster with two Standard B2ms nodes (2 vCPUs, 8 GiB) on Azure CNI and Istio 1.18.3. Two namespaces hold sleep, not-sleep and echo-server pods; the second has echo server v1 and v2. The code is on his GitHub (MD-AZMAL/ambient-mesh-deep-dive).

1. **Install and enrol.** `istioctl install --set profile=ambient` with an ingress gateway, the Gateway API CRDs, then Prometheus, Grafana and Kiali. Labelling a namespace with `istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient` puts it in the mesh; ztunnel logs show inbound and outbound connections with identities.
2. **L4 policy.** An empty AuthorizationPolicy denies everything, so curl fails with exit code 56. A second policy allows only the sleep service account in ns1 to reach echo in ns2; not-sleep and even same-namespace callers stay blocked.
3. **Ingress.** A standard Istio Gateway and VirtualService, plus a policy allowing the ingress gateway's service account. The browser gets a response with Envoy headers.
4. **L7 policy.** `istioctl x waypoint generate` for the echo service account emits a Kubernetes Gateway with class istio-waypoint. Once the waypoint exists, calls get an RBAC access denied until an L7 policy allows GET. GET succeeds, POST is denied.
5. **Canary.** A VirtualService with a 90/10 split and a DestinationRule for subsets v1 and v2, the same YAML a sidecar mesh uses. Out of 100 requests, 91 reached v1; the v2 count came back at 16, which he waves off as approximation.
6. **Observability and debugging.** Prometheus shows L4 TCP metrics from ztunnel and L7 metrics from the Envoy-based gateway and waypoint. Kiali draws the graph, Grafana has the control-plane and mesh dashboards, and `istioctl proxy-status` and `istioctl proxy-config all` show what each Envoy knows. Ztunnel is not Envoy, so it is skipped there.

## Who should watch

Teams running sidecar Istio who wince at every upgrade, and anyone choosing a mesh who wants to see ambient mode do real policy work rather than a hello world. Note the date: this is Istio 1.18 with experimental waypoint commands, so check current docs before copying flags.

Title: Your LLM feature can't be unit tested, so instrument it like prod
Description: Christine Yen (Honeycomb) at Conf42 Incident Management 2023 on running LLM features with tracing, rich metadata and SLOs instead of unit tests
Body:
An LLM is a black box behind an API, just like your payments provider, except it is not predictable, not reproducible and not explainable. At Conf42 Incident Management 2023, Christine Yen, CEO of Honeycomb, argued that this breaks unit tests, staging and early access programs at once, and that the tools that still work are the ones SREs already have: instrumentation, observability and SLOs.

Her evidence is Honeycomb's own Query Assistant, which turns plain-English questions into Honeycomb queries. It shipped in May 2023 after about six weeks of development, followed by eight weeks of iterating on it in production.

## Why does an LLM break the usual testing toolkit?

Yen lines up a normal REST API against an LLM on three properties. With a normal API you can scope the range of inputs; an LLM invites free-form natural language from users, so no test suite covers the long tail. A SaaS API is deterministic and ideally idempotent; an LLM drifts as the provider changes the model under you. A spec makes a normal API explainable; with an LLM, a small change to the prompt can produce a very different answer.

Retrieval augmented generation adds one more layer: your app pulls extra domain context into the prompt, which is one more moving part between what the user typed and what came back. Her conclusion is blunt. Staging won't tell you whether the feature behaves, and early access programs only delay the failures until a larger crowd of users does things nobody expected.

## Treat the LLM like a dependency you can't open

You can't put instrumentation inside MySQL or your payment provider either. What you can do is record everything around the call: who made the request, from where in the code, with which parameters, how long it took and what came back. For LLMs her list is user and team IDs, the full user input string, the extra product context added to the prompt, token usage, LLM latency, the full LLM response, parse and validation errors, and user feedback.

Honeycomb's trace for one Query Assistant request runs from the user's click through dynamic prompt building, the OpenAI call, response parsing and validation, and finally query execution. The OpenAI call is one small span near the bottom; everything above it is the app's own prompt-building work, and each of those spans is something that can go wrong. User feedback came from yes, no and not-sure buttons, so a single bad answer can be traced back to the input and the prompt that produced it.

She is also relaxed about what counts as an error. "Not every exception is exceptional. Not everything exceptional is captured as an exception," Christine Yen said at Conf42 Incident Management 2023. Early on you don't know which failures matter, so capture them openly and correlate them back to what the user was trying to do.

## An SLO at 75% is still an SLO

The SRE idea she zooms in on is the service level objective. The Query Assistant team set an SLO on the share of requests that complete without an error, and set the initial baseline at 75%, because it shipped as an experimental feature and the goal was to climb. At the time of the talk compliance was closer to 95%. The SLO gave them a baseline at release and a way to see whether each round of prompt changes moved the number, which matters when, in her words, you will break one thing while fixing another.

## Duolingo and Intercom found the slow part wasn't the model

Two Honeycomb customers back the approach. Duolingo, whose LLM features are mostly on mobile, cared about latency and found that total latency depended far more on the work they controlled, building the prompt and gathering context, than on the LLM call itself. Intercom, iterating on an LLM-backed chatbot, recorded time to first token, time to first usable token, model version and algorithm version on every interaction, traced with the rest of the application, so one lever pulled could be tied to one result seen.

## Who should watch

SREs and product engineers who were handed an LLM feature without an ML team behind them. The talk is about practice, not Honeycomb features; Yen says up front the techniques should transfer to any LLM and observability stack.

Title: Knative gives you scale-to-zero on your own cluster, and minScale to undo it
Description: Karan Jagtiani (HackerRank) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on running your own serverless platform on Kubernetes with Knative Serving, scale-to-zero and cold starts
Body:
Serverless from a cloud provider means someone else owns the knobs. At Conf42 Kube Native 2023, Karan Jagtiani, SDE 2 at HackerRank, shows how to run serverless inside your own Kubernetes cluster with Knative Serving: a pod that scales to zero while you watch, wakes up on a curl, survives a load test, and then gets a minimum scale so the cold start stops hurting. The pitch is control. With Knative you keep the scale-to-zero economics and decide how scaling behaves yourself.

It is an introductory talk with a hands-on demo on a local kind cluster, so you can follow along on a laptop.

## Why not just use Lambda?

He starts from the with-server world: provision a VM, configure it, install the app and its dependencies, then maintain and scale it forever. Serverless (AWS Lambda, GCP Cloud Functions, Azure and Vercel functions) moves all of that to the provider. "Contrary to popular belief, serverless is actually a misnomer," he said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023: the servers are still there, just behind the scenes.

The trade-off is that hands-off can become hands-tied. When the provider's scaling behaviour does not fit you, there is little you can change. Knative, an open-source serverless platform for Kubernetes written in Go, is the answer for teams that want that configuration in their own YAML.

## What does Knative Serving actually give you?

Knative has two parts, Serving and Eventing; the talk covers only Serving. Its features as he lists them: scale down to zero and back up, YAML-based configuration that looks like any other Kubernetes object, the same rollout strategies you know from Deployments, and easy integration with service meshes and monitoring, tracing and logging tools.

A Knative Service has revisions (versions of your app), a route and a URL. Traffic can be split between revisions, say 80% to one and 20% to the next, which makes A/B tests and canaries a matter of config.

## The demo: from zero to 4,390 requests per second

Prerequisites are Docker, kind and the Knative client `kn` (Homebrew on a Mac), plus the quickstart plugin. `kn quickstart kind` builds a kind cluster on Kubernetes 1.25.3, installs Knative Serving, the Kourier networking layer that exposes services outside the cluster network, and Eventing. A look at the knative-serving namespace shows the pods, services and horizontal pod autoscalers that manage the workloads.

The hello-world service is a short YAML file using the `serving.knative.dev/v1` API, which looks almost exactly like a plain Kubernetes manifest. He diffs before every apply (a habit worth stealing), applies, and watches the pod run, then terminate a few seconds later because nothing is calling it. `kubectl get ksvc` shows the URL; one curl returns a hello-world response and a pod appears again. Scale-to-zero, demonstrated rather than described.

Then a load test with hey: about 10 seconds at 100 concurrent requests. The slowest request took 1.6 seconds, and the report showed 4,390 requests per second in total.

## How do you kill the cold start?

That 1.6-second slowest request is the cold start: the first requests wait while Knative scales up from zero. The fix is a second YAML with autoscaling annotations:

- target of 10 concurrent requests per pod,
- target utilisation of 80%, so a new pod starts at 8,
- minScale of 2, so it never drops to zero,
- panic window and panic threshold percentages for sudden bursts.

Applying it creates revision two with two pods that stay up. A describe on one pod explains why each shows two containers: your user container plus queue-proxy, the sidecar Knative injects. The same load test then shows a much lower slowest request and slightly better throughput, though he does not read out the new figures.

## Who should watch

Kubernetes engineers curious about serverless without leaving the cluster, and anyone who has felt a Lambda cold start and wondered what owning the dial would look like. It skips Eventing entirely, and production installs (done by hand rather than with quickstart) are mentioned but not shown.

Title: Kubernetes cuts your inner loop from 70 iterations a day to 40
Description: Edidiong Asikpo (Ambassador Labs) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on the slow Kubernetes inner dev loop and closing it with Telepresence intercepts
Body:
Moving to Kubernetes quietly takes away about 30 code iterations a day from every developer. At Conf42 Kube Native 2023, Edidiong Asikpo, Developer Advocate at Ambassador Labs and CNCF ambassador, lays out the arithmetic of the inner dev loop, compares local and remote development honestly, and then shows the middle path with Telepresence, the CNCF tool Ambassador Labs maintains. Expect a vendor demo, but one built on a problem every Kubernetes team recognises.

## Where do the 30 lost iterations go?

The talk splits developer experience into the inner loop (code, build, test, until you are happy enough to push) and the outer loop (merge, canary, deploy). Cloud native changed both: more steps in the inner loop, and developers dragged into the outer one.

The worked example: six hours of coding a day and a five-minute loop. Three minutes writing code, one building and reloading, one checking the change, ten to twenty seconds committing. That gives about 70 iterations a day, and the only tax is the commit. Containerise the same workflow and every change now waits to be built into an image, pushed to a registry and deployed to a cluster before you can see it. Iterations drop from 70 to 40.

The usual reaction is to treat the wait as a break: "let me go grab a cup of coffee. Let me quickly watch like a Netflix episode while my code is containerizing." The cost spreads further than the developer. Frontend engineers wait for backend previews on a shared environment or code against mocks; backend engineers wait for CI/CD to deploy before they know their change works; releases slow down, and users sit with bugs longer.

## Local or remote: pick your pain

Running everything locally keeps breakpoints, hot reload and fast logs, and it costs nothing in clusters. But the mock API scripts must stay current across a whole team (stale mocks are how bugs reach production), and the laptop turns into a space heater. Remote development fixes the maintenance and the temperature, since CI keeps shared dependencies fresh, but every developer needs a cluster, the build-push-deploy loop is back, and so are the 40 iterations.

## What is the remocal option?

Telepresence connects a laptop to a cluster with a two-way proxy. You run only the service you are changing locally; everything else stays in a shared cluster. That combines low cost, low maintenance, a normal laptop temperature and a fast loop, which Ambassador Labs calls remocal development.

There are two intercept modes. A global intercept sends all traffic for a cluster service to your local copy. A personal intercept only reroutes requests that carry a specific HTTP header, so colleagues on the same shared cluster keep hitting the real service. Under the hood a sidecar agent next to the service checks each request and hands matching ones to the traffic manager, which forwards them to the laptop.

## The demo, step by step

The demo app, Edgycop, has a data processing service that the presenter owns, a very large Java service owned by another team (no code access) and a very large data store holding years of critical test scenarios. Neither of the large ones fits on a laptop.

- `telepresence connect` merges the laptop's routing table and DNS with the cluster, so the Java service answers to its cluster DNS name with no port-forwarding.
- The local data processing service starts on port 3000 with `python3 app.py`.
- `telepresence intercept` on that service with port 3000 creates a global intercept: the web app's colour flips from green to blue, served from the laptop.
- `telepresence leave`, then a personal intercept with an HTTP header: the page stays green until a browser header extension adds the key-value pair.
- Change blue to orange in the code, save, reload, and the change is live in the cluster flow. No image built.

A customer before-and-after follows: from running every microservice locally to running one, and from code-build-push-deploy-wait-test to code-intercept-test. The company is not named and no numbers are given.

## Who should watch

Developers on teams where a one-line change still means waiting for an image build, and platform teams weighing shared dev clusters against per-developer ones. If you already use Telepresence, Skaffold or Tilt daily, the iteration arithmetic is the reusable part: it is a good slide to show a manager.

Title: cdk8s turns 45 lines of Kubernetes YAML into 13 lines that say what you meant
Description: Robert Hoffmann (AWS) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on cdk8s and cdk8s+, writing Kubernetes manifests as typed, reusable code instead of copy-pasted YAML
Body:
An HTTP echo server on Kubernetes takes about 45 lines of YAML: a Deployment, a Service and an Ingress, with the same label and port repeated everywhere and names that must match by hand. At Conf42 Kube Native 2023, Robert Hoffmann, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, rewrites it with cdk8s, then with cdk8s+, and lands at about 13 lines of TypeScript that read like a sentence. His argument is less about saving keystrokes and more about writing infrastructure for humans.

He opens by confessing he hates YAML, and that there were times he "could swear that yaml, it really stands for yelling at my laptop." A crowd-pleaser, and a fair description of the problem.

## What is wrong with plain Kubernetes YAML?

His list is short and familiar. One logical change means edits in several places. That leads to copy-paste, or to a templating engine. Sharing needs a special package manager such as Helm. The total is high cognitive load spent on details nobody cares about, like making sure the Service selector matches the pod labels.

## How does cdk8s work?

cdk8s (Cloud Development Kit for Kubernetes) is an open-source framework and CNCF sandbox project. You write code in TypeScript, Python, Java or Go, run `cdk8s synth`, and get plain vanilla Kubernetes manifests with no trace of where they came from. It sits next to AWS CDK and CDKTF (which outputs Terraform), and shared constructs live on Construct Hub at constructs.dev.

The lifecycle he walks through:

- `npm install -g cdk8s-cli`, then `cdk8s init typescript-app` (or go, java, python) to scaffold a project.
- `cdk8s import` to generate classes for a given Kubernetes API version. The neat trick: feed it a CRD and you get classes for that too. His example is the Jenkins operator, so Jenkins instances become typed objects.
- Write a Chart class (one Chart becomes one manifest) and add constructs to it, then instantiate an App.
- `cdk8s synth`, then deploy however you already deploy: `kubectl apply` on the dist folder, or commit the output to Git and let your GitOps tooling pull it.

Because it is a real language, you get code completion, inline docs and types. You can pull the port and labels into one variable. You can skip naming the Service at all: cdk8s generates a unique name and you reference it from the Ingress. Package the result as your own construct and publish it to an internal or public artifact repository like any library.

## Where do the 13 lines come from?

From abstraction, which he calls the main benefit of programming that the first rewrite has not used yet. cdk8s has construct levels. L0 is the bare API object. L1 is the auto-generated Kubernetes kinds (`KubeDeployment` and friends) produced by import. L2 is handcrafted, high-level constructs, and that is cdk8s+.

With cdk8s+, the echo server is a `Deployment` with a container and a call to `exposeViaIngress`. Under the hood it still creates the Deployment, Service and Ingress and wires the labels, ports and references between them. You never see that wiring, and since it is the same every time, as he put it, "You can only mess it up." He ties it to Robert C. Martin's clean code: the code tells a story (create a deployment, expose it via ingress) that a reviewer can read, instead of a bag of objects linked only by matching strings. Teams can bake security defaults into their own constructs and hand them out as a platform.

## When should you not use it?

He is upfront about three cases. You like your existing tools: fine, but cdk8s can import existing YAML manifests, so mixing is allowed and a small new project is a good place to try it. You don't like coding: control flow can make infrastructure code complicated, though in his experience cdk8s code reads top to bottom. And you author Helm charts: cdk8s can deploy a chart with parameters but cannot create one, which at the time was the area of planned features he wanted Helm users' feedback on.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers drowning in Helm templates and Kustomize overlays, and developers who keep avoiding the Kubernetes side of their service because of the YAML. It is a clear, well-paced 101 with code on every step; if you already ship cdk8s, the construct-levels section is the part worth your time.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Abhishek Gupta on [removing YAML by writing Go code](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2022_Abhishek_Gupta_building_apps_removing_yaml_writing_go_code) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022.

Title: The OpenTelemetry Collector config is where you swap observability tools
Description: Jhonnatan Gil Chaves (Globant) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on Kubernetes observability with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Jaeger and Grafana on EKS
Body:
If you want to see what a full open-source observability stack looks like on Kubernetes before you instrument a single service of your own, this is the talk. At Conf42 Kube Native 2023, Jhonnatan Gil Chaves, DevOps Engineer at Globant, builds an EKS cluster, installs the official OpenTelemetry demo with one Helm chart, and walks through metrics in Prometheus, traces in Jaeger and dashboards in Grafana. His most useful point: once the OpenTelemetry Collector sits in the middle, changing backends is a config change, not a project for every development team.

It is an introductory talk with a long demo. The first half is a Kubernetes and observability primer; the second half is where the value is.

## Why do you need eyes inside the system?

He opens with a short tour of Kubernetes architecture (control plane, etcd, kubelet, kube-proxy, pods) and then the CNCF glossary definition of observability: a system property that defines how well the system generates actionable insights from its external outputs.

His picture of the problem is a request travelling from customer to firewall, load balancer, frontend, backend, database and archive, split across microservices. Any hop can fail, and without instrumentation the engineer in the middle (his "spidey guy") has no way to tell which one. Hence the golden triangle: logs as unstructured records of events, metrics as structured quantitative measures (CPU, memory, disk), and traces as the record of how one request jumps between services. Traces are the hard one, he says, and the one that pays off most in distributed systems.

## How big is the open-source menu?

He counts the CNCF's observability and analysis category at the time: 98 monitoring tools, 21 for logging and 18 for tracing, paid and open source mixed. His picks are short: OpenTelemetry for instrumentation, filelog for logs, Jaeger for traces, Prometheus for metrics and Grafana on top. OpenTelemetry gives you auto-instrumentation (one line, or a sidecar on Kubernetes) and manual instrumentation for the parts auto can't see, depending on how mature the team is. eBPF gets a mention as the other approach, focused on efficiency, with a pointer to further reading rather than a deep comparison.

## The Collector is the seam

The architecture section is the part to rewatch. The OpenTelemetry demo ships microservices in .NET, C++, Erlang, Go, Java, JavaScript, Kotlin, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust and TypeScript, all exporting to an OpenTelemetry Collector. The Collector config defines receivers, processors and exporters; Prometheus gets the metrics, Jaeger gets traces over gRPC, and Grafana reads both.

Don't like Jaeger? Remove it from the pipeline and add another exporter. The services don't change. As he put it, you "remove this responsibility for the development team and you add this responsibility for the it guy." That is the real argument for OpenTelemetry in a polyglot shop, and it is made with a working example rather than a slide.

## What does the demo show?

The cluster comes up with eksctl on Kubernetes 1.27, about 20 minutes of waiting compressed into a cut. Then `helm repo add` for the OpenTelemetry charts, one `helm install` of the demo, and a `kubectl port-forward` to reach the web store and Grafana. He browses the shop to generate traffic and tours the preinstalled dashboards: per-service CPU and memory recommendations, error rate and latency; the Collector's own receiver, processor and exporter stats, including accepted versus refused data; and span metrics with per-endpoint latency.

The finale is a Jaeger trace for a single request fanning out to checkout, cart, product catalog and currency services, which is the moment the golden-triangle diagram turns into something you can click. The demo code is on his GitHub (jthan24/conf42-kubenative-observability), with a sensible warning not to run it in production.

## Who should watch

Engineers starting on Kubernetes observability who want the shape of an OpenTelemetry pipeline end to end, and team leads deciding whether to standardise on the Collector. If you already run OpenTelemetry in production, skip to the demo or pick one of the deeper talks below.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Nicolas Frankel on [tracing with OpenTelemetry](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Nicolas_Frankel_opentelemetry_tracing).
- Zameer Fouzan on [OpenTelemetry tracing for beginners](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2024_Zameer_Fouzan_opentelemetry_beginners_tracing).

Title: GitOps flips the pipeline from push to pull, and it is still not magic
Description: Frederic Harper (Kubefirst) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on GitOps as pull-based CD with Git as the only source of truth, pros and cons included
Body:
The one change that makes GitOps different from the DevOps you already run: the CD side stops pushing and starts pulling. At Conf42 Kube Native 2023, Frederic Harper, Principal Developer Advocate at Kubefirst, gives a 30-minute, deliberately honest intro to GitOps: the four OpenGitOps principles, a real repository layout, a live Argo CD demo with a live-demo hiccup, and a list of cons that most GitOps talks politely skip.

It is a first talk on GitOps, and it says so. If you already run Argo CD or Flux in production, this one is a refresher; if you are about to, it is a good evening.

## What actually changes when you go from DevOps to GitOps?

In the familiar setup, application code sits in Git and a CI/CD pipeline validates it and pushes it somewhere. Infrastructure as code (Terraform is his example) joins it in the repository. GitOps splits CI from CD: CI keeps doing whatever it did, but the CD part now lives inside the cluster and pulls the desired state from Git, which becomes the source of truth instead of the server.

That has a side effect security people like. Your CD pipeline no longer needs credentials to the cluster, because nothing reaches in from outside. As he puts it, the agents run inside the cluster, so there is "no need for the CD to have access to the server."

## What does a GitOps repo look like in practice?

He opens the repository the Kubefirst CLI generated for his own cluster, as one example rather than a sales pitch. A registry folder holds the Kubernetes YAML that Argo CD reads, using the app-of-apps pattern. A Terraform folder manages three things: the Git repositories tied to the cluster (via a Terraform provider), the users (add a developer by committing a file), and secrets in HashiCorp Vault wired to the preinstalled apps. Users managed by commit sounds odd at first; he admits it, then explains why it is the point.

## The four principles, and why the fourth one matters

He walks through the OpenGitOps principles: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, and continuously reconciled. The last one does the heavy lifting. Agents compare the cluster's actual state with what Git declares and keep applying the declared state, which kills cluster drift.

His description of drift is painfully familiar: something breaks in a pod, you SSH into prod, fix it, "it's going to be beautiful and you're going to forget about it." That fix now lives only on one server. With GitOps, there is nothing on the server that Git does not know about.

The listed benefits follow from that: familiar Git workflows, change history and easy reverts, pull requests as code review for infrastructure, reproducible environments, simpler access control, and a stateless disaster-recovery story because there is no server state to recover.

## So what are the cons?

This is where the talk earns its keep. The learning curve is steep if Git, infrastructure as code or DevOps practice are new to you. Every change goes through a PR, which is more approval layers (a feature to him, friction to some teams). Customising the process is harder, the model is Kubernetes-centric, and things can still go wrong between Git and the CD agent depending on your tooling. And the closing caveat, which belongs on a sticker: "it's not magic. It doesn't fix bad practices."

## The demo, hiccup included

In Argo CD on a local k3d cluster, he adds a Flappy Bird Helm chart as a single YAML file, commits straight to main ("the unthinkable", strictly for the demo), and syncs. Argo CD briefly shows the app out of sync, a page-not-found appears, a chart version gets fixed, and then it deploys. It is a fair picture of what reconciliation feels like on a real afternoon.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving onto Kubernetes who keep hearing GitOps and want the model, the trade-offs and one concrete repository layout in half an hour. He points to the OpenGitOps project, Weaveworks' awesome-gitops list and the open-source Kubefirst repo as next steps.

Title: From Ballerina service to running pod without writing a line of YAML
Description: Anuruddha Liyanarachchi (WSO2) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on Ballerina, a language whose compiler writes your Dockerfile and Kubernetes manifests
Body:
Anuruddha Liyanarachchi, Technical Lead at WSO2, demoed at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 the party trick that makes Ballerina interesting to Kubernetes people: write an HTTP service, run bal build --cloud=k8s, and the compiler hands you a Docker image, a Deployment, a Service and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, ready for kubectl. The broader pitch is a language built for integration, where network endpoints, JSON and concurrency are first-class rather than bolted on through a framework.

It is a WSO2 talk about WSO2's language, half overview and half live demo, with the demo the stronger half.

## What is the integration gap?

His framing: modern apps are mostly conversations with endpoints (databases, SaaS APIs, devices), and "integration is the discipline of resilient communication between endpoints," Anuruddha Liyanarachchi said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023. Doing it well means transactions, compensation, circuit breakers, discovery, protocol handling and mediation.

Historically you picked one of two sides. ESBs, EAI and BPM tools understand integration but aren't agile. General-purpose languages like Java and Node are agile but don't understand integration, so you add Apache Camel or Spring Integration and inherit their complexity and learning curve. WSO2 says it has worked on more than 1,000 integration projects and that nearly every one landed on one side of that gap. Ballerina, developed at WSO2 since 2016 and first released in February 2022, is its attempt to close it.

## What makes Ballerina different?

- **Network primitives in the language**: services, resources and clients are syntax, not annotations.
- **Structural, flexible typing**, used both for static checking and for describing service interfaces.
- **Type-safe, declarative handling of JSON, XML and tables**, plus language-integrated queries.
- **Code and sequence diagram are the same program.** The VS Code extension renders any function as a sequence diagram and lets you edit either side. His example pulls open pull requests from GitHub and writes them to Google Sheets.
- **Concurrency** through language-managed threads called strands, with safety checks.

The tooling list is long for integration work: OpenAPI, GraphQL and AsyncAPI client and service generators, a FHIR/HL7 tool, EDI tooling, a graphical data mapper, entity-relationship diagrams generated from records with SQL to match, remote debugging and an architecture view across multiple services.

## How many ways can you ship it?

bal build gives an executable JAR; bal build --graalvm a native image; --cloud=docker generates the Dockerfile and image, and combining the two gives a GraalVM container. --cloud=k8s adds Kubernetes manifests. There is built-in support for AWS Lambda and Azure Functions too. Programs emit OpenTelemetry-compatible observability data without extra code, and logs can be shipped to Elasticsearch.

## What does the demo build?

A geodata service on port 9090, on Ballerina Swan Lake Update 7. Pass it an IP address and it calls IP-API for latitude and longitude, passes those to a weather API, and returns a merged record: city, country, ISP, temperature, conditions. The API key is a Ballerina configurable read from the environment. curl locally says one IP is in the United Kingdom, where it is raining heavily, which is the most believable output of any demo at the conference.

Then Kubernetes, on Rancher Desktop. He adds a readiness resource through the graphical editor and watches the code appear, then a Cloud.toml with the image name and tag, a ConfigMap reference for the API key and a readiness probe. The first build fails, and the useful part is why: the compiler checked the probe path against the actual service resources and caught his typo. Fixed, the build produces the image and manifests: a ClusterIP Service on 9090, a Deployment with the ConfigMap injected and a 30-second readiness delay, and an HPA. kubectl create, wait out the probe, expose as a NodePort, and the same curl works against the cluster.

## Who should watch?

Integration developers stuck between an ESB and a pile of Spring config, and Kubernetes folks curious what a language with deployment knowledge baked into the compiler looks like. If you already write Ballerina, it is a summary of the toolchain.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Anupama Pathirage on [Kubernetes deployments with Ballerina](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Anupama_Pathirage_kubernetes_ballerina_deployments) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

Title: Run the end-to-end tests before CI does, with KUTTL and a kind cluster
Description: Ram Mohan Rao Chukka (JFrog) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on moving Kubernetes end-to-end tests to the laptop with KUTTL to cut broken builds
Body:
Ram Mohan Rao Chukka, Senior Software Engineer R&D at JFrog, answered the question every team lead eventually shouts across the office, who broke the build, at Conf42 Kube Native 2023. His answer: whoever pushed code whose end-to-end tests only ever ran on the remote CI server. The fix his team adopted is KUTTL, the KUbernetes Test TooL, which lets developers run the same Kubernetes end-to-end suite locally against a throwaway kind cluster before opening a pull request.

It is a practical talk with a live demo: the problem, the tool's three building blocks, and a suite that installs JFrog Artifactory four times and checks it came up.

## Why do end-to-end failures cost so much?

Because of the round trip. In the usual flow, a developer writes the feature and unit tests, pushes, opens a PR, and the end-to-end tests run on CI, sometimes for hours. If one fails, they dig through remote logs, fix, push again, wait again. Chukka says his team found most developers weren't running integration and end-to-end tests locally because the environments were too hard to set up and administer.

The broader goal is a development environment that is set up with a single click, lets you develop and test locally, and matches production, so a new joiner spends minutes rather than a day or two following wiki pages, and production bugs reproduce on a laptop. Local end-to-end testing is the missing piece: run the suite, fix with git commit --amend until it passes, then open the PR.

## What is KUTTL?

A toolkit from the KUDO project (kudobuilder on GitHub) for writing tests, mainly designed for Kubernetes operators and controllers but able to test any Kubernetes object declaratively. The appeal is that tests are YAML, not Go or Java code polling the API server. "So Kuttl provides a Yaml based declarative way of doing testing, which would mean you don't need to learn a new language," Ram Mohan Rao Chukka said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023.

Install it with Homebrew from the kudobuilder tap, as a kubectl plugin via krew, or as a Go library for API integration. It has three parts:

- **TestSuite**: the suite config. Set startKIND to true and KUTTL spins up a kind cluster on Docker Desktop for you; set it false to use an existing cluster. It holds the test directories, setup commands and a timeout (300 seconds in his example, after which the suite fails).
- **TestStep**: the actions, including arbitrary commands, so a Helm install or a shell script fits in.
- **Assert**: the state you expect. For a StatefulSet, readyReplicas: 1.

Tests can run in parallel; his example suite uses eight.

## What does the demo show?

kubectl kuttl test creates the kind cluster, runs the suite's setup (adding the JFrog Helm repo), then four tests that each install Artifactory, a stateful application, into a fresh namespace and assert the replica is ready. He watches it in K9s while it runs, which takes five to ten minutes. As each assertion passes, KUTTL deletes that test's namespace. At the end it emits a report in XML or JSON for CI, plus detailed console logs. Change the expected replica count to two and the failure says exactly what was expected and what it found.

A tip from the docs he shows: kind can preload images so repeated runs don't pull them every time. Beyond install tests, he notes KUTTL can assert on API responses too.

## Who should watch?

Teams shipping Helm charts or operators whose PRs keep failing in CI on things a local run would have caught, and anyone who has written a few hundred lines of Go just to check a pod became ready. If your end-to-end suite already runs locally in minutes, you are ahead of the talk.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Rohit Mishra on [how Kubernetes operators work](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Rohit_Mishra_deepdive_kubernetes_operators) at Conf42 DevOps 2024.
- Julien Breux on [testing with Testcontainers](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Julien_Breux_test_testcontainers_container) at Conf42 Golang 2024.

Title: Move Kubernetes troubleshooting into the chat where the team already is
Description: Maria Ashby (Kubeshop) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on five Kubernetes troubleshooting practices and running them from Slack with Botkube
Body:
Maria Ashby, Developer Advocate at Kubeshop working on the open source Botkube project, argued at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 that Kubernetes troubleshooting is slow less because of the bugs and more because of the workflow: alerts in one tool, kubectl in another, context in somebody's head and a teammate in a different time zone. Her five best practices boil down to putting the alerts, the commands and the history in one shared place, and her demo puts that place in Slack.

It is a vendor talk for an open source tool, short and practical: five principles, then a live setup.

## Why does a five-step fix take a day?

Her example is OOMKilled. The textbook procedure has five steps: identify the terminated pod, check its memory usage, read its logs, update the image, raise the memory limit. Five steps sounds manageable, she says, until each one fans out into sub-steps, and then you multiply it across several clusters, several observability tools and a team with uneven Kubernetes experience. That is how minutes become hours or days.

Her framing of the developer experience problem is the line many platform teams will recognise: "nowadays if you're a developer working with kubernetes, you're almost forced to be kubernetes expert just to know the status of your applications," Maria Ashby said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023.

## What are the five practices?

1. **Centralise monitoring and observability**, so everyone works from one shared context and source of truth.
2. **Keep incident response and collaboration in one place**, not split across an alerting channel and a separate war room.
3. **Establish a feedback loop**: keep a record of past incidents and commands so you learn from them. Ashby's background is industrial and systems engineering, and she puts it in those terms: "you can't have continuous improvement without having data to back it up."
4. **Streamline command execution**, so one command can run against multiple clusters instead of being repeated per cluster.
5. **Automate observability and delivery**, so the routine first moves of every investigation happen without a human typing them.

None of these need Botkube. They are worth stealing whatever chat tool and bot you use.

## How does Botkube map onto them?

Botkube connects a cluster to Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord or Mattermost. Sources (Kubernetes events, Prometheus, plus a plugin system) push alerts into channels; executors (kubectl, Helm, plugins) let you act on them from the same thread. You can route alerts per channel, so the front-end channel doesn't drown in everything the platform channel needs to see. A hosted web app keeps an audit log of events and commands across clusters, which is her feedback loop, and handy for spotting whose command ran just before things fell over.

Actions handle the automation: her example runs kubectl logs automatically whenever an error event arrives, so the logs are already in the thread when someone looks. With alerting and actions in place, she says, the five-step OOMKilled routine shrinks to two.

## What does the demo show?

A fresh instance created in the web app, added to a Slack workspace and a production channel, installed into the cluster with a copy-paste Helm command. Then, in Slack: a ping, the help listing, kubectl get pods built with interactive buttons instead of typing, a failing pod's alert, a describe, log output filtered down to the lines that matter, a Helm list, and an automation that runs describe whenever a resource such as an Ingress is created. Executors can be trimmed in the web app if you want a read-only channel. The last trick is a ChatGPT-backed plugin called Doctor, asked what a Kubernetes Ingress is, as documentation without leaving the chat.

The intro promises a Microsoft Teams and Azure setup; the demo itself runs on Slack.

## Who should watch?

Platform teams supporting developers who don't want to learn kubectl, and on-call engineers tired of copying logs into chat by hand. If your team already runs mature ChatOps, the five practices are the reusable part.

Title: Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: teams have to want the platform
Description: The Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 roundup - 12 talks on platform adoption, APIOps and ChatOps, AWS networking, service meshes, cost and incidents.
Body:
[Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023](https://www.conf42.com/platform2023) went out on September 7 with 12 talks, at a moment when platform engineering was still busy explaining how it differs from DevOps with a new logo. The answer the speakers kept giving was practical: a platform is a product, its users are other engineers, and if those engineers don't want to use it, it doesn't matter how good the Terraform is. Around that sat a solid layer of plumbing (AWS networking, service meshes, microservice calls) and the operational questions every platform team inherits: cost, observability and incidents.

Speakers came from Kong, AWS, Expedia Group, Citigroup, Silicon Valley Bank, Zuhlke Group, Mattermost, MY.GAMES, EPAM, Solo.io, Fiberplane and Coralogix.

## How do you get teams to adopt a platform?

[Caio Medeiros Pinto](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Caio_Medeiros_Pinto_3_practices_to_ensure_a_smooth_platform_engineering_ad) of Citigroup gave the getting-started talk, built on his own experience: three practices for getting a platform team adopted, and a frank view on who needs one. In his framing, platform engineering is for medium and big companies, and the main ways it fails are lack of time and old ways of working and thinking, with adoption itself as the second big risk.

[Romano Roth](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Romano_Roth_the_digital_factory) of Zuhlke Group zoomed out to the digital factory: the industrialisation of software development, with platform engineering as its foundation so teams can actually do DevOps at scale. His line on the human side is the one platform teams should tape to the wall: the teams need to love the platform.

## Self-service, through chat and pull requests

Two talks showed what self-service looks like when it lives in the tools people already use. [Spiros Economakis](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Spiros_Economakis_building_a_platform_with_selfserve_powers_using_chatops_) of Mattermost described building Mattermost Cloud with a platform-as-a-product mindset, then giving engineering and non-engineering teams self-serve powers through ChatOps and GitHub bots, so people trigger platform workflows from chat without knowing what runs underneath.

Gold sponsor Kong brought the API version. [Rick Spurgeon](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Rick_Spurgeon_apiops_amplified_ai_rapid_api_delivery) showed APIOps, DevOps and GitOps principles applied to the API lifecycle, with a chat-based AI tool (Chatblade on the command line) drafting a new API spec, Kong's declarative tooling bridging spec and config, and GitHub Actions deploying through a Kong Konnect hosted control plane. An API built by asking an API for help is a pleasingly recursive demo.

## The network under the platform

[Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Samuel_Baruffi_aws_networking_simplified_a_comprehensive_tour_of_key_featu) of AWS gave a clear tour of AWS networking, from regions and availability zones through VPCs, endpoints and gateways to Transit Gateway and VPC Lattice for service-to-service connectivity. [Atif Siddiqui](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Atif_Siddiqui_cloud_network_segmentation_in_pursuit_of_zero_trust) of Silicon Valley Bank built on the same pieces with a security goal: network segmentation as a zero trust tenet, opening with IBM's figure of $4.35 million for the average data breach and ending with a design of four Transit Gateway route tables (dev, QA, UAT, prod spokes) where all traffic crossing a VPC boundary is inspected.

One layer up, [Rohit Ghumare](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Rohit_Ghumare_sidecarless_service_mesh__is_it_a_dream_or_a_reality_) of Solo.io asked whether a sidecar-less service mesh is real yet, walking through the overhead, cost and operational complexity of sidecar proxies and how Istio's ambient mode, helped by eBPF, takes them out of the pod. [Oresztesz Margaritisz](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Oresztesz_Margaritisz_aspects_of_microservice_interactions) of EPAM explained why all those network calls are costly in the first place, through five forces: latency, availability, reliability, queuing theory and Conway's law. Some rules you can't bend; some problems turn out to be easy once you name them.

## Shipping a game without downtime

[Dmitrii Ivashchenko](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Dmitrii_Ivashchenko_building_a_scalable_ecosystem_for_highloaded_multiplay) of MY.GAMES brought the most concrete platform of the day, the one behind a high-load multiplayer game. Automation is at the centre: TeamCity as the linchpin of CI/CD, git hooks enforcing coding standards before code leaves a laptop, a backend broken into independent services coordinated through Photon Cloud for real-time play, and a game update system built for zero downtime.

## What does the platform cost, and who pays when it breaks?

[Vaibhav Chopra](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Vaibhav_Chopra_optimise_your_platform_cost) of Expedia Group argued for a cost culture rather than quarterly clean-ups, citing Gartner's estimate of close to $600 billion in public cloud spend for 2023 and the FinOps maturity split of 71% crawl, 25% walk and 3% run. His order of operations: cost transparency first, optimisation second, prediction and visualisation after, with compute and spot instances as the first targets.

[Nicolas Takashi](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Nicolas_Takashi_observability_strategies_to_not_overload_engineering_teams) of Coralogix compared three ways to give teams observability without asking each engineer to instrument everything: a proxy, OpenTelemetry and eBPF. And [Ivan Merrill](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2023_Ivan_Merrill_incident_response_lets_do_science_instead) of Fiberplane, drawing on 15 years of monitoring in the financial sector, brought Karl Popper to incident response: stress makes on-call decisions worse, so treat hypotheses as things to falsify, borrow from safety engineering, and stop spending an hour on the wrong theory because the dashboard looked convincing.

## Thanks to the sponsors

[Kong](https://konghq.com/) and [Sleuth](https://www.sleuth.io) were the gold sponsors, with [unpack.tech](https://www.unpack.tech/) as newsletter partner, alongside media partners including [Manning](https://www.manning.com), [Packt](https://www.packtpub.com/), [bpb online](https://bpbonline.com/), [Infosec Conferences](https://infosec-conferences.com), [Dev It Jobs](https://devitjobs.uk/), [Glorium Technologies](https://gloriumtech.com/) and [CodeCrafters](https://codecrafters.io/?r=2qF).

Every talk is on the [Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 page](https://www.conf42.com/platform2023) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCD1FfkoF8-6lJPzNFia-KV). The series returned a year later as [Conf42 Platform Engineering 2024](https://www.conf42.com/platform2024).

Title: Zero trust for microservices without touching a line of Java
Description: Jonathan Vila (Sonar) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on zero trust for Kubernetes microservices with Istio, Keycloak tokens and no app code changes
Body:
Jonathan Vila, Java Champion and Developer Advocate at Sonar, made the case at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 that perimeter security fails the moment one service inside the cluster is compromised, and that you can fix it without rewriting the services. His demo takes two plain Quarkus REST services with zero security code, puts them in an Istio mesh, and ends with every call, external or internal, rejected unless it carries a valid Keycloak token, and egress blocked to everything except an allow list.

He is upfront that it is a simple introduction to zero trust architecture and that his way is not the only way. His stated goal is to spark curiosity, and the demo does the sparking.

## What is wrong with a secure front door?

He opens with the numbers on his first slide: more than 4,100 publicly disclosed data breaches in 2021, exposing 22 billion records. Then the classic setup: a gateway checks every user against the IAM system, and once you are past it, service A calls B, B calls the database, nobody asks again.

His analogy is an office building with security at the entrance and nowhere else. Badge in, and you can walk into almost any room. "But what if I leave the toilet window open?" Anyone who climbs through has the same run of the building. In cluster terms, the window is a CVE like Log4Shell: an attacker lands in service B, and because everything inside trusts everything else, B can now reach service C, its database and the other one too. He notes 866 CVEs in 2022 scored close to Log4Shell.

## What does zero trust actually require?

"So what we are going to do is to assume that everyone in the system could be an attacker," Jonathan Vila said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023. In practice that means:

- **Strong identity for every service**, and authentication on every call, internal included, via mutual TLS or tokens.
- **Know the whole architecture**, so your policies don't block legitimate traffic.
- **Explicit policies** on who can call whom. The product catalogue service never needs the salaries service, so it should not be able to reach it even if someone takes it over.
- **Egress control**: most services have no business calling the internet.

Doing that inside each application is expensive: TLS libraries in every service, legacy code you are afraid to touch, third-party software you have no source for, and a patching treadmill every time a TLS CVE lands.

## How does Istio do it without code changes?

Istio injects an Envoy sidecar into each pod and routes all traffic through it, so authentication, authorization, observability, canaries and rate limiting happen in the network layer. The application has no idea. istiod translates Istio's smaller config objects into Envoy's much hairier ones.

The demo, on a local cluster, runs in stages:

1. Two identical Quarkus services (endpoints hello and echo) answer curl from outside, from each other, and happily call the internet.
2. Label the default namespace for istio-injection and delete the pods; they come back with two containers each. Nothing is secured yet.
3. Apply a RequestAuthentication naming Keycloak as the JWT issuer for workloads labelled app: quarkus, plus an AuthorizationPolicy requiring a token. Now curl gets RBAC access denied, from outside and from inside a pod. Fetch a token from Keycloak, pass it in the Authorization header, and it works again.
4. Switch Istio's outbound traffic policy from ALLOW_ANY to REGISTRY_ONLY in the config map and add a ServiceEntry for google.com. From inside the pod, Google answers and Oracle doesn't.

Kiali, installed with Helm alongside Prometheus, then shows the denied calls on the service graph.

## What does it cost you?

He doesn't pretend a mesh is free. It adds a network layer that can break things when misconfigured, and the configuration surface is large. The upside: you can roll it out gradually (mTLS first, then tokens, then encryption, then who-talks-to-whom policies), and Envoy's filters, including custom ones written in WebAssembly, let you enrich or transform traffic without touching services.

## Who should watch?

Developers and platform engineers running JVM microservices on Kubernetes who have a gateway and a nagging feeling. The demo files are in his repository linked from the talk, which makes it an easy afternoon proof of concept.

- Thibault Koechlin on [crowd power and zero trust architecture](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Thibault_Koechlin_crowd_power_internets_zero_trust_architecture) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021.

Title: Six Kubernetes security tools, one UI - a guided tour with m9sweeper
Description: Jacob Beasley (M9sweeper) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on securing Kubernetes cloud, cluster, container and code with open source tools
Body:
Jacob Beasley, project maintainer of the open source m9sweeper platform, ran what is really a Kubernetes security workshop at Conf42 Kube Native 2023: the four Cs of cloud native security (cloud, cluster, container, code), and for each one the CNCF-world tool that checks it, demoed through m9sweeper's UI. kube-bench, kube-hunter, kubesec, OPA Gatekeeper, Trivy and Project Falco all appear, live. The abstract calls it a lightning talk; the recording is a full workshop, so budget the time.

Beasley says he has run Kubernetes since 2016, holds the CKS and CKA, and leads the SRE team that maintains m9sweeper, so this is a vendor-of-sorts talk for an open source project, and the advice holds whether or not you install it.

## Where should you start locking down?

The API. Almost everything in Kubernetes security comes back to who can talk to the API server and what they can deploy through it. "The majority of our efforts revolve around making sure that access to that API is limited and that users can't deploy bad things with that API," Jacob Beasley said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023.

His baseline before any tooling:

- **Don't expose the API to the internet.** VPN or at least an IP allow list, so a future zero-day finds nothing to hit.
- **Don't make everybody an admin.** Map identity provider groups to namespaced roles.
- **Protect etcd** like the database it is: anyone who can edit it can bypass the API entirely.

He then walks through RBAC vocabulary (Role versus ClusterRole, RoleBinding versus ClusterRoleBinding, users living in your identity provider, service accounts for apps) with a pod-reader role bound to a user named Jane.

## Why run benchmark tools instead of a checklist?

Because Kubernetes has too many settings for a checklist to survive contact with an upgrade. kube-bench, from Aqua Security, runs the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark against your nodes; he recommends running it daily so configuration drift shows up. His demo flags check 3.2.11, kubelet server certificate rotation not enabled, on an Azure Kubernetes Service cluster where not every finding is yours to fix. kube-hunter does the attacker's view: it starts a pod and checks what an app inside the cluster can learn, and in his demo it finds an auto-injected service account token and an API that reveals the Kubernetes version, handy for picking an exploit.

## How do containers actually break out?

He explains the isolation stack: cgroups for CPU and memory, chroot for the filesystem, namespaces for processes, networking and mounts, then Kata Containers or gVisor if you want more. The easy breakout is a root container mounting the host's root filesystem through a hostPath volume. The fix is a security context with allowPrivilegeEscalation false, runAsNonRoot true and privileged false, dropping Linux capabilities you don't need (NET_ADMIN deserves a hard look), care with hostPath, and minimal service account permissions, because a service account that can create pods can create a privileged one.

kubesec scores pod manifests against these rules. Pointed at Project Falco's own pod, it scored minus 32 (minus 39 for criticals, plus 7 for passes), which is fine: Falco legitimately needs to be privileged. Everything else should not look like that.

## How do you enforce policy instead of hoping?

Pod Security Admission, the replacement for Pod Security Policies, gives three presets per namespace via the pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label: privileged, baseline and restricted. Start with baseline. For anything finer, OPA Gatekeeper: constraint templates hold the Rego, constraints hold the parameters. His demo requires a cost-center label on every pod outside the system namespaces (for the FinOps we are all being told to do, he notes), then lists violators, starting with the ingress controller nobody can bill. m9sweeper adds time-limited exceptions on top.

Network policies get a section too, with a fair caveat: they cannot target external hostnames, which is why people reach for Istio egress gateways or Cilium.

## What about images and runtime?

Trivy scans every image running in the cluster, can block deployments over a severity threshold, and m9sweeper wraps it with an exception request flow that emails the security team. Project Falco watches kernel calls via eBPF and Kubernetes audit logs for suspicious behaviour, such as a process opening a file for writing where it shouldn't. Falco is chatty by default; m9sweeper hashes event metadata into a signature so you can group repeats, tune noise per environment and get alerted only on new anomalies.

## Who should watch?

Platform engineers setting up a cluster's security baseline, and anyone studying for the CKS who wants every tool on the syllabus shown working. You can follow along in the free m9sweeper lab on Killercoda.
