Title: Three ways to get telemetry without asking developers to write any
Description: Nicolas Takashi (Coralogix) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on zero-code observability from proxies, OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation and eBPF
Body:
Ask a product team to spend a sprint adding HTTP latency metrics and watch the ticket sink to the bottom of the backlog. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023, Nicolas Takashi, Senior Platform Engineer at Coralogix and a contributor to Prometheus Operator and OpenTelemetry, demos three ways a platform team can hand developers request rates, latency histograms and traces without a single line of instrumentation code: the web proxy, OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation and eBPF. His conclusion is that you rarely have to pick just one.

The talk is almost all live demo, built on open source tools (Prometheus, Jaeger, Grafana, Cilium), with a toy e-commerce checkout that calls a payment service.

## Why should the platform own the boring telemetry?

Takashi splits observability into infrastructure (pods scaling, Kafka disk throughput) and application observability, which is the hard part: p99 latency per service, messages produced to a broker, orders per minute. Frameworks often don't expose any of it, so someone has to instrument code, and that someone would rather ship features. He shows the meme of a product manager hearing "we need to instrument our code" and admits it gets low priority automatically.

His fix is to treat telemetry like CI or Kubernetes: something the platform serves. "You want to consume observability as a service," Nicolas Takashi said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023. Standard technical signals (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka, DB latency) come from the platform, in the same shape whatever language a service is written in, and engineers spend their instrumentation effort only on the business paths they care about.

## The proxy you already run is a telemetry source

Strategy one uses the Nginx (or HAProxy) you probably already have. The demo is a Go checkout and payment service behind an ingress proxy, plus an egress proxy acting as an ambassador container, a bit like a service mesh sidecar. An Nginx image with OpenTracing modules emits spans to Jaeger, and a Prometheus exporter turns Nginx access logs into request counts, status codes and response sizes. Load comes from Vegeta.

You get standard metrics for SLOs and a service map in Jaeger. The limit is honest: the traces only show hops between proxies, so you can't debug what happens inside a service. Two practical tips: if you start today, use the OpenTelemetry Nginx module rather than OpenTracing, and once status codes and paths live in metrics, consider dropping the 200-status access logs to save on storage and network.

## Auto-instrumentation rewrites your code at runtime

Strategy two is his favourite. A plain Flask app, with no OpenTelemetry, Prometheus or Jaeger code in it, gets the OpenTelemetry distro installed in its Docker image and is started through the `opentelemetry-instrument` wrapper. The agent patches the Python code at runtime to start trace contexts and propagate headers on HTTP calls and Kafka messages, the same trick commercial vendor agents use.

Spans go over OTLP to the OpenTelemetry Collector, which he describes as a receive, process, export pipeline. The neat bit is the spanmetrics connector, which acts as both exporter and receiver: it turns spans into call counts and duration histograms and remote-writes them to Prometheus. That powers Jaeger's Monitor tab, an APM-style view by service and operation. In the demo, p99 latency came out around 8 ms for checkout and about 1.5 ms for payment, all without touching the app. On Kubernetes, the OpenTelemetry Operator can inject the instrumentation from a pod annotation instead.

He has strong views on the standard: "And if you are using a vendor which is not supporting open telemetry format, I do recommend you move away from this vendor because it's not good for you."

## eBPF watches from the kernel

Strategy three runs on minikube with Cilium, the eBPF-based CNI, and its Hubble sub-project, which turns network flows between pods into metrics. The traffic comes from Cilium's Star Wars demo, with an X-wing and a TIE fighter sending HTTP requests to the Death Star. The Hubble UI shows who talks to whom, and the Grafana dashboards show L7 HTTP metrics by source and destination workload, with status codes and p95/p99 latency, ready for SLOs and alerts. It's application-level data, not load balancer data, and the language doesn't matter.

He's candid about the gaps. In his setup Cilium only gives metrics, not traces or logs, and the OpenTelemetry eBPF agent was still immature when he recorded the talk. He still calls eBPF a technology you must watch, profiling included.

## So which one?

His comparison table says: proxy and eBPF are technology-agnostic, auto-instrumentation depends on the language. Auto-instrumentation and eBPF give real context propagation, the proxy only between proxies. All three run on Kubernetes, VMs or bare metal, and all produce multiple telemetry types. Then he argues for combining them: proxy metrics for latency closest to the customer, auto-instrumentation for traces, eBPF for network and kernel-level data, and default dashboards and alerts on top so teams get observability on day one.

## Who should watch

Platform teams building a paved road who want a concrete starting point for default telemetry. If you already run the OpenTelemetry Operator across your fleet, the first two demos will be familiar; the comparison and the combine-them argument are still worth the time.

Title: Kubernetes, translated into vSphere for the VM admin
Description: Julia Furst Morgado (Veeam) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 maps Kubernetes onto vSphere concepts, from kube-apiserver as vCenter to pods as VMs
Body:
Julia Furst Morgado, Global Technologist at Veeam, gave the virtualization crowd a Rosetta Stone at Conf42 Kube Native 2023: kube-apiserver and etcd are your vCenter and its database, kubectl is your vSphere Client and esxcli, a pod is roughly a VM, and a worker node is an ESXi host. Her point is that Kubernetes is compute, storage and networking, the same three things a vSphere admin already manages, behind a different API.

It is an introductory talk aimed squarely at people who know VMware well and Kubernetes not at all. If that describes you, or the colleague you keep trying to recruit to the platform team, this is the one to send.

## How did we get from racks to pods?

She traces four stages: physical servers with one application each, virtualization with a full guest OS per VM, cloud as VMs on demand, and containers that share the host kernel and carry only what the app needs. A slide makes the key point that none of these have gone away. The difference she draws is the useful one: a VM virtualises hardware to run many operating systems, while a container virtualises an operating system to run many workloads on one OS instance. That is why containers are light enough to pack many onto a single server or VM, which in most shops will itself be running on vSphere.

## What maps to what?

Her translation table, from the architecture section:

- **kube-apiserver + etcd** ≈ vCenter and its configuration database. The API server is the front end of the control plane; etcd is the distributed key-value store that holds the cluster's state.
- **kubectl** ≈ vSphere Client and esxcli.
- **Pod** ≈ VM, the unit that hosts workloads.
- **Worker node** ≈ ESXi server, running a container runtime (Docker, containerd, CRI-O), the kubelet as the node's agent, and kube-proxy forwarding traffic to pods the way a load balancer fronts VMs.
- **Scheduler** ≈ the placement decision you make when sizing a new VM in vSphere.
- **Pod YAML** ≈ creating a VM with PowerCLI: you declare the name, image, arguments and resources.
- **PersistentVolumeClaim** ≈ the VM's data disk, with the PersistentVolume behind it playing the datastore or NFS export.

The declarative model is the big mental shift. You don't start five instances, you tell Kubernetes you want five, and it keeps reconciling to that number when things break.

## Isn't Kubernetes only for stateless apps?

No, and she calls this out directly. "The biggest myth in the Kubernetes world, and even in the virtualization operations infrastructure world, is that Kubernetes is only for stateless applications," Julia Furst Morgado said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023.

A plain pod with attached storage keeps its data across restarts, but not its identity: it may come back with a new hostname. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable, predictable identity, so in her three-node database example a terminated member comes back as itself and reattaches to the same storage. Deployments handle the stateless side, with ConfigMaps for settings, Secrets for credentials, and rolling updates without downtime.

## How does traffic get in, and who can talk to whom?

Services give a stable endpoint in front of pods that come and go, with ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer types; Ingress routes HTTP paths such as domain.com/gallery and domain.com/basket to different services. Her WordPress example contrasts one monolithic VM with separate pods per component that scale independently. Network policies control pod traffic at OSI layers 3 and 4, and the default, if a namespace has none, is that all ingress and egress is allowed, which is worth knowing before an auditor points it out.

## Who should watch?

vSphere admins being asked to support Kubernetes, and platform engineers who need a shared vocabulary with the infrastructure team. Kubernetes regulars can skip it. She closes by saying hybrid estates running both VMs and Kubernetes are the likely future and mentions Kasten by Veeam for migration and data management, briefly.

- Koray Oksay and Batuhan Apaydin on [running VMs as Kubernetes workloads with KubeVirt](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Koray_Oksay_Batuhan_Apaydin_kubevirt_vms_kubernetes_workloads) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.
- Mary Grygleski on [stateful microservices on Kubernetes with Open Liberty](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Mary_Grygleski_stateful_microservices_open_liberty_kubernetes) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021.

Title: Your tables are APIs, so give them contracts and SLOs
Description: Antoni Ivanov (VMware) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on APIs for data, data SLOs and running the DevOps cycle on pipelines with Versatile Data Kit
Body:
Antoni Ivanov, Staff Engineer at VMware working on the open source Versatile Data Kit, argued at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 that data engineering is missing the thing software engineering takes for granted: APIs. A table that a BI dashboard or an ML model reads from is an interface between two applications, and it deserves a schema, written semantics, SLOs and a release process, just like a REST endpoint. The second half shows how VDK lets a platform team bolt those guarantees onto data pipelines without data engineers having to learn Docker.

He opens with Moneyball, the Oakland Athletics and on-base percentage, to make the obvious-but-true point that data beats gut feeling. Then he gets to the part where the data has to actually be correct.

## Where are the APIs in a data pipeline?

He walks through an e-commerce example. Every application throws off data: the OLTP database, Kafka events, log files, click streams, metrics. Data teams ingest that into a data lake (Snowflake, Redshift and friends), transform it into a dimensional model, train models, and feed BI tools and data-driven products. Each arrow in that diagram is two applications communicating, so each is an API, and in his view almost none of them are treated as one. The source side is the worst: the application developer who owns the OLTP schema rarely thinks of it as a published interface.

His API for a dataset has three parts, shown with a single All Products entity:

- **Schema**: product_id as a UUID, name as a string, category, price as a decimal.
- **Semantics**: product_id unique across all records, name a non-empty string with the latest official name, category from a predefined list, price a positive decimal in a given currency. Be as specific as possible.
- **Access**: SQL tables, pandas DataFrames, Parquet or Arrow.

## What does an SLO for a table look like?

Semantics become accuracy rules, and accuracy rules become data accuracy SLOs. Add the more familiar ones: availability (his example, the products table queryable 99.9% of the time) and freshness (inventory changes visible in the table within one hour). How fresh is fresh enough depends on the consumer: hours for some, seconds for others. Put API and SLOs together and you have what the industry calls a data contract; he points to Chad Sanderson's blog posts for the long version.

## How does the DevOps cycle map onto data work?

Flatten plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor, and the data journey drops in: plan is discovering and exploring data, code and build are ingestion and transformation logic in SQL or Python, deploy is putting the data to use in reports and models, operate and monitor is managing the data so it stays accurate, secure and available.

The friction he describes is a wall between teams. Data teams know the domain and optimise for speed; infrastructure and operations teams optimise for reliability and security. When the lines blur you get stalled development on one side and inefficient operations on the other.

## What does Versatile Data Kit actually do?

VDK is an SDK for writing data jobs in Python and SQL (he compares it to Spring for data), plus a control service and operations UI that deploy and monitor those jobs on Kubernetes. It integrates with Snowflake, Postgres, MySQL and Spark for heavy lifting. The key bit is plugins that intercept both data and metadata.

Demo one: a data team keeps writing SQL big enough to knock over the shared database. Instead of finding out in production, the platform team installs a query-validation plugin that intercepts every statement and rejects ones over a size threshold, so the developer gets the error while running the job locally. "The query wouldn't leave their work environment," Antoni Ivanov said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023. The same hook can enforce data quality rules and data API checks as the model is being written.

Demo two: the control service builds jobs through Docker images, so the operations team can extend the builder image to run standard system tests and strip unneeded execution privileges before any job is released. Fail the tests and the job never deploys. Data engineers never see the containerisation, cron jobs or Kubernetes objects.

He is candid that APIs for data are an open problem and that much of this is direction rather than finished product, and he asks for input on the project's GitHub.

## Who should watch?

Data platform engineers and SREs who inherited the data team's pipelines, and anyone trying to turn data contracts from a slide into something enforced.

Title: During an incident, try to disprove your hunch, not prove it
Description: Ivan Merrill (Fiberplane) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on applying Karl Popper's falsifiability to incident hypotheses
Body:
The most expensive hour in an incident is the one spent proving the wrong theory. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023, Ivan Merrill, Head of Solutions Engineering at Fiberplane, argues that responders should borrow from science: write down a hypothesis, then try to disprove it, following Karl Popper's theory of falsifiability.

Ivan spent 15 years in the financial sector on monitoring and observability, rolling out tools and joining incidents where the stakes were high. The talk mixes those war scars with the resilience engineering research of Richard Cook and John Allspaw.

## Why are incidents so hard?

He uses Allspaw and Cook's definition: incidents are a set of activities, bounded in time, related to an undesirable system behaviour. Not one thing, and not just something broke. And from Cook's How Complex Systems Fail: catastrophe is always around the corner, because the potential for catastrophe is a hallmark of complex systems. Firefighters don't each grab a hose and spray random walls, and tech incident response, still young next to aviation, healthcare or emergency services, too often descends into exactly that.

## What goes wrong in the room?

Ivan lists the pitfalls he has seen:

- **Over-reliance on dashboards and runbooks.** Every team's dashboard is green while the incident rages, the watermelon effect: green outside, red inside. Mean time to innocence is low for everyone. Runbooks are useful, but if the only skill is if X then Y, nobody builds troubleshooting skill or updates their mental model.
- **Guesswork.** Failing over to the second site sometimes works. That is luck, and luck teaches nothing.
- **The wrong hypothesis.** Ivan said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: "Spending a long time on the wrong hypothesis is a massive time sink and can be really, really costly for organizations." Confirmation bias makes us collect evidence for what we already believe.
- **Fear of failure.** Even at 99% certainty, fear of consequences delays action. Responders need psychological safety.

Postmortems have their own traps. Hindsight makes the answer look obvious, so record the context of each decision. Normative language ("The team missed this obvious error") replaces learning with blame; human error should rarely be the conclusion. Mechanistic reasoning collapses a set of contributing factors into one root cause, a Scooby-Doo ending where it was the regional database failure all along.

## Where do humans fit?

Cook's above-the-line, below-the-line model: code and infrastructure are below the line, and we only infer them through our interactions. Humans are the adaptive part of the system, and every change we make adds new ways to fail. Fix the small failures and the next one takes something bigger.

Research on troubleshooting (Jonassen and Hung) finds experienced people lean on case-based strategies, cycling through hypotheses from past incidents. That experience is hard to transfer, and people leave.

## How does falsifiability help?

Map the scientific method onto the incident. The observation is undesirable behaviour. Research means checking monitoring and observability. Form the most likely hypothesis, then experiment, and the key move is in his own words: "we attempt to disprove the hypothesis, right? Disprove, not prove." If it falls, you learned something; take the next one. The first hypothesis you can't disprove becomes the working theory, to narrow or act on.

His written example: a possible explanation for a high error rate is high database latency backing up requests and filling the API's DB connection pool. You can disprove it by checking available connections in the pool and comparing database latency with an earlier period.

Why bother writing it down? It kills bad lines of investigation early, adapts as the incident changes, gives decisions a shared formal language, offers psychological safety through documented reasoning, avoids normative language and leaves context that defeats hindsight bias.

To generate hypotheses he borrows Allspaw's heuristics: look for changes first, then widen the net (many shallow hypotheses, perhaps one or two per team, disproved fast) and remember Occam's razor. He closes with Cook: "All practitioner acts are a gamble." Science can't remove the gamble, but recording your reasoning shrinks it.

## Who should watch

Anyone on call, incident commanders and people who run postmortems. No tooling pitch, despite the vendor badge.

Title: One query, one endpoint - a GraphQL primer for Kubernetes teams
Description: Akshay Bhat (Hasura) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on GraphQL basics and running the Hasura GraphQL Engine on Kubernetes
Body:
Akshay Bhat, Developer Advocate at Hasura, spent his Conf42 Kube Native 2023 slot on the case for GraphQL as the API layer for workloads running on Kubernetes, and on Hasura's GraphQL Engine as the way to get one without writing the resolvers yourself. The core idea fits in one sentence, and he gives it: with GraphQL, "the key idea is to post a query to an HTTP endpoint instead of hitting different HTTP endpoints for different resources."

Set expectations correctly. This is a short introductory talk and a vendor talk: most of it explains GraphQL from scratch, the Kubernetes part is an overview, and the closing section is about Hasura. The abstract promises more depth on combining the two than the recording delivers.

## Why GraphQL instead of another REST endpoint?

Bhat uses the classic example: fetching a user's profile and their address. In REST that is two resources and two calls. In GraphQL it is one query, posted to one URL, that names exactly the fields you want (id, name, address, street, city) and gets back JSON in the same shape as the query. You think of your data as a graph, not a list of URLs.

He lists four benefits:

- **No over-fetching**, because the client names the fields.
- **Fewer round trips**, because related data comes back in one call.
- **Less waiting on the API team**: a front-end developer who needs one more field does not need a new endpoint built for them.
- **Self-documenting schemas**, which is what lets tooling do autocompletion, exploration and code generation.

His mapping for REST people: GET becomes a query, POST becomes a mutation, and subscriptions, for watching data change, have no clean REST equivalent.

## Where does Kubernetes come in?

He gives a quick tour of Kubernetes as the orchestrator (scheduling, scaling, self-healing restarts, the control plane and worker nodes), then names two pain points for teams building on it: data retrieval and API complexity, which he says grow faster than linearly with cluster size. His answer is GraphQL's three verbs: flexible queries for retrieval, mutations to create, update and delete through one well-formed request, and subscriptions for real-time updates in monitoring and management. The agenda promised case studies; in the recording they stay at this level, without a specific deployment walked through.

## What does Hasura add?

Hasura's GraphQL Engine connects to your data sources, such as Postgres or existing REST APIs, and generates the GraphQL schema for you, so the boilerplate for fetching, filtering and pagination disappears. On top of that he highlights subscriptions for live updates, fine-grained authorization rules on the schema, and built-in monitoring and observability of the API.

The demo is brief: Hasura's guide for running the engine on Kubernetes, then a Postgres database connected, its orders and assignment tables tracked, and a query run against them from the console. The links he leaves behind are Hasura's Introduction to GraphQL tutorial and its Kubernetes deployment guide.

## Who should watch?

Kubernetes and back-end engineers who keep hearing GraphQL in design reviews and want the 15-minute version, or teams already sitting on Postgres who want to know what Hasura does before they try it. If you already run GraphQL in production, the more architectural talks below will serve you better.

Title: Istio ambient mesh, or how to stop doubling your container count
Description: Abdel Sghiouar (Google) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on Istio ambient mesh, which swaps per-pod sidecars for per-node ztunnels and waypoint proxies
Body:
Abdel Sghiouar, Senior Cloud Developer Advocate at Google, co-host of the Kubernetes Podcast from Google and a CNCF Ambassador, used his Conf42 Kube Native 2023 talk to explain Istio ambient mesh: the mode that removes the sidecar from every pod and moves the mesh into a per-node proxy called ztunnel, with an optional per-namespace waypoint proxy for layer 7 work. The pitch is the same control plane, a much cheaper data plane, and no pod restarts to join the mesh.

It is an introduction, with no demo, and it moves fast. He says so himself and suggests slowing the video down.

## What does a sidecar actually cost?

He starts with classic Istio. The control plane, istiod, is a stateless deployment in the istio-system namespace. The data plane is Envoy, the proxy open-sourced by Lyft, injected as a second container into every pod in a labelled namespace. Each sidecar downloads its config, policies, the full routing table and certificates for mTLS, then talks directly to the other sidecars' pod IPs instead of the Service's cluster IP. That every-pod-to-every-pod pattern is where the word mesh in service mesh comes from.

Sidecars carry three problems, in his telling:

- **They are invasive.** Labelling a namespace does nothing until you restart the workloads, so teams tend to bundle an Istio rollout into a cluster upgrade, which is two big changes at once and a change manager's nightmare.
- **Protocol gaps.** He first says TCP, then corrects himself to UDP, as the traffic sidecar Istio can't handle.
- **Resources.** Citing the Istio 1.18 benchmark, he puts a sidecar at roughly 0.3 to 0.4 vCPU and 40 to 50 MB of memory for a service handling 1,000 requests per second, per pod.

"Essentially the moment you add istio, you're doubling up the number of containers in your cluster and that's an issue," Abdel Sghiouar said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023.

## How does ambient mesh split the work?

The design goals: non-disruptive to workloads, interoperable with sidecar-based Istio (because real adoption is a migration), and simple to switch on and off. The data path is split into two layers.

- **ztunnel**, a new proxy written in Rust, runs as a DaemonSet, one per node. It is stateless, handles authentication and encryption, and covers layer 4 policy and telemetry. It also keeps the workload identity, so the receiving pod still sees the caller's service account rather than the node's.
- **Waypoint proxy**, still Envoy, runs per namespace and only when you need layer 7: authorization policies that read HTTP headers, advanced traffic management. Also stateless, also scalable.

So if all you wanted from Istio was mTLS, you run the secure overlay and never deploy a waypoint. Joining the mesh no longer means restarts: Istio's CNI redirects pod traffic to the local ztunnel.

## What is HBONE?

The tunnel protocol between ztunnels and waypoints. With sidecars, every client connection to a different port opens a new TCP connection between proxies. HBONE multiplexes the traffic over a single mTLS connection using HTTP CONNECT, which he argues performs better than sidecar-to-sidecar connections.

## Why does Gateway API show up in a mesh talk?

Because Istio is moving its traffic management onto it. He walks through the old way, a VirtualService and DestinationRule sending 95% of traffic to service B v1 and 5% to v2, then introduces the Kubernetes Gateway API as the successor to Ingress: GatewayClass from the infrastructure provider, Gateway for the load balancer, HTTPRoute (plus TCP and TLS routes) owned by each app team, and cross-namespace routing that Ingress could not do. Header-based canaries and weighted splits are native fields instead of vendor annotations that never agree with each other.

The reasons for adopting it are refreshingly short. Reason one, he says, is that no one needs more CRDs. Reason two: Gateway API is an upstream API that every cluster will eventually ship with. He notes Istio and Linkerd both support it for routing already.

## Who should watch?

Platform engineers who skipped Istio because of the sidecar tax, and existing Istio users wondering what ambient changes. If you already run ambient in production, this is a refresher; if you have never touched a mesh, the first ten minutes double as a decent primer.

Title: You can't optimise a cloud bill you can't attribute
Description: Vaibhav Chopra (Expedia Group) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on tagging, chargeback and a cost culture built top-down and bottom-up
Body:
Quarterly cost-cutting sprints treat the symptom; the bill grows back by next quarter. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023, Vaibhav Chopra, Engineering Leader at Expedia Group, argues for a cost culture where efficiency is part of every feature, and lays out the order to get there: know the cost, analyse and predict it, optimise it, then make it everyone's job.

It is a framework talk in the FinOps tradition, and a sensible checklist for a platform team that has just been handed the cloud bill.

## Why bother?

Because cloud is a big slice of operating expenses. Vaibhav quotes Gartner's April 2023 forecast that worldwide public cloud end-user spending would reach nearly $600 billion in 2023. He frames FinOps as DevOps for money, finance and engineering at one table, and cites the FinOps Foundation's maturity assessment: 71.3% of organisations in crawl, 25.3% in walk and only 3.4% in run. Crawl means teams are just getting educated; run means cost is aligned with organisation-wide OKRs set by leadership.

## Step one: know your cost

Vaibhav said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: "Our first target always should be the cost transparency." Optimisation comes after you have a baseline. The flow:

1. Define metadata tags (domain, application) for every cloud resource, whether EC2, S3, EBS or anything else.
2. Enforce them with guardrails and policies so untagged resources don't slip through.
3. Split cost by stage: development, operational and maintenance, including staging that must mirror production and workloads that could run on demand as functions.
4. Visualise it, with traffic trends next to cost trends.

## Step two: analyse and predict

Go from coarse to fine: by domain, then application, then resource type (object storage, compute, networking). For unit economics, form a FinOps focus group mixing finance and cloud people, and agree a cost attribution model that leadership can read at a glance.

Then the data habits: reconcile cloud billing against your own usage data daily or weekly, charge costs back to the owning application or domain (teams don't own a cost they never see), name the top idle and underutilised resources, factor in seasonality such as a festival sale, and predict a quarter ahead before trusting longer forecasts.

## Step three: quick wins, then strategic ones

Short term is the infra layer. Compute is the first bet: idle resources and right-sizing, visible through open source tools such as Grafana and cAdvisor on Kubernetes. Balance spot and on-demand, keeping critical workloads off spot. Switch off what isn't used, like dev environments at weekends. Scale vertically as well as horizontally. And set log retention policies, a cost most teams forget.

Long term is the application layer, designed with cost in mind: language choice (he mentions Rust for resource efficiency), cost as a real factor in buy-versus-build, database choice and sharding, NAT gateway and Transit Gateway traffic, third-party API calls, and data transfer, retrieval and archive costs.

## How do you make it stick?

Run both directions at once. Top-down: put cost into org-wide strategic initiatives, add cost KPIs to OKRs, and add cost optimisation to the definition of requirements so every new task asks whether it could cost less. Bottom-up: show the cost impact of a Terraform or Ansible change at commit time, add retention policies and stale-PR cleanup to CI/CD (his example: dev cluster labs cleaned up after seven days without activity), and alert on thresholds, such as an app that hasn't used its requested CPU and memory in 15 days. Then put the money next to the cores, because people act once they see what their idle requests cost.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers asked to bring the bill down, and managers who want a FinOps vocabulary. There are no case-study savings figures; the value is in the structure.

Title: Your accessibility scanner will happily pass a terrible site
Description: Erissa Duvall (CVS Health) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023 on why automated scanners miss most accessibility bugs and what a real test plan adds
Body:
Erissa Duvall, Accessibility Engineer at CVS Health, gave a first-principles accessibility testing talk at Conf42 Kube Native 2023, and its most memorable moment is a demo: two web pages that look identical, one built from proper semantic HTML and one built almost entirely from divs and spans, and both scoring zero issues in axe DevTools. The takeaway is blunt. Automated scanners are a useful floor, not a verdict, and a real test plan needs humans, assistive technology and users with lived experience.

It is billed as a 101 and it is one: definitions, guidelines, test-plan principles and a tour of free tools. That makes it a good first talk for any team that has just been handed an accessibility ticket and a deadline.

## What counts as a disability, for testing purposes?

Duvall frames disability as a mismatch between a person and their environment, which is a practical definition for engineers because it tells you where the bug is. She sorts the cases by type (hearing, vision, mobility, comprehension), by time (temporary, situational, permanent) and by visibility. A parent carrying a child has a situational mobility impairment; someone panicking has a temporary comprehension one. Your users hit these every day without ever filling in a form about it.

The business case comes with sources. She cites an American Institutes for Research estimate of about $490 billion in disposable income for working-age US adults with disabilities, and the CDC figure of roughly one in four people having a disability.

## Why does accessibility get a reputation for being expensive?

Because teams find the problems last. Her argument for shifting left is the same one you already accept for security and performance: a semantic mistake caught in design is a one-line change, the same mistake found in production is a rewrite.

"Usually it's not accessibility itself that's expensive," Erissa Duvall said at Conf42 Kube Native 2023. "It's the fact that people wait until the very end, find out that they've made a huge blunder, and then they're having to go back and redo everything."

## How much can automated testing catch?

Not much: she puts it at somewhere in the 30% to 37% range of accessibility issues. Scanners also test only what is on the page at that moment, so modals, frames that appear after a click, and layouts that reflow at different sizes slip through. They cannot tell whether an image should be decorative or informative, or whether its alt text means anything at all.

Hence the good-site/bad-site demo. The bad page has null alt attributes on informative images, no nav elements, no headings and a footer that is a div with a list in it. The good page has a header, meaningful alt text, two navs told apart with an aria-label, sections labelled with aria-labelledby and a proper h1-h2-h3 hierarchy. To a screen reader user, one page has a table of contents and the other is a wall of text. To axe DevTools, they are both fine.

## What does a real test plan look like?

Her principles:

- **Shift left**, into design and discussion, not just code.
- **Balance manual and automated** testing rather than trusting the green tick.
- **Nothing without us**: involve people living with disabilities early, and more than one of them, since the same condition presents differently in different people.
- **Screen reader and keyboard first**, because content that works well there tends to work with other assistive technology too.
- **WCAG as a starting point**, not the finish line. Version 2.1 underpins most regulations; AA is the usual target, and the guidelines themselves warn that chasing full AAA can create problems elsewhere.
- **Test across environments**: JAWS, NVDA and Narrator on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iOS, TalkBack on Android, plus multiple browsers.

For ready-made plans she points to VGAR (Visa Global Accessibility Requirements) and the Section 508 ICT Testing Baseline for Web.

## Which free tools are worth installing today?

The tour covers Chrome DevTools rendering options (vision-deficiency emulation, paint flashing), Lighthouse, the accessibility features built into Windows and macOS, the Colour Contrast Analyser from TPGI, Microsoft Accessibility Insights (browser extension, Windows app, CI pipeline option, open source), WAVE, axe DevTools, the W3C Markup Validation Service, and bookmarklets, including ANDI from the US Social Security Administration, used for Section 508 testing. For reading she recommends Inclusive Design Patterns and Inclusive Components by Heydon Pickering and Form Design Patterns by Adam Silver. The links collect on her site, corgidev.com.

## Who should watch?

Developers and QA engineers new to accessibility, and platform teams wondering what to put in the pipeline. Experienced accessibility specialists will know most of it, but the demo is a handy thing to show the colleague who thinks a Lighthouse score of 100 means the job is done.

Title: Istio ambient mesh swaps a proxy per pod for a proxy per node
Description: Rohit Ghumare (Solo.io) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on the cost and latency of sidecars and how Istio ambient mesh removes them
Body:
Every pod in a classic Istio mesh carries an extra Envoy container, and you pay for each one in CPU, memory and milliseconds. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023, Rohit Ghumare, Developer Advocate at Solo.io and Google Developer Expert for Google Cloud, explains why the sidecar became a tax and how Istio ambient mesh moves the data plane out of the pod.

This is an introductory, concept-level talk. If you have never quite understood what a mesh does or why ambient mode exists, it is a quick on-ramp.

## Why a service mesh at all?

Rohit starts with the questions every microservice estate eventually asks: how do you observe interactions between services, secure them, handle timeouts and failures, and control traffic? Before a mesh, developers wrote that operational code into the business logic. A mesh, in his slide's words, is a programmable framework to observe, secure and connect microservices. It handles service discovery and load balancing, mutual TLS between services, traffic shaping and shifting, intention-based access control, metrics and resilience features such as failover.

## What is wrong with sidecars?

In standard Istio, each application pod gets an Envoy proxy as a sidecar, and all L4 and L7 traffic goes through it. That is the data plane. The control plane, istiod, pushes configuration and policies, issues certificates and keeps track of the mesh, separate from the proxies.

Rohit names four costs. Operational complexity, especially in large enterprise deployments where a request hops through several gateways. Applications that have to be mesh-aware. Latency, because every call goes app to sidecar to sidecar to app. And plain cost: deploy the Bookinfo sample and count the extra container in every pod. Changing mesh settings also meant restarting pods.

## What does ambient mode change?

Ambient mesh is an open source contribution to Istio from Solo.io and Google, announced the year before the talk, that defines a sidecar-less data plane. It slices the layers. A per-node component handles L4 (the secure overlay, TCP routing and mutual TLS) by default, and L7 processing is added only where you ask for it with a policy. Rohit said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: "Now you have the proxy for the entire node, right?"

He calls that per-node proxy ztunnel. Applications on the node talk through it, so L4 metrics and mTLS come for free, and you add L7 features like retries or failure handling by configuration. Because the proxy is decoupled from the application, adding a new app to the mesh or upgrading the mesh no longer means restarting your pods. He points to a Solo.io blog post on what ambient mesh means for your wallet for the CPU and memory savings, and to eBPF as the way to speed the data plane up inside the kernel.

On observability, the trade-off is honest: without sidecars you scrape application metrics plus what the node-level proxy provides, and one open question is whether that is enough for troubleshooting or whether BPF can fill the gaps.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers weighing a mesh for the first time, or teams already on sidecar Istio who want the reasoning for ambient mode before reading the docs. Expect diagrams, not benchmarks you can reproduce; for hands-on practice Rohit points to the free ambient mesh workshop and certification at Solo Academy.

Title: Queuing theory explains why your autoscaler won't fix latency
Description: Oresztesz Margaritisz (EPAM) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on latency, availability maths, queuing theory and back pressure between microservices
Body:
Autoscaling buys you throughput, not latency, and most teams find out the hard way. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023, Oresztesz Margaritisz, Chief Software Engineer at EPAM, works through the forces behind every service-to-service call (latency, availability, reliability, queuing theory and Conway's law), then shows four production fixes, ending with a noisy client tamed by per-API-key RabbitMQ queues.

The first half is the physics. The second half is war stories, with numbers.

## What can't you negotiate with?

**Latency.** Light needs about 27 ms to cross the US and back in theory, more like 41 ms in fibre, and 50 to 60 ms between AWS regions in practice. Under load, cross-region replication can stretch to 500 to 600 ms. Every synchronous multi-region write pays it. Research on page load time shows more bandwidth stops helping early, while lower round-trip time keeps helping. That is why scaling out won't fix latency.

**Availability.** Four components at 99% each give a single machine 96%. A client-server-database chain of 99% parts drops to 88.5%. He built a microservices availability simulator to check such numbers.

**Reliability.** A write can fail on the way in, during processing, or on the way back, and in that last case the client can't know whether to retry. That is why two-phase commit struggled at scale and why at-least-once delivery beats exactly-once in practice. A page that needs 100 requests, each 99% reliable, succeeds well under half the time.

## Why think in marbles?

His queuing model uses orange marbles in and green marbles out. With 100 ms per item, one worker does 10/s and eight items take 800 ms. Two parallel workers give 20/s and 400 ms. Split the work into two 50 ms stages and you also get 20/s, but latency stays at 800 ms. Oresztesz said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: "So interestingly, latency did not change, but throughput increased." That, he argues, is the quiet trick of reactive libraries. Separate queues also give each producer its own quality of service, so one greedy client can't starve the rest. And when arrival rate beats departure rate for long enough, you will fail unless you add back pressure or rate limiting.

On Conway's law: service ownership need not mean schema ownership. Move it to whichever side changes more, and use contract tests, schema registries or schema federation as the number of teams on each side grows.

## What did it look like in production?

- **Rapid read protection** (from Cassandra): the coordinator fires a backup request when a replica is slow. With 99% per node, the query lands near 99.99%, and p99 improves.
- **CQRS for a read-heavy, almost immutable workload**: writes go through Amazon SQS to DynamoDB, which smooths bursts and keeps write capacity low. Reads hit Hazelcast replicated across read nodes, so new nodes warm up from their peers and a cache miss gets pushed proactively to the others.
- **A client library from hell**: a shared library downloaded and unzipped a config archive from S3 at startup, slowing every dev environment and failing health checks during deploys. It had no off switch but a configurable URL, so they shifted left with a containerised mock S3 sidecar holding an empty archive and a real one.
- **Region pinning**: a cookie marks a user's home region, and only users whose shopping cart lives in the other region pay the roughly 60 ms cross-region read. An auction system used the same idea, writing bids to the Kafka cluster where the auction started and mirroring them out with MirrorMaker.

## How do you tame a client that sends 15,000 requests at once?

The finale. One client fetched its recent keys, then fired about 15,000 value lookups at once. DynamoDB autoscaling lagged and throttled. A statistics write in the same path forced write capacity to match read capacity.

Step one moved the stats write to its own thread, which leaked memory through Java's effectively unbounded queue (it is sized to the maximum integer) until the orchestrator killed the pods. Step two used Resilience4j: a bulkhead capped at 25 queued items inside a circuit breaker, after which write capacity could finally drop. Retries gave no fairness. Per-instance rate limiting broke as autoscaling added instances. Istio's Redis-backed rate limiting changed the API to HTTP 429s, so they skipped it.

Back to queuing theory. The default client timeout was 30 seconds ("for every library it looks like timeout is 30 seconds"), so 15,000 items means 500 operations a second: 4 ms per item with two workers, a realistic 10 ms with five. The fix was RabbitMQ request-reply queues per API key, with overflow settings and per-queue prefetch, and workers that nack when DynamoDB throttles. In his sandbox rebuild, five workers finished the burst in 30 seconds, as designed, and one run even hit 500 ops/s.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers who own service-to-service traffic, or whoever is about to answer a latency problem with more pods. His slides list plenty of references, and the sandbox is on his GitHub.

Title: Blue-green deploys for a mobile game stuck in app store review
Description: Dmitrii Ivashchenko (MY.GAMES) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on CI/CD, a Vert.x game backend and zero-downtime alpha/beta server switches
Body:
When the client update you need takes days to clear app store review, the server has to carry the fix. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023, Dmitrii Ivashchenko, Lead Unity Developer at MY.GAMES, walks through the three pillars behind a high-load mobile multiplayer game: CI/CD for a large team, a backend built to scale out, and a blue-green deployment scheme where QA flips servers from a game tool.

It is a practitioner's tour of a real stack, with the trade-offs left in.

## How do you keep a big game team shipping?

The CI/CD principles are on one slide: containers for reproducible CI and staging, an emulator farm for testing, test and production servers deployable at the click of a button, as many checks as possible at the merge request stage, and infrastructure as code throughout.

They run both TeamCity (configuration in Kotlin DSL) and GitLab CI (YAML, handy for checks after a push). Autobuilds on the develop and stable branches validate and build server configs, build the server and clients for PC, Android and iOS, launch a server and upload clients to App Center, so a fresh client-server pair with the latest changes appears every one or two hours. On-demand servers give each TeamCity user an isolated, named VM for experiments, deleted automatically twice a week, on Thursday and Saturday nights.

Quality gates sit on both sides of the push. A Unity validation system checks assets and configs for problems such as broken links, with critical validators enforced in builds and merge request pipelines. Client git hooks (installed and auto-updated by a small binary) check commit messages and files; server hooks protect branches, require a rebase before push, validate branch names and enforce commit message formats with regular expressions.

## What runs behind the game?

The backend is Eclipse Vert.x for messaging and clustered runtime storage, Hazelcast as the in-memory data grid underneath it, Apache Kafka as the log broker, PostgreSQL for persistent data and Ansible for configuration. An account server handles authentication and knows every game server. Each game server is a cluster of nodes whose components (front-end TCP gateway, dispatcher, scheduler, DB operation executor, resource system, log system, game mechanics) talk over a common event bus. Gametool ETL moves logs from Kafka into its own database; Gametool Web is the admin console. Services cover PvP, leaderboards, friends, replays, mail, chat, matchmaking, clans and push notifications, with Photon Cloud for real-time multiplayer.

Dmitrii is candid about Vert.x. It supports many languages on a reactor pattern, but code gets complicated when your language isn't fully supported. Quasar was the alternative, but it wasn't actively maintained when they started in 2017. Testing surfaced a lock queuing issue in Vert.x that they reported and the developers fixed. Prometheus and Grafana helped tune the configuration. The current hardware comfortably supports 150,000 concurrent users. When CPU runs out, add servers; PostgreSQL is the likely first bottleneck, eased by deferred synchronisation through Hazelcast.

## Why go blue-green?

Two reasons. Downtime is expensive, as Dmitrii said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: "Even a minute of downtime can have significant financial implications for us". And store review means several server versions must run at once.

The mechanics use a client, two servers named alpha and beta, and the account server, which only stores each server's address and status. Alpha is live, beta stopped. To switch, beta goes live, alpha is marked stopped and broadcasts a reconnect, and clients ask the account server again and land on beta. Players shouldn't notice.

Two refinements followed. A staging status lets QA test the new server first; ordinary players can reach it only by naming it in their login request. And a client mid-battle can ignore the reconnect and finish on the old server.

## How do versions fit in?

They refused to maintain both forward and backward protocol compatibility. The rule: "Client of version X will only connect to server of the same version X". Server changes within a version are fine if the protocol doesn't change. For a 2.0 release, beta goes live after QA as a soft update for a slice of players; fixes go out by moving players with the same blue-green process to a third server, gamma; 1.0 players stay on alpha until a hard update blocks old clients and prompts an upgrade.

The account server keeps its state in its own database, so its instances are stateless, and QA specialists run the whole process from the game tool. The bonus Dmitrii highlights: sometimes a small change to server responses can persuade a buggy client to behave, buying time until the store approves the fix.

## Who should watch

Game backend engineers, and anyone shipping to clients they don't control, such as mobile apps, TVs or embedded devices. The version-pinning rule alone is worth the half hour.

Title: Eight ways floating point lies to you, and the Rust crates that help
Description: Prabhat at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on floating-point pitfalls, from rounding and cancellation to equality tests, and the Rust tools that contain them
Body:
`0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3`, and in 1991 a cousin of that bug sent a Patriot missile defence system off target. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, Rust developer Prabhat maps the ways floating-point arithmetic goes wrong, one issue at a time, and pairs each with a fix from Rust's standard library or its crate ecosystem.

He is upfront about the format: this is a map, not a textbook. He wants you to know which problem you are looking at and where to search next. Most of it applies to any language; the solutions lean on Rust.

## Why care about the last bit?

The opening case is the Patriot failure in the Gulf War. The system tracked incoming Scud missiles using time measured in tenths of a second, and a tenth cannot be stored exactly in binary. The rounding error grew the longer the system ran, and because the radar predicted a missile's position from that time, the prediction drifted away from where the missile actually was.

## How is a float built?

A quick IEEE 754 refresher. Single precision is 32 bits: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits (biased by 127) and 23 significand bits. Double precision is 64 bits: 1, 11 and 52. The standard also defines extended precision (80 bits or more). Everything else in the talk follows from the significand having a fixed number of bits.

## The problems, and what to reach for

- **Limited precision.** Real numbers that don't fit get rounded. Fixes: fixed-point arithmetic with scaled integers (think cents, not euros), arbitrary-precision crates such as num-bigint, and picking `f32` or `f64` deliberately.
- **Rounding errors.** They accumulate across operations. Use decimal arithmetic via rust_decimal, round only when presenting results, avoid divisions where a multiplication will do, and consider interval arithmetic with the inari crate.
- **Loss of significance.** Subtracting two nearly equal numbers throws away the significant bits, also known as catastrophic cancellation. Reorder operations so the subtraction happens late, rewrite the formula algebraically, approximate functions with a Taylor series (his favourite, straight from first-year engineering), or go arbitrary precision with rug or rust-gmp.
- **Associativity.** His example adds the same three numbers grouped two ways and gets 1 in one case and 0 in the other. As he said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023: "So changing orders can lead to different results." Group explicitly with parentheses, order operations so the least lossy parts come first, and look at fused multiply-add, which multiplies and adds with a single rounding (Rust exposes it as `mul_add` on `f32` and `f64`).
- **Equality.** "Trust me, this one is the one which most of you will come across if you ever will work with the floating point numbers in your code," Prabhat said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023. Never `a == b`; compare `(a - b).abs()` against an epsilon (the standard library already ships `f64::EPSILON`), use relative error when magnitudes vary, use ULP comparison via the float_cmp crate's `ulps_eq`, or a fixed tolerance your domain can justify.
- **NaN and infinity.** Zero divided by zero or the square root of a negative number produce special values; `is_nan()` and `is_infinite()` let you check before they spread through a calculation.
- **Compiler optimisations.** Optimisers may reorder or combine float operations and change the result. He points at function attributes such as `#[inline(never)]` and `#[target_feature]`, plus RUSTFLAGS passed to the LLVM backend. This is the thinnest section, closer to a reading list than a recipe, so check the current Rust documentation before changing build flags.
- **Accumulated errors in loops.** Iterative sums drift. His fix is Kahan (compensated) summation, which carries the lost low-order bits forward in a second variable.

## The checklist to keep

He closes with the summary you'd pin above your desk: choose the float type for the precision you need; reach for rug, num-bigint-dig, inari, float_cmp or rust_decimal when accuracy matters; never compare floats directly; run error-propagation analysis to estimate how much error a calculation can accumulate; use Kahan summation in iterative code; control compiler float behaviour explicitly; and test numerical code with diverse inputs, edge cases included, so you don't ship your own Patriot.

## Who should watch

Developers about to write their first financial, scientific or sensor-handling code in Rust, and anyone who has stared at `0.30000000000000004` and wondered how deep the hole goes. Numerical analysts won't learn much new, but the crate list is handy.

Title: A lazy tester, a Java prototype, and a testing language in Rust
Description: Atmaram Naik (Sedin Technologies) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on writing Journey, a scripting language for test data, mocks and load tests, in Rust
Body:
Testers repeat the same chores all day: create test data, poke an API, stand up a fake for a third-party service. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, Atmaram Naik, Test Manager at Sedin Technologies, tells how automating those chores turned into the Journey programming language and its compiler, corr, written in Rust by someone who had never written Rust before. It has since been used at his past and present employers for test data, service virtualization and load testing.

The talk is a project story with demos, not a language-design lecture, and it is candid about what went wrong along the way.

## What does Journey actually do?

The demo uses a to-do REST API on localhost. Running the `create to do` command, the tool stops and asks for a title of type string, then creates the item. `get all to dos` prints the list. `create multiple to dos` asks how many, then whether you want random names, and fills the server with a dozen entries.

The trick is what Atmaram calls correlation. A script refers to `title` without defining it, and the runtime asks whoever invoked the command. As he said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023: "Whatever is not known it will ask the user." Types are checked too: declare an `id` as a positive integer, type text, and it asks again. The create script is eight lines; the list script is six, using a `matching body object result` clause to capture the response.

The reveal at the end: the to-do server itself is written in Journey. It listens on port 9001, matches requests, keeps the to-dos in a temporary variable and responds with 201, 200 or 404. That is the service virtualization feature in miniature.

## Why did the Java version have to go?

The first pilot was plain Java and entirely config-driven: commands were folders and files in a fixed structure, and even control structures lived in config. Colleagues liked the idea and used it on a real project, but the feedback was consistent: commands were hard to write, you had to learn the conventions, everyone needed the right Java version installed, and the tool was restrictive.

So he switched from config-driven to code-driven commands, which meant writing a language, and wrote down what its host language needed: native cross-platform binaries for Mac, Windows and Debian, memory safety for a highly programmable tool, high concurrency for mock servers and load tests, good CLI libraries, systems-level reach, little or no GC footprint (load tests care about every virtual user), and type safety.

## Why Rust over C++ and Go?

All three passed the native-binary, concurrency and CLI-library checks. The difference was enforcement. In C++ memory safety is the programmer's job. Go is memory safe but lets you escape it, and its garbage collector periodically scans the heap. Rust is memory safe, forces it on you through the borrow checker, and has no GC. Rust won despite his inexperience with it.

## What did the project look like?

Three crates and one plugin: corrs, a WebSocket server so commands could be triggered from messaging apps; corr, the compiler that builds distributable packages; a library holding the parsing and execution logic; and an IntelliJ IDEA plugin written in Kotlin for syntax support.

Features came and went with demand. One employer's product integrated with third-party systems that had poor sandboxes, so he added service virtualization and used it to fake more than ten of them. Test data went straight into databases. A WebSocket load-testing need arrived, and because the tool already ran on Tokio's event loop, spawning scripts as virtual users was a small step. corrs was removed for low adoption. A CI/CD pipeline builds a Homebrew formula, Windows installers and Debian installers, because his teams used all three platforms.

## How was Rust as a first-timer?

Honest answer: the usual fights with the compiler, then reward. He needed nightly for some language features and libraries, and where crates were missing or immature he wrote quick ones himself, such as async-rdbc. The stack: nom for the parser and AST, Tokio, hyper, serde and serde_json, clap, futures, async-trait, async-recursion, fake for generated data and mockito for test doubles. Unit, integration and end-to-end tests were the safety net for a side project he might not touch for months; the demo run shows 263 passing.

His verdict, as he said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023: "The feared learning curve with Rust had a minimal impact as the programming settles."

## Who should watch

Testers and QA engineers who script their way out of repetitive work, and anyone weighing Rust for a first real project. If you want parser theory, look elsewhere; if you want to see how a side project survives real users, this is a good half hour.

Title: Mattermost's internal platform is a GitHub label and a slash command
Description: Spiros Economakis (Mattermost) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on dogfooding the SaaS platform as an IDP via GitHub bots and ChatOps
Body:
The best internal developer portal might be the one nobody has to open. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023, Spiros Economakis, Head of Cloud Infrastructure at Mattermost, explains how his team built Mattermost Cloud once for paying customers and then reused the same SaaS platform as the internal platform for developers, sales, support and DevRel, driven entirely from GitHub labels and chat slash commands.

The team motto is build once and for all. The talk is a real case study with real bot names, and it doubles as an argument for dogfooding.

## How did Mattermost Cloud come together?

Spiros walks the software development lifecycle. Planning looked at team capacity, structure, cost and milestones, under a Dev and Ops collaboration model. Requirements (the ideal customer profile, SLOs and SLAs, incident response, scale to thousands of workspaces, security and compliance) led them to add an SRE team that takes code into production once production readiness reviews pass. Four teams came out of it, including SRE, automation and tooling, and delivery.

The design runs on AWS with RDS Aurora and Kubernetes. A command-and-control cluster hosts the customer portal, customer web server and the provisioner, the central point of management that tells the Mattermost operator in worker clusters to create a customer's workspace. A fleet controller does housekeeping, hibernating and deleting inactive workspaces.

## Why test on the production-grade platform?

Testing a SaaS platform at scale with full automation would take a lot of effort, cost a lot and slow the launch. So they chose not to over-automate. They automated the critical paths and used the SaaS platform itself as the golden path for dev, support and demo environments. Internal users became early adopters on a platform identical to the customers' one, which surfaced bugs early and kept the same SLO mindset in test environments.

## What does self-serve look like for developers?

The constraint: developer experience happens only in tools people already use daily, which at Mattermost means GitHub and Mattermost itself.

**Spinwick** is a GitHub bot that watches pull request labels. Add the setup cloud test server label and it comments that it is creating a server; about a minute later it posts the access link and shared credentials. Spiros said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: "So if I remove the label, it's going to destroy the server." Merging or closing the PR destroys it too. Forgotten PRs are handled by the same fleet controller that hibernates idle customer trials, and later deletes them.

**Mattermod** automates the rest of the PR workflow with slash commands in comments: checking that open source contributors signed the contributor agreement, updating a branch from its target, cherry-picking a fix onto release branches (his example is release-8.0), running and cancelling end-to-end tests on the SaaS platform, and labelling stale PRs.

## And for people who never open GitHub?

ChatOps. The Cloud Bot plugin creates and manages test environments from any Mattermost channel or a DM to the bot. Type `/cloud create test-con42`, get an installation started, check `/cloud list`, then receive a DM with URL and credentials when it is ready. Flags compose richer setups for sales or support, for example `/cloud create cloudweek --license e20 --test-data --size miniHA --filestore bifrost`. A monitoring control plane lets anyone read their workspace and provisioner logs.

So the internal developer platform turns out to be a set of small services (Spinwick, Mattermod, Cloud Bot and a few more) over the customer platform. Three control planes, customer, developer and non-developer, all hit the same IDP without knowing what runs underneath.

## What did they learn?

Flexibility and reuse gave confidence that daily changes were stable. The experience has to live where people already work, not in one more new tool. Run surveys and listen to internal and external customers. And use your own product, which Spiros calls the only way to know if what you built is meaningful for customers.

## Who should watch

Platform teams designing self-service before they buy a portal, and anyone with a SaaS product wondering whether its own platform could be the internal one.

Title: Unit tests that read like sentences, built from a doorknob
Description: Joe Skeen (World-Class Engineers) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on four keys to unit testing, from use-case sentences to nested Rust test modules and macros
Body:
Most developers agree unit tests matter and quietly dread writing them. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, Joe Skeen, Developer and Mentor at World-Class Engineers, argues the dread is a skills gap, not a character flaw, and fixes it with a bathroom doorknob: write the behaviour as plain sentences first, then turn each sentence into a Rust test whose name reads back as that sentence.

Joe has been writing code for nearly 30 years, and his diagnosis is blunt. As he said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023: "I've come to the conclusion that most developers are uncomfortable with unit testing simply because they never learned how to do it well." Self-taught developers never hear the term, CS courses mention it without making it stick, and bootcamps leave it off the critical path to a first job. Add a management edict demanding a coverage number and you get people who associate tests with punishment.

## Key 1: break it down into sentences

His running example is a privacy doorknob, the kind with a push button on the inside. Before any code, he names the parts (inside knob, outside knob, push button, latch bolt; the latch plate belongs to the door frame, so it's outside the unit) and starts writing behaviour:

A privacy doorknob, when the push button is not pressed, when the user turns the inside knob, should also turn the outside knob.

Each sentence immediately suggests the next one. Should it retract the latch bolt? Does direction matter? Clockwise on the inside means counterclockwise on the outside. Then the pressed state: the outside knob shouldn't turn at all, while turning the inside knob pops the button out. Then the odd cases: a pin in the outside hole, closing the door on a locked knob, a user applying excessive force. Those last ones are a conversation for the business analyst, which is the point. Given/when/then works too if you prefer BDD phrasing.

It also makes his case for unit tests over end-to-end ones: try listing every permutation for the whole door and the pile becomes unmanageable, while each component can be specified on its own.

## Key 2 and 3: treat test code like production code, and ignore the coverage number

The flat list of sentences is already unreadable, so he nests it: doorknob, then button state, then action, then expected outcomes. Duplication in tests deserves the same DRY instinct as anywhere else.

And coverage isn't the goal. Start from use cases, he says, and you end up close to 100% coverage as a side effect. As he put it at Conf42 Rustlang 2023: "You're not testing to get a certain percentage of code coverage."

## Key 4: arrange, act, assert, then let Rust do the boilerplate

The Rust part is where the talk earns its place at a Rust conference. The nested sentences map directly onto nested `mod` blocks inside `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`, with the last clause as the test function name. The test runner output then reads as the original sentence, something like `when_the_push_button_is_pressed::when_the_user_tries_to_turn_the_outside_knob_clockwise::should_not_retract_the_latch_bolt`. A failing test tells you which requirement broke, in words a non-technical person can follow.

From there he refactors step by step:

1. Each test does arrange, act and assert inline.
2. An `action()` function moves into the module whose name describes that action, so renaming `turn_outside_knob` touches one place.
3. An `arrange()` function moves up to the module that describes the state, here the pressed push button.
4. A `macro_rules! it` macro takes the test name, arrange and action functions, and finally an assertion closure, so every test is one line.

Once that structure exists, he says, AI code completion becomes useful; starting from scratch with AI-written tests disappointed him. His claim on speed: "once you get some momentum, you can pump out over 100 top quality unit tests in under an hour."

## Can you overdo it?

Yes, and he says so. For a function that strips vowels, test classes of input, not every string: empty, some vowels, only vowels, no vowels, very long, and Unicode such as emoji. Ten tests or a hundred is fine, as long as each one is there for a reason.

He admits he's still new to Rust and that the knob implementation could be more idiomatic. That doesn't matter much; the testing approach transfers to any language, and the nested-module trick is a cheap way to get RSpec-style readable test names out of plain `cargo test`.

## Who should watch

Anyone who writes tests because the pipeline makes them, and team leads looking for a way to teach it. Mocking, async and multithreaded testing are out of scope; he leaves those for another talk.

Title: AWS networking in one sitting, from reserved IPs to VPC Lattice
Description: Samuel Baruffi (AWS) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on the core AWS networking toolbox, from VPCs and endpoints to Transit Gateway and VPC Lattice
Body:
Every AWS subnet quietly eats five IP addresses before you deploy anything, and that is one of the gentler surprises in AWS networking. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023, Samuel Baruffi, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS working with global financial services customers, gives a fast tour of the core networking toolbox: VPC basics, security groups and NACLs, gateways and endpoints, Transit Gateway, hybrid connectivity, VPC Lattice and traffic visibility.

It is a survey, not an in-depth design session, and Samuel says so up front: networking fundamentals, not application architecture. As a map of which tool solves which problem, it is a very good one.

## What sits under a region?

At recording time AWS had 32 regions, 102 availability zones and more than 450 points of presence, with Israel the newest region. Each region has two independent, fully redundant transit centres connecting it to the global network; each AZ is one or more data centres with independent power, networking and connectivity.

A VPC is regional and spans the AZs you pick; subnets live in one AZ and are public or private. The primary CIDR block can't be changed, only extended with secondary blocks. In every subnet AWS reserves five addresses: the network address, the VPC router, two reserved for AWS, and the broadcast address. Public IPs come and go with instances; Elastic IPs stay with your account, which is why he recommends them. IPv6 runs dual-stack, with a /56 on the VPC and /64s on subnets.

## Security groups or NACLs?

Both, at different layers. Security groups attach to resources and are stateful: open the port you need and the return traffic is handled. By default nothing comes in and everything goes out. On opening a port to 0.0.0.0/0, Samuel said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: "Unless you know what you're doing, you should always avoid to do zero zero."

The underused trick is referencing groups instead of IPs. His example: the database security group allows TCP 3306 from the web server security group, so it keeps working as instances scale or change IPs. Self-referencing rules let every member of a group (his slide uses a Hadoop cluster) talk to each other. NACLs work at the subnet level and are stateless, so you must allow the ephemeral return ports too.

## How do you leave the VPC, and how do VPCs meet?

- **Internet gateway** for public subnets; **NAT gateway** (in a public subnet, one per AZ for redundancy) gives private IPv4 subnets outbound-only access; the **egress-only internet gateway** does the same job for IPv6.
- **VPC peering** is one-to-one, non-transitive and costs only data transfer. Fine for two VPCs, painful for five, where each VPC needs four peering connections.
- **Transit Gateway** replaces the mesh with one attachment per VPC and central route tables, and peers across regions for multi-region or DR designs.
- **VPC endpoints** keep AWS API calls off the internet. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink ENIs in your subnet) cover most services but cost money; gateway endpoints only do S3 and DynamoDB and are free. Endpoint policies, in the same JSON as IAM, restrict who can use them.
- **PrivateLink** lets a SaaS provider put its app behind a Network Load Balancer and expose it into consumer VPCs privately.

For hybrid: Direct Connect is a private fibre to a Direct Connect location, private but not encrypted by default (add an IPsec VPN on top); Site-to-Site VPN runs IPsec over the internet; Client VPN gives remote developers OpenVPN-based access with split tunnelling and Active Directory or federated auth. Route 53 Resolver handles DNS inside the VPC at the VPC+2 address.

## What does VPC Lattice change?

Lattice, introduced the year before the talk, is service-to-service connectivity across accounts and VPCs without peering, Transit Gateway routes or worrying about overlapping CIDRs. It works at layer 7, so it does path-based routing (his example sends /api/parking and /api/inventory to services in different VPCs), and it applies IAM-based policies so billing can call parking but not inventory. Samuel calls it a mindset change in how you architect.

He closes with VPC Flow Logs (enable them everywhere, query them in CloudWatch or S3) and Traffic Mirroring, which copies every packet to an inspection appliance without touching production traffic.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who inherited an AWS account and want the whole map in one sitting, and anyone who has nodded through a networking review without knowing why NACLs need ephemeral ports.

Title: Rust's ownership rules, explained from the memory leak up
Description: David Oyinbo (HeySummit) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on how ownership and borrowing replace both manual frees and the garbage collector
Body:
Every systems language has to answer one question: who frees the memory? At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, David Oyinbo, Senior Frontend Developer at HeySummit, walks through Rust's answer for people who know the other two. C++ makes you call `delete` yourself; garbage-collected languages do it for you at a time of their choosing. Rust's ownership and borrowing system does neither, and the compiler enforces it.

It is an introductory talk, and a tidy one: a leak, a fix, a comparison with TypeScript, a threading example, then a tour of the optimisations the compiler does so you don't have to.

## Why not just use a garbage collector?

David starts with a C++ snippet that allocates on the heap and never frees. Wrap the allocation in a `while (true)` and you have a crash on a timer. The consequences he lists are the familiar ones: less available memory, slower execution, crashes, resource saturation and code that's painful to maintain.

The garbage collector fixes the leak and adds three problems of its own: runtime overhead, unpredictability and resource spikes when it decides to run. That makes it a poor fit for low-latency work such as games, which is why those teams historically stayed with C++ and manual memory management. Rust's pitch is the third option: no collector, no manual frees, and you can still drop a value yourself if you want to.

## Own it, or borrow it

The core rule fits on a sticky note. As David said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023: "Any data I own, the moment I'm going out of scope, I'm going to destroy them basically and deallocate the memory."

His examples make the consequences concrete. Pass a `String` into a function by value and it moves; the function drops it when it returns, and touching the original afterwards is a compile error ("value has already been moved"), not a dangling pointer at runtime. Pass a reference instead, as in his `calculate_length` example, and the function only borrows: it doesn't own the value, so it doesn't free it, and the caller can keep using the string.

## The TypeScript comparison is the best part

The section worth the evening is a small `User` class with a `set_age` method. In TypeScript, he wants one function that must not modify the user and another that may. `Object.freeze` stops the first function from mutating it, and then breaks the second one too, because frozen is frozen for everyone.

In Rust the intent lives in the signature. A function that takes `&User` cannot mutate it, and the code won't compile if it tries; a function that takes `&mut User` can. David's point: you can tell what each function will do to your data without reading its body, which the TypeScript version can't promise.

## What about threads?

Moving a value into a spawned thread with the `move` keyword works for one thread. Add a second, and the compiler points out that the first thread already took ownership. The fix he shows is `Arc`, the atomically reference-counted pointer: clone it once per thread, move each clone in, and ownership is shared safely.

## What the compiler does for you

The second half covers optimisations Rust applies largely without your help:

- **Zero-cost abstractions**: ownership itself costs nothing at runtime. David also argues that Rust iterators are at least as fast as the loop you would write by hand, where in Java or C# the hand-written loop usually wins.
- **`#[inline]`**: a hint to copy a function body to the call site. The compiler may ignore it depending on function size, optimisation level and target; it pays off for small, frequently called functions.
- **Constant propagation**: with `const` values, an expression like `2 * radius * PI` can be computed at compile time.
- **`const` and `static`**: both feed the optimiser. One detail to correct when you watch: the talk says a `static` lives on the heap, but statics sit in the binary's static memory for the whole run of the program.

He closes with where Rust already runs: Redox OS and Tock OS, Microsoft rewriting core Windows libraries, Actix and Rocket for web servers, plus databases, games, embedded, blockchain and networking.

## Who should watch

Developers coming from TypeScript, Java or C# who keep hearing about the borrow checker and want the why before the how. Experienced Rustaceans will know all of it, though the TypeScript-versus-Rust mutability example is a handy one to borrow (pun accepted) for teaching.
