Title: Every packet that crosses a VPC boundary gets a firewall
Description: Atif Siddiqui (Silicon Valley Bank) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on Transit Gateway route tables and blackhole routes for zero trust segmentation
Body:
A flat network is a gift to an attacker who gets one foothold. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023, Atif Siddiqui, Senior Principal Software Engineer at Silicon Valley Bank, shows how to segment an AWS estate with AWS Transit Gateway: two route tables, centralised inspection firewalls, and blackhole routes so dev cannot reach prod even by accident.

He opens with the bill. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach report put the average breach at $4.35 million, up 2.6% on the year before. The talk is a short, dense design walkthrough, and the design is the payoff.

## Is zero trust a new idea?

No. Atif traces the term to 1994, when Stephen Paul Marsh used it in his doctoral thesis on quantifying trust. John Kindervag's 2010 Forrester paper, Build Security Into Your Network's DNA, coined the zero trust model, and Atif counts NIST's Zero Trust Architecture publication in August 2020 as the real endorsement. The principles: never trust, always verify; verify explicitly; least privilege; minimise the blast radius by segmenting access. This talk is about that last one: split the network into smaller segments so lateral movement gets hard.

## How does Transit Gateway route traffic?

Transit Gateway, announced at re:Invent 2018, is a managed layer 3 router in a hub-and-spoke model. The common setup provisions it in a foundational network account and shares it to spoke accounts through Resource Access Manager. The vocabulary matters:

- **Attachment**: how a VPC (or Direct Connect gateway, VPN, peering) connects. A VPC attachment shows up as ENIs, one per availability zone you specify.
- **Route table**: every routing decision comes from one. The default table can be purged and replaced.
- **Association**: binding an attachment to a route table. One attachment, one table.
- **Propagation**: the gateway learning routes from attachments. Static routes beat propagated ones, and more specific routes win.

## What does the design look like?

The ground rules: AWS Organizations with one account per environment, so an app with dev, QA, UAT and prod has four accounts. Two Transit Gateway route tables, Spoke and Inspection. Three traffic patterns to inspect: on-prem, inline (account to account) and egress to the internet. Three sets of firewalls sit in their own VPCs in the network account.

The rule that does the work, Atif said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: "The strict control that is being enforced is that all traffic crossing a VPC boundary must be inspected." That includes two VPCs in the same account; they still talk through a firewall.

The Spoke table holds the application VPC attachments, and its static routes push traffic to the right firewall by specificity: the AWS range goes to the inline firewall, the rest of the private range is treated as on-prem, and everything else is egress. The Inspection table holds the firewall attachments and routes inspected traffic to its final hop, one route per application VPC CIDR, appended as new accounts are onboarded. Each application VPC's own route table sends anything non-local to the Transit Gateway, which then owns transit routing.

He deliberately leaves out ingress from the internet and the on-prem plumbing (Direct Connect, VPN, SD-WAN with Transit Gateway Connect); each is a talk of its own.

## How do you stop dev from talking to prod?

Here the design pays off. Swap the single Spoke table for four (dev, QA, UAT and prod spokes), associate each environment's attachments with its own table, and add blackhole routes for the other environments' CIDRs. Dev can then only route to dev, and there is no network path from a dev account to anything non-dev. Want separate firewalls for production and non-production? Deploy a second set of egress, inline and on-prem firewalls in their own VPCs and add a second Inspection table. The design stretches without a rewrite.

## Who should watch

Cloud network and platform engineers building a multi-account AWS landing zone, especially in regulated industries. You should already know what a CIDR is; Atif does not stop to explain.

Title: On AWS Lambda you pay for memory times milliseconds, which is why Rust fits
Description: Roman Boiko (AWS) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on why Rust suits AWS Lambda pricing, rewriting only hot functions, cargo lambda and Rust Lambda extensions
Body:
AWS Lambda bills you for memory multiplied by time, so a language that needs less of both pays twice. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, [Roman Boiko](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Roman_Boiko_serverless_workloads), Senior Specialist Solutions Architect for Serverless at AWS, makes the case that Rust is the best fit for Lambda functions, shows how to start one with cargo lambda, and points to a second, less obvious use: Lambda extensions.

He admits he started out sceptical about using Rust as his main language for Lambda, and changed his mind because of how the Lambda runtime runs your code.

## How does Lambda pricing reward Rust?

The only hardware knob on a Lambda function is memory, up to 10 GB, and CPU is allocated in proportion to it. At about 1,800 MB you get the equivalent of one full vCPU, and at the maximum you get six. Billing has two parts: the number of requests and duration in GB-seconds, metered per millisecond. So 100 ms at 2 GB costs the same as 200 ms at 1 GB. If a function runs faster and in less memory, you pay less on both axes, and that is where Rust comes in.

As evidence he points to public comparisons: a Hello World benchmark across runtimes and head-to-heads of Python and Node.js against Rust, plus a quote from Alan Ning of Tenable.io: a 75% reduction in CPU usage and a 95% reduction in memory usage in production after moving to Rust.

## Do you have to rewrite everything?

No, and his customer stories are the most useful part of the talk. One customer ran mostly on Node.js until certain workloads needed lower latency. After rebuilding some of them in Rust, they got the same or better performance at lower memory settings than on Node or Go, and the bill fell with it.

Another team had a Node.js serverless app with hundreds of functions but found that "almost every request coming into their system hit those two or three lambda functions." They rewrote only those three in Rust, got large latency and cost gains because those were the hottest paths, and kept Node.js everywhere else. His advice: if you've already invested in serverless, find the most critical functions and rewrite those first.

He adds a sustainability angle. Serverless already avoids running idle resources around the clock, and more efficient code helps further. The slides quote AWS's Shane Miller and Carl Lerche estimating that broad adoption of C and Rust could cut compute energy use by 50%. And even if you never write Rust yourself, Lambda isolates workloads in Firecracker microVMs, which are written in Rust.

## What does a Rust Lambda look like?

Rust on Lambda runs as a custom runtime, but you don't build one yourself. The open source Rust runtime for AWS Lambda handles the protocol, and `lambda_http` adds a layer for API Gateway events. His sample is the classic API Gateway to Lambda to DynamoDB app, using the AWS SDK for Rust.

- Bootstrap with cargo lambda (`cargo lambda new`), which also builds, tests locally, cross-compiles for x86 and Arm, and deploys. It doesn't care whether you use Terraform, SAM or CDK.
- The handler gets the event, can log to CloudWatch with `println!` or the tracing crate, use the ephemeral `/tmp` file system and call other services, and returns a `Result`.
- `main` is annotated with `#[tokio::main]`. Create SDK clients and load configuration there, during the init phase, so later invocations reuse them.
- Package as a zip (his suggested default) or a container image.

## Extensions are where Rust is hard to argue with

Lambda extensions are companion processes in the same execution environment: they capture diagnostics, instrument code, fetch configuration or secrets, or add security guardrails. External extensions run as a separate process and can be in a different language from the function. The catch is that they share memory, CPU and disk I/O with your function, so a heavy extension slows it down. That's why he sees many extensions now written in Rust. cargo lambda can bootstrap one too, with handlers for invoke and shutdown events.

His favourite example is the Lambda Web Adapter, written by a colleague: a Rust extension that turns API Gateway events back into ordinary HTTP calls to a port inside the sandbox, so Express.js, Flask or PHP apps can run on Lambda without code changes.

## Who should watch

Teams already on Lambda looking at cost or latency, and Rust developers curious about serverless. It's a clear AWS-focused introduction rather than a benchmark study.

Title: Rust got into a nuclear lab through the data pipeline, not the reactor
Description: John Darrington (Idaho National Laboratory) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on getting Rust into a risk-averse nuclear lab and a reactor digital twin in under 6 months
Body:
The nuclear industry is about as hostile to new programming languages as an industry can be, and Rust got in anyway. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, [John Darrington](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_John_Darrington_nuclear_rust), Lead Digital Systems Architect at Idaho National Laboratory (INL), tells how his digital engineering department introduced Rust, starting with a data loader, and ended up shipping a working digital twin of the AGN-201 research reactor in less than six months.

## Why is change so slow in nuclear?

He opens with Fukushima Daiichi in 2011: a 15-metre tsunami cut the power supply to three reactors, all three cores largely melted within three days, and cold shutdown took until December. His point is that every industry has accidents and the good ones learn from them, and software, which runs through all the other industries, should too.

Then he describes the culture he works in: risk averse, slow to change, run by committees, with fixed ways of doing things and ancient protocols. The same microcontroller has been used for 20 years and nothing has happened, so it must be safe. His reply is the best line of the talk: "if something's worked for 20 years, that doesn't necessarily mean it's better. It just means it's worked for 20 years," John Darrington said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023.

## The case for a new language, as written in 2022

He shows his original 2022 pitch slides unedited, which is a nice touch. The department ran a lot of Node.js and Python. Node is single-threaded, good for async I/O but wrong for heavy computation. Python needs a runtime that doesn't fit microcontrollers or lightweight data acquisition systems, and it is permissive enough that code from data scientists, who mainly want something that works, easily ships with bugs. C++ tooling was hard to learn. And because the goal was a digital twin that could eventually feed back into and control a physical reactor, the language had to be safe and performant.

The memory safety numbers did the rest. Citing Okta: roughly 70% of CVEs at Microsoft are memory safety issues, two-thirds of Linux kernel vulnerabilities, 70% of Chrome security bugs, and more than 80% of exploited zero-days found in the wild. That was the stick. Getting rid of a whole class of bugs was the carrot.

## What they built first

Rust arrived three months after those discussions, in DeepLynx, INL's open source, ontology-driven data lake, which was originally pure Node.js. The first piece was a fast PostgreSQL loader for tabular and time series data into a TimescaleDB-backed cluster, patterned after TimescaleDB's own concurrent loader and shipped as a native Node module, so no separate service. Since then Rust has picked up the new time series and tabular data model with Delta Lake integration, a RedisGraph fast loader, and an experiment with llama-rs for LLM integration.

Two more tools: Serval, a WebSocket multiplayer game server for AR/VR digital twin sessions and the DeepLynx 3D viewer, and the DeepLynx Loader, a Python and C# module, written in Rust, that caches data from the lake into DuckDB, so data scientists can query with SQL without hammering the lake. It now sits in many of INL's ML and AI pipelines.

## The reactor

The AGN-201 is a five-watt research reactor at Idaho State University in Pocatello. INL built its digital twin around DeepLynx and a lot of Rust. A Rust file watcher and data acquisition tool ran on a very small machine next to the reactor and pushed readings to the data lake. Jupyter notebooks, run through Papermill, did anomaly detection on the data via the DeepLynx Loader. The same loader, as a C# module, fed an AR view on a Microsoft HoloLens. Regulations stopped them short of closing the feedback loop into the reactor, but he says they got everything up to that point.

The results he claims: launched in under six months, though DeepLynx already existed, with speed and accuracy of data maintained and no code written five times in five languages. He's honest that this excludes ramp-up time, and his experience is that "people pick up rust fairly quickly when they are motivated and they have a problem to solve."

## Lessons for anyone selling Rust internally

Find what drives the people making the big decisions and use it. Have a game plan with room to experiment. Prototype early and often, and give people real problems rather than expecting them to learn Rust over a weekend. He doesn't hide the rough spots either: async, some libraries, the trait system and proc macros.

## Who should watch

Engineers trying to bring Rust into conservative, regulated organisations, and data teams wondering where Rust fits next to Python and Node.

Title: A platform nobody is forced to use is the base of the digital factory
Description: Romano Roth (Zuhlke Group) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on the digital factory, with an opt-in platform team as its foundation
Body:
If your platform team needs a mandate to get users, you have built another silo with a nicer logo. That is the core of Romano Roth's talk at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023. Romano, Chief of DevOps and Partner at Zuhlke Group, describes a digital factory, the end-to-end machine from board-level idea to shipped product and back again, and puts an opt-in platform team at its foundation.

Romano has been at Zuhlke for 21 years. He runs the monthly DevOps Meetup Zurich, presides over DevOpsDays Zurich and has a YouTube channel with more than 100 videos on DevOps, platform engineering, architecture and leadership. He knows the walls he is about to describe.

## What breaks the value stream?

He opens with the picture most consultants see on day one. The business writes plans into Word documents and Jira tickets and throws them over the wall of confusion to development. Development builds something and throws it to testing, which tests something and throws it to operations, which says it will never work in production and then makes it work anyway. The customer looks at the result and says that is not what they wanted. Every handover is a wall, and the walls come from the silo org chart.

DevOps, in his definition, is a mindset, a culture and a set of technical practices to continuously deliver value. He skips the DevSecOps vs BizDevOps naming war: any team needed for the product belongs in it, so just call it DevOps. He cites the State of DevOps research and the book Accelerate for the payoff, including the 973 times higher deployment frequency for high performers.

## Why doesn't DevOps scale on its own?

His two failed scaling patterns are familiar. A central DevOps team between dev and ops is a fine starting point but just another silo. Fully cross-functional product teams fix the walls but bring inconsistency, redundancy and a heavy cognitive load: every team ends up integrating and maintaining its own continuous delivery pipeline (continuous exploration, CI, CD and release on demand), even on all-in-one platforms that still need third-party tools bolted in.

Then come the symptoms he sees at clients. Onboarding takes weeks or months before a new engineer has access to the repo, pipeline and Kubernetes cluster. A new cluster, VM or database takes ages to provision and then has to be configured by hand from a Word document or Jira ticket. Switch on vulnerability scanning, license compliance and software composition analysis and you get a flood of findings nobody can triage. The outcome: slow time to productivity, slow time to market, low quality and no standards.

## What is a digital factory?

Romano builds the picture top-down. The board has a vision (his example: a small drone company that wants more market share). The portfolio level holds the big initiatives and picks the most promising one, a drone that can lift heavy weights. Product managers turn it into features, features become user stories, teams build them. If the idea needs a new team, the platform engineers give it a working platform, CI/CD pipeline included. The product ships, and then feedback flows back to every level, customer feedback and telemetry alike, so the board can check whether its hypothesis was right and decide whether to keep investing.

That loop is the digital factory. The platform team builds API gateways, CI/CD pipelines, repositories, synthetic test data and Kubernetes clusters, creating value for product teams, who create value for customers. Product teams still build and run what they make.

## Why must it be opt-in?

This is the line worth remembering. Romano said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: "They don't need to use it, they can use it. They need to love that product." And, a moment later: "So the platform itself is a product and you should never force the teams to use this platform."

He is also clear that a platform is not the whole factory. It needs the right architecture for scalability, quality standards and APIs, data pipelines that feed decisions, customer experience built on that data, agile program delivery across teams, and product management connecting strategy to execution.

## Who should watch

Leaders who have to explain to a board why a platform team is worth funding, and platform engineers who want the big-picture framing. It is a concept talk with no demos, and a clear one.

Title: One Rust codebase, two jobs. Aurora's smart contract is also its indexer
Description: Michael Birch (Aurora Labs) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on traits, generics and conditional compilation that let one Rust codebase be a Wasm contract and an indexer
Body:
If your code can't do I/O without asking for it in the type signature, it can run anywhere you can supply the I/O. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, [Michael Birch](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Michael_Birch_smart_contracts_indexers_crosscompilation), Senior Software Engineer at Aurora Labs, shows how Aurora compiles the same Rust business logic into a WebAssembly smart contract on NEAR and into a native indexer that serves a low-latency Ethereum RPC.

His takeaway is broader than blockchain: "you can write your business logic in a way that uses pure reusable code by abstracting away platform specific effects," Michael Birch said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023. He's been writing Rust since 2018, after functional programming in Scala, and the talk is aimed at blockchain developers, Rust experts and FP fans at once.

## Why a smart contract needs an indexer

He keeps the blockchain primer short. A blockchain is an append-only structure with immutable history, transactions run in a virtual machine and change global state, and a smart contract is a program for that VM. Users read state through an RPC, which is slow because it takes several network hops and only eventually consistent.

Indexers fix specific queries by keeping their own view of the state. His example is Etherscan listing every token an account holds, which the chain can't answer directly because the mapping is reversed: each token knows its holders, but nothing indexes tokens by holder. Since an indexer has to understand the contract's state anyway, contract and indexer are always coupled. So why not build them from one codebase? Less code to maintain, and an indexer that can simulate whole transactions off-chain.

## The Rust toolkit

Three pieces make it work:

- **Compilation targets.** `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown`, then `cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- **Conditional compilation.** `#[cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")]` picks per-target code, but it's verbose and awkward in an IDE, which usually shows one branch at a time. So keep it to the edges.
- **Type generics with trait bounds.** Define an `IO` trait with `read` and `write`, write `get_balance<I: IO>` against it, then implement `IO` once for Wasm (host functions) and once for native (a database).

## The functional programming idea underneath

Push environment-specific effects into traits, implement them only at the boundaries, and the core becomes pure. That buys three things. It's easier to test, because storage can be a HashMap in memory. It's easier to reason about, because a function without the `IO` bound can't be doing I/O, which he ties to the principle of least authority. And it's easier to reuse, which is the point of the talk.

## What Aurora actually does

Aurora is an Ethereum scaling solution: an EVM written in Rust, compiled to Wasm and deployed as a smart contract on NEAR. To work with Ethereum tooling such as MetaMask and Hardhat it has to expose the Ethereum RPC. A proxy translating Ethereum RPC calls into NEAR RPC calls would be slow, especially for heavy methods that simulate entire transactions. So Aurora runs the engine code itself as an indexer.

The open source aurora-engine code shows the pattern for real. `get_balance`, `set_balance` and `add_balance` are generic over `IO`. On Wasm, a field-less singleton `Runtime` struct implements `IO` by calling NEAR's storage host functions. On the indexer side, the struct holds a RocksDB handle plus extra state: full state history, because users can simulate against older blocks, and an in-memory transaction diff, so simulations don't write to the database. Reads check the diff first, then walk the database history backwards.

## Not just storage

The same trick covers other effects. Environment data such as block height, signer and time comes from host functions in the contract, and from the block being indexed (or defaults, for simulations) in the indexer. NEAR's cross-contract calls are asynchronous promises; the indexer can't simulate those, so it gets a no-op implementation, which works because most Aurora transactions stay inside the EVM. All of it composes into the big `submit` entry point, too large to duplicate. The payoff is RPC methods like `eth_estimateGas`, which sets up the environment, opens state at a chosen block and calls `submit` without copying any engine logic.

## Who should watch

Rust developers who target Wasm, blockchain engineers maintaining contracts and indexers separately, and anyone who wants a practical case for effect abstraction in Rust. He suggests the same pattern for web and mobile apps sharing a core, or embedded code shared with a hardware simulator.

Title: Platform adoption needs tool champions, not unicorns
Description: Caio Medeiros Pinto (Citigroup) at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023 on three practices that keep a platform team adopted, staffed and trusted
Body:
Building the platform is the easy half. Getting the rest of the company to use it, and keeping the platform team from burning out while they do, is where most efforts stall. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023, Caio Medeiros Pinto, DevOps & EE Lead at Citigroup, boils his fix down to three practices: customer-centric leadership, using your own platform, and forming a champion per tool.

He speaks from the trenches: enablement work at Red Hat's Open Innovation Labs, then running a platform-as-a-service team that gave development teams CI/CD and code versioning as a service. This is a people-and-process talk, short on YAML and long on the ways adoption goes sideways.

## Who is platform engineering actually for?

Caio starts from the platformengineering.org definition (designing and building toolchains and workflows that enable self-service for engineering organisations) and lists three reasons companies want it: standardisation and control, lower cognitive load for product teams, and more reliable, stable platforms.

He is blunt about scope. Platform engineering, he says, is "something for medium and big companies, it's not for small companies". A company with three to five teams won't fund a team that only serves internal customers. The trouble starts when you have dozens of teams, each with its own habits.

## The three roadblocks

He groups the failure modes into three:

- **Lack of time and high demand.** Product teams have no time to become experts in secret management or deployment tooling, so tech debt piles up. And when the platform works, demand grows: more teams, more questions, more requests, until the shiny strategic platform becomes the single point of failure.
- **Ways of working and thinking.** Detractors who prefer the old way, compliance flows that slow everything down, oddly specific requirements, clashing priorities, and language barriers between teams in different countries.
- **People.** Rotation, motivation, cognitive limits, and what he calls market temptation: your best platform engineers get poached.

## Practice one: lead like the customer is down the hall

The platform team's customer is the product team, and the leader's job is to keep the team close to that customer and steer by objectives that make priorities obvious. The platform should fit this company's policies and ways of working, not a vendor's idea of the average company. Onboarding should be smooth enough that a team plugs its application in and gets back to its core business. This is the answer to the time-and-demand problem: someone has to decide what the platform team does next, and that decision should come from what customers actually need.

## Practice two: eat your own platform

Define metrics for how teams use the platform, then apply the same metrics to the platform team. A platform team that tells everyone to use the platform but doesn't use it to build the platform is selling something it has never tried. Caio adds showcases and demo days so the team can show its wins from its own experience.

## Practice three: one champion per tool

A platform is a toolbox (his slide example: Kibana, Kubernetes, Grafana), and nobody can be deep in every tool. Everyone on the team is T-shaped with a shared general knowledge, and each tool gets a champion who owns its training, documentation structure and configuration. The leader delegates and trusts. The catch is that champions must share what they know. Caio said at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2023: "We don't want to generate people that cannot be replaced or people that cannot have a background backup, right?" A champion who hoards knowledge is just a bus factor of one with a better title.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers starting a platform team, and platform leads whose adoption numbers are stuck. If you want architecture diagrams, this isn't that talk. Caio also points to further material: Manuel Pais on platform as a product, Mallory Haigh on DevOps and platform engineering, the Puppet State of DevOps Report 2023, and Nicki Watt on people, process and platform.

Title: Numerical Rust is fast by default. Measure before you make it faster
Description: Felipe Zapata (Altas Technologies) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on a workflow for numerical Rust, from MVP to perf, criterion, proptest and Maturin
Body:
The most expensive line in a numerical codebase is the one somebody optimised on a hunch. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, [Felipe Zapata](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Felipe_Zapata_numerical_applications), Software Engineer at Altas Technologies, lays out a workflow for numerical applications in Rust: start correct, profile, benchmark, then optimise, and lean on battle-tested libraries for anything harder than a few lines.

He comes at it from scientific simulation, with a background in physical chemistry, and has written numerical code in C, Haskell, Fortran, Python and Rust before moving to autonomous trading systems in Rust and Python. His philosophy for dealing with messy real-world problems is one of the better lines of the event: "I firmly believe that intelligence is just a robust methodology to recursively improve upon my stupidity," Felipe Zapata said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023.

## Why Rust for number crunching?

Speed and the ownership model, yes, but he calls the tooling Rust's killer feature. Anyone who has built Fortran or C++ projects knows CMake, and next to it Cargo is light years ahead. The abstract puts it more memorably, asking whether you'd rather sell kombucha than use CMake again.

## Step one is a boring MVP

The general algorithm starts from a correct but probably slow version, often a Python prototype from a research team, and turns it into a Rust MVP in baby steps:

- Run Clippy, which suggests more performant patterns.
- Don't fight the borrow checker. Before scattering references and removing clones, write correct, readable code. Humans are bad at guessing where the time goes.
- Use battle-tested libraries for performance-critical operations.

Then decide whether it's fast enough. Sometimes it is, or throwing hardware at it is fine.

## Profile, then benchmark, then optimise

If not, measure. Felipe Zapata uses perf on Linux and visualises its output as flame graphs. He explains how to read them: they come from stack sampling, common frames are merged, and bar width is time spent in that call, while the x axis is not time at all.

Benchmarking comes next, with criterion, which gives statistical confidence on the size of an improvement or regression. His toy example benchmarks a one-dimensional convolution on arrays of 100 Gaussian random numbers: set a baseline, change the code, rerun. The first change gave a meagre 2.5% improvement and the second none. The warning that comes with it is worth the talk: benchmarks assume an otherwise idle machine. "if you just stop Spotify, for instance, you will see an increase in performance of 15%." Run them on a separate VM or box.

His three most important optimisations are choosing the right algorithm, choosing the right algorithm, and asking someone else to check you chose the right algorithm. After that come the smaller ones: preallocate vectors with `Vec::with_capacity`, swap HashMap's default cryptographic hash for a non-cryptographic one, and read the Rust Performance Book.

## Testing numbers is its own job

He suggests three complementary strategies. Let an LLM generate unit tests, which he finds fantastic for this. Hunt for edge cases that cause numerical instability. And use property testing with proptest, inspired by Python's Hypothesis: his example generates random float vectors of length 0 to 1,000 and checks that a min function's result is no larger than every element and a max function's result no smaller, with proptest shrinking any failure to a minimal case.

A footnote on floating point: rounding errors are always there and they accumulate, so read what numerical analysis says about your algorithm, and use rust_decimal for financial calculations.

## Build or borrow?

His rule of thumb: for anything other than trivial algorithms, use a third-party library, even one written in C or C++. Implementing an algorithm yourself is a great way to learn it, but well-known libraries have been through many cycles of errors and fixes. His favourite crates: the ndarray family, Rayon for data parallelism, Polars, rustc-hash, approx for comparing floats, and ordered_float.

Finally, bring Rust to the people writing the numerics. Most quants, scientists and engineers write Python, and Maturin makes it easy to ship Rust as Python modules, which he calls a win-win for both communities.

## Who should watch

Scientists, quants and engineers moving numerical code from Python, Fortran or C++ to Rust, and anyone who benchmarks on a laptop with a browser and music open.

Title: Describe a Rust struct in XML, get the getters and setters for free
Description: John Rexes Murro (Amdocs) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on rustxmlproto, a protobuf-inspired tool that generates Rust structs, enums and traits from XML
Body:
Protocol Buffers taught a generation of engineers to describe data once and generate the code. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, [John Rexes Murro](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_John_Rexes_Murro_code_prototyping_xml), Software Engineer at Amdocs, applies that idea to Rust itself: rustxmlproto, an experimental tool that takes an XML model of a struct, enum or trait and generates the Rust module for it, constructor, getters and setters included.

It's a learning project, and he says so. "I started this project few months after I learned about Rust, and this I've done to explore more about the language itself," John Rexes Murro said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023. He adds that he had come across code generators at previous companies but hadn't seen one written in Rust for generating Rust.

## Why XML, when protobuf exists?

The talk opens with a quick protobuf refresher: a `.proto` definition of a `Person` with a name, an `int32` id and an email, and the builder code that uses it. He notes protobufs are much faster than XML and JSON for serialization. rustxmlproto isn't trying to compete on the wire. It borrows the workflow, not the format: you model the object in XML, a familiar and tool-friendly format, and get Rust source out.

## The XML schema in five elements

The format is small enough to cover in one talk:

- **`<prototype>`** is the required root. Its `name` attribute names the object and the generated module, `class` picks struct, enum or trait, and `visibility` sets the scope.
- **`<includes>`** lists imports, with `<within/>` for modules from your own crate and `<extern/>` for external crates. A `scope` of all imports everything, or `objects` names the items you want.
- **`<members>`** declares fields. The child element's tag is the data type (for example `String` or `u32`), with `name` and `visibility` attributes.
- **`<functions>`** declares extra methods beyond the generated constructor, getters and setters, with `<parameters>` for their arguments.
- **`<procs>`**, named after procedural macros, holds `<derive>` for derive traits, `<serde>` for Serialize and Deserialize implementations, and `<custom>` for any other macro.

Visibility has a small vocabulary that maps onto Rust's: mod (module only, also the default when you leave it out), crate, external and global, plus private.

## What using it looks like

In the demo, a `TestProto.xml` file defines a struct visible inside the crate, imports `Serialize` and `Deserialize` from serde as an external crate, derives `Debug`, `Serialize` and `Deserialize`, and declares three members: a `String` name visible externally, a `String` current address visible in the crate, and an `i32` id with the default visibility.

In `main.rs` you bring in the proto macro and call `import_proto!` with the object name, and the generated type is ready: `TestProto::new(...)` builds an instance, getters read fields, and `set_name`, `set_current_address` and `set_id` change them. The demo checks each step with `assert_eq!`, printing a pass message for each of six test cases and stopping at the first failure.

## Who should watch

Rust learners curious about code generation and macros, and engineers who maintain lots of boilerplate structs and wonder whether to model them outside the code. It's a short walkthrough of an experimental project, not a production library pitch, so treat it as a source of ideas rather than a dependency to adopt.

Title: LanceDB rewrote its C++ core in Rust in under a month and got faster
Description: Lei Xu (LanceDB) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on rewriting LanceDB from C++ to Rust, hand-tuned SIMD k-means and a vector index built for S3
Body:
Most rewrite stories end with a small performance apology. This one ends with a speed-up. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, [Lei Xu](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Lei_Xu_lancedb_oss_serverless_vector_db), creator and CTO of LanceDB, explains how his team threw away a C++ implementation of the Lance columnar format, rebuilt it plus vector search in Rust in less than a month with two engineers, and ended up with better performance than the original.

"We were surprised that the performance was actually better than our original C implementations," Lei Xu said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023. The team had no Rust experience before the rewrite started in January 2023.

## What LanceDB is

He describes it as SQLite or DuckDB, but for vectors: an open source, in-process vector database, with no server and no Kubernetes to run. It does vector search, SQL and full text search, and stores multimodal data (images, text, video) alongside its embeddings. The vector index was cloud native from day one, so data and index can live directly on S3 and still answer quickly. It sits on Lance, a columnar format compatible with Apache Arrow, which he says matches Parquet on scans and delivers 2,000 times faster point queries.

## Why they left C++

CMake came first. Lei Xu is blunt that fighting the C++ build system while trying to ship to customers was the main reason to try Rust. Cargo, by contrast, made high-quality libraries easy to pull in. He also credits the compiler's error messages and Rust's opinionated habits around modules, tests and benchmarks for saving the team arguments about code standards. Two more reasons were specific to a database: Rust embeds cleanly into other languages for multi-language SDKs, and `std::arch` gives direct access to SIMD instructions in the standard library.

## Building a vector index that lives on S3

A vector database finds the nearest neighbours in a space of hundreds to thousands of dimensions. A typical LanceDB dataset, per his slides, has 768 to 1,536 dimensions and 500,000 to a billion float32 vectors. The curse of dimensionality means you can't be both perfectly accurate and fast, hence approximate nearest neighbour indexes. Putting everything on S3, with its random I/O latency, adds a second problem on top.

LanceDB's first index is IVF_PQ. K-means splits the space into Voronoi cells, product quantization compresses the vectors inside each cell, and a query scans only the few partitions closest to it. The on-disk layout keeps the IVF centroids at the start of the file, opens it once and caches them, then scans the chosen partitions and does a merge sort for the final result. Metadata filters are applied at the end for hybrid search.

## Yet another k-means, on purpose

The team wrote its own k-means on top of arrow-rs and tuned it by hand: SIMD distance functions for x86_64 and aarch64, L1/L2 cache-friendly layouts and manual loop unrolling. He reports it beat NumPy, Arrow and LLVM auto-vectorization in their benchmarks, all on stable Rust.

The tooling he praises is concrete: `#[cfg(...)]` for multi-architecture code (a relief after C's defines), `#[inline]`, `cargo bench` as part of the development culture, `cargo flamegraph`, and the Compiler Explorer at godbolt to check the generated assembly uses the right instructions. His one wish was generic specialization, which C++ has and stable Rust doesn't.

## The rest of the stack

SQL comes from sqlparser-rs and DataFusion, full text search from tantivy with customisations, and async I/O from tokio, futures and object_store. The Python and TypeScript SDKs use PyO3 and Neon, and there's a Rust crate too. His closing argument: only C, C++ and Rust can realistically build a multi-language in-process database, and the choice was obvious. He ends by announcing LanceDB Cloud, a managed service you reach by changing the connection URL.

## Who should watch

Database and search engineers, anyone weighing a C++ to Rust rewrite, and people who want a quick primer on how IVF_PQ indexes work. It's a mix of architecture and performance tuning, with no live demo.

Title: Deta.Space or Shuttle.rs? Pick by storage, limits and who owns the app
Description: Peter Kehl at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on choosing between Deta.Space and Shuttle.rs for Rust web apps, by storage, memory limits, privacy and sharing
Body:
Two platforms that both run Rust web apps can still be wrong for each other's users. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, [Peter Kehl](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Peter_Kehl_detaspace_shuttlers), a Rust software developer, compares Deta.Space and Shuttle.rs feature by feature, and his conclusion is that the choice comes down to storage, memory and threads, mixing in non-Rust components, and who is meant to own each running copy of the app.

He likes both. "Spoiler alert. I love them both," Peter Kehl said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023. He built four small apps to find out, two per platform, across three web frameworks (Axum, Actix Web and Warp): system info pages, an HTTP header dump and a small WebDAV file share. His slides note they were updated in mid-August 2023, and he warns that both platforms are works in progress, so treat the numbers below as a snapshot from then.

## What the code looks like on each

On Deta.Space you write a Spacefile, a short YAML file, read the `PORT` environment variable and serve. No platform crates are needed, so your code stays portable. Rust support was new at the time, and builds against the default glibc target sometimes failed, so his advice was to build for the MUSL target, which is statically linked and doesn't use glibc.

Shuttle.rs goes the other way. There's no mandatory config file (a `Shuttle.toml` only holds an optional app name). Integration happens through Shuttle's own crates, such as `shuttle-axum` or `shuttle-actix-web` plus `shuttle-runtime`, and a `#[shuttle_runtime::main]` attribute on the function that serves your app. The default path is well documented and works out of the box. The catch is anything non-default, such as custom headers or MIME types: the framework tutorials won't tell you how to wire it through Shuttle's types.

## What they share

Both deploy to Linux containers you can develop for locally on Linux, macOS or Windows. Neither gives you sudo or Docker-level customisation, and "Neither of the platforms shows IP addresses coming from the client." So rate limiting or geo-IP logic needs a proxy that injects the client IP in a header, such as Cloudflare. Both have helpful Discord communities.

## Where Deta.Space wins

- **Private apps.** An app can be visible only to its owner, and you can deploy unpublished test versions of a public one.
- **Mesh design.** An app can have up to five micros (computes), each with its own limits and language, some of them private. That makes it easy to put an access-control proxy in front of a third-party app.
- **Personal copies.** Users can clone a published app into their own isolated instance without developer skills, and a marketplace lists shared apps.
- **Scheduled actions** with one-minute granularity, and no restrictions on Rust version or channel.

The trade-offs: storage is only Deta's own NoSQL Deta.Base and file storage Deta.Store APIs, which tie your code to the platform, there's no Postgres or MySQL without a connection pool manager, and no background tasks, Discord bots or WebSockets.

## Where Shuttle.rs wins

- **Rust first.** It's Rust only, with tutorials on middleware, security and cryptography.
- **Long-running work.** Background tasks, Discord bots and WebSockets are fine.
- **Richer storage.** Postgres (shared or dedicated), MySQL and MariaDB as dedicated instances, Turso via a dedicated crate, MongoDB, and the Shuttle Persist key-value store.

The trade-offs: crates and the Rust version are pinned (1.70 at the time), and the procedural macros pull in roughly 300 to 600 dependencies, so the first local build is slow. There's no `/tmp`, only `/dev/shm`. Sharing an app means publishing the source for others to deploy themselves. On pricing he only notes that the planned limits weren't enforced yet.

## The numbers that might decide it

From his comparison tables: Deta.Space allowed 250 MB of RAM per micro per execution and a 20-second timeout, against usually up to 6 GB per container on Shuttle. Shuttle allowed 4 threads per project versus 1,024 per micro on Deta.Space. Deta.Space capped HTTP payloads at 5.5 MB. Shuttle's free tier had 10 GB of storage.

## Who should watch

Rust developers picking a place to host a side project or small service, and anyone who wants a model for comparing platforms by design rather than by marketing page. Expect a careful feature comparison, not a demo.

Title: A bootloader should do almost nothing, and Rust helps it do that safely
Description: Yashwanth Singh M (Bosch Global Software Technologies) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on rustBoot and Secure Building Blocks, signed firmware and safe updates
Body:
The safest bootloader is the one with the least code in it. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, [Yashwanth Singh M](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Yashwanth_Singh_M_sbb_secure_building_blocks), Firmware Security Engineer at Bosch Global Software Technologies, presented Secure Building Blocks (SBB), an open source set of modular security components for embedded, IoT and automotive systems, and spent most of the talk on its centrepiece: rustBoot, a standalone secure bootloader written entirely in Rust.

## Why Rust, when the field already runs on C?

He starts by admitting the burden of proof. In automotive and embedded work, tried and tested C code is already running in the field, so a new language has to justify itself. The team shortlisted systems languages without a garbage collector, then looked at the data on memory safety. The figures he cites: around 70% of high-severity bugs in Chromium are memory safety bugs, Apple's OS releases show roughly 60% of vulnerabilities in that class (60.4% for version 14, 66.3% for 12), and Project Zero found memory corruption at the root of 68% of the issues it tracked.

His argument is that Rust removes that class by construction. Pointers are checked at compile time unless you opt into `unsafe`, `Send` and `Sync` stop data races at the type level, and the compiler can verify the absence of undefined behaviour. He estimates the language handles about 70% of the problem. The other 30% is design, which is where SBB comes in.

## Secure Building Blocks, plugged in where needed

SBB is meant to slot into existing stacks rather than replace them: secure boot, secure update, trusted firmware, secure authentication, secure communication, secure storage and secure processing, each as its own block. The crypto is designed to be swappable. If an elliptic curve breaks tomorrow, a different curve, or eventually a post-quantum algorithm, should drop in without rewriting the system. The benefits he lists include a smaller trusted computing base, less boot time complexity and no vendor lock-in.

## The bootloader that refuses features

rustBoot's design goals come from one idea: a bootloader handles only the bare essentials and offloads the rest to the firmware. No network stack, no USB, not even UART unless it's needed. His reasoning: "if you increase the size of your bootloader, you're going to increase the attack surface." Every protocol you add gives an attacker another way in.

The other goals follow from that: comply with the key requirements of the IETF SUIT standard, keep updates reliable, be predictable as well as fast, and use zero dynamic memory allocation, so no heap. Updates matter because the hardware outlives the crypto: "Hardware can stay for hundreds of years, but your software has to be updated every single time."

At the time of the talk rustBoot supported Arm Cortex-M and Cortex-A parts from families including STM, nRF, NXP, Raspberry Pi and ESP, aarch64 Linux booting, multi-slot flash partitioning, elliptic curve signatures via the RustCrypto crates, anti-rollback through version numbers, power-interruptible updates with fallback, and its own Rust-based signing tool. Arm TrustZone support was in a pull request.

## How a signed boot actually works

The middle of the talk is a clear walkthrough of the chain of trust. Immutable ROM code, flashed at manufacture, is the root of trust. It holds a public key, typically in one-time programmable fuses, where integrity matters and confidentiality doesn't. The developer signs a digest of the firmware with a private key, and at boot the digest is recomputed and checked against the signature before control moves on.

rustBoot splits execution into two stages. In the pre-handover stage, the boot ROM hands control to rustBoot, which checks every byte of a 256-byte header on the firmware: magic bytes, image size, timestamp, image type, the firmware digest, the digest of the embedded public key and the signature. In the post-handover stage, the firmware runs and uses a tiny rustBoot API to trigger and confirm updates. A new image downloads into an update partition, control returns to the bootloader, it verifies the image and swaps the partitions. A failed check or an interrupted update rolls back to the previous firmware.

## Who should watch

Embedded and firmware engineers weighing Rust for security-critical code, and anyone who wants a plain-language tour of secure boot. Secure communication, storage and processing are left for another talk.

Title: Twenty small CLI tools are a better Rust tutorial than a big project
Description: Jim Lynch at Conf42 Rustlang 2023 on learning Rust through 20 small, test-driven CLI exercises, from argument parsing to a travelling salesman solver
Body:
The fastest way out of tutorial purgatory is a pile of small, finished programs. At Conf42 Rustlang 2023, [Jim Lynch](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Jim_Lynch_building_cli_tools), a software engineer with about ten years in the trade, walks through his open source set of 20 Rust command line exercises, each one small enough to finish in an evening and each one a reason to write tests.

He's upfront about where he's coming from. "I wouldn't consider myself a rust expert," Jim Lynch said at Conf42 Rustlang 2023, after a language path that went from ActionScript 3, Java and VBA through TypeScript and Clojure to Rust. That makes this a good first talk for people who have read the book and still haven't shipped anything.

## Why a CLI tool, of all things?

Because it's what `cargo new` gives you anyway. A command line tool is the default project shape, it's small and isolated, and it lets you practise one thing at a time. In his words: "These CLi tools are usually small, isolated projects, which makes it easy to just practice one specific thing."

There's also a practical payoff. Rust has no garbage collector or virtual machine to boot, so a CLI written in it starts instantly. Tools in Go, Python or Node.js often carry a split second of startup delay, and Jim points out that some people find exactly that annoying. He also brings up the well-known Discord post about moving a service from Go to Rust, where garbage collection showed up as regular latency spikes.

## The exercises are really about testing

The part worth stealing is the framing. Each exercise is a chance to practise "not just writing the rust code to complete the task, but also to practice writing automated tests to make sure your rust code works." The slides push it further: use the exercises to practise TDD.

His practical advice is to put tests where Cargo expects them:

- Unit tests live in the same file as the code they test, for example `src/lib.rs`, under `#[cfg(test)]`.
- Integration tests go in a `tests/` folder next to `src/`.
- Get used to the testing macros such as `assert!`.

The README in the repo also shows how to get code coverage with tarpaulin and, if you want to get serious, mutation testing.

## What's in the box

Every exercise has the same parts: a title, a made-up real-world backstory, the goal, suggestions for tests, a list of the skills it practises, sometimes a bonus idea, and a hints file for when you're stuck. The idea is to build your own Rust toolbox, a folder of working snippets you can copy from next time.

The 20 exercises climb gently:

- **Basics**: hello world, splitting code across files and modules, argument parsing with positional args and long or short flags, reading environment variables (so your API keys never end up hard-coded and pushed).
- **Text and data**: a table of chairs rendered in the terminal, Fibonacci, an apology letter generator with placeholders and file I/O, a birthday countdown with date handling.
- **Interactive**: a yes/no prompt that waits for input, an agile stand-up questionnaire, a pizza order, a higher-or-lower guessing game and a five-letter word game.
- **Real-world I/O**: an image resizer, a GitHub project scaffolder, a JSON GET request, reading and writing an S3 bucket, database CRUD with any database you like, and an audio stutter effect.
- **The finale**: the travelling salesman problem over a weighted graph.

## How to use it

Fork [rust-cli-exercises](https://github.com/JimLynchCodes/rust-cli-exercises) so you can push your own solutions, install the toolchain with rustup, then run `cargo run` and `cargo test` in each project. The exercises are independent, so do them in any order. His own answers live in a separate [rust-cli-examples](https://github.com/JimLynchCodes/rust-cli-examples) repo, which he describes as his personal solutions rather than the only or best ones. Both are MIT licensed, and he would like more contributors, from typo fixes to new exercises. For the database exercise in particular he'd like to see examples against lots of different databases.

## Who should watch

People learning Rust who want a structured set of small wins, and anyone who mentors juniors and needs a ready-made exercise list. It's an overview of the exercises, not a live-coding session. Rust veterans can skip it.

Title: A quantum career built on Friday evenings, then four steps to copy it
Description: Alberto Garcia Garcia (Accenture) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on growing a quantum career before the jobs exist, and four steps to start now
Body:
Full-time quantum jobs are scarce, so the people who hold them mostly started before anyone paid them to. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, Alberto Garcia Garcia, Quantum Computing Iberia Lead at Accenture, tells his own route from physics student to leading a quantum team, shows what that team builds for clients, and ends with four steps for anyone who wants in.

The abstract promises a talk about the quantum talent problem and a looming quantum winter; what you get is mostly a career story plus a tour of Accenture's quantum practice. Both are useful, as long as you know which one you are watching.

## How do you get into quantum without a quantum job?

His timeline, roughly: physics at Universidad Complutense de Madrid from 2012, falling for quantum mechanics in his third year, then an Erasmus final year at TUM in Munich, taking every quantum subject he could. He wanted the quantum computing group at the Max Planck Institute but ended up in nuclear physics, analysing collision data from CERN's ALICE experiment, and wrote his thesis on quantum cryptography and the BB84 protocol.

Academia had to wait for personal reasons, so he joined Accenture's consulting finance practice in Madrid in 2017. That September, a managing director decided to start working on quantum computing; Alberto asked to join, and with a colleague co-founded the quantum computing team for Iberia. For the next few years his day job was data science, data engineering and BI in the applied intelligence department, while quantum happened on Friday afternoons, evenings and Saturday mornings. Sundays were off limits: "Sundays I need to rest because otherwise I get crazy," Alberto Garcia Garcia said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023.

Along the way: his first quantum project at BBVA in 2018, teaching in the Quantum Technologies master at Universidad Politécnica de Madrid from 2019, a master's in theoretical and computational chemistry to go deeper into drug discovery and protein folding, and in 2022 the move to Accenture's global quantum team, finally 100% of his time. His group has since become a Next Gen Computing team covering neuromorphic computing, quantum security, HPC and confidential computing too.

## What does a consulting quantum team actually build?

He argues for top-down over bottom-up. Startups tend to take an algorithm and look for a use case; Accenture starts from the business problem and picks the algorithm that fits. The demos he shows:

- **Currency arbitrage** as a QUBO on a D-Wave annealer, finding the most profitable exchange cycle.
- **Molecular comparison** for virtual screening, combining Unity rendering with Qiskit on PubChem data.
- **Battery power scheduling**: when to charge and discharge against volatile energy prices, run on Fujitsu's Digital Annealer and Microsoft's QIO.
- **Aircraft loading** for an Airbus challenge, as a hybrid QUBO on D-Wave.
- **PFAS chemistry**, not quantum but HPC: a record-breaking simulation of carbon-fluorine bond breaking on millions of vCPU cores on AWS, with Good Chemistry's iFCI algorithm and ICHEC.

He also cites an Accenture survey from the New York metro area in which 97% agreed quantum computing will bring growth comparable to what AI did.

## The four steps

His advice is blunt about the market: positions are few, hard to get, and usually want quantum plus something else. So: start studying quantum technologies now; apply to any open quantum position; add other skills (data science for applications, engineering for hardware); and stay tuned. The reason to start early: "when this moment arrives and you want to start, there will be a lot of people that already learn quantum computing and will be in front of you in this race."

## Who should watch

Students and early-career engineers weighing a move into quantum, and anyone curious how a consultancy turns QUBOs into client demos. If you want benchmarks rather than a career map, see Peter den Haan's talk below.

Title: The quantum revolution needs mixed teams, not a room of show-offs
Description: Sara Marzella at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on why inclusive teams build better quantum tech, and which jobs quantum will change first
Body:
Every conference veteran knows the question that is not a question: the one asked by someone who already knows the answer and wants the room to know it too. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, applied mathematician Sara Marzella uses that small, familiar failure to make a bigger argument: quantum technology will reshape enough of our lives that it has to be built in inclusive, mixed teams, and the professions it touches go well beyond physics.

It is a short talk, built on three years of personal experience rather than data, and it does not pretend otherwise.

## What does a bad technical room look like?

Sara has worked, learned and tutored across ages, genders, cultures, religions and backgrounds, and she has also been in rooms that were mostly male, heterosexual, white and cisgender. Her description of the latter is uncomfortably precise: stagnant air, competition, people defending their own work until it went stale, speakers aiming to show superiority rather than give something to the audience.

Her diagnosis of what makes the inclusive rooms work is awareness of difference: knowing your own physical and cognitive peculiarities goes hand in hand with respecting other people's. That leads to open-mindedness and a willingness to share, for two reasons. The second is that collaboration is crucial. The first is the line worth printing out: "the knowledge and skills you build during your life are unique. No one can steal them from you, so don't be afraid to share them," Sara Marzella said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023.

She credits those environments with how she learned: senior people who took time with her doubts, taught her to build a demo without arrogance and let her make her own mistakes, and less technical but socially skilled people who helped her build a network.

## Why does this matter more for quantum?

Because the stakes are high. Sufficiently powerful quantum computers could help discover new materials against climate change and new medicines for diseases that are incurable today. Her warning comes from the technology next door: "We should not remain deaf to the lessons artificial intelligence are imparting to us right now." AI, she argues, has been built poorly, filled with dangerous biases, under-legislated, and hyped into places it does not belong, wasting money and time. Diverse teams, drawing on experts from many fields and identities, are how you spot the grey areas before they backfire.

## Which jobs will quantum change?

The second half is a useful checklist, and the part engineers will get the most from:

- **Post-quantum encryption.** Banks and security companies are already moving, because data stolen today and undecryptable now will probably become decryptable in a few years.
- **Data management and architecture.** The one she says people consider much less: outdated architectures and data catalogues already struggle on current systems and would make quantum algorithms unusable on them. Time to modernise before the hardware arrives.
- **Graphics and interfaces.** Quantum systems have to be usable, so integrated classical-quantum interfaces will ease the transition.
- **Technology translators.** People with hybrid knowledge of quantum computing and finance, chemistry or telecoms, who can tell when and how a quantum approach actually applies.

That data-readiness point deserves more airtime than it gets. Anyone who has migrated a legacy data warehouse knows the hardware is rarely the slow part.

## Who should watch

Team leads, community organisers and anyone hiring into quantum or AI who wants a short, personal case for building mixed teams on purpose. If you came for circuits, there are none; come for the data-architecture warning instead.

Title: Five problems, seven annealers, one Gurobi baseline, and a pizza parlour
Description: Peter den Haan (Objectivity Ltd, part of Accenture) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 benchmarks quantum and quantum-inspired annealers against Gurobi
Body:
Ask whether quantum computers are useful today and you get "now" or "in 20 years", depending on who is selling. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, Peter den Haan, Quantum Computing Specialist at Objectivity Ltd (part of Accenture), answers with a benchmark: quantum and quantum-inspired annealers against five optimisation problems under fixed timeouts, with Gurobi as the classical yardstick. His bottom line: annealers already bring business value, if you pick the right problem and the right machine.

He is a physicist with a PhD in quantum electrodynamics in anti-de Sitter space and twelve years as a software developer, and the talk reads like that: rigorous, practical and allergic to hype.

## Why annealers first?

Gate-based machines sit at about 100 noisy qubits with limited circuit depth. Annealers are single-purpose optimisation hardware, simpler to scale and less bothered by noise, which is why Peter sees them as the earliest commercially useful quantum tech. You start in a superposition, slowly morph the Hamiltonian into one that encodes your problem, and the adiabatic theorem says you end near its minimum. "Slowly enough" is the catch, and he admits there is an art to it. A surprising number of problems fit, including all of Karp's 21 NP-complete problems, per Andrew Lucas's Ising formulations paper. D-Wave's hardware has 5,614 qubits.

## What got tested?

The contestants: the D-Wave hybrid cloud service, the raw D-Wave QPU, Microsoft's Quantum Inspired Optimization on Azure, 1QBit, Toshiba's SQBM+, the startup Quantagonia, and Gurobi. Fujitsu was left out for commercial reasons, not technical ones. The problems: a Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, feature selection for ML, the travelling salesman, bin packing, and a pizza parlour integer linear program (which pizzas to make from which ingredients to maximise returns).

## What did the numbers say?

- **Spin glass.** A perfect annealer case and a nightmare for Gurobi. D-Wave hybrid and Toshiba held 100% solution quality up to 10,000 variables; Microsoft QIO slipped to 97% and 91% at the largest sizes; Gurobi to 97% and 96%. The raw QPU stopped at about 100 variables.
- **Feature selection.** D-Wave hybrid stayed at 100%; Toshiba fell to 82% and 78% at 3,000 and 10,000 features; Gurobi held until 79% at 10,000.
- **Travelling salesman.** D-Wave hybrid kept 100% up to 300 cities, which is about 90,000 binary variables. Gurobi dropped to around 20% at 100 and 300 cities within the timeout. The QPU managed size three.
- **Bin packing.** The naive encoding gives a rough energy surface and almost everything struggles beyond ten items; even D-Wave hybrid slid to 93% and 88%. A two-step reformulation into graph covering is in progress.
- **Pizza parlour.** Not annealer territory, and Gurobi "blows all of them out of the water". D-Wave hybrid still hit 100% up to 100,000, falling to 68% at 300,000; the rest struggled once integers were encoded into binary.

## Why can't a 5,614-qubit QPU handle 100 variables?

Connectivity. Quantum-inspired annealers let any variable interact with any other. Real hardware connects only certain qubits, so you embed your problem by chaining several physical qubits into one logical qubit with strong couplings. A fully connected spin glass burns qubits fast. The hybrid service hides this behind classical compute, and QPU time is measured in milliseconds.

## So, are annealers useful?

Yes, with caveats. In a pilot for a manufacturing customer already running Gurobi, an annealer was very competitive because complex constraints made the problem hard to crack algorithmically. "So don't count them out, but be aware, use the right tool for the job," Peter den Haan said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023. His ranking: D-Wave is the only quantum show in town, mostly as a hybrid; Toshiba is the strongest after it; most business problems need classical pre-processing to fit current hardware.

And the line to send to whoever calls quantum a 2040 problem: "So don't let anyone tell you that you are working on an abstract problem that will already only carry fruit 20 years from now."

## Who should watch

Anyone deciding whether to spend real budget on quantum optimisation, and OR folks who want to see Gurobi measured fairly against the new kids. This is the most data-heavy talk of the event.

Title: Quantum-inspired algorithms trade some speed-up for scale you can use today
Description: Abhigyan Mishra (BosonQ Psi) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on why NISQ limits push quantum-inspired optimisation onto classical hardware
Body:
If today's quantum hardware cannot hold your problem, borrow the physics and run it on the GPUs you already have. That is the pitch Abhigyan Mishra, Qiskit Advocate at BosonQ Psi (BQP), makes at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023: quantum-inspired algorithms give up part of the theoretical speed-up in exchange for scalability, and for expensive industrial optimisation problems that trade is often worth taking.

He spends the first half on why the NISQ era hurts, and the second on what quantum-inspired actually means. It is a teaching talk with a practitioner's bias toward optimisation.

## Why can't we just run it on a quantum computer?

His tour of NISQ (noisy intermediate-scale quantum) limits is the clearest part:

- **Scale.** Around 120 usable qubits is, by his estimate, roughly the upper limit right now, and not every physical qubit is usable: some go to error correction, ancillas and support qubits.
- **Noise.** Qubits decohere and lose their state, and every gate adds error on top of the last one's. That caps circuit depth, and more qubits usually means deeper circuits.
- **Error correction.** Today's codes are not good enough, and the better the fidelity you want, the more qubits they eat.
- **Calibration and variability.** A qubit is a concept; the physical particles playing the role never behave perfectly identically.
- **Connectivity.** If two qubits are not neighbours on the chip, you route through SWAP gates, each built from three CNOTs. In his worked example, one logical two-qubit operation across the chip costs 48 physical gates.

## So what is quantum-inspired, then?

Classical algorithms that simulate selected quantum-mechanical principles to get a performance benefit. The two he leans on are superposition and tunnelling. Superposition gets simulated by keeping amplitude-like parameters (the alpha and beta of a qubit state) for each candidate and nudging them toward better solutions, so one step effectively explores several candidates. Tunnelling is borrowed for annealing: instead of climbing the hill out of a local minimum, the search is allowed to go through it. Entanglement, he says, is close to impossible to simulate classically, so quantum-inspired methods don't rely on it.

The trade-off, in his words: "On a real quantum hardware. We expect huge performance bonus, but scalability is an issue." Quantum-inspired flips it: smaller gains, real scale.

He also files QAOA, VQE and quantum neural networks under the quantum-inspired umbrella and calls them "quantum ready", meaning the same algorithm can move to real hardware once it exists. That is a looser use of the term than many would choose, but the point stands: design for both.

## Where does it pay off?

His speciality is quantum-inspired optimisation, split into evolutionary methods (quantum-inspired genetic algorithms, particle swarm, wolf optimisation) and annealing. The argument is about cost per evaluation. Gradient methods get stuck in local minima on non-convex functions; genetic algorithms escape them but burn compute evaluating whole populations. Simulated superposition lets a smaller population cover more ground, so the search converges in fewer generations.

The use cases he has worked on are airfoil and topology optimisation, where each fitness evaluation is a heavy simulation. "And the function which I'm trying to optimize is so computationally expensive that even if I'm able to reduce it by ten generations, the convergence rate, that means a lot," Abhigyan Mishra said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023.

He closes on why he likes the field: "So quantum inspired is sort of like one of my favorite things, because I get to enjoy quantum computing, and yet I don't have to worry too much about scalability."

## Who should watch

Engineers with nasty combinatorial or simulation-driven optimisation problems who keep being told to wait for fault-tolerant hardware. Also anyone who wants a patient, from-the-basics explanation of why NISQ machines struggle. If you want benchmarks, pair it with Peter den Haan's talk below; this one is conceptual.

Title: Teaching BB84 by making students race to decrypt a message
Description: Myron Giannakis (IEEE Branch of University of Patras) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on a Qiskit game that teaches BB84 quantum key distribution
Body:
The fastest way to make students learn a cryptographic protocol is to hide a secret message behind it and promise bragging rights. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, Myron Giannakis, computer engineering student and coordinator of the quantum computing students' group at the IEEE Branch of University of Patras, shows how he built exactly that: a Qiskit implementation of the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol, turned into a race to decrypt his message.

The talk has two halves: the theory of BB84, then the code and how it became a game. It is a student project explained by its author, and that is its charm.

## BB84 in one paragraph

BB84 comes from Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard's 1984 paper and was the first quantum cryptography protocol. Two parties share a secret key over two channels: a quantum one and an authenticated classical one. Security rests on the no-cloning theorem: you cannot copy a quantum state, so an eavesdropper only gains information by disturbing the signal, and that disturbance gets noticed.

The mechanics, as Myron walks through them: Alice picks a random bit string and, for each bit, randomly applies a Hadamard or the identity gate. Bob randomly applies a Hadamard or not before measuring. Where their gate choices match, Bob gets Alice's bit; where they differ, he gets a coin flip. They then compare gate choices (never the bits) over the classical channel and keep only the matching positions. On average, half the qubits make it into the key.

## What changes when the payload is a whole message?

His variant departs from BB84 in two ways. First, Alice sends characters, not bits: each character becomes a 7-qubit circuit holding its ASCII code, and every gate applied to a circuit is applied to all seven qubits. Second, instead of distributing a key, the protocol transmits the entire message. Since about half the characters arrive intact each round, the program keeps resending the ones that failed, which by his reckoning takes on the order of log x rounds for a message of length x.

The code is small and readable:

- a `CryptoCircuit` class that extends Qiskit's `QuantumCircuit`, with methods to initialise a state, add (or not) a Hadamard, get measurements and visualise the Bloch vectors;
- a `BB84` class with static methods for the sender, the receiver and the classical channel, each given only the information it would really have; the classical channel returns the indices of correctly transmitted characters, never the characters;
- a `main` loop that repeats the transmission until the whole message is through.

A nice touch: he uses the simulator's ability to peek at states without collapsing them, something no real quantum machine allows, to make the game easier to build and more instructive to play.

## How did it become a game?

He ran only the sender, saved the circuits to a quantum_channel file and the gates to a classical_channel file, and handed them out with a Jupyter notebook. Players got the circuit class and an empty receiver and classical-channel method to write themselves, plus their own main function. "This whole thing was done in the form of a competitive game where winner would be the first person to manage to decrypt my initial message," Myron Giannakis said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023.

That is a good design for a teaching exercise: you cannot win without understanding which half of the information the classical channel is allowed to carry.

## Who should watch

Anyone running a university club, a meetup or an internal guild and looking for a hands-on first quantum exercise that is not another Bell state. The code lives in the team's [Quantum Cryptography Game repository](https://github.com/IEEE-SB-UPatras-Quantum-Computing/Quantum-Cryptography-Game) on GitHub. If you already teach QKD, the 7-qubit-per-character twist is worth stealing.
