Title: Quantum machine learning is older than you think, and has five SDKs
Description: Karthiganesh Durai (BosonQ Psi) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on QML techniques, the Qiskit, PennyLane and TensorFlow Quantum stack, and its history since 1995
Body:
Quantum machine learning did not start with the generative AI boom. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, Karthiganesh Durai, Chief Quantum Architect at BosonQ Psi (BQP), gives a compact tour of QML: what it is good for, which techniques exist, which SDKs you can install today, and a timeline that starts in 1995.

It is a short survey talk, closer to a well-organised map than a tutorial. No code, but plenty of names worth searching for afterwards.

## What is QML, in one breath?

His definition: a research area that explores the interplay of ideas from quantum computing and machine learning. Machine learning revolves around algorithms, model complexity and computational complexity; quantum computers bring parallel processing, and superposition and entanglement are what the industry is using to build more efficient ML algorithms. His headline claim is that QML is becoming a base building block for many scientific solutions built on quantum computing.

The application list is broad: classifying nanoparticles at the subatomic scale (where, as he points out, the data is already quantum information rather than classical data), molecular modelling for drug discovery, weather forecasting, recommendation, space exploration and even large language systems.

## Is half of this just old names with a quantum prefix?

Karthiganesh gets there first. "it is very fancy to prefix the word quantum in front of any technique or any tool," Karthiganesh Durai said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023. Support vector machines become quantum SVMs, neural networks become quantum neural networks.

But he argues QML has its own approaches too. His list: quantum binary classifiers, the Grover search algorithm (which he calls fundamental to most QML solutions), quantum-enhanced reinforcement learning, quantum sampling, quantum neural networks, quantum convolutional and dissipative quantum neural networks, hidden quantum Markov models, explainable QML, quantum transfer learning, quantum GANs and fuzzy cognitive maps.

## What can you actually pip install?

This is the most practical stretch of the talk:

- **IBM Qiskit** has machine learning libraries for quantum SVMs, nearest neighbours and neural networks, plus helpers such as the ZZ feature map for encoding classical data, which make it easy to build quantum counterparts of classical models.
- **Xanadu PennyLane** is a Python package that connects to various quantum computers and has the most QML-specific functionality of the bunch.
- **TensorFlow Quantum** from Google, the natural pick if your classical ML already lives in TensorFlow.
- **D-Wave** has its own machine learning libraries, and **PyQuil** from Rigetti rounds out the list.

He also mentions Q# and Amazon Braket, and lands on the safe summary: "So almost all quantum computing platforms have their QML capabilities." He even asks viewers to tell him about the frameworks he missed, which is a refreshingly honest thing to say in a field that ships a new library every week.

## A timeline that predates most of your dependencies

The history section is the part most people will not know. Theoretical work goes back to 1995, with Kak's biologically inspired work. In 2009 D-Wave demonstrated detecting cars in digital images. In 2013 Google and NASA started the Quantum Artificial Intelligence Lab. 2014 brought an all-optical linear classifier, a perceptron that could learn a classification boundary, and quantum genetic algorithms for matching and optimising a dual-motor electric vehicle powertrain. Between 2015 and 2018 came generative models trained for handwritten image generation and traffic flow optimisation on a quantum annealer; 2019 to 2021 brought an experimental demonstration of a quantum speed-up in reinforcement learning time, the quantum neuron and the TensorFlow Quantum release.

The growth curve is the punchline: by his count, QML has been publishing around 1,200 papers a year over the last four years.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and ML engineers who keep hearing about QML and want the vocabulary and the toolchain in one sitting. If you already train variational circuits in PennyLane, you will know most of it; the timeline is still a nice thing to have in your back pocket.

Title: Quantum accelerometers want to navigate without a single satellite
Description: Amit Modhwadia at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on quantum accelerometers, ultracold atoms and GPS-free navigation that is hard to jam
Body:
GPS works until somebody jams it, and then your very expensive ship is guessing. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, Amit Modhwadia, a computer science undergraduate and Qiskit Textbook contributor, gives a short, brisk introduction to quantum sensors and the case for a quantum accelerometer as a navigation system that needs no outside signal at all.

It is a lightning-length talk, a few minutes long, and an intro rather than a full lecture. If you have never looked at quantum sensing because it sits outside the qubits-and-gates conversation, it is a good first stop.

## What is a quantum sensor, exactly?

Amit's definition: an advanced sensor technology that detects changes in motion, force, and electric and magnetic fields by collecting data at the atomic level. The trick is that it uses properties of quantum mechanics, such as entanglement, interference and state squeezing, to beat the precision limits of conventional sensors.

He sorts the field by what gets measured: acceleration, force, and magnetic and gravitational fields. The rest of the talk sticks with acceleration, because that is the one that matters for navigation.

## How does a quantum accelerometer measure anything?

The accelerometer he describes uses ultracold atoms. Cooled to extremely low temperatures, the atoms start showing their quantum nature and behave like waves. As they move through the sensor, a series of laser pulses forms what he calls an optical ruler, and that ruler lets the atoms' acceleration be measured very precisely.

So far, so physics. The engineering payoff comes next.

## Why would anyone give up GPS?

Most navigation today leans on a global navigation satellite system such as GPS. Amit's comparison is blunt: for a precise fix you need four to five satellites, the whole system depends on an external source, and anything that depends on a signal from orbit is easy to jam or spoof.

A quantum accelerometer is self-contained. "It is independent navigation using quantum accelerometer," Amit Modhwadia said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023. The recipe is old-fashioned dead reckoning with a much better instrument: start from a precisely known position, measure acceleration very precisely, and combine the two to work out where you are in 3D space. No satellites, nothing to intercept, nothing to jam.

For anyone who has fought sensor drift in an inertial navigation system, that is the whole point. Dead reckoning lives and dies by how accurate the accelerometer is, so a sensor that reads motion at the atomic level is exactly the upgrade that approach has been waiting for.

## Is any of this real yet?

Amit points to work from Imperial College London: the UK's first quantum accelerometer for navigation has been demonstrated by a team there, and a prototype quantum sensor built at Imperial, with potential application in GPS-free navigation, has been tested in collaboration with the Royal Navy.

He is honest about the catch, too. "But the quantum sensors are quite big. So this is the disadvantage of quantum sensors," he said. The trade-off as he frames it: bulkier hardware in exchange for navigation that is more accurate and much harder to hack.

## Who should watch

Anyone curious about quantum technology that is not a quantum computer, and engineers working near navigation, defence or resilient positioning who want the one-paragraph version of why atom-based sensors keep showing up in the news. If you already know your atom interferometers, this one will be too short for you; it is a primer, and it says so by finishing in a few minutes.

Title: The Impact of Quantum Computing on Cybersecurity: Threats and Opportunities
Description: guest post by Myrtle Bautista
Body:
## Quantum computing has taken the world of IT security by storm with its revolutionary new capabilities.

Using quantum-level calculations promises to revolutionize how we secure data and protect ourselves from cyber threats. But what is quantum computing? What are the potential risks and opportunities it offers for cybersecurity?

In this blog post, we'll explore the potential implications of quantum computing for our online safety, analyzing both threats and possibilities that could arise due to technological advances.

## Opportunities of Quantum Computing on Cybersecurity

### Improvement of Encryption Algorithms

Quantum computing offers a unique solution for encrypting valuable data. By harnessing the power of quantum algorithms and advances in mathematics, it is possible to protect data with higher levels of security than ever before.

While traditional encryption tools provide a certain level of protection, they can be rendered useless by sophisticated computer attacks and hackers. However, using quantum computing to improve existing encryption algorithms can protect data against even the most powerful forms of attack.

### Identification of Malicious Codes

[Quantum computing](https://www.conf42.com/2022-06-29-quantum-world-2022) is an exciting new technology that can revolutionize how malicious code is identified and removed from computers. By utilizing the laws of quantum mechanics, this technology allows thousands of calculations to be done simultaneously, far outpacing conventional computing power.

Using quantum-based algorithms, malicious code can be analyzed more quickly and accurately than ever before, potentially helping to curb the spread of dangerous viruses and malware.

This could make our online world safer and open up many possibilities for making faster breakthroughs in other areas, such as machine learning and data analysis.

### Analyzing Large Data Sets

This powerful technology combines principles of quantum mechanics with modern computing to enable us to tackle problems that would be difficult, or even impossible, for classical computers.

By taking advantage of the unique properties of quantum physics, a single quantum computer can analyze massive amounts of data far more effectively and efficiently than traditional technologies.

### Use in Quantum Machine Learning Algorithms

Quantum computers have been touted as the future of computing, capable of performing calculations that traditional computers could not possibly manage. However, these quantum machines are also being developed with another application in mind -- quantum machine learning algorithms.

This means using quantum computers to improve artificial intelligence, allowing for smarter and more robust AI systems. The potential for this technology is immense, with many experts expecting it to revolutionize [machine learning](https://www.conf42.com/2022-05-18-machine-learning-stronger-than-ever) in the same way quantum computing will revolutionize computing itself.

### Creating More Efficient and Secure Algorithms for Authentication

Quantum computing makes possible the creation of more powerful algorithms that promise to revolutionize authentication processes. With its ability to store and process large amounts of data, quantum computing can generate stronger cryptographic keys, providing an unprecedented level of security for authenticating users.

In addition, quantum computing algorithms can help reduce authentication times to nearly instantaneous levels due to their capacity to process big datasets quickly. Thus, leveraging quantum computing enables developers to create more efficient and secure algorithms for accurately authenticating individuals in record time.

Developers must also engage in continuous security monitoring, which could lead to an entirely new horizon regarding digital security and privacy within many industries - from financial services to healthcare and transportation.

## Threats Posed by Quantum Computing on Cybersecurity

### Breaking Through Traditional Encryption Methods

Cybercriminals have a whole new tool at their disposal which is quantum computers. These ultra-powerful machines can easily crack through traditional encryption methods, making the valuable data stored in such systems vulnerable to attack.

It's like having a master key that can open any door on earth. The rewards for bad actors could be immense, so companies must update their security measures to cope with this new technology to ensure the safety of their information and customers.

Thankfully, the development of protection mechanisms is advancing right alongside quantum computing, so let's hope these criminal masterminds aren't able to exploit the situation before these safeguards are in place.

### DNNs Will Be More Difficult to Evaluate

Recent advances in quantum computing have led to concerning implications for cybersecurity, especially with regard to the defense mechanisms used by businesses. A further issue is posed by Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which are already a difficult security component to evaluate.

With quantum computing powering the computational models of these DNNs, their evaluation will become more difficult, as it may be impossible to determine all possible outcomes of a complex network.

Businesses looking to safeguard their data should now have comprehensive defenses that use up-to-date security evaluations and components to defend against increasingly powerful hacker networks.

### Web Interactions Will Be At Risk

As quantum computers become stronger and more efficient, it will undoubtedly be challenging as web interactions become increasingly vulnerable to intrusive quantum computing attacks.

The most pressing worry is that when conventional security measures are overpowered by quantum computing power, our most sensitive data will be at risk, especially because so much of our lives now transpire online.

Suppose a quantum computer goes rogue and hacks our banking information, social media accounts - or even worse - national secrets. In that case, it will take an even higher level of tech-savviness to protect us from harm in the new age of cybersecurity risks.

## Conclusion

As quantum computing matures and gains traction, it will likely have a major impact on cybersecurity, positively and negatively. It could be used to improve the security of digital systems or even assist with encryption in unprecedented ways. Yet, it threatens to provide malicious actors with new means of bypassing existing cyber defenses.

Regardless, businesses must be vigilant about preparing for these changes to ensure their systems remain safe from intrusion and disruption. 

##**This guest post was written by Myrtle Bautista**

Title: RSA is safe from today's 433 qubits - your stored traffic is not
Description: Husayn Gokal (CodersHQ) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on how Shor's algorithm threatens RSA, why it can't yet, and NIST's post-quantum replacements
Body:
Breaking RSA with Shor's algorithm is a numbers game, and in 2023 the numbers did not add up. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, Husayn Gokal, an ambassador at the UAE's CodersHQ who also leads the QWorld chapter QuAE, puts the figures side by side: around 20 million qubits to crack RSA in hours, about 9.2 years with 2,000 qubits, and IBM's biggest machine at the time had 433 noisy ones. The catch is store now, decrypt later, which is why the NIST post-quantum algorithms matter today and not in ten years.

It is a short introductory talk, a good first explanation of the threat for developers who have never looked at it. Specialists will want to fact-check a couple of the simplifications, noted below.

## Which encryption is actually at risk?

The classical public key trio, each with its home turf:

- **RSA** (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman): web browsers, email, VPNs.
- **Diffie-Hellman**: key exchange in TLS, SSH and IPsec.
- **ECC** (elliptic curve cryptography): Bitcoin, Ethereum and the rest of the crypto-asset world.

All three rest on maths problems, factoring and discrete logarithms, that classical computers cannot solve in reasonable time at real key sizes. Gokal makes the point visually: factoring 15 by brute force is trivial, and then he puts an RSA-sized modulus with its two factors on screen, each factor a wall of digits.

## How does Shor's algorithm change the maths?

His explanation is that a quantum computer can test all the candidate factors at once rather than one at a time, with the toy factoring of 15 needing about eight qubits. Take that as the popular shorthand. Shor's algorithm actually turns factoring into period finding and extracts the period with a quantum Fourier transform; superposition alone does not let you read out every answer at once. The conclusion is the same either way: a big enough, good enough quantum computer factors RSA moduli in polynomial time.

## How many qubits does it take?

This is the useful part of the talk. Classically, the search is basically infinite. With about 20 million qubits, he cites an estimate of around 9 hours to break RSA. With a more realistic 2,000 qubits, about 9.2 years. "So basically infinity, but it still takes 9.2 years with 2000 qubits," Husayn Gokal said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, and by then most stolen secrets would be worthless.

Then reality: the largest IBM machine had 433 qubits, and they are error-prone. Noise limits scaling, error correction and mitigation are not good enough yet and can stretch computation time a lot, and the hardware lives in dilution refrigerators to keep environmental noise out. "It's a very difficult task to actually remove or prevent errors in a quantum computer," he said.

## So why worry now?

Store now, decrypt later (SNDL). Encrypted traffic is easy to capture by sniffing a network, and an attacker who cannot read it today can simply keep it: card data, transactions, anything long-lived, waiting for the day the qubits and the error correction exist. The data you encrypt in 2023 has to stay secret for as long as it is valuable, not just until the next hardware announcement.

## What replaces RSA?

NIST ran a global competition to pick classical algorithms that resist quantum attack, and he walks through the winners:

- **CRYSTALS**: covers key encapsulation (Kyber) and digital signatures (Dilithium), with several implementations, and his personal favourite.
- **Falcon**: compact digital signatures, so less storage and faster sending and verifying.
- **SPHINCS+**: hash-based digital signatures, a different mathematical foundation from the lattice-based schemes.

He also gives QuAE a closing plug: the group runs hackathons with CodersHQ, Qiskit-basics meetups, and once demoed NYU Abu Dhabi's two-qubit NMR quantum computer, a SpinQ machine, live on Zoom.

## Who should watch

Developers and students who want the quantum threat to cryptography explained in one short sitting, with real numbers attached. If you are already planning a migration, go to the inventory-and-crypto-agility advice in the related talks.

Title: Quantum readiness - build an office, sign a vendor, or join a network
Description: Abdullah Alsalman at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on three routes to quantum readiness for sectors and a proposed international quantum standards body
Body:
Abdullah Alsalman's talk at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 boils quantum readiness down to a choice of three routes for an industry sector or organisation: build an in-house quantum computing office, contract with an established quantum company, or plug into national and international quantum organisations. He then goes a step further than most readiness talks and proposes something that does not exist yet: government standards for the field and an international Quantum Computing Standards organisation (QCS) that would certify sectors.

It is a short, high-level governance talk of roughly ten minutes. The abstract promises real-world examples and a detailed analysis of the pros and cons of each route; the talk itself stays at the level of a framework, so treat it as a structured checklist rather than a case study.

## Why prepare before the technology is ready?

His reasons are the standard ones, stated plainly: quantum computing can disrupt industries and markets, proactive preparation is the way not to fall behind, specialised experts and consultants can guide sectors through the complexity, and every sector needs a foundational understanding of the concepts to spot where quantum could make the biggest difference.

## What does readiness buy you?

Three benefits, as he frames them:

- **Competitiveness**: better-informed decisions, cost reduction and room to explore new applications.
- **Security**: robust frameworks, risk assessments and governance that protect data against quantum-era threats and keep the organisation compliant.
- **Structured data**: data prepared for quantum algorithms, which he argues speeds processing and surfaces insights in large datasets.

## Which of the three routes fits?

- **A dedicated quantum computing office.** An in-house team that writes tailored strategies, keeps sensitive work confidential and drives collaboration inside the sector. The most control, and presumably the biggest investment.
- **Contracts with quantum computing companies.** Partnering with established vendors gives access to proven technology and expertise and speeds things up, with the vendor helping assess what the sector actually needs.
- **Engagement with quantum organisations.** National and international bodies that guide sectors on risks and opportunities. His examples are the US National Quantum Coordination Office and the European Quantum Flagship.

He leaves the weighing to the audience: the right mix depends on a sector's needs, goals and resources.

## What is the QCS proposal?

Two recommendations aimed at governments rather than individual companies. First, government standards for the quantum computing field, to give guidance, reduce risk and make knowledge exchange the norm. His reasoning is about duplicated effort. "We don't want two companies work to solve the same solution," Abdullah Alsalman said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023; shared standards would let organisations swap knowledge and spread out across different problems.

Second, an international Quantum Computing Standards organisation, modelled on bodies like ISO, that would publish standards, provide guidance and certify sectors that meet them. He ties it to the Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) principles, so the body would also anticipate the consequences of quantum services, not just their technical quality. He admits establishing it would be hard, and argues it would still be a significant step towards safe adoption across sectors and countries.

## Who should watch

Policy people, public-sector technology leaders and anyone drafting an organisation's first quantum strategy who wants a simple frame for the build, buy or join decision. Engineers looking for technical depth will find more in the related talks.

Title: Encrypt and mask database columns in a proxy, not in a thousand services
Description: Trista Pan (SphereEx) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on column encryption and dynamic data masking for MySQL and PostgreSQL via ShardingSphere-Proxy
Body:
If you have a thousand microservices and a new rule that customer addresses must be encrypted at rest, you are not going to patch them one by one. Trista Pan, co-founder and CTO of SphereEx and a PMC member of Apache ShardingSphere, used her Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 talk to show the alternative: put a SQL-aware proxy between the applications and MySQL or PostgreSQL, and let it encrypt, decrypt and mask specific columns with no application code changes.

It is a short, practical session, despite the event's name, and has nothing to do with qubits. The architecture comparison in the middle is the part worth keeping even if you never run ShardingSphere.

## Where in the data lifecycle does each control belong?

She starts from data lifecycle management: generate or collect, store and manage, share and use, then archive or destroy. Each phase gets its own controls. Collection needs trusted data sources. Storage and movement need encryption in transit (SSL/TLS, which most databases already support through configuration) and at rest. Sharing needs masking, because production data used for analytics, testing or training should not carry real SSNs into a test environment; masking scrambles the values while keeping their structure usable. And at the end, data you no longer need should expire or be archived, ideally automatically, with time-to-live settings on table rows. On algorithms she recommends the mature, popular ones such as AES over inventing your own.

## Application, proxy or database: where should encryption live?

Her comparison of the options is the most reusable part:

- **Application level.** Fine for a small case: developers call AES in the code. It does not scale across many services.
- **Proxy level.** A database proxy, firewall or gateway encrypts and masks on the way through. No application changes, and because a good proxy understands the query, policies can target individual columns.
- **Database level.** Depends entirely on what your database supports, and many encrypt or decrypt everything wholesale, which is inflexible.
- **File or disk level.** Even blunter: the disk has no idea which bytes are a user's private data, so it encrypts everything and you pay the performance cost on all of it.

She picks the proxy, for the two reasons above: zero code changes and partial, policy-driven encryption.

## How does ShardingSphere-Proxy do it?

Apache ShardingSphere is a top-level Apache project, a distributed SQL engine for sharding, scaling and encryption on top of existing databases, which she says has more than 1,500 contributors. It ships two clients: ShardingSphere-JDBC, a lightweight Java framework you pull in through Maven, and ShardingSphere-Proxy, which presents itself as a MySQL or PostgreSQL server. Applications connect to the proxy exactly as they would to the database; the proxy parses each statement, rewrites it, and handles sharding, read/write splitting, distributed transactions, encryption and masking. Helm charts and operators deploy it on Kubernetes in one step.

Rules are written in DistSQL, ShardingSphere's SQL dialect. Next to a normal `CREATE TABLE`, you create an encrypt rule naming the column and algorithm (AES in her example) and a mask rule for the column to mask.

## What does the demo show?

A `t_user` table with user id, name, telephone and address. Address gets an encrypt rule, telephone a mask rule. Insert rows through the proxy and query them back through the proxy: the address comes back as plain text, because the proxy fetched the ciphertext and decrypted it, while the telephone comes back partly masked. Query the database directly and the picture flips: the address column is ciphertext, and the telephone is stored in full, since masking is applied dynamically on read, not on write.

"Therefore for your application everything is transparent," Trista Pan said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, while anyone who reaches the database itself, an attacker included, gets ciphertext. The steps (deploy the database, deploy the proxy, register the instance with DistSQL, create the table with both rules, insert, select) are in the deck so you can repeat it yourself.

## Who should watch

Platform and database engineers facing a compliance requirement across many services, and anyone weighing proxy-level encryption against application or disk encryption. If you need key management, rotation or performance numbers, the talk does not cover them; bring your own questions to the ShardingSphere docs.

Title: Do quantum ethics now, before quantum repeats machine learning's mistakes
Description: Roberto Magnani (AEIT Milan and EuropIA) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on the security, fairness, privacy and energy ethics of quantum computing
Body:
Machine learning was wired into business processes long before most organisations understood how much damage it could do. Roberto Magnani's argument at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 is that quantum computing is the chance to do it the other way round: work out the ethics while the machines are still small. An advisor at AEIT (the Italian association for electronics, electrotechnics, informatics and telecommunications) and a member of EuropIA, he covers four areas, safety, security, privacy and fairness, then adds energy, regulation and a concrete role for organisations: the digital ethics officer.

It is a policy and governance talk, dense with references, and the cryptography section is the most practical part for engineers.

## What does quantum break first?

Public key cryptography. RSA, elliptic curves and discrete-log schemes get their strength from problems that Shor's algorithm solves quickly on a big enough quantum computer, so asymmetric crypto needs new maths. Symmetric crypto is hit by Grover's algorithm, but key and digest size decide the damage: AES with 256-bit keys is considered quantum safe. He maps the exposure to real systems: banking leans on symmetric crypto for core applications, connected cars on asymmetric crypto for vehicle-to-everything messages and firmware integrity, and blockchains on both public keys and hash functions, which means redesigning them around post-quantum cryptosystems.

The numbers he cites: breaking today's 80-bit-security systems classically costs somewhere between tens of thousands and hundreds of millions of dollars, and 112-bit systems should stay safe against classical attack for 30-40 years. On the quantum side, researchers estimate 160-bit elliptic curves fall to a 1,000-qubit machine and 1024-bit RSA to roughly 2,000 qubits.

## What should a security team do about it?

Follow the standards work and start the inventory. He walks through NIST's first four quantum-resistant algorithms: CRYSTALS-Kyber for general encryption, chosen for small keys and speed; CRYSTALS-Dilithium as the primary signature algorithm, FALCON where smaller signatures are needed, and SPHINCS+ as a backup because it is hash-based rather than lattice-based like the other three. At the time of the talk NIST was asking experts to explore them but not to bake them into systems before the standard was final.

The migration steps, borrowed from IBM's introduction to quantum safe: discover and classify your data, build a crypto inventory (protocols, algorithms, key lengths, providers), then embrace crypto agility, running classical and quantum-safe algorithms side by side through what will be a multi-year transition. He also notes the physics route, quantum key distribution over fibre with photon polarisation, where any eavesdropper disturbs the key and gives themselves away.

## Where are the less obvious ethical risks?

- **Access.** Few people or small companies will ever own a quantum computer, so who gets the knowledge and the cycles matters. The slides add the geopolitical angle: a quantum arms race with national programmes spending billions, and the militarisation risk that comes with it.
- **Bias and fairness.** Quantum machine learning inherits classical ML's bias problems (sample, labelling and historical bias) and is being aimed at the same high-stakes decisions: credit, hiring, sentencing. He points to research on formally verifying the fairness of quantum decision models, built on tensor networks in Google's TensorFlow Quantum and tested on income prediction and credit scoring. His mitigations are diverse teams, internal ethical guidelines, representative data, bias detection and external audits.
- **Privacy and explainability.** Faster processing of huge data volumes is an incentive to harvest even more of it. And the black-box problem gets worse. "With quantum computers, explainability is more of a physics problems than a programming problem," Roberto Magnani said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023.
- **Energy.** Cryogenic cooling is power-hungry, manufacturing has a raw-materials footprint, and quantum machines are nowhere near classical efficiency. He asks for efficiency research, renewable power, lifecycle assessments, recycling and policy standards.

## Which rules already apply?

The EU AI Act targets AI, but he expects it to shape quantum applications too, especially its banned uses: real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces, biometric categorisation by sensitive traits, predictive policing, emotion recognition at work, school, borders and in law enforcement, and indiscriminate scraping of biometric data. He also cites the Rome Call for AI Ethics, signed in 2020 by the Pontifical Academy for Life, IBM, Microsoft, FAO and the Italian innovation ministry, with its six principles: transparency, inclusion, accountability, impartiality, reliability, and security and privacy.

## What should an organisation actually change?

Appoint someone, or a team, to own it: a digital ethics officer, an idea from a January 2023 workshop in Dublin. The role needs deep knowledge of the company's digital processes, identifies the ethical exposure of projects, leads governance, advises across the organisation (not just developers), and builds evaluation and control tools. Above that, enterprises should agree in advance on the trigger events, a technical breakthrough or a competitor's move, that would make them act or invest more.

## Who should watch

Security architects starting a post-quantum migration plan, engineering leaders building governance for AI and quantum work, and anyone who thinks ethics can wait until the hardware is ready.

Title: The skill AI teams share is a 1965 model of team development
Description: Scott M. Graffius (Exceptional Agility) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on why Tuckman's five phases of team development make AI teams succeed
Body:
Out of 111 skills that AI teams draw on, Scott M. Graffius argues one decides whether they succeed, and it is not a framework or a model architecture. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 the agile project management consultant, author and founder of Exceptional Agility makes the case that team development is what successful AI teams have in common, and walks through Bruce W. Tuckman's five phases with concrete things to do in each.

Yes, it is a people talk at a quantum conference. It is also a well-researched one: Graffius built it from 117 sources, most published in the previous ten years, with a full bibliography in the deck. One of them is the SRE Team Lifecycles chapter of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, so the ops crowd is in good company.

## Why soft skills, of all things?

He starts with a chart of 111 hard and soft skills that show up in AI teams, explicitly not exhaustive and never identical between two teams. At the category level, soft skills win, and he lines up support from Computerworld, the book chapter *In the AI Era, Soft Skills are the New Hard Skills*, and the United States Artificial Intelligence Institute, which puts soft skills at the top of its most-wanted AI skills. Narrow that down and you get the team itself: IBM calls the team a key driver of a successful AI project, Microsoft warns not to underestimate team dynamics, and MIT calls teamwork crucial.

## What are the five phases?

Tuckman, a Princeton psychology PhD, published forming, storming, norming and performing in 1965. In 1977 he and Mary Ann C. Jensen added adjourning, so anything you read describing four phases is the original, superseded version. Performance across the phases follows a curve: lowest in storming, highest in performing. Graffius uses the characteristics of each phase as diagnostic criteria, so you can tell where a team actually is. There is no fixed duration: storming might last a business day or the whole project.

## Forming: what should a lead do first?

Forming happens whenever a team assembles or someone joins or leaves. Expect eagerness, politeness, safe topics, and a normal amount of anxiety and questioning. Whoever takes the lead (title does not matter: engineer, Scrum Master, PM or business analyst) should be visible, facilitate interactions, share everything already known about values, process and deadlines as early as possible, set clear expectations and answer questions fast. He also defends the humble icebreaker. "Icebreakers aren't just for people who have never worked together before," Scott M. Graffius said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023; a two-minute one gives an established team a fresh start too.

## Storming: how do you get out of it?

Resistance, lower participation, conflict over opinions, jockeying for position and high emotions are all normal here. Two strategies stand out. First, actively request and encourage feedback, through any channel, any time, and then visibly handle it, rather than parking issues until a retrospective weeks away. Second, build trust by honouring commitments. His example is a new team whose first five daily stand-ups get cancelled in a row: no single cancellation is a problem, but the pattern tells people what your commitments are worth. As he puts it, "honoring your commitments goes a real long ways to building trust".

## Norming and performing: what changes for the leader?

In norming, the second most productive phase, cohesion develops, purpose and goals are understood and earlier anxiety fades. The lead recognises individual and team efforts, offers learning opportunities and feedback while the work is live, and starts stepping back to monitor the team's energy.

Performing is the peak, which the literature correlates with happiness and success, the opposite of burnout. The team shows interdependence and self-management, high motivation, trust and empathy, and consistently ships. Here the advice is minimal intervention: lead from the side, celebrate successes during the work rather than only at the end, and encourage collective decision-making (which a performing team is probably doing already).

## Why does adjourning matter?

Because projects end and teams disband, and that can bring real sadness, which is why some call it the mourning phase. It applies even when the same people carry on together, since it marks the end of a sprint, iteration or R&D cycle. Run a retrospective or post-project review and fold the lessons into future work, acknowledge individuals, and celebrate publicly. A leader thanking the team at a company meeting does more than please the team; it shows everyone else what the company values.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, tech leads, Scrum Masters and anyone forming a new AI or ML team. If you have already run a team through Tuckman's model, the value is in the specific strategies per phase and the bibliography.

Title: Could quantum processing pull more out of LIGO's laser light?
Description: Archit Srivastava (Hewlett Packard Enterprise, AiQyaM) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on using quantum signal processing in gravitational wave detection
Body:
Most quantum use-case talks stop at portfolios and delivery routes. Archit Srivastava went somewhere stranger at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023: gravitational wave observatories, where quantum noise is one of the main enemies, and where he proposes adding quantum processing before and after the measurement to separate signal from noise. A full stack data engineer at Hewlett Packard Enterprise and founder of the quantum hardware community AiQyaM, he is upfront that this is a research direction, not a result.

The title, In Ignotis, means into the unknown, and the talk is honest about how much of it is unknown. Treat it as a well-illustrated introduction to how detectors like LIGO work plus a sketch of where quantum computing might plug in.

## Why put quantum and astrophysics in the same talk?

Because they sit at opposite ends of physics. Astrophysics deals with black holes and relativity on cosmic scales; quantum physics with the very small. Quantum gravity is the hypothetical theory joining them, with the graviton as its predicted particle, and Srivastava's longer-term hope is that better detection tools could one day help test it experimentally.

He also does a quick tour of today's quantum computers for context: the gold "chandelier" of a dilution refrigerator with the chip near absolute zero at the bottom, cloud access from IBM, Google, Microsoft and Amazon through SDKs such as Qiskit, PennyLane and Braket, and architectures from superconducting and trapped ions to photonics and D-Wave's annealers.

## How does a gravitational wave detector actually work?

Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime predicted by Einstein's general relativity, sent out strongest when massive bodies such as two black holes or neutron stars spiral into each other and merge. Everything that moves makes them; it is only a question of mass. "Even if I am moving my hand, it is creating gravitational wave ripples in the spacetime fabric," Archit Srivastava said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, but a hand is nowhere near massive enough to be noticed.

The detectors are laser interferometers. A beam splitter sends light down two long vacuum arms, mirrors bounce it back, and when a wave passes, the mirrors shift by a minuscule amount and the light intensity at the detector changes. LIGO's first two sites, Livingston and Hanford, have kilometres-long arms; Virgo in Europe, the underground KAGRA in Japan, the 600-metre experimental GEO 600 in Germany and the planned LIGO-India site in Maharashtra join them. The space-based LISA is meant to escape the arm-length limits of building on Earth. Multiple sites matter because only a signal common to all of them counts as a wave, not a passing car.

## Where does quantum noise come in?

The list of noise sources is long: seismic, gravity gradient, suspension, mirror coating Brownian noise, thermal effects from lasers heating mirrors that weigh tons. One of the biggest contributors is quantum shot noise, caused by quantum vacuum fluctuations, since the instrument is counting photons. Detectors already fight it with squeezed states of light, which raise the signal-to-noise ratio and help pick out faint wave signatures, and machine learning is already used to identify the waves of interest among the noise.

## What is the proposal?

Two places to add quantum processing around the photodetector measurement:

- **Quantum signal pre-processing**: process the light before measurement to extract quantum information potentially hidden in the wave, using Hilbert space for a wider spectrum of data. He cites the GEO 600 team's work as the inspiration.
- **Quantum signal post-processing**: today's post-processing is classical, including its machine learning steps. A quantum equivalent, with quantum machine learning in place of classical models, might speed up processing and improve signal isolation, so errors are separated more efficiently.

The foundation he points to is the 16-metre frequency-dependent squeezing experiment for the A+ upgrade of Advanced LIGO, together with GEO 600's efforts. His picture is a modular setup: optical or software stages, each targeting a particular quantum algorithm or optical technique, that could be swapped in after a wave is isolated.

## What does it add up to?

His conclusions are carefully hedged: these methods might help explore quantum gravity, might lead to a hypothesis for experimentally proving gravitons, and may improve gravitational wave detection along the way. He also makes the spin-off argument familiar from CERN and LIGO: the engineering built for fundamental physics tends to end up in medicine and elsewhere.

## Who should watch

Physics-curious engineers who want a clear explanation of interferometric detection, and quantum people looking for a less crowded application area to read about. Anyone wanting a worked quantum algorithm or measured speed-up will not find one here.

- Karthiganesh Durai on [quantum machine learning as the next big thing](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Karthiganesh_Durai_qml_next_big_thing), the post-processing ingredient here.

Title: Developer observability, or how to stop redeploying just to add a log line
Description: Shai Almog (debugagent.com) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on developer observability, a fourth pillar for injecting logs and metrics into production.
Body:
Every developer knows the loop: a bug shows up only in production, the logs don't say enough, so you add a log line, open a PR, wait for review, wait for CI, deploy, wait for the bug to happen again, and find out you logged the wrong thing. Shai Almog, founder of debugagent.com and author of Practical Debugging at Scale, argued at Conf42 Observability 2023 that developers need a fourth pillar of observability next to logs, metrics and traces: one that lets them add a log or metric to running production code without a redeploy.

## What's wrong with the three pillars?

Nothing, for Ops. Almog calls logs, traces and metrics fantastic and essential. His complaint is that they are static. You can't add a log to a production system without a code change, and the same goes for metrics and custom spans.

He draws the path a single log line takes: development, pull request, review (sometimes two), merge, CI/CD and QA, production, then waiting for an end user to reproduce a flaky bug, only to discover the log missed the key value. Back to square one. "That's the CICD cycle of death," Shai Almog said at Conf42 Observability 2023, and he notes it gets nods from every crowd he shows it to.

## Why logging everything makes it worse

The obvious workaround is to log more, just in case. Almog's numbers for why that hurts: "Logging ingestion alone can account to a third of the total cloud costs." He also quotes a Reddit poster from r/devops: "A team just set a log level too high and burned through $100,000 in days." Overlogging slows the application, needs more resources, and still doesn't capture what you need, because privacy and security rules stop you from logging the truly valuable data. You end up with a bigger haystack and the needle still missing.

## The tools speak Ops, not code

His second complaint is the audience. Developers write logs, but Ops ingests them and SREs handle the incidents, so developers are guessing what someone else will find useful. The tooling talks about agents and entry points, not source lines. With microservices and serverless, many developers can only check their code through tests. And the hardest production bugs aren't crashes: they are cache misses or a stale cache that makes an item vanish from a listing, only in production. Ops can flush the cache, which he calls a blunt instrument.

## What developer observability looks like

The principle is to meet developers where they work, in the IDE or a browser, in terms of lines of code. You inject a log, metric or snapshot at a line in production, without changing the code. That cuts two stages out of the cycle: you can sit on a call with the customer while they reproduce the bug and add another log on the spot if the first wasn't enough.

He admits injecting is a scary word (a former employer banned it) and spends real time on security:

- **A management server in the middle.** Developers talk to the observability backend, never to production servers, unlike remote debugging.
- **A sandbox** that throttles an action using too much CPU and blocks expressions that try to change application state.
- **An administrative log** of every operation, so misuse leaves evidence.
- **PII reduction** that recognises patterns like credit card numbers and keeps them out of logs.
- **Block lists**, the most important one: stop anyone from adding logs to sensitive files, classes or packages, so a disgruntled developer can't print every password on the login path.

## The Lightrun demo

He demos Lightrun, noting he used to work there but no longer does. In IntelliJ IDEA, against a remote prime-counting app that prints no logs, he right-clicks a line and adds a log of a variable. It lands in the application log in order with the existing logs, ready for Elastic or piped back to the IDE. Tags let one action target a group of servers, say 500 tagged production out of 1,000. When his log burns too much CPU, the sandbox pauses it and restores it later on its own.

His favourite use isn't debugging at all: put a metric on a block of code to find out if it's ever reached before you change or delete it.

## Who should watch

Backend developers who debug production through other people's dashboards, and SREs who keep getting asked to raise log levels. It's a well-argued case for a tool category, with one vendor demoed, so treat the demo as an example rather than a recommendation.

Title: Quantum computing in one sitting, from Shor to a three-qubit Qiskit circuit
Description: Emmanuel Samir Harris at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on quantum basics, key algorithms, hardware, error correction and a first Qiskit circuit
Body:
If you want the whole field mapped on one page before diving into any part of it, Emmanuel Samir Harris's talk at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 is that page. The freelance software developer runs from qubits and a short history through Shor's and Grover's algorithms, hardware types, the Qiskit and Cirq frameworks and error correction, to a small Qiskit circuit and the challenges still blocking large machines. The takeaway is a sober one for a talk whose title promises to unleash quantum power: the applications are real candidates, but scale and noise decide when any of them pay off.

Be clear about the scope: this is a survey for newcomers, closer to a well-organised lecture than a field report. There are no benchmarks, and the success stories stay at the level of an unnamed leading airline.

## What do you need to know first?

A qubit, unlike a bit, can sit in a superposition of zero and one, which lets a quantum computer work on many possible inputs at once for certain problems. Qubits can be built from trapped ions, superconducting circuits or single photons, and all of them are fragile: noise and error make it hard to hold a quantum state for long, which is why so much research goes into error correction and qubit quality.

The history segment runs from Richard Feynman's early-1980s proposal to simulate quantum systems with quantum hardware, through Peter Shor's 1994 factoring algorithm and Grover's search, to the first NMR and ion-trap experiments in the 1990s and IBM's 5-qubit and 16-qubit machines in 2016 and 2017.

## Which algorithms matter, and why?

Two do most of the work in the talk:

- **Shor's algorithm** factors large integers efficiently, and since much of today's encryption rests on factoring being hard for classical computers, it would render many current schemes insecure.
- **Grover's algorithm** searches an unsorted list of N items in roughly the square root of N steps instead of N. Harris first calls this an exponential speed-up, then states it correctly later in the talk as a quadratic one, which is the version to remember.

Around them he lists the usual application areas: quantum simulation for drug discovery (with the caveat that modelling large biological systems precisely is still hard), route and supply-chain optimisation, quantum annealing for logistics and finance, fluid dynamics for aerospace, robotic control, quantum machine learning, and cryptography in both directions, breaking current schemes and building quantum key distribution and quantum-resistant encryption.

## What does the hardware and software stack look like?

On hardware he contrasts superconducting qubits, popular because they scale but troubled by stability and noise, with trapped ions, which hold coherence longer. Topological qubits and photonic machines are the bets further out.

On software, Qiskit from IBM Quantum gives a high-level, accessible environment for building circuits and running them on simulators or real hardware; Cirq from Google offers lower-level, gate-by-gate control. Both come with active communities, tutorials and hackathons.

## How does error correction help?

Qubits are disturbed by their environment, by hardware imperfections and by the fragility of the states themselves, and errors get more likely as machines grow. Quantum error correction codes add redundancy so errors can be detected and corrected without directly measuring the fragile state. The best known is the surface code, built on a two-dimensional grid of qubits; colour codes and other topological codes are also being explored. Fault tolerance, he argues, is the milestone that turns quantum computing from experiment into infrastructure.

## What does the demo show?

A Jupyter notebook with Qiskit: a three-qubit, three-bit `QuantumCircuit`, an X gate on qubit 1, Hadamards on all three, a CNOT from qubit 0 to 1, and measurement of everything, printed as an ASCII diagram. It is adapted from the Qiskit circuit-visualisation docs, and it is a sensible first step. "When building a quantum circuit, it is often helpful to draw the circuit," Emmanuel Samir Harris said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, and calling `print` or `draw()` on the circuit is how you do it.

## What still stands in the way?

Scaling up qubit counts, improving qubit stability and coherence times through materials science and engineering, and building the software tools that make all of it usable. His answer is collaboration across academia, industry and government, and across physics, computer science, mathematics and engineering.

## Who should watch

Developers and students who want a structured overview before picking a direction, or a refresher on the vocabulary before reading papers. If you already write Qiskit, the more specialised talks below will serve you better.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Abhigyan Mishra on [algorithms for quantum benefit in the NISQ era](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Abhigyan_Mishra_algorithms_quantum_benefit_nisq_era).

Title: An observability platform is a pipeline, and AIOps is its last stage
Description: Sameer Paradkar (Eviden) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on building an enterprise observability platform, from OpenTelemetry signals to AIOps.
Body:
Monitoring tells you what broke and when; observability is supposed to tell you why and how, ideally before the customer notices. Sameer Paradkar, IT architect at Eviden, an Atos business, used his Conf42 Observability 2023 talk to lay out what an enterprise-scale observability platform is made of: the telemetry it ingests, the pipeline that turns it into insight, the KPIs it moves, the tooling options, and AIOps as the stage after it.

This is an architect's overview for large estates, not a hands-on build. Expect reference architectures and comparison tables rather than code.

## Why bother beyond monitoring?

His opening argument is commercial. Unavailable or slow systems cost revenue, and users are impatient: if a page takes more than two or three seconds to load, he said, "the users would just run away from the portal." In an estate of application servers, databases, load balancers, network gear, IAM, integration and data warehouses, on premises and in the cloud, nobody can track the full stack by hand. The platform's job is to find the needle in the haystack and give one pane of glass over all of it.

He contrasts the two approaches column by column: monitoring is reactive, situational, speculative and built on data silos and sampling; observability is proactive, predictive, data-driven, keeps data in one place and instruments everything. Monitoring handles known unknowns, observability is meant for the unknown unknowns. His deck cites a Gartner prediction that by 2024, 30% of enterprises running distributed architectures would adopt observability techniques, up from less than 10% in 2020.

## The three signals, OpenTelemetry style

The foundation is the OpenTelemetry framework driven by the CNCF, which he describes as the set of practices ISVs, open source tools and hyperscalers all have to align with. Metrics are numeric values over time (CPU, memory, network bandwidth). Logs are timestamped records of events, call stacks included. Traces follow a user request end to end across nodes and services. Everything else, from user experience to KPIs, is derived from these three.

## What does the platform actually look like?

Paradkar's reference architecture is a funnel in four stages:

1. **Ingestion and collection** of logs, APM data, metrics, uptime and user experience data.
2. **Aggregation and processing**: raw data, then cleansed, then aggregated.
3. **Analysis**, where machine learning looks for anomalies, patterns and root causes.
4. **Alerts and dashboards** for the ops and SRE teams.

Alongside sits self-healing infrastructure: rules and policies that roll out a fix without the service desk or level 1 and 2 support getting involved. His logical architecture adds synthetic data to the list, six data types in all, and he notes the volumes run into terabytes and petabytes. His conclusion: "I think there is no way but to leverage automation."

## Which KPIs does it move?

He maps the platform to the non-functional numbers leadership cares about: customer experience, MTTR (down), MTBF (up), reliability and availability against your target nines, performance and scalability. Many tools ship templates for these KPIs, so you customise rather than build from scratch.

## Open source, hyperscaler or ISV?

The tooling comparison is the most reusable part of the talk. For each stage his deck lines up three options:

- **Open source hybrid**: Logstash for logging, Prometheus for application monitoring, Jaeger for tracing, Nagios for infrastructure, JavaMelody or Apache SkyWalking for user experience, Elasticsearch to analyse and Kibana to visualise.
- **Open source ELK**: Logstash with Filebeat and Metricbeat across the collection stages, then Elasticsearch and Kibana.
- **Azure native**: Azure Monitor, Application Insights, Log Analytics and Power BI. On the ISV side: Dynatrace, AppDynamics and New Relic.

His advice is to decide case by case: more focused, concrete products bring more features, and the right mix depends on your requirements.

## AIOps as the next maturity stage

The close frames AIOps as stage two: observability plus ITSM plus automation, observe, engage and act, heading towards autonomous operations. His deck includes an automated cloud remediation example where problem-to-fix time drops from 60 minutes of triage and developer remediation to 9 seconds with auto-ticketing and automated remediation, a claimed reduction of up to 99% in incident response time.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering managers planning an observability platform for a large, mixed estate who want a vocabulary and a checklist. Engineers already running OpenTelemetry in production will find it high level.

Title: A 31-minute queue for a 2-second run, and why quantum is still worth it
Description: Michal Jankowski (Objectivity, part of Accenture) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on why the quantum hype is justified and how to run a first PoC
Body:
Is quantum computing real or hype? Michal Jankowski of Objectivity, part of Accenture, answers both at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023: the hype is huge, it is also justified, and the cheapest way to find out what it means for your business is a proof of concept on a cloud quantum service. He backs that with two Objectivity PoCs, one of which cut a manufacturer's production-planning calculation from 4 hours to 90 seconds.

Jankowski builds quantum services at a custom software house, so read the optimism in that light (he says as much himself). What makes the talk useful is that he shows the unglamorous mechanics, queue times and noisy results included.

## Can you really run code on a quantum computer today?

Yes, and without a credit card. He builds a one-qubit circuit in IBM Quantum Composer: initialise to zero, apply a NOT (X) gate, measure. The composer shows the OpenQASM 2.0 code and a simulated result before you even log in. Then he sends it to real hardware, the seven-qubit IBM Oslo, with more than 300 jobs ahead of his.

The result is a good reality check. The job waited about 31 minutes in the queue and ran for 2 seconds, executing the circuit 1,024 times. A perfect machine would return 1 every time; this one returned 1 roughly 95% of the time, the rest lost to noise and short coherence times. Classical computing says two plus two is four. Quantum computing, in his framing, says it is four with 95% or 99% probability, depending on the device.

## Why now and not in ten years?

He gives three reasons:

- **Quantum runs in the cloud.** Besides vendor clouds, Microsoft Azure Quantum offers six hardware providers (among them Toshiba, QCI, Rigetti, Pasqal and IonQ) billed by usage. For a consultancy, that turns a quantum PoC into one more line on the client's existing cloud invoice instead of a new procurement and legal review.
- **Vendors are hitting their roadmaps.** IBM and others keep shipping processors with more qubits, which buys room for error correction and bigger problems.
- **The focus has shifted to interconnecting processors.** He compares it to his own path from a Commodore 64 and an Intel 286 to multicore CPUs: at some point clock speed stopped mattering and architecture took over. He sees the same move in quantum.

He also cites the surveys: in IQM's State of Quantum 2022, 63% expected commercial quantum computing within five years and 90% expected their operations to be transformed by 2030; EY and Capgemini point in the same direction.

## How do you check whether a technology is real?

Before touching any code, he talked to organisations already using quantum devices and asked blunt questions: what has been done, is it delivering value, how hard is it to learn, how long did that take, are you still using it, how much does it cost? Only the answers convinced him to build a quantum division. It is a reusable checklist for any shiny technology, not just this one.

## What did the PoCs actually do?

The first came out of a pre-Christmas hackathon: plan the CEO's trip around Objectivity's offices to wish staff merry Christmas in person, balancing people's availability against flights and shuttles, with a choice to optimise for price, flight time or CO2. The problem goes to a D-Wave quantum annealer over an API and returns in seconds, which is the real point of the demo: quantum slots into an existing application like any other service.

The second was for a manufacturing customer whose production-planning optimisation took 4 hours on classical methods and blocked them from extending the model. The quantum approach brought the largest models down to 90 seconds and, more interestingly, produced multiple solution scenarios, so the customer can score what-if options instead of adding new dimensions to the model.

## What is the adoption path?

Four stages: awareness, discovery (a prioritised backlog of use cases and a business case to find a sponsor), PoC on real data, then production. His most honest point is about failure. "Even if you will be not successful with the quantum projects, there is a huge chance that you will figure out something that will increase the value of the classical solution to your organization," Michal Jankowski said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023.

His verdict: roughly two to five more years before the technology is mature for general purposes, good today for narrow optimisation cases, and at minimum it belongs on your radar.

## Who should watch

Engineers and tech leads who want to see what a first quantum job looks like end to end, and anyone asked to evaluate a quantum PoC. If you already submit jobs to IBM Quantum, the second half on the PoCs and adoption stages is the part for you.

Title: GitOps is a reconciliation loop, and the loop is blind without observability
Description: Alejandro Mercado (KMMX) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on why GitOps needs observability, with an Argo CD demo of desired vs actual state.
Body:
GitOps keeps two versions of the truth, and only one of them lives in Git. Alejandro Mercado, Sales & DevOps Engineer at KMMX, argued in [his Conf42 Observability 2023 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2023_Alejandro_Mercado_unlocking_gitops) that Git holds the system's intended state while observability holds its actual state, so a GitOps controller that can't observe is a controller that can't reconcile. He backed it with a short Argo CD demo of a cluster drifting out of sync.

He warns up front that this is a big-picture talk: the forest rather than one tree. If you want deep internals of a GitOps controller, this isn't it. If you want a clear mental model of where observability plugs into GitOps, it is.

## Why does GitOps depend on observability at all?

The core image of the talk is the reconciliation loop. On one side sits the desired state, declared in manifests in a Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, any repo, it doesn't matter). On the other side sits the current state of the cluster. In the middle, a control plane added to Kubernetes compares the two and adjusts when they differ.

That comparison is observation. Mercado calls the loop the keystone of GitOps: you observe, and if the two states differ, you adjust. His four closing takeaways spell it out. You can't do GitOps without observability. Git is the single source of truth for intended state, observability for actual state. Internal observability lets the GitOps controller spot configuration drift. External observability lets operations staff and other systems see changes in the cluster.

## Monitoring looks back, observability looks ahead

Before GitOps, he spends some time on the difference between monitoring and observability. Monitoring, in his framing, is mostly post-mortem: diving into an ocean of log lines after something broke, passively gathering data that turns out to be mostly noise. Observability actively gathers what is relevant, from the three pillars of metrics, traces and logs, so the team knows about a problem before a user reports it. Noise, he points out, drowns operations people and AI tools alike.

## The four OpenGitOps principles

Mercado recommends opengitops.dev, the vendor-neutral set of open standards and best practices, and walks through its principles:

- **Declarative**: the desired state lives in manifests, not imperative commands.
- **Versioned and immutable**: the state is stored with full history, so rollbacks work like reverting a commit.
- **Pulled automatically**: software agents pull the desired state from the source rather than having it pushed at them.
- **Continuously reconciled**: agents keep observing the actual state and apply the desired one when they drift apart.

He lists the payoff companies are chasing: better security and compliance, more collaboration, less manual oversight, faster deployments and higher reliability.

## What does drift look like in Argo CD?

The demo uses Argo CD on a ready-made environment from the Codefresh GitOps training at learning.codefresh.io, which saves you from building a cluster first. He forks an example repository, creates an application pointing at a simple Go web app with one replica and a service on port 8080, and the UI immediately shows it as out of sync, in yellow. A click on Sync brings the actual state in line with Git.

The point he makes along the way: change the replica count in the manifest to two, five or twelve and the cluster is out of sync again until the loop catches up. In real life you don't sync by hand. As he put it, the idea is that you are not going to wake up every morning to sync every cluster; you let the controller do it. Health status turns red when a pod fails, and rollbacks work from the UI or the CLI. He also mentions Flux, Harness, Jenkins and Codefresh among the tools that apply the same pattern, and Helm as an easy way to install Argo CD.

## Does GitOps replace DevOps?

No, and he is firm about it. After a tour of the ever-growing list of Ops (DevSecOps, DataOps, AIOps, NoOps, and the Triceratops joke), he lands on the relationship. GitOps, he says, is a companion to DevOps. "Gitops without DevOps does not have a future," Alejandro Mercado said at Conf42 Observability 2023. GitOps is a way of doing releases and managing clusters inside a DevOps culture, not a successor to it.

## Who should watch

DevOps engineers and platform teams who have heard GitOps pitched as a deployment tool and want the observability angle, and anyone who needs a gentle first look at Argo CD's sync and health views. Experienced Argo CD users won't learn new mechanics here, but the desired-versus-actual framing is a handy way to explain GitOps to the rest of the team.

Title: Executives don't need superposition, they need the right questions
Description: Vardaan Sahgal (Womanium) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on what non-technical leaders should know before spending on quantum computing
Body:
You don't know how your phone works either, and you still make decisions about phones. That is the premise of Vardaan Sahgal's talk at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023: an executive's job is not to understand Shor's algorithm but to know which business problems quantum might help with, how far off that help is, and how not to get dragged onto the hype train. Vardaan Sahgal is software head at Womanium, a Washington, DC nonprofit, leads its Quantum Solutions Launchpad and is an IBM Qiskit Advocate.

It is a short, explicitly non-technical session, and the second half is a pitch for Womanium's programmes. Engineers looking for circuits should look elsewhere; engineers who need to explain quantum to their VP may find the framing useful.

## Why should a leader care at all?

He opens with money rather than physics. Worldwide public investment in quantum technologies has passed $36 billion, and an EY survey of 501 executives found 97% expect quantum computing to disrupt their sectors to a high or moderate extent. Add more than 100 active players, startups with heavy capital behind them and pure-play quantum companies going public, and his estimate is that early advantages could show up in the next four to five years.

## What is quantum computing, at board level?

His analogy is a maze. A classical computer walks it path by path until it finds the exit. The tempting explanation is that a quantum computer checks every path faster, and he rejects it: the quantum machine is built differently and changes the rules of the game. For an executive, he argues, the mechanism can stay a black box, the same way the electronics inside a laptop do.

Then the necessary cold shower. No Schrödinger's cat doing your daily tasks, no Mars colonies, no time travel, no robot overlords. "Quantum computers are, they are not magic. They are still very much science," Vardaan Sahgal said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023. Classical and quantum machines will coexist, each in its own domain, and a realistic quantum advantage is still a long way off.

## Where will the first wins come from?

Optimisation and chemical simulation lead, followed by quantum machine learning and cryptography, with finance, healthcare, engineering and defence as the industries most exposed. He leans on a McKinsey analysis of sectors quantum could affect in the next five to ten years, and then on four short case studies:

- **Optimisation**: Volkswagen exploring smart traffic management, and Quantum-South using quantum annealers in a hybrid approach to plan cargo loading in passenger aircraft holds. His rule of thumb: any problem that boils down to minimising a cost function, from staff timetables to delivery schedules, is worth at least trying on quantum.
- **Drug discovery**: Fujitsu pairing quantum computing with its digital drug platform, with the wider point that cheap, accurate chemistry simulation spills over into materials science, food technology and nanotechnology.
- **Finance**: JPMorgan Chase, QC Ware and the University of Paris combining deep reinforcement learning with quantum computing to improve a deep hedging model. The slides note honestly that today's prototype machines are not powerful enough to run financial applications like this at scale.
- **Security**: ID Quantique as an early quantum cryptography adopter, and SoftBank with SandboxAQ combining classical encryption with post-quantum cryptography, so systems stay secure against quantum attacks without giving up classical guarantees.

On security his message is the familiar one, and still correct: a quantum computer that breaks today's encryption is likely decades away, but the time to prepare is now.

## What should an executive actually do?

Get educated before getting excited. Understand the principles, the risks and the realistic scope of advantage, so decisions inside the organisation are informed rather than hype-driven. The rest of the talk lays out Womanium's three offerings: an annual month-long workforce training programme for technical people (over 2,000 participants from 80+ countries a year, per the slides), an on-demand executive education course tailored per organisation, and the Quantum Solutions Launchpad, which assembles a remote team to build a first quantum project for a company. He stresses that the organisation is a nonprofit whose funds go to scholarships, that it can give a vendor-neutral view of SDKs and hardware services, and that the client keeps full IP ownership of the project.

## Who should watch

Executives, investors and policymakers who want a jargon-free 25 minutes on where quantum stands, and engineers who need an analogy for their leadership. Anyone wanting evidence beyond press-release case studies will want a more technical session alongside it.

Title: Start your quantum journey before the hardware is ready, not after
Description: Daniel Goldsmith and Pippa Spencer-Williams (Digital Catapult) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 on why business users should upskill for quantum now
Body:
Quantum computers today are small, noisy and of little direct use to most businesses, and that is exactly why Daniel Goldsmith and Pippa Spencer-Williams of Digital Catapult think you should start learning now. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023 the pair walk through what a qubit actually is, why the current NISQ machines are limited, which near-term use cases look plausible, and how Digital Catapult's free quantum Technology Access Programme (qTAP) gets end users hands-on before they have to bet any money.

It is an introduction pitched at business and technical decision makers, not physicists. If you already know your Hadamard from your CNOT, skip to the second half.

## What is a qubit, minus the maths?

Daniel Goldsmith, Senior Quantum Computing Technologist, uses a thought experiment he calls the quantum egg timer. It starts full and ends empty like the kitchen version, but because sand comes in lumps (quantum means a lump) it cannot be half full halfway through. Measure it then, and half the time it is full, half the time empty. A qubit driven by a pulse of exactly the right frequency and duration lands in the same kind of superposition.

His one-line version of why that matters: classical computers read a book letter by letter. "Whereas quantum computer is like reading the whole book all at the same time," Daniel Goldsmith said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023. He adds entanglement, notes that it underpins quantum key distribution, and then walks a two-qubit circuit (a Hadamard gate, a controlled two-qubit gate, a measurement) mainly to show where today's hardware runs out of road.

## Why can't today's quantum computers do much yet?

Three reasons, all visible in that tiny circuit:

- **Noise limits gate depth.** Stack too many gates and the signal washes out.
- **Too few qubits.** Useful work needs thousands of error-free qubits; IBM's Osprey had 433 noisy ones in 2022.
- **Limited connectivity.** A qubit may talk to only two or three neighbours instead of all of them.

The history slide runs from Feynman and Deutsch in 1985 through Shor's algorithm in 1994 and Grover's search in 1996, to the number fifteen being factorised on an NMR machine in 2002. The speculative end of the timeline puts a commissioned fault-tolerant quantum computer around 2035, with a question mark. Getting to millions of qubits, he stresses, needs fundamental research breakthroughs, error correction (grouping physical qubits into logical ones) chief among them.

Until then the workhorse is the variational quantum algorithm: a parameterised circuit runs, a classical optimiser scores the output and feeds new parameters back, and the loop repeats. A quantum computer trained by a classical one, which is a nice inversion of the usual hype.

## Which use cases are realistic in the near term?

Pippa Spencer-Williams, Senior Innovation Partner, takes the business half. Her three buckets:

- **Optimisation** via quantum annealing or variational algorithms: energy networks with ever more assets on them, telecoms networks, parcel and air cargo routing, factory flows.
- **Simulation of physical systems**: computational fluid dynamics over an aerofoil or a hull, and molecules for drug discovery, since a molecule is itself a quantum system.
- **Quantum machine learning**: speed, accuracy and scalability gains for existing ML workloads; network fault detection is one application being evaluated.

## What should a business do today?

Two things. First, sort out your encryption. Shor's algorithm could undermine RSA within a decade, the slides warn about store-now-break-later attacks, and the migration is not quick. "There is massive amounts of information encrypted using the RSA encryption today," Pippa Spencer-Williams said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2023, and replacing all of it will take a long time, so the inventory should start now.

Second, avoid future shock. If quantum suddenly matters to a core business process, how long would your team need to catch up? Her argument is that a small investment in education today is cheaper than being on the back foot later.

## What is qTAP?

The programme is part of Digital Catapult's Quantum Data Centre of the Future project, which embeds a quantum computer in a classical data centre. qTAP runs for five months with 5-12 end-user participants, picked through an application, a questionnaire and a one-to-one interview. It moves through onboarding, discovery (education, masterclasses, hands-on training), experimentation on simulators, and demonstration, in three streams: fault tolerant, optimisation and quantum machine learning. Participants run algorithms on an ORCA photonic quantum computer, with consortium partners including ORCA, Riverlane, KETS, BT and PQShield. The 2023 open call opened in July.

## Who should watch

Managers and architects being asked whether quantum is worth a budget line, and anyone who wants a gentle, accurate primer on NISQ limits before reading vendor roadmaps. Researchers will find nothing new in the physics.
