Title: From useless Lambda logs to real observability in a few clicks
Description: Pawel Piwosz (Spacelift) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on observing AWS Lambda with X-Ray, Lambda Insights and Powertools, from cold starts to structured logs
Body:
Deploy a Lambda behind API Gateway with a 20-line SAM template and the default telemetry tells you it ran, how often and for how long, and nothing about why one invocation took longer than another. At Conf42 Observability 2023, Pawel Piwosz, Developer Advocate at Spacelift and an AWS Community Builder, walked that function from near-useless defaults to proper observability: X-Ray tracing, Lambda Insights for cold starts, JSON access logs with trace IDs, and AWS Lambda Powertools inside the code.

The first half is his philosophy of observability; the second is the AWS walkthrough. He had joined Spacelift only days before, so the talk is about AWS, not Spacelift.

## Why do we see less than we used to?

On bare metal you could observe everything from the air conditioning to each user's behaviour. Virtual machines hide the layer below; containers hide more (on Fargate, almost everything); with serverless you hand over code and an API endpoint and see nothing else. Fewer interactions, less access, more tools, and the idea that central logging is passé.

He blames part of it on a misreading of agile: self-organising teams monitoring only their own component. "Yes, but on the end of the day, it's the company who sell the product, not the team," Pawel Piwosz said at Conf42 Observability 2023. Decoupling into microservices and functions adds complexity to communication between components and between teams, with Conway's law lurking.

## What makes a log structured?

A structured message is not yet a structured log. Wrapping a syslog line into JSON is his tongue-in-cheek hint for becoming a senior engineer, and also a real upgrade, since downstream tools stop pattern-matching text. A structured log goes further, adding the surrounding information: who, which resource, which gateway, what outcome.

He's equally blunt about tools: "observability is not Grafana on kubernetes. If you have Grafana on kubernetes, you don't have observability." Logs (not just errors to save money), metrics (with context, relevant to the business) and traces (to answer the customer who swears his request was slow) all need to be consistent across the system and built for automation, because you want to sleep at night. Logs give the surroundings, traces the path, metrics the scale. His own framework, MEAL (metrics, events, logs, actions), adds the fourth part: act on what you collect, automatically where you can.

## Turning on the lights, click by click

The issue he chases is the cold start, visible to experienced eyes but hard to measure by default.

- **X-Ray on the function and on the API Gateway stage**: request paths, response distributions and per-invocation traces. One click for the Lambda, two for the API, and you've become a regular engineer. The traces show gaps, but not whether a gap is a cold start.
- **Lambda Insights** (enhanced monitoring): memory, CPU time, network I/O, duration and init duration. Init duration is the cold start, so now you can see which invocations paid it.
- **API Gateway logs**: CloudWatch logs plus a custom JSON access log format with `$context.xrayTraceId` added, so one trace ID follows the request everywhere. Contributor Insights then slices the data further.

That covers the outside of the request. For the inside, AWS Lambda Powertools (Python, TypeScript, Java and .NET), added as a Lambda layer, gives traces into sub-functions, custom metrics such as how often a sub-function was called, and consistently formatted logs. The SAM template grows from 20 to 67 lines, partly because he spells out the log format across several lines. His dev.to series has the full Python implementation.

## Where does the data go next?

Everywhere: CloudWatch, Athena, OpenSearch, Kinesis and QuickSight, Timestream with Grafana, or Prometheus, plus alarms that trigger Lambdas. Instrumentation options beyond Powertools include Jaeger, Prometheus and OpenTelemetry; all-in-one options include Honeycomb, Dynatrace and Splunk. He signs off with DevOps Borat's question about who monitors your monitoring server.

## Who should watch

Engineers running Lambda behind API Gateway with only the default metrics, and anyone who needs the argument for structured logs and traces spelled out for their team. If you already ship Powertools everywhere, the first half's opinions are the main draw.

Title: Students monitor, teachers observe. Observability 101 with RisingWave
Description: Ritvi Mishra (Major League Hacking) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on observability basics for newcomers, with a RisingWave and generative art project
Body:
A class monitor watches the room for a while; the teacher keeps observing even when she isn't trying to keep order. At Conf42 Observability 2023, Ritvi Mishra, a coach at Major League Hacking, used analogies like that one to explain observability to people with no production experience, then sketched a learning project that feeds click data from a generative art front end through the RisingWave streaming database and back into the art.

This is explicitly a 101. Ritvi says up front that it's for people coming from a non-production background, and that she is learning observability on the go herself. Experienced SREs can skip it; students and career changers are the audience.

## How do you explain observability to a non-engineer?

She starts with an intuition exercise: pause the video and write down the first word that comes to mind when you hear observability, then compare at the end. Then the analogies. A status page with a green all-systems-OK badge is not observability. Fast fashion is closer: brands correlate runway trends, social media, influencers, what customers browse and stitching lead times to push new clothes out in about three weeks. Lots of signals, constantly correlated (she notes it's not an environmentally friendly example).

And the classroom. "Students monitor, but teachers observe" is the line most likely to stick with the audience she's addressing.

## Where does the word come from?

From control theory: Rudolf E. Kálmán introduced observability in 1960 as a measure of how well a system's internal states can be inferred from its external outputs, the mathematical dual of controllability. For software she adds conditions: you can understand the inner workings and whatever unpredictable state the application got itself into purely by interrogating it with external tools, without shipping new code to do so. She also notes you don't always need it, for example in a monolith that isn't serving lots of users.

## Monitoring versus observability

"Observability is way more than just monitoring," Ritvi Mishra said at Conf42 Observability 2023. Her framing: monitoring tracks predefined metrics, where a metric is a single number with optional tags for grouping and searching. Observability is about being ready before the system reaches a state you couldn't predict, by collecting widely and correlating. She leans on the idea that every application has irreducible complexity, and the only question is whether the user, the application developer or the platform developer deals with it.

Her treatment of cardinality and dimensionality is the loosest part of the talk. She describes high-cardinality data as rare data; the more common definition is a field with many unique values, like user or request IDs. The conclusion lands in the right place, though: rich, high-dimensional telemetry is what lets you find patterns you didn't know to look for.

## Four steps and a streaming database

Her recipe for an observable system has four steps: instrumentation, data correlation, incident response, and AIOps (which she says she hasn't explored much). For correlation she likes a streaming database, and RisingWave in particular: open source, runs locally or in its then-beta cloud, ingests event streams and keeps materialized views fresh in real time. She points newcomers at the clickstream analysis example in its docs as a front-end observability starter.

## The generative art project

The project is presented as a block diagram rather than a demo (she estimates a full demo would take another 40 minutes). A React front end draws a small algorithmic spiral. Click events are instrumented and sent to RisingWave, which maintains a materialized view over them. Instead of an incident response stack, the correlated data is fed back into the art as an extra parameter, with new parameters generated separately for comparison. Start with one click, add more data, and watch how correlation changes the output. It's a toy, but a nicely visual way to see the pipeline end to end.

## Who should watch

Students, hackathon folks and anyone outside engineering who keeps hearing the word observability. If you already run production systems, try one of the related talks instead.

Title: CloudWatch ships zero alarms. SLIC Watch writes them at deploy time
Description: Diren Akkoc (fourTheorem) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on SLIC Watch, which generates CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for serverless apps on deploy
Body:
Open the CloudWatch console on a freshly deployed serverless app and you'll find plenty of metrics and exactly zero alarms. At Conf42 Observability 2023, Diren Akkoc, Junior Cloud Software Developer at fourTheorem, showed SLIC Watch, the company's open-source plugin that reads your CloudFormation template at deploy time and adds sensible dashboards and alarms for every resource in the stack.

It's a short talk and an honest one about scope: CloudWatch is powerful, but it's a kit you have to assemble. SLIC Watch assembles a sensible default version for you. Diren maintains the plugin, and she also used the stage to encourage more women to speak at technical events.

## What does CloudWatch give you out of the box?

The AWS-native observability stack covers logs with Logs Insights, metrics, dashboards, alarms, canaries and distributed tracing with X-Ray. The good: metrics are generated automatically for every service. The less good: dashboards are organised by service, not by your application, and there are no alarms, which she says is fair, since what to alert on depends on your application's context. "Cloudwatch is already a super powerful tool, but it's a toolkit," Diren Akkoc said at Conf42 Observability 2023.

## Why doing it by hand hurts

The manual route: research the available metrics, decide thresholds, write infrastructure as code for application dashboards and for every service metric alarm, then update it all whenever you add a service or even a single Lambda function, for every stack. One Lambda throttles alarm in CloudFormation is a screenful of JSON with a metric math expression for throttles as a percentage of invocations; now multiply by every function.

The AWS Well-Architected Framework's operational excellence pillar and the Serverless Lens tell you which metrics matter, and the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) frame them. They still don't pick thresholds for you. Her advice is to treat observability like unit tests: maintain it and keep it current, and it pays you back.

## How does SLIC Watch work?

Most AWS infrastructure-as-code tools (Serverless Framework, AWS SAM, CDK) end up as CloudFormation stacks. On `sls deploy` or `sam deploy`, your YAML becomes a very big JSON template. SLIC Watch hooks into the framework's deploy lifecycle, inspects that template for each resource type, and adds dashboards and alarms, so the very big JSON becomes an even bigger one, and that is what gets deployed.

It comes with sane defaults, and everything is configurable: change the thresholds, or disable specific dashboards and alarms. Point it at an SNS topic and every alarm is delivered there, ready to wire into AWS Chatbot, Opsgenie or PagerDuty. The before-and-after is the point of the demo: an empty alarms page becomes a list of relevant alarms, plus one dashboard covering the whole stack, so you scroll one page instead of hopping between console tabs.

## Who should watch

Teams on Serverless Framework or SAM who have been meaning to set up CloudWatch alarms, and anyone who has copy-pasted the same alarm block across twenty functions. Her one takeaway: "observability is your friend from day one." If you already have a mature alerting setup, the talk mostly confirms you did the work SLIC Watch automates. The plugin lives at fth.link/slic-watch.

Title: SLOs for 1,000 engineers need formulas, time ranges and raw histograms
Description: Fred Moyer at Conf42 Observability 2023 on SLO and error budget formulas that scale across 1,000+ engineers, and why averaged percentiles lie
Body:
Average two servers' p95 latencies and you can be off by almost 100%. At Conf42 Observability 2023, Fred Moyer, an SRE observability engineer who has spent years rolling SLOs out to organisations of more than 1,000 engineers, distilled that work into a short list: SLI, SLO and error budget formulas that humans and code can both parse, an explicit time range on every objective, and raw histograms instead of percentiles for latency.

He calls it the greatest-hits version of the SLO talks he has given over the past six or so years, and his opinions are his own, not his employer's.

## Why the books weren't enough

When Fred was first asked to bring SLOs to a 1,000+ engineer organisation, he went back to the sources: the Google SRE book, the SRE workbook, and Liz Fong-Jones and Seth Vargo's talk "SLIs, SLOs, SLAs, oh my!". He found no prescription. The books were vague on concrete SLIs, and some workbook examples had subtle omissions. Then came what he calls the Cambrian SLO explosion, with SLO conferences and Alex Hidalgo's book, but he still needed formulas that left little room for creative variance across hundreds of teams.

## The formulas he shipped

He picked the SLI definition that splits good requests from bad ones, which he found more practical than the SRE book's "measurement of system performance". Each SLI is a metric identifier, an operator and a value: `home page request response code != 5xx`, `home page request served in < 100ms`.

An SLO is then a success objective, the SLI and a period: 99.95% of home page requests served in under 100 ms over the last 24 hours. Leave the period out and it isn't an SLO, and he sees that omission constantly, in the literature too. Use the same SLI with different periods for different audiences: a week for an engineering manager scheduling reliability work, a month for a director, a quarter for a VP reporting upwards.

The error budget is the inverted SLO: 1 minus 0.9995 gives 0.05%, so out of a million requests only 500 may be slow or fail. Alert when, say, 80% of the budget is spent, or when the burn rate predicts exhaustion before the period ends. An untouched budget is a signal too: a miscalibrated SLO, too little feature work, or a case for deliberate burns like Google's Chubby. Combining both conditions gives one SLI for latency and availability: not a 5xx and served in under 100 ms.

## Where does 99.95% come from?

An engineering VP he worked with set three and a half nines as the bar, and Fred argues that's what enterprise customers demand. With the objective fixed, the SLI's threshold is the only variable, so he calibrates it: take a period of known good performance, set 99.95%, and iterate over latency values until the numbers match (100 ms, in his example). He built a dashboard so teams could do exactly that.

## Why averaged percentiles lie

The talk opens with an RRD graph from the dot-com era, when bandwidth was billed at the 95th percentile, the habit that StatsD later carried into latency with p95 in 2011. His 2019 SREcon example: one bimodal fast server and one slower one. Averaging their p95s gives about 430 ms; computing p95 over the combined raw values gives 230 ms. "And many, if not all, of the monitoring and observability tools out there will happily let you use an averaging function for percentiles generated from different hosts, nodes or clusters," Fred Moyer said at Conf42 Observability 2023. Fine on one node, wrong the moment nodes behave differently.

The fix is histograms with latency bands. He compares log-linear histograms (OpenHistogram's circllhist), Prometheus-style cumulative histograms, and an inverse cumulative variant he designed, tagging a 125 ms sample as above 10, 50 and 100 ms. The SLI is then plain counting: sum of requests under 100 ms divided by all requests, times 100, at least 99.95. Fast, exact, arbitrary precision. Sketches and approximations (t-digest, DDSketch, HDR Histogram) do well on one node, but across hundreds of asymmetric nodes or arbitrary windows their errors are likely unbounded, so he recommends raw histograms. He also points to Adrian Cockcroft's work splitting bimodal latency into normal distributions with the R mixtools package, a path to per-mode SLOs such as cache versus block device writes.

## SLOs across a distributed system

Give every service an SLO and error budget, third-party vendors included, then roll error rates up from upstream towards the client. In his example the in-house backend runs at 0.1%, but a third party pushes the mid tier to 1%, past its 1% budget, so that's where the reliability work goes. "The goal here is not to assign blames to teams or to different services. It's to prioritize reliability work," he said.

## Who should watch

Anyone writing SLOs for more than a handful of teams, and anyone whose latency SLO is built on averaged percentiles.

Title: Image scanning stops at deploy time. Falco watches the syscalls after
Description: Thomas Labarussias (Sysdig) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on runtime security with Falco, eBPF and Falcosidekick, from syscall to alert to automated reaction
Body:
You scan your images and enforce admission policies, and then a container in production spawns a shell, installs curl and pokes the Kubernetes API. At Conf42 Observability 2023, Thomas Labarussias, OSS and Ecosystem Advocate at Sysdig (the company that created Falco), showed how Falco catches that in real time by watching system calls through an eBPF probe, and how Falcosidekick turns its alerts into notifications and automated reactions.

Thomas was an SRE for over eight years and created Falcosidekick and its UI, so this is a tour from someone who built half the ecosystem.

## What is runtime security, exactly?

His definition: all the tools and procedures you put in place to secure an application, containerised or not, during its lifetime in production. That's different from image scanning in CI and from admission policies with tools like Gatekeeper. It is about what the application does while it serves real traffic.

The signal is the syscall, the kernel's API: every process creation, network connection and file read or write goes through one (glibc or musl being the SDK in his analogy). Falco, a CNCF incubation-level project with 5.8k GitHub stars and 60M+ pulls at the time, reads those syscalls and matches them against rules.

## Why eBPF?

eBPF runs programs inside the Linux kernel without changing kernel code or loading a module. Probes attach to hooks (syscalls, file system, network, or custom ones), and before anything runs the kernel checks it. "All the code you write for your EBPF probe will be verified by the Linux kernel," Thomas Labarussias said at Conf42 Observability 2023. The verifier rejects infinite loops and anything that could hurt stability or performance; approved code is compiled to bytecode and runs in a sandbox. A new CO-RE (compile once, run everywhere) probe was in development, so one build would serve any kernel from 5.8 onwards instead of one per kernel version.

## How does a rule fire?

Only the probe lives in kernel space. Falco itself runs in user space with fewer privileges, on two libraries: libscap reads syscall events from the driver's ring buffer, and libsinsp enriches them with machine state (container ID and name, pod name, namespace, labels), filters them and extracts fields for the rules.

Rules are YAML, readable even without a Linux background. The classic `Terminal shell in container` rule combines macros: `spawned_process` (`evt.type in (execve, execveat)`), `container` (`container.id != host`) and `shell_procs` (`proc.name` in a list of shells from ash to zsh). The output template fills in `%user.name`, `%proc.cmdline` and `%container.id`; each rule has a priority and tags, including MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs. The default ruleset ships around 70 rules covering privilege escalation, sensitive file access, shells, SSH binaries, binary mutation and symlinks, some disabled by default because they're noisy until you add your own exceptions. Lists, macros and rules can all be overridden or appended.

## From alert to action

Falco detects; Falcosidekick notifies. It forwards alerts to chat, Elasticsearch or Loki, Kafka, NATS or Pub/Sub, on-call tools (PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Grafana OnCall), S3-style storage, and exposes a Prometheus endpoint for alert stats. Falco runs as one instance per node, all feeding a single Falcosidekick, which can for instance send everything to Elasticsearch but page only on alerts above critical. Route alerts into Lambda, OpenFaaS, Knative, Argo Workflows or Tekton and you get reaction: terminate the pod, apply a network policy to isolate it, scale a group.

Falco has also grown past syscalls. Plugins (shared libraries in user space) bring in Kubernetes audit logs, AWS CloudTrail, GitHub webhooks, Docker events and Nomad events, the last built with HashiCorp. falcoctl installs plugins and rules and keeps them updated. "It means right now with Falco you can protect all stages from the development to the production," he said.

## The demo

A two-node cluster runs Falco as a DaemonSet (one pod per node), plus Falcosidekick, its UI with Redis storage, and a separate Falco with the EKS plugin. Thomas plays the attacker inside a pod: opening a shell, installing curl, trying the Kubernetes API (blocked, but detected) and opening a file under /etc for writing. Each is flagged instantly with user, namespace, pod, image and command line, and the Falcosidekick UI shows them with filters and charts, alongside the audit-log event for the exec. Getting started is one Helm install with Falcosidekick, its UI and the eBPF driver enabled; he says it's running in less than two minutes.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers running Kubernetes who have build-time controls but nothing watching production, and SREs curious how eBPF-based detection works under the hood. A good first talk on Falco.

Title: One giant trace or span links? Tracing event-driven systems with OTel
Description: Henrik Rexed (Dynatrace) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on tracing event-driven architectures with OpenTelemetry, and when span links beat one end-to-end trace
Body:
Propagate trace context through a message broker and you get exactly what you asked for: one end-to-end trace, minutes long, in which the publisher's work is a sliver too thin to see. At Conf42 Observability 2023, Henrik Rexed, Cloud Native Advocate at Dynatrace, walked through tracing an event-driven architecture with OpenTelemetry both ways, a single propagated trace versus separate traces joined with span links, and why choosing between them is a design decision, not a default.

Henrik brings 15+ years of performance engineering and runs the Is It Observable YouTube channel; the demo code is public in the isItObservable/tracing_eda GitHub repository.

## Why does he call observability an art?

The opening is a story about drawing a web server's health. In 1999, with top and nmon, all he had were points. Stored history plus CMDB metadata gave him lines, APM tools around 2010 added distributed traces and real user monitoring, and indexed logs around 2014 filled in a bit more. Even then, the picture never showed the surroundings. "Observability is not a science. Observability is like an art," Henrik Rexed said at Conf42 Observability 2023.

The art supplies are logs, events (Kubernetes, CI pipelines), metrics, traces and profiling, plus context: namespace, pod, version, region. His complaint is the common setup where Prometheus holds metrics, Jaeger holds traces and Elasticsearch holds logs, and nothing connects them. OpenTelemetry fixes the format, not the storage: the SDK is the guitar, the Collector the amplifier that adds effects and feeds as many backends as you like. At the time traces were stable in most languages, metrics nearly so, logs still under construction and continuous profiling only at the spec stage.

## The OTel tracing pieces that matter here

A compact refresher: auto-instrumentation covers Spring, Django and friends; a trace is a list of spans glued by a context holding the trace ID and span ID; the TracerProvider brings a span processor, sampler, exporter and resource (minimum: `service.name`); and a propagator injects the context on the way out and extracts it on the other side.

Sampling gets a warning worth remembering. With AlwaysOn, AlwaysOff, ParentBased, TraceIdRatioBased and the parent-based combinations, ratios multiply along a chain. In his five-service example (A at 50%, then 25%, 50%, 10%, 10%), 1,000 requests yield just one end-to-end trace that reaches service E.

## Option one: propagate the context through the broker

The demo runs a publisher and two consumers (one REST, one database) over a Solace pub/sub broker, next to the OpenTelemetry demo app, with Dynatrace as the backend. Because the messaging SDK didn't propagate context automatically, the publisher writes the trace ID and span ID into message properties, and each consumer reads them, rebuilds a span context and continues as a child.

It works: one trace shows the publisher and both consumers. It is also the minutes-long trace from the top of this post, and the publisher's few hundred milliseconds of work are impossible to optimise in it. Henrik's verdict on whether it's a useful trace: no.

## Option two: span links

A span link records a relationship between spans without making one the parent of the other. The publisher code doesn't change. The consumers still extract the context, but now start a new trace and attach a link to the publisher's span. The result is three short traces, one per service, and in Dynatrace a link on the consumer trace jumps back to the publisher trace. Now the bottleneck is obvious: the publisher spends most of its time connecting to the pub/sub broker.

## What do span links cost you?

Two things, and he's candid about both. The relationship is one-way in practice: from a consumer it's easy to find the publisher, but from the publisher you can't see how many consumers a message triggered. And sampling decisions are now made per trace, so you may keep the consumer trace and lose the publisher's, or the other way round. "That's why it's an art to do observability," Henrik Rexed said at Conf42 Observability 2023.

His takeaways: keep instrumentation vendor-agnostic (no vendor libraries or exporters), give metrics enough dimensions and logs enough context, add span attributes, and design the tracing approach around how your system actually behaves.

## Who should watch

Anyone instrumenting Kafka, Pulsar, Solace or any queue-based system who has stared at an unreadable mega-trace. Also a solid half-hour OpenTelemetry tracing refresher, sampling maths included.

Title: ChatGPT for observability is useful, non-deterministic and no panacea
Description: Gareth Emslie (Dynatrace) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on where ChatGPT fits in observability and why prompt engineering decides if it helps
Body:
Ask ChatGPT the same question twice about a latency problem and you get two different answers, which is a strange property for something you want in an incident workflow. At Conf42 Observability 2023, Gareth Emslie, a cloud strategist at Dynatrace, looked at where large language models could genuinely help operations teams, and concluded that they can, but only with careful prompt engineering, new skills and an honest view of the risks.

He opens with a disclaimer that the views are his own, not his employer's, and the talk stays vendor-neutral. It dates from mid-2023, so the model details are a snapshot of the GPT-3.5 era.

## Why bother with better observability?

Gareth starts with Werner Vogels' line that everything fails all the time, then backs it with 2022's hyperscaler outages. A Google Cloud maintenance event in us-west caused raised latency for 3 hours and 22 minutes. A Traffic Director code change produced elevated errors for 2 hours and 35 minutes, hitting customers such as Spotify and Discord. An Azure power oscillation in East US 2 lasted around 12 hours. A London heatwave broke data-centre cooling for Google Cloud and Oracle, and an AWS power failure in us-east-1 took down EC2 instances behind Webex, Okta, Splunk and BambooHR. The lesson he draws: the hyperscaler won't architect your reliability for you.

The money follows. Gartner put downtime at $5,600 per minute in 2014. Citing Pingdom, he gives hourly costs today of around $260,000 in manufacturing, $450,000 in IT, $3 million in automotive and up to $5 million for enterprises. Add multicloud complexity, an explosion of data and alerts, team silos and weak correlation, plus 199,889 people laid off by 715 tech companies in 2023 alone (his layoffs.fyi figure, with the institutional knowledge that leaves with them), and he expects outage risk to grow.

## How does ChatGPT work, briefly?

A compact primer for the non-ML crowd: deep neural networks, pre-training on data that is filtered, deduplicated, redacted of PII and tokenised, then reinforcement learning from human feedback. GPT-1 had 117 million parameters; GPT-3 has 175 billion and trained on 570 GB of filtered text taken from 45 TB of raw data. Training can cost in excess of $20 million in energy. ChatGPT is GPT-3.5 fine-tuned on dialogue, an autoregressive transformer using self-attention.

He's equally direct about the flaws: nonsensical answers, sensitivity to small prompt changes, verbosity, trouble with ambiguity, and exposure to prompt injection. And no, it is not Skynet.

## Where could it help operations teams?

Four use cases: a conversational interface for querying observability data in natural language; code generation for the scripts developers and ops engineers write; intelligent problem remediation, suggesting fixes in custom code; and enriching problem tickets and alerts with extra context for faster remediation.

Then the catches, shown from his own sessions. Responses are non-deterministic, and operations engineers expect a system to give the same guidance for the same input. And ChatGPT needs a lot of context: asking why latency appeared between application layers turned into a long thread of follow-up questions. You'd get there eventually, but nobody has time for that on every incident.

## Prompt engineering is the actual work

Drawing on Microsoft's guidance, Gareth lists the design basics: be specific, be descriptive, double down by repeating what you want, put things in the right order, and give the model an out ("I don't have enough information"). The implementation side: prime the model with a system prompt, provide few-shot examples, repeat key instructions at the end to counter recency bias, define the output format (JSON, CSV), and break tasks into smaller steps.

He closes with the hyperscalers' bets (Microsoft's $10 billion into OpenAI and Prompt flow, Amazon Bedrock and CodeWhisperer, Google's PaLM 2 announcements) and his verdict. "Do I think that large language models are a panacea? No, I don't," Gareth Emslie said at Conf42 Observability 2023. Prompt engineering may need reskilling and tooling that doesn't exist yet, and protecting IP, data privacy and security needs careful thought.

## Who should watch

SREs and observability leads who were handed an LLM project and want a sober framing, or anyone who wants a quick history of where the LLM-for-ops conversation stood in 2023. Practitioners already running LLM pipelines will find the primer basic.

Title: Put the ML model inside the event stream with Pulsar Functions
Description: David Kjerrumgaard (StreamNative) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 on Apache Pulsar Functions in Java that run sentiment analysis on streaming tweets
Body:
You do not always need Apache Flink to add a model to a data stream. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2023, David Kjerrumgaard, Developer Advocate at StreamNative, Apache Pulsar committer and author of Pulsar in Action, showed how a Pulsar Function written in Java can bundle a third-party NLP library and score the sentiment of every tweet as it arrives, with no separate stream processing cluster.

The first half explains Pulsar and why it suits event-driven microservices; the second is a live demo you can clone.

## What do event-driven microservices need?

In an event-driven architecture, services never call each other directly. They publish events (an item placed in a cart, an order checked out) to a broker that delivers them to whoever subscribed, asynchronously and loosely coupled. Split that by business unit into microservices and you get his summary: "event driven microservices need an event bus to interact with one another," David Kjerrumgaard said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023. The bus is also what lets those services be written in any language.

## Why Pulsar for the bus?

Pulsar started at Yahoo in 2012 as a cloud-native messaging and event streaming platform, and it supports both styles natively: classic pub/sub queuing like RabbitMQ or IBM MQ, and Kafka-style streaming. Topics live under namespaces under tenants, so a single cluster can host several departments in isolation, with security and retention policies set per namespace.

The architecture is the part he stresses. Brokers are stateless; messages are persisted to Apache BookKeeper. If a broker dies, another takes over its topics, because the data was never on it, which also lets Pulsar scale dynamically under Kubernetes. A metadata store ties it together and is pluggable: historically Apache ZooKeeper, with etcd as an option and Oxia, StreamNative's newer and more scalable store, which he recommends.

## What are Pulsar Functions?

A serverless compute framework inside Pulsar itself; think AWS Lambda wired to topics. You declare input and output topics, implement one method, and the framework handles consumers and producers. Each incoming message triggers your code, which can publish to an output topic and an optional log topic. Functions can be chained, output of one into input of the next, and run as Kubernetes pods.

They are meant for lightweight stream processing: event-driven microservices, transformations, ETL, enrichment. The SDK (Java, Python and Go) adds one-to-many output, stored state and content-based routing. For ML the key detail is packaging: every third-party library must ship inside one artifact. For Java that is an uber JAR or a NAR file; he prefers NAR.

## The demo: sentiment on a simulated stream

The [sentiment-analysis repo](https://github.com/david-streamlio/sentiment-analysis) has two Maven modules. The function implements Pulsar's `Function` interface, typed from `String` in to a user-defined `AnalyzedTweet` out, initialises an open source NLP library once behind a guard, and returns the tweet text with its sentiment. The second module is a Pulsar IO source that simulates tweets from a local file, because the Twitter API now cuts you off after about a thousand tweets a month.

After `mvn clean package` builds both NARs, he starts a local Pulsar standalone in Docker (with volumes mapped to the build target directories, and the function worker enabled, which standalone mode turns off by default). `pulsar-admin sources create` starts the simulator, a consumer confirms tweets flowing in, and `pulsar-admin functions create` deploys the function from its NAR with input and output topics. On the output topic each tweet arrives labelled neutral, positive and so on, and the `stats` command reports processing latency.

## Who should watch

Java developers who want ML inference in a streaming pipeline without running a separate processing engine, and teams already on Pulsar who have not tried Functions. The model is deliberately simple; the point is the plumbing.

Title: Observe your APIs from the gateway, not from every service
Description: Bobur Umurzokov (Apache APISIX) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on getting logs, metrics and traces from API gateway plugins with no service code changes
Body:
Every request already passes through your API gateway, so why instrument each service separately? At Conf42 Observability 2023, Bobur Umurzokov, Developer Advocate for Apache APISIX, made that case and then demonstrated it: three APISIX plugins (HTTP Logger, Prometheus and Zipkin) give an ASP.NET Core Web API logs, metrics and traces without a line of code changing in the service.

It's an introductory talk with a project-specific demo, so expect APISIX throughout. The idea transfers to most modern gateways.

## Monitoring versus observability, for APIs

Bobur starts with why APIs deserve the attention: every service used today "either uses an API or we can assume that it's API itself," Bobur Umurzokov said at Conf42 Observability 2023, and "the success of your services depends on the integrity, availability and performance of your APIs."

Traditional API monitoring tracks what you already know to measure, like requests per second or errors per second. It tells you something is wrong, not why. Observability is the part that helps you investigate the unknown unknowns, and it isn't only for engineers: product teams want adoption and usage, sales and growth teams want to see free trials and expansion, security teams want to spot API threats.

## Why the gateway is the easy place to start

The gateway sits between every client and every upstream, so it can collect the data for all the services behind it. It also already handles the other cross-cutting concerns (authentication, authorisation, traffic control), and most observability platforms (Prometheus, SkyWalking, OpenTelemetry and others) integrate with it.

Apache APISIX itself is, in his words, one of the fastest-growing top projects of the Apache Software Foundation. Beyond the bundled plugins you can write custom ones in Java, Python, Go or JavaScript, or chain existing plugins in the dashboard's drag-and-drop plugin orchestration, for example running a second plugin only after JWT authentication succeeds.

## One plugin per pillar

- **Logs**: the logger family includes http-logger, tcp-logger, udp-logger, kafka-logger, rocketmq-logger, clickhouse-logger, google-cloud-logger, skywalking-logger and error-log-logger. The HTTP Logger plugin pushes request logs as JSON to an HTTP or HTTPS server.
- **Metrics**: the Prometheus plugin exposes the gateway's metrics for scraping, ready to graph in Grafana.
- **Traces**: the Zipkin plugin reports spans to a Zipkin collector, following the Zipkin API specification. SkyWalking and OpenTelemetry tracers are also available.

## How much setup is the demo?

Not much. Docker Compose runs a product API (one endpoint returning a product list, in-memory database), APISIX, etcd, Prometheus, Grafana and Zipkin. Through the APISIX Admin API, protected by an API key, Bobur creates an upstream pointing at the product API (round-robin by default, irrelevant with one node), then a route that references it.

Each pillar is then one curl call that adds a plugin to the route's `plugins` object. The HTTP Logger ships request logs to a mockbin.org endpoint; the Prometheus plugin exposes metrics including the per-route HTTP status counter, browsable in the Prometheus UI; the Zipkin plugin sends the trace of a call to the products endpoint to the Zipkin UI. To end, all three go onto one route in a single request. One honest moment: the Grafana dashboard shows up empty because the APISIX config still needed its Prometheus settings wired up.

The code is in his apisix-dotnet-docker repository on GitHub, on the api-observability branch.

## Who should watch

Teams running many small services behind a gateway who want baseline API telemetry before (or instead of) instrumenting each service, and anyone evaluating APISIX. The gateway sees the edge, not what happens inside a service, so this complements SDK instrumentation rather than replacing it for deep traces.

Title: Keyword search finds nothing for fast animals, and a vector database finds a cheetah
Description: Zain Hasan (Weaviate) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 on how vector databases embed, index and search unstructured data, then feed LLMs context
Body:
Search 100,000 Wikipedia paragraphs for the exact string "fast animal" and you get an empty list. Ask a vector database for the concept and you get a gazelle, a cheetah and a bobcat. Zain Hasan, Senior Developer Advocate at Weaviate, used that contrast at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 to explain what vector databases are, how they scale to billions of objects, and why they became the memory layer for large language models.

It is a genuine intro, as the title promises, with a live demo that goes further than most.

## What is wrong with keyword search?

Keyword search is string matching. Search a set of articles for Python and it will not find one titled programming languages for data scientists, and it cannot tell the snake from the language anyway. Semantic search understands both the query and the documents and matches on meaning. Hasan remembers his first encounter with the idea as a light bulb moment: "why doesn't everybody just use vector databases?"

## How does a vector database understand data?

Two hurdles stand in the way. First, making sense of unstructured data: text, images, audio, video. A machine learning model turns each object into a vector, and in the resulting vector space similar things land close together (the word cat near a photo of a cat, far from banana). Real spaces run to 300, 600 or 2,000 dimensions; more dimensions preserve more of the original, like summarising a book in a chapter instead of a page.

Second, doing it at scale. A vector database stores both the objects and their vectors, supports full CRUD as data changes, combines similarity search with structured filtering (only animals, then the ones you can cook), and answers many queries per second. Brute-force comparison against every vector would take hours, so it uses approximate nearest neighbour search, HNSW in Weaviate's case: a layered graph where you enter at a sparse top layer and descend, doing far fewer distance computations. The price is in the name: approximate, not guaranteed exact.

## What does Weaviate add?

Weaviate is open source and modular: plug in an open model such as ResNet-50, one from Hugging Face, or a hosted one from OpenAI, Cohere or Google's PaLM (integrated, he notes, the week before), or bring your own vectors. Supported modalities are whatever your model understands. Results can be piped onward, to re-ranking, question answering or an LLM.

## The demo

On Weaviate Cloud Services, Hasan loads 100,000 Wikipedia paragraphs with a schema that sets a multilingual text vectorizer and dot-product distance, batching 100 objects at a time. A query for a programming language used for machine learning returns Python, then C++, then central processing unit. Because the model is multilingual, he queries for great movies in Chinese and Hindi and vacation spots in Farsi and still gets relevant English articles back.

Then generative search, or retrieval augmented generation: find famous basketball players, then have OpenAI's model write interview questions for each one from the retrieved paragraph. A grouped task sends 15 retrieved documents at once to ask which player was most accomplished. The retrieval is not flawless (basketball's inventor James Naismith shows up among the players), which is a fair reminder that the LLM's answer is only as good as the context.

As Zain Hasan said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023, "vector databases essentially act like long term memory for these large language models." Instead of copying relevant documents into a chat window by hand, the database does the filtering over millions of documents.

## Who should watch

Engineers who keep hearing about RAG and want the fundamentals in one sitting, and anyone choosing between keyword and semantic search. It is a vendor talk that shows Weaviate, but the concepts carry over to any vector database.

Title: Observability starts with the business process, not the tool config
Description: Aswin Kumar (Infosys Limited) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on a business-architecture blueprint for end-to-end, persona-based observability
Body:
Most observability programmes start as a tool rollout: pick a vendor, install the agents, build some dashboards. At Conf42 Observability 2023, Aswin Kumar, Senior Director at Infosys Limited, argued for the opposite order: start from the business processes (procure-to-pay and friends), work out which applications, events and teams sit under them, and only then wire up monitoring, so that a slow API can be traced to the business function it is hurting.

It is a short, high-level talk, closer to an architecture briefing for leads and architects than a hands-on session. No code, no demo, no numbers.

## What changed in observability?

Aswin lists four shifts. SRE as a function is maturing, with processes and engineering teams working together on the ground. System health is now being correlated with business metrics such as sales, manufacturing output and customer experience. Generative AIOps (his term) promises insights from large language models and deep learning over the flood of operational data. And enterprise architecture has started to treat observability as a design input rather than an afterthought. "Observability is key in the design stage and that's how enterprise architects are working," Aswin Kumar said at Conf42 Observability 2023.

## Why one layer of monitoring isn't enough

The picture he paints is familiar to anyone in a large enterprise: online, cloud, SaaS, partner and B2B applications (payments, supply, logistics) all feeding systems of record in the data layer, with cloud scale multiplying the transactions. His answer is multilayer observability, covering front-end applications, the integrations between them and the cloud underneath, with end-to-end visibility of each transaction and the business function it serves.

## The three-level blueprint

The reference architecture has three levels:

- **Environments and teams**: dev, QA and production, with DevOps, QA and SRE teams working in them.
- **Events**: application logs, traces, network events, security threats, incidents, problems, storage data and user experience data, all of which need capturing and correlating. He notes that tools such as OpenTelemetry already do much of the collection.
- **End-to-end business observability**: end-user experience, application performance, infrastructure, security monitoring, ITSM process performance and cloud monitoring, correlated together.

The gap he points at sits at the top. "But these applications do not have end to end business observability," Aswin Kumar said at Conf42 Observability 2023. The applications running under a business process are each monitored on their own, so no one can tell which process is hurting when one of them degrades.

## Personas and planned self-healing

Two things make the approach distinctive in his framing. First, the views are persona-based: the head of DevOps, ITSM, SRE, network operations and cloud monitoring teams each get the slice of end-to-end observability they need. Second, once the architecture is in place, the patterns it reveals feed automation planning, from partial automation to self-healing, or runbooks SREs execute when an anomaly fires.

The claimed payoffs: AI/ML is easier to apply because logs, traces and metrics are collected together; incidents, whether security, application or cloud, get deeper correlation; and business process automation can find value-stream improvements, tie KPIs and SLAs to applications, and give teams a shared view of which business process is impacted and what to fix first.

## Who should watch

Enterprise architects and observability leads who have to sell observability to the business, or who inherited a tool-first rollout and want a framework for reorganising it. Engineers looking for implementation detail won't find it here; the talk stays at the blueprint level.

Title: Your app only writes logs? Teach the OTel Collector to emit traces
Description: Alberto Gastaldello and Andrea Caretta (Liquid Reply IT) at Conf42 Observability 2023 on patching an OTel Collector exporter to turn logs into trace spans
Body:
Some applications will never be instrumented: the vendor forbids agents, the code is closed, and all you get is a log stream. At Conf42 Observability 2023, Alberto Gastaldello and Andrea Caretta of Liquid Reply IT showed a way around that: if the logs already carry a trace ID, span ID and parent span ID, a modified OpenTelemetry Collector exporter can turn each log line into a real trace span and ship it to a tracing backend, next to the original log.

It's a short, focused talk: a quick tour of the pillars and OpenTelemetry, then the hack, then a demo.

## Why traces, and why OpenTelemetry?

Andrea opens with the theory. Observability is a property of the system, not something you install. "It's a system attribute, of course, not an activity or a tool," Andrea Caretta said at Conf42 Observability 2023. RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) describe the symptoms; USE metrics (utilization, saturation, errors) help with root cause; logs are the system's diary. Traces are the pillar that ties one user action to the last query it fired at the database, a cause-and-effect view of a single request rather than an aggregate.

They focus on traces for a practical reason: at the time of the talk, tracing was the only OpenTelemetry signal whose spec had reached stable. Andrea also points out that new enterprise software increasingly emits OpenTelemetry data out of the box, often because those vendors won't let anyone install a monitoring agent on their product.

## How does a trace hang together?

Alberto covers the plumbing every tracing newcomer needs: a trace is the request's full record, spans are its units, and the W3C Trace Context `traceparent` and `tracestate` headers carry the context between services. The trace ID names the whole tree, each span gets its own span ID, and the caller passes its ID on as the parent span ID.

The demo app is Sock Shop, with the orders, shipping, queue-master and carts services auto-instrumented by the OpenTelemetry Kubernetes operator. One checkout click produces the same trace in Dynatrace and in Grafana, which is the point of a standard data format: the backend stops mattering.

## The hack: crossing from the logs pipeline to traces

Collector pipelines are split by signal. Receivers, processors and exporters are wired per pillar in the YAML `service` section, and a trace stays a trace, a log stays a log. "What we found out breaks this model," Alberto Gastaldello said at Conf42 Observability 2023.

The team picked the exporter, the last point before data leaves the Collector, and built a version that reads the trace ID and span ID from a log record and writes them out as the key values of a span. The log still goes to Loki; the new span goes to Grafana Tempo and to Dynatrace. A broken end-to-end trace, with a gap where the log-only application sits, now has a properly formed span in the middle.

The sample input is an RFC 5424 syslog line with an `[opentelemetry trace_id=... span_id=... parent_span_id=...]` structured-data block, received by the Collector's syslog receiver on UDP. The config also shows the `transform` processor rewriting log attributes (setting severity, normalising `/user/{userId}/list/{listId}`-style routes) before export.

## Did it work?

In the demo they run their compiled Collector locally, and a Python script plays the uninstrumentable app, sending syslog events to it. In Grafana a Loki query finds the logs, and the Tempo integration jumps straight from a log to the trace with the same ID. Dynatrace shows the same trace under distributed traces.

The talk doesn't show the exporter's code or discuss upstreaming it, so treat it as a proof of concept and a pattern rather than a component you can download.

## Who should watch

Anyone stuck with a black-box application in the middle of an otherwise traced system, and anyone who wants a compact refresher on Collector receivers, processors and exporters. If your logs already carry trace context, this is a cheap way to get those hops back into your traces.

Title: A heart failure classifier in a Colab notebook, step by step
Description: Yogesh Seenichamy (State Farm) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 on building a Keras neural network that predicts heart disease from patient records
Body:
Heart disease causes one in five deaths in the United States, and the traditional ways of spotting heart failure early, clinical assessment, imaging and biomarkers, are slow, costly or not specific enough. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2023, Yogesh Seenichamy (State Farm) built a small neural network in Google Colab that predicts heart disease from routine patient data and reached about 79% accuracy in a handful of lines.

It is a beginner's walkthrough, and an honest one: he says plainly which choices were arbitrary and where a real project would go further.

## What problem is the model for?

His numbers frame the stakes: one in five US deaths caused by heart disease, roughly 655,000 a year, and an average cost of $30,000 to treat heart failure. Clinical assessment relies on a doctor's reading of symptoms, history and an exam, which can lead to inconsistent diagnoses; imaging such as CT and MRI is expensive; biomarkers are not specific enough. Delays in diagnosis lead to worse outcomes. Machine learning, he argues, can spot patterns across many records that a single assessment misses, and published work already finds ML more accurate than traditional models for this.

## What data does it use?

The dataset is the Kaggle heart failure prediction set, which combines records from several hospitals in the UCI Machine Learning Repository into one larger table, giving him more rows than any single source. Each row is a patient: numeric fields such as age, resting blood pressure, cholesterol and maximum heart rate, categorical ones such as sex, chest pain type, resting ECG result and ST slope, and a heart disease label of 0 or 1.

## How is the network built?

Preprocessing is the classic sequence. Neural networks want numbers, so categorical columns get one-hot encoded: the chest pain column becomes one column per type, with a 1 in the matching one. Inputs are everything but the label. Scikit-learn's `train_test_split` holds out 20% for testing (around 800 training rows and 200 test rows by his estimate), and a `StandardScaler` keeps the inputs small.

The model is a Keras `Sequential`: an input layer sized to the features, two hidden layers of 16 neurons with ReLU, and one sigmoid output neuron that reads as the probability of heart disease. He compiles with the Adam optimiser and an accuracy metric, then trains for 100 epochs with a 33% validation split. Predictions above 0.5 count as heart disease.

Yogesh Seenichamy said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 that "we got an accuracy of around 79%, which isn't too bad considering how few lines of code this really is." He is upfront that the architecture was not tuned: "to be honest, a lot of the choices are arbitrary." Trying different layer sizes and settings is the obvious next step.

## From notebook to something people can use

The last step is deployment: host the trained model behind a simple web form where someone enters their age, blood pressure and the other fields and gets a prediction back. He built one while comparing models. The Colab notebook is linked from his slides.

## Who should watch

Students and developers who want to see a complete, small supervised learning project on medical data from CSV to prediction. Practitioners will know every step; the value here is the clarity. Keep in mind it is a learning exercise on a public dataset, not a validated clinical tool.

Title: Video is static content too, and generative AI could change the format
Description: Gaurab Patra (Flurgo) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 on GANs and LLMs combining into tools for crowdsourced, interactive multimodal content
Body:
Text, images, video, and then nothing new for a long time. Gaurab Patra, co-founder of Flurgo, argued at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 that the next mainstream content format will be interactive, and that generative AI, GANs and language models together, is what finally makes it cheap enough to create. He ends with a demo: a gamified startup idea validator assembled from generated images and GPT-4.

This is a vision talk with a founder's thesis, not a technical walkthrough. Expect broad strokes on the models and a concrete example at the end.

## Why does content need a new format?

He opens with the attention problem. By the time his talk ends, he says, almost 10,000 hours of content will be uploaded to YouTube, almost 6 million Instagram stories posted, almost 700 million messages sent and almost 20 million swipes made on dating apps. A creator, brand, marketer or employer has to stand out in that. His claim is that formats have stalled: "I consider video is also static content," Gaurab Patra said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023, because nothing has fundamentally changed how content is made or consumed since. Interactive video exists, but making it, from ideation to implementation, is still too complicated.

## From touchscreens to no interface

The first third maps how humans talk to machines. Human-to-human communication is multimodal: speech plus facial expressions, gestures, eye motion and touch. Human-to-machine interfaces are catching up step by step: graphical interfaces you tap and pinch, voice assistants like Alexa, gesture control in augmented reality, Google's Project Soli (a miniature radar sensor that reads hand gestures), brain-computer interfaces and haptics. The end state he calls no interface, connected sensors and models that act on your behalf.

## What generative AI brings

The middle section is a primer. GANs, introduced by Ian Goodfellow and colleagues in 2014, pit a generator against a discriminator until the fakes pass. Language models are transformers that use self-attention to predict the next token from a learned probability distribution. He sees GANs' iterate-and-refine loop as a mirror of how human creativity works, and the pair, combined, as the engine for multimodal interfaces. He also sides with the camp that bigger is not the only way forward: privacy and on-device inference push for smaller, different architectures.

Open research areas he lists: more stable training (avoiding mode collapse), explainability, multimodal generation, controlled generation and incorporating prior knowledge such as knowledge graphs.

## Where does the crowd come in?

Crowdsourced interactivity means different people contribute what they are good at, interfaces, backgrounds, the logic of how objects interact, with AI doing the heavy lifting in between. He applies it to idea generation, fast experimentation, refinement (extending a background, sharpening an image, tuning animations), multimodal interfaces and personalisation, such as an employee onboarding flow that adapts to each new hire.

## The demo

His example starts with Stable Diffusion images of a unicorn running on Mars, ice and marble, then extends one into an endless scene for a platformer-style backdrop. GPT-4 turns a prompt for a gamified startup idea validator into UniCorner: it asks a founder for their idea (a decentralised investment platform), follows up on weak spots such as fractional ownership being illegal in India, and scores the founder's clarity. Flurgo is wiring those pieces into one creation tool. His closing line is the slide's: cooperate with machines, don't operate them. In the talk: "You will rather cooperate with your machines."

## Who should watch

Product people and creators curious where generative tools might take content formats, and anyone wanting a gentle tour of GANs and LLMs side by side. Engineers after implementation detail will find little here.

- Michal Mikolajczak on [what generative AI means for tomorrow](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Michal_Mikolajczak_unveiling_tomorrow_generative).
- Yashwanth Kotha on [dynamic user interfaces](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Yashwanth_Kotha_dynamic_user_interfaces).

Title: Set your first SLO below where the graph already sits
Description: Muhammad Jihad (SocketSpace) at Conf42 SRE 2023 on building a first SLO from the four golden signals, and why its target starts below today's average
Body:
The most common first-SLO mistake is picking 99% because it sounds right, then discovering the service has been sitting at 90-95% all along and was in breach from day one. Muhammad Jihad, CEO of SocketSpace, used his [Conf42 SRE 2023 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Muhammad_Jihad_starting_slos_implementation) to walk through a first SLO built from the Google SRE book and workbook, ending with a worked example that turns a 95% target into a concrete count: 432 bad five-minute windows a month.

It is a beginner's talk, and it says so by doing it: definitions, a formula, one example, done.

## What problems is an SLO supposed to solve?

Jihad starts with three arguments every tech company has had. A third-party provider says its service will be down "for a while", and nobody knows if that means a minute or two years. Product and operations debate whether a new deployment is stable, because product wants to change things fast and operations wants to keep things steady. And the two sides don't share a definition of down. An SLO gives all three a number to argue about instead.

## Where do you get your first SLI?

He quotes the book's definitions, then gives his own: the SLI is "The Metrics that you want to observe", and the SLO is the target value or range for that metric. If you don't know which metrics to pick, start with the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Errors include the implicit kind, an HTTP 200 with the wrong content, and saturation is how full the service is. If you collect nothing yet, deploy Prometheus or use a service mesh on Kubernetes.

Building the SLI is two steps. The specification says what you observe, such as HTTP responses that are not errors, meaning 2xx or 3xx. The implementation says where and how you get it, from API gateway metrics, the service mesh, or a WAF or cloud proxy, and in Prometheus that means writing PromQL. The generic formula is good events divided by total events, times 100%.

## Which time windows do you need?

Two. The aggregation window is how often you evaluate a point, since requests don't arrive at a constant rate: every one, five or ten minutes. The SLO window is the period you judge the target over: a week, a month, a year, but not the ten years a web server may have been running.

## Why put the target below the average?

His boundary rule: visualise the SLI over the chosen window, find its average movement, and put the first SLO below it, around the minimum point. Put it above and the service breaches by default. "If you put the boundaries on top of your average movement, then by default your system was breaching the SLO," Jihad said at Conf42 SRE 2023. First SLOs commonly start at 90%, then move up through 95%, 99% and 99.5% as tuning lifts the normal behaviour.

## How do you know you breached it?

The worked example uses five-minute aggregation, a 30-day window and a 95% SLO. The allowance is (1 - 0.95) x 30 days = 36 hours. At five minutes per point, that is 36 hours / 5 minutes = 432 points. If more than 432 five-minute points fall below 95% within 30 days, the SLO is breached. In general: the SLO is breached when the count of points below target exceeds (1 - SLO) x SLO window / aggregation window.

Back to the three arguments. The partner can't be down for a while, it can be down for, say, five minutes. Errors after a deploy are fine as long as the SLI stays above the SLO. And down now has one definition for everyone, which leaves room to agree on experiments.

He flags the follow-ups as the next topics in his series: error budgets and error budget policies (which he says make breach detection cleaner than counting dots), SLOs for services that depend on each other, alerting on SLOs, and canary releases that improve SLOs without killing agility.

## Who should watch

Teams that have Prometheus and dashboards but no SLOs yet, and engineers who need to explain error budgets with arithmetic rather than slogans. Experienced SREs will want the more advanced follow-ups instead.

Title: BERTopic is a pipeline of swappable parts, and HDBSCAN is the clever one
Description: Abhiram Ravikumar and Jaspal Singh Jhass (Collinson) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 on BERTopic topic modelling and how HDBSCAN finds clusters
Body:
Nobody can read a million product reviews, but a topic model can tell you which thousand to read. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2023, Abhiram Ravikumar, Cloud Machine Learning Engineer, and Jaspal Singh Jhass, Lead Data Scientist, both at Collinson, ran BERTopic over Amazon Alexa reviews and then took apart the clustering step inside it, HDBSCAN. The takeaway: BERTopic is modular, so every stage can be swapped when something better comes along, and HDBSCAN earns its place by not forcing every point into a cluster.

## Why topic modelling for reviews?

The framing is an Amazon Echo Dot. One review praises it for helping kids learn general knowledge and English; a tweet complains it will not work with the customer's phone and support will not pick up. Both matter, and nobody can sift hundreds of thousands of them by hand. A topic model has to cope with messy, unstructured text full of emojis and hashtags, and pull out themes worth acting on.

## What makes BERTopic a good fit?

Ravikumar walks the pipeline: embed documents with sentence transformers (or a count vectorizer), reduce dimensions with UMAP, cluster with HDBSCAN, then describe each cluster with c-TF-IDF, a class-based variant of TF-IDF that avoids centroid-based keyword extraction. The selling point is that each block is replaceable. Unhappy with UMAP, try PCA. If a better clustering algorithm shows up next year, drop it in. As he put it at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023, "new advancements in clustering can be adapted very easily."

He also explains why not k-means: it makes you choose the number of clusters, forces every point into one with no outliers, and assumes neat spherical clusters. Real review data does none of that.

## What did it find in the Alexa reviews?

The hands-on part runs in Google Colab on the Kaggle Amazon Alexa reviews dataset, using its verified reviews column. After a vectorizer config and a `fit_transform`, the biggest topic (284 reviews) is about loving Alexa and the Echo Dot, and the intertopic distance map places Hulu and streaming next to the Fire Stick. The find he highlights is a gift topic: plenty of customers bought the device for friends and family. The notebook is on GitHub.

## How does HDBSCAN find dense regions?

Jhass takes over, telling the audience to get their swimsuits ready, and starts from DBSCAN, which grows clusters by drawing a fixed-radius circle around each point. It is robust to outliers and needs no cluster count, but you have to pick the radius, and it is slow.

HDBSCAN drops the fixed radius. The core distance of a point is the distance to its k-th nearest neighbour; the mutual reachability distance between two points accounts for both of their core distances. His analogy is people in a park whose arm lengths differ: whoever you can reach is close. A minimum spanning tree over those distances links everything by the shortest paths, lifting it gives a cluster hierarchy, and pruning by a minimum cluster size condenses the tree. Clusters are then kept by a stability score that combines density and how long a cluster persists in the hierarchy. Points that belong nowhere stay as outliers.

On his benchmark chart HDBSCAN beats DBSCAN on speed as data grows, with k-means fastest but worst at clustering. For very large datasets he points to cuML's GPU-accelerated HDBSCAN. One assumption to remember: BERTopic treats every document as having one topic.

## Who should watch

Data scientists doing review mining, support ticket triage or survey analysis, and anyone who has used BERTopic as a black box. The HDBSCAN half is one of the clearer spoken explanations of the algorithm around.

- Daniel Svonava on [vector ops for embedding-powered apps](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2023_Daniel_Svonava_vector_ops_embeddingpowered_apps) at the same event.

Title: Every extra nine cuts your error budget by ten, and costs about ten times
Description: Ramon Medrano Llamas (Google) at Conf42 SRE 2023 on building an SLO step by step, from critical user journeys to SLIs, targets and alerts
Body:
Ask product how reliable the service should be and the answer is the highest possible. Ramon Medrano Llamas, Senior Staff SRE at Google working on identity, has a way to end that meeting: put the price on the table. In his [Conf42 SRE 2023 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Ramon_Medrano_Llamas_reliability_production) he builds one SLO end to end on a demo shop, and his central warning is that each added nine cuts the error budget to a tenth and multiplies operational cost by roughly ten.

It is a compact workshop for people who know the acronyms but have never shipped an SLO, built on a demo app you can deploy yourself.

## Why not just aim for 100%?

Medrano Llamas opens with his thesis: the most important feature of any system is its reliability towards its users, and he includes security in that, because users must trust you with their payments and their files. Then the hard question, what level of reliability do we need? 100% is wrong because nothing in a distributed system is unbreakable. A shrug and a wait-and-see is wrong too, because then nobody can set expectations.

The terms get a 30-second tour. Critical user journeys (CUJs) are the functionality users care about. SLIs are metrics describing the user experience of that functionality, which can be as broad as checkout or as narrow as storing one value in a Redis cache. SLOs are the targets. SLAs are the contract, with refunds or credits when you miss. And SLOs are the lingua franca across the product lifecycle, from concept and business case through development and operations to market, discussed by product, dev and SRE alike.

## Which user journeys come first?

The example is Hipster Shop, the microservices demo in Google Cloud's Cloud Operations Sandbox, a click-to-deploy playground with synthetic load where you can inject faults and watch the SLIs move. Its CUJs are browsing products, adding to cart and checking out. Ordered by business impact, checkout comes first, since that is where the sale happens, then add to cart, then browse.

The word to stress is user. A CUJ that names your Redis cache leaks your abstractions. For infrastructure teams, the user is often another product: for his authentication service, Gmail is the user, and its journey is credentials being issued so it can reach mailboxes.

## How do you turn a journey into an SLI?

Metrics should be as simple as possible but rich enough to capture what users expect. Pick the type first: request/response services get availability, latency and quality; data pipelines get freshness, coverage, correctness and throughput; storage gets throughput and latency. Then the specification, for availability the proportion of valid events served successfully. Then the implementation, where the trade-offs live: application metrics scraped by something like Prometheus, logs (slower but more precise), front-end infrastructure metrics, synthetic clients, or client-side instrumentation, which is the only option that sees last-mile network latency.

For checkout, the SLI covers the front end and the checkout service, and counts requests to the checkout service's response counts that don't return a 5xx, measured at the Istio service mesh.

## Where does the hard part start?

Setting the target. The example SLO is 99.9% of checkout requests successful over the past 28 days, leaving 0.1% as an error budget to spend on faster rollouts or riskier schema changes. Go to four nines and the budget is a tenth of that, with operational complexity and cost growing roughly tenfold.

His tactic is to get product, developers and SRE in one room. "Sure, we can do like five, six nines, but this is going to cost you this much headcount, this much development time," Medrano Llamas said at Conf42 SRE 2023. Things balance quickly after that. Journeys at the top of the list get tighter SLOs; accessory ones get more headroom. Pick a measurement period too, a sliding window or a calendar month.

Then alerts become almost trivial: fire when the SLI sits under the SLO for a window, from five minutes to an hour, with smaller windows for higher SLOs.

## Who should watch

Teams writing their first SLO, and anyone who needs a clean five-step process (journeys, SLIs, targets and windows, dashboards, alerts) to show their product manager. He closes by pointing to Google's four SRE books, free at sre.google.

- Jayaganesh Kalyanasundaram on [product management in SRE](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Jayaganesh_Kalyanasundaram_product_management), including a rollback SLO that started at 40%.

Title: A Google rollback SLO started at 40%, and a PM made that survivable
Description: Jayaganesh Kalyanasundaram (Google) at Conf42 SRE 2023 on what a dedicated product manager does for an SRE team, from user journeys to error budget fights
Body:
Jayaganesh Kalyanasundaram's team at Google set a 99.99% SLO on rollbacks in their CI/CD platform, measured from the click to a finished rollback, and found the real success rate was about 40%. His [Conf42 SRE 2023 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Jayaganesh_Kalyanasundaram_product_management) is about how a dedicated product manager helped them through that and similar moments, and why SRE teams that build internal platforms should think of themselves as product teams.

Kalyanasundaram, a Technical Lead at Google, walks through the four SRE principles one by one and shows where product management changed the outcome in each. It is a short, practical talk with one very good story in the middle.

## Whose definition of the rollback journey wins?

Principle one is SLOs with consequences. In the monolith days, one service-level measure covered the whole user experience. With microservices and platforms that monitor each service by default, SLOs tend to shrink to the boundaries of individual services.

His example is the rollback button. Engineers wanted to measure from the click until the right RPC reached the right system. Managers and tech leads wanted to wait for the workflow that performs the rollback to start. The product manager's view was that a rollback is a journey: the user clicks, and the rollback actually happens. Three teams, three definitions.

The PM's answer was a framework of written critical user journeys, an explicit document describing each journey end to end. That aligned everyone on what each SLO meant, and it became a way to measure product quality: if the product offers 15 journeys and SLOs govern five, two thirds of the product could break without anyone being alerted.

## How do you get the team off the pager?

Principle two: SREs must have time to make tomorrow better than today. Early on, the SRE team is the "pager monkey", and improvement needs error budget. If your SLO allows five minutes of downtime a month and you have burned four by day ten, there is one minute left for twenty days.

An error budget policy that stops feature work and redirects the team to reliability is the right call, and a hard conversation. So is announcing that a whole quarter goes to postmortem action items that have been ignored for two years. Kalyanasundaram argues these are conversations best had wearing the product manager's hat, and his PM handled the stakeholders.

## Why lower an SLO from four nines to 45%?

Principle three is the ability to regulate workload, which depends on a shared responsibility model and leadership buy-in. Here the rollback story continues. Over half the failures came from users who lacked permission to roll back that microservice; as he puts it, someone working on Google Search shouldn't be able to roll back a YouTube service. The product worked as designed, but users were still unhappy.

The fix was UX: a big red bar telling users they don't have access, so they stop trying. Until it shipped, the team loosened the SLO from four nines to 45%. "Having a target of 40% makes you look really bad before the upper management," Kalyanasundaram said at Conf42 SRE 2023. Getting management to accept that took stakeholder management, which is exactly the job of a PM.

The team also wrote launch requirements for its own internal SRE tools: integration tests, SLO coverage and named early-access customers before anything ships, so the product doesn't get brittle with each launch. On automation, he names four themes that recur across SRE teams, CI/CD, monitoring, capacity planning (a cricket match spiking traffic to YouTube is his example) and incident management, and argues that building them once as horizontal products saves every vertical team from maintaining its own.

## And blamelessness?

Principle four is that failure is an opportunity to improve. You have already paid the price in an outage, so write the blameless postmortem, share it widely, and treat human errors as system problems. The goal is better MTTD and MTTR, and ideally the action items mean you never meet that failure again.

His closing observation: across Google, senior engineers and leads often end up informally wearing the product management hat for SRE, and training them in it pays off.

## Who should watch

Teams that run internal platforms (CI/CD, deploy tooling, observability) and SREs who keep losing the feature-versus-reliability argument. The rollback SLO story alone is worth bringing to your next SLO review.

- Ricardo Castro on [alerting on SLOs and error budget policies](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2022_Ricardo_Castro_alerting_slos_error_budget_policies) at Conf42 SRE 2022.
