Title: LLMs reason better when you stop asking them to do arithmetic
Description: Logesh Kumar Umapathi (Saama Technologies) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 on eliciting LLM reasoning with prompting, fine-tuning, iteration and tools
Body:
A 175-billion-parameter model can still fumble taking the last letter of three words. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2023, Logesh Kumar Umapathi, Lead ML Research Engineer at Saama Technologies, toured the research on getting reasoning out of large language models, from chain-of-thought prompting to agents that call tools. The thread running through it: play to the model's strengths and hand its weaknesses to something else.

It is a literature review of roughly a dozen papers, delivered as a guided reading list. Umapathi works on biomedical NLP and code generation and maintains mutate, an open source package for synthesizing data with LLMs.

## Why does reasoning need eliciting at all?

He opens with a small ChatGPT experiment: asked to concatenate the last letters of a short list of words in one go, the model got the letters wrong. Broken into three questions (what are the words, what are their last letters, now join them), it got every step right. His explanation is that these models are trained for completion, not reasoning: "It still has the tendency to do text completion."

Reasoning in the literature is measured in three buckets: mathematical (GSM8K, SVAMP, AQuA, MAWPS), commonsense (ARC, CSQA, StrategyQA, with questions like whether Aristotle would have used a keyboard) and symbolic (last-letter concatenation and coin flips from Wei et al.). In the GPT-4 technical report he cites, the state of the art on GSM8K and ARC sat at 96% and 92%.

## Prompting the model to show its work

Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) gives few-shot examples that spell out intermediate steps, and the model imitates them. Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) samples several reasoning paths instead of one greedy answer and takes the majority vote.

The paper that gives this post its title is PAL, program-aided language models (Gao et al., 2023). Chain of thought still leaves the arithmetic to the LLM, and as Logesh Kumar Umapathi said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023, "So we all know that llms lack even simple arithmetic abilities." PAL has the model write the solution as a Python program and lets the interpreter compute the answer, which beat chain of thought across the math benchmarks. Plan-and-Solve prompting (Wang et al., 2023) fixes zero-shot chain of thought by asking the model to first devise a plan, then carry it out step by step.

## Teaching smaller models to reason

The fine-tuning section covers models that learn from their own correct answers. Ni et al. (2023) fine-tune GPT-Neo 2.7B on self-sampled solutions that match the gold answer, plus partially correct ones whose intermediate steps match. STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022) bootstraps rationales and, when the answer is wrong, hints the correct answer so the model writes a rationale for it; GPT-J's few-shot-then-fine-tuned score went from 5.8 to 10.7. Fu et al. (2023) distil chain-of-thought steps from GPT-3 into T5 and Flan-T5 models, and Distilling Step-by-Step (Hsieh et al.) trains small models on labels and rationales as separate tasks, letting them beat few-shot results from a 540-billion-parameter model.

## Solving it in rounds, then with tools

Least-to-most prompting (Zhou et al., 2022) first asks for sub-questions, then answers them in sequence. Plan, Eliminate, and Track (Wu et al., 2023) splits an embodied agent into planner, eliminator, actor and tracker modules, which he compares to Auto-GPT and BabyAGI. Describe, Explain, Plan and Select (Wang et al., 2023) plays Minecraft with an explainer that diagnoses failed plans before replanning.

Tool use closes the talk. ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) interleaves thoughts, actions such as a Wikipedia search and observations until the model emits finish. Chameleon (Lu et al., 2023) has the LLM compose a sequence of tools, such as a text detector, knowledge retrieval, a table verbalizer, a Python program and a verifier, for science and tabular math questions.

## Who should watch

Engineers building on LLMs who want the research lineage behind today's agent frameworks in one sitting. It is from April 2023, so it predates much of what came next, but the papers it covers are still the foundation. Bring a notebook for the citations.

- Aditi Godbole on [prompt engineering challenges and best practices](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Aditi_Godbole_promptengineering_challenges_bestpractices).
- Jonathan Harel on [the rise of AI agents](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Jonathan_Harel_rise_ai_agents).

Title: At 2am, check the login-to-dashboard ratio before the logs
Description: Gonzalo Maldonado (FireHydrant) at Conf42 SRE 2023 on business value proxy metrics, alerts that tell on-call whether an incident is actually hurting the business
Body:
Your test suite has 800 tests for the user model, 80 for the login endpoint, 40 for the React login component and eight Playwright or Cypress end-to-end runs. Then someone uploads a button colour that matches the background and nobody can log in. Gonzalo Maldonado, Staff Engineer at FireHydrant, used his [Conf42 SRE 2023 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Gonzalo_Maldonado_incidents_align_platform_product_engineering) to propose the metric that catches that: a business value proxy metric (BPM), a simple ratio that tells you whether the system is still doing its job for the business, and is good enough to page on.

The talk is built as a choose-your-own-adventure, and the joke works: the first run-through ends with you losing.

## How does the 2am adventure go wrong?

Your pager buzzes. You revert the latest code and pray; it doesn't help. You look deeper, find a typo, ship a fix. Your shift ends in 30 minutes, so you go back to bed. The next engineer reverts your fix, causing a bigger outage, and your main customer calls demanding an explanation. The rest of the talk is about the option he calls something else.

## Why do severe incidents get through good defences?

Maldonado uses James Reason's Swiss cheese model, with unit tests, synthetic tests and monitoring as the slices. "Bacteria cause cheese, and bugs create incidents," Maldonado said at Conf42 SRE 2023. You can't predict where the holes are, and when they line up, three good layers act like none.

The standard responses all have a catch. More monitoring helps, but the wrong metric leads to the wrong fix. Anomaly detection fires on all the noise distributed systems produce: unreliable networks, power fluctuations in a data centre. Asking developers to instrument their apps without guidance is expensive and possibly misleading. He also warns about survivorship bias: like armouring the right parts of an aircraft, look at what isn't failing too, because that may be the load-bearing part.

And testing alone won't catch a deleted S3 bucket, a route misconfiguration or a DNS issue.

## What is a business value proxy metric?

He admits he made the name up. His login example: of the people who reach the login page, how many reach the dashboard? Work out the normal ratio, say 70%, and alert when it moves sharply either way. Up to 80 or 90% might mean your simpler login flow is paying off. Down might mean someone deleted a button. A suspicious value might mean login is broken and unauthenticated users are landing straight on the dashboard. One ratio catches all three.

He anchors business value in Coda Hale's definition: "Business value is anything which makes people more likely to give us money." And code generates business value when it runs, not when it is written or tested.

From there platform engineering and product management become BFFs, business focused friends, and he maps the RARR metrics onto BPMs: retention is logins per hour, activation is sign-ups per hour, revenue is subscriptions per day, referral is marketing page views. Product teams are already moving from user stories to capabilities with measurable signals and experiments, so platform teams measuring the same signals puts both sides on one dashboard.

## What does FireHydrant's dashboard look like?

They call it mission control: a small board of BPMs where a spike, such as a large orange one on login, prompts the obvious questions. Did someone ship something? Did a feature flag flip? Back at 2am, the third option is to check mission control first. If the BPMs look normal, mute the alert and deal with it in business hours. If one looks off, correlate it with other signals, fix it, and go back to sleep trusting the BPMs to alert if anything else breaks.

## How do incidents feed the loop?

His closing tips: capture learnings in incident management software, so people can join mid-incident and catch up from the record. In every retrospective, ask which BPM would have caught this, and add it. Tie BPMs to the company's KPIs, OKRs or V2MOMs, and share them with product and other departments. Use the same tooling for business metrics as for infrastructure, OODA loops included. And finding the root cause is not enough: preventive measures, BPMs, tests and dashboards matter as much as the bug fix.

## Who should watch

On-call engineers tired of being woken by alerts that don't matter, and platform teams that want a shared language with product. The talk is about a practice, not FireHydrant's product.

Title: In the year of efficiency, SRE beats another dashboard
Description: Fabio Alves (FIAP) at Conf42 SRE 2023 on why SRE and well-defined SLOs, not dashboards, are the way to save money in a year of layoffs and budget cuts
Body:
Spring 2023 was the year of efficiency: budgets reviewed, hiring frozen, layoffs announced by the tens of thousands. Fabio Alves, MBA Professor at FIAP and a technology executive, used his [Conf42 SRE 2023 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Fabio_Alves_improve_efficiency_crises_time) to argue that the structural answer to that pressure is investing in SRE, with SLOs at its core, rather than cutting people or buying another reporting tool.

It is a business case talk, aimed more at the people who sign budgets than at the people who hold the pager.

## From digital transformation to digital efficiency

Alves starts with a timeline. Virtualization, the mother of cloud computing, ended the era of buying a server before starting a project. Waterfall gave way to agile, agile brought DevOps and the end of the silo between development and operations, then came mobile and the iPhone. Covid-19 accelerated everything: a hot market, quiet quitting, developers holding two or three jobs at once, and a wave of Web 3.0, metaverse and NFT talk.

Then the bubble burst. Recession in many countries, inflation, budget cuts, and the layoff figures he puts on screen: about 27,000 positions at Amazon, 10,000 at Microsoft, 10% of the workforce at Salesforce, around 13% at Meta, 19,000 at Accenture. ChatGPT arrived at the same time and made everyone feel pressured to be more effective. He calls this the age of digital efficiency.

His motivation is personal. At a large company he worked at a few months earlier, he was responsible for a savings strategy, and the expectation was that adopting Power Platform and dashboards would make developers more efficient. He disagreed, and left. "I believe that you should do something more structural," Alves said at Conf42 SRE 2023.

## What is the business case?

His list of reasons is a chain: more reliable systems mean fewer incidents, faster resolution keeps products available, and SRE and DevOps together raise agility. Collaboration between ops and dev builds trust and, he argues, lowers pressure on teams afraid for their jobs. The financial side is reduced downtime costs, better resource allocation (time moves from fixing bugs to building features), better scalability and lower maintenance costs.

He makes a specific point about consulting firms. When clients cut technology spend, consultancies feel it first, and when buyers pay the same money either way, a firm that ships with SRE practice (lower MTTR, better security, more reliable architecture) stands out.

He quotes adoption results for Google, LinkedIn, Netflix and Dropbox, such as a 50% lower incident rate at Google and 90% fewer outages at Dropbox. He gives no sources for these, so treat them as illustrations rather than benchmarks.

## Where are most companies on SRE maturity?

From a state of SRE survey he cites, 6% of organizations are immature, 32% emerging and 42% maturing, which he reads as 80% of the market still having savings available from adopting SRE alongside DevOps. On where SREs spend their week, reducing MTTR leads at around 67-70%, followed by building and maintaining automation code at 60%, and security and running experiments to reduce production failure risk at over 50%.

## Why SLOs are the main event

The same data shows 75% of respondents use SLOs to evaluate service levels, and Alves calls the SLO the heart of SRE, because it produces the error budget that makes experimenting, and occasionally being wrong, safe. The difficulty is data: too many sources, too many metrics, monitoring tools that don't make the SLO easy to get. He suggests SLO families for business and end-user views (availability, engagement, satisfaction, conversion), for performance (utilization, response time, traffic, saturation, success rate) and for mobile apps (adoption, availability, response time, crashes and the app store rating). Targets come mostly from end-user experience (26%), historical data and industry standards (24%) and current system behaviour (20%).

He ends on AIOps, which he expects generative AI to accelerate, and FinOps to stop unnecessary cloud spend.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers who need language to defend reliability work during a budget review. Practising SREs will find the SLO material familiar and the business framing useful.

Title: A fast detector plus a picky classifier beats one big vision model
Description: Argo Saakyan at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 on cascading a high-recall detector into a crop classifier to cut false alarms without losing speed
Body:
A camera running around the clock sees more than 2 million frames a day, so even a tiny false positive rate turns into a steady stream of fake alarms. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2023, computer vision engineer and researcher Argo Saakyan showed a cheap way out of the usual speed-versus-accuracy trade-off: run two neural nets in cascade, a fast detector tuned for recall and a classifier that only checks what the detector flags.

It is a short, practical talk with one technique, explained well.

## What problem does the cascade solve?

His running example is weapon detection on security cameras in a school or shopping centre. Paying guards to watch every screen is expensive, so a model watches the streams and alerts an operator. Two requirements pull against each other. The system must be fast, because more cameras means more frames per second per server and hardware is not free. And it must not cry wolf, because "that's more than 2 million frames per day per camera," Argo Saakyan said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023. A faster net usually means a less accurate one, and a more accurate one usually means more GPUs.

## How do the two models split the work?

The first model is a detector that runs on every frame, downscaled to 640 by 640. It is tuned for high recall at the expense of precision: it should almost never miss a gun, and it is allowed to mistake a phone for one.

The second model is a classifier that runs on the detector's crop, taken from the full-resolution frame, and only when the detector fires. Its job is to confirm or reject. It is trained not just on the target class but on the things the detector keeps confusing with it: phones, umbrellas, bags, plus a catch-all class for everything else.

## Why is it fast and more accurate?

Speed first: the system runs at the speed of the detector, because "So 99% of the time second net is idle." That also means you can pick a really fast detector, since the classifier catches its mistakes.

Accuracy comes from several places at once: it is effectively an ensemble; the classifier sees a higher-resolution crop than the downscaled detector input; each model is trained on its own data; and each can be chosen for what it is good at instead of one model having to do both jobs. The classifier is also easy to retrain on real cases after deployment. His reported metrics show recall dipping slightly and precision rising noticeably, which is the trade you want when a human operator reviews every alert.

## Data and deployment advice

For the detector, collect data as close to inference as possible: similar cameras, mounted at realistic heights and angles, with objects at realistic distances (nobody holds a gun 10 cm from a ceiling camera). For the classifier, run the detector with a low threshold to harvest plenty of false positives, look for recurring confusions such as phones, and give each its own class.

On deployment he recommends converting models to NVIDIA TensorRT, which he says makes them two to five times faster with less VRAM, and serving them through a model server such as Triton. His starting picks: YOLOv8 for the detector (it comes in sizes from nano to extra large and converts to TensorRT easily), EfficientNet or EfficientNetV2 for the classifier, and Makesense.ai for labelling.

## Who should watch

Engineers shipping object detection on video where alerts reach a human: security, retail, industrial inspection. If you already run detector-plus-verifier pipelines, this will be familiar; if your answer to false positives has been a bigger model, it is a useful 15 minutes.

Title: Keep your PostgreSQL, add a compute layer, call it distributed
Description: Trista Pan (SphereEx) at Conf42 SRE 2023 on turning existing PostgreSQL or MySQL into a sharded, highly available database on Kubernetes with ShardingSphere
Body:
When a single PostgreSQL instance runs out of road, the usual options are a new distributed database vendor or a cloud provider's one-stop product. Trista Pan, Co-founder & CTO at SphereEx and a PMC member of Apache ShardingSphere, used her [Conf42 SRE 2023 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Trista_Pan_achieve_scalability_availability_database_infrastructur) to pitch a third: keep the databases you trust as storage nodes, put Apache ShardingSphere in front as the computing layer, and get sharding, read/write splitting and failover without moving off MySQL or PostgreSQL.

It is a project talk from one of its maintainers, so expect ShardingSphere front and centre, with a demo on Kubernetes at the end.

## What does a database SRE actually measure?

Pan frames the problem through database reliability engineering, which she treats as a subset of SRE with one big difference: databases are stateful, so connections and persistence change the game. The SLIs from the DBRE literature (latency, throughput, availability, scalability, efficiency) are high level, so she lists the practical needs for a database on the cloud instead: large data to manage, efficient queries, data security, traffic governance, elastic scaling, backup and recovery, metrics, portability and out-of-the-box deployment.

Each maps to a technique: data sharding for scale, replicas with read/write splitting and a traffic strategy for availability and throughput, encryption for security, a monitoring stack, and Helm charts or operators on Kubernetes for deployment. End users care about none of it. They want the query answered, fast.

## How do you split compute from storage?

Distributed databases, she points out, tend to split into computing nodes that take client traffic and do the global query work, and storage nodes that persist data and compute locally. Her proposal is to let your existing PostgreSQL or MySQL clusters play the storage role, since they are already proven in production, and add ShardingSphere as the computing nodes. The two together behave as one distributed database.

The application stops caring which instance is the primary, which is a replica, or which shard holds a row. It sends queries to ShardingSphere, which routes them, rewrites them for the right shard, spreads reads across replicas, and notices when a PostgreSQL instance crashes so it stops sending queries there.

She also answers the worry that a young project might vanish or go closed source with community numbers: "It has been open source for six years and it's the Apache top level project and it's already received more than 400 contributors," Pan said at Conf42 SRE 2023, adding nearly 18k GitHub stars and close to 50 releases at the time.

## JDBC driver or proxy?

ShardingSphere comes in two clients. ShardingSphere-JDBC is a lightweight implementation of the JDBC interface for Java applications. ShardingSphere-Proxy is deployed on its own and acts as a database server, so applications in Go, Rust or anything else can use it. Both carry the same features: sharding, read/write splitting, data migration, encryption and masking, SQL audit, a SQL firewall and traffic governance.

Configuration happens through DistSQL, ShardingSphere's own SQL dialect for the distributed layer. In the demo, one statement creates a sharded `t_user` table keyed on the user id with a mod algorithm, splitting one logical table into four physical tables across two PostgreSQL groups. Another declares a write data source, read data sources and a random load balancing strategy across three replicas.

## What does the Kubernetes demo deploy?

The ShardingSphere on Cloud repository provides Helm charts and an operator. The demo deploys two PostgreSQL clusters of a primary and a replica each as storage nodes, two ShardingSphere-Proxy instances plus the governance center as computing nodes, registers the databases, creates the sharded table, inserts test data, previews how a SELECT will be routed, and runs it. The storage nodes can be RDS on AWS or Google Cloud, or PostgreSQL inside the cluster, which is her no-lock-in argument.

## Who should watch

DBAs moving toward DBRE, and platform engineers asked to run PostgreSQL on Kubernetes at a size one instance can't handle. If you want a vendor-neutral survey of distributed databases, this isn't it.

Title: Your reliability metric is missing the people who fix the outage
Description: Emily Arnott (Blameless) at Conf42 SRE 2023 on defining reliability as product health, customer happiness and sociotechnical resilience
Body:
Ask ten engineers to define reliability and you get ten answers: uptime, error rate, latency, customer expectations. Emily Arnott, Community Manager at Blameless, used her [Conf42 SRE 2023 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Emily_Arnott_new_reliability) to put a third leg under the usual two. Reliability is product health, judged against customer happiness, and prioritized by sociotechnical resilience: whether your team can respond quickly, confidently and effectively when something breaks.

That third ingredient is the point of the talk. She calls it the "secret sauce" of the new definition, and most of the talk goes into making it concrete.

## Why add people to a technical definition?

Because you already do it everywhere else. Arnott's extended example is flying. You assume the airline's systems assign seats and print boarding passes, that the plane is stocked, and that the airline knows what you want. You also assume, without ever thinking about it, that the pilot can fly, the crew shows up on time, and the airport staff knows what to do.

Then she runs the US holiday travel meltdown of December 2022 through the three buckets. A once-in-a-generation winter storm and a spike in demand sit on the product health and customer side. Scheduling and seat-assignment systems hit their limits, cancellations cascaded through connecting flights, and passengers got late, conflicting messages. On the sociotechnical side, work the systems normally did automatically fell to people who weren't trained for it, at airlines that had cut staff during the pandemic and were now stretched too thin. The same three-way breakdown, she argues, explains a bad cell phone provider, a car nobody can repair, or a building whose elevator stays broken.

## Which service should get your spare engineering cycles?

Her technical example is three services. Service A has good health, middling user demand and low team resilience: it is unlike anything else in the company, with no runbooks and no escalation path. Service B is OK on health, high on demand, and well understood by the team. Service C is in bad shape but is a new feature few customers use, closely modelled on B, so engineers are confident fixing it.

Monitoring alone says fix C. Customer expectations say B. Sociotechnical resilience says shore up A before it breaks, with guides and practice. Arnott admits the answer is not clean, and that is the lesson: the framework surfaces deficiencies that dashboards alone hide.

## What questions make up each bucket?

- **Product health:** telemetry, code stability and the four golden signals (latency, error rate, traffic, saturation).
- **Customer happiness:** user journeys broken into steps and ranked by importance, with targets such as a login page that has to work 99% of the time within a latency budget. Importance comes from observing and surveying users; there is no universal formula.
- **Sociotechnical resilience:** how effective incident response is, whether service ownership is clear, whether priorities are aligned and severity scales consistent, whether on-call loads are balanced and fair, whether people are burnt out, whether they have runbooks and past cases to consult, and whether the team still works if someone is suddenly away.

## How do you measure it?

With numbers that take effort to collect. She suggests three questions: what are the sources of manual labour for each type of incident, how many incident hours has each engineer actually spent responding (not just shifts held), and how much time has the team spent fixing each service. Each points at an action. Lots of manual steps means automate. A permanently busy incident team means hire. A service that has barely gone down means nobody knows how to fix it, so run drills and write runbooks now.

"It's in the process of gathering this data and having these conversations that you can start to really figure out where your strategic priorities should lie," Arnott said at Conf42 SRE 2023.

## Who should watch

SRE leads trying to justify reliability work against feature work, and anyone whose reliability reporting stops at the dashboard. It is a framework talk with no tooling; the airline section alone is a useful story for a leadership deck.

Title: In Polars, method chaining is how the query planner gets to help
Description: Matt Harrison (MetaSnake) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 on Polars, with tight types, chained lazy queries, and why apply is the slow path
Body:
Matt Harrison, the Python and data science trainer behind MetaSnake and author of Effective Pandas, took a US government fuel economy dataset through Polars 0.17 at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023. The takeaway: write Polars as one long chain, because chaining is more readable and it hands the lazy query engine everything it needs to skip work.

He has opinions to back it. He has worked with data since 1999, built his own OLAP engine in Python in 2006, and has written several books on pandas. This talk is a live notebook, not slides.

## How much memory do the right types save?

The dataset has 41,000 rows and 83 columns. Harrison keeps a subset of columns, which weighs about 8 MB, then tightens the types step by step. Polars checks casts strictly, unlike pandas 1: converting combined mileage to `Int8` fails because values reach 131, so he moves to an unsigned 8-bit integer, which goes up to 255. Mileage, cylinders and displacement become `UInt8`, range, fuel cost and year become `UInt16`, and the frame drops to about 5.8 MB without losing data.

Strings get the same treatment. Drive, make and model become categoricals (4 MB). Then he uses the `str` expression namespace to pull the number of speeds out of the transmission column with a regex and a boolean for manual gearboxes, and selects only the columns he needs: about 2.5 MB. Nulls in drive and cylinders turn out to be mostly electric vehicles, so he fills them deliberately. A timestamp column with EDT and EST suffixes gets string replacements, `strptime` with UTC, then a conversion to New York time.

## Why chain at all?

Harrison wraps the parenthesised chain in a function and then shows the payoff. Swap `read_csv` for `scan_csv`, make it lazy, end with `collect`, and nothing runs until the end. Polars then reads only the columns the chain uses out of the 83, and can do predicate pushdown on top.

The usual objection is that chains are impossible to debug. He disagrees: a `pipe` step can print the shape at any point, and another can save the intermediate frame to a global for inspection. "So I don't think that chaining is necessarily hard to debug," Matt Harrison said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023.

## Where does Polars get slow?

Function application. Converting miles per gallon to litres per 100 km with `apply` took 4 milliseconds; the same result as plain arithmetic (235 divided by the column) took 150 microseconds. Each `apply` pulls values out of the Arrow memory that Polars implements in Rust, turns them into Python objects, runs your function and writes them back. His advice: "You want to try and avoid crossing that, what I would call the rust to python boundary there."

## Aggregation, pivots and the pandas escape hatch

The last part covers `group_by` with `agg`, a `when`/`then`/`otherwise` expression that labels makes as US or other (it trips over the categorical type until he casts back to a string), and a `pivot` to get one column per country. Polars has no plotting, so he hands results to pandas with `to_pandas`, sets the year as the index, sorts it (Polars does not keep group order, because that would cost speed) and plots. The charts show combined mileage climbing around 2008 to 2010.

## Who should watch

pandas users weighing Polars, and anyone who learned Polars from the docs and never saw why lazy mode cares about chaining. It is a hands-on intro at the 0.17 API, so expect some method names to have moved since; the ideas have not.

Title: Separation of duties is good security and a breeding ground for gaps
Description: Saurabh Bangad (Google) at Conf42 SRE 2023 on keeping enterprise teams split by compliance rules from splitting on goals, metrics and change management
Body:
ISO 27001 tells you to separate duties so no single person or party makes a business-critical decision alone. It is good advice, and it is also how a bank ends up with developers, operators, security and audit all working on the same service with different goals and a grey no-man's-land between them. Saurabh Bangad, Technical Account Manager at Google Cloud, used his [Conf42 SRE 2023 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Saurabh_Bangad_divided_responsibilities_united_devops__cultures) to argue you can keep the controls and still get the collaboration back, through SRE and DevOps culture rather than another reorg.

He calls it a short refresher for people in enterprises and large organizations, and it is: a compact checklist, no tooling demo.

## Why do split teams pull in opposite directions?

The usual way to separate duties is to let developers ship features and make operators responsible for maintenance and reliability. Developers get rewarded for velocity, operators for stability, fewer incidents and minimal outages. Those incentives are not aligned, and at enterprise scale it multiplies: different people own prod and non-prod, many applications talk to each other, and independent security and auditing teams each hold a piece of the decision.

Least-privilege policies add to it. Giving people only what they need is sound security, but it can make one party more powerful than another and quietly reduce collaboration.

## The grey areas are where the risk lives

Bangad's central picture is the wall between teams. Every responsibility that nobody documented or acknowledged is a gap, and he treats each one as a risk that can trigger at any point. Communication gaps also undo automation: when two parties share one workflow, human intervention becomes part of the normal path. He quotes Carla Geisser of Google SRE on exactly that, and cites Google internal data from 2011-2018 that roughly 70% of outages are due to changes in a live system. If changes are not coordinated, he says, an outage is close to certain.

Step zero is a blameless culture: postmortems that fix processes and systems, not people, psychological safety so people can ask questions and admit failures, and no celebration of heroism. "Short term it works well, but medium and long term heroism for celebration of heroism doesn't go anywhere," Bangad said at Conf42 SRE 2023.

## What does the fix look like?

His culture checklist has seven items: a sense of joint ownership and accountability, treating it as "our joint" problem because the teams' destinies are intertwined, agreed golden signals as core metrics, communication methods that work across teams, mutually agreed change management practices, rewarded continuous improvement, and revisiting all of it after every reorg or major change. That last one, he says, matters most in enterprises where reorgs are common.

On communication he is specific:

- **Bidirectional channels.** Shared Google Chat spaces or Slack channels with threaded discussion. Tickets and email are one-way and formal; keep them for tracking, not collaboration.
- **Joint artifacts.** Jointly owned documentation pages, shared roadmap items and common, reusable tooling, so documentation is not a set of islands.
- **Forums for changes.** Regular syncs where teams say what they will deploy and what impact upstream and downstream teams should expect.
- **Informal learning.** Lessons learned, TGIFs, brown bag sessions and shadowing, so one team spends time in the other's shoes.

## The "be careful" list

The best part is the cautions, because collaboration has its own failure modes: meetings with no outcomes that turn into toil, approvals that made sense before a reorg and now just slow things down, fancy but unnecessary tooling, no incentive to shrink the grey areas, and contradicting metrics. His maintenance window example is the one to remember: three dependent teams each take a different day, Monday, Wednesday and Friday, each window looks fine to its owner, and end users get three outages in one week.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers in regulated enterprises where compliance dictates the org chart. If you already run shared SLOs across dev and ops, the cautions list is still worth the time.

Title: They fly now?
Description: What the actual...
Body:
#What the actual…

Therapist: "Golangs flying alien spaceships don’t exist, therefore they can’t hurt you."
Me: "But… but I saw them abducting a cow!"
Therapist: "Mhm… And how does that make you feel?"

Well, I don’t know about you, but this flying Golang makes me feel a bit uncomfortable. Might need to bring that up in my next therapy session.

Title: Renaming ops to SRE changes the door sign, not the work
Description: Ricardo Castro (FanDuel/Blip.pt) at Conf42 SRE 2023 on the anti-pattern of rebranding an operations team as SRE while tools and processes stay the same
Body:
Plenty of companies have an SRE team that used to be called Operations last quarter, and still does exactly what Operations did. Ricardo Castro, Founder & CTO at FanDuel/Blip.pt, spent his [Conf42 SRE 2023 talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Ricardo_Castro_antipattern_roadblocks_rebranding_operations_team) on that anti-pattern: the rename that leaves the tools, processes and day-to-day interactions untouched. His fix starts with asking why you want SRE at all, before you pick a single tool.

It is a short, accessible talk, closer to a primer than a teardown, and a good one to send to a manager who has just ordered new business cards.

## How did we get here?

Castro opens with a quick history lap: TCP/IP in 1983, the web at CERN in 1989, the first big internet companies in the late 90s, cloud computing making massive scale available to everyone, and the term DevOps in 2009. Google, facing massive growth in 2003, handed Ben Treynor Sloss a production team, and his definition stuck: SRE is what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team.

The principles he lists are the familiar ones from the book: embrace risk, define SLOs, eliminate toil, monitor, automate, own release engineering, and strive for simplicity. Then he names the culprit behind the hype and the confusion at once. The 2016 Site Reliability Engineering book and its companions gave everyone a view inside Google, but they hold so much material that most organizations struggle to adopt even part of it, or to translate Google's reality into their own.

## What makes something an anti-pattern?

He quotes his favourite definition: an anti-pattern is "a solution that initially looks like an attractive road lined with flowers, but further on leads into a maze filled with monsters." His example is the QWERTY layout. It was a sensible pattern for mechanical typewriters, where typing too fast jammed the type bars. We kept it for computers out of habit, and a pattern became an anti-pattern.

Rebranding ops as SRE fits the same mould, and Castro generalizes it to rebranding X to Y: agile and CI/CD have suffered the same treatment. The team gets a new name, maybe adopts Terraform, a configuration management tool or Kubernetes, and the daily work stays the same.

## How do you get out of it?

His remedies, in order:

- **Educate yourself.** Read the books, but also find out what other organizations tried, what worked for them and what didn't. "Google is an amazing technology company, but most of the things will not be applicable to our own reality," Castro said at Conf42 SRE 2023.
- **Start with why.** What problem is SRE supposed to fix? Adopting a methodology because someone else did is how the rename happens in the first place.
- **Apply Pareto.** 80% of the results come from 20% of the effort, so map a few SRE practices onto the problem you actually have.
- **Use the Eisenhower matrix.** Urgent and important gets done, urgent but unimportant gets delegated, neither gets dropped. The planning win is in the important-but-not-urgent quadrant, because that work turns urgent if you ignore it.
- **When in doubt, invest in observability.** You cannot define, measure or assess reliability with SLOs without the data, and the data is what lets you change a system with less risk.

## The rest of the rogues' gallery

He closes with the other SRE anti-patterns he covers in his other talks: missing observability, not assessing user satisfaction, poor incident management where teams put out one fire and move to the next without learning, the SRE hero who fixes everything alone, and poor automation.

## Who should watch

Engineering leaders about to stand up an SRE function, and engineers on a freshly renamed team wondering why nothing feels different. Experienced SREs will know the material; the value is in the framing, and in having a talk to point at.

Title: Your MLOps stack should be designed around the ML engineer's morning
Description: Noa Goldman (Dagshub) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 on designing MLOps around ML engineers' flows, from versioned data to simple deploys
Body:
Most MLOps tooling debates are about which tool. Noa Goldman, Lead Product Manager at Dagshub and a former software developer of about eight years, spent her Conf42 Machine Learning 2023 talk on a different question: what should the experience of building a model feel like for the ML engineer doing it? Her answer is a product manager's answer: stop choosing features, start mapping flows.

It is a UX talk about MLOps, not a tool tour. She says up front that by approaches she does not mean specific tools or technical integrations.

## Why is MLOps so hard to assemble?

Goldman draws the lifecycle as three blocks: data (ingest, curate, annotate), experiments (code, train and tune, track and evaluate) and models (containerize, deploy, monitor, collect production data). Every step has a pile of open source and paid options, and stitching them together is, in her words, almost impossible to get right on the first go. On top sit the human problems: data quality, model selection, explaining results to people who are not ML engineers, and a field where team standards and best practices still have not settled the way they have in software development.

## Treat your data like you treat your code

Her strongest idea comes straight from her software background. ML engineers should be data centric, which means constantly collecting new data from many sources, and that only stays manageable with data versioning: clear diffs between dataset versions, reproducible datasets, and the collaboration tools developers take for granted, such as pull requests, comments and issues on data.

Versioning alone is not enough. Engineers also need to find the data points that matter, so she argues for visualisation that shows the data next to its enrichment (metadata, annotations, predictions), fast filtering and sorting, and then an obvious next step: send the subset to annotation, or download it to retrain.

## Experiments are a communication problem

Experiment tracking is the most mature part of the stack, she says, so the gap is not the hyperparameter table. It is the meeting afterwards. An engineer who believes a model is the right one still has to convince a manager, so tracking tools should produce visual outputs that non-ML stakeholders can read, ideally exportable, without the engineer walking someone through three tools.

## Deploying without filing a ticket

For models she borrows from production software practice: a model registry as the one place where every version lives with its details, plus a deployment path ML engineers can use themselves. If a model misbehaves in production, rolling back should be fast and should not require a DevOps engineer. Even where the full process can't be self-service, engineers should be able to do most of it and understand the rest.

## Simplicity is a feature

The closing section is the one worth stealing for any internal platform team. Goldman thinks many tools are missing simplification: so many capabilities that the core workflow gets buried. "Make sure you don't add extra abilities and features just because you think someone thinks it's cool," Noa Goldman said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2023. Her other rule: integrate tools ML engineers already love. If the team lives in pandas, pick tools that behave like pandas, so the new thing feels like home rather than homework.

The method behind all of it: think about what an ML engineer is trying to do when they wake up with a task, map that step by step, and build or buy for the flow instead of the feature list.

## Who should watch

Platform and MLOps teams building internal tooling, and anyone choosing an ML platform for a team. Expect principles and a product mindset rather than demos or code. Hardcore infrastructure engineers looking for architecture details can skip it.

Title: Your deploys-per-day target has no finish line until an SLO draws one
Description: Mandeep Ubhi (DevSRE.org) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023 on taming unintentional chaos in product development with SLOs, toil work and focused monitoring
Body:
Ten deploys a day becomes fifteen, then twenty, because nobody ever wrote down what good enough looks like. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023, Mandeep Ubhi, Founder and CTO of DevSRE.org, called this kind of everyday disorder the "chaotic cat": unintentional chaos that walks into a team as quietly as Tom stalking Jerry. His argument is that SRE practices, moved left into the product lifecycle, are how you bell it.

The talk is short and concept-led. Chaos engineering, which Ubhi has written a book about, injects failures on purpose; this talk is about the failures nobody planned.

## Which cats are we talking about?

Ubhi picks three themes.

**Speed.** Without a defined target for deployment frequency, teams chase an undefined one, and every number is never quite good enough. His slides ask the pointed question: do customers even care whether you are in the Elite category?

**Dependencies.** On other internal teams, on vendor products and vendor APIs. A feature can be finished and still stuck because an approval or an upgraded vendor API hasn't arrived, and incident time goes into finding the right team rather than fixing anything.

**Measuring everything.** Modern tooling lets you measure almost anything, so teams do. "In my experience, measuring everything is as bad as measuring nothing," Mandeep Ubhi said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023. Nobody can say which dashboard panels actually help.

## Why does product versus service matter?

His root cause is a missing distinction. We talk about site or service reliability, rarely product reliability. A service is a running instance of a product; cloud providers build products, and customers consume them as services. Reliability, availability and performance matter once the product runs, so the question is how to build them in during development rather than treat SRE as an operations afterthought.

The bridge is the SLO, which he calls a balancing lever and a common language between the product paradigm (innovation, speed) and the service paradigm (stability). His example is a team adding multi-factor authentication to a login module. The user expectation is that login completes; the SLI is the ratio of successful login requests; the SLO is that 99% of logins, averaged over the previous 30 days, succeed. The product team can be as innovative as it likes as long as the new feature keeps that number, and the error budget is the margin.

## What counts as toil, and what doesn't?

Chasing dependencies and waiting on other teams falls into the SRE bucket called toil: manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, without enduring value, and growing linearly with the service. His slides separate it from overhead, which needs conscious attention, can't be automated and has strategic value. Examples of toil: setting up environments to reproduce a production issue, upgrading libraries to meet a mandate such as TLS 1.3 by Q2, and work about work, such as one-pagers on login latency.

He is realistic about it. Toil can't be eliminated, only reduced, and it shrinks through engineering (the whole lifecycle), not just automation scripts. His tips include setting toil-reduction goals once a quarter with monthly checkpoints, keeping a few hours aside for Friday hackathons, inviting experts from other teams to run dojos (and sponsoring lunch), borrowing extra people for a breather, and, the honest one, lowering the SLO.

## How do the three themes resolve?

- **Speed**: the number of deployments is whatever the SLO allows. As long as deploys don't break the SLO, keep deploying; now there is a finish line.
- **Dependencies**: go with data. His example is a gaming app that integrates Discord. Rather than waiting on the vendor, probe the downstream dependency (or use its public status data), build trending data, and set your own SLOs with it in mind. He notes the approach has trade-offs.
- **Measuring everything**: tune monitoring to SLOs, add dependency monitoring (often missing next to application and infrastructure monitoring), and define SLOs for new features up front so they are baked into the code. The result is a higher signal-to-noise ratio and, over time, better MTTR and MTBF.

## Who should watch

Team leads and engineering managers who feel their team is busy but not moving, and developers who think SRE is somebody else's job in production. It stays at the level of concepts and examples, so pair it with a hands-on SLO implementation talk.

Title: Go has a garbage collector, and you can still leak memory
Description: Liam Conroy Hampton (Microsoft) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on Go memory management, from stacks and heaps to leaky globals, defer and pprof
Body:
A garbage collector frees memory nobody references. It does nothing for memory you still reference and never use again. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Liam Conroy Hampton, Senior Regional Cloud Advocate at Microsoft, gives an introductory tour of how Go manages memory, the patterns that leak anyway, and how to catch a leaky function with pprof.

## Why care, if the runtime cleans up?

Liam's reasons are leaks, security holes and slow systems, plus cost: in cloud native environments, memory you waste is memory you pay for. His learning goal for the talk is simple, understand Go's memory model and how to manage memory in it, and he is clear that this is the surface, not the whole ocean.

## Stacks, heaps and goroutines

The refresher covers the two places memory lives. The stack holds local variables and call frames, last in, first out, fast and fixed in size; Liam cites about 8 MB as the default on a typical Linux distribution. Goroutines, Go's lightweight threads that sit a layer above the operating system's, start with far smaller stacks, which is a big part of why spawning thousands of them is cheap. The heap holds dynamically allocated, longer-lived data. It grows and shrinks at runtime, which makes it flexible and slower. Short-lived data on the stack, long-lived on the heap.

Go's model rests on three things: the garbage collector reclaiming memory automatically, goroutines for concurrency, and channels for passing data between goroutines safely, without races or hand-rolled locking. For allocation, `new` gives you a zero-valued variable of a type to use later, and `make` builds slices, maps and channels ready to use straight away.

## How do you leak memory in a garbage-collected language?

A leak, in Liam's definition, is memory that is still referenced but no longer needed, so nothing frees it, and eventually the program crashes or the system crawls. His usual suspects: goroutines that never terminate and keep holding their allocations, global variables assigned once and never touched again, and infinite loops.

The code examples make the global case concrete. A struct with a 100 MB byte slice declared inside `main` is fine: when the function ends, the collector reclaims it. The same 100 MB in a package-level variable stays put after the work is done, because the collector sees it as still reachable. The fix is to give the allocation a local scope. A recursion example with a huge call count makes the same point about runaway growth; the fix there is fewer calls or a controlled loop.

The other habit is `defer`. Open a file, check the error, `defer file.Close()`, and the file is closed when the surrounding function returns, even if it fails halfway. The same goes for sockets and database connections, which Liam flags as a security issue as much as a memory one.

## Playground demos, then pprof

In the Go playground Liam runs two goroutines that print task one and task two, and on the second run task two finishes first, which is the point: no ordering guarantee. A channel example sends 42 from one goroutine and reads it in another, and a pointer example takes the address of an int holding 27 and adds 2 through the pointer to get 29.

The finale is the useful bit. A small program imports `net/http/pprof` with a blank identifier, serves it on port 6060 from a goroutine, and calls a deliberately leaky function in a loop. `go tool pprof` against the heap endpoint, then `top`, puts the leaky function at the top of the list with 91% of the memory, and the number climbs the longer it runs. If you have never opened pprof, this is a two-minute reason to.

## How other languages do it

A short comparison rounds things out. Rust uses ownership and borrowing, so the compiler decides when memory is freed. Python combines reference counting with a cyclic garbage collector that periodically finds unreachable objects. Java, with a stack, a heap and a mark-and-sweep collector, is closer to Go than people expect. Liam describes Go's collector as using a stop-the-world technique; in practice it is a concurrent mark-and-sweep that stops the world only briefly.

## Top tips

Use `defer`. Use the collector wisely: "The garbage collector handles most of it for you," Liam Conroy Hampton said at Conf42 Golang 2023, but churning through lots of short-lived objects still slows a program down. And monitor memory with the tools you have, pprof first.

## Who should watch

Go developers early in their journey, or anyone coming from Java or Python who wants a quick map of where Go's memory goes. Readers who already tune GOGC can skip to the pprof demo.

Title: Psychological safety in SRE teams can be measured, and it drops fast
Description: Florian Hoeppner, Marco Torre and Alexander Schaper (Accenture) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023 on measuring psychological safety in SRE retros
Body:
A team that was doing well had a data leak, and within one retrospective its psychological safety score fell off a cliff, with finger pointing at the two people supposedly responsible. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023, Florian Hoeppner, Marco Torre and Alexander Schaper of Accenture showed that drop on a chart, then walked through how the team recovered, making the case that culture in SRE teams can be measured, not just discussed.

The three bring different angles: Hoeppner covers SRE tech strategy, Torre is an SRE subject matter expert, and Schaper leads Accenture's psychological safety capability. The result is one of the few culture talks that comes with a dataset.

## Why does SRE need psychological safety at all?

Hoeppner sets the scene: most companies run two operating models side by side (waterfall, ITIL and large on-prem teams next to cloud, agile, DevOps and SRE squads), responsibilities keep shifting towards cloud providers, and smaller batches mean more changes hitting production. In that setting, communication across silos is how problems get found.

Torre brings in Amy Edmondson's definition: psychological safety is the belief that you won't be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns or mistakes. SREs are paid to raise uncomfortable concerns about reliability with the business and architects. He also links it to SLOs and error budgets, which only work if a team feels safe taking calculated risk in production.

They contrast the traditional and SRE approaches across four dimensions: blame (finger pointing versus taking responsibility without fear), mistakes (hidden versus discussed openly), feedback (critical versus focused on learning), and management (micromanaged versus trusted). Structure matters too. When a team owns something end to end, there is less "it's networking" and fewer people outside the team to blame.

The research numbers they cite: 76% more engagement, 11 times more innovation, 50% higher productivity, and a 67% higher probability that employees apply a newly learned skill when they feel psychologically safe. That last one matters most for anyone rolling out SRE, a new role that asks everyone to learn new skills.

## How do you measure something this soft?

Schaper's answer is a survey tool Accenture uses called the Insight Scan. "It's 15 questions that generates real time data on team level psychological safety and motivation," Alexander Schaper said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023. It tracks factors such as courage, vulnerability and accountability, and places a team on a two-axis map of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation, with four zones:

- **Fear**: teams freeze or take irresponsible risks, and leaders have to hold them accountable.
- **Apathy**: disengaged, struggling to do their job.
- **Comfort**: comfortable, but not stretched.
- **Flow / learning**: high on both axes; they take accountability themselves, learn from mistakes and communicate proactively.

## What happened to the team in the case study?

The team was a product engineering group under pressure from growing pandemic-era online sales. Over a 12-week journey it ran three or four data-driven retrospectives and postmortems, anonymous where it counted, using online whiteboards. The 12 weeks are deliberate: the research they draw on says teams internalise new behaviours after repeating them for about three months.

After the data leak, the facilitated retrospective asked which ways of working led there, how much the team wanted to own the decision, and what each individual could do better. Courage, vulnerability, inclusion and collaboration were the low scores. The fixes were partly tactical (tighter feedback loops, visualising risks in tickets) and partly about leadership framing uncertainty. The team returned to the flow zone.

Then it dropped again, this time into apathy, with no incident at all, just a change of strategy. Schaper's point is that psychological safety is not something that stays once you've achieved it; a leader's words or a shift in direction can move it.

## What should a retro look like?

Their best practices: anchor the conversation in anonymous, team-level data, not who said what; bring a neutral facilitator, especially when the low safety comes from the leader; let people comment anonymously instead of expecting them to unmute; leave with specific improvement ideas and named owners; and start with micro-actions, such as committing to raise one concern in the next postmortem.

Across their projects the slides report psychological safety up 30% on average, motivation up 57%, and two in three teams reaching the flow zone in about 12 weeks, with the biggest gains in purpose (+54%), relatedness (+45%), accountability (+44%) and courage (+37%). Hoeppner closes on the enterprise view: transformations stall when people don't feel safe enough to take risks, and SRE, still new in most companies, is exactly that kind of transformation.

## Who should watch

SRE managers whose postmortems have turned into quiet blame sessions, and leaders rolling out SRE across an organisation. Note that the measurement tool is Accenture's own; the practices around it are transferable.

Title: Your webhook is a public URL, so sign it and keep it thin
Description: Marvin Collins Hosea (AppsLab KE) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on securing webhooks with timestamped HMAC and thin payloads, and scaling them with a broker
Body:
A webhook endpoint is a URL anyone on the internet can POST to, and nothing in the mechanism tells either side who is on the other end. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Marvin Collins Hosea, founder of AppsLab KE, walks through the ways to fix that, from one-time tokens to mutual TLS, and lands on a clear default: an HMAC signature with a timestamp, on a payload that carries almost no data.

## Why webhooks instead of polling?

Marvin starts with the basics for anyone new to them. The term goes back to Jeff Lindsay in 2007, and a webhook is a reverse API: the client registers a URL and the provider calls it, usually with a JSON body in an HTTP POST, when something happens. Polling means asking the server over and over whether anything changed, which wastes resources on both sides. Or, as Marvin put it at Conf42 Golang 2023, "webhooks is kind of don't call me, I will call you". His use cases: killing polling, moving data automatically on events, integrating systems, and driving triggers and actions in another application.

## What exactly is insecure about them?

"By default, webhooks does not come with security implementation and this is a big challenge," Marvin Collins Hosea said at Conf42 Golang 2023. The producer can't verify it is sending to the right destination, and the consumer can't verify the message came from the expected source. Anyone can pose as either side and push malicious data into the receiving application. Unlike an authenticated API endpoint, the webhook URL is simply out there, so every request needs proof of origin.

## Five ways to secure a webhook, ranked

Marvin goes through the options in rising order of strength:

- **One-time verification.** The provider issues a token at setup (revocable) and the client checks it on every request. Weak, because the provider can't see how the client stores it, and the endpoint stays exposed to DDoS and server-side request forgery. He names Zoom as a user.
- **Verification token, or shared secret.** A secret sent in a header on every request and compared by the client. Common, and still not enough on its own.
- **HMAC.** The provider computes a hash signature of the body with a shared key and puts it in a header with a timestamp; the client recomputes it and compares. Messages older than the allowed window get dropped, which shuts the door on replay attacks. He points to GitHub, Shopify and Slack.
- **IP allowlisting.** Easy to defeat with IP spoofing, and painful to maintain whenever addresses change.
- **Mutual TLS.** Both sides verify each other's certificates. Very secure (DocuSign uses it, he says), but certificates expire, rotate and get revoked, and every time that means setup work again, which hurts a high-volume webhook service.

## The default he recommends

Which one is best depends on what the payload exposes, Marvin says. For most data, his answer is HMAC with a timestamp plus a thin, dataless notification: the webhook only says that an event happened, and the client fetches the actual resource through the authenticated API. A leaked or forged notification then carries almost nothing worth stealing.

The Go demo is short. A `getSignature` function takes the plain-text body and the shared secret, builds a new HMAC with Go's crypto packages, writes the data and hex-encodes the result. That goes into a signature header on the request (the example names it `Conf42-Signature`), and the receiver repeats the computation over the body with its copy of the key and compares. One thing to add in your own code: compare the two with `hmac.Equal` rather than `==`, so the check runs in constant time.

## Scaling the thing

The scalability list is short and practical: keep payloads minimal, put a load balancer in front, push events through a message broker (he mentions NATS, which his team implemented, as well as RabbitMQ and Kafka) instead of sending straight from the service, cache data that rarely changes so each delivery doesn't hit the database, and monitor response times and errors so you find the bottleneck before your consumers do.

## The parting checklist

Authenticate both ends. Encrypt data where needed and send less of it. Use timestamps against replays. Ship SDKs and good documentation so integrators get the verification right. Log and trace webhook events like any other event-driven flow, and give every event an ID so you can track it back to its origin.

## Who should watch

Developers building a webhook provider for the first time, or consuming one and wondering how much to trust it. It is a survey with a small code sample, not a production implementation.

Title: Accessibility programs fail on two things, attitude and expertise
Description: Cam Beaudoin (Accelerated Accessibility) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023 on building an accessibility program that pays off for the business
Body:
Imagine being a developer handed a spreadsheet with 800 accessibility defects and no plan for fixing them. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023, Cam Beaudoin, owner of Accelerated Accessibility, used that scene from his IBM consulting days to open a talk on building accessibility programs that don't waste time and money, and on why disability inclusion is a business case rather than charity.

This is the one talk at the event that isn't about systems. It is about people, which is the point he makes in his first story.

## Why does accessibility start with a handshake?

Beaudoin came to accessibility as a junior developer at IBM in Toronto, assigned to fix defects for a banking client. He read the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG, about an inch thick when printed) and started fixing bugs without ever meeting a user who would benefit. Then Tom, a blind colleague who travelled between IBM offices teaching accessibility, arrived. Beaudoin's boss walked up, said hello and stuck out his hand, and Tom had no way of knowing it was there. Beaudoin went back to his desk and searched YouTube for how to shake hands with a blind person. (The answer: ask "can I shake your hand?")

His lesson is that the discomfort around the word disability, and the fear of saying the wrong thing, is what produces unconscious bias and exclusion. It is fine to ask, to be wrong and to learn.

## What does the framework look like?

From his IBM work and conversations with chief accessibility officers at the CSUN Assistive Technology Conference, he built what he calls the Accelerated 180 framework, aimed at getting a program started in as little as eight weeks:

- **Know your current situation.** Which laws apply: AODA in Ontario, the Accessible Canada Act, Section 508 and the ADA in the US. Run a maturity model assessment of every part of the business, and anchor the work in your DEI initiative.
- **Define the destination.** Decide early what stakeholders and executives need reported, build a coalition of allies, and secure buy-in before the formal executive presentation.
- **Be realistic about time.** He plans six to 18 months for a rollout, and accessibility work is never done.
- **Pick one measurable outcome.** Not a vague goal of making the whole organisation accessible, but something like adding automated accessibility checks to the CI/CD pipeline and cutting the defect count from 300 to 80 in six months.

Large organisations often use a hub-and-spoke model, with a central accessibility team lending experts to projects. Smaller ones can start with one to three champions who consult across HR, development and procurement.

## What happens when you skip it?

His cautionary tale is Target. In 2006 the National Federation of the Blind filed suit over thousands of access barriers on the website, where blind users with screen readers could not even complete checkout, and the case became a $6 million settlement. Target's response was a real program rather than a panic audit. Today it commits to WCAG, works with advocacy groups, runs an accessibility centre of excellence and speaks at CSUN about its progress.

## Why do programs fail?

"Number one is attitude, number two is expertise," Cam Beaudoin said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023. The attitude side is familiar to anyone who has shipped software: it's boring, it's extra work, and the developer was only following a design that wasn't accessible to begin with. He reframes it around fairness, better code (following the HTML standard properly, and not making buttons out of divs, solves most problems) and our future selves, since age brings disabilities to almost everyone. The expertise side means knowledge bases, clear owners and, above all, involving people with disabilities in testing your products.

Intuit is his scale example: it went from three people caring about accessibility to more than 1,200 accessibility champions, with gates in its release processes and guidance built into its design system and content rules. It still isn't perfect; a deaf intern pointed out the onboarding videos had no captions, and they got fixed.

## Where is the business case?

His numbers: the US Office of Disability Employment Policy ranks people with disabilities as the third largest market segment in the US, he puts the discretionary income of working-age people with disabilities at $21 billion, and one in seven people worldwide has a disability, according to the World Health Organization. Selling to government, higher education and many large companies requires a VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template). Microsoft is his headline case: its AI for Accessibility program was a $25 million, five-year investment, and the Xbox Adaptive Controller came from an employee, Bryce Johnson.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers who own a product's front end, SREs whose pipelines could carry accessibility checks, and anyone who has to make the case for accessibility to leadership. It is a business and culture talk with no code or tooling walkthroughs.

Title: Go and Apache Pulsar from go mod init to a Kubernetes pod, no Dockerfile
Description: David Kjerrumgaard (StreamNative) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on building Pulsar producers and consumers in Go, packing them with buildpacks, and deploying to Kubernetes
Body:
Apache Pulsar does queues and streams on the same topic, and Go is a first-class client for it. At Conf42 Golang 2023, David Kjerrumgaard, developer advocate at StreamNative, Apache Pulsar committer and author of Pulsar in Action (Manning), builds a Go producer and consumer, containerises both without writing a Dockerfile, and ships them to Kubernetes with config pulled from ConfigMaps. It is an end-to-end walkthrough, from `go mod init` to `kubectl logs`.

## What makes Pulsar different from Kafka or RabbitMQ?

Pulsar started at Yahoo in 2012, and its party trick is a two-tier architecture. The brokers that serve messages are stateless, and the data lives in a separate layer built on Apache BookKeeper, whose storage nodes are called bookies. A metadata store ties the two together. Because no broker owns any data, any broker can serve any topic, load rebalances on its own, and you scale brokers and storage separately, which plays nicely with Kubernetes autoscaling.

The same split gives tiered storage (offload old data to S3 and keep it for much longer, more cheaply), geo-replication and multi-tenancy from day one. Data is organised as tenant, then namespace (topics that share policies), then topic. On the client side, pluggable protocol handlers let MQTT, RabbitMQ, Kafka and native Pulsar clients publish to or consume from the same topic. Four subscription types pick your semantics: exclusive, failover and key-shared give ordered, Kafka-style streaming, and shared gives a classic work queue.

## Why Go for Pulsar apps?

The official Go client covers producers, consumers and readers, and Go is one of the three languages supported by Pulsar Functions, the lightweight serverless framework David compares to AWS Lambda. He doesn't cover Functions in this talk, but flags them as the next thing to try.

## The producer and the consumer

The code is deliberately plain. Both apps read their settings (broker URL, topic, subscription name) from a properties file through a small utility module, so nothing about the cluster is hard-coded. The producer creates a client, then a producer on `public/default/purchases`, and loops forever, sending a message every 5 seconds: a username as the key, a purchased item (a book, an alarm clock, batteries, a gift card) as the raw byte payload.

The consumer subscribes to the same topic with a named subscription and reads from a message channel. Each message is printed and then acked, so the broker won't redeliver it; a negative ack asks for redelivery when processing fails. The named subscription is what lets a consumer that disconnects pick up exactly where it left off, which the demo shows more than once as message IDs carry on across restarts.

## Containers without a Dockerfile

For packaging David uses Cloud Native Buildpacks instead of Docker. "Instead, buildpacks automatically detect the language and framework your application is using and will automatically containerize it for you with a single command," David Kjerrumgaard said at Conf42 Golang 2023. One `pack build` per app, with a builder image, detects Go, fetches a Go runtime and builds the binary inside a cached layer. The first run spends a while downloading the builder, and that wait is in the video. Both images run locally under Docker before he tags them and pushes them to Docker Hub.

## Kubernetes, with config outside the image

The deployment manifest puts producer and consumer in one pod as two containers. The properties files become two ConfigMaps (`kubectl create configmap` from the files) mounted where the apps expect them, so you can point at another broker or topic without rebuilding. Then `kubectl apply`, `describe` to check images, limits and mounts, and `logs` per container: the producer publishing every 5 seconds, the consumer keeping up.

## Who should watch

Go developers new to Pulsar who want a working mental model of the architecture and a template for a deployable app. Expect a narrated walkthrough, not a production design. The speaker works at StreamNative, a Pulsar company, but the talk sticks to open source Apache Pulsar and buildpacks.

Title: Make docs part of code review, or watch your SRE playbooks rot
Description: Yury Nino (Google) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023 on the documents SRE teams need across a service's life, and how to keep them alive
Body:
Every team has a playbook that was correct on the day it was written. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023, Yury Nino, Cloud Infrastructure Engineer at Google Cloud, mapped the documents an SRE team needs across a service's life, from onboarding to decommissioning, and closed with the rule that keeps them from dying: if a change alters how someone has to behave, the change must include the doc update.

The talk builds on Google's "Why SRE documents matter" article and the Seeking SRE book. It is a catalogue with a point of view, useful as a checklist for any team auditing its own docs.

## Why do SRE documents matter, and why do they decay?

Nino opens with the Stack Overflow 2022 developer survey: respondents named technical documentation as the top resource for learning to code, and the same people ranked documentation as the number two challenge they face. Missing, incomplete or outdated docs hurt velocity, quality and, for SREs, reliability.

The deeper problem is tribal knowledge. Operational principles passed on verbally have to be relearned, painfully, through trial and error. And documentation competes for time. The slides put SRE operational work at 35% of the week, leaving 65% for development, and documentation has to come out of that development budget. Many engineers also suspect it won't count in a performance review or promotion case.

## What documents does a service need?

She sorts them into six groups.

**New service onboarding.** The core is the production readiness review (PRR), with documents answering pointed questions: the request flow from user to front end to back end, and which requests have different latency needs; expected traffic and growth during and after launch; single points of failure and how you survive an unavailable dependency; which manual processes remain and how they will be automated; which third-party code, data or services you depend on, and which partners depend on you. Alongside sit an SRE role document, written so developers don't equate SREs with an ops team, and an engagement model covering takeover criteria, SLO and error budget negotiation, launch and freeze criteria, status reports, staffing and roadmap planning.

**Running a service.** Service overviews (architecture, dependencies, owners, links to dashboards), playbooks with verification, troubleshooting and escalation steps for each alert, postmortems (timeline, user impact, root cause, action items), technical, escalation and on-call policies, and SLAs.

**Products SREs build.** Concept guides, quickstarts, how-tos, developer guides, codelabs, FAQ and support pages (with escalation flows and on-call info), and API references.

**Reporting service state.** A quarterly service review and presentation covering performance, sustainability, risk and production health, plus on-call tickets, postmortems and SLO performance. It is also the team's chance to show the value of SRE.

**Running the SRE team.** A team site and a team charter: the space the team operates in, its top two or three services, its principles and its links. At Google, she notes, many teams keep docs next to source code in an internal platform.

**Onboarding new SREs.** On-call checklists covering production concepts, the front-end and back-end stack, automation, tooling and monitoring, and role-play training such as the Wheel of Misfortune, where a hypothetical on-call engineer works through a scripted outage, which also tests whether people can find the right documents under pressure.

## How do you keep documents alive?

Her recommendations, drawn from what Google learned:

- **Communicate the value.** Leadership funds docs when you show data on their quality and impact; functional data is the convincing kind.
- **Create one repository.** Information scattered across sites, heads and Drive folders is information nobody finds. Interview stakeholders, inventory what exists, do a gap analysis, set up a structure, track the migration, archive the dead, and watch search terms and analytics.
- **Use templates.** With a good template, writing a simple doc is like filling in a form, and readers know where to look. The SRE book includes several, including a playbook template.
- **Define success metrics.** A service overview has high impact if people use it and incidents get resolved faster.
- **Work with technical writers.** They should partner with SREs on operational and product docs and improve the tooling.
- **Require docs in code review.** Nino is honest about the motivation problem: "Documentation is like testing. Nobody really wants to do it," Yury Nino said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023. Code review is the lever: not every change needs a doc update, but any change that makes a developer, SRE or user behave differently does.

## Who should watch

SRE leads setting up a new team or taking over services, and anyone who has opened a playbook mid-incident and found a command for a cluster that no longer exists. If you already run PRRs and docs-as-code, the value is the checklist itself.
