Title: TDD on a real Go handler, five failure modes before one line of code
Description: Ivan Pesenti (Sorint Lab) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on test-driving a Gin and Gorm update handler, with sqlmock standing in for PostgreSQL
Body:
Most TDD tutorials stop at a function that adds two numbers. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Ivan Pesenti, a software developer at Sorint Lab, skips FizzBuzz and test-drives the hardest handler in a to-do REST API, the edit route, through red, green and refactor, with a mocked PostgreSQL behind it. The takeaway: list every outcome first, then let the tests drag the design out of you.

## What does TDD actually ask of you?

Ivan opens with the three rules and takes them literally. No production code unless it makes a failing unit test pass. No more of a unit test than is enough to fail, and compilation failures count. No more production code than is enough to pass that one test. His first test fails because the handler doesn't exist yet, which by rule two is a perfectly good red.

A clean test, in his checklist, follows Arrange, Act, Assert, has no code smells (a function with a pile of parameters gets a struct), no magic numbers or magic strings, a name that tells you its input and output, and the F.I.R.S.T. principle: fast, independent, repeatable, self-validating, thorough. On coverage he pushes back on the 100% obsession: cover the critical business logic. If you follow TDD strictly you land near 100% statement coverage anyway, because no code exists without a test.

His sharpest line is the one people forget: "test driven development is not about testing but about designing," Ivan Pesenti said at Conf42 Golang 2023. The tests are the feedback loop that shapes the solution.

## Five scenarios, decided before the code

The route is `PUT todos/:id` with a JSON body of description, completion flag and due date. Before writing anything, Ivan lists every outcome:

- id not an integer (say, `abc`): 400 Bad Request
- payload not valid (an empty description): 400 Bad Request
- database error: 500 Internal Server Error
- to-do not found: 404 Not Found
- happy path: 202 Accepted, empty body

If you can't name the scenarios, he argues, you can't do TDD. Each one becomes a test, then just enough handler code, then cleanup.

## The toolbox

Production code uses Gin, Gorm and Gorm's Postgres driver. Ivan picked Gin partly because Gorilla Mux had just been publicly archived, and he puts Gin at roughly 70,000 GitHub stars against Gorilla Mux's 20,000. Tests use the standard `testing` package (no framework needed in Go, which he counts as a win), `net/http/httptest` for recorders and requests, testify's `assert`, and DATA-DOG's go-sqlmock. The mock is the design point: you program against an abstraction and push the choice of database engine to the end of the project.

## The refactor phase does the real work

The demo is a patient loop. A recorder and a Gin test context, a failing test, `c.String` with a 400, then out go the magic numbers in favour of `http.StatusBadRequest` and a constant for the error string. Two tests that cover the same scenario get merged. Ivan reminds you that tests are code too: you can adjust, delete or improve them as long as every scenario stays covered. Later rounds add sqlmock expectations for Gorm's queries, a DTO struct for the payload, and finally a `repo` package that pulls the database logic out of the handler.

## Proving the 500 path for real

The wiring at the end is where it stops being a toy. Postgres runs in Docker, Gorm runs auto-migration, and a middleware injects the Gorm DB into each request. Ivan wraps it with a 5-second context timeout and a deferred cancel, as a habit for any IO. Postman then walks through each scenario. The database error is the awkward one to trigger by hand, so he adds `SELECT pg_sleep(10)` to the repo, and the request hangs, then comes back as a 500 with context deadline exceeded. A timeout you've watched fire is worth ten you've only configured.

## Who should watch

Go developers who know TDD in theory but have only ever applied it to katas, and anyone who wants to see Gin handlers tested without a live database. It is a long, code-heavy demo; have an editor open.

- Julien Breux on [testing with Testcontainers](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Julien_Breux_test_testcontainers_container), for when the mock isn't enough.

Title: Every SRE practice is a change, and CI/CD is where changes travel
Description: Safeer CM (Flipkart, CD Foundation) and Garima Bajpai (Crowdbyte Solutions) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023 on CI/CD as the SRE-DevOps overlay
Body:
The SRE-versus-DevOps debate usually ends in a Venn diagram. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023, Safeer CM, Senior Staff SRE at Flipkart and a CD Foundation ambassador, and Garima Bajpai, founder of the Canada DevOps Community of Practice (Crowdbyte Solutions), drew it differently: the overlap between the two is change, and the pipeline that carries change, CI/CD, is where the two disciplines actually meet.

The talk comes in two halves. Safeer covers the here and now: which SRE and DevOps practices run through the pipeline. Garima takes the longer view: operating models, measurement beyond DORA, SBOMs and net zero.

## Why is change the common thread?

Safeer starts with two short lists. The SRE principles from the Google SRE book: embracing risk, SLOs, eliminating toil, monitoring, release engineering, automation and simplicity. The common DevOps practices: collaboration, continuous improvement, monitoring and automation. The two meet on shared ownership, observability (SLOs on the SRE side, DORA metrics on the DevOps side), automation and platform engineering, and above all on change.

Change is what delivers business value, whether new features or stability work. It is also what causes outages, bugs, SLA breaches and lost reputation. Software change management (Git, pull requests, peer review) tracks and accepts the risk; release management takes it the rest of the way. CI/CD, in Safeer's words, "is the vehicle of all changes in your software infrastructure," he said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023. Both disciplines also prefer small incremental changes, and the only way to do that sustainably is a fully automated pipeline.

## Which practices live in the pipeline?

His tour of the overlay:

- **Testing.** Functional tests (unit, integration, smoke, regression) mostly run in CI; non-functional tests (performance, scalability, resilience, security) run at different deployment stages, some after production deploys. In organisations with both teams, DevOps usually drives the functional side and SRE the non-functional one.
- **Application configuration.** Config files, environment variables, external key-value stores or feature flags: pick a method, stay consistent, and make every change versioned and auditable.
- **Infrastructure.** Configuration management (Ansible playbooks, Salt states) for bare metal and VMs; infrastructure as code with Terraform or AWS CloudFormation; network as code for devices.
- **GitOps.** Desired state declared, versioned and immutable in Git, pulled automatically by agents that continuously reconcile drift. A CI/CD system is the natural way to implement it.
- **Everything as code.** Policy as code, SLOs as code (tracking SLOs across many services by hand gets tricky), dashboards and observability config as code, and the pipelines themselves as code, which makes onboarding new projects easier.

His summary: codify as many SRE and DevOps practices as you can, and let the pipeline evolve as the organisation's maturity grows. He also introduces the Continuous Delivery Foundation, the Linux Foundation's vendor-neutral home for Jenkins, Jenkins X, Screwdriver, Spinnaker, Tekton, Pyrsia, Ortelius, Shipwright and CDEvents.

## What comes after DORA?

Garima frames the pressure on both disciplines: exponential tool growth in roughly a decade, complexity and cognitive load, cloud costs pulling finance and engineering together (FinOps), and a skills shortage. She reads the history as two reinforcing pushes: DevOps for developer productivity and lead time, SRE for reliability and customer experience. To get the full value of DevOps at scale, she argued, SRE has to be built in: "the integration of SRE practices is essential. Everybody agrees to that today," Garima Bajpai said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023.

Her caution is the law of diminishing returns: past a point, more tools, people and practices lower productivity. To find the optimal operating model, ask why you deploy, what (monoliths or microservices), where, across how many clouds, and how often. The common core she proposes is continuous delivery built on the four GitOps-style principles: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled.

For measurement she argues for going beyond DORA. Functional advancements include cross-cloud ("supercloud") delivery, event-driven pipelines, progressive delivery combined with machine learning, and the SBOM. She cites Gartner: by 2025, 60% of organisations buying mission-critical software would mandate SBOM disclosure in their contracts, up from less than 5% in 2022. Operational measures include portability, flow-optimised and observable delivery, resource-optimised infrastructure and real-time scaling. She closes with net zero: map the carbon footprint of products and services, find hotspot features and decarbonise them, with SRE leading the way.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE leads deciding what belongs in the pipeline versus in a runbook, and anyone explaining to management why SRE and DevOps teams should share one delivery system. The first half is concrete; the second is strategic and forward-looking, so expect frameworks rather than YAML.

Title: An SLO is an API contract for how a service behaves at runtime
Description: Prathamesh Sonpatki (last9.io) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023 on SLOs as runtime promises that keep business, engineering and ops in balance
Body:
Your API docs promise that POST /users returns 201 on success and 400 on bad input. They say nothing about whether it answers in one second or five during peak hours, or whether a tenth of requests may fail on weekends. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023, Prathamesh Sonpatki, Developer Evangelist at last9.io, argued that service level objectives are exactly that missing half of the contract: a written agreement about how an endpoint behaves at runtime.

It is a short, non-technical talk, with no dashboards or PromQL, and it makes a tidy case for why SLOs are an organisational tool before they are a monitoring feature.

## Why does everyone's wish list collide?

Sonpatki opens with four wish lists. The developer wants bug-free code and the latest tools. The DevOps engineer wants infrastructure that scales without the cloud bill exploding. The team lead wants deadlines met, tech debt contained and a motivated team. The product leader wants velocity, adoption and external commitments kept. Each list ends with the same word: but.

To explain why, he brings in Jens Rasmussen's model of how accidents happen. A system operates inside three boundaries: economic failure (spend too much and the company shuts down), unacceptable workload (push people 24x7 and they leave), and acceptable performance or safety. Push hard on one axis and the operating point drifts towards another boundary, until something breaks. In software terms: business pushing features until tech debt causes failures, or engineering chasing perfection until delivery stalls.

## How do negotiations become contracts?

Teams handle boundaries by negotiating, and the examples will sound familiar: we can ship with a few bugs; we can deploy but the AWS bill goes up for two or three weeks; we can roll out to the new customer if the team works the weekend, again. A negotiation that both sides accept becomes a contract.

In code, the closest thing to a contract is an API interface. Sonpatki's point is that the status codes are only the static part. The runtime part looks like this, from his example for POST /users:

- Uptime 90%, so 10% of requests are allowed to fail.
- Every weekend, 20% of requests are allowed to fail.
- During peak hours, latency can vary between 1,000 and 5,000 ms.

Write those down and the consumer stops expecting the impossible. That runtime interface is what SRE calls an SLO: a target for a health indicator over a time window, such as availability above 99.99% over one day, or latency under 4,000 ms over seven days.

## Why does every extra nine need a budget line?

Once a promise is explicit, you can ask what it costs. "Because we have to remember that not every nine is free," Prathamesh Sonpatki said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023. Going from three nines to four or five means more time, money, people and possibly hardware. An SLO tells you whether that spend is needed at all.

It also settles arguments that otherwise run on opinion. If a service sits at 80% availability, shipping new features on top of it is unlikely to pay off, because they will inherit the same failures; fix reliability first. The same numbers answer whether you can promise 99.9% to an enterprise customer, where engineering should focus next sprint, and whether to build or buy a component you lack the people to make reliable.

## From promises to policies

The next step is to codify promises as organisational policy. Tiered services are his example: a P0 service gets 99.99% availability, a P3 gets 90%, and everyone knows not every service is a priority. Tiers can follow the customer too: paid versus pilot, enterprise versus self-serve, alpha versus generally available.

He also warns against top-down targets. Start from a baseline of what you have now and climb what he calls the ladder of reliability one rung at a time: 90% to 95% to 99%, not 90% straight to five nines, which ends in tears.

The boundaries from Rasmussen's model never go away. What changes is that contracts and policies create a tension that keeps the operating point inside them, with every function working to the same objectives instead of against each other.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and product leaders who need a vocabulary for reliability trade-offs, and SREs who have to sell SLOs inside the company. Engineers looking for implementation detail should pair it with a more hands-on SLO talk.

Title: Golings teaches Go by handing you broken programs
Description: Mauricio Antunes (Globo) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on Golings, a rustlings-style CLI that teaches Go through small exercises with fast compiler feedback
Body:
The fastest way to learn a language is to have its compiler yell at you, early and often. That is the whole premise of Golings, and at Conf42 Golang 2023 its author, Mauricio Antunes, a software developer at Globo, demos it in a short, hands-on talk: install the tool, fix a couple of broken exercises, then write a brand new one live.

If you have used rustlings for Rust (or ziglings for Zig), you already know the shape. Golings is the Go version: a binary plus a folder of small programs that don't compile or whose tests fail, ordered from easiest to hardest. Your job is to make them pass, one at a time.

## Why build it at all?

Mauricio's reason is fast feedback. Books carry the theory you need, but they make you read a lot before you type anything, and experienced developers picking up a new language want to get to the code. "I created golings because I believe in fast feedback while learning new programming language," Mauricio Antunes said at Conf42 Golang 2023. Go, with its quick compiler and clear error messages, is a good fit for that loop.

## How does a Golings session go?

You install the binary with `go install` or grab a release for your OS and architecture, clone the repo, and run `golings run next`. It compiles the next unfinished exercise and prints the compiler error. In the demo the first exercise is about variables: a `Printf` call formats an integer, but the variable it needs has no name. Stuck? `golings hint` prints the hint stored for that exercise in the index file, here a gentle reminder that variables in Go have names.

Once the program compiles and prints what it should, you delete the not-done marker comment from the file, and only then does Golings move you on. Forget the comment and you stay put, which is a neat way to make the learner confirm they understood the fix, not just that it compiled. `golings verify` runs every exercise from the first one onwards and stops at the first that still fails, so you always know where you are.

## The honest limitation, and the workaround

Mauricio is upfront about the weak spot of any tool like this: the checker is the compiler. "It must obey the compiler and if the compiler is happy, you will succeed," he said, so an exercise can pass without the learner doing what the author intended. His fix is plain and practical: write comments in the exercise that spell out the expected output, so the target is clear even when the compiler would accept something else.

## Writing your own exercise, live

The second half of the talk is the part contributors will want. Mauricio adds a third struct exercise on camera: the program must print a person's full name, so the learner has to add a method to a struct. He copies an existing exercise into a new folder, rewrites the message and fields, registers it in the index file with a hint (a skeleton of a method on a struct, enough to point someone at the right chapter of a book without giving the answer away), and runs it on its own with `golings run`.

Golings works with any folder of exercises plus its own index file, so you can build a private course for your team. If your exercises would help other learners, he invites a pull request to the upstream repo.

## Who should watch

People teaching Go, or onboarding a team onto it, and anyone who learned Rust through rustlings and wants the same thing for Go. It is a short, practical demo, not a tour of the tool's internals.

Title: How HCL turned chaos experiments into an SRE training path
Description: Chandra Dixit (HCL Cloud Native Labs) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023 on using chaos engineering to upskill 1,000+ SREs, from pod deletes to GitOps workflows
Body:
Teaching a thousand engineers SRE is hard to do with slides alone; breaking things in front of them works better. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023, Chandra Dixit, SRE Architect at HCL Cloud Native Labs in London, told how his team made chaos engineering a standard part of its SRE enablement programme, growing from manual pod deletes to chaos workflows checked into Git and run by Argo.

It is an enablement story more than a technical deep end: what a large services company did to make a niche practice routine, plus one worked example of a chaos workflow.

## What does Cloud Native Labs actually do?

The labs, in Frisco, London and Noida, cover cloud native strategy, prototyping and workforce modernisation. Dixit's part is the culture side: DevOps and SRE upskilling. The SRE services come in three groups: enablement (skill assessment, custom learning journeys, certification), advisory (consulting on chaos engineering, tooling, automation strategy and operating models), and maturity assessment (third-party reviews of architecture and automation, then coaching).

The numbers on the slides: 100+ customers, 1,000+ SREs enabled through the certification programme, 20+ SRE cohorts, and chaos environments showcased in 100+ client engagements.

## How did the chaos practice grow?

The timeline is short and specific:

- **August 2021**: exploring products, concepts and installation methods.
- **October 2021**: chaos engineering added to the SRE Associate training path.
- **November 2021**: simple hands-on experiments, such as pod delete and node shutdown.
- **December 2021**: workflow-based experiments, combining several faults to get closer to what a real production failure looks like.
- **February 2022**: part of the standard Cloud Native Labs stack shown to clients, then client-specific use cases.

The progression ran from VM-based experiments in the spirit of Chaos Monkey, to Kubernetes faults (killing pods, blacking out services, dropping DNS), to workflows wired into CI/CD with Jenkins, GitHub Actions and Argo CD. The domains covered Azure, AWS, Kubernetes, and private cloud and on-prem setups, because a good share of client environments still live there.

The method behind each experiment is the classic loop: form a hypothesis, choose a blast radius, test and observe, and feed what you learn back into the service.

## What does a chaos workflow look like?

The example uses LitmusChaos with GitHub Actions, Argo Workflows, Prometheus and Grafana against the Sock Shop microservices demo app:

1. A developer writes a workflow in YAML (take one service down, watch the others, take the next one down) and checks it into the repository.
2. GitHub Actions picks up the change and submits the workflow to the Argo server.
3. Argo runs it, and Litmus creates its custom resources: ChaosExperiment definitions, a ChaosEngine as the running instance, and ChaosResult objects with the outcome.
4. Those spawn ordinary Kubernetes jobs and pods that inject the faults.
5. The impact on the golden signals shows up on Grafana dashboards.

The design goal is that chaos rides along with delivery. "The flows that are designed for chaos, they run in production after the service has been deployed," Chandra Dixit said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023. If the service survives, the deployment goes ahead. The safety valve is just as important: if the blast radius grows too big or latency climbs too far, the experiment can be aborted and the chaos engine stopped.

## Which tools?

Dixit name-checks LitmusChaos, Chaos Mesh, Gremlin, Harness, Azure Chaos Studio and AWS Fault Injection Simulator. What he likes about the current crop: many are open source with enterprise versions available when you need support, they run on lightweight, managed and on-prem Kubernetes alike, they expose detailed APIs and CRDs for scripted scenarios, they support GitOps and Prometheus out of the box, and the documentation is good, which he notes is not a given in open source. Native tools such as Azure Chaos Studio are the easy pick for experiments inside that cloud.

## Who should watch

People building an internal SRE academy or a chaos engineering programme in a large organisation, who want a realistic timeline and a reference workflow. If you already run Litmus in production, the workflow section is familiar ground, and the rest is about enablement rather than new technique.

Title: Hide the transaction in the context, keep the repository clean
Description: Ilia Sergunin (Avito) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on transaction management in Go with repositories, a context-based transaction manager and unit of work
Body:
Every Go repository pattern tutorial looks clean until the second table, and then `*sqlx.Tx` starts leaking into every method signature. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Ilia Sergunin, Senior Software Engineer at Avito, walks one shop example from a naive repository to nested transactional use cases. His answer is to store the transaction in `context.Context` behind a transaction manager, and to reach for unit of work when business transactions run long.

Avito runs Go in more than a thousand microservices and handles about 300 million visits a month. His team's own domain, reselling smartphones, has more than 20 states between seller and buyer, so the problem is not academic.

## What should a repository hide?

Saving, loading and mapping, so use cases think about the domain and not the database. One repository per model, because a repository that handles several models becomes a super-repository that is hard to change and test. His `User` has a nested `Profile` in the domain, but they are two tables in the database, and the repository converts between the two views. That alone needs a transaction, so a failure between the two writes cannot corrupt data.

## How does the transaction leak?

Step by step. Registration must save the user and publish a message to a queue, so it begins a transaction and passes `tx` into the repository and the publisher. The repository interface now knows about database transactions. Then the business adds checkout without registration, a use case that calls the registration use case. Now each use case needs if/else logic to decide whether it owns the transaction or joined one. "But as we know, with great business logics comes great legacy."

His wish list: a simple repository with no transaction argument, nested transactional use cases, transaction control hidden away, and a database you can swap without rewriting use cases.

## Which fixes don't work?

He tries them in order. A `WithTransaction` closure removes the begin/commit/rollback boilerplate but still ties use cases to `sqlx.Tx`. A factory method that returns a repository bound to a transaction adds a temporal dependency: call it in the wrong order and you are outside the transaction. Reflection that injects the transaction into repositories works, but reflection is no golden path and the transaction still travels through use cases.

Other languages don't help much. SQLAlchemy passes the session explicitly. Django and PHP use globals because each request gets its own thread or process. Java and C# use thread-local storage. Go has no goroutine-local storage, getting a goroutine ID takes hacks that a new release could break, and the Go team discourages it on purpose.

## Why is context the right place?

Because request-scoped values that die with the request are the accepted exception to the advice against storing anything beyond primitives in a context. The transaction manager checks the context for an active transaction, starts one if there is none, and puts it in the context. Repositories pull the transaction from the context, or fall back to the plain DB connection, through a small getter interface. Nested use cases join the outer transaction automatically.

To make it testable he turns the closure into a `Manager` interface with `Do` and `DoWithSettings` (nested transactions, read-only, timeouts), a generic `Transaction` interface, and per-database settings. A generic `TxDecorate[In]` wraps any use case that follows one convention, a `Handle` method taking an args struct, so transaction handling disappears from use case bodies entirely. The result is Avito's go-transaction-manager library, with adapters for `database/sql`, sqlx, GORM, MongoDB and Redis.

## What does it cost?

He is candid about the drawbacks. It needs Go 1.13 or newer. Other drivers need their own adapter, about 70 lines each. The overhead is about 17%, or roughly 5 microseconds, on an in-memory SQLite benchmark. A benchmark against sqlmock showed only 3.4%, but mostly because the mock is slow, and against file-backed MySQL the overhead disappears into I/O. You must pass context everywhere. And long business transactions are out, because a database transaction holds a connection. In his line count comparison the manager wins once you pass about 1.8 nested scenarios.

## When do you need unit of work?

When a business transaction must span slow calls, such as an external service. Martin Fowler defines the pattern as "maintaining a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinating the writing out of changes and the resolution of concurrency problems." In Go that means `RegisterNew`, `RegisterDirty`, `RegisterClean`, `RegisterDeleted`, `Commit` and `Rollback`. Commit opens one short database transaction and writes everything in batches, so updates stay atomic.

The catch is complexity: a full version needs an identity map, a mapper registry and data mappers, plus a plan for auto-increment IDs (generate them in the app). His simplified version just queues callbacks and fits on two slides. For SQL databases he points to `freerware/work`.

## Who should watch?

Backend engineers building service layers in Go who have felt `tx` creep through their code. Dense slides, but every step is motivated by a concrete business change.

Title: Observability is the SRE muscle you build with cAdvisor and Grafana
Description: Jhonnatan Gil Chaves (Globant) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023 on observability as the core of SRE, from DORA metrics to a Prometheus demo
Body:
When a request fails, the ticket bounces from ops to the developers, who reply that it works on their machine, while the actual culprit is a firewall rule somebody changed yesterday. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023, Jhonnatan Gil Chaves, DevOps Engineer at Globant, made the case that observability is what ends that ping-pong, and then built a small local stack with cAdvisor, Prometheus and Grafana to show where to start.

This is an introductory talk: a tour of the concepts followed by a hands-on Docker demo. If you already run OpenTelemetry in production, it is a refresher; if your team is still debating whether it needs observability at all, it is a useful one.

## Where does observability sit in SRE?

Gil Chaves starts from the CNCF glossary definition of site reliability engineering and its contrast with DevOps: "While DevOps focuses on getting code to production, SRE ensures that code running in production works properly." DevOps gets you to push code to dev, staging and production easily. What happens after the deploy is the SRE question, and most of the answer is performance monitoring, alerting, debugging and troubleshooting.

He then brings in the DORA metrics as the way to locate your team: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, time to restore service and change failure rate. His warning is about the measuring, not the metrics. To compute them you have to connect the repository, the commit conventions, the requirements tool (Jira, Confluence or whatever you use) and the incident history. That plumbing is the hard part, and doing it tends to expose how many of a company's process definitions only exist on paper.

## How is observability different from APM?

He treats observability as a property of the system: the degree to which it generates actionable insights from its external outputs. APM shows you what is happening inside components; observability adds alerting and, eventually, automated remediation for alerts you have learned to recognise. It also has a selling point for managers and security teams: give a team a dashboard and it can see how its application behaves in production without access to the infrastructure or the code.

The golden triangle is the familiar three signals:

- **Logs**: unstructured, text-based records of events, good for troubleshooting and spotting trends.
- **Metrics**: structured numbers aggregated over time, good for anomalies and performance targets.
- **Traces**: the path of a request between services, with timing and context.

Traces are where he places the real effort. "That is the biggest challenge here because you need to instrument your application," Jhonnatan Gil Chaves said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023. That means a conversation with developers and architects about frameworks and patterns, not a toggle in a console. For tracing he points to OpenTelemetry, which he describes as the second most active CNCF community after Kubernetes.

## What does the demo build?

The demo runs on Docker and comes with a repeated disclaimer: it is for a local proof of concept, not production. The steps:

1. **cAdvisor** first, which collects container metrics from the Docker host and exposes them.
2. **Prometheus**, started with a mounted config that scrapes cAdvisor at your machine's internal IP; the targets page shows both endpoints.
3. **Grafana** on port 3000 (admin/admin, the default you should change anywhere but a laptop), with Prometheus added as a data source on port 9090.
4. Two community dashboards imported by ID, giving two views of the same Docker metrics.

He finishes by opening Grafana alerting: rules for the behaviour you care about, and contact points that route to Alertmanager, email, Discord, Slack, Telegram, PagerDuty, Kafka or a custom webhook payload.

## What is the takeaway for a team?

His closing advice is less about tools than direction. Observability has to be tied to business value and the organisation's goals, not built because a stack exists. Invest in the right tools, prioritise data quality, and keep the approach collaborative and data driven. The CNCF's observability catalogue lists more tools than anyone could evaluate, so pick based on the team's expertise.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving from DevOps work into SRE, and teams that want a first Prometheus and Grafana setup running in an afternoon. The transcript is rough in places and the talk leans on definitions, so experienced observability folks can skip to the demo.

Title: Go and Redis, and why your read replicas are probably idle
Description: Abhishek Gupta (AWS) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on using Redis from Go with go-redis, from data structures and pipelines to cluster gotchas
Body:
You added read replicas to your Redis cluster, and with default client settings every read still goes to the primary. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Abhishek Gupta, Principal Developer Advocate at AWS, gives a practical tour of Redis from Go: which client to pick, how the core data structures map to go-redis calls, two demos (a worker queue and a WebSocket chat), and the production gotchas that trip up newcomers, the idle replicas included.

## Why do Go and Redis fit together?

His answer is simplicity. Redis is a key-value store whose values are the data structures developers already use daily: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, plus streams, geospatial indexes and HyperLogLog. Go keeps its tooling and language small. He also stresses that "contrary to popular opinion, redis is not just a cache." It is a solid messaging platform, can be made highly available with replication or cluster mode, and can persist to disk.

Some context from the talk: Redis was open-sourced in 2009 and has topped the DB-Engines charts since 2013. He cites the claim that 75% of CNCF projects are written in Go.

## Which Go client should you use?

- **go-redis**: the most popular, well documented, and now under the official Redis GitHub organisation. He uses it throughout.
- **Redigo**: stable and long-lived, but its API is too loosely typed for his taste, and the deal-breaker is no Redis Cluster support.
- **rueidis**: newer, supports RESP3 features like client-side caching, and builds commands with a builder pattern that keeps type safety. Its site has benchmarks against go-redis.

## What do the basics look like in go-redis?

Connect with `NewClient`, then issue a `Ping`, because creating the client does not open a connection and failing fast is good practice. Strings use `Set` and `Get`, with an optional TTL after which Redis deletes the key for you. `HSet` accepts key-value pairs, a slice, a map or a struct with `redis` tags, which is the natural way to store objects. Sets get `SAdd`, `SCard` for unique counts and `SIsMember`.

Two features he urges you to try yourself. **Pipelines** batch commands into one round trip; his demo inserts a million keys. "If you do not invoke the exec function, your pipeline will not get executed." **HyperLogLog** counts unique items in near-constant space: a million fake IP addresses took about 50 MB as a set and only a fraction of a megabyte with `PFAdd`.

## What do the demos show?

**Worker queue on lists.** A producer registers fake users and workers send welcome emails to a mock SMTP server, using a Go library that speaks the Celery protocol over a Redis list. Start a second worker and the jobs spread across both automatically. Inside `redis-cli` you can see the `celery` list (139 tasks at that moment) and base64-decode a JSON task payload.

**Chat with pub/sub and WebSocket.** Each gorilla/websocket connection is mapped to a username. Incoming messages are published to a Redis channel, and a broadcaster goroutine subscribed to that channel pushes each message to every connected user. Redis absorbs the fan-out that makes stateful WebSocket servers hard to scale.

## What goes wrong in production?

- **Wrong connection mode.** Standalone, cluster and Sentinel need different constructors (`NewClient`, `NewClusterClient`). go-redis v9 also offers a universal client. Some providers hide the mismatch behind a generic error.
- **Networking.** With Amazon ElastiCache, nodes live in a VPC, so Lambda, EKS or ECS clients need the right VPC and security group setup. Read your provider's docs.
- **Scaling.** Redis is in-memory and single-threaded, so more RAM helps and more cores barely do. Add replicas for read-heavy loads. Write-heavy loads need Redis Cluster with more shards, since each shard has one primary that takes writes.
- **Idle replicas.** Cluster clients route reads to primaries by default, so new replicas will "sit idle, believe it or not." In go-redis set `ReadOnly`, or `RouteByLatency` or `RouteRandomly`, which enable it too.
- **Hash slots.** Redis Cluster has 16,384 slots, and multi-key operations fail across slots. Hashtags like `{customer42}` force related keys into one slot.
- **Sharded pub/sub**, added in Redis 7, scales pub/sub in a cluster with the same hashtag trick. `ForEachShard` and `ForEachMaster` fan bulk operations out across goroutines.

## Who should watch?

Go developers starting with Redis, and teams that already run it and want a checklist for cluster mode. Seasoned Redis operators will know most of the gotchas, but the go-redis specifics are handy.

Title: Quality gates are a speed feature, not a checklist
Description: Craig Risi (REPL Group, Part of Accenture) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023 on automated quality gates that let CI pipelines say no fast
Body:
Most teams treat quality control as the slow bit at the end of a sprint, where testers get two days to do two weeks of work. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023, Craig Risi, QA Architect and Senior Manager at REPL Group, Part of Accenture, argued the opposite: move those checks into the CI/CD pipeline as automated quality gates, and they stop slowing you down and start speeding you up.

Risi, who also wrote the book Quality by Design, spends a good third of the talk on software design before he touches a pipeline. That is deliberate, and it is the part most CI talks skip.

## What is a quality gate, in pipeline terms?

He describes it as a change control with entry and exit criteria: a stage is not allowed to pass the ball to the next stage until certain measures are met. The twist is that nobody signs it off by hand. "What I want to talk about now is really something that can actually be driven by your CI CD pipelines," Craig Risi said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023.

His reasons for bothering: acceptance criteria get measured automatically, the shift-left mindset gets enforced rather than preached, and the late-cycle crunch shrinks because fewer defects reach the testers in the first place. He also likes gates for the boring human failure: a known major bug forgotten on release day.

## Why does he start with architecture?

Because you cannot gate what you cannot test. His building blocks come before any YAML: clear completion criteria, a testable architecture, a strong unit test base, automated integration tests, and small, frequent releases. His rule of thumb for testability is pointed. If you can't write unit tests that get a part of the system to 90 to 100% code coverage, there's a good chance the design needs rethinking.

He also pushes testers away from the instinct to test everything end to end. Long cross-service tests are slow and flaky, which is exactly what you don't want in a pipeline. Instead, isolate one system (its service, its database) and mock the dependencies, so teams working on system one and system two get fast feedback independently.

## What should the gates actually check?

His list of checks: build health, infrastructure health, test results, code coverage, security scans, service performance, and incident and issue management. The gate types follow the pipeline: setup and checkout, build, unit and CI tests, static analysis, environment readiness, pre- and post-deployment checks, automated integration tests, dynamic code analysis and non-functional tests.

A few of his concrete targets and opinions:

- **100% unit test pass rate with 90% code coverage**, counting statement, branch and decision coverage, not just one of them. Coverage is a poor metric only when used alone, he argues.
- **Security scans from the first commit.** He describes projects that added scanning three or four months in and found big failures in code written at the very start.
- **Service performance in unit tests.** A test that used to finish in milliseconds and now takes 10 to 20 seconds is a gate failure, not a curiosity.
- **Smoke tests right after deployment.** If the basic checks fail, don't run the rest; downstream results will be noisy anyway.
- **Load tests rarely.** He would not run load tests on every pipeline run, because loading a shared system disrupts other teams; run them for big changes.
- **Issue tracker as a gate.** With traceability in place, a major open bug against code in the release can stop the deployment.

## What does it look like in code?

The examples are in Azure DevOps YAML, though he says the same works in GitLab or Jenkins. Pre-deploy jobs run shell scripts that check the server and database are up; post-deploy jobs run smoke tests. A coverage task uses Cobertura with a target of 90 and a required pass rate of 100, and a scan step reads the critical, high, medium and low findings and stops the build if anything severe appears. His point is that the YAML is the easy bit; getting the processes and test design right is the work.

## And after the gate fails?

The closing section is about observability for the pipeline itself. Unit test output, integration results, scan reports and performance data usually land in different places. Collect them into one location through APIs, add alerting and dashboards, and you can ask useful questions, such as which gate failed most often across a thousand pipeline runs this month, and whether the gate is too strict or the team is doing something wrong. Keep a data retention policy too; years of CI data are rarely worth keeping.

## Who should watch

QA leads and developers building their first serious pipeline, and SREs who inherit pipelines that pass everything. It is a broad overview rather than a close study of any one tool, and it is honest about legacy systems: gates still work on big applications, they just look different.

Title: GPT reads your Azure AD logs so the analyst doesn't have to
Description: Clay Langston (oak9) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023 on few-shot prompts, regex drafts and a Kibana plugin that summarises raw log events with GPT
Body:
A raw Azure AD event that says a user was disabled is technically readable, if you have spent a few years staring at Azure logs. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023, Clay Langston, Security Engineer at oak9, showed how to hand that event to GPT and get back a sentence an analyst understands at a glance, and how to wire the trick into Kibana so it happens on every log.

It is a short, practical talk recorded in spring 2023, in the GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 era, and the advice on prompts, parameters and privacy has aged better than the model list.

## What is an LLM actually good at in a log pipeline?

Langston starts by lowering expectations. A large language model generates likely strings that follow an input string. "It's important to note that these are not magic, they are not self aware," he said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2023. Likely is not the same as accurate, so he puts LLMs in workflows where a human reviews the output, and he is blunt that better prompts give dramatically better results.

Then comes the claim the whole talk hangs on: "Where GPT really shines is summarizing large amounts of data into something human readable." Field extraction and regex writing are useful side quests; summarisation is where the model earns its tokens.

## Why does one example beat a long instruction?

The prompt section is a clean demo of single-shot versus few-shot. Asked for a list of characters from Dune as usernames (first initial plus surname), the model returns something that only loosely matches. Add one worked example, Paul Atreides becomes patreides, and the list snaps into the right format.

He applies the same move to logs. Give GPT a raw log event plus a handful of fields and values you want extracted, and it fills in the rest of the fields. Ask it to write regexes for each field and the results are mixed, but, in his words, a great jumping-off point for building your own extractions. Nobody should paste those regexes into production unread; everybody should enjoy not writing the first draft.

For volume, he points at OpenAI fine-tuning: a tuned model is "many shot", trained on more examples than fit in a prompt. That gives higher quality results and cuts cost, because you stop paying for the same examples inside every prompt.

## How do you get it into Kibana?

Kibana plugins are written in TypeScript, and Elastic publishes a template plugin on GitHub (elastic/template-kibana-plugin), so Langston built on that and added the OpenAI API calls. The plugin takes the original log event, asks GPT for a description and stores it next to the event. The Azure AD example came back naming the directory service the log came from, converting the timestamp into something readable, and saying who the acting user was, who the target was and how the operation ended.

Two caveats come with the plugin. The token limit counts what you send plus what comes back, so a fat raw event may not fit: trim it to what is necessary. And raw events carry client IDs and usernames you may not want to ship to a third party: find and replace sensitive data before the call.

## Which knobs matter?

He walks through the OpenAI parameters, most of which have equivalents in other LLM APIs:

- **Temperature** (0 to 2): keep it low where determinism matters, such as field extraction and regexes; raise it for human-readable summaries.
- **Top P**: restricts answers to the most probable slice, 0.1 being the top 10%. Tune either Top P or temperature, not both.
- **Frequency and presence penalties**: less repetition, more new topics.
- **Model**: at recording time he recommended GPT-3.5 Turbo for bulk log work because it is capable and cheap, GPT-4 for summaries that need real sophistication, and the 32K-context GPT-4 for very large log files.

## What about the data you are sending?

The closing section is the one security engineers will nod along to. OpenAI said API content was not used to train new models, but it did not say logs or other properties of the requests were not retained. Sending keys, secrets, client IDs or usernames to a third party is always a risk. If that is a deal breaker, his suggestion is Stability AI's open source models running on your own hardware.

## Who should watch

SREs and SOC analysts who live in ELK and want a weekend project that makes raw events readable, and anyone writing their first log-summarisation prompt. Skip it if you want benchmarks or a production rollout story; this is a well-scoped how-to, not a case study.

Title: Keep your Postgres, put a stateless sharding proxy on Kubernetes
Description: Trista Pan (SphereEx) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on turning existing PostgreSQL or MySQL into a distributed database with Apache ShardingSphere on Kubernetes
Body:
The usual answer to an overloaded Postgres is a migration to a new distributed database. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Trista Pan, co-founder and CTO of SphereEx and a PMC member of Apache ShardingSphere, argues for a cheaper route: keep your PostgreSQL or MySQL instances as the storage layer, and add a stateless computing layer, ShardingSphere-Proxy, that runs where Kubernetes is actually good, with stateless pods.

Honest scope: there is no Go code in this one. It is an architecture talk aimed at whoever owns the database your Go services talk to.

## Why are databases awkward on Kubernetes?

Kubernetes was built for stateless services. Databases add data persistence, primary/replica state management, and backup and restore to a point in time. These come on top of the monitoring, HA, deployment, scaling and security that every workload needs. Vendors who run their distributed databases on Kubernetes lean on PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims and StorageClasses, StatefulSets and pod identity. It works, but it is the hard way.

Trista Pan said at Conf42 Golang 2023 that "Kubernetes currently is not so good to help you manage the stateful databases," and the rest of the design follows from that sentence.

## What is the trick?

Split the database the way distributed systems already do. She points to the high-level designs of systems like MongoDB and CockroachDB: computing nodes route and process queries, storage nodes persist data. If you accept that model, your existing Postgres or MySQL cluster can be the storage nodes, and you only need to add global computing nodes on top.

ShardingSphere-Proxy is that computing layer. It is stateless, so it belongs in Kubernetes. For storage you have two options: run PostgreSQL in the cluster too, or, as she recommends, keep using managed RDS from your cloud and point the proxy at it. Applications connect to the proxy with their standard database driver and see a single logical database, whatever language they are written in.

The benefits on her list: keep the databases you already run, upgrade to a distributed setup at low cost, gain SQL audit, traffic governance and elastic scaling, sidestep the stateful-on-Kubernetes headache, deploy out of the box, and avoid lock-in.

## What is Apache ShardingSphere?

An Apache top-level project, open source for five or six years at the time of the talk, whose own tagline is to "Transfer any monolithic databases into a distributed one." It comes in two forms. ShardingSphere-JDBC is a Java driver embedded in the application. ShardingSphere-Proxy is a standalone database proxy for any language, including Go. Either way you get data sharding, read/write splitting, distributed transactions, data encryption and masking, SQL audit and firewall rules, and elastic scale-out across MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server.

## How does a sharded query actually run?

You define tables with DistSQL, ShardingSphere's SQL dialect: instead of a plain `CREATE TABLE` you declare a sharding table rule. In her example the logical table `t_user` is backed by four physical tables spread across two PostgreSQL clusters, each with a primary and a replica. The application sees one table.

When a query arrives, the proxy works out which instances hold the rows, sends the query to one or more of them, and merges the partial results into the final result for the application.

## How do you deploy it?

The `apache/shardingsphere-on-cloud` repository provides Helm charts and an operator to deploy, scale in and scale out the proxy cluster. The demo, which she ran out of time to show live but documents step by step, goes like this:

1. Deploy two PostgreSQL clusters (primary plus replica) with the Bitnami Helm chart.
2. Deploy two ShardingSphere-Proxy nodes plus governance with the operator chart.
3. Register the PostgreSQL resources with the proxy.
4. Create the `t_user` sharding table.
5. Inspect the metadata.
6. Insert test data.
7. Preview the routing.
8. Run the select.

## Who should watch?

Platform and database engineers with a growing Postgres or MySQL fleet who want sharding without a rewrite, and teams weighing whether to move databases into Kubernetes at all. Go developers looking for code should pick another talk.

Title: Count heap objects, not bytes, when Go's GC hurts your p99
Description: Nishant Roy (Pinterest) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on diagnosing Go garbage collection pressure and cutting heap objects with pprof and struct changes
Body:
If your Go service has a fine median and an ugly p99, the garbage collector is a prime suspect, and the number to watch is how many objects live on the heap, not how many bytes. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Nishant Roy, Engineering Manager for the ads serving platform at Pinterest, explains how Go's GC steals from your program under memory pressure, how to prove it is the culprit, and the changes that cut heap objects by around 20% without touching the logic.

Context for the stakes: his team's Go systems power an ad delivery business of over $2 billion a year.

## How does Go's GC end up slowing your program?

By default the collector runs whenever the heap has grown 100% since the last cycle. It uses a tricolour mark algorithm (white is collectible, black is in use, grey is undecided), which lets it run concurrently without the long stop-the-world pauses Java was famous for. It aims to use no more than 25% of available CPU.

The trouble starts when allocation outpaces cleanup. The GC then recruits your goroutines to help with marking, which keeps the heap in check and also slows your program down. Marking means scanning every object on the heap, so cost grows with the object count. Anything that escapes a function's scope, as decided by escape analysis, ends up there.

## How do you prove the GC is the problem?

Three steps. **Observe**: GC pressure shows up as high tail latency, typically p99, because collections are infrequent and only hit the last percent of requests. **Measure**: run with `GODEBUG=gctrace=1` to get a line per GC cycle with phase timings, CPU share and heap sizes before and after (he credits Ardan Labs' write-up for explaining the format). **Align**: line those cycles up against latency spikes. He ran a background goroutine that printed p90 and p99 latency at regular intervals next to the gctrace output and looked for correlation.

## Which tools show where the objects come from?

`runtime.MemStats` first. The three fields he watches are `HeapObjects` (his success metric for every optimisation), `HeapAlloc` (what triggers the next GC) and `HeapSys` (memory obtained from the OS, which is a blocking request if it keeps climbing). In his toy example a single `runtime.GC()` drops `HeapAlloc` from about 929 KB to 112 KB.

He also mentions the newer soft memory limit, which triggers GC at a heap size you choose instead of at 100% growth. Useful as a quick fix, but tuning actual heap usage gives more consistent wins.

Then pprof. Register the handler, run `go tool pprof -inuse_objects` (or `-alloc_objects`) against `/debug/pprof/heap`, and use `-http` to open the web UI. The graph view showed `bufio.NewReaderSize` responsible for about 45% of heap allocation in one example, and the flame graph makes the widest allocators obvious. In the CLI, `list` on a function gives allocations line by line.

## What actually reduces GC work?

Three levers: fewer objects on the heap, a lower allocation rate, and smaller data structures.

**Fewer long-lived objects.** Compute per-request data on demand instead of keeping it in a giant long-lived map. That costs more compute per request but trades unpredictable tail latency for predictable per-request work. Avoid nested pointers, because each referenced field becomes its own heap object. And watch strings: Nishant Roy said at Conf42 Golang 2023 that "Strings and binaries are treated as pointers under the hood."

That last point is his best example. A catalog map keyed by a string that encoded product ID and seller ID was switched to a struct key holding the two IDs. Total objects in the profile went from 132 million to 106 million, about 26 million fewer and roughly 20% of the heap. "So we didn't actually change that much, we just changed how we're representing the exact same data."

**Lower allocation rate.** Object pools help with bursts of short-lived objects, with two warnings: the GC will not clean the pool for you, so misuse leaks memory, and objects returned unsanitised can leak one user's personal data into another user's request. Use them last.

**Smaller structs.** Removing four unused fields shrank his example struct from 64 to 40 bytes, because unused fields still hold default values. Reordering the remaining fields to avoid alignment padding (bools together, then int32s, then the int64) took it to 24 bytes, a 62% drop per object. Go's allocator does not reorder fields for you.

## Who should watch?

Engineers running high-throughput Go services with tail latency problems, and anyone who has stared at a pprof graph without a plan. His conclusion is balanced: for most programs the Go GC needs no attention at all.

Title: TDD in Go starts with a test that is supposed to fail
Description: Mohammad Quanit (timegram) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on test-driven development with Go's testing package, httptest and table-driven tests
Body:
Most teams write the code, then the tests, then discover the edge case in production. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Mohammad Quanit, Product Engineering Manager at timegram, makes the beginner's case for flipping that order in Go, and shows the three testing styles you need to start: plain unit tests, HTTP handler tests with `httptest`, and table-driven tests. Every demo includes a deliberately failing assertion, which is the most TDD thing about it.

This is an introduction, and it says so. If you already write table-driven tests every day, skip to the frameworks and best practices at the end.

## Why bother writing tests first?

His argument is that writing the test first forces you to think like the user of the code and enumerate the cases a feature has to cover before you build it. That catches errors earlier, keeps code modular and refactorable, and cuts debugging time because you already know where the failure can hide. He also says it plainly: "TDD is not just part of merely testing mechanism." It is a way of designing software, a mental model that feels overwhelming at first and gets easier with practice on side projects.

The motivations on his list: a shorter feedback loop when requirements change (you tweak the existing test rather than writing a new one), a lower cost of change, and confidence that a shipped feature does what it should. His team at timegram had just started adopting TDD on their own product. "Test cases should be mandatory for every company," he says.

The cycle itself is the familiar one: write the test, watch it fail, write the production code, run everything, then refactor either side.

## What does the built-in testing package give you?

More than people remember. Tests live in files ending in `_test.go`, functions start with `Test` and take a `*testing.T`, and `go test` finds and runs them. `-v` shows each step, `-cover` reports coverage, and the same package runs benchmarks for performance work.

His first demo has a `HelloWorld` function and a `Sum` over a slice. The `Sum` test passes in five numbers that add up to 15 and asserts 16, so `go test -v` shows one pass and one failure reported through `t.Errorf`. He uses `t.Run` for subtests to keep cases separated.

## How do you test an HTTP handler?

With `net/http/httptest`. His service uses gorilla/mux and has a handler that returns posts from a public JSON API. The test builds a request with `http.NewRequestWithContext`, creates an `httptest.NewRecorder` (a `ResponseWriter` that records what the handler wrote), calls `ServeHTTP` on the handler, decodes the body and checks that exactly 100 posts came back. Change the expectation to 101 and the test fails with a clear message. The same approach covers status codes and specific fields.

One caveat a reviewer would raise: because the handler fetches from a live public API, this is closer to an integration test. In a real TDD loop you would stub that dependency, which is exactly what his later advice on mocks is for.

## Why do gophers love table-driven tests?

Because adding a case becomes one line. He defines a slice of structs with a description, two inputs and an expected value, loops over it with `range`, and runs each entry under `t.Run(tc.description, ...)` so every case shows up by name in the output. One plus two and three plus four pass. He adds ten plus 45 expecting 70, and the output tells you exactly which row broke and that it got 55.

## Which frameworks and practices does he recommend?

For when the standard library feels thin: Gomega for matchers, GoCheck as a richer testing library, Testify for assertions and mocks, GoMock for dedicated mocking, and Ginkgo for BDD-style specs.

His best practices: write the test before the code, keep tests small and focused, run `go test -v`, mock dependencies to simulate real behaviour, check `go test -cover`, automate tests in CI, and keep tests updated whenever requirements or library versions change.

## Who should watch?

Developers new to Go or new to TDD who want a guided tour of the standard tooling in one sitting. Experienced gophers will find little new, but it is a good link to send a junior colleague.

Title: The Go SaaS toolbox, from config file to metered Stripe bill
Description: Huseyin Babal (Kubeshop) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on the tools that take a Go SaaS from config and logging to GoReleaser, Terraform Cloud and Stripe billing
Body:
Writing the Go service is the easy 20% of a SaaS product. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Huseyin Babal, Principal Cloud Engineer at Kubeshop, walks through the other 80% with a sample quiz app called Quizzer: configuration, logging, release artifacts, linting, CI, infrastructure, secrets, DNS, TLS and, because the point is to get paid, usage-based billing with Stripe.

It is a breadth talk. Each tool gets a few minutes and one config file, which is exactly what you want when assembling a stack for the first time.

## What does the app itself need?

Start with `go mod init` against your GitHub path. For configuration he uses koanf to unmarshal a YAML file into a Go struct, with methods on the struct (a `DSN()` for the Postgres connection string, for instance). Following the twelve-factor app, every value can be overridden by an environment variable, where an underscore stands for YAML nesting, so `APP_PORT` maps to `app.port`. That is what makes the same image configurable as a Kubernetes pod.

Logging is Uber's zap, with one detail worth remembering: fast loggers buffer, so `defer logger.Sync()` before exit or you lose the last lines. Log with key-value context (which customer, which session) so you can filter in Elasticsearch or Graylog later.

In the Quizzer demo the rest is GORM with `AutoMigrate` on Postgres, Fiber for the REST endpoints, and a Prometheus metrics endpoint via `promhttp`. Wrappers around third-party libraries live in packages named after the technology plus an x, like `loggerx`.

## How do the artifacts get built?

GoReleaser does binaries and Docker images from one `.goreleaser.yml`: a build per entry point under `cmd/`, a Docker section that references builds by id, image tags templated from the Git tag, a build argument that tells one shared Dockerfile which module to copy, and `extra_files` to put the config YAML into the Docker context. It can also announce releases to Slack or Discord.

Quality checks are golangci-lint with its own YAML. In GitHub Actions the pipeline checks out code, sets up Go, runs the golangci-lint action, sets up the QEMU emulator for Docker builds, logs in to GitHub Container Registry with the repo token, and runs the GoReleaser action with `release --clean`. The workflow needs read access to contents and write access to packages. A tag produces a GitHub release and a container package.

## Where does it run?

On Kubernetes, created by Terraform Cloud connected to the repository: a workspace runs `plan` on each change, and in the demo it creates a GKE cluster and node pool once he applies. From there:

- **Argo CD** deploys the Helm chart through an `Application` resource pointing at the chart repo, version and target namespace.
- **External Secrets** syncs the database password and Stripe key from Vault, AWS or GCP secret managers into Kubernetes secrets, so nobody creates them by hand.
- **Cloudflare**, through its Terraform provider, creates the A record so customers never see the load balancer IP.
- **cert-manager** with a Let's Encrypt issuer puts TLS on the ingress, so traffic is HTTPS from Cloudflare to the service.

Huseyin Babal said at Conf42 Golang 2023: "If I have them in my code base I can easily sync everything to my production with single push or single tag."

## How does the billing work?

This is the section most Go talks skip. Stripe models it as a subscription to a plan, subscription items as line items (cost per request, cost per storage), and usage records for metered billing. Customers subscribe through a Stripe Checkout link, so payment details never touch your servers. A webhook tells you which customer picked which plan.

Your only job is metering. In Quizzer, an hourly cron job counts questions per customer and sends that number to Stripe as a usage record with the `increment` action. At the end of the billing period Stripe multiplies the total by the unit price, charges the customer and notifies them. In his words: "You do nothing if you use stripe, almost nothing."

## Who should watch?

Go developers about to launch a side project or a first SaaS product, and anyone who wants one reference stack to compare theirs against. Expect breadth over depth: the abstract mentions vulnerability scanning, but the talk does not show it.

Title: A paying SaaS in 30 days, and the code was the easy part
Description: Sam Williams (Complete Coding) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on launching a serverless SaaS on AWS in 30 days and finding paying users fast
Body:
Sam Williams gave himself 30 days to build a startup and get someone to pay for it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, the founder of Complete Coding tells how that went: a serverless app on AWS, built in days rather than months, that ended the month with 300 free users, six paying users and $140 in revenue. His conclusion is that serverless made the building the least of his problems; finding a painful problem and getting it in front of people was the real work.

This is a founder's story, not an architecture walkthrough: the talk is about scope, validation and marketing.

## Why a 30-day limit?

Williams has a list of failed startups that all went the same way: months of evenings and weekends, a launch, then a few free users and nobody paying. So he borrowed Pieter Levels' 30-day rule (Levels shipped twelve startups in twelve months) and adapted it to four challenges a year around consulting and his YouTube channel. A paying user within 30 days means the idea is worth pursuing; none means move on.

He named three challenges up front: keep the architecture simple enough that building doesn't eat the month, find a problem painful enough that people pay to fix it, and get the product in front of people, which is hard for someone who calls himself a developer through and through.

## Where did the idea come from?

LinkedIn. Creator advice says to comment on posts from five or ten creators in your niche, because their audience then sees you. Another post showed a creator spending one and a half to two hours a day writing comments, which nobody with a job can justify. Williams pasted a post into ChatGPT with a prompt to act as a software engineer and write an engaging comment, and the result, though wordy, had more depth than the canned replies other tools produced. The product became LinkedIn Power Tools.

## Validation, half done

Technical validation was easy for him: five years of serverless proof-of-concept work, prior Chrome extensions with user login, and a working ChatGPT test. Customer validation was partial. Both LinkedIn posts came from people already paid to grow accounts, and the comments under them were full of people wanting to comment more but lacking the time. What he admits he should have done is message those commenters, ask how much time they have and what they would pay, and consider selling to copywriters and ghostwriters as a B2B tool. Landing pages, presales and surveys help, but talking to the target customer matters most.

## The build: three days to an extension

The MVP was a Chrome extension that adds a button under LinkedIn posts, sends the post text to an API, and types the generated comment back into the comment box. He deliberately avoided full automation, partly to keep users from getting blocked and partly so they add their own voice. Sam Williams said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023: "So I did something a little bit cheeky. I added a fake typing speed." The comment appears word by word, people read it as it types, and they edit what doesn't sound like them.

The extension and APIs took about three days. He then recorded a demo and posted it to LinkedIn: over 17,000 views and 52 comments, some enthusiastic, some telling him to burn it with fire. A website-builder landing page turned that into a waitlist of 25 for the beta and 69 by launch. For the real site he bought a React template rather than spend the month on CSS, and for billing used Stripe with a custom webhook-driven subscription integration, which took a couple of days of business logic on top of the serverless plumbing.

## Launch, first payment, and the marketing wall

He launched on day 17. Three days later he had over 100 free users and no paying ones, until a notification one night announced the first payment. The most valuable feature after launch came from beta feedback: per-comment tone of voice, including adding a question or a quote, which drew far more replies from original posters. A month after the challenge, the product was still doing over $120 in monthly recurring revenue.

He credits two unfair advantages: years of shipping serverless MVPs, and 14,000 LinkedIn followers who happened to be exactly the target audience. That second one is also the limit, since posting to your own network doesn't scale, and SEO, ads or affiliates need more than 30 days. His next plan is a month spent only on marketing, more customer conversations, and a B2B model, because at $30 a month a consumer product needs huge numbers of users.

## Who should watch

Developers with a side-project graveyard, and anyone who thinks the infrastructure is what's stopping them from launching. Serverless gets credit for speed and pay-per-use cost when nobody shows up, but the useful parts are the validation mistakes and the scope cuts.

Title: Your internal platform has a chasm to cross, and sticks come last
Description: Omer Kahani (Snyk) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on using the technology adoption lifecycle to get R&D teams onto an internal developer platform
Body:
A platform team that ships a great tool nobody migrates to has shipped nothing. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Omer Kahani, Staff Software Engineer in the Platform Infra Group at Snyk, borrows the technology adoption lifecycle from product marketing and applies it to R&D: segment your teams into innovators, early adopters, majority and laggards, treat each group differently, and reach for mandates only after everything else.

His framing is platform as a product. Snyk's infra group is three teams that don't do company-wide ops or on-call; they build a paved path to lower cognitive load for everyone else. So the only way their work creates value is adoption, whether the change is a minor version bump of a Helm chart that provisions Postgres or a new Git branching strategy.

## Who goes first?

The model dates from 1957 and was popularised by Crossing the Chasm. Kahani's twist is mapping it onto teams rather than customers, and redoing the mapping before every migration, because teams change behaviour over time.

**Innovators** are excited by novelty and will tolerate bugs and missing docs. They become design partners: one or two teams to test assumptions with while you build. Pick teams whose applications carry little or no customer risk, and who can free time in their sprint to pair with you.

**Early adopters** still like new things but need a real problem solved. They are the group for a proof of concept just before GA, and the group that validates the onboarding guides the majority will rely on. Again: teams with trust in you and time to spare.

## The majority is where projects die

In the model the majority is about 68% of the population, and it cares about its day job, not your tool. Kahani sees two failure modes: a product that doesn't solve a problem (user research and design partners should catch that), and a migration that is too difficult. The value of any tool is reduced by the effort of adopting it, so a great product with a painful migration delivers almost nothing. Omer Kahani said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023: "Good product and low migration effort should be our goal."

Two practices from Snyk lower that effort. First, self-serve migration: when the internal deployment tooling gained new options that required every application team to change its deployment configuration, the platform team opened the pull requests for them automatically, so migrating became a review and a click on merge. Second, docs tested by someone forbidden to improvise: a team member follows the guide word by word, doing nothing that isn't written down, and every place they get stuck is a doc bug.

## Laggards usually have a reason

The classic model says laggards hate change. Kahani's version is kinder and more accurate for R&D: the last team may run a production-critical application that can't afford downtime, own a legacy system nobody fully understands, or be on the hook for a major milestone with no room to touch its deployment process. What helps them is just-in-time knowledge: pair with them, bring the migration expertise, and let them bring the application context.

## Trust first, sticks last

For the majority he adds two more levers. Trust: celebrate early adopters publicly (at Snyk, the R&D sprint demo) and make it a rule that every PoC ends with as many people as possible hearing about it. Pick early adopters that represent as many use cases and groups as possible, and recruit the people others already listen to; at Snyk those were group-level staff engineers. When the infra group set out to replace the continuous delivery system, everyone in the group had been at the company under a year, so they took their blueprints to those staff engineers early, asked where they saw problems, and used the answers to prioritise and to spot early adopters. Those engineers later turned up in Slack threads pointing people at the infra group.

Then sticks: a realistic support deadline (with two-week sprints, give four to six weeks or more so teams can plan it in) and, if needed, senior management asking teams to make time. Omer Kahani said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023: "Sticks are not excuse for not doing anything else." Done in that order, the stick lands on people who already trust the product, and frustration stays low.

## Who should watch

Platform and infra engineers with a migration on the roadmap, and engineering managers who keep being asked to mandate one. It is a short, practical talk with no tooling to install, just a framework you can apply to your next deprecation.
