Title: Build pipelines that fail like go test, not like Bash
Description: Robert Pajak (Splunk) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on goyek, a Go library for build automation compared with Make and Mage
Body:
Every Go repo has a Makefile that someone is afraid to touch. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Robert Pajak, Senior Software Engineer at Splunk and the author of goyek, runs the same three-target build (all, fmt, test) through Make, Mage and goyek, and shows why he ended up writing his own library: build tasks should read, log and debug like ordinary Go tests.

He is upfront that this is partly an advert for his project, and the comparison is fair to the alternatives.

## What is wrong with Make?

Nothing fatal. His demo Makefile has an `all` target depending on `fmt` (imported from a shared file so several repos can reuse it) and `test`, which has to run `go test` with coverage, remember the exit code in a shell variable, still produce the HTML coverage report, and only then exit with the saved code. A `help` target parses double-hash comments to print usage, and the shared file pins the shell to Bash because macOS defaults to zsh.

That is the problem in miniature. Anything beyond trivial logic sends him to the docs, old Makefiles or Stack Overflow. Debugging means printing to the console. And making one Makefile behave on Linux, macOS and Windows is hard. Meanwhile most Go programs that stick to the standard library just work everywhere, which is why some SREs he heard from write Go tools instead of shell scripts.

## Why not Mage?

Mage was the first Go-native option he found: plain exported Go functions become Makefile-like targets. Running it through a `mage.go` wrapper with `go run` even pins every developer to the same Mage version through Go modules.

His verdict: "For me, mage is too magical." Target discovery needs special build tags, which often breaks IntelliSense in VS Code or GoLand. Reusing targets from another package needs a magic import comment. Logs from concurrent targets interleave. Without verbose mode a failing build tells you almost nothing, not even which target failed. And the `sh` package has so many near-identical run functions that he never knew which one to call. He respects its community (50+ contributors, 3k+ stars) but never used it in production.

## What does goyek do differently?

"It took me one year to create initial version of Goyek," he said, and the design borrows from the standard packages every gopher already knows. Tasks are registered with `goyek.Define` much like Cobra commands, with a name, usage and dependencies. Actions receive a `*goyek.A`, which behaves like `testing.T`: `cmd.Exec` runs a shell-style command and marks the task failed on error without stopping, and there are `Skip`, `Fatal` and `Helper` methods. Flags use the `flag` package. Extensions are middlewares in the style of `net/http`.

The result feels like `go test`. A quiet run prints only the failing task and its output. A verbose run prints everything, Make style. Log lines carry file name and line number, and a function marked as a helper drops out of those locations, just as in tests. Since goyek uses no build tags, IntelliSense works, and since the pipeline is just a Go program, he sets breakpoints in VS Code and steps through a failing `go test` call live.

His bonus example adds a spell task that installs misspell, finds every Markdown file with a `filepath.WalkDir` helper and fails on a typo. goyek also dogfoods itself: its own build pipeline is written in goyek.

## So should you drop Make?

He hasn't. He still uses Make, in Go and non-Go repos alike, for simple jobs like setting up local Kubernetes clusters or validating protobufs. Make is concise and language-agnostic, and you can always call a Go program from it instead of writing complex Bash. goyek earns its place once the build has real logic, with if statements, loops and reusable pipelines shared across repositories. His own slide lists its main downside as being unpopular.

## Who should watch?

Anyone maintaining a Makefile that has grown into a Bash program, and platform teams standardising builds across many Go repositories. Even if you never adopt goyek, the critique of Mage and the go test-style output model are worth borrowing.

Title: A self-service DBaaS is a YAML file, a Git repo and an operator
Description: George Hantzaras and Dan Mckean (MongoDB) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on building a self-service DBaaS with the Atlas Kubernetes Operator and Argo CD
Body:
Every internal developer platform eventually gets the same ticket: a team needs a database, and needs it today. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, George Hantzaras, Director of Engineering for Kubernetes at MongoDB, and Dan Mckean, Senior Product Manager at MongoDB, show how to stop answering it by hand: a developer commits a short custom resource to a Git repo, Argo CD applies it to the cluster, and the MongoDB Atlas Kubernetes Operator turns it into a managed database through the Atlas API.

It is a compact talk, under half an hour, and about two-thirds of it is vendor-neutral thinking about why a database-as-a-service (DBaaS) is the hardest part of an IDP. The last third is MongoDB's own tooling, so expect Atlas to be the database in the example.

## Why build the platform on Kubernetes at all?

Their opening number comes from internaldeveloperplatform.org: 95% of internal developer platforms are built on top of Kubernetes. The reason they give is less about containers and more about extensibility. An operator extends the Kubernetes control plane with product-specific logic, paired with custom resources that describe what you want; the operator watches those resources and acts on them, from deploying an app to taking a backup or running an upgrade.

The part that matters for a DBaaS is that operators can manage things that don't live in the cluster at all. A custom resource can describe a database running in a managed cloud service, and the operator calls that service's API to make reality match. The payoff, in their words, is that external resources get "the same tooling, processes, permissions and automation" as everything else in the cluster.

## Why is the database the risky part of an IDP?

Most applications need a database, and databases are among the most complex services to deploy and run, especially on day two: upgrades, backups, resizing. That makes centralising them valuable, and also dangerous. The questions they raise are the ones platform teams actually argue about: how much configuration do you expose? Security, sizing, performance, backup, sharding and resilience are each a knob a developer can get wrong.

Their observation is that many companies settle on fairly strict templates, such as T-shirt sizes for database deployments with guidance on which size suits which use case. Troubleshooting is the other tension: least privilege says few people should hold the keys, but a central team holding all of them becomes the bottleneck. The common split they describe is loose rules in pre-prod, where developers can break things and fix them, and tight rules in production.

## Self-service, but with oversight

Dan Mckean said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023: "Self service is nearly always faster, as we haven't got to wait for someone else to become free to do what we need them to." It also frees the central team to work on support and on improving the platform instead of fulfilling requests.

They list three ways to offer it, each trading central-team effort against how much the user must know: published assets such as Helm charts that users customise themselves, a GitOps workflow with Argo CD or Flux, or a portal or marketplace that hides the complexity entirely.

## The build: YAML, Git, Argo CD, operator

The architecture has three steps: the developer defines what database the application needs, the request becomes a resource Kubernetes understands, and Kubernetes creates the deployment. With the operator alone, that resource is an `AtlasDeployment` custom resource: a name, an instance size, a cloud provider and a region, applied with `kubectl`. The operator compares desired and current state and calls the Atlas API.

That still leaves every developer holding a YAML file locally and running `kubectl` by hand, so the second half of the design moves it into GitOps. The prerequisites are an Atlas account and API key, a Kubernetes cluster with the Atlas Kubernetes Operator installed, Argo CD, a dedicated infrastructure-as-code repository and an Argo CD Application pointed at it (repo URL, revision, sync policy). From there, the flow is a pull request: merge to the watched branch, Argo CD syncs the new custom resource, the operator creates the cluster, users and databases. Code review becomes the approval process, which is a neat way to get central oversight without a ticket queue.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers designing the data layer of an IDP, and anyone weighing how much database configuration to expose to product teams. The first half applies to any database and any operator; the second half is most useful if you run MongoDB Atlas. The pattern of operator plus GitOps for external resources carries over to other managed services.

Title: Every migration lags its source, so plan the lag on purpose
Description: Sindhuja Nagarajan (Chargebee) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on a process-first playbook for data, cloud and SaaS migrations, change data capture included
Body:
A migration means running two systems at once: double the infrastructure and double the operational problems, until the old one is finally switched off. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Sindhuja Nagarajan, Data Migration and Data Engineering Lead at Chargebee, offers a process-first way to think about them. Whatever you are moving, database, cloud, application, SaaS business process or storage, the same problems come back and the same systematic answers apply.

She is upfront that it is not a deep technical talk. "This is fully process driven," Sindhuja Nagarajan said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. Think of it as a checklist from someone who has run these projects, especially business-process migrations between SaaS tools, which she calls her specialty.

## Assess first, plan next

Her first rule is to inventory before you plan. List environments, dependencies, server types and CI/CD pipelines, not just the front end and the back end. Her warning is about the small script nobody mentions that keeps something vital running: if it is not in the assessment, it will not be in the new environment either.

Then plan end to end. Moving the data and pointing the application at the new target is not the plan. The plan is how business as usual (BAU) runs on the target, which problems from the source you fix on the way, how users of every kind are onboarded and tested, and how CI/CD changes. Security and governance shape every decision, down to physically moving a storage disk. Her slides add a mantra that rings true: execution is the easiest part.

## Test in phases, then audit

Build a pipeline, transform, test, repeat. Bring in UAT and beta users, and test for every persona: database administrators, application administrators and end users, with enough data to prove the target can run BAU. For storage, test at byte level. Open the business reports and check they make sense to a layperson as well as an administrator. Then finish every migration with a post-migration audit.

## Why can't the target ever catch up?

Change data capture is, in her words, the most fundamental problem. The source keeps changing while you migrate, sometimes for months of parallel running, and you have to move that delta too. There are two main approaches:

- **Log based:** read the source's logs, reverse-engineer the changes and apply them to the target.
- **Query based:** query for changes made between the last run's timestamp and now, and copy them over.

Her honest point is that you will always lag the source; the question is how small and controlled that lag is when you cut over, minutes or seconds with minimal data loss. Many databases and cloud services ship prebuilt CDC pipelines. Your other choice is offline (stop the source, bring the target up, move the remaining delta) or online, service by service.

## Database and cloud specifics

For database migrations, her slides list three properties: complete (all specified data arrives), duplicate free (each record migrated exactly once, which matters most when you use the migration to clean up indexes or schema), and ordered (changes applied in the order they happened at the source). Plenty of ETL tools exist, from free to fully featured.

For cloud migrations she organises everything around the six Rs: rehost (lift and shift, good between equivalent cloud providers), replatform (CI/CD, automated testing, containers), repurchase (swap an old e-commerce system for a SaaS one), retain, retire and refactor. For a startup, she jokes, if you are not building in the cloud, where are you building?

One caveat: the recording ends in the middle of the six Rs, so the later sections on application, business-process and storage migrations appear only in her slides (online versus offline storage moves, encryption in transit and at rest, persona testing and audit again).

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads facing their first big migration who want a structured checklist rather than a tool tutorial. If you have already lived through a CDC cutover, you will mostly be nodding along.

Title: Debugging is broken by people and process before it is broken by tools
Description: Elinor Sapir (Rookout) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on why classroom debugging fails in the cloud and how people, process and tools fix it
Body:
If a study is right that 75% of developer time goes on solving bugs, your team has a day and a quarter a week for new code. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Elinor Sapir, Director of Solution Architecture and Partnerships at Rookout, uses that figure (credited to Coralogix) to argue that debugging deserves the attention we give to features, and that most of what holds it back is human, not technical. Her fix comes in three pillars: people, processes and tools.

It is a short talk, aimed more at engineering managers and team leads than at the person holding the debugger, and she says so by framing everything as what managers should focus on.

## Why is debugging so painful?

Sapir names three problems, drawn from working with teams from small startups to Fortune 500 companies.

**It is less fun.** Ask a room whether they would rather work on a bug or a feature and features win. "Our engineers often get less satisfaction from fixing broken things rather than creating new, shiny features," Elinor Sapir said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. Lower motivation means a slower workflow. People like new clothes more than getting old ones mended, too.

**It is stressful.** Serious bugs come with stakeholders, customer complaints and real consequences. She uses an XKCD strip where one developer asks another to look at a bug and gets back panic that it might be one of the ones proving the whole project is broken. Debugging can feel like Jenga.

**The tools do not fit.** She shows a debugging exercise that a top US engineering school gives first-year computer science students: confirm the input, step over, check the output. Fine for a local app you control. Useless for a cloud native production system you cannot recreate locally, or for code that behaves differently once it runs as a serverless function.

## People: market the bug

Her first suggestion is almost marketing. Do not hand out a bug with a defeated look; sell what is interesting about it, whether that is the challenge or the users it affects. A friend of hers prefers bugs to features because they are usually well defined, the challenge excites him, and he knows the fix matters to someone. Make the whole team own a bug rather than one unlucky developer. And create a safe space: managers should build trust with stakeholders and, when needed, keep product and business people from nagging the engineers doing the fix.

## Processes: adjust the backlog for real

When bugs come in, actually adjust the sprint commitment and the backlog, and tell everyone. Agree with the rest of the company on how bugs get prioritised; not everything needs fixing right away, and some things need not be fixed at all. And do the groundwork before a developer starts, just as nobody builds a house before the land has been surveyed: hand them all the information you have about the bug.

## Tools: a cloud native toolbox

Tools are the easiest place to see results. If your team ships serverless functions, give them a way to debug serverless functions. If a deployment takes two weeks, adding a log line and waiting two weeks for data is not a debugging strategy, so give them a way to debug live environments. Integrate the tools into daily work and train people with shared use cases, because nobody should be learning a tool at 3am while everything is on fire. Her closing rule: "Data is gold, but too much will weigh you down." Collect it where it makes sense and keep it accessible.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and team leads whose bug backlog keeps losing to the roadmap. If you want a technical walkthrough of production debugging, pair it with the hands-on talks below.

Title: One Gin router, two main.go files, a gqlgen API on AWS Lambda
Description: Durgaprasad Budhwani (Tech9) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on running one Go GraphQL codebase locally and on AWS Lambda with gqlgen, Gin and SAM
Body:
The annoying part of serverless Go is rarely the handler. It is testing it without deploying it every five minutes. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Durgaprasad Budhwani, Chief Technologist at Tech9, shows a small trick that fixes most of that: put your routes in one shared file, then give the app two entry points, one that listens on port 8080 on your laptop and one that hands the same router to AWS Lambda. On top of that he builds a GraphQL to-do API with gqlgen and DynamoDB and deploys it with AWS SAM.

## What changes when a Gin app moves to Lambda?

Less than you would think. He starts with the canonical Gin hello world, a router with one GET route that runs on `:8080`. The Lambda version imports `aws-lambda-go` and the `awslabs/aws-lambda-go-api-proxy` adapter for Gin (it also supports Fiber and Gorilla), wraps the router with `ginadapter.New`, and calls `lambda.Start` with a handler that takes an API Gateway proxy request and returns `ginLambda.ProxyWithContext(ctx, req)`.

As Durgaprasad Budhwani said at Conf42 Golang 2023: "Only a small kind of a wrapper is required when we are running this code for the AWS lambda."

The one Lambda-specific habit he stresses is where to put the setup. Router construction goes in `init`, so it runs once per execution environment instead of on every invocation, which trims cold start cost for the calls that follow.

## How do you test it without deploying?

He mentions LocalStack as the heavyweight option, then shows the lighter one, which follows AWS's own advice to keep initialisation separate from business logic. The routes live in `router.go`. A `local` main calls the router and runs Gin on 8080, so `go run` gives you a normal HTTP server. A `lambda` main builds the same router and passes it to the proxy adapter. Same code, two front doors.

## Which deploy tool?

For a proof of concept he picks AWS SAM over Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi or the CDK. `sam init` scaffolds a project, and the `template.yaml` (a CloudFormation template with SAM shortcuts) names the code path, the handler, the `go1.x` runtime and the architecture. He picks Arm over x86_64. A catch-all API event creates the API Gateway, and `sam build` plus `sam deploy` print the endpoint URL with its default `Prod` stage.

## Where does gqlgen fit?

He gives the GraphQL background briefly: built at Facebook in 2012, open-sourced in 2015, one schema that defines your models, queries for reads and mutations for writes, and resolvers in place of REST controllers. gqlgen is the schema-first Go library that generates type-safe server code from that schema.

`go run github.com/99designs/gqlgen init` scaffolds the project. The useful details are all in `gqlgen.yml`: where the `.graphqls` schema files live, where generated code and models go, and `autobind`, which tells gqlgen to reuse your existing model structs instead of generating duplicates. The generated resolvers come as stubs to fill in.

His demo stores to-dos in DynamoDB through the `dynamo` wrapper library, behind a small to-do service that adds and lists items per user. That service is injected into gqlgen's base `Resolver` struct, which is the dependency injection point gqlgen gives you. Gin serves two routes, a GET for the GraphQL playground and a POST for the query endpoint. Asking for only `text` and getting only `text` back is the GraphQL selling point in one screenshot.

## What changes for the GraphQL deploy?

Very little. The router moves into the shared file again, the local and Lambda mains stay thin, and the SAM template gains an IAM role allowing get, put, query and update on the DynamoDB table. Two events are needed, GET for the playground and POST for everything else, since "in graphql everything is mostly a post operation." He then queries the deployed API Gateway URL from a GraphQL client extension in Chrome.

## Who should watch?

Go developers about to put their first HTTP service on Lambda, and anyone curious about gqlgen's workflow. The code-sharing layout is the part to steal. The closing minutes are a pitch for Tech9, and the serverless benefits section covers ground most viewers already know.

Title: Your remote debug port is an open door, and breakpoints break prod
Description: Shai Almog (debugagent.com) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on debugging Kubernetes in production with kubectl debug, port-forwarded JDWP and developer observability
Body:
Production bugs are rarely crashes. They are the bug that only hits one user, on a Tuesday, when the moonlight meets the water at 37.5 degrees. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Shai Almog, founder of debugagent.com and author of Practical Debugging at Scale, walks the ladder of Kubernetes debugging: from `kubectl exec`, to ephemeral containers with `kubectl debug`, to JDWP over a port-forward, and finally to developer observability tools that give you breakpoints that never stop the app.

His starting point is cultural. Too many developers treat production as somebody else's problem, the ops team's universe. His view is that the product is not perfectly running unit tests; it is the thing running in production, and R&D needs to be there.

## Why not just exec into the container?

`kubectl exec` feels like a local shell, and that is the trouble. Even on staging, which he treats as the dress rehearsal for production, you should not disrupt other people. The tool you want is usually not in the image, and installing it pulls dependencies that might break the running process. Minimal images may have nothing at all, which is great for resources and miserable for "an old Unix guy" who wants strace. And when the container has crashed, there is nothing to exec into.

## Ephemeral containers: debug next to the pod, not in it

`kubectl debug` opens a prompt much like `exec`, but in an ephemeral container beside your pod, which he calls the Keyser Söze of containers. Ephemeral containers existed before, but were painful to use. You can preinstall anything, it is gone when the pod goes, and you can share the process namespace and filesystem, so you can look into a crashed container without touching it. You can also pick your own base image: debug an Alpine container from Ubuntu, or use KoolKits, the batteries-included debug image he helped launch while at Lightrun.

## The problem with JDWP

For a JVM app, the classic next step is a debugger. That means restarting the process with debugging enabled, which you may not be able to do, and then working in the command-line JDB. He has written Java since the first beta and had never used JDB before; he likes GUIs.

So he exposes JDWP the safer way: `kubectl port-forward` to tunnel the remote debug port to localhost (the Kubernetes equivalent of an SSH tunnel), then a stock IntelliJ IDEA remote-debug configuration on port 5005. It feels exactly like a local debugger. And it is still not fit for production:

- You need that restart, and you cannot leave JDWP running. "If we open the server to remote access with JDWP, we might as well hand the keys to the office to hackers," Shai Almog said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023.
- Breakpoints stop threads, which no cloud workload likes. He retells a story, possibly an urban legend, of a rail system that fell into the ocean while its engineer sat on a breakpoint.
- Stability: an expensive or wrong breakpoint condition, or even loading a watch variable, can take down the app.
- Privacy: a breakpoint on the login path can read user credentials, and because everything is writable you can raise your own permissions by setting a variable.

Then multiply it by Kubernetes scale, where your code is a tiny box in a huge architecture running in places you cannot name.

## Observability is the new debugging, mostly

Observability fills the gap, with two caveats. Cost: he says logs alone can be 30% or more of total cloud spend, which is not what the cloud promised. And most of it is built for ops. It tells you an endpoint is unhappy, not which line of code or why one specific user sees stale data after a cache flush. His fix is organisational too: vertical teams with SREs embedded, developers reading production logs, and shifting both left and right.

## Breakpoints that don't break

Developer observability tools work in developer terms, source files and line numbers. He demos Lightrun, his former employer, saying he no longer works there and that other tools exist. From IntelliJ he adds a log line to a running prime-counting service without a restart; it lands in order with the existing logs and can be shipped to Elastic. Tags apply actions to groups of servers (500 of 1,000 tagged production), and developers never get direct access to the production machine because everything goes through a management server. Expressions are read-only, and when a log eats too much CPU the agent throttles it for a while.

Snapshots are breakpoints that do not stop: stack and variables, with conditions. His best example is a conditional snapshot on one user ID, set with a one-week timeout, so you can go home and come back when that user reproduces the bug. Counter metrics count how often a line runs, which is the number you want before deprecating an API.

## Who should watch

Java and Kubernetes developers who still SSH in to debug, and SREs who want developers sharing the production load. It is a broad tour, and the last third is a product demo.

Title: Observability eats 20-30% of the cloud bill, eBPF wants it back
Description: Shahar Azulay (groundcover) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on eBPF observability for Kubernetes, collected out of band and processed where the data lives
Body:
Observability now costs teams something like 20 to 30% of what they pay their cloud provider, a figure his slides credit to Charity Majors of Honeycomb. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Shahar Azulay, co-founder and CEO of groundcover, argues that the cause is architectural: SDK instrumentation tied to the dev cycle, raw data shipped to a vendor, and pricing by volume. His proposed fix is eBPF, collecting data out of band from the kernel and boiling it down on the node before anything is stored.

It is a vendor talk, and the second half is groundcover's design, but the diagnosis is worth hearing whichever tool you run.

## How did observability get this expensive?

"That's unheard of, and I think most teams are even not aware of it," Shahar Azulay said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 about that 20-30% figure. Worse than the size is the unpredictability. Volume-based pricing assumes you know how many log lines and gigabytes you will ingest next month, and one engineer's cardinality mistake can raise the bill by 30%.

Cloud native made it worse. He cites an O'Reilly report showing observability data growing faster than business data, and a 2022 Kong survey putting the average company at 184 microservices. Following one customer request now means tracing dozens of components, each producing its own logs and spans.

## Why the dev cycle is the bottleneck

Observability was designed to be part of development: developers add an SDK, decide what to measure, and build their dashboards. That works for one team. In a company where the data science team writes Python, the web team Node.js and the backend Go, nobody is asking whether all that data is needed, and the SRE who gets woken up at night cannot force a team maintaining legacy code to instrument it. Blind spots and surprise costs follow.

He adds two more problems with legacy tools: harder organisational alignment, and privacy, since logs and traces that may contain PII leave your Kubernetes cluster for the vendor's storage. Adoption shows the gap: a DevOps Pulse 2022 survey on his slides has 67% of teams on logs, against 22% using APM.

## What eBPF changes

eBPF runs sandboxed programs inside the Linux kernel. Azulay quotes Brendan Gregg's comparison: eBPF does to Linux what JavaScript does to HTML. Instead of waiting years for a feature to go through the kernel community and into distributions, you load a program from user space, the verifier checks it is bounded and safe, it is JIT-compiled to machine code, and maps carry data back to user space. BPF dates to 1993, eBPF to 2014 (the year Kubernetes was born), and kernel 4.14 in 2017 is where the observability features matured.

Why bother with the kernel? Efficiency, compared with SDK overhead that is hard to even measure. Safety, since the program cannot crash your application the way a bad SDK or kernel module can. And coverage: a Kubernetes node can host 150 containers, and eBPF sees all of them out of band without touching a single runtime or image. That hands the SRE a uniform approach they can roll out alone, without convincing every team first.

## Process the data where it lives

His second target is the centralised architecture: ship everything to the vendor, let it compute insights there. It brings random sampling (keep half a percent, and hope the one-in-10,000 bug is in it), raw storage (why store every span just so the vendor can compute a P50 latency?), and rigid collection that records the same detail for 10,000 healthy 200s as for one 500.

groundcover's answer is span-based metrics computed in the eBPF agent on the host, plus variant-depth capturing: full payload and logs for a failed request, CPU usage and other requests to the server for a P95 latency event, and about a 1% sample of normal traffic. Data is stored in your own cloud account, while groundcover runs the control plane and the UI as SaaS, so logs and traces never leave your environment.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform leads staring at an APM invoice, and anyone who wants a quick primer on why eBPF matters for observability. Expect a product pitch at the end, and no code.

Title: Rust has no Lambda runtime, so ship your own inside the binary
Description: Luciano Mammino (fourTheorem) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on writing AWS Lambda functions in Rust with Cargo Lambda, SAM and power tuning
Body:
AWS Lambda bills you for memory multiplied by time, and Rust is very good at using less of both. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Luciano Mammino, Senior Architect at fourTheorem, AWS Serverless Hero and co-author of Node.js Design Patterns, shows how to run Rust on Lambda even though AWS has no managed Rust runtime: you compile the runtime and your handler into one binary, and Cargo Lambda makes that nearly painless. Then he pairs it with AWS SAM for the rest of the infrastructure and with Lambda Power Tuning to find the cheapest memory setting.

## Why Rust on Lambda at all?

His argument starts with the pricing model. You pick memory, you pay memory times milliseconds, and CPU is not a separate knob: it scales with memory up to six vCPUs. His worked example, 512 MB running for the full 15-minute maximum, comes out at less than a cent. So the two dimensions you pay for are exactly the two Rust is good at, raw performance and a small memory footprint.

He also likes Rust for reasons beyond the bill: no null, an error-handling system that makes you deal with the missing value, a modern toolchain with Cargo built in, and an ecosystem he found surprisingly mature for a language first released in 2015. He has no hard benchmark for it, but in his own measurements cold starts are very good. The case is strongest for functions that run thousands or hundreds of thousands of times a day.

## How do you run Rust without a Rust runtime?

Lambda's managed runtimes cover Node.js, Python, Java, .NET, Go and Ruby. Rust goes through a custom runtime, built with the AWS Lambda Rust Runtime library. Your `main` calls `lambda_runtime::run` with your handler, so the runtime and your code end up in one process and one binary.

He is fair about the trade-off. With a managed runtime AWS patches security for you; with a custom one, applying updates means recompiling and shipping a new version yourself. In exchange you get better performance (less message passing between runtime and handler) and more control: middlewares, generic services, even a web framework embedded in the function.

## Cargo Lambda, from new to deployed

Cargo Lambda is a Cargo subcommand for creating, testing and deploying Rust functions, and its best trick is cross-compiling for Linux on ARM from Windows, macOS or Linux. ARM is generally cheaper on Lambda and can be faster. The commands map to the lifecycle: `cargo lambda new`, `watch` (a local emulator that restarts on every change), `invoke`, `build --release` and `deploy`.

The live demo scaffolds an SQS-triggered function with the event types already wired in (lambda_events, lambda_runtime, Tokio, tracing), loops over the records, logs each message ID and body as structured logs, and returns the number of messages processed. The first `invoke` with an empty payload fails to deserialise, which is Rust being Rust in the best way. A copy-pasted JSON event with curly quotes fails too, which is the web being the web. After the fix the function reports two messages processed locally, gets deployed with its role and log group created for it, and gives the same answer in the AWS console.

## SAM for everything that is not the function

Real projects need buckets, tables, permissions and more than one function, so he reaches for AWS SAM: YAML templates that transform into CloudFormation, so you keep rollbacks and change sets. With experimental features enabled, recent SAM versions build Rust functions through Cargo Lambda, so you get SAM's infrastructure and Cargo Lambda's emulator and cross-compilation together.

His full example is personal. He is from Sicily, near Mount Etna, and built a Lambda that runs every hour, pulls earthquake data for Italy and nearby, filters by distance and magnitude, and on a match emits an EventBridge event that logs it and emails him through SNS, so he can call his family straight away. The repository is public.

## Where is the memory sweet spot?

Because CPU follows memory, more memory can be cheaper if it makes the function finish much faster. You cannot work it out in advance, he says; you measure. AWS Lambda Power Tuning is a Step Functions workflow that runs your function across memory configurations and plots time against cost. In his example the sweet spot sits around 1024 MB, where execution time has dropped sharply and cost is only starting to climb.

## Is learning Rust worth it?

He does not pretend it is easy, especially coming from JavaScript or Python, and he has been learning it in his spare time for about three and a half years. His answer is still yes: "learning rust on its own, it's a good investment," Luciano Mammino said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, because it also changed how he writes Python and Node.js.

## Who should watch

Serverless developers with a hot, expensive function, and Rust developers curious about Lambda. Some of the tooling was marked experimental at the time, so check current docs before copying commands.

Title: From flag.StringVar to ten fake people in XML, one commit per slide
Description: Abhisek Pattnaik (Impelsys) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on building Go CLI apps with the standard flag package, custom values, embed and goroutines
Body:
Most Go CLI tutorials either stop at `flag.String` or jump straight to Cobra. At Conf42 Golang 2023, Abhisek Pattnaik, Senior Software Engineer at Impelsys, takes the middle road: he builds a random test data generator that writes XML plus its XSD schema using mostly the standard `flag` package, and every code step is a tagged commit in his repository that matches a slide number.

That last detail makes it a workshop you can actually follow along, rather than a talk you nod through.

## Why build CLIs in Go at all?

His pitch is short. "Go provides reliable, efficient and scalable CLI application development," he says, with a rich standard library for text, files and data, and built-in plus third-party modules for parsing arguments. A single static binary is the rest of the argument.

## How far does the standard flag package go?

Further than most people use it. He starts with `flag.StringVar` and a default of world, for the inevitable greeter, and then works through what the package already supports:

- **Typed values**: strings, ints, booleans, floats and `time.Duration` via `DurationVar`.
- **Aliases**: bind the same variable to `--name` and `-n`. The catch is that the help output lists them as two separate flags, so he brings in `rsc.io/getopt` for cleaner aliasing and usage text.
- **Help when called bare**: check `os.Args`, and if no arguments were passed, print `flag.PrintDefaults()` as if the user had typed `-h`.
- **A name for your tool**: `flag.NewFlagSet` gives the CLI a proper name in its usage output.
- **Custom types**: implement the two-method `flag.Value` interface (`String()` and `Set(string) error`) and a flag like `--address` can parse an address written as street, city, state, pin code and country straight into a struct. `flag.Func` covers the one-off case, such as pulling a number out of an arbitrary string.

The JSON example is the most practical one. An input file has an `aliases` field that is sometimes a comma-separated string and sometimes an array. A custom unmarshaller reads it as `any`, checks which shape arrived, and normalises both into a string slice, all behind a `flag.Var` so the CLI just takes `-i input.json`. He then opens the `flag` package source to show how parsing and the built-in help flags work under the hood.

## How does it turn into a data generator?

The second half builds the actual tool. A min/max random number CLI comes first, then `brianvoe/gofakeit` for realistic fake data: fill a struct with `faker.Struct`, use struct field tags as hints so a street looks like a street, or call faker functions directly. For inspecting the results he recommends `go-spew`, `valast` and `litter`.

`//go:embed` bundles a `person.schema.json` into the binary, which the tool writes out when you pass `--generate`. The layout follows convention: `cmd/` for the entry point, `internal/` for code nothing else may import, and a Makefile that builds into `bin/`.

## How does the concurrency part work?

He generates N people sequentially, then with a `sync.WaitGroup` and one goroutine per record, then with a buffered channel as a semaphore so `-c 3` caps the work at three goroutines at a time (the default is eight). It is the classic bounded-concurrency pattern, shown on a problem small enough to read in one screen.

The finale writes N records to XML with an embedded XSD alongside, refuses to overwrite existing files unless you pass `-f`, and accepts a prefilled `input.json` (scaffolded with `-g`) so fields like first and last name stay fixed while the rest is randomised.

## What should you take away?

His closing advice is the one most CLIs ignore: keep the user experience in mind and "provide clear and helpful error messages when commandline arguments are incorrect." For anything bigger than this, he points to Cobra.

## Who should watch?

Go developers who have written a `main.go` with two flags and want to know what comes next, and anyone who needs a quick fake-data generator for tests. If you already ship Cobra-based tools, the `flag.Value` and bounded-concurrency sections are still worth the time.

- Robert Pajak on [goyek, using Go for automation](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2023_Robert_Pajak_goyek_automation) instead of Makefiles.

Title: AWS CDK lets you do anything, which is exactly the problem
Description: Ran Isenberg (CyberArk) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on AWS CDK best practices from three years in production, from one stack per app to cdk-nag
Body:
AWS CDK turns infrastructure into real code, and real code can do anything, including delete your production table during a refactor. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Ran Isenberg, Principal Software Architect in CyberArk's platform engineering group and an AWS Community Builder, shares the CDK practices he collected over almost three years of taking services from development to production: one stack per application, constructs split by business domain, environment-aware configuration, cdk-nag security tests, and unit tests that guard logical IDs.

His opening story explains the enthusiasm. For the first AWS CDK Day, he and two colleagues built an audit-service proof of concept wiring IoT, Kinesis, Lambda, API Gateway, Elasticsearch and S3 together, in three days, with little prior experience of those services. Then comes the Spider-Man line, credited to "AWS Uncle Ben": with great power comes great responsibility.

## Why one stack, not several?

His default: one CDK app per business domain, one repository, one CI/CD pipeline, one owning team, and one stack. The reason is blast radius. With two stacks, a critical fix in the second one can be blocked because the first stack fails to deploy.

Split into a new app and repository only when another team will maintain it or it has become its own business domain, and do not over-split. Cross-repo features then need feature flags, and deploy-time values like an API Gateway URL have to travel through SSM or Cloud Map. Project layout is three folders, `cdk`, `service` and `tests`, because he wants infrastructure and business code owned by the same developers.

At CyberArk, the platform team turned this into a self-service CDK template project with internal training, which he says reduced the cognitive load on developers and sped up development. The open-source version is his AWS Lambda Handler Cookbook, a complete API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB service with its pipeline and tests.

## Constructs are your microservices

Do not define every resource in the stack, just as you would not write a 10,000-line function. Constructs are his micro or nanoservices, with one exception: a Lambda layer shared by several constructs can live at stack level. Platform teams can publish organisation-approved constructs as a versioned library (a Python one at CyberArk): WAF rules for API Gateway or CloudFront, SNS to SQS with encryption at rest, an AppConfig construct, a Datadog log shipper, a PII sanitizer. The catch is versioning, since an upgrade that changes a logical ID can delete a stateful resource.

How to split an app into constructs? By business domain. In his CRUD example, the API Gateway and Lambda functions own the Aurora Serverless database, while the SNS, SQS and Lambda messaging path is its own construct. Aurora still gets its own construct because it is complicated and worth sharing across the organisation.

## Configuration that knows where it is running

Jenkins injects a profile (dev, test, production) as an environment variable, and the CDK code adapts: point-in-time recovery off for an ephemeral dev DynamoDB table and on in production, removal policy destroy in dev and retain in production. Separate AWS accounts per environment shrink the blast radius of a breach.

## Least privilege, by hand

Never hard-code secrets in CDK code or config files. Keep them in your CI secret store, pass them into the stack, deploy them to Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store as encrypted strings, and let Lambda fetch them by name. Do not put secrets in Lambda environment variables.

Security defaults vary by service: new S3 objects are encrypted by default, but SNS encryption at rest is off until you turn it on. He runs cdk-nag before every deploy, synthesising the CloudFormation template and checking it against the AWS Solutions and HIPAA rule packs, so an overly permissive role or a public bucket fails the build.

His favourite example: `table.grant_read_write_data(role)` is readable, but when he only needed `GetItem` and `PutItem` it granted something like eight or ten permissions he did not need. Write inline policies against the specific table ARN instead. "I think it's going to make you a better developer since you understand Im policies better," Ran Isenberg said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023.

## Tests that catch the deletion before CloudFormation does

Renaming a construct or moving a resource changes its logical ID, so CloudFormation deletes and recreates it: fine for a Lambda, terrible for a table full of production data or a cross-account trust role. He has also seen an exception in CDK code that did not fail the deployment and quietly removed resources from the stack. His fix is CDK infrastructure unit tests that synthesise the template and assert that critical resources (the REST API, the DynamoDB table) exist with unchanged logical IDs, plus a cdk diff step in the pipeline to make changes visible, retain policies, and backups via point-in-time recovery or AWS Backup.

The closing tips: explore a new service in the console first, drop to L1 `Cfn` constructs when the higher-level ones hide a setting, tag at stack level, and resist clever abstractions in infrastructure code. He prefers more duplication if it reads more easily.

## Who should watch

Teams already shipping with CDK, especially in Python, and platform engineers building templates or shared construct libraries. It assumes you know what a construct is.

Title: A data mesh is domain-driven design for your analytics, not a product
Description: Ismael Hommani and Charles-Alban Benezech (Wescale) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on data mesh as DDD for analytics, built on AWS or GCP Dataplex
Body:
If a vendor offers you a data mesh in a box, keep your wallet closed. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Ismael Hommani and Charles-Alban Benezech of Wescale explain data mesh, the idea Zhamak Dehghani introduced in 2019, as domain-driven design applied to analytics: an answer to an organisational scaling problem, not a technical one. Then they sketch what a data domain could look like on AWS, and demo GCP Dataplex as one of the enablers.

The talk is built around a quote from Efrat Goldratt-Ashlag: "There is no sense in talking about the solution before we agree on the problem and no sense talking about the implementation steps before we agree on the solution." They follow it in that order.

## What problem does data mesh solve?

Hommani starts with the classic loop: users generate operational data in relational databases, an ETL pipeline moves it into a data warehouse, analysts mix it with third-party dimensions, and product owners turn the insights into features. Operational and analytical systems want different things: entities and consistency on one side, facts, dimensions and the broad picture of the business on the other.

He names two problems with the ETL bridge. First, the whole business domain gets poured into one warehouse, and keeping it coherent is hard. Second, coupling: the table schema becomes a contract with the pipeline, so a DBA cannot change a table that hundreds of pipelines read from. Data lakes fix the coupling (extract and load raw data, transform later) but tend to turn into a data swamp.

The deeper issue is Conway's law. Data engineering, DBA and data science teams are split by technology and talk through Jira tickets, so the data science team asks the data engineers for new dimensions that mean nothing to them in business terms. The central team becomes a bottleneck, people build it themselves, and you get shadow IT and several sources of truth. "So I would say that the problem is not really technical," Ismael Hommani said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. The tech scales; the organisation does not.

## Why domain-driven design is the key

Dehghani worked at Thoughtworks, and the speakers see no coincidence in a software design consultancy coining the term. DDD has a strategic phase (split the business domain into subdomains, agree on a ubiquitous language in a multidisciplinary team, draw bounded contexts) and a tactical one (hexagonal architecture, CQRS, event sourcing). Bounded contexts communicate through contracts such as an anti-corruption layer, an open host service and a published language, and each context has exactly one owning team, accountable for its SLAs and SLOs.

Data mesh applies the same thinking to analytics. Data domains are really data bounded contexts; the mesh's nodes are the domains and its edges are the flows between them. Inside a domain you can still run a plain ETL pipeline. On top of domain ownership come three more pillars: data as a product, a self-serve platform and federated computational governance (naming rules, API quotas, how domains talk to each other).

Their caveats are the useful part. Unlike a service mesh, you cannot install a data mesh on your cloud platform. There are enablers, but no data mesh ready solution. And if your business domain is simple, the classic ETL-centric approach is perfectly fine.

## What would it look like on AWS?

Benezech takes over for a possible implementation, and they stress the word possible. Every domain needs a catalog, a marketplace where producers publish data products with a schema, an API, a refresh frequency and the transformations to apply, so subscribers can consume them without asking the data team. Subscribers can build new products on top of existing ones, as long as that lineage is declared. An orchestrator drives the ETL stages, checks each one, updates the catalog (last refresh time, for example) and offers an admin panel for debugging stuck jobs.

His AWS sketch for one domain: catalog and orchestrator on the Serverless Framework with Lambda, API Gateway and DynamoDB; Spark on EMR for transformations; S3, Redshift or Aurora PostgreSQL as the store depending on data size and query concurrency (Redshift for large SQL workloads, Aurora when many queries run at once); and an exploration service on ECS containers rather than Lambda, because some jobs run long.

## GCP Dataplex as an enabler

Hommani closes with a GCP Dataplex demo. Dataplex is a logical layer over BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Data Catalog and IAM: a lake maps to a data domain, zones split it logically, assets (a BigQuery dataset, a storage bucket) can come from different GCP projects and arrive with technical metadata. The demo shows permissions per zone and asset, catalog search, and a business glossary with terms, relationships and a steward who owns each definition.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects being asked to do a data mesh, and developers who already know DDD and want to see how it maps to analytics. Light on code, strong on the why.

Title: Your microservices lost the database rollback, sagas buy it back
Description: Dmitry Khorev (Mero) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on the saga pattern, compensating transactions, and choosing choreography or orchestration
Body:
Split a monolith into microservices and the first thing you lose is the free rollback your database gave you. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Dmitry Khorev, Senior Software Engineer at Mero, gives a compact introduction to the saga pattern: a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event that triggers the next, with compensating transactions to undo the work when a step fails. He runs one stock-trading example through choreography and orchestration so the trade-offs are concrete rather than abstract.

It is an intro talk, and says so in the title. If you already run sagas in production, this is a refresher; if you are about to split your first service off the monolith, it is a good 20 minutes.

## What breaks when the transaction crosses services?

Khorev starts with ACID and a monolith. A trading app has an order service that coordinates a fiat currency service (does the buyer have the money?), a stock service (does the seller have the shares?) and an audit service that writes one audit record per operation. In the monolith that is four writes in a single database transaction. A race condition leaves a buyer short of funds? Throw an exception, the database rolls back, nothing moved.

Now give each service its own database. The happy path still looks fine, but his failure case is the one every team eventually ships: the order service cannot reach the currency service, the stock service goes ahead anyway, the audit service logs the stock movement, and the shares changed hands while no money did. As he puts it, transactions within a single service are usually ACID, "but cross service data consistency requires a cross service transaction management strategy."

## Sagas trade rollback for compensation

A saga is that strategy. Each service commits its own local transaction and publishes a message or event. When a step fails, the saga runs compensating transactions that counteract the earlier steps. In his example the stock service rejects the transfer, the audit service marks the earlier logs as rejected, the currency service writes a reverse transfer between the two accounts, and the order service learns the trade was fully rolled back. Nothing is deleted; new records cancel the old ones, which is also what your auditors want.

## Choreography: no boss, many listeners

In choreography, services exchange events over a shared message broker with no central controller. His event names make it readable: the order service emits `ORDER_CREATE`, the currency and stock services listen and emit `CURRENCY_TRANSFERED` and `STOCKS_TRANSFERED`, the audit service listens to everything and finally emits `ORDER_COMPLETE`. On failure the stock service emits `ORDER_CANCEL`, and everyone who already did work runs their compensation.

Pros: good for simple workflows with few participants, no extra service to run, no single point of failure. Cons: the workflow gets confusing as steps are added, participants consuming each other's events can form cyclic dependencies, and integration testing needs every service running. His events map for just four services already takes some effort to document, which is the honest warning.

## Orchestration: one service that knows the plan

In orchestration a central orchestrator tells each participant which local transaction to run, tracks the state of each task and drives recovery. In his error path the transfers succeed but the audit check fails, so the orchestrator sends `ORDER_CANCEL` to everyone who already acted, waits for confirmations, and only then tells the order service the trade is cancelled.

Pros: suits complex workflows and participants added over time, no cyclic dependencies because the orchestrator depends on the participants and not the other way round, and participants do not need to know about each other. Cons: more design work for the coordination logic, and the orchestrator is a new point of failure.

## What to get right before production

His closing checklist is short and correct. Sagas require a new way of thinking about consistency, they are hard to debug, and the complexity grows with the number of participants. Handle transient failures and make steps idempotent so retries do not double-transfer money. And add observability to track the saga workflow from day one, not after the first mystery imbalance.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers about to split a service that touches money, stock or anything else that must add up, and anyone who needs a clear diagram to explain sagas to their team.

Title: A watch mode for Golings, and the fsnotify events that went missing
Description: Lais Lima (Globo) at Conf42 Golang 2023 on building an interactive watch mode for the Golings CLI as her first open source contribution
Body:
Your first open source pull request is rarely a typo fix that merges in an hour. For Lais Lima, a software engineer at Globo, it was a watch mode with an interactive prompt for Golings, a CLI that teaches Go through broken exercises you fix one by one. At Conf42 Golang 2023 she walks through how she built it with fsnotify, goroutines and an infinite loop, and the bug that cost her the most time.

It is a short, honest talk from someone shipping her first contribution, and it is better for that.

## What is Golings, and what was missing?

Golings works like Rustlings for Go. Each exercise is a Go file that does not compile or fails a check. `run` compiles an exercise and tells you whether it passes, `list` shows the exercises available, and `hint` gives you a nudge when you are stuck.

The issue she picked asked for a `watch` command: save the file you are editing and the exercise reruns automatically, while you can still type `hint` or `list` into the same terminal without stopping the watcher. Two jobs at once, which in Go means goroutines and channels.

## How do you watch a directory tree in Go?

Her watcher uses the fsnotify package, which listens to operating system file events. The first surprise: adding a directory to an fsnotify watcher does not cover its subdirectories. Golings keeps each exercise in its own folder, so a watcher on the root saw nothing. The fix was to walk the exercises tree with the `filepath` package and add every directory to the watcher individually.

From there the loop is small. Range over the watcher's events, keep only write events, and push the changed file name into a channel that the function received as a parameter.

## How does the interactive mode share the terminal?

The CLI body creates that channel, starts the watcher, and runs a goroutine that ranges over the channel and reruns the next exercise every time a file name arrives. Because the watcher lives in its own goroutine, the main flow is free for the prompt: a `bufio` reader calling `ReadString` until the user presses Enter, inside an infinite loop, with a `switch` that maps `list`, `hint` and quit to their commands.

It is a good minimal pattern for any developer tool that needs to react to file changes and keyboard input at the same time.

## Which parts were actually hard?

She lists three, and only one is technical.

**Understanding the issue.** She first read it as a request for flags after `watch`, as in a CLI flag that switches modes. It only clicked when the maintainer sent her a video of the same feature in Rustlings. Her lesson is about writing clear issues as much as reading them.

**Finding the time.** Between tech communities, family, content production and work, Lais Lima said at Conf42 Golang 2023 that "it took me about three months to actually finish my contribution." Coming back after a break meant forgetting what she had been thinking, so next time she plans to organise the schedule first.

**The missing events.** In a stripped-down reproduction she saved a file five times and the watcher printed one event before the program finished; in a second run, two saves printed nothing at all. Since a buffered channel should hold every value you send it, she suspected the OS notifications, her machine's M1 chip or her own code. The talk does not claim a root cause, which is refreshingly honest. Anyone who has fought editors that save via rename-and-replace, or event coalescing on macOS, will recognise the shape of the problem.

## What did she take away?

Ask for feedback early: "Maybe they can see things you're not seeing." Learn how Go actually behaves around channels and OS notifications, which her day job rarely touched. And treat open source as active learning, where you read up on something and immediately apply it.

## Who should watch?

Go beginners, and anyone sitting on their first open source contribution and wondering whether it is worth the effort. Experienced gophers will get the fsnotify subdirectory gotcha and a clean watcher-plus-prompt pattern in a few minutes.

Title: Twenty-five years of HTTP caching RFCs, and the two that matter now
Description: Sylvain Combraque at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on HTTP caching from RFC 2616 to ESI, Cache-Status and targeted Cache-Control headers
Body:
Most teams treat Cache-Control as a header they copy from Stack Overflow and never read again. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Sylvain Combraque, a freelance Go architect, creator of the Souin HTTP cache and maintainer of its Caddy cache module, walks through the history of HTTP caching standards, from HTTP/1.1 in 1999 to the two RFCs Mark Nottingham published in June 2022, with a live Edge Side Includes demo in the middle. The takeaway: the newest headers finally let each cache layer in your stack get its own instructions and tell you what it did.

He apologises up front for his accent ("I'm also a french baguette, so sorry for my baguette accent," Sylvain Combraque said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023), then spends 30 minutes being very precise about headers.

## Why did HTTP/1.1 need to standardise caching at all?

Before 1999, HTTP/1.0 left most of the behaviour to providers, so each CDN and proxy did things its own way and supporting all of them was painful. RFC 2616 (HTTP/1.1, released the same month as The Matrix, he notes) defined the grammar of requests, responses and headers, and made the first attempt at standard caching. Its caching section opens with a line he clearly likes: "Caching would be useless if it didn't significantly improve performances."

He extends it for today: if your cache server is slower, more energy hungry or more expensive than your upstream, you may not need it either.

## The Cache-Control directives, request versus response

The most useful part for practitioners is the tour of directives and how they mean different things depending on context:

- `no-cache`, `no-store`, `max-age` and `no-transform` work on both sides. `no-transform` means the cache must not add or strip headers or gzip the body.
- Request-only: `max-stale` (accept a stale response up to x seconds stale), `min-fresh` (he admits he has no use case for it) and `only-if-cached`.
- Response-only: `public` versus `private` (shared caches versus the browser), `must-revalidate`, `proxy-revalidate` and `s-maxage` for shared caches.
- `cache-extension`, which lets a cache system define its own custom directives.

He also digs up the forgotten `Warning` header, which let a cache return a stale response with a warning attached. He only learned it existed by reading the RFC, and suspects most applications have never sent it.

## Edge Side Includes still earns its keep

ESI dates from 2001 and was never a ratified RFC, yet most CDNs and cache servers support it. The idea: cache a page as a template and fetch only the dynamic fragments. An article page is served from cache, the ESI processor finds an `esi:include` pointing at a dynamic user fragment, fetches it from upstream and splices it in. The browser never sees the tags. He covers `alt` fallbacks, `onerror="continue"`, `esi:try` / `attempt` / `except` blocks, comments, and variables pulled from cookies, host and path.

The demo runs Caddy as the proxy with his ESI module built from source, serving a page that exercises every tag. It fails once, he blames the demo effect, finds the wrong port, and it works on the retry, which is the most honest live demo genre there is.

## RFC 7234: Age and invalidation

The 2014 HTTP/1.1 caching RFC replaced the earlier rules with more detail. It added the `Age` response header (how many seconds the response has been stored) and spelled out invalidation: cache a `GET /books/1`, and a `PUT`, `POST` or `DELETE` on the same resource must invalidate it. He also covers `stale-while-revalidate`, which serves the stale copy while refreshing in the background, so clients still get data when the upstream is down.

## Cache-Status and targeted Cache-Control

The two 2022 RFCs are why the talk is worth watching now. Cache-Status gives each cache in the chain a standard way to report what it did: `hit`, `fwd` (forwarded, with a reason), `fwd-status`, `ttl`, `collapsed`, `key` and `detail` (for example, storage unreachable). He notes that the `Age` header plus the `ttl` should equal the storage duration.

Targeted Cache-Control solves layered caching. Picture client, CDN, Varnish, Caddy, upstream. The upstream sends `Cache-Control`, `CDN-Cache-Control`, a Varnish-specific and a Caddy-specific header, each with its own duration: Caddy keeps the response for an hour, Varnish for five minutes, the CDN for two minutes, and the browser stores it but must revalidate because of `no-cache`. A cache that does not recognise its targeted header falls back to plain `Cache-Control`.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers running more than one cache layer, and anyone who has debugged a stale response by deleting things until it went away. It is a standards walkthrough with one demo, not a tuning guide.

Title: Stop tossing webhooks at ServiceNow - an observable ITSM framework
Description: Matt Morris (RapDev.io) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on rich two-way observability-ITSM integrations, shown with Honeycomb and ServiceNow
Body:
The standard integration between an observability tool and an ITSM tool is a webhook that turns an alert into a ticket, which is DevOps' old toss-it-over-the-wall problem wearing a new badge. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Matt Morris, Principal Solutions Engineer at RapDev.io, proposed what these integrations should do instead, a checklist he calls the Observable ITSM Framework, and demoed his own Honeycomb-to-ServiceNow integration doing most of it.

He anticipates the eye-roll at the word ITSM in his first minute. The talk earns the patience.

## Why did ITSM and observability drift apart?

Morris's backstory: Dev and Ops merged into DevOps, SRE gave it practices, workloads moved from on-prem to lift-and-shift cloud to cloud native, and monoliths became microservices. Each shift weakened a pillar of classic ITSM. Change management is no longer the toll gate before production when CI/CD ships many times a day. The CMDB's value rests on an accurate inventory, and keeping one current for ephemeral cloud resources is near impossible and hard to justify. Service maps drawn the traditional way don't fit anymore, and leadership loses the big picture.

His point is that the observability side already has the data to fix all of that; nobody is using it.

## What's wrong with today's integrations?

They are built to check a box rather than to drive outcomes. A webhook plus a little host data strips out the context, and responders end up switching between tools to work out what an incident means, where it came from and who is affected. "Observability is about context rich data. Don't listen to those people who try to tell you it's about three pillars," Matt Morris said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. Meanwhile the ITSM team stays on an island, its processes seen as red tape, and both tools leave value on the table.

## What should the integration do?

His framework, version 1.0, groups the requirements:

- **Changes and deploys.** Create change records automatically from CI/CD and show them as markers in the observability tool. Attach an SLO to a change request, and if it burns after the change, back it out. Open a change in the observability tool to see its effect on real users.
- **Service components and maps.** Create CMDB records for every entity and SLO the observability tool sees, from telemetry, auto-refreshed so they never go stale. Build maps from host attributes and parent-child relationships in traces. Setup in five minutes or less.
- **Incidents.** Create rich incidents, directly or via event management, with the affected services, entities and SLOs, plus responsible team and severity set from the alert payload by the teams who write the alerts.
- **Troubleshooting.** One click from any detected incident back to the exact view in the observability tool, and one click from a user-reported incident too.

## What does the demo show?

Setup: import an update set from his repo into ServiceNow, add a Honeycomb API key, choose whether to populate the CMDB. That is the whole install. Behind the scenes it registers alert recipients in Honeycomb and imports observed entities into the CMDB.

Then four scenes. A new microservice demo service appears in ServiceNow with a service map drawn entirely from Honeycomb telemetry, down to Kubernetes pods and nodes. An SLO burn alert, routed to an assignment group named in the alert itself, lights up the frontend node on the map, and an Open in Honeycomb button jumps straight to the affected SLO. A change request for the cart service's caching, once moved to Implement, links to a live Honeycomb query of transaction counts and a duration heatmap two hours either side of the change, scoped to the cart service. And a user-reported incident that only says the demo app is slow still gets a one-click route into Honeycomb, where a latency spike from earlier in the night shows up when you zoom out to the last 8 hours.

The user-reported case is the one most integrations skip, and it is the one that wins over service desks.

## Who should watch

SREs whose company runs ServiceNow and who are tired of tickets with no context, and ITSM leads wondering why engineers route around their processes. Expect one vendor pairing in the demo; the framework itself is tool-agnostic.

Title: Infrastructure-from-code wants your Lambda to stay unnamed
Description: Ala Shiban (Klotho) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on infrastructure-from-code: tools that infer cloud resources from app code, four ways to build them
Body:
Infrastructure as code still means somebody writes the Lambda, the API Gateway and the IAM policy by hand. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Ala Shiban, co-founder of Klotho, who previously led teams on Visual Studio at Microsoft,, mapped the state of infrastructure-from-code (IfC) in 2023: tools that read your application code, work out which cloud resources it needs, and create and maintain them for you. His short tour covers what IfC is, the four ways tools try to do it, and the nine dimensions that separate them.

## How is infrastructure-from-code different from infrastructure-as-code?

With IaC (Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, CDK) you describe the infrastructure and then wire the application to it through injected configuration or environment variables. IfC flips the direction: the application code is the input, and the tool infers the infrastructure. Shiban admits the name is not great, and his slides spell out the longer version: infrastructure, inferred, from application code.

His example is a plain Python app using the Redis SDK and FastAPI. Run an IfC tool over it and out come an API Gateway, a Lambda to run the code, an ElastiCache instance behind the Redis calls, plus the VPCs and policies that make it deployable. "Nowhere did it say Lambda," he points out, and depending on the tool you can swap the underlying technology without touching the application code. The aspiration is what he calls universal backend code: one codebase that runs on different clouds, services and architectures and adapts as requirements change.

## Why bother: the 63% problem

The pitch starts with an old joke. If you got a dollar for every tool that promised you could just focus on the business logic, you would be rich: VMs, SOA, microservices, containers, Mesos, serverless, now Kubernetes. The slides list 24 steps for moving a modest app onto Lambda, DynamoDB, SNS and then EKS, and step 14 is a cheeky note that there are so many steps you did not even notice it. Then come the follow-up requests: run it on Azure and GCP too, add multi-region, split that service in two, merge those three to save money, add gRPC.

The number behind the joke comes from Klotho's own research: "only 63% of engineering capacity in midsized companies is dedicated to feature development," Shiban said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. The rest goes on plumbing like the list above.

## Four ways to infer infrastructure

Shiban sorts the tools into four approaches, each with its catch:

- **SDK based.** Developers call a custom SDK, and the tool infers infrastructure from how the code uses it. Predictable, but the SDK is always one step behind new cloud features, and you give up the breadth of community libraries.
- **Language based.** A new cloud-centric programming language with distributed-computing constructs built in. Elegant, but developers abandon years of ecosystem expertise, and the company now hires for a language few people know. Sometimes this works out, as with TypeScript, and often it does not.
- **Annotations based.** Annotate existing code, for example marking a Node.js event emitter as pub/sub so the tool backs it with SNS, SQS or Kafka. The developer still just emits events. The cost is heavy static analysis across an exploding set of libraries, languages and clouds, and an annotation system that keeps wanting to grow into a full DSL.
- **Hybrid / framework based.** Mixes of the above, such as an SDK with some annotations.

## Nine ways to compare the tools

He then compares the 2023 players along license (open source, source available, closed), languages supported, developer interface, security (most generate least-privilege IAM policies from the dependency graph they already computed), IaC support, low-level configurability, hosting model (PaaS, self-hosted, or both), backing technologies (proprietary, preselected or adaptable), and cloud portability. The full matrix lives at klo.dev/ifc.

## What happens to the platform team?

His answer is reassuring for infra people. Platform teams keep writing organisation-specific Terraform where it matters, and run an IfC tool in the middle that translates developer code into cloud resources using their standards and enforces policy per team or technology. Developers write application code, platform teams set the rules, and the two work together while staying independent. Keep in mind it is a co-founder of one of the IfC tools giving the overview, though he spends most of the time on the category rather than on Klotho.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who want a vocabulary for the IfC tools pitching them, and developers tired of writing IAM policies. At under 20 minutes it is a quick taxonomy, not a tutorial for any single tool.

Title: Record production traffic, replay it as API tests with the DB mocked
Description: Barkatul Mujauddin (Keploy) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on turning recorded API calls into tests, with database responses captured as mocks
Body:
Record-and-replay testing sounds like free coverage until the replayed request asks for a user who doesn't exist in your test database. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Barkatul Mujauddin, DevRel Intern at Keploy, walked through why plain record-replay is expensive and flaky, how capturing the database's answers alongside each request fixes the state problem, and demoed Keploy doing exactly that for a Java app on Postgres.

Honest scope: the abstract promises a broad tour of API testing types and test-writing tips, but the talk is mostly one approach, record-replay with dependency mocking, followed by a demo of the speaker's company's open source tool.

## Why do teams under-test their APIs?

His diagnosis is short: strict timelines. Limited time means limited testing, which means regressions. What would actually help is three things: real-world functional tests, tests that are easy to create and update without hand-writing them, and test infrastructure that sets itself up.

## Why does plain record-replay hurt?

The classic version: capture user traffic hitting version 1 in production, set up a shadow or snapshot database in a non-production environment, replay the traffic against version 2 and compare responses. The upsides he credits are real. It is low code, coverage is high because you exercise every flow users actually take, and you discover user flows nobody coded for on purpose.

The downsides are why few teams keep it running. Snapshot databases are expensive and need regular refreshes, the comparison layer is work, and the dependency state (databases, internal and external APIs) makes tests flaky. That makes it, in his words, fine for load and stress testing but "not suitable for functional testing", Barkatul Mujauddin said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023: when one API breaks, many recorded calls fail and you debug each one. Writes are tricky too.

## The fix is a virtual database

The step he proposes: if you are already recording API requests and responses, record the database queries and their responses too, and package them with the test case. His example is a `getGames` call for user Thomson that returns cricket, volleyball, carrom and boxing in production. Replay it in a test environment where Thomson doesn't exist and the app answers that the user was not found. Replay it with the captured MongoDB response served as a mock and you get the same four sports, every time.

That trade has its own costs, which he lists: you need support for every kind of dependency your app talks to, and the mocks are brittle when your API schema changes, so you re-record. In return you don't replicate a whole database, and storing just the query data is cheap.

## What does the demo show?

Keploy, as he describes it, converts API calls into test cases, mocks external dependencies automatically and detects noise. The demo uses a Java employee-management sample doing CRUD against Postgres:

1. Add the Keploy dependency and middleware, download the agent JAR from Maven Central and pass it as a `-javaagent` VM option.
2. Set the Keploy mode environment variable to record, with denoise on so timestamps and random values don't break comparisons.
3. Make a POST to add an employee and a GET to fetch it; each produces a test case with request, response and the captured Postgres query as a mock.
4. Switch to test mode and run: both pass.
5. Break the code by changing the queried field from the first name to `name`, stop Postgres entirely, and run again. The tests still run without the database, because the mocks stand in for it, and one fails with a null first name, which is exactly the regression you want caught.

That last step is the best minute of the talk.

## Who should watch

Backend developers who have no API regression suite and no time to write one, and teams who tried snapshot-database replay and gave up. If you want a survey of contract testing, fuzzing or test design, this isn't it.
