Title: Ballerina makes the network and JSON part of the language
Description: Anupama Pathirage (WSO2) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on Ballerina, a language where services, clients, JSON and code-to-cloud artifacts are built in
Body:
Most backend code is plumbing: call an endpoint, bind its JSON to a struct, reshape it, call another endpoint. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Anupama Pathirage, Director of Engineering at WSO2, presented Ballerina, an open source language designed around that plumbing, where services, clients, JSON and XML, transactions and even the deployment artifacts are language features rather than libraries.

It is an overview of the language by the team that builds it, so expect breadth over depth, and a short mention of WSO2's Choreo platform at the end.

## What problem is a new language solving?

Her framing: we went from mainframes to client-server to the cloud, and the unit we think in moved from libraries to APIs. Every backend now talks to many systems over many protocols and data formats. On one side sit integration products such as ESBs and BPM tools, powerful but not very cloud native. On the other sit general-purpose languages and frameworks, flexible but without the right abstractions for this domain. Ballerina aims for the middle.

WSO2 had watched integration developers hit the same walls since around 2010, started the language in 2016, shipped the first version in 2019 and the Swan Lake major version in 2022. The syntax is C-family and should feel familiar.

## Data oriented, not object oriented

Pathirage calls Ballerina data oriented. The argument: we used to ship code over the network in RPC style and stopped for security reasons, so now we move data, and the language should make that data easy to model, access and transform. JSON and XML are built-in types alongside string and int, and there is a language-integrated query syntax that looks like SQL for filtering and reshaping data that arrives from the wire.

The type system doubles as a schema language. When an HTTP client call returns JSON, you bind it directly to a record type you defined, with no explicit casting or mapping code; the slides compare it most closely to TypeScript, where data binding is just a type cast.

## Services and clients are keywords

A service is a first-class construct, and what kind of service it is depends on the listener you attach. Attach an HTTP listener and you write resource functions named after HTTP methods (`get`, `post`) plus a path; the listener handles the network details and converts your return values. RPC-style services such as gRPC use remote methods instead. Clients are a language concept too, for gRPC, WebSocket, GraphQL and more, so calling an endpoint and binding the response is a line or two.

Concurrency comes through asynchronous calls, workers and strands (logical threads multitasked cooperatively), with compile-time checks on mutability to catch concurrency bugs before runtime. Transactions get their own syntax that delimits the atomic block.

## The diagram is the code

The feature that gets the most airtime is graphical parity. Every program has an automatically generated sequence diagram in the VS Code plugin, with vertical lines for workers and endpoints and horizontal lines for the calls between them. Her example program pulls from GitHub and writes to Google Sheets. The diagram is editable, and edits generate code, so the two stay in sync. There are also architecture views for multi-component apps and a drag-and-drop data mapper for converting large payloads between types.

## Observability and code-to-cloud

"Every ballerina program is automatically observable by any open telemetry tool," Anupama Pathirage said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, covering metrics (Prometheus, Grafana), tracing (Jaeger) and logging, switched on or off rather than wired up.

For deployment, `bal build` with the cloud option generates Docker and Kubernetes artifacts from the code itself (Dockerfiles, deployment and service YAML), with `Cloud.toml` to tune values such as memory. That removes a hand-off between developers and deployment engineers.

## Is it a JVM language?

Today the compiler is written in Java and emits JVM bytecode, which gives you Java interop. But the semantics were designed to be independent of Java and the JVM: nBallerina, a native implementation, was in progress, and a native flag already produced GraalVM native executables. The platform around it includes OpenAPI, GraphQL and gRPC tooling, a test framework with service mocking, standard and extended libraries of connectors, and Ballerina Central for sharing modules.

## Who should watch

Integration developers tired of writing mapping code by hand, and language nerds curious what a type system designed around network data looks like. If you want the concurrency model in detail, she says herself it is too much for a short session.

Title: From loopback to Gateway API, Kubernetes networking without sidecars
Description: Federica Ciuffo (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on how Kubernetes networking went from ingress to service mesh to Gateway API and VPC Lattice
Body:
Every step away from the monolith buys flexibility and sells you a networking problem. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Federica Ciuffo, Senior Containers Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS, traced how Kubernetes application networking grew from CNIs and ingress controllers to sidecar service meshes and then to the Kubernetes Gateway API, ending with Amazon VPC Lattice as a Gateway API implementation that connects services across clusters and VPCs without sidecars.

It is a history-of-the-stack talk with an AWS destination. Lattice was in preview at the time, announced at re:Invent 2022.

## How did we get here?

Ciuffo walks up the ladder one rung at a time. In a monolith, components talk over loopback interfaces and a load balancer or proxy handles client traffic. Containerise the pieces and put them in Kubernetes, and pods talk through a CNI (Amazon VPC CNI, Cilium, Calico), while an ingress controller watches Ingress objects and creates, updates or deletes load balancers for you.

Then the pattern she sees at medium and large AWS customers: microservices spread across several clusters, VPCs and accounts, written in different languages, owned by small DevOps teams. Now you need connectivity and routing, visibility into service-to-service traffic, and security and compliance that don't depend on each team getting it right. One load balancer per service doesn't scale, and shared ingress only goes so far.

## What did the sidecar buy us?

The sidecar proxy pattern puts a proxy in every pod and sends all traffic through it, decoupling networking from application code. Her example: when the backend team ships a new version, the frontend team no longer has to change code to point at it; the proxy handles the switch. Logs come out in one consistent format because it is the same proxy everywhere.

Add a control plane for all those proxies and you have a service mesh (AWS App Mesh, Istio, Consul, Linkerd, Kong on her slide). The use cases she lists: weighted routing for blue/green and canary releases, retries, circuit breaking and rate limiting, allow lists, TLS at the proxy so application teams don't carry it, mutual TLS for service identity, tracing without touching application code, and multi-cluster active/active setups. Envoy, born at Lyft in 2016 and a CNCF graduated project, is the usual data plane, and Istio with Kiali is the common combo on EKS.

## What's still wrong with meshes?

Three things, per her slides. You have to deploy and maintain sidecars at scale. Meshes only cover container workloads, not AWS Lambda or plain Amazon EC2. And before you install one, you still need inter-VPC networking (transit gateways, peering) that isn't mapped to application or security needs.

## Gateway API: networking objects that match your org chart

The Kubernetes Gateway API, a SIG Network project, took the lessons from Ingress and split the job into objects: a GatewayClass formalises the type of load-balancing implementation, a Gateway requests a point where traffic enters and is translated to Kubernetes Services, and HTTPRoutes map requests from a Gateway to Services. "A nice feature to the Kubernetes Gateway API is that it is role oriented," Federica Ciuffo said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023: infrastructure providers, cluster operators and application developers each own their layer. Implementations include Istio, NGINX, HAProxy and now Lattice.

## Where VPC Lattice fits

Amazon VPC Lattice is a layer 7 networking fabric across VPCs and accounts, with no sidecars and no proxies to manage, working across EC2, EKS, ECS and Lambda. Its pieces: a service network (a logical boundary across VPCs and accounts for common access and observability policies), services (units of application on any compute), a service directory, and IAM-based auth policies at the network or service level.

The AWS Gateway API controller maps the Kubernetes objects onto it. Apply a Gateway and the controller creates a service network and associates the VPCs of your EKS clusters, much like attaching them to a transit gateway. Apply an HTTPRoute and it creates Lattice services as targets, including services exported from one cluster and imported into another. The result is cross-cluster routing defined in Kubernetes YAML, without setting up transit gateways or peering, and without running a mesh.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers on EKS weighing a mesh against Gateway API, and anyone who needs the ingress-to-mesh-to-Gateway-API story in one sitting. If you are not on AWS, the first two thirds still stand on their own.

Title: Hudi, Iceberg or Delta Lake? Pick the table format by workload
Description: Satish Mane and Rajeev Jaiiswal (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on building a lakehouse on S3 and choosing between Hudi, Iceberg and Delta Lake
Body:
A data lake is cheap until a customer invokes their right to be forgotten and you have to find and delete one person's rows across a lake full of Parquet files. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Satish Mane and Rajeev Jaiiswal, Senior Solutions Architects at AWS, laid out how open table formats turn an S3 data lake into a lakehouse with transactions, and how to choose between Apache Hudi, Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake: Hudi for streaming and CDC, Iceberg for schema and partition evolution, Delta Lake if you live in Spark.

It is a two-part architecture talk with an AWS slant: Jaiiswal covers the data lake, Mane the lakehouse and the formats.

## Why a data lake first?

Jaiiswal starts from the legacy setup: an operational database feeding a reporting database and data marts. Its four problems: analytics cycles that take weeks or months, scaling that means buying hardware and licences ahead of time, poor fit for machine learning and ad hoc data science queries, and an inability to keep up with changing business needs.

The data lake answer: keep data in its original form and format, apply structure only when you read it (schema on read), and open it up to many users. On AWS that means Amazon S3 as storage decoupled from compute, the AWS Glue Data Catalog for metadata, and AWS Glue, Amazon EMR and Amazon Athena for processing. He reminds the audience why formats matter: CSV is row storage and human readable, while Parquet is columnar, compresses each column better and suits bulk processing. And the warning that applies to every lake: without a catalog you can't manage data, find it or control access, and without governance you have a swamp.

## Where regular data lakes break

Mane lists the failures that push teams towards a lakehouse:

- **Record-level changes.** Under GDPR and CCPA you must change or delete a customer's data on request, and that is hard in a plain lake.
- **CDC pipelines** and late or erroneous data that needs rewriting.
- **Reprocessing** missing or corrupted data after job failures.
- **No schema enforcement on write**, so low-quality data gets in.
- **Performance**: you need to know the partition layout to avoid full table scans and listing every file.

Open table formats address these with ACID transactions written to a log as a single source of truth, DML, concurrent reads and writes, schema evolution and enforcement, engine neutrality, and time travel for audits, rollbacks after a bad write and reproducible reports.

## Two ways to build a lakehouse on AWS

The ready-made route pairs Amazon Redshift for transactional warehouse work with an S3 data lake, joined through Redshift Spectrum: raw data stays in the lake, processing happens in the warehouse. The do-it-yourself route puts one of the three open table formats directly on S3 and optionally adds Redshift for low-latency OLAP on business-ready data. The comparison table in the slides sums it up: lake and lakehouse cost $, the warehouse $$$, and only the plain lake is rated difficult to operate.

## How the three formats differ under the hood

This is the part worth the watch.

- **Apache Hudi** uses a timeline-based transaction model, offers both MVCC (snapshot isolation between one ingestion writer and many readers) and file-level optimistic concurrency, time travel by commit time, and schema evolution but no partition evolution. Auto file sizing and compaction avoid small files; its default index maps record keys to file groups, so use monotonically increasing keys (a timestamp prefix) for range pruning.
- **Apache Iceberg** "follows snapshot based transaction model", Satish Mane said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023: every change writes a new metadata file and commits with an atomic pointer swap, retrying if the base snapshot moved. Time travel works by snapshot ID or timestamp. Expiring old snapshots and compacting files are manual Spark jobs. Column value ranges and partition fields let queries skip files.
- **Delta Lake** logs operations in JSON, checkpoints into Parquet every ten commits, uses optimistic concurrency and time travel by timestamp or version. It is copy-on-write with no compaction, so you run `VACUUM` and `OPTIMIZE` yourself; Z-ordering colocates data-skipping statistics.

On AWS integration at the time: Athena had read-write support for Iceberg but read-only for Hudi and Delta Lake, Redshift Spectrum could read Hudi and Delta Lake, and EMR and Glue could read and write all three, with AWS Lake Formation permissions on some combinations.

## So which one?

Hudi for streaming, IoT and CDC, thanks to its indexes, auto file sizing and the bundled DeltaStreamer ingestion tool. Iceberg when schema and partition evolution matter: hidden partitioning means queries don't need the exact partition key, and you can change the partition column and it simply starts writing to new partitions. Delta Lake when your platform is built around Spark, since it keeps table state in its log and checkpoints rather than a central metastore.

## Who should watch

Data engineers on AWS deciding on a table format, and anyone who has been asked to make an S3 lake GDPR-compliant. Expect architecture and comparisons, not a demo.

Title: Service Weaver - write a modular monolith, deploy microservices
Description: Robert Grandl (Google) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on Service Weaver, a Go framework that writes like one binary and runs like microservices
Body:
Google looked at why its own teams split applications into microservices and found that many of the reasons don't survive contact with the data. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Robert Grandl, Software Engineer at Google, presented Service Weaver, a Go framework built on that finding: you write your application as a modular binary, and the runtime decides how to deploy it as a set of connected microservices.

It is a framework introduction by one of its authors, with code, deployment commands and a benchmark against the classic Online Boutique demo.

## Are your microservice boundaries real?

Grandl's opening is the most quotable part. Teams give three reasons for splitting beyond scalability and fault tolerance, and Google's analysis undercuts each one. Different languages per service? The vast majority of teams use only one language. Different rollout schedules? A significant fraction of teams release all their microservices together. Very frequent releases of some services? Only a tiny fraction of microservices are released that often.

Meanwhile the split has a price: versioned upgrades and backward compatibility between instances at different versions, multiplied configuration, IDL and protocol plumbing, and API hardening, where "once a developer splits into microservices and deploys them, it is incredibly difficult to change the APIs because of versioning concerns", Robert Grandl said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. End-to-end and local testing get hard too.

A monolith fixes most of that and brings back the problems microservices were invented to solve. Service Weaver tries to sit in between.

## What does a Service Weaver app look like?

An application is a set of components that call each other, a bit like actors. A component is a plain Go interface, say a `Cache` with a `Put` method. The implementation is a Go struct that embeds `weaver.Implements[Cache]`, which is how the framework recognises it. In `main`, `weaver.Init` starts the app, `weaver.Get[Cache]` returns a handle, and from then on you make ordinary method calls. A code generator does the rest: encoding, stubs, registration.

Deployment is one binary and a small `weaver.toml`: the binary name, optional colocation groups (put two chatty components in one process) and an optional rollout duration. Then:

- `go run .` runs everything in a single process.
- `weaver multi deploy` runs it as multiple processes on one machine.
- `weaver ssh deploy` runs the same binary across machines listed in a file.
- `weaver gke deploy` runs it on Google Cloud, where the deployer builds containers, places components into pods, replicates them and load-balances traffic.

Every component runs at the same code version, and rollouts are blue/green. At the time the deployers covered a local machine, an SSH cluster and Google Cloud, with AWS and Azure pitched as relatively easy to add.

## What do you get for free?

Each component has a logger; metrics include counters, gauges and histograms, plus default metrics for throughput and latency between components. Tracing uses OpenTelemetry once you install a handler in `main`, and then covers HTTP requests and component method calls. `weaver gke profile` profiles every process and merges the result into one profile. The dashboard draws the call graph between components with metrics on each edge.

Testing uses the `weavertest` package, which runs unit tests in single- or multi-process mode by swapping `weaver.Init` for `weavertest.Init`. To check for version-skew bugs, `weaver gke-local` simulates multiple application versions running at once.

One caveat he is careful to state: the framework doesn't hide the network, and developers should treat method calls as remote by default, even though calls within one process are optimised to local calls.

## How do the numbers look?

The benchmark used Online Boutique, eleven microservices, rewritten in Go for a fair comparison, on the Google Cloud deployer. Per the slides, against the non-Weaver version:

- 99th percentile latency: 520 ms, down to 130 ms (Weaver split) and 14 ms (Weaver merged), up to 37x.
- Median latency: 40 ms to 12 ms and 6 ms, up to 7x.
- Autoscaled to 21 VMs versus 10 and 5, up to 4x fewer.
- Go code: 2,647 lines versus 2,117, up to 1.25x less, since there are no protos, service discovery or encoding boilerplate.

The gains come from an encoding with no versioning overhead, a custom TCP-based transport with built-in load balancing, colocation, and routing that improves cache hit ratios.

## Who should watch

Go developers maintaining a fleet of services that always ship together, and anyone who has lost a sprint to protobuf version skew. If your services genuinely use different languages and release cycles, his own data says you are in the minority this framework isn't for.

Title: You have pipelines. That doesn't mean you do CI/CD
Description: Ricardo Castro (FanDuel/Blip.pt) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on why build/deploy automation isn't CI/CD, and how trunk-based work and fluid PRs get you there
Body:
Ask a room who practises CI/CD and every hand goes up, because every team has a Jenkins somewhere. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Ricardo Castro, Principal Engineer, SRE at FanDuel/Blip.pt, argued that most of those hands belong to teams with build and deploy automation, not continuous integration, and that the thing standing in the way is usually the pull request workflow, not the tooling.

The talk mentions no tool, no pipeline and no YAML on purpose, and that is the point.

## What counts as CI, by the book?

Castro starts with definitions, leaning on Dave Farley: continuous integration is about keeping a clear picture of how your changes work alongside everyone else's as they progress, and continuous delivery is the ability to get changes of all types (features, configuration, bug fixes, experiments) into users' hands safely, quickly and sustainably. Continuous deployment, where it is distinguished at all, is the fully automatic last step.

Then the rule of thumb that does the damage: integrate code from every developer on the team at least daily, and get it in front of users at least daily. He adds the speed targets he cites: Farley's CI under 5 minutes, Charity Majors' whole CI/CD loop under 15 minutes, and the DORA report's elite performers going from code to production in under an hour.

## Why feature branches and PRs fight CI

The typical workflow is a main branch, a feature branch for an entire feature, a pull request, a code review, a merge. Castro walks through the cost. You open a PR and wait for someone to pick it up, 10 minutes, an hour or a week. Then come the back-and-forth rounds. Now multiply by a team of five or six people, each supposed to integrate several times a day, each interrupting the others for reviews. How many reviews can anyone actually do in a day?

The usual escape is batching changes, which means you are no longer doing CI. And the review itself is asynchronous with no two-way conversation.

## What are the alternatives?

**Trunk-based development.** Commit to main, or use short-lived branches merged straight back. He cites the State of DevOps data: trunk-based development predicts higher throughput and better stability, plus higher job satisfaction and lower burnout.

**Pair programming** to keep the review without the queue. He takes on the standard objections. Wasteful? He points to John Nosek's "The case for collaborative programming". Uncomfortable? Most people who try it find otherwise, though that one is personal preference. Bad for focus? He cites a comparison of solo and pair programming in the Journal of Educational Computing Research showing pairs sustain better focus. Time zones in remote teams are the objection he grants.

**Fluid pull requests**, the middle ground he credits to a colleague and has used for years: policies set up before development say which changes are low risk and can be merged automatically (documentation, say), which are critical and need a review, and who the right reviewer is. You trust developers to merge before review, and you track the PRs that still need a look after the merge.

## So where do the tools fit?

Borrowing Simon Sinek's golden circle: the why of CI/CD is building better software, the how is faster feedback, and build servers and pipelines are the what. They help with speed and effort, but they aren't the practice. "CI CD is not about a tool, it's about a practice," Ricardo Castro said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023.

Why do teams stop at automation? Because automation alone is already valuable, because people lack trust in each other and reach for rules, and because the rest takes investment.

## Who should watch

Team leads whose "CI/CD" consists of a pipeline and a PR queue that takes a day to clear, and anyone about to argue for trunk-based development who wants the citations. His reading list: the Continuous Delivery and Continuous Integration books and Accelerate.

Title: A side project with no time budget should be a monolith
Description: Bervianto Leo Pratama (Mitrais) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on moving a Lerna side project to a .NET monolith because his time, not scale, was the constraint
Body:
The scarcest resource on most side projects isn't CPU, it's the evenings. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Bervianto Leo Pratama, Software Engineer at Mitrais, told the story of moving his self-hosted password manager from a Lerna monorepo of Vue.js and Feathers.js to a single .NET web app, and his takeaway is refreshingly unfashionable: re-scope to the time you actually have, and don't be shy about starting with a monolith.

It is a short talk, a lightning-length case study rather than a tutorial, and it says what it needs to.

## What was he building?

The goal is a simple service to manage his personal passwords and secrets, in the spirit of LastPass or Bitwarden, but open source and self-hostable. The third goal is the one that drives everything else: easy to manage, which for him means something he can develop and run with limited time.

## Why did the Lerna setup stall?

The original structure was a Lerna monorepo with a `packages/` folder holding a Vue.js frontend and a Feathers.js backend, plus a database: three tiers, two projects. Two problems piled up.

First, context switching. His day job is .NET, so every session on the project meant switching his head into Node.js, then into frontend, then back to backend. Second, operations: with two projects to ship, he spent about a year thinking about the deployment target and the CI/CD strategy and never implemented either, because managing multiple projects alone was too much. Capacity, in the human sense, was the real bottleneck.

## Why a monolith, and why .NET?

He expects the obvious objection and answers it directly. Microservices might be the textbook answer, but with limited time they are hard for one person to run. A monolith means one service to deploy, and "it's more manageable for a person with limited time", Bervianto Leo Pratama said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. The new shape is two-tier: a web app, with the database as a separate service.

.NET won on familiarity, and because a .NET solution with multiple projects in one repository feels close to the Lerna pattern he was leaving, which made the move less of a rewrite of habits.

## Where did it land?

It shipped, which is more than the old setup managed. The app runs on AWS: Azure DevOps runs the pipelines, the web app is containerised with Docker and pushed to Amazon ECR, and AWS App Runner serves it from that image. The repository, `bervProject/SimplePasswordManagerService` on GitHub, is open for contributions and feedback.

Next on his list is clean architecture: separating the business logic from infrastructure such as the API and the database, moving towards modularity step by step rather than in one heroic weekend.

## What's the lesson?

Two lines from his summary are worth keeping on a sticky note. Re-scope your project to your available time and your needs. Don't hesitate to start from the monolith, and split it into services later if the project ever earns it.

Mixing Azure DevOps with AWS hosting also makes a quiet point: for a one-person project, pick the tools you already know on each layer rather than buying into a single vendor's whole stack.

## Who should watch

Anyone with a half-finished side project and an over-engineered architecture diagram for it. If you want deep .NET or AWS detail, this isn't that talk; it is about scoping decisions.

Title: Stop chaining Lambdas by hand and let a state machine hold the state
Description: Oskar Neumann (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on AWS Step Functions as the orchestrator that replaces chained Lambdas, queues and DB bookkeeping
Body:
Every serverless app starts as one Lambda function and ends as forty, talking to each other through queues, a DynamoDB table and a prayer. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Oskar Neumann, Solutions Architect at AWS, walked through AWS Step Functions as the place to put that coordination: a state machine that owns sequencing, retries, branching and error handling, so your functions can go back to doing one thing each.

It is an AWS talk about an AWS service, and a well-organised tour of it: the why, the Amazon States Language, data flow between states, workflow types and the tooling.

## Why not just call the next function?

Neumann opens with the familiar wish list: sequence task A before B, retry what fails, catch errors, run things in parallel, choose a branch based on a result. Then he walks through the four ways people usually get there without an orchestrator, and what each costs.

- **Method calls** glue functions together, but you lose small independent functions that do one thing well.
- **Function chaining** synchronously doesn't scale; asynchronously, error handling gets hard and finding out about failures needs extra plumbing.
- **Coordination through a database** (DynamoDB or a relational one, SQL transactions) works and people get good results, but it is a lot of work.
- **Coordination through queues or streams** means bookkeeping: catch the failure, write the state back to the queue, and build timeouts and retries yourself.

His conclusion: "Business workflows are rarely sequential from start to finish", Oskar Neumann said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, so isolate tasks into logical components and centralise orchestration in a workflow.

## What a Step Functions workflow is made of

A workflow is a state machine of states joined by transitions, written in the Amazon States Language (ASL), which he describes as assembly for the workflow. You can drag and drop it in Workflow Studio, write the JSON, or generate it with the CDK or the Data Science SDK for Python.

The running example is an image pipeline: extract metadata with a Lambda function, check the image type (fail if unsupported), store the metadata, then in parallel run recognition and generate a thumbnail, and finally add the recognised tags. The eight state types do the rest: Task, Choice, Wait, Parallel, Map, Pass, Succeed and Fail.

Integrations come in two flavours. Optimized integrations (17 services per the slides) get extra Workflow Studio support but no performance benefit; SDK integrations reach over 200 AWS services and over 10,000 API actions directly, so you write fewer Lambda functions whose only job is calling an API. On top of that sit three patterns: request-response, run a job and wait (`.sync`), and wait for a callback with a task token.

## The JSONPath plumbing is where people get lost

The most practically useful section is the anatomy of a state. Input flows through `InputPath` (select part of the input), `Parameters` (build the key-value pairs passed to the integration), the integration itself, `ResultSelector` (reshape the task result), `ResultPath` (merge the result back into the input, or overwrite it) and `OutputPath` (filter the final output). Each uses JSONPath starting with `$`. The context object (`$$.Execution.Id`, start time and more) and intrinsic functions such as `States.Format` and `States.StringToJson` let you massage data without a Lambda in between.

If you have ever lost an afternoon because `ResultPath` silently replaced your whole input, this part is for you.

## Standard or Express?

The slides spell out the trade-off. Standard workflows run up to 365 days at over 2,000 execution starts per second, with executions kept for 90 days and visual debugging; good for IT automation, order processing, billing, ML training. Express workflows cap at 5 minutes but start over 100,000 executions per second, with logs only in CloudWatch; good for event-driven microservices, IoT ingestion and high-volume processing.

## Patterns and best practices

Catch and Retry blocks (with interval, max attempts and backoff rate), nested child workflows for building big flows out of small ones, and tooling: Workflow Studio, the AWS Toolkit for Visual Studio Code, SAM or CDK, and Step Functions Local as a JAR or Docker image with mocked service integrations. His closing list is short and worth pinning: pick the right workflow type, set timeouts so executions don't get stuck, pass large payloads through S3, watch the history quota, and handle Lambda service exceptions such as throttling.

## Who should watch

Developers whose serverless app has outgrown one Lambda calling the next, and architects deciding between Step Functions and hand-rolled queue choreography. Seasoned Step Functions users will mostly be reviewing.

Title: A placeholder pod turned a four-minute scale-up into seven seconds
Description: Chris Nesbitt-Smith (UK Government) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on keeping a spare Kubernetes node warm with low-priority placeholder pods
Body:
Cluster Autoscaler only adds a node once a pod is already pending, so every scale-up starts with a wait. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Chris Nesbitt-Smith, a consultant to UK government who has run Kubernetes in production since version 0.4, shows a cheap hack around that: a big, low-priority placeholder pod that holds a spare node and gets evicted the moment real work needs the room. In his live demo, the second node's pod went from about three to four minutes to 7 seconds.

## Where do the minutes go?

Nesbitt-Smith starts from scheduler basics and one rule he would settle for if you remember nothing else: set requests and limits on every container. "So if you don't specify requests and limits, Kubernetes will play completely blind," Chris Nesbitt-Smith said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. Nodes get oversubscribed and you end up firefighting.

With requests set, Kubernetes looks like a reasonably skilled Tetris player, fitting app blocks onto node boards. The catch is that the board is smaller than the box says. An 8 GB, 2 CPU node won't fit four 1.5 GB pods, because memory and CPU are reserved for the operating system, the kubelet and the eviction threshold. His AWS example: about 255 MB for the kubelet plus 11 MB per pod the instance can run, 100 MB for the OS and another 100 MB for eviction. The fourth pod goes pending and a new node is ordered.

Then the timeline, starting from a traffic spike: roughly 90 seconds for the HPA to decide to add pods, about 30 seconds for Cluster Autoscaler to request a node, three to four minutes for the machine to boot, another 30 seconds to join the cluster, and then an image pull onto a cold node.

## Is failing a few requests really that bad?

To make the trade-off tangible, he built a fake Kubernetes scheduler library that simulates days of scaling in milliseconds, and a game on top of it called Black Friday: you are the SRE team for a retailer with a three-tier app facing spikes on Black Friday and Cyber Monday. In his run, under-provisioning cost $1,154 in SLA penalties while the company still came out about $15,000 ahead of having no autoscaling at all. The point is that just enough infrastructure, not maximum safety, wins the game.

His other way to stack the odds is not to scale at all: size nodes so the workload fits, using an instance calculator his team built to compare how efficiently different instance types pack a given pod shape, with or without DaemonSets and agents.

## How does the placeholder trick work?

Run a placeholder pod sized to fill a whole node, so nothing real can share it, with a PriorityClass of -1. Every other pod, even ones with default priority, outranks it. When real pods need space, the scheduler evicts the placeholder, the real pods start right away on the warm node, and the now-pending placeholder makes Cluster Autoscaler order the next node. You are always one node ahead.

The live demo on Linode is honest about live demos: one cluster's timer never loaded and he fell back to a second cluster. Without the placeholder, scaling from one replica to five filled the first node within seconds and left the fifth pod waiting about three minutes. With the placeholder, the fifth pod was running in 7 seconds.

A recorded HPA run tells the same story under load. Without the placeholder, served requests per second flatten for roughly four minutes while nodes boot. With it, the curve keeps climbing. Traffic sometimes outpaces even the spare node, so new nodes fill before a placeholder can land, but there is always a node request in flight and no requests fail.

## What does it cost?

A node doing nothing but holding a placeholder is money spent on purpose, the same logic as a hot spare in a RAID array. His suggestion for getting value back: replace the placeholder with real low-priority work that can stop and start, such as housekeeping, analytics or machine learning jobs, or less critical services, so the shopping cart preempts the internal tools. Asked about oversubscribing VMs underneath Kubernetes, his answer is short: you are in for a bad day.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose HPA reacts fine but whose users still wait minutes during spikes, and teams sizing node pools for the first time. It works with any cloud's Cluster Autoscaler; no extra tooling needed.

Title: Change data capture without polling, built on Apache Pulsar
Description: Mary Grygleski (DataStax) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on log-based change data capture with Apache Pulsar and why batch ETL can't keep up
Body:
If your downstream systems learn about database changes from a nightly batch job, they are always a day behind the truth. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Mary Grygleski, Streaming Developer Advocate at DataStax, made the case for log-based change data capture (CDC) carried by Apache Pulsar: detect a change once, ship it as an event, and let a broker that separates compute from storage do the heavy lifting.

It is an introductory talk that starts from first principles, then lands on DataStax's own CDC for Astra DB, so expect a vendor tour in the second half.

## What is CDC actually for?

Grygleski frames CDC as four steps: detect changes in a source of truth (a database, a data lake, a warehouse), capture them, transform them (filter, map, enrich, sometimes remediate), and propagate them to downstream systems that become derived data sources. Before you groan that this is just ETL with a new hat: she spends a good chunk of the talk explaining why it isn't.

ETL, she argues, still has its place, but it is batch-shaped. Data gets bundled, shipped through transformation, then loaded, which eats network bandwidth, needs heavy setup and, in the enterprise flavour, expensive licences. "ETL traditionally is a very slow type of processing because it is synchronous in nature," Mary Grygleski said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023.

## Why log-based beats polling and triggers

The talk walks through the usual ways of detecting a change. Polling with a SQL query on a timestamp column works, but you only find out as often as you poll. Database triggers tie you to one database's quirks and limitations. The preferred route is the transaction log.

Her example is small and clear: client one sets `x = 1`, client two sets `x = 2`. Both writes land in the transaction log in order, the CDC system replays them downstream in that same order, and a query against the target always returns the latest state, `x = 2`. No polling loop, and the ordering guarantee comes for free from the log. That ordering matters more than it sounds: she points out that a debit and a credit on the same account have to arrive in the order they happened, or your derived data is fiction.

## What a modern CDC system needs

Her checklist for a cloud native CDC pipeline: lean on resources (public cloud bills by usage), responsive, elastic enough to shrink and grow with traffic, and resilient when a node dies. For the messages themselves: guaranteed delivery (at least once or exactly once, defined properly), asynchronous and loosely coupled producers and consumers, pub/sub for scale, and preserved message order.

No single legacy system meets that list, so her pitch is to rethink the job: treat CDC as an event-driven problem.

## Where Apache Pulsar fits

Pulsar, created at Yahoo, donated to the Apache Software Foundation in 2016 and a top-level project since 2018, ticks most of those boxes by design. The points she leans on:

- **Compute and storage are separate.** Brokers are stateless; Apache BookKeeper stores the messages and Apache ZooKeeper holds cluster metadata. Scaling brokers doesn't mean rebalancing partitions.
- **Guaranteed delivery.** If a message reaches a Pulsar broker, it will be delivered to its intended target.
- **Pulsar Functions** handle the transform step inside the cluster, with no external dependencies.
- **Tiered storage** moves cold data off warm storage to cheaper places such as S3 or HDFS.
- **Multi-tenancy** and client libraries in Java, C#, Python and Go, plus community ones.

The slides add native geo-replication and four subscription modes (exclusive, failover, shared, key_shared), with a dig at Kafka's fit for queuing.

## The Astra DB part

The last section shows CDC for Astra DB, DataStax's managed Cassandra: create a database and a table, create a streaming tenant in Astra Streaming (managed Pulsar), enable CDC on the table, transform with Pulsar Functions and write to a sink. The documented example uses Elasticsearch as the sink. She runs short on time and points to the docs rather than walking through every step, and also mentions Luna Streaming for self-managed Pulsar on Kubernetes and the plain open source route on your laptop.

## Who should watch

Engineers who still move data around with batch jobs and want a clear mental model of log-based CDC, and anyone weighing Pulsar against Kafka for a streaming backbone. If you already run Debezium in production, the first half will be familiar ground.

Title: A string parsed as a long cost $10,000 and nobody noticed for 12 hours
Description: Yoav Nordmann (Tikal Knowledge) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on catching data anomalies in minutes with Apache Pinot and StarTree ThirdEye
Body:
One new field, one wrong data type, one phone model. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Yoav Nordmann, a tech lead and group leader at Tikal Knowledge, opens with an ad tech incident: a parameter sent as a string and parsed as a long, only for one iPhone model, in a pipeline handling a million events per second. The talk is about making sure that kind of silent data break shows up in minutes, using Apache Pinot as the fast store and StarTree ThirdEye on top for anomaly detection and root cause analysis.

## Why do data anomalies go unnoticed?

The cost of the original bug is the hook. "Needless to say, that this problem went unrecognized for 12 hours, after which we lost about $10,000 of billing data," Yoav Nordmann said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. Five days of work to recover it went nowhere.

Nordmann describes the usual fate of a data issue as a black hole. Most issues are never noticed. Some are noticed but nobody finds the root cause, so they come back. Only a few get both found and fixed. His goals are to remove the black hole, cut time to detect, and cut time to resolution. A second example from the same company: one user's daily bulk download slowed everyone else's queries, and the team learned about it a day later, when a batch job finally parsed the previous day's latency logs.

## Why does the store matter as much as the detector?

ThirdEye is an anomaly detection, monitoring and interactive root-cause analysis platform, and it queries its data source constantly, so that source has to answer in under a second. That source is Apache Pinot, a real-time distributed OLAP datastore.

Nordmann explains the problem Pinot solves with slice and dice. Three dimensions give 7 combinations, five give 31, seven give 127, and real data has many more. Keep data raw and you get flexibility but high latency; pre-aggregate or cube it and you get speed but lose flexibility. Pinot aims for the middle, between joined and aggregated data, through pluggable indexes: inverted, forward, range, text, JSON, geospatial, timestamp, Bloom filters and the star-tree index.

Its credentials come from LinkedIn, where it started as an internal analytics database and grew to serve user-facing analytics. The LinkedIn figures he quotes, about a year old at the time: 200,000+ queries per second, a peak ingestion rate of over 1 million events per second, and over 20 billion records scanned per second.

On licensing: Pinot is open source. ThirdEye comes from StarTree, which offers both as SaaS, under a community license that lets you use it freely but not resell it as a SaaS product.

## How does ThirdEye define an anomaly?

Three layers. An alert template is detection boilerplate (create an anomaly if a metric exceeds a maximum). An alert fills it in (revenue above 20,000, checked hourly). An anomaly is what the pipeline finds (revenue was 30,000 on a given Thursday between 9pm and 10pm). Detectors include threshold, mean-variance, percentage and absolute change rules, plus a proprietary Holt-Winters rule in the commercial edition; you can plug in your own.

Root cause analysis compares the anomalous period with a baseline as a heat map, deep red for big drops and intense blue for big rises, with top contributors listed. Subscription groups push anomalies to email, Slack or a webhook. And for the skeptic's question, what if the baseline was a holiday, you record events (holidays, releases) so they show up in the analysis.

## What does the demo show?

A K3s cluster on his laptop running Kafka, Pinot and ThirdEye from StarTree's quick start. Telegraf sends the laptop's CPU metrics to Kafka; a real-time Pinot table ingests them, over 10,000 rows and growing every few seconds. In ThirdEye, an alert using the StarTree threshold template sums system CPU usage against a threshold of 170, evaluated every minute, which is the shortest interval ThirdEye supports. He opens a live anomaly, compares it against a baseline, marks one as not an anomaly (the count drops from 16 to 15) and shows the merge settings that fold nearby anomalies into one.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who have shipped a schema change and found out from finance. The demo is small, one laptop's CPU, so treat it as a tour of the concepts rather than a benchmark.

Title: Keep your Postgres, add a compute layer, call it distributed
Description: Trista Pan (SphereEx) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on turning existing PostgreSQL or MySQL into a sharded database with Apache ShardingSphere
Body:
You don't have to migrate to a new distributed database to get one. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Trista Pan, Co-Founder and CTO of SphereEx and a PMC member of Apache ShardingSphere, shows how to treat your existing PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server or Oracle instances as storage nodes and put ShardingSphere in front of them as the compute layer, deployed on Kubernetes with one Helm command.

It is an architecture talk for people who still love their monolithic database and are running out of room in it.

## Why not just pick a NewSQL database?

Pan sets the scene with big data's five Vs (value, veracity, volume, velocity, variety) and the usual split between OLAP, analysing large datasets quickly, and OLTP, many users writing transactions, which is where MySQL, PostgreSQL and Oracle live and where this talk stays.

The pressure is familiar. Services became microservices on Kubernetes that scale in and out; the database is still one machine, struggling with terabytes and petabytes. Distributed databases such as CockroachDB solve that if you start fresh. "But I guess most of us are still in the progress of the evolution, right?" Trista Pan said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. Most teams have years of PostgreSQL or MySQL, the tools and the DBAs who know them, and no appetite for overturning all of it.

## Where does the "distributed" part come from?

Her answer borrows the design most distributed databases already use: separate compute from storage. Your existing database instances become the storage nodes; they persist data and do local computing. What's missing is a global compute layer that knows where each row lives, and that's the role of Apache ShardingSphere.

The benefits on her slide: reuse the databases you have, upgrade at low cost, keep the mature ecosystem around them, gain SQL audit, traffic governance and elastic scaling, and avoid lock-in. It also helps with moving to the cloud gradually: storage can stay on premises or in RDS while the compute nodes run on Kubernetes.

ShardingSphere, an Apache top-level project open source for more than six years, comes in two flavours:

- **ShardingSphere-JDBC**, a lightweight driver that Java applications use through the standard JDBC interface.
- **ShardingSphere-Proxy**, a database proxy any application can connect to.

Both offer data sharding across instances, distributed transactions, read/write splitting (updates and deletes go to the primary, selects spread across replicas with random or round-robin strategies, no separate load balancer), and data masking and encryption: because the layer sits between application and database, it can encrypt on the way in and decrypt on the way out, so the database never stores plain text.

## What does a sharded table look like?

The demo design uses two PostgreSQL clusters, each a primary and a replica, deployed with the Bitnami chart, plus two ShardingSphere-Proxy compute nodes and a governance component, installed from the shardingsphere-on-cloud Helm charts. You register the PostgreSQL resources with the proxy, then create a sharding table in ShardingSphere's DistSQL dialect.

The example table `t_user` uses a hash-mod strategy on its sharding column to split into four physical tables spread over the two clusters. The application sees one logical table. The proxy parses each query, routes it to the shard that holds the rows, and sends selects to replicas, which is where the higher QPS comes from.

One caveat: Pan runs out of time before the live demo and leaves the eight steps on her slides (deploy, register, create the table, show metadata, insert, preview routing, run a select) to do yourself. The talk explains the design; the slides carry the commands.

## Who should watch

Teams with a large PostgreSQL or MySQL estate who are being asked to scale out without a rewrite, and platform engineers wondering how a database can live partly on Kubernetes. Pan gave related ShardingSphere talks at Conf42 Golang 2023 and SRE 2023 if you want more depth.

Title: Watch Karpenter shrink an EKS cluster you forgot to shrink
Description: Samuel Baruffi (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on installing Karpenter on EKS and letting consolidation pick cheaper nodes live
Body:
Scaling up is the easy half of autoscaling; the money leaks out on the way down. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Samuel Baruffi, Senior Global Solutions Architect at AWS, explains why Cluster Autoscaler struggles on EKS and then spends the second half of the talk in a terminal, installing Karpenter and watching its consolidation feature move pods onto fewer, cheaper nodes without being asked.

## Where does Karpenter sit among the autoscalers?

Baruffi starts from EKS basics: a managed, single-tenant control plane per cluster, data plane nodes in your VPC as self-managed or managed node groups, four supported Kubernetes versions at a time. Then the three Kubernetes autoscalers: HPA adds pods, VPA resizes them, and Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes by bumping an Auto Scaling group when pods go pending.

That works for most workloads, but AWS hears the same three complaints. Node group sprawl, because Cluster Autoscaler can only add more of the same instance type, so GPU jobs, web apps and batch each get their own group, and Spot and On-Demand can't share one managed node group. Slow response for spiky work such as ETL or GPU training, where slow scale-up delays data scientists and slow scale-down wastes expensive accelerators. And the difficulty of balancing utilisation, availability and cost across AZs. His slide puts a number on it: nearly half of AWS Kubernetes customers say configuring cluster autoscaling is challenging.

## What does Karpenter change?

Karpenter replaces Cluster Autoscaler and has no groups. It watches for unschedulable pods, bin-packs them, and calls the EC2 Fleet API for just-in-time capacity that fits their requests and constraints. Going straight to Fleet avoids Auto Scaling group API limits, and Karpenter binds pods to the new node early, so image pulls start before the node reports ready, which shaves seconds off startup. "The goal is to launch 1000 pods within 30 seconds," Samuel Baruffi said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023.

Configuration is two objects: a Provisioner (what may be launched) and an AWSNodeTemplate (how: subnets, security groups, tags, AMI). His Provisioner examples:

- **Capacity type**: allow Spot and On-Demand together, and Karpenter favours Spot, falling back to On-Demand only when Spot isn't available.
- **Architecture**: arm64 Graviton and amd64 in one provisioner, chosen per pod.
- **Instance shape**: restrict sizes, families, generations and CPUs; restrict AZs.
- **Expensive hardware**: a separate GPU provisioner with a taint, so only pods with the matching toleration land there.

For removal there are two mutually exclusive options. `ttlSecondsAfterEmpty` deletes a node that has run only DaemonSets for N seconds. Consolidation, which he recommends, also replaces underused nodes with cheaper ones. `ttlSecondsUntilExpired` rotates nodes after a set age, a handy way to roll out new AMIs.

## What does the demo show?

The setup is a small managed node group to host Karpenter itself, plus eks-node-viewer, an open source tool that shows each node's instance type and the cluster's cost per hour and month as it changes. Karpenter installs from a Helm chart; Spot interruption handling needs an SQS queue and EventBridge rules created beforehand. It runs as a two-replica Deployment in active/standby, not a DaemonSet (he first tails the standby pod's logs and finds nothing, a mistake everyone makes once).

The first Provisioner is Spot-only, Linux, amd64, 2xlarge and up, C, M and R families, capped at 1,000 CPUs and 8 TB of memory, with a 30-second empty TTL. A pause-container deployment scaled from 0 to 1 to 10 replicas brings up Spot nodes within about a minute, the logs showing each step: found provisionable pods, computed new nodes, discovered the security group and AMI, created a launch template, launched. Scale to zero and the nodes vanish 30 seconds later.

Then he switches to On-Demand with consolidation enabled. Scale to 10 replicas and a second node appears. Scale down to 6 and Karpenter notices everything fits on the bigger node, moves the pods and deletes the smaller one. Scale to 3 and the remaining node sits at 40% utilisation, so Karpenter cordons it, launches a cheaper instance, moves the pods, and only then removes the expensive one.

## Who should watch

EKS operators who want to see Karpenter's behaviour before trusting it with production, especially consolidation. His takeaways: use Spot for stateless workloads spread across nodes and AZs, avoid it for single-pod stateful apps, keep a broad default provisioner plus specific ones for constraints like GPUs, and pair Karpenter with HPA. At the time Karpenter supported only AWS as a provider.

Title: Karpenter deletes the node group, and that is the whole trick
Description: Yael Grossman (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on groupless Kubernetes autoscaling with Karpenter, Spot and Graviton
Body:
If you have ever maintained twelve Auto Scaling groups so that Cluster Autoscaler can tell a 4xlarge from an 8xlarge, this talk is for you. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Yael Grossman, Specialist Solutions Architect for Flexible Compute at AWS, explains why Karpenter drops node groups entirely and asks EC2 for exactly the instances your pending pods need, and how that makes Spot and Graviton easy to adopt.

## What are we actually optimising?

Grossman defines efficient autoscaling as three related goals plus one constraint. Scale: pay only for what the business needs right now. Density: pick the right instance and bin-pack containers into it. Flexibility: be willing to use whichever of many instance types is cheapest, which is where Spot and Graviton come in. The constraint is operational overhead, because the platform engineer choosing an autoscaler already has a ton of other tasks.

She also decodes the EC2 naming convention on the way: in m6g.xlarge, the family sets the CPU-to-memory ratio, the size sets the CPU count, and the g says Graviton.

## Why is Cluster Autoscaler hard to configure?

The Kubernetes scheduler matches pods to nodes, but it doesn't create nodes. Cluster Autoscaler fills that gap by bridging pods to Auto Scaling groups: a pod goes pending, Cluster Autoscaler picks a group, bumps its desired count, waits for the instance to bootstrap and join, and the pod schedules.

The catch is in how it picks. It simulates how much capacity each group will return, so every group must be homogeneous. "So you need to run each auto scaling group with homogeneous instance types," Yael Grossman said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. You can mix c5.2xlarge and c6.2xlarge, but not 2xlarge with 4xlarge. Need small and large nodes, multiple availability zones, On-Demand and Spot? Multiply the groups, and then keep their AMIs and configuration up to date. Her slides show the result: a cluster with a dozen groups across two AZs, and a note that nearly half of AWS Kubernetes customers say configuring cluster autoscaling is challenging. It also fights Spot best practice, which wants you diversified across sizes as well as families.

## How does Karpenter do it differently?

Karpenter watches for unschedulable pods too, but then calls the EC2 Fleet API directly with a request built from those pods' requirements. No pre-built list of instance types, no group in the middle. Scaling decisions happen in seconds even in large clusters, and different applications can share infrastructure.

Configuration is a Kubernetes custom resource, the Provisioner. Left at defaults it can choose from all 600+ EC2 instance types (metal excluded). You can narrow it by attributes, cap the resources a team's workloads may provision, or set a time-to-live after which nodes are replaced. Karpenter reads the usual pod constraints: resource requests, node selectors, affinity, taints and tolerations, topology spread.

Grossman describes three layouts:

- **Single provisioner** for many workloads, mixing Spot and On-Demand or Graviton and x86, maximising sharing.
- **Multiple provisioners** for isolation: GPU nodes you don't want shared because they're expensive, security boundaries, team separation, different AMIs.
- **Prioritised (weighted) provisioners**, for example running 30% of a deployment on Graviton and the rest on x86.

## Why does this make Spot and Graviton easier?

Spot instances can be interrupted with a two-minute notice, so the workload must tolerate moving. Modernised containers usually do: stateless, fault tolerant, bin-packed across sizes and AZs. Karpenter bakes in the Spot playbook: all instance types by default, the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy that picks the deepest capacity pools, and built-in interruption handling. The discount is up to 90%.

For Graviton, AWS quotes up to 40% better price performance, list prices around 15-20% lower than equivalent x86 instances, and up to 60% better energy efficiency. If you already build multi-architecture images, a provisioner that allows Graviton, Intel and AMD lets Karpenter pick whichever is cheapest, and the container runtime pulls the matching image.

## Who should watch

EKS operators still running Cluster Autoscaler with a pile of node groups, and anyone who wants to try Spot without hand-building the diversification. It is a conceptual talk from AWS, with no live demo; for a hands-on install, the companion Karpenter talk at the same event goes further.

Title: SolarWinds shows why CI can't be your only security scan
Description: Sven Ruppert (JFrog) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on software supply chain security, SLSA, SAST vs DAST, and scanning binaries before CI
Body:
Sven Ruppert recorded this one on a multi-day hike through the Swedish woods, and the trail ends at a lake just as the talk does. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, the JFrog Developer Advocate makes the case that software supply chain attacks have changed who gets targeted, that your dependencies are the low-hanging fruit, and that the CI pipeline is too late to be the first place you scan.

## Why would anyone attack a 20-person company?

Ruppert opens with geopolitics. Attacks used to be about money: a big company, a ransom. Now groups and even governments are involved, and ransomware increasingly wants to cause damage rather than collect payment. Big targets have hardened their own systems, so attackers walk down the supply chain to the weakest link. "Now you are target because you are a political target," Sven Ruppert said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. If you deliver software to a large company that some government dislikes, your 20-person shop is in scope.

## What does SLSA give you?

For the developer view of the chain, he leans on SLSA, the Linux Foundation project that maps the path from source to production: code review against malicious commits, a hardened source server, a build system that could be compromised or fed overlaid source, a repository of dependencies and binaries, then delivery. Between those steps he wants a zero trust environment. What developers directly control is narrower: the source code they write, and the binaries they produce and consume.

SLSA itself is documentation, not an implementation: levels from zero to four to calibrate where you are and what the next step is, plus a catalogue of source, build and dependency threats with real examples. It was in alpha at the time, and he recommends it anyway. He also points to Pyrsia, a decentralised package network started by JFrog in which randomly selected peer nodes build the same commit and compare fingerprints before a binary is distributed. Compromising exactly those nodes is hard.

## Which kind of testing first?

Ruppert walks through four approaches:

- **SAST** (static) scans source, configuration and binaries without running anything. It sees everything you give it and can start with the first line of code, but has no runtime context.
- **DAST** (dynamic) attacks a running system from outside through its API, like a hacker would. No knowledge of internals needed, but it only reaches what the API exposes.
- **IAST** (interactive) combines the two, a kind of security debugging. You can't just buy it; you need highly skilled people, or you'll test something and wrongly believe it's secure.
- **RASP** (runtime protection) is an agent in production that spots attacks and either alerts or shuts the system down. It is the last layer, never the only one.

His recommendation: start with static scanning, and start with dependencies. You write thousands of lines; you import millions. Add the base image in your Dockerfile's `FROM`, Helm charts, the operating system, and the binaries of the CI and dev tools themselves.

## Why isn't CI enough?

He calls CI "a security gateway for everything", and you should scan there on every build. But the SolarWinds case shows its limit. Attackers didn't steal data from SolarWinds; they modified the CI environment that built the Orion platform, so every build produced a compromised binary, and the automatic updates shipped it. By Ruppert's account, Orion had 300,000 customers, and within days over 15,000 networks were infected. That led to the US executive order on cybersecurity and the SBOM requirement for software used by the US government.

The lesson he draws is that you defend in two directions: don't consume malicious or vulnerable components, and don't distribute them. So scan earlier as well.

## What does scanning earlier look like?

This part shows JFrog's tooling. Keep every binary (Maven, NuGet, Debian, Docker) behind one central repository, Artifactory, instead of pulling straight from Docker Hub or Maven Central, and scan there with Xray, which uses the dependency managers' metadata (transitive dependencies, scopes, linking) instead of looking at a lone binary. Build Info, which JFrog had before SBOMs were mandatory, stores each build's dependencies, environment and agent next to the binary, so a CVE published tomorrow points at the Helm chart in production without rescanning anything.

Earlier still: a free IDE plugin that shows the dependency tree and vulnerabilities the moment you add a line to your POM, a CLI audit of a freshly cloned repository, and on-demand scans of a local Docker image or JAR whose reports can be shared with colleagues. Wherever you scan, read the CVSS base metrics, which describe the worst case, and adjust them for your environment: a network-exploitable flaw matters less on an air-gapped system.

## Who should watch

Developers who want the supply chain vocabulary (SLSA, SBOM, SAST versus DAST) in one sitting, and teams deciding where to put scanners. The second half is JFrog-specific; the first half works with any tool stack.

Title: Security writes the zero trust policy, platform teams make it real
Description: Steve Judd (Jetstack, a Venafi Company) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on why platform engineers should implement zero trust in Kubernetes
Body:
Zero trust in Kubernetes stalls less on tooling than on ownership. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Steve Judd, Chief Architect at Jetstack, a Venafi Company, argues that security teams know which policies a cluster needs but rarely have the Kubernetes depth to implement them, and that the people who do are the platform engineers. His answer to "shift left" is to shift sideways, to the platform team.

It is a short talk built on conversations Judd has as a consultant with security teams trying to bring zero trust into Kubernetes estates. Treat it as a framing talk, not a tutorial.

## What does zero trust actually mean?

Judd starts with Forrester's definition: a security model that denies access to applications and data by default, and grants access to networks and workloads only through policy informed by continuous, contextual, risk-based verification of users and their devices. His short version: never trust, always verify, every time.

Four principles sit under it:

- **Least privilege.** Give a requester exactly the access the request needs. His example: don't hand everyone cluster-admin, because for sure they don't need it.
- **Per-request authentication and authorisation.** Every call, not once per session.
- **Identity-based.** Machines need identities as much as people do: servers, VMs, IoT devices, pods. In practice that means X.509 certificates.
- **Context-based.** Where is the request coming from, and is that normal for this identity? A UK-based user suddenly calling from Russia should change the answer.

The goal of all four is to stop lateral movement: an attacker who lands on one server shouldn't be able to wander on to the next.

## Why is it hard in a cloud native estate?

Judd lists four challenges. Machine identities are multiplying fast (pods, jobs, services), and if each needs a certificate that is issued, renewed and revoked, doing it by hand is not an option. Access control raises questions of level, updates and enforcement. Shift-left security sounds right, but development teams have competing priorities. And someone has to own governance: who defines the policies and checks they are enforced?

## What does Kubernetes give you out of the box?

Three native features. RBAC, which can be very granular about what a workload may do. Network policies, which define which pod talks to which pod on which port, provided your CNI driver implements them, and not all do. And pod security, where the manifest declares the constraints containers must run under and the Pod Security Admission controller refuses pods that don't comply.

Then three add-ons. cert-manager, which Judd calls the de facto tool for X.509 certificates inside a cluster.  A service mesh such as Linkerd or Istio for mutual TLS between workloads and traffic policies that go beyond network policies. And policy-based admission controllers such as Kyverno and Gatekeeper for richer rules every deployment must meet.

## So who should hold the pen?

This is the talk's real point. "Security teams deeply understand what security policies need to be introduced, what they look like, but they aren't necessarily the right people for actually implementing those policies," Steve Judd said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023.

Platform engineers already have three things the job needs: Kubernetes expertise, automation know-how, and familiarity with the tools that run, or should run, in the cluster, Istio, Linkerd and cert-manager among them. Security keeps the lead on defining policy; platform engineering implements and probably enforces it. The closing slide puts the onus on security teams to reach out first and collaborate.

It is a tidy answer to the governance question too: the team that owns the golden paths is also the team that can make the secure path the default one.

## Who should watch

Security leads planning a zero trust programme for Kubernetes and wondering why tickets to app teams go nowhere, and platform teams who want vocabulary for the conversation. If you want YAML, pair it with one of the hands-on talks below.

Title: The OWASP Serverless Top 10, mapped to five open source tools
Description: Shlomi Kushchi (Jit) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on covering the OWASP Serverless Top 10 with ZAP, dependency-check, Gitleaks, Prowler and AirIAM
Body:
Ten risks, five free tools, one table. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Shlomi Kushchi, System Architect at Jit, takes the OWASP Serverless Top 10 and assigns each risk to an open source scanner: OWASP ZAP, OWASP dependency-check, Gitleaks, Prowler and AirIAM. The takeaway is that a handful of scheduled scans covers most of the list, as long as you know which tool watches which door.

He frames it with a Home Alone metaphor: your application is the house, the family has left, and you need to know where the burglars will try first.

## What changes when the app goes serverless?

Kushchi starts with a typical AWS serverless shape: users hit an API gateway, static assets come from S3, logic runs in Lambda functions, data sits in managed databases. Compared with a classic app, four things differ. The shared responsibility model shifts so that the cloud provider handles the OS, network and platform, leaving you mostly responsible for the application logic. Functions are ephemeral. The attack surface grows, because every function, bucket and third-party service is another entry point. And you get finer-grained control, which is only a benefit if you use it.

The perimeter to protect includes the CI/CD pipeline, user and admin access (MFA, least privilege), public resources such as IPs and buckets, and third-party services.

## How does the Top 10 group?

The list Kushchi uses is the OWASP Serverless Top 10, which reuses the 2017 web Top 10 categories. He sorts the ten into four domains:

- **Your code**: injection, XML external entities, cross-site scripting, insecure deserialization, components with known vulnerabilities.
- **Identity and access**: broken authentication, broken access control.
- **Data**: sensitive data exposure.
- **Logging and monitoring**: security misconfiguration, insufficient logging.

A detail worth stealing from the misconfiguration slide: the risk includes denial of wallet, not only DDoS. Max concurrency and timeouts on a function are a security setting when someone else can trigger it a million times on your bill.

## Which tool covers what?

- **OWASP ZAP** attacks your web app and API from outside, finds SQL injection, XSS and friends, and takes a Swagger/OpenAPI spec. Its blind spot: it only tests what sits behind an API gateway, so async flows go untested.
- **OWASP dependency-check** compares your packages against the NVD. Kushchi's argument for scheduled dependency scans is blunt: because it's open source, it's scanned all the time. "And common threats are common," he adds.
- **Gitleaks** finds secrets in git history. The debug password that slipped into a commit is there forever once pushed. "If you find them, you need to make sure you mitigate it properly, replace the secrets, invalidate them," Shlomi Kushchi said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, then check whether anything was compromised and add a pre-commit hook so the next one never leaves the laptop.
- **Prowler** scans the cloud account itself, AWS and Azure, with roughly 200 checks and AWS Organizations support. It covers what ZAP can't see: internal resources, async flows without an API gateway, unencrypted storage, missing CloudTrail logs.
- **AirIAM** from Bridgecrew compares IAM roles and policies with what CloudTrail says was actually used, and flags the excess.

Least privilege shows up in almost every row. For injection, ZAP detects the missing input validation and AirIAM limits the blast radius if one slips through. The same few tools keep reappearing across risks, which is the point: you don't need ten products for ten risks.

## Where does Jit come in?

The last few minutes are the vendor part: Jit orchestrates these same open source tools as a security plan defined as code, per environment, triggered by events or schedules, with guidance on fixing what they find. It is brief, and everything before it works without Jit.

## Who should watch

Teams running Lambda-style workloads who want a starter security checklist with a free tool per line. Security specialists will find the material familiar; the value is the mapping, which makes a good one-page plan for a team that has none.

Title: Your NetworkPolicy does nothing until your CNI says so
Description: Reza Ramezanpour (Tigera) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on securing Kubernetes with small images, private registries, Calico policies and monitoring
Body:
A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is a polite request. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Reza Ramezanpour, Developer Advocate at Tigera, walks from the container image to the cluster network to monitoring, and builds a locked-down three-node lab on camera: images from a private registry, a default-deny policy, and Prometheus metrics that are off until you turn them on. The core lesson is that each layer has a default that works against you.

It is an introductory talk with a long demo, and it is Calico-centric, since Ramezanpour works on Project Calico. The title promises ten best practices; the talk delivers them as themes rather than a numbered list.

## What does Calico actually bring?

Ramezanpour opens with the project: an open source networking and network security layer for containers, VMs and host workloads, on x86 and ARM64, with four pluggable data planes. The standard one uses iptables; the eBPF one can replace kube-proxy entirely, preserve source IPs and do direct server return; a Windows data plane builds on Microsoft HNS; and VPP was in beta at the time. The project counted 9,000+ Slack members, 550+ contributors and over 2,000,000 nodes running Calico every day.

## Start with the image: smaller is safer

The container section has three rules: put the application in an image, include as little as possible, and scan it. The demo makes this concrete. He compiles the same hello world application twice, once on `ubuntu:latest` and once on `scratch`, then scans both with the Tigera image scanner. The Ubuntu image comes back with two vulnerabilities in a program that prints one line. The scratch image has none, because it contains nothing he didn't put there, and it is much smaller too.

Then registries. Public ones are convenient and cheap; private ones give the control that banks and government agencies need for compliance and data protection. Most manifests on the internet point at a public registry (the Tigera operator manifest pulls from quay.io), so the demo mirrors every Calico component, and later the node exporter image, into a private registry on another Multipass VM. The Calico Installation resource has a `registry` field that redirects the whole install there, and a `describe` on a Calico pod proves the image came from the private side.

## Who enforces the policy?

Here is the trap in plain Kubernetes. "Kubernetes doesn't enforce these policies on its own, and it delegates the responsibility to the CNI plugins," Reza Ramezanpour said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. Pick a CNI without policy support and your carefully written YAML is decoration.

Even with enforcement, the built-in resource has gaps he lists: no explicit action attribute (allow or deny is implied), no node-specific policies, and nothing that applies to the cluster as a whole. Calico adds its own NetworkPolicy (namespaced), GlobalNetworkPolicy (cluster-wide) and host endpoint policies that cover non-namespaced things such as host processes and network interfaces. Segmentation, in his framing, combines namespaces, labels, security policies and RBAC, so a compromised pod can't wander laterally.

In the demo he creates a monitoring namespace, a ClusterRole, a ServiceAccount and the binding, then applies policies: one letting host-network pods reach the local host IP, then the classic default deny that blocks all namespaced traffic except DNS lookups to CoreDNS.

## Monitoring is off by default

The last layer is visibility, split into infrastructure monitoring (host, network, storage) and application monitoring (leaks, errors, crashes). Calico components can expose Prometheus metrics, but the default configuration disables them; two configuration values and a Service per component fix that. Node exporter, installed by Helm from the private registry, covers the VMs, and the Prometheus UI confirms both feeds.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to Kubernetes networking who want to see image hygiene, private registries and default-deny policies wired together in one lab. Everything in the demo is in a public GitHub repository (frozenprocess/Tigera-Presentations), so you can rerun it at your own pace. If you already run Calico with GlobalNetworkPolicies in production, this will be familiar ground.
