Title: The scikit-learn features data scientists forget, plus a deep learning map
Description: Jose Manuel Ortega at Conf42 Python 2023 on the machine learning lifecycle and the Python libraries for each stage, from pandas profiling to PCA and Keras
Body:
Python won machine learning on readability and libraries, but the libraries are the part people only half know. At Conf42 Python 2023, Jose Manuel Ortega, a Python developer and security researcher from Spain and author of a Spanish-language book on big data, machine learning and data science with Python, walks through the stages of a data science project and the Python tool that fits each one, with the most time spent on the scikit-learn features that even experienced practitioners skip.

It is an introductory survey, a good map for someone starting out or filling gaps, not an in-depth study of any single library.

## Which library for which job?

Ortega opens with the case for Python: simple, readable, general purpose, and fast to prototype in, with use cases from spam filters and recommendation systems to personal assistants and fraud detection. His map of the ecosystem: Keras, TensorFlow and scikit-learn for machine learning; NumPy and SciPy for scientific computing; OpenCV for computer vision; NumPy and pandas for data analysis; NLTK and spaCy for natural language processing.

NumPy's n-dimensional array comes first. Jose Manuel Ortega said at Conf42 Python 2023: "The main advantage of Numpy is its speed, mainly to the fact that it is developed in C programming language". pandas builds on it, and its DataFrame, a size-mutable two-dimensional table, handles reading formats, selecting subsets, filling missing data, grouping and joining. A tip worth stealing: pandas profiling produces an exploratory data analysis report as interactive HTML in a few lines, `ProfileReport(data)` and `to_file('output.html')`.

## The lifecycle, in five steps

He describes the machine learning lifecycle as a cyclical process: define the objectives, acquire and clean the data, build the model by picking an algorithm and a target variable, interpret and communicate the results, and implement, document and maintain the project. On interpretation he makes a practical point: the more interpretable the model, the easier it is to meet regulatory requirements and explain its value to management.

## scikit-learn's hidden gems

The meat of the talk is scikit-learn beyond `fit` and `predict`. Experienced practitioners, he warns, rarely know all of what the package can do, and he lists six features:

- **Pipelines**: `make_pipeline` chains estimators (his example is `Binarizer()` then `MultinomialNB()`), so feature selection, normalisation and classification run as one fixed sequence and are easier to track.
- **Grid search**: `get_params()` shows an estimator's hyperparameters; a search combines an estimator, a parameter space, a sampling method, a cross-validation scheme and a score function.
- **Validation curves**: `validation_curve` plots one hyperparameter against training and validation scores. Both low means underfitting; high training with low validation means overfitting.
- **One-hot encoding** with `OneHotEncoder` for categorical columns.
- **Dataset generators** for artificial data of controlled size and complexity.
- **PCA**: standardise with `StandardScaler`, then `PCA(n_components=2)` and `fit_transform`, using explained variance to choose how many dimensions to keep.

He adds statsmodels for statistical models, linear fits and exploratory analysis.

## Deep learning: TensorFlow, Keras, PyTorch, Theano

TensorFlow builds networks out of tensors and has grown an ecosystem, including TensorFlow Lite for phones and IoT devices; since 2.0, Keras is its main high-level API and, he suggests, the best starting point for beginners, with the Sequential API for a simple stack of layers. His comparison table puts Keras as simple and readable but slower, with TensorFlow and PyTorch fast but harder to read. He closes with Theano, its NumPy integration, transparent GPU use and symbolic differentiation, and the extensions built on it.

## Who should watch

Python developers moving into data science who want one tour of the tools and the order in which they are used, and scikit-learn users who have never touched pipelines or validation curves. Seasoned ML engineers will know most of it.

Title: Kubernetes Secrets sit in etcd as base64, so run Vault next to them
Description: Michael Levan at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on why default Kubernetes Secrets aren't safe and how to install and unseal HashiCorp Vault with Helm
Body:
Anyone who can read etcd can read your Kubernetes Secrets. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Kubernetes trainer and consultant [Michael Levan](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Michael_Levan_kubernetes_secret_management_vault) made the short case for moving secrets to a third-party store, picked HashiCorp Vault for a reason more teams should use (it's the boring, heavily supported option), and installed and unsealed it live on a managed cluster.

Set expectations: this is a short, hands-on session, and it stops once Vault is running and unsealed. The title promises secret management the right way; what you get is the first step, done cleanly. Injecting secrets into pods is left for another day.

## What's actually wrong with Kubernetes Secrets?

Levan starts with a broader definition than usual. Secrets aren't only passwords and API keys; "secrets are really anything that you don't want in plain text," Levan said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, even a username you'd rather keep paired with its password.

Kubernetes has a Secret resource in its core API group, but by default those values are stored unencrypted in etcd, the cluster's data store, as plain base64. So a service account, an engineer or an attacker with access to etcd has your secrets. For production, he recommends a third-party secrets provider, and points out that the Kubernetes documentation itself says much the same.

## Why Vault, of all the options?

Not because it's new. You can deploy it without paying anything, and there's a deep pile of documentation, getting-started guides, production write-ups, videos and courses. "I'm always thinking about not what the latest and greatest is, but what's actually supported heavily," he said of his consulting work. A tool with that much community knowledge behind it is easier to run well, and easier to hand over.

## The install, step by step

He uses Helm rather than raw manifests, so the release can be versioned, upgraded and rolled back.

1. Add the HashiCorp Helm repo.
2. Install the vault chart as a release named vault, with the UI enabled, the UI service type set to LoadBalancer, into a vault namespace created on the fly.
3. Watch the namespace with kubectl. The pod reaches Running but shows 0/1 ready, which is the first thing that confuses newcomers.

He's on AKS, but notes any managed Kubernetes service works the same way. Opening the load balancer IP on port 8200 shows the Vault UI, up but sealed, which explains the 0/1.

## Unsealing, from outside the pod

Instead of shelling into the container, he runs `vault operator init` through kubectl exec. That prints the unseal keys and the initial root token. Then he runs the unseal command three times with three different keys, and the status ticks from one of three to two of three to unsealed. Back in the UI, the root token logs him in, and the pod finally reports ready.

It's the part of Vault that trips people up the first time, the idea that a running Vault server is not yet a usable one, and seeing it on a real cluster makes it click. In production you'd keep those keys and that root token far away from a terminal recording.

## Who should watch

Kubernetes users who have never deployed Vault and want to see the minimum path to a working, unsealed instance. If you need the next steps, Kubernetes auth, policies and the agent injector, watch the companion talk below.

Title: An IP address, a port and IMDSv1 were all the attackers needed
Description: Nader Zaveri and Brandan Schondorfer of Mandiant (Google Cloud) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on how attackers chain SSRF with IMDSv1, and how to shut it
Body:
The attackers in this story never needed a username or a password. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, Nader Zaveri (Senior Manager, Incident Response & Remediation) and Brandan Schondorfer of Mandiant (Google Cloud) walk through a real intrusion where an SSRF bug plus the AWS instance metadata service in version 1 handed over EC2 role credentials, and the S3 data went out shortly after. The fix is a setting most environments still haven't flipped: require IMDSv2.

## What is the metadata service, and why is it a target?

Every cloud VM can ask a link-local address (169.254.169.254) about itself: IP, subnet, availability zone, and on AWS the temporary credentials of the instance role plus any user data script. AWS, Azure and GCP all have one. The address is not routable, so on its own it is harmless. Pair it with an application that can be tricked into making requests for you (server-side request forgery) and the outside world can read it.

Zaveri's point is that your vulnerability scanner stays quiet about it. He cites a Datadog study published just before the talk: 93% of EC2 instances across 600+ organisations still allowed IMDSv1, and 95% of those organisations had at least one such instance. Version 2 exists since November 2019, shipped after the Capital One breach used exactly this trick, but v1 stays enabled by default. "This is not a vulnerability. It is a misconfiguration," Nader Zaveri said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023.

User data makes it worse. Startup scripts written in Bash or PowerShell routinely carry clear-text passwords, and anyone who can query the metadata service can read them.

## How did the attack actually go?

Schondorfer covers the forensics. A CVE in Adminer, the database management tool, disclosed in February 2021, allowed SSRF, and a proof of concept followed. Within about three months, a group Mandiant tracks as UNC2903 was spraying it across AWS address space; Mandiant's threat intel matched around 2,100 IP addresses scanning for the same thing. The attacker ran the PoC on an operational relay box, pointed the vulnerable Adminer login (with the driver set to Elasticsearch) at it, and the credentials came back on screen. From there it was the AWS CLI: list the buckets, copy the data. Reconnaissance to exfiltration took roughly three hours.

The demo reproduces this with IMDSv1 on, then repeats it with IMDSv2 required. The second run errors out: v2 needs a PUT to get a session token first, rejects requests carrying an X-Forwarded-For header, and the relay can't do either.

## Why is it so hard to investigate?

There is no HTTP log of who asked the metadata service for a token, and nothing you can turn on to get one. The team stitched the story together from three sources: web logs showing a 302 redirect and a 403 (which looked like failures and were the opposite), VPC flow logs showing the EC2 instance unexpectedly talking to the internet, and S3 object-level data events lining up with the copies. GuardDuty's InstanceCredentialExfiltration findings (inside and outside AWS) fired, but after the credentials were already taken. An alert, Zaveri notes, is not prevention.

Azure and GCP get partial credit: both require a metadata header and reject forwarded requests, though Zaveri points to research on abusing Azure managed identities and on adding SSH keys at GCP project level once you are on the box.

## What should you do on Monday?

The talk ends with a checklist:

- **Find it.** Security Hub, a CloudWatch metric for IMDSv1 use, an AWS Config rule, or open source tools such as Prowler, Metabadger and CloudMapper. `describe-instances` shows `HttpTokens: optional` for the exposed ones.
- **Remove or restrict it.** If nothing needs the metadata service, disable the endpoint. If something does, require tokens, limit the hop count to 1, and restrict access with iptables and IAM.
- **Keep it fixed.** Service control policies that refuse to launch instances without IMDSv2, the same guard in Terraform or CloudFormation, or IAM policies for single-account shops. Scan user data for secrets with Scout Suite.

There is also a side lesson on patching priority. Zaveri tells of a vulnerability disclosed on October 21, a PoC on the 27th, and a client breached on the 28th. "So it's only so much you can be ahead of these vulnerabilities," he said, which is why a published proof of concept should move a CVE to the top of the queue, and why the configuration fix matters more than any single patch.

## Who should watch

Anyone running EC2 who hasn't checked `HttpTokens` lately, and incident responders who want to know which AWS logs will and won't help them. It is a practical, front-line talk with two short demos, not a theory lecture.

Title: Exploits arrive in 30 days, fixes in 246. Security as code closes the gap
Description: Christoph Hartmann (Mondoo) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on security as code: one policy checked from the IDE through CI/CD to production
Body:
Most security tooling only notices a public bucket once it's public. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, [Christoph Hartmann](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Christoph_Hartmann_security_as_code), Co-Founder and CTO of Mondoo and co-creator of InSpec, argued that security as code should do for security what Terraform did for infrastructure: one policy, written once, that checks the Terraform file in your IDE, the pipeline in CI and the live AWS account in production.

It's a vendor talk that ends in Mondoo's open-source cnspec, but most of it is the case for why the current split between platform and security teams keeps failing, and that part is worth hearing whatever tools you use.

## Who is he, and why policy as code?

Hartmann started at Deutsche Telekom, securing critical infrastructure across Europe through automation that people told him wouldn't work. That became the DevSec Project and InSpec, an early policy-as-code engine started around 2014-15 to turn long, boring PDF requirements into automated checks. His company, Vulcano Security, was acquired by Chef Software, where he was Director of Engineering and InSpec was sold to Fortune 500 companies and the Department of Defense.

## Why do fixes lose the race?

His numbers paint the gap. CVE publications grow about 20% year over year, with over 25,000 in the last year alone. Around 25% of CVEs have known exploits; per his slides, 14% of exploits appear before the patch, 23% in the first week after the CVE and 50% in the first month. Against that, NTT Application Security puts the average time to fix a high-severity vulnerability at about 246 days.

Meanwhile ransomware is a business, with sales quotas, playbooks, customer support and affiliate programs. In an independent survey of 1,100 IT and security professionals, Hartmann said 80% had been ransomware victims and more than 60% paid. And Microsoft's Cyber Signals report attributes 80% of attacks to outdated software and misconfiguration, which is to say, avoidable ones.

## Two teams, two ends of the pipeline

The structural problem is where each team looks. Developers and platform engineers live in local development, Git and CI; security teams watch production, where the attack surface is. Take a storage bucket that mustn't be public. Security checks the setting in AWS, Google Cloud or Azure and files a ticket. Platform engineers think in Terraform and want to be told what to change in HCL, not which dashboard toggle is wrong.

So, he said, "we have to deploy a vulnerable software in order to detect the vulnerable software so that we can essentially fix the vulnerable software, which is not making any sense." Hartmann is careful to blame the tooling, not the people: when the tools don't fit together, each side goes to management to complain about the other.

## What security as code needs

He defines it as integrating security controls and practices into the software development process through code and automation, and lists four ingredients: static and dynamic testing of Terraform and Kubernetes manifests, package vulnerability management for containers at build and at runtime, continuous testing of running systems such as AWS and Microsoft 365, and secure coding practices like input validation and proper review.

Every phase needs checking, not just the first. A supply chain attack can change something after it looked fine in Git, so "correct in Git" doesn't mean correct in production. And a container that passed CI picks up new CVEs a week after deployment.

His four tests for tooling: access (developers and security engineers use the same tools), coverage (build and runtime, or you rebuild the silos), automation (security fits the pipeline you have) and extensibility (an open-source foundation, not hard-coded rules).

## What it looks like in cnspec

The demo turns the bucket rule into a single policy with variants per technology. Against AWS, it checks that S3 buckets have block public ACLs and block public policy enabled. Against Terraform, the same GraphQL-based query language finds the public access block resources and checks those arguments are true, so the problem shows up in the IDE before anyone runs apply. The policy is one shared rule; the variant that runs depends on what you point it at. That's the alignment he's after: exceptions get agreed once, in code, rather than negotiated per tool.

Mondoo publishes hundreds of policies with thousands of checks in its open-source registry and on GitHub, alongside cnquery query packs for asset inventory and incident response.

## Who should watch

Security engineers whose findings keep bouncing off platform teams, and platform engineers who want security feedback before the deploy, not after. The first half is useful even if you never touch cnspec.

Title: Your runbook should be a Jupyter notebook you can actually run
Description: Doug Sillars (unSkript) at Conf42 Python 2023 on turning runbooks into Python Jupyter notebooks that automate CloudOps work, from pod logs to AWS quotas
Body:
A runbook is a checklist, and a Jupyter notebook is a checklist that executes. At Conf42 Python 2023, Doug Sillars, Head of Developer Relations at unSkript, makes the case for writing operational runbooks as Python notebooks, then demos unSkript, the company's open-source runbook automation tool built on Jupyter, from a Kubernetes log check to an AWS service quota report that refreshes itself daily.

It is a vendor talk showing the speaker's own product, and an open-source one, with a practical idea underneath that works whatever tool you use.

## Why runbooks, and why the usual way fails

Sillars opens with a figure: application support and operations take up to 55% of developer time. Good internal documentation cuts that down. He leans on a well-known blog post by an SRE at some of the world's busiest gambling sites, where downtime is directly lost money: with good runbooks, issues were resolved faster, escalations were simpler, onboarding and training got easier, and the docs stayed current because people used them.

The catch is the price. That engineer's boss gave him a seven-month kick-off to review every outage of the previous 18 months and write hundreds of runbooks, then 10% of his time to keep them up to date. Most teams get nothing like that, so the question is how to get there faster.

## What notebooks get right

His list of why Jupyter suits the job: notebooks live online, so the runbook isn't stuck on someone's laptop during an outage; they are plain Python, with no domain-specific language and no YAML; markdown cells document each step and its inputs; and because every step is code, every step can be automated.

The first example is a Kubernetes health check: list the pods, fetch each pod's logs, scan the last hour for warnings with a small Python script, and post them to Slack. As Doug Sillars said at Conf42 Python 2023, "nobody reads the logs", so a scheduled job that reads them for you is the point. Three of its four actions were prebuilt; he wrote the last one and opened a PR to the open-source repo.

## Building a runbook in minutes

The live demo runs the Docker install of unSkript. Credentials for clouds, databases, observability and CI/CD tools, Kubernetes and Slack are stored once, so actions never show a key; anything missing can go through a REST API or SSH. Input parameters such as the AWS region feed every action. He drags in a prebuilt action to filter EC2 instances in us-west-2, saves the result to a variable, prints it, and shows that the next step could restart those instances (he declines, since some are in production).

## Service quotas: the limit you find out about by failing

The best example came from a customer whose automations failed because they had quietly hit AWS service quotas. Elastic IPs for EC2, for instance, are limited to five per region, and each quota hides behind a service name and an opaque code such as L-CEED54BB. His runbook gets each VPC quota, checks usage, flags anything past 50%, and can request an increase: NAT gateways per availability zone sat at four of five, he asked for ten, and AWS answered with a 200 and queued the request.

Then he went further. Iterating over all 222 AWS service names collects roughly 2,600 quotas, which an action writes to a Google Sheet, run every day; in the week he had been running it, four or five new ones appeared daily. The output also feeds the unSkript docs, so the codes can be looked up without the API calls.

## Who should watch

SREs, DevOps and platform engineers whose runbooks live in a wiki nobody trusts, and Python developers who keep getting dragged into operations. Expect a product demo, but the pattern of runnable, documented, schedulable notebooks is the takeaway.

Title: Your config management runs hourly. Your drift runs continuously
Description: Ben Rockwood (Mondoo) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on cnquery and cnspec, open-source GraphQL queries and assertions across clouds, hosts and GitHub
Body:
Infrastructure as code told us a comforting story: declare the state, apply it, done. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, [Ben Rockwood](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Ben_Rockwood_posture_management), VP of Engineering and Operations at Mondoo, called that story a farce, because nobody applies it continuously, and pitched the missing piece: a Kubernetes-style reconciliation loop for security posture everywhere, built on two open-source Mondoo tools, cnquery and cnspec.

It's a vendor talk introducing the company's own projects, but Rockwood spends the first third on how to think about security, and that part travels well beyond Mondoo.

## Security without the scary statistics

He skips the usual ten minutes of breach numbers ("you know that the world is a scary place") and offers three short definitions instead. Security is protecting what matters, including the work you've done; security for its own sake is going in circles. Compliance "really is about doing what we say we do," Rockwood said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. If a written procedure is outdated or ridiculous, change the procedure, and treat the auditor as the person who points that out. Posture is situational awareness: we can't stand on a factory catwalk and watch virtual infrastructure hum, so we need tools that see inside it.

Most posture problems, he argues, are one of two things. Outdated software, because most attackers are opportunists hunting known vulnerabilities, not researchers inventing new ones. And misconfiguration, the more egregious of the two: "your biggest threat is your kids leaving the door open," he said. One of the most common ways ransomware attacks begin is an open RDP port.

## Why not just use the tools you have?

Because you have too many. Plenty of good tools scan AWS, or Terraform, or a Kubernetes cluster, or containers, and each does its slice well. Stitching them together is a job nobody has time for. Rockwood's answer is extensibility, which in his view means open source. The goal is assurance: knowing what you built is still in the state you built it, without adding a recurring "go check that thing" to your own to-do list. Configuration management runs every hour or six or 24, finds drift, puts it back, and the drift returns.

## cnquery: GraphQL for your infrastructure

cnquery is a GraphQL interface to, in his words, all the things. GraphQL's appeal over REST is that you ask for exactly the fields you want. Ask the users object for name, uid and shell and you get back a list of users with just those three fields; add a filter on name and ask for star, and you get one user with every attribute.

The demos scale up from there. In a shell over SSH, he queries listening ports not bound to localhost and returns address, port and protocol. Point cnquery at an Ansible-style inventory and the same query runs across the fleet, which beats scanning from outside: you see the ports the host actually has open. Then the same syntax against a GCP organisation lists every Cloud Run service with its annotations, and it works the same way for AWS and Azure.

## cnspec: the same queries, as assertions

cnspec, the sibling, turns queries into pass/fail checks. His best example is offboarding. Assert that a given username (his own, in the demo) does not exist on a host, because somewhere an old Ansible role or Chef cookbook still defines that departed employee, and the next run will quietly recreate the account. Were you looking for that? Another check runs against the Mondoo HQ GitHub organisation and asserts that two-factor authentication is required. Scanning GitHub settings is something he says few tools do well.

You don't have to write queries from scratch: there are ready-made query packs for cnquery and policies for cnspec on GitHub. The integration list on his slides covers AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, Docker and registries, VMware, GitHub, GitLab, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Okta, Slack, Linux, macOS, Arista, DNS, TLS, Terraform and Vagrant. Mondoo calls the approach extensible security posture management, XSPM: open source so anyone can extend it, cloud native, and covering the whole stack rather than one cloud or one layer. Mondoo's commercial platform adds reporting and visualisation on top.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers tired of running five scanners with five query languages, and SREs who already think in reconciliation loops and want one for compliance. If you want to see the tools in more depth, his colleague's security-as-code talk at the same event pairs naturally.

Title: Formula One brags about pit stops, not tyre uptime. Neither should you
Description: Mohammed Aboullaite (Spotify) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on ten Formula One safety measures mapped to DevSecOps, from canaries to reverse uptime
Body:
In 2020, Romain Grosjean's Haas hit the barrier at the Bahrain Grand Prix and turned into a fireball, and he walked out of it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, [Mohammed Aboullaite](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Mohammed_Aboullaite_move_fast_build_things), Backend Engineer at Spotify and a Google Developer Expert in cloud, used that crash to ask what software would look like if we designed it with the FIA's devotion to driver safety. His answer is ten Formula One safety measures, each mapped to a DevSecOps practice, and one idea worth stealing outright: reverse uptime.

It's a metaphor talk, and an enjoyable one. Most of the mappings are familiar practices; the F1 framing is what makes them stick.

## Safety, not security

Aboullaite came to this through Drive to Survive during the pandemic. He noticed the sport talks about safety, not security, and the dictionary explained why. Security is the state of being free from danger; an internet-facing system never is. Safety is being protected from danger, which is achievable. His thesis: "good architecture should allow people to move as fast as they can in a safe manner," Aboullaite said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. The FIA's own record backs him: as safety regulations piled up over the decades, deaths fell and the gaps between fatal incidents grew, while the cars kept getting faster.

## Five measures before the crash

**The six-point harness, released with one hand.** The driver needs help to put it on and one push to get out. That's push-to-deploy, and the lesson is automation: let a pipeline, not a person, check for vulnerabilities.

**Stringent dynamic, static and load testing.** Teams test cars in heat, rain, wind and cold tracks. The software version is a trusted, repeatable and adversarial CI/CD pipeline, plus canary deployments with error, latency and business thresholds that roll back automatically, because production is the only environment that behaves like production.

**A deformable crash structure around the cockpit.** The car is designed around a piece whose only job is protecting the driver. In software that's designing for failure: mTLS so traffic inside the cluster is encrypted even if an attacker gets in, and micro-segmentation that keeps data as far from the internet as possible.

**The five-second exit.** Drivers who can't get out of the car within 5 seconds don't race that day. That's testing for failure, which is chaos engineering: start by adding a few seconds of latency, take notes, fix, then grow to killing databases, instances and regions.

**Constant tyre monitoring and replacement.** Pit crews celebrate how fast they swap tyres, not how long a set lasted. "Why in the hell we as software engineers brag how long our servers and containers and instances have been running," he asked. He extends pets versus cattle to chickens: cheaper and faster to raise, which is to say containers.

## Reverse uptime is the idea to steal

Picture an attacker with root on one node, quietly using it as a base to attack the rest of the cluster. Now replace that node every day. The attacker loses their foothold and has to start over, daily. Aboullaite calls the maximum node lifetime reverse uptime. Pair it with base image freshness and you get a bound on exposure: even for a zero-day, once the image is patched, the longest a vulnerable node survives is the reverse uptime. You can't backdoor a system that keeps being rebuilt.

## Five measures after the crash

**The seat lifts out with the driver.** Modular cars and loosely coupled systems both make emergencies survivable: fewer dependencies to patch, failure isolation, independently evolvable services.

**HANS, the head and neck support,** spreads crash forces across the body. Elastic design does the same for load: load balancers, autoscaling, request timeouts, circuit breakers and exponential backoff. Degraded is better than down.

**Fire-resistant suits** keep the driver's body under 41 degrees for at least 11 seconds. In security terms, contain the attacker: least privilege, defence in depth, zero trust with no implicit trust between services, and a hardware security module holding the key for password hashes so stolen database dumps are useless outside your cluster.

**A fire suppression system** the driver or a marshal can trigger. That's access policy: allow-list service-to-service calls, RBAC and ACLs, neither too strict nor too optimistic.

**A data recorder** in every car. No system goes to production without monitoring and logging, especially security logging.

He closes with IBM's cost of a data breach figures: an average attack costs more than $4 million, and breaches took more than 280 days to detect.

## Who should watch

Engineers making the case for DevSecOps to a team that thinks security slows them down, and anyone who likes their architecture advice with a bit of motorsport. Security specialists will know every practice; reverse uptime is the part to take home.

Title: Base64 is not encryption, so put Vault in front of your pods
Description: Alain Lompo (ISO-GRUPPE) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on HashiCorp Vault internals and injecting secrets into Kubernetes pods with the agent injector
Body:
A Kubernetes Secret is a base64 string with good intentions. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, [Alain Lompo](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Alain_Lompo_managing_secrets_hashicorp_vault_kubernetes_clusters), Software Developer at ISO-GRUPPE, walked through how HashiCorp Vault works inside, from the seal to the expiration manager, and then the commands to get a secret from Vault into a running pod through the Vault agent injector, with Kubernetes service accounts doing the authentication.

It's a structured guide rather than a war story. Lompo, who works in the public sector and has 20 years of software development, training and consulting behind him, runs the demo as annotated command slides instead of a live terminal, which makes it easy to follow and easy to copy.

## What's wrong with Kubernetes Secrets?

They're the natural default because every distribution ships them, but the protection is thin. The values are not encrypted, "they are simply base 64 encoded, which means that anybody that can access them can also decode them," Lompo said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. Before picking a tool he suggests four questions: what are you storing (passwords, API keys, TLS certificates, GPG keys, runtime arguments), what storage options exist, how will the asset be used, and how does your application framework accept external configuration?

## How does Vault protect data at rest?

The architecture section is the part people usually skip in the docs and shouldn't. Vault treats its storage backend as untrusted, so everything passes through an encryption layer, the barrier, before it's written. A compromised backend gives an attacker ciphertext.

A Vault server starts sealed. At initialisation it generates an encryption key that protects all data; that key is protected by a root key stored alongside the data, and the root key is in turn encrypted by the unseal key. The unseal key is split with Shamir's secret sharing into shards, and a quorum of shards is needed to rebuild it. Once unsealed, Vault loads its audit devices, auth methods and secret engines, all of which are themselves stored in Vault, guarded by ACLs and tracked in audit logs.

## Tokens, policies and leases

Requests flow through the core, which enforces ACLs and makes sure audit logging happens. Auth methods are pluggable: username and password, GitHub, AppRole, LDAP and more. Policies are named ACL rules over paths, and Vault denies by default: no explicit policy, no access. The built-in root policy is the exception that permits everything.

A successful login returns a client token, used like an auth cookie on later requests, possibly with a lease that needs renewing. Secrets work the same way: when a secret engine returns a secret, the core registers it with the expiration manager and attaches a lease ID. Let the lease lapse and the secret is revoked for you.

## Getting a secret into a pod

Containers are ephemeral and a bad place to keep their own secrets. Lompo covers Vault as a KMS plugin for Kubernetes, CRD-and-operator approaches, and the most common path, the agent injector, which mutates pods to add a sidecar that fetches secrets. The nice consequence: a legacy app can get its secrets from Vault without knowing Vault exists.

The demo sequence is the useful bit to bookmark:

1. Enable a KV v2 secret engine at the path `internal` and put a database username and password at `internal/database/config`.
2. Enable the Kubernetes auth method and point it at the cluster's API host.
3. Write an `internal-app` policy granting only `read` on `internal/data/database/config`.
4. Create a Kubernetes auth role bound to the `internal-app` service account in the `default` namespace, with that policy and a 24-hour TTL.
5. Create the service account, deploy the app with it, then patch the deployment with `vault.hashicorp.com` annotations (agent-inject, role, and the secret path).

After the patch, the secret appears as a file under `/vault/secrets/` in the app container. The Kubernetes auth backend's main benefit, in his summary, is the end of manual token distribution: pods authenticate with their own identity, and tokens renew automatically.

He closes with a GitOps pipeline: Sealed Secrets encrypts values before they reach Git, Argo CD picks up the change, secrets land in Vault, and a CSI driver mounts them into pods.

## Who should watch

Engineers who know Vault exists but have never read past the quick start, and teams still committing base64-encoded Secrets. Vault operators will know the architecture already; the injector walkthrough is a decent refresher.

Title: Introverts should skip the hallway and give the talk instead
Description: Matt Harrison (MetaSnake) at Conf42 Python 2023 on consulting as an introvert - attitude, investing in yourself, investing in others
Body:
If working a conference crowd sounds like punishment, Matt Harrison has a workaround: be the person on stage, and let the people come to you. At Conf42 Python 2023, Harrison, a Python and data science corporate trainer and consultant who runs MetaSnake and has written several Python and pandas books, walks through how he built a consulting practice without enjoying sales or large groups.

He frames it as his own story, not a formula, and says so early: four kids, anecdotal data, and a US-centric view of the paperwork.

## Why consult, and why not?

The definition is simple: people pay you for your expertise. The upside, for him, is money, control over his time (he went skiing the morning of the recording) and autonomy over the work. The downside is sales, marketing, the invisible work of running a company, and competing in a global market that can look like a race to the bottom.

His first steps, if you try it: get an accountant, form an LLC (in the US), list the company on LinkedIn so people see you do work on the side, and if you go fully solo in the US, find a health insurance broker. The common thread is to pay professionals rather than save money doing their job badly.

## Attitude: there is more than enough work

Riffing on Drew Conway's data science Venn diagram, he reduces consulting to three things: attitude, investing in yourself and investing in others. The attitude is an abundance mentality: even in a season of layoffs, companies have small jobs they would rather hand to a consultant than hire for, and he says he has more work than he can do.

The conference advice is the sharpest part. Attending as a plain attendee is mostly a waste for him, because group small talk does not suit him. Speaking flips it. Matt Harrison said at Conf42 Python 2023: "Be the one who's dispersing the wisdom, and then people will come to you." He goes in with a goal, expects business from his talks, and says that while he gets pitched on LinkedIn constantly, 90%+ of his work comes from his network or conference work. Write down your goals; a goal with no action is a wish.

## Invest in yourself, including in a Windows laptop

Two cautionary stories. Asked to record the first Python course for Pluralsight, then a .NET shop, he recorded it on Linux; they wanted Windows, he refused, and he has heard the course that someone else made instead earned on the order of a million dollars or more. The lesson: buy the tools your client's world uses. The second story is better: turning a conference tutorial into a book. A book works like a business card, self-publishing is easy, and publishers watch Amazon rankings, so a self-published hit can get picked up.

He also argues introverts can lead. His onion skin of open-source participation runs from people who have heard of a project, to users, to bug filers, to PR authors, to committers at the centre, and he tells of a colleague who set out to become a core Python committer and did. Public work counts too: blog posts, tweets, open-source contributions, talks, screencasts, books. And take care of your body; his first book gave him sore fingers and sent him down a keyboard rabbit hole.

## Invest in others

Other Python trainers are partners rather than competitors. Ask people what you can do for them without expecting payment, run a mastermind group with people doing similar work, give clients a fair price and drop the ones who don't return the favour, and teach: he has taught Python, data science and drone programming to third to sixth graders. He recommends Mark Beckner's The Coder's Path to Wealth and Independence as the book that started him down this road.

## Who should watch

Developers thinking about moonlighting or going independent, and anyone who has stood alone at a conference coffee break wondering what the point was. No billing templates here, despite the abstract's promise; it is mindset and the first practical steps.

Title: Security fits in one design-doc question, if it's the right one
Description: Wiktoria Dalach at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on asking how the CIA of a project can be broken, at design time instead of the last sprint
Body:
Security is an ocean, and you are one developer with a deadline. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, software and security engineer [Wiktoria Dalach](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Wiktoria_Dalach_security_nightmare) offered a way to stop drowning: sort every threat into confidentiality, integrity or availability, and put a single question in your design template: how can the CIA of this thing be broken?

It's a short, friendly talk aimed at product teams more than security specialists, and it works because the speaker has sat on both sides of the review.

## Why does the last-sprint security review keep happening?

Dalach opens with a scene every engineer knows. Monday of the final sprint: two bugs, the docs, then release. Tuesday: the engineering manager suggests running it past security first, which means you must. The security team reads the half-written documentation and hands back a pile of bugs. At the retro everyone agrees this was painful, and by the time the meeting-room door closes everyone has forgotten.

She spent about a decade building software, mostly backend, before moving to a security team. The switch taught her the political half of the problem: as an engineer she was a peer in design meetings; as a security engineer she was another stakeholder getting pushback. And product people, she says, treat security as purely an engineering problem, while engineers scoping an MVP shelve security features under nice-to-have.

## The low-hanging fruit

Before the main idea, four basics:

- **Access control.** Roles don't have to match the org chart. A senior engineer doesn't need production access to customer data to see their feature, and the CEO doesn't need access to every AWS instance.
- **Secure your APIs.** An internal address nobody else knows is not authorisation. She calls skipping auth on internal services the easiest way to cause a data breach.
- **Misconfiguration hurts.** Default settings and plain-text credentials are what turns a server compromise into an admin-account compromise.
- **Let the machines work for you.** DAST throws malicious input at the running app; SAST reads the code base and can sit in your pull request workflow, flagging a fresh SQL injection before review. Small startups trade speed against security, but in a growing organisation, the earlier these tools arrive, the more the culture grows with them.

## One ocean, three buckets

The main idea is the CIA triad, and the move is to use it as a question rather than a checklist. There are infinitely many threats, but each falls into one of three buckets: confidentiality (secrets stay secret), integrity (we get what we expect) and availability (we can always reach the information). She declines the obvious spy joke in favour of the Spice Girls.

"Instead of looking at security as an ocean, you can use the question," Dalach said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. It works for front end, back end, cloud or not, junior or director, engineer or designer. Expanded per bucket, it gives you concrete prompts:

- **Confidentiality:** who can see this resource, how do we store credentials, what goes into the logs?
- **Integrity:** who can create, update and delete it, what happens when malicious data arrives via a form, could we spot someone deleting all of a customer's resources?
- **Availability:** is this endpoint rate-limited, what happens when a product we depend on is down, how long does the database migration take?

## When to ask it

At design time, which is what shifting left means. Her aside on the SDLC is the one engineers will nod at: it's drawn as a cycle, but in a decade of shipping she has mostly seen a timeline, analyse to release, then on to the next project. Changing a sketch means moving a few lines; changing shipped code is slow, expensive and stressful.

To make it stick, present the triad to your peers, discuss it with your team, and add a security section with that one question to the templates you already write: solution briefs, enhancement proposals, RFCs. Her closing line on the slides: move fast and break things is over.

## Who should watch

Product managers, designers and engineers who only meet security at review time, and security engineers looking for a lightweight way into the design process. Seasoned threat modellers will find it familiar; the value is in how cheap she makes it to start.

Title: CNCF graduated images look safer until you check what's in memory
Description: Yiscah Levy-Silas (ARMO) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on scanning 43,539 public images and why most scanner CVEs aren't exploitable
Body:
The most common high-severity CVE in public container images lets an attacker change the colours of your terminal. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, [Yiscah Levy-Silas](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Yiscah_LevySilas_unpacking_open_source_security), Software Engineer at ARMO and a Kubescape maintainer, compared CNCF graduated projects with the general population of public images and repos. The graduated projects come out ahead, but by much less than the raw scanner output suggests, because most of what scanners flag is never loaded or never reachable.

It's a research talk built on ARMO's own Kubescape data, and an honest one: she sets out to show the CNCF looking good and ends up qualifying her own headline.

## How big is the data set?

Big enough. Kubescape results stored in the ARMO platform covered 179 container registries and 43,539 images, plus 1,914 Git repositories holding 164,887 YAML files and Helm charts. The most scanned image was Argo CD at 19,426 scans, followed by Bitnami Redis, Argo's argoexec and several Prometheus images. In the graduated subset, Argo and Prometheus dominate, with core Kubernetes images such as kube-proxy behind them.

A detail worth knowing: Kubescape uses Grype for image scans, and Grype splits the usual low band into negligible (CVSS 0-2) and low (2-4). Medium was the most common severity in the general sample; negligible in the graduated one.

## Which top CVEs actually matter?

This is the good part. ARMO went through the top-ten high and critical CVEs by hand.

- **BusyBox, CVE-2022-28391**, in nearly 37,000 images. Remote code execution if you run netstat to print an attacker-controlled DNS record to a VT terminal. "Alternatively, the attacker can also change the colors of your terminal. Cute." Nobody runs netstat in a pod that way, so: barely relevant.
- **Libgcrypt, CVE-2021-33560**, in nearly 15,000 images. A real ElGamal side-channel that leaks private keys, but libgcrypt is there for GPG verification of APT/YUM packages, which uses public keys. She calls it not exploitable in about 99.99% of Kubernetes clusters.
- **SQLite, CVE-2019-8457**. Code execution via a crafted query, which assumes the attacker already has SQL injection.

After that filter, two of the general sample's top ten looked likely exploitable. Her slides label the threshold, a probability above 0.1, as a gut feeling, which is refreshingly candid.

The graduated sample's top hit was stranger: a 2015 protobuf heap overflow. It turned out to be a false positive, with Grype misreading a Go package as the C/C++ one (there's an open Grype issue for it). Five of that top ten survived the filter.

## What changes when you check memory?

"A vulnerability that an image scanner has returned is not always an exploitable security issue," Levy-Silas said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. ARMO's answer was a work-in-progress project called Sneeffer, which uses eBPF to see which files a running container actually loads, filters the image SBOM down to those packages, and feeds that back to the scanner. In one NGINX container, the scanner reported nearly 400 vulnerabilities; four were in memory.

Recalculated with relevancy, graduated projects are still better overall, but for critical and high CVEs the gap mostly closes. Her explanation for the original gap is plausible: CNCF projects are mostly Go on empty base images, with no distro packages bringing their own CVEs. The flip side is that a Go binary loads as a whole, so it's harder to tell which parts are unused.

## Are the YAML files any better?

Slightly. In the general sample the most failed control was immutable file systems (understandable, they are fiddly), then resource limits, then running as root and allowing privilege escalation. Graduated projects failed resource limits most, then missing readiness probes and immutable file systems, with somewhat better non-root and privilege escalation settings. A random workload failed 38% of relevant controls in the general sample and 35% in the graduated one.

## Who should watch

Anyone triaging a scanner report with four digits in it, and platform teams deciding how much to trust "it's a CNCF project" as a security argument. Pairs well with her colleague's cluster statistics.

Title: Every one of 10,000 scanned Kubernetes clusters was misconfigured
Description: Rotem Refael (ARMO) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on what Kubescape found scanning 10,000+ Kubernetes clusters, and why DevOps now owns the fix
Body:
If your cluster passed every security check, you'd be the first. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, [Rotem Refael](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Rotem_Refael_scanning_10k_kubernetes_clusters), Director of Engineering at ARMO, shared what the open-source scanner Kubescape found across more than 10,000 Kubernetes clusters: 100% had at least one misconfiguration, 65% had at least one high-severity one, and half failed 14 or more controls.

It's a short talk built around a data set. ARMO makes Kubescape, so the tool gets its pitch, but the numbers are the reason to watch.

## Who owns Kubernetes security now?

Not the CISO, Refael argues. Survey data on her slides puts DevOps (and its DevSecOps and other Ops cousins) as the role most responsible for container and Kubernetes security, and Kubescape's own users match: a bit over 60% of the people scanning were DevOps. "DevOps are the new security personas," Refael said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023.

The other half of her framing is a quote from Gartner on the slides: through 2025, more than 99% of cloud breaches will have a root cause in customer misconfigurations or mistakes. So the job splits in two. Posture management finds known vulnerabilities and misconfigurations early, ideally in CI/CD. Runtime protection catches what you couldn't know ahead of time, through behavioural analysis and network segmentation.

## Where the data comes from

Kubescape, a CNCF sandbox project installed with a Helm chart, scans clusters (plus Git repositories and container registries) against frameworks including NSA, MITRE and ARMO's own best practices, and reports to the ARMO platform. The data set skews small: most users ran a single cluster, 33% ran two to four, and about a third of clusters had fewer than five nodes. Roughly half the users were in North America and a third in Europe.

Scores are risk scores, so lower is better. Keep yours below 30; above 60 puts you in the worst 5%, below 10 in the best 10%.

## The misconfigurations that keep showing up

The top five: privileged containers, cluster-admin bindings, missing resource policies, containers without an immutable file system, and ingress and egress not blocked. Then the percentages:

- 63% of clusters exposed workloads outside the cluster without proper ingress blocking.
- 63% had workloads without proper resource limits, which she flags as a security problem as well as a noisy-neighbour one.
- 37% had applications with credentials in configuration files. Kubescape greps for passwords, JWTs and private keys, and keeps finding them.
- 35% ran workloads with insecure capabilities, and 23% ran applications with dangerous Linux capabilities.

"So, running privilege container is a big no no," Refael said. Her slides spell out why: a privileged container cancels the container isolation concept and leaves you exposed to kernel vulnerabilities. The fix is boring and well known: run as a non-root user and group, and set allowPrivilegeEscalation to false.

## And the images?

Worse. 63% of containers had one or more vulnerabilities, 46% had at least one critical, and 53% had at least one remote code execution vulnerability. The usual suspects at the top of the list were glibc and libpcre. Her rule is simple: a critical CVE is mandatory to fix, especially an RCE.

Her closing point is about volume. Teams are drowning in findings, which is why ARMO was working on vulnerability relevancy, flagging only what actually loads into memory at runtime. She saved that for a follow-up talk.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers who inherited cluster security without asking for it, and anyone who needs numbers to justify an afternoon of fixing securityContext blocks. If you already run Kubescape or a similar scanner in CI, the stats are the value, not the method.

Title: Engineers spend half the week writing, so make it count for your career
Description: Lauren Hayward Schaefer (Grammarly) at Conf42 Python 2023 on five kinds of writing that grow an engineer's career and three ways to write better
Body:
Knowledge workers report spending about 20 hours a week on written communication, roughly half the working week. At Conf42 Python 2023, Lauren Hayward Schaefer, Developer Advocate at Grammarly and a former software engineer, argues that this writing is the cheapest career lever most engineers ignore, and lays out five kinds of writing that build scope and influence, plus three ways to get better at it.

It is a career talk rather than a technical one, full of personal stories, and it starts with the most relatable one: forwarding her professor's thesis feedback, with a celebratory note meant for her mum, straight back to the professor.

## Answer one question a day

Her first strategy is to write to help your users, internal or external. Early in her engineering career, her manager told her she needed to show scope, and suggested answering questions on the company's user forums. She set a goal of one answer a day, often coding the solution first to check it worked. Over time she ranked in the top 1% of forum users by reputation points, people in other offices started recognising her name, and her manager's next suggestion, writing for the company blog, became part of the path to developer advocacy.

The menu is wide: forum answers, blog posts and tutorials, documentation, replies to bug reports, reason-for-outage reports, user emails, Slack or Discord chats, a newsletter. Her tip for finding the time is to read your career ladder; almost every technical one she has seen asks you to demonstrate scope and influence, and this is a way to do it.

## Writing in public is the scary one

Strategy two is writing to educate the tech community: Stack Overflow and DEV answers, open-source discussions, short posts on LinkedIn or Twitter, tutorials, even a book. The payoff is helping others and becoming known as the go-to person on a topic. She is honest about the cost: mean comments happen, and one can sit in her head for days. Her mitigations are a technical review from a trusted colleague and a copy edit before publishing.

## The 3am phone call is a documentation bug

Strategy three is documenting team knowledge. Answered a question twice? Put it in a README or wiki and point people there. Made a decision? Write a paragraph on what you chose and bullets on what you rejected and why. And document processes, because, as Lauren Hayward Schaefer said at Conf42 Python 2023, "it's nice to feel needed, but it's not nice to feel needed at 03:00 a.m."

## Compliments and the brag document

Strategy four is writing to encourage teammates. By her own account she is quick to criticise and slow to praise, so she made it deliberate: celebrating wins in team chat and thanking people publicly. A Friday calendar reminder works, and copying both managers on a thank-you email gives everyone visibility.

Strategy five is recording your accomplishments. Her advice is plain: "Do not waste your performance review." Log what you did and who you helped weekly or monthly, keep a doc just for compliments, group items into themes at review time, and update your CV or LinkedIn while the impact is fresh. She got her last two jobs through LinkedIn.

## Three ways to write better

Don't be a jerk, intentionally or accidentally: be empathetic, use inclusive language (she points to Google's developer documentation style guide), and get a second reader for tone. Practise: she ran a personal blog at two posts a week for a little over a year, which never made her internet famous but built her voice and speed. Educate yourself: a writing partner, an AI writing assistant, books such as Docs for Developers, workshops.

## Who should watch

Engineers who want the next level and suspect that shipping code alone won't get them there, and anyone who dreads their performance review. It pairs well with a calendar, since she ends by asking you to pick one strategy for the next month.

Title: Kubernetes features without the Kubernetes chores, on Azure Container Apps
Description: Bojan Vrhovnik (Microsoft Azure) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on running revisions, autoscaling, secrets and Dapr in Azure Container Apps without touching a cluster
Body:
At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, [Bojan Vrhovnik](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Bojan_Vrhovnik_azure_serverless_container_apps), Senior Cloud Solution Architect at Microsoft Azure, took a three-service app from his laptop to Azure Container Apps (ACA) and fixed it one revision at a time. The takeaway: ACA gives you traffic splitting, KEDA-style autoscaling and a managed Dapr sidecar while the Kubernetes API server stays out of reach, which is the point.

It is a demo-heavy talk and a Microsoft product talk. Most of the runtime is spent in the Azure portal, so expect clicks, not YAML.

## Where does ACA sit next to AKS?

Vrhovnik's framing is control versus focus. Azure Kubernetes Service is infrastructure-focused: full access to the API server, high control over the cluster, node-based pricing, and you install and maintain KEDA, Dapr or a service mesh yourself. ACA is a serverless abstraction built on top of Kubernetes, priced on consumption, with Envoy (ingress and traffic splitting), KEDA (event-driven autoscale) and Dapr managed by the platform. You deploy with the portal, the CLI or infrastructure-as-code templates, and no Kubernetes manifests.

The use cases he lists are the usual suspects: public APIs with blue-green or A/B rollouts, web apps with custom domains and certificates, background jobs that scale down to zero when they finish, queue readers, and microservices that want retries and service-to-service calls without writing the plumbing.

## Environments are namespaces, revisions are snapshots

An environment is the virtual network boundary around a group of container apps, with shared logging to Log Analytics. In Kubernetes, he said, "we achieve the same logic with the use of namespaces."

Revisions are the part worth watching. Each one is an immutable snapshot of the container app. He builds a small ASP.NET Core app in two versions, deploys both as revisions, switches the app to multiple-revision mode and splits traffic 50/50, so every other refresh through the Envoy ingress shows a different page. No Helm charts, no Ingress objects. Then he adds an HTTP concurrent-requests scale rule with a minimum of two and a maximum of ten replicas.

## The bigger demo breaks on purpose

The second half deploys a work-task app: a web front end on SQL Database, an internal reports API, and a background stats service that writes daily JSON files. All three images come from Azure Container Registry, and the stats service gets no ingress at all. Nothing works at first, because nothing is configured, and the log stream tells you so.

The fixes come in order. Connection strings go into ACA secrets and get referenced from environment variables. "Connection strings are sensitive data so what we need to provide is a way to secure that data," Vrhovnik said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. The API key and hash salt follow, then the reports API URL, and the dashboard finally shows stats. The background service, which wrote to a local file system that no longer exists, gets a new image tag that writes to Azure Blob Storage.

## Why Dapr shows up at the end

The blob fix works, but it hard-wires a storage implementation and three new settings into the container. Swap the store for Cosmos DB and you rebuild the image again. "This is where DAPR shines," he said. With the Dapr sidecar enabled on the app, the code calls a generic state API over HTTP and the component in the environment decides it is Blob Storage, scoped to the one app allowed to load it.

The demo then fails in the most realistic way possible: the sidecar can't get a token. He creates a user-assigned managed identity, grants it a data contributor role on the storage account, puts its client ID in the component, attaches the identity to the app and restarts the revision. Then the request comes back. Continuous deployment from GitHub Actions, tagging images with the commit ID, closes the talk. The demo code is on his GitHub.

## Who should watch

Developers and platform teams on Azure who want containers in production without owning a cluster, and anyone curious what Dapr looks like when someone else runs it. Experienced Kubernetes operators who want API server access will find the AKS comparison the most useful five minutes.

Title: You can't tame SSH keys, so stop trying and issue certificates
Description: Linda Ikechukwu (Smallstep Labs) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023 on why SSH keys don't scale and how short-lived SSH certificates fix sprawl and TOFU
Body:
Every authorized_keys file is an access list nobody audits. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2023, [Linda Ikechukwu](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Linda_Ikechukwu_introducing_ssh_certificates), Developer Advocate at Smallstep Labs, argued that SSH keys have a design flaw you can't operate your way out of, and that SSH certificates, signed by your own SSH certificate authority and short-lived by default, are the fix.

It's an explainer with a clear point of view and a vendor at the end: the last part covers Smallstep's own tools. The first two thirds stand on their own as a good primer.

## Are SSH keys really that bad?

Not on a small scale, and she says so. For ten to 20 devices or a home lab, well-managed keys are probably the simplest answer, especially now that servers can enforce hardware-bound private keys. The trouble starts at fifty, hundreds or thousands of servers and users. Do you hand out a dongle to everyone who needs a shell?

She gives three reasons keys break down in larger organisations.

**Key management is manual labour.** A developer runs ssh-keygen, sends the public key to an operator, and the operator pushes it into the authorized_keys file on every host they need. Teams paper over this with an AuthorizedKeysCommand script or Ansible runs that keep files in sync, and it's still messy. Can you list every key that opens a door in your infrastructure, and who owns it? Her slides quote NISTIR 7966: many organisations don't even know how many SSH keys they have.

**Keys never expire.** As long as the public key sits on a host, the private key works, including after its owner has left. Revoking means editing every server, and first working out which key was theirs. The slides cite an ssh.com analysis of 15,000 servers where 90% of the three million keys granting access to production were no longer used.

**Keys train people to type yes.** The first-connection warning is the client telling you it can't prove the server is yours. Nobody checks the fingerprint, the host key lands in known_hosts, and you've just done trust on first use, TOFU. "The truth is you can't tame ssh keys," Ikechukwu said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023. "They just have a rudimentary fundamental design flaw."

## What is in an SSH certificate?

A public key plus metadata, signed by a CA. She walks through a decoded user certificate: the type (user or host), the public key, the signing CA, a key ID that shows up in SSH logs, a validity window, principals (which users or hosts it can access) and extensions such as agent and port forwarding. One detail people trip over: you can't reuse your X.509/TLS CA, because OpenSSH uses its own, simpler certificate format.

Setup means configuring sshd on each host to trust the CA's public key for user certificates, and adding the CA to each client's known_hosts for host certificates. Hosts get a certificate when deployed and renew it on a timer; users get one when they need it. Then the handshake carries on like public key auth.

## What do you actually get?

Three things, in her order. TOFU goes away, because both sides verify each other against the CA. Static keys in authorized_keys go away, and since the certificate says who it belongs to, logs and audits get useful. And certificates expire: set them to 16 hours, or shorter for sensitive hosts, and a stolen credential dies on its own schedule rather than yours.

## Tooling, open source and otherwise

The open-source list: ssh-keygen itself, Netflix BLESS (a CA running in AWS Lambda with IAM), nsheridan/cashier, Uber's pam-ussh and Smallstep's step-ca. Her caveat is fair: the foundations exist, but dashboards, visibility and auditing are yours to build.

The pitch for Smallstep's paid product is SSO for SSH. A developer types ssh, signs in with the company identity provider, the OIDC token buys a fresh key pair and a 16-hour certificate held in memory in the SSH agent, and the day's sessions need no further login. Offboarding falls out for free: remove the user from the IdP and their SSH access ends. She also shows an Indent integration that lets approvers grant on-demand access from Slack.

## Who should watch

Anyone still distributing public keys by hand or Ansible, and anyone who has ever answered yes to that host-key prompt without reading it. Experienced PKI people can skip to the tooling list.

Title: Animated charts let business users explore data without getting lost
Description: Peter Vidos (Vizzu) at Conf42 Python 2023 on building animated, two-way interactive Streamlit explorers with ipyvizzu and a few lines of Python
Body:
Most dashboards answer one question and then make you squint at a new chart for the next one. At Conf42 Python 2023, Peter Vidos, Founder and CEO of Vizzu, shows the alternative his team built: ipyvizzu, an open-source charting tool that morphs one chart into the next with animation, now running inside Streamlit through a two-way component. His argument is that animation keeps people oriented, so non-technical users can explore a dataset on their own.

This is a demo-heavy talk by the tool's creator, and it was the first public showing of the Streamlit integration.

## How does ipyvizzu work?

Vizzu's core engine is written in C++ and compiled to WebAssembly for the browser. It started as an in-house tool, became an open-source JavaScript library in September 2021, and then reached data scientists as ipyvizzu, an extension for Jupyter and similar notebooks. ipyvizzu-story, a presentation layer for building animated slide-style stories in a notebook, followed at EuroPython.

The whole API is essentially one method. `animate` takes the data, the chart configuration and the style, plus optional animation options. Call it once and you get a chart; call it again and ipyvizzu morphs the first chart into the second. It remembers the previous state, so each call only says what changes.

## Titanic, one call at a time

The first notebook demo uses the Titanic dataset loaded with pandas. A bar chart of passenger count by sex gets the survived category added to the x axis and the colour channel, and the bars split into stacked bars. Move survived to the y axis and it becomes a grouped bar chart. Switch the geometry to circles, map the count to marker size, flip to polar coordinates: each step animates from the last.

A second notebook on music-format revenue uses presets instead of raw channels (a grouped bar chart, a split column chart, a stream graph), a custom colour palette, US short-scale number formatting, and an event handler that only labels years divisible by five. Filtering down to vinyl and streaming reads like zooming in, which is his point: since every transition is animated, nobody needs it explained. Peter Vidos said at Conf42 Python 2023 that the stream graph is the phase "my wife calls when the elephants kiss."

## What the Streamlit component adds

The streamlit-vizzu component was built by Zachary Blackwood, a senior data scientist at Streamlit, and is installable from pip. It is bi-directional: Streamlit widgets drive the chart configuration, and clicks on chart markers send data back to the app. The repo ships five sample apps:

- A minimal app where a Swap checkbox flips the axes and a click reports the value of the clicked bar.
- The music revenue data with a year slider and tooltips, a controllable cousin of the racing bar chart.
- A drill-down in about 45 lines: click a marker, the chart filters to that category and swaps the x axis; click elsewhere to go back.
- A sales explorer with four products and four regions, where radio buttons, a multiselect and a colour picker switch between sales and revenue, sort, filter, and change coordinates, and the title updates as items are removed.
- A larger music-history explorer with a year range slider, inflation adjustment and a sidebar of options.

One practical tip from the code: the animation delay defaults to about a second, so for an interactive explorer he sets it to 0.1 to make the chart feel responsive.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and analysts who build Streamlit apps for business stakeholders and want those users to explore rather than file requests for another chart. The demos are concrete and the code is shown next to each app. The live demo also hits a transition glitch, which he owns cheerfully, so expect the occasional rough edge in what was then a fresh integration.

Title: PyO3 turns Rust into a Python module with annotations, not glue code
Description: Moshe Zadka (Twisted) at Conf42 Python 2023 on wrapping Rust for Python with PyO3 and maturin - prototype in Python, move hot paths to Rust
Body:
Writing a Python extension used to mean C, reference counting and a long afternoon. At Conf42 Python 2023, Moshe Zadka, Principal Engineer and long-time Twisted contributor, shows the PyO3 route instead: you keep your Rust code, sprinkle a few attributes on it, run maturin, and `import` the result like any other module. Moshe Zadka said at Conf42 Python 2023: "Using rust in Python is surprisingly easy."

It is a short, code-first talk built around one deliberately small example, which is exactly why it works as a first look at PyO3.

## Why would a Python developer want Rust at all?

Zadka's pitch for Rust is a rare combination: a low-level language with zero-cost abstractions that is also memory safe. Sometimes, as he puts it, the "algorithm needs to go vroom", and that algorithm often runs on untrusted data. His prototypical case is low-level parsing of some new, odd format: no high-level library exists yet, so you go byte by byte, and you want that loop to be both fast and incapable of turning bad input into a security issue.

Python sits at the other end. It is easy to start, supports tight iteration loops, and then hits a speed cap. Rust is fast and safe but has a learning curve (mutable references, then the borrow checker and lifetimes) that makes it awkward for prototyping, because every interface change also means changing the types.

## The toy example: does a character appear more than N times?

To stay on the slides, the demo is a counter. Given a character and a threshold, it answers whether the character appears at least that many times, optionally resetting the count on spaces or newlines. The twist is that it only needs a yes or no, so it can stop as soon as the threshold is hit instead of reading the whole input.

The Rust side is plain: an enum `Reset` with `NewlinesReset`, `SpacesReset` and `NoReset`, a `Counter` struct holding `what`, `min_number` and `reset`, and a `has_count` method that loops over `data.chars()`. The helpers show off Rust features a Python developer will enjoy reading: a `match` on a tuple of (character, reset mode) decides when to zero the count, and `&mut u64` at both the call site and the signature makes it obvious which function may change the counter. Zadka is upfront that the code style and API are shaped to fit slides, not to be best practice.

## Wrapping it: attributes in the Rust file, nothing else

The PyO3 part is the punchline. There is no separate Python wrapper and no glue layer; the wrapping lives inline in the Rust source, so the binding changes whenever the code does.

- `use pyo3::prelude::*;` pulls in what you need.
- `#[pyclass]` on the enum, plus `#[derive(Clone)]` and `#[derive(Copy)]`, because PyO3 needs to copy it and there is only one sensible way to do that.
- `#[pyclass]` on the struct and `#[pymethods]` on its `impl`, with a `#[new]` constructor so Python can create a `Counter`.
- A `#[pymodule]` function that adds both classes and returns `Ok(())`, where the `?` turns a registration failure into a Python exception.

If the Rust code is someone else's, you write a thin Rust layer of your own around it and decorate that.

## Building it with maturin

`maturin develop` is the equivalent of `pip install -e` into the current virtual environment (rerun it after changes; it is fast). `maturin build` produces a wheel, including a manylinux one, though it is CPU-specific: supporting more architectures and operating systems means building on each. From Python it is then `import counter`, `counter.Counter('c', 3, counter.Reset.NewlinesReset)`, and `has_count` returns `True` for three c's on one line and `False` when a newline sits between them.

Zadka skips benchmarks on purpose, saying measurements were beyond the scope of the talk, but argues that an equivalent pure-Python loop would be much slower, and that the Rust version cannot hit an out-of-bounds error or a memory bug.

## Who should watch

Python developers who have a hot loop, a parser, or a Rust crate they would like to call, and who want to see how little ceremony the binding takes. Expect one worked example end to end, not a performance study. The workflow he lands on is the useful part: prototype in Python, move the bottlenecks to Rust.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Tim McNamara on [getting the most out of zero-cost abstractions](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2022_Tim_McNamara_maximum_benefit_zerocost_abstractions) at Conf42 Rustlang 2022.
- Dmitry Kudryavtsev on [speeding up Node.js with Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2022_Dmitry_Kudryavtsev_supercharge_nodejs), the same idea for JavaScript.
- Everett Pompeii on [catching performance regressions](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2023_Everett_Pompeii_catch_performance_regressions) at Conf42 Python 2023, for when you want proof that the Rust port paid off.
