Title: gRPC in Python, from one .proto file to interceptors and the browser
Description: Aditya Mattos (Kandji) at Conf42 Python 2023 on when gRPC beats REST, and how to build a Python gRPC server and client with protoc and interceptors
Body:
If your services spend their day calling each other, gRPC is worth a look, and in Python it takes one `.proto` file and a `protoc` command to get going. At Conf42 Python 2023, Aditya Mattos, Staff Software Developer at Kandji, gave a no-prior-knowledge-required introduction: why gRPC exists, where it hurts, a working Python server and client, interceptors, and how browsers get in through gRPC-Web.

It's a 101 and a good one, with a live demo built on Poetry.

## How did we get from SOAP to gRPC?

Mattos opens with a short history of web APIs. SOAP, from the late nineties and early 2000s, used XML and WSDLs shared between server and client: clumsy and error-prone. REST arrived in the late 2000s, modelling APIs as resources with JSON on the wire, and became the default. GraphQL, from Facebook, lets a client walk a graph and fetch what it needs in a single round trip, which is why it's popular on mobile and wherever bandwidth matters. Apache Thrift (Facebook) and gRPC (Google) solve the same problem, strongly typed and high-performance APIs, and gRPC won on adoption, so that's the talk.

## What you get, and what you pay

The advantages, in his order:

- **HTTP/2 natively**: binary framing and compression make messages smaller, and many calls multiplex over one TCP connection.
- **Code generation**: share the protobuf file and the client generates a stub instead of re-implementing the API.
- **Strong typing**: the protobuf specifies message types, eliminating a big class of untyped errors seen with REST.
- **Streaming**: unary plus bidirectional duplex streaming.
- **Deadlines**: the client tells the server how long to hold the connection; set a one-second timeout and the server can give up after a second.

The costs are just as concrete. It's newer, with bugs (patched quickly, he says). Browsers can't call it natively. You can't just fire up a client and hit an endpoint: you need the proto file and a generated stub first. It's more complicated than REST, and fewer of your users will know how to call it. His use cases follow: service-to-service calls in a microservices architecture (shared protobufs make malformed requests rare), point-to-point real-time communication, and low-latency applications. "Anywhere that you need fast speed, gRPC is usually going to outperform an equivalent REST API," Aditya Mattos said at Conf42 Python 2023.

## The demo: one service, one method

The demo project defines a `Greeter` service in a protobuf file with a single `Greet` method that takes a `GreetingRequest` with a `name` string and returns a `GreetingResponse` with a `greeting` string. That's the entire API. Install `grpcio-tools` and `mypy-protobuf`, run `protoc`, and you get generated Python files "not really meant for human consumption" (his words) that your code imports.

The server side implements `Greet` in its own file under a services folder (a convention of his, one file per method), returning hello plus the name. A `server.py` starts a gRPC server on a thread pool and calls the generated `add_GreeterServicer_to_server`, which he compares to adding a URL path in Django. The client opens an insecure channel to localhost on port 50051, wraps it in the generated `GreeterStub`, builds a request and calls `Greet`. Poetry scripts run both, the name goes in, the greeting comes back, and the project is on GitHub.

## Middleware that lives on both ends

The advanced section is interceptors, gRPC's take on middleware, except that unlike the middleware on most REST services they can live on the client as well as the server. A client interceptor can attach credentials to every message, and a server interceptor can validate them. Typical uses: logging, monitoring, authentication, validation and tracing.

There are four kinds. A client unary interceptor might add device type and OS metadata to a call; a server unary interceptor checks for a valid token and either lets the call continue or ends it. On streams, a client stream interceptor can add a checksum to each video packet it sends, and a server stream interceptor verifies it and asks for a resend if it doesn't match.

## Getting browsers in with gRPC-Web

Because gRPC was designed machine to machine, browsers need gRPC-Web: a slightly different wire protocol that works over HTTP/1.1. The web app generates a client from the same `.proto` file, and a proxy such as Envoy translates on the server side. In exchange, the front end gets the small binary messages too.

## Who should watch

Python developers who've only built REST and want to know whether gRPC is worth it for their internal services, with enough code to start a prototype the same afternoon. If you already run gRPC in production, the interceptor section is the only new ground.

Title: One login for every region - the identity platform behind OwnBackup
Description: Hila Israeli (OwnBackup) at Conf42 Python 2023 on one global identity platform with Okta, mTLS and FastAPI for users spread across regional silos
Body:
Data residency rules can leave a SaaS company with one customer and a separate user account for every region and product they buy. At Conf42 Python 2023, Hila Israeli, Senior Software Engineer at OwnBackup, told how her team fixed that with a platform: one global identity service in front of the regional silos, built on Okta, mutual TLS and FastAPI, which ended up changing how the company sells.

She tells it as a story with three characters, and it's a short talk; expect architecture at the whiteboard level rather than code.

## Why does John have six accounts?

John runs a small company using a backup and recovery product. He signs up in the US region. His company grows and serves customers worldwide, so he signs up again in the EMEA region and the Australian region, adding every employee each time. Then the company buys a security product with a different UI, and John repeats it all again. Adding or removing a user means doing it everywhere.

The reason, explained by Alice, the principal engineer of the tale: regulations keep user data inside its geographical region, so each region is a web server on EC2 with its own database and distinct URL. Like islands, a user on one knows nothing of the same email and username on another. Developers suffer too. Products written at different times in different technologies mean that reusing another product's ability is so awkward that people rewrite the same code again and again.

Victoria, the VP of product, sets the vision: a single login with one username and password for all regions, products and supported SaaS providers, centralized account and user management, one modern UI, and secure throughout.

## Don't build the identity layer, rent it

Alice's first problem is identity. Every database has its own version of each user, so the regions must be merged into one identity per user, with one global service for authentication, authorization, passwords, central account configuration and security settings like MFA, SSO and expiration. That, Israeli points out, is exactly what an identity provider is for, and OwnBackup uses Okta.

The login flow is standard OpenID Connect on top of OAuth 2: redirect to the Okta login page, return with an authorization code, exchange it along with the Okta app's client ID and secret for a JWT, and the regional service validates the token before starting the session.

## Fixing the problem you just created

A global user service talking to every region creates a new problem: that traffic must be secure. They use HTTPS with mTLS, so client and server each validate the other's certificate against the certificate authority, not just the client checking the server. Authentication isn't authorization, though, so services also use machine-to-machine tokens. The backup service in one region asks Okta's authorization server for, say, read permission on the global user service, receives a JWT, forwards it in the headers, and the global service validates it before answering.

## Gunicorn, FastAPI and Kubernetes

The platform is now the system's front door, serving thousands of customers across products and regions, so it has to be scalable, highly available and resilient; nobody wants John staring at an error page on login. OwnBackup split the monolith into microservices on managed Kubernetes (Amazon EKS) for self-healing, rolling updates and scaling with demand. Docker images build from a base image that's rebuilt occasionally, with separate service and test images, stored in ECR. Each container runs Gunicorn with FastAPI, chosen for performance and for its plugins: Pydantic for validation and serialization, SQLAlchemy for the database, middleware, and auto-generated OpenAPI docs that other teams in the company can integrate against.

## The part sales noticed

The payoff goes beyond fewer passwords. John gets one login, central user management, consistent security settings across the system and cross-product features: data in his backups can now be scanned and potential risks flagged to the security product. And once he's logged in, he sees the other products, can read about them and start a free trial without talking to a salesperson. Signing up to a new region and adding existing users is simple, so upselling gets easier, and new products launch faster because R&D focuses on business logic while the platform handles identity. "A successful product is a product that generates new revenue streams," Hila Israeli said at Conf42 Python 2023.

## Who should watch

Engineers at multi-product or multi-region SaaS companies stuck with per-region user stores, and anyone making the case for a platform team to people who care about revenue as much as architecture. Identity specialists will find the OIDC and mTLS parts introductory; the value is in seeing the pieces assembled and the business case made.

Title: A Raspberry Pi, Kafka and 120 dry readings keep the houseplants alive
Description: Danica Fine (Confluent) at Conf42 Python 2023 on an event-driven houseplant alerting pipeline with a Raspberry Pi, Apache Kafka, ksqlDB and Telegram
Body:
Danica Fine owns three or four dozen houseplants, and after going back to the office she came home to a badly wilted one she'd forgotten to water that morning. At Conf42 Python 2023, the Senior Developer Advocate at Confluent showed what an engineer does next instead of buying a gadget: a Raspberry Pi with soil moisture sensors, Apache Kafka, a ksqlDB query and a Telegram bot that messages her when a plant is genuinely dry.

It's the most fun way to learn the three pieces every streaming pipeline needs (getting data in, processing it, getting it out), and she says as much at the end.

## Kafka in three words

Before the build, a compact primer. Her definition of Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform, and each word gets a section. Streaming, as in the shift from batch to real-time processing. Event, which is the mindset: "In order to use Kafka successfully, you really need to start thinking in events," Danica Fine said at Conf42 Python 2023. An event has a when, a who or what, and supporting details: her umbrella plant at 2:30pm yesterday, 19% moisture. And events are immutable; watering the plant to 70% doesn't erase yesterday's dry reading, it just appends a new fact.

Distributed covers the rest. Topics are split into partitions, which are the immutable append-only logs; consumers track position with an offset and can share partitions or read independently from the start. A topic is a log, not a queue: reading doesn't delete anything. Partitions spread across brokers for parallel consumption, and replication (factor three in her example) promotes a follower when a broker dies.

## The hardware fine print

To avoid running infrastructure on her first hardware project she used Confluent Cloud for Kafka, managed Kafka Connect and ksqlDB in the browser. The sensors are I²C capacitive moisture sensors, a couple of dollars each, wired through a breadboard onto one input channel and addressed individually. The catch she didn't read in advance: the address can only be set to one of four values, so the first version monitors four plants.

Readings get an Avro schema (moisture percentage, the temperature the sensor gives for free, and a plant ID), because schemas tell downstream systems what to expect. Since she owns the code on the Pi, the producer API beats Kafka Connect: the script uses the confluent-kafka Python library and a serializing producer, looping every 30 seconds over the sensors.

Plant metadata (scientific, common and given names, and low and high moisture thresholds) also goes in through a producer, a slightly guilty choice for slow-changing reference data that would normally live in a database. With four plants, a database was overkill. Working out each plant's thresholds took a fair amount of letting plants dry out and checking the numbers.

## Making the Pi event-driven too

The first version had a hard-coded sensor-to-plant mapping in the collection script, so swapping a plant meant running a script, editing code and moving a sensor. She fixed both ends with Telegram. A bot built with the Python Telegram library walks her through a conversation (essentially a finite state machine of handlers, one per field) and produces new plant metadata to Kafka from her phone. A second conversation writes sensor-to-plant mappings to their own compacted topic, which keeps the latest value per key.

The collection script then consumes that topic with a non-committing consumer that always starts from the earliest offset, so the script stays stateless: on start-up it blocks until it has mappings for all four sensors, then checks for new ones between readings. A moved sensor propagates within 30 seconds.

## Six-hour windows and EMIT FINAL

Processing happens in ksqlDB, which she picks over hand-rolled consumers and Kafka Streams (Java and Scala) because it's SQL and runs in the Confluent Cloud console. Metadata becomes a table keyed by plant ID, readings a stream; thanks to Avro and the schema registry she typed only the key, not the ten or so fields. A stream-table inner join with `EMIT CHANGES` enriches every reading as it arrives.

The alert query is where the domain thinking shows. A reading every 30 seconds would mean an alert every 30 seconds, and the cheap sensors throw false highs and lows, though the trend is clearly downward. So: tumbling six-hour windows, count readings below the plant's low threshold per plant, and fire if there are at least 120, an hour's worth. `EMIT FINAL` waits for the window to close before emitting, so she gets one message per plant per six hours at most. "I love this feature," she said.

The last hop is the fully managed HTTP Sink connector in Confluent Cloud, pointed at the Telegram bot endpoint for her chat ID, pulling the alert text out of each message.

## Who should watch

Python developers who've heard of Kafka but never built anything with it, and anyone who wants a home project that teaches producers, consumers, compaction, windowed aggregation and connectors in one go. Her Linktree points to the collection scripts, bot and SQL.

Title: Tracing a pollution spike upstream through the sewer with ML
Description: Alex Smolyak (Kando) at Conf42 Python 2023 on using sensors, lab samples and machine learning to detect, classify and trace wastewater pollution
Body:
Somewhere upstream of every wastewater treatment plant, a factory may be discharging something the plant can't handle, and nobody can see it because the whole system is underground. At Conf42 Python 2023, Alex Smolyak, Data Director at Kando, walked through the data science that turns sewer sensor readings into an answer to three questions: is something happening, what is it, and where is it coming from?

It's an overview of a production ML pipeline in an unusual domain, told without code; he notes some of the algorithms are standard scikit-learn and NetworkX and others are proprietary.

## Why should anyone care what's in the sewer?

Two flows meet in the pipes. Domestic wastewater is what goes down your drain. Industrial wastewater comes from factories that use water in their processes and discharge it afterwards, sometimes carrying pollutants. Treatment plants cope with the usual ones, but every so often a pollutant exceeds its type or limits, and treatment, a delicate multi-step process where each step handles one kind of contaminant, gets damaged. In extreme cases the plant stops working; more often the effluent quality drops, and that water goes on to irrigate crops or back into rivers and reservoirs.

So Kando's users, the treatment facilities, need an alert that something is happening, a description of the event (category, intensity, likely damage), and the source. The source matters twice: it lets the plant check that the pollution makes sense for that producer and contact the facility to fix its pretreatment, and if something illicit is going on, regulators need to know whom to act against.

## Three data sources

Smolyak lists them:

- **Open data** about the deployment area: the mix of sanitary and industrial sources, where people live, what the industrial facilities do, and the surface topology that shapes the sewer network.
- **Kando's own sensors**, some off the shelf and some built to its specifications, producing time series that need to be understood over time.
- **Lab samples**, from Kando's own database plus external sources: a bit of wastewater sent for analysis, recording which pollutants were found where and when.

## Where to put the sensors

Deployment is a planning problem before it's a monitoring one. Combining the customer's network data with open data on industry and population produces a map of which locations matter, where fine resolution is needed and where an overall glance will do, traded off against the cost of deployment.

## Finding the event in the noise

Then come the time series, and the honest difficulty. "It's not that easy to know when something is taking place that is out of the ordinary versus kind of just the regular bits and pieces of what happens throughout the day," Alex Smolyak said at Conf42 Python 2023.

The event-detection process has three steps. Outlier-detection metrics generate candidate segments. The top-scoring candidates go to internal expert labellers, who name the event type when they can (often, not always). Then the labelled patterns are matched against the large pool of unlabelled data to enrich the dataset, with internal validation and corrections along the way.

## Cheap sensors trained to read like expensive ones

Classification goes two ways. The first is classic regression: train readings from an easily obtained signal to predict a hard-to-obtain one, using a subset of locations and events. Once trained, the cheap, data-rich sensors can stand in for accurate but cumbersome ones that are hard to maintain, making signals available that would otherwise be very expensive or almost impossible to get. The second is classification proper: with a large enough labelled or semi-labelled dataset, events are classified in real time by pollution type.

## Climbing the ladder upstream

Localisation is the part that sounds most like detective work. Sensor coverage is broad near the treatment plant and thinner close to individual factories, so an event is usually first seen somewhere downstream. Knowing the event's type, open data on the facilities suggests which producers could plausibly generate it, and the signals are pattern-matched further and further upstream, rung by rung, until the system can point to the specific or most likely source.

His takeaway is that the essence of the work is "to combine relatively easily obtainable data, whether through proprietary or available sensors, with intelligent processing techniques", so treatment plants get clear information they can act on with the industries around them.

## Who should watch

Data scientists working on sensor or IoT time series, especially with scarce labels and a mix of cheap and expensive measurements, and anyone curious about ML outside the usual web and fintech domains. Expect the pipeline's shape, not implementation details.

Title: Put the model inside the stream with Pulsar Functions in Python
Description: Tim Spann and David Kjerrumgaard (StreamNative) at Conf42 Python 2023 on Python microservices that run ML on Apache Pulsar event streams
Body:
A Pulsar Function is one Python method that runs every time an event lands on a topic, and that's enough to put a sentiment model in the middle of a live stream. At Conf42 Python 2023, Tim Spann, Principal Developer Advocate at StreamNative, and his colleague David Kjerrumgaard, an Apache Pulsar committer and author of Pulsar in Action, showed how to build ML-enhanced streaming apps as small Python microservices on Apache Pulsar, with Kafka, MQTT, WebSockets and Apache NiFi plugged in around them.

Spann admits up front the title is as long as he could fit. The talk is a Python client tour more than an ML talk: the models are small, the plumbing is the point.

## Why Pulsar, according to the person who wrote the book?

Kjerrumgaard takes the first part. Per his slides the project has 560+ contributors, 10,000+ commits, 7,000+ Slack members and 1,000+ organizations using it. The architectural pitch is decoupled storage and compute: brokers scale up for a burst and back down while the data stays in the storage layer (Apache BookKeeper), so topics can be repartitioned without downtime. Geo-replication has been there since Pulsar's Yahoo days in 2012, built for full-mesh replication across eight data centres, alongside replicated subscriptions and failure-aware clients that switch to a standby cluster without DNS shuffling.

Three features matter most for Python developers. The schema registry is built in, so Avro, JSON or Protobuf producers and consumers check compatibility on connect. Protocol handlers let Kafka, MQTT and AMQP clients talk to Pulsar natively; "Pulsar is the first and only messaging system that supports multiple messaging protocols natively," David Kjerrumgaard said at Conf42 Python 2023. And tiered storage offloads old data to S3, Google Cloud Storage, HDFS or NAS for 30 or 90 days or longer, and reads it back in place without rehydrating a broker first.

## A function is a lambda on a topic

Pulsar Functions are the lightweight stream processing layer, in Java, Python or Go. You implement one method; it runs for each event on the input topics, and whatever you return is published to the output topic. Third-party libraries work inside it, which is the ML hook. The example is a `Chat` class whose `process` method parses the JSON message, runs VADER's `SentimentIntensityAnalyzer` on the comment, labels it Positive or Negative and returns JSON.

Deploying it is one `pulsar-admin functions create` command: auto-acknowledge on, point to the Python file and class, the input topic, an output topic, and a log topic so anything logged through the context lands as data in a topic, not in a log file you have to go and find.

## The Python client, from hello world to OAuth

Spann's half walks through the `pulsar-client` library (2.11 at the time; `pip install` works on Mac, Windows, Raspberry Pi and Ubuntu, and only exotic hardware needs a C++ build). A producer is four lines: create a client, create a producer on a `persistent://` topic, send, close. For a cloud cluster you add SSL and `AuthenticationOauth2` with an issuer URL, private key and audience.

Schemas are Python classes extending `Record`; wrap one in `AvroSchema` or `JsonSchema` and the first send registers version one of the schema, creating the topic too if you have permission. His advice on mixing formats is blunt: "Create a new topic for everything you're doing," Tim Spann said, since a cluster can have millions of them. Consumers subscribe with a name, loop on `receive()` and acknowledge each message individually, which lets you leave an odd-looking message unacknowledged for someone to inspect later.

The same topics take other protocols: paho-mqtt for IoT devices (handy, though he warns it can be a little lossy), `websocket-client` with base64 payloads for talking to a pure JavaScript front end, and `kafka-python` pointed at Pulsar as if it were a Kafka bootstrap server.

## From stock ticks to a live table

The walk-through app takes stock trades from a REST feed, builds a `Stock` record with a timestamp-plus-UUID key, and sends it with JSON schema. A web page using jQuery and DataTables subscribes over a WebSocket with a shared subscription and adds a row for each message as it arrives. Apache NiFi does the ingest and routing around it, with guaranteed delivery, backpressure and data provenance, and it moves images and PDFs as easily as rows. Spann flags Python-based NiFi processors as coming in the next release. "But face it, most people use Python," he said.

## Who should watch

Python developers who need to get events in and out of a broker without writing a JVM service, and teams on Kafka curious what Pulsar offers. If you want deep ML, the models here are deliberately simple; the reusable part is the pattern. Spann's GitHub (tspannhw) has the sensor, thermal camera and transit examples.

Title: Word of The Hour - one vocabulary word, 30 social feeds, every hour
Description: Michael Wehar (Swarthmore College) at Conf42 Python 2023 on the Python behind Word of The Hour, and an API that adds its words to your own apps
Body:
Every hour, Word of The Hour posts one vocabulary word with English definitions and translations into over a dozen languages, across web, Android, iOS, Slack, Roku, Fire TV, Electron and more. At Conf42 Python 2023, its creator Michael Wehar, a professor at Swarthmore College, showed where Python does the work behind the project, and introduced a small Word of The Hour API that lets any Python app pull in the current word with one call.

It's a short, friendly talk: part tour of a hobby-scale multi-platform product, part invitation for Python developers to build language tools with it.

## Why one word an hour?

The goal, as Wehar puts it, is that language learning is tough, so the tool serves small, digestible content on a regular interval to keep learners going. Roku turns out to be one of its most popular platforms, where it runs as an active screensaver; the word of the hour sneaking onto the living-room TV is the kind of spaced repetition nobody has to schedule.

## Picking 200,000 words down to one

Python handles three jobs, and the first is choosing the words. The pipeline starts with data on over 200,000 words, generates features for each (based on frequency, dependency between words, and the contexts a word appears in), then ranks and filters them. The toolkit is plain standard Python: file IO to read the text and language data, dictionaries mapping each word to what's known about it, sorting to rank, and regex to detect patterns in the data. "In Python, all of these things are readily available," Michael Wehar said at Conf42 Python 2023.

## Crowdsourcing 40 languages through Google Sheets

The second job is translations. Users submit them into Google Sheets for 40 languages, and Python scrapes the sheets and merges the results with past submissions. The project has received over 35,000 crowdsourced translations, many of them edited and re-edited since, so the real count of contributions is higher. Two groups of volunteers stand out: Portuguese and Cornish. Yes, Cornish.

The flow is: read past data, request the sheets, filter submissions against basic quality standards, then commit the result to git, so every change is recorded and there's a checkpoint to see how the data looked at any point in time. It's a low-tech, sturdy setup: a spreadsheet as the contribution UI and git as the audit log.

## Posting to 30 pages every hour

The third job is distribution: posts to about 30 social media pages every hour, using each platform's API plus the Word of The Hour API or direct endpoints to fetch the current word. Wehar is candid that not all of this is Python today. One platform used to get images posted from Python every hour or few hours, and the Discord bot that posts hourly is Python, but other feeds run on other stacks. Adding a new page in Python means input arguments to choose where and how to post, some text formatting to satisfy each platform's rules on characters and patterns, and that platform's API.

## The API: call fetch and you're done

The part he was most excited to present is the Word of The Hour Python API on GitHub (MichaelWehar/Word-of-The-Hour-API). Clone the repo, import `WothAPI`, call `fetch()`, and you get a dictionary with the keys `word`, `definitions` and `translations`. His demo runs a `test.py` with four checks: the current word, whether there's a German translation, all translations, and the definitions. The word on the day was grant, and it had no German translation yet; crowdsourcing welcome.

## Who should watch

Python developers looking for a small, real dataset to build a language tool, bot or widget around, and anyone running a side project across many platforms who wants to see how little machinery it can take. It's short, and it isn't an NLP talk, so don't expect models or embeddings.

Title: The case for testing in production, made to a sceptical boss
Description: Vipin Jain (Metacube Software) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on chaos testing in production as a vaccine for distributed systems
Body:
Ask most managers whether testers may run experiments on production and the answer arrives before the question ends. Vipin Jain, QA Head and Product Delivery Manager at Metacube Software, spends his Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 talk building the argument for yes: chaos testing as a vaccine, a small, deliberate dose of harm that leaves the system more resistant to the real thing. It is an introductory talk, aimed squarely at testers and the people who sign off on their test plans.

## Why the vaccine metaphor?

He wrote the original paper during the pandemic, when everyone was talking about immunity, and the metaphor holds up well. In his words at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023: "like a vaccine, we inject harm into the system to build the system's immunity." The harm is concrete: added latency, a CPU failure, a network black hole, injected to find weaknesses before they become unplanned downtime.

The history is the familiar one, told briskly. Netflix built Chaos Monkey in 2010 after moving to AWS, randomly terminating instances to make sure the service survived it. The Simian Army followed in 2011 with Janitor Monkey, Conformity Monkey, Chaos Kong (drop a whole AWS region), Latency Monkey and friends. By 2020, he notes, chaos engineering had made it into the AWS Well-Architected Framework.

## Five principles, with the traps called out

Jain walks through the principles of chaos engineering one at a time, and the useful part is where he says how teams get them wrong:

- **Build a hypothesis around steady-state behaviour.** His template is a fill-in-the-blank sentence: under these circumstances, the security team is notified. The team agrees on what goes in the blank before anyone injects anything.
- **Vary real-world events.** Two failure modes here: variables picked because they are easy to inject rather than because they teach the most, and engineers picking variables from their own experience instead of the user's.
- **Run experiments in production.** Staging and production differ in ways nobody predicts, so confidence built in staging is confidence in staging. He is honest that regulation or technical barriers sometimes rule this out, and adds a firm limit: "If we know that an experiment is going to generate an undesirable effect on the production system or the outcomes, then we should not run that experiment."
- **Automate and run continuously.** Dependencies change underneath you, noisy neighbours saturate the network, downstream responses grow extra fields, and the engineers who knew the system leave. Only continuous experiments notice.
- **Minimise the blast radius.** Control groups, shadow traffic, excluding high-value requests such as transactions over a hundred dollars, and the sampling and sticky sessions Netflix's chaos team used.

## The known-unknowns matrix, applied to a database

The section he calls his favourite maps a real scenario onto a two-by-two of things you are aware of and things you understand. Region A runs a primary database with two replicas on semi-synchronous replication; Region B holds a pseudo-primary and two pseudo-replicas.

- Known known: when one replica dies, it is removed, a new one is cloned from the primary and added back.
- Known unknown: the clone happens and the logs confirm it, but nobody knows the average time from failure to a replica back in the cluster. Minutes? A day?
- Unknown known: two replicas dying at once has never been tried, so the time to clone both is a guess, though the pseudo-region is known to be recording every transaction.
- Unknown unknown: lose the whole Region A cluster and nobody knows whether Region B fails over cleanly, because nobody has ever dared to try.

That last box is the argument for chaos testing in one line.

## Selling it to the business

He closes with the benefits split by audience (fewer outages for customers, less lost revenue and fewer ruined weekends for the business, fewer incidents and a lighter on-call load for engineers) and the eight fallacies of distributed computing as a source of experiment ideas: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, and the rest. Packet loss and latency attacks test exactly the applications that wait forever for a packet or retry too aggressively once the network comes back.

## Who should watch

QA engineers and test leads who need the vocabulary to pitch chaos testing to management, and anyone new to the field. Practitioners who already run game days will find the principles familiar; the database matrix is the bit worth borrowing.

Title: Nobody ships the end-to-end ML pipeline; split it into three
Description: Jim Dowling (Hopsworks) at Conf42 Python 2023 on replacing the monolithic ML pipeline with feature, training and inference pipelines on a shared feature store
Body:
The end-to-end ML pipeline from the MLOps diagrams is a myth, according to Jim Dowling, CEO of Hopsworks. At Conf42 Python 2023 he argued that real systems are three separate Python programs (a feature pipeline, a training pipeline and an inference pipeline) glued together by a feature store and a model registry, and that you can build one without becoming an infrastructure engineer.

"You don't need to become a dockers or a Kubernetes expert in order to do ML ops," Jim Dowling said at Conf42 Python 2023. The talk is his case for that claim, followed by a credit-scoring demo.

## What's wrong with one big DAG?

He starts with the diagrams: Google's MLOps chart, Databricks' version, the classic TensorFlow Extended flow where data enters on the left and a served model leaves on the right, all in one orchestrated graph. "I've never seen an end to end pipeline written like this," he said. Kubeflow Pipelines gets singled out for promising reusable components that save you rebuilding each time, which he has never seen happen in practice.

His objection is coupling. Training deep learning models wants GPUs; feature engineering doesn't, so a single pipeline ends up burning GPUs on pandas. New data might arrive daily while predictions run hourly. "Inference should not be coupled to feature engineering when they run at different cadences," he said. A monolith also stops you reusing features across models and makes a minimal viable ML product harder to reach.

For developers, he says, MLOps comes down to testing, versioning and small changes: get a working system with a baseline, then improve it, with features and models both tested and versioned so you can upgrade one without breaking the other.

## The FTI pattern

His replacement is what he calls the FTI pattern:

- **Feature pipeline**: reads raw data, computes features (and labels, for supervised learning) and writes a DataFrame to the feature store. It's operational, so you schedule it with Airflow or something like Modal on an hourly or daily cron.
- **Training pipeline**: selects features and labels from the feature store, trains the model and saves it to a model registry. It can run on a laptop or in Colab, on demand, when the model goes stale.
- **Inference pipeline**: reads new features and the model, makes predictions and writes them where a dashboard or an operational system will use them, logging as it goes.

On the feature side he compares the options honestly. Pandas tops out around 10 GB and Polars around 100 GB, per his slides. Spark scales but is harder to debug and operate. SQL has low overhead but turns things like embeddings into UDF misery. Flink gives low-latency features on clusters of 10,000+ nodes, at the price of complexity and a Java-centric API.

## Point-in-time joins and the skew you didn't notice

The feature store earns its place in the middle of the talk. Tables of features are feature groups, each with a primary key and, ideally, an event-time column. Selecting features from several groups into a feature view lets the store do a point-in-time correct join, so no row picks up values from its own future. That's data leakage, and writing that join by hand is a wall of SQL; in the Hopsworks Python API it's a select and a join on two feature groups.

The feature view also carries model-specific transformations. Features are stored untransformed (a categorical column stays unencoded, because CatBoost wants it raw and gradient-descent models want it encoded), and the view applies a label encoder or standard scaler when it reads training data, batch inference data or an online feature vector. Do that by hand in two places and the training and inference code drift apart, which he calls skew. Because scaling needs state such as the training set's mean, the predictor class initialises the feature view at the training dataset version the model was trained on.

## The demo: credit scores on free tiers

The demo is the credit-scoring tutorial from the Hopsworks tutorials repo, run in notebooks on his laptop. A backfill pipeline reads CSVs of loan applications, bureau balances, credit card data and payment installments into feature groups; one has 72 features. A second feature pipeline generates synthetic rows from the historical distributions, a handy trick when the real data can't leave the bank. He creates a feature view with a label encoder on categorical columns and a standard scaler on numerical ones, creates a training dataset with an 80/20 split, trains a scikit-learn random forest or XGBoost model, and registers it. The batch inference notebook pulls the model and the new data and writes predictions.

He sketches a serverless stack around it: Modal schedules the pipelines, Hugging Face Spaces hosts the UI, and Hopsworks' free tier (25 GB of storage) holds features and models. He counts 40 or 50 public examples built this way, including air quality predictions for Poland and an electricity price forecast for New York.

## Who should watch

Data scientists whose notebook model never made it to production, and ML engineers drowning in orchestration YAML. It's Hopsworks' API on screen, but the FTI split applies with any feature store, or with none. His serverless-ml.org course is the follow-up.

Title: Gojek's A/B testing platform hit 2 million RPM by moving into a sidecar
Description: Riteek Srivastava (Gojek Tech) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on scaling an A/B testing platform from 100K to 2M RPM with a sidecar
Body:
An experimentation service is one more network call in the middle of every flow it touches, so it has to be fast for everybody, including the client running two experiments next to the one running hundreds. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023, Riteek Srivastava, Lead Software Engineer at Gojek Tech, tells how Litmus, Gojek's A/B testing platform, went from about 100K requests per minute in 2019 to about 2 million in 2022, and why the architecture that finally scaled was the one that pushed the work out to the clients.

## What does Litmus do?

Litmus does two things: experiments (A/B tests with two or more variants) and releases (a staggered rollout of the winning variant). His example is Gojek's driver allocation algorithm: instead of shipping a tweaked algorithm straight to production, you run old against new for a few weeks and let booking conversion decide.

The detail that shapes the whole design is targeting rules. Experiments carry rules such as an app version newer than 3.12, a platform in Android or iOS, or a latitude/longitude inside a set of circles. Every request has to evaluate the rules of every experiment a client runs, which makes the service CPU-intensive and makes response time proportional to the number of experiments. The non-functional targets were low latency, high availability, high throughput and weak (eventual) consistency.

## Why splitting reads and writes was not enough

Version one was a single Litmus server cluster on a Postgres primary, serving both the portal where experimenters edit experiments and the clients asking which variant to use. The traffic was lopsided. Srivastava said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023: "The read throughput is around six to seven x larger than the write throughput." Sharing one cluster meant heavy reads could starve writes, a single deployment touched both paths, and the primary database took everything.

Version two separated write servers (portal, primary database) from read servers (clients, replica). Each side could scale and deploy on its own. Two problems remained. All clients still shared the read cluster's CPU, so a client with hundreds of experiments slowed down a client with two. And it did not scale horizontally, since every new server opened more Postgres connections until the database's maximum knocked servers over. Both architectures held up to roughly 500K throughput within the SLA.

## How fast was it growing?

Fast, and unevenly. Active experiments went from 178 to 739 to about 1.8K by the end of 2022, with about 1.6K active releases. Year-end peak throughput:

| Year end | Peak throughput |
|---|---|
| 2019 | ~100K RPM |
| 2020 | ~500K RPM |
| 2021 | ~1.1M RPM |
| 2022 | ~2M RPM |

The distribution of experiments per client was just as skewed, and so were the expectations: a heavy client might accept a 50 ms p99, a light one has no reason to.

## The sidecar: every client pays for its own rule parsing

Version three runs a Litmus sidecar next to each client process. The sidecar polls the write servers every few seconds (configurable, five in his example) for that client's experiments, stores them in BadgerDB, and does the rule parsing locally. Clients never touch the database, so the platform scales horizontally; the write servers alone hold the database connections. A client with a hundred experiments gives its sidecar more resources, a client with two gives it one core or less, and neither affects the other's response time.

In PACELC terms, the sidecar chooses availability over consistency during a network partition and consistency over latency otherwise, a choice the team made after surveying its clients. Because the platform team now ships code that runs on other teams' servers, every sidecar reports to central monitoring on New Relic and Grafana. The screenshot that closes the talk shows about 1.61 million RPM at a p99 of 9.52 ms.

## Who should watch

Engineers designing any high-read, CPU-heavy internal platform: feature flag services, config services, authorization. It is a system design story rather than a chaos engineering talk, compact, with the numbers to back each architectural step.

Title: Fake 60,000 employees across every CPU core with Faker and pandas
Description: Mario Garcia (Percona) at Conf42 Python 2023 on generating test data for MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB with Faker, pandas and multiprocessing
Body:
Your schema is ready and your app is half-written, but the tables are empty. At Conf42 Python 2023, Mario Garcia, Technical Evangelist at Percona, walked through a small Python data generator that fills MySQL, PostgreSQL or MongoDB with realistic fake rows: Faker makes the data, pandas holds it, and `multiprocessing` spreads the work across every core but one.

It's a practical, follow-along talk with a public repo (mattdark/data-generator on GitHub), not a theory lecture. Bring a terminal.

## Dataset or generator?

Garcia lays out the two options. Grab a dataset from somewhere like Kaggle and massage it with pandas before inserting it, or generate your own. Percona has a data generator in one of its repositories, but it only works for MySQL, which is the gap the talk fills: one approach that covers Postgres and MongoDB too.

The dependencies are short: pandas, SQLAlchemy, tqdm for a progress bar, Faker, plus the drivers PyMySQL, psycopg2 and pymongo. He uses Anaconda with an `environment.yml` (Python 3.10), but a `requirements.txt` and pip work the same. For MySQL and Postgres you create the `company` database up front; MongoDB creates the database and the `employees` collection when the script first writes.

## What Faker actually gives you

Faker works through providers and their properties. Initialise a `Faker()` generator, call `fake.name()` in a loop, and you get ten random names that change on every run. The built-in providers cover person (name, first and last name), address (address, city, country), job, company and internet (email, company email), and the community maintains more. The demo table uses eight of them: first name, last name, job, company, address, city, country and email.

## Divide the rows, not the patience

Generating rows one at a time on a single core is the slow part, and by default Python uses one core. His fix is to split the job. The script reads `cpu_count()` and subtracts one, so on a 16-core machine it uses 15 and leaves one free. "This way we avoid that the computer freezes when using all the cpu cores available," Mario Garcia said at Conf42 Python 2023.

Each worker runs a `create_dataframe` function that builds its share of the 60,000 records (60,000 divided by the worker count, so 4,000 each on 15 cores) into a pandas DataFrame, and a `multiprocessing.Pool` maps it across the workers. `pd.concat` stitches the pieces into one frame. He shows the effect in Percona Monitoring and Management: every core busy at once instead of one pegged and the rest idle.

## One DataFrame, three databases

The connection module uses SQLAlchemy's `create_engine` and `sessionmaker` for MySQL (`mysql+pymysql`) and Postgres (`postgresql+psycopg2`), and `MongoClient` from pymongo for MongoDB.

For the schema he skips SQLAlchemy's schema definition language (it covers MySQL, Postgres and SQLite, not MongoDB) and leans on pandas instead. A plain dict maps each column to a SQLAlchemy type such as `String(50)` or `String(200)`, and `DataFrame.to_sql` writes the table with `if_exists='append'` and that dict as `dtype`. For MongoDB, `to_dict('records')` turns the frame into a list of dicts and `insert_many` drops them into the collection.

The last step fixes what `to_sql` leaves out: a primary key. MySQL gets `ALTER TABLE employees ADD id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY FIRST`, so the column lands at the front. Postgres has no AUTO_INCREMENT, so it gets `ADD COLUMN id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY` instead, one of those small dialect differences that bites at 5pm on a Friday.

## Who should watch

Developers who need a populated database for testing, schema validation or a demo, and anyone who hasn't used Faker yet. Experienced pandas users will notice the DataFrame is filled cell by cell with `.loc`, which is the main reason it needs all those cores; the structure of the script is the useful takeaway. The repo, the Faker provider docs and SQLAlchemy's schema docs are in his resources list.

Title: 60 bugs found before production by putting chaos in the build
Description: Ravi Bellam, Chris Ashton and Rohith Gundreddy at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on nominal and disaster chaos scenarios in CI/CD with Azure Chaos Studio
Body:
Fifty-five services onboarded, 60 previously undetected bugs found and 22 critical issues kept out of production: those are the numbers behind this three-speaker talk at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023. Chris Ashton, Ravi Bellam and Rohith Gundreddy explain how they moved chaos engineering out of the occasional game day and into the CI/CD pipeline, using Azure Chaos Studio, and how they split their scenarios so the pipeline runs the cheap ones on every build.

## Why shift chaos left at all?

Chris Ashton opens with the case for doing chaos early. Injecting faults in production can be fun and is valuable, but it can also cause the outage you were trying to prevent. His advice is blunt: "Add chaos engineering to your CI CD pipeline, test in a pre production environment." Most teams he describes do it in the integration stage, layered on top of the stress or performance benchmarks they already run, so they can compare the baseline with and without chaos.

He then tours Azure Chaos Studio, at the time of the talk in public preview: a managed service with an Azure portal UI and Azure Resource Manager APIs, role-based access control both on which resources can be targeted and on who can run which faults, and two kinds of faults. Agent-based faults run on Windows or Linux VMs (CPU, memory and disk I/O pressure, network delay, blocked IP addresses). Service-direct faults need no agent: shutting down VMs, a Cosmos DB failover, a Redis reboot, Chaos Mesh faults on AKS, and network security group rules. The neat trick is combining NSG rule faults with Azure service tags, which have a regional component, so you can cut off Cosmos DB in a single region and rehearse a regional failover.

## Nominal scenarios for every build, disaster scenarios on a schedule

Ravi Bellam covers how to scale adoption across hundreds of services, starting with the economics. Ravi said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023: "Our data suggests the cost of problem skyrockets as the software engineering progresses." The organisational answer is one shared platform instead of every team building its own fault tooling, and a split of scenarios by risk:

- **Nominal scenarios** are quick and low-risk: CPU, memory and disk I/O pressure, dependency disruption. They run in CI/CD as part of build qualification.
- **Disaster scenarios** are the big ones: Azure Active Directory or DNS outages, load balancer failures, Availability Zone and data centre loss, and load-driven cascading failures. They run in staging or a sandbox, and only move towards production once teams have repeated them and recovered with confidence.

The pilot picked critical services that together covered the compute, networking, storage and authentication stacks, so the standards would generalise. Telemetry before, during and after each experiment tracks whether resilience holds over time. The team also fed features back into the product, including faults for Cosmos DB failover, network security groups, Key Vault access denial and certificate rotation. At the time of the talk: 55 services onboarded and 65 more in progress, six using nominal scenarios for build qualification and two running monthly disaster validation.

## What the experiments actually caught

Rohith Gundreddy, an engineering manager on a key management platform, brings the concrete results. The service has a data plane on VMs, control and management planes on Service Fabric-backed VM scale sets, Cosmos DB and Azure Storage for data, a DNS-managed load balancer in front, and Azure Active Directory for auth. Each stack gets its own nominal and disaster standards, and the team also combines them, for instance load plus faults, because some failures only show under pressure.

Two findings stand out. Replicating 99% CPU pressure across the fleet in pre-production surfaced operation failures: higher latency was expected because hardware constraints prevented auto-scaling, outright failures were not. And slow packet transmission between compute and storage under heavy traffic crashed the services, which then failed to recover on their own. Rohith said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 that "these type of bugs are difficult to detect unless a real world event occurs", and now that scenario runs continuously in CI/CD.

To make it routine, the team built and released internally an Azure DevOps extension for Chaos Studio. Official builds run load, performance and nominal chaos scenarios in pre-production before they can ship, and disaster scenarios run automatically every two weeks.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE leads who need to sell chaos engineering to many teams at once, and anyone on Azure wondering what Chaos Studio can disrupt. The first third is a product tour; the payoff is the nominal-versus-disaster split and the pipeline numbers.

Title: Your benchmarks belong in CI, next to your unit tests
Description: Everett Pompeii (Bencher) at Conf42 Python 2023 on catching performance regressions in CI with pytest-benchmark and continuous benchmarking, not in production
Body:
You run unit tests in CI so a feature regression never reaches users. Everett Pompeii, founder and maintainer of the open-source tool Bencher, used his Conf42 Python 2023 talk to argue that benchmarks deserve the same treatment, and showed how to go from pytest-benchmark on a laptop to continuous benchmarking that raises an alert before a slow commit ships.

It's a compact, code-first talk, and yes, it is built around FizzBuzz.

## How does a performance regression hide for three weeks?

Pompeii frames everything around one line: "Detection is a prerequisite to prevention." You can catch a slowdown in development, in CI or in production, and it usually ends up being production, where users already feel it whether or not your observability tool noticed first.

To make the point he tells a story (flagged in the slides as a work of fiction, any resemblance to your last incident entirely coincidental). A Flask calendar API gets a fun notification feature: v1 returns Fizz when the day of the month is divisible by 3. Users love it, so v2 adds Buzz for 5 and FizzBuzz for both. Then v3, FizzBuzzFibonacci: on days divisible by 7, return the nth Fibonacci number. It ships, users love it, and three weeks later production is on fire. After a day of digging through three weeks of commits, the culprit turns out to be the textbook recursive `fibonacci(n)` that calls itself twice per step.

## Micro benchmarks with pytest-benchmark

The fix starts locally. He picks pytest-benchmark because it plugs straight into pytest (airspeed velocity, asv, gets a mention as the other well-known option). You install it with pip, write a test that takes a `benchmark` fixture, and hand it the function to time; his test loops over every 7th day of the month calling `fibonacci`. Run `pytest fun_notification.py` as usual. The naive version took over a tenth of a second for that loop, which is not what you want on a hot endpoint.

Two flags make it useful over time. `--benchmark-autosave` writes results to a directory you can commit to git, and `--benchmark-compare=0001` puts a new run side by side with a saved one. Swap in a memoised Fibonacci, keep the benchmark untouched, rerun, and the comparison shows the drop directly.

He separates micro benchmarks (unit-level, one function) from macro benchmarks (integration-level, say the whole Flask endpoint that reads the date, calls the function and returns JSON). Macro benchmarks catch regressions in the libraries you depend on too, at the cost of more noise and larger numbers. Same mechanics, same trade-off as unit versus integration tests.

## Why local benchmarks aren't enough

Fixing the Fibonacci function made him a firefighter for a fire he lit. His review slide sums up the gap: production is too late, and development is local only. Saved results on one laptop are tied to that machine and hard to share across a team, so nobody else sees the trend.

## Continuous benchmarking with Bencher

The answer is to run the benchmarks in CI and track them. Rewinding the story, he adds a benchmark at v1 that calls `fun_notification` for every day 1 to 31. In CI, install the Bencher CLI (a Debian package from the GitHub releases) and wrap the pytest call in `bencher run`, with pytest-benchmark writing `--benchmark-json results.json` and Bencher reading the file in and storing the results.

At v2 nothing needs doing; CI just keeps recording. At v3 the naive Fibonacci lands way outside the distribution of earlier runs. You set a threshold, and a result beyond it triggers an alert, in CI, before customers see it. He keeps the statistics light: reruns vary a little, the averages of v1 and v2 sit close together, v3 is out in the tail.

He's upfront that asv also has basic continuous benchmarking if you want something simpler, and that Bencher is his own project.

## Who should watch

Python developers who've lost an afternoon hunting for whatever got slow, and teams that already gate merges on tests but treat performance as something to check in a dashboard after the fact. If you've never written a benchmark in Python, this doubles as a quick pytest-benchmark tutorial.

Title: A good chaos experiment is one you expect to pass
Description: Narender Gakka (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on running chaos engineering as a program, from game day to pipeline
Body:
If you already know an experiment will break production, don't run it: go fix the bug. That is the rule Narender Gakka, Solutions Architect at AWS, puts near the start of his Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 talk, and the rest of it follows from there. Chaos engineering, in his framing, is a program of controlled experiments the system should tolerate, scaled across teams, and ending in automation. Randomly switching things off in prod is not on the list.

## What chaos engineering isn't

He opens by retiring the cartoon version: chaos engineering is not the thing that blows up production. AWS frames it with a shared responsibility model for resilience. AWS owns the resilience of the facilities, the network and the storage; you own where you put your EC2 instances, where your data lives and how you fail over. The questions he asks are the ones that keep architects up at night. What happens to your database when the Redis cache in front of it fails? Does injected latency between two microservices turn into a retry storm? Can you fail over to another Availability Zone, or another Region, inside your SLA?

The reason to answer them with experiments rather than good intentions is a line AWS likes to repeat. Gakka puts it this way: "You need mechanisms which come into play, and those mechanisms can be built using chaos engineering and the continuous resilience." He also cites Gartner's I&O leader's guide: 40% of companies would adopt chaos engineering as part of their DevOps initiatives in 2023, and the guide puts the reduction in unplanned downtime at 20%.

## Four prerequisites, and the fourth is the one people skip

Before the first experiment he wants four things in place:

- **Monitoring and observability.** Metrics alone are the known knowns; you need metrics, logs and traces correlated end to end (AWS X-Ray or an open source equivalent) so a CPU spike can be traced to a restarting Kubernetes node and a wall of HTTP 500s.
- **Organisational awareness.** A small central team builds common faults and guardrails, then the development teams run experiments themselves, because they already hold the IAM permissions and know their own workloads. Executive sponsorship makes it stick.
- **Real-world faults.** Bad deployments and expired credentials, infrastructure failures, data and state problems such as a database running out of disk, third-party dependencies like an identity provider, and the unlikely-but-possible loss of a whole Region.
- **Remediation.** Findings that touch resilience or security should outrank new features. As Gakka said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023: "There's no point finding it, but not fixing it, right?"

## What does a well-written hypothesis look like?

The worked example is a payments workload on Amazon EKS across several Availability Zones, behind Route 53 and an Application Load Balancer, with Aurora and managed Kafka behind it. The experiment is a brownout: the point where clients give up waiting while the server keeps burning cycles on requests nobody will read.

The steady state is a business metric, not a CPU graph: transactions per second for payments, orders per second for retail, stream starts for streaming. The hypothesis is specific enough to fail. At 300 transactions per second, with 40% of the nodes terminated, 99% of API requests should still succeed and return within 100 milliseconds; nodes should come back within five minutes and pods should be scheduled and serving traffic within eight. The experiment template adds the duration, the fault isolation boundary and the alarms that stop and roll everything back.

## From a staging game day to a production canary

The execution flow checks the system is healthy, checks the experiment is still valid (someone may already have fixed the bug), then builds a control group and an experiment group from synthetic resources, so a fresh cluster with the same code takes the fault while the real one keeps serving customers. Load comes first, the fault second. The tool is AWS Fault Injection Simulator, which calls AWS APIs directly, integrates Litmus Chaos and Chaos Mesh for Kubernetes faults, and reaches EC2 through Systems Manager; its stop conditions are the CloudWatch alarms that define your steady state.

Production gets extra guardrails: no first runs at peak hours, tighter permissions, a changed fault isolation boundary, and a canary that moves a small slice of real traffic into the control and experiment groups before any fault is injected. Then a correction-of-error review, and finally pipelines, because faults do not wait for deploys.

## Who should watch

Teams who want to start chaos engineering on AWS and need the process more than the tooling: how to plan a first game day (he budgets one to three weeks of preparation), whom to invite, and how to write a hypothesis that can actually fail. It is a methodology talk with FIS as the tool, not a live demo.

Title: Swap the vulnerability checklist for one question about the CIA triad
Description: Wiktoria Dalach at Conf42 Python 2023 on replacing endless threat lists with one design-phase question - how can the CIA of this project be broken?
Body:
You can't memorise every vulnerability, and Wiktoria Dalach says you don't have to. At Conf42 Python 2023, the backend engineer turned security engineer argued that one question, asked at design time, does more for a product team than any checklist: how can the confidentiality, integrity and availability of this project be broken?

It's a short talk, under 20 minutes, and it is aimed at developers, product managers and designers rather than security specialists. That's the point.

## Why does the security review always land in the last sprint?

Dalach opens with a scene most engineers have lived through. Monday of the final sprint: two bugs left, docs to finish, release in sight. Tuesday: the engineering manager asks for a quick security review before shipping. The review asks about the unfinished documentation, and the two bugs become a swarm. The retro agrees this was a terrible idea, and the next project repeats it.

Having moved from roughly a decade of backend work to her company's security team, she saw the same organisation from both sides. As an engineer she was a peer; as a security engineer she was suddenly the stakeholder with questions, the one blocking things. Her diagnosis has two parts. Product people treat security as purely an engineering problem, while engineers, busy scoping an achievable MVP, file security features under nice-to-have, where they stay. And security itself is an ocean: application, cloud and infrastructure security, vulnerabilities, threats and an acronym soup. In her first six months on the team she was googling three to ten acronyms a day.

## Infinite threats, three buckets

The hopeful part is the CIA triad. There's an infinite number of threats, new library vulnerabilities every week, but every one of them breaks one of three properties:

- **Confidentiality**: secrets stay secret.
- **Integrity**: you get what you expect, and your data isn't lost or tampered with.
- **Availability**: you can always reach the information, at 10pm or 3am.

Instead of walking a list of known vulnerabilities and ticking off the ones you don't have, you step back and ask the single question. "It's so powerful because it works for everything," Wiktoria Dalach said at Conf42 Python 2023. Backend, frontend, mobile, cloud or not, junior or director, product manager or designer, the question still applies.

## What the follow-up questions look like

Answering it means digging into each bucket with questions specific to your project. Her examples:

- Confidentiality: who can see this resource? How do we store credentials? Do we log sensitive data?
- Integrity: who can create, update and remove a resource? What happens when malicious data comes in through a form? Is the input sanitised? Are we protected against XSS?
- Availability: is this endpoint rate limited? What happens when an external product is down? How long does this database migration take?

She makes a special plea for the third bucket, because developers hear the word availability and mentally hand it to the infrastructure team. But every library and SaaS you add is a dependency. Her example is the feature flag service: if it goes down, does your whole product go down with it? "Don't skip it when you do this CIA questioning with your team," she said.

## Shift left by editing a template

The timing is where the triad pays off. Her version of shift left: the development lifecycle is really a timeline (analyse, design, develop, test, maintain, then on to the next project), and the last-minute review sits at the expensive right-hand end. In design, a change means editing a document or a diagram. Just before release, it means rework, stress and a slipped date; after release, worse.

Her implementation advice is refreshingly low-tech. Present the triad to your peers, discuss it with your team, invite the security team into design discussions, and make it part of the process, because "Security cannot be just an ad hoc action." The cheapest lever: add a CIA section to your doc templates, whether solution briefs, enhancement proposals or RFCs, asking how the new feature could break each of the three. Run that discussion with frontend engineers, designers and product in the room, not just the backend folks; the goal is a compromise between business and security that everyone understood before the first line of code.

## Who should watch

Developers and product people who find security overwhelming, and tech leads who keep losing the last sprint to a surprise review. Security engineers already fluent in threat modelling will know the material, but may borrow her framing for their next internal pitch. It's an intro, and a good one.

Title: Autoscaling won't save an overloaded service, but load shedding can
Description: Tanveer Gill (FluxNinja) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on graceful degradation with adaptive concurrency limits and prioritized load shedding
Body:
Once median latency reaches the timeout, half your requests fail, and a little more traffic takes availability to zero. Tanveer Gill, co-founder and CTO of FluxNinja, used his Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 talk to build that result from Little's Law, explain why autoscaling alone cannot fix it, and show how adaptive concurrency limits and prioritized load shedding keep a service useful while it is overloaded.

The last third demos Aperture, the open-source project from his own company. The first two thirds are vendor-neutral load management theory and worth the time on their own.

## What actually happens when a service is overloaded?

Every service has a concurrency limit: thread contention, context switching, garbage collection and I/O contention cap how many requests it can process in parallel. Little's Law, L = λW, ties it together: requests in flight equal average throughput times average response time. If L is capped by resources and W is set by the workload, maximum throughput λ follows. Anything beyond it queues.

So there is an inflection point. Below the concurrency limit, latency is flat. Above it, every extra request adds queueing delay. Gill's chart plots throughput against median latency and availability (requests served within the timeout), and the curve is brutal: when median latency equals the timeout, availability is 50%, and it falls to zero quickly after.

In microservices this spreads. A failing service A drags down service B that depends on it, and failure also spreads laterally: lose a few instances of A and the rest take their load, overload, and fall over in turn.

## Why isn't autoscaling enough?

Gill likes autoscaling for persistent demand changes and cloud costs, but lists three limits:

- It is slow to respond, especially for services that take a while to become available.
- It is capped by resource quotas, often shared across many microservices.
- It can amplify load on dependencies, moving the overload downstream.

The third is illustrated by the Pokémon GO migration to Google Cloud Load Balancer, the case study from the Google SRE Workbook. Scaling the load balancing layer let more traffic through to backends that could not take it, which prolonged the outage. "Auto scaling is not a complete solution on its own, but rather a piece in the larger load management puzzle," Gill said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023.

## Why not just set a concurrency limit?

Cap in-flight requests and shed the rest, and availability for admitted requests stays at 100% even when incoming throughput is far above capacity. The catch is the number. Too low and you reject requests you could have served; too high and the service slows to a crawl. And in a system with constant deployments, autoscaling, new dependencies and changing machine types, any static value goes stale. Hence the need for limits that adapt - which also protect against performance regressions, not just traffic spikes.

## How does Aperture adapt the limit?

An Aperture agent runs next to the service; on each request the service asks it whether to admit or drop. Policies are declarative and drawn as a circuit graph. The one shown queries the service's response time from Prometheus with PromQL, smooths it with an exponential moving average, compares the current value with the long-term trend to detect overload, and feeds an AIMD concurrency controller inspired by TCP congestion control: ramp the limit up gradually, back off multiplicatively when latency deteriorates. It integrates with language frameworks or slots into an Envoy service mesh without code changes.

The demo service handles only 10 concurrent users. A k6 load generator alternates 5 users for two minutes with 30 users for one minute. Without the policy, latency balloons during each burst; with it, Aperture starts dropping requests as response times turn and latency stays in a reasonable range.

## Who gets dropped first?

That is the question that makes this graceful degradation and not just rejection. Borrowing from weighted fair queuing in packet scheduling, Aperture lets you rank workloads: checkout above recommendations, subscribed users above guests. In the demo, with equal numbers of guests and subscribers and subscribers given four times the priority, subscribers got roughly four times the acceptance rate during overload.

## Who should watch

SREs and backend engineers whose overload plan is to add replicas, and anyone who wants a crisp explanation of why latency falls off a cliff. Watch the first half even if you never touch Aperture; watch the second if you want adaptive limits without writing your own controller.

Title: QA engineers should estimate testing, then say the number out loud
Description: Grzegorz Niczyporuk (Swing Development) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on why test estimation matters and how to defend it from "can you do it faster?"
Body:
Project managers ask developers how long a feature will take, and almost never ask the testers. Grzegorz Niczyporuk, QA Manager at Swing Development with more than twelve years in testing, used his Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 talk to argue that QA engineers should estimate their work, communicate the estimate loudly, keep it updated - and know how to defend it.

It is a non-technical talk about a professional habit, built on experience rather than formulas. He says up front that you can find the estimation methods on Google; what he offers is the approach.

## Why estimate testing at all?

He opens with fortune tellers. Poland, he says, has around 75,000 fortune tellers, bioenergy therapists and seers, and 56% of citizens use their services at $1 to $250 a visit. Yet in the QA job descriptions he read, test estimation never appears. His theory is blunt: nobody cared in previous projects, so testers stopped offering numbers.

Estimating is guessing, he admits, but guessing with rules. He gives four reasons it pays off: resource management (spare capacity on project A can support project B, and a tight deadline on A can borrow help), safety for the business, which knows when testing ends instead of wondering what the testers are doing, professionalism, because accurate estimates come from experience, and knowledge, because estimating forces you to understand what you actually test.

## What goes into the number?

The trap he keeps hitting: someone sees one test takes an hour, needs 20 runs, and writes down 20 hours. His analogy is a room of 100 people. One photo takes about 10 seconds. A photo of every person is not 1,000 seconds, because setup and teardown change. The sum of single task estimates is not the total.

A real estimate also includes the supporting work around execution: writing test cases, tracing them to requirements, reporting bugs and results, writing and discussing the test report. And it carries a buffer for what nobody can predict, from an unavailable environment to a requirement that turns out to be wrong.

## When and by whom?

When is not about project phase, but about what is happening around you. How stable are the test environments? He mentions a summer when the server room's air conditioning had to be shut down and the machines slowed. How stable is the application? Is half the team being pulled onto other projects, as happened during COVID-19?

Who should estimate: the QA engineers, ideally the experienced ones who know the project and the environment, though a newcomer can still estimate less accurately. Above all, people who are engaged and care about quality beyond the 8-to-4 shift. And the company culture matters: if nobody asks how long testing needs, be the one who starts telling them.

## Communicate, monitor, update

"The biggest sin about the test estimation or about the activities which we actually perform as a QA is the fact that we are not talking about this," Niczyporuk said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023. Say it out loud, even if nobody asked: one week, a full 40 hours. Then track progress against it, as ISTQB foundation material says, and update it. He borrows the cone of uncertainty from SAFe: early estimates have wide margins, and they narrow as you run tests and learn. Telling your PM you need two more days two weeks before the deadline is a very different message from telling them the day before release.

## How do you answer "can you do it faster?"

Every PM, PO or Scrum Master will eventually ask. He offers four answers:

- **Tell them what they already know**, fortune-teller style: it is a new project, the test plan they agreed covers critical functions, the risks and client impact are real.
- **Add a buffer that can be cut**, so the manager gets a win. He admits it is not very elegant.
- **Ask for priorities**: accept the shorter window, ask what to focus on, and put that decision in the test report.
- **Use your own authority**: if your estimates have held over many deliveries, say so. "So I know that it will just take that much time," as he put it. He recommends this one most, because it builds your reputation as someone who knows what they are doing.

## Who should watch

QA engineers and test leads who never get asked for an estimate, or get theirs cut, and PMs who want to understand what a test estimate should contain. It is a talk about professional practice, not tooling or chaos experiments, despite the event it aired at.
