Title: A first chaos engineering talk on AWS, from Chaos Monkey to an AZ failure
Description: Shirisha Vivekanand (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on chaos engineering basics and FIS experiments for CPU stress and AZ failure
Body:
If your team has heard the phrase chaos engineering but never run an experiment, this is a good place to start. Shirisha Vivekanand, Solutions Architect at AWS, used a Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 talk to cover the what, why and how of the discipline, a short history of its tools, and two AWS Fault Injection Simulator experiments on a three-tier ECS application: CPU stress and the loss of half the EC2 fleet.

It is an introductory talk, and honest about it. Seasoned chaos engineers will recognise every slide; teams on AWS looking for the first step get a clear map.

## Why does AWS frame chaos as Well-Architected advice?

Vivekanand starts with Werner Vogels' line that everything fails all the time, and with the AWS Well-Architected Framework's six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability. Three matter here, and the reliability pillar spells the practice out: run tests that inject failures regularly into pre-production and production environments. Chaos engineering is AWS's own advice, written down.

The business case is the cost of downtime. For Amazon.com's retail business, Vivekanand notes, even a few minutes of outage can hit revenue hard. "Waiting for the next costly outage is not an option," Vivekanand said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023. The alternative is to cause the failure yourself, in working hours, rather than let it find you at 3 a.m. on a weekend.

## What does an experiment look like?

Five phases: understand the steady state, form a hypothesis, run the experiment (usually by injecting faults), verify the results, and improve. The events worth simulating fall into three groups: hardware failures such as a server dying, software failures such as malformed responses, and non-failure events like a traffic spike or a scaling event. Anything that can disturb the steady state is fair game.

## Where did the tools come from?

The history tour is short and useful for newcomers. Netflix built Chaos Monkey around 2010 and the Simian Army added failure modes in 2011. Chaos Toolkit arrived in 2017 with an open API for developers and CI/CD integration, and Chaos Mesh brought experiments to Kubernetes in 2019 without changing the application's deployment logic. Kolton Andrus, who had built fault injection at Amazon, co-founded Gremlin, a hosted failure-as-a-service platform for hosts, containers, functions and Kubernetes primitives. Then there is AWS Fault Injection Simulator, with actions, targets (often picked by tags), experiment templates and stop conditions to keep the blast radius in check.

## Two experiments on a three-tier app

The test bed is a multi-AZ application: an Internet gateway, an Elastic Load Balancer in front of a web tier on ECS, another load balancer in front of an ECS application tier, and Amazon Aurora underneath.

**CPU stress.** Hypothesis: if CPU on a compute resource is under stress, the website stays available thanks to the system's built-in capacity. The FIS template uses a prebuilt action that runs an AWS Systems Manager command under the hood; you type start to confirm and watch the spike on the ECS monitoring dashboard or a custom one. Network packet loss works the same way through SSM.

**Availability zone failure.** The second experiment mimics losing an AZ by removing it from the auto scaling group's configuration and triggering a database failover. Hypothesis: terminating 50% of the EC2 instances across the web and application tiers does not hurt availability, and auto scaling brings capacity back. You watch healthy hosts drop in the ECS cluster, instances terminate and reappear in EC2, the auto scaling group count dip and recover, and the user's view through a CloudWatch Synthetics canary probing the endpoints.

## Once is not enough

The closing point is the one most teams miss. Recovery designs rest on assumptions that age: a replication job that finishes within the steady-state window today may not once the data grows. So run experiments regularly, bring in people who do not know the system for game days, wire tests into CI/CD starting with staging, and do not trust manual runbooks that silently go stale. She ends on Casey Rosenthal and Nora Jones: chaos engineering is about making the chaos already in the system visible.

## Who should watch

Teams on AWS new to chaos engineering, architects who want the Well-Architected angle to pitch it internally, and anyone who needs a short history of the tools. If you have already run FIS in anger, you know most of this.

Title: The chaos experiment went fine until nobody could find the runbook
Description: Yury Nino (Google) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on a documentation framework for chaos engineering, from team charters to postmortems
Body:
A planned chaos experiment turns into a customer-facing outage, and the fix sits in a script nobody on the team knew existed. Yury Nino, Cloud Infrastructure Engineer at Google and a long-time chaos engineering advocate, opened her Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 talk with that story and used it to argue a point the discipline tends to skip: chaos needs its own documents, and she proposes a framework for which ones.

It is a structured, practical talk: one cautionary tale, then a checklist of documents mapped to the stages of a chaos exercise.

## How does a controlled experiment become real chaos?

The story is fictional but painfully familiar. On a Friday at 13:50, a co-host announces the exercise in the chaos engineering Slack channel. At 14:00 they run the prepared commands to unplug some network links in production while the note taker records the time. At 14:15 all looks well: evidence collected, hypothesis confirmed, recovery prepared.

At 14:30 production does not return to steady state. The chaos lead stops the experiment, but an automated recovery procedure has already brought the isolated region back online, and customers notice. The failure is in a new component with no documentation. The development team does not answer the page. After 90 minutes the team finds a document with commands to restart the new service, runs it and crosses their fingers. It works.

"Luckily, all the characters and episodes in this story are fictional," Nino said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023. Her postmortem of the story: teamwork, communication channels and the experiment's isolation went well; knowledge of the automated recovery script, the unavailable dev team and the missing docs did not. First action item: a meeting between the dev and SRE teams, then document the new service.

## Why bother writing it down?

Teams tend to keep operational knowledge as nuggets passed verbally to new members, and when it is not written down, it has to be relearned painfully through trial and error - exactly what happened on that Friday. Documentation helps developers talk to each other, helps future engineers maintain the code, helps onboarding, and helps you learn from mistakes. She leans on an ACM Queue article on SRE documentation for the argument that high-quality docs keep teams from that decay as they scale.

She is explicit about scope: these are not the documents for building and operating systems, but the documents for the chaos.

## Which documents, and when?

The framework sorts documents into four stages:

- **General**: a team charter (vision, how the team operates, its top services, key principles), a production readiness review (architecture and dependencies, capacity planning, failure modes, processes and automation, external dependencies), and technical design documents. A design doc describes the system's steady state, which makes it gold for chaos engineers.
- **Before the chaos**: chaos policies (goals, what steady state means, SLOs and SLIs, outage and escalation policies), service agreements with user and internal targets, and on-call policies covering training, shifts, pager load and compensation.
- **During the chaos**: the chaos engineering design, which she calls the most important document of all - application, hypothesis, environment, duration and load, results, observability and actions. "It is like an airplane black box," she says. Next to it sit playbooks for each alert (verification, troubleshooting, escalation) and incident management documents covering hand-off, escalation, responsibilities and dashboards.
- **After the chaos**: postmortems (what went well, what didn't, lessons, prioritised action items) and reliability reports for management, with each indicator's collection method, formula, targets, data source and revision date.

The playbook is where the opening story turns. Had the engineer in it had one, Nino says, the incident could have been resolved in minutes rather than after a frantic intranet search. She also gives technical writers a role: partnering with chaos engineers on operational docs and improving the tooling around them.

## Who should watch

Teams about to run their first game day in production, SRE leads who want a checklist before they let anyone unplug anything, and anyone who has ever searched the intranet during an incident. It is a framework talk, so expect lists of sections rather than tools; pair it with a hands-on talk and you have both halves.

Title: One bad pod owns your cluster, and PSP's replacements won't save you
Description: Chris Nesbitt-Smith (UK Government) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on the death of PodSecurityPolicy and why cluster-enforced policy is not real security
Body:
A vanilla Debian container with one hostPath volume is enough to take over a Kubernetes cluster, no tooling required. Chris Nesbitt-Smith, a consultant with the UK Government and a Kubernetes user since 0.4, shows it live at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023, then walks through what replaces the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy - and finishes by arguing that none of the replacements gives you real security on their own.

He warns early that he has opinions, and he is not lying. It is a fast, funny, recorded-in-a-room talk that takes you on what he calls a roller coaster: problem, solution, problem, tool, problem.

## What can one bad pod actually do?

PodSecurityPolicy let cluster admins limit what pods could do: run as root, open host ports, mount certain volume types. Nesbitt-Smith shows what happens when those limits are missing. On a fresh kind cluster, he starts a plain Debian pod that mounts the host's root filesystem, then puts the host's binaries on his path, symlinks in the kubelet's config and uses the kubelet's own certificates to talk to the API server.

From there he can list every pod and node. The API server rightly refuses a kubectl exec from a kubelet, but that barely matters: impersonating a node, he can relabel it, pull workloads onto the node he owns, talk to the container runtime socket, cordon and drain every other node and copy their taints and tolerations onto his own. A pod on the host network is a quieter path to the same end: grab port 443 or 80 once the real ingress pod is gone and sit between your users and your apps. "You can be kind of one bad pod away from losing absolutely everything that you own," he said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023.

## Why did PodSecurityPolicy die?

PSPs existed since Kubernetes 1.0 and never left beta. They were deprecated in 1.21 and removed in 1.25. The idea was sound; the usability was not:

- The policy is tied to the user who created the pod, not the workload. Nobody creates pods - deployments, stateful sets and jobs do, so the identity in play is a controller's service account.
- Some fields do not just accept or reject; they mutate the pod, which the docs do not make clear.
- With several overlapping policies, evaluation order is confusing and in some ways unpredictable.
- It only applies to new pods, so a policy change can break a running workload silently until the next reschedule, when a node fails at the worst possible moment.

## What replaces it?

The built-in answer is Pod Security Standards with Pod Security Admission: three fixed levels. Privileged is anything goes, baseline stops the obvious attacks and most workloads should run there unchanged, and restricted is the one to aspire to. Fixed, universal levels are easy to communicate and test. The catch: they apply per namespace, via a label, with no fine-grained exemptions. One workload that cannot meet restricted drags its whole namespace down a level. His verdict on who benefits is dry: mainly vendors shipping software onto Kubernetes, who can prove it runs under restricted.

For everything else there is a long list of admission tools - Kyverno, Kubewarden, OPA Gatekeeper, jsPolicy, Polaris and more - or your own webhook, which is just something that answers 200 or not 200. There is no like-for-like mapping from PSP, and he recommends refactoring tangled old policies rather than porting them. Still, he built a converter that takes an existing PSP and emits Kyverno, Kubewarden or Gatekeeper policies, and demos it in the browser, bugs and all; some mappings fail because of limits in the engines themselves.

## So should you migrate at all?

Here is the twist. "Using a cluster enforced policy does not guarantee any real security," he says, and the cure may be worse than the disease. The vulnerabilities trending in the wild - PwnKit, Dirty Pipe, Dirty COW - are attacks admission policy would not stop. The answers, he says, "are simple, but not necessarily easy", and he runs out of time before giving them, leaving a list instead: seccomp, AppArmor, SELinux, kernel-level protection, eBPF, version-controlled policy as code, GitOps, testing, secure by design, zero trust, and the cultural change that has to go with it.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who still have PSP-shaped holes in their mental model of Kubernetes security, and anyone who thinks an admission controller is the end of the story. The demo alone is worth showing to whoever keeps asking for cluster-admin. The ending is a tease, so budget time for the follow-up reading.

Title: Chaos-test the ingress controller, the data plane must keep proxying
Description: Jintao Zhang (API7.AI) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on using LitmusChaos to prove Apache APISIX Ingress keeps serving traffic when its controller fails
Body:
An ingress controller has one job that matters, and Jintao Zhang knows it: "Proxy traffic is the most important capability so I write it three times," he said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023. Zhang, Technical Expert at API7.AI, Apache APISIX PMC member and a Kubernetes Ingress-NGINX maintainer, showed how the APISIX Ingress project used LitmusChaos to check that traffic keeps flowing when the controller itself misbehaves - and the bug it turned up.

It is a compact maintainer's talk: one open-source project testing another, with a clear method you can lift for your own controllers and operators.

## Where can an ingress controller break?

Zhang starts with the basics. An Ingress is a deliberately simple Kubernetes resource holding routing rules. It does nothing on its own: an ingress controller watches those resources and translates them into proxy configuration. Real deployments need more than the spec offers (access limits, authentication), so controllers extend it with annotations, and every controller does it differently.

Apache APISIX Ingress uses APISIX as the data plane, with nearly 100 built-in plugins, and accepts three configuration styles: plain Ingress, the Gateway API and its own CRDs. The architecture choice that makes the chaos story interesting is the separation of planes. The controller handles routing rules but carries no traffic; every client request goes through the data plane. A retry module re-syncs rules to the data plane once the control plane comes back.

## Which experiments are worth running?

This is the part to steal. Zhang walks the path a configuration takes: user applies Ingress, Gateway API or CRD objects, kube-apiserver authenticates and stores them in etcd, the controller watches and translates, the data plane routes client requests upstream. Then he crosses out what does not need an experiment:

- If kube-apiserver fails, writes fail. Obvious, so no experiment.
- If the data plane itself crashes or loses its network, traffic stops. Also obvious.
- Bad configuration is already covered by end-to-end tests.

What is left is the interesting question: when the ingress controller has a problem - a DNS error, a network interruption, its pod killed - can the data plane still proxy requests normally? The hypothesis follows the template: when the controller pod gets hit with fault X, the client's request still gets a normal response.

His method is the standard five steps, done properly: define the system under test, choose the right experiment, establish a hypothesis, run it (in a controlled environment such as staging, with SLOs in mind), and evaluate the results against the hypothesis.

## Why LitmusChaos?

LitmusChaos is a CNCF incubating chaos framework for Kubernetes, declarative and extensible. Asked why he picked it, Zhang's answer is refreshingly unmarketed: it has the functions he needs and he knows it best. Experiments can be built in the ChaosCenter portal or submitted as YAML manifests, and can be scheduled. He calls out Litmus probes - pluggable checks attached to the chaos engine that decide whether an experiment passed. Results come from the built-in statistics reports; Prometheus and Grafana integration exists, but his scenario did not need it.

## What did it find?

The experiments built confidence that the data plane holds when the controller fails, which matters for a project with many production users. They also found a real bug: after the ingress controller pod was restarted multiple times, configuration could become invalid. The GitHub issue on the project's tracker describes `resolveGranularity: service` no longer taking effect after repeated restarts of the controller. It has been fixed.

Next steps at the time: run the Litmus experiments in the APISIX Ingress project's CI and publish reference docs and examples so users can run the same chaos in their own environments.

## Who should watch

Maintainers of Kubernetes controllers and operators, platform teams running an ingress or gateway, and anyone who wants a worked example of scoping chaos experiments by ruling out the obvious first.

Title: A meta operating system for apps spread from cloud to IoT
Description: Radoslaw Piliszek (7bulls.com) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on NebulOuS, an EU-funded meta OS that brokers apps across cloud, fog, edge and IoT on Kubernetes
Body:
Not every workload belongs in a public cloud region, and not every on-prem rack deserves to be thrown away. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Radoslaw Piliszek, SysAdmin and Programmer at 7bulls.com, introduces NebulOuS, an EU-funded open source project building a meta operating system that places one application across public clouds, private data centres, edge sites and IoT devices, with Kubernetes as the backbone.

Honest scope: the talk was recorded a few months into a three-year project. It's strong on definitions and goals, and the architecture is, in his words, still early.

## What is a cloud continuum?

Piliszek borrows the definition from Sergio Moreschini et al. (IEEE Access, 2022): an extension of the traditional cloud towards multiple entities such as edge, fog and IoT that provide analysis, processing, storage and data generation capabilities. The word he underlines is data. As he puts it, "it's actually no computation without the data": data is generated by humans or sensors, stored transiently or persistently, moved between nodes, and processed by people or automation. Where each of those happens is the thing to optimise.

He lays out the layers: public clouds; fog (your data centres and private clouds, OpenStack included); edge, meaning smaller sites, micro data centres and telco multi-access edge computing; and finally the IoT devices producing much of the data. Then he separates the terms that tend to get blurred: multi-cloud is two or more public clouds, hybrid cloud is a public cloud plus something that isn't one (possibly just a data centre not even managed like a cloud), and the continuum generalises both. "So you have the cloud continuum when you just go mix and match as you wish," Radoslaw Piliszek said at Conf42 DevOps 2023.

## Why isn't the cloud enough?

He lists technical constraints a cloud-only design can miss: latency and bandwidth, specialised hardware such as FPGAs, and IoT devices that rarely talk to the cloud directly. Then the non-technical ones: GDPR, CCPA, PCI DSS, HIPAA and internal compliance rules, sometimes requiring data to stay off the cloud entirely. And there's the business side: companies that haven't migrated and want to keep their existing investment, and companies leaving the cloud after a cost explosion, often having learned the hard way what lift-and-shift costs.

## What does meta operating system mean here?

He builds the term up from Wikipedia's definition of an operating system, software that manages hardware and software resources and provides common services to programs, and adds the Greek prefix meta, meaning after or beyond. A meta operating system manages sets of computer resources and provides common services to the programs running on them. NebulOuS's full name spells out the job: a Meta Operating System for Brokering Hyper-Distributed Applications on Cloud Computing Continuums. Brokering here means picking the best mix of resources for a given application.

## What is the project actually building?

From the talk and its slides:

- **Who and when**: a consortium of 16 organisations, academic and business, tool providers and use-case owners, running September 2022 to August 2025, funded by the European Union.
- **Licence**: developed in the open under the Mozilla Public License 2.0.
- **Directions of work**: modelling the infrastructure, application requirements and data streams so the platform can assure quality of service; multi-criteria decision-making to compare offers; security across the continuum; and service level agreements based on smart contracts, so violations are detected automatically rather than argued over in a PDF.
- **Building blocks**: reuse of open source multi-cloud components from earlier EU projects (Melodic, Functionizer and Morphemic, the last still in progress at the time) and Kubernetes. Applications are modelled declaratively in YAML, GitOps-friendly, using Kubernetes custom resource definitions with custom controllers.
- **Open call**: a 1.35 million EUR fund for nine grants, with the first round planned for 2024, for teams bringing an IoT-to-edge-to-cloud use case to test the platform.

The architecture sketch is a two-layer orchestration. A Kubernetes-driven core takes descriptions of the available infrastructure, the application and its data streams. Each site (public cloud, private cloud or data centre, edge or fog node) runs its own local Kubernetes cluster federated with the core. The core makes the first placement decision and the local clusters handle the rest. The team was also working out fault tolerance, so a site cut off from the core keeps running and optimising locally, possibly in a degraded mode.

## Who should watch

Architects dealing with data that can't or shouldn't all go to one public cloud: IoT, regulated data, latency-sensitive workloads. It's a good primer on continuum vocabulary and on how an EU research project frames the problem, not a product demo.

Title: Your internal developer platform needs a product manager
Description: Gal Bashan (Cisco) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on why platform engineering becomes another silo unless the IDP is run as a product, with a PM
Body:
DevOps was supposed to break down the silo between dev and ops, and mostly renamed it. SRE did the same. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Gal Bashan, Head of Engineering at Cisco, asks how platform engineering avoids becoming the third rebrand of the same wall, and his answer is that the internal developer platform (IDP) has to be treated as a product, with a product manager in charge of it.

## Why does every new practice end up as two groups again?

Bashan's history runs from the dev and ops silos of the 1990s and 2000s, through DevOps around 2008, to SRE around 2018. He cites a Humanitec benchmarking study putting the share of organisations that reached the DevOps ideal (every developer builds and runs what they ship) at around 3%. The rest fell into one of two patterns: a new DevOps team wedged between dev and ops as a third silo, or ops abolished on paper, with a few senior developers running a shadow ops operation nobody else understands.

SRE went the same way, because being Google isn't easy. Platform engineering pitches golden paths and paved roads built by a platform team. His question, posed for the whole session, is how we avoid seeing the same two-box diagram in two years' time with "platform engineering" written in one of the boxes.

## How do you know the platform is working?

He measures an IDP on three things: does it make building more secure, more cost-effective, and does it improve developer experience. The first two are easy to see. Developer experience is harder; cycle time, MTTR and PR or release frequency all help, but his favourite signal is attrition. Plenty of things drive it, he admits, but a team with a good developer experience doesn't see high attrition.

## Should the platform team solve problems nobody has?

The first story is from Epsagon (since acquired by Cisco), an observability company built heavily on AWS Lambda and Kinesis. A senior developer with spare time built a tool to stream sampled traces from Kinesis to local machines for debugging. A month or two later, nobody used it. Debugging on Lambda was fine, and pulling traces locally took about ten lines of code anyway.

"Just because we can solve something doesn't mean that we should solve something," Gal Bashan said at Conf42 DevOps 2023. The list of possible developer pain is long: infrastructure toil, Helm charts, boilerplate for new services, key management, missing alerts on RED metrics, code ownership, cognitive load, hard-to-write tests. Developers know which of these hurt, so ask them: interviews, retros, recent bugs and their root causes. Start from the problems, not from the solutions.

Even with the right problem, he warns against three traps: building every request one user makes, spending six months forcing a shiny technology onto the problem, and building the solution that would suit you rather than the developer you interviewed.

## Does agile still apply to internal tools?

His second story comes from his army unit, with the domain changed to bagels for security reasons. Many vendors, many proprietary bagel formats, so the team spent about six months building a generic bagel library to serve every project. The developer who wrote it came from one project, and it fitted that project perfectly. The other projects tried it for two weeks, found it too complex and too generic, and abandoned it.

The lesson is plain: an internal platform is no excuse to disappear into the lab for six months. Pick the most important pain point and the simplest solution, ship an MVP to your internal customers, get feedback, and only then move on to the next step.

## Who does that job?

Problem validation, solution validation, iterative delivery and go-to-market add up to a job description he recognises: product manager. Then he takes on the four objections you'll hear from a head of product:

- **It's another headcount.** Ask what's more expensive, one PM or a whole platform team building something nobody uses.
- **Engineering managers can do it.** Interviewing users well is a real skill, and EMs already carry people development and execution.
- **Developers know what developers want.** Then why does Elasticsearch, a product for developers, employ product managers?
- **The platform is mandatory anyway.** Then the developers will have a bad time, and so will the platform team.

That PM should be measured against the same three criteria: security, cost and developer experience.

## Who should watch

Platform team leads and engineering managers about to staff an IDP effort, and anyone who needs arguments for a platform PM. It's a talk about practice and organisation, with no tools or architecture shown.

Title: Your DORA metrics lie unless the team trusts each other
Description: Tomasz Manugiewicz (Grand Parade / William Hill) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on trust, not tooling, as the real lever of a DevOps transformation
Body:
Any team can hit a great deployment frequency: split the user stories small enough and the chart goes up and to the right. Tomasz Manugiewicz, General Manager at Grand Parade / William Hill, used his Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 talk to argue that a DevOps transformation runs on trust between people, and that without it even your metrics turn into theatre.

This is a culture talk, not a tooling one. No YAML, no pipelines, and a former Java developer explaining why "works for me" was never a deployment strategy.

## Why is trust the bottleneck?

Manugiewicz starts from the VUCA world (volatile, uncertain, complex, ambiguous) and offers his own engineering version, MUCA: market dynamics, unknown requirements, complex problems and ambiguous estimations. Then he reads the Agile Manifesto line by line and finds trust in every one. Individuals and interactions need people who trust each other; customer collaboration needs a customer you are not fighting over every feature; working software needs investors who trust you with their money.

The silos are where it breaks. He remembers a competition, about 15 years ago, between developers and QA: developers shipped a jar and declared it bug-free, QA sent back a pile of Jira tickets. The same blame game repeats between the people who deploy and the people who run production. DevOps, as he puts it, is just development plus operations: a shared goal, shared responsibility and shared ways of working. The tool chain is the easy part.

## What is trust made of?

His model has two pillars. The cognitive one is competence: skills, knowledge, experience and the results you show. The emotional one is character: intentions, openness and honesty, together adding up to integrity. Trust is competence plus character. Engineers tend to over-invest in the first and forget that the product owner in a planning meeting may be worried, or excited, about a feature the team considers a nightmare.

He applies it to the three things a transformation changes: team structure (he points to the book *Team Topologies*), process adjustments that will meet resistance from people who like the old way, and the tools review engineers love. Each needs trust in a different direction. The payoff is autonomy, the stage in the DevOps evolution model where individuals can work without manual approval from outside the team - the green button in Jira someone has to click before every release.

## Where does it get built?

Quoting Brené Brown, he says trust is not built in big sweeping moments but in tiny everyday ones. His two examples are the most practical part of the talk. Pair programming carries a fear of being assessed, for the senior as much as the junior, and behind it a fear of rejection. Code review raises the question every author has felt: are they reviewing my code or me? "If we will be brave enough to show ourselves, then it helps building trust," Manugiewicz said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023.

That leads to vulnerability. In engineering, a vulnerability is a flaw to be found and fixed. In people, it means showing a weakness and not rushing to patch it. Retrospectives only work when people do that.

## How do metrics get gamed?

The closing argument lands hardest for anyone with a DORA dashboard. Deployment frequency and lead time for changes can be inflated by slicing work into tiny chunks. Mean time to recover can be shaved by deploying a fix behind a feature flag the client cannot see yet and stopping the clock there, before the final tests. "Give me your metrics and I will tell you whatever you want to hear," as he puts it. Honest numbers need a team that trusts each other enough to show the bad ones.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers starting a DevOps transformation, team leads whose metrics look suspiciously good, and engineers who have been on either side of a dev-versus-QA standoff. If you want an implementation guide, look elsewhere; this is about the people the implementation depends on.

Title: DevOps fixed the outer loop and made the inner loop longer
Description: Arsh Sharma (Okteto) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on moving dev environments into the Kubernetes cluster so the inner loop runs against production-like infra
Body:
CI/CD pipelines and staging environments made shipping faster, but they did nothing for the minutes a developer spends between hitting save and finding out whether the code works. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Arsh Sharma of Okteto argues that DevOps shortened the outer feedback loop while the inner one got longer, and that the fix is to run dev environments in the same cloud where everything else already lives.

It's a short talk: a quick history lesson, the problem from both sides, and a demo of the open source Okteto CLI. Expect a vendor's own tool front and centre.

## How did DevOps end up leaving developers out?

Sharma starts with the history. Containers merged application developers and application builders, packaging shifted left, and teams iterated faster because a hand-off disappeared. Ops still owned clusters and deployments, so DevOps set out to make developers self-sufficient, with ops building the processes developers rely on. In practice most organisations settled on two of them: CI/CD pipelines and staging environments.

Both help, he says, but both sit far away from the moment code is written. You commit and push before CI sees anything; you wait for access and a build before staging does. Meanwhile development happens on a laptop that looks nothing like a cluster running Kubernetes. Reproducing a production bug means asking ops for a local cluster, and minikube or kind will never quite match what production runs.

Ops doesn't win either. They configure an environment per developer, and those environments aren't reproducible. Terraform standardises the infrastructure, he notes, not the application on top of it.

## Why put the dev environment in the cluster?

"So why shouldn't your dev environments live there too?" Arsh Sharma said at Conf42 DevOps 2023, after pointing out that production, staging and CI already run in the cloud. The industry agrees development should happen in a production-like environment; he asks why we've been so slow to actually do it.

The Okteto CLI model splits the work. Ops writes an Okteto manifest once, with everything needed to stand up a dev environment, including how to deploy the application, the part that used to take synchronous calls between ops and developers. The environment is deployed into a Kubernetes cluster, and a two-way file sync connects the developer's local files to the code running there.

## What does the demo show?

He uses a movie rental app made of several microservices. After setting a context (he uses Okteto Cloud, but says any cluster works, AWS, Google Cloud or vanilla Kubernetes), a single `okteto up` builds each service from its existing Dockerfiles and deploys the lot with Helm. The manifest's dev section declares which folders sync and which ports forward.

Okteto then asks which service you want to work on. He picks the front end, the running container is replaced by a dev container, and he gets a terminal inside it plus an endpoint for the app. From there it feels local: `yarn`, `yarn start`, refresh. He uncomments a discount coupon banner, it appears on the live endpoint; comment it out again and it's gone. Every other service keeps running in the cluster, so nobody had to bring up the back end and database by hand first.

## What's the payoff?

His recap: you get to the code-writing phase without local configuration, the environment matches production, and feedback arrives on save instead of after a pipeline run. Ops moves from building environments one developer at a time to maintaining the tooling. His closing argument is about mindset more than speed: if you're shipping for the cloud, developing in it means fewer surprises when the code gets there.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers tired of helping developers fight their local cluster, and teams whose microservice count has outgrown docker-compose on a laptop. It's a quick introduction to the idea plus one tool, not a comparison of the options; the questions about cluster cost and multi-tenancy are left for another day.

Title: One Log4Shell weekend, two teams, and what DORA says about the gap
Description: Nathen Harvey and Amanda Lewis (Google Cloud) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on why capabilities like CI and loose coupling decide how a CVE weekend goes
Body:
The same CVE can cost one team a day and another team three weeks, and the difference is rarely heroics. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Nathen Harvey and Amanda Lewis, both Developer Advocates at Google Cloud working on the DORA research program, skip the usual tour of the 2022 Accelerate State of DevOps report and act it out instead: a fictional Log4Shell incident, two teams in the same company, and the capabilities that separated them.

The framing is the report's own headline finding: context matters. So they tell a story, disclaimer for the lawyers included.

## What happened when Log4Shell landed?

It starts on Friday 10 December 2021, with a calendar full of coffee chats and holiday shopping. Harvey plays the incident commander who goes through all five stages of grief, from hearing about it on Twitter to declaring an incident, then reaches for an OODA loop: observe, orient, decide, act.

The orient step is where the first lesson lands. About 400 production applications were potentially affected. The punchline that SBOMs answered the question in two minutes is quickly withdrawn: they only had a good SBOM for one application, and it wasn't in production yet. Everything else meant calling in subject matter experts for the weekend, and it took until Monday morning to settle on the two most critical systems: the order management system (OMS) and the e-commerce front end.

## Why did the modern microservices site take the longest?

The website was the newer system, 27 microservices in 27 repositories, built by a vendor that was no longer engaged. "Ultimately, we paid for functionality, not knowledge or documentation," Nathen Harvey said at Conf42 DevOps 2023.

There was no automated build and no automated test suite. The team upgraded Log4j in one service, deployed to staging, and everything broke, because the services were tightly coupled. The feedback mechanism was refreshing the page: "500 was not the number of orders we received. Instead, it was the server error code that we got," Harvey said.

Then came the process. The fixes were ready on a Friday, which ran into the no-deploy-Fridays rule; the change approval board met only on Tuesdays and Thursdays, convened an emergency session on Monday, asked for more manual testing, and finally chose to hold everything until the Log4j releases settled. There were four of them, the last on 28 December. The slides put the website's numbers bluntly: lead time of one to two months, deployments once or twice a year, a change failure rate of about 50%, and 20+ days stuck at the CAB. The team ended up, in Harvey's word, crispy.

## And the legacy system?

The OMS was older, bigger and closer to a macroservice, but its team had spent two years going from quarterly to weekly releases. The components were loosely coupled, with automated builds and tests. On Monday the team upgraded Log4j in the first of three affected components, CI built the JAR, ran tests, deployed to a test environment, and the CAB rubber-stamped it. A test failed on the second component; the team swarmed the broken build, found a well-hidden bug, and shipped by Wednesday. The third component went out on Thursday. Slide figures: one-week lead time, 15% change failure rate, restore in under a day, four days at the CAB.

Both teams had a change approval board. Only one of them experienced it as an obstacle. Lewis mentions hearing of a team that took the CAB off the critical path, leaving it to handle only the unusual changes, and saw deployment frequency rise 800x.

## What does the DORA research add?

Lewis and Harvey then map the story onto the 2022 findings:

- **Delivery performance drives organisational performance only when operational performance is also high.** Reliability practices (targets, reviews, toil reduction, re-prioritising when targets are missed) follow a J-curve: early adopters may see setbacks before the gains arrive.
- **Technical capabilities build on one another.** Teams strong in practices like version control and loosely coupled architecture show 3.8 times higher organisational performance.
- **Supply chain security hinges on continuous integration.** Teams above average on both CI and security practices had the best organisational performance, and generative, high-trust cultures (per Westrum's typology) were more likely to adopt the security practices in the first place. Better security practices also lowered burnout.

The advice that follows is the opposite of a maturity model. "And in fact, there is no one size fits all roadmap or maturity model for you to follow," Harvey said at Conf42 DevOps 2023. Start from the outcome you want to improve, work back to the capability that's holding you back, invest there, and don't try to boil the ocean.

## Who should watch

Anyone who has to argue for CI, decoupling or a lighter change process with someone who controls the budget. The story makes the case better than a scatter plot does, and the OMS team's week is a useful target to point at. If you've already read the 2022 report closely, the new material is the narrative, not the data.

Title: AWS FIS terminates real instances, so bring stop conditions
Description: Samuel Baruffi (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on AWS Fault Injection Simulator templates, targets, stop conditions and a live instance kill
Body:
An auto scaling group with two instances sounds redundant until one of them dies during a traffic spike. Samuel Baruffi, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, used his Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 talk to walk through AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS), the managed chaos service, and then killed one of his own two nginx instances live to show that redundant and fine are different things.

It is a vendor talk about an AWS service, given by AWS, and it is a clear one: the building blocks, the safety rails and a demo that does not go perfectly, which is the point.

## Why do teams struggle to run chaos on their own?

Baruffi opens with how many steps hide inside one client-to-server message: the network delivers, the server validates, updates state, replies, the client validates and updates its own state. Every step can fail, and then you multiply by thousands of microservices. Traditional tests verify known conditions; they do not tell you what happens when a disk fills because log rotation was never set up.

AWS, he says, collected four complaints from customers who tried chaos engineering on their own: stitching together tools and homemade scripts, needing lots of agents and libraries to start, ensuring safety, and reproducing real-world events that are rarely a single failure but several, in sequence or in parallel.

## What are the building blocks?

FIS has four components, defined in JSON or YAML so they can be version-controlled and code-reviewed:

- **Actions**: the fault to inject, namespaced as `aws:<service>:<action>`, with parameters such as duration or the share of requests to throttle. Actions can run in parallel or in sequence (a wait action can follow a stop-instances action). Some host-level actions on EC2 go through the Systems Manager agent.
- **Targets**: which resources get hit, by resource IDs, tags and filters, with a selection mode - all, a count, a percentage or random. His example picks exactly two running EC2 instances in us-east-1a tagged environment=test, in one VPC.
- **Experiment templates**: actions plus targets, an IAM role, and the stop-condition alarms.
- **Experiments**: a snapshot of a template each time it runs, with who started it, status and results.

The supported faults at the time included EC2 API errors and throttling, latency injection, killing ECS containers, terminating EKS nodes, and the newer network disruption and EBS I/O pause actions.

## Real faults need real guardrails

The detail that matters most: faults are injected at the service control plane level. Terminate an instance in an experiment and AWS terminates the instance. There is no metric trickery, so a sloppy target filter is an outage you scheduled yourself.

The safeguards are CloudWatch (or third-party) alarms wired up as stop conditions, with EventBridge telling FIS to halt and roll back. IAM decides who can start experiments, and tag policies can restrict which resources are fair game - only instances tagged as test, say. "I highly recommend every single time you create a stop condition," Baruffi said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023, while skipping one for the demo. The console asked him twice whether he was sure.

## From one-off experiments to CI/CD

His adoption path runs from one-off experiments (verify a new service, expose monitoring blind spots) to game days that rehearse a promotion day or a launch, then to automation: experiments on a recurring schedule, experiments triggered by events like an auto scaling action, and a stage in the CI/CD pipeline that runs experiments against every staging deploy. The more automated it gets, the more the stop conditions earn their keep, because nobody is watching the button.

## What did the demo show?

Two EC2 instances running nginx behind a load balancer, in two availability zones, with an auto scaling group at desired and minimum capacity two. Hypothesis: lose one instance under load and the application stays up. The template targets instances by tag, filters on running state and selects 50%.

Under synthetic load from Lambda functions, FIS terminated one instance. The application stayed up, and the auto scaling group started a replacement, but the dashboard told the real story: more than half the requests returning HTTP 500s or failing to connect, CPU on the survivor above 60%, and response times up to a 2.6-second maximum and a 1.3-second average. His fix as the owner: more instances across three or four availability zones. Hypothesis disproved, which is the useful outcome.

## Who should watch

Teams on AWS that want managed chaos rather than a folder of scripts, and anyone who wants a clear mental model of templates, targets and stop conditions before touching the console. Non-AWS shops will get less from it.

Title: Start a platform team with one happy pilot team and free tools
Description: Serg Hospodarets (William Hill) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on why platform engineering and how to start, from Docusaurus to Backstage and JHipster
Body:
DevOps tells you what culture to aim for; it does not tell you how to get there across a hundred teams. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Serg Hospodarets, Global Head of Engineering at William Hill, argued that platform engineering is that how, and then built a slice of one live: an application template from JHipster, published through Backstage, pushed to GitHub and deployed to AWS by its own pipeline.

He has gone from developer to leading organisations of more than 100 engineers and is still hands-on, which shows in the demo.

## Why platform engineering?

He asked ChatGPT what DevOps is and got a methodology: culture, guidance, and no starting point. Meanwhile the number of tools in the cloud native catalogue has exploded, and teams adopted them independently. The result is cognitive overload, no way to align architecture, no way for security and ops to roll out scans, patches or central monitoring (think Log4j, or a vulnerable dependency of a dependency in npm), and a business asking you to operate twice as fast, at the same quality, for less.

His analogy: DevOps is to platform engineering what ECMAScript is to JavaScript in the browser, a standard and an implementation. He cites the State of DevOps report for data showing platform engineering's impact on development velocity.

## Who is the platform for?

Treat the platform as a product. The main customers are internal developers, and the main metrics are their net promoter score and adoption. Before building one, settle the prerequisites: common CI/CD (GitLab, GitHub), cloud provider, target tech stack. If those are not decided, check whether you need a platform yet. His rough threshold: an engineering organisation of at least about 50 people, starting with 5 to 10 platform engineers drawn from a product team that already builds something reusable, plus ops and security.

The most important early decision is the pilot customer. Pull, never push: find a team that wants your solution and make it the happiest customer ever, because when someone else does the demo it is ten times more trusted than when you shout about your own platform. Eventually security and ops become customers too, delivering their own work through the platform.

## The tools, stage by stage

His maturity model runs from childhood to adolescence to maturity, and almost everything he shows is free:

- **Discoverability first.** A simple versioned docs site with Docusaurus (or Slate for API docs). Later, Backstage, open sourced by Spotify, as a scalable developer portal; Roadie if you want it as paid SaaS.
- **Front end.** Storybook as the component playground, plus your own React or Vue app templates.
- **Services.** JHipster generates monoliths, microservices and micro frontends from a CLI or the web, with authentication, database, caching and pre-commit static analysis bundled, and can wire in CI/CD and cloud providers.

The demo combines them. A Spring Boot and React app generated with JHipster becomes a Backstage software template; creating an app from it publishes a repository to GitHub, whose workflow installs dependencies, runs Terraform and deploys the front end to S3 behind CloudFront. The first attempt fails, and he takes it in good humour before the second run goes through.

## The million-dollar question is upgrades

Upgradability is where he gets most emphatic. By his figures, the yearly cost of updates for internal customers runs up to $20,000 for a small platform, around $80,000 for a medium one and half a million dollars or more for a large organisation, before you count the friction. Backstage does not solve this. JHipster's upgrade flow creates a branch with the new template version applied to each product's code base, codemods via Codeshift handle code transformations, and Renovate keeps dependencies current across languages.

## Tips from experience

Serg Hospodarets said at Conf42 DevOps 2023: "Treat your platform as a product as soon as possible." Business rarely cares about technology, so solve a business problem. Give internal teams Slack support and a developer portal, invest in a platform product manager, ship predictable releases with demos and newsletters, pair developers with UX for UI adoption, and get top-down support for bottom-up enablement. His jackpot strategy: deliver the platform to your company's external customers, and you stop being a cost centre. On his slides: prefer a golden path over a golden cage, and aim for a thinnest viable platform.

He collected the tools in an awesome-platform-engineering repository on GitHub, and he closes with: "The best day to start is always today."

## Who should watch

Engineering leaders deciding whether to fund a platform team, and the first engineers on one who need a tool list and a sequence.

Title: Run incident response, observability and capacity planning on yourself
Description: Julie Gunderson (AWS) and Ana Margarita Medina (Lightstep) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on applying reliability practices to humans to prevent burnout
Body:
We put more care into our clusters than into the people who run them. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Julie Gunderson, Senior Developer Advocate at AWS, and Ana Margarita Medina, Staff Developer Advocate at Lightstep, took the practices engineers already trust (incident response, observability, capacity planning, blameless postmortems) and applied them to human systems, with burnout as the incident to prevent.

It opens with a true story. At a conference in Spain, a friend went for a swim and asked Medina to keep an eye on them every five to ten minutes. Then came the beach balls, frisbees and margaritas, and the bobbing head was gone. She had, as Gunderson puts it, literally forgotten a human.

## The technical side, briefly

Gunderson starts with the AWS Well-Architected Framework's definition of reliability: a workload performing its intended function correctly and consistently when it is expected to. Systems keep getting more interconnected (the death star diagrams of large microservice estates), so one failure cascades. The design principles follow: automatically recover from failure by watching KPIs that measure business value, test recovery procedures (both speakers have taught chaos engineering for years), scale horizontally so no single resource is a single point of failure, stop guessing at capacity, and manage change through automation.

Then the pivot. Humans are complex systems too, circulatory, respiratory, muscular, digestive, nervous, and a failure in one cascades into others.

## What does incident response look like for a person?

Incident response did not come from tech. It grew out of the Incident Command System, created after the 1970s wildfires in southern California, when thousands of firefighters knew how to fight fires alone or in small groups but had no common framework to work together. The phases are familiar: prepare, detect, assess, respond, resolve, recover, learn.

Gunderson maps each phase onto life, because life happens: illness, a family matter, burnout, a power cut just before you were due to give a conference talk. Write a personal incident plan. Watch for signals. Decide the severity (a two-hour power cut versus a long health crisis). Mobilise the right people, a colleague who can take your talk, family, friends, medical professionals. Respond, and then actually recover rather than sliding back. Finally, reflect with a postmortem on yourself.

## Burnout is the outage

Medina takes burnout. Herbert Freudenberger, one of the first to write about it, in a 1980 book, defined it as the "state of mental and physical exhaustion caused by one's professional life". She argues it reaches beyond work, into parenting, community work and social life. Ana Margarita Medina said at Conf42 DevOps 2023: "Burnout is not depression, but it can definitely lead you there." A Yerbo survey she cites found two in five tech workers at high risk of burnout, and she suspects the number is higher for people who get paged. The warning signs: exhaustion, loss of concentration, lack of motivation, alienation, frustration, physical symptoms, low self-esteem and substance abuse.

## Observability and capacity planning for humans

Your body ships with observability out of the box, but its signals are biased by perception: an ordinary day can still produce a panic attack. Medina's suggestion is to add telemetry deliberately: wearables like the Apple Watch, Fitbit or Oura ring for heart rate and sleep, plus logging through food, mood, habit and connection tracking. Did the 11pm donut make you cranky this morning?

Capacity planning carries over too. Humans have a maximum capacity, physical, emotional, financial, educational. Know your values, count your spoons, and put on your own oxygen mask first.

## Be blameless, with yourself too

Gunderson brings it back to the beach. A blameless postmortem asks how and what, not why, and looks at the conditions: frisbees, sunscreen, people, and one person as a single point of failure. The same applies when you lie in bed replaying the day. Julie Gunderson said at Conf42 DevOps 2023: "Be kind to yourself. Practice blamelessness."

To move from reactive to proactive, they suggest building human connection, setting goals, keeping a personal board of directors of past managers and peers, and prospection, borrowed from future-directed therapy. And because it is a DevOps conference, `kubectl apply -f humans.yaml`, with resource limits set.

The ending resolves the story: the lost swimmer was Gunderson. Her location was shared with Medina, but her phone was on the beach. She came out a quarter of a mile away, uneaten by sharks.

## Who should watch

On-call engineers, SREs and the people who manage them. It is light on tooling and heavy on practical self-care, and it closes with mental health resources (Open Sourcing Mental Health among them) and a reminder that it is OK to ask for help.

Title: Pre-aggregate your telemetry before a thousand dashboards ask
Description: Shay Lin (Confluent) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on serving Kafka telemetry at scale by pushing predefined aggregations through Kafka Streams
Body:
Chaos experiments are only as good as the metrics you read during them, and at cloud scale the metrics platform is its own reliability problem. Shay Lin, Staff Software Engineer at Confluent, used a Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 talk to show how Confluent stopped answering the same telemetry query over and over: it computes predefined aggregations once, with Kafka Streams, and publishes the results back through Kafka and into Apache Druid.

It is a short talk, closer to an architecture sketch than a tutorial, and a useful one for anyone whose observability store is starting to sweat.

## Why does telemetry need its own architecture?

The abstract puts the scale up front: at Confluent, raw telemetry flows in at 5 million metrics per second. Lin starts from the SRE's view of a hypothetical global Kafka deployment, where a product manager asks to roll a feature out tomorrow and the boss asks what happens if us-west-2 goes down. Answering either needs telemetry from clients and brokers, and the questions people ask of it fall into four patterns: facts (total network bytes in the last hour), trends (CPU over seven days), diagnosis (a point-in-time value) and attribution (does the CPU trend correlate with fetch requests?).

A plain data store handles the first two. Attribution pushes you to a time-series-optimised OLAP store, and the example is Druid: data streams into segments in near real time, and a query engine fetches from the right ones.

## What breaks when everyone asks the same question?

Segments fill up constantly. Lin compares it to a stream of water filling bottles: each has a capacity, so a full one is pushed aside and a new one starts. At millions of events per second, Lin notes, you can pile up petabyte-scale data within an hour.

Meanwhile the consumers multiply: billing, SREs running continuous monitoring, and external customers who want to see their own Kafka cluster (and nobody else's). The result: repetitive queries on hot entities, rising compute and serving costs, metric definitions that must stay consistent, and more customers depending on the platform staying up. The quiet killer is the third one - billing and a customer computing the same metric two different ways.

## How do pre-aggregations fix it?

Raw segments still land in Druid. But instead of serving the same heavy query to every consumer, Confluent publishes predefined aggregations that everyone reuses. The pipeline is event-driven: when a segment fills, it emits a signal, and a set of Kafka Streams topologies picks it up.

- A central registry holds the metric definitions, so there is one answer to what a metric means.
- A global task manager splits the work into the smallest units, based on how many clusters to aggregate and the metric granularity in space and time.
- A second sub-topology runs the processing with external compute.
- The results are published to Kafka for consumers and back into Druid as aggregation segments.

One detail worth stealing: the output uses OpenTelemetry, so the pipeline has to respect counter versus gauge semantics and keep state, or consumers end up with duplicated data over time.

## What about the alternatives?

Lin is fair about other routes. Offline roll-ups are built into some stores: Apache Pinot's Star Tree index can reduce, say, five dimensions to three in background tasks, and Druid supports custom roll-up ingestion too. Online stream processing (Flink, Kafka Streams) is the other path. The lesson from their proof of concept: "your partition strategy should be highly coherent with how you're aggregating your data," Lin said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023. Get that wrong and you replicate the data set through every processing step, which is slow and expensive.

The closing trade-off is a curve: the more compressed the aggregate, the narrower the use cases it serves; the more dimensions you keep, the broader. Picking which aggregations to predefine is the actual design work.

## Who should watch

Platform and observability engineers running a metrics store that serves both internal teams and customers, and anyone weighing Druid or Pinot roll-ups against a streaming pre-aggregation layer. Chaos engineers get the framing - telemetry as the foundation of experiments - but little chaos itself.

- Yoav Nordmann on [anomaly detection with Apache Pinot and ThirdEye](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Yoav_Nordmann_anomaly_detection_apache_pinot_thirdeye) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2023.

Title: Your CI/CD is designed by your org chart, so plan it there
Description: Pawel Piwosz (EPAM Systems) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on designing CI/CD at enterprise level, a mind map from Conway's law to SBOMs
Body:
Most CI/CD gets designed from three inputs: some code, a list of environments and whichever tool the team knows. Pawel Piwosz, Lead Systems Engineer at EPAM Systems, used his Conf42 DevOps 2023 talk to step back to the helicopter view and treat CI/CD as an architecture problem for the whole organisation, with a mind map that covers everything from Conway's law to software bills of materials.

There is no pipeline YAML here and no tool tutorial. That is the point.

## Why start with the organisation?

Because of Conway's law: the design of a system mirrors the communication structure of the organisation that builds it. If two components must talk to each other closely and the teams that own them do not talk, it will not work. That leads straight to Team Topologies, the book by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, and its team types, including the platform team that he thinks is often misunderstood under the current hype.

His own credentials fit the theme: DevOps Institute ambassador, AWS Community Builder and CD Foundation ambassador.

## The areas you have to decide on

The core of the talk is a walk through the branches of his framework. A few of them, with the questions he asks:

- **Environments.** Who owns each one, how is it structured, who has access? You may have full control over dev and QA and none over production, where only automation deploys.
- **Branching strategy.** Trunk-based, Gitflow, per story, or per environment, which he describes as Gitflow multiplied by the number of your environments. Plus pull request design, approvers, protected branches, escalation paths and feature toggles. A small codebase may not need Gitflow; AWS CodeDeploy nudges you towards a particular strategy.
- **Delivery strategy.** Continuous delivery has a manual stop; continuous deployment has none. Any manual test means no continuous deployment. Deployment strategies matter across teams: if two tightly coupled services deploy one with canary and the other with recreate, expect trouble.
- **Artifact management.** Naming conventions, versioning, access, and whether the store is loosely integrated (CodePipeline with artifacts in S3) or built in (Azure DevOps).
- **Quality gates.** If you promise a delivery every five minutes, you cannot have a four-hour test suite in the gate.
- **Constraints.** A cat-pictures site and a space mission do not share a CI/CD, nor does a company that must keep artifacts and backward compatibility for 20 years or push software to millions of cars. No cloud allowed? Then no hosted CI services.
- **Releases and rollbacks.** Pawel Piwosz said at Conf42 DevOps 2023: "Release doesn't mean deploy, right?" A change committee in your SDLC rules out continuous deployment. Rollback can mean rolling back or rolling forward, which gets interesting when two microservices pick different ones; then add RTO, RPO, zero-downtime requirements and what happens to databases.
- **KPIs, monitoring and measurement.** SLAs, SLOs and SLIs constrained by how fast your process can restore. Monitoring of pipelines is technical; measurement is operational, with the four DORA metrics split into throughput (deployment frequency, lead time) and stability (time to recover, change failure rate).
- **Value streams and tools.** CI/CD is usually a big chunk of the value stream, so its waste and bottlenecks are the value stream's. Three teams paying for three different CI tools means fragmented knowledge and three licences where one might do.

## Security closes the map

Security is the biggest branch of the latest version of his framework. Beyond securing the tools, pipelines now have to produce SBOMs, already required for work with the US government, and to guard against injection during pipeline runs. He asks how many teams check their dependencies, and the dependencies of those dependencies, especially in the Python and JavaScript ecosystems.

## What is the mind map for?

He maps those branches against architecture quality attributes such as scalability, interoperability, usability and security, and uses it as what he calls a Rosetta Stone of CI/CD: one picture that lets business people, stakeholders, engineers, architects and security sit in the same room and agree on what is possible. Pawel Piwosz said at Conf42 DevOps 2023, "this is not about ordering all teams to use Jenkins." It is about collaboration, tooling included.

## Who should watch

Architects, DevOps leads and engineering managers about to standardise delivery across many teams, or anyone who has to explain to stakeholders why CI/CD is more than a pipeline.

Title: Before you bake in reliability, ask what it means to people
Description: Ricardo Castro (FanDuel / Blip.pt) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on starting a reliability engineering practice, from first questions to SLOs
Body:
Handed the job of implementing reliability engineering, most people reach for the Google SRE book and start copying. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Ricardo Castro, Principal SRE at FanDuel / Blip.pt, laid out what he actually does instead: start by asking people what reliability means, then work through a set of habits, cultural and technical, that get a practice going and keep it running.

It is a practical playbook rather than theory, and it suits anyone who has just been given the title.

## Why not just do what Google does?

Castro's context is quick. The DevOps movement took shape around 2007 and 2008 and got its name around 2009, yet many organisations still struggle to implement it, because DevOps is a culture rather than a set of steps. When Google published the Site Reliability Engineering book in 2016, describing both a practice and a role, companies grabbed it as a recipe. The catch: the book covers a lot, and Google's problems are not most companies' problems, so translating it to your own reality is hard.

## The first two questions

Before any tooling, he goes around asking two things. Ricardo Castro said at Conf42 DevOps 2023 that he asks people "what does reliability mean to you and what does reliability mean to the organization?" The answers reveal people's expectations, whether a common language for reliability exists, and whether there is a mismatch between what engineers think and what the organisation wants. Ask enough people and you find clusters with different definitions, which tells you how to approach the rollout.

## Ask, expose yourself, then educate yourself

The first tips are about learning the company before changing it.

- **Ask questions.** "We mustn't be afraid to ask questions, no matter how stupid they might seem", in a meeting or in an incident. He uses the career cold start algorithm popularised by Meta's CTO: book 30-minute meetings and ask what you need to know to do your job, what difficulties you will run into, and who you should talk to next. Patterns appear, and you build a map of who does what.
- **Expose yourself.** Sit in meetings, incident bridges and incident reports. Listen far more than you speak, and take a lot of notes. The goal is empathy as much as knowledge.
- **Educate yourself.** The SRE book, Implementing Service Level Objectives by Alex Hidalgo, a Coursera course on reliability engineering taught by Google engineers, and local meetups where you can ask what worked and what did not.

## Earn trust, then make the work visible

Next comes earning a place. Attack recurring pain points early to reduce toil and prove value, but time-box it, or firefighting becomes all your team ever does. Make yourself available through a Slack channel, office hours or a mailing list, an open door policy for anything reliability related. Communicate extensively through talks, newsletters, documentation, blog posts and periodic surveys against a reliability maturity model, so reliability stays on people's minds and nobody thinks it is one team's job.

Make reliability work visible by tracking it with whatever the company already uses, Jira or Trello tickets and epics, in the same agile process, so it is never obscure. Find your niche: if a cloud engineering or DevOps team already owns an area, do not compete with it; pick something unowned, observability for example, and collaborate where you overlap. And promote independence with docs, videos, tools, CLIs, bots and training, so your team never becomes the bottleneck.

## The technical anchors

Three tips are about the engineering itself. Adopt a reliability framework, SLOs being the popular choice, so development and operations teams share a language and can prioritise: inside your reliability target, ship features; below it, invest in operational work. Get executive support by meeting executives regularly and backing claims with data, with DORA metrics as a translation layer between engineering and business outcomes. And invest in observability (metrics, logs, traces, continuous profiling) to improve time to detect and time to repair and to cut change failure rate, with OpenTelemetry and automatic instrumentation to get started quickly. He recommends the Observability Engineering book from the Honeycomb team.

None of these are one-offs, he stresses, and most run in parallel.

## Who should watch

Engineers starting or inheriting an SRE or reliability function, and managers who need to explain what that team will actually do in its first months.

Title: Terraform in a pipeline is CI/CD; GitOps means a controller reconciles it
Description: Roberth Strand (Amesto Fortytwo) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on real GitOps for Terraform with Flux and the TF-controller on Kubernetes
Body:
Putting your Terraform in Git and running it from a pipeline is good automation, but it is not GitOps. Roberth Strand, Principal Cloud Engineer at Amesto Fortytwo and a maintainer of the OpenGitOps project, made that case at Conf42 DevOps 2023 and then showed how to get the real thing: Terraform modules reconciled by a Kubernetes controller, using Flux and the TF-controller from Weaveworks.

Strand is home alone with his dog for the recording, so the demo has a small risk of barking. It survives.

## Why is a Terraform pipeline not GitOps?

GitOps, coined by Weaveworks in 2017, describes an operating model, not a storage location. Roberth Strand said at Conf42 DevOps 2023 that if you put stuff in Git and run pipelines, "it's just CI CD at that point." GitOps is about the continuous deployment part: you stop writing imperative steps for where and how to deploy.

The OpenGitOps working group under the CNCF pinned that down as four principles:

- **Declarative.** You describe how the system should look, not the steps to get there.
- **Versioned and immutable.** Each desired state supersedes the previous one in full, so you keep a complete history and can roll back. Git fits, but an S3 bucket or Azure blob storage would too.
- **Pulled automatically.** Software agents fetch the desired state; nobody pushes it.
- **Continuously reconciled.** Agents keep making the observed state match the desired state.

Kubernetes is where this works best today, simply because the tools exist there. The two big ones, Argo CD and Flux, are both graduated CNCF projects. The demo uses Flux, because the Terraform tooling is built on it; Argo CD users can still do Terraform, just not with these tools.

## How do Flux and the TF-controller fit together?

Flux is a set of controllers. The source controller pulls the latest state from version control into the Kubernetes API, the Kustomize controller applies plain or Kustomize-templated manifests, and the Helm controller manages Helm releases. The TF-controller sits on top: it uses the source controller to fetch your HCL and adds a Terraform custom resource, so a root module becomes an object in the Kubernetes API.

It also handles lifecycle. If you do not configure a backend, the Terraform state is kept in the cluster as a secret (fine for demos, not what you want in production). The plan is stored as a secret too, which matters: an unsaved plan can produce a different result the next time you run apply. And resources can declare dependencies on each other.

## The demo: from hello world to a dependency chain

On a local kind cluster, watched through k9s, Strand bootstraps Flux against his own GitHub repository, with the TF-controller installed by a Helm release in the same bootstrap. A Kustomization that depends on the Flux system one avoids complaints about the missing CRD.

The first Terraform object is a greeting module, a hello world that takes inputs and writes the output to a Kubernetes secret. It is set to approve plans automatically, and he explains why: Roberth Strand said at Conf42 DevOps 2023, "I feel that the entire idea behind Gitops is that deployment should be continuous and it should just work."

The second example is closer to real life. A shared resources root module creates Azure resource groups, a virtual network and security groups, using Terraform Cloud as the backend, and exports the subnet ID and resource group name to a secret. A workload module that builds a VM depends on it, reads those outputs as variables and takes its admin password from a secret created out of band. Each run spins up a runner pod, executes, then disappears. The workload waits on its dependency, then runs on the next reconcile, set to a minute.

## Why should a platform team care?

Strand builds platforms on Kubernetes, and his point is about the people. Many infrastructure engineers find a programming language a steep climb but are comfortable with Terraform. If they write a module with clean inputs and outputs, the platform team can run it continuously through this machinery without anyone learning a new language.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who already run Flux and want Terraform under the same reconciliation loop, and anyone whose team says it does GitOps because the HCL lives in a repo.
