Title: Chaos testing belongs in your load tests, not just in production
Description: Pablo Chacin (Grafana Labs / K6) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 on shifting chaos testing left into k6 tests developers already write
Body:
Most catastrophic failures in distributed systems come from error handling code nobody tested. Pablo Chacin, Technical Lead for Chaos Engineering at Grafana Labs / K6, used his Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 talk to argue that chaos testing should move left, into the load and functional tests developers already run, and showed how the k6 disruptor extension injects faults straight from test code.

The pitch is modest on purpose: before you break production on a Tuesday, check that your service survives the incident you already had.

## Why not just do chaos in production?

Chacin does not argue against production experiments. "Nothing can substitute testing this real stuff," he says. His problem is the adoption bar. He lists four obstacles: experimenting in production assumes battle-tested procedures many teams do not have, the blast radius of killing instances or disrupting the network is hard to predict, results are hard to reproduce, and the tools seem built by and for SREs and DevOps engineers, so developers cannot use them on their own.

Learning from real incidents has its own limits. They are stressful, unpredictable, and you do not get to choose what or when you learn. Game days help, but only for failures you can already imagine.

## Does testing known faults actually help?

This is the honest question at the centre of the talk: if modern systems fail in unpredictable ways, is testing predictable faults in staging just false confidence? Chacin answers with the 2014 USENIX OSDI paper by Yuan et al., *Simple Testing Can Prevent Most Critical Failures*. In that study, 92% of catastrophic failures came from incorrect handling of non-fatal errors, and in 58% of cases the fault could have been caught by simple testing of the error handling code.

The study gets better (or worse, if it is your code). In 35% of cases the error handler fell into one of three patterns: it overreacted and aborted the system on a non-fatal error, it was empty or only logged, or it carried a FIXME or TODO comment. Everyone has written at least one of those this year.

So chaos testing shifts the emphasis from experimentation to verification: from hunting unknown faults to making sure known ones are handled. He frames four tenets: incremental adoption, application-centric testing (faults described as latency and error rates, not infrastructure), chaos testing as code in the tools developers already use, and controlled, reproducible faults with a small blast radius. As he put it, "You cannot be confident from flocky test" - flaky chaos is just noise.

## The Sock Shop incident, replayed in k6

The demo uses the Sock Shop, a polyglot microservices e-commerce demo on Kubernetes. The invented incident: long-running queries overload the catalog database, adding up to 100 milliseconds of latency and some HTTP 500 errors. The catalog team fixes the root cause; the front end team wants to know how its own service copes.

The baseline is a plain k6 load test in JavaScript against the front end: zero errors, about 50 milliseconds of latency. Then the same test gets a second scenario that calls the disruptor, which installs agents in the pods behind the catalog service and injects 100 milliseconds of extra latency plus 10% HTTP 500 responses for the duration of the test. No extra tooling, no separate pipeline: the fault lives in the test file.

The result: latency up by the injected 100 milliseconds and an error rate at the front end of almost 12%. The front end was passing the catalog's errors straight through, with no retries. "I wouldn't be surprised if we find a two to comment in the error handle code," Chacin said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2023 - the transcript garbles "TODO", but the joke lands.

From there, the team can add retries, raise the error rate in the test and tune the fix before it turns into a retry storm.

## Who should watch

Developers and QA engineers who own a service but not the chaos tooling, and SRE teams trying to get product teams to care about failure handling. It is a short, clear talk with one worked example, not a tour of the disruptor's internals. If you already run k6, this is the cheapest chaos experiment you will ever set up.

Title: The real bill for instrumentation is distraction, not Datadog
Description: Prathamesh Sonpatki (Last9.io) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on the hidden cost of instrumentation and why emitting less telemetry is the fix
Body:
Everyone knows telemetry costs money. Prathamesh Sonpatki, Community and Dev Evangelist at Last9, used his Conf42 DevOps 2023 talk to argue that the money is the visible part: the hidden cost of instrumentation is the engineering attention it eats, and the fix is to emit less, on purpose.

It is a short, opinionated talk, closer to a checklist you can take to a planning meeting than a tooling tour.

## Why instrument at all?

He starts with the case for it: you need to know the application runs as expected, you may owe customers proof against an SLA, and SREs need to sleep. Prathamesh Sonpatki said at Conf42 DevOps 2023: "Hope cannot be the strategy." Reliability starts with instrumentation because you can only improve what you measure.

Then the complication. Your application is not standalone, it is a burger: the bun is the cloud or VM, the patty is your code, the mayo is RDS and the other data stores, the ketchup is third-party services. Often you run several burgers that talk to each other. Monitoring only the patty misses requests dropped at the load balancer or database IOPS stuck below threshold, which is how you end up with full stack observability, on infrastructure that scales up and disappears on its own schedule.

## Six pillars, and nobody uses them all

Beyond logs, metrics and traces, he adds the three extra pillars from Yuri Shkuro's six pillars of observability: profiling, external events and exceptions. Logs are easy to adopt but inconsistent across services. Metrics give the aggregate view and benefit from standards like OpenTelemetry and OpenMetrics. Traces follow a workflow, say a payment from authentication to the notification job, but left unchecked they behave like debug logs in production. Continuous profiling has an overhead you pay all year for the two or three times you use it. External events (deployments, config changes, a cloud instance being reprovisioned) are rare and need precise capture. Exceptions go to tools like Sentry and Rollbar.

His informal survey: most teams use three or four of the six at a time, never all of them.

## C.O.S.T., and the cost hiding behind it

The apparent costs get an acronym: Cardinality and churn, Operations, Scale, Tuning and toil. The cardinality number is the one to remember: a three-node Kubernetes cluster with Prometheus ships around 40k active series by default, before a single custom metric. The instrumentation stack is one more system to run, and it has to scale with the app, because being blind on New Year's Day or during an India against Pakistan World Cup final is a business problem, not just an engineering one.

The hidden cost is distraction. He lists the messages every team has received: cut the Datadog bill before next month, treat the log pile-up as a P0 or the vendor charges double, ignore the release because Prometheus is missing metrics and we are blind. Teams may emit huge volumes and use 10% to 20% of it, but they pay for all of it. Then comes fatigue: duplicate alarms, logs that contradict each other mid-incident, dashboards nobody reads.

## What does less look like?

His model is the Apple Watch: it shows vitals such as heart rate and sleep, and you go for the X-ray or the ECG only when a vital is off. Focus on the smallest set of data that gives early warnings, then dig deeper when needed.

The plan of action: plan what to measure and why, emit only what you need, observe and track usage, prune unused metrics aggressively, store less for less time, and spend where the value is. Then make it organisational: access policies (full detail for a window, aggregates after), data storage policies such as one-day log retention, and shared standards. Prathamesh Sonpatki said at Conf42 DevOps 2023 that "instrumentation is not just instrumenting, it is actually a liability that we have to worry about as builders of software."

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers facing an observability bill or a cardinality problem, and engineering managers who need language for why telemetry work keeps landing on the roadmap.

Title: Generate SDKs as a service, then trace them before your users do
Description: DeveloperSteve Coochin (Lumigo) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on OpenAPI Generator as a containerised SDK service, traced and tested end to end
Body:
Hand-maintaining SDKs in a dozen languages is a slow way to make your API less popular. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, DeveloperSteve Coochin, Senior Developer Advocate at Lumigo, walked through the setup he used at a big telco: OpenAPI Generator run as a containerised service that turns an API spec into SDKs automatically, with distributed tracing across the API, the generator and a test harness so you know how the generated code behaves before anyone installs it.

The talk opens with his disclaimer: he loves tech jokes. Why do devs prefer dark themes? Because light attracts bugs. The rest is more useful.

## What makes an API worth adopting?

Coochin has run hackathons for large companies around the world and lists four things a good API needs. DeveloperSteve Coochin said at Conf42 DevOps 2023 that "a good API really needs to provide a valid service", and provide it in a valid way. Then it needs good documentation, which for him means sample code and video tutorials next to the written docs. Then integration options for the platforms and languages your users actually work in (survey them, or offer a request form). And then SDKs, the part he has spent many hours building, debugging and fixing by hand.

## From a bash loop to a containerised generator

OpenAPI Generator, which he calls one of the most amazing open source communities he has contributed to, loads an OpenAPI spec (and legacy Swagger 1 and 2 specs, depending on the target language) and generates SDKs, with documentation, in more than 50 languages. Each language has its own template and its own sub-community under the core maintainers, and the templates are customisable. He points to Square, which published its own Mustache templates for the SDKs it generated and took community contributions to them.

His first version was the CLI (a `brew install` away) driven by a bash script: one YAML or JSON configuration per language sitting in a folder, the script loops through them, and out comes a stack of SDKs. If you are still on Swagger 2, he recommends upgrading to OpenAPI, which gives the generator more to work with.

The later version runs the generator as a deployable container. The flow: an API (his example is a Lambda with DynamoDB behind it; the Pet Store demo works if you have none) publishes its spec, the containerised generator outputs SDKs, and each generated SDK is deployed into a Lambda that exercises its functions.

## Why trace all three parts?

He calls this full circle observability, and it is where the Lumigo angle shows: distributed tracing, agentless, across managed services. Tracing the API shows each invocation through API Gateway, the Lambda and the database, with memory, cost per call and cold starts. Tracing the generator in its container (ECS in the example) shows resource use and the jobs that get stuck on a particular part of a spec. Tracing the test Lambda shows how the SDK performs inside an application, which is what users complain about when an SDK pulls in a heavy library or eats memory.

None of this has to run constantly. Regeneration only needs to happen when a new API version lands, ideally in staging.

Two lessons from experience are worth the video on their own. When generating 40 to 50 SDKs at a time across languages and products, he got the Python ones working first because Python was the strictest; once those were happy, the other languages usually followed. And he once shipped SDKs without testing them fully. The support inbox told him exactly how many people used them.

## Who should watch

API product teams and developer experience engineers who maintain SDKs for public or partner APIs. It is a practitioner's story with a vendor's tracing tool in the observability half; the generator part is fully open source and stands on its own.

Title: DataOps is the old dev-versus-ops wall, rebuilt between data and infra teams
Description: Antoni Ivanov (VMware) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on DataOps with Versatile Data Kit, letting infra teams set policy while data teams just deploy
Body:
Data engineering has rebuilt the wall that DevOps spent a decade tearing down, only this time it stands between data teams and infrastructure teams. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Antoni Ivanov, Staff engineer at VMware, argued that DataOps should borrow DevOps' lessons rather than reinvent them, and showed how the open source Versatile Data Kit (VDK) splits the work: data people write and deploy jobs, infra people encode their best practices as plugins that apply to every job.

It is a short talk, a concept introduction rather than a hands-on demo, but the framing is clear.

## Why do data projects fail so often?

Ivanov opens with the gap: we are nowhere near as efficient at shipping data projects as software. He cites industry studies that put the share of data and AI projects that never reach production at somewhere between 60 and 80 percent. DataOps promises to fix that, and its goal is about the only thing its proponents agree on: the most efficient creation of business value from data. How to get there is still contested.

## Two heroes with conflicting goals

His diagnosis is the same tension DevOps addressed twenty or thirty years ago, with different job titles.

- **Infrastructure and operations teams** know how to provision containers, virtual machines, networks, Spark and Kafka clusters, and CI/CD. They understand performance details such as big files for Kafka versus small files for HDFS. They optimise for reliability, availability and security.
- **Data teams** (data engineers, scientists, analysts, analytics and ML engineers) hold the domain knowledge: how to join datasets, report numbers and build predictive models. They optimise for agility, because a business that cannot get data fast enough stops using data.

Put those goals side by side and you get a wall of conflict and blurred lines of responsibility: operations debugging data engineering work, and data engineers provisioning infrastructure. Inefficient operations on one side, stalled development on the other.

The lesson he takes from DevOps is the slogan on the wall of every data mesh talk. Antoni Ivanov said at Conf42 DevOps 2023 that "we need to start treating data as a product", not a side effect produced somewhere between the source and the report.

## How does Versatile Data Kit split the work?

VDK has two halves, each automating and abstracting one journey.

- **The Data SDK** automates the data journey: a library for extracting, transforming and loading data in SQL and Python, with a plugin framework so others can extend it. Infra teams who know, for instance, that you cannot send very large messages into Kafka can write a plugin that checks the data before it is ever sent.
- **The Control Service** automates the DevOps cycle: data jobs are created, deployed and managed in a runtime environment on a schedule or manually, with automatic versioning and deployment behind a REST API.

The example on the data side is a lineage plugin. Because plugins can intercept every SQL query sent to the database, even when a job runs locally during development, an infra team can collect lineage information across all jobs without the data team changing a line.

On the DevOps side, the plan, code, build, test, release and deploy steps collapse into one click or one CLI deploy command for the data team. Operators extend the process by swapping the job builder image at install time (`helm install --set job-builder=my-job-builder-image`), for example to add standard system tests or to strip execution privileges so no job can run arbitrary files.

## Who should watch

Platform and infrastructure engineers supporting data teams, and data engineering leads who keep getting pulled into infrastructure work. It is a framing talk with a project pitch, so expect concepts and a few code snippets rather than a live build.

Title: A production-ready Kubernetes stack from Terraform plus Argo CD app of apps
Description: Abhimanyu Selvan (DigitalOcean) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on Kubernetes Bootstrapper, Terraform and Argo CD wiring a day-two-ready cluster
Body:
A bare Kubernetes cluster is the easy part. The ingress controller, certificates, runtime security, metrics and alerting that make it production-ready are where teams lose a week picking tools from the CNCF catalogue. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Abhimanyu Selvan, Senior Developer Advocate at DigitalOcean, demoed Kubernetes Bootstrapper, an open source framework that gets from nothing to a cluster ready for day two operations in three steps: Terraform for the infrastructure, Argo CD for everything installed on it, and Robusta for observability.

It is a demo talk, almost entirely in the terminal and the Argo CD UI, and it delivers on the title.

## Why bother with a bootstrapper?

Selvan starts with the problem anyone who has scrolled the CNCF cloud native map knows: it does not fit on one screen. A production stack needs infrastructure, security, authentication, observability, releases and deployments, and every one of those has a dozen candidate tools. Picking them and making them work together as one package is the real cost. The bootstrapper's answer is a curated set of battle-tested open source apps that are easy to enable or disable, wired together so the result works on the first apply.

## Step one: Terraform builds the cluster and installs Argo CD

The repository has an infrastructure directory with Terraform modules for DigitalOcean. You copy the sample variables file, adjust the cluster configuration, then plan and apply. The plan spins up a Kubernetes cluster, a DigitalOcean container registry, and installs Argo CD automatically. Once it finishes, the cluster ID is printed in the terminal; update your kubecontext and k9s shows a cluster with Argo CD already running.

## Step two: one parent app installs the rest

This is the core of the design. Argo CD's documented cluster bootstrapping pattern, app of apps, uses a parent application (here called bootstrap) that declares child apps beneath it. The project structures it as a Helm chart, so a single values file carries flags to enable or disable each component. In the demo the children are cert-manager, Let's Encrypt, the metrics server, Traefik as the ingress controller and the Trivy operator for runtime security.

Selvan is firm about the workflow this implies. Argo CD watches the repository, so a change only happens when it is pushed to the branch Argo CD tracks. Abhimanyu Selvan said at Conf42 DevOps 2023: "So whatever is in git is going to be synchronized with your cluster." Flip a flag locally and forget to push, and nothing changes. The payoff is an audit trail of who committed what, with Git as the source of truth.

In the Argo CD UI the bootstrap project fans out into a bootstrap resources app (ingress resources and certificates) plus each child, all synced and healthy.

## Step three: observability with Robusta

The last piece is Robusta, an open source Kubernetes monitoring automation platform that ships with the Prometheus stack and Grafana dashboards. Running `robusta gen config` walks through an interactive setup, including a Slack integration and whether to install kube-prometheus-stack, and writes a generated values file used for the Helm install. Once deployed, Grafana dashboards are there out of the box and cluster warnings land in a Slack channel.

## Who should watch

Engineers who need a sane default Kubernetes stack on DigitalOcean, or anyone who wants to see the Argo CD app of apps pattern driven by Helm value flags end to end. It assumes basic Kubernetes and Terraform knowledge. If you already run a mature GitOps platform, this is a quick reference rather than new ideas; if you are on another cloud, the Argo CD half carries over and the Terraform half needs rewriting.

Title: Measure DevSecOps maturity from the tools, not from a survey
Description: Sandeep Panghal (Tata Consultancy Services) and Juan Antonio Conde (Zurich) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on DataHook, DevSecOps metrics pulled from tool APIs
Body:
Most DevSecOps maturity assessments are a questionnaire filled in once a year by people who would rather be shipping. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Sandeep Panghal, Senior Engagement Manager at Tata Consultancy Services, and Juan Antonio Conde, Head of Application Portfolio Composition at Zurich Insurance Group, showed the alternative Zurich built with TCS: DataHook, a tool that computes maturity metrics automatically from the data teams already produce in Jira, code quality, security and testing tools, through their APIs.

It is a short case study, closer to a briefing for a CTO than a technical walkthrough, and it is honest about that.

## What question was Zurich trying to answer?

Panghal opens with the questions a CIO of a global insurer actually asks. How mature is the organisation in DevSecOps against industry standards? Which business units, applications or platforms deliver slower and with lower quality, and which are the top class? Where should the next investment go? Can I compare business units with each other, and with other insurers?

Zurich could not answer any of that cleanly. The problem statement had four parts: no standard set of development metrics across the organisation, no harmonised view of DevSecOps adoption, metrics produced with heavy manual effort because the data sat in many sources, and teams spending their time producing measurements instead of delivering product. That last point is the one most engineers will recognise: the dashboard becomes the job.

## How does DataHook work?

Conde describes the design brief they settled on after talking to stakeholders across Zurich and to outside consultancies: automate how metrics are produced, stay tool agnostic, and keep the metric definitions flexible so they can change later. DataHook was built from scratch to that brief. It is cloud based and meant to scale, it hooks into any tool that exposes an API (DevOps platforms, code quality, security testing, other testing tools), and it can feed any BI tool.

A few design choices stand out:

- **Secure by design**, meaning one business unit's data is not shown to another. Benchmarks are presented from group level down to teams without breaking that anonymisation.
- **Error reports aimed at the teams.** When an application's data does not show up on the dashboard, the team gets a readable report explaining why and how to fix the way they record their work.
- **Design thinking and UX principles** applied to the dashboards, because the audience runs from application teams to business unit IT heads to group leaders.

At the time of the talk the tool measured nine metrics and was ready to take on more.

Juan Antonio Conde said at Conf42 DevOps 2023 that with the tool "we have been able to produce metric at a scale almost with no effort or with a very little effort on the team side."

## What did it change?

The outcome slide carries the real numbers:

- 200 applications from 12 business units assessed for DevSecOps maturity across four classes.
- A monthly onboarding ratio of plus 20%, with onboarding of new applications semi-automated through Azure Pipelines.
- Metrics for customer value, organisational effectiveness and service quality measured continuously from several toolsets, with global, business unit and department benchmarks.
- The Lead Time To Market KPI down 9% over nine months.
- Up to a 10% month-on-month increase in technical debt identified for more than 20 business areas over a year.

That last figure is the interesting one. A tool that only reported good news would be a vanity dashboard; one that surfaces technical debt growing at 10% a month in some areas is doing its job.

## Who should watch

Engineering leaders and platform or DevOps enablement teams in large organisations who are being asked for a maturity score and dread the survey. Do not expect code, an architecture diagram or a product you can download: DataHook is Zurich's internal capability, and the talk is about the problem, the design principles and the results.

Title: VSHN built APPUiO Cloud docs-first and let Conway's law win
Description: Adrian Kosmaczewski (VSHN AG) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on building the APPUiO Cloud OpenShift platform with the Three Ways, async work and trust
Body:
The first thing VSHN built for its new OpenShift platform was not a cluster. It was the documentation. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Adrian Kosmaczewski, Developer Relations at VSHN AG, tells how the 50-person Zurich company that calls itself The DevOps Company used Gene Kim's Three Ways to build APPUiO Cloud with a small team, fully async, and why he thinks writing skills and trust matter more than any tool in the stack.

It is a company story, so expect some pride and a product at the end, but the process details are concrete and transparently shared.

## What kind of company builds like this?

VSHN (pronounced like vision) was founded in 2014, has been self-funded since day one, and profitable and growing since 2017. It sells DevOps as a service around Kubernetes and OpenShift; "Everything we do runs on Kubernetes," Kosmaczewski said. Decisions are made by consensus under sociocracy, with any employee able to file a VSHN Improvement Proposal as a Jira ticket. The company handbook runs to 573 pages in print. It worked remote and asynchronous before the pandemic, so when Switzerland sent everyone home in March 2020, nothing changed.

## Why a new product instead of a migration?

APPUiO, a 2016 joint venture with Puzzle ITC, packages Red Hat OpenShift for companies without the staff or budget to run it, as a shared public platform, managed clusters or self-managed with training. APPUiO Public ran on OpenShift 3. Given the architectural changes in OpenShift 4, they built APPUiO Cloud from scratch rather than migrating it, launched it in September 2021, moved customers over, and fully decommissioned APPUiO Public in September 2022. It is an entry-level, pay-per-use platform for the long tail of OpenShift users (startups, CI/CD, mobile back ends, education, resellers), running in cloudscale.ch's Aargau zone and Exoscale's Geneva zone, with honest restrictions: best-effort SLA, fair-use policy, no privileged containers and 72 hours of log retention.

## The principles of flow: write it first

The first value stream was the product documentation, written and commented on asynchronously until everyone agreed, from product owners to the DevOps engineers who would run it. Then they structured the team before designing the system, so the architecture mirrors the team on purpose. "We do not fight Conway's law. We embrace it," Kosmaczewski said at Conf42 DevOps 2023. The output is three public documentation sites, for product owners, system engineers and end users, which he calls great marketing tools.

Automation comes from Project Syn, the GitOps tool suite VSHN started in 2019 to manage hundreds of clusters from one place: commit to Git, and within seconds every cluster has the change. They use it to roll the same Kyverno security policies out to every zone, and to write down the differences between the two cloud providers.

## The principles of feedback: everything as code

Observability was built in from the start, reusing OpenShift's management stack. Policies, builds, configuration, infrastructure and documentation all live in Git, with GitLab CI building, testing and deploying them. Even the docs are pipelines: AsciiDoc sources, Antora to assemble them, and style and syntax checks on every push.

## Continual learning: the CPU pricing mistake

The best story is a failure. After launch, they found their pricing had not accounted for CPU requests properly, and some users were consuming disproportionate amounts of CPU without knowing it, with VSHN covering the cost. The fix, from May 2022, counts CPU requests beyond the zone's fixed memory-to-CPU ratio as memory-equivalent usage. They changed the cluster policies, updated the docs, told every customer openly, and absorbed some of the cost. "We didn't lose a single customer because of it," he said.

## Crunchy details

The team, called Aldebaran, was one project and product manager (CTO and co-founder Tobias Brunner), one product owner, three core DevOps engineers (six now) and a system architect, plus three to five engineers from other teams and marketing and sales help. The stack: Red Hat OpenShift 4.11, Kyverno, Keycloak, Vault, Rook (which won their storage benchmark against Ceph and Longhorn), Isovalent Cilium Enterprise, K8up for backups (a CNCF sandbox project VSHN started), Project Syn and Antora. First discussions were in February 2021; later came AppCat for requesting S3 buckets and databases in YAML, the Vertical Pod Autoscaler and user workload monitoring.

## Can anyone copy this?

Yes, with three caveats: writing skills (documentation is a deliverable, reviewed and proofread, not a chore), the cloud native open source ecosystem to stand on, and trust, which he ranks above flat hierarchies. "You cannot really go full async if you do not trust your teams."

## Who should watch

Engineering leaders curious about async, consensus-run teams, and platform teams launching an internal or public product. Skip it if you want a deep technical OpenShift build.

Title: Monitoring tells you the soup is salty, observability says who did it
Description: Sarah Morgan (TelemetryHub by Scout APM) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on how observability differs from performance monitoring, and where OpenTelemetry fits
Body:
Cooking at home, you know exactly who put the salt in. In a restaurant kitchen, with an order passing through half a dozen stations, a too-salty soup is a mystery. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Sarah Morgan, Senior Product Manager at TelemetryHub by Scout APM, uses that analogy to separate performance monitoring from observability: monitoring answers the questions you knew to ask, observability lets you answer the ones you did not, and buying a tool gets you neither by itself.

It is an introductory talk from a vendor that builds on OpenTelemetry, and she is clear that OpenTelemetry is not the only route.

## Why did monitoring stop being enough?

Morgan starts with why anyone should care: her figures put debugging at around 25% of a developer's time and downtime at roughly $5,600 per minute, and nobody takes a job hoping to be woken at night. Performance monitoring was born in the data center, for monoliths you could run locally and step through with a debugger. It answered three questions well: what is the current state, what do the trends say, and when should I be alerted. She still remembers the exact pager model she carried.

Distributed systems broke that model. They bring scalability, faster deploys and smaller pieces that new hires can learn quickly, but understanding a request from start to finish gets hard. Ephemeral resources make it worse: "So you can't set a monitor for something that you can't see." And a container that shuts down to save money should not page anyone.

## Is observability just monitoring with a new name?

Partly, and she is relaxed about it. Monitoring is one aspect of observability. The term itself comes from R. E. Kalman's 1960 work on the general theory of control systems: how well a system's internal states can be inferred from its external outputs. Her rules of thumb are that observability is never done, it is not all or nothing, it is a spectrum from opaque to transparent, and "the outcomes are more important than the labels," Morgan said at Conf42 DevOps 2023.

The real difference is the unknowns. Monitoring answers a known question, like average response time. Observability, with high-cardinality data, lets you ask why only one customer is having a problem. Logging everything is not the answer either; that builds a haystack that leaves you data rich and information poor.

## What do you need to know at 3am?

Her nightmare scenario is a page where the runbook just says restart the service. To actually fix things you need to know who is impacted (a canary in production can wait, your biggest customer onboarding new users cannot), whether you have what you need to resolve it, where the problem is, when it started, and how you got there. She also tells the story of Bob, the one engineer who understood a legacy part of the platform. If Bob leaves, nobody can see inside it.

## Metrics, traces and logs

- **Metrics** are aggregate, low-cardinality data: cheap to store, good for alerting and autoscaling, bad for diagnosis because the connective detail is gone.
- **Distributed traces** follow a request across services, made of spans, held together by propagated trace and span IDs. Her checkout example hops through customer IDs, SKU lookups and inventory checks.
- **Logs** hold the high-cardinality detail (user ID, organisation ID) and become much more useful once they carry trace IDs.

"Just because you have purchased an observability platform or tool doesn't mean that your system is observable," she says. Pick tools for your size: no need to buy a Ferrari when a Smart car will do.

## Where does OpenTelemetry come in?

She calls it the second most active CNCF project after Kubernetes, backed by more than 130 companies, with a shared definition of signals, a shared protocol, per-language SDKs and auto-instrumentation. Getting a Python app instrumented takes a few lines. The collector receives, processes and exports data, and can send it to several back ends at once. The main payoff is vendor neutrality: if you outgrow a back end, you point the data elsewhere instead of ripping out proprietary agents.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers who hear observability and monitoring used interchangeably and want a clear mental model, and teams weighing OpenTelemetry before choosing a vendor. Practitioners already running tracing will know most of it.

Title: Humana put the change board inside the pipeline, and patented it
Description: Rupesh Kumar and Andrew Foster (Humana) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on scaling DevOps in a regulated insurer with Greenlight API, a pipeline compliance gate
Body:
In a regulated health insurer, releasing software usually means leaving your pipeline to fill in a change ticket. Humana decided its engineers should never have to. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Rupesh Kumar, Principal DevOps Engineer, and Andrew Foster, Director of DevOps Engineering, both at Humana, describe how the Fortune 41 company scaled DevOps from 2018 onwards, with a patented pipeline task called Greenlight API that encodes the company's SDLC, security and change rules so a release can go to production straight from the pipeline.

## What does DevOps look like at an insurer?

Humana serves 5.1 million individual and group Medicare Advantage members, plus military families through Tricare, and works with the federal government, so traceability and audits are not optional. Foster's team owns all the DevOps platforms across open systems, mainframe and Salesforce, and calls itself the IT team for the IT teams. Its mission: give engineers the most compelling development experience possible, and get out of their way.

Kumar opens with culture: "we say that culture is pretty much everything to do with DevOps," he said at Conf42 DevOps 2023, tying Humana's company values (cultivate uniqueness, rethink routine, inspire health, thrive together, pioneer simplicity) to the DevOps model the team runs: listen to engineers actively, empower them with tools and platforms, guide them with standards for branching, progressive delivery, GitOps, environments and microservices, measure with data and OKRs, and improve by cutting cognitive load.

## Three moves that made it scale

Foster credits three things.

- **Alignment and feedback.** In 2018 Humana achieved unusual alignment across its engineering community, then kept it with tight feedback loops: regular updates to leaders and regular sessions with engineers.
- **Engineer-first platforms.** The rule from the start: to release to production, an engineer should never leave their native tooling for a CMDB or change management tool. Security and quality posture has to show up inside the workflow, with separate experiences for open systems, mainframe and Salesforce engineers.
- **Automated SDLC and smaller releases.** One component, one repo, one pipeline, which maps source code to application components and pushes teams towards smaller, more iterative releases.

## How does Greenlight API work?

Greenlight API (GLAPI, US patent 11467810) is a required, enforced task in every pipeline. From the first commit and build, it tells developers which parts of the Humana SDLC they have satisfied and which they have not, across plan, build, accept, deploy, run and feedback. Its checks include traceability to a business requirement, source code policy, security and quality scanning, releasing from the main branch, unit test coverage, no open defects, security and performance gates, approval validation and release within a maintenance window. An integration with ServiceNow opens the change order automatically and sends it through approval.

The result, in Foster's words: "So literally, DevOps do not have to leave their pipeline interface to release software in a certified and trusted way at Humana."

## What's in the open systems toolchain?

The developer experience is a fully integrated stack: Azure Repos and GitHub for code, Azure Boards for planning, Azure Pipelines for CI and CD, SonarQube, Checkmarx, AppScan, Contrast and Burp Suite for code and runtime security, JFrog Artifactory and Xray for open source packages and CVE blocking, LaunchDarkly for feature flags, qTest and Azure Test Plans, Tosca and Selenium for testing, LoadRunner, Dynatrace and Keptn for performance testing and SLO enforcement, and Splunk for events. A developer control plane lets teams self-serve things like SonarQube projects and Artifactory repos. Teams own their pipelines, because the pipeline is part of the application; Greenlight API is the guardrail on that ownership.

## What did it deliver?

Kumar puts the scale at more than 1,600 applications and components, more than 300 teams, more than 10 million lines of code, over 17,000 CI/CD pipelines and over 24 tools run by the DevOps platform team. For teams fully adopting the DevOps capabilities, they report a 56% improvement in automation over manual release processes, a better than 80% improvement in process, wait and lead time, and more than 97% of eligible releases going to production through DevOps pipelines month over month. Kumar closes with the reminder that "DevOps is certainly a journey and not a destination."

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps leads in regulated industries who are stuck between auditors and engineers. It is an enterprise case study rather than a technical deep look at GLAPI's internals, but the list of automated checks alone is worth stealing.

Title: From dotnet new to Azure Container Registry, one Dockerfile at a time
Description: Hamida Rebai (Microsoft) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on containerising .NET microservices with Docker and pushing images to Azure Container Registry
Body:
Microservices and containers get mentioned in the same breath so often that it is easy to forget they are separate decisions. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Hamida Rebai, Microsoft MVP in Developer Technologies and a cloud application architect, makes the distinction explicit, then walks through containerising an ASP.NET Core Web API with Docker and publishing it to Azure Container Registry and Docker Hub, from both Visual Studio 2022 and Visual Studio Code.

It is a beginner-to-intermediate talk: a theory half on microservices and containers, then a long, click-by-click demo.

## What makes a service a microservice?

Her checklist: services are small, independent and loosely coupled; each is a separate code base a small team can manage; each deploys independently; each persists its own data rather than sharing a data layer; they talk through well-defined APIs and hide their internals; and they do not need to share a technology stack. Around them sit management (placing services on nodes, detecting failures, rebalancing), service discovery, an identity provider and an API gateway.

The gateway gets the most attention. Without one, clients call front-end services directly, which couples them to how the back end is decomposed and makes refactoring harder. With one, you get a single entry point that can also handle authentication, logging, SSL termination, rate limiting and load balancing. And a caveat she is careful to state: "The microservices architectures offer tremendous benefits, but it's not a silver bullet," Rebai said at Conf42 DevOps 2023.

## Containers are not only for microservices

A container packages an app with its configuration and dependencies into one deployable unit, with a much smaller footprint than a VM image. An image is the immutable snapshot a container runs from; it can be duplicated, shared or deleted, never changed. Her practical point for .NET shops: you can containerise a monolith just to get isolated test environments and kill missing-dependency surprises in production, even on the traditional .NET Framework with Windows containers, without migrating to .NET 6 or 7 first. For new services, she recommends the latest .NET.

## A multi-stage Dockerfile, line by line

The demo starts from the ASP.NET Core Web API template with Docker support enabled (or added later via Add, then Docker Support). She explains the generated file:

- A build stage based on the official .NET 7 SDK image, so all build tooling comes from Microsoft's image.
- `WORKDIR` so later commands can use relative paths.
- Copy only the `.csproj` files and run `dotnet restore` first. Each command creates a cached layer, and project files change rarely, so restores are reused.
- Copy the rest of the source and run `dotnet publish`.
- A runtime stage with its own working directory, port 80 exposed, and an `ENTRYPOINT` running the published DLL.
- A `.dockerignore` to keep the build context small.

In VS Code she does the same with the Docker extension's add-Dockerfile command, builds with `docker build -t`, and runs the container from the terminal.

## Tags, registries and where to run it

"Docker tags are just an alias for an image id," she says, comparing them to Git commits: several tags can point at the same image. She adds a second tag through the Docker extension, then creates an Azure Container Registry in the portal (Basic, Standard or Premium SKU, optional private networking and customer-managed keys) and again with `az acr create` in Azure Cloud Shell. Publishing works from Visual Studio's Publish dialog or by pushing from VS Code; the same flow targets Docker Hub for public images.

Her closing map of Azure options: Container Registry for private images, Docker Hub for public ones, Azure Container Instances or App Service for a single container, and Azure Kubernetes Service for full orchestration with autoscaling and service discovery. For the in-between, she points to Azure Container Apps, because, in her words, "The problem is Kubernetes is extremely difficult to use".

## Who should watch

.NET developers containerising their first service, or teams on the classic .NET Framework wondering whether Docker is worth it before a migration. Experienced container users can skip to the Dockerfile walkthrough.

Title: From zero GitHub stars to 17,000, the ShardingSphere way
Description: Trista Pan (SphereEx) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on growing an open source community, from project value and docs to a contributor path
Body:
Apache ShardingSphere started with zero stars on GitHub. By the time Trista Pan, Co-Founder and CTO of SphereEx, spoke at Conf42 DevOps 2023, it had more than 17,000 stars, more than 400 contributors and a commercial company built on top of it. Her talk is a practical playbook for getting an open source project there: be genuinely useful, invest in the boring assets, and give people a visible path from user to committer.

Pan is an Apache Member, an Apache Incubator mentor and on the ShardingSphere PMC, so most of the advice comes through the lens of the Apache Software Foundation.

## What does a healthy community look like?

She starts by defining the target before the tactics. A healthy, active open source community scores well on code quality, a clear license and copyright, documentation and articles, a place for people to discuss and report issues, and above all people: users, evangelists, contributors and committers. A project maintained by one person is not a community, however good the code.

ShardingSphere is her worked example. It turns a monolithic database such as MySQL or PostgreSQL into a distributed one, adding features like automatic data encryption and decryption, SQL audit and auto scaling on Kubernetes. Beyond the GitHub numbers, it has many releases, GitHub Actions guarding quality and an Apache license that companies are comfortable with.

## Start with the value

The first question is whether the project solves real problems for many people, because usefulness is what brings users and, eventually, monetisation. ShardingSphere's usefulness in the database space is what let SphereEx exist. Value also has to keep up with trends: she points to established Apache Java projects working out how to move onto Kubernetes. Projects that stop evolving and lose their maintainers end up in the Apache Attic, frozen.

## The kernel and the shell

She splits project assets into two layers.

- **The kernel** is the infrastructure: code hosting, CI/CD, tests, license and copyright, and an issue and feedback platform. She recommends GitHub for the templates and Actions marketplace, with the caveat that this is not a pitch. Language choice matters too; a niche language shrinks the pool of potential contributors.
- **The shell** is what lets others understand the project: user documentation, articles, a code of conduct, milestones and plans. ShardingSphere spent three years building its documentation base.

The part people forget is community documentation: how to get involved, how to raise a first pull request, which areas a newcomer can own. "So you need to pave the way for your contributors to come here," Pan said at Conf42 DevOps 2023.

## Give contributors a path

The Apache Way she cites is community over code, earned authority and open communication. In practice: discuss in the open rather than in small private groups, and make the ladder visible, from user to contributor to committer to PMC member, voted on by the PMC. Recognition and swag matter, because everyone needs positive feedback. Her best case study is one of SphereEx's own: a developer who started as a contributor, was voted onto the PMC for his work, and was then hired by SphereEx as a developer manager.

Outside the project, she pushes promotion: social media, Slack, blogs, long-form articles, a book, conference talks. Her articles led Delivery Hero's Korea branch to adopt ShardingSphere in production, and JD.com used it with MySQL to build a sharded system, a case MySQL itself published.

Her closing advice is patience: "be patient with the progress", keep doing the routine work, and let it compound.

## Who should watch

Maintainers of a young project who want more than drive-by users, and developer relations people at open source companies. Note that the abstract also promises career advice for women in tech and fundraising tips; the recorded talk sticks to community building.

Title: DataOps plus data mesh, or the data team that owns its infra
Description: Agita Jaunzeme (VMware) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on combining DataOps and data mesh so domain teams own pipelines and infrastructure
Body:
On her first day as a junior DevOps engineer, Agita Jaunzeme was handed seven to ten printed pages of manual deployment steps and told, at 6pm, that they had to be run four more times that day. Three months later she had automated every step. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Jaunzeme, community manager for VMware's open source Versatile Data Kit (VDK) and a former DevOps engineer, takes that lesson to data teams: combine DataOps with data mesh so that the people who own the data also own the pipelines and the infrastructure, and the dependencies between teams disappear.

She says up front that the talk is beginner friendly, aimed at DevOps engineers curious about data and data engineers curious about DevOps.

## What DevOps taught her

Two things, from two projects. The first was automation. After that long evening repeating the paper checklist, she started scripting it, from copying files and renaming folders up to editing the code, until the deployment could run around 280 times in 2 hours with nothing left for her to do. Her takeaway, as she said at Conf42 DevOps 2023: "if something can be written on paper, it can be definitely automated."

The second was collaboration. On a large Chef infrastructure automation project in Germany, she commuted weekly from Latvia, because everyone doing any kind of automation sat in the same room. When something broke, they fixed it together on the spot. That proximity, physical or virtual, is the part she carries into data mesh.

## What does DataOps change?

DataOps is the data engineering equivalent of DevOps: speed up data deployments while improving quality, with pipelines and jobs that run automatically instead of hand-run data work. It reduces dependencies between data teams and infrastructure teams, but does not remove them. In her ideal, "data pipelines and infrastructure are built and maintained by the same people", which she admits is not always the case.

She notes that the community has not agreed on a DataOps lifecycle and offers her own: plan, code, orchestrate, test, deploy, execute, monitor and feedback. She maps it onto VDK as an example:

- **Code**: data jobs in Python and SQL, interchangeably, whose steps run in the alphanumeric order of their file names. `vdk run` executes the whole pipeline locally.
- **Orchestrate and deploy**: code goes to Git, and VDK's control service sets up the infrastructure and schedules the jobs on Kubernetes, through staging to production.
- **Monitor**: failing jobs send an alert to a configured email address with the job name and error type, including whether it is a user, configuration or platform error.

## Where does data mesh fit?

Data mesh, introduced by Zhamak Dehghani in 2019, is a platform architecture built on domain ownership, self-service and data as a product: each business domain builds and maintains its own pipelines. On its own, it still leaves domain owners waiting on whoever runs orchestration, testing and CI/CD. Hence her DataOps mesh: data mesh supplies governance, self-service, data as a product and domain ownership; DataOps supplies CI/CD, testing, observability and orchestration. If the domain team owns all of it, there is nobody left to wait for. VDK supports this with team ownership on every data job, plus shared templates and plugins.

## What could go wrong?

She names two risks honestly. Skills: one person would need domain knowledge, data engineering and DevOps all at once. Her team's answer is tooling that lowers the bar to basic Python and SQL, plus the DevOps habit of learning new tools every week. Trust: management may not want domain teams to hold full power over infrastructure, with the risk of accidental deletion that comes with it. Rules and guardrails help, but she leaves that question open.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who keep filing tickets with an infrastructure team, and DevOps engineers moving into data platforms. It is a conceptual overview with one tool as the worked example, and it ends with a polite request to star VDK on GitHub.

Title: Spend 10% more up front and skip 90% of the incidents
Description: Sinan Kucukkoseler (Shopify) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on shipping fast without breaking things via priorities, walking skeletons and safe integrations
Body:
Sinan Kucukkoseler once watched an experiment tell his team that users did not want a feature. They later found out the users would have liked the idea fine; the feature was just slow, so they dropped off. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, the Senior Software Engineer at Shopify uses lessons like that to argue for moving fast without breaking things, built on one rule of thumb: more often than not, spending 10% extra time and effort prevents 90% of the issues you would face later.

He has the background for it: ten years in tech, ThoughtWorks across Turkey, Germany, India and Spain, then New Relic, whose telemetry pipeline he describes as running perhaps the biggest Kafka cluster in the world, and now the Shop app team at Shopify, which processes more than 20 million order-tracking status updates.

## Why not just move fast and break things?

Facebook's old motto made sense for a company inventing new user habits, and Facebook itself later moved to "move fast with stable infra". Kucukkoseler gives three reasons stability matters even when speed is the goal. Users now expect a quality threshold. Experiments are only valid if the experimental feature meets your current quality bar, as his slow-feature story shows. And morale: a team that ships things that break often spends its time fixing them, and that wears people down over months.

## Plan around priorities, not heroics

His team motto is that a team "should be doing the most important thing at any given time." On a Wednesday morning, someone will have to pick between a security fix and a performance optimisation. Rather than relying on each engineer to guess right, set the priorities between time, performance, scope, quality and security up front and broadcast them. A 20-minute conversation is enough; trade-off slider workshops are optional.

For design he borrows evolutionary architecture from ThoughtWorks: accept that architecture is a living thing, and change it consciously with a fitness function that encodes those priorities (high throughput over low latency, say, or data security over usability). Start with low complexity, because a system that hides its behaviour, like a chessboard mid-game to a novice, is hard to grow.

## Tough parts first, on a walking skeleton

When splitting work, prioritise the parts with high value and high complexity: the ones that connect the pipes, the risky ones, the ones holding unknowns. Do not build the car's parts separately and bolt them together in the final week. "I think you should really consider having a walking skeleton from week one," Kucukkoseler said at Conf42 DevOps 2023.

## Treat integrations as where incidents live

Integrations are where most incidents happen, so he splits their protection by direction:

- **Downstream**: timeouts, retries, back-off policies, circuit breaking. Do not wait 30 seconds on a failing service; time out and use the resource for something else.
- **Upstream**: bulkheads, load shedding, rate limiting, so a flood in one place cannot eat every resource.

The key point is timing. Build these while you build the integration, not in the week before release, so you can test and tune them.

## Decide at 2pm what you would do at 2am

Map the failure scenarios before they happen: a sudden spike in ingress load, the database as a bottleneck, a throttled downstream API, an unavailable cache cluster, a cloud provider incident. Decide the response as a team and write a runbook, instead of leaving it to whoever gets woken at 2am on a Saturday. His supporting patterns: auto-scaling with warm-up before known peaks, immutability so parts of the flow can be retried when (not if) something fails, compartmentalising work so you can deprioritise or scale it separately (50 million notifications without scaling the whole app), and runtime configuration for kill switches and thresholds without a deploy.

## Observability on day one

Add metrics while you build, not when productising. Start with the question of how you would know the thing works: an API success rate, a p95 response time, requests per second. Emit data generously, alert from day one so you can tune the alerts, make performance tests a gate if performance matters, and run game days.

## Who should watch

Tech leads planning a new service inside an existing large system. Much of it is familiar material, but the ordering and the emphasis on building safeguards early make a good checklist.

Title: Your CI/CD platform is production too, so trace it and predict it
Description: Michele Dodic and Francesco Sbaraglia (Accenture) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on tracing Jenkins with OpenTelemetry and predicting CI/CD health with ML
Body:
The moment you most need your pipeline is the outage, when a hotfix has to ship now. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Michele Dodic, SRE DevOps Specialist at Accenture, and Francesco Sbaraglia, SRE Tech Lead at Accenture, treat the CI/CD platform as the critical system it is: instrument Jenkins with OpenTelemetry, define KPIs for the platform itself, and train a model to predict its health half an hour ahead.

It is a vendor-specific demo (Splunk Observability Cloud and Splunk IT Service Intelligence on top of the OpenTelemetry collector), but the KPI list and the architecture carry over to any stack.

## Why watch a pipeline at all?

Sbaraglia lists the challenges: SRE and DevOps teams need a CI/CD platform that is reliable with predictable failures, data for proactive capacity management, and a working path to deploy hotfixes and bugfixes during outages. And yet, "Most of the time the CI CD platform is black box," Sbaraglia said at Conf42 DevOps 2023.

## Which KPIs describe a CI/CD platform?

Their architecture is a standard one: a commit triggers Jenkins, which spins up a dynamic agent pod on Kubernetes and deploys to production. What they add is telemetry from every run, and a KPI set for the platform:

- Speed of the CD pipeline, and hotfix/bugfix deployment speed in particular. A faster hotfix deploy is directly a lower MTTR.
- Build and test success rate.
- Deployments per month, per pipeline and per application.
- Lead time from commit to deployment.
- Change success rate: successful builds or deployments over the total.
- Availability of the CI/CD platform itself.

A side benefit: the engineer deploying no longer opens Jenkins to check on a release, because the status lives in the observability platform. In a light moment, they also asked ChatGPT to suggest SLIs for a CI/CD platform and compared its list with theirs.

## One agent on the controller, not one per worker

Dodic walks through the OpenTelemetry side: logs, metrics and traces (their golden triangle) next to the golden signals of latency, traffic, errors and saturation. The collector enriches all three signals uniformly, so they carry the same attribute names describing the Kubernetes pod they came from. The practical win is that OpenTelemetry is attached to the Jenkins controller, and "we don't have to install anything on each single Jenkins agent."

In Sbaraglia's part of the demo, each pipeline run becomes a trace with a span per stage. Pod allocation comes first, which is where a saturated Kubernetes cluster shows up as a slow start. Checking out the Jenkinsfile took around 16 seconds, compiling the deployment YAML 47 seconds, and both are visible as candidates for trimming. One stage is an SRE gate: if the production service has already consumed its error budget, the pipeline blocks the deployment. Out of the box they also get request rate, latency and error rate for the Jenkins controller.

## Can a model see a pipeline outage coming?

Their AI-driven approach runs in three stages: observe, engage, act. Two service health KPIs feed it: CI/CD pipeline reliability and an end-to-end score from a scheduled smoke-test pipeline that exercises every stage of a fake build. In Splunk ITSI, the KPIs roll up into a service tree (Vault for secrets, the Kubernetes cluster, Jenkins) with a health score.

Dodic then trains a random forest regressor on 14 days of KPI data with a 70/30 train/test split, checks predicted average and worst-case health on the test set, and applies the model to predict the Jenkins reliability service's health score for the next 30 minutes. From there the plan is predictive alerting and zero-touch automation: scripts that fix the platform or add resources before the disruption lands. The automated remediation was out of scope for the demo.

## Who should watch

Platform teams who own Jenkins or another shared CI system and get blamed when it is slow, and SREs curious what tracing a pipeline looks like. Expect a guided demo, not a deep look at model accuracy. Their closing advice fits the scope: "start simple and scale fast."

Title: Your Kubernetes cluster is the new pet, and it should go
Description: Chris Nesbitt-Smith (UK Government) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on why hand-built Kubernetes clusters became pets, and why vanilla managed services win
Body:
Kubernetes was supposed to turn our servers into cattle, and it did. The trouble, Chris Nesbitt-Smith argues at Conf42 DevOps 2023, is that the cluster itself became the pet. The consultant, working with UK Government among others and running Kubernetes in production since version 0.4, gives a short, very funny and slightly self-loathing talk with a blunt answer to its own title question: "Is it time to put your Kubernetes cluster down? Yes, it is."

## Where did the pet come from?

He starts with the history of pets versus cattle, usually traced to Bill Baker of Microsoft around 2006. Pets are Bob the mail server: when Bob goes down, the CEO cannot get his email and the sysadmins perform resuscitation rituals into the night. Cattle are web01 to web100, taken out the back and replaced. Kubernetes handles this beautifully for nodes and workloads, which get arbitrary names and are rescheduled when they fail.

So where is the pet? Look at what you do first with a brand-new cluster. It is not deploying anything the business cares about. It is installing the add-ons needed before it can run workloads at all, and the trend towards features living out of tree (flex volumes, policy, most of the SIG projects) makes that list longer. Then you need dev, integration, staging and QA clusters, plus separation between teams. Then an upgrade lands that patches a vulnerability you care about, and you are testing every app against every permutation.

That is day-two operations, and it is where versions drift and teams pick different ingress controllers (Kong here, NGINX there, Apache and Envoy elsewhere), each for good reasons. "Congratulations, you're now the proud owner of a pet shop," Nesbitt-Smith said at Conf42 DevOps 2023. Automate the creation and you have a pet factory.

## The grey layer that delivers nothing

His model of a cloud estate has three tiers. Apps are what the boardroom can name: the website, the shopping cart, customer service tools. Infrastructure should be a commodity you consume with an SLA from the cloud vendor. Sandwiched between them sits the grey layer of operational enablers: log aggregation, certificate issuers, security policy, monitoring, service mesh. That is where the DevOps or SRE team lives, and unless your business is building those products, it delivers zero business value. Worse, by running it yourself you assume you are more competent than your multi-billion-dollar cloud vendor and tear up the shared responsibility model you moved to the cloud for.

It also wrecks hiring. The job spec becomes Kubernetes plus a CKA, on AWS, with Linkerd in some places and Istio in others, a mix of pod security policy, Kyverno and OPA, Terraform, Helm, Jenkins and GitHub Actions in a monorepo. You are back to hunting unicorns, and each new hire brings their own favourite tools to the pile.

## A Helm chart horror story

The sharpest rant is about abstraction. Operators that create CRDs for other operators, mutating admission controllers, and Helm, which he calls a string-based templating engine where every community chart ends up exposing every parameter. His example: a nested chart maps a database replica count to a string value, a dependency that does not follow semver renames that value, and your three replicas silently become one. A plain YAML patch against the Deployment object, with a stable versioned API and schema validation, would never have done that.

## So what should you do?

"Bin it. Bin it all, kill it with fire, and then learn to love vanilla." Keep it simple, embrace the shared responsibility model, and "Make your cloud vendors do more than just provide compute." A cluster earns the right to live only if you can bring it back immutably from code without anyone noticing. It is not exciting, he admits, and magpie engineers who chase shiny things may find the job less fun.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE leads deciding how much of the cluster add-on stack to own, and anyone whose cluster has a name. It is opinion rather than a migration guide, and it is short enough for a coffee break.

Title: Page on burn rate, not on CPU: SLO alerts that let you sleep
Description: Joe Blubaugh (Grafana Labs) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on SLOs, error budgets and multi-window burn-rate alerts that only page for real user pain
Body:
If your pager goes off because CPU is high while checkout works fine, your alerts are measuring the wrong thing. At Conf42 DevOps 2023, Joe Blubaugh, Principal Software Engineer at Grafana Labs, argues that service level objectives are the cure for noisy on-call: alert on the symptoms users feel, measure how fast you are spending your error budget, and only wake someone when that spend is fast enough to matter.

Blubaugh has spent ten years building and running distributed systems at Google, Twitter and startups, and he describes his relationship with on-call as love/hate. The talk is short, practical and ends with a table you can paste straight into your alerting rules.

## Why is bad on-call a retention problem?

He opens with burnout, citing a figure that 75% of software engineers show symptoms of it. The causes he lists (unclear expectations, lack of autonomy, inability to unplug, inability to ship) map almost one-to-one onto bad on-call: nobody knows who owns the alert, you get paged at 3am for minor things, and you spend the day firefighting instead of committing code. People quit, and the institutional knowledge walks out with them. As he puts it, "No matter how good your system documentation is, you can't recover from huge turnover."

A good on-call shift, in his framing, has the right people on call for the right systems, and every alert is meaningful and actionable.

## What goes into an indicator?

A service level is about the quality of service a system gives its users, not about a single microservice. You build an indicator in three steps: a prose question (can users sign in?), the metric that answers it (a `login_requests_count` counter), and some math that turns it into a number between 0 and 1, such as non-5xx requests over all requests in a PromQL ratio. Common shapes are ratios (successful over total requests), thresholds (backup throughput over 40 Gbps) and percentiles (p99 latency under 500ms).

## How strict should the objective be?

Less strict than your VP of engineering wants. His downtime table makes the point: 99% over 7 days allows 1 hour 41 minutes of total downtime, 99.9% over 28 days allows 40 minutes, and five nines over 28 days leaves you 25 seconds. His advice is to look at the last few months of the indicator, pick a target you already roughly meet, leave a safety margin and tighten later. A blanket top-down rule that every service must hit 99% sabotages a team on day one, before anyone knows how the system actually performs.

## Alerting is triage, not maintenance

The core of the talk is the split between symptoms and causes. Pods running out of memory is a cause; checkout being broken is a symptom. Causes belong in regular system check-ups during working hours. Symptoms are what should page. "Alerting is not about maintaining systems," Blubaugh said at Conf42 DevOps 2023, and then the line that gives the talk its title: "You shouldn't be getting up at three in the morning for maintenance tasks. You should be getting up at three in the morning when something is broken."

## Burn rate, with two windows

Treat the objective as a budget and errors as spending, like a startup's cash burn. He sorts burn into four buckets: sustained high or transient extremely high burn should wake you; sustained moderate burn is for the morning, but must be prioritised; sustained low burn is check-up work; transient moderate blips should not alert at all, because big systems always have a switch being replaced somewhere.

To avoid paging too early or too late, each alert checks the burn rate over a short and a long window at once. The long window stops brief spikes from paging; the short one makes the alert resolve quickly once things recover. His severity table:

| Short window | Long window | Burn rate | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 minutes | 1 hour | 14.4x budget | urgent |
| 30 minutes | 6 hours | 6x budget | high |
| 2 hours | 1 day | 3x budget | moderate |
| 6 hours | 3 days | 1x budget | low |

## Who should watch

Teams whose pager is mostly noise, and anyone about to introduce SLOs and wondering where to start. It is an introduction, not a tour of tooling, and it is about 20 minutes well spent before you rewrite your alert rules.

Title: Python plus Apache Pulsar is enough for a one-person streaming app
Description: Tim Spann (StreamNative) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on streaming apps in Python with Apache Pulsar, from schemas and functions to MQTT, Kafka and a Raspberry Pi
Body:
Real-time data apps usually take a team, but Tim Spann, Developer Advocate at StreamNative, argued at Conf42 DevOps 2023 that a small one can be built by one person with Python and Apache Pulsar as the hub in the middle. His talk walks through what a Pulsar message carries, how schemas, functions and protocol handlers work from Python, how to script a cluster's setup, and ends with a Raspberry Pi tracking the planes over his house in New Jersey.

As he put it: "if the application is small enough, you could do this by yourself."

## Why Pulsar as the hub?

His pitch is DevOps-shaped. Compute and storage are separate layers, so you can partition, rebalance and scale without taking things down. Clusters are managed from one place through REST endpoints, command-line tools or your automation of choice. Geo-redundancy is built in, and old data can be tiered off to cloud storage or Hadoop automatically. His community numbers: 560+ contributors, 10,000+ commits, 7,000+ Slack members and 1,000+ organisations using it.

## What goes into a message?

The value is raw bytes, so anything fits, though JSON, Avro or Protobuf are the sensible choices. Then:

- **Set a key.** It helps partitioning, compaction, lookups and debugging, and the table API can keep the latest value per key. His advice is to always set one.
- **Properties** for extra key-value pairs, within reason; "don't put a whole database in there."
- **A producer name**, otherwise you get a generated one.
- **A sequence ID**, assigned for you to keep ordering.

The schema registry is built in. In Python you define a record class, pass the schema to the producer, and Pulsar versions it; a message that doesn't match the contract is rejected. Avro, Protobuf and JSON are supported by default.

## Functions are your own little Lambda

Pulsar Functions are where Python earns its place. A function is a class with a process method called for every message; the return value goes to the output topic, a context object gives access to topics, logs and state, and logs can be routed to their own topic, which another function can consume. His example runs the VADER sentiment library on a JSON field and adds the score to the output. Deploying is one CLI command naming the Python file, class, input topics, log topic and output topic, with options such as auto-ack. Functions can run inside Pulsar, on Kubernetes, or under the open-source Function Mesh project.

## Speak MQTT, Kafka or WebSockets

Protocol handlers let existing clients talk to Pulsar unchanged: MQTT (MoP) for devices, AMQP (AoP) for older enterprise systems, Kafka (KoP) so standard Kafka libraries, Python's included, treat Pulsar as a broker, and WebSockets. He shows each from Python: Paho MQTT on port 1883, a WebSocket client sending base64-encoded payloads in a JSON envelope, and the stock kafka-python library.

## Scripting the cluster

Pulsar is multi-tenant, so setup is a short script: create a tenant, a namespace, then topics named persistent://tenant/namespace/topic (persistent means kept until acknowledged or expired). The newer Pulsar shell runs these admin and messaging commands interactively or as a batch. The Python client supports Python 3; he suggested starting new projects on 2.11 and matching older clusters otherwise. Consumers get a subscription, a cursor in the broker, so a client that reconnects resumes where it left off.

## The Raspberry Pi demo

A PiAware USB stick and antenna pick up aircraft near Newark and JFK, and a short Python app polls the device's local API, adds device stats like temperature, sets a unique key per record and sends the raw JSON to Pulsar, where a function cleans it up for Spark or Flink. A second app streams sensor readings with required fields because they land in a data lake. Others pull from WebSockets and Mastodon. Every one follows the same three steps: make a record, set a key, send it.

## Who should watch

Python developers new to streaming, and anyone choosing between Pulsar and Kafka who wants to see the developer experience. Pulsar regulars will know most of it; the code is in his GitHub, and the free Apache Pulsar in Action book he plugs covers the rest.

Title: Tell Melodic your deadline and budget, and it picks the cloud machines
Description: Maciej Riedl (7bulls.com) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on Melodic and Morphemic, open-source multi-cloud deployment that reconfigures apps from live metrics
Body:
Most autoscalers react to CPU. Melodic reacts to whether your job will finish on time and what it costs. Maciej Riedl, Software Developer at 7bulls.com, demoed the open-source platform at Conf42 DevOps 2023: you describe the application and its constraints once, in a cloud-agnostic model, and Melodic solves for the cheapest set of machines across providers that meets them, then keeps re-solving as metrics arrive. Its extension, Morphemic, adds forecasting so the reconfiguration can happen before the load shows up.

One note on scope: despite the serverless in the title, the demo deploys virtual machines for a Spark workload. The ideas, constraint solving and a utility function over live metrics, are the point.

## What do you give it?

Cloud credentials (the demo has AWS plus an OpenStack cloud at the University of Oslo) and a model of the application written in CAMEL, a cloud-agnostic modelling language. The model holds the components, hardware requirements as ranges rather than hard-coded values (minimum and maximum RAM, for instance), custom variables, and the metrics to collect. There is a drag-and-drop CAMEL Designer for people who'd rather not write it by hand. Upload, pick the credentials, press the big green button.

## What happens after the green button?

The deployment view shows five steps, and he walks through the main ones:

1. **Fetching offers.** Melodic asks each cloud provider what machines and operating systems it offers.
2. **Generating the constraint problem** from the limits in the CAMEL model.
3. **Reasoning.** A solver finds concrete values for the variables that maximise a utility function.
4. **Deploying.** Machines are started, software such as Java installed, and metric collection wired up.

"Best" is whatever you define. The utility function can be far more elaborate than a price-to-performance ratio, and there is a graphical tool for building custom ones. With no metrics yet, the first solution is minimal: one master, one worker.

## The demo: 576 computations in 60 minutes

The test application is Genome, which Riedl described as a real-case scenario built with the University of Bialystok: feature selection over large genomic and genetic data sets, an exhaustive search over tuples that is expensive but easy to parallelise. A Spark master schedules the jobs, and Melodic decides how many workers there should be.

The run starts with 576 computations and a CAMEL constraint that they all finish within 60 minutes, at the lowest cost. Grafana shows six application metrics, including time left and estimated time. With one worker, estimated time is above time left, so Melodic reconfigures on its own, running the same reasoning and deploying steps with real data this time. Worker cardinality goes from one to two, estimated time drops below time left, and the indicator turns green. The master stays at one, the limit set in the model. Riedl's point, as he said at Conf42 DevOps 2023: "So you can see I haven't interfered with the application at all from the moment I started it."

The same loop can scale down: if the job is running far ahead of the deadline, a worker can be stopped to save money.

## Morphemic adds forecasting

Morphemic, the extension, brings a forecasting module. A larger Genome run, almost 800 simulations over seven to eight hours, shows predicted metric values from several time-series models: ARIMA, TFT, N-BEATS, CNN and Prophet, combined by an ensemble because some single models are not very accurate. The value is proactive scaling: if requests always climb after 5 p.m., the platform learns that and adds nodes before the spike. Also in development, he said, is changing the architecture itself, for example moving a component from CPU to GPU nodes.

## Who should watch

Teams running batch or scientific workloads with deadlines across more than one cloud, and anyone curious about deployment as an optimisation problem rather than a rule-based autoscaler. The talk shows the dashboards and the loop, not the CAMEL model in depth.
