Title: Terraform feature flags are just count, a ternary and a YAML file
Description: Prabesh Thapa at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on building feature flags in Terraform with count, conditional expressions and a config.yaml of toggles
Body:
Terraform has no feature-flag keyword, and it doesn't need one. Prabesh Thapa, an SRE and DevOps engineer, showed at Conf42 DevOps 2023 that the whole pattern comes down to the count meta-argument, a conditional expression, and a place to keep your flags, ideally a config.yaml that describes the whole environment at a glance.

It is a short, beginner-friendly talk with a DigitalOcean demo, and the code is on GitHub.

## Why flags in infrastructure code?

Feature flags, also called toggles or switches, have long been used in application code to turn features on and off without new code, fed from config files, environment variables or platforms like LaunchDarkly. Thapa's argument is that the same benefits carry over to infrastructure: provision resources selectively per environment (a small instance on dev, a bigger one on prod), scale up or down without code changes, control rollouts with blue-green or canary patterns, and debug more easily because you know which change was switched on when.

## The trick is count = 0

The count meta-argument creates a given number of identical resources, and works on every resource type and on modules. The detail that makes flags possible: "if we set count to zero, then the resource will not be created at all." Combine that with Terraform's conditional expression, `condition ? true_val : false_val`, and you have a toggle. Count plus conditional expression equals feature flags.

## Three kinds of toggle

**Environment toggles.** A variable called env defaults to dev. One DigitalOcean droplet resource, the puny VM (s-1vcpu-1gb), gets a count of 1 when env is dev and 0 otherwise. Another, the beefy VM (s-4vcpu-8gb), gets a count of 3 when env is prod and 0 otherwise. Run plan with the default and you get one small droplet; override env to prod and you get three big ones.

**Resource toggles.** Same mechanism, but keyed on a dedicated flag rather than the environment: a load balancer with `count = var.provision_lb ? 1 : 0`, the flag living in a locals block.

**Module toggles.** Pass count to a module and the whole module becomes optional, which Terraform has supported since version 0.13. His demo gates a load balancer module and a database module this way.

He also points to further uses: blue-green deployments with DigitalOcean floating IPs, and canary releases with AWS ALB target groups.

## Where should the flags live?

Two options. Flags in a locals block in main.tf are simple, and you reference them as `local.feature_flags.provision_lb`. His favourite is a config.yaml loaded with `yamldecode(file("config.yaml"))`, holding the environment name, the feature flags (provision_lb, provision_db) and the network layout of regions, VPCs, availability zones and subnets. His reason: you get a complete picture of the infrastructure without digging through variables and Terraform files. In the demo, flipping provision_lb and then provision_db to true in the YAML is all it takes for the next plan to add the load balancer and the database.

## Who should watch

Terraform users who copy whole directories per environment, or who comment out resources to disable them. Experienced HashiCorp users will know the pattern; this is a tidy refresher with a config-file layout worth borrowing.

Title: Start OpenTelemetry tracing with a Java agent, then add spans by hand
Description: Nicolas Frankel (Apache APISIX) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on OpenTelemetry tracing across APISIX, Kotlin, Python and Rust, auto then manual instrumentation
Body:
Auto-instrumentation is the free lunch of distributed tracing: one Java agent on the command line and your Spring Boot service shows up in Jaeger with spans you never wrote. Nicolas Frankel, a developer advocate with more than 20 years as a developer and architect, built a four-service demo at Conf42 DevOps 2023 to show how far that gets you with OpenTelemetry, and where you need a dependency and a couple of annotations to see what happens inside a component.

It is billed as a practical introduction and is exactly that: observability history and concepts first, then a working stack of Apache APISIX, Kotlin, Python, Rust and Jaeger under Docker Compose.

## From wall-of-screens monitoring to tracing

He starts with the old model, people watching dashboards and spotting the slight anomaly that means trouble, which stops working once a request crosses a network of components. Observability has three pillars. Metrics have moved from CPU and memory to higher-level ones like requests per second or orders. Logging raises the questions of what to log (auto-instrumented logging is easy but can leak passwords into logs), which format (write JSON directly rather than parsing human-readable lines later), where (to the console, in a container world), and how to ship, store, search and eventually delete it.

Tracing is his focus, and he offers his own definition: "tracing is a set of techniques and tools that help follow a business request across the network through multiple components."

## Traces, spans and the W3C spec

Zipkin, Jaeger and OpenTracing pioneered the field, each with its own interfaces. The W3C Trace Context specification standardised the two key concepts. A trace is the whole business transaction from entry point to the most deeply nested component and back. A span is one part of that trace inside a single component, linked to its parent span, so the parent-child chain reconstructs the flow.

OpenTelemetry implements that spec and goes beyond HTTP, for example through Kafka. It came from merging OpenTracing and OpenCensus, is a CNCF project under the Apache license, and its collector simply accepts and stores data in OpenTelemetry format. Jaeger and Zipkin both added OpenTelemetry-compatible collectors, so migrating an existing tracing setup is mostly a matter of formats and ports.

## The demo: one request, four runtimes

The request enters through Apache APISIX, which is built on Nginx with OpenResty and LuaJIT for Lua scripting, and ships an OpenTelemetry plugin. Its config names the service, points at the collector and sets sampling per route; the demo samples 100%, which he flags as not what you want in production, and adds the route ID, request method and a custom header as span attributes.

Behind it sits a catalog service in Kotlin with Spring Boot, WebFlux, coroutines and R2DBC over H2, which calls a Python pricing service (Flask) and a Rust stock service (Axum). Jaeger runs as the all-in-one image.

For the JVM, auto-instrumentation is a Java agent: a multi-stage Dockerfile builds with a JDK, runs on a JRE, downloads the agent from GitHub and starts the jar with it. Developers write nothing. The first Jaeger trace already shows APISIX, the catalog, Spring's proxied repository calls, and the calls to stock and pricing, one going straight to the service and one back through the gateway. That is a feature: "In case you misconfigure something, you can check it through the traces," Frankel said at Conf42 DevOps 2023. The trace also shows the pricing and stock calls running in parallel, a cheap check that the coroutine code does what you meant.

## Manual spans for the inside of a component

To see inside the catalog, he adds the OpenTelemetry annotations dependency and marks handler methods with @WithSpan, capturing the product ID with @SpanAttribute. One honest detail: he had to change the method signature to pass the ID explicitly just so it could be captured, since annotating the whole product object would record a memory reference. The rerun shows the extra spans and the custom header that the first run missed because of a header-name mix-up. Python got the same treatment, with the query logged manually.

His advice on order: auto-instrumentation doesn't couple your code to OpenTelemetry, so do it right away; add manual spans where you need business detail.

## Who should watch

Developers and SREs who haven't wired up tracing yet, especially on the JVM. If you already run OpenTelemetry in production, it is a refresher; the polyglot demo code is on GitHub.

Title: Flux or Argo CD? Both deploy 200 apps in 90 seconds, so pick by model
Description: Ismael Hommani and Clement Loiselet (WeScale) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 compare Flux and Argo CD by model, user experience and a 200-deployment benchmark
Body:
Flux and Argo CD answer the same question, how to do GitOps on Kubernetes, with very different philosophies, and that difference should drive your choice more than speed. Ismael Hommani and Clement Loiselet of WeScale, who run both in production, made that case at Conf42 DevOps 2023: their benchmark found both tools deploy roughly 1,400 objects in about a minute and a half, while Argo CD used close to three times Flux's memory day to day.

They open with one firm rule, which Hommani said at Conf42 DevOps 2023: "we strongly discourage you to install both on Kubernetes cluster."

## Why GitOps at all?

The classic push pipeline imperatively describes how to deploy, needs kubectl and cluster credentials inside the CI runtime, and has to be rewired for every new platform. GitOps flips that: an agent in the cluster pulls declared state from Git and reconciles it. No deployment tooling or secrets in the pipeline, and Git permissions become the collaboration model between dev and ops. Kubernetes suits it because it is already declarative and runs reconciliation loops.

## How do the models differ?

Both tools are operators, but they model GitOps differently.

**Flux** is a set of small CRDs from the GitOps Toolkit. Sources say where to watch: GitRepository, Bucket, OCI repositories, HelmRepository and HelmChart. A Kustomization says which path in a source to apply; a HelmRelease wraps a Helm release. Kustomizations can contain further sources, so the cluster's state becomes a directed acyclic graph, with explicit dependsOn ordering between objects of the same kind. Create a cycle and the Kustomization at its origin fails to sync.

**Argo CD** centres on one CRD, the Application: sources (plain YAML, Kustomize, Helm, Jsonnet, plus config management plugins) and a destination cluster, which need not be the one Argo CD runs on. Applications can point to other Applications (the app-of-apps pattern), sync phases can run hook jobs such as creating a database before a sync, and AppProjects group applications with permissions and allowed namespaces, clusters and resource kinds.

Hommani's summary: Flux is keep-it-simple, built from things a Kubernetes person already knows, while Argo CD adds a logical layer that makes Kubernetes an implementation detail, which suits developers who don't care about Kubernetes and explains why it ships with a UI.

The same split shows up in fleets and tenancy. Argo CD is multi-cluster and multi-tenant by design, with AppProjects, RBAC and SSO in its UI. Flux needs an instance per cluster, though a central root repository holding every installation's source can manage them all; tenants are emulated with Kubernetes RBAC plus Git provider permissions on per-tenant repositories.

## What is each like to run?

Loiselet took the user-experience half. Flux installs via its CLI bootstrap or Terraform and syncs from a root repository from the start, including its own manifests, so you can pre-load a repo and stand up a pre-production cluster from production's manifests fast. Developers need only Git: "They only need to know about a git commit git revert." There's no UI out of the box (Grafana dashboards or the separately installed Weaveworks web UI fill the gap), and no safety net: delete a manifest in Git and it's gone from the cluster.

Argo CD installs with Helm or plain manifests, needs no initial repository, and comes in HA, non-HA and core-only (no UI) flavours; he recommends non-HA. It doesn't manage itself. Configuring an Application has many options, but the web UI helps, and the defaults are cautious: it won't prune removed resources unless told to, and syncs can require a manual button press, handy for production.

One warning applies to both: using a GitOps tool to upgrade itself is risky, because a broken upgrade leaves nothing to revert with. Use a second tool, and read the release notes.

## The benchmark

On AWS EKS with five t3.large nodes, they deployed 200 deployments (one pod each, roughly 1,400 Kubernetes objects) from 100 Git repositories and 100 Helm releases, comparing Argo CD 2.6.0 (non-HA) with Flux 0.38.3, core components only:

| Phase | Argo CD | Flux |
|---|---|---|
| Idle | 240 MiB | 300 MiB |
| Initial sync | 3.9 CPU, 2.2 GiB | 2 CPU, 1.2 GiB |
| Day to day | 0.3 CPU, 1.4 GiB | 0.3 CPU, 500 MiB |

Both took about 1 minute 30 seconds to deploy everything. The day-to-day row matters most, since that is where the tools spend almost all their time. They attribute Argo CD's appetite to its do-everything Application design and note that its memory grows with the number of objects tracked.

## So which one?

Argo CD if you want manual gates before production, a rich UI for developers, and defaults that won't delete things by accident. Flux if your users know Kubernetes well, understand that Git changes hit the cluster directly, and Git plus Kubernetes RBAC is enough.

Title: Let the cluster's Kubernetes version pick its add-ons, not a human with kubectl label
Description: Gianluca Mardente (Cisco Systems) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on Sveltos, which deploys add-ons across many clusters and relabels them from runtime state
Body:
Running ten or a hundred Kubernetes clusters is easy now; keeping the same CNI, policy engine and other add-ons consistent across all of them is not. Gianluca Mardente, Principal Engineer at Cisco Systems, used his Conf42 DevOps 2023 talk to introduce Sveltos, his open-source project that deploys add-ons from one management cluster to every cluster matching a label selector, and that can set those labels itself based on what each cluster is actually running.

It is a short, focused tour of the project's core objects, illustrated with a Kyverno, Calico and Gatekeeper example.

## Where does Sveltos run?

Sveltos is installed in a management cluster and manages add-ons in the clusters it can reach. It has built-in support for Cluster API, so any Cluster API-provisioned cluster is picked up with no extra steps. Other clusters, such as GKE or EKS, are registered with Sveltos and get their own SveltosCluster resource in the management cluster.

## One ClusterProfile, many clusters

The main object is the ClusterProfile. Its spec has two parts: a cluster selector, which is a plain Kubernetes label selector, and a list of Helm charts. His example selects clusters labelled environment production and deploys the Kyverno chart, version 2.5.0. Label two workload clusters, and Sveltos notices the match and installs Kyverno on both.

Per-cluster values come from the management cluster at deploy time. For Calico, the profile tells Sveltos to read the pod CIDR from the Cluster instance's spec (the clusterNetwork pod CIDR blocks) at the moment it installs Calico. Besides the Cluster object, Sveltos can read from the infrastructure provider instance, the KubeadmControlPlane and Secrets.

## What happens when someone kubectl-deletes an add-on?

Sveltos installs an agent in each managed cluster with one job: watch every resource Sveltos deployed and report changes. In the demo an admin runs kubectl delete on the Kyverno deployment. The agent flags the drift, the management cluster reconciles, and Kyverno comes back. In Mardente's words, "there is absolutely no admin intervention that is needed."

## Classifiers: labels from runtime state

The part that sets Sveltos apart is the Classifier. With hundreds of clusters, he argued, "we cannot expect those management cluster admin to be the only one in charge of setting the labels on each clusters." A Classifier describes a runtime condition and the labels a matching cluster should get.

His example: one Classifier matches Kubernetes versions from 1.24 up to (but not including) 1.25 and adds the label gatekeeper=v3-9; a ClusterProfile for that label installs Gatekeeper 3.9.0. A second Classifier matches 1.25 and above and sets gatekeeper=v3-10, tied to a profile with Gatekeeper 3.10.0. Upgrade one cluster from 1.24.2 to 1.25.2 and the chain runs on its own: the cluster stops matching the first Classifier, gets the new label, matches the other profile, and Gatekeeper is upgraded. Nobody has to remember to relabel a cluster after an upgrade, which is exactly the step people forget. Classifiers can also match on any Kubernetes resource present in the cluster, not only the version.

## Snapshots and rollback

A Snapshot resource tells Sveltos to record the deployed configuration on a schedule (hourly in his example). With sveltosctl, the CLI he wrote for the project, you can diff two snapshots and roll the configuration back to an earlier one. The abstract also describes a DryRun mode that previews which charts and resources would change in which clusters; the talk itself doesn't demo it.

## Who should watch

Platform teams running Cluster API or a fleet of managed clusters who are tired of per-cluster add-on scripts. If you already run Argo CD ApplicationSets or Flux, the Classifier idea is the part worth stealing. Docs and examples live at projectsveltos.io and github.com/projectsveltos.

Title: Your forgotten DNS records are someone else's free subdomain
Description: Simon Gurney (Punk Security) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on subdomain and NS takeovers, why DevOps delegation multiplies them, and DNS Reaper
Body:
Delete the GitHub Pages site, forget the DNS record, and anyone can serve content from your subdomain with no proof of ownership. Simon Gurney, co-founder of Punk Security, demoed exactly that at Conf42 DevOps 2023, then went one level up and brute-forced an AWS Route 53 name-server delegation. His point: the DevOps habits of buying SaaS instead of building and letting teams own their own DNS make these leftovers more common, and a scheduled scan catches them cheaply.

## A two-minute refresher on how DNS resolves

He starts with the plumbing, because the attacks live in it. 13 root servers, hard-coded into resolvers as root hints, point to the TLD servers (Nominet runs .co.uk). The TLD servers hold NS records pointing at wherever you host your zone, such as Azure, AWS or Cloudflare, and that zone holds the A, AAAA, CNAME and NS records you actually edit. Everything along the way is cached, which matters later: adding a record takes effect fast, removing one lingers.

## Attack one: the GitHub Pages leftover

A subdomain CNAMEs to GitHub Pages, and the site is gone (or was never set up). Ping it and you get one of GitHub Pages' handful of IPs; browse it and you get GitHub's 404 page. That is a detectable condition. In the demo he adds the domain to his own repository's Pages settings, GitHub checks only that DNS points at GitHub Pages, and his content is live. "So as an attacker with no authentication, no method of proving that that domain is mine, I can serve content for it."

## Attack two: brute-forcing a Route 53 delegation

NS delegation is how central ops gives a dev team its own zone: create a hosted zone for a dev subdomain in AWS, copy its four name servers into an NS record in the parent zone. The trap is a mismatch. In his demo the zone is created under one name and the parent's NS record points at a different one, so the name servers listed in the parent know nothing about it.

An attacker reads those name servers with nslookup, then keeps asking Route 53 for a hosted zone with that name, deleting every zone that lands on the wrong servers and keeping the ones that match until all four are covered. The servers are less random than you'd expect, so he puts it at around five minutes, slowed mainly by AWS rate limiting. His Python script for this is deliberately unreleased. There are mitigations on AWS's side, such as recently deleted zones being held back, so not every finding is exploitable.

## How is DevOps making it worse?

Three ways, by his account. Core-versus-context thinking, which he credits to Gene Kim, pushes teams onto SaaS for blogs, forums and auth, so more records point at services that later get dropped. Ticket handoffs between developers and the ops team that owns DNS leave gaps of a week or two, a race an attacker can win. And Terraform plus copy-paste makes a wrong NS block hard to spot in a pull request, while per-PR environments make delegation more common than ever. He is clear that he still advocates infrastructure as code.

## What can an attacker do with it?

Credible phishing links on your real domain; his examples from HackerOne disclosures include signup.uber.com. With an NS takeover they control MX records too, so they can send and receive mail from that subdomain. The nastiest one pairs a takeover with loosely scoped cookies: a session cookie set on the parent domain (leading dot) is sent to every subdomain, so "just by having an image tag we can steal their session tokens," Gurney said at Conf42 DevOps 2023. His demo removes the dot and the cookie stops flowing.

## Defence is mostly hygiene

DNS is treated as set-and-forget, so audit it and add a removal step. Run a bug bounty, and widen pen tests beyond web apps to DNS, git and other auxiliary services. Then automate: Punk Security's open-source DNS Reaper runs in Docker, pulls records from AWS, Azure, Cloudflare, DigitalOcean, zone transfers or BIND files, and checks them against nearly 60 signatures, matching both the record and the web response. It reports potential and confirmed findings to screen, CSV and JSON; his demo scan took 1.68 seconds. Run it as a pipeline step after DNS changes to fail a bad deployment, or as a one-off audit of years of accumulated records.

## Who should watch

Anyone who owns a DNS zone with more than a handful of records, and platform teams that hand out delegated zones. The DNS primer is gentle enough for newcomers; the Route 53 brute force will interest the experts.

Title: When security bans your temporary IP allow-list, move the build agent into the VNet
Description: Hong Bu (Microsoft) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on why a customer forced a self-hosted Azure DevOps agent inside the VNet and how to build one
Body:
A Microsoft-hosted Azure DevOps agent lives on the public internet, and a customer's zero-trust security team will eventually notice. Hong Bu, Senior Program Manager at Microsoft, told that story at Conf42 DevOps 2023: a mid-project ban on her team's deployment workaround, a week of building a self-hosted agent pool inside the customer's virtual network, and a recorded demo of both the workaround and the fix.

Her first takeaway: security is the first thing to consider in a project, not the last.

## Why the hosted agent couldn't deploy

The customer ran an Azure web app in front of resources inside a VNet. Deployments to an App Service go through its SCM site, the engine behind App Service deployments, and the customer had locked the SCM site so only requests from their virtual network were allowed. The Microsoft-hosted agent running the team's pipelines sits on the public network by design, so deployments failed with an IP-forbidden error.

The team had picked the hosted agent for good reasons: many ready-made VM images, pre-installed tools and runtime dependencies, and Microsoft maintains and patches it for you.

## The workaround that got a high-severity ticket

The first fix was simple. Every hosted agent run gets an IP address, so the pipeline added that IP to the SCM site's access rules for the deployment window and removed it afterwards. In the demo she does it by hand, then shows the practical version: a PowerShell script that fetches the agent's runtime IP, adds the rule and removes it after the deployment.

It worked, until the customer's security team, running regular scans, raised a high-severity ticket. Even a temporary allow rule for a public IP broke their zero-trust policy. She explained the short window and Microsoft's own protections; they answered that nobody could guarantee the agent wouldn't be attacked during that window. As she put it, "I know this is something that I cannot further negotiate."

## Building the self-hosted agent pool

The replacement was a self-hosted agent pool on a virtual machine scale set inside the same VNet, which the SCM site allows by default. The cost is that you own everything the hosted agent gave you for free, and you discover missing tools the slow way, when the pipeline fails on the new agent. The team split in two for a week: one half kept developing in their own subscription, the other built and tested the agent until every pipeline ran cleanly. They held the project timeline.

The demo walks through the steps:

1. Build a custom VM image with the tools your pipelines need (hers was about 8 GB). She recommends the GitHub actions/runner-images repository for step-by-step guidance.
2. Publish the image to an image gallery in Azure.
3. Create a virtual machine scale set from that image, inside the VNet that the SCM site allows.
4. In Azure DevOps project settings, add a new agent pool linked to the scale set. Its agents show up once the VMs are running.
5. Change the pool name in the pipeline YAML from the default hosted agent to the new pool, and rerun.

The scale set lets the pool scale in and out with the pipeline workload, which takes some of the sting out of running your own agents.

## Talk to the security team on day one

Her takeaways: cloud security is a shared responsibility, every organisation has its own requirements, and their security teams are busy, so start the conversation early. A self-hosted agent is more work than a hosted one, but it avoids big losses later. Her summary: "No pains no gains."

## Who should watch

Anyone running Azure DevOps against locked-down customer or enterprise networks, and program managers who want a concrete example of security requirements arriving late. If you already run self-hosted agents in a VNet, the demo will be familiar; the story is the useful part.

Title: Every microservice adds a pipeline, so plan the pipelines first
Description: Gaston Cacheffo (Globant) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on planning microservice CI/CD with trunk-based branches, promoted artifacts, templates and APM
Body:
Every microservice you add is another repository, another pipeline, another set of variables and another place for logs to hide. Gaston Cacheffo, Tech Manager at Globant, used his Conf42 DevOps 2023 talk to hand teams a planning guide for exactly that multiplication: how to set up branches, pipelines, configuration, QA and tracing so that shipping many small services doesn't take more ceremony than shipping one monolith.

It is a practical checklist rather than a tutorial on any single tool, built with Globant solution architect Luis Pulido, and it reads like the notes of someone who has sat through a few too many release-planning meetings.

## Why do microservices make DevOps harder?

The benefits are the familiar ones: fault isolation, data isolation (each service owns its domain and schema), independent scaling and independent deployment. The catch is that each of those multiplies the components a team must operate. As Cacheffo put it, the relation between microservices and DevOps is a multiplier: "Your team will have to deal with the microservices the more components in your architecture."

His list of challenges is honest. Developers burn time merging code across feature, hotfix, dev, release and main branches. Small changes get bundled into a giant release that has to travel through every environment together. Retro-compatibility stops being optional because services are promoted independently. QA becomes a bottleneck when validation is manual. Database changes need extra coordination. And debugging gets slow because the logs are no longer in one place.

He opens the challenges section with a question worth asking your own team: "have you ever thought about how much time a developer dedicates to exclusively code new features?"

## Fewer branches, more automation

The branch strategy is the base everything else automates on, so he argues for trunk-based development (or something close, like GitHub flow) and against elaborate branching models. "The more branches, the more automation complexity," Cacheffo said at Conf42 DevOps 2023. He points viewers to Viktor Farcic's DevOps Toolkit channel for the longer argument.

Three supporting habits:

- **Git tags for versioning.** Tags need no commits, and the version can flow into pipeline triggers, environment config, logs and traces.
- **Build validation on pull requests.** Pipelines that check for vulnerabilities, regressions, build integrity and performance become part of the PR completion policy.
- **Version your APIs.** When a change can't stay backwards compatible, publish a new API version through the API manager and give consumers room to migrate.

## Keep the services small by moving roles out

Lightweight microservices means stripping out anything that isn't the service's job. Authentication and app roles go to the API manager or an external identity provider (he names Google, Facebook, Microsoft and Okta), with JWT claims passed down in headers. His advice on writing your own IdP is blunt: you will spend a lot of time and probably end up halfway there with something insecure.

## Build once, promote the artifact

On pipelines, split integration from deployment and promote the same artifact through environments instead of rebuilding per stage. His reasoning is incident-shaped: during a production outage you don't want to hear that "code shouldn't be there" or that it isn't what was tested. Shared pipeline templates let one change roll out to every service. Schema changes run from the pipeline with tools such as Flyway or Liquibase, and API definitions are extracted at build time (Swashbuckle for .NET, the springdoc OpenAPI Maven plugin for Spring Boot) and pushed to the API manager.

Configuration gets a simple two-by-two policy: sensitive values go to a vault whether or not they vary by environment, non-sensitive environment-specific values go to a pipeline library or variable group, and the rest stay in app property files. Shared infrastructure settings such as base URLs and external domains can live in Kubernetes ConfigMaps so they change independently of service releases.

## QA, tracing and the feature-flag endgame

QA belongs close to developers and automated; UAT is for business users. For observability he prefers an APM tool over plain logs, with business events sent there instead of dashboards querying the service databases, plus daily ingestion caps and sampling in production. Feature flags are his candidate for the holy grail of microservices: they separate business releases from continuous deployment. The closing list covers canary deployments, a configuration server, infrastructure as code and a center of excellence to standardise all of it.

## Who should watch

Team leads and platform engineers about to split a monolith, or already drowning in per-service pipelines. Experienced platform teams will recognise most of the list; the value is having it in one place to argue from.

Title: Put the Sec in DevOps by upskilling one developer, not the whole team
Description: Greta Jocyte (Microsoft) at Conf42 DevOps 2023 on bringing a security mindset to dev teams with playbooks, threat modelling and automation
Body:
Most developers aren't trained in security, and sending a whole team on a two-week course isn't going to happen. Greta Jocyte, Senior Technical Program Manager at Microsoft, used her Conf42 DevOps 2023 talk to lay out a cheaper path: write down your engineering practices, threat model the big changes, automate the boring checks, and get at least one person on the team properly upskilled so the knowledge spreads from there.

Her team works in a code-with model, with Microsoft engineers building alongside customers' developers, so these are habits she has had to install in other people's teams, not just her own.

## How expensive is getting this wrong?

She sets the stakes with the IBM Security report for 2022: the average cost of a data breach globally is 4.35 million USD, rising to 5.57 million USD for organisations with high compliance failures. The figure that worries her more is time: "on average it takes 227 days for a team to be able to remediate that breach."

## Write the practices down

Her first recommendation is the least glamorous one: document your engineering best practices. She once joined a team with a high security bar that had never written any of it down, which made it hard to keep up and turned onboarding into chaos. Starting points she names are the OWASP Top 10, the SANS Top 25 and Microsoft's own CSE Engineering Playbook.

What goes in: a pull request policy (how many reviewers, how to write constructive review comments), logging and error handling, and a vulnerability management policy that says how long you have to fix a finding of a given severity and what the escalation path is when you can't. The question she wants every developer to ask before committing is whether they have reviewed those practices.

## Threat model before the security team does

Threat modelling should happen for any major architectural change, with a framework such as STRIDE or MITRE ATT&CK, and tools like OWASP Threat Dragon to walk you through it. Her story here is the best part of the talk. A customer required threat models for major changes, so her team documented a whole platform, held meetings with the customer's security team and waited for weeks, almost months. The answer: the security team couldn't do it, because they had only ever worked with on-premise systems.

So the team ran the threat model itself, using one or two people with expertise, checked it with a Microsoft security expert and handed it back. It built trust with the customer, and the developers kept thinking about hardening for the rest of the build. That is where her central tip comes from: "I also highly recommend that you upskill at least one developers that is able to go through a threat modeling exercise."

The engineer's checklist for any new component is short: is the data encrypted at rest, is it encrypted in transit, and who has access and how is that enforced?

## Automate, then ask what the tools miss

The automation list is practical: container and dependency scanning, static code analysis, git commit hooks with credential scanners (her demo uses git-secrets, installed with a single make install), automated secrets rotation and pre-built security frameworks instead of home-made auth. For container scanning she names Trivy, Aqua, the Dependency-Check plugin for SonarQube and Mend (formerly WhiteSource). Then the caveat: tools have gaps, so the developer question is what your automated tools are not catching.

## Your cloud defaults are not your cloud provider's problem

Infrastructure is the last pillar: Kubernetes security practices, runtime security and binary authorisation, and the cloud provider's security configuration. Security in the cloud is shared, and she calls out Azure directly: many Azure services ship with a setting that lets services from other tenants or subscriptions talk to yours, and she disables it on every customer engagement. She also warns against over-engineering, such as recommending VPNs to a junior team with a simple setup; a phased plan that the team can maintain beats a perfect one it can't.

## Who should watch

Team leads and engineering managers who want a starting plan for DevSecOps without hiring a security team. Security specialists will find it introductory; the threat-modelling story is worth the time either way.

Title: Zero trust for IoT means a quarantine group for the chatty device
Description: Syed Rehan (AWS) at Conf42 Web 3.0 2022 on applying zero trust to IoT fleets with least-privilege policies, Device Defender ML Detect and quarantine
Body:
A compromised IoT device should not be bricked, it should be quarantined: cut down to a deny-all policy while it keeps doing its job offline. At Conf42 Web 3.0 2022, Syed Rehan, Senior Global IoT Developer Evangelist at AWS, [maps zero trust principles onto IoT fleets](https://www.conf42.com/Web_30_2022_Syed_Rehan_zero_trust_security_iot) and then demos the AWS IoT tooling that audits devices, spots anomalies with machine learning and moves misbehaving things into isolation.

It is a vendor talk, built on AWS services throughout, but the principles transfer to any fleet.

## What does zero trust mean for a device?

Syed starts from two definitions. NIST SP 800-207 moves defences from network perimeters to users, assets and resources, with no implicit trust based on network location or ownership. The UK's NCSC puts it more bluntly, and so does he: "Always assume network is hostile and each request is verified."

From there, five protection principles: paranoia (internal and external threats always exist), assume every device is hostile, a gatekeeper that authenticates and authorises every request, trusted devices are never trusted, and a guard that updates policies dynamically when a device is compromised or a laptop is stolen. He specifically calls out gatekeepers that cache an authorisation for days: authenticate every time.

## Which IoT practices carry the weight?

His list of AWS IoT security best practices is long, and a few stand out:

- **Decouple ingestion from processing.** Keep the control plane separate from the data plane, so you can lock a device out without touching the telemetry path.
- **Design for offline behaviour.** His example is his own internet-connected humidifier: locked out of the cloud, it should still humidify.
- **Lean data at the edge.** Filter and enrich locally (AWS IoT Greengrass runs compute at the edge), send only what matters to the cloud.
- **Personalise per device category.** A car, a fridge and a microwave need different policies and different responses.
- **Least privilege.** On wildcard policies he is direct: "if applying a star for everything, it's just not the right way to do."
- **Secure credentials at rest** with a hardware TPM, or a software one if the device has none.

## Let a model do the watching

The argument for machine learning is reaction time: a model can spot a compromise and quarantine a device faster than a human on call. Where devices are too small for ML, AWS IoT Device Defender security profiles watch metrics instead, notify through SNS, log to CloudWatch and trigger Lambda to move the device. Where they can, models are trained in the cloud with SageMaker and run as inference at the edge, even on a microcontroller or a Raspberry Pi.

## What the demo shows

The demo uses the open source AWS IoT Device Client and Greengrass to emulate real devices sending temperature, pressure and humidity:

- **Audit.** Device Defender checks against 14 best practices, ad hoc or on a schedule. His run flags devices sharing a certificate and an overly permissive policy, and a mitigation action fixes the policy.
- **Rule-based versus ML Detect.** Rule-based profiles need you to set thresholds (say, three authorisation failures in five minutes). ML Detect only asks how many data points raise and clear an alarm, but the model "needs 25,000 data points" before it activates, so his advice is to run a rule-based profile in the meantime.
- **Quarantine.** For a device whose policy allows every action on every IoT resource, a mitigation action adds it to a quarantine thing group whose policy is deny-all.
- **One view.** AWS Security Hub pulls Device Defender findings in alongside EC2 and S3 ones.

He also mentions AWS IoT secure tunneling for getting into a quarantined device over SSH tunnelled through MQTT to restore its firmware or state.

## Who should watch

Teams running device fleets on AWS IoT, and anyone writing a zero trust policy that has to cover things, not just people. If you are not on AWS, the first half is the portable part.

Title: Zenroom signs Ethereum and Bitcoin transactions from plain-English scripts
Description: Andrea D'Intino (Forkbomb) at Conf42 Web 3.0 2022 on Zenroom, a deterministic crypto VM scripted in English-like Zencode for multi-chain interop
Body:
A one-megabyte virtual machine that does ECDSA, zero-knowledge proofs and post-quantum signatures, and that you program in sentences. At Conf42 Web 3.0 2022, Andrea D'Intino, co-founder of Forkbomb, gives [a quick, demo-driven tour of Zenroom](https://www.conf42.com/Web_30_2022_Andrea_DIntino_zenroom_cryptographic_vm_blockchain_interop) and the open source stack around it, from browser-side signing to blockchain oracles.

It is a short talk, almost entirely live in the browser, and it moves fast.

## What is Zenroom, physically?

Zenroom is written in C, so it builds for servers on every architecture, as libraries for Android and iOS, and as a WebAssembly module packaged on npm for the browser and Node.js. It even runs on small Cortex-M chips. The binary is around a megabyte and a computation needs roughly 500 KB of RAM.

The property Andrea stresses most is determinism. As he said at Conf42 Web 3.0 2022: "It's fully deterministic, meaning that given the same inputs, you will get the same output on any platform you run it on, which is crucial for a blockchain virtual machine."

## What can it compute?

The crypto menu is long:

- Signatures: ECDSA (as used by Bitcoin and Ethereum), EdDSA, Schnorr.
- Post-quantum: Dilithium signatures, one of the algorithms picked in the NIST competition, plus Kyber for key exchange.
- Hashes and key derivation: SHA-256, PBKDF, HMAC and more.
- Advanced flows: zero-knowledge proofs including zk-SNARKs, multi-signatures and verifiable credentials.
- Blockchain interop: key generation, addresses and signed raw transactions for Ethereum and Bitcoin, with Hyperledger Fabric, Hyperledger Sawtooth, IOTA and Planetmint (a rewrite of BigchainDB) also covered.

## Smart contracts in Given, When, Then

The most interesting feature is Zencode, the English-like language inspired by BDD and Gherkin, which he says is designed to be read and written by people with no programming background. A script has three phases: Given loads data and is strictly read-only, When does all the computation, Then formats and prints the output.

In the Apiroom online playground he runs a cookbook example: load a keyring, a string nested in a JSON object and an array of strings, sign both with ECDSA, print the results. The output footer reports the Zenroom version, git commit, loaded curves, memory use and execution time, and every run in the browser takes between 30 and 40 milliseconds with the same memory footprint. That is the WASM build doing real signing client-side.

The obvious application, in Andrea's words, is a browser-based multi-blockchain wallet: think MetaMask that also speaks Bitcoin and Fabric, running in a browser or a PWA, and with small changes in React Native or on a backend.

## Oracles, storage and a DID method

The rest of the tour covers Forkbomb's ecosystem, all open source:

- **Zenswarm**, built for the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure (EBSI): a swarm of blockchain oracles that wrap a Zenroom microservice in a Node.js app. An oracle listens to a chain, an event triggers a Zencode contract, and the oracle replies, either bridging to another chain or feeding the chain data from the internet. A dashboard monitors each oracle.
- **Distributed storage**: a Tarantool-based key-value store for caching and sharding, where both storing and retrieval follow policies coded in the application.
- **A W3C DID method**: first built so oracles could announce themselves to the network, and being generalised to people, services and objects. DID documents embed public keys for every signature scheme Zenroom supports, Dilithium included, and are anchored on a blockchain so their validity can be checked at any time.

## Who should watch

Developers who need cryptography or multi-chain signing in places where a full crypto library is awkward: the browser, mobile, embedded chips, or a team where not everyone writes code. Do not expect a close look at any single primitive; it is a capability tour with live proof that it runs.

- Luis Cardoza Bird on [building blockchains in Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Luis_Cardoza_Bird_building_blockchains) at Conf42 Golang 2021.
- Michael Birch on [turning smart contracts into indexers with cross-compilation in Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Michael_Birch_smart_contracts_indexers_crosscompilation).

Title: Every new line of code is as risky as it was in 2016
Description: Jon Peck (GitHub) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on developer-first security, with dependency, secret and CodeQL scanning before code reaches main
Body:
Years of AppSec spending have not made new code any safer. Jon Peck, Senior Manager of Enterprise Advocacy at GitHub, opened his Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 talk with that trend: vulnerabilities still grow linearly with lines of code. "In other words, every line of code written today still has the same risk of introducing a vulnerability as it did in 2016. More code, more problems." His answer is developer-first security: catch flaws on the branch, inside the tool developers already use, before anything merges to main.

To set expectations: this is GitHub making the case for GitHub Advanced Security. The framing is broadly useful, though, and the three checks he describes map onto whatever stack you run.

## Why bolt-on security makes things worse

His numbers on the state of AppSec: 85% of applications still contain a security issue, more than 80% of code bases are open source, 44% of developers are not trained to code securely, and 93% of DevSecOps implementations are not optimised. Flaws in applications are consistently the number one attack vector for breaches, and most of the code in any project comes from people outside your company whose security standards you don't control.

The scenario he describes is painfully familiar. You finish a two-week sprint, ship, and start on the next features. Then security arrives with a huge review and a pile of findings, and the next sprint is gone, spent untangling code you wrote two weeks ago. Faced with the choice of shipping with possible vulnerabilities or stopping the presses, about half of companies ship. It is a logical business decision, and an expensive one: fixing a flaw costs 10 times more once it reaches QA and 100 times more in production, and an exploited production bug can sink a company.

## Three checks before merge

Developer-first security, in his framing, needs two things: visibility across a very large number of projects to learn which nudges developers act on, and being the tool they already live in rather than another one they learn to ignore. The checks run on the feature branch:

**Dependency scanning.** Every change to a dependency manifest is scanned, whether it's a risky Node module or an insecure PHP version in a Dockerfile, and the fix arrives as a pull request. Dependency vulnerabilities get fixed 4.5 times faster this way. The detail worth stealing is the compatibility score: GitHub looks at how many unit tests keep passing when other projects take the same security update, so a developer can see how likely the bump is to just work before clicking merge.

**Secret scanning.** Every push is scanned for tokens and blocked if one is found, until it is removed or allow-listed; history gets scanned too. We have all pasted a token in, meaning to remove it before committing, and forgotten. The problem with secret scanning is false positives: flag every random-looking GUID or hash seed and developers turn the scanner off. Instead of guessing from randomness, GitHub works with dozens of secret providers on precise patterns for each of their token types, and you can add custom patterns.

**Code scanning with CodeQL.** CodeQL analyses what the code means, not just its text. It can answer questions such as whether input from an API or form travels down some execution path into a database query without sanitisation. Over 2,000 queries ship with it, covering the OWASP Top 10 and beyond, and they run on every pull request, blocking it when needed. His slides credit it with a 72% fix rate on potential vulnerabilities.

## The Mars rover story

His centrepiece: after NASA's Curiosity rover launched in 2011, a manual code review found a bug that could have stopped the parachutes from deploying, on a project with a total estimated cost of $2.5 billion. The fix went up as an over-the-air update in flight, and the tooling now in CodeQL found 30 variants of the same flaw that the manual review had missed. It is the strongest argument in the talk for variant analysis: once you find a bug, query for its siblings.

## Who should watch

Security leads making the case for shifting checks into the pull request, and teams already on GitHub weighing Advanced Security. It is a short product-led talk; for hands-on CodeQL, pair it with the demo below.

Title: No team wants your platform capability? You're building the wrong thing
Description: Geert-Hinke Addink (Qxperts) and Hylke Stapersma (Nationale-Nederlanden) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on building an internal platform teams adopt willingly
Body:
An internal platform that has to be forced on teams has already lost. Geert-Hinke Addink, product owner at Qxperts, and Hylke Stapersma, product owner for the CDaaS platform and pipeline enablement at Dutch insurer Nationale-Nederlanden, used their Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 talk to share what building continuous delivery platforms in a large, regulated, federated enterprise taught them: build trust before building features, find a launching customer for every capability, and measure whether people are actually happy.

The subtitle on their opening slide sets the tone: a tale of beautiful vistas and open sewers. It is a lessons-learned talk, light on tooling and heavy on organisational reality.

## Why is platform engineering hard in a big enterprise?

Their setting will be familiar to anyone in banking or insurance: a federated organisation with many internal customers, regulation from the financial sector and privacy rules, centralised IT run as a cost centre (with a whiff of ivory tower), and limited speed of innovation.

The dream is frictionless delivery of business value. They use curling as the picture: the platform team sweeps so the stone slides across the ice with almost no resistance. The reality is a priority paradox, where everything is a priority because everyone has their own yearly goals, plus existing investment in tools, a transformation that has to happen while the shop is open, and real difficulty working out who the customer even is. The loudest teams are not the only users; security, compliance and architects are customers too. And smart teams have usually built their own workarounds, which deserve respect rather than demolition.

## Seduce, don't force

The rainbows-and-unicorns half is product thinking applied to a platform. Be customer centric, treat users as partners, and win adoption rather than mandating it. Balance opinionated requests against the underlying problem, and urgent asks against the long-term vision. Find the value proposition unique to your context: for a startup that may be speed, for a regulated company it may be security and compliance delivered as a service. Focus on capabilities, not tools, because everyone thinks their favourite tool is the best one.

Self-service is what lets a platform scale without the platform team becoming the bottleneck, and waiting times are the enemy. Their supermarket line: you get annoyed waiting a minute at the checkout, so imagine waiting four weeks for a new project to be available on a platform.

## Lessons from the trenches

The first lesson surprised one of them: he expected to earn trust by shipping capabilities, but relationships mattered more. Talk to people, explain the vision, and accept it takes a long time. Find the people who actually influence the organisation, who are often quieter than the vocal teams. Pace change to the organisation; for a new compliance check, educate teams and give them a help channel rather than blocking pipelines overnight, or you become a platform of frustration.

Then deliver small and often, each capability with at least one launching customer. "If you can't find a team that is willing to use your capability, you're probably building the wrong stuff," Geert-Hinke Addink said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022. The launching customer is a partner, not the boss of the roadmap; the platform team plays devil's advocate for every other user. And staff the team with people who love hard problems.

Their design principles: a strong authorisation model as the foundation, built to evolve as tools get replaced; fewer touchpoints through event-driven automation that works beside the tools people already use; working standards that balance simplicity with compatibility; and don't fix things that work.

## Community and the complexity diet

They push one chat channel for all platform questions, and ask people who DM a question to repost it there so others learn too. A question asked over and over is a signal about your docs or the experience, not an annoyance. Platform teams should eat complexity so feature teams can focus on core rather than context, ideally until the platform is like electricity from a socket. Silence can be a good sign, if your other metrics show people are using it.

## What do they measure?

Two kinds of metrics. From the system: start simple (users, projects), then move to DORA metrics, software delivery performance and instrumentation of how capabilities are used. From the people: start with a coffee and a chat, then customer engagement and Net Promoter Score, because promoters are how a platform spreads in an organisation too big to reach everyone yourself.

## Who should watch

Platform product owners and leads in large or regulated companies, especially early in a build. Startups with one platform team of three can take the principles and skip the politics.

Title: Scaffold-ETH takes a dApp from yarn chain to a public URL in one sitting
Description: Kevin Jones (NGINX) at Conf42 Web 3.0 2022 on building, testing and shipping an Ethereum dApp with Scaffold-ETH, Hardhat and a self-adapting React UI
Body:
The hard part of a first Ethereum project is usually the plumbing, not the Solidity. At Conf42 Web 3.0 2022, Kevin Jones of NGINX, who is also a developer advocate for Scaffold-ETH, [live-codes a smart contract](https://www.conf42.com/Web_30_2022_Kevin_Jones_build_ethereum_easily_scaffoldeth) from a hello-world to a pay-to-write contract with an owner-only withdraw, deploys it to a testnet, verifies it on Etherscan and pushes the front end to a public URL, all in one session.

It is a hands-on beginner talk, and a good one: about five minutes of web1-to-web3 context, then mostly terminal and browser.

## What do you need before you start?

Git, Node.js 16 or newer, and a current Yarn. Scaffold-ETH bundles the rest: Hardhat as a local Ethereum Virtual Machine with play ether, React for the front end, and the Solidity compiler, which also generates the contract's ABI and injects it into the front end so you never wire that up by hand.

The workflow is three terminals (Kevin runs them in tmux):

- `yarn chain` starts the local Hardhat chain.
- `yarn start` starts the React app on localhost:3000.
- `yarn deploy` compiles and ships your contract to the chain; `yarn deploy --reset` forces a fresh copy.

## The UI writes itself

The detail that sells the tool is the Debug Contracts tab. It reads your contract and renders a form for every variable and function. Kevin removes `payable` from a function, redeploys, and the value field disappears; he puts it back and it returns. As he put it at Conf42 Web 3.0 2022, "the UI is adapting based on our smart contract so that we can test it."

The app also ships a burner wallet. Every new incognito window gets a fresh identity, which makes testing access control as easy as opening a second window, and a faucet button tops it up from Hardhat.

## From janky access control to Ownable

The live-coding follows a sensible arc:

1. **Hard-coded boss.** A `require` that `msg.sender` equals a pasted address. It works, and Kevin calls it janky.
2. **OpenZeppelin Ownable.** Inherit the standard contract instead, and the UI immediately grows `owner`, `transferOwnership` and `renounceOwnership`. One gotcha: Hardhat deploys from the first of its 20 built-in accounts, so the contract is owned by a Hardhat key until you call `transferOwnership` in the deploy script.
3. **Pay to write.** A `price` in ether and a `require` on `msg.value`. The UI's conversion button handles the ether-to-wei maths (ten to the 18th), which trips up everyone once.
4. **Get the money out.** Without a withdraw function the balance is a black hole. He adds one that uses `call` to send the contract's balance to the sender, guarded by the `onlyOwner` modifier. His summary of the result: "now we have this vending machine that's kind of in the cloud."

## Shipping it

For a real network you want your own deployer key, not one everybody's Hardhat has: `yarn generate` creates a mnemonic-based account and `yarn account` shows its QR code, which he funds with Goerli testnet ether from a phone wallet. Change the network in `App.jsx`, run `yarn deploy --network goerli`, then `yarn verify` so the source shows up on Etherscan with the green check mark. Finally `yarn build` and `yarn surge` (or `yarn ipfs`) publish the front end.

The demo even fails once in a useful way: a withdraw from MetaMask errors with an unpredictable gas limit because ownership had moved. He transfers ownership back and drains the contract, which is a better lesson in `onlyOwner` than any slide.

## Who should watch, and what next

JavaScript and React developers curious about Ethereum who want the whole loop once, end to end. Experienced Solidity devs can skip it. Kevin's next steps are Solidity by Example and the challenges on SpeedRunEthereum.com (an NFT, a staking app, a token vendor, a dice game), which lead into the BuidlGuidl. Goerli has since been retired, so pick a current testnet when you follow along.

Title: An error nobody traces is both happening and not happening
Description: DeveloperSteve Coochin (Lumigo) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on tracing a Flask app from local debugging to OpenTelemetry on AWS ECS
Body:
If a deployed app throws an error and nobody is watching, your users still see it; they just assume that's how the app works. DeveloperSteve Coochin, Senior Developer Advocate at Lumigo, built his Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 talk around that idea, which he calls Schrödinger's rules of observability, and demonstrated it with a small Flask app that throws errors on purpose, first locally and then on AWS ECS with OpenTelemetry tracing.

Two notes on scope. The abstract mentions Node.js, but the demos are in Python; a Node.js version of the tracer exists and gets a mention. And the cloud demo uses Lumigo's own OpenTelemetry distribution and free tier, so it doubles as a product walkthrough.

## Build small, with big ideas

Before the code, a lesson from years in digital agencies (organised chaos, in his words): scale has to be designed in early. "And so you might be building that application for only ten users now, but you have to build small now, but with big ideas later." Skipping that is how tech debt starts.

He pairs it with his Friday night rule: you are halfway through a game when the message arrives that something in production is down. Avoiding that message is the whole job. Murphy's law says it arrives then or at 2am, and probably both.

## Local debugging is the easy part

On a laptop you have plenty of tools: `print()`, `logging.warning()`, `pdb`, `pprint()` and the debuggers in VS Code or Eclipse. The demo app, Schrödinger's App, is a Flask to-do list on SQLAlchemy with get, post, update and delete routes, plus a few traps. Add a to-do called cat and you get a button that steps through the 4xx HTTP status codes one click at a time. There is also a route that returns 418, I'm a teapot, his favourite status code.

The live demo misbehaved for a moment, a 400 that did not appear when it should have, which he put down to browser caching. It made his point better than a script would have: even locally, you need to see what was actually returned.

## Why does the cloud change everything?

Locally you caused the error, so you know where it came from. A deployed cloud native app touches many managed services that change underneath you, and it-was-working-on-my-machine stops being a defence. Distributed tracing turns one transaction into a map across every service it touched, and it can now be done agentless, without running an extra monitoring service on your infrastructure.

The standard that makes this portable is OpenTelemetry, around since 2019 and part of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. Its main selling point for him is vendor neutrality: the instrumentation is the same whichever backend you send traces to, so you are not locked in to an observability vendor.

## Three steps, no code changes

Setting up the Lumigo OpenTelemetry tracer for Python is short: install it with pip, reference it in the code, and set two environment variables, `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` and `LUMIGO_TRACER_TOKEN`. Beyond importing the library, he added no tracing code.

The second demo runs the same app containerised on ECS, with an extra to-do (meow) that sends messages to Amazon SQS. In the UI the meows appear to work fine. In the transactions view, the simulated 401s and 402s show up as errors, and the meow requests show the full path from the Flask app into SQS. The same view would show calls out to email, SMS or payment services like Stripe, which is where e-commerce apps hide their most expensive failures.

## Who should watch

Python developers about to deploy their first containerised service, and anyone still debugging production by grepping logs. If you already run OpenTelemetry in production, this is an introduction you can skip. The demo app is on GitHub as developersteve/Schrodingers-Python-App if you want something that fails on demand.

Title: A 15-year-old pen tester shows how your login form falls over
Description: Francesco Vecchi at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 demos XSS, SQL injection, broken auth and LFI from the attacker's side, then the cheap fixes
Body:
`' OR 1=1--` in a password field still gets you into an admin account on a deliberately vulnerable app, and Francesco Vecchi, a 15-year-old student pen tester and web developer, demonstrated it live at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022. His talk walks through four classic web vulnerabilities from the attacker's chair in Kali Linux (cross-site scripting, SQL injection, broken authentication and local file inclusion), then lists the habits and free tools that stop them.

Nothing here is new to a seasoned AppSec engineer, and that is the point: these are the bugs that keep turning up in real breaches, shown by someone who exploits them for practice.

## How does an unsanitised comment box steal cookies?

He starts with stored XSS. A comment form posts user input to an API, and if neither frontend nor backend sanitises it, whatever HTML the attacker typed is rendered for every visitor. His sample payload is an image tag with an invalid source, so the browser fires the `onerror` handler, which sends `document.cookie` to the attacker's server.

On OWASP Juice Shop he shows the search bar rendering injected heading tags, the quick way to confirm a field is not sanitised before trying JavaScript.

## Why SQL injection is worse

The same root cause, an unsanitised input, gets more dangerous when the input lands in a query. The leading quote closes the password string, `OR 1=1` makes the condition true, and `--` comments out the rest. On Juice Shop that login lands him in the admin account.

"Just signing into someone's account is really the least you could do with an SQL injection vulnerability," Francesco Vecchi said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022. He then captures a request from DVWA in Burp Suite, feeds it with the session cookie to sqlmap, enumerates the databases and tables, and dumps the users table, MD5 password hashes included.

## Broken authentication has four flavours

He lists insecure cookies, unsafe password policies, no request limits on login and sign-up (which leaves brute forcing running all night), and passwords stored in plain text. Plain text makes every other bug worse: an SQL injection that would have leaked hashes now leaks the passwords themselves. His fixes: hash passwords (bcryptjs for a Node.js backend), set a password policy, log and rate-limit requests, and issue unique, unguessable cookies such as JWTs. The insecure cookie demo is a `privilege` cookie set to `user`; change it to `admin` and see what happens.

## One `include` away from `/etc/shadow`

The local file inclusion example is a few lines of PHP that include whatever file the request names. With path traversal on a parameter, he reads `/etc/passwd` on DVWA and explains how pairing it with `/etc/shadow` lets an attacker crack the hashes. Point the same parameter at an attacker-hosted reverse shell and LFI becomes remote file inclusion.

## What should developers actually do?

His prevention list is practical and mostly free:

- Listen to your package manager: read what `npm install` warns about and ask a senior developer when it looks serious.
- Get code reviews done, and keep libraries updated. He mentions Tomcat bugs with ready-made Metasploit modules and a Grafana path traversal exploit.
- Schedule a pen test before a new branch goes public. No budget? Run scanners: Nmap scripts, Nessus, or the slower but more thorough OpenVAS, plus Masscan to check for ports you did not mean to open.
- Behind Cloudflare or another WAF, check SecurityTrails and ZoomEye to see whether your origin IP has leaked. He found a real server IP that way on an engagement.
- Put an access control list in front of services like MySQL; on one engagement an ACL is what stopped him.
- Plan for lateral movement. "But it's usually that one vulnerable machine that allows the attackers to get access to everything else using privilege escalation." He shows LinPEAS output and mentions BloodHound for mapping a network.

## Who should watch

Junior web developers, and anyone who wants to see what an attacker's workflow with Burp Suite and sqlmap actually looks like. Security pros can skip it, or send it to the frontend team.

Title: Developers often know they're shipping the vulnerability
Description: Joylynn Kirui (Microsoft) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on defensive programming, ten secure coding standards and running CodeQL in the IDE
Body:
There are roughly 570 developers for every security researcher, so nobody is going to review your code for you. Joylynn Kirui, Senior Cloud Security Advocate at Microsoft, made that the starting point of her Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 talk on defensive programming: secure coding standards every developer follows, plus a static analysis tool running in the IDE so the bug never reaches a commit. The demo uses CodeQL in Visual Studio Code to find a cross-site scripting flaw.

It is a compact, introductory talk: a stats-heavy case for shifting left, a checklist, and one short demo.

## Why shift left at all?

The numbers on her slides make the case. From Threat Stack (2018): 52% of companies sacrifice cybersecurity for speed, 57% of ops teams push back on security best practices, and 44% of developers are not trained to code securely. 80-90% of the code in new applications comes from open source, so unchecked dependencies are a major source of vulnerabilities. There are about 40 million professional developers and about 70,000 security researchers.

Then the cost curve, citing NIST and the Ponemon Institute: a defect costs $80 to fix in development, $240 at build, $960 in test, $7,600 at deploy, and millions after a breach. Fixing a security defect in production costs 60 times more than in development, enterprises that extend security into development see 80% fewer security incidents, and 62% of enterprises have not integrated security into the development phase.

Her most uncomfortable observation came from experience rather than a survey. Developers usually push vulnerable code knowingly: "In most cases, they already know that there's a vulnerabilities in their code."

## What does defensive programming look like before commit?

She splits the lifecycle into pre-commit (threat modelling, IDE security plugins, pre-commit hooks, secure coding standards, peer review), commit (static analysis, security unit tests, dependency management, credential scanning), deploy (infrastructure as code checks, dynamic scanning, cloud configuration checks, security acceptance tests) and operate (monitoring, threat intelligence, blameless postmortems).

Threat modelling comes first: scope which endpoints are public and which threats each exposed API faces, then design defences. Her secure coding standards, roughly ten of them:

- Validate input: "Make sure that you never trust what a user is inputting." Check lengths and character sets.
- Manage authentication and passwords properly, never transmit passwords in the clear, keep secrets in a vault such as Azure Key Vault.
- Sanitise data before passing it to other systems, with allow lists, deny lists or escaping.
- Least privilege, and deny access by default (zero trust).
- A secure architecture everyone follows, such as the OWASP secure architecture practices.
- Defence in depth across application, data, APIs and containers.
- Strong encryption, protected databases and signed code.
- Code quality standards and peer review before commit.

## The CodeQL demo

CodeQL treats code as data. You install the CodeQL extension in VS Code, download the CodeQL CLI and put it on your path, then build a database for the project with `codeql database create`, giving it a name and the language (Java in the demo). Add that database in the extension, clone the community query repository, and right-click a query to run it. She ran the cross-site scripting query for CWE-79, and after a few minutes it pointed at the lines where a user-provided value reached the output.

The point she stresses is that you are not limited to the community queries. If you spot a mistake you made once, you can write a query to find every other place you made it. The same engine runs in GitHub Advanced Security, alongside secret scanning and Dependabot dependency scanning.

## Tools are not enough on their own

She closes on people: a checklist alone does not work. Run regular security training (she has run a monthly developer all-hands on security best practices), and grow security champions inside development teams who meet more often and push their peers to take security seriously.

## Who should watch

Developers new to secure coding and teams choosing a first SAST tool. If you already run CodeQL in CI, the IDE workflow is the bit worth a look.

Title: Coding got you the job, influence gets you the career
Description: Tom Henricksen (Code is Easy) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on why developers stall without soft skills, and his LUCK model for building influence
Body:
The skills gap that stalls most developers is not another framework. Tom Henricksen, Human Skill Enabler at Code is Easy, used his Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 talk to argue it is people: "Coding skills got you the job, influence will get you the career." He gets there through a string of career stories, including being fired, and lands on a four-letter model, LUCK, for building influence.

This is a storytelling talk, not a technical one. It is short, funny in places, and more honest about its speaker's own mistakes than most career advice.

## How does a developer end up with a skills gap?

Henricksen started out sure he just needed to know more tech. Java, Linux and SQL were all ticked off; humans were not. Early mentors taught him the wrong lesson well. One DBA fixed his problems in seconds and left without explaining. An architect would refuse to help anyone who asked a question they could have researched, the "bozo bit" of developer folklore. The conclusion he drew at the time: earn respect through technology, keep your head down.

Then, as a technical lead, his annual review told him his credentials were solid but he was failing at delegation. He was doing a ten-minute upgrade himself because explaining it would take as long, and quietly enjoying being the only one who could. Meanwhile a teammate had already scripted the deploy-and-update-dependencies chore he was still doing by hand.

## Bank tellers or financial planners?

The story that frames the talk comes from a leader he coached, John, whose IT team worked transactionally. In John's words, his team was like bank tellers: someone hands over a request and they process it. He wanted financial planners, who build a relationship and anticipate needs. Henricksen admits he thought the empathy angle would not work. It did: as the team learned what the community directors they supported were juggling, those directors started trusting the team to fix things without hovering, and John was given more responsibility.

The contrast is a developer called Eric, technically brilliant and so abusive the company let it slide because he was productive. And a coding hero called Dave, whose three-week bike trip across several states forced his manager to set up knowledge transfer sessions, which made the team more resilient. If your bus factor is one and the one is cycling across America, you find out fast.

## Adding code is easy

Even in the technical parts the talk keeps circling back to judgement. He mentored a developer who added a loop he could not explain; deleting it fixed the bug. "Adding code is easy. Knowing what to keep is hard," Tom Henricksen said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022. He leans on Steve McConnell's Code Complete (learn the kinds of mistakes you make), Greg McKeown's Essentialism on the editor's role, and a think, apply, reflect loop.

## What getting fired taught him

As a manager of software development, his boss walked him into the HR director's office on a Friday morning in May. His two lessons: he had not asked enough questions, so his team lacked clarity and did not execute; and relationships matter, because reaching out to his network afterwards turned up plenty of opportunities.

## LUCK, the three core soft skills plus one

Communication, relationships and influence each get a core habit, plus a bonus:

- **Listen** to what is being said, ask good questions, seek clarity. He cites The Pragmatic Programmer on digging for requirements.
- **Understand their interests**, illustrated by tilting a television so a toddler could keep watching Elmo.
- **Connect** on a personal level, like learning that a tight-lipped project manager shows Welsh springer spaniels.
- **Knowledge**: apply it.

The closing story ties it together: a strong but silent developer on a 60-day performance improvement plan, who stormed out of the first meeting. Daily check-ins, team working agreements and coaching turned it around.

## Who should watch

Developers who feel stuck despite being good at the work, and new tech leads who still do everything themselves. Senior people will recognise every character.
