Title: Your roadmap needs a roadmap for how you'll ship it
Description: Steve Pereira (Visible Value Stream Consulting) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on flow engineering, four team maps that end in a flow roadmap
Body:
Every organisation has a feature roadmap. Almost none has a map of how the work actually gets out the door. Steve Pereira, founder of Visible Value Stream Consulting, used his Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 talk to walk through flow engineering: four collaborative maps (outcome, value stream, dependency, capability) that narrow a team from everything-is-on-fire down to one constraint, and then into what he calls a flow roadmap.

It is a short, practical tour of a facilitation method, not a security talk, which makes it a nice palate cleanser at a DevSecOps conference. Nothing here needs a tool more advanced than a whiteboard.

## Start with one outcome, not a backlog

The opening is relatable: a giant backlog, staff cuts, reorganisations, leadership asking for more, quality slipping, everyone firefighting. The first map, the outcome map, gets every stakeholder in a value stream (design, development, quality, product, leadership) on one surface to dump pains, goals, questions, ideas and context. Then the group picks a single target. His example is releasing twice as often.

Around that target the team writes down why it matters (to customers, to the team, to the business), what obstacles stand in the way, and which investigations could test a way past them. He notes you can run this map on its own when a team just needs to clear the air.

## Measure the gaps, not just the steps

The value stream map lays out every activity in one workflow, say a release or a single story's path through a sprint, and measures two things: how long each step takes, and how long the work waits between steps. Those two numbers alone usually point at one hotspot.

His tip for teams that can't agree on what a value stream is: pick one customer outcome, internal or external, and work backwards from it. Whatever makes that outcome happen is your stream.

## The hotspot is usually someone else's queue

In his example the hotspot is environment setup, and the dependency map shows why: the team waits on the data team for refreshed and cloned data, and on the DevOps team for everything else, both of whom are busy. "Often I find the biggest delays are connected to external dependencies," as he put it in the wrap-up.

The capability map then asks, per dependency: who owns the relationship, is there a backup when that person is on holiday, what skill does the team have, and what support (APIs, documentation, tooling) is missing. Those factors roll up into a score, and a simple two-factor matrix sorts the work into now, next and later. Sometimes the answer is not to take the work over but to change something on your side that makes the other team's job easier.

## Collective flow comes first

The flow roadmap holds milestones, measures of progress and an owner for each action, sharp in the short term and deliberately vague further out. "This is the roadmap for how you're going to ship all those features," Steve Pereira said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022.

His argument for why it matters is about people as much as throughput. Collective flow means minimising delays and waste across the stream; personal flow means engagement, the sweet spot between challenge and skill. "But personal flow, I believe, starts with collective flow." An engineer who is constantly interrupted by a broken workflow can't find flow, however good their headphones are. When the workflow is fixed, he says, cycle times, lead times and fix times go down and deployment frequency goes up, though the talk gives no figures.

He also points to the Thoughtworks Technology Radar adding path to production mapping as a sign the industry is catching up with end-to-end flow thinking. And because the method was developed during the pandemic, it works remotely across time zones as well as in a room.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, team leads and platform teams who suspect their real bottleneck is a handoff, not the code. If you have run value stream mapping before, the dependency and capability maps are the new part.

Title: Redundancy buys reliability and a bigger attack surface
Description: Kalyan Dhokte (Cognizant Technology Solutions) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on why SREs should own security in the pipeline, chaos experiments included
Body:
Every replica you add for availability is one more thing an attacker can poke. Kalyan Dhokte, Practice Head for SRE in Digital Engineering at Cognizant Technology Solutions, argued at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 that this is exactly why security belongs on the SRE's plate: reliability already means protecting systems from unauthorized attacks, so in practice SRE ends up implementing the DevSecOps principles anyway.

It is a framework talk with a case study at the end, not a tour of one tool. The useful part is how concretely he maps SRE habits (toil reduction, SLOs, chaos engineering, blameless postmortems) onto security work.

## Where do reliability and security pull in opposite directions?

He names two trade-offs that anyone who has run production will recognise. "While redundancy is going to increase the reliability, it also increases the attack surface," Kalyan Dhokte said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022. The second is logging: verbose logs shorten MTTR during an incident, and those same logs are a target for attackers. His point is not to pick a side but to strike the balance deliberately, rather than discover it during a breach.

The backdrop is complexity. Microservices, service meshes, serverless and continuous delivery mean the system changes faster than anyone can hold it in their head. His slide of complexity sources reads like a year of on-call: Kubernetes upgrades, WAF and firewall outages, expired certificates, misconfigurations, regulatory audits, changing deployment tools. You can't simplify a system without changing it, and changing it adds complexity, so his advice is to navigate it, with security context applied to every change.

## Why do DevSecOps programmes fail?

He lists the symptoms bluntly. Teams blame security for slowing projects down and route around it. "Security reviews of new applications take weeks and then also produce little actionable information." Authentication and authorization behave inconsistently across products. Large parts of the portfolio carry vulnerabilities nobody has found, and the vulnerability list grows as more applications reach production.

The diagnosis: misaligned teams, every team reinventing the security and reliability wheel, both disciplines brought in too late, and not enough automation. The remedy is to embed SREs in development teams, create shared standards and accelerators, and automate security scans, observability and resiliency testing.

## What does the pipeline look like?

He lays out a full plan-to-monitor stack, with value stream management on top: threat modelling and resilient design patterns at planning, IDE security plugins and pre-commit hooks while coding, SAST at build, DAST and chaos security experiments at test, then policy compliance, scheduled audits, fuzz testing, WAF, pen testing and automated security monitoring in production. He also stresses not starting from scratch: document the people, process and tools you already have, then adapt them.

## The case study: YAML validation and security chaos

Three pieces stand out. First, a threat modelling tool at the plan stage. Second, a YAML validator plugin in an Azure pipeline that checks Kubernetes manifests against a security context schema before release: run as non-root, read-only root file system, privilege escalation set to false. Failures go straight back to the developer as a report.

Third, security chaos engineering with tools like Chaos Slinger and Gremlin. Two scenarios are described step by step. In one, the tool picks network security groups tagged for chaos, randomly opens or closes ports, and the team checks whether the security center raises an alert. In the other, it flips an S3 bucket ACL from allow to deny and watches AWS CloudWatch and the security center for the event. The test categories follow STRIDE-like lines: spoofing, tampering with data stores like S3, RDS and Redshift, data leaks through default security groups, denial of service, privilege escalation, and assigning a public IP to an internal resource.

The underlying idea is a nice one: the experiment doesn't only test the system, it tests whether your detection notices. If nobody gets paged when a port opens, that's the finding.

He closes with automated root cause analysis dashboards that use anomaly detection and suspect ranking built with Python and scikit-learn, and the Andrew Widdowson line that "SRE work is like being a part of the world's most intense pit crew."

## Who should watch

SRE leads and platform teams being asked to take on security, and security teams wondering how to get SREs on side. It is broad rather than deep; the chaos scenarios and the security context validator are the parts you can copy on Monday.

Title: Cloudsmith: 10 ways to make your software pipeline more observable
Description: Manage All Of Your Artifact Repositories, in the Cloud
Body:
#### Security into your software supply chain means visibility into how an artifact is built, packaged and signed.

A considerable part of the reason supply chain attacks are such a threat is that we are missing information to decide if the software we develop and use is safe.

Audit logs, SBOMs, automation, and package management are all essential aspects to bring visibility into your software supply chain so you can answer questions like:

- What are my build steps?
- Who wrote the code, who built that code, and who approved the code?
- What 3rd party dependencies do I use in my software, how trustworthy are they, and am I up to date?
- How do I trace my build from source to deployment?
- What vulnerabilities are in my code?

More than inspecting, scanning, and monitoring historical data, this information can be ingested by observability tools that can help you gain insights, identify unusual behavior and possibly prevent a software supply chain attack.

I've listed 10 ways to make your software pipelines more transparent and generate the information needed to gain your observability insights:

**1 Automated Build Steps**

Automate your builds using a CI/CD tool like Jenkins, CircleCI, or BuildKite. Make sure all the other tools you use in your build process, including your package repositories, tests and code scanners, facilitate automation using APIs, CLIs, and webhooks.

Having your build steps codified with no manual steps means they can be logged with timing and authentication information. You can gather unusual login attempts, policy changes, or build patterns. Using in-toto attestations at each build step can make this information verifiable and thus more trustworthy.

**2 Audit Logs**

Audit logs capture all actions the system, users, and service accounts perform for compliance and troubleshooting purposes.

All your build tools should produce audit logs, including your CI/CD, packaging, deployment, and cloud infrastructure tools.

Audit logs can be forwarded to the Security Incident and Event Management (SIEM) for visibility, tracking, and managing of security incidents. SIEM tools also provide next-generation detection, analytics, and response.

**3 Package Management**

It's much more difficult for people and scanners to figure out what is installed on a system when software is installed using scripts instead of a package manager.

A software package, artifact, or image is the output of building software- it groups files containing your software along with the metadata about the software and dependencies in a well-defined format.

A package manager is a software tool that uses the power of automation to create, upload, install, upgrade, and configure software packages. Most software languages, containers, or operating systems have a corresponding package manager, e.g., NPM, NuGet, Maven, or RPM.

Dependencies installed with a package manager ensure consistency and transparency in how software is included in your product and give a straightforward way to access your package's metadata, including version information, license information, dependencies, environment state, etc.

Let's make it easy to figure out what is on our system by installing software with a package manager.

**4 Versioning Software and Version Control**

Consistently versioning your software product releases, e.g., [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/), lets you keep track of all the changes and progress you make. For consumers of your software, the version numbers should inform them of when it's imperative to update and if there are backward compatibility issues.

Mistakes in build can be a hassle, but if at all possible and avoid republishing your builds.

**5 Pin your builds**

For visibility into your supply chain, we need to know all the 3rd party dependencies in your software. Some package managers, such as pip and npm, do their best to resolve package information look-ups when explicit guidance isn't provided. This means that a different dependency can be included in your software depending on when you build it e.g. if a dependency has a new update.

If you pin your dependencies to an exact version in your manifest files, no matter when you build your code, the same top-level dependencies should be pulled in, making your build more transparent and consistent.

**6 Automated dependency updates**

You need to know when your dependencies have updates for visibility into your software build.

The previous step recommended pinning your builds, but if you have many dependencies, it can be very difficult to update each one manually.

Several update tools help you check for updates in your code base, including Renovate and Dependabot (GitHub).

**7 Scorecards**

[Scorecard](https://github.com/ossf/scorecard) is an automated tool that gives developers a score on how safe their dependencies are. Understanding the trustworthiness of your dependencies is vital to improving the security posture of your project.

**8 Sign your artifacts**

Signing a package/artifact/image lets people know that this package was signed by a person or organization and proves that the code was not tampered with after it was signed.

There are issues with signing, including a lack of understanding of the signing process, cost, complexity of managing keys, implementation of code signing pipelines, and the lack of verification of signatures.

Recent developments in signing to reduce the complexity of signing and remove the cost barrier to signing with the [Sigstore](https://www.sigstore.dev/) project have invigorated efforts to sign artifacts.

**9 Generate SBOMs**

A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) lists all the components in your software. The notion of the SBOM was popularized by the Whitehouse when it was namechecked in an [Executive Order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/05/12/executive-order-on-improving-the-nations-cybersecurity/) last year on improving software security.

An accurate SBOM would improve the transparency of your supply chain, which could allow for:

- Earlier identification of potentially vulnerable systems
- Support informed decisions for 3rd party dependencies
- Incentivize secure software development practices.

[Tooling around generating an SBOM](https://cloudsmith.com/blog/how-to-generate-and-host-an-sbom/) is still evolving, but hopefully, it will be integrated into build tools, making this process accurate and automatable.

**10 Provenance of your built artifacts**

It is no longer just about the published artifact at the end of your software pipeline. Instead, it is about providing the tools to ensure artifact integrity across the supply chain.

Information demonstrating the supply chain provenance of a built artifact includes a combination of the steps above, including signing, build attestations, and SBOMs.

Provenance allows you to know and prove the origin of your software.

Monitor and Observe your Software Supply Chain

Some of this information isn't so easy to generate but will help us monitor and observe our software supply chain, which will ultimately help secure it. This information will help us:

- Monitor software supply chain more effectively
- Enable visibility for DevOps, security analysts, and developers into the entire build process
- Find and connect events in our build and trace them back to the source
- Detect and mitigate against vulnerabilities earlier
- Detect and alert for unusual login activity or build activities

Observability tools are promising to answer questions relating to the information that your system is generating, even questions that are not currently anticipated- what could this do for our software supply chain?

For more content like this, visit our blog [https://cloudsmith.com/blog/](https://cloudsmith.com/blog/)
_By Ciara Carey, Developer Relations, Cloudsmith_

Title: Your fitness band's BLE encryption ends at the phone's Bluetooth stack
Description: Meghana Rao and Ananya M Gowda (Deep Armor) at Conf42 Web 3.0 2022 on how any Bluetooth-permitted app can read a wearable's decrypted data
Body:
Bluetooth Low Energy encrypts the link between your fitness band and your phone, and that is exactly where the protection stops. At Conf42 Web 3.0 2022, Meghana Rao and Ananya M Gowda, security analysts at Deep Armor, show a malware app on an ordinary Android phone reading step counts and calories off a paired Xiaomi Mi Band 2, in real time, without breaking any crypto at all.

The lesson is about trust boundaries, not radio hacking: the wearable trusts the whole phone, and every app on it.

## Why are wearables hard to secure?

Ananya opens with the shape of an IoT ecosystem: nodes with sensors, gateways, a smartphone and a cloud backend, all talking different protocols. Fitness trackers are the case study, because people wear them all day and they collect geolocation, biometric data, sensor readings and sometimes payment details.

The challenges she lists are familiar to anyone who has shipped hardware. Traditional secure development lifecycles assume long-lived products with stable requirements, while gadgets ship fast and change constantly. A developer has to pick from 30 to 40 protocols. Firmware runs on microcontrollers with a limited software stack, so asymmetric crypto and trusted execution environments are often too heavy. And IoT security research is still young.

## How does BLE pairing protect the link?

BLE is the lightweight, low-power subset of classic Bluetooth, running in the 2.4 GHz band and governed by the Bluetooth SIG. Its security rests on Secure Simple Pairing, in four flavours:

- **Just Works**: for devices with little or no UI, and the weakest, prone to man-in-the-middle attacks.
- **Numeric Comparison**: a display with a yes/no button.
- **Passkey Entry**: a six-digit PIN.
- **Out of Band**: keys exchanged over another channel such as NFC or Wi-Fi Direct, the strongest option.

After pairing, traffic is encrypted with AES-128. The known weaknesses follow: the link is only as strong as the pairing method, eavesdropping on pairing can expose the keys, and then there is the fourth item on their list, the apps on the phone.

## The attack: no sniffer, just an app

Meghana runs the demo. The setup is a Mi Band 2 on firmware v1.0.1.81, the Mi Fit app v5.5.2 on a current Android phone, and Deep Armor's custom malware app configured with the band's Bluetooth address. An attacker sniffing the air near the band gets only ciphertext, encrypted with the long-term key. The problem sits one layer up: the phone's Bluetooth stack decrypts the BLE traffic before handing it to the app, and as Meghana Rao said at Conf42 Web 3.0 2022, "any app residing on the phone can sniff and fetch all the data that is being exchanged."

She waves her wrist to rack up steps. The count climbs in Mi Fit and, at the same moment, in the malware app's logs: 1026 steps and 30 calories in both. The malware reads the same GATT characteristics the legitimate app uses, identified by their UUIDs for step count and heart rate.

## Why does any app get this access?

On Android, all an app needs is the BLUETOOTH and BLUETOOTH_ADMIN permissions; on iOS, the Core Bluetooth framework. With those, any app can read or write the BLE channel just like the vendor's own app. Android's documentation even warns that apps holding these permissions should not misuse them, which is a policy, not a control.

In Meghana's words, the "device is trusting entire phone and all the apps on it." The fix is to shrink the trust boundary from the phone to the companion app: encrypt the payload with an app-specific key on top of the BLE link-layer encryption, so only the legitimate app can read what the band says.

## Who should watch

Mobile and firmware engineers building companion apps for wearables or any BLE peripheral, and security folks who threat-model IoT products. It is a 101 on BLE pairing plus one clean, memorable demo. Their closing advice is to bring device, phone, protocol and cloud into the secure development lifecycle and to run security continuously in CI/CD.

Title: Red team your own AWS account and tell nobody first
Description: Josh Armitage (Contino) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on a surprise red team against a consultancy's own AWS - 12 minutes to identify, 88 to contain
Body:
The blue team didn't know it was a blue team until 10:03 on a weekday morning in 2019, when a virtual machine booted in a serverless-first company's AWS account. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Josh Armitage, Distinguished Technologist at Contino and author of O'Reilly's *Cloud Native Security Cookbook*, tells the story of the day he and a colleague hacked the AWS environment of the cloud consultancy he then worked for, with only the leadership team in on it, and how that one morning built a security culture that outlived his time there.

## Why attack yourself?

The goal was to shift learning left. The middle of a real incident is the most expensive moment to learn your incident response process. And for a consultancy, Armitage says, you shouldn't tell clients to adopt practices you're unwilling to try on yourself.

Everyone knew security was everyone's responsibility, and there was an incident response process; nobody knew how it held up. The company had also grown from about ten people to about 30, and his rule of thumb is that processes break at around 3x. So instead of writing new ones from their heads, they would test, then build the process around the evidence.

## How do you set it up fairly?

Some choices worth copying:

- **Everyone in one room.** This was before COVID, and the consultants were normally scattered across client sites, so they gathered everyone in the office for high-bandwidth, face-to-face communication.
- **Senior engineers lose their access.** Only junior staff could change the environment, so the seniors had to work through them, pair-programming style. Nobody got to sit back while the five most experienced people handled it.
- **Leadership leaves the building.** The three directors went with the red team to a coffee shop next door, deliberately leaving a vacuum to see who would step up.
- **Rules of engagement.** The CEO set a financial limit (no crypto mining, which in 2019 was tempting) and the explicit aim was a stretch, not demoralisation. You win or lose together.

They also picked four measures for next time: time to identify, time to contain, percentage of intrusions detected (including the cleanup afterwards), and who would take responsibility.

## What happened on the day?

At 10:03 they booted the VM, which fired a Slack alert, and sent a phishing email. Six minutes later someone noticed; a minute after that a second person joined, and the red team promptly killed both their access. Soon came the call to down tools and mob the problem, and five minutes after that someone called the CEO, step one of the incident response process. Armitage watched him look at his phone, put it down and go back to his coffee.

The first response structure was one person with about 20 people reporting into him, which collapsed under its own chatter. After a regroup they polled who still had AWS access and split leadership from communication: one person made calls while a second filtered the information coming to him. They also unmasked a colleague who had been tipped off in advance and was relaying news to the red team, and moved off Slack, which the red team could read.

Meanwhile Armitage broke out of AWS altogether. An engineer had stored his GitHub credentials in Parameter Store, encrypted with KMS, but with a key policy open to any principal in the account. His lesson: KMS (and its equivalents in GCP and Azure) is fundamental, and you need to be really good at it.

The blue team declared victory at 10:57. They were wrong. After the red team got more brazen and posted a selfie in Slack, containment came at an hour and 28 minutes. Time to identify was 12 minutes, and the blue team found about two thirds of what the red team had done.

## Why the red team stayed ahead

His explanation uses John Boyd's OODA loop: observe, orient, decide, act, and whoever loops faster wins. The blue team lacked visibility and tooling, so everything was manual, while the red team created things faster than defenders could find them. The painful part: useful tools existed, but on individual laptops from client work, never shared in common repositories.

When someone objected that the scenario wasn't realistic, he pointed out it started from a single person's compromised credentials. As Armitage said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, "If you're not testing it with realistic scenarios, then you don't have a process at all." Backups never fail; restores do.

## From exercise to myth

Every gap went into a backlog of Jira tickets, and picking one up between engagements became a rite of passage. The day turned into company legend: years after he left, new employees still knew who he was and what he did. It started a tradition of CTFs, game days and more red team events. His closing chess analogy: novices see pieces, masters see patterns. In a real incident, which do you want next to you?

## Who should watch

Security and platform leads planning a first game day, and anyone whose incident process only works on paper.

Title: Constant patching isn't technical debt, it's technical inflation
Description: Giulio Vian (Unum) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on why continuous updates aren't technical debt, and what rebuilding production every day takes
Body:
Nobody chose to depend on a library that got a critical CVE last Tuesday, so calling the cleanup "technical debt" blames the wrong people. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Giulio Vian, Principal DevOps Engineer at Unum, argues that the constant stream of patches is a different phenomenon, closer to inflation than to debt, and that naming it properly changes how you plan, budget and automate.

It's a short, sharp talk: some data on how often each layer of your stack changes, an argument about words, and the engineering consequences.

## How often does your stack actually change?

Vian splits any runtime environment into three layers, each with its own patch stream: the operating system, the application stack or runtime, and the libraries. He went through public release histories to measure them. Average days between patches, from his slides:

| Layer | Platform | Patched every (avg.) |
|---|---|---|
| OS | Alpine | 52.2 days |
| OS | Ubuntu / Amazon Linux | about 22 days |
| Runtime | Chrome | 14 days |
| Runtime | Node.js / Go | 25-26 days |
| Runtime | MongoDB / .NET | 5-6 weeks |
| Runtime | Java | 12 weeks |

Windows Server gets the monthly Patch Tuesday. MongoDB is there as a stand-in for all the databases, caches and queues a modern application leans on. Libraries are the fastest-growing layer: citing Sonatype, he shows open source repositories recording 50%, 70% and even 90% more downloads from 2020 to 2021, and JavaScript applications pulling in hundreds of libraries where Java or .NET use tens. Average it all out and something in your stack needs patching roughly every day. Traditional monthly patching no longer keeps up.

## Why isn't that technical debt?

Debt has three ingredients, he says: will (you chose to borrow), principal (a known amount) and interest (growing cost as time passes). Ward Cunningham's technical debt fits all three. A team knowingly takes a cheaper, suboptimal design, has an estimate for both paths, and pays more the longer it waits to refactor.

A patched base image has none of that. Nobody decided to take it on, there's no principal, and no new domain knowledge or user feedback is involved; it's adaptation to the environment. So he borrows (pun intended, as he puts it) from economics instead. Depreciation captures software losing value over time, but it's an accounting schedule disconnected from outside events. Technical inflation does capture them: something outside your control erodes the value of what you built, with high-inflation periods (a new attack technique, a technology leap) and calm ones. Or call it what finance already understands: higher operational costs to keep the lights on.

As Vian said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, "Perfectly working software weakens over time and need continuous maintenance." His slide puts the conclusion more bluntly: we must rebuild production frequently, and it is not our fault.

## What does continuous update look like in practice?

He defines continuous update as the need to update a system frequently independent of source code changes, which makes it neither continuous delivery nor continuous deployment. Architecture decides who carries it. A monolith on a VM lets operations patch the OS and runtime while developers only rebuild for library changes. A microservice in a container image bundles all four layers, so every patch anywhere means rebuilding and redeploying the image. He calls that an interesting downside of containers, and of immutable infrastructure in general.

Rebuilding everything every day is the simple answer and it doesn't scale to an enterprise portfolio. The smarter version needs a bill of materials on steroids, with reverse indexes: from library to binaries (an SCA tool), OS API to binaries (SAST), binary to pipelines (the artifact store) and pipeline to repos. Then automatically update every reference, whether `pom.xml`, `.csproj`, `package.json`, Dockerfile base images, Ansible, Puppet or Chef, Terraform, CloudFormation or ARM templates, and kick off the pipelines.

## The flip side

Automating this exposes new problems. Think Log4j: you can't approve 100 pipelines one at a time, so you need an expedited approval process covering every impacted component. You need a test harness strong enough to trust a patch without a human. A single library upgrade across a large Java estate can start a build storm, hundreds of builds queued for hours, followed by simultaneous deployments that spike disk, network and CPU in production. Every rebuild also produces new images, and image technology isn't yet optimised for frequent small changes. His hopeful note: memory-safe languages such as Rust may mean fewer security patches in a few years.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers who have to justify patching work to the business, and platform teams designing SBOM-driven rebuild automation. The vocabulary alone is worth having for the next budget meeting.

Title: The digital nomad's first rule is to ask for the absurd
Description: Arafat Khan (Shopify) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on working remotely from a ski hostel and across Canada by negotiating stays and testing cities cheaply
Body:
A hostel that would charge $3,600 for a month on Booking.com agreed to $1,200 cash because a regular guest simply asked. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Arafat Khan, a production engineer at Shopify (Terraform, Kubernetes "and a lot of other buzzwordy stuff", in his words), tells how a lonely pandemic year turned into a run of remote work from a ski resort, Vancouver and Calgary, and what rules he took from it.

This is not a technical talk. It's a personal story with practical tactics, and an unexpected one to find at a DevSecOps conference, which is part of its charm.

## How did it start?

In early 2020 Khan lived in Ottawa, worked in Shopify's office there and had a full social life. Then came COVID and working from home alone. When his father and sister fell ill with COVID in India, he was thousands of miles away and unable to help, while his local friends were moving cities and changing jobs. His coping mechanism was skiing at Mont-Tremblant in Quebec, a two-hour drive away, where he stayed at the same hostel every weekend and found the connection he'd been missing. His family recovered, and the weekends got longer.

Eventually he proposed paying the owner directly for a month. The owner took a day and came back with $1,200, about a third of the online price. Khan agreed his working hours with his employer, set up a desk and skied before and after work, for two months, "before the partying and the fun got the better of me".

## The rules he took away

He frames the lessons as rules of digital nomadism:

1. **You can live almost anywhere if you negotiate.** He started emailing hotels, guesthouses and Airbnb hosts with a short introduction and asking for a call and a monthly rate. Places that make their money on weekends would often offer 50% to 60% off for a reliable tenant who stays a month and takes care of the place. Cut out the middleman.
2. **Never be afraid to ask for the absurd.** As Khan said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, "The absolute worst that someone can say is no." His illustration is a former intern colleague who leased farmland in Surrey, one of Canada's most expensive property markets, for one dollar, by befriending the owner and promising to build an organic farm (the owner got the produce for free).
3. **Skip the remote-work resorts.** The places marketed to nomads with fast Wi-Fi, a pool and a spa cost around $7,000 a month in his searches. Pair a cheap place to sleep with a coworking membership instead.
4. **Minimalism is hard but worth it.** Before flying 3,000 km from Ottawa to Vancouver he listed everything he owned, marked what he used daily or weekly, and gave away or sold the rest, including his bike. He landed with two bags, a laptop, a ski bag and ski boots.
5. **Treat the apartment search as an optimisation problem.** Write down the constraints (in his case $900 to $1,300 a month, furnished, decent Wi-Fi, month-to-month) and turn them into a template message for landlords. In Vancouver that got a $1,100 Airbnb month down to $700.
6. **Stay legal.** Taxes differ by province and state; many countries allow a 90-day visit but not work. Email the embassy, talk to your employer, and don't risk a career for a few fun trips.

## Cheap experiments before big moves

The last rule is the most transferable. Google Flights' explore feature, with Vancouver as the origin and Canada as the destination, turned up $100 return flights to Calgary. A four-day weekend there went so well that he moved. The same logic, he says, applies to gym memberships and apps: buy monthly, prove it works, then commit annually.

## The fine print

He is honest that rebuilding your life in a new city over and over is taxing, mentally and physically, and that it isn't for everyone. His closing reframes travel as seeing the world with new eyes, which you can also do on your usual commute, and ties it to ikigai: what you love, what you're good at, what you can be paid for and what the world needs. For him, that's travel. The talk ends with a pitch for Shopify's careers page.

## Who should watch

Remote engineers who keep thinking about working from somewhere else and haven't worked out how, and anyone who needs a reminder that the worst answer to a polite request is no. If you're after DevSecOps content, this is the evening's palate cleanser.

Title: A placeholder pod turns a four-minute node wait into seven seconds
Description: Chris Nesbitt-Smith (UK Government) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on why Kubernetes node scaling takes minutes and how low-priority placeholder pods pre-scale
Body:
The Kubernetes cluster autoscaler only adds a node once a pod is already stuck pending, and by then your users have been waiting for minutes. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Chris Nesbitt-Smith, a consultant to UK Government who has run Kubernetes in production since version 0.4, explains where those minutes go and shows a pattern that keeps a spare node warm: a big, low-priority placeholder pod. In his live demo, scaling onto a new node went from close to four minutes to about seven seconds.

It's a fun, demo-heavy talk, complete with a Black Friday game and a candid running commentary on the demo gods.

## Why does the scheduler need requests and limits?

The scheduler doesn't know how much CPU and memory a pod uses; you have to tell it. Without requests and limits, he warns, Kubernetes plays blind, nodes get oversubscribed and you spend your days firefighting. If that's the only thing you take away, he says, the talk was worth it. Requests are the initial ask; limits are where CPU gets throttled and memory overruns get the container killed. With them, Kubernetes turns out to be a reasonably skilled Tetris player.

The catch is that a node's spec sheet is not what your pods get. Memory and CPU are reserved for the operating system, the kubelet and the eviction threshold. His example: on an 8 GB, two-CPU node you might expect four pods of 1.5 GB and a quarter CPU to fit, but one stays pending and triggers a new node.

## Where do the minutes go?

He adds up the scale-out path. About 90 seconds for the horizontal pod autoscaler to react, around 30 seconds for the cluster autoscaler to ask the cloud for a node, three to four minutes for the machine to boot, another 30 seconds to join the cluster, plus pulling your image onto a machine with an empty cache.

To make that cost tangible he built a fake Kubernetes scheduler library (appvia's cloud-spend-forecaster) that simulates days of scaling in tens of milliseconds, and a game on top of it called Black Friday. You run SRE for a retailer with a three-tier app facing Black Friday and Cyber Monday spikes, and tune node counts and scaling thresholds. His run failed some requests and paid $1,154 in SLA penalties, yet ended about $15,000 ahead of having no autoscaling at all. Just enough infrastructure, not perfect infrastructure, is the goal.

## Option one: don't scale

It sounds flippant, but a correctly sized node might hold your whole workload. With so many instance types on offer, he demos the Learnk8s Kubernetes instance calculator, which shows how efficiently pods of a given shape pack onto instance types across AWS, GCP and Azure, accounting for reserved resources and DaemonSets.

## Option two: scale before you need to

The placeholder pattern: deploy a pod sized to fill a whole node, give it a priority class of minus one, and let it sit there. When real workload arrives, the scheduler evicts the placeholder to make room, the placeholder goes pending, and the cluster autoscaler boots a fresh node for it. As Nesbitt-Smith said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, this keeps you "always one step ahead."

On a real Linode cluster, scaling a deployment from one to five replicas took about three to four minutes without the placeholder, because the fifth pod had to wait for a node. With it, the pod landed on the spare node in about seven seconds. A recorded HPA demo under ramping traffic tells the same story: without the placeholder, served requests per second flatten for the four minutes of node boot; with it, traffic climbs steadily with no failed requests, even when the HPA outpaces the node provisioning.

## What does the spare node cost?

Money, obviously, and he says so when asked: it's a hot spare, like the spare drive in a RAID array, except you're saving minutes rather than a trip to the data centre. His better answer is to make the spare capacity useful. Instead of an idle placeholder, run low-priority work that tolerates being stopped (housekeeping, analytics, machine learning, less important services) and let priorities express what the business cares about, such as the shopping cart over the service desk.

And a short answer to a question about oversubscribing VMs in VMware under Kubernetes: you're in for a bad day. Kubernetes needs real resources and the most accurate information you can give it.

## Who should watch

Anyone running bursty workloads on the cluster autoscaler, and teams arguing about cost versus latency during scale-out. Karpenter users will still find the timing breakdown and the priority trick useful.

Title: Azure security starts with deleting your storage account keys
Description: Radu Vunvulea (Endava) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on Azure security practices - Key Vault, RBAC, short-lived SAS tokens, column encryption and WAF
Body:
Moving to Azure doesn't move your security to Microsoft, and the leadership that budgets as if it does is where most cloud breaches start. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Radu Vunvulea, Group Head of Cloud at Endava and a Microsoft Azure MVP who has run commercial workloads on Azure since 2011, walks through the security practices he sees missing most often in real projects, from secrets and role-based access to storage, SQL and edge protection.

It's a practitioner's checklist rather than a deep architecture talk, built from things he keeps finding on customer systems.

## Why the shared responsibility model still needs saying

Engineers know it. Management often doesn't, and assumes the cloud provider handles security once the contract is signed, so nobody funds hardening. The provider covers the physical data centre and the fabric; the network, VMs, configuration, workloads and data are yours. His framing for everything that follows: four pillars (networking, operations, monitoring, cloud platform), then storage, data, compute and identity on top, then the application.

He backs the urgency with three numbers: around 80% of security breaches involve privileged credentials, around 49% of databases are not encrypted, and around 25% of organisations have cryptojacking activity in their environment. The first one has an uncomfortable example: does your product manager really need access to the subscription, the repo and the pipelines?

## Secrets: Key Vault, then never a password again

Every secret needs a policy for where it lives and how it's encrypted. On Azure that means Key Vault (or Dedicated HSM for stricter compliance), with separate vaults for anything holding real customer data and for dev and test. Accessing a vault still needs credentials, so store the client ID, secret and tenant ID in the developer's user-scoped environment variables, not in files.

Better still, skip credentials altogether. With Azure RBAC and managed service identities, an Azure Function can reach Azure SQL or Storage with no username or password stored anywhere. A role assignment ties together the principal (user, group or service), the role and the scope, down to read-only access on specific tables, so a compromised function stays boxed in. The learning curve is real; the payoff is that there's nothing left to steal.

## Keep secrets out of the repo

Working from home means a developer clicks one bad link and an attacker has the app repo, the infra repo and maybe the subscription. Scan every push and pipeline run, and reject commits that contain an Azure storage key or a database password, whether in Terraform, ARM, C# or Java. He compares several scanners and picks two: git-secrets, easy to set up and great for teaching, but basic once you need custom rules; and SpectralOps, paid, with a strong UI for reporting and an ML engine that cuts false positives, more suited to large programmes with several teams on one repo.

## Configuration is sensitive even without secrets

Application configuration reveals how the system talks to itself. His example: an attacker with config access flips logging to verbose and reads the architecture out of the logs. Centralise it in Azure App Configuration (or AWS AppConfig) and store Key Vault references instead of values, so reading a secret needs access to both services. Each component can be limited to its own secrets.

## Storage and SQL: the basics people still skip

He still sees projects authenticating to storage with the account name and key. As Vunvulea said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, "Don't use accounting key." For third parties, use shared access signatures scoped to specific rights, an IP and a short window; he recommends five to 15 minutes, because issuing another one is cheap. For long-lived service access, use RBAC. Storage firewall rules are crude, which he describes as "Windows XP firewall like because basically you are just whitelisting the IPS", but they still shrink the attack surface.

For Azure SQL: encrypt data and backups (he once watched a security specialist crack a SQL backup's password hash in a 90-minute session using tools found online), manage firewall IP rules by company ranges rather than each remote worker's home IP, use Azure AD identities, turn on threat detection, and use column- and cell-level protection so support staff can work on databases with customer data without seeing the sensitive columns.

## Push the rest to the platform

Rather than hand-coding OWASP protections into every API, put Azure Application Gateway's WAF in front. Microsoft Defender for Cloud scans the infrastructure for misconfiguration against standards such as PCI DSS 3.2, scores you and often fixes the finding in one click. Azure Advisor adds reliability, performance and cost recommendations on top. His closing pointers: Skyhigh Networks' Azure security guide, Microsoft's security best practices, the Cloud Adoption Framework and the Well-Architected Framework.

## Who should watch

Teams running production on Azure who suspect their basics have gaps, and architects who need a short list to take to management. If you already run managed identities everywhere, the storage and SQL sections are the quickest wins to check.

Title: Wrap the secret scanner, then send its findings to the backlog
Description: Audrey Long (Microsoft) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on wrapping Yelp's detect-secrets for Azure DevOps and turning scan results into backlog bugs
Body:
When security engineers make up around 1% of an organisation, the only security that scales is the kind developers can drop into a pipeline without reading a manual. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Audrey Long, Senior Security Software Engineer in Microsoft's Commercial Software Engineering group, shows how her team wrapped Yelp's open source detect-secrets scanner as an Azure DevOps extension, with simple inputs, an allow list for false positives and findings that land in the backlog as bugs.

She is clear that the tool is an example, not the product. As Long said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, "I'm not trying to sell you a tool here. Instead I'm trying to sell you an idea".

## What goes wrong without it?

Her list of common missteps is the usual rogues' gallery, each with a reason it matters. Stored test passwords teach an attacker your password structure. Secrets in open source repos show how the code works and where it breaks. Default and reused passwords are rampant in IoT configuration files. And security tacked on at the end, rather than shifted left into requirements, is still the norm.

Her fix is an adversarial mindset: threat modelling to find the entry points, then countermeasures built into the DevSecOps pipeline, and above all tooling that is easy enough that developers actually use it.

## Is there one tool that covers it all?

No, and she says so plainly. Static analysis, dynamic analysis, infrastructure as code, credential scanning, container scanning and open source scanning each need their own tools, and new ones appear seemingly every week. So her team built a reusable, plug-and-play foundation for command-line scanners rather than betting on one.

The pipeline is the same for each tool: research which scanner fits the job, read the inputs from a configuration file, run the scanner CLI with a deliberately chosen configuration, convert its report into something the Azure DevOps dashboard can display, generate a readable report, and push findings into the Azure DevOps backlog. The configuration step gets her sharpest criticism of her own field: too many security engineers unbox a tool and let the default configuration do the job.

The backlog step is the one she calls novel, and it's the most useful idea in the talk. Pipelines break and nobody fixes them; a work item with a line-level finding attached is something a team actually schedules.

## What does the demo show?

The target is OWASP WebGoat, the deliberately vulnerable application she recommends to anyone evaluating security tools. It contains about 150 secrets, which makes it a good way to see what a scanner really catches. The extension's inputs are intentionally few: what to scan (the whole repo by default), a word list as an allow list to skip known false positives, and an option to report findings as warnings instead of failing the build. She makes a point of the naming too: allow list and disallow list, not the older terms.

The results show up in the Azure DevOps dashboard line by line, and from there one click creates a bug that appears in the backlog linked to the finding. At the time of the talk the extension was not yet publicly downloadable, with release promised soon.

## What's next for secret scanning?

Her forward look: better entropy engines that recognise strings resembling secrets, machine learning models to cut false positives, and secure-by-default pipelines, because she still meets strong engineering teams whose pipelines run no security checks at all. She also wants security research to be less siloed, with teams sharing the tooling and vulnerabilities they find.

## Who should watch

Security engineers supporting many development teams, and Azure DevOps shops that want credential scanning in the pipeline. The abstract mentions pre-commit hooks; the talk itself focuses on the pipeline extension and its architecture, so look elsewhere for hook setup.

Title: After serverless, the infrastructure is inferred from your code
Description: Domenico Musto (Chronomics) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on platform as code and infrastructure from code, demoed with Pulumi and Serverless Cloud
Body:
Twenty years ago in Naples, a power cut threatened the one server that authenticated a region's broadband users, so Domenico Musto unplugged it, took it on his scooter and rode through traffic to his parents' house. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Musto, Principal Engineer at Chronomics, uses that story to open a talk about how far we've come since, and argues that even serverless still splits the world into infrastructure and application. His bet for what comes next: platform as code and infrastructure from code, both demoed live in TypeScript.

## What happened to Argo?

The server was called Argo, lived in an air-conditioned room, and had been patched and reconfigured for years until nobody knew what was on it. There was no second Argo and no way to rebuild one in time. So Argo went to his bedroom, the broadband partners were given his home IP address, and the service came back. Then Argo's fan was too loud to sleep through, so it moved to the living room, with a little more downtime.

"So what did I do? I unplugged Argo," Domenico Musto said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

The point: there was a time when servers were long-lived pets and whole businesses depended on one box.

## How far has the dev/ops gap closed?

He tracks the distance between developers and operations through four eras. Physical servers: two different jobs, with code handed over as a package. Virtualisation: both sides start scripting and configuration as code, so the gap shrinks a bit. Docker: the biggest shift in his view, because environments become ephemeral, you talk about processes, memory and CPUs instead of named servers, and tools like Helm are shared by both sides. Functions as a service: no servers at all, but in his opinion less impactful than Docker.

The gap is still there in serverless, he argues, because the tooling is split. His example is a TypeScript Lambda next to a YAML Serverless Framework config: two languages, two mental models, infrastructure versus application.

## What is platform as code?

Three properties: you code the system rather than infrastructure or application, in a single language, and you deploy it as one atomic unit through a single CI/CD pipeline. He demos it with Pulumi, specifically its metaprogramming side rather than its Terraform-style use, and says up front that he has no commercial relationship with either tool and that others implement the same patterns.

`pulumi new typescript` creates an empty project. He writes an Express-like HTTP route returning JSON with Pulumi's cloud package, sets AWS as the provider and `eu-west-1` as the region, and `pulumi up` works out the API Gateway, REST API, permissions and stage on its own. He never mentions Lambda. Then he declares an SQS queue with a callback that runs on each message, and shares a constant between the route and the handler, all in one file. The infrastructure still runs in his own AWS account, and the queue is still explicit, so some infrastructure knowledge remains.

## And infrastructure from code?

The next step: the application comes first, the infrastructure becomes a side effect inferred from it, and the system is decoupled from any cloud provider, which here means you no longer own the account it runs in. His example is Serverless Cloud, a then-new offering from the company behind the Serverless Framework.

The CLI creates a TypeScript app connected to a personal sandbox with a live URL, and every save syncs to it within moments. He builds a hello-world API, then store-data and get-data endpoints with the built-in data primitive (he assumes DynamoDB underneath but doesn't know or care), a schedule that runs every minute with its logs streaming into his terminal, and a query over users. A share command clones the environment, data included, for a teammate or QA. Deploying to prod creates that environment on the fly and deliberately doesn't copy the data.

He notes in passing that the instant cloud sync also answers serverless's weak local-development story.

## Who should watch

Developers who feel that writing YAML for every Lambda is a tax, and platform engineers wondering where IaC is heading. It's a forward-looking opinion talk with two demos, not a comparison of tools, and both tools have evolved since 2022, so read it for the patterns. He also admits that after 20 years in the industry he still can't write a simple regular expression, which makes him easy to trust.

Title: A crypto checkout where the merchant never touches crypto
Description: Filipe Castro (Utrust) at Conf42 Web 3.0 2022 on accepting crypto payments at checkout while settling in fiat, with no volatility risk for the merchant
Body:
The most practical idea in crypto payments is that the merchant never has to hold any crypto. At Conf42 Web 3.0 2022, Filipe Castro, founder and special projects director at Utrust, [makes the case](https://www.conf42.com/Web_30_2022_Filipe_Castro_cryptocurrency_confidence) for a payment gateway that takes Bitcoin, Ethereum or stablecoins from the buyer and drops fiat into the merchant's bank account, so the shop gets the new customers without the price chart.

Honest scope up front: this is a vendor talk. The first half is a short primer on what makes digital assets different, the second half is the pitch for Utrust's gateway (which he mentions was about to be renamed xMoney). It is short, and it is clear about what it is selling.

## What actually changes when value moves on a blockchain?

Filipe's framing is that your home banking app shows you a representation of money, while a blockchain transfer is the money itself moving between two parties, closer to handing over cash than sending a request to a bank. That is why self-custody matters, and why he reaches for the old line: "not your keys, not your crypto."

He is careful not to lump everything together. Bitcoin and Ethereum float; USDC and USDT are stablecoins pegged one to one to the US dollar ("not all the times", he adds, and wisely leaves that for another talk). Issuer risk matters for stablecoins the same way it matters when comparing a US dollar with a Venezuelan bolivar. He sketches the narrative arc Bitcoin went through, from payments to speculation to inflation hedge to store of value, and expects central bank digital currencies to arrive as hybrids of centralised and decentralised parts.

## Why would a merchant bother?

His answer is the audience: young, digital-native buyers who already hold crypto. The numbers he puts up come from third-party studies cited in his deck: nearly 32% of US small businesses accepting cryptocurrency, merchant transaction volume up 100% in a year, and an average ROI of 327% for merchants who accept crypto. They are presented without much methodology, so treat them as the industry's own optimism rather than settled data.

The more interesting argument is about intermediaries. Plenty of people already pay with crypto, he points out, just through linked cards that convert to fiat behind the scenes, so the buyer pays a conversion fee and the merchant pays card rails on top. Cut out layers and you cut costs.

## How does the gateway work?

The pitch is a crypto-to-bank gateway that works at checkout or through invoicing:

- The buyer pays from any wallet, with no ecosystem lock-in.
- The merchant is settled in fiat, so volatility is Utrust's problem, not theirs.
- No chargebacks, and blockchain screening for anti-money-laundering checks.
- Plugins for the common e-commerce platforms, plus an API for custom integrations, with no blockchain expertise needed on the merchant side.

On pricing, his words: "Merchants only pay 1% of any transacted volume."

## The float trick, run in reverse

The sharpest bit of the talk is about float. Legacy processors, Filipe says, earn on the money in transit between the buyer paying and the merchant being paid: "these funds in transit can be used and reinvested to generate additional revenue." His proposal is to pass that yield to the merchant instead, which in principle can push the effective processing fee towards zero, or past it. It is optional, and he presents it as a fairer version of a model that already exists, not a new invention. Whether the economics hold up is a question for your finance team, but it is a neat example of how the payment rail shapes the business model.

## Who should watch

E-commerce and payments engineers who get asked whether the shop can take crypto and want the merchant-side view in under 15 minutes. If you want to know how stablecoins hold their peg or how settlement works under the hood, this is not that talk; it stays at the product level.

Title: The backend changed the API again, so sign a contract first
Description: Julio Cesar Abalde Reyes (Sngular) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on API-first OpenAPI contracts and Node.js tools for codegen and mock servers
Body:
Every frontend team knows the sprint-end surprise: the backend renamed a field, nobody told you, and the integration day turns into a hunt. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Julio Cesar Abalde Reyes, head frontend developer at Sngular, argues that the fix is an agreed OpenAPI contract before anyone writes code, and shows two Node.js command-line tools his team built so frontend developers can work from that contract without installing a Java toolchain.

"The problem is not usually a technology problem, it's a communication problem," Julio Cesar Abalde Reyes said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

It is a short talk with a quick demo, best taken as a pitch for the API-first workflow plus a look at open source tools from the Sngular team.

## What goes wrong without a contract?

He names two pains. The first is waiting: until the API exists, the frontend either writes its own mocks, which usually drift from the final API and cost extra work at integration, or waits and blocks the whole team. Waiting also means you discover design gaps late, when the API lands and the UI needs something it doesn't provide. The second is the silent change: a difference in the API, now or months later, can break the frontend, and if nobody catches it early it surfaces at integration time with the whole team under stress.

## How does API first fix it?

The two teams negotiate the API signature until they agree. From then on, both sides build in parallel against the same contract, the API is designed and documented up front, and the risk drops because everyone must honour it. A team that changes the API without telling the other breaks the build before integration, especially once the checks run in the CI/CD pipeline.

The contract format is an OpenAPI specification file (formerly Swagger): endpoints and methods, parameters, input and output schemas, authentication, plus contact and licence details.

## Why build new tools?

Contract tools already exist, he notes, citing Spring Cloud Contract and Pact, but almost all of them run on the JVM. Asking frontend developers to install the Java world to read a YAML file is a non-starter, so the team wrote the tools in Node.js, which every frontend machine already has.

## What do the tools do?

**openapi-nodejs-cli**, published on npm as `@corunet/openapi-nodejs-cli`, reads a spec and generates client code, an Express server skeleton and interfaces for the schemas, in JavaScript or TypeScript, with Angular service files as an option. In the demo the generated server endpoints simply throw a not-implemented error, ready for your database code; the client and interfaces mean both sides speak the same types.

**openapi-contracts-nodejs-cli**, still in development at the time, does two jobs. First, it launches a mock server straight from the spec as soon as the contract is signed: in the demo it reads the routes and starts in memory in about two seconds, and Postman calls return list and single-item responses. POST and PUT bodies are validated against the spec, so a missing mandatory field returns an error naming the key, and an extra field not in the spec is rejected too. Second, it will validate a real API server against the contract, so drift shows up in the development flow instead of at integration.

## Who should watch

Frontend leads who keep getting burned by unannounced backend changes, and teams that want contract testing but have no JVM in their JavaScript workflow. Don't expect a deep comparison with Pact or a production case study; the value is the workflow and a starting point in the team's GitHub repositories.

Title: Your org's GitHub Actions secrets are one forked PR away from leaking
Description: Ranjan Mohan (Menlo Security) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on org-wide GitHub Actions templates, scheduled reports and keeping secrets away from forks
Body:
A pull request from a fork can carry its own edited workflow file, and that workflow can read your secrets. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Ranjan Mohan, Senior Security Engineer at Menlo Security, shows how he runs GitHub Actions across the 30 repositories of padaiyal, an open source organisation of Python, Java and JavaScript libraries he has built with friends for three years, and which settings stop that fork from walking off with the credentials.

It's a getting-started talk with a security engineer's priorities: half of it is templates and schedules, the other half is what not to trust.

## Where should shared workflows live?

Mohan's first question for any action: do you reuse it across repositories in the same organisation? If yes, put it in the organisation's special `.github` repository, which also holds the org profile README and the issue and pull request templates. Its `workflow-templates` folder holds his three templates: a Maven build, a Maven package publish and a Python build.

Each template comes as three files: the YAML, an SVG icon and a properties JSON with the name, description and categories. The JSON's file patterns field is the neat part: any repository containing a `pom.xml` gets the Maven build suggested automatically. Inside the template, the `$default-branch` variable is replaced with the actual default branch when someone sets it up.

He is honest about the limit. Templates make setup easy, but if the original YAML changes, he said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, "you would need to manually propagate the changes to all the repositories using the action."

## What does a real Java pipeline look like?

The Maven template triggers on pushes and pull requests to the default branch and runs on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS with JDK 14.0.1. The steps: checkout, a git command to pull submodules, JDK setup, a Maven dependency cache so later runs skip the downloads, Checkstyle for linting, PMD for static analysis, the JUnit tests, and JaCoCo to enforce code coverage. The pass or fail status then gates merges, which is the part that turns a pipeline into continuous integration.

## A workflow that writes its own README

His second example is a report repository. On top of push and pull request triggers it has a daily cron schedule and `workflow_dispatch` for manual runs, which he triggers live. The job installs cached dependencies, generates a report on every repository in the organisation (maintained or not, public or private, open issue counts) and commits it back as the README. The result shows the run timestamped minutes earlier. It's a handy template if you need a cheap org dashboard.

## How does a fork steal a secret?

Organisation secrets reach the runner as environment variables, which keeps them out of the repository. The catch: he opens a merged pull request that came from an outside contributor's fork, and points out that whoever controls that branch also controls the workflow file in it. They could edit it to read the secrets and send them to a server of their own.

The allow-list settings (only actions from this organisation, or from GitHub and verified creators) help, but don't stop that. The setting that does is under organisation settings, Actions, fork pull request workflows from outside collaborators. Of the three levels (approval for contributors new to GitHub, for first-time contributors, or for all outside collaborators) his recommendation is the strictest: require approval for all outside collaborators, so nothing runs until a person has looked at it.

The other one: workflow permissions. His report job needs read and write because it pushes the README. Anything that only builds should keep the default token read-only.

## Who should watch

Maintainers of open source organisations and anyone who accepts pull requests from forks into repositories with secrets. If you already have fork approvals and a read-only token, the template tricks are the new part. His links cover GitHub's starter workflows, the org report and the padaiyal Java and Python templates.

Title: A real-time scrum poker app in Remix, built from plain HTML forms up
Description: Dave Bitter (iO) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on building a multi-user real-time Remix app on forms, server state and progressive enhancement
Body:
The usual knock on Remix is that it's great for a dashboard with a form and not much else. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Dave Bitter, Developer Advocate at iO in the Netherlands, answers it by building something deliberately interactive: a multi-user, real-time scrum poker app for remote estimation sessions that works without client-side JavaScript first and only then gets optimistic UI and live updates layered on top.

The stack is Remix, Supabase for data and Tailwind for styling. The app has four features: create or join a session, cast a vote, toggle vote visibility, clear the round.

## Why build on web fundamentals?

The talk opens with a Twitter argument: someone told him Remix is a framework for over-engineered websites, and that web apps will inevitably fail at being native apps. His reply is the thesis of the talk. Remix counters over-engineering by going back to what the browser already does well (forms, HTTP, cookies), then progressively enhancing toward modern UX. Build every layer so it works, rather than building the fancy version and trying to degrade it gracefully later.

"It's not about your user not having client side JavaScript, it's about reducing the complexity of your app," Dave Bitter said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

The anecdote that sells it: a colleague's two-month-old Remix app loaded as a blank page. He suggested turning JavaScript off, and the whole app worked again, because the server routes and actions were doing the real work.

## How do forms work in Remix?

File-based routing gives an index page and a dynamic `session/$id` route. The create-session form is a Remix `Form` with `method="post"`, which renders a native form element. No `preventDefault`, no event listeners. An exported `action` function on the server reads the form data, inserts the session through the Supabase client and returns a redirect, or returns an error object that the page reads with `useActionData`. Without JavaScript that's a full page post; with it, Remix does the same round trip without the reload.

Two forms on one route share one action through an old trick: a hidden `form_type` input and a switch statement. The invite link uses the native Web Share API on phones, the clipboard when JavaScript is available, and the plain URL otherwise. On the index page `useSearchParams` reads the session ID during server-side rendering, so the create form is hidden and the join form is prefilled and focused before the page arrives. No `useEffect` flash.

## Interactivity without client state

Data comes in through a `loader` (think `getServerSideProps`) and `useLoaderData`. The voting grid turns out to be just a fieldset of radio inputs over the Fibonacci numbers, which already guarantees one active vote; CSS makes them look like cards. `useSubmit` on change posts the form immediately, and a small CSS trick (a no-JavaScript data attribute on the body, plus helper classes with a 500 ms delay so the bundle can load) shows a manual submit button only to users without JavaScript. The admin's show and clear buttons are two more micro-forms with the same hidden-input trick.

## Who is allowed to vote?

His first version passed the username in a query parameter, so anyone could vote as anyone or become admin. The fix needs no sign-up: a cookie-based server session stores a user ID and username per session ID, and the action reads identity from the session rather than from the request body. The loader also strips user IDs from the votes it sends back, so the client only ever sees names and efforts. For defence in depth, the Supabase policies block everything, and only a server-only key (in `process.env`, in a `.server.ts` file) can bypass them.

## Making it fast and live

A full round trip per click feels slow, so `useTransition` (the Remix API at the time) provides optimistic UI: while a form is submitting, read its form data on the client and show the new vote straight away. Real-time comes last, through a custom Supabase subscription hook. His first attempt pushed every change into client state and hit ordering problems as people spammed the buttons. The better fix reuses what already exists: on any change, `useFetcher` reruns the route's loader and the page renders the fresh server state.

"Databases are perfect at keeping the latest state," he said.

In the test run with his team, colleagues tried to break it with things like DROP TABLE in the form fields (they didn't) and hammered the free Supabase tier with clicks, so he throttled the refresh. With optimistic UI on your own vote, nobody notices a second's delay on someone else's.

## Who should watch

React developers who reach for client state and an API layer for every button, and anyone who has only seen Remix demos with a single form. Some APIs have since moved (Remix was folding into React Router even then), but the order of operations he argues for is the part that lasts.

Title: Anonymise your logs without asking developers for a release
Description: Leonid Yankulin (Google) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on moving log anonymisation out of app code into a DevOps-owned pipeline with Cloud DLP
Body:
If the fix for a social security number in your logs is a new application release, the fix is in the wrong place. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Leonid Yankulin, Developer Relations Engineer at Google, compares three ways to anonymise PII, PHI and other sensitive data in logs, and argues for the one where the DevOps team owns it end to end and the application code doesn't change.

It's a compact architecture talk: one problem, three designs, and a Google Cloud reference implementation with the code on GitHub.

## Why are logs a compliance problem at all?

Logs usually show up in compliance programmes as evidence (audit trails, investigations), not as data that must itself comply with GDPR, HIPAA or PCI DSS. Yankulin splits the controls into preventive, detective and corrective, and splits the log lifecycle into access and ingestion. Access is the easy half: IAM, audit logs and storage controls work the same under most regulations. Ingestion is where it gets specific to industry and geography, because that is where you detect sensitive values and then either drop them or obfuscate them.

Obfuscation has a catch engineers will recognise. If an application (wrongly, as he admits many still do) uses a social security number as the user's identity, simply masking it breaks troubleshooting, because you can no longer follow one user's transactions. The masked value has to stay unique and stay the same for the same user.

The cost side, from his slides, cites a Coalfire report: for most organisations, growing compliance obligations now eat more than 40% of the security budget.

## Option one: let the developers do it

The engineering-first answer is to put detection and masking right where log lines are written. Yankulin lists what goes wrong. The R&D team owns a piece of specialised compliance logic it may not have the knowledge for. It runs inside the business process and eats its CPU. Any regulation change means a new application version even though nothing in the business changed. Different regions with different rules mean either messy configuration or several implementations. And it never sees the logs your load balancer and other infrastructure produce.

## Option two: a DLP service in the middle

Delegating to a data loss prevention service, commercial or in-house, moves the running and maintenance to DevOps, runs outside the application's resources and scales better across regions. It still leaves work for developers: the DLP needs structured logs with metadata about the source (which service, where, which environment), and the log shipping has to be redirected to it. And infrastructure logs are still not covered.

## Option three: push it into the cloud's log pipeline

His preferred design routes all log ingestion, application and infrastructure, through a proxy in front of the log backend and into DLP first. Managed platforms already add metadata and structure; elsewhere Fluentd or Fluent Bit can reformat stdout logs before forwarding. The pitch, as Yankulin said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022: you can do it "in a scaled and flexible way without changing single line of code and keeping all the work within the DevOps team".

The Google Cloud reference architecture uses four managed services: Cloud Logging, whose log router replaces the hand-built proxy; Pub/Sub; Dataflow, the managed Apache Beam; and Cloud DLP for the detective and corrective controls. The streaming pipeline unpacks each Pub/Sub message, aggregates log entries into large batches, sends each batch to the DLP API, then writes the processed entries to a log storage bucket.

The batching is the practical detail worth stealing. Cloud APIs have quotas, and most providers charge per call, so sending many entries per request saves money each month and keeps up with log-heavy applications.

## Who should watch

Platform, SRE and DevOps engineers who have been handed a compliance requirement for logs, and anyone running in several regions with different rules. It's a design walkthrough with no live demo; the implementation is in the linked repo.
