Title: SRP, YAGNI and a pacifier on a strap, clean code for tired parents
Description: Ben Tlusty (Forter) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on five clean-code principles, from SRP to Tell Don't Ask, explained in code and with a toddler
Body:
A toddler turns a tidy living room into a monolith in minutes, which is roughly what a few fast-moving sprints do to a codebase. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Ben Tlusty, Senior Software Engineer at Forter, takes five classic principles (single responsibility, the Boy Scout rule, KISS, YAGNI and Tell, Don't Ask), shows each as a before-and-after code refactor, then shows how he applied the same idea at home in his first, very tired year as a father.

The title promises seven and delivers five. That's the first joke: a tired father who forgot how to count. It is a short, light talk, and a good one to send a junior developer.

## Where does the mess come from?

His starting point is honest: the mess is fine at first, because you want to move fast. Once you reach a certain size it starts eating productivity, and, as with a house with a newborn, you can't fix everything at once, so you prioritise. His two takeaways up front: fight coupling as hard as you can where it applies, and keep the code simple and be kind to whoever reads it next. Kind in the code, he clarifies, not only in code reviews.

## One responsibility, one function

The single responsibility example is a function that fetches a user and their location, needing the whole user object just to read an IP, and returning two unrelated objects. The fix splits it in two: one function validates and normalises the user, the other enriches a location from just an IP, so anyone can reuse it without a user ID.

"Always remember if there is an and or an or in the function name," Ben Tlusty said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

The home version: the trolley, the laptop and the dishes don't belong in the living room, and the toys get their own room. The living room isn't empty, it's just doing one job.

## Leave it better than you found it

The Boy Scout rule example is adding a profit calculation to a file where the surrounding code is cryptic. The task is the new function with tests. The bonus is fixing the typo in a default date and renaming `acc`, `row` and `r` to names like total income and expense. Nobody asked, and the next reader will thank you. At the campsite, the family picks up litter even when it isn't theirs.

## Simple beats clever

KISS gets a single invoice function that computes every section, which grows long and is hard to test because you run the whole thing every time. Split it into one function per section, test each one, and as a bonus you can reorder the sections. At home: instead of stashing pacifiers in every closet and cot, put a strap on the one pacifier. Problem solved.

## You ain't gonna need it

This is the most relatable code in the talk. A feature needs one thing, get a user by ID from the database. The first draft has a base repository interface, a user repository extending it and a Prisma ORM with its setup code. He strips it step by step: drop the interface built for a single method, drop the ORM for plain SQL, then ask why it's a class at all and not a function. He admits he has written the bloated version himself. The rule, from his slides: always implement things when you actually need them, never when you just foresee that you may need them.

The parenting version is a spreadsheet of every food a baby should try in the first year, tracked with special cups to catch a salt allergy that most children don't have. They end up eating off the floor anyway.

## Tell, don't ask

The last example is caller code that checks whether a task is not started, created before January 2022 and has no subscribers, and then closes it. That logic belongs inside the task class, so the caller just tells the task to close. His toddler is the purest tell-don't-ask client he knows: no questions, just demands.

## Who should watch

Junior and mid-level developers who know the acronyms but haven't seen them applied to small, believable JavaScript and TypeScript snippets, and anyone who wants a gentle refresher with a few laughs. Senior engineers won't learn new principles here, but they might borrow the analogies for their next mentoring session.

Title: A GitHub Actions tour where the missing secret is an empty string
Description: Chris Ayers (Microsoft) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on GitHub Actions end to end - triggers, needs, contexts, secrets, environments, matrices and act
Body:
Drop a valid YAML file into `.github/workflows` and it simply starts running: no registration step, no "new pipeline" button. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Chris Ayers, Senior Customer Engineer at Microsoft on the FastTrack for Azure team, gives a demo-driven tour of CI/CD with GitHub Actions, from YAML indentation to approvals, dynamic deployment outputs and running workflows locally.

It's an introduction, and a well-paced one. Every concept comes with a workflow from his public demo repo that he runs live.

## How does a workflow actually start?

Workflows are event driven, and the list of events goes well past push and pull request: creating a branch or tag, someone forking the repo, a project card moving, a comment, a cron schedule. His favourite is the one people forget. As Ayers said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, "out of the box. There's no manual way to trigger a workflow. You have to add workflow dispatch if you want to manually trigger a workflow."

Filters narrow things down further: only the main branch, only `release/**`, only v2 tags, only when JavaScript files change. A workflow holds one or more jobs, each job runs on its own runner, and jobs run in parallel unless `needs` says otherwise. In his three-job demo, job three finished first, which is exactly the point.

## What do you get on a hosted runner?

A GitHub-hosted runner is a VM with roughly two CPU cores and 7 GB of RAM in his description, on Linux, Windows or macOS, with an almost comical amount of software preinstalled: Docker, kubectl, npm and CLI tools for pretty much every cloud. The job log links to the runner image's full software list, so you can check before you install anything. Self-hosted runners have whatever you put on them.

Steps can be shell commands in bash, cross-platform PowerShell, Python or Perl, or actions from the Marketplace. He pins `checkout` to a specific commit SHA in one demo, and points out that Marketplace actions must live in public repos, so you can read the code and the open issues before trusting one.

## Variables, contexts and the secrets hierarchy

Environment variables can be set at workflow, job and step level, and the lower level wins: his "hello from" demo prints the step value over the job value over the workflow value. Expressions handle string formatting, `contains`, `endsWith`, JSON parsing and joins, and contexts expose the repo, the run, jobs, steps and secrets.

Secrets follow the same layering across organisation, repository and environment. Two details are worth the price of admission. A secret that doesn't exist comes back as an empty string rather than an error, so nobody can probe for secret names. And GitHub masks known secret values in the logs. He prefers passing secrets through environment variables rather than command-line arguments, in case something lists processes on the box, while admitting that one is a debate.

## Build once, deploy with approvals

His .NET example is the pattern he uses on every CI platform: a build job that restores, builds, tests, publishes and uploads two artifacts, the app and its infrastructure as code. Then a deploy job that `needs` build, targets an environment with a required reviewer and a main-branch-only rule, logs into Azure, deploys an ARM or Bicep template and reads the generated web app name from that step's outputs, because the name differs per environment. A known-good binary means you can redeploy without rebuilding.

He uses the older service-principal login in the demo and tells everyone to look at OpenID Connect instead, where Azure and GitHub trust each other and no password is stored at all.

Matrices get a quick tour too: one job definition fanned out to six runs across Node versions and operating systems. Container builds use the Docker login and build-push actions for Docker Hub or Azure Container Registry, with a Trivy scan before the push, and GitHub's Super-Linter covers everything else.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving to GitHub Actions from Azure Pipelines, Jenkins or GitLab, and anyone who has copied workflows without knowing why the secret came back blank. Experienced Actions users will mostly enjoy the closing tips: GitHub Skills (training courses that run on Actions events) and `act` for running workflows locally in containers.

Title: Cypress tests that survive a refactor, and a few that run in production
Description: Rob Richardson (Shoreline.io) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on Cypress end-to-end tests, custom commands, fixtures and data-cy selectors
Body:
The point of end-to-end tests is to let you refactor mercilessly without spending the following week cleaning up regressions. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Rob Richardson, Developer Advocate at Shoreline.io (and a former Gulp contributor), walks through Cypress from `npm install` to a TypeScript test suite against TodoMVC and a Hacker News PWA, then lands on the practices that keep such a suite from becoming its own fragile tower.

It's a hands-on intro aimed at people who haven't written a Cypress test yet, and his slides and code are on robrich.org.

## Why Cypress rather than Selenium?

He places end-to-end tests among the other kinds (function, component, service, API), each with its own tools, and then compares the end-to-end options fairly:

- **Selenium** invented the category and uses WebDriver, which has all but become a web standard. But it moves the mouse and waits, so slow APIs lead to longer timeouts or reruns: slow and brittle.
- **Cypress** runs a browser plugin that watches the DOM and continues as soon as it settles. The trade-off is the browser list it chose to support: Chrome, Firefox, Edge and its built-in Electron, but not Safari or IE. The API feels like jQuery, which he admits is a little dated.
- **TestCafe** uses CSS selectors and feels native, but you shim data between a browser context and a test context.
- **Playwright** builds on the Puppeteer approach and supports lots of languages, though its assertion style feels odd if you grew up on Mocha and Chai.

Cypress is built on Mocha and Chai, so anyone who knows Mocha, Jest or Jasmine will feel at home.

## What does a first suite look like?

`npm install cypress`, then `npx cypress open` starts the runner and can scaffold example tests. Tests run in a clean browser instance with no cookies or plugins from your daily profile. You click through each step, see where it clicked, open DevTools and set breakpoints, and read the console output for each step.

His TodoMVC suite (the AngularJS implementation, though you can swap frameworks) shows the idioms: `beforeEach` visits the page, the first test checks the URL (which caught the site moving from HTTP to HTTPS while he was writing the talk), then type a todo with `{enter}`, toggle it complete and assert the `completed` class, delete one. That last one needs `force: true`, because the destroy button only appears on hover and Cypress fires JavaScript events, not real mouse moves. Notice there is no `await` anywhere; Cypress queues the commands.

For TypeScript, a `tsconfig` in the Cypress folder extends the root one and adds the Cypress types. In his project (an older Cypress) `cypress.json` and a plugins file set up the folders; newer versions merge the two.

## Mock the API, then test it for real too

The Hacker News PWA is the more interesting test, because you don't know what today's stories are. `cy.intercept` with a regex answers the request with a fixture whose first story has a known title, so you can assert the component renders it. Then a second test lets the real API through and checks there are 30 stories.

"If we only mock out all of our API requests, we won't be able to validate that our site works, only that our site works if we assume the API behaves that way," Rob Richardson said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

## The practices worth stealing

- **Select by `data-cy` attributes**, not long XPaths that break when the markup moves. A side benefit: the attribute documents that a test depends on that element.
- **Custom commands for frequent tasks**, such as a `todo add` command with a TypeScript declaration file. It's the page-object idea from Selenium, and a refactor touches one place.
- **Log in once**, save the token and reuse it (or fetch one from a test API), instead of logging in at the start of every test. Test the login itself separately.
- **Fixtures for mock data**, such as standard users and result sets, so tests stay short and legible.
- **Run some tests in production.** A walk from the home page to the shop, the cart and almost-checkout every 15 minutes or every hour tells you the site is down before customers do.

That last point flips the usual worry about test hooks shipping to production. "So maybe having our test content in production is actually a good thing," he said.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers who rely on manual clicking before a release, and teams on Selenium wondering what they'd gain. The Cypress specifics are from 2022, so check the current config layout, but the testing advice hasn't aged.

Title: Strip the YAML and every CI pipeline is the same pipeline
Description: Lionel Lonkap Tsamba at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on universal CI/CD pipelines - name the intent, hide the tooling, and stay platform agnostic with Dagger
Body:
Put a Jenkinsfile, a GitHub Actions workflow and a GitLab CI file side by side and squint: they are the same document in three dialects. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Lionel Lonkap Tsamba, a senior DevOps and cloud engineer consultant, argues that a CI/CD pipeline should be written in the language of intent, with the tool-specific noise generated or hidden, and shows how Dagger makes the result portable between CI platforms.

It's a short talk built on one observation from writing a lot of pipelines for a lot of clients, and he offers the ideas openly: copy them, steal them.

## What do all those manifests have in common?

His opening exercise is the whole thesis. Look at the Jenkins and GitHub Actions manifests long enough and, as Lonkap Tsamba said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, "when you remove the noise, we are only left with name of stages and actions". GitLab CI is the same again. So if you had a way to express only the intent, a tool could produce the rest.

From the dictionary definition of universal (understood by all, applicable everywhere) he derives two principles. A universal pipeline is built around a ubiquitous language that is semantically correct, and it is platform agnostic.

## Name stages after what they mean

The first principle is about words. His reference pipeline goes trigger, source, create, verify, review, deliver, then a manual approval and a go-live stage. Source holds the sanitising, linting and code analysis; create compiles code and docs and runs unit tests; review puts the build into a QA environment; deliver packages it and pushes it to an artifact repository. Continuous deployment, in this framing, is just the same pipeline with the manual approval removed.

The point of picking verbs carefully is that someone new to the project can read the workflow and know what it does without opening a single script. That is a domain-driven design idea (the ubiquitous language) applied to YAML, and it holds up.

## Make, Projen and a disciplined repo

To keep the manifest that clean you need a task manager in between, so the CI file calls intents and the intents call implementations. His choice is `make`: a near-empty root Makefile that includes per-step makefiles from a tasks folder, each of which only calls a script in a scripts folder. The scripts can be in any language. The resulting GitHub Actions workflow reads like the stage list above.

For spreading the pattern he recommends a project generator, specifically Projen, the project behind the AWS CDK. His reason is a sharp one: most generators only help at bootstrap, so when the template improves, every project stamped from it is left behind. Projen keeps generated projects in sync with their template.

## Where does Dagger fit?

The second principle, platform agnostic, needs something that runs the same on every CI system. His pick is Dagger, a programmable CI/CD engine with SDKs for CUE, Go, Node.js and Python, running everything in containers under the hood so a pipeline behaves the same from one CI to the next.

The demo compares two GitHub Actions workflows in one repo. Both share a composite `prepare` action that installs Node.js (and, for the Dagger path, Python and the Dagger SDK, pinned to the same Python version used in development). The plain workflow runs the steps directly; the Dagger one only calls a Python script: an async function that opens a client, builds a container on a Node 18 image and runs the scripts inside it. Both runs publish a new package version, and the demo gods cooperate.

Because the pipeline is code, he notes, you can imagine testing the pipeline itself, and Dagger can partly replace the task manager: name the script well and the semantics survive.

## What he took away

His lessons are about people more than tools: focus on semantics over technology, and take onboarding seriously. If you go the Dagger route, pick abstractions that don't confuse newcomers; if you go the task-manager route, name the actions well. He closes with two open explorations: a universal project folder structure for any language or framework, and a language-neutral documentation spec, something like Javadoc for everything.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers who maintain pipelines for several teams or several CI vendors, and anyone about to migrate from one CI system to another. It's an ideas talk with a small demo, not a Dagger tutorial.

Title: Give each frontend its own serverless backend, and three ways to feed it
Description: Roman Boiko (AWS) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on building the backend-for-frontend pattern with API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB and Step Functions
Body:
When the web team and the mobile team both call ten microservices directly, every new field becomes a cross-team negotiation and a pile of glue code in the client. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Roman Boiko, Senior Specialist Solutions Architect for Serverless at Amazon Web Services, shows how to build the backend-for-frontend (BFF) pattern on AWS serverless services, with a concrete answer to the question most BFF diagrams skip: how does the data get into the BFF in the first place?

It's an architecture walkthrough with diagrams. The abstract mentions a live demo, but the recording sticks to patterns and service choices.

## What problem does a BFF solve?

The pattern comes from Sam Newman. Each type of client (web, iOS, Android) gets its own thin backend, owned by the frontend team, that consumes the downstream microservices and serves exactly the shape of data that client needs. The frontend talks to one endpoint, is decoupled from how the microservices are built, and the team can change its own presentation logic without waiting on anyone. The web BFF and the mobile BFF can call different services and store different data.

Why serverless for it? The usual reasons (no servers to patch, automatic scaling up and down, availability and security built into the managed services) plus one he stresses for BFFs specifically: pay per use makes a dev environment per developer and plenty of test environments cost a fraction of always-on infrastructure.

## The starting stack

The simplest BFF is API Gateway as the front door exposing a REST API, Lambda functions for the business logic and transformations, and a DynamoDB table holding the data this frontend needs. The missing piece is a set of event consumers that fill that table from the backend microservices.

## Three ways to get data from microservices

This is the most useful part of the talk, because it maps to what your downstream teams can actually offer:

- **Events.** If the microservices already publish events, route them through Amazon EventBridge, match the ones you care about with rules, and send them to a Lambda that transforms and stores them.
- **Webhooks.** If a team can send HTTP requests, give them a Lambda Function URL, a then-recent feature that exposes a function over HTTP directly, no API Gateway needed. Your function can enrich the payload with extra calls before writing it.
- **Polling.** If all they have is an API (REST, gRPC or a queue), use EventBridge Scheduler with a rate or cron expression to trigger a Lambda that queries them on a schedule.

All three land in the same DynamoDB table, so the frontend sees one API no matter how messy the backends are.

## What do you add before production?

Authentication through Amazon Cognito: the frontend shows the login form, gets a JWT, and API Gateway checks it on every call. Credentials for the downstream services go in AWS Secrets Manager, not hard-coded in a function. Observability comes from CloudWatch logs and metrics, which API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB emit by default, plus AWS X-Ray, which assigns a trace ID at API Gateway and follows the request through Lambda and DynamoDB so you can find the slow hop.

## Where Step Functions fit

For a BFF that has to orchestrate rather than just read a table, he brings in AWS Step Functions: a state machine with a visual editor, built-in parallel branches, timeouts and retries, and a direct integration with API Gateway. You can fan out to several APIs in parallel, aggregate the responses and return them synchronously, or accept the request asynchronously and answer right away.

His example is a travel booking saga: hotel, flight and car hire booked as one trip, with a compensating cancel step for each so a failure rolls back what already succeeded.

"If I can't book a car, probably I'm not interested in going to Grand Canyon," Roman Boiko said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

## Who should watch

Frontend and full-stack developers who own (or are about to own) the layer between their UI and a crowd of microservices, especially TypeScript teams on AWS. It is AWS-specific and stays at the architecture level. He closes with pointers to Serverless Land patterns, the Well-Architected serverless lens and a TypeScript Lambda sample repo, and notes the same approach works as a backend for micro frontends.

Title: Two hours a week for security? Then automate, but secure the pipeline too
Description: Joshua Arvin Lat (NuWorks Interactive Labs) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on the attacks Kubernetes, serverless and ML systems face, and what to automate
Body:
In most companies, security gets the hour or two left over after the build work is done. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Joshua Arvin Lat, CTO of NuWorks Interactive Labs, AWS Machine Learning Hero and author of *Machine Learning with Amazon SageMaker Cookbook*, argues that the only realistic answer is automation - but only after you know which attacks your particular system invites, and only if the automated pipeline itself is locked down.

The talk runs in three parts: why security gets squeezed, what attacks look like against Kubernetes, serverless and ML systems in the cloud, and which automation is worth building.

## Why does security always lose the priority fight?

He starts with an unflattering but familiar ranking. Business owners put short-term financial goals first, long-term goals and customer happiness next, and compliance and security last, on the theory that there's nothing to secure if there's no business. In his example, of a 40-hour week, maybe 35 to 38 hours go to building and one or two to everything else. Nobody prevents attacks in an hour a week.

His opening example is the ML engineer's nightmare. A team pulls a model from the internet and loads it with a library that will happily execute a payload embedded in the file. The payload opens a reverse shell to the attacker's machine, which then behaves like an SSH session into your server. The developer ignored the library's warnings because the deadline came first. Within an hour or so, he says, the whole cloud account can follow, because a reverse shell is only the first link in the attack chain: scanning, exploitation, privilege escalation, lateral movement, exfiltration.

## What attacks should you expect in the cloud?

His core point is that you should design security for your own system rather than copy another company's. The attacks differ by architecture:

- **Kubernetes on AWS.** The public-subnet instance is the obvious risk, but a badly configured cluster is the less obvious one. Teams adopt the shiny tool, put it on their CVs, skip hardening the production configuration, and get attacked a month or two later. Add ineffective logging and monitoring, sensitive data exposure, network misconfiguration, unsecured CI/CD and insecure secret storage.
- **Serverless.** The provider owns the servers, so security lives in your code: code injection, SQL injection (which developers new to serverless may assume is a solved problem), broken authentication from credentials shipped in the frontend, and denial of wallet, where an attacker who can't get code execution settles for making your Lambda run endlessly. His illustrative bill goes from $50 a month to $1 million.
- **Machine learning.** Even a well-secured inference endpoint can leak through crafted inputs: model inversion, model extraction, membership inference and attribute inference attacks against data and model privacy.

On secrets, he's blunt about received wisdom like putting everything in environment variables. "Best practices from an engineering end may not really be best practices, especially if proven wrong by real attacks," Lat said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022.

## Should you automate everything?

No - only where it makes sense. If something is repetitive and eats time you could spend on more important work, automate it, but do the arithmetic first: five engineers spending a month on automation have a cost in salaries and overheads that the automation has to repay.

Automated pipelines are where it usually pays off. His model pipeline runs dependency and code checks automatically after a push, then a manual approval step where a security engineer runs further checks, then deployment. Without it, teams deploy, run a vulnerability assessment afterwards, roll back, and spend one to two weeks remediating.

## Who secures the pipeline?

The catch is that the pipeline is now a target. He describes poisoned pipeline execution, where an attacker gets their commands run by the pipeline itself, for example through a poisoned configuration file pushed alongside the code. The defence is least privilege for every IAM entity, human or machine, so no cloud resource holds more permissions than it needs and a compromised one can't escalate.

From there the talk moves on to building your own tools where it's cheaper (an automated data integrity checker, automated vulnerability management and report generation), securing infrastructure as code, watching for privilege escalation and continuous security monitoring.

## Who should watch

Developers and DevOps engineers on AWS who own security by default and want a map of what can go wrong across Kubernetes, serverless and ML workloads. It's a broad survey rather than a hands-on tutorial, and the ML attack section is the part you're least likely to have heard before.

Title: 45 lines of Kubernetes YAML become 13 lines of TypeScript with cdk8s
Description: Robert Hoffman (AWS) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on writing Kubernetes manifests as real code with cdk8s and cdk8s+ instead of hand-copied YAML
Body:
A trivial echo server on Kubernetes (one Deployment, one Service, one Ingress) takes about 45 lines of YAML, and most of them are the same label, port and name typed three times. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Robert Hoffman, Senior Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, rebuilds that echo server with cdk8s, the Cloud Development Kit for Kubernetes, and then with cdk8s+, where it shrinks to about 13 lines of TypeScript that read like the sentence you'd say out loud.

"I know some engineers who swear that Yaml stands for yelling at my laptop," Robert Hoffman said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

## What's actually wrong with YAML?

His teardown of the echo server is the most useful five minutes for anyone who has debugged a Service that selects zero pods. The `app: echo` label has to match between the Deployment and the Service. The container port appears in the Deployment, again in the Service, and again in the Ingress. The Service name has to be typed identically in the Ingress. None of it is DRY, all of it is copy-paste, and a typo in any copy fails quietly.

He sums it up as: YAML is static (no real conditionals or variables), it promotes copy-paste, it is hard to customise and share because there's no native inputs and no YAML package manager, and Kubernetes itself adds a high cognitive load with all its dials and knobs.

## How does cdk8s work?

cdk8s is an open source framework (a CNCF sandbox project) where you model Kubernetes resources as classes in TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java or Go. The workflow:

1. Install the CLI with `npm install -g cdk8s-cli` (Homebrew works too).
2. `cdk8s init typescript-app` scaffolds a project; Go, Java and Python templates exist.
3. `cdk8s import` generates classes for the Kubernetes API version you target. Hand it a CRD file, his example is Jenkins, and you get typed classes for your operators' custom resources too.
4. Write the code, then `cdk8s synth` writes plain manifests to the `dist` folder.
5. Deploy them with `kubectl apply` or your GitOps pipeline.

The important design choice is step 4: the output is vanilla YAML with no runtime dependency on cdk8s, so linters, policy checks and GitOps controllers don't know or care how it was produced. You can also mix it with existing YAML in the same deploy.

Even the generated level-1 classes such as `KubeDeployment` help. Your IDE now offers autocompletion and inline docs for every property, the port becomes one variable, the labels are defined once, and the Service exposes a generated, collision-free name for the Ingress to reference. No more naming things by hand, the famous hard problem.

## Where cdk8s+ earns its keep

Constructs come in levels. L0 is the bare API object, L1 the auto-generated one-to-one classes, and L2 the handcrafted high-level APIs of cdk8s+. With the L2 Deployment you give it the image, the args and the port, then call the expose-via-ingress helper with a path and a prefix match. The Service, the Ingress, every label and every name reference are generated for you. That's the drop from 45 to 13 lines: roughly a factor of three less to write.

He ties it to Robert C. Martin's Clean Code: the code should tell a story a teammate (or you, a year later) understands at a glance. Here the story is literally create a deployment, expose it via ingress.

Because they're packages in your language's registry, constructs can be shared like any library. Constructs Hub (constructs.dev) collects community-published ones.

## When should you not use it?

He gives three honest reasons. You're happy with your current tools (though you can mix and match). You don't like coding, which is fair, because code means abstraction.

"Abstractions are nice when they work and you really hate them when they do not work," he said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

And you author Helm charts: cdk8s can deploy and use Helm charts as an end user, but it can't author their internals.

## Who should watch

TypeScript developers who got handed a Kubernetes cluster, and platform teams tired of reviewing copy-pasted manifests. It's an introduction with one worked example rather than a production migration story, and it comes from an AWS architect, though cdk8s itself works on any cluster, not just in the cloud.

Title: Two-person approval on AWS, built from nothing but IAM tags
Description: Yoav Yanilov (Axiom Security) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on control tags, a tag-based control plane that makes AWS ABAC scale and enforces two-person approval
Body:
Who in your organisation can delete a production RDS cluster? The honest answer is usually some admin role, and nobody is quite sure how well it's guarded. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Yoav Yanilov of Axiom Security presents control tags, a tag-based control plane on top of AWS IAM that he and Itamar Bareket (now CTO of MobiMatter) built at Similarweb. It fixes the integrity hole in tag-based access control, and then uses the same trick to require two admins for destructive actions.

## Why is ABAC on AWS broken?

The naive service control policy denies `rds:Delete*` unless the principal carries an admin tag. Fine, until you ask who can set that tag. Without extra logic, some privileged role will eventually find an indirect path - passing a role to a Lambda, say - to tag something as admin and walk around the guard.

So every SCP needs a second statement saying only admins can tag admins. Multiply that by tens or hundreds of SCPs and you have tedious, error-prone copy-paste. Yanilov's diagnosis is a missing separation of concerns: the access control logic (who can do what, given tags) is the data plane; the tagging integrity logic (who may set which tags) is a control plane, and it should be written once.

## What are control tags?

He borrows from Unix paths. If Alice owns `/home/alice`, she can write anywhere under it but not in `/home/bob` or `/system`. Translated to IAM: every principal playing the game gets a tag `swctl/v1/meta/grant_path` whose value is its grant area, and nobody can add or remove anything under `meta`. Control tags are simply tags that start with `swctl/`.

One control tags SCP then enforces two rules: you can't touch `swctl/` tags without a grant path, and any control tag you set or remove must sit inside your grant path (with a short allow list of legacy tags like team, role and environment, so Terraform and friends keep working). Attach it to the account or OU alongside your feature SCPs, and those feature SCPs shrink to pure access control. The RDS example becomes one statement requiring `swctl/v1/admin/rds_deleter`, which anyone granted that path or a parent of it can hold.

## How do you require a second admin?

Approvals are easy in GitHub, where a pull request is a multi-step process. In the cloud, "destroying an RDS cluster is one single API request, so it either succeeds or fails," Yanilov said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022. There's nowhere to hang an approve button.

The answer is a 2PA ticket: Alice tags Bob's role with `swctl/v1/admin/2pa/ticket` and a value of the form `by/alice/PAYLOAD/for/bob`. The live demo shows him failing to delete an S3 bucket, his co-presenter running an approval script, and the delete then succeeding. A 2PA SCP gives the ticket its guarantees:

- **Identity integrity.** Only principals tagged as identity brokers (your OIDC or SAML providers) may call `sts:SetSourceIdentity`, and source identities are sticky once set. No source identity, no 2PA tagging.
- **Anti-reflexive.** You can't issue a ticket for your own source identity.
- **Anti-forgery.** The by section must be your own identity, so CloudTrail always shows who approved whom.
- **Payload-bearing.** The payload carries a TTL. A Lambda runs every 30 minutes across the organisation and strips tickets that have expired or that claim to expire more than four hours ahead.

The data plane is then tiny: deny `s3:DeleteBucket`, `rds:DeleteDBInstance` and `rds:DeleteDBCluster` unless you hold a ticket issued for your own source identity. Pasting the same condition into the control tags SCP lets two collaborating admins step outside their grant paths, which also solves the chicken-and-egg problem of who grants the first grants.

## What are 2PA seals?

The second use case targets specific resources. A seal tag on a Secrets Manager secret lets an admin describe it but not reveal it or remove the seal without a ticket; he says that's how they store manual recovery keys. A `deny_trust_update` seal on an IAM role blocks changes to its trust policy without approval, which shuts down a whole class of privilege escalation.

Combine the two and you get the trust relay pattern: a super admin role that can only be assumed with a ticket and whose trust policy is sealed. Map it to `system:masters` in the EKS aws-auth ConfigMap, map the regular admin role to an ordinary group, and logging into the cluster as a cluster admin now takes two people. The same works for HashiCorp Vault.

He finishes with a cat-and-mouse walk-through of a compromised admin chasing a sensitive bucket: bucket policy, role assumption, trust policy edits, `kubectl` tricks and even a freshly created SAML provider all fail at a different layer. They've run it in production for more than two years with a team of more than ten admins.

## Who should watch

AWS platform and security engineers who already write SCPs and have felt the who-tags-the-taggers problem. If IAM condition keys are new to you, watch an IAM primer first; this one assumes fluency.

Title: A browser metaverse in Babylon.js, from hello-world sphere to live video
Description: Griffin Solot-Kehl (Dolby.io) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on building 3D worlds in the browser with Babylon.js, video textures and live streams
Body:
You don't need a game engine install or a beefy GPU to put people in a shared 3D space; a browser tab with WebGL will do. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Griffin Solot-Kehl, Developer Advocate at Dolby.io, builds up a browser-based metaverse in Babylon.js live in the playground: a lit sphere first, then imported models, animated characters, video on the walls, and finally a sub-second live stream mapped onto a 3D surface.

It is a demo-heavy beginner's tour of Babylon.js, with the last third showing where Dolby.io's streaming and spatial audio plug in.

## What is Babylon.js, and who uses it?

A JavaScript library for 3D rendering on HTML5 and WebGL, backed by Microsoft. Games are the obvious use, but he lists education, blockchain and data visualisation too. The showcase includes a Minecraft recreation, Temple Run, a 3D Space Invaders, a Google Earth-style globe and a virtual art gallery, which is the bit that starts to smell like a metaverse. If it runs HTML5 and WebGL, it runs Babylon.js.

## How does a scene come together?

Everything lives in one `createScene` function, and the playground walkthrough is a good 10-minute primer:

- **Scene** from the engine, with nothing in it yet.
- **Camera**: a `FreeCamera` placed with a `Vector3`. Calling `attachControl` hands it to the mouse, keyboard or a game controller, so you stop editing coordinates and re-running.
- **Light**: a `HemisphericLight`, the usual stand-in for the sun, with an intensity that defaults to 1.
- **Meshes** from `MeshBuilder`: a sphere whose segment count trades smoothness for rendering cost (32 looks round, 2 looks like a rock), a box, a ground plane.

"Lights are very important because without lights, you won't be able to see anything," Griffin Solot-Kehl said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022. Anyone who has stared at a black WebGL canvas for an hour knows he's not joking.

From there he moves to real assets: `ImportMesh` loads a model an artist built in a tool like Maya (his demo is a detailed skull from the community gallery), so nobody has to assemble a face from boxes. The inspector gives you a scene tree, materials and textures, plus screenshot, video, GIF and export tools. Saving a playground gives it a shareable hash URL, which is how the Babylon.js community trades examples.

## Does it do VR?

Yes, out of the box. Playground scenes can be viewed on a Google Cardboard, and WebXR (the replacement for WebVR) covers Oculus, Valve Index and HTC Vive headsets. He shows a car scene with a VR goggles button and flags that its `createDefaultVRExperience` call is the older API: check the docs for the current way.

## Making it move: render loops and video textures

Animation runs through `scene.onBeforeRenderObservable`, a loop inside the render function that reacts to input. His demo character idles, walks and turns from the keyboard and dances on a key press, all without a manual re-render. The slide's practical warning: remember to add a stop command.

Video works the way HTML5 video does, except the output is a texture. `BABYLON.VideoTexture` puts a clip on a plane, a box or someone's head, with play and pause wired to GUI buttons in the scene. In his VS Code walkthrough he scales the 16:9 frame down so it doesn't cost too much to render, and uses the double-side option so the video shows on both faces of the plane.

## Live streams as textures

"I don't think it would be that much of a metaverse if we only had pre recorded videos," he said.

This is the Dolby.io part. Swap the texture's source from a local file to a Dolby.io stream URL (free API credentials, a token for auth) and the same `VideoTexture` code shows a live broadcast; he starts his own camera stream from the dashboard and it appears inside the scene. The pitch is latency: a DJ greeting a virtual crowd reaches them in milliseconds rather than the seconds traditional streaming takes, which matters for concerts, lectures, live sports and auctions. Spatial audio goes one step further: feed object positions from Babylon.js into Dolby's communications SDK and each voice comes from where that avatar stands. He points to odyssey.stream as a customer example.

## Who should watch

Web developers who have never touched 3D and want a gentle, code-on-screen start, and anyone building virtual events who wants to see live video inside a WebGL scene. It's an intro, and the streaming section shows the speaker's employer's product, so evaluate that part alongside alternatives. His self-paced workshop repo is linked at the end.

Title: No security team? Four controls and the tools you already pay for
Description: Roman Zhukov (Intel) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on how a DevOps team without security staff can cover SAST, SCA, secrets and vulnerability scans
Body:
A full secure development lifecycle has a long list of controls, and a small company with no security staff will implement none of them if it tries to do all of them. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Roman Zhukov, Product Security Manager at Intel, offers the short version: four controls - static analysis, software composition analysis, roles and secrets, and vulnerability scanning - plus two bonuses, mostly using features already built into GitHub or GitLab and free open source tools.

His abstract pitches this as cheap automation that addresses 80% of the security concerns in a development pipeline. He speaks for himself, not Intel, and says up front there's no marketing in it.

## Is security really the thing slowing you down?

He opens by knocking down five myths R&D teams hold about security: that security people and their tools are aliens, that it's security versus features, that yet another vulnerability won't get exploited, that security has no clear metrics, and that it's boring. His counter is that security done inside DevOps speeds delivery up.

The example everyone remembers is Log4Shell. Without DevSecOps, by his slides: three days of inventory just to learn whether you're affected, a week for an out-of-cycle release including approvals, tests and scans, and the bonus surprise of third-party dependencies nobody had updated in years. With continuous security in place, stored scan logs and a known component list, inventory takes a day and the out-of-cycle release two or three.

He also cites Veracode's State of Software Security report from February 2022 for the most common bug classes, which have barely changed in decades: buffer overflow and underflow, error and input handling, crypto implementation, and web classics like CRLF injection, XSS and SQL injection.

## Which four controls first?

A heavyweight SDL is right for big companies; he points to Intel's own SDL and its 2021 white paper on software supply chain threats. A popular industry diagram counts 17 DevSecOps controls. For everyone else, he picks four: SAST, SCA, roles and secrets, and vulnerability scanning.

His first rule: "don't try to buy and to implement a lot of security tools," Zhukov said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022. Look at what your development platform already does. On GitHub that means CodeQL for static analysis, Dependabot (and Renovate) for dependencies, built-in secret scanning, role management, and the security overview, much of it free for open source projects. GitLab has its own equivalents. Turning these on costs small teams almost nothing.

## What if you need more than the built-ins?

His free and open source list, with the caveat that free plans vary by language and use case:

- **Static analysis:** SonarQube (free plan), Bandit for Python, RIPS for PHP, Semgrep for C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python and Ruby. He prefers tools built for your specific language - one size doesn't fit all.
- **SCA:** Snyk and Debricked (free plans), OWASP Dependency-Check and Dependency-Track, and Intel's open sourced CVE Binary Tool for binaries, an area he says lacks good tools.
- **Secrets:** GitGuardian (free plan), Gitleaks, Whispers, detect-secrets, and Vault for secrets management.
- **Vulnerability scanning:** OpenVAS, Nmap with extensions, ThreatMapper, Nuclei and OWASP ZAP.

The point of the list is that these tools are developer-centric, easy to automate in a pipeline, and don't need deep security expertise to run.

## The two bonuses

**Containers and Kubernetes.** Pick base images responsibly (scratch, distroless or busybox), verify them with Docker Bench, Clair or OpenSCAP, and check Cosign or Docker Content Trust signatures. Follow Docker's security guidance and the OWASP cheat sheet, lint with Hadolint, Dockle, Trivy or KubeLinter, run rootless and avoid privileged containers. Make sure secrets are really gone from YAML, image layers, Helm charts, environment variables and even release notes. At runtime, apply the Kubernetes, OpenShift, Rancher or NSA/CISA hardening guides, plus a service mesh, OPA, Calico, Falco and Kube-bench.

**Trusted artifacts.** SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) asks you to keep provenance: metadata on how, when and by whom each artifact was built. He argues SLSA level 2 is not a big deal for most teams, since it needs version control, a scripted build on a build service, and authenticated, service-generated provenance. SLSA GitHub Actions automate the provenance, in-toto handles attestation and Cosign signs and verifies.

## Who should watch

DevOps engineers and engineering leads at small and mid-sized companies who've been handed security with no security hire. It's a curated checklist with links, not a deep technical talk, and that's exactly what makes it useful as a starting point.

Title: Your users' browsers can run the SQL your server keeps doing
Description: Gaurab Patra and Bhagyajit Jagdev (Techweirdo Consultancy) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on in-memory SQL analytics in the browser with AlaSQL
Body:
Every laptop that opens your dashboard has more compute than it needs to render a table, and most apps still ship every filter and GROUP BY back to the server. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Gaurab Patra, Co-Founder of Techweirdo Consultancy, and Bhagyajit Jagdev, SDE III there, make the case for pushing that work to the client with AlaSQL, an open source in-memory SQL database that runs in the browser and in Node.js.

It is a short, focused introduction. The speakers say up front that they won't compare AlaSQL with other browser SQL libraries; this is about one tool and the use cases where it fits.

## Why analyse data on the client at all?

Gaurab Patra frames it with the edge: data is increasingly produced outside the data centre, on phones, laptops, watches, consoles and home appliances, and anything that runs JavaScript can process some of it.

"It will not be cloud versus edge, it will be cloud with edge," Gaurab Patra said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

The other argument is about sharing analysis. When an analysis is written in JavaScript, the person you send it to isn't looking at a static chart; they are running it live, and can query the data, tweak assumptions and ask their own questions in the browser.

## What AlaSQL actually is

The library was written by Andrey Gershun, with the first commit in October 2014, originally to bring NoSQL-style capabilities to browsers when few engines offered them. Later milestones added foreign keys and unique, not-null and check constraints, and TypeScript syntax support in version 0.4.0.

The feature list that matters here:

- Plain SQL against JSON arrays, relational tables and nested JSON, plus schemaless and graph data.
- Import, export and direct queries over Excel (xls and xlsx), CSV, JSON, TAB, IndexedDB, localStorage and SQLite files.
- User-defined JavaScript functions inside queries, for the cases standard SQL can't express.
- A real engine underneath: statements are parsed into an abstract syntax tree, compiled, WHERE expressions are pre-filtered for joins, joined tables are pre-indexed, and indexes are hash tables stored in a plain JavaScript object.

## Where does it fit, and where doesn't it?

The fitment list is honest: use it when you don't need persistent storage or permanent results, when query speed matters, and when you want joins, filtering and grouping in memory. The typical pattern is to hit the server-side database once for an initial filter, bring the slice back, and run every subsequent sort, search and aggregation locally. Processing a local file, pre-processing large data at the edge, lightweight ETL and BI-style fat clients all qualify.

Bhagyajit Jagdev's demo loads a local file and runs a duplicate search plus count, sum and average. Those are easy in plain JavaScript, he points out; joins across two files are where SQL starts paying for itself. He also shows the two directions of the trade: crunch data on the client before sending a smaller result to the server, or ship a dataset down once and stop round-tripping every time the user changes a filter.

The limitations are the ones you would guess, and it's good that they are said out loud. Pulling a large dataset from server to browser takes time, and that wait is the app's problem. Joins across three or four uploaded files slow down as the record count grows. And joining a subselect doesn't work.

## Who should watch

Front-end and full-stack developers building reporting screens, admin tools or multi-tenant dashboards where every user wants a slightly different cut of the same data. It is an intro to one library, light on benchmarks, so treat it as a map of what AlaSQL can do rather than a performance study.

Title: Your CI/CD server is a gold mine, so stop leaving it on the network
Description: Mike Guthrie (NetFoundry) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on making CI/CD, monitoring and data tools dark with zero-trust networking and OpenZiti
Body:
The security audit covers the production app; the CI/CD server that can deploy code anywhere usually isn't in scope. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Mike Guthrie, Senior DevOps Engineer at NetFoundry, argues that DevOps tooling is the softest and richest target in most infrastructure, and shows how his team took theirs dark - no ingress at all - using the open source zero-trust networking platform OpenZiti.

Full disclosure, which he gives himself: NetFoundry develops OpenZiti, and his team was asked to dogfood it. He describes himself as a skeptical DevOps engineer, not a salesperson, and the most interesting part of the talk is what the migration was actually like.

## Why are DevOps tools the target?

"Pretty much every single tool that we use is an absolute gold mine for an attacker," Guthrie said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022. His list is uncomfortable reading:

- **CI/CD** is an automated code injection system that builds and executes code in every critical place.
- **Monitoring** is a data mining platform with an inventory of everything important, often with remote execution.
- **ETL** is a pile of loosely hacked-together scripts with access to every business-critical data source, feeding a **data warehouse** that lumps it all in one place.
- **Config management** is root access to everything, which makes it the ideal place to plant a crypto miner or a rootkit.
- **Developer access** tends to be all or nothing, because nobody wants friction when production is down.

His gut check: would you turn a pen tester loose on your monitoring or CI/CD system? Most people pass audits by narrowing the scope to the public-facing app. He points out that real breaches have come in through monitoring updates and CI/CD systems precisely because they reach everywhere.

## What does making it dark mean?

His definition of zero trust is the useful kind: assume the network is already compromised, including everything inside the castle walls. Peered VPCs don't count, since compromising one side compromises the other. VPNs that expose a whole private network don't count either.

In OpenZiti there are no IPs and ports to manage, only services and identities. Every laptop, phone, server or application is an identity; everything dials out to a fabric mesh, and nothing can talk until a service policy (an AppWAN, in NetFoundry's terms) says so. Policies work on tags: identities tagged `#datawarehouse` can reach services tagged `#datawarehouse`, much like Active Directory groups but at the network layer. Firewalls and security groups are set to no ingress.

## Good, better, best

He lays out three levels of darkness:

- **Good: network access.** A tunneller or edge router in each data center, no ingress, no peering. Identities reach only the specific services they're granted, which he calls a VPN on steroids that is easier to manage. It solves the classic headache of granting acquired companies or contractors access to one thing without exposing the whole data center.
- **Better: host access.** The tunneller runs on the host itself (a systemd service on Linux, an agent on Windows, a sidecar for containers) and services terminate on localhost, so traffic is never unencrypted off the box. Works for SSH, web access and the rest.
- **Best: application embedded.** Using the Ziti SDK, each application is itself an identity, giving end-to-end encryption from one app to another with no open ports anywhere. This is what NetFoundry considers true zero trust.

## What happened when they switched?

NetFoundry moved its data warehouse and ETL runners, CI/CD system, SSH (dark bastions, a bastion with no open ports), company chat (they replaced Slack with Mattermost, reachable only over Ziti), Grafana, and developer support access via sidecars.

He expected breakage. Instead, because identities and policies could be set up and verified before going dark, they watched traffic shift onto the overlay and knew users had migrated before closing the doors. Switchover day for the data warehouse was a non-event. By the third migration, his slides say, they were moving users without telling them. New tools now start dark from day one; Grafana was spun up that way with minimal effort. With fake DNS names for intercepts, outsiders can't even resolve the services. The bonus: no more red tape for punching holes in firewalls, and audits are easy when the firewall rule is no ingress, full stop.

## Who should watch

DevOps and platform engineers who own CI/CD, monitoring and bastions and suspect they're over-exposed. It's a product-led talk about OpenZiti, but the threat model for DevOps tooling and the good/better/best ladder apply whatever overlay you choose.

Title: Serverless means you test in the cloud, not on your laptop
Description: Gareth McCumskey (Serverless) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on why serverless teams should develop in the cloud, write less code and ship continuously
Body:
Everyone knows the brochure version of serverless: no servers to patch, pay per use, autoscaling for free. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Gareth McCumskey, Developer Advocate and Customer Success Engineer at Serverless Inc. (the makers of the Serverless Framework), skips quickly past those and spends his time on the benefits you only notice after years of building with Lambda: you stop pretending your laptop is production, bad code hurts less, and you write a lot less of it.

He has been building serverless apps since 2016, and the talk reads like the lessons of a team that has shipped a lot of them, for themselves and for customers.

## What does he mean by serverless?

Not lifting your Express monolith and dropping it into a Lambda. His definition is architectural: break the application up so that cloud services do the work your code used to do. On AWS that means S3 and CloudFront for the static front end, API Gateway receiving HTTP requests and routing them with no web server or routing code of yours, Lambda running the handlers, and DynamoDB as the fully managed data store. Cloud native, in the sense that the app is built around the services rather than merely hosted on them.

A framework ties it together. His example is a short Serverless Framework config that, with one `serverless deploy`, creates the API Gateway endpoint, uploads the handler, and wires up the IAM policies. Anyone on the team can deploy the same file into their own AWS account. You could click it all together in the console, he concedes, but then you can't share it or debug it sensibly.

## Why stop emulating the cloud locally?

This is the sharpest part of the talk. The classic flow (build locally, bundle a release every two weeks, toss it over the wall, watch it break in production) comes from the gap between two environments. Serverless makes that gap wider, because cloud services are hard to run on a laptop, and he treats that as a feature rather than a problem.

"So a better development model is to push the changes to the cloud and rather test there," Gareth McCumskey said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

What you can't reproduce locally is the list that bites: IAM permissions between services, the latency between services (IAM adds some of its own), concurrency, API validation. His loop is `serverless deploy function` to push a single function in seconds, then invoke it or curl it, tail the logs in the cloud, and repeat. Your dev stage differs from production only in configuration.

## Is bad code really less dangerous on Lambda?

His argument: on a shared server, one user hitting a terrible loop eats CPU for every other user on that box, and autoscaling just spreads the pain across more swamped machines. Each Lambda runs in its own tightly constrained Firecracker micro-VM, has a timeout even if you never set one, and is ephemeral, so a slow execution doesn't linger for weeks. He cites research showing noisy-neighbour effects on Lambda are barely detectable.

He is careful not to say optimisation is dead, only that it stops being the thing that eats your sprint.

"I've never met a single MD of a company that is going to be happy to hear that you need to spend two to four weeks on optimizing code," he said.

## Less code, fewer bugs

The single largest cause of platform failures, in his view, is code written by developers. Serverless lets you delete whole categories of it: API Gateway handles paths, CORS and responses; DynamoDB tables are designed around your query patterns instead of hand-written SQL; S3 replaces the scary file-system code. And the Serverless Framework adds no code of its own to what ships, it only packages and configures.

"When you have a bug, it's usually not the framework that you installed three weeks ago, it's the chunk of code that was released last week," Gareth McCumskey said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

## Continuous delivery falls out of it

Because the infrastructure is part of the service, a schema change or a new endpoint isn't a ticket for another team and a maintenance window. Deploy is a command (or a merge to GitHub that a CI/CD tool turns into that command), and small microservices keep each deploy's blast radius small. Big-bang releases built up over two to four weeks go away.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers who have used Lambda a bit and still develop against a pile of local emulators, and leads trying to explain to a team why serverless is more than a billing model. It is a concepts talk with AWS examples, not a coding session, and it comes from the framework vendor, so read the framework parts with that in mind.

Title: How HMRC's paved road lets a small AppSec team cover 1,000 microservices
Description: Ben Conrad (HMRC) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on how an opinionated tax platform makes central AppSec possible across 1,000+ microservices
Body:
A central AppSec team can't review 1,000 microservices one by one, unless they are all built the same way. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Ben Conrad, Head of Product for HMRC's Multi-channel Digital Tax Platform (MDTP), and Gerald Benischke, the AppSec lead who calls himself the platform's "appsec snooper", explain how the UK tax authority's opinionated platform turns application security from an impossible audit into a set of searchable, platform-wide tools.

The talk's conclusion fits on one line from their final slide: the paved road helps, tooling helps, experienced engineers help.

## What is MDTP?

MDTP is HMRC's platform as a service, running for eight to ten years and hosting nearly all of its customer-facing digital services. Infrastructure, logging, metrics, alerting, CI/CD, testing and prototyping templates come out of the box, and nearly all of it is self-service. The catch: services must be written in Scala with the Play framework.

It runs on AWS, but developers never get AWS credentials. "They are writing services to run on MDTP," Conrad said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, which is why HMRC could in principle move the whole platform to another cloud without services changing, and has done a move like that before.

The stakes are real. The services process data for around 45 million UK taxpayers and about 5 million companies, and handle payments of hundreds of billions of pounds a year. The threat list on their slide runs from rogue engineers (whose credentials can be stolen) and script kiddies (a constant stream of requests that seem convinced HMRC is a WordPress site) through fraudsters and hackers to nation states.

## How big is the problem?

Over 1,000 microservices, around 200 created in the year of the talk, roughly 340 of them frontends, which, they joke, speaks to how inventive the country is at coming up with new taxes. The abstract puts it at about 100 teams and around 1,500 deployments a month. Their slides add 36 million lines changed in 12 months, by 640 authors, across 1,187 repositories.

They're clear that change volume is not the security problem. A change freeze would make the platform more vulnerable, not less, since many deployments are upgrades away from known-vulnerable versions. The approach is trust, but verify.

## What does the tooling look like?

Because everything is Scala and Play, the team can search for problems across hundreds of services at once. The tools they show:

- **Bobby rules** fail any build that uses a dependency the platform has banned. It's a blunt instrument, so they announce deprecations ahead of time. It doubles as a way to enforce platform upgrades.
- **Leak detection** watches GitHub commits (HMRC codes in the open, per the GDS standards) and alerts both the service team and the security team on Slack when something looks like a secret.
- **The catalogue**, an in-house, mostly auto-generated inventory of every service, with a **dependency explorer** that searches the dependencies of all services. When Log4Shell landed over Christmas 2021, they knew in about ten minutes that no service used the vulnerable log4j-core library.
- **A risk ledger**, which started as plain spreadsheets listing where risky code could live: which services parse XML, generate files, store data, call third parties. Remembering that for 20 microservices is possible; for 1,000 you need a list.

## Why don't they trust CVSS scores?

This is the part every vulnerability-management team should hear. JFrog Xray had the data but the reports were unreadable at that volume. So AppSec went through each flagged CVE by hand, in spreadsheets, and found that CVSS was not a predictor of risk: some of the worst issues didn't have the worst scores, and some of the scariest-looking ones weren't an issue on the platform at all. Their plea is not to write policies that wave through anything scored below eight. From those spreadsheets came an MVP in under a month that lets service teams see their own vulnerabilities, with the AppSec team's assessment attached.

## Where should security specialists sit?

They borrow from Team Topologies: service teams are stream-aligned, AppSec is an enabling team. One expert per team is unaffordable across 100 teams and wastes time on the same issues; a central team becomes a bottleneck and lacks context. The paved road is what makes the middle ground work, since one team can turn over stones across a uniform stack, then find the owning team's Slack channel in the catalogue and talk to them without blame. The same platform built some Covid services in about four weeks.

Their advice for starting an AppSec team: collect threat intelligence first. Find out which services write files or talk to a sensitive backend, make a list, use a spreadsheet, then automate it.

## Who should watch

Platform teams and security leads in large organisations, especially public sector, wondering how to scale AppSec without hiring a security engineer per team. It's light on code and heavy on organisational design that actually shipped.

Title: Validating a hex colour at compile time, and other TypeScript type tricks
Description: Serhii Bilyk (catchts.com) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on type-level TypeScript patterns, from inference priority to compile-time hex validation
Body:
TypeScript can reject `#GGG` as a colour before your code ever runs, if you're willing to write the types for it. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, [Serhii Bilyk](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Serhii_Bilyk_safer_typescript), who writes about advanced TypeScript on his blog catchts.com, worked through a series of type-level patterns that make APIs safer: underused inference tricks, key filtering, a cast-free `includes` for tuples, and recursive types that build number ranges and validate strings.

Fair warning: this is an advanced talk, delivered at speed in the TypeScript playground. If generics with conditional types make your eyes water, start with something gentler. If you answer TypeScript questions on Stack Overflow for fun, this is your evening.

## Two tricks the docs don't explain

First, `Lowercase<string>`. Applied to the general `string` type it used to do nothing, but since TypeScript 4.8 it works as a constraint: a variable typed that way errors if you assign an uppercase string.

Second, inference priority. Take select props with a generic value that must be one of the options. Pass options red and yellow with a value of green and TypeScript happily infers all three. Intersect the value's type with an empty object and its inference priority drops, so TypeScript infers the options first and then rejects green. The same `T & {}` intersection also means non-nullable, and TypeScript itself redefined the built-in `NonNullable` utility that way. Bilyk points to a Stack Overflow answer and a post on his blog for the why.

## Accept only the keys whose values are strings

A common question: a function should take an object and only those property names whose values are strings. He builds it from two popular utilities, `Values` (a union of all values) and a filter that keeps keys whose value extends a given type. The detail that makes it work is an intersection telling the compiler that the object's value at that key really is a string, so inside the function you get string methods like `charAt` and `includes`, and with a number filter, `toFixed` and `toLocaleString`.

## Why does includes fail on readonly tuples?

Someone asks once a week, he says. Instead of an `as` assertion, he curries it: a `withTuple` function captures the tuple with a rest parameter for inference and returns a type guard. After the check, the string narrows to the tuple's members.

## Interfaces aren't a matter of taste

His most opinionated point: "using interfaces in typescript is more safer than using types," Serhii Bilyk said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022. Use `type` for aliases and utilities, `interface` for object shapes. The reason is index signatures. A function taking `Record<string, unknown>` may mutate whatever it's given. An object typed with a `type` alias passes straight in and can be mutated, by you or by the colleague who joins a year later and likes mutation. An interface isn't indexed by default, so TypeScript rejects the call. He's seen this cause runtime errors and production bugs.

## Recursion: ranges, coordinates and a hex validator

Tail-recursion optimisation in recent TypeScript versions lets a recursive type build a range of numbers up to around 1,000, where older versions gave up after a few dozen. The pattern: keep an accumulator tuple and stop when its length matches the target.

The same idea handles repeated patterns that template literal types can't express directly, such as coordinate strings with comma-separated pairs joined by semicolons. He generates a union of valid lengths, two numbers, four, six, never odd counts.

The finale is a hex colour map validator. Build the allowed characters from a 0-9 range wrapped in template literals plus `a` to `f` in both cases, compute a string's length with a recursive type, then check each character. Each validator returns the string itself or `never`, so intersecting them reads like a sentence: the result is the string if every check passed, `never` otherwise. Add a hash prefix, infer the object through a helper function that just returns its argument, and an invalid hex value becomes a compile error.

## Who should watch

Library authors and developers who design typed APIs and want concrete patterns, not theory. His blog has longer write-ups of each one.

Title: Exclude, customise, create - taming IaC scanner noise with KICS
Description: Gabriel Manor-Liechtman (Jit.io) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on cutting IaC scanner noise by customising and writing your own KICS queries in Rego
Body:
An IaC scanner with 1,600 built-in checks will find problems on its first run. It will also flag things your organisation does on purpose, and that noise is what makes developers stop reading the findings. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Gabriel Manor-Liechtman, Technical Leader at Jit.io, shows how to fix that with KICS, the open source IaC scanner from Checkmarx: exclude the checks you don't need, customise the ones you only half need, and write your own Rego queries for the rules nobody else knows about.

The whole talk is told through Breaking Bad. Gus Fring runs his laundromat and chicken empire as code, and his problems are your problems with better production values.

## What does KICS actually catch?

Gus's first incident traces back to one character: an asterisk in the actions of an IAM policy in his Terraform. KICS flags exactly that. "You should never put wildcard in the actions portion," Manor-Liechtman said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022.

KICS runs as a GitHub Action, locally, or in any CI system as a Docker image and one command. It ships more than 1,600 security and misconfiguration tests across Ansible, Azure Resource Manager, CloudFormation, Dockerfile, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, OpenAPI, Google Deployment Manager, gRPC and Terraform. He shares the most common findings in Jit's metrics, led by missing global security definitions in OpenAPI v2, EC2 instances with public IPs, Azure instances using basic authentication and Kubernetes containers with privilege escalation allowed.

## When do you exclude a check, and when do you rewrite it?

That fourth one is Gus's next problem. The privilege escalation check is correct in general, but some of his containers legitimately need different treatment. Excluding the query entirely is the easy fix, and he regrets it, because now nothing checks privilege escalation at all.

The better move is to customise. Every KICS query is two files: `metadata.json` (query name, ID, severity, category, description and a docs URL) and `query.rego`, the policy itself. KICS is built on Open Policy Agent, which treats any config as a JSON tree and evaluates Rego rules against it; KICS supplies libraries that convert YAML, Terraform, Pulumi and others into that tree first. The built-in privilege escalation rule walks the Kubernetes document, iterates over the containers, and returns a result when `allowPrivilegeEscalation` is true. A returned result is a failure; no result is a pass.

His custom version adds one condition: only fail when the container name starts with a given prefix (in the story, the Regalo trucks). Copy the original query from the KICS repo, edit it, mount it over the original path in the KICS container, and the scanner uses your version. The same pattern works for, say, allowing a few named S3 buckets to be public while still catching the rest.

## How do you write a query from scratch?

For Gus's new head of security, Mike, every API endpoint must carry a specific inspection header, which no built-in check knows about. Manor-Liechtman's advice is to treat a new query like a unit test: before writing any Rego, list every configuration that could be harmful (no headers, headers without the right one, the right one with the wrong schema).

The KICS repo has a template query to start from, including a test folder for positive and negative cases: an OpenAPI path with no header that should produce a finding, and one with the header that shouldn't. You fill in the metadata, generating the ID with the KICS CLI, and pick the platform. His first policy checks that the document is OpenAPI 3, collects every path, and returns a missing-attribute result for any endpoint without a `parameters` key. KICS also ships test tooling you can run with `go run` instead of a full scan.

To ship custom queries, copy your assets folder over the KICS image's own assets in a Dockerfile, or have a CI pre-step clone your queries repository and mount it at runtime. Your queries override the built-ins with the same path and add the new ones.

## Gus's protocol

The closing rule is one line: exclude, customise, create. Find what developers complain about and exclude what you don't need; customise what's almost right so developers know exactly what to fix; then create the rules specific to your organisation. He points out the same three moves apply to almost every security automation tool, not only KICS.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevSecOps engineers running IaC scanning who are drowning in findings, and anyone curious how OPA and Rego work in practice. You'll get the most from it if you've seen a Terraform plan and a Kubernetes manifest; Breaking Bad knowledge is optional but rewarded.
