Title: TypeScript's red squiggles, no build step: the JSDoc route in four stages
Description: Austin Gil (Akamai Technologies) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on adopting TypeScript type checking incrementally in plain JavaScript with JSDoc
Body:
You can get most of what TypeScript gives you without writing a line of TypeScript or adding a build step. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, [Austin Gil](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Austin_Gil_jsdocs_typescript), Senior Developer Advocate at Akamai Technologies, laid out the path he follows on his own projects: JSDoc comments in plain JavaScript, checked by the TypeScript engine, adopted one file at a time and ending in CI checks and published type definitions.

It's aimed at people who haven't tried TypeScript, tried it and didn't like it, or are curious. If you already love TypeScript, Gil says up front that this may not be for you. His dog Nugget appears throughout, partly, he admits, to win the dog more Instagram followers.

## What's wrong with just using TypeScript?

Nothing, mostly. Gil likes what strong types bring: red squiggles for typos and type mismatches, safer refactors, IntelliSense that teaches you an API, faster onboarding, CI that blocks type errors from reaching production, easier maintenance of code you haven't touched in six months, and generated docs.

What he doesn't like is the tooling. JavaScript runs anywhere you paste it, in the browser, on the server, on embedded devices, even in space for NASA. TypeScript needs a transpilation step, has a learning curve for junior developers who likely know JavaScript better, and adds noise to the code. So he takes the best of both.

## Stage one: check a single file

The starting point is VS Code, which already runs the TypeScript language engine behind IntelliSense. That engine won't flag passing the number 2 to a `yell` function that expects a string, until you add a `// @ts-check` comment at the top of the file. Then the red squiggles appear, including for reassigning a string property to a number.

JSDoc tells the checker what you meant. A `@type` comment above a variable can allow a string or a number; a function doc block with `@param` and `@returns` makes `yell` reject numbers. It's all comments, so the code still runs anywhere. For complex objects, `@typedef` defines a type, such as a dog with a string breed, numeric age and optional name, and types can be imported from other files or from a `.d.ts` file.

## Stage two: check the whole project

Adding the comment to every file gets tedious. You can tick the implicit-project-config check-JS setting in VS Code for yourself, or, his preference for teams, add a `tsconfig.json` with `checkJs` set to true in the compiler options.

## Stage three: fail the pipeline on type errors

This is where you first need to install anything. A CI runner has no TypeScript engine, so you add the `typescript` package as a dev dependency, a `ts` script in `package.json`, and in `tsconfig.json` the files to check plus `allowJs` and `noEmit`, since there's no TypeScript to compile into JavaScript. Running the script reports each error by file, line and column, and as a required pipeline step it stops a type error before deploy.

## Stage four: ship types for your library

For library authors, flip `noEmit` off and turn on `declaration` and `emitDeclarationOnly`, with an output folder for the definitions, then point the `types` field in `package.json` at that folder. Consumers get types; you never wrote TypeScript.

## Do you have to choose?

No, and that's his main point. "I like this approach because you can do it incrementally and you don't have to rewrite your whole code base all at once," Austin Gil said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022. You can mix the two and move to TypeScript syntax later. He finds JSDoc better for describing objects and methods, while TypeScript is far better at typecasting, and the TypeScript team won't support every JSDoc feature. He's had no trouble on large JavaScript projects either way, though neither catches every bug, and both can eat hours that add nothing for the user. He writes the process up on his blog as TypeScript the easy way.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers and library authors who want type safety without a compile step, and team leads looking for a low-friction way to introduce types.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [TypeScript's Strict Compiler Options](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Daniel_Danielecki_TypeScripts_Strict_Compiler) by Daniel Danielecki at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.
- [How typescript improves Developer Experience](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Kacper_Szewczyk_31_typescript_developerexperience_improvement) by Kacper Szewczyk at Conf42 JavaScript 2024.

Title: A DevSecOps program where the dashboards do the arguing
Description: Evan Gertis (Inner Growth Training & Services) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on building a DevSecOps program on scans, reports and weekly security reviews
Body:
Most security programs fail in the meeting, not the scanner. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Evan Gertis, founder and CEO of Inner Growth Training & Services, describes how he took a mid-sized organisation from no security program to automated scanning, weekly security reviews and a SIEM, and his thesis is that reports, not arguments, are what move developers and managers.

His refrain, repeated at the end of nearly every section: "Real leaders show they don't tell," Gertis said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022.

Fair warning on scope: the title promises a zero-trust pipeline, and zero trust gets a brief demo at the very end, where the pipeline is taken off the public internet behind a zero-trust client. The bulk of the talk is the program around it, delivered with a lot of motivational-speaker energy (you will be asked to clap and pound your chest).

## What are the five takeaways?

He opens with them, which is helpful:

1. Automated scanning removes manual labour.
2. Application security reviews increase accountability, but they need a security champion.
3. Vulnerability reports land better when backed by easy-to-read metrics, here from Veracode dashboards and JFrog Xray reports.
4. Penetration tests fill the gaps automated scanning misses.
5. Pen test results need systematic logging behind them.

His framing of the problem is the human one: "The weakest element in any process is the human," he says, so the process has to give people structure and a reason to own their fixes.

## Which tools did the pipeline use?

The stack is commercial and specific:

- **Veracode** for SAST, DAST, software composition analysis and container scanning, with a fix button that shows developers how to remediate each finding. One line in a bash script kicks off container scanning; at the end of his demo, 19 microservices were being monitored.
- **Burp Suite** for a manual pen-testing workflow that targets what SAST and DAST miss: proxy for reconnaissance, scanner for crawling and scoping, repeater for modified requests, intruder for automated attacks. He demonstrates SQL injection, repeatedly.
- **JFrog Xray** with Artifactory and a Jenkins pipeline: configure build info, publish it to Artifactory, scan, and stop vulnerable builds before production. Reports download as PDFs for the people who need them.
- **Elastic as a SIEM**, fed by CloudTrail and the Filebeat AWS module, with ALB access logs in S3, all deployed with Terraform. Compliance follows the free CIS Foundations Benchmark, which he recommends as a first project for a new security engineer building a program from scratch.

The logging closes a loop he likes: the SQL injection he pops with Burp shows up in the SIEM dashboards, so the pen test report has evidence behind it.

## What did the numbers look like?

He shows before-and-after figures from the organisation. A repository with over 254 Jackson Databind vulnerabilities had cleared them, and the others alongside them, after six months of the program. The organisation's Veracode score went from 58 to 94. One dashboard showed 1,675 vulnerabilities remaining with over 1,547 closed, and all the high-severity ones removed. The end state, in his telling, was a Veracode level three certification with automated remediation and full SIEM monitoring.

## How do the weekly reviews work?

This is the part worth stealing regardless of tooling. Application security reviews run weekly over Teams, Zoom or Hangouts, are recorded, and have minutes distributed before and after. Everyone reads the previous minutes and comes ready to answer the questions they own; there are five questions every member answers, drawn from leadership research he offers to share. Remediation work goes into a ticketing system automatically, so tickets carry enough detail for a developer to fix the issue without another meeting. His advice for the review itself: show the scan results and say nothing, and let the silence do the work.

## Who should watch

Security engineers asked to stand up a program from nothing at a mid-sized company, who want a concrete tool list and a meeting cadence to copy. If you came for zero-trust network architecture, this isn't that talk, and if motivational asides grate, keep a finger near the skip button.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Tanya Janca on [adding DAST to CI/CD](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Tanya_Janca_dast_cicd) without slowing the pipeline down.
- Jon Peck on [securing the software factory](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Jon_Peck_securing_software_factory).

Title: Write a Svelte compiler in 40 minutes, and finally get what compile means
Description: Li Hau Tan (Shopee) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on building a tiny Svelte compiler live, from parser to analysis to generated JavaScript
Body:
Everyone says Svelte is a compiler. Few people could write one. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, [Li Hau Tan](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Li_Hau_Tan_svelte), a Svelte maintainer and engineer at Shopee in Singapore, live-coded a stripped-down Svelte compiler that turns a counter component into plain DOM instructions, and showed why the analysis step is what makes the output small.

It's in the spirit of build-your-own-React: no slides about Svelte's API, just a parser, an analyser and a code generator written in one sitting. If you have ever nodded along when someone says Svelte compiles the framework away, without knowing what that means, this fixes it.

## Why compile a UI framework at all?

Tan's path is a familiar one. jQuery let him find elements and change them by hand, which got messy as apps grew. React let him describe the view as a function of data and diff virtual DOM snapshots, but because React can't know in advance which elements or handlers you'll use, its runtime has to prepare for everything. For a small app the library can outweigh your code.

Svelte's pitch is to write declarative components but get the lean, direct DOM code you'd have written with jQuery. The component he compiles is the classic counter: a script block with a `counter` variable and increment and decrement functions, two buttons with click handlers, and a div showing the count.

## What does a compiler actually do?

"It takes your code, parse it, analyze it, and finally generate an output," Li Hau Tan said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022. Parsing produces an abstract syntax tree (abstract because it keeps meaning, not semicolons). Analysis walks the tree to find which variables are declared, used and changed. Generation uses the tree and the analysis to write optimised JavaScript.

Before writing any of it, he designs the output: a function returning an object with `create`, `update` and `destroy` methods. Create builds elements with `createElement` and `createTextNode`, attaches listeners and appends to the target; destroy removes listeners and children. Update takes the list of changed variables and refreshes only the text nodes that depend on them.

## How do you parse a template into a tree?

You start with a grammar. He shows Backus-Naur form on JSON first (an object is braces around a property list, a property list is a property or a property list plus a comma and a property), then writes one for his mini Svelte: fragments made of scripts, elements, expressions or text; elements with tag names, attribute lists and child fragments.

The parser is a pointer `i` into the source string and three helpers: `match` checks what's at `i`, `eat` matches and advances or throws a syntax error, and `readWhileMatching` consumes characters against a regex and returns them. Then there's one function per grammar rule, recursion doing the rest. JavaScript inside script tags and curly braces goes to Acorn, because nobody is writing a JS parser on stage.

## How does it know what changes?

Variable names aren't enough: a local `let counter` inside a function shadows the top-level one. Scopes are subtrees of the AST, and he uses the periscopic library to map scope-creating nodes to their scopes, then estree-walker to traverse depth-first, tracking the current scope on enter and leave. An `UpdateExpression` whose variable resolves to the root scope is a change. A second walk over the template marks variables used in attributes or expressions.

## Where does the small output come from?

Code generation pushes strings into create, update and destroy arrays per node type: elements, text, `on:click` attributes (strip the first three characters for the event name), and expressions, which become text nodes plus an update instruction only if the variable changes. For the script, he rewrites the AST to insert a `lifecycle.update(['counter'])` call after each change, but only for variables the template uses, then prints it back with escodegen.

The payoff demo: modify only a local variable and the update call disappears and the update method is empty. Remove the counter from the template and the code stops calling update at all, even though the variable still changes. That's the Svelte idea in miniature: generate only the code the component needs.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers who use Svelte, Solid or any compiled framework and want to understand the machinery, and anyone curious about writing a parser. He continues the series, including reactive declarations and server-side rendering, in a Build your own Svelte playlist on his YouTube channel.

Title: Publish the container images that fail your scans (with a different key)
Description: Adrian Gonzalez (Microsoft) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on securing containers across four phases, from Dockerfile to registry, CI pipeline and production
Body:
Container security isn't one scanner in one pipeline step; it lives in four places, and most teams only cover one or two. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Adrian Gonzalez, Principal Software Engineering Lead at Microsoft, walks through all four - building images, securing the registry, the CI pipeline and production - with the Dockerfiles, Docker commands and Azure DevOps tasks he actually uses.

His closing advice frames the whole thing. "Decisions are all about ratios between convenience and security," Gonzalez said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, and his rule is to start weighted towards security, because shifting towards convenience later is cheaper than recovering from a breach.

## What goes into a secure image?

Four habits for the Dockerfile:

- **Stay current.** Recent OS and container tooling versions, installed the boring way: remove old versions, add the GPG key, set up the repository, pin the Docker Engine and Compose versions you want.
- **Run as a non-root user.** Create the user and group, switch to root only for the steps that need it (his Golang example installs dependencies as root), then switch back before the image is done. A few non-root users with sudo is acceptable, but keep them few and segmented.
- **Pull from trusted registries**, on-prem or in a public cloud such as Azure, AWS, Google or JFrog Artifactory.
- **Keep it lean with multi-stage builds.** His Node example builds with Yarn and all its npm packages, then copies only the build output into an `nginx:alpine` image. Fewer dependencies, fewer CVEs.

## How do you lock down the registry?

A private registry, he points out, is just a registry with stronger network policy around it: firewalls, source IP ranges, port policies. Security partly by nobody knowing it exists. On top of that, sign images with Docker Content Trust (`docker trust key generate`, add the signer, `docker trust sign`), so consumers get a chain of custody and know who to call when an image turns out to be bad.

Access control is where he gets granular. In Azure Container Registry an account is an ID plus roles, and a role is permissions on an asset. The least privileged key can only pull one image; a contributor key covers a couple of repositories; the most dangerous key is anything scoped to the whole registry, even if it can only pull.

## What does the pipeline actually do?

His CI agents get the same treatment: a pull-only key for most pipelines, a contributor plus image signer key for pipelines that push (so consumers know which pipeline produced an image), and an owner key that only a DevSecOps automation provisioning new repositories should ever hold.

The pipeline itself has four steps on every container code change:

1. **Build** with `docker build`.
2. **Test** the container like code, with tox driving pytest and the testinfra package: files exist, environment variables and ports are right, the process user is correct. He catches his own sample test asserting the user *is* root and suggests asserting it is not.
3. **Scan** with Trivy, twice: once that passes on low and medium findings, once that fails the build on anything high or critical. He also lists Aqua, the Dependency-Check plugin for SonarQube and WhiteSource as alternatives.
4. **Version and publish.**

## Why publish images that failed?

This is the least obvious idea in the talk. In his experience "it's worthwhile to publish even the images that failed previous tests" - tagged with a failed suffix, pushed by a separate key into a separate repository - so the people fixing them can pull the exact broken image and troubleshoot it. Passing images get a specific version (semver or the CI build ID) plus `latest`. He's wary of `latest`: it's convenient, which is exactly why a vulnerability pushed there reaches far more consumers than one pushed to a pinned version.

## What about production?

Three controls: network segmentation down to individual containers (he calls it nano-segmentation), resource quotas because a container has no CPU or memory limits by default and a hijacked one can starve its neighbours, and continuous monitoring. For the last he uses Microsoft Defender for Containers, which covers environment hardening, ongoing vulnerability assessment (new CVEs keep appearing for images that passed CI months ago) and runtime threat protection mapped to the ATT&CK for Containers matrix.

His team-level takeaways: make everyone aware of the practices, use RBAC so nobody can switch off pipeline control gates in a hurry, and hold each other accountable.

## Who should watch

Developers and DevOps engineers shipping Docker images, especially on Azure. The pipeline examples are Azure DevOps and Azure Container Registry, but the Docker, Trivy and testinfra parts transfer anywhere. A solid end-to-end checklist rather than an exhaustive treatment of any one phase.

Title: You don't need Python to ship an ML feature, just a place to run the model
Description: Joshua Arvin Lat (NuWorks Interactive Labs) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on running ML inference from JavaScript in the browser, on mobile and in the cloud
Body:
A team of five JavaScript developers asked to add machine learning doesn't have to stop and learn Python first. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, [Joshua Arvin Lat](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Joshua_Arvin_Lat_mlpowered_applications), CTO of NuWorks Interactive Labs, AWS Machine Learning Hero and author of Machine Learning with Amazon SageMaker Cookbook and Machine Learning Engineering on AWS, mapped out where a JavaScript team can train and run models: in the browser, on the phone, and in the cloud, and what each choice costs.

It's an architecture-level overview, not a coding session. If you want to know which option fits your app before you open the docs, this is the right half hour.

## Can you even build ML apps in JavaScript?

His answer is yes, because the libraries and tools exist. He starts with a gentle introduction for front-end developers: the cat versus not-cat classifier you can't hard-code, a model trained on 100,000 images, a 90% evaluation score meaning roughly nine right answers out of ten. He's quick to add that the real process is circular, because a deployed model can degrade within two weeks to a month and needs refreshing.

Then the case for JavaScript: the team already uses it heavily and its pipelines are built around it, nobody has to learn a new language, and you get one thing Python can't easily give you, inference in the browser.

## What do you gain by running the model in the browser?

In server-side inference, the browser sends the image to a server holding the model and gets back a one or a zero. In browser inference, the model loads with the page and predictions happen on the client. Lat lists the wins: it works offline once loaded, latency improves without a round trip, no inference servers are needed, and user data never leaves the device, which helps with privacy. TensorFlow.js and ONNX Runtime Web are his examples, and they sit next to React, Vue or Angular like any other library.

The catch is model security: once the model is in the browser, anyone can download it. And size matters. If the page takes five minutes to load because the model is huge, the model belongs on the server.

Mobile is the same trade. With on-device machine learning, say React Native with TensorFlow.js, inference happens inside the app with the same benefits: offline, private, faster, serverless.

## When does the cloud win?

When the data and models get big. A resource-hungry algorithm on a large dataset struggles on a small machine, while the cloud lets you choose the size and type of resources. His favourite example is hyperparameter optimisation: 100 training configurations at one hour each is 100 hours in sequence, or maybe one to 1.5 hours run in parallel.

SageMaker, the AWS platform he wrote a book on, has an SDK for JavaScript, not only Python, because the heavy lifting happens inside the service and the SDK just calls the API. Deploying a trained model to a real-time or serverless endpoint takes a few lines of configuration and, by his estimate, 30 minutes to an hour, against three to five days for building your own inference server with Express. For lighter cases, a Lambda function in JavaScript can load the model and serve predictions behind API Gateway, with container image support for more complex setups, or process streaming records one at a time, or sit behind a GraphQL API.

## How do you choose?

Start from business requirements, including security, before the cool technical solution. Everything is a function of time, so a team already fluent in Python or R shouldn't switch to JavaScript just because it can. "Choosing the right solution starts first by knowing what's possible," Joshua Arvin Lat said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

His three common patterns: train and deploy on the server; train on the server and run inference in the browser (keeping the model small); or train on the server and ship the model to the phone for on-device inference. Training in the browser or on the device is the exception, worth it when the user's confidential data can't be sent to a central server. If all you have is a hammer, everything becomes a nail.

## Who should watch

JavaScript and Node.js teams handed their first ML feature, and architects deciding where inference should run. Data scientists will find the ML parts basic.

Title: Your SRE stack already has a place for security scans
Description: Anais Urlichs (Aqua Security) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on wiring Trivy scans into the Prometheus and Grafana stack SRE teams already run
Body:
SRE teams obsess over what a healthy service looks like and rarely ask whether it's a secure one. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Anais Urlichs, Developer Advocate at Aqua Security and a CNCF ambassador, argues the two questions are the same question, and walks through ten steps for putting open source security scanning into the observability stack an SRE team already has.

Her one takeaway, in her words: "only secure services are healthy services," Urlichs said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022.

## Where were the security tools?

The talk starts from her own SRE stint at a startup running tenant clusters inside superclusters across regions such as Frankfurt, New York and London. The observability stack was textbook: Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger, Grafana Loki for logs, Helm and Terraform for management, GitLab CI/CD. The team gave a KubeCon North America 2021 talk about its operators and observability. What nobody talked about was security tooling; at one point an intern set up kube-bench, and that was about it.

So she lines up SRE goals against security goals. Scaling services means keeping them secure as replicas come and go. Visibility into what's deployed, where and by whom is also security posture. Reducing log noise maps onto reducing vulnerability fatigue. Runbooks for incidents can just as well define who does what when a critical CVE lands.

## Ten steps, one scanner

Her worked example uses Trivy, Aqua's all-in-one open source scanner (she stresses that everything she shows is free on GitHub, no sign-up). Trivy covers git repositories and filesystems, container images, Dockerfiles, IaC, Kubernetes manifests, SBOMs, AWS accounts and in-cluster scanning.

The steps, roughly:

1. **Understand your need.** Team size, industry and regulation, tech stack, company goals, budget and expertise all shape which tools fit. She borrows four needs from a Wise Engineering blog post: assign ownership of vulnerabilities, get a global view of the security state, build dashboards per audience, and stop making people learn yet another UI.
2. **Choose a scanner.** Tools differ in installation (CLI vs Kubernetes operator), scan coverage, integrations and audience. Be wary of anything that gets broad privileges inside your cluster and sends the results elsewhere.
3. **Set it up properly.** She runs the Trivy Operator via Helm in its own namespace plus CLI scans in CI/CD, and tests edge cases in a small environment first.
4. **Build a dashboard.** The operator writes its findings as Kubernetes custom resources - vulnerability, exposed secret, RBAC and config audit reports - which you can read as YAML and export as Prometheus metrics. Her community Grafana dashboard showed 175 vulnerabilities in the demo cluster.

Steps five to ten cover triage, alerting, correlating metrics, ownership, tuning and going beyond scanning.

## How do you avoid vulnerability hell?

175 findings is already more than anyone will read. She cites Alex Jones tweeting a scan with over 550 vulnerabilities, of which only three were critical. Her strategies: ignore everything but criticals at first, don't scan everything at once, filter to vulnerabilities that have a fix available (one Trivy flag), and split findings by team and application so each one has context and an owner. Ideally the person who already manages a resource owns its vulnerabilities.

## Why do vulnerabilities need alerts?

This is the sharpest point in the talk. You have to define deployment resources, or the app doesn't run and customers complain. Nobody has to define security scanning for the app to work; customers only notice security when their data leaks. That asymmetry is why she wants you to "make your vulnerabilities scream at you": alerts you can't ignore, then correlation between the vulnerability dashboard and the deployment dashboard, so a jump in criticals points straight at the new ReplicaSet that caused it.

Her final steps are cultural: don't roll out lots of new tools at once, reuse existing workflows and platforms, accept that the setup will differ for every team, and don't stop at scanning. Tracee, Aqua's runtime security and forensics tool, catches someone exploiting a misconfiguration rather than just the misconfiguration itself.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers on Kubernetes who own Prometheus and Grafana and have been told security is now also their job. It's a practical, opinionated playbook built around one vendor's open source tools, so expect Trivy specifics rather than a tool comparison.

Title: One React editor, four homes: Red Hat's multiplying architecture
Description: Saravana Balaji Srinivasan (Red Hat) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on running the same micro-frontends in VS Code, browser and GitHub extensions and the web
Body:
Red Hat's business automation editors have to run as a VS Code extension, a Chrome or Firefox extension, a GitHub extension and a plain web app, all from the same components. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, [Saravana Balaji Srinivasan](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Saravana_Balaji_Srinivasan_platform_freedom_microfrontends), Software Engineer at Red Hat, explained the framework his team built on top of micro-frontends to make that work, which they call the multiplying architecture, and the webpack feature that fixed its last big problem.

The talk is partly a micro-frontends primer and partly a case study from migrating jBPM, Red Hat's legacy business automation product, to a stack that can keep up with future technology.

## Why those four platforms?

The components are developer tooling: editors such as the DMN editor, which shows business rules graphically, and the BPMN editor. Developers live in VS Code, the browser and GitHub, so that's where the editors had to go. The requirements were multiple distributions with minimal code changes, plus a bridge to future tech stacks, so a team on React today could move to Vue later.

## How do you split a front end?

Srinivasan compares three strategies. A modular monolith breaks the front end into smaller UIs that share libraries but stay tightly coupled in one app. An integrated application splits them into separate apps composed at build time. Micro-frontends split the UI into separate applications composed at runtime, in the sense of Cam Jackson's definition: independently deliverable front-end applications composed into a greater whole.

He's practical about granularity. In the DMN editor the header is small, so whether it deserves its own micro-frontend is a team decision; an e-commerce header with profile, search and nested dropdowns clearly does. He also covers the backend-for-frontend pattern (BFF, as he notes, not best friends forever): each micro-frontend talks only to its own BFF, which translates backend responses, and micro-frontends talk to each other only through the container app shell.

## Runtime or build-time integration?

Runtime integration loads a deployed bundle like `c.js` into the container when needed: teams deploy whenever they like, but the setup is more complex. Build-time integration ships components as npm packages: easy to set up, but every change or new dependency means rebuilding the whole application.

Then there's styling, where one micro-frontend's CSS can override another's. Iframes isolate them, but he doesn't want to go back there. "I feel that nobody will prefer to use iframes," Saravana Balaji Srinivasan said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022.

## What is the multiplying architecture?

The answer is abstraction, which he ties to Ralph Johnson's line that architecture is about the important stuff. The framework has four parts:

- **Channel**: the platform, such as the VS Code extension, browser extension, GitHub extension or online web app.
- **View**: the React web components.
- **Envelope**: the layer between channel and view that passes data both ways.
- **Editor**: the tool itself, for example the BPMN or DMN editor.

The envelope renders components in a div rather than an iframe and isolates their context, so teams stay autonomous with their own release cycles, and the whole thing is TypeScript, so it's type safe. In the code walkthrough from the kie-tools examples, each micro-frontend has an API folder with abstract methods the channel exposes to the envelope and the other way round, an embedded component that kicks off the view, and an envelope folder holding the React view. The same to-do list micro-frontend then runs inside a VS Code extension and in a web app that lists the other examples (a ping-pong demo and a base64-to-PNG converter).

## What broke when it all came together?

Duplicated libraries. Three micro-frontends each depending on React meant three copies of React in the container, and a bundle that kept growing. The fix was Module Federation, added in webpack 5: the `ModuleFederationPlugin` declares the remotes for each micro-frontend and shares dependencies like React across them, which also gives runtime integration. On the React side, lazy imports load each micro-frontend only when its route is visited.

With that in place, the team got multiple distributions with minimal code changes, runtime integration, autonomous teams, no duplicate libraries, and the bridge to future stacks they wanted.

## Who should watch

Front-end architects weighing micro-frontends, and anyone who needs one UI to ship as a web app and as editor or browser extensions. The examples are in the kie-tools repository under kiegroup on GitHub.

Title: Most of your DAST scan doesn't belong in the release pipeline
Description: Tanya Janca (We Hack Purple) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022 on adding DAST to CI/CD by scanning only what matters there and running the rest elsewhere
Body:
The fastest way to lose friends on a DevOps team is to drop a full dynamic scan into their release pipeline. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2022, Tanya Janca, founder and CEO of We Hack Purple and author of *Alice and Bob Learn Application Security*, explains how to add DAST to CI/CD anyway: keep the pipeline scan small, fast and accurate, and move everything thorough and slow to places nobody is waiting on.

It's a short, practical talk, and refreshingly honest about the trade-offs. Janca works for a DAST vendor and says plainly that one tool is not enough.

## How slow is too slow?

She opens with her own war story. On the OWASP DevSlop open source project she added a dynamic scanner to the pipeline of an app that did almost nothing, and the build went to nine minutes. Her collaborator pointed out it used to take one minute. "So you added 900%," as she retells it, and that was with the scan rushed. As the app grew, so did the wait.

The lesson she took: if security wants to be allowed to run tests in a DevOps pipeline, security has to follow DevOps rules. That means accuracy (no flood of false positives), speed and automation. Her DevSecOps additions are testing from multiple angles, good relationships between security and the people who build software, and fixing bugs as early in the SDLC as possible.

## Why start with DAST at all?

Her argument for DAST as the first tool is about attackers, not tooling. A dynamic scanner pokes a running app with requests and reports what breaks, and anyone can learn to point one at your site in under an hour. Most apps on the internet have no CDN, WAF or RASP in front of them. So the bugs a DAST finds are the ones a bored stranger finds, and she'd fix those first, ahead of bugs that need a copy of the source code or weeks of effort to exploit.

## Three ways to make the pipeline scan fast

Checking every box and clicking go is fine when you're playing with the tool by hand. In a pipeline it's how you get uninvited from coffee. Instead:

- **Refine the scope with a HAR file.** Record an HTTP archive of the feature you're shipping this sprint and feed it to the scanner, which then tests only that. If QA already records Selenium sessions, reuse them.
- **Only test what worries you.** Every AppSec team has a short list of findings that must never reach production. Test for those in the release pipeline; everything else goes to a pipeline nobody waits on, or an overnight run.
- **Uncheck the tech you don't use.** A Ruby app on MongoDB doesn't need WordPress, SQL Server or Java tests. She estimates that alone buys maybe 10 or 15% - small, but every bit of speed helps.

## The rest of the scanning happens off the critical path

The talk's most useful reframe: "you don't have to put everything in a CI CD to be doing DevOps," Janca said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022. Scheduled scans of 100% of your apps every Sunday give you a pile of reports on Monday to triage into backlogs. One-off manual scans cover cases like due diligence: she once ran a quick assessment of a company a client was about to buy, and the findings fed into renegotiating the price. Pen testers bring 20 or 30 tools and a lot of manual work, none of which you can automate into a pipeline.

She maps it onto the SDLC: security regression tests alongside unit tests, scans against the dev server or localhost, a full-blast scan or manual pen test during testing, a tuned scan in the pipeline for every release, and scheduled weekly scans in production. Running the slow, thorough stuff outside the pipeline, she argues, is more respectful of DevOps processes, not less.

## One tool is never enough

DAST is where she starts, not where she stops. She runs through the rest of the toolbox: SAST for the code your team wrote, software composition analysis for the libraries you didn't (including newer tools that check whether a known vulnerability is actually reachable), IAST from inside the running app, and secret scanners for the API keys someone committed on a Friday.

## Who should watch

Security engineers about to ask a DevOps team for pipeline time, and DevOps engineers who've been handed a scanner and a deadline. It's an approachable 101 on where DAST fits, with concrete tuning tips rather than product demos. Pentesters won't learn much new.

Title: Nine drawing algorithms, one canvas, and a lot of Math.random()
Description: Michael Wehar (Swarthmore College) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on nine JavaScript algorithms that draw generative artwork on an HTML canvas
Body:
A spiral is a few lines of code away from a straight line: grow the radius, raise the transparency, swap the increment for a trig function. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, [Michael Wehar](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Michael_Wehar_algorithmically_generated_visual_designs), Visiting Assistant Professor at Swarthmore College, presented a research project with John Mancini, Maya Newman-Toker and Alyssa Zhang: nine JavaScript algorithms that generate visual designs, and an open-source framework you can use to write your own.

It's a short, friendly talk, more creative-coding workshop than conference keynote, and it ends with a live tutorial that turns a dot into a spiral.

## What were they trying to find out?

The team wanted to bring artists and computer scientists together to understand drawing processes, and to see how far programming goes as a tool for making art. Their open questions were plain ones. "What kinds of designs and artworks can algorithms generate?" Michael Wehar said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022. Can they be appealing? And can the drawing process get better from user feedback?

## What do the nine algorithms draw?

Each one is a procedural process that draws lines and basic shapes onto a digital canvas, inspired by mathematical concepts, natural phenomena or artistic trends. The set: Wrapping Paper, Vines and 70's Funk by Alyssa Zhang; Geometric Patterns, Overlapping Tiles and Trees by Michael Wehar; Spiderwebs and Fractals by Maya Newman-Toker; and a Game of Life by John Mancini and Wehar.

Every algorithm takes a list of parameters, and the demo shows why that matters: the same Geometric Patterns code with different parameters produces a different picture. Wrapping Paper overlaps shapes systematically until the result looks like, well, wrapping paper. According to the abstract, they used the algorithms to build a dataset of over 1,000 generated artworks for reviewers to compare and rate, to find which parameter choices people respond to.

## How does the framework work?

The drawing program runs an algorithm on an HTML canvas and shows the image forming in real time. An algorithm is an object with a fixed set of methods: initialize, start, pause, reset and draw one step. The front end calls draw one step on a timer and the picture grows.

The repo, under the Algorithmically-Generated-Artwork organisation on GitHub, has a detailed README and pairs of algorithm and params files. Newcomers should start with the dots example.

## From a dot to a spiral, live

The tutorial is the best part, because it shows how little code a design needs. Wehar starts with the dots algorithm and tweaks its params: transparency to one turns every circle black, radius 50 fills the canvas, a larger speed value adds a delay in milliseconds so you can watch it draw.

Then he edits the algorithm. Track the brush position starting at the centre of the canvas and increment it: a line. Wrap around at the edges: a line that keeps going. Add `Math.random()` noise: a jittery line, and with a bigger x step, stripes. Move x by ten each step and y by ten times the cosine of an angle that cycles from zero to two pi as steps go by: overlapping waves. Finally, grow the circle radius and transparency each step, stop wrapping, change the increment functions, and the canvas draws a spiral.

## Who should watch

Developers who want a gentle way into generative art, teachers looking for a canvas project for students, and anyone who'd like to contribute an algorithm or a pull request to an open-source drawing framework. The team was also looking for reviewers to rate generated images.

Title: He rebuilt Node's URL parser in Rust, then in JavaScript. C++ still won
Description: Yagiz Nizipli at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on building a spec-compliant URL parser for Node.js in Rust/WebAssembly, then JavaScript, and what the benchmarks said
Body:
Every request your Node.js server handles goes through a URL parser, and in 2022 the one in Node was slow enough that its maintainers opened an issue about it. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, [Yagiz Nizipli](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Yagiz_Nizipli_performant_url_parser), Node.js core collaborator and member of its performance team, told the story of trying to beat it twice: first in Rust compiled to WebAssembly, then in plain JavaScript. Both lost to the native C++ version, and the reasons are the useful part.

It's a rare honest benchmark talk. Nizipli doesn't hide the losing numbers, and the micro-optimisations he found along the way apply well beyond URLs.

## Why does a URL parser matter so much?

"URL parsers are the most important functionality for a web server," Yagiz Nizipli said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022. Walk through an OAuth flow and every arrow between user agent, client and authorisation server carries a URL that something has to parse. That makes the parser the baseline cost of every network request.

It's also the part nobody wants to touch, because it's complex and bug-prone. Nizipli found that an IPv4 address with more than four parts was handled differently in Node than in Chrome and Safari, and filed issues about Node's URL implementation not matching the specification. Those were later fixed.

## Isn't it just a regex?

No. The WHATWG URL specification defines a state machine with around 20 states: scheme start, no scheme, special authority, relative, file paths that behave differently on Windows and Unix, fragments. He reads a couple aloud, and the no-scheme state alone brings in opaque paths and base URLs. Special schemes imply default ports (80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS), so the parser has to know which is which.

## Why didn't Rust plus WebAssembly win?

The issue that started it, opened by James Snell of Node's technical steering committee, suggested a big speed-up from porting the parser to WebAssembly. The precedent looked good: undici, Node's HTTP client, compiled llhttp to WebAssembly and saw a 1,329% boost. Nizipli chose Rust, partly because it's fast and partly, he admits, because he wanted to learn it.

The catch is the boundary. WebAssembly talks to JavaScript through shared memory, so strings must be encoded from UTF-16 to UTF-8 and back, and Node's `TextEncoder` and `TextDecoder` are themselves implemented in C++. The whole point was to remove the C++ bridge, and the bridge came back through text encoding. In his rough benchmark, the Rust version was slower than native for the URL constructor and 86% slower for `URLSearchParams.set()`, because every getter and setter crosses the boundary.

## How fast can pure JavaScript get?

His second attempt became the url-state-machine npm package, a spec-compliant URL state machine in JavaScript. It came out about five to six times faster than the whatwg-url library, and still well behind Node's native implementation. The optimisations that got it there are the talk's best takeaways:

- **Functions over classes.** Up to Node 18, a class with private fields was 55% slower than the equivalent function and prototype.
- **Switch versus if.** With more than ten branches, `switch` was faster; with fewer, `if` won. Benchmark it, because V8 changes.
- **Numbers, not strings, for states.** Comparing strings means checking length and every character; switching states to numeric constants gave a large speed-up.
- **`slice` over `substring`**, which was faster for computing the fragment.
- **Check for `undefined`** instead of the spec's code point helpers, which means drifting from the spec's wording, with the risk of Unicode edge cases that are hard to track.
- **Memoise.** Set a special-scheme flag once when the scheme changes, instead of looking it up in an object every time.

## What were the final numbers?

Around 2,000 lines of code, more than 800 benchmarks, 99.9% spec compliance (the one failing test involves UTF-8 and UTF-16 encoding), and 733 web platform tests passing. Those tests covered only 96% of his code, which he argues is a gap in the web platform tests themselves. The work was his graduation thesis, and he thanks Matteo Collina and James Snell from Node.js.

His conclusion: until V8 improves for these operations, JavaScript can't match the native C++ parser.

## Who should watch

Node.js developers who care about hot-path performance, and anyone about to propose rewriting something in WebAssembly for speed without measuring the boundary cost first.

Title: Real awk in the browser, and no server doing the work
Description: Robert Aboukhalil (Chan Zuckerberg Initiative) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on compiling C command-line tools to WebAssembly for sandbox.bio
Body:
The terminal in a sandbox.bio tutorial isn't a simulation. When you pipe `awk` into `head`, the real tools run, compiled from C to WebAssembly, inside your browser, with no server doing the computation. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, [Robert Aboukhalil](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Robert_Aboukhalil_interactive_commandline_tutorials_webassembly), Senior Software Engineer at the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, explained how he built it, and spent just as much time on when WebAssembly is the wrong tool.

Sandbox.bio hosts interactive command-line tutorials aimed mostly at bioinformaticians, with general ones on `awk` and `jq` too: instructions on the left, a live terminal on the right.

## What is WebAssembly, practically?

Aboukhalil's framing is refreshingly flat: it's another language the browser runs, next to HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Nobody writes it by hand. It's a compilation target, best supported today from C, C++ and Rust. He gives three reasons it has mattered: reusing existing desktop and command-line code without a rewrite, replacing slow JavaScript computation with faster code in some cases, and portability to any runtime, from Cloudflare and Fastly at the edge to Node and Deno.

## How do you get a C tool into the browser?

For C and C++ his pick is Emscripten. He walks through a bioinformatics tool written in C. Normally you'd build it with GCC; with Emscripten you swap in `emcc`, a wrapper around the compiler, and output a `.js` file instead of a binary, which gets you both the `.wasm` module and JavaScript glue that initialises it, calls functions and handles the file system.

The other flags barely change. Instead of linking zlib with `-lz`, you ask Emscripten for its port with `-s USE_ZLIB=1` and skip compiling zlib yourself; libpng and SDL work the same way. Since command-line tools expect files, Emscripten provides an in-memory virtual file system: you mount a user's local file onto it and hand the path to the tool as usual. Calling the tool becomes `Module.callMain()` with an array of arguments, and Emscripten converts those strings into what the module understands, because WebAssembly only deals in numbers. There are wrappers for the rest of the build too: `em++`, `emar`, `emmake`, `emcmake`, `emconfigure`.

He's honest that his example is the easy case. Threads, SIMD beyond 128 bits, inline assembly and sockets all make compiling harder, sometimes impractical.

## What does the app around it look like?

Xterm.js draws the terminal. Aboukhalil parses each command line into an abstract syntax tree to handle pipes, substitutions and variables, then walks it: call `awk`'s main with its arguments, feed the output into the `head` module. A background process saves the virtual file system's state to IndexedDB, so edits to a tutorial file survive a page refresh.

## Why not run the commands on a server?

Without WebAssembly, every command goes to a server that has to spin workers up and down to run arbitrary user input, and track every user's file state. With it, the server only serves static assets, which can sit behind a CDN. His list of wins: much cheaper, easy to scale to millions of users, safer because untrusted commands run inside the browser's sandbox, more responsive, and simpler state. The costs: tutorials use small subsets of large datasets, and every tool must compile to WebAssembly, which he calls the biggest drawback.

## When shouldn't you use it?

Three warnings. Too little computation (a Rust front-end UI compiled to WebAssembly adds complexity and overhead with no speed-up) or too much (two dozen CPUs and 50 GB of RAM) both miss the sweet spot of audio and video processing, games, simulations and playgrounds. Second, if someone already compiled the tool, use their library, such as sql.js or Pyodide. Third, don't try to swap your Nginx, Postgres and Flask containers for wasm binaries. "I think most people in the field agree that webassembly will not replace containers," Robert Aboukhalil said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022. Outside the browser, he sees it fitting two jobs: safely running user-provided code, and edge computing, where its fast start-up beats a container.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers curious about WebAssembly who want a concrete Emscripten workflow and an honest list of limits. He covers the topic in depth in his book Level up with WebAssembly, and his open-source biowasm library has more examples of compiling complex tools.

Title: Your paying customers deserve the static page too
Description: Eric Burel (LBKE - Vulcan) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on segmented rendering, static pages for personalised content via a tiny rewrite server
Body:
Most sites serve anonymous visitors a fast, prerendered page and logged-in, paying customers a slower one rendered per request. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, [Eric Burel](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Eric_Burel_segmented_rendering), founder of LBKE in Montpellier and maintainer of Vulcan.js, named that the rich guest, poor customer problem and showed the fix he calls segmented rendering: one URL per segment plus a small rewrite server, so personalised pages can be static too.

He also teaches Next.js at Human Coders and is part of Devographics, the collective behind the State of JS surveys, and it shows: the talk is half rendering theory, half a working Next.js demo you can clone.

## What counts as personalisation?

Anything that adapts the site to who the user is, usually known from a cookie. His running example is a theme picker with three starter themes (fire, water, grass), but the same shape covers language, paid versus free content, and A/B test buckets. Each is a cookie whose value puts the user into a segment that many other users share.

## Why do customers get the slow page?

Burel lays out the rendering triforce in Next.js: client-side rendering, per-request server-side rendering, and static site generation. The first two are dynamic, so they can read the request and adapt, but they cost a computation per request or per interaction. Static generation is fast because the HTML already exists, and that's exactly why it can't adapt: by the time the request arrives, the page is done.

So teams use static renders for public pages and dynamic ones for personalised content. Personalised content is for the people who log in, pay and hand over their data, and they get the worse performance. Hence rich guest, poor customer.

## Why not just put the segment in the URL?

The first try is the familiar `/fr/` pattern: put the theme in a route parameter and prerender each variant. Fine for languages, broken for the rest. Users can edit the URL to reach paid content. They can see their A/B bucket, which ruins the test. And with several parameters the URL turns into a path like `/fr/dark/my-company/a/my-article`.

The second try adds a proxy server that reads the cookie and rewrites the URL on the server side. A rewrite, he stresses, not a redirect: the user never sees the parameter, can't alter it, and the server can compute it from a session token. That's the whole pattern. If 3 million users pick the fire theme, there's one render for all of them.

## What does it look like in Next.js?

Next.js middleware plays the proxy, running at the edge and written in JavaScript rather than Nginx config or an AWS gateway. The middleware reads the theme cookie, validates it, and rewrites the request to the matching variant. The page then uses `getStaticPaths` and `getStaticProps` to prerender each theme. He deliberately leaves the grass theme out of the prerendered paths to show incremental static regeneration filling it in on first request and caching it, which is also the answer to sites with too many variants to build ahead of time. A small bonus: the theme switch goes through an edge API route that sets the cookie, so the demo works with JavaScript disabled. The live demo and code are public (lbke/segmented-rendering-demo).

Vercel sells the same idea as edge personalisation; Netlify and Eleventy have their own edge takes. Burel prefers a vendor-neutral name.

## Is SSR really just caching?

His conclusion reframes the whole debate. "So static rendering is just server side rendering cached at build time," Eric Burel said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022. Per-request SSR is a cache miss. The cache key is the full request, not just the URL, and the middleware's job is to translate a request into a URL that works as that key. He bets on a future unified server-rendering API covering static, per-request and everything between, and notes that Next.js 13, released as he recorded, was already heading that way.

## Who should watch

Front-end and full-stack developers on Next.js or any Jamstack setup who run A/B tests, paywalls or i18n and have accepted slower pages for logged-in users as the price.

Title: When the queue backs up, split it before you buy more workers
Description: Dmitry Khorev (Mero) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on scaling event-driven NestJS apps by separating queues before throwing workers at the backlog
Body:
A traffic spike in an event-driven app rarely breaks anything loudly. It just makes your most important event wait behind everyone else's. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, [Dmitry Khorev](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Dmitry_Khorev_scalable_eventdriven_applications_nestjs), Senior Software Engineer at Mero, used a small NestJS demo to show the fix that works first: give mission-critical events their own queue, then scale workers only where the backlog actually is.

It's a short, practical talk: a quick tour of what NestJS offers, a recap of architecture styles, then a Docker demo you can run yourself from his GitHub repo (dkhorev/conf42-event-driven-nestjs-demo).

## What does NestJS bring to event-driven work?

NestJS is a Node.js back-end framework inspired by Angular and built around TypeScript and decorators. Khorev's list of reasons to use it starts with dependency injection, which takes away the chore of wiring a class dependency tree by hand, and continues with abstracted database integration, caching, config, API versioning, queues, and a choice of Express or Fastify for the HTTP server.

For event-driven architecture specifically, the draw is integration. NestJS wraps the Bull package for Redis-backed queues and ships transports for Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ, MQTT and NATS. Setting up a queue is three steps: install `@nestjs/bull` and `bull`, connect to Redis, register the queue. A service then type-hints the queue in its constructor and the container injects it; a decorated processor class consumes it.

The messaging side has one distinction worth remembering. A client proxy can `send`, which behaves like a synchronous request routed over the broker and waits for the listener's answer, or `emit`, which is fire and forget (or a durable queue event, depending on the transport). On the consumer side, `@MessagePattern` handles the request-response style and lives in a controller; `@EventPattern` can sit in any class and returns nothing.

## Monolith, microservices or events?

Khorev runs through the usual options: a modular monolith, microservices with their own stores talking over HTTP or messaging, event-driven services that emit and stop caring who listens, and the mix most long-lived projects end up with. His argument for NestJS here is that its module system makes it easy to start as a monolith and pull a unit of work out later.

## What happens when traffic triples?

The demo models a trade flow: an API gateway hits a trade service, which emits an event that four other services consume. A side application, his channel monitor, prints each queue's waiting and processed jobs plus the number of workers online. He calls that monitor a powerful pattern for observability and for autoscaling on queue metrics.

Under normal load the waiting count sits at zero. Then `make start-issue1` triples the event flow, jobs pile up, and the trade confirmations, the one event that matters to a user staring at a spinner, queue behind everything else, because a single worker processes events with no priority.

## Which fix comes first?

He lists five options: a bigger worker, more workers, application optimisation, separate queues, and event prioritisation. On the first one he's blunt. "In the node js world, this is rarely a good solution unless you are processing high cpu intensive tasks," Dmitry Khorev said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022. More workers is valid but not always cost effective, and profiling can eat a week for a small win.

So step one is queue separation: the producer emits trade confirmations to a new trades queue, a new Trades service listens to it, and the default listener doesn't change at all. After that, whatever the spike, trades keep flowing and the trades queue shows zero waiting. Step two is targeted scaling: three workers on the default queue only, and over time both queues drain to zero. Prioritisation is the next step he leaves to you, delaying logging and internal metrics in favour of integrations and notifications.

## Who should watch

Node.js developers new to NestJS who want to see queues and brokers wired up in minutes, and anyone whose event-driven system treats every event as equally urgent. It's an intro, not a production war story.

Title: When the client wants a working prototype by Monday, Meteor.js
Description: Arman Murzabulatov (Rabobank) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on why Meteor.js suited a fast-pivoting startup, plus a live React and MongoDB to-do app build.
Body:
Some startups pick a stack for scale. Arman Murzabulatov's picked one for weekends. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, the Rabobank Senior Software Engineer (and former co-founder and CTO of a SaaS startup) explains why Meteor.js fit a company that went from a Startup Weekend hackathon through an incubator, an accelerator and demo days in four or five months, then builds a reactive to-do app with React and MongoDB on screen to prove the point.

Fair warning on scope: the abstract promises a look at trade-offs against traditional stacks and a strategy for migrating off Meteor later. The talk is mostly the startup story and the official Meteor tutorial, live, with migration covered in a sentence. Watch it for the second part.

## What does a startup need from a stack?

His requirements came straight from the constraints. No budget for dedicated developers meant students, interns and freelancers, so one language across the whole stack, and ideally one person able to handle all of it. A quick learning curve to onboard fresh graduates. Rapid prototyping, because as Arman Murzabulatov said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, "you would need to show working prototype by Monday morning." And a prototype that can grow into the product, not one you throw away once the market niche is found.

One more constraint was specific to them: the product was a personality-assessment platform handling data close to mental-health records, so they couldn't put it on someone else's cloud and needed full control over hosting. Meteor ticked every box. It's a full-stack JavaScript framework on Node.js and MongoDB, cheap to self-host, and it works with React, Vue, Svelte or its own Blaze. His slides say steep learning curve, but he means the friendly kind: about a week to go from zero to 90%. It starts as a monolith, which he says you can decompose later.

## The demo: CRUD from scratch

`meteor create` scaffolds an app with React by default; `meteor run` serves it on localhost:3000. The layout is client, server and imports (UI components and API code). Hot module replacement is on out of the box, so edits land in the running app with state intact.

From there he follows the official tutorial step by step:

- **Collections.** Declare a Mongo collection for tasks in imports/api. Meteor has already set up MongoDB for you. A `Meteor.startup` hook seeds it with a few tasks if it's empty.
- **Reading.** Replace the hard-coded array with `useTracker` from the react-meteor-data package, which ships in the React skeleton. Data changes trigger re-renders, so the list on screen is live from MongoDB. He inspects the same documents with `meteor mongo` or NoSQLBooster on port 3001.
- **Creating.** A small form component with `useState`; on submit, ignore empty text, insert the trimmed text with a createdAt timestamp, reset. Sort by createdAt descending, in standard MongoDB syntax, so new tasks go on top.
- **Updating.** A checkbox toggles an isChecked field with a Mongo `$set`. Refresh the browser and the state is still there.
- **Deleting.** A cross button calls remove by id. The demo also includes a live bug where the delete button toggles the checkbox instead, because the wrong handler was wired up. It is the most relatable moment of the talk.
- **Filtering.** A hide-completed toggle adds a not-equal-to-true query on isChecked.

## What the demo skips

Writing to collections straight from the client is tutorial-grade convenience. Arman notes that he skipped Meteor methods and publications, which are what secure the backend, and accounts (email and password, GitHub, Facebook logins). The tutorial covers both, and you'll need them before anything goes near production.

## Who should watch

Founders and solo developers choosing a stack for an MVP, and anyone curious how Meteor's reactivity feels with React hooks. If you already know Meteor, there's little new; if you want the trade-off analysis the abstract mentions, you'll have to do it yourself.

Title: A side-project startup stack for about $70 a month
Description: Anton Kalik (Amenitiz) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on the stack behind a word-translation app - Koa, Apollo GraphQL, MongoDB, React and AWS.
Body:
How much stack does a small startup really need? Anton Kalik, Senior Software Engineer at Amenitiz, answers with a concrete example at Conf42 JavaScript 2022: the backend and desktop client for a word-translation and vocabulary-training app that his brother started as an iOS app. It's a full-stack JavaScript tour - Koa and Apollo Server over MongoDB, a React client with Apollo Client, all on AWS - built in about three months and running for roughly $65 to $70 a month at the start.

It's a show-and-tell rather than a set of new ideas, and the value is in seeing every layer wired together in one place.

## Start with the algorithm, then the architecture

His first step wasn't choosing tools. It was writing the basic logic for the problem at small scale, then growing that into an architecture that can scale. The resulting picture is plain: a database, a server, and clients (desktop React now, with room for React Native or native iOS and Android). He runs three AWS instances - client, server and database - connected through Route 53, with security rules and nginx in front. Locally, Docker Compose brings up Mongo.

## The server: Koa, Apollo, resolvers

He picked Koa over Express because, in his opinion, it's simpler and faster and its middleware chain is easy to follow. The Koa app connects to the database, adds middleware (graphql-upload for file uploads among them), and mounts Apollo Server on an `/api/v1/graphql` path.

Apollo builds an executable schema from type definitions and resolvers, formats errors, and builds a context per request. That context is where auth lives: the token comes from the Authorization header, gets validated, and the resulting session (or null) is passed to every resolver along with the models. Resolvers then split into queries for reads and mutations for writes, with subscriptions possible. Whatever a resolver returns has to match the shape the GraphQL schema declares.

The data model is small and multi-language: a word has an id, a creation date and translations (a language code plus a value), and belongs to a stack, the collection a user trains with. A stack has a title, an optional subtitle, a creation date, its words and its author. His example resolver fetches the words of a stack with cursor-based pagination; a mutation updates the user and then returns fresh statistics by reusing an existing query.

## The client: Apollo Client, context, styled-components

On the React side the tree is a stack of providers: Apollo Provider with the Apollo Client, a context provider for global state (useReducer with actions and dispatchers rather than Redux), a styled-components theme provider for light and dark themes, and global styles. He notes you could lean on Apollo's own cache for state instead; he prefers keeping state, queries and styles in separate places.

The Apollo Client is assembled from links: an HTTP link to the server's GraphQL path, an error link that surfaces GraphQL and network errors, and an auth link that adds the token to the Authorization header. The cache is set up for relay-style pagination on the list fields, so infinite scrolling through a word list fetches more as you go. GraphQL fragments built from schema types (a user fragment, a word fragment) are reused across `useQuery` calls such as fetching the session, while a sign-up mutation just asks for the token and user id.

## A folder rule worth copying

It's "very important to keep good structure in your applications," Anton Kalik said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, and his one strong rule is about components: every component gets a capitalised folder with an `index.js` implementation, a unit test and a styled-components file, always the same three. Components (reusable, atomic) and views (what a route shows) live in separate folders but follow the same pattern. On the server, resolvers, mutations and utilities get the same treatment.

## The rest of the toolbox

Nodemailer for transactional email such as password resets, PM2 to keep the server running in production, CircleCI for deployment, Jest for unit tests plus Testing Library or Enzyme for React. His advice for choosing: when you need to ship a startup fast, pick familiar, well-supported tools. Postgres instead of Mongo works too; you'll just want an ORM.

## Who should watch

Developers about to build their first full-stack JavaScript product who want a reference wiring of GraphQL end to end, auth context included. Experienced GraphQL users will find it familiar territory.

Title: Approve travel requests without leaving Slack, built with Bolt.js
Description: Alba Rivas (Salesforce) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on building Slack apps with Bolt.js - Events API in, Web API out, Block Kit UIs in between.
Body:
Every approval flow that makes people open another tab is a small productivity tax. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Alba Rivas, Principal Developer Advocate at Salesforce, shows how to cut it by building a Slack app with Bolt.js, Slack's official framework. Her demo app, Ready to Fly, lets employees create travel requests and managers approve or reject them without leaving Slack, with Salesforce as the backend. The pattern underneath is simple enough to learn in one sitting: listen to the Events API, do your business logic, answer through the Web API with a Block Kit UI.

Context for the Salesforce angle: Salesforce had acquired Slack the year before, and the talk opens with the company's forward-looking statement slide. The backend is Salesforce because that's her day job, but she is clear you can swap in Postgres or any database you like.

## What does the demo do?

Ready to Fly lives in the app's Home tab. After a one-time authorisation that maps the Slack user to a Salesforce user (specific to her backend, skippable with yours), the first tab lists your own travel requests: origin, destination, start and end dates. A second tab shows requests to review from the people you manage, with approve and reject buttons. Creating a request opens a form with dates, estimated cost and an approver list populated from Salesforce. And it works the other way round: approve a request in Salesforce and the requester gets a Slack notification.

## How does a Slack app actually work?

Two APIs, one in each direction:

- **Events API**, subscription-based. You choose which events Slack publishes to your app, such as `message`, `reaction_added` or `user_join`. Each arrives as JSON with everything about the interaction.
- **Web API**, for acting on Slack: `chat.postMessage`, `reactions.add`, or queries like `users.info`.

Your client app sits between them. Bolt.js, available for JavaScript, Python and Java, wraps both APIs behind a listener pattern and is maintained by Slack's developer relations team, so new platform features land there first. As Alba Rivas said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, "it abstracts you from the implementation details of those APIs." Ready to Fly is a Node.js app running on Heroku.

## Block Kit, and the tool that writes it for you

Plain-text replies are possible, but richer surfaces - modals, messages, the App Home tab - are built with Block Kit, a JSON description of UI blocks. Nobody wants to memorise block syntax, so she leans on Block Kit Builder (app.slack.com/block-kit-builder): drag elements in, copy the generated JSON out. For Node.js there's also Slack Block Builder, a community open-source library with a SwiftUI-like syntax that produces the same JSON more robustly than hand-written literals.

## Reading the code

The repository (github.com/trailheadapps/ready-to-fly) has a force-app folder for the Salesforce side and the Node.js app in its own folder. The `app.js` entry point imports from the Bolt module, initialises the app, registers listeners and calls `start` on a port. Strip out the Salesforce integration and it's only a few lines.

The rest follows a folder structure recommended by Slack's developer relations team: a listeners folder with one handler per user interaction, and a user-interface folder with the Block Kit surfaces. Her walkthrough of the `app_home_opened` listener shows the full loop in one place: the event fires when a user opens the Home tab, the handler authorises with Salesforce, queries that user's travel requests, builds the Block Kit view, converts it to JSON and publishes it through the Web API - refreshing the screen only for the user who triggered the event.

## Where to go next

The README has setup instructions to clone and run it yourself. For more examples there's github.com/slack-samples. She also points to Slack's next-generation development platform, built in collaboration with Deno and in beta at the time, plus a Code Live series, a blog post series and a Trailhead project on the same app.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers asked to build an internal Slack integration, and anyone who wants a quick mental model of Slack's two APIs. The code is Node.js, but the Events-in, Web-API-out pattern carries over to Bolt for Python and Java.

Title: A linter for your website's carbon footprint
Description: Katarzyna Wojdalska (ec0lint) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on what a page view emits and how lighter libraries, WebP, WOFF2 and a linter cut it.
Body:
Your linter already nags you about unused variables. Katarzyna Wojdalska, co-founder and CEO of ec0lint, wants it to nag you about moment.js, PNGs and TTF fonts too, because each of them has a measurable carbon cost. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022 she walks through where the internet's emissions come from, how to estimate what one page view emits, and the frontend changes that shrink it, then shows ec0lint, the open-source ESLint- and Stylelint-style tool her team built to flag them.

## Where does a web page's CO2 come from?

Digital ecology, as she defines it, studies how digital systems and the natural environment depend on each other. It is explicitly not about using the internet less; it's about greener habits. Emissions come from three places: data centres (the cloud is a building that is powered and cooled around the clock; she cites them at 1% of world electricity use), the network that carries the data, and end devices. Her slides put the ICT industry at 4% of all greenhouse gases.

Then the number that frames the talk: 250,000 new web pages are published every day. On her slides, a page view generates 1.8 g of CO2, which adds up to 216 kg a year at 10,000 views a month - about the same as driving 900 km in a petrol car. The abstract quotes a heavier average (4.6 g per view), but the talk works with the lower figure.

## How do you estimate it?

She recommends the Website Carbon Calculator for its transparent method and walks through its formula. First visits are 25% of traffic and transfer the full page; returning visits are 75% and transfer about 2% of it thanks to caching. Multiply the weighted data by end-user traffic energy (0.81 kWh per GB) and by grid intensity (a global average of 442 g per kWh). The useful bit for engineers: the dominant term is page size, which is the thing you control.

## What actually moves the number?

Her slides come with per-asset figures, and they're the best part of the talk:

- **Libraries.** moment.js weighs 4.23 MB and 1.48 g of CO2; lodash 1.41 MB and 0.5 g; axios 0.44 MB and 0.16 g. Ask whether you need the library at all, or whether plain JavaScript or the built-in fetch does the job.
- **API calls.** Fewer calls, and cache on both the frontend and the backend.
- **Images.** The same image is 2,111 KB as PNG (6.05 g) and 200 KB as WebP (0.57 g), or 126 KB as SVG (0.26 g).
- **Video.** WebM.
- **Fonts.** System fonts beat hosted ones. WOFF2 beats WOFF beats TTF: Montserrat drops 69% just by changing the format. As Katarzyna Wojdalska said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, "a user will not see the difference."
- **Colours.** Offer a dark mode; on OLED screens, darker pixels use less energy.
- **Hosting.** Check the data centre's power usage effectiveness (lower is better) and whether it runs on renewables. The Green Web Foundation keeps a directory.
- **Tracking.** Collect less user data. She cites USA Today, which loaded 91% faster after the EU introduced GDPR.

The payoff is not only carbon. Lighter pages save energy, load faster and help SEO, and her slides cite the statistic that 53% of users leave a site that takes longer than three seconds to load.

## ec0lint, the linter

Nobody remembers all of that, hence the tool. ec0lint pairs with ESLint for JavaScript, and ec0lint-style with Stylelint for CSS. It suggests changes such as replacing heavy library functions and validating font, image and video formats. Planned rules on her roadmap include video autoplay, lazy loading, dark mode control, a CO2 module, CI/CD reports and React, Angular and IDE plugins. Getting started is an npm install of ec0lint, ec0lint-style and the recommended config, an `npm init @ec0lint/config`, then `npx ec0lint .` and `npx ec0lint-style` on your CSS.

Her team's estimate is that ec0lint could cut emissions by up to 88%, based on comparing heavy websites with lighter ones. Applied to the 250,000 daily new sites, it turns 220 million petrol-car kilometres a year into 26 million. That is a projection, not a measurement, and she presents it as a goal.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers who want a concrete, numbers-first case for performance budgets, and teams that need a sustainability argument their product manager will accept. The habit tips at the start (emails, tabs, keeping a laptop six years instead of four) are a warm-up; skip ahead to the websites section if you're short on time. For more, she recommends Tom Greenwood's book Sustainable Web Design.
