Title: Promises run too early and type errors as any. fp-ts fixes both
Description: Naty Rocha (Stack Builders) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on lazy, typed alternatives to promises - fp-ts Task, TaskEither, RemoteData and Fluture.
Body:
A JavaScript promise starts running the moment you create it, its errors are typed as `any`, and nothing stops you from leaving off the `.catch()`. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Naty Rocha, Software Developer at Stack Builders in Quito, Ecuador, walks through a React demo that pits promises against the functional alternatives in fp-ts (Task, TaskEither, RemoteData) and the Fluture library, one downside at a time.

It is not an anti-promise rant. She credits promises with killing callback hell, being declarative, and having railway-oriented control flow, where a failure switches the computation from the success rail to the error rail. Her slides list the downsides she then demonstrates: eager evaluation, error types, unchecked exceptions, poor referential transparency, and nesting that gets complicated.

## Why does laziness matter?

In fp-ts, a Task is the lazy cousin of a promise. As Naty Rocha said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, "A task is basically a promise that can never fail," and its main benefit is that it runs only when you call it. Her demo assigns a fetch promise to a constant, saves the file, and the request fires on page load anyway. The equivalent Task sits there until a button click (or a `useEffect`) runs it. Remove the thunk that wraps it and the type checker complains that a Task can't be a promise.

Laziness pays off in composition. With fp-ts `pipe`, she maps and filters a not-yet-run Task of GitHub repositories, keeping only the JavaScript ones and then just their names, and calls the Task at the very end of the pipe. With a promise you have to wait for the data before you can start shaping it.

## Refactoring that doesn't change behaviour

Referential transparency is the subtle one. She builds an array of two promises and gets both results. Then she does the obvious refactor - extract the promise into a function and reuse it - and gets only the first result back, because the promise already ran. Do the same refactor with Tasks and you get both results, as you would expect. A refactor that changes the output is exactly what the functional crowd means by a lack of referential transparency, and it's a neat ten-second demo of why they care.

Short-circuiting tells the same story. `Promise.all` over several delayed promises plus one rejection reports the failure but still evaluates the rest. A sequenced array of Tasks stops at the first failure and never runs the remaining ones. You can also traverse, or run Tasks in parallel, when that's what you want.

## TaskEither makes the error part of the type

TaskEither is a Task that can fail, with the result typed as Left for errors and Right for success. A promise's `.catch` hands you an `any`. A TaskEither declares the error type and the success type (an array of GitHub repositories in her demo), and you can't map over it directly: you fold it, giving one function for the Left and one for the Right, each returning a React node. Try to return something that isn't the declared error type and the compiler stops you. With promises, the loading, error and success states are yours to track by hand.

RemoteData, from the fp-ts-compatible remote-data-ts library, goes one step further and splits a request into four states: initial, pending, failure and success. Fold it and the compiler makes you handle all four. Her demo throttles the network so you can watch it move from not called to loading to success, then breaks the URL to get the failure branch.

## Futures you can cancel

Fluture's Future has the same laziness and composability, plus cancellation. Running a Future with `fork` returns a cancel function. Her example waits three seconds before resolving, with a cancel handler that clears the timeout. Click cancel and the Future never resolves. She points to reactive UIs like React or Vue, where a user clicks away from the thing that started a request.

## The honest caveats

Her conclusions are balanced. The learning curve is steep. Documentation for these libraries can be hard to understand, though the types do a lot of explaining. And use them with caution: dropping them everywhere without good practice is overkill. Learn the functional basics first. Next stops on her list: Effect-TS, RxJS, algebraic data types, and io-ts for validation.

## Who should watch

TypeScript developers tired of `any` in their catch blocks, and React developers juggling isLoading flags. If you've never seen fp-ts, the demo-driven format makes it far less intimidating than the docs.

Title: Visual tests for every Storybook story, zero new test code
Description: Andrew Knight (Applitools) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on visually testing Storybook components across 10 browser configs with Applitools Eyes.
Body:
A button that quietly goes from round to rectangular passes every functional test you have. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Andrew Knight, developer advocate at Applitools and better known as the Automation Panda, shows how to catch that class of bug by visually testing every story in a Storybook component library across browsers, without writing a single new test case. It's a vendor demo: the tool is Applitools Eyes and its Storybook SDK, and the talk is a clean end-to-end walkthrough of it.

## Why components need eyes, not just asserts

Andrew draws the line between a web element (one HTML tag) and a component (a unit of UI made of elements, from a styled button up to a header or sidebar). Component libraries exist so a round blue button is defined once and reused everywhere. The flip side: break the component and you break every page that uses it.

Some regressions are loud, like a CSS typo that makes the button enormous. Others aren't: a colour shift, a changed corner radius. Clicking through the Storybook viewer by hand catches some of them, but it doesn't scale with a big library, and doing it again in every browser is a grind. The fix he proposes is snapshot comparison: a known-good baseline next to the latest checkpoint, with the differences highlighted.

## How much setup does it take?

Very little, which is the point of the talk:

- `npm install` the Applitools Eyes Storybook package. It works for any project with a Storybook library - React, Angular or Vue.
- Add an `applitools.config.js` with a concurrency setting (free accounts get one) and a batch name for the dashboard.
- Set the `APPLITOOLS_API_KEY` environment variable from a free account.
- Run `npx eyes-storybook`, pointing it at the static files directory with the `-s` option.

The SDK starts Storybook, finds every story and tests each one. His demo library has four components (button, header, scroll button, text input) but nine stories, because the button alone has five variants. As Andrew Knight said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, "you won't even need to write a single line of new test code."

## Baseline, checkpoint, thumbs up or down

The first run marks all nine as new: those are the baselines. The second run, with no changes, marks all nine passed. Then he turns the primary button flaming red. Seven pass, two are unresolved: the button story and the header, where Eyes narrows the difference down to the sign-up button. Unresolved means a human decides. Thumbs up makes the checkpoint the new baseline; thumbs down keeps the old one and records a failure.

The second experiment is sneakier. He changes the header title and deletes the `justify-content` rule from the header wrapper, so the buttons slide from the right edge to sit beside the title. Match levels help sort out what kind of change that is. Strict looks for anything a human eye would notice. Content focuses on text and colour. Layout ignores the text and highlights only what moved - here, the buttons. He cares about both, stays on strict, and gives both header stories a thumbs down as a real visual bug.

## 90 snapshots in 37 seconds

Everything so far ran in Chrome. Adding a browser list to the config - five desktop browsers with viewport sizes and five mobile devices, each with a set screen orientation - turns nine stories into 90 tests. On the Applitools Ultrafast Grid the whole batch took 37 seconds, against what he estimates could be several minutes to an hour for traditional cross-browser runs. Testing big components with responsive layouts in isolation means a broken breakpoint shows up before it spreads to every page.

## Where does it fit in the pipeline?

Andrew puts visual component tests between integration and end-to-end tests, since components are UI units. Run them in CI. His example repository has a GitHub Actions workflow on Ubuntu that checks out the code, sets up Node.js, installs dependencies and runs the same command, triggered when a pull request opens; the API key is the only input it needs.

## Who should watch

Frontend teams with a Storybook library and no visual regression coverage, and anyone weighing a visual testing tool. It's a product demo, so treat it as one, but the baseline-checkpoint workflow and the strict-content-layout distinction apply to any visual testing setup.

Title: Solid.js looks like React, and that's the trap
Description: Travis Waith-Mair (Plex) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on Solid.js for React developers - signals, memos, effects, and the habits that break reactivity.
Body:
Solid.js reads like React and runs nothing like it. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Travis Waith-Mair, Senior Software Engineer at Plex and author of the Bedrock Layout primitives library (written for React, ported to Solid), gives React developers a fast tour of Solid's fine-grained reactivity and, more usefully, the React habits that silently break it.

His framing is a language-learner's one. Spanish has false friends: universidad is university, presidente is president, and embarazada is very much not embarrassed (it means pregnant). Solid has false friends for React developers, and familiarity is exactly what gets you in trouble.

## Same JSX, different engine

Solid uses JSX, components and props. A simple component can be valid in either framework, and `createSignal` looks a lot like `useState`. But Travis is clear that Solid is not a drop-in replacement the way Preact is: you can't swap the import and go.

The difference is under the hood. React's virtual DOM flags a component whose state changed, re-renders, and touches the real DOM only at commit time. Solid has no virtual DOM. It is a compiled framework, and at compile time it wires its reactive primitives so that only the parts of the page that depend on a changed value get updated. As Travis Waith-Mair said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, "Your component only renders once and then it never renders again."

## Three primitives, no dependency arrays

Everything in Solid breaks down into a signal, a memo or an effect:

- **Signal**: `createSignal(0)` gives you a getter and a setter. The value is a function call, `count()`.
- **Effect**: `createEffect` reruns when the signals it reads change. His example sets `document.title` from the count. No dependency array, because Solid already knows what the effect reads.
- **Memo**: `createMemo` is effect plus signal - it reruns only when its inputs change and returns a signal. Good for expensive calculations.

In the counter demo, clicking the button doesn't rerun the `Counter` function. The effect reruns, the paragraph showing the count updates, and nothing else is touched.

Because components run once, the rules of hooks don't apply. You can create an effect inside an `if`. You can lift a signal out of the component to module scope and import it into two components, and both stay in sync: a common way to do simple global state, with more sophisticated stores in the docs for bigger cases.

## The false friends

**Don't return early.** In React, a loading guard that returns before the main JSX is normal. In Solid, the component never reruns, so when the data arrives, the rest of the component never happens. Use control-flow components instead: `<Show>` with a `fallback`, plus `Switch`, `For`, error boundaries and `Suspense`.

**Don't compute outside JSX or primitives.** Deriving a double count as a plain constant from `count()` captures the value once and loses reactivity. Wrap it in a function, or put the expression right in the JSX.

**Don't destructure props.** This is the one that catches nearly every React developer. A reactive prop is compiled into a getter that calls the signal, so destructuring in the signature (or right after) reads it once and freezes it. Treat every prop as if it were a signal: use `props.name` in the JSX. When you need to split or merge props, `splitProps` and `mergeProps` do it safely.

**Forget useRef and useCallback.** No rerenders means no need to keep identities stable. Assign a ref to a plain `let`, focus it in `onMount`, and pass functions directly.

If that's too much to remember, there's `eslint-plugin-solid`, the equivalent of React's hooks lint rules.

## Why bother?

React has the market share. Travis's case for Solid: the highest satisfaction rating in the State of JS 2021 results, in its first year on the list; performance by default from creator Ryan Carniato, without making developer experience pay for it; and an ecosystem with routers, UI components, tooling and starters. SolidStart, a meta-framework in the same spirit as Remix or Next, was in beta at the time.

## Who should watch

React developers curious about signals, or about to touch a Solid codebase. It's a short intro with real code, and the gotchas section alone will save you an afternoon of wondering why your loading spinner never goes away. Next stops he recommends: the solidjs.com tutorial, the playground, and the Solid Discord.

Title: Internationalise first, translate later - the i18n checklist
Description: Mayank Kumar (Rakuten India) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on i18n vs l10n, key-value configs, partial translation, RTL layouts and locale pitfalls.
Body:
A user who can't read your site in their language doesn't file a bug; they open your competitor's site. Mayank Kumar, Senior Software Engineer II at Rakuten India, opens his Conf42 JavaScript 2022 talk with exactly that scene, then gives a compact, practical checklist: internationalisation (i18n) is the architecture that makes a new locale a config change, localisation (l10n) is the translation and testing you do on top, and doing them in the wrong order costs you.

It's an introductory talk, and a tidy one. If you've never shipped a second language, this is the map.

## What's the difference between i18n and l10n?

The numeronyms first: 18 letters between the i and the n, 10 between the l and the n. Internationalisation is the process of making localisation possible - building the platform so that adding German or Japanese tomorrow needs no change at runtime or deployment time. Localisation is translating into specific locales, chosen by the markets you're targeting, followed by thorough testing.

Two scope rules. Text isn't the only thing to internationalise: images, currency, numbers and punctuation all vary by locale, and whatever you don't internationalise now you can't localise later. And not everything should be localised. As Mayank Kumar said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, "there are some technical terms, some names which should not be localized." Decide early what sits outside the scope.

The business case on his list: global reach, customer satisfaction, avoiding content that is fine in one culture and offensive in another, and a much shorter time to market. If the app already ships in English, German and Dutch, launching in Chinese is adding a locale, not building a new app.

## The process, in four moves

1. Pull every hard-coded string out of the code into key-value configs (.json or .properties). The `<div>` with Hello World becomes a lookup of a key like `hello_content`.
2. Translate the configs, with context.
3. Read the user's language preference and pick the right config.
4. Localise numbers and currency, and support switching at runtime (a translate-to-English action or a language dropdown).

His number example renders the same value in German, Japanese and English formats: the currency symbol moves, and dots and commas swap roles. JavaScript's built-in locale functions, such as `toLocaleString`, do this for you, so don't hand-roll it.

## Where does it hurt?

- **Retrofitting.** Adding i18n to an existing app means first finding every static string. Starting a new app this way is far easier.
- **Context.** Import and export mean one thing in a data app (CSV in, Excel out) and another in a shipping business. Translators who don't know your product need that context with every string.
- **Cost that recurs.** Third-party translation isn't a one-off: every release adds strings. Still cheaper than a new app per market, he argues.
- **Testing.** Translated text breaks layouts built around an assumed string length.
- **Partial translation.** His favourite real case: admins who all read English, end users who don't. Translating admin pages is wasted money. Either split resources into admin and end-user files and load end-user only, or admin plus end-user, depending on who logs in, or namespace the keys with a prefix and send only the end-user ones for translation.

## Right-to-left is more than text alignment

He illustrates RTL with a three-panel energy-drink ad: read left to right, a tired man drinks and perks up; read right to left, the drink knocks him flat. For Arabic, Hebrew, Urdu and Farsi the whole layout mirrors: sidebar on the right, menus starting from the right, right-aligned input, text flow, and slideshow navigation that goes the other way.

The browser tooling: the HTML `dir` attribute set to rtl, the `<bdi>` element for mixed-direction content (the browser's bidirectional algorithm decides), and the CSS `direction` property. For custom CSS, his team splits direction-specific rules (float, margin-left, padding-right and friends) out of a common stylesheet, then loads common plus LTR or common plus RTL per user. It is a simple pattern that keeps the direction logic in two small files.

## Three rules to tape to the monitor

- Translate whole messages. Concatenating separately translated fragments loses the meaning.
- Think in locales, not languages: en_US and en_GB are both English and still differ.
- Never design around string length.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers about to add a second language, and anyone inheriting an app with strings baked into the templates. Seniors who've done this before will find little new, but it's a good link to send a team before the retrofit starts.

Title: Teaching JavaScript to art students who never wanted to code
Description: Marcell Endrey (Wise) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on what worked teaching code to non-programmers - p5.js, sprites, no semicolons, and a browser sandbox.
Body:
If your students will never write code for a living, you can throw out half of what you'd call good practice. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Marcell Endrey, Frontend Developer at Wise, describes three semesters of teaching beginner programming to Hungarian university art students (plus one semester of high schoolers), and the deliberate shortcuts that made it work: no `var`, no semicolons, everything global, and sprites instead of coordinates.

The course started in the fall of 2016, when he tagged along as a mentor for a friend's class and then took it over. The university gave him nearly free rein: attendance was mandatory, everything else was his call. So the goal was not a skill level. It was a sneak peek into coding and a feeling of success.

## What does success look like when nobody wants to be a developer?

No exam at the end. Homework every week and a final task, but no fixed point the class had to reach. The mindset was safety: there are no stupid questions, trying beats getting it right first time, and the teacher admits he works by trial and error too. Code, he told them, isn't written top to bottom; you put something out there and massage it until it behaves.

That framing drove the hardest design call. Wrap an awkward framework function in a friendlier helper, and students understand it faster, but they'll never find that helper in the official docs. Marcell chose the bubble: his own conventions and helpers, because walking away believing you can do this mattered more than matching patterns seen elsewhere.

## Why p5.js over Processing?

The circle of people teaching these workshops used Processing, a framework built for teaching beginners. Marcell switched to its JavaScript port, p5.js, even though Processing had the bigger community and tooling. Java's verbosity was the problem: type names like void, String and int are not everyday words for an art student, and you have to remember that String is capitalised and int isn't.

JavaScript let him strip variables down to a name, an equals sign and a value. Dropping `var`, `let` and `const` puts everything in global scope, which he concedes you'd never do in production. But as Marcell Endrey said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, "understanding variable scope was just too big of a hurdle."

Semicolons went too, via automatic semicolon insertion, since the class would never write the corner cases where it bites. The reason is wonderfully physical: on a Hungarian keyboard many special characters, curly braces included, sit behind AltGr, and students wasted real time hunting for them. If you've ever watched someone search for a backtick, you know.

## Sprites beat coordinate geometry

Why not Python, which the stripped-down code resembles? Because of p5.play, an open-source extension that adds sprites. Processing's own hello-world example has more numbers than letters, which is a hard sell when your message is that you don't need to like maths. Sprites are actors: put one on the canvas, move it, rotate it, change how it looks, let two collide. It is much closer to how people think about things in a space. The idea borrows from Logo's turtle graphics, the first language Marcell learned: if you can drive a remote-control car, you can drive the turtle.

JavaScript also lives in the browser students already use. Open the console on any page and you can change it, which shows how close programming is to everyday life. The console is a REPL, too: tell your sprite to do something, it does it and stays there, and you keep giving instructions. He points out that the official Python tutorial starts the same way, with the interpreter as a calculator.

## Ditch Git for a URL

Previous courses saved code on pen drives or pushed it to GitHub through GitHub Desktop, on shared university machines. Git cost too much time for a first course. Marcell moved everything to JS Bin, an online sandbox: log in anywhere and your programs are there, versioned. Stuck on homework? Send the teacher the URL. Want it on your phone? Open the URL. Nothing to install.

## Did it work?

Honestly, not always. One class didn't want to code at all, even during the course, and that semester failed; he says he gave up on them because they gave up on it. But classes with zero background and some willingness went well, and in one semester his course got the university's highest teacher satisfaction score for groups of 10 to 15 students.

## Who should watch

Anyone running a bootcamp, an intro workshop, or onboarding non-engineers onto a codebase. It's a short, candid talk with a reusable principle: decide what the learner needs to feel, then remove every obstacle that doesn't serve it.

Title: Six questions to ask your code before someone else has to read it
Description: Chris Miller and Liz Kaufman (School Of Code) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022 on six questions that make code readable by juniors, teammates and non-developers.
Body:
Most clean-code advice is written for the author. At Conf42 JavaScript 2022, Chris Miller (Internal Services Lead) and Liz Kaufman (Lead Coach and Head of Bootcamps), both of School Of Code, turn it around: the test of your code is whether someone else - a junior, a teammate, a product owner, or you in six months - can pick it up. They frame it as six questions, talked through as a conversation between a developer of 22 years and a coach who has taught over 300 bootcampers.

The questions: is your plan extensive enough to help someone else, is your code abstracted enough to minimise (mental) load, encapsulated enough to be clear, tested enough to be confident, documented enough to help, and clear enough that a non-developer can understand it. Chris put the last one at the end on purpose because it is the scary one.

## Why plan before you type?

Liz's argument is simple: for anyone new to code, the logic is hard and the syntax is hard, so doing both at once is a recipe for trouble. Break the logic down until it won't break down any further, then layer the code on top.

They demo it live on a calculator that handles whole numbers only and does add, subtract, multiply and divide. Walking the plan step by step finds the pitfall before any code exists: three divided by two. Now you have a decision to make (round up, round down, or switch to floats) and, as Liz points out, an early, honest conversation with whoever wrote the brief. Pitfalls in the plan are cheaper than pitfalls in production.

Chris adds a rule worth stealing: if your plan uses words the team won't know (his example is a PHP trait attached to an abstract class), put the definitions or a docs link right in the plan. A senior forgets what a junior doesn't know, and a junior sometimes has the idea the senior missed.

## How much abstraction is enough?

Chris defines abstraction as showing what's needed now and hiding what isn't. Liz describes the moment bootcampers learning Express move from one big app.js to separate routers and models: everyone panics, then a few hundred lines later everyone gets it. Her caveat is the useful part: hidden must not mean lost. Name the function for what it does and keep a folder structure that leaves breadcrumbs, so going under the hood is not a black box.

On naming, Chris notes the code doesn't care - you could call your users fish. Liz makes the same point in class by renaming a variable potato and running it anyway. Names are for people, so pick them with people.

Encapsulation gets the OOP and functional view side by side. Chris offers a checklist from OOP that still works if you swap class for file: all related things easy to identify, unrelated things easy to tell apart, and "no data should be accessible that's not needed" - the user's password never travels to the front end. Liz's functional take: a methods file shouldn't know it lives in a router. When one of their database providers went down, only the connection string had to change, which they recognise as dependency inversion explained in plain words.

## Tests for confidence, not for coverage

Liz pushes back on the school of thought that every second of code needs five seconds of tests: everything is a trade-off, including testing. The goal is confidence that the user gets what they need and that a teammate can add a feature without breaking your work from two days ago. They lean on Kent C. Dodds' line about tests resembling how the software is used, and on the QA-engineer-walks-into-a-bar joke, where every edge case is covered and the bar burns down when a customer asks for the bathroom. Chris's practical fix: put unfinished work in front of a user as early as possible, so the final user acceptance test is short.

## Documentation that answers why

The sweet spot sits between commenting every `1 + 1` and writing nothing. Chris's rule: docs tell you how to get set up and what the code does; comments are for the why. His example is a value converted from integer to string to float, which looks daft until a comment explains that the calculation, the front end and the database each needed a different type. Liz wants verb-tense function names (greet, calculate, add) and then parameters that finish the job - not `add(x, y)` but first number and second number.

## Who should watch

Juniors, bootcamp grads, and the seniors who pair with them. It is a conversation, not a code-heavy talk, and the hit-by-a-bus question at the end is the one to take to your next retro. As Chris Miller said at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, "If you were hit by a bus tomorrow, could anybody else pick up your work?"

Title: Let the pipeline size its own Spark cluster, one millisecond per record
Description: David Joyce (Spectrum Labs) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on Argo Workflows that size elastic Spark clusters from a per-record cost estimate
Body:
Most data scientists do not want to know how many Spark executors their job needs; they want the job to finish. At Conf42 Kube Native 2022, David Joyce, Principal Data Engineer at Spectrum Labs, showed how his team built a framework on Argo Workflows where a developer declares one number - how long a single record takes to process - and the pipeline works out the cluster size, partition count and node type at runtime.

It is a practical, demo-heavy talk: three live demos, real YAML, and an honest list of what hurts.

## Why does a trust and safety company need big batch pipelines?

Spectrum Labs builds B2B trust and safety technology. Gaming apps, dating apps and social platforms send text conversations, and deep learning models flag toxic behaviour such as bullying, hate speech or threats, triggering either a human moderator or an automated action. Training those models means preprocessing, training and validation runs over large labelled datasets, and data scientists need to kick off, monitor and troubleshoot those runs themselves.

The team was already on Kubernetes, which made Argo Workflows the obvious pick. Joyce's pitch for it is short: it is container-native, open source, installs via a Helm chart, and every task runs in its own pod, so tasks can be sized independently. Tasks pass data either as string parameters or as file artifacts, which Argo stores in its artifact repository and drops onto whichever pod needs them.

## How do you go from Argo basics to a Spark job?

The first demo is the hello world: a DAG packaged as a Helm chart, where one task downloads a file from S3 with the S3 CLI and registers it as an artifact, and the next prints the first lines of it. Helm templating plugs in values from the values file, which is the hook everything later builds on. The workflow is kicked off with a plain curl against Argo's web server, then watched in the read-only Argo UI.

The real workload is Iroh, a pipeline that feeds model training. It runs preprocessing, in-house language detection, cleaning and tokenisation, then downloads embeddings for every token. Inputs can be tens of millions of human-labelled records and the output can pass 100 GB once embeddings are attached, so it runs on Apache Spark, deployed through the Kubernetes Spark operator as a custom resource.

The team wrapped all of the Spark operator manifest - image, main class, driver and executor settings, the standard config nobody wants to retype - into reusable workflow templates. "You can configure a spark job or spark pipeline with a couple of lines of Yaml", Joyce said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022, and the deployed result is a fully scalable Spark pipeline.

## Where does the elastic sizing come from?

The key value in the config is the time to process one record, in milliseconds (100 ms in his example). Before the Spark task runs, preprocessing steps count the records: first by asking the internal catalog whether the file has been seen before, otherwise by opening it, and for files above a size threshold by estimating. Records times per-record cost gives total work, and the framework sizes the cluster, picks the partition count, and chooses between spot and on-demand node types to match.

In the demo nobody set executor counts in the values file, yet the job ran with five executors of 15 cores each and finished a dataset of a couple of hundred thousand records in nine minutes.

## What else is in the framework?

Spectrum Labs is mostly a Scala shop, and the surrounding tooling shows it:

- **Argonaut CLI**: data scientists write instructions in YAML or JSON; the CLI turns them into a protobuf message, serialises it as a hex string and passes it as the workflow's string parameter. The first task converts it back and hands it down as a file artifact.
- **Shared libraries** for converting between protobuf messages and Argo file artifacts in any task.
- **Cron cleanup jobs** for headless Spark applications and long-running workflows.
- **A Datadog agent** on each pod, so metrics and logs land in one place.
- **Minikube** to run the whole thing locally.

The third demo adds Argo Events: a file dropped into an S3 bucket starts the Iroh workflow. One gotcha worth knowing - Argo Events would not listen to S3 directly, so the S3 event publishes to SQS and the sensor listens there. Kafka is another source they use.

## What hurts?

Joyce closes with four honest pain points. The Spark operator is not a native Argo component, so killing a workflow does not always kill the Spark job - hence those cleanup cron jobs. YAML is easy to typo, which is why local Minikube matters: "we can get feedback on these kind of errors in seconds rather than minutes." Argo is newer than Apache Airflow, with good docs for Workflows 3.x but far fewer Stack Overflow answers. And running Spark on your own Kubernetes instead of EMR means a lot of platform tuning, including custom Spark configuration so jobs survive spot instances.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers choosing a batch orchestrator on Kubernetes, and anyone tired of hand-tuning executor counts. If you already run Airflow, the challenges section is the fair comparison.

Title: From testing circuit boards to DevOps - learn the concepts before the tools
Description: Megha Kadur (TechWithMegha) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on switching from electronics to DevOps, and what she wishes she had learned first
Body:
Most people switching into DevOps start by asking which tools to learn. Megha Kadur, a tech YouTuber behind TechWithMegha, did the same, and her Conf42 Kube Native 2022 talk is about why that is the wrong first question. She came from about three years in electronics and communication engineering, testing product and component specifications, with no IT background, and her advice is to understand what DevOps is solving before collecting Jenkins, Docker and Kubernetes badges.

This is a career story plus a DevOps primer, aimed squarely at people at the start of the path. Experienced engineers will know every concept in it; the useful part for them is a clear picture of what a newcomer finds hard.

## Why DevOps exists, in her framing

Kadur took a step back after drowning in search results about tools and cloud providers, and started from a plain software release cycle: idea, planning, code, test, package, deploy, monitor. Then the problems that cycle tends to produce: changes that are hard to track, slow manual testing, incremental builds that are hard to manage, inconsistent environments, and the blame game, where development says the code works on their machine and operations says the environment is fine.

Megha Kadur said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022: "DevOps is not a particular team nor a person. It's the state of mind and we work in collaboration to solve the issues and deliver the product on time."

## The concepts, mapped to tools

The middle of the talk is the map she built for herself, concept first and tool second:

- **Version control**: Git, with GitHub for hosting and collaboration. Her verdict: you will need it for your entire DevOps journey, so learn it.
- **Cloud**: AWS, GCP and Azure. She started on Azure and found the concepts carry over; mostly the names and interfaces change.
- **Infrastructure as code**: CloudFormation, Google Deployment Manager, Azure Resource Manager. The benefits she lists are speed, lower cost, efficiency and consistency, because a configuration file deployed again and again does not make the mistakes a manual process does.
- **Containers**: Docker, packaging software with its dependencies so it runs the same in dev, QA and production.
- **Orchestration**: Kubernetes, explained from cluster to node to pod, including that a container that dies in a pod gets restarted.
- **Configuration management**: Ansible, Chef, Puppet, SaltStack.
- **CI/CD**, which she calls the backbone of DevOps: Jenkins first for her, then Azure build and release pipelines, with CircleCI, Drone and GitHub Actions as alternatives.
- **Monitoring and logs**: Grafana, Prometheus, the ELK stack, Splunk.

## What she wishes she had known

The last section is the one worth sending to anyone planning the same move:

- **Learn a programming language.** On her first project her build and release pipeline kept failing with different errors, and without programming knowledge she could not tell whether the code or her pipeline configuration was at fault.
- **Understand the concepts before the tools.** Tools get you through the interview checklist; concepts let you relate tools to problems and actually bring the DevOps culture to a project.
- **Learn a scripting language.** Several pipeline steps needed scripts, and she had to learn scripting on the job to write them.
- **Communicate and collaborate.** Technical knowledge you cannot convey does not help much, and she had to work on this deliberately early on.

## Who should watch

People in another engineering discipline, or fresh graduates, wondering whether DevOps is reachable without an IT background. Also worth sharing with whoever mentors juniors: the pipeline story is exactly the kind of blocker that a short explanation from a senior can save weeks on.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Rupesh Kumar and Andrew Foster on [Humana's DevOps journey](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Rupesh_Kumar_Andrew_Foster_humana_devops_journey) at Conf42 DevOps 2023, the same transformation seen from an enterprise.
- Tomas Fernandez on [technical writing as a career path](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Tomas_Fernandez_technical_writing_ai_career_path), for the communication half of her advice.

Title: Why your CI server shouldn't hold the keys to your cluster
Description: Utibeabasi Umanah (Matrica Labs) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on GitOps with Argo CD, pull-based deploys and catching configuration drift
Body:
Everyone has changed something in a cluster by hand and forgotten about it. At Conf42 Kube Native 2022, Utibeabasi Umanah, DevOps Engineer at Matrica Labs, gives a compact introduction to GitOps with Argo CD, and the most useful idea in it is about security, not convenience: a pull-based deployment means your CI server no longer needs credentials to your Kubernetes cluster.

This is a short, first-steps talk, about ten minutes, aimed at engineers who have heard the word GitOps and want the shape of it before trying it.

## What is GitOps, in one paragraph?

A continuous delivery strategy where infrastructure and application configuration are defined as code and stored in a version control system such as Git, which becomes the single source of truth: whatever the repository defines is what runs. Umanah lists the payoffs as faster and safer deployments, easy rollbacks, better traceability and an easy way to eliminate configuration drift. Argo CD, Flux CD and Jenkins X are the common tools; the talk sticks to Argo CD.

## Push versus pull

In a push setup, a CI/CD pipeline builds the app and then runs kubectl against the cluster to deploy it. Jenkins is the example, and Jenkins therefore needs access to the cluster.

Utibeabasi Umanah said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022: "But this isn't entirely safe because let's say your Jenkins server gets hacked, the hacker would have access to your cluster."

In a pull setup, software running inside the cluster watches the Git repository and redeploys when it changes. Nothing outside needs cluster credentials. That is the model Argo CD implements.

## How does Argo CD work?

Argo CD runs as a Kubernetes controller. It continuously compares the live state of each application with the desired state in Git; an application that deviates is marked OutOfSync, and Argo CD shows the difference and syncs it back, manually or automatically. Bump an image version in the repo and the change reaches the cluster without anyone running kubectl.

The features Umanah walks through:

- Kustomize, Helm, Jsonnet and plain YAML as sources; Argo CD renders the right manifests from whatever you have.
- One Argo CD installation deploying to multiple clusters.
- Basic username and password auth by default, with SSO via OIDC, OAuth2, LDAP, SAML 2.0, GitHub, GitLab, Microsoft and LinkedIn.
- Rollback, or roll anywhere, to any configuration committed to Git.
- Health status of deployed resources, automated drift detection and visualisation.
- A web UI and a CLI for automation and CI integration.
- Webhooks from GitHub, Bitbucket and GitLab, and parameter overrides, for example Helm values.

## The quick look

The demo is a tour of the Argo CD web UI with three applications: one created from the CLI, a declarative one and a Helm demo. Argo CD flags one as out of sync, meaning the cluster does not match the repo, and offers a manual sync, while the other two show healthy. From the same UI you can create applications, roll back and sync; the CLI does the same from a terminal.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to GitOps who want the vocabulary (desired state, drift, OutOfSync, push versus pull) in ten minutes. If you already run Argo CD, the related talks below go further, from Flux comparisons to event-driven microservices.

Title: Turn the databases you already run into storage nodes
Description: Trista Pan (SphereEx) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on Apache ShardingSphere as a computing layer that shards and routes traffic to existing databases
Body:
The usual route to a distributed database is a migration. Trista Pan, Co-Founder and CTO of SphereEx, proposes skipping it: keep your MySQL or PostgreSQL cluster exactly as it is, treat each instance as a storage node, and put Apache ShardingSphere in front as the computing layer that shards data, splits reads from writes and governs traffic. At Conf42 Kube Native 2022 she walks through that architecture and how it deploys on Kubernetes with Helm and an operator.

It is an architecture talk. The ten-step demo is outlined at the end but not run live, so expect diagrams and reasoning rather than a terminal session.

## What problem is it solving?

Pan says the most common request from the ShardingSphere community is how to upgrade an existing monolithic MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle or SQL Server cluster into a sharded, distributed one, and then govern the traffic, because sharding makes the topology between applications, compute and storage complicated.

She lists the needs for a database on the cloud and pairs each with an answer: large data to manage and efficient queries (data sharding); traffic governance (high availability, read/write splitting, traffic strategies, SQL audit); elastic scaling (resharding for computing and storage nodes separately); and out-of-the-box deployment (Helm and an operator on Kubernetes).

## Compute and storage, pulled apart

The core idea is a reframing of what a database is. Every database has computing and storage. A monolithic database keeps both in one instance on one machine; a distributed one splits them and deploys them separately.

Trista Pan said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022: "So could we just regard such monolithic database as the storage nodes of a new distributed database system, right?"

No changes to the existing databases. ShardingSphere-Proxy pretends to be a MySQL or PostgreSQL server to the application and connects to the real instances behind it; a governance component keeps metadata in sync across proxies. Because compute and storage are split, they scale independently. More query load means more proxies; more data means more database instances, and ShardingSphere reshards the existing data across old and new nodes.

## How does one SQL statement travel?

The application talks only to the proxy. For a query, the proxy uses the sharding algorithm to find which databases hold the data, fetches from each, merges the partial results and returns one answer. On top of that it reads the statement type. SELECTs go to replicas by default (randomly or by another strategy you configure in YAML, or to primaries if you prefer). INSERT, UPDATE and other changes always go to the primary, which replicates them. The aim is to use both replica and primary capacity for throughput. If a primary crashes, ShardingSphere is aware of the database roles and reroutes traffic, though she notes that the availability of PostgreSQL or MySQL themselves still needs other tools.

ShardingSphere offers two clients: ShardingSphere-Proxy, used here, and ShardingSphere-JDBC, which does the same work inside a Java application.

## Where Kubernetes comes in

ShardingSphere ships Helm charts that deploy the proxy cluster in one command, and the ShardingSphere operator, which she describes as a DBA on Kubernetes: it keeps the proxies highly available and scales computing nodes in or out. For the demo outline, the PostgreSQL chart deploys two PostgreSQL clusters (primary plus replica each) as storage, then the operator, two proxies and governance. The steps go on to test the operator's high availability, register the PostgreSQL resources, create a sharded t_user table, insert data, preview the SELECT routing and run the query.

She also points to the project's community as a reason to trust it, with more than 400 contributors on GitHub at the time.

## Who should watch

Engineers with a monolithic MySQL or PostgreSQL that is outgrowing one primary, curious whether a proxy layer can buy sharding without a rewrite. The transcript-level detail is thin in places and there is no live demo, so pair it with the ShardingSphere docs; her follow-up talk below goes further on the Kubernetes side.

Title: From a curl loop to a Slack alert - Kubernetes monitoring with operators
Description: Twinkll Sisodia (Red Hat) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on wiring Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana into a cluster with operators
Body:
Monitoring a Kubernetes app takes three custom resources and a role binding before the first alert fires. At Conf42 Kube Native 2022, Twinkll Sisodia, Software Engineer at Red Hat, builds that pipeline end to end on an OpenShift Dedicated cluster: an observability operator deploys Prometheus and Alertmanager, ServiceMonitors and PrometheusRules tell them what to watch, alerts land in Slack, and the Grafana operator turns the same metrics into a dashboard.

It is a beginner-friendly, demo-led talk. If you have never connected the Prometheus custom resources together, this is a clear 20-minute map of which piece does what.

## Why monitor at all?

Sisodia frames it with security cameras.

Twinkll Sisodia said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022: "we have few tools like Prometheus Grafana which is like cctvs for our system."

The things worth catching are concrete: CPU, memory or storage approaching critical limits, and Kubernetes resources such as pods and deployments failing or not running at the desired count. Prometheus, originally built at SoundCloud, stores metrics as time series with labels, and was designed for dynamic container environments where servers come and go and nobody can see inside every one by hand.

## Which pieces do you need?

Three Prometheus Operator resources carry the setup:

- **ServiceMonitor**: which services Prometheus scrapes, via a namespace selector, a label selector (here the label for an app called blue) and the endpoint port. A PodMonitor does the same for pods.
- **PrometheusRule**: recording rules, which precompute frequently used queries, and alerting rules with thresholds. The demo rule fires a low-load alert once the app sees more than 20 requests per minute, with medium and high tiers above it.
- **Alertmanager config**: receivers and routing. Here a secret holding the Slack API URL and the channel; PagerDuty and others work the same way.

On the Grafana side, the Grafana operator needs a Grafana instance, a data source pointing at the Prometheus service URL with type Prometheus, and dashboards.

## The demo: blue app, monitor namespace

The architecture is simple and realistic. The blue application runs in its own blue namespace; the observability operator and its Prometheus and Alertmanager instances live in a monitor namespace. Sisodia creates the ServiceMonitor, the PrometheusRule and the Alertmanager secret, then the step that is easy to forget: a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding so the monitor namespace may scrape metrics from the blue namespace.

Port-forwarding Prometheus shows the alerting and recording rules and the blue app up under targets. Then the load test, which is a curl loop of about 25 requests. Within 25 to 30 seconds the low-load and medium-load alerts pop into the Slack channel, each with its metadata: alert name, container, endpoint IP and namespace.

For Grafana, the operator is installed from OperatorHub into the same monitor namespace, then an instance and the data source. After a port forward to 3000 and a data source test, an imported dashboard shows recent alerts and their states, requests per minute for the blue app, response status, process CPU, and the up metric: one each for Alertmanager, the blue app and Prometheus.

## Who should watch

Developers and new SREs who have heard of Prometheus and Grafana but have not connected ServiceMonitors, rules and Alertmanager receivers to a real app. It is OpenShift-flavoured (OperatorHub, an OpenShift Dedicated cluster) but the custom resources are the same on any Kubernetes with the Prometheus Operator. Experienced operators of a monitoring stack will find nothing new; the full hands-on steps are in the speaker's GitHub repository.

- Rob Richardson on [horizontal autoscaling with Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2022_Rob_Richardson_horizontal_autoscaling), which puts the same Prometheus metrics to work scaling pods, at the same event.

Title: Validate Kubernetes manifests in the editor, not in the cluster
Description: Ole Lensmar (Kubeshop) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on the Kubernetes manifest lifecycle, four kinds of validation, and Helm plus Kustomize
Body:
A misspelled ConfigMap name can cost an afternoon, because Kubernetes' error messages will not tell you that is the problem. At Conf42 Kube Native 2022, Ole Lensmar, CTO of Kubeshop, walks through the life of a Kubernetes manifest, from kubectl-generated YAML to the object running in etcd, and makes one argument throughout: validate early, in your editor, against the YAML that will actually be applied, not the templates that produce it.

It is a manifest 101 that does not stay at 101 for long, with a short demo in Monokle, Kubeshop's open-source Kubernetes IDE.

## What is in a manifest?

The basics, done carefully. Every manifest has a kind and an apiVersion, metadata with a required name and an optional namespace (the pair must be unique: one pet store Service per namespace), optional labels and annotations, and the spec (or data) carrying the actual properties. The apiVersion and kind select the schema, which is JSON Schema as used by OpenAPI 3.0, with some limitations.

His warning on versions is the practical bit: the apiVersion is not the Kubernetes version. Kubernetes 1.24 accepts both v1 and v1beta1 of CronJob, and v1beta1 is gone in 1.25, so a cluster upgrade can break manifests that never changed. Use the latest stable apiVersion and check what your cloud provider's Kubernetes supports.

Objects reference each other in three common ways: by name (a ConfigMap ref), by object reference (name plus kind and API group, as in a roleRef) and by label selectors, which make one-to-many links. And once deployed, Kubernetes adds a status property and more metadata, so the object in the cluster never quite matches the file on disk.

## Four layers of validation

Lensmar splits validation into four:

1. **Syntax**: is it valid YAML or JSON?
2. **Schema**: are the properties and their values right for this kind and version?
3. **Links**: do the references point at objects that exist? Tricky, because the target may live in the cluster or another namespace, not in your files, and some references are optional so you only get a warning.
4. **Policy**: performance, resource allocation, security, networking, and team rules such as naming and labelling, typically written for Open Policy Agent in Rego.

OPA policies can run in a cluster gate, which helps, but by then you have to go back, fix and redeploy. In the demo he generates an Nginx Deployment with kubectl create deployment and a client-side dry run, and the schema check immediately flags null values kubectl wrote. Enabling an OPA rule flags that the process can elevate its own privileges; setting allowPrivilegeEscalation to false in the security context clears it, and the next rule (default capabilities not dropped) lights up straight after. Deployed to minikube, the live object shows everything Kubernetes added.

## Helm, Kustomize, or both

For dev, staging and production from one set of manifests, he lays out four approaches: YAML-native (Kustomize, yq), custom templating (Helm, Jsonnet), generating from code (cdk8s, Dekorate) and abstraction layers (Acorn). All of them end as YAML or JSON. Kustomize applies overlays to base manifests and is built into kubectl; his demo previews the same Deployment as one replica in dev, three in staging and five in prod. Helm packages an application as a chart with Go templates, parameterised by a values file and shared through repositories; even Minecraft has a chart.

The pattern he likes is both: Helm to package the app, Kustomize to overlay runtime settings the chart's authors never anticipated. He concedes it sounds complicated and is complicated. Either way, add a preview step to the lifecycle and validate the rendered output.

## Validate before you deploy

His tooling map is candid: kubectl creates and applies but does not help with editing or validation; IDE plugins can cover most of the lifecycle if you cobble them together and keep them compatible; validators like Trivy and Kubescape validate; Lens and k9s inspect clusters but are not built for authoring. On CI and in-cluster checks he does not mince words: from his point of view they come a little too late. You shouldn't be deploying things that have errors. Treat manifests like source code linting, in the IDE first, automated as a safety net.

And GitOps comes last, once the team is ready for it.

Ole Lensmar said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022: "Gitops is similar to maybe like adopting agile. It's not something that just one person does."

## Who should watch

Title: Kubernetes has no users, and your homelab still needs them
Description: Matt Williams (Infra) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on least privilege in a homelab Kubernetes cluster, from kubeconfig certs to SSO with Infra
Body:
Everything in Kubernetes is a resource, except the users. At Conf42 Kube Native 2022, Matt Williams, Evangelist at Infra, argues that even a homelab cluster made of a 2011 Mac Mini and a few Raspberry Pis deserves users, roles and single sign-on, shows how tedious that is with the built-in tooling, and then demos Infra, his employer's open-source tool, doing it in a few minutes.

The real title, he admits up front, should have been: why would I want single sign-on, or roles, or users? And the whole talk is about Kubernetes.

## What is a homelab, anyway?

Whatever you have. Williams is refreshingly unglamorous about it: no rack required. His first lab was a used Cisco 2600 with analog phone cards for learning fax over IP, which he says sounded like a jet engine. Today's is a Mac Mini as the workhorse, a Raspberry Pi by the utility sink next to a fly swatter, Proxmox for virtualisation, TrueNAS, Portainer, and a stack of clusters on minikube, kind, MicroK8s and k3s. Home Assistant runs the lights and an old iPad on the wall shows which bins the trash trucks take this week. Free tiers across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud round it out, and his AWS bill is about $0.53 a month.

The limit, he says, is your budget and maybe the approval levels of your significant other.

## Why bother with roles at home?

Kubernetes lets a hodgepodge of machines act as one cluster, so he deploys every side project and every tool he finds online the same way. That is also the risk: if one of those tools gets compromised while running as admin, it can reach the secrets and data of everything else on the cluster.

Matt Williams said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022: "Kubernetes is just remote execution as a service."

If everything shares the same credentials, one compromised job or user compromises the whole environment. At work there is the other case: a user who is fired, not hacked, and still holds admin.

## What a user really is

There is no user resource. A user is a signed certificate in a kubeconfig file, which holds clusters, users and the contexts that link them. A role is a set of resources and verbs; his example ClusterRole, marketing-dev, allows get, watch and list on pods.

Creating a user by hand is not hard, just tedious: generate a key with openssl, create a certificate signing request, submit it to the cluster, approve it with kubectl certificate approve, fetch the signed cert, build a kubeconfig and distribute it. Then, because possession of the cert is access, repeat that every five to 30 minutes so a removed user really loses access. That is how teams end up giving everyone admin.

There is prior art for automating it: a script by Brendan Burns, one of the creators of Kubernetes. It runs the same steps but skips the hardest part, distributing the config file.

## The Infra demo

The second half is a vendor demo, clearly labelled as such. Infra is open source and free, self-hosted or as Infra Cloud, which was in beta at the time. Williams installs the Infra server on Docker Desktop with a Helm chart and a small values file defining one admin user (password password, which he notes you would never do outside a demo). He then installs a connector per cluster with an access key, adds a user and a dev group, grants the group view on the whole cluster and gives one user exec on the default namespace.

On the terminal, infra login writes the clusters, contexts and user into the kubeconfig, and infra list shows exactly which roles a user holds where. The connector adds exec, port-forward and logs roles on top of Kubernetes defaults like view, and any custom role becomes grantable once it carries the Infra label. In real setups users and groups come from an OIDC provider such as Okta, Google or Azure AD instead of being typed in.

## Who should watch

Anyone with a home or team cluster where every kubeconfig is cluster-admin. The first half, on what users and roles are in Kubernetes and why hand-rolled certs do not scale, is useful whatever tool you pick; the second half shows one tool.

Title: Base64 is not encryption - secrets in Docker and Kubernetes
Description: Jose Manuel Ortega at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on keeping secrets out of images and repos with Docker secrets, Sealed Secrets and Vault
Body:
A Kubernetes Secret manifest stores your password as base64, which anyone with a terminal can reverse in one command. At Conf42 Kube Native 2022, security researcher Jose Manuel Ortega surveys how to keep credentials out of Docker images and source repositories: Docker secrets in Swarm, Kubernetes secrets mounted as volumes, Bitnami's Sealed Secrets for anything you want to commit to Git, and dedicated managers from HashiCorp Vault to the cloud providers' own.

It is a survey talk, a map of the options with the commands for each, rather than a single deep build.

## Why secrets at all?

Ortega starts from the twelve-factor rule that configuration lives in the environment, separate from code. The example is the database connection every app has: hostname, username, password, and a different server for development, testing and production. With secrets, each environment hands the app its own values and the code never needs to know where it is running.

Jose Manuel Ortega said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 that "secrets play a critical role in security when storing sensitive data separately from application code."

He compares a secrets manager to a personal password manager, working at the application level instead of for a person.

## What do Docker secrets actually do?

Docker's secrets are created and managed separately from applications, follow least privilege and need-to-know access, and hold anything that fits in a string or a binary blob: credentials, SSH keys, TLS certificates. The catch is that they only exist in Swarm mode. A standalone docker run container cannot use them, so the flow is docker swarm init, docker secret create from a file, then a service granted access to it.

Under the hood the managers replicate secrets with Raft, encrypted, and send them over mutual TLS. A service sees the secret as a file in an in-memory filesystem, by default under /run/secrets/ with the secret's name; when the task stops, the decrypted secret is unmounted and flushed from the node's memory. Nodes only get secrets they are managers for or that their running tasks were granted.

His best practices from this part:

- Remove secrets you no longer need with docker secret rm, after stopping the services that use them; Docker refuses to delete a secret a running service holds.
- Rotate rather than delete-and-hope when a live service needs a new value.
- Change the mount target and file mode per service if the app expects the secret at a specific path.
- In Docker Compose, prefer external secrets; a file-based secret bypasses most of the benefits and leaves you protecting that file on every host yourself.

## Kubernetes: volumes and Sealed Secrets

In Kubernetes, kubectl sends the Secret to the API server and it lands in etcd. Mounting it as a volume makes each key appear as a file in the container. The problem is the manifest: base64 values are trivially reversible, so it cannot go into Git as is.

Sealed Secrets is the fix he walks through. A controller in the cluster holds a private key; kubeseal encrypts the Secret with the cluster's public certificate into a SealedSecret resource that only that controller can decrypt. You apply it with kubectl, and the encrypted manifest is safe to push to a repository.

## The heavier tools

For more than Kubernetes-native secrets, Ortega tours the dedicated managers:

- **HashiCorp Vault**: encryption as a service through its transit engine, secrets generated on demand (for example AWS or SQL database credentials), replication across data centres, built-in revocation and access control. On first start it generates an encryption key protected by a master key, split by default into five key shares, any three of which unseal it.
- **Keywhiz**: infrastructure secrets, GPG keyrings, database credentials and TLS keys, with a JSON API, a CLI and an automation API, holding all secrets in memory only.
- **AWS Secrets Manager** with client-side caching libraries and VPC endpoints to keep traffic inside the AWS network, and **Azure Key Vault** for apps on Azure.
- **Akeyless Vault**, adding zero-trust application access and FIPS 140-2 certified app-level encryption.

The conclusion is the one to tape to the monitor: never store secrets in environment variables of the system, in the application or in source control, and pick a manager, because leaked credentials make the whole application vulnerable.

## Who should watch

Developers moving from docker run to an orchestrator who have not yet decided where credentials live, and teams adopting GitOps who need a story for secrets in Git. It is an overview: if you already run Vault in production, the related talks below go further.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Alain Lompo on [managing secrets with HashiCorp Vault in Kubernetes clusters](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Alain_Lompo_managing_secrets_hashicorp_vault_kubernetes_clusters).
- Sam Gabrail on [secrets management for GitOps with Argo CD and the Vault injector](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Sam_Gabrail_secrets_management_gitops_argocd_hashicorp_vault_injector).

Title: Pulsar on Kubernetes - stateless brokers, bookies and Function Mesh
Description: Tim Spann (StreamNative) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on running Apache Pulsar on Kubernetes and building streaming apps with Pulsar Functions
Body:
Apache Pulsar fits Kubernetes well because it splits the work that a messaging system usually piles onto one node: stateless brokers route messages, BookKeeper bookies store them, and a metadata store keeps track of both. At Conf42 Kube Native 2022, Tim Spann, Developer Advocate at StreamNative, walks through that architecture and then shows how to build the apps on top, with Pulsar Functions in Python and Java deployed through Function Mesh.

Tim Spann said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022: "Pulsar, as opposed to some other streaming and messaging system, was from the very beginning designed to run natively in the cloud and in containers."

It is a short, brisk talk, more architecture tour than tutorial. The abstract mentions Apache NiFi; the talk itself sticks to Pulsar, its functions and connectors.

## Why does the split matter on Kubernetes?

Spann goes layer by layer. Protocol handlers let the same cluster speak Pulsar, Kafka, MQTT and AMQP 0.9.1. Brokers handle routing and connections; they hold a cache but no real storage, so they are stateless and easy to scale up and down with the number of messages or clients. Topics are broken into segments, which keeps them movable.

Storage lives in Apache BookKeeper. A group of bookies forms an ensemble that stores a ledger. Metadata and service discovery for both Pulsar and BookKeeper go to a pluggable metadata store: ZooKeeper historically, and now etcd too, which he points out is the natural pick on Kubernetes since you already run it. Offloading moves older data from local or Kubernetes storage to tiered storage: S3, HDFS, Azure, MinIO or anything S3-compatible.

Because data is in segments on bookies, topics can be redistributed while the cluster runs. That is the scaling point he stresses: scaling down matters as much as out, and Pulsar can shrink a cluster without someone moving data by hand. StreamNative ships Pulsar operators for this, and the monitoring is the standard Prometheus and Grafana pairing, with CLI tools and REST endpoints for admin work.

## Pulsar Functions are lambdas that read topics

The app side is Pulsar Functions, written in Java, Python or Go, with any third-party library. A function consumes from one or more input topics, runs your logic on each message and publishes to an output topic, optionally with a log topic. Inputs are not hard-coded: a new data feed that wants your spell-checking or ETL function just gets added as another input topic.

The Python example is barely Pulsar code at all. A class subclasses Function, and its process method gets the input and a context. The function runs VADER sentiment analysis on a comment and returns JSON. The context is where the platform features live: logging, shared state, and sending to other topics. In the Java weather function, the context sends a message to a topic that does not exist yet, and Pulsar creates it, as long as security allows that, with a key, properties and a schema built from a plain Java bean.

## Function Mesh and connectors

Function Mesh, another StreamNative project, is the Kubernetes-native way to run many functions and chain them into a pipeline, declared in YAML (everyone's favourite, as Spann says) and applied with kubectl. The function mesh operator connects to a Pulsar cluster that can sit in an adjacent Kubernetes cluster, so compute scales separately from data. StreamNative dogfoods functions for its source and sink connectors (MongoDB, MySQL, Kafka and more).

The demo is small: a one-pod Python app serving a page whose JavaScript opens a websocket to Pulsar and streams the data in as it arrives, plus the open-source management console browsing tenants, namespaces and topics. Pulsar is multi-tenant, so one cluster can serve, for example, a tenant for Kafka users and another for public data.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers weighing Pulsar against Kafka on Kubernetes, and developers who want to see how little code a streaming function needs. Expect architecture and code snippets, not a production runbook; the examples live in his FLiPN-Conf42-KubeNative-2022 repo on GitHub.

Title: Your printers and cameras are the attacker's favourite foothold
Description: Brian Contos (Phosphorus Cybersecurity) at Conf42 Incident Management 2022 on what interrogating two million IoT devices says about enterprise security
Body:
Somewhere on your network there is an APC UPS whose username and password are both apc, in lowercase. At Conf42 Incident Management 2022, Brian Contos, Chief Security Officer at Phosphorus Cybersecurity, drew on five years of research and over two million interrogated devices to argue that enterprise IoT security is roughly where IT security was in 1995: nobody knows what they have, firmware is ancient, default passwords are the norm, and attackers know it.

He works for a vendor in this space and says so; the last part of the talk describes the category of product Phosphorus sells, and names competitors too. The first two thirds are threat intelligence.

## What counts as XIoT?

He uses XIoT for three overlapping groups: enterprise IoT (printers, VoIP phones, KVM switches, UPSes), network devices (NAS, wireless access points, load balancers, switches) and OT, the PLCs and SCADA kit in manufacturing, energy and utilities. They are purpose-built, they mostly run Linux, Android, BSD or a real-time OS such as VxWorks, they're networked, and they can't run endpoint security.

## How bad are the numbers?

An admittedly unscientific Shodan search turned up about 5 million exposed cameras, over a quarter of a million VoIP phones, about 83,000 printers and, for reasons he can't explain, more than 13,000 UPS systems.

Inside organisations, the Phosphorus data is worse:

- About three to five XIoT devices per employee, so a 10,000-person company has 30,000 to 50,000.
- When asked to guess their count up front, organisations are consistently off by 40% to 60%.
- About half the devices run default passwords, and for UPS systems it's close to 100%.
- 26% run end-of-life firmware; the other 74% have firmware that is six years old on average.
- About 50% carry CVSS 8 vulnerabilities and another 18% carry 9s and 10s, so 68% have high or critical CVEs.

On getting in, Brian Contos said at Conf42 Incident Management 2022 that you check whether a device is internet-accessible and whether it runs default credentials: "That's all the hacking is involved, if you can call it hacking."

On the APC defaults, Phosphorus has a standing offer: find one UPS with the password changed and everyone in the company gets a steak dinner. "We've been eating a lot of chicken."

## What are attackers doing with them?

Mostly using them as a quiet base. His case studies:

- **Fronton**, an XIoT hacking tool built by contractors for Russia's FSB, later stolen and leaked online by the Digital Revolution group.
- **Hikvision**: in August 2022, over 80,000 cameras were found exposed and vulnerable to a critical command injection flaw, across more than 2,000 organisations in about 100 countries, with a patch available since September 2021. In his testing, some banned camera brands switch the indicator light to red, meaning off, while continuing to record and send audio and video.
- **Mirai** (2016): Shodan, Telnet and a handful of common passwords were enough to build a botnet that hit Reddit, Netflix, Sony, PayPal, Twitter and GitHub. Because of white-labelling and shared libraries, the same weaknesses spread to printers and phones, and he still finds devices with Mirai on them.
- **QuietExit**, reported by Mandiant in May 2022: attackers got in through a laptop, pivoted to network devices and cameras, installed Dropbear SSH for reverse tunnels, then used those devices to call Exchange and Microsoft 365 APIs and pull email from executives, corporate development and security staff. They stayed undetected for over a year and a half.
- **RSOCKS**, a Russian botnet made up mainly of OT devices, rented out from about $30 a day and taken down by the US, UK, Germany and the Netherlands.
- **The Siemens S7 crash**: unauthenticated packets to TCP port 102 knock a PLC over, so it can't raise an alarm when a set point is breached. Siemens' advice was 1995-grade: update firmware, enable access control, set a password, disable protocols you don't use.

Some organisations only notice their cameras mining cryptocurrency when the power bill arrives.

## Which devices are the worst?

KVM switches (one shipping on an Ubuntu release about a decade old), lights-out management ports (iDRAC, iLO, IPMI) with no password, smart racks whose firmware updates need a power cycle so nobody schedules them, and physical access controllers. On one engagement at a large financial services company, his team could open and close 6,400 doors, front door included, without hacking anything.

Printers are promiscuous: wired, wireless, Bluetooth, every protocol, plus a 60-80 GB disk to hide in. One customer had hundreds compromised, used to pull data from IT systems and exfiltrate it over ICMP. VoIP phones and video-conferencing kit share builds, including one major vendor's phone shipping with undocumented SSH and a default login. And the top offender is security cameras: laptop-class hardware, thousands per enterprise (one casino has over 50,000), and nobody agrees whose job they are.

## What actually fixes it?

His remediation sequence: discover by talking to each device in its own protocol rather than scanning (malformed packets can crash a 1990s PLC) or sniffing encrypted traffic or trusting MAC prefixes; update firmware with path awareness, including downgrading to dodge a fresh CVE, and with 100% device identification so a $2 million MRI machine never gets printer firmware; harden (for example only SSH and HTTPS on ports 22 and 443); enrol credentials into existing PAM tools such as CyberArk with each device's password quirks; fix expired, self-signed and outdated-TLS certificates; re-interrogate daily to catch drift from a paperclip reset; and report trends into Splunk or ServiceNow. VLANs alone, he says, are a sandwich bag duct-taped over a bleeding hand.

## Who should watch

Security and incident response teams whose asset inventory stops at laptops and servers. Read the final section as a product category overview from someone who sells in it.

Related talks: [Jonathan Williams on IoT security threats](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2021_Jonathan_Williams_IoT_Security_Threats), [Andrey Slastenov on IoT, 5G and DDoS threats](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Andrey_Slastenov_iot_5g_devices_ddos_threat_landscape), and [Antoinette Hodes on IoT devices and saving toasters](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Antoinette_Hodes_iot_devices_saving_toasters).

Body:
# Jeli: goodbye post-mortems, hello Opportunities to learn

We've lived it just as you do: Incidents happen, despite the best plans and practices. They rarely go as imagined. Afterwards, a hapless engineer gets assigned to run a post-mortem meeting. The meeting isn't fully attended. The resulting report gets filed away where few will read it.

Our decades of combined experience in incident analysis at Jeli tell us that teams need mission-critical tools to adapt to continuously changing complex systems. That's why we give away a free IR Bot and offer a [free trial package](https://www.jeli.io/pricing) for small companies that includes our Narrative Builder, timelines, tags, investigator notes and multi-channel support. These are the very basics every company should have.

### We think big about the little things

Response teams are made of people, not machines and apps. We know, with cross discipline research backing us up, that people on distributed teams need an environment that supports them in ways that lead to better performance, more productivity, and much higher job satisfaction. These go together. We've baked that into our company culture and our product.

What creates that productive environment for learning and improving?

- **Make everyone feel safe sharing the truths:** Team members need _psychological safety_ — the certainty that they can do their jobs, speak necessary truths, and have potentially challenging conversations without repercussions. [Amy Edmondson](https://amycedmondson.com/) at Harvard Business School is a leading author on the topic with more than 20 years of research. Learning, she says, happens when high performance expectations and psychological safety are combined. She provides this helpful X/Y infographic that resonates with us.

![](./assets/custom/jeli blog item 1.PNG)


_Infographic of how psychological safety and performance standards combine to create a Learning Zone. Source:_ [_Amy Edmondson_](https://amycedmondson.com/)_, Harvard Business School_

- **Share**** findings effectively:** Burying a retrospective report doesn't lead to improved performance, increased productivity, or a healthier work environment. Our [Conf42 keynote](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2022_Vanessa_Huerta_Granda_sharing_Incident_findings_effectively) by Jeli Solutions Engineer Vanessa Huerta Granda will get to the nuts and bolts of how to ensure that your learnings from incidents reach the most people and have the deepest impact. (For starters: craft a short abstract as your incident's elevator pitch. Use it to get those who didn't attend the retro to decide to learn more about the incident and get behind your proposed solutions.) Vanessa has a lot more to share — don't miss her talk!

- **Learn across incidents over time:** We call it cross-incident analysis, or XIA, in our work. Jeli's tools are designed and built knowing that incidents don't live independently of one another. They're best viewed as a connected series of events to be analyzed as a whole. Seeing incidents as part of a connected whole helps you avoid fixing one thing by breaking another, identify organizational contributing factors (code freezes!), and develop a long-term big picture of how best to deploy your organization's talent and budget — over time, a series of minor issues can wreak unseen havoc on costs.

### We want to learn with you

No one person or group has more than a fraction of the knowledge, experience and insights we share as a group, often without knowing it. We're always eager to connect and learn with others. Please join us for [Vanessa's keynote](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2022_Vanessa_Huerta_Granda_sharing_Incident_findings_effectively) and [get in touch](https://www.jeli.io/contact) to stay connected!
