Title: Write Kubernetes apps in Go and let cdk8s worry about the YAML
Description: Abhishek Gupta (AWS) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on cdk8s, defining Kubernetes apps, reusable constructs and CRDs in Go code instead of YAML
Body:
Helm and Kustomize take some of the pain out of Kubernetes manifests, but what you write is still YAML. At Conf42 Kube Native 2022, Abhishek Gupta, Principal Developer Advocate at AWS, shows the alternative: define the application in Go with cdk8s, the CNCF's Cloud Development Kit for Kubernetes, and have it generate the YAML for you. His pitch is less removing YAML than pushing it behind the scenes, so it is no longer in your face all the time.

Abhishek Gupta said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022: "I'm a developer, I like to write code and the last time I checked, YAML isn't really a programming language."

The talk is about 20 minutes and almost all live coding, from an empty directory to a Kafka cluster on a local kind cluster.

## How does cdk8s work?

The workflow fits in a sentence: bootstrap a project, write code that describes your Kubernetes resources, run synth to turn it into YAML manifests, and deploy those however you like, with kubectl or a GitOps pipeline. cdk8s runs locally and the YAML it produces works on any cluster.

The code is a tree of constructs. Basic constructs (a Deployment, a Service, an Ingress, a persistent volume) go into a chart, which is itself a construct, and one or more charts go into an app, the root of the tree. Go is a first-class language; cdk8s also supports Python, TypeScript and Java.

## The low-level API is honest, cdk8s+ is pleasant

Gupta starts with cdk8s init for a Go app and writes the obligatory Nginx deployment against the low-level API. It works, and anyone who has written a manifest will recognise every field: labels, selectors, containers, images. It is also, as he warns, going to get pretty verbose once you build serious things from those primitives.

So he switches to cdk8s+, the higher-level API. A Deployment gets a container added and is exposed through a Service, and the boilerplate (selectors, matching labels) disappears. cdk8s synth writes the manifests into a dist folder, and the generated Deployment and LoadBalancer Service look exactly like what you would have written by hand. Port forward, and Nginx answers.

## Constructs are where the reuse happens

The WordPress demo is the most convincing part. First as two charts, one for MySQL and one for WordPress, with secrets, deployments, persistent volumes and claims, and services. Then folded into a single custom construct: a function that returns a construct (not a chart) and stands up the whole stack. Another team calls it like any built-in construct and gets a working WordPress with a database behind it. Gupta's point: you do not want multiple teams in your organisation writing that stack over and over. He ends the demo by publishing a post live from the WordPress admin console.

## CRDs become typed APIs

The advanced demo imports custom resource definitions. Using Strimzi, the operator for running Apache Kafka on Kubernetes, he runs cdk8s import against the Kafka and KafkaTopic CRD YAML straight from GitHub. That generates Go packages, and a Kafka cluster with ZooKeeper, its version, broker replicas and server config becomes ordinary Go code. Synth, apply, wait for the operator, then a console producer and consumer pass a hello-world message across the new cluster.

He closes on a reframing: infrastructure is code, as opposed to infrastructure as code. The difference is a real programming language with functions, types and packages instead of templated text.

## Who should watch

Go developers who write Kubernetes manifests and resent it, and platform teams thinking about how to hand application teams a reusable building block instead of a folder of templates. It is a hands-on introduction: GitOps integration, testing and packaging constructs get only a mention.

Title: Use chaos experiments to train on-call engineers, not just systems
Description: Eran Levy (Cyren) at Conf42 Incident Management 2022 on On-Call Like a King, workshops that replay real incidents with chaos experiments
Body:
Chaos engineering is usually sold as a way to make systems more resilient. At Conf42 Incident Management 2022, Eran Levy, Director of Engineering at Cyren, described using it to make people more resilient: a series of workshops called On-Call Like a King, where engineers work through simulated versions of recent production incidents in a real environment, with the tools they'd use on a real shift.

It's a talk about a practice and how to run it, not about a chaos tool. The workshops started as a way to give on-call engineers confidence and turned into a training ground for cloud native skills.

## Why do engineers need this now?

His argument starts with how much the job has grown. Engineers design, develop, release and support what they ship; throwing artifacts over to operations is over, and teams own the full lifecycle. In his words: "We ship products and not just code."

That ownership comes with depth. A service is one link in a chain of dependencies - the deep systems idea he borrows from Lightstep. An order service fetches from one service, then another, then produces an event for a third. "Deep systems are complex and you should know how to deal with them," Eran Levy said at Conf42 Incident Management 2022.

His example of what that looks like on call: back pressure burning your SLO, trouble in one availability zone, and a third of your deployment unable to reschedule because the cluster has no node capacity. Debugging that means knowing about regions and AZs, pod affinities, pod statuses and how to read cluster events, on top of YAML, Helm, ingress and sidecars. Frameworks hide some of it, but being blind to them can hurt you one day, or more likely one night. He also points engineers at the fallacies of distributed computing.

## How is a workshop run?

Some context first. Cyren runs weekly on-call shifts, plus a team monitoring systems 24/7, with three severity levels running from business-impact alerts down to service-owner alerts, and playbooks for the alerts. In a severity one, the priority is getting the system back to normal, and the on-call engineer leads, communicates the business impact and pulls in the service owners when specialist knowledge is needed.

Each session follows the same shape:

1. **Intro and motivation**: why we're here, what happens next. Keep it short and clear so people stay focused.
2. **Recent changes**: a chance to share architecture changes, platform improvements or process updates such as a new on-call procedure.
3. **At most two incident simulations in at most 60 minutes.** Longer sessions lose people. If the team works hybrid, do it in the same room; he found the in-person communication made a real difference.

## How close to production should it be?

As close as you can manage. They run the experiments in one of their load test environments, since nothing is identical to production anyway and they've never needed production for this. Prepare the experiment so it runs in a few clicks. And don't rush to buy a tool: they started by simulating incidents manually two years earlier and only recently moved to LitmusChaos, though Gremlin or others would do. What matters is that engineers practise instead of watching slides.

Each challenge opens with a deliberately minimal brief, the way a real incident arrives: say, back pressure from a certain UTC time, the alert, and the matching Grafana dashboard. Then engineers get time alone to investigate - cluster metrics, dashboards, logs, service status - and to think about customer impact, which he says engineers aren't always aware of, along with whether there's a workaround while the fix lands.

## The facilitator's job

The facilitator pauses, asks someone to show their progress or the tools they're using, and steers. His prompts: have one engineer walk through the Grafana dashboard to check, another share their log queries, a third show how they found the trace. Point at architectural details you want people to learn, such as an async channel, and invite them to suggest designs or raise challenges - some of which end up on the technical debt list. Keep an eye on the clock.

The side effects are where it pays off. Engineers swap the CLIs and tricks that make debugging easier, and that know-how goes back into the playbooks (he shows their playbook template). At the end of each challenge someone presents the end-to-end analysis, which helps people who won't ask questions in a big room, new joiners and juniors. Record it and share notes: people watch the recordings later, and they become onboarding material.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers who own an on-call rotation and want a repeatable training format, and teams moving onto Kubernetes whose engineers have never debugged a scheduling failure. It's process-heavy and light on code. His closing advice from the slides: start quick and dirty, and measure how the sessions help.

Title: Your autoscaler is only as smart as the metric you feed it
Description: Rob Richardson (Jetpack.io) at Conf42 Kube Native 2022 on picking the right metric for the Kubernetes HPA, and the pitfalls once it scales
Body:
A horizontal pod autoscaler watching CPU on an I/O-bound service will sit at its minimum pod count forever while users queue up outside. Rob Richardson, Developer Advocate at Jetpack.io, makes that the centre of his Conf42 Kube Native 2022 talk: Kubernetes can scale your pods for you, but only if you pick the metric that matches how your workload actually gets busy, and only if you fence in the ways it can go wrong.

It is a practical tour of the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, with live demos on minikube, from built-in CPU metrics to Prometheus-driven scaling, then the pitfalls: runaway scale, slow scale, sloshing and scale to zero.

## Why isn't autoscaling just a button?

Richardson starts with the history. We used to over-provision for Black Friday because getting a new server took weeks. Utility billing changed that: buy what you need, hand it back when demand eases. He notes that teams now run machines hot, and 80 or 90% utilisation is not unusual.

The catch is that Kubernetes cannot guess what busy means for your service. He walks through three cases. A CPU-scaled service that mostly waits on an external data store never looks loaded, so it never scales. A service scaled on concurrent requests, behind a framework that caps concurrency and pushes back to the load balancer, never crosses its threshold either. The one that works scales on a message queue length, because that metric is the business concern: emails waiting to be sent.

## What does the setup need?

The checklist is short and easy to get wrong:

- Turn on the metrics server first (kubectl top pods tells you if it is there).
- Scale something that knows how to build pods: a Deployment, StatefulSet or DaemonSet.
- Set resource limits, because utilisation targets are a percentage of them. With a 0.5 CPU limit and a 50% target, a quarter of a CPU per pod is the line.
- Remove the replicas field from the Deployment and let the autoscaler own the count.

By default the HPA checks metrics every 15 seconds and, after a scaling change, waits five minutes before the next one. Both are configurable.

## Beyond CPU and memory

The metrics side has three APIs: resource metrics (CPU and memory via the metrics server and cAdvisor), custom metrics (for example via the Prometheus adapter) and external metrics (queue lengths, load balancers, cloud resources). Richardson installs Prometheus and the Prometheus adapter from the prometheus-community Helm charts and annotates the pods so Prometheus discovers them, with a reminder that the annotation values must be quoted strings, not a boolean and an integer. He also tours a collection of adapters: HTTP JSON, InfluxDB, AWS SQS queue length, Istio, and a schedule-based scaler for clusters nobody uses overnight.

## The pitfalls

**Scaling too high.** An attack, a bug or going viral can all drive pods up. Set a max replica count that matches your budget, and accept that the system may be less available past it. With several metrics, Kubernetes uses whichever demands the most pods, so a quiet CPU graph does not mean the scale-up was wrong.

**Scaling too slow.** Missing metrics count as the best case: 0% when scaling out, 100% when scaling in. Pods that are slow to publish metrics will not trigger action.

**The reset to one pod.** A hard-coded replicas line means every deploy throws away the autoscaled pods. The fix creates a small edge case on the very first deploy, which he is happy to live with.

Rob Richardson said at Conf42 Kube Native 2022: "I'd rather have 15 seconds of only one pod than have it reset to one on every deployment."

**Sloshing.** The docs call it flapping; Richardson prefers water pushed up a beach. A slow-booting Java app is not live after 15 seconds, so the HPA adds more, then has too many, then scales down, and round it goes. The stabilisation window is the brake; he sets one to 600 seconds for such an app.

**Scale to zero.** The HPA stops at one pod. Getting to zero needs a reverse proxy that holds the request and wakes a pod, which means reaching for Knative or KEDA. If you only have one microservice, he suggests just leaving it running may be simpler than running their pods.

## Who should watch

Engineers who have an app on Kubernetes and a vague HPA with a 50% CPU target copied from a tutorial. It is an intro-to-intermediate talk with working YAML and kubectl, not a cluster-autoscaling talk: node scaling is explicitly out of scope.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Chris Nesbitt-Smith on [proactive cluster autoscaling in Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Chris_NesbittSmith_proactive_cluster_autoscaling_kubernetes), the node side Richardson leaves out.
- Raja Ganesan on [cluster autoscaling with Karpenter](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Raja_Ganesan_cluster_autoscaling_karpenter).
- Giovanni Paolo Gibilisco on [using ML to tune Kubernetes apps](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Giovanni_Paolo_Gibilisco_ml_automatically_tune_k8s_apps), for the resource limits the HPA depends on.

Title: Turn your OpenAPI spec into tests and stubs, then skip integration testing
Description: Hari Krishnan (Polarizer Technologies) at Conf42 Incident Management 2022 on contract-driven development to catch API breaks before integration
Body:
A broken API contract is an incident that has already been written; it's just waiting for deployment. At Conf42 Incident Management 2022, Hari Krishnan, Founder and CEO of Polarizer Technologies, made the case for contract-driven development: treat the OpenAPI specification as an executable contract, generate provider tests and consumer stubs from it, and check two versions of the contract for backward compatibility before anyone writes code. The goal is to deploy microservices independently, with compatibility problems caught on a laptop or in CI rather than in a shared integration environment.

All the demos use Specmatic, an open source tool that reads OpenAPI (or WSDL) specs, so this is a tool-led talk as much as a methodology one.

## Why do hand-rolled mocks break integration?

His setup is the familiar one. A mobile app (the consumer) needs data from a backend (the provider). Waiting for the provider is sequential and slow, so the consumer team stands up a mock server. The trouble is that the mock only reflects the consumer's assumptions: maybe they send the product id as a string when the provider expects an integer, or expect name and price when the provider returns name and SKU. The provider, meanwhile, is built with no emulation of the consumer at all. Nobody finds out until both land in integration testing, which then gets blocked for everyone, or worse, until production.

Writing an OpenAPI spec reduces the ambiguity, but a spec only describes the API. Enforcing it is the part teams skip.

## Contract as test, on the provider side

He points Specmatic at an e-commerce spec (products and orders, CRUD operations) stored in a Git repo, and runs it against a Kotlin Spring Boot app through its JUnit support; the tool itself is a language-agnostic executable. Without writing a test, he gets twelve generated scenarios, one per operation, each sending a request built from the schema and validating the response. Hari Krishnan said at Conf42 Incident Management 2022: "That's money for nothing and tests for free."

Then the useful part. Happy paths are not where trouble lives; in his words, "Incidents do not happen in the happy path scenarios." Turning on generative tests for boundary conditions raises the count to 26 tests, and only 16 pass. One negative case sends a null to a field the spec says must not be null, and the app answers with a 500 Internal Server Error instead of a 400, because nobody wrote the null check. That's the kind of bug that becomes a production incident, found with zero lines of test code.

## Smart mocks, on the consumer side

For the consumer, a 30-40 line products spec becomes a local stub server with one command. Ask it for a product and it generates schema-valid strings for name and SKU; drop request/response JSON files into a products_data folder (named by convention after the spec) and it returns specific examples, such as The Mythical Man-Month for id 1.

The trick is that the stub validates your examples. When he edits an example to return name and price, the running stub rejects it immediately: price is not part of the contract. The wrong assumption from the opening story is caught before the mobile team builds against it. The same expectations can be set dynamically over HTTP for component tests, slotting into the arrange step the way Mockito does in a unit test.

## Is this change backward compatible?

Comparing two versions of a contract, no code involved, answers a pop quiz of escalating difficulty:

- **Adding a required request field**: obviously breaking, and the comparison says the new contract expects a key the old one didn't send.
- **Making an optional nullable field optional and non-nullable**: also breaking, since old clients may still send null - less obvious, and flagged correctly.
- **Making fields of a shared address schema optional**, when that schema appears in requests and responses, at several levels of nesting, and possibly across files via remote references: he admits he can't work that one out in his head, which is the point of having a tool do it.

## Keep the contract in one repo

All of that falls apart if the provider updates the wrong file or the consumer builds against an old spec someone emailed. So the specs live in a central contract repository under version control, with pull requests, linting (he mentions Stoplight Spectral) and an automated backward-compatibility check against the previous version before merge. In each service's CI, consumers run component tests against the contract stub, and providers run contract tests before their component tests. When both pass, deploying to integration should be uneventful.

## Who should watch

Teams with many services whose shared integration environment is permanently red, and tech leads who own API versioning. You'll want basic OpenAPI knowledge; contract-testing experience helps but isn't required.

Related talks: [Navendu Pottekkat on SRE best practices for API design](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2022_Navendu_Pottekkat_sre_best_practices_api_design), [Barkatul Mujauddin on API testing](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Barkatul_Mujauddin_api_testing), and [Prathamesh Sonpatki on policies and contracts in distributed systems](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2023_Prathamesh_Sonpatki_policies_contracts_distributed_systems).

Title: Ship your policy like a dependency, with semver and Renovate PRs
Description: Chris Nesbitt-Smith (UK Government) at Conf42 Incident Management 2022 on versioning policy as code so teams can test, update and prove compliance
Body:
Writing policy in YAML instead of a Word document is not the same as treating it like software. At Conf42 Incident Management 2022, Chris Nesbitt-Smith, a consultant who has spent much of his career across UK government and large organisations, argued that most policy as code is done wrong, and showed a working fix: publish the policy as a versioned dependency, with tests and release notes, and let Renovate open the pull requests that tell every team where they stand.

## A lift full of stakeholders

He opens with an imaginary lift. A CIO who doesn't know what teams are doing or how much risk they're carrying, because changing policy is slow and hard to communicate and people go off and do their own thing. A product manager who sees the bureaucracy as designed to slow them down. A Python developer who wants to know which rules exist and which ones they can bend. And a cleaner whose instructions arrive as memos on a noticeboard, compiled into a manual that goes wrong whenever a memo is missed - the week they forgot the third-floor meeting room had become the war room, and wiped every board in it. He turns out to be the lift engineer, there because it only goes to the top floor. It's a long bit, and it lands.

## Where does policy as code go wrong?

Policy tends to be emotionally led rather than a proportionate control, which invites case-by-case exemptions and grows like case law until nobody can measure compliance. Putting it in code is the right instinct, but the detail matters. Chris Nesbitt-Smith said at Conf42 Incident Management 2022: "Throwing some curly braces or yaml at something doesn't inherently fix things."

Three failure modes stand out:

- **Secret policy.** Security teams hide the rules so an adversary can't use them, and developers reverse-engineer them by hitting the wall. That is the opposite of shifting left.
- **Half-applied deployments.** If one resource is rejected midway through a deployment, the app lands in an inconsistent state. If that causes downtime, was the policy worth more than the outage? And smart engineers start finding creative routes around the system.
- **Warnings nobody reads.** Soft-launching new rules as warnings only works if someone reads build logs of green builds, which in a working CI/CD setup nobody should need to.

## Treat it like every other dependency

His list of what policy should easily be: visible, communicable, consumable, testable, usable, updatable and measurable. The steps map onto things software teams already do.

**Make it visible**, at least inner source to employees and suppliers, open source if you're brave. Visible policy with known gaps beats downtime, workarounds and what he calls opaque legacy exemption spaghetti soup.

**Version it with semver.** His running example is a department label on every resource. Requiring the label is 1.0.0. Restricting it to a fixed list of departments is a breaking change, 2.0.0. Fixing a misspelt department name is 2.1.0. Adding a department is 2.1.1, a patch anyone can take.

**Publish it as a dependency**, the way ESLint sits in a JavaScript project, **with tests** whose passing and failing cases double as examples of good and bad. Teams run the same checks on a laptop and in CI.

**Let bots update it.** Dependabot or Renovate opens the pull request when a new policy version ships, possibly auto-merged. And once policy is a dependency, the software bill of materials work you started after Log4j (CVE-2021-44228 and friends get the obligatory memes) tells you who runs which version across the estate.

## The demo: Checkov, Kyverno and a bit of bash

He builds a real example in the policy-as-versioned-code GitHub organisation, using Terraform checked by Checkov and Kubernetes checked by Kyverno, while stressing the tools are interchangeable. The policy repo has tagged, signed releases 1.0.0 through 2.1.1 with release notes. Three pairs of app and infra repos pin different versions; Renovate's open pull requests show each one where and why it would fail the next version, so the open PRs become the compliance report. A containerised checker, held together with some bash he asks you not to judge, evaluates a repo against its pinned policy version locally or in CI.

Kubernetes admission control lets several policy versions coexist in one cluster: one cluster accepts every version, another only 2.0.0 and up, tested in CI with kind. Cloud providers' own policy engines can't be evaluated locally the same way, which he flags as an open gap where contributions are welcome.

## Policy that carries its reason

The last idea is the best one. If each policy carries the risk it mitigates, a team that wants to do something outside it doesn't need an exemption; it opens a reasoned pull request against the policy. When the risks change - a new privacy regulation, a marketing win that brings in more data - the policy moves with them. He admits the culture change behind that is a series of talks in itself, and closes with the tongue-twister from his abstract: "Purposeless policy is potentially practically pointless policy."

## Who should watch

Platform and security teams who own guardrails and are tired of exemption spreadsheets, and developers who keep hitting policies they can't see. Bring some familiarity with Kubernetes admission controllers and Terraform.

He came back to Conf42 with [pod security policy](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2023_Chris_NesbittSmith_pod_security_policy). For the tooling side, pair it with [Noaa Barki on OPA, Conftest and Gatekeeper](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Noaa_Barki_open_policy_agent_conftest_gatekeeper_kubernetes_policy_in_action) and [Ismael Hommani and Tanguy Combe on compliance as code with Cloud Custodian](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2021_Ismael_Hommani_Tanguy_Combe_compliance_as_code_cloud_custodian).

Title: Retire the giant Jenkins box and let spot agents scale from zero
Description: Valera Bronshtein (Memphis{dev}) at Conf42 Incident Management 2022 on replacing one oversized Jenkins server with EC2 spot fleets that idle at zero
Body:
Every startup has the Jenkins server that started small and grew into a monster nobody dares reboot. At Conf42 Incident Management 2022, Valera Bronshtein, Head of DevOps at Memphis{dev}, showed how his team split theirs into a small coordinator plus EC2 spot fleets in Auto Scaling groups that sit at zero instances most of the month, and took the CI bill from about $1,016 a month to well under $100.

It is a short, practical war story with a live demo, not a survey of CI tools. Memphis{dev} builds an open source real-time data processing platform, and like most startups it set up its first CI quick and dirty.

## How did one Jenkins become a problem?

They installed Jenkins and used it as it was, without much configuration. It worked, until builds got slower and the disk filled too fast. So they kept scaling it up into what he calls the Jenkins ninja: a c5a.8xlarge with 32 vCPUs and 64 GB of RAM, on demand, all month. The next size up was 64 vCPUs, and he didn't want to go there.

The big box brought three problems:

- **Single point of failure.** One broken build can take down every other pipeline, which is tolerable on a Tuesday and much less so in the middle of a release.
- **No parallelism.** One build eats all the resources, or two builds both want MongoDB on the same port, and the rest wait in line.
- **Endless monitoring.** The CI server is effectively production for the DevOps team, so someone has to watch it all the time.

## Why not just run it on spot?

He priced it: the same c5a.8xlarge as a spot instance all month comes to around $427 instead of $1,016. But a single spot instance gets reclaimed exactly when you need it, which by Murphy's law means in the middle of a release. He has been there and does not recommend it.

## Turning one ninja into many

The goals were high availability, parallel builds for a shorter time to market, and a dedicated compute node per pipeline type, so a nightly backup job doesn't run on a 32-core machine. On availability he is refreshingly unsentimental about agents: if a pipeline kills a node, throw it away. As he put it at Conf42 Incident Management 2022, "I want to destroy it and create another one."

The flow:

1. Someone clicks Build Now in the Jenkins UI.
2. The pipeline is pinned to a fleet group, and the EC2 Fleet plugin talks to AWS.
3. The fleet maps to an Auto Scaling group, which starts the right launch template with its instance type, network and security groups.
4. The launch template's user data script installs the build's prerequisites (the right Java version, Node.js libraries) and raises an OK flag when it's done.
5. A prefix start-agent command on the Jenkins side checks for that flag, every five seconds or so, and only then starts the pipeline on the new agent.

The detail worth stealing: the Auto Scaling group can list several acceptable instance types, so when one spot type isn't available it picks another and the pipeline never notices.

## What does the bill look like after?

The heavy fleet still uses c5a.8xlarge spot instances, but its minimum and desired capacity are zero. Valera Bronshtein said that "on a day to day basis I have zero instances up." His deliberately pessimistic model - four release peaks a month, five spot instances each, four hours of intensive work per instance - comes to about $40.65 a month. In practice, he said, peaks use two or three instances for less time.

He pre-empts the obvious objection: the coordinator is still running all month. True, but it is now a t3.medium (2 vCPUs, 4 GB) on demand at about $35 a month, and since it only runs plugins and routes pipelines to fleets, he says a t3.micro would do. Add the two together and you're at roughly $76 against $1,016 - a cut of more than 90%, and one that grows as the build load does.

## The demo

Two pipelines that both back up a GitHub repository: one bound to the big fleet (capped at five instances) for builds, end-to-end tests and image work, and one bound to a small fleet (capped at two) of t2/t3-class instances for cron jobs. He shows the cloud configuration in Jenkins (region, credentials, Auto Scaling group name, the OK-flag check) and the two Auto Scaling groups in AWS, then runs both pipelines; the small fleet scales up from zero and the instance removes itself a few minutes after the job finishes.

## Who should watch

Anyone still paying for a large always-on Jenkins controller that does the building itself. It is AWS- and Jenkins-specific, and the numbers are his own estimates from the AWS pricing calculator, so run your own. The incident-management connection is indirect: fewer single points of failure in the pipeline means fewer release-day incidents.

Related talks: [Ankit Jain on automating merges to keep builds healthy](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2022_Ankit_Jain_automate_merging_keep_builds_healthy), [Maksymilian Kalek on AWS cost efficiency](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Maksymilian_Kalek_aws_cost_efficiency), and [Michael Levan on cost and resource optimisation](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Michael_Levan_cost_resource_optimization).

Title: An extra nine can cost ten times more for $900 of value
Description: Ricardo Castro (Anova) at Conf42 Incident Management 2022 on building reliability from metrics up to SLOs, error budgets and burn-rate alerts
Body:
Reliability is whatever your users say it is, and chasing nines they never asked for is an expensive hobby. At Conf42 Incident Management 2022, Ricardo Castro, Lead SRE at Anova, builds the full SLO stack step by step - metrics, SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, SLAs, burn-rate alerts and error budget policies - and runs the back-of-the-envelope numbers on why another nine may not be worth it.

It is a structured introduction, a good first SLO talk for a team that keeps hearing the acronyms. Anova works in industrial IoT, ingesting data from industrial sensors and turning it into services customers use to run their infrastructure, so every one of those services has to be reliable.

## What does a supermarket have to do with microservices?

His opening analogy: a supermarket is a microservices architecture. You walk in, shop, pay and leave, but behind that someone placed purchase orders, transported and unloaded stock, filled the shelves and staffed the tills. When paying takes too long, that is latency. When the yoghurt is past its expiry date, that is an error.

He prefers Alex Hidalgo's definition from Implementing Service Level Objectives to the dictionary's: the question is whether the service is doing what its users need it to do, not whether it is behaving well.

## From a metric to a promise

The stack climbs one rung at a time:

- **Metric**: a measurement, nothing more. Memory use, request time in milliseconds, count of HTTP 500s, age of a message arriving at a Kafka cluster.
- **SLI**: turns a metric into a binary good or bad event. A request answered within 200 ms is good; a Kafka message older than five minutes is bad.
- **SLO**: how often the SLI has to be good, over a window. For example, 99% of requests answered within 200 ms over 30 days.
- **SLA**: an SLO with a penalty attached, such as a 30% discount, and usually looser than the internal SLO so you breach the SLO first and still have room before the contract bites.

His tips for good SLOs start with the one to remember if you forget the rest. Ricardo Castro said at Conf42 Incident Management 2022: "always, always and always focus on the users." Users define the reliability of the service.

From there: list critical user journeys, order them by business impact, pick the SLIs that track them, keep it to three or four SLOs for most services, write an SLO document (he shows the template from Google's SRE workbook: authors, approvers, review date, SLIs, rationale, error budget, caveats), and review them periodically.

## How expensive is one more nine?

Three nines of uptime allows about eight hours of downtime a year; four nines cuts that to roughly 52 minutes; five nines leaves about five minutes. His two scenarios for going from three to four nines on a service with $1 million of revenue: the improvement in value is around $900. Then the rule of thumb that each extra nine costs ten times more: if running the service costs $1 million, the extra nine costs around $10 million. Rough numbers, he says, but worth doing before anyone promises five nines in a meeting.

## Alerting on what users feel, before it's too late

Classic threshold alerts (CPU above 80%, too many 500s) don't track the user. Alerting when the SLO itself is breached does, but only once you're already in trouble. Alerting on error budget consumed is better: email at 25% burned, a Slack or Teams message at 50%, PagerDuty or Opsgenie at 75%. That still says nothing about speed, though, and if you'd end the window with budget to spare, you probably don't want the page at all.

Hence burn rate: how fast the error budget is being consumed. A burn rate of one spends the budget exactly over the window; a burn rate of two over a four-week window empties it in two weeks. The final refinement is multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting: a fast-burn alert for sudden spikes, such as a 2-hour window evaluated every five minutes firing at a burn rate of 10, and a slow-burn alert for steady leaks, such as a 4-hour window firing at a burn rate of 2.

## What happens when the budget runs out?

That gets decided in advance, in an error budget policy. His example: if a service has exceeded its error budget for the preceding four-week window, all changes and releases stop except P0 issues and security fixes until it's back within its SLO, and the team may move from feature work to reliability work depending on the cause. The value is that everyone agreed to it before the incident.

## Why bother

His closing case: SLOs measure reliability through the users' eyes, tie reliability work to business goals, give engineers, product and business people one shared language, and make the reliability-versus-features call a decision instead of an argument.

## Who should watch

Teams starting with SLOs, and anyone who has to explain to leadership why four nines is a budget question. Engineers already running multi-window burn-rate alerts will find it familiar.

He returned to the topic at Conf42 SRE 2022 with [alerting on SLOs and error budget policies](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2022_Ricardo_Castro_alerting_slos_error_budget_policies). Pair it with [Fred Moyer on SLOs and error budgets at scale](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2023_Fred_Moyer_slos_error_budgets_scale) and [Jeff Nickoloff on reliability management](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2022_Jeff_Nickoloff_reliability_management).

Title: Most of incident response happens before the pager goes off
Description: Hila Fish (Wix) at Conf42 Incident Management 2022 on a structured incident flow, the qualities of an incident manager and day-to-day prep
Body:
In school, the theory went that listening in class gets you half of the exam prep for free. Hila Fish, Senior DevOps Engineer at Wix, applies the same idea to on-call at Conf42 Incident Management 2022: if you do the boring work on ordinary days and follow a structured flow on bad nights, incidents get shorter and you get more sleep. Fifteen years in tech, as she puts it, means a lot of production incidents.

## Can an incident really follow a structure?

Incidents are full of unknowns, which is exactly why she wants a fixed flow around them. Everything fails all the time, so the ad hoc, putting-out-fires mindset doesn't scale; a business mindset does, because downtime means lost data, lost revenue and breached SLAs. Her flow (credited to an OnPage article) has five pillars, each with questions to ask yourself while the alerts are still red:

- **Identify and categorise.** Do I understand the full extent of the problem? If not, gather more information before diving in. Can this wait for business hours? A 4am page for something minor means the severity or the runbook is wrong, so change it. Was I notified through the expected channel? Hearing about it from a user complaint rather than PagerDuty is a note-to-self to fix.
- **Notify and escalate.** Who needs to know during the incident (customer success when users are hit) and in general (teams that care about the system's health)?
- **Investigate and diagnose.** Focus on the relevant information, because the rest throws you off course. Prioritise root causes over surface symptoms: restarting the same service on the same server three times and going back to bed is a band-aid, not a fix.
- **Resolve and recover.** Pick the fastest fix that doesn't compromise the system's health and stability. If a night-time patch went in, the permanent fix is an action item.
- **Close.** Be an end-to-end communicator: tell the support teams it's resolved, and use them as a kind of QA in case users still see problems. Tune the alerts, update or write the runbook, and file the ticket that prevents the next one.

On postmortems she cites the Zeigarnik effect, from psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik: people remember more details of an ongoing task than of a finished one. So write the notes as soon as possible, and if there is no postmortem, still share the knowledge in a runbook or a daily brief.

## Who runs the war room?

Once more than three or four people are involved, someone has to be the incident manager: calm, dividing the work, and willing to send people away when their part is done, because too many people are too noisy. Her story here is a good one. New at a company, sitting quietly on a Zoom war room during a critical AWS issue, she watched everyone pull in different directions. She stepped in, took the incident manager role, handed out log checks, and asked someone to write down the startup order the application needed, since no runbook existed for it. Things started moving.

## What makes a good incident manager?

Her list: think on your feet, separate relevant from irrelevant information (the better you know the system, the easier that gets), operate under pressure, work methodically, be humble, keep a can-do approach, own what you escalated, communicate well, lead without authority, and care.

The pressure point comes with a second story. On her first on-call shift at another job, about 100 alerts filled the screen, so she called the engineer who'd been there two years. He stared at the wall of alerts, marvelled at how many there were, and froze. Her lesson: "stress is a symptom of being out of control, and collection of relevant data will help you decrease stress levels."

On humility she is blunt. Fixing it alone to be the hero misses the point; during an incident, she said, "it's not your time to shine." Escalating keeps the business healthy, and ownership means checking back ten or fifteen minutes later that the person you escalated to is actually on it.

## What does proactive look like?

After an incident: an on-call handoff summary in the team channel, postmortem notes, tickets that stabilise the environment, fixes for false-positive alerts (don't leave them for the next on-call, who will leave them for the next one), runbooks, candidates for self-remediation, and a write-up of how you reasoned it through.

Day to day: read every handoff, not just the one before your shift. Know the escalation contacts for services outside your own realm before 3am, not during it. Learn the architecture's weak spots and blast radius, learn the application flows so you can follow the logs along them, and know what your teammates and deployments changed in production. The pager will call you whether or not you made the change.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to on-call or about to run their first war room, and leads who want a checklist they can hand to the team. It's practical, structured and light on tooling.

Related talks: [Lisa Karlin Curtis on using incidents to level up your teams](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2022_Lisa_Karlin_Curtis_incidents_levelup_your_teams), [Kurt Andersen on the varieties of incident response](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2022_Kurt_Andersen_varieties_incident_response), and [Nick Mason and Emily Arnott on too many people in an incident](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2022_Nick_Mason_Emily_Arnott_too_many_people).

Title: Run towards the fire - incidents are the fastest way to grow engineers
Description: Lisa Karlin Curtis (incident.io) at Conf42 Incident Management 2022 on why incidents speed up careers and how to open them up to the whole team
Body:
Lisa Karlin Curtis, Technical Lead at incident.io, made senior faster than she expected, and when she looked back at why, the pattern was incidents. At Conf42 Incident Management 2022 she made the case that incidents are the densest learning an engineer gets, and that most teams quietly lock their juniors out of them.

The story that opens the talk is a good one. Early in her career at GoCardless, the API slowed to a crawl. One endpoint kept timing out, so the team disabled it to get the system back. The real cause turned out to be Postgres switching the query plan for one query from expensive-but-manageable to not manageable at all; a subtle change to the query pushed the database back to the old plan. She watched from the sidelines taking notes, and afterwards asked a senior engineer on her team what a query plan was.

## What does an incident actually teach you?

She lists six things, and each one comes back to that API outage.

**Incidents broaden your horizons.** Engineers live among black boxes: languages, frameworks, databases. You learn the interface and move on, because otherwise nobody would ship anything. Lisa Karlin Curtis said at Conf42 Incident Management 2022: "Incidents force you to open the black boxes around you, peek inside and learn just enough to solve the problem." Reading up on query plans paid off. It was not their last query-plan incident, and she started writing code that scaled the first time instead of by trial and error in production.

**Incidents teach graceful failure.** A key follow-up was a statement timeout on every database call, so a bad query gets a few seconds and then gets cancelled. Cancelling queries on purpose sounds odd until the alternative is losing the whole API. You don't need to know which query will go bad, only that one eventually will. As she put it, "A degraded service is far better than a completely absent one."

**Incidents allow blue-sky thinking.** Disabling an entire endpoint is something you'd never do on a normal Tuesday, and in context it was the right call. Her comparison is a surgeon: nobody amputates by choice, only because the alternative is worse.

**Incidents make you better at observability.** She admits to shipping plenty of useless log lines and metrics. Good observability needs empathy for whoever is debugging at 2am, and the people who do it well are pattern-matching on incidents they've lived through.

**Incidents build your network.** She hadn't known the name of the account manager whose partners were worst hit, despite sitting on the product team that served partners. Most of the finance, risk, support and marketing people she knew at GoCardless, she met in incidents.

**Incidents let you learn from the best.** The people who get pulled into a bad incident are the ones everyone trusts with the hardest problems, and they are usually too busy to shadow any other way.

## How do you open incidents up to everyone?

GoCardless let anyone follow incident channels. Many teams don't: private channels by default, invite only, an in-group that handles everything while everyone else stays out of the way. Her four fixes:

- **Declare lots of incidents.** She calls it the single most impactful change to an incident process. A low bar means the process gets practised, so the big one runs like a well-oiled machine. The corollary: "the first step is to stop counting incidents." If more incidents look bad on a dashboard, nobody declares the small ones.
- **Encourage everyone to participate.** Public channels by default. Twenty people piling into a minor incident is too many, but most can take two or three juniors tagging along, who can save questions until it's resolved. Debrief documents and post-incident reviews count too, and a reading list of the best debriefs makes good onboarding.
- **Show your working.** Every command run and every theory disproved goes into the channel, even if that means a 10pm conversation with yourself. It helps the handover, and it teaches everyone else how you approached the problem.
- **Watch out for the hero.** The engineer who fixes things before anyone notices burns out, gets less credit as it becomes normal, and takes the learning away from the team. It's good job security and a bad team.

She does mention her employer's product as one way to keep incidents central and visible; the rest of the advice is tool-agnostic.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers deciding who gets into incident channels, and junior engineers wondering whether lurking in one is allowed. It is short and full of stories, with no slides of process diagrams.

Related talks: [Vanessa Huerta Granda on sharing incident findings effectively](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2022_Vanessa_Huerta_Granda_sharing_Incident_findings_effectively), [Einat Mahat on on-call heroes and effective practices](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Einat_Mahat_oncall_heroes_effective_practices), and [Ramon Medrano Llamas on postmortem culture at Google](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2022_Ramon_Medrano_Llamas_postmortem_culture_google).

Title: Your postmortem report is not the finish line, it's the first draft
Description: Vanessa Huerta Granda (Jeli.io) at Conf42 Incident Management 2022 on sharing incident findings in formats each audience will actually read
Body:
Most incident reviews end with a lovingly written document that goes to Google Drive to die. At Conf42 Incident Management 2022, Vanessa Huerta Granda, Solutions Engineer at Jeli.io, argued that the review is only half the work: the learnings change nothing until they reach the people who can act on them, and each of those people needs a different format.

She opens with her own history. Her team was running good retrospectives and learning plenty, but the recommendations went nowhere. Engineers pointed at reports full of error screenshots and timestamp timelines that never said what was actually needed, and the non-engineers couldn't see why any of it mattered - the company was still making money. Once the team started rewriting reports, adding abstracts, sending weekly updates and building cases for long-term fixes, the recommendations slowly started landing in quarterly plans. Not all incidents went away, but the loop of the same incidents over and over did.

## Why isn't a report in the drive enough?

Because availability is not readership. Vanessa Huerta Granda said at Conf42 Incident Management 2022: "having something available to me doesn't mean that I'm going to read it." Her inbox isn't at zero, and neither is anyone else's.

She leans on Jeli's Howie guide for the principle. In her words, "your work should not be completed to be filed. It should be completed so it can be read and shared across the business." The reasons to share go beyond tidiness: transparency, letting affected teams know about findings that touch them (part of a just culture), giving executives a TL;DR when you need buy-in, and covering everyone who missed the review because they were on PTO, heads-down, or busy with the next incident.

## Who is reading, and why?

Her analogy is the movies. Some people watch the full 120 minutes, some want a ten-episode podcast about it, some want a five-minute review before spending $12 on a ticket and another $12 on popcorn. Incidents have the same spread: engineers, managers who give context to others, executives who approve changes, technical and non-technical stakeholders, and outside parties such as customer support and the PR folks writing tweets while the site is down.

Each of them reads with a purpose: an action is requested, they need to know, it's an update, or you want to change their mind. Her example for the last one is gloriously specific: telling Jen's boss not to fire Jen, because the report shows it wasn't her fault.

## Six formats, from longest to shortest attention span

- **Report**: the most in-depth artifact, built around a narrative timeline told from several points of view, not a start-middle-end log. Written to be commented on, linked from PRs, and read asynchronously.
- **Abstract**: one or two paragraphs on what happened, why anyone should care and the contributing themes. Her personal favourite, and the one she sends to leadership. It is, she said, "your incidents elevator pitch."
- **Summary**: more context from the review meeting, action items with who suggested them, and key takeaways. When she shares one she tags people and tells them why it concerns them.
- **Recording**: the review call itself, best shared with timestamps (impact at minute ten, action items at minute 25). Good for responders who missed the meeting; leadership won't watch an hour of it, and that's fine.
- **Weekly update**: every incident analysed that week, each with its abstract, a link to the report and fields such as teams impacted. Great for large orgs with many incidents, where managers skim for their own technologies.
- **Presentation**: the chance to walk a wider audience through the timeline and the themes, tuned to whether the room is technical or business.

## From one incident to a case for change

The first five formats cover single incidents. The interesting part is what happens across many. She dislikes the postmortem that turns into an action items factory, where half the tickets will never be done and people lose faith in the process. With a sample size of one you can't propose a reorg; with a body of well-written reports you can spot macro trends and argue for structural change.

Her example: an organisation where only a few trusted people could declare an incident. As the company grew, that gate was delaying the response to high-impact incidents. Across many reports it showed up not as a root cause but as a contributing factor, so she took the case to engineering leadership, up to the CTO, with a checklist anyone can reuse: what is the suggestion, who needs to approve it, what do they need to see, what is it based on, what could go wrong, what is the end game, and who does the work. The team proposed trying it for a quarter and revisiting. It worked.

## Who should watch

Anyone who writes postmortems that nobody opens, and anyone running a learning-from-incidents programme who needs leadership to fund the follow-ups. It is short, practical and tool-light.

Pair it with [Lisa Karlin Curtis on using incidents to level up your teams](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2022_Lisa_Karlin_Curtis_incidents_levelup_your_teams), [Amir Shaked on creating a learning culture](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2022_Amir_Shaked_create_learning_culture), and [Andre Carvalho on getting insights through reports](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Andre_Carvalho_insights_through_reports).

Title: A Rust blog that serves from RAM and beats nginx at static files
Description: Xe Iaso (Tailscale) at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 on a Rust blog engine that renders compiled templates from RAM faster than static file servers
Body:
Xe Iaso's blog is dynamic, written in Rust, and so fast that readers assume it is a static site. At Conf42 Rustlang 2022, Xe, Archmage of Infrastructure at Tailscale, walks through how it works: Markdown loaded into RAM at startup, templates compiled to Rust functions, and a post lookup that is technically O(n) and in practice constant time. Then comes the hosting history that explains why it ended up that way, Kubernetes included.

## How can a dynamic site beat a static one?

Posts are Markdown with YAML front matter, written in Emacs. They are parsed with comrak, extended with custom HTML elements that lol_html rewrites through a bank of templates, which is how the conversation snippets and AI-generated hero images get onto the page. The page templates use ructe, which compiles a template syntax over HTML into Rust code. Loading the homepage calls a function that renders straight into a string buffer, from data already in memory.

Xe said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "Turns out serving things out of ram is very fast." To check, Xe benchmarked the site against nginx, OpenResty, Tengine, Apache, the Go standard library, warp and axum. None was faster except a Go binary with the whole site compiled into it, at about 200 MB, which was not viable.

ructe has costs: you declare types inside templates and must make sure the generated code imports the traits you need. Xe has been moving to maud, a procedural macro that turns its own DSL into HTML at compile time, with components as plain Rust functions. The short codes already use it.

## The linked list that should be a problem

Every post lives in memory in the moral equivalent of a linked list (a Vec of posts on the slides), so showing a post means walking the list. That sounds terrible for a high-traffic blog until you look at the analytics: the most read post is almost always the newest one, which sits at the front. At almost 300 posts, it is fine. Xe admits it may need rethinking one day.

Startup reads every post from disk with Tokio spreading the work across all cores, so loading is up to twelve times faster than doing it serially. Xe also credits Rust with lower cognitive load: a line of Rust that would be about 50 lines of Go.

## Stateless, mostly

Because everything is loaded into RAM, the site is stateless and can move to any server. The same in-memory data feeds RSS, Atom and JSON Feed, the last with a custom extension carrying extra front matter such as stream recordings, slides and series names.

The state lives in a separate personal API called mi, after the Toki Pona word for me. It handles POSSE (publish on your own site, syndicate elsewhere), announcing new posts on Twitter and Mastodon automatically, and receives and stores Webmentions, which the blog fetches at startup. The trade-off is some delay before a new mention shows up, which Xe accepts to keep the blog easy to move. Patreon remains manual, because its API does not let you create posts.

## How did it get here?

The history is the most fun part. Heroku's free tier hosted the first version, built on Lapis, a Lua web framework inside nginx, which parsed Markdown on every page load. It barely survived its first Hacker News front page; caching rendered HTML in OlegDB, a key-value store written in C by friends, is what got it through. Then Dokku, a self-hosted Heroku clone, because many apps could share one 5 dollar server. Then a rewrite in Go, nerd-sniped by people in the Go community Slack wanting a standard library web app example, first with PureScript and React and then plain server-rendered HTML for readers whose browsers skip JavaScript. That is where everything moved into RAM.

Traffic kept growing, past 100 GB a month for a mostly text site, with less than one post in ten going viral but each time all at once. When the Docker host started falling over, Kubernetes on DigitalOcean was next. Xe said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "So I decided to commission a freight train to mail a letter and I set up a Kubernetes cluster with digitalocean." It worked, with GitHub Actions continuous deployment, until stuck mounts and no root access made outages worse than on a single server. Now it runs on one big NixOS server, with nginx routing to a Unix socket.

## Who should watch

Anyone running a content site who reaches for a CDN or a static generator by reflex, and Rust web developers who want a real, opinionated example. Xe said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 that "dynamic web apps can be very fast, especially if they are built to purpose." The talk is the proof, with jokes.

- Haseeb Majid on [reproducible development environments with Nix](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Haseeb_Majid_using_nix_reproducible) at Conf42 Golang 2024.
- Leigh Capili on [cloud native Nix](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Leigh_Capili_cloud_native_nix_development) at Conf42 Kube Native 2024.

Title: EpiRust: shrinking a 10 GB grid on the way to 100 million agents
Description: Jayanta Kshirsagar and Sapana Kale (Thoughtworks) at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 on scaling the EpiRust epidemic simulator with hash maps, Rayon and Kafka
Body:
Simulating every person in a city of 3.2 million, hour by hour for 45 days, starts with a grid that eats 5 to 10 GB of RAM. Jayanta Kshirsagar and Sapana Kale of Thoughtworks' Engineering for Research team tell the story at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 of how EpiRust, their open-source agent-based epidemic simulator, went from that grid to a hash map of a few hundred MB, then to parallel and distributed engines aimed at 100 million agents.

They keep it technical on purpose: the Covid-19 disease model is out of scope. This is a scientific computing case study.

## What is EpiRust simulating?

Agent-based modelling builds the society bottom-up. Every individual gets a home, maybe a workplace, a schedule and some characteristics; they commute, sit next to strangers on transport, meet colleagues and go home to their families, and each interaction is a chance for the disease to spread. Government interventions like lockdowns, masks and vaccination can be modelled too.

Stripped down, the engine is two loops: an outer loop over simulated hours, an inner loop asking every agent to perform its routine and updating infections, then bookkeeping and interventions at the end of each hour.

The scale grew in steps: 1,000 identical agents, then 10,000 with heterogeneity (age, essential workers), then Pune at 3.2 million, then Mumbai at 12 million with long commutes, with the 100 million agents of Maharashtra and multiple cities as the target. Kshirsagar said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "Scale and performance became the issue pretty quickly for us."

## Why is it so expensive?

The numbers from their slides: 45 days is 1,080 simulated hours. At 1,000 agents that is about 7 million behaviours to execute; at 1 million, about 7 billion; at 100 million, about 700 billion. The grid is also sparse, mostly empty cells, so memory matters as much as compute.

There is a subtler problem. The inner loop moves agents one after another, but real people move at the same time, so naive iteration makes the result depend on order. EpiRust uses double buffering: agents read neighbour positions from a read buffer and write their new position to a write buffer.

## How did memory drop from gigabytes to megabytes?

The first Pune implementation stored the grid as a 2D matrix, 5,660 by 5,660, which is 32,035,600 cells and 5 to 10 GB of RAM. Replacing it with a hash map from point to citizen made the number of entries equal the number of agents, kept lookups O(1), and brought memory down to a few hundred MB. They then benchmarked hashers, including hashbrown with AHash, FxHash and FNV, since the hash is never exposed outside the simulator and does not need to be cryptographic.

## How did throughput scale up and then out?

Because each agent's update reads only from the read buffer, the inner loop parallelises. Kale walks through two versions: a map-reduce that updates agents in parallel and writes them serially to avoid collisions, and Rayon parallel iterators over a DashMap, a concurrent map that handles both steps. On 5 million agents both roughly doubled the serial throughput, and on 64 cores they performed about the same.

Scaling up stops at the biggest machine you can get, and different cities can need different parameters anyway. So they split geography into engines, each with its own configuration, running in distributed mode. Commuters crossing between engines travel as messages over Kafka, and an orchestrator keeps the engines in step hour by hour, so someone leaving at hour 24 arrives on time.

The slides have the payoff: Mumbai as 24 engines of 0.5 million agents ran at a throughput of 0.57, while 100 engines of 100,000 agents (10 million in total) reached 3.03. Running 100 engines by hand is not an option, so EpiRust is containerised and runs as Kubernetes jobs packaged in a Helm chart, with Kafka in the cluster and the ELK stack, Prometheus and Grafana for logs, metrics and alerts.

## What did Rust bring?

Kale credits C-like performance with no runtime or garbage collector, memory safety without C and C++ debugging sessions, Cargo and the crate ecosystem (Rayon, Tokio), and concurrency that fails at compile time. Kale said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "With the fearless concurrency, we could easily go with the parallel implementation and most of the errors were coming at the compilation time."

## Who should watch

Anyone writing simulations or other compute-heavy scientific code, and Rust developers who want a real-world story of the hash map, Rayon, then distribution progression. The code is on GitHub under thoughtworks/epirust.

Title: Neon or WebAssembly? Two ways to put Rust under Node.js
Description: Dmitry Kudryavtsev (Forter) at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 on speeding up Node.js with Rust native modules via Neon versus WebAssembly
Body:
Rust can speed up a Node.js service in two quite different ways, and the right one depends less on raw speed than on where the code has to run. Dmitry Kudryavtsev, Senior Software Engineer at Forter, compares them at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: native modules built with Neon, and Rust compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-bindgen, measured on the same recursive Fibonacci and then weighed on reusability, ergonomics, standard library access, portability and browser support.

## Why bring Rust into JavaScript at all?

JavaScript is everywhere, from the browser to Node.js on the backend to desktop apps via Electron and Tauri, and it is not going away. It is also slow at CPU-bound work like image processing or 3D rendering. Native modules have long been the escape hatch, traditionally in C or C++. His case for Rust over them: modern tooling with Cargo, a rich standard library, and memory safety, so no segfaults.

## Path one: a native module with Neon

Neon is the glue layer between the two worlds. The Rust side has the plain Fibonacci function, then a glue function that converts JavaScript numbers into Rust types and the result back, then a main that exports it to JavaScript under a name of your choosing. The neon team's cargo-cp-artifact tool builds a dynamic library wrapped in the Node API, and from JavaScript you simply require it and call it like any other function.

## Path two: WebAssembly

WebAssembly is a portable binary format, executed by a VM that ships in every major browser and in Node.js. It can be written directly in AssemblyScript, but the interesting part is that it is a compilation target for languages like Rust. With wasm-bindgen the Rust version is the same function plus one macro.

## What did the benchmark show?

He ran each version with hyperfine, three warm-ups, taking the mean:

| Fibonacci | Node.js | Native Rust | Rust Wasm |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30th | 165.2 ms | 161.5 ms | 163 ms |
| 44th | 5.846 s | 2.271 s | 3.286 s |
| 46th | 15.038 s | 5.721 s | 8.317 s |

At small inputs there is no difference worth the effort. At the heavy end native Rust took about 60% less time than Node.js and Wasm about 45% less. Then the honest conclusion. Kudryavtsev said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 that "benchmarks like this are useless." They prove a point; run your own against your real workload before adding a native build to your pipeline.

## So which one?

His comparison, in order:

- **Performance:** native wins, as native beats any VM. Wasm is still fast and a good middle ground.
- **Reusability:** it is complicated. A native Rust library can be reused through FFI from Java or Swift on mobile; Wasm only runs where there is a Wasm VM.
- **Ergonomics:** Wasm. wasm-bindgen converts basic types for you, while Neon needs a hand-written glue layer that gets messy with error handling, because JavaScript values can be anything.
- **Standard library:** native. Wasm has no file system, networking or OS access. WASI is the proposal to fix that and was still in development; embedding a virtual file system does not help with dynamic files on disk.
- **Portability:** Wasm. Native modules are tied to the host architecture, so a build from an M1 MacBook will not run on an x86_64 Windows machine. Compile them in the target environment, for example the same Alpine Docker image you run in production.
- **Browser:** Wasm only. Native modules work in Node.js because of N-API; browsers have no FFI.

His two mental models sum it up. Native modules extend your Node.js code with things JavaScript cannot do well. Kudryavtsev said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "webassembly is meant to replace non performant Javascript code." Image manipulation or heavy visualisation in the browser is the classic case.

## Who should watch

Node.js developers with a hot function they would like to make faster, and Rust developers asked to help them. It is a clear, short decision guide; the blog posts it is based on carry the code and the GitHub repos.

- Thorsten Hans on [going serverless with WebAssembly](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Thorsten_Hans_serverless_webassembly) at Conf42 Golang 2024.

Title: Rust on AWS Lambda answered in 4 ms where Node took 60
Description: Luca Bianchi (Neosperience) at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 on why Rust cuts Lambda cold starts and run time, and how to start with AWS SAM
Body:
On AWS Lambda you pay per millisecond and wait on every cold start, so the runtime you pick shows up on the bill. Luca Bianchi, CTO at Neosperience and an AWS Hero, makes the case at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 that Rust is the unfair advantage among Lambda runtimes: in his comparison it was at least twice as fast as equivalent Node.js code, and in the best case 4 ms against 60 ms.

A note on scope: the abstract describes a Kinesis churn-prediction pipeline and a Python comparison. The talk as recorded is shorter and simpler, a serverless primer, a DynamoDB example scaffolded with AWS SAM, and a Rust versus Node benchmark. Treat it as a first talk on Rust for Lambda.

## What does serverless remove from your plate?

Bianchi peels the stack layer by layer: no servers to buy, no VMs to size (so no paying for idle and no VM disaster recovery), no operating system to patch, no schedulers or containers to manage. What remains is your code, invoked by the platform. Borrowing Patrick Debois's term, he goes one step further. Bianchi said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 that "serverless is serviceful because you can focus directly on what is providing added value for your customers."

In practice that means configuring managed services rather than writing them: Amazon API Gateway for REST and websockets, AWS AppSync for GraphQL, with scaling, firewalls and monitoring that come with them, and business logic in Lambda functions.

## Where does the time go in a Lambda?

Each invocation runs in a micro virtual machine that Lambda builds on demand: start the container, the runtime, any extensions, then your initialisation code, then the handler. The first part is the cold start. You hit it in two ways: a function nobody has called for a while (he puts it at roughly 30 minutes), and, more worryingly, scaling out. On Black Friday every new concurrent request can mean a new unit of compute and a new cold start, sometimes costing seconds.

You cannot pick CPUs on Lambda, only memory, and CPU scales with it. Across configurations from 128 MB up to 1 GB, his chart shows Java slowest and Ruby, Node.js and Python in between, with Rust ahead at every step.

## Why Rust, beyond raw speed?

Static typing matters more in serverless than people expect, he argues, because the development loop bounces between your laptop and the cloud. Every error the compiler catches is a deploy you did not have to make. Add good tooling and a busy crate ecosystem and Rust is a comfortable fit.

## How do you start?

AWS SAM has a Rust template. Run sam init, pick the template and the architecture (Lambda supports x86_64 and arm64), and SAM writes the template file it later turns into CloudFormation, plus a project skeleton. His example takes an HTTP request and writes an item to DynamoDB:

- the lambda_http crate for the request handler and runtime, the AWS SDK for DynamoDB, and Tokio to make main async;
- clients and environment variables set up in main, so they persist across warm invocations until the runtime is torn down;
- the runtime started with a closure that passes the DynamoDB client, the table name and the request to the handler;
- a handler that parses the body, builds a PutItem request with the builder pattern, matches the result and returns a 200 or a 500 for API Gateway.

## The numbers

On that sample, his Rust versus Node comparison shows Rust at least twice as fast in the worst case. Bianchi said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "But in the best case scenario rust is more than 1000% faster than node so it is four milliseconds compared to 60 milliseconds". He adds that Node cold starts can stretch towards a second. With per-millisecond billing, that gap is money once functions run at scale.

## Who should watch

Developers already on Lambda with Node or Python who want a quick, practical argument for trying Rust, and Rust developers looking for the shortest path to a deployed function. Experienced serverless engineers will know the first half.

- Roman Boiko on [why to use Rust for serverless workloads](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Roman_Boiko_serverless_workloads) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023.
- Dmitry Kudryavtsev on [speeding up Node.js with Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2022_Dmitry_Kudryavtsev_supercharge_nodejs), if you would rather keep Node and swap out the hot path.

Title: Smart contracts under a kilobyte, and references to data that isn't there
Description: Andrei Marinica (Elrond) at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 on a Rust smart contract framework where the VM owns the data and types are handles
Body:
Some of Elrond's smart contracts compile to 800 or 900 bytes of WebAssembly. Andrei Marinica, Core Team Software Developer at Elrond, explains at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 how the team's Rust framework gets there: the contract never touches its own big numbers, the VM does, and Rust's type system is bent far enough to give ownership semantics to data that lives somewhere else entirely.

He pitches it at Rust programmers rather than the blockchain crowd, and it shows: this is a talk about generics, macros and transmute, with a blockchain as the excuse.

## Why does contract size matter so much?

Elrond runs contracts as WebAssembly on Wasmer, under its own VM, Arwen. Contracts are stored on chain and JIT-compiled to machine code when run. Two costs follow: JIT compilation is not free when you want thousands of contract calls per second, and on-chain storage is expensive because every node replicates it. So bytecode size is a first-class goal, next to speed, and next to a third one he states bluntly from the slides: devs cannot be trusted to optimise this themselves. The framework has to do it.

## The contract is the recipe, the VM is the kitchen

The trick is to strip everything heavy out of the contract. Big-number arithmetic, crypto functions and memory allocation all live in the VM. The contract holds integer handles, asks the VM to add big int five to big int seven, and gets a handle back. Marinica said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "the smart contract never even sees these numbers." In his metaphor the contract is the recipe and the VM does the cooking.

Rust makes that bearable to program against, because operator overloading lets developers write a plus between two BigInt values as if they were local. When millions of dollars flow through the code, readable code is a safety feature.

## 300+ easy steps, grouped into six

His summary of three years of framework work: make it fast, make it pretty, make it testable, make it interoperable, make it composable, make it escape. Some highlights:

- **Contracts are traits.** The implementation is generated, so the same trait can compile to WebAssembly for the chain or to a plain library for unit and integration tests.
- **Proxies are generated too.** Calling another contract looks like calling a method, with the transaction plumbing hidden in an auto-generated proxy. The same proxies let off-chain code call contracts almost like a database query.
- **Modules caused stray endpoints.** Splitting a contract into modules via supertraits worked, but every endpoint in a crate was always exported, so including one module from a library dragged in callable endpoints you never meant to ship. The fix was serious metaprogramming: macros generate ABI generators per module, a meta crate calls them for the whole contract, and the wasm crate is generated from that ABI. Endpoints in modules you did not include never reach the binary.

## Three times they nearly broke Rust

**A fat Result.** Error handling with Result inflated bytecode with branches on every return. On a blockchain you want failures to crash immediately anyway, so contracts use a panicking error handler whose error type is the never type. A Result whose error can never exist compiles down to just the value, and he says that cut about 20% off some contracts.

**Vararg madness.** Endpoint argument loaders should hard-code each argument when there are no varargs and loop when there are, decided by type alone, because the macros cannot know. The solution is a compile-time fold over tuples nested inside tuples, as deep as needed, so each level can peek at what comes after it and every branch resolves during monomorphisation.

**Owning stuff that isn't there.** A ManagedVec of BigInt lives in the VM, so what should getting element i return? There is nothing in contract memory to point at. They built a ManagedRef type with a lifetime and, when it must behave like an ordinary reference, transmute it. Marinica said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "You can trick rust into thinking there's something there where there's nothing there, so you can work with reference to nothing." He calls it the closest they got to the limits of the language.

## Who should watch

Rust developers who enjoy type-level tricks, and anyone building a framework on top of WebAssembly where binary size is a cost. You do not need to care about blockchains; you do need to be comfortable with generics.
