Title: A finite state machine inside Redis, live-coded in Rust
Description: Brian Sam-Bodden (Redis) at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 on writing a Redis module in Rust with a custom data type, commands and hash event hooks
Body:
Redis lets you add your own data types and commands, and you no longer need C to do it. Brian Sam-Bodden, Developer Advocate at Redis, spends his Conf42 Rustlang 2022 session live-coding a Redis module in Rust from cargo new to a working finite state machine that manages the state field of ordinary Redis hashes.

It is a demo talk: one terminal, one editor, the whole module built step by step.

## Why would you write a Redis module in Rust?

Redis is a key-value database whose values can be strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, geospatial indexes, HyperLogLogs and more. The modules API extends that with new data types and commands; Redis itself ships modules such as RedisJSON, RediSearch, RedisGraph, RedisTimeSeries, RedisAI, RedisGears and RedisBloom.

Until recently that API was for C programmers only. Redis has been building a Rust bridge for it, published as the redis-module crate, and the reason is safety. Sam-Bodden said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "Redis modules run in the same memory space as Redis." A leak or a bad pointer in your module is a problem for the whole server, so memory safety is a requirement, not a nicety.

## What gets built?

A toy job state machine with three states (sleeping, running, cleaning) and three events (run, clean, sleep). The definition is JSON: a name, the key prefix of the hashes it governs, the field that stores the state, the states and the events with their from and to states. The module exposes four commands:

- **FSM.CREATE** parses the JSON with serde and stores it as a custom Redis data type.
- **FSM.INFO** reads it back and serialises it to JSON.
- **FSM.ALLOWED** checks whether an event can apply to a given hash in its current state.
- **FSM.TRIGGER** applies the event and writes the new state into the hash.

Plus one implicit behaviour: when a new hash with a matching prefix is written, the module sets its state field to the initial state, which is the first state in the definition.

## The details you only learn by doing it

Before the module, he gives a quick Redis CLI tour on Redis 7.0.4: strings, colon-separated key namespaces, the NX and XX flags on SET, and hashes. Sam-Bodden said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "Hashes are kind of the workhorse of Redis." They are what most clients map objects to, which is why the state machine targets them.

The build itself is full of small, useful facts:

- The crate type must be cdylib so Redis can load it with the loadmodule flag; MODULE LIST confirms it is in.
- A custom data type name must be exactly nine characters, and types carry a version number so you can handle older encodings later.
- Each command is registered in the redis_module macro with its name, backing function, a write or readonly flag, and the first key, last key and key step. FSM.ALLOWED takes three arguments but only two of them are keys.
- Keys are opened through the context, writable for create and read-only for info, and he uses the guard crate to avoid nested lets around Redis results.
- The prefix-to-machine lookup lives in a plain Redis hash the module writes on create, so an incoming hash event can find its state machine with one HGET. Watching the server log, you see the module receive events for that mapping hash too, which is ignored because its prefix matches no machine.

The finale runs the whole loop: create the machine, write a job hash, see it start in sleeping, ask whether sleep is allowed (no) and run is allowed (yes), trigger run, and read the hash back in running.

## Who should watch

Rust developers who use Redis and have wondered what server-side logic would look like if it lived next to the data. It is an intro to the modules API by example, not a production guide; the state machine is deliberately a toy and the source is on his GitHub.

- Karthik Reddy Beereddy on [self-healing streaming with Redis](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Karthik_Reddy_Beereddy_streaming_redis_selfhealing) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025.

Title: Zero-cost means zero extra cost, and a dozen ways to collect on it
Description: Tim McNamara (AWS) at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 on idiomatic Rust tips, from Clippy pre-commit hooks and newtypes to enum dispatch
Body:
A zero-cost abstraction is not free; it is just something you could not have written better by hand. Tim McNamara, Senior Software Engineer at AWS, opens his Conf42 Rustlang 2022 talk with that definition and then spends half an hour on practical ways to write Rust that stays fast and stays readable for the next person on the team.

It is a tips talk built from before-and-after code, so it rewards having an editor open.

## What does zero-cost actually promise?

McNamara said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "So zero cost, in the sense of zero cost abstractions actually means zero additional cost." He suggests zero marginal cost as the more precise phrase, and adds the trade-off that makes Rust Rust: the cost is measured at runtime, so it is fine for builds to take longer if the program runs faster.

His three go-to references are the Rust API Guidelines, the Clippy lint index (hundreds of checks, each with an explanation) and the idiomatic-rust repository.

## Idioms are for your teammates

McNamara said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "Programming is a team sport, and writing software is easier than reading software." So follow the conventions. Java-style getters and setters mostly do not belong in Rust, with an exception for wrapper types like the NonZero integers or Cell, where a get method returning the inner value makes sense. Use the as, to and into naming conventions for conversions.

The underrated one: eagerly implement the common traits (PartialEq, Clone, Hash) on your public types. Because of the orphan rule, your users cannot implement a foreign trait for your foreign type; their only way out is a newtype wrapper, which is just annoying.

He also shares his git pre-commit hook: cargo fmt check, then cargo check, then Clippy, in that order of cost, with an environment variable escape hatch for when you really need to commit something broken.

## Small changes that help callers

Accept a string slice rather than a reference to a String, and a slice rather than a reference to a boxed value. Deref coercion means callers holding the owned type can still call you, so the narrower signature costs nobody anything.

For generic functions, he shows a monomorphisation trick: keep the generic public function as a thin shim that converts its input and calls a private non-generic inner function marked not to inline. Only the shim gets copied per type; the body exists once.

## Make the compiler do the testing

He nudges towards formal methods via the cheapest possible entry point, readme-driven development: write the document describing how the program should behave before writing it. Then property testing with the proptest crate, and fuzzing, which he says is far easier than it sounds.

The type-system tips are the strongest section:

- **Newtypes.** Two thermometers both read 20, one in Celsius and one in Fahrenheit, and the naive average is 44. Wrapping f32 in unit types turns that logic bug into a compile error, which is the better failure.
- **Return enums, not booleans.** A bool ten lines after the call that produced it tells you nothing; a two-variant enum documents itself.
- **Make illegal states unrepresentable.** Instead of a validate method people forget to call, put validation in the constructor and return a Result. His example is a building whose height must be non-zero.
- **Option around a reference is free.** References are never null, so the compiler uses the spare bit pattern and the Option takes no extra space.
- **Do not fake inheritance with Deref.** It is a known antipattern; use a trait with a default method or write the facade by hand.

## The third kind of polymorphism

Everyone knows generics (static dispatch) and trait objects (dynamic dispatch). McNamara argues for a third: an enum that lists every concrete type, matched in the calling code. The enum_dispatch crate removes the boilerplate, and he cites its benchmarks showing around ten times speed-ups even over the static dispatch case. He pairs it with design advice: if your trait needs more than two or three methods implemented, it is probably too broad. Most standard library traits need just one.

## Who should watch

Rust developers past the borrow-checker stage who want their code to read like the ecosystem's. Beginners get a lot from the newtype and constructor sections; experienced Rustaceans will likely argue with at least one tip, which he explicitly invites.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Joe Skeen on [unit testing in Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Joe_Skeen_love_unit_testing) at Conf42 Rustlang 2023.
- Shriram Balaji on [rustc, symbols and static libraries](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Shriram_Balaji_unlinked_rustc_symbols), for what monomorphisation leaves in your binary.
- Andrei Marinica on [pushing Rust to the limit in a blockchain environment](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2022_Andrei_Marinica_blockchain_environment), where the never type and monomorphisation go much further.

Title: How to Make SPA Apps SEO Friendly
Description: a guest blogpost by Sammy Lin
Body:
## How to Make SPA Apps SEO Friendly
The evolution of web apps has recently brought about an interesting twist. As developers became ever more reliant on client-side Javascript for creating dynamic web pages, a new pattern of development emerged. This new pattern was great for developers and clients alike.
However, Googlebot wasn’t so fond of it. This client heavy pattern, known as the single page application (SPA), essentially builds and renders an entire website on the client. In most cases, the only real work happening on the server is client-side API calls for data retrieval.

### Why Are SPAs Bad for SEO?
SPAs and SEO don’t always play well together, and it’s common for poorly configured [SPA
SEO](https://www.ohmycrawl.com/spa-seo) to rank poorly with Google or other search
engines. To understand why, we need a quick refresher on how an SPA works. SPAs use an
empty shell pattern, which means that an empty HTML shell is sent to the client at initial page
load.

### What the Client Receives When They Request an SPA
When you request a page that utilizes the SPA pattern of development, you’ll receive something that looks like this:
```
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
<title>Example SPA Shell</title>
</head>
<body>
<div id='root'>
</div>
<script src=”/spa-script.js”></script>
</body>
</html>
```

After the initial page load, the **spa-script.js** script is ran, which populates the `root div` tag
with all the guts of the site. This means the navigation bar, footer, images, and everything else
isn’t rendered until the browser finishes processing this script.
It’s a simple concept that works well at first glance. However, Google wants content fast, and
the extra time it takes to process all that Javascript before the content is displayed hurts page
rank for a number of Google SEO web metrics.

### Ways to Load Content More Efficiently in an SPA to Enhance SEO
SPA frameworks like React have devised a number of ways to increase SEO performance while
leveraging all the benefits that come with the SPA pattern. These techniques can be broken
down into 3 main categories:

1. CDN caching and prerendering services.
2. Dynamic loading.
3. Isomorphic development.

These techniques are often used in conjunction with one another to increase SEO performance,
which usually has the added benefit of enhancing user experience.
Let’s take a closer look at each technique and how they solve our SEO woes.

#### CDN Caching and Pre-Rendering Services
One popular and fairly simple technique is to utilize caching services, which saves a pre-
rendered copy of our SPA that is ready for the client (and search engines) to consume. This
improves SEO because the Javascript is already processed into static content, which is readily
available for crawler consumption.
The workflow for this solution looks something like this:

1. The SPA website is built and launched.
2. A prerender service such as prerender.io is used to store and serve a static “prerendered” copy of the website.
3. This new endpoint is configured with a CDN such as Cloudflare to serve the content even faster.

For small sites that utilize content that doesn’t change frequently, such as a blog or small business page, this solution works great. However, this option comes with limitations that make it a poor choice for sites more dynamic in nature.

The prerender.io service will only render your page one to three times per day. So, if you have
content that is changing rapidly, such as an auction site or social media platform, three renders
a day isn’t even close to keeping up with the rapidly changing data.

#### Dynamic Loading of Components
Most SPA frameworks come equipped with some form of dynamic or “lazy” loading
functionality. Since React is the most popular SPA framework to-date, we’ll use it for our
example.

When using React, code is broken up into components. Each component usually consists of
some bit of code that is eventually rendered into pure HTML. The problem is, all these
components are indiscriminately packaged up into a code bundle that’s processed on the client.
Instead of loading all of this code as one linear chunk, we can gain significant SEO performance
gains if we prioritize the order in which our code is loaded.
As an example, we can load our navigation bar and footer first, then load the body content
once these two components are rendered. This helps boost an SEO metric called first contentful
paint (FCP), which is an important Google ranking factor.
Here’s an example of what this would look like in a simple React implementation:

```
import React, { Suspense, lazy } from 'react';
import Navbar from './Navbar';
import Footer from './Footer';
 const MainContent = lazy(() => import('./MainContent'));
 const App = () => {
        
    return(
        <>
            <NavBar/>
            <Suspense fallback = {<div>Content is loading...</div>}>
                <MainContent/>

            </Suspense>
            <Footer/>
        </>
    );
    
}
 export default App;

```
As can be seen in the above code, we are importing the `lazy` and `Suspense` components from
the React framework. We then wrap our `MainContent` component, telling React to __only
load__ this component once all other components on the page are finished rendering.
This is a simple technique often overlooked by novice React developers that can significantly
increase SEO performance in React apps.

### Isomorphic Development for Increasing SEO Performance

Isomorphic development is just a fancy way of saying “what can be done on the client can also be done on the server.” In the case of React, this means that we can utilize React code on the server. This opens the door for two patterns of development that can increase SEO performance; static site generation (SSG) and server side rendering (SSR). Each technique can be defined as follows:

- **Static Site Generation (SSG)**: SSG is similar in concept to prerendering, but it is much more powerful. SSG is implemented by creating server code that renders all of your SPA code into pure HTML at build-time. This means the developer can code the entire site using a framework like React, then run a “build”, which essentially converts all that code into static HTML files which are then served from a hosting provider.
- **Server Side Rendering (SSR)**: SSR is similar to SSG because most of the work happens on the server. However, instead of everything being processed at build-time, it is processed at “run-time”, during each request that is made by the client. This means that when you request a page, the server converts all of the code into HTML on the fly, then sends the result to the client.

SSG is typically faster than SSR, but it comes with the same pitfalls as the prerendering option. Although SSG can handle more dynamic data than a prerendering service, you are still limited

by the number of builds your server can process before the overhead becomes too cumbersome. SSR is currently the most scalable solution because you can handle much of the rendering on the server real-time, while dictating which code you’d like to process on the client.

### Overview SPA Technology and SEO Implications

Leveraging SPA technology is beneficial for both the developer and end-user. For this reason, developers have worked hard to come up with solutions for the inherent SEO pitfalls of this design pattern.

The techniques mentioned in this article can be used to significantly increase SEO performance, while leveraging all the great features that come with SPA frameworks such as React. As usual, if the problem is understood, it can be overcome.

The SPA paradigm is here to stay. While it can be tricky understanding which implementation is best for you, the payoff is usually worth the hard work.

To learn more about Javascript SEO, visit [OhMyCrawl.com](https://www.ohmycrawl.com) for more information.

Title: Render video frames as SVG, encode them with libav, skip the browser
Description: Dmitriy Kovalenko (Lightsource) at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 on building videos from code in Rust with SVG frames, libav encoding and a GPU renderer
Body:
The most popular video editors people use for TikTok-style content render their frames through a browser, HTML and CSS. Dmitriy Kovalenko, Lead Software Engineer at Lightsource, used his Conf42 Rustlang 2022 talk to show the alternative he spent about a year and a half building: fframes, a Rust framework where every frame is an SVG, rendering is parallel on the CPU (or tessellated on the GPU), and encoding goes straight through libav instead of a pile of PNGs on disk.

It doubles as a compact primer on how video actually works, which is reason enough to watch it.

## Why Rust for video at all?

His argument is about memory, not fashion. Kovalenko said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022: "you will notice that the main problem of video is memory and garbage collector." A 4K frame is a loop over roughly 8 million pixels, and you do that for every frame. A runtime that pauses to collect garbage mid-render is a runtime that drops frames.

## What is a video file, really?

He walks through it from the container down. MP4 is a container, not a codec; it holds an image stream and an audio stream, each split into frames with separate presentation and decoding timestamps, because an encoder may need the next frame to decode the current one. Audio frames bundle samples, typically 48,000 per second. The codec is the maths for making a sequence of images smaller: HEVC (H.265), his pick for the codec that should be used everywhere, has a specification of over 700 pages.

Nobody wants to implement 700 pages, so libav (the library half of FFmpeg) does it. The lazy path is one FFmpeg command over a folder of numbered PNGs, which is how many free mobile and web editors work. The faster path calls libav's C API from Rust and encodes manually: raw image, convert to YUV, send to the encoder, get a packet, stamp it, write it to the container. The YUV step gets a nice history detour: it is a leftover from analogue TV, where colour had to ride on top of a black-and-white signal without breaking old sets.

## Why SVG for frames?

The frame-rendering problem is where the talk gets opinionated. Kovalenko said at Conf42 Rustlang 2022 that "today, surprisingly, browser is still the most popular way to render any kind of static content." OBS overlays and GitHub's social preview images are both rendered in a browser.

His list of requirements for a frame format: fixed dimensions, easy to animate, GPU-friendly, specified, and above all debuggable. SVG ticks every box. In fframes you write SVG inside a Rust macro, with Rust expressions and animations inline, and the same definition feeds two things: a Wasm bridge that drives a live editor preview, and a renderer that turns frames into images for the encoder. You can design a frame in Figma, copy it as SVG and paste it into the macro.

For rendering he started on resvg, the Rust SVG library with around 1,500 tests that he says renders SVG more precisely than Chrome, and now runs his own fork tuned for sequential frames, so unchanged parts are not re-rendered.

## CPU first, GPU when it blurs

The CPU renderer simplifies SVG ahead of time to plain paths, then uses Rayon to give each core its own chunk of frames; the chunks are encoded so they can be concatenated at the end. That is fast until you hit shadows, gradients and blur, which force multiple passes over every pixel. For those he built a GPU renderer from scratch that tessellates paths into vertices and indices. He is upfront that it was not yet fully compatible with SVG, and that on a simple hello-world video the parallel CPU path is still competitive; the GPU wins on full-page blurred gradients.

Audio gets the same treatment: decode, mix, encode, plus an API that hands you frequency data so you can draw a visualiser. That was how the project started, as a podcast visualiser, and he quotes an hour of podcast video rendered in about 15 minutes on CPU alone.

## Who should watch

Rust developers curious about multimedia, and anyone generating video from data who is currently shelling out to a headless browser. It is part product launch (fframes opened its beta at the talk), part codec primer; the primer stands on its own.

Title: Quantum computing will touch every security domain, not just RSA
Description: Robert Slade at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2022 on why quantum decryption is far off while quantum's effect on every security domain arrives sooner
Body:
Ask most people what quantum computing means for security and you get one answer: it breaks encryption. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2022, malware researcher Robert Slade argued that [universal quantum decryption](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2022_Robert_Slade_implications_for_security) is a long way off, and that the more interesting story is the dozen other places quantum machines will show up first: risk management, intrusion detection, biometrics, disaster response, forensics, and the brand new attack surface of the machines themselves.

Slade, a CISSP, structures the talk by security domain, and he says up front that it grew out of a set of blog posts he wrote years earlier. Expect a brisk tour with opinions, not maths.

## Quantum cryptography is not what you think

His first job is to separate two things that keep getting conflated. Quantum cryptography is real, but it is the BB84 key-exchange protocol: elegant, able to detect eavesdropping, used by a handful of Swiss banks and sold commercially.

"Quantum cryptography is not cryptography. It is basically just key exchange," Robert Slade said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2022.

It also needs dedicated single-mode fibre, which prompts his best line of the night: "if you've got dedicated, single mode fiber optic cable, why do you need cryptography, for crying out loud?" And as always in crypto, the implementation is what gets attacked, and quantum key distribution has collected plenty of implementation attacks.

Quantum decryption, on the other hand, is hypothesised. The brute-force, drop-the-key-out-in-one-step attack is limited to Shor's algorithm and similar approaches, which today means RSA is the exposed one. By the time a machine is big enough, he expects quantum-resistant algorithms to be in place.

## What can quantum machines actually do?

He is blunt about the hardware. The gate-based machines of the day were barely past 100 qubits, test beds rather than workhorses. D-Wave's Orion line is an adiabatic machine that looks for the lowest-energy state, more an analogue quantum coprocessor than a full quantum computer, in the same family as the spaghetti sorter and the slide rule: special-purpose and very effective at that purpose.

From that he pulls three general capabilities that drive the rest of the talk: least-path problems (the travelling salesman; he cites a Norway tour of roughly 28,000 towns that took classical machines about a decade), simulation (climate and weather models, recalculated cell by cell), and pattern matching, where people are good and computers have been bad.

## Domain by domain

Mapped onto security, the list is long:

- **Risk management**: instead of shuffling budget between controls in a giant spreadsheet, hand the whole model to a least-energy solver and get the optimal allocation in one shot.
- **Access control**: better biometric matching, fewer false positives and negatives, plus information-flow and covert-channel analysis.
- **Intrusion, malware and botnets**: pattern matching for detection, malware family attribution, and command-and-control and ownership analysis for fast-flux botnets. Spam filtering, already straining Bayesian analysis, gets a new tool too.
- **Business continuity**: impact analysis, testing plans by simulation, and real-time re-routing of disaster resources when the hurricane lands 20 miles from where it was forecast.
- **Cryptography**: quantum devices as sources of genuinely random, even tunably random, numbers, and simulation to find implementation flaws.
- **Law and investigation**: new forensic tools, and a new problem explaining their output to a court.

## The bad news is architecture

"In terms of security architecture, the news here is probably all bad," he said. New architectures bring new vulnerabilities, noise, and hybrid quantum-classical systems that are harder to troubleshoot. Physical security gets strange: by his figures room temperature is 100 times hotter than interstellar space, and interstellar space is 1,000 times hotter than the core of a running Orion device. Lose power or cooling and you lose the computation outright. For the foreseeable future these will be remote, time-shared machines, so the data flying between classical and quantum halves needs protecting and authenticating.

He also raises a testing problem that has only grown since: how do you check the output of a system built to give answers you could not compute classically? His tentative answer is to cross-check, the way D-Wave votes across repeated runs, by running a neural network and a quantum assessment side by side and seeing whether they agree.

## Who should watch

Security managers and CISSPs who want a structured map of where quantum lands in their domains, and anyone who needs a calm counterweight to quantum-apocalypse headlines. If you want post-quantum migration steps, pair it with a more hands-on talk.

Title: To scale quantum computers, first build a network that teleports
Description: Sam Samuel (Mobility Business Group, Cisco) at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2022 on why scaling quantum computers needs quantum networks and repeaters
Body:
You make a bigger computer by joining computers together, and quantum computers are no exception, except that the wire has to carry entanglement. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2022, Sam Samuel, CTO of the Mobility Business Group at Cisco, walked from qubit basics through the threat to today's ciphers to the hard part: [the quantum communication challenges](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2022_Sam_Samuel_communication_challenges_scaling_quantum) that stand between a lab machine and a quantum internet, which he puts roughly a decade out.

A long, deliberately general talk; networking engineers get the most from the second half.

## Where is the money going?

He starts with investment. His chart counts about $1.5B in quantum startups, split roughly $950M into hardware, $300M into software and $200M into quantum communication and internet companies.

## Neven's law and the cipher clock

Classical chips follow Moore's law, doubling per generation. Samuel contrasts it with Neven's law, named after Hartmut Neven, who noticed that the classical machines used to verify his quantum results were running out of steam far faster than expected: quantum computing power grows doubly exponentially, 2, 4, 16, 256 and onward.

Point that at factorisation and the RSA and elliptic-curve key exchanges in networks today start to look mortal, through Shor's algorithm. Symmetric ciphers are hit by Grover's algorithm instead, which is far less effective against longer keys. No doom, though: NIST's post-quantum competitions aim to keep defenders ahead. The real risk he flags is harvest-now, decrypt-later, where traffic is siphoned off and stored until a bad actor has a quantum computer to spend on it.

## Why connect quantum computers at all?

Partly for raw scale, and partly because current machines are specialists: some are good at annealing and optimisation, others at factoring, rarely both.

"there's no such thing as a general quantum computer," Sam Samuel said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2022.

So programs get split and routed to the right machine, which is a networking problem.

## Teleportation, then entanglement swapping

The core of the talk is a careful, slide-by-slide build of the mechanics. The no-cloning theorem means an unknown quantum state cannot be copied, which is great for eavesdropping resistance and terrible for the usual store-and-forward networking. Instead you distribute a maximally entangled Bell pair to both ends of a link, perform a Bell state measurement between the qubit you want to send and your half of the pair, send two classical bits to the far end, and apply a local operation there. The state shows up at the far end without ever crossing the link, and since the classical bits travel no faster than light, relativity survives.

To go further, you chain segments. With pairs A, B and C, an entanglement-swapping measurement joins A to B, a second joins the result to C, and you have end-to-end entanglement. Swapping also doubles as routing: with quantum memories and a high enough entanglement distribution rate, you can steer entanglement to any source and sink you choose. The catch, from the paper by Sourabh Kumar, Nikolai Lauk and Christoph Simon that got Samuel interested in the field, is that entanglement generated at a given rate only propagates so far, so long links need quantum repeaters to regenerate it.

## What breaks first: qubits or the network?

Both, in different ways. On the qubit side: errors programming initial states, decoherence from coupling with the environment, lifetimes measured in microseconds to milliseconds, gate operation errors, and photons absorbed by the fibre. Fidelity, a number between 0 and 1, tracks how healthy an entangled pair still is.

On the network side: pairs need high fidelity and purity before they set off; quantum error correction helps against decoherence, noise and loss but needs even more qubits; and synchronisation has to be far tighter than anything in today's networks, because a qubit's shelf life starts the moment it is entangled and every operation has to finish before it expires.

## How far away is the quantum internet?

He leans on the 2016 work by Muralidharan and colleagues, which sorts repeaters into first, second and third generations depending on how error correction is applied to loss and operational error. Today, by his account, the field is still scratching around at first-generation repeaters.

"I think we are talking maybe ten years or so before we start to get to a reliable network at reasonable entanglement rates that can start to teleport at reasonable rates," he said, and then a few more years before a full quantum internet.

His closing sketch is a virtualised quantum data centre: a programmer writes an ordinary program, a compiler splits it into classical and quantum parts, and a manager places them. That leaves four open problems: compiling for mixed classical and quantum execution, networking quantum computers within a data centre, extending the rate and range of quantum links cost-effectively, and virtualising quantum data centre resources.

## Who should watch

Network engineers and architects who want the teleportation and repeater story explained by someone from a networking company, and security people curious about the harvest-now risk.

Title: Restarting the server is a haymaker, and other lessons from the ring
Description: Paul Marsicovetere (Formidable) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on five combat sports principles that apply to incident response
Body:
Boxing and SRE share more than bad sleep. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Paul Marsicovetere, Senior Cloud Infrastructure Engineer at Formidable in Toronto, mapped five combat sports principles onto incident response, plus a bonus from Mike Tyson. It's a short, light talk, and the haymaker metaphor alone is worth keeping for your next incident review.

Before Formidable, Paul spent three years in SRE at Benevity in Calgary, and he is clearly a serious MMA and boxing fan. Thankfully, as he notes, SRE rarely involves bodily injury, depending on where you work.

## Sometimes you're the hammer, sometimes the nail

Some days you add an availability zone for redundancy, speed up slow database queries, or ship a backup and restore setup you trust. You're the hammer. Other days a cloud region goes intermittently dark or your DNS disappears, and you're the nail. You can't architect around every outage, and your next one is never far away. Paul's advice is to roll with the punches and not be too hard on yourself, because the good days come back around too.

## Don't throw and hope, aim and fire

Fighters are tempted by haymakers, the wild swing that might end the fight. The SRE haymakers are familiar: bump the CPU or memory and see, kill processes to free resources, or turn it off and on again. They can buy debugging time, and sometimes they even work. But as a default response they are not a long-term tactic. Precision beats power and timing beats speed: investigate, find the root cause or causes, then fire the fix through monitoring, alerting or a code deployment.

## Don't react, respond

Paul's joke here is that this isn't another JavaScript framework. In the ring, an uncontrolled reaction can cost the fight or expose a flaw. In an incident, it's the urge to believe everything is collapsing, or to start blaming colleagues, vendors or the code, and blame is very hard to undo. A measured response keeps the team focused and shows calm leadership. That is why it is called incident response, not incident reaction.

"So remember to take a moment to breathe, think, plan and then respond accordingly," Paul said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022.

## It only takes one punch to change a fight

One well-placed command can end an incident: a firewall rule, upgrading or downgrading a package, moving traffic from one availability zone to another. The same is true in reverse. Paul's warning is against cowboy moves mid-incident, like updating a database row or restarting a server without telling anyone. Talk to the team, get agreement, then press Enter.

## The fight is won or lost in preparation

Fail to prepare, prepare to fail. For SRE, that means game day exercises for disaster recovery, so a real outage feels less unfamiliar and the team has already rehearsed its roles and coordination. It also means deploying to pre-production or staging before production, and automated tests in pipelines. Paul admits the trade-off with deployment velocity, but argues it builds confidence and means less winging it.

## The bonus round

Mike Tyson's line closes it: everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face. Failing tests, a wrongly sized scaling group or an expired SSL certificate can derail the best launch plan. Adapting gets easier with experience, but the random punches never stop. Protect yourself at all times.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to on-call, and team leads looking for a memorable way to talk about incident behaviour. It's a culture talk with no tooling or numbers, short enough to watch between pages.

Title: Software quality has a quality problem, and openness might fix it
Description: Andrew Knight (Applitools) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on Open Testing, sharing tests, results and suites the way we share source code
Body:
We open-source our code but lock our tests behind company doors. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Andrew Knight, Developer Advocate at Applitools and director of Test Automation University, made the case for Open Testing: share the tests themselves, their results and eventually whole reusable test suites, to get the same benefits open source gave developers.

It's a talk of ideas rather than tooling, and Andrew says so: the goal is to start conversations.

## What did open source teach a calculator kid?

Andrew builds his argument from three personal lessons. On a TI-83 Plus in high school, TI-BASIC programs couldn't hide their source, so every program copied over a link cable could be opened and studied: open source helps me learn. In college, JUnit showed him that free code written by others could carry his own project: open source helps me become a better developer. And after he and his team released Boa Constrictor, a .NET implementation of the Screenplay pattern, in October 2020, community pull requests added interactions his own company then used: open source helps me become a better maintainer.

## Why does testing need this?

His diagnosis is the line of the talk. "Software quality has a big problem with quality," Andrew said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. Test repositories are full of copy-pasted setup steps, static variables and singletons instead of dependency injection, flaky suites where a 90% pass rate counts as a good day, and tests that cover nothing valuable. Because tests are private, nobody can show good practice at scale, and tutorials are toy examples.

## How open can testing get?

He lays out a ladder, starting from the worst case: testers alone own the test cases and the automation, and everyone else sees only failure percentages and bug reports.

1. **Openness in collaboration.** The three amigos (business, development, testing) shape features together with question storming and example mapping. His Q2 colleague Steve started booking half-hour example mapping sessions, once dropped a story with no business value and saved two weeks of work, and ended up switching to a software engineer in test role.
2. **Specification by example and living documentation.** Example cards get refined into Gherkin's Given-When-Then, which works as requirements, acceptance criteria, test cases, automation and documentation at once. SpecFlow+ LivingDoc turns those scenarios into a searchable site with pass/fail results that non-programmers can read.
3. **Sharing tests and results with customers.** At Q2 his team shared that LivingDoc report with specific PrecisionLender customers every two-week release; even a vice president could read it, and it built trust without exposing automation code. The catch: public results only help if they can be trusted.
4. **Sharing tools and frameworks.** Already true for JUnit, pytest, Selenium, Playwright and the rest.
5. **Shared test suites for common behaviour.** Every shopping cart works the same way, so why does every team rewrite the same cart tests? He imagines machine learning models that learn common workflows and generic suites, which he calls ROAST (run-on-any-system tests), for login, search, cart and payment, which might cover a quarter, a third or half of what's worth testing.

## Should anything stay closed?

He raises security himself: fully open tests might reveal vulnerabilities, and visible coverage gaps might invite attackers. He has no answer and says so. He ends with three questions for your team: how open is your testing today, what small step could you take (try example mapping, join a mob session), and what would radical openness look like. Openness is a means to an end, and the end is quality.

## Who should watch

Test leads and SDETs, and SREs who rely on test signals they can't see. Readers who want a framework walkthrough should look elsewhere; this is the argument for a culture change.

Title: Deploy is not release, and feature flags are how you prove it
Description: Travis Gosselin (SPS Commerce) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on feature flags that unblock pipelines, and the costs nobody demos
Body:
Fully automated CI/CD pipelines still stall at the last step, because someone has to decide when a feature is allowed out. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Travis Gosselin, Principal Software Engineer at SPS Commerce, showed how feature flags remove that gate by separating deploy from release, and then spent a good part of the talk on what the simple if/else demos leave out.

SPS Commerce runs a retail network of over 4,200 retailers, and Travis reports about 1,000 changes to production a month with a change failure rate around 2 to 2.1%.

## What is the gate that blocks the pipeline?

Travis draws the familiar picture: main is always deployable, short-lived feature branches come back through pull requests, semantic versioning tags a build, and it auto-deploys to dev. Then it stops. The gate might be a product owner who wants the feature out next Tuesday, a coordinated release with a UI that isn't ready, or a bug found in dev. Meanwhile the next feature branch lives longer than it should, other services wait on contracts, and when a critical bug fix arrives the pipeline is blocked. You end up cherry-picking from tags and hoping.

The fix is to wrap the new code path in a flag that defaults to off, so you can merge and deploy straight to production without releasing anything. In a mature setup the flag moves to a feature decision provider, a small service you ask whether feature one is enabled, in which environment, for whom. The gate now sits beside the pipeline instead of across it.

## What do flags actually buy you?

Using Martin Fowler's four types (release, operational, experiment, permission), the list is long: shorter branches, true CI, rollback by toggle instead of redeploy, A/B tests and canaries, testing in production for one user. SPS Commerce went from five environments to two by targeting features contextually.

There's a culture shift too. Travis leans on progressive delivery, with release progressions and progressive delegation: hand the switch to whoever owns the feature, often the product owner, so the engineer isn't waiting to be asked. He links it to the State of DevOps metrics (deployment frequency, lead time, time to restore, change failure rate) and notes the counterintuitive result his own numbers bear out: deploy more often and you fail less.

## The honeymoon is over

His simple example: a SetupUser method that sends a welcome email through SendGrid if a flag is on and local SMTP if it's off. A global flag lets you ship, but to test the SendGrid API key in production you'd have to turn it on for everyone. Pass the user context into the check and you can enable it for Travis alone.

Then the costs. Complexity shifts left into the code. Reasoning about the system is no longer binary; you need observability that says whether a feature was on for that user, in that environment, at that time. Flags need lifecycle management and removal. And a flag is still a code change: "I have broken production with a feature flag. Absolutely," Travis said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022.

On build versus buy, he avoids undifferentiated engineering. Options run from key-value stores (AWS Parameter Store, Azure App Configuration, Consul, etcd) to open source providers such as Unleash to full services; SPS Commerce uses LaunchDarkly. He also cites the Thoughtworks Tech Radar's advice to start with the simplest possible toggles.

## Flags beyond the if statement

The second half is a tour of patterns. UI routing with LaunchDarkly's React router component, where a single-page app open for weeks needs a live websocket or long-polling connection to pick up flag changes. API flags for preview endpoints, shifting v1 users to v2, or quietly fixing a 200 that should have been a 204 while watching error rates. A strangler migration from a monolith to a new scheduling API using a write-to-both flag and a read flag, which surfaced production load problems they could only have found in production. Kill switches, log verbosity, sunsetting features, timed holiday releases.

The architecture warning is about user context. If one app identifies Travis by user ID and another by first and last name, targeting is inconsistent and you may pay a provider for two users. SPS Commerce only targets individual users when they're internal; external customers are enabled per organisation.

## Who should watch

Teams with CI/CD that still batch releases, and anyone about to roll flags out beyond one team. It's practical, honest about the costs, and light on vendor pitch.

Title: Your CPU limit can turn 100 ms into 3.6 seconds, so test it
Description: Henrik Rexed (Dynatrace) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on validating Kubernetes requests, limits and quotas with chaos and load tests
Body:
Henrik Rexed, Cloud Native Advocate at Dynatrace, opened his Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 talk with a measurement that should worry anyone who copies resource limits from a blog post: the same workload answered in about 100 milliseconds without CPU limits and close to 3.6 seconds with them, purely from CPU throttling. His fix is not to drop limits, but to stop guessing them and prove them with chaos experiments plus a steady load test.

## How does Kubernetes end up killing your workload?

Henrik starts with a refresher on pod states (pending, creating, running) and then the eviction story. One app on a node eats resources, the node comes under pressure, and Kubernetes evicts a pod and reschedules it elsewhere. On a good day users barely notice. On a bad day every node is saturated, or your taints and tolerations leave nowhere to go, and the evicted workload simply doesn't come back.

Eviction follows quality of service classes, which come from what you declare. Requests equal to limits makes a pod Guaranteed, requests below limits makes it Burstable, nothing at all makes it BestEffort, and eviction goes in that order: BestEffort first, Guaranteed last. Add resource quotas per namespace so one team's app can't starve another's.

## Requests are Tetris, limits are a contract

His analogies are good. Requests tell the scheduler the shape of the piece so it can play Tetris with your nodes; without them it places a small square that later turns into a huge block. Or a box of chocolates where you only discover the liqueur after biting. Over-requesting is safe but wastes nodes, since the reserved capacity is never used by anyone else.

Limits are the contract on top of that. Memory is easy: load test, see the peak, set it, and if you set it too low you get an OOMKill event. CPU is harder because of the CFS quota inherited from Docker: a core is sliced into 100 ms periods, and a limit of 20 lets you run for 20 ms per period before you're paused. That pause is throttling, and it's where the 3.6 seconds came from. Henrik still recommends limits, at least for memory, as an industry best practice; the lesson is to measure them, not skip them.

## Which experiments validate the settings?

The chaos workflow is classic: write a hypothesis, predict the behaviour, decide what to measure, define the experiment and its rollback, then run it. His three Kubernetes hypotheses: with the right requests and limits the app stays stable; a node drain during maintenance causes no user impact; and under node pressure, correct pod priorities mean no downtime.

To test eviction and maintenance together, drain some nodes, then apply node CPU and memory stress while a constant load test runs. No spike test. "I want to run in a non production environment and I need to measure the user, the impact on the user," Henrik said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. Compare runs with and without limits, watch throttling, tune.

## What do you need to observe?

Metrics and Kubernetes events, layer by layer like an onion: user response time and failure rate, node CPU, memory and pod counts, pod requests and limits against actual usage, and container CPU throttling. On the events side: node pressure, failed scheduling, eviction, OOMKill, unhealthy.

The stack in his demo setup: LitmusChaos (its ChaosHub ships 50+ Kubernetes experiments, including node drain, node CPU hog and node memory hog), k6 for load with its Prometheus output, the Prometheus operator with its Kubernetes metrics exporter, node exporter and cAdvisor for throttling, plus exporters for Litmus and k6, all feeding Prometheus or Dynatrace. Tooling runs on labelled nodes so the experiments don't knock over the observers.

## Removing the human from the pipeline

Running all this from Jenkins still leaves a person staring at dashboards before approving. Henrik closes the loop with Keptn, the CNCF project Dynatrace started, used here as a quality gate: after the test, the pipeline sends Keptn an event, Keptn evaluates the SLIs and SLOs you defined (pod failures, node pressure under 1%), scores the run, and returns pass or fail.

## Who should watch

Platform teams setting defaults for requests and limits, and SREs who suspect throttling behind mystery latency. Expect a methodology talk with a practical toolchain, not a live demo.

Title: Using chaos experiments to train on-call engineers, not just systems
Description: Eran Levy (Cyren) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on On-Call Like a King, workshops that replay real incidents with chaos experiments
Body:
Chaos engineering is usually sold as a way to harden systems. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Eran Levy, Director of Engineering at Cyren, showed it working on the people instead: a workshop series called On-Call Like a King, where engineers investigate simulated production incidents in a test environment before they meet the real thing at 3am.

The takeaway is refreshingly low-tech. You don't need a chaos platform to start; Cyren began by reproducing incidents by hand.

## Why do cloud native engineers need this?

Eran's framing: engineers no longer throw artifacts over the wall to operations. They design, build, release and support their services, and those services sit in what he calls deep systems, a long chain of dependencies on top of a platform. His example scenario: you're on call, back pressure is burning your SLO, and a third of your deployment can't reschedule because of node availability in one availability zone. Knowing your programming language well doesn't help. Knowing AZs, pod affinities, pod status and how to read cluster events does.

So the workshops have two goals: practise on recent production failures, and learn cloud native practices and tooling along the way.

## How is a session run?

Cyren's on-call setup frames it: weekly engineering shifts, a NOC watching 24/7, severity one to three alerts mapped to business impact, and alert playbooks. The toolbox includes Jaeger, Kibana and Grafana.

Each workshop has three parts: an intro that restates the motivation and agenda, a slot for announcements (on-call process changes, architecture updates), then the challenge. The challenge is capped at two incident simulations and the whole session at 60 minutes, because concentration drops after that. If the team works hybrid, run it when people share a room; Eran found it much more productive.

The incidents run in a non-production environment that is close to real. The experiments are prepared in advance so they can be launched in a few clicks. Cyren recently adopted LitmusChaos, but Eran's advice is not to rush into tooling or spend time building it. Pick any chaos tool you like, or simulate the incident manually as Cyren did for the first two years.

## What makes the challenge work?

The facilitator shows a minimal incident brief, a few alerts and their Grafana dashboards, because that's all you get in a real page. Then engineers get time to dig alone: cluster metrics, logs, service status. Eran pushes them to think about customer impact, since in a severity one the on-call engineer has to communicate it and look for a workaround, and many engineers aren't used to that.

Then pause and talk. Ask one person to show their Grafana dashboard, another their Kibana query, a third how they find the trace in Jaeger. "We have found out that the discussions around the incidents is a great place for knowledge sharing," Eran said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. People swap CLI tools, someone spots an architectural oddity, and occasionally a suggestion lands on the tech debt list.

The facilitator has to moderate, because the conversation gets heavy and the hour flies. At the end, someone presents the end-to-end analysis, which helps juniors and new joiners who won't ask questions in a big group. Record it and share notes; Eran found people rewatch the recordings, and they become onboarding material.

## What came out of it?

The playbooks improved. Each workshop surfaces know-how that goes back into Cyren's incident playbook template, which covers how to detect the issue, assess customer impact and communicate. And on-call engineers say they feel more comfortable in their shifts and know which tools they have. The talk shares no metrics on that, and the summary slide's own advice is to measure how the sessions help.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and SRE leads who own on-call onboarding, and teams with chaos tooling that only ever gets pointed at infrastructure. It is a process talk, light on tooling detail.

Title: A postmortem without action items is just a well-formatted diary
Description: Ramon Medrano Llamas (Google) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on blameless postmortems and why action items decide whether you learn anything
Body:
Writing the postmortem is the easy half. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Ramon Medrano Llamas, Senior Staff SRE at Google in Zurich, walked through how Google writes, reviews and uses postmortems, and his main point was blunt: the document only matters if the action items get prioritised, done and closed. Everything else is paperwork.

It's a compact, practical tour of the process described in the Google SRE books, from the person who has to live with it on the authentication stack.

## Why does Google write postmortems at all?

The starting point is error culture. Disks, machines and network links fail all the time underneath you, so 100% is the wrong reliability target for nearly everything, and the gap between the SLO and 100% becomes the error budget you spend on features, changes and rollouts. When something does fail, the postmortem is the written record: what state the system was in, what people did before and after, the user impact, the root causes and the trigger.

Ramon draws a clean line between those last two. The root cause is the latent flaw, maybe a bug committed years ago. The trigger is whatever finally exercised it: a feature flag flipped, a new version, a change in customer behaviour. Aviation and medicine have done this for decades; IT is catching up.

## Blameless means fixing systems, not people

The talk is firm on blamelessness. Someone will always have pushed the release or pressed the button, but that person is not the root cause; the system that let one push take it down is. "So just to emphasize, let's fix systems and processes, not people, right?" Ramon said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022.

The less-quoted corollary: don't celebrate heroism. If your reliability depends on one person who can be paged at any hour and pulls long nights, that dependency is itself a flaw. Action items that try to fix humans are a smell; fix the playbook, protect the dangerous flag, automate the risky step.

## When should you write one, and who owns it?

Define the criteria before the incident: users affected, revenue lost, a severity scale. If the criteria are met, a postmortem is mandatory. If they would have been met without luck, you should write one. Near misses and interesting alerts are optional, lightweight write-ups with relaxed review, and they double as training material for new on-callers and a risk register for the service.

One person owns it, typically the incident commander or a tech lead or manager, and coordinates contributions from every team whose service caused or felt the outage. Readers come in three tiers: the team (every detail), the wider company (directors, architects, with an executive summary) and customers (a differently structured, higher-level document to regain trust, sometimes required by an SLA).

## What goes in it?

The minimum is root cause, trigger, impact tied to business metrics, an action plan, and lessons learned split into what went well, what went poorly and where you got lucky. The luck column is the useful one: every lucky break is a candidate action item, because nobody wants reliability that depends on luck.

The worked example is the Shakespeare search outage from the SRE book: down for 66 minutes after a newly discovered sonnet sent traffic through the roof, an estimated 1.21 billion queries lost, a cascading failure from a file descriptor leak, mitigated by sending traffic to a sacrificial cluster and adding 10x capacity. Ramon admits the timeline is his favourite part, because it shows the outage started long before anyone was paged.

## Action items are the whole point

The process is draft fast (dump every log and graph into the doc before you lose them), analyse, review, publish, then execute. "There's no difference between nothing and a postmortem without action items," he said, paraphrasing Ben Treynor Sloss's line that to users a postmortem without follow-up is indistinguishable from none.

To get root causes worth acting on, he recommends Five Whys, starting from the impact and asking until the answer is actionable, since there is almost always more than one cause. Balance band-aids with long-term fixes, think beyond prevention to detection and mitigation, and add a Detect-type item whenever users noticed before your monitoring did. Then review open items regularly and give executives visibility so closing them gets rewarded.

Google also keeps postmortems alive after publication: review clubs, a postmortem of the month, and Wheel of Misfortune sessions that replay an old incident to train new team members.

## Who should watch

Teams starting a postmortem process, or teams whose postmortems quietly die in a shared drive. It is a 101 with Google's templates attached, not a story of a novel incident.

Title: Uranium draws quantum circuits and simulates 27 qubits in a browser tab
Description: Radu Marginean at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2022 on Uranium, an open-source visual circuit editor with a Rust simulator running in the browser
Body:
Most quantum algorithms are easier to understand as a picture than as a list of gate calls. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2022, software developer Radu Marginean showed [Uranium](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2022_Radu_Marginean_uranium_visual_platform), an open-source, free platform that pairs a drag-and-drop circuit editor with a simulator written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly: up to 27 qubits in the browser, 32 offline, and export to Qiskit and OpenQASM when you want to leave.

It is a short talk, half motivation and half guided tour of the editor. If you have ever built a Grover circuit gate by gate in code and lost track of which qubit was which, it is aimed squarely at you.

## Why draw circuits at all?

Marginean opens with two textbook circuits and makes the case that their structure is visual. Grover search on five qubits is a layer of Hadamard gates that puts the register into superposition, then an oracle that flips the phase of the state you are looking for, then the diffusion operator that inverts the amplitudes around their mean, repeated a few times so the marked state grows more likely with each round. Quantum phase estimation follows the same opening move: Hadamards on the control register, controlled-U operations on a target prepared in an eigenstate of U, phase kickback writing the phase bit by bit into the controls, and an inverse quantum Fourier transform before measurement.

Both algorithms also show up as building blocks inside bigger ones. That reuse is the core of his argument: if circuits are built out of smaller circuits with recognisable shapes, the tool should let you see and compose those shapes. In his view existing editors are rather limited here.

"Uranium is a platform that intends to fill this unoccupied space," Radu Marginean said at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2022.

## What the editor actually does

The demo covers the productivity features that separate a real editor from a toy:

- Drag a gate in once, then duplicate it, generate an array of copies, or select a region to copy, paste or erase.
- Save small circuits in a project and reuse them as gates inside a larger circuit from the same project.
- Generate circuits programmatically from a small Python API and import them into a project.
- Add any number of controls to a gate, in the Z basis and also in the X or Y basis, and group gates into an aggregate gate that shares one set of controls (his example is a Steane error-correction code).

The gate catalogue is long and goes past the usual suspects: square roots of the Pauli gates, the two extra Hadamard variants that rotate around the diagonals of the YZ and XY planes, iSWAP and parametric swaps, Ising gates native to trapped-ion hardware, the cross-resonance gate native to superconducting devices, plus Givens and Magic gates for chemistry-flavoured work.

## Measurement gates select a subspace, they don't sample

One design choice is worth knowing before you click around. Uranium displays probability distributions rather than sampled shots. With no measure gates, you see results over the full Hilbert space of the circuit; adding measure gates narrows the output to the subspace they cover. The editor also lets you switch between big-endian ordering, which most textbooks use, and little-endian ordering, which many hardware platforms use. Anyone who has stared at a reversed bitstring from a real device will appreciate that toggle.

## How fast is a browser simulator?

Faster than you would guess. The Rust simulator runs as WebAssembly, and Marginean's figure is a 20-qubit circuit with 300 gates simulated in under a second. He put it more simply: it "runs very fast in your browser, surprisingly fast."

For anything beyond that, Uranium can send a circuit to IBM Quantum devices straight from a project, using your own account. On his basic account he only saw real devices up to seven qubits, but IBM's cloud simulators, including a tensor-network simulator for up to 100 qubits, are also on the list. The roadmap he sketched: editing circuits with hundreds or thousands of qubits, and running semi-classical algorithms such as VQE and QAOA on the simulator.

## Who should watch

Students and developers learning quantum algorithms who want to see what a circuit does without writing a notebook first, and anyone teaching the subject. If you already live in Qiskit, the export path means you can sketch in Uranium and keep your existing workflow.

Title: Valid Go is not correct Go, and staticcheck guards the gap
Description: Xe Iaso (Tailscale) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on go vet and staticcheck blocking the trivial Go bugs that page SREs at 3 a.m.
Body:
Code that never reaches production cannot page you at 3 a.m. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Xe Iaso, Archmage of Infrastructure at Tailscale, showed three Go bugs that compile cleanly and fail at runtime, how go vet and staticcheck catch them in CI, and why this is ultimately a talk about SRE health rather than linters.

## Why doesn't the compiler catch these?

The Go spec describes valid programs, not correct ones. "The specification doesn't define what correct go code is, it only defines what valid go code is," Iaso said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. Proving correctness is an open research problem that, in Iaso's words, small scrappy startups like Google, Microsoft and Apple struggle with. Rust and Haskell make these mistakes harder, not impossible. Static analysis is the pragmatic middle path: closer to correct without porting everything to Rust.

Go also leaves these checks out of go build on purpose. The Go team would rather you compile buggy code than have the compiler reject valid code by accident, trusting tests, tools and human review to sit between the programmer and production. A subset of go vet checks with no known false positives runs automatically under go test; the rest belong in CI.

What static analysis can prove: resources you forgot to release, typos the compiler cannot see (often struct tags), invalid constants such as time formats, URLs and regular expressions, and a wide range of predictable crashes.

## Bug one: the deferred close in the wrong place

Reading an HTTP response body without closing it leaks the connection, and eventually the server runs out of sockets at 3 a.m. The obvious fix, deferring the body close right after the GET call, is also wrong: if the request failed, the response is nil and the deferred close panics on the way out. go vet flags it with `using resp before checking for errors`. Move the defer below the error check and it behaves.

## Bug two: the shadowed type assertion

Go lets you scope variables to an if statement, which makes it easy to shadow a variable with a type assertion of the same name. When the assertion fails, the inner variable is a zero-valued int, so the error branch reports an unexpected type of int, about a value that was never an int. It will confuse you thoroughly. staticcheck catches it; the fix is to give the asserted value its own name, such as xInt.

## Bug three: the nil that isn't nil

A custom error type with a pointer receiver, returned from a function whose return type is the error interface. If the function returns a nil pointer of that concrete type, the interface box still exists, so the not-nil check passes and calling Error() panics with a nil pointer dereference. staticcheck reports `doWork never returns a nil interface value`. Returning an untyped nil instead fixes it.

## Why is this an SRE talk?

Because the pager is a health problem. Iaso describes burnout from on-call that severely affected their health, a near panic attack the last time the pager went off, and permanent career changes made to never be in that position again. Pages should be for things that are measurably novel, not for errors that tooling could have blocked. Static analysis in CI will not make things perfect, but trivial errors stop shipping and people sleep better. "When the machines come to take our jobs, I hope that this is one of the first that they take," Iaso said.

Iaso closes by asking Go shops to sponsor Dominik Honnef, staticcheck's author, on GitHub: the better he sleeps, the better you sleep. For other languages, the honest advice is to research the equivalent tools with your team, because it is worth the teething pains.

## Who should watch

Go developers who have not added staticcheck to CI yet (there is a GitHub Action for it), and anyone who needs a persuasive case for why on-call sleep is an engineering concern.

Title: Run towards the fire - incidents are the fastest way to grow engineers
Description: Lisa Karlin Curtis (incident.io) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on incidents as the fastest way to level up engineers, if everyone can join in
Body:
The fastest way to become a senior engineer may be to lurk in incident channels. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Lisa Karlin Curtis, Product Engineer and employee number two at incident.io, explained how incidents accelerated her own career, what exactly they teach, and how teams can stop keeping those lessons inside a small group of heroes.

## The day she learned what a query plan was

The story that opens the talk is from her early days at GoCardless. The API, effectively the whole product, slowed to a crawl. One endpoint was sending a query to a large Postgres database whose query plan had flipped from expensive-but-manageable to unmanageable, with no recent change to blame. No statement timeout meant the database kept grinding long after the caller had given up. A subtle query change brought back the good plan. She watched from the sidelines taking notes, and afterwards asked a colleague what a query plan was.

That pattern repeated. The step changes in her ability to handle bigger problems and reason about tradeoffs came from incidents she took part in or watched, and she made senior faster than she expected.

## What do incidents actually teach?

Five things, in her telling.

- **They broaden your horizons.** Engineers live among black boxes: languages, frameworks, databases. "Incidents force you to open the black boxes around you, peek inside and learn just enough to solve the problem," Karlin Curtis said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. After that outage she read up on query plans, and it paid off in the next query plan incident and in writing code that scaled the first time. Incidents also ignore team boundaries, which teaches the wider system faster than any architecture diagram.
- **They teach graceful failure.** The key follow-up was statement timeouts on every database call: you do not need to know which query will be bad, only that one will be. She also heard the options the responders discussed and discarded, and why.
- **They teach debuggability.** Useful logs and metrics come from empathy for whoever will debug this later, and that is built from pattern matching on past incidents.
- **They build your network.** Stress forges connections quickly. Most of the non-engineering people she knew at GoCardless she met during incidents, which later gave her a friendly face in support, sales or risk.
- **They let you learn from the best.** Big incidents pull in the people with the most context, who are otherwise too busy to shadow.

## How do you make incidents accessible?

At GoCardless she could open any incident channel. Many teams run private, invite-only channels, so juniors who want to watch never know an incident is happening, or an in-group handles everything and newcomers, even senior ones, struggle to get in. Her fixes:

- **Declare lots of incidents.** A low bar means more practice, so the response is smooth when a big one arrives, and more learning opportunities.
- **Encourage everyone to participate.** Public channels by default. Twenty people in a minor incident is too many, but a few juniors tagging along is fine; they can ask someone not actively responding, or save questions for afterwards. Read debriefs, attend reviews, and give new joiners a list of the best past write-ups.
- **Show your working.** Post the commands you ran and the theories you disproved, even when you are alone in the channel at 10 p.m. talking to yourself. It protects you from false memories and teaches everyone reading.
- **Watch out for heroes.** The engineer who quietly fixes everything burns out and takes the learning away from everyone else.

Her closing line for the heroes: "If you think that you get a lot of recognition for resolving incidents, imagine how much you'll get for leveling up your whole team so they can do the same."

## Who should watch

Engineering leads deciding whether incident channels should be public, and juniors wondering if it is okay to watch. It is, and the talk tells you how to do it without getting in the way.

Title: One engineer, six weeks, a whole R&D org moved from Bitbucket to GitLab
Description: Hila Fish (Wix) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on running a solo SCM migration like a real project - plan, milestones, training, handoff
Body:
Engineers learn to write code; nobody teaches them to run a project end to end. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Hila Fish, Senior DevOps Engineer at Wix, described how, at a previous employer, she moved an entire R&D department's code from Bitbucket Cloud to self-hosted GitLab on her own in a month and a half - planning, implementation, training and handoff included - and turned it into a set of project management habits any engineer can steal.

The twist that shaped everything: she had told the company she was leaving before the project started, and they asked her to do it anyway. So the documentation had to be good enough that nobody would need to call her.

## Ask three questions before planning

Pre-planning was three questions. What is the deadline? Why are we migrating - on-premise to cloud, SaaS to self-hosted, or something internal? Any limitations? That last one decides real choices: GitLab ships as Omnibus for VMs or a Helm chart for Kubernetes, and a company with no Kubernetes should not adopt Kubernetes and a new SCM at once. "A goal without a plan is just a wish," Fish said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022.

## Turn the plan into milestones managers can read

A high-level plan is for the person doing the work; managers want milestones and dates. Hers ran roughly from early June to mid July:

1. Terraform code for dev and production GitLab projects (dev for testing upgrades and letting people play).
2. A dedicated slot for networking troubleshooting, because another team owned the network and other teams are potential bottlenecks.
3. GitLab up and running: DNS, certificates, SAML.
4. First bare repo migration with GitLab's Bitbucket importer.
5. Backups, restores and monitoring - full system, repo and branch restores tested, with her own step-by-step restore procedure because the docs were thin.
6. Second repo migration with the Jenkins pipeline working end to end.
7. Training, gradual login and continuous migration, team by team.
8. Migration done, documentation and handoff.

The largest back-end repo took several hours to import in a dev test, and nobody could push to Bitbucket during a migration, so she ran it on the Israeli weekend, Friday and Saturday. A happy Sunday followed.

One planning doc held everything: first steps, out-of-scope to-dos, a read-more list for later, audit considerations, known issues, an access map of inbound and outbound connectivity, the LDAP groups, and a repo tracker her manager added to ease his mind.

## Communicate more than feels necessary

Working alone made status updates the job. Weekly meetings, ad hoc ones for blockers, Jira tickets for everything including requests to other teams so they could work in parallel. She brought R&D team leads into the folder structure decision, since permissions were set per folder and they own the code, because she wanted them on board rather than handed a decision from outside.

## Read the docs, then write better ones

GitLab was new to her, so documentation drove decisions: a non-default database version that would allow the upgrade path to version 14, and high availability left off because it was not yet GA, with a comment in the Terraform code to turn it on later. Monitoring for the Kubernetes deployment was not built in, so she wrote dashboards and alerts herself. A limits issue her team raised even changed GitLab's official documentation.

For R&D: a training session (pull requests are merge requests now), a dev instance to practise on, an onboarding doc for repointing local clones, and a Slack channel with known GitLab issues pinned. For her own team: documentation covering upgrades, certificates, SAML and what to send GitLab support to skip the ticket ping-pong.

## Who should watch

Any engineer handed a migration with a deadline and no project manager. The GitLab specifics are a bonus; the milestone plan is the takeaway.
