Title: The OpenTelemetry Collector was the one piece that just worked
Description: Dave McAllister (NGINX) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on instrumenting NGINX MARA with OpenTelemetry - traces, metrics, logs and the gotchas
Body:
Adding observability to an existing microservices app is less about picking a tool and more about surviving the language-specific gotchas. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Dave McAllister, Senior OSS Technical Evangelist at NGINX, reported how his engineering team instrumented NGINX MARA, the Modern Application Reference Architecture, with OpenTelemetry - and why the OpenTelemetry Collector ended up carrying most of the weight.

He is upfront that it is a point-in-time snapshot, from work done five or six months before the talk, in a project that was moving fast.

## What were they instrumenting?

MARA is a production-ready reference setup on Kubernetes, built around a banking app: a Python front end, a back end split between Python and Java (Spring Boot), and two PostgreSQL databases, with NGINX open source handling application networking, plus load generation and CI. Two languages and two frameworks meant any solution had to handle both and carry context across the hops.

The team started with a feature checklist across Elastic APM, Grafana, Graylog, Jaeger, OpenCensus, OpenTelemetry, StatsD, Zipkin and others, then threw it away: "this chart is very pretty and honestly kind of meaningless," McAllister said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, because Zipkin and Elastic APM solve different problems. The OpenCensus and OpenTracing sites both pointed to OpenTelemetry anyway.

## Logs: it works, but it eats resources

OpenTelemetry logging was in early beta, so they did not trust it for production. Logs went through Filebeat as a Kubernetes DaemonSet into Elasticsearch (deployed via the Bitnami chart with separate ingest, coordinating, master and data nodes) and Kibana. It worked, but it was resource hungry, and queries outside the preloaded indexes got awkward.

## Tracing: Python easy, Java less so

Tracing had hard requirements: it must not hurt quality of service, and it must cover both languages. The OpenTelemetry Collector worked as both agent and aggregator, feeding Jaeger. Python was straightforward: a couple of files, a requirements update, Bunyan for JSON logs, and trace IDs attached to log lines so a problem can be traced back through context.

Java was the hard part. Greenfield Java is fine; their existing Spring app was not. Spring Cloud Sleuth adds trace and span IDs, but its OpenTelemetry autoconfig was a milestone release tied to old OpenTelemetry versions, and they had to pull from Spring snapshots. Their workaround became a common telemetry module that adds standard trace names across languages, a no-op tracing implementation to measure the overhead of tracing, an error handler that writes to both logs and traces, extra attributes such as service name and instance ID, and the trace ID in a comment before every SQL statement, so you know which request produced which query. NGINX also has an OpenTelemetry module, published on the NGINX GitHub.

## Metrics: easy, with caveats

They skipped Python metrics as not meaningful for the goal. Java already used Micrometer, the default metrics API in Spring, which exports Prometheus and StatsD. Because the Collector ingests Prometheus, StatsD or OTLP, Micrometer and OpenTelemetry were never in conflict: Micrometer to a Prometheus exporter, then into the Collector, and from there to any backend.

## What would he change?

A more central store with easy correlation instead of several tools with different query languages, and a look at Loki, Graylog or the newer OpenTelemetry logging. The headline is simple: "the open telemetry collector is the thing that made this actually work," he said. The other lesson: auto-instrumentation is great when it gives you what you want, and you still need trace IDs in your logs.

## Who should watch

Teams retrofitting tracing into a polyglot Kubernetes app, especially with legacy Spring in the mix. Some version details have aged; the architecture choices have not.

Title: Kubernetes ships 1,277 metric names per node and dashboards use 307
Description: Aliaksandr Valialkin (VictoriaMetrics) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on why Kubernetes monitoring is hard - metric bloat, churn, no standard
Body:
Kubernetes monitoring is hard mostly because Kubernetes exports far more than anyone looks at. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Aliaksandr Valialkin, Founder and CTO of VictoriaMetrics (and author of the Go libraries fasthttp, fastcache and quicktemplate), measured the bloat, explained why pod churn hurts every time series database, and asked the community to agree on a lighter standard.

He is a database vendor talking about a problem his database exists to solve, and he is candid that VictoriaMetrics' own exporter has the same disease.

## How many metrics does a cluster really emit?

The numbers grow by the release. Unique metric names exposed by Kubernetes components grew about 3.4x, from roughly 150 in Kubernetes 1.10 in 2018 to more than 500 in 1.24. node_exporter grew 4.5x over five years. On Kubernetes 1.24 every node exports at least 2,459 series before you count a single application metric, and across the clusters VictoriaMetrics could get data from, the realistic average was around 4,000 per node.

Layers explain why: hardware, VM, pod, container, application, each wanting its own observability. Deploy one container with three replicas and cAdvisor alone adds 629 new series. The application's own metrics come on top.

## Why does pod churn hurt so much?

Churn is old series being replaced by new ones, and monitoring systems hate it because it costs memory and CPU. Kubernetes generates it in two ways: every deployment (even changing an image tag) and every horizontal pod autoscaling event creates new pod names, and therefore a fresh set of series. The new series per event scale with container metrics plus application metrics, multiplied by replicas and by deployments.

Prometheus 2.0 was redesigned largely to cope with this, Valialkin notes, and churn and cardinality are still not solved there or anywhere else. VictoriaMetrics itself started as a fix for Prometheus 1.x cardinality problems and uses a per-day inverted index against churn.

## Do we need all these metrics?

There is no easy answer, he admits: no, because rules and dashboards touch only a fraction; yes, because you might need one later. Grafana's Mimirtool settles it empirically by scanning alerting rules, recording rules and dashboard queries, then generating an allowlist; Grafana's own example cut a small cluster from 40,000 active series to 8,000. In kube-prometheus-stack, one node exposes 1,277 unique metric names, and 307 of them are used in rules and Grafana dashboards. About a quarter.

He points the finger at his own project too: VictoriaMetrics' exported metric names grew about 3x in four years, and only around 30% are used by its own dashboards and rules.

## Why is there no standard?

"Unfortunately, there is no established standards for metrics at the moment," Valialkin said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. Google's four golden signals, Brendan Gregg's USE method and Weaveworks' RED method compete, so nobody follows one, metrics drift over time, and most community Kubernetes dashboards on grafana.com are out of date. Microservices pile on: per-instance metrics, correlation across services, network monitoring, noisy neighbours and a service mesh layer that also needs watching.

His fix list: fewer exposed metrics, fewer histograms (the biggest cardinality offender), fewer per-metric labels (does every metric need every pod-level label?), less churn from HPA and deployments, and a community standard for Kubernetes monitoring.

## Who should watch

Anyone paying for a Prometheus-compatible backend by the series, and platform teams wondering why the monitoring stack costs more than the cluster it watches.

Title: Dynamic alerting needs high school statistics, not machine learning
Description: Abhijeet Mishra (last9.io) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on smoke detectors that alert on rate, spikes, seasonality and missing metrics
Body:
Static thresholds made sense when Nagios checks returned 0, 1 or 2 and nobody had written a line of YAML. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Abhijeet Mishra, Software Engineer on Last9's core data science team, argued that modern systems need dynamic alerting - and that you can build it from standard deviations and percentiles rather than a fleet of machine learning models.

## Why don't static thresholds work any more?

Because the honest answer to every threshold question is that it depends. A handful of 5xx errors is noise at millions of requests and an SLO breach at hundreds. Container restarts matter relative to the desired count. One second of latency is too slow for an e-commerce page, fine for a data crunching job and blazing fast for a video editing pipeline. "There are no sitting ducks anymore. The ducks are armed and dangerous," Mishra said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022.

## Aren't SLOs enough?

No, because SLOs are lagging indicators: they tell you how the system did, not how it is about to do. His analogy is weather: a wet car means it rained, clouds and lightning mean it might.

He also separates request-based from window-based SLOs. A shop that serves 99% of requests successfully on a sale day can still have had a 30-minute window where every request failed and customers left for good; the request-based SLO looks fine. A window SLO - at least 99% of one-minute intervals over 24 hours had a success ratio of 95% or more - catches it. Payments care about successful transactions, so request-based fits; a streaming service cares about uninterrupted viewing, so windows fit.

## What does a smoke detector look for?

Machine learning is ruled out on cost: one model per metric, trained and maintained, gets expensive fast as components multiply. Instead, Last9's smoke detector treats an anomaly as a deviation in one of three characteristics.

- **Rate.** Standard deviation over a sliding window flags sudden change. Worth it for a jump in 4xx errors or RDS queue depth; not for CPU going from 20% to 50%, unless it keeps climbing and stays there.
- **Amplitude.** Percentile-based cutoffs on historical data, for example the 95th percentile as an upper bound that adjusts as new values arrive. This stops a sparse-traffic service from paging every time it gets its first request in an hour.
- **Time of day.** The 4 a.m. database backup spikes network I/O every morning and fools both detectors above. Seasonality fixes it: to judge a value at 6:30 p.m., compare it with values from 6 to 7 p.m. in the past week. The window size depends on how predictable traffic is: an hour for a sports stream with known start times, 3 to 5 hours for e-commerce weekends and holidays.

Combining characteristics adds context, and the number of characteristics firing at once gives a severity signal.

## What if the metrics stop arriving?

Every method above assumes data is flowing. Loss of signal is its own alert. For a high-traffic service, any gap is suspicious. For a Lambda that fires roughly hourly, track the time between data points with percentile cutoffs: nothing for 75 minutes is fine, nothing for two hours is a problem.

Mishra ends without a silver bullet, and admits he still uses static thresholds for basics like uptime.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose on-call rotation is drowning in threshold alerts, and teams about to buy an anomaly-detection feature who want to know what is likely inside it.

Title: Teams say MTTR is improving while their incidents get longer
Description: Dotan Horovits (Logz.io) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on the DevOps Pulse survey, where 64% of teams took over an hour to recover from incidents
Body:
Ask engineers whether they are getting better at incident recovery and most say yes; ask them how long recovery takes and the answer got worse. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Dotan Horovits, Principal Developer Advocate at Logz.io, tested five common assumptions about cloud, Kubernetes and observability against Logz.io's annual DevOps Pulse survey of more than 1,000 engineers, from startups with a dozen people to enterprises with 5,000 or more.

It is a short talk, about ten minutes of numbers, and it holds up as a snapshot of where the industry stood in 2022.

## Is everybody on AWS?

Mostly. AWS grew from 66% to 71% of respondents. Google Cloud and Azure both jumped from roughly 11-12% to around 30% (32% and 29%), with Google Cloud overtaking Azure for second place. Everyone else was close to zero, with VMware the one showing some strength.

## Is everything containerised?

It is happening across company sizes. Over 50% of respondents said more than half their apps run in containers, and 30% said more than three quarters do.

## Is Kubernetes a piece of cake?

No. Respondents reported trouble across the board, led by security and by monitoring and troubleshooting, followed by networking, cluster management and storage. "Everyone's moving to containers, as we've seen, but still don't know how to manage them," Horovits said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022.

## Are logs and metrics still enough?

Logs (about 88%) and metrics (about 80%) remain the default. The story is tracing: 48% now do some distributed tracing, up from 26% in the previous survey and 19% the year before that, and 70% of those not yet tracing plan to start within one or two years. APM, often seen as old-school, is used by 43%. The number Horovits liked most: 21% use all of the above, which he reads as a real step towards full observability built on correlated signals rather than logs alone. He also notes tracing adoption has been slower than people predicted in earlier surveys, even if it is clearly picking up.

## Are we getting better at MTTR?

Here the survey argues with itself. 68% said they are improving mean time to recovery: 14% greatly reduced it, 23% are making great strides, 31% are slowly making progress. Yet 64% reported that recovering from production incidents took more than an hour, up from 47% in the previous report. Horovits suggests the growing adoption of Kubernetes and cloud native architectures may be part of the cause. Either way, the perception gap is the most useful slide in the talk: if your team feels faster, measure it.

One more stat from the opening: the respondent pool moved from 86% male to 79% male and 15% female, which Horovits called encouraging.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers making the case for tracing or for better incident tooling, and anyone who wants a quick reality check on 2022 adoption numbers. The full report, with sections on security, data volumes, cost and team structure that the talk skips, was linked at the end.

Title: Prometheus doesn't take logs, so parse them into metrics first
Description: Samuel Arogbonlo (O(1) Labs) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on turning logs into Prometheus metrics with Vector, and actionable alerts
Body:
Your logs know why the server crashed; Prometheus only understands numbers. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Samuel Arogbonlo, Senior Infrastructure Engineer at O(1) Labs (the team behind Mina Protocol), walked through using Vector, the open source observability data pipeline, to turn log lines into metrics Prometheus can scrape - and argued that the metrics you choose and the alerts you set matter more than the plumbing.

This is a short introductory talk: a good first look at the log-to-metric pattern, not a deep configuration walkthrough.

## Why bother with log metrics at all?

Arogbonlo lists the use cases he sees: cutting total observability cost, improving performance and reliability of the observability stack, switching vendors without disrupting workflows, better data quality, and consolidating agents so you are not running one per tool.

His case for logs in SRE is the crash you cannot catch live. When a server dies before you can log in, restart it, tail the logs, and wait: the last line before it falls over often names the culprit, whether that is the image, the config or memory. Metrics are the other half, with a firm rule borrowed from the SRE literature on his slides: each exposed metric should serve a purpose, and you should resist exporting metrics just because they are easy to generate.

## The pipeline in five steps

Vector sits between your servers and Prometheus. "Prometheus does not accept logs, it accepts metrics," Arogbonlo said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, and Vector is the converter. His best practices, in order:

1. Set up the source and web server configuration in vector.toml; a handful of lines in the docs gets it running.
2. Parse the logs before transforming them. Unparsed lines cannot become metrics, and he has seen people skip this step and wonder why nothing arrives.
3. Count deliberately. Decide what you actually want - request status, service status, how many 200s versus 404s - and count those components and strings, rather than shipping everything and drowning in it.
4. Expose the result with Vector's Prometheus exporter sink so Prometheus can scrape the URL.
5. Check the scrape on a dashboard before trusting it.

## Alert on what needs a human

The last practice is the one with the most opinion in it. A Kubernetes pod that restarts and recovers by itself should not page anyone; a crash loop or a down service should. Set thresholds that catch problems before users feel them without causing alert fatigue, and route notifications to the team that can act, in time, including whoever is on call. His closing line, from the slides: a good monitoring system pays dividends, and it is worth iterating until you get it right.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to Prometheus or to Vector who want the shape of a log-to-metrics pipeline in one sitting. If you already run Vector in production, the alerting section is the part to keep; the rest will be familiar.

Title: Treat your metrics like Terraform treats your infrastructure
Description: Piyush Verma (last9.io) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on openmetrics-exporter, observability as code in HCL instead of one exporter per source
Body:
Every new thing you want to observe usually means another exporter binary, and another binary that can quietly die. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Piyush Verma, Founder and CTO of last9.io, presented openmetrics-exporter (OME), a framework born at Last9 that turns metric collection into declarative HCL files: pick the metrics you care about, correlate sources, and emit them in OpenMetrics format for any Prometheus-compatible agent to ship.

It is a talk about his company's open source tool, and it says so. The interesting part is the argument behind it.

## Are you paying to store metrics nobody reads?

Verma opens with `go_gc_duration_seconds`, the metric every Go exporter emits and almost nobody alerts on. Multiply that by every exporter you run and the store fills with free, unused data. "40% of your metrics might not even be accessed ever," he said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, a figure he attributes to what Last9 observed across its customers. The symptom everyone recognises: the dashboards are getting slower.

The EKS example makes the duplication concrete. CloudWatch reports on the cluster, kube-state-metrics and cAdvisor report on the same cluster to Prometheus, and someone correlates the two by eye in Grafana. Meanwhile the CloudWatch-scraping exporter raises the AWS bill on every pull, and you may not know if it is lagging or has crashed.

His summary of the problem: sources keep changing, there is no correlation between them, metrics explode, and every new source needs a new exporter.

## Declare, plan, dispatch

The workflow borrows from Terraform on purpose. You declare a scraper with a source and its gauges, counters and histograms, each carrying a source-specific query and dynamic labels. A resources block lets one file run across every load balancer you have. You run a plan locally, then dispatch, and OME serves the selected metrics on an `/openmetrics` endpoint for Prometheus agent, Grafana Agent or vmagent to carry away.

Correlation happens in the same file. Throughput can come from CloudWatch and latency from a PromQL query, emitted under the same label set; if the scrape fails, both fail together. Two scraper properties handle sources whose values change after the fact: lookback re-reads a past window and re-emits corrected values with their original timestamps, and lag holds a pipeline until the data has settled. Most exporters stamp data with the scrape time; OME keeps the source timestamp.

For a faster feedback loop, every run can generate a Grafana dashboard from the file, so you check that you did not use an average where you meant a max before shipping. Scrapers can become modules, referenced by remote URL and reused, with a public catalogue of curated metric sets. Sources include Prometheus, Google Stackdriver, Amazon CloudWatch, Redshift and other SQL databases.

## Why HCL and not YAML?

The slide's punchline: YAML gives you job security, HCL lets you concentrate. The real reason is that HCL has expressions - joins, splits, format strings, conditionals - so small transformations live in config rather than in a fork of someone's exporter. It also fits existing editors and GitOps pipelines, as with Terraform, Consul and Nomad.

On performance, Verma quotes a single machine with about six cores and 6 GB of RAM running 500 scrapers and emitting three to four million data points.

## Who should watch

SREs whose Prometheus bill or dashboard load times are growing faster than their system, and anyone running a zoo of single-purpose exporters. Expect a tool tour rather than a vendor-neutral survey.

Title: LinkedIn's Hodor sheds just enough traffic to keep services alive
Description: Bryan Barkley and Vivek Deshpande (LinkedIn) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on Hodor, zero-config overload detection and load shedding
Body:
When a LinkedIn service drowns, something called Hodor holds the door. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Bryan Barkley (Senior Staff Engineer) and Vivek Deshpande (Senior Software Engineer) of LinkedIn explained Hodor - Holistic Overload Detection and Overload Remediation - a framework that spots overload from several root causes and drops just enough requests for the service to recover, with no per-service thresholds to tune.

The no-tuning part is the point. LinkedIn runs hundreds of services on tens of thousands of machines, and hand-configuring each one was never going to happen. Everything shown runs on the JVM, though the ideas travel.

## What counts as overloaded?

Barkley defines it as the point where a service can no longer serve traffic with reasonable latency. The resources that run out can be physical (CPU, memory, network, disk I/O) or virtual (threads, pooled DB connections, semaphore permits). The causes vary too: a 5x traffic spike, a slow downstream applying backpressure up the call chain, or a noisy neighbour on the same host eating CPU while your own metrics look innocent. That spread of causes is why the framework has to be holistic.

Hodor has three parts: overload detectors, a load shedder, and a platform adapter that wires them into Rest.li (LinkedIn's open source RPC framework), gRPC and HTTP servers such as Play.

## Three detectors, one for each way to run out

The CPU detector is the clever one. A lightweight heartbeat thread, running at the same priority as application threads, sleeps for 10 ms and checks whether it woke up on time. If the 99th percentile of a second's worth of wake-up delays exceeds 55 ms, that window is in violation; eight consecutive violating windows and the service is overloaded. Deshpande's rationale: it measures CPU that is actually usable. "Just because you see 30% free cpu on something like top command does not mean that it is useful cpu," he said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. It also works the same on bare metal, VMs or cgroup quotas.

The GC detector tracks the amortised percentage of time spent in garbage collection, in tiers: 10% or more for 30 seconds counts as overload, a lower tier such as 8% needs 60 seconds. The thread pool detector watches queue wait time, which catches a slow downstream without knowing anything about it. In the production cases shown, p90 and p99 latencies jumped by up to 900% when these detectors fired.

## How much traffic should you drop?

Hodor limits concurrency rather than a percentage of requests. The shedder cuts aggressively and lets traffic back in conservatively; a percentage-based shedder kept chasing changing traffic levels in their experiments and lost. Dropped requests return 503 before any business logic runs, so clients can retry them on a healthy host. To stop that turning into a retry storm when the whole cluster is hot, both client and server keep retry budgets.

## Monitoring mode found bugs nobody knew about

Rollout started with detectors in monitoring mode for at least a week per service, correlating firings with latency, CPU and GC data. Some services were not ready, nearly always because of GC, and fixing that often cut CPU use as a side benefit. One team quoted on the slides found that detectors had surfaced behaviour its owners did not know about. The best example: a forgotten setting that periodically wrote thread dumps to disk, freezing the JVM for seconds at a time without ever showing up in high-percentile metrics.

## The 20% that saved the other 80%

The flagship LinkedIn.com app hit a new bug during a data-centre traffic shift. Hodor shed about 20% of requests for a while, and SREs concluded that without it a minor incident would have been a major outage. The team counts over 100 such saves. Next on the list: traffic tiering (drop prefetch and offline requests first), latency-confirmed detection to cut GC false positives, a Netty event-loop detector, and feeding overload signals into autoscaling, which Barkley warns can push the problem further downstream.

## Who should watch

Anyone running a large JVM fleet, or anyone who has tuned a rate limiter per service and hated it. The heartbeat detector alone is worth the 25 minutes.

Title: The biggest base image ended up the safest container
Description: Martin Wimpress (Slim.ai) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on container hardening, comparing base images by CVEs, and slimming a Python image
Body:
Smaller is safer, says the adage, and Martin Wimpress spent his Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 talk testing it. Wimpress, Senior Director of Developer Relations and Community at Slim.ai, built the same small Python Flask app on four base images, scanned each one, and found that Ubuntu 22.04, the largest of the four, had no critical or high vulnerabilities. After slimming it with the open-source DockerSlim, it came out within 5 MB of a slimmed Alpine image with zero known vulnerabilities.

It is a vendor talk (the analysis runs in Slim.ai's SaaS and Docker Desktop extension), but the practices and measurements hold up without the product. The title promises five practices; Wimpress admits at the end that he gave you more than five.

## The Dockerfile basics that matter for security

His starting Dockerfile already follows the usual rules: official base image, a work directory, layers ordered to minimise cache invalidation, files copied only when needed, an exposed port, an ENTRYPOINT for proper signal handling. Then the security-specific changes:

- **Run as nobody.** Without a USER line the app runs as root, and an attacker who gets in has the container and every tool shipped in it. The unprivileged nobody account exists in Debian, Ubuntu, RHEL, Alpine and distroless.
- **Pin the base image.** The latest tag means no single source of truth for your bill of materials and surprise major-version bumps. He pins to a specific distro and language version (python:3.9.13-slim-bullseye) and lets security scanning drive updates.
- **Do run apt-get upgrade.** The old advice was to avoid it. His point: vendors refresh base images under the same tag, but there can be days between a fix landing in the package repositories and the new image reaching the registry. On a pinned, stable base, upgrades are security and severe bug fixes only.
- **Watch the layer cache.** Docker reuses a cached layer if the command text hasn't changed, so your apt-get line keeps installing old packages after the distro has shipped fixes. Keep your normal build, and add a nightly rebuild with the pull and no-cache flags.
- **Skip recommended packages.** On Ubuntu, installing Python with the no-install-recommends option saved about 266 MB.

## What is actually in the image?

Scan every production image and generate SBOMs in the pipeline. For the talk he used docker scan (powered by Snyk) and docker sbom (powered by Syft), and mentions Trivy, Grype and Clair as alternatives worth trying.

"Knowing what's inside your container is critical to securing your software supply chain," Wimpress said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022.

## Four base images, scanned

The regular python:3.9.13-bullseye image is 915 MB. With the app and its eleven pip dependencies, the slimmer candidates came to 62 MB on Alpine 3.15, 72 MB on distroless, 135 MB on python slim-bullseye and 139 MB on Ubuntu 22.04. The vulnerability counts don't follow the sizes:

- Alpine: 0.
- Ubuntu 22.04: 15, none critical or high.
- Distroless (Debian 11): 46, three critical and seven high, and with no apt-get inside, hard to patch.
- python slim-bullseye (Debian 11): 84, thirteen critical and three high, all in system packages.

Why does Ubuntu beat its own parent? Wimpress, a Debian contributor himself, credits the commercial security team: Canonical commits to SLAs for mitigating critical and high vulnerabilities over a release's supported life, as do Red Hat and SUSE, while Debian is a community project doing its best. He gives one example: the glibc CVE-2021-3999 was still present in the Debian 11 images, already mitigated in Ubuntu, and never present in Alpine because it uses musl.

## So why not just use Alpine?

Because of musl. Python, Node and some other languages can build much more slowly on Alpine and hit runtime bugs that come from musl versus glibc.

"Personally, I do not recommend using Alpine for Python apps, but it can be great for Go and Rust," Wimpress said.

## Slimming: Ubuntu's patching with Alpine's footprint

DockerSlim analyses what the app actually uses, through static and dynamic tracing, and builds a new single-layer image containing only those files. On this simple app the reductions were 3 to 6 times (Ubuntu went from 139 MB to 25 MB); he says complex applications often see 10 to 30 times. Slim.ai's report on the top 100 public container images found more and more test, QA and infrastructure tooling left in production images, which is exactly what an attacker wants to find.

The catch: scanners often can't assess a slimmed image because the package metadata is gone, so checking is manual. In the demo he searches the Ubuntu image for the Python mailcap module, which carried two of the low-severity findings, finds it in the original and not in the slimmed one. The app never used it, so the vulnerability left with it. The same check cleared the medium findings in e2fsprogs, libsqlite3 and perl-base.

## Who should watch

Anyone who writes Dockerfiles for production, especially Python teams that picked Alpine for its size. The base-image table and the layer-caching point are worth the time even if you never touch Slim.ai.

Title: A bootstrap team, an SRE in every squad, and predictions over pages
Description: Rohit Sinha (T-Systems International) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on rolling out SRE in a services company with bootstrap SREs and ML predictions
Body:
A product company can stand up a central SRE team and spread the practice from there. A services company, where every customer unit runs its own P&L and behaves like its own little firm, can't. Rohit Sinha, Director of Cloud Application Services at T-Systems International, described at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 how his organisation dealt with that: a small bootstrap team of experienced SREs mentoring a designated SRE in every squad, plus data science that predicts failures so engineers stop waiting for incidents.

His framing is that SRE is a cultural and data shift more than a technology one, and the talk is honest that the predictive part was still work in progress.

## How do you roll out SRE across customer units that act like separate companies?

Each customer unit delivers similar services slightly differently, at different levels of tooling and SRE maturity. The answer was the bootstrap site reliability engineer: a group of ten to twelve SREs, mostly hired from outside because they had done it before, acting as the ideological mentors of the whole SRE community. Sinha calls them the horizontal SREs. The vertical ones are designated SREs inside every squad of every customer unit, trained by the bootstrap group, which also introduces the new tooling and the analytics. In a company Sinha puts at $5 billion, that is a lot of squads. Ideally everyone would be an SRE, he says, but that is a maturity target, not reality.

## Why does he call automation an output?

He lists four transformation drivers (cultural shift, technology refresh, data and visibility engineering, process and automation) and insists the first is the hardest. Culture here means throwing a lot of not-my-problem out of the window, reskilling people, and replacing consequence management (finding the culprit) with a culture that accepts failure.

Automation comes last on purpose. "Automation is after you know what you need to do and then automation does what it does," Sinha said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. Analysis decides what is worth automating. He also wants processes measured and, where needed, removed: too many stage gates turn structure into shackles.

## What is visibility engineering?

It is his name for the data layer that gives SREs something better than Excel. The first stage was ITSM analysis: a machine learning model, with separate pipelines per customer because each has different incident thresholds and ways of working, that categorises incidents automatically from historical records, showing what the problem is rather than where. The data is integrated across customers rather than centralised, because GDPR and many different toolchains rule out one big data lake. Sinha is explicit: they are not building a data lake.

The second stage is log analysis with dynamic, moving-average thresholds and predictions, correlating dependent and independent variables across component and system data. The abstract adds the details the talk skips: ARIMA as an example model, data captured every five minutes, and a correlation matrix of around 20 to 30 parameters per machine.

## What does an operator do with a prediction?

This is the question most AIOps pitches dodge, and the best part of the talk. ITIL is built around incident and change management, and problem management is reactive. If a prediction says something will break eight to ten hours from now, what is the standard procedure? Their answer: when a prediction says it will go wrong (Sinha mentions a 75% mark), the squad's SRE leads a project to bend the trend down before it becomes an incident. That only works if the predictions are accurate, which is why he says organisations need to invest in data science.

The second process change was a failure budget for application change management. Each team gets credits based on its historical change performance; while it has credits it can move through the quality gates freely, and after a breach or two it goes back to the full gates. It is a neat way of rewarding teams that have earned the right to take risk.

## What went wrong?

His challenges list is candid: people use transformations to chase numbers when the return is long-term, heavy governance gets in the way, organisations work from spreadsheets instead of tools, and leaders avoid bold decisions. His closing analogy for error budgets is a smartwatch: you look at the numbers every day to see whether you are improving.

## Who should watch

Leaders rolling out SRE in a large IT services or managed-services organisation, and anyone wondering how ML predictions fit into an ITIL world. Engineers looking for implementation detail on the models will find the talk light on it.

Title: LMAO, or how not to burn out on a 365-day pager
Description: Richard Lewis (3Cloud) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on LMAO, logs, metrics, alerts and an observability tool, plus playbooks and drills
Body:
In his first IT job, around 2011, Richard Lewis was on call 365 days a year, 16 hours a day, with a physical pager, no remote access and no logging framework. He burned out in six months. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, Lewis, now a Senior DevOps Consultant at 3Cloud, turned what he and his boss built after that into a short, fast acronym for anyone carrying a pager: LMAO, for logs, metrics, alerts and an observability tool.

It is a short talk with more war stories than tooling, aimed at on-call engineers and the people who schedule them.

## What fixed the burnout?

He didn't quit; he told his boss what was wrong, and the boss listened. They added a logging framework first (log4net) and then fixed the rotation by hiring and spreading the load. The first lesson of the talk is the scheduling one.

"You can't have a person on call 24 hours a day, 365 days a year," Lewis said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. If you try, they leave, and they take their tribal knowledge with them.

## L and M: what happened and when

Logs and metrics answer the basic questions: what happened, how many errors, how many requests, when, and for how long. It is the briefest section; the interesting parts are about what you do with them.

## A: pages, tickets and alert fatigue

Lewis splits alerts into pages (the network is down, the website is offline) and tickets (the disk behind the website is at 80% and climbing, the e-commerce site is slow but up). Managing them well comes down to four habits: schedule people sensibly, avoid alert fatigue, collect data on the alerts you send and keep reducing them, and be careful adding new ones.

The reduction ideas are practical. If CPU alerts keep firing, look at autoscaling. If traffic rises at the same hours every day, autoscale for that. If a disk fills up, write a runbook that heals it automatically. Every alert should exist to make someone act.

## O: one dashboard, or nine

He pulls up the monitoring section of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation's product map and counts about nine products on it that he regularly recommends to clients, with the caveat that there is no single right tool, only the right tool for the cost and the moment. Two dashboards illustrate what good looks like. A New Relic one lines up policy violations, synthetic check failures and errors per minute next to deployment notes, so the first question in an incident (what did we just change?) has an answer on screen. A Grafana one embeds wiki links, documentation, an architecture diagram, service up/down history and the 200 versus 500 status codes, so whoever is on call has everything in one place.

## Playbooks: where you keep them matters

Every application should have its own playbook. His contents list: links to the observability tools for that application, its golden signals and their normal range, notes from previous outages and postmortems, the application owner's contacts, and third-party escalation paths such as cloud premium support or your payment provider.

The placement advice is the subtle bit. If the playbook lives inside a network that you reach through Azure AD and Azure AD is the thing that's down, you can't read the playbook. He prefers somewhere outside the network but still behind single sign-on: Confluence, a hosted wiki, SharePoint or a Microsoft Teams wiki.

## Practise like a tornado drill

Growing up in the US Midwest, Lewis did tornado drills at school until crouching in the hallway was muscle memory. That is his case for chaos engineering: controlled experiments that find single points of failure early and test your documentation and processes. He points to Gremlin and to Microsoft's chaos engineering service for tooling.

After real outages, run the postmortem within a day or so while memories are fresh: what went right, what went wrong, where you got lucky. He likes the Google SRE book line that the cost of failure is education. Then update the playbooks and put a revision date on them. A playbook untouched for six months means either a quiet system or an undocumented one.

## Who should watch

On-call engineers early in their career and managers who build rotations. Experienced SREs know the ideas, but the burnout story is worth sending to whoever is planning your next rotation.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Julie Gunderson on [postmortems, continuous learning and blameless culture](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Julie_Gunderson_postmortem_continuous_learning_blameless_culture) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2021.

Title: Stop bolting reliability onto every API endpoint
Description: Navendu Pottekkat (API7.ai) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on moving API auth, rate limits, canaries and circuit breakers into an API gateway
Body:
If every microservice carries its own copy of auth, rate limiting and monitoring, written in whichever language that team picked, reliability work scales with the number of services. Navendu Pottekkat, Developer Advocate at API7.ai and a contributor to Apache APISIX, argued at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 that this is the core reliability problem of traditional API architectures, and that the fix is to move those concerns into an API gateway and manage them in one place.

He keeps it vendor-neutral on purpose: APISIX gets a mention at the start and the end, but the practices apply to any open-source gateway or a cloud provider's.

## Isn't reliability just uptime?

His first move is to widen the definition. A 99.9% uptime SLA is a myopic view; for an API, reliability also means consistency (clients get reproducible results), availability, low latency, security and status (both the team and API consumers can see whether it is up and whether redirects are in place).

"A service with a high latency is almost equal to service that is not working," Pottekkat said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. For the client app waiting on your response, slow and down look the same.

## What goes wrong without a gateway?

Every improvement has to be added to each service separately. The endpoints may use different languages and libraries, so nothing is plug and play, and the reliability tooling has to scale with the API. Monitoring means instrumenting every service, security and authentication mean configuring each one, and releases become stressful because you are aiming for zero downtime with no request dropped mid-transition. The gateway turns that into one common entry point that routes to back-end services by configuration.

## The practices, one at a time

**Authentication.** The gateway authenticates every request, from basic schemes such as a JWT or a cookie in a header to external identity providers such as Active Directory, then passes what it learned to the services behind it. Authenticated requests also make monitoring finer-grained.

**Rate limiting.** He files it under security and reliability both: it stops intentional and accidental misuse, denial of service included, and protects the back end from sudden traffic spikes. Excess requests are either rejected with an error status or, if clients can tolerate the latency, delayed until the services can take them.

**Monitoring and observability.** Instrument the gateway and you see all traffic: metrics for reliability and scaling decisions, plus logs and traces that follow one request from the gateway through the services and back. The point he stresses is avoiding silent failures.

**Canary releases.** All traffic goes to the version 1 upstream; when version 2 is ready, the gateway sends it a small share, increasing it as results stay good, possibly automatically. If something breaks, version 1 is still on standby and rollback is a configuration change.

**Circuit breaking.** With several upstreams behind the gateway acting as a load balancer, one that is down or slow must be cut off. Otherwise requests pile up on it, retries exhaust resources, and the failure spreads to the healthy upstreams like dominoes. The gateway routes around the failed upstream, periodically checks it, and sends traffic back when it recovers.

**Changing paths.** Renaming an endpoint normally means chasing every client to update code. Instead, configure the gateway to redirect the old path to the new one, return a redirect status, and add a deprecation message. Old clients keep working while they migrate.

## Who should watch

Teams with a growing number of services that still handle auth and rate limiting in application code, and SREs making the case for a gateway. If you already run Kong, APISIX or a cloud gateway with these features on, the talk is a checklist rather than news.

Title: New on the ops team? Write the runbook nobody has yet
Description: Kazuki Higashiguchi (Autify) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on three habits that get a new team member into on-call and troubleshooting fast
Body:
The newest person on a DevOps team is the one least able to judge whether an alert matters, and often the best placed to write down how things work. Kazuki Higashiguchi, a backend engineer at Autify, turned that into three habits in his Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 talk: open problem reports even when you don't understand them, write down what you learn, and write the runbooks your team is missing.

It is a short, practical talk aimed at engineers joining a team, built on his own experience at Autify (an AI-based test automation platform, where backend engineers also handle infrastructure, incidents and on-call) and on a well-chosen shelf of SRE books.

## Why is joining operations so hard?

He starts from the troubleshooting model in Google's *Site Reliability Engineering* book: a problem report, then telemetry and logs, then the current state, possible causes, a controlled change and the observed result. The process is generic; the knowledge isn't.

Take an alert that CPU utilisation is over 90%. Before deciding whether to act, you need answers you don't have yet: has the team seen this before, which workflow uses the server, do customers hit it or is it internal, is it a known issue? Mike Julian's *Practical Monitoring* splits alerts into those meant to wake someone up (all web servers down) and those that are FYI (an overnight backup failed, look at it next business day). Telling them apart depends on knowing the system's failure patterns. The same gap shows up in diagnosis: when queue processing stops and waiting events pile up, you need to know what the queue carries, the known causes, and whether retries are implemented.

## Tip one: open the alert anyway, with a timer

Click into problem reports even when you can't fix them. Each one teaches you a failure pattern. The guard rail is a time box.

"It's a good idea to set a time box, in other words a time limit, for example 30 minutes, as too much time may interfere with your main work," Higashiguchi said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022.

## Tip two: make your learning visible

After digging into an alert, open a blank page (Autify uses Notion for knowledge and Datadog for observability, so sometimes it is a Datadog investigation note) and write down the architecture you discovered, related metrics, and similar past cases. The notes help you, and they show your peers how much of the system you understand, which is how you earn their trust for on-call.

He also leans on Lorin Hochstein's chapter in *97 Things Every SRE Should Know*: the best skill transfer comes from watching experts solve real problems and documenting how they did it. Autify works remotely, so his version is asking a colleague on Slack how they investigated an issue after the fact, then writing it up.

## Tip three: write the runbook

A runbook turns knowledge held by subject-matter experts into a shared asset, and writing one is how you take over an operation. It also attacks the anti-pattern Jeffery D. Smith's *Operations Anti-Patterns, DevOps* calls Only Brent knows: knowledge pooling around a few key people who become valuable and overloaded at once.

Higashiguchi cites *Software Engineering at Google* on timing: the first time you learn something is the best time to improve the docs, before you forget what was confusing. Of the questions *Practical Monitoring* says a good runbook answers, he recommends newcomers take two: what dependencies the service has, and what its infrastructure looks like. Both force you to organise your picture of the architecture. And for the fear of writing something imperfect, he quotes *Seeking SRE* on Anne Lamott's idea that a rough first draft beats a perfect document that doesn't exist.

## Who should watch

Engineers in their first months on a team with on-call, and leads planning onboarding. Senior SREs won't learn new techniques, but might steal the reading list and the idea of making the new hire own the runbook gaps.

Title: A smart city ML stack on OpenShift, deployed by one Ansible playbook
Description: Karan Singh (Red Hat) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 on an edge-to-core licence plate pipeline with Kafka, Ceph and OpenShift
Body:
Karan Singh, Senior Principal Architect and Developer Evangelist at Red Hat, starts an Ansible playbook against an empty OpenShift cluster at the beginning of his Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 talk, and by the end it has stood up an entire edge-to-core smart city stack: licence plate recognition at the edge, Kafka moving events to the core, Ceph object storage, and Superset and Grafana dashboards on top. The point is the architecture, and that you can rebuild all of it with one command.

It is a live demo with simulated traffic, and an OpenShift-and-Red-Hat-tooling talk, which he does not hide. The pattern itself (edge inference, buffered event streaming, cheap object storage, federated SQL) travels to any Kubernetes.

## What is the city actually trying to do?

The business case is modelled on London's Ultra Low Emission Zone. Cameras at toll locations recognise passing vehicles and read their plates, so the city can charge an entry fee, add a dirty-vehicle charge for cars that miss emission standards, and flag wanted vehicles to officials. Each toll location is an edge site; fee calculation, business rules and analytics happen at the core.

The second half of the design is the ML loop: store vehicle images, plate images and plate strings centrally, retrain the model to improve accuracy, and push the new version back out to hundreds or thousands of edge sites. Edge sites can be a three-node OpenShift cluster or a single-node one.

## How does data get from edge to core?

At each edge site, video frames go through a licence plate detection model, which crops the plate region and passes it to an OCR model that reads the characters. The result, with a timestamp and coordinates, is produced to a local Kafka cluster.

Edge networks drop out, so the design leans on Kafka to buffer.

"We need to build this loosely coupled system that should handle the network disruptions, right?" Karan Singh said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022.

Kafka MirrorMaker then moves events asynchronously from the edge clusters to a central Kafka cluster at the core. From there, custom consumers (Python, Go or Quarkus apps) can run business logic such as wanted-vehicle notifications, and Secor, a Kafka consumer, writes everything to Ceph object storage for long-term retention of what is, after all, government data.

## The analytics layer

On top of the object store sits Open Data Hub tooling. Starburst runs distributed SQL across heterogeneous sources, so one query can join PostgreSQL tables with data sitting in S3-compatible buckets. Apache Superset serves the reporting views for managers; Grafana handles the real-time operations dashboard, which Karan admits is his favourite.

The demo dashboards are fed by a load generator in place of real cameras, so the numbers are made up, but they show the kind of questions the stack answers: roughly £215,000 in toll fees and £100,000 in pollution fees collected from about 45,000 vehicles, one station taking 22% of the city's traffic (time for another lane?), and which car makes are most common. Kafdrop shows the raw LPR topic messages, with timestamp, event ID, plate, detection status and station, at both the edge and the core, so you do not need kafkacat to check that MirrorMaker is doing its job.

## Eight Ansible modules, 36 pods

The automation is deliberately boring. The playbook creates databases, edge and core Kafka clusters, the microservices (LPR, events, image server, load generator, Secor), Open Data Hub and the Grafana dashboards. It does that with eight modules: k8s to apply YAML for secrets, deployment configs, services, image streams and build configs; k8s_info to read objects back, for example database credentials; set_fact for state; command for the bits with no module, such as Superset data imports; copy, add_host and s3_sync to seed images into object storage; and pause to let things settle.

The finished environment runs 36 pods.

"It has taken 15 minutes to deploy the entire setup that we have shown," Karan Singh said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022.

The code is in an open Git repository, and he invites pull requests.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers building data pipelines that start outside the data centre, and anyone who wants a worked example of Kafka MirrorMaker for edge-to-core replication. Data scientists looking for model training detail will not find much; the models are a box in the diagram.

Title: Alert on how fast the error budget burns, not on CPU
Description: Ricardo Castro (Anova) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on going from metric thresholds to multi-window burn-rate alerts and error budget policies
Body:
A CPU at 80% at 3am is not an incident if no user notices. Ricardo Castro, Lead SRE at Anova, used his Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 talk to walk the whole ladder from metric thresholds to multi-window, multi-burn-rate SLO alerts, and then to the part most teams skip: an error budget policy that says in advance what happens when the alert fires.

If you have read the Google SRE workbook chapter on alerting, this is the same progression, explained patiently with good examples. If you haven't, it is one of the clearer half-hour introductions to it.

## Why does an IoT company care?

Anova runs industrial IoT services: data from industrial sensors, processed, stored and fed into machine learning and applications for its customers. Castro gives the (admittedly dated, he says) figures of more than 2,000 customers in more than 80 countries and over a million monitored assets. That is a lot of things that can be quietly unreliable.

He borrows his definition from Alex Hidalgo's *Implementing Service Level Objectives*: a service is reliable if it does what its users need it to do. His warm-up analogy is a supermarket as a microservices architecture, where a half-hour queue at the till is latency and an expired yoghurt is an error.

## From metric to SLA in five steps

The foundations come with concrete examples worth reusing:

- **Metric**: a measurement of an event, such as request duration or how old a message is when it reaches a Kafka cluster.
- **SLI**: a binary good/bad judgement on that event, such as served within 200 ms, not a 500, Kafka message younger than five minutes.
- **SLO**: how often the SLI must be good over a time window, such as 99% of requests within 200 ms over 30 days, or 99.99% of Kafka messages younger than five minutes over 24 hours.
- **Error budget**: 100% minus the SLO.
- **SLA**: an SLO with consequences, like a 30% discount or a fine.

"SLAs are nothing more than an SLO that has consequences when that SLO is not met," Castro said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. SLAs should be looser than SLOs, so a broken SLO still leaves time to fix things before the contract is breached.

## Why each alerting approach falls short

This is the core of the talk. Metric thresholds page you for things users don't feel. Alerting when the SLI drops below the SLO target is better, but by then users are already unhappy.

Alerting on budget consumed is the next step, and Castro shows routing by level: 25% burned sends an email to the team, 50% posts in Microsoft Teams, 75% goes to PagerDuty. The flaw is that it says nothing about speed. If you would still finish the window with budget left, why get woken at 3am?

Burn rate fixes that. A burn rate of one spends the whole budget exactly by the end of the window; a burn rate of two over a four-week window empties it in two weeks. But a single burn-rate check has its own blind spot: evaluate it hourly, and a budget burned in 30 minutes produces no alert at all.

The last rung is multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting. A fast-burn alert over short five-minute windows at a burn rate of ten catches the catastrophic spike; a slow-burn alert over a 24-hour window, checked every five minutes, at a burn rate of two catches the steady leak.

## The policy is what makes the alert mean something

An alert you trust still needs an agreed response. Castro's error budget policy examples: if the service exceeded its budget over the preceding four weeks, freeze changes and releases except P0 issues and security fixes until it is back within SLO, and possibly move people from features to reliability; if one incident consumes more than 20% of the budget in four weeks, hold a postmortem with at least one P0 action item. He walks through the example policy document from Google's SRE book: authors, reviewers, approvers, revision date, scope, goals and non-goals, what counts as missing the SLO, and outage and escalation policies.

The payoff, as he frames it, is less alert fatigue, a shared language for reliability between engineering and product, and a clear rule for when reliability work beats feature work.

## Who should watch

Teams that have SLOs on a dashboard but still page on CPU. Experienced SLO practitioners can skip to the burn-rate section and the policy document.

Title: Stale dashboards are downtime too, so data needs its own SRE
Description: Miriah Peterson (Weave) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on data reliability engineering, data downtime and SLOs for pipelines
Body:
Web services brag about five nines; data rarely gets close. Miriah Peterson, Senior Data Reliability Engineer at Weave, argued at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 that the fix is to treat data systems as an engineering problem and borrow the SRE playbook: define data downtime, measure it with the golden signals, and wrap pipelines in SLAs, SLOs and SLIs. Her second claim is about people: the pipelines in the middle of a modern data stack need a specialist who is neither a DBA nor a classic SRE.

It is a short, clear introduction, about twenty minutes, with one worked example you can copy.

## What counts as data downtime?

Reliable data is more than an available database. Peterson lists accuracy, freshness, latency, availability, duplication and missing data. For downtime she uses the definition from Barr Moses, CEO of the data observability company Monte Carlo: any period when your data is partial, erroneous, missing or otherwise inaccurate. A dashboard that loads fine but shows last Tuesday's numbers is down.

As with services, the target is not 100%. She quotes *Database Reliability Engineering* by Laine Campbell and Charity Majors on systems without failures becoming brittle, and argues for error budgets that give a trained team room to respond before consumers notice.

## The golden signals, applied to data

Latency, traffic, errors and saturation map neatly onto data services: queries on a store taking too long, a model taking too long to train, a data gateway with unexpected latency, an API gateway returning 400s and 500s it shouldn't, a service with more or less traffic than expected. Metrics and metadata become the picture; anomalies become alerts worth investigating.

## A pipeline SLO you can steal

Her example is a pipeline that pulls CRM data, trains a lead-scoring model and publishes revenue dashboards for sales leaders.

- **SLA**: the revenue dashboard has data no older than one day.
- **SLO**: the pipeline extracts from the CRM and completes transforms, training and analysis at least once a day, and can be triggered manually if something fails.
- **SLIs**: errors in the pipeline (training didn't finish, a transform didn't run, the CRM connection failed) and timeouts on the CRM or on writes to the data store, each alerting someone that manual intervention is needed.

The point of the gap between SLO and SLA is time: the automation fails, the alert fires, and a human reruns the job before the 24 hours are up and anyone in sales notices.

## Who owns reliability for which data?

Peterson splits data work into three stacks. The **software data stack** (databases behind microservices, caches, browser storage) belongs to SREs. The **enterprise data stack** (large distributed databases, warehouses for BI, SAP and Oracle) belongs to DBAs or database reliability engineers who can shard and tune queries. The **modern data stack** is everything else: ETL for data scientists, ML pipelines, data gateways guarding golden datasets in a data mesh. That is where she places the data reliability engineer, with skills in ingress and egress, streaming and batch transformations, storage varieties, governance, analysis, automation, monitoring and architecture. Her phrase is data in motion rather than data at rest.

"Any service that relies on data to function needs to have some kind of data reliability in place," Peterson said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. As analytics data ends up inside software products and ML models ship to production with back-end teams, she says the work can move from trivial to a hard requirement quickly.

## Who should watch

Data engineers being paged for stale dashboards, and SREs who have just inherited a pipeline. If you already run data SLOs, the talk is a quick confirmation; if you don't, the CRM example is a template for your first one.

Title: Fail over on the data plane and keep a big red button
Description: Christian Elsen and Lerna Ekmekcioglu (AWS) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on fast multi-region routing and failover with no control plane dependency
Body:
A multi-region architecture only helps if users reach the nearest region quickly and you can move them off a broken one while half of the cloud's APIs are struggling. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, AWS solutions architects Christian Elsen (Principal, networking specialist) and Lerna Ekmekcioglu (Senior) showed how to do both with AWS Global Accelerator and Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller. Their summary: minimise hops before the AWS backbone, remove control plane dependencies from disaster recovery, and build a big red button for manual failover.

It is an AWS talk about AWS services, with three recorded demos. The control plane versus data plane idea travels well beyond AWS.

## Why not just let users cross the public internet?

Every hop between a user and your endpoint adds latency. Global Accelerator hands you two static anycast IP addresses, announced from AWS edge locations at the same time, so a user in Jakarta enters the AWS network at the Jakarta edge and rides the backbone the rest of the way. The talk puts the network at 96 points of presence in 84 cities across 46 countries. The headline figure: about 60% faster p50 download time for a 100 KB object, from third-party real-user measurements. The accelerator sits in front of ALBs, NLBs, EC2 instances or Elastic IPs.

## Blue/green across two regions with traffic dials

Global Accelerator has two controls. A traffic dial per endpoint group (a region) runs from 0% to 100%, default 100%, and applies only to traffic already headed to that group by proximity and health. Endpoint weights inside a group run from 0 to 255 (default 128), so traffic splits by each endpoint's share of the total.

That makes a multi-region blue/green deployment simple. Both regions serve live traffic at version 1. Dial us-west-2 to 0%: Japanese users still enter at Tokyo or Osaka but get routed to us-east-1, and you upgrade us-west-2 to version 2. Then do the same for us-east-1, then dial it back to 100%. Nobody's connection changes entry point, only where the backbone takes it. The demo shows a CloudWatch dashboard moving from a 50/50 split to 100% on one side and back over two to three minutes per shift. One gotcha from the demo: the dials act on traffic already directed to the group, so a 50/50 split means setting both regions to 50% explicitly.

## What should a failover depend on?

Here the talk gets more interesting. Every AWS service has a control plane (create, modify, delete: launching an EC2 instance, changing a security group) and a data plane (keep running what exists: reading an EBS volume, routing packets by existing VPC routes). The analogy is a flight: takeoff and landing need the control tower, but a plane in the air has its fuel and instruments and keeps flying if the tower goes quiet. Data planes are built for availability, control planes favour consistency, so recovery should lean on the data plane.

Route 53 Application Recovery Controller applies that. It has readiness checks (configuration drift, capacity, routing policies across replicas, or cells), routing controls (on/off switches for manual failover of a whole stack), and safety rules, such as refusing to switch every routing control off at once and stop all traffic. Each routing control maps to a Route 53 health check, and health checks live on the Route 53 data plane with a 100% uptime SLA. So even when you cannot edit the public hosted zone, flipping a routing control forces the health check unhealthy and the failover DNS record answers with the standby region. The controller itself runs as a cluster with endpoints in five AWS regions; one reachable endpoint is enough to change state.

"We can imagine each of these routing controls to be like a circuit breaker," Christian Elsen said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022, in a demo that fails a tic-tac-toe game over from us-east-1 to us-west-2 with one switch.

## Why a manual button?

The talk makes the case that a regional failover is often a conscious human choice, based on application metrics or a gray failure that automation cannot judge well. Routing controls also cover maintenance traffic shifts and the case where your monitoring is what failed. The target audience they name, regulated industries such as payments and trading, is exactly where a reliable manual lever matters.

## Who should watch

Cloud and SRE teams running, or about to run, active/active or active/standby on AWS. If you are not on AWS, the control plane versus data plane section is still worth twenty minutes of your DR planning.

Title: Renaming your ops team to SRE is anti-pattern number one
Description: Niladri Choudhuri (Xellentro) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on the SRE anti-patterns he keeps meeting, from renamed ops teams to tiered support
Body:
The quickest way to adopt SRE is to change the job titles on the operations team and carry on as before. Niladri Choudhuri, CEO of Xellentro, opened his Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 talk with exactly that as the first of ten anti-patterns he sees when talking to teams that say they practise SRE. The rest of the list is a tour of the ways organisations keep the vocabulary and skip the change.

It is a talk of principles and stories rather than tooling, and a fast one: each anti-pattern gets a few minutes.

## Why isn't a renamed ops team doing SRE?

Choudhuri goes back to why Google created the role: growth that traditional operations could not keep up with. SRE is about reliability *as the system scales*, whether that is new users (Zoom after lockdown started), a rising incident count, new technology or a faster stream of features. SREs automate to cut toil so people can spend their time on making the system more reliable, and they need the psychological safety to break things and learn, because a failure is the system's problem, not the person's. He also cites Google's 2020 book *Building Secure and Reliable Systems*: a system that is not secure is not reliable either.

## Should users find the outage before you do?

No, and the fix is SLOs plus alerts you can act on, on the service rather than on individual metrics. His analogy is the cockpit: hundreds of gauges, and the pilots watch four or five. Everything should be logged and traced, not everything should page. The goal is a shorter MTTR, which needs a shorter MTTD, which needs end-to-end knowledge of the system and of what normal looks like for each customer persona.

"Everything doesn't need to be alerted, everything needs to be logged, everything needs to be traced, but not alerted," Choudhuri said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022.

## Measuring only up to your own edge

Four nines on your servers mean little if the customer reaches you over mobile data with 95% availability. He argues for SLOs set with product teams from real data, and never 100% unless you build pacemakers or aircraft. Customer experience is a journey: Spotify sells a listening experience, not a song; Uber sells a trip from booking to payment.

His best story here came from Mehdi Daoudi, founder of Catchpoint. A client saw slow responses from California on AWS; AWS sent server logs showing all was well. Only the Catchpoint end-user data convinced AWS to dig, and it took five days to find that a change had routed Californian traffic to a server in Asia instead of North America. The server metrics were green the whole time.

## Alerts: fewer, specific, and carrying evidence

Three anti-patterns cover alerting. False positives are worse than no alerts. A pager that rings all the time burns productivity, since nobody actually multitasks. And an alert that only says something is wrong wastes the responder's first minutes: it should carry the health information needed to diagnose, because a long MTTR eats the error budget that would have paid for features, security patches and chaos engineering.

## Pets, cattle and poultry

The configuration management trap gets the talk's best anecdote. Early in his career he asked for a memory upgrade from 4 MB to 8 MB; the engineer took the 4 MB chip out of the desktop of a colleague who was away at a client for a month. When the colleague came back his machine would not boot, and nobody remembered why. Multiply that by millions of components and you get the case for infrastructure as code and immutable infrastructure: pets (named servers), then cattle (VMs), then poultry (containers), replaced rather than changed.

## Incidents without tiers, fixes beyond the point

SREs belong in incident response, but not in an L1-to-L4 ladder. He wants one cross-functional team that owns the system end to end and swarms an incident, with Google's incident command roles for the big ones, and blameless postmortems shared across the organisation. He points to Monzo publishing a postmortem openly, which brought a reply from maintainers of the open-source component involved.

From there: think beyond point fixing (no release ships without a tested rollback script), stop treating the root cause as the place where you stop asking questions, and don't become a production-readiness gatekeeper that slows the flow. The final anti-pattern is treating SRE as automation alone: hiring developers to automate everything without measuring whether the automation helped. He has seen automation that made the work take longer than before.

## Who should watch

Managers and team leads starting an SRE practice, or anyone who suspects their SRE team is the old ops team with new titles. Practitioners will know most of the list, but the Catchpoint story is a good one to bring to the next SLO meeting.

Title: A hackathon random forest that questioned the obvious mail route
Description: Aditi Ramaswamy and Anisha Biswaray (Lob) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 on using historical USPS data to rethink print partner routing
Body:
The closest print partner is not always the fastest one. Aditi Ramaswamy, Software Engineer, and Anisha Biswaray, Business Analyst, both at Lob, show at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 how a two-day hackathon project, a plain scikit-learn random forest over historical USPS scan data, cut transit-time prediction error from 1.43 days to 0.86 and suggested that Lob's geolocation-based routing might be leaving time on the table.

It is a short talk with one idea, and the idea is the title: companies without an ML team sit on data they never analyse, and the analysis can be surprisingly cheap.

## The traveling mailpiece problem

Lob generates mail digitally and sends it to print partners, who put it into the USPS network. Anisha frames this as the traveling salesman problem with stamps: a mailpiece hops through distribution centres, most of those hops belong to USPS, but one choice is Lob's, which print partner the piece starts from. Lob's routing engine used a modified geolocation algorithm to pick the partner closest to the destination. Reasonable, and, as Aditi puts it, with a twist worthy of M. Night Shyamalan, maybe not the best approach.

## How messy is USPS data?

Very. Anisha lays out the scale: the network covers nearly 42,000 destination ZIP codes, arranged under 29 national distribution centres (NDCs) and 450 sectional centre facilities. Millions of mailpieces move through it every day, and each one can generate up to 105 different operation codes describing what stage of the process it is in.

"So, as you can see, this particular system has been built to create messy data," Anisha Biswaray said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022.

Their way through was to keep only the highest-fidelity signals: the entry and exit scans. The target metric became transit time, the difference between the earliest and latest operation-code timestamps for each piece. A fancier version using vectors of op codes and specific network routes was discussed and parked; the first iteration used only the print partner's ZIP code and the destination ZIP code, for partners with solid history.

## What did the model find?

Aditi, who describes herself as an ML student with a couple of classes behind her, fed those two features into a random forest regression in scikit-learn. Because of Databricks memory limits she used only half the data, 500,000 data points. The error dropped from 1.43 days with the non-ML averaging method to 0.86 days.

The more interesting result is what the model implies. Print partners geographically further from the destination sometimes had lower transit times. Historical data captures what geolocation cannot, such as seasonality: the nearest partner might get swamped around Christmas, and a farther one would get the letter there sooner.

They are careful about scope. At the time of the talk the model had not been plugged into the live router, so there were no production delivery numbers yet, only the prediction error and the hypothesis it supports.

## The takeaway is about who gets to do ML

No calculus, no custom model; the hardest part was choosing the features. The baseline project took two days during a work hackathon.

"A company doesn't need to have an ML focus, or a dedicated ML department, or even an ML expert in order to make breakthroughs and improvements to their processes using machine learning tools," Aditi Ramaswamy said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022.

## Who should watch

Engineers at companies with a pile of operational data and no data science team, and anyone who needs an example to convince a manager that a hackathon on ML is not wasted time. Practitioners looking for modelling depth will find it light; that is the point.
