Title: Observability starts with a user who feels awesome
Description: Rajalakshmi Srinivasan (Site24x7, Zoho Corp.) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 on why user experience is the reason to observe anything
Body:
Most observability talks open with a dashboard. Rajalakshmi Srinivasan, Director of Product Management at Site24x7 (Zoho Corp.), opened hers at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022 with a book about users: Kathy Sierra's *Badass: Making Users Awesome*. Her argument is that metrics, traces and logs only matter because a happy user stays, and that the job of an SRE team is to keep that user feeling capable rather than stuck on a spinner.

It is an introductory talk with a vendor close, and it says so: the last few minutes are about Site24x7's own platform.

## Why does a book on product design open an SRE talk?

Sierra asks whether you want users to feel the product is awesome, the company is awesome or the brand is awesome. Her answer is none of those: you want them to feel that *they* are awesome. Users who feel that way evangelise, tolerate problems, resist the competition and answer each other's questions before your support team gets there.

Srinivasan backs the point with figures from a Forbes roundup of digital experience statistics: 89% of companies have adopted a digital-first strategy, 86% think cloud technology is critical for digital transformation, 67% of consumers will pay more for a great experience, and 83% of enterprise workloads run in the cloud. Her conclusion is that the experience you give customers now shows up directly in the business, which is what she means by an experience-driven economy.

## Observability, monitoring, analysis: a three-layer stack

Her model is a stack. Observability is the bottom layer: a system has to expose some API or protocol before anyone can watch it. Monitoring sits on top and collects the metrics that fit the component. Analysis sits on top of that, and without it the first two layers are a storage bill.

"If you're not going to do anything with the data that you're collecting, do not collect it," Srinivasan said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2022. That sentence alone would save a fair number of observability budgets.

## Where do DevOps and SRE split?

She tells the familiar story of developers throwing builds over the wall to operators, and adds a number from her own shop: Site24x7 went from roughly one build every three months to three or four builds a day, which is what forced the two roles together. DevOps then picks up security and becomes DevSecOps.

Her short version of the difference: "if DevOps is about principles of what to be done, SRE is about how you do things." In Java terms, she says, SRE implements DevOps. The SRE needs end-to-end visibility from the end user through the application and platform down to the infrastructure, because the outage can come from a customer's ISP, an endless loop in the code, a database connection nobody closed or a bad switch port.

## The three pillars, with a cost column

The pillars section is a tour more than a revelation, but it is a well-organised one. Metrics change with the component (CPU and memory for a server, response time and call counts for an application, connections and slow queries for a database), and she groups them as availability, security, performance, scalability and cost. Two numbers she gives: the industry expects about two seconds of response time, and surveys suggest around 30% of purchased cloud resources go unused, which is the case for watching cost as closely as uptime.

Traces exist because microservices in short-lived containers, each possibly in its own language, turn one slow call into a cascade. Logs are where everyone looks first anyway; log management, in her phrase, is turning unstructured data into structured data, with audit trails as a side benefit when a customer asks who changed what and when.

## What AIOps is supposed to add

The closing section lists what AI can do on top of the pillars: forecasting capacity from past traffic (the next new-year sale), routing alerts by severity, correlating data across tools and test results, dynamic thresholds per transaction, and chatbot integrations into Slack or Microsoft Teams. Her caveat is the useful part: an AI system is only as good as its training data, and the point is to stop false alerts, not create new ones. The goal she names is moving from reactive to proactive.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to observability, or managers who need the user-experience argument for funding it. Seasoned SREs will know the pillars already; stay for the build-cadence number and the cost-metrics framing.

Title: Finding solar-ready rooftops with image segmentation
Description: Harika Chebrolu (Red Hat) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 on a computer vision pipeline that scores rooftops for solar panel installs
Body:
Working out whether a roof can carry solar panels still takes someone a day or two per building, and that slowness shows up in the bill. Harika Chebrolu, Senior Software Engineer at Red Hat, proposes at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 a computer vision pipeline that segments rooftop images, classifies each roof, estimates the usable area, colour and material, and turns that into an energy estimate investors and utilities can act on.

It is a short talk and a solution design rather than a production case study: no dataset sizes, accuracy figures or deployment story. What it gives you is a clear sketch of how the pieces fit.

## Why is rooftop solar hard to sell?

Her problem statement is about information, not panels. Investors, policymakers and the railway and electricity departments that could fund solar lack data good enough to pick viable, cost-effective sites, so high-potential projects stay undeployed. The manual assessment of each roof is slow, and the cost lands in sales.

"This has resulted to the cost of sales taking up to 30% to 40% of the total project cost, significantly worsening the unit economics of solar projects," Harika Chebrolu said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022.

The abstract adds the technical wrinkle: existing approaches are sensitive to noise from varying ground and climate conditions and from shadowing.

## Training and prediction, the classic split

The pipeline starts with unlabelled, unprocessed rooftop images. They are annotated (material, roof type), then cleaned: noise removal, brightening, greyscaling, watermark removal. Features are extracted, the available roof area is calculated, and the data is split 70% for training and 30% for testing. A held-back unseen set checks the trained model in the prediction phase, whose output is an energy variable that points to the best place for the panels.

## Four kinds of roof

The interesting part is the classification step. Cleaned images go through a YOLACT instance segmentation model that sorts each roof into one of four classes:

- **Flat**: no equipment, an empty plate of a roof.
- **Heavy industrial**: lots of equipment and pipework.
- **Low clutter**: a few pieces of equipment or pipes.
- **Existing solar**: panels already installed.

The segmented image then feeds three estimators. Available rooftop area comes from Mask R-CNN or a greyscale-based method, depending on the images and the accuracy needed. Colour comes from the CIE76 colour-difference formula. Material comes from k-means clustering over the annotated data. Combined with factors supplied by the electricity department, these give an energy estimate per roof.

The end product, as she describes it, is a deep vision engine that property owners and energy departments can run across a portfolio of buildings to rank roofs by return on investment and carbon reduction, instead of sending someone up a ladder for each one.

## Who should watch

Engineers curious about applied computer vision in renewables, or anyone sketching a similar geospatial scoring pipeline who wants a checklist of stages. If you need validation results or a reference implementation, this talk does not have them.

Title: A snapshot is worth a thousand assertions
Description: Andrew Knight (Applitools) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 on visual AI testing that catches the UI bugs locator-based tests miss
Body:
Your login test passes while the logo on the login page is plainly wrong. Andrew Knight, the Automation Panda, Developer Advocate at Applitools and director of Test Automation University, uses exactly that bug at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 to show why locator-based assertions miss visual breakage, and how visual AI snapshots replace pages of brittle checks with one line.

It is a testing talk at an ML conference, and it is a demo of his employer's product, Applitools Eyes. The argument about what assertions can and cannot see holds whatever tool you use.

## Why do functional tests miss visual bugs?

Andrew reduces all testing to one formula: interaction plus verification. Automation scripts both, which means humans still write the checks and fix them when they break.

"Paradoxically, test automation isn't fully autonomous," Andrew Knight said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022.

His example is a four-step smoke test against the Applitools demo banking app, in Java with Selenium WebDriver and JUnit: load the login page, verify it, log in, verify the main page. Verifying the login page means waiting for five elements by locator: logo, username, password, sign-in button, remember-me checkbox. Verifying the main page is, in his word, a doozy: a regex for the banner that says your nearest branch closes in so many minutes, lists of menu items mapped and compared, transaction status pills filtered against an allowed set. And it still ignores dates, amounts and descriptions, a risk-based trade-off every tester makes.

Then he swaps in a second version of the login page with a different logo, a different sign-in button and a shifted checkbox. The test still passes, because every locator still finds its element. If it clicks, it works, and the visuals are a blind spot.

## Pixel diffs are too fragile, which is where the AI comes in

Visual testing compares a baseline snapshot with a new checkpoint. Humans have always done it by eye, and do it well, but they do not scale to CI that deploys several times a day. (He brings in the legend of John Henry, who beat the steam drill and died of exhaustion, as the cautionary tale.)

The obvious automation, a pixel-by-pixel diff, fails on its first real test. His demo is a pair of underwater octopus pictures with ten differences. Shifted a few pixels to the side, the pixel comparison flags nearly every pixel as different and finds none of the ten. Applitools' visual AI, in strict mode, pinpoints all ten and ignores the noise. That, he argues, is what makes automated visual testing usable: highlight missing elements, colour changes and skewed layouts, not padding shifts no human would notice.

## What the code looks like after

The migration is small. Add the eyes-selenium-java3 Maven dependency, set an API key as an environment variable, configure a VisualGridRunner (concurrency of 5 in his code) and a browser config (Chrome at 800 by 600), and open an Eyes object per test. Interaction methods stay. Verification methods collapse: the five waits on the login page become one window snapshot call, and the long main-page method goes the same way.

"If a picture is worth a thousand words, then a snapshot is worth a thousand assertions," Andrew Knight said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022.

In the live run, the first execution creates baselines. The second passes. The third, with the altered login page, comes back unresolved, with the icon, the button text and the checkbox shift highlighted. He gives it a thumbs down, and the next run with the same change fails automatically.

## Cross-browser testing without rerunning the test

The last trick relies on the difference between a screenshot and a snapshot. A snapshot captures the DOM, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, so Applitools' Ultrafast Grid can re-render it on browsers you do not have locally. He adds five desktop browsers (Chrome, Firefox, IE 11, Edge, Safari) and five emulated mobile devices, runs the test once locally on Chrome, and all ten checks finish in 46 seconds, against several minutes for ten conventional UI runs.

His closing point is about adoption: teams think visual testing is for mature automation shops, and he argues the opposite. Start with a smoke test that visits pages and snapshots them, which he calls 80% of the value for 20% of the work, then add traditional assertions later. Visual testing does not replace functional testing; it makes it stronger.

## Who should watch

Test automation engineers drowning in locator maintenance, and front-end teams who keep shipping CSS regressions that green builds never caught. The code is Java, but the pattern carries to any language.

Title: Catching factory defects with 30 images and a serverless pipeline
Description: Mohsin Khan (AWS) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 on product defect detection with Amazon Lookout for Vision and serverless AWS services
Body:
A scratched circuit board costs a manufacturer far more once it ships than while it is still on the line. Mohsin Khan, Solutions Architect at AWS, shows at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 how to catch defects with Amazon Lookout for Vision, which builds a custom anomaly model from as few as 30 images, and how to wrap it in a fully serverless pipeline that stores results, emails quality managers and feeds dashboards.

It is an AWS talk about AWS services, and it says so. Lookout for Vision itself has since been retired by AWS, but the event-driven architecture around it (S3, Step Functions, DynamoDB, Firehose, SNS, CloudWatch) is the part you can reuse with any vision model.

## Why does quality cost so much?

Mohsin opens with the money. Citing Aberdeen Strategy & Research, many organisations carry true quality-related costs of 15% to 20% of sales revenue, and some go as high as 40%. U.S. manufacturers paid an estimated $26 billion in warranty claims in 2018. The metrics behind those costs are defect rework, scrap, customer returns, warranty complaints and corrective action processes.

The two existing answers both have a weakness. Manual inspection, inline or end-of-line, is agile and flexible but limits throughput, is subjective, and has a feedback loop of days, hours or minutes. Classic machine vision is fast and repeatable but needs high upfront spend and purpose-built hardware, and does not adapt.

## Lookout for Vision in four steps

The pitch is a managed service with no ML expertise required: create a model from as few as 30 images, train in the cloud, use lower-resolution cameras, and let process engineers and operators send feedback in real time to improve the model. Its use cases range from surface defects (a scratch) and shape defects (bad solder) to the absence or misalignment of parts in a blister pack and consistency problems in a steel coil.

The demo walks through printed circuit boards with scratches, bent pins and improper soldering:

- Create an S3 bucket and a project, then a dataset from two S3 folders named normal and anomaly; Lookout for Vision infers labels from the folder names.
- Click train, then read precision, recall and F1 score in the console.
- Run a trial detection on new images, mark each prediction correct or incorrect, and fold that feedback into the next model version.
- Start the model from the CLI and call DetectAnomalies on an image to get a binary normal/anomalous result with a confidence score.

That binary result drives what the quality manager does next: classify, grade, bin and ship, rework, scrap, investigate the process, or improve the model.

## What the serverless architecture looks like

The more interesting half is the solution architecture, built around four personas: the camera or client app, data science admins, business users and quality managers.

1. The camera calls API Gateway (optionally through a custom Lambda authorizer) to get a signed S3 URL, then uploads the image with metadata such as camera ID, assembly line ID and image ID.
2. The S3 upload event starts an AWS Step Functions workflow with three Lambda steps: call DetectAnomalies, write the result to DynamoDB, publish to an SNS topic that emails operators (or texts them, or hits your own HTTP endpoint).
3. A DynamoDB stream feeds a Lambda that enriches each record and hands it to Kinesis Data Firehose, which batches records into an S3 data lake for Amazon QuickSight.
4. CloudWatch collects logs, dashboards and alarms, for example when defects exceed a threshold.

A small static front end behind CloudFront and Cognito lets admins start and stop the model without the console. Apart from the QuickSight visuals, the whole thing deploys from one CloudFormation template, published on GitHub as the amazon-lookout-for-vision-serverless-app sample.

## The demo, end to end

The second demo uses a metal casting dataset of more than 6,000 images. A Python script plays the camera, uploading images with metadata; emails arrive with the image ID, its S3 location, the timestamp and the confidence score, while the CloudWatch dashboard counts processed images and detected anomalies. QuickSight shows records by assembly line, results over time and the confidence distribution.

Then comes the step every cloud bill wants you to remember:

"Once we've done with the inferencing, we can stop the model so that we don't incur any sort of additional cost," Mohsin Khan said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022.

He closes with edge inference for low-latency lines or patchy connectivity, with a reference architecture built on AWS IoT Greengrass and IoT SiteWise.

## Who should watch

Engineers building inspection or anomaly pipelines in manufacturing, and anyone who wants a clean reference for an event-driven ML inference flow on AWS. If you need to train vision models yourself, look elsewhere; this is about wiring a managed model into production.

Title: Stop mocking the backend and run the real cluster locally
Description: Robert Stein (Blueshoe) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on replacing mocked APIs with a local copy of the production Kubernetes setup
Body:
A mocked API is a second implementation of your backend that nobody owns. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Robert Stein, Managing Director at Blueshoe, a Munich cloud-native development agency, argued that front-end developers should work against a local replica of the real Kubernetes setup, and demoed it with Keycloak, a federated GraphQL gateway and Blueshoe's own open source tool, Unikube.

Stein is the front-end person at Blueshoe, which moved from monoliths to microservices around 2018 and ended up on Kubernetes. (He also bakes sourdough and will talk to you about it on LinkedIn.)

## What's actually wrong with mocks?

He lists the options a front-end developer has: read the docs and hope CI catches it (nobody really does this), mock the API, or run a development backend on a VM, Docker Compose, or a local or shared cluster. Blueshoe started with mocks like everyone else, because they're quick and many frameworks have mocking built in.

The bill arrived later. Every change to a real response has to be mirrored in the mock, and it's never clear who does that: the front-end developer who uses it, the back-end developer who owns the API, or QA. When the two drift, teams lose time working out which response is the right one. Stein said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "mocking APIs is fairly simple, it's quick to set up, and still it's pretty hard to keep your code and your mocking service, the result of it in sync."

And a good mock is more than a JSON body. CORS, timing, and SSL certificates behave differently in production, and a static response won't show you any of it.

## Environment parity, beyond the container

Docker made the runtime reproducible, but a service-oriented system is more than its containers: caches, OAuth, S3 storage, external services. If your laptop has a volume where production has S3, your code has to behave differently, and that difference is where bugs live. Blueshoe's goal is environment parity: development, integration and production should look alike not just in the runtime but in orchestration and in the services themselves.

The pragmatic bit: your DevOps colleagues already wrote the Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts. Reuse them for development instead of maintaining a parallel fake world.

## The demo: production, minus the secrets

Their platform runs the same Kubernetes setup in development and production; only the secrets differ. Requests hit a gateway backed by Keycloak for authentication with JSON Web Tokens, then Apollo, which federates the GraphQL interfaces of the back-end services into one schema. A front-end developer can ask for an organization and all its projects in a single query across services.

Unikube, which Stein describes as a thin layer around k3d, takes the charts, values and development secrets that the DevOps team registered in its platform and builds the environment locally. He authenticates the CLI through the browser, brings up the project with a command that feels like Docker Compose, lists the exposed ingress paths (front end, gateway, Keycloak), logs in through the real Keycloak, and runs queries and mutations against the real GraphQL API in the cluster on his machine. Then he starts the webpack dev server and works against it.

He admits the demo was sluggish with OBS recording and a full cluster running on one laptop. That's the honest trade-off: parity costs RAM.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers in microservice teams tired of mocks drifting from reality, and platform teams wondering how to give them a production-like environment without making them Kubernetes experts. It's a short talk, and Stein is upfront that this flow works for Blueshoe and might not for you. It also names k3d and Minikube as alternatives.

Title: Search for animals, find the article about dogs
Description: Laura Ham (SeMI Technologies) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 on how vector search engine Weaviate finds meaning in unstructured data
Body:
Search a keyword index for animals and an article about how dogs were domesticated never shows up, because it never uses the word. Laura Ham, ML Product Researcher at SeMI Technologies (the company behind Weaviate), uses that one example at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 to explain vector databases from first principles, then queries a live Weaviate instance to prove the point.

It is an introduction with live demos, and in hindsight a well-timed one: this is 2022, a few months before vector databases became the default answer to every retrieval question. If you want the mental model in 30 minutes, it holds up.

## Why does unstructured data break normal search?

Laura splits data into two camps. Structured data is the rows-and-columns table with an ID, a name and a city: quantitative, easy to store and query. Unstructured data is what she calls data found in the wild: long text documents, raw sensor data, images, video, audio, social media. The information is in there, but a relational schema has nowhere to put it.

Her dog article is the whole argument in one search box:

"As humans, we know that animals are related to dogs, that dogs are a type of animal, so that maybe we want to see this article as a result," Laura Ham said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022.

She points out that you already use a vector search engine every day: Google, which answers an abstract question with a concrete sentence pulled from a web page. The catch, per her slides, is that Google only indexes an estimated 0.004% of unstructured data, because the rest sits inside companies that would rather Google did not read it. Hence open source vector search you can run on your own data.

## How a vector database stores meaning

Weaviate runs data through a machine learning model as it is stored and places every object in a high-dimensional space, around 300 dimensions in her example, where position encodes meaning. The word chicken sits next to a photo of a chicken and near wolf, dog and cat, and far away from apple and banana. A query goes through the same model, lands somewhere in that space, and the engine returns its neighbours: search for kitten, get cat.

She contrasts this with a graph database. Weaviate keeps graph-style classes and relations (an article has an author and a category), but each object also gets a vector, so the category Nature lands near environment and animals and far from laptop and technology.

The pipeline she lays out has four steps:

1. **Pick an encoder (retriever) model.** Dense retrievers such as BERT, Sentence Transformers or ResNet-50 for images; or sparse retrievers like TF-IDF and BM25 that use word frequencies and skip the neural network.
2. **Import and vectorise** your data automatically.
3. **Vectorise the query** with the same model.
4. **Retrieve** with approximate nearest neighbour search, using cosine distance and an HNSW index, which keeps it fast even at millions or billions of objects.

On top of retrieval you can add reader models (question answering, named entity recognition) that extract answers from the retrieved objects, or generator models that write new text such as summaries.

## What the demo shows

Weaviate exposes RESTful endpoints for CRUD and a GraphQL API for queries. Laura's demo dataset is about 3,500 news articles. A plain Get query lists titles with no machine learning involved. Add a nearText filter for animals and the dogs article comes back first, followed by a piece about cattle, ranked by distance in vector space. Ask for certainty, a score from zero to one, and the top hit comes back at 79%.

Then she switches to question answering: who is the king of the Netherlands? Weaviate retrieves an article about the Dutch royals and a question answering model extracts King Willem-Alexander from its first sentence. A second public demo indexes all of English Wikipedia.

## What else Weaviate does

The end of the talk covers multimodal search (index images and text together, search one with the other), out-of-the-box vectorisers including Hugging Face models, OpenAI models and SeMI's own Contextionary, bring-your-own custom models, or no model at all if you supply vectors yourself. Weaviate can also classify data automatically, with kNN classification when you have labelled examples or zero-shot classification when you do not.

## Who should watch

Engineers who keep hearing about vector databases and want the plain explanation of embeddings, ANN and HNSW, plus a quick look at a real query API. If you already run a RAG stack in production, this is the prequel.

Title: Back up the whole Kubernetes app, not just the volume
Description: Michael Cade (Kasten by Veeam) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on protecting and moving whole Kubernetes apps, including data that lives outside the cluster
Body:
Kubernetes gives you high availability and fault tolerance, but not backups and not disaster recovery. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Michael Cade, Senior Global Technologist at Kasten by Veeam, made the case for protecting the whole application (deployments, services, ingress, config maps, secrets and persistent volumes together) and showed Kasten K10 moving a stateful app from GKE to EKS and backing up a database that lives outside the cluster in Amazon RDS.

## Why isn't Kubernetes enough on its own?

Cade's framing comes from years in data management across physical, virtual and cloud. None of those platforms has gone away, and none of them stops accidental deletion, malicious insiders, ransomware or a security breach. Containers versus VMs is the wrong argument; the data still has to live somewhere, and it still needs a copy you can restore. Cade said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "No one really cares about the backup, you only really care about the restore, but you have to back up to be able to restore."

He separates three jobs that often get blurred: backup and restore, disaster recovery (fire, flood, the region that isn't there anymore), and application mobility, moving data to cut risk or cost or to use a service another cloud does better, or cloning it to put a copy to work.

## Demo one: Pacman moves clouds

His mission-critical application is Pacman: a Node.js front end and a MongoDB database holding the high scores on a persistent volume claim. After racking up a score, he switches to an EKS cluster where the Pacman namespace doesn't exist, and runs a K10 import policy that restores the whole application there.

The useful detail is transformation on restore. The source might use one storage class and a load balancer; the target can come up on a different storage tier with different settings, and the policy can be scheduled for recurring DR copies. Once restored in EKS, the deployments for Pacman and Mongo are there, and so are the high scores. For a real migration you'd also repoint DNS, which he flags as part of the process.

## Why does CSI matter here?

He takes a short detour through the storage stack: persistent volumes, claims, and the Container Storage Interface. CSI lets storage vendors ship drivers outside the Kubernetes release cycle, unlike the old in-tree provisioners, and volume snapshot classes give a fast recovery point. Fast, but not sufficient: he wants an export to object storage or another storage layer as well, not just a snapshot sitting next to production.

## Demo two: the database isn't in the cluster

Plenty of teams run the app in Kubernetes and the database somewhere else. His second demo is a GKE cluster whose app talks to a Postgres database in Amazon RDS, wired up through a config map for the connection and a secret for the credentials. A K10 policy, selected by namespace or labels, snapshots the RDS instance, exports it to S3, and can restore the dvdrental database into a stateful set on EKS.

The argument for doing it this way rather than with an RDS-only tool: a point solution protects the database and knows nothing about the front end, the other microservices, or the logs and metrics that make up the application. He'd rather recover an application as an application.

## Stateless is a myth (sometimes)

Cade also pushes back on the idea that only stateful workloads need protecting. Stateless apps still have logs and configuration worth keeping, and with 100 or 200 namespaces you may have the source code but not know which version was running where. Load balancer and IP settings matter during a cross-region recovery too. He sums up the Kubernetes situation with a line that stuck: there's no shining green button that makes backups unnecessary.

## Who should watch

Platform teams running databases on Kubernetes, or Kubernetes apps backed by managed databases, who haven't yet rehearsed a restore into another cluster. It's a vendor talk built on K10 demos; he mentions the open source Kanister project for the data-service side and says the whole-application approach applies whatever tool you use.

Title: How Wix moved 2,000 services to managed Kafka without downtime
Description: Natan Silnitsky (Wix) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on a live, automated, reversible migration to multi-cluster Confluent Cloud
Body:
Wix moved the Kafka traffic of 2,000 microservices from self-hosted, one-cluster-per-data-center Kafka to a multi-cluster Confluent Cloud setup with traffic flowing the whole time. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Natan Silnitsky, a backend infrastructure team lead at Wix, explained how a replicator with offset mapping, an orchestrator and their own client layer kept it lossless, and how a Kafka bug on Christmas Eve 2021 started deleting records.

Silnitsky said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "This was the most challenging project I have ever led."

## Why leave self-hosted Kafka?

Growth. Per cluster, Wix went from around 5,000 topics and a little under half a billion messages a day in 2019 to more than 20,000 topics and over 2.5 billion messages a day. The metadata load made broker restarts slow enough to hurt production. The plan: split into more, smaller clusters per data center, grouped by SLA to shrink the blast radius, and let Confluent Cloud handle broker balancing, version upgrades, capacity changes and tiered storage for long retention.

Developers pick a cluster by adding a logical cluster name to their producer or consumer spec, and a back office shows which cluster a topic lives on.

## Greyhound was the lever

Wix doesn't use the Kafka client directly. Greyhound, its open source layer on top of the Kafka SDK, is a library for JVM services in Scala and Java and a sidecar-style service for Node, Go and Python. Because every service talks to Kafka through it, the migration team could tell Greyhound, from outside the service, to unsubscribe from one cluster and subscribe to another. No code change, no redeploy.

## How do you switch consumers without losing a message?

The first plan was to drain a whole data center and switch with no traffic. It was dropped: some services relied on a single data center, and flipping everything at once was neither gradual nor easy to roll back. So they migrated live.

- A **replicator service** consumes each partition from the self-hosted cluster, produces to the matching partition in Confluent Cloud, and records an offset mapping (offset 57 in the old cluster maps to, say, offset 5 in the new one).
- A **migration orchestrator** asks the replicator to copy all topics for a consumer group, waits for zero lag, then asks Greyhound to unsubscribe from the old cluster.
- Once no pod is subscribed to the old cluster, it tells Greyhound to subscribe to Confluent Cloud from the mapped offsets: no lost messages, no duplicate processing.
- Producers come later and are simpler: flip the state and restart.

The scripts check state themselves but deliberately don't self-heal. On anything unexpected they stop and alert the person running them, who has a ready-made rollback. Practise the whole forward-and-back dance on test topics first, fed with relayed real production traffic, and build a dedicated dashboard that shows only what the migration operator needs.

## The Christmas Eve bug

Producers can only move once all of a topic's consumers have, so the replicator kept picking up more topics, and its single consumer group grew huge. Replication stopped with a sync group error: the maximum message size between the group and the broker was too small for that many partitions. They raised message.max.bytes dynamically from 1 MB, and it worked.

On Christmas Eve 2021 the same error came back, and they bumped it again, from 4 MB to 8 MB. Then records started vanishing far faster than retention allowed, including from compacted topics that were the source of truth for some data. The cause was a bug in certain Kafka versions. Silnitsky said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "if you change these configuration dynamically twice, it reverts the log configuration to be the default." Every topic's cleanup policy and retention fell back to cluster defaults.

They got lucky: the change hadn't been made in every data center, so records were restored from another one. The fix was a dummy per-topic config change on every topic, then a rule of no more dynamic config changes; instead the replicator was split into several consumer group shards, each owning a set of topics.

## What they kept afterwards

The migration plumbing became a feature. Greyhound can now be told externally to switch a consumer's cluster, skip corrupted messages, or throttle processing rate per pod to protect a struggling database.

## Who should watch

Anyone planning a Kafka cluster migration, self-hosted to managed or just splitting a cluster. The offset mapping and the rollback discipline transfer directly; the Christmas Eve story is a reason to check your broker version before touching dynamic configs.

Title: The ML made the pods bigger, and the bill dropped by half
Description: Giovanni Paolo Gibilisco (Akamas) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on ML tuning of Kubernetes and JVM settings together to cut cost within SLOs
Body:
The cheapest configuration for one Java microservice turned out to be a bigger pod, not a smaller one. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Giovanni Paolo Gibilisco, Head of Engineering at Akamas, showed how an ML-driven optimisation of nine Kubernetes and JVM parameters found a setup that ran a business-critical service at almost half the baseline cost, with the latency spikes gone, after 34 experiments and about 19 hours.

Before the case study, he spends the first half on the Kubernetes resource model, and that part is worth the watch on its own.

## Why is Kubernetes tuning so easy to get wrong?

He walks through the facts in order:

- **Requests drive capacity, not usage.** Kubernetes schedules on requests with no overcommit, so a cluster can be full while CPU utilisation sits at 10%.
- **CPU and memory limits fail differently.** Hit the CPU limit and the container is throttled; hit the memory limit and it's killed. No slow swapping, the pod just disappears.
- **Throttling starts early.** Gibilisco said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 that in Akamas' lab research they "found that cpu throttling start when cpu usage is as low as 30% of the limit", because of how the Linux kernel enforces CPU limits. That means latency spikes and SLO breaches with no obvious CPU pressure.
- **Removing limits isn't the fix.** Engineers at Buffer dropped CPU limits and got lower latency, but one runaway container can then starve its neighbours or even make the kubelet unresponsive.
- **The VPA only sees resource usage.** In their test, the Vertical Pod Autoscaler saw CPU below 50%, halved the CPU request, and the service's latency shot through its SLO. It doesn't know response time exists.

## The case: a B2B authorisation service on Azure

The real-world example is a European vendor of accounting, payroll and business management software, running Java microservices on Azure and AWS Kubernetes services. The target was a business-critical B2B authorisation service on Azure. Goal: minimise cloud cost. Constraint: throughput, response time and error rate may not degrade more than 10% against the baseline.

The ML could touch nine parameters at once: CPU and memory requests and limits on the container, plus five JVM options including heap sizes, garbage collector and heap region size. Each iteration was automated in five steps: apply the configuration through the Kubernetes API, run the customer's existing JMeter load test, collect KPIs from Elastic APM, score the run on Azure prices, and let the optimiser pick the next candidate.

## What the baseline was doing wrong

The baseline asked for 1.5 CPUs and 3.42 GB of memory, with limits of 2 CPUs and 4.39 GB. The JVM had a 0.5 GB minimum heap and a 4 GB maximum, so the heap could outgrow the memory request. Autoscaling ran through KEDA on CPU and memory, with thresholds measured against requests, not limits.

Under load, two things went wrong. Every scale-out caused a big response time spike, because a fresh JVM starting up burns CPU and gets throttled. And after the load dropped, the replicas never scaled back in: memory use stayed above the threshold relative to the request, partly because the max heap sat above it. You pay for idle pods and still breach the SLO.

## The counterintuitive winner

The best configuration, found at experiment 34, raised both CPU and memory requests and limits. The max heap went up 20% but now sat inside a 5 GB memory request, and the min heap was set close to the max to avoid garbage collection churn at startup. One pod carried the full load test, autoscaling never fired, and response time stayed within the SLO with no spikes. A fixed bigger pod beat a smaller pod that kept triggering scale-outs.

A second configuration, found at experiment 14 after about 8 hours, went the other way: a much smaller CPU request, still a large memory request, and the parallel garbage collector. It was cheaper than the baseline, more resilient (the scale-out spike was under half the baseline's) and it scaled back to one replica properly. Different goals, opposite shapes, which is his point about why humans struggle to do this by hand.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who set requests and limits by copying the last service's YAML, and anyone running JVMs in containers. The first half is vendor-neutral and teaches the resource model well; the second half shows Akamas' approach on a real customer.

Title: When DynamoDB fails at 2:32am, the answer is upstream
Description: Erez Berkner (Lumigo) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on tracing managed services end to end so you know which users a failure hurts
Body:
PagerDuty fires at 2:32 in the morning and DynamoDB is throttling. Do you wake the team or go back to sleep? At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Erez Berkner, CEO and co-founder of Lumigo, argued that you can only answer that if your tracing reaches past the failing service to the customer-facing API that started the request, and he laid out three ways to get there.

The talk is broader than its title. DynamoDB is the example, but the real subject is everything you consume as a service: queues, storage, Snowflake, Stripe, Twilio. You can't install an agent there, you don't own the server and you didn't write the API. Berkner lumps all of it under serverless in the wide sense, and the problem is the same everywhere: the thing that broke is a black box, and the thing you care about (who got hurt) is several hops away.

## What should you be able to see when a managed service breaks?

Berkner's target is what he calls a virtual stack trace. In a monolith you could read the call stack and see which function called which. In a distributed system he wants the same view across services: the inputs, outputs, environment variables, logs and exception for every hop along the failing request. Distributed tracing gets you the path; the virtual stack trace adds the payloads at each step.

With that, the 2:32am question becomes answerable. Trace upstream from the DynamoDB error, find that it sits behind a business-critical, customer-facing API, and you know it can't wait until morning.

## Three ways to build it, with honest trade-offs

**Cloud-native tools.** CloudWatch and friends, plus your own logging of requests, payloads and exceptions around each Lambda and managed call. It's in the same cloud, supported by AWS and fine for dev and early production. It breaks at scale because the only thing joining your logs is the clock. Berkner said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "when you have millions or billions, you can no longer connect the dots via timestamps." AWS X-Ray helps, but in his view it doesn't follow requests well across services such as DynamoDB, S3 and EventBridge.

**Homebrew and open source.** Zipkin, Jaeger and, his recommended starting point, OpenTelemetry. You get a tailored system that isn't tied to one cloud, and OpenTelemetry is a standard many vendors support. The catch is that it's high-touch and doesn't solve managed services: you still have to carry a correlation ID through S3, EventBridge and Kinesis yourself. He points to Yan Cui's writing on passing correlation IDs through microservices as the reference for doing that properly.

**Third-party SaaS tools built for cloud-native.** Low-touch, opinionated, with preconfigured alerts and more than tracing (cost, latency breakdowns). The costs are another platform in your stack, data leaving your account (check their GDPR and ISO 27001 posture), and features you may not need yet.

## The demo: from an empty field to its source

Here the talk turns into a Lumigo walkthrough, and it's his own product, so weigh it accordingly. The dashboard is about cloud-native signals rather than CPU and I/O: failed invocations, cold starts, timeouts, runaway cost, the slowest services among dozens. He opens a live error in a Lambda that posts to social media, has Lumigo rebuild the whole transaction, then clicks through it hop by hop.

The Lambda failed because a run ID was an empty string. The Lambda's input event shows it arrived empty, the EventBridge message that triggered it was already empty, and so on upstream, past a DynamoDB write that failed with a key schema mismatch and then succeeded on retry, out to an SMS sent through Twilio. It's a good illustration of the point: the service that throws is rarely the service that's wrong.

## What to take home

Berkner closed with three points. Expect more than a log aggregator; Berkner said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "Don't settle for what you used to have with having logs out there in a log aggregator and that's it." Build observability in during dev and pre-prod rather than after the first outage. And ask the community, because plenty of teams have already solved what you're facing.

## Who should watch

Teams running Lambda, Step Functions-style event flows or anything heavy on managed services who still debug by grepping CloudWatch log groups. The three-option comparison is useful whatever you pick; the second half is a vendor demo, and he says so.

Title: One Slack-like messenger, three ways to spread its data across the globe
Description: Denis Magda (Yugabyte) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on designing geo-distributed apps for latency, resilience and GDPR with three multi-region data modes
Body:
Pick the wrong region pair and every request pays for it: on Google Cloud, Oregon to Mumbai is about 220 ms round trip, Oregon to Tokyo about 90. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Denis Magda, Director of Developer Relations at Yugabyte, designed a Slack-like corporate messenger that serves users worldwide, survives region outages and keeps European data in Europe. The useful part: each microservice gets the multi-region data mode that matches its needs, not one mode for everything.

The talk is language-agnostic architecture; the data layer is the speaker's own YugabyteDB.

## What do regions and zones actually cost you?

He grounds everything in Google Cloud numbers. From Oregon, a round trip to North Virginia takes about 60 ms, to Tokyo about 90 ms, and to Mumbai about 220 ms, with London in between, because inter-region links are not equal. Inside a region, zones are separate physical locations with round trips under 5 ms, so three zones let you survive a zone outage cheaply. Local zones and edge nodes in big metros such as Seattle, Atlanta, London and New York exist for single-digit-millisecond latency, mostly gaming and streaming.

## Why not just ship it in one zone?

The default deployment, one region and one zone, fails three ways. The zone goes down and so does the app. Six months in, the startup expands to Europe and has to meet GDPR with an architecture that cannot. A year and a half in, users in Japan, Singapore or India get a slow app because every request crosses an ocean. Multi-zone fixes the first; multi-region fixes all three at the price of higher latency on average.

## Match the data mode to the microservice

The messenger has four services: messaging and profile (mission-critical), plus reminders and status (utilities). YugabyteDB, a distributed SQL database that reuses PostgreSQL's query layer on top of its own sharded storage, offers three multi-region layouts, and each service gets one.

- **Geo-partitioned single cluster, for messaging and profile.** One cluster spans continents, with groups of nodes pinned to geographies. Tables are partitioned on a country column, so rows for UK, France, Italy or Germany live on European nodes. Writes stay transactional, Europeans read and write locally, and GDPR residency comes from the schema. Denis Magda said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "We cannot afford losing any message."
- **Primary cluster with read replicas, for reminders.** Writes go to the primary in North America; a user in South Korea creating a reminder has the write forwarded there. Reads hit local replicas. A worker next to each replica wakes every minute, bulk-reads the reminders that just expired, and notifies those users, so bulk reads never cross the ocean.
- **Standalone clusters with async replication, for status.** Statuses change rarely, everyone reads them often, and nobody minds if a colleague's "in a meeting" shows up five or ten seconds late in another region. Each region gets its own cluster, with uni- or bidirectional asynchronous replication.

## Then the boring, essential layers

Every microservice runs an instance in North America, Europe and Asia, co-located in the same region as the database nodes it talks to, to keep that under-5 ms hop. How you run them (App Engine, an AWS or Azure equivalent, or Kubernetes, which he expects most will choose) and how they talk (message brokers, gRPC, sidecars) is left to you.

In front sits a global cloud load balancer with a single anycast IP. A European user's request goes to the European service instance, which reads from European nodes. If that region fails, the balancer redirects traffic to the next-nearest location.

His closing argument is to design for this before you need it. Denis Magda said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "then you will become the victim of your own success." An app that starts in one region across three zones but can stretch to Europe next month is in a far better place than one that needs a redesign. For further reading he recommends Architecting for Scale and Designing Data-Intensive Applications, and there is a Gitpod sandbox for trying the deployment modes.

## Who should watch

Architects of apps that will outgrow one region, and anyone who needs GDPR residency without running a separate product per continent. It is a design talk using YugabyteDB as the example; the patterns apply to any distributed SQL database.

Title: Infrastructure as code builds the Lego bricks, not the toy
Description: Adarsh Shah (zLifecycle) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on how software engineering history shaped infrastructure, and why environment as code comes next
Body:
Your Terraform is declarative and idempotent; the Jenkins pipeline that runs twelve Terraform stacks in the right order is neither. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Adarsh Shah, founder and CEO of zLifecycle, traced how each big software engineering practice eventually reached infrastructure, and argued that the next step is environment as code: one declarative definition of a whole environment, reconciled by a Kubernetes-style controller.

## Which software practices has infrastructure already borrowed?

He starts by noting that software itself borrows: waterfall from construction, lean from Toyota, incident handling from airlines. Then he walks a timeline of six practices, roughly dated: version control in the 1970s, deployment pipelines around 1991, microservices around 2005, containers around 2013, Kubernetes in 2014 and GitOps in 2017. The first three have already reached infrastructure through infrastructure as code.

- **Version control.** Application code stopped living on whoever deployed last long before infrastructure did, which kept being clicked together in consoles. IaC put it in source control. His advice: everything goes in, even the bash script you run once in a while.
- **Pipelines.** IaC pipelines bring static analysis and unit tests, then temporary environments for compliance, integration, security and smoke tests, then production deployment and another smoke test. Changes become repeatable and auditable.
- **Microservices.** One Terraform root with networking, EC2, S3 and the database means one state file and slower runs as you grow. Splitting into separate runs (networking, then compute or Kubernetes or Postgres, then Kubernetes add-ons) gives loosely coupled pieces you can change alone.

## Where does micro-IaC break down?

The split creates a dependency graph, and someone has to walk it. With today's tools that means hand-rolled pipeline logic in Jenkins or CircleCI that runs networking first, then the cluster, then the add-ons, and also handles teardown and partial failures. Adarsh Shah said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "You have to write a lot of custom code to provision an entire environment."

He is careful about scope: for a simple setup, plain IaC and a pipeline do the job. The pain starts with many divergent environments, each with networking, databases, SageMaker, Kubernetes clusters and buckets, and it typically ends with a dedicated team babysitting pipelines.

## What is environment as code?

His definition: an abstraction over IaC that declares an entire environment, paired with a control plane that tracks state for the whole environment and the relationships inside it, detects drift and reconciles, keeping loose coupling, idempotency and immutability at the environment level. Adarsh Shah said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "So infrastructure as code automates various Lego pieces." Environment as code automates how the pieces connect into the toy, and the toy is what a product team wants.

## Borrowing package managers, Kubernetes and GitOps

The remaining three practices map onto that idea.

- **Package managers.** Containers, Helm and Kustomize tamed dependencies between microservices. Environment as code packages every component in an environment with the dependencies between them. His example is zLifecycle's own format, a Kubernetes custom resource listing the environment name, team and components, each with a type (Terraform here) and a `dependsOn`, such as EKS depending on networking.
- **Kubernetes controllers.** A control loop observes the environment, detects drift from the desired state in Git and reconciles, running each Terraform component in order with its own state while tracking state for the environment as a whole. He recommends an approval step showing the plan first, because reconciliation can mean destroying things, and you do not want that happening to a database unreviewed.
- **GitOps.** Push the environment definition to a branch, run validation, open a pull request, get it approved, merge; the control plane watches the repository and builds the environment.

## Who should watch

Platform teams running many environments out of a tangle of Terraform stacks and pipeline glue. It is a conceptual talk with a clear timeline and one example format from the speaker's own company, not a product demo or a tool comparison.

Title: Your ML pipeline is an attack surface, not just a workflow
Description: Joshua Arvin Lat (NuWorks Interactive Labs) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 on how ML systems get hacked and the layers that stop it
Body:
A model file you downloaded can open a port on your training server. Joshua Arvin Lat, CTO of NuWorks Interactive Labs, AWS Machine Learning Hero and author of Machine Learning with Amazon SageMaker Cookbook, spends his Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 talk showing where ML systems get compromised, then lists the defences, most of them cheap or free.

The examples lean on AWS (SageMaker, EC2, Lambda, Amazon Inspector), but the attack paths apply to any cloud or a rack in the basement.

## Best practices are not a security test

Joshua's starting point is that following best practices does not make a system secure; testing it does. He compares it to load testing: nobody should promise a client 100 concurrent users without running the load test, and nobody should claim a system is secure without scanners and assessment tools that check the assumption.

He also explains why security rarely gets attention. Companies rank short-term and long-term financial objectives and customer happiness first, and he estimates that 90% to 95% of a team's focus goes there. Compliance, security and operational excellence fall to the bottom of the list, right up to the breach that makes customers stop trusting the company.

## Think like the attacker in the DMZ

The core of the talk is the cybersecurity attack chain. An attacker given five servers starts with what is visible and reachable, exploits a weakness, escalates privileges, moves laterally toward the servers that talk to the databases, then exfiltrates passwords and data, and uses compromised machines to attack the next ones. Phishing an employee is just another way in. The practical consequence: whatever sits in the public subnet, the DMZ, is high risk and gets the most layers.

## Where ML-specific payloads hide

Then he maps that thinking onto the ML workflow. A data scientist's Jupyter notebook runs on infrastructure, pulls in libraries, packages, custom code and datasets. Each of those is a place for a payload. His example: a malicious dependency or pre-built model that, once loaded, opens port 4000 so the attacker can connect and run commands as if the machine were their own. If the instance's IAM role is too generous, that attacker can now delete or create resources, with no API keys needed.

Training jobs and inference endpoints have the same problem at a different layer. Custom container images built by someone else, the dataset, the custom code and the configuration are all inputs.

"So be very careful because these input parameters are also the areas where your hacker might insert a payload or a malicious script," Joshua Arvin Lat said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022.

Even a container that is clean today will collect known vulnerabilities as its libraries age. And serverless does not mean unhackable: a Lambda function behind API Gateway still runs your code, and your code can still be vulnerable. Pipelines inherit all of this plus the orchestration tool itself, whether that is an ML service or open source tooling on Kubernetes.

## The defences, in order of usefulness

- **Network isolation.** An XGBoost training job has no reason to call the internet. With isolation on, a malicious payload cannot phone home, exfiltrate data or fetch more scripts, while nodes in a distributed training cluster still talk to each other.
- **Manual approval in CI/CD.** Fully automated pipelines with nobody looking can ship code that redirects your users to a malware site.
- **Automated vulnerability management.** Amazon Inspector scans servers and container images from the inside on every change, so a vulnerable library is caught before deployment. Expect 1,000 or 5,000 findings, and budget time to triage which ones are exploitable and which fixes break the app.
- **Infrastructure as code.** Layered templates for resources, network and security config let you spin up separate environments for penetration testers and load tests, and roll security changes through staging before production.
- **Account action monitoring and least-privilege IAM.** Collect and analyse logs fast, and assume a weak password like 123456 will be found.

He also argues for training teams on the last 50%: the scaling, troubleshooting and hardening that turn something working on a laptop into a production system.

## What does all this cost?

Joshua splits cost into infrastructure and people. Do the free items first (network isolation and a sane IAM configuration often cost nothing), then justify the paid ones. For people, he suggests something like 80% builders to 20% maintainers, and planning ahead, since security vendors and audits usually mean long-term contracts.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and data scientists who deploy their own models, and platform teams inheriting an ML stack. Security specialists will find the attack-chain material familiar; the value is in the ML-specific entry points.

Title: Cloud agnostic starts with the database you didn't pick
Description: Handoyo Sutanto (Lyrid) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on four engineering decisions for cloud-agnostic apps and what portability costs up front
Body:
The lock-in usually arrives on day one, the day you pick a database that only one cloud runs. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Handoyo Sutanto, CEO and CTO of Lyrid, laid out the four engineering decisions his company made to run on several public clouds at once: control your stack, hide cloud APIs behind abstraction libraries, design microservices to be replaceable, and rehearse your migration every month. He also lists what that costs.

He defines cloud agnostic as using two or more public clouds for your workloads, and comes to it as a platform engineer with more than 15 years of building cloud systems, from data centres up.

## Why bother with more than one cloud?

His case for it: freedom over tooling, choice on region and price, scaling that follows the workload (Lyrid leans on Kubernetes autoscaling), and long-term savings because you can switch providers when a better deal appears. Those are the promises; the useful part of the talk is how to earn them.

## Decision one: a stack you control

Before writing any code, pick technologies that exist everywhere. Compute, storage, database and network are, in his words, the lifeblood of the application. The classic trap is a managed database that only runs on one vendor: the easiest to integrate, the hardest to move. His advice is to start small with a distributed database you run yourself, open source, with high availability and redundancy, which can grow without downtime and spread across clouds later.

## Decision two: abstraction libraries everywhere

Wrap anything that might need to move behind a generic interface. ORMs are the familiar example (Prisma for Node.js, SQLAlchemy for Python, Entity Framework for .NET), and Lyrid applies the same idea to messaging. Its job distribution runs on Google Pub/Sub but can switch to AWS SQS or a self-hosted Redis pub/sub, which is how the team moves workloads that need global distribution or on-premises deployment.

## Decision three: replaceable microservices

Embrace distributed architecture and small components that run on any system, with distributed storage that keeps copies for durability and recovery. During development he asks one test question of every service. Handoyo Sutanto said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "Can this same code or API run on another cloud platform? If not, why is that?" Then fix the answer before production.

## Decision four: rehearse the move

Most teams end up on one region and one provider anyway. The fourth decision is a plan B: pick a target cloud or technology and run the migration as a test about once a month, starting small with the pieces that move easily.

## What does Lyrid's own stack look like?

Kubernetes as the base, MongoDB and MinIO for data and object storage. A MongoDB instance inside each Kubernetes cluster acts as a globally distributed read-only cache. Build and deploy jobs are spread through Google Pub/Sub, with Redis pub/sub as the drop-in for development and for customers who need more security.

The demo is his own product. He deploys a Next.js template whose `package.json` has no cloud SDK at all, just a Lyrid definition file. The source lands in MinIO, container builds run on Lyrid's cluster, and the platform creates the cloud-specific services, for example AWS Lambda. After adding an IAM role for each cloud account and setting the execution policy to all clouds, refreshing the endpoint shows requests load balancing between AWS, Google Cloud and Lyrid's own Kubernetes cluster.

## What does portability cost?

He is upfront about it. Without one provider's security model, zero trust becomes the baseline: never trust, always verify, HTTPS everywhere, with cert-manager and Let's Encrypt between machines, plus container scanning, hardening and RBAC on the clusters. Every extra cloud costs integration time because providers differ in small ways; on AWS his team found Kubernetes ingress load balancers come with public DNS names instead of public IPs. Monitoring is cloud-specific, so they standardised on Prometheus and Grafana. And there is complexity, a slightly higher upfront cost, and data transfer charges that are hard to predict.

Handoyo Sutanto said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "Just like everything else in the world, nothing is perfect, not even cloud agnostic."

## Who should watch

Architects weighing multi-cloud against the convenience of one provider's managed services, and anyone writing the "can we leave AWS?" section of a risk register. Expect principles plus a vendor demo, not a migration war story.

Title: Strangling a monolith one URI path at a time with Refactor Spaces
Description: Lerna Ekmekcioglu (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on the strangler fig pattern, moving a Spring Boot shop's basket to Lambda with Refactor Spaces
Body:
Nobody gets to rewrite the monolith in one go, so the question is which piece leaves first and how its callers never notice. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Lerna Ekmekcioglu, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, answered with the strangler fig pattern: put a reverse proxy in front of a Spring Boot monolith, then route one URI path at a time to new services. The demo moves a shopping basket to AWS Lambda and DynamoDB using AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces, which builds the proxy and networking for you.

## What does an overgrown monolith cost?

The speaker, who brings 18 years in technology and financial services, lists the symptoms from personal experience. Many developers push through one shared release pipeline, so upgrading a shared library means convincing everyone to upgrade at once, and an urgent fix ships alongside everybody else's changes. Feature requests pile up. Releases happen a couple of times a year, so each one is huge, risky to deploy and risky to roll back. Lerna Ekmekcioglu said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "So you may typically see in this scenario teams prefer to fix forward, which is pretty high risk as well, but it's easier."

The fix is not a big bang. Refactor incrementally, and only where it buys the business something: speed, agility, or independent scaling.

## Why move the basket first?

Lerna Ekmekcioglu said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "Independent deployment is the heart of microservices." That brings a smaller blast radius per deployment, teams that choose their own stack, and the chance to scale the busy functions without scaling the whole app.

The sample is the Unicorn Shop: Spring Boot, MySQL and a Bootstrap front end, on EC2 in its own VPC. It has controllers for inventory, basket, users and health, and three tables: unicorns, users, and an association table for basket contents. The basket is the business-critical part that has to survive Black Friday, so it goes first.

Before cutting, the speaker lists the questions to answer: which stack suits the new service, how existing MySQL data moves to the new store, what extra network chatter between monolith and microservice does to performance, and how to switch over without breaking the existing REST contract.

## A proxy keeps the API contract

The contract is the monolith's REST API: POST to a user path to register, POST to a login path, GET on unicorns for the home page, and the basket actions all hanging off one basket path. Step one is a reverse proxy that sends everything to the monolith. Step two is the new service behind the same proxy, with only the basket path routed to it. Clients see the same URLs throughout.

You could build that with Amazon API Gateway by hand, defining every resource and method. Refactor Spaces does the plumbing instead:

1. Create an environment in an account that becomes the environment owner; it gets a Transit Gateway in your own account, which you can customise.
2. Add the accounts that hold the monolith and the new services.
3. Create an application, which provisions the proxy: API Gateway, a VPC link and a Network Load Balancer.
4. Add services; Transit Gateway bridges their VPCs across accounts.
5. Add routes: a default route to the monolith, then specific paths to the new service.

## Routes are path plus HTTP verb

The new basket is three Lambda functions (add, remove, get) on DynamoDB, serverless so it scales for spiky sales days and you pay for what you use. Routing matches the basket URI path combined with the verb: GET goes to the get-cart function, DELETE to remove-cart, and additions to add-to-cart. Everything else falls through to the monolith on EC2. In the shop, basket actions now hit Lambda while browsing and login still hit Spring Boot, and users cannot tell.

The demo runs everything in one account for simplicity, but the recommendation is one account per application per environment: a contained blast radius, isolation by security and data profile, and separate service quotas per workload. Adding the next microservice later means sharing the environment with its account, defining the service and adding its routes.

## Who should watch

Teams that have lifted and shifted a monolith to AWS and now need a safe first cut, especially in regulated industries. It is a clear walkthrough of an AWS service with a workshop you can follow in your own account (and clean up afterwards), not a discussion of domain boundaries or data migration in depth.

Title: Terraform's ugly side is a huge state and a nervous Ctrl+C
Description: Hila Fish (Wix) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on Terraform practices from quick wins to long-haul structure, and how Wix runs Terraform as a platform
Body:
You change resource X, run a plan, and Terraform announces it will change Y. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Hila Fish, Senior DevOps Engineer at Wix, sorted Terraform habits into the good, the bad and the ugly, from fixes that take a minute to code structure you have to plan for. Her main point: small states and a structure planned ahead are what let Wix run Terraform as a platform for every team.

She works with open-source Terraform only and uses AWS examples, but says the practices apply to any cloud provider.

## Which quick wins pay off in minutes?

Three, each in good, bad and ugly flavours.

- **Version locks.** Lock Terraform, provider and module versions, the way `requirements.txt` or a package lock does. Bad is a constraint loose enough to let breaking changes through. Ugly is no lock at all; Hila Fish said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "Trust me, it is really really ugly."
- **Tags.** Tag everything so costs can be filtered by owner and project. Set defaults such as `managed_by` at provider level so every resource inherits them, and fail pull requests that skip tags. Inconsistent tags are bad; none at all is ugly, and the FinOps team will not thank you.
- **Remote state.** Keep state in a remote backend such as S3, secured (it holds secrets), versioned, and locked during writes. Local, unbacked-up or unlocked state is the ugly version.

## What should be second nature?

Use official community modules before writing your own: they are battle-tested, maintained by someone else and come with linters and formatters already wired up. If you must write one, keep it stateless, generic and DRY.

On variables and locals, she gives module variables a default or validation so a missing input does not break the module, and uses locals as constants that enforce conventions, such as a bucket naming scheme. The live layer, where modules are called, should hold no logic, use tfvars files per region or other breakdown, and reuse environment variables that already exist. File layout follows community modules: `main.tf`, variables, data and outputs, with side resources such as security groups in their own file, and sub-modules once `main.tf` gets crowded (the community IAM and EKS modules split node pools out this way).

Terraform is not a programming language, but the usual code rules apply: source control, KISS, DRY, idempotent modules. She points out that HashiCorp moved the same way: until Terraform 0.13, released in August 2020, you could not use `for_each` on modules.

## How Wix structures Terraform for the long haul

Wix lays out its live code by team, project, cloud provider and region, so a path reads like `bi/airflow/aws/us-east-1`. Each state covers one project in one region, which keeps it small, and each folder has its own CODEOWNERS entry so teams approve their own pull requests. That is what makes it Terraform as a platform: independence for teams, less load on the DevOps group. Accounts are currently handled at region level, which she admits is not great, and a restructure is under way.

The ugly alternative is a structure that allows huge states, which breed surprise dependencies. Hila Fish said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "I'm like what? I changed x not Y."

Workspaces isolate state and suit the same code for many customers (one GCP project per customer) or one service in many regions. But they hide each other from anyone who forgets to list them, and HashiCorp's own documentation says they are not a suitable isolation mechanism between staging and production. If you use them, wrap Terraform in a script that selects the workspace for you. The one use everyone agrees on: a throwaway workspace to test a change before applying it to default.

## Never Ctrl+C a running apply

Run Terraform remotely so there are no local credentials and there is an audit trail. Apply from a saved plan file so you know exactly what lands. Set a timeout: she once had an apply waiting on an auto scaling group of spot instances until the price dropped. Hila Fish said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "And the ugly here is to execute locally and click control c while terraform is running." Interrupted applies corrupt state and cause conflicts.

## Enforcement is the one with no bad side

The community AWS autoscaling module runs a checklist on every pull request: docs, `terraform fmt`, lint, end-of-file checks. Copy that for internal modules with pre-commit hooks or CI, add drift alerts to Slack, and make main the source of truth. At Wix, a push runs checks and a plan, and `atlantis apply` both applies and merges, so what is merged is what is deployed.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose Terraform codebase grew faster than its structure, and platform teams about to open Terraform to other teams. Dense, practical and opinionated, with a real company layout to borrow.

Title: Apache Pulsar for Python people, where the consumer picks the semantics
Description: Tim Spann (StreamNative) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on Apache Pulsar basics for Python developers, from schemas and functions to Presto and Flink SQL
Body:
In most messaging systems the shape of the topic decides how you consume it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Tim Spann, Developer Advocate at StreamNative, gave a Pulsar 101 for Python developers whose most useful idea is the opposite: in Apache Pulsar the consumer chooses whether a topic behaves like a Kafka-style ordered stream or a free-for-all work queue. Around that he shows schemas as plain Python classes, serverless functions, and SQL over live topics with Presto and Flink.

## Why one messaging platform instead of three?

Pulsar started at Yahoo, which could not find a single system that met all its needs and did not want to run several. The architecture separates compute from storage. Brokers route messages, cache and load-balance topic segments, and need little disk, so they scale up and down cheaply. Apache BookKeeper "bookies" hold the messages and cursors. Old data can tier off to S3-style object storage or HDFS, so replaying years of events does not mean buying years of SSDs. The metadata store is pluggable, with ZooKeeper, RocksDB and etcd implementations at the time.

## The consumer decides how a topic behaves

Subscriptions are where the flexibility lives. Exclusive and failover subscriptions give guaranteed order with a single active consumer and a standby, which is how you get Kafka-style streaming. Shared subscriptions turn the topic into a work queue: a thousand small apps grabbing whatever is next, order be damned. Key_Shared splits the difference with many active consumers but order per key; his example is change data capture with the table name as key, so every table's rows arrive in sequence.

Tim Spann said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "But remember it's the consumer that decides that." The producer never has to know.

He also argues for always setting a message key, auto-generated if nothing better exists, plus properties for metadata and a producer name so you know who sent what when debugging.

## A schema is just a class

The Python demo is short. Install the `pulsar-client` library with pip, define a schema by writing a class with the weather fields, and pass it to the producer as a JSON schema; switching to Avro is a one-word change. Topic names follow Pulsar's multi-tenant layout of tenant, namespace and topic, which is how one cluster carries hundreds of thousands of topics and keeps teams apart. A loop reads a sensor, builds a record, and sends it with a key.

## Functions, protocol handlers and SQL on topics

Pulsar Functions are the Lambda or database-trigger equivalent, written in Java, Python or Go. His sentiment-analysis function parses incoming JSON and returns a sentiment to an output topic. The demo wires it to an HTML form over WebSockets: type a question, a function scores it, a separate consumer pushes the answer back to the page. By default functions run inside the broker; Function Mesh runs them on Kubernetes instead.

Protocol handlers implement MQTT, Kafka, AMQP and others in full, not as thin converters. Tim Spann said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "And what's cool is it doesn't matter how your data gets into or out of pulsar, you pick the library you're comfortable with."

For queries, Pulsar SQL is Presto (Trino) underneath and reaches data already in tiered storage, including metadata such as event time, message ID and key; his count query ticks from 81 to 83 rows as the sensor keeps sending. Flink SQL runs the same select continuously, and a Flink catalog lets you join topics with other stores. Spark covers micro-batch ETL.

## Who should watch

Python developers who need messaging and have only seen Kafka, and anyone comparing streaming platforms who wants to see Pulsar's moving parts in 30 minutes. It is a 101 with a vendor advocate's enthusiasm, and the demos run live, including a slightly too warm 82-degree room.
