Title: A Kubernetes cluster is a bunch of YAML, so manage the fleet from Git
Description: JJ Asghar (IBM) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on GitOps for fleets of Kubernetes and OpenShift clusters, pull versus push, and a live Argo CD demo
Body:
Everyone was told to run one big cluster with namespaces, and almost everyone ended up with separate dev, QA and production clusters on different clouds anyway. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, JJ Asghar, Developer Advocate at IBM, made the case that GitOps is how you keep that sprawl consistent, explained why pull beats push, and installed Argo CD live on an OpenShift cluster to prove the point. His summary: GitOps is the CD half that most teams claiming CI/CD never finished.

## CI is standard, CD is not

He separates the two terms people say in one breath. Continuous integration is everywhere: GitHub Actions, Travis, CircleCI, low overhead, peace of mind. Continuous delivery is a mature process most teams have not reached, where green tests on main mean the code simply goes out. In his framing, GitOps is that missing CD portion, applied to cluster configuration as well as applications.

He is blunt that it is not something you dip a toe into. When you choose GitOps you change your deployment process and mechanisms completely, which is also what buys you a true history of every deployment.

## Why should a cluster pull instead of being pushed to?

A traditional pipeline pushes the new build to the servers. GitOps flips that: an agent inside the cluster polls the Git repository and pulls changes in at its own rate. The consequences he draws out:

- Your application has to tolerate being updated at any time, which is an engineering problem and a reason to keep QA in the loop.
- Air-gapped clusters become possible: the agent pulls from a security-scanned cache instead of the open internet.
- A pull can refuse to apply a change that breaks things, where a push lands on top of whatever is running.

JJ Asghar said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "Because what is a Kubernetes cluster but a bunch of yaml." Which makes fleet management a text-editing problem with an audit trail.

## Flux, Jenkins X or Argo CD?

He names three tools. Flux CD is the lightweight, CLI-based one he calls the granddaddy of them all, and he is impressed by it. Jenkins X is the next generation of the Jenkins ecosystem, a natural fit if you already live there, but prescriptive about how you work. Argo CD is the one that made GitOps click for him, so the demo uses it.

## Two commands and a link to Google

Installing Argo CD on his 17-day-old OpenShift cluster is a namespace plus one `kubectl apply` of the stable manifests. JJ Asghar said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "Argo CD is just two commands, which is always fun." It does not need to be exposed to the internet; he reaches the UI through a port forward. By default it gets cluster-admin rights, worth knowing before you copy the demo into production.

The use case is deliberately small: a ConsoleLink resource, managed with Kustomize, that adds a menu link in the OpenShift console. He creates an Argo CD application against his GitOps tutorial repository with automatic sync and self-heal, syncs it, and the link to Google appears. He edits the YAML in Git to point at Bing, Argo CD flags the app out of sync, and the change lands. On a fleet, every cluster running Argo CD with that configuration would pick it up without anyone logging in, which is the point he wants you to imagine at scale: an internal privacy page or a logo change across every cluster.

He ran out of time for the second demo, a small Flask app in the same repository, and points to Christian Hernandez's Argo CD tutorials at Red Hat, on which his own repository is based.

## Is GitOps DevOps 2.0?

No, he says. GitOps is a natural progression with real strengths, and he believes it will be how fleets of clusters are maintained, but DevOps covers much more than keeping infrastructure in line. The lesson he carries over from configuration management is consistency: developers touching many clusters expect the same interface and the same things installed on each.

## Who should watch

Teams with two or more clusters who still deploy by pushing from CI, and OpenShift users who want to see Argo CD on their platform. It is an introduction with a live, unrehearsed install, small demo and all.

Title: Homer imagined self-driving ships before anyone said AI
Description: Vasco Veloso (ING Bank) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 on 2,800 years of AI in myth and fiction, and why explainability is the real lesson
Body:
Artificial intelligence is not a new idea, only a new name. Vasco Veloso, Senior Software Engineer at ING Bank, makes that case at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022 by walking from Homer's Iliad to the Terminator, and then lands somewhere far less mythical: biased training data and why explainable models matter.

It is a history-and-ideas talk, not a technical one. No code, no benchmarks. What it offers instead is perspective, which is rarer in a machine learning track than it should be.

## Was AI really invented in the 1950s?

Vasco's answer is no. The concept, he argues, has lived in our collective imagination for millennia; the field just gave it a label. His first exhibit is Hephaestus in the Iliad (8th century BC), whose furnaces know what he needs before he asks, and whose tripods walk themselves to the assembly of the gods and back. That is autonomous navigation, written down before the alphabet had settled.

The better example is the Odyssey, where the Phaeacian ships have no pilots and no rudders and simply know where their passengers want to go, mist or no mist.

"Almost 3000 years ago, Homer was imagining a fully autonomous sea vessel and a telepathic one at that," Vasco Veloso said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022. His dry follow-up: today we have prototypes, and they are nowhere near that spec.

## From animated statues to training data

The tour moves on to 1754 and Condillac's Traité des Sensations, which imagines a statue with an empty soul that learns all human knowledge if you feed it one sensation at a time. Vasco draws the obvious line to how we train models today: feed in information piece by piece until the model has learned what it can. We have only built specialists, not the statue, but the principle holds up surprisingly well.

Chess runs through the whole story as humanity's favourite intelligence test. The 18th-century Mechanical Turk turned out to be a strong human player hidden in a box. Leonardo Torres Quevedo's 1912 automaton genuinely played, if only the king-and-rook versus king endgame, and always won. IBM's Deep Blue finished the job by beating Garry Kasparov in 1997. The reason for the obsession, as Vasco puts it, is that chess is too combinatorially large to brute-force with textbook game theory, so a machine winning at it meant something.

## Fiction keeps asking whether the machines will be kind

The middle of the talk is a reading list. Isaac Asimov's positronic robots bound by the three laws of robotics show that the fear of AI as a weapon is decades old. HAL 9000 in Arthur C. Clarke's 2001: A Space Odyssey defends itself against a crew that wants to unplug it. Skynet in The Terminator and the machines of The Matrix are the familiar catastrophes, and Daniel H. Wilson's Robopocalypse adds a program that suffocates its own creator before escaping into the internet.

Vasco is clear that not every fictional AI is a villain. His favourite is Marvin the Paranoid Android from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, who uses a tiny fraction of an enormous brain and found his most interesting conversation partner in a toaster. Ian McEwan's Machines Like Me, the Swedish series Äkta människor (Real Humans) and Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? push the question the other way: if synthetic humans can be good, what rights do they have, and what makes us human at all?

## Where the history meets your model

The last third is the part engineers should not skip. Vasco brings the philosophy down to the algorithm level with two failures. During the 2020 lockdowns, an algorithm used to predict UK exam grades produced results skewed by where students lived and which school they attended, and was overturned in favour of teacher assessment. In the US, a healthcare risk model used past healthcare spending as a proxy for future need, and so underestimated risk for patients who had spent less, mostly Black patients according to Scientific American.

The idea behind each algorithm was sound; the data taught it something else. That leads to explainability, black-box versus white-box models, and his blunt point about datasets:

"Every single data set is biased because someone had to make a decision on which data was present there," Vasco Veloso said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2022. His concrete advice: if you are grading academic performance, a postcode has no business in the feature set, because the model will happily find the correlation.

## Who should watch

Anyone who wants a well-told history of AI as an idea, and teams that need a non-technical way to open the conversation about bias and explainability. If you want architecture diagrams, pick another talk from the event.

Title: 300 lines of CloudFormation YAML, or under 30 lines of CDK
Description: Robert Hoffmann (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on replacing hand-written infrastructure templates with code, using AWS CDK and its level 2 constructs
Body:
A load balancer in front of an auto scaling group of EC2 instances sounds like a whiteboard sketch. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Robert Hoffmann, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, showed that it took him more than 300 lines of CloudFormation YAML, and under 30 lines with the AWS Cloud Development Kit. His argument: general-purpose languages beat configuration languages because of the abstractions that come with them, not because of the syntax.

## Where did 300 lines of YAML come from?

The architecture fits on a slide: internet, load balancer, several VMs for resilience. Robert Hoffmann said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "But the thing that stuck out to me most was that I had to write over 300 lines of yaml."

The hidden cost is everything around the boxes on the diagram. A VPC needs subnets, routing and internet connectivity. The load balancer needs a security group and a target. The auto scaling group needs a launch template, a scaling policy and an IAM role for its instances. Each of those is its own resource, wired to the others by hand. He frames the history as a career path: the lucky engineer who did it manually, the bash engineer, the YAML engineer, and finally the software engineer who models infrastructure in code. As a former web developer working in JavaScript and TypeScript, he knew which one he wanted to be.

## How does CDK turn code into a deployment?

You write a CDK app in TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java or C# (Go was in developer preview at the time). The app contains stacks, and the stacks contain constructs: classes that represent resources, such as an S3 bucket. `cdk synth` runs your program and produces a CloudFormation template, which the CloudFormation service then deploys. It is one more step than writing the template yourself, but you only ever touch the code. Pulumi takes a similar approach, and he says most of the talk applies to it too.

## Level 2 constructs do the busy work

Constructs come in three layers:

- **Level 1**: generated one-to-one from CloudFormation resources. No savings, just types.
- **Level 2**: hand-written representations of AWS services with sane defaults and best practices built in.
- **Level 3**: opinionated patterns that cover a whole architecture, such as load balancer plus auto scaling group in one class.

The demo stays on level 2. One line creates a VPC with public and private subnets, routing and internet connectivity, spread over two availability zones. The auto scaling group takes the VPC, an instance type picked from an enum (so no typo-driven failed deployment), a machine image and the subnets. The load balancer gets `addListener` on a port, `addTargets` pointing at the auto scaling group, and a convenience call that opens the default port to any IPv4 address and configures the security groups to match.

## Infrastructure code that reads like a story

The best part of the talk is a small detour into Robert C. Martin's Clean Code: code that is easy to read is easy for someone else to extend. The listener and target calls read as one sentence: the load balancer takes traffic on port 80 and sends it to the instances, while CDK writes the wiring underneath. Robert Hoffmann said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "You can really tell a story by code if you write good code."

His celebration got a mixed review at home. Robert Hoffmann said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "So you can come home from work earlier today and do the dishes."

## When should you not use it?

He is honest about the trade-off: if your team is fluent in CloudFormation or Terraform and not keen on debugging code, CDK may not be your thing. You do not have to choose, though. A platform team can stay on Terraform while a product team builds its new application in CDK. And CDK is not only for AWS: cdk8s generates Kubernetes manifests and CDK for Terraform writes Terraform in your language of choice, with shared constructs on Construct Hub at constructs.dev. For a hands-on start he points to cdkworkshop.com.

## Who should watch

Developers who have been handed infrastructure work and dread the YAML, and teams weighing CDK or Pulumi against Terraform. It is an introduction with one worked example, which is exactly right for that audience.

Title: Your production container has no vim, and that is fine
Description: Shai Almog (Lightrun) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on debugging Kubernetes in production with kubectl debug, KoolKits images and developer observability
Body:
You `kubectl exec` into a misbehaving pod to change one log level and find there is no editor, no htop and no debugger. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Shai Almog, Developer Advocate at Lightrun, showed three answers in increasing order of scale: `kubectl debug` with ephemeral containers, the open-source KoolKits images that fill those containers with tools, and developer observability for bugs you cannot pin to one pod.

## Why is Kubernetes harder to debug than a box?

He names three problems. Scale: the failure might be on any of hundreds of pods. Depth: it can sit in the orchestrator, the container or the code, and each layer needs a different skill set. And the bare-bones container: lean images are good practice, but once you are inside one, there is nothing to work with except luck with the logs.

Installing tools by hand inside the live pod is the obvious fix and the wrong one. Shai Almog said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "We don't want people in production just installing packages left and right, even if it's cleaned up." A pod's state should be described by its manifest, not by whoever ran `apt-get` last.

## Ephemeral containers: bring your own toolbox

`kubectl debug` adds an ephemeral container to a running pod. It vanishes when the pod is destroyed, it works on crashed pods and on bare images, and it can come from a completely different image with a full distro inside. He notes the feature arrived in Kubernetes 1.23, so hosted clusters need checking first.

His demo starts with the `busybox` image that the `kubectl debug` docs reference. Technically you are now in a new container rather than the app's, and you still have no vim. You could build your own debug image, but as he points out, everyone wants roughly the same tools.

## KoolKits: one opinionated image per runtime

That is the gap KoolKits fills: curated, platform-specific images for `kubectl debug`, built on Ubuntu so you get a desktop-grade distribution. There are four:

- **Go**: a Go debugger, pprof and friends.
- **JVM**: SDKMAN!, jmxterm, honest-profiler, VisualVM.
- **Node.js**: nvm, 0x, vtop.
- **Python**: pyenv, ipdb, IPython.

All of them add the basics (vim, htop), networking tools such as traceroute and nmap, and clients for PostgreSQL, MySQL and Redis. With access to the main container's file system and process namespace, he edits the log level from INFO to ERROR with vim, and mentions profiling, GDB or JDB, and JMX operations through jmxterm. The package list is open to pull requests.

## What about bugs on a hundred pods at once?

A debugger only helps if you know which server shows the bug, and attaching one in production risks a stuck breakpoint or an expensive condition. Shai Almog said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "JDWP itself is literally an open invitation for hacking." Logs rarely contain the line you need, and APM-style observability is built for the big picture, not for one variable in one method.

His answer is what he calls developer observability. Shai Almog said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "With developer observability, we flip that, we ask questions and then instrument based on those questions."

This part is a demo of his employer's product, Lightrun, with an agent in every pod and actions created from the IDE. Unlike `kubectl debug`, the agent has to be installed before the problem happens. He shows:

- **Injected logs** with expressions in curly braces; expressions that are too expensive or change state are rejected, and a log point pauses itself when CPU use crosses a threshold.
- **Snapshots**: stack trace and variables like a breakpoint, without stopping the server.
- **Conditional snapshots** that fire for one user ID only, for the bug only one customer sees.
- **Metrics**: counters per line, method duration, and timing for a code block, piped to StatsD or Prometheus.
- **Tags** that group agents (production, green, blue) so one action runs across many pods.

## Who should watch

Developers who own services on Kubernetes but do not live in it, and platform teams deciding what debugging access to give them. The first half is vendor-neutral and immediately useful; the second half is a product demo, clearly labelled as such.

Title: Kubernetes policy that runs on your laptop, in CI and in the cluster
Description: Noaa Barki (Datree) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on enforcing Kubernetes policy with OPA, Conftest, Gatekeeper and Argo CD, from local test to cluster
Body:
One missing memory limit is enough to take every node in a cluster out of memory. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Noaa Barki, Developer Advocate at Datree, walked through the policy-enforcement stack that stops that kind of mistake: Open Policy Agent as the engine, Conftest on the laptop and in CI, Gatekeeper inside the cluster, and Argo CD to make Git the only way in. Her takeaway: validate Kubernetes resources like source code, as early as possible, and then treat the policies themselves as something that has to be managed.

## Which manifest would you deploy?

She opens with a game: two manifests side by side, pick the safe one. A CronJob with `concurrencyPolicy` set to allow, so failed runs pile up instead of being replaced; she tells the story of Target, whose one failing CronJob created thousands of constantly restarting pods and pulled a few hundred CPUs into the cluster. A CronJob where the right setting sat in the wrong place in the YAML, which she says took Zalando's API server down. A pod with no memory limit, the Blue Matador story. The point of the quiz is that all three look harmless in review.

Noaa Barki said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "Trust me, nobody is immune to Kubernetes misconfiguration." Before Datree launched, she says, the team read more than 100 Kubernetes failure stories, and the pattern behind them was missing policy enforcement.

## Why the CI check should also be a local test

Her two beliefs are shift left and GitOps: every config file goes through CI exactly like application code. The less obvious argument is cultural. If the policy check runs as a local testing library, developers use it the way they already use unit tests: run it on their machine, open a pull request, expect CI to run it again. That lets the DevOps team hand responsibility to developers instead of guarding every manifest themselves.

## OPA is the engine, Conftest makes it usable

OPA is a general-purpose policy engine that decouples policy decisions from the services that enforce them. You can embed it as a Go package or run it as a daemon and query it over HTTP with JSON input. Policies are written in Rego, which she notes is inspired by Datalog.

For Kubernetes, raw OPA is a lot of work. Noaa Barki said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "And I do enjoy crossfit training and I do enjoy heavy lifting, but not when it comes to my Kubernetes cluster."

Conftest is the lighter option: write Rego rules (her examples block running as root and require an app label on every deployment), put them in a `policy` folder, and run `conftest test` against your files. It handles JSON, XML, Dockerfiles and YAML, and it can push and pull policy bundles to a Docker registry, which is how her GitHub Actions example shares one policy set across repos.

## CI is not enough while kubectl exists

Anyone with cluster access can still run `kubectl apply` and skip the pipeline. Gatekeeper closes that gap: it is a validating admission webhook, so every create, update or delete goes through OPA before it reaches etcd. Policies live in a ConstraintTemplate CRD with the Rego inside, and a separate Constraint says which kinds it applies to; her example requires an owner label on every namespace.

The cost is duplication. The same rule now exists as a Rego file for Conftest and as a ConstraintTemplate for Gatekeeper, across many repositories. Rego itself gets hard once a rule needs ranges, unit checks or comparisons across files, so her advice is to start from policies someone has already written.

## Or make Git the only door

The alternative to guarding the cluster is to stop people writing to it. With Argo CD, the cluster pulls from a Git repository and overrides manual changes when it drifts, so a separate GitOps repository (config apart from application code) becomes the single source of truth. Run Conftest in that repository's CI and policy enforcement covers everything that can reach production.

She ends on centralised policy management: who may change a policy, which ones fail most, and whether developers know how to fix a failure. Git and email do not answer those. That is where she brings in Datree's open-source CLI, which ships built-in rules for Kubernetes and Argo CD, runs locally, in CI or as a pre-commit hook, and checks each file in three steps (valid YAML, valid Kubernetes or Argo CD resource, policy). The final section is a pitch for her employer's tool; the first three quarters are a vendor-neutral tour.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers about to roll out policy as code for Kubernetes, and anyone deciding between CI checks, admission control and GitOps. It is an overview with configuration examples, not a Rego tutorial.

Title: Epsagon forked OpenTelemetry, regretted it, and became a distribution
Description: Yosef Arbiv (Cisco) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on Epsagon's path from proprietary tracing SDKs via OpenTelemetry forks to an OpenTelemetry distribution
Body:
Forking an open source project feels like a shortcut right up to the moment upstream ships its next release. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Yosef Arbiv, R&D Team Leader at Cisco and lead of the SDK team at Epsagon, told the story of how Epsagon went from proprietary tracing SDKs to forks of OpenTracing and OpenTelemetry, and finally to building on OpenTelemetry as a distribution and contributing upstream, with a lesson at the end of each act.

It is a short, honest talk about how a vendor should use open source, and the mistakes are the useful part.

## What did Epsagon build?

Epsagon gave teams with many cloud services and frameworks a view of who talks to whom, where the errors are and how to troubleshoot. Customers imported Epsagon's SDKs without changing their code, and the SDKs, built by Arbiv's team, instrumented the application, created traces and sent them to Epsagon's backend.

## Act one: build your own, then open it

Epsagon started about four years before the talk, aimed at the then-new serverless market. There was no industry standard for distributed tracing; most customers had logs or non-distributed traces. OpenTracing was on the table, but it was backed by a single company that happened to be a competitor, and it lacked automatic instrumentation. Epsagon wanted minimal code changes, so it wrote its own auto-instrumenting libraries.

The plan to ship them closed-source didn't survive customers, who refused to install closed packages in their code and wanted to read and fix it. So the libraries went open source, with hopes of a small community around them.

Lessons: decide carefully which parts of a product should be closed, because defending the wrong part is a problem. And building an open source community is hard work. "It is much easier to join a community than to create one on your own," Yosef Arbiv said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022.

## Act two: fork fast, maintain forever

Serverless made Epsagon popular but the market was too small to build a big business on. Moving into Kubernetes meant a Java agent, which was too complex to write from scratch, so Epsagon took OpenTracing code, added what its backend needed, and shipped a working Java agent.

Then OpenTelemetry arrived, built from OpenTracing and OpenCensus, and caught on quickly. Epsagon did the same trick again: take the OpenTelemetry libraries, change them a bit, add the Epsagon-specific features. New libraries appeared fast. Maintaining them did not go so well, because the community kept moving and the forks kept falling behind.

Lessons: "So I really suggest not to use forks when possible," Arbiv said. And tech debt is a tool, not a sin, as long as you keep it under control; growing it without control is the problem.

## Act three: become a distribution, then a contributor

With the fork overhead no longer scaling, and customers wanting their own OpenTelemetry traces shown alongside Epsagon's, the team ran an experiment with a new Java agent. This time OpenTelemetry was a dependency, not a copy: Epsagon packaged it as a distribution, collected the extra data it needed through an extension, and kept the OpenTelemetry trace structure. The agent was quick to build, easy to update, and the backend could now accept plain OpenTelemetry traces too.

Just as they were about to rebuild more libraries that way, Cisco announced it was acquiring Epsagon. The Epsagon product stopped, and the team moved to a new full-stack observability product that supports OpenTelemetry natively, with Epsagon's libraries as distributions on top.

They also joined the community properly: contributing features and fixes, working with maintainers, and learning from the AppDynamics team and other Cisco groups already deep in OpenTelemetry. Arbiv says being part of something bigger has been good for his developers too.

## Who should watch

Anyone at a company building a product on top of an open source project, especially in observability. The fork-versus-distribution choice applies well beyond OpenTelemetry. There is no code on screen; it is a story with lessons, not a tutorial.

Title: Your 10-second average just ate the alert - observability is a data problem
Description: Dave McAllister (NGINX) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on how sampling, aggregation, drift and skew quietly hide the data observability depends on
Body:
A 10-second average of 13.9 requests per second looks calm. The individual measurement that crossed 30, exactly where the alert was set, is gone. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Dave McAllister, Senior OSS Technical Evangelist at NGINX, used examples like that to argue that observability is first a data problem: sample, aggregate or collect too slowly, and you build your own blind spots.

It is a talk about the statistics underneath your dashboards rather than any particular tool, delivered by someone who has been an open source geek since before it was called open source.

## Why does cloud native make this harder?

McAllister frames it with the Cynefin framework (credit to Kevin Brockhoff for the drawing). A monolith is a simple system: categorise, respond, fix. Microservices add complication, elastic and ephemeral infrastructure adds a second dimension, and together they land you in a complex system where you probe before you can sense and respond. Things you want to inspect may already have scaled away, failures seldom repeat exactly, and multitenancy hurts.

Monitoring watches the known failure modes; observability is the data that lets you ask about the ones you didn't predict. Both depend on how much of that data you actually keep. His sizing example: hundreds of services, kilobytes of metadata per transaction, and a single application can produce megabytes per second, or 300 GB a day.

## Rule one: use all of your data to avoid blind spots

Metrics, traces and logs overlap: logs and traces yield metrics, metrics point you at the right trace or log. Cardinality matters, so a CPU figure can be sliced down to a core on a specific VM. He wants streaming rather than batch, full-fidelity data, and open standards so you are not locked in.

The usual ways of taming volume all throw something away. Filters smooth sharp edges or remove outliers, and trace sampling routinely misses edge cases and intermittent failures. The arithmetic is blunt: keep 5 of 100 traces at random and you have a 95% chance of missing the outlier. Sampling that decides after seeing a trace catches known errors, but you are hunting unknown unknowns.

His side-by-side shows it. The sampled run of an application put trace durations in the one-to-two-second range with one exception. The unsampled run of the same app showed a trace taking around 29 seconds. "And in an ecommerce world, 29 seconds is known as a lost sale," Dave McAllister said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022.

Metrics are not a full escape hatch. Infrastructure metrics are usually unsampled, but metrics derived from traces (rate, errors, duration) inherit the sampling, and duration is probably the most important signal for user experience. His answer to noise is better visualisation, not less data.

## Rule two: operate at the speed and resolution of your app and infrastructure

He borrows the von Neumann bottleneck as an analogy: how fast data arrives is usually lower than the resolution the data has, and both limit what aggregation, analysis and visualisation can tell you.

That is where the alert-eating average comes from. Over ten seconds of requests per second, the 10-second average is 13.9 and the 95th percentile 27.5. Split into two 5-second windows, the averages are 16.4 and 11.4. None of these numbers shows the point above 30. Multiply that by hundreds of thousands of requests.

His guidance:

- **Accuracy and precision are different.** Accurate means the number is correct; precise means it is consistent from one measurement to the next. Aggregation can damage both.
- **Keep the raw points.** Native (collection) resolution and chart resolution will rarely match. If you throw away data points, you cannot reconstruct what happened.
- **Granularity is a trade-off.** Finer granularity gives more potential precision, and more data.
- **Watch drift and skew.** On VMs and networks you don't control, data sources run ahead or behind. Drift keeps growing; skew is a one-off out of line. Keeping all the data is again the easiest way to see them.

## Can you trust your predictions?

Most alerting is predictive, and predictions are only as good as the data. Stationary signals suit static thresholds; otherwise look for sudden change, linear trends (resources running out), or seasonal patterns compared against history. Expect false positives and negatives whichever you choose. For historical baselines, use the median, not the mean, because outliers drag the mean around.

He closes with Brian Kernighan's 1979 line about careful thought and judiciously placed print statements being the most effective debugging tool, and his own update: "observability is the new print statement."

## Who should watch

SREs tuning trace sampling or alert windows, and anyone who has trusted a p95 panel without asking what it aggregated. No product pitch, just the maths behind the graphs.

Title: Cloud tagging starts with one rule - tag everything new from today
Description: Tim Davis (env0) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on why resource tags pay off for finance and security, and how to tag a backlog in baby steps
Body:
The tag field is the one box everybody skips when deploying a cloud resource, because nothing breaks if you leave it empty. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Tim Davis, DevOps Advocate at env0, argued that this small piece of metadata is how you stop finance and security from asking you what everything is, and that the way out of an untagged estate is a single rule: tag every new resource from today, then chip away at the backlog.

It is a short, lighthearted talk, closer to a pep talk with a plan than a technical walkthrough, and that's fine for the subject.

## What is a tag, really?

Davis keeps the definition minimal: a tag is a filter. A small piece of metadata attached to a cloud resource that does not change how it is deployed or what runs on it, only how you find it. Every major public and private cloud has them, and while not every resource type is taggable, the ones you use most are.

He comes at it from an infrastructure career (systems administration, architecture, then VMware's cloud and developer advocacy team), and his lens is that infrastructure exists for the application that runs the business.

## Who benefits from your tags?

The selling point is selfish in the best way: make other people's lives easier and they stop interrupting yours.

- **Finance.** Reports on what each team, application or resource type costs, such as whether databases are overspending this month or what all those Lambda functions add up to.
- **Security.** What is deployed, what it is connected to, whether something sits on the VPC it shouldn't. With tags, they click the resource or filter a report instead of asking you.
- **Managers.** Who, Davis notes dryly, can run report after report to justify their existence.

## How do you tag an estate that has no tags?

Treat it like any other DevOps change: people and process first, tooling after. "Remember, DevOps is a marathon. It's not a sprint," Tim Davis said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, before checking whether the audience got the joke.

The plan is baby steps:

1. **Stop the bleeding.** From today, tag every new resource. The untagged backlog stops growing.
2. **Agree a structure first.** Decide on your tagging scheme before you start applying it everywhere.
3. **Start broad.** Tag all production resources with environment as the key and prod as the value, then do the same for dev, QA and staging. Many teams already split environments by account or cloud, which makes this quick.
4. **Move inward.** Then function: web servers, databases, what each one runs.

How many tags, and which? He gives the engineer's answer, it depends, and declines to prescribe a scheme for you.

## Which tools help?

Infrastructure as code makes automatic tagging easy. He names Yor from Bridgecrew, Terratag from env0, the default tags you can set for the AWS provider in Terraform, tags in Pulumi, PowerShell for Azure and PowerCLI for VMware. Those tools help with both halves of the job: new deployments and updating the existing backlog systematically.

His closing philosophy fits on a sticky note. Work hard today to be super lazy tomorrow.

## Who should watch

Teams that have just been asked by finance for a cost breakdown they cannot produce, and engineers who want a quick argument to bring to their next planning meeting. If you already enforce tagging policies in CI, you can skip it.

Title: StackHawk didn't need faster laptops, it needed Kubernetes to carry the deps
Description: Zachary Conger (StackHawk) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on moving local microservice dependencies from Docker Compose to Kubernetes, then to Kotlin tooling
Body:
When the laptop fans start sounding like a jet engine every time you run a test, the instinct is to order bigger laptops. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Zachary Conger, Senior DevOps Engineer at StackHawk, told the story of how the company kept local development on laptops while its microservice count grew: first Docker Compose overlays, then Kompose pushing the dependencies into per-developer Kubernetes namespaces, and finally a Kotlin CLI that replaced a sprawling pile of shell scripts.

It is a candid, three-iteration history with trade-offs at every step, which makes it more useful than a tool pitch.

## What was the platform?

StackHawk builds a DAST scanner on top of the open source OWASP ZAP project. The architecture, greenfield about three years before the talk, has a run-anywhere scanner, a React single-page UI, and Kotlin microservices behind REST APIs on Kubernetes. Builds run in AWS CodeBuild on GitHub webhooks, across separate build and runtime AWS accounts with production and several staging environments. Gradle builds the JVM code, and a growing bash library handled environment lookups, artifact pushes and deploys.

Developers built and tested locally, then let automation take over. That lasted a couple of weeks.

## Iteration one: Docker Compose overlays

The problem: service A does little without services B, C and D running. Each repository got its own Compose file describing how to run that service (image from ECR with the latest tag, a reserved port such as 3200, its dependencies), and a local start script pulled the Compose files of every dependency and merged them using Compose's overlay feature. The service you were working on stayed out of the mix and ran from the IDE against everything else on localhost.

It worked for another four or five weeks, until the containers grew and Docker Desktop and the IDE started fighting over memory.

## Iteration two: dependencies in Kubernetes, code on the laptop

"Well, it turns out we do not need faster laptops," Zachary Conger said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. The team wanted to keep local IDEs, debuggers and profilers, so it kept the merged Compose file and fed it to Kompose, which generates Kubernetes manifests from Compose files. A script applied the resulting deployments and services to a namespace named after the developer and set up kubectl port-forwards, so the dependencies looked exactly as if they were still on localhost.

Laptops cooled down, the IDE got its memory back, and UI developers, who needed the whole stack, benefited most. This setup held for about two years.

## Why did the shell scripts have to go?

Because shell scripts don't scale. The bash library had grown big, each project had its own scripts calling it, and everything depended on a list of CLI tools sensitive to versions and to whether you were on macOS, Linux or Windows. New developers had to install the AWS CLI, Terraform, Docker Compose, Kompose and more before writing a line of code.

Meanwhile Gradle had been quietly absorbing the work. StackHawk wrote its own Gradle plugins in Kotlin, which gave it the AWS, Kubernetes and GitHub APIs directly: authenticate to CodeArtifact, push and pull containers and S3 objects, look up environments, deploy workloads, even open pull requests. The team moved the remaining functions into that Kotlin library and built a new CLI on top. It is strongly typed, testable, talks to cloud APIs instead of shelling out, and is written in the language every developer on the team already knows.

## What the Kotlin version adds

The dev environment command became a subcommand of the new CLI, with its own YAML config tuned to StackHawk's services. Sensible defaults for CPU and memory requests (so the cluster can autoscale as environments come and go), common environment variables and pod permissions are baked into the library and can still be overridden. Highlights:

- **Three run modes.** Bring the dependencies up in Kubernetes, in a local Compose-like setup, or natively on the JVM, which is the lightweight choice when you need only a couple of services.
- **Snapshots.** Database state with sample users and scans can be backed up to S3 and restored the next time, so you don't rebuild test data every morning.
- **Gradle integration.** The same environments serve as ephemeral test environments, static UAT environments, or a source of manifests for Argo CD or Flux.
- **Small automations.** Pushing an image to an ECR repository that doesn't exist yet now creates the repository first.

Ideas on his list: a web UI, environments for product and support teams, CRDs and a controller that snapshot and reap environments left running too long, and self-service repos, pipelines and EKS clusters. He calls the result what it became, an internal developer platform.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers at startups whose microservices are outgrowing laptops, and anyone deciding between remote dev environments and keeping the local loop. It is a story, not a product demo, and the lessons transfer even if you don't write Kotlin.

Title: If you write CloudFormation by hand, AWS CDK is the easy upgrade
Description: Roy Tal (Firefly) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on why CloudFormation users should move to AWS CDK, and how importing an existing template works
Body:
Anyone who has maintained a few thousand lines of CloudFormation YAML knows the feeling Roy Tal describes. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Tal, Engineering Team Lead at Firefly, made a short, enthusiastic case for the AWS Cloud Development Kit: write AWS infrastructure in a real programming language, keep CloudFormation as the engine underneath, and bring existing templates along with a single import.

It is a compact talk aimed squarely at CloudFormation users, with a small demo. Teams on Terraform or Pulumi will get less out of it than the abstract suggests.

## What is a CDK, and what is the AWS one?

Tal treats CDK as a concept first: any infrastructure-as-code tool where you write the infrastructure in code (TypeScript, Python, Go, Java, .NET) instead of a configuration language like YAML or JSON. The AWS CDK is AWS's implementation, built natively for AWS and set to succeed CloudFormation there. CDK for Terraform and cdk8s for Kubernetes are other implementations of the same idea, and he says those fit better if AWS isn't your target.

He came to it from the re:Invent show floor, where visitors to Firefly's booth kept asking about CDK, and Firefly's own product tracks a cloud footprint across Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, CDK and Helm, so drift between code and cloud is his day job.

## How does it work under the hood?

The AWS CDK sits on top of CloudFormation. You define constructs, the AWS resources, in code; anything CloudFormation can create, CDK can. Then two commands: cdk synth turns the code into what will be deployed, and cdk deploy creates CloudFormation stacks that create the resources. A bootstrap stack, CDKToolkit, sets up supporting resources such as the S3 bucket CDK uses. Tal calls the synthesised output a state file; strictly, synth emits CloudFormation templates, and CloudFormation keeps track of what is deployed.

## Who should use it, and when?

His answer is direct. Every CloudFormation user, because migration is easy and the experience stays AWS-native. AWS-focused DevOps and SRE teams, even if they are on Terraform or Pulumi today. And curious infrastructure people in general. The moments to switch: now, if you have CloudFormation projects, and at the start of any new AWS infrastructure project.

The pros he lists:

- **Languages.** TypeScript (the original), JavaScript, Python, Java, .NET and Go.
- **No DSL.** Big CloudFormation projects get painful as dependencies and cross-references between resources pile up; code handles that structure better.
- **Multi-region.** Instead of reaching for StackSets, which he calls a patch over CloudFormation, you write reusable code and deploy it per region.
- **AWS-native.** On AWS, the best-integrated option.

The con is the flip side: it is AWS-only, so multi-cloud teams should look at the other CDKs.

## The demo: import a template, deploy it as CDK

The demo stack defines an S3 bucket and an SQS queue in code, plus an import of an existing CloudFormation template that defines an EC2 instance. After synth and deploy, the AWS console shows two stacks: CDKToolkit, and the app's stack containing the bucket, the queue and the imported EC2 instance, now managed from CDK code. That import is the strongest argument in the talk: you do not have to rewrite a template before you can start working in CDK.

The abstract also promises a migration story from Terraform and Pulumi and Go code samples; the talk does not get to those.

## Is it worth adopting early?

Tal's closing takeaway is about timing. "I absolutely recommend you to use the CDK now instead of later on," Roy Tal said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, calling CDK a technology still in its first steps. For CloudFormation shops he pushes even harder.

## Who should watch

Engineers maintaining CloudFormation who want a short, opinionated nudge and a look at the import path. Those already comparing CDK with Terraform in depth will want a longer talk.

Title: Why Oak9 moved its API monolith off Fargate onto EKS and Argo CD
Description: Ramesh Patel (Oak9) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on leaving a Fargate monolith for EKS microservices, deployed by Jenkins and Argo CD
Body:
Build times are usually the first honest signal that a monolith has outgrown its home. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Ramesh Patel, Director of Cloud and DevOps at Oak9, explained in a short talk why the cloud security company moved its API off an AWS Fargate cluster and onto Amazon EKS, with Argo CD deploying the new microservices, and then showed a change going from commit to cluster in about 30 seconds.

This is a lightning-length talk: a few minutes of context, an architecture before-and-after, and a demo. Watch it for the shape of the migration, not for a detailed playbook.

## Who is Oak9 and what were they running?

Oak9 is a SaaS product for cloud security, covering the path from writing code to production, with integrations into CI/CD tools and its own CLI. The stack is polyglot: Angular and Node on the front end, .NET Core for the API and Lambdas, Python for the automation behind its security blueprints, Go for the CLI binary, and most of the infrastructure on AWS.

The starting point was a typical event-driven AWS architecture, with the core API running as a monolith on a Fargate cluster.

## Why break up the monolith?

Patel gives four reasons, all familiar to anyone who has watched a .NET build crawl:

- **Build time.** Builds had grown too long, which slowed deployments and stretched the time to ship features.
- **Onboarding.** A huge API codebase made it hard for new developers to get going, and meant longer builds and test runs.
- **Coupling.** The team wanted a loosely coupled architecture.
- **Team independence.** Teams needed to ship without waiting on each other.

## What does the new architecture look like?

The Fargate cluster is replaced by an EKS cluster, and Argo CD deploys microservices into it following GitOps principles. Kustomize handles environment overlays, and Jenkins stays in the picture as the CI half.

The abstract mentions breaking the monolith apart with domain-driven design and the hurdles along the way. The talk itself does not cover those; it sticks to the before and after diagrams and the deploy flow.

## The 30-second deploy

The demo is a minimal Nginx service serving a hello world page. Patel edits the index.html, which starts a Jenkins pipeline with two stages: build the Docker image, then call the Argo CD binary to push the new image tag. In Argo CD's UI the project picks up the new image and syncs to the cluster automatically.

"So within a matter of 30 seconds we were able to tag an image, build an image and push an image to kubernetes," Ramesh Patel said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. It is a deliberately tiny service, so treat the number as the pipeline's overhead rather than a benchmark for a real build.

## Who should watch

Small teams on ECS or Fargate wondering when Kubernetes starts paying for itself, and anyone who wants a quick look at Jenkins handing deploys to Argo CD. If you want the gritty migration details, pair it with a longer GitOps talk.

Title: Start on App Runner, graduate to ECS and Fargate when the startup grows
Description: Maish Saidel-Keesing (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on taking a startup from an App Runner website to ECS and Fargate as needs grow
Body:
Most container platform talks start with the cluster. Maish Saidel-Keesing, Senior Enterprise Developer Advocate on the Amazon ECS service team at AWS, started his Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 talk with a three-person startup that just needs a website by Friday. His pitch: begin with AWS App Runner, where the build system, pipeline, load balancer and autoscaling are AWS's problem, and move to Amazon ECS and AWS Fargate once the company needs private data and background work.

It is an AWS story told through an imaginary company, AnyCompany, with a live App Runner demo in the middle. Expect a guided tour of AWS services, not a neutral comparison.

## Who is AnyCompany and what do they need?

AnyCompany promises to take any product to market in under eight weeks. The founders are Scott (CEO and, by necessity, CMO), Diane (CTO) and Alice (VP of engineering, still a coder). Their six-month plan is topped by one item: a web presence, fast.

Alice's requirements are relatable. Containers, because she trusts them. No infrastructure to babysit. Something that copes with load if the product takes off. "And the most important thing as a developer, git flow for life," Maish Saidel-Keesing said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022.

## What does App Runner actually run?

App Runner takes either an image from Amazon ECR (public or private) or a source repository such as GitHub, and handles the path from a push to a running service. You configure CPU and memory, the port, a health check, autoscaling and deployment mode (manual, or automatic on every new image tag or commit).

Under the hood, the container runs as a Fargate task in an AWS-managed VPC across several subnets. Users resolve the service through Route 53 to a Network Load Balancer, a managed router spreads requests across containers, and outbound calls go through a managed NAT gateway. Autoscaling is driven by concurrent requests per container. Saidel-Keesing notes App Runner can scale down to zero when nobody is calling, so there is nothing to pay for idle requests. He is upfront that App Runner was a fairly new service, built on mature AWS building blocks.

The sweet spot he describes: stateless web applications and REST APIs serving HTTP, long-running, with state in an external store such as DynamoDB or RDS.

## The demo: a boilerplate site becomes AnyCompany's

Alice clones a Node.js boilerplate site, a script adds a Dockerfile and a build script, and the image goes to a private ECR repository tagged both latest and with a timestamp. A second script rebrands the template, a rebuild leans on Docker layer caching, and the push is quick because most layers are already there.

In the App Runner console, the service is wired to the ECR tag, so every push deploys. He walks through the options that matter: an IAM role to pull from ECR, an optional instance role for calls to AWS APIs, encryption with an AWS-owned or your own key, public networking or a custom VPC, and a custom domain via a Route 53 record instead of the default awsapprunner.com name. Deployments are blue-green: the old version keeps serving until health checks pass on the new one, which is why the live site briefly still shows the unbranded template.

## When does ECS enter the story?

Six months later AnyCompany has teams, customers and two new requirements: security (no customer PII on the front page of the New York Times) and data that has to be stored and processed. App Runner's VPC support lets the front end reach a private RDS database without exposing it to the internet, and ECS on Fargate runs the background tasks that turn that data into business insight.

His ECS primer is compact. ECS is the managed control plane, Fargate the managed data plane, so there are no AMIs or container hosts to maintain. A task is one or more containers, identical tasks form a service that ECS can attach to a load balancer, and services live in a cluster. "A cluster is simply a logical grouping," Saidel-Keesing said. Tasks run on EC2 or Fargate, with EC2 Spot, Fargate Spot and Savings Plans for cost.

Fair warning: this part is brief. The abstract suggests a longer ECS and Fargate growth story, while the talk spends most of its time on App Runner.

## Who should watch

Small teams choosing their first AWS container service, and anyone who wants a quick feel for App Runner's console and deployment model. Engineers already running ECS in production will find little new.

Title: Let your SD-WAN read Kubernetes labels, then scale bandwidth with replicas
Description: Alberto Rodriguez-Natal (Cisco) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on CN-WAN, which maps Kubernetes service metadata to per-microservice SD-WAN policies
Body:
Your SD-WAN probably terminates right in front of a Kubernetes cluster and has no idea what is behind it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Alberto Rodriguez-Natal, Tech Lead in Cisco's enterprise networking CTO team, showed how to change that: harvest labels and annotations from Kubernetes services and turn them into per-microservice SD-WAN policies, and even scale WAN bandwidth up and down with the replica count.

It is a networking talk for cloud native people, and a cloud native talk for networking people, with Cisco's open source Cloud Native SD-WAN (CN-WAN) project as the worked example.

## What problem is SD-WAN solving here?

A WAN connects geographically spread locations: branches, headquarters, the cloud, remote workers, IoT devices. SD-WAN builds that network in a software-defined way, connecting any location over whatever transport is available (internet, MPLS) with services such as security on top. The classic picture is two SD-WAN edges, one near the users and one near the application, and a controller that stitches a tunnel between them.

The catch is the application end. If it runs on Kubernetes, it is not one monolith but a collection of services, and a voice stream, a chat service and a file transfer want very different treatment from the network. Rodriguez-Natal describes SD-WAN and Kubernetes as two systems deployed side by side that are agnostic to each other. Nothing says they have to stay that way.

## How CN-WAN wires the two together

The flow has two teams and a few components:

1. **DevOps deploys** a service as usual, exposed as a LoadBalancer, with labels and annotations in the YAML.
2. **The CN-WAN Operator** watches the cluster for exposed services, extracts that metadata and writes it into a service registry.
3. **The CN-WAN Reader** reads the registry.
4. **The CN-WAN Adapter**, specific to each SD-WAN vendor's API, passes the application information to the SD-WAN controller.
5. **NetOps** writes controller policies that match the metadata.

His example is a video conferencing app with four microservices: voice, video, slides and chat. NetOps defines policies per metadata value, for instance minimal latency and no drops for real-time traffic, lots of bandwidth for file transfer. When DevOps deploys a service tagged accordingly, the right flow lands on the right policy without a ticket going back and forth.

CN-WAN is one route. Some SD-WAN products are growing their own Kubernetes awareness; CN-WAN is for those that have none.

## Can the network autoscale like a deployment?

The second example moves from the overlay (edge to edge, over an underlay you don't control) to the underlay itself, using connectivity providers that expose APIs to the SD-WAN. Here CN-WAN reads one more thing from Kubernetes: the replica count.

"Kubernetes is very good to scale applications both horizontally and vertically. Why we cannot do the same on the network, right?" Alberto Rodriguez-Natal said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. As replicas grow, the bandwidth requested from the provider grows. As they shrink, the bandwidth shrinks too, which is where the cost saving comes from. Paying for WAN capacity that tracks your HPA is a pleasant thought for anyone who has signed a fixed bandwidth contract.

## What comes next?

His closing question is service mesh metadata: if SD-WAN can learn from Kubernetes services, it could learn from the mesh too. He says Cisco's team was working on it at the time and leaves it as an open direction rather than a demo.

## Who should watch

Network engineers whose WAN carries traffic to Kubernetes apps, and platform teams who want a say in how that traffic is treated. It is an architecture walkthrough with two clear examples, no live demo, and it is Cisco's own open source project on show.

Title: Karpenter skips the node group and picks the instance itself
Description: Raja Ganesan (AWS) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on how Karpenter provisions right-sized nodes without node groups, versus Cluster Autoscaler
Body:
Cluster Autoscaler assumes every node in a group is a twin. Karpenter does not believe in groups at all. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Raja Ganesan, Cloud Architect at AWS, walked the same scheduling problem through both autoscalers, and the difference is the whole argument: Karpenter reads the pending pods, picks an instance type that fits them, and asks the cloud provider for it directly.

It is a clear, explainer-style talk aimed at people who run Kubernetes nodes and pay for them.

## Why autoscale nodes at all?

Ganesan starts with the honest alternative: some sites simply over-provision. The reasons to do better are resiliency against failures and interruptions, cost (run the cluster at the right size) and predictable availability. He splits Kubernetes autoscaling into two families, scaling pods and scaling the nodes under them, and both Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter belong to the second.

## The same nine pods, two autoscalers

His example runs on AWS. A cluster has one t3.medium node, and two workloads with four and five replicas are pending, each replica asking for 250 millicores of CPU and 1 GB of memory.

With Cluster Autoscaler, the cluster is a node group of one to ten t3.medium instances. Cluster Autoscaler watches the API server, works out what the Auto Scaling group's launch template offers, and raises the desired count until the pods fit. It ends up adding three more nodes of exactly the same size, because it assumes every node in a group is equivalent. Several matching groups mean it needs expanders to pick one. An unavailable instance type means retries against a preconfigured timeout. Zone balance relies on the provider's own rebalancing, which on AWS can terminate nodes to even things out. And it is happiest when workloads have no zone-specific storage or zone affinity.

With Karpenter there is no node group. It watches for pods marked unschedulable, totals what they need, and calls the EC2 Fleet API directly. In the example it might pick a single m5.xlarge with 4 vCPUs and 16 GB, a different size from the existing t3.medium, which fits all nine replicas at once. When a node is empty, Karpenter removes it.

## What you actually configure

The unit of configuration is a Provisioner, a Karpenter custom resource that uses well-known Kubernetes labels such as zone, instance type and operating system. The API names are the 2022 ones, so check them against the current docs. Nodes go away in three ways: a TTL after which Karpenter drains and deletes the node, an empty-node TTL, or a manual delete.

A few details stand out:

- **Spot first.** With both spot and on-demand allowed, Karpenter prefers spot and falls back to on-demand when spot capacity isn't there. Use it for workloads that tolerate interruption.
- **Upgrades by expiry.** The simplest node upgrade is the expiry TTL: replacement nodes pick up the latest AMI from the launch template.
- **Launch templates.** On AWS, Karpenter creates them for you with the latest EKS-optimised AMI and encrypted EBS volumes. If that is not what you want, bring your own. Bottlerocket is supported the same way.
- **One Provisioner or many.** One is enough for most sites. Separate ones make sense for CPU versus GPU nodes, or per team for cost attribution, but keep them mutually exclusive. If several match a pending pod, Karpenter picks one at random, which is a fun thing to discover during a cost review.
- **Topology spread over affinity.** For availability across zones and capacity types, Karpenter recommends topology spread constraints rather than pod affinity.

## Where the speed comes from

Ganesan's recap names three gains: any instance type the provider offers, not one size per group; no extra orchestration layer such as Auto Scaling groups, so "when there are failures, your retry time is considerably reduced," as Raja Ganesan said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022; and pods bound to a node as soon as it is launched, so the kubelet can prepare the runtime and pull images while the node is still coming up.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers on EKS weighing Karpenter against Cluster Autoscaler, and anyone who has stared at a node group full of half-empty instances. It is a conceptual walkthrough with a worked example, not a live demo.

Title: Can you do GitOps with Terraform and no Argo or Flux?
Description: Jim Sheldon (Harness) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on two Terraform repo layouts for Kubernetes, and whether a Git-driven pipeline counts as GitOps
Body:
Deleting a YAML file is the one change most Kubernetes CD pipelines quietly ignore. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Jim Sheldon, Developer Advocate at Harness, showed two ways to lay out Terraform repositories for Kubernetes resources, and why the directory-per-environment layout turns a deleted file into a clean destroy instead of an orphaned deployment. He then asked the awkward question: is any of this actually GitOps?

It is a short, demo-heavy talk. The stack is Terraform, GitHub, Docker, the Terraform Kubernetes provider and Drone CI, with the podinfo microservice as the guinea pig.

## Why manage Kubernetes resources with Terraform at all?

There is no shortage of tools for Kubernetes manifests, and Sheldon admits Terraform is "yet another tool to add to the pile". His argument is organisational: if a team already lives in Terraform, the Kubernetes provider lets it manage deployments, stateful sets and services the same way it manages everything else. The workflow is not Kubernetes-specific either. He used the same pattern at a previous company with the GitHub provider, managing every GitHub repository as code.

Drone gets a short introduction: open source, container native, written in Go, started in 2012 and acquired by Harness in August 2020. It needs only a server and a runner, works with GitHub, Bitbucket and GitLab, and runs builds on Windows, Mac and ARM.

## Layout one: a tfvars file per environment

The first repository keeps one set of Terraform files and one tfvars file per environment, with pods in a demo-dev and a demo-prod namespace. Sheldon edits the message in the deployment file, commits to main, and Drone clones, sets the kube config, initialises and applies to dev. Promotion to prod is a Drone promotion of the same build, which runs the same steps with the prod tfvars file.

His verdict: it works well for a small set of tightly coupled resources, and when every environment runs all the time.

## Layout two: a directory per environment

The second repository has separate dev and prod directories with nearly identical files; the namespace in locals.tf is the main difference. The commit-and-apply loop looks the same. The difference shows up when he wants dev gone. He renames the file with a destroyed suffix (his habit, so it is obvious what is running), opens a pull request, Drone runs a plan that says it will destroy the deployment, and the merge removes it.

This is the bit worth the price of admission for anyone who has fought pruning in a CD pipeline. "If you delete a YAML file, your CD pipeline doesn't have it there. It can't run Kubectl delete on the file," Jim Sheldon said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. With Terraform, everything is an apply, and a removed file means Terraform removes the resource.

The directory layout also allows a pull request flow for prod, which the tfvars promotion did not, and tearing down dev when nobody uses it saves money.

## So, is it GitOps?

Sheldon holds his own demo against the four OpenGitOps principles: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled. He gives himself the first two. Pulled automatically, not really: the pipeline runs on commit and promotion events. Continuously reconciled, no: nothing compares the live state with the desired state between commits.

Rather than concluding that you therefore need Argo CD or Flux, he turns it into the question he wants the audience to leave with: can you follow GitOps without them? Not everything runs in a Kubernetes cluster, and Argo had a high-profile security vulnerability shortly before the talk. Git as the single source of truth still brings its benefits, whichever tool applies the change.

## Who should watch

Teams already on Terraform deciding how to structure environments, and anyone wondering whether their pipeline-driven setup deserves the GitOps label. Expect a practical demo with Drone, not a tour of reconciliation controllers. It is a Harness developer advocate showing Harness-owned Drone, and he says so.

Title: Multicloud as a move button for your containers
Description: Gilbert Cabillic (ScaleDynamics) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on provisioning across AWS, Azure, GCP and OVH and moving containers on metrics and carbon
Body:
Picking a cloud is easy. Changing your mind six months later is the expensive part. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Gilbert Cabillic, founder and CEO of ScaleDynamics, demoed a container platform built around that problem: provision resources on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud or OVH from one console, deploy with one command, and move a running container to a different machine, region or provider with a button, guided by metrics that include an estimate of its carbon footprint.

It's a product demo from start to finish. What makes it worth a look is the set of criteria he uses for choosing where workloads should run.

## Why would one app need several clouds?

His framing: each application has different requirements, so the best place to run it changes. He cites a figure of 97% of companies needing multicloud and hybrid management, and lists the criteria behind those choices:

- **Performance**: CPU, RAM, GPU, disk type and speed, network.
- **Cost**.
- **Managed services**: a specific database or API only one provider offers.
- **Certification**: some workloads, such as medical data, must run on hosting certified for them.
- **Carbon footprint**, for companies that treat it as a requirement.

Add the shift from monolithic VMs to containers, with reusable components you can patch one at a time, and you get his pitch: containers, managed across clouds.

## How does provisioning work?

The platform has two parts: a web console for organisations, members and rights, projects, environments and API keys for CI/CD, and an SDK and CLI called Warp for Linux, macOS and Windows that developers use to deploy, build and read logs.

A project is whatever unit you choose: a backend, a website, a payment microservice. An environment says where it runs. When creating one you pick what to deploy (static hosting, a managed Node.js server, an HTTP service built from a Dockerfile, or a Node.js module called directly from JavaScript), then the provider, the region (London on AWS, in the demo) and a machine size from the catalogue. Click order and the machine is provisioned and configured to accept containers, with nothing else to set up. Shared resources exist for testing.

The demo deploy follows the getting-started guide, which promises a live Node.js server in under three minutes. He edits the hello message, runs deploy, and the platform builds the Docker image, ships it to the chosen resource, then sets up DNS and the TLS certificate. A testing domain is used when you don't give your own.

## What does the move button actually do?

He then moves the running Node.js container from the shared resource to a new AWS machine. Gilbert Cabillic said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "So the move button is able to move across multicloud, multi cloud regions and is very flexible internally." It handles scaling up when load climbs, scaling down when it falls, and switching providers for cost or performance, say from a small AWS machine to a small Azure one.

On the hard part, he is brief: "The platform manage all the redirection of the traffic for you." The next deployment goes to the new resource automatically.

## When should you move?

The console shows per-container metrics: CPU load, memory, request counts, request execution time, data in and out, downtime and restarts. His rule of thumb: around 80% CPU means upgrade, back at 10% means downgrade, so you pay for the right size at the right time.

The carbon estimate is the unusual part. It's computed in real time from a model per resource type (CPU architecture and type, RAM, disk type and size) combined with the actual CPU load and the data sent and received. He compares it to Google's carbon footprint reporting, viewable by day, week and month. Moving to a different region becomes a carbon decision as much as a latency or cost one.

## Who should watch

Small teams who want multi-provider hosting without running Kubernetes themselves, and anyone thinking about carbon as a placement signal. The abstract's cost comparison and dynamic failover are not demoed in depth; the recording covers provisioning, deployment, the move and the metrics.

Title: An ingress controller that never reloads, and can live outside the cluster
Description: Wei Jin (API7) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on the design of the Apache APISIX Ingress controller - dynamic config, plugins, a decoupled data plane
Body:
Kubernetes already has plenty of ingress controllers, so why build another? At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Wei Jin, Software Engineer at API7, Apache APISIX PMC member, Apache SkyWalking committer and the founder of the Apache APISIX Ingress controller, gave three reasons: configuration changes apply without reloads, one readable resource can describe a complex route, and the controller is split from the proxy, so the gateway can even sit outside your clusters. It's a short, focused talk, best watched by people choosing an ingress for a new platform.

## What is APISIX Ingress?

Apache APISIX is a dynamic, real-time API gateway and a top-level Apache project. Its data plane handles traffic with a large plugin library; its control side exposes an Admin API. The ingress controller is the bridge to Kubernetes. It usually sits at the edge of the cluster as the entry point, forwarding requests to services.

The mechanism is a standard controller loop. It watches the Kubernetes API server for Secrets, Endpoints and Ingress objects, plus its own custom resources such as ApisixRoute, ApisixUpstream and ApisixTls. It converts and diffs them, then pushes the result into the APISIX cluster through the Admin API. You can configure it with plain Ingress resources or with the CRDs.

The feature list he gives: dynamic configuration, service discovery, flexible load-balancing strategies, built-in health checks, traffic splitting, more than 70 official plugins and support for custom ones.

## A short history

He wrote the first line in 2019. The project was donated to the Apache Software Foundation in December 2020 and, after half a year of community polishing, shipped its first GA release in June 2021. At the time of the talk, 1.4 was the latest release and 1.5 was on the way, with a steadily rising contributor curve.

## Why another ingress?

First, everything in APISIX takes effect dynamically, with no reload when the configuration changes. Anyone who has watched a proxy reload drop long-lived connections will see why that's the headline.

Second, readability. His traffic split example is one resource in two parts: a match section with the routing rules and a backends section with the weights between upstreams. The whole canary is one declarative file you can read top to bottom.

Third, plugins as the extension model. Want CORS or URI rewriting on that route? Add a plugin to the same declaration. There's no code embedded in your YAML, just a few named variables per plugin, which keeps the configuration general and readable.

## Can the gateway live outside the cluster?

This is the most interesting design choice. Unlike ingresses that bundle controller and proxy into one deployment, APISIX Ingress keeps them separate. Wei Jin said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "The advantage of this is that you can deploy them together or separately."

Together, it behaves like any other ingress for one cluster. Separately, the APISIX cluster runs outside Kubernetes and fronts traffic for several Kubernetes clusters at once. All routing is managed in one gateway cluster, and you save a forwarding hop. The catch is the one he names: you have to sort out networking between the gateway and the clusters.

## What was next

Two items on the roadmap: support for the Kubernetes Gateway API, and a deployment mode without etcd, aimed at people who'd rather not run another stateful store. "I think users who mind etcd being stateful will be happy to hear about that."

## Who should watch

Platform engineers comparing ingress controllers, and teams with multiple clusters who'd like one gateway in front of all of them. It is a brisk overview, not a tutorial, so pair it with the project docs.

Title: DevOps means self-service, and Crossplane hides the 500 lines of YAML
Description: Viktor Farcic (Upbound) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on internal developer platforms as the point of DevOps, demoed with Crossplane and Argo CD
Body:
Handing a developer an AWS account and a Kubernetes manual is not shifting left, it's shifting blame. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Viktor Farcic, Developer Advocate at Upbound (the company that founded Crossplane), argued that the one thing that matters in DevOps is self-service: an internal developer platform (IDP) that wraps the ops tooling into services application developers can consume without becoming experts. Then he skipped most of his slides and built one live.

## What is DevOps actually for?

Say DevOps and people list tools: containers, Kubernetes, CI/CD, monitoring, infrastructure as code, service mesh. Farcic's point is that those are operations tools. DevOps is about making application developers self-sufficient, and no single person can master that whole list. Viktor Farcic said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "We cannot shift left by saying, now you do it."

The alternative is services. Need a cluster? There's a form with three or four fields. Need an application? Same. Ops, SREs and platform people stop answering Jira tickets for clusters and put that knowledge into the platform instead. The payoff he lists is the usual set of delivery metrics: shorter lead time, higher deployment frequency, lower MTTR and change failure rate.

## Why does the API have to be Kubernetes?

His IDP has a user interface (web, CLI, IDE, whatever people use), an API, desired state in Git, and actual state in the providers: AWS, Azure, Google, on-prem, Splunk, Elastic. The contested part is the API: "that API must be Kubernetes, simply because that's the only API that we have today that is widely accepted."

He's careful about what that means. This Kubernetes cluster is not where your applications run; they might be on Lambda, VMs or RDS. It's a control plane. Custom resource definitions describe what something can be in your company, such as what a cluster means there, custom resources in Git say what something is, and controllers converge the actual state to match. Argo CD or Flux syncs Git into the cluster; Kubernetes syncs the cluster into the world.

At that point he abandons the slides, "because I get nervous speaking for too long without touching my keyboard."

## The demo: a cluster from a short manifest

As a developer, he writes a short manifest for a CompositeCluster, a Crossplane composite resource definition someone in ops already prepared. He picks the AWS composition and asks for medium nodes and a minimum of three. Done by hand, he reckons, that's around 500 lines of YAML or HCL. A second resource, GitOps, asks for Argo CD in that cluster pointed at his repository.

He pushes to Git. Argo CD picks it up, Crossplane does the rest. (He did it in advance, as it takes 20 to 30 minutes.) Behind the short manifest: an EKS cluster, node group, subnets, IAM roles and policy attachments, plus Helm charts so the cluster is production-ready on arrival. Argo CD is already running inside it, empty, waiting.

## What the ops side writes

The operator's half is a composite resource definition with an OpenAPI schema (id, version, node size, minimum nodes) and one or more compositions implementing it for EKS, GKE or AKS. The composition maps user-facing words to provider details, so small, medium and large become specific t3 instance types. The developer never sees it.

## An app with a database, in 30 lines

Next he copies about 30 lines of YAML into the apps directory Argo CD watches: an App claim (a backend with an image, host and port) and an SQL claim for PostgreSQL on AWS that writes its connection string into a secret the app reads. Commit, push. Argo CD shows two manifests; Crossplane expands them into a deployment, service, ingress, VPC, subnets, internet gateway, security groups, route tables, a DB subnet group and an RDS instance. The app is ready first; RDS takes about ten minutes, as RDS does.

The split is the lesson: developers push short YAML to Git, and the complexity lives in compositions owned by the people who understand it.

## Who should watch

Platform teams figuring out what their platform's API should be, and anyone still provisioning clusters from tickets. The abstract mentions Backstage; the demo sticks to Crossplane and Argo CD, with the UI layer left as an exercise. Crossplane is open source and was donated to the CNCF.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Leonardo Murillo on [GitOps across clouds with Crossplane and Flux 2](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Leonardo_Murillo_gitops_multicloud_crossplane_flux2) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2021.
