Title: Apache Pulsar does pub-sub and queues because storage moved out
Description: Mary Grygleski (DataStax) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on event streaming basics and how Apache Pulsar's split of compute and storage fills Kafka's gaps
Body:
Most messaging systems pick a side: streaming or queuing. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Mary Grygleski, Streaming Developer Advocate at DataStax and president of the Chicago Java Users Group, made the case that Apache Pulsar does both, and that the reason is architectural: its brokers keep no state, and Apache BookKeeper does the storage. It's a fundamentals-first talk that builds from what an event is up to where Pulsar beats Kafka, and where it doesn't.

## What counts as an event?

She goes to the dictionary, and not the first definition. Merriam-Webster's fourth sense calls an event a point in spacetime: three coordinates of place and one of time. That's how computing treats events too, occurrences pinned to a moment.

Her argument for event-driven systems is that they are closer to how people work. Synchronous HTTP is a walkie-talkie: one side talks, says over, and waits. Real conversation doesn't block.

From there, the vocabulary. Event stream processing acts on a continuous series of data points. Complex event processing (CEP) spots patterns in those streams as they arrive, for things like security monitoring. Event-driven means a sender publishes and whoever is interested subscribes; message-driven means sender and receiver already know each other's addresses. Batch processing still has its place, she says, for systems of record and big ML training sets.

## Pub-sub versus queues

Streaming, in her framing, is pub-sub: publishers send to a topic on a broker, subscribers opt in. Queuing is asynchronous service-to-service communication where messages wait first in, first out until one consumer processes and deletes them, which is how you buffer spiky workloads.

Kafka is the obvious comparison and she is fair to it. Mary Grygleski said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "Kafka does its job perfectly well, but there are certain limitations."

## How Pulsar is built

Pulsar started at Yahoo, went to the Apache Software Foundation in 2016 and became a top-level project in 2018. The architecture has three parts:

- **Brokers** are stateless. They take messages from producers, dispatch them to consumers and handle topic partitioning, so scaling them is quick.
- **Apache BookKeeper** stores the log: write-ahead journals for fast, durable writes and ledgers for segment-based storage, with tunable ensemble size, write quorum and ack quorum. Her joke is that nobody likes doing the accounting, so Pulsar hands the bookkeeping to BookKeeper.
- **Apache ZooKeeper** keeps the cluster metadata and coordination, keeping order in the zoo.

On top: Pulsar Functions for lightweight in-cluster transformation, tiered storage that offloads ageing data to cold storage, multi-tenancy with tenants and namespaces (finance, marketing, engineering) and soft or hard isolation, built-in geo-replication, pluggable authentication and end-to-end encryption.

The four subscription types are where streaming and queuing meet: exclusive (one consumer), failover (one primary with a standby), shared (consumers split the messages, queue style) and key-shared (messages routed to consumers by key).

## So is it better than Kafka?

Her honest answer: "I wouldn't say it's like all better. Sometimes it depends on what your scenario is, right?" Her list of reasons to consider Pulsar: you need RabbitMQ-style queues and Kafka-style streams together, geo-replication should be easy, multi-tenancy is a must, you want to keep messages for a long time without offloading them to another system, and your own benchmarks show lower latency and higher throughput.

The Kafka pain points she names are about growth. Kafka's partition-centric storage means planning topics, partitions and brokers up front, rebalancing affects connected clients, and geo-replication through MirrorMaker is not ideal, which is why companies like Uber built their own. Pulsar's segment-centric storage in BookKeeper makes adding nodes less disruptive. She also positions Pulsar as a drop-in next to existing Kafka, JMS and RabbitMQ estates rather than a rip-and-replace.

## Who should watch

Engineers who know Kafka and want a clear picture of what Pulsar does differently, or anyone who wants the streaming vocabulary sorted out in one sitting. She runs out of time before the demo, and the close covers DataStax's Astra Streaming and Luna Streaming briefly.

Title: When Apex is too slow, Salesforce Functions bring Node and Java
Description: Alba Rivas (Salesforce) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on Salesforce Functions, elastic Node.js and Java compute built on Kubernetes and Buildpacks
Body:
Finding the five schools closest to a point, out of a JSON file with thousands of them, is the kind of job you don't want running inside a CRM transaction. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Alba Rivas, Principal Developer Advocate at Salesforce, showed how Salesforce Functions moved that kind of compute-heavy work out of Apex into elastic Node.js and Java functions that still run next to your Salesforce data. It's a clean, demo-led walkthrough: anatomy, invocation, deployment.

## What is a Salesforce Function?

She starts with the generic definition: "A function is a short lived executable that is invoked on demand." Serverless, so nobody manages servers, and elastic, so it takes more or fewer resources as demand changes.

For non-Salesforce people she adds the context. Salesforce is a CRM (sales, service, marketing, commerce) and an application platform. You build on it with low-code tools or with code: Lightning Web Components in JavaScript on the front end, and Apex, an object-oriented, Java-like language, on the back end. Functions, available since late 2021, added a second back-end option.

Three things set them apart, in her telling. They run inside the Salesforce trust boundary and work with your records (accounts, leads, whatever you store) through an SDK. Alba Rivas said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "Your data never goes out from Salesforce, which means that it's going to be safe." And you write them in JavaScript or Java instead of Apex.

## What's it built on?

The interesting part for a cloud-native crowd: open source all the way down. Kubernetes runs the containers, Cloud Native Buildpacks turn function source code into container images, and the CloudEvents specification standardises the event payloads.

## Anatomy of a function

The Node.js demo's entry point is index.js. It loads the JSON of schools with latitude and longitude, then exports an async function taking three parameters:

- **event**: the payload the function was invoked with, here a latitude and longitude.
- **context**: the link back to Salesforce, used to query or write records.
- **logger**: logging, which can feed a log drain.

The function computes the nearest schools and returns them. The Java version is near-identical: override an apply method that takes the event and context, with Log4j handling logging.

Why a function and not Apex? Because finding the nearest points is compute-intensive, which is the reason she gives for doing it outside Apex.

## How do you invoke and deploy one?

Functions are invoked from Apex, synchronously or asynchronously; at the time that was the only entry point, with more planned. Synchronous: instantiate the function by project and function name, call invoke with a payload, get the result. Asynchronous: the same call with a callback that runs when it finishes. A Lightning Web Component or a low-code screen calls the Apex.

Deployment uses the Salesforce CLI and VS Code extensions:

1. Create a scratch org, an ephemeral development environment.
2. Create a compute environment, the Salesforce-managed Kubernetes and Buildpacks infrastructure where functions run, linked to the org.
3. Commit to git, since deploys use git-tracked changes, much like Heroku.
4. Run sf deploy functions against the org.

In the demo, a Lightning Web Component takes her current location and returns the ten nearest schools. Functions also run locally for testing, which saves a lot of deploy-and-wait.

## Who should watch

Salesforce developers who have hit Apex limits, and platform engineers curious how a SaaS vendor packaged Kubernetes, Buildpacks and CloudEvents into a FaaS product. A note from the present: Salesforce has since retired Functions, so watch this for the design and the integration pattern rather than as a getting-started guide. The sample code lived in the Functions Recipes repo under trailheadapps on GitHub.

Title: Sharding and encrypting PostgreSQL without touching the application
Description: Trista Pan (SphereEx) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on putting Apache ShardingSphere Proxy in front of PostgreSQL to shard tables and encrypt columns
Body:
Your application sees one table called t_user with readable phone numbers. PostgreSQL sees four physical tables spread over two instances, with the phone column stored as ciphertext. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Trista Pan, CTO and co-founder of SphereEx and an Apache Software Foundation member, showed how Apache ShardingSphere Proxy sits between the two and does the translation, so sharding and column encryption become configuration instead of application code.

It's a practical, architecture-first talk with the setup steps laid out, aimed at teams whose single primary-plus-replicas PostgreSQL cluster is starting to feel small.

## What problem is it solving?

She starts from the standard setup: one primary, one or more replicas for availability and read traffic. Modern apps want more from it: horizontal scale-out as the data grows, faster reads, elastic capacity, and sensitive fields encrypted and decrypted automatically. ShardingSphere's answer is a layer that turns an existing database into a distributed system and adds features around it: sharding, distributed transactions, SQL audit, a database gateway, and shadow databases for load testing.

The features are independent, which is the design idea she stresses most: "you can pick up some features and group these features into a complete new solution." Here, the pick is sharding plus encryption.

On the project itself, she cites over 15,000 GitHub stars, around 318 contributors, more than 14 releases and over five years as open source, mostly written in Java.

## Proxy or JDBC driver?

ShardingSphere comes as two clients:

- **ShardingSphere-Proxy** runs as its own server and speaks the PostgreSQL (or MySQL) protocol. You connect to it with psql or any admin tool as if it were a normal PostgreSQL instance. The proxy plus your PostgreSQL instances together form the distributed database.
- **ShardingSphere-JDBC** is a lightweight driver embedded in a Java application, deployed on the same machine. It implements most of the JDBC interface and works with PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle and SQL Server.

The demo uses the proxy.

## How does encryption work in the proxy?

The encryption case doesn't even need sharding: one application, one proxy, one PostgreSQL. Trista Pan said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, "So you cannot store the plain text into your postgresql, right?" The proxy encrypts the telephone column on write and stores ciphertext; on read it fetches the ciphertext, decrypts it and returns plain text. The application never handles keys or crypto calls.

She also sketches the database gateway: the proxy splits traffic between a primary and its replicas by weights you configure, acting like a load balancer that understands SQL.

## The setup, step by step

The combined demo has two PostgreSQL storage nodes, demo_ds_0 and demo_ds_1, behind one proxy. A logical t_user table maps to physical tables across both, with the phone column encrypted. The recipe:

1. Prepare the PostgreSQL storage nodes.
2. Deploy one or more proxies. You can cluster several for more compute; the demo uses one, set up from the quick start or SphereEx's one-command Python deployment tool, which also brings up the governance centre.
3. Log in to the proxy as you would to PostgreSQL.
4. Register the storage nodes as resources.
5. Create the sharding rule and the encrypt rule with DistSQL.
6. Create the tables.
7. Insert test rows.
8. Compare views.

DistSQL is ShardingSphere's own SQL dialect for managing the distributed layer. It looks like PostgreSQL SQL but creates sharding rules, encryption rules and distributed schemas, and reports cluster state (two storage nodes, one compute node, and their status). The proxy still accepts standard PostgreSQL SQL for everything else.

The payoff: select through the proxy and you see one t_user with readable phone numbers. Log in to a physical PostgreSQL node and there is no t_user at all, only the numbered physical tables, with the phone column as opaque strings. It's the database equivalent of a magician showing you both sides of the trick.

## Who should watch

PostgreSQL users who need scale-out or column-level encryption and don't want to rewrite the data access layer. She runs out of time before narrating the full test script, so have the ShardingSphere docs open alongside.

Title: Serverless lost the perimeter, so your function has to defend itself
Description: Tal Melamed (Contrast Security) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on the serverless security top 10 and a Lambda exploit triggered by an email file name
Body:
A file name in an email turned a call-for-papers system's private S3 bucket public. That's the demo at the centre of Tal Melamed's Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 talk, where the Senior Director of Cloud Native Security Research at Contrast Security walked through the serverless security top 10. His thesis: serverless hands the servers to the cloud provider, but your code still runs, still has bugs, and now has no perimeter to hide behind.

Melamed has worked on serverless security for years, including at the testing startup he co-founded before Contrast acquired it, and it shows. This is a practitioner's list with AWS examples throughout.

## Why serverless security is different

A real serverless app is a tangle of Lambdas wired to API Gateway, S3, DynamoDB, SNS, SES, IoT rules and more, with no single logic flow to guard. Functions are read-only, ephemeral environments with a writable /tmp folder, no SSH, and their permissions sitting in environment variables as keys. Forrester, he notes, put regular serverless use at a quarter of developers.

The structural problem is the entry points. Tal Melamed said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "because actually with serverless we kind of lost the perimeter." You don't control the network in front of the function, so the code has to secure itself.

## The first six, in order

1. **Event injection.** Classic SQL, NoSQL, command and code injection, arriving from new places: S3 files, emails, MQTT, pub/sub, even voice commands through Alexa. The rule hasn't changed: "never trust, pass or make any assumption regarding input." Validate with allow-lists inside the function, and use API Gateway JSON models where you can.
2. **Broken authentication.** Functions are stateless and often reachable through side doors. His diagram shows a locked-down Lambda that an open SES or SNS trigger can still invoke. Use Cognito or another identity service, signed JWTs, and assume zero trust.
3. **Sensitive data exposure.** Data left in /tmp, unencrypted environment variables, public buckets, and the source code itself living in the environment. Delete /tmp files after use, encrypt with KMS, use a secrets store, and let Macie find sensitive data in buckets.
4. **Over-privileged functions.** His favourite. He thinks "more than 90%" is too kind: "I'd say more than 95% or 99% are misconfigured." The blast radius of every other bug is set by the function's IAM role. His example goes from s3 wildcard on action and resource, to one bucket, to a single GetObject on one bucket. Doing that by hand only works for a handful of functions; automate it.
5. **Vulnerable dependencies.** Small functions pull in big dependency trees. Scan before deploying, patch or replace.
6. **Insufficient logging and monitoring.** CloudWatch is there by default, but with millions of invocations you need automation to learn anything from it.

## How does an email become a public bucket?

The demo targets a CFP system: you email a PDF, a Lambda stores it in S3 and replies. Send a known-malicious PDF and a second Lambda flags it with a VirusTotal link. Then Melamed sends a file whose name carries a command injection. The scanning function downloads and runs his payload, which does two things. It emails the sender a fake acceptance with a $300 honorarium link, a ready-made phishing campaign against every other submitter. And it flips the submissions bucket to public, so he can browse and download everyone's papers.

None of it needed the attacker to reach the function directly. The email service did that for him, and the function's broad permissions did the rest.

## The last four

- **Open resources**: queues, SNS topics, buckets and API Gateways simply left open.
- **Denial of service versus denial of wallet**: Lambda had a 1,000 concurrent executions limit per account at the time, so a flood can starve every function, and because you pay per invocation, an unauthenticated endpoint hammered for a week shows up on the bill.
- **Insecure shared space**: warm runtimes are recycled between invocations, so whatever one request left in /tmp, the next may read.
- **Insecure secret management**: hard-coded secrets are common because stateless functions make storage awkward. Use a secrets manager or a vault, or at least encrypted environment variables.

## Who should watch

Anyone shipping Lambdas who has never asked what their functions are allowed to do. For practice, he points to OWASP's Damn Vulnerable Serverless Application, deployable in one click, never into a production account. The close covers Contrast's own testing approach, briefly.

Title: Your service mesh wants a new tablecloth every three months
Description: Tim Szigeti (Cisco) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on why service meshes and microservices break old networking and security habits, with Istio demos
Body:
You don't upgrade a service mesh, you replace it, and at the usual mesh release cadence that means doing it every quarter on every cluster. That's the sharpest point in Tim Szigeti's Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 talk. The Principal Technical Marketing Engineer and Director of Technical Marketing at Cisco walked through why microservices break networking and security habits built over 30 years, then demoed two tools from Cisco's emerging technologies and incubation group: Service Mesh Manager and Secure Application Cloud.

Be clear on the format: the first half is a solid explainer, the second half is a product tour.

## Why does the old playbook stop working?

He starts with the familiar arc: apps tied to hardware, then VMs with their stacks of operating systems to license and patch, then containers that virtualise the OS instead. Split a monolith into containers and you get portability, continuous delivery and rollbacks by changing pointers. You also get a whole new set of internal connections that used to be function calls on one server, and every one needs authentication, encryption, observability and traffic management.

A service mesh such as Istio or Linkerd makes that consistent. It also brings its own problems.

## The tablecloth problem

Network engineers are used to upgrading routers in place. Immutable infrastructure says you can't do that to a mesh. His analogy is a wine-stained tablecloth at a fancy restaurant: nobody yanks it out from under the plates. They set a new table, move everything over, then seat you. A mesh upgrade is the same: stand up a new mesh, deploy new service instances on it, shift workloads gradually, retire the old one.

Then the cadence. Meshes typically have three-month lifecycles with two supported versions, the current and the previous, so, as Tim Szigeti said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, "this forces you to upgrade your mesh every three months." Cluster by cluster. He mentions customers with over 100 clusters.

Two more pain points: observability split across Prometheus and Grafana for metrics, Kiali for topology and Jaeger for traces, each cluster-scoped; and the advanced cases, canary rollouts that start at 20% of traffic and circuit breakers that cut a degrading service before it drags users down.

## What the mesh demo showed

Service Mesh Manager is Cisco's enterprise Istio distribution. Szigeti claims a few firsts for it: active-active multi-primary control planes across clusters, multiple gateways per mesh per cluster, and Istio tuned to carry asynchronous, Kafka-style traffic as well as request-reply, instead of running a separate event mesh.

The demo runs two AWS clusters with 18 services and 11 workloads in one integrated view. He injects 2,000 ms of latency into 100% of a healthy service's transactions and watches the health score slide, then scrolls a timeline back to an earlier incident on the booking service. Finally he splits traffic across three versions of a movie service, 60/30/10, from a form instead of by editing VirtualService weights in YAML.

## Where do you put the firewall now?

The security half opens with microservice dependency graphs from Monzo, Netflix and Amazon, each scarier than the last. "Where is the perimeter of this application that you stick firewalls around it?" Customers' biggest complaint, he says, is plain lack of visibility, across containers, libraries, orchestration and APIs. The answer he argues for is shifting security left into CI/CD and arming developers, not just SecOps.

Secure Application Cloud is built agentless: it uses native Kubernetes API server mechanisms and needs one pod per cluster rather than an agent on every node, with optional Istio integration through an Envoy module that adds DNS-based egress policy. For APIs, it scores third-party endpoints using Cisco Talos, Umbrella and BitSight data so developers can pick the safer one. The demo maps findings to MITRE ATT&CK, applies a fix for defence evasion in one click, flags a privileged, root, public Nginx workload, finds an API still on a deprecated TLS version open to POODLE and BEAST, and builds a geolocation policy that blocks APIs hosted in one country.

## Who should watch

Network engineers moving into Kubernetes, and platform teams weighing whether running Istio themselves is worth the quarterly upgrade cycle. The tablecloth analogy alone is worth stealing for your next architecture review.

Title: Moving Java to the cloud needs a flight plan, with stops
Description: Otavio Santana (Zup Innovation) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on a staged flight plan for Java teams moving to the cloud, from first MVP to GitOps
Body:
Nobody flies from São Paulo to Japan without stops, and Otavio Santana thinks your Java estate shouldn't move to the cloud in one hop either. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, the Distinguished Software Engineer at Zup Innovation, Java Champion and Apache and Eclipse committer, laid out a survival guide for Java architects: a staged flight plan that takes a team from no cloud at all to an optimised, hybrid setup, one level at a time.

It's an architect's talk, not a coding one. Expect trade-offs, a maturity model and a reading list, not a demo.

## Why move at all?

He starts with the history: the Agile Manifesto in 2001, DevOps around 2010 putting operations into the loop, then security moving from reaction to prevention. The cloud fits that arc as delegation. His definition is short. Otavio Santana said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022: "But to me cloud is basically somebody else's problem." The pizza-as-a-service analogy follows: on-premises is baking at home, IaaS hands off the hardware, PaaS (Heroku, Platform.sh) the operations too, and SaaS hands off everything.

What you want from all that delegation, in his framing, is faster innovation without hurting stability. He's candid that it rarely goes to plan: aim for Apollo, end up as Icarus.

## Cloud native means whatever your book says

The funniest section is his tour of definitions. Pivotal, the CNCF and several books all define cloud native differently, some as infrastructure, some as a whole philosophy of software development. His conclusion is that nobody agrees, and that is fine. His own working definition: "So to me cloud native is a set of good practice to optimize an application in the cloud through three steps, containers, orchestration and finally automation."

Every choice along the way is a trade-off between complexity, risk, cost and knowledge. SaaS costs more and carries less risk; IaaS is cheaper and leaves you with more details to handle. He leans on Fundamentals of Software Architecture here: everything is a trade-off.

## The flight plan, level by level

The core of the talk borrows from the Richardson maturity model for REST and applies it to cloud adoption. Each level answers three questions: where are we, where should we go next, how do we get there?

- **None**: no cloud yet. Learn the method first: build a small MVP, prepare it, take it to production, expand, optimise, then make it self-sustaining.
- **Initial**: measure risk and complexity before moving more. He recommends A Philosophy of Software Design, because complexity is where the risk hides.
- **Automation**: move the applications and make CI/CD the normal way of shipping, on whichever provider you use.
- **Observable and modifiable**: infrastructure as code, then GitOps, with Git as the single source of truth for developers and operations. His example: upgrading from Java 11 to Java 17 is a pull request; CI runs, the merge deploys, and if production disagrees, a git revert takes you back. The old works-on-my-machine joke stops working once the machine is code.
- **Optimisation**: hybrid cloud, managed services where your team lacks the depth, and simplicity everywhere else.

## Don't copy Netflix

His microservices advice is the part to tape to the wall. Read the microservices books, he says, and notice that every one of them warns you that a monolith is sometimes the right call: "just because Netflix and Amazon are using it does not mean that you are Netflix and Amazon." Conway's law gets a mention too: the software follows the shape of the organisation. Beyond that, the classics: Effective Java by Joshua Bloch, domain-driven design, Clean Code and Clean Architecture by Robert C. Martin. Read them once, then read them twice.

## Who should watch

Java architects and tech leads planning a migration who want a framework for sequencing it. If you came for the DevSecOps material in the abstract, note that the recording is the Java cloud survival guide its title promises; security appears as one stop on the history tour rather than the topic.

Title: RBAC as a Go sidecar with OPA, not a library in every service
Description: Federico Maggi (Mia-Platform) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on distributed RBAC built as a Go sidecar with embedded Open Policy Agent and Rego policies
Body:
Adding role-based access control to a platform made of many microservices in many languages forces two awkward questions: where does the code live, and what happens when it goes down? At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Federico Maggi, Senior Technical Leader at Mia-Platform, walks through how his team answered both: a Go sidecar next to each service that owns a resource, embedding Open Policy Agent and evaluating Rego policies on every request.

It is a design story, with the rejected options left in, which is the most useful part.

## Why did they need RBAC?

Mia-Platform users configure microservices, define data models, deploy, monitor and scale services on Kubernetes. Letting everyone do everything is not safe, so the team defined personas: owners who can do anything, developers limited to certain configuration and environments, and guests with read-only access to a subset. Each API got a permission, permissions were grouped into roles.

Then they noticed APIs behave in two ways. Some must be blocked outright for the wrong users. Others are open to many users but must show each one different data. That gave three requirements:

1. Allow or deny a request.
2. Filter data before it is fetched from the database, so services only ever handle authorised data.
3. Rewrite the response body for field-level visibility.

## Where does the code go?

Their first idea was to embed RBAC in each service. That means duplicated code, or libraries in every language the platform uses, a barrier to adopting any new language until its library exists, and a risky change to many existing codebases.

The second idea was one central RBAC service, scaled horizontally. Two problems: every service would need code to call it, and it is a single point of failure. "No matter the scaling, if it goes down, everything is down," Federico Maggi said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022.

So they chose the sidecar pattern. The RBAC container runs in the pod of every service that owns a resource, intercepts all incoming requests, checks them and either proxies them to the application container or rejects them on the spot. The project configuration service, for example, is the one that blocks a user without permission from changing a project's configuration. They wrote it in Go, for a low resource profile with high request throughput.

## Why OPA instead of a custom rules engine?

Writing the sidecar from scratch would have meant a big configuration format mapping every API to actions and filtered properties. Instead they adopted OPA, whose Rego lets them write policies as code, test them and ship them. The Go SDK is the key: beyond just running policies, they can isolate the engine, precompile policies for faster evaluation, prepare data stores and build dynamic input per request.

For each request the sidecar gathers the headers, the full URL and its parameters and the request body, fetches the user's role bindings from a database, and evaluates the configured policy. The three examples map to the three requirements:

- **Allow**: take the project ID from the path, iterate over the user's bindings, and allow only if one matches that project and carries the project view permission.
- **Query generation**: using OPA's unknowns, the policy returns conditions rather than a yes or no, and the sidecar turns them into a query passed to the service so data is filtered at the source.
- **Response rewriting**: in the response flow, the policy gets the original body and drops a field, the sales forecast in his example, from each document with a list comprehension.

## What did they get?

Policies as code with tests that guard the authorization model against regressions, all policies in one place with shared Rego functions, and per-service scaling: the busiest services get more resources for their sidecar, quieter ones stay lean. The extra hop added very low latency in their measurements, though the talk gives no figure. He also wrote a longer post on the Mia-Platform blog.

## Who should watch

Platform and backend engineers designing authorization for polyglot microservices on Kubernetes. Familiarity with RBAC helps; you'll come away with a pattern and the reasons behind it.

Title: Scan the RDS snapshot, not the database, to find what will leak
Description: Mor Manor (Imperva) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on scanning RDS snapshots in an isolated VPC to tie misconfigurations to the sensitive data at risk
Body:
Most cloud security reviews check the walls and forget to check what's inside. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Mor Manor, Head of Innovation & Operations at Imperva, showed Imperva Snapshot, a tool that restores a copy of an AWS RDS or Aurora snapshot into a throwaway VPC, scans it, and tells you which misconfigured databases hold the data you'd least like to read about in the news. The takeaway: a misconfiguration only tells you half the risk. You also need to know what sits behind it.

It's a product talk, and he says so. The parts worth your time are the scanning design and the findings from real users.

## Why look at the data, not just the config?

He opens with two numbers: over 31 billion records compromised in 2020, most of them in cloud breaches, and Gartner's prediction that through 2025, 99% of cloud breaches would trace back to customer mistakes. Then two stories. A marketing firm leaked over 340 million personal records in June 2019 from a database that was simply publicly accessible. A financial firm exposed 7 million usernames and passwords in July 2020 through an unencrypted database and a public S3 bucket.

His point is that neither team lacked a firewall. They lacked visibility. So the tool reports on three things side by side: misconfigurations and bad practices, known vulnerabilities (CVEs, patch state), and the data itself, meaning classification, PII and PCI counts, and compliance level.

## How do you scan a database without its password?

This is the clever bit, and the part Imperva filed a patent for. The tool never asks for database credentials. It takes an existing snapshot, restores it into an isolated VPC, and resets the master password on the restored copy. Production is never touched.

The whole flow runs from public CloudFormation templates. A root template collects parameters, a setup template checks the prerequisites (the database is RDS or Aurora, a snapshot exists, a VPC is available, everything sits in one region), and an installer template creates three Lambdas:

- **Sandbox**: builds the networking, restores the snapshot into the isolated VPC, and deletes every resource it created at the end.
- **Scanner**: resets the master password on the restored copy, then runs the assessment and data classification queries.
- **Reporter**: collects the results and emails a PDF.

The isolation is strict: new security groups and route tables, no internet gateway, and IAM roles scoped only to the resources created for the scan. It also doesn't need admin permissions to run.

## What did the scans actually find?

The three anonymised examples rhyme, which is the point. A marketing organisation had excessive permissions, an unencrypted database, a publicly available snapshot and over 200 known vulnerabilities, sitting on over 1.2 million email addresses, over 500,000 personal identifiers and over 100,000 phone numbers. Mor Manor said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, "the database itself is not even encrypted. Easy win for the bad guys."

A financial firm had the same pattern plus disabled notifications for security group changes, with 500 passwords, 100 credit cards and almost 2,000 mobile numbers found. A cloud services company had close to 100 known vulnerabilities and 20,000 email addresses. Lining up posture against content is what lets you decide which database to fix first.

## The three settings to check today

His closing advice needs no tool at all. Watch for excessive permissions. Don't leave snapshots public: if you share one between environments, "make sure that if you make a snapshot publicly available for a certain amount of time, change it into a private mode right away." Encrypt the database and its snapshots. And turn on notifications for security group changes on your databases.

A public snapshot is the database backup equivalent of leaving the house key under the doormat, and then posting a photo of the doormat.

## Who should watch

AWS operators and security engineers who run RDS fleets, and anyone who has ever made a snapshot public for a quick test. The abstract also promises a research piece on a vendor misconfiguration and the disclosure process; the recording sticks to the tool and the user findings. It's AWS-only (RDS and Aurora).

Title: One Rego policy gate for every security scanner in your pipeline
Description: David Melamed (Jit) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on Open Policy Agent as a single decision point for SAST, secrets, SCA and DAST results in CI
Body:
Four security scanners in CI means four config formats and four ideas of what failing means. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, David Melamed, co-founder and CTO of Jit, shows how to collect all of their output and let Open Policy Agent decide, from policies written once in Rego and kept in a central repository, whether a pull request passes.

"But what if there was a way to write simple policies using a single language for all your security tools?" David Melamed said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. The rest of the talk is that idea, built and run.

## What is OPA, in two examples?

Open Policy Agent is a cloud native, open source policy engine meant to unify policy enforcement across the stack: API gateways, message brokers, the Kubernetes API server, CI/CD. You write policy in Rego, a declarative language, and services offload the decision to OPA through an API. Main uses: authorization, SSH access, admission control and data filtering.

His first example is classic authorization. A salaries service receives a request from user1, asks OPA, and OPA combines the input, a role mapping (user1 is an employee, user2 an admin) and a policy saying only admins see salaries. Answer: deny.

The second moves the same idea to security results. Bandit, a Python SAST tool, writes JSON with totals per severity. A Rego rule says deny if high severity is above zero. The sample report has four highs, so the test fails.

## What does the pipeline do?

The demo app is a tiny Python serverless function that returns the current time, defaulting to Berlin unless you pass a time zone, run locally on LocalStack through docker-compose. The GitHub Actions workflow triggered by a pull request has four scanner jobs and one policy job:

- **SAST with Bandit**, an open source Python tool with 35 built-in rules, output saved as a JSON artifact.
- **Secrets with Gitleaks**, which knows many well-known secret patterns (GitHub personal access tokens, Slack tokens, AWS keys) and also searches Git history, for the secret you committed and then forgot.
- **Dependency checks with OWASP Dependency-Check**, with its own vulnerability database cached between runs.
- **DAST with OWASP ZAP**, which needs the app deployed to LocalStack inside CI first, then attacks the resulting URL; it handles web apps and APIs via OpenAPI or Swagger definitions.
- **Policy evaluation**: pull the policies from the central repo, download the artifacts, and run conftest, which uses OPA under the hood, against each report.

The policies are deliberately simple. The SAST package has two rules: no medium and no high findings. The secrets package fails on any secret in the serverless YAML file, and on any finding whose rule is the AWS access token. That second one is the useful pattern: if a scanner is noisy, a policy can fail only on the findings you care about.

He first runs the whole workflow locally with act, the local runner for GitHub Actions: two tests, one pass and one fail, because Bandit found a medium severity issue. The same thing happens on GitHub in the PR.

## Why centralise the decision?

One language, one decision point, and policies that differ by context without reconfiguring every tool; some repos are more critical than others. Rego packages can grow more complex rules, and OPA can even make HTTP calls to other services if a decision needs more data. Jit builds this into its platform as part of its security plans, which he mentions at the end.

## Who should watch

Teams already running several scanners who are tired of tuning each tool's pass and fail settings, and anyone curious what OPA looks like outside Kubernetes admission control.

Title: Start network automation with Ansible by automating your show commands
Description: Jason Belk (Cisco) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on Ansible for network engineers, from inventory and Jinja2 templates to pre and post change checks
Body:
You don't have to hand your next change window to a robot to get value from automation. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Jason Belk, Senior Technical Advocate in Cisco's learning and certifications organisation, makes the case that network engineers should start with Ansible by scripting what they already do (pushing a few config lines, running verification commands) and then demos it against a Cisco IOS XE sandbox router.

## Why Ansible, for network people?

Ansible is a free, open source command line tool for runbook-style automation, owned by Red Hat and used for more than ten years across compute, cloud and storage. It keeps no state database: each run loads your inventory and variables, connects to the devices and does the work. Your compute and storage colleagues are probably using it already, which can mean existing licences and in-house help.

His real argument is about adoption. Playbooks are easy to read and share, so you can borrow other people's. You can begin with the exact lines from your change request, let it run your verification commands on 30 devices at once and save the output, and still make the change by hand. "So that way you can start having automation trickle into your existing workflows," Jason Belk said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. Templating comes later, once you trust it.

## The building blocks

- **Inventory**: INI or YAML, listing devices and groups (for example an IOS XE group) with connection details. He uses plain-text credentials for the demo and points out you would not in production.
- **Playbooks**: ordered tasks run against hosts or groups. Each task checks whether the configuration is present and only pushes it if not.
- **Modules**: the workhorses inside tasks, over 750 of them, from IOS configuration to Webex Teams, Slack and ServiceNow.
- **ansible.cfg**: defaults such as the inventory location, custom module paths or turning off host key checking in a lab.
- **Templates and variables**: copy a running config, swap the values that change (interface name, IP, subnet, description) for Jinja2 variables kept in YAML per device, group or region, and loop over lists. This is where he says productivity takes off.
- **Facts**: unless you switch them off, Ansible parses the running config and operational data into standard variables at runtime, such as OS version or serial number, for reports and decisions.

## What do the three demos do?

All run from VS Code against a Cisco DevNet sandbox IOS XE router.

1. **Configure interfaces**: the cli_config module renders a Jinja2 template with loopbacks 100 to 104, their descriptions and IPv4 addresses, and pushes them. He previews the render in TD4A, the Template Designer for Automation, a tool built by someone at Red Hat. Run it a second time and Ansible reports changed=false: the config is already there, nothing sent.
2. **Build a report**: the ios_facts module gathers facts, prints the hostname and OS version, creates an outputs directory and fills a template with model, version, serial number and every interface.
3. **Pre and post checks**: before the change it runs show ip interface brief, show interfaces and show ip route and saves the output into a timestamped per-device directory. It makes the change, runs the same commands again, then a Linux diff shows exactly that loopbacks 100 to 104 appeared and came up. He resets the shared sandbox first with what he calls a good citizen playbook that removes the loopbacks again, which is a polite habit worth copying.

The abstract sums up the low-risk entry point well: start "even if it is just grabbing “show” commands to put into a file and view the differences between the state before and after your change."

## Who should watch

Network engineers who keep meaning to start with automation and don't know which tool to learn first. It is a 101 with working examples; if you already template your configs with Ansible, skip it. The code is on GitHub.

Title: Five open source security scanners, picked after testing hundreds
Description: Aviram Shmueli (Jit) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on the five open source security tools Jit chose for SCA, secrets, IaC, DAST and containers
Body:
For every security problem there are dozens of open source tools, and most comparison posts never ran them. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Aviram Shmueli, co-founder and CPO of Jit, shares the shortlist his team arrived at after researching and trying hundreds of tools on real projects while building Jit's continuous security platform: one pick for each of five categories, and a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs all five in parallel.

## How did they judge the tools?

The criteria are worth stealing for your own bake-off: a high true positive rate with few false positives, usability and output that makes sense, easy CI integration, a large community and regular maintenance, a reputable company behind the tool (it tends to create a standard), GitHub stars as a popularity signal, and free licensing with a preference for permissive ones such as MIT and Apache.

He calls the approach minimum viable security: a few simple controls baked into config files, apps and CI/CD.

## The five picks

| Category | Contestants | Pick |
|---|---|---|
| Dependency check (SCA) | Retire.js, OWASP Dependency-Check, npm audit | OWASP Dependency-Check |
| Secret detection | git-secrets (AWS Labs), detect-secrets (Yelp), Gitleaks | Gitleaks |
| Infrastructure as code | Checkov (Bridgecrew), KICS (Checkmarx), tfsec (Aqua Security) | KICS |
| Runtime (DAST) | OWASP ZAP, Nikto, Arachni | ZAP |
| Container scanning | Trivy (Aqua), Clair (Quay) | Trivy |

The reasons, briefly:

- **OWASP Dependency-Check** for efficacy and ease of use. On a project using adm-zip, the Node.js zip library, it flags three critical CVEs.
- **Gitleaks** for its detection rate, CI friendliness, almost 100 contributors and reports in several formats. It finds secrets through many regular expressions plus entropy; his sample AWS key matches the AWS access token rule.
- **KICS**, in a category where he says all three tools are great, for an exceptional detection rate and for severity ratings, which help DevOps people who are not security experts prioritise. A Terraform module with unencrypted EBS data comes back as medium, with a description and fix guidance.
- **ZAP**, around for over a decade, for authenticated and unauthenticated scanning, API scanning, fuzzing and a large community. It catches a missing Content-Security-Policy header.
- **Trivy** for efficacy and easy CI integration; it finds a vulnerable library in an image based on Debian 11.3.

## What does the pipeline look like?

A GitHub Actions workflow triggered on push, with five jobs running in parallel: Gitleaks, ZAP, KICS, Dependency-Check and Trivy. One whitespace commit later, the secret scanner reports a password in the Dockerfile on line eight (without printing the secret), KICS reports an unencrypted DynamoDB table as medium, and the Dependency-Check report lands as an artifact. The demo repo is public.

"And it's very possible to build an entire security program only by using open source solutions," Aviram Shmueli said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. Jit's pitch, in the last minute, is the layer on top: managing the security plan, automating it and putting findings into the pull request instead of making developers dig through each tool's CI output.

## Who should watch

Small teams setting up their first security checks in CI and wanting a defensible default per category. It is a short talk; the table above is most of the value, the demo is the proof it runs.

Title: Breakpoints in a Kubernetes sidecar setup, from your laptop
Description: Michael Schilonka (Unikube) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on Gefyra, debugging a FastAPI app behind an OAuth2-Proxy sidecar in Kubernetes from local VS Code
Body:
The bug only happens in Kubernetes, because only Kubernetes has the sidecar that sets the header your code chokes on. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Michael Schilonka, Managing Director at Unikube, shows how Gefyra lets you run the container on your laptop as if it lived in the cluster's namespace, intercept the real traffic, and hit a breakpoint in VS Code.

## What is Gefyra for?

His team built it to let developers work against Kubernetes from day one instead of a docker-compose approximation of production. They had used Telepresence 2 for a while and were not satisfied with its features and approach, so they wrote their own.

The goal is to keep the tools developers already use: their IDE, hot reloading, the source tree mounted into the dev container, overridden environment variables, an interactive shell, easy logs, and a debugger attached to the container under development. Gefyra creates a dedicated Docker network on your local host and, through a sidecar that carries a VPN connection to the cluster, makes the local container behave as if it ran inside a Kubernetes namespace.

## What is the demo setup?

A local k3d cluster, brought up with Getdeck, another of their open source tools, which pulls five sources together (Helm charts, plain YAML and the demo app) plus the Kubernetes dashboard. Inside:

- **Keycloak** as the identity provider, with a realm, an OAuth2 client and a test user.
- **OAuth2-Proxy** as a sidecar in the same pod as the app, so every request is authorised before it reaches the backend, and the backend never has to implement the login flow.
- **A FastAPI backend** on port 8155, the container Gefyra will take over.

The sidecar pattern scales the pair together: every replica gets a proxy and an app. Logging in through the OpenID Connect flow works, then requesting an item returns an HTTP 500.

## Where was the bug?

In a classic anti-pattern: an if/else that behaves differently when an access token is present. Locally there is no token, so the dev path never touches it. In the cluster the sidecar forwards the token and the code reads it, and blows up.

The Gefyra flow is four commands. Up installs the operator and local infrastructure. Run starts a container from the same image in the right namespace, here with the working tree mounted, debugpy waiting on port 5678 and Uvicorn started with reload. Bridge intercepts the app container in the deployment's pods and tunnels its traffic to the local instance. Down tears it all down when you are done.

With VS Code attached through a remote attach launch config, a breakpoint on the items route catches the next real request. Inspecting the decoded JSON web token shows the key is email with a lowercase e; the code asked for an uppercase one. One character fixed, Uvicorn reloads, and the page still returns 500, because he forgot to save the file. A very honest demo. Saved, it works.

## Why it matters

"So there's no need anymore for a docker compose or vagrant setup or any custom scripts that create a developing infrastructure which is not really matching your production systems," Michael Schilonka said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. The pattern is language-agnostic; Python is just the example.

## Who should watch

Developers whose services sit behind sidecars, auth proxies or meshes and who debug with print statements and redeploys. It is a hands-on demo, and the repo is public if you want to follow along.

Title: Ghost assets are gone from AWS but alive in your Terraform
Description: Naor Paz (Firefly) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on ghost assets, the top five types in 100+ AWS accounts, and how to detect, fix and prevent them
Body:
Drift gets all the attention, but the scarier case is the resource that no longer exists at all. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Naor Paz, Director of Product at Firefly, defines ghost assets (cloud resources created by Terraform, deleted by hand or by API, and still sitting in the code and state file) and ranks the five types that turn up most often across more than 100 AWS production accounts.

## How is a ghost different from drift?

Drift is about changes to existing assets. The familiar story: you created everything with code, then patched something in the console. "When we want to make just a small patch here and there, we tell ourselves that we'll add it to the code later, but we usually never do," Naor Paz said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. Next terraform plan, you face a list of manual changes and a choice between reverting and codifying.

A ghost is about existence. The asset was removed outside of code, so it is gone from the cloud but present in the code and the state. That leaves two ways to get hurt:

- You meant to delete it, and the next terraform apply quietly brings it back, with its cost and its attack surface.
- You did not mean to delete it, and something you need (a backup, a Lambda function, a database replica) is missing when you need it.

## Which ghosts show up most?

From Firefly's customer data, the top five:

1. **EC2 instances**. Deleted by accident, they take down whatever they ran, from a web server to a database, and a quiet internal service can stay missing for days or weeks. Revived by accident, that forgotten test box costs three to four digits a month and may sit on the internet running old, unmaintained code. A fun detail: EC2 was the second AWS service, launched in August 2006, right after S3.
2. **IAM policies**. Deleting one revokes its permissions from everything attached, which breaks production processes and customer access. Worse for security: explicit deny statements always beat allows, so a deleted policy can remove a guardrail and leave excessive permissions behind.
3. **SQS queues**. Producers can't send, consumers can't read, jobs already in the queue stop.
4. **CloudWatch metric alarms**. Lose the alarm and the first sign of trouble is the SLA breach.
5. **Security groups**. Losing one can cut needed access, and because an asset can have several, it can go unnoticed. AWS won't let you delete a group that is still attached, which keeps this one lower on the list.

## How do you bust them?

He groups the answers into detect, alert, fix and prevent, and covers four options:

- **Firefly**, his company's platform, with a free tier. The inventory filters to ghost assets, Slack alerts fire when a codified asset disappears, and each ghost links to the stack, state file and Git line that created it. To revive it, run terraform apply with a target on that one resource; to bury it, a button opens a pull request that removes the resource block.
- **Lock the cloud**: no non-read console access, only IaC makes changes. It is the ultimate prevention and also expensive, especially when PagerDuty wakes you at 2am and you would rather click than write Terraform.
- **ClickOps**, an open source tool that reads CloudTrail logs to detect console actions, deploys across accounts with AWS Control Tower, alerts through a Slack webhook and ships as a Terraform module with its own Lambda.
- **driftctl**, open source, works from state files, but you schedule it yourself and build your own alerts. He adds a warning: state files can hold sensitive data, so handle them carefully.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams with Terraform estates that predate strict IaC discipline, which is most of them. It is short and concrete, with a clear product section in the middle. His sign-off is the Firefly blessing: may your infrastructure never drift.

Title: A 20-second bug fixed with routing rules, not a redeploy
Description: Jason Dudash (Red Hat) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on Istio service mesh, from the fallacies of distributed computing to canaries, circuit breakers and mTLS
Body:
A user profile service that takes 20 seconds to answer is a bad day. Fixing it by shifting traffic back to the old version, with no code change and no redeploy, is the point of Jason Dudash's talk at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. The Chief Architect at Red Hat explains why service meshes exist and then demos an Istio-based mesh on OpenShift: finding the slow version, rolling it back, canarying the fix, tripping a circuit breaker and turning on mutual TLS.

He warns up front that it is a fire hose. It is, in a good way.

## Why do microservices need a mesh at all?

His starting point is the fallacies of distributed computing, identified more than 25 years ago: the network is not reliable, latency is not zero, bandwidth is finite, security gets overlooked. Microservices make those problems bigger, because one application becomes many small services with chains of network calls between them. Everything looks fine in dev and QA, then production load arrives. "And scaling up isn't like the solution that fixes a lot of the problems you have," Jason Dudash said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022.

The historical fix was libraries baked into every service, Netflix's Eureka and Zuul being the famous ones. That works until you also write services in Go and Node.js and have to replicate the same plumbing in every language. The mesh moves it into the platform.

His analogy: a small town gets by without traffic lights, a city does not. Police, speed limits, bike lanes and stoplights are the control plane; traffic cameras are the observability.

## Data plane and control plane

Under the hood, each application pod gets an Envoy sidecar, a fast proxy that accepts new configuration through an API without reloading. That is the data plane. Policy lives in the control plane, which pushes it to all proxies, so you never configure hundreds of proxies by hand. Once services are in the mesh, policy changes need no new code, no rebuild and no redeploy.

## What does the demo show?

The app is a small boards application with single sign-on, a UI, a board service backed by MongoDB, and a user profile service running in two versions. Load comes from a couple of shell loops.

- **Find the problem**: Kiali draws the service graph with traffic and success rates. Grafana shows user profile v2 taking 20 seconds against three to five milliseconds for v1. The distributed tracing view confirms it at the end of the call chain.
- **Roll back by routing**: a destination rule and virtual service flip all traffic to v1, and the profile page loads again. Kiali even flags a deliberately broken destination rule.
- **Canary the fix**: v3 is deployed and gets 10% of traffic while v1 keeps 90%, then 50/50, then all of it.
- **Circuit breaking**: an outlier section in the destination rule ejects failing instances. He deletes the v3 pod mid-load; v3 starts throwing errors and the traffic lands back on v1.
- **mTLS**: before, any container in the cluster can curl the services. A PeerAuthentication policy plus destination rules for mutual TLS, and the same curl fails because it is not a known mesh identity. The OpenShift console can do the same with checkboxes. He also points at request authentication for validating JSON web tokens and authorization policies for access control.

## Who should watch

Developers and architects who have heard the term service mesh and want to see what it does in 30 minutes, and teams on OpenShift weighing whether to turn Service Mesh on. It is an introduction with a solid demo, not an operations guide for running Istio at scale.

Title: A service mesh moves five jobs out of your code, but not telemetry
Description: Rosemary Wang (HashiCorp) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on what a service mesh replaces in application code, shown with Consul and Envoy
Body:
Most service mesh material is written for the operator who installs it. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Rosemary Wang, Developer Advocate at HashiCorp, flips that: she maps each thing developers already do in code (service discovery, load balancing, security, traffic management and telemetry) to what the mesh does instead, with a live Consul and Envoy setup running Java and .NET versions of the same service.

The takeaway: the mesh can take over most of that work, but tracing still needs your application's help.

## How did she end up with a mesh?

A security engineer told her "we must have a service mesh". What they actually wanted was mTLS between every service, and the application team's objection was fair: refactoring every app to load and validate certificates would take forever. Digging in, she found that encryption was one of five ways services depend on each other, and each was handled by a different tool or library.

The mesh answer is a proxy (Envoy in her demo) next to every application instance, through which all traffic flows, plus a control plane that pushes configuration to those proxies. On Kubernetes an annotation injects the proxy; on a virtual machine running an older app, Consul can run it as a process sidecar.

## What does each job look like on both sides?

- **Service discovery**: Spring has Eureka and an annotation; not everything is Spring, or even Java. In the mesh, proxies register the service, and Envoy's admin endpoint shows the service-to-IP mappings Consul pushed out.
- **Load balancing**: Spring gives you Feign clients. In Consul, a service splitter sends 50% to v1 and 50% to v2, which turns into Envoy weights of 5000 and 5000. Her curl loop alternates between the Java and the .NET backends behind one name.
- **Security**: in .NET, certificate validation is custom code. In the mesh, mTLS happens between proxies, with one caveat she spells out: traffic between a proxy and its own application instance is not encrypted. API authorization moves too: a Consul intention lets the report service call the expense service only on the trip endpoint with a GET, and Envoy enforces it as a filter.
- **Traffic management**: watch the vocabulary. An Envoy circuit breaker sets maximum pending and concurrent connections; outlier detection is what ejects an instance after, say, more than three HTTP 500s. Together they make the circuit breaker pattern. In Consul that is a passive health check.

## Why telemetry is the exception

"Just because you have a service mesh doesn't mean that you get telemetry out of the box," Rosemary Wang said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022. Traces have to be propagated by the application, so you still instrument it: OpenTelemetry libraries in .NET, the OpenTelemetry agent for Java.

Two practical lessons from her setup. First, the instrumentation's trace format must match the tracer configured in Envoy. Older Envoy versions mostly spoke Zipkin, so she standardised on Zipkin spans as the lowest common denominator and sent them to Jaeger. Second, merge your application's Prometheus metrics into the proxy's metrics endpoint (Consul has an annotation for it), so Prometheus scrapes one place and the app itself stays off the network. With every hop instrumented, from the Kong gateway through the proxies to the database call, the full trace finally shows up.

## Who should watch

Developers who have been handed a mesh and told to use it, and platform engineers who need to explain to app teams what to delete and what to keep. She is explicit that this is not a verdict on whether you need a mesh: most apps end up with some logic in code and some in the mesh.

Title: Before you containerise it, ask why five times
Description: Rajalakshmi Srinivasan (Site24x7, Zoho Corp.) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on Kubernetes adoption, its real costs and what a container monitoring tool must cover
Body:
Moving a monolith to containers is easy on a whiteboard and expensive in production if you skip the question of why. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Rajalakshmi Srinivasan, Director of Product Management at Site24x7 (Zoho Corp.), walks from client-server to serverless, puts numbers on Kubernetes adoption, and lists what a monitoring tool has to do before you trust your cluster to it.

It is an overview talk with 22 years of industry experience behind it, and it ends with her own product, so expect a vendor close.

## How fast is Kubernetes actually spreading?

She compares VMware's State of Kubernetes reports for 2020 and 2021. Organisations running Kubernetes in production grew from 59% to 65%. On-premises deployments were at 64% in 2020 and are slowly shrinking as workloads move to the cloud, but they have not gone away: Kubernetes is also how teams who can't leave their own data centre get a foot on the path.

Lack of experience and expertise is still the top deployment challenge, cited by 65%. The benefits from the same survey: 58% saw better resource utilisation, 48% easier upgrades and maintenance, 46% a shorter development lifecycle, 41% managed to containerise a monolith, 39% said it enabled the move to the cloud and 28% cut their public cloud bill. She adds a separate estimate that close to 30% of cloud resources are simply wasted.

## Where does it go wrong?

Her list of challenges comes from Site24x7's customers and from moving their own setup to containers: missing expertise, deployment complexity that the architecture diagram hides, monitoring that gets bolted on after the first production outage, security across pod, node, cluster and service, regional compliance, a feeling of lost control over a black box, and scaling cost.

The last one is the most useful warning. Not every workload belongs in an auto-scaled container. Some apps are cheaper on a fixed server or on-premises, and adopting the newest stack because it is new is how teams end up with a bigger bill and the same app. "Don't do things just because somebody else is doing," Rajalakshmi Srinivasan said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022.

## What should container monitoring cover?

She maps it onto the three pillars of observability:

- **Metrics**: availability (the industry expects four nines for nodes, pods and clusters) and performance, because a component that is up but slow is still a problem.
- **Traces**: when a page takes 10 seconds, you need the container and the line of code, even when each microservice is written in a different language.
- **Logs**: collected centrally and turned from unstructured text into something you can query, because nobody can remote into every short-lived container.

On top of that, she wants the tool to act, not only watch. Her examples: restart a pod automatically once it fails to respond three or five times in a row, and run a cleanup script when node CPU goes above 90%.

## The ICE checklist

Her shorthand for choosing a tool is ICE. Integration: import and export with your in-house metrics and third-party alerting, no data silos. Customisation: change what the dashboards show. Extension: APIs to build your own views, and they have to work, not just exist.

## The product part

The close is about Site24x7, which she describes as an AI-powered full stack monitoring tool hosted in Zoho's own data centres: ten of them in five regions (US, Europe, China, India and Australia), with data kept inside the region you pick. She frames the whole decision with the golden circle from Start With Why and finishes with the Red Queen's line about running twice as fast to get anywhere, which she credits to Alice in Wonderland. Pedants will note it is from Through the Looking-Glass; the point about keeping up still stands.

## Who should watch

Ops leads and engineers early in a Kubernetes migration who want adoption numbers and a checklist for monitoring. If you already run Prometheus, tracing and central logging, the first half will be familiar.

Title: Cloud breaches are not misconfigured servers, they are bad design
Description: Josh Stella (Snyk) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022 on cloud control plane compromise attacks and five fundamentals, built on policy as code, to prevent them
Body:
When a breach headline says misconfiguration, the misconfigured server is usually just the doormat. At Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, Josh Stella, Chief Architect at Snyk (and co-founder of Fugue before it joined Snyk), argues that the real damage comes from cloud control plane compromise: attackers using stolen API keys against the cloud provider's own APIs, and getting away with it because of identity and permission design.

## Why doesn't data centre security carry over?

He starts with what changed. Data centre gear was bought, racked and cabled by humans, lived three to five years, got names, and was defended mostly at the network with firewalls and intrusion detection. Cloud resources are an API call away, live for hours, minutes or seconds, never get named, and there are far more of them: Snyk manages millions of resources for its customers. They are also more varied, with a dozen managed databases at one provider alone, each reached through a control plane that has nothing to do with the TCP/IP network your old tools were watching.

Programmable infrastructure cuts both ways. Mistakes happen at the speed of electrons, but you can also test and check things with decades of software engineering practice.

## How do attackers work now?

The older pattern was targeted: pick a victim, hunt for a hole, exfiltrate slowly. His example is North Korea's hack of Sony Pictures. The common pattern now is automated: scan everything public for a known weakness, build a list, pick from the list, then smash and grab. The Capital One attacker was not after that bank in particular; she was collecting anything vulnerable.

His breakdown of the headlines:

- **Twitch**, 125 GB of data and source code, reported as server misconfiguration. He calls that nonsense: no single server should be able to download all your source code. That is an access control design mistake.
- **Capital One**, blamed on a misconfigured WAF. The WAF was the foothold; the target was S3. According to a Department of Justice filing, a running virtual machine had IAM keys with S3 list permissions.
- **Uber**, where API keys stored in GitHub repos did the work.

"You're going to have misconfigured servers. You don't have to shoot yourself in the foot with bad architecture," Josh Stella said at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022.

The path is always the same: initial penetration (an open port during a maintenance window, an application vulnerability like Log4Shell, long-lived keys in source control), then discovery and lateral movement, then data out through API calls that perimeter tools never see.

## What are the five fundamentals?

Snyk's answer, drawn from its most successful customers, puts policy as code at the centre, surrounded by four verbs:

1. **Know your environment**: every resource, its current state, and how it changed over time. S3 list permissions are fine for a human at the console and dangerous on an internet-facing VM; only the combination makes it a risk.
2. **Prevent error**: check Terraform and CloudFormation with policy as code before deploy, inside the CI/CD pipeline.
3. **Empower developers**: one customer has over 2,000 application developers and a cloud security and platform team of about three people. The only way that scales is guidance delivered by the tooling, in the editor and the pipeline, not in emails.
4. **Measure what matters**: risk differs by data set; a small table can have a huge blast radius. Track fixes quantifiably.

Why code and not spreadsheets of rules? "If you're not doing policy as code, the hackers are faster than you because they're doing exploitation as code," he said. Any human in the loop makes you slower than the attacker.

## Who should watch

Cloud security and platform teams who keep getting asked to fix misconfigurations one ticket at a time, and developers who own their Terraform. It is a methodology talk, no demo; the product mentions are light.

Title: Nine Go gotchas that compile fine and still bite
Description: Ranjan Mohan (Menlo Security) at Conf42 Golang 2022 on Go gotchas from variable shadowing and shared slices to defer, loop closures and recover
Body:
Go is famously simple, which is exactly why its sharp edges catch people off guard. At Conf42 Golang 2022, Ranjan Mohan, Senior Software Engineer at Menlo Security, ran through a set of Go gotchas, each one a short program that looks innocent, runs, and prints the wrong answer, followed by the fix.

It is a compact, demo-driven talk aimed at beginners and at anyone who arrived in Go from Python or Java with their old reflexes intact.

## Why did my input change?

The opener squares a list of numbers inside a function and prints the original afterwards: it has been squared too. Mohan frames it as pass-by-reference. The precise version is that Go copies the slice header, but the header points at the same backing array, so a function that writes into its input mutates the caller's data. Same root cause in his slicing demo: `names[:2]` has length 2 but capacity 4 and the same address as the original, so writing to the slice writes to the original.

## Why does an all-negative check say true?

A function sets `result := true`, loops, finds a negative number, and inside the `if` writes `result := false`. The colon makes it a new variable in the inner scope, shadowing the outer one, so the function returns true. The fix is plain `=`. "So be careful when redeclaring variables using the shorthand notation," Ranjan Mohan said at Conf42 Golang 2022. Of all the bugs in the talk, this is the one most likely to be in your code right now.

## Strings, operators and overflow

Three quick ones. `len` on a string counts bytes, not characters, so a single visible symbol can report 3; use `utf8.RuneCountInString` when you mean characters. The caret is Go's bitwise NOT when used with one operand and XOR with two, which surprises anyone expecting `!`, `~` or exponentiation.

The third is better. A loop sums numbers, and a `switch` case sets the sum to the maximum unsigned integer and calls `break` when it sees that value. The output is 9, not the max. In Go, `break` inside a `switch` exits the switch, not the loop, so the loop keeps adding and the sum wraps around past zero. The fix is a labelled loop and `break` with the label.

## When does defer read its arguments?

Immediately. He defers a goodbye function with a joined list of names, changes the names afterwards, and the deferred call still prints the original: arguments to a deferred call are evaluated at the `defer` statement, not when it runs. Multiple defers run last-in, first-out, like a stack.

## Goroutines in a loop

The classic: start goroutines inside a `for ... range` loop that print the index and name, and they all print the last element, because the closures share the loop variables. His fix is to copy them into fresh variables inside the loop body; the output then shows every value, in a scrambled order, because goroutines run concurrently. Worth knowing when you watch it today: Go 1.22 changed loop variables to be per-iteration, so on modern toolchains this bug is gone, but you will still meet the copy idiom in older code.

## Recover only works in a deferred call

Finally, calling `recover` next to or after a `panic` does nothing; the panic propagates up the stack and the program dies. Put `recover` inside a deferred function and it catches the panic and hands you its value.

## Who should watch

Go beginners, reviewers who want a checklist of things to look for, and people preparing for Go interviews. It is under 20 minutes, mostly live code, and he planned to publish the samples on GitHub.

Title: Put a Go slice under a microscope and it starts sharing memory
Description: Jesús Espino (Mattermost) at Conf42 Golang 2022 on how slices, maps and channels really behave in memory, read straight from the runtime with unsafe
Body:
You use slices, maps and channels every day; Jesús Espino wanted to see what they look like from the inside. At Conf42 Golang 2022, the Staff Engineer at Mattermost used `unsafe` to read the Go runtime's own structures out of memory and print them after every operation, showing exactly when a slice reallocates, how a map grows without stalling, and where a blocked goroutine actually waits.

The method is the fun part: a scalpel function casts a pointer to the value into a copy of the runtime's internal struct, a microscope function prints it, and the subject gets poked between prints. Everything is reproducible from his GitHub repo.

## Why does append change the address?

A slice is three words: a pointer to an array, a length and a capacity. An empty `[]int` has length and capacity zero. Append one value and the runtime allocates room for one. Append four more and the array address changes, because the old allocation was full: the runtime reserves a bigger chunk and copies everything over. After five appends the slice has length 5 and capacity 8, so the backing array holds 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 followed by three zeros. Growth is never one slot at a time, because "you don't want to resize the slice with every single insertion," Jesús Espino said at Conf42 Golang 2022.

## When is a subslice a window, and when is it a stranger?

This is the section that justifies the talk. Take `s[1:4]` and its array pointer is exactly 8 bytes after the original's (one int64 in), with length 3 and capacity 7. Write to the subslice's index 0 and the original's index 1 changes. Append 6 to the subslice and it overwrites the original's fifth element, because the subslice's end is not the original's end.

Then append enough to the original to force a resize, and the two silently stop sharing memory: changes to one no longer show in the other. A subslice is a window onto its parent only until either side reallocates. Espino's advice is not to rely on this behaviour for anything, which is the right advice and also the reason to know it exists.

## How does a map grow without freezing?

The map header holds the element count, B (log2 of the bucket count), an approximate overflow-bucket count, a random hash seed, pointers to the current and old bucket arrays, and an evacuation counter. The random seed, generated per map, is one reason map iteration order is unpredictable.

Each bucket holds eight keys and eight values in parallel arrays, plus a few top bits of each key's hash and an overflow pointer. Insert nine entries and B goes from 0 to 1. When one bucket fills before the whole map justifies growing, the runtime chains an overflow bucket instead. Real growth doubles the bucket array, moves the old one to old buckets, and evacuates entries gradually on later operations, so a big resize becomes a period of slight slowdown rather than one long pause. Worth knowing when you read his slides today: this is the bucket design of the runtime at the time, and Go 1.24 later replaced it with Swiss tables.

## Where does a blocked goroutine go?

For channels he dissects a buffered `chan int32` with capacity 4 (an unbuffered channel behaves the same with a zero-sized buffer). The header has the queue count, buffer size, element size (4 bytes), a closed flag, send and receive indexes into a ring buffer, and two wait queues of parked goroutines.

Fill the buffer with four values and the fifth sender parks itself on the send queue. A receiver takes the oldest value, sees a sender waiting, wakes it, and its value drops into the freed slot, so the count stays at 4 while both indexes move one step. Drain the channel completely and the reader parks on the receive queue instead. Close it and every parked receiver wakes up with the zero value.

## Who should watch

Go developers who want a mental model of the runtime that holds up under debugging. His own conclusion is refreshingly modest: you may never need this at work, but the trade-offs the Go team made show up in behaviour that will one day surprise you. His other tip: reading the Go runtime source is less scary than it sounds, and it is how he built the talk; in his words, "reading the go runtime code is not complicated."
