Title: Peernet makes UDP act like TCP, in pure Go
Description: Akilan Selvacoumar (Peernet) at Conf42 Golang 2022 on a pure-Go p2p file-sharing protocol with NAT hole punching, decentralized search and UDT
Body:
Peernet is a peer-to-peer file-sharing protocol written entirely in Go, and its most interesting trick is moving the transport layer's job into the application. At Conf42 Golang 2022, Akilan Selvacoumar, a core developer at Peernet, toured the protocol's design: per-peer blockchains for metadata, NAT traversal, keyword search without a central index, a content-addressed file store, and a pure-Go implementation of UDT for reliable transfers over UDP.

It is a project tour from the people building it, ending with a live demo of the command-line client and a call for contributors.

## Why pure Go?

Portability. One static binary runs on Windows, Linux, an Android phone or RISC-V, with zero configuration. The core library ships inside the command-line binary, and anything else, including Peernet's own (proprietary, Windows-only at the time) browser app, talks to it over a local REST API. Go developers can also import the packages directly.

## A blockchain that is allowed to shrink

Each peer keeps its own blockchain holding file metadata and profile information, and shares it with other peers, so search can look up who has what. "I like to think of blockchain as a fancy link list," Akilan Selvacoumar said at Conf42 Golang 2022.

The unusual part is that it is mutable. Delete a file and its entry goes away; the chain gets a new version number, which propagates to the network within about a minute. The whole network ends up as a forest of small per-peer chains rather than one global ledger.

## The packet is designed to look like nothing

The design goals read like a security checklist: handshake on the first packet, no eavesdropping or spoofing, no forged messages from a peer pretending to be another, detect tampering and bit flips, keep packets small. Each packet carries a random number against replay attacks, a protocol version, a command, a sequence number, the payload size, and random padding so a router cannot fingerprint Peernet by packet size.

Most commands are encrypted with Salsa20. File transfers, at the time of the talk, were not: encrypting every one of thousands of small packets cost too much CPU, and he lists that as an open problem the team was still working on.

## Finding peers behind NAT

Discovery starts centralized and stops there. A new node bootstraps from root peers (Peernet ran some, but a private network can use a box in your house), then nodes swap peer lists. On a LAN it uses IPv4 broadcast and IPv6 multicast.

To get through NAT it tries UPnP first, asking the router to open and map a port, which only works if the router supports it and someone left it on. Otherwise it falls back to UDP hole punching via a rendezvous node, the same technique WebRTC relies on. Being UDP-native is what makes this easy.

## Search without Google

Decentralized search is deliberately simple. On upload, the file name is split on spaces, dashes and underscores into words, and each word becomes an index pointing at the file's hash. A search query is lowercased and stripped the same way, matched against the index table, and the hashes are resolved to metadata via the blockchains. Files themselves live in the warehouse: content-addressed by hash, deduplicated, and seekable, so a peer can serve just part of a file.

## UDT: congestion control you can edit

The backbone of file transfer is UDT, which makes UDP reliable with acknowledgements, negative acknowledgements and congestion control, all in user space. "We want UDP to act like TCP," Akilan Selvacoumar said at Conf42 Golang 2022. Living in the application layer means the team can tune packet and window sizes per connection, for example sending bigger packets to nearby peers, without touching the kernel, and the same code runs on every platform. He believes Peernet was the only project running UDT fully in pure Go.

The demo shows `go build` on the command-line repo, the status command listing nodes by public IP, and a probe file transfer command that measures speed and verifies the transfer by hash.

## Who should watch

Networking-curious Go developers, anyone who has fought NAT, and people looking for an open-source p2p codebase to contribute to. His suggested extensions include a decentralized game engine loading maps from the nearest peer and better, ranked search.

Title: Call it payment_avocado and keep coding, on the choice paradox
Description: Fabricio Buzeto (bxblue) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on beating developer choice paralysis by storing, delaying and modelling decisions
Body:
Pick PayPal and you now have to pick a queue; pick Kafka and you now have to pick a language. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, [Fabricio Buzeto](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Fabricio_Buzeto_learning_to_overcome_the_choice_paradox), CTO at bxblue, argues that every engineering decision spawns more of them, and that the cure for freezing up is less about willpower and more about giving your brain somewhere safe to park what it's worried about.

It is a human-side talk with code examples, built on Barry Schwartz's The Paradox of Choice and David Rock's Your Brain at Work. No chaos experiments here, unless you count your own head.

## Why do more options make it worse?

He walks through Schwartz's main points. We tie freedom of choice to well-being, yet more choice doesn't seem to make us better off. Buyer's remorse drives a lot of it: we stall because we want to avoid regretting the pick. His example is painting a house grey when there are endless greys; an architect's short palette makes the decision possible.

Too many options lead to analysis paralysis, where fear of a mistake outweighs the value of deciding on time. Freedom feels like the opposite of commitment, so committing feels like a loss. Rules aren't a lack of choice: early Twitter's 140-character limit, in his telling, fed creativity rather than killing it. And then there's fear of missing out on the option you didn't consider.

## What is your brain doing meanwhile?

He is upfront that he isn't a neuroscientist, then gives a working model with two parts. The prefrontal cortex does reasoning: energy hungry, synchronous and low on working memory, so it copes by chunking big ideas into small ones (Brasília is in Brazil, which is in South America). The hippocampus stores memories and connects them asynchronously, which is why the forgotten milk surfaces in the middle of your flow state and breaks it.

His prescription is to make both feel safe. Store information outside your head somewhere you trust. Review and re-evaluate those notes, and write them so you understand them later. And delay decisions, which only calms the brain if the delayed decision is written down and reviewed.

## What does that look like in code?

Three examples, all on a loan-evaluation method. First, naming: he can't think of a good name for a payment amount, so he picks a silly one on purpose.

Fabricio Buzeto said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022: "So I'll just make a mark here, I'll just call payment avocado."

It will never survive code review, not even his own, so it works as a reminder. He finishes the feature and comes back to rename it installment_monthly_value, which says both the period and the loan context. He pairs this with the Pomodoro technique: 25 minutes on, 5 off, a 15-minute break after four, with review and replanning built in.

Second, a refactor: when new behaviour has to land in code you don't trust, isolate the old code behind an old_evaluate method, add the new path, and only then decide what the structure should be. In his case it ended up as evaluator objects mapped to scores.

Third, slicing a task: two new steps (request documents, process information) between cart and payment. Top down, bottom up or vertical slice depends on context, for example shipping document collection first so the anti-fraud team can process documents by hand while the automation is built. No clear answer, which is the point.

## How do you actually choose?

Chunk the problem, ask people who have been there, then weigh options with a method: pros and cons, AHP, conjoint or cost-benefit analysis. He considers most methods variants of the analytic hierarchy process and shows a payment-gateway matrix scored on team familiarity, coverage and pricing, with totals of 8, 7, 7 and 5. The best part, he says, is writing the criteria, because that is where you model the problem. The ranking is a starting point for negotiation; a contact at Stripe might change the pricing score.

His closing advice is to look for help, try different methods, and stop overthinking.

Fabricio Buzeto said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022: "If you're overthinking, you are not choosing."

A choice can be an experiment, and you can come back and make a different one.

## Who should watch

Developers and tech leads who lose afternoons to small decisions, and managers who want a vocabulary for decision fatigue on their team. It is light on research depth and heavy on habits you can try the next morning.

Title: Go testing from first test to Ginkgo, minus the copy-paste
Description: Francisco Daines (Walmart) at Conf42 Golang 2022 on Go unit testing basics, table-driven tests, testify mocks, test packages and BDD with Ginkgo
Body:
If your Go test file is the same function copy-pasted forty times with different numbers, this talk is your intervention. At Conf42 Golang 2022, Francisco Daines, Principal Software Engineer at Walmart and maintainer of the Arch-Go architecture testing tool, walked through testing in Go from the first `go test` to behaviour-driven development with Ginkgo and Gomega, with live demos at every step.

It is a 101 and says so in the title. It is also a well-ordered one, and the section on where to put your test files is worth it even for people who have been writing Go for years.

## Why bother: the death spiral

Daines opens with Kent Beck's "no time for testing" death spiral from *Test-Driven Development: By Example*: more stress means less testing, less testing means more errors, more errors mean more stress. Automated tests break the loop because the computer can rerun the same battery in seconds after every change.

He also gives the two arguments that work on non-engineers: fewer production errors save money, and shipping more often with higher quality keeps customers. On strategy, he shows Mike Cohn's testing pyramid next to Kent C. Dodds' testing trophy and declines to crown a winner. "There is no rule of thumb to select the right testing approach," Francisco Daines said at Conf42 Golang 2022.

## The standard library goes a long way

Everything starts with the built-in `go test` tool and the `testing` package, nothing to install. The first demo is an `AddNumbers` function: a file ending in `_test.go`, a function starting with `Test`, and a check that fails. He then swaps the bare fail call for `t.Errorf` so the failure tells you expected 55, got 56, on which line.

Next comes the fix for copy-paste tests: table-driven tests. Define a slice of structs with inputs and expected results (1, 2, 3 gives 6; 1 and 100 give 101; an empty input gives 0), loop over it, and run each row as a subtest with `t.Run`. Adding case number 101 becomes one line. He names each subtest after its input, so a failure points straight at the offending row.

He also covers testable examples: functions named `Example...` that print to standard output, are checked against an `Output` comment, and show up on the package's Go documentation page with a runnable playground. Tests and documentation in one function.

## Assertions and test doubles, via testify

For assertions he prefers testify. The demo highlights the difference between `assert.Equal` on two slices, which cares about order, and `ElementsMatch`, which does not, plus `Contains` and friendlier failure output.

The test doubles section lists the five variants (dummy, fake, stub, spy, mock) and then makes the design point that actually matters: you can only stub a dependency cleanly if your business code depends on an interface, not on a concrete SQL driver. With that in place, a stub is just a struct in the test file that satisfies the interface. Mocks go one step further with testify's `mock` package: bind specific inputs to specific return values, limit how many times a call may happen, and fail the test when the code calls the mock with arguments nobody configured.

## Where should test files live?

Go convention puts tests in the same directory and the same package as the code, and the compiler leaves `_test.go` files out of builds. Daines recommends the other allowed option: same directory, but a separate package with the `_test` suffix. That way the tests can only reach exported functions, so you test the package's public interface, and you drop back to the internal package only when a private function genuinely needs exhaustive tests.

## BDD with Ginkgo and Gomega

The closer is behaviour-driven development, aimed at the gap between acceptance criteria written in human language and tests written in code. His example is a user story about a dean checking scholarship eligibility (medicine students with a GPA over 80 qualify), turned into `Describe`, `Context` and `It` blocks with Gomega expectations, so each test reads like its acceptance criterion.

## Who should watch

Go newcomers, and teams where testing is still the thing that happens when there is time. Experienced gophers can skip to the test-package and mocking sections.

Title: What chaos experiments actually find, and what to do with it
Description: Vishnu Vardhan Chikoti (Fanatics) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on the weaknesses chaos experiments keep exposing and how to fix and share them
Body:
Most chaos engineering talks stop at the moment the fault is injected. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, [Vishnu Vardhan Chikoti](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Vishnu_Vardhan_Chikoti_utilising_results_from_chaos_experiments), Senior SRE Manager at Fanatics, covers the bit after: the weaknesses that four or five years of experiments kept turning up, how to get the fixes prioritised, and why the results need to travel beyond the team that ran them.

He brings 17 years across investment banking, product development and SRE (Goldman Sachs, Bank of America and DBS among them), and co-wrote Hands-On Site Reliability Engineering. The talk is a practitioner's checklist rather than a tool demo.

## Why the tool is the easy part

Engineers reach for a tool first. His advice is to think about scope before you pick one. A tool that works for one team may not cover the whole organisation, because runtimes vary (VMs, on-prem, cloud, Kubernetes), architectures vary in how they handle HA and replication, and each service implements the standard patterns to a different level of maturity. A result from one blast radius doesn't automatically carry over to another set of applications.

Then come the policies: what the infrastructure team allows, which experiments security permits, and how runs fit change and incident processes. A tool's capability means little if policy forbids using it.

He runs through the options, from Chaos Monkey and the Simian Army to Chaos Monkey for Spring Boot (add it to the pom and faults start appearing), Alibaba's ChaosBlade with JVM-level faults, Pumba for Docker, Chaos Mesh, Litmus and chaoskube for Kubernetes, T-Mobile's Monarch for Cloud Foundry, VMware's Mangle and the Chaos Toolkit. Under the hood, he notes, most of them lean on the same operating system features.

## What do experiments actually expose?

The core of the talk is a list of findings, which doubles as a list of hypotheses worth testing:

- **Reconnect failures**: the database blips and the app never reconnects, or hangs.
- **Timeouts**: inject network delay and see whether the UI shows a proper message or a bare error page.
- **Crashes** in a service, UI or mobile app under the injected condition.
- **Primary election and split brain**: take the primary down and check a replica gets promoted; cut the network between them and see whether a replica wrongly promotes itself. His fix is three nodes, so a replica can check with its peer that the primary is still alive.
- **Autoscaling and HA**: under CPU pressure or lost instances, does capacity come back?
- **Exception handling**: a buy that succeeded on the server but failed on the way back leaves the user guessing what happened.

Then the second-order checks. Was the error logged in your observability data? Did a monitor fire? Did the alert go through the right channel: message, email or page? Did the errors count against the error budget? Did auto recovery trigger and bring the instance back? He has seen teams with observability set up and no monitors on top.

## One fault at a time

Vishnu Vardhan Chikoti said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022: "if you inject too many failures parallel at the same time, you don't know what went wrong and what would have actually caused it."

A good rule for anyone tempted to make the first game day a grand finale.

## How do the fixes get done?

A weakness found by an experiment lands in the technical backlog, where it competes with features. His answer is to size it by imagining the same failure across the whole estate instead of the small blast radius you tested. Modest issues fit in the 20% of a sprint set aside for tech work; bigger ones justify more than that.

Finally, share. Write up which experiments ran, what the system did and what you changed, because the same architecture patterns are usually copied across the enterprise, and the bug you found in one service is probably waiting in several others.

## Who should watch

Teams that have run a few experiments and wonder what to do with the results, and SRE leads building a chaos practice across many teams. If you have never injected a fault, start with the basics first and come back.

Title: Why a startup might pay its data collectors in tokens
Description: Ignas Galvelis (Sky) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on using blockchain incentives, ordering and on-chain governance to crowdsource data
Body:
Google gets its data handed to it in a convenient format; a startup has to go and fetch it. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, [Ignas Galvelis](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Ignas_Galvelis_application_for_blockchain_in_crowdsourcing_data), Software Developer at Sky, argues that a crowd, paid in tokens and coordinated on a blockchain, can collect and analyse data that a small team never could, and gives a quick tour of which chains suit the job.

Expect an introduction. It is a conceptual walk through blockchain properties and trade-offs, with no code or architecture, and it sits at the edge of a chaos engineering lineup: the resilience here is about a data supply that survives a messy world.

## Why is data sourcing hard for small teams?

He opens with a world that won't hold still: companies rise and fold, governments and policies change, and new data sources keep appearing, each with its own format, language and legal regime. He cites 2.5 quintillion bytes generated every day. Some data also resists quantification, which hurts when, say, building an inflation figure means knowing a product's category, units and currency.

Ignas Galvelis said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022: "If you are the scale of Google, everyone will try to serve you."

A startup gets no such help. Organisations guard their data silos, add scraping protection and reshuffle their UIs to break scrapers. His point is that none of that works against a crowd, because a human can always read what the site shows a customer and write it down in a usable form.

## What does a crowd add?

Four things, in his framing. Collection scales with the number of contributors, as long as the incentive works. Humans get around quantification resistance. Analysis can be crowdsourced too, so a small company doesn't need to hire every specialist up front; experts do a small piece of work and share in the result. And a crowd can report offline events as they happen, before they show up online.

## Where does the blockchain come in?

He goes through what blockchains are good at and maps three of those onto crowdsourcing:

- **Incentives**: reward contributions with a token, ideally one that appreciates, and let people trade it for money.
- **Ordering**: transactions in a block are ordered, so it is easy to prove who submitted a piece of data or work first and reward the pioneer.
- **On-chain governance**: votes are provable, which is how DAOs run. The catch he flags is that blockchain voting is public; private voting needs something like zero-knowledge proofs.

He is just as clear on the weak spots. Large, queryable data doesn't fit on a chain, since every node keeps a copy, so most projects lean on centralised storage or something like Filecoin. Changes are expensive because history is kept. And Vitalik Buterin's trilemma applies: of decentralised, scalable and secure, pick two.

## How decentralised is decentralised?

He reaches for the Nakamoto coefficient, which counts how many entities across mining, clients, developers, exchanges, nodes and ownership would need to collude to control a chain. His figures put Avalanche at 26, Solana at 19 and Polygon at 2, with Bitcoin highest, even though a handful of large mining pools could in principle attempt a 51% attack. His argument for why they don't is economic: the attack would crash the price of what they mine.

## Which chain, then?

A short buyer's guide follows. Ethereum has the best documentation and community, sets Solidity as the standard, and is expensive to transact on. Binance Smart Chain is a cheaper Ethereum fork that is more centralised. Solana is fast and has been knocked over by denial-of-service attacks. Cardano, his favourite, writes peer-reviewed papers before code and uses mathematical proofs, at the cost of congestion when its first popular exchange launched. Chainlink provides the oracles that let smart contracts query the outside world.

His worked example is Crowdflation, an open-source project building a decentralised autonomous organisation that crowdsources prices into an alternative inflation index, paying participants in a token. For learning, he points to Emurgo's courses and Buildspace.

## Who should watch

Engineers curious about where crowdsourcing and blockchain actually fit together, and anyone who wants a compact overview of chain trade-offs as they stood in early 2022. If you want implementation detail or failure-injection content, look elsewhere on the lineup.

Title: Distributed sagas bolted onto Istio, without redeploying the app
Description: Alparslan Avci (Zapata Computing) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on running distributed sagas from an Envoy Lua filter in Istio, backed by Hazelcast
Body:
Split a shop into microservices and the first failed checkout teaches you about the dual write problem. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, [Alparslan Avci](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Alparslan_Avci_distributed_transactions_in_service_mesh), Software Developer at Zapata Computing, shows a way to get saga-style compensation into an existing Istio deployment by putting the logic in the sidecar: an Envoy filter that tracks each transaction and calls the compensation endpoints when a service returns a 500.

It is a short, demo-heavy talk: one theory section on two-phase commit versus sagas, then a live Kubernetes cluster with Kiali open.

## What does the dual write problem look like live?

The demo is a toy e-commerce site: a front end service that calls a user service, a product service and a banking service, each with its own database. The banking service is rigged to fail. The product starts with 10 in stock and the user with 10,000 pounds of credit. He buys three, pays part from credits and the rest from the bank, and gets an internal server error.

Back on the main page, the stock reads seven and the credit reads 7,000. Nothing was bought, yet two services committed their half of the purchase. That is the whole problem in one screen, and a neat target for a chaos experiment too: kill one hop and see what your data looks like afterwards.

## Two-phase commit or sagas?

He walks through both. Two-phase commit runs a prepare phase and a commit phase through a coordinator, which buys strong consistency and read-write isolation. The price: it blocks, it needs XA-compatible data sources, and the coordinator becomes a scaling limit and a single point of failure.

Sagas give each service its own local transaction. When one step fails, the services that already succeeded run compensation actions, which are new code that semantically undoes the work rather than a database rollback. His analogy is booking a trip: meeting, flight, hotel, transport. If the hotel fails, it cancels itself, then calls the flight's cancellation, which cancels the meeting. Sagas come as orchestration (one component drives the flow) or choreography (services react to events). You get asynchronous, scalable, heterogeneous-friendly transactions, and you pay with eventual consistency, stale reads and compensations that can fail themselves.

## Where does the saga logic live?

This is the interesting bit. In Istio every pod gets an Envoy sidecar, and all east-west traffic goes through those proxies. Envoy supports filter chains, so he writes an EnvoyFilter custom resource, an HTTP filter in Lua that runs before every operation on the pods.

The filter has two functions. On each request it reads the transaction ID from a header and records the call with a small companion service, which keeps transaction state in a three-replica Hazelcast cluster. On each response it checks the HTTP status. On a failure it looks up the transaction in Hazelcast and calls the compensation action on every endpoint that took part.

Then he reruns the purchase on the same running application.

Alparslan Avci said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022: "we haven't redeployed our application. We have just applied filter."

This time he buys four, the banking service fails again, and stock stays at seven and credit at 7,000. Kiali's graph shows the banking service failing, then the user and product services getting their compensation calls.

## What the demo leaves to you

The filter coordinates; it does not write your compensations. Each service still needs an undo endpoint that knows what undo means for its data, and the eventual-consistency window is still there. Keying everything off a status code also means a 500 from a timeout behind an already-committed write deserves some thought before production. As a pattern, though, moving saga plumbing into the mesh is a clever way to retrofit it onto services you'd rather not touch.

## Who should watch

Engineers running Istio who keep hitting partial writes across services, and anyone who wants a quick, concrete refresher on two-phase commit versus sagas. If you want production-grade saga frameworks, this is a proof of concept, not a library tour.

Title: Data is the bottleneck now, and SpongeBob explains why
Description: Joe Karlsson (SingleStore) at Conf42 Golang 2022 on reliability, scalability and maintainability when data, not CPU, is the constraint
Body:
Cloud made CPU cheap; data stayed stubborn. At Conf42 Golang 2022, Joe Karlsson, Senior Developer Advocate at SingleStore, gave a gentle introduction to data-intensive applications, built on the three pillars from Martin Kleppmann's *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*: reliability, scalability and maintainability. And yes, every pillar gets a SpongeBob SquarePants analogy.

Honest scope first: the abstract promised a build with Redpanda, SingleStore Pipelines, stored procedures and a Grafana dashboard. The recording is a conceptual talk instead, with no demo and no Go code, and a fair amount of SingleStore pitch along the way. Treat it as a primer on how to think, not a tutorial.

## What makes an application data-intensive?

Karlsson's working definition has five triggers: lots of data, data streaming in fast, low-latency queries that matter, complex queries across many sources, or heavy parallelism and concurrency. The one-line version:

"data intensive applications is where data is the main constraint or bottleneck," Joe Karlsson said at Conf42 Golang 2022.

His argument is that with Kubernetes and the cloud you can throw nodes at compute, but you cannot throw nodes at a data model that was wrong from day one. He opens with the volume problem: roughly 80 zettabytes of data created in 2022, heading for about 175 zettabytes by 2025.

## Reliability: humans are the flakiest component

Hardware fails, software fails more, and people fail most. He points to Netflix's Chaos Monkey as the case for designing systems that survive losing machines, including the database tier, and walks through SingleStore's approach of replicating data across leaf nodes so a dead node triggers re-election instead of downtime.

The bigger point is about people. "humans tend to be the least reliable component of any system," Joe Karlsson said at Conf42 Golang 2022. His remedies are unglamorous and correct: admin interfaces that make the wrong thing hard, automated tests, and full sandbox environments for trying things safely.

He also makes a sidebar that deserves its own talk: databases tend to get left out of the DevOps conversation, and leaving the most important part of the system to manual processes is how human error gets into your data.

## Scalability: the Twitter timeline problem

The best section is the classic Twitter example from Kleppmann's book. Version one: store tweets, join against a follows table at read time. With a few thousand tweets posted per second against roughly 300,000 timeline reads per second (his figures, which he admits are a few years old), the joins could not keep up.

Version two: fan-out on write. Each new tweet gets copied into every follower's timeline cache, like a letter photocopied into thousands of mailboxes. Reads become cheap; writes explode. A user with 30 million followers turns one tweet into 30 million writes.

Twitter's answer was both: fan-out for most accounts, read-time merge for the handful of celebrities. Karlsson's takeaway is that real systems end up hybrid, after you measure where the load actually lands. He also sketches the scale-up vs scale-out choice and argues for horizontal, node-based scaling.

## Maintainability: the bill comes after launch

Most software cost is maintenance, not the first build, so he splits maintainability into operability (routine tasks are easy), simplicity (fewer moving parts) and evolvability (you will need to change it, and data is sticky). His practical advice: plan for the load you expect in five years, assume real-time analytics will become a requirement even if it isn't one today, and resist the urge to overcomplicate things to look smart.

## Who should watch

Developers who have built a few CRUD apps and are about to meet their first real data volume. If you have already read Kleppmann's book, this is a quick, friendly refresher with cartoon breaks; the Go content is limited to the advice that Go is a good language to build a learning project in. His closing homework: build something real, like a stock ticker or a streaming Twitter analysis, on a free developer tier.

Title: ML models have no steady state, so chaos testing has to change
Description: Soumen Chatterjee and Nathalie Rauschmayr (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on adversarial inputs and catching them in deep layers with SageMaker
Body:
A speed limit sign that reads 80 to you and stop to the model is a chaos experiment you didn't schedule. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, Soumen Chatterjee, a partner solutions architect at AWS, and Nathalie Rauschmayr, Senior Applied Scientist at AWS, ask what chaos engineering means for machine learning, then show a working way to spot adversarial inputs in production: compare a deep layer's activations at inference with those from training, using Amazon SageMaker Debugger and Model Monitor.

The first half reframes chaos engineering for ML; the second half, Nathalie Rauschmayr's, is the technical meat.

## Why doesn't classic chaos engineering fit ML?

Soumen Chatterjee starts from Werner Vogels' line that everything fails all the time, then explains why ML fails differently. Traditional software is deterministic and tested with unit, regression and integration tests. ML systems are stochastic and probabilistic, shaped at every stage by the data that flows through them, and the model is only one part of the system next to data preparation, training, tuning, deployment and monitoring.

That breaks two steps of the usual chaos loop. Soumen Chatterjee said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 that "there is no as such steady state, because models are not steady": a model at 98% accuracy today may not stay there. And verification isn't a pass or fail; you inspect metrics and plots summarising performance, closer to error analysis than to a test report.

He sorts ML use cases into four categories (when you can't code it, can't scale it, need to personalise, or can't track it) and shows how each is exposed: manipulated images in manufacturing quality checks, spam that slips past a filter, misread signs in automated driving. The attacks come in three predominant kinds: evasion, poisoning and model extraction.

## How small can an attack be?

Nathalie Rauschmayr's examples make the threat concrete. A starfish image from the Caltech 101 data set is classified correctly; after a projected gradient descent (PGD) attack the image looks the same to a human, and the prediction is wrong. The epsilon parameter sets how much noise is added, and she explains that "The higher the amount of noise, the more likely the attack is going to be successful." Only when epsilon is raised further do visible artifacts appear. The German traffic sign data set gives the scary version: the 80 km/h sign classified as a stop sign after a near-invisible change.

## Where do adversarial samples give themselves away?

Not in the input. A t-SNE embedding of clean and attacked test images shows the two distributions overlapping completely, so anything that inspects the raw images won't separate them.

Inside the network it's different. Repeating the analysis on activations from a ResNet-18, layers 0 and 4 show no difference, layers 8 and 12 begin to cluster apart, layer 14 more so, and layer 15, the penultimate layer before classification, separates them clearly. It makes sense: an attack has to change the representation that reaches the classifier, while early layers only learn basic features. The detector is a two-sample test with maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a kernel-based measure of similarity between distributions, comparing deep-layer activations captured during validation with those captured at inference.

## The SageMaker pipeline

The production version uses two SageMaker features. Debugger, with its open-source, framework-agnostic smdebug API, records tensors: a hook configuration takes a regular expression of the layers to capture and an S3 output path, both during training and on the deployed endpoint. Model Monitor normally compares captured requests with a baseline computed from training data, flagging, say, a column that was always 0 to 10 in training and suddenly arrives between -100 and 100.

Here a custom Model Monitor job runs the MMD test every hour, writes violations and the most likely adversarial images to S3, and publishes metrics to CloudWatch. In the demo, the first hour is clean; then adversarial samples hit the endpoint and the detection rate sits at roughly 100% from 5 to 6 a.m., falls off, and by 7 a.m. the attacker is gone. The same smdebug trial object lets you pull the recorded tensors for further t-SNE analysis.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and MLOps teams responsible for models in production, and SREs who've inherited one. The first half is conceptual; stay for the second, which is a reusable detection pattern with specific layers, tests and AWS services. It closes on chaos engineering as a continuum: build ML systems that withstand turbulent conditions and adversarial inputs every time they run.

Title: Can your AIOps tool tell a chaos experiment from an outage?
Description: Michele Dodic (Accenture) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on testing an AIOps setup with Litmus latency injection and Splunk Observability
Body:
If you've bought into AIOps to predict failures, the obvious test is to cause one on purpose. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, Michele Dodic, SRE DevOps Engineer at Accenture, does exactly that: inject 4,000 milliseconds of network latency into one microservice with LitmusChaos and check whether Splunk Observability's anomaly detection notices, and whether it can see that a chaos experiment is running at all.

The talk pairs two ideas usually kept apart, AIOps and chaos engineering, and argues observability is where they meet.

## What is AIOps here?

The definition used is a practical one: machine learning and analytics applied to IT operations to prevent degradation and failure. The model ingests historical and real-time logs, metrics and text, and produces actionable insights such as anomaly detection, root cause identification and reduced alert noise, ideally with auto-remediation and self-healing on top. The setup is familiar to anyone who has been on call: an SRE buried in tools, tickets, incidents and mail, wondering why it has to be like that.

Chaos engineering comes in through the security chaos engineering definition, adapted from Netflix's: experimenting on a distributed system to build confidence in its capability to withstand turbulent and malicious conditions. The loop is steady-state posture from observability, hypothesis, continuous verification, lessons learned and mitigation, then round again.

## The hypothesis: AIOps will notice

Two questions drive the demo. How does AIOps react to a chaos experiment? And can it recognise that an experiment is running, through observability alone? The hypothesis: run an experiment and AIOps will detect it, and the experiment will either fail or stay under control.

The test bed runs in minikube:

- **Online Boutique**, Google's microservices demo shop, with around ten to eleven services.
- **Splunk Observability**, fed through the OpenTelemetry Collector, with its AIOps component on top.
- **Locust**, simulating 30 users with a spawn rate of two.
- **LitmusChaos**, injecting the faults.

Of the golden signals, latency is the target. Even before the experiment, Splunk's service map shows its root-cause tracing at work, following trouble from the front end down to the payment service: shoppers can browse and fill baskets but may fail at checkout.

## The alert arrives before the spike

The experiment is a Litmus workflow with network latency on the cart service: 200 seconds of chaos, 4,000 milliseconds of added latency, and the cleanup option enabled to restore the environment afterwards (the tip worth remembering from the demo). On the Splunk side the detector uses the sudden change condition for unexpected latency increases; a historical anomaly condition would instead learn from past latency patterns.

As Locust's failure count climbs, the latency dashboard shows a red alert triangle and a critical alert email arrives: latency over the last eight minutes is more than three deviations above the norm. On the chart, the alert lands before the largest latency peak. The speaker reads that as the model predicting trouble before the error, and points to the runbook field in the alert settings, where Splunk can be told to remediate, for instance by resetting the failing node. Michele Dodic said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 that "we're shifting from a proactive to a predictive paradigm".

## Recognising the experiment itself

For the second question there's a simple dashboard counting pod launches in the Litmus namespace, which lists every chaos experiment run in the past week. The talk concludes the hypothesis is proven. A skeptical viewer will note this half is a counter on observability data rather than machine learning, though it does show the experiments are visible in the same pane where incidents land.

## Who should watch

SREs evaluating or running an AIOps platform who want a repeatable way to check that it reacts to real degradation. It's a single-vendor demo (Splunk Observability with Litmus) on a toy shop, so treat it as a pattern to copy rather than a benchmark. The closing advice is sensible for any of this: "start simple and scale fast".

Title: The chaos experiment that broke before the chaos started
Description: Rain Leander (Cockroach Labs) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on trying to run Gremlin against CockroachDB, and what the failed setup taught
Body:
Sometimes the first chaos you meet is your own setup. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, Rain Leander, Developer Advocate at Cockroach Labs, set out to point Gremlin's fault injection at CockroachDB and report what broke. What broke first was the lab: serverless, Docker, macOS and AWS each blocked the experiment in a different way, and the talk is an honest account of that.

A fair warning, then. The abstract promises a series of Gremlin experiments helping CockroachDB evolve; the talk itself is about getting to the starting line, with full disclosure up front that it's about failure, mistakes and lessons learned. Seen as that, it's a short, useful field report.

## Two ways people arrive at chaos engineering

Rain Leander opens with a distinction worth keeping. Some people come to chaos engineering out of curiosity and want to try the tools on projects they have. Others arrive after a catastrophic production event and want checks so it never happens again. This experiment came from the first camp; anyone in the second is invited to watch at one and a half speed and go and play with their own environment.

## Four attempts at a test bed

The starting point was a Medium post on hardening CockroachDB with Gremlin: three Ubuntu instances in an AWS VPC, the open-source CockroachDB and a free Gremlin account. The plan was to keep it cheaper and simpler, on a laptop and on familiar platforms rather than AWS. In order:

- **CockroachDB Serverless.** Great for a developer who wants to point an app at a database and stop thinking about sharding or replication, but there's no way to give Gremlin the access it needs, since its agent requires its own team key and identification, as any API would.
- **Self-hosted CockroachDB in Docker on a Mac.** Gremlin doesn't support macOS, so Gremlin went into Docker too. Getting the CockroachDB containers and the Gremlin containers to see each other proved beyond the speaker's Docker experience, and one CockroachDB node kept failing whatever resources it was given.
- **Kubernetes on minikube.** That fixed the failing node, for reasons the talk admits it can't explain.
- **AWS, as in the original post.** Three instances and a CockroachDB install later, Rain Leander said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 that "It was an incredibly painful 6 hours of my life", and the deadline for the conference had arrived.

The serverless lesson is the one with legs beyond this talk: the more a managed service hides its infrastructure, the fewer handles a host-level chaos agent has to grab.

## If the plan fails, keep the goal

The lessons are short and motivational: if the plan doesn't work, change the plan, not the goal; winners fail until they succeed; fall down seven times, get up eight. The quotable version is "If the plan doesn't work, change the plan, not the goal."

There's also a candid engineering one: the unexplained Docker node failure might be an older open-source version, a resource limit, or the setup itself, and finding out is on the to-do list. Admitting Docker turned out to be harder than expected is the sort of thing most conference talks edit out.

## What were the next steps?

The plan from there: try Netlify, Vercel or Heroku with a small app such as a leaderboard (Netlify and Gremlin had a brand-new relationship but no documentation yet), try other tools such as Chaos Toolkit, Jepsen or Litmus, find someone who knows Docker well enough to make the containers talk, and ask the Conf42 audience for help, which the talk does directly.

## Who should watch

People starting out with chaos engineering who want reassurance that tooling friction is normal, and anyone choosing a platform for a chaos lab. If you want a demonstration of Gremlin attacks on CockroachDB, this isn't it; it's a brief, good-humoured story of what stood in the way.

Title: Make the chaos experiment the gate before production
Description: Akram Riahi (WeScale) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on running Litmus 2 chaos workflows in Jenkins and promoting only images that pass
Body:
QA tests check the failures you already thought of. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, Akram Riahi, SRE and chaos engineer at WeScale, shows how to catch some of the others: a Jenkins pipeline that injects a LitmusChaos workflow into every build on Kubernetes, promotes the image to production only if the experiment passes, and reports the verdict to Slack.

He is upfront that this is a talk about the how, not the why, and most of it is a demo built from work he did with a client to test application resilience before promotion.

## Why put chaos in the pipeline at all?

His framing is a choice teams face: write custom scripts and tests, which costs time, money and often consultants, or adopt chaos engineering's hypothesis-and-experiment approach. The worry is whether developers and SREs can realistically do that every day while shipping lots of code. His answer is to make injecting chaos as easy as a push or a pull request, so developers can do it as often as they like.

## What is a Litmus chaos workflow?

LitmusChaos is an open-source, Kubernetes-native chaos framework (a CNCF sandbox project that had moved to incubation). Its ChaosHub collects ready-made experiments for Kubernetes, AWS and more: CPU hog, memory hog, network latency, pod delete, with a blast radius that can grow from a pod to a node.

A chaos workflow chains experiments together with whatever preconditioning steps they need, in parallel or in series. His example: if your app is sensitive to CPU and memory, run CPU hog and memory hog in parallel, then add network latency in series after them. Workflows can be written as code or built in the Litmus ChaosCenter portal, which also handles teams, connected clusters, Grafana observability and a GitHub integration that pushes new workflows into your repository.

## The pipeline, stage by stage

The demo stack is AWS EKS built with Terraform, Grafana and Prometheus for monitoring, Jenkins triggered from GitHub pull requests, Docker Hub as the registry, and Slack for notifications. A push or pull request runs:

1. Prepare, with a Slack message that the pipeline has started.
2. Build the image and push it to dev.
3. QA tests (skipped over in the talk).
4. Update the deployed app with the new image.
5. Inject chaos by applying the workflow, a Kubernetes custom resource, from a script.
6. Pass: tag the image for prod, push it and promote the deployment. Fail: the app isn't resilient, and Slack hears about it.
7. Clean up the workflow and the ChaosResult resources, then send Slack the QA and chaos reports.

Communication is a theme he keeps returning to. Akram Riahi said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 that "communication in chaos engineering is very important", so that nobody is surprised by an injection and teams can work on resilience together.

## What does the demo show?

The app is a deliberately tiny PHP and Apache page saying hello. The workflow has three steps: install the experiment, run pod CPU hog, and revert by removing the runners and resources it created. The chaos engine targets the app's namespace, label and deployment kind, with a 60-second chaos duration on one CPU core. In ChaosCenter he rebuilds the same workflow, notes where a steady-state probe (HTTP, command or Prometheus) would go, and gives the experiment a weight of 10 out of 10 for the resilience score because CPU matters most for this app.

A pull request run ends with Slack reporting the pod CPU hog experiment with a Pass verdict and a resilience score of 100. He then edits the greeting, pushes to master and walks the pipeline again, watching the Litmus runners appear in their namespace while the experiment runs. A laggy connection delays the final Slack message, a small reminder that notification paths need watching too.

## Who should watch

Teams already on Kubernetes and Jenkins who want a concrete template for chaos as a pipeline gate. It's a beginner-friendly, demo-heavy walkthrough; one CPU experiment on a hello-world app shows the pattern but not how to pick thresholds for a real service. His closing advice: start injecting, automate more, and keep improving alerting and monitoring, because the experiments will expose things you forgot.

Title: One git tag decides the account, region and Terraform state
Description: Lerna Ekmekcioglu and Jack Iu (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on multi-region Terraform pipelines split into cells by region and environment
Body:
Deploying the same infrastructure to one AWS region is easy. Doing it across several regions, several business units and dev, QA, staging and prod without drift is where teams get hurt. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, Lerna Ekmekcioglu, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, and Jack Iu, Solutions Architect at AWS, show a Terraform-built CI/CD pipeline where a single git tag tells the pipeline which account, which region and which Terraform state to touch, and every boundary is a cell that contains failure.

Both work with financial services customers, and it shows: the design leans on multi-account isolation, early security scanning and the pipeline as the only way to change anything.

## Why go multi-region at all?

Jack Iu sets the scene: at the time AWS had 84 availability zones in 26 regions, and a well-built multi-AZ deployment is the right answer for most workloads (it's how Amazon.com runs). Customers go multi-region for three reasons: to put compute closer to users in a global expansion, to give mission-critical applications extreme resilience, and to meet business continuity, disaster recovery and regulatory requirements. The price is complexity: consistent infrastructure across many regions, business units and SDLC environments, plus a delivery strategy that holds it all together.

## How does a git tag drive the deployment?

The workflow has four steps: infrastructure as code, a git tag, a pipeline trigger, and the deploy into the target account. A central tooling account holds the Git repository (AWS CodeCommit) and the pipelines (AWS CodePipeline and CodeBuild). Target workload accounts exist per business unit and per environment; the examples are a research unit publishing to external clients and a risk unit with internal-only data.

Engineers work trunk-based with short-lived branches and merge requests. To release, they tag main with a convention of environment and deployment scope, team, then version, such as `dev_eu-central-1/research/1.0`, or `dev_global/research/1.0` for account-wide resources like IAM roles. A CodeBuild job captures the tag plus a full clone, drops them into a versioned S3 bucket per environment, and that bucket is the pipeline's source stage. The version number matters because you always want to know what's deployed in an account.

## Lint, scan, plan, approve, apply

The pipeline stages are deliberately boring in the best way:

- **IaC lint** with TFLint: static analysis for errors such as illegal instance types, deprecated syntax and unused declarations. Failures stop the pipeline.
- **IaC security scan** with Checkov, which ships thousands of ready-made policies and produces a JUnit XML report. A public S3 bucket or a security group open to the world stops the run here, rather than at the traditional late security gate just before production.
- **Build**: `terraform plan`, a manual approval where a DevOps lead reviews the plan, then `terraform apply`.

The last security rule is that the pipeline is the authoritative source for deployment. IAM roles and policies let the pipeline deploy into target accounts and stop individuals from making changes there by hand.

## Bulkheads, from twelfth-century ships to Terraform state

The idea that ties it together is cell architecture. Lerna Ekmekcioglu compares it to bulkheads, the vertical partitions used in shipbuilding since the twelfth century and on the International Space Station: group what belongs together and keep the blast radius small. It's applied at every level:

- **Accounts** per business unit and environment, each with its own security and access profile.
- **Pipelines per region**: each region's pipeline deploys only to its own region, so trouble in region one doesn't stop deployments to regions two through n.
- **Pipelines per environment**: dev pipelines only take dev-prefixed tags and dev buckets, so a broken dev pipeline can't touch production.
- **State**: Terraform state in S3 with DynamoDB locks, one set per environment, and the S3 key built from the git tag's environment, team and region. Doing state surgery on research dev in eu-central-1 can't affect research dev in us-east-1, and adding ap-southeast-1 writes a brand-new state file.

In Terraform the provider is parameterized by region and assumes an IAM role in the target account, and two module namespaces separate global resources (scoped to the account) from regional ones (scoped to account and region). The sample workload is a VPC from versioned modules up to an external application load balancer, and the demo walks a tag through lint, the Checkov report, plan approval and apply into eu-central-1 until the load balancer answers.

## What's the takeaway?

Lerna Ekmekcioglu said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 that "the most important takeaway about multi region deployments is that we should be making sure that we are consistent with our deployments". Pipeline as the single source of truth, code structured for reuse, and security shifted left.

## Who should watch

Platform and cloud teams running Terraform on AWS across several accounts and regions, particularly in regulated industries. It's a reference architecture with a working demo, not a chaos engineering talk, though every design choice is about containing failure.

- Ana Van Straaten on [going multi-region](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Ana_Van_Straaten_going_multi_region) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022.
- Kyle Shelton on [disaster recovery preparedness](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Kyle_Shelton_disaster_recovery_preparedness), from the same event.

Title: Red teaming finds 35 bugs, fixes five, and bills you $64,000
Description: Kim Carter (BinaryMist) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on OWASP PurpleTeam, security regression tests that run in your build pipeline
Body:
Security defects are cheapest when you find them the day you write them, and most teams find them months later in a two-week pentest. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, Kim Carter, Lead Security Engineer at BinaryMist, shows OWASP PurpleTeam, a developer-focused security regression testing CLI and backend that sits in your build pipeline and tests web applications and APIs as you build them.

It's the creator's own tour: the architecture, the setup, and a full test run against a deliberately vulnerable app.

## What does late security testing really cost?

The economics carry the talk, and he attributes the figures to statistics collected in his book series, Holistic Info-Sec for Web Developers. A typical six-month project for a small to medium web app or API gets a red teaming engagement of about two weeks at roughly $20,000 a week, so about $40,000. It typically finds five critical, ten high, ten medium and ten low severity bugs. The business fixes only the five criticals, and by now each costs more than 15 times what it would have when introduced: five bugs, times 15, times $320 (about two developer hours) is $24,000.

Kim Carter said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 that "this is too expensive, it's too late, and too many bugs are left unfixed". PurpleTeam's pitch is to move that discovery into the pipeline, with reports that show how to reproduce each attack and tips on not introducing the same class of bug again.

## How is it built?

The CLI is the front end. Headless in a pipeline, or with a terminal UI when run by hand, it sends a job file to the backend. The job file is where the build user configures test sessions without writing tests, including alert thresholds per tester that decide whether a run passes.

Behind it, a Node.js orchestrator dispatches work to three testers: an application tester, a TLS tester (in production for months by then) and a server tester that was not yet implemented, with Nikto planned. The app tester spins up one set of OWASP ZAP and Selenium containers per test session, launched by Lambda functions (SAM CLI locally, Lambda and ECS in the cloud), and tears them down afterwards. Testers groom their feedback and publish it to Redis; the orchestrator relays it to the CLI by long polling or server-sent events, configurable, with little practical difference between them.

Locally you set up the Docker network, the Lambda functions, the stage-two containers, the orchestrator, the testers and firewall rules. In the cloud you install the CLI, configure it and write a job file.

## Watching a run fail, on purpose

The demo runs against OWASP NodeGoat, brought up with clean state by the PurpleTeam infrastructure-as-code system-under-test project. Two app test sessions (a low-privilege user hitting the profile route, an admin user hitting profile then memos) and one TLS session run in parallel. Donut meters show progress per tester, a running statistics panel shows bug counts against thresholds, and a new bugs counter shows anything above the threshold.

All three sessions fail because defect counts exceed their alert thresholds, which is exactly what the tool is for. The outcomes archive holds HTML and Markdown reports from ZAP, CSV, JSON and HTML from the TLS emissary testssl.sh, and NDJSON results from Cucumber. Alert thresholds are the brownfield trick: an app with known defects can still pass while new ones fail the build.

## A four-year side project, given away

The backstory is honest. PurpleTeam grew from a proof of concept in the book, mostly built seven days a week as a second full-time job. He donated the local version to OWASP in Q1 2021, launched the cloud version commercially in Q4 2021, couldn't get the publicity to make it viable, and donated the cloud SaaS to OWASP in Q1 2022. He invites contributors and offers mentoring for those who want to learn security by building it.

## Who should watch

Developers and DevSecOps engineers who want automated security regression tests in CI, especially Node.js shops. It's a dense walkthrough of one open-source tool rather than a general security talk.

Title: Server-driven UI lets the backend ship your mobile screens
Description: Lucas Fonseca (Zup Innovation) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on server-driven UI, so mobile apps can change screens and run A/B tests without a store release
Body:
Your backend can deploy ten times a day; your app ships when Apple and Google say so. At Conf42 Mobile 2022, Lucas Fonseca, Developer Advocate and iOS Specialist at Zup Innovation, argues that server-driven UI closes that gap: the server returns not just the data but the screen itself, so one app binary can run many layouts, experiments and flows, all changed from the backend.

The talk is half concept, half live demo with Beagle, Zup's open-source server-driven UI framework, including a demo glitch that every mobile developer will recognise.

## Why is hypothesis testing so expensive on mobile?

Fonseca frames everything around a fictional flower shop that wants the same experience on every platform, continuity when a customer moves from phone to desktop, layouts that change per business rule, and updates that reach customers immediately. Each of those is a hypothesis to test: SMS is an effective channel for people over 35; a 20% discount is enough to move customers from a physical to a fully digital solution; value proposition A, B or C communicates best; raising prices by 1.5x makes customers perceive more value and convert more.

A hypothesis needs a metric and a criterion before it becomes a thesis, and that means shipping variants. On the server side that is ten deploys a day. On mobile it is about two releases a week, gated by store review. Feature flags help with releasing functionality, but he notes they still don't give full control over review and releases, and the SMS-style tests are easy on the backend while A/B/C screen tests drag the front end and the stores into it.

## What does server-driven UI change?

The idea, in his framing, is to bring the backend's dynamism to the front end. With one version of the app installed, you can run several versions of the same screen in production with different UIs, vary screens by region or country, or give each user their own flow.

Lucas Fonseca said at Conf42 Mobile 2022: "we can have two versions or three versions, ten versions in production of the same screen but with different uis".

He names Swiggy, Flipkart and Spotify among the companies doing native server-driven UI, and points to frameworks such as Flipkart's Proteus, Facebook's Litho and Airbnb's Lona alongside Beagle.

## What do you need before you start?

Two things. A design system, where every piece of UI (buttons, labels, colours, text inputs, fonts, icons) is a component you can compose into layouts. And a JSON contract, so the backend and the front end agree on which component to render.

He is just as clear on when not to bother:

- the app has no mature design system, or the design system itself changes all the time;
- the screens and flows are static and rarely change;
- the source code has no layers separating business rules from UI, so fix the architecture first;
- the service layer can't handle scaling and A/B testing.

That last point is the honest part of the pitch: you are moving UI work onto the backend, so the backend has to carry it.

## The demo: a Kotlin BFF that draws iOS screens

Beagle runs as a dependency on both sides. On the server, a Spring backend-for-frontend describes screens in a Kotlin DSL and serialises them to JSON; on the device, Beagle deserialises them into native components and uses Facebook's Yoga library to lay them out with flexbox. Fonseca shows a login screen (navigation bar, text input, biometric login button), translates its text to English, adds a password field, and the iOS app picks up each change after a backend restart, with no new build. A condition component validates the input and shows an alert on a wrong value, and a send-request action can call other services, so flows and logic live on the server too.

Mid-demo, macOS decides it is a good moment for Siri to pop up, and the emulator needs a reinstall. Server-driven UI does not, sadly, extend to the presenter's laptop.

## Who should watch

Mobile teams whose product people want weekly experiments that the release train can't deliver, and backend engineers about to be asked to own screen layouts. It is a concept-and-demo talk, not a production war story: expect the case for SDUI and a working Beagle example, not migration lessons or performance numbers.

Title: Backups aren't a DR plan, and an untested DR plan isn't either
Description: Kyle Shelton (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on picking a DR strategy from RTO and RPO, then proving it with chaos experiments
Body:
A disaster recovery plan you've never exercised is a document, not a capability. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, Kyle Shelton, a chaos and reliability engineering builder at AWS, makes the case for choosing a DR strategy by cost and risk, then using chaos engineering to run the fire drills that prove it works before the next big service event does it for you.

He has the background for the metaphor: in the Navy, he says, firefighting exercises were constant, because you practise for the day you actually need to put out a fire.

## High availability and disaster recovery are different jobs

He opens by separating two things teams often blur. High availability improves uptime by removing single points of failure and adding redundancy. Disaster recovery is the set of plans and policies that bring workloads back when things go down anyway. Backups alone don't count as a DR plan; DR has to be clearly defined and practised often.

Resilience in the cloud also works differently from on-prem. He recalls building applications at Verizon in a 40/40 distributed model so nothing ran above 40% capacity. In the cloud, you plan instead for specific failures: an instance stop or start, instance degradation, an availability zone problem, a service event, or a regional event like the one AWS had in December 2021.

## Which DR strategy do your RTO and RPO buy?

Everything starts with two numbers. Recovery time objective (RTO) is the acceptable delay between interruption and restoration. Recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable time since the last recovery point, in other words how much data you can afford to lose. From there he walks up the cost ladder:

- **Backup and restore**: back up data and applications to the DR region and restore when needed. Fine when recovery can take hours, up to 24.
- **Pilot light**: the critical core always runs in the DR region, ready to scale to full production. Works when RPO is in minutes.
- **Warm standby**: a reduced but fully functional copy always running, scaled up on recovery. More expensive.
- **Active-active**: the workload serves traffic in multiple AWS regions, RPO near zero and RTO in seconds, with users and data kept in sync and traffic shifted by Route 53 or Global Accelerator. The most expensive, reserved for the most critical workloads.

The criticality of the workload decides where you sit. Safety-related systems get a very different answer from an internal report generator.

## Start with an instance, not a region

His chaos advice is conservative by design. Test regularly in non-production as part of the integration and deployment lifecycle, and when you touch production, don't make the service unavailable for customers. Start small, by stopping instances or failing a host, then work up to availability zone failures and only later to regional ones. Isolate failures, know your risk appetite, and always have a backout and rollback plan.

Then quantify. How long until the failure is detected and someone is notified? Should the status page change? How long does auto-recovery take, and is it partial or full? Kyle Shelton said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 that "if you have a recovery objective of ten minutes and your auto recovery takes 20, then you're going to have to go back to the drawing board".

## Every escalation should end with a runbook

Experiments feed post-incident reviews, which AWS calls COEs (correction of errors): blameless, structured, with the event, the impact, five whys, the observability data to back it up, and corrective actions someone actually follows through on. In one SRE role he met NOC engineers every two weeks to go over each escalation and write a runbook for it, so no repeat escalation should arrive without one. Anything that keeps coming back and needs a human is toil to automate.

## Put fault injection in the pipeline

To get started, he suggests recurring experiments run like other machine-led tests (unit, regression, integration, load), placed late in the CI/CD pipeline because fault injection needs longer runtimes to collect enough data. The reasoning for automating it is the best line of the talk: it's easy to slow down the pipeline to run only once a year, but hard to speed up a manual process to run it many times a day. He points to an AWS chaos engineering workshop that uses the CDK to build the infrastructure, the pipeline and the fault injection from a single repository so all the parts are versioned together.

## Who should watch

Teams that have a DR document and a vague feeling it might work. The talk is short and strategic: no live demo, but a clear framework for matching DR spend to RTO and RPO and a sensible order for introducing failure.

Title: BLoC in Flutter is events in, states out, and no setState
Description: Abhishek Doshi (Somnio Software) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on Flutter state management with BLoC, from widget state to a counter app without setState
Body:
Every Flutter tutorial starts with a counter app and a call to setState, and every growing Flutter app eventually regrets it. At Conf42 Mobile 2022, Abhishek Doshi, Senior Flutter Engineer at Somnio Software and a Google Developer Expert for Dart and Flutter, explains what state actually is in Flutter, why it needs managing, and how the BLoC pattern (Business Logic Components) splits the work into events going one way and states coming back.

It is an introductory talk: a good first session if you have written some Flutter widgets and keep hearing that you should use BLoC without knowing what it buys you.

## What counts as state in Flutter?

Doshi starts from the basics. In Flutter everything is a widget, and the properties of a widget are its state: the text you type into a text field is that field's state. He gives state three jobs. It holds information about the widget that can be read synchronously when the widget is built. It rebuilds the UI when you need it to, which is why setState exists. And it gives you control over the widget's lifecycle, which cuts both ways: mismanage it and the app can crash or leak memory.

State can live in one widget, one file or the whole app, depending on how you lay out the UI. That flexibility is exactly where the trouble starts.

## Why not just pass data down the tree?

His example is the one every Flutter developer hits. Two screens, passing data from page one to page two at navigation time: easy. Five screens, and page five needs something from page one: you don't want to thread it through pages two, three and four. State management gives you access to that data wherever you need it, and the same applies to the classic async case of showing a loader while an API call is in flight and updating the UI when the data lands.

He lists the options (Provider, Riverpod, Redux, RxDart, BLoC) and notes that all of them sit on Flutter's InheritedWidget under the hood. BLoC can be built by hand with streams and sinks, but the flutter_bloc package already wraps them.

## The six names you need to know

Most of the talk is a glossary, and a useful one. The core idea is a one-way loop, and the Google sign-in example makes it concrete: the UI adds a sign-in event carrying parameters such as a user id or email, the BLoC processes it (an API call, say), and sends back a success or failure state.

Abhishek Doshi said at Conf42 Mobile 2022: "event is something that you send from UI to block, and state is something that you send from block to UI".

Around that loop sit four widgets:

- **BlocProvider** supplies a BLoC instance to the widget tree. Wrapping MaterialApp gives one state for the whole app; wrap a single page instead if you want several instances of the same BLoC.
- **BlocBuilder** rebuilds the UI from the current state.
- **BlocListener** reacts to state without rebuilding, which is what you want for navigation, such as going to the home page once sign-in succeeds.
- **BlocConsumer** is builder plus listener, for when you need both.

The builder-versus-listener split is the bit worth remembering. Navigation inside a builder is a classic source of odd rebuild bugs, and the talk gives a clean rule for where each kind of reaction belongs.

## The counter app, without setState

The demo converts the default counter app to BLoC. A BlocProvider hands a counter BLoC to the home page, the event is an enum with an increment value, the BLoC maps the increment event to a new state with the incremented value, and a BlocBuilder renders that integer in a Text widget. The floating action button just adds an event. The whole file is 43 lines with formatting, and setState appears nowhere.

One caveat he flags himself: the demo uses the older mapEventToState style of the flutter_bloc API, and newer versions have simpler code, though the concept is the same. He is also candid about the cost: as an app grows, the sheer number of BLoCs, events and states can get confusing.

## Who should watch

Flutter developers who are past their first app and want a mental model of state management before choosing a package, and anyone coming from web development (he compares widgets to HTML tags). If you already ship BLoC in production, this is too basic for you; the 2022-era API in the demo is also worth noting before you copy it.

- Frank Courville on [the power of state machines in Swift](https://www.conf42.com/Mobile_2022_Frank_Courville_swift_power_of_state_machines), the same event-to-state idea on iOS.
- Joshua Arvin Lat on [state management in React, Angular and Vue.js](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Joshua_Arvin_Lat_State_Management_React__Angular_Vuejs) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.
- Nicola Zaghini on [cross-platform with React Native](https://www.conf42.com/Mobile_2022_Nicola_Zaghini_dreaming_reactnative_crossplatform), for the other side of the cross-platform debate.

Title: Once a human is paged, the outage lasts at least 20 minutes
Description: Ayelet Sachto (Google) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on cutting incident impact by shrinking time to detect, time to repair and failure frequency
Body:
Failures will happen, so the useful question is how much they hurt. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, Ayelet Sachto, Strategic Cloud Engineer at Google (and at the time an SRE on GKE SRE in London), splits the painful window into three parts you can attack separately: time to detect, time to repair, and time between failures.

Her most quotable number comes from Google's own experience. Ayelet Sachto said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 that "once a human is involved, the outage will be at least 20 to 30 minutes", which is the case for automation and self-healing in one sentence.

## What counts as an incident?

She starts with definitions, briefly. An incident is an issue escalated because it's too big to handle alone and needs an immediate, organised response; not every page becomes one. Then the vocabulary: SLIs tell you how the service is doing right now, SLOs set a target over a window, SLAs say what you'll do (a refund, say) if you miss it, so SLOs must be stricter than SLAs. User happiness is measured per user journey, and the ones that matter most are critical user journeys.

## Time to detect: alert on what users feel

Time to detect (TTD) runs from the moment an outage starts to the moment a human is notified. Her levers:

- Align SLIs as closely as possible with what users expect, whether those users are people or other services, and review them periodically.
- Align alerts with SLOs.
- Pick the measurement strategy that fits the data: streams, logs or batch processing.
- Balance speed against noise. Alerting too fast causes alert fatigue, alerting too slowly hurts customers.

Noisy and non-actionable alerts are, she says, the complaints Google hears most often from operations, DevOps and SRE teams alike. Only page on things that need immediate action, send them only to the owners, and route the rest to the right place: a ticket, a dashboard, or a metric you pull when debugging.

## Time to repair means mitigate, not fix

Time to repair (TTR) runs from the alert to mitigation, and she stresses that word. It's not the time to land a code fix; it's the time to stop the customer impact, for example by shifting traffic to another region.

This part is mostly human. Unprepared on-callers mean longer repairs, so train them: disaster recovery testing, shadowing, Wheel of Misfortune exercises. Use a clear incident process; Google's IMAG protocol is based on the Incident Command System used by firefighters and medics, with defined roles, tasks and communication channels. Write playbooks, start simple, and let new joiners update them during onboarding (see it, fix it). Watch shift load, because exhausted responders repair slowly. And build dashboards per audience: a manager's SLO view is not a troubleshooting dashboard.

## Time between failures: ship smaller, break on purpose

Time between failures runs from the end of one outage to the start of the next. Beyond fixing what risk analysis turns up, she recommends avoiding global changes, using progressive and canary rollouts over hours, days or weeks, wiring automated testing and automatic rollback into CI/CD, building in redundancy and graceful degradation, and practising chaos engineering and automated disaster recovery tests to find issues before they find you.

## Let the postmortems choose your priorities

The last tool is the blameless postmortem: assume good intentions and fix the system that allowed the incident, not the people. Her practical tip goes further: once you have a critical mass of postmortems, mine them for patterns and let them decide where to invest. She encourages customers to keep a shared repository and share it broadly across internal teams.

## Who should watch

On-call engineers and team leads who want a structured way to argue for investment in alerting, training or rollout tooling. It's a well-organised overview rather than a deep technical talk, and it comes with a curated list of Google SRE resources.
