Title: Chaos testing without observability is just chaos
Description: Narmatha Bala (Microsoft CSE) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on golden signals, SLOs and alerts that make chaos tests readable
Body:
Breaking a system on purpose only teaches you something if you can see what broke. That's the whole argument of Narmatha Bala, Senior Software Engineering Manager at Microsoft CSE, at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022: before you inject a single fault, know what normal looks like, which signals will move, and who gets paged when they do.

Narmatha Bala said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 that "chaos engineering without doing observability will just lead to chaos". Her talk is a compact checklist for avoiding that, drawn from her work running the observability chapter of the CSE Engineering Playbook.

## What does "normal" look like?

Chaos experiments start from a steady state and a hypothesis, then measure the deviation. Her definition of observability fits that loop neatly: the ability to answer new questions with existing data. To describe normal she uses three groups of attributes:

- **Service health**: is the API answering 200 OK?
- **Resource health**: CPU, memory, disk I/O under stress.
- **Business transaction KPIs**: logins per second, searches per second, whatever the business actually counts.

None of these helps much on its own. They become useful when they land on a dashboard built for a specific stakeholder. An SRE running a chaos test needs a different view from everyone else, and throwing every metric onto one combined dashboard serves nobody. Alerts, in her framing, are the end result of a dashboard.

## The golden signals, with numbers attached

To decide what to measure she reaches for Google SRE's four golden signals: traffic, latency, errors and saturation. Her worked example sets a baseline of roughly 200 requests per second, 500 milliseconds per request, zero errors, CPU under 20% and memory under 50%. Then the chaos test pushes traffic to 500 or 600 requests per second, and you watch how latency drifts, whether timeouts start appearing, and which resources saturate first.

## Logs that don't talk to each other aren't observability

The most relatable part is a story from earlier in her career. The team had logs and alerts in place and felt confident, until production troubleshooting showed the logs were atomic: no correlation between components, no context, so finding the cause took far too long.

An actionable failure, as she defines it, is one where the time from spotting a problem to recovering from it is minimal. That takes logs with enough runtime context to point at the problem area, correlation of cause and effect across components, and ingestion plus analytics engines that can actually crunch the volume. Logging everything isn't the same as being able to read it.

## Use SLOs to decide when chaos is allowed

She runs through the SLA, SLO and error budget basics with a mapping provider and a ride-sharing app: the SLA promises maps available 99.99% of the time and two weeks' notice before API changes, the SLOs are what the provider's team must hit to keep that promise, and the error budget at 99.99% works out to about 52 minutes a year.

The chaos-specific twist is how SLOs shape the experiment. Before testing, they tell you which failures are critical for users (is a little buffering on a streaming service an incident, or does it fix itself?). During testing, they tell you when not to inject: if user experience is already deteriorating, adding more uncertainty is the wrong move. And with live feedback from the golden signals you can decide whether to turn the traffic up or back off.

## Treat each chaos run as an audit of your alerts

A chaos test is also a rehearsal for your alerting. While the system degrades, she suggests asking: which alarms are missing, are they measuring causes or only symptoms, are the thresholds right, and does each alert reach the team that owns the fix? A threshold set too low brings alert fatigue, and people stop reacting to pages. Better to discover that during a planned experiment than at 3am.

Her closing advice: start small with the auto-instrumentation your tooling already gives you, correlate distributed logs and traces, iterate on instrumentation as you find gaps, and celebrate the learnings when something turns out not to work.

## Who should watch

Intermediate practitioners whose chaos experiments produce more confusion than insight. It's a short, principles-level talk with no tool demos, and a good companion to anything more hands-on.

Title: A native diehard's case for React Native: the killer feature is OTA updates
Description: Nicola Zaghini (Phorest Salon Software) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on why over-the-air updates, not code reuse, sold React Native for 4,000 white-label apps
Body:
Code reuse is the reason everyone gives for cross-platform, and according to Nicola Zaghini it is the wrong one. At Conf42 Mobile 2022, Zaghini, Engineering Manager at Phorest Salon Software and a native mobile engineer for most of his 13-year career, told how he pitched React Native to his CTO to save a product line of thousands of white-label apps, and why the feature that sold it was over-the-air updates.

He frames it as the talk he wished he had heard four years earlier, aimed squarely at skeptical native developers.

## Why did a scalability problem need a new framework?

Zaghini spent years in the airline industry; if you have checked in for a flight on your phone, he says, there is a fair chance you used an app he built or architected. At Phorest, which makes software for hair, beauty, barber and spa businesses, he inherited a consumer product line headed for retirement. Every one of Phorest's 8,000-plus customers was eligible for its own branded native app. Now picture a single bug fix: rebuilding and resubmitting thousands of apps through two app stores. That does not scale, whatever your architecture.

## Does React Native feel native?

His first job was convincing the CTO that quality would not suffer. His argument: with React Native, users touch the real native components. A scroll view bounces like a UIScrollView because it is one; labels are UILabels, buttons are UIButtons. There is no embedded browser and no custom widgets drawn on an OpenGL canvas that feel subtly too fast. His metaphor is puppets: the native components are the puppets, the JavaScript engine is the puppeteer you never see, and the bridge is the strings.

The numbers he shows are not a proof of concept: more than 4,000 apps live in the stores, about 12,000 daily active users and around 2,000 appointments booked per day, taking payments too, with theming per brand.

## What changed for the developers?

He goes through the developer experience point by point. TypeScript, not JavaScript: typed and modern enough, he says, that Swift and Kotlin developers will not miss their old language. IDE support for debugging, completion and refactoring that he rates better than Xcode (he used AppCode back then for refactoring alone). Fast Refresh, which looks like a nice gimmick until you go back to compiling. React itself, declarative and even better with hooks. A large community for when you get stuck. His verdict made it onto a slide. Nicola Zaghini said at Conf42 Mobile 2022: "no money can convince me back to the previous way of working."

## What goes in the CTO pitch?

Quality first, then the metrics. 98% code reuse in a typical app, with platform checks rare. But reuse is not the killer feature; what it implies is. A 50% cost reduction, which he says you can push further because React is fast to build with: his product owner and designer, also from native, were shocked to find the iOS app already ran on Android. A 50% time-to-market reduction when two developers share one codebase. Full resource utilisation, since any engineer can fix any bug. Uniformity and feature parity by design, which two separate codebases rarely achieve.

Then the real differentiator. Over-the-air updates shrink lead time and raise release frequency, the two numbers behind software delivery performance. Native fixes wait days for review, even with expedited requests to Apple. With OTA, he ships mission-critical fixes in about 30 minutes: find the code, write a test, fix, QA, out. Within the store rules: no big new features over the air, but tweaks to declared features and bug fixes are fine.

## How do you build the team?

For the existing codebase, either extend it in a hybrid (brownfield) setup, replacing native chunks one at a time, or rewrite, remembering you now work at twice your usual speed. His warning: do not plan to live with the hybrid forever.

For people, you need buy-in, and you should expect both leavers and new converts. His story: during a React Native R&D spike at a previous company, his best Android engineer declared a bridging task impossible, asked for three more days, came back with a clean working solution, and later left for a company already doing React Native. He would not go back either.

The golden rule: keep experienced native iOS and Android developers on the team, because React Native has a native half to tame, and hire engineers with native experience who want to leave their comfort zone.

## Who should watch?

Native mobile developers who are sure cross-platform is a toy, and engineering managers who maintain two codebases or many branded apps. If you want a deep technical comparison of renderers, look elsewhere; this is a decision story with numbers.

Title: Chaos on serverless means breaking config and code, not hosts
Description: Gunnar Grosch (AWS) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 on serverless chaos via config and code faults, with AWS FIS as the stop button
Body:
You can't SSH into a Lambda function to kill a process, so how do you run chaos experiments on it? At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022, Gunnar Grosch, Senior Developer Advocate at AWS, answers with two live demos: break the configuration around your functions and break the code inside them, and let AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) roll everything back when an alarm fires.

The method stays the same as on servers. Gunnar Grosch said at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022 that "the chaos engineering part is the same no matter if it's serverless or if it's say, server full". What changes is where you're allowed to put your hands.

## What do you lose when there's no server?

Serverless removes the undifferentiated heavy lifting of running servers, and with it your access to the environment. On EC2 or containers, environment manipulation (stressing CPU, killing processes) is often where teams start. On Lambda, DynamoDB, API Gateway, S3, SQS and SNS that door is closed.

That leaves three fault-injection techniques:

- **Configuration manipulation**: throttling, concurrency limits, denying access with IAM or resource policies, VPC attachments, CORS mistakes.
- **Network manipulation**: packet loss, bandwidth limits, latency, blocked connectivity via security groups, NACLs, network firewalls, HTTP proxies or NAT instances.
- **Code manipulation**: different API responses, disk exhaustion, corrupted messages, injected latency.

The hypotheses come from a list of serverless weak spots he walks through: error handling (are your dead-letter queues actually catching anything?), timeout values that are only right in steady state, events and messages that go missing when something fails, and third-party dependencies you simply trust to be there.

## Latency is the Swiss Army knife

His favourite single experiment is adding latency to a function. One fault simulates several failures at once: slow runtime or code, slow upstream and downstream integrations, timeouts that are set too tight, and cold starts.

## Demo one: set Lambda concurrency to zero, then undo it

The example app is deliberately plain: API Gateway in front of a Lambda reading from DynamoDB, plus an SQS queue drained by another Lambda into a DynamoDB table. The questions: what if SQS can't invoke the function because it's throttled, what if that invocation stops entirely, what if the function loses its DynamoDB permissions?

You could flip reserved concurrency to zero in the console and remember to flip it back. Instead he runs an FIS experiment template that uses the SSM start-automation-execution action. An SSM document sets the function's concurrency to zero, sleeps, then rolls back. In the demo the function shows as throttled for a one-minute experiment, then returns to its original setting without anyone touching it.

The point of using a managed service rather than CLI commands is the safeguards. He describes them as a blast-radius guard, saying "they act as this automated stop button".

## Demo two: failure-lambda behind a parameter

For code faults he shows failure-lambda, an npm package for Node.js functions (there is chaos-lambda for Python). You install it, import it, and wrap your handler. Its behaviour lives in a JSON parameter in Parameter Store or AWS AppConfig: enabled or not, a failure mode, a rate, and mode-specific settings.

On a small demo site with three identical functions loading images from DynamoDB, normal invocations take roughly 150 to 200 milliseconds. He then turns on:

- **latency** between 100 and 400 milliseconds on function one, which visibly slows down next to the other two;
- **status code** 404 at a rate of 0.5 on function two, so about half the requests fail to load a new image;
- **deny list** for S3 and DynamoDB on function three, which then stops loading images entirely.

Doing that by editing parameters by hand is, as he admits, very manual. So he moves it into FIS too: one route is an SSM document that writes a new parameter value and a rollback value, the other was an experimental put-parameter action AWS was trying out at the time. Finally he adds a CloudWatch alarm as the stop condition, forces the alarm state from the CLI, and FIS halts the experiment and restores the parameter on its own. That last trick, testing the stop button by pressing it on purpose, is worth stealing.

## Who should watch

Teams running Lambda-heavy, event-driven systems who have read the chaos engineering principles and wondered how any of it applies without hosts. It's a practical, demo-driven half hour, and it is AWS-specific: FIS, SSM, Parameter Store and CloudWatch all appear by name.

Title: Four Swift features that quietly do something else, explained in SIL
Description: Pawel Lopusinski (Glovo) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on four Swift surprises, from structs turning into NSObjects to autoclosure retain cycles
Body:
A pure Swift struct with no inheritance can pass an `is NSObject` check, and that is one of the tamer findings in this talk. At Conf42 Mobile 2022, Pawel Lopusinski, iOS Developer at Glovo with about nine years of iOS behind him, took four everyday Swift features, bent them until they looked broken, then read the Swift Intermediate Language (SIL) to show why they actually behave as designed.

Bring a coffee; this one rewards attention. All samples come from Swift 5.5.1.

## What is SIL, and how do you read it?

SIL is the intermediate step between your Swift source and the binary, where the compiler optimises and synthesises the generated parts, such as Codable conformances. Lopusinski uses SIL Inspector by Alex Blewitt (tip: it did not work when run from Xcode for him, but the built binary runs fine standalone) and Matt Godbolt's Compiler Explorer in the browser, which maps code to assembly.

## How does a struct become an NSObject?

Swift has no base type; Objective-C has NSObject and `id`. Swift's `Any` holds anything, `AnyObject` only classes. Cast an Int to NSNumber and bridging kicks in: the object is both NSNumber and Int, and also passes as Float, because the runtime checks whether the value can be represented without losing precision, not what it originally was. A 1.5 is a Float but not an Int.

Then the custom types. Assigning a plain struct to `AnyObject` fails, but the error comes with a fix-it suggesting an explicit cast, and once applied it compiles. Ask whether that struct is an NSObject and the answer is yes. The Swift source explains it: classes are passed to Objective-C unchanged, types conforming to a private bridging protocol use their own bridging, and anything else gets boxed in an NSObject subclass. The reason is Swift Evolution proposal 116, which changed `id` to import as `Any` instead of `AnyObject`, so structs could go straight into things like an NSError user info dictionary.

## Why does an autoclosure leak?

`@autoclosure` wraps the entire expression in a closure, so it may run later, more than once, or never. Pawel Lopusinski said at Conf42 Mobile 2022: "Whenever we see a method being called, we assume that it happens immediately." Autoclosure breaks that assumption, and Xcode's autocomplete just shows a plain String parameter.

His example: a class sets up a closed-source SDK in its init and passes it a method call on self through an escaping autoclosure. Because the whole expression is wrapped, self is captured strongly, and the class also holds the SDK strongly: a retain cycle. The usual weak-self closure, called inline, does not fix it. SIL shows your inner closure captures self weakly, but the generated autoclosure around it still captures self strongly. The fix is to define the weak closure outside the autoclosure expression, so the autoclosure only captures that closure. His API advice: if you make an autoclosure escaping, name the parameter so callers can tell.

## Which default value wins in a subclass?

A `DatePrinter` with a default argument of the current date, and an `EpochDatePrinter` subclass overriding the method with a new default. Call it through a variable typed as the base class and the output looks stitched together: the subclass's implementation with the base class's default.

SIL explains why. The default value is not part of the method at all; it lives in a separate generator function chosen at the call site. The method is dispatched dynamically, but the default is picked statically from the type the compiler sees. Is that a bug? He leaves it open, noting that Kotlin rejects default values in overriding methods outright, and that protocols instead of inheritance avoid the trap.

## Can one type have two properties with the same name?

Sort of. Swift forbids overloading properties, yet a protocol with an optional `String?` requirement, a default implementation in an extension returning nil, and a conforming struct that declares a value without a type annotation gives you two. The struct's property is inferred as non-optional String, does not match the requirement, and the compiler happily uses the protocol default for it. Which value you get depends on the static type: direct access on the struct returns the string, access through the protocol existential goes through the witness table to the default nil.

Declaring the conformance in an extension gets you a near-miss warning, but stored properties cannot live in extensions, so the common pattern of declaring them in the type definition hides it. It gets nastier with third-party protocols and associated types; it was raised on the Swift forums and turned out to be required for library evolution, not a bug.

## Who should watch?

Intermediate and senior iOS developers who want to know what the compiler really does with features they use daily. Newcomers get a tour of `@autoclosure` and protocol extensions; everyone else gets a reason to open SIL Inspector.

Title: Your loading screen is already a state machine, so write it like one
Description: Frank Courville (School of Swift) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on turning state diagrams into Swift enums, wrapper classes and composable child state machines
Body:
Every iOS app has a screen that loads remote content, fails, retries, comes back empty and finally shows data, and almost none of them call it what it is: a state machine. At Conf42 Mobile 2022, Frank Courville, Chief Instructor and Content Director at School of Swift, showed how to draw that state diagram and translate it into Swift with two pieces, a state definition enum and a wrapper class, and then how to keep big state machines manageable by nesting smaller ones.

It is a clear, code-first talk with a sample project behind it.

## What is wrong with coordinators?

Courville opens with the coordinator pattern in UIKit, popularised by Soroush Khanlou back in the Objective-C days, and still his go-to pattern. Its weak spots: nothing in a coordinator tells you the order of view controllers, you wade through several files to see how each one talks to it, and it is hard to test whether a flow still works after a change. State machines answer all three.

His definition: a pattern to represent a finite number of states and enforce known transitions between those states. Finite, because you model your problem, not the world. Known, because every transition has a name. Enforced, because nobody can reach in and set an arbitrary state. The traffic light is the textbook case: green, amber, red, each transition labelled by the timer that fires it.

## How do you turn a diagram into Swift?

Draw the remote-content diagram first: loading, error, empty and data, with arrows for received error, retry, received empty data and received data. Then part one, the state definition enum. The states are the cases; the transitions are a nested `Event` enum (did receive error, did trigger reload, did receive empty data, did receive data), scoped inside the state enum because nothing else should use it. A mutating `handleEvent` switches over the tuple of current state and event:

```swift
mutating func handleEvent(event: Event) {
  switch (self, event) {
  case (.loading, .didReceiveError): self = .error
  case (.loading, .didReceiveData): self = .data
  case (.loading, .didReceiveEmptyData): self = .empty
  case (.empty, .didTriggerReload), (.error, .didTriggerReload): self = .loading
  default: break // log the invalid transition
  }
}
```

The compiler insists the switch is exhaustive, which he counts as the compiler being on your side. Listing every combination is wordy but forces you to revisit them when states are added; a default case is shorter.

## What should an invalid transition do?

Not crash, he argues. A `fatalError` suits very strict applications, but UI race conditions can trigger an invalid transition and take the app down for nothing. Ignore it and log, to Crashlytics or another remote log if you want to audit production behaviour, and at least to the console so you notice during development.

## What does the wrapper class add?

Part two, `RemoteContentStateMachine`, holds the state privately, starting in loading, and tells the outside world about changes. Combine, RxSwift or a closure would work; he uses a weak delegate with a `didSet` on the state so a notification is never forgotten. Public methods (receive error, reload, receive data) are the only way in. `receiveData` is where light business logic belongs: an empty array sends the empty-data event, anything else sends the data event. A `start` method controls when the initial state goes out.

A container view controller adopts the delegate and swaps between loading, error, empty and data child view controllers, each self-contained and reusable elsewhere. Side effects live there too: entering loading fires the network request. A single giant view controller becomes small parts, and the state machine is trivially easy to test.

## How do you stop a state machine from growing out of control?

With a war story. Courville once worked on a large multinational's Internet of Things app with about a dozen devices, each with its own pairing flow, and new devices arriving practically every quarter. Frank Courville said at Conf42 Mobile 2022 that its state machine "was like 5000 lines long and incredibly difficult to modify without introducing bugs."

His fix is composition. Complex state machines contain sub-machines, so extract them. In the example, empty and data become one loaded state whose associated value is a child state machine with its own states (empty, data, refresh) and events, adding pull-to-refresh. The parent's `handleEvent` simply forwards the relevant events to the child.

He closes with implicit state machines to look for in your own code: an onboarding flow where back should not always mean the previous screen, form field validation from empty through entering data and validating to valid or error, and the push-notification priming prompt before the system one.

## Who should watch?

iOS developers with tangled view controllers or coordinators they cannot test. The pattern is not Swift-specific, but Swift enums with associated values make it particularly clean.

Title: iOS gives you the Secure Enclave; the rest of the app is on you
Description: Julio Cesar Fernandez Munoz (Apple Coding Academy) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on how iOS security works and what developers must add with CryptoKit
Body:
The iPhone's hardware security is excellent, and it still does not protect the JSON file your app writes to disk. At Conf42 Mobile 2022, Julio Cesar Fernandez Munoz, Swift Developer Evangelist and podcaster at Apple Coding Academy, walked from the history of iOS security to the code a developer has to write: file protection classes, hashing and encryption with CryptoKit, and the easy leaks through app snapshots and backups.

Roughly half background, half Swift code you can lift into a project.

## How did iPhone security get here?

He starts with Darwin, the BSD-based kernel under every Apple OS, then goes back to the first iPhone, which was far less secure than the phones of 2022. No third-party apps (the official answer was web apps), but code signing from day one: only code signed by Apple would run. A crypto coprocessor held two AES keys burned into the chip, a global GID key and a per-device UID key. Everything else was weak by modern standards: the passcode sat in the keychain unhashed, so clearing that record opened the phone to anyone; the keychain was an SQLite database where only password items were encrypted, all with one key; and the file system was not encrypted at all.

The modern picture rests on the Secure Enclave, introduced with the A7: a black box that encrypts and decrypts on request, holds Touch ID and Face ID data, and never lets keys leave the chip, with a unique key per file. On top sit entitlements controlling access to things like iCloud, ASLR, and execute-never memory pages so injected code cannot run.

## What does App Transport Security force on you?

All networking goes through URLSession, so Alamofire and AFNetworking are wrappers around it. ATS has required modern TLS, strong certificate keys and forward-secret key agreement since the end of 2016, with narrow exceptions such as localhost while debugging.

## Which file protection class should you use?

This is the most practical section. There are four classes:

- **None**: no encryption beyond the file system being mounted.
- **Complete until first user authentication**: the default. Encrypted until the first passcode entry after boot, then readable even while the phone is locked, which is what music, podcasts, Bluetooth and location need.
- **Complete unless open**: encrypted when locked, except files already open, which are encrypted once the process closes them. Good for background uploads and downloads.
- **Complete**: encrypted and unreadable whenever the device is locked. His choice for most data.

In code, that is a write with the atomic option (write to a temporary file, then move it into place) plus complete file protection.

## What should you never store in plain files?

Anything sensitive. JSON, plists, Core Data and SQLite are all readable by anyone who gets at the files. Audit what the app stores before writing it, keep some data only on the server or in memory, use the system containers (keychain, HealthKit) where they exist, and encrypt local databases. Realm takes an encryption key; with Core Data you build a transparent encryption layer yourself. Even enum raw values in a sensitive data set should not be readable strings.

## How do you hash and encrypt with CryptoKit?

Three building blocks, all in a few lines:

- **Random bytes** from `SecRandomCopyBytes` into a byte array, turned into `Data`: cryptographically secure random numbers to use as keys.
- **Password hashing** with HMAC-SHA256 and a symmetric key, stored as Base64, and validated by recomputing the authentication code, never by decrypting.
- **Encryption** with AES-GCM (or ChaCha20, the other algorithm he recommends), which gives confidentiality and integrity together and parallelises well. Seal the data with a key and authenticating data, store the combined sealed box, and open it later with the same pair. RC4 and 3DES are out.

## What about screenshots and backups?

When an app goes to the background, iOS snapshots its last screen for the app switcher. In SwiftUI, the `privacySensitive` modifier blurs a view in that state; in UIKit, observe the will-resign-active notification, cover the screen with a blank view controller, and dismiss it on did-become-active. And mark key files as excluded from backup through their URL resource values, because an unencrypted iTunes backup is the easy way into an app's files.

## Is any of this enough?

No device is ever 100% secure, he says, and patching fast is the only defence against zero-days. His closing advice is to wrap these practices in your own Swift package and reuse it, keep third-party libraries updated, or skip them and go native. Julio Cesar Fernandez Munoz said at Conf42 Mobile 2022: "we don't know who is behind a third party library and we are relying on their good faith and good security practice blindly."

## Who should watch?

iOS developers who store anything sensitive on the device and have never chosen a file protection class on purpose. Security engineers will know the theory; the CryptoKit and snapshot code is the reason to watch.

Title: Getting your first iOS job? Record the interview and pick the supervisor
Description: Ivan Besarab (Innit.inc) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on starting as an iOS developer, from courses and GitHub to the first job and career moves
Body:
The most useful career tip in Ivan Besarab's short Conf42 Mobile 2022 talk costs nothing: record your technical interviews. Besarab, iOS Team Lead at Innit.inc, with seven years as an iOS engineer and about six teaching iOS courses, lays out a three-stage roadmap for people starting out (education, first job, building a career) with networking running underneath all three.

It is a ten-minute talk for beginners, and it says so. No code, just the advice a team lead gives a junior over lunch.

## What should you learn first?

Start by finding out whether coding is for you: anyone can code, so give it a shot. Pick a course with no prerequisites and work through it lesson by lesson, assignment by assignment. Besarab prefers small chunks. The order he recommends is basics, then object-oriented programming together with UI (SwiftUI or Interface Builder, it does not matter which), then patterns, from delegation up to MVC, MVP and MVVM.

He measures the result by three things. The most important is being able to solve problems on your own: take a loop over a collection and work out the multidimensional version, search well, and adapt a Stack Overflow answer to your code. Second, a GitHub profile; as a hiring lead he wants to see how your study progressed through demo projects. Third, optional but a large plus, an app you actually shipped to the App Store, linked from your resume.

How long it takes varies. Some of his students became developers in two or three months, others took a year. Quality matters more than speed.

## How do you get through the first interview?

Collect the technical requirements from real job ads into a list, then work through the blind spots. You do not need to know all of Foundation and UIKit, just the general things: how arrays and dictionaries work, objects versus structs, what Swift is.

Then the tip. Ivan Besarab said at Conf42 Mobile 2022 that you should "record your interview to get back to any question at any time." A failed interview becomes study material, on top of whatever feedback the interviewer gives you.

When the company asks whether you have questions, ask about the team you would join and, if possible, talk to its members. For a first job you will stay six months to two years, and a good supervisor bends the learning curve sharply upward. Besarab is blunt about the alternative: starting as the only developer on a team was not a good experience for him, and he does not recommend it. Finally, do not accept the first offer. Ask for another week, compare, then decide.

## When is it time to move?

His red flags: your skills have not improved in two years, or your work has turned into routine tasks with no challenge. Then ask for a different team or change company. He also interviews at other companies about every six months, even when he is not planning to leave: he learns something every time, sees what other teams are building, and an offer in hand is a good argument for a raise.

## Why does networking sit under everything?

Because a lot of his career decisions came from the people around him. Hackathons, conferences and meetups are where those connections start. His summary: invest in education, avoid being a solo developer on your first job, take on challenges, and remember that IT is as much about people as about software.

## Who should watch?

People learning iOS development or just past their first course, and anyone mentoring them. Experienced developers will not learn new Swift here, though the six-monthly interview habit might start an argument at your next one-on-one.

Title: A video editor inside your Android app, in five steps and one SDK
Description: Giovanni Laquidara (Huawei) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on adding video editing to an Android app with HMS Core Video Editor Kit, from setup to timelines
Body:
Building video editing into an Android app from scratch means timelines, codecs, effects and a UI people can actually use. At Conf42 Mobile 2022, Giovanni Laquidara, Developer Advocate at Huawei, showed the shortcut his employer sells: HMS Core Video Editor Kit, which gets a working editor screen into an app in five steps, plus a lower-level SDK for teams that want their own UI.

To be clear about scope: this is a vendor walkthrough of Huawei's own kit. Laquidara says it runs on Android smartphones from Android 7 up, not only Huawei devices.

## Why would an app need an editor at all?

His starting point is that video is now the main content on phones, and the videos people share are rarely raw recordings: they add stickers, sound effects and text. Standalone editors exist, the social apps build their own, and Laquidara argues the Android editors on Google Play often lag behind their iOS counterparts because the work is hard. A drop-in kit is his answer for teams that want editing as a feature rather than a product.

## What are the five steps?

Before step one there is a prerequisite: a Huawei ID and access to the AppGallery Connect developer console, which he says takes a couple of days.

1. **Console setup.** Create the app in AppGallery Connect, enable Video Editor Kit under Manage APIs, note your API key, and download `agconnect-services.json`, the configuration file that plays the same role as Google's services JSON.
2. **Gradle.** Add Huawei's Maven repository and the AppGallery Connect plugin to the project build file, then apply the plugin and add the Video Editor UI SDK as a dependency in the app build file.
3. **Permissions.** The list looks long, and he explains each one: internet because the kit is API-based, external storage read and write to import material and export the result, microphone to record voice-over, and vibrate, which is how the editor tells users they dropped a sticker or text outside the allowed area.
4. **Export callback.** A mandatory `MediaExportCallback`, so the SDK knows what to do once a video is exported. His sample just logs.
5. **Launch.** Set a license ID (an identifier for your user, which you can use to assign quotas; a random UUID works for a demo), set the API key, register the callback, and launch the editor activity.

The result is a full editor screen: import clips, arrange them on a timeline, add stickers, effects and text, then export.

## Can you change what users see?

Partly, from the console. Stickers, effects and other material come from Huawei's library, and the Video Editor Kit section of AppGallery Connect lets you choose which are available to your users. Custom material was not supported yet. Giovanni Laquidara said at Conf42 Mobile 2022: "But you still cannot upload your own resources." No custom PNG or GIF stickers; he described that as a future feature.

## And if the stock UI does not fit?

That is what the second SDK is for, which Huawei calls the fundamental capability SDK. Swap the UI dependency for the plain video editor SDK and you get the engine without the screens. The structure is worth knowing even if you never touch this kit, because it is how most editing engines are shaped:

- A `HuaweiVideoEditor` object, created once and initialised with its environment, attached to a layout of your own (a LinearLayout is enough) as its display.
- A timeline inside it, made of lanes: a video lane for clips, images and transitions, an audio lane for music and sound, a sticker lane for stickers and text, and effect lanes for sound and video effects.
- Append methods on each lane to add your own assets, playback control with a play callback and a play-timeline call taking start and end times, and an export manager that writes the final file with the properties you choose.

Both flavours are in Huawei's HMS Core GitHub organisation as a video editor demo, with the UI demo and the SDK demo in separate directories.

## Who should watch?

Android developers who need video editing as a feature, not as their core product, and are fine with a Huawei account and a Huawei-hosted service behind it. If you want to understand editing internals, the lane-based timeline model is the useful part; the rest is setup.

Title: Imposter syndrome never leaves, so learn to read it as a signal
Description: Mihailo Joksimovic (JAGGAER) at Conf42 Python 2022 on why imposter syndrome can't be beaten, only fought, and six tools for doing it
Body:
You do not get rid of imposter syndrome; you learn to fight it. That is the premise of Mihailo Joksimovic's talk at Conf42 Python 2022. The head of platform development at JAGGAER, drawing on more than seven years of therapy, argues the feeling is less a verdict than a signal that you are leaving your comfort zone, and offers six practical tools for living with it.

There is no Python in this talk, and that is fine. It is a personal, candid one, and he admits that preparing it triggered one of his biggest imposter attacks yet.

## How does a fast career turn into burnout?

His story will sound familiar to plenty of engineers. Programming since he was six, he climbed quickly and was a team lead by his early to mid 20s, leading people around ten years older. He assumed it was luck and that he had to prove himself, so he worked ten to 12 hours a day. Past the point of diminishing returns, productivity dropped, the inner voice got louder, and his only answer was more work.

It ended with a morning when he felt physically sick at the thought of one more day at the office. He quit, bought a motorcycle, partied for months, then hit wild daily mood swings. A friend suggested professional help, and what he expected to fix one problem became seven years of therapy, which he calls one of the best things he ever did for his life and career. Therapy gave him names for it: burnout, perfectionism, imposter syndrome, and a concept he calls mental debt, which builds up like tech debt from intellectual work until it threatens the whole codebase, so to speak.

His perfectionism self-test hits home: have you ever had code that solved the problem on time, then rewritten it until the deadline anyway?

## Where does the feeling come from?

He traces the term to a late-1970s study of around 150 highly successful women who, despite recognition, all reported feeling like frauds; later work found it gender neutral. The more successful people are, he says, the more intense the feeling.

For the why, he leans on evolution and a lab study in which mice whose dopamine centres were stimulated to feel good all the time stopped looking for food and starved. Discomfort is what makes you move. "If you sucked at your job, you wouldn't feel like a fraud," Mihailo Joksimovic said at Conf42 Python 2022.

## The toolbox

- **Acknowledge it.** Everyone has it and always will. Engineers rarely share these feelings, and the isolation makes them worse, which is why he asked viewers to post theirs in the conference Discord.
- **Read biographies.** Honest ones show almost every successful person felt it; the difference is how they dealt with it.
- **Discipline.** His number one tool: a fixed daily slot, say 6 to 7 pm for job applications or writing, whether you feel like it or not. Motivation is optional in his version; the slot is not.
- **Review your successes.** He journals a few times a week in the Day One app and schedules monthly or quarterly reviews of what he actually achieved.
- **Do something you suck at.** His was the guitar. Watching yourself improve while the doubts stay put proves the doubts are not data.
- **Therapy.** He has done rational emotive behaviour therapy, gestalt and psychodrama, and recommends it to anyone who can afford it.

His reading list: Tim Ferriss's Tools of Titans, Extreme Ownership, Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow (it took him about four months), and Atomic Habits.

## Who should watch

Engineers newly promoted to lead, anyone who has rewritten working code out of dread, and managers who want language for what their team is not saying out loud.

Title: Migrating a seven-year-old Android app to Compose, one screen at a time
Description: Ahmed Tikiwa (Luno) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on moving an XML app to Jetpack Compose screen by screen with ComposeView, state hoisting and lazy lists
Body:
You do not have to rewrite an Android app to get it onto Jetpack Compose. At Conf42 Mobile 2022, Ahmed Tikiwa, Senior Software Engineer (Android) at Luno, showed how he moved Up Next TV Series Manager, a side project in production on Google Play since 2015, from XML layouts to Compose one screen at a time, keeping fragments and Jetpack Navigation in place until the very end.

It is a practitioner's migration log, with the code for every screen and the gotchas he hit along the way.

## Why bother leaving XML?

Tikiwa's case against the imperative approach is the familiar one: an XML tree of widgets, `findViewById` to walk it, and manual `setText` calls to keep it in sync with state. Set a value on a node that has already been removed and you get an exception; the more views, the more maintenance. Compose replaces that with Kotlin functions that describe the UI for a given state. He quotes Monzo on how much easier code is to trace when it all lives in Kotlin, often in one file, and Twitter on collapsing a theming layer spread over several XML files into one Kotlin file.

He also admits he put off learning it. When he did, it was the official Compose pathway on the Android Developers site (quiz and badge included) plus two Udemy courses, because he learns visually.

## Which migration strategy?

The Android docs offer two: bottom-up (buttons and text views first, then their parents) and top-down (fragments and containers first, then the small pieces). Interoperability is what makes either possible: Compose code can sit next to XML, because Google knows a full overhaul is expensive.

Tikiwa went screen by screen. In each fragment's layout he deleted everything (TextViews, RecyclerViews, a NestedScrollView, the ConstraintLayout, a LinearProgressIndicator) and left a single `ComposeView` as the container. The fragment references it through data binding and calls `setContent`. Once navigation moves to Compose Navigation, the fragments and the ComposeViews go away.

## What broke?

Composition disposal. By default, Compose disposes of the composition when the view detaches from the window, and inside a fragment that is not what you want. Ahmed Tikiwa said at Conf42 Mobile 2022: "without adding this set view composition strategy, my app actually crashed." The fix is `setViewCompositionStrategy` with `DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed`.

Theming was the other bridge. Wrapping each screen in `MdcTheme` from the Material theme adapter reads the existing XML theme and maps it onto Compose's Material theme, so migrated and unmigrated screens look the same. Once everything is Compose, he can write his own theme files and drop the adapter.

## What does a migrated screen look like?

The search screen is the worked example. `SearchScreen` gets its ViewModel through `hiltViewModel()`, turns the ViewModel's LiveData into state with `observeAsState`, and lays out a full-screen `Surface` with a `Column`. A `Box`, Compose's FrameLayout, stacks the progress indicator on top of the results so the list does not jump when loading finishes.

The core concept is state hoisting: keep composables as stateless as possible and push state up to the caller. His rule of thumb is that state comes down and events go up. `SearchArea` takes the results plus two callbacks, `onTextSubmit` and `onResultClick`, and `SearchScreen` decides what they mean: tell the ViewModel about the query, or call the NavController to open show details. The query itself lives in `rememberSaveable`, so it survives process recreation.

The RecyclerView, adapter, view holder and item layout all disappear in favour of `LazyColumn`. The dashboard reuses one `ShowsRow` composable built on `LazyRow` for yesterday, today and tomorrow's schedule. The Trakt favourites screen uses `LazyVerticalGrid`. Small reusable pieces such as a `SectionHeadingText` keep headings consistent across the app.

## What is left?

His to-do list is honest: the toolbar and bottom app bar, Compose Navigation with `Scaffold` instead of `Surface`, replacing `observeAsState` with mutable state, animations, and tests for the composables. The app is now open source, with the migration on a feature branch. His advice is to go step by step: early composables feel like a lot of code, but once they are reusable, the next screen goes much faster.

## Who should watch?

Android developers with a large XML codebase who want to start on Compose without a big-bang rewrite. If you already write Compose daily, the ComposeView and theme adapter sections are still a useful checklist for the legacy corners.

- Abhishek Doshi on [managing app state with BLoC in Flutter](https://www.conf42.com/Mobile_2022_Abhishek_Doshi_Manage_blocks_of_your_app_bloc__flutter), the same declarative ideas on another toolkit.
- Nicola Zaghini on [React Native and cross-platform](https://www.conf42.com/Mobile_2022_Nicola_Zaghini_dreaming_reactnative_crossplatform) at Conf42 Mobile 2022.

Title: Dev containers turned a failed hackathon into 3-hour onboarding
Description: Yshay Yaacobi (Livecycle) at Conf42 Python 2022 on dev containers, SOPS, Tilt and k3d for repos that build and run on day one
Body:
The company hackathon for Tweak, an open-source feature management project, produced very few features. Most developers spent the day trying to build and run it. At Conf42 Python 2022, Yshay Yaacobi, Co-Founder and CTO of Livecycle and Tweak's creator, showed how dev containers fix that: the whole development environment, runtimes, tools, IDE extensions, secrets, even a Kubernetes cluster, lives in the repo and starts with the editor.

It is a demo-heavy talk, four projects of rising complexity, and every tool in it is open source. "I'm not selling anything," he said.

## Why is a new codebase so painful?

He lists what anyone who has joined a team will recognise: the wrong OS, a missing or conflicting SDK (Python 2 or 3?), package managers throwing errors that feel random, a README full of magic scripts, a root CA to install. Then debugging will not attach, autocomplete is broken, file watching and hot reload fail, and integration tests do not run. And you do it all again in a few months because the project or your machine drifted.

His target is an environment that is consistent, reproducible, isolated and self-contained, which sounds a lot like containers. VS Code's remote containers feature gets there: the UI stays local while the extensions, language server, debugger and terminal run inside the container.

## Four demos, rising complexity

**An old Go CLI.** A devcontainer.json points at a Dockerfile that installs Go with modules disabled, the dep tool and zsh plugins, plus the right VS Code extensions. Go is not installed on his laptop, yet the terminal, autocomplete and tests all work inside the container.

**A Python Flask email sender.** New problems: secrets and a server you need to reach. Secrets live in the repo encrypted with Mozilla SOPS (here with a GPG key; it can also use AWS KMS or HashiCorp Vault). Keys stay readable, values encrypted, so diffs and history still make sense. An init script decrypts them into an env file for Flask. A committed launch.json gives everyone the same debug setup, and VS Code forwards port 5001 from the container automatically, breakpoints included.

**Tweak itself.** Several microservices in different languages, databases and messaging. The dev container runs Docker in Docker, installs .NET, Go, Node.js and Tilt, and a Docker Compose file describes the stack. Tilt adds the feedback loop: rebuild images on code change, hot reload for the editor UI. Cloud dependencies are swapped for compatible local ones, MinIO for Amazon S3 and an OpenID Connect mock server for Google sign-in.

**A Kubernetes cost-monitoring tool.** k3d creates a k3s cluster with a registry inside the dev container, Helm installs Prometheus, and Tilt builds, pushes and deploys. Delete the cluster, rerun the init, and in under a minute everything is back.

## What it buys a real team

At Livecycle, with tens of microservices in Go and TypeScript, custom Kubernetes resources and a CI engine, he reports a build-run-test loop of under 10 seconds, onboarding a new developer in under 3 hours (including provisioning an AWS machine), and adding a new tool in under five minutes. The setup works on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

He lists the costs too: the initial setup takes time, some tools are bleeding edge, the environment is more code to maintain, and the approach leans on VS Code, Docker and Linux. Alternatives he mentions include Gitpod, Theia and JetBrains Gateway.

## Who should watch

Tech leads tired of the onboarding wiki, maintainers who want contributors to get past the build step, and platform teams standardising developer environments. The examples and slides are on his GitHub.

Title: Android accessibility checks are one Espresso line away
Description: Nav Singh (Manulife) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on making Android apps accessible in XML and Compose, and testing it with TalkBack, Scanner and Espresso
Body:
Most Android teams already have Espresso tests, and most of those tests could be checking accessibility for free. At Conf42 Mobile 2022, Nav Singh, Mobile Software Engineer at Manulife (and a GDG Montreal organiser and Google Developer Expert for Android), walked through the attributes that make an Android UI usable with a screen reader, then showed how to catch the misses with TalkBack, Accessibility Scanner and a single line in your UI tests.

It is a hands-on introduction, mostly XML views with a look at Jetpack Compose, ending in a live demo in Android Studio on a mirrored Pixel.

## Why should a product team care?

Singh gives two reasons. Reach: according to the World Bank, 15% of the world's population has some type of disability, a user base many apps never considered. And versatility: accessible apps are easier for everyone, whether they are on a D-pad, a keyboard or one-handed on a bus.

On Android the main channel is spoken feedback: TalkBack reads out whatever is on screen as the user moves through it. Everything else in the talk is about making that readout make sense.

## What should you fix first?

He lists four basics.

- **Task flows.** Important tasks such as resetting a password should not hide five or six taps deep behind a drawer, settings and profile. Users leave, and leave a bad rating on the way out.
- **Touch target size.** Fancy custom views drawn at 20 by 20 dp are hard to hit. Material guidelines say at least 48 dp. Stock buttons and Material Compose components already meet it; your custom view probably does not.
- **Labels.** Images that act or inform need a content description; decorative ones should be hidden from accessibility services.
- **Focus-based navigation.** Screen readers and D-pads follow the order of elements in the XML. If your layout needs another order, define it.

## Which attributes do the work?

The XML tour is the reference section of the talk:

- `android:contentDescription` for meaningful images, and `importantForAccessibility` set to no (or a null description) for decorative ones.
- `focusable` and `screenReaderFocusable` (Android P and up) to control what TalkBack stops on, and `accessibilityHeading` (also P and up) for heading-to-heading navigation through long text like terms and conditions.
- `nextFocusForward`, plus the up, down, left and right variants, for custom focus order.
- `labelFor` to tie a TextView label to an EditText in older layouts that predate TextInputLayout.
- `accessibilityLiveRegion` for views that appear conditionally, such as a login error. Polite waits for TalkBack to finish its current sentence; assertive interrupts it.
- Marking a list item's parent as focusable so a contact row with name, surname and date of birth is read as one item instead of five.

In Compose the same ideas live in `contentDescription` and `semantics`, with properties for headings, live regions and focus order via focus requesters. His sample code is on GitHub.

## How do you test it?

Manual first: turn on TalkBack and walk the app screen by screen. Then Accessibility Scanner from the Play Store, which snapshots a screen and flags colour contrast (with the current and suggested ratio and colours), touch target size and missing labels, in a report you can share with the team. Android Studio's lint already warns about missing descriptions and contrast problems while you edit XML. Google Play's pre-launch report adds an accessibility section before release. And user testing with real people.

The automated part is the hook. Nav Singh said at Conf42 Mobile 2022: "there is only a single line of code that you need to add and there is one dependency that you need to add to your build file and you will be good to go." Enable Espresso's accessibility checks, set them to run from the root view so one narrow test still audits the whole screen, and suppress known results by matcher (a specific contrast issue on a specific view id) when you need to.

The demo is honest about how this goes. After fixing the contrast and the missing description, he reran the tests expecting green, and both failed: a Compose view still lacked a label readable by screen readers. Which is exactly the point of putting the check in CI.

## Who should watch?

Android developers who have never turned TalkBack on in their own app, and teams that want accessibility regressions to fail a build rather than reach a user. Compose-only teams will want the Compose docs alongside it, since most examples are XML.

Title: Your APM says what broke, not which line, so ask the server
Description: Shai Almog (Lightrun) at Conf42 Python 2022 on continuous observability, adding logs, snapshots and metrics to running production code
Body:
An APM dashboard can tell you a web service got slow. It cannot tell you which line of code did it. At Conf42 Python 2022, Shai Almog, Developer Advocate at Lightrun, made the case for continuous observability: instead of instrumenting everything up front, you ask the running server a specific question, a log line, a snapshot, a counter, and it instruments just that spot, with no redeploy.

Honest scope: this is a vendor talk, and the demos are Lightrun's product, but the argument about where APMs and logs run out applies whatever tool you use.

## Why are logs and APMs not enough?

Almog loves APMs and says so. "When I started, we used to monitor the server by kicking it and listening to see if the hard drive was spinning properly," Shai Almog said at Conf42 Python 2022. Kubernetes-scale deployments made dashboards essential. But the dashboard is a check engine light: it points at a performance problem or an error spike, then you drop from a jet engine to stone tools, grepping logs and hoping the line you need is there.

Usually it is not, because you cannot log everything: billing and performance would suffer, and nobody knows in advance where the bugs will be. So the loop is add a log, go through CI/CD and QA, reproduce in production with fingers crossed, repeat. That can take hours per round while the bug stays live.

APMs have their own physics problem. The more you instrument, the more runtime overhead, the more hosts, the more complexity. "By observing, we effectively change some of the outcome," he said, a line he thinks Schrodinger should have delivered. Vendors let you tune the ratio of observability to performance, which means less data exactly when you need more.

Traditional debuggers are no answer either: insecure remotely, they can block a server, and they stop at one machine and one language.

## How continuous observability works

The developer works in the IDE (he demos PyCharm and VS Code) through a plugin. Requests go to a management server, SaaS or on premises, which talks to a small agent on the production or staging servers. Developers never touch production directly; ops keep the line between dev and ops, they just connect the agent. Because the tool is surgical, it costs almost nothing when idle and only pays overhead at the one spot you asked about.

## What he showed

- **Dynamic logs** in a Flask hello world: inject a log of any expression at runtime, piped to the IDE or merged with the app's own logs.
- **Snapshots:** like a breakpoint that does not break. It captures the stack and variables without stopping the thread, so no user waits on your debugging. Conditions can narrow it to one user.
- **Apache Airflow:** workers are short-lived, so by the time you set a snapshot the worker is gone. Tags apply actions to every agent that comes up with that tag.
- **Polyglot:** the same log flow on a Kotlin prime counter, and metrics on a Java demo: counters, method duration and tic-toc timing of a code block, which can be piped to StatsD and Prometheus.

## The safety bits

Expressions run in a sandbox; anything too expensive or that changes state is rejected. The agent pulls requests from the server rather than the other way round, so the server can sit behind a firewall. PII redaction masks patterns such as credit card numbers before they reach logs, and a blocklist stops developers from placing actions in sensitive files, classes or methods. Supported runtimes at the time: JVM languages, Node.js and Python.

## Who should watch

Python and backend developers who live in the add-a-log-and-redeploy loop, and SREs deciding how much production access developers should have. If you want a vendor-neutral survey, look elsewhere; if you want to see the idea working end to end, this is a tidy demo.

Title: Your app's carbon footprint starts on the iPhone battery screen
Description: Manuel Carrasco Molina (StuFF mc) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on what developers and their companies can do about CO2, from battery drain to flights
Body:
Manuel Carrasco Molina has been writing software for 24 years and building for the iPhone since 2008, and at Conf42 Mobile 2022 he used his slot for something other than SwiftUI: a call for developers to treat CO2 as a technical concern. His argument is that every developer has two levers, the code and the company, and that both are bigger than they look.

Be warned, this is not a green-software benchmarking talk. Carrasco Molina describes himself as a political (h)activist: ten years with the Green party in Germany, local and regional council seats, and a sideline filming climate protests. About half the talk is activism; the other half is a checklist an iOS team can act on the same week.

## Why bring climate into a mobile conference?

He opens with the curve everyone has seen: warming at roughly 1.2 degrees, with 1.5 as the line to hold. Then he gets local. The lignite pit a few kilometres from his home, which he calls the biggest polluter in Germany, produces as much CO2 every year as New Zealand. Next to it, what is left of the Hambach forest, saved by years of protest. His point: activists and politicians move these decisions, and Germany's coal exit discussion moved from 2045 to 2030 because people pushed.

He does not ask anyone to go vegan tomorrow. He took years himself, through pescatarian and vegetarian stages, before going vegan.

## What can you change in the code?

This is the part iOS developers will bookmark.

**Look at the battery list.** Settings, then Battery, is where users go when their phone dies early, and you do not want your app on it. His example is the Tagesschau news app, which had drained 27% of his battery in only 18 minutes of use. Something in there was working far harder than the user. He wants developers to profile energy in Xcode, where his example shows an app hitting location 30% of the time, and wants users to report hungry apps to their developers.

**Keep it small.** Open the network inspector and you will probably find a 4 MB picture that could be 600 KB. Question the 100 MB video on the front page, and never autoplay it, which is bad for the planet and for the user.

**Respect OLED.** A dark pixel on an OLED screen is a pixel that is switched off, so dark mode saves real energy on every iPhone since the X.

**Ship less often.** He turned off automatic app updates, partly to avoid the apps that ship a new build every two-week sprint whether you need it or not, and partly because each manual update reminds him to delete apps he never opens.

## And the company?

Run on 100% renewable energy, ideally from your own solar panels, otherwise from a pure renewable provider, not a mixed utility that also digs coal. He credits Apple for going carbon neutral and says it is not enough: he wants companies to aim for 200% renewable and carbon negative, as Ecosia does. Ecosia is also his search engine tip: founded by Christian Kroll, built on Bing results, and putting 80% of its profits into planting trees.

The rest of the list is office culture: vegan catering, bulk breakfast cereal in 10 kg packages, ceramic cups, reusable pizza packaging. And remote work: his company was moving into an office for 35 people with 70 employees. When you do commute, walk, bike or take the train, an EV is the worst acceptable case. He stopped flying in 2018 and took the train all day to iOSDevUK in Wales.

His closing ask is about what we build. Carrasco Molina said at Conf42 Mobile 2022: "Make an app that does good for the world, not just the next useless app."

## Who should watch?

Mobile developers who want a concrete energy checklist, and engineering leads who set office, travel and hosting policy. If you came for measured carbon numbers per API call, this is the wrong talk; it is a wake-up call with practical tips attached.

Title: A live Wikipedia edits dashboard in Python, Kafka and Pinot
Description: Mark Needham (StarTree) at Conf42 Python 2022 on building an auto-refreshing analytics dashboard with Streamlit, Apache Pinot and Apache Kafka
Body:
Real-time, user-facing analytics sounds like a platform team's six-month project. At Conf42 Python 2022, Mark Needham, Developer Relations Engineer at StarTree, built one in a single demo: the Wikimedia recent changes feed streamed into Apache Kafka, ingested into Apache Pinot, and queried by a Streamlit app that refreshes every 5 seconds. Almost every piece of glue is a Python library.

It is a demo-led talk with the code on GitHub (mneedham/pinot-wiki), so you can follow along afterwards.

## What does user-facing analytics actually require?

He starts from Gartner's definition of real-time analytics, logic and math applied to data for making better decisions quickly, then adds the user-facing part: giving analytical queries to end users, not just internal analysts. That means two things at once. Data must be queryable as soon as it arrives, and queries must come back in milliseconds while lots of users run them concurrently.

His examples are familiar. The Uber Eats restaurant manager dashboard shows missed orders, inaccurate orders and downtime that need attention now. LinkedIn runs three flavours: the member-facing who-viewed-your-profile page, a recruiter dashboard, and internal product and BI tools.

## The pipeline, piece by piece

- **Source:** Wikimedia publishes every change to its properties over HTTP using server-sent events. A Python script reads it with requests and an SSE client.
- **Kafka:** the same script, wrapped in a while-true loop to reconnect on drops, pushes each event onto a Wikipedia events topic with a Kafka producer and flushes every hundred messages.
- **Pinot:** a schema defines dimension fields (id, wiki, user and so on) and a timestamp column; a real-time table points at the Kafka topic. Segments are set to 1,000 records, which he notes is far smaller than production but good for a demo.
- **Streamlit:** a script that queries Pinot through its Python client, loads results into a data frame and draws Plotly charts.

Everything runs locally from a Docker Compose file: ZooKeeper, Kafka, and the Pinot controller, broker and server.

## What the dashboard showed

Within minutes the overview counted around 2,000 changes in the last minute by 398 users across 61 domains. Bots made 27% of changes, humans 73%, and one top editor had made 548 changes in roughly seven minutes. The surprise for Needham was where the edits happen: mostly on Wikimedia Commons and Wikidata, not Wikipedia itself. The final tab is a drill-down, the pattern every analytics dashboard ends up needing: pick a user, see which properties they touch and what kinds of changes they make.

## Why Streamlit carries the front end

The app is plain procedural Python: an auto-refresh call, a title, a sidebar of radio buttons mapped to functions, SQL queries with a GROUP BY, data frames, charts. "It's just that streamlit is making it super easy to render it to the screen," Mark Needham said at Conf42 Python 2022. He admits one non-Python ingredient: a bit of YAML to wire Pinot to Kafka.

## Who should watch

Application developers and data engineers who have a stream and want to see something on screen fast, and Python developers curious about Pinot as a serving layer. It is an introduction: no tuning, indexing strategy or scaling numbers, just the shortest path from events to an interactive dashboard.

Title: Teaching OOP in Python to stop a 69% dropout rate
Description: Tiago Bacciotti Moreira at Conf42 Python 2022 on an eight-step way to teach object-oriented programming in Python that keeps students engaged
Body:
Brazilian technology courses lose students fast, and the first programming class is part of the reason. At Conf42 Python 2022, Tiago Bacciotti Moreira, who has taught Information Systems at the State University of Minas Gerais since 2010, walked through the pedagogical approach he built for teaching object-oriented programming in Python: start easy, raise the difficulty in small steps, work in groups, and use the tools real teams use from week one.

It is a teaching talk, built on a classroom experience rather than code, and it is refreshingly practical.

## Why do students drop out?

He cites a Brazilian survey showing a 69% dropout rate among technology course students, at a time when remote work had opened jobs to people in small towns like his. Many students arrive with weak foundations in math and logic from school, many work during the day to support their families, and the first months of programming become the place where they quit or switch to a course with less math.

Part of the problem, he argues, is the first language. Brazilian colleges long used C or Java for first contact. Put the Java hello world next to the Python one and count the concepts a beginner must accept on faith: class, void, main, String. Python's version is just print.

## The method, step by step

His proposal has eight steps.

1. **Easy to get started.** No local installs of IDEs, libraries and MySQL. Students use Repl.it, an online editor, from the first minutes of class, at home or on their lunch break.
2. **Clear problem definition.** Students often start typing before they understand the task, so each exercise is written to be understood first.
3. **Increasing difficulty.** The first exercise adds two numbers, the next converts metres to millimetres, and over nine exercise lists it climbs to a full create, retrieve, update, delete application. He borrows this from gamification, his master's topic: too easy loses motivation, too hard makes students give up.
4. **Collaborative work.** Students work in groups and are encouraged to search online and discuss solutions, with the teacher supervising.
5. **Real-world practices and tools.** Everyone opens a GitHub account and publishes their code.
6. **Multidisciplinary.** SQL, web, programming, requirements analysis and project management mixed, the way a real team works.
7. **All open and published.** Exercises, slides and code on GitHub, classes recorded on YouTube.
8. **Online classes,** forced by the pandemic.

"So everyone is encouraged to use GitHub from the first week," Tiago Bacciotti Moreira said at Conf42 Python 2022. He adds that the teacher stays central even with all the tooling: students look for solutions, but someone has to guide the search.

## What the students build

The intermediate exercises include a tic-tac-toe game (with no computer intelligence, but plenty of arrays and conditionals) and a currency quote lookup against a Brazilian public web service. The course ends with a CRUD application, which he treats as the proof that someone can work in a language: joining code and a database to record, retrieve, list, update and delete data.

The side effect he enjoyed most: after he blogged about the approach, students from other Brazilian states started emailing him for help with the exercises, having followed the recorded classes on YouTube.

## Who should watch

University and school teachers running a first or second programming course, and anyone designing onboarding for junior developers. The same principles, a zero-install start and a steady difficulty ramp, apply well outside the classroom.

Title: Your one UX hire is not a unicorn, so stop treating them like one
Description: Jessica Wirt (truematter) at Conf42 Mobile 2022 on why no single person can do UX alone, and how to make one UX hire count
Body:
Plenty of companies hire one UX person and expect them to fix the whole product. At Conf42 Mobile 2022, Jessica Wirt, Content Strategist at truematter, explained why that person does not exist, and how a team with budget for only one UX hire can still get most of the benefit: hire for the gap you actually have, put them inside the team, and let them spread the know-how.

It is a short, practical talk aimed at the people who write the job description and own the org chart, not at designers.

## Why can't one person do UX?

Because UX is a property of the whole product team, not a job. Wirt starts with what UX is not. It is not a band-aid you slap on a badly built product. It is not a phase at the end of a project. And it is not something one person does alone. In her words, "there is no such thing as a UX phase or quick UX tag on to make surface level changes."

She splits the hands-on product team into five disciplines: developers, visual designers, content strategists, user researchers and information architects. Inside each one sits a smaller group of people who do that job with users in mind. A UX developer guards against features nobody needs and builds toward consistent, usable patterns. A UX-minded visual designer thinks in tasks, not just tone and style. User researchers watch real people use the product and get surprised regularly, because people never use software the way you expect.

Wirt is an example herself: her title is UX strategist, but her background is content strategy. That, she argues, is where the value is: someone with a home discipline who also really knows UX.

## What does good UX actually buy you?

She shows a before-and-after of a healthcare website truematter rebuilt, the before being the familiar wall of links with no CMS behind it. The numbers she quotes from truematter client projects: a 45% increase in site traffic, a 65% reduction in maintenance over time, and a 465% increase in mobile use on a site similar to the healthcare one. Those come from a consultancy describing its own work, so treat them as what a full team can achieve, not a promise.

## How do you make a single UX hire work?

This is the useful half. Her process has four steps.

**Identify your gaps.** Before writing the job ad, map your team onto the five disciplines. Her example team is Romeo, a front-end developer, and Juliet, a back-end developer, which covers exactly one of the five. Also look for untapped skills: a developer who used to do visual design is a discipline you no longer need to hire for.

**Prioritise by upcoming work.** A team of developers about to build a pile of forms will find the code easy and the copy hard, so hire a content strategist or information architect. A patient-facing healthcare app leans on design and on understanding patients, so hire a visual designer or a user researcher.

**Support the new hire.** This is where most companies get it wrong. Wirt said at Conf42 Mobile 2022: "You treat your new hire like a UX unicorn, they will start to act like one." The unicorn's habitat, she adds, is the magical forest of LinkedIn, and you will not hear from them again. So never park the UX person on an island outside the team structure. Put them inside an existing team, doing real discipline work from day one, including reviewing other people's work.

**Share the know-how.** Be realistic: one person will not turn the team into UX professionals. The target is a UX-happy team, where one person is the expert and everyone else applies the basics. That progress may be what earns the budget for the second hire.

## Who should watch?

Engineering managers and product leads on mobile and web teams who are about to open a UX role, or who already have one and wonder why it is not working. Designers will recognise all of it; the talk is for the people around them.

Title: The snake game is secretly a math lesson
Description: Jeronimo Medina Madruga at Conf42 Python 2022 on teaching math with Python, games and music instead of a hundred repeated integrals
Body:
Students do not hate math, they just cannot see where it lands. At Conf42 Python 2022, Jeronimo Medina Madruga, drawing on his master's research in mathematics education in southern Brazil, argued that Python's open ecosystem lets teachers connect formulas to things students care about: a character's jump, a Street Fighter frame, a song, a snake game.

He says up front it is a light, non-technical talk: a tour of the problem and the tools, not a deep look at any one library.

## What is wrong with the way math is taught?

His research reading points to a gap. Teachers report that most students do not actually hate math, but they struggle to see where concepts apply. Repetition (hundreds of calculus exercises) and abstraction (x, y, delta, square roots) are the first suspects. Meanwhile assessments such as PISA show many developing countries stalling, while new jobs increasingly sit in STEM. He borrows Seth Godin's line that the economy has changed but the school has not.

The fix he proposes is not burning the books. It is praxis, mixing practice and theory, and making the student the protagonist: project-based learning, gamification, flipped classrooms. He illustrates praxis with Cobra Kai's rival dojos having to teach together, which is a better analogy than it has any right to be.

## Where does the math hide?

His examples are the good part. A quadratic equation stops being a ritual when it becomes the arc of a jumping character or a basketball throw. Fighting games run on frame data, which is arithmetic under pressure. Music is formulas, rhythm and tempo.

## Why proprietary math software does not fit

He is blunt about cost. In Brazil a US dollar was worth almost six reais at the time, so imported hardware plus yearly licences is out of reach for most public schools. Many tools are not translated, which matters where few students and teachers are fluent in English, and school hardware is old, so software must be light and run on Linux. He also compares drill-style tools to the Skinner teaching machine: useful for right or wrong, useless for understanding why an answer was wrong.

## The open toolbox

He deliberately starts outside Python: Logo (over 50 years old), Scratch from the MIT Media Lab, and Sonic Pi for making music in code. Then the Python side:

- Python Tutor, to visualise what a program does with its variables;
- the turtle module, Logo inside Python;
- the math and itertools modules for functions, permutations and combinations;
- JythonMusic as a Python alternative for music;
- BlockPy and EduBlocks, block programming that generates real Python and eases the jump from Scratch;
- Pygame for building games, and Anaconda with Jupyter notebooks as an interactive digital classroom.

"Python should not be seen only as a calculator," Jeronimo Medina Madruga said at Conf42 Python 2022. His argument is that the language matters less than the ecosystem: most of the time a teacher does not need to build anything, only to find the right package and read its documentation.

## The snake game

His closing example is a snake game of about 100 lines, which he says people can write in an hour and a half. Reading keys, direction, speed: it is vectors all the way down. "The snake game isn't only about the snake game, it's about math," he said, and the students often only notice afterwards.

He ends with a reading list: Al Sweigart's Invent Your Own Computer Games with Python, Peter Farrell's Math Adventures with Python, and Amit Saha's work on doing math with Python.

## Who should watch

Teachers and teacher trainers looking for free, Linux-friendly ways to bring programming into math lessons, and developers who volunteer in schools. If you want a Pygame tutorial, this is the map, not the territory.
