Title: Your Python profile is lying by omission, and eBPF fills in the C
Description: Yonatan Goldschmidt (Granulate) at Conf42 Python 2022 on PyPerf, an eBPF profiler that samples every Python process plus native and kernel stacks
Body:
Most Python profilers show you Python frames and politely hide everything underneath. At Conf42 Python 2022, Yonatan Goldschmidt, Principal Engineer and research team lead at Granulate, showed why that is a mistake: PyPerf, an open-source eBPF-based profiler his team extended, samples every Python process on a box at once and stitches Python, native and kernel stacks into one flame graph. His own toy function turned out to spend its time in places he did not expect.

It is a short, focused talk and a good first look at what eBPF changes for profiling.

## Why not just use cProfile?

He starts with the two families of Python profilers. Deterministic profilers such as cProfile (plus Pyinstrument and Yappi) instrument every call. They are accurate and versatile in development, but intrusive: they may need code or deployment changes, and his slides put the overhead at up to 2x slower code. Not something you attach to production.

Statistical profilers like py-spy take samples at an interval from outside the process. No code changes, negligible overhead on the application itself, production safe. The catch is that py-spy still costs the system: it reads the interpreter's memory through system calls. Goldschmidt's team hit that wall profiling a large CPython application with hundreds of threads at high frequency, where py-spy simply was not fast enough. It is also per process: 50 Python applications means 50 py-spy instances.

## What eBPF brings

eBPF grew out of the Berkeley Packet Filter, the in-kernel virtual machine that tcpdump used for socket filters. Today its programs can attach to almost any point in the kernel, and a verifier ensures only safe programs run: no arbitrary syscalls, no arbitrary memory writes. For a profiler the key property is speed of access. An eBPF program can read the memory of the running Python process far faster than an external tool making system calls. His quick demo was opensnoop, a few lines of bpftrace that hook the open syscall and print every file opened on the machine.

## PyPerf: from proof of concept to system-wide profiler

PyPerf started as a proof of concept in the BCC repository (there is a Ruby sibling, rbperf). Granulate took it much further:

- support for all current CPython versions;
- system-wide: one PyPerf profiles every Python process on the host;
- native stacks, so C extensions such as json, pickle and NumPy, interpreter code and native libraries show up;
- kernel stacks, so you see the system calls your code triggers.

He notes these were relatively easy to add precisely because PyPerf runs on eBPF; a user-land profiler would have struggled to get there.

## Native code is not noise

The best part of the talk is a small exercise. He shows a short Python function and asks you to guess where the time goes, then reveals the native profile. String concatenation with += dominated, which he half expected. What surprised him was how much time went to calls to chr(), to loading globals, and to the % operator, while the comparison he had suspected barely registered.

"From our experience, we know that taking the native profile into account is very important when you want to truly understand what's going on," Yonatan Goldschmidt said at Conf42 Python 2022. The profile handed him a ranked to-do list: replace += with a join, cache the chr() results, then avoid the % operator. Many profilers drop native frames on the theory that you cannot change C code anyway. His point is that the C code tells you which Python line to change.

## Who should watch

Python engineers chasing CPU in production, and anyone who has stared at a py-spy flame graph and wondered what the interpreter was really doing. It is an introduction, not an eBPF internals session. PyPerf ships as part of gProfiler, Granulate's open-source, system-wide profiler that also covers Java, Go and Ruby.

Title: Don't touch the tested container, bolt a Python sidecar onto the pod
Description: Moshe Zadka (Palo Alto Networks) at Conf42 Python 2022 on small Python sidecars for readiness, metrics and scheduled jobs in Kubernetes pods
Body:
The application is built, the container passes its tests, and now someone wants readiness checks and Prometheus metrics. At Conf42 Python 2022, Moshe Zadka, Principal Engineer at Palo Alto Networks, made the case for leaving that container alone and adding a small Python sidecar to the pod instead, and set himself the challenge of fitting each sidecar's code on one slide.

It is a fast, funny talk with a Kubernetes refresher up front and a party trick at the end.

## What do you need to know about pods first?

A pod is the unit Kubernetes runs, though not usually what you configure. Its containers always share a network namespace, so 127.0.0.1 is the same for all of them; they may share the process namespace and volume mounts; they never share the filesystem. Readiness answers whether the pod is good, and it matters because a Service routes only to good pods. TCP and HTTP checks are the norm, and he steers people away from command checks.

A sidecar is not a Kubernetes type, just a shape your YAML takes: an extra container next to the one that does the work. He is cheerfully uninterested in arguing what counts as a true sidecar. The classic example is a web app caching to files, with a sidecar that deletes the old ones.

## Why split it out at all?

Three reasons. Each container gets its own resource limits, which helps capacity planning. Restarts and logs stay separate, so dashboards and tools like Prometheus see each one clearly. And both containers stay simple, with Kubernetes handling the supervision you would otherwise write yourself.

Python fits the job because sidecar needs show up late, when the schedule is tight, and because the sidecar is often owned by a different team (infrastructure, SRE) and has to keep up as the main container changes. Quick prototyping and quick iteration matter more than raw speed here.

## The sidecars on a slide

All of them talk to the main container over localhost with httpx, served by Pyramid where they need an endpoint.

- **Readiness.** Fetch a JSON value from the app and raise an exception if it is not 5, so the framework returns a 500. His exception of choice is dividing one by zero, the shortest code that raises in Python.
- **Metrics.** A Prometheus client registry with a latency gauge, fed by a synthetic request to the app on every scrape, so you see slowdowns even if the app never measures itself.
- **Scheduler.** Call the app's flush-queues endpoint every 60 seconds. A CronJob would start a new pod; this has to flush the queue inside each running container.

## How do you read a log you can't see?

The finale is a log analyser for a container that writes to /var/log/something on its own filesystem, with no shared volume allowed. With shareProcessNamespace enabled on the pod, the sidecar reads the inode of its own root under /proc, loops over the other processes until it finds one whose root differs, and reads the peer's log through that process's root link, counting lines and posting them to a metrics endpoint every minute.

"That you can do the impossible in three slides, not even full slides worth of code," Moshe Zadka said at Conf42 Python 2022, admitting he had failed his one-slide rule.

## Make your containers sidecar friendly

His closing advice is aimed at whoever builds the main container: treat containers as black boxes and keep them simple, but give them good internal APIs, for example on a separate port that is exposed only to peers in the pod. Packaging into containers is good; packaging into separate containers is better.

## Who should watch

Python developers who deploy to Kubernetes, and SREs who keep being asked to add health checks to images they did not build. The code is written for slides, not production, as he says himself.

Title: Stop picking the best forecaster and let a network blend them
Description: Pawel Skrzypek (Omphalos Fund) and Anna Warno (7bulls.com) at Conf42 Python 2022 on ensembling time series forecasters, up to a neural ensembler
Body:
Which forecaster is best? Depends on the week. At Conf42 Python 2022, Pawel Skrzypek, CEO of Omphalos Fund, and Anna Warno of 7bulls.com showed why the winning answer in time series is usually several forecasters combined, and how a small neural network trained as the ensembler beat every simple combination on a real cloud-resource dataset.

Pawel gives the theory in about ten minutes; Anna spends the rest on a production case study.

## Why did ensembling win the M4 competition?

Ensembling simply means combining the outputs of several forecasters to get better accuracy and, just as important, more stable results, because one model having a bad period gets outvoted. The simple forms are voting for classification, averaging for regression, plus stacking and bagging.

Pawel's point is that the breakthroughs in the M4 and M5 competitions, run by forecasting veteran Spyros Makridakis, leaned on cleverer ensembling. The hybrid exponential smoothing model that won M4 rated every model on every series during training with sMAPE, after each epoch, and kept a set of the best models per series for the final prediction. N-BEATS, its successor, ensembles up to 100 models trained on different subsets of the data, different loss functions and different horizons, so no single wrong model can spoil the forecast. For the financial series he works on, he says, ensembling significantly improves both accuracy and robustness.

## The real problem: forecasting cloud usage in real time

Anna's case is a system that forecasts cloud resource usage and decides whether to scale, say, the number of instances. Several forecasters, among them the Temporal Fusion Transformer and N-BEATS, are trained independently and each sends a prediction on the same clock, every 10 seconds for example. The ensembler has to turn those into one number.

Real time makes it messy. Predictions go missing because of delays or a model that is not ready yet, the solution has to work across applications and metrics, and it must survive a forecaster that goes badly wrong.

"Large predictions error can lead to bad decisions and be very costly in cloud computing environment," Anna Warno said at Conf42 Python 2022.

## Simple ensembles: good, but never consistently best

The demo dataset is 6,000 rows of CPU usage predicted by five forecasters on a test set. The simple ensemblers are naive mean, mean over the best subset of forecasters (scored by mean absolute error on a training window), mean over the best n on the last k steps, weights found with linear programming (positive, summing to one), and weights proportional to each model's scores.

Across five metrics, linear programming wins most often, while mean over the best subset tends to win on sMAPE, and which method leads changes from one stretch of the series to the next. Ensembles beat the best single forecaster, but there is no single best ensemble.

## The neural ensembler

So Anna trains one. Each input has a past part, holding every forecaster's errors (real minus predicted), the real values and a time index, and a future part with every forecaster's predictions. She tried fully connected networks and 1D convolutional networks with and without residual connections and attention. The 1D CNN with residual connections came out on top, with attention adding little.

For the missing-prediction problem, a second model is trained with random forecaster columns zeroed out and a mask marking which ones are absent; it keeps returning good results when inputs drop. On the comparison plot the deep learning ensembler is the best method throughout, where the simple ones swap places. Her caveat: it needs a reasonable amount of data before it can be trained, so simple ensembles are the place to start.

## Who should watch

Anyone running more than one forecasting model in production, especially for autoscaling or finance. It assumes you know what TFT and N-BEATS are; it does not show code.

- Andrei Stroganov on [ML ensemble performance](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Andrei_Stroganov_ml_ensemble_performance).

Title: A correlation heatmap hides structure that a stock network shows
Description: Kalyan Prasad (Creative Crewz) at Conf42 Python 2022 on turning ETF return correlations into NetworkX graphs and minimum spanning trees
Body:
A correlation matrix of 40 assets is 1,600 numbers, and a heatmap of it only tells you how close pairs are. At Conf42 Python 2022, Kalyan Prasad, Data Scientist and Analytics Manager at Creative Crewz, showed how to turn the same correlations into a network with NetworkX, prune it, and end with a minimum spanning tree where equities, bonds, commodities and currencies fall into readable clusters.

The first half is a gentle tour of graph theory; the second half is a notebook you can follow line by line.

## Why model markets as networks?

He starts with Leonhard Euler and the Königsberg bridge problem, where four land masses and seven bridges became the first nodes and edges. A network is a system of nodes connected by links, and both can carry metadata: his example is two people who connect at a conference, with age and location on the nodes and the date they met on the edge.

Finance picked this up after the 2008 crisis, when economists came to see the architecture of the financial system as central to systemic risk. Interbank networks, stock correlation networks and agent-based models followed. He also covers the three centrality measures you meet first: degree (the most connected node), closeness (the fastest communicator) and betweenness (the most influential, the one sitting on the most shortest paths).

## The warm-up: who owns Tesla and Google?

Section one uses the yfinance library to pull the institutional holders of Tesla and Google, concatenates the two DataFrames, and builds a graph with `nx.from_pandas_edgelist`, holders as sources and companies as targets. Colouring the two companies red and the holders green makes the shared owners visible at a glance. It is deliberately small, a template for exploring who holds what.

## From heatmap to graph

Section two is the real case: daily prices for 40 ETFs across 1,013 rows, from January 2013 to December 2017. Prices become daily log returns so assets can be compared, then pandas computes the pairwise correlation matrix. A seaborn clustermap shows the expected blocks, with international equity ETFs moving together and safe havens moving against equities.

His complaint about the heatmap is that it is one-dimensional: it shows how close assets are, not the shape of the whole system. So the matrix becomes an edge list and a graph of 39 nodes and 741 edges. Drawn with circular, random, spring and spectral layouts, it is a hairball.

"All these plots look pretty fancy if you observe them and they looks pretty fancy, but they actually fail to convey the information which we are actually looking from our network graph," Kalyan Prasad said at Conf42 Python 2022.

## How do you make the network readable?

Four steps, each a small function:

1. Drop weak edges: anything with absolute correlation under 0.5 goes, which removed 530 of the 741 edges.
2. Colour edges by sign, green for positive and red for negative correlation.
3. Scale edge width by correlation strength, and node size by the number of strong links, so heavily connected ETFs such as VGT and DIA stand out.
4. Switch to the Fruchterman-Reingold layout, which pulls strongly correlated nodes together, so gold sits with commodities and BND with the bond funds.

The last cluster of equities is still too dense to label, so he finishes with NetworkX's built-in minimum spanning tree. It keeps just enough edges to connect every node, and the result shows clear groups of equities, bonds, commodities and currencies.

## Who should watch

Python developers curious about graph analysis, and finance people who live in correlation matrices and want another lens. The finance theory is light; the value is the notebook, which goes from raw prices to a clean minimum spanning tree in a few dozen lines.

Title: Python is secure by design, its third-party packages are not
Description: Gajendra Deshpande (Eyesec Cyber Security Solutions) at Conf42 Python 2022 on scanning Python code and dependencies with Bandit, Safety and Semgrep
Body:
Python's popularity makes it a target, and the soft spot is rarely the interpreter. At Conf42 Python 2022, Gajendra Deshpande, founder and managing director of Eyesec Cyber Security Solutions, toured three free tools for finding the weak spots in your own code and in the packages you install: Bandit, Safety and Semgrep.

It is a practical, command-by-command introduction, aimed at developers who have never run a security scanner over a Python project.

## Where do the vulnerabilities come from?

His framing is that open source is not insecure because the code is visible. Python, like other big open-source projects, has a large community watching it and bug bounty programmes behind it. The risk arrives with third-party packages written by people who may not know secure coding principles, or published deliberately by attackers.

The abstract puts a number on it: a large-scale static analysis of PyPI by Jukka Ruohonen, Kalle Hjerppe and Kalle Rindell found at least one security issue in about 46% of the packages scanned. In the talk he adds press coverage of dependency confusion via PyPI, packages stealing credit card data, and remote code execution findings.

## Bandit: what does it check?

Bandit parses each file into an abstract syntax tree, runs plugins against its nodes and writes a report. `bandit -r <path>` scans a project; `-p` runs a profile such as shell injection only; `-b` compares against a JSON baseline so known non-issues, like a clear-text password in a unit test, stop showing up.

The plugins are grouped by ID series: B1xx miscellaneous, B2xx framework misconfiguration, B3xx blacklisted calls, B4xx blacklisted imports, B5xx cryptography, B6xx injection, B7xx cross-site scripting. His examples include `assert` and `exec` use, bad file permissions, binding to all interfaces, hard-coded passwords, try-except-pass, Flask with debug left on (B201), certificate checks disabled, weak SSL versions and keys, subprocess calls with a shell, and raw SQL or `mark_safe` in Django. You can also write custom tests with Bandit's decorators.

## Safety: are my dependencies known to be vulnerable?

Safety checks installed packages against Safety DB, an open database of known vulnerabilities in Python packages built from CVEs and changelogs, with an API key option for a commercial feed. `safety check` scans the active virtual environment, `-r requirements.txt` scans a requirements file, and you can pipe in `pip freeze`. His run checked 221 packages and flagged an outdated whitenoise; installing the deliberately vulnerable insecure-package demo pushed it to 222 and added a second finding. The fix in both cases was an upgrade.

He stresses one nuance that is easy to miss: Safety DB lists affected versions, not packages to avoid. Some of the most popular packages appear in it; check which versions are hit and upgrade.

## Semgrep and the house rules

Semgrep is an open-source static analyser for 17-plus languages, with more than a thousand community rules and rules that look like the code they match. It covers OWASP Top 10 classes such as SQL injection and broken authentication, and its online playground is the quickest way in.

His closing guidelines are short. Maintainers should keep their packages secure. Developers should scan dependencies before using them and keep scanning afterwards.

"Periodically scan your environment, that is, even after upgrading it, because the new packages may come up with new vulnerabilities," Gajendra Deshpande said at Conf42 Python 2022.

Beyond that: scan packages before and after upgrades, sign and verify packages with PGP keys, upload with Twine, and install only from trusted sources, never from nulled copies. The abstract also promised a section on GPG signing for PyPI and conda; in the recording it is one line in that checklist.

## Who should watch

Python developers and team leads who want a scanner in CI by the end of the week. Security specialists will know the tools; the Bandit plugin tour is still a handy checklist.

Title: Malicious packages have authors, so hunt them like attackers
Description: Tzachi Zornstain (Checkmarx) at Conf42 Python 2022 on why malicious open-source packages need threat hunting, not patch management
Body:
Removing a malicious package from a registry fixes one package; the person who published it moves on to the next. At Conf42 Python 2022, Tzachi Zornstain, who leads software supply chain research at Checkmarx, argued that the open-source ecosystem treats malicious packages like vulnerabilities to patch, when they are the work of attackers who can be tracked and hunted.

He comes from malware research at McAfee, Symantec and Palo Alto Networks, and the talk reads like it: attacker habits, indicators of compromise, and a call for the data researchers need to do the job.

## How do attackers get code into your build?

He walks through two attack patterns, both of which he says show up weekly rather than in theory.

**Dependency confusion.** A project mixes internal packages with public ones, and by default nothing marks which is which. An attacker guesses the name of an internal package, registers it on npm or PyPI with a very high version number, and an artifact server told to take the latest version pulls the attacker's copy. In his words this is often not a bug but a feature. The case he describes had odd version numbers, names that pointed at the targeted organisation, and code that stole the developer's SSH keys and sent them to a server the attacker controlled. Checkmarx released an open-source tool, Dustilock, to flag configurations that expose internal package names.

**Account takeover.** The compromise of the popular npm package ua-parser-js added a password stealer and a crypto miner, and drew an advisory from CISA. Two weeks later the same actor hit coa and rc, this time with a bug that made the attack fail while still breaking build servers worldwide.

## What gave the hijacked releases away?

The attacker took over the npm account but not the GitHub one. Normally a maintainer tags a release on GitHub and pushes it to npm, so the two line up; during the attack three new versions appeared on npm with no matching code on GitHub. Three versions, he notes, so that whatever update policy you use, you pick one up.

That gap became ChainAlert, a free early-warning service from Checkmarx for the open-source community. It watches new releases and, when one has no corresponding code or activity on GitHub, opens an issue for the maintainer and for projects that depend on the package. It does not call the release malicious; it asks whether it was expected.

## Why are these attacks so slow to detect?

Two reasons. The ecosystem is reactive: it waits for someone to report a package, which stretches the time to detection. And it leans on static signatures, which attackers bypass easily.

His alternative is hunting. Starting from a package already listed in the Backstabber's Knife Collection, a research dataset of removed malicious packages, his team pulled its metadata (account, description, repository, homepage, owner) and its indicators of compromise (URLs, domains, IPs, cryptocurrency addresses), built a fingerprint, and searched other registries. They found related packages still live years after the first was removed, and had them taken down from PyPI, npm and RubyGems.

"Those are attackers. And we need to change our mindset about how do we approach attackers and how do we track them, how do we hunt them down," Tzachi Zornstain said at Conf42 Python 2022.

## The ask

The talk ends as a call to action: the major registries should keep a central repository of removed malicious packages with their full metadata, so researchers can hunt the people behind them. The abstract also promises a StarJacking demo and a broader look-ahead; the recording sticks to the attacks, ChainAlert and the hunting case.

## Who should watch

Security engineers and platform teams who own a package mirror or an artifact server, and anyone who thinks their software composition analysis already covers malware. It is a short talk and a useful reframe.

Title: Shrink the pandas DataFrame before you rent a bigger machine
Description: Marco Carranza (Teamcore Tech) at Conf42 Python 2022 on pandas memory tricks, then Vaex, Modin and PySpark as data outgrows one machine
Body:
The script works on the sample file and crashes on the real one. At Conf42 Python 2022, Marco Carranza, technical co-founder of Teamcore Tech, laid out a ladder of fixes for data that has outgrown memory: six pandas tricks first, then vertical scaling in the cloud, then Vaex, Modin and finally PySpark. His recurring advice is to climb only as far as you need, and to optimise the DataFrame before throwing money at it.

He has used Python for more than 15 years, and Teamcore runs sales data from retail stores through machine learning models, so the examples come from people who actually hit these limits.

## How much memory can a few lines of pandas save?

More than you would guess, and he brings the numbers:

- **Sparse columns.** A column full of NaN values switched to a sparse dtype used 41% less memory.
- **Sampling.** `DataFrame.sample` gives a uniform sample whose descriptive statistics and histograms track the full data; taking the first thousand rows does not, and he shows the two diverge.
- **Load only the columns you need.** A 3.8 GB text file with 77 columns took 4.5 GB in memory; keeping four columns brought it to a little over 300 MB. You can do this at read time.
- **Smaller numeric types.** A column holding values from one to nine stored as int64 used 196 MB; as int8 it used 24 MB, an 87.5% cut from one line.
- **Categoricals.** A two-value text column went from 142 MB as object to 2.4 MB as category, a 98% reduction.
- **Chunked reads.** A file of almost 4 GB read with `chunksize` in blocks of 500,000 rows, aggregating each block and releasing it before the next.

## When is a bigger machine the right answer?

Sometimes. He is candid that the easiest fix for missing RAM is renting more, and cloud notebooks make it trivial: Binder, Kaggle Kernels, Google Colab, Azure Notebooks, with machines past 1 TB of RAM. No code changes, and you pay only for what you use.

"Of course, if you forget to turn off your machine, you'll have to pay that too," Marco Carranza said at Conf42 Python 2022.

The catch is that unoptimised code stays unoptimised. Long term it is expensive, it does not scale well and it is not production ready.

## Vaex, Modin or PySpark?

Each gets a pros-and-cons pass:

**Vaex** works with datasets larger than memory, where the limit is the size of your disk. It memory-maps the data and never copies it into RAM unless asked, computes lazily with virtual columns, and claims statistics at up to a billion rows per second. It prefers HDF5, and `vaex.from_csv(..., convert=True)` converts a big CSV in chunks on the fly. The syntax is close to pandas but not identical, and the project is younger.

**Modin** keeps the pandas API: change the import to `modin.pandas` and your code uses every core instead of one, with Dask or Ray to spread work across a cluster. The project quotes a 4x speed-up on an 8-core machine. The costs are cluster setup, the usual distributed-systems debugging, and memory needs as high as pandas'.

**PySpark** is the all-in option when data and computation both have to be distributed. It brings a mature ecosystem and Hadoop integration, but you rewrite your pandas code in a different syntax, small datasets run slower than in pandas, MLlib has fewer algorithms, and Spark is hungry for RAM.

## Who should watch

Analysts and data engineers whose notebooks have started to swap, and anyone about to propose a Spark cluster for a 4 GB CSV. The pandas section alone pays for the half hour. He signs off with Donald Knuth's line about premature optimisation, which is fair warning not to start at the top of the ladder.

Title: Stop tracking ML experiments in a spreadsheet, let DVC bundle them
Description: Milecia McGregor (Iterative) at Conf42 Python 2022 on DVC experiments that snapshot code, data and hyperparameters so any model can be rebuilt exactly
Body:
Every data scientist has had the eureka model: great accuracy, and no idea which combination of code, data and hyperparameters produced it. At Conf42 Python 2022, Milecia McGregor, Developer Advocate at Iterative, showed how DVC experiments turn each training run into a bundle of code, data and config, so a good result can be reproduced exactly instead of reconstructed from memory.

It is a short, practical talk built around one workflow: queue a batch of hyperparameter values, run them all, compare the table, repeat. If you have ever kept a spreadsheet with a commit hash in one column and a Google Drive zip link in another, this one is for you.

## Why is experiment tracking hard in the first place?

Her framing is that the experiments pile up faster than you notice. You tune hyperparameters, spot a line of code you could change, and then fresh data arrives from production. Each change is layered onto the last, and after a few hundred runs nobody can say which state of the world produced the best model. The cost lands at deployment, as an unexplained accuracy drop or an environment difference nobody wrote down.

The fix she proposes is to treat every experiment as one bundle: the dataset, the hyperparameters, the code and, if you start from one, the model. She also covers the two classic tuning strategies the demo uses. Grid search tries every combination, so it is guaranteed to find the best one in the grid; random search samples the same value sets at random and, run for about the same time, often lands on better combinations because it covers a wider spread.

## What does DVC actually record?

DVC is open source and sits on top of Git, which she sums up as Git for your data: Git versions the code, DVC versions the data, and an experiment ties them together with the parameters. There is no library to import into your training script and no tracking server to call, a point she makes directly against MLflow's API calls. Everything runs locally, with optional remote storage on AWS, GCP or Azure.

The workflow in the demo is a handful of commands:

- `dvc exp run` runs the training script and snapshots code, data and configuration as metadata attached to the resulting model.
- `dvc exp run --queue` lines up experiments with different hyperparameter values; queued runs get their own IDs and can be pushed to a bigger machine or a GPU.
- `dvc exp run --run-all` executes the queue, and `dvc exp show` prints a table of every run with its parameters and metrics (average precision and ROC AUC in her example).
- `dvc plots diff` takes two experiment IDs and plots them side by side from the JSON or TSV metrics your training script already writes.

She runs three rounds of this, including a random-search round that turns out worse than an earlier run, which is the point: the table tells you which direction to tune next, or that it is time for a different algorithm or more data.

## The spreadsheet has to go

The closing argument is blunt. Any run in the table can be rebuilt from its experiment ID with a few DVC commands, so the bookkeeping that eats an afternoon becomes a lookup.

"Please don't use spreadsheets to keep up with your machine learning experiments when we have stuff that'll do it for you now," Milecia McGregor said at Conf42 Python 2022.

She adds a reason to care about data versioning in particular: when data drift hits production, you still have exact copies of the datasets from before the drift. And she ends with a nudge engineers need more often than they admit, that using an existing tool is not cheating and that an hour spent trying one is cheap even if it does not fit.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and ML engineers who run more than a few experiments a week and still track them by hand. It is an intro to DVC experiments, not a comparison of MLOps platforms; as a developer advocate for the company behind DVC she is open about her preference.

Title: Kubernetes is an API to compute, and OpenShift ships the rest
Description: JJ Asghar (IBM) at Conf42 Python 2022 on taking a tiny Flask app from a GitHub repo to a live OpenShift route with webhook-driven rebuilds
Body:
Most Python developers who end up on Kubernetes want the shortest path from a git repo to a URL, and as little YAML as possible. At Conf42 Python 2022, JJ Asghar, Developer Advocate at IBM, gives a fast vocabulary tour of containers, Kubernetes and OpenShift, then deploys a one-file Flask app to OpenShift from the web console in a few clicks, with a GitHub webhook that rebuilds it on every push.

It is an intro talk and says so: the goal is to get your developers to focus on code, not the cluster. If you already run production clusters, the demo will feel familiar. If you are the Python person who just inherited a namespace, it is a friendly half hour.

## What is Kubernetes, in one sentence?

JJ's mental model is the most useful thing in the talk. Kubernetes is not a platform you learn piece by piece; it is a thing you hand a declaration to, and it goes and runs your pods somewhere on its nodes.

"If you anchor your thoughts and kind of build up your knowledge around that simple concept where all Kubernetes is, is an API to compute, everything else kind of just falls into place," JJ Asghar said at Conf42 Python 2022.

From there he builds up the pieces in order. Containers follow the OCI spec, so whether you build with Docker, Podman or Kaniko, the image runs anywhere with a container runtime. The smallest unit Kubernetes actually knows about is the pod, not the container, and a deployment keeps the requested number of replicas running. KubeDNS gives services internal names. Namespaces let you slice one cluster into your app and my app, or dev, QA and prod, which also means UAT no longer lives on a machine under someone's desk.

## Why OpenShift instead of plain Kubernetes?

Upstream Kubernetes is deliberately small: it orchestrates containers, and security, ingress and the rest are your job. OpenShift is Red Hat's opinionated, supported distribution on top. JJ's pitch is buy versus build: you get the integration work done and enterprise support behind it, at the price of some strong opinions.

Two OpenShift features carry the argument. Projects extend namespaces with real RBAC (tie them to Active Directory groups so devs reach payment-dev and only ops reach payment-prod), and they are cheap enough to use like git feature branches: spin one up, push code, test, merge, delete. Routes replace hand-maintained Ingress YAML, which he calls the hardest thing in Kubernetes to understand and which grows unruly once you pass 30 or 40 services.

He also name-checks the ecosystem you will meet next: Helm as the package manager (a GitLab install is one chart), Istio for the service mesh (wait until you are comfortable before going there), and Knative for scale-to-zero serverless on your own cluster.

## The demo: from repo to route

The app is a few lines of Flask from his cloud-native Python example repo. In the OpenShift developer view he creates a project, picks "from git repository", and pastes the URL. OpenShift detects a Python app, builds it on a Universal Base Image (Red Hat's minimal image, which he compares to Alpine), creates the deployment and service, and ticks a box to expose a public route. The image lands in OpenShift's built-in registry, so the code never leaves the cluster.

The part that sold him on OpenShift is the build webhook. Every build config comes with a webhook URL; paste it into the GitHub repo's webhook settings, edit the app's text, commit to main (he tells you not to do this in real life), and a new build starts on its own. The rollout spins up the new pod before killing the old one, and liveness and readiness checks keep users from seeing the gap.

The whole thing takes about 20 minutes on screen, including a wait for the build that he fills with Jeopardy music.

## Who should watch

Python developers new to containers who want the words (pod, namespace, route, build config) attached to something they can click. Teams weighing upstream Kubernetes against a supported distribution get a candid buy-versus-build framing from someone at IBM. Platform engineers can skip it.

Title: Run a Flask app inside Google Colab and share it through ngrok
Description: Shweta Mishra (Tata Consultancy Services) at Conf42 Python 2022 on serving a Flask app from Google Colab with a public ngrok URL, no local setup
Body:
Colab gives you a free Python machine in the browser, but localhost on that machine is somebody else's localhost. At Conf42 Python 2022, Shweta Mishra, Software Developer at Tata Consultancy Services, shows the workaround in a short live-coded session: write the templates, start Flask in a thread inside the notebook, and punch a public URL through ngrok so you (and anyone you send the link to) can see the page.

It is a beginner talk and a short one. If you have never served a web page from a notebook, it is a tidy ten minutes; if you deploy Flask for a living, skip ahead to the related talks below.

## Why not just pip install Flask locally?

Her framing is setup cost. Shweta Mishra said at Conf42 Python 2022: "Flask is a python framework that allows you to build web application." The catch, in her words, is that using it locally means installing a pile of libraries and dependencies that take time and disk space. Google Colab, an online Jupyter notebook, already has Python ready, so the only missing piece is a way to reach the server.

## Templates live in a folder, even in a notebook

Flask's render_template looks for HTML in a templates directory, and Colab doesn't care that you're in a notebook. She creates the folder with a shell mkdir -p cell, then uses Colab's write-file cell magic to drop an index.html into it: a heading, a bit of inline CSS, nothing fancy. One typo in the cell magic (a missing percent sign) gets fixed live, which is the most honest moment in any notebook demo.

## Flask in a thread, ngrok in front

The Flask code itself is small. She imports os and threading so the server runs in a separate thread and doesn't block the notebook, installs an ngrok Python wrapper, and builds the app with a single route that renders index.html on port 5000. More routes (an about page, a home page) are just more decorated functions.

The ngrok part has the one gotcha worth knowing. ngrok used to work anonymously; by the time of the talk it wanted an authentication token from your ngrok account, pasted into the notebook before connecting. She also hits the other gotcha live: a token she had already used refused to work again, so she swapped in a fresh one.

## Two URLs come out

Run the cell and you get two addresses: the localhost URL, which only the Colab VM can open, and the ngrok URL, which anyone can. She notes the ngrok link stays reachable for about six hours, which is plenty for showing a prototype to a colleague and not a hosting plan. Without ngrok you would only get the localhost address, and nobody can see that but the VM.

## Who should watch

Students, data people who live in notebooks and want to show a quick HTML front end, and anyone who needs a throwaway shareable demo without a laptop setup. It is not about production Flask: no WSGI server, no deployment, no security.

Title: The startup security team is you, so let the pipeline do the nagging
Description: Ryder Damen (Indeni Cloudrail) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on securing a startup cloud alone with pipeline scanners, CSPM, IaC and SOC 2 tools
Body:
One DevOps engineer can't make a startup's cloud fully secure, and Ryder Damen says so on his second slide. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, the DevOps engineer turned developer advocate at Indeni Cloudrail lays out what one person realistically can do: put scanners in the deployment pipeline, scan the live cloud, move infrastructure into code, buy tooling for the SOC 2 chores, and push application security back to the developers who write the code.

## Who is this talk for?

His past self: a DevOps engineer at a scaling startup without a security background, who knows to keep ports closed and limit blast radius but is no AppSec expert. His career ran from biomedical engineering through web development to DevOps at several startups. The list of things he has been asked to do in that job runs to dozens of items, from migrating everything to AWS and then to GCP, to resetting the breakers after the machine learning engineers all trained at once. His favourite: catching an Uber with the company server in the trunk.

He splits startup security into three buckets: application, infrastructure, and other.

## Application security: turn the scanners on, but don't fail the build yet

Application security covers your source code (the OWASP Top Ten, unsanitised inputs, SQL injection, XSS), your application composition (that Python package last updated in 2008), and penetration testing. He recommends an annual pen test even though it can cost anywhere from about $7,000 to $50,000. Day to day, you won't have time to test the app yourself, so wire tools into the pipeline: GitHub's dependency alerts and Snyk for vulnerable packages, OWASP ZAP for web application testing.

The important part is rollout. You probably weren't the first hire, so expect hundreds or thousands of findings on day one. Ryder Damen said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "Don't allow any of these tools to fail your pipeline."

Instead, surface the findings, set a deadline, and on that deadline fail the pipeline no matter what. To get there, borrow the most senior engineer for half a day to triage, then double your own estimate, because upgrades have a way of breaking four other packages. Ryder Damen said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "you will fix one vulnerability and five new more will come up."

If management won't release engineers for a week, ask for a day at a time and pair with whoever owns the code.

## Infrastructure security: scan what's live, and what's about to be

If you are on one of the big three clouds, it is very easy to build an insecure environment by accident. Two layers of tooling help. Cloud security posture management (CSPM) tools such as Orca Security, Cloudrail and Aqua scan the running cloud against a policy you define and report drift, like a machine in the wrong subnet. But those issues are already in production.

That is the real argument for infrastructure as code. Repeatable infrastructure in version control is nice; being able to scan it before it ships is better. He names tfsec, Cloudrail and Checkov by Bridgecrew. He admits he resisted Terraform for a long time because it looked overwhelming, and that it was easier than he feared.

## The other bucket: everything SOC 2 asks about

Anything that's neither app nor infrastructure tends to land on DevOps at a startup with no IT team: endpoint monitoring for encrypted drives and firewalls, who holds the office keys, office Wi-Fi, the production server on a desktop under someone's desk. He likes Kolide, which lives in Slack and pings a new hire every day until their laptop is compliant (normally his job), and Vanta and Secureframe for SOC 2 compliance, which scan cloud accounts for gaps like missing VPC flow logs and let auditors self-serve.

## Practices that make it survivable

Keep production infrastructure as simple as possible and try the shiny things in a sandbox, even if they'd look good on a CV. Prefer managed services: AWS ECS on Fargate instead of EC2-backed ECS, a bit more expensive but someone else patches it. Ryder Damen said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "You ship the blame and the responsibility to AWS, and for me, that's worth a couple extra hundred dollars a month."

Get teammates to review your Terraform even if they don't know it well. Shift left in a literal sense: shift responsibility for application security onto the engineers writing the code, and make it your job that the pipeline fails when they forget. And keep showing management that more people in this role would be worth it.

## Who should watch

The lone DevOps or platform engineer at a scaling startup who just inherited security and a SOC 2 deadline. Security specialists will find it basic; that's the point. He works for Cloudrail and mentions it among the tools, but the advice holds without it.

Title: A bank's security pipeline that every release must pass and no team can edit
Description: Manuel Schuller at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on a shared security pipeline that gates every bank release and an immutable bill of materials
Body:
Compliance at a bank works when the project team can't opt out of it and doesn't have to design it. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Manuel Schuller, Senior DevOps Evangelist and DevOps Institute ambassador, describes how a bank he worked with split delivery into two pipelines: an application pipeline each team shapes as it likes, and one security pipeline, owned by transversal teams, that every release has to pass. The payback, in his fair-case model, came after five months.

## Why one pipeline per team doesn't scale in a bank

He sets the scene with three decades of release tooling: from job-based scripts, to pipelines with stages and access rights, to automated testing, approvals and audit trails, to model-based platforms that separate deployment from release. Each step answered a real problem. At enterprise scale in financial services the problem is spread: a central tools group making choices away from the people who ship, several clouds and Kubernetes flavours (OpenShift, Tanzu, Rancher), and business units with their own stacks, licences and release habits. Getting everyone to the same level of control by persuasion is hopeless.

So the bank quantified the cost of the status quo (spending, lack of visibility, morale, lost business and lost people) and modelled a return on investment. Not the best case, not the worst, a fair case, which broke even after five months of full use.

## What sits in the security pipeline?

Five stages agreed with the security people: development, integration, delivery, pre-production and production, each with scans and checks. The example tools are SonarQube, Checkmarx and an IQ server for dependency analysis, though he stresses any tool could slot in. The development stage starts with an entry check that the developer has done the security training, so they can read the findings, and ends with an exit gate that blocks delivery if the thresholds of three static analysis tools aren't met. Pre-production runs DAST and its own rules before anything moves on.

Three properties make it work. The checks are generic across technologies, they are flexible enough to cover each team's process, and they can change at any time, even between two deliveries. And the project team can't touch them. Manuel Schuller said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "I cannot bypass these checks."

## How do two pipelines stay in step?

The application pipeline keeps whatever stages the department has used for years. The two are synchronised at the gates: to start the QA stage, the application pipeline waits for the security pipeline's integration checks to pass. The production handoff is where it gets serious. It requires a bill of materials, an entry in the CMDB, a check that this information is immutable, and an SKU, because at this bank nothing reaches production without one.

He notes the security pipeline isn't the only one. Other control pipelines run in parallel the same way, so a green light to production means every bank-level control has been met, whatever the department or technology.

## The bill of materials as yet another artifact

Since the US executive order of May 12, vendors have to publish a bill of materials for what they sell. Schuller treats the BOM as a meta-artifact describing every artifact used or generated to deploy the application, a nod to Unix's Yacc: yet another artifact. It used to describe how software was built; now it describes how software is released, including the results of every scan along the pipeline. Because that content grows over time, it has to be stored immutably so the audit trail survives. He calls it the single source of software delivery proof.

## Lessons learned

Three, on one slide. Implement now, even with a minimal set of tools, because the return is fast. Follow the state of the art company-wide, because competitors already do: CI five years ago, CD two years ago, release orchestration, DevSecOps and value stream management today. And let embedded controls spread the culture. Teams were wary at the start, afraid of the constraint. Manuel Schuller said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "we have a queue of people asking to be embedded into the system."

The bottleneck now is onboarding capacity, not willingness.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevSecOps leads in banks, insurers and other regulated shops who need controls that apply across many teams without owning every team's pipeline. It is a process and lessons-learned talk, not a tool tutorial.

Title: If you can't manufacture an IoT device securely, it isn't secure
Description: Jonathan Williams (Twilio IoT) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on threat models, secure boot and secure factory provisioning as day-one IoT design
Body:
IoT security fails long before a hacker shows up: it fails when the MVP ships without it. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Jonathan Williams, Product Manager in Twilio's IoT and wireless business unit, makes the case that device security has to be a system component from the first design review, and that a device you can't provision securely in the factory can't be trusted in the field.

## How big is the problem?

He opens with the numbers. According to the figures he cites, 1.51 billion IoT devices were breached in the first six months of 2021, up from 639 million in the same period of 2020, while the count of connected devices is predicted to reach 50 billion by 2030. Meanwhile device builders treat security as the hoops you jump through after the features work, and retrofitting it into an existing product is hard and expensive.

## What do real incidents teach device builders?

Three cases, none strictly IoT, all with lessons that transfer. Zoom's early client vulnerabilities across Mac and Windows, which the company turned around by taking security seriously fast, with plenty of sleepless nights along the way. Hikvision's connected cameras, compromised through a weak password implementation and a cookie backdoor that the US Department of Homeland Security rated as remotely exploitable with a low level of skill; attackers really did access users' footage. And the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack: nearly 100GB of data stolen, the pipeline shut for six days, and a ransom of 75 bitcoin, then $4.4 million. He squints and calls the pipeline's computerised equipment an IoT-style device, which is fair enough.

His framing is deliberately not finger-pointing: this happens to someone every day, and it could be you.

## Start with the threat model

Before choosing chips or protocols, decide what you are protecting and from whom. The scale runs from accidental misuse and sloppy defaults (the default password), through rogue employees and untrusted manufacturing partners (the territory ISO 27001 covers), to state-sponsored attackers decapping silicon and injecting power glitches to read flash. The defences differ by orders of magnitude, so the answer shapes everything after it.

Some basics now come from regulation. Legislation in California, Australia and, more recently, the United Kingdom targets weak and default passwords, and standards such as Arm PSA and ISO 27001 cover specific technical and people risks. His take: if you can't jump through those hoops, you probably aren't ready to ship.

## Seven properties, plus two more

For the device itself he leans on Microsoft's white paper on the seven properties of highly secure devices: a hardware-based root of trust, a small trusted computing base, defence in depth, compartmentalisation, certificate-based authentication, renewable security and failure reporting. Microsoft uses custom silicon to get there; Williams notes they can be achieved in other ways.

He adds two that he considers non-negotiable: secure boot and secure factory provisioning. Building secure products at scale means a production process that produces trusted devices even in an untrusted factory, which also protects customer IP and keeps grey-market units from existing. If you can't be sure the device runs your code, you can't trust anything else about it. Jonathan Williams said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "I like to think if you can't manufacture it securely then it certainly isn't secure."

His cautionary example is the many industrial deployments built on the Raspberry Pi, which supports neither secure boot nor a secure factory provisioning step. Great for getting a use case running; secure by design, not really.

## Why teams stay on insecure platforms

The sunk cost of the hardware or software approach already chosen, plus pressure to ship, keeps teams on the insecure path into production. He suggests asking blunt questions at any stage: what happens if our devices are hacked, and is the risk of not switching really worth it? The earlier, the cheaper.

## Who should watch

Embedded engineers, hardware product managers and CTOs of connected-device startups who need a compact checklist and a few memorable incidents for the next roadmap argument. It is a short, high-level talk. The last minute points at Twilio's Microvisor and Super SIM, so expect a brief product mention.

Title: DevOps was never just automation, and cloud engineering says so again
Description: Matty Stratton (Pulumi) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on cloud engineering as DevOps' CALMS principles applied to build, deploy and manage
Body:
DevOps got shrunk to one letter of its own acronym. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Matty Stratton, Staff Developer Advocate at Pulumi and global chair of DevOpsDays, argues that cloud engineering is not a new movement but a way to take DevOps back: apply software engineering practice to infrastructure, applications and compliance alike, and keep all five CALMS principles in play instead of only the A.

## How did we get here?

He opens with a short history lesson. Paul Hammond and John Allspaw's Flickr talk at Velocity 2009 on ten deploys a day, the tweet from Andrew Clay Shafer that is the first known use of the word DevOps, and the birds-of-a-feather session on agile system administration that exactly one person attended: Patrick Debois, who went on to start DevOpsDays in Ghent. The name DevOps exists because agile system administration was too long for a conference. By the 10th-anniversary event in Ghent in 2019, the organiser-only day zero had more people in the room than the entire first DevOpsDays.

His point is that the talks from that first event could run at a conference today. We have been discussing the same ideas for over a decade.

## What is CALMS, and which part got lost?

CALMS is culture, automation, lean, measurement and sharing (John Willis and Damon Edwards proposed CAMS in 2010; Jez Humble added the L). Stratton insists the letters carry equal weight. Then he lists what the industry did with it instead: DevOps as automation, DevOps as Kubernetes, DevOps without culture (one enterprise voice once claimed culture was for yoghurt), and DevOps as something you can buy.

He is pragmatic about job titles, though. Matty Stratton said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "most of the people who have the title DevOps engineer didn't give that title themselves."

His second reason for not fighting the title is better. Matty Stratton said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "the title DevOps engineer gets you 20% to 30% more money. So go get paid."

The portmanteau problem gets its own slide of escalating names, from DevSecOps and BizDevOps to DevSecDBOpsOps and DevOpsDevOps. Words are hard, he concludes, and then offers more words.

## Build, deploy, manage, each through CALMS

Cloud engineering, as he defines it, means standard software engineering practices and tools across infrastructure, application development and compliance, to tame the complexity of the modern cloud. He splits the work into build, deploy and manage, and walks each one through all five CALMS letters.

**Build** is about shared services platforms and reusable infrastructure components written in ordinary programming languages, so teams inherit the whole ecosystem of IDEs and test tools. Culture here means focusing on your differentiator: unless you are a CI vendor, building pipelines is not what makes you special. He used to ask public sector customers whether they were the US Department of Continuous Delivery.

**Deploy** means the same way every time, and he means every time. If your process has a break-glass path for emergencies, that tells you two things: the process is too slow, and everything will become an emergency. Security is just another aspect of quality, so it belongs in the pipeline. And his favourite line on checklists: humans should define them, software should tick the boxes.

**Manage** is where DevSecOps lands. Treat policy like infrastructure, as code rather than prose in a PDF on a SharePoint you can't open, and check it both before and after deployment. Automated gates also beat audits that rely on a sysadmin remembering whether they did x, y and z every time. Matty Stratton said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "policy as code is executable documentation of your policy."

## Who should watch

Anyone tired of arguing about what DevOps means, team leads trying to explain why a platform and a pipeline are not a culture, and security engineers who want policy treated like code. It is a principles talk with no product demo, despite the Pulumi badge. Pair it with your next reorganisation meeting.

Title: Encrypt data at rest high in the stack or accept a bigger attack surface
Description: Senthil Raja Chermapandian (Ericsson) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on four layers for encrypting data at rest and what each one costs you
Body:
Where you encrypt matters as much as whether you encrypt. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Senthil Raja Chermapandian, Principal Software Engineer at Ericsson, slices a cloud-native application into four layers (microservice, database, volume, disk) and shows that each place you can encrypt data at rest trades attack surface against effort. The higher in the stack the encryption happens, the less an attacker can read; the lower it happens, the easier it is to switch on.

He builds cloud-native AI/ML platforms at Ericsson, the kind that chew through batch and streaming data at scale, so the question of where that data sits encrypted is a day-job one. He also maintains kube-fledged, an open source project for caching container images on Kubernetes worker nodes. The talk is a compact, vendor-neutral map rather than a tool demo.

## What are the four layers?

The model is simple. At the top is the microservice holding the business logic. Under it is the database that stores the state. Under that is the volume the database writes files to, carved from a physical or virtual disk. At the bottom is the disk itself. Data can be encrypted at any one of those points, and everything above that point handles plain text.

## Encrypting in the microservice: least exposed, most work

When the application encrypts before writing, the data travels through every lower layer already encrypted. That gives the smallest attack surface of the four patterns. The bill comes in three parts. The database can no longer sort or search the data, because it only sees ciphertext. Retrofitting existing applications that already talk to a database is expensive. And key management becomes the application's job: it has to track which key encrypted which piece of data, even if it delegates storage of the keys to an external key management service.

Senthil Raja Chermapandian said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "at the very first layer itself where the data is generated, the data is getting encrypted and as the data cases through the underneath layers it passes in an encrypted fashion, which means the attack surface in this case is the least."

## Letting the database do it: plug and play, with a catch

Database-level encryption needs no application rewrite and no changes to storage or infrastructure, which makes it close to plug and play if your database supports it. The catches are specific. Most implementations require running the database containers in privileged mode, which many organisations' security rules forbid in production. Most wrap dm-crypt under the hood. Support in open source databases is limited, so this route often means commercial plugins or enterprise licences. And performance on encrypted data varies a lot between engines, so test before you commit.

## Volume-level encryption: the cloud default

This is the pattern you meet most in public clouds, where volume services encrypt natively and some providers let you bring your own keys. Many third-party storage providers support it too, and so do open source options. On Kubernetes the gotcha is the CSI layer: not every CSI plugin exposes the full encryption feature set of the storage behind it, so check what your provisioner supports per volume or per storage class, or be prepared to write your own plugin. The bigger limitation is control. If your software ships into environments you don't run, it can't assume the volumes it gets will be encrypted.

## Disk-level encryption: simplest, and the widest open door

Kernel modules intercept writes and encrypt at the disk. It is mature, well tooled, and LUKS gives you a standard Linux format, which keeps things portable. But it needs control over infrastructure that application teams often don't have, and it has the highest attack surface: the microservice, database and volume layers all handle plain text, so an attacker who gets into any of them reads everything. It protects you against someone walking off with a disk, and not much more.

## Who should watch

Platform and application engineers deciding where encryption at rest belongs in a Kubernetes or cloud stack, and anyone who has ticked the encrypted-at-rest box on a compliance form without asking which layer did the ticking. It's an overview: no benchmarks, no code, but a clean framework for the design conversation.

Title: Treat Terraform like code, and never hand-edit the state file
Description: Eran Bibi (Firefly) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on Terraform habits for immutable infrastructure: modules, remote locked state, data blocks and drift checks
Body:
Most Terraform pain comes from a handful of habits: one giant file, a state file on someone's laptop, and a colleague who fixes production in the console. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Eran Bibi, co-founder and CPO of Firefly, shared his short list of lessons from writing Terraform for immutable infrastructure, ending with the one he rates most important: "just treat your infrastructure as code, the same as any other code."

A note on scope: the abstract promises a single-tenant SaaS case study with Kubernetes and Step Functions. The talk itself is a compact list of practical tips, without that worked example. Come for the checklist, not the case study.

## What does immutable mean here?

The concept, as he puts it, is that "you cannot change or alter any configuration after you are provisioning a server." Instead of patching and reconfiguring servers over time, you replace them. You get consistency and predictability, and when something breaks you build new infrastructure rather than reasoning about how each server has diverged. The examples are Terraform, but he says most tips carry over to Pulumi and CDK.

## Keep the blast radius small

- **Modules.** Split the monolithic Terraform file into a root module and child modules (networking, storage) you can reuse across projects.
- **DRY.** Minimise duplicated code, even on a project you think you will finish and forget.
- **Logical separation.** Changes usually touch certain resources, so separate them; a typo in one module should not take down the whole application.
- **Consistency.** Read up on naming conventions before the first project, use variables in a consistent order, and check the Terraform Registry before writing a module someone has already written.

## The state file deserves respect

The state file is how Terraform knows the current state of your cloud and plans the next change, so most of his tips are about protecting it:

- **Use remote state** as soon as more than one person runs Terraform against the same infrastructure. He prefers an S3 bucket as the backend.
- **Back it up.** On S3, turn on bucket versioning so you can roll back to an earlier revision if the state is damaged.
- **Lock it.** With S3, add DynamoDB for state locking, so a second engineer gets a locked message instead of a corrupted file.
- **Do not edit it by hand.** It is human-readable JSON, which is exactly why people try. To bring existing resources under management, use `terraform import`. "I didn't face any situation that required a manually modification of state file," Eran Bibi said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, adding that he knows plenty of people who tried and ended up with a corrupted deployment.

## Ask the cloud instead of hardcoding

Data blocks work like a query language over provider APIs. His example: instead of a hardcoded list of availability zones that someone has to update by hand, query `aws_availability_zones` filtered to available ones and feed the result into a variable. Data sources also let projects share information with each other.

## Drift will happen anyway

Once you commit to infrastructure as code, every change has to go through the pipeline, and you should put guardrails in place so nobody can alter infrastructure directly in the console, CLI or API. Even with education and guardrails, though, drift happens: a manual change, or a third-party tool such as a CSPM creating resources on its own. So run tooling that continuously compares your state and HCL against what is actually deployed.

## Give IaC the full CI treatment

His closing tip is the one that ties the rest together. Whatever your application code gets in CI (reviews, static analysis, linters, scanners) your Terraform should get too. He names Terrascan and Checkov for security scanning and Infracost for cost projections, plus proper peer review on every pull request, something teams tend to be looser about for infrastructure. In his experience, once the team started treating IaC as just more code, quality improved steadily.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving from a first Terraform project to a shared one, and team leads who want a short checklist to hand out. Seasoned Terraform users will know most of it; the talk runs well under half an hour.

Title: Start DevSecOps by scanning your binaries, not your source code
Description: Sven Ruppert (JFrog) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on SAST-first quick wins after SolarWinds, and why build info beats a bare SBOM
Body:
If you are starting security from zero, the quickest win is scanning the binaries you already depend on for known vulnerabilities. That is the answer Sven Ruppert, Developer Advocate at JFrog, gave at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 to the question he says he gets at every conference: where are the low-hanging fruits? He also argued that build info, the full record of how a binary was made, is a better weapon than the SBOM the US executive order on cybersecurity asks for.

The talk was recorded on the second day of a hiking trip in the German woods, which makes it the only supply chain security talk where the speaker packs up his tent at the end.

## What did SolarWinds change?

His starting point is the SolarWinds attack. SolarWinds, with roughly 300,000 customers, sells network management software that runs with administrative rights. The attackers did not look for a hole in that product; they broke into the company's CI environment and made it inject compromised code into every build. The signed, legitimate-looking update then went out through automatic updates, and around 15,000 to 20,000 customers installed it. The malware stayed quiet for two weeks, then started pulling other binaries, so every infection looked different and cleaning up often meant rebuilding the infrastructure from scratch.

The new lesson: you have to protect yourself against consuming compromised components and against distributing them. "Did you ever check if your compiler is not compromised?" Sven Ruppert asked at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021. The same goes for CI agents, their firewalls and their own known vulnerabilities.

## Which of SAST, DAST, IAST and RASP comes first?

He walks through the four families:

- **SAST** scans every component statically, from the first line of code, across your libraries, operating system, compiler, tooling and CI. It misses runtime context, but it is fast and robust. One caveat: source code scanning still leans on pattern matching and machine learning, and "it's too early to just trust the scan of your source code." Binary scanning, by contrast, works on known fingerprints.
- **DAST** attacks a running system from outside using common vulnerability patterns. It needs something close to production, takes a long time, cannot see inside, and is slow to pick up new attack vectors.
- **IAST** combines both into something like a security debugger, but needs skilled people to drive the interactive part.
- **RASP** is an agent in production that monitors data flows and can shut the system down during an attack. Good as an add-on, a bad place to start, and dangerous if teams start believing it will catch everything.

His order: SAST first, then DAST, then IAST if you have the people, then RASP. Two reasons. Known vulnerabilities vastly outnumber unknown ones, so fight those first, using a vulnerability database merged from several sources, since any single one is a subset. And across the whole stack (application, OS, Kubernetes, virtualisation), he estimates that 99% of what you run is binaries, not code you wrote. Scan what you ship, in the IDE as soon as a dependency is added.

## Why build info instead of a bare SBOM?

The executive order requires an SBOM for software the US government creates, operates or uses: every component with version, origin and fingerprint. Because so many companies sell into that chain directly or indirectly, he expects it to reach almost everyone, including European vendors like his employer's customers.

His point is that an SBOM is a subset of build info, which also records the timestamps, operating system and patch level, agent name, compiler and library versions used to produce a binary. That context is what you need for a postmortem on a compromised build. And because build info is immutable, you can keep correlating it with fresh vulnerability data. "So you don't need to scan production, you just need to hold build info," Sven Ruppert said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021.

To make that work you need one place that stores every binary across tech layers (Docker images, Maven dependencies, Debian packages) so you can follow the full impact graph: this JAR is in this web archive, in this Docker layer, in this image, in this Helm chart, running in production. Build info can be generated with free tools, which he suggests open source maintainers start doing now.

## Who should watch

Teams that have no security tooling yet and need a defensible first step, and anyone who needs a plain-language walkthrough of SolarWinds and the executive order. Experienced AppSec engineers will know the taxonomy already.

Title: Kubernetes only protects itself, so scan the container in four places
Description: Rob Richardson (Cyral) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on where to put container scanning (pipeline, registry, cluster, admission webhook) and a pragmatic fail policy
Body:
Kubernetes keeps Kubernetes running; what happens inside your container is your problem. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Rob Richardson, Developer Advocate at Cyral, Microsoft MVP and Docker Captain, explained what container scanning actually does, the four points where you can run it, and why "fail on any CVE" is a policy most teams will regret. The demo wires the open source scanner Anchore into a scripted build and into GitHub Actions.

## Doesn't Kubernetes handle this?

No. The control plane microservices exist to keep the cluster alive and do nothing for the process in your pod. Once an attacker pops one container, every other container is reachable over the network by default, in Docker and in Kubernetes alike. "Namespaces are not a security boundary, they're an organizational boundary," Rob Richardson said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021. If you want to restrict east-west traffic, that is a service mesh's job.

A container looks a lot like a Linux machine, with a file system, users, processes and ports, and the usual hardening still applies: do not run as root, remove extra users and unused software, keep packages current. What changes is how. Containers are ephemeral, immutable and deterministic, so "we don't run patch Tuesday inside of a container"; you build a new image and replace the old one. A compromised container is evicted, not scrubbed, though you still chase whatever it pivoted to.

## What does a scanner do?

Two things. It inventories the image (OS packages plus every app ecosystem inside it, including the Node libraries your back-end image ships for the front end), then compares that list of names and versions against a vulnerability database. Because images are deterministic, the inventory stays valid for that image hash forever. You do not need to rescan; you re-compare the saved inventory against the latest vulnerability data and find out which running images became vulnerable overnight.

Container scanning sits alongside the other pipeline checks he runs through quickly: unit and integration tests, static analysis, license analysis (does that GPL library make your system open source?), then a policy step that weighs all the results against the organisation's risk tolerance. His slides on robrich.org link several tools per category.

## Where should you scan?

Scanning is slow, so placement matters. If your build takes ten minutes and the scan takes ten, either accept twenty or move the scan downstream.

1. **In the pipeline**, after the image is built and before it is pushed, so vulnerable images never reach the registry.
2. **In the registry**, periodically, to catch images that were pulled from Docker Hub and pushed without going through your build.
3. **In the cluster**, too late in theory, but the only place to catch pods that reference public registries directly.
4. **In a Kubernetes validating admission webhook**, the last gate before a pod starts. Mutating webhooks run in series and can rewrite the YAML; validating webhooks run in parallel and each one says yes or no. An image you have seen before can be checked against stored results in time; a brand-new one cannot be fully scanned in a webhook's time budget, so you reject it and let the pod retry once the scan finishes.

Which ones you need depends on what flows where. If every image, including third-party ones, is rebuilt in your pipeline, the pipeline may be enough.

## Should one CVE fail the build?

His pragmatic answer is usually no. A known vulnerability with no fix does not mean you stop shipping, and the new image may still be safer than what runs in production. One middle ground he suggests: block high-severity findings and anything that already has a patch. The same logic applies to purging the registry: remove vulnerable images that are not in use, but do not delete the one production needs to restart a pod.

## The Anchore demo

Anchore is free, open source and, in his words, "definitely not fast," with docs that are not great either. It starts from a Docker Compose file that runs the same image several times with different arguments, which he notes looks more like a distributed monolith than microservices. The docs promise a feed sync of about ten minutes; his ran from the 20th to the 23rd.

The scripted build runs image add, image wait, then exports vulnerabilities and the package inventory to JSON, fails on findings, saves both files tagged with the image hash, and only then pushes. The GitHub Actions version skips the feed sync entirely, uploads the reports as build artifacts on every run, and exposes a fail-build flag he could not get to work. One finding worth knowing: Anchore reads package manifests, so a JavaScript file dropped straight into a public folder went unnoticed.

## Who should watch

Developers and platform engineers adding scanning to an existing Docker and Kubernetes pipeline, and anyone writing the policy for what a scan failure means.
