Title: A TACO gives security, compliance and devs one language for pipelines
Description: Peter Maddison (Xodiac) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on TACO, a control model that turns regulated-bank governance into automated pipeline checks
Body:
In a bank, the thing slowing your delivery down is rarely the tooling; it is five departments using five vocabularies for the word safe. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Peter Maddison, Managing Partner at Xodiac, presented TACO (Traceability, Access, Compliance, Operations), a set of pipeline controls he has used at several banks to give architecture, security, compliance and developers a shared definition of a good pipeline, and then automate it.

This is a people-and-process talk. There is no demo, and the main artefact is a spreadsheet of controls, which he offers to send to anyone who fills in his feedback form.

## Why do DevSecOps efforts stall?

His opening claim, backed by McKinsey and Boston Consulting Group research on failed transformations, is that efforts fail from a lack of clarity, not a lack of tools. Developers, testing, operations, security, compliance and architecture all want a safe delivery system, and all describe it differently. "You can have the best security team and the best delivery team and still fail at being able to deliver securely," Peter Maddison said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021.

The symptoms will be familiar to anyone who has worked in a regulated shop. A delivery team asks which standard applies and gets pointed at a 300-page book that references 200 more. A technical review board leads to an architecture review board, and a decision on whether you may even try something takes three, six, nine or twelve months. His goal for security is to move "from this idea of being the department of no to the department of yes."

## Controls belong all along the pipe, not at the end

Using a generic pipeline from an IT Revolution white paper (source repository, build, dependency management, package, artifact repository, non-production and production deploy), he argues that controls only at the production gate cannot tell you how secure anything is. Linting and SCA at the repository, open source scanning in dependency management, SAST and DAST through the build: each stage feeds information back to the team.

Small batches matter for controls too. Peer review is a good control only if the change is small; a developer who submits every two weeks hands reviewers a few thousand lines and gets a rubber stamp.

Automated pipelines also make governance visible. At one bank his team started with the Hygieia dashboard, found that keeping it in step with every upgraded tool was a job in itself, and switched to pulling logs from each tool into their own dashboards. Those showed deployment frequency going from once every six months to once a month within six months, a number that helped adoption more than any audit report.

## What goes in the TACO?

The four groups, each with its own short list of controls:

- **Traceability**, identify what happens in the pipe: chain of custody (he has tagged everything back to a Jira ticket), test results visible to all, deployed version tracked, every change recorded.
- **Access**, secure the delivery process: source code managed, creator tracked and code signed, build once and deploy many with immutable artifacts, deployments by pipelines only.
- **Compliance**, validate the payload: peer review, code scanning, artifact scanning, data management.
- **Operations**, record and monitor: validate the target, validate quality, check it works, watch it live.

The model maps onto existing compliance frameworks as a straw man the organisation can adapt. His spreadsheet records, for every control, why it exists, what the control is, where its evidence is stored, what happens on pass and on fail, and who owns it. When a control fails, the build breaks and the result goes back to the team. He points to Capital One's published pipeline gates and Nationwide's lean controls, where control tickets land in the delivery team's backlog, as similar real-world sets.

## The paved road is an invitation

A standard pipeline with TACO built in becomes the easy button for teams that are struggling. Faster teams get the guidelines instead and can build their own, as long as the controls are there. In a company with 20,000 developers and every version of every tool, he notes, nobody reaches uniform compliance, so frameworks have to bend.

His advice for getting started: it is not about keeping audit off your back, start with one team or one value stream, and engage leaders on the conversation rather than the tooling. A new scanner that floods teams with false positives and never feeds back into their work adds reports, not safety. "Safety is about behavior, not just tools," Peter Maddison said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, adding that teams need to be able to admit mistakes without 300 approvals.

## Who should watch

Engineering leaders, platform teams and security people in banks, insurers or anywhere with an audit function, especially if you are the one translating regulation into pipeline steps. Hands-on engineers looking for tool configs can skip it.

Title: Let a script read
Description: Christopher Van Der Made (Cisco) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on automating threat hunting by turning tweets and vendor blogs into enriched cases
Body:
There is more threat intelligence published every day than any security operations centre can read. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Christopher Van Der Made, Developer Advocate for security at Cisco, showed Python scripts that pull indicators out of #opendir tweets and research blogs, check them against your own environment through the Cisco SecureX APIs, and only alert a human, at high priority, when a machine in your network actually touched one.

The tooling is Cisco's, and he says so up front, but the pattern ports to any platform with an enrichment API.

## Why automate the hunt?

He starts with the asymmetry. Attackers "can do a million attempts to hack you, but they only need one to succeed," Christopher Van Der Made said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021. Defenders have to stop all of them, with analysts who are scarce and expensive. After five years as a consulting systems engineer, he says, he met few customers with a truly well-staffed SOC.

Threat hunting, in his framing, is proactive: form a hypothesis (say, a new malware campaign is hitting us), investigate its tools and techniques, then enrich and test it against your own data and global intelligence. That last step is the one machines are good at. He cites the Hunting Maturity Model from Sqrrl's threat hunting framework, where level 0 relies on automated alerts and little data collection and level 4 automates most of the successful analysis, and argues you can borrow level 4 habits without the full governance programme.

## The pyramid of pain decides what to automate

The pyramid of pain ranks indicators by how much it hurts an attacker when you find them. File hashes are trivial to change, which is why polymorphic malware exists; IP addresses and domain names are cheap too. Network and host artefacts start to annoy, tools more so, and tactics, techniques and procedures hurt most. His split: automate collection and blocking for the bottom four layers, and hand analysts bite-sized cases so they can spend their time on the top two.

## How SecureX does the plumbing

SecureX, which comes included with Cisco security products, is an aggregation layer, not a SIEM. "We don't gather data. We pull data when we need it, and we push data when we need it," Christopher Van Der Made said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021. It queries local telemetry from products such as AMP and firewalls and global intelligence from Talos, and can push response actions like blocks.

Everything is described in CTIM, the Cisco Threat Intelligence Model: observables (domains, IPs, hashes), judgements and verdicts about them, and sightings. A target sighting is the one that matters, meaning a device in your organisation contacted the observable. The APIs follow the OpenAPI spec with OAuth2, and there are three ways in: the raw APIs, a low-to-no-code orchestrator, and relay modules for deeper integrations.

## The demo: #opendir to Webex

The first script watches the #opendir hashtag, where researchers post fresh malicious domains and IPs. On each run it fetches only tweets newer than the last seen ID, cleans them, sends the text to the Inspect API, which extracts observables (even defanged IPs) as CTIM, then enriches them. Every tweet with observables becomes a case in Casebook and a Webex Teams message; when there are target sightings, both get a high-priority tag. He tweeted a known-malicious domain before the session, and the live run picked it up and flagged it high priority because his demo environment had contacted that domain earlier.

The second script does the same for RSS feeds from Talos, Fortinet's FortiGuard and Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, using the Python feedparser module and saved feed metadata so posts are not imported twice. It matters even for Cisco customers, he notes, because a blog about a zero-day can reveal a connection your product logged weeks before the block existed. A third outline routes MSSP events into ServiceNow, and closing the ticket triggers responses in SecureX. All the code is on his GitHub.

## Who should watch

SOC engineers and threat hunters who want a concrete starting point for automated enrichment, and anyone curious how indicator feeds become tickets. If you do not run Cisco gear, watch for the loop, not the product; he lists alternatives including CrowdStrike Falcon, Cortex XDR and TheHive.

Title: One operator, four secret stores, and developers who never see the value
Description: Jhonnatan Gil Chaves (AppGate) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on syncing cloud and Vault secrets into Kubernetes with External Secrets Operator
Body:
Every cloud has its own secret store, and Kubernetes has its own Secret object, and the glue between them is where passwords end up in Git. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Jhonnatan Gil Chaves, DevOps Engineer at AppGate, showed how the External Secrets Operator pulls secrets from AWS, Azure, Google Cloud or HashiCorp Vault into a cluster, and how that lets the security team own the values while developers only ever reference a name.

It is an introductory talk with a live demo, aimed at teams that have Kubernetes running and secrets scattered across providers.

## Which secret stores does it cover?

He starts with a tour of the four backends most teams will meet:

- **AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store**: hierarchical storage for configuration and secrets, stored as plain text or encrypted with a key managed in AWS, readable from Lambda, EC2 or a cluster through IAM users and roles. Read-only access for the application, write access for the security team.
- **Azure Key Vault**: vaults for software- and HSM-backed keys, secrets and certificates, plus managed HSM pools for HSM-backed keys only, with access controlled by Azure RBAC.
- **Google Cloud Secret Manager**: a central place and single source of truth for API keys, passwords and certificates, with audit across Google Cloud.
- **HashiCorp Vault**: a unified interface to any secret, encrypted before it hits storage, with an audit log, running on premises or in the cloud. He suggests a separate cluster just for Vault, owned by the security team, with dev, staging and production kept apart.

The common thread across all four is granular access: the security team updates the secret, the application reads it, and nobody in between needs to.

## Where does Kubernetes fit?

A Kubernetes Secret keeps sensitive data out of the pod spec and the container image, and reaches the container as an environment variable, a file or a mounted path, depending on how the application was built. What Kubernetes does not do is fetch that value from your cloud's store. That is the job of the External Secrets Operator: an operator, following the Kubernetes control loop, that reads from the external API and writes the value into a native Secret.

The architecture is three steps. Define the secret in your provider, describe in YAML where to fetch it from, then consume the resulting Secret in your workload.

## What does the demo show?

The live part uses Vault as the backend:

1. Create a secret in Vault.
2. Add the external-secrets Helm repository and install the chart into its own `external-secrets` namespace.
3. Create a Kubernetes Secret holding the Vault token, and a SecretStore that points at the Vault server and path and authenticates with that token.
4. Apply an ExternalSecret that references the store, fetches one property from the Vault secret and writes it into a new Kubernetes Secret.
5. Deploy an nginx pod that reads the value through `secretKeyRef` into an environment variable, then confirm with `kubectl describe` that it arrived.

He splits the YAML deliberately. The token file belongs to the security team, the SecretStore configuration to operations, and developers only reference the synced Secret in their deployment. Developers and IT never learn the database password, as Jhonnatan Gil Chaves said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021: "Just the secure team and the application. No more."

One caveat for anyone copying the demo: the Vault token used is the root one, which is fine on a laptop and a bad idea anywhere else. In production you would give the operator a scoped auth method and policy.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers new to Kubernetes secrets who want to see the External Secrets Operator wired up end to end in under half an hour. If you already run it across clusters, you will not find much new here.

Title: PIACERE, an EU-funded plan to make DevSecOps one pipeline
Description: Radoslaw Piliszek (7bulls.com) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on PIACERE, a Horizon 2020 framework that models, verifies, sandboxes and deploys IaC
Body:
DevSecOps has no complete standard, so a consortium of twelve European organisations decided to build one. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Radoslaw Piliszek, IT systems architect at 7bulls.com, presented PIACERE, a Horizon 2020 research project that wants to take infrastructure from a cloud-agnostic model to verified, sandbox-tested, monitored deployments in a single framework.

Be clear on the scope: this is an architecture tour of a project one year into a three-year run, not a demo. He says so himself. "So we are presenting how we are thinking about it, but not how it works already," Radoslaw Piliszek said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021.

## What is PIACERE?

The name stands for Programming trustworthy Infrastructure As Code in a sEcuRE framework. The consortium spans academia, business and government, is led by Tecnalia from Spain, and runs from December 2020 to November 2023. 7bulls.com, a certified research and development centre in Poland and France, owns the integration work and the Canary Sandbox Environment. The talk was prepared with his colleague Paweł Skrzypek.

The case for it is the usual DevSecOps one, sharpened for software-defined infrastructure: frequent builds and deploys widen the attack surface, mixed on-premises, edge and multicloud estates add risk, and companies still struggle to bolt security onto DevOps. He acknowledges the XKCD comic about competing standards multiplying, and answers it by saying this end-to-end piece has not been done yet.

## Why snowflakes are the enemy

The goal he dwells on is killing snowflake servers: hand-tuned machines built for one purpose, cared for by an admin who has since left, and drifting quietly away from every standard you set. Anything you are not monitoring can hurt your security.

His fix is GitOps with teeth. A single repository is the source of truth, merge requests are the approval gate, and repository permissions are the access control, borrowing the desired-state model from Kubernetes. "The best way that we have as a humanity developed so far is the usage of version control systems," Radoslaw Piliszek said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, and he calls this accountability the one point to take away if you take nothing else. Subversion users are welcome, he adds, since the principle is what counts.

## How the pieces fit together

The design-time half:

- **DOML**, the DevSecOps Modelling Language, describes applications and infrastructure, including security rules, at an abstract, environment-agnostic layer and a concrete layer. You can still reach for a provider-specific feature, at the cost of portability for that part. Modelling tools live in a web IDE built on Eclipse Theia.
- **The infrastructure code generator** turns DOML into runnable IaC, starting with Terraform and Ansible, rather than replacing those tools.
- **The Verification Tool** statically checks both the model and the generated IaC for correctness, known vulnerabilities and security best practice.

The runtime half:

- **A runtime controller** based on BPMN drives the deployment workflow once a verified change lands in the repository.
- **The IaC Executor Manager** runs Ansible and Terraform, understands their state and output, handles reconfiguration and scaling, and is the only component that pulls credentials, for example from HashiCorp Vault.
- **The Canary Sandbox Environment** has a provisioner for opinionated, minimal OpenStack and Kubernetes environments, plus a mocked-cloud tool for checking how IaC behaves against fake provider APIs without calling AWS. Static analysis misses things; dynamic tests get closer to production behaviour.
- **The Infrastructural Elements Catalogue** stores provider offers, what was deployed where, and historic performance and security metrics.
- **The Infrastructure Advisor** deploys monitoring agents during the IEM run, self-heals small discrepancies, and feeds a machine-learning optimiser that trades off cost, performance and availability.

## Is it worth your time?

If you design internal platforms, the talk is a useful checklist of the stages a full DevSecOps flow needs: model, generate, verify statically, test dynamically in a sandbox, deploy with scoped credentials, monitor and optimise. If you want working code and benchmarks, this is the wrong talk; the project was a year old and the diagrams were the deliverable.

Title: SAST sees three apps where your serverless system has one
Description: Tal Melamed (Contrast Security) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on why SAST, DAST and IAST miss serverless flows, and testing from inside the cloud instead
Body:
The classic application security toolbox was built for an HTTP request going in and a response coming out, and serverless apps mostly do neither. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Tal Melamed, Senior Director of cloud native security research at Contrast Security, walks through why SAST, DAST and IAST each fall short on AWS Lambda, and argues for testing that connects to the cloud account and simulates events against the functions themselves.

He has been in serverless security for about five years, through two startups that were acquired (one by Check Point, one by Contrast Security), and he leads the OWASP Serverless Top 10 project. The last part of the talk shows his employer's approach, so expect a vendor section; the first two thirds stand on their own.

## What changes when there is no server?

A small serverless application, he says, already means a couple of dozen APIs and functions, 200 to 300 resources in total, and he has seen customers with millions. Everything is event-driven: a file upload, a database row change, an IoT rule or a log line can run your code. "The problem is that where your code is could also be your mistakes," Tal Melamed said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021.

He lists the Lambda details that matter for an attacker. The environment is read-only except for `/tmp`. You cannot SSH in. Execution data is supposed to be temporary, but AWS recycles warm environments between invocations, so anything your code leaves in `/tmp` can be read by the next event if the code is exploitable. The code itself and the function's credentials both sit inside the runtime, the credentials as environment variables.

## Least privilege, one function at a time

The single biggest problem is the policy attached to each function. A function that only writes one item should get `PutItem` on one table, with the table taken from the environment variable, not a wildcard action on a wildcard resource. That way an attacker who manages to run arbitrary code gets blocked by the cloud when they try a scan or a delete.

Easy for one function, hard at scale, and the internet does not help. He shows the Stack Overflow answers that fix an access-denied error by granting `dynamodb:*`, or by attaching the AWSLambdaFullAccess managed policy, which included wildcards across CloudWatch, DynamoDB, Lambda, logs and S3 before AWS deprecated it.

## You lose the perimeter

In a monolith, input validation, DLP, IPS and the firewall all sit at the load balancer. Serverless removes that choke point, since a function can be triggered by a database change with nothing in between. "When you talk about serverless, you lose the perimeter," Tal Melamed said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021. Security has to move into each function, and with hundreds of functions, anything done by hand simply will not get done.

His risk list mirrors the OWASP work: event injection, broken authentication, sensitive data exposure, over-privileged functions, vulnerable dependencies, insufficient logging, open resources, denial of service and denial of wallet, insecure shared space and insecure secret management.

## Why the usual scanners miss it

He takes a three-function iRobot registration flow from an AWS case study and runs the traditional tools against it in his head:

- **SCA and image scanning** covers around 10% of the app, and only finds problems you imported.
- **IaC scanning** is as far left as you can go, but sees configuration only, with zero code coverage and no prioritisation.
- **IAST** needs a server to instrument; on Lambda it is overkill.
- **SAST** sees three separate apps, because the queue that links the functions lives in configuration, not code. No source, no sink, plenty of false positives and false negatives.
- **DAST** can only hit the one function with an API, and gets back a 200 or a 403 while the rest of the flow happens out of sight. In one 200-function system he saw, about ten had APIs.

## Testing from inside the account

The alternative he presents connects to the account through a CloudFormation template, discovers resources, triggers and policies, builds a graph of what talks to what, then simulates events against each function and checks the cloud to see whether the attack worked, such as a file written or a table touched. It re-runs on every deployment and can generate least-privilege policies from what the code actually needs. He also mentions his earlier Black Hat demo of hacking a Lambda function by talking to an Alexa device.

For hands-on practice, he points to DVSA, the Damn Vulnerable Serverless Application he created, which deploys in a few clicks. Install it in a throwaway AWS account, never in one holding real data.

## Who should watch

AppSec engineers inheriting a serverless estate, and Lambda developers who copy IAM policies from Stack Overflow. Skip the last ten minutes if product demos are not your thing.

Title: Your Terraform pipeline needs three scanners, not one
Description: Pawel Piwosz (EPAM Systems) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021 on running Checkov, TFSec and Terrascan side by side, because each catches different misconfigurations
Body:
No single free Terraform scanner is enough. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2021, Pawel Piwosz, Lead Systems Engineer at EPAM Systems, ran Checkov, TFSec and Terrascan against the same deliberately broken templates, got three different answers, and concluded that you need all three in the pipeline before you can be roughly 90% sure your infrastructure code is clean.

His working definition of the tool sets the tone. "Infrastructure as code is a fast, dynamic, programmable way to deploy hidden misconfigurations everywhere," Pawel Piwosz said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021.

## How bad is the misconfiguration problem?

He opens with numbers, mostly from 2020 reports. The IBM and Ponemon Institute study puts the average breach at 280 days from start to containment, 207 of them spent just finding it, and attributes 19% of breaches to cloud misconfiguration. Imperva's 2019 leak of API keys and TLS certificates came from a network misconfiguration, a hardcoded API key and unencrypted records, and took ten months to spot. Capital One, the same year, exposed more than 100 million records through IAM policy mistakes and unencrypted storage.

A Sonatype survey of 300 professionals adds the day-to-day picture: 36% had suffered a serious breach from cloud misconfiguration, and almost half of the teams saw more than 50 misconfigurations a day. Only 33% check templates manually before deployment; 27% check after. And 4% reported spending more than 500 hours a week on infrastructure-as-code security, which he translates as twelve people doing nothing else.

IAM and security groups top the list of offenders. The security group failure mode will be familiar to anyone who has ever needed to test something quickly and did not know their own IP address.

## Why does dev count as production?

His rule is to control everything before it deploys, and to treat the first environment in the chain with production-level suspicion. He asks whether you would open an account at a bank whose dev and QA environments had just been exposed.

"If we deploy templates, it is already too late," Pawel Piwosz said at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021.

That means shift left for infrastructure too: static analysis in CI/CD, pipelines that break on findings, and policy engines such as Open Policy Agent for enforcement across environments.

## What does each scanner actually find?

The demo uses the Accurics test templates, which are written to be problematic, and runs each tool with defaults only. He says the beauty lies in simplicity, so no tuning.

- **Checkov** (Bridgecrew, Python): 44 checks passed, 58 failed, each with the resource, file, line and a fix guide. It also flags things like a missing security group description, which he points out is not really a security issue, so skipping checks matters.
- **TFSec** (Aqua, Go): ten critical findings plus high, medium and low, fewer than Checkov but not a worse tool. It is happiest with Terraform installed.
- **Terrascan** (Accurics, now Tenable): 38 policies violated, 20 high, 13 medium and 5 low. The slowest of the three, but it can run as a standing API server the pipeline calls.

Then all three go into an AWS CodePipeline built with CloudFormation, running in parallel after the source step. All three emit JUnit reports and all three can fail the pipeline. On a different repository the reports showed Checkov at 20 failed and 84 passed, Terrascan at 14 failed and 16 passed, and TFSec at 11 failed with no pass count, which he dislikes because it makes trend metrics harder.

The live demo also fought back: a Vagrant box refused to cooperate, and the fallback EC2 instance went up with a wide-open security group, which he flagged on camera as exactly what not to do.

## Scanners do not see drift

Drift, the undocumented manual change nobody can explain, is the harder half. Someone always holds elevated privileges, and detection tools miss things; even CloudFormation's own drift detection catches a lot but not everything. He points to driftctl and to paid offerings from Bridgecrew and Accurics for continuous monitoring, and argues for everything as code: policy, security, drift detection and remediation.

His closing line is the one to tape to the monitor: "please do not pretend that you have security."

## Who should watch

Teams that already ship Terraform through CI and want a quick comparison of the free scanners, with real output. It is an intro-level demo, not a tuning guide.

Title: JavaScript's weird parts stop being weird when you think like the compiler
Description: Rob Richardson (Cyral) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on hoisting, scope, this, the event loop and async/await, explained through how the engine runs code
Body:
Most of JavaScript's famous weirdness is the engine doing exactly what it was designed to do. At Conf42 JavaScript 2021, Rob Richardson, Developer Advocate at Cyral, walks through hoisting, var versus let versus const, the meaning of this, the event loop and async/await with one habit: pause, think like the compiler, and predict the output before the answer appears.

It's a quiz-style talk. Each snippet is followed by a let's-think-like-the-compiler walkthrough and his refrain, is that what you got? Rob credits Jonathan Mills' talk on JavaScript's scary side as the starting point.

## Why is JavaScript like this?

Brendan Eich wrote it in ten days about 25 years before the talk, and the engines (V8, SpiderMonkey, Chakra, JavaScriptCore) copied it with remarkable fidelity, bugs included. Rob points out that the early cross-browser pain was mostly the DOM, not the language. And JavaScript ships as source code, running on a machine the developer has long left, so its instinct is to keep going. Hence automatic semicolon insertion: semicolons are required, Rob says, "the engine does require it. It's just really good at putting them in place if you don't."

He warms up with the classics from the Wat video: undefined used to be an ordinary variable you could assign to, typeof null is object, and typeof NaN is number.

## Why does hoisting work?

The engine works in two phases: the first pass allocates every variable it finds, the second runs the code. Use a var before its declaration line and you get undefined, not an error, because the slot already exists. Hoisting is the story we tell to explain that. Rob calls it a convenient lie: once you picture the two passes, you don't need it.

From there he runs a set of variations on one foo variable, declared inside or outside a function, inside curly braces or not, or never declared at all. The undeclared case is the trap. Assigning to a variable that doesn't exist quietly creates a global; reading one that doesn't exist throws a ReferenceError. "Javascript tries to correct whenever it can, and it can create new variables," Rob Richardson said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021, but it can't make up a value to read. Two developers who both forget to declare i will overwrite each other's loop counter.

## What changes with let and const?

They are scoped to curly braces, which feels natural if you come from C#, Java or C++. Forget the declaration and a let example still leaks a global; declare it properly and you get the ReferenceError you wanted. const stops you reassigning the binding (the object it points to can still change). His practical warning: if Babel was compiling your const down to var, reassignments never failed. Change the build to target modern JavaScript and a batch of TypeErrors appears. Babel didn't break anything; the bugs were always there.

## What is this, really?

His one-line definition: "This is the thing to the left of the dot." Call a method through the object and this is the object; copy the method into a variable and this becomes the global object; put it in an event listener and this is the button. Wrap it in setTimeout and you lose the context, because the callback runs as a plain function call. Then the tools: call sets this and runs the function right away, bind returns a new function with this fixed, and arrow functions capture this where they are defined. That's why a find-and-replace from function to arrow functions can break an app, and why binding an arrow function again does nothing: this is already fixed.

## How does the event loop explain setTimeout of zero?

Using an online event loop visualiser, he shows the call stack, the callback queue and the web APIs waiting on outside events. Nothing in the queue runs until the stack is empty, which is why a loop scheduling ten timeouts logs ten, ten times. On a Node server, one request counting to a million or processing an image blocks every other request. A setTimeout of zero or process.nextTick isn't pointless: it gives the thread back so others can run.

## Do you need a big-bang rewrite to adopt async/await?

No. He calls async/await "clearly stolen. I mean inspired by" C#, and in JavaScript it sits on promises and generators, so the two mix freely: call an async function without awaiting and you get a promise you can chain then on, and await any old promise-returning library. For parallel work, start the tasks without awaiting, then await Promise.all on the three promises: three one-second tasks finish in about a second, not three.

## Who should watch

Developers who know JavaScript by habit and want the mental model behind it, interview candidates who'll meet these puzzles, and anyone who has had an arrow-function refactor go wrong. Experienced engine people won't learn much new, but the predict-the-output format makes it a good talk to watch with a team.

Title: Treat your tech debt like an error budget, and spend it
Description: Alexandre Omeyer (Stepsize) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on managing tech debt by size, with ownership, sprint budgets and quarterly business cases
Body:
Zero tech debt isn't a goal, it's a sign you're shipping too slowly. At Conf42 JavaScript 2021, Alexandre Omeyer, co-founder and CEO of Stepsize, distils interviews with more than 300 engineering leaders into a practical playbook: sort every piece of debt by size, give each size its own process, and treat the debt you're willing to carry the way SRE teams treat an error budget.

Honest scope: Stepsize sells an editor-first issue tracker for tech debt, and the talk ends with a short pitch for it. The first 90% is product-neutral and useful whatever tool you use.

## What counts as tech debt?

His working definition is short: "tech debt is code that you've decided is a liability," Alexandre Omeyer said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021. It exists because software is written against our current understanding of a problem, and that understanding moves faster than the code. He leans on Martin Fowler twice: software exists in a world of uncertainty, and it can take a year on a project before you understand what the best design should have been.

Using Fowler's technical debt quadrant, he separates debt worth taking on (prudent and deliberate: ship now, deal with the consequences) from mess that shouldn't be called debt at all (reckless: no time for design). The best teams, he says, refuse to file sloppy code under tech debt.

## Why should anyone outside engineering care?

He knocks down three myths: that debt is always bad, that it's only engineering's problem, and that managing it slows you down. "if you have zero tech debt, you should truly ask yourselves if you're going fast enough," he said. Debt never hits zero anyway; one engineering leader he interviewed describes it as entropy in the code base.

The numbers he brings: Gartner's claim that leaders who actively manage tech debt get at least 50% faster delivery; Stripe's finding that engineers spend 42% of their time fixing the past; and Stepsize's own survey, where two thirds of respondents said they'd ship twice as fast with debt under control and 15% said three times as fast. The cost spreads: more bugs, performance issues and downtime create more work for QA, SRE, support and account managers, and in the end unhappy customers.

## Is it a culture problem or a code problem?

Culture first. If paying down debt never helps anyone's career, nobody volunteers. The trait he singles out is ownership, quoting Snyk chief architect Gareth Visagie: ownership is a leading indicator of engineering health. He backs it with Microsoft research on Git history: the buggiest files were those where the main contributor made less than 60% of the edits. But he doesn't argue for one owner per file, which wrecks your bus factor. The target is collaborative ownership: a main contributor with more than half the edits, and the code owned by a team.

## How big should the tech debt budget be?

Teams often set aside 10% to 20% of each sprint, but Alexandre cares less about the exact figure than about how you think about it. Google doesn't aim for 100% uptime; at 99.99% it has about 52 minutes of downtime a year, and leaving that budget unspent is a missed chance to take risks. Debt works the same way: hover near the most you can tolerate, pay back when you're in the red, take on more when you're in the green. To scope it, take the parts of the code base that have debt and overlap them with what the roadmap says you'll touch. Fix the debt that's in your way and leave the rest.

## Small, medium or large?

- **Small**: fix it on the spot as part of the ticket. Follow the Boy Scout rule, and no approval needed.
- **Medium**: fits in a sprint, so it goes through sprint planning just like feature work. James Rosen, an engineering manager at Everlane, pointed out to him how much time PMs spend curating features compared with how little goes into making the case for debt. No wonder so little engineering time ends up on it.
- **Large**: a quarterly session with engineering and product leadership, where engineering managers make the business case: which priorities the debt puts at risk, whether and how fast it gets worse, and what it has already cost. Approved items go on the roadmap like any feature.

He's blunt about the tooling gap: the tech debt epic in Jira, he says, is where thousands of tickets go to die. That is the opening for Stepsize, which lets engineers log debt from the editor, tied to the code, and push it into Jira sprints.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and tech leads who need language to take tech debt to product, and engineers tired of the one tech debt sprint a year. The size framework and the business-case questions are worth stealing even if you never install the product.

Title: Your fake checkbox div needs more JavaScript than the real thing
Description: Austin Gil (Reveal Biosciences) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on enhancing native HTML forms with JavaScript instead of rebuilding them, so they work without it
Body:
The best JavaScript for a form is the JavaScript that builds on the form the browser already gave you. At Conf42 JavaScript 2021, Austin Gil, Senior Full Stack Developer at Reveal Biosciences, distils a year of writing about HTML forms into one rule: use JavaScript only for improvements that don't break native functionality, accessibility, semantics, performance or security. Progressive enhancement, with working code.

He opens with the line the rest of the talk hangs on: "the first rule of JavaScript is knowing when to use it, and therefore knowing when not to use it." JavaScript costs extra requests, more bytes, render blocking, runtime work and the chance of an error that stops everything, and it may be disabled or blocked entirely.

## What does HTML already give you for free?

A lot: input state, clickable labels, keyboard navigation and focus, screen reader support, consistent behaviour across browsers, implicit submission on Enter, and validation through required, minlength, maxlength, min, max, type and pattern. "validation built into HTML costs us zero," Austin Gil said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021. There are 24 kinds of form control to pick from.

So why do we still see a div pretending to be a checkbox? Styling, mostly. He cites Greg Whitworth's 2019 survey of 1,400 respondents: styling was the top reason people rebuild native controls, and the select was the control they rebuilt most. Making the fake one accessible means a role, aria attributes, a tabindex and separate click and keydown handlers, against an input and a label. CSS has caught up a lot (pseudo-classes such as valid, invalid and focus-within, appearance none, the visually hidden input plus sibling selector trick), and Open UI is working on proposals to make select, checkbox and file inputs styleable.

## How do you customise validation without losing the native behaviour?

The browser's ValidityState API, one of his favourites, sits on every input's validity property: a set of true/false flags matching the HTML attributes. His recipe:

- Add the novalidate attribute from JavaScript, so the native popup is suppressed only when the script is running.
- On submit, call checkValidity on the form; if it fails, focus the first invalid input, which also scrolls to it, just like the native behaviour.
- Toggle aria-invalid, and attach error messages with aria-describedby and a live region so assistive technology hears them.

His case against reaching for a validation library first: less to download, nothing new to learn, no dependency to keep patched, and a fallback if JavaScript fails. The server validates anyway, so the front end only needs to help the user.

## Why wrap every input in a form?

"I would argue that almost every input would actually benefit from having a form HTML tag wrapped around it," he said. You get native validation, Enter-to-submit without a keydown listener, and a fallback submission if your script dies. His generic fetch handler then reads everything from the markup: the URL from the action, the method from the method attribute, the payload from FormData. GET requests put the data in the query string; POST sends FormData for multipart (file) forms and URLSearchParams otherwise. He calls preventDefault only at the end, once everything has worked.

He's honest about the limits: HTML forms only do GET and POST, nested objects and arrays don't fit, GraphQL needs its own format, and the backend has to tell a fetch request (JSON back) from a native submit (redirect back).

## What else can JavaScript add?

Things HTML can't do alone: show/hide password toggles, auto-growing textareas, input masks, Ctrl+Enter to submit, repeater fields, a beforeunload warning when a half-filled form is about to be lost, and backing up non-sensitive form data in localStorage and restoring it when the user comes back.

## Where do component frameworks come in?

This, he says, is where the real superpowers are. In a Vue example he makes label and name required props, generates an id when none is given, runs validation on blur by looping over the validity flags (rangeUnderflow becomes a message about the min value), and renders errors with role alert tied to the input via aria-describedby. A form component adds custom events for valid and invalid submissions. You get the same quality everywhere, and a bug fix in one place fixes every form. The examples come from Vuetensils, the Vue library he maintains.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers who reach for a form library by reflex, anyone building design-system inputs, and teams who have lost signups to an ad blocker breaking a JavaScript-only form (which happened to Austin himself). There's a lot of code in a short talk; the slides are worth keeping open.

Title: Clean code is a habit, so let a Git hook build it for you
Description: Karan Balkar (LTI) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on making clean code automatic with Husky hooks, ESLint, Prettier, commitlint and nvm before the first feature
Body:
Clean code doesn't fail for lack of principles; it fails because nobody checks before the commit. At Conf42 JavaScript 2021, Karan Balkar, a software engineer at LTI who builds React Native apps, argues that writing clean code has to become a habit, and that the reliable way to build the habit is to wire it into the repository: Husky Git hooks, ESLint, Prettier, commitlint and a pinned Node version, all set up before development starts.

This is an introductory talk, and it says so: it skips the why and what of clean code and goes straight to the how, at the level of setup commands rather than war stories.

## Why does code that works still disappoint?

Karan walks through a typical day: commit, pull request, review comments, refactor, approval, pipeline, QA, production. When the release goes live, it feels like the job is done. His point is that this flow quietly rewards working code over maintainable code. Developers focus on making it work, little time goes to refactoring, and there are few or no pre-commit checks. Principles such as DRY, KISS, SOLID and separation of concerns are known, but teams tend to adopt them near the end of a project, or after launch.

## What does habit psychology have to do with linting?

He borrows the four-stage habit loop popularised by James Clear (cue, craving, response, reward) and maps it onto code. The cue is the mechanical stuff: dead code, unused variables, formatting, custom rules. The craving is maintainable code with fewer bugs. The response is the tooling: Git hooks and linters. The reward is consistency, saved effort and cost, and higher quality. "writing clean code also needs to be, or become a habit," Karan Balkar said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021, and the trick is that a hook doesn't need willpower.

## What goes in the toolbox?

- **Husky** runs scripts on Git events such as pre-commit and pre-push. He recommends the then-current version 6 over version 4: the setup changed significantly and is less tied to the JavaScript ecosystem. Running npx husky-init adds a prepare script that calls husky install.
- **A pre-commit hook running ESLint with the fix flag**, so whitespace and variable declaration problems are cleaned up before code is committed.
- **ESLint and Prettier**: ESLint finds problems without running the code, Prettier formats it. Create React App already ships an ESLint config, and rules live either in an .eslintrc file or an eslintConfig field in package.json.
- **commitlint** with the conventional config, because meaningful commit messages are, in his words, one of the most often neglected tasks, and they are what lets someone trace an issue years into a project.
- **nvm** to pin the Node version per project (his example is 14.17.3), so developers on Windows, Linux and macOS stop hitting dependency and version conflicts.

## When should a team set this up?

Before the first feature. His closing advice is that teams should configure the environment and the clean-code tooling before development begins, and that "refactoring should definitely be made a continuous process" rather than something left for the end. If the hooks exist on day one, nobody has to argue about them on day ninety.

## Who should watch

Developers and leads setting up a new JavaScript or React project who want a checklist of guardrails, and juniors who haven't met Git hooks yet. If your repo already runs lint-staged in CI with conventional commits, you won't find anything new; the value here is the habit framing and a compact setup list, not depth on any one tool.

Title: Your first dev job is a communication job with some code in it
Description: Riaz Virani at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on five habits for a first dev job, from asking for help with a deadline to writing pseudocode before syntax
Body:
Most advice for new developers ends at the offer letter. At Conf42 JavaScript 2021, Riaz Virani, a freelance web developer who has also worked as a CTO and project manager over about twelve years in the industry, picks up where that advice stops: five habits for surviving the first year, and most of them are about talking, not typing.

It's a short, story-driven talk. A bootcamp graduate called Ruby (he's a Ruby developer, so yes, that's the joke) lands her first job and walks into each of the five problems in turn. Riaz is upfront that many first-year failures are really failures of the people onboarding them, but a junior can only control their own side, so that's what the tips cover.

## How do you ask for help without looking like a fraud?

The first tip, ask and you shall receive, deals with the two failure modes he sees most. One is the developer who says they're still working on it at every stand-up for three days while getting nowhere. The other is the one who gives up and hands the ticket back. "You cannot wait forever to ask for help, or you cannot just throw your hands up and give up," Riaz Virani said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.

His fix is a script, not a pep talk. At stand-up: say what you're working on, which approach looks best so far, that you'll keep at it today, and that if it's still stuck, "I'd like to grab someone else from the team really quickly tomorrow to talk it through and get me unstuck." The word unstuck matters: you're asking for the next piece of information, not for someone to do the ticket. From the manager's chair, he says, that sentence does their job for them: the risk is flagged, there's a timebox, and the next step is already planned.

## What do you do with a pull request that comes back with 20 comments?

Write now, worry later. Ruby's first PR comes back covered in comments, and she wonders whether she wants the job at all. Riaz asks reviewers to add a line of encouragement when they're marking up a newcomer's work, but he knows a junior can't count on that. What they control is how they respond. "You're going to write a lot of mediocre code as you improve," he said, and that's what learning looks like. His comparison is the gym: you don't quit because you can't do someone else's pull-ups on day one. The thing people do notice is whether you take the feedback and get better.

## Why go deep instead of wide?

Ruby's bootcamp taught her seven languages and frameworks, and now everything at work feels too advanced. Riaz's view is that juniors rarely fail from too little variety; they fail because they don't know any one thing well enough to be useful. His example comes from Rails teams, where backend-heavy developers often hack the CSS together. If you happen to like CSS and design, offer to own that. A clear area of expertise earns credibility, the rest of the stack sinks in while you work, and when you do ask for help people see someone worth teaching.

## Are senior developers always right?

No, and his fourth tip, don't put your teammates on a pedestal, is about saying so early. When a senior developer's suggested approach isn't working, either the idea was wrong or you misunderstood it, and both get sorted in one conversation. Wait three days and it becomes a politics problem, because now the senior has to explain why nobody noticed. "Your job is to communicate about the code across your team," he said. In his experience, half the time the senior admits their approach was wrong.

## The one tactical tip

Pseudocode is your friend. Write the logic out in plain-language comments first, then translate it into the language. Experienced developers don't think about syntax any more; new ones spend half their attention on where the closing parenthesis goes. Splitting the logic from the syntax turns one hard task into two easier ones. His summary: "So the point here is, syntax sucks."

## Who should watch

Bootcamp graduates and anyone in their first months on a team, plus the leads who onboard them: Riaz suggests experienced developers spend a minute remembering their own first job, so they understand what new teammates are going through. Don't expect JavaScript content; the advice works in any stack. The stand-up script alone is worth the half hour.

Title: Keep WordPress for the editors, serve the readers static files
Description: Colby Fayock (Applitools) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on running WordPress headless behind Next.js, so every page is built at compile time and served from storage
Body:
WordPress is still where most content lives, so stop fighting it and stop letting it serve your pages. At Conf42 JavaScript 2021, Colby Fayock, Developer Advocate at Applitools, shows how to keep WordPress as the editing tool, pull its content through WPGraphQL at build time, and ship a fully static Next.js site that scales the way a bucket of files scales.

The talk is a pitch plus a demo: why headless WordPress still makes sense, then a fresh site spun up from his open source Next.js WordPress Starter, then a smaller starter dissected line by line.

## Why bother with WordPress at all?

He opens by addressing the CMS in the room. Citing BuiltWith, he notes that almost 35% of the top 1 million sites run WordPress, and that it's detected on at least 28 million sites. Developers may cringe, but clients already know the editor, the plugin ecosystem is enormous, and almost any problem you hit has a search result. Many newer headless CMSs, he argues, are built for developers, which is a poor fit when the people publishing aren't technical.

What WordPress is bad at is serving traffic. Every page is a server hit; caching plugins help but still serve from a server; and the day a post goes viral is the day your readers pay for it in timeouts.

## What does going static actually buy you?

He frames it with three of the AWS Well-Architected concerns: performance, reliability and cost. A static HTML file from storage or a CDN is just fast, and it doesn't fall over. "That static site will survive that Reddit hug of death when your post ultimately goes viral," Colby Fayock said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.

On cost he is blunt: "Storage is cheap. It's really, really cheap." The WordPress server is still there, but it now only answers content editors and build-time requests, so its traffic drops to almost nothing.

## How does the plumbing work?

WordPress has shipped a REST API since 4.7, so it can already act as a headless CMS. Colby goes one step further with WPGraphQL, a plugin created by Jason Bahl, which adds a GraphiQL explorer to the dashboard. In the demo he clicks together a query for posts (id, slug, title, excerpt, content) and gets content back as an HTML string, which means WordPress still decides what a post's markup looks like.

On the Next.js side the key choice is getStaticProps over getServerSideProps. The server-side version renders on every request; the static version runs at compile time, so the visitor gets a file from storage. Individual posts use a dynamic route file named after the post slug, with getStaticPaths listing every slug at build time and getStaticProps fetching each post by that slug through Apollo Client.

## What about search on a static site?

The WordPress API has search, but calling it at runtime would defeat the point. His fix is a custom webpack compiler in the starter that fetches every post at build time and writes a static search index, which the browser loads into memory or fetches asynchronously when someone searches. It's a neat trick, and a good example of pushing work to build time.

## What comes in the box?

The Next.js WordPress Starter is created with yarn create next-app from the GitHub template, then pointed at the WordPress GraphQL endpoint through an environment variable in a local env file. On the first yarn dev it pulled posts from a fresh WP Engine instance and also generated social sharing images, the search index, a sitemap and an RSS feed. It works with plugins such as Yoast and ACF. Because the full starter is a lot of code for a short talk, he then spins up a second, basic starter that does the same data fetching with far less around it.

His closing line sets the scope fairly: "the goal here wasn't to get you all over to jump over to WordPress, but to show you the flexibility of it and why it's still compelling."

## Who should watch

Front-end developers inheriting a WordPress client, agencies whose editors won't give up the WordPress admin, and anyone new to Next.js data fetching who wants to see getStaticProps and getStaticPaths used on a real CMS. If you already run a headless setup, the search index trick is the part to take home. Note it predates incremental regeneration being the default answer to stale static content.

Title: Elm's pitch for the front end - if it compiles, it works
Description: Jordane Grenat (Viseo) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on Elm, a typed functional language for web apps that rules out null crashes at compile time
Body:
JavaScript can never take a mistake back, and Elm can. That's the core of Jordane Grenat's case at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: Jordane, a web software engineer at Viseo, argues that Elm, a statically typed functional language built only for web applications, trades JavaScript's eternal backward compatibility for a compiler that refuses to ship whole classes of bugs, null crashes first among them.

The talk is half argument, half live coding: a tour of the syntax in the Elm REPL, then a small heads-or-tails game built step by step in the editor.

## What's wrong with JavaScript, in his framing?

Backward compatibility is both the web's best feature and its curse. Because nothing can be removed, the oddities stay forever. His opening example: in JavaScript, null greater than zero is false, null equal to zero is false, yet null greater than or equal to zero is true. The language only grows, and you end up learning callbacks, promises, generators and async/await, then which one to use when, then a framework, then a bundler.

The dynamic nature also hurts tooling: editors can only help so far, dead code elimination is guesswork inside a module, and the feedback loop often runs through the browser. And npm packages can do almost anything once installed. But his main complaint is confidence. "I will even bet my house that the majority of bugs in JavaScript are caused by null pointer exception," Jordane Grenat said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.

## How does Elm get rid of null?

It doesn't have one. Elm has Maybe, a custom type that is either Nothing or Just a value, and because the type says a value can be missing, the compiler forces you to handle that case. Jordane quotes Tony Hoare calling the null reference his billion-dollar mistake, then shows why Elm can't make it.

The same idea runs through custom types. His JavaScript example models a remote string with three variables (the value, an isLoading flag, an isError flag), which allows nonsense states like loading and errored at once. In Elm it becomes one type: not loaded, loading, loaded with a string, or error with a code and message. Impossible states simply can't be written down.

The numbers he cites come from NoRedInk, an e-learning platform and big Elm user: over three years, about 62,000 JavaScript runtime exceptions from roughly 17,000 lines of JavaScript, against almost zero from about 200,000 lines of Elm.

## Why does he call functional programming honest?

He skips the academic definition. A JavaScript sendEmail function might throw if the address is missing, and you won't know without reading the body. In Elm, side effects are declared in the types, so a function can't quietly call the network. "In elm you don't execute side effects, you let the runtime execute them," he said. The coin flip in his demo shows how: the update function returns a command, a recipe for a random coin, and the runtime runs it and sends the result back as a message.

That loop is the Elm Architecture: a model holding all state, a view function rendering it to HTML, messages from user events, and an update function returning the next model. If it reminds you of Redux, that's because Redux took it from Elm.

## The compiler as pair programmer

Much of the demo is the compiler talking back. Concatenating strings with plus gets an error that points at the exact spot and tells you to use the double-plus operator; a list mixing strings and numbers gets an error with a link explaining what to do instead. "In elm the errors will guide you to working code," he said, and the heads-or-tails game grows by adding a state, watching the compiler list every case you forgot, and fixing them.

Two details stood out. The package manager enforces semantic versioning: the compiler works out whether your change is a patch, minor or major release, so an update can't silently break your app. And publishing a package requires documentation.

## Where does Elm hurt?

He's fair about the costs. Governance is essentially one person, the language's creator Evan Czaplicki, so you take his direction or leave it. Some find it verbose because everything is explicit. And talking to JavaScript is asynchronous message passing, which takes getting used to.

## Who should watch

Front-end developers tired of chasing undefined in production, teams with complex UI state and frequent refactoring, and anyone who wants a gentle on-ramp to typed functional programming. He adds that writing Elm made his JavaScript more readable, and points to his GitHub workshop for a hands-on start. React and Redux users will recognise more of it than they expect.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Daniel Danielecki on [TypeScript's strict compiler](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Daniel_Danielecki_TypeScripts_Strict_Compiler), the same safety argument from inside the JavaScript world.
- Sergii Zhuravel on [Redux tools for React-Redux apps](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Sergii_Zhuravel_Reduxtools_ReactRedux_apps), the architecture Elm inspired.

Title: Giving a JavaScript app spidey senses with anomaly detection
Description: Ron Lyle Dagdag (Spacee) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on anomaly detection for JS apps, from outlier basics to Azure Anomaly Detector on a Raspberry Pi
Body:
Spider-Man's spidey sense is the tingle that says something is wrong before he can say what. At [Conf42 JavaScript 2021](https://www.conf42.com/js2021), Ron Lyle Dagdag, Lead Software Engineer at Spacee and a Microsoft MVP, argued that anomaly detection is the same superpower for an application, and showed a JavaScript app on a Raspberry Pi flagging a bad temperature reading through Azure's Anomaly Detector API.

The talk is half primer, half demo. If you've never thought about outliers beyond a threshold alert, it's a good map of the options; if you have, skip to the Pi.

## What counts as an anomaly?

Dagdag's definition: identifying unexpected items or events that differ from what is normal, under two assumptions, that anomalies are rare and that they differ significantly from normal instances. For developers, he says, the human version is experience. "It's that gut feel and vibe or intuition that you learn through time," Ron Lyle Dagdag said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.

He sorts outlier causes into artificial and natural, and the artificial list is a useful checklist for anyone cleaning data: data entry errors (100,000 typed as 1,000,000), measurement errors, experimental errors such as starting collection late in a sprint, intentional outliers like students under-reporting alcohol consumption, data processing and extraction errors, and sampling errors, such as measuring athletes' heights with a sample made up mostly of basketball players.

## Rules, statistics or machine learning?

- **Rule-based systems** set thresholds and limits (alert above a temperature). They need industry experts to describe the known anomalies, require labelled data, and don't adapt when patterns change.
- **Statistical techniques** flag points that deviate from the mean, median or quantiles, or from moving averages, with low-pass filters such as Kalman filters and histogram-based outlier detection. Their big advantage: they're interpretable, so you can explain the formula to your boss.
- **Machine learning** comes supervised (decision trees, SVMs, LSTM forecasting), unsupervised (k-means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN) or self-supervised (LSTM autoencoders), with density-based, clustering-based, Gaussian, one-class SVM and PCA-based approaches.

His rule for choosing: anomaly detection fits when you have very few positive examples, many kinds of anomaly and anomalies nobody has seen yet, as in fraud detection, machinery, data centre monitoring and IoT. Supervised learning fits when positives are plentiful and future ones will look like the training set, as with spam, weather prediction or cancer classification.

The first demo is deliberately small: an npm statistics package filters outliers out of an array of numbers, run line by line in a Jupyter notebook through tslab, a TypeScript and JavaScript kernel.

## Why time series, and why IoT?

Logs, stock prices, sales and sensor readings are all values indexed by timestamp. IoT makes it urgent: sensors are cheap, networks are fast, and these systems are becoming critical, as anyone who has hunted for the TV remote while the smart speaker was down knows. He calls that the Internet of Broken Things.

He walks through four time series anomaly types: outliers, spikes and level shifts, pattern changes (a kink in a garden hose slowing the flow) and seasonality (ice cream in summer, pizza around the Super Bowl), plus the difference between univariate detection, the focus here, and the harder multivariate case.

## A Raspberry Pi with a red X

Azure Cognitive Services' Anomaly Detector does real-time or batch detection over REST, needs no labelled training data, adapts to new data, and has adjustable sensitivity. Behind the API it picks from a gallery of algorithms, including Fourier transformation, extreme studentized deviate, STL decomposition, dynamic threshold, z-score and SR-CNN, depending on whether your series shows seasonality. The limits: granularity from minutely to yearly (custom intervals such as every five minutes need a flag), and between 12 and 8,640 points per request.

The demo runs on a Raspberry Pi with a Sense HAT. JavaScript reads the temperature every minute into a timestamped array, creates the client from an endpoint and key (the resource is set up through the Azure CLI), and asks whether the last point is anomalous. The real reading, 34.275, isn't. Changed to 134, it is, and the Sense HAT's LED matrix lights up with an X. SDKs exist for C#, JavaScript and Python, there are Docker containers for running at the edge, and it integrates with Power BI and Azure Databricks for streaming. Metrics Advisor, then in preview, adds a portal for root cause analysis.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers working with IoT, telemetry or business metrics who want something smarter than static thresholds, and anyone who needs a clear tour of anomaly detection methods before picking one. The code is on his GitHub.

Title: Incremental static generation is not just a Next.js trick
Description: Rishi Raj Jain (Layer0 by Limelight Networks) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on incremental static generation for Nuxt.js by caching SSR pages at the edge
Body:
Incremental static generation (ISG) usually arrives bundled with one framework and one host. At [Conf42 JavaScript 2021](https://www.conf42.com/js2021), Rishi Raj Jain, Solutions Engineer at Layer0 by Limelight Networks, showed the same idea working for Nuxt.js: render a page on first request, cache it at the edge, and serve every later visitor a static copy, without rebuilding the site.

It's a short, focused talk from a vendor's engineer, and the implementation runs on Layer0. Still, the pattern underneath, server-rendered once and edge-cached after, is the useful part, and he's upfront about its drawbacks.

## What is ISG, and why did it need freeing?

Next.js introduced the idea as Incremental Static Regeneration: create pages after the site is built, so you only build the pages you need but still get static speed on dynamic ones. He calls it the best of both worlds. The catch, in his framing, is that it's a feature of both your framework and your infrastructure, and some platforms support it only for Next.js. Layer0 describes itself as an all-in-one Jamstack platform to develop, deploy, preview and monitor front ends. "Our jam is to bring large and complex websites that serves up to millions of pages into subsecond loads," Rishi Raj Jain said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.

## Two flavours of first visit

He uses the official Next.js static tweet example, which builds a page per tweet ID, to explain the two fallback modes:

- **fallback: true**: the first visitor to an unbuilt page gets a placeholder while the page builds in the background. The rendered page and its data response are cached, so the next visitor gets the static build.
- **fallback: blocking**, the preferred mode: the first request is server-side rendered and the browser waits for the finished page. Later visits are served the static HTML.

Either way, someone pays for the first render.

## What you gain, and what you give up

The benefits: pages on demand, a minimal static build, no full rebuild to add content, faster deployments, and on Layer0, purging by regular expression through the console or REST API, or keeping the cache across deployments.

The drawbacks, which he lists himself: the first user always sees a fallback or waits; some users will see stale data; and ISG breaks the immutability of deploys, since what's served depends on what was cached rather than only what was built. Layer0's answer to the last one is letting you choose whether the cache survives a deployment.

## How do you build it with Nuxt?

The demo rebuilds the static tweet idea around Medium: enter a Medium handle and get a page listing that user's posts. The first load fetches the page's data JSON, renders the page, and requests the same page again in the background so it lands in the edge cache. On reload, the timing comes in at 29 milliseconds.

The recipe has four steps:

1. **API routes**: Nuxt's `serverMiddleware` property in `nuxt.config` points at a custom Express server that does the data fetching.
2. **Dynamic pages**: a file such as `pages/blog/_slug.vue`, with `asyncData` for fetching, so the request is server-side rendered (or blocks client-side navigation) and users only see a finished page. Layer0 deployments expose an API URL environment variable for server-side fetches.
3. **Fetch the page again once mounted**, the step he calls the most critical: that second request ensures the page is built at the edge and ready to serve as if static.
4. **Configure Layer0's EdgeJS routes**: dynamic blog paths are cached at the edge with revalidation, not cached in the browser, served from the static folder when present, and otherwise rendered by the app, meaning Layer0 asks Nuxt to render the page and stores the result. API routes can get the same caching treatment.

## Who should watch

Nuxt and Vue developers who envied Next.js its ISR, and anyone weighing static builds against server rendering for a site with too many pages to prebuild. It's brief, so pair it with a longer ISR talk for the trade-offs.

Title: Quick Apps bring the WeChat mini program idea to Android
Description: Martin Alvarez-Espinar (Huawei Technologies) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on Quick Apps, Vue-like light apps for Android that run without installation
Body:
The cheapest app install is the one that never happens. At [Conf42 JavaScript 2021](https://www.conf42.com/js2021), Martin Alvarez-Espinar, Web Standards Manager at Huawei Technologies, introduced Quick Apps: light applications for Android written with web technologies and a Vue.js-style framework, which users open by scanning a QR code or tapping a link, with no marketplace detour and no install step.

It's an overview of a platform his employer backs, delivered by someone who also works on the W3C MiniApp standardisation effort. Expect concepts, architecture and capabilities, not a live coding session.

## Why light apps at all?

The friction he targets is the classic one: find the app in a marketplace, download it, install it, and lose a share of users at every step. In Asia the alternative is already mainstream. WeChat launched mini programs five years before the talk, letting developers ship games, shops and payment flows inside the super app, and "nowadays WeChat has more than 3.2 million mini programs," Martin Alvarez-Espinar said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.

The field he maps is crowded: mini programs and mini apps from WeChat, Alipay, Baidu and 360, Facebook Instant Games, Uber Eats inside the Uber app, progressive web apps (where the browser plays super app), KaiOS apps, Apple's App Clips, Android Instant Apps, Fire OS web apps, WebAPK, and Quick Apps, which run on top of Android itself.

## A W3C standard to tame the fragmentation

At the W3C, he explains, the MiniApp work collects requirements from mini app vendors to standardise the common core: the package format, delivery and how the metadata is described, coordinated with the group behind progressive web apps so the two stay aligned. Quick Apps are one implementation of that standard.

## What does a Quick App look like to a developer?

If you know Vue, you know most of it. The framework follows the model-view-viewmodel pattern, and a page has three parts: a template using a domain-specific markup close to HTML with mustache-style data binding, a script exporting the page's data and handlers, and styles in CSS, with Less and Sass preprocessing built in. His example is a page whose button swaps a title to hello world. Virtual DOM updates keep refreshes fast.

Underneath, the platform runs two engines in separate threads: a JavaScript engine (V8) for page logic and a render engine for templates and styles. User events flow from the renderer to the logic and data flows back. A JavaScript bridge connects both to the operating system's native APIs. That split, he argues, is where the near-native performance comes from.

Built-in components cover the basics (text, span, links, inputs, forms) and native-style extras such as tabs, a drawer, swipers, pull-to-refresh, maps, camera, video and star ratings. You can write and share your own components too. The API list is long: calendar, contacts, alarms, battery level, network type, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, local storage and databases, sharing with other apps, push notifications and running in the background, plus vendor services such as payments, accounts, ads and AI speech recognition. He also cites an estimate that a Quick App needs only 20% of the code lines of an equivalent native app.

## The product lifecycle comes with it

Much of the talk is about everything after the code. Discoverability: widgets, global search results on the device, links from websites and other apps, and listings in app marketplaces with an open button instead of install. Acquisition: one click from a banner to a running app, and one-click login if the device already has an account. Monetisation: in-app payments, ads and rewarded videos for casual games. Retention: a prompt to save a home screen shortcut, remembered state, push notifications and banners in other apps. The use cases he has in mind are task-oriented: paying for parking or checking live traffic while out and about.

## What's missing?

Reach. "So far, quick apps is only supported by Android devices, but there are billions of Android devices out there, so this is a good start," he said. The goal is a universal platform aligned with W3C standards, and he's frank that it needs more documentation, more code and examples, and a bigger community. That's the pitch for the OW2 Quick App Initiative, a vendor-neutral open source group anyone can join.

## Who should watch

Mobile and front end developers curious about the mini app model outside China, and anyone following the W3C MiniApp work. If you only target iOS, the architecture is still worth seeing next to App Clips and PWAs.
