Title: A production front end on AWS, written in TypeScript with CDKTF
Description: Denis Artyuhovich (DAZN) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on building S3, Route 53, CloudFront and ACM hosting for a JS app with CDK for Terraform in TypeScript
Body:
For a lot of front end engineers, infrastructure as code is still something the platform team does in a language they never learned. At [Conf42 JavaScript 2021](https://www.conf42.com/js2021), Denis Artyuhovich, Senior Software Engineer at DAZN, set out to change that: in one talk, he builds production-ready hosting for a React app on AWS, in TypeScript, using CDK for Terraform (CDKTF), and explains each AWS service as it goes in.

It's a live, step-by-step build. By the end the app sits in a private S3 bucket behind CloudFront, on a custom domain with an SSL certificate, with Terraform state stored remotely.

## Why automate the clicks at all?

At DAZN, a sports streaming service running on smart TVs, phones, laptops and consoles, he describes hundreds, probably thousands of features and infrastructure changes that can land several times a day. Doing that by hand means someone forgets to document a checkbox, or the AWS console UI changes and someone ticks the wrong box and the site goes down. "It's increasingly crucial to automate literally everything, what can be automated," Denis Artyuhovich said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.

He contrasts imperative scripts (full control, but you maintain every step, and it scales badly) with declarative tools, where you describe the end state and providers do the work. Terraform is the declarative one, with more than 1,000 providers, and CDKTF lets you write it in TypeScript.

## Step one: a bucket, deliberately insecure

The project starts with Create React App and the TypeScript template, then `cdktf init` with the TypeScript template in a terraform folder. The first errors come from the React project's types and go away with `skipLibCheck` set to true in the tsconfig. The AWS provider goes into `cdktf.json`, and `main.ts` holds a class extending `TerraformStack`.

The first resource is an S3 bucket named after the domain, configured as a website with an index document and a public-read ACL, "because who cares about security, right?" he jokes, promising to fix it later. He does. The loop is build, synth, then `terraform init` once and `plan` and `apply` thereafter. Deployment of the app itself stays separate: an `aws s3 sync` of the build folder, because deploys happen far more often than infrastructure changes and usually belong to CI or a deploy dashboard.

## Why did the DNS step fail on purpose?

Next comes Route 53: a hosted zone for a subdomain and an A record aliasing to the bucket. The apply fails at validation, intentionally. He bought the domain from a different registrar, which he calls a common case, so the hosted zone's NS values have to be copied to that registrar by hand (his has no API and no Terraform provider). Wait for the name servers to update, rerun apply, done.

## CloudFront, a wildcard certificate and no public bucket

A bucket in us-east-1 is slow for users far away, and there's no HTTPS. So he adds an ACM wildcard certificate with its DNS validation record and validation resource. ACM for CloudFront requires the us-east-1 region, so if your bucket lives elsewhere you need a second provider. Then a CloudFront distribution with the bucket as origin, a default root object, no geo restrictions yet, default cache behaviour for GET, HEAD and OPTIONS only, a redirect to HTTPS and a default TTL of one day. Ordered cache behaviours can override that per path, for example to never cache `index.html`. Route 53 now aliases to the distribution.

Finally, security: an origin access identity, a policy document allowing it to get and list objects, and a bucket policy attaching it. Redeploy the files without the public ACL, and the S3 URL returns access denied while the domain keeps working through CloudFront.

## State belongs in a remote backend

Working alone, local state is fine. With a team it needs a shared home, and not GitHub, since state holds sensitive information. Terraform supports DynamoDB, S3 and its own cloud. He adds an S3 backend with three parameters (a separate bucket, a key and a region), runs `terraform init` again, and lets it copy the local state over.

## Why TypeScript instead of HCL?

No new language to learn; autocomplete and typings that replace trips to the Terraform docs; real modules, functions and array methods instead of one folder of HCL where you can't tell what depends on what; sharing through npm; and tests in the same language. He also wants front end teams to own monitoring and alerting as code (New Relic, Sentry, PagerDuty).

His caveat is fair: Terraform is mature, but CDKTF was still in beta at the time. The synthesized Terraform JSON is the stable part. If minor CDK issues are unacceptable, stay on HCL and migrate later.

## Who should watch

Front end developers who deploy to AWS and want to understand what's underneath, and teams that want infrastructure in the same language as their app. If you already run Terraform, the CDKTF workflow and TypeScript structure are the new parts.

Title: Your framework is tech debt, and the browser is the way out
Description: Andrew Desmarais (Meltwater) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on building whole apps with web components, from Shadow DOM and slots to routing and state
Body:
Andrew Desmarais opens with a line designed to start arguments: every front end framework you pick is a future rewrite. At [Conf42 JavaScript 2021](https://www.conf42.com/js2021), the Principal Software Engineer at Meltwater, a full stack developer of 17 years who started on back ends, made the case for building your next application on web components and the platform alone, then answered the questions people always ask him about routing, styles and state.

It's an opinionated talk, and he means it to be. It's also short on hand-waving: each objection gets a concrete tool or a few lines of config.

## Why treat framework code as debt?

"Every line of front end code is tech debt when it's written in a framework," Andrew Desmarais said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021. His exhibit is AngularJS: the best option of its day, adopted widely for enterprise software, deprecated years later, with end of support set for December 31, 2021. Every one of those apps had to be rewritten into something, and he'd like that something to be web components.

The general charges: frameworks equate to vendor lock-in, upgrade fatigue is real (skip upgrades and you skip security patches and speed improvements), and every framework drags in a dependency tree you don't control, which is how left-pad broke builds across the web. And in the framework wars, he says, you always pick wrong.

## What's actually in the box?

Web components are four pieces of the platform:

- **Custom elements**: your own HTML tags. The only rules are all lowercase and at least one hyphen, so even a tag called `t-` is valid, to his visible dismay. Lifecycle methods (`connectedCallback`, `disconnectedCallback`, `attributeChangedCallback`) will feel familiar to anyone coming from a framework.
- **Shadow DOM**: a miniature DOM isolated from the main document. Styles inside it don't leak out, so you can use plain class names, or even tag selectors, with no build tooling to obfuscate them.
- **Slots**: consumers bring their own content, like content projection in Angular, children in React or slots in Vue. His card component takes a title, image and description and handles the layout.
- **Templates**: predefined HTML cloned quickly for faster rendering.

The documentation, he points out, is MDN, which beats most framework docs.

## Is it enterprise ready?

YouTube is built on web components, which he shows using the Web Component DevTools extension to inspect attributes, properties and slots. The Nintendo web store is too. Browser support covers all major modern browsers, with polyfills for IE11 if you must. And the upgrade problem flips: when something needs patching, the browser vendors ship it.

Delivery can be a single script tag pointing at native ESM, with markup that stays plain, readable HTML. If you want bundling and minification, he shows webpack doing it in nine lines of config and Rollup with Terser in 13.

## But how do I handle templates, routing and state?

The second half is his answer to the people he has to convince:

- **Dynamic templates**: it's just JavaScript, so template literals cover most cases. For more, lit-html at about 6 KB adds template rendering plus data, event, attribute and property binding; µhtml-style libraries at around 2 KB go smaller.
- **Data binding**: a web component is an object like any other, so grab it with a query selector and set complex data on a property.
- **Routing**: the standalone Vaadin Router gives child routes, fallback routes, route parameters, redirects and lazy loading of bundles, for example only loading the second page of a wizard when someone navigates there.
- **Sass**: you need a build step. Webpack does it with sass-loader and raw-loader so the stylesheet imports as text for the shadow root's style tag; Rollup's Sass plugin with output set to false is simpler.
- **State**: keep it simple. He uses singletons, for example one user service instantiated once and referenced anywhere. Redux works but is usually overkill; on GraphQL, Apollo's caching covers it.

## Who should watch

Teams staring at an AngularJS (or any ageing framework) rewrite, and developers building design systems that have to work across several frameworks. If you're happily shipping React, it's still worth half an hour to hear the counter-argument made well.

Title: vee-validate v4 turns a Vue form into one place to declare fields
Description: Abdelrahman Awad (Octopods) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on vee-validate v4, from search-and-replace adoption to schemas, the composition API and devtools
Body:
Forms break in boring ways: someone adds a field, forgets to bind it, forgets to send it, and the API quietly receives less than the user typed. At [Conf42 JavaScript 2021](https://www.conf42.com/js2021), Abdelrahman Awad, Senior Frontend Engineer at Octopods, who created vee-validate and has maintained it since 2016, showed how version 4 of the library attacks that friction, and why it's built composition API first.

It's the author explaining the design of his own library, which at the time pulled around 1.4 million downloads a month and 8.6k GitHub stars. You get both the what and the why.

## What makes forms hard?

Awad names five pain points. Value tracking: native HTML forms track values for free, but JavaScript forms need two-way bindings kept in sync, and checkboxes, radio buttons and file inputs each have quirks. Validation and error messages: sync or async pipelines, global string rules or explicit functions, and messages that are hard to normalise once localisation enters (not every language lets you write a field-neutral sentence). UI and UX: "Users hate filling out forms," Abdelrahman Awad said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021, and as he adds, developers usually do too. Organisation: an admin dashboard with dozens of CRUD forms, each in create and edit modes. And debugging: most libraries give you nothing when a form refuses to submit.

The goals follow from that: reduce friction on those points, handle the common 80% of UI, UX and developer experience needs, offer a progressive API in the spirit of Vue itself (drop it in from a CDN, or build a full single-page app), and design composition first.

## Declare a field once and you're done

A typical form has three sections: the markup that binds state, the state declaration, and the code that collects values before submission. vee-validate v4 collapses them. Swap the native form element for the `Form` component and inputs for `Field`, give each field a name, and the library creates the model, binds the input and retrieves the value on submit. Names double as paths in the model tree, so object and array syntax produce nested values, such as an array of links. Adding a field means adding one element.

## Three ways to express validation

Awad came to the front end via backend work, and the library supports the validation styles each ecosystem prefers:

- **JavaScript functions**, the baseline: return true for valid, or a string as the error message. That also opens the door to libraries such as validator.js.
- **Laravel-style string rules**: define the rules from the companion rules package once at your app's entry point, then write required and email as a compact piped string. Useful in apps with many forms.
- **Schema validators** such as Yup and Zod, per field or, better, one object schema for the entire form. That removes the back and forth between script and template, and lets you express conditions like a field being required when another value is above five.

## Progressive enhancement, inferred from your intent

The neat part is the plain server-rendered form, posting to a register endpoint on Laravel, Rails or plain PHP with full page reloads. Replace the elements with `Form`, `Field` and `ErrorMessage` components, add a schema, and if there's no submit handler the library validates on submit, shows errors when invalid, and otherwise lets the native full-page submission go ahead as if there were no JavaScript at all. Add a handler and it calls it only when the form is valid, always preventing the native submit.

For UX there are meta flags (valid, submitting, touched, dirty, validated) to disable buttons or show spinners, and an invalid-submission hook he uses in three lines to scroll a long form to the first broken field. The library ships no form generator, but he shows an eight-line one driven by a schema object, and points to FormVueLate for generators with first-party integration.

## Why composition first?

The components API is itself built on the composition API, so the two mix freely. `useField` gives a custom input its value and error message; `useForm` takes a validation schema and returns a `handleSubmit` that validates before running your callback. The before and after is the payoff: a verbose form of `Field` and `ErrorMessage` pairs becomes three one-line custom inputs for name, email and password. He's explicit that this is the point: use it to build your own components, and reach for other libraries if you only want to validate plain JavaScript values.

Finally, a Vue devtools plugin adds a vee-validate inspector that shows forms and fields as nodes, red when invalid and green when valid, with values, errors and meta flags, plus buttons to clear or force-validate. His demo finds a mismatched confirm-password in seconds.

## Who should watch

Vue developers building anything bigger than a login form, especially admin dashboards and multi-step flows. Developers on other frameworks will still recognise the problem breakdown.

Title: A front end developer's cloud wish list, answered by git push
Description: Maxim Salnikov (Microsoft) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on shipping a front end app with Azure Static Web Apps, from first push to global hosting and local emulation
Body:
Front end developers want their app online, fast, everywhere and on HTTPS, and most of them would rather not become DevOps engineers to get there. At [Conf42 JavaScript 2021](https://www.conf42.com/js2021), Maxim Salnikov, Developer Engagement Lead at Microsoft in Norway, framed that as a wish list and walked through how Azure Static Web Apps covers it, using a tool he built for his other life as a hobby DJ and music producer.

It's a Microsoft speaker showing a Microsoft service, and he says he helped shape it with feedback and some of the architecture. Read it as a short, practical product walkthrough.

## The app behind the demo

Salnikov needed a BPM counter for live audio, to know roughly how fast the music he was producing on the fly was before mixing it with an existing track. He couldn't find one, so he wrote BPM Techno: pure web technology, no back end for the core feature. It captures the audio stream in the browser, applies filters and calculates peaks. It's a progressive web app, installable and offline-capable, because all the analysis happens on the device.

Then the usual question: it works on localhost 3000, so how does he share it with every DJ on the planet, and add a few features (thumbs up or down on a detection, user accounts with stats), while staying a front end developer?

## What does a front end developer want from a cloud?

His list, which he argues applies equally to a solo developer and an enterprise team:

- **Hosting**: fast, reliable, geo-distributed, ready for single-page apps and server-side rendering, custom domains, a free SSL certificate.
- **Deployment**: fully automated, with staging environments, and no DevOps skills required.
- **Feature helpers**: serverless API endpoints, authentication through providers such as GitHub or Twitter rather than a hand-built login and password reset flow, role-based access, and tools to mimic all that on a laptop, ideally offline.
- **A generous free tier**: a hobby project gets evenings, not dollars. His only spend so far was the domain.

## How do you get from repo to global hosting?

Setup starts from the VS Code extension (open the project, press plus, create static web app) or the Azure portal. Either way you point it at the code repository, confirm where the front end code lives (handy in a monorepo) and where the build artifacts land (the build folder for a Create React App project), and wait. The app comes up on a generated test hostname, distributed over multiple data centres, and you can attach a custom domain afterwards.

Deploying a fix is one step: push to the branch you chose. "And you know folks, there is no step number two, this is only thing you need to do," Maxim Salnikov said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021. Under the hood, a GitHub Actions workflow file appears in your repo when you connect the resource. It installs npm modules, runs the build (npm run build by default, or your own command) and copies the artifacts out. You don't have to read it on day one, but you can tune it. Azure Repos and Azure Pipelines can run the same flow if your code doesn't live on GitHub.

## Can you run it all locally?

That's the job of the Static Web Apps CLI, which he strongly recommends installing globally. It gives you a `swa` command that serves the app, emulates authentication and authorization, and serves or proxies API requests. For a Create React App project it's one line: `swa start` pointed at the dev server on localhost 3000, the npm start command, and an `./api` folder for the functions.

## The demo

The live app listens to the microphone through the browser with a spectrum analyser running. Talking produces nonsense BPM, clapping produces visible peaks, and his own sample track settles at 120 BPM after a moment, which is what he produced it at. The thumbs-up button calls an API endpoint that's part of the same app. The code is a classic React application plus a service worker for offline use; to make it work on Static Web Apps he only had to supply the build command.

His demo repository, which he describes as an end-to-end journey through staging environments, authentication and API functions, is open source, alongside Microsoft Learn paths and the service docs.

## Who should watch

Front end developers with a side project that deserves a real URL, and teams evaluating static hosting with built-in APIs and auth. If you already deploy to a static host from CI, the local CLI and provider-based auth are the parts worth your time.

Title: Point it at a database, get REST, GraphQL and gRPC for free
Description: Joe Wingard (CMI/Compas) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on Service Engine, which surveys a database and auto-provisions validated REST, GraphQL and gRPC CRUD
Body:
Most data access layers are the same CRUD endpoints written again for every table, with validation that drifts from the schema it's supposed to mirror. At [Conf42 JavaScript 2021](https://www.conf42.com/js2021), Joe Wingard, Associate Director of Engineering at CMI/Compas, presented Service Engine, his open source Node.js application that connects to a database, surveys its tables, views and materialized views, and provisions REST, GraphQL and gRPC interfaces with full CRUD and validation, without you writing the endpoints.

It's an author's tour of his own project (his first npm package, he notes), focused on the REST interface, with the other two described as working the same way.

## How does it know what to serve?

At startup Service Engine runs migrations, then a database survey query against the internal tables. For every resource it collects the field names, whether each accepts null, and whether it belongs to a primary or unique key. That material builds Joi validators for each resource, and only then are the services published: REST and GraphQL on port 8080, gRPC on 50051.

Anything Knex supports works: PostgreSQL (including PostGIS), MySQL, SQLite, Oracle, Redshift and SQL Server. It ships three ways: the npm package, a Docker implementation that also builds the generic public image, and a template repo that uses that image, which is what Wingard uses himself. Running it is an env file plus one docker command.

On boot you also get a health check route, an auto-generated OpenAPI 3 document (render it like Swagger UI, or import it into Insomnia or Postman), the `.proto` file gRPC clients need, and a GraphQL Playground when the node environment isn't production.

## A URL that reads like a WHERE clause

The core idea, as he puts it, is that "the exercise is to build a rest query and generate SQL and then execute it." The path names the resource as schema and table; query string keys name fields, with an optional dot suffix for the SQL operator. His example searches for engineers in New Jersey or Pennsylvania with a handle like `sudo%`: a plain field means equals, `state.in` takes several values, `handle.like` does pattern matching.

Supported operators cover the comparisons, not, like, null and not null, in and not in, range and not range. Some take a fixed number of arguments: range needs exactly a lower and an upper, and sending more gets a verbose 400. With PostGIS and geometry fields you also get bounding box, radius (a lat/long centre plus metres) and custom polygon queries in WKT.

Query-wide context (page, limit, orderBy, fields, separator) is prefixed with a pipe, a deliberate choice to avoid colliding with real column names. Fields work on every action, not only reads.

## What gets validated, and where?

Every request, REST, GraphQL or gRPC, goes through one chain Wingard summarises as normalize, validate, build SQL. A call for a resource that doesn't exist fails early with a 400. Otherwise it becomes a standard query object, which the validators check field by field: missing required fields, a string that can't be cast to a number, an unsupported operator, a geo operator on a non-geometry field or a non-PostGIS database, an orderBy on a field that isn't there. Only valid objects reach the query builder.

Single-record read, update and delete exist only for keyed resources; unkeyed tables and views still get create and search. Create accepts one record or many. Three headers help with debugging: every response carries a request UUID that is also injected into every log line, `x-get-sql` returns the generated SQL, and `x-get-count` returns the unpaginated total, which he suggests sending only on the first page to save a database query. Swap `service` for `debug` in the path and the whole chain runs but stops short of execution.

## Middleware for the keys users never see

The feature he clearly built for himself is middleware: a function that receives the validated query object before SQL is built and can modify it. His real use was appending a partition key to inbound queries, invisible to the caller, to optimise them. Redactions hide fields from responses, permissions restrict CRUD per resource (whole service read-only, a couple of tables writable), and aggregate or subquery resources can be predefined in configuration.

## What will bite you

GraphQL SDL accepts only a narrow character set, so table or field names with spaces won't provision. Startup migrations need a database user allowed to create objects; he recommends disabling them and running migrations once from CI/CD rather than from every container in a cluster. MySQL and SQLite can't return fields on mutations, so you get a 201 with no body; Postgres can, and is his recommendation for new projects. His deployment picture puts several instances, one per database, behind a reverse proxy so callers see one data access layer, and he says "you get a lot of wins by deploying a system in this manner."

## Who should watch

Backend and full stack developers who maintain internal data APIs, and anyone curious about schema-driven API generation.

Title: Storybook replaces the local hacks you write to see a button state
Description: Milecia McGregor (Iterative) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on component-driven development with Storybook in Redwood, from generated stories to documented states
Body:
Every front end developer has hard-coded a prop, faked an API response or flipped a boolean in a running app just to see what a component looks like in a state the real data won't produce today. At [Conf42 JavaScript 2021](https://www.conf42.com/js2021), Milecia McGregor, Developer Advocate at Iterative, argued that Storybook makes that dance unnecessary, and showed how Redwood wires it in from the first command so you never have to retrofit it.

It's a friendly, hands-on talk: a short case for component-driven development, a live build of one button component in a fresh Redwood app, and a slide on adding Storybook to a project that isn't Redwood.

## What does component-driven development buy you?

McGregor's framing is that most of us already do it without naming it. Instead of pages that each carry their own self-contained components, you build loosely coupled pieces that accept props and handle whatever state the data arrives in. A component written for the reporting page then also works on the settings page, because it was never tied to one page's data.

Storybook is the tool that lets you develop those pieces in isolation. Her example is the humble button, with a primary state, a secondary state and a dark mode variant. Without isolation, checking each one means running the whole app, changing data, calling APIs or tweaking code by hand. "With storybook, you don't have to do all of the spaghetti code locally," Milecia McGregor said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.

## Documentation and tests come along for free

The benefit she thinks gets overlooked is documentation. A new teammate, or you six months later, won't remember which props a component takes, what values they accept or what they do. A story records each state with the props that produce it, so the catalogue doubles as a living reference and, as business needs change, a history of how the component evolved.

Testing gets easier for the same reason. If a button needs to switch to a differently coloured loading state while data arrives, you can test that component on its own without rendering the full page or mocking a pile of APIs.

## Redwood generates the story before you ask

Redwood, in her words, is a full stack JavaScript framework (or a full stack Jamstack one): a React front end, a GraphQL server on the back end and Prisma handling the database, all present the moment you create an app, with Storybook included. Nothing is hidden; you can edit every generated file.

The demo runs `yarn create redwood-app` (with an optional TypeScript flag), then `yarn redwood generate page home /` for the root route. Redwood writes the page component, a test file and a Storybook story, and updates the routes. `yarn redwood storybook` starts the Storybook server, and the home page appears there already. She points out the use for permission-dependent pages: toggle a report page's columns per role in the story, without touching the app.

Then the button. `yarn redwood generate component` produces the same trio of component, test and story. The component takes two props, a type and a label, and a styled-components wrapper changes background and text colour based on the type. In the story she builds a template that takes args, binds a primary export to it, then copies it for secondary and dark. All three appear in Storybook side by side, no app changes required.

She mentions one more Redwood command that takes a GraphQL schema and generates the server types, resolvers, pages and components that fetch the data. It isn't demoed, but it explains why she says Redwood makes development oddly fast.

## Not on Redwood?

Storybook drops into an existing React (or other framework) project with one command run at the project root that writes the configs. She adds the honest caveat that you will then debug it, "because it's never that easy."

## Who should watch

Developers who haven't tried Storybook yet, and teams with a component library that lives only in people's heads. If you already run Storybook daily, the Redwood generators are the new part. Tables, she notes, benefit most: missing columns and odd empty states are exactly what's hard to force in a running app.

Title: A/B test code is a sandcastle, so build it to wash away
Description: Bill Coloe (Lovevery) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on writing A/B test code that ships fast, avoids flicker and survives single-page apps
Body:
Most front end code is written to last. A/B test code is written to be thrown away, and that changes almost every decision you make about it. At [Conf42 JavaScript 2021](https://www.conf42.com/js2021), Bill Coloe, Front End Optimization Engineer at Lovevery and a veteran of several conversion rate optimization agencies, walked through how an experiment goes from hypothesis to live variation, and what a developer has to get right along the way: snippet placement, a real build step, and code that copes with pages that re-render under your feet.

It's a practical talk built around one example, adding a mini cart to the header of a demo apparel store, run through Optimizely. Coloe is clear that the platform choice matters less than people think: "at their core they all do the same thing."

## Why does the testing snippet have to block rendering?

The first rule surprises developers trained to make every script async. With client-side testing, the platform snippet goes as high in the document as possible and loads synchronously. Otherwise users get a glimpse of the original page before their variation swaps in, the flicker that makes an experiment look broken and skews its results.

"So it's very important that this script is implemented synchronously," Bill Coloe said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021. The trade-off is honest: yes, it's render blocking, which is exactly why the variation code you ship through it has to be small and fast. He also flags the classic beginner mistake of dropping the snippet into a tag manager, which quietly makes it async. The one exception he allows is a test that only touches elements below the fold.

## What does a developer need before writing a line?

A test plan. Coloe's template restates the hypothesis (if we add a mini cart to the header, users will find checkout easier and order conversion rate goes up), then lists the problem, devices, targeting, key metrics, duration until statistical significance, mockups of control and variation, dev specs and QA stories. With that in hand the developer knows exactly what to build, and the QA team knows what to break.

He then walks the execution order every platform shares: the snippet loads, checks the URL against the targeting rules, checks the audience (desktop only, in his example), checks traffic allocation, and only then picks a variation. Allocation doesn't have to be 100%: to limit risk you might expose 10% of traffic, split 50/50 between control and variation.

## In-house or third party changes everything

An in-house developer has source code access. That allows hide/show tests (ship the new component hidden, reveal it with one CSS rule in the variation), deploys synced with the main site, and redirect tests for full page redesigns. A third-party developer only has the live page: every change is injected JavaScript, you hunt for global functionality to hook into, and a client deploy can remove a dependency your variation relied on without anyone telling you. Coloe spends most of the talk on the third-party case, because it's the harder one.

## A build step for code you'll delete

You can paste one long IIFE into the Optimizely editor, CSS assembled through string concatenation and all. Coloe shows it, then shows why you shouldn't: past a small experiment it gets unwieldy. His preferred setup is a webpack project per experiment, with imported CSS and HTML, transpiling and npm packages, compiled into a single bundle you paste into the variation. A preview link built from the variation ID (the `optimizely_x` and `optimizely_token` query parameters) then lets designers and QA see the real experience before launch.

For single-page apps, where virtual page changes re-render components and wipe your changes, he lists four tools: mutation observers, intersection observers, overriding the XHR prototype to hook into completed requests, and polling functions that wait for a condition before running a callback.

## Sandcastles, not houses

The best line of the talk is borrowed. Coloe quotes his former coworker Aaron Montana, who contrasts the architecture analogies of normal software with experiments: "Experimentation, however, is the art of building sandcastles." The point is velocity: build quickly, learn, and let the tide take it. A winning variation can run at 100% for a short while, but it belongs in the core team's roadmap as a permanent change, not living on in the testing tool.

His remaining tips are the kind you learn from incidents: avoid concurrent tests on the same page, namespace classes, IDs and globals, QA on real devices, check logged-in and logged-out states, and when a bug report comes in, first opt out of the testing platform to confirm it isn't already on the control. Keep a hypothesis library, prefer small changes so a result can be attributed to one thing, and make sure the page has enough traffic to reach significance at all.

## Who should watch

Front end developers who have just been handed their first experiment ticket, and agency developers who write variations against sites they can't see the source of.

Title: Only tests left? Write them first, and let bowling prove it
Description: Tal Doron (NICE) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on why developers dislike tests and how TDD with business-flow tests fixes it, live-coding the bowling kata in Jest
Body:
If you have ever said "I've finished, it's working.. only tests left" at a stand-up, Tal Doron, Principal Software Engineer at NICE, would like a word. In his Conf42 JavaScript 2021 talk, [I've finished, it's working... only tests left..!?](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Tal_Doron_only_tests_left), he explains why so many developers dislike writing tests, then live-codes Uncle Bob's bowling kata in Jest to show the alternative: tests first, written against business flows rather than code structure, so that when the code works the task really is done.

Doron spent years as a backend developer before becoming a technical coach, running an agile software engineering training across NICE's R&D teams and then pairing with those teams on their own backlog. The talk feels like a condensed version of that class.

## Where is the love?

He surveyed several hundred developers before the talk. About 45% said they like writing tests, 50% said they don't but see the value, and about 5% hate it. He suspects the sample is biased towards people who care about testing, and still concludes that roughly 55% of developers do not like something they spend a lot of their time doing, which is how it ends up done badly.

He blames two effects:

- **The afterthought effect.** Tests written after the code mean reworking code you already know works, and treating test code as a second-class citizen with no design principles. Under deadline pressure, there is no time to test, which causes defects, which causes more stress, and an incomplete suite that nobody trusts.
- **The unit effect.** Read the test pyramid as an order to test the smallest units in isolation and you get piles of mock objects, a massive number of tests, and refactoring hell: nobody refactors when it means rewriting three or four hundred tests. Units pass, integration breaks, trust drops again.

## Kent Beck's two rules, plus three

The fix is Kent Beck's TDD: write new code only when an automated test has failed, and eliminate duplication by refactoring before you continue. Red, green, refactor, with design thinking saved for the refactor step. Doron adds three guidelines that carry most of the weight:

- A unit is a business flow, and tests should not know the structure of the code.
- Mock objects are only for external boundaries: databases, I/O, streams, other services. Never an internal layer.
- Test code is as important as production code, and gets the same clean-code treatment.

## The bowling kata, test by test

The kata (code katas being Dave Thomas's idea, this one from Bob Martin) asks for two methods, roll(pins) and score(), for a ten-frame game with spares, strikes and a possible third roll in the last frame. Doron starts from the simplest flow, a gutter game scoring zero, and makes it pass by returning 0. A game of all ones forces a running total. A third test exposes that a module-level score is shared between players, so he refactors to a class with a beforeEach, then removes duplication in the tests too.

Spares force the switch from iterating over rolls to iterating over frames, and he replaces a comment with an extracted, well-named method, his rule being that comments are only for what readable code cannot say. Strikes follow, the loop index becomes frame, and then he adds a perfect game expecting 300. It passes without any code change: the implementation is already complete.

Should he keep adding tests? Doron said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: "So I want my test suite to be small but very powerful." Every test is code you maintain; an edge case like the perfect game earns its place, a pile of redundant ones does not. As for the if/else chain that the open-closed principle frowns on, he is relaxed: the rules of bowling are a closed set.

## Who should watch

Developers who write tests last and resent it, and teams whose unit suites make refactoring scary. If you have never watched someone do TDD for real, the live kata is the main event. His closing advice: go for business flows over unit tests, stop mocking everything, and practise on katas until test-first is muscle memory.

Title: Stop writing web tests in your backend's language
Description: Dmitry Vinnik (Facebook) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on user-centric web testing in JavaScript, from Jasmine and Jest to WebDriverJS, Protractor, TestCafe and Cypress
Body:
A Java backend does not mean your web tests should be in Java. Dmitry Vinnik, Developer Advocate on Facebook's open source team, made that his starting point at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 in [Modern Web Testing: Going Beyond Selenium](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Dmitry_Vinnik_Web_Testing_Selenium): test web apps the way users see them, in JavaScript at every level of the pyramid, and pick your end-to-end framework for the app you will have in two years, not just the one you have today.

## The pyramid you draw versus the one you have

Everyone knows the test pyramid: lots of cheap, fast unit tests with low confidence, fewer integration tests, and a handful of slow, expensive end-to-end tests that give the most confidence. Vinnik points out that most teams actually run one of its anti-patterns:

- **Ice cream cone**: few unit tests, more integration tests, a big end-to-end suite and manual testing piled on top. He has worked at companies where this was the reality.
- **Hourglass**: lots of unit and UI tests, very few service tests.
- **Cupcake**: an inverted pyramid with a massive layer of manual testing.

The way out, he says, starts with deciding what you are actually testing. His running example is the classic to-do app.

## Why JavaScript, even with a Java backend?

Matching the test language to the backend is the mistake he wants gone. The user experiences the frontend, so tests should speak about what the user sees. He ties this to three ideas: a hybrid model where developers test and testers develop instead of throwing code over a wall, the ubiquitous language of domain-driven design (if the user says account, the test should say account too), and user-centric testing.

In practice that means JavaScript throughout. Unit tests in Jasmine check a single function, such as one that creates a to-do item, without caring which services sit behind it. Integration tests use Jest snapshot testing: render a React component to JSON, save it, and catch any change to its structure, class names or styles.

## End-to-end: tasks, not keystrokes

At the top of the pyramid the focus moves from developers to users. Describe tasks (user enters a username, user presses OK) rather than interactions like sending keys to a field, and use the screenplay pattern rather than page objects when you structure test code.

He then walks the tool ladder:

- **WebDriverJS**, the official Selenium bindings for JavaScript: still the de facto standard, generic and well integrated, with ID, CSS and XPath locators. The old promise manager is gone in favour of async/await. Generic is also its limit.
- **Protractor**, from the Angular team: everything WebDriverJS has, plus Angular-specific locators and knowing exactly when the app is ready, so no explicit waits. Point it at React and you end up switching off the synchronisation it was built around.
- **TestCafe** and **Cypress**: both handle waits well, run tests in parallel, give fast feedback and support recording. TestCafe's recorder is a good way to move manual testers into automation; Cypress, he notes, was getting more traction online.

## How do you choose without regretting it?

The patterns that matter are waits, parallel execution, rapid test development and recording or IDE support. Then come his rules. Vinnik said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: "Don't try to fit a thing into a use case that doesn't work." Avoid mixing several test tools in one infrastructure, which makes a complex system at least twice as hard to test. Look at GitHub stars, npm downloads and integrations, but run a proof of concept before migrating. Think about cost of transition (betting on Protractor is risky if the company may move to React), count the hours spent maintaining Selenium tests before deciding a move to Cypress is worth it, and be honest about team skills: for a team of non-JavaScript developers, the whole JavaScript argument may not be worth the trouble.

## Who should watch

Teams with a Selenium suite and a nagging feeling they should move, and QA engineers in hybrid teams choosing between Cypress and TestCafe. Note it was recorded when Protractor was still maintained; the selection advice outlives the tool list.

Title: A promise won't save your frozen UI, a Web Worker will
Description: Atila Fassina (SAP) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on concurrency vs parallelism in JavaScript and moving heavy work into Web Workers, with Comlink for types
Body:
Wrapping a huge computation in a promise does not stop it freezing your UI; it just freezes it slightly later. Atila Fassina, Lead Frontend Engineer at SAP, shows exactly that in his Conf42 JavaScript 2021 talk, [Multi-Thread demystified](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Atila_Fassina_MultiThread_demystified), then moves the same task into a Web Worker in about ten lines of React and TypeScript. His point: leaving the main thread is cheap, and more frontend developers should keep it in their toolbox.

## Concurrent is not parallel

He starts by separating the two ideas. Concurrent threads are like chat threads: you can switch between them fast enough that nobody notices, but you never reply to two at once; they compete for one engine. Parallel threads are a one-person band playing accordion, keyboard and trumpet at the same time.

setTimeout, setInterval and promises are all concurrent. A setTimeout callback arrives late if a long task is running, setInterval stays on schedule at the expense of everything else on the main thread, and promises are more efficient but behave the same way in nature. For real parallelism in the browser, the main tool is Web Workers, and they are what UX loves: nothing running in a worker blocks interaction with the page.

## What changes inside a worker

The rules he lists are the ones that bite in practice:

- **Different global scope.** No window; a DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope or SharedWorkerGlobalScope instead, reachable as self for isomorphic code. Shared workers are, as far as he knows, gone from WebKit, so not an option in Safari.
- **Data is copied, not shared.** Messages go through postMessage and the structured clone algorithm, so the main thread and the worker hold perfect copies, never the same instance. Wait for the result before touching the data again.
- **Errors are silent unless you listen.** A runtime error in the worker does not block the main thread, which also means nobody hears it fail unless you handle the error event.
- **No DOM.** Only thread-safe APIs are available, which is fine, because UI work belongs on the main thread.
- **CSP is not inherited.** In nearly every case the worker does not inherit the page's Content Security Policy, so set the right headers on the worker script request, or it runs as if there were none. The exceptions he names are workers from UUID origins and inline workers embedded in the page.

## The demo: three ways to run one big task

A stopwatch keeps the recording honest. Run the task synchronously and the UI freezes; every click on the button lands at once when it finishes. Run it in a promise and nothing improves, because the task is too big to interleave. Run it in a Web Worker and the UI stays responsive with a loading state while the work happens in the background.

The plain version is short: the worker listens for the message event and posts back the result; the React component creates the worker from a URL its bundler understands (Parcel 2 in his case, webpack works too), posts the task size and sets state when the message returns. No dependencies.

What bothered him was postMessage accepting anything. Comlink fixes that by wrapping the worker in a Proxy-based remote procedure call: expose an object with your task in the worker, export its type, then wrap the worker in the main thread with that type as a generic. Calls become strongly typed promises, and the click handler just becomes async. Comlink needs Proxy support, so Internet Explorer 11 is out without a polyfill.

## There is more under the hood

importScripts loads third-party code into a worker (handle the network error, or it surfaces as a runtime error that stops the thread), workers can spawn subworkers, and service workers and audio worklets also run off the main thread. Fassina said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: "I just want to make it very clear that getting out of the main thread is very doable and cheap". He is not arguing for heavy computation on the client, only for using a worker when you do need it.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers with one expensive operation that makes the page stutter (parsing, sorting, number crunching), and React developers who have never created a worker. The concurrency analogies make it a good first talk on the topic.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Tamas Piros on [speeding up JavaScript with WebAssembly](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Tamas_Piros_Supercharge_Web_Assembly), from the same event.
- Lorenzo Pieri's [Node.js event loop fairytale](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Lorenzo_Pieri_nodejs_eventloop_fairytale) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023.

Title: Your React app is slow because of your re-renders, not React
Description: Assaf Krintza (Livecycle) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on cutting React reconciliation work with production builds, React.memo, children props and local state
Body:
A demo running at 11.4 frames per second, then noticeably smoother once served as a production build, without changing a line of code: that is how Assaf Krintza, co-founder of Livecycle, opens the practical half of his Conf42 JavaScript 2021 talk, [React is Killing your Performance and it's Your Fault](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Assaf_Krintza_React_Performance). The title is the thesis. React's reconciliation is efficient but not free, and most slow components are slow because of how we trigger it.

## Declarative comes with a runtime bill

React lets you describe the UI instead of calling document.createElement and friends. To keep that promise, every prop or state change triggers a render that builds a new element tree, diffs it against the previous one, and turns the difference into the minimum DOM calls. The diff is fast, but it runs on every update, so the cheapest re-render is the one that never happens.

Before any of the tricks, his ground rules. Krintza said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: "Optimize only when needed, because most of the times those optimizations, they don't matter unless they do." Premature memoisation adds bugs and complexity and can even slow things down. In his experience the most expensive work in a frontend is usually DOM changes rather than React itself, so rule those out first, and use the React DevTools extension to investigate.

## Check you are not benchmarking the dev server

The first demo draws random coloured circles every frame. Under the Create React App dev server, Chrome's FPS meter shows 11.4. Serve the same app as a production build from a plain HTTP server and the frame rate goes up by somewhere between 50% and 100%. The dev server does a lot of work for warnings and tooling. He admits this is the one he always forgets.

## React.memo, and how it bites

A pure component (same props and state, same output) can be wrapped in React.memo so React skips the render when the props have not changed. His demo is a draggable wrapper around an artificially slow child. Dragging updates the wrapper around 60 times a second, and without memo the slow child re-renders every time even though its text prop never changes. Wrap it, and dragging is smooth.

Two catches:

- **The comparison is shallow.** Props are compared by reference, so mutating an object prop (a size object with height and width, in his example) while using memo produces a UI that never updates. Create a new object with the spread operator instead.
- **Children are always new.** A component that takes children gets new element objects on every render, so memo always fails its comparison and only adds the cost of checking.

## Decouple the child, push state down

Two refactors often beat memo. First, pass the slow component in as children instead of rendering it inside the draggable. The draggable becomes a generic component, and since the child element is created by the parent, dragging no longer re-renders it.

Second, do not keep state higher than it needs to be. His last demo has a button that sets a random text colour, with that colour state living in a parent that also renders the slow component, so every click re-renders both. Moving the colour state into its own small component means the click only re-renders that component.

His summary fits on a sticky note: use the production build before optimising, use React.memo where props are stable, decouple children from their wrappers, and keep state as low as possible.

## Who should watch

React developers who reach for a library or a memo for every problem, and anyone whose app has one sluggish interaction they cannot explain. The demos are small and easy to reproduce at home. The talk predates React 18, but the reconciliation basics it explains still apply.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Travis WaithMair's [intro to Solid.js for React developers](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2022_Travis_WaithMair_solidjs_react) at Conf42 JavaScript 2022, a framework built to avoid re-renders altogether.
- Tejas Kumar on [React Server Components](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Tejas_Kumar_react_server_components) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023.
- Daniel Espino Garcia on [levelling up your React hooks](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Daniel_Espino_Garcia_18_reacthooks_improvement_development) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024.

[Watch Assaf Krintza's talk](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Assaf_Krintza_React_Performance)

Title: Why your design system breaks micro frontends, and the split that fixes it
Description: Azizi Yazit (Trovicor Intelligence) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on a provider-consumer design system with headless UI for independently deployed micro frontends
Body:
Micro frontends promise independent deployments, then a shared design system quietly takes them away: bump the button package and every app has to rebuild. Azizi Yazit, GUI Architect at Trovicor Intelligence, tackled that tension in his Conf42 JavaScript 2021 talk, [Design System For Micro-Frontends](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Azizi_Yazit_System_MicroFrontends). His answer is to split the design system in two: a slow-moving provider with tokens and headless logic, and a consumer layer each team owns.

## What both sides want

He sets up the two definitions first. Micro frontends are independently deployable frontend apps modelled around business domains, valued for incremental change, independent deployment and autonomous teams. A design system is a collection of reusable components guided by clear standards, with documented components, a living style guide (Storybook in his examples) and a single source of truth for design. He then scores two common ways of shipping a design system against the three micro frontend goals.

## Centralised: versioned packages

A core team maintains the components and publishes them to npm or an internal registry like Verdaccio or Nexus; apps pick a version in package.json. Incremental change is easy, since each app upgrades when it wants. But every change means consumers recompile and redeploy, contributions go through pull requests reviewed by the core team, and teams have to coordinate on who stays on which version. Not independent, not autonomous.

## Independent: Module Federation

With webpack 5 Module Federation, the design system deploys like an app and consumers fetch components over the network at runtime. No recompiling. The catch: there is only one live version, so a breaking change pushed by accident hits every consumer at once. Avoiding that needs coordinated releases across teams and a lot of testing across all the apps, which is the coupling micro frontends were meant to remove.

## The provider-consumer split

Yazit said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: "Then my recommendation is to use a design system called provider consumer design system."

The **provider design system** holds what rarely changes: the colour system, spacing system, icons, typography and fonts, small atomic components meant to be customised, and composite components built with two patterns:

- **Headless UI**: the provider ships the UI logic and interaction handling, and the consumer decides the look and feel. He shows a combobox built this way in React, Angular and Vue.
- **Compound components**: a complex component delivered as a set of named parts (header, body, title) the consumer assembles.

Each team's **consumer design system** customises the atomic components and implements the composite ones on top of the headless logic. The split is abstraction versus implementation: the provider owns behaviour, the consumer owns appearance.

Because the provider changes rarely, keeping it as a versioned npm package (with the recompile that implies) is acceptable. Day-to-day UI changes live in each team's consumer layer and deploy with that team's app, so one team's breaking change no longer cascades into everyone else's.

## Who should watch

Frontend architects running, or about to run, micro frontends with a shared component library, especially across different frameworks. It is a short, conceptual talk with diagrams and brief headless UI snippets, not a full implementation.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Tomasz Krajewski on [micro frontend foundations](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Tomasz_Krajewski_Micro_Frontends_foundations), from the same event, including a design system shared across apps.
- Milecia McGregor on [using Storybook to maintain components in Redwood](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Milecia_McGregor_Storybook_Redwood), also at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.
- Elena Shabanova on [building a design system in limited timeframes](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Elena_Shabanova_building_design_system) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024.

Title: Micro frontends, or how to swap Angular for React one app at a time
Description: Tomasz Krajewski (Frontend House) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on micro frontend foundations, shell apps, mixed-stack teams and step-by-step migration
Body:
If your backend went microservices years ago and your frontend is still one big app, Tomasz Krajewski, Tech Lead at Frontend House, has a short primer for you. His Conf42 JavaScript 2021 talk, [Micro Frontends - foundations](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Tomasz_Krajewski_Micro_Frontends_foundations), walks from monoliths to distributed systems to micro frontends, then makes the case with four use cases, the strongest being a technology migration done piece by piece instead of a rewrite.

It is a foundations talk, as the title promises: concepts, diagrams and trade-offs rather than code. A good first talk on the topic, and a quick one.

## Monolith versus distributed, the honest version

He starts with the two shapes most of us know. The monolith, with a Ruby on Rails app as the example, puts frontend, backend and database in one application: easy to start, simpler data security, a reduced choice of technologies, little modularity, and hard to scale as complexity grows. The distributed approach splits functionality into microservices (patients, hospital, payments, auth in his healthcare example) behind an API gateway, with GraphQL federation as an example of the pattern. It scales and performs under heavy traffic, but costs more complexity up front, is harder to debug, harder to prove secure, and response time grows with the number of nodes a request crosses.

## So what is a micro frontend?

The same distributed idea, applied to the web app. Instead of one app containing every module, you build separate micro apps (in his example schedule, video call, user profile and notifications), and a shell app composes them, playing the role the API gateway plays on the backend. The user sees one app. Each micro app can talk to microservices directly, through a single API, or get its data from the shell.

His pros and cons list is short. Each module is a self-contained app with its own ecosystem and its own API integration, modularisation makes scaling easy, and independent teams can work on the same frontend. The catch is that good communication between apps is the key, and the architecture is complex to set up. Frameworks help: Bit, webpack 5 with Module Federation, single-spa and OpenComponents. He has used Bit with React and recommends its tutorials.

## Why would you want one?

Four reasons, all from the healthcare example:

- **Independent teams on mixed stacks**: a React team owns the schedule app, an Angular team the video call app, a vanilla JS developer the shell. Staffing gets easier because teams do not all need the same skills.
- **Technology migration**: move from Angular to React one module at a time, starting with the schedule app behind an adapter.
- **Reusable micro apps**: the same video call app inside the patient, doctor and ambulance driver apps, as long as it exposes the right communication interface.
- **One design system across apps**: three apps with the same branding share a component package documented in Storybook, which becomes the foundation of a design system.

The migration case is the one that sells it. Krajewski said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: "So following the rule, make an evolution, not a revolution." Teams can also try a different technology on one module without rewriting the whole app.

He closes with companies that use the approach, among them Zalando, Microsoft, Leroy Merlin and Starbucks, and a final rule: choose your technology with surgical precision, picking the one that fits each business problem.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers and leads who have heard the term and want the map before choosing a framework, or who need a quick explainer to share with a team considering the switch. If you already run Module Federation in production, skip ahead to the related talks.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Azizi Yazit on a [design system for micro frontends](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Azizi_Yazit_System_MicroFrontends), from the same event.
- Trishul Goel on [destructuring frontend monoliths with micro frontends](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Trishul_Goel_monolith_Microfrontends), also at Conf42 JavaScript 2021.
- Maksim Zemskov's counterpoint, [scaling an application without micro frontends](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Maksim_Zemskov_glorious_monolith_scaling_application_microfrontends), at Conf42 JavaScript 2023.

Title: Distributed tracing in Node.js starts with one tracer file
Description: Michael Haberman (Aspecto) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on how OpenTelemetry traces requests across Node.js services, and the one file you need to start
Body:
Logs tell you which line in service A threw; metrics tell you DB1 is running hot; neither tells you that service B and service C were both hammering service A when it happened. Michael Haberman, co-founder and CTO of Aspecto, used his Conf42 JavaScript 2021 talk, [Distributed tracing for Node.js using OpenTelemetry](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Michael_Haberman_distributed_tracing_OpenTelemetry), to show how traces fill that gap and how little code it takes to get them: a single tracer file per service.

It is a beginner-friendly introduction. You do not need deep Node.js experience; the focus is on what traces are, how context moves between services, and a short live demo with Jaeger.

## Why another signal when we have logs and metrics?

His scenario: an alert says service A cannot write to DB1. Logs send you to the throwing line, and you start the familiar game of walking back through files to see what led there. That works inside one process. Metrics might show high CPU or a traffic spike, which raises the next question: which endpoints in service A hit DB1, and is the traffic even HTTP, or a Kafka message? Two upstream producers, and you cannot tell which one caused it.

A trace is the story of one request across services: B called A, A queried DB1, in sequence or in parallel, with requests and responses attached. Haberman said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: "We need logs, metrics and traces in order to understand how an incident occurs." The goal he names is lower MTTR: see the failing hop and what led to it, fix it faster.

## How does a trace survive the hop between services?

OpenTelemetry, a CNCF project and the standard way to collect traces (it also does metrics and logs, but traces are the most mature part), runs as an SDK inside each service. When service A calls service B, OpenTelemetry injects its context into the request headers, a breadcrumb saying A sent this call. Every action is a span; all spans of one request share a trace ID. A's span has no parent because it is the root; B reports its own span with A's span ID as the parent, and B's database query names B's span as its parent. The tracing backend rebuilds that parent-child tree into the timeline view.

## The demo: two services, one file each

The demo has an item service whose data endpoint calls a user service, which picks a random user from a mock list. Each service imports a tracer file with its service name, and that is the whole integration. The tracer file sets a Jaeger exporter (Jaeger visualises traces; run it locally, in production, or swap in a vendor backend), the service name so spans can be told apart, and the instrumentations to load. He uses only HTTP and Express, but there are instrumentations for Kafka, MongoDB, Redis, the AWS SDK and more.

Two tricks round it off:

- **Logs inside traces**: grab the active span and add an event with the random number picked, so the trace explains why that user came back.
- **Traces inside logs**: on an error, print the current trace ID in the log line, then paste it into Jaeger to see the whole request that failed. In production that means your log tool (Kibana, say) links to the right trace.

The code is in Aspecto's OpenTelemetry bootcamp repository on GitHub, whose first episode closely matches the demo.

## Who should watch

Node.js developers on a microservices team who still debug by grepping logs across services, and anyone who has heard of OpenTelemetry but never wired it up. If you already run tracing in production, this is a refresher.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Nicolas Frankel's [practical introduction to OpenTelemetry tracing](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Nicolas_Frankel_opentelemetry_tracing) at Conf42 DevOps 2023.
- Roni Dover on [OpenTelemetry from code to prod](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Roni_Dover_observant_developer_opentelemetry_from_code_to_prod) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2022.
- Shai Almog on [debugging Node.js in production with Lightrun](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Shai_Almog_Debug_NodeJS_Lightrun), from the same event.

Title: Your CSP allows Google Analytics, so does the skimmer
Description: Amir Shaked (PerimeterX) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on why Content Security Policy allowlists leak data and how to make CSP worth having anyway
Body:
A strict Content Security Policy that allows Google Analytics also allows an attacker to send your users' passwords to their own Google Analytics account. Amir Shaked, Senior VP R&D at PerimeterX, demonstrates exactly that in his Conf42 JavaScript 2021 talk, [CSP is broken, let's fix it](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Amir_Shaked_CSP_broken), and then spends the rest of it explaining why CSP is still worth deploying, as long as you stop treating it as the last line of defence.

## The CSP rollout story nobody has told

He opens with a fairy tale: read every directive across CSP 2 and 3, deploy in report-only mode, collect a day of reports into some Lambda functions, mark the legitimate resources, flip to blocking, and nothing breaks. Shaked said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: "I think nobody ever said that story when it comes to CSP."

The real story he sees more often: a merchant gets a call from the credit card company about stolen cards, and the investigation finds no breach of the site itself, only a compromised third-party vendor injecting code into the frontend and sending data to a new destination. That is precisely the attack CSP was designed to stop, and in some of those cases CSP was in place.

## How many sites actually use CSP properly?

Very few. From his crawl of HTTP Archive scans over two years, about 690,000 domains sent a CSP header at all, out of roughly 6 million scanned. Most of those use it only as a replacement for older headers: frame-ancestors for framing, upgrade-insecure-requests and mixed-content blocking for HTTPS. Only about 17% go further and use default-src and friends to control where content loads from and goes to.

Among the ones that do, many policies allow unsafe-eval and unsafe-inline in default-src, which switches the protection off while keeping the header. At the strict end are nonces and hashes for allowed scripts, which very few sites use. He also found over 700 distinct directive names in the wild, against around 30 that exist, plus plenty of policies broken by invalid syntax. His plea: run your policy through Google's CSP Evaluator before shipping it.

## Why are CSP reports so hard to read?

Three reasons. Reports are full of noise from extensions, ads and proxies injecting code unrelated to your site; a domain with very few reports is probably noise. Browsers disagree: Chrome sends one report for a repeatedly blocked resource, Firefox sends them repeatedly, and Safari may give you only the truncated top-level domain instead of the full blocked URI. And nothing authenticates the reporter, so anyone can post fake violations. If you auto-allowlist domains by report volume, someone can try to game that into allowlisting theirs.

## Browser bugs and the allowlist flaw

Implementation gaps are real. He walks through a CVE his team reported about a year before the talk: under a policy that looked very strict, appending a script element one way was blocked while another call path loaded and ran the same unauthorised script. It has since been fixed. Sites that used nonces or hashes for inline scripts were not vulnerable, which is his argument that a really strict policy also protects you from browser bugs.

The deeper problem is the allowlist itself. Google Analytics was the most commonly allowed target in his data, and anyone can open a free account. Because the tracking ID is just a parameter, injected code can send collected data, username and password in his demo, to the attacker's own property. You cannot pin the allowed destination to your ID, because CSP source matching ignores query strings. After PerimeterX published the method, other vendors found it in use by attackers within days.

Sources are at risk too: an allowed vendor can be compromised, a long-forgotten allowlisted domain can lapse and be bought by someone else (an allowlist never reports the entries nobody uses any more), and in 2021 a vulnerability in Cloudflare's cdnjs could have let anyone replace libraries served from it, since fixed.

## How to make CSP worth having

- Filter reports instead of reading every violation.
- A/B test the policy: run a stricter report-only policy beside the blocking one, and drop domains that stop producing reports.
- Use different strictness per page: checkout and login pages get the strictest policy and the fewest libraries, Google Analytics included.
- Add nonces and hashes on those sensitive pages, where the work stays manageable.
- Clean up regularly, and comment on CSP 3 while it is still a draft.

His three takeaways: skimmers are a growing risk every time you add a JavaScript library, CSP is not a silver bullet, and you need a checklist for your own site.

## Who should watch

Frontend and security engineers who own a CSP header, or are about to inherit one. The Google Analytics demo alone is worth the time.

Title: Eight workers, 28 shuffle shards and one unlucky customer
Description: Andrew Robinson (AWS) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on shuffle sharding, which shrinks a poison request's blast radius to one customer
Body:
One bad request should cost you one customer, not the whole fleet. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, [Andrew Robinson](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Andrew_Robinson_fault_isolation_shuffle_sharding), Principal Solutions Architect on the AWS Well-Architected team, shows how plain sharding cuts the blast radius of a poison request from 100% of customers to 25%, and how shuffle sharding takes the same eight servers and cuts it much further.

It is a short, focused explainer: one worked example, the arithmetic behind it, and pointers to the code and labs where you can try it. No product pitch beyond the AWS resources he names.

## Why does a fleet without sharding fail all at once?

Robinson opens with the Werner Vogels line he likes to quote: "we need to build systems that embrace failure as a natural occurrence". Then he sets up the usual horizontally scalable service: eight worker nodes behind a load balancer, any worker can serve any request.

That design handles a dead node well. Lose one and the other seven absorb the work with only a little slack capacity. It handles a bad customer terribly. A poisonous request, a flood from a single user or a denial of service that crashes one worker will crash the next one it lands on, and the next. In his words, "the failure is everything and everyone, the whole service goes down and every customer using it is impacted."

## What does plain sharding buy you?

Split the eight workers into four shards of two (his example colours them orange, blue, green and red) and pin each customer to one shard. Now the poison request only takes out its own shard. Robinson said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "So we've been able to reduce the impact of the failure here from 100% to just 25%."

The bill comes in capacity. Each shard is only two nodes, so a single node failure costs that shard half its capacity. You need more pre-provisioned headroom per shard, or faster scaling, to cover it. As the customer count grows you add shards, and the impact scales roughly with customers divided by shards.

## How does shuffle sharding beat that?

Same eight workers, eight customers, A to H. This time every customer gets a virtual shard of two workers, and the pairs overlap differently. Customer A shares one worker with B and another with F. B shares one with A and another with G.

When A sends the poison pill, A's two workers go down. B and F each lose one of their workers but still have the other, so they keep running at reduced capacity. Everyone else doesn't notice. Customer A is still in trouble, but customer A caused it.

The arithmetic is where it gets fun. Eight workers give 28 unique pairs, so 28 possible shuffle shards, and a failure that follows one customer's combination hits a far smaller slice of the fleet. Robinson puts it at "seven times better than what that regular sharding would offer you", with the same hardware. Add workers and customers and the number of combinations grows much faster than the fleet, so the impact keeps falling. Combinatorics, for once, on the side of the on-call engineer.

## Can you try it without building it yourself?

Robinson points to Route 53 Infima, an open source library from AWS Labs for the AWS Java SDK. It applies shuffle sharding to compartmentalise your endpoints and bakes in the decision tree for removing failed ones, so Route 53 can stop sending traffic to a poisoned endpoint quickly. It is Maven-based and, by his account, takes minutes to get running.

He also notes the idea isn't tied to Route 53: other DNS services or your own load balancer can distribute requests and drop failed endpoints the same way. For more depth he recommends the Amazon Builders' Library article on workload isolation using shuffle sharding, and the AWS Well-Architected Labs reliability pillar, which has a hands-on fault isolation with shuffle sharding lab built on AWS load balancers.

## Who should watch?

Anyone running a multi-tenant service where one noisy or malicious tenant can take everyone down, and anyone who has nodded along to blast radius talk without doing the maths. It is a concise introduction, so if you already run cell-based architectures you will know the idea; the eight-worker example is still a good one to borrow for explaining it to your team.

- Josh Stella on [minimizing the blast radius of a cloud breach](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2021_Josh_Stella_Minimizing_the_Blast_Radius_of_a_Cloud_Breach) at Conf42 DevSecOps 2021.
