Title: Hexagonal Lambdas, where adding a cache means touching one adapter
Description: Luca Mezzalira (AWS) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on structuring AWS Lambda code as ports and adapters so it can evolve one file at a time
Body:
Most Lambda handlers in the wild cram the entry point, the DynamoDB call and the domain object into one file, and then everyone wonders why a small change breaks three things. Luca Mezzalira, Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, used his Conf42 JavaScript 2021 talk, [Embracing Hexagonal Architecture with Serverless](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_Luca_Mezzalira_hexagonal_architecture_serverless), to show the fix: structure each function as ports and adapters, so the business logic never knows which database or API it talks to, and every later change lands in one small file.

## Why do serverless codebases rot?

He starts from the definition of evolutionary architecture (guided, incremental change across multiple dimensions) and two familiar failures. In three-tier apps, the presentation and data layers leak into the application layer until the lines blur. And in one migration he describes, moving workloads from containers and VMs to Lambda was hard because the code was tightly coupled to the infrastructure it ran on. The typical handler he shows mixes a submit function that is really a DynamoDB write with a value object, all in the file that is also the Lambda entry point.

## Domain, ports, adapters, in plain JavaScript

The hexagon has three parts:

- **Domain logic**: what the function is actually for, where the value lives.
- **Ports**: the only way in or out of the domain. In Java or TypeScript they are interfaces; in Node.js with ES6 they are simply functions.
- **Adapters**: the classic adapter pattern, mapping external contracts to internal ones and acting as an anti-corruption layer.

Primary actors (a frontend, another service, a queue) trigger the function; secondary actors (a database, a third-party API, a queue it writes to) are the ones the function calls. Why a hexagon and not layers? Per Alistair Cockburn, who created the pattern, the shape was mostly a visual device: more sides to draw more interactions on.

The trade-offs are honest: you build more layers up front, and the pattern gives you no opinion on how to structure the business logic itself.

## The demo: one requirement, one file

The demo is a stock converter Lambda. An HTTP request hits an adapter, which pulls out the stock ID and passes it through a port to the domain. The domain fetches the stock value from DynamoDB via one port and adapter, live currency rates from a third-party API via another, applies the rates and returns. The project has three folders (adapters, domain, ports) plus an `app.js` entry point that does nothing but hand the stock ID to an adapter.

Then traffic grows and the third-party service starts throttling. The fix is a cache-aside pattern on Amazon ElastiCache for Redis: check the cache, otherwise call the API and store the response with a 20-second expiry. The domain does not change. The port changes one import to point at a new adapter, and Mezzalira keeps the old adapter around so he can revert quickly. The same structure in a container on Amazon ECS has the same entry point, which is what makes extracting pieces into Lambda later straightforward.

## Where else it pays off

He walks through the use cases he has found:

- **Testing**: separate tests for adapters and business logic, so CI and local runs can focus on the part that changes most.
- **Changing the trigger**: going from API Gateway calling Lambda synchronously to API Gateway feeding Amazon SQS, with the client polling for results.
- **Service migration**: from self-managed MongoDB on EC2 to Amazon DocumentDB, with the adapter querying the new database first and falling back to the old one, branch by abstraction style.
- **Modernisation**: carving bounded contexts out of a modular monolith into microservices, then out of a container into Lambdas. Be pragmatic: if a service is mostly reads, move the reads into one Lambda and everything else into a second.
- **Hybrid**: the same business logic on Lambda and on Knative on premises, with only the adapters swapped.

Hexagonal architecture dates from 2005, and onion and clean architecture both build on it to add the opinionated business-logic structure it lacks. His view is that a well-divided Lambda keeps cognitive load so small that you rarely need that extra structure.

## Is this the official AWS way to write Lambdas?

No, and he says so. Mezzalira said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: "As usually in architecture, the context is king, and based on the context you take these kinds of decisions." Use it for workloads that will evolve and change often; for a proof of concept or a function that just fetches some JSON, it is overkill.

## Who should watch

Node.js developers writing their tenth Lambda and dreading the first refactor, and teams planning a container-to-serverless move. The code walkthrough is short and readable.

- Yan Cui on [patterns for efficient serverless development](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Yan_Cui_patterns_efficient_serverless) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2024.
- Rafal Leszko on [architectural caching patterns for Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Rafal_Leszko_architectural_caching_patterns_kubernetes), for more on cache-aside and friends.
- Mihaela-Roxana Ghidersa on [the many faces of architecture](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_MihaelaRoxana_Ghidersa_many_faces_architecture), from the same event.

Title: The architect is a role, not a title (and not the architecture police)
Description: Mihaela-Roxana Ghidersa (Strongbytes) at Conf42 JavaScript 2021 on why architecture belongs to the whole team and architects must stay close to the code
Body:
Plenty of developers spend their first project never meeting the architect. Mihaela-Roxana Ghidersa, Technical Lead at Strongbytes, did exactly that for over a year, and her Conf42 JavaScript 2021 talk, [The (too) Many Faces Of Architecture](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2021_MihaelaRoxana_Ghidersa_many_faces_architecture), is the argument that it should never happen: architecture is a structure the whole team builds on, the architect is a flexible role rather than a title, and developers who never look up from the IDE pay for it later.

Fair warning, as she gives it herself: this is not a technical talk. There are no patterns or diagrams of the "best architecture". It is about people, roles and decisions, which is the part of the job the internet has far fewer tutorials for.

## Where does architecture end and design begin?

Her working definition: architecture is the base structure, the high-level units, how they relate and how they evolve, decided with the whole product in view, stakeholders included. System design sits at the code level: what each class and module is for, and which design patterns fit. She leans on Grady Booch (significance is measured by the cost of change) and on Simon Brown's version of the same test: if you cannot reverse a decision without a lot of effort, it is architecture. In her words, "You can't change an architectural decision in an afternoon."

That is why the first step is deciding what is significant and why. She gives Darwin a software job, too: the system that survives longest is the one whose architecture predicts and adapts to change, so the goal is an architecture that "anticipates change and evolution in a cost efficient way".

## Three myths she wants dead

She lists the beliefs she picked up early and had to unlearn once she started asking questions above her task list:

- Software architecture is inflexible and forever.
- Architecture is the architect's problem, not mine.
- Architecture is not about coding, so architects never look at the code.

The fix for all three is the same: developers look up, architects look down. When she started asking why the system was shaped the way it was, she went from complaining about problems to proposing fixes, and says she liked the job more for it.

## The architect does not architect the architecture alone

Her sharpest line is aimed at the lone-genius model. Ghidersa said at Conf42 JavaScript 2021: "We need to just quit this mindset that the architect architects the architecture."

She contrasts the old model (a title, the most experienced person, the one who defines and guards the architecture) with the one she wants: a flexible role that uses the team's technical expertise while growing the team, and that understands the developers' perspective. Owning the whole stack is unrealistic; pair programming, code reviews and the occasional look at the codebase are how an architect keeps their vision grounded in what real people can implement. As for guarding: "Is architecture something so fixed and hard to implement that it needs someone to guard it?"

## Leadership over management, expertise over know-it-all

Two principles carry the second half. Leadership over management: communication, influencing, coaching, delegation, and giving the team a direction they understand. She recounts a team that barely talked to its architect until she went and asked for explanations, after which the rest of the team said they had wanted the same context all along. Expertise over know-it-all: a pragmatic view of requirements and constraints, spotting high-risk areas, managing technical debt before it damages the architectural vision, and owning the system's evolution.

On decisions she is practical: gather feedback from the whole team, avoid getting emotionally attached to your choices, and delay commitments to the last responsible moment, or better, build evolvable structures so that late changes stay cheap. She also rejects the idea that self-organising teams make the role unnecessary for complex, evolving products, because somebody has to stay engaged with the product as team members come and go.

## Who should watch

Mid-level developers wondering what growing into architecture actually means, and architects who suspect they have drifted into abstractions. Her closing advice for each group: developers should think globally and implement towards the big picture; architects should keep working on abstractions but get their hands dirty in the code from time to time.

Title: Terraform brought the cluster back; GitOps would have brought the apps
Description: Ricardo Castro (FARFETCH) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on GitOps principles, Flux, Argo CD and Jenkins X, and rebuilding a cluster from git
Body:
The story starts with a reviewed pull request and a production Kubernetes cluster that disappeared. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Ricardo Castro, Senior Site Reliability Engineer at FARFETCH, uses that outage to explain GitOps: Terraform rebuilt the cluster, but getting the applications back exposed a disabled pipeline, a deploy that reported success on an app that did not work, and manual changes only one team remembered. GitOps closes that gap by making git the single source of truth for everything running in the cluster.

Despite the yea-or-nay title, this is a yea: a gentle introduction to the principles, a short survey of tools, and a live Flux demo, not a debate.

## What makes something GitOps?

Ricardo lists four principles. The whole system is described declaratively:

> "declarative means that the configuration is guaranteed by a set of facts instead of a set of instructions"

Ricardo Castro said that at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021. Instead of launching a server, installing a package and starting a service, you declare the state you want. Second, the canonical desired state is versioned in git, so a rollback is a `git revert` and signed commits show who changed what. Third, approved changes are applied automatically, so nobody outside the cluster needs credentials to deploy. Fourth, software agents check that reality matches the repo, alert on drift (for example to Slack) and can reconcile it.

The benefits he claims follow from those: faster deploys, developers who push code instead of containers and can be productive without knowing Kubernetes internals, a free audit trail for compliance, and a shorter recovery after a meltdown, because the whole system can be rebuilt from one place.

## Flux, Argo CD or Jenkins X?

All three watch one or more git repositories and apply what they find to Kubernetes, and all support Helm and Kustomize:

- **Flux**, from Weaveworks, the company that coined the term GitOps, keeps clusters in sync with sources of configuration.
- **Argo CD** works the same way at a high level but comes with a UI and more integrations out of the box.
- **Jenkins X** is, in his words, the next evolution of a tool that has had a bad reputation for years, rebuilt for the cloud with GitOps pipelines and preview environments.

In a typical pipeline, a merged PR builds an image and pushes it to a registry, a tool commits the new version to the config repo, and the in-cluster agent picks it up and deploys it.

## What does the demo show?

He creates a local cluster and bootstraps Flux against a repo whose staging cluster folder declares a `GitRepository` source pointing at the podinfo sample app, plus three Kustomizations for the web app: a common one (namespace, service account), a backend and a frontend. The interesting bit is `dependsOn`: the backend waits for common, the frontend waits for the backend, and Flux's kustomize-controller applies them in order. A port-forward later, podinfo answers and exposes Prometheus metrics. That is the missing half of his opening story: point a fresh cluster at the repo and it rebuilds itself.

## What about secrets, Terraform, and push versus pull?

Three questions he says always come up:

- **Secrets.** Encrypt them and keep them next to the code with Sealed Secrets or SOPS, decrypted by an in-cluster agent, or fetch them at runtime with the Vault Agent Sidecar Injector.
- **GitOps versus infrastructure as code.** IaC usually manages infrastructure only, and its source of truth is sometimes split between a git repo and a database. GitOps can manage the entire cloud native stack.
- **Push versus pull.** Agents pull changes from git, so you never open the cluster to an outside tool or person. That is a real security win.

## Who should watch

Teams with infrastructure as code but hand-maintained deploy pipelines, which describes the start of his story. If you already run Flux or Argo CD, you will know most of it; if you are deciding whether to start, it is a well-paced introduction.

Related Conf42 talks: [Leonardo Murillo on multi-cloud GitOps with Crossplane and Flux 2](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Leonardo_Murillo_gitops_multicloud_crossplane_flux2), [Ismael Hommani and Clement Loiselet comparing Flux and Argo CD](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Ismael_Hommani_Clement_Loiselet_flux_argocd), and from the same conference [Dewan Ahmed on deploying to many clusters with ApplicationSets](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Dewan_Ahmed_deploy_applications_clusters_appset).

Title: The ISS is microservices in orbit, technical debt included
Description: Robert Barron (IBM) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on what the International Space Station's modular design teaches SREs about reliability
Body:
The International Space Station's main oxygen generator is old enough that it is hard to find anyone on Earth who still knows it well. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Robert Barron, an AIOps and SRE solution architect at IBM who helps clients adopt SRE, tells the history of space stations as an architecture story: monoliths, sidecars, modular microservices, and the technical debt that orbits with them.

It is a history talk with lessons attached rather than a technical walkthrough, and a fun one: space exploration is his hobby, and it shows.

## Spacecraft are stateless, space stations are not

His first distinction: a mission like a Moon landing is a deployment pipeline. You launch, reach the target, do the work and come home, and if it fails you retry from the start. Apollo 13 was not repaired; Apollo 14 flew its mission instead. A space station is a stateful application with data, crews and a huge investment, so when something breaks you recover in place.

## Monolith, sidecars, microservices

Space stations went through three generations. The 1970s stations were monoliths, launched in one piece and often impossible to resupply. Salyut 6 and 7 were transitional, a core station with sidecar modules added for engineering and science. Mir, the ISS and China's Tiangong are modular, built in stages.

Skylab is his monolith example: the top third of a Saturn V turned into a station, so roomy that astronauts tested a jetpack and ran laps inside, and launched with all its equipment and supplies at once. The ISS is bigger overall but each module is far smaller. It took nearly 50 shuttle and rocket flights between 1998 and 2011, with solar panels moved as power needs grew, life support and engineering first, then science and commercial payloads, and standard payload racks that let experiments be swapped like containers. One planned module never flew: a dedicated habitation module turned out to be unnecessary, so astronauts sleep wherever they find space.

## Three oxygen systems and a lesson in debt

Oxygen is the resiliency case study. The original system, Elektron, inherited from Mir, makes oxygen from water but leaves a byproduct that clogs the system, technical debt since 1998. A 2006 Oxygen Generation System used the same idea with less maintenance. A 2018 system from ESA changes the approach entirely, turning carbon dioxide into oxygen and producing water for the other two. Behind all three sit chemical oxygen generators and bottled oxygen. In more than 20 years, there has never been a serious oxygen problem for the crew.

But Elektron is still meant to supply over half the oxygen, its experts are disappearing, and the less modular Russian segment makes parts hard to replace.

> "Technical debt is the biggest problem that we have in the industry. It's crippling."

Robert Barron said that at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021. His fix is ESA's: do not solve the same problem better every time, change the design so the problem never appears.

## Spacesuits, CIMON and a drilled hole

Three smaller stories carry the rest. A spacewalk was postponed in 2019 because the two astronauts scheduled for it, both women, could not each assemble a suit in the right size from the spare parts on board, most of which had been sized for men. That is resource management: you never know when you will need a new node for your Kubernetes cluster, or a smaller spacesuit.

CIMON, a free-flying assistant that shows astronauts manuals and troubleshooting steps, does most of its AI work on Watson in the IBM Cloud, hundreds of kilometres below. His point is lowering the cost of learning: we cannot staff every on-call rotation with astronauts.

And in 2018, an air leak was traced to a hole that had been drilled, not punched by a micrometeorite, in a recently docked spacecraft. No public explanation has ever been published. Blameless postmortems are the goal, he says, but sometimes politics sits above the incident and you cannot stay as detached as you would like.

## Politics shipped the station

The station was proposed in 1969, announced in 1984 and cancelled in 1993, decades of design without construction. What finally got it built was international cooperation, chiefly between the United States and Russia. The business of the ISS is being international. For SREs, that means aligning reliability goals with what the business is actually for.

> "Don't decide your technology before you decide what you want to do with it."

## Who should watch

SREs who like their lessons with a story, and anyone who has to explain technical debt to people who sign budgets. The oxygen systems are a ready-made slide for that meeting.

Related Conf42 talks: [Giulio Vian on technical debt as a metaphor](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Giulio_Vian_technical_debt_right_metaphor_continuous_update), and from the same conference [Dmitry Vinnik on broken windows in legacy systems](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Dmitry_Vinnik_broken_windows_legacy_systems__poor_quality_gaps) and [Quintessence Anx on effective incident response](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Quintessence_Anx_dont_panic_effective_incident_response).

Title: Four YAML mistakes that took real Kubernetes clusters down
Description: Noaa Barki and Shimon Tolts (Datree) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on lessons from 100+ Kubernetes postmortems and policy checks before deploy
Body:
A CronJob left on the default concurrency policy once produced more than 4,300 pods stuck restarting. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Noaa Barki, full-stack developer at Datree, and Shimon Tolts, Datree's co-founder and CEO, turn more than 100 Kubernetes postmortems into a game show: she shows a manifest, he guesses the mistake, and each wrong answer is a real outage. The conclusion is that these failures are too easy to make for humans to catch reliably, so you should check for them automatically before deploy.

Expect a vendor angle at the end: Datree's product is an open source CLI that scans Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts. Shimon built it after a misconfiguration reached production while he ran an infrastructure engineering department of 400 engineers, and he had no good way to stop the next developer repeating it.

## What's wrong with this CronJob?

Round one is a CronJob that runs every minute with nothing unusual in it. The bug is what is not there: `concurrencyPolicy` defaults to `Allow`, so if a run fails or overruns, Kubernetes starts another one next to it. The speakers credit this one to Target: a single failing CronJob, 4,300+ restarting pods, a cluster down and a large CPU bill.

> "never ever trust the default configuration"

Noaa Barki said that at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, with a caveat they both agree on: `Allow` exists for a reason, and a daily job may be fine with it. The point is to know what the default does before you rely on it.

## And this one, which looks correct?

Round two has the right settings in the wrong place. Zalando, an online fashion company with over 6,000 employees, had the correct concurrency configuration for a CronJob, but indented outside the CronJob spec. Kubernetes ignored it, applied the defaults, the job created thousands of pods, and the API server ran out of memory. Noaa compares it to the days before TypeScript, when one missing semicolon broke everything and nobody could see why. A human reviewer misses it; a schema check does not.

## A wildcard host, and a pod with no limits

Round three: an Ingress with the host set to `*`, which can send every request in the cluster to one container. In the speakers' telling, one developer did exactly that and took the whole cluster down, reportedly the company's first Kubernetes mistake. Their lesson is about people more than YAML: once developers own infrastructure as code, DevOps has to hand over the knowledge and the tools. As they put it, a great Java payments engineer is not automatically a Docker or Kubernetes expert, and should not have to be one to ship safely.

Round four: a harmless-looking pod with no resource limits. Blue Matador, a small startup, ran a third-party app in a pod like that, and nothing stopped it taking over the node. They point out that VMs force you to choose CPU and memory, but Kubernetes will happily schedule a pod with no limits, and some software, RabbitMQ in their example, grabs as much memory as it can by default.

Their list of who this has happened to includes Google, Spotify, Datadog and Toyota. It can happen to anyone.

## How do you stop the next one?

Three steps. Define your policies, and decide which apply to which workloads, since a frontend is not a batch job. Run them on every change: pre-commit hooks, local runs, CI. Developers already run `npm test` before pushing, so this feels familiar. Then manage the policies centrally, because 500 repositories should not need 500 pull requests when you upgrade Kubernetes.

The tools they compare:

- **OPA Gatekeeper**: an admission webhook in the cluster, with policies written in Rego. It protects production but finds problems only at the end of the line.
- **Conftest**: also OPA and Rego, but it tests any structured file (YAML, JSON, Dockerfiles) locally or in CI, like unit tests for manifests. Policies can be pushed to and pulled from a Docker registry. You write all the rules yourself.
- **Datree**: works in CI or locally like Conftest, ships with predefined rules and rule packs, supports custom rules in YAML or Rego, and adds central management.

## Who should watch

Platform teams handing Kubernetes to application developers, and anyone who has typed `kubectl apply` and hoped. It is quick and funny, and the four examples make good onboarding material.

Noaa went deeper on the policy tools in [Open Policy Agent, Conftest and Gatekeeper in action](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Noaa_Barki_open_policy_agent_conftest_gatekeeper_kubernetes_policy_in_action). See also [Ara Pulido on policy as code with OPA Gatekeeper](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Ara_Pulido_poilcyascode_kubernetes_opa_gatekeeper) and, from the same conference, [Itiel Shwartz on troubleshooting Kubernetes independently](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Itiel_Shwartz_troubleshoot_K8s_independently).

Title: A WAR file in a container is a first step, not a migration
Description: JJ Asghar (IBM) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on the gotchas enterprises hit moving a monolith to Kubernetes, from doubled schedulers to the CCB
Body:
One enterprise JJ Asghar worked with had a three-node Kubernetes cluster where only one node ever did any work. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, the IBM Cloud developer advocate explains why: they had wrapped a Java monolith, scheduler and all, in a container, so every job spawned another process inside the same pod. His talk is a tour of the gotchas companies hit when they assume bare metal to VMs is the same as VMs to containers.

The stories come from several real companies, merged into one fictional conglomerate, AsgharLabs, to keep the guilty anonymous.

## What questions should you ask after containerizing?

JJ usually arrives after a few migrations that were declared successful and asks deceptively simple questions:

- **Who containerized your app?** Developers, operations, or a centre of excellence that lacked the skills of either? With strong separation of powers, you need to know who built the container and why they made the choices they made.
- **Why did you containerize it?** Often because an executive read that the stack had to be next gen. His view: if you are making money and do not need to, you should not.
- **Where did you deploy it?** Some clouds give you all you can eat in year one and then the bill jumps. Did anyone compare providers, or was the choice forced on you?
- **What did you actually containerize?** In one conversation the answer was an EAR or WAR file shoved into a container and pushed to Kubernetes, followed by confusion about why nothing improved.

## Replatform, repackage, refactor

His architecture path, with WebSphere as the canonical example (he works at IBM, after all): replatforming the legacy app into a container on OpenShift or Kubernetes is a fine first step but gains you almost nothing. Repackaging the EAR into a few WARs lets parts talk and scale independently, and the return on investment starts. Real benefit comes from refactoring with the strangler pattern, peeling features off into microservices and letting Kubernetes do the scheduling, so releases stop being big-bang events every few months.

That also means auditing what you are doubling up on. The idle nodes came from an in-app Java scheduler competing with the Kubernetes scheduler. The same goes for the F5 in front of a cluster that already has ingress. The punchline: that company still had not broken out the scheduler, because it was harder than they thought and other priorities won.

## Why is everything so complicated now?

> "your app has already probably always been this complicated. You just now get to see into the complication"

JJ Asghar said that at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021. Microservices spread knowledge that used to sit with two or three enterprise architects, which kills tribal knowledge and exposes bottlenecks. The cost is captured in a slide quote from Robb Kidd: you had one ornery bull mastiff, now you have 13 yipping chihuahuas to feed. And a line JJ borrowed from elsewhere:

> "We replaced our monolith with microservices, so every outage is like a murder mystery."

The answer is standardised logging and standardised APIs between teams, so people can reconstruct what happened.

## What has to change in the culture?

The change control board has to go. JJ remembers being the operations person woken at 3am on a Saturday to ship code a room of managers had thumbs-upped; that does not survive releasing ten to fifteen times a day. Replace it with CI/CD pipelines, agreed formatting and linting (he credits `go fmt` for how readable Go is at 3am), and real collaboration rather than status meetings and Jira tickets. One subsidiary rotated one engineer between tribes every sprint; onboarding became negligible and velocity jumped.

Monitoring changes too: Nagios will not cut it, and a single pane of glass is mostly for marketing. Expect several tools and people who know them. Money changes as well: you cannot depreciate cloud spend, so build a bridge to your CFO and accounting team. And if you run plain upstream Kubernetes, support may in practice be Stack Overflow; managed services or OpenShift give you someone to call.

## Who should watch

Architects and SRE leads at enterprises with a containerised monolith that did not deliver the promised savings. It is a stories-and-questions talk, light on code, heavy on the conversations you should have before the next sprint. His closing advice: ask whether you need to at all, and if you do, look for optimisations instead of features for a while.

Title: Helm, Linkerd, KEDA, Flux, KUDO, Meshery - a CNCF tour in one sitting
Description: Annie Talvasto (CAST AI) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on six CNCF projects worth knowing, with live Helm and Linkerd demos
Body:
The CNCF project map is the cloud native equivalent of a restaurant menu with hundreds of dishes. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Annie Talvasto, CNCF ambassador and product marketing manager at CAST AI, picks six projects off it (Helm, Linkerd, KEDA, Flux, KUDO and Meshery), explains what each is for in a few minutes, and demos two of them live on an Azure Kubernetes cluster.

Expectation management, in her words: it is a wide overview, not a deep look at any single project, and she is picking by excitement and community size rather than science.

> "I don't have a PhD on how to select CNCF projects, nor is it fortune telling."

Annie Talvasto said that at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021. Project maturity levels below are as of the talk; several have moved on since.

## How does a CNCF project grow up?

Three stages: sandbox (innovators and techies), incubating (early adopters), graduated (early and late majority, production ready). At the time she counted roughly 40 to 50 sandbox projects, 20 to 30 incubating and around 14 graduated, compared with one or two graduated projects (Kubernetes, maybe Prometheus) when she started talking about CNCF a few years earlier. The CNCF 2020 survey she quotes put containers in production at 92%, up from 84% the year before, and Kubernetes in production at 83%, up from 78%.

## Helm: package management for Kubernetes

Helm is Homebrew or Chocolatey for Kubernetes: charts describe complex apps, give repeatable installs, in-place upgrades and easy rollbacks. It was already graduated and passed a million downloads a month in 2019. She adds a nod to Artifact Hub, a sandbox project that replaced the per-project hubs (Helm Hub among them) with one place to find charts.

The demo: start from an empty cluster, add the Bitnami repo, `helm install` WordPress, and shortly after there is WordPress plus MariaDB with admin credentials stored as Kubernetes secrets. The demo effect made one command slow, and she narrated through it.

## Linkerd: the service mesh that tries to stay out of your way

Linkerd had graduated about a month before the talk. Its pitch is reducing the mental overhead of a mesh: install in seconds into one namespace, add services one at a time, and get success rates, request volume and latency per service without configuration. It uses its own purpose-built proxy, linkerd2-proxy, rather than Envoy.

> "security is not an extra, it's a default"

The demo runs the Emojivoto sample app, where bots vote for emojis in the background, then uses `linkerd top`, `linkerd tap` and the Linkerd dashboard, with Prometheus-backed charts of success rates and request volume, to watch the traffic live.

## KEDA: scale on events, not CPU

Kubernetes' default autoscaling reacts to CPU and memory, which is late for event-driven work. KEDA, freshly promoted to incubating, watches event sources through pluggable scalers and scales before CPU even moves. Its principles: rebuild nothing Kubernetes already offers, stay single-purpose and non-intrusive, work with any container. Public case studies at the time: Alibaba Cloud and CAST AI, her own employer.

## Flux: git push as the only deploy command

Flux replaces `kubectl apply`, `kubectl set image` and `helm upgrade` with commits. Git holds the desired state, which doubles as a save point: lose a cluster, point a new one at the repo, and everything that lived in Kubernetes comes back (stateful data not included). The practices she lists: declarative descriptions, configuration in source control, agents that reconcile and alert on drift.

## KUDO and Meshery: operators and many meshes

KUDO, the Kubernetes Universal Declarative Operator, attacks stateful apps. Writing a custom operator for Kafka or Cassandra can take thousands of lines of code; KUDO lets you define lifecycle plans declaratively and manage them with kubectl. Meshery, accepted into the sandbox weeks before the talk, is a management plane for teams that ended up running more than one service mesh in the same cluster: it supports over ten meshes and already had 15 maintainers and 300+ contributors.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to the cloud native ecosystem who want a guided shortlist, and SREs who know Kubernetes but have not looked past it in a while. Seasoned CNCF watchers will know most of it; the demos are the fun part.

To go deeper on two of these, see [Leonardo Murillo on multi-cloud GitOps with Crossplane and Flux 2](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Leonardo_Murillo_gitops_multicloud_crossplane_flux2) and [Rosemary Wang's introduction to service mesh](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Rosemary_Wang_introduction_service_mesh). From the same conference, [Ricardo Castro weighs GitOps](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Ricardo_Castro_GitOps).

Title: SQL Server HA/DR on AWS, from VSS snapshots to distributed AGs
Description: Asif Mujawar (AWS) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on SQL Server HA/DR on AWS, tier by tier, and how a passive secondary halves the licence
Body:
Microsoft SQL Server has more high availability options than most teams have runbooks for, and almost all of them were designed for a single data centre with a SAN. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Asif Mujawar, Senior Specialist Solutions Architect for databases at AWS, maps each one onto AWS, from backups and snapshots to failover cluster instances and distributed availability groups, and ends with a licensing trick: a truly passive secondary can halve the cores you pay for.

It is an AWS talk by an AWS architect, so the services are AWS's, but the decision tree (what fails, what protects you from it, at what RTO) carries over to any platform.

## RDS or EC2?

The first fork is who does the undifferentiated heavy lifting. Amazon RDS for SQL Server is managed and licence-included: backups, patching and Multi-AZ come with a checkbox. SQL Server on EC2 is a VM you run yourself, with bring-your-own-licence as an option. You pick EC2 when you need what RDS does not offer, such as Always On setups you design yourself, log shipping, or third-party maintenance scripts like Ola Hallengren's.

## Which HA/DR tier do you need?

Asif sorts the options into three tiers by what they protect:

- **Simple**: VM and guest-level failures. On AWS, EC2 auto recovery moves an instance to a healthy host, the cloud's answer to vMotion, plus backup and restore.
- **Standard**: adds SQL Server instance failures, via failover cluster instances (FCI) or basic availability groups.
- **Mission critical**: adds database-level protection with availability groups, aiming for seconds of RTO, zero data loss, minimal downtime for planned maintenance and readable replicas for read scaling.

## Backups are half the story

On RDS, automated daily snapshots are kept for seven days by default and up to 35. Need ten years for compliance? User-initiated snapshots survive even deleting the instance, so a scheduled job can take them and expire them. Transaction log backups every few minutes give point-in-time restore into a new instance.

On EC2, the server-level backup is an EBS snapshot: incremental, point-in-time, and with fast snapshot restore to skip the lazy-loading performance lag. For consistency, use VSS-enabled snapshots; AWS Systems Manager can install the agent, flush buffers, pause I/O, snapshot and resume in under 10 seconds with one API call. With hundreds of instances, State Manager targets them by tag, maintenance windows keep backups out of business hours, and rate controls stop every instance backing up at once. Native backups go to S3 and age down through Infrequent Access and Glacier so ten-year retention does not cost premium storage prices.

Restore is the other half: he argues for automating it with Systems Manager Automation documents, because a tested workflow removes human error in the middle of a disaster.

## FCIs, and when a stretch cluster stops being a bad idea

Failover cluster instances (since SQL Server 2008) share storage between nodes. On AWS that can be multi-attach EBS, Storage Spaces Direct, or Amazon FSx for Windows File Server as an SMB share, which also lets you provision throughput for the whole file system rather than per volume. Put the file share witness in a third AZ to keep quorum safe from split brain.

On premises, stretch clusters are usually a no. He speaks from experience:

> "I've been bitten myself in the past when I did decide to do these stretch cluster"

Asif Mujawar said that at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, explaining that network blips cause false failovers. AWS's low-latency links between AZs, he argues, make a multi-AZ FCI stretch cluster practical.

## DR and availability groups

For region-level disasters: log shipping (around since SQL Server 2000, four steps, schedules as short as five minutes, and a pause button when you spot corruption), and CloudEndure Disaster Recovery for block-level replication, which is a paid service for DR but free for migration.

Availability groups replaced database mirroring. Basic AGs in Standard edition allow two replicas and one database, with no readable secondary. Full AGs replicate synchronously across AZs behind a listener, so the application never notices a failover. Across regions, either stretch one cluster with an asynchronous, manually failed-over replica, or use a distributed AG: two independent clusters, with a forwarder replica in region B feeding its local secondary, so a region swap keeps the same protection. On RDS Multi-AZ, a mirroring failover takes one to two minutes because of DNS propagation; with Always On, it is under 10 seconds.

## The licence maths

Two Enterprise nodes, both used (OLTP on one, reporting on the other), means licensing 12 cores. Keep the secondary passive and license only 6, then spin up a licence-included reporting instance from a VSS snapshot when needed, possibly downgrading to Standard edition.

## Who should watch

DBAs and SREs moving SQL Server estates to AWS, or inheriting one there. It is a long, option-by-option tour, so keep a notepad handy for your RTO and RPO targets.

Title: Agile got Scrum; Vishnu Vardhan Chikoti proposes Arctic for SRE
Description: Vishnu Vardhan Chikoti (Fanatics) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on Arctic, an SRE adoption framework built on visibility and accountability
Body:
Ask five people what SRE is and you get availability, golden signals, ops automation, infrastructure automation, or simply a new title for production support. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Vishnu Vardhan Chikoti, Senior SRE Manager at Fanatics and co-author of Hands-On Site Reliability Engineering, argues that enterprises need what agile teams got from Scrum and Kanban: a framework. He calls his Arctic, and it rests on two pillars, visibility and accountability.

Worth knowing before you press play: by his own account the framework was freshly conceptualised and not yet used in any enterprise. This is a proposal to seed discussion, not a case study, and the goal-setting part promised in the abstract does not get much airtime.

## Why would SRE need a framework?

His starting point is the pile of questions every transformation hits. How is SRE different from ITIL, or from DevOps? How do we structure teams? Is capacity planning already done during performance testing? Can a service have several SLOs, and is it fine to measure only critical services? Books, videos and blogs answer these one at a time. A framework, in the Spring Boot or Scrum sense, gives you the basic structure to build on so each enterprise does not reinvent the plan before starting.

## Visibility: what is actually in place?

The first pillar is an honest inventory, because most organisations already do some SRE practices under other names (often via ITIL or product engineering standards), and nobody needs to boil the ocean on day one. Arctic sorts it into three lists:

- **Practices**: monitoring, observability, SLOs, measured SLIs and error budgets, incident response and management, blameless postmortems, change and release management, toil elimination, capacity planning, infrastructure automation, AIOps, ChatOps, chaos engineering, security, regulatory compliance.
- **Tools and platforms**: alerting, alert correlation, on-call, runtime platforms such as Kubernetes or OpenShift, ticketing, self-healing, CI/CD, backup and recovery, patching, fault injection, even natural language understanding so a chat bot treats restart, reboot and bounce as the same request.
- **Policies and procedures**: incident management, change management, error budget policy, and an SRE onboarding procedure.

On the monitoring versus observability argument he offers a tidy image:

> "monitoring is the microscope and observability is the slide under the microscope"

Vishnu Vardhan Chikoti said that at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, as part of a list that treats tracing, logging and metrics as the raw material monitoring depends on.

Visibility also covers the value a transformation delivers, measured rather than asserted: toil eliminated, and reductions in MTTA, MTTD, MTTI, MTTR and MTBF, faster closure of postmortem action items, and fewer SLO breaches and exhausted error budgets.

## Accountability: who owns what?

The second pillar is structure. He walks through central SRE, SRE split by function (infrastructure, data, a tools team that integrates vendor and in-house tooling), embedded SREs in product teams, and federated SRE for large organisations, where each vertical runs its own team. His rule for the federated case: tooling can vary, but culture, principles, policies and procedures stay standard.

Then the roles nobody writes down. Who decides which services onboard first, and who does the onboarding? How does SRE hear about a business launch that ships as a flag flipped in a UI rather than a release? Who has the final word when SRE teams have conflicting priorities?

## What goes with it, and what to avoid?

Arctic is meant to sit next to other frameworks: Scrum for an SRE tools team, Kanban for teams juggling interrupts and engineering work, Microsoft's SPACE framework for measuring developer experience, design thinking and design sprints for new dashboards or practices. He also flags the chicken-and-egg problem of an incident knowledge base nobody uses until it has enough in it.

Hiring needs evangelists, strategists and specialists, not one mythical SRE who knows everything. And three things to avoid: bandwagon tool choices, over-engineering past the SLO (100% is the wrong target), and running traditional and SRE policies side by side after the switch.

> "There's no need to do something because someone else is doing."

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and SRE leads planning an adoption, or halfway through one and wondering what they missed. The visibility checklist alone makes a decent maturity self-assessment.

Pair it with two other talks from the same conference: [Cristina Buenahora Bustamante on evangelising a culture of ownership](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Cristina_Buenahora_Bustamante_evangelizing_culture_ownership) and [Joshua Arvin Lat on pragmatic SRE on Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Joshua_Arvin_Lat_Pragmatic_Site_Reliability_Engineering_Kubernetes). For the toil line item, [Mandi Walls on automation and toil](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Mandi_Walls_automation_toil).

Title: 35 load tests, 24 hours, 77% better cost efficiency on Kubernetes
Description: Stefano Doni (Akamas) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on letting ML tune container limits and JVM flags against SLOs instead of hand-tuning
Body:
Nobody hand-tunes 800 JVM flags; they copy the ones from the last service and hope. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Stefano Doni, CTO of Akamas, shows the alternative: an SRE writes down the goal and the SLOs, and a machine learning optimiser runs load test after load test until it finds a configuration that beats the baseline. On Google's Online Boutique demo, it found one that improved cost efficiency by 77% in about 24 hours.

This is a vendor talk: the optimiser is Akamas's own product, and the results are from the company's runs. The method behind it is worth knowing regardless of the tool.

## Why is configuration an SRE problem at all?

Stefano anchors it in the Google SRE book's tenets: change velocity within SLOs, capacity planning, efficiency. Configuration hits all three. He shows a Java service whose CPU use dropped 75% after a JVM reconfiguration on day three while serving the same load, and another where the baseline configuration crashed under load and the tuned one held.

Three things make it hard. The parameter count keeps exploding:

> "a JVM has more than 800 parameters, a MySQL database more than 500"

Stefano Doni said that at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, adding that AWS shipped over 100 new EC2 instance types in a single year. Effects are counterintuitive, too: in one example, allocating less memory to a MongoDB database made it run much faster. And release cadence has gone from months to days, so manual tuning by an expert falls behind every sprint.

## How does the optimisation loop work?

Five steps, fully automated: apply a configuration (JVM options, Kubernetes resource settings), apply a workload with an existing load testing tool, collect KPIs from existing monitoring, score the result against the goal, and let the ML pick the next configuration to try. Brute force is not an option when the space has billions of combinations; the optimiser learns which parameters matter and converges.

The SRE's job moves up a level: define the goal, the constraints and the load scenarios, then review what comes out.

## What did it find on Kubernetes?

The target was Online Boutique, ten microservices in Go, Node.js, Java and Python, with Locust for load, Prometheus for pod metrics and Istio for service-level metrics. The optimiser tuned 22 parameters (CPU and memory limits per container) while watching 275 KPIs.

The goal was to maximise frontend throughput divided by cloud cost, priced at AWS Fargate rates of $29 per CPU per month and about $3 per GB of memory. Constraints: p90 latency at or under 500 ms and a Locust failure ratio at or under 2%.

After 35 iterations in 24 hours, cost efficiency went from 0.29 to 0.52 transactions per second per dollar per month. The best configuration cut CPU limits for most services but raised CPU and memory for two under-provisioned ones, product catalog and recommendation. Throughput also rose 19%, and p90 latency peaks fell 60%. That is the part a human tuner rarely gets right: shrinking everything except the two services that were quietly the bottleneck.

## And on the JVM?

The second case kept container sizes fixed and tuned 32 JVM options on the Java ad service, with one SLO: average response time no higher than 100 ms. The baseline sustained 74 TPS before breaking the SLO; the best configuration reached 95 TPS, a 28% gain. The winning changes: max heap up roughly 250%, garbage collector switched from G1 to Parallel, fewer GC threads, and adjusted heap regions and object ageing thresholds. Eight options turned out to matter most.

## Who should watch

SREs who own capacity planning and are tired of resource limits set by folklore, and performance engineers curious how goal-driven optimisation is framed. Bring your own scepticism about the numbers being a vendor's showcase, but the goal and constraint definitions are a good template for any tuning exercise, automated or not.

From the same conference, [Hari Krishnan on shift-left performance testing](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Hari_Krishnan_shift_left_performance_testing) and [Suraj Muraleedharan on the performance of container workloads](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Suraj_Muraleedharan_performance_container_workloads) pair well with this. For the money side, see [Michael Levan on Kubernetes cost and resource optimisation](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Michael_Levan_cost_resource_optimization).

Title: Your mobile app is a distributed system you cannot roll back
Description: Pranjal Deo (Google) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on mobile SRE, where rollbacks are near impossible and old app versions never die
Body:
Server-side SRE assumes you can push a fix and know it landed. Mobile takes that away. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Pranjal Deo, SRE Program Manager for client infrastructure and Firebase at Google, explains why a native app behaves like a distributed system of billions of machines you do not control, and shares three real Google outages, including one where the only fix left was asking users to upgrade.

The talk is based on an article Pranjal co-authored, Engineering Reliable Mobile Applications, and it is the practical sequel: what server-side habits break on phones, and what to do instead.

## Why isn't server-side availability enough?

Because users judge the service by the device in their hand. Pranjal describes incidents where server instrumentation looked perfectly healthy while users saw blank screens, a maps app crashing in a new city, or an update that quietly wrecked battery life. None of that shows up in data-centre dashboards.

So the monitoring has to live on the device: crash reports, counts of attempts and errors around key entry points, and UI test probes that run critical user journeys on emulated devices. All of it has to respect privacy, and all of it costs the user battery and data. One trick worth stealing: include config state as a metric dimension, so after a fix you can look only at the devices that have picked it up. Google's mobile config is polling-based, so clients fetch at convenient moments for battery and bandwidth, and it can take several hours for client metrics to normalise after a fix.

Resource use is treated as reliability too. Google apps have been blocked from release for battery regressions as small as 0.1%.

## Why are rollbacks off the table?

On the server, rollback means you are off the bad version. On Android and iOS the standard is to roll forward and hope people upgrade, and the user holds the upgrade button. Some disable auto-updates, some have no storage, some are on metered data. Old versions pile up.

> "Anything that causes users to not upgrade is similar to accumulating tech debt."

Pranjal Deo said that at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, and the release advice follows from it: staged rollouts (with a beta pool, since developer devices are not representative), A/B experiments with randomised populations to escape the bias toward newer devices and better networks, and feature flags that ship dark in the binary so a rollback is a flag ramp-down instead of a new release. For the noise of the upgrade itself, Pranjal mentions shipping a placebo binary to the control group, with caution.

## What did the outages teach?

**The Doodle with no colour (2016).** The Android Google Search app (AGSA) fetched a new Doodle config that lacked its colour field, and the app crashed. Crash spikes arrived at midnight in each time zone as Doodles launched. Fixing the config did not stop it, because clients cached the config. A client fix followed, then a repeat outage months later on older versions without that fix, then server-side guardrails. Lesson: client fixes never reach everyone.

**Four characters, two weeks (2017).** A four-character change to a legacy config, tested locally but not canaried, reached a wider population and older app versions that could not handle it. Those versions crashed on startup, read the cached bad config, and crashed again before they could fetch the fixed one. Recovery meant sending users notifications to upgrade. Lessons: validate a config by exercising it before it becomes active, make caches expirable without user action, and monitor crash recovery rates, because recovery that fires often hides a real failure.

**The comb (Firebase Cloud Messaging).** A new Google Play services release kept calling FCM registration, and the graph showed teeth of a comb as the app exhausted its quota, got topped up, and hammered again. Throttling saved other apps. Google turned it into a rule:

> "Mobile apps must not make service calls during upgrade time"

New service calls must instead ride an independently ramped experiment, and release metrics must prove an upgrade added none.

## Who should watch

Mobile engineers who get paged, and backend SREs whose biggest client is an app. The five takeaways (resilient apps, on-device monitoring of critical journeys, flag-gated releases, planning for the app's load on servers, and client-side incident playbooks) make a good checklist for a release review.

Title: A 524 MB Java base image is a reliability problem, not a disk problem
Description: Dmitry Chuyko (BellSoft) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on shrinking Java containers with Alpine musl builds and GraalVM native images
Body:
Pull the default `openjdk` image and you wait 28 seconds on a 100 Mbps link for 524 MB that your three-kilobyte Spring Boot app sits on top of. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Dmitry Chuyko, Senior Performance Engineer at BellSoft, argues that the base image is where Java container reliability is won or lost, and walks through two roads to small ones: a JDK built for Alpine's musl libc, and GraalVM native images that start in a twentieth of a second.

It is a vendor talk in the sense that the examples use BellSoft's Liberica JDK and its Native Image Kit, but he says up front that the advice applies to any OpenJDK distribution.

## Why should an SRE care how big a base image is?

His iceberg picture of a Java container: scratch, an OS, OS packages, the JRE, libraries, a framework, and a tiny tip of business logic. A Spring Initializr sample compiles to a 37 MB fat jar, but the thin jar with the actual application code is 2.7 kB. Everything else is the iceberg.

Multiply the iceberg by the fleet. A quarter of a gigabyte per pull times 1,000 simultaneous deploys is a quarter of a terabyte on the wire, and that traffic lands on shared hardware, shared I/O limits and registry quotas that your neighbours also depend on. Smaller images make every deploy faster and the registry bill smaller. Docker Hub's rate limits from November 2020 made the point more painfully: he recommends a proxy, a mirror or a private registry you can get an SLA for.

## Is Alpine just a smaller Debian?

No, and that is the interesting part. Alpine Linux is built on musl libc and BusyBox, and the base image is 5.6 MB on disk (2.7 MB on the wire), smaller even than Google's distroless base. JEP 386 ported the JDK to musl in JDK 16, so the JVM no longer needs a glibc compatibility layer. BellSoft's `liberica-openjdk-alpine-musl` image for JDK 15 comes in at 107 MB on disk, and the pull took about 4 seconds.

> "So in 4 seconds on 100 megabytes network you get working OpenJDK in a container."

Dmitry Chuyko said that at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, then spent a good part of the talk on why size alone is the wrong metric. The traps he demonstrated:

- **Stale images.** One slim JDK 8 image he compared was on 8u262 while another was on 8u282, about a year of security updates behind.
- **Missing tools.** The same image rejected `-XX:StartFlightRecording`: no JDK Flight Recorder, a free OpenJDK diagnostic that simply was not included.
- **Compressed `rt.jar`.** A JDK 8 image that compressed its standard library jars looked smaller on disk, but Spring PetClinic started in 6.81 s versus 6.03 s, a 12.6% penalty, and the double compression made the image bigger over the wire.
- **No debug symbols.** async-profiler on one image showed 85% of samples as an opaque `libjvm.so`; on an image with symbols shipped in the release build, you see the C2 compiler's internals by name.

> "The key here is having debug symbols."

The DIY route fails too: `apk add openjdk8` on stock Alpine gave him a `jcmd` that was not on the path and a stack trace instead of the JVM's uptime.

## What happened to Graal after JDK 16?

JDK 16 removed the experimental AOT compiler and the Graal JIT from OpenJDK (JDK-8255616). He is clear that this is not the end of Graal: JVMCI, the interface for Java-based compilers, still ships, and GraalVM development continues upstream. It only means nobody copies Graal's source into the OpenJDK repo any more. Oracle's GraalVM Enterprise Edition sits under OTN and Java SE subscription terms, while Community Edition is GPLv2 with the Classpath exception; Liberica Native Image Kit is built on Community Edition and adds Alpine musl and AArch64 targets.

## How small does a native image get?

He built Spring's `gs-rest-service` guide with Spring Native 0.10.3, either through Cloud Native Buildpacks (`BP_NATIVE_IMAGE=true` and `mvn spring-boot:build-image`) or by hand inside an Alpine container. The result: a 57 MB executable on a 5.6 MB Alpine base plus 7 MB of runtime libraries, starting in 0.055 seconds, with a further drop in PetClinic's memory footprint.

The trade-off he names honestly: a classic JVM container lets you update only the thin top layer, while a native image has to be shipped whole on every change, and you lose the standard JDK diagnostic tools. New nodes, on the other hand, pull far less.

## Who should watch

Anyone running Java on Kubernetes who has never looked at what their `FROM` line drags in. The talk is dense with real `docker` and `objdump` output, so it rewards watching with a terminal open.

Pair it with [Nicolas Frankel on migrating an app to Quarkus, Kotlin and GraalVM](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Nicolas_Frankel_app_migration_cloud_quarkus_kotlin_hazelcast_graalvm), [Frank Kriegl comparing HotSpot, GraalVM and OpenJ9](https://www.conf42.com/Enterprise_Software_2021_Frank_Kriegl_hotspot_vm_graalvm_openj9), and, from the same conference, [Suraj Muraleedharan on the performance of container workloads](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Suraj_Muraleedharan_performance_container_workloads).

[Watch Dmitry Chuyko's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Dmitry_Chuyko_chasing_the_grail)

Title: Clickstream to dashboard in five minutes, with one Lambda as the only code
Description: Shubhankar Sumar (AWS) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on near real-time ecommerce clickstream analytics with Kinesis, Glue and QuickSight
Body:
Analytics is usually the feature a team gets to after the budget has gone. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Shubhankar Sumar, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, shows a near real-time clickstream pipeline for an ecommerce site built almost entirely from managed AWS services: CloudFront real-time logs into Kinesis Data Streams, Kinesis Data Firehose with one Lambda transform into S3, AWS Glue to catalogue it, and Amazon QuickSight via Athena on top. A click shows up on a dashboard in about five minutes.

He is careful with the word: near real time, not real time. That honesty is the most useful framing in the talk, because it tells you which half of the problem this architecture solves.

## Why does freshness matter?

His case study is Epic Games and Fortnite, a free-to-play game whose revenue depends on keeping players engaged, which in turn needs an up-to-the-minute view of player satisfaction. He cites more than 125 million players in under a year and a data lake on Amazon S3 holding over 14 petabytes and growing about 2 petabytes a month. Shubhankar Sumar said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "So the value of data diminishes over time."

He maps use cases to latency budgets: messaging between microservices and in-app notifications need milliseconds, IoT ingestion and change data capture tolerate seconds, and classic ETL into a data lake can live with minutes to days. Streams are increasingly replacing message queues as the event backbone between services, because the same stream later feeds analytics.

## What does a streaming system have to guarantee?

Three requirements: data produced, captured and processed in milliseconds; a system that scales with ingestion and lets you build applications directly on the collected data rather than chaining feeds (each hop adds latency); and ordering, so the application can tell the story of what happened, and when, relative to everything else. Ingestion, processing and analytics should be decoupled so that processing never stalls the stream.

On the AWS side, the Kinesis family covers it: Data Streams to collect and store (retention configurable up to 365 days, so streams can be replayed), Data Firehose to load into S3, Redshift, Elasticsearch or Splunk with optional serverless transforms, batching, compression and encryption, Data Analytics for SQL and Java applications, Kinesis Video Streams, and Amazon MSK for teams who prefer Kafka. He quotes Data Streams making data available to S3 or Lambda within about 70 milliseconds of collection.

## How is the demo wired?

The site is a single page in an S3 bucket behind CloudFront with AWS WAF in front, listing products with Buy and View details buttons. The steps:

- **Kinesis Data Streams** sized by average record size and records per second, which determines the shard count.
- **CloudFront real-time log configuration** with a sampling rate (he uses 100%), the request fields to capture (the URI query parameters matter most, plus country, port, IP), and the stream as the endpoint.
- **Kinesis Data Firehose** consumes the stream, invokes a Lambda per record to extract product ID, name and status, and writes to S3 under year, month, day and hour prefixes, with a separate bucket for processing errors.
- **AWS Glue** workflow with a crawler builds a database and a partitioned table from those prefixes, rerun on a schedule as new data lands.
- **QuickSight** reads through Athena rather than straight from S3, so the dataset can join other sources, and shows clicks by day, hour and product.

Where do the five minutes go? Firehose buffers for at least a minute before delivering, the crawler run adds a few more, and the dashboard refresh the rest. Shubhankar Sumar said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "So if you see the entire end to end architecture, there was no coding involved, only the lambda was used just to manipulate the click stream". He sketches one extension for that Lambda: count clicks without purchases on a high-value product in DynamoDB and send an SNS alert past a threshold.

## Who should watch

Teams that want product analytics without standing up a streaming platform, and engineers new to the Kinesis family who want to see how the managed pieces connect. It is an AWS architect showing AWS services, and the demo is deliberately small, so treat it as a reference architecture rather than a production design for scale or cost.

## Related Conf42 talks

- Mark Needham on [a real-time analytics dashboard with Streamlit, Apache Pinot and Kafka](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2022_Mark_Needham_realtime_analytics_dashboard_streamlit_apache_pinot_apache_kafka) at Conf42 Python 2022.
- Sagar Sudhir Behere on [streaming real-time analytics](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sagar_Sudhir_Behere_streaming_realtime_analytics).
- Ozioma Uzoegwu on [observability for serverless applications](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Ozioma_Uzoegwu_observability_serverless_application) at the same event.

Title: Legacy code is code without tests, and the windows break in three places
Description: Dmitry Vinnik (Facebook) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on fixing legacy systems with approval tests, domain-driven design and less stress
Body:
A broken window nobody fixes invites the next one, and a legacy module nobody tests invites the next shortcut. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Dmitry Vinnik, Developer Advocate on the Facebook open source team, applies broken windows theory to software in three layers: the code, the team that works on it, and the individual engineer, who breaks too if the first two stay broken.

## What makes code legacy, and should you fix it at all?

He takes Michael Feathers' definition. Dmitry Vinnik said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "Legacy code, if you were to define it, is simply code without tests." That sets up the catch-22: legacy code is rarely testable without refactoring, and refactoring without tests risks changing behaviour, which is the one thing users care about. They don't care that you moved a button; they care that login still works.

So his first answer to whether to fix it is the contractor's: it depends. Weigh the cost of transition against the return, avoid the popularity contest of rewriting for every new framework, and always put doing nothing on the list of options. When you do touch it (a feature, a bug fix, an optimisation), that is the moment to change its legacy status. His rules: no Chia Pet pattern of bolting code onto the side just to make it testable, avoid glue such as non-thread-safe singletons, keep changes single-goal rather than massive pull requests, and accept better over best. Find the seams, the units of behaviour users actually touch, and grow your toolbox (SOLID, delegation, builders).

The everyday code smells are the cracks: duplication, giant classes that ignore object orientation, YAGNI violations (delete it, source control remembers), and comments that restate a getter and rot. He leans on The Pragmatic Programmer and Martin Fowler's Refactoring, plus habits like minimal responsibilities, private by default, encapsulated collections, design by contract and Java's Optional instead of null.

## How do you preserve behaviour while you change it?

With characterisation tests built on domain-driven design: know the domain (taxes, accounting), dogfood the product and use the same names in code as the domain experts use out loud. He swaps the classic unit/integration/end-to-end pyramid for a domain-driven one:

- **Domain-enforcing unit tests,** written as an auditor would and as if it were your last day, using invariant and approval testing. His QuickTheories example claims adding two positive integers yields a positive integer, and the framework falsifies it after two examples by finding the overflow. Schema validation with a JSON schema validator fits here too.
- **Component approval tests:** text-based, snapshot and visual tests. His demo uses open source BackstopJS to screenshot a small app at tablet and phone sizes and diff the changes, with Applitools as the option for scale. It is approval testing because a human approves the baseline.
- **End-to-end task tests** that describe user tasks (enter username, enter password) via the screenplay pattern rather than individual clicks via page objects, split by user dimension: Protractor for the web client, REST Assured for APIs.

## Why are the teams part of the problem?

Conway's law: lots of untested, unowned code usually mirrors silos. The team-level pitfalls are one-size-fits-all, dogmatism, and design stagnation (someone else wrote it, don't touch it). His remedies: ubiquitous language across engineers, tests and domain experts, bounded contexts (sales and support need different fields for the same customer), a context map kept current as documentation, and design with an expiry date, like a note to re-evaluate a function in a couple of years. On communication he prefers asynchronous pings over surprise calls, response time over reach time, faces over avatars, and the art of unsent letters before replying angrily.

## And the engineer?

The last third is about stress. Short-term stress has a purpose; long-term stress must go. He recommends a single place for notes, distraction-free phones kept at arm's length, noise control, library rules and office hours for the legacy expert. His arithmetic on overwork is blunt. Dmitry Vinnik said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "You have 100% to spare." Give 150% today and you have 50% tomorrow.

## Who should watch

Engineers inheriting an untested system, and leads trying to stop a codebase from sliding. The testing section is the densest; the team and stress sections are broader advice that will land differently depending on where you are.

- JJ Asghar on [migrating a monolith to cloud native](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_JJ_Asghar_migrating_monolith_cloudnative_stumbling_blocks) at the same event.

Title: Overcooked is incident command training, and nobody wants to do the dishes
Description: Austin King (OpsDrill.com) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on party games, co-op games, tabletops, fire drills and game days for incident response
Body:
Soccer teams drill penalty kicks and firefighters set buildings on fire to practise walking in and out. SRE teams mostly wait for the next outage. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Austin King, founder of OpsDrill.com and a former Amazonian who worked on Prime Now, lays out a ladder of games for practising incident response, from Jackbox to Amazon-scale game days, each one aimed at a specific skill.

## What has to be in place first?

Two prerequisites: an incident management framework your company agrees on (he points to PagerDuty's open-sourced response training), and everyone trained on it, so that from the CEO down people know what an incident commander is. On top of that sit the human factors of resiliency: psychological safety, blameless postmortems, a growth culture, tight feedback loops and shared ownership, so you do not depend on one hero who can never take a holiday.

Then the incident skills. Responders need curiosity and problem solving; he has watched teams accept the first hypothesis (it's probably networking) and lose 45 minutes to an hour and a half before looking elsewhere. Incident commanders need communication, delegation and coordination. And everyone needs knowledge of the specific system, captured in runbooks. Weakness here shows up as longer MTTR, the bystander effect on the call, and the blame game about who pushed on Friday at four.

## Which games train which skill?

He arranges them like Maslow's hierarchy, each level building on the one below:

- **Trust and safety: party games.** Jackbox, played over Zoom, is a team favourite; in its drawing game being bad at drawing is the point, and laughing at stick figures builds the safety to be wrong in front of each other.
- **Communication: asymmetric co-op games.** In Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes, one player sees the bomb and the others hold the defusal manual. Saying there is a yellow wire is not enough; the experts need orientation, order and colour, under a timer. It is a bridge call with a bigger penalty for ambiguity.
- **Delegation: role-based co-op games.** Overcooked starts calm, then time pressure and running out of clean plates force someone to act as chef and assign people to stations. Austin King said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "And it turns out in the game, just like real life, nobody wants to do dirty dishes." Teams with an incident-commander figure get further than teams where everybody does everything.
- **Skills and knowledge: ops drills,** which is where the real systems come in.

## What are the ops drills, from cheapest to scariest?

**Tabletop exercises** need only a scenario, a call and a dungeon master, perhaps helped by the Backdoors and Breaches card deck from the security world. His example scenario: customer video uploads stop being encoded to the right codec, and the team talks through what they would check. It needs nobody's buy-in and surfaces missing metrics and stale runbooks. His best tip is the invite list: bring an executive, legal and marketing. Executives who have seen the process are less likely to storm a real incident call making demands, and more likely to prioritise operational work over features. Legal and marketing get to think through a scenario like three months of lost customer data with broken backups before it happens.

**Fire drills** page the on-call engineer to execute a specific runbook, or break a node in staging to test the alarm, the page and the failover, which often reveals that staging has no paging or monitoring wired up.

**Chaos testing** is the disciplined version, with Netflix and Gremlin as the reference points; run it as a team exercise and it doubles as a stepping stone to continuous chaos.

**Game days** are the big ones. His first was in 2008 on Amazon retail: paged at 10:30 in the morning, two months into the job, on his first on-call day, because someone had cut power to an entire building on purpose. Prime Day game days are announced and planned, simulating its odd traffic, a single hot product per hour, and the permutations of fallback feature flags.

The abstract also promises outage simulation as a research topic; the recorded talk sticks to the games and drills above.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers building on-call culture, especially for remote teams, and incident commanders looking for low-cost practice. The game recommendations are concrete enough to try at the next team social.
