Title: The on-call bot that phones you and closes the incident by voice
Description: Arthur Grishkevich (Dasha.ai) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on a voice AI app that calls on-call engineers and acks Better Uptime incidents
Body:
Most paging tools can phone you. Very few let you talk back. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Arthur Grishkevich, Citizen Developer Advocate at Dasha.ai, demos a conversational voice app built on his company's platform: Better Uptime detects an outage, a webhook triggers a phone call, and the on-call engineer asks for the status of Kubernetes and TLS, acknowledges, notifies the team and resolves the incident, all by voice, with the transcript emailed afterwards.

This is a vendor talk showing Dasha's own tooling, and it is honest about that. What makes it worth a look is the shape of the integration rather than the brand.

## Why talk to your incident tool?

His use cases: get notified, handle incidents on the go when you are away from the keyboard, avoid tab-switching at your desk by asking for the state of vital services out loud, tell the bot to notify all or some colleagues, and dictate notes during the incident that land in your inbox (or wherever you keep incident records). He is clear on why not just use Better Uptime's own voice alerts: those tell you an incident started or was resolved, and that is all.

## What happens in the demo?

Two Node.js servers run locally behind ngrok: a hello-world server that Better Uptime monitors, and a webhook listener that launches the Dasha app. He kills the hello-world server, the webhook fires, his phone rings. He asks for the Kubernetes cluster status (up), then TLS and health checks (certificate active, health checks not responding), confirms an acknowledgement, which the app sets in Better Uptime, asks it to notify team members, and finally confirms a resolve. The script even has an Easter egg for his exclamation mid-call, asking whether he used the wrong terminal again. A transcript of the whole call arrives by email a moment later.

## How is it built?

Three parts. Dasha Studio is a VS Code extension where you write the conversation in DashaScript, a domain-specific language that models the conversation as nodes and states, some of which never speak and only compute or call external functions. The SDK is imported into Node.js for APIs and telephony. The Dasha cloud supplies the speech-to-text, text-to-speech, intent and entity recognition.

The details that transfer to any chatops or voice design:

- **Filter the webhooks.** Better Uptime sends webhooks for every state change; the listener only launches a call when an incident is created, not when it is acknowledged or resolved. Skip that and the bot phones you to say you just fixed it.
- **Digressions for commands.** Resolve, acknowledge and ignore are digressions, nodes reachable from any point in the conversation and triggered by intents, so the engineer does not have to walk a phone menu.
- **Closed entity sets.** Status questions require both a status intent and a named entity from a closed set (Kubernetes, TLS, health check), so the bot only answers about services it knows.
- **Confirm before acting.** Every action asks for confirmation; only then does an external function in `index.js` call the Better Uptime API with the incident ID and a bearer token.

Training data lives in a `data.json` of example phrases per intent, which the platform uses to recognise wording that differs from the examples but means the same thing. Phone number, name and API tokens sit in an env file.

Arthur Grishkevich said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "Took me probably around five or 6 hours to build this entire thing and I'm not a very experienced software engineer". The source and a README tutorial are on GitHub.

## Who should watch

Title: Argo CD ApplicationSet is a factory for Applications, and nothing more
Description: Dewan Ahmed (Red Hat) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on Argo CD ApplicationSet generators deploying many apps to many clusters from one resource
Body:
One Argo CD Application maps one Git path to one cluster. That stops scaling the day you have a second cluster or a monorepo. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Dewan Ahmed, Developer Advocate at Red Hat, starts from GitOps first principles, demos plain Argo CD on OpenShift, and then shows how the ApplicationSet controller generates whole fleets of Applications from one templated resource, using the list and Git directory generators.

## What does GitOps on Kubernetes actually need?

He borrows a one-slide definition: Git is the single source of truth, Git is the single place where you operate (create, update, destroy environments), and every change is observable and verifiable. The bill of materials is Git repos, clusters, an optional manifest generator such as Kustomize, a CI tool, and a way to group Kubernetes resources. With one firm rule attached: CI servers should not do CD, because orchestrating direct cluster updates as CI jobs is an anti-pattern.

Argo CD, which started at Intuit and has contributions from IBM, Red Hat and others, is a Kubernetes controller that compares the live state against the desired state in Git. The case for it: developers deploy with the git push they already know, SSO through OIDC or OAuth2, multi-tenancy and RBAC, audit trails, rollback as a matter of returning to a commit, and `argocd app diff` to see drift. Resource hooks let you run scripts before, during and after a sync for deployments more complex than a rolling update.

## What does the Argo CD demo show?

On OpenShift, the Red Hat OpenShift GitOps operator installs an Argo CD instance and the ApplicationSet controller out of the box. He creates an Application pointing at a Kustomize nginx path, syncs it manually, then bumps replicas from one to three with a direct push to main. The app turns out of sync, the diff shows the replica count, one click fixes it.

The second run uses automated sync with prune and self-heal. He deletes the service with `oc delete service` and it simply comes back; the app never even shows as out of sync. Prune is the mirror image: delete a resource from Git and Argo CD removes it from the cluster.

## So what is an ApplicationSet?

The questions it answers: how do you deploy Applications to many clusters at once, deploy many Applications from a single monorepo, let unprivileged cluster users deploy, and do all of that from a single custom resource? An ApplicationSet holds a template that looks like a normal Application spec plus generators that produce parameters to fill it. A list generator with three entries of cluster name and URL yields three Applications; adding a cluster means adding a list entry.

Dewan Ahmed said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "The application set controller can thus be thought of as an application factory, taking an application set resource as input and outputting one or more Argo CD application resources that correspond to the parameters of that set."

The scoping matters for anyone worried about blast radius. The controller only creates, updates and deletes Application resources in the Argo CD namespace. It does not touch other Kubernetes resources, does not connect to clusters (they must already be registered in Argo CD) and does not work in other namespaces. Argo CD still does the actual deploying. The generator list in his slides: list, cluster, Git (directory and file), matrix, SCM provider and cluster decision resource.

## What does the multi-cluster demo look like?

Remote clusters can only be added through the CLI, not the UI: `argocd login` (which, he warns, is picky about the URL, so drop the https), then `argocd cluster add` with the remote context, which creates a service account, cluster role and binding on the remote side. The list generator then deploys a guestbook app to the local cluster and an engineering-prod remote cluster. Delete one of the generated Applications and the controller recreates it, which is the point.

The Git directory generator takes every folder under a path, here Helm, Jsonnet and Kustomize versions of guestbook, and produces one Application each. On OpenShift, target namespaces need creating up front with the managed-by label so OpenShift GitOps may deploy into them. A matrix generator example is in his demo repository, written for vanilla Kubernetes.

## Who should watch

Teams already on Argo CD who are copy-pasting Application manifests per cluster, and anyone new to GitOps who wants a clean 101 followed by the multi-cluster step. OpenShift users get the operator-specific details as a bonus.

Title: Your laptop is the flaky dependency, so put the dev environment in the repo
Description: Yshay Yaacobi (Livecycle) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on dev containers, SOPS, Tilt and k3s for self-contained repositories
Body:
The hardest part of contributing to a complex project is often getting it to run at all. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Yshay Yaacobi, CTO and co-founder of Livecycle and creator of the open source feature flag service Tweak, argues for the self-contained repository: everything needed to build, run, debug and test the code lives in the repo, inside a VS Code dev container. He shows it on five open source projects of rising difficulty, all with free tools.

## Why did the hackathon fail?

His origin story is a company hackathon for Tweak (naturally, a tweakathon). Dedicated backlog, fresh docs, printed t-shirts, very few contributions. Most developers spent their time failing to run the project, and the ones who got there found debugging and code completion broken.

He then lists the onboarding ritual everyone recognises: wrong OS instructions, the wrong Python or Node version, package installs failing with errors that are not random but sure feel that way, magic scripts, a database to install, breakpoints that never hit, hot reload broken by websockets. Then you leave for a few months and do it all again. Yshay Yaacobi said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "Our own machines are usually polluted and overloaded with tools, which is really terrible."

What he wants instead is development environments that are consistent, reproducible (destroy and rebuild, like servers), isolated from each other, self-contained, and hard to break. Containers already gave applications those properties; VS Code's develop-inside-a-container feature extends them to the IDE, with the UI on your machine and the backend (file editing, terminals, language servers, extensions) in the container next to the code.

## What do the demos add, one layer at a time?

- **An old Go project** (image to ASCII art, pre-Go modules) runs on a Windows host with no Go installed. The `.devcontainer` Dockerfile installs Go, turns modules off, adds the `dep` dependency manager and sets up the old GOPATH-style workspace, so every contributor gets the same shell, extensions and autocomplete.
- **A Flask app that sends mail through SendGrid** adds secrets, debugging and ports. The API key sits in the repo encrypted with Mozilla SOPS, decrypted into an env file on init. A `launch.json` gives breakpoint debugging, and port 5000 is forwarded from the container. SOPS also integrates with cloud key services such as AWS KMS and Key Vault, which turns key storage into an access-control problem.
- **Habitica**, a large gamified task manager, needs Docker Compose: MongoDB, Mongo Express for visibility, seed data imported when the container is created, and Traefik as a reverse proxy routing subdomains of localtest.me (a wildcard DNS name that resolves to localhost) to each service on one port.
- **Tweak itself** runs Docker-in-Docker, so the project has its own daemon, with .NET 5, Go, Node.js and Yarn installed and Tilt rebuilding images or hot-reloading code on every change. Cloud dependencies are mocked with wire-compatible stand-ins: MinIO for object storage, NATS for messaging, Redis, and an OIDC mock server.
- **Kubecost** needs a real Kubernetes cluster with metrics server and Prometheus. Inside the dev container he runs a k3s cluster with a local registry, and Tilt builds, pushes and swaps the image on each Go change. He deletes the cluster and has a fresh one answering in under 20 seconds.

His point on Kubernetes is practical: local distributions (minikube, Docker Desktop, MicroK8s, kind, k3s) all differ, especially if your code talks to the Kubernetes API, so pinning one distro and version in the repo removes a whole class of works-on-my-machine.

## What does it buy a real team?

Livecycle's own setup has many microservices, custom Kubernetes resources and controllers, a GraphQL engine and a CI system. He quotes a full teardown and rebuild under 15 minutes, about 10 seconds from code change to running tests, and new developer onboarding, including provisioning on AWS, under 3 hours.

He is clear about the costs: the initial setup takes work, some tools are bleeding edge, it is tempting to keep adding tools because installing is free, the definitions are coupled to VS Code, there are performance and security trade-offs, and native mobile development is a hard case he is not optimistic about.

## Who should watch

Anyone who maintains a repository other people struggle to run, platform teams thinking about developer experience, and open source maintainers who want contributors past the README. The demos are dense and practical, and the examples are on GitHub.

Title: An empty folder to a green Kubernetes deploy, no slides allowed
Description: Rob Richardson (Cyral) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 live-codes a .NET app, multi-stage Dockerfile and GitHub Actions deploy to Kubernetes
Body:
Some talks explain CI/CD. This one builds it, from an empty folder, while you watch. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Rob Richardson, Developer Advocate at Cyral (and Microsoft MVP and Docker Captain), skips slides entirely and live-codes a .NET website, a multi-stage Dockerfile, a Kubernetes manifest and three GitHub Actions workflows: deploy on main, build-only for pull requests, and per-environment deploys through GitHub environment secrets.

## Why spend time on .dockerignore?

He scaffolds an MVC site with `dotnet new mvc`, then goes straight to the files people skip. The `.gitignore` drops `bin`, `obj` and user-specific files. The `.dockerignore` starts as a copy, since Docker falls back to `.gitignore` if there is none, and then adds debug-only content: `appsettings.Development.json` and `launchSettings.json`, which have no business in a production runtime image.

Rob Richardson said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "In fact, if you know these four commands, you can probably read pretty much any docker file and understand what's going on." The four are FROM, COPY, RUN and CMD.

## How do you get a small image that still caches well?

The first Dockerfile builds from the .NET 5.0 SDK Alpine image and runs restore, build, test (in release mode) and publish as separate RUN layers, so Docker caches each. Then two refinements that are worth the price of admission for anyone new to containers:

- **Multi-stage build.** The SDK stage is named `build`; a second stage starts from the ASP.NET Alpine runtime image and copies only the published `dist` output across. Source code and build tools never reach production.
- **Restore before copy.** Copy only the `.csproj`, run restore, then copy everything else. Changing a JavaScript or `.cshtml` file no longer re-downloads every NuGet package, and a failed build, test or publish stops the pipeline before any runtime image exists.

## What does the GitHub Actions workflow do?

Starting from the publish-a-Docker-container template, the main-branch workflow checks out the code, logs in to the container registry with a marketplace action, sets the Kubernetes context from a kubeconfig stored as a secret, builds and tags the image with the commit SHA (so a running container traces straight back to its source), pushes it, substitutes registry URL, cluster URL and image tag into the Kubernetes YAML with sed, and runs `kubectl apply`.

The ordering of that substitution is the sharpest detail in the talk. He does it after the push on purpose: if the manifest ever slipped past `.dockerignore` into the image, it would carry placeholders, not secrets. Which is exactly what happened, as he later notices he forgot to ignore the YAML file. Belt, braces, and a live demo that proves why.

The build goes green, `kubectl get all` shows the service up, and while ingress DNS propagates he uses `kubectl port-forward` to the service on local port 8080 to show the page. He also adds a README status badge, and a moment of honesty in the test step: Rob Richardson said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "There are no failing tests because there are no tests."

## What about pull requests and other environments?

The PR workflow is the main one with things deleted: no registry login, no cluster login, no push, no secret replacement, no deploy. It still runs the full Dockerfile, so a syntax error or failing unit test fails the PR. For a develop environment, rather than duplicating the workflow with develop-flavoured secret names, he uses GitHub environments: secrets with the same names and environment-specific values, so one workflow file deploys both branches.

## Who should watch

Developers taking their first container to Kubernetes through GitHub Actions, and anyone who wants to see a sensible Dockerfile built up step by step. Seasoned platform engineers will know the moves, but the secret-ordering trick and the environment-secrets pattern are worth a look. The code is on his GitHub, linked from robrich.org.

Title: One open source scanner, three places to catch the hard-coded password
Description: Filipi Pires (Talkdesk) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on running the open source Horusec SAST scanner from the CLI, VS Code and GitHub Actions
Body:
The cheapest place to find a password in clear text is before it leaves the developer's laptop. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Filipi Pires, Principal Security Engineer at Talkdesk, gives a demo-heavy tour of Horusec, an open source static analysis tool, and runs the same scan three ways: from the command line, inside VS Code, and as a GitHub Actions gate that fails the build when it finds something.

## SAST, DAST, IAST: which one runs where?

He starts by putting everyone on the same page. SAST, static application security testing, reads source code (or bytecode and binaries) before anything reaches production, as part of a secure software development lifecycle. DAST tests exposed interfaces from the outside, so it needs a published URL or a running binary. IAST combines the two, and SCA and container scanning fill in more gaps. This talk lives entirely on the SAST side.

## What does Horusec actually check?

Horusec, maintained by the Brazilian company ZUP Innovation where Pires used to work, does three kinds of analysis: static analysis of the code itself, leak detection (credentials, private keys, hard-coded passwords, including in Git history), and a dependency audit for vulnerable third-party libraries. His list of supported targets runs from C#, Java, Kotlin, Python, Ruby and Go to JavaScript, JSON and shell, plus Terraform and Kubernetes files.

The detail worth noticing is that Horusec is an orchestrator of engines, not one engine. The demo output shows findings from Horusec's own engine next to Bandit for Python and a Go engine, all in one report. Filipi Pires said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "From my perspective, it's pretty nice because you can combine all those engines."

## How does the CLI demo go?

The install is a curl of a binary moved into the local bin. `horusec start` scans the current directory; `-p` points it at another project path, `-a` takes an authorisation token to ship results to the Horusec web manager, and `-o` changes the output format, for example for SonarQube. He positions the two as complementary: SonarQube for code quality, Horusec for security, since it was built by a security team.

His demo repository on GitHub (deliberately vulnerable code in Go, Java, Node.js and Python, free to reuse) produced ten findings: one critical, two high, three medium and four low. The critical one is the classic, a hard-coded password in a Python file, reported with the file, line and a link to CWE-798. A Java file gets flagged for an insecure random number generator, and a JavaScript file for passing input to a shell. He makes a good point about the CWE links: for developers without a security person nearby, the MITRE pages are a free course in why the finding matters and how to mitigate it.

## And inside the editor and the pipeline?

The VS Code extension runs the same analysis and puts the finding on the offending line, with the same CWE reference on hover. He notes a normal scan takes 30 to 40 seconds, slower in his demo only because he was streaming from a virtual machine.

The pipeline step is the payoff. A GitHub Actions workflow installs Horusec with curl and runs the start command with `-e true`, which makes the job return exit code 1 when vulnerabilities are found. He pushes the workflow, the job runs in about a minute, finds the same clear-text password, and breaks the build. The documentation also covers CircleCI, Jenkins, Azure DevOps, GitLab CI and AWS CodeBuild, plus a Docker image.

## Who should watch

Developers and SREs who want a first, free security gate in their pipeline, and anyone who has never seen a SAST tool run end to end. It is an introductory demo with a strong accent on getting started; it does not cover tuning false positives or the web manager in depth.

Title: Stop running terraform apply for everyone else
Description: Andrew Kirkpatrick (PartnerStack) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on self-service Terraform via pull requests with Atlantis, Terraform Cloud and env0
Body:
Codifying your infrastructure does not stop the Slack messages asking you to change it. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Andrew Kirkpatrick, Staff Engineer at PartnerStack, shows how to hand those requests back to the people making them: wrap the hard parts in Terraform modules, let a central executor run plan and apply from pull requests, and keep the SRE as the reviewer rather than the typist. He compares Atlantis, Terraform Cloud and env0, demos all three, and explains why PartnerStack picked Atlantis.

## Why isn't infrastructure as code enough?

Andrew Kirkpatrick said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "So infrastructure as code solves some problems, but not all problems." A codified estate tells you which line of HCL is which bucket, but the requests still arrive by Jira ticket, Slack message and tap on the shoulder: a new VM for capacity, a database setting, a test environment. That is toil, and it is the old dev-versus-ops wall in a new outfit.

What actually needs an infrastructure engineer, he argues, is a short list: changes made safely, tracked to a person or team, reproducible for rollback, peer reviewed like application code, and approved by the right chain of command. None of that requires the SRE to type the command.

## Modules as classes of HCL

His mental model: code is what you want to be true, state is what someone last made true, the APIs are what is true now. Writing Terraform from scratch is daunting for an application developer, so the trick is modules that expose a few attributes and force the rest. His DigitalOcean VM example makes the name configurable, derives backups and monitoring from an environment string, interpolates CPU and memory into the size, and pins region and image so every VM comes out the same. The developer gets a server in the right VPC with the right security groups without knowing either exists.

## Why not just run Terraform in CI?

You can, but HashiCorp's own docs list the traps, and he walks through them. The plan and the apply have to happen on the same commit with a plan file carried between machines. The approval may come hours or days after the plan, when state may have moved. Two PRs against the same project need an order. A CI system built to validate every commit as golden is a slightly odd home for a workflow that pauses for a human.

## Atlantis, Terraform Cloud, env0: what's the difference?

- **Atlantis** is a Go application that answers webhooks from GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket. You comment `atlantis plan` and `atlantis apply` on the PR and it replies with output as comments plus a status check. It adds project locks separate from Terraform state locks, so a second PR touching the same project is told to wait its turn. Apply requirements reuse your VCS rules: approvals, code owners, mergeability.
- **Terraform Cloud** runs as SaaS, on premises (enterprise plan) or hybrid with agent pools. It has an API, a CLI, approval screens in its own UI, protection against accidental destroys, and status checks but no PR comments. Gotchas he hit: no symlinks, and only its enhanced backend, so it would not read his remote state from a GCS bucket.
- **env0** is built around organisation templates: one-to-many copies of a project as ephemeral environments, with cost limits, time-to-live and per-user environment caps. It comments on PRs but has no status check, and keeps state inside env0, so it suits on-the-fly environments more than long-lived infrastructure.

The demos are refreshingly mundane: delete a Google Cloud DNS record via a PR, get told by Atlantis that someone has to approve before apply, then open a second PR to restore the record and watch it bounce off the lock.

## What does it cost you?

The upside: occasional contributors can make infrastructure changes without a fully configured workstation, every change gets review before execution, and VCS integrations give you audit trails into tools like Jira. The downsides are honest. Module development is slow if every iteration goes through a remote executor, so he builds modules locally first. Security controls move from cloud accounts to your Git host. The executor holds a skeleton key, so its credentials need the same Vault or external-secrets treatment as everything else, and it should not live on the cluster it manages. And badly segmented projects produce terrifying plan output; picture a reviewer reading a plan that wants to remove a hundred servers they never touched.

PartnerStack chose Atlantis because it is open source, free, actively maintained, and its custom workflows let them run arbitrary scripts around plan and apply, for things like special AWS tokens or multiple Kubernetes clusters.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who are the human bottleneck for Terraform changes, and teams choosing between these three tools. It is a 2021 comparison and he says himself that Terraform Cloud and env0 were moving fast, so check current feature sets, but the CI-versus-executor reasoning holds up.

Title: Empty queues, angry nurses, and the SLO that finally measured the right thing
Description: Marco Coulter (Tech-Whisperer.com) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on Goodhart's law and SLOs negotiated across code, infra and business
Body:
Your dashboard can be green while your users are running down the stairs. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Marco Coulter, Technical Evangelist at Tech-Whisperer.com and a former bank CTO, uses a hospital lab system to show how a well-meant metric turns into a target nobody should be chasing, and how to build SLIs, SLOs and SLAs that stay honest: measure across code, infrastructure and the business, then negotiate the numbers instead of using them as a club.

## How do you hit your SLA and still fail the customer?

Coulter's story comes from a service provider that ran IT for every hospital in an Australian state. Lab results travelled from the lab's Unix systems through message queues into the mainframe holding patient records, all of it nominally speaking HL7. In practice, malformed messages from proprietary software got stuck in the queues, and the fallback was a nurse physically running from a high ward down to the lab in another building.

So the contract said: if the queues went above 100 messages, the provider refunded money. Coulter wrote a bash monitor, icons went green to yellow to red, and the team even built capacity plans to keep queue processing fed. The queues stayed empty. The nurses kept calling to say the system sucked. Transactions were timing out before they ever reached a queue.

That is Goodhart's law, which he only learned the name of years later. Marco Coulter said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "Basically, Goodhart's law says that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Queue length was a fine measure of queue health. As a target for the whole application it was useless. His fix is the framing of the talk: let SLIs stay measures, and make the SLOs the goal.

## What does an SLI look like when it's written properly?

Before the three dimensions, a quick shared vocabulary: SLIs work better as percentiles than averages, they nest from the code and infrastructure up to the customer, SLOs are the limits that would keep a typical customer happy if barely met, and the SLA says what happens once the budget is spent. He also argues that full outages are rarer now, so slowdowns matter, and successful customer requests make a better goal than raw uptime.

His code-level example spells out three things: the transaction (well-formed HL7 updates for Labs), the reaction (an OK response) and the source (the APM tool, a single source of truth so SREs and developers don't argue from different data). The SLO is 99.9% of those, and the SLA is a looser 99.1% over the previous 28 days, leaving reaction room. He deliberately avoids a good-over-bad ratio here, because the malformed messages came from lab software his team could not patch.

## Why did five minutes beat thirty seconds?

The infrastructure dimension uses a performance curve rather than one threshold: 90% of lab updates within 30 seconds, 99% within a minute, 99.9% within five minutes. The SLA only commits to the five minutes, and that number came from watching the nurses, not from the hardware. Their benchmark was the roughly ten minutes it took to run to the lab when the system was down, so five minutes made them happy and saved infrastructure spend.

Marco Coulter said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "It doesn't always have to be as fast as possible, just as fast as necessary." He contrasts it with his bank trading systems, where latency was the competitive edge and cost came second.

## Can you measure impatience?

The business dimension is the best bit. The team owned the patient record application, so they added a repeat-lookup counter: a nurse reopening a record because the result was not there yet was the earliest sign of an unhappy ward. The first version kept failing for records that were fine, because one or two nurses hammered Enter without waiting, so the measure gained a "beyond 10 seconds" condition. The SLA window of eight hours came from the nurses, who thought in shifts.

## Negotiation is an SRE skill

The last third is about getting those numbers agreed. Know your own team's maturity, risk tolerance and peak periods first, profile the people you will negotiate with, and find a facilitator, ideally someone from outside who can politely shut down long introductions. His meeting flow runs warm-up, test drive with one real SLI/SLO/SLA, assess (and capture assumptions, which is why SLA footnotes outgrow the SLA), propose, recur, agree on the record. One practical hint: predictability often beats speed, and a spread wider than six standard deviations signals a low-capability process.

## Who should watch

Anyone writing their first SLOs, and anyone whose SLAs have become a weapon between teams or vendors. The hospital story is the clearest Goodhart example you will hear in an SRE talk, and a whole section on negotiation is something few SRE talks bother with.

Title: Measure the process, not the people - cycle time in four segments
Description: Yishai Beeri (LinearB) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on cycle time as the first engineering metric, split into coding, pickup, review, deploy
Body:
If you measure only one thing about your engineering process, Yishai Beeri, CTO of LinearB, wants it to be cycle time: how long a piece of work takes from the first line of code to running in production. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 he splits it into four segments (coding, pickup, review, deploy), explains what blows up each one, and argues that a metric on a dashboard is only the first step. The bigger gains come from flagging the specific pull request that is stuck, while it is stuck.

This is a vendor talk, and LinearB's product shows up in the numbers and the closing pitch, but the segment advice works with any tooling.

## Why not measure developers?

Because you get what you measure. Count lines of code, commits or pull requests and people optimise for those, and you build a Big Brother culture where developers feel stack ranked. Yishai Beeri said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "Instead of focusing on individual metrics, instead of focusing on technical metrics like code lines, like commits, things that are easy to game and that don't really get you any benefit, you should be measuring the process."

The process view targets three productivity killers:

- **Context switches.** Reloading a task into your head is a real tax; he cites research putting it at 20 minutes or more to get back into something.
- **Work in progress.** Starting things is the fun part; finishing needs reviews, merges and deploys, so WIP piles up unless the team is deliberate.
- **Dead value.** Code that is merged but not deployed for hours, days or months. Nobody learns anything from it, and the more of it waits, the riskier the deploy.

Cycle time, familiar from the Accelerate book and the DORA metrics, captures all three.

## Coding: blame the requirements first

Coding runs from the first commit on a branch to opening the pull request. It's calendar time, not effort: two hours of coding followed by two days of negotiating a missing edge case with product is a two-day coding phase. His fixes are better requirements up front, chopping work into small standalone slices that can be reviewed, merged and deployed on their own, and refactoring the hairy parts of the codebase that make every change slow.

## Pickup: nothing happens here, so shrink it

Pickup is the wait between opening a pull request and someone starting to review it. It's pure waiting. Comments an hour or two after you wrote the code are cheap to address; comments after the weekend are not. Teams improve it with coordination, so nobody has to nag, and with deliberate context switching: do reviews at the start of the day, after lunch or after a meeting, when you've already switched context anyway.

## Review: done beats started

Review is the back and forth between author and reviewers until the merge. Long review times point to three things: a culture that values starting over finishing, a bottleneck of too few reviewers (add more, or relax the review requirements), or a change built the wrong way, which is cheaper to catch with a design check before the code is written than in the pull request.

## Deploy: kill the dead value

Here the remedies are well known: CI/CD, reliable and comprehensive tests, and small work items that are easy to test, deploy and roll back.

## What does a short cycle time buy?

Predictability, whatever your method; a shorter learning loop from production (did that change actually cut CPU or database load?); better team communication, which remote and hybrid work makes harder; lower WIP; fewer, cheaper context switches; and lower delivery risk. He mentions customers that get a typical change through in a day or less.

The numbers come from LinearB's customer base, so read them as vendor figures. The slides show average cycle time improving by 18.5% or more for 80% of organisations in the first month, rising to 48% by month four, and by 75% or more for half of them. A 75% cut, he notes, is a four times shorter cycle: one day instead of four.

## Why a dashboard isn't enough

A dashboard someone checks every two or three weeks is a lagging indicator: by the time it shows pickup is high, those pull requests are already late. And delays are not spread evenly; it's an 80/20 case where a few stuck changes drag the average. His progression is metrics, then insights, then action, then automation: alert the team in Slack, where they already work, when a specific pull request has waited past a threshold, say five or ten hours. That real-time nudge is the second big jump he says they see in customer data.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers starting to measure delivery who want a metric that won't poison the culture, and SREs who own the deploy end of the pipeline. If you already track DORA metrics, the segment breakdown and the pickup tips are the parts to steal.

Title: You can't run 10,000 RPS on a laptop, but you can disprove things there
Description: Hari Krishnan (Polarizer Technologies) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on shift-left performance testing by falsifying hypotheses locally
Body:
Shift-left performance testing sounds impossible: production is a hybrid cloud with load balancers and firewalls, and your laptop is, in Hari Krishnan's case, an 8 GB MacBook Pro gasping under a Gatling run. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Hari Krishnan, CEO of Polarizer Technologies, argues you don't need to reproduce production locally. You scale down the trend instead of the load, use your laptop to falsify performance hypotheses cheaply, and save staging for verifying the ones that survive. Then he shows a dockerized setup, Perfiz, that turns existing Karate API tests into Gatling performance tests.

## Why late performance testing breaks your sprints

The usual cycle: developers write code, a performance tester builds an environment and scripts, load hits staging or production, a report comes back, the developer digests it. Finding issues that late means an equally long loop to fix them, and the higher environments are contested, with every developer queueing to check their own fix.

In a sprint it gets worse. Feature one goes to the performance tester, the developer moves on to two, three and four, and the feedback on one and two lands mid-sprint when nothing can change. Sprint three becomes the hardening sprint, a washout spent fixing earlier work.

## Scale down the trend, not the problem

How do you scale down a pair of KPIs like throughput and latency? Keep the aspect ratio? Keep RPS and relax response time? His honest answer: you can't, not in a truly representative way. What you can scale is the shape of the expected behaviour, and use it to invalidate hypotheses.

The logic is the green apple. To verify that all green apples are sour you would have to eat every one; to falsify it, one sweet apple is enough. Hari Krishnan said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "on the left hand side we're learning through falsifiability, and on the right we are confirming our learning through verifiability."

His first example: as throughput rises exponentially, response time should degrade only logarithmically, at loads up to 10,000 RPS. Locally he tests the same trend at much lower rates and finds latency degrading exponentially, so the hypothesis is disproved without touching staging. He fixes it on the laptop. The local pass is inconclusive, so he verifies in the higher environment, where it holds until about 1,000 RPS and then falls off. Back to the laptop to reproduce and fix. Staging only got used where it was strictly needed.

## The with-and-without experiment

His favourite is the A/B check. The system hit 10,000 RPS at 80% CPU; a cache was supposed to deliver 1 million RPS at the same utilisation. Neither number fits on a laptop. At whatever max CPU your machine reaches, measure RPS without the cache (X) and with it (Y). If X is less than Y, the cache makes a difference and is worth taking upstream. If not, you've learned it locally, and he has seen many caches that were, in his words, just there for moral support.

## Repurpose the API tests

The other half of shift left is effort. Developers write API tests; performance testers write load scripts that generate the same requests and assert less about the response. On one team he worked with, developers wrote Karate API tests while the tester wrote Gatling scripts in Scala: duplicated work, inconsistent coverage, and a tester without the developer's view of the architecture. His fix is to reuse the API tests as perf tests, like turning a road car into a rally car.

Tool sprawl (load tool, metrics store, dashboards, glue code) gets one answer: containerize the whole setup and develop it locally like code, so the same stack runs on a laptop and in staging.

## The Perfiz demo

Perfiz, which his team built on those principles, takes a Karate feature file and runs it as a Gatling simulation via the Karate-Gatling integration, configured with a YAML file and no Scala. Metrics go to Prometheus and the results show up in Grafana in real time. The demo uses the Karate demo Spring Boot project: init, point the YAML at the greeting feature, start the stack in Docker, run the test, and watch one constant user for 30 seconds then three for 15 seconds appear in Grafana. API test to performance test in about five minutes.

## A template for scientific rigor

He closes on mindset: performance testing as a learning activity through spikes, not a verification step at the end. His continuous evaluation template lists the problem, baseline and target KPIs, the hypotheses, one falsifiability and one verifiability experiment per hypothesis, and the validated learning. Walking it through the cache example uncovers a near-100% miss rate from a TTL that's too short, then 40% misses from evictions, tested locally by shrinking the cache rather than growing it, before the target 10x on staging.

## Who should watch

Developers and performance testers tired of hardening sprints, and teams using Karate who want load testing almost for free. The falsify-locally idea is worth the time even if you never touch the tool.

Title: Check engine light, roadside assistance, Carfax - alerts aren't incidents
Description: Chris Riley (Splunk) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on why alerts, incident response and incident management are three different things
Body:
If your team uses the words alert, incident and ticket interchangeably, Chris Riley, Senior Technology Advocate at Splunk, has a car analogy for you. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 he separates the three: an alert is the check engine light, incident response is roadside assistance, and incident management is the Carfax history of everything that ever happened to the car. Treat them as one thing, usually by running response out of a ticketing system, and on-call gets slower and noisier than it needs to be.

It is a short, opinionated framing talk rather than a tooling walkthrough. The abstract also mentions on-call scheduling, shift-left and machine learning; the talk itself sticks to the core distinction.

## Why the 1998 Honda doesn't need observability

The setup is his own garage envy. When something broke on a 1998 Honda Accord, it was fairly clear what and how to fix it. A 2020 Tesla has the same brakes and tires plus a pile of software running in a cloud native way, so a check engine light alone won't tell you what's wrong. That's the monolith versus microservices story.

In the monolith days there was always the Billy Bob server that had to be restarted every two weeks, after which everything was magically better. Alerts carried enough context because the infrastructure never changed. With many small services wired together in ways nobody can hold in their head, there is no Billy Bob service to go and poke. As he puts it, we can't expect to go and find the problem; the problem has to find us, with enough context to resolve it quickly. And the first service to scream, often the API gateway, may have nothing to do with the cause.

## The point of all this is on-call

He is refreshingly blunt about the goal. Chris Riley said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "Nobody wants to be paged at night. Being on call sucks."

Everything the industry builds in monitoring and observability, in his view, serves a better on-call experience: ideally never woken up, and if you are, you're the right person, with enough data to fix it or to know exactly who can. Going from an alert straight to logs doesn't get you there any more. He admits his curmudgeon reflex about the word observability (it's just monitoring, and yes, people abbreviate it o11y), then concedes the term exists because what monitoring has to do has changed.

## Alerts, incidents and tickets, separated

- **Alert, the check engine light.** A system says something is wrong. You get a pointer, not a diagnosis.
- **Incident response, roadside assistance.** Mobilising the right help quickly. Maybe they jump the battery on the spot; maybe they tow you to the shop, where diagnostics pour out.
- **Incident management, the Carfax.** Born from ITSM and driven by a ticketing system: the historical record of what happened, useful later.

An incident is not just an alert. It can be many alerts aggregated by rules that decide when something is significant enough, which means less noise. It carries more context, linked to previous incidents, Confluence articles and runbooks, which means it can drive action. He is still amazed by teams that get 1,000 alerts a day and ignore them; his advice is to fix those first.

## What a slow incident looks like

He describes two mobilisation anti-patterns. Spray and pray blasts the whole organisation and hopes someone picks it up, common in NOC-style setups; the back and forth across people and tools typically ran about six hours and five reroutes, an average he says his team has seen consistently with customers. Lazy mobilisation always calls the one person who fixes everything, which works until you burn them out. And resolution means everything is green again, not just that the service was restarted, because in microservices the failure cascades and recovery takes time.

The model he wants instead flows from observability (alerts with context) to incident response (mobilisation and action) to incident management (the long-term record): alerts roll up into incidents, incidents link to a dashboard, the dashboard leads to logs or traces and spans, and then you act. The aim is to compress the time between those steps and shrink the noise at each.

## Who should watch

Teams whose incident process is a monitoring dashboard plus a ticket queue, and anyone who needs a clean way to explain to management why paging and ticketing are different tools. Experienced incident commanders will know the content, but they may borrow the Carfax line.

Title: Container observability on AWS, down to the alarm that fixes itself
Description: Suraj Muraleedharan (AWS) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on logs, metrics, traces and SLOs for container workloads with CloudWatch and X-Ray
Body:
Observability is not a new set of signals, argues Suraj Muraleedharan, Senior DevOps Consultant at AWS. Logs, metrics and traces have always been there; observability is correlating them into one picture of the system. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 he applies that to container workloads on AWS: how to log so the logs are useful, how CloudWatch metrics, alarms and anomaly detection fit together, what X-Ray adds, and how to set SLOs without promising more nines than you can pay for. The most practical bit is an alarm that triggers a Lambda function to repair a broken security group.

It is a fundamentals talk mapped onto AWS-native tooling, with the SRE vocabulary at the end.

## What should good logging look like?

He splits logs into four categories, the same split the CNCF observability white paper uses: application logs, system logs (from the OS or AMI), audit logs (who did what, AWS CloudTrail being one example) and infrastructure logs (from Terraform, Chef or CloudFormation runs). Then the hygiene list:

- Change log levels per environment. In production, keep to errors; trace, debug and info belong in lower environments. Too much logging costs performance through file I/O.
- Never print sensitive information, and have a mechanism that checks for it.
- Use one consistent format via Log4j, Logback or your framework of choice, so the people analysing centralized logs can extract fields.
- In containers, write to stdout and let a DaemonSet aggregate, for example with Fluent Bit, into CloudWatch Logs or Elasticsearch.

## Metrics: alert now, plan later

Metrics serve two jobs in his framing: real-time monitoring and alerting (CPU past a 70% threshold, too many 404s or 500s) and trend analysis for right-sizing, such as starting a new app on two vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM and growing from the historical data. In CloudWatch, metrics are grouped by namespace and dimension, from defaults like API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, DynamoDB and EBS to custom ones like Container Insights and Prometheus.

Container Insights gives one view of an EKS or ECS cluster: CPU, memory, network, node count, disk and cluster failures. Performance events arrive in the embedded metric format, structured JSON that carries high-cardinality data. On plain EC2 the CloudWatch agent ships logs to the same place.

## Alarms that do more than page

He distinguishes metric alarms from composite alarms, which combine alarm states with a rule expression. Thresholds come with a choice: fire on the first breach, or only after the value stays over the line for several periods (his example uses three). Anomaly detection draws a band from statistical and machine learning models, two standard deviations wide in his example, and alerts when the metric leaves it.

What an alarm triggers is where it gets interesting. Beyond SNS email and Auto Scaling (scale out at 90% CPU, back in around 50%), he walks through automated remediation from an AWS blog post on incident management: a microservice behind an Application Load Balancer times out because traffic can't reach it, the alarm notifies an SNS topic, a Lambda function receives it, recognises the security group as the culprit and fixes the inbound or outbound rules. Or send the alert to Slack and do it ChatOps-style.

## Tracing with correlation IDs

X-Ray ties a chain of calls together through a trace ID in the X-Amzn-Trace-Id HTTP header, works with API Gateway and Application Load Balancer, and draws a service map where healthy services are green and failing ones red. His example, the Scorekeep sample app, breaks one request into DynamoDB session, update and put calls with timings for each.

## How many nines can you afford?

The SRE part is short and sensible. Don't track every metric; pick a few indicators that matter. Have as few SLOs as possible, agree them with every stakeholder, and spell out the conditions under which they hold. Define an error budget, which the slides set per quarter, as the objective measure of how unreliable a service may be.

Then the cost question. Suraj Muraleedharan said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "the more available that you want to have your application, sometimes the cost associated with it is also high." Before you sign up for 99.9% or 99.95%, ask who owns disaster recovery, whether the run team has runbooks, how the build team hands over, and whether the team can ship fixes on its own. (One correction for note-takers: the talk puts 99.9% at about four and a half hours of downtime a year; the usual figure is closer to nine hours, while four and a half matches 99.95%.)

For hands-on practice he recommends the AWS observability workshop at observability.workshop.aws, a self-paced lab of about three to four hours.

## Who should watch

Teams running containers on EKS or ECS who have CloudWatch switched on but not much more. Engineers already deep in OpenTelemetry will find the AWS specifics more useful than the definitions.

Title: Feed your eBPF counters to a clustering model and let it judge
Description: Sujith Samuel (Ericsson) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on clustering eBPF data to tell healthy system behaviour from bad, starting at XDP
Body:
eBPF already tells you how many times a file was opened or which IP sent a packet. Sujith Samuel, Principal Software Engineer at Ericsson, asks what happens if you stop just graphing those numbers and hand them to a clustering model instead. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 he sketches the idea: eBPF programs generate data points about system behaviour, a model trained on labelled examples groups them into healthy and unhealthy clusters, and a time series check on top flags when traffic is drifting towards trouble, such as an incoming DDoS.

Set expectations accordingly. This is a concept talk with an eBPF primer, not a results talk: no model, accuracy figures or production numbers are shown. The eBPF half is concrete; the machine learning half is a proposal.

## eBPF in four sentences

eBPF programs are event driven: they run when the kernel or an application passes a hook point such as a system call, a function entry or exit, a kernel tracepoint or a network event. You write the program, compile it to bytecode, and the verifier rejects anything that could step out of bounds, because the code runs in the kernel. Programs pass data back to user space through maps. His example counts how many times the kernel function behind execve is entered: a kprobe looks up a counter in a map, increments it and writes it back.

## Where does the clustering come in?

The machine learning part starts with the Iris dataset, the first clustering example most of us met: plot sepal and petal measurements and similar flowers land close together. Swap petals for system signals (network calls, file opens, database reads) and you have the pitch. Sujith Samuel said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "So EBPF can help us understand the basic characteristics of a system behaving right now."

The workflow he proposes:

- eBPF generates the data points.
- You label an initial set as positive or negative behaviour.
- A clustering model learns the boundary between good and bad.
- In production, live eBPF data runs through the model to classify behaviour in real time.

Because scoring every packet makes no sense at volume, a time series algorithm on top looks for a gradual build-up of abnormal requests, which is how you might spot a denial-of-service attack before it lands.

## Why start at XDP?

His worked use case is network traffic. XDP (express data path) is the earliest point where the kernel can intercept a packet, before socket buffers are allocated. An eBPF program attached there writes packet details such as source IP, bytes and time into a map; a user space program reads the map and pushes the data to a store such as Redis, where the clustering system decides whether the request belongs to a normal cluster.

The same hook can act, not just observe. Keep a list of known malicious IPs in a BPF map, and the program returns XDP_DROP for matches, XDP_TX to bounce a packet out without climbing the stack, or XDP_PASS to let it continue. Updating the blocklist means updating the map, and the filter picks it up dynamically. Dropping traffic before the kernel spends memory on it is the cheapest firewall you'll run, and he says it is a use case his team is exploring across their systems.

## Cilium and Pixie already do the collecting

For observability today he points to two open source tools built on eBPF. Cilium hooks network events at the NIC and kernel, tracks pod traffic through ring buffers, and exposes it through the Hubble API, CLI and UI, alongside load balancing, network policy and bandwidth management. Pixie runs Pixie Edge Modules as daemons on every node, collects metrics, events, traces and logs, and lets you query them with Pixie scripts that return JSON. He says his team uses both, and their fundamentals, for the observability side of their SRE work.

Other use cases he lists: catching performance degradation (fewer database reads than the expected minimum), checking for malicious traffic, and preventive maintenance when an API's mix of GET and PUT calls stops matching what is expected.

## Who should watch

SREs who know eBPF by reputation and want a quick primer with a networking example, and anyone toying with anomaly detection on kernel-level signals. If you want a finished ML pipeline, this is the whiteboard version.

Title: Observing a serverless app you can't SSH into
Description: Ozioma Uzoegwu (AWS) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on serverless observability with CloudWatch, X-Ray, ServiceLens and OpenTelemetry
Body:
Serverless hands most of the stack to the cloud provider, which also means there's no box to log into when a request goes missing between API Gateway and DynamoDB. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Ozioma Uzoegwu, Solutions Architect at AWS, walks through how to observe a serverless application on AWS: built-in and custom metrics in Amazon CloudWatch, structured logs, tracing with AWS X-Ray, CloudWatch ServiceLens to tie them together, and the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry for teams that don't want to be locked into one toolset.

It is an AWS services tour aimed at builders new to the topic, organised around a troubleshooting workflow that is worth stealing on any platform.

## What does observability mean for a pile of functions?

His serverless app is the classic one: static frontend on AWS Amplify Console, auth with Amazon Cognito, API Gateway in front of Lambda functions, data in DynamoDB, perhaps a Step Functions workflow (his example runs sentiment analysis on submitted feedback, stores it and notifies the owner via Amazon Chime). The developer's job is to understand latency, bottlenecks and failures between those services.

For the definition he borrows his colleague Nathan Peck's magic box: you inherit a box that turns a green circle into a pentagon ten milliseconds later, the people who built it have left, and there are no docs. One day it takes 2 seconds, another day it returns a blue hexagon, and then it catches fire. Ozioma Uzoegwu said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 that good observability "allows you to answer questions you did not know you need to ask."

## The troubleshooting workflow

The structure of the talk is the workflow itself: a question or an alarm, then a service map to find where to look, then traces, then trace analytics, then logs for the root cause. Each AWS service is slotted into a step.

## Metrics: built-in first, then your own

CloudWatch runs at a scale he quotes from AWS: more than 1 quadrillion metric observations, 3.9 trillion events and 100 PB of logs ingested each month. For serverless, the built-ins cover Lambda (invocations, errors, throttles, duration, concurrent executions), API Gateway (latency, 4xx and 5xx errors) and DynamoDB (consumed and available capacity units), with per-service and cross-service dashboards.

Built-ins don't cover business metrics such as revenue, daily sign-ups and page views, or operational ones such as time to recover or pages per incident. Those need custom metrics. You can call the PutMetricData API from the AWS SDK, which pushes synchronously and is charged per metric and per call, or use the CloudWatch embedded metric format: write structured JSON logs that carry the metrics, and CloudWatch extracts them for you. Client libraries exist for Node, Python and Java.

## Logs and alarms

API Gateway logs at error or info level, set per stage or overridden per method. Lambda logs go through your language's console logging or the embedded metric format, and can be exported to Amazon OpenSearch Service or S3. CloudWatch Logs Insights then queries up to 20 log groups at once; his examples list the 100 most expensive invocations by billed duration and chart average, max, min and p90 duration in five-minute windows. Alarms come with static thresholds or CloudWatch anomaly detection, which learns a metric's pattern and alerts when it breaks.

## Traces and the single pane

X-Ray is a checkbox (or an infrastructure-as-code setting) on Lambda; API Gateway adds the tracing header to HTTP calls. A trace shows each hop with its latency, and X-Ray analytics compares trace sets across time ranges or by attributes such as status code or a custom username. ServiceLens joins metrics, logs and traces in one place. In the demo he filters traces down to Firefox users on Windows, picks the p95 to p99 slice, and follows one request from API Gateway through Lambda to DynamoDB, logs included.

## Why OpenTelemetry?

He cites a survey: 50% of companies use at least five observability tools, and within that group, 30% use more than ten. Each means another SDK or agent, more compute, and manual correlation between tools. OpenTelemetry standardises how you instrument, collect and export metrics, logs and traces. AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry is AWS's upstream-first, supported distribution, shipped as a Lambda layer so you don't touch function code, exporting to CloudWatch, X-Ray, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, OpenSearch or partner tools. Amazon Managed Grafana handles the dashboards.

For further reading he points to Lambda Powertools and the AWS Lambda Operator Guide.

## Who should watch

Developers starting their first production serverless app on AWS, and SREs inheriting one. If you already live in X-Ray, the OpenTelemetry section is the part to skip to.

Title: Murphy's laws of observability, and why your sampled traces lie
Description: Dave McAllister (Splunk) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on ten Murphy's laws for observability, from sampling blind spots to OpenTelemetry
Body:
Dave McAllister, Senior Technical Evangelist at Splunk, opens his Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 talk with the law everyone knows and the corollary that makes it hurt: whatever can go wrong will go wrong, at the worst possible time. He then hangs a tour of modern observability on ten Murphy's laws of his own. The most useful lesson sits at law six: sampled data told him latency was one to two seconds, while the full data showed 95th percentile traces at 29 to 40 seconds.

## The fifth way to fail

Law one is the cleanest description of SRE work going. Dave McAllister said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "So far I have yet to hear a better description of the life of an SRE." The law: if you see four ways a procedure can go wrong and guard against them, a fifth, unprepared for, will promptly develop. The job is to mitigate the four and be ready for the fifth.

That readiness is data. His framing is the familiar one (metrics tell you whether you have a problem, traces where it is, logs why) with an important widening: observability should use any data that helps you infer what the system is doing, and it works as a proxy for customer happiness.

## Why monitoring stopped being enough

Law two, every solution breeds new problems, gets a Cynefin framework walk-through. We moved from monoliths to microservices and, at the same time, onto elastic and ephemeral cloud infrastructure. In his words, we changed two variables at once, something you'd never do in math class. Failures stop repeating exactly, debugging gets painful, and the system lands in the complex domain: probe, sense, respond.

Law three, you never run out of things that can go wrong, maps to the known/unknown grid. Monitoring covers the things you know to watch, such as disk or memory running out. Observability is what lets you do forensics on an unknown unknown, then move it into the known categories so the next person doesn't start from scratch.

## Scale, drift and the 30-millisecond Lambda

Law four (nothing is as easy as it looks) and law five (things get worse under pressure) are about complexity and scale. A front page for a single product on a major ecommerce site can touch around 43 microservices, each calling four to eight more, and then 100,000 transactions arrive at once. No one holds that in their head, which is why service maps and the RED pattern (rate, errors, duration) matter: RED shows him a 25% error rate, the service map shows where transactions stop.

Ephemeral compute makes it worse. A warm-start AWS Lambda can start in about 30 milliseconds and finish in about 1.2 seconds, gone before you look. Correlating across VMs, containers and pods depends on timestamps, so clock drift and skew become observability problems. And his demo environment has 2,247 instances, which nobody watches by eye.

## Sampling and averages hide the incident

Law six, if it's not in the computer it doesn't exist, is the heart of the talk. He compares the same environment with head-based sampling and without. Sampled: latency of one to two seconds and about one error. Unsampled: 95th percentile traces between 29 and 40 seconds and plenty of errors, against a 3.7-second threshold he cites as the point where people abandon carts. Saving data only when you see an error doesn't help either, because with an unknown unknown you don't yet know what counts as an error.

Law seven, availability is a function of time, separates accuracy (the measurement is correct) from precision (it is consistent with the others), with an archery example. Then the numbers: ten seconds of requests average 13.9 per second with a 95th percentile of 27.05; split into two five-second windows that becomes 16.4 and 29.2, then 11.4 and 19.4. Look only at the aggregates and you miss the single second that crossed his alert trigger.

## OpenTelemetry is the thing you do first

Law nine, whenever you set out to do something, something else must be done first, comes with a hardware-store confession about PVC glue and plumber's putty. The thing to do first is correlation. Observability 1.0 meant a separate agent and back end per signal; the 2.0 version he describes is built on OpenTelemetry, the merger of OpenTracing and OpenCensus. The collector takes in data in whatever protocol you have, processes it (sampling included), and exports OTLP, Jaeger or Prometheus, so existing setups don't need to be torn out.

He closes with axioms: numbers are tools, not rules; prediction is only as good as its data; Baker's law (misery no longer loves company, now it insists on it) as the case for sharing data rather than just results; and his corollary to Hill's commentaries: if it doesn't matter, it does not matter, until it does.

## Who should watch

Anyone deciding how much telemetry to sample or how to set alert windows. It is a vendor-neutral talk, light on product and heavy on the reasons full-fidelity data matters.

Title: The tester who found the root cause was missing logs, not bugs
Description: Parveen Khan (ThoughtWorks) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on how a tester pushed her team from Ctrl+F in Notepad++ to observability
Body:
A board full of tickets marked blocked is usually read as a complex product. Parveen Khan, Senior QA Consultant at ThoughtWorks, read it as a team that couldn't see inside its own system. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 she tells how, as the tester on a microservices invoicing product, she went looking for observability, built a proof of concept with open source tools, and moved the team from no visibility to centralized, structured, queryable logs. Her takeaway for testers: the problem is yours too, even if nobody files it under testing.

This is an introduction to observability, told through one team's story. If you already run traces in production, the value is in the tester's angle.

## Why do you slow down on a foggy road?

She opens with an analogy borrowed from another speaker. On a foggy road you slow down, not because you're a bad driver or the car is slow, but because you can't see. Pilots fly through clouds because they have instruments. Microservices and distributed systems are faster cars: simpler to develop piece by piece, but when you distribute a system you also distribute the places where it can go wrong. Observability is the instrument panel.

## What did no visibility look like?

The team she joined was new, on an automated invoice system built as microservices. Production issues arrived daily. Developers spent days or weeks investigating, couldn't find the cause or even the location, and marked tickets as blocked. A conversation with a developer was her light-bulb moment: the product wasn't the problem, the lack of visibility was.

They did have logs, written with NLog, but stored separately per service. The only way to read them was to open them in Notepad++, one tab per service, and search with Ctrl+F. "Can you imagine?" she asks, and anyone who has done incident response from a text editor can. Her fix list follows directly: centralize the logs, and make them searchable by structuring them.

## Logs, metrics, traces, and the questions they answer

The middle of the talk is a clear primer. A log is a message with a timestamp and a payload. Metrics are numbers over time, at system level (memory used by a process), application level (requests per second, an API's error rate) or business level (how long a user takes to log in). They aggregate well but can't tell you which customer hit the problem at a given moment. Traces can: a trace follows one request end to end, which makes it the most valuable signal when debugging.

Parveen Khan said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "So trace is kind of like telling you a story which gives more low level details."

With that data in place you can ask questions such as why something is broken, which services yours depends on and which depend on yours, what went wrong in a release, or why performance degraded over a quarter. And like DevOps, she argues, observability is a culture and mindset change rather than a set of tools.

## What's in it for testers?

Plenty, in her experience. Browser devtools only show so much when something looks wrong in the UI; observability tools let a tester follow the request under the hood and put that evidence in the bug ticket, which saves developers time. Exploring logs, metrics and traces also teaches how the system communicates, and testers are well placed to spot where more instrumentation is needed. It supports testing in production too, so teams shift right as well as left.

She cites a tweet making the point that good debugging and good exploratory testing are often indistinguishable; developers just call it debugging.

## A proof of concept, not a finished migration

She is honest about the ending. When she left the team, they weren't at full observability, but they had taken the first steps: structured, centralized logs that could be queried, with next steps planned. The route there was her own: reading, trying tools, building a proof of concept with open source tools and presenting it to the team, instead of deciding it wasn't a testing problem.

## Who should watch

Testers and QA engineers on distributed systems who rely on the UI and the API alone, and team leads wondering whether observability belongs only to ops. It is a gentle first talk on the subject, not a tooling comparison.

Title: Your SLIs are fine. Are your Survival Level Indicators?
Description: Alayshia Knighten (Honeycomb.io) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on Survival Level Indicators, the human SLIs that warn of burnout first
Body:
The talk title promises service level indicators. Within a minute Alayshia Knighten, Team Lead for Onboarding Engineering at Honeycomb.io, admits the bait and switch: at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 she talks about Survival Level Indicators, the signals that tell an engineer whether they are actually okay. Her argument is short and hard to dispute: SLOs measure customer success, and customers are only as successful as the people building and running the systems they use.

It is a short, personal talk, closer to a team-lead conversation than a technical session. That is the point.

## What is a Survival Level Indicator?

She gives it a formula, because this is an SRE conference. Alayshia Knighten said at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021: "It's the me factor divided by valid moments."

The me factor is your core values, what intrigues you, your mantra and your tolerance levels: the good parts of you that you bring to work. When work compromises it (her example: being told to skip your child's graduation or a trip planned for months because there are things to do), the best parts of you stop showing up, and the private Slack channels get spicier.

Valid moments are the costs you have decided are justifiable. Being on call might be fine for you and a dealbreaker for someone else. Working extra hours for a while can be fine if it pays off later. Invalid moments are whatever you decide they are, and she is candid about where her own line sits: "My tolerance on invalid, non justifiable moments is pretty low nowadays."

So the indicator is personal by design. Nobody else gets to set your threshold, which is also why nobody else will notice when you cross it.

## Calibrate expectations before they calibrate you

Her first tactic is mutualistic expectations: define what you want early and keep recalibrating, because people's needs change as much as their lives do. Some want leadership, some want harder technical problems, some want a lighter load, especially when they are doing the job of nine people. The opener she suggests is not a complaint but a question: tell your boss where you see yourself, where you think you are now, and ask whether they agree. It starts a conversation and shows you are thinking ahead.

It works the other way too. As she puts it, "it's not cool to force someone into leadership, yet it's totally cool to encourage them" - ask people where they want to be and what is holding them back. She also recommends a personal README: how you work, what you value, how and when to reach you. Boundaries, written down before anyone tests them.

## Protect the calendar, then leave it

The practical part of the talk is about time:

- **No meeting Wednesdays.** If you have them, defend them; if you don't, create them. One day without meetings gives you room to get real work done.
- **Plan the week.** Spend a little time at the end of one week or the start of the next deciding which tasks are actually required and which meetings actually need you.
- **Get a hobby.** Something to look forward to that has nothing to do with work. Hers is a newly bought Kamado grill and an ambition to become a grill guru.

## Watch the people next to you

Survival is not only self-service. She describes noticing colleagues sending smoke signals and asking them to do something non-work related on Zoom for 30 minutes. And if you know someone hasn't taken time off, tell them to. The work will still be there; their sanity might not be.

She closes with a Louisiana metaphor: the me factor is a gumbo, and its ingredients change over time. Taste it now and then. If the job no longer fits your expectations, that is allowed too - sometimes you outgrow a season, and the conversation with your boss is about whether the recipe can change.

## Who should watch

Engineers who haven't taken a vacation in nine months, and the leads who should have noticed. There is no tooling here, just a framework you can apply in your next one-to-one, delivered with enough humour that it never turns into a lecture.
