Title: Your one-off chaos experiment expired when the other team deployed
Description: Gunnar Grosch (AWS) at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021 on automating chaos experiments by schedule, by event and in the delivery pipeline
Body:
A chaos experiment you ran last month proved something about a system that no longer exists. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2021, Gunnar Grosch, Senior Developer Advocate at AWS, makes the case for automating chaos experiments and shows three ways to do it with AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS): on a schedule, on an event, and as a stage in the delivery pipeline. The safety net that makes all three possible is the stop condition.

## Why aren't one-off experiments and game days enough?

Gunnar starts from the two use cases he sees most: one-off experiments (built from a past outage, a new feature or the services that hurt customers most when they fail) and periodic game days that rehearse a launch or a traffic spike. They get you far, he says, and for many teams they are enough.

Then he builds an ecommerce example to show where they run out. The product service is well architected: instances in Auto Scaling groups across Availability Zones, Amazon Aurora with replicas. Add CI/CD and the team deploys daily, several times a day, sometimes hourly. Add cart, order, user, search and recommendation services, each with its own codebase and team, all depending on each other. His learnings from that picture:

- Frequent deployments are hard to cover manually.
- Covering an extensive set of experiments is time-consuming.
- Unknown parts of the system might change, because other teams ship too.
- Systems are getting too complex for anyone to hold a mental model of them, let alone keep the docs current.

He also ties automation back to the science: repeating an experiment is how you tell a fluke from the normal case.

## Three ways to automate an experiment

**Recurring scheduled experiments.** A small serverless app: an Amazon EventBridge (CloudWatch Events) schedule rule, cron syntax, triggers an AWS Lambda function that starts a FIS experiment template. The demo template stresses CPU and memory on the product service instances once a day. Whatever your teammates and third parties changed since yesterday, the experiment checks again.

**Event-triggered experiments.** The same Lambda, wired to an event pattern instead of a clock. In the demo, an EC2 Auto Scaling launch event fires the experiment: he bumps an Auto Scaling group's desired capacity from two to three, EventBridge catches it, and FIS starts stressing instances. The pattern can be any AWS service event or a custom one, including business events such as items added to a cart. It answers the awkward what-if-this-while-that-happens questions, even when the trigger lives in a different part of the system.

**Continuous delivery experiments.** The one he gets most questions about. A pipeline that deploys to staging and production gets an experiment stage after staging, implemented as an AWS Step Functions state machine that starts the FIS experiment and watches it. He edits code straight in GitHub, as one does for a demo, and the commit goes through, the experiment passes, production deploys. On the second run he flips the stop-condition alarm with the AWS CLI; FIS halts the experiment, the stage fails, and the change never reaches production.

## Stop conditions are what make automation safe

Nobody watches an automated experiment, so it needs an alarm that stops it. What the alarm watches is, in his words, "the traditional it depends answer": fewer users adding items to the cart, or a technical signal such as CPU above a threshold. In the pipeline demo, the stop condition doubles as a deployment gate.

## Keep the manual experiments

Gunnar is clear that automation adds to the practice rather than replacing it. One-off experiments and game days remain the core, the main source of learning and of confidence. The path he suggests: design an experiment by hand, run it, then promote it to run every day, every hour or on every deploy. His takeaways: automation covers a larger set of experiments, it verifies assumptions over time, and safeguards and stop conditions are key to doing it safely.

## Who should watch

Teams that already run chaos experiments on AWS and want them to keep up with their deploy rate. The demos are AWS-specific, but the schedule, event and pipeline patterns translate to any fault-injection tool or homegrown scripts, as he points out.

Title: Check SageMaker for a two-line fix before you build it yourself
Description: Joshua Arvin Lat (NuWorks Interactive Labs) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on shipping ML on SageMaker by reusing built-in features, with time as the metric
Body:
Most ML teams lose months to plumbing that already exists. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, Joshua Arvin Lat, CTO of NuWorks Interactive Labs, AWS Machine Learning Hero and author of the Machine Learning with Amazon SageMaker Cookbook, argues for a blunt rule: before building anything, check whether Amazon SageMaker already does it in two or three extra lines of code. His metric for picking an approach is time.

It is a practical tour of the SageMaker Python SDK, with code from the book's GitHub repository (PacktPublishing/Amazon-SageMaker-Cookbook, about 80 recipes), not an architecture talk. Expect estimators, `fit`, `deploy`, and a running count of how few lines each feature adds.

## Why is time the metric?

A slow build pays for infrastructure, overhead and salaries the whole way, and the requirements may move before you finish.

"If you can build something in 3 hours, I would prefer that over something which can be built in three months," Joshua Arvin Lat said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021. His summary of the cost side: "time will always be a multiplier".

The opening example makes the point with a lookup table. Anomaly detection maps to the SageMaker Random Cut Forest algorithm, product recommendation to Amazon Personalize, forecasting to SageMaker DeepAR, image and video analysis to Amazon Rekognition, document classification to the BlazingText algorithm and translation to Amazon Translate. His claim: even a newcomer gets a working proof of concept in four to eight hours, and spends the tuning budget only after approval.

## Infrastructure is one line of config

He leads with the compute abstraction. Each stage of the workflow declares its own instance type and count: two instances for data preparation, six for training and tuning, one small one for the endpoint, since inference rarely needs the training hardware. Changing any of those is a single line.

Training instances are transient. They are created for the job and deleted when `fit` returns, so nobody writes cleanup code and nothing idles on the bill. So he recommends going bigger: an ml.m5.2xlarge that runs for two minutes barely registers on the bill and cuts training time. Deploying a DeepAR forecasting model is one `deploy` call with an instance type and count, then a wait of roughly three to five minutes for a production endpoint.

You also don't have to start over. SageMaker takes its 17 or so built-in algorithms, your own container image (an R script included), or your existing TensorFlow, PyTorch, MXNet or Hugging Face code with minimal changes.

## The features worth knowing about

He runs through the catalogue (Processing, Experiments, Feature Store, Autopilot, Studio, Model Monitor, managed spot training, Data Wrangler and more), then shows a few in code. The mindset behind all of them: the cool custom solution loses to whatever solves the problem fastest and cheapest, and some other AWS customer has probably asked for your feature already.

- **SageMaker Debugger**: about three extra lines on the estimator. In his example it saves a snapshot every two steps to Amazon S3 and applies a rule that flags a loss that stops decreasing, handy when the failing job is a distributed run.
- **Automatic model tuning**: three to four lines on top of the same estimator. He sets continuous and integer ranges for three hyperparameters, min_child_weight and eta among them, calls `fit`, and after 15 to 20 minutes gets the best model by the objective metric (validation AUC in his case).
- **SageMaker Clarify**: bias detection before and after training, plus explainability via SHAP values. Configure the data and SHAP configs, run the explainability job, wait three to seven minutes, and get a ranking of which features drove the output, without learning SHAP first.

## Deployment has more shapes than one endpoint

The deployment section is a menu of patterns: a model inside an AWS Lambda function (cheap, minus the other SageMaker features), Lambda calling a SageMaker endpoint to pre- and post-process data, API Gateway mapping templates calling the endpoint with no Lambda at all, and a model in AWS Fargate. On the SageMaker side there are multi-model endpoints (several models behind one endpoint, which cuts cost), multi-container endpoints, A/B testing with production variants, and Lambda's container image support.

## Retraining should not be a calendar reminder

The last part covers automation: new data lands in S3 each month and a better model gets swapped in without anyone rerunning a notebook. Option one combines the SageMaker SDK with the AWS Step Functions Data Science SDK for a linear train, build and deploy pipeline you can trace in Step Functions. Option two is SageMaker Pipelines, the dedicated service, with a graph view where clicking the train step shows its metrics. By his count it costs roughly two to three lines per step, chained together and started with `execute`.

## Who should watch

Engineers and data scientists who are new to SageMaker, or who have used it only for training and haven't touched the rest. It is a 2021 snapshot of a service he says ships something new every month, so check the current docs. If you already run SageMaker Pipelines in production, you can skip it.

Title: Kubeflow as the middle road between managed ML and DIY
Description: Mofizur Rahman (IBM) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on Kubeflow as a portable, open source end-to-end ML platform on Kubernetes
Body:
If your models behave differently on a laptop, a GPU training box and the production cloud, every difference is a future outage. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, Mofizur Rahman, Developer Advocate at IBM and a contributor to Kubeflow's manifests and deployment work, argues for Kubeflow as the end-to-end ML platform that keeps those environments the same, without the lock-in of a managed service or the upkeep of building your own.

Rahman comes from containers and infrastructure, not data science, and the talk reads that way: platform trade-offs first, then components, installation and a short demo on IBM Cloud.

## Why is ML a platform problem now?

He starts from the familiar diagram where the ML code is a small box surrounded by data verification, serving and monitoring. Ten years ago, he says, IBM spent hundreds of millions of dollars a year on ML research without much direct business impact. Now ML is core to the business, so it needs the same discipline as software: version control, continuous testing, delivery and rollback. That is MLOps, which he defines with the CD Foundation's MLOps special interest group as applying DevOps principles to ML applications.

"We can't just build the model on our local laptop and just deploy it into production just by copying some files over," Mofizur Rahman said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021. An end-to-end platform should cover ingestion, cleaning, transformation and validation, training (distributed if needed), serving, monitoring and logging, and give you a loop to improve each step.

## Buy, build, or something in between?

Managed platforms such as Google Cloud AI Platform, IBM Cloud Pak for Data with Watson Studio, Amazon SageMaker and Azure Machine Learning are fully managed, integrate with the rest of the cloud, scale with it and come with enterprise support. The costs: price, vendor lock-in (you end up doing one cloud's version of ML, not ML), no faithful local replica of the environment, closed source components and models and code that may not move.

DIY is what Uber did with Michelangelo, and Netflix, Airbnb and Lyft built their own too. You get full control and no lock-in, and you pay in engineering hours forever. Eventually you are maintaining an ML platform instead of your business.

His wish list sits between the two: scalable infrastructure, the tools data scientists already use, open source, industry backing, an option to pay for enterprise support, and portable models and code.

## How does Kubeflow fit the list?

Kubeflow is an open source, curated set of ML tools and frameworks for Kubernetes, and Kubernetes does a lot of the work. Pods and nodes scale. Kubernetes skills are easy to hire for, which he frames as scaling the team as well as the cluster. The platform is composable, so you pick the pieces you need, and multi-tenant, so one installation gives each team member their own namespace. The portability argument is the central one: run Kubeflow locally, on a GPU training cluster and in the cloud, and the gap between experiment, training and production shrinks.

The components he lists: a central dashboard; notebook servers for Jupyter, VS Code through code-server and RStudio; TensorFlow, PyTorch, XGBoost and MXNet; pipelines on Argo or Tekton; serving with KFServing or Seldon; ML Metadata; Feast as a feature store; Istio for networking, with Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring.

Installation goes through the manifests repository with kustomize and kubectl, on any Kubernetes including minikube, or through the Kubeflow Operator for Kubernetes and OpenShift. The manifests were restructured around the 1.3 release, out about a week before the talk, to make maintenance, modularity and first-time installs smoother.

## What is still painful?

He is candid. Kubeflow has many moving parts, each with its own release cycle and upgrade path, so maintaining a distribution for your company is a big job. Distributions on IBM, AWS, GCP and Azure differ slightly, so moving from minikube to a cloud is close to, but not exactly, one to one. End users mostly do not feel this; maintainers do.

## The demo

On IBM Cloud with App ID for authentication (Dex is the default), Rahman logs in as two users to show separate namespaces and notebooks on one cluster, runs a coin-flip pipeline written in the Python DSL on KFP Tekton, and points at Katib for hyperparameter tuning and KFServing for serving.

## Who should watch

Platform teams weighing a managed ML service against Kubernetes, and data teams that already run Kubernetes. If you want a deep look at Kubeflow pipelines, this is the overview, not the tutorial.

Title: TensorRT turns RetinaFace from 81 FPS into 190 on one GPU
Description: Aditya Lohia (Tod'Aers) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on cutting deep learning inference latency in Python with NVIDIA TensorRT and DeepStream
Body:
The accurate model is often the one you cannot deploy, because it is too slow for real time. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, Aditya Lohia, Machine Learning Engineer at Tod'Aers, shows how NVIDIA TensorRT and DeepStream close that gap from Python, with his own benchmarks: RetinaFace with a ResNet-50 backbone on a GTX 1080 goes from 81 FPS in FP32 to 190 FPS in INT8.

It is a compact, practical talk from someone who uses TensorRT in industry, and it is honest about the trade-offs.

## Where does the latency come from?

Lohia defines latency as the time to process a single image or video, and throughput as the time to process the whole dataset, the two being inversely related. In a typical pipeline the bottleneck is usually model inference, and he lists four ways to attack it:

- **Weight quantization** to FP16 or INT8, either after training or with quantization-aware training. INT8 is much faster but costs accuracy. "I generally find that float 16 is the best method to go because it preserves my accuracy," Aditya Lohia said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, adding that it gives him 1.5 to two times the speed of FP32.
- **Pruning** layers and connections that experiments show you can skip. In the best case you can remove up to 99% of connections and keep accuracy.
- **Knowledge distillation**, transferring what a large ResNet learned into a small one such as ResNet-18 that would otherwise plateau below the big model's accuracy.
- **Framework-based deployment**, the subject of the talk.

## What does TensorRT actually do to your model?

TensorRT is NVIDIA's SDK for high-performance inference, written in C++ with Python bindings: an optimizer that rewrites the model and a runtime that executes the resulting engine. It imports from TensorFlow, PyTorch, MXNet, ONNX and others. The optimizations:

- **Precision calibration.** To quantize to INT8 with minimal accuracy loss, TensorRT calibrates weights and activations on a representative sample of the input data. No retraining, no full training set, no parameters to tune.
- **Kernel auto-tuning.** From hundreds of specialized, often hand-tuned kernels, it picks the fastest for the target GPU, input size, filter size, layout and batch size. That is also why an engine built on one GPU cannot run on another model of GPU.
- **Dynamic tensor memory**, allocating memory per tensor only for the time it is used.
- **Multi-stream execution**, processing several input streams in parallel.
- **Layer and tensor fusion.** Frameworks launch one CUDA kernel per layer, and the launches plus the memory reads and writes between layers cost more than the computation. TensorRT fuses convolution, bias and ReLU vertically into one CBR block, merges layers with the same input and filter size horizontally into one wider kernel, and removes concatenation layers by writing straight into preallocated buffers. His analogy is one trip to the supermarket instead of three.

His fusion counts: VGG19 drops from 43 layers to 27, Inception V3 from 309 to 113, ResNet-152 from 670 to 159.

## How do you get a PyTorch model into TensorRT?

The easy route is PyTorch to ONNX, then the ONNX parser builds the engine. The network definition API in C++ or Python takes more work and gives marginally to considerably better speed and accuracy, depending on the model.

His benchmarks, batch size one on a GTX 1080 unless noted:

| Model | Precision | Input | FPS |
|---|---|---|---|
| RetinaFace ResNet-50 | FP32 | 640x480 | 81 |
| RetinaFace ResNet-50 | INT8 | 640x480 | 190 |
| RetinaFace MobileNet 0.25 | FP32 | 640x480 | 400 |
| YOLOv5-s | FP16 | 608x608 | 142 (188 at batch 8) |
| YOLOv5-l | FP16 | 608x608 | 30 |

Even YOLOv5 large runs in real time on a five-year-old card. His practical advice: try every precision and do not dismiss INT8, set the workspace size, use Docker because installation is slow without it, and serialize the engine. "Do not build an engine for each inference as that is an overhead," he warned.

## DeepStream for the rest of the pipeline

Once inference is fast, everything around it becomes the bottleneck. DeepStream is NVIDIA's streaming analytics framework, built on GStreamer with GPU-specific elements, for Python or C++, on edge or cloud. It captures RTSP, HTTP or file streams, decodes on the GPU, does scaling, dewarping and cropping on the GPU, batches automatically, runs TensorRT or Triton models, tracks objects, then renders to screen or sends results to the cloud or disk. NVIDIA's purpose-built models run at about 1,100 FPS on a T4 and 95 FPS on a Jetson Nano, before any pruning.

## Who should watch

Engineers whose PyTorch or TensorFlow model works and is too slow, especially on NVIDIA edge hardware. His RetinaFace TensorRT conversion code is on GitHub for anyone who wants to follow along.

- [Ron Lyle Dagdag on leveraging machine learning with ONNX](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2021_Ron_Lyle_Dagdag_Leverage_Power_ONNX), the format that feeds TensorRT's parser, also at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021.
- [Eduardo Dixo on object detection with transformers and CNNs](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2021_Eduardo_Dixo_Object_Detection_Transformers_CNNs_Drone_Case_Study), detectors that would need exactly this treatment to run live.

Title: ONNX is the PDF of machine learning models
Description: Ron Lyle Dagdag (Spacee) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on ONNX and ONNX Runtime for training in one framework and deploying anywhere
Body:
Train in whatever framework your data scientists like and run the model wherever your app lives: that is the promise of ONNX, the Open Neural Network Exchange. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, Ron Lyle Dagdag, Lead Software Engineer at Spacee, explains when ONNX is worth it, how to get models into it and how to run them with ONNX Runtime, then demos a model trained in ML.NET from C# and served from Python.

It is an introduction aimed at software engineers who have to ship someone else's model, and it comes with the best bakery metaphors of the event.

## What problem does ONNX solve?

Dagdag starts with the basic split: training frameworks produce a model, and a runtime uses it for inference inside an application. The trouble is the number of each. Data scientists train in PyTorch, Keras, TensorFlow or scikit-learn; the model has to run on a laptop, a phone, the cloud, a GPU, FPGA or ASIC, even a microcontroller. ONNX sits in the middle as an open format for both neural networks and traditional ML models.

His analogy is the PDF: write in Word or anything else, export, and any viewer on any device can display it. ONNX began as a partnership between Microsoft and Facebook and is a graduate project of LF AI, with about 11,000 GitHub stars, almost 2,000 pull requests and around 200 contributors at the time of the talk.

When to reach for it: a model trained in Python that must run in a C#, Java or JavaScript app; inference latency too high for production; deployment to IoT and edge devices or a different OS and hardware; combining models from different frameworks in one pipeline.

## How do you get an ONNX model?

Data scientists are the bakers, he says, the people who perfect the secret recipe. To get the recipe into ONNX:

- Download a pre-converted model from the ONNX Model Zoo, such as ResNet, for vision or sound.
- Export from a service such as Azure Custom Vision, where you upload and tag photos and get a model back.
- Convert from a training framework: load the model, convert, save. PyTorch has a built-in exporter, Keras goes through ONNXMLTools, TensorFlow converts from the command line, scikit-learn uses skl2onnx.
- Use ONNX as an intermediate step, for example PyTorch to ONNX to TensorFlow, or ONNX to Core ML.

Netron is the tool he wants every software engineer to know. Open an ONNX file and it shows the graph plus the input and output names and shapes, so you can integrate the model without chasing the data scientist for the training code.

## Where should inference run?

"What is the difference between a baker and starting a bakery?" Ron Lyle Dagdag said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021. Baking the model and running the business around it take different skills, and both are needed. Deployment is the software engineer's bakery: VMs, Windows, Linux and Mac, phones, edge devices.

His second food analogy: McDonald's bread is made centrally, Subway bakes it in the store. Cloud inference means shipping data to the model; edge inference runs it close to the user, on the phone, the camera or a gateway. Reasons for the edge are low latency, not paying to ship every video frame to the cloud, working without a connection, and privacy rules about personal data or geography. For the cloud, there are ONNX Docker images, a minimal base one and an ecosystem one with the converters preinstalled.

## ONNX Runtime everywhere

ONNX Runtime is Microsoft's open source, MIT-licensed inference engine for ONNX models, with pluggable hardware accelerators. Its website generates install instructions for your OS, language, architecture and accelerator, CUDA or OpenVINO for example, so a PyTorch model can use OpenVINO through ONNX without a separate conversion. It ships in Windows 10 as WinML for desktop apps, sits alongside DirectML on DirectX 12 for games, and ONNX.js runs models in the browser or Node via WebGL and WebAssembly.

## The demo: C# trains, Python serves

On a Binder-hosted Jupyter notebook with .NET Interactive, Dagdag loads a 30-row CSV of years of experience against salary, trains a regression with ML.NET (the usual fit-and-transform pair) and converts it to ONNX in one call. Netron shows the graph: only years of experience feeds the regressor, and the salary input is an unused stub. A second notebook switches to Python, installs onnxruntime, creates an inference session, reads input names, shapes and types, and returns a salary prediction for ten years, then three and a half.

The recap is the thesis: "It separates out how you train it and how you would run and do inferencing on that model," he said.

## Who should watch

Application developers who keep receiving models in frameworks their stack does not speak, and teams eyeing edge deployment. ML researchers will know most of it.

Title: Forecasting after M4, and why the naive baseline comes first
Description: Pawel Skrzypek and Anna Warno (7bulls.com) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on ES-Hybrid, N-BEATS, TFT and ensembling for time series forecasting
Body:
Machine learning took over time series forecasting in 2018, and ensembling is still the cheapest accuracy you can buy. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, Pawel Skrzypek, CTO at 7bulls.com, reviews the methods that won the M4 and M5 competitions, and data scientist Anna Warno then forecasts air pollution with N-BEATS and the Temporal Fusion Transformer, ending with an ensemble that beat the best single model by more than 15% on mean absolute error.

Two talks in one: a short literature review, then a practical session with real data, missing values and all.

## What changed with the M4 competition?

For a long time statistical methods dominated forecasting, typically ensembled, and ML trailed. Skrzypek dates the break to 2018 and the M4 results. The M competitions, run by Professor Spyros Makridakis of the University of Nicosia, are the most prestigious benchmark in the field; M4 asked for forecasts on about 100,000 series. First and second place went to hybrid methods mixing statistics and ML, and M5 was dominated by pure ML.

The methods he covers:

- **ES-Hybrid**, Slawek Smyl's M4 winner: Holt-Winters exponential smoothing for preprocessing, feeding an LSTM with dilations and residual connections, ideas borrowed from CNNs for images, and heavy ensembling of the best models per series.
- **N-BEATS**, pure ML, published after M4 and claiming better results on its data. Stacks of blocks with residual links, trend, seasonality and generic block types for some explainability, transfer learning, and ensembles of over 100 models.
- **GluonTS**, a ready framework rather than a method, with transformers among its models, probabilistic forecasting and cloud training. Not easy to use, he says, but easier than compiling research code yourself.
- **The Tsetlin machine**, based on stochastic learning automata. It learns a probability distribution per parameter and updates it after every prediction, so it retrains as it goes, a different approach from gradient descent that is useful as one more voice in an ensemble.

At AI Investments, his team applies these to financial series and reports over 60% accuracy on long test periods.

## Start with missing data, then the naive forecast

Warno picks a public air quality dataset because it is multidimensional, hard and big enough: around 40,000 hourly rows and about 15 columns, six pollutants, six weather variables and date fields. It looks like noise until you aggregate it by week.

Missing data gets serious attention. Bar plots, heatmaps and a dendrogram show which columns lose values together (the weather ones, strongly correlated). Histograms of consecutive gaps show most are short, but runs of 60 exist. Short gaps get interpolated, and she compares forward fill, linear and higher-order splines on artificially removed values. Long gaps are not filled at all: the series is split into two. Then normalisation, sometimes Box-Cox, and hours and days encoded on the unit circle so 23:00 sits next to midnight.

The target is nitrogen dioxide, six hours ahead, evaluated with a rolling window on a train, validation and test split. First come two naive predictors, last value and same hour the previous day, plus classical models such as SARIMA, Prophet, TBATS and exponential smoothing. "So it's a good practice to start first with naive prediction," Anna Warno said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, because metrics that look fine at first glance can hide a model worse than repeating yesterday. MASE builds that comparison into the metric.

## N-BEATS or TFT?

They complement each other. N-BEATS is univariate and interpretable through its trend and seasonality blocks. The Temporal Fusion Transformer handles multivariate data with categorical, continuous and static inputs, has a variable selection network, accepts known future inputs for conditional forecasts and explains itself through attention. Training uses early stopping, learning rate scheduling and gradient clipping, with Optuna for search when time allows.

TFT with quantile loss scored the best mean absolute error. The naive baselines sat around 25, so the networks clearly learned something.

## Ensembles of near-identical models

The step Warno calls extremely effective for the effort is ensembling. Models with the same architecture differing only in loss function (quantile, MAE, RMSE and a custom delayed loss) combined for more than 15% MAE improvement over the best single model. Even the worst TFT, the one trained with the delayed loss, contributed positively.

TFT's interpretability closes the talk. The most influential time point was 168 hours back, a seven-day lag that suggests weekly seasonality, and the most important feature was the target, NO2, itself.

## Who should watch

Anyone forecasting with ARIMA and wondering what the neural methods add, and ML engineers who want a disciplined workflow: gap analysis, baselines, rolling evaluation, then ensembles. Note the speakers work on forecasting commercially, so the method picks reflect their own stack.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: Ten ways ML projects fail, and domain knowledge fixes the worst
Description: Karl Weinmeister (Google) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on ten common ML project failures, from missing baselines to drift, and the tools that help
Body:
Most ML projects stall for reasons that have nothing to do with the algorithm. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, Karl Weinmeister, Engineering Manager for Cloud, AI and ML at Google, walks through ten things that go wrong with ML projects, grouped into building a model, model accuracy, transparency and fairness, and MLOps, each paired with a practice and a Google Cloud tool.

It is a checklist talk with a Google Cloud slant: every problem gets a product, mostly from Vertex AI. The practices underneath travel well beyond it.

## Building a model: goals, prototypes, training time

**1. No goal, no baseline.** Your model has to serve a business goal, and you need to know how the current approach performs, whether manual, rule-based or an older model, to know whether you have improved anything. He recommends a 30-minute DeepMind video on product management for AI and draws three lessons: stay focused on the goal but flexible on tactics, set milestones you can adapt because research is hard to schedule, and involve users at every stage. He adds a quick fit test: predictive analytics on historical data, unstructured data such as images and text, automation of manual steps, and personalisation are good ML territory.

**2. Skipping the prototype.** Start simple. A quick prototype exposes data access problems, unknown integration points and accuracy ceilings early. BigQuery ML trains models from SQL in the data warehouse, and AutoML gives a performance baseline plus feature importances that hint where feature engineering could pay off.

**3. Training takes days.** When every experiment means waiting until tomorrow, iteration dies. Serverless training on Vertex AI spreads jobs over GPUs and runs hyperparameter tuning, and Cloud TPUs are there for heavier workloads.

## Accuracy: imbalance and the plateau

**4. Imbalanced data.** In fraud detection a model that calls everything benign scores well and is worthless. The TensorFlow tutorial on imbalanced data covers class weighting, oversampling, undersampling and synthetic data with packages such as SMOTE. Weinmeister says class weighting worked best for him. In AutoML, switching the optimisation objective to area under the precision-recall curve helps the minority class, and the confusion matrix shows which class is losing.

**5. Accuracy stops improving.** This is the one that kills projects, and his answer is the most useful part of the talk. Modelling flight delays, he joined BigQuery public weather data to airports by latitude and longitude. It helped, but not much: a study he cites puts extreme weather at about 6% of the root causes of delays, while the biggest cause is the aircraft arriving late. Better data engineering would follow the chain of inbound flights instead. "So that's my number one tip is look at improving domain expertise for the problem you're trying to solve," Karl Weinmeister said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021. More and more varied data, feature engineering, removing features that overfit, other architectures, tuning and ensembling come after that, with AutoML as a gut check of what the data allows.

## Transparency and fairness

**6. The model does not serve all users well.** Use a responsible AI framework and ask the questions early: who is the user, what are the risks, how was the training data collected, sampled and labelled. The What-If Tool slices data and lets you change inputs to see how predictions move, so it is almost like a debugging tool for your model. TensorFlow Model Analysis reports metrics per slice; in the Chicago taxi tips example, trips at 5 and 6 a.m. are rare, which shows up as uneven accuracy by hour.

**7. The model ships with no documentation.** Software ships with docs, models usually do not. Explainable AI shows which features drive predictions, and model cards, with a Model Card Toolkit that can plug into a TensorFlow Extended pipeline, record data collection, performance curves and architecture.

## MLOps: bad models, drift and traffic spikes

**8. A bad model reaches production.** Vertex Pipelines codifies the build steps and adds CI/CD-style guardrails and tests before deployment.

**9. Accuracy drifts downward.** Unlike a unit test, ML degrades gradually as the world shifts. Continuous evaluation samples predictions against ground truth, and continuous training retrains on a schedule or when enough data changes, with the trick being neither too many models nor stale ones. Vertex Model Monitoring watches for drift and training-serving skew.

**10. Inference load is spiky.** Vertex Prediction endpoints autoscale between a minimum and maximum node count, with logging and GPU options.

## Who should watch

Team leads and engineers starting their first production ML project, especially on Google Cloud. Seasoned MLOps people will recognise most of the list, but the flight delay story is worth the time.

Title: On drone footage, CNN detectors still beat the transformer
Description: Eduardo Dixo (Continental) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet and DETR detecting cars in VisDrone aerial images
Body:
Cars seen from a drone are small, and small objects are where the Detection Transformer struggles. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, Eduardo Dixo, Senior Data Scientist at Continental, fine-tunes two CNN detectors and DETR on the VisDrone aerial dataset and reports a clear result: the off-the-shelf CNNs make strong baselines, while DETR does well on large cars and poorly on small and medium ones.

It is a well-structured talk that doubles as a refresher on how these architectures work, with the configuration details you need to reproduce the experiment.

## Why are drone images a hard detection problem?

Object detection means locating every object with a bounding box and classifying it, with any number of objects at different poses and scales, which makes it harder than image classification. VisDrone adds its own trouble: nearly 6,000 training images and 500 validation images captured in varied weather and lighting, different scene densities, objects at very different scales depending on altitude, and motion artifacts from moving cars or the drone itself. Boxes are annotated for occlusion and truncation. Dixo keeps one of the ten categories, cars, with applications such as road safety, traffic monitoring and finding free parking spots.

## Two stages or one?

The first model is Faster R-CNN, a two-stage detector. A backbone such as ResNet extracts high-level feature maps. A region proposal network slides over them, generating k anchor boxes per position with an objectness score and box coordinates. Region-of-interest pooling then cuts fixed-size features for each proposal and a classifier head predicts class and refined box. Proposals cut the candidate set, which removes many false positives.

Dixo uses Detectron2, the PyTorch-based detection library, with a ResNet-50 backbone and a Feature Pyramid Network, because cars appear both tiny and large and FPN builds semantic feature maps at every scale. The walkthrough covers registering a COCO-format dataset, inheriting a model config, loading pretrained weights from the Detectron2 model zoo, setting learning rate, iterations, batch size and decay steps, one class, and launching the default trainer.

The second is RetinaNet, a one-stage detector that samples a dense grid of candidate locations. One-stage detectors used to trail two-stage ones in accuracy, and RetinaNet's authors blamed class imbalance: most candidates are easy background that floods the loss. Their focal loss down-weights well-classified examples. In Detectron2 the change is mostly config.

Both reached good COCO average precision and were closely matched; RetinaNet was better on larger objects and worse on smaller ones. Data augmentation with flips and random brightness, saturation and contrast, which Detectron2 supports and libraries such as Albumentations and Kornia extend, did not improve either model, even with longer training.

## How does DETR see an image?

Dixo then builds up to transformers: encoder and decoder, multi-head self-attention, residual connections and layer norm, positional encodings because attention ignores order, and the cost that the attention matrix is quadratic in sequence length. Self-attention gives every position a global receptive field in one layer, where CNNs need deep stacks to get there.

DETR runs a CNN backbone, flattens the feature map's height and width into a sequence for the encoder, and feeds the decoder a set of learned object queries, which must outnumber the most objects any image contains. Predictions come out in parallel as a set, matched to ground truth with a bipartite, Hungarian-algorithm loss.

He uses the Hugging Face implementation, following Niels Rogge's example notebooks, with a dilated ResNet-50 backbone to raise resolution for small objects. On a V100 he caps image size at 1,100 pixels and drops batch size from four to two to avoid running out of memory.

## What the numbers say

DETR's average precision was very poor next to the CNNs: decent on large cars, very low on small and medium ones. Inference shows duplicate boxes that non-maximum suppression could remove, plus missed detections. "To conclude, we see that CNNs make for very powerful baselines," Eduardo Dixo said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021.

His next steps: a bigger backbone such as ResNet-101, combining other public drone datasets such as UAVDT, using temporal cues from video to cut false positives, and trying newer architectures like the Swin Transformer and Focal Transformer. He expects something FPN-like to do for transformers what it did for CNNs on multi-scale detection, and sees transformers as a framework that may unify vision and language work.

## Who should watch

Computer vision engineers choosing a detector for aerial or small-object data, and anyone who wants Faster R-CNN, focal loss and DETR explained in one sitting. It is a 2021 snapshot, so treat the DETR verdict as the baseline later small-object work was measured against.

Title: Monitor what your ML pipeline ships, not just what it burns
Description: Hila Fox (Augury) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on monitoring the detection lifecycle of an AI engine with Grafana alerts and deploy tags
Body:
CPU graphs will not tell you that a detector quietly stopped finding broken pumps. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, Hila Fox, Squad Leader and backend developer at Augury, explains how her squad monitors the output of the company's AI pipelines as a product: count what the models emit, track each detection through its lifecycle, and alert when the statistical shape of that flow changes.

It is a practitioner talk from a team that owns the layer between the AI engine and the customer-facing apps, and it lands on a pattern any ML team with downstream consumers can copy.

## What does the AI engine do?

Augury sells machine health for manufacturing: its own IoT sensors (vibration, temperature and magnetic field) on motors and pumps, a node that collects their data over Bluetooth and sends it to the cloud, an AI engine that diagnoses it, and a line of human vibration analysts on top. The customers are large manufacturers, including Pfizer and Heineken, which as Fox puts it keep the beer and the toilet paper coming.

The numbers explain why monitoring matters. Augury has more than 50 million hours of machine monitoring and over 80,000 machines diagnosed. Each machine produces about 1.3 million points per hour, reduced to roughly 1,000 features per hour by a feature extraction model. Dozens of algorithms sit on top: semi-supervised anomaly detectors that learn a baseline per machine and aim for high recall, and fault detectors matching the signatures of specific faults such as bearing wear. Three algorithm squads, three product squads and a data engineering team all touch the flow.

## Why is the detection management layer the risky bit?

Every hour, every detector outputs detections with a confidence. They all land in the detection management layer, which decides what reaches customers and analysts. "So we can even call this maybe a single point of failure," Hila Fox said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021. It consumes from many producers, publishes to many consumers, and contains logic of its own.

That logic filters hard: 99.87% of detections never get past it, which is the point, since customers should only see what they need to act on. It also means a silent failure upstream looks exactly like a quiet week.

Fox splits risk into expected changes, such as new features, which you can de-risk with staging, dry runs in production and feature switches, and unexpected ones. Those include bad deployments where a detector simply stops emitting, interface changes between squads, and configuration changes. Her real example: a DevOps security change stopped two detectors from generating detections. The new monitoring caught it, the change was reverted, and it was reapplied properly.

## Black box, white box, or both?

Citing the Google SRE book's split between white-box monitoring (internal metrics like CPU and memory) and black-box monitoring (externally visible behaviour), Fox argues the detection management layer is both. It is a consumer of the AI engine, which makes it look like black-box monitoring, and it applies product logic that decides what users see, which makes it look like white-box monitoring.

So the team monitors that internal product process. They found patterns they could commit to statistically across the machine pool, not per machine: how many detections arrive per detector, how many are filtered by low confidence, how many are filtered by machine state (a machine already alerted on does not need a second alert), and how many are propagated. Those lifecycle states became metrics in Graphite, visualised in Grafana.

## Getting proactive with alerts

The first alerts covered one detector, bearing wear, with four rules: not too many and not too few detections arriving, a limit on filtered detections, and bounds on propagated ones. They went to a Slack channel called detections monitoring. Absolute thresholds made it noisy at first, and the team was considering a switch to percentage change. Once it calmed down, Fox ran a workshop with the algorithm team and they added dashboards and alerts for every detector.

The trick worth stealing is Grafana annotations. Every service posts a deployment tag on release with the Git hash, the person who deployed and the service name, drawn on the graphs. When detections drop off a cliff, the culprit is a vertical line away, and the fix starts with a direct message instead of an investigation.

Her conclusions: keep customers at the centre, internal teams included, aim for fast response rather than a zero-bug product, and make it easy for teams to talk to each other. The org grew from eight people on the diagnosis flow to seven squads, which is when this stops being optional.

## Who should watch

Teams whose models feed other teams or customers, and SREs asked to put an ML system on call. Expect architecture and practice, not code.

Title: Multilingual NLP in Python means stitching libraries together
Description: Gajendra Deshpande (KLS Gogte Institute of Technology) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on multilingual NLP pipelines and the Python libraries that power them
Body:
No single Python library does multilingual NLP end to end, so you build a pipeline out of several and hard-code the gaps. That is the honest conclusion of Gajendra Deshpande, Assistant Professor at KLS Gogte Institute of Technology, at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, after a tour of the steps and packages for processing text that arrives in many languages and many formats.

It is a survey talk with short code snippets, useful as a map of the tools rather than a deep treatment of any one of them.

## Why is more than one language so much harder?

Deshpande opens with a quick glossary of NLP building blocks: tokenization, word embeddings, sentence similarity on a zero-to-one scale, normalization, lemmatization versus stemming (running becomes run; stemming just chops characters and is less accurate), language detection, dependency parsing, named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging. He separates transliteration, writing Korean in English script, from translation, turning Korean text into English.

Then the problems that multiply with each language. The same sentence can mean different things across languages, and context matters even within one. Grammars, word order and reading direction differ, left to right or right to left. People who speak several languages mix them, and code-mixed text trips up libraries that cannot identify the borrowed words. Translation is not word for word, so semantics have to survive the trip. And libraries cover some languages well and others barely.

## A pipeline for multi-source, multilingual text

His worked scenario is generating a summary from sources in mixed formats and languages:

1. Collect the information source, which may be text, audio, video or images.
2. Extract the text.
3. Identify the language, hard-coding features where detection falls short.
4. Translate everything into one source language. He calls this the very important step, since processing needs a single language.
5. Process the text: tokenize, lemmatize, count word and sentence frequencies, run n-gram analysis, pick the top n sentences.
6. Translate the summary into the target language.

## Which libraries cover which step?

- **Googletrans 3.0.0** for detection and translation through the Google Translate Ajax API. It auto-detects the source, translates Korean to Japanese or Latin to English, and can rotate between service URLs. The warning matters: it is unofficial and unstable, with a 15k character limit per text, so for real requirements he points to Google's official Translate API.
- **SpeechRecognition** for audio, wrapping engines that work offline (CMU Sphinx, Snowboy hotword detection) and online APIs from Google, Microsoft, IBM and others.
- **pytesseract** for text in images, a wrapper for Google's Tesseract OCR that reads anything Pillow and Leptonica can open. Three lines get you a string.
- **Beautiful Soup 4** for web pages. It gives you the browser-rendered HTML, so the real work is stripping unwanted code and navigating to the right element.
- **Stanza** from Stanford, formerly Stanford NLP, a full neural pipeline with pretrained models for 66 human languages.
- **iNLTK** by Gaurav Arora, for Indic languages, native and code-mixed, such as Hinglish.
- **Indic NLP Library** by Anoop Kunchukuttan, covering script conversion, transliteration and translation across Indo-Aryan and Dravidian languages. India has around 22 official languages.
- **Polyglot** by Rami Al-Rfou, with tokenization for 165 languages, language detection for 196, sentiment analysis for 136 and named entity recognition for 40.

## The feature gaps are the real finding

The most concrete moment is a side-by-side in Stanza. Deshpande runs the tortoise-and-hare story in English and gets part-of-speech tags, lemmas, named entities and dependencies. He runs the same story in Hindi: tagging and lemmas work, named entity recognition is not supported. Polyglot shows the same pattern, with feature coverage dropping off sharply from tokenization to tagging.

"So there are various libraries offering different features, but not a single library offers all features," Gajendra Deshpande said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021. He reads that as an invitation as much as a limitation: the missing features are where contributors are needed, and Hindi NER in Stanza is one he names directly.

## Who should watch

Engineers starting a project that must handle Indian languages or code-mixed text, and anyone who needs a quick inventory of free Python tools for getting text out of audio, images and HTML. If you already run transformer-based multilingual models in production, this is background, not news.

Title: CNNs do your feature engineering, if you feed them enough images
Description: Milecia McGregor (Iterative) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on how convolutions and max pooling work, with a PyTorch MNIST model tracked in DVC
Body:
A convolutional neural network finds its own features, which is why it beats a hand-tuned pipeline on images, and why it needs a lot more data to do it. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, Milecia McGregor, Developer Advocate at Iterative working on DVC, gives a compact introduction to CNNs and then builds one in PyTorch for MNIST, running the training as a DVC experiment.

It is a first talk on CNNs, not an advanced one, and it says so in its structure: neural network basics, what convolutions and max pooling do, use cases, code, takeaways. McGregor's background is mechanical and aerospace engineering, then ML work on an autonomous car that interacted with pedestrians, and CNNs are her side-project hobby.

## What does a convolution actually do?

A filter, a small matrix such as three by three, slides across the image in steps called strides. At each position it takes the dot product with the filter-sized patch under it. One row done, it drops down and repeats until the whole image is scanned. The result, the convolved feature, is a smaller representation of the image that keeps what matters: edges, large shapes, the big features that define the picture.

The point, in her framing, is context. Flatten an image to one dimension for a regular neural network and you throw away the spatial relationships. Keep two dimensions, convolve, and the network squeezes the image down to the features that matter while doing much of the preprocessing for you.

Max pooling is the second ingredient. It returns the largest value in each kernel-sized patch, which cuts the compute needed for the next layers and acts as a noise suppressant: the maximum stands for the boldest feature in that region.

## 1D, 2D or 3D?

McGregor sorts CNNs by dimension. 1D networks suit time series data, 2D networks are the standard for image labelling and classification, and 3D networks process volumes such as CT scans and MRIs, where the filter becomes a cube scanning chunks of a cube, used for things like tumour detection.

Her use cases are the classic ones: handwriting recognition, autonomous cars, parts identification on a camera line, reading digits on cheques deposited at an ATM or in a mobile app, and post offices sorting handwritten and printed addresses.

The catch she is careful to state: CNNs save you the feature engineering, but on small datasets a regular neural network can do better. Her rule of thumb is that under roughly 10,000 images you may not get the best accuracy from a CNN.

## The code is mostly knowing your data

The live demo is a small PyTorch module. One input channel, because MNIST is greyscale (RGB would need three), eight output channels, a kernel size of three and padding so the edges of each digit are not lost. Then a max pool layer, a second convolution going from eight channels to 16, linear layers, and a forward pass with ReLU activations.

The useful lesson comes from breaking it. McGregor changes the output channels from eight to nine, the kernel size, then 16 to ten, and each run fails on mismatched shapes, because the input of each convolutional layer has to match the output of the previous one. "So you see, you really have to know the data you're working with to get the right values," she says, before settling for a learning rate change that trains to 83% accuracy.

## Why run it through DVC?

Because that flailing is the job. "Pretty much all of model making and machine learning is just experimenting with different values," Milecia McGregor said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021. DVC detects the code or hyperparameter change, reruns the training stage, and keeps a table of every experiment, so when a model gets good you can see exactly which change made it good.

Her closing advice is pragmatic: compare a few algorithms before you commit to a CNN, use existing libraries such as PyTorch or TensorFlow instead of writing the maths yourself, and break problems into reproducible steps. "You don't have to write everything from scratch to prove that you're just this great ML engineer," she adds, which is permission many of us needed in 2021 and still do.

## Who should watch

Developers who use image models without knowing what a kernel or a stride is, and anyone who wants a gentle look at experiment tracking with DVC. Practitioners who already tune CNNs for a living can skip it.

- [Eduardo Dixo on object detection with CNNs and transformers on drone footage](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2021_Eduardo_Dixo_Object_Detection_Transformers_CNNs_Drone_Case_Study), the next step up, also at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021.

Title: Stop shipping models, start shipping pipelines with SageMaker
Description: Antje Barth (Amazon Web Services) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021 on replacing hand-built models with SageMaker Pipelines and approval gates
Body:
The unit of work in machine learning should be the pipeline, not the model. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2021, Antje Barth, Senior Developer Advocate for AI and ML at Amazon Web Services and co-author of the O'Reilly book Data Science on AWS, makes that case and then builds it live: a BERT review classifier trained, evaluated, gated, registered and pushed through staging to production with Amazon SageMaker Pipelines and SageMaker Projects.

It is a vendor talk on AWS tooling, and a well-paced one. The first ten minutes are tool-agnostic MLOps thinking that applies whatever you run.

## Why do models take months to reach production?

Barth starts with the people, not the tooling. "So while most of the time we tend to focus on the technology, people and process are equally, if not more important," Antje Barth said at Conf42 Machine Learning 2021.

Her picture of the status quo is a relay race with too many baton passes: a data engineer hands a raw dataset to a data scientist, who iterates on features and experiments until a model scores well, then throws it over to an ML or DevOps engineer for deployment. To that engineer the model is opaque, so questions bounce back. A software engineer then changes the application that calls the model, and someone else has to operate and monitor it. Each handoff costs time, and teams that rarely talk produce rework.

She also flags the parts of the ML lifecycle that do not look like software delivery: longer experimentation cycles, data processing code alongside training code, and the fact that the model is usually a small part of the system that consumes it. Enterprise process belongs in the pipeline too, so a new model might automatically open a change ticket or wait at a manual approval step.

## Phase one: orchestrate the steps you already do

The first demo turns the manual workflow into a DAG. The use case: classify product review text into a one-to-five star rating by fine-tuning a pretrained BERT model from Hugging Face on a subset of a public reviews dataset, three product categories only so training stays short.

The steps, each a SageMaker job wrapped as a pipeline step:

- **Feature engineering** as a SageMaker Processing job using a prebuilt scikit-learn container. It turns raw text into BERT embeddings and splits the data 90% training, 5% validation, 5% test. Instance count is a parameter, so scaling the job out is a matter of setting one to five or ten.
- **Training** with the built-in TensorFlow estimator, one epoch for the demo, with regex patterns that pull validation loss and accuracy out of the logs. Step caching skips steps whose inputs have not changed when the pipeline reruns.
- **Evaluation** as another processing job that writes an evaluation JSON report.
- **A condition step** that checks validation accuracy against a threshold. Pass, and the model is registered in the model registry and a deployable model object is created. Fail, and the pipeline ends, or messages the data scientist if you wire it up.

The threshold is honest demo material: "In this case, I'm using 20% as my minimum accuracy to check against," Barth said, with the caveat that real use cases should set the bar much higher. Registered models land as pending manual approval, so a human looks at the metrics before anything ships. SageMaker also tracks lineage: every artifact each step consumed and produced, from the raw data and Docker image to the features and model artifact.

## Phase two: let commits and drift trigger the pipeline

The second phase adds automated quality gates on model performance and bias, deployment strategies such as A/B tests or bandits, integration tests with pass/fail gates, and model monitoring whose drift alerts can kick off a retraining pipeline. Code changes become the other trigger.

The second demo shows that with SageMaker Projects. A built-in template creates two AWS CodeCommit repositories, one for model build and training and one for deployment, plus the CodePipeline and CodeBuild wiring. Barth copies the same pipeline code from the first demo into the build repo, pushes, and the training pipeline runs on its own. The deploy pipeline sits in a failed state until a model is approved, which is the correct behaviour.

Deployment is two-stage. Approving the model package through the API sends it to a staging endpoint, where a TensorFlow predictor returns five stars for the sample review "this is great". A second approval, the kind an integration or DevOps team would own after running its tests, promotes it to production.

## Who should watch

Teams on AWS who still train in notebooks and deploy by hand get the most out of it, as do platform engineers designing the approval flow between data science and operations. If you are not on AWS, the first section and the staging-then-production gate design still transfer.

Title: Thirty clusters per workshop is how you end up building a cloud
Description: Mofizur Rahman (IBM) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on how workshop cluster automation grew from Bash into a Go cloud interface on top of IBM Cloud
Body:
Nobody sets out to build a cloud on top of their own cloud. At Conf42 Golang 2021, Mofizur Rahman, Developer Advocate at IBM, told [how his team did it anyway](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Mofizur_Rahman_cloud_cloud_native): a two-person side job of creating Kubernetes clusters for workshops turned into a Go backend and a React UI that mimics IBM Cloud, with bulk creation, round-robin placement across data centres and Ansible post-provisioning. Then, refreshingly, he spends the second half arguing you probably shouldn't do the same.

His working definition: a cloud is someone else's computer, on demand, with some way for users to reach it.

## What problem forced it?

The numbers, from his slides: an average of 10 to 20 workshops a month, two to four a week, each needing about 30 Kubernetes or OpenShift clusters (the most they had done was around 150). Subnets, volumes per data centre and clusters per account all have limits, and there were no workshop metrics. The team owning all this was two people, for whom it wasn't the main job.

## Why weren't the obvious fixes enough?

He walks through three generations.

**The worst solution:** click each cluster into existence in the console and grant every attendee access by hand. He estimates four hours per workshop for the workshop lead and account owner, two full working days in a four-workshop week. Clusters created on Friday for a Monday workshop burn money all weekend, and anything needing Istio or Knative on top was out.

**The passable solution:** the CLI in a Bash script, a config file per workshop request (reused to delete the resources afterwards), a GitHub repo to track requests, and a small web app where attendees enter their email and get added to the account with the right permissions. Since it's a for loop, five clusters or 500 cost the same effort. Mofizur Rahman said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "So not always like a full blown software solution is the best answer, but this is good enough for most cases."

The catch: someone's laptop has to run it, Bash error handling is thin, and it's still manual.

**The current solution:** a React UI that looks like IBM Cloud, a Go API that wraps the IBM Cloud APIs, and AWX, the open source upstream of Ansible Tower, running jobs and post-provisioning playbooks. Things the real console didn't offer: delete many resources at once, ask for N clusters, spread them round-robin across, say, all North American data centres to dodge subnet and volume limits, and tick post-provisioning tasks such as Knative, OpenShift versions, Cloud Paks or the Cloud Native Toolkit. Anyone can now be taught to spin up resources in about five minutes, and because it's their own code they can add retries and rate limits.

## What does the Go side look like?

A monorepo. The main app is a REST API built with Echo, serving the React front end on port 9000. Authentication is borrowed from IBM Cloud itself (log in with your IBM ID), which neatly removes the hardest part of building a cloud, user management. Most endpoints are thin wrappers over the IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service API, built by reading its Swagger docs, and a second package does the same for AWX: list workflow job templates and launch them. New post-provisioning steps are just new Ansible playbooks. The project is open source.

## What was still missing?

Scheduling, metrics and self-service. The UI still needs a human, so weekends and time zones still cost money; he reckons creating clusters three hours before a workshop would roughly halve its cost. The roadmap: GitHub workshop requests turned into cluster requests by a cloud function, with manual approval; scheduled creation and deletion; opening it to other teams; and completion metrics to right-size requests (asked for 50 clusters, used 30, get 35 next time). The single app was being split into provisioner, scheduler, reclaimer and notifier services.

## Should you build your own cloud interface?

His checklist: your cloud has no easy way to do what you need, you keep writing custom code against it, other teams do the same, and you struggle to keep resources in check. Even then, infrastructure as code comes first (Terraform, Pulumi, Ansible, Chef, Puppet, plus CI/CD from GitHub Actions to Tekton), and a custom solution belongs at the bottom of the list. Mofizur Rahman said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "So all code is technical debt."

The reasons to do it anyway are real: six teams maintaining six scripts is a bigger dependency than one tool, most teams shouldn't need to understand raw cloud resources, and a wrapper can answer questions the console can't, such as who last used a resource and whether its size was approved. His considerations: do only what is necessary, expect cloud APIs to change under you, solve your problem and your neighbours', not the general cloud problem, and don't start by building the cloud.

## Who should watch

Developer relations and platform teams who provision environments for other people, and anyone whose Bash script has quietly become critical infrastructure.

Title: A few lines of Go, 829 lines of CloudFormation, thanks to the AWS CDK
Description: Vincent Lesierse (AWS) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on defining AWS infrastructure in Go with the CDK, from construct levels to a Lambda URL shortener
Body:
If your infrastructure is a pile of YAML templates that only one person dares to edit, the AWS CDK offers to turn it into Go you can autocomplete. At Conf42 Golang 2021, Vincent Lesierse, Solutions Architect at AWS, explained [what the Cloud Development Kit is and how it works with Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Vincent_Lesierse_building_applications_cloud_AWS_CDK), which was in preview at the time, and then deployed a URL shortener written in Go as a Lambda function, behind API Gateway, backed by DynamoDB, all defined in one Go file.

## How did we get from wikis to classes?

He sketches the history of infrastructure in five stages. Manual: wikis, playbooks and someone clicking through the console. Scripted: Bash, fine until it grew and the advice became don't touch it. Declarative: CloudFormation and Terraform, with state management, rollbacks and drift detection, whose success produced templates too big to maintain. Generators: Troposphere and GoFormation, code that emits the JSON or YAML. And abstractions: the AWS CDK and Pulumi, frameworks for building your own reusable infrastructure components.

The CDK's pitch is your language (Python, TypeScript, Java, C#, JavaScript and Go), your IDE with autocomplete, inline docs, testing, linting and a debugger, and sane defaults so you can start safely without reading every page of documentation.

## What are L1, L2 and L3 constructs?

The CDK has three parts: the core framework (an app holding stacks, each mapped one to one to a CloudFormation stack, ideally split by lifecycle, network apart from cluster apart from application), the AWS Construct Library, and the CLI. Constructs come in three levels:

- **L1**: generated straight from the CloudFormation resource specification, prefixed Cfn (`CfnBucket`, `CfnInstance`). Full control, and you need to know every property.
- **L2**: higher-level constructs scoped to one service. A single `NewVpc` line gives you a VPC across two availability zones with 65,536 IPs split equally between four subnets, an internet gateway and route tables, per AWS security best practices. Vincent Lesierse said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "Anyone who actually build a VPC for scratch and cloudformation, I think you can relate."
- **L3**: opinionated compositions across services. His example takes two parameters, an ECS cluster and a Docker Hub image name, and produces a VPC, application load balancer, security groups, Fargate service, task definition, IAM roles and policies and log groups, which the slides put at an 829-line CloudFormation template, 37 resources by his count.

L3 is also where your platform team publishes its own abstractions, publicly or inside the organisation.

## What does the Go workflow look like?

Install the CLI with npm, then `cdk init app --language=go`, which scaffolds a `go.mod`, `cdk.json`, a git repo and a sample stack with an SNS topic. Build with `go build`, `cdk synth` to produce CloudFormation templates and assets (a cloud assembly), `cdk diff` to see what will be created, updated or deleted, and `cdk deploy` to push it.

The URL shortener stack replaces the sample topic with:

- A DynamoDB table with a string partition key named slug. Strings go through `jsii.String` because the generated Go bindings take pointers, the one Go-specific wrinkle he points out.
- A `GoFunction` from the Lambda Go construct package, with its entry pointing at the plain Go application in the project and the table name injected as an environment variable, so a renamed table follows automatically.
- `table.GrantReadWriteData(handler)`, which creates the IAM role and least-privilege policy for you.
- A Lambda proxy integration on an API Gateway v2 HTTP API, using payload format version 1.0 because the Lambda Go library had not yet moved to v2.
- A `CfnOutput` with the generated API URL.

`cdk deploy` stops to ask before applying IAM changes, then creates the change set. A curl POST returns a slug, and visiting it returns a 301 redirect to the original URL.

## Where to go next?

He points at AWS Solutions Constructs, open source architecture patterns built on L3 constructs; the public CDK roadmap; awesome-cdk and CDK Patterns for community constructs; the CDK Workshop and the examples repo; and cdk8s, which applies the same idea to Kubernetes manifests.

## Who should watch

Go developers on AWS who maintain CloudFormation or Terraform by hand and want to see how much of it the CDK writes for them, and platform teams thinking about publishing their own L3 constructs. If you are already on the TypeScript CDK, the Go-specific parts are pointers and the GoFunction bundling.

Title: WebRTC is a networking toolkit, not just video calls, and Go has Pion
Description: Sean Dubois (Apple) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on what WebRTC solves (NAT traversal, congestion control, head-of-line blocking) and building with Pion in Go
Body:
Most engineers file WebRTC under browser video calls and never look again. At Conf42 Golang 2021, Sean Dubois, a developer who works on the Pion project, made the case that it is really a general-purpose, always-encrypted peer-to-peer transport, and that [Pion turns it into a plain Go API](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Sean_Dubois_WebRTC_secret_power) you can use for robots, cloud gaming, file transfer and censorship circumvention.

Pion is an open source collective for real-time communication in Go, driven by individuals rather than a single company. His abstract put its size at the time at 7k GitHub stars. The talk is a tour: who builds with it, what WebRTC actually solves, a few lines of API, and a gallery of projects.

## What does WebRTC give you?

An end-to-end secure connection between two peers, with no optional mode: if you use WebRTC, the connection is encrypted. Over it you can send any number of audio and video tracks, and binary data that can be lossy and unordered if you want it to be. Sean Dubois said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "If you think if you're building a real time system like a video game, you don't care these, the player was 2 seconds ago."

He also pitches it as a cross-language channel: a Go process and a Python, TypeScript or Java one can exchange data directly, with no pub/sub broker or HTTP layer in between.

## Which problems does it solve that you didn't know were solvable?

- **NAT traversal.** Every outbound packet opens a temporary hole in your NAT so the server can reply. A STUN server tells you your public IP and that hole, which you can share with another peer, so two machines with no public IP on different networks can connect. He calls it an automatic port forward.
- **Staying connected on the move.** ICE restart measures connection quality and switches routes on the fly, Wi-Fi to cellular, and unlike transport-level tricks, your application knows it happened and can, say, drop video quality on a metered link.
- **Congestion control.** Measuring bandwidth once is meaningless: his example measures 50 megabits a second, then other users at different hops eat into it. Receiver feedback (packets received, packets lost, delay) lets the sender keep adjusting bitrate.
- **Head-of-line blocking.** With TCP, message one must arrive before message two. In WebRTC you choose per message: telemetry can be sent with max retransmits of zero so new data flows unblocked, while important data is resent until acknowledged.
- **Existing protocols.** WebRTC bundles RTP, RTCP and SRTP, so it plugs into existing VoIP systems and can even bring in a plain old telephone call.

## How much Go does a connection take?

Peers first exchange metadata (where they are, which codecs they support), known as signaling. The caller creates a peer connection and an offer, sends it, and sets the remote description from the answer; he counts six lines of code per side. After that, create data channels (he recalls a limit of about 65,000), each with its own lifetime and priority settings, send hello world when one opens, and print messages in the other side's handler. The same Go code compiles to WebAssembly and runs in the browser.

Video is a track you write media into. His demo reads an IVF file, a container of raw media frames, frame by frame onto the connection, and WebRTC handles bandwidth estimation and loss.

## What are people building with it?

The list is the fun part:

- Formant's agent on a Boston Dynamics Spot, driven from a browser with audio and video streamed back.
- Headroom's conferencing, with raised-hand detection, speech to text and eye-contact measurement.
- Piepackr, multiplayer NES and Game Boy games in the browser, the couch-co-op experience over the network.
- Neko, a shared remote browser for watching a movie or browsing with a friend; CloudMorph, open source cloud gaming running Diablo II and StarCraft.
- Snowflake, Tor's censorship-circumvention transport, which is hard to block because it looks like all the other conferencing traffic.
- Webwormhole for file transfer, a terminal shared to a browser without a central server, ASCII video calls in a terminal, security cameras that get mandatory encryption and NAT traversal, and a VR theatre that staged Shakespeare.

His wish list includes a project to connect two hosts or containers directly, multi-cloud, with no central relay.

## Who should watch

Go developers building anything real-time or peer-to-peer, and anyone who has stood up a relay server only because two machines couldn't reach each other. You won't leave able to implement congestion control, but you will know it exists and where to start: the Pion community's book, WebRTC for the Curious, and the awesome-pion list on GitHub.
