Title: mTLS gRPC behind NGINX Ingress on KinD hinges on one controller flag
Description: Mahendra Bagul (InfraCloud Technologies) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on running an mTLS Go gRPC server behind the NGINX Ingress Controller on a local KinD cluster
Body:
Getting mutual TLS working between a gRPC client and a server inside Kubernetes is mostly a question of who terminates TLS, and the answer you want is nobody in the middle. At Conf42 Golang 2021, Mahendra Bagul, an engineer at InfraCloud Technologies, [built the whole setup on a laptop](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Mahendra_Bagul_KinD_nGinx_Ingress_Controller_Secured_gRPC_server): a three-node KinD cluster, the NGINX Ingress Controller in SSL passthrough mode, a Go gRPC server holding its own certificates, and a Node.js client presenting client certificates from outside the cluster.

The talk is a demo with a short theory primer up front. If you already know Kubernetes basics, the value is in the specific annotations, flags and port mappings, which are exactly the things that cost an afternoon when you get one wrong.

## What is the target architecture?

The primer covers the Kubernetes control plane and worker nodes, NodePort services (the crude way to expose an app, not one he recommends for production) and Ingress as a URL map deciding which service a request reaches, with an ingress controller such as NGINX doing the work. KinD, Kubernetes in Docker, runs every node as a Docker container; originally built for testing Kubernetes itself, it is now common for local development and CI.

The final deployment: a namespace for the demo holding the Go gRPC server deployment, a service in front of it, an Ingress pointing at that service, two ConfigMaps (server address and port, plus a small JSON employee database) and a Secret with the server certificates mounted into the pod. The client runs locally and calls the server through the Ingress host over port 443.

His mTLS explanation is the one to show a junior: client and server each hold a certificate signed by a common certificate authority. The server presents its certificate and the client validates it against the CA; then the client presents its own and the server validates that. Only when both checks pass does the client reach the protected resource.

## Which settings make passthrough work?

Since the client certificate has to reach the Go process, the Ingress must not offload TLS. The pieces that make that happen:

- **KinD config**: one control-plane node and two workers, an `ingress-ready` node label so the NGINX controller lands where it can be reached, and extra port mappings so 443 on the laptop reaches the cluster.
- **NGINX install**: apply the controller manifest, then `kubectl wait` on the ingress-nginx namespace for the controller pod to be ready.
- **The flag**: edit the controller deployment and add `--enable-ssl-passthrough` to its arguments. Mahendra Bagul said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "This needs to be added as an argument to the ingress NgINX controller, otherwise your SSl pass through mechanism will not work." He adds that it was a major blocker when he first did this for real work.
- **Ingress annotations**: GRPC as the backend protocol, passing the client certificate to the upstream, a reference to the secret holding the certificates, and a TLS host that matches an `/etc/hosts` entry on the laptop.

Certificates come from two shell scripts in the repo: one generates the root CA, server and client CAs, certificates and chain with OpenSSL; the other recreates the namespace and loads them as Kubernetes secrets.

## What do the Go server and Node client do?

The contract is a small `employee.proto` in proto3: a `GetDetails` RPC that takes an employee id and returns id, email, first name and last name. The Go server uses protoc-generated code, builds a certificate pool from the mounted files, assembles a `tls.Config` and starts the gRPC server with those credentials. Inside `GetDetails` it first validates the client certificate, including its common name, and only then looks the employee up from the ConfigMap data.

The Node.js client loads the same proto with the grpc-js library, creates SSL credentials from the CA chain, client key and client certificate, and dials the Ingress host on 443. Ask for employee 2 and the record comes back from a pod in the KinD cluster.

## Who should watch

Go developers who need mTLS between services and want a local, reproducible environment to prove it before touching a shared cluster, and platform engineers wiring gRPC through NGINX Ingress for the first time. If you run a service mesh that handles mTLS for you, this is the manual version of what it hides.

Title: Your architecture rules belong in CI, not on a Confluence page
Description: Francisco Daines (Walmart) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on Arch-Go, his tool that checks Go code against architecture rules written in YAML, in CI
Body:
Every team has architecture rules, and most of them live in a wiki nobody opens after the second sprint. At Conf42 Golang 2021, Francisco Daines, Senior Software Developer at Walmart in Chile, presented [Arch-Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Francisco_Daines_archgo_architecture_tooling_test_guidelines_automation), an open source testing tool he wrote that keeps those rules in a YAML file in the repo and fails the build when the code drifts from them.

He is upfront about the lineage: Arch-Go is strongly inspired by ArchUnit, the Java library for architecture tests. The talk is a tour of what the Go version checks and how to wire it in.

## Why can't code review catch this?

He lists four problems with architecture guidelines as most teams keep them:

- **Versioning.** If you believe in evolutionary architecture (he recommends the book by Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons and Patrick Kua), the rules change, and those changes need recording.
- **Outdated guidelines.** Francisco Daines said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "In a daily basis we work with the code base, not with the confluence system." A couple of months later the document describes a different codebase.
- **Quality degradation.** Code review and pair programming are good, but with many rules, someone forgets one in some pull request, and nobody notices the drift.
- **Metrics.** If you want to know whether guideline compliance correlates with lead time or other delivery metrics, you have to measure compliance first.

The rules he means are the ones you would otherwise write in prose: in a layered service, presentation packages may only call business logic; persistence calls nobody; a clean architecture codebase has its own version of the same constraints. Or, from his abstract, the classic unwritten rule: "Don't call repository components from components in the presentation packages".

## What can Arch-Go check?

You install it with `go get`, drop the YAML rules file in the project root and run `arch-go`. Every rule is evaluated, so the result lists all the gaps rather than stopping at the first, and the run ends as succeeded or rejected. There are five rule types:

- **Dependency rules**: which packages a package should only depend on or should not depend on, by pattern, plus an allow-list of external modules. His example permits the go-sql-driver MySQL package and forbids another MySQL client.
- **Content rules**: a package should only contain, or should not contain, functions, methods, interfaces or structs. Put a struct in an interfaces-only package and the check fails.
- **Function rules**: maximum parameters, maximum return values, maximum lines per function and maximum public functions per file, for teams that prefer passing a struct over a parameter list.
- **Naming rules**: structs implementing a given interface must match a pattern, so implementations of a `Processor` interface end in Processor. He notes this is a judgment call, since a struct implementing two interfaces is free to be named anything.
- **Cycle rules**: no import cycles. Because the Go compiler already refuses import cycles, he flags this one as under evaluation and possibly deprecated later.

## Why does it describe rules in plain English?

YAML lets you write the same document many ways, block style or inline, and both versions pass the schema. So `arch-go describe` prints the rules in human language, which is the version you can hand to a product owner or another team. A `--html` flag writes a report modelled on the PIT mutation-testing coverage report from the Java world, still a work in progress at the time.

## Where does it run?

The continuous part of the title is simply a pipeline step: after unit and integration tests, before deploy. Because it is one command, he shows it running in GitHub Actions, CircleCI and Bitbucket Pipelines, and in a Docker container. His backlog for the project included validating the rules file itself, JSON as well as YAML, more naming rules and a minimum version check for external dependencies.

## Who should watch

Tech leads on Go codebases with more than one team committing, and anyone who has left the same layering comment on a pull request more than twice. If your service is three packages and one developer, you probably don't need it yet.

Title: Give every domain its own state machine and let errors climb the tree
Description: Ilya Kaznacheev (MTS Cloud) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on running managed Kubernetes cluster creation as DDD aggregates with one state machine per domain
Body:
Creating a Kubernetes cluster for a customer is one long process made of dozens of small ones that fail independently. At Conf42 Golang 2021, Ilya Kaznacheev, Technical Lead of the managed Kubernetes service at MTS Cloud, showed [how his team rebuilt that process](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Ilya_Kaznacheev_ddd_fsm_state_machine) around a domain-driven design aggregate in which every entity (cluster, node group, node) has its own finite state machine, and events and errors move up and down the tree.

He promised a minimum of theory and kept the promise: one definition, then the architecture they actually ran, and the four problems they hit on the way.

## Why weren't steps and a pipeline enough?

The MVP created a cluster in three steps separated by Kafka messages, and a crash or restart killed the whole process with no way to resume. As a cloud provider they could not just call Terraform; they wanted low-level control for speed and resilience, which meant many granular operations.

Version two split creation into a pipeline of steps sequenced over Kafka, so a crashed instance's work could be picked up by another. It looked good in theory. In practice some steps were sets of parallel operations, others were chains that depended on several components, and the more complex the logic got, the worse it fit.

A worker node shows why. It is created in four stages (virtual machine, operating system, environment and application configuration, running), and each can fail differently: an OS start failure means a restart or deleting the VM, a configuration error means retrying setup. Those failures can happen at once across many nodes, which you cannot manage from one place.

## What does one state machine per domain look like?

The aggregate root is the cluster, addressed by cluster id, holding load balancers, masters and node groups of workers. His example is a real cluster with three masters and five workers in two groups. Each domain gets its own state machine and a state column in the database, so every entity has a clearly defined state between events.

Success propagates upwards. A node that reaches running escalates the change to its node group; the group moves to running only once all its nodes have, then escalates to the cluster, which moves once all groups have.

Errors propagate the same way, and this is where the design earns its keep. A node can only decide about itself, so it runs the error transition for its current state and escalates. The node group can replace the broken node or roll back the group; if that is not enough, the decision goes to the cluster level, which sees everything. Decisions then travel back down as events.

Ilya Kaznacheev said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "However, unlike pipelines and sagas, the state machine allows you to solve one very important task, error handling."

## Which problems showed up in production?

Four, each with a fix you can lift:

- **Race conditions.** Parallel handlers fought over the same aggregate. The fix is a database lock on the root element, with every change in one ACID transaction. It costs parallel throughput, acceptable for them; if it isn't for you, lock a parent of the domain being changed, never a child, or you invite deadlocks.
- **Lost consistency between Postgres and Kafka.** A transition could send a Kafka message, then the transaction rolled back, and the world heard about a state the database never saved. The fix is the outbox pattern: messages go into a table in the same transaction, and a separate job ships them to Kafka.
- **One-at-a-time VM creation.** Dozens of VMs per cluster created individually hurt infrastructure availability. Batch events keep the logic in the domains but move message sending up to the list level, a small, deliberate leak in encapsulation.
- **Late or wrong error messages.** What he calls state-matched error processing: error handling always depends on the current state of the domain, so a late error from a slow queue, or a mislabelled one from a buggy sender, is ignored (and can be logged or traced) when the current state has no transition for it.

## How does it look in Go?

Refreshingly plain. The domains live inside hexagonal services with a CQRS model, synchronous queries and asynchronous commands. Ilya Kaznacheev said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "We just use long switch cases to describe each state machine."

Easy to read and easy to troubleshoot, in his words. Next on their list were distributed transactions built on these domain state machines, already working in parts of their infrastructure, and generating state diagrams from code instead of drawing them by hand in Mermaid.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers running long, failure-prone workflows: provisioning, payments, order pipelines, anything where saga diagrams have started to sprout exceptions. You will not get a library; you will get a design that holds up when ten things fail at once.

Title: A blockchain is a linked list with hashes, so build one over gRPC
Description: Luis Cardoza Bird (DEVotion) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on building a toy blockchain in Go and serving it over gRPC with a streaming endpoint
Body:
Strip away the white papers and a blockchain is a list of blocks where each one carries the hash of the one before it. At Conf42 Golang 2021, Luis Cardoza Bird, founder of DEVotion, a mobile and Go developer active in GDG and JUG Nicaragua, took that minimal definition and [live-coded a small blockchain in Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Luis_Cardoza_Bird_building_blockchains), exposed through a gRPC service with a unary call to add blocks and a server-streaming call that sends the chain to a client.

It is a hands-on beginner session: no consensus, no peers, no mining, one server holding one chain in memory. As a first project for protobuf and gRPC streaming in Go, it is a tidy one, and the code is on GitHub as BlockchainsOnTheGo.

## What is in a block?

His model has three fields per block: the data, the previous block's hash, and the block's own hash computed from the two. The first block, the genesis block, has no predecessor, so it gets a hard-coded value. Luis Cardoza Bird said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "These three components are needed to build a single block, just a block, not a blockchain."

The property he leans on is that each block depends on the previous one: move block 1002 into another position and its previous-hash no longer matches, so the chain is visibly broken. In the talk he describes the hash step as encryption and mentions RSA, PBKDF and Argon2 as options; the code itself uses SHA-256, which is a hash function, and that is what the integrity check actually needs. Worth knowing before you repeat the slide in a design review.

He also draws the line between a chain and a database: a blockchain stores information in a deliberately simple structure, fine for small records such as credentials, while a database handles the richer querying you would normally want.

## Why Go, and why gRPC?

The Go pitch is the usual one, said with conviction: a low learning curve, a compiler that cross-builds for Windows, Linux and macOS on 32 and 64 bits, static strong typing, and goroutines.

For gRPC he sums it up as HTTP/2 plus remote procedure calls plus protocol buffers, against the REST habit of HTTP/1.1 and JSON. His four selling points are a faster HTTP/2 connection, a framework that is easy to understand, services that can be rearranged without big client or server changes, and protobuf making testing and inspection easier. He also corrects a common assumption: the g in gRPC changes from release to release (good, great, genius), and in his telling it never stands for Google.

## How is the service built?

The walkthrough runs in four files.

- **The proto**: a `Block` message (previous hash, data, hash), request and response messages, an empty `ChainRequest` to play the role of a GET, and a `Blockchain` service with three RPCs: `AddBlock`, a server-streaming call that sends the chain block by block, and a plain call that returns it as a repeated field. A small `generate.sh` runs `protoc` with the Go gRPC plugin. His warning about the generated `blockchain.pb.go`: edit it and the next generate run wipes your changes.
- **The chainer package**: `Block` and `Blockchain` structs, `getHash` (SHA-256 over previous hash plus data, hex-encoded), `makeBlock`, `makeBlockchain` to seed the genesis block, and `appendBlock`, which takes the last block's hash and appends a new one. He points out the package is reusable as is.
- **The server**: listen on TCP port 8004, create a `grpc.NewServer`, wrap the chain in a server struct and register it. `AddBlock` appends and returns the hash; the streaming method ranges over the blocks and sends one a second, the sleep added so the stream is easy to watch.
- **The client**: two flags, `-start` to add a block every second with the current time as data, and `-stream` to receive the chain and print previous hash, data and hash until it hits end of file.

Run both and you watch new hashes appear on one side and the chain stream past on the other.

## Who should watch

Go developers who want a small, end-to-end gRPC example with server streaming and a data structure more interesting than a to-do list. If you are after distributed ledgers, consensus algorithms or smart contracts, this is not that talk; it is a linked list taught to speak protobuf.

Title: Your terminal is a teletype in disguise, and Go can build one
Description: Ishuah Kariuki (Hover Developer Services) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on the Linux TTY subsystem and building a small terminal emulator in Go on a PTY
Body:
Every time you open a terminal you are talking to a piece of software pretending to be a 1960s printing typewriter. At Conf42 Golang 2021, Ishuah Kariuki, Principal Backend Engineer at Hover, explained [how the Linux TTY subsystem got that way](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Ishuah_Kariuki_tty_linux_terminal_emulator_basics) and then live-coded a working, if rough, terminal emulator in Go: a bash process on a pseudo terminal, two keyboard callbacks and two goroutines.

Half history lesson, half codelab, recorded (by his own admission) slightly out of breath after an evening run. He describes himself as a triathlete in active training, which explains it.

## Why is it called a TTY?

TTY stands for teletype, a printing device resembling a typewriter used to send and receive telephonic signals, popular in the early to mid 20th century. When 1960s computers became fast enough to interact with users in real time, engineers reused teletypes as input and output devices instead of inventing new ones: they were already on the market, people knew how to use them, and keyboard in, paper out fit the bill. His favourite artefact is teleprinter output of the original Oregon Trail from 1971, which ran on a mainframe and was played on paper.

Video terminals such as the VT100, one of the first to support ANSI escape codes, later replaced paper, but the plumbing stayed.

## What sits between the keyboard and bash?

The physical setup is a terminal wired to the computer over a UART, and the kernel-side TTY device has three parts:

- **UART driver**: moves bytes between the terminal and the line discipline, keystrokes in and output back.
- **Line discipline**: buffers what you type until you press enter, handles editing keys like backspace and clear line, and echoes keystrokes back so you can see them.
- **TTY driver**: hands the characters to the foreground process, usually the shell or one of its children.

When hardware terminals gave way to software, the first terminal emulators lived in the kernel too, which made them rigid: nobody could build on top of them. The fix was the pseudo terminal. Emulation moves to userland, the line discipline and session management stay in the kernel, and the link is a pair of files, the PTY master (attached to the emulator) and the PTY slave (attached to the program you want to control). He is careful to separate this from the shell, which is just another userland program, bash or zsh or fish.

## How small can a Go terminal emulator be?

The codelab uses the creack/pty package for the pseudo terminal and the Fyne UI toolkit for the window, and grows in three steps.

First, create an `exec.Cmd` for `/bin/bash`, start it on a PTY slave and keep the returned master. Write `ls` plus a carriage return to the master, sleep a second, read the bytes back and paint them in a label. It works, and the stray carriage return shows up in the output too.

Second, wire the keyboard. Fyne needs two callbacks: one for special keys, so enter sends the carriage return that tells the line discipline the command is ready, and one for runes, which writes every ordinary character straight to the master. A goroutine sleeps a second, reads up to 256 bytes and refreshes the UI. The result is interactive and chaotic: a long-running `ping` only ever shows its latest line, with no history.

Third, split the work across two goroutines. One reads runes from the master through a `bufio` reader into a buffer of lines (a slice of rune slices), starting a new line on every newline character and dropping the oldest once it holds ten. The other wakes every 100 milliseconds, joins the buffer into one string and redraws. Now new commands print in order, with history, and foreground programs stay in the foreground.

Ishuah Kariuki said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "This is a very rudimental terminal."

He is upfront about the gaps: no ANSI escape code handling, no tab, backspace, delete or arrow keys, and no signal interrupts such as Ctrl-C or Ctrl-Z. That last one is the honest answer to the question his abstract asks, why signal interrupts exist; the talk sets up the line discipline that would handle them rather than implementing it.

## Who should watch

Go developers who use terminals all day and have never looked under the hood, and anyone who has wondered what a PTY actually is. If you want escape-code parsing or a production-grade emulator, this is the foundation, not the building. His reading list is a good next step: The TTY demystified by Linus Åkesson tops it.

Title: Kafka is a log, and Go makes you want schemas for it
Description: Lorna Mitchell (Aiven.io) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on Apache Kafka from Go, Avro schemas with a registry, and describing streams with AsyncAPI
Body:
Apache Kafka will happily store whatever bytes you hand it, and that is exactly the problem. At Conf42 Golang 2021, Lorna Mitchell, Developer Advocate at Aiven, gave [a practical tour of Kafka for Go developers](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Lorna_Mitchell_go_big_apache_kafka_open_source): the mental model, a producer and consumer in Go, the tools she keeps around for poking at topics, and then the part most intros skip, enforcing a payload format with Avro and a schema registry and describing the whole thing with AsyncAPI.

The examples come from a public repo for an imaginary factory, Thingum Industries, whose machines (the MagicMaker3000 among them) report oven temperatures as JSON.

## What is Kafka, if not a database or a queue?

Her framing is the one worth stealing for your next onboarding doc. Lorna Mitchell said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "We know it isn't a database and it isn't a queue, although it can look a bit like both of those concepts. I think it's a log."

From there the pieces fall into place. Producers append to a topic, data is immutable once written, consumers read. Topics are sharded into partitions, usually by message key, for two reasons: spreading data across the cluster, and keeping order, since order is preserved within a partition. The rule she repeats until it sticks is one consumer per consumer group per topic partition. Her railway example makes consumer groups concrete: one sensor reading feeds both the platform arrivals board and the control room map, each its own group. Replication factor is set per topic and applied per partition, and the more precious the data, the higher it should go.

One number to remember: the typical maximum message size is one megabyte. In her words, if you're sending files, you're doing it wrong.

## How much Go does a producer take?

Not much. She uses confluent-kafka-go for the client, with a shout-out to Shopify's Sarama as another good option. The producer is a config map with the broker URI from an environment variable plus SSL certificate paths for a hosted cluster (a local Docker Kafka needs none of that), a deferred close, then a struct marshalled to JSON and handed to `Produce`. The consumer is similar: a group id, `auto.offset.reset` set to earliest so it reads the topic from the beginning (handy for re-auditing transactions, and for conference demos), and a `ReadMessage` loop.

For poking at a cluster she keeps three things handy: the shell scripts that ship with Kafka, kafkacat as a single CLI for producing and consuming, and Kafdrop, a web UI that runs from a Docker container. Hosted platforms usually have their own topic browser too.

## Why do schemas matter more in Go?

Kafka does no validation and no transformation: rubbish in, rubbish out. Schemas are optional, but compressed formats like Protobuf and Avro need one, and she finds them most useful when several teams share a topic. Lorna Mitchell said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "When you come to do it from go, the schema becomes oh, we should all do it this way."

Avro strips repeated field names and compresses the payload, which helps under that one-megabyte ceiling. The producer registers the schema with a registry, then prepends a zero byte and a four-byte schema id to the serialised record; the consumer reads the id, fetches the schema and rebuilds the message. Her registry is Karapace, Aiven's open source one, and the Go side uses srclient for the registry plus gogen-avro, which turns an `.avsc` file into a `MachineSensor` struct that knows how to serialise itself, doc strings carried over as comments.

Her rules for evolving schemas are short: aim for backwards-compatible changes, rename by adding the new field and keeping the old one, optional fields are safe, every change is a new version, and Avro's defaults and aliases help.

## Where does AsyncAPI fit?

The closing section treats internal consumers a few hops away on the org chart as third parties. AsyncAPI, the sister spec to OpenAPI for event-driven systems, describes brokers and auth, topics and whether you publish or subscribe, and payloads, and a `$ref` can point straight at the Avro schema file. From that one document you can generate code, integrations and documentation with the examples rendered beside the fields.

## Who should watch

Go developers about to touch their first Kafka topic, and anyone whose team argues about message formats in Slack. If you already run a schema registry in production, the Avro wire-format walkthrough and the AsyncAPI section are still worth the time.

Title: Ent is an ORM for Go that thinks in graphs, and it starts in four commands
Description: Dmitry Vinnik (Facebook) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on Ent, the open source ORM for Go, from go get to your first generated schema and query
Body:
If your Go service talks to a database and you are still hand-writing the glue between structs and tables, Ent wants a word. At Conf42 Golang 2021, Dmitry Vinnik, Developer Advocate on the open source team at Facebook, gave a short, fast introduction to [Ent](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Dmitry_Vinnik_ent_making_data_easy), the entity framework Facebook open sourced for Go: a graph-flavoured ORM where you describe a schema in Go and let code generation write the rest.

It is a quick-start talk, under ten minutes, and honest about it. Expect the shape of the workflow and the reasons to try it, not migrations at scale or benchmark tables.

## Why bother with an ORM at all?

Dmitry starts from the textbook definition (he credits Wikipedia, with a straight face, as the best online source ever): object relational mapping is a technique for converting data between incompatible type systems using object-oriented languages. His plain version is a `User` entity in code with an id, a first name and a last name, a `users` table with the same columns, and the ORM sitting between them so you never write the transaction or constraint plumbing by hand.

The argument for caring is that almost everything is data. He points at a Google Cloud integration diagram, an AWS startup use case and Scribe, Facebook's own log processor, as examples of systems that are mostly pipes for data. If data is the important part, the tool that maps it is important too.

Dmitry Vinnik said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "Everything is about data, big or small. Most applications are data driven."

## What does the first ten minutes with Ent look like?

The workflow he demonstrates is short enough to memorise:

- `go get` the Ent CLI.
- Initialise a project (his was called `entgotalk`), which gives you a module file.
- Initialise an entity, here `User`, which generates a schema file with placeholder fields.
- Add the fields you want (age, name) and run Ent's generate step.

Generation writes all the supporting code, and at that point the project is already usable. Creating a user means opening a client (he connects to SQLite) and chaining setters for the attributes before saving. Reading one back is a generated query function plus a where clause, which he compares to writing the query against the database directly, except it lives in typed Go code.

That is roughly where the demo stops, by design. For the rest he sends you to the Ent documentation at entgo.io, which he rates highly: step-by-step tutorials (a to-do app, querying and mutating data), GraphQL and Relay integration, schema and migration docs, graph traversal, and a testing section he was glad to see on the main page. Dmitry Vinnik said at Conf42 Golang 2021: "No production code should be left untested, I believe."

## The community pitch

The last stretch is about joining rather than consuming: Ent's newsletter, blog, Twitter account and Slack. His call to action has three steps, experiment with the tools, join the Ent community, contribute back, and he spells out the open source ladder from user to contributor to maintainer.

## Who should watch

Go developers who have not picked a data layer yet, or who have only seen ORMs in Java or Python and want to see how Go's code generation culture changes the shape of one. If you already run Ent in production, you will not learn much new here; the talk is a doorway, not a manual.

Title: Put a Go service in an SGX enclave with one extra command
Description: Moritz Eckert (Edgeless Systems) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on confidential computing in Go with EGo, covering enclaves, remote attestation and sealing
Body:
The cloud is other people's computers, and confidential computing is how you stop those people from reading your data while it is being processed. At [Conf42 Golang 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Moritz_Eckert_confidential_computing_Intel_SGX_security_cloud_native), Moritz Eckert of Edgeless Systems showed how EGo, their open source modified Go compiler, turns an ordinary Go HTTP service into an Intel SGX enclave: build with ego-go, add an ego sign step, then ego run. He then added remote attestation over TLS and encrypted state on disk, each in a few lines.

Edgeless Systems is a startup from Bochum, Germany, founded in 2019 with about ten engineers, building open source confidential computing tools.

## What problem does confidential computing solve?

Your workload in the cloud shares hardware, hypervisors and operating systems with people you have never met, and with other customers' code separated only by ordinary isolation. For individuals that means breach risk. For companies it also means lost value: regulated data that can't move to the cloud, or data two firms could analyse together if neither had to trust the other.

The hardware answer is the enclave, which he defines by four properties:

- **Isolation** from everything else on the machine.
- **Runtime memory encryption**, so even direct memory access sees no plaintext.
- **Sealing**, persisting state encrypted so only the enclave can read it back.
- **Remote attestation**, proving to an outside party which code and data are running.

Examples from the talk include Germany's electronic health records and e-prescriptions, Signal's private contact discovery, and wallets on commodity cloud CPUs instead of special hardware. The bold forecast he quotes, from a cloud security manager, is that the cloud will be fully confidential in five years.

## Why Go, and what EGo changes

Confidential computing is a cloud technology, and cloud native means microservices. "Most software there is written in Go," Moritz Eckert said at Conf42 Golang 2021. When Edgeless started there was no Go support for enclaves, so they built it: a modified compiler, SGX-specific tooling, and libraries for code inside and outside the enclave. Install from the snap store or a Debian package, and Microsoft's Azure confidential computing docs point to it too.

## Demo one: a key-value store, now in an enclave

The demo app is a small HTTP secret store backed by a Go map and saved to a file. Normally you build with go build. For the enclave you build with ego-go build, then run ego sign, which produces a signing key pair and an enclave.json configuration with SGX parameters, then start it with ego run. The client works unchanged. The docs at ego.dev explain every configuration field, and the same flow works for bigger apps; their usual showcase is HashiCorp Vault.

## Demo two: how does the client know it's the real service?

An enclave in the cloud is useless if a malicious copy can sit in its place and collect secrets. In remote attestation the service produces a signed identity report, a quote in SGX terms, and the client checks it before sending anything. EGo hides this in TLS. On the server, one call creates a TLS config that embeds the quote in the certificate, and ListenAndServe becomes ListenAndServeTLS. OpenSSL shows the quote as a binary extension in the certificate. On the client, a matching call creates a TLS config with a verify function that checks the security version, product ID and signer ID, the last from ego signerid. Set a secret, and the verified connection carries it end to end.

## Demo three: sealing state to disk

The demo still wrote its map to disk in plaintext. EGo's crypto package offers sealing tied either to the product key, meaning any instance of this service, or to a unique key for one specific instance. He seals with the product key before writing and unseals on load. One gotcha he points out: EGo doesn't mount the host file system by default, so nothing leaks by accident, and the file lands in memory until you declare a mount point in enclave.json. After a restart the encrypted state loads back correctly.

## From one enclave to a cluster

Scaling to four pods means the instances must attest each other and sync state, and outside clients should still see one service. That is MarbleRun, which he calls the control plane for confidential computing. It works with Kubernetes and existing service meshes and extends confidentiality, integrity and verifiability to the whole deployment.

## Who should watch

Go developers handling sensitive data in the cloud, and platform engineers wondering what SGX looks like in practice. The demos are short and real; you need no hardware security background to follow them.

Title: Generative art in Go is simple steps, repeated until it's art
Description: Preslav Rachev (PSV) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on making generative art in Go with image.Image, the gg library and WebAssembly
Body:
Go is the language of web servers and containers, and Preslav Rachev, founder of PSV, wants you to use it to paint. At [Conf42 Golang 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Preslav_Rachev_order_and_chaos_create_immersive_generative_art) he tells how he ported his old Processing sketches to Go, why Go's tiny image interfaces suit generative art, and then renders a few pieces live, including one compiled to WebAssembly and running in the browser. The talk grew alongside a self-published book on graphics and generative art in Go, his first product after going solo.

## From Processing to Go

His story starts in the early 2000s with a kid wanting to make video games, first in Pascal, then in Processing, the MIT-born language that simplified Java for artists and non-programmers. His first Processing sketch pulled a colour palette from a source image and scattered semi-transparent rectangles to build a layered effect, the same sketch that later inspired the book. During his master's he studied under one of the German pioneers of computer graphics and art, then spent years as a Java developer.

Go arrived with a job switch in late 2018. He liked its simplicity enough to try translating the old sketches. It worked, and that is the whole origin story.

## What makes art generative?

His own definition: a balance between procedure and randomness, the result of simple steps multiplied many times over, a complex organism of tiny actors interacting sequentially and concurrently. He notes that last part sounds a lot like Go itself. "It's like you don't have to write complex code to achieve complexity," Preslav Rachev said at Conf42 Golang 2021. You write simple things and repeat them, each step building on the one before.

## The standard library gets you surprisingly far

Go's graphics basics fit on one slide: three interfaces. To count as an image, a type implements three methods, and colour is just as small. He calls them the Reader and Writer of the graphics world, and the payoff is composability. Two examples:

- **Filters as images.** A filter wraps its source image and implements the same interface, so it can go anywhere an image is accepted.
- **A circular cutout**, the example also used in Go's documentation, wraps a source and returns zero opacity for every pixel outside the circle.

For real drawing he uses gg, a 2D library whose procedural API feels like Processing: shapes, fonts, basic filters, opacity. It is the main library in his book and, in his words, indispensable.

## A live sketch, from a random photo

The demo sketch takes its palette from a random photo pulled through the Unsplash API, an image nobody looks at, used only for its colours. A set of parameters drives each iteration: canvas size, initial alpha, minimum and maximum polygon edges. Every update picks a random source pixel, finds the matching spot on the canvas and draws a polygon in that colour. Two invented knobs give it character. A stroke inversion threshold adds borders once polygons get small, so the result looks more sketched. Stroke jitter nudges each shape a random distance from its source position. Each iteration shrinks the brush and raises the alpha, and the render speeds up as the polygons shrink.

Because the palette is random, he has no idea what will come out either. The first result is too dark for his taste; the second comes out black and white. Meanwhile a WebAssembly build in the browser draws a Perlin-noise piece that imitates scattered brush strokes, on a site anyone can use to generate their own.

## Who should watch

Go developers who want a weekend project that is not another CRUD service, and creative coders curious whether Go can replace Processing. There is little theory and a lot of showing. For further reading he recommends The Nature of Code by Daniel Shiffman, a Processing book whose ideas carry over to Go, and he flags genetic algorithms as his next topic.

Title: Python's pickle is a tiny virtual machine, so he wrote one in Go
Description: Marco Nicola (EXOP) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on GoPickle, a pure Go unpickler that loads Python pickle data and PyTorch models without Python
Body:
Python's pickle format is not really a data format. It is a program for a small stack-based virtual machine. At [Conf42 Golang 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Marco_Nicola_deserializing_python_objects_with_GoPickle), Marco Nicola, a software developer at EXOP with more than 20 years of experience and a focus on NLP, showed how that insight let him write [GoPickle](https://github.com/nlpodyssey/gopickle), a pure Go library that reads pickled Python data, custom classes included, and loads PyTorch models without running Python at all.

## Why do Python projects pickle instead of using JSON?

A plain dict of strings, numbers and a mixed list goes to JSON with no fuss. Define a small Greeter class with a name and a greet method, and json.dumps gives you an error. Real code makes it worse: classes from third-party libraries that can't export themselves, one object referenced twice that should still be one object after a round trip, and a list that contains itself. Pickle handles all of that, which is why NumPy, PyTorch and pandas use it behind their save and load functions.

## A pickle file is a program

Instead of mapping objects onto a format and parsing it back, pickle.dump writes a sequence of instructions, each a one-byte opcode with optional operands. pickle.load hands that program to an unpickling machine with a stack and a side area called the memo; when the program ends, the stack holds one object, the result. Python's pickletools module will print an annotated listing if you want to see the opcodes in your own files.

The machine is deliberately dumb. "In no way you can perform any sort of looping or testing. There are no conditionals, there are no arithmetic instructions, and no function calls," Marco Nicola said at Conf42 Golang 2021. The program runs once, start to finish. There are six protocol versions, 0 to 5, each adding instructions and each backward compatible with the ones before.

That simplicity is what made a Go port realistic. The whole pickle.py in CPython 3.9, serialisation and deserialisation together, is under 2,000 lines.

## The wish list behind GoPickle

The trigger was spaGO, a machine learning library for Go he works on, which needed to load pretrained PyTorch models, and PyTorch serialisation leans heavily on pickle. Rather than a Python script that converts files to something Go-friendly, he wrote down a wish list: support every pickle protocol, handle basic types out of the box, be easy to extend with custom types, never run Python, and have minimal dependencies with no unsafe or cgo. Nothing existing fit, so he wrote it, as a port of the Unpickler class from CPython's reference implementation. It only deserialises for now.

## How do custom Python classes map to Go?

Basic types map directly: booleans, ints, floats, strings, and None to nil. Dicts, lists and tuples get structs from the gopickle/types package; a Python dict becomes a types.Dict of key-value entries. He admits some of those types are unpolished and unoptimised, since the goal was a working machine first.

Unknown classes fall back to generic object and class types, which is sometimes enough. The Greeter class is not, and the load fails with a panic saying BUILD requires a PyDictSettable instance. The fix mirrors what Python does:

- A Greeter struct with a Name field implements PyDictSet, emulating assignment into an object's __dict__. When the key is _name, it stores the value as a string.
- A GreeterClass empty struct implements PyNew, emulating __new__, and returns a fresh Greeter.
- On an Unpickler built with pickle.NewUnpickler, a FindClass callback maps module __main__ and name Greeter to GreeterClass.

Run Load, assert the result to a Greeter pointer, add a Greet method, and Go prints the same greeting Python did. Other callbacks cover persistent IDs, pickle extensions and specific instructions, but he says most real cases need about as much customisation as this.

## The PyTorch payoff

Once the unpickler worked, loading PyTorch models took little code, so it ships inside GoPickle as a pytorch subpackage with a pytorch.Load function covering a subset of models. spaGO uses it to download compatible pretrained models from Hugging Face, convert them to its own format, and run text classification, question answering, translation and named entity recognition from Go. His to-do list is honest: more tests, better docs and error messages, more Python and PyTorch classes, and performance work.

## Who should watch

Go developers who inherit pickle files from a data science team, anyone serving PyTorch models from Go, and people who enjoy finding out that a familiar format is secretly a bytecode interpreter.

Title: A new CISO's first 90 days, measured, assessed and planned
Description: Gordon Rudd (Stone Creek Coaching) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on a CISO's first 90 days, using a measure-assess-plan loop
Body:
The CISO job is not the rock star job people imagine; most days you are underwater and slightly behind the curve. At [Conf42 Golang 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Gordon_Rudd_306090dayplan_careerdevelopment_ciso_career_mapping_ciocareermapping_cyberse), Gordon Rudd of Stone Creek Coaching, who has coached CISOs, CTOs and CIOs for 15 years, gives would-be and new security chiefs one loop to run on: measure what is in place, assess the gap, plan the work and work the plan. He calls it MAP.

Fair warning for a Go audience: this is a leadership and career talk with only a short Go aside. It is dense, opinionated and practical, and it reads like a checklist from someone who has sat through a lot of board meetings.

## Start by deciding what kind of CISO you are

Before mapping the organisation, map yourself. He splits the role three ways: the technically oriented, hands-on CISO who is often a one-person band; the policy-oriented business information security officer who stays at the C-level; and the strategically oriented one who looks ahead at new things. Then comes what he calls an agonizing self-appraisal, SMART goals with dates on them, and an accountability partner or coach. Not your boss, he adds, because the boss rarely has an ear for why you're late.

He also lists nine things to watch constantly, from the tone from the top and GRC to employee ownership, solving problems without buying new tech, and automating everything you can.

## What the first 90 days should cover

The 30-60-90 day plan should already exist before day one; you brought it to the interview, and it doubles as a way to find out what your manager expects. Then you measure: strategic and tactical plans, budget, policy and procedure analysis, managed and unmanaged assets, vulnerability assessment processes, staff skills, access controls. You learn the change management process and where security fits into it. You check compliance (NYDFS, CCPA, GDPR) and the backup plan, which in a ransomware incident will either save you or kill you. Then you write a corporate information protection plan and walk it up through management until the board blesses it.

## The habits he puts numbers on

The useful bits are the specific rules of thumb:

- **Behavioural analytics take time.** Learning what normal network traffic looks like takes six to nine months, and he sees many AI installs taking nine to twelve months before the false positives are worked out. If a salesperson promises less, look at them funny.
- **Scan in slices.** Turn a vulnerability scanner on the whole network at once and users will think the network is down. Scan a different small segment every day.
- **Train five days every three months**, and train two people for every job: two is one and one is none.
- **Re-justify technology every 18 months**: is your firewall vendor still the best answer?
- **Know your burn rate**, what the security program costs per day or month, and what the organisation gets for it.
- **Ask the CFO what a material loss is.** One answered 25,000; five years later the same question got 300,000. Risk appetite moves.

## Communicate, or the board will guess

Boards may get 700 to 1,000 pages to read before each meeting, so set a predictable reporting cadence instead of flooding them: monthly to the committees that meet monthly, quarterly to the audit committee, an annual summary for the board. Each report covers the asset inventory, threat, vulnerability and patch status, risk assessments and upcoming contract changes, with at least one slide per security domain and a written document behind it. "don't be afraid to communicate because if you don't communicate they're going to speculate," Gordon Rudd said at Conf42 Golang 2021.

His Spectre and Meltdown story shows why. Patches existed, but in his tests they would have made production servers so slow users would think they were down, so he went to the board and explained why they would rely on perimeter defences and behavioural analytics instead.

## Build unicorns, don't hire them

On hiring he is blunt: the unicorn employee wants too much money and leaves the moment someone offers 20% to 25% more. "Stop looking for the unicorn. Start building your team," he said. A simple skills matrix (person, role, skills, current and ideal capability, development action) plus certifications that match your framework do the job. He calls the CISSP the usual cert, citing a figure of almost 69% of CISOs holding it.

The Go moment comes in the log aggregation section: friends in forensics told him they were moving from Python to Go because it is quicker to learn and does the same work in fewer lines.

## Who should watch

Senior engineers eyeing a security leadership role, and new CISOs who want a checklist for the first quarter. If you came for Go code, this is not that talk.

Title: Post-quantum crypto in Go is faster than you'd think, just bigger
Description: Mathilde Raynal (Kudelski Security) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on crystals-go, a side-channel-hardened Go port of the Kyber and Dilithium schemes
Body:
Post-quantum cryptography has a reputation for being slow. At [Conf42 Golang 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Mathilde_Raynal_quantumresistant_native_go_programs), Mathilde Raynal of Kudelski Security presented crystals-go, a Go port of the lattice-based Kyber and Dilithium schemes, which in her benchmarks ran faster than RSA and ECDSA from Go's crypto packages. The catch is bandwidth: keys, signatures and ciphertexts are much larger. Bolted into WireGuard, it added 0.2 ms and two extra IP packets.

The library came out of her master's thesis, a joint project between Kudelski Security and EPFL.

## Why bother before quantum computers exist?

Quantum algorithms break public-key schemes such as RSA outright. Symmetric ciphers and hash functions are weakened rather than broken and can be fixed with longer keys. Public-key cryptography is everywhere: password managers like gopass, SSH, encrypted email, VPNs, cryptocurrencies. Making RSA itself quantum-resistant by growing its keys is no answer, since that would take 1 TB keys.

The timing argument is the one engineers should take home. Research and standardisation, then deployment, then a complete transition across security infrastructure is a long road, and nobody knows when a scalable quantum computer will reach attackers. "the correct answer actually was yesterday," Mathilde Raynal said at Conf42 Golang 2021, on when to start. Her cautionary tale is Git's slow move away from SHA-1, which stayed in use long after it was known to be weak. Crypto agility, swapping primitives in running systems, is hard, and that is the reason to start early.

## Signatures and key encapsulation, the two jobs to replace

A short refresher maps out what has to be swapped. Public-key crypto does authentication through digital signature algorithms (DSA), and encryption mostly in hybrid form: public-key cryptography is too slow for bulk data, so a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) safely moves a symmetric key, and symmetric encryption does the rest.

The CRYSTALS suite covers both. Dilithium is the signature scheme and Kyber the KEM. Both were finalists in the NIST post-quantum competition, which her abstract notes started in 2016 with 105 candidates and narrowed to 15 finalists in 2020. Kudelski picked them for their simplicity, tight security proofs and versatility. Their one real drawback is output size.

## An API that makes you pick a security level first

The port from the C reference implementation is not a line-by-line translation. The team added countermeasures against published side-channel attacks and used Go's own features for speed and reliability. Using it takes two steps. First you choose a security level, which fixes every internal parameter so you can't mix them up: NewDilithium2, 3 or 5, and NewKyber512, 768 or 1024. Then you call the core methods:

- **Dilithium**: KeyGen returns the verification and signing keys, Sign takes the secret key and message, Verify returns a boolean.
- **Kyber**: KeyGen returns a key pair, Encaps takes the public key and random coins and returns a ciphertext plus shared secret, and Decaps recovers the same shared secret from the ciphertext with the secret key.

## The numbers, at the recommended level

Her figures for the middle security level:

| Scheme | Runtime (ms) | Sizes (bytes) |
|---|---|---|
| Dilithium | KeyGen 0.4, Sign 1.8, Verify 0.5 | public key 1,952, signature 3,293 |
| Kyber | KeyGen 0.4, Encaps 0.2, Decaps 0.3 | public key 1,184, ciphertext 1,088 |

Against Go's ECDSA (for Dilithium) and RSA-OAEP (for Kyber) at equivalent classical security, crystals-go came out faster on runtime and clearly worse on bandwidth. The WireGuard experiment is the practical test, and the overhead of 0.2 ms and two IP packets is small enough to call it practical. Her closing advice reaches past this library: implementation security is the part people overlook, so pick crypto libraries that take side channels seriously.

## Who should watch

Go developers who own anything with TLS, SSH, signatures or VPN tunnels and want a clear 101 on why post-quantum migration is a today problem. You don't need lattice maths; she skips it on purpose. The code is open source at [kudelskisecurity/crystals-go](https://github.com/kudelskisecurity/crystals-go).

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: Skaffold makes your laptop's Kubernetes feel like production
Description: Matan Cohen (Wix) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on Go development on local Kubernetes with Skaffold, Helm for dependencies and Bazel for smart rebuilds
Body:
Your local setup can be fast or it can be like production, and most teams pick one. At [Conf42 Golang 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Matan_Cohen_skaffold_helm_kubernetes_local_development), Matan Cohen, Software Development Team Lead on the production platform at Wix, shows how his team gets both: Go services running on a local Kubernetes cluster with Skaffold, external dependencies pulled in with Helm, and Bazel deciding exactly which services a change needs to rebuild. Three live demos, all on Docker for Mac.

## What should a local dev setup optimise for?

His team owns developer experience for Wix's production engineers, so he starts with requirements. "you must have velocity, good experience and a fast feedback loop," Matan Cohen said at Conf42 Golang 2021.

He then places the usual options on a scale from nothing like production to exactly like production: running your code through tests, running a single service as a binary or container, a dockerised environment with the service plus its database and queues, and finally all services with full integration. The goal was to keep the feedback loop of the first option while getting as close as possible to the last.

## Skaffold watches, rebuilds, redeploys and cleans up

Skaffold, Google's tool for Kubernetes development, watches your files and continuously redeploys every change to a cluster, local or remote, then cleans up when you stop. He calls the idea continuous development. Setup is Docker for Mac with Kubernetes enabled, Skaffold from brew, and the Cloud Code extension for VS Code or IntelliJ.

The first demo uses Cloud Code's Go guestbook template: a backend, a frontend and MongoDB. The skaffold.yaml has two parts, build pointing at the artifacts and deploy pointing at the Kubernetes manifests. One skaffold dev builds both images, deploys all three pods, and serves the app on localhost, with Lens showing the pods. Then the loop:

- Rename the app in the frontend, and Skaffold rebuilds only the frontend.
- Add a ping handler to the Go backend, and only the backend is redeployed.
- Change a port in a Kubernetes manifest, and it redeploys almost instantly since no image needs rebuilding.

The part that sells it is debugging. Running on Kubernetes in debug mode from the IDE, he sets breakpoints in both the frontend and the backend handler, posts a guestbook entry, and steps from one service into the other inside the cluster. Cross-microservice debugging, on a laptop.

## How do you bring Postgres, Kafka and Redis along?

Skaffold is pluggable at every stage: build with the local Docker daemon, Google Cloud Build, Kaniko or Bazel; tag with Git commit IDs, SHA256 hashes or a Go template with env variables; deploy with kubectl, Helm or Kustomize. For dependencies he picks Helm, the Kubernetes package manager, with charts found on Artifact Hub (formerly Helm Hub).

A second file, skaffold-services.yaml, lists Helm releases with no build artifacts. skaffold run -f deploys it once without watching, unlike skaffold dev. He adds PostgreSQL, then Kafka and Redis, and one more run brings up Kafka with ZooKeeper and a Redis master and replica. The chart parameters still need tuning, he notes, but the shape is right. skaffold delete removes it all.

## Bazel knows which services a package change touches

Skaffold can tell which service changed, but not which services depend on a shared package you just edited. That is where Bazel, Google's language-agnostic build tool, comes in. Each directory has a BUILD file declaring its targets, which are generated rather than written by hand, and Bazel caches every layer of the dependency tree. At Wix, he says, backend groups mostly writing Scala cut their CI build times from hours to minutes after moving to Bazel.

The third demo has two services and two packages. Service one uses a sum package; service two uses sum and a multiply package. Edit sum and both services rebuild. Edit multiply and only service two does. Edit service one and nothing else moves.

## Who should watch

Go developers on Kubernetes teams whose local setup is docker-compose plus hope, and platform teams designing developer experience. The demos are mostly YAML and terminal, with very little Go code on screen.

- Haseeb Majid on [reproducible development with Nix](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Haseeb_Majid_using_nix_reproducible) at Conf42 Golang 2024.

Title: No cache in Traefik, so he learned Go and wrote one
Description: Sylvain Combraque (Les-Tilleuls.coop) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on learning Go by building Souin, an HTTP cache for Traefik, plus the basics that tripped him up
Body:
Some people learn a language from tutorials. Sylvain Combraque, a software developer at Les-Tilleuls.coop, learned Go because his reverse proxy had no cache. At [Conf42 Golang 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Sylvain_Combraque_Souin_feedback) he tells how that gap in Traefik became Souin, his open source cache system written in Go, and then live-codes the Go basics he wishes someone had shown him first: GOPATH, goroutines, WaitGroups, channels and the built-in test runner.

## Why write a cache, and why in Go?

He had used Traefik since version 1.4 and contributes to it as a helper and ambassador. Traefik is container-first: it detects deployments, follows scaling and load balances on its own, which makes it the pivot point of the infrastructure. What it did not have was an internal cache, so every request had to resolve its backend service, costing milliseconds each time. After many nights searching, everything he found was either not efficient enough or a proof of concept.

His abstract lists the language shortlist. PHP got a no, Node.js got a laugh, C++ was too much to learn on the side. Traefik itself is written in Go and Go fits a Docker setup, so Go it was. At the time of the talk Souin was at version 1.5.2 with more than 100 GitHub stars, and its releases are named after beers, which he puts down to liking beer.

## The environment variables that confused him first

His first lesson for newcomers is that Go is organised by environment variables. GOPATH tells Go where binaries, sources and dependencies live, under three folders: src for readable sources with dependencies, pkg for compiled package objects, and bin for finished binaries. GOROOT points at the SDK. GOOS picks the target operating system and GOARCH the architecture, and together they give you cross-platform builds, Windows binaries from a Mac included. Build a full matrix and you get hundreds of binaries, one for every system you could want.

## Goroutines need someone to wait for them

The live demo builds up concurrency one mistake at a time. A function with a ten-step loop runs in sequence from main. Put go in front of it and it runs concurrently, but main finishes first: the detached loop gets through about four iterations before the process exits, because starting the goroutine takes a few microseconds and the main loop doesn't wait.

A time.Sleep of one second hides the problem. "So that's not a really clean way to do that," Sylvain Combraque said at Conf42 Golang 2021, and he replaces it with a sync.WaitGroup: Add before launching, pass the WaitGroup as a pointer so it is not copied, defer Done inside the goroutine, and Wait in main.

## Channels, deadlocks and the zero value

Channels come next, described as a pipe between main and your goroutines that you push data into and pull from. The first attempt deadlocks on purpose, since nothing is left to send. Once a goroutine sends a value, the receive returns one and true for an open channel. Close the channel and the same receive returns zero, the default for int, and false. It is a short, useful demonstration of the two-value receive that beginners tend to skip.

## Tests come in the box

He admits he came from an environment that did not test much, so the built-in test runner was a discovery. He writes a few toy functions, including a FizzBuzz variant, and tests them with the plain testing package in files ending in _test.go, then shows a test failing when he changes the expected value. For the next step he points to golint, go vet, goimports and gofmt, Avelino's awesome-go list, and coding katas on Codewars. The Souin repository has a fuller example with a web server sending JSON.

## Who should watch

Developers who learn best by building something real, and Traefik users curious where Souin came from. The Go section is introductory; skip ahead if goroutines and channels are already second nature.

Title: Learn Go concurrency by making merge sort stop waiting
Description: Jayaganesh Kalyanasundaram (Google) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on learning goroutines and channels by rewriting merge sort three times
Body:
The fastest way to understand Go channels might be to write the same merge sort three times. That is the path Jayaganesh Kalyanasundaram, a software engineer in site reliability engineering at Google, walks in his [lightning talk at Conf42 Golang 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Jayaganesh_Kalyanasundaram_concurrency_for_beginners): sequential, then goroutines with a WaitGroup, then channels that let the merge start before either half is finished.

It is a short beginner-track talk, and it is honest about where he started. Coming from C++, his first read of Go was C++ performance with syntax closer to Python, with structs plus interfaces standing in for classes.

## Version one: merge sort as a syntax exercise

Merge sort is his standard first program in any new language because it touches functions, variable declaration and slice manipulation in one go. Sort splits the slice at the midpoint, recurses on both halves and calls Merge, which walks the two sorted halves with two indices and copies the smaller element each time. Nothing concurrent yet, just a check that you can read Go.

## Version two: the go keyword, and a wait that costs you

Then he found the go keyword. Having written multithreaded C++ with the threads library, the contrast stuck with him. "Though it wasn't rocket science, it wasn't as intuitive and easy as just using the go followed by the function name," Jayaganesh Kalyanasundaram said at Conf42 Golang 2021.

The second version sorts each half in its own goroutine. A sync.WaitGroup gets Add(2), each goroutine calls defer wg.Done(), and wg.Wait() blocks until both halves are sorted before Merge runs. He takes a moment to explain defer as the last statement to run in its scope, which is exactly what a beginner needs to read this code.

He also points at the weak spot: the merger needs two fully sorted slices, so the program sits idle at wg.Wait(). Concurrency, but with a traffic light in the middle.

## Version three: channels as water pipes

His mental model for channels is a pipe, with a sender at one end and a receiver at the other. The rules he lists:

- A channel has a buffer, the length of the pipe, and it can be zero.
- If the receiver is not receiving, the sender blocks.
- If the sender is not sending, the receiver waits indefinitely.
- The sender can close the channel to say it is done, and the receiver learns that once the data has drained.

The final Sort takes a channel instead of returning a slice, and closes it with defer when done. It creates two buffered channels sized to each half, launches both recursive sorts with go, and Merge reads from both channels as values arrive. Sorting and merging now overlap with no blocking wait. His summary of the journey goes from sequential sort with a blocking merge, to concurrent sort with a blocking merge, to concurrent sort with a non-blocking merge. He points to the Go blog post on sharing memory by communicating as the reason this beats shared memory with lock contention.

## Where channels paid off in real work

The closing anecdote is the most useful part. His team had an internal CLI with one frontend and several backends compiled into a single binary. Each backend call took minutes, and a full run could take half an hour to an hour, which meant staring at a blank screen. Each backend got a channel to the frontend and pushed progress whenever it hit a milestone; the frontend aggregated them for the user. No separate logging pipeline, no extra database.

## Who should watch

Developers who know basic Go syntax and want to see goroutines, WaitGroups and channels click into place on a problem they already understand. It is about ten minutes. People who already use channels daily will not learn much new.

Title: From go mod init to a scratch container in one sitting
Description: Huseyin Babal (Hazelcast) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on Go basics for beginners, from modules and table tests to cross-compiled binaries in Docker
Body:
Most Go intros stop at Hello World. At [Conf42 Golang 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Huseyin_Babal_development_for_beginners), Huseyin Babal, Software Development Team Lead at Hazelcast Cloud, runs the whole beginner loop in one session: start a module, write variables and functions, test them with table tests, measure coverage, and ship a binary in a multi-stage Docker build on a scratch image. It is a 101, and a well-ordered one: theory first, then the same steps live in GoLand.

## What does a Go project need before the first line of code?

A Go binary from golang.org and a module. He opens with go mod init plus a version control URL, which leaves you with a single go.mod file holding the module path and Go version. Dependencies appear there under require, and go list -m all shows both your direct dependencies and the recursive ones they pull in. GitHub is the common case, but GitLab, Bitbucket or a self-hosted VCS work too.

For editors he lists vim-go (with :GoRun), GoLand with a run configuration, and VS Code with Ctrl+F5. Then the first rule worth remembering: a package named main builds an executable; any other name, such as a math package, is a library.

## The syntax tour, with the gotchas newcomers hit

The language section moves quickly through the parts that trip people coming from other languages:

- **Variables**: var with a type, or := to declare and assign in one go. Slices with or without a preset length, two-dimensional slices, and maps (student ID to name, in his example).
- **Functions**: multiple return values (he compares them to Scala tuples) and the visibility rule. A function name starting with a lowercase letter stays private to the package; an uppercase one is exported.
- **Control structures**: if and switch without parentheses, a for loop that doubles as the infinite loop when you drop the condition, and range as Go's stand-in for for-each.
- **The compiler is strict**: declare something and not use it, and the build complains. The underscore is how you tell it you don't care about the index.

The live demo earns its keep with a deliberate mistake. He declares a slice with length two, assigns a third element, and gets an index out of range panic. Remove the extra line and the missing values fall back to zero, the default for int. Small thing, exactly the kind of thing a beginner needs to see once.

## Tests that tell you what broke

Testing uses the built-in testing package, with testify for assertion-style checks and mockery or golang/mock for mocks (he leaves mocking for another session). The first example tests a Fibonacci function that should return 610; the second turns it into a table test, a slice of structs with input and expected values looped over in one function.

In the demo he plants wrong expected values in the table on purpose, watches the test fail with the wanted and got numbers, and fixes the table. His aside on the workflow is the right instinct for beginners. "But normally you don't change test code most of the time," Huseyin Babal said at Conf42 Golang 2021.

Coverage comes from go test -cover, and -coverprofile writes a file for an HTML report or a CI tool such as Sonar to enforce thresholds. His demo package sits at 50% because the multiply function has no test yet.

## Why cross-compiling matters for containers

He skips CI products and goes to what they all consume, the artifact. go tool dist list prints the supported OS and architecture pairs (darwin/amd64 in his case), and setting those for go build gives you a binary for that target. That binary is what makes Go containers small: a first stage builds from the golang image and runs go mod download and go build, and a second stage starts from scratch, copies only the binary and sets it as the entry point.

## Who should watch

Developers new to Go who learn best by watching someone type, and anyone who wants the modules-to-container path in one place. Experienced Gophers can skip it.

Title: The MySQL Shell speaks Python now, and you can teach it new tricks
Description: Dave Stokes (Oracle) at Conf42 Python 2021 on the MySQL Shell's Python mode, the X DevAPI document store and writing your own plugins and reports
Body:
If your mental image of the MySQL client is a monochrome prompt that only takes SQL, Dave Stokes wants a word. At Conf42 Python 2021, the MySQL Community Manager at Oracle gave a quick tour of the new MySQL Shell (mysqlsh): three modes (SQL, JavaScript and Python), a NoSQL JSON document store through the X DevAPI, and a plugin and report system you extend in a dozen lines of Python. The pitch for Python developers: your scripts, your libraries and your database live in the same prompt.

It is an introduction, and he says so up front, with a safe harbor statement about future releases.

## What's different from the old client?

Anything before MySQL 8.0 shipped a simple command-line editor. The new shell switches between modes with a command (py for Python, js for JavaScript, sql for the old-timers), and code from one mode can be called from another. Running SQL from Python mode is a method call on the session, and the output can come back as a table or, once you change the result format, as JSON.

He points out the defaults visible in the status command: connections are encrypted with AES 256, the character set is utf8mb4 (all four planes of Unicode, so yes, emojis), and compression is on. If you want to pin TLS versions, cipher suites or compression algorithms such as LZ4 and Zstandard, you can. The first time you connect, the shell offers to store your password hashed, and you can pipe a Python file straight into mysqlsh.

## Two protocols, one database

The shell offers two session types: classic on port 3306, which MySQL has used for its 25 years, and the X DevAPI on port 33060, which carries both SQL and NoSQL traffic. You can open several sessions at once, of either type, against one server or many, and use one to feed another.

The X DevAPI is the part that will surprise people who think of MySQL as strictly relational. Get a collection, find documents with a bound parameter, limit the result, all without writing SQL. He stresses that it's not an ORM but a clean-sheet protocol built on Google protobufs, with protection against most SQL injection built in. Dave Stokes said at Conf42 Python 2021, "Once again, if you don't like SQL, you do mysql without SQL."

His use case for this is refreshingly honest: the project where the boss says start coding now, we'll tell you what you're building next week. Create a collection, add a document, store data without designing relations or indexes. Each document gets an _id, which is the primary key for the InnoDB storage engine; supply your own or let the server generate it.

## Keeping JSON honest

Schemaless storage has an obvious failure mode, and he names it: JSON by default is very loosey goosey. The answer is JSON Schema validation, credited to the json-schema.org folks. You attach a schema when creating a collection, and documents that don't match are rejected. His example is a geographic coordinate with required latitude and longitude fields, type checks, and range checks of -90 to 90 and -180 to 180.

## Extending the shell in Python

This is the section Python developers came for. You can define extension objects and reports in Python or JavaScript, use them from either language, and persist them as plugins that load every time the shell starts. His example is a show_tables function that grabs the current session, tells you to connect if there isn't one, runs a query against the world database and dumps the rows; registering it on a plugin object with a name and a help string takes about a dozen lines.

Reports are registered with register_report and get the reporting facility for free: options with shortcuts (a limit flag, say), arguments, help text, and output types of list, report or print. His sessions report queries the sys schema's session view, and with the watch command it reruns every 2 seconds, like top for your database connections.

## The utilities that save a migration weekend

The shell also ships utilities. checkForServerUpgrade checks a 5.7 server before a move to 8.0, including new reserved words and character set problems. importJson loads a JSON file into a collection, importTable splits a data file and loads it with multiple threads, exportTable dumps a table fast, and there are instance, schema and table dump utilities, with a dry-run option and Oracle Cloud bucket support. For anyone still scripting mysqldump, that list alone is worth the watch.

For further reading he points to the MySQL Shell 8.0 manual and to Frédéric Descamps (lefred) and his GitHub collection of shell plugins.

## Who should watch

Python developers who touch MySQL and still alt-tab to a separate client, DBAs who write maintenance scripts, and anyone curious about MySQL as a document store. The talk is a feature tour rather than a deep technical session, and it closes with Oracle cloud credit and startup program offers plus a plug for his book on MySQL and JSON.
