Title: Go is a great first language, once you hide the terminal
Description: Miriah Peterson (Weave) at Conf42 Golang 2021 on teaching Go to people who have never coded, with a free, open source zero-to-hero course
Body:
Go's learning material assumes you already know what a function is and where your terminal lives. At [Conf42 Golang 2021](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Miriah_Peterson_from_zero_to_hero_learning_go), Miriah Peterson, a data engineer at Weave, argued that Go is actually an ideal first language for complete beginners, and that the real barrier is the tooling around it. Her answer is a free, open source tutorial that teaches programming first and the Go toolchain second.

She speaks from experience. Go was the first language she used professionally, learned at her first tech job. "if anybody ever asks me, I say my first programming language was Go, which is very, very uncommon," Miriah Peterson said at Conf42 Golang 2021.

## Why is Go hard for beginners if the language is simple?

Her diagnosis: the official resources target people who have used a command line before and understand types and functions. Hello World in most languages means pressing a button. In Go, a newcomer first has to install a binary, set up a GOPATH, and learn to run the go tools. Each step raises the bar before a single line of code runs.

The usual workaround is a paid bootcamp or course, which she sees as a real problem for people from low-income backgrounds, people working full time or single parents. Her alternative is what she calls open source learning: the same free blog posts, tutorials and examples experienced developers rely on every day, but written for people who are just coming in.

## Teach programming in the playground, the toolchain later

The course, [published on GitHub Pages](https://soypete.github.io/Golang_tutorial_zero_to_hero/), runs in a deliberate order. Part one is plain programming, done in Go Playground or Go Play Space so nobody has to install anything: Hello World dissected line by line, then types, functions, conditionals and loops. She avoids the term control flow on purpose, because computer-science vocabulary is one more barrier. Conditionals come straight after functions, which is where learners start to feel they can tell a program what to do. Loops come last, since you need everything before them to use them well.

Only then does the terminal show up. Her own fear when starting out was concrete. "I thought I was going to click a wrong button. I thought I was going to nuke my computer," she said. Part two covers bash basics (pwd, cd, cp, mv, rm), Git, installing Go with the right paths, and picking an editor. She recommends VS Code to beginners while admitting she uses Vim herself. She also points out that people from bootcamps often have never touched a terminal, which costs them jobs.

Part three writes a small Go server using only the standard library, a chat server, so the first real project is an API that prints messages and lives in Git.

## From writing code to being employable

The title promises a hero, not just someone who can write code, so the later parts cover what makes someone hireable:

- **Dependencies** with Go modules and pkg.go.dev, using a library outside the standard library (testify, a mock server, or in her case machine learning libraries).
- **Checking your code** with go vet, gofmt and goimports, plus the strict community linting habits Go developers are known for.
- **Testing** with go test and the built-in coverage tool, with the lesson that testable functions are small and do one thing. She built a simple web crawler on her Twitch stream as the practice project.
- **Deploying** a service in a Docker container, and stopping there. Cloud and servers are left for learners to explore.

She is upfront that the course is unfinished and has no education theory behind it, only her own path. Contributions are the point: someone needs to write the Chromebook section, for example, because a cheap Chromebook may be the only machine a learner has. The next planned feature is an embedded playground so readers can run code beside the text.

## Who should watch

Anyone mentoring a career changer, running a meetup study group, or wondering whether Go is a sensible first language. It is a short, opinionated talk about curriculum design, with no deep Go internals. Experienced Gophers will mostly find a contribution opportunity.

Title: Python best practices, timed with a stopwatch instead of argued in a PR
Description: Ranjan Mohan (Thales) at Conf42 Python 2021 on Python habits that pay off, from fail-fast checks to lazy imports, lru_cache and join, each one benchmarked
Body:
Most Python style advice arrives as a code review comment with no evidence attached. At Conf42 Python 2021, Ranjan Mohan, Senior Software Engineer at Thales, took a handful of those comments (use built-ins, fail fast, import late, cache pure functions, join strings, reach for generators) and ran each one against a timer or a memory counter on screen. The takeaway: most of the folklore holds up, a couple of results are closer than you'd think, and readability still wins the tie-breaks.

He opens with an honest caveat that many benchmark talks skip: his execution times don't exclude CPU context-switch time, so the numbers are indicative. He leans on the gaps being large enough that the noise doesn't matter, and for most of the examples it clearly doesn't.

## Is failing fast actually faster?

His example converts years to months. The fail-late version checks the valid case first, computes, and raises in the else branch; the fail-fast version checks for the invalid input first and raises immediately. Run over a thousand invalid inputs (from -1000 up to -2), fail-fast came out at more than a 50% cut in average time.

The fine print is the useful bit. That result assumes the failure check and the validity check cost about the same. If your validity test is much cheaper than your failure test, the ordering flips. So the rule is really: put the cheap check that rejects the most traffic first.

## What does a top-of-file import cost?

The most practical number in the talk. A baseline function that does nothing rounds to zero milliseconds; a function that imports numpy and urllib took about 264 milliseconds on the first call. Now picture a call chain crossing several modules, each with heavy global imports it doesn't need for the path being run, and those hundreds of milliseconds stack into seconds.

His advice is to import expensive libraries inside the method, class or block that needs them. He admits the trade-off (you lose the tidy list at the top of the file) and argues IDEs and dependency tools make that list less important than it used to be. Anyone who has watched a CLI tool take two seconds to print its help text will nod along.

## When should you reach for lru_cache?

For a pure function, where the same input always gives the same output. His demo sums the first n Fibonacci numbers recursively, once plain and once wrapped in an LRU cache holding 128 entries. The uncached version's time rises exponentially with n; the cached one stays close to zero throughout.

The one caveat he gives: skip the cache when the input objects are expensive in memory, because the cache will happily hold on to them. For a function taking a single integer, Ranjan Mohan said at Conf42 Python 2021, "you could jolly well use a cache to improve performance by several manifolds."

## Loops, comprehensions or map?

The test squares a list of numbers, run for input sizes from zero to 1 million in steps of 10,000. List comprehension was the clear winner, the plain for loop sat in the middle, and map was slowest. Then he argues against his own chart a little: he still prefers map for cleaner code, says its advantage shows up at much larger inputs, and warns that comprehensions with several conditions or nested objects become a cognitive-load problem for the next reader. Use comprehensions freely for simple cases, in other words, and stop when they need a comment to explain them.

## Strings, dictionaries, generators and membership

"Any PR where I see string concatenation about 90% of the time, I see a comment that says use join, don't use plus," he said, and the benchmark backs up the reviewers: concatenating lists of 1 to 1,000 strings with plus is erratic and trends upward, while join stays close to zero.

The dictionary example is more nuanced. Counting fruit with an explicit membership check versus dict.get with a default gives mixed results per operation: get can lose on updates because of the extra indirection for the default. Averaged over adds and updates together, get comes out ahead, and it fits on one line.

Generators versus building a list shows the memory side: the list's size grows steadily with the number of values, while the generator object stays constant because it produces values only when iterated. And for checking whether a value is in a large list, the in keyword beats a hand-written for loop on both time and readability.

## Who should watch

Python developers in their first couple of years, and reviewers who want numbers to point at instead of an appeal to authority. It's a short, demo-driven talk; experienced Pythonistas will know the rules, but the import-cost and fail-fast caveats are worth the time. He also mentions sharing the repository with the code and a best-practices markdown file.

Title: Reference counts free most Python objects. Cycles need the collector
Description: Nisarg Shah (Fountain9) at Conf42 Python 2021 on how CPython allocates memory, counts references and uses a generational collector to break cycles
Body:
Python has no free(), and most of the time it doesn't need one: an object dies the moment nothing points to it. At Conf42 Python 2021, [Nisarg Shah](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Nisarg_Shah_memory_understanding), then a computer science undergraduate and Software Developer Intern at Fountain9, walked through how CPython stores objects, how reference counting frees them, and why a second, generational garbage collector exists to clean up the reference cycles counting can never catch.

It's an introductory internals talk, built on the CPython developer guide's garbage collector design page, which he recommends reading next.

## What is a Python object, in memory terms?

Everything is an object. Assign 9 to a variable and CPython creates an object with a unique id, a type, a value and a reference count; id() and type() show the first two. Objects and instance variables live on the heap, while each function call gets a stack frame that is destroyed when it returns. Because objects nest freely (lists in dicts in lists), allocation has to be both smart and fast, which is the job of pymalloc, CPython's allocator sitting on top of the general-purpose one.

Why not let developers manage it? Long-running processes with hundreds of objects need a lot of memory, and freeing the wrong object by hand means a crash and a long debugging session. Automatic tracking takes that off the programmer.

## Watching the reference count move

His examples run on Python 3.8.5. Bind 19 to a, then b = a, and id(b) matches with a count of two. Then c = 19 lands on the same object too and the count reaches three, which works because CPython caches small integers, so treat that one as an implementation detail rather than a rule. Check with sys.getrefcount and you get four, not three, because passing an object into a function adds a reference for the duration of the call. Copy a list with copy.copy and the ids differ: a new object. Rebind l1 to a new list and its id changes.

The count goes up on assignment, on appending an object into a container and on passing it as an argument, and down on del and when a function's locals go away. When it hits zero the object is freed immediately, which he names as the algorithm's big advantage. Globals keep their count above zero until the program ends.

## Why reference counting isn't enough

A list that appends itself, or two objects pointing at each other, never reach zero, even after the rest of the program has forgotten them. Reference counting can't see cycles, so CPython adds a generational, trace-based collector. "Now, one thing to note is that this algorithm does not run in real time," Nisarg Shah said at Conf42 Python 2021. It runs periodically, while reference counting runs on every change.

New objects go into generation 0. When the collector runs, survivors move to generation 1 and then generation 2, where long-lived objects stay until the program exits. Each generation has its own counter and threshold, and crossing a threshold triggers a scan of that generation.

## How the collector finds a cycle

This is the most useful part. For a scan, every container object gets a second counter, gc_refs, initialised from its real reference count. The collector then walks the objects and subtracts every reference that comes from inside the group being scanned. Whatever is still above zero is referenced from outside, so it's alive. Zero doesn't yet mean garbage, only that nothing outside points at it directly, so those objects move to a tentatively unreachable list.

A second pass, driven by each type's tp_traverse, starts from the objects known to be alive and pulls back anything they can reach. In his four-link example, links two and three are rescued because link one, held by a variable, reaches them. Link four, referenced only by itself, stays unreachable and is freed.

For hands-on follow-up he points to gc.collect() and gc.garbage, the devguide's design document and Medium's Python memory model posts.

## Who should watch

Python developers who have never looked below the object model, people chasing memory growth in long-running services, and anyone preparing for interviews where the question about reference cycles will come up. CPython core developers will know all of it.

Title: Python is how architects get skyscrapers out of drawing tools
Description: Tadeh Hakopian (HMC Architects) at Conf42 Python 2021 on using Python with Dynamo, Rhino, Blender and Ladybug Tools to design buildings faster
Body:
A modern building ships with thousands of drawing sheets, and the architects producing them have quietly become Python programmers. At Conf42 Python 2021, [Tadeh Hakopian](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Tadeh_Hakopian_Skyscraper_coding_architecture_blender_pythonweb_data_analysis__machine_l), Design Technology Manager at HMC Architects, toured the Python tools that let building architects script geometry, automate BIM models and run daylight and energy studies, and his one-line takeaway is that Python makes it possible.

It's a short showcase rather than a tutorial: lots of tools, a few snippets, and a strong pitch for open source in an industry built on proprietary suites.

## Architects and architects

He opens with the overlap between building architects and software architects: Christopher Alexander's pattern language, which influenced both. A pattern that has proved reliable can be reused at any scale without reinventing the process, and that's a design philosophy either kind of architect will recognise.

The problem is volume. Drawing, feedback and revision worked when a house needed about 20 drawing plans. Today's projects run to 2,000 or more 30x40-inch sheets. "Now you need thousands, literally thousands," Tadeh Hakopian said at Conf42 Python 2021. He calls the traditional process wasteful and limited, and it's why computational design, generating designs from inputs and parameters with a computer, has spread through the profession over the past decade.

## From diamonds to a twisting tower

The first examples are small. In Rhino and Grasshopper, a Python script places points in a diamond, joins them into planes, then repeats the shape into a curtain wall. "Just simple scripting has gone a long way," he said.

The bigger lever is building information modelling (BIM): a 3D model tied to a relational database that knows each wall's size and each floor's material, so the drawings carry the data. Revit is the largest BIM platform, and Autodesk's Dynamo add-in puts visual, low-code scripting on top of it. His tower workflow feeds in coordinates plus the levels and walls he wants and extrudes them through 100 levels into a full skyscraper, complete with elevations for the documentation set.

Dynamo was his gateway to programming, and its Python node, running IronPython, was his gateway to Python. One example takes a 100-foot rectangle, sets an origin and rotation axis, and loops through floors with a fixed rotation step to make a twisting tower. The visual graph can do it too, with more nodes and less fluency. He jokes the script is simple enough to teach a child.

The slides add pyRevit, an open-source rapid prototyping environment that lets people build Revit add-ins in Python instead of C# and the SDK. Since, by the slides' count, 90% of an architect's work is documents, that one matters for productivity.

## Open formats, open tools

Blender, open source and scriptable in Python, is gaining ground with designers. The BlenderBIM add-on writes Blender geometry out as IFC, the open BIM format, which Revit and Archicad can read, so a design can start in free tools and still land in the enterprise suite. In a few steps you go from massing to floor plans and sections. He calls that world candy.

## Daylight, energy and feedback from the finished building

Sustainable design gets the last section. Ladybug Tools, written in Python and runnable in any geometry engine (pip install lbt-ladybug), simulates sun and daylight inside the design environment, so you don't have to export to another package, and can lay out options to pick from. Honeybee, from the same developer, visualises daylight and energy analysis. On a tall tower, one floor's study often holds for every floor with the same orientation, shading aside.

After handover, Python collects metered energy data per floor and plots kilowatt-hours over time, so the team checks the building against the design instead of assuming it works. His vision for the future is Python as glue: XML, CSV, HTML and JSON from BIM and design models into pandas, then into analysis and Matplotlib charts, and out of the proprietary formats that used to box architects in.

## Who should watch

Architects, BIM managers and computational designers wondering where to start with Python, and software engineers curious how their language is used in building design. Developers looking for deep code will find a menu, not a meal. The credits slide, thanking pyRevit, Revit Python Wrapper, BlenderBIM and Ladybug Tools contributors, doubles as a reading list.

Title: Stock forecasting where the naive baseline wins on error and loses money
Description: Paweł Skrzypek and Anna Warno (7bulls.com) at Conf42 Python 2021 on ML time series forecasting, N-BEATS and a reinforcement learning trading agent
Body:
In stock prediction, the model that predicts tomorrow equals today often posts the best error metrics and is useless for investing. At Conf42 Python 2021, [Paweł Skrzypek](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Pawe_Skrzypek_Anna_Warno_ai_forecasting_methods_investments_portfolio_optimization), CTO, and Anna Warno, data scientist, both of 7bulls.com, surveyed the machine learning methods that overtook classical forecasting in the M4 and M5 competitions, then built a Python pipeline from yfinance data to N-BEATS forecasts to a toy reinforcement learning agent that trades.

Skrzypek gives the map and Warno the hands-on half. The demo is deliberately small, and they say so.

## Why did machine learning take over forecasting?

Until a few years before the talk, Skrzypek says, statistical methods ruled: ARMA and ARIMA, exponential smoothing, ARCH/GARCH, the Theta method. The M competitions, organised by the University of Nicosia and Professor Spyros Makridakis, changed that. M4 ran on 100,000 time series of varying length and frequency, its first and second places went to hybrid methods, and M5 was dominated by machine learning. On finance specifically: "for financial time series we are able to achieve over 60% of the accuracy, which is a very significant number for the financial time series," Paweł Skrzypek said at Conf42 Python 2021. Low for most series, but a real edge in portfolio construction. He mentions a first version of their platform already deployed for an investment fund in Luxembourg.

## Five methods worth knowing

- **ES-RNN hybrid**, the M4 winner by Slawek Smyl of Uber. Its exponential smoothing preprocessing is learned by backpropagation together with the network weights, it has its own way of ensembling and assigning models to series, and it uses residual, dilated LSTMs with attention.
- **N-BEATS**, pure machine learning, built from stacked blocks for trend, seasonality and generic patterns, with explainability, transfer learning and ensembling.
- **Facebook Prophet**, generalised additive models in a library. The easiest to start with, and it gives uncertainty intervals, not just a point.
- **GluonTS**, a full probabilistic forecasting framework with many models and transformations, cloud support and a strong research community. Harder than Prophet, much more powerful.
- **Tsetlin machines**, stochastic learning automata (an idea dating to the 1960s) that learn a probability distribution for each feature. The odd one out, and he treats it as such.

## From yfinance to N-BEATS

Warno's pipeline uses yfinance (Yahoo Finance data, for learning purposes) for daily open, high, low, close and volume, QuantStats for its 20-odd ready-made plots and metrics, and statsmodels for seasonal decomposition, transformations and outlier detection. She thinks statsmodels does a fine job of replacing R for classical analysis. A Kalman filter gets a mention for its smoothing.

The target is the closing price at daily and weekly frequency, which she calls very noisy and very hard to predict. Data splits into train, validation and test. Benchmarks first: naive (repeat the last value), exponential smoothing and ARIMA. Then N-BEATS from PyTorch Forecasting, built on PyTorch Lightning.

The punchline is in the comparison table. "naive method achieves surprisingly good scores. However, from investor point of view, its prediction is worthless," Anna Warno said. A model with good mean absolute error may only be the series shifted by a day, so she adds the metric investors care about: how often the model gets the direction of the move right. The numbers, she stresses, are examples that vary a lot between stocks.

## A reinforcement learning agent, kept honest

The last step treats the market as a game where profit is the score. Instead of an existing environment such as FinRL, she writes a minimal OpenAI Gym environment for one stock. The observation is past prices, shares and cash held, time remaining and the forecasts from the previous step. The reward is cash plus shares at the current price. Actions buy or sell a percentage: sell up to 100% of holdings, buy at most three shares a day. Episodes last 20 days to keep training short. The agent is PPO from Stable Baselines3 with small multilayer perceptrons, evaluated on the last 365 days with 365 different start dates.

Against buy-and-hold and a simple last-n-values rule, over four runs on randomly chosen companies, the agent is not the worst. She is explicit that this proves nothing, since fair comparison is hard, but it suggests the approach has potential.

## Who should watch

Python developers moving into time series, quants curious which ML forecasters are worth trying, and anyone about to report a stock model's MAE without checking the naive baseline. Skip it if you want a production trading system; this is a map and a sandbox.

Title: Counting trucks from orbit to measure a lockdown's economic cost
Description: Aakash Gupta (ThinkEvolve Consulting) at Conf42 Python 2021 on measuring economic activity from open satellite data via NO2, truck counts and surface water
Body:
Economists struggle to see a policy's impact on the ground; satellites see it from orbit. At Conf42 Python 2021, [Aakash Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Aakash_Gupta_Abha_Porwal__Apsal_K_earth_observations_measuring_economic_indicators), CEO and co-founder of ThinkEvolve Consulting, and interns Abha Porwal and Apsal K showed how open Earth observation data and Python can stand in for economic indicators: NO2 over industrial belts, trucks counted on highways from 10-metre Sentinel-2 pixels, and surface water measured with Google Earth Engine.

It's three talks in one: a survey of proxies, then two hands-on Python projects, then a refreshingly long list of everything that can go wrong.

## Which signals from space track the economy?

Gupta's list of proxies: air pollution over industrial belts, water quality, ESG signals such as deforestation and mangrove loss, surface water levels, and vehicle density on highways and at airports. The hypothesis is simple. "Measuring pollution can be a very good measure of identifying ongoing economic activity," Aakash Gupta said at Conf42 Python 2021.

The headline example uses Sentinel-5P NO2 composites of the Indian subcontinent. April 2019 shows red over the Delhi belt, the leather and tanning areas south of Varanasi, the steel and coal region around Jamshedpur, Mumbai, Gujarat, Hyderabad and Karachi. April 2020, after India's strict late-March lockdown, shows a sharp drop. The team saw the same in Germany and Wuhan, and no such effect where lockdowns were loosely enforced.

The rest of the tour moves fast: clearer, less turbid Venice canals once the boats stopped; a floating algae index over Lake Victoria from Sentinel-2 L2A; synthetic aperture radar, which sees through cloud, to track field-hospital construction in Spain and Wuhan; a Planet hackathon app built in 2020 to flag Amazon logging in near real time; and car and aircraft counts from 30-centimetre imagery with open-source detectors covering more than 60 vehicle classes, or Picterra if you prefer low-code.

## Counting trucks with pixels too big to see them

Very-high-resolution imagery costs money, and at Sentinel-2's 10 metres you can't see a car. Abha Porwal's project uses a quirk of the sensor instead. Sentinel-2's detectors sit in two parallel arrays, so each band sees a pixel at a slightly different moment. A moving truck lands in a different place in each band, which leaves a rainbow-like smear in RGB.

The pipeline is all Python:

- **xcube**, which serves Earth observation data as an analysis-ready cube on top of xarray, Zarr and Dask, plus the xcube_sh plugin to pull cubes from Sentinel Hub on the fly.
- **An OpenStreetMap road mask** built with the Overpass API from highway and motorway tags, for a bounding box around Visakhapatnam.
- **Six bands** (B02, B03, B04, B08, B11 and the SCL scene classification), with NDVI, NDWI and NDSI masks to remove vegetation, water and snow.
- **Thresholds on the blue-green and blue-red ratios**, since the moving-object signature is a pixel where blue beats green and red. Each truck shows up as one to three pixels.

One date in June produced 195 trucks for the region, and comparing 2019 with 2020 put the lockdown drop at up to 26%. She is upfront that counts are approximate at 10 metres and that clouds decide which dates you can use. The output is a relative truck density, not a census.

## Measuring water with Earth Engine

Apsal K uses Google Earth Engine through its Python API and geemap, the Jupyter-friendly wrapper. Draw a rectangle on the map, compute NDWI from Landsat 8's bands 3 and 6, count pixels above a threshold (conventionally 0.2 or 0.3) and multiply by pixel area to get surface water, plotted from January to May. Counting water bodies goes through OpenCV and scikit-learn: grayscale, smooth, threshold, then connected component analysis, keeping blobs above a minimum size. NDWI overestimates near built-up land, and small or oddly shaped ponds slip through.

## What breaks with open satellite data?

Gupta's closing list is worth the watch on its own. Revisit gaps mean you may get no image for your period, especially in remote areas. Ageing sensors produce bad data, so you need anomaly detection. Cloud cover makes optical imagery hard over equatorial belts and rainforests such as Indonesia, Myanmar and Cambodia. "You may notice a large gap during revisit times and you may not get an image for the period of interest," he warned. Commercial providers prioritise industrial and urban areas, and local law matters: in India, imagery finer than 50 centimetres goes through the national remote sensing agency, and defence sites must be blurred.

## Who should watch

Data scientists curious about geospatial work, economists and analysts looking for alternative data, and Python developers who want a tour of xcube and Earth Engine. No remote sensing background needed, though it helps to know what a spectral band is.

Title: Your first data pipeline can run on Google Sheets and a cron job
Description: Hui Xiang Chua (Essence) at Conf42 Python 2021 on starting data engineering side projects with Python scraping, ETL into Google Sheets and Data Studio
Body:
You don't need a warehouse budget to practise data engineering; a free spreadsheet API and a scheduled script will do. At Conf42 Python 2021, [Hui Xiang Chua](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Hui_Xiang_Chua_data_engineering_projects), Senior Analytics Manager at Essence in Singapore, showed two side projects built that way: a daily scraper that collected 1,680 Towards Data Science headlines into Google Sheets, and an image pipeline that produced the average face of each party's candidates in Singapore's 2020 general election.

It's a beginner-friendly, code-on-screen talk. Experienced data engineers will spot the shortcuts; that's rather the point.

## What does a data engineer actually do?

She frames the job as plumbing: pipelines that move data rather than liquid or gas, so data scientists and analysts get a consistent flow. At work her team pulls campaign data from advertising platforms through their APIs into a warehouse on Google Cloud Platform. The pattern is ETL, extract, transform, load, automated as much as possible to save time and keep things consistent and accurate. The transform step is where test records and junk get cleaned out. "So the data warehouse should be the place where there is a single source of truth and it should contain the most accurate data," Hui Xiang Chua said at Conf42 Python 2021.

For a side project with no budget, her suggestion is to swap the warehouse for Google Sheets (the API is free) and the BI tool for Google Data Studio (also free).

## Use case one: scraping a Medium publication every day

The target is Towards Data Science: author, recency and post title for every new article, plus a timestamp column for when the script ran. The stack is Beautiful Soup and Selenium for scraping, NumPy and pandas for transformation, and gspread with gspread-dataframe to write to the sheet. She walks through the Google API setup, the downloaded JSON credentials file and the spreadsheet scope, and flags authentication as the step that makes or breaks the whole thing. Without it, nothing is automated.

The scraping is where the real-world mess shows:

- **The page only loads about ten articles**, so Selenium clicks Show more 20 times, with a two-second sleep between clicks to look less like a bot (which, she admits, it is).
- **The text under the a tags is noisy**, with image captions mixed in. The pattern she found: three blank elements between posts. The script finds runs of three identical elements and takes the fields after them.
- **When a caption sneaks in first**, the title shifts position. Captions are under 20 characters, so an if-else on length picks the right line.
- **Overlap between days** is handled by appending to the existing sheet data and dropping duplicates on author and title in pandas.

Scheduling is plain Windows Task Scheduler pointing at the virtualenv's Python and the script. Her honest assessment of the output is roughly 90 to 95% clean data, with outliers left for manual fixes. Over six weeks the sheet collected 1,680 articles, enough to start text mining for the hottest topics in data science, and Data Studio put a friendlier interface on top.

## Use case two: ELT, and an average face

The second project flips the order to extract, load, transform, which she relates to data lakes, while noting that in her own work it's ETL most of the time. The source is The Straits Times' interactive page of GE2020 candidates. Selenium runs headless with the GPU disabled so the scrolling page loads fully, Beautiful Soup collects the img tags, a bit of trial and error finds where the candidate photos start and end in the list, blank alt texts are skipped, and each image is saved with the candidate's name and the extension taken from the URL. The transform is an open-source face-averaging library from GitHub, run once per party with at least ten candidates. She credits the wonders of open source for making it quick.

## The order she recommends

Start from the analysis you or your data science team want to do, work out what data that needs, then write the Python that automates the ETL or ELT. She covers more of this on her blog, Data Double Confirm.

## Who should watch

Analysts and data scientists who want a portfolio project that proves they can feed their own models, and students looking for a first pipeline. Production data engineers can skip it, or send it to the intern.

Title: Stop writing tests by hand and let Hypothesis pick the inputs
Description: Zac Hatfield-Dodds (Australian National University) at Conf42 Python 2021 on property-based testing, the Hypothesis ghostwriter and adaptive fuzzing
Body:
Most automated test suites automate one thing: re-running examples a human picked. At Conf42 Python 2021, [Zac Hatfield-Dodds](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Zac_HatfieldDodds_stop_writing_tests_fuzzing_propertybased_testing), a researcher at the Australian National University and a maintainer of Hypothesis, argued for automating the rest: let the computer choose the inputs (property-based testing), write the test code (the Hypothesis ghostwriter) and decide what to run (adaptive fuzzing with HypoFuzz).

The title is provocative on purpose. He wants you to keep testing, just not by typing out input-output pairs.

## What's left to automate in a test suite?

Testing, in his definition, is running code to see what it does: choose inputs, run, check the result, repeat. Tools like pytest automate the repeat. Choosing inputs, deciding what to run and writing assertions for a particular output are still manual.

He shows this by growing a test for sorting. Hard-coded examples become a parametrised test, which scales but still needs every expected output worked out by hand. Without the answers, you can compare to a trusted implementation (the pre-refactor version, a single-threaded one, a slow bubble sort). Without that, check that the output is in order. But the empty list is always in order, so check the length. Then that the set of elements matches, which lets an evil sort turn 1, 2, 1 into 1, 2, 2. Finally, compare collections.Counter of input and output. Two properties, ordered output and the same elements, are the full definition of sorting, and he has just invented property-based testing.

## Let the random number generator be the pessimist

The remaining flaw is that you still pick the inputs, so you'll never test anything you didn't think of when writing the code. Hypothesis takes a description of the data instead: lists of mixed integers and floats, or lists of strings. Run the sort test with it and it fails at once, because NaN compares unequal to itself. His starter plan has three steps: pip install hypothesis, skim the docs, find lots of bugs.

## A ghostwriter for the test you were going to skip

The Hypothesis ghostwriter writes tests from a function signature. Pointed at sorted, it immediately covers the key and reverse arguments his hand-written demo forgot. It can also generate tests for idempotence (sorting twice changes nothing), equivalence between two implementations, commutative and associative properties, and the one he recommends to everyone: round trips, such as save then load or compress then decompress. "So for pretty much everyone I would recommend writing these round trip tests," Zac Hatfield-Dodds said at Conf42 Python 2021, because IO and persistence cross many abstraction layers and break more often than you'd expect.

The JSON round-trip demo is the best part. Hypothesis reports two distinct failures: NaN isn't equal to itself, and infinity with allow_nan off is invalid under strict JSON. Patch those with an assume and it finds a third: a list containing NaN does compare equal to itself, because CPython's list equality checks identity first as a performance shortcut. The real fix is to stop generating NaN at all.

## Migrating an existing test, one refactor at a time

You don't have to throw out your suite. His example is git-like business logic: create an empty repo, check out a new branch, assert it's active. Make the branch name a parameter, then a Hypothesis strategy that returns the same name, so nothing changes yet but the intent is clearer. Then widen the strategy. Git's real branch-name rules are long, so he settles for ASCII letters of reasonable length, and finally any repository, not just an empty one.

## Fuzzing all night

The last step hands the choice of what to run to the machine. Google's Atheris wraps libFuzzer and runs one function for hours or days, which suits C extensions and sanitisers, and it works with Hypothesis-generated inputs. HypoFuzz, his own pure-Python tool at hypofuzz.com, runs a whole test suite at once and spends time on the tests making the fastest coverage progress. In the live dashboard, run on hypothesmith, his generator of Python source code, it had found a failure in the black formatter. "This is genuinely a new bug to me, and so I'm going to have to go report that after the talk," he said.

## Who should watch

Any Python developer who writes pytest tests, especially for parsers, serialisers, data pipelines or financial code. It's one of the clearest introductions to property-based testing you'll find, from the person who maintains the main library for it.

Title: A decade of mistakes, and the CEO who wanted servers in a nuclear silo
Description: Bojan Miletic (Softerrific) at Conf42 Python 2021 on ten years of career mistakes, from deleting production to a nuclear silo pitch, and the lessons
Body:
The best career advice often comes from someone who ran sudo rm -rf / on a production server and lived. At Conf42 Python 2021, [Bojan Miletic](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Bojan_Miletic_server_nuclear_silo), CEO of Softerrific, told a decade of his own mistakes as anecdotes, from that midnight deletion to talking a blockchain CEO out of buying a decommissioned nuclear silo, with a plain lesson after each.

There is no code in this one. It's a story talk, and a funny one, about the non-technical things that sink technical projects.

## How do you learn Linux administration?

His way: in the middle of the night, deleting a directory with sudo privileges and a path that turned out to be the root of the disk. For a brief moment there was nothing on the hard drive and the site kept serving from memory. Then came a new server, all the requirements, the deployment, the permissions and a DNS switch, in one panicked sitting. "If you want to switch from Red Bull or coffee, I warmly recommend deleting production servers," Bojan Miletic said at Conf42 Python 2021.

The early-career hits keep coming: two or three weeks writing code in plain Notepad and uploading it over FTP straight to production (safe enough, he jokes, because the client was asleep in the USA), versioning by copying files with a timestamp until a YouTube video introduced him to version control, and discovering git branches roughly two years after that.

## Why do teams build the wrong thing?

His first startup was a search engine that returned listings in under 15 milliseconds and had no monetisation plan, which they noticed after a year and a half. His takeaway isn't a 50-page business plan, just knowing how the thing will make money before you build it. Staffing it with juniors led by him, at six months of experience, taught him that "Seniors are expensive, but they are less expensive than juniors."

The second startup, a social network, adds three more. Hype-driven tech: they picked MongoDB, and two years later most of his database code was turning it back into a relational model. His rule now is that in 95% of cases a relational database is perfectly fine, and if you do pick NoSQL, know why. Ship to users early: they spent a year and a half before anyone used it, then nobody did. And talk to your team: when he asked each of 15 people what they were building, he "got 15 different answers, myself included".

## How do you say no to a client?

Consulting brought the best stories. Clients skim a 20-page proposal for the price, so talk to them first and find out what they actually care about and fear; compete on price alone and someone will always be cheaper. One client wanted a three-dimensional video player; Bojan spent two weeks on it, and by the time he had a design the client had forgotten asking. Another client's friend said Python was no good because his company used Java, until Bojan asked to speak to the friend directly.

Then the title story. At the 2018 blockchain peak, the CEO of a client building a new blockchain wanted to move everything from AWS into a nuclear silo, which apparently sell decommissioned for about 800,000. Technical arguments about configuring AWS security went nowhere, so he switched to a metaphor: "using nuclear silos to secure your blockchain servers is the same thing as buying a dog and putting it next to your computer to ward off the hackers." It worked. The real problem, he notes, was that nobody was using the blockchain. Find product-market fit first, then solve its problems.

## Know your limits, and keep your evenings

He closes on limits. His teenage Flash website was five megabytes of unstoppable music that took 20 minutes to load on a friend's dial-up, and the only frontend he'll now admit to writing is a red CSS background. A no-fixed-hours experiment with a junior team ended in chaos and 12 to 14-hour days, so they went back to regular hours. His final point, made at a programming conference: personal life matters more than your programming skills.

## Who should watch

Junior developers who want the mistakes without paying for them, first-time founders and tech leads, and freelancers learning to handle clients. Senior engineers will laugh in recognition.

Title: Pythonic code is a quality bar, and linters are the lint filter
Description: Ammara Laeeq at Conf42 Python 2021 on what makes code Pythonic, how the Zen of Python, PEP 8 and linters enforce it, and the idioms worth adopting
Body:
Writing Python and writing Pythonic code are not the same thing, and the gap shows up in maintenance budgets. At Conf42 Python 2021, [Ammara Laeeq](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Ammara_Laeeq_tools_tips), a Python developer from Pakistan with more than six years in the language, made the case that idiomatic code is a quality signal, showed the three tools that keep a codebase honest (the Zen of Python, PEP 8 and linters), and finished with a long run of before-and-after idioms.

It's a fundamentals talk, pitched at developers who came to Python from C++ or Java and still write it with an accent.

## What makes code Pythonic?

"Any program, function or block of code that follows style guidelines and make use of Python's unique capabilities or language features is said to be pythonic code," Ammara Laeeq said at Conf42 Python 2021. She ties it to code quality, which she defines in three parts: it does what it's supposed to do, it has no known defects (her analogy is a detergent that's fine on everyday laundry and useless on a hard stain), and it's readable, maintainable and extendable. The last one matters most, because the person who wrote the code won't be around to maintain it forever. Bad quality costs you clarity, efficiency (maintenance costs skyrocket) and your credibility as a programmer.

## Three tools, from philosophy to enforcement

**The Zen of Python.** Tim Peters' aphorisms, printed by typing import this in a shell, and sung as lyrics by Barry Warsaw in May 2020. She walks through the practical ones: explicit is better than implicit (name variables for what they hold), flat is better than nested (itertools.product instead of nested loops), errors should never pass silently unless explicitly silenced.

**PEP 8.** One statement per line, four spaces per indentation level, spaces over tabs, 79 characters per line and 72 for comments and docstrings (PEP 257 covers docstrings), imports at the top and one per line with standard library first, then third party, then your own, and no wildcard imports. Pick one string quote style and stick to it. Naming gets a full checklist: short lowercase modules, PascalCase classes without the word Class, an Error suffix on exceptions, SNAKE_CASE constants, self and cls as first arguments, a trailing underscore to dodge keywords (class_, not clss), and one or two leading underscores for non-public and name-mangled attributes. She also recommends a single point of return per function, which is more of a house preference than PEP 8, and early-return fans will have opinions.

**Linters.** Her best analogy: lint is what sticks to clothes in the washing machine, and the lint filter is what saves them. She splits lint into logical (errors, dangerous patterns, unintended results) and stylistic (convention violations), then maps the tools: IDEs mostly stylistic, Pylint both, pycodestyle stylistic, pydocstyle for docstrings, PyFlakes logical.

## When should the linter run?

She weighs three moments: as you write, when you check in, and when tests run. Linting only at test time means a big pile of fixes a couple of times a sprint. Her pick is the daily check-in. "So in my opinion, the best choice is to use the option of when it's checked in," she said, because half an hour at the end of the working day keeps quality up with the least effort.

## The idioms

The second half is a catalogue, each with the non-idiomatic version first:

- Swap with a, b = b, a, no temp variable.
- Don't compare to True, False or None with ==; use is not rather than not ... is; treat empty sequences as false.
- Replace chains of or comparisons with in.
- Loop with for element in my_list, reversed() for backwards, enumerate() when you need the index.
- for ... else for search loops, so the else runs only when the loop never broke.
- iter() with a sentinel and functools.partial to read a file in 32-byte chunks.
- startswith and endswith over slicing, join over += in a loop.
- Context managers for files, locks, ignoring a specific OSError, redirecting stdout and temporary decimal contexts.
- List multiplication, star-unpacking with _ as a throwaway, list comprehensions and dictionary idioms.

Her closing caveat is the right one: these are powerful constructs, to be used where they help, not for the sake of using them.

## Who should watch

Developers in their first year or two of Python, team leads writing a style guide, and anyone who still writes for i in range(len(x)). Seasoned Pythonistas will know most of it, though the for-else and iter-with-sentinel sections catch plenty of people out.

Title: Your Python build probably isn't reproducible. Bazel gets you most of the way
Description: Gaspare Vitta (FCA Fiat Chrysler Automobiles) at Conf42 Python 2021 on hermetic, reproducible Python and Flask builds with Bazel
Body:
Run the same commit on two machines and you will most likely get two different builds. At Conf42 Python 2021, [Gaspare Vitta](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Gaspare_Vitta_Reproducible_Builds_Bazel), CI/CD Engineer for Autonomous Driving at FCA Fiat Chrysler Automobiles, showed how Bazel makes a Python project hermetic down to the interpreter, built a Flask app that hashes identically across clean builds, and then admitted, to his credit, that it still wasn't fully reproducible.

That last twist is the reason to watch. Most build talks stop at the green checkmark.

## What counts as reproducible?

He uses the Reproducible Builds project's definition: given the same source code, build environment and build instructions, anyone can recreate bit-by-bit identical copies of all specified artifacts. The pay-off is a smaller attack surface, knowing exactly which sources an artifact came from, and much faster builds because intermediate artifacts can be cached safely.

Two enemies stand in the way. The first is inputs that aren't source code: compilers, build tools, third-party libraries. Every reference has to be unambiguous, pinned to an exact version or hash, and ideally checked into source control. That's what hermetic means, and it buys you cherry-picking: check out a two-month-old release, fix a bug and rebuild it with the compiler it was built with, not today's. The second enemy is internal randomness. Timestamps are the usual culprit, and he's blunt about them: you're already tracking the environment in version control, so get rid of them. Initialise your variables too.

## How does Bazel enforce it?

Sandboxing. Bazel runs each action in a working directory that contains only the declared inputs, so a compiler can't wander off and read something you forgot to list; undeclared input means a failed build. Caching is the other half, and he cites up to 50 times faster repeated builds.

The walkthrough builds everything from the WORKSPACE file:

- **The interpreter itself.** An http_archive rule downloads the Python 3.8.3 tarball from python.org, pinned by SHA-256, and runs configure, make and make install as patch commands. The host Python is never used.
- **Python rules.** rules_python 0.1.0, also fetched by hash.
- **A toolchain.** py_runtime points at the freshly built interpreter, py_runtime_pair wraps it (Python 3 only), and register_toolchains goes at the very end of WORKSPACE, a placement he stresses.
- **Dependencies.** A requirements.txt with every package, child dependencies included, pinned with hashes, loaded through pip_install with the interpreter target overridden to the one Bazel built. No virtualenv, no manual pip install: you list deps on the target and you're done.

A small pytest target checks that the running interpreter is the Bazel one and the version is 3.8.3. Then a Flask app prints both interpreters side by side: Bazel's 3.8.3 and the 3.8.5 from pyenv on his Mac.

## So is it reproducible?

He builds, takes the MD5 of the binary, runs bazel clean --expunge_async, builds again from scratch, and gets the same hash. Done? Not quite. Building Python through patch commands means it's compiled with whatever GCC and system libraries the host has, and those aren't pinned. His three ways out: run Bazel inside a Docker image with a pinned GCC, check in a precompiled interpreter binary, or use Nix and its Bazel rules to bring system packages in hermetically.

"From now on, don't take for granted that your build is reproducible, since most probably is not," Gaspare Vitta said at Conf42 Python 2021. The example code is on GitHub at gasparev/reproducible-python-bazel, ready to reuse as the base for your next project.

## Who should watch

Python teams in regulated or safety-critical work (he builds for autonomous driving, where knowing exactly what went into a binary isn't optional), monorepo owners eyeing Bazel, and anyone whose CI has ever behaved differently from a laptop. It's code-heavy: expect Starlark, not slides about philosophy.

Title: Production Celery is a pipeline, a retry policy and a memory cap
Description: Vishrut Kohli (Grofers) at Conf42 Python 2021 on turning Celery into a production-ready task queue with pipelines, tuning, retries and monitoring
Body:
Getting a task onto a queue is the easy part; keeping the workers that consume it fast, honest and alive is where teams lose sleep. At Conf42 Python 2021, [Vishrut Kohli](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2021_Vishrut_Kohli_productionready_distributed_task_queue_system_celery_django_queing), Software Engineer at Grofers, walked through a Celery setup in five steps: build it as a pipeline, tune it, make it resilient, plan for the SOS moment, and monitor it. His definition of production-ready is four words: efficient, scalable, transparent, resilient.

It's a practical, config-level talk with a running e-commerce warehouse metaphor and, as promised on the agenda, bad jokes.

## Why put a queue in front of the database at all?

His opening story is a mall with an IoT sensor at the door that fires an API request per visitor and bumps a counter in the database. It works until he streams a football match, the crowd arrives, and concurrent requests time out on database locking. The counter comes out low. The fix is a task queue: the web server enqueues and returns 200, and the database consumes at its own pace. Real time becomes eventually consistent, which is fine when you only read the count once, at closing time.

On brokers he keeps it simple: RabbitMQ if you need several workers on different queues and persistence across shutdowns (at the cost of more setup and upkeep), Redis if you want a quick messaging system that's easy to run.

## One big task is worse than a pipeline of small ones

The warehouse has three jobs: picking, packing, delivery. One worker doing all three scales only by cloning the whole worker. Split into a pipeline of specialised tasks and you get three wins he lists: you can see the bottleneck and scale just that stage, each stage can run on hardware that suits it (more CPU here, more memory there), and retries restart from the last succeeded step instead of from the beginning. For a sale-day spike he prefers horizontal scaling, a second makeshift warehouse, since the load drops back afterwards.

## Measure first, then batch and pick the right pool

"It is always better to benchmark before moving to any further optimization because in my experience I have seen if we go by intuition, either we end up over optimizing the system or optimizing wrong parts of the architecture," Vishrut Kohli said at Conf42 Python 2021. In his load test the picking worker had far more queued tasks than any other stage, so that's where he started.

The tuning list:

- **Batching.** An order aggregator task chunks orders so one picker grabs ten at a time, cutting trips to the aisle (the database) tenfold. The trade-off: retries and failures now happen per batch, so one bad order retries all ten.
- **Split IO-bound from CPU-bound work.** Gevent or eventlet pools for tasks that wait on IO; the prefork pool, built on multiprocessing, for number crunching. It's the -P and -c flags on the worker command.
- **Use -Ofair** when task durations vary, so work goes to free workers rather than round robin. It costs some coordination but behaves far more predictably.
- **Ignore results you never read.** CELERY_IGNORE_RESULT saves calls to the result backend.

## Retries need backoff, jitter and late acks

Software errors are inevitable, as he quotes Sentry. Start with automatic retries and a circuit breaker (his example: five retries, then give up). With a 10-second interval, five linear retries give a downstream service about 50 seconds to recover; exponential backoff at 10, 20, 40, 80 and 160 seconds stretches that to 160. Turn on late acknowledgement so a task isn't marked done until a worker actually finishes it, which saves it when the worker dies mid-flight. Add retry jitter so two tasks that deadlocked don't retry in lockstep and deadlock again. Whatever still fails goes to a dead letter queue.

## When memory climbs and nobody owns the leak

His SOS step: check CPU and memory first. High memory that your own code can't explain is often a leak inside a C-based library. Celery's --max-tasks-per-child and --max-memory-per-child recycle the worker process once a threshold is hit, which clears it out without anyone finding the leak. For watching it all he uses Flower, which can purge queues, show acknowledgement rates, manage workers and expose an HTTP API to feed your own alerts, with the RabbitMQ admin panel as a broker-level alternative.

## Who should watch

Python and Django developers who already run Celery and want a checklist of the settings that matter, or anyone about to put their first background worker into production. If you've tuned prefetch and pools for years, it's a refresher.

Title: Streamlit lets data scientists skip the frontend ticket
Description: Steven Kolawole (SCITYLANA) at Conf42 Python 2021 on building data apps in plain Python with Streamlit, and where its convenience runs out
Body:
Steven Kolawole, a data scientist speaking from Lagos, Nigeria, made the case at Conf42 Python 2021 for Streamlit as the shortest path from a notebook to a shareable data app: a Python script with a few st. calls becomes an interactive web page, with no HTML, CSS, JavaScript or Flask in sight. His honest conclusion: it is superb for showing a model or an analysis quickly, and the wrong tool once you need custom layouts or real application features.

It is a beginner-friendly talk with a couple of live demos, and it closes with a cons list, which is more than most framework talks offer.

## What problem is Streamlit solving?

He describes the usual route from analysis to app. Explore in .ipynb files. Share notebooks if your audience can read them. For a wider audience, copy the functions into a .py file, wrap them in Flask, then build a frontend with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, likely plus a framework. In an organisation you hand a specification to the software engineering team instead, get a polished app a week or two later, and hear that the next update can happen in two or three months.

His pain points are relatable: the back and forth over specs, no way to ship your own updates, and the small matter that most data scientists are not designers. He jokes that he cannot tell blue from yellow and is bad at UI design. Most would rather spend the time on insights and models.

## How little code is a Streamlit app?

After pip install streamlit, running streamlit hello opens a gallery of demos in the browser, including an animated plot he says takes under 15 lines. Your own app is a hello.py that imports streamlit as st, run with streamlit run.

His best demo has a story behind it. His younger sister was starting out in data science and working through statistics and probability, so he built her a page where she could see the distributions she was studying. A title, a line of text, an st.selectbox offering normal or uniform, NumPy generating random samples, and st.line_chart drawing them. Switch the select box and the chart redraws.

> "It's quite amazing that we're able to come up with this little app in less than six lines of code."

Steven Kolawole said that at Conf42 Python 2021. Widgets such as checkboxes, select boxes, sliders and charts are ready-made methods, and Streamlit works with Plotly, Bokeh, pydeck, Matplotlib and seaborn, as well as pandas and scikit-learn.

## Real apps from the gallery

He tours the community gallery, with examples from NYC Uber ride-sharing data to computer vision and finance. Two examples stand out. Streamlit's own self-driving car demo runs semantic search over the Udacity self-driving car dataset and a real-time YOLO object detector in under 300 lines of code. A friend's Lagos apartment price estimator, built on property listing data, takes city, number of bedrooms, bathrooms and toilets, and whether you want an estate, then returns an estimated price and a range, in roughly 100 lines.

## Where does Streamlit stop being the answer?

His cons list:

- **The convenience-flexibility trade-off.** The UI is generated for you, so you cannot freely rearrange it, for example placing charts side by side as you like.
- **Upload size.** His slides cite a 50 MB maximum for data upload.
- **Limited support for video and animation.**
- **No complex app features.** User authentication, newsletter subscriptions or chatbots belong in Flask or Django.

His verdict is still positive. For an NLP model he wanted to check, he could spin up an app in under 30 minutes, against a Flask route that needs a frontend stack which can take months or years to master.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and ML engineers who want a demo or internal tool without filing a frontend request, and anyone new to Python data apps. If you already ship Streamlit apps, the cons list is a useful checklist to show your manager.

Title: Shopyo wants to give Flask the structure Django ships with
Description: Abdur-Rahmaan Janhangeer (Compiler Alchemy) at Conf42 Python 2021 on Shopyo, a framework adding Django-style modules, boxes and commands to Flask
Body:
Abdur-Rahmaan Janhangeer, founder of Compiler Alchemy, a Shopyo maintainer and a member of the Python user group of Mauritius, used his Conf42 Python 2021 talk to pitch Shopyo, version 3.9.4 at the time: a framework built on Flask that borrows Django's code organisation, shareable modules and management commands while staying a Flask app underneath. His pitch is simple. Flask developers should not have to pick between flexibility and a sensible project layout.

It is a short talk by a maintainer about his own project, and it is upfront about when you should not use it.

## Why do people pick Django, and why do they pick Flask?

He starts with the Stack Overflow survey, where Flask and Django top the Python web frameworks, and with what draws people to each. Django gets you started quickly under pressure. It is mature, widely adopted in production, has a package for nearly everything (geospatial being a field where Django is often the only choice), scales in code organisation as the app grows, and has already fixed the common security holes you would otherwise rediscover yourself.

Flask gets ten lines to a running app and then stays out of your way. You pick plugins like ingredients and roll your own style. The catch, unstated but implied, is that every Flask project ends up rebuilding the same scaffolding.

## What does Shopyo add?

Shopyo's answer is to make that scaffolding the default. A Shopyo app is a set of modules, and each module looks familiar to any Django developer: static, templates and tests folders, a view, models, forms, an info.json describing the module. Even the view file is optional, so a module can exist purely for organisation. Modules can be shared between Shopyo projects, and a concept called boxes groups modules into a higher level of organisation that can also be shared.

Out of the box you also get migrations, asset management with collectstatic and a get-asset helper so the same code works in development and production, a theming system switchable from an admin panel, mail, secrets management, config profiles, an application factory, and starter fixtures for login, logout and an admin user. The part he stresses most is the project's own documentation and tests: Sphinx is set up by default, along with test fixtures, so neither gets forgotten. Commands mirror Django's: start a new project, initialise the database, run the dev server, migrate.

## Is it reliable?

The question he says people ask silently is whether a new framework is safe to bet on. Shopyo does not maintain its own middleware. It leans on Flask-Login, Flask-Admin, Flask-Migrate, Flask-WTF, SQLAlchemy and Flask-Mailman, all long-lived packages. And it tries to stay transparent: what Shopyo does is visible in app.py and can be changed.

Why not just use Django, then? Because you want the Flask ecosystem and SQLAlchemy, and more power on top of them.

## Who should use it, and who should not?

He answers the intimidating-file-tree objection himself.

> "If you want something maybe very simple, maybe this is not the project."

Abdur-Rahmaan Janhangeer said that at Conf42 Python 2021. Shopyo is aimed at Flask projects that will grow into many features and many contributors, where the Django-style layout pays for itself. A single-endpoint microservice does not need boxes.

## Who should watch

Flask developers who keep copying the same blueprint, migration and auth setup into every new project, and Django developers curious about what Flask looks like with familiar furniture.

Title: Kafka from Python, explained one pizza order at a time
Description: Francesco Tisiot (Aiven.io) at Conf42 Python 2021 on Apache Kafka for event-driven apps - topics, partitions, consumer groups and Kafka Connect
Body:
Francesco Tisiot, Developer Advocate at Aiven, gave Conf42 Python 2021 an introduction to Apache Kafka for Python developers, with every concept acted out by pizza orders in Jupyter notebooks. His case for Kafka is about latency: batch pipelines add a delay between an event happening and anyone knowing about it, and for many events, a stolen credit card or a delivery rider's position, a late answer is a useless one.

It is a beginner-friendly talk that still covers the parts people get wrong in production: partitioning and ordering, offsets, and consumer groups. The managed Kafka in the demos is Aiven's, shown briefly. Everything else is plain kafka-python.

## Why not just write to the database?

The old way, as he puts it, is an application that collects a few records, pushes them to a database in a batch, and reads in batches too. The delay is the batch time, anything from milliseconds to hours. Event-driven applications react the moment something happens and usually emit events that other applications react to in turn: an order goes to the restaurant, a finished pizza summons a courier.

> "The information has value only if delivered on time."

Francesco Tisiot said that at Conf42 Python 2021, talking about the courier's GPS position. Ten minutes old, it is just trivia.

## What Kafka actually is

At heart, an append-only, immutable log. Event zero goes in, then event one, and nothing gets updated in place. If reality changes, you write a new event. Different kinds of events go in different logs, called topics. Kafka runs as a cluster of brokers, and each topic is copied across them according to its replication factor. Lose a broker and Kafka notices the missing copy and rebuilds it elsewhere.

To Kafka, an event is a key-value pair of bytes, typically up to about a megabyte. JSON is readable but repeats every field name on the wire. Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry keep the schema out of the payload. Producers need to know where the brokers are, how to authenticate and how to serialise. Consumers need the same plus which topics to read, and they commit offsets back to Kafka so a crashed consumer resumes where it stopped.

The first demo has a good gotcha. A new consumer does not see the order sent before it subscribed, because by default it starts at the end of the topic, not the beginning. Set auto_offset_reset to earliest if you want history.

## Partitions buy throughput and cost you global ordering

A topic must not be limited to one broker's disk, so it is split into partitions, and those are what actually live on the nodes. The producer picks a partition by hashing the key, so the same key always lands in the same partition. That matters because Kafka guarantees ordering only within a partition. Three events across two partitions can come back blue, red, yellow instead of blue, yellow, red. The design question becomes which events need relative ordering: all of Luigi's orders, yes; Luigi's versus Mario's, nobody cares.

The payoff is parallelism. More partitions mean more producers and more consumers working at once. Consumers in the same group split the partitions between them without overlap. In the demo, two consumers each own one partition, keys route as predicted, and when one consumer dies its partition moves to the survivor after a timeout. Retention can be set by time, by size, or both, and the first limit reached wins.

## Consumer groups and Kafka Connect

Reading a message does not delete it. Two pizza makers in one consumer group share the orders. A billing application in its own group gets a full copy at its own pace. He shows both at once, with the billing consumer reading from the earliest offset and catching the order the first consumer missed.

The last section is about writing less code. Kafka Connect moves data between Kafka and other systems with a config file: change data capture from an existing database into Kafka, or out to any JDBC database, PostgreSQL, BigQuery or S3. The demo sends records with their schema embedded, configures a JDBC sink with auto-create, and a pizza table appears in Postgres and keeps filling as new orders arrive.

As an Italian, he would like it noted that the pineapple and chocolate pizzas in the demo are allowed, just not in Italy.

## Who should watch

Python developers who keep hearing Kafka and want the mental model in under an hour, plus anyone about to choose a partition key. Seasoned Kafka operators will know all of it.

Title: Python forensics tools have to hold up in court, not just run
Description: Gajendra Deshpande (KLS Gogte Institute of Technology) at Conf42 Python 2021 on building cyber forensic tools with hashlib, Whoosh, Pillow and Mutagen
Body:
Gajendra Deshpande, Assistant Professor at KLS Gogte Institute of Technology, showed at Conf42 Python 2021 how far you get toward a cyber forensics toolkit with the standard library and a handful of pure-Python packages. His framing is the part most developers never think about: forensic code is only useful if its output is admissible, so the investigation process and the legal standard come before the first import.

It is an introductory talk, a tour of small, readable examples rather than one finished application, and it works well as a map of which library does which job.

## Why does a court care which language you used?

He starts with the investigation process: identification, collection, validation, examination, preservation and presentation. The procedural details are the kind you only learn from people who have done it. If a machine is off, do not turn it on. If it is on, do live forensics or pull the plug, because a clean shutdown changes the evidence. Collect the most volatile evidence first. Work only on an image, never the original, and store seized drives in antistatic or Faraday bags.

Then the legal angle. In US federal courts, the Daubert standard governs expert testimony: has the technique been tested in the field, peer reviewed, does it have a known error rate, standards and general acceptance? He cites Brian Carrier's 2003 paper, which concluded that open source tools may meet those guidelines more clearly than closed source ones. That is an argument for Python with a caveat he states himself: it is not automatic. The program must be explainable in words, testable, with error rates calculated and validated independently.

## Hashes are how evidence proves it was not touched

The validation step is the most concrete demo. With hashlib and SHA-256, he hashes a sentence built from two concatenated strings and the same sentence written in one go: the digests match. Add one trailing space and they do not. Scale that up to a disk image and you have the check that the analysed copy is identical to the seized original. He notes that the use of hash algorithms is recognised in Indian law under the Information Technology Act 2000.

> "You cannot perform forensics analysis on the original data. You need to perform forensic analysis on the copy of the data."

Gajendra Deshpande said that at Conf42 Python 2021, and it is the rule the whole toolkit is built around.

## A library per evidence type

The rest is a walk through the toolbox:

- **Built-ins first.** dir() lists what you already have. range() can generate address lists, and the os module lists directory contents without any third-party dependency.
- **Search and indexing.** A plain line-by-line keyword search over files gets you clues. Whoosh, a pure-Python search library by Matt Chaput, adds fielded indexing, BM25F scoring and a query language. It has not been updated since 2016 but still works.
- **Images.** Pillow reads EXIF data, including GPS tags, so a photo from a seized phone can say where it was taken.
- **Screens.** pyscreenshot grabs the full screen or a bounding box. He is clear that performance is not the goal in forensics. Preserving the evidence is.
- **Audio and documents.** Mutagen identifies audio files by content rather than extension (renaming a file does not fool it) and reads bitrate and length. PyPDF extracts PDF metadata.
- **Executables.** pefile parses Windows Portable Executable headers, sections and resources, and can flag suspicious or malformed values and detect packers.
- **Text at scale.** A disk image holds far too much text to read by hand, so NLP libraries do the triage with tokenisation, n-grams, part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition. He separates English-first tools (NLTK, spaCy), multilingual ones (Stanza, Polyglot) and Indian-language ones such as the Indic NLP library.

## Who should watch

Python developers curious about digital forensics, and students who want a reading list of libraries. If you already run a forensics lab, the Daubert section is the part worth the time.

Title: git commit --amend does not delete your secrets
Description: Rob Richardson (Cyral) at Conf42 Python 2021 on what lives in the .git folder - objects, refs, hooks, config, index, reflog - built up from an empty repo
Body:
Rob Richardson, Developer Advocate at Cyral and Microsoft MVP, spent his Conf42 Python 2021 talk opening every file in a .git folder, starting from an empty directory and a git init. The moment that lands hardest: amend a commit to strip out a secret you checked in, and the old commit, its tree and the blob with the secret are all still sitting in the objects folder. Rewriting history is not deleting it.

There are no slides. It is a terminal, VS Code pointed at the .git folder itself, and a visualiser he wrote, Git Explorer, that draws the object graph. If you have ever typed git commands without knowing what they do on disk, this is the talk that fills in the picture.

## What is actually inside a commit?

He makes one commit and goes hunting in .git/objects. The commit hash's first two characters are a folder and the rest is a file. Open it and you get binary noise, because it is zlib-compressed, so he inflates it with a tiny script of his own. Then he switches to the built-in way: git cat-file -t for the type, -p for the contents.

Three node types fall out. A commit holds the author, committer, timestamp, message, parent and a pointer to a tree. A tree is a directory listing of names, permissions and hashes. A blob is the file content. Each commit of a single root-level file creates three nodes, which is why two commits leave six objects. You only need enough of a hash to be unique, which is why logs show seven characters.

Watching the graph grow explains a lot of Git's behaviour. git add creates the blob straight away, before any commit exists. A commit adds the tree and commit nodes. Identical content is stored once and reused: the same file in two folders is still one blob.

## Why --amend leaves the secret behind

He modifies a file, commits, notices a secret, removes it and amends. git log shows a clean history. Git Explorer shows the orphaned commit still there, its tree pointing at the blob with the secret line.

> "If I've pushed this repository into a public spot, or if I've shared this with anyone, even if it's just on my local machine, I should probably consider those secrets as exposed."

Rob Richardson said that at Conf42 Python 2021. Dangling objects do get collected by git gc eventually, which Git runs on its own from time to time. Even after he runs git gc by hand at the end and everything is packed into one pack file and its .idx, the dangling commit with the secrets is still there. Rotate the key.

## Branches are name tags

The refs folder demystifies the rest. A branch is a file containing a commit hash. HEAD is a file that usually says ref: refs/heads/main, and the scary detached HEAD message just means it holds a hash instead. Tags are the same idea in refs/tags. He moves main with git update-ref, what he calls a ninja move: it does no merge and reconciles nothing, it just picks the label up and drops it somewhere else. A bare repository created as a local server is simply the contents of a .git folder with no working directory, and pushing to it creates remote-tracking refs under refs/remotes/origin.

## Hooks, config, index, reflog

Hooks are shell or Perl scripts with a .sample suffix. Remove the suffix and they fire, pre-commit, prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg and pre-push among them. You cannot commit .git itself, so to share hooks you use a package that symlinks them from a committed folder (he shows a Node one and notes Python has equivalents).

Config cascades: the system file from the Git installer, then the user file in your home directory, then the repository's own, which is where a work email overrides a personal one. .git/info/exclude is a private .gitignore. He tells of one machine that seemed possessed until someone emptied its exclude file. The index, read with git ls-files --stage, maps every working file to a blob hash so Git can skip unchanged files.

Finally, recovery. He moves a branch away from a commit, then gets it back with git reflog, checks out the hash and creates a branch. The reflog keeps a history for HEAD, every branch and every remote, as long as garbage collection has not got there first.

## Who should watch

Anyone who uses Git daily and still treats reset, amend and detached HEAD as superstition. Python developers get a bonus: the hooks section points at tools to share pre-commit hooks across a team.
